Persist in implementing the political responsibility for governing the Party 坚持落实管党治党政治责任 Nie Pingping Writing in the People's Daily (22 September 2026), Nie Pingping, a professor at Nanjing University, examines the last of the "fourteen adherences" in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: persisting in implementing political responsibility for governing the Party. Nie argues that this item is the logical conclusion and anchor of the whole system, because it turns theory and deployment into action. For a ruling party of more than 100 million members, the author holds, vigilance in governing the Party cannot be relaxed for a moment. The commentary has four parts. It first explains why responsibility links theory to practice, then describes the mechanisms through which political responsibility is carried out. It goes on to set out a four-step chain of responsibility and ends with proposals for tightening responsibility further, based on Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Nie draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on volumes of Xi Jinping's selected writings on Party building. Nie argues that the first thirteen adherences set the leadership, strategy, values and the seven areas of Party building, and that responsibility is the "rigid force" that converts them into an operable, checkable and accountable system. Three mechanisms are said to do this work: pressure transmission, running from the central leadership to grassroots organisations; rigid constraint through accountability rules; and systemic integration, in which Party committees bear primary responsibility, secretaries are the first persons responsible and discipline commissions supervise. Responsibility is then divided into knowing, bearing, discharging and being held to account for it, a closed loop that Nie says rests on institutions. The author contrasts this with Western public-governance theory, where responsibility is described as dispersed and legal or contractual, whereas the Party's political responsibility is described as centralised and answerable to the people's fundamental interests. Nie calls for responsibility to be tightened in line with the "three more" requirements: more resolute implementation of central decisions, more effective confinement of power within institutional "cages", and a clearer and firmer anti-corruption struggle. Nie reads the Party's history as showing that Party building is strong when responsibility is firmly applied and falters when it slackens, and concludes that this is how the Party will remain the core of leadership guiding Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the Party presents responsibility, accountability and discipline as the working core of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Upholding rule by institutions and rule by Party regulations in governing the Party 坚持制度治党、依规治党 Li Binxiong This commentary, originally published in the People's Daily, sets out what it means to govern the Party through institutions (zhidu zhi dang) and through Party regulations (yi gui zhi dang), why this matters and how to do it. Li Binxiong argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has treated this approach as the long-term and fundamental basis of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In Li's account it is an important component of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building. The piece is organised in three parts, each built around quotations from the Selected Writings of Xi Jinping on Party Building. The first part defines the concept and its features. The second explains its significance for the Party's leadership, for Party building and for long-term rule. The third sets out practical requirements. In the first part, Li defines institution-based governance as the Party using rules and systems to guide, regulate and safeguard its governance, and regulation-based governance as doing the same through intra-Party regulations. Li cites Xi's view that regulations and institutions are fundamental, comprehensive, stable and long-term, and presents four requirements: rules to rely on, rules that must be followed, rules strictly enforced, and violations investigated. In the second part, Li argues that this approach turns the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds into institutional norms, secures the Party's comprehensive leadership and helps the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. It is also said to support the Party's self-purification and to align state law with Party regulation. On practice, Li calls for three things. First, a sound institutional system built on systemic, dialectical and bottom-line thinking, balancing strict management with care for officials and keeping rules up to date. Second, stronger institutional awareness and enforcement, so that rules are not treated as soft advocacy but as binding constraints. Third, a clear responsibility system with enforcement duties and strict accountability, including investigation of leaders where enforcement fails. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style statement of how the Party's regulatory approach to self-governance is justified and what its stated implementation priorities are.

Persist in advancing the three-pronged approach of not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt as an integrated whole 坚持一体推进不敢腐不能腐不想腐 Song Xueqin This commentary, published in the People's Daily, takes up the Party's principle of advancing, as one whole, the aims of making officials not dare to be corrupt, not able to be corrupt and not want to be corrupt. Song Xueqin argues that the principle is both a basic guideline of the anti-corruption struggle and an important strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In the author's account it is an original theoretical result of Xi Jinping's leadership of that struggle, and it has shifted corruption governance from treating symptoms to addressing symptoms and root causes together. The article has three parts. The first sets out the principle's standing and its theoretical underpinnings. The second explains how the three components work in practice. The third assesses the current situation and proposes measures. Song draws on passages from the second volume of Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Party Building, and on Party figures such as the 2025 number of people who turned themselves in. Song describes the three components as interdependent: not daring is the precondition, not being able is the key, and not wanting is the foundation. Deterrence through strict punishment clears existing corruption and curbs new cases. Institutional constraints, by closing gaps in how power is allocated, exercised and supervised, move governance from passive punishment to active prevention. Ideological education and a culture of integrity are said to produce voluntary self-discipline, which Song calls the most durable barrier. The author contends that fragmented or one-dimensional governance can no longer meet current needs. In the author's view the approach also differs from Western parties' reliance on external checks and purely legal restraint. Song states that the anti-corruption struggle has won an overwhelming victory that has been consolidated, but remains severe and complex, with old corruption not yet cleared and new cases emerging. The author calls for stronger centralised Party leadership and responsibility systems, close attention to new and hidden forms of corruption, and use of the "four forms" of supervision and discipline. Further proposals include tighter rules on power and joined-up supervision, harsher punishment of bribe-giving, and tailored integrity education. Song concludes that these efforts will provide political assurance for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and policy agenda behind the three "nots" formula in Party anti-corruption discourse.

Using strict discipline to govern the whole Party 坚持用严明的纪律管全党治全党 Wang Yong This commentary, first published in the People's Daily, argues that using strict discipline to manage and govern the whole Party is a key part of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building and the fundamental measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Drawing throughout on the first volume of the Selected Writings of Xi Jinping on Party Building, Wang Yong holds that the Party, as a Marxist party built on revolutionary ideals and iron discipline, depends on discipline to answer the question of what it relies on to govern itself. The article has four parts. It first reviews discipline building since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then links strict discipline to the Party's advanced and pure character and to its governing capacity. It next discusses extending discipline to every member, cadre and organisation, and closes with the joint use of Party discipline and state law as 'two yardsticks'. Wang's central claim is that theory and practice in discipline building have reinforced each other. On the theoretical side, the author stresses that political discipline is the most important and fundamental discipline, and notes that the 19th Party Congress (2017) put discipline building into the overall plan for Party building. On the practical side, Wang lists regulations such as the Disciplinary Action Regulations, political inspections and the eight-point rules, and says these ended a previous 'lax and soft' approach. Wang also presents strict discipline as a response to the 'four tests' and 'four dangers' and as the basis for cadres to act boldly. Discipline must apply to everyone, with no exceptions and no blind spots. Wang says the Disciplinary Action Regulations, revised in 2015, 2018 and 2023, express the principle that discipline is stricter than law and comes before it. The merged work of discipline inspection commissions and supervisory commissions is said to link Party discipline with law enforcement. Wang concludes that when discipline is strong the Party is strong, and that strict discipline is a historical lesson of the Party's growth. The author presents it as protecting Chinese modernization and keeping the Party advanced and pure, citing 101.286 million members and 5.431 million primary-level organisations at the end of 2025. Read the original if you want an official Party-school account of how current discipline building is framed, including its institutional and legal-regulatory components.

Persisting in making Party conduct building regular and long-term 坚持推进作风建设常态化长效化 He Husheng This commentary, published in the People's Daily, takes up one of the "fourteen persistences" that the author identifies in Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: making the building of Party conduct (zuofeng) regular and long-term. He argues that Party conduct is the Party's image and bears on its survival. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), he says, the Central Committee has pursued conduct building continuously, and the task now is to fight a protracted campaign so that it supports the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the principle matters. The second explains its theoretical content, drawing on several texts in the Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Party Building. The third proposes practical paths for carrying it out. On significance, He gives three reasons. Conduct building keeps the Party's flesh-and-blood ties with the people, and the public fears campaigns that leave only a superficial effect. Conduct problems are stubborn and recurrent, so one-off drives cannot remove them. And because conduct problems are at root problems of Party spirit, conduct building drives Party building as a whole. On content, He treats "regular" (changtaihua) and "long-term" (changxiaohua) as one unit. Regularity means continuous attention to thinking, supervision and discipline, and routine self-examination in Party life. Long-term effect means moving from treating symptoms to tackling root causes through Party regulations, so that cadres move from "not daring" to "not being able" and finally to "not wanting" to violate norms. For practice, He calls for three things. Cadres should temper their Party spirit and put political cultivation first. Regulations should be improved and enforced rigidly, so that the "four undesirable work styles" cannot mutate in hidden forms. Chains of responsibility should be tightened, and unhealthy conduct and corruption should be investigated and handled together. He concludes that this approach will let good Party conduct set the tone for social conduct and customs and create a good environment for high-quality development. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-building discourse frames conduct building, discipline and institutional constraint in the Xi era.

Persisting in building a high-calibre cadre corps capable of shouldering the great task of national rejuvenation 坚持建设堪当民族复兴重任的高素质干部队伍 Liu Jingbei This commentary, first published in the People's Daily, asks how the Party should build a cadre corps able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu Jingbei argues that selecting and appointing officials is a historic Party tradition, and that Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building supplies the guiding principles for doing so. Liu presents strict governance of officials as the key to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article is organised as seven study themes drawn from Xi's writings, including the Selected Works on Party Building. They cover the principles of selecting and appointing officials, the criteria for a good cadre, the primacy of political standards, the "five systems" of cadre work, strict management combined with care, talent strategy, and the training of young cadres as successors. Liu's core move is to set out a chain running from selection to management. Political loyalty comes first, including support for the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and failure on this standard means a one-vote veto. Around it Liu arranges five systems: cultivating quality, assessing and knowing cadres, selection and appointment, strict management, and positive incentives. Each is paired with a named risk, such as promoting officials with problems, mismatching people and posts, or going through the motions. Liu also holds that strict supervision and encouragement to take responsibility are inherently unified, and that protecting officials who act, and clearing those falsely accused, belongs to management. For talent work, Liu lists eight elements of Xi's thinking and calls for more active, open and effective talent policies to support Chinese modernization. For young cadres, Liu proposes long-term planning, strict selection, graduated training in hard posts, bold and timely promotion, and constant supervision, which Liu likens to tending a field. The aim is reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics, so that the "red country" never changes colour. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned statement of current Party doctrine on cadre selection, management and succession.

Upholding the building of an organisational system that is connected from top to bottom and effective in execution 坚持健全上下贯通、执行有力的组织体系 Zhang Peng This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2026, explains one of the "fourteen upholds" of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: keeping up the effort to build an organisational system that is connected from top to bottom and strong in execution. Zhang Peng argues that a tight organisational system is the strength of a Marxist party. In the author's account, it is a precondition for upholding the leadership of the Party Central Committee and for pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece has two main sections. The first sets out why such a system matters: Zhang cites Xi's statements on organisation, the size of the Party, and the risks it faces on the new journey. The second addresses how to build the system and what it is meant to achieve. It treats the Central Committee, the intermediate Party committees and grassroots organisations in turn, and then links the system to Party leadership, Party discipline and national rejuvenation. Zhang's central claim is that organisation turns scale into strength. The article cites 101.286 million members and 5.431 million primary organisations at the end of 2025. It says that this size brings problems of managing members, covering new sectors and tackling lax discipline, and that a tight system can convert size into quality and political advantage. The Central Committee is described as the brain and hub, with the Party's leading position resting on the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Zhang assigns each level a role in carrying out central decisions: central bodies are the "first kilometre", local committees the "middle section" and grassroots branches the "last kilometre". Each level must avoid specific failures: obstacles, blockages and broken links. The author also stresses a priority on the grassroots, including rectifying weak and lax branches. Zhang concludes that the Party's overall leadership and all its work depend on a strong organisational system. The article cites poverty alleviation, the response to the pandemic, disaster relief and technological breakthroughs as examples of organisational strength becoming national governance capacity. It calls for a complete system of organisational rules and for stricter enforcement of democratic centralism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party organisation is justified as the basis of leadership and governance in the Xi era.

Persist in forging strong Party spirit 坚持锤炼坚强党性 Chen Jiaxi This commentary, published in the People's Daily, asks why and how Communist Party members and cadres should keep forging "strong Party spirit" (dangxing). Chen Jiaxi argues that doing so is a foundational task of the Party's new great project of self-building in the new era and an important part of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building. In Chen's account, strong Party spirit guarantees the Party's advanced nature and purity and its capacity to lead and govern. The article has three parts. It first sets out why forging Party spirit is necessary, then analyses the internal logic of Xi Jinping's statements on it since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally proposes practical requirements for the new journey. It draws on quotations from Xi Jinping, including texts in the Selected Works on Party Building. On necessity, Chen names three requirements: strengthening political building and unity around the Party Central Committee, building an ideological barrier for long-term rule and advancing the Party's self-reform, and shaping cadres who are loyal, clean and ready to take responsibility. On logic, Chen reads Xi's remarks as answering questions of essence (Party spirit is ultimately a question of standpoint, tested by public versus private interest), of mechanism (a lifelong task, combining self-discipline with institutional constraint) and of cultural roots (Party-spirit education as the Communists' "study of the mind", linked to Chinese self-cultivation traditions). Chen holds that this moves Party-spirit work from individual self-improvement to the strategic level of a long-ruling party. Chen proposes four practical paths: arming members with theory through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, tempering them through rigorous inner-Party political life, testing them in practical work for the people, and reinforcing them through discipline and supervision. The author concludes that members should treat Party-spirit cultivation as a lifelong task and convert it into strength for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building discourse presents Party spirit, loyalty and self-reform as linked themes.

Persistently using the Party's innovative theory to unite hearts and forge souls 坚持用党的创新理论凝心铸魂 Feng Yanli Feng Yanli, writing in the People's Daily (10 September 2026), takes up the task of using the Party's innovative theory to "unite hearts and forge souls", which the article calls the fundamental task of the Party's ideological work. Feng argues that this task gives Party building in the new era an ideological foundation and spiritual support. The commentary opens with Xi Jinping's remark that a strong theory gives the world's largest Marxist governing party clear direction, unity and confidence. The piece has four parts. The first explains what the formula means. The second presents it as an answer to major questions facing a long-governing Marxist party. The third reviews practical results since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The fourth sets out how theoretical armament should be pursued further. Feng draws throughout on Xi Jinping's writings on Party building. Feng reads the formula in three ways: as a scientific orientation grounded in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, as a strategic measure for strengthening the Party's foundations, and as a requirement of unified thinking and firm belief. "Uniting hearts" is defined as unifying thought, will and action. "Forging souls" is defined as firming ideals and convictions. The two are said to support each other. Feng says the formula answers three questions: how to forge the soul (belief rests on theoretical clarity), how to consolidate the foundation (theoretical identification builds political identification, inside and outside the Party), and how to stay evergreen (clear theory and firm belief drive the Party's self-reform). As evidence, Feng cites firmer ideals among Party members, stronger unity, and better links between study and practice through campaigns such as the study of Party history and the theme-based education campaign. Feng calls for deeper, more practical and more heartfelt theoretical study. Party members should read original works and study genuinely, understand, believe and apply the theory. Study should be tailored to different groups, with leading cadres as the "key minority", and should reach enterprises, villages, schools, communities and online platforms in accessible forms. Study should also connect with investigation and research and with concrete work, so that it supports Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official press frames ideological education and theoretical study in the new era.

Marini's theory of super-exploitation and its contemporary value Theoretical innovation grounded in the dilemma of dependent development in Latin America 马里尼的超级剥削理论及其当代价值——基于拉丁美洲依附发展困境的理论创新 Liu Xi Why did economic growth in mid-twentieth-century Latin America bring deepening poverty rather than general prosperity? Liu Xi takes up this question through Ruy Mauro Marini's theory of super-exploitation, set out in Dialectics of Dependency. The article argues that the theory is an independent and still valuable contribution: dependent capitalism offsets value lost in unequal international exchange by pushing workers' wages below the value of labour-power. The article has three parts. It first reconstructs Latin American debates over whether super-exploitation fits Marx's Capital, both on its nature and on whether it is general or exceptional. It then sets out Marini's main contributions: an independent category, a mechanism for peripheral accumulation, and an account of structural inequality in the capitalist system. Finally it assesses the theory's present-day value, drawing on Foster, Harvey and John Smith. On the nature of super-exploitation, Liu contrasts Hugo Figueira Corrêa and Marcelo Dias Carcanholo, who treat it as pre-capitalist 'plunder' and a temporary deviation, with Jaime Osorio, who sees it as exploitation specific to dependency. Liu sides with the view that it combines the features of plunder with the substance of exploitation, and that it is the law of surplus value working under unequal conditions in the world market. Core countries keep labour relations relatively mild by shifting contradictions onto the periphery, while peripheral capital compensates by cutting labour-reproduction costs. Liu also presents Marini as extending Marx's remark in Capital, Volume III, on wages pushed below the value of labour-power as a counteracting factor to the falling rate of profit. In this reading Marini turned an incidental fluctuation into a standing feature and gave exploitation analysis a spatial dimension. Liu concludes that super-exploitation explains twenty-first-century imperialism, including global value chains, financial expansion, platform and gig work, and value transfer without direct colonisation. The article also holds that it underpins solidarity among workers in the Global South, illustrating this with Brazil's 'economic miracle' of 1964–74. It calls on the global left to build an internationalist alliance against imperialism and neo-colonialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language survey of the Latin American dependency debate and of how Marini's concept is being applied to the contemporary world system.

Lenin's critique of the Proletkult and its implications for China's cultural construction 列宁对“无产阶级文化派”的批判及其对我国文化建设的启示 Yang Yinyin Yang Yinyin asks what Lenin's struggle against the Proletkult (the "proletarian culture" current led by Bogdanov) can teach China about cultural construction today. The article treats the Proletkult as a representative form of cultural nihilism. It argues that Lenin's critique remains instructive for developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and for building a strong cultural nation, and it links this to Xi Jinping's calls to oppose cultural nihilism and to carry forward Chinese culture through "creative transformation and innovative development". The article first reconstructs Lenin's criticism in four parts: Machism as the philosophical error behind the Proletkult, its "independentism" towards the Party, its nihilism towards cultural heritage, and its "closed-door" sectarianism towards practice and the people. It draws on Bogdanov, Lebedev-Polyansky, Pletnev, Lunacharsky and others, and on Lenin's writings, letters and marginal notes, including the 1920 resolution on proletarian culture. A final section derives four lessons for China today. Yang's core argument is that each Proletkult error had a Leninist answer. Against Machism's "elements" and claimed neutrality, Lenin asserted the Party-mindedness of philosophy and the guidance of Marxist theory. Against demands for "complete autonomy", he placed the Proletkult organisations under the People's Commissariat for Education and the "general direction of the Russian Communist Party". Against the slogan that the past is poison, he insisted that proletarian culture must absorb and remake all that humanity has produced, including bourgeois specialists and old intellectuals. Against laboratory-style culture-making, he held that culture comes from the practice of the people, including peasants and intellectuals. Yang adds that the Proletkult was not uniform: Lunacharsky and Bogdanov accepted inheriting the past, but only after proletarian ideology had been established, which Yang says wrongly separates two processes that should run together. Yang draws four lessons for China: guide cultural work with Xi Jinping Thought on culture; strengthen the Party's centralised leadership over propaganda and ideological work, including its "cultural leadership"; hold to both the "soul" of Marxism and the "roots" of excellent traditional Chinese culture, while learning openly from other cultures; and root culture in the people. On the last point Yang criticises current closed-door and elitist tendencies, citing repetitive television fantasy plots and elite-oriented literature, and calls for better public cultural services. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Lenin's polemics with Bogdanov and Pletnev, and of how they are used to frame current Party cultural policy.

Socialist ideology as an enabler of "value alignment" in large AI models 论社会主义意识形态赋能人工智能大模型“价值对齐” Gao An'an Gao An'an takes up the "value alignment" problem in large AI models, first formulated by Stuart Russell in 2014. The article argues that Western states, led by the United States, have turned alignment into a political project for technological hegemony and for exporting their ideology as "universal values". Gao contends that China urgently needs its own alignment scheme with socialist ideology at its core, and that existing Chinese research, which the author describes as mostly defensive (engineering control, legal sanction, moral restraint), has not shown how socialist ideology can actively empower alignment. The article has three parts. The first sets out why socialist ideology is the right "alignment target", the second proposes three practical principles, and the third sets out four paths for embedding socialist ideology in models. A short conclusion looks ahead to further research. Gao draws on Marx and Engels, on speeches by Xi Jinping, and on Chinese regulations and standards on generative AI. The author also uses cases such as ChatGPT, Amazon's recruitment algorithm, Anthropic's "constitutional AI" and DeepSeek. Gao argues that capitalist ideology, with its priority on profit maximisation, tends to make AI a tool of exploitation. Socialist ideology, in the author's account, supplies basic value resources (the core socialist values and the "common values of all mankind" across individual, group, national and global levels), steers both the training and the post-deployment stages of alignment, and points toward the final aim of "machines for people" and human liberation. The three principles are balancing innovation with safety and control, combining positive incentives with negative sanctions, and combining industry self-governance with social co-governance, the last aimed at easing the "alignment tax". The four paths aim to make models "virtuous", "emotional", "refined" and "orderly": ethical training and review, emotion computing, cultural-meme extraction and generation, and institutional design, support and criticism. Gao concludes that alignment is becoming a permanent and demanding undertaking. It faces unresolved technical and ethical difficulties and a persistent mismatch between machine rationality and human value systems. The author calls for research to move from theory to technical practice, and for sustained effort toward human–AI coexistence and the digital-intelligent advance of civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholarship links AI governance, ideological security and concrete technical proposals for alignment.

Digital-intelligence empowerment of whole-process people's democracy and the prevention of its risks 全过程人民民主的数智赋能及其风险防范 Yang Kangkang Yang Kangkang asks how "digital-intelligence" technology, meaning the combination of digital technology and artificial intelligence, can strengthen whole-process people's democracy without damaging its socialist character. The article's thesis is that the technology brings real strategic opportunities but is a "double-edged sword". On Yang's account, it can be put to good use only under Party leadership and a "people first" orientation, with institutional safeguards. Working within a historical-materialist framework, the article has three parts. The first sets out three opportunities: new democratic forms, higher governance efficiency and wider channels for participation. The second identifies three risks: "digital-intelligence alienation", the "digital-intelligence divide" and "digital-intelligence monopoly". The third proposes practical remedies. Yang draws on Party documents, Marx's concept of alienation and examples from Western countries. On opportunity, Yang argues that big data, algorithms and generative AI can link the five democratic stages (election, consultation, decision-making, management and supervision), lower participation costs and sort public concerns quickly. On risk, the author holds that over-reliance on the technology can distort the authenticity of democracy, objectify interaction and expose privacy. Divides in access, skills and intelligence between urban and rural areas, regions and age groups may create "democratic stragglers". Citing Western cases, Yang says platform capital can use data and algorithms to steer elections, and that this is a negative example for China, where the people's congress system is described as preventing such control. Yang's remedies are to uphold Party leadership and the people-centred approach, and to treat technology as an auxiliary, service-oriented tool. The article also calls for stronger privacy protection, including a right to be forgotten, and for algorithm audits with third-party review and "democratic value impact assessments". It further proposes inclusive digital training, offline channels alongside online ones, and "subject reshaping" rather than AI replacing human participants. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of socialist democracy frames AI governance, the digital divide and platform power in terms of Party leadership and Marxist theory.

What is distinctive about the world view contained in Chinese modernization? 中国式现代化中蕴含的独特世界观独特在哪里 Tian Pengying Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization contains a distinctive world view, outlook on values, history, civilization, democracy and ecology, Tian Pengying asks what makes the world view distinctive, since the article treats it as the leading and decisive one among these six. The author argues that it is the overall and fundamental understanding of the modern world, of the path of modernization and of its general laws, and that it surpasses existing modernization theory, Western theory in particular. The article presents it as a major innovation in world modernization theory and practice and as an answer to the question of where world modernization is heading. The article is organised around five pairs of features that the author says the world view holds together: universality and particularity in choosing a path; historicity and contemporaneity in the logic of evolution; autonomy and inclusiveness in creating models; progressiveness and advancedness in grasping the essence of modernization; and reflexivity and transcendence in constructing the ideal. Tian draws on Marx, Engels, Hegel and Xi Jinping, and sets Chinese modernization against Western and capitalist modernization throughout. Tian argues that modernization is not a multiple-choice question. Its general laws are shared, but each country's path is shaped by its history, institutions, conditions and external environment. Chinese modernization is said to follow the general laws while rejecting imitation of the West, to grow out of continuous Chinese civilization rather than break with it, and to combine independence with openness, so that China neither exports a model nor imposes one. Its core is said to be modernization of people, which Tian explains through three questions: for whom, by whom and shared by whom. On this reading the people are both the purpose and the main force of modernization. Capitalist modernization, in Tian's account, mistakes capital accumulation for development and reproduces alienation between people and nature, society and themselves. Tian concludes that this critique leads beyond capitalist modernization to a new form of human civilization. It also leads to the common values of all humanity and to a community with a shared future for mankind, which the article calls China's answer to the question of what world to build and how. The author expects the world view's explanatory and practical power to grow as Chinese modernization advances, and to supply a scientific methodology for civilizational progress. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical statement of how Chinese modernization is distinguished from Western modernization theory, framed through paired dialectical categories.

Digital socialism or digital utopia? The predicament of foreign left-wing theories of digital socialism and how to resolve it 数字社会主义还是数字乌托邦？ Xu Tao Foreign left-wing scholars have responded to platform, data and surveillance capitalism by proposing various versions of "digital socialism". Xu asks whether these blueprints are realistic or merely utopian, and whether they can break free of capital's domination. The article argues, from a Marxist standpoint, that they largely end as "digital illusions": they depart from historical materialism, from the objective conditions of scientific socialism, and from a sober view of technology. Xu nonetheless credits them with returning thinking about future society to a Marxist vocabulary. The article first maps four strands. The critical communication school (Christian Fuchs, Michael Kwet) advocates media democracy and a digital commons. The "new planned economy" current (William Paul Cockshott, Allin Cottrell, Evgeny Morozov) revisits the socialist calculation debate with algorithms and feedback infrastructure. Left accelerationism (Nick Srnicek, Alex Williams, Aaron Bastani, James Muldoon) pursues full automation and "platform socialism". Digital social democracy (Jeremy Rifkin, Paul Mason, Michael A. Peters) envisages a gradual "post-capitalism". Xu then criticises these strands and proposes remedies. The critique has three parts, which Xu calls myths. The theoretical myth is that they distort the laws by which social formations succeed one another: digital technology, Xu says, continues capitalism's internal contradictions on the basis of private ownership. The practical myth is that they replace the proletariat with abstract subjects such as Fuchs's "playbour", prefer reform to abolishing capitalist relations of production, and lack a unified proletarian party. The technological myth is that they are over-optimistic about technology, ignoring algorithmic discrimination and AI risks, and slide into a "convergence theory" that blurs the difference between socialism and capitalism. Xu proposes four corrections: return from a "digital revolution" to an "institutional revolution"; move from the "aphasia" of class to its "presence"; turn from Western experience to that of the Global South, especially socialist countries' digital modernisation; and unite theoretical critique with organised practical movement. The conclusion says technology should be neither rejected nor expected to bring about institutional change automatically; its potential should be steered towards social emancipation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western left debates on digital socialism, platform socialism and fully automated planning.

Mao Zedong's initial blueprint for socialist agricultural and rural modernization and its historical lessons 毛泽东对社会主义农业农村现代化的初步擘画及历史启示 Xia Shaoguang Marking the 70th anniversary of the compilation of The Socialist Upsurge in China's Countryside (compiled late 1955, published early 1956), Xia Shaoguang asks what Mao Zedong's editorial notes to that volume reveal about his plan for modernizing agriculture and the countryside. The article argues that the notes set the fundamental direction of cooperativization, sketched a comprehensive blueprint, and offer lessons that remain relevant for building a strong agricultural country today. The article first places the volume in the context of the 1950s: the two-step path Mao outlined at the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949), the general line for the transition period, and disputes within the Party over cooperatives. It then examines Mao's notes, which Xia summarises as "twelve unities", and the institutional advantages and Party working style the book displays. It closes with three historical lessons. Xia's central claim is that Mao's notes treat modernization as a balanced whole. The "unities" include Party leadership with mass contact, productive forces with changes in relations of production, bold construction with thrift, economic work with ideological and political work, exploiting nature with ecological protection, and bold planning with continual revision. Others pair patient persuasion with firm struggle, economic with social development, and the interior with minority regions. Xia reads the book as showing the advantages of public ownership over smallholder farming, which was vulnerable to disaster and polarisation, and as embodying the mass line, fact-based investigation and a plain Marxist writing style. The author endorses the 1981 Party resolution's verdict that the socialist transformation was a great historic victory. Xia draws three lessons. The achievements of Mao's leadership should be assessed in a long historical view, and the author opposes "historical nihilism" that exaggerates errors. Xia also claims four forms of progress for the Chinese path compared with traditional small-peasant production, capitalist modernization, Soviet agricultural stagnation and other agrarian countries' development. Finally, today's rural revitalization should follow Mao's balanced approach: keep the collective basis of agriculture, resist land privatization, loosen management systems, and uphold Party leadership in the countryside. Xia presents this as continuing Mao's blueprint. Read the original if you want a Party-line reappraisal of Mao's agricultural cooperativization, with close textual use of the volume's editorial notes.

America's financial hegemony, financial colonization and international anti-hegemony action 美国的金融霸权、金融殖民与国际反霸权行动 Yan Jingfeng Yan Jingfeng asks what underpins US financial hegemony, how Washington uses it to extract wealth from the rest of the world, whether it is truly unbreakable, and how other countries are resisting it. The article's thesis is that this hegemony rests on a large supporting system and operates as a form of 'financial colonization', but that it is deeply fragile and not indestructible. The article has four parts. It first sets out six pillars of the hegemony: the dollar-centred financial system, military power, the science and technology system, discursive power, control of international financial and credit-rating institutions, and an alliance network. It then describes the mechanisms of financial colonization, analyses the hegemony's internal weaknesses, and surveys international moves to break it, citing figures on dollar reserves, payment systems and central bank digital currencies up to 2026. In Yan's account, financial colonization works in four ways: neoliberal ideology and institutions such as the IMF and World Bank bring other states under US control; seigniorage, 'fleecing' cycles of interest-rate change and the 'IOU' character of US debt extract wealth; financial sanctions punish challengers; and digital finance, including dollar-backed stablecoins, extends the system. Drawing on Marx's analysis of credit and capital, Yan then argues that financialization hollows out US industry, which weakens the technological and military bases of dollar power, widens inequality and political polarization, and leaves the US dependent on extracting wealth abroad. Sanctions on Russia since 2022, the article argues, undermine confidence in the dollar. Yan identifies the resistance as de-dollarization: diversifying settlement currencies and reserves, building independent payment systems such as CIPS and BRICS Pay, and using digital finance, while relying on real-economy strength, military modernization and the loosening of US alliances. The author presents China's Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind and renminbi internationalization as part of this response. Yan concludes that only comprehensive national strength can counter financial hegemony, and, citing David Harvey, warns that a declining hegemon may turn to harsher coercion. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of dollar hegemony as neo-colonialism, with data on de-dollarization measures.

The philosophical foundation of Marx's revolution in the theory of the modern state and its contemporary value An examination centred on The German Ideology 马克思现代国家观革命的哲学奠基及其当代价值——以《德意志意识形态》为中心的考察 Li Yingrui Li Yingrui asks what The German Ideology contributed to Marx's theory of the modern state and whether that theory remains valid 180 years later. The article argues that the materialist conception of history, first set out systematically in this work, provided the philosophical basis for a revolution in how the modern state is studied. In Li's account, it also yielded the first reasonably complete and systematic statement of Marx's state theory, which the author holds is still explanatory today. The article has three parts. The first treats the materialist conception of history as a new worldview and methodology, examined at three levels: ontology, epistemology and axiology. The second reconstructs four theses on the state in The German Ideology, tracing them through the Holy Family, the Communist Manifesto, Capital, the Civil War in France and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. The third draws out the present-day value of these ideas for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li argues that Marx grounded the state in practice and material production rather than in speculative premises such as the Hegelian absolute spirit. This is the core of the shift from a Hegelian to a materialist approach. The author states that the modern state arose from the division of labour and from "pure private property", and that it has a dual character: it performs social functions but is essentially a class instrument and an "illusory community". It will be replaced by a "real community" once production develops, and the proletariat must first seize political power. Li also stresses the diversity of modern state forms. On this view, Marx and Engels distinguished the capitalist modern state from the new socialist state of the dictatorship of the proletariat, and China's system is presented as its Chinese, contemporary form. Li concludes that Marx's state theory is scientific, practical and open, and that claims it is outdated are mistaken. The author calls for three tasks in further deepening reform: holding firm to the Four-sphere Confidence and rebutting distortions of the socialist system, using problem-oriented institutional reform to adapt the relations of production to the productive forces, and putting social fairness and the people's wellbeing at the centre of modernizing national governance. Read the original if you want a close Chinese reading of The German Ideology as the foundation of Marxist state theory, and an example of how that theory is tied to current Party discourse on institutions and governance.

The dialectical implications of the Communist Party of China's self-reform 中国共产党自我革命的辩证意蕴 He Changyu He Changyu takes up the Party's self-reform, which Xi Jinping describes as the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. Earlier scholarship has located its philosophical basis in the mass view of history. The article argues that it can also be read through the logic of materialist dialectics, and that self-reform is an application and development of dialectics in Party building. The article is organised around three questions. The first asks what self-reform is, using dialectical logic. The second asks why the Party must undertake it, through several dialectical relationships. The third asks how it should be advanced, through paired practical principles. The author draws on Marx, Engels, Hegel, Mao Zedong and Xi, and repeatedly contrasts the case of the Soviet Communist Party's collapse. On definition, He holds that self-reform is a substantive, object-oriented revolution aimed at specific problems: wavering ideals, disregard of political discipline, lack of competence, and poor conduct. It is also a revolution of negation of the negation that ends in self-affirmation, which the author distinguishes from the historical nihilism said to have destroyed the Soviet party. It is also a long-term undertaking that is always under way. On necessity, He argues that it follows from the unity of Party spirit and the people's character, from long-term rule combined with consensus among the people, which is needed to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall, and from the unity of upholding fundamental principles and innovation. On method, He proposes combining the main thrust with the strategic goal (the 'unique challenges of a large party'), intra-Party supervision with supervision by the people, organisational drive with individual initiative, and strict management with caring support. He concludes that self-reform is the Party's 'second answer' to the historical cycle, building on the 'first answer' of people's supervision, which it does not replace. In He's account, internal causes work through external conditions, so the two forms of supervision must reinforce each other. The article's practical proposals include clear assignment of responsibility, higher standards for senior cadres, heart-to-heart talks and early correction of minor errors. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the Party's anti-corruption and self-discipline agenda is justified in terms of dialectical method.

The cultural self-awareness behind the formation and continuation of the Chinese Communists' spiritual lineage 中国共产党人精神谱系生成与赓续的文化自觉 Xu Yan Xu Yan asks why and how the "spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists" (a series of named "spirits" such as the Long March spirit and the Yan'an spirit) came into being, and how it can be continued. The article argues that earlier studies describe individual spirits or their functions but do not explain the internal cultural driver. Drawing on Fei Xiaotong's concept of "cultural self-awareness", Xu holds that the lineage is the product of the Communist Party's conscious cultural creation as a historical subject. The article adopts a three-part framework of awareness of formation, awareness of value and awareness of practice. It opens with a review of case studies and holistic studies of the lineage, then moves through the historical genesis of the lineage, its value structure and contributions, and finally the paths for its continuation in the new era. Examples run from the Long March, the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" spirit and the reform and opening-up spirit to the poverty-alleviation spirit. On formation, Xu argues that the Party achieved a "double transcendence": a practical overcoming of hard realities and a sublating critique of dogma, such as the "encircling the cities from the countryside" strategy and the debate on the criterion of truth. The Party also drew on two sources, Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture, through the Two Integrations. On value, Xu identifies three layers: ideals and convictions, a people-first stance, and seeking truth from facts together with hard struggle. Xu claims the lineage builds national cohesion and offers a spiritual reference beyond Western modernity and the logic of capital. On continuation, Xu proposes four paths. These are upholding the Party's cultural leadership and the Party's self-reform; deepening the Two Integrations for innovative transmission; embedding the lineage in Chinese modernization through high-quality development, common prosperity and the modernization of people; and building new narratives and digital communication. Xu concludes that the cultural self-awareness lens moves research from historical narrative toward analysis of mechanisms and supports building China's independent knowledge system. Read the original if you study Party spirit-building, ideological education or the Party's account of cultural subjectivity and want a detailed example of how these are framed.

The problems of the "platform rent thesis" in the light of Marx's theory of the circuit of capital, and how to correct them 马克思资本循环理论视域下“平台租金说”的问题及其矫正 Huang Zaisheng Are the huge profits of giant digital platforms best understood as "digital surplus value" or as "digital ground rent"? Huang Zaisheng takes up this debate and argues that the "platform rent thesis" (data rent, "cloud rent", the "techno-feudalism" line) misreads digital capital. In Huang's account, the thesis stays inside the sphere of circulation, ignores digital labour and the platforms' productive activity, and so cannot show the full circuit of digital capital. The author proposes to correct it with Marx's theory of the circuit of capital. The article has four parts after the introduction. It first sets out the thesis's four "rents" (data, cognitive or knowledge, transaction and traffic, and cloud) and contrasts them with what the author calls four productive roles of platforms. These are forming data factors, researching and developing digital-intelligent technology, producing digital space, and supplying services. It then explains how the thesis reduces the circuit of digital capital and why it errs, and what harm follows. Finally it offers a corrected account. Huang draws on figures on platform R&D spending, AI model output and cloud-computing revenue, and cites Evgeny Morozov's criticism of techno-feudalism. Huang's central move is that the thesis treats platforms as pure intermediaries, a new commercial capital whose circuit collapses into M–M′, like interest-bearing capital. The author traces this to three sources: free services that obscure production, platforms' self-description as mere "markets", and a mechanical reading of Marx's claim that circulation creates no value. Against this, Huang argues that platforms commodify digital-intelligent services (business intelligence, precision marketing, cloud computing) and that digital labour creates value, from user-generated data and crowd-sourced labelling to algorithm development. Digital capital is therefore a composite. It runs the full industrial circuit M–C…P…C′–M′. It also acts as commercial capital with a "dual circulation" pattern. In addition, it shows features of fictitious capital under the "growth first, profit later" model. The author concludes that the thesis, if left to spread, would saddle platform economies with a bad reputation, erase the value contribution of digital labour and mislead regulators. Huang adds that the virtualisation of digital capital, driven by data worship and "intelligence fetishism", carries the seeds of a digital-capitalist economic crisis. The author presents this as a way to understand digital capital in China's socialist market economy and to promote high-quality development of the platform economy. Read the original if you work on digital capitalism, rent versus surplus-value debates, or Chinese Marxist readings of the platform economy.

"Quasi-feudal" phenomena in digital space production in Western countries and China's response 西方国家数字空间生产“类封建”现象与中国应对方案 Long Yu Long Yu asks what happens when digital space production in some Western capitalist countries takes on a "quasi-feudal" form, and how China should respond. Starting from Marx's remark that space is an element of all production, the article argues that a few digital technology oligarchs enclose digital territory, seize the gains of technological progress and extract rent from everyone who enters their space. Long's answer is that China should use the advantages of its socialist system to prevent this pattern. The article has three parts. The first describes the main features of the quasi-feudal pattern: a digital enclosure movement, new relations of personal dependence, and digital ground rent. The second identifies three crises hidden in it: technological monopoly, human alienation and imbalanced governance. The third sets out a Chinese approach built on high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, the management of attention and an open digital ecosystem. Long draws on Meta, Amazon, Google and Apple as examples, and on thinkers such as Cédric Durand, Yuval Noah Harari and Jonathan Crary. Long describes oligarchs as "digital lords" who act as legislator, enforcer and judge through user agreements. In this account, other capitalists become "digital vassal capitalists", digital workers become a "digital proletariat" and consumers become "digital serfs" who work unpaid by generating data. Using Marx's theory of absolute, differential and monopoly rent, Long argues that digital space rent is the economic realisation of ownership of digital space and is a redistribution of surplus value created by living labour. Capital accumulation thus shifts from "exploiting profit" to "seizing rent". Long stresses that this is not a reversion to feudalism but a product of capital's own logic, which produces technological hegemony, attention manipulation and closed ecosystems that spill power into politics and global governance. For China, Long proposes making full use of the new whole-nation system (xīnxíng jǔguó tǐzhì) to combine an enabling government with an effective market, and regulating digital capital through anti-monopoly law. Long also calls for algorithm governance, cultivating "deep attention" and raising public digital literacy. On data, the article advocates compliant data circulation, trusted data spaces, privacy-preserving computing, open-source models and interoperability, in order to secure fairness and justice in digital society. Read the original if you want a Marxist rent-theory account of platform power, or want to see how a Chinese scholar links critique of Western digital capitalism to domestic policy proposals.

How Chinese modernization resolves the modernization predicament of the Global South, and why it matters 中国式现代化对全球南方现代化困境的破解及其意义 Dai Xuehong Dai Xuehong asks why the countries of the Global South have struggled to modernize and how Chinese modernization answers that predicament. Opening from Xi Jinping's remarks on the collective rise of the Global South, the article argues that Western modernization created a structural predicament for latecomers. In Dai's account, Chinese modernization has broken through it and offers the wider South a path, momentum and theory. The article has three parts. The first sets out four sources of the predicament: predatory colonial expansion, the "core–periphery" structure, the capitalist system of global accumulation, and ecological imperialism. The second pairs each with a Chinese answer. The third describes the world significance of that answer under three headings: path options, development momentum and theoretical contribution. Dai draws on world-systems and dependency theory (including Samir Amin), Marx's theory of capital and the notion of metabolic rift. In Dai's reading, Western modernization depended on plunder, then on unequal exchange and conditional aid that locked the South into dependence, and on shifting capital's crises and pollution southwards. Chinese modernization is said to answer these with peaceful development, independent self-reliance combined with opening up, a people-centred approach that "harnesses" capital under a socialist framework, and harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. Dai holds that China has crossed the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, which the author treats as structurally similar to the situation of the Global South. Its aid carries no political conditions, and the Belt and Road Initiative supplies public goods. Dai also says it breaks the Western monopoly on modernization discourse, and presents the Four Global Initiatives as a theoretical contribution. Dai concludes that Chinese modernization is not a model to be exported but offers distinctive path choices, such as a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, ecological harmony and peace. It also supplies momentum and theoretical resources for the South's collective modernization, with a community with a shared future for mankind as its goal. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship uses dependency and world-systems arguments to present Chinese modernization as a response to the Global South's development problems.

A detailed investigation of Ren Bishi's return to support the Central Red Army's Long March 任弼时等率部回援中央红军长征一事详考 Ren Xiangyuan Peng Yu The article takes up a little-documented episode of Red Army history. In 1941–42 the historian Ye Huosheng heard comrades of the former Second Front Army recall that Ren Bishi, leading the Sixth Army Corps on its westward expedition, turned back to support the Central Red Army's Long March. The authors, from the Ren Bishi Memorial Hall, argue that the episode really happened and set out to establish it from Nationalist and Communist documents, telegrams, battle reports and memoirs. The study follows the Sixth Army Corps from its departure in August 1934 to its meeting with He Long's Second Army Corps on 24 October 1934. It has three parts: the existence and content of the recall orders of 3–4 October; the decision taken by Ren, Xiao Ke and Wang Zhen at Houchang on 4–5 October; and the military significance of the marches and battles from 5 to 24 October. The sources include the Central Revolutionary Military Commission's telegrams, Otto Braun's (Li De's) recollections, Xiao Ke's and Zhang Ziyi's memoirs, and Nationalist battle reports and recollections. The authors first compare the Commission's orders with the corps' route. Up to 2 October the route matched the instructions. Only the three urgent telegrams of 3–4 October forbade a move west across the Wu River and ordered the corps to Jiangkou, and the authors treat these as the recall orders. They link the orders to the Central Committee's decision to break out, and cite Xiao Ke and others to argue that the corps was meant to provide a foothold in western Hunan and to scout the route. The authors infer that the Army Corps' military and political committee gave up a feasible Wu River crossing at Houchang and turned northeast. No source records the discussion directly, so they reason from circumstances: the corps' leaders had foreseen a westward shift of the Central Red Army, and they were told to reach the new area by mid-October. They then show that the breakout at MaSangchangping and the Jiagou gorge, at heavy cost at Ganxi, drew off large Nationalist forces. They cite Li Jue's and Yang Shangkun's memoirs to argue that this eased the Central Red Army's passage through the first blockade lines. The authors conclude that the episode is genuine military history. In their account the Sixth Army Corps took heavy losses but completed its task: it joined the Second Army Corps, served as a scout and diverted enemy troops. They present the episode as showing the political loyalty, firm conviction and spirit of sacrifice of Ren, Xiao Ke, Wang Zhen and their troops. Read the original if you work on Long March history or Ren Bishi and want a source-based reconstruction of the Sixth Army Corps' movements in October 1934.

How the Red Army built discipline on the Long March 长征路上红军如何开展纪律建设 Liu Jie Marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory in 2026, Liu Jie asks how the Red Army kept itself together under extreme pressure. The author argues that strong discipline-building was an important guarantee of victory, citing Zhu De's remark that on the Long March "we lived by discipline". Observing discipline is presented as a core part of the Long March spirit and a key to reading the Long March "miracle" and passing on the Party's red genes. The article is a short commentary built around three practices drawn from the Party Central Committee and Central Military Commission record: discipline education, combining work style with discipline in mass work, and strict supervision and enforcement. Liu draws on Red Army orders, the newspaper Red Star, proclamations issued in Yi and Hui areas, and individual disciplinary cases. It closes by linking these experiences to present-day Party governance. On education, Liu describes a layered system: written directives such as the 1934 political-work instruction, case-based articles in Red Star, and memorable slogans like the "Eight Points for Attention on entering Zunyi" for a largely illiterate army. On mass work, the author argues that publicly announcing ethnic and discipline policies before entering Yi and Hui areas gave local people a concrete standard by which to monitor the army. Liu says that the army's conduct then won trust, with Yi and Hui youths joining it. On enforcement, the author points to inspection teams at corps, division and regiment level, and to public trials and executions of personnel for extortion, embezzlement and dereliction of duty. Liu concludes that firm Party spirit, good Party conduct and strict Party discipline explain how the Party has endured, and that each generation has its own Long March. The author calls for sustained full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, citing Xi Jinping on strict supervision as a weapon of the Party's self-reform. Liu also urges handling violations early and in small matters, and neither wronging the innocent nor excusing the guilty. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of Long March discipline cases and how they are used to support current Party-discipline messaging.

The distinctive contribution of the Long March Spirit to inheriting and carrying forward the great founding spirit of the Party 长征精神对传承弘扬伟大建党精神的独特贡献 Wang Binglin Marking the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March, Wang asks how one specific form in the Spirit Genealogy of Chinese Communists inherits and extends the great founding spirit of the Party. The author treats the founding spirit as the source and the genealogy as the stream that flows from it. Wang argues that earlier studies tend to read single spirits statically or list them chronologically, and that the Long March Spirit's bridging role has been under-examined. The thesis is that the Long March Spirit inherits the founding spirit in every dimension and also enriches it through its own distinctive features. The article has four parts. It first sets the four components of the founding spirit (upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, being loyal to the Party and true to the people) against Long March episodes. It then examines what is unique about the Long March Spirit, then its influence on Chinese society from the revolution to the present, and finally its international dissemination. The evidence ranges from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping to accounts by foreign journalists, scholars and politicians. In the author's reading, the Long March Spirit is distinctive for three reasons. It carries a historical turning-point character, because the Zunyi Meeting ended dogmatic leadership and began genuinely independent exploration. It also fuses Party spirit with the national spirit, which Wang calls the highest embodiment of that spirit. And it has unusual reach, since, unlike regional or sector-specific spirits, it worked at the level of the whole revolution and spread through texts, poetry, songs and slogans. Wang then traces how the 'new Long March' idiom was used from Deng Xiaoping's 1978 speech through later leaders to Xi Jinping's image of each generation's own Long March. The author also cites the naming of rockets, submarines, parks and hospitals after the Long March. Wang adds that Snow, Salisbury and Brzezinski, the Comintern's reassessment, and Time magazine's 1999 listing helped spread the founding spirit abroad. Wang concludes that the Long March Spirit turns the abstract founding spirit into concrete, widely felt strength, and that it has become a shared spiritual asset of humanity. The author suggests it can feed a community with a shared future for mankind and broaden the founding spirit's reach abroad. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how the Long March is used in official discourse and how its foreign reception is presented, with many cited sources.

Characteristics of the Central Committee's meetings during the Long March 长征时期中共中央会议特点论析 Li Zequan Li Zequan asks what distinguished the dozens of important meetings the CPC Central Committee held during the two-year Long March, and why they proved decisive. Earlier scholarship, the author notes, has mostly catalogued their number, type, date, place, topics and participants. Li instead identifies three defining features: fixing on the most important agenda item and pursuing it to the end, handling the tactics of inner-Party struggle correctly, and upholding democratic centralism. The article is organised around these three features. It draws on more than twenty meetings, from Tongdao, Liping and Zunyi through Lianghekou, Eijie (Russian-border) and Maoergai to Wayaobao after the Central Committee reached northern Shaanxi. It concentrates on Mao Zedong's role and on the conflicts with the 'Left' dogmatist leadership of Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De), and with Zhang Guotao. It closes with the contemporary lessons the author draws. On the first feature, Li argues that the 'first agenda item' was line and leadership. Before arrival in Shaanxi the issue was the military line, and afterwards the political and organisational lines. The author also points to the tight, sustained pace of meetings, such as six in eleven days at Zhaxi. On the second, Li contends that at Zunyi Mao won over Zhang Wentian, Wang Jiaxiang and Zhou Enlai, and confined the meeting to the military line without attacking the earlier political line. In dealing with Zhang Guotao, Li says, Mao combined principle with flexibility and refused expulsion so as to preserve Party and army unity. On the third, Li reads Zunyi as a victory of the majority over a small minority. Li cites the enlarged-meeting format used in 14 sessions and the Gougba meeting, where Mao accepted a vote against him and then persuaded colleagues. Zhang Guotao's defeat is likewise attributed to his violating democratic centralism. Li concludes that these meetings were the most critical factor in turning the Long March from crisis to success and in establishing Mao's correct line and leadership. The article presents them as a guide for improving decision-making today. It calls for the traditions of the Long March to be carried forward under the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and for formalism and bureaucratism in meetings to be opposed. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how Long March meetings are interpreted in current official scholarship, including the Zunyi, Gougba and Zhang Guotao episodes.

A historical examination of the building of daily-life discipline in the Red Army during the Long March 长征途中红军生活纪律建设的历史考察 Li Anfeng Sun Huitong Li and Sun take up a topic they say has received little attention. Scholarship on the Long March has concentrated on policy, key meetings, the Long March spirit, leaders and military command, while the daily-life discipline that governed Red Army conduct has been neglected. Drawing on published archives and memoirs, they argue that the Party Centre steadily built up this discipline in response to changing circumstances, and that it was an important guarantee of the march's success. The article has three main parts. The first explains why daily-life discipline arose: the pressure of Nationalist encirclement and harsh terrain, the need to forge a reliable force, the need to win popular support, and the need to hold the army together. The second describes how the discipline was constructed, as an integrated system of regulation, propaganda, leadership example, enforcement and supervision. The third assesses results. A short conclusion draws lessons for the present. The authors' central claim is that daily-life discipline was not an external restraint but became an internalised habit and value, moving from "being made to obey" to "wanting to obey". They point to directives of the General Political Department on ethnic minorities and grain purchases, to the Red Star newspaper, songs and slogans, to Mao Zedong's stretcher and Peng Dehuai's mule as examples set by leaders, and to inspection teams, local work departments, Communist Youth League members and complaints from local people as a multi-layered supervisory system. They also cite Zhang Guotao's challenge to the Centre as a case of indiscipline that failed. The authors report four results: the trust of local people, who supplied food and information; an upright style within the army; large-scale recruitment, which they put at about 20,000 for the First Front Army alone; and stronger combat capacity, illustrated by the 34th Division at the Xiang River. They conclude that strict discipline is the basis of victory and of a strong army. They call for carrying this "red gene" into military education, in support of building a world-class army and of national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the Red Army's everyday conduct rules were framed, propagated and enforced during the Long March, as presented in current Chinese military-history scholarship.

Combining an efficient market with an effective government to promote "Little Giant" enterprises 有效市场与有为政府结合 推动“小巨人”企业发展 Zeng Xiankui This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2026, asks how policy can best support the specialised, refined, distinctive and innovative "Little Giant" enterprises. Zeng Xiankui argues that these firms are a backbone of the real economy, especially manufacturing, and matter for advanced manufacturing, supply-chain resilience and new quality productive forces. In Zeng's view, the core task is an efficient industrial ecosystem that joins firms' rapid short-term growth with long-term sustainability, and the key is to combine market mechanisms with a more proactive government. The piece sets out four lines of action: fiscal and tax tools, support for technological innovation, a wider industrial ecosystem, and locally tailored development models. On the first, Zeng proposes rewards and subsidies to ease the weak finances of small and medium-sized firms, support for digital transformation and technical upgrading, and fiscal rewards or tax relief for firms that reach R&D thresholds. On innovation, Zeng wants government to broker cooperation with universities and research institutes, fund major technological projects, open large research instruments to shared use, and strengthen intellectual property protection so that competition rewards the strongest firms. On the ecosystem, Zeng calls for easing constraints on talent, capital and data through special loans, support for listing, postdoctoral workstations and fast-track channels for senior talent, together with graded cultivation systems and a "one enterprise, one policy" officer system. Zeng concludes that regions should build on local industrial bases and resource endowments, giving the example of eastern regions backing "Little Giants" in artificial intelligence and robotics, and should design systematic policy packages suited to local difficulties. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style account of the policy instruments Chinese commentators link to the "Little Giant" programme.

New requirements and tasks for accelerating the building of a modern economic system 加快建设现代化经济体系的新要求和新任务 Qiao Xiaonan Written in the wake of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) and its Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan, this article asks what it takes to achieve a "major breakthrough" in building a modern economic system by 2030. Qiao Xiaonan argues that only by combining breakthroughs in key areas with coordinated advance across the whole system can China release its economic potential. The result, Qiao contends, would be an effective improvement in the quality of growth alongside a reasonable increase in its quantity, supporting decisive progress towards basically realising socialist modernization. The article has four parts. The first explains why the modern economic system underpins Chinese modernization, and reads it through a systems perspective as six "systems" and one "mechanism": industry, urban-rural and regional development, green development, opening up, income distribution, a unified market, and the economic institutions. The second concerns technological and industrial innovation, new quality productive forces and the green development system. The third deals with strategic economic layout, and the fourth with production relations suited to new quality productive forces, including distribution, urban-rural and regional coordination, and the market economy. Qiao's central claims are several. Growth remains a necessary basis for development: with 2024 per capita GDP of US$13,445, the article holds that average annual growth of 4.5–5 per cent is still needed to approach the level of moderately developed countries. A country of over 1.4 billion people cannot rely on export-led growth, so the domestic cycle must be strengthened, and investment in things must be balanced with investment in people. Drawing on Marx's theory of machine industry, Qiao argues that intelligent production raises the organic composition of capital, reduces employment absorption and the labour share and widens income gaps. Common prosperity, income rising in step with growth, and a high-level socialist market economy are therefore presented as conditions for accommodating advanced productive forces. Qiao concludes with a programme: self-reliant science and technology, an "AI Plus" initiative, a manufacturing-centred industrial system that does not neglect traditional industries, carbon peaking and neutrality, a unified national market, institutional opening up and an income distribution tilted towards labour. Throughout, the article presents the Party's leadership and an effective market working with an enabling government as the framework. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy rationale, from within the Chinese academy, for the 15th Five-Year Plan's economic priorities.

On the new form of scientific socialism in the twenty-first century 论二十一世纪科学社会主义的新形态 Wu Haijiang Wu Haijiang asks what historical position Chinese modernization occupies in the long development of scientific socialism, and what theoretical narrative should accompany it. The article argues that Chinese modernization has opened a new form of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. In Wu's account this form rests on the achievements of developed socialism with Chinese characteristics, aims to surpass contemporary capitalism, and looks towards the next stage of socialism. The article has three parts. The first treats Marxism as a "historical science" and traces scientific socialism through three forms: the classical conception built on developed Western capitalism and the Paris Commune, the twentieth-century practice in backward countries such as Russia and China, and the emerging twenty-first-century form. The second part explains how Chinese modernization creates this new form.
