The third part turns to building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system for scientific socialism, covering its context, methods and points of focus. Wu's central argument is that Chinese modernization has solved three major problems of scientific socialism: how socialism should relate to capitalism, how to avoid the ills of capitalist modernization, and how to defend the socialist system against risks. It has also answered new questions of the era, namely the Chinese, world, people's and epoch questions, in the setting of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes unseen in a century. The author lists new features in path, theory, institutions and culture, including the Two Integrations, the socialist market economy and whole-process people's democracy. For the knowledge system, Wu draws on narratology to describe scientific socialist narrative as both factual and normative. The article proposes methods that unite critique with construction, upholding fundamental principles with innovation, and a Chinese standpoint with openness. Wu names three priorities for the new knowledge system: the new possibilities Chinese modernization opens for scientific socialism, the social effects of the technological revolution (digital productive forces and artificial intelligence), and new changes in contemporary capitalism such as financialization and populism. The conclusion presents the new form as a new version of modern human civilization and as a "Chinese sample" of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese theorists place Chinese modernization within the genealogy of scientific socialism and frame an autonomous knowledge system.

The Party and the Red Army's practice of close unity during the Long March, and its lessons 长征时期党和红军发扬紧密团结精神的实践探索和启示 Li Zequan Marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March, Li Zequan asks how the Party and the Red Army sustained close unity under near-annihilation, and what this offers today. Li argues that close unity was a major internal cause of the march's turn from strategic retreat to a victorious advance north against Japan. The article ties this to the Great Long March Spirit, which Xi Jinping summarised as including taking the overall situation into account, strict discipline and close unity. The article has three parts. The first describes four manifestations of unity: the cohesion of the central leadership, co-ordination among the Red Army forces, solidarity within the ranks, and bonds with the civilians along the route. The second gives three causes: shared ideals and convictions, correct Party leadership, and strict discipline. The third draws four lessons. Li draws on episodes such as Xu Haidong's loan to the Central Committee and the "half a quilt" story, and on recollections by Li Xiannian, Peng Dehuai, Chen Yun and others. Li's central claim is that unity was produced through principled, well-handled struggle rather than the absence of conflict. After the Zunyi Meeting, Mao Zedong and others rejected the "Left" military line but did not fully repudiate the "Left" political line or strip its leaders of other posts. Li presents this as necessary to keep figures such as Zhang Wentian and Wang Jiaxiang on side. Against Zhang Guotao's split, the Central Committee combined firmness with flexibility. It treated the dispute as an intra-Party contradiction and declined to expel him, and Li credits this with bringing the Fourth Front Army north. Li adds that leaders' own conduct (Zhou Enlai giving up the post of general political commissar, Zhu De, Ren Bishi and He Long resisting the split) and democratic centralism guaranteed the outcome. Li lists the lessons as: set a correct strategic line, conduct correct inner-Party struggle, have leading cadres show Party spirit and model unity, and uphold democratic centralism. The article closes by saying that the Party is still "on the Long March", with new mountain passes and rivers to cross. It calls for carrying forward this spirit to consolidate unity among the Party, the army and the people in pursuit of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of the Zunyi Meeting and the Zhang Guotao split, and of how contemporary Chinese scholarship draws lessons from them.

The Long March spirit in Chen Yun's writings on the Long March and its contemporary value 陈云长征著作中蕴含的长征精神及其当代价值 Zhao Dan Li Jinhui Chen Yun took part in the Long March and supported Mao Zedong at the Zunyi Meeting. He later wrote three accounts of it: Notes on Accompanying the Army to the West (Jianwen lu), the Outline for Conveying the Enlarged Politburo Meeting at Zunyi, and the Report on the Long March of the Red Army and the Zunyi Meeting. Zhao and Li note that existing scholarship treats these texts mainly as propaganda and historical sources. They argue that the Long March spirit embodied in them has been neglected, and that the texts remain valuable today for understanding and promoting that spirit. The article appeared in 2026. The article has three main parts. The first reads Chen Yun's writings against the five components of the Long March spirit as set out by Xi Jinping. The second sets out the works' contemporary value. The third proposes practical ways to promote the spirit in the new era, and a short closing section places this within the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In the first part, the authors pair each component with episodes Chen recorded. These include the crossing of the Dadu River and the Luding Bridge, the sacrifice of a division at the Xiang River, and the criticism of "dogmatism" for directing the army as if along a line drawn in pencil. They also cite the Zunyi Meeting's correction of errors, soldiers' discipline and equal treatment with officers, ethnic unity with the Miao and Yi, and Mao Zedong's gift of clothing to a destitute old woman. In the second part they argue that the works supply reliable historical evidence, preserve emotional memory through humane details, and serve as lively texts for communication. They stress that Chen's account reached Paris and Moscow in March 1936, before Edgar Snow's interviews, and was praised by the Comintern. The authors call for collecting, protecting and digitising Long March documents, and for using the sources in education, including short videos and micro Party lessons. They also call for micro-level narratives and plain language in place of abstract preaching. In addition, they urge the Party to seize leadership of ideological work, to build the image of a great Party through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, and to take control of international discourse so as to counter Western discursive hegemony. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based reading of Chen Yun's Long March texts and the official line on using them in education and external communication.

The Long March Spirit in the process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context: logic, value and contemporary expression 马克思主义中国化进程中的长征精神：逻辑理路、价值意蕴与当代表达 Zhu Hong Li Xiaokang Zhu Hong and Li Xiaokang ask what role the Long March Spirit (1934–36) plays in the process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. They argue that the Long March moved the Party from a "dogmatic" Marxism towards a practice-based, nationalised one, and from passive imitation to active creation. In their account it launched the first historic leap in this process, and the spirit it produced is a concentrated form of the early intellectual achievements of that process. The article has three parts. The first sets out five logics of the spirit: practical breakthrough and theoretical self-awareness, theoretical innovation, the formation of an ideological line, the mass line, and a cultural logic. The second discusses its value under three headings: a spiritual foundation (ideals and hard struggle), a methodological root (seeking truth from facts and independence), and organisational support (the mass standpoint and solidarity). The third examines its contemporary expression. A short conclusion follows. The authors' central claim is that the Party's break with Soviet and Comintern models, marked by the Zunyi Conference (1935), produced the line of "seeking truth from facts" and independence. In their reading this line was later systematised in Mao Zedong's philosophical and strategic writings, the Yan'an rectification campaign and the 1945 Seventh Congress. They trace its continuation through reform and opening up and the Three Represents, then the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For the present day they say the spirit informs poverty alleviation, rural revitalisation, the Belt and Road Initiative, red tourism, ideological and political education, technological self-reliance and the international presentation of China's experience. Zhu and Li conclude that the Long March marked the logical starting point and methodological foundation of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. They treat Chinese modernization as a new "Long March", and call on the Party to strengthen theoretical self-awareness, cultural confidence and its people-centred stance. Revisiting the spirit is, in their words, a reconfirmation of the laws of theoretical innovation, not mere commemoration. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated journal links the Long March to successive stages of Sinicised Marxism, including its present-day uses in education, development policy and external communication.

The historical contribution of the Long March to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and its lessons for today 长征时期中国共产党推进马克思主义中国化时代化的历史贡献与当代启示 Li Zhaoyang Guo Shasha Marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory, Li and Guo ask how the Chinese Communist Party advanced the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times during the Long March, even though the Party had not yet formally posed the question in those terms. They argue that the Long March's victory was in a real sense a victory for that adaptation and an important part of its first historic leap. The article is organised around four contributions. It treats the break with dogmatism as the ideological foundation, the establishment of a strong leadership core as the organisational foundation, the mass line as the popular foundation, and the Long March spirit as a source of motivation. It draws on events from the Xiang River battle to the Zunyi Meeting, on recollections by Chen Yun, Geng Biao and others, and on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The authors argue that the "Left" dogmatism of the Party's provisional central leadership, under Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De), brought heavy losses. In their account, doubts grew through the Tongdao change of direction and the Liping and Houchang meetings, and Zunyi then ended that line's control and marked a turn in the ideological line toward seeking truth from facts. They attribute the earlier setbacks to an immature central leadership and to mechanical obedience to the Comintern, and cite Deng Xiaoping to the effect that no leadership before Zunyi was truly mature. The mass line is presented as both a value ("everything for the masses, everything relying on the masses") and a method ("from the masses, to the masses"). The authors illustrate it with the Red Army's discipline, its ethnic policy toward minority groups, and its use of local knowledge to cross the Wu River. Drawing on Xi Jinping's 2016 account of the Long March spirit, the authors propose five lessons for adapting Marxism today. These are to uphold Party leadership as the guide to direction, to hold to ideals and convictions, to practise seeking truth from facts, to put the people first, and to keep a fighting spirit. They tie these to the Two Integrations, Chinese modernization and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-history article links Long March episodes to the current theory of adapting Marxism, or if you want its sources on Zunyi and the mass line.

Digital socialism or digital utopia? The predicament of foreign left-wing theories of digital socialism and ways out of it 数字社会主义还是数字乌托邦？——国外左翼数字社会主义理论的困境及破解 Xu Tao Xu Tao asks whether the digital socialism proposed by left-wing scholars outside China can break the grip of capital and move socialism from theory to reality, or whether it is only a utopian fantasy. Starting from the rise of 'platform', 'data' and 'surveillance' capitalism, the article argues that these schemes depart from historical materialism and ultimately amount to a 'digital utopia'. Xu nonetheless credits them with a critical and constructive dual stance. The article first maps four strands of digital socialism. These are the critical communication school (Christian Fuchs's 'digital/communication socialism' and Michael Kwet's 'digital commons'); the 'new planned economy' (William Paul Cockshott, Allin Cottrell, Evgeny Morozov); left accelerationism (Nick Srnicek, Alex Williams, Aaron Bastani, James Muldoon, with full automation and 'platform socialism'); and digital social democracy and 'post-capitalism' (Jeremy Rifkin, Paul Mason, Michael A. Peters). It then critiques them on three fronts, theoretical, practical and technological, and closes with four proposed corrections. Xu's critique rests on three 'myths'. Theoretically, the schemes treat socialism as the outcome of technological evolution rather than of the natural-historical movement of productive forces and relations of production, and digital technology remains inside capitalism. In practice, they replace the proletariat with abstract subjects such as Fuchs's 'playbour', favour gradual reform over abolishing capitalist relations of production, neglect land, factories and industrial and finance capital, and lack a unified proletarian party. Technologically, Xu finds them overly optimistic about tools that embed capital's logic and carry risks such as algorithmic discrimination and opaque AI decision-making. Xu also sees a drift towards 'convergence theory', which erases the difference between socialism and capitalism. Xu proposes four moves. The first is to return from a 'digital revolution' to an 'institutional revolution' aimed at capitalist relations of production. The second is to move from 'class silence' to 'class presence', restoring the proletariat as political subject. The third is to shift from Western experience to the experience of the Global South, especially socialist countries, and Xu says this also answers 'data colonialism'. The fourth is to unite theoretical critique with organised practical movement, moving from the 'weapon of criticism' to the 'criticism of weapons'. Xu rejects both nostalgia for a pre-digital society and the expectation that technology will deliver socialism automatically. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western digital-socialist theories, with a typology of their main thinkers and a critique grounded in historical materialism.

Mao Zedong's initial blueprint for socialist agricultural and rural modernization and its historical lessons 毛泽东对社会主义农业农村现代化的初步擘画及历史启示 Xia Shaoguang Marking the 70th anniversary of the compilation of The Socialist Upsurge in China's Countryside (1955–56), this article asks what Mao Zedong's editorial notes to the volume reveal about his plans for agricultural and rural modernization. Xia argues that in these notes Mao set the basic direction of cooperativization, sketched an initial blueprint, drew out the contradictions driving the process, and foresaw its prospects. The article holds that this legacy still guides rural work today. The article first explains why agricultural cooperativization became the route to modernization, drawing on the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949), the general line for the transition period, and early mutual-aid experience. It then recounts how Mao selected 176 of more than 200 reports and wrote notes for 104 of them. The central sections set out twelve unities in the notes, discuss the book as evidence of socialist institutional advantages and of the Party's style of work, and close with three historical lessons. In Xia's reading, the twelve unities show Mao's approach of balanced planning (tongchou jiangu). Examples include Party leadership with close ties to the masses, developing productive forces with changing relations of production, bold construction with frugality, economic work with political and ideological work, and exploiting nature with protecting the environment. Others pair patient education with firm struggle, economic with social construction, the interior with ethnic minority regions, and the enthusiasm of all ages and classes. The author argues that the book embodies the mass line, seeking truth from facts through investigation, and a plain writing style. Xia cites the 1981 Resolution on Party history as endorsing cooperativization as a great historical victory. Xia draws three lessons. Mao's achievements should be assessed in a long historical perspective, and Xia opposes what the article calls historical nihilism. Comparing social systems, the author finds four kinds of progress: over small-peasant production, over capitalist modernization's rural crises, over Soviet agricultural lag, and as a world-historical example for agrarian countries. Finally, rural revitalization today should keep collective ownership as its basis, resist land privatization, and uphold Party leadership in the countryside. Read the original if you want a Party-line reading of Mao's 1955–56 editorial notes and of how they are linked to current rural revitalization policy.

US financial hegemony, financial colonization and international action against hegemony 美国的金融霸权、金融殖民与国际反霸权行动 Yan Jingfeng Yan Jingfeng asks what underpins US financial hegemony, how Washington uses it to extract wealth from the rest of the world, whether it is as solid as it looks, and how other countries are resisting it. The article's thesis is that this hegemony rests on a large, mutually reinforcing support system and operates as a form of financial colonization, but that it is deeply fragile and not unbreakable. The article has four parts. It first sets out six supports of US financial hegemony: the dollar-centred financial system, military power, scientific and technological innovation, discursive power, control of international financial and credit-rating institutions, and an alliance network. It then describes the ways the US exercises control, harvests revenue, sanctions challengers and rebuilds its hegemony digitally. A third part identifies internal weaknesses, and a fourth surveys de-dollarization and other counter-measures. Yan describes financial colonization as a form of neo-colonialism. In the author's account, the US collects seigniorage, shifts its crises abroad through interest-rate cycles and quantitative easing, and treats Treasury bonds as unredeemable IOUs. The author argues that the same logic erodes the base of hegemony. Financialization hollows out industry, which weakens technological and military capacity. It also widens inequality at home and leaves the US dependent on extracting wealth abroad. Sanctions, such as those on Russia after 2022, are said to push other states away from the dollar. Yan reports that countries are diversifying settlement currencies and reserves, buying gold, and building independent payment systems such as CIPS, PAPSS and BRICS Pay. The article also points to non-dollar stablecoins and central bank digital currencies. It argues that the Fourth Industrial Revolution lets major powers build up real-economy strength and military capacity, and that alliance ties loosen as interests diverge. The author lists China's Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind, renminbi internationalization and defence modernization as responses. The article ends with David Harvey's warning that a declining hegemon may turn more coercive, and cites the US–Israeli strikes on Iran as confirmation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of dollar hegemony and de-dollarization, with the author's data on reserves and payment systems.

The "woke" turn of Western liberalism and its likely trajectory 美西方自由主义的“觉醒化”转向及其发展趋势 Lai Qingli Lai Qingli asks how to understand the renewed split of liberalism in the United States and Western Europe since the 2008 financial crisis. The article argues that wokeism has become the banner of a polarised liberal left, which now faces a polarised, populist liberal right in what Western commentators call an "inner Cold War" or "culture war". Lai concludes that this division is a recurrence of older liberal splits driven by the contradictions of the capitalist mode of production, and that a new ideology will eventually emerge. The article has three parts. The first treats wokeism as a new form of progressivism and describes its meaning, motives, principles and historical narrative, and how it draws on cultural Marxism and other Marxist resources. The second sets out three disputes between left and right: over identity (liberalism or "new communism"), over content (liberal "civilisation" or Marxist "culture"), and over orientation (opposing right-wing hegemony or building a left-wing one). The third places the present split in the history of liberalism, from classical liberalism against progressive liberalism around 1900, through progressivism against neoliberalism after the oil crises, to neoliberalism against wokeism after 2008. Lai argues that the left and right differ over the meaning of freedom, its institutional vehicle (market or public power), its path of realisation and its values. In this reading, wokeism keeps Marxist anti-oppression language but replaces ownership of the means of production with race, gender and ecology as the markers of oppression, and moves the struggle to culture. The right, for its part, labels this communism and accuses the left of censorship and cultural hegemony. Lai maintains that each earlier split came from crises of capitalism, and that after 2008 both liberal traditions lost legitimacy at once, so that class conflict was displaced by identity politics. Lai outlines three possible futures: a new left or right idea becomes dominant; the two camps merge anew, since both are said to rely on the state and on individualism; or a replacement ideology appears. The author holds that the fragmentation of ideology signals a new historical period, not the end of history. The new ideology, Lai asserts, can be neither a cycling liberalism nor populism or fascism, but only twenty-first-century scientific socialism, oriented to the free and all-round development of the human being. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of wokeism and the Western culture wars as a symptom of capitalist crisis.

The Lebanese Communist Party's new explorations of the path of national democratic revolution 黎巴嫩共产党对民族民主革命道路的新探索 Wang Ximan Liu Ziwei Wang Ximan and Liu Ziwei ask how the Lebanese Communist Party (LCP), founded in 1924, has developed its path of national democratic revolution, and above all how it has done so since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe. They argue that the LCP has applied Marxism-Leninism to Lebanon's specific conditions and produced a distinctive revolutionary theory. In their assessment the party has made real gains but still faces serious obstacles. The article has four parts. It first periodises the LCP's history in three stages: national revolution dominant (1924–1946), democratic revolution dominant (1947–1989), and the organic combination of the two since 1989, tracing the party's twelve congresses. It then sets out the party's post-1990 theory, followed by its practice in mass struggle, parliamentary and extra-parliamentary politics, and Arab and international solidarity. It closes with an evaluation of the party's progress and its challenges. The authors report the LCP's view that Lebanon is a dependent capitalist state under a confessional (sectarian) power-sharing system. Its two tasks are to break dependence on imperialism and to overthrow the confessional system, and it advances a programme of national and social liberation. In the authors' account the party treats dependence as the root problem and sectarianism as the tool of exploitation that imperialism manipulates. The party puts the working class and its party in the lead and relies on a "class–political alliance" as its organisational form. It prefers peaceful transition through combined parliamentary and mass struggle and rejects civil war. The authors describe practical steps: the October 2019 uprising, and a revised electoral strategy that won the party its first two parliamentary seats in 2022. They also describe its leading role in the Arab Left Forum and its hosting of international communist meetings. The authors judge that the LCP has enriched national democratic revolutionary theory in the Arab world and played a positive role in Lebanon, the Arab region and the international communist movement. They list six constraints: limited party strength (about 30,000 members), a shrinking and divided working-class base, a weak alliance, entrenched confessionalism, an unstable Arab left, and prolonged regional turmoil. They conclude that the road remains long and arduous. Read the original if you study communist parties in the Middle East, or want a Chinese academic account of the LCP's theory, strategy and difficulties.

The core meaning, inner logic and practical path of building a culturally strong country in the new era 新时代文化强国的核心意蕴、内在逻辑与实践进路 Luo Yuting Wu Linlin Taking its cue from the proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), the article asks what it means to build a culturally strong country and how this should be done. Luo and Wu argue that the core of a cultural power is spiritual strength, which they break down into four capacities: ideological guidance, spiritual cohesion, value appeal and international influence. In their view these four, developed in step, are the key marker and lever of cultural-power building. The article has three parts. The first places a culturally strong country within a modernized strong country and treats spiritual strength as the measure of national strength, drawing on Xi Jinping, R.S. Cline, Joseph Nye, and the historical views of Sun Yat-sen, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. The second sets out how the four capacities relate to one another. The third proposes four practical paths. On the core argument, the authors say a country's cultural strength cannot be judged by the scale of the culture industry or the number of cultural products. It depends on whether a spiritual force pervades society and shapes people's inner world. They describe the four capacities as progressive. Ideological guidance, grounded in Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is the foundation. Spiritual cohesion, built on shared ideals and convictions, is the core. Value appeal, rooted in people-centred practice, is the focus. International influence is the outward expression. They add that rising international influence in turn strengthens the other three. The practical path has four parts. The authors call for the Party's theoretical innovation through the Two Integrations, and for using advanced ideas to win over the masses through accessible language and digital media. They also call for sustained practice of socialist core values, and for multi-channel civilizational exchange and mutual learning that keeps the subjectivity of Chinese culture and aims at mutual understanding rather than cultural hegemony. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of the official framework of the "four forces" of cultural power, and of how Chinese scholars link Party theory, values and external communication.

On systems thinking in the five-year plans of the new era 论新时代五年规划的系统思维 Ha Zhanrong Zhang Ying Written after the adoption of the 15th Five-Year Plan Outline in March 2026, the article asks what systems thinking contributes to China's five-year planning. Ha and Zhang argue that the plans' success as a mode of governance rests on systems thinking, which serves as their epistemological and methodological foundation. They contend that existing scholarship studies individual plans or the history of planning but neglects this feature, and they treat each plan as a layered, rigorously structured systems project. The authors examine the plans along three dimensions: the overall arrangement of plan content, the linkage of the planning system, and the coordination of planning actors. Their examples come mainly from the 12th to the 15th Five-Year Plans, with illustrations from provincial and city plans, annual plans, special and regional plans, and the mid-term evaluation of the 14th plan. On content, the authors identify four nested subsystems: guiding purpose, deployments, indicators and means. Each, they argue, balances a pair of tendencies: economic development with human development, overall advance with key breakthroughs, anticipated with binding indicators, and an effective market with a proactive government. On system linkage, they describe four kinds of connection: across time between successive plans, between short-term plans and long-term goals, vertically from national to provincial and county levels, and horizontally among development, spatial, special and regional plans. On actors, they describe a chain in which the Party proposes the Recommendations, the government drafts the Outline and the people's congresses approve it. The Party then exercises overall leadership in implementation, with government organising and congresses supervising. Evaluation by government, with Party approval and review by congress standing committees, feeds the next plan in a cycle of drafting, implementation, evaluation and redrafting. In the article's account this arrangement overcomes problems of Western capital-led development and of policy discontinuity in multiparty systems. The authors conclude that content, system and actors depend on one another and together form the complete shape of the five-year plan as a systems project. They hold that grasping these features helps convert the institutional advantages of planning into national governance capacity and supports the modernization of the national governance system and capacity. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars present five-year planning as systems engineering, with concrete examples from recent plans.

Moving forward through reflection and critique, debate and reconstruction: developments in foreign Marxism in 2025 在反思与批判、争论与重构中不断前行——2025年国外马克思主义发展动态 Wang Xuedong This is an annual survey of Marxist scholarship outside China in 2025, published in World Socialism Studies in 2026. Wang sets it against deepening global ecological crisis, accelerating technological revolution, sharper gender and racial problems in Western societies, and unusual intellectual ferment. The survey holds that foreign Marxism advanced through reflection and critique, debate and reconstruction, and that this is how the theory builds its explanatory, critical and practical force. The review is organised around four fields: Frankfurt School critical theory, ecological Marxism, Marxist feminism, and research on digital capitalism. For each it reports new books, seminars and journal articles, naming scholars from Germany, Britain, the United States, Canada, Italy, Japan and elsewhere. A short conclusion draws out four general features of the year's work. Wang reports the main debates in each field. On critical theory, scholars such as Lukas Meisner and Lauren Langman affirm its emancipatory value, while Lois McNay, Amy Allen and John Bellamy Foster criticise its normative turn and Western Marxism's "four retreats" (from class struggle, from anti-imperialism, from materialism and from reason). In ecological Marxism, Ian Angus and Foster defend Marx's ecological thought and the Anthropocene concept; Jason W. Moore rejects the latter, and Kohei Saito's degrowth communism is judged by Roulx and Fritsch to be original but ahistorical and strategically hesitant. On digital capitalism, Christian Fuchs's account of digital labour is set against the claims of Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean that capitalism has become technofeudal or neo-feudal. Nicholas Gane and Radhika Desai reject that claim, arguing that rent, monopoly and profit remain capitalist categories. In Marxist feminism, Wang covers renewed interest in the 1970s wages-for-housework movement and the turn towards intersectionality. Wang's conclusion identifies four features: the established currents and their core issues still dominate; historical and contemporary studies coexist; reflective and critical work sets the tone and drives theoretical innovation; and the practical guidance of these theories remains weak. Examples given are the unclear measure and path of degrowth, the difficulty of uniting different gender groups, and the problem of organising digital workers to strike. Wang also evaluates individual positions, finding Foster's critique of Western Marxism apt and Fuchs's digital socialism somewhat utopian. Read the original if you want a map of the year's debates in foreign Marxism, with named scholars and titles, as seen from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

The Latin American Left's view of indigenous peoples: problems, perspectives and evolution 拉美左翼的土著观：问题、视角与流变 Huang Yunhe Li Ziying Huang Yunhe and Li Ziying ask how left-wing Latin American thinkers have understood the "indigenous question", a problem they say remains unresolved from Bolivian protests to the Zapatista movement. They group these views under the label "the Left's view of indigenous peoples" and argue that it is not a unified system but a constructed object made up of differing positions. Their thesis is that the views evolved through three stages, mechanical, reformist and revolutionary, tracking the Latin American localisation of Marxism. The article has three parts. The first examines three core issues: who counts as "Indian" (Pozas and Horcasitas, Lombardo Toledano, Álvaro García Linera, Mariátegui), how the question should be characterised (José Antonio Arze, Mariátegui) and what solutions are proposed. The second traces the three-stage evolution, using Toledano and Arze for the reformist view and Mariátegui and García Linera for the revolutionary one. The third sets out the general features and limits of these views and draws lessons for Marxist research. The authors report a broad consensus among left-wing scholars that the indigenous question is at root socio-economic, tied to land tenure, rather than racial or cultural, which they present as what separates the Left from liberal and positivist views. The "mechanical" view, shaped by Eurocentrism, expects indigenous people to be proletarianised and dissolved as a group. The "reformist" view, which the authors attribute to Soviet-centrism, seeks integration into capitalist national modernisation and is judged to have denied indigenous agency. The "revolutionary" view of Mariátegui and García Linera treats indigenous people as historical subjects: Mariátegui through a worker–peasant alliance and a non-capitalist path, García Linera through Marxism fused with Indianismo and the ayllu tradition, in a "communitarian socialism". The authors describe the views as subjective, plural and critical, and identify four weaknesses: thin theory, a lack of practice, one-sidedness (neglect of culture and identity) and departures from scientific rigour, such as Mariátegui's reliance on Sorel's myth. They nonetheless argue that studying these views supplements research on foreign Marxism. It also shows, they say, how Marxism must avoid both "narrow localisation" and "dogmatic universalism", which they link to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and it can help move past a binary of Chinese and Western Marxism. Read the original if you study Latin American Marxism, Mariátegui or García Linera, or want to see how Chinese scholars use this case in debates about localising Marxism.

Mao Zedong and the narrative construction of the Long March as a revolutionary epic A perspective from conceptual history 毛泽东与长征革命史诗的叙事建构——基于概念史的视角 He Yuqian Li Baogeng Marking the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory, He and Li ask how Mao Zedong turned "Long March" from a plain descriptive verb into a core concept of Chinese Communist Party ideological discourse. They argue that existing scholarship stays at the level of philological dating of early terms and text-by-text reading, and lacks a theory of how a historical event became a political symbol. Using conceptual history, they claim that Mao, adapting the term to successive stages of national rejuvenation, built the Long March into a revolutionary epic. The article moves chronologically. It begins with dictionary and encyclopaedia definitions and the early labels "breakthrough" and "westward advance", then traces the first documented uses of "Long March" in 1935. It next follows Mao's usage during the march, in the Wayaobao report of December 1935 and the Edgar Snow interviews of 1936. It then covers the Yan'an and civil-war years, and finally the period after 1949, ending with three lessons and a link to the present. The core move borrows a speech-act framework in four stages: "speaking to refer to things", "speaking to promote action", and "speaking to accomplish things". The authors say Mao first gave the term a political meaning at Hadapu and in his "manifesto, propaganda team, seeding machine" formulation. In 1939 he made it a call to action, linking it to youth, the United Front and "permanent struggle". The authors read the 1949 remark that victory was only "the first step" of the Long March as the start of the "new Long March" discourse. After 1949 the concept is said to extend to hard work, seeking truth from facts and economic construction, including Mao's 1961 remark on the Long March and practical experience. The authors conclude that the concept's changing meaning shows the Party combining Marxism-Leninism with Chinese realities. They draw three lessons: meaning grows out of revolutionary practice, national rejuvenation is the organising axis, and theoretical innovation keeps pace with the times. They link the "new Long March" to present tasks such as poverty alleviation and building a modernized socialist country, and cast the story as an example of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you study Chinese Communist Party discourse, Mao Zedong Thought or the Long March as political symbol, and want a conceptual-history reading with dated primary-source citations.

The historical evolution of Tanzania's "Ujamaa" socialism and its lessons 坦桑尼亚“乌贾马”社会主义探索的历史嬗变与启示 Yan Shudi Yan Shudi asks what Julius Nyerere's Ujamaa (village-based) socialism in Tanzania achieved and why it failed, and what its legacy offers to Africa today. The article argues that Ujamaa failed in practice but left lessons on post-colonial modernization and an ethos of self-reliance and fairness that still shapes Tanzanian public life. Yan contends that these lessons can help break Western discourse hegemony and point towards a socialist modernization suited to Africa. The article has three parts. The first sets out Ujamaa's origins in Tanzania's colonial economic and social structure, the Arusha Declaration, Nyerere's three principles (equality, democracy, universal participation in labour) and the reasons for failure. The second traces the aftermath: the turn to IMF and World Bank structural adjustment after 1985, echoes of Nyerere in opposition and ruling-party rhetoric, and Ujamaa survivals in village practice such as village assemblies and land governance. The third draws four lessons for Tanzania and Africa, ending with China–Africa cooperation. Yan rejects explanations that blame only Nyerere's personal outlook, official incompetence or outside interference, and stresses the structural obstacle of bringing a largely autonomous peasantry into state management, citing Samir Amin. The failure is traced to forced resettlement from 1967, scarce funds spent on moving people rather than on agricultural productive forces, family plots outcompeting collective fields, and poorly qualified local officials, corruption and a "kulak Ujamaa" of richer peasants. Yan also faults the one-sided plan that put all development into agriculture without an industrial base. After liberalisation, the author says, poverty, land sales to foreign capital and weak land titling persisted, while the ruling party's rhetoric of Nyerere coexists with a still neoliberal core. Yan proposes that Tanzania's ruling party abandon neoliberalism, draw up a systematic socialist development plan and protect Ujamaa legacies such as village assemblies and cooperatives. For Africa generally, Yan calls for a balanced industrial strategy, firm adherence to the socialist path, cultural confidence, and the joint pursuit of Pan-Africanism and socialism. The article closes by urging African states to learn from the experience of socialism with Chinese characteristics and to build modernization with China within a community with a shared future. Read the original if you study African socialism, Nyerere's Tanzania, or how Chinese scholars draw lessons from the Global South for world socialism.

The line, strategy and policy outlook set by the Ninth Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea 朝鲜劳动党九大确立的路线、战略及政策展望 Li Chengri Qian Zhengyu The article examines the Ninth Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPK), held in Pyongyang in February 2026, and what it signals for the DPRK's development strategy, China–DPRK relations and the situation on the Korean Peninsula. Li and Qian argue that the congress consolidated Kim Jong Un's leadership, set a gradual path of high-quality development, and confirmed the Party's existing political line while adjusting its foreign policy. The text is organised in five parts. It covers leadership and personnel changes, the new five-year economic plan, Party building and the 'three revolutions', foreign policy, and a closing outlook that places the congress after the Seventh (2016) and Eighth (2021) Congresses. The authors draw on DPRK official reports, including Kim's work report on the Eighth Central Committee. First, the authors describe a further concentration of leadership. Kim was re-elected General Secretary. A generational turnover of senior figures such as Choe Ryong Hae and Pak Jong Chon took place, and Kim Yo Jong became head of the General Affairs Department. They also note that the share of military cadres fell, with no military figure on the Presidium for the first time, while economic officials gained ground. Second, they report Kim's assessment that the 2021–2025 plan was largely completed. They cite housing construction, the '20×10' regional development policy and tourism projects. The next five years are defined as a stage of consolidation and step-by-step high-quality development. Third, the authors describe the revised Party rules, which write the 'five great Party-building lines of the new era' into the charter and reaffirm the ideological, technical and cultural revolutions, with ideological work first. On foreign relations, the authors report a priority on friendly ties with neighbouring countries and a division of labour among Kim Song Nam, Choe Son Hui and Kim Yo Jong. They note a hard line towards the United States that leaves room for improvement if Washington drops hostile policy. They also note that South Korea is defined as the 'most hostile' state and 'primary enemy'. They conclude that the congress marks more institutionalised rule and a steady line of gradual development, and that China–DPRK cooperation will deepen. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of the Ninth WPK Congress, including its personnel changes, economic targets and foreign-policy lines.

The development, theory and practical experience of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) An interview with Samik Lahiri, Central Committee member of the CPI(M) and former member of the Indian parliament 印度共产党（马克思主义）的发展历程、理论主张与实践经验 Lin Wen Zhao Lijun This is an interview, conducted by Lin Wen and Zhao Lijun and published in World Socialism Studies in 2026, with Samik Lahiri (b. 1967). Lahiri is a Central Committee member of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), CPI(M), editor of its Bengali daily Ganashakti, and a four-time member of the Lok Sabha between 1996 and 2009. The interviewers ask him to explain the party's history, its theory of Indian society, its record in government and its view of China's path. The interview has three parts. The first covers the party's origins, its membership (1.019 million as of 2024), the Telangana uprising, land reform in West Bengal and the party's turn to parliamentary struggle, as well as its relations with Maoist armed groups. The second turns to class analysis, caste, land concentration, urban–rural gaps, Hindu nationalism, the long rule in West Bengal and Kerala, the 2011 defeat, the theory of the people's democratic revolution and BRICS. The third records the party's views on socialism with Chinese characteristics. Lahiri says the party defines India as a state ruled jointly by the bourgeoisie and landlords, led by big capital and increasingly tied to imperialism and neoliberalism. In his account, caste, landlessness and the urban–rural divide are not separate from class struggle but reinforce exploitation, so anti-caste and anti-communal struggles must be joined to class struggle. He presents parliamentary work as a necessary means, not the only path, towards the people's democratic revolution, which he describes as an intermediate stage of land revolution, curbs on monopoly capital and resistance to foreign capital. He attributes the 2011 loss in West Bengal to detachment from rural people, the Singur and Nandigram land acquisitions, neglect of urban and youth demands, and a coalition of anti-communist forces. He condemns Maoist armed struggle as left adventurism and says the party opposes the BJP while refusing a permanent alliance with the Congress. On China, Lahiri says the party broadly endorses socialism with Chinese characteristics as a distinctive attempt to build socialism in a relatively backward country, accepting the primary stage of socialism and the use of the market. He also notes widening income and regional gaps and the need to fight corruption. He reports a CPI(M) delegation visit to China in September 2025, and praises the CASS World Socialism Forum for challenging Western discourse on modernization and democracy. Read the original if you want a first-hand account of how a leading Indian communist party explains its history, its setbacks since 2011 and its stance towards the Chinese Communist Party, as presented to a Chinese academic audience.

Origins and discursive evolution of the Chinese Communist Party's concept of the "political check-up" 中国共产党政治体检概念的源流考释与话语变迁 Wu Zongwei The "political check-up" (zhengzhi tijian) entered Party discourse in 2018, when Xi Jinping called on members and cadres to undergo regular check-ups to "sweep away political dust". It was written into Party regulations in 2019 and restated in 2024. Wu asks where this concept comes from and how its meaning developed. Wu argues that, although the term appeared only in the new era, related ideas and practices run through the Party's whole history, and that the concept matured through inheritance and innovation rather than appearing without precedent. The article is a conceptual history in five parts. It first traces the concept's sources in classical Chinese culture and in Marxist writings on Party building. It then follows its development through the New Democratic Revolution, the period of socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and finally the new era. On the sources, Wu reads the term as a medical metaphor applied to politics and finds precursors in the traditional ideas of self-examination (canxing), official assessment (kaoke) and public critique (qingyi). Wu also draws on Marxist writings about Party spirit, criticism and self-criticism, and ideological struggle and political education. For the revolutionary period, Wu argues that struggle was itself the test of members' loyalty, and that the Party built a system of political screening covering admission, assessment and purges. In the socialist period the equivalent expressions were \"passing the socialist test\" and \"clearing up politics\", which the author says combined institutionalised screening with campaign-style purification. Wu acknowledges that the latter caused harmful consequences. In the reform era, \"democratic appraisal\", \"checking against standards\" and \"Party-spirit analysis\" made the practice more regular, with clearer standards. For the new era, Wu identifies three innovations: a statement of the concept's function (for individuals, for intra-Party political life and for selecting cadres), explicit standards (Central Committee requirements and Party rules, the people's expectations, and the example of revolutionary forebears), and methods (political inspection tours, organisational life and mass supervision). Wu concludes that the century-long history should be viewed objectively and as a whole, despite detours and misunderstandings, so that its revolutionary and political significance is properly understood. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language genealogy of this Party-building term and its precursors, from imperial-era ideas to current Party regulations.

Theoretical construction and practical paths of the historical outlook of the Chinese nation in the new era 新时代中华民族历史观的理论构建与实践路径 An Beijiang An Beijiang takes up the contest over historical narrative in international ideological struggle. The article argues that hostile forces inside and outside China use erroneous narratives to dismantle the pluralistic and unified pattern of the Chinese nation and to deny the continuity of Chinese civilization. In response, An proposes building a correct historical outlook of the Chinese nation, centred on "diversity in unity" and the "five commonalities", to safeguard ideological security and forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first analyses the manifestations and spread of historical nihilism and "Western-centrism" in four areas: deconstructing the national pattern, denying civilizational continuity, discrediting the historical roots of China's path, and the channels of dissemination. The second sets out the core content and theoretical foundations of the proposed outlook. The third lays out construction paths at the levels of the state, scholarship, media and education. In An's account, the targeted narratives include "conquest" or "colonial rule" readings of the Yuan and Qing dynasties, an absolutised use of Benedict Anderson's "imagined communities", "rupture" and "foreign origin" theories of civilization, and "empire" analogies for governance. An says these spread through academic packaging, popular culture, emotive social media, "index traps" such as human-rights indices, and AI-generated content. Against them, the author grounds the outlook in historical materialism, with the people as creators of history. It treats diversity in unity as the nation's historical gene, the "five commonalities" (shared territory, state, history, culture and spirit) as its historical main line, and the idea of great unity (dayitong) as the ideological guarantee of civilizational continuity. An calls for a national historical narrative system with assessment and early-warning mechanisms, and for a national index-analysis centre to track Western indices. The article also proposes national interdisciplinary research platforms, field stations in border areas, a national communication project with digital platforms and youth-oriented content, stronger international communication, integrated history education, and the creative use of cultural relics. The author concludes that building and spreading this outlook is a basic, strategic task for countering attempts to use history against China. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences scholar frames history, ethnicity and ideological security, and what concrete institutional measures are proposed.

The historical position of Leninism and its contemporary significance 列宁主义的历史地位及其当代意义 Wang Xiaoju Wang Xiaoju asks how Leninism should be assessed historically and what it means today. The article argues that Lenin advanced Marxism to a new stage, that Leninism made an original contribution to Marxist theory, and that inheriting, defending and developing it remains a major task for the prospects of world socialism. In Wang's view it also bears on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and on Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out Leninism's historical position under five headings: Marxism adapted to its era, to Russia, to practice, to the future, and to internationalism. The second surveys and rebuts anti-Leninist currents, from Khrushchev and Gorbachev to Russian historians, Vladimir Putin, Western scholars such as Erich Fromm and Karl Korsch, and some Chinese scholars. The third turns to four present-day implications. Wang's central claim is that Leninism is Marxism developed for the age of imperialism and proletarian revolution, and confirmed in practice by the October Revolution, the New Economic Policy and the founding of the USSR. Wang cites Lenin's theory of imperialism, his view that socialism could first win in one country, and his notion that each nation would reach socialism in its own way. Wang treats the evaluation of Lenin as a political question as well as a scholarly one, and rejects what the article calls historical nihilism. Putin's remark that Lenin's national self-determination planted a 'bomb' under the Soviet state is rejected as untenable. Wang argues that the federation Lenin proposed was meant to secure the Soviet state against intervention, and that the USSR's dissolution cannot be blamed on Leninism. For the present, Wang argues that Leninism offers a basis for understanding world history, including the continuing validity of the 'two inevitables' of Marx and Engels. It also gives a scientific basis for reading the changing world order, including digital and platform capitalism, and supports a fairer international order and multilateralism. For Chinese modernization, Wang draws on Lenin's formula for learning from foreign technology and management, and on the New Economic Policy as an inspiration for the socialist market economy. Wang calls for close reading of the classics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences historian defends Lenin against Russian, Western and Chinese critics and ties Leninism to current Chinese policy.

The contemporary situation and clarification of Lenin's theory of imperialism From the perspective of the dialectical relationship between politics and economics 列宁帝国主义理论的当代境遇与澄清——以政治与经济的辩证关系为视角 Xiao Bin Zheng Yongliang Xiao Bin and Zheng Yongliang take up a charge made by a number of Western scholars: that Lenin's theory of imperialism over-emphasises economics and neglects geopolitics and the theory of the state. The authors argue that this charge rests on a misreading of historical materialism, and that returning to Lenin's method remains necessary for understanding present-day imperialism, including the post-2000 expansion of US-led capitalism. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the political and economic sides of Lenin's theory: the political hegemony contained in imperialism's economic features, the revolutionary potential in its parasitism and decay, and Lenin's critiques of Hobson, Hilferding and Kautsky. The second surveys Western criticisms: Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin, John Willoughby, Vivek Chibber, Ashman and Callinicos on 'state instrumentalism'; and Noonan, Morgenthau, Schumpeter and Waltz on 'economic reductionism'. The third offers a reply and restates the method. The authors' central move is to argue that critics split politics from economics mechanically. They hold that Lenin saw imperialism as a structural fusion of the state with monopoly capital, citing his remark that the state merges ever more closely with the capitalist alliances, and not as simple state subordination. They also hold that Lenin stressed the relative independence of politics. On the post-1945 'informal empire', they accept that it rests on state coordination through Bretton Woods, NATO and cultural industries. They maintain, however, that its base is still highly financialised monopoly capital, so stressing state 'autonomy' alone slides into political voluntarism. The authors then draw four methodological lessons: historical materialism applied to a new stage; a totalising political-economy critique; the dialectic of necessity and contingency, structure and agency; and the rise from the abstract to the concrete. The authors conclude that a new theory of imperialism should refine state theory and geopolitical analysis without abandoning Lenin's core categories of monopoly, finance capital and capital export. These should be examined under financialisation, globalisation, informatisation and neoliberalism. They warn that abandoning the totalising method leads either to political idealism that reduces everything to state power, or to fixation on fragmentary phenomena such as derivatives, digital technology and cultural discourse. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of Lenin against Western state-centred and realist critics, and a detailed account of the critics' arguments.

A review of the 12th National Congress of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party 老挝人民革命党第十二次全国代表大会述评 Xu Qinfa Yuan Liduo Xu and Yuan review the 12th National Congress of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP), held in Vientiane on 6–8 January 2026 under the theme of strengthening Party leadership, building an independent and self-reliant economy, consolidating people's democracy and advancing steadily towards socialism. The authors argue that the congress was a milestone that both summarised five years of experience and set out a blueprint for Laos's socialist cause, and that it combines continuity in basic principles with adjustments in development paths. The article has four parts. It first sets out the congress's background, covering the 70th anniversary of the Party and the 50th of the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Laos's economic and financial difficulties, the international environment, the congress's democratic-centralist preparations (834 delegates, a Central Committee enlarged to 73 members, Thongloun Sisoulith re-elected General Secretary) and reported achievements since 2021. It then examines the 'six basic lessons', the 'three development stages' with 'ten key tasks', and finally compares the 12th Congress with the 11th. In the authors' account, the six lessons, drawn from the Party's 70 years and 50 in power, form a preliminary theoretical framework: Party leadership as decisive, Party unity, a national defence and security line linked to the mass line, respect for objective economic laws and science, rule of law under Party leadership, and self-reliance combined with international cooperation. The strategic framework runs from a long-term vision to 2055 of an upper-middle-income country near high-income status, through a 2026–2035 plan, to the 2026–2030 five-year plan aiming to leave least-developed status and reach growth above 6 per cent. The comparison with the 11th Congress is the article's main analytical move. What stays constant is the socialist orientation, Marxism-Leninism and Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, Party leadership and the socialist-oriented market economy. What changes is a shift from growth and opening towards independence and endogenous drive, stricter Party building against ideological degeneration, higher-quality human resources and poverty reduction, and a more proactive, diversified foreign policy. The authors conclude that the congress's strategy is systematic, scientific and pragmatic, and that it reflects a dialectical unity of continuity and innovation. They present it as an exploration of a Lao path to modernization that enriches understanding of the laws of socialist construction and Party governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned Chinese account of the LPRP's 12th Congress, including its documents, statistics and policy targets, and how Chinese scholars frame Laos's socialist development.

Western distortions of the history of the Second World War: manifestations, effects and responses 西方错误二战史观的表现、影响及应对 Huang He Huang He asks how the Western-centred account of the Second World War took shape, what it does politically, and how China should answer it. The article argues that after 1945 the West built a narrative in which a global people's war against fascism became a story of civilisational victory led by a few "democratic" states. In Huang's view this narrative is an instrument of discourse power and ideological competition, not neutral history. The article has three parts. The first sets out six forms of what Huang calls the erroneous Western view of the war. These are the marginalising of the Eastern Front and the Soviet role, the "Soviet–German collusion" thesis, the "atomic bomb ended the war" thesis, the sidelining of China's war of resistance, the erasure of left-wing resistance movements, and the erasure of colonial peoples' contributions. The second part examines the effects, and the third proposes national strategies. Huang's central argument is that this narrative has been institutionalised through textbooks, commemorations, films and museums, and that it feeds historical nihilism in China. By recasting the resistance as "externally led", it is said to weaken the standing of the Communist Party as its mainstay. The article also says the narrative weakens China's historical voice and softens international consensus on Japan's responsibility, so that it becomes a strategic risk. The evidence includes the Eastern Front battles, Tsuyoshi Hasegawa's argument that Soviet entry mattered more than the bombs for Japan's surrender, and figures on China's role. These figures are that China tied down over 60 per cent of Japan's army and suffered 35 million casualties. Huang proposes three responses. The first is a Chinese narrative with global reach, built on rigorous scholarship and framed through shared international themes such as total war and anti-colonial struggle; the English edition of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' New History of the Second World War (2025) is cited as an example. The second is stronger history education, including a unified database of wartime archives, revised school curricula, and cross-departmental oversight of history content in media and online platforms. The third is wider international communication through touring exhibitions, scholarly exchange and local exchanges in Britain and Southeast Asia. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar frames Western war memory as an ideological security issue and what policy measures the article proposes.

New changes in the accumulation model of financial imperialism under digital production and their implications 数字化生产下金融帝国主义积累模式的新变化及其启示 Chen Hao Zhong Jinchen Chen Hao and Zhong Jinchen ask whether digital production has altered Lenin's basic definition of imperialism or the foundations on which international financial monopoly capital accumulates. Their answer is no: digital capital, which they describe as financial capital in a digital shell, continues the monopoly logic Lenin identified. The form, content and characteristics of financial imperialism nonetheless need to be re-examined, and the article does so in order to draw lessons for China. The article first returns to Marx's account of the "social productive power of capital" and extends it to digital production, arguing that digital capital is the key to understanding contemporary financial imperialism. It then analyses two interacting logics, the expansion of digital hegemony and the export of digital capital. Next it sets out five changes in accumulation, covering new domains, mechanisms, methods, channels and frontiers, with cases and data from the United States. It ends with measures for China. The central claim is that digital hegemony reinforces a "centre–periphery" structure, while digital capital export deepens a "digital–financial" logic. In the authors' account, the centre extracts value through rent-seeking, data pricing power and platform monopolies, and peripheral countries are fragmented into dispersed "points" dependent on the centre. Finance securitises data, collects "circulation rents" through platforms such as the GAMMA firms, and pushes accumulation into digital space, including the sea and outer space. The authors hold that these incomes redistribute surplus value rather than create new value. They argue that this deepens the separation of the real from the virtual economy, adds speculation and parasitism, and breeds the risk of a global digital crisis. For China, the authors call for breaking the technological monopoly through key core technologies and new quality productive forces, and for steering finance to serve the integration of the real and digital economies. They also urge cautious opening of financial-sector foreign ownership, a strong state-capital role as "patient capital", public control of data resources, and a national big-data platform led by "digital central enterprises". Beyond this, they propose building a digital community with a shared future, closing the digital divide with the Global South, and reforming IMF quota formulas. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist political economists extend Lenin's theory of imperialism to data, platforms and digital finance, and the policy conclusions they draw.

Paths to modernization in developing countries and their lessons: the cases of India, Brazil and South Africa 发展中国家现代化路径选择及其经验教训——以印度、巴西、南非等国的现代化为例 Chai Shangjin Zhou Tong Chai Shangjin and Zhou Tong ask what developing countries can learn from the modernization experience of India, Brazil and South Africa, which they describe as among the faster-developing emerging economies. They argue that although these states were shaped by Western influence, their choices of path carried distinct regional and national features. In the authors' view this shows that modernization is not equivalent to Westernization, and that Chinese modernization widens the options open to developing countries. The article is organised in five parts. Three country sections trace each case from colonial beginnings to the present: India from British rule through Nehru's state-led mixed economy to market reforms from the 1980s; Brazil through commodity exports, import-substitution industrialisation, neoliberalism and Workers' Party governments; and South Africa through mining, apartheid and the post-1994 ruling alliance. A fourth part draws general lessons and an analysis of setbacks, and a fifth turns to implications of Chinese modernization. On successes, the authors identify three common features: breaking free of Western models to seek paths suited to national conditions, tackling the main social contradictions that threaten stability, and combining market mechanisms with state planning and regulation, partly learning from socialist countries. On failures, they point to Western-style multiparty parliamentary systems that produce factional strife and leave even left-wing governments unable to change the capitalist character of the state. They also cite unresolved ethnic, religious, caste and racial divisions, and Western economic and political pressure, including neoliberal reform, which they say causes policy swings and the 'middle-income trap'. Drawing on this comparison, the authors propose five lessons from Chinese modernization: put the people first, uphold independence and diversity of paths, combine adherence to fundamentals with innovation, ensure firm leadership by a strong political party, and promote shared benefits through peaceful development and a community with a shared future for mankind. They conclude that a major lesson of India, Brazil and South Africa is the lack of a strong party leadership core able to sustain national political consensus. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar frames comparative lessons from major Global South states in support of Chinese modernization.

Basic paths for the orderly connection of Party discipline and state law in the new era 新时代党的纪律与国家法律有序衔接的基本路径 Wang Yong Bi Lanxin How should Party discipline and state law be linked so that the two work together without displacing each other? Wang and Bi take up this question of "discipline–law connection" (jifa xianjie). They argue that the connection has moved from a principle to be advocated to a mechanism to be implemented. Even so, they hold that institutional design, drafting procedures and enforcement still need strengthening if intra-Party supervision and state supervision are to be integrated. The article has three parts. It first sets out the value of the connection, then identifies four priority problem areas, and finally proposes remedies for each. It traces the policy line from the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2014) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Along the way it covers the revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of January 2024 and the Supervision Law. The authors ground the connection in three needs. Drawing on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, they present discipline as essential to a Marxist party's vanguard character. They also treat the connection as a component of the socialist rule-of-law system with Chinese characteristics and as a requirement of the joint effort against corruption. They then name four weaknesses: blurred boundaries (Party discipline spilling over into society, or "discipline replacing law" and the reverse); poor enforcement links in case transfer, evidence conversion and cooperation; unclear allocation of responsibility among Party discipline, administrative sanctions and criminal liability; and weak awareness and skills among officials. Their remedies include applying "law reservation" and proportionality limits, and keeping discipline stricter than, and ahead of, the law. They also propose joint meetings, joint case teams and a shared clue platform, different conversion rules for physical and verbal evidence, and early involvement of procuratorates. Finally, they propose training, publicity and stronger accountability. Wang and Bi conclude that clear boundaries, working mechanisms, defined responsibilities and stronger awareness together make the connection operate stably. They present this as serving full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the legal governance of power. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-school account of how discipline inspection, supervision and judicial organs are meant to coordinate in practice, including proposed procedures on case transfer, evidence and sanctions.

The dialectical unity of cultural diversity and the common values of all humanity 论文化多样性与全人类共同价值的辩证统一 Zou Guangwen Han Danyang Zou and Han ask how cultural diversity and the common values of all humanity can be held together under economic globalization, which they say both enriches cultures and sharpens conflicts between them. Their thesis is that the two are dialectically united: diversity supplies the experiential soil from which shared values grow, while shared values give diversity a normative framework. They present this as grounded in Marxist historical materialism and in Xi Jinping's statements on civilizational exchange. The article has three parts. The first treats cultural diversity as the basis of civilization, tracing its mixing through exchanges of peoples, species and ideas, and then lists modern challenges in the economic, political, cultural and ecological fields. The second sets out why a bottom-line consensus is needed and how the common values of all humanity (peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy, freedom) take shape over time and space. The third draws out the dialectic between diversity and unity and warns against two extreme attitudes. Zou and Han argue that capital's standardizing logic, Western claims to political universality, algorithmic recommendation and fossil-fuelled climate change each erode diversity. Against this they ground common values in Marx's idea of the human species-essence formed through practice, and in shared existential threats such as ecological and security crises. The authors say these values are not fixed dogma but evolve, combining traditional wisdom with modern practice, as in the move from the idea of harmony between heaven and humanity to the slogan that clear waters and green mountains are invaluable assets. They hold that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers a model for going beyond Western 'universal values'. The authors conclude that cultural relativism, which they say shields backward institutions, and cultural hegemonism, which packages one civilization's values as universal, must both be rejected. Common values should be sought in the 'commonality within difference' through economic interdependence, political trust and mutual learning among cultures. They call for cultural subjectivity and the creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture, in pursuit of the ideal of 'each beautiful in its own way, all beautiful together'. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholars connect the discourse on common values to cultural diversity and a critique of Western universalism.

The inherent logic of the theoretical system of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化理论体系蕴含的内在逻辑 Bao Xinjian Bao Xinjian asks what internal logic underlies the theoretical system of Chinese modernization, which the article presents as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author argues that this system contains a historical, theoretical, practical and contemporary logic, and that its essence lies in the Two Integrations: combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The introduction traces the Party's exploration of modernization from the 'four modernizations' under Mao Zedong, through Deng Xiaoping's 'Chinese-style modernization' and the three-step strategy, to Xi Jinping's formulations. The body then sets out five 'adherences', each treated as one strand of the system's logic: national conditions, a people-centred orientation, civilizational foundations, reform as driving force, and problem orientation. Bao contends that national conditions are the logical starting point. China is a socialist developing country of over 1.4 billion people still in the primary stage of socialism, so it must follow general laws of modernization without copying Western models. The author reads the five Chinese characteristics set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022) as showing the unity of the universal and the particular. The people-centred strand is grounded in the Marxist idea of the people as historical subject. Bao lists six elements of traditional culture (humanism, moral self-cultivation, family-state sentiment, renewal, harmony, holistic thinking) and five features of Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness) as the cultural root of Chinese modernization. On reform, Bao stresses a 'competent market' and 'capable government', new quality productive forces and the modernization of institutions. The final strand names problems still to be solved, among them uneven development, institutional obstacles, outdated thinking, formalism and corruption. Bao concludes that the theoretical system gives the Two Integrations richer content and shows the 'truth-power' of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times in building an autonomous body of knowledge. The author holds that Chinese modernization, led by the Communist Party, has broken the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers developing countries a Chinese approach. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party theorists organise the logic of the Chinese modernization theory.

An analysis of the roots of the degeneration of Karl Kautsky's view of Marxism 卡尔·考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源论析 Zhuang Wencheng Why did Karl Kautsky, a leading theorist of the Second International and the German Social Democratic Party who once contributed importantly to Marxist theory, end up opposing Marxism? Zhuang argues that the shift came from an incomplete and wavering grasp of Marxism's basic principles. The author reads this as the product of both theoretical roots and personal, subjective factors set against the transition from peaceful capitalism to imperialism. The article has three parts. The first sets out four theoretical roots of Kautsky's degeneration. The second turns to three subjective factors in his character and politics. The third draws lessons for the Chinese Communist Party's theoretical innovation in the new era, and a short conclusion follows. On the theoretical side, Zhuang says Kautsky made Marxism's scientific character positivist, treating it as an empirical science rather than a philosophy and reducing historical materialism to a method. He is said to have made its revolutionary character abstract: his stance moved from delaying revolution to obstructing, opposing, attacking and finally slandering it. He is said to have vulgarised the Marxist view of development through Darwinian evolutionism and dissolved its class character through the theory of "ultra-imperialism" and "pure democracy". Citing Lenin's criticism, Zhuang presents Kautsky's war-time and post-1917 positions as a blurring of the class nature of war and democracy. On the subjective side, Zhuang points to his weak theoretical independence, which left him under outside influences such as Bernstein's. The author adds that he failed to grasp imperialism and revisionism as products of the new epoch, and lacked the practical ability to apply theory, preferring a compromise that kept the Party formally united. Zhuang concludes that Kautsky's case warns that theory loses vitality once it departs from Marxism's essential attributes. The author calls for unwavering adherence to dialectical and historical materialism, to the unity of science and revolution, of thorough theory and conscious practice, and of class character and popular character.
