The article ties this to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to Chinese modernization, and to the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-scholarly account of Kautsky as a negative example, and of how it is used to frame current theoretical innovation.

Constructing the false legitimacy of ideology: how American cultural hegemony is built, and its crisis 建构意识形态的虚假正当性：美国文化霸权的建构方式及其危机 Ye Rurong Ye Rurong asks through which cultural practices the United States has built a false legitimacy for its ideology, which epistemological traps keep reproducing it, and how current "America First" policies erode it. The article argues that US cultural hegemony rests on a carefully constructed ideological legitimacy that is false in nature. In the author's account, this legitimacy is now being dismantled by Washington's own turn to open, unilateral dominance, which puts its cultural hegemony in structural crisis. The article begins with Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony and with the distinction between "legitimacy" (zhengdangxing) and legality. It argues that the former is actively created by rulers rather than inherent. Ye then sets out three routes of construction after the Second World War: legitimating liberal values, legitimating a consumerist way of life, and controlling the means of cultural communication. A third section identifies three epistemological traps, and a fourth examines three reversals in recent US policy. On the construction side, Ye contends that consumer goods and media products carry capitalist ideology. Consumers who buy their symbolic meanings take on that ideology, and US dominance of media standards and agenda-setting makes communication one-directional. The traps are an illusion of shared interests, between workers and capital and between the hegemon and subordinate states. They also include a claim of "value neutrality" voiced by new "organic intellectuals" and a false "universalism" that Ye describes as an ideology directed at non-Western societies. On the crisis side, the article describes a move from "consistent interests" to "America First", from "depoliticisation" to "pan-politicisation" (visa limits, cultural decoupling, technology controls), and from "universal values" to "American exceptionalism" (tariffs, withdrawal from agreements and organisations). Ye says these moves strip away the disguise and push the US from hegemony towards "non-hegemonic domination". Ye concludes that these shifts have accelerated the collapse of false legitimacy rather than rescuing US hegemony. In the author's view, the crisis breaks the Western monopoly on global discourse, opens a new historical opportunity for world civilisation, and gives China a key window to step outside Western-set frameworks and build its own discourse system. Read the original if you want a Chinese Gramscian reading of US soft power, and of its decline under Trump-era policy, as a case of ideological legitimacy crisis.

The history, present and future of the Danish communist movement An interview with Lotte Rørtoft-Madsen, chair of the Communist Party (Denmark) 丹麦共产主义运动的历史、现状与未来——访共产党（丹麦）主席洛特·于特夫特·麦德森 An De Zhao Dingqi This is an interview, published in World Socialism Studies (2026, no. 1), in which two Chinese researchers question the chair of the Communist Party (Denmark), identified in the Chinese text as Lotte Yutefute Maideseng. They ask about the history of Danish communism, the party's current situation, Danish social movements and capitalist crisis, and the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The interviewee presents a movement that is divided and not yet in a position to lead, but that she sees as growing. The first part runs from the founding of organised communism in 1919 to the present. It covers the interwar years, the wartime resistance against German occupation, the Cold War splits, the Sino-Soviet divide and the Maoist-oriented groups of the 1960s. It then turns to the crisis after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern European socialist regimes. The later parts take up the party's present tasks, the Nordic welfare state, the far right, and China's role in the world. On history, the interviewee stresses that the Danish resistance succeeded through a broad popular front, which she attributes to communist initiative and links to the Comintern's 1935 strategy. She traces the later fragmentation into three parties and the 2006 merger that created the Communist Party (Denmark), and says the party aims to shift the balance of forces towards the working class through an anti-monopoly alliance. On welfare, she argues that the Nordic system was won by organised labour through class struggle, not granted by the bourgeoisie, and is not a bridge to socialism. She adds that it is being dismantled now that the pressure of European socialism has gone. She describes neo-fascism as fed by decades of neoliberalism, and holds that a full communist revival in Denmark would be premature to proclaim. On China, she calls the 1949 revolution one of the twentieth century's most important events and describes China as upholding socialism while Europe's collapsed. She presents China as a counterweight to the transatlantic alliance and says her party opposes what she calls a new Cold War and interference in China's internal affairs. She says her party will counter rumours about China in the Danish left. Read the original if you want a Danish communist leader's account of her party's history, strategy and view of China, as presented to a Chinese academic audience.

On the cultural subjectivity of the Communist Party of China 论中国共产党的文化主体性 Liu Hongchang The article takes up "cultural subjectivity", which Liu calls a signature concept of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. It asks what the Communist Party of China's (CPC) cultural subjectivity consists of. Liu defines it as the Party's inherent cultural consciousness and capacity as the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture. The article argues that this subjectivity has been formed, consolidated and developed through more than a century of cultural practice led by the Party. Liu distinguishes three nested levels of cultural subject: the Chinese nation, the Chinese people and the Party. The Party's cultural subjectivity is then analysed through four attributes: cultural consciousness, cultural autonomy, cultural creativity and cultural transcendence. Each is broken into sub-dimensions and illustrated with episodes from the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods up to the new era. The sources are speeches by Xi Jinping, works by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, Party congress reports, the Constitution and passages from Marx and Engels. Consciousness is shown in the Party's acceptance of cultural missions, its changing view of culture's place (from a supporting instrument to a goal, a livelihood matter and a productive force), and its grasp of the laws of cultural development. Autonomy means keeping cultural identity and shedding the dependence of late-developing countries. Liu contrasts the CPC's self-chosen path with the Kuomintang's alleged dependence on imperialism and feudal forces, and traces the Party's cultural strategies from the 1950s to the goal of a cultural powerhouse by 2035. Creativity covers people-centred cultural values, new content (revolutionary and socialist culture, and the creative transformation of traditional culture) and methods such as the Two Integrations. Transcendence rests on the relative independence of culture from the economic base, citing Marx on Greek art and Engels on philosophy. Liu argues that the Party has made culture advance beyond its material conditions, and that this is also embedded in constitutional and legal cultural institutions. Liu concludes that the Party's cultural subjectivity is closely tied to the fate of Chinese culture, and that the Party's leadership of culture, rooted in a people-oriented value stance, underpins the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text presents Party leadership over ideology and culture, together with the defence of cultural security against Western infiltration, as essential to this subjectivity. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Chinese Party scholarship frames the CPC as a cultural agent, along with its periodisation of Party cultural policy.

The Communist Party of China's historical process, basic experience and practical paths in building an international united front 中国共产党推动构建国际统一战线的历史进程、基本经验和实践路径 Wang Xinying Zhang Xianyan Wang Xinying and Zhang Xianyan ask how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has built an international united front over its history, and how it should build a new one today. They argue that the united front, long treated by the Party as a key instrument of revolution, construction and reform, has always had an international dimension. Placing the question against the interwoven "two overall situations" (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and profound global change), they hold that the Party's historical record offers lessons and a practical route for the present. The article has three parts. The first periodises the history: the New Democratic Revolution (including the anti-Japanese war and the world anti-fascist front), socialist revolution and construction (anti-hegemony fronts, the "intermediate zone" and "three worlds" theories), reform and opening up (peace and development, partnerships, a harmonious world), and the new era (shared human values, a community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative and the four global initiatives). The second part distils three lessons. The third proposes four practical paths for the present. On experience, the authors identify three points. First, the CPC has handled self-reliance and the international front dialectically: independence and leadership are preserved inside the front, while international aid is treated as necessary though not a substitute for self-reliance. Second, domestic and international fronts must be coordinated, as in the mutual reinforcement of the anti-Japanese national front and the world anti-fascist front. Third, strategic principle (peace, anti-hegemony, solidarity with colonial and developing countries) must be joined with tactical flexibility, shown in Mao Zedong's wide 1964 definition of anti-imperialist forces and the 1970s cooperation with Western states against Soviet hegemony. For the new era the authors propose four paths: take a community with a shared future for mankind as the guiding goal and supply international public goods; make Global South countries the main targets of the front; build issue-based coalitions on development, climate and, in the authors' account, selected areas of China–US cooperation; and shape China's national image through a shift from "unilateral telling" to "shared narrative". The authors conclude that China should use the united front's distinctive strengths to secure a favourable international environment for national rejuvenation and for world peace and development. Read the original if you want a Party-centred, periodised account of Chinese united front thinking in foreign affairs, from Mao to the present, and its policy recommendations.

Mao Zedong's wisdom of struggle and its contemporary value 毛泽东的斗争智慧及其当代价值 Chen Long Chen Long asks what lay behind Mao Zedong's approach to struggle and what it offers the Party today. Starting from the 2021 Party resolution on history, which holds that all achievements came through continuous struggle, the article argues that Mao's "wisdom of struggle" is not personal calculation or mere stratagem. In Chen's account it is a multi-dimensional whole made up of an ideological foundation, value orientation, strategy and method, and fighting spirit. The article first traces the objective and subjective conditions that shaped this wisdom: China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal condition, the lessons of two victories and two defeats in the revolution, the absence of precedent for building socialism, and Mao's early reading, Hunan culture and personal temperament. Four sections then take up the ideological foundation, the values, the strategic and tactical methods, and the spiritual will. A final section draws five lessons for the present, set within Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chen contends that Mao's wisdom has a double theoretical root: struggle must be guided by scientific theory, and new theory must be created in struggle, as in On Practice, On Contradiction and On the Ten Major Relationships. Its values are a bright future for China, socialism and communism, and serving the people wholeheartedly, with policy set independently from investigation of actual conditions. On method, Chen stresses unities of strategic judgement and tactical decision, of principle and flexibility, and of unity and struggle, together with the formula "just, advantageous, restrained" and the pursuit of initiative. Chen presents the spirit of struggle as public-minded conduct, courage that does not fear ghosts, and confidence in victory grounded in a scientific view of contradictions. For today, Chen calls for grasping the new historical characteristics of the great struggle and seizing initiative, and for consolidating the theoretical foundation through Xi Jinping's innovative theory. Chen also stresses keeping a socialist direction and upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee, citing the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and for training cadres through practice and reviving their fighting spirit. Chen concludes that learning from Mao's wisdom will help the Party win new victories in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how Party scholarship presents Mao's thought on struggle as a resource for current Party-building and ideological work.

Two paths beyond modernity: Marx and Strauss 超越现代性的两条道路：马克思与施特劳斯 Hao Zhichang Liu Xiaona Hao Zhichang and Liu Xiaona compare how Karl Marx and Leo Strauss diagnose the crisis of modernity and what each proposes in response. The article argues that the two thinkers represent opposed directions: Strauss seeks a return to classical political philosophy, while Marx seeks to go beyond capitalist modernity through social revolution. The authors hold that the difference rests on rival views of history, and that Marx's historical materialism reaches the deeper root of the crisis. The article has three main sections and a conclusion. The first sets out Strauss's critique of historicism, his account of the 'quarrel between ancients and moderns', and his appeal to natural law, teleology and the best regime. The second presents Marx's analysis of capital, its 'great civilising influence', its limits in production, consumption and human relations, and the abolition of capitalist private property and the restoration of individual ownership. The third weighs the two paths as a choice between value reconstruction and social transformation, and briefly sets aside Nietzsche, Heidegger, Löwith and Arendt. It closes with Baudelaire's view of modernity and a remark of Althusser's. In the authors' reading, Strauss treats the crisis as theoretical: modern historicism dissolves any standard of good and bad, and an 'eternal history' embodied in the classical best regime is the remedy. The authors judge this a one-sided, partly romantic and conservative, ultimately utopian approach that never reaches the real source of the crisis. They cite Engels to argue that social change originates in modes of production and exchange, not in ideas, and note that Western cultural traditions existed long before modernity arrived. Marx, by contrast, locates the crisis in the capital relation, so overcoming it requires changing the material mode of production. The authors add that Strauss's charge that Marx's future humans are 'last men' fails, since Marx envisages free, many-sided activity. The authors conclude that the crisis of modernity is total, at once theoretical and practical, and that Strauss and Marx complement each other. Strauss lacks a dimension of practical reality; Marx's project should absorb Strauss's ethical concern and his reminder not to forget inherited human values. Even so, they insist on viewing Strauss through Marx's lens, discarding his unrealistic social imagination, and judge that the most urgent crisis is capital's 'colonisation and control' of life. Read the original if you study Marxist critiques of Western conservative thought, or want a Chinese academic account of how Marx and Strauss can be set against each other on modernity.

The determination of time in Marx's theory of value 马克思价值理论中的时间规定 Pan Yuwen Pan Yuwen asks what role time plays in Marx's theory of value at a moment when algorithmic management, affective and creative labour, and the blurring of work and life are putting the labour-time standard under strain. The article argues that time is not a neutral, natural yardstick in Marx. Pan contends that Marx offers a critique of time as a historically produced and socially coercive measure, one that remains explanatory under digital capitalism. The article first reviews three readings of the "value–time" problem: the traditional reading, the New Reading of Marx, and Autonomism. It then reconstructs how time became the measure of value in classical political economy, from the Physiocrats through Adam Smith and David Ricardo. Finally it returns to Marx's account of socially necessary labour time, the "temporalisation" of labour and the "crisis of measurability", and applies these to digital capitalism. Thinkers engaged include Rubin, Sweezy, Backhaus, Postone, Negri and Hardt, Foucault and Sohn-Rethel. Pan argues that the traditional reading treats time as a technical unit, the New Reading plays down labour time in favour of value-form analysis, and Negri and Hardt reject "time-as-measure" as a flaw in Marx. Each, in Pan's view, misses Marx's critique. Pan reads Marx's dual definition of abstract labour, as physiological expenditure and as a purely social relation, as the key to the problem. Concrete labour becomes abstract labour time through a process of temporalisation, illustrated by Taylorism, which sets the time a task "should" take. Socially necessary labour time therefore does not record pre-existing labour. It produces abstract reality and disciplines labour towards the demands of valorisation. On this reading the "crisis of measurability" is a recurrent feature of capitalist production, not a novelty of immaterial labour, and Pan holds that it does not refute Marx. Immaterial labour, Pan says, extends temporal domination by turning all of a worker's time into potential surplus labour time. Pan concludes that Marx's value theory contains a deeper critique of time than either the New Reading or Autonomism supplies. Abstract value-time, detached from natural and lived time, is presented as a mechanism of abstract domination over labour and life. Pan treats this critique as a resource for understanding and resisting contemporary temporal domination and for rethinking the real possibility of free time. Read the original if you work on value theory, the New Reading of Marx, Autonomism or the political economy of digital labour and want a detailed argument that socially necessary labour time is a mechanism of domination rather than a neutral measure.

Rethinking the consistency of Marx's and Engels's philosophical thought 马克思恩格斯哲学思想一致性再思考 An Qinian An Qinian takes up the long-running claim that Marx's and Engels's philosophies differ fundamentally or even oppose each other. The article argues that this "Marx–Engels opposition thesis" is untenable and that their philosophical thought is wholly consistent. In An's view, most defenders of consistency have simply stressed their close collaboration, whereas a targeted theoretical rebuttal built on their own texts remains underdeveloped. The article first sets out two representative versions of the opposition thesis: Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness (1923), and the American Marx scholar Norman Levine's work from the 1970s and 1980s, with brief mention of Terrell Carver. It then makes two moves: it argues that the thesis conflicts with the historical record, and that it rests on misreadings of Marx. It ends by suggesting what a fuller account of their unity would require. On the historical record, An notes that Engels criticised abstract materialism for setting nature against humanity in 1844, before Marx's Theses on Feuerbach. Both men said they were in full theoretical agreement from 1844, and The German Ideology, which they co-wrote, develops the practice-centred view. Engels's account of labour in the transition from ape to human, and his 1890 statement on the decisive role of production, are cited as evidence that he never abandoned that view. For An, the main misreading is to treat Marx's criticism of old materialism as a rejection of it. Marx wrote that it understood reality only as object, and An reads "only" as meaning that he accepted the material world as independent of human will. Marx therefore viewed the world from two angles, matter and human practice. Labour in Capital is itself a material exchange between natural forces, so practice does not contradict a materialist ontology or the dialectics of nature. The difference in emphasis arises because Marx had to found historical materialism, centred on human emancipation, while Engels later defended dialectical materialism against neo-Kantians and Dühring. An concludes that the two did not oppose each other but each developed different aspects of shared ideas. He adds that Soviet and Chinese philosophers have not yet built a systematic theory unifying practical materialism, dialectical materialism and historical materialism. He links this task to the ecological crisis, the "one-dimensional man" and the risks of artificial intelligence. He also links it to Xi Jinping's account of Chinese modernization, which he says calls for a philosophy combining humanism with scientific rationality. Read the original if you want a detailed textual rebuttal of Lukács and Levine, or an account of how Chinese philosophers frame the unity of practical and dialectical materialism.

A historical examination of the Communist Party of China's upholding of cultural leadership since reform and opening up 改革开放以来中国共产党坚持文化领导权的历史考察 Yang Fengcheng Zhang Zhiqiang Yang and Zhang ask how the Communist Party of China has understood and upheld its cultural leadership (wenhua lingdaoquan, often rendered cultural hegemony) since reform and opening up. They note that the Party named "the CPC's cultural leadership" as an explicit proposition only in Xi Jinping's June 2023 speech at a symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Taking an intellectual-history approach, they argue that the Party's exploration moved through challenge, innovation and gradual maturity, and that it now forms a systematic theory. The article divides the period into three stages. The first covers the early reform years of ideological emancipation and the return to order after the Cultural Revolution. The second runs from the 1990s to the early 2000s, under the socialist market economy and all-round opening up. The third is the new era under Xi Jinping, set against what the authors call great changes unseen in a century and the Party's push to strengthen its overall leadership. Each stage is tied to leaders' statements and Party documents. In the authors' account, early reform leaders such as Deng Xiaoping upheld cultural leadership through the Four Cardinal Principles, opposing both "Left" and Right deviations. They also held that literature and art should neither be subordinate to politics nor detached from it, and that journalism is the Party's mouthpiece. Their fourth measure was building socialist spiritual civilization. From the 1990s the emphasis shifted to "building rather than criticising" and to establishing a leading role amid pluralism, summed up as one dominant strand with many coexisting ones, an image of a wild-goose formation replacing a single rigid line. The authors also list advanced socialist culture, the core socialist value system, and the claim that "only by occupying the market better can more ground be occupied". In the new era they describe a strengthened socialist ideology, core socialist values, control of public opinion on the internet, and comprehensive Party leadership over propaganda, ideology and culture, including its personnel. They present this last stage as a historic shift in the ideological situation. The authors conclude that early problems were largely legacies of history, while later ones, such as cultural pluralism and cultural markets, were new and called for fresh thinking. They say the Party under Xi has now set out fundamental principles, key tasks and institutional safeguards, which marks a new stage. They add that new situations will keep arising and that the Party must uphold fundamental principles while innovating. Read the original if you want a Party-historical account, built from official texts, of how the concept of cultural leadership developed from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping.

Examining the practical dimension of ideological and political theory courses in schools in the new era 新时代学校思政课教学的实践维度审视 Xu Yanguo Xu Yanguo takes up the place of practice in the teaching of school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke), whose core content is now Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Starting from the practical character of the Party's innovative theory, the article argues that these courses are at root the teaching of truth, and that truth must withstand the test of practice. Teaching should therefore be organised around a practical logic rather than treating practice as a supplement to theory. The article has three parts. The first traces course construction from the early People's Republic to the present, through the teaching of Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, to the introductory course on Xi Jinping Thought. The second looks at practice as teaching content in the first classroom (textbooks, lesson plans, assignments, assessment) and in the second classroom (off-campus practice teaching). The third examines method, teachers, organisation and assessment. Xu reads the history of the curriculum as showing that the courses have always taught Marxism and its latest Chinese adaptations, so that the Party's theory persuades students through its demonstrated strength in practice. The goal is for students to internalise ideals and convictions and then act on them. Xu proposes practice bases tied to first-classroom content, with front-line practitioners joining teachers, and a teaching logic that runs from practice to theory and back. Theory teaching is likened to the skeleton and practice teaching to the muscle, the bridge from the abstract to the concrete. Xu notes that many teachers go from school to school with little social experience, and urges field research for them. Xu also wants practice written into course standards and assessed for courses, teachers and students, not just exam scores. Xu concludes that traditional teaching treated practice as a supplement, and that, with the 15th Five-Year Plan period under way, a practice-based "big ideological and political course" matters for Party governance. Mastering and truly believing theory both depend on practice, which Xu compares to travelling ten thousand miles alongside reading ten thousand books. Xu calls for active exploration of organising these courses around practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames the practice dimension of ideological and political courses, including a historical survey of curriculum documents and concrete proposals on teaching content, teacher training and assessment.

The implications of capital power in Foucault's theory of power: a reflection from Althusser's perspective 福柯权力理论中的资本权力意蕴——基于阿尔都塞视角的反思 Dong Jianming Dong Jianming asks how Michel Foucault's analyses of power, especially his biopolitics, can be related to Marx's critique of political economy without simply grafting one onto the other. The article argues that Louis Althusser's theory of repressive and ideological state apparatuses can serve as a theoretical bridge. Through it, Dong contends, the 'capital power' implicit in Foucault's account becomes visible, and the basis is laid for a theory of capital power consistent with Marx. The article has three parts. The first presents Foucault's method (archaeology and genealogy), his rejection of both 'economism' and the 'economic functionality' of power, and his resulting 'non-economic' analysis of power. The second turns to Althusser's analysis of power in terms of the reproduction of the conditions of production, and the third reconstructs Foucault's themes through that lens. It addresses disciplinary power and biopolitics, the 'war' model of power, and liberal governmentality, and ends with remarks on digital capitalism and socialist governance. Dong argues that by detaching power from economic analysis Foucault produced a 'descriptive theory' of power, in Althusser's sense of a first stage that has not yet become theory proper. Althusser, by contrast, insists that critique of oppression must not replace critique of exploitation. He shows how repressive and ideological state apparatuses reproduce labour-power and the relations of production. Read this way, Dong claims, Foucault's disciplinary and biopolitical techniques serve to reproduce capitalist conditions of production; his proposition that power is war expresses class struggle; and his 'naturalness' of society and population is an ideology produced by the bourgeoisie, so that his history of power is in fact the history of capitalism's self-reproduction. Dong concludes that a sound theory of capital power must tie power mechanisms to exploitation and capital's logic and must retain class analysis, since Marx held that population without classes is an abstraction. It should also avoid confusing critique of capital with critique of digital technology, as in Byung-Chul Han's Heideggerian approach. Socialism, Dong adds, cannot simply adopt liberal governmentality; it must work towards a proletarian state apparatus beyond the bourgeois one, a point the author says matters for China's modernization. Read the original if you study Foucault–Marx relations, Althusser's state apparatus theory, or Chinese Marxist debates on power and governance.

On the logical evolution of Lukács's ethical thought 论卢卡奇伦理思想的逻辑演变 Yan Yan Liu Danfei Yan and Liu take up a common periodisation of Georg Lukács's ethics: a Romantic phase before Marxism, a revolutionary ethics after his turn to Marxism, and late cultural critique and democratic politics. They argue that this scheme hides the links between the phases. In their view, the evolution of Lukács's ethics, its substance and its present-day relevance can be understood only within an overall 'individual–class–species' (ge ti–jieji–lei) framework. They also hold that Lukács never built a systematic Marxist ethics, but his critique of dogmatised Marxism opened a path for constructing one today. The article follows Lukács's ethics chronologically in four parts. It begins with the metaphysical individual ethics of Soul and Form and Theory of the Novel and its move towards the proletarian class ethics of 'Tactics and Ethics'. It then examines the ethical predicament of History and Class Consciousness. Next it treats the late works: the Aesthetic, the Ontology of Social Being and The Process of Democratization. It closes with an assessment. The authors draw on commentators such as István Mészáros, Ágnes Heller, Norman Levine, György Márkus and Gareth Stedman Jones. The authors present Lukács's shifts as responses to the problems of his time and to impasses in his own theory, not as irrational breaks. In History and Class Consciousness, individuals are subordinated to the class and the Party. Class consciousness is treated as the proletariat's 'ethics', and Lenin's idea of 'injecting' it from outside is endorsed. The authors see the book's real difficulty as the relation between material base and consciousness: Lukács tried to resolve capitalist contradictions through consciousness, which underestimated capital's logic. After 1956, influenced by the 1844 Manuscripts, he replaced 'class' with 'species'. Aesthetics then sought the unity of individual and species, and the later democratization work tied socialist democracy, teleology and non-alienated labour to that unity, extending to everyday life. Yan and Liu conclude that Lukács's work has a deeper continuity, which they call a steadfast 'cultural watchfulness' grounded in concern for human existence and fate. They cast the Ontology as overcoming the subjectivism of History and Class Consciousness, and The Process of Democratization as a development of Leninist state theory. They add that his ethics strongly influenced Western Marxism, especially Eastern European neo-Marxism, and that, as Lukács himself said, theoretically mistaken parts often have the greatest influence. They therefore call for a critical attitude. Read the original if you study Lukács, the history of Marxist ethics, or how Chinese scholars read the continuity of his thought across his career.

"The warmth and cold of revolution": clothing and bedding supply for the people's army in the revolutionary war years “革命的冷暖”：革命战争时期人民军队被服供给问题研究 Qi Xiaoguang Qi Xiaoguang takes up a basic but little-studied question in the logistics history of the people's army led by the Chinese Communist Party: how it obtained clothing and bedding (quilts, blankets, uniforms) during the revolutionary wars. Qi argues that the problem affected soldiers' survival and the army's capacity to keep fighting. In Qi's account, solving it required mass mobilisation of production and the gradual building of supply institutions, and the process shows the army's revolutionary optimism and the close bond between army and people. The article follows the army from the Jinggangshan base area to the final stage of the civil war and has four main sections. The first describes the hardships of supply in the Soviet period and the Long March, the War of Resistance against Japan and the War of Liberation. The second traces the move towards self-sufficient production behind enemy lines, with mass participation. The third examines how supply standards and management were systematised. A short conclusion reflects on the symbolic meaning of clothing. Qi draws on recollections of commanders such as Xu Xiangqian and Nie Rongzhen, Party directives, military orders and folk songs. Qi's core claim is that shortage drove self-reliance. Early supply depended mainly on capture from the enemy, then on the Nationalist blockade and the later cutting-off of funds, especially after the Southern Anhui Incident of 1941, pushed the army towards full self-supply. Qi describes army workshops, production competitions and above all the labour of peasant women, tailors and villagers, summed up in the phrase that the "largest clothing factory is the masses". Qi then shows how, after the 1940 logistics meetings, supply became standardised: unified management, issue by unit level, fixed quotas and service lives for items, accounting and discipline rules, economies in cloth use, and, in 1949, nationwide unified standards. Uniform styles and colours moved from disorder to regularity. Qi concludes that clothing was both a soldier's means of survival and a carrier of political identity, revolutionary feeling and class belonging. Patched uniforms and the labour of people at the rear are presented as a "living fossil" of revolutionary spirit and of the "fish and water" relationship between army and people. Qi sees the history as reflecting the Party's political skill in mobilisation, institution-building and revolutionary narrative, with continuing spiritual value today. Read the original if you are interested in the social and institutional history of Communist military logistics, or in how current Party-history scholarship frames material culture and army–people relations.

Mao Zedong's planning and direction of the strategic offensive during the War of Liberation 解放战争时期毛泽东关于战略进攻的谋划与指导 Peng Houwen Peng Houwen asks how Mao Zedong planned and directed the People's Liberation Army's shift to the strategic offensive in the War of Liberation (1946–1949). The article argues that the PLA went on the offensive before its strength had overtaken that of the Nationalist (Kuomintang) forces. Its main forces moved to exterior-line operations and carried the war into Nationalist-held areas, which Peng presents as a vivid application of Mao's military strategic thought. In Peng's account this reversed the course of the war and hastened the fall of the Nationalist regime. The study is organised around three turning points, drawn mainly from Mao's telegrams and Central Committee directives. The first is the southern-front operational plan of 22 June 1946, drafted on the eve of the full-scale civil war. The second is the Central Committee meeting of 21 November 1946, which adopted the line of "overthrowing Chiang Kai-shek". The third is the Xiaohe Conference of 21–23 July 1947 in northern Shaanxi, which fixed the offensive's overall deployment. Peng's central claim is that Mao's thinking moved in stages. The 1946 southern plan was defensive in strategy but offensive in form, and it pointed south into Nationalist territory. As military victories mounted and the peace talks collapsed in November 1946, the aim changed from securing peace and democracy to overthrowing Nationalist rule. Mao then set out a blueprint: destroy 70 to 80 Nationalist brigades, bring the two sides' strength into balance, and push beyond the Yangtze within three to five years. Peng then identifies a further shift after Liu Bocheng and Deng Xiaoping's forces crossed the Yellow River on 30 June 1947. Mao no longer waited to crush the Nationalist offensives in Shandong and northern Shaanxi, or for overall superiority. Peng attributes this to two causes: the liberated areas' resources were close to exhaustion, and inner-line operations in Shandong were going less well than expected. Peng concludes that the Xiaohe Conference settled the offensive's goals, policy and concrete plans. Its principles were set out in Mao's directive of 1 September 1947, "The Strategic Policy for the Second Year of the War of Liberation". Three armies then advanced into the Central Plains, and by October 1947 the PLA's slogan was to overthrow Chiang Kai-shek and liberate all China. In Peng's reading, the Nationalist regime's collapse was by then clearly in prospect. Read the original if you study Mao's military thought, the Party's documentary record of the War of Liberation, or the decision-making behind the 1947 advance into the Dabie Mountains and the Central Plains.

Debate, reflection and exploration in British and American communist historiography since the Second World War 二战后英美共产主义史学的争鸣、反思与探索研究 Yang Ningcong Li Jing Yang Ningcong and Li Jing ask how the historiography of communism in Britain and the United States developed after 1945, at a time when such scholarship declined elsewhere in the West along with the communist parties. They argue that the two countries' scholarship shows striking parallels, rooted in similar party experiences of political line, ideology and Soviet and Comintern influence. They present its history as a movement from Cold War distortion through critique and renewed dispute to self-reflection. The article is organised chronologically in four stages. It begins with the traditionalist school of the 1950s and 1960s (Henry Pelling, Leslie Macfarlane, Walter Kendall, Theodore Draper). It then covers the revisionist critique of the 1970s and 1980s (Kevin Morgan, Nina Fishman, Maurice Isserman) and the renewed quarrel after the opening of Russian archives following the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Finally it turns to reflection and new directions since 2000. The authors contend that the traditionalists, writing under anti-communist Cold War pressures, chose sources selectively and portrayed the parties as Moscow's puppets, spies or subversives. In their account, the revisionists, helped by the decline of McCarthyism, new archives and the arrival of New Left scholars, stressed a bottom-up view, party autonomy and the movements' progressive record. They add that this view neglected the role of the Soviet Union and the Comintern. After the archives opened, the traditionalists (Keith Laybourn, Harvey Klehr, John Earl Haynes) reread them to confirm old claims about funding, centralism and espionage. Revisionists such as Morgan, Andrew Thorpe and Ellen Schrecker answered that funding did not prove subversion and that Comintern influence worked through negotiation. They also held that the Cold War stemmed from a manufactured 'red scare'. The authors credit twenty-first-century historians with calling for a paradigm shift beyond archive worship and for a less partisan stance. These historians also want both Moscow's leading role and the parties' autonomy integrated into one account. The authors describe new departures: journals such as American Communist History as shared forums, comparative and interdisciplinary work, document-based and oral history, and treating communism as a belief system. Further themes are placing the Comintern within the framework, studying Stalinism's influence, relating communism to other social movements and the labour movement, drawing lessons from the movements' weak position, and recovering their historical contributions. They conclude that it remains uncertain whether a more objective history will end the disputes, and that historians carry a moral responsibility to the communists who made sacrifices. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Anglo-American scholarship on communist parties, with named authors, works and debates to follow up.

The scientific meaning, constraints and realisation path of common prosperity in spiritual life A reading based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 精神生活共同富裕的科学内涵、制约因素及实现路径 Li Suxia Zhang Xun Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) statement that material poverty and spiritual poverty are both alien to socialism, Li Suxia and Zhang Xun ask what Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 can contribute to understanding common prosperity in spiritual life. They argue that the Manuscripts, where Marx first used the phrase "spiritual wealth", already contain a coherent picture of such prosperity, grounded in the opposition between labour and capital. The authors present this as having present-day significance for Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first defines the concept; the second identifies what constrains spiritual common prosperity under capitalism; the third sets out how it can be realised. A short conclusion places Marx's approach against ancient Greek and modern philosophy and links it to the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilisation. Throughout, the authors rely closely on passages from the Manuscripts on estranged labour, private property, Hegel and the French workers' associations. On the concept, the authors hold that spiritual common prosperity means the completeness of human life-expression, realised through labour, social interaction and the satisfaction of spiritual needs. It also means a harmonious relation with nature, which Marx calls humanity's "inorganic body", and a dialectical unity of content and form, reached through critiques of German classical philosophy and Hegel. On constraints, they identify estranged labour, private property and the logic of capital. Estranged labour in four forms impoverishes workers' spiritual life; private property makes society's spiritual life materialistic; capital's logic makes collective spiritual life hypocritical, through dehumanising domination, the hoarding and squandering of wealth, and a rigid division of labour. For realisation, the authors derive three conditions from Marx: securing free time for the proletariat, sublating private property, and uniting the proletarians. They summarise this as a sequence of criticising estranged labour, sublating private property and uniting the proletarians. They conclude that this sequence points from estrangement to freedom and from the individual to the common. Read the original if you want a close, text-based Chinese reading of the 1844 Manuscripts used to ground the Party's current language of spiritual wealth.

Marx and Engels's twofold critique of capitalist civilization 马克思恩格斯对资本主义文明的双重批判 Chen Gaohua Zhou Hang Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that capitalist civilization rests on a system of capitalist exploitation and cannot overcome the barbarism within it, Chen Gaohua and Zhou Hang ask how Marx and Engels themselves criticised capitalist civilization. They argue that the critique has two sides: the violent expansion of capitalist civilization abroad, and the barbarism it produces inside capitalist society. Capitalism, in their reading, is a civilization that is at once civilized and barbarous. The article first reconstructs Marx and Engels's criteria for calling a society civilized, drawing on their reception of Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society. It then treats the two critiques in turn: expansion through colonies, slavery and the world market, and the condition of workers under capital. The authors confine their account to the European capitalism of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and they do not treat it as all forms of capitalism or of human civilization. A short conclusion extends the argument to digital capitalism, ecological crisis and neo-colonialism. On the criteria, the authors say Marx and Engels did not take civilization to mean reason, refinement or technology. They defined it by social relations: a society counts as civilized when the division of labour, exchange and commodity production are fully developed, and capitalism pushes all three furthest. On expansion, the authors cite Marx on India, Turkey and China and on slavery as the pivot of modern industry. In this reading, civilizing rhetoric masks plunder and monopoly, and colonies show the hypocrisy that is veiled at home. On internal barbarism, the authors argue that the "civilizing" of capital turns domination into contractual, legitimate and hidden order. Progress enlarges capital's power over labour rather than enriching workers, so that, as Marx put it, the more civilized the worker's product, the more barbarous the worker. The authors conclude that Marx and Engels exposed the capitalist civilization of their time as a unity of civilization and barbarism, and they claim that recognising this breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. They say the contradictions persist in new forms: algorithmic and platform exploitation, ecological crisis, and technological, financial and cultural hegemony that draws developing countries into new dependency. Only by seeing through capitalist civilization's hypocrisy, they argue, can civilizations overcome estrangement and conflict through equal dialogue and mutual learning. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Marx and Engels used "civilization" and "barbarism", set in the context of current Chinese debates over civilizations.

Building a narrative system for the international communication of the Global Governance Initiative 全球治理倡议的国际传播叙事体系建构 Qi Weiping Wang Yuqi Xi Jinping put forward the Global Governance Initiative at the "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Plus" meeting in September 2025. Qi Weiping and Wang Yuqi ask how it can be communicated abroad, and approach the question through narrative theory. They argue that an abstract value core reaches international audiences only when it is turned into narrative text that can be decoded. A systematic narrative, in their view, would help close the gap between China's contributions and its discourse power in global governance. The article has three parts. The first sets out the logic behind the narrative: the domestic and external needs that drive it, the signifier and signified of the Initiative as a communicable text, and its potential to build cognition and identification among audiences. The second sets out a narrative framework built on system, identity and issue narratives. The third turns to practical mechanisms: coordinating narrators, segmenting audiences and combining narrative methods. The authors claim that China's governance practice has not translated into discourse power, because Western states and media recast it as a "China threat" and exclude it from core rule-making. They characterise Western narratives (liberal internationalism, radical republicanism, cosmopolitan democracy) as having failed to meet governance deficits. In their framework, the system narrative presents the UN-centred order as legitimate but in need of reform, and opposes hegemonic powers' generalisation of special rules. The identity narrative casts China as participant, promoter and leader, the UN as the authoritative actor, and the Global South as an increasingly important force. The issue narrative addresses spatial, temporal and object-based issues. For delivery, party and government, mainstream media and think-tank scholars are to speak in coordination. Audiences are to be divided by Global North and South, by cultural capital, and by big-data user profiles. Competitive and cooperative, rational and empathetic, diachronic and synchronic narration are to be combined. The authors conclude that effective international communication is a way to project a credible image of China and to move beyond Western governance narratives. They call for the narrative framework to be set out fully and for narrative techniques to be mastered. They stress that treating the Initiative as a text does not deny its ideological or institutional forms. Communication is one link in turning ideas into material practice, alongside ideational and institutional practice. Read the original if you study Chinese international communication, discourse power, or how Chinese scholars apply narratology to foreign-policy initiatives.

Socialist culture with Chinese characteristics for a new era: connotation, functions and guiding principles 新时代中国特色社会主义文化：内涵、功能与遵循 Shang Zhixiao Shang Zhixiao examines a concept given prominence by the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025): "socialist culture with Chinese characteristics for a new era". The article asks what the concept means, what work it does and what should guide its development. Shang argues that the term gathers earlier formulations into one overarching idea, and that developing such a culture is now the central task of cultural construction in the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The article has three parts. The first traces how Xi Jinping introduced the term in 2023 and used it again in 2024, and how the Fourth Plenum made it a core planning concept. The second sets out four functions drawn from Xi's formulation: ideological guidance, spiritual cohesion, value appeal and international influence. The third turns to guiding principles for implementation. On meaning, Shang reads the concept through three anchors. Its essential character is socialist culture, since in the Marxist view culture takes its nature from the social formation on which it rests. Its practical basis is socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization. Its historical position is the new era and the decisive stage of building a culture-strong nation by 2035. The term, Shang argues, narrows in extent but deepens in content compared with older labels. The four functions are said to form one whole, each tied to a different dimension: shared ideals, national identity, core socialist values and cross-civilisational exchange. For implementation, Shang calls for adherence to the "three upholds" guidelines (serving the people and socialism, letting a hundred flowers bloom, creative transformation and innovative development). Shang also calls for cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. The author further urges linking past and present, China and abroad, and gives priorities: promoting core socialist values, developing cultural undertakings and industries, using digital technology, and strengthening international communication. Shang presents all this as implementing the Plenum's spirit and supporting Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the new term consolidates earlier cultural vocabulary and how it is tied to cultural-policy priorities up to 2035.

Distinctive advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics, viewed through social development 从社会发展看中国特色社会主义制度的显著优势 Qin Gang Qin Gang asks where the institutional advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics come from, how they show up in social development, and what lessons they offer. Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that institutional advantage is a country's greatest advantage, the article argues that these advantages are comprehensive. In Qin's account they rest on scientific socialism, Chinese cultural tradition, accumulated practice and the achievements of human civilisation, and are confirmed by results in economic and social development. The article has three parts. The first traces four sources of the system's advantages: the institutionalisation of scientific socialist principles, the transformation of excellent traditional culture, the lifting of socialist practical experience into institutions, and the integration of civilisational achievements, including capitalist ones. The second part identifies five manifestations: centralised and unified leadership by the Party Central Committee; the people's principal position; concentrating resources on major undertakings; combining an effective market with a capable government; and scientifically drawn and effectively implemented national development plans. The third part draws four lessons. Qin argues that Party leadership is the system's greatest advantage, since it produces unified will and common purpose, and that democratic centralism reconciles democracy with efficiency. The author presents the national-plan procedure (Party proposal, State Council drafting, National People's Congress approval) and the 'whole-nation chessboard' approach as sources of stability and rapid breakthroughs, citing projects from the 'two bombs and one satellite' programme to high-speed rail and poverty alleviation. The system is said to have solved the market–government problem and to have absorbed capitalist-era institutions such as the rule of law and modern enterprise systems by stripping out their original institutional character. Qin presents this as a transcendence of capitalism's internal contradictions. The lessons Qin draws are that institutions must be built on specific historical conditions, with principles adapted rather than copied. They should take the people's well-being as their ultimate yardstick, be tested by practical results through pilot experiments and evaluation, and be improved through reform that perfects the system without overturning its basic framework. Qin concludes that the system secures China's rejuvenation and offers 'Chinese wisdom' and a 'Chinese approach' for humanity's search for fairer, more efficient and more inclusive institutions. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Party-school scholarship explains the sources and merits of China's institutional system, with the official vocabulary used throughout.

High-quality Party building leading high-quality development: theoretical logic and strategic paths 高质量党建引领高质量发展：理论逻辑与战略路径 Tang Huangfeng Han Zixi Tang and Han take up Xi Jinping's 2025 formula of "leading high-quality development through high-quality Party building". They ask why the quality of Party building should shape the quality of economic and social development, and how the link can be strengthened. Their answer is that the Party's leadership is the fundamental tie between the two, so that improving Party building turns the Party's political and organisational strengths into development momentum and governance capacity. The article has three parts. It first sets out the theoretical logic, tracing it through Marx, Engels and Lenin on the active role of the superstructure, then through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. It then assesses the current situation, giving achievements and problems. It closes with strategic paths along four dimensions: political and ideological guidance, institutional arrangements, working mechanisms, and cadre capacity. The authors cite examples such as industrial-chain Party alliances in Jiangsu. The core argument is that the formula follows the Marxist principle that the superstructure acts back on the economic base, and that a ruling party is the concrete agent of this. The authors describe the formula as continuing the tradition while innovating on it in five areas: Party leadership, Party organisations' functions, the driving mechanism of the Party's self-reform, the orientation towards new quality productive forces, and systemic method. They present the two sides as mutually dependent. Party building supplies direction, organisation and institutions, while development results serve as the yardstick of Party-building quality. Against the achievements they set four problems: superficial understanding of "Party leadership", organisational coverage that is formal rather than effective, weak resource integration and merely formal fusion with business, and thin personnel capacity. The authors cite figures showing that misconduct such as inaction or false action made up 84.1 per cent of the formalism and bureaucratism cases handled in November 2025. The authors propose that Party organisations change how they understand the link between Party building and development, and that institutions be built into corporate governance, science and technology, and emerging sectors. They also call for more flexible, networked working mechanisms and for cadres who combine political and business competence, selected and assessed under a correct view of performance. They conclude that Party building should be embedded in every stage of development through organised, institutionalised channels. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party-building scholarship justifies and operationalises Party leadership of the economy, including its diagnosis of grassroots problems in new economic and social organisations.

The composite narrative of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的复合叙事 Zhao Yong He Zhengtao Zhao Yong and He Zhengtao ask what kind of story Chinese modernization tells, and how it differs from the narratives that have dominated accounts of modernization. Using narratology, they argue that Chinese modernization forms a new narrative paradigm, a "composite narrative" (fuhe xushi). In their account it is composite in four dimensions: narrator, narratee, story and discourse. The authors present it as going beyond the logic of capital and as promoting the coexistence of plural civilizations. The article has four parts. It first analyses Western modernization narrative, both classical modernization theory and the postmodern narrative that arose in reaction to it, along the four narratological dimensions. It then sets out how the composite narrative takes shape in each dimension, in the form of a community of narration, a community of shared values, a social organism and a space-time continuum. A third part gives its philosophical grounding, and a fourth its significance for the world. Marx, Engels, Lenin, Hegel, Habermas, Žižek, Byung-Chul Han and Xi Jinping are among the sources drawn on. Zhao and He argue that classical narrative has an abstract, elite narrator, a hidden narratee, a single storyline of capital accumulation and an omniscient viewpoint. Postmodern narrative, they say, dissolves narrator, narratee and chronology into fragments and ends in a "narrative vacuum". The Chinese composite narrative is said to respond with the people, led by the Communist Party, as the real narrators. It treats civilizations as both narrators and listeners, runs economic, political, cultural, social and ecological storylines in parallel ("parallel" rather than "serial" development), and joins past, present and future while remaining rooted in China and open to the world. The authors insist this is not eclecticism. They ground it in the concrete universal, the unity of subjective narrative and objective reality tested in practice, and a systems approach. The authors conclude that the composite narrative breaks the discursive monopoly of "modernization equals Westernization" and moves beyond capital logic with "the people first" as its anchor. They also hold that it offers the Global South a model for pursuing modernization with autonomy, balancing growth and equity. They further claim that it anticipates a general trend toward a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese theorists apply narratology and Marxist philosophy to present Chinese modernization as a distinct discursive paradigm.

The discourse of the "salient hallmark" of the Communist Party of China in the new era: construction and effectiveness 新时代中国共产党“显著标志”话语建构及效能 Lin Jianhua He Xihui How should the Communist Party of China be described and labelled? Lin and He take up this question through the phrase "salient hallmark" (xianzhu biaozhi), which Xi Jinping has repeatedly used since the 18th Party Congress (2012), usually prefaced by "distinguishing it from other political parties". The authors argue that this discourse is a comparative, value-laden, historical and forward-looking concept that expresses the Party's nature, purpose and mission. They present it as a resource for building an autonomous body of knowledge in Party history and Party building. The article has four parts. It first sets out four types of "hallmark": courage in self-reform, standing firmly with the people, promoting the Party's glorious traditions and fine work style, and letting self-reform lead social revolution. It then analyses how the discourse is constructed, identifies three regularities in its construction, and ends with six functions or effects of the discourse. It cites Mao Zedong's 1945 report On Coalition Government and Xi's speeches, Party resolutions and the Party Constitution. On construction, the authors argue that the discourse rests on the Party's nature, with its purpose (serving the people wholeheartedly) as its value core. It carries historical continuity, citing Mao's 1945 use of "salient mark" and the investigation-and-research campaigns of 1960–61 and 2023. It is also developmental, responding to new-era questions: self-reform answers how to govern the Party, and the people's standpoint answers whom the Party serves. The regularities are that the discourse serves full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, applies historical materialism, and stresses the initiative of individual Party members. Its effects, in the authors' account, are building ideological consensus, political mobilisation, consolidating long-term governance by winning popular support, distinguishing Party culture, raising Party soft power and shaping a better Party and government work style. Lin and He conclude that the discourse has theoretical, methodological and practical value. In their view, studying such identifying concepts can supply a paradigm for an autonomous knowledge system in Party history and Party building, and the hallmark discourse can strengthen Party members' commitment, deepen Party–mass ties and support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a close account of how Party theorists treat Xi's "hallmark" formulations as a discourse system and what functions they assign to it.

Paths to enhancing the Communist Party of China's international discourse power: reflections based on the new form of human civilization 论中国共产党国际话语权的提升路径——基于人类文明新形态的思考 Wang Qiang How can the Communist Party of China turn its achievements into greater influence over international opinion, rules and agendas? Wang Qiang argues that the new form of human civilization supplies both the value core and the strategic angle for this task. In Wang's account it lets the Party move from reactive rebuttal to initiative in the international ideological struggle. The article has three parts. The first sets out how the new form of human civilization supports the Party's discourse power, through its theoretical roots and its claimed transcendence of capitalist modernization. The second analyses structural obstacles: Western discourse hegemony, the gap in cross-cultural understanding, and weaknesses in international communication. The third proposes a four-in-one path of value guidance, practical support, innovation in communication and a win-win pattern. Wang grounds the new civilizational form in historical materialism, the Two Integrations and Chinese modernization. Wang lists its defining traits as putting the people first, peaceful development, win-win cooperation and a shared destiny, and contrasts each with a capitalist logic of capital, hegemony and zero-sum games. The proposals follow three shifts. The first is from 'geyi' (explaining Chinese ideas through Western categories) to 'reverse geyi', which means producing core concepts across languages and building an autonomous knowledge system. The second is from supplying public goods to leading a development paradigm, for example presenting the Belt and Road Initiative as a development philosophy set against the 'Washington Consensus' and seeking rule-setting power in areas such as AI governance. The third is from issue-based alliances to a 'community of consensus', through a Global South development community, layered dialogue, 'translator-type' scholars and institutional platforms. Wang concludes that raising the Party's discourse power is no longer a technical matter of telling China's story in language the world understands. It has become a question of exchange between civilizations, which needs long-term strategic planning rather than piecemeal tactics. The article presents this as serving national rejuvenation and China's contribution to humanity's shared challenges. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links civilizational theory to concrete proposals on international communication and conceptual strategy.

The narrative structure and contemporary value of the discourse of "standing on the side of human civilizational progress" “站在人类文明进步一边”话语的叙事结构与时代价值 Lü Liexia Against the background of accelerating global change, the article asks how the Chinese Party-state's political formula of "standing on the side of human civilizational progress" can be understood and conveyed as a coherent discourse. Lü argues that the formula, used by Xi Jinping and in the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, answers the question "where is human civilization heading?" and offers a Chinese approach to building a new order among civilizations. The article has three parts. The first traces the discourse's origins in theory (Marxist world-history and civilizational-interaction theory), in history (lessons from socialism's development and the Soviet collapse) and in present needs (geopolitical conflict and the rise of the Global South). The second sets out its narrative structure as four linked layers: ontological, epistemological, axiological and practical. The third assesses its contemporary value for Marxist theory, for Chinese civilization and for global civilizational governance. Lü's central move is the four-layer structure. Ontologically, civilization is a balanced whole of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilizations, within a single human community. Epistemologically, it rests on equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness, and rejects linear history and the "clash of civilizations". Axiologically, it promotes "common values of all humanity" against what the author calls capitalist "universal values", an ideological tool of hegemony. Practically, it is carried out through the four global initiatives (security, development, civilization, governance) and the Belt and Road Initiative. Lü also holds that China's own path, built on Chinese modernization and the Two Integrations, disproves the "end of history" thesis and offers developing countries an alternative. Lü concludes that the discourse extends Marxist world-history theory by stressing the conscious agency of civilizational actors and a "harmony and coexistence" model of interaction. It also guides the creative transformation of Chinese civilization and gives global governance an action framework built on consultation, fair rules and balanced development. The author presents it as a public good that China offers to humanity at a historical crossroads. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese theorists systematise Xi Jinping's civilizational rhetoric into ontology, epistemology, axiology and practice.

The core meaning, historical necessity and scientific method of upholding the Party's cultural leadership 坚持党的文化领导权的核心要义、历史必然性和科学方法 Chen Wanqiu Chen Wanqiu asks what it means to uphold the Party's cultural leadership, why this is historically necessary, and how it should be done. The article treats the Party's cultural leadership (cultural hegemony in the sense of leading influence) as an extension of political leadership and as a proposition Xi Jinping put forward in the new era. Chen argues that existing scholarship has examined its origins, texts and countermeasures but rarely interpreted it through historical materialism, and sets out to do so. The article has three parts. The first sets out the core meaning from three Marxist angles: the contradictory movement between social being and social consciousness, the internal logic of strengthening the Party's overall leadership, and the principle that the people are the creators of history. The second presents four grounds for historical necessity, and the third proposes methods built on Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Chen draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and on the Party's record from the revolutionary period to the present. Chen's central claim is that, because consciousness reacts back on social being, contesting cultural leadership means contesting the power to shape people's thinking. Giving it up, in this reading, would expose society to capital's logic, Western values and historical nihilism, and would shake the socialist system. Chen also holds that cultural leadership cannot be separated from the Party's overall leadership, and that it expresses the cultural agency of the people rather than simple administrative interference. For practice, Chen distinguishes three linked powers: leadership (the goal), management (the institutional support, including control of the internet and online literature and art) and discourse (the means of narrative and interpretation). Chen adds two further requirements: a path of socialist cultural development with Chinese characteristics, aimed at building a culturally strong country by 2035, and the organic union of the "soul line" (Marxism) and the "root line" (traditional Chinese culture) in the Second Integration. Chen concludes that upholding cultural leadership is not an expedient but a fundamental matter for the fate of the Party and country, supported by the claim that the Party's undertakings have advanced when it used cultural power well and met setbacks when it did not. The article presents this as essential to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and as guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese Party theorists ground cultural leadership in historical materialism and translate it into policy on media, the internet and discourse.

A historical-materialist interpretation of spatial ethics 空间伦理的历史唯物主义阐释 Li Jiali Li Jiali asks how spatial ethics, meaning the ethical values built into the spaces people produce, can be grounded in historical materialism. The author argues that space is a product of human practice rather than a neutral container. On this basis Li presents China's rural revitalization strategy, the people's city concept and the community with a shared future for mankind as answers to the problem that go beyond Western spatial theory. The commentary opens with the new urbanization drive and the goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan outline, which Li reads as a people-centred spatial ethics. It then notes that Western spatial production theory, critical urban theory and spatial justice theory expose alienation but, in Li's view, neglect the human subject. Marx and Engels wrote no dedicated treatment of space, but Li finds spatial factors in their critique of capitalism: the labourer's body, town and country, and the world market. The core argument has three steps. First, the real individual is the logical premise, since space gains an ethical character only through practice, and ethics unfolds at three scales: bodily, urban-rural and global space. Second, social being is the objective basis of content. Ethical demands arise from concrete conditions, such as the body as an instrument of capital, structural urban-rural divides and unequal relations between core and periphery. Third, the free and all-round development of the human being is the value goal. Li concludes that clarifying the premise, basis and goal of spatial ethics lets space confirm human essential powers and unites theory with practice. The 15th Five-Year Plan goals for countryside, city and world are described as grounded in real needs and as a critique and transcendence of the capitalisation of space. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars frame spatial theory within historical materialism and current planning language.

The 180th anniversary of The German Ideology: retrospect and prospect 《德意志意识形态》问世180周年：回顾与展望 Zhao Yulan Marking 180 years since Marx and Engels began writing The German Ideology in 1845–46, Zhao Yulan offers a short retrospective and research outlook in a newspaper commentary. The author treats the work as the birthplace of the materialist conception of history. The main claim is that Chinese scholarship has long tracked international editorial work and should now aim to lead as well as follow, above all by settling its own edition and by debating the editors of the second Marx-Engels Complete Works historical-critical edition (MEGA2). The article first traces the work's publication history. It runs from the single chapter Marx published in 1847, through the partial printings by Mehring, Bernstein and Mayer in the early twentieth century, to Riazanov's 1924 and 1926 publication of the 'Feuerbach' chapter and Adoratsky's 1932 MEGA1 volume, the first complete edition in the original language. It then follows the post-1962 rearrangements of the 'Feuerbach' chapter by Bagaturia and Taubert and the 2017 MEGA2 volume. Finally it sets out the Chinese editions, from Guo Moruo's 1938 translation to the 1960 first Chinese Complete Works, the 1988 new 'Feuerbach' chapter, the 2003 selection and the 2009 Collected Works. Zhao argues that the 2017 MEGA2 volume largely returns to the MEGA1 logical structure. In Zhao's reading, it nonetheless rests on a judgement that the text was a quarterly-journal project made up of separate texts, and it inserts Engels's notes on Feuerbach into the 'Feuerbach' chapter, which undermines the chapter's status as a chapter. The second Chinese Complete Works, which is based on MEGA2, should therefore follow MEGA2 for textual content but decide its own arrangement through independent research. Zhao also contends that Chinese scholars have already made a case for treating the text as a 'work' rather than a 'quarterly', and doubts that the order in which the manuscripts were written shows a major 'Stirner shock' to Marx. Zhao concludes that the work remains an important growth point for Marxist research. The author calls for a new Chinese complete edition, for international dialogue in which Chinese scholars lead the discussion, and for continued study of the text's documents, theory and contemporary value. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-authored overview of the editorial history of The German Ideology and of how Chinese scholars position themselves toward MEGA2.

Grasping the great significance and key requirements of Party building leading grassroots governance 深刻把握党建引领基层治理的重大意义与重要要求 Tan Xiaoyan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 3 August 2026, asks why Party building should lead grassroots governance and what that leadership requires. Tan Xiaoyan argues that, amid a changing social structure, more diverse popular demands and growing pressure to control risks, grassroots governance has an increasingly foundational and strategic place in national governance. The author concludes that Party building must lead it, as a safeguard for Chinese modernization. The piece has two parts. The first sets out the significance of Party-led grassroots governance, which the author calls political, theoretical and practical. The second turns to four requirements: improving the system of overall Party leadership, pursuing reform and innovation, serving and benefiting the people, and putting risk prevention first. Tan frames the whole discussion with Xi Jinping's statements on grassroots work and on the Party's roots among the people. In the first part Tan gives four reasons. Grassroots Party organizations, which the author says numbered 5.431 million at the end of 2025, are the foundation of the Party's long-term rule. Grassroots governance underpins the modernization of national governance. Rising popular expectations require responsive services. Grassroots units are also the first line of defence in coordinating development and security. In the second part, Tan proposes that major grassroots matters be decided by Party organizations after discussion. The author also calls for trimming township and sub-district administrative structures, giving them fuller powers and cutting formalistic burdens. Tan further urges combining self-governance, rule of law and moral governance, and strengthening emergency management, using the updated 'Fengqiao experience' and big-data tools. Tan concludes that the Party's organizational strengths must be converted into governance capacity at the grassroots, so that effective governance supports high-quality development and a high level of security. The author holds that the people should be the judges of results, and that governance should be tested by whether people gain real benefits and whether their rights are protected. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of the current Party-building approach to grassroots governance, including its institutional proposals on township powers, burden reduction, cadre training and risk control.
