Engels's critique of "True Socialism" and its lessons for today 恩格斯对“真正的社会主义”思潮的批判及其启示 Fu Chenchen Fu Chenchen examines how Engels criticised "True Socialism", a current of 1840s German thought that tried to graft English and French utopian socialism onto German idealist philosophy. The article argues that Engels's first systematic critique, in the preface and concluding remarks of his 1845 text Fragments on Fourier's Trade, exposed the current as an abstract, ethicised, anti-proletarian doctrine. Fu also argues that this critique still offers methodological lessons for ideological work in the new era. The article has four parts. It first traces the historical formation of True Socialism: the split of the Young Hegelians (Strauss, Bauer, Feuerbach) and the way utopian socialism was received and distorted in a Germany with a weak bourgeoisie and a large petty bourgeoisie. It then sets out four theoretical features of the current, drawing on figures such as Karl Grün, Hermann Kriege and Friedrich Beck. A third part analyses Engels's methods of critique, and the last turns to present-day implications. Fu identifies the four features as follows: an abstract theory of human nature with a moralising bent; a "supra-class" ethical utopia of universal love in place of class struggle; a vulgarising misreading of Fourier; and, at root, the conservatism of the German petty bourgeoisie. In Fu's account Engels's method rests on historical materialism, class analysis and scientific abstraction, which he sets against the "empty abstraction" of True Socialism. Fu stresses Engels's contrast between Fourier, who reached his vision of the future after correctly understanding past and present, and the True Socialists, who arbitrarily arrange history and then point to where the future should go. Fu also cites the position of True Socialists during the 1844 Silesian weavers' uprising as evidence of the current's reactionary function. In the final part Fu draws three lessons for China today, each tied to statements by Xi Jinping. These are to uphold historical materialism against historical nihilism and abstract speculation; to treat theoretical resources scientifically and avoid vulgarised readings or mechanical grafting of Western concepts; and to hold to Party spirit and a people's standpoint against ideological deception. Fu links petty-bourgeois illusions to what the article calls "welfare populism", "universal values" and ideological infiltration. Read the original if you want a close textual study of Engels's Fragments on Fourier's Trade, or an example of how classical critiques of rival socialisms are applied to present-day ideological work in China.

On the relationship between the "two inevitabilities" and the "two never wills": a reflection based on Marx's idea of bypassing the capitalist "Caudine Forks" 论“两个必然”与“两个决不会”的关系——基于跨越资本主义制度“卡夫丁峡谷”设想的反思 Li Jian Li Jian takes up a gap in Chinese scholarship on the "two inevitabilities" (capitalism will inevitably perish, socialism will inevitably triumph) and the "two never wills" (no social order perishes before all the productive forces it can contain have developed; no new relations of production appear before their material conditions mature). Existing work, the author says, analyses their logic at the level of what ought to be and neglects how the "two never wills" actually serve as conditions for the "two inevitabilities". Li argues that Marx's late idea of bypassing the capitalist "Caudine Forks" does not overturn this condition. It deepens it and shows a special route to realising the "two inevitabilities" in backward countries. The article has three sections. The first reads the relationship through historical materialism, tracing the two formulas to the Communist Manifesto, Capital and the 1859 Preface. The second examines how the Russian-commune idea both challenges and sustains the framework. The third draws lessons for building the theoretical system of Chinese modernization, citing Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Engels's 1885 letter to Vera Zasulich. Li's central move is to reject two misreadings of the "two never wills": a dogmatic \"capitalist-conditions theory\" requiring every country to pass through full capitalism, and an abstract talk of \"general material conditions\" detached from history. The Caudine Forks idea is said to acknowledge diverse paths and multiple sources of the material conditions, which can be partly absorbed from capitalist civilisation abroad and combined with reactivated communal forms. Li then argues that it leaves the framework intact on four grounds. The bypassable path is particular while the unbypassable law is universal, a dialectical \"concrete universality\" rather than an either/or. What can be bypassed is capitalist relations of production and their suffering, not the development of productive forces. Subjective initiative operates within objective limits, which Li reads into Marx's remark that a society can shorten and lessen the birth-pangs. The classical and bypass paths are complementary, operating at different analytical levels. Li concludes that the Russian-commune idea upholds both the trend and its preconditions while extending historical materialism's grasp of diversity. For Chinese modernization, Li draws three implications. It is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. It must proceed from national conditions, separating socialism's unchangeable essence from its selectable forms. It must follow the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, using capital while ultimately transcending capital's logic. Li adds that replacing capitalism is a long, peaceful competition. Read the original if you study the Marxist theory of non-capitalist paths, the Caudine Forks debate, or how Chinese scholars link Marx's late writings to Chinese modernization.

Why stand first? Rethinking "Marxism is the unity of standpoint, viewpoint and method" A reconsideration of the priority of standpoint in Marxism 为什么首先是立场？ Zhao Jiwei Zhao Jiwei asks why, within the familiar formula that Marxism is a unity of standpoint, viewpoint and method, standpoint should come first. The article answers that standpoint is the "soul" and commanding element of the other two, and that the proletarian and people's standpoint is the premise on which Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character rests. Zhao presents this as a response to Western tendencies to weaken or dilute that standpoint. The article opens by criticising several Western positions. These are radical-left thinkers such as Jacques Rancière and Antonio Negri, who replace the proletariat with plural subjects; Western Marxism, which rejects the dictatorship of the proletariat; and scholars who treat Marxism only as philosophy. Three sections follow, each tied to a question: standpoint and values (whom Marxism serves), standpoint and method (how the world is understood), and standpoint as the link between science and revolution (how the world is changed). The evidence includes the Communist Manifesto, The German Ideology and Capital, and comparisons with Adam Smith, Ricardo and List. It also draws on Bernstein, Rosa Luxemburg, Habermas, the Paris Commune, Lenin, and the Chinese Communist Party. Zhao argues that Marxist viewpoints, including historical materialism and the theory of surplus value, are theoretical expressions of the proletarian standpoint rather than neutral knowledge. Bourgeois economics and philosophy that claim neutrality are said to defend capitalism, so the same object analysed from different standpoints yields different conclusions. On method, Zhao holds that contradiction analysis and class analysis serve the aim of overthrowing exploitation. Detached from standpoint, they become abstract tools, as in Bernstein's treatment of surplus value or Habermas's recasting of economic crisis as an administrative problem. Method in turn gives standpoint cognitive tools and practical routes, such as the mass line, and tests it in practice. Zhao reads the Paris Commune's failure as a case of unclear theoretical standpoint, and presents reform and opening up as a contemporary example of scientific and revolutionary unity under a people-centred standpoint. Zhao concludes that standpoint is the "soul", viewpoint the "body" and method the "application", and that their unity must have standpoint as its axis. Only by holding to the proletarian and people's standpoint can viewpoint stay scientifically oriented and method serve human emancipation. Without it, the article warns, theory hardens into dogma or degenerates into a narrow sectarian movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-theory argument for the priority of class standpoint, including its critique of Western Marxism and post-Marxist thought.

The three-dimensional innovation of the Marxist worldview and methodology in contemporary China 当代中国马克思主义世界观和方法论的三维创新 Liu Zhuohong Following the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), which called for upholding and applying the worldview and methodology of contemporary Chinese Marxism, Liu asks in what ways that worldview and methodology represent an innovation on Marx's own. The article argues that the innovation has three dimensions: it is epochal (shídàihuà), national (mínzúhuà) and popular (dàzhònghuà). Liu presents the "six musts" as the concentrated expression of this worldview and method. The article is organised in three sections, one for each dimension. The first traces how Marx and Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping each analysed their own epoch. The second takes up the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The third examines how theory is made accessible to ordinary people, drawing on the Yan'an period and on present-day media. Liu argues that epochal innovation comes from answering the questions of the age. Marx grounded the concept of an epoch in the contradictions of modes of production, Lenin in imperialism, Mao in war and revolution, and Deng in peace and development. For Xi's era, Liu pairs each of the "six musts" with a classical Marxist counterpart, for example people-centredness with the mass view of history and global vision with "workers of all countries, unite". On the national dimension, Liu claims Marxism and traditional culture converge on materialism, on practice (set against the Western speculative tradition) and on human development, and that each "must" fuses a Marxist idea with a Chinese one, such as the "people as the foundation" tradition. On the popular dimension, Liu holds that the people-centred character of Marxism underlies the whole set, and calls for building on Yan'an methods such as Ai Siqi's Mass Philosophy, audience-specific communication, and online and local-cultural carriers. Liu concludes that the three innovations are complementary. The first gives theory its contemporary content, the second gives it a distinct cultural character, and the third lets the people accept and own it. Together they are said to make the theory more vital and to root it more deeply in China. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how the "six musts" are linked to the Second Integration and to the popularisation of Marxism in China.

Promoting new major progress in building a Beautiful China 推动美丽中国建设取得新的重大进展 Xiong Huanhuan This commentary, published on Guangming Online in August 2026, takes up the Beautiful China Construction plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, issued in July 2026. The authors argue that the plan sets out a clear roadmap for ecological protection over the next five years and a weighty promise to the people. They treat 2030 as a key stage for achieving a fundamental turn for the better in the ecological environment. The piece has three sections. The first describes a space–air–ground–sea integrated monitoring network. The second looks at air, water and marine targets and at whether residents actually feel improvements. The third places Beautiful China within Chinese modernization and global sustainable development. On monitoring, the authors cite targets for 2030: 6 new ecological satellites, national monitoring points rising from 33,000 to over 50,000, and a "1+7+N" operating mechanism, with human involvement in key national operations cut by 70%. They describe a shift from manpower and experience to computing power and data-driven decisions. On public benefit, they list targets of PM2.5 below 27 micrograms per cubic metre, 85% good air days and 85% good surface-water bodies, and stress that residents' own sensations should be the final judge. They also describe a move from key regions to nationwide control and from large rivers to rural areas. The authors conclude that monitoring makes problems visible, governance action makes them manageable, and public experience tests whether they are properly resolved. They contend that China, rather than following the Western path of pollute first and clean up later, has launched a green transition and offers wisdom and a model for global sustainable development. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of the plan's monitoring and pollution-control targets and how they are presented to the public.

Cultivating a culture of innovation: inheriting the innovation genes of fine traditional Chinese culture 培育创新文化 传承中华优秀传统文化的创新基因 Zhang Xiaoping Cui Yi Zhang Xiaoping and Cui Yi take up Xi Jinping's call, made at the national science and technology conference, to cultivate a culture of innovation and to inherit the innovation genes of fine traditional Chinese culture. Their thesis is that such a culture is neither a break with tradition nor a simple return to the past. Guided by the Two Integrations, it should reactivate the reformist spirit in traditional culture and combine it with the scientific and revolutionary character of Marxism, producing an innovation culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article opens by naming three values of cultivating innovation culture: for national strategy (science and technology self-reliance), for the social ecosystem, and for the integrated development of education, science and talent. It then has three main sections. The first identifies innovation genes in traditional thought. The second sets out three components of innovation culture in the new era. The third proposes four practical paths, labelled root, foundation, environment and force. The authors argue that the Chinese tradition contains innovation genes in three pairs of ideas. 'Shengsheng' (ceaseless generation) and 'ri xin' (daily renewal) supply the motive force. 'Hetong' (harmony without uniformity) and 'tongbian' (change through interconnection) supply the developmental logic. 'Zhixing' (knowing and doing) and 'gezhi' (investigating things) supply a practice-based orientation. Innovation culture in the new era is then defined by three elements: valuing science and pursuing innovation as its value cornerstone; encouraging exploration and tolerating failure as its institutional guarantee; and daring to break new ground and be first as its practical character. They link each element to Marxist epistemology, in which truth develops through struggle with error, and to traditional ideas of perseverance. The four paths are to draw on the innovation spirit of classical texts, to build innovation into education and the training of top talent, to reform institutions toward flexibility, tolerance of error and classified evaluation, and to open up to exchange with other civilisations. The authors hold that this combination can make innovators of the broad population and support technological self-reliance and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style argument draws on Confucian and Yijing concepts to frame current science and education policy.

The epochal basis, guiding principles and strategic measures of high-quality economic development 经济高质量发展的时代依据、指导原则与战略举措 Liu Wei Writing in the context of the Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), Liu Wei asks how China should understand and achieve high-quality development. The article argues that three elements form one logical system: grasping China's new historical position is the epochal basis, applying the new development philosophy is the guiding principle, and building the new development paradigm is the strategic measure. Together, Liu says, they answer why, on what principles and how high-quality development should proceed in order to advance Chinese modernization. The article follows this three-part structure. The first section reviews the achievements that, in Liu's account, define the present position: GDP above 140 trillion yuan in 2025, the elimination of absolute poverty, a complete industrial system and expanding opening up. The second section treats the origins and content of the five-part new development philosophy and its link to high-quality development. The third discusses the new development paradigm, its basis in China's status as a large economy, and the relations it requires to be balanced. Liu draws on figures for GDP, trade, manufacturing, research spending and consumption throughout. Liu's central argument is that the shift from rapid growth to high-quality development is demanded by changed conditions. Growth driven by factor inputs and low costs is no longer sustainable; reaching the 2035 modernization target needs about 4.8 per cent annual growth, which the old model is said to deliver at only around 4 per cent. Liu adds the pressure of the dual carbon goals, imbalances in development, Western containment and the technological revolution. The new development paradigm, presented as an extension of Marx's theory of capital circulation, is meant to turn this philosophy into practice. Its core is to strengthen the domestic circulation through a unified national market, integration of scientific and industrial innovation, secure industrial and supply chains and a dynamic balance of supply and demand, while promoting mutual reinforcement with international circulation. Liu concludes that the Party's approach reflects a unity of historical, theoretical and practical logic and is a component of Xi Jinping's economic thought. The article also calls for coordinating relations between domestic demand and supply-side reform, self-reliance and openness, rural revitalization and urbanization, and market-economy reform and high-level opening up. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how the logic behind the 15th Five-Year Plan's economic approach is framed, with extensive statistics on China's development.

The mode of existence of modern humans and its transformation in the perspective of the critique of political economy 政治经济学批判视域中现代人的存在方式及其变革 Huang Zhijun Starting from the claim that Chinese modernization requires the modernization of the human being, Huang Zhijun asks three questions: who the modern human is, in what fundamental way modern humans exist, and how the transformation of that mode of existence can be grasped at the level of practical principle. The article argues that Western Marxists, working with Marx's concept of alienation, offered a forward-looking but ultimately purely theoretical critique. In Huang's reading, Marx instead follows the logic that the sublation of self-alienation takes the same path as self-alienation itself, and this logic yields both a critique and a real prospect of change. The article first compares three answers to what a modern human is: Adam Smith's self-interest, Hegel's self-consciousness, and Marx's production of exchange value. It then examines the modern mode of existence in three spheres taken from Marx's critique of political economy: the mode of material production, the mode of social interaction, and the mode of spiritual life. It next sets out how each sphere might be transformed and closes with implications for the modernization of the human being. Huang's central move is that Smith grasps the human through things and Hegel through spirit, while Marx finds the inner measure of modern humans in the production of exchange value, an alien yardstick that rules over them. In material life, ends and means are inverted, and the division between productive and non-productive labour reflects the capitalist's standpoint. In social interaction, money and credit exert an abstract domination. In spiritual life, labour is split between a reified, profit-oriented form and a non-alienated form. Huang argues that the conditions for overcoming these predicaments are created by the same epoch that produces them. Material life would move towards common production, social interaction towards a new system beyond money and credit, and spiritual life towards the satisfaction of individual needs and all-round development. Huang concludes that Marx surpasses Smith's and Hegel's idealist accounts and that change must rest on new modes of production and interaction, so that people move from subordination to a position as subjects. For the modernization of the human being, Huang draws three implications: a people-centred approach, a community with a shared future for mankind, and spiritual abundance for the people, so that development moves from the realm of necessity towards the realm of freedom. Read the original if you work on Marx's critique of political economy, alienation theory or the philosophical foundations of Chinese modernization and want a systematic Marxist account of modern human existence.

The theme, main thread, historical experience and contemporary features of the Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation 中国共产党推进理论创新的主题主线、历史经验和时代特点 Ai Silin Zhang Chuanquan This article asks what has driven and shaped the Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation over more than a century. International communication strategies of Yan'an woodcuts during the War of Resistance 抗战时期延安木刻的国际传播策略 Xue Dong This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2026, asks how Yan'an woodcuts reached foreign audiences during the War of Resistance against Japan. The security implications of new quality productive forces 新质生产力的安全意蕴 Qi Guang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, asks how development and security relate in the case of new quality productive forces. Understanding in depth the thesis that "upholding Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics" 深入理解“坚持党的领导是中国特色社会主义最本质的特征” Gong Yun This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, explains a thesis placed first among the "fourteen upholds" of Xi Jinping's Party-building thought, which a national Party-building conference in June 2026 formally set out. Carrying forward the great Long March spirit to build a firm ideological foundation of ideals and convictions among young people 弘扬伟大长征精神 筑牢青年理想信念根基 Song Xiaodong Song Xiaodong, a researcher at Beihang University's School of Marxism, takes up how universities can use the Long March spirit to strengthen the ideals and convictions of young people. Grasping the rich meaning of the Communist Party of China's outstanding qualities 深刻把握中国共产党的优秀特质的丰富意蕴 Chen Jinlong This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the six "outstanding qualities" of the Communist Party of China that Xi Jinping set out in his speech marking the Party's 105th anniversary. The Party's self-reform focuses on governing power 党的自我革命重在治权 Wu Yijun Liu Zhiqi This newspaper commentary takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that the Party's self-reform 'focuses on governing power', because the "Four Forms of Decadence" mostly stem from privilege-seeking thinking and corruption is chiefly the use of power for private gain. A historical analysis of who proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance 工农联盟提出和创建的历史辨析 Li Wei Who first proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance? The article argues that the alliance was proposed and created by Lenin, not by Marx and Engels or by the nineteenth-century European socialists and workers' parties, who never developed it in theory or practice. Li first sets out two conflicting readings in Soviet and Chinese editorial prefaces: Lenin's 1894 work is said to have first proposed the alliance, while the prefaces to Marx and Engels's Selected Works credit Marx's The Class Struggles in France and The Eighteenth Brumaire. The article then reviews how Marx and Engels's views on the peasantry changed between 1848 and the 1890s. It examines Engels's 1894 "The Peasant Question in France and Germany", and closes with Lenin's creation of the alliance and its development by Mao Zedong and later Chinese Communists. Li argues that passages usually cited for an early alliance idea come from the 1848 revolutionary period and were later revised by Marx and Engels themselves. Li notes that Marx deleted one such passage from the 1869 edition of The Eighteenth Brumaire. After the Paris Commune, they concluded that peasants could obstruct workers' revolutions. Reading Engels's 1894 text, Li finds that the European parties took up the peasant question only after half a century, and that they regarded peasants essentially as voters to be won in parliamentary elections. In Li's account, the worker-peasant alliance instead grew from armed struggle against landlords and the bourgeoisie, from proletarian leadership of the peasantry in the bourgeois-democratic revolution, and from the Leninist party. Only Lenin's Bolsheviks, in Li's view, found "the correct way of approaching the peasants". Li concludes that the alliance emerged only when the proletarian revolution reached a higher stage, and that Europe's early workers' movement had no peasant movement to learn from. Li treats this as no fault of Marx and Engels, since each era solves the tasks it is able to pose. The article presents the Chinese Communists under Mao Zedong as the culmination of the alliance in practice and theory, and refers to Xi Jinping's thought as guiding its current consolidation. The value orientation of closely combining investment in things with investment in people 投资于物与投资于人紧密结合的价值旨归 Wang Wencheng This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 8 June 2026, asks what value order should govern the relation between material capital accumulation and human development. Decoding "Chinese governance" and building "Chinese scholarship" An interview with Xue Lan, senior professor of humanities and social sciences at Tsinghua University 解码“中国之治” 构建中国之学 Zhang Sheng This is an interview, published in Guangming Daily on 28 May 2026, with Xue Lan, a senior professor of humanities and social sciences at Tsinghua University who works in public administration. The threefold core meaning of practice as the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy 实践作为马克思哲学基石的三重核心要义 Hu Bo Hu Bo asks what makes the concept of practice the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy and what it contains. Hu identifies three closely linked core meanings: practice as the human mode of life-activity, as the foundation of the real world, and as the true force that transforms it. Hu draws mainly on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and Capital-era passages on labour. Idealism, old materialism and religious theology serve as foils throughout. In the first section, Hu holds that practice differs from animal instinct because it combines two attributes: thinking initiative (purposes and plans guide action) and sensuous reality (subject, object and means are all real, so ideas can be realised). Practice is therefore neither pure mind nor mindless matter. Hu also stresses its purposiveness, with a final purpose in the freedom and emancipation of all humanity. The second section argues that nature in the human sense and society are products of generations of practice, so idealism, which makes spirit the origin, and old materialism, which reduces the world to mechanical matter, both miss the real basis of history. The third section claims that practice is the force that changes the world, so philosophy's task becomes changing it rather than merely interpreting it. Hu concludes that emancipation requires a two-way movement between theory and reality: thought must press towards reality, and reality towards thought. This means shifting from speculative justification to concrete, historically specific programmes, which Hu sees in Marx's empirical study of capitalism. It also requires practitioners to be consciously guided by truth rather than partial desires or narrow experience. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style exposition of the practice concept in Marx's early philosophy and its link to emancipation, as presented in a Chinese Party-press venue.

Building an international communication narrative system for the four global initiatives 构建四大全球倡议国际传播叙事体系 Qiu Gengtian Chong Juan This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 2 July 2026, asks how China should communicate the Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, Global Civilization Initiative and Global Governance Initiative to foreign audiences. They want the initiatives presented as open platforms and public goods, not as an exclusive "small circle" or a tool of hegemony. On content, they say narratives should show the initiatives as a response to global problems, as practical support for building that community (material, security, spiritual and institutional dimensions), and as a path to cooperation, illustrated with concrete joint projects in each field. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-school scholars frame the communication strategy for China's global initiatives.

On the wealth attributes of lucid waters and lush mountains 论绿水青山的财富属性 Liu Yan Liu Yan takes up Xi Jinping's claim that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" and asks what it means that lucid waters and lush mountains (green mountains and clear waters) are at once natural, ecological, social and economic wealth. The article argues that this claim of multiple wealth attributes is the foundation of the idea. In Liu's reading, it extends Marx's category of wealth in an ecological direction and goes beyond the limits of Western economics. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical meaning of the claim through three dimensions of wealth: its essence, its content and its measure. The third discusses the theoretical value of the idea for reconstructing the view of wealth, with attention to accumulation, distribution and the inheritance of wealth. Liu draws on Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, the Grundrisse and Capital, and on texts collected in the Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Ecological Civilization. Liu makes three main moves. First, wealth is defined as an advanced form of productive forces consistent with green development, with high-quality ecological products and services answering the people's need for a better life, and with a measure that reflects the contribution of resources and the environment. Third, the article contrasts this with Western modernization, which it describes as relying on resource extraction and as oriented to capital accumulation, and with "zero growth" and "degrowth" theories (Jason Hickel and Kohei Saito are named). Liu concludes that the claim points to a new path of accumulation through green and low-carbon development, with innovation-driven growth and intensive rather than extensive models. It makes ecological justice a principle of distribution, covering fairness within and between generations. Liu presents it as a basis for Chinese modernization and as a reference for other developing countries. Read the original if you want a close account of how current Party ecological theory is tied to Marx's concepts of wealth, use-value and the measure of wealth.

Taking the path of health development with Chinese characteristics is an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization 走中国特色卫生与健康发展道路是中国式现代化内在要求 Wang Xiufeng This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 4 June 2026, takes up Xi Jinping's call of 6 March 2026 to "unwaveringly follow the path of health development with Chinese characteristics" on the way to building a Healthy China by 2035. Read the original if you want to see how an official-media commentary connects the Healthy China 2035 goal to the established themes of Chinese modernization.

The threefold core meaning of practice as the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy 实践作为马克思哲学基石的三重核心要义 Hu Bo Hu Bo asks what makes practice the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy and what distinguishes it from all earlier philosophy. According to Hu, the concept carries three closely linked determinations: a theory of human essence, a theory of the foundation of the world, and a doctrine of human liberation. This short theoretical piece in the Guangming Daily has three sections, one for each determination. The first treats practice as the human mode of life-activity. The second treats practice as the basis on which the real world arises and develops. The third treats practice as the real force that transforms the world. Hu draws mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach, and contrasts Marx with idealism, old materialism and theological accounts of creation. In the first section Hu says that, for Marx, free and conscious activity is the species-character of humans, unlike the instinctive behaviour of bees or spiders. Practice combines two attributes: thinking initiative, which includes purposiveness and an ultimate aim of universal human freedom and liberation, and sensuous reality, which turns ideas into actual things. In the second section Hu argues that nature as humanised nature and society as the sum of social relations both come from practice. Idealism reduces the world to spirit and old materialism reduces it to mechanical matter, and Hu holds that both lack a theory of practice. In the third section Hu contends that practice makes humans the makers of their world, so philosophy's task becomes changing the world rather than only interpreting it. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese restatement of the standard Marxist-philosophical reading of practice, as it appears in the Party press.

Using New Era civilised practice to consolidate the grassroots foundation of Chinese modernization 以新时代文明实践夯实中国式现代化的基层基础 Li Dingyi This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 2 June 2026, asks how New Era civilised practice (a grassroots programme of propaganda, cultural and volunteer work) can be made to work in depth. From Yan'an to Xibaipo: an important exploration by Chinese Communists in establishing a correct view of performance 从延安到西柏坡：中国共产党人树立正确政绩观的重要探索 Wu Yin This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 3 June 2026, asks how the Communist Party of China forged and held to a "correct view of performance" (zhengjiguan) between the Yan'an period and the Xibaipo period. The author presents this trajectory as historical experience for establishing and practising a correct view of performance in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Party discourse draws on the revolutionary period for lessons on cadre conduct and assessment.

A great expedition that opened a new situation: the Red Army's Long March, its strategic shift and historical significance 开创新局的伟大远征：红军长征实现战略大转移及其历史意义 Luo Pinghan Gao An'yi This newspaper article by two Party historians argues that the Red Army's Long March was more than a feat of preserving the revolution's seed of fire. They say that Japanese aggression, the Huabei Incident of 1935 and the rise of the Sino-Japanese national contradiction to the principal contradiction made north China the front line. The Long March, they write, moved the revolution 'from south to north' geographically, 'from narrow to broad' politically and 'from passive to active' strategically. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party historians present the Long March's strategic logic and significance.

Using digital empowerment to promote high-quality development of discipline inspection and supervision work 以数字赋能推动纪检监察工作高质量发展 Gong Bihan Gong Bihan takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, to grasp new trends in corruption and innovate methods. The piece examines four areas: the fundamental guiding principle, the value orientation, the mechanism through which digital tools work, and the practical path of implementation. It is a short newspaper commentary built as four numbered sections. Gong holds that digital systems must stay under the Party's centralised, unified leadership and serve full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, with its political requirements built into the algorithms. The value orientation is a people-centred approach, with data monitoring of livelihood areas such as education, healthcare, pensions and rural revitalisation, and online platforms that lower barriers to public participation. On mechanism, Gong describes anti-corruption penetration deepening from static structure to dynamic process to underlying logic. Gong presents this as converting institutional strengths into governance effectiveness and consolidating the Party's anti-corruption gains. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated researchers frame digital technology in anti-corruption supervision.

People's wellbeing first: an important contribution of Chinese modernization to the world 民生为大：中国式现代化的重要世界贡献 Xin Xiangyang This commentary, published in the People's Daily, takes up Xi Jinping's formula that in Chinese modernization 'people's wellbeing comes first' (minsheng wei da). Each presents one respect in which the principle is said to contribute globally: making the people the main force of modernization in a populous country, reconciling economic vitality with social order, addressing the principal contradiction of society, and advancing balanced, inclusive and sustainable global development. Xin first contrasts Chinese modernization with the Western path, which the author describes as built on colonial plunder, capital-centred logic and exploitation that left most people outside modernization. Second, the author argues that it resolves the common dilemma of vitality versus order by combining investment in things with investment in people, resolving disputes at the grassroots and developing whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary presents Chinese modernization's livelihood agenda as a global contribution.

The Holy Family and the formation of the materialist conception of history 《神圣家族》与唯物史观的形成 Gong Qin This short commentary in a Chinese academic newspaper asks what role Marx and Engels's The Holy Family (1844–45) played in the formation of the materialist conception of history. Gong Qin argues that the book is a key link in that process. Its "real humanism" is a key step towards a science of real human beings and their historical development, going beyond Feuerbach while still showing his influence. The book's main target is the Berlin "Free" circle around the Bauer brothers, whom Marx and Engels treat as a caricatured completion of Hegelian dialectics in a philosophy of self-consciousness. Gong organises the discussion around three questions: what real humanism is, how humanist materialism relates to historical materialism, and how to understand Marx's critique of the "mystical side" of Hegel's dialectic. The article draws on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach, Engels's later work on Feuerbach and the afterword to the second edition of Capital, Volume I. On the first question, Gong notes that contemporaries such as Ruge and Stirner read Marx and Engels as members of a Feuerbachian "humanist school", stressing the "humanism" in the phrase. Gong stresses its "real" side: the distinction between interests and ideas, and the claim that history originates in material production. On the second, Gong argues that Marx moved from using "materialism" pejoratively to engaging French and English materialism, linking it to humanism, the critique of private property, socialism and communism. The Holy Family and the Theses on Feuerbach thus mark a move from reflecting on humanist materialism to historical materialism. On the third, Gong reads the critique of Hegel's "speculative structure" (the hypostatisation of ideas and the turning of substance into subject) as a long exploration. It ran through the analysis of civil society and material production and ended in Capital's historical, materialist and dialectical exposure of the capitalist mode of production. Gong concludes that the decisive step beyond Feuerbach was the construction of a dialectical, historical and practical materialism within the critique of political economy and the exploration of socialist and communist practice. Rereading the book today, Gong says, means taking from Marx and Engels the habit of starting from reality, grasping social structure and historical trends, welcoming dialogue between different views, and advancing theoretical innovation with methodological self-awareness. Read the original if you want a compact orientation on how The Holy Family connects Feuerbach, Hegel's dialectic and the emergence of historical materialism, as seen by a Chinese scholar of Marxist intellectual history.

Historical laws and the historical subject from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域中的历史规律与历史主体 Wang Su Wu Jinjing This short commentary asks how historical materialism relates objective historical laws to the people who make history. Wang and Wu argue that the scientific character of the theory lies in the dialectical unity of the two: laws give social change its direction and necessity, while the people, as the historical subject, are the material force that recognises, applies and realises those laws. The article is organised into three pairs of unity: the constraint of laws and the initiative of the subject; the necessity of laws and the subject's capacity to choose; and social progress and the free and all-round development of the human being. It draws mainly on Marx and Engels, including the 1859 Preface, Engels's idea of the resultant of many wills, and Marx's three stages of human development. In the authors' account, laws set a boundary of possibility, since practice cannot overleap the limits of the productive forces or the sequence of social formations. Within that space, the subject's cognition and choices shape the path, form and pace of development. Class position affects how different classes understand and act on laws, so class struggle becomes part of how they unfold. Choices that accord with laws advance society, while those that violate them are eventually corrected by historical necessity. Laws are not fate; they come alive only through the practice of millions. The authors conclude that the realisation of laws and the development of the subject are mutually reinforcing. Greater understanding of laws lets people align relations of production with the productive forces and the superstructure with the economic base, speeding progress. Freedom is thus not escape from necessity but, in the authors' phrase, necessity that has been recognised. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese textbook-style statement of how law and agency are reconciled in historical materialism.

"Human–AI synergy" and the transformation of forms of labour “人智协同”与劳动形态的变革 Zhu Hongwei Zhu Hongwei, writing in the China Social Sciences Journal (April 2026), asks how large AI models are changing labour. The article begins from the State Council's opinion on the "AI+" initiative, which calls for new forms of human–machine collaboration. Zhu argues that AI is shifting from tool to "collaborative subject", which frees workers for creative labour but also lets the logic of capital penetrate production and creates interlinked systemic risks. The piece first describes the new forms of collaborative labour. It then sets out three risks of capital's penetration and closes with three institutional responses. Zhu holds that human–AI synergy builds on the strengths of both sides, opening a \"missing middle\" of tasks neither can do alone. Living labour remains the only source of value, since intelligent machines are objectified knowledge and fixed capital that raise efficiency without creating new value. The three risks follow from this: gains captured by capital and technical elites, which Zhu says produces \"intelligent poverty\"; labour substitution and worker \"deskilling\", with a structural mismatch between scarce high-end and surplus low-end jobs; and flexible work that conceals capital's domination, leaving gaps in rights protection. Zhu calls for institutional innovation to regulate capital and steer the technology. Proposals include curbing the disorderly expansion of AI capital, distribution by data contribution, ethical review of AI, technical support for weaker groups, and digital-literacy training. The aim is \"co-evolution\" that serves human development. Read the original if you want a short Marxist account of AI-era labour that rests on the labour theory of value and fixed capital.

Free time and human digital existence 自由时间与人的数字化生存 Wen Quan This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how digital technology affects free time, which Wen Quan treats as the key condition for people's free and all-round development. Wen argues that digital technology holds real potential to release people from necessary labour, but that, fused with the logic of capital, it fragments, accelerates and empties out time. The piece moves in three steps. It first sets out Marx's view of time as "the space for human development" and of free time as leisure plus time for higher activity. It then examines the potential and the predicament of free time in the digital age, drawing on Nicholas Negroponte's Being Digital. Finally it considers how free time might be rebuilt. In Wen's account, automation, remote work and online learning widen the forms free time can take. Yet "digital labour" quietly turns life time into production time: work messages arrive at night, and platforms convert users' browsing and likes into data for profit. Algorithms on the production side drive delivery workers towards "self-exploitation", while consumption-side recommendation feeds produce "filled" rather than self-determined time. Wen reads this time alienation as an extension of capital's logic, so attention should shift from the technology itself to the social relations and power structures in which it is embedded. Wen calls for vigilance against virtual time displacing real creative practice and against "digital addiction". The author also proposes institutional safeguards for workers' time rights, a fair allocation of time and a narrower digital divide. Wen concludes that, with technical progress, institutional protection and awakened time-consciousness, free time can be freed from digital capital, so that people "dance with bits" rather than being devoured by them. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist reading of platform labour, algorithms and leisure that is organised around Marx's concept of free time.

The idea of human emancipation in The German Ideology 《德意志意识形态》中人的解放思想 Yang Fan This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how Marx and Engels treat human emancipation in The German Ideology. Yang argues that the work completes a revolution in the conception of history and moves emancipation away from abstract moral appeals or changes of ideas. It places emancipation within the objective laws and practical process of social development. The article proceeds in four steps. It starts from the premise of the "real individual", then turns to the division of labour, private property and alienation. It next discusses the growth of productive forces and the revolutionary proletariat, and ends with the "genuine community" and the free and all-round development of the individual. Yang's central argument is that emancipation must be examined through material production and social relations rather than through self-consciousness or an abstract human essence. In this account, the involuntary division of labour and the private property it produces turn labour into an alien power, and the worker, the capitalist and the relations between people are all alienated. Emancipation requires highly developed productive forces and world-wide intercourse. Capitalist large-scale industry creates universal alienation but also the material and subjective forces to overcome it, above all the proletariat. The result Yang describes is "autonomous activity" and a genuine community, in contrast to the illusory community of class society, in which individuals gain freedom through their association. Yang concludes that the idea combines a revolution in the view of history with a lasting practical movement. It remains, the author says, a basic theoretical resource for criticising capitalist modernity and for exploring humanity's future. Read the original if you want a brief, orthodox Chinese overview of how The German Ideology links the real individual, alienation and communism.

From Yan'an to the world: the international dissemination of Chinese literary theory 从延安到世界：中国文论的国际传播 Deng Haili Writing in a newspaper commentary, Deng Haili asks what the 80-year translation and circulation of Mao Zedong's Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art can teach about taking Chinese literary theory abroad. Deng argues that the Talks' international career offers a historical model for telling China's story well and building Chinese discourse and narrative systems. The piece surveys English translations in two groups: those led by the Chinese government and those produced by foreign research institutions and scholars. It runs from versions around 1950 to the Harvard multi-volume edition of Mao's writings completed in 2023. Deng describes the official translations of the 1950s and 1960s, including the Foreign Languages Press Selected Works of Mao Zedong, as state-level cultural dissemination. In Deng's account they served Cold War solidarity with Western leftists, sinologists and Third World revolutionaries. Foreign-led translations, by contrast, moved from political-historical readings, as in the 1952 Harvard documentary history, to aesthetic ones. Bonnie McDougall's 1980 translation criticised ideologically biased scholarship and stressed the text's aesthetic content. Deng presents the Harvard edition under Stuart Schram as combining political, historical and aesthetic perspectives. Deng concludes that international dissemination is a complex process of discourse generation, re-signification and cultural dialogue, not simple language conversion. In this reading the Talks moved from a revolutionary document to a theme in world literary theory, showing the vitality of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Deng sees lessons for helping Chinese culture "go out" and "go in" and for mutual learning among civilisations. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the Talks' English translation history and how a Chinese scholar frames its lessons for international communication.

From the critique of religion to the critique of fetishism 从宗教批判到拜物教批判 Zhu Linlin This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how Marx's early critique of religion relates to his mature critique of fetishism. Zhu argues that the two are continuous: religious critique was the starting point and model, and the critique of fetishism is its culmination, in a sense a radicalised version of it. The article follows Marx's path from the 1840s to Capital. It covers his place among the Young Hegelians, the 1843 Introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, On the Jewish Question, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and the theory of fetishism in the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital. Zhu's central move is to treat the theory of alienated labour as the bridge. Marx saw religion as alienation of human essential powers, and found the same structure in the state and in capitalist production, where the worker's product confronts him as an alien power. Later Marx distinguished commodity, money and capital fetishism, and the article cites the 'automatic fetish' of M–C–M′. Zhu holds that fetishism resembles religion but is more fundamental and concealed, because it is an objective illusion rooted in capitalist relations of production, a 'secular religion'. Zhu concludes that Marx's philosophical revolution was a continuing critique, not a new system. It asks where abstract powers such as God, value and capital come from, and it exposes ideologies that present historical social relations as eternal natural order. Real emancipation, Zhu says, requires changing the relations of production that keep generating fetishes. Read the original if you want a concise outline of the continuity between Marx's early alienation theory and his theory of fetishism.

The fetishism dilemma of the digital age and how to resolve it 数字时代的拜物教困境及其破解思路 Zhang Huaming Zhang Huaming asks why people come to treat algorithms, data and platforms as mysterious, autonomous powers, even though these are products of human labour. The commentary argues that this "digital fetishism" is a new form of Marx's commodity fetishism. It hides real power relations and exploitation behind digital symbols, and Marx's critical method can demystify it. After recalling Marx's account of commodity fetishism in Capital, Volume I, the article identifies three layers of digital fetishism: data, algorithms and platforms. It then sets out how to critique them and closes with institutional proposals. Zhang holds that data value comes from users' unpaid "digital labour", while the exchange of "free services" for data only appears equal. Algorithms, on this account, are not neutral. They carry the stance of their authors and the intentions of capital, and they extend control over couriers, consumers and public opinion. Platforms present themselves as public infrastructure while concentrating capital and exploiting small producers such as couriers and drivers. The chain "commodity–money–capital" thus becomes "data–algorithm–platform capital", and the core remains that relations between things mask relations between people. Zhang calls for "demystification" through the labour theory of value, for recognising users as digital labourers, and for restoring human agency. Proposed measures include exploring public ownership of data through public data pools or data trusts, independent algorithm audits, recognised worker status and social insurance for platform workers, and making giant platforms public, like utilities. Zhang stresses that the aim is not to reject technology but to make it serve people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a concise Marxist-political-economy treatment of digital capitalism and platform labour, with concrete policy proposals.

Engels's historical-materialist interpretation of the "ideological battlefield" 恩格斯对“思想战场”的唯物史观阐释 Wei Qiang Wei Qiang, a professor at Chongqing University, asks how Engels's 1855 study The Armies of Europe, written at Marx's request during the Crimean War, treats what the author calls the "ideological battlefield" (sixiang zhanchang). Wei's thesis is that, although the phrase is not an explicit term in Engels's text, it runs through it as an analytical thread. Armies' ideas, discipline, cohesion and morale, Wei argues, are social forms of consciousness shaped by mode of production, class relations and tradition. On this reading Engels widened military struggle from armed confrontation into a total contest between material and spiritual forces. The short commentary first sets out the historical occasion: the war made Europe's armies of about two million men open to comparative study. It then follows three themes in Engels's text: national military characteristics, discipline, and morale and will. Examples include French, British, Russian, German and Austrian forces, with the British stand at Inkerman cited as a case. The piece closes by drawing a lesson for contemporary military affairs. Wei's central claim is that Engels grounds the ideological battlefield in social being. National traits such as French dash, British tenacity or Russian passive obedience are, in Wei's account, products of civilisation level, economic structure and political system, and not racial endowments. Engels's contrast between feudal discipline based on corporal punishment and bourgeois discipline based on contract and duty to the state is read as reflecting different relations of production. Multinational Austria shows, for Wei, that coercive discipline without shared interests breaks down under strain. Morale is presented as ideological identification turned into combat power, the political awareness of whom one fights for, which can offset material inferiority. Wei concludes that, whatever the technology, war's agent remains human beings, and that the initiative on the ideological battlefield is as important as on the armed one, or more fundamental. Winning hearts, holding ideological leadership and cultivating spiritual cohesion are described as lasting core issues of military struggle. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese reading of Engels's military writings that stresses morale, discipline and ideology, and want to see how it is tied to present-day military ideological work.

Making the responsibility for governing the Party effectively a reality 推动管党治党责任落实到位 Wang Xipeng Writing in the People's Daily (29 May 2026), Wang Xipeng takes up the relationship between the responsibility for managing and governing the Party and the effort to form and act on a correct view of performance. The article argues that the two are mutually reinforcing: the tighter and more concrete Party governance is, the steadier a correct performance outlook becomes, and the more it yields achievements that benefit the people and are recognised by them. The piece is a commentary in three parts. The first sets out five ways in which Party governance supports a correct performance outlook: political guarantee, ideological foundation, work-style safeguard, a yardstick for testing results, and institutional safeguard. The second turns to how responsibility is to be enforced, and the third to democratic centralism as the basis of scientific decision-making and practical implementation. Wang's central claim is that a performance outlook is a "soft constraint" that Party governance turns into a "hard" one, through quantified assessment, accountability and personnel decisions. The author describes distortions such as vanity projects, falsified data and formalism as ultimately problems of Party spirit, and treats failure to pursue full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as itself evidence of a wrong performance outlook. Responsibility must run vertically through every level and horizontally across clearly defined bodies: Party committees bear primary responsibility, secretaries are first responsible persons, other leaders carry "one post, two responsibilities", and discipline commissions supervise. Wang also argues that democratic centralism, combining collective leadership with individual division of responsibility, prevents both one-man rule and diffusion of responsibility. Wang concludes that democratic centralism should run through the whole process of creating achievements: collective wisdom to judge at the decision stage, divided responsibility at the implementation stage, and institutional constraint at the oversight stage. This, the author holds, removes the ground for a distorted performance outlook and encourages foundation-laying, long-term work that answers to history and the people. Wang also stresses that strict management should be combined with care for officials, so that rigour does not stifle initiative. Read the original if you want to see how official Party-building discourse in 2026 links cadre evaluation, accountability systems and democratic centralism to the idea of a correct performance outlook.

Drawing on traditional Chinese thought on clean governance 汲取中华传统廉政思想养分 Sun Dawei This newspaper commentary, published in Henan Daily in 2026, asks how the clean-governance thought of China's traditional culture can feed the building of a culture of integrity in the new era. Sun argues that five strands of that thought, though limited by their time, still offer a systematic resource. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping on learning from the history of anti-corruption work. The article takes five strands in turn, each tied to one representative figure and one dimension: public-mindedness and integrity (Cao Duan, Ming dynasty; power), diligence and integrity (Kuang Zhong, Ming; performance of duty), loyalty and integrity (Zhen Dexiu, Southern Song; political allegiance), filial piety and integrity (Huang Tingjian, Northern Song; family ethics) and purity and integrity (Zhou Dunyi, Northern Song; inner cultivation). Each section ends with a present-day problem among Party members and cadres. Sun presents each pair as mutually dependent. Public spirit is the basis of integrity, and integrity gives public spirit substance. Diligence secures integrity, and integrity directs diligence. Loyalty and integrity imply each other, though Sun notes that Zhen's loyalty was owed to the feudal monarch. Filial piety is the emotional root of integrity. Inner purity is needed for integrity, which in turn makes purity concrete. Sun links these to current failings: obstructive red tape, passivity, double-dealing, nepotism and family-based corruption, and cadres who refrain from corruption only under pressure. Sun concludes that Party members should unite public spirit with integrity, combine diligence with honesty, join absolute loyalty with self-discipline, run clean households, and move from "not daring" and "not being able" to corrupt to "not wanting" to. The article calls for passing on these "integrity genes" and strengthening conscious commitment to clean governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars use classical Chinese ethics to frame contemporary anti-corruption education.

A historical analysis of who proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance 工农联盟提出和创建的历史辨析 Li Wei Who first proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance in the history of the international communist movement? Li Wei notes that Soviet and Chinese editorial prefaces give two contradictory answers: Lenin in 1894, or Marx in 1850. The article argues that Marx, Engels and the European socialists of the nineteenth century never formulated or built such an alliance, and that Lenin first tried and partly solved the problem in practice and theory. Li first reviews how the Soviet Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute and, later, China's Central Compilation and Translation Bureau interpreted the classics in prefaces to the Selected Works and Collected Works. He then traces the nineteenth-century record, from the 1848 revolution through the Paris Commune and Engels's 1895 Introduction to Marx's The Class Struggles in France to Engels's 1894 essay on the peasant question in France and Germany. The second half turns to Lenin, the Bolsheviks and the Chinese Communists, ending with Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. Li argues that the oft-cited 1848–52 remarks on peasants joining workers reflect the thinking of Marx and Engels as young men, and that they later revised it. Li points to Marx's deletion of a passage from the 1869 second edition of The Eighteenth Brumaire and to his 1875 judgement that peasants can obstruct workers' revolutions. On Li's reading, Engels's 1894 essay shows that European socialist parties took up the peasant question only late and treated peasants chiefly as voters in parliamentary contests. Lenin, by contrast, fought for proletarian leadership in the bourgeois-democratic revolution and treated the land question as its core. He then drew on 1905 Moscow uprising and armed struggle to form peasant, worker and soldier soviets, whose alliance carried the October Revolution. Li concludes that the alliance emerged from revolutionary practice against landlords and the big bourgeoisie, and marks the passage of Marxism into the era of Leninism. The Chinese Communists, in Li's account, then brought it to completion through rural revolutionary bases and land reform. Li adds that the absence of the idea among Marx and Engels is no cause for regret, because each era sets its own historical tasks. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based challenge to the view that Marx originated the worker-peasant alliance, or want to see how Chinese editorial prefaces shaped that view.

Grasping the contemporary value of Chinese modernization from the depth of world history 从世界历史纵深把握中国式现代化的时代价值 Zhang Guanzi Writing in People's Daily, Zhang Guanzi asks what Chinese modernization means when set against the long history of world modernization. The commentary argues that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of "modernization = Westernization" and offers the world a new option. Zhang holds that the limits of the Western model are increasingly visible and that other countries are looking for new paths. The piece has three parts. The first revisits world modernization as a process pursued jointly by all of humanity rather than by the West alone. The second sets out how Chinese modernization is said to surpass Western theory and practice. The third discusses its influence on the global modernization process. Zhang draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on Marx, Engels and Immanuel Wallerstein. Zhang argues that Western modernization did not develop in isolation. It drew on inventions from other civilizations, such as Chinese papermaking, printing, the compass and gunpowder, and it pulled Asia, Africa and Latin America into a world market. In this account Western modernization is one particular form, driven by the unlimited expansion of capital. Zhang says it produced alienation, wealth polarisation and, through war, slave trading and colonialism, long-term underdevelopment elsewhere. Chinese modernization is said to surpass it in three ways: putting the people first instead of capital, harmonious coexistence instead of benefiting oneself at others' expense, and openness and inclusiveness instead of systemic monopoly. Zhang cites the Belt and Road Initiative as an example of the last. Zhang concludes that Chinese modernization has exposed the myth of a single Western model and confirmed that paths to modernization are diverse. It also offers a development philosophy and approach to governance, including a strong political core, long-term strategic continuity and a socialist market economy combining an effective market with an enabling government. In Zhang's view, the modernization of more than 1.4 billion people will reshape the global modernization landscape, and a community with a shared future for mankind will open opportunities for the Global South. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary presents the world-historical significance of Chinese modernization.

The crisis of capitalism and the failure of its governance An interview with the German sociologist Wolfgang Streeck 资本主义的危机及其治理失败——访德国社会学家沃尔夫冈·施特雷克 Qin Shiya This is an interview, conducted in early 2022 by Qin Shiya of the journal World Socialism Studies, with the German sociologist Wolfgang Streeck, formerly director of the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Societies in Cologne. It asks how capitalist crises and the way states manage them should be understood. Streeck's answer is that the remedies adopted since the 1970s only postpone crisis, while hollowing out democracy and deepening inequality. The conversation moves from a definition of capitalism to the sequence of postwar state forms. It covers the role of private and public debt, the passage from the tax state to the debt state, the consolidation state and a tentative central bank state, and the link between economic and democratic crisis. It then turns to the prospects for collective action by workers, the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic, the risk of inflation, and Streeck's current research. Streeck defines capitalism as an economic system committed to the unlimited accumulation of private capital, on which social and political stability then depend. When accumulation stalls, crisis follows. Debt, he says, has been central from the start: it imposes work discipline, and public borrowing replaced taxation of capital, so that owners lend to the state and pass the claims on to their heirs, which in his account widens inequality. He argues that the neoliberal turn weakened unions and collective bargaining, which he calls pillars of capitalist democracy, and that globalisation and European monetary union removed economic decisions from democratic control. Since 2008, he says, central banks have injected newly created money to offset weak demand and inflate asset prices, so the rich grow richer while accumulation continues. He doubts that this can last, since pandemic-related supply disruptions are bringing inflation back. Streeck foresees no orderly replacement of capitalism. Borrowing Gramsci's notion of the interregnum, he expects a long post-capitalist period of disorder, an "age of entropy", in which crises are the new normal and change is rapid but uncontrollable. He is cautiously optimistic that people will keep organising to resist. Read the original if you want a leading critical sociologist's account of debt, central bank policy and democratic erosion in Western capitalism, as an example of Western critical scholarship presented to a Chinese Marxist readership.

The "five organs", "six viscera", "four beams" and "eight pillars": focal points for building an autonomous knowledge system of Chinese discipline inspection and supervision studies “五脏”“六腑”“四梁”“八柱”：构建中国纪检监察学自主知识体系的着力点 Sun Dawei After discipline inspection and supervision studies became a first-level discipline in September 2022, building its autonomous knowledge system became a shared task for the field. Sun Dawei asks where the effort should concentrate. The article argues that existing studies treat only the discipline system and pick scattered points, and proposes a three-dimensional framework. It links the "five organs" and "six viscera" to the disciplinary system, the "four beams" to the academic system and the "eight pillars" to the discourse system. The article first reviews work by Wang Xu, Chen Yafei, Guo Weilu, Zhang Zhen, Jiang Laiyong and Xu Yuzhen, and finds it fragmented. It then draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on an autonomous knowledge system, which the author reads as comprising disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. Three sections follow, each defining its metaphor, assessing current progress and naming a priority for the future. The metaphors are borrowed from sociologists. Fei Xiaotong's "five organs" are five kinds of institution: learned societies, research institutes, departments, libraries and documentation centres, and publishing houses. His "six viscera" are six core courses. Chen Guangjin's "four beams" are theoretical, historical, methodological and applied knowledge. The "eight pillars" are the distinctive concepts, judgments, propositions and categories, together with the representative works, scholars, schools and doctrines. Sun reports that the organs have grown quickly, citing the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision Association, new institutes at universities, the publisher China Fangzheng Press and new journals. The viscera lag because courses are poorly designed and theoretical talent is scarce. Applied, historical and methodological knowledge have advanced through practice, integrity-culture work and survey research. Theory remains the weakest beam, still shaped by Western frameworks such as principal–agent theory. In the discourse system, annual anti-corruption buzzwords remain political language that has not yet been turned into academic concepts. Sun concludes that the priorities are to strengthen the six viscera, to develop theory with Chinese characteristics, and to turn political discourse into systematic academic concepts. These steps, Sun argues, would make the system more systematic, original and fit for its time, and would support international communication of Chinese anti-corruption discourse. Sun ties the task to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese legal and Party-discipline scholar sets out an agenda for building a new discipline, or if you follow the institutional growth of anti-corruption scholarship in China.

Polishing the "golden calling card" of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation 擦亮中央八项规定这张“金色名片” Lü Yongxiang This newspaper commentary asks how the Central Committee's eight-point regulation on Party conduct, issued after the 18th Party Congress (2012), can keep advancing the Party's self-reform. Lü Yongxiang calls the regulation a "golden calling card" and a fulcrum for changing how the Party is governed. The author argues that thorough implementation of its spirit gives the Party's self-reform a concrete lever and supplies a conduct guarantee for building a strong country and national rejuvenation. The piece is set against the learning and education campaign on implementing the regulation, which the whole Party began in March 2025. After a short opening on the regulation's record since 2012, it sets out three orientations for implementation, each tied to a different foundation of self-reform: values, integrity and institutions. First, Lü holds that putting the people first must be the value stance. Officials should check whether their view of power, of performance and of career has been distorted, and should deal with formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. Second, the author urges a mechanism for investigating work-style problems and corruption together, so that the chain from bad conduct to corruption is cut. This means tracing the funds, participants and interest exchanges behind banquets and gifts. Third, Lü stresses making conduct-building regular and long-term. The author points to Party regulations on accountability, thrift and official reception, and to case analysis that finds the institutional roots of recurring problems. Lü concludes that work-style building is a protracted struggle and that the regulation is a long-term "iron rule", not a short-term measure. The author calls for combining reform spirit with strict standards, and for linking conduct, discipline and anti-corruption work. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official line on how the eight-point regulation is tied to the Party's self-reform and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Advancing the Party's self-reform requires systematic guidance 推进党的自我革命要实现系统化指引 Liang Fei This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (26 March 2026) asks how the Party should govern itself in the new era. Liang Fei argues that Xi Jinping's call for "five more steps into place" in advancing the Party's self-reform gives systematic guidance on this question. The author presents the five as the key practical levers for applying Xi's thinking on the Party's self-reform. The article draws on Xi's remarks at the 21st group study session of the Political Bureau of the 20th Central Committee. There, Xi called self-reform the Party's "second answer" to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. The five areas are understanding, Party spirit, regulated exercise of power, strict supervision and discipline, and fulfilment of responsibility for Party governance. Liang groups them under three headings: motivation, rigid constraints, and coordination of the governance system. Liang's central claim is that governance effectiveness depends on moving from piecemeal to systemic governance. Awareness and Party spirit are treated as the ideological drive, which turns external pressure into internal motivation. Regulating power and joint investigation of misconduct and corruption, with Party supervision linked to other forms of supervision, supply the rigid constraints. A closed loop of assigning, performing, supervising and holding to account responsibility ties the system together. Liang assigns each element a role: understanding answers "why", Party spirit "who", power regulation "what", supervision "how well", and responsibility "relying on whom". Liang concludes that the five steps form an organic whole and must be pursued with a systems outlook, so that the elements resonate together. The aim, in the article's account, is a governance pattern that covers all content, all objects, the full chain of responsibility and every institution. This would strengthen the Party's creativity, cohesion and combat capacity and support the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars frame the "five steps" as a systematic governance framework.

Gathering the strength of Chinese modernization through high-quality labour and creation 以高质量的劳动创造汇聚中国式现代化奋进伟力 Li Yuyan This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 7 May 2026, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that high-quality development depends on high-quality labour and creation. Li argues that such labour runs through the course of Chinese modernization, expresses its people-centred values, drives high-quality development and points towards common prosperity and the all-round development of the individual. The piece has three main sections. The first treats high-quality labour as an expression of the people-centred requirement, the second as the core engine of high-quality development, and the third as a condition of common prosperity and all-round human development. It closes with a brief call to action. Li draws on Marx's account of labour as free, conscious activity and contrasts this with alienated labour under capital-driven older modernization. In this reading, high-quality labour returns labour to its authentic form: knowledge-based and skilled, marked by craftsmanship, and aimed at real social needs. Li links it to new quality productive forces, citing more than 220 million skilled workers at the close of the 14th Five-Year Plan. On distribution, the author holds that distribution according to labour, a rising labour share in primary distribution and better skill-grade systems enlarge the middle-income group and produce a cycle of creation, sharing and re-creation. Li concludes that Chinese modernization is achieved by doing, not waiting. The author calls for promoting the model-worker, labour and craftsmanship spirits, strengthening protection of workers' rights, and fostering a social climate that respects labour and skills. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary connects Marxist labour theory to current policy themes.
