Persist in investing in people to promote the development of new quality productive forces 坚持投资于人 促进新质生产力发展 Cheng Shuang Zhang Yongqiang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 7 May 2026, asks how "investing in people" relates to new quality productive forces. Cheng and Zhang argue that the two form an organic unity. In their account, investing in people is a precondition for high-quality development and for building China into a modern socialist country. They take their cue from the 15th Five-Year Plan outline, which lists the talent pool as an advantage and calls for investing in things and in people together. The piece has two parts. The first sets out four reasons why investing in people and new quality productive forces belong together. The second turns to four practical requirements, which cover local-government assessment, the direction of investment, the integrated development of education, science and technology, and talent, and the institutional setting for innovation. The theoretical argument rests on Marx and on Xi Jinping's statements. The authors say investing in people helps relations of production fit the demands of the productive forces, because it raises workers' standing and skills and lets knowledge and technology share more fully in distribution. They cite Marx's Capital on training for skilled labour-power to claim that such spending is a productive investment with a multiplier effect, not mere welfare. They also hold that workers' free and comprehensive development upgrades consumption and widens demand. In their reading this creates a loop running from human capital to effective demand to better supply, and it pushes reform of income distribution and property rights. Retraining is meant to ease skill mismatches and prevent large-scale unemployment as traditional industries are upgraded. In practice, the authors propose adding "people-centred" indicators, such as the share of human-capital investment, to assessments of local governments. They would tie the results to officials' promotion, project approval and fiscal transfers. They also call for balancing priority fields such as artificial intelligence with basic training, and for balancing present needs with future ones. Other proposals include merging the education, innovation and talent chains through industry-education integration, reforming ownership and profit-sharing for職务 research results, and adopting tolerant, error-correcting supervision. Read the original if you want to see how Party-state scholars connect human-capital policy, Marx's labour theory and local cadre evaluation to the new quality productive forces agenda.

Integration and symbiosis: advancing university–enterprise collaborative education 融合共生 推动校企协同育人 Bi Tianshu Writing in Guangming Daily on 24 March 2026, Bi Tianshu, president of North China Electric Power University, argues that industry-oriented universities should deepen collaboration with enterprises in training talent. Starting from the proposal in the outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan to integrate scientific and industrial innovation, Bi holds that such collaboration can link the education, talent, industry and innovation chains and support the building of a leading education country. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out the value of collaborative education, then proposes three changes of mindset, and finally outlines three directions for practice. On value, Bi presents collaboration as the link joining national strategy, industrial upgrading and the university 'Double First-Class' initiative, through shared mission, aligned responsibility and common development. On ideas, Bi urges universities and firms to move from short-term 'project-based' or 'order-based' cooperation to long-term strategic coordination, to treat each other as interdependent partners sharing teachers, resources and results, and to replace 'adaptive' training with innovation-led training aimed at 'bottleneck' technologies. On practice, Bi calls for three shifts: from a discipline-driven to a strategy-driven training system, from single-point cooperation to an ecosystem covering the whole industrial chain, and from serving industry to enhancing national competitiveness, including exporting technologies and standards through the Belt and Road Initiative. Bi concludes that collaborative education should become a vehicle for national competitiveness and a foundation of educational strength. Read the original if you want a concise statement, by a university head, of how Chinese industry-oriented universities frame cooperation with enterprises under the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Using a "broad view of employment" to connect the whole cycle of educating students 以“大就业观”贯通育人全周期 Ning Depeng This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 24 March 2026, asks how universities should respond to a record graduating cohort, which the author gives as 12.7 million, 480,000 more than the previous year. Ning Depeng argues that employment work must stop being treated as a graduation-season task and must be built into the whole cycle of educating students through a "broad view of employment". The author ties this to the demand of new quality productive forces for composite and innovative talent. The piece is organised under four headings: running through the whole process, breaking down barriers, balancing hard and soft skills, and precise services without interruption. It addresses university administrators and employment offices, with concrete measures on admissions, curriculum, assessment and career guidance. Ning's central move is to bring employment quality forward to the start of training. This means linking admissions plans to national strategy, judging institutions by employer feedback, salary growth and social contribution rather than first-job rates, and fostering lifelong learning. The author then calls for dismantling disciplinary boundaries through new interdisciplinary fields, micro-majors, AI and digital literacy for all students, and university–enterprise cooperation. Ning also proposes a two-wheel approach: hard skills through project-based learning and simulation, and soft skills through a "second-classroom transcript" and ideological and political education that encourages graduates to work in areas of national need and in remote or grassroots posts. On services, the author recommends career education from freshman year, differentiated guidance for students seeking stable posts, new sectors or start-ups, regulated support for platform and flexible work, and big-data matching with a "one student, one policy" ledger for those facing difficulty. Ning concludes that these measures would raise talent-training quality and so support high-quality and full employment. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese education scholar translates national employment and industrial policy into university practice.

The operating system of Western discursive hegemony in the digital age and China's response 数字时代西方话语霸权的运行体系及中国应对 Qiu Weidong Qiu Weidong takes up what the article calls an anomaly in international communication. In the author's account, Western hegemonic states, whose capital-centred expansion produced dependency and "disaster capitalism", still dominate global discourse through "universal values". Meanwhile socialism with Chinese characteristics, which has overcome the problems of being "beaten" and "starved", is still "scolded" abroad. Qiu argues that Western discursive hegemony in the digital age is an extension of the capitalist mode of production, serving capital's limitless accumulation, and that China needs a systematic response. The article first describes four features of digital-age Western hegemony: widening of fields, technological reinforcement, reaching down to mass audiences, and multi-actor collusion. It then analyses how the hegemony operates in three steps: packaging culture, monopolising communication carriers, and disciplining audiences' cognition. The final part sets out China's response in three areas: a discourse system, a communication system and an identification system. Qiu's core claim is that digital technology lets "instrumental rationality" mask capitalist "value rationality". Indices such as Freedom House and Polity IV are presented as objective, but the author says they embed Western values in their weighting and data selection. Qiu adds that government strategy papers, academic gatekeeping, NGOs and platform firms such as Google and Meta form a "digital closed loop". Western dominance is said to rest on first-mover advantage in capital accumulation, not on institutional superiority. The author cites English-language dominance of online content, the concentration of platforms and news agencies, and technology blocs. In education, culture and social life, algorithms are said to deprive audiences of the chance to test ideas in practice. Qiu proposes three paths. The first is an autonomous philosophy and social science knowledge system, built with digital tools and the Two Integrations, so that China has "reasons it can state". The second is to use new quality productive forces for core technology breakthroughs, industrial coordination and a public-interest communication base, including a "Digital Silk Road", so that messages "travel". The third is precise communication: varied actors, audience profiles and algorithmic delivery, and agenda-setting that combines fact-based rebuttal with positive constructive themes. Qiu holds that together these would shift China from reactive self-justification to active leadership. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of digital media, indices and platforms as tools of hegemony, together with a concrete policy agenda for international communication.

The relationship between digital capital and financial capital in the digital economy 数字经济下数字资本与金融资本关系研究 Cai Wanhuan Cai asks whether digital capital is a higher form than financial capital, and whether it replaces financial capital in the way financial capital once displaced industrial capital. The article answers that digital capital has neither replaced nor simply merged with financial capital. In Cai's account it is the dominant form of capital, but it operates under the control of financial capital and serves as a tool for extracting profit under new technical conditions. The article first reviews two positions in current scholarship. One holds that digital capital has taken over the top of the capital hierarchy, moving towards 'data capitalism'. The other holds that the two are deeply fused, and it names several hybrid forms: financial-monetary capital, digital financial capital, 'financial-digital capital' and the 'digital-financial' complex. Cai then defines digital capital through Marx's three dimensions of capital: value that yields surplus value, value in motion, and a social relation embodied in a thing. The article ends with proposals for governing digital capital under the socialist market economy. Cai makes three main moves. First, digital capital is a relation of production: data are privatised as means of production, algorithms control the labour process, and platforms monopolise exchange. Exploitation therefore extends from paid wage labour to the unpaid labour of platform users. Second, Cai traces how financial capital drives platform development. Venture capital funds loss-making start-ups in the hope of future monopoly rents, and platforms later become channels for financial gains through public listings, embedded finance and crypto-assets. Cai concludes that the platform 'technological revolution' is a shell for financial capital's accumulation regime. Third, drawing on Marx's phrase that money is 'the power of all powers', Cai argues that financial capital remains dominant because it is the form freest of material constraints. Digital technology extends money's reach through payment data and consumer credit. Cai notes that data are non-rivalrous and shareable and that digital networks call for socialised use, which sits uneasily with private monopoly. For socialist market conditions, the author calls for public digital capital to take the leading position. Four institutional measures are proposed: a structural separation of data property rights, a unified national data market with data pricing, 'traffic lights' for private digital capital, and a national data-value sharing fund. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy argument that platform and digital capital remain subordinate to financial capital, together with Chinese policy proposals on data governance and capital regulation.

The distributional paradoxes of capitalist intelligentization and their alternative 资本主义智能化的分配悖论及其替代方案 Yang Tianyu Does artificial intelligence (AI) necessarily worsen income distribution? Yang Tianyu, writing in Marxist Studies (2026, no. 1), argues that it does not. Western economists describe three biases of AI, toward capital, toward skills and toward tasks, but Yang holds that these arise from the capitalist relations of production in which AI is used, not from the technology itself. Socialist intelligentization, the article claims, offers a workable alternative. The article starts from Marx's distinction between machinery and the way machinery is used, and from the principle that distribution is determined by the structure of production. It first analyses how AI restructures the capitalist labour process, then its effects on labour–capital relations and class structure. It next examines three Western remedies (social security, shorter working days and basic income) and finally sets out a socialist alternative, drawing on China's experience. In Yang's reading, the capital bias is a rise in the rate of surplus value. AI raises it through relative surplus value, through algorithmic control of working time and intensity, and through labour displacement that sharpens competition among workers. Employment becomes de-materialised and fragmented, bargaining power shifts to capital, and a new labour aristocracy faces a digital proletariat. Yang argues that each Western remedy collides with capital's pursuit of a higher rate of surplus value. Shorter hours cut surplus labour time, while the tax rises needed to fund basic income erode competitiveness. Fragmented employment also undermines social security and trade unions. Yang contends that under public ownership with the state sector in the leading role, and under Party leadership, these paradoxes can be resolved. State capital returns can fund a basic income that is a form of "capital income" rather than welfare, supplement flexible workers' social insurance, and support working-time reduction and wage consultation. Yang adds that a state fund for creative work could address alienated labour and promote people's free and all-round development. Policy proposals include socialising new AI means of production, universal basic income, and a shift from profit to social value. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy account of AI and inequality that defends a socialist alternative against Western technology-centred analyses.

Lenin's thought on strengthening the Party's political development and its contemporary value 列宁关于加强党的政治建设思想及其当代价值 Yue Kui Yue Kui asks what Lenin contributed to the idea of the Party's political development (dang de zhengzhi jianshe), and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. The article argues that, although the classical Marxist authors did not use the term, Lenin's practice in leading the Russian Bolsheviks produced a coherent set of principles. Yue presents these as a creative development of Marxist party theory and as a theoretical basis for the Chinese Party's current work. The article first notes that the 19th Party Congress (2017) placed political development first among the Party's building tasks and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) made it the lead for all Party building. It then reconstructs Lenin's thought under four headings: the Party's supreme leading position, ties with the masses, a stable leadership group with a core, and a correct political programme with strategy and tactics. It also treats iron political discipline. The final section turns to three present-day lessons. On leadership, Yue reads Lenin's idea of the Party's "general leadership" and his claim that the dictatorship of the proletariat is the proletariat's leadership in politics as placing political leadership above all other forms. On the masses, Yue stresses Lenin's call to work wherever the masses are, including in reactionary trade unions and bourgeois parliaments, and his criticism of "Left" communists who withdrew. Yue also cites his view that a party's treatment of its own mistakes is the surest test of its seriousness. On leaders, Lenin is said to reject both the cult of personality and nihilism about leaders' roles, while requiring a stable leadership group with a "first violin". Yue presents Lenin's demand for "iron" discipline and obedience to the central organs as a condition for winning and holding power. Yue draws three lessons for the present. The Party must be upheld as the "supreme political leading force", a formulation written into the Party Constitution at the 20th Party Congress. The Two Upholds, which Yue reads as inheriting Lenin's "iron discipline" and leader authority, must be put into practice. And "the people's hearts are the greatest politics", which Yue links to closed-loop mechanisms for responding to public needs, such as assessment based on the public's sense of gain and security. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory scholar reads Lenin's texts on party leadership, discipline and the masses to support current Party-building doctrine.

Marx and Engels on Party-spirit cultivation in the proletarian party and its implications 马克思恩格斯无产阶级政党党性修养思想及其启示 Zang Xiuling Zang Xiuling takes up the question of what Marx and Engels said about cultivating "Party spirit" (dangxing) in a proletarian party, and what this means for the Communist Party of China today. Writing against the background of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) and the study campaign on the central Party's eight-point regulations, Zang argues that Marx and Engels, though they used the word "Party spirit" only three times, set out a coherent early framework for it. In this reading, the framework is the intellectual source of the Chinese Party's own conception of Party-spirit cultivation. The article first defines Party spirit as a party's essential, class-based attribute, and Party-spirit cultivation as the long-term self-remodelling of members. It then arranges Marx and Engels's scattered statements under four headings: political, theoretical, disciplinary and moral cultivation. Evidence comes from the Communist Manifesto, the rules of the Communist League and the First International, Engels's "On Authority", the Paris Commune, and the struggles against Bakunin, Lassalle, Proudhon and Weitling. A final section draws practical lessons for Party members. Zang argues that political cultivation is the core. It covers a standpoint serving the great majority, a direction that links immediate and final goals, the authority of a centralised leadership, a correct programme, and the "two most radical ruptures" with traditional property relations and ideas. Theoretical cultivation rests on a scientific worldview that keeps the party pure and turns a class "in itself" into one "for itself". Disciplinary cultivation combines intra-party democracy with centralism, serious Party life, and enforcement through supervision and recall, as in the Commune. Moral cultivation means selflessness, loyalty and the status of "public servant", protected in the Commune by universal suffrage and workers' wages for officials. Zang concludes that Party spirit does not persist automatically over time or grow with rank, so cultivating it is a lifelong task. Following Xi Jinping, Zang recommends that members place political cultivation first and study the classics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Members should also uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, apply democratic centralism, and cultivate the virtues of serving the people, loyalty to the Party and personal probity. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese reading of Marx and Engels's party-building texts and the way it is tied to current Party discipline and ideology campaigns.

On the new form of scientific socialism in the twenty-first century 论二十一世纪科学社会主义的新形态 Wu Haijiang Wu Haijiang asks what historical position Chinese modernization occupies in the development of scientific socialism and what kind of theoretical narrative should accompany it. The article argues that Chinese modernization has opened a new form of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. In Wu's account, this form rests on the achievements of a developed socialism with Chinese characteristics, aims to surpass contemporary capitalism, and looks towards the next stage of socialism. The article first traces scientific socialism through three historical forms. These are the Marx–Engels conception tied to mature Western capitalism and the Paris Commune, the twentieth-century practice in Russia and China, and the present form. It then examines why Chinese modernization can claim to create a new form, looking at the difficulties it has resolved, the era in which it unfolds, and its innovations in path, theory, institutions and culture. The last third turns to narrative and to building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system of scientific socialism, covering its necessity, its basis, its methods and three priority areas. Wu contends that the new form answers three long-standing problems. The first is how to position socialism against capitalism: Wu describes a socialism that grew outside the capitalist system, uses markets and other capitalist instruments, and keeps its own goals. The second is how to avoid the ills of Western modernization, through a modernization of a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony with nature and peaceful development. The third is how to defend the socialist system, through a people-centred stance, the Party's overall leadership, and reform and opening up. Wu also reads the "two great trends", the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and changes unseen in a century, as the setting that links China's questions with the world's. Wu proposes building an autonomous knowledge system of scientific socialism guided by three methodological pairs: criticism with construction, upholding fundamentals with innovation, and subjectivity with openness. Its priorities should be the new possibilities opened by Chinese modernization, the social effects of digital and AI-driven technological revolution, and new features of contemporary capitalism such as financialization. The aim is a Chinese model of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists periodise scientific socialism and frame a research agenda around Chinese modernization.

The civilisational significance of building a community with a shared future for mankind and the path to putting it into practice 构建人类命运共同体的文明意蕴及践行理路 Liu Yang Drawing on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, Liu Yang asks what kind of world is to be built and how, and argues that a community with a shared future for mankind is best understood as a project of civilisational renewal. In Liu's reading, its purpose is to move beyond the modern civilisation shaped by Western-centrism and to plan the course of twenty-first-century human civilisation as a whole. The article treats this as the deeper aim behind the concept, beyond its role in global governance. The article has three parts. The first sets out the background: the "changes of the world, of the era and of history" and the intellectual sources of the concept, namely Marx's thought on civilisation and the Chinese tradition of "all under heaven as one family". The second compares the concept with Western civilisation on five dimensions: nature, values, content, mode of interaction and goals. The third turns to practice and proposes five "communities" to be built through the four global initiatives (on development, security, civilisation and governance). Liu's central contrast is between what the article calls a "deconstructive" Western civilisation and a "constructive" one. Western civilisation is described as driven by capital and marked by universalism, uniformity, hierarchy and short-termism. It is said to rest on a "centre–periphery" order and on the "end of history" thesis. Against this, the community with a shared future for mankind is credited with mutual learning among civilisations, shared human values of peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom, balanced development across economic, political, cultural and ecological fields, and equal participation in governance. Liu presents this as a sublation of Western civilisation and as the basis of a "new form of human civilisation". On the practical side, Liu proposes a community of ideas built on dialogue, a development community aimed at the unequal division of labour in global industrial chains, and a security community. Liu also proposes an ecological community resting on "common but differentiated" responsibility, and a cooperative community suited to the shift of power toward the Global South. Liu concludes that capitalism is not the end point of civilisation and that the "end of history" has failed. The community with a shared future for mankind is presented as China's contribution to human civilisation and a banner for its direction in the twenty-first century. Its ultimate horizon is said to be the "association of free individuals". Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship frames the concept as a civilisational alternative to the West, with a ready-made programme for implementing it.

The civilisational narrative and political-cultural logic of building the Chinese national community 中华民族共同体建设的文明叙事与政治文化逻辑 An Beijiang An Beijiang asks what historical and cultural meaning, and what practical logic, lie behind the building of the Chinese national community (zhonghua minzu gongtongti jianshe), which the article presents as a strategic task of the Party's ethnic work in the new era. Existing research, An says, approaches the topic from theory and practice and from many angles but seldom examines this historical-cultural dimension. The article argues that the project rests on the idea of great unification, takes cultural identity as its core, uses interaction, exchange and integration among ethnic groups as its practical path, and draws on cultural empowerment as its driver. The article starts from the idea of great unification (dayitong) and traces a shift from the concept of "all under heaven" to a view of unity, from the Zhou enfeoffment system and Confucian and Mencian thought through the Qin-Han county system to the Tang, Yuan and Qing. It then discusses cultural identity and its ethical dimension, the Marxist theory of the nation, and the historical record of ethnic interaction. It ends with contemporary measures: ethnic embeddedness, a shared spiritual home and the mining of cultural resources. An's central claim is that, unlike Western nation-state theory, great unification stresses historical continuity and political unity. In An's account, frontier and non-Han dynasties from the Northern and Southern Dynasties to the Liao, Jin, Western Xia and Yuan all claimed legitimate succession to "China" and adopted Han institutions and Confucianism, so that the community formed through institutional innovation and value reconstruction rather than simple assimilation or conquest. An reads Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin as treating the nation as a historical community whose formation depends on long interaction. The Party's term "interaction, exchange and integration" is said to avoid equating integration with assimilation, since integration does not erase differences. An concludes that the project links past and present and offers a "Chinese approach" to governing a multi-ethnic state, achieving political integration without eliminating difference. An proposes embedded social structures and communities, regular education and publicity, preserving historical memory and heritage, and socialist core values as the basis for value consensus. An also calls for opposing narrow nationalism and for creative transformation of traditional culture under the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of borderland studies draws on dynastic history and Marxist nation theory to ground current ethnic policy.

Innovative paths for integrating red cultural resources into university ideological and political theory courses 红色文化资源融入高校思政课教学的创新路径 Zhang Xiaozhi Zhang Xiaozhi, an associate professor at a school of Marxism, asks how "red cultural resources" (the heritage of the Chinese revolution) can be built into university ideological and political theory courses. The article argues that this should rest on the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, and proceed on four levels: content, teaching model, carriers and mechanisms. In Zhang's view, doing so helps train a new generation able to shoulder the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a short practical commentary organised around four proposals. Each is given a three-part formula: a "history–theory–reality" curriculum, an "immersive–interactive–research-based" teaching paradigm, a "digital–networked–social" set of communication platforms, and a "process-based–comprehensive–developmental" evaluation system. It closes with a brief statement of the results Zhang says such integration has achieved. On content, Zhang calls for going beyond simply telling stories, by linking the Jinggangshan and Yan'an spirits to Marxist views of practice and the masses. Content should be tiered by discipline and year of study, for example the "two bombs, one satellite" spirit for science and engineering students, and drawn from local resources such as Gannan, Shanghai and Jiaxing. On method, Zhang proposes VR/AR simulation labs, practice bases at memorials and former revolutionary areas, debates, historical dramas, flipped classrooms and student research projects. Platforms would include a national open digital archive, short videos, WeChat columns, live lectures, and cooperation among universities, government and enterprises. For evaluation, Zhang proposes that process-based assessment make up at least 50 per cent of the final grade, with indicators covering knowledge, ability and values. Long-term tracking of graduates through surveys and interviews would feed back into course reform. Zhang concludes that the integration has already made abstract theory more vivid, raised classroom participation and strengthened students' patriotism and ideals. Read the original if you want a concise inventory of the teaching methods and assessment schemes currently promoted for Party-directed ideological courses in Chinese universities.

Passing on the red gene to build a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation 传承红色基因构筑中华民族共有精神家园 Ma Xingyu Ma Xingyu asks how state-owned enterprises can pass on the "red gene" and so help build a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation. This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in March 2026, argues that corporate culture is a key force for carrying on red heritage and strengthening national spirit. It takes Baotou Iron and Steel (Group), known as Baogang, as its single case. The piece has three parts. The first traces how Baogang's history became a "red resource". The second shows how that resource became identification with the company's culture. The third explains how Baogang's culture helps build the shared spiritual home. Ma draws on Halbwachs's account of how historical memory is activated through narration and commemoration. Ma argues that the story "All pulling together to build Baogang" rose through four levels: individual builders' oral histories, artistic representations, internalisation in company histories, exhibition halls and ceremonies, and finally recognition in national narrative as a "historical tale" and red resource. Baogang then joined this inheritance of dedication and hard struggle to the new development philosophy. In Ma's account, "pulling together" now means collaborative research, industrial-chain coordination and company–locality co-prosperity. The author claims this gives a multi-ethnic workforce a "community" in practice, ties national and company identity together, and strengthens the sense of the Chinese nation as one family. Ma concludes that Baogang has both grounded and elevated the shared spiritual home by turning historical memory into an ideological resource within present-day corporate culture. Read the original if you want a brief case study of how Chinese state-enterprise culture is linked to ethnic unity and red heritage.

Enhancing the value appeal of socialist culture in the new era 提升新时代社会主义文化的价值感召力 Feng Lihua This newspaper commentary asks how the value appeal (jiazhi ganzhaoli) of socialist culture can be raised in the new era. Feng argues that this appeal is the core measure of a culture's vitality and influence, and that raising it is essential to building a strong socialist cultural nation and to steady progress of Chinese modernization. The piece takes its cue from the recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee. The article is organised in three parts: the theoretical source of the appeal, its core task, and the practical paths to strengthen it. It ends with a short summary of the whole project. Feng locates the source of value appeal in the Two Integrations, especially the integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. In the author's account, this produces a "new cultural organism" with firm cultural subjectivity, free of cultural "apprenticeship" and dependence, and it contributes to a new form of human civilization that goes beyond the Western path of capital logic and materialism. The core task is to internalise the core socialist values as national consensus and to turn them into people's civility. The paths are stimulating cultural creativity, including through AI and digital technology, deepening reform of cultural institutions under Marxism's guiding role in the ideological sphere, and building Chinese discourse and narratives to solve the problem of being unable to be heard abroad. Feng concludes that raising value appeal is a major undertaking tied to the future of the nation and its spirit. It calls for cultural consciousness and confidence, institutional reform and a modern communication system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary links cultural confidence, core socialist values and international communication.

Empowering ideals-and-convictions education for young people through red venues 以红色场馆赋能青少年理想信念教育 Li Nan This short newspaper commentary asks how red venues (museums, memorial halls and similar sites of Party history) can strengthen ideals-and-convictions education for young people. Li Nan argues that these venues are a core base for patriotic education and a "second classroom" for ideological and political education. The piece opens from Xi Jinping's call to use red resources and from the recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan. The article first sets out the educational value of red venues on three levels: cognition, value guidance and practice. It then turns to two sets of measures, one on venue design and one on new educational forms and routes. Li contends that red venues convey historical understanding, offer moral exemplars and let young people turn patriotic feeling into action. Because young people now want personalised, interactive and immersive experiences, Li says venues must be a two-way space. Proposed measures include digital reconstruction of historical scenes, VR/AR and 3D rendering, and symbolic rituals such as oath-taking. They also include big-data analysis to tailor content, and tasks, debates and short-video creation to spread red culture through "buzz" dissemination among peers. Li concludes that red venues should pursue high-quality development by innovating on a foundation of fidelity to tradition. They should become places where the red gene is passed on and ideals are nurtured, supplying spiritual motivation for a new generation to take on national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-education writing links museum design, digital technology and youth engagement.

Cultivating a high-spirited and striving ethos across the whole nation 涵养全民族昂扬奋发的精神气质 Wang Weiguo This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today, takes up a phrase from the Party Central Committee's recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan: the call to cultivate a high-spirited, striving ethos across the whole nation. Wang Weiguo argues that national rejuvenation needs spiritual as well as material strength. In Wang's account, this ethos reflects the character of an era and shapes a nation's future. The call is presented as guidance for advancing Chinese modernization, in which material and cultural-ethical progress are coordinated. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundations of the call. The second names its core requirements. The third proposes practical paths for putting it into effect. Wang draws on Marx, on Xi Jinping's remarks on Chinese civilization, and on classical Chinese sayings about self-improvement, renewal and the people as the foundation of the state. Wang grounds the call in three sources. It puts into practice the Marxist view that the masses make history, by stirring the people's historical initiative. It is a contemporary expression of the vitality and continuity of Chinese civilization. It is also a requirement of common prosperity in spiritual life. The core requirements are three qualities: resolve (zhiqi), meaning unity and the will to overcome difficulties; backbone (guqi), meaning self-reliance, rejection of dependence and fearlessness under external pressure; and confidence (diqi), which Wang says rests on long cultural accumulation, economic strength and a solid scientific and technological base. For practice, Wang calls for three steps. First, study the Party's innovative theory and master the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method. Second, build a healthy social atmosphere by coordinating urban and rural cultural-ethical development and weaving core socialist values into all areas of social life. Third, encourage people to strive in the economy, society and people's livelihood, through high-quality development, deeper reform and opening up, and shared social governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the 15th Five-Year Plan's cultural goals to Marxist theory, traditional culture and policy practice.

Realising modernization in which humans and nature live in harmony 实现人与自然和谐共生的现代化 Ke Changwan Writing in the China Social Sciences Today (24 March 2026), Ke Changwan argues that Chinese modernization is a modernization of harmony between humans and nature, and that building a solid ecological security barrier is both an inherent requirement and an important safeguard of it. The commentary takes its cue from the recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). The piece is organised in three parts: why ecological security underpins national security and the nation's lasting development; which guiding ideas should govern the work; and what practical path to follow. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on the Party and State Council opinion on comprehensively advancing the building of a Beautiful China. Ke contends that ecological security, as part of the holistic approach to national security, is a bottom line that protects territorial, resource, food, economic and social security. On ideas, the author calls for the "two mountains" principle, an integrated approach to mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts, and development planned within resource and environmental carrying capacity. In practice, Ke proposes a "three zones and four belts" spatial pattern with firm ecological red lines, tighter control of environmental, biological and climate risks, stronger legal, monitoring and emergency systems, and active participation in global ecological governance. Ke concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on ecological civilization should guide efforts to build the barrier with greater resolve, laying an ecological foundation for the nation's lasting development and offering "Chinese wisdom" for a clean and beautiful world. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholarship links ecological security to the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Making good use of fine traditional Chinese culture to cultivate the political virtue of officials 善用中华优秀传统文化涵养为政之德 Yang Kui This newspaper commentary asks how leading cadres can draw on fine traditional Chinese culture to cultivate zhengde, the political virtue of those who govern. Yang argues that traditional ideas such as "governing through virtue" and "the people as the foundation of the state" retain contemporary value. In Yang's view, they help officials form a correct view of performance and improve the modernization of national governance, in line with Xi Jinping's call to use traditional culture to "rectify the mind and clarify virtue". The piece has three parts. The first sets out what traditional culture contains on political virtue, under three heads: governance of the state, benefit to the people, and self-cultivation. The second argues that these ideas still have vitality today. The third turns to practice and sets out how Party members and cadres should apply them. Yang draws on Confucius, the Guanzi, Fan Zhongyan and other classical sources. The author claims these ideas match the Party's demands for loyalty to the people, practical and clean conduct, and fairness. After creative transformation, Yang says, they have merged with the core socialist values. They supply a moral foundation for national development, social stability and cadre self-discipline. The practical section lists four requirements: put the people first, favour practical work over formalism and bureaucratism, exercise power impartially and for the public good, and plan for the long term. Yang concludes that cadres should draw on traditional wisdom on the principle of making the past serve the present while preserving what is sound and innovating. The aim is to sustain their bond with the people and strengthen their ability to carry out their duties. Yang holds up historical figures such as Bao Zheng and Yu Qian, and Party models such as Jiao Yulu and Yang Shanzhou, as mirrors for cadres. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present traditional culture as a resource for official ethics and cadre education.

Turning the Party's strategy for governing Tibet in the new era into concrete practice 把新时代党的治藏方略转化为具体实践 Yao Yu Writing at the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026), Yao Yu asks how the Party's strategy for governing Tibet in the new era should be understood and put into practice. The newspaper commentary argues that Xi Jinping's directives on Tibet work, centred on four major tasks (stability, development, ecology and strengthening the border), give Tibet's long-term stability and high-quality development a clear direction. Yao holds that these tasks should be pursued in close connection with Tibetan realities and with the aim of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first explains the strategy, summarised by Xi Jinping as the "ten musts", and the five principles Yao singles out. The second reviews what Yao describes as achievements in Tibet in each of the four areas, with figures for 2025. The third links the four tasks to the work of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and ends with four proposals. Yao presents the five principles (governing Tibet by law, enriching the people and rejuvenating Tibet, long-term building of Tibet, winning hearts and minds, and strengthening foundations) as an interlocking system that provides a methodology for Tibet work. The article cites figures as evidence: regional GDP of 301.89 billion yuan... as reported, 303.189 billion yuan, growth of 7.0%, urban per capita disposable income at 104.1% of the national average, more than 50% of land placed under ecological red lines, and 12.52 million... as reported, 125,200 km of roads. Yao also reports public satisfaction with security above 99% and the development of border villages such as Yumai. Yao then argues that each of the four tasks is itself a concrete way of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Stability enables exchange among ethnic groups, shared development gives a material basis, ecological protection serves the national community, and guarding the border expresses patriotism. Yao proposes four lines of work: keep law at the centre and improve institutional safeguards, including integrating the sense of community into national, cadre and social education; use culture to build a shared spiritual home, drawing on the "old Tibet spirit" and the "two roads" spirit; promote mutual embedding through everyday contact, moving from shared space to shared hearts; and use the common cause of socialist modernization to bring all ethnic groups into local economic construction and its benefits. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Tibet policy is framed in 2026, with the statistics and policy language used to present it.

Three paths to strengthening the reach and influence of Chinese civilization 提升中华文明传播力影响力的三条路径 Han Han Writing in China Social Sciences Today (20 March 2026), Han asks how Chinese civilization can be communicated abroad more effectively during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). Han argues that the declining discursive dominance of the West and the rise of the Global South create an opening, but that the task now is to move from breaking through to building a lasting position, and from broad coverage to deep recognition. The answer is three mutually supporting paths, framed by the Plan's call for a Chinese discourse and narrative system. The commentary is a short policy-oriented piece. It takes each path in turn: regional and country studies, culture–technology integration, and a plural ecosystem of narrators. Han draws on phrases from the Outline of the Plan and on public figures for online-game, micro-drama and web-literature revenue. The first path uses area studies to overcome the "cognitive discount" that cultural products suffer abroad. Han calls for in-depth country research, country-specific or region-specific strategies, and measuring recognition and goodwill rather than output volume. The second path treats technology as a core variable. Han points to AI-driven content generation, immersive experiences such as digital museums, and online games, citing 2025 overseas revenue of US$20.455 billion for self-developed games. The third path draws on enterprises, local and grassroots actors, and outside voices such as foreign influencers and scholars. Han holds that the mainstream media's "solo" can no longer cover the whole field. Han concludes that the paths answer three questions: precise communication addresses whom to speak to, technology-driven innovation addresses how, and ecosystem communication addresses who speaks. Capitalist states' self-diagnosis of the contemporary crisis: an analysis based on mainstream Anglo-American media 资本主义国家关于当代危机的自我诊断：基于英美等主流媒体的解析 Chen Huiyuan Why have mainstream Anglo-American media and commentators begun publishing what Chen Huiyuan calls "pathology reports" on their own system, after the post-Cold War confidence of Fukuyama's "end of history"?
