Qiao cites later policies such as the Third Front, "preparing for war and natural disasters, and doing everything for the people", the "two fists and one backside" formula, and civil-military integration. Qiao concludes that the thought still has "lasting theoretical vitality" and draws four implications for Chinese modernization. These are to keep a bottom-line mindset and plan security in advance; to treat national-defence modernization as part of overall modernization; to build civil-military and peacetime-wartime integration, including new quality productive forces and new quality combat capability; and to pursue self-reliance in core technologies while opening up critically. Qiao also calls for data-property, distribution and security systems that spread the gains of the digital economy fairly, and for adapting people's war to new fields of competition. Read the original if you study Mao Zedong Thought or Chinese defence-economic thinking, or want to see how current security and technology policy is linked to Mao-era ideas.

How Mao Zedong summed up the experience of revolutionary war: a reading of the telegrams he drafted for the Central Committee and Military Commission during the War of Liberation 毛泽东如何总结革命战争经验——解放战争时期代为中央（军委）起草电报解读 Chen Dong Chen Dong asks how Mao Zedong drew lessons from fighting during the War of Liberation (1946–49). The source base is the large body of telegrams he drafted on behalf of the Central Committee and the Central Military Commission. Chen argues that Mao built a mechanism of four linked stages: acquiring experience, summing up experience, reviewing experience and learning experience. In this account, summation stopped being a post-war retrospective and became a method of leadership that ran through the whole war. The article begins with Mao's 1965 remark that he lived by 'summing up experience'. It then moves through the war's phases. It first treats how the Party was led to acquire experience for new tasks: siege warfare with explosives, the shift from dispersed guerrilla to concentrated mobile warfare, 'warfare without a rear', and the reporting system. Next come the strategic lessons Mao summed up, then the review of failures, and finally the channels through which lessons were passed on. It closes by linking this method to Xi Jinping's present-day remarks on experience. Chen's central claim is that operational principles came out of concrete battles and were then turned into directives for the whole army. Examples include concentrating superior force to destroy the enemy one by one, drawn from the Longhai railway, Dingtao and northern Jiangsu engagements, and the 'mushroom' tactics of wearing the enemy down. They also include the 'ten major principles of operation'. Reviewing experience was handled from the top down through criticism of unprepared battles, failure to concentrate force and complacency, with the Jinmen defeat as the main warning. It was also built into routine practice, through reviews in the pauses between battles and a reporting system that demanded analytical reports. Learning ran through four channels: circulating successes, forwarding subordinates' reports, promoting model battles, and exchanging approaches between theatres. Chen says this let the centre guide the war without 'remote control' and sustained morale. Chen concludes that Mao's treatment of wartime experience followed Marxist epistemology and let the Party correct its strategy and tactics continuously. The article presents this as a tradition the Party has inherited in the new era. It cites Xi Jinping on piloting reforms by 'crossing the river by feeling for the stones', and on treating failed experience as valuable. Read the original if you want a source-based account, built on Mao's telegrams, of how experience was turned into command doctrine in the Chinese civil war.

The major significance of Mao Zedong's discourse system of "the people" 毛泽东人民话语体系的重大意义 Li Youxin Lei Chengwen Li Youxin and Lei Chengwen examine Mao Zedong's discourse system centred on "the people", which they describe as comprising discourses of the people as subject, people's democracy, serving the people and the mass line. The article argues that this system transformed Marxist class discourse into a people-centred political discourse suited to Chinese conditions. It further holds that the system is the ideological source and value foundation of the discourse system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article begins with the concept of "the people" within the whole discourse system, then contrasts it with classical Marxist class discourse. It traces how the content of "the people" shifted across the stages of the revolution (from the New Democratic revolution through the anti-Japanese and liberation wars) and into socialist construction. It then turns to what the discourse says about the Party's nature, stance and purpose, and ends with its legacy under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The authors argue that in the classical works of Marx, Engels and Lenin the peasantry was an ally but not an independent historical subject. Mao, analysing semi-colonial, semi-feudal China, where the proletariat was small and the peasantry the great majority, made peasants a main revolutionary force. He also defined "the people" through the "enemy, us, friends" distinction, so that the concept was historical and dynamic rather than tied to a single class. The authors describe four levels of the system: a historical view (the people as the driving force of history), a value orientation (serving the people wholeheartedly, written into the Party constitution at the Seventh Party Congress in 1945), an institutional design (people's democratic dictatorship) and a practical method (the mass line). On this basis they say the discourse defined the Party as a vanguard that represents the broadest people's interests, in contrast to what they portray as bourgeois parties serving particular interests. The authors conclude that Mao's system gave the discourse of socialism with Chinese characteristics its people-centred ideological base, its core topics and its principles of plain, popular expression. They present later leaders' formulations, including Xi Jinping's "people first", as inheriting and deepening it. They add that, in a setting where China's international discourse power is described as relatively weak, it offers resources for building a discourse system with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from a Mao Zedong Thought research centre, of how the concept of "the people" is used to link Mao's revolutionary theory to today's Party discourse.

Digital technology empowering primary-level Party building: advantages and pathways 数字技术赋能基层党建的优势及进路 Gao Qi Nie Hongna Gao Qi and Nie Hongna ask how big data, artificial intelligence and related technologies can be used to raise the quality of primary-level Party building, and what risks must be managed along the way. Their thesis is that digital technology offers three distinct advantages (integration, precision and interactivity), but that these are accompanied by five risks that call for deliberate countermeasures. The article, published in Theoretical Horizons in 2025, presents itself as offering theoretical grounds and practical reference for the digital transformation of grassroots Party organisations. The article opens by citing Xi Jinping's call for full online and offline coverage of Party organisations and several Party documents on primary-level Party building. It then moves in three steps: the technological advantages, the risks, and a set of corresponding remedies. The authors draw illustrations from cloud storage, integrated digital Party-building platforms, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection's 2015 anti-'four undesirable work styles' app, and VR and metaverse training. On advantages, the authors argue that integration breaks down hierarchical barriers to information sharing and converts resources into practical effectiveness. Precision shifts work from experience to data and from after-the-fact exposure of misconduct to early-warning systems. Interactivity turns one-way governance into interactive governance and enables immersive training. On risks, they identify a 'technology-first' tendency in which instrumental rationality displaces value rationality, digital formalism (such as compulsory app check-ins and 'digital traces'), data-security weaknesses linked to outsourced platforms, algorithmic bias and 'information cocoons', and digital divides, especially between urban and rural Party members. The remedies follow the risks. The authors call for embedding a people-centred value orientation in technology design, reforming assessment systems and the view of performance, and establishing tolerance-for-error and correction mechanisms. They also call for stronger data and system security, algorithmic ethics rules with monitoring and accountability, and tiered digital-skills training with long-term incentives for Party members and cadres. Digital tools, they stress, remain auxiliary to serving the masses and winning hearts. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how digitalisation of grassroots Party organisation is being justified and where its problems are officially acknowledged.

The ideological value of Party conduct building 党的作风建设的意识形态价值论析 Cao Jinlong Liu Jianjun Cao Jinlong and Liu Jianjun ask what ideological significance the Communist Party's work on its "style of conduct" (zuofeng jianshe) carries beyond its place in Party discipline. They argue that conduct building is part of ideological work as well as of Party building. In their view it has three kinds of ideological value: it shapes the Party's image, it expresses the Party's nature and purpose, and it helps guard against ideological risks. The article starts from the Party's long record of emphasising good conduct, including the practices of linking theory with practice, staying close to the masses, criticism and self-criticism, and plain living. It also covers the work since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, notably the Central Committee's eight-point regulations. The argument is organised in three parts: the direct value of image-building, the core value of reaffirming Party spirit and purpose, and the potential value of preventing risk. Historical examples include the contrast between "Yan'an style" and "Xi'an style", and a series of education campaigns since 2013. The authors' first move is to treat the Party's conduct as its image. They trace the shift in official wording from conduct "affecting" the Party's image to conduct "being" the image, and say that people judge the Party by the behaviour of its members. Where conduct matches ideological propaganda, they argue, ideology gains recognition and cohesion, and where it does not, trust is lost. Second, they follow Xi Jinping in holding that conduct problems are at root problems of Party spirit. They link such problems to a weakened commitment to the people's standpoint and say they damage the Party-masses relationship, which underpins the Party's legitimacy. Third, they list internal and external ideological risks, including "Westernisation", "colour revolution", social trends and digital platforms. They describe formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance as an especially dangerous internal risk. They argue that a disciplined Party is the precondition for resisting external ones as well. The authors conclude that conduct building is both a way of solving present problems and a pre-emptive move against future risks. They contend that the greater the risks and tasks on the path of building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the more conduct building must be strengthened. They say this would raise the cohesion and guiding force of socialist ideology. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-building scholars link discipline and conduct campaigns to the Party's legitimacy and ideological security.

Systematically constructing a long-term mechanism for Party conduct building 论党的作风建设长效机制的体系化建构 Wang Jianqin Writing after the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (October 2025), Wang Jianqin asks how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) can be made routine and lasting, and argues that a mature long-term mechanism has now taken shape. In Wang's account, the Eight-point Regulations adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012) served as the anchor that moved conduct building from 'frequent campaigns' to 'long-term governance'. The article presents this mechanism as an institutional guarantee for upholding the Party's overall leadership and for implementing the 15th Five-Year Plan. The article is organised around four components of the mechanism. These are the creation of Party regulations, the internalisation of values, the execution of rules, and supervision. Wang first traces how the Eight-point Regulations changed the way intra-Party regulations are drafted, then examines education and demonstration effects, then responsibility systems and monitoring, and finally the supervision system and its link to state supervision. Wang's central claim is that the Eight-point Regulations combined rigidity with effectiveness. They carried no 'trial' label, were framed around concrete problems, and were revised through a standing practice at the start of each Politburo term. Wang describes a 'small incision' drafting method, a 'core norm plus supporting rules' structure, and phased development from 2013 to 2027. On implementation, Wang stresses a 'dual-responsibility' arrangement. It pairs the 2019 trial regulations on responsibility for enforcing Party regulations with the regulations on Party committees' principal responsibility for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It is backed by five linked steps, including joint supervision and the 'one case, two investigations' accountability rule. Wang adds big-data monitoring that targets hidden variants of the 'four forms of decadence', and list-based governance. In supervision, the author argues that the Eight-point Regulations widened the scope of intra-Party oversight. They also helped align it with the national supervision reform through joint investigation of misconduct and corruption. Wang concludes that the mechanism has matured into an integrated whole, moving from treating symptoms to addressing root causes. In the author's view it shows the Party's historical consciousness in carrying out the Party's self-reform. Wang expects it to supply institutional support for the Party's leadership system, major national strategies, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and Chinese modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party discipline and conduct rules are designed, enforced and supervised, and how this work is justified institutionally.

New problems in building an intelligent society and ways to resolve them 智能社会建设面临的新问题及破解思路 Wang Wei Wang Wei asks how China can build an "intelligent society" (one organised around AI, the Internet of Things and blockchain) while managing the "growing pains" it brings. The article argues that this transition is a product of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Wang contends that it is strategically necessary, but that it generates ethical, social, security and governance risks. These, in Wang's view, call for a response built on the rule of law, people-centred priorities, multi-party governance and innovation. The article has three parts. The first sets out why an intelligent society matters, drawing on Marx's remark about the hand-mill and the steam-mill, Xi Jinping's statements and examples such as smart factories, urban command centres, online medical services and assistive technologies. The second catalogues problems under three headings: ethics (algorithmic bias, privacy leakage, the weakening of human agency through algorithmic substitution), social structure (structural unemployment, the gig economy, the digital divide) and security and governance (cyberattacks, deepfakes, lagging regulation, public distrust). The third proposes four pathways: top-level design, value orientation, governance mechanisms and innovation. Wang's central move is to treat these problems as technological alienation under unequal power relations rather than as neutral side effects. The author therefore calls for anti-monopoly enforcement, data-ownership rules and benefit-sharing, together with guarantees of people's rights to be informed, to choose and to opt out. Concrete proposals include tiered regulation with sandbox testing for high-risk fields and negative lists for low-risk ones, digital-literacy programmes, portable social-security accounts, a pilot of universal basic income and three-dimensional education reform. Governance, Wang argues, should rest on cooperation among government, enterprises, academia and the public, with ethics review built into research and an "ethics veto" for high-risk technologies. The author also stresses self-reliance in core technologies such as AI security, privacy computing and trustworthy blockchain. Wang concludes that intelligent technology should serve human liberation and all-round development, in line with Marx's vision of a community in which each person's free development is the condition for all. The article presents its proposals as consistent with Xi Jinping Thought and Chinese modernization, and as a way to ensure that intelligence benefits the people, social progress and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a policy-oriented Chinese Marxist account of AI governance, with specific institutional proposals and the official sources it cites.

Safeguarding and improving people's wellbeing in the course of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化进程中的民生保障和改善 Zhao Jiping Zhao Jiping asks how livelihood protection (minsheng) should be advanced in the coming Fifteenth Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030), after the achievements of the Fourteenth. Writing under the guidance of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), the author argues that safeguarding and improving people's wellbeing is both an essential expression of common prosperity and a yardstick of Chinese modernization's success. The article holds that this work needs forward-looking and systematic planning. The article first sets out why livelihood work matters to Chinese modernization. It then reviews Fourteenth Five-Year Plan results in education, employment and social security, citing official figures. Next it identifies challenges for the Fifteenth Five-Year Plan period: population ageing, low fertility, regional, urban–rural and group inequalities, and the effects of digital technology and artificial intelligence on jobs. It closes with four policy directions. Zhao presents livelihood work as the starting and ending point of Chinese modernization, a foundation of social stability and an engine of growth, because better livelihoods lift consumption and domestic demand and create new service markets. The review of achievements cites, among other figures, preschool gross enrolment of 92%, higher-education gross enrolment of 60.8%, 59.21 million new urban jobs, and basic pension insurance coverage above 95%. On challenges, the author stresses that 60-and-over residents reached 22.0% of the population by 2024, that public services remain unequal across regions and between town and country, and that automation may bring structural unemployment. Zhao proposes combining doing one's best (jinli'er wei) with acting within one's means (liangli'er xing), so that spending stays fiscally sustainable. Further proposals are a population service system covering all people and the whole life cycle, balanced policies to narrow urban–rural and regional gaps, and institution-building as the main line, so that livelihood protection is stable, predictable and systematic. Read the original if you want a Party-school overview of Fourteenth Five-Year Plan livelihood statistics and the policy agenda for the Fifteenth Five-Year Plan period.

The three perspectives on the concept of productive forces in Marx and Engels 马克思恩格斯生产力概念的三重视域 Zhang Lin Fu Guowei Marx and Engels never fixed a single definition of "productive forces", although the concept runs through their political economy, historical materialism and scientific socialism. Zhang Lin and Fu Guowei argue that the concept must be read in context, as a theoretical grasp of real material production rather than an abstract category. Their thesis is that three perspectives – political economy, historical materialism and scientific socialism – each use it differently, yet are united in the mission of interpreting and changing the world. The article takes each perspective in turn and then draws out lessons for the present. The first part covers the labour-productivity analysis in Capital and the 1857–61 manuscripts. The second covers the German Ideology and the 1859 Preface on the "sum of productive forces" and social revolution. The third covers the idea of "new productive forces" and the social nature of productive forces. A final section applies these ideas to new quality productive forces. In the political-economy perspective, the authors say, productive force is chiefly the productivity of labour. It governs the magnitude of commodity value and makes surplus labour and surplus value possible. Under capitalism it appears as the "productive power of capital", an expression of the alienation of workers from the forces they create. In the historical-materialist perspective, the sum of productive forces determines social conditions, and the contradiction with relations of production supplies the "productive-force basis" for revolution. This has a qualitative side (the relations become fetters) and a quantitative side (no formation perishes before it has exhausted its capacity). In the scientific-socialist perspective, Marx and Engels distinguish the quantity and quality of productive forces and hold that new forces arise within old modes of production. They also argue that capital obscures the social nature of productive forces, which communism would release. The authors draw three implications for developing new quality productive forces, which they present as a conceptual innovation on Marx and Engels. First, capital should be harnessed and regulated, with state-owned, private and "patient" capital each given a role under the basic socialist economic system. Second, further comprehensive deepening of reform is needed to build new relations of production in the economic, legal, ecological and cultural fields. Third, development should aim at people's free and all-round development, with shared outcomes and public ownership as the safeguard. Read the original if you want a close textual tracing of Marx and Engels on productive forces, and an example of how Party-school scholars connect it to current policy on new quality productive forces.

Marx's theory of artistic production and its contemporary value 马克思艺术生产论及其当代价值 Han Xiao Han Xiao asks what Marx's theory of artistic production says and what it offers to cultural work in China today. The article argues that the theory, first formulated with the concept of "artistic production" in the 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, matured together with historical materialism. In Han's account, it explains the relation between artistic and social production and the laws governing art, and it gives guidance for building a socialist culture with Chinese characteristics. The article first traces how the theory took shape. It starts from the 1844 manuscripts, where art is treated as a special mode of production, and moves to The German Ideology, where the division between material and mental labour yields two types of production. It then turns to the Introduction, where Marx sets out the uneven relation between material and artistic production. Han then examines the features of artistic production under capitalism and ends with three lessons for socialist art in the new era. Han's central move is to contrast two positions. In The German Ideology, material production has priority and shapes mental production. In the Introduction, Marx observes that art's flourishing is not proportionate to material development, and cites Greek epic and Shakespeare. Han explains this through early division of labour, the Greek orientation towards use-value, and the soil of myth, which disappears once nature is mastered. Han reads this as Marx's guard against economic determinism and as an illustration of the relative independence of social consciousness. Under capitalism, the author says, art is produced for profit, ruled by the law of value, and organised as a "mental production branch". Artists become wage-like producers, as in Marx's distinction between productive and unproductive labour. Art's own nature still resists capital's reifying rule. Han draws three implications for art in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Art must be grounded in material and economic development while balancing material and cultural-ethical progress. It must unite social and market value, with economic returns subordinate to social benefit, citing Xi Jinping. It must also follow the principle of "art for the people", which Han sets against art's subordination to capital. Han links the unevenness of material and artistic production to the principal contradiction of Chinese society as the article presents it. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Marx's Introduction on Greek art and uneven development, and how it is tied to current cultural policy.

Foucault and Marx: from Capital to the genealogy of power 福柯与马克思：从《资本论》到权力谱系学 Ouyang Qian Was Foucault a Marxist, an anti-Marxist, or something in between? Ouyang Qian takes up this long-contested question and argues that the answer should start from Foucault's own statements. The article focuses on Foucault's remark that his work on disciplinary power was guided by Volume II of Capital, which he called a genealogy of capitalism. Ouyang concludes that Foucault used Marx selectively and that the two thinkers' critiques of capitalism are complementary. The article first surveys Western views on the relationship, from claims that the two are unconnected to Jacques Bidet's reading of a relation both close and exclusionary, and Étienne Balibar's reading of Foucault's work as a confrontation with Marx. It then sets out the French intellectual context: the post-war prestige of Marxism, Sartre's "horizon", the structuralist turn, and the shock of May 1968. Next it examines what Foucault said about Marx, before comparing Capital Volume II with Foucault's analysis of power under three headings. It ends by applying both thinkers to digital capitalism. Ouyang argues that Foucault separated Marx from "Marxism", rejected economic determinism, the base–superstructure model and utopian teleology, and kept Marx's critique of political economy and historical analysis as a toolbox. Since Foucault never explained the debt to Volume II, Ouyang offers a tentative comparison. Capital's circulation corresponds to power as flow and network. Reproduction of capital corresponds to the reproduction of "docile bodies" and qualified subjects through disciplinary institutions. Circulation obstacles and crises correspond to the inevitability of resistance within power relations. In Ouyang's formulation, Marx deals with the power of the economy and Foucault with the economy of power, and Foucault preferred to cite Marx "secretly". Ouyang proposes combining the two: Marx's macro-level analysis of class and exploitation with Foucault's micro-level analysis of discipline and biopolitics. The article argues that this combination explains digital capitalism, where data serve as a factor of production and source of surplus value, platforms accumulate monopolistically, and algorithms act as invisible overseers of labour. It contends that both critiques remain valid while private ownership of the means of production, capital logic and unequal power relations persist. Read the original if you study Foucault's relation to Marx, or want a Chinese philosophical reading that links Capital Volume II to the analysis of power and digital capitalism.

How non-productive platforms take part in the distribution of surplus value 非生产性平台如何参与剩余价值分配 Lin Guangbin Xiong Youcheng Lin and Xiong ask how platform firms that do not directly produce material goods nevertheless earn large profits. Using the framework of Marxist political economy, they argue that only platforms whose digital labour is productive labour create surplus value, while "non-productive" platforms obtain income by redistributing value created elsewhere. That income, in their account, combines commercial profit with a new form of digital ground rent. The article first defines platforms, platform enterprises and the platform economy, and lists the benefits and risks usually attributed to them. It then divides platforms into productive types (industrial internet, B2B e-commerce, cloud and R&D platforms) and non-productive types (e-commerce and O2O, social and content, gig-economy platforms). It examines three kinds of digital labour: building information technology, providing digital services and producing digital commodities. It ends with a discussion of the contradictions this appropriation produces and with policy proposals. The authors argue that service platforms resemble merchant capital: they speed up circulation and share in industrial profit but create no new value. They reject the "audience commodity" thesis, holding that users' spontaneous data are by-products rather than purposive labour. Only data processed by hired workers into digital commodities carries surplus value. Drawing on Marx's theory of rent, they then say that platforms act as "virtual landlords": entry fees correspond to absolute rent, differences in platform efficiency to differential rent, and tiered or dynamic commission rates to monopoly rent. Such rent rests on separating data ownership from usufruct, on "data enclosure" through user agreements, and on two-sided lock-in and winner-take-all competition. Lin and Xiong say this appropriation brings wasteful competition, heavier burdens on producers and pressure on workers such as delivery riders. The authors also stress that the productive/non-productive division is a neutral economic description, and that real platforms are often hybrids. They propose limiting private monopoly over data, for example by requiring leading platforms to open non-core data interfaces. They also call for mandatory disclosure of commission structures, a multi-party regulatory framework, and a special fund drawn from rent-type income to improve social insurance for platform workers. Read the original if you want a Marxist rent-theory account of platform commissions, or a case against the "audience commodity" view of digital labour.

From "coping with virtual shocks" to "mastering the symbiosis of the virtual and the real": the social quasi-reality turn in ideological and political education 从“应对虚拟冲击”到“驾驭虚实共生”:思想政治教育之社会拟现实转向探究 Lu Lan Lu Lan asks how ideological and political education should respond as digital-intelligent technologies reshape human interaction and draw learners from physical into virtual space, a drift the article calls "spatial escape". The author proposes a "social quasi-reality turn" as a new concept and analytical framework. It would move the field from merely coping with virtual shocks to mastering a symbiosis of the virtual and the real. The article defines social quasi-reality, sets out why the turn is needed, and describes what it changes in practice. It places the concept against policy documents, including the national education digitalisation strategy launched in 2022 and the State Council's August 2025 opinions on the "AI Plus" initiative. Its sections cover the concept's structure and theoretical roots, the technological and disciplinary drivers of the turn, and the new educational scenes it makes possible. The author also lists the risks. Lu holds that social quasi-reality is a new reality nested inside existing society, not a copy of it. It is distinct from VR/AR "simulated reality", which reproduces the world as a digital scene. The author grounds it in Marxist practice theory and historical materialism and rejects Baudrillard-style "hyperreal" nihilism. The author argues that educators can neither intervene directly in real society nor in virtual society, so the quasi-reality layer is the interface where values become symbols, experience becomes narrative and contradictions become spectacle. Intervening at this layer would turn educators from passive responders into active architects. The author describes the resulting changes as multiple and virtual educational subjects, fragmented and customised content, a shift from authority-led transmission to intersubjective "meaning negotiation", and "liquid narrative" anchored by core socialist values. The author also names risks: algorithmic black boxes, the dilution of educators' discourse power, and the loss of critical reflection. Lu concludes that the aim is to strengthen the real with the virtual, not to replace it. Embodied presence and face-to-face emotional exchange remain irreplaceable, and moral education must stay at the centre of technological innovation. The author calls for embodied scenes, personalised AI-assisted provision, cross-disciplinary tools for tracking value shifts in virtual communities, and an autonomous knowledge system for ideological and political education. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars theorise digital technology, AI and ideological work, or how the field is being repositioned around the "AI Plus" policy.

Beyond the logic of capital: innovation and development in the people-centred path of new-type urbanization 超越资本逻辑：以人为本的新型城镇化道路的创新与发展 Yao Changcheng Yao Changcheng asks how China's people-centred new-type urbanization can avoid the urban crises of capitalist countries. The article argues that urbanization everywhere is driven by capital's general features, but that capital's specific character differs by ownership system. Under capitalism this produces an urbanization governed by the logic of capital, while under socialism with Chinese characteristics it produces one governed by a people's logic, in which the author sees an innovation in Marxist political economy. The article distinguishes "capital in general" (profit-seeking, motion, limitlessness) from "capital in particular" (the class content set by ownership relations). It uses Lefebvre's contrast between the use value and exchange value of space, plus David Harvey's "spatial fix" and Arghiri Emmanuel's unequal exchange. Cases include British, Japanese, Swedish, Spanish and Australian new towns and vacant housing, Japan's land-price bubble, and urbanization in Latin America and Southeast Asia. It ends with policy measures and lessons for developing countries. Yao's central claim is that capitalist urbanization lets exchange value swallow use value, favours "land urbanization" over "people's urbanization", and produces dormitory towns, "ghost cities" and bubbles. Unequal exchange between cities and countryside, arising from differences in the organic composition of capital and in wages, is said to reinforce the gap. In China, the author argues, state capital predominates, Party leadership amplifies capital's "people-oriented" character, and the principle "housing is for living in, not for speculation" restores use value. The contradiction between the two kinds of urbanization therefore remains but is not systemic and can be corrected through a "capable government" and an "effective market". Drawing on Lefebvre, Yao also says cities should move from "dominating space" to "appropriative space" guided by spatial justice. Yao proposes balanced urban–rural development, fair distribution within urban space, a shift from "utilizing" capital to "harnessing" it, steering finance towards county towns and the countryside, wider public-service provision, and regulated capital in urban renewal. The article presents four features of China's model as lessons for developing countries: multi-centre city clusters, institutionalised control of capital, urban–rural integration, and coordination with new-type industrialization. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy account of urbanization that applies Marx, Harvey and Lefebvre to China and contrasts it with capitalist and developing-world cases.

The free-time dimension of promoting common prosperity in spiritual life 促进精神生活共同富裕的自由时间向度 Li Mengyun Li Mengxi Li Mengyun and Li Mengxi ask how common prosperity in spiritual life, which they treat as an indispensable dimension of common prosperity, can be promoted through the category of free time. Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) formulation that Chinese modernization requires both material abundance and spiritual richness, they argue that existing studies of digital technology, culture and ideological education neglect time. Their thesis, drawing on Marx, is that spiritual prosperity depends on people having free time they can control, rather than on endless involution. The article first defines spiritual common prosperity as a state in which all people, through linked spiritual production, enjoyment and exchange, meet diverse spiritual needs and move towards free and all-round development. It then sets out three roles of free time in Marx's thought: restoring human essence, enabling all-round development, and driving a good life. Next it examines three mechanisms linking free time to spiritual prosperity, then three obstacles, and finally proposes remedies. The authors link free time to three elements of spiritual life: meeting multidimensional needs, ensuring full enjoyment of spiritual resources, and enabling deep spiritual exchange. They identify three obstacles. Under the logic of capital, time is alienated and spiritual needs shrink. Digital technology squeezes free time, citing a figure of 53.8% of urban young people working over 41 hours a week and “996” overtime, and induces involution. A culture of pan-entertainment turns free time into consumption time and leaves exchange shallow. Their remedies are to use artificial intelligence and new quality productive forces to cut necessary labour and raise spiritual production, while keeping a human-centred logic and preventing the capitalisation of AI. They also call for moderate labour combined with leisure, with individuals, firms and government acting together. The authors call for stronger working-time rules, including revising the Labour Law, limiting overtime, regulating paid leave, stricter labour inspection and a fuller social security system. They also propose public cultural provision, education that fosters a correct view of time and criticises “ineffective involution”, and AI-assisted online spaces for healthy spiritual exchange. They conclude that both the quantity and the quality of free time matter, and that wealth should be measured by free time rather than labour time. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical account of how free time, AI and overwork are being tied to the Party's goal of spiritual common prosperity, including concrete policy proposals.

The historical turn in Marx's view of morality: from value critique to practical generation 马克思道德观的历史转向:从价值批判到实践生成 Gu Qingqing The article takes up the dispute that began in Anglo-American scholarship in the 1970s over 'Marx and justice' and widened into a quarrel between moralist and non-moralist readings of Marx. Gu notes that Allen Wood and Richard Miller, among the analytical Marxists, treated Marx's theory as a pure science of history and so morally neutral. Gu replies that this view rests on fragmentary, ahistorical readings of isolated concepts. The author argues that Marx's moral outlook underwent a historical turn, developing in step with historical materialism, from abstract value judgement to a practical ethics. Gu traces this turn through four stages: an idealist view of morality in Marx's youth, a radical-liberal view, a revolutionary-humanist view, and finally a practical view of morality. Each stage is tied to texts and circumstances. The author discusses Marx's school essays, his work on the Rheinische Zeitung (the press-censorship and wood-theft debates), the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and finally the Communist Manifesto and Capital. In Gu's account, the early stages rest on Christian love, Enlightenment humanism, Kantian-Hegelian rationalism and Feuerbach's anthropology, and all of them judge society from an abstract standard of human nature or reason. Contact with material interests and political economy weakened that footing. Gu argues that from the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology onwards Marx treats morality as ideology, a product of material production and class position, and no longer as the foundation of society. In this account, Marx criticises moralising approaches that preach mutual love, and treats the aim of human emancipation as something that emerges from the contradictions of capitalist production, with the proletariat's revolutionary practice as its carrier. Gu concludes that the practical view of morality unites scientific and evaluative elements, class character and popular character, and realism and idealism. The author holds that it dissolves the moralist/non-moralist dispute, since Marx's ethics is neither Kantian deontology nor utilitarian consequentialism but a practical ethics inseparable from the working class's self-emancipation. Communist ethics, on this reading, is a necessary outcome of historical contradictions rather than a utopian postulate, and it offers a perspective on contemporary moral dilemmas. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-by-text periodisation of Marx's moral thought and a Chinese response to the analytical-Marxist debate on Marx and justice.

Spirit-building and image construction of the Communist Party of China in the Yan'an period 延安时期中国共产党的精神塑造与形象建构 He Husheng Cao Weiqing This research article asks how the Communist Party of China's spirit and its public image shaped each other in the Yan'an period (1935–48), and what that interaction means today. He and Cao argue that Party members under Mao Zedong's leadership developed the Yan'an spirit, and that this spirit was the inner core around which the Party built three images: a leadership image, a revolutionary image and an advanced image. They note that existing scholarship describes these images but rarely links them to the Yan'an spirit. The article has three main parts. The first treats the Yan'an spirit as the core and value guide of image-building, tracing its origins in model figures and in Mao's essays. The second examines the three images in turn. The third draws lessons for the Party's spiritual inheritance and image-building in the new era, including international communication. The authors draw on Mao, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Yan'an-period sources such as the Liberation Daily and the labour-model campaigns. The central claim is that a party's image is the practical form of its spirit. The authors say the Yan'an spirit grew from exemplars such as Norman Bethune, Zhang Side and the labour model Zhao Zhankui, then was condensed into four elements: a correct political direction, an ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, the fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and a self-reliant, hard-working pioneering spirit. The leadership image rested on the line of all-out resistance, Mao's theoretical works and his personal example in the production campaign. The revolutionary image rested on the Rectification Movement and self-criticism, which the authors present as the Party leading social revolution through self-reform. The advanced image rested on communist ideals joined to concrete goals, expressed in the proposition of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. The authors conclude that the new era should carry forward these practices in four ways. The Party should rely on its leading core, draw on exemplars, combine internal improvement with external perception, and build the image systematically. They add that the image depends on governing capacity, on serving the people's fundamental interests, and on interaction between the Party and the people. They also call for stronger research on the Party's spiritual lineage, use of digital media and a modern international communication system. Read the original if you study Yan'an-period Party history, or want to see how Chinese scholars link Party spirit to political image-building.

The theoretical content and global significance of the distinctive view of democracy embodied in Chinese modernization 中国式现代化蕴含独特民主观的理论内涵与世界意义 Wang Jing Wang Jing asks what distinguishes the view of democracy embodied in Chinese modernization from the liberal-democratic view that grew out of Western modernization, and why this matters beyond China. The article argues that because capital logic dominates Western modernization, liberal democracy functions as an ideology serving capital accumulation. In Wang's account, the Chinese view is a distinctive, people-centred view of democracy that surpasses it in theory and in practice and offers a model to late-developing countries. The article first reviews Western democratic theory: transition theorists, postmodern scholars and left-wing deliberative democrats. It judges them unable to transcend liberal democracy because they lack a grounding in democratic practice and do not grasp its capital logic. It then traces how liberal democracy took shape from Montesquieu, Locke and Rousseau to Schumpeter and Dahl, and sets out the Chinese view in terms of democratic values, subject, institutions, process and evaluation. It ends by discussing the view's global significance. Wang criticises four "myths" of Western liberal democracy. These are the property-rights myth, which subordinates democracy to the market; electoral supremacy, which reduces democracy to elite competition for votes; the history of democracy as a Western story that justifies "democracy export" and capital expansion; and the "end of history" meta-narrative. Against these, the author presents the Chinese view as grounded in historical materialism and the Two Integrations. It treats the people as the real political subject, relies on the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation and whole-process people's democracy, and judges democracy by whether people actually run their own affairs. Wang adds that liberal electoral systems have aggravated ethnic division and polarisation in late-developing states, whereas the Chinese approach links democracy with ethnic unity and the building of a sense of community of the Chinese nation. Wang concludes that the word "distinctive" does not imply exceptionalism. It marks a systematic difference between a people-centred and a capital-centred democracy, and a Chinese cultural subjectivity that the "Second Integration" establishes. The author claims that this democracy is more broadly, deeply and truly democratic, and that its universality comes from practice. It is therefore presented as a model for developing countries seeking their own paths. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of the official Chinese critique of Western liberal democracy and of how Chinese scholars frame the global claims of whole-process people's democracy.

The principled contribution of the common values of all humanity to the Marxist theory of value 全人类共同价值对马克思主义价值学说的原理性贡献 Chen Shuguang Chen Shuguang asks in what sense the common values of all humanity go beyond the Western claim to "universal values", and in what sense they develop the Marxist theory of value. The article argues that core values are always regional, national and historical, so no value model that transcends time and space exists. In Chen's account, the common values are a shared consensus across geographical and institutional boundaries, distinct from a supra-historical "value in general", and they make an original contribution to Marxist value theory. The article opens with a critique of Western "universal values" (freedom, democracy, human rights, equality, fraternity), tracing them from the Renaissance and Enlightenment. It then briefly argues that traditional Chinese ideals such as "great harmony under heaven" are also local and need modern transformation. Next it draws on Marx and Engels to expose the gap between bourgeois principles and practice. It turns to the Party's formulation of common values under Xi Jinping, and closes with three claimed theoretical advances. Chen's central claim is that Western "universal values" are a false universalism: a particular, capital-serving value system dressed in the form of universality, following Marx and Engels on how a rising class presents its interests as common. By contrast, the common values of peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom are described as a "true" universality that contains difference. Three advances are named. First, they combine value in general with value in particular, drawing a "concentric circle" between civilisations. Second, they separate value ideas from their forms of realisation, so that different countries may pursue different paths. Third, they separate ideological from human attributes: the common values stand for a human standpoint and are said to be only weakly ideological, whereas "universal values" express a capital standpoint and socialist core values a people's standpoint. Chen concludes that the common values and the core socialist values are two complementary pillars of the Marxist theory of value in the new era. The first provides a value base for a community with a shared future for mankind, and the second sets values for the nation. The author insists that advocating common values does not mean exporting China's system or ideology. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Party School scholar builds a Marxist case against "universal values" and for the Party's common-values concept, with extensive citation of Marx and Engels.

A critique of the ideological logic of cognitive capitalism 认知资本主义的意识形态逻辑批判 Deng Bojun Deng Bojun asks how ideology operates under "cognitive capitalism", a concept taken from the French scholar Yann Moulier-Boutang and used for a capitalism in which knowledge, information and data replace material resources as the main means of production. Deng's thesis is that its ideology has shifted from visible repression to hidden production: capital no longer coerces workers from outside but makes them "voluntarily" accept domination. In this reading it remains, in essence, the dictatorship of the bourgeoisie in a new form. The article first contrasts industrial and cognitive capitalism, then traces a lineage of ideology critique from Marx and Engels' "false consciousness" through Althusser's ideological state apparatuses to Foucault's technologies of the self. It then examines how the ideology is generated: the new form of the means of production (data, algorithms, intellectual property), changed labour forms such as "immaterial labour" and "play labour", and the role of knowledge production, algorithms and platforms. It goes on to "colonisation" in the economic, political and cultural spheres, and ends with strategies of resistance. Deng's central claim is that the non-rival nature of data forces its monopolisation to be dressed in a rhetoric of knowledge sharing and liberation. Platforms, algorithmic management, user agreements and a "knowledge–power–capital" alliance with academia and the state then turn exploitation into self-exploitation. Deng treats algorithmic rent as surplus value from appropriated "general intelligence", producing real subsumption of cognitive production. The article describes platforms as "digital landlords" and creators as "digital tenants", and presents the new ideology as the "de-ideologisation of ideology", in which capital's logic appears as natural common sense. Deng proposes a systematic "decolonisation" of the cognitive sphere. Its elements are public ownership of data, democratised algorithms, open collaboration, digital unions and cognitive-labour cooperatives. Legal measures include knowledge-commons legislation, cognitive-labour rights and rules for platform power. Technical proposals include decentralised data, algorithm and platform governance, plus cross-border cooperation against tax arbitrage and infrastructure monopolies. Deng frames this as proletarian class struggle in the cognitive domain, aimed at seizing control of cognitive means of production and moving toward socialism and communism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of data, algorithms and platforms that combines Marx, Althusser, Foucault and Heidegger with concrete legal and technical proposals.

Mao Zedong's initiation of the Party's cultural leadership: a historical examination and its present-day implications 毛泽东开启党的文化领导权的历史考察与现实启示 Shu Jin Shu Jin asks how the Chinese Communist Party came to establish its cultural leadership, and what that history means today. The article argues that Mao Zedong, in both a historical and a logical sense, opened up the proposition of the "Party's cultural leadership", defined as the Party's authority over ideological work, management and discourse. It contends that this proposition answered the question "Where is China heading?" and the dispute over ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, and that it underlies Xi Jinping's present emphasis on upholding that leadership. The article first sets out the theoretical sources of the proposition: historical materialism, Engels's late account of the superstructure's relative independence, and Lenin's view of the proletarian party's cultural force and of writing as a "cog and screw". It then traces the historical background of modern China's semi-colonial position and Mao's New Democratic cultural programme of 1940. Next it turns to practice: the Yan'an Rectification Movement, the 1942 Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art, intellectuals, and Party newspapers and propaganda work. The final sections draw lessons for the present. Shu's central claim is that the proposition arose from both theory and revolutionary need. In the author's account, Mao showed that the bourgeoisie could no longer lead the new culture after the May Fourth Movement, so that leadership fell to proletarian ideas, exercised through the Party. Mao then made this concrete by establishing Marxism's guiding position through its adaptation to Chinese conditions, with Mao Zedong Thought written into the Party constitution in 1945. He also united intellectuals with workers, peasants and soldiers, and applied the mass line to propaganda. Shu presents these steps as turning an earlier passive response to the "ancient–modern, Chinese–Western" dispute into active leadership. Shu concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Culture continues this line and that the Party's cultural leadership must be upheld as the political guarantee of cultural work. The author calls for balancing Party spirit with the people's character, and for the Two Integrations, especially the second, to settle the old dispute, in service of Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Shu stresses that consolidating this leadership is a long and arduous task. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-historical account of how Mao's cultural programme is linked to Xi-era cultural doctrine.

The War of Resistance against Japan and the theoretical foundation of the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 抗日战争与马克思主义中国化第一次历史性飞跃的理论奠基 Tian Keqin Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (1931–1945), this article asks how the war and the Chinese Communist Party's adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions shaped each other. Tian argues that the war posed objective demands that pushed the Party to apply Marxist principles to China's concrete realities. In the author's account, this laid the ideological and theoretical groundwork for victory in the war and, ultimately, in the New Democratic Revolution. The article is organised around what it calls three basic questions of the Chinese revolution: the united front, armed struggle and Party building. It then turns to how the Party's understanding of the New Democratic Revolution deepened. The narrative runs from the Mukden Incident and the Xi'an Incident to the formation of the second Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, the Zunyi and Wayaobao meetings, and the Yan'an period. Tian draws heavily on Mao Zedong's writings of the late 1930s and early 1940s. Tian makes three main moves. First, the Party built a Sinified theory of the united front, summarised in six regularities: the national bourgeoisie can join for a time, the content of the front changes, some comprador groups may be allied with, the big bourgeoisie must be restricted, and the worker–peasant alliance and the petty bourgeoisie are the base. Second, Mao's protracted-war strategy, the three stages of the war, and the strategic status of guerrilla warfare developed Marxist theory on armed struggle into a doctrine of people's war. Third, the Party formally put forward the proposition of Sinifying Marxism, and the rectification movement fixed seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance as basic stances. Mao's analysis of China as a colonial, semi-colonial and semi-feudal society then underpinned the concept of New Democracy as a transitional stage between that society and socialism. Tian concludes that the war proved Marxism to be a powerful intellectual weapon for the Chinese people, and that the Party developed itself while upholding the national cause. The article ties this to the present, urging continued Integration of Marxist principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a Party-historiographical account of how the wartime period is presented as the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context.

Artificial intelligence and the realisation of general intellect 人工智能与一般智力的实现 Chen Junkun Chen Junkun asks how Marx's concept of "general intellect" (一般智力), set out in the 1857–58 manuscripts, can help in understanding artificial intelligence. The article argues that AI is the contemporary objectified form of general intellect. In Chen's reading, it sublates the natural-intelligence form of general intellect and creates a potential bridge between human and machine intelligence. This, Chen holds, should be the starting point for thinking about the relation between the two. The article begins with the "Fixed capital and the development of the productive forces of society" section of the manuscripts. It criticises existing debates, including the Italian autonomist and cognitive-capitalism readings and Paolo Virno's, for neglecting the critique of capitalism and for treating machinery as a mere instrument. It then reconstructs three dimensions of general intellect in Marx. It next turns to AI: the contradiction in the term "artificial intelligence", the traditional division between humans and things, and the challenges facing that division. Chen argues that for Marx general intellect is objectified, "living" knowledge. It is general, in the sense of being universally applicable, because of historical accumulation of social knowledge. It takes independent form in the automatic machine system. Marx's real concern, Chen stresses, is its capitalist application as fixed capital, which produces labour's real subordination to capital while also undermining capitalism's own basis. Chen reads AI's advance as dissolving the worldview that sharply separates human and thing, since intelligence no longer belongs only to humans and AI may become a potential subject. Two obstacles remain: the embodiment of human intelligence, which ties into the human appropriation of things, and capitalist applications of AI, which reinforce the opposition. Under capitalism, shortened necessary labour time extends relative surplus-value time; under socialism, Chen says, it can become free time for all-round human development. Chen concludes that in the near term human and artificial intelligence will probably stay different, each ahead in some domains. Drawing on the Chinese Room argument, Chen cautions that intelligent behaviour does not necessarily mean AI possesses general intellect, and that calling AI another subject may be premature. Chen nonetheless holds that human–machine interaction shows "intersubjectivity" and a relation of symbiosis. Chen calls for a worldview that moves beyond the strict human/thing divide, towards human–machine symbiosis and mutual benefit. Read the original if you want a close reading of Marx's "general intellect" applied to generative AI and to the philosophical question of human and thing.

A historical-materialist reflection on the development of artificial intelligence 人工智能发展的历史唯物主义审思 Lan Yang Lan Yang asks how artificial intelligence (AI) should be understood, steered and socially managed, taking as the starting point Xi Jinping's remark of April 2025 that AI is a strategic technology that deeply changes how people live and produce. The article argues that historical materialism's "dual-scale" theory of technology, a material scale and a scale of human relations, offers the key to this question. Lan contends that, on this basis, AI can be developed so that its economic, social and ethical value are united. The article first reconstructs Marx's account of technology. It then applies the two scales to AI in turn: AI as a breakthrough in productive forces, and AI as a new confirmation of humanity's essential powers. It then looks at the opportunities and risks arising from the unity of the two scales, contrasts capitalist and socialist institutional settings, and closes with three practical directions: following the material scale, following the scale of human relations, and making use of socialist institutions. On the material scale, Lan argues that AI is continuous with Marx's "machine" and extends accumulated technique. It also marks a leap that improves labourers, means of labour and objects of labour and the way they combine. On the scale of human relations, AI is distinctive because it simulates mental labour, supplies momentum for restructuring relations of production through data, and may reduce socially necessary labour time and help sublate alienated labour. Following Marx, Lan holds that technology does not by itself bring about free and all-round human development. Under capitalist private ownership, the author argues, AI fuses with digital monopoly and capital logic, producing algorithmic surveillance, structural unemployment and polarisation. Under socialism, in Lan's account, public ownership as the mainstay, the steering of capital and a people-centred orientation bring AI into line with common prosperity. Lan calls for training composite talent and human–machine cooperation, developing new intelligent tools and expanding data as an object of labour. The article also rejects both technological omnipotence and romantic technophobia, and insists that AI is a simulated intelligence that extends human brainpower. It further calls for law, ethics and governance, macro-regulation against monopoly, a unified market and employment-friendly policy and social security. The author concludes that overcoming the capitalist application of technology and sublating technological alienation constitute the world-historical significance of developing AI under socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist theorist uses Marx's view of technology to frame AI governance and policy in Chinese official terms.

The inner logic of the intelligent society, a community with a shared future for mankind, and a new form of human civilization 智能社会、人类命运共同体与人类文明新形态的内在逻辑 Wang Shuixing Wang Shuixing asks how artificial intelligence, a community with a shared future for mankind and a new form of human civilization are related, and what the AI era means for the future of humanity. Drawing on the materialist conception of history, Wang argues that AI itself and its application are two different things. Applied under the logic of capital, AI may create existential risks. Applied under socialism, it can help build a true intelligent society and a new form of human civilization. The three, Wang claims, shape one another. The article first distinguishes two possible paths for the intelligent society in a world of 'one globe, two systems'. It examines digital capitalism through Marx's notions of living labour, the 'illusory community' and the 'civilization of capital'. It then sets out the socialist alternative, the 'civilization of labour' and Marx's 'real community'. The final sections turn to China: AI governance initiatives, data sharing, computing power, algorithms, and the treatment of capital under Chinese modernization. Wang's central claim is that AI cannot replace living labour as the source of surplus value. Capitalist use of AI therefore changes the form of exploitation, not its essence, and produces more 'superfluous people', social division and a gap between production and consumption. Only a society based on public ownership of data, computing power and means of production, with algorithms that carry the people's collective will, can qualify as truly 'intelligent'. AI can then free people from alienated labour and give them free time, so that labour becomes a first necessity of life. In this reading, the new form of human civilization is one in which the logic of labour dominates the logic of capital. Wang concludes that AI is a 'historical lever' that can lift human civilization, but only within a community with a shared future for mankind. The author does not expect a worldwide socialist revolution to follow automatically. Capital and labour will keep contesting for a long time, so a system for governing capital, including intelligent capital, is needed. Countries should also be free to choose AI policies suited to their level of development. Wang presents China's AI initiatives and 'AI+' cooperation as practical steps towards this goal. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical case, from within Chinese academia, for linking AI, the community with a shared future and civilizational change.

How is Marx's critique of fetishism possible? 马克思的拜物教批判何以可能 Liu Zhaofeng Liu Zhaofeng takes up a question about Marx's critique of fetishism that, in the author's view, Chinese scholarship has neglected: what exactly the critique targets, why Marx arrived at it, and under what conditions and with what mode of thinking it became possible. The article argues that the critique has two objects: the fetish character of commodities, money and capital, and fetishist ideas about them. It holds that these ideas are a specific kind of misrecognition, not 'worship' and not psychoanalytic 'fetishism'. The article opens with a short review of Chinese research and its shortcomings, then clarifies the concepts. It criticises early Chinese readings, including Chen Duxiu's 1923 lecture and 1930s writers, that treat fetishism as worship, and Jean Baudrillard's psychoanalytic reading in his critique of the political economy of the sign. It then traces Marx's path from the Rheinische Zeitung through the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right to The German Ideology. Next it examines the historical conditions for unmasking fetishism, and finally the 'Trinity Formula' as a case study of fetishist thinking. Liu's central claim is that the fetish character of commodity production exists wherever commodities are produced, but it can only be exposed once commodity production has become general under capitalism. By comparison, the author notes, corvée labour makes exploitation visible, while wage labour presents unpaid labour as paid. Marx's distinctive method is to keep historical self-awareness and to separate the material elements of production from their social forms. With this method he shows that value, money and capital forms are specific and historically transient. Liu reads the Trinity Formula (capital–interest, land–rent, labour–wages) as the concentrated case of fetishist ideas, because it confuses material elements with social forms and makes the capitalist mode of production seem eternal. The author attributes this confusion to the empiricism of bourgeois economists and, more deeply, to their bourgeois standpoint. Liu concludes that taking up the critique of fetishism follows from the internal logic of historical materialism, since only this critique can reveal the secret of capitalist production. Researchers should avoid equating fetishism with worship or object-love. Mastering Marx's critique, and clearly distinguishing material elements from social forms, is presented as the way to avoid fetishist ideas and keep historical awareness. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of the conceptual and methodological preconditions of Marx's fetishism theory, especially its use of Capital and its manuscripts, and a critique of the 'worship' reading in Chinese scholarship.

The civilisational implications of building a community with a shared future for mankind and the path to realising it 构建人类命运共同体的文明意蕴及践行理路 Liu Yang Drawing on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, Liu Yang asks what the idea of building a community with a shared future for mankind means for the course of human civilisation. The article argues that the idea is not only a framework for global governance but a plan to move beyond Western-centric modern civilisation and to rethink 21st-century civilisational development as a whole. Liu holds that it answers the question of what kind of world to build and how to build it. The article has two main parts. The first explains why the idea arose, through three 'changes' (changes in the world, in the era and in history) and through its two intellectual sources: Marx's thought on civilisation and the conception of civilisation in traditional Chinese culture, joined by the Two Integrations. The second sets the idea against what Liu calls the defects of Western civilisation, then lays out five practical tasks tied to the four global initiatives (on development, security, civilisation and governance). Liu's central claim is that Western civilisation, driven by capital, is 'deconstructive', 'universalist', 'single-dimensional', 'hierarchical' and 'short-sighted'. Against this, the community with a shared future is said to offer a constructive view of civilisation, common values of all humanity in place of 'universal values', a balanced view of economic, political, cultural, social and ecological development, and equal, consultative relations between states. Liu reads this as a sublation of Western economic rationality, and presents the 'end of history' thesis as having failed amid current crises. The practical path has five parts: a community of ideas built on shared values, a development community that corrects the unequal global division of labour, a security community with a new security outlook, an ecological community based on 'common but differentiated' responsibility, and a cooperation community in which power shifts from Western dominance toward 'multi-party co-governance' with a stronger Global South. Liu concludes that the idea redraws the future of world civilisation and offers new choices and Chinese wisdom for overcoming civilisational difficulties. It presents the idea as part of creating a new form of human civilisation and as a step toward the Marxist ideal of an 'association of free individuals'. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars link Xi Jinping's foreign-policy concepts to Marxist civilisation theory and to a critique of the West.

The civilizational narrative and political-cultural logic of building the Chinese national community 华民族共同体建设的文明叙事与政治文化逻辑 An Beijiang An Beijiang asks what historical and cultural foundations, and what practical logic, underlie the current policy of building the Chinese national community (Zhonghua minzu gongtongti jianshe). The author notes that existing research approaches the topic from many angles but rarely addresses its historical-cultural meaning. The article's thesis is that this project rests on the idea of grand unification, takes cultural identity as its core, uses exchanges, interaction and integration among ethnic groups as its practical path, and draws on cultural empowerment as its source of innovation. The article opens with the Confucian-era "all under heaven" outlook and its development into the doctrine of grand unification (da yitong), traced from the Zhou, the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods through the Qin-Han, Tang, Yuan and Qing dynasties. It then treats cultural identity, citing non-Han dynasties' claims to legitimacy and their adoption of Confucianism. A third section sets out Marxist theories of the nation, from Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin, and reviews the history of ethnic interaction, including migration, frontier settlement and trade. The last section turns to present-day measures. An argues that grand unification was never simply territorial expansion. In the author's account it combined institutional innovation (commanderies and counties, the examination system, flexible frontier arrangements) with ideological integration. Because rulers of non-Han origin also claimed the mantle of "China", political consensus formed around shared cultural standards rather than lineage. The author presents the community as the product of long interaction that produced a "pluralistic yet unified" pattern. They also present the current term "exchanges, interaction and integration" as the Marxist theory of ethnic fusion combined with the Chinese idea of harmony, and as distinct from assimilation. For the present, An proposes a socialist core values-led consensus, the retelling of historical narratives around the pluralistic-unified pattern, the exploration of shared cultural resources, and the building of mutually embedded social structures and communities. The author also calls for a move from "physical superposition" to "chemical reaction", and for opposing narrow nationalism. The author concludes that the approach offers a Chinese solution for governing multi-ethnic states and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account that links imperial-era unification thought, Marxist nation theory and current ethnic policy.

Building a strong cultural self for contemporary China 构建当代中国强大的文化自我 Shen Xiangping Shen Xiangping takes up a concept he reads out of Xi Jinping's thought on culture: the "cultural self", meaning a nation's firm self in the cultural sense. He argues that the new cultural mission of the new era, namely promoting cultural prosperity and building a strong cultural nation, amounts to building a strong cultural self for contemporary China. In his view this is the fundamental task of cultural construction today. It then takes each of the five questions in turn, relating them to the Two Integrations and to Xi's wider strategic framework. Shen's central claim is that cultural subjectivity is the foundation of the cultural self. In his account, the Communist Party rebuilt it in modern form after it had nearly been lost, and consolidated it through the Two Integrations, above all the second. Contemporary Chinese culture, he says, is a "new cultural life-form" whose lifeblood is Marxism as its soul, excellent traditional Chinese culture as its root, and present-day practice as its vitality. Its essence is socialism with Chinese characteristics under Party leadership. Its core is Chinese values: core socialist values, common values of all humanity, and the primacy of the people. Shen presents it as a culture at "the height of principle", citing Marx, with the free and all-round development of the person as its aim, in contrast to a Western modernity he characterises as capital-centred. Shen proposes that confirming the cultural self in practice follows the "7+1" requirements Xi set out. He highlights four tasks: strengthening cultural identity across ethnic groups, stimulating cultural creativity through information technology and AI, raising soft power through opening up while insisting on China's own discourse, and keeping the person at the centre of cultural work. He ends by calling for long-term mechanisms in institutions, policy, talent and evaluation. Read the original if you want a detailed look at how Chinese philosophers systematise Xi Jinping's cultural thought around the concepts of cultural subjectivity and the cultural self.

Artificial intelligence and the transformation of teaching paradigms in ideological and political education 人工智能赋能思想政治教育教学范式变革 Yuan Ke Huang Tenglong This newspaper commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2026, asks how artificial intelligence (AI) can drive a systematic change in the teaching paradigm of ideological and political education. In Yuan and Huang's account, platforms, virtual simulations and case libraries have eased the limits of time, space and uniform supply in traditional teaching, but problems remain: fragmented applications, content that does not match needs, and weak institutional links. They call for a system of technology, content and mechanisms, with the leading role of value guidance combined with students' and teachers' actual needs. Read the original if you want a concise view of how official policy language frames AI in Chinese university ideological and political courses.

Promoting the effective integration of the ideological and political classroom and the social classroom 促进思政课堂和社会课堂有效融合 Wang Jindong This newspaper commentary takes up a call in the proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan, adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), to integrate the ideological and political classroom with the social classroom. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-line ideological education policy is justified and operationalised in universities.

Governing the country through planning: an institutional guarantee for advancing Chinese modernization 规划治国：推进中国式现代化的制度保障 Tang Yalin Writing after the National People's Congress passed the National Development Planning Law on 12 March 2026, Tang Yalin argues that "governing the country through planning" is the dynamic mechanism that moves Chinese modernization forward step by step.
