Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars present the Five-Year Plan as an institutional system and as a model with wider relevance.

The new development model underpins the building of a strong economy 新发展模式支撑经济强国建设 Chi Fulin Chi Fulin takes up the 15th Five-Year Plan outline's call for more growth models led by domestic demand, driven by consumption and based on endogenous growth. Chi's core argument rests on the claim that strong economies draw on domestic demand, especially consumption. Chi concludes that the next five to ten years are a historic window for economic transformation. Domestic reform and high-level opening up are presented as mutually reinforcing, and Chi links imports and services trade to China's influence in setting global trade rules. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese reform-minded economist, writing in the Party's leading economic daily, turns the 15th Five-Year Plan's domestic-demand agenda into specific targets and policy proposals.

Strengthening the scholarly foundations to release the educational vitality of ideological and political courses 厚植学理根基，释放思政课育人活力 Feng Xiujun Writing in Guangming Daily, Feng Xiujun, dean of the School of Marxism at Renmin University of China, asks how ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) in schools and universities can meet the new demand for "connotative development". Feng argues that this development depends on winning by quality and persuading through reasoning, and that both rest on deeper theoretical and teaching research. Feng presents the courses as combining politics, ideology, scholarship and professional skill, and as requiring a unity of "the way", "learning" and "technique". Feng wants each to be converted into the next, and research on how the Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought course relates to other courses, and across undergraduate, master's and doctoral stages. On teaching, Feng says the notion that pedagogical research is not scholarship must be overcome. The author proposes studying students' thinking, using AI-based learning data, and mastering the shift from knowing to believing to acting, so that abstract theory becomes concrete narrative in youth-friendly language. Feng concludes that the courses' persuasive power comes from rigorous research at all three levels, and that this is what will move teaching from supplying content to shaping values. The author also calls for the courses to adopt digital and intelligent technologies, combining case-based, inquiry-based and experiential teaching. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Marxist-studies administrator links theory, textbook and pedagogical research in ideological and political education.

How to better explain theory to young people 如何更好地把理论讲给青年听 Yanhe Lecturers' Group, Renmin University of China This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 17 March 2026, is written by Renmin University of China's "Yanhe Lecturers' Group", a student-led theory outreach team. It asks how the Party's innovative theory can be presented in ways that suit young people's habits of thought and reception. The authors argue that youth, as a generation that grew up with the internet, resist rigid preaching but want vivid ideas, and that young lecturers have a distinct advantage in speaking to their peers. It is organised around three problems the group says it has tried to solve: the gap between theoretical discourse and young people's lives, the competition for attention in the modern media environment, and the mismatch between uniform supply and varied audiences. The group therefore links the plenum's decisions to real issues and uses a chain of theory point, real-life scene, case and action implication, with everyday phrasing such as ecological civilization being a "grand chorus" rather than the government's "solo". On the second, it combines online booking platforms with on-site lectures, and ties talks to grassroots Party and Youth League meetings so that a single talk becomes regular study. The authors conclude that accuracy and depth must be combined with lively expression, flexible organisation and precise targeting if the popularisation of theory is to persuade and take root. Read the original if you want a short, practice-based example of how Party-sponsored student lecture teams describe their methods for youth theory outreach.

Better realising the strategic guiding role of national development plans on the track of the rule of law 在法治轨道上更好发挥国家发展规划的战略导向作用 Li Yuju Chen Zhichao This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 17 March 2026, discusses the Law of the People's Republic of China on National Development Planning, adopted at the fourth session of the 14th National People's Congress. Li and Chen argue that the law is a milestone: it puts a long-standing governing method of the Party on a legal footing and, in their words, uses the stability of law to meet external uncertainty. They present it as an institutional guarantee for scientific plan-making and effective implementation as the 15th Five-Year Plan period begins. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the law is urgently needed for the modernization of state governance. The second explains the law's basic spirit and main provisions. The third turns to practical requirements for putting the law into effect. It leans throughout on quotations from Xi Jinping on planning, the rule of law and the socialist market economy. On the need for the law, the authors give three reasons: it advances the construction of a law-based China, it improves the socialist market economy by giving firms stable expectations and drawing limits around government powers in planning, and it strengthens macroeconomic governance by keeping national goals from being diluted by administrative level or local interests. For implementation, the authors call for annual plans and all other plans to be linked to the national plan, with binding targets broken down year by year. They also call for consistency checks on fiscal, monetary, industrial and other policies, and for funds, land, credit and data to follow major projects, while projects that diverge from the plan are denied approval. They further urge local plans to follow higher-level ones, and full-cycle monitoring, mid-term and final evaluation, and accountability for formalism, illegal approvals and vanity projects. Creating a sound rule-of-law environment to promote high-quality development 为推动高质量发展营造良好法治环境 Feng Lixia Writing in the People's Daily (13 March 2026), Feng Lixia takes up how law can support high-quality development. The commentary opens by noting that the Fourth Session of the 14th National People's Congress had just passed three laws at once: the Ecological Environment Code, the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, and the National Development Planning Law. Feng's thesis is that the socialist market economy is in essence a "law-based economy", and that building one is the way to create a good rule-of-law environment for high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the socialist market economy is a law-based economy, drawing on Xi Jinping's statements from 2014 to 2024. The second follows the rule of law through four links of economic circulation: production, distribution, circulation and consumption. The third sets out practical paths for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030), organised around legislation, law enforcement, the judiciary and law-abidingness. Feng argues that markets operate through legal forms, so a socialist market economy needs law to protect property, secure fair competition and keep the economy circulating. Building a law-based economy depends on combining an "effective market" with a "capable government". Feng reads this as a government that does what the law requires and nothing the law has not authorised, and that uses law to mark the boundary between government and market. Feng adds that improving the business environment means unified market rules, enforcement standards and judicial criteria, and clearing away local rules that obstruct a unified national market. For each link of the economy Feng gives legal tasks: equal protection of property, including the Private Economy Promotion Law in force since 20 May 2025; distribution rules covering all three distributions; credit systems and action against local protectionism in circulation; and consumer-rights protection. For the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Feng calls for higher-quality legislation in key, emerging and foreign-related fields, to support new quality productive forces. Feng also calls for service-oriented, standardised enforcement, and for the judiciary to avoid treating economic disputes as crimes. Feng also wants the Fengqiao experience developed in dispute mediation, and a culture of compliance and good faith among firms. Feng presents this as both a practical route to balancing development and security and a long-term task for modernising national governance by 2035. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary links Xi Jinping's economic thought and legal thought, and how it frames law for market regulation, property protection and enforcement.

How to combine strict management with care and balance incentives with constraints 怎样做到严管厚爱结合、激励约束并重 Wang Ruijun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts, Wang Ruijun takes up a line from the Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025): combine strict management with loving care, and give equal weight to incentives and constraints, so as to stimulate the endogenous drive and overall vitality of the cadre corps. Wang argues that strictness and care are not opposites but a single unity, and that the 15th Five-Year Plan period requires cadres who dare to take responsibility and know how to deliver. The article has three parts. It first describes the challenges facing cadres in the new era and the problems Wang sees in the cadre corps. It then explains why strict supervision and encouragement of initiative are organically unified. It closes with four practical areas of work for Party committees and organisation departments: Party-spirit training, incentives and care, enforcement of rules, and motivating cadres to act. Wang names several problems: formalism and bureaucratism, a lack of capability, passive attitudes of "doing less so as to err less", and a minority who treat strict constraint as an excuse for inaction. The causes lie in distorted views of political achievement, weak skills, and inadequate systems that do not coordinate material, spiritual and promotion incentives. Wang also calls for a performance-and-merit approach to appointments, support for grassroots cadres, lighter formalistic burdens, and checks on "top leaders" through power, responsibility and negative lists. Cadres should also be assessed on livelihoods, ecology and public satisfaction, and be led to build new quality productive forces and pursue high-quality development. Read the original if you want a representative example of current Party-building discourse on cadre management, including its institutional measures and official vocabulary.

Understanding the major significance of "upholding the organic unity of governing the country by law and governing the Party by regulations" 深刻理解“坚持依法治国和依规治党有机统一”的重大意义 Zhou Yezhong This article from Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 24) explains why Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law treats the organic unity of governing the country by law and governing the Party by regulations as a core principle. Zhou Yezhong argues that the principle is a theoretical innovation that sets Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law apart from Western legal theory. It is now listed as the "twelfth upholding" in the 2025 edition of the Study Outline on that thought. The article has four sections. The first presents the principle as a core element of Xi's legal thought. The second presents it as a distinctive strength of "governance by the Communist Party of China" and of "Chinese governance". The third treats it as a practical way to address problems specific to a large party and a large country. The fourth presents it as China's contribution to the rule-of-law civilisation of humankind. Zhou's central claim is that the principle joins political logic and legal logic. Placing Party-regulation governance alongside state-law governance, in Zhou's account, brings both governing the Party and governing the country onto a legal track. The result is a "grand rule of law" with both Party rules and state law. Zhou sets this against Western theory's habit of treating law and political parties as relatively separate. Zhou also links the principle to the "two answers" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Law-based governance gives practical force to the first answer, popular supervision of government. Regulation-based Party governance is described as the legal instrument for the second, the Party's self-reform. Zhou adds that it addresses the "unique problems of a large party" and the governance problems of a large country. Zhou concludes that the principle gives world party governance a legalised path built on intra-Party regulations. These emphasise duties that come before rights, self-discipline, and Party discipline stricter than state law. In Zhou's view it also offers non-Western countries experience in exploring their own legal paths. It further shows that Party and law are mutually reinforcing, not opposed. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party-theory case for combining Party regulations with state law, and of how it is contrasted with Western legal thought.

Why strict supervision and enforcement of discipline is a sharp tool of the Party's self-reform 从严监督执纪为什么是党的自我革命的利器 Cai Jue This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the 21st collective study session of the Political Bureau that strict supervision and enforcement of discipline is a "sharp tool" of the Party's self-reform. The piece, written by Cai Jue for a university research centre on the Party's innovative theory, argues that supervision and discipline are what keep the fight against corruption from becoming a formality. In its account, they are essential to ensuring that the Party never degenerates in character. The article has three parts. The first sets out why strict supervision and discipline matter, the second identifies their core requirements, and the third proposes practical paths. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on the record of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the first part, the author gives three reasons. Strict discipline is said to be needed to preserve the Party's vanguard character and purity. It is also described as the key to winning popular trust, and as a guarantee of long-term governance and Chinese modernization. The second part sets three requirements: strictness across the board and to the end, catching problems early and keeping supervision regular and lasting, and strict enforcement with every violation investigated. The author treats the "four forms" of supervision and discipline as the means of applying this. The third part is the most practical. It calls for tackling Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together, with ideological education, the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and regular discipline education. It also calls for linking the Party's internal supervision with external forms such as people's congresses, audit and public opinion, with special focus on the "key minority" of leading cadres. It further proposes investigating and handling misconduct and corruption together, since the author treats them as sharing one root. Finally, it asks for a disciplined inspection and supervision force that is itself subject to the strictest constraint. Cai concludes that the depth of the Party's self-reform depends directly on how effective strict supervision and discipline are. The author calls for keeping up this strictness, presented as a permanent task, against complacency and against any expectation that the campaign will ease. The text is a Party-theory commentary rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register account of how current Party discourse links discipline, supervision and anti-corruption to the idea of self-reform.

A powerful domestic market as the strategic support of Chinese modernization 强大国内市场是中国式现代化的战略依托 Guo Liyan Guo Liyan, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts, examines the proposition in the Party Central Committee's recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) that "a powerful domestic market is the strategic support of Chinese modernization". The author argues that, as uncertainty grows, the market becomes a scarcer strategic resource. Over the next five years, Guo contends, China should hold to expanding domestic demand as its strategic base and move the domestic market from "big" to "strong". The article has four parts: the meaning and features of a powerful domestic market; why building one is necessary and urgent in the 15th Five-Year Plan period; the internal and external conditions; and concrete measures. It is a policy commentary that follows and explains the Central Committee's recommendations, and it cites figures such as an economy of 140 trillion yuan by the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan and fixed-asset investment of 50 trillion yuan. Guo defines "big" as aggregate size, market capacity and growth speed, and "strong" as quality, structure, competitive advantage and global influence. Building such a market is described as a systemic project that upgrades supply, distribution, circulation and demand systems together, including raising the household and labour share of income and moving consumption from subsistence to development-oriented spending. The author says a strong market supports people's needs, technological self-reliance and supply-chain security, and helps unblock circulation. It also helps counter de-globalisation and is described as open rather than closed. Guo sees opportunities outweighing challenges, citing a middle-income group projected above 800 million and the most complete industrial system. The challenges listed are unconverted demand potential, urban–rural gaps, weak brands, local protectionism and market fragmentation, and incomplete new infrastructure. Guo's proposals include a special action to boost consumption, better government investment that links "investing in things" with "investing in people", and removal of barriers to a unified national market. They also include stronger private-sector vitality through the Private Economy Promotion Law, a national data market, and modern infrastructure such as 5G-A, 6G trials and intelligent connected transport. The author presents these as the practical path to turning market-size advantages into industrial competitiveness. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese policy thinkers frame domestic demand and market-building for the 2026–2030 plan period.

The distinctive strengths of China's governance as seen in the 15th Five-Year Plan 从“十五五”规划看中国之治的显著优势 Li Zhijun Li Zhijun asks what the drafting and implementation of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) reveals about the strengths of China's system of governance. Writing after the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) adopted the Party's Recommendations for the plan, Li argues that the plan's compilation logic and implementation mechanisms show four "unities" that together demonstrate the distinctive advantages of China's governance. The article is a commentary in four sections, each opening with a statement by Xi Jinping. They treat scientific decision-making, strategic coordination across successive plans, overall planning that looks both inward and outward, and the conversion of blueprints into results. Li draws on the 14 five-year plans since 1953, the consultation timetable for the 15th plan, and the content of the Recommendations on industry, markets, opening up, security and the rule of law. First, Li holds that top-level design and consultation with the public are combined. Central leadership, in Li's account, can rise above departmental interests, while consultation rounds (provincial research teams, an online solicitation, circulation of a draft) embody whole-process people's democracy and a "democracy first, centralism after" method. Second, long-term layout and continued effort are joined: Li presents the 14th, 15th and 16th plans as successive steps towards basic socialist modernization by 2035, citing growth and social insurance figures from the 14th plan period. Third, Li describes a plan that rests on domestic conditions, such as a unified national market and new quality productive forces, while expanding opening up and handling development and security together. Fourth, Li points to the planning law draft, task lists divided among central, local and departmental levels, and monitoring and evaluation, as a closed loop that turns plans into action. Li concludes that the plan shows the advantages of Party leadership and the socialist system, including the ability to concentrate resources on major tasks and to implement decisions. Li calls on readers to rally around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to study the plenum's spirit. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary presents the planning system as evidence of governance strengths, and how it frames the 15th Five-Year Plan.

How the CPC Central Committee's organs established themselves in Shanghai after the failure of the Great Revolution 大革命失败后中共中央机关在上海何以立足？ Ma Xiaohan After the failure of the Great Revolution in 1927, the CPC Central Committee moved from Wuhan back to Shanghai and went underground. Ma Xiaohan asks how the Party sited and shielded its organs under the White Terror. The article argues that the Party moved from improvised methods, such as using members' homes and borrowed or feigned shops, to a mature model of 'independently run businesses', and that this model explains how the centre survived in Shanghai until 1933. The study covers the Central Committee's Shanghai organs from 1927 to 1933. It begins with the early Party's two cover strategies in the foreign concessions, 'using the family to cover the Party' and 'using commerce to cover the Party'. It then follows the post-1927 stage of 'family-style organs', the reorganisation after the defection of Gu Shunzhang in 1931, and the later results of the business model. Evidence includes memoirs, Party circulars, the 1928 'Common Knowledge of Secret Work' and accounts by defectors and Guomindang agents. Ma's central claim is that each model's weaknesses led to the next. 'Family-style organs' (large pretend families, or real or pretend couples) helped with tenancy checks but depended on neighbours and comrades, left the Party short of funds and exposed it to informers. Ma cites the betrayal of Luo Yinong in 1928 as an example. From 1928 the Party therefore pursued 'socialization of organs' and 'professionalization of members', opening real shops, clinics, bookshops, antique dealers and 'husband-and-wife' stores, while borrowed or feigned cover remained a supplement and a risk. Ma credits independent businesses with three benefits: safer cover (the Central Committee survived nearly three years after Gu's defection), closer links with the masses, and financial self-reliance, including 'red-white trade' with the Soviet areas. Ma concludes that independent business combined security, economic autonomy and mass work, and that the Party's adaptability and resilience in extreme conditions rested on it. The author adds that the experience laid a foundation for hidden-front work in the War of Resistance and the civil war. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of the Central Committee's underground arrangements in Shanghai, including named safe houses, shops and Special Branch practices, as seen through Party-history writing in the journal Documents of the Party.

From domestic confrontation to international debut: the CPC and the question of representation at the San Francisco Conference 从国内交锋到国际亮相：中共与旧金山会议代表权问题 Zhou Tianyu Zhou Tianyu asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) handled the composition of the Chinese delegation to the 1945 San Francisco Conference, which founded the United Nations, and how its propaganda changed along the way. Existing scholarship has examined the delegation's makeup, the Party's fight to attend and Dong Biwu's activities in the United States. Zhou argues that it has paid less attention to the link between the Kuomintang–CPC talks on a "coalition government" and the delegation question, and to the propaganda around Dong's trip. The article contends that the episode shows the CPC growing from a party with little international experience into one with both international and domestic horizons. Drawing on archival documents, the article follows events from the Dumbarton Oaks talks of 1944 to the conference of mid-1945. It covers the CPC's growing foreign-affairs work after the Kuomintang's military collapse in the Henan–Hunan–Guangxi campaign and the arrival of the US Army observer group in Yan'an. It then traces the failed talks mediated by the US envoy Patrick Hurley and the Yalta announcement. The last sections cover the naming of Dong Biwu as delegate and his publicity work on the way to and in San Francisco. Zhou's central claim is that the Party's approach had two phases. From mid-February to late March 1945, the CPC treated the delegation list as a political instrument. It demanded that the Kuomintang receive at most one third of the seats and that the CPC, the Democratic League and non-party figures hold the rest. It tied this demand to "coalition government" in the Yan'an press and English-language broadcasts, in order to expose one-party rule and mobilise domestic opinion. Zhou argues that this pressure, together with the Democratic League's lobbying and Roosevelt's suggestion, helped lead Chiang Kai-shek to accept one Communist delegate, though far fewer than the CPC wanted. In the second phase, once Dong was named, the Party shifted its main audience abroad. Despite Kuomintang obstruction, Dong spoke to the American press and overseas Chinese and distributed 5,000 copies of an English booklet on the liberated areas. Zhou concludes that the Party moved from "exposing the Kuomintang" to "constructing the image of the liberated areas". In this reading, the episode taught the Party a lesson in linking international and domestic issues that proved useful in the Civil War period. Read the original if you study CPC diplomacy, the Kuomintang–CPC negotiations of 1944–45 or early Communist propaganda, and want an archive-based account of the San Francisco delegation dispute.

Techniques of rapid night marching in mountain terrain by the Red Army 红军山地夜路快速行军技术探赜 Niu Zelin Niu Zelin takes up a question that, the author says, has not yet received detailed scholarly study: how did the Red Army march quickly along mountain roads at night during the Agrarian Revolutionary War (the Soviet period of the late 1920s and 1930s), and how was that capacity built? Facing a much stronger Nationalist army, the Red Army had to rely on mountain and night marches to turn passivity into initiative. Niu argues that these marches rested on concrete technical training, field expedients and organisational discipline, not simply on evasion. Drawing on historical sources, diaries and memoirs, the article starts from the strategic shift of going "up the mountains" after 1927, associated with Mao Zedong. It then moves through training (hill-climbing, physical competitions, military geography courses), guides and local recruitment, bridging and river crossing, and signalling by flags, bugles and relayed orders. It goes on to route choice, night-march methods, examples of speed, and the political work and discipline behind the pace. The core argument has three parts. First, Niu holds that route selection decided outcomes: circling and detour tactics worked in the first four encirclement campaigns, but straight-line marching under Li De and Bo Gu in the fifth campaign lost the Red Army its flexibility, while the post-Zunyi Conference manoeuvres, notably the four crossings of the Chishui River, regained it. Second, night marching was drilled for secrecy: silent movement, soldiers dyeing clothing and horses, limited torches, and white towels as guides, with the 1931 passage between enemy forces and the Gansu night escape as cases; Niu also notes risks such as getting lost, bad weather and slow bottlenecks. Third, the article cites daily marching rates of roughly 80 to over 100 li and the 240-li dash to the Luding Bridge, and attributes this speed to political work, singing, strict discipline and detailed crossing regulations. Niu concludes that the Red Army's way of marching was meant to find favourable moments to fight, and that it grew from the reality of enemy strength and Red Army weakness, as well as from the adjustment of strategy by Mao Zedong and Zhu De. The author adds that this style shaped later Chinese military practice, citing a US veteran's memoir about Chinese night flanking marches in Korea. Read the original if you are interested in the tactical and logistical detail of Red Army marching, with its sources, rather than in strategy alone.

"Making the Party truly mass-based": the development paths of the Chinese Communist Party's early grassroots organizations “使党真正群众化”：中国共产党早期基层组织的发展路向 Yi Fenglin How did the Chinese Communist Party build grassroots organizations during its founding years and the Great Revolution (1924–27)? Yi Fenglin argues that existing scholarship has examined local cases, operating mechanisms and individual explorations, but has not synthesised the multiple paths and underlying logic at both macro and micro levels. The article contends that the Party's early grassroots development combined several paths, and that together they produced what the Party then called its "massification" (qunzhonghua). The article draws on Party documents, regional committee circulars and reports, Comintern resolutions and membership statistics. It covers five dimensions: the shift in recruitment method from traditional social ties to a more revolutionary and standardised approach; expansion into new regions and sectors; the balance between quantity and quality of members; the working of democratic centralism between higher and lower organizations; and the role of the Comintern. Yi's first main point is that early recruitment relied on networks of schoolmates, fellow-townspeople and workmates, as in Jiangxi, which helped secrecy. After the May Thirtieth Movement this was judged inadequate: in 1926 the Shanghai regional committee and Chen Duxiu called for recruiting through the branch's collective work. Second, the Party extended from core cities to surrounding regions and from factories to schools, villages and offices, supported by study societies, trade unions and peasant associations. The article cites membership rising from 994 before the Fourth Congress to 57,967 before the Fifth, with workers at 53.8 per cent. Third, active recruitment targets and shortened probation periods were followed by branch reorganisation, member education, vetting and anti-corruption measures. Regular reports, special commissioners and inspections sustained democratic centralism, though Yi notes that the Comintern's excessive focus on workers and its failure to guide organizational policy after the 1927 coup had negative effects. Yi concludes that these varied paths rooted the Party in grassroots society and reflected Marxist guidance together with an ability to adjust organizational policy to revolutionary conditions. The article presents a balanced growth in numbers and quality as the Party's overall approach. Read the original if you study early Chinese Communist Party history, organizational development, or the documentary sources on regional Party committees in the 1920s.

Publication, distribution and dissemination of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong in China's border ethnic minority regions 《毛泽东选集》在边疆民族地区的出版发行与传播 Di Hongxu Wang Xinyi How did the Selected Works of Mao Zedong reach China's border ethnic minority regions, and what did their spread do for national cohesion? Di and Wang note that earlier research has concentrated on translation and publication of the ethnic-language editions. They argue instead that publication, distribution and study of the Selected Works in these regions turned Party theory into a resource for governance and culture, and strengthened identification with the Party, the state and the Chinese nation. The article covers roughly 1951 to 1965, from the first volume's release to the completion of the four-volume set. It first traces translation and publishing: Uyghur, Kazakh, Mongolian, Tibetan and Korean editions, with figures for Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Tibet. It then examines the media and distribution channels, the Party-led study system, and the effects on ideological identification, cadre training, new socialist culture and ethnic relations. Examples come from Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia, Ningxia, Tibet, Yanbian, Guangxi, Yunnan and Hainan. Di and Wang describe a combination of organised promotion and popular response. Local newspapers, radio in minority languages, Xinhua Bookstore working groups and mobile book-sellers carried the volumes to remote areas. Party committees set study plans, and workplaces, schools, newspaper-reading groups and night classes took up the texts. The authors say the study was adapted to local language and production conditions and was not mere indoctrination. They report that, by their account, the books shaped a concrete sense of belonging to the Party and the new China, equipped growing numbers of minority cadres, and supplied authoritative arguments against both "Han chauvinism" and "local nationalism". Evidence includes sales figures, reported readers' comments and accounts of local practice. The authors conclude that the Selected Works served as both a cultural product and a guiding ideological banner, and that their circulation built an ideological foundation for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. They call for inheriting and developing the useful practices of this period and for new ways of strengthening national cohesion today. Read the original if you study the history of Party theory dissemination, ethnic-minority policy in the 1950s and 1960s, or Chinese official scholarship on the sense of community of the Chinese nation, and want the regional examples and figures.

The genesis and logic of upholding the Party's cultural leadership 坚持党的文化领导权的发生逻辑 Tian Xuming Tian Xuming examines why the Communist Party of China (CPC) now stresses upholding its cultural leadership (wenhua lingdaoquan, often rendered cultural hegemony), a concept the article calls an original idea of Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The author argues that the concept is both a product of applying Marxist party theory to Chinese cultural work and a response to the Party's own history and to present-day demands. Tian contends that a party holding cultural leadership can guide social values, command discursive authority, unite the people, integrate resources and resist cultural colonisation. The article moves in three steps. It first reconstructs the theoretical sources in Marx, Engels and Lenin. It then surveys the CPC's practice from the May Fourth period through the Party's founding, the Gutian Conference, the Yan'an rectification, the post-1949 years and reform and opening up, citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Finally it explains, under three headings, why the concept is stressed in the new era. On the classics, Tian reads Marx and Engels' claim in The German Ideology that the ruling material force is also the ruling intellectual force, and Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force when it grips the masses, as implying that the proletarian party must contest cultural leadership. Lenin is presented as making this explicit: he opposed the Proletkult's claim to cultural autonomy and demanded that publishing and libraries be Party institutions. In Tian's account, the CPC's history shows the same pattern, with cultural struggle opening the way for each stage of its work. For the new era, Tian gives three reasons: safeguarding the Party's governing security, citing Xi's remark that regimes often collapse first in the ideological sphere and the author's view of the Soviet collapse; meeting the inner requirements of Chinese modernization; and answering the great changes unseen in a century, in which the author sees Western cultural infiltration as a continuing means of containing China. Tian concludes that a party's strength lies not only in organisation but in its ideological and cultural leadership, and that the CPC must keep strengthening this leadership to secure its long-term rule and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Tian says the concept supplies a political guarantee for building a socialist cultural power. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how Chinese scholars trace the lineage of the cultural leadership concept from Marx and Lenin through to Xi Jinping's era.

Understanding the "Second Integration" through the grand historical outlook 以大历史观理解把握“第二个结合” Gao Changwu Gao Changwu asks how the "Second Integration", the combination of the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, should be understood. The article, published in Party Literature in 2025, answers that it must be read through the "grand historical outlook" (da lishi guan). Gao treats this as a way of placing the concept in long historical time, a broad field of view, a coherent internal structure and a layered set of goals. The author presents the Second Integration as an original, signature theoretical innovation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, especially of Xi's thought on culture. The article is organised around four senses of the "grand" in the outlook: looking far, looking wide, looking through, and looking deep. The first section traces the idea from the Party's early explorations to its formal announcement on 1 July 2021 and its later elaboration. The second examines its significance for the Party, the country and the world. The third analyses its internal structure as an integrated whole of standpoint, viewpoint and method. The fourth sets out its aims in three dimensions. Gao argues that the Second Integration should be seen as a line, not a point. Mao Zedong's 1938 call to inherit China's cultural heritage critically, the 1943 call to join Marxism-Leninism deeply with China's history and culture, and examples such as seeking truth from facts and regional ethnic autonomy are read as earlier stages. Xi's statements from 2012 to 2021 then led, in Gao's account, from quantitative accumulation to a qualitative leap. Gao claims that the concept answers three questions: what the Party is, where China comes from and is going, and what is to be done about the world. It is said to establish cultural subjectivity, to explain why socialism with Chinese characteristics is a necessary road, and to supply ideas for a community with a shared future for mankind. Its goals are said to run from theoretical innovation, through cultural innovation, to the evolution of civilisation, with theory as the basic dimension. Gao concludes that the Second Integration must be upheld and deepened on the new journey. This means holding to Marxism as the "soul-root" while keeping Chinese traditional culture as the "root-vein". The author calls for creative transformation and innovative development of that culture, for building a socialist cultural powerhouse, and for further resolving the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western. Seen from a long historical perspective, the concept is said to open space for Chinese modernization and for a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-historical account of how the Second Integration is traced and framed in official theory, with dated citations from Mao and Xi.

Digital rentier capitalism: three manifestations, formation mechanism and internal contradictions 数字食利资本主义的三重表现、形成机理和内在矛盾 Hao Ruilin Han Wenlong Hao Ruilin and Han Wenlong ask what is new about the rentier character of capitalism in the digital age, how these changes arise, and how China should respond. Working from Marxist political economy, they argue that contemporary capitalism has produced a 'digital rentier capitalism' distinct from the industrial and financial capitalism of earlier eras. In their account it is driven by capital's own movement and produces contradictions that advanced capitalist states try to push outward onto the world. The article first sets out three changes in the rentier economy: the mode of rent-seeking, the source of profit and the rentier class itself. It then explains the formation of this system through the rise of digital capital, platform accumulation, the merger of digital and financial capital, and the union of capital with political power. It goes on to analyse the contradictions and their external transfer, drawing mainly on US examples, and ends with proposals for China. The authors contend that rent has shifted from financial speculation to technology patents, platform monopolies and data. Profit now draws on 'digital gig workers', whom platforms control by algorithm without employing them, and the rentier bloc has become a 'technology–finance–politics' alliance. They hold that digital capital arises as users' unpaid data labour and replicable digital products are turned into data commodities and then data capital. The central contradiction, in their reading, is between increasingly socialised production and private ownership of platforms, technology and data. They say this stifles innovation, depresses workers' consumption and breeds social anarchy. They add that it also drives de-globalisation, 'digital colonialism' and political interference abroad, which in turn split the imperialist camp and prompt resistance in developing countries. Hao and Han argue that China's basic socialist economic system and its technological strengths put it in a favourable position to resist these pressures. They propose building a community of digital destiny through international technology cooperation and rule-making. They also call for regulating capital and guarding against its disorderly expansion, and for building new production relations. These would include rights protections for platform workers and clearer ownership, use and income rights over data. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist political-economy analysis of platform and data capitalism, and the policy conclusions it draws for China.

Five theses on the development of the contemporary world socialist movement: an analysis based on foreign left-wing forces 当代世界社会主义运动发展“五论”——基于国外左翼力量的分析 Zhuo Mingliang Zhuo Mingliang asks how foreign left-wing forces, mainly communist and workers' parties and left-wing intellectuals, assess the state and prospects of world socialism more than thirty years after the Soviet collapse and the upheavals in Eastern Europe. The article argues that these forces see the movement as moving out of its trough and as holding a historic opportunity. It also holds that they see the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era as a major driving force of that revival. The article starts from Xi Jinping's formulation that the world still lives in the historical era Marxism identified, and from the trend of "the East rising and the West declining". It organises the foreign left's views into five "theses": on opportunity, on methods and paths, on China's significance, on difficulties, and on the way forward. The evidence is a long series of statements by leaders of communist parties in Germany, Italy, Britain, Nepal, Cuba, Colombia, Ireland, Greece, Sri Lanka and elsewhere, plus some scholars. Zhuo also cites Western opinion polls on young people's attitudes to socialism. Zhuo reports that foreign leftists regard the "end of history" thesis as refuted by capitalist crises, protest movements and China's development. On method, they call for ending dogmatism and applying Marxism to national conditions. They also call for learning from the Communist Party of China through equal, voluntary exchange, without copying or sanctifying its experience. On China, they are said to see its successes as proof of the truth of scientific socialism and as a refutation of capitalism's permanence, and to expect Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to gain wider international influence. On difficulties, the article lists anti-communist legislation and repression, Western media campaigns against socialist states, persistent dogmatism and sectarianism, and a "double split" at national and international levels. For the way forward, the article reports four proposals from foreign left forces. They are to strengthen party-building and the vanguard role, to create new forms and principles of international unity based on diversity, to build consensus among communists, and to defend the international reputation of China and other socialist countries. Zhuo concludes that most foreign leftists remain revolutionary optimists, but that revival will be long and conflictual. In the author's view, "capitalism strong, socialism weak" will remain the main pattern for a long period, while "the East rising, the West declining" is the increment that points to the future. Read the original if you want a dense, quotation-based record of how foreign communist parties and left intellectuals are presented in Chinese scholarship, and of how they are cited to support China's role in world socialism.

A study of Lenin's thought on building grassroots organisations of the proletarian party 列宁无产阶级政党基层组织建设思想研究 Fang Guangshun Wu Gaojie Fang and Wu ask how Lenin conceived the building of grassroots Party organisations, which they treat as a matter of life and death for any proletarian party. They argue that Lenin built on Marx and Engels's organisational theory and, before and after the October Revolution, developed a systematic body of thought on grassroots organisation. In their account this thought laid the political and organisational foundation for the revolution's victory and then guided the Bolsheviks as a ruling party. The article moves through the Bolshevik experience in sequence. It begins with the status and functions of grassroots organisations, then turns to their political, ideological and organisational construction. It then covers style of work, discipline and the fight against corruption. It also discusses how organisational forms were adjusted to the Party's central tasks in the revolutionary period, the civil war and the New Economic Policy. A closing section links the findings to the Communist Party of China. The authors' central claims are that Lenin saw the grassroots branch as the Party's basic cell, a bridge to the masses and a fighting fortress. On this reading, the Party is the sum of its organisations, and every member must belong to one. Lenin fought the Mensheviks' "autonomy" and rejection of discipline, and insisted on democratic centralism, adherence to the Party rules and the authority of the Central Committee. The authors say he extended branches to villages, cities, trade unions and the Red Army. He demanded quality over quantity in recruitment, through trials, a longer probationary period, strict sponsor rules and purges informed by non-Party opinion. They also report his campaign against bureaucracy, factionalism and corruption, including harsher punishment for Communists than for non-members. In their reading, branch priorities shifted with the Party's central tasks: seizing power, supporting the front, and then consolidating Soviet power and strengthening factory and rural branches under the New Economic Policy. The authors conclude that the Communist Party of China inherited and adapted these practices. Citing Xi Jinping, they list five lessons: stress the status of grassroots organisations, prioritise political and ideological work, perfect the organisational system, use style, discipline and anti-corruption as levers, and tie grassroots building to the Party's central tasks, extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party downward. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Lenin's writings on branch organisation are used in Chinese Party-building scholarship.

The Global Security Initiative: China's proposal for a security order in a multipolar world 全球安全倡议：构建多极世界安全秩序的中国方案 Eduardo Regalado He Qin The article asks what the Global Security Initiative, proposed by Xi Jinping in 2022, offers as an alternative to the Western-dominated security order. The authors argue that the Initiative is a comprehensive Chinese proposal that treats security and prosperity as global public goods. They hold that it reflects a shift from a unipolar to a multipolar order driven by China's rise, and that its success depends on the willingness of states to build security consensus and trust. The text first sets out China's economic, technological and military rise and the Initiative's six core principles and five dimensions of security: political, economic, social, environmental and digital. It then places the Initiative in a non-Western tradition of international relations, drawing on the idea of tianxia, and contrasts it with NATO-style collective security. A third section describes implementation through the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the Belt and Road Initiative and BRICS, and through bilateral defence dialogue, exercises and security assistance. The longest section turns to Latin America and the Caribbean. The authors argue that the Initiative rests on three principles: sustainable security, interdependence and non-interference. They present these as distinct from Western approaches that separate security from development, bypass multilateral bodies and justify intervention through liberal interventionism and the "responsibility to protect". In their account, Latin American states find the Initiative congenial because it matches their own traditions of sovereignty and self-determination. They cite Nicaragua and Venezuela as endorsing it, and note that the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC)–China Forum documents and Chinese support for a Latin American zone of peace point the same way. Three cases illustrate practice: the Chinese deep-space station in Neuquén, Argentina, the ECU911 security system in Ecuador, and biotechnology cooperation with Cuba. The authors also say Latin American states are growing more cautious as they balance between China and the United States. The authors conclude that the Initiative is a programmatic statement of a non-confrontational security philosophy that casts China as a guardian of stability and a development partner. They say that, in Latin America, aligning security concepts and interests could help root the Initiative in regional needs. Read the original if you want a Chinese-Cuban co-authored account of how the Initiative is presented to the Global South, especially the Latin American cases and the contrast drawn with Western security thinking.

Marx and Engels's thought on the international unity of the proletariat and its contemporary value 马克思恩格斯无产阶级国际联合思想及当代价值 Shu Xin Yang Zhouyu Shu Xin and Yang Zhouyu ask how Marx and Engels's idea of the international unity of the proletariat arose, how it was carried by successive international organisations, and what it offers communist parties today. They argue that the idea gives the parties a resource for overcoming disagreements and strengthening solidarity amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century. Their central claim is that the form of international unity must change with the movement's tasks, while its essence stays the same. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the theoretical and practical logic of the idea from The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto and Capital. The second traces its historical carriers: the Communist League, the First, Second and Third (Communist) Internationals, compared by membership, programmes and achievements. The third turns to the period since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and to the organisational forms and disputes of the present. On theory, the authors argue that world history, the capitalist world system with its internal contradictions, and the mission of human emancipation make proletarian unity necessary. In practice, they say, bourgeois anti-feudal struggle gave workers their first, spontaneous unity, large-scale industry supplied the means of communication, and conscious intellectuals provided doctrine. Drawing on Engels's insistence that the Second International take a loose form, they hold that the essence of unity is voluntary cooperation based on common interests. They add that the highly centralised model of the Third International suited a period of revolutionary upsurge and is not suited to the present. They therefore reject calls for a new Third International-style body, as the 'centre–periphery' model of Soviet leadership dissolved after 1991. The authors describe today's system as a multi-level network of bilateral and multilateral party ties, regional or issue-based platforms, and the annual International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. They report that this meeting was held 23 times between 1999 and 2023. They discuss the sharp split over the Ukraine crisis at the 2023 meeting and the dissolution of the Initiative of European Communist and Workers' Parties. They call for a broad, loose organisational form and for parties to put their own national struggles first while keeping the shared goal of human emancipation in view. They also urge parties to set aside disputes and seek common ground while respecting differences. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Marx and Engels's internationalism is applied to present divisions among communist parties, including the Ukraine dispute.

Practice and reflection on socialist reform in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe: goals, paths and results 苏联与东欧国家社会主义改革的实践与反思：目标、路径与成效 Xiang Zuotao Zhang Jihong Xiang and Zhang ask why the nearly half-century of reform in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe failed to deliver its goals, and what lessons this holds for existing socialist states. They treat these reforms as ruling-party attempts to resolve the contradiction between backward productive forces and advanced socialist institutions, through partial adjustment of the relations of production and the superstructure. Their thesis is that reform fell short because of dogmatism, a rigid opposition to capitalism, a bureaucratic privileged stratum and Soviet control over Eastern Europe. The article first sets the Soviet model in historical context. It contrasts Western 'capital accumulation' industrialisation with Russia's position as the 'weakest link' and Lenin's late idea of combining Soviet power with capitalist technology. It then surveys reform from the mid-1950s in politics, economy, ideology and foreign relations. The cases include Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev, and Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia, the German Democratic Republic and Yugoslavia. It then assesses outcomes and analyses the causes of failure. The authors argue that the Stalin-era system suited early industrialisation but became a fetter once mobilisation advantages were exhausted. Reforms rehabilitated victims of repression, restored some intra-Party democracy, devolved enterprise powers, introduced market elements and improved living standards. Yet the planned economy kept its dominance, state and enterprise remained fused, heavy industry stayed favoured, and the ideology swung between loosening and tightening. Cited figures show Soviet growth of total social product falling from 7.4% to 6.3% and then 4.2% across successive five-year plans. Gorbachev's 'democratisation' and 'openness' are described as lacking institutional limits and ending in the abandonment of the Party's leadership. In Eastern Europe, the authors describe Soviet 'limited sovereignty' and the interventions in Hungary and Czechoslovakia as constraints on autonomous reform. The authors conclude that the Soviet model's achievements were a stage-bound result of 'catching up' through institutional mobilisation. Its fatal flaw was to treat that experience as absolute, which stifled institutional vitality. Citing Engels, they hold that socialism is a society in constant change, and they call for 'reform is always on the road' as a theoretical commitment to keep relations of production and the superstructure aligned with productive forces. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Soviet and East European reform, with country-by-country examples across four policy fields.

Marx's social republic: radical republicanism and socialist political institutions 马克思的社会共和国：激进共和主义与社会主义政治制度 Bruno Leipold What political institutions did Marx think socialism needs? Bruno Leipold argues that Marx's answer, drawn from his reading of the Paris Commune, owes much to the radical and most democratic strand of the republican tradition. Marx called the resulting regime the 'social republic', and Leipold holds that it rests on his conviction that ordinary people can govern and administer themselves. The article draws mainly on Marx's The Civil War in France and its two drafts, and acknowledges that these give scattered sketches rather than a blueprint. It organises Marx's views in three dimensions: popular delegation in place of representative government, legislative supremacy combined with a critique of the separation of powers, and popular control of the state's administrative and coercive organs. Along the way it compares Marx with Rousseau, Félix Pyat, Ernest Jones, the American Anti-Federalists and Tocqueville. First, Leipold shows that Marx endorsed binding mandates, recall and short terms, which conflict with the core principle of representative government as described by Bernard Manin. Leipold traces this to a revolutionary-republican tradition running from Marat to the Commune, and notes Marx's early criticism of Hegel and his parallels with Rousseau. Second, Marx criticised the 1848 French constitution's strong presidency and attacked the separation of powers because it shifted power to an executive prone to escape popular control. Leipold reads this alongside Pyat, Jones and the Anti-Federalists, who also preferred simple, legislature-centred government. Third, Marx wanted the standing army replaced by a citizen militia and officials elected, recallable and paid workers' wages, which Leipold reads as de-professionalising public functions. Leipold concludes that Marx's most important insight about the Commune is that socialism needs a distinctive political structure: the working class cannot simply take over the ready-made state machinery but must transform it into genuinely democratic institutions. He suggests that the Commune's de-professionalised administration recalls the rotation principle of ancient Athens and Marx's youthful classical republicanism. Both socialists and republicans, he argues, can draw on this account when thinking about institutional design. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Marx's Commune writings connect to republican constitutional debates from Rousseau and the French Revolution to 1848.

Marx and Engels on the scientific character of Marxism In commemoration of the 130th anniversary of Engels's death 马克思恩格斯论马克思主义的科学性质——纪念恩格斯逝世130周年 Liu Zhenying Ma Yongjun Marking 130 years since Engels's death, Liu and Ma ask in what sense Marx and Engels regarded their theory as a science, and why Engels credited the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value with turning socialism from utopia into science. They argue that Marxism is a living, historical science whose object is practice itself. Its scientific status therefore rests on a criterion of demarcation different from both modern natural-science models and Western philosophy of science. The article begins with Lenin's tribute and Engels's own modest ranking of himself below Marx. It then moves through Marx and Engels's concept of a single "science of history", their critique of the thing-in-itself and of naturalistic views of history, and the end of philosophy as a "science of sciences". It goes on to Capital's account of overproduction and the limits of capitalism, then to the historical conditions of scientific socialism, and ends with the adaptation of Marxism to China. The authors contend that nature and humanity form one historical science, because the nature we know is already shaped by human practice. Truth is therefore not the match of thought to a human-independent objective reality but its fit with actuality and process, tested through practice. Engels's example of artificially produced alizarin is read as turning the "thing-in-itself" into a "thing-for-us". On this basis, historical materialism is a worldview and method applied in the specific sciences, and surplus-value theory is its first successful application. The authors argue that capitalist overproduction, which arises when profit ends, could be met by taking unprofitable firms into state ownership. They stress that socialism became scientific only when objective and subjective conditions had matured, and that theoretical necessity differs from practical necessity, which needs proletarian revolutionary struggle. The authors attribute the twentieth-century failure of socialism to prevail to the abandonment of two subjective conditions by Western workers' parties: proletarian internationalism and a scientific communist programme. They credit Lenin with restoring both, and conclude that Marxism cannot simply be copied in China. They present Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They link common prosperity and Chinese modernization to the shift from scarcity to a new principal contradiction. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical reading of Engels's epistemology and its tie to current Party theory.

Optimising and strengthening the discursive power of the Communist Party of China in the all-media era 全媒体时代中国共产党话语权优化与提升分析 Wu Yangsong Wu Yangsong asks how the Communist Party of China can consolidate and raise its discursive power (huayuquan, the capacity of its language to shape public understanding) now that the "all-media" environment has changed how information is produced and spread. The article argues that this environment has reset discourse production, interaction and power relations, and that the Party must therefore strengthen its discursive consciousness, discourse system and discursive capabilities together. The article is built in three steps. It first describes how the all-media era, driven by network, digital and intelligent technologies, has transformed the Party's discursive environment. It then sets out four new features of the discourse field and four resulting challenges. Finally it proposes remedies under three headings: discursive consciousness, the discourse system (theme, content, form) and discursive capability (production, communication, struggle, governance). Wu holds that, unlike in the era of newspapers, radio and television, discourse production is no longer one-directional, and communication has shifted from top-down "one-to-many" to networked "many-to-many". In this setting the public's sense of itself as a speaker has grown, and attention has turned to everyday life, entertainment and emotion. In the author's account, this tests the consensus-building quality of Party discourse, weakens its dominance, and exposes its cohesion and practical effect to deconstruction, rumour, commercial traffic logic and what the article calls hostile forces. The remedies include overcoming the habit of doing rather than speaking, balancing lofty ideals with livelihood concerns, making content fact-based and problem-oriented, and using popular, vivid forms. Wu also calls for original concepts, agenda-setting, segmented and dialogic communication, a readiness to confront erroneous trends, and law-based content review and governance of online discourse. Wu concludes that building discursive power in the all-media era is a complex systemic project requiring simultaneous change in how the Party thinks about, structures and conducts its speech. The proposals are presented as the Party's task of leading the production, spread and governance of discourse, not merely reacting to it. Read the original if you study Chinese Party communication, ideological work or online public opinion management and want a detailed statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar frames the Party's discursive challenges and responses.

On the common features of socialist modernization 论社会主义现代化的共同特征 Yin Xiaoen Qin Xuan Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization shares common features with other countries' modernization while having its own national characteristics, Yin Xiaoen and Qin Xuan ask what features all socialist modernization has in common. They note that Chinese scholarship is rich on world modernization and on Chinese distinctiveness but thin on this question. Their thesis is that these features unite the basic principles of scientific socialism with the general laws of modernization, and form requirements every socialist country must follow. The article proceeds through a historical survey followed by a structural analysis. The survey runs from Marx and Engels's theoretical outline of socialist modernization, through post-1917 Soviet industrialization and the Soviet model spread to Eastern Europe, Cuba and China, to the post-1991 shift towards all-round social development, which the authors trace through Chinese Party Congress documents. The second half sets out three dimensions (people, material things, institutions) and five paired unities that distinguish socialist from capitalist modernization. The authors argue that the common features changed by stage: industrialization with priority for heavy industry under the Soviet model, then comprehensive social development after the Soviet and East European upheavals. The Soviet model, in their account, ignored institutional modernization and so slowed material progress and emptied all-round human development of content. Capitalist modernization, by contrast, achieved material abundance at the price of human alienation. Socialist modernization must therefore integrate the modernization of people (the fundamental goal), of material things (the material base) and of institutions (the fundamental guarantee). The five unities are advanced productive forces with advanced relations of production; material abundance with all-round human development; objective historical development with human agency; the integrity of civilizational forms with the coordination of civilizational processes; and critique of capitalist modernity with constructive building of an ideal society. The authors conclude that socialist modernization has always sought the free and all-round development of the individual, while its features have evolved in stages and do not rule out national particularity. They call for firm adherence to fundamental and basic institutions, adaptive adjustment of important ones, and the development of new quality productive forces. They also call for systematically absorbing the achievements of capitalist civilization, as Lenin and Deng Xiaoping urged, while curbing capital's negative effects. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese theoretical account of how socialist modernization is defined against both capitalist modernization and the Soviet model.

The philosophical foundations of a theoretical narrative of Chinese modernization: based on a critique of Western-centrism 中国式现代化理论叙事的哲学基础——基于对西方中心主义的批判 Sun Hui Sun Hui asks how a self-reliant, original theoretical narrative of Chinese modernization can be built when Western-centrist accounts have long distorted the interpretation of China's modernization. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that Chinese social science is still in a position of 'having reason but being unable to state it', the article argues that Western-centrism must first be criticised and overcome at the philosophical level. Only then, Sun contends, can theoretical confidence and methodological awareness be established. The article first dissects Western discourse through three questions: the source of China's modernizing drive, the choice of path, and the global impact. It traces three foundations of that discourse: a fragmented view of history, linear historicism and teleology, and a narrative of civilizational superiority. Sun then sets out an alternative based on the 'grand view of history' and applies it to the same three questions. The article engages Fairbank, Levenson, Pomeranz, Huntington, Hegel and Fukuyama, and draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi. In Sun's critique, the 'impact–response' paradigm, the 'high-level equilibrium trap' and the 'Great Divergence' all fix on the nineteenth-century 'time lag', which strips Chinese civilization of its subjectivity. Hegelian teleology is said to underlie the equation 'modernization = Westernization', and civilizational-conflict theory conceals the contradictions of capital-centred Western modernity. Against these, Sun draws on historical materialism. The Western impact was an external condition, not the first mover. China's modernization is said to arise from 'economic necessity' in its own social contradictions, and the Party's activation of the 'cultural subjectivity' of Chinese civilization through the Two Integrations turned it from passivity to initiative. Sun presents Chinese modernization as Engels's 'third conception' of industrialization, uniting the development of productive forces with their ownership by the people. Sun concludes that Chinese modernization is the self-sublation, self-development and self-transcendence of Chinese civilization. In the author's account it creates a new form of human civilization across five spheres: material, political, cultural-ethical, social and ecological. Because it is people-centred rather than capital-centred, Sun says, it avoids the Western pattern in which a strong state inevitably seeks hegemony, and it offers answers to modernity's problems. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese theorists use historical materialism and the 'grand view of history' to rebut Western accounts of China's modernization.

Quasi-cause of affect, or empty set of the state of the situation? A comparison of Deleuze's and Badiou's conceptions of the event 是情动的准原因，还是情势状态的空集?——德勒兹与巴迪欧事件观比较 Sun Lin Sun Lin compares the conceptions of the event in Gilles Deleuze and Alain Badiou. The article starts from what it calls the "overflow" of presence, the problem both thinkers share with phenomenology, structuralism and post-structuralism after Hegel and Marx. Its thesis is that the two form a "paradoxical pair": both stand on a materialist ground, criticise Hegel's "One" and rebuild the Spinozist trinity, yet Deleuze moves toward a "relative nothing" and Badiou toward the "void" or empty set. Sun notes that the comparison is well established abroad, citing Badiou and Žižek, but has barely begun in Chinese scholarship. The body has three parts: the rebirth of the subject (body, intuition, difference); the rifts in the object (repetition, multiplicity, exception); and the event's inner drive (immanence, power, cause). A final section sets out similarities, differences and implications, with references to Spinoza, Bergson, Husserl, Heidegger, Foucault, Althusser and Lacan. In Sun's reading, Deleuze starts from the body and temporal intuition. Difference is infinitesimal and the event is a "quasi-cause", an immanent force (affect) that repeats creatively and moves toward a unified ideal event. Badiou rejects intuition and repetition. He works with set theory: the event site is a multiple on the edge of the void, "fidelity" and "generic forcing" proceed from there, and the event ruptures the "state of the situation" rather than flowing from it. Sun argues this makes Deleuze's epistemology closer to Foucault's, with a break that does not sever, and Badiou's closer to Althusser's structural rupture. Sun finds four points of agreement with historical materialism. These are that history develops from within, that capitalist ideology and reification must be opposed, that the new subject rests on a community of individuals, and that creative collective action and mutual love drive world history. The differences are continuity versus rupture, "relative nothing" versus void, and how a rupture can be acted on. Sun adds that Badiou proclaims himself anti-humanist but in practice sides with Sartre. The article ends with a warning not to let historical materialism drift from the dialectic of productive forces and relations of production. Read the original if you work on Deleuze, Badiou or French post-war philosophy and want a Chinese Marxist reading that links their ontologies to Hegel, Spinoza and historical materialism.

Marx's critique of the "universal opulence" of national economics and its implications: the logical link between labour, wealth and capital 马克思对国民经济学“普遍富裕”的批判及其启示——基于劳动、财富及资本的逻辑关联 Yan Jinggao Yan asks why national economics (the author's term for classical political economy) set "universal opulence" among all social classes as its goal, and why Marx held that goal to be unattainable under capitalism. The article argues that Marx, by clarifying what is specific to the capitalist mode of production, exposed the goal as a theoretical fiction. Marx then sketched a communist vision of "wealth for all", which Yan reads as supplying the institutional preconditions of shared wealth and as theoretical support for common prosperity in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article first reconstructs the logic of national economics through Smith, Ricardo, Sismondi, Say and List. Yan identifies "three consistencies": between labour savings and wealth accumulation, between wealth accumulation and capital accumulation, and between labour savings and capital accumulation. It then turns to Marx's critique in the 1844 Manuscripts, the Grundrisse and Capital. The final sections draw out contemporary implications, including a discussion of welfare capitalism and of capital under China's socialist market economy. Yan's central move is that Smith's "general labour" is in fact wage labour. Where national economists observed natural economy, individual production and direct appropriation of natural objects, Marx saw capital as a social power that commands labour. On this reading, the worker's wealth becomes "another's thing", and the accumulation of capital is the unpaid appropriation of surplus labour. The three consistencies are therefore illusory for the working class, whatever they describe for the bourgeoisie. Yan also takes up welfare capitalism, which seems to refute Marx. In Yan's account it rests on exploitation displaced abroad and on internal polarisation and fiscal conflict. Yan adds that rising living standards, in Marx's cottage-and-palace comparison, do not amount to cross-class opulence. Yan contends that Marx's "wealth for all" goes beyond material abundance to the free development of all people, and requires social ownership of the means of production. Yan warns against a dogmatic reading that equates capital with absolute domination. Under China's basic socialist economic system, citing Xi Jinping, capital is said to be one production factor among others rather than an all-controlling power. Yan concludes that the Two Unwaverings allow capital to play a constructive role, so that the consistencies Marx denied under capitalism become possible and "wealth for all" can become common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Marxian reading of classical political economy that ends in a Party-line account of capital in contemporary China.

Debt and the mode of human existence from the perspective of the critique of political economy 政治经济学批判视域中债务与人的存在方式研究 Huang Zhijun Huang Zhijun asks how debt shapes the way human beings exist, and argues that the question belongs to the critique of political economy rather than to moral philosophy or conventional economics alone. Moral readings, in Huang's view, attend only to creditors and debtors as moral persons, while economics treats debt as an accounting or lending category. The article claims that, seen through the critique of political economy, debt affects people's moral existence, their economic existence and what Huang calls the "texture" of existence (cunzai zhigan), the felt sense of living in contradiction. The article, published in Philosophical Research in 2026, begins with debt as a social relation and with accounts that trace morality to primal debt, including Indo-European etymologies of guilt and debt, David Graeber and Nietzsche. It then turns to Marx's 1844 remarks on credit and to the later analysis of interest-bearing capital and the credit system in Capital. It surveys debt by purpose, subject and object (personal, household, corporate, national and international debt), and engages Adam Smith, Keynes, Thomas Piketty, Dirk Ehnts-style debt critics such as Steffen Steuerlechner's namesake Steuerl, and Ray Dalio. Finally it considers existence at macro and micro levels. Huang makes three main moves. First, against Nietzsche's view of morality as originating in debt, Huang follows Marx's claim that credit is the political-economic judgement on a person's morality: under credit, the poor person's virtues and life activity become security for the rich, so that people themselves become money, a deeper self-alienation than the Saint-Simonians imagined. Yet Huang insists that modern credit also requires honesty, citing the personal bankruptcy rule of the "honest but unfortunate" debtor, and that creditors' conduct in collection also needs moral scrutiny. Second, modern debt is profit-seeking and consumption-driven, so debtors may be sufferers or beneficiaries. Third, Huang contrasts Marx's focus on production with Piketty's focus on distribution, and endorses Steuerl's point that over-indebtedness must be addressed; real solutions lie in raising productive capacity, not in more financialised products. Huang concludes that debt is a double-edged outcome of capital's credit logic: it can improve living standards and open conditions for development, but it also deepens anxiety, inequality and crisis, leaving people between a stretched present and an overdrawn future.
