Distinguishing reasonable from excessive, productive from consumer and voluntary from forced debt is, in Huang's view, necessary, and ultimate resolution lies in the self-negation of capital's development. Read the original if you want a philosophical reading of debt that links Marx's early and late writings to contemporary debates on financialisation, household debt and bankruptcy law.

A critique of positive philosophy: Feuerbach and Marx 肯定哲学批判：费尔巴哈与马克思 Liu Senlin Liu Senlin takes up Feuerbach's little-studied 1838 essay "Critique of Positive Philosophy", the first Young Hegelian review of the late Schelling's positive philosophy. The article asks what the essay reveals about Feuerbach's shift of thought and about the path from Hegel through Schelling and Feuerbach to Marx. Liu argues that the essay criticises Schelling's positive philosophy and, beyond it, the "negative" speculative philosophy that Hegel represents, while pointing towards a "new and only positive philosophy". The article reconstructs the essay's two senses of the relation between "philosophy" and "speculation", then traces its echoes in Marx and Engels. It draws on The Holy Family, The German Ideology, Marx's letter to Feuerbach, Feuerbach's later writings on Hegel, and commentary by Frank, Xian Gang and Wang Ding. It also brings in Stirner, whose key concepts Liu presents as reversed borrowings from Schelling's Philosophy of Revelation. Liu's core claim is that Feuerbach inherits Schelling's stress on sensuousness, becoming and existence but finds Schelling's positive philosophy half-hearted: still subordinate to negative philosophy, bound to religion and myth, and prone to arbitrary subjectivity. Feuerbach wants to free it and reduce theology to anthropology. Liu uses Marx and Engels's remark that Feuerbach "first attacked Hegel" with sober philosophy against drunken speculation to argue that it refers to this essay, not to the 1839 critique of Hegel. In Liu's account, Feuerbach's overcorrection against subjectivity pushes him into contemplative naturalism. He drops the subjectivity and active practice that Schelling, Hegel and Stirner kept, and Marx later criticises this. Liu concludes that Marx and Engels corrected Feuerbach in several ways. They replaced "positive philosophy" with positive science, treated the sensuous as needing critical reflection and as practice, and combined sensuousness with rationality and essence. Marx's Hegel, Liu says, is the Hegel already criticised by Schelling and Feuerbach, so historical materialism emerged from reworking the Hegel–Schelling dispute over negative and positive philosophy. Read the original if you study the Hegel–Schelling–Feuerbach–Stirner–Marx lineage and want a detailed textual argument about how Marx's practical materialism emerged.

Reflections on modernization based on the revolution in Marx's term "metabolism" 基于马克思“物质变换”术语革命的现代化思考 Ye Haitao Ye Haitao asks what Marx's concept of "metabolism" (wuzhi bianhuan, literally material exchange) can reveal about two centuries of modernization and the ecological crisis that accompanied it. The article argues that Marx critically remade a physiological and chemical term into a historical-materialist category, and that this category lets modernization be read as the social reshaping of the relationship between humans and nature. On that basis Ye contends that capital-led Western modernization opened an irreparable "metabolic rift", while Chinese modernization, defined by harmony between humanity and nature, forms a new historical pattern of metabolism. The article first traces how the concept took shape in Marx's work from the London Notebooks of 1851 through the 1857–58 manuscripts to Capital. It draws on Daniels, Moleschott and Liebig, then reviews how John Bellamy Foster, Paul Burkett and Saito Kohei, with Alfred Schmidt and others, developed metabolic rift theory. It then applies the concept to the history of Western industrialization and ends with a three-stage account of China's own path, from the socialist revolution period through reform and opening up to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Ye holds that Marx's concept has three levels: natural metabolism, social metabolism and the human–nature metabolism mediated by labour. The author treats the last as the most basic. Under capital, primitive accumulation, enclosures and the commodification of nature broke older forms of metabolism and wedged a rift between people and the land. In Ye's reading this rift widened into global ecological crisis, a case of "reflexive modernization". Ye therefore takes "capital-centredness" to be the chief defect of Western modernization. Against it, Chinese modernization is said to be "people-centred" and to combine purposiveness with conformity to natural law. The slogan "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" is presented as resolving the apparent conflict between growth and environmental protection. Ye concludes that human–nature relations are the basic dimension of any modernization, and that the establishment of the socialist state system gives Chinese modernization an institutional basis for going beyond Western modernization ecologically. The author adds that metabolism in China is still "in progress" rather than complete, and points to Marx's vision of associated producers rationally regulating their exchange with nature. Chinese modernization is described as offering Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach toward that goal. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist philosopher links metabolic rift theory from Western ecological Marxism to official ecological civilization discourse.

The emergence, true meaning and practical path of the ecological wealth outlook of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化生态财富观的出场逻辑、本真涵义与实践路径 Liu Ying Liu Xigang Liu Ying and Liu Xigang ask how the relationship between ecology and wealth should be understood within Chinese modernization, and argue that an "ecological wealth outlook" has taken shape as a concentrated expression of its essential requirements. Starting from Xi Jinping's 2018 statement that lucid waters and lush mountains are both natural and ecological wealth and social and economic wealth, the authors present this outlook as the unity of three things: a necessary logic of emergence, a distinctive meaning and a systematic practical path. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the historical, theoretical and practical logic by which the outlook emerged: the Party's attention to ecology from the new-democratic revolution to the new era, Marxist views of nature and wealth, and present resource and environmental bottlenecks. The second sets out the outlook's meaning along three dimensions: goal, core and demand. The third proposes a path of "directional guidance, multi-dimensional drivers, institutional safeguards". The authors contrast the outlook with a Western "material wealth outlook" that, in their account, serves capital valorisation and treats unprocessed nature as outside social wealth. Against this, they say the ecological wealth outlook aims at harmony between humanity and nature and holds material, spiritual and ecological wealth to together make up social wealth. Its core, they argue, follows a logic of people rather than capital, aiming at common prosperity and fairness towards future generations. Its demand is the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilization. For practice, the authors propose building the goal of ecological wealth creation into every stage, field and driving force of modernization. They add three drivers: an effective market, a capable government and the endogenous energy of the people. They also propose institutional safeguards: stronger ecological laws, a fair distribution system for ecological wealth, and assessment and supervision of cadres, including lifelong accountability for ecological damage. The authors conclude that putting this outlook into practice is a cornerstone for the sustainable development of socialist modernization and for achieving economic growth together with environmental protection. They treat it as a Marxist-grounded alternative to the Western modernization model. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how current Party theory links ecological civilization, the theory of wealth and Chinese modernization, including its proposals on law, distribution and cadre assessment.

Accelerating the green transformation of the development model against the background of new quality productive forces: rationale and pathways 新质生产力背景下加快发展方式绿色转型的理与路 Hu Changsheng An Xiaoxing Hu Changsheng and An Xiaoxing ask how the green transformation of the development model can be accelerated now that new quality productive forces have become a Party priority. They argue that the two are not separate, one-directional agendas but mutually constitutive: green transformation supplies the ecological foundation and value orientation of new quality productive forces, while the latter supply innovation and technical support. The article, published in 2025 in the Journal of Harbin Institute of Technology (Social Sciences), builds on Xi Jinping's statement that new quality productive forces are themselves green productive forces. The article is organised in three parts. It first sets out three logical reasons why green transformation is necessary: it is an essential requirement of new quality productive forces, an expression of their value stance, and a way to consolidate their green foundation. It then examines four dimensions of transformation (greening of economic growth, remaking the three elements of productive forces, resource conservation and intensive use, and green restructuring of production functions and consumer preferences) before analysing obstacles. It closes with practical paths in education, ecology, industry, institutions, consumption and international cooperation. In the authors' account, conventional growth theory treats natural resources as unlimited exogenous inputs and equates GDP growth with development. New quality productive forces, by contrast, bring ecological boundaries into endogenous growth, so that environmental quality drives rather than constrains growth. The authors identify five obstacles: a tension between economic rationality and ecological rationality, in which market prices and national accounts fail to capture ecological value; path dependence and weak industrial coordination; technological and talent bottlenecks amid external technology restrictions; institutional gaps in structure, timeliness and policy coordination, including data rights; and weak public understanding of green living. The authors also stress the inertia generated by China's parallel pursuit of industrialization, urbanization, agricultural modernization, informatization and greening. To respond, Hu and An propose integrating green education, green technology and green talent training; building systemic ecological governance with digital monitoring; developing green industries with price signals, subsidies and tax incentives; deepening institutional and legal innovation; promoting green consumption and lifestyles; and expanding international green cooperation, including through the Belt and Road Initiative, standard-setting and communication of Xi Jinping's ecological thought. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese policy-academic account of how green transition is linked to the concept of new quality productive forces, with detailed lists of obstacles and measures.

The jurisprudential logic of implementing the core socialist values in judicial adjudication 司法贯彻社会主义核心价值观的法理逻辑 Wang Jianguo Zhang Qianyi Wang and Zhang ask how courts can apply the core socialist values in individual judgments without turning them into empty slogans or letting them displace legal rules. They argue that the values hold the position of a "quasi-source of law" (zhun fayuan). In their account, this status permits a supplementary role in legal reasoning, but never a role as the basis of a judgment, and needs a systematic method to be applied reliably. The article starts from the policy trajectory since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the 2018 constitutional amendment and the Supreme People's Court's guidance documents. It then analyses six batches of model cases, 64 in total, issued by the Supreme People's Court, together with data on judgments published on the national court judgments website. Using these materials, it identifies recurring problems in current practice and proposes a reconstructed reasoning framework. The authors find that only 13 of the 64 model cases mention the values in the "judgment result" section, and that in some of these the values made no real difference to the outcome. In ordinary judgments they identify three faults: equating the values' legal meaning with moral meaning, "rule escape" (citing the values where a clear statutory rule exists), and "label-sticking" citation without reasoning. Their remedy has three parts. First, the twelve keywords should be turned into a concrete pairing of "motive plus specific behaviour pattern". Second, judges should choose keywords step by step from the citizen level, through the social level, to the national level. Third, the traditional judicial syllogism should be recast as a "recursive four-step syllogism" (digui si duan lun), in which a values-based second minor premise is added and combined with comparison to similar cases. The authors conclude that citing the values adds legitimacy and persuasiveness to judgments, but that vague invocation or substitution for legal norms undermines the stability and authority of law. They call for a complete methodology, along with regular revision and clearing of model and database cases, so that procedural fairness secures substantive fairness. Read the original if you study Chinese judicial practice, the legal status of ideological values, or the detailed analysis of Supreme People's Court model cases and the proposed reasoning model.

Systems integration in advancing comprehensive deepening of reform: theoretical foundations, objectives and practical path 系统集成推进全面深化改革的理论根基、目标指向与实践进路 Zhang Yonggang Jia Yunfei The article takes up the methodological question raised by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for strengthening "systems integration" so that reforms in different fields work together efficiently. Zhang and Jia argue that systems integration has become the core methodology of further comprehensively deepening reform. In their account, reform logic is shifting from early "breakthroughs at key points" towards "systemic coupling" and overall effectiveness, which they present as a response to fragmented and department-bound reform. The authors build a three-part framework: theoretical foundations, objective orientation and practical path. The foundations section covers Marxist systems thinking, traditional Chinese philosophy, modern systems science and the Party's own practice. The objectives section treats three goals: improving socialism with Chinese characteristics as an institutional system, modernizing national governance, and high-quality development. The practical section is organised around top-level design, coordinated advance and dynamic adjustment. Zhang and Jia derive three features of systems integration (wholeness, systemic interconnection and dynamism) from each of their four sources. They draw on Engels, Marx, Bertalanffy and Laozi and Zhuangzi's idea of the unity of heaven and humanity. They illustrate these features with examples such as the "streamline administration, delegate power, improve regulation and services" reforms, the national unified market, rural revitalization and regional coordination. The three objectives are described as a closed loop in which institutions provide the vehicle for governance and governance underpins development. On practice, the authors describe the fundamental, basic and important institutions as trunk, branches and foliage of one system. They call for reform goals to be ranked by level, stage and priority, for measures to be coordinated across and within fields, and for monitoring and feedback mechanisms so that reform can adapt to changing conditions and to people's needs. The authors conclude that systems integration gives reform a distinctive logical framework, one that helps turn institutional strengths into governance effectiveness and supports Chinese modernization. They call for adherence to systems thinking and stronger systems integration as national governance continues to be modernized. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link the Party's reform method to Marxism, classical Chinese thought and systems science, and how that method is applied to policy fields.

Advancing the Party's self-reform by improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 以健全全面从严治党体系推进党的自我革命 Sun Daozhuang Zhao Fuke Xi Jinping has described improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the "effective path" to advancing the Party's self-reform. Sun and Zhao note that existing scholarship mostly studies how to build this system in practice, while the basic question of why it is an effective path has not been settled. They answer by asking what makes it effective, in what sense it is a path, and how it can drive the Party's self-reform. Their thesis is that the system's own properties match the inner demands of self-reform. The article, published in the Journal of Harbin Institute of Technology (Social Sciences Edition), is organised in three steps. It first sets out the criteria of effectiveness: results, speed, cost-benefit and overall function. It then treats the system as a path formed by history, theory and practice, and surveys the Party's rigorous self-governance from the Mao Zedong period through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally it describes the system's structure and proposes ways to improve it. The authors argue that effectiveness has three parts: strengthening the Party's overall leadership, pooling the forces of Party governance and securing long-term rule. They say it also needs speed, quality, controlled cost and returns that the people can see. They describe a vertical hierarchy of institutions, from the Party Constitution and democratic centralism down to Party regulations. It spans six areas of Party building and runs through a "establish–implement–revise" cycle. Three features, in their account, link the system to self-reform. Its integrated, interlocking nature ties self-reform to the Party's mission of social revolution. Its linkage reflects the dialectical "self-negation" by which the Party must overcome corruption, which they define as the alienation of power. Its emergence and adaptability allow gains to accumulate like compound interest and let the Party respond to new risks. The authors call for refining the vertical institutional system, planning the six areas systematically, and strengthening the supply, operation and updating of rules. They also call for using AI and big data in Party governance. They conclude that the system's central task is to bring Party power within the rule of law, so that power belonging to the people stays under popular control and reflects the people-oriented nature of Party rule. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building scholarship justifies the system through systems theory, dialectics and cost-effectiveness reasoning, or want to track the official vocabulary around the Party's self-reform.

Three-dimensional interpretation of shaping the image of a Marxist party from the perspective of self-reform in the new era 新时代自我革命视域下马克思主义政党形象塑造的三维阐释 Xu Fengzhen Zheng Pei'e Xu Fengzhen and Zheng Pei'e take up the relationship between the Communist Party of China's self-reform and the shaping of its image as a Marxist party. Starting from the 2021 Party resolution's conclusion that an advanced Marxist party is forged through constant self-reform, they argue that the two are bound by an internal logic: the process of self-reform is itself the process of building the Party's image. They treat this as necessary for keeping the Party advanced and pure, and for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The article is organised around three questions: why, what and how. The first part sets out the value of image-building, the second describes how it has appeared in practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and the third proposes ways to deepen it. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on Party documents, regulations and statistics, such as figures on Party membership, intra-Party regulations and anti-corruption cases. On the first question, the authors hold that Xi Jinping Thought on self-reform supplies theoretical guidance, while the spirit of self-reform supplies moral support. They say this spirit shapes the Party as responsible, mission-driven and clean. On the second, they link each strand of Party building to a specific image: political building to a Party that takes charge of the whole situation, ideological building to firm belief, organisational building to tight organisation, conduct to a clean political climate, discipline to strict order, institutions to rule-based governance, and anti-corruption work to integrity. On the third, they propose that the Party solve the "unique problems of a large party" through the "six always" questions, tell the story of its self-reform, and use home-hosted diplomacy, new media and scholarly exchange to spread it. They also suggest recasting that story in terms that international audiences can accept, with anti-corruption cooperation as an example. The authors conclude that self-reform and image-building are an organic whole, with theory, practice and values reinforcing one another. They call for the Party to keep pursuing self-reform without pause, so that it becomes a Marxist governing party that is vigorous, trusted by the people and able to withstand all tests. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party-building scholarship links discipline, anti-corruption and institutional reform to the Party's public image and external communication.

The Global Governance Initiative offers Global South countries development opportunities and momentum for cooperation 全球治理倡议为全球南方国家提供发展机遇和合作动能 Wang Bo This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 11 March 2026, argues that the Global Governance Initiative, which it presents as China's latest public good for the world after the "three major initiatives", gives the Global South new development opportunities and momentum for cooperation. Wang Bo contends that it helps move the international political and economic order in a more democratic, just and reasonable direction. The piece first describes the case for reform: the Global South's growing weight, and a governance system that Wang says is still dominated by Western countries. It then sets out the initiative's five core principles, four ways it benefits the Global South, and China's own practice as a Global South member. Wang cites figures that the Global South accounts for over 40% of world output and 80% of global growth contribution over the past 20 years. Against this, the author says the current system fails to reflect that shift and cannot handle problems such as climate change and public health crises amid unilateralism and protectionism. The five principles are sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centred approach and action orientation. The four benefits are practical development support, stronger solidarity and South-South cooperation, a higher status and voice that closes the "representation deficit", and greater mutual learning among civilizations. Wang concludes that China is both proposer and practitioner, pointing to the Belt and Road Initiative, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the New Development Bank, the Paris Agreement and the Kunming-Montreal biodiversity framework. The author reports support from over 150 countries and organisations and a UN "Group of Friends" with over 40 founding members. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the initiative is presented to a domestic audience in official commentary.

Advancing the building of the Chinese nation as a community and realising national rejuvenation 推进中华民族共同体建设 实现中华民族伟大复兴 Wang Zhimin Published in the People's Daily on 12 March 2026, this commentary takes up the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee's (2025) recommendation for the 15th Five-Year Plan to "forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation" and advance the building of the Chinese nation as a community. Wang argues that this task is the core requirement of ethnic unity work in the coming five years. In Wang's account, it is also the mainline of the Party's ethnic work and a necessary condition of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first traces the Party's leadership of ethnic work from its founding through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second assesses the theoretical and practical strength of Xi Jinping's ideas on ethnic work, including their relevance for other countries. The third sets out five areas of work for the Chinese modernization drive. Wang's central claim is that the idea of building the community is a product of the Two Integrations, which join Marxist ethnic theory with China's concrete realities and its fine traditional culture. In this reading, the path differs both from the Western "one nation, one state" model and from the ethnic governance of feudal dynasties. Wang cites results as evidence: 31.21 million people in ethnic minority areas lifted out of poverty, and the combined GDP of the five autonomous regions rising from 6,012.9 billion to 8,376.6 billion yuan between 2020 and 2024. Wang contrasts this with other states that, in the article's account, pursue forced assimilation, tolerate separatism or practise divide-and-rule, and presents China's approach as a model for global ethnic governance. For future work, Wang calls for strengthening Party leadership and national security safeguards in ethnic affairs. Other proposals are to build a shared spiritual home through cultural identity, to speed high-quality development in ethnic areas, to promote interaction and mixing among ethnic groups through mutually embedded social structures, and to govern ethnic affairs by law, including a planned law on promoting ethnic unity and progress. Wang presents these as the way to gather strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of current Party discourse on ethnic policy, with the official statistics and policy priorities for the 15th Five-Year Plan period.)

The development and practice of the theory of Party-spirit cultivation in the new era 新时代党性修养理论的发展与实践探析 Zhu Yan Zhou Zhudong Huang Li Zhu Yan, Zhou Zhudong and Huang Li ask how the theory and practice of Party-spirit cultivation (dangxing xiuyang) have developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They argue that Xi Jinping's statements on the subject, which call it the \"study of the heart\" of Communists and a lifelong required course, form an original body of ideas. In the authors' account, these ideas are part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and guide the Party's self-reform. The article first sets out why cultivation is needed and what it means, then lists three routes: theoretical study, tempering through work practice, and criticism and self-criticism. It then reviews how the Central Committee has strengthened Party spirit through eight rounds of concentrated education campaigns between 2013 and 2025, the anti-corruption drive, and Party regulations. The final sections assess results in six areas: theoretical, political, moral, disciplinary and work-style cultivation. The authors' central claim is that Party spirit does not rise automatically with seniority or rank and must be built through lifelong effort. They treat campaigns, such as the mass-line campaign of 2013 and the study of Party discipline in 2024, as the main vehicle for concentrated education. Daily branch study and Party school training provide the regular kind. Anti-corruption work targets the \"key minority\" of leaders, grassroots \"flies and ants\" and fugitives abroad. The article cites official figures: 4.648 million cases filed since 2012 and 97.4 per cent satisfaction in a 2022 survey. Rules are to be made systematically and enforced strictly, so that discipline becomes a \"high-voltage line\". The authors conclude that cultivation is a systematic, long-term project. They call for better institutional supply, for including it in the modernization of state governance capacity, and for turning Party spirit from an \"organisational requirement\" into a \"value pursuit\". They also urge the \"key minority\" to set an example, and they want problems of \"disconnect between knowing and doing\" and formalism to be resolved. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the post-2012 education campaigns and anti-corruption statistics are presented as evidence of improved Party discipline and conduct.

Basic experience of the Communist Party of China in Party-spirit education 中国共产党党性教育的基本经验 Han Qiang Ma Jingming How has the Communist Party of China (CPC) cultivated "Party spirit" (dangxing) in its members over more than a century, and what lessons follow? Han Qiang and Ma Jingming define Party-spirit education as the Party's internal education of members, with leading cadres as the main focus, aimed at preserving its character as the vanguard of the working class, the Chinese people and the Chinese nation. They argue that political cultivation comes first, and they draw out six basic experiences from this history. The article opens with the 2023 revised regulations on cadre education and Xi Jinping's December 2024 remarks on lifelong self-cultivation. It cites 2024 discipline-inspection figures (877,000 cases filed) to show that the anti-corruption situation remains severe and that this education is never finished. It then moves through the Party's history, from the Anyuan and Beijing Party schools of the Great Revolution period through Yan'an to the present, and cites the key regulations and five-year plans of the Xi Jinping era. The core claim is that Party spirit is not innate and does not rise automatically with seniority or rank, so it must be built through education and practice. The authors list the experiences: keep ideals and convictions at the centre; uphold Party leadership and the authority of the Central Committee; test Party spirit in practice; safeguard unity as the Party's life; use persuasion and the formula "unity–criticism–unity", learned after past excesses such as the expanded anti-rightist campaign; and rely on institutional safeguards. They add that confronting major questions of each era produces ideological unity. In their account the Yan'an rectification campaign is the model of concentrated education. Party schools, cadre academies and the national Party-education plans carry out the work. The authors conclude that Party-spirit education is a key means of keeping the Party advanced and pure. They call for continuing its traditions while widening content and methods. They also call for tackling superficiality, formalism and activity-for-its-own-sake, so that cadres are moved for a lifetime rather than for a moment. They want a multi-actor, multi-channel pattern consolidated, with lasting mechanisms. Read the original if you want a Party-school perspective on how Chinese scholars summarise the history, institutions and regulations of Party-spirit education.

Ancient Chinese supervision systems: evolution, characteristics and lessons 中国古代监察制度：演变、特征及启示 Qu Xiaoshuang Qu Xiaoshuang asks what the long history of supervision (jiancha) institutions in ancient China can teach contemporary China. The article argues that these institutions, which arose early and were tightly designed, served to protect imperial power and discipline officialdom. In Qu's reading, they remained dependent on the monarch and so could never effectively restrain supreme power, while offering experience that is relevant to deepening supervision reform today. The article first defines supervision power as a power parallel to legislative, executive and judicial power. It then traces five periods: the Pre-Qin beginnings, formation under the Qin and Han, maturity under the Sui and Tang, transformation under the Song, and full elaboration under the Ming and Qing. It also discusses debates over when the system originated. Qu singles out the Han, Tang and Ming as the most typical stages. Qu draws out three threads. First, supervision officials sent to the localities repeatedly acquired military and administrative power, as with Han regional inspectors, Tang military governors and Ming–Qing governors-general and governors. The author argues that this produced separatism and corrupt officialdom and reflected a flaw in one-directional, top-down supervision. Second, the inspection tour (xunshi) system developed from temporary dispatches to standing, professionalised practice, and Qu compares it with the Party's present system. Third, supervisory officials were selected, promoted, rotated and punished under strict rules, with high rank and rewards to motivate them. Qu concludes that ancient supervision, rooted in imperial power and an integrated power structure, lacked internal checks and could be turned into a weapon of factional struggle. Qu contrasts this with the Party's full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the 2018 Supervision Law and the Party's self-reform. The article calls for strengthening Party leadership of discipline inspection and supervision, building a Party-regulation system, and developing discipline inspection and supervision studies as a discipline that draws on ancient experience. Read the original if you study the history of Chinese supervision institutions or how Party scholars draw on imperial-era practice to frame current anti-corruption reform.

A theoretical account of how the Eight-Point Regulation has changed China 八项规定改变中国的学理化阐释 Gao Yazhou Sang Xuecheng The article asks how and why the Central Committee's Eight-Point Regulation on improving Party conduct and staying close to the masses, adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012), has changed China. The authors say existing scholarship covers its content, origins and implementation, but has not explained the underlying mechanism. They argue that a modest rule on conduct became a lever for the Party's self-reform and for wider social change, and that this rests on uniting the "power of truth" with the "power of personality". After a literature review, the article is built in three parts. The first sets out what the regulation changed in three dimensions: the governing actors (Party cadres), the organisation of power and public spending, and social customs. The second explains why it could have such effects. The third proposes ways to turn the new conduct into lasting custom, which the authors call "transforming conduct into custom". The core argument is that the regulation joins the truth of correct theory with the personal example of the Party's fine traditions, and turns the principle of putting the people first into concrete daily rules. The authors say it worked through a governing logic of three steps: starting from "key small matters" such as banquets, official cars and meeting styles, building a systematic network of rules, and enforcing them rigidly through accountability, routine supervision and special campaigns. They add that it spread through pressure and example from the "key minority" of leading cadres to the Party majority. In the authors' account this moved discipline from external constraint towards habit, and its example influenced government conduct and then popular customs. For lasting effect, the authors call for three things. The first is more precise rules, with refined implementation measures, list-based management and feedback on rectification. The second is education: theoretical study and Party-spirit training so that cadres move from outside constraint to inner conviction. The third is cultural work, including a culture of integrity, drawing on traditional and revolutionary resources, and public opinion that supports the rules. Read the original if you want a Party-school scholarly account of how the Party explains the Eight-Point Regulation's wider effects and its plans to make it permanent.

A systematic account of how the Communist Party of China can achieve long-term governance 中国共产党何以能够实现长期执政的系统性认识 Jian Jiaojie Liu Jingbei Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that achieving long-term governance is a fundamental question the Party must answer, the authors ask why the Communist Party of China (CPC) is able to govern over the long term. They argue that existing scholarship explains mainly why long-term governance is necessary and how to achieve it, but not why it is possible. Their answer is that the Party, as a mission-driven party, has unified political, historical and practical logic into a distinctive system of governing advantages. The article reviews recent studies and then builds a composite analytical framework: Party authority, Party adaptation, value consensus, institutional resilience and civilizational genes. Each element corresponds to one of five sections: Party leadership, self-reform, the supremacy of the people, the socialist system, and the Two Integrations. The sections draw on the Party's history from the new-democratic revolution through the post-1949 period and reform and opening up to the post-18th Congress (2012) era. On leadership, the authors hold that centralised and unified leadership, with the Party Central Committee at its core, gives strategic continuity, mass mobilisation and the capacity to concentrate resources, and they contrast China's stability with what they call Western turmoil. On self-reform, they present it as the Party's defining political strength and its "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall, advanced through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On the people, they describe a shift from "representing" to "becoming" the people, realised through whole-process people's democracy, and set it against Western party systems they portray as serving narrow interests. The socialist system and the Two Integrations, especially integration with fine traditional Chinese culture, are said to supply institutional durability and cultural legitimacy. The authors conclude that long-term governance rests on unifying five things with it: Party leadership, the supremacy of the people, institution-building, cultural integration and self-reform. They warn that global uncertainty, heavy reform tasks and problems peculiar to a large party threaten this governance. They call for continued strengthening of governing capacity, the Party's overall leadership, risk awareness and a firm people's stance in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how current Party-building scholarship justifies the CPC's long-term governance through a five-part framework.

A scientific path for implementing democratic centralism in the new era 新时代贯彻民主集中制的科学路径 Wu Hui Ding Yongqiang Wu Hui and Ding Yongqiang ask how democratic centralism, which they call the Communist Party's fundamental organisational principle and leadership system, can be carried out more effectively in the new era. Following Xi Jinping's remark that it must be advanced through both cadres and mechanisms, they argue that persistent implementation problems can be solved only through a systematic path: educating and training leading cadres, having leaders set an example, and building up institutions. The article opens by setting out four reasons the principle matters: it upholds the authority of the Party Central Committee, underpins the modernisation of state governance, joins scientific decision-making to efficient execution, and sustains a clean political ecology within the Party. It then examines four shortcomings that Xi Jinping has identified since 2013, and their causes. The remainder is divided into two parts, one on leading cadres as the "key minority" and one on institutional mechanisms. The authors describe the four shortcomings as too little promotion of democracy, too little correct centralisation, too little criticism and too little strict discipline. They attribute these to weak Party spirit, unclear theoretical understanding, imprecise institutional design (for example vague definitions of "major matters") and lax enforcement of accountability. For cadres, they propose training in theory, Party rules and working methods, drawn from Mao Zedong's "Methods of Work of Party Committees" and the "sixteen-character principle". They also call for example-setting by Politburo members, by first secretaries ("squad leaders" rather than "patriarchs") and by team members. For institutions, they propose collective-leadership rules, wider participation by Party members and Party congress delegates, and the Two Upholds. They add a request-and-report system with "must request", "should report" and "no need to request" lists, together with supervision, graded accountability and an early-warning system with indicators such as collective-decision rates and the share of dissenting views adopted. The authors conclude that democratic centralism is the Party's greatest institutional advantage. They call for institutional confidence and continued refinement of the system, so that democracy and centralism are united and the Party becomes "a piece of hard steel", providing institutional support for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-school account of how the current leadership proposes to operationalise democratic centralism, including its proposed lists, indicators and accountability measures.

The historical significance and lessons of leading the troops to Jinggangshan and the Tongdao change of course 引兵井冈与通道转兵的历史意义及启示 Zhang Youliang Writing in a Party-school journal in 2025, Zhang Youliang takes up two turning points in the history of the Communist Party of China: Mao Zedong's decision in 1927 to lead the Autumn Harvest Uprising troops to Jinggangshan, and the change of the Central Red Army's route at Tongdao in December 1934. Zhang argues that the two events are comparable, since each combined historical necessity with contingency, and that both opened the way to revolutionary victory. The article draws lessons from them for present-day officials. The article compares the two events under three headings borrowed from the traditional triad of favourable timing, terrain and human harmony: deep historical causes, geographical and popular advantages, and Mao's personal role. It then moves to lessons. It is organised as a parallel narrative, from the failed attacks on cities and the Wenjiashi and Sanwan decisions to the Xiang River defeat and the emergency meeting at Tongdao, followed by a set of contemporary implications. On causes, Zhang holds that the Party's dependence on Comintern instructions and the successive 'Left' errors of Qu Qiubai, Li Lisan and Wang Ming produced the failures that forced both changes of course. On terrain and people, Zhang cites Jinggangshan's remoteness and economic base, local armed forces under Yuan Wencai, Tongdao's strategic position and the weak Guizhou forces, and the loss of confidence in Bo Gu and Otto Braun among Red Army commanders. On Mao, the article stresses his insistence on turning from cities to the countryside, his reorganisation of the army at Sanwan, and his persuasion of colleagues on the long march. Zhang presents the Tongdao decision as the start of Mao's emergence as the core of the leadership. Zhang draws five lessons: seeking truth from facts; adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; the Two Establishes and the importance of a leadership core; the Party's self-reform; and the ability to recognise, adapt to and initiate change amid a rapidly shifting international environment. The author links these to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Party-history account that ties the Jinggangshan and Tongdao decisions to current Party doctrine on leadership and self-reform.

Why Soviet-area cadres developed a good work style, and what it means for today 苏区干部好作风成因及时代启示 Xiao Xiaohua Xiao Xiaohua asks why cadres in the Central Soviet Area (1931–34) acquired the work style summed up in a Xingguo folk song, and what that experience offers Party building today. The article holds that the style, which it defines as wholehearted service to the people, truth-seeking and pragmatism, hard struggle, honesty in office and striving for first-class work, followed from the Party's nature and purpose and was then shaped by its environment, leadership example, institutions and cultural inheritance. The article, published in the Journal of the Jinggangshan Cadre Academy of China in 2025, works through five sets of causes. These are the Party's class character, ideals and mission; the political atmosphere inside the Party; the example set by leaders such as Mao Zedong, Zhu De and Zhou Enlai; systems of education, supervision and discipline; and inherited resources. These include the Jinggangshan period, traditional Chinese culture, and Hakka and Luling local culture. A final section draws lessons for the present. Xiao's central argument is that style expresses a party's nature and purpose. The Soviet constitutional documents defined the regime as a democratic dictatorship of workers and peasants, and revolutionary conviction gave cadres their resolve. Xiao then shows how organisational life, criticism and self-criticism, and model-praising newspaper columns kept the Party's political atmosphere healthy. Leaders led by example in studying theory, conducting investigations, doing voluntary labour and saving grain and oil. Education programmes, inspection bodies, audit and anti-corruption regulations and inspection tours added institutional constraints. Xiao also argues that traditional values such as seeking truth from facts and putting the people first were transformed into the new style. Xiao draws four lessons for the new era, linking them to the Eight-point Regulation and Xi Jinping's statements. They are to arm cadres theoretically with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; to keep close ties with the people and oppose formalism and bureaucracy; to have leading cadres set an example as a "lead goose"; and to build a mechanism of education, restraint, supervision and punishment, with zero tolerance for violations. Xiao adds that culture, including the Soviet Area spirit, should be drawn on to purify the Party's political ecology. Read the original if you study the history of Party work style and discipline in the Central Soviet Area, or how Party scholars link revolutionary-era experience to current campaigns.

Practical paths and significance of carrying forward the Long March spirit in the new era 新时代传承长征精神的实践路径与意义探析 Zhu Hong Li Wenjia Zhu Hong and Li Wenjia ask how the Long March spirit, long treated mainly through historical study and commemoration, can be turned into a working resource under socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. They argue that the spirit is a dynamic structure that has moved from political mobilisation to governance guidance. In their account it is now embedded in institutions, culture and communication, and supports Chinese modernization. The article first traces the spirit through four stages: its original formation during the Long March of the 1930s, its deepening in socialist construction, its extension in the reform and opening up period through the idea of a "new Long March", and its dual institutional and cultural embedding since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out a five-part structure of belief, organisation, action, communication and cohesion. Finally it examines four fields of value (political, social, cultural and international) and illustrates them with cases such as Ninghua's "Long March College", Ruijin volunteer teams, Guangxi's Xiang River memorial sites and the Guizhou Long March National Cultural Park. The core argument is that each dimension of the structure has its own route of transmission. Belief is cultivated through renewed ideological and political education, including integrated courses, case banks and experiential or digital "memory communities". Organisational capacity is carried by turning red resources into institutions through legislation, cadre-training academies and grassroots Party building. Action appears in social collaboration, for example volunteers invoking the spirit during the 2021 Zhengzhou floods. Communication and cohesion rely on digital re-creation, immersive red culture-and-tourism, and international outreach such as the "Long March" rockets and the Belt and Road Initiative. The authors also note a tension between authoritative narratives and user-generated reinterpretation online. The authors conclude that the Long March spirit has moved beyond static commemoration to become a cultural gene of institutional design and a support for the national narrative. They call for it to move past ritualised and symbolic communication and be integrated more fully into the systems of governance, cultural innovation and international communication. In their view this would turn it from red memory into a civilisational resource and from national spirit into a global value. Read the original if you want a survey of how Chinese scholars and local institutions describe the practical institutionalisation of Party spirit, with many regional examples.

Turning the institutional advantages of Party leadership over economic work into governance effectiveness: a perspective from the Five-Year Plans 切实把党领导经济工作的制度优势转化为治理效能——基于五年规划的视角 Wu Zhiyuan Wu Zhiyuan asks how the institutional advantages of Party leadership over economic work can be converted into effective governance, and takes the Five-Year Plans as the vehicle for answering. The article argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the system of Party leadership over the economy has matured, but that weaknesses lie mainly in implementation: Wu lists institutional failure, idle or empty institutions and distorted execution. The Five-Year Plan, Wu contends, is the key mechanism by which Party leadership is embedded in economic governance. The article opens by justifying its focus on execution rather than institutional design, offering four reasons: advantages must be proved through governance, the same institution performs differently in practice, designers should think like implementers, and economic governance is under pressure. It then analyses the Plans at three stages: drafting, framework and content, and implementation safeguards. A later section draws practical lessons for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), using the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) as its starting point. Wu argues that the drafting procedure (Party Central Committee proposal, State Council outline, National People's Congress approval) embodies the Party's "overall command and coordination" and the relations between Party and government and between Party and masses. The Plans are also said to apply four governance methods: systemic, law-based, comprehensive and source governance. In Wu's reading, this unites Party leadership, the market's decisive role and an effective government, and lets the Plans overcome both "government failure" and "market failure". Because the National People's Congress must approve a plan, Wu calls it a "compulsory" legal route from institutional advantage to governance effectiveness. For the 15th Five-Year Plan, Wu calls for strengthening Party leadership across the plan cycle, enforcing implementation responsibilities, monitoring and evaluation, and incentives and constraints. Wu also urges attention to a people-centred orientation, the development of new quality productive forces suited to local conditions, and a unified planning system that respects regional characteristics. Wu adds that governance, reform and policy must be deployed together. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the Five-Year Plan is presented as a mechanism of Party leadership and of what its authors expect of the 15th Plan.

High-quality development as the theme of the 15th Five-Year Plan period: historical evolution, theoretical meaning and practical requirements “十五五”时期以推动高质量发展为主题：历史演进、理论内涵和实践要求 Zhang Peng Following the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), whose Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan name high-quality development as the theme of economic and social development for 2026–2030, Zhang asks how this theme emerged, what it means and what it requires in practice. The article argues that the theme is both a precise reading of China's current stage and a strategic choice aimed at basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035. It builds a framework that unites historical, theoretical and practical logic. The article has three parts. The first traces three historical stages: the early People's Republic (restoration and heavy industry, solving the problem of 'having or not having'), the reform era from 1978 (growth-centred, with the first signs of attention to quality in successive plans), and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part sets out the theoretical content of high-quality development and its links to the new development philosophy, the new development pattern and new quality productive forces. The third part turns to the practical requirements drawn from the Recommendations' 'five orientations' and their twelve areas of strategic tasks. Zhang's central claim is that high-quality development is a 'brand-new development theory' that enriches Marxist principles. In this reading it embodies the new development philosophy's five dimensions (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing), the dialectic of 'effective improvement in quality and reasonable growth in quantity', and a people-centred orientation. The author says it surpasses the older 'growth equals development' view and cites China's Human Development Index rise from 0.713 (2012) to 0.788 (2023). New quality productive forces supply the new momentum, and the domestic–international 'dual circulation' is presented as a development of Marx's reproduction schemes. The practical requirements range from the real economy, modern industry and domestic demand to reform, innovation, opening up, common prosperity, cultural development and strengthening Party leadership. Zhang concludes that high-quality development is a long and arduous task requiring a self-reliant Chinese economics, better policy tools and precise implementation. The author claims it offers Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to world development, and challenges the notion that modernization equals Westernization. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the 15th Five-Year Plan's guiding theme is justified historically and theoretically, and of its policy agenda.

The generative mechanism, value implications and practical requirements of the "Second Integration" “第二个结合”的生成机理、价值意蕴和实践要求 Su Xinghong Chen Ruixia Su Xinghong and Chen Ruixia take up the "Second Integration", the proposition that Marxism should be combined with China's fine traditional culture, which they call the signature proposition of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. They argue that existing scholarship has treated its political and theoretical logic well but its philosophical underpinnings only weakly. Their thesis is that, read through ontology, axiology and a theory of practice, the Second Integration is necessary, needed and workable. The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these philosophical levels. The first addresses its generative mechanism through Marxist practice-ontology. The second addresses its value implications, covering socialism with Chinese characteristics, cultural subjectivity and the modern transformation of Chinese civilisation. The third addresses its practical requirements. On the first point, the authors treat Marxism as the universal law of human history and fine traditional culture as the particular law of the Chinese nation, so that the universal shows itself through the particular. They list seven Marxist-compatible elements in traditional culture, including worldview, dialectics, epistemology, people-based thinking and the Confucian "Great Harmony". They also claim that Chinese thought indirectly fed into Marxism through Hegel and utopian socialism, and they cite Marx's and Engels's many references to China. They further trace the idea through Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of Marxism's adaptation to China and the way later Party leaders reworked classical Chinese expressions. On value, they argue that the Second Integration is the "golden key" to understanding the Chinese path, consolidates cultural subjectivity (standpoint, awareness, innovation) and gives the modern transformation of Chinese civilisation its direction, standpoint and openness. In practice, they propose adapting Marxist cultural theory to China and to the times, creating a new cultural form of Chinese modernization, answering real problems at home and globally, and combining safeguarding fundamentals with innovation under Party leadership. The authors conclude that the Second Integration is the necessary route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, for modernising traditional culture and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They describe it as the greatest asset for building a strong socialist cultural nation and call for continued work on the cultural path, theory and institutions. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of Marxism grounds the Second Integration in philosophical categories and in claims about Marxism's links to Chinese thought.

How should the vulgarity of vulgar economics be understood? An analysis based on Capital and its manuscripts 如何理解庸俗经济学之庸俗性？——基于《资本论》及其手稿的辨析 Wang Fengming Qin Yifan Marx's label "vulgar" for post-classical bourgeois economics has long been attacked, notably by Ludwig von Mises and the Austrian school, as a narrow and unscientific smear. Wang Fengming and Qin Yifan argue that such attacks misread the concept, and that existing Marxist defences are also insufficiently precise. They hold that "vulgar" in Marx's critique of political economy carries three progressive determinations rather than a merely rhetorical or literal meaning. The authors first assess two readings: "vulgar" as superficial phenomenalism, and the more influential "double meaning" reading combining phenomenalism with apologetics. They find the second flawed, because Marx also names conciliatory (reconciling) economics as a second school, and because class standpoint is itself something to be explained by economic relations. Drawing on Capital and its manuscripts, including Theories of Surplus-Value, they then examine cases: Say and utility theories of value, Malthus and the Ricardian school, Senior's abstinence theory, John Stuart Mill's profit-sharing, Bastiat, and conceptions of capital in Quesnay and Ricardo. The three determinations are these. First, in theoretical content, vulgar economics stays with surface description and opposes analysis of essence. The authors argue, for example, that utility theory confuses use-value with value and phenomenon with essence. Second, in theoretical substance, it is a systematised bourgeois ideology, in apologetic form (Senior, Bastiat) or conciliatory form (J. S. Mill), the latter emerging after the 1848 revolutions as an adjustment within capitalism's limits. Third, in theoretical aim, it naturalises, absolutises and eternalises the capitalist mode of production. The authors say classical economists shared this tendency, but Marx did not blame them, because capitalism was then immature and its contradictions had not yet appeared through crises and class conflict. The authors conclude that the three determinations move from description to class analysis to the underlying economic relations, which reflects Marx's historical materialism: economic structure shapes class structure, and class interest shapes ideas. They cite David Harvey's remark that neoclassical economics is almost identical to the vulgar economics Marx criticised. As long as capitalist relations are reproduced, they argue, vulgar economics will be reproduced too, so criticising it is a protracted ideological struggle. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reconstruction of Marx's concept of vulgar economics, with detailed case studies and a reply to Austrian-school objections.

The Communist Party of China's exploration of an independent Chinese knowledge system in the Yan'an period 延安时期中国共产党对中国自主知识体系的探索 Dong Jia Wen Ruiqin Taking up Xi Jinping's 2022 remark that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's own independent knowledge system, Dong Jia and Wen Ruiqin look for its historical roots in the Yan'an period (1935–1948). They argue that the Communist Party of China was both the leading force and a direct builder of such a system. In their account, this period settled key terms, concepts and methods of what they call the Yan'an chapter of an independent knowledge system. The article begins with the background: the modern clash between Chinese and Western learning, the May Fourth critique of tradition, and the failure of earlier reform and revolutionary programmes. It then traces the early Party's wish to adapt foreign theory, from Yun Daiying and Li Dazhao to Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. The body is organised around the contribution of Mao Zedong Thought, the academic climate fostered by Party leaders, and the movement for the sinification of scholarship. The authors' core argument has several parts. Knowledge is independent, they say, when it rests on Chinese experience and addresses Chinese problems, and when it is systematic, as Mao and Ai Siqi stressed. Mao, Zhang Wentian, Zhou Enlai and others encouraged scholars such as Fan Wenlan, He Ganzhi and Hou Wailu, and set up research bodies such as the Central Research Institute. The Party then guided the movement for the sinification of scholarship, begun in Chongqing, towards the 'new-democratic culture' of Mao's 1940 essay. The authors present this as a shift from a vague appeal to a leading framework that combined inheriting the national heritage with localising foreign learning. They also note that some works over-emphasised service to current politics. The authors conclude that Yan'an built on Marxism as the guiding principle, critically inherited traditional culture, grounded scholarship in practice, and raised professional standards. They cite Hou Wailu and Hu Sheng to argue that scholars had moved from imitating the West to using their own methods. For the present, they call for continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era running through teaching and research. They also call for greater international academic influence. Read the original if you want a detailed account, with many period sources, of how Yan'an-era Party leaders and scholars shaped the idea of an independent Chinese knowledge system and how it is used in current discourse.

The holistic reconstruction of ecological civilization in the age of artificial intelligence 人工智能时代的生态文明整体性重构 Li Juan Li Juan asks what happens to ecological civilization when artificial intelligence stops being a mere tool and becomes a structural force. Existing research, the author says, mostly stresses technological empowerment and digital transformation of ecological governance. Li argues instead that AI, especially strong AI, acts as a quasi-subject, turning the human–nature relationship into a three-way structure of human, intelligent agent and nature. Ecological civilization therefore needs its basic structure re-examined, not just a technical upgrade. The article, from a historical-materialist standpoint, first sets out the debate on whether AI has subjectivity, then argues for its quasi-subject status at the ontological, cognitive and practical levels. It then examines five areas of reconstruction: the goals and training of AI; technological ethics and ecological justice; AI hallucination and decision-making; hidden energy consumption; and the public's ecological awareness, ecological culture and environmental participation. It draws on Marx and Engels, and on Western writers such as Kate Crawford, Virginia Dignum and Lewis Mumford. Li's core move is that AI learns from natural data, analyses connections among natural information, and adjusts its effects on nature toward set goals. This makes AI a new active element in ecosystems, though one whose abilities are bounded by human design. Li therefore calls for ecological goals to be built into all AI systems, with measurable indicators for value alignment. The author warns of algorithmic bias that marginalises fragile regions and endangered species, of hallucinations that distort environmental decisions, and of systemic high energy use. Li proposes data representativeness, bias correction, expert verification, accountability chains and full life-cycle environmental disclosure in response. On the public side, Li calls for higher environmental literacy that reads "data nature" critically, for AI-assisted green lifestyles, and for the modern transformation of traditional Chinese ecological culture. Li also proposes recognising both explicit expression and implicit behavioural data as forms of participation, which the author links to whole-process people's democracy. Li concludes that AI's reconstruction of ecological civilization does not diminish humans, who remain the ultimate responsible subjects and must keep the quasi-subject within technological ethics and a framework of green AI governance. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of AI as an ecological actor, with concrete governance proposals on bias, hallucination and energy use.

The Chinese nation's tradition of great unification thought and its modern development 中华民族大一统思想传统与现代发展 Zhu Handmin Zhu Hanmin asks how the tradition of "great unification" (da yitong) arose in Chinese thought and how it carries on in the present. The article argues that this tradition is a pluralistic-yet-unified body of ideas. It took shape among the pre-Qin philosophers, was fixed in the Western Han, and has been continued and developed in Xi Jinping's cultural thought. Zhu proposes reading that thought through the continuity and development of Chinese civilization. The first half looks at the Spring and Autumn and Warring States thinkers, the classifications of them by Sima Tan and Ban Gu, and the Gongyang commentary's use of the term "great unification". It then turns to Dong Zhongshu's synthesis in the Han. The second half moves to the modern period: Liang Qichao's 1902 concept of the "Chinese nation", Sun Yat-sen's "five-race republic" and the failed attempts to rebuild unity. It ends with the People's Republic and Xi Jinping's statements on modern governance, national community consciousness and modern Chinese civilization. Zhu's central claim is that the philosophers' pluralism did not split Chinese civilization. In Zhu's account, the schools shared an origin in Three Dynasties civilization, and each hoped to unify the realm in its own way: Confucian "unity", Mohist "agreeing with the superior", Legalist centralised law, Daoist unity in the "Way". Dong Zhongshu then absorbed Mohist, Legalist, Huang-Lao Daoist and Yin-Yang ideas into a Confucian-centred system joined to centralised rule. Zhu adds that the ideal of "following the ways of antiquity" let the tradition change form with circumstances, and that it parallels the formation of a many-in-one Chinese nation, citing Fei Xiaotong. Zhu concludes that the PRC's system inherits this tradition while drawing on modern institutional achievements. The article names the single-state form, regional ethnic autonomy and the people's congress system. Citing Xi Jinping, Zhu presents Chinese modernization, the forging of a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation, and the Second Integration (of Marxism with traditional culture) as continuations of great unification. Zhu holds that unity and diversity are dialectically linked in modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a Chinese intellectual-historical account of how the idea of great unification is tied to current official theory on national unity and civilization.

On relational civilization and its place in the new form of human civilization 论关系文明及其在人类文明新形态中的地位 Qiu Gengtian Qiu Gengtian asks what "relational civilization" is, why it should be built, where it sits within the new form of human civilization, and how it can be created. The article, guided by the Marxist conception of civilization and Xi Jinping's thought on culture, argues that civilization has so far been built mainly through domain-specific forms. It contends that the growing "disharmony" of development calls for a distinct civilization of human relations, to stand alongside the existing five. The article begins from the contradiction of today's world, which Qiu summarises as insufficient development and discordant development. It defines relational civilization and sets out its practical, theoretical and institutional components. It then grounds the concept in Marx's theory of "all-round production" and in classical Marxist ontology, and traces precursors in Chinese tradition, communicative-practice philosophy and the Party's record, from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence (1954) to the global initiatives. The last sections discuss its theoretical and international significance and how to build it. Qiu's central move is to place relational civilization in the logic of production. Material, spiritual and ecological civilization rest on their own forms of production, and relational civilization rests on the production and reproduction of human relations. Because the existing five civilizations are domain-based and "entity-type", the author holds that they cannot cover relations between domains or relations such as international ties. Relational civilization is therefore a "relational" form that cannot be reduced to social civilization. Qiu also cites relational ontology, arguing that matter exists as both entity and relation. Together these give a "5+1" structure, and the author argues that the new form of human civilization would be incomplete without it. On the practical side, Qiu proposes a shift in ideas from egocentrism to symbiosis (gòngshēng zhǔyì), and a shift in practice from mutually harmful to mutually beneficial development. Qiu presents China's development as a leading example of relational civilization and links the concept to the Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. Qiu says it also enriches Marxist civilization theory. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar derives a new sixth civilization from Marxist production theory and ties it to China's foreign-policy concepts.

On the major significance of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind for world modernization 论人类命运共同体理念对世界现代化的重大意义 Wu Zhongmin Wu Zhongmin asks what the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind means for the course of world modernization. The article argues that the concept is more than a diplomatic slogan: it concerns how modernization worldwide can be advanced as a whole. In Wu's view, without building such a community world modernization has no future, and the concept is an original Chinese contribution that fits historical materialism and the basic trend of modernization. The article first sets out the historical and practical grounds for the concept, then examines its effects on four conditions of sustainable world modernization. It then turns to the obstacles to building the community and to what states should do. It draws on Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping, together with cited Western scholarship on globalization, and gives figures for China's GDP and trade for 2018–2023. Wu grounds the concept in historical materialism. Modern large-scale industry and the market economy produce economic globalization, which makes states mutually dependent. This globalization spreads social risks and ecological damage that no single state can handle alone. On that basis, Wu says the concept supports four things: a healthy world economy through free movement of production factors and fair competition instead of jungle-law zero-sum play; a more balanced modernization that gives developing countries a voice; harmony between humans and nature; and a just international order. Wu presents the concept as going beyond the principles of sovereignty, equality and peaceful coexistence, which aim only at passive coexistence, by pursuing active common prosperity. The article describes China as a responsible leader on ecology and as an example of fair-competition cooperation, and it describes US hegemony and withdrawal from climate agreements as obstacles. Wu concludes that the community is the direction of history but will take a long and difficult process. The article names three obstacles: no world government with enforcement power, slow cultural adaptation, and tangled disputes that feed reverse globalization. It proposes that states build an economic community of shared destiny as the foundation, jointly govern risks to deepen mutual empathy, and build a fair order through multilateral consultation centred on the United Nations. Wu adds that the UN needs reform, with better global governance and a stronger voice for developing countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese sociologist's systematic case linking the community with a shared future for mankind to theories of modernization and globalization.

Chinese modernization and the logic of value change in creating a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化与人类文明新形态创造实践的价值观变革逻辑 Yuan Zushe Yuan Zushe asks what Xi Jinping means when he lists a distinctive 'outlook on values' among the features of Chinese modernization, and how that outlook differs from the values behind Western modernization. Drawing on Marxist historical materialism and modern value philosophy, the article argues that Chinese modernization has identified and practised a genuinely universal 'true value'. In Yuan's account, this has corrected the value basis of Western modernization and supplied the value logic for creating a new form of human civilization. The article begins with the place of values in modernization, drawing on Ulrich Beck, Jürgen Habermas, Cyril Black, Talcott Parsons, Anthony Giddens and Jacques Derrida to describe the costs of Western modernity. It then turns to the value premises of Enlightenment modernity, quoting Marx and Engels on capitalism's productive power and on the general law of capitalist accumulation. The second half sets out the value content of Chinese modernization, first in four points, then in three claimed contributions, and finally in six areas of value change. Yuan argues that Western modernization rests on one-sided values: capital logic, wealth maximization, individualism and hedonism, and the slide from a market economy into a 'market society'. In the author's reading, this produces ecological crisis, spiritual emptiness, an 'acquisitive personality' and claims to 'universal values' that serve narrow national interest. Chinese modernization is said to unite three value sources: the Marxist ideal of the free and all-round development of the person, excellent traditional Chinese culture, and the common values of all humanity. It is also said to offer a relational, 'public value' logic and to rest on a socialist market economy that differs in kind from a market society. The six areas of change are ecological harmony, social justice and common prosperity, development aimed at a better life, a people-centred approach, common values of humanity with a community with a shared future for mankind, and a pluralist view of civilizations. Yuan concludes that the values in Chinese modernization are 'Chinese values'. The author presents them as the outcome of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as the basis for Chinese discourse power on values. They are also described as a way past the binaries of universalism versus particularism and efficiency versus equality. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher builds a value-theoretic case for Chinese modernization and how the article frames Western modernity critically.

The spiritual force for achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation: structure, roots and driving mechanisms 实现中华民族伟大复兴的精神力量：结构、根源与动力机制 Wang Yongyou Wei Mingyong Wang Yongyou and Wei Mingyong take up the call in the 20th Party Congress report (2022) to strengthen the spiritual force for achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They note that existing scholarship deals mainly with its meaning, how it arises, its sources and ways of promoting it, but has not analysed its structure, roots and driving mechanisms. Their thesis is that this force is a complex system that can be understood through three analytical lenses, and that such an analysis is a precondition for strengthening it in the drive to build a modern socialist country. The article is organised in three parts. The first analyses the internal structure of the spiritual force along three dimensions: its agents (individual, group and nation), its sources of motivation (material, psychological and spiritual needs) and its functions. The second traces four roots: material, ideological, institutional and cultural. The third sets out three driving mechanisms, namely guidance, incentive and publicity. The argument draws throughout on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping. On structure, the authors argue that individual, group and national strength relate quantitatively, as accumulation, and qualitatively, as consolidation. Human needs, rising with the productive forces, are the source of the force, which performs four functions: spiritual guidance, cohesion, creativity and fighting capacity. These are described as subjective in content but objective in essence, and as mutually reinforcing. On roots, the authors rely on the claim that social being determines social consciousness. They hold that economic achievements since reform and opening up, the Party's innovative theory, the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Chinese traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture together generate the force.
