Chen says the thought combines the universal with the particular, finding models among the masses and then using them to guide the general run of work, as in the campaigns to learn from Dazhai and Daqing. It also unites historical continuity with responsiveness to the times, so that models shift from national heroes in wartime to technical models in construction. On practice, Chen describes the selection of individual and collective models, and a dissemination system of newspapers, radio, television, commendation meetings, artistic performances and voluntary service. The author adds that models were to be brought into family, school and social education. Chen concludes that this thought remains valuable for ideological guidance, moral construction, talent cultivation and social governance. Present-day figures such as Fang Zhimin, Lei Feng, Jiao Yulu, Yuan Longping and Tu Youyou, along with community and rural cadres, are offered as models that would firm up ideals, foster patriotism, support the core socialist values, promote all-round development and innovation, and improve grassroots governance. The author calls for creative methods suited to the new era in service of the Chinese Dream and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Party-oriented account of how Mao's model-citizen campaigns are being reinterpreted for ideological and political education today.

Mao Zedong's exploration of Party propaganda work in the Yan'an period and its contemporary implications 延安时期毛泽东对党的宣传工作的探索及其当代启示 Zhao Daixing Nie Jiahua How did Mao Zedong lead the Communist Party's propaganda work during the Yan'an period, and what does it offer propaganda work today? Zhao and Nie argue that Mao treated propaganda as a "major task" of the revolution. In their account, flexible strategies and wide use of available resources broke the Japanese and Kuomintang news blockade, built a positive image of the Party and won domestic and international sympathy. The article first sets out Mao's view of propaganda as a vehicle of ideological leadership, tied to political, military and diplomatic work. It then examines the Yan'an situation and the principles Mao drew from it, the mobilisation of different propaganda actors, and the strategies used, including domestic methods and outreach abroad. It closes with lessons for the present, linked to statements by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors' central claim is that Mao's work rested on a sober reading of the situation: attacks on the Party abroad, Kuomintang smears, and subjectivism, sectarianism and "Party stereotyped writing" inside the Party. From this came three principles: Party leadership, seeking truth from facts, and distinguishing audiences ("look at the target before shooting the arrow"). Mao also drew on cadres, journalists, writers, theorists, students and correspondents under the slogan of "opening the door" to run newspapers. The authors add vivid language, popular forms, newspapers and radio, and foreign journalists such as Edgar Snow and Anna Louise Strong, plus overseas Chinese. They cite figures such as nearly 30,000 correspondents by 1945. Writing against the background of the "two overall situations", the authors propose four lessons. These are upholding Party leadership and top-level design; mobilising diverse actors, including self-media, foreign influencers and overseas Chinese; adopting a "user mindset" and new discourse for differentiated audiences; and following communication laws with a full-media system using AI, big data and short video. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Mao's Yan'an propaganda experience is being tied to current propaganda and communication policy.

Mao Zedong's exploration of and contribution to inheriting and developing China's fine traditional culture after 1949 A text analysis based on volumes 4–9 of the Chronology of Mao Zedong 新中国成立后毛泽东对传承与发展中华优秀传统文化的探索及贡献 Liu Yanwu Liu Yanwu asks how Mao Zedong approached the inheritance and development of China's fine traditional culture in the years after the founding of the People's Republic, and why Chinese communists present themselves as its faithful heirs. The article, published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2025, argues that Mao and his generation made a preliminary but distinctive contribution within the Two Integrations: combining Marxism's basic tenets with Chinese realities and with traditional culture. Liu also holds that this contribution was uneven and marked by errors. The study takes volumes 4–9 of the Chronology of Mao Zedong as its source and extracts 289 entries from 1949 to 1976 concerning traditional culture. Liu sorts them by theme (theoretical background, policy, remoulding of old culture and intellectuals, key fields, cultivation, commentary, practice) and by period: 67 entries for 1949–1956, 137 for 1957–1965 and 85 for 1966–1976. Entries about errors already judged in the Party's 1981 historical resolution are excluded. Method follows grounded-theory coding, in three stages: initial, focused and theoretical. Liu's reading draws out several threads. On policy, Mao's slogans "let a hundred flowers bloom, weed through the old to bring forth the new" and "make the past serve the present, foreign things serve China" called for critical, discriminating use of the heritage. Liu cites Mao on protecting cultural relics and museums, reforming old education and intellectuals, and promoting opera and traditional Chinese medicine. Mao judged traditional figures and works by four yardsticks: popular character, historical context, the needs of the present, and comparison with the West. Liu also counts 42 entries where Mao used classical allusions to explain international and domestic affairs. Liu concludes that the policies protected many relics and advanced opera and Chinese medicine. The author also says Party understanding of cultural laws was still limited, so interference in the arts was excessive, the "hundred flowers" line was not well carried out, and the material heritage was better protected than traditional ideas, which were often criticised. Liu cites Xi Jinping on the continuity of the pre- and post-reform periods. The article names four factors for further study: politics, the principal contradiction, the Party's historical position and intellectuals. Read the original if you want a source-based, coded survey of Mao's remarks on traditional culture, with specific entries and an official-line assessment of its mistakes.

The Chinese Communists' theoretical exploration of the people as the main body: a three-dimensional analysis Political integration, institutional construction and value guidance 中国共产党人民主体思想的理论探索历程 Zhang Ruoyun How has the Communist Party of China understood "the people" as the main body (renmin zhuti) of history and development, and how has that understanding changed over a century? Zhang argues that the Party's thinking evolved through three core values, "each in its proper place", common prosperity and shared development. Over this course, the Party moved from a strategy of mobilisation to a role of value guidance, uniting the people as subject of material production, holder of political power and realiser of values. The article, published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2025, proceeds chronologically and is organised around political integration, institutional construction and value guidance. It covers the New Democratic Revolution and the Anti-Japanese War, then the early reform and opening-up period, and finally the digital economy of the "new era". Zhang draws on Mao Zedong's class analysis, Marx's remarks on distribution and ownership, Xi Jinping's statements on sharing, and figures on income distribution, taxation and migrant workers. Zhang makes three main moves. First, for the wartime years, Mao's picture of a society "small at both ends, large in the middle" is said to have led to a "double recognition" of class identity and political rights, through rent and interest reduction and the "three-thirds" system, producing the united front as a new political community. Second, after reform and opening up, "allowing some to get rich first" is presented as legitimising socialism through growth while distinguishing inequality from unfairness; it also reshaped the people into four identity groups, and the author flags unresolved tensions in primary, secondary and tertiary distribution. Third, digitalisation produces four new groups, including platform workers and "new workers", and moves the core value from common prosperity to shared development, with data rights framed as a successor to "land to the tiller". Zhang concludes that through economic empowerment, political confirmation of rights and value empowerment, the Party has united the people as material, rights-bearing and value-bearing subject. The people thus become an end, not a means, and the "revolutionary community" gives way to a "community with a shared future for mankind". Read the original if you want a periodised account of how Party scholarship frames the people-centred idea, with the wartime class data, distribution figures and digital-economy case material that support it.

The 15th Five-Year Plan: the internal logic and practical path of a "strong domestic market" and the new development pattern “十五五”规划：“强大国内市场”与新发展格局的内在逻辑与实践路径 Li Jiangtao Qian Junhao Li Jiangtao and Qian Junhao take up the call of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) to "build a strong domestic market and accelerate the construction of a new development pattern" for the 15th Five-Year Plan period. They argue that a strong domestic market is not a stand-alone policy choice but a structural necessity, set by China's stage of development, a changed international environment and the laws governing a large economy. It is presented as the key lever for achieving both an effective improvement in quality and a reasonable growth in quantity, and so for high-quality development. After a short review of Chinese literature linking the strong domestic market to the new development philosophy, the article first explains why the strategy is needed. It looks at the external environment, domestic structural problems, the sequence of Party decisions since 2020 and the advantages of a country with over 1.4 billion people. It then sets out a four-part analytical framework of demand, supply, driving force and security. This framework is filled out through four areas and nine focal points, each with concrete policy measures. The core argument rests on two moves. First, the authors hold that the old international-circulation model of "both ends abroad" no longer fits, given external shocks and Western technology controls and decoupling, so domestic circulation must offset international uncertainty. They cite figures such as foreign-trade dependence falling from 55.5% in 2008 to 32.5% in 2024, and domestic demand contributing an average of 98.3% of growth since the international financial crisis. Second, they argue that demand and supply must reinforce each other: consumption and investment are to be expanded by linking improvements in people's livelihoods with consumption, and "investment in things" with "investment in people". They note a 2024 household consumption rate of 39.9%, about 28 points below the United States. The proposed measures include a unified national market, macroeconomic governance centred on consumption, and security in food, energy and industrial chains. The authors conclude that building a strong domestic market will gradually reduce reliance on external markets and produce a higher-level dynamic balance in which demand pulls supply and supply creates demand. They describe it as essential to Chinese modernization and as a route to security, resilience and sustainable prosperity. The article also calls for further research that quantifies the contribution of the new development philosophy to market efficiency. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented account of how Chinese economists frame the 15th Five-Year Plan's domestic-demand strategy, including its statistics and nine-point agenda.

The endogenous logic and basic experience of the Communist Party of China in establishing cultural confidence since 1949 An interview with Professor Zhang Ji of the School of Marxism, Hebei Normal University 新中国成立以来中国共产党确立文化自信的内生逻辑与基本经验——访河北师范大学马克思主义学院张骥教授 This is an interview, published in Studies on Marxism, with Professor Zhang Ji of the School of Marxism at Hebei Normal University, a specialist in Marxist cultural theory and cultural soft power. The interviewers ask how the Communist Party of China has established cultural confidence since 1949, what logic underlies the process and what lessons it offers. Zhang answers that the process unites theoretical, historical and practical logics and reflects both inheritance of Marxist cultural thought and fine traditional Chinese culture and a firm belief in creating modern culture. The conversation opens with the meaning of cultural confidence. Zhang defines it as a people's, state's or party's strong identification with its own cultural ideals and values, and presents it as the most basic of the Four-sphere Confidence. It then takes up the theoretical logic, the historical logic across three periods, and the practical logic of the present. The final questions concern the experience gained: Party leadership, people-centredness, innovation, the Two Integrations, and the balance between material and spiritual civilisation. On theory, Zhang sets out Marx and Engels on the two-way relation of culture and the economy and on human beings as the subjects of culture. He then covers Lenin on the Party's cultural leadership, on seizing bourgeois cultural achievements and on respecting the pace of cultural work. Zhang adds Mao Zedong's cultural policies, Deng Xiaoping's spiritual civilisation, later leaders' contributions and Xi Jinping's thought on culture, together with fine traditional culture as the "cultural gene" of the Party. Historically, he traces a progression from cultural self-awareness and self-reliance to cultural self-direction, strength and confidence. He admits that cultural work in the early decades took some detours. For the present, he points to the Two Integrations, to the "two overall situations" of national rejuvenation and global change, and to cultural subjectivity as the root of confidence. Zhang names comprehensive Party leadership as the first lesson, exercised through political leadership, ideological guidance, mass organisation and social mobilisation. He adds the people's主体 role, innovation in keeping with fundamental principles, and coordinated material and spiritual progress. He lists domestic challenges, including coexisting cultures, digital cultural security, cultural arrogance or inferiority, historical nihilism and weak identification. Internationally he cites cultural competition and the struggle for discourse power, which he says call for exchange and mutual learning. Read the original if you want an authoritative Chinese academic statement of how Party theorists periodise and justify the Party's cultural policy from 1949 to the present.

Theoretical innovation and global significance of Chinese modernization from the perspective of the Global South 全球南方视角下中国式现代化的理论创新与世界意义 Wang Yashan Wang Yashan asks what Chinese modernization's theoretical innovations mean for the Global South, at a time the author describes as one of declining Western hegemony and the collective rise of developing countries. The article argues that Chinese modernization, built through the Two Integrations, breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. In Wang's account it offers Global South states a non-dependent path and supports reform of global governance. The article first clarifies the concept of the Global South, tracing it from its 1969 origin through the 1977 Brandt Line and the 1974 declaration on a New International Economic Order to its present use. It then sets out the internal and external tensions the concept faces. Wang next examines Chinese modernization in five dimensions: Party leadership and politics, the economic system, ecology, a conception of civilization, and common prosperity. The final sections discuss its practical effects and its discursive significance. Wang defines the Global South as a successor to the Third World: a bloc of emerging and developing countries, formerly structurally marginal, that now carries an anti-dependence and decolonial charge. The author stresses its heterogeneity, citing divergent Latin American paths and states that remain dependent on Western security ties. Wang also holds that Western discourse tries to depoliticise the concept and spreads narratives such as the 'debt trap'. Against this background, the article contends that Chinese modernization transcends the single logic of capital. It does so through Party leadership, a basic economic system with public ownership as the mainstay and an 'effective market and capable government', green development, and common prosperity. Wang argues that these offer lessons for avoiding the 'middle-income trap'. Wang concludes that Chinese modernization breaks the Western monopoly on defining modernization and promotes a decolonial turn in Global South theory. The article points to the Belt and Road Initiative, South-South cooperation mechanisms and the Global South think-tank alliance as practical channels. It also quotes Xi Jinping that each country is best placed to judge which modernization suits it, and calls on Global South states to remain independent. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal links Global South discourse to Chinese modernization and presents it as a development model.

Autonomous modernization of the Global South: meaning, logic and development path 全球南方自主现代化：内涵、逻辑与发展路向 Tian Wei Tian Wei asks how the Global South can escape dependence on Western modernization and build its own path, and why that path must be "autonomous". The article argues that existing scholarship on Global South modernization (classical modernization, dependency, world-systems and latecomer-advantage theories) mostly criticises the West. In Tian's account, it neglects the South's own agency and has not produced a self-constructed discourse. Tian proposes a theory of autonomous modernization that would move the South from being theorised by others to theorising itself. The article first reviews the literature and its limits. It then defines autonomous modernization and treats the Global South in three dimensions: as an economic, a political and a cultural category. It next sets out the internal logic of autonomous modernization in five pairs: lawfulness and purposiveness, diachronic and synchronic, autonomy and commonality. The final sections discuss multilateralism, a shared theoretical narrative, and a "new form" of world modernization. A closing section places Chinese modernization within this framework. Tian defines autonomous modernization as modernization that fits national conditions, balances universality with difference and independence with inclusiveness, and builds its own discursive power. Drawing on Marx's analysis of capital, the author traces the North–South divide to the capitalist mode of production. Tian holds that neoliberalism, debt and premature deindustrialisation deepened dependence, and that decolonisation turned the South into a political category of collective resistance. The cultural category rests on a shared identity of the marginalised. Tian argues that the South has moved from being forced into Western modernization, to criticising it, to shaping its own. It should pursue strategic autonomy and avoid both wholesale Westernisation and closed-door exclusion of the West. Tian concludes that there is no genuine world modernization without Global South modernization, and that the South must unite development with autonomy through multilateralism. Proposals include strengthening BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the Belt and Road Initiative and the "G77 plus China" format, plus a Global South research centre. They also include a joint theoretical narrative that rejects capital-centred, polarising and expansionist modernization. China, as a Global South member, is said to offer new models through Chinese modernization and the four global initiatives. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar builds a theory of Global South modernization and links it to Chinese foreign policy.

The metaphorical narrative of Marx's critique of false ideology and its inner logic 马克思虚假意识形态批判的隐喻叙事及其内在逻辑 Xue Yonglong Why does Marx's critique of false ideology rely so heavily on metaphor, and what does that reliance accomplish? Xue Yonglong argues that metaphor in Marx is neither decoration nor an aesthetic extra. It is a way of piercing appearances, and it runs through the critique from its theoretical premise to its mechanism and its historical outcome. Three metaphors, the "caricature", the "hat" and "Prometheus", form a linked and progressive critical system. The article opens with the paradox that theorists distrust metaphor yet use it at decisive points, citing Althusser as an example. It then explains why Marx turned to metaphor: to overturn the apologetic discourse of speculative philosophy and bourgeois political economy, and to make capital's abstract domination perceptible. The author describes a movement in Marx's metaphors from "unveiling of cognition" to "construction of thought" to "summons to action". The three images are then analysed in turn, with reference to The Holy Family, The Poverty of Philosophy, Marx's doctoral dissertation and the Communist Manifesto. Derrida, Debord, Jameson and Hayden White are drawn in as commentators. Xue reads the "caricature" as exposing the premise of false ideology: Bruno Bauer's self-consciousness philosophy exaggerates one side of Hegel and elevates spirit above reality, which turns real people into abstractions. The "hat" ("if an Englishman transforms men into hats, a German transforms hats into ideas") reveals the mechanism. People are first reduced to things, as Ricardo saw, and then things are raised into ideas, as Hegel did. The author presents this as reification and "abstract domination", in which domination by things is in fact domination of people by people. "Prometheus bound" points to the outcome: the proletariat is both sufferer and liberator, and its suffering must become universal and provoke it to rebellion. Xue adds that the three images move from surface description to essence and follow the dialectic of contradiction: its emergence, its development and its resolution. Xue concludes that Marx's aim was not to abandon ideology or merely to judge whether an ideology is false. It was to expose the roots and operation of falsity and to show the necessity of escaping the "rule of ideas". The author holds that false ideology survives today in more hidden forms. These include Western scholars who beautify capitalism, consumerism that disguises "capital's needs" as "individual needs", and technological alienation and digital hegemony. Read the original if you study Marx's theory of ideology, his textual use of imagery, or the way Chinese scholars apply his critique to contemporary capitalism.

On the divergence of digital governance under capitalism and socialism 论资本主义与社会主义两种制度下数字治理的分野 Wei Shiguo Wei Shiguo asks whether the present split between "Chinese governance" and "Western disorder" in the digital field is a passing difference in policy or the product of two fundamentally different historical logics. The article argues for the second answer. In Wei's account, digital capitalism arose as a crisis-driven rescue plan for capitalism after 2008 and is heading towards extraction, monopoly and alienation. China's socialist digital governance, by contrast, is presented as a conscious adjustment of the relations of production to new productive forces. Wei says existing scholarship either criticises Western digital capitalism at the level of phenomena (surveillance business models, antitrust remedies) or lists the strengths of Chinese digital governance, and lacks a unified Marxist comparative framework. The article first sets out a historical-materialist framework in which data and digital platforms are the key means of production, with "data reification" and "data fetishism" as updates of Marx's commodity fetishism. It then analyses digital capitalism, drawing on Shoshana Zuboff, Nick Srnicek and Yanis Varoufakis, and illustrates it with the Google and EU Digital Markets Act cases, Cambridge Analytica and the gig economy. It then turns to China's institutional practice and closes with a comparative table. Wei's central move is to treat ownership and control of data and platforms as the decisive question. Under digital capitalism, private capital monopolises them, and network effects leave the state a passive, belated regulator. Wei cites the 2024 US ruling against Google, whose remedies were later limited, and the EU's fines on Apple and Meta, which Wei calls small relative to global revenue. For China, the article cites the National Data Administration (2023), public data authorised operation (such as Beijing's financial data zone) and the digital yuan (e-CNY) as a mutually supporting system. Wei contrasts "the logic of capital" with "the logic of the people" across five dimensions: core logic, data ownership, institutional actors, value realisation and systemic consequences. Wei concludes that the digital-field divergence reflects the logic of the people sublating (surpassing) the logic of capital. The article defines a "new form of socialist digital civilization" by three features: a public-led, public-ownership-based set of production relations, a shift in value goal from extracting profit to creating social value, and governance that moves beyond the state–market opposition. Wei adds that China's exploration offers Global South countries a way to avoid becoming "data colonies". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar frames a capital-versus-people comparison of digital governance, including the specific cases and policy documents it uses.

The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of "Chinese experience" and "Chinese theory" in the New Democratic Revolution period 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党对“中国经验”和“中国理论”的探索 Zhou Jiabin Zhou Jiabin asks how the Chinese Communist Party (CPC) came to summarise its revolutionary practice as "Chinese experience" and raise it to "Chinese theory" with a world-wide significance. Noting that existing scholarship mostly treats these concepts from a domestic ("China dimension") angle, the article takes the "world dimension" and looks back to the New Democratic Revolution period (1921–1949). Its thesis is that the current stress on "Chinese experience" and "Chinese theory" under Xi Jinping has deep historical roots and developed through five stages. The article periodises the CPC's exploration into germination (1921–1922), initial stage (1922–1928), development (1928–1935), maturity (1935–1945) and deepening (1945–1949). It follows the Party's relations with the Comintern, with episodes such as Zhang Tailei's revision of the Comintern's classification of colonial and semi-colonial countries, the May Thirtieth Movement and proletarian leadership, armed separatist bases and the Soviet regime, the Zunyi Meeting, the Sinification of Marxism, Mao Zedong Thought, and Liu Shaoqi's 1949 "formula" of the revolutionary road. It also draws on evidence of how other communist parties received Chinese experience. Zhou argues that the Party moved from individual to organisational summaries of experience, and from applying existing Marxist-Leninist positions to original innovation, notably armed separatism, which departed from the Russian model of armed uprising. After the Zunyi Meeting, in the author's account, a strong sense of the revolution's own subjectivity emerged, and Mao's formulation of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context turned scattered experience into systematic theory. The author reads the theory of New Democracy as one drawn from Chinese experience but meant to apply to colonial and semi-colonial revolutions generally. By 1949 the Party, Zhou says, treated propagating this experience abroad as a responsibility, citing Stalin's remarks on a division of labour and messages from parties such as Thailand's. Zhou draws three lessons for the present. The formation of Chinese experience and theory was historically necessary, driven by practical needs of the communist movement and by Marxism's own demand for unity of the universal and the particular. It was a long process combining continuity and stages. And the two are related as source and stream, root and crown: experience is the basis of theory, and theory is its systematised result. The author calls on the Party to dig deeper into Chinese practice, refine theory from it and advance adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of the Comintern relationship and of how the Chinese revolution is presented as an internationally relevant source of theory.)

The Communist Party of China's development concepts and their development in the new era 中国共产党发展理念及其在新时代的发展 Qiu Gengtian Qiu Gengtian asks what the Communist Party of China's "development concepts" are, why they arose and how they have changed since 1949, especially in the new era. The author argues that these concepts form a coherent system of Marxist ideas about China's development. They have been continuous in basic orientation while changing with practice, and today they are centred on Chinese modernization and the new development philosophy. The article follows a method that unites logic and history. The article first sets out four dimensions through which the Party leads development: practice, theory, discourse and emotion. It then describes the content of the concepts as four theoretical blocks: ontology, epistemology, axiology and methodology. It identifies five features (practical, people-oriented, dialectical, stage-specific, innovative) and four logics (practical, political, reform and world). It ends with the concepts' evolution from the revolutionary period through the reform era to the present. Qiu holds that practice and theory are the two original sides of development, while discourse and emotion are derivative. Development ontology, the author argues, gives development supreme status as both end and means, a "fundamental law" for solving all problems, and Qiu cites the cost of earlier neglect of productive forces. Development epistemology is framed through information theory: knowledge removes blind spots and uncertainty and so makes development safer. Axiology asks "development for whom" and answers with the people-centred approach; methodology stresses overall planning and systems thinking. The political logic treats development as the "greatest politics" that must prove the superiority of socialism, and the world logic ties China's progress to its contribution to humanity. Qiu concludes that, since the 20th Party Congress (2022), modernization has been the "main thread" and "underlying colour" of the Party's development concepts. The author therefore calls for those concepts to be built into a theoretical system of Chinese modernization, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On this view the new development philosophy is the main form of development thinking in the new era. Its five concepts (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) are matched to the dynamics, relationships, ecology, external environment and common prosperity of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists organise the philosophy of development from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping.

The ecological narrative of Marxist productive-forces theory 马克思主义生产力理论的生态叙事 Shen Guangming Shen Guangming takes up the charge, made by some Western ecological scholars, that Marx's theory of productive forces contains anti-ecological elements. The article asks two questions: whether productive forces have an ecological character, and how ecological problems relate to productive-force development. Shen argues that, although Marx never used the word "ecology", his account of nature, of the contradiction between humans and nature, and of its resolution fits the core of ecology, and that this is concentrated in his productive-forces theory. Ecological crisis, on this reading, results from the anti-ecological form of capitalist productive forces. The article is a textual and conceptual argument that moves from Marx's materialist view of nature and his concept of labour as metabolism (material exchange) between humans and nature to a typology of productive forces. It distinguishes labour productive forces, capitalist productive forces and green productive forces. It then turns to China, treating the Xi Jinping formulation that new quality productive forces are "in themselves green productive forces" as a major theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Shen holds that labour productive forces are the power by which humans exchange matter, energy and information with nature, and so have an ecological character, while also having an economic character that can clash with it. Under capitalism, value valorisation drives production for production's sake, technology for technology's sake and consumption for consumption's sake, which Shen says breaks the metabolic relation. Green productive forces, by contrast, must respect ecosystem carrying capacity, ecological laws and humanity's free development. Shen holds that these conditions can be met only through public ownership of the means of production, which allows common control of metabolism and inheritance of capitalism's developed productive forces. Capitalist "green" policies and technologies, in this view, cannot escape the logic of capital. Applying this to China, Shen proposes three tasks for cultivating new quality productive forces: a green transformation of the mode of production (adjusting economic and energy structures, building green industrial chains, extending this abroad through the Belt and Road Initiative and South–South cooperation), green innovation in science and technology, and a green revolution in lifestyles. Shen concludes that Marxist productive-forces theory is a resource for understanding and addressing ecological crisis, and that new quality productive forces are themselves green productive forces. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reply to Western ecological critiques of Marx and a theoretical account of how the green dimension of new quality productive forces is justified.

Engels's original contribution to the materialist foundations of dialectics 恩格斯对塑造辩证法的唯物主义根基的原创性贡献 Zhao Zhen Marxist dialectics is usually said to have inverted Hegel's idealist dialectic, but how that inversion was achieved is seldom spelled out. Zhao Zhen argues that Engels carried out the decisive part of this work. By studying the dialectics of nature, Engels is said to have given Marxist dialectics its solid materialist base and, on that base, a general theory of dialectics that goes beyond Hegel. The article begins with Hegel. It places his dialectic within modern philosophy's turn from ontology to epistemology. It then follows Engels's materialist reconstruction through natural science, the three laws of dialectics, the relation between natural and historical dialectics, and the dialectic of objective world and human thought. It also answers critics from Western Marxism, including Lukács, Alfred Schmidt and Norman Levine. Zhao's central claim is that Hegel's dialectic was a dialectic of reason, not of the world. For Hegel, the question "how do we know the world" became "how is the world constructed", so worldview was reduced to a footnote of epistemology. Engels therefore could not simply swap concepts. He had to start from facts and, by inductive generalisation from physics, chemistry and biology, show that dialectics exists objectively. He drew the three laws from nature and history, which turned dialectics into a scientific theory, though Zhao notes he had not yet fully separated the unity of opposites from the negation of the negation. Against Lukács and others, Zhao contends that natural and historical dialectics are not two dialectics but one materialist dialectic in different fields. Nature acquires dialectical significance in its relation to humanity, so Engels never imposed dialectics on nature. Engels also divided dialectics into an objective and a subjective form, with thought required to master the first. Zhao says this division completed work Marx had left undone, since Marx used dialectics directly in political economy. Zhao concludes that dialectics, for Engels, is not an eternal truth or a new metaphysics but an open scientific theory. It rests on natural science, is confirmed by its advances (Zhao cites relativity and quantum mechanics), and is enriched by them. Some of Engels's specific scientific points may be outdated, but scholars today should use materialist dialectics to address the philosophical problems of science in their own time. Read the original if you are interested in the Engels–Marx debate, in replies to Western Marxist critiques of the dialectics of nature, or in a Chinese reading of how Hegel's dialectic was turned materialist.

The meaning of cultural subjectivity from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域下文化主体性意涵阐析 Guo Chao Guo Chao takes up the question "what is cultural subjectivity?", a concept Xi Jinping put forward when he said that any culture that is to stand firm and travel far must have its own subjectivity. The author notes that existing scholarship approaches it from philosophy, history, Chinese modernization and the Two Integrations, but rarely from historical materialism. The article argues that cultural subjectivity is an ideational superstructure rooted in material production, whose true bearer is the people, whose core is cultural leadership, and which develops through exchange with other cultures. The article is organised around four relationships, each treated as a separate perspective. These are cultural subjectivity and economic subjectivity (material production), and cultural subjectivity and human subjectivity (the "real human being"). The other two are cultural subjectivity and cultural dominance (ideology), and cultural subjectivity and cultural inter-subjectivity (world history). In its closing summary the author says the four parts answer, in turn, where cultural subjectivity comes from, whose it is, what its essence is and how it develops. Guo first argues that economic subjectivity, meaning a nation's autonomy over its economic path and resources, determines cultural subjectivity. Cultural subjectivity in turn acts back by setting direction, building consensus and supplying spiritual impetus, so historical materialism is not economic determinism. Second, because culture cannot itself be a subject, cultural subjectivity is in essence human subjectivity, ultimately that of the people under Party leadership. The author traces how the people built it across the revolutionary, socialist, reform-era and new-era periods. Third, the author names five components: cultural self-awareness, autonomy, dominance, innovation and transcendence. Of these, cultural dominance ("one dominant, many coexisting") is the core. Fourth, drawing on Marx's world-history theory, Guo argues that subjectivity and inter-subjectivity are mutually dependent. The author reads the Qing closed-door policy and Western "cultural hegemony" as two ways of severing the two. Guo concludes that consolidating the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation requires strengthening its material base, including through new quality productive forces. It also requires upholding the Party's cultural leadership, advancing the "second integration" of Marxism with traditional culture, and embedding core socialist values. Externally, the author calls for equal treatment, mutual learning and shared benefit among civilizations, and for better international communication of Chinese culture. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese theorists derive cultural subjectivity from historical materialism, and how they link it to Party leadership and cultural dominance.

The moral and institutional predicament of American religion seen through the "baby formula appeal experiment" 从“奶粉求助实验”看美国宗教的道德与制度困境 Zhu Shuochen Zhu Shuochen takes up a viral TikTok "social experiment" from November 2025 to ask why the universal moral claims of American religious organisations break down when confronted with urgent suffering. A Kentucky addiction counsellor, Nikalie Monroe, phoned about 40 religious and charitable bodies posing as a mother of a two-month-old unable to buy formula after the federal government shutdown suspended SNAP benefits. Zhu argues that the mostly cold or bureaucratic responses expose the hypocrisy of American religion and reflect structural features of capitalist society rather than individual failings. The article first narrates the experiment and its reception. By the 43rd video, the author reports, 33 institutions had refused or offered no immediate help, mostly wealthy mainstream Protestant churches, while ten, including small working-class and Black congregations, mosques and temples, offered help at once. It then analyses the causes at several levels: theology and ethics, organisational form, economic base, politics and ideology. A final section applies Marxist atheism to two questions: whether religion can be a reliable moral source, and whether social security can be entrusted to religious charity. Zhu's central moves are these. Large churches, he says, have become professionalised non-profit enterprises, and under neoliberal welfare outsourcing (from Berger and Neuhaus's \"mediating structures\" to Charitable Choice) the state shifts responsibility to them, and they in turn push it back onto the individual through procedures and membership screening. Prosperity theology, religious consumerism and the alliance of evangelical churches with the Republican Party further instrumentalise charity. The author explains the better response of small groups by their organisational form, not by greater virtue. Drawing on Engels on class morality and Marx on religion as the \"opium of the people\", Zhu concludes that religious morality is a superstructural idea determined by the economic base and serves as a \"safety valve\" that manages the symptoms of poverty without touching its roots. Entrusting social security to religious charity is therefore, in the article's view, utopian in theory and bound to fail in practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-atheist reading of a recent American media event and its use of the \"opium\" thesis in a contemporary case.

Jean Meslier's militant atheism and its lessons: a study centred on the Testament 梅叶的战斗无神论思想及其启示——以《遗书》为中心的考察 Yan Li Li Huiqin Jean Meslier (1664–1729) was a village priest in Champagne who, according to the authors, outwardly performed his duties for forty years while privately hating the feudal nobility and the Church. His manuscript Testament (Mémoire), first published in full in the Netherlands in 1864, is the focus of this research article. The authors argue that Meslier's atheism was not a purely philosophical position but a direct weapon against exploiting-class society. They also claim it carries practical lessons for atheist education in China today. The article first reviews earlier scholarship. It finds Soviet and French work on Meslier's politics and philosophy, and Chinese studies of his political thought, common prosperity thought and materialism, but no systematic study of his atheism in China. It then proceeds in four steps: Meslier's critique of religion as fabrication; his exposure of the alliance of royal and priestly power; his critique of rural social relations and absolutism; and his call for revolution and a society based on common property. A final section assesses his influence, limits and present-day relevance. On religion, the authors report Meslier's claims that religions are human inventions, that blind faith is the root of error and deceit, and that visions, revelations, covenants and prophecies in the Old Testament are false. He also offers a test of prophecy: a prophecy that fails is not genuine. He then argues that the 'art of governing' underlies popular misery, and that religion and government are 'accomplices' who protect each other. Nobles, clergy ('parasites') and the king live off peasant labour. From this follows his rejection of any reform: he urges the people to unite, to seize freedom by violent revolution, and to replace private property with communal ownership in federated communes based on equal labour and enjoyment. The authors credit Meslier with helping move French thought from deism to thoroughgoing atheism, influencing Diderot and Holbach, and anticipating later utopian socialists. They note limits: he did not observe the rising bourgeoisie and capitalist relations, and he misunderstood the roots of religion, so he could not find the path to its disappearance. For today, they draw three lessons: affirm human value and a people-centred approach in atheist education; resist illegal religious and superstitious activity while guiding religion to adapt to socialist society and pursuing the sinicization of religion; and keep the critique of theology thoroughgoing, grounded in materialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Meslier's Testament, or want to see how current Chinese atheist-education writing draws on Enlightenment radicalism.

On the historical entanglement of science and theology 论科学与神学的历史纠缠 Zhang Peifu Zhang Peifu asks how science and theology have related to one another across human history, and what the historical record implies about their boundary. The article argues that the relationship has moved from simple to complex and from conflict towards dialogue and coexistence. Even so, Zhang maintains that the two are fundamentally different paradigms, and that science has increasingly become the driving force of social progress while theology has not shaped its mainstream methods. The article first traces a historical sequence: a shared origin in antiquity (Egyptian calendars, Mesopotamian astrology, Greek natural philosophy, Chinese astronomy-astrology), medieval Europe's subordination of science to Christian theology, and the early modern rupture associated with Copernicus, Vesalius, Galileo, Newton, Laplace and Darwin. It then covers the nineteenth-century missionary transmission of Western science to China and twentieth-century developments, including American anti-evolution legislation, historical revisions of Galileo and Newton, and science–theology dialogue around ecology and physics. In the middle section Zhang sorts scholarly views into three schools: the conflict thesis, the integration thesis and the independence thesis, citing figures such as Mach, Merton, Polkinghorne, Einstein, Sarton and Whitehead. Zhang then argues that science and theology differ in kind and sets out the contrast through worldview (materialism versus idealism), values, epistemology and method, and conceptions of truth, summarised in a table of some twenty dimensions. In this account science is open, falsifiable and critical, while theology is closed, dogmatic and grounded in revelation. Zhang adds that twentieth-century philosophy of science, especially logical positivism, sharpened the demarcation, and that modern science is institutionally separated from theology. Zhang concludes that theology has not substantively shaped scientific research and that science has greatly improved human life. The article endorses Engels's remark that God fares worse among natural scientists who believe in him than anywhere else, and cites Russell, Comte and Hawking against the idea that science ends in theology. Zhang also cites Engels to explain why scientists who are materialists in their work can fall into mysticism: crude empiricism that despises theory. Read the original if you want a broad, Marxist-inflected survey of the science–religion debate, including its Chinese episodes, and an example of how Chinese scholars argue for a categorical distinction between scientific and theological thought.

Paths to governing grassroots religious affairs according to law 基层宗教事务治理法治化路径研究 Fang Ye Zhang Liang Fang Ye and Zhang Liang ask how religious affairs at the grassroots (township, street, village and community level) can be brought fully within the rule of law. They note that religious activity mostly arises at this level, yet scholarship has paid it little attention. Their thesis is that grassroots governance should move from "controlling" religion to "managing it well", through a "five-in-one" path of Party leadership, legal system, enforcement, judicial safeguards, and legal and atheist education. The article first sets out why rule-of-law governance of grassroots religion matters at three levels: advancing the Sinicization of religion, strengthening rule-of-law construction in the religious field, and improving practical governance. It then identifies five groups of problems drawn from the authors' fieldwork: organisational leadership, the body of law, enforcement capacity, judicial protection and legal awareness. A final section offers counter-measures for each problem, illustrated with local cases such as Zhejiang, Shaanxi's Yulin and Hangzhou. On the diagnosis, the authors describe responsibility systems that weaken at village level ("hot at the top, cold at the bottom"), laws that are fragmented, declaratory or silent on new matters such as illegal religious activity and internet religion, and understaffed, campaign-style enforcement. They also report that judicial remedies are scarce, so disputes go to religious figures for mediation, and that believers and cadres alike have weak legal awareness, citing the Shi Yongxin case. For remedies, they propose "integrating", "refining" and "filling gaps" in legislation, permanent joint and cross-regional enforcement, diversified legal aid and open courts, and tailored Marxist atheist education, including school courses for young people. The authors conclude that improving grassroots rule of law in religious affairs requires system-wide thinking under Party leadership, with concrete measures: performance indicators, grid management, more staff and big-data platforms, local regulations that conform to higher law, and legal publicity delivered through accessible forms. They present this as part of making religion fit socialist society and modernising national governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, fieldwork-based Chinese policy account of how local religious affairs are administered and what reforms are being proposed, with provincial examples.

A contemporary examination of "fortune-telling": theoretical evolution, pseudoscientific nature and countermeasures “算命术”的当代审视：理论演变、伪科学本质与应对策略 Yang Huicong Why do highly educated people with good scientific literacy still believe in fortune-telling? Yang Huicong argues that sociological and psychological studies explain this only from the outside, because they presuppose that fortune-telling is false, a premise believers reject. In Yang's account, today's believers see their faith as rational and even scientific, so anti-superstition work must engage the internal logic of fortune-telling and show that it is pseudoscience. The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2026, first traces the history of divination. It moves from the official tortoise-shell and yarrow-stalk divination of the pre-Qin period, through the spread of fortune-telling among ordinary people and its codification in the Sui, Tang and Song, to the scholarly schools of the Ming and Qing. It then describes the present: online platforms, an industry with tiered pricing, learning communities, and a clientele that is younger and better educated. Finally it analyses why the claim to be scientific fails and proposes responses. Yang argues that fortune-telling grew with productive forces, literacy, the imperial examinations and printing, and increasingly wears a "scientific cloak", including modern borrowings from quantum mechanics and relativity. Its foundations are said to be self-contradictory: the "four identical birth-chart" problem undermines the doctrine of innate endowment, and even Ji Xiaolan's explanation leaves the outcome unspecified. Its symbols are ambiguous alone and in combination, and the same sign can mean good or bad fortune. Because failed predictions can be explained away, and practitioners mix in ordinary experience and publicise only their hits, apparent verification is unreliable. Yang holds that this is why it fails even Popper's falsifiability test in practice. Yang concludes that basic science education is no longer enough and calls for stronger Marxist atheist education. The proposals are to explain fortune-telling through historical materialism, as a premodern attempt at prediction that offers psychological comfort rather than useful guidance. They also include deeper science popularisation, teaching critical scientific thinking and frontier theories so they are not vulgarised, and more targeted anti-superstition publicity that explains why something is superstition, using vivid cases that expose practitioners' tricks. Read the original if you want a Chinese atheist-education perspective on why educated young people turn to fortune-telling, or details of its online industry and arguments against it.

The historical logic, theoretical content and contemporary lessons of Ya Hanzhang's thought on atheist propaganda and education 牙含章无神论宣传教育思想的历史逻辑、理论内涵与当代启示 Li Yong Peng Qinghai Li and Peng take up Ya Hanzhang (1916–1989), an ethnologist, scholar of religion and Tibetologist who became a pioneer of atheist propaganda and education in the People's Republic. They note that earlier scholarship has treated his work on nationality theory and Tibetan studies, but that his thought on atheist education has not been examined systematically. Their thesis is that this thought is an important result of adapting Marxist atheism to Chinese conditions and still offers guidance for ideological work today. The article first traces Ya's life. It covers his youth in Gansu, his time as a monk at Labrang Monastery, his move to Yan'an and Party membership in 1938, and his work on nationality questions and in Tibet after 1951. It then turns to his later roles at the Institute of Ethnology and in the Chinese Atheism Society, including his book Atheism and the Problem of Religion and the multi-volume History of Chinese Atheism. The last part draws out lessons for the present. In the authors' account, Ya's thought has three parts. The first is theory: using dialectical and historical materialism, he traced the origins of theism, criticised Feuerbach's view of religion, and held that "socialist society is not a period of religion's disappearance". On that basis he defended freedom of religious belief and distinguished religion strictly from feudal superstition. The second is the study of inherited atheist heritage, both foreign (the French Enlightenment, Spinoza, Epicurus) and Chinese. Ya was the first to urge using China's own atheist tradition, and he described Confucius as an atheist. The third is a set of practical principles. These are to avoid offending believers, to target peasants and herders, to use varied cultural forms, to institutionalise the work, and to link it with science popularisation. Ya held that atheist education does not conflict with the policy of freedom of religious belief but implements it fully. The authors conclude that Ya's thought offers three lessons for the new era: keep Marxism as the guiding ideology, so that atheist education stays legitimate; fight online superstition and strengthen grassroots, especially rural, positions; and extend Marxist atheist education to young people through the curriculum and new media. They cite the 2018 rural revitalisation guidelines and the 2021 guidelines on ideological and political work as consistent with this. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned account of how a founding figure of Chinese atheist studies framed religion policy, superstition and atheist education, and how that legacy is being used in current ideological work.

Strengthening the Party's ideological and political work in the new era requires stronger atheism education 加强新时代党的思想政治工作必须加强无神论教育 Dou Gaofei Dai Lixing Prompted by the Regulations on Ideological and Political Work of the Communist Party of China, issued by the Central Committee in September 2025, which call for strengthening atheism education, Dou and Dai ask why such education is indispensable to the Party's ideological and political work. They argue that Marxist atheism is the philosophical foundation of the Party's worldview, and that the pressure of theistic currents of thought now makes atheism education urgent for consolidating the Marxist ideological base. The article is organised in two halves. The first sets out why atheism education is necessary: the Party's nature, theoretical sources and purpose; its role in ideological security, the convictions of Party members and cadres, and social norms. It then traces atheism education through the New Democratic Revolution, the socialist period, early reform and opening up, and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second half diagnoses current problems and proposes remedies. The authors argue that atheism is inseparable from the Party's founding mission. In their reading, Marxism treats religion as an illusory reflection of social contradictions, and the Party seeks real-world liberation through practice and the people's own efforts rather than spiritual consolation. They identify three sets of problems: misunderstandings among some cadres, such as equating atheism with simply denying religion's existence, or treating freedom of religious belief as permission for Party members to believe; weak methods, content and teaching staff; and poor accountability mechanisms. They maintain that atheism education does not oppose believers, since atheists and believers share fundamental interests and religious freedom is protected. The authors propose four lines of work: deepen theoretical research across disciplines; use new media, VR and big data to reach audiences; target leading cadres, young people and the new economic and social sectors; and build lasting mechanisms for responsibility, assessment, funding and supervision. They treat atheism education as a long-term systematic undertaking, not a temporary campaign. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party-aligned scholars justify and plan atheism education within current ideological work, including its historical narrative and proposed institutional measures.

Atheism education in ideological and political work 论思想政治工作中的无神论教育 Zuo Peng Liu Yuxiang In September 2025 the Central Committee issued the Regulations on Ideological and Political Work of the Communist Party of China. Among nine main contents, it lists strengthening dialectical and historical materialist education and atheism education, the first time atheism education has entered an intra-Party regulation. Zuo and Liu argue that atheism education is the starting point and cornerstone of ideological and political work. They hold that it needs to be made routine and long-term so that Marxist atheism stays the dominant mainstream ideology among the people. The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2026, has four parts. It first sets out why atheism education matters, then explains what it should teach, where it should be concentrated, and what guarantees it needs. It draws heavily on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping. Its practical section singles out four of the Regulations' seven fields: government organs and public institutions, schools, rural areas and the internet. The authors give four reasons for strengthening atheism education. It consolidates Marxism's guiding position, it forms a defence against religious spiritual temptation and what the authors call infiltration by hostile foreign forces, it underpins the modernization of national governance, and it mobilises people for Chinese modernization. On content, they argue that there are no gods and that humans created them, tracing religion from tribal to national to world religions. That people believe in gods is also a fact, they say, which stems from incomplete scientific knowledge, from social suffering and from religion's role as ideology and culture. They conclude that the contradiction between non-existent gods and believers can be resolved only by protecting freedom of religious belief. This freedom includes the freedom not to believe, and religion is expected to die out naturally in the long run, not by being abolished. For practice, the authors call for atheism content in Party school curricula, in school courses and campus safety work, in rural cultural activities and customs reform, and in online atheism publicity and the law-based governance of online religious information. They also propose four guarantees: clear and firm Party leadership, an organisational system in which propaganda, united front, education and other departments share responsibility, the rule of law in religious affairs, and a Marxist atheism discipline with trained personnel. Read the original if you want to see how Party scholars justify and plan the institutionalisation of atheism education and its handling of religion in schools, villages and online.

Clarifying three misconceptions about the Yan'an Rectification Movement 澄清对延安整风的三个误识 Zhu Jun Marking the 80th anniversary of the end of the Yan'an Rectification Movement (1942–45), Zhu Jun takes up what the article calls misreadings and deliberate distortions of this episode in Chinese Communist Party history, circulating in Chinese and foreign scholarship. The author argues that these accounts amount to historical nihilism, whose real aim is to deny Mao Zedong's contribution to the revolution and, through that, the historical legitimacy of Communist Party rule. Drawing on historical sources, Zhu seeks to refute three claims. The article is organised around three charges: that the movement was a power struggle against Wang Ming, that it was a campaign of persecution through criticism and self-criticism, and that it was a vehicle for a Mao personality cult and Mao's personal dictatorship. Zhu treats the rectification's origins, its method of starting with senior cadres, the 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party, and the Seventh Party Congress. Sources include Mao's speeches, accounts of Ren Bishi, Zhou Enlai, Zhang Wentian and Bo Gu, and Stuart Schram's biography of Mao. On the first charge, Zhu argues that the Comintern and the Party already backed Mao as leader by 1938, so there was nothing to fight over. In this reading, the target was subjectivism, whether leftist or rightist, and the policy was to attack the errors while keeping the people. On the second, the author presents criticism and self-criticism as a principled, comradely method, citing the self-examinations of senior leaders. On the third, Zhu distinguishes rational respect for a leader from blind worship. Mao's prestige is explained by wartime conditions, the Comintern's dissolution in 1943 and the rivalry with the Nationalists. Citing Mao's refusal of a birthday celebration, the author says the movement guarded against a personality cult. Mao Zedong Thought, Zhu adds, came out of collective drafting under democratic centralism, which restrains personal arbitrariness. Zhu concludes that Mao's leadership position rested on political, ideological, mass and practical foundations and was chosen by history and the people. The author holds that a proletarian party needs a firm leadership core whose authority is upheld. Closing in the present, Zhu calls for a deeper grasp of the Two Establishes and a stronger consciousness of the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party historiography currently rebuts Western and Chinese critical accounts of the Yan'an period and ties them to present-day political principles.

African scholars' perceptions and assessments of Chinese modernization 非洲学界关于中国式现代化的认知评价 Wang Mingdong Lan Yang This article, published in World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 12), is a literature review of how scholars, think-tank researchers, commentators and political figures in Africa have assessed Chinese modernization. Wang and Lan start from the observation that Africa, the continent with the largest concentration of developing countries, has looked to China's 'development miracle' for lessons. They aim to offer an African perspective on the meaning and global contribution of Chinese modernization. Their overall finding is that most African scholars reach objective and positive conclusions, and that the research is gradually deepening. The review is organised in three parts followed by an assessment. It first covers African views of China's achievements: the economy, governance and democracy, common prosperity, and peaceful development. It then turns to explanations of China's success, grouped under leadership, guiding ideology, the people as the main body, the political system, policy adjustment and traditional culture. The third part covers the global significance Africans attach to Chinese modernization. Most of the material is quotation from named commentators in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, Rwanda, Zimbabwe and elsewhere. In the authors' account, African commentators credit above all the leadership of the Communist Party of China, the Two Integrations of Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture, a people-centred approach, and a political system suited to national conditions. Several of them are reported to describe whole-process people's democracy as different from Western democracy. Many are said to see the Belt and Road Initiative and China's global initiatives as expanding China–Africa cooperation. The central lesson the authors draw from these voices is that 'modernization is not Westernization'. Africa should choose its own path, borrowing from China without copying it wholesale. In their closing assessment, Wang and Lan characterise the scholarship by 'three comparisons' (past and present, China and the West, China and Africa), 'four combinations' of methods and 'three expansions' of scope. They concede that some scholars are influenced by negative opinion, and that others offer only shallow praise because the concept is recent. They argue that behind the research lies a growing African insistence on autonomy and independence in modernization. They end by quoting Xi Jinping that Africans have the greatest say on which path suits Africa, and by calling for deeper China–Africa cooperation. Read the original if you want a catalogue of African voices on Chinese modernization, as seen through a Chinese academic lens, with many named sources.

Communicative capitalism, neofeudalism and the latest developments in capitalism An interview with the American Marxist political theorist Jodi Dean 交往资本主义、新封建主义与资本主义的最新动态——访美国马克思主义政治理论家乔蒂·迪恩教授 Wang Yin Chang Yutong This is an interview, published in World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 12), in which Wang Yin and Chang Yutong question Jodi Dean, a Marxist political theorist who teaches politics at Hobart and William Smith Colleges in the United States. Dean is known for the concepts of "communicative capitalism" and "neofeudalism". The interview asks her to explain them, to assess where capitalism is heading, and to comment on communism and on China. The questions move from communicative capitalism and its link to Habermas, through artificial intelligence and the "attention economy" of her book Blog Theory, to neofeudalism as a tendency inside capitalism. They then turn to her new introduction to The Communist Manifesto, her reading of Marx on communism, and her book Comrade. The last two questions invite her impressions of socialism with Chinese characteristics and of Chinese modernization. Dean says communicative capitalism arises from the fusion of democratic ideals and capitalist logic. Openness, inclusion and participation are realised materially through global networks, yet this produces tech billionaires, the far right, lost trust and isolation, not a more rational society. She reads Habermas materially, as the ideology of "technoculture". She sees AI as a bid by tech firms and the US government to restore growth and hegemony after 2008, with job losses, damage to education and heavy resource use. Neofeudalism, in her account, is an internal tendency of capitalism: growth slows, accumulation depends on rents, services and finance, and asset-holders use the state to redistribute wealth upwards. She tracks it across the state, class relations, space and subjectivity, citing Trump, Musk, Adani and Modi as examples. Dean argues that the Manifesto is still relevant, perhaps more than in the nineteenth century. She holds that communism requires public ownership and planning, cannot be built in one country alone, and keeps the principle "from each according to ability, to each according to need". She presents "comrade" as a distinct political bond that helps build communist habits. On China, she says her expertise is not modernization theory and her view is intuitive. She credits the Communist Party's leadership and its use of markets within a planned, collective framework, and contrasts this with what she calls the anarchic and imperialist character of Western capitalist modernization. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist's own short statement of communicative capitalism and neofeudalism, or her views on China as put to a Chinese journal.

The theoretical implications and institutional advantages of the Communist Party of China's consolidation of cultural subjectivity in the new era 新时代中国共产党巩固文化主体性的理论蕴涵与制度优势 Wang Zhen Wang Zhen asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) consolidates what Xi Jinping calls the 'cultural subjectivity' (wenhua zhutixing) of Chinese civilisation, and why it is able to do so. The article argues that this consolidation rests on a historical-materialist foundation, on the Party's integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, and on its accumulated theory of cultural construction. It adds that the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics give the project a distinctive advantage. The author writes under the guidance of Xi Jinping's cultural thought. The article has three main parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundations, drawing on Marx and Engels's views of practice, objectification, the masses and social intercourse, and on the 'second integration' with traditional thought (Laozi, Xunzi, the idea of great unification, the continuity of civilisation). The second traces the Party's thinking on culture through the New Democratic revolution, the socialist period and reform and opening up, up to the new era, and summarises three theoretical features of current practice. The third turns to institutions and sorts them into fundamental, basic and important systems. In Wang's account, culture is the objectified product of labour and practice, so a nation's cultural subjectivity is created by the people and has to be defended by them. Wang adds that it is not closed: cultural intersubjectivity and mutual learning among civilisations are needed. Drawing on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, the author claims the Party has consistently sought a leading role for Marxism within cultural diversity. The new-era theory is characterised as seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times and putting the people first. On institutions, Wang argues that the socialist system and Party leadership secure cultural security and direction, that the people's congress system and consultative bodies bring in popular input, and that public ownership keeps the products of labour in the people's hands. Wang also lists the system for cultivating core socialist values, heritage-protection inspection and integrated education, science and talent development. Wang concludes that the Party's consolidation of cultural subjectivity has a theoretical basis and institutional guarantees that other approaches lack. Wang presents these as turning into momentum for cultural innovation and for building a strong cultural nation. The article treats this as showing the world significance of a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory scholar links historical materialism, traditional Chinese philosophy and the institutional order to the Party's current cultural policy.

An analysis of the roots of the degeneration of Karl Kautsky's view of Marxism 卡尔·考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源论析 Zhuang Wencheng Karl Kautsky was a leading theorist of the Second International and the German Social Democratic Party and once contributed significantly to Marxist theory. Zhuang asks why his understanding of Marxism changed over time until, in the article's account, he ended up opposing it. The thesis is that the root lies in an incomplete and unsteady grasp of Marxism's basic principles, which Zhuang traces to three sources: his misreading of Marxism's essential attributes, a vulgar evolutionary view of development, and the pressures of the transition to imperialism together with his own personal weaknesses. The article first examines how Kautsky understood the essential character of Marxism. It then follows what Zhuang calls the parabolic course of his political outlook, from the revolutionary tactics of the 1905–1909 period to his wartime and post-1917 positions. Zhuang draws on Kautsky's own writings, on remarks by Lenin, and on his intellectual biography, including his father's nationalism, Darwinism and his friendship with Bernstein. The final sections draw lessons for developing Marxism today. Zhuang's central move is that Kautsky turned Marxism into a positivist empirical science. He denied it was a philosophy, reduced historical materialism to a method, and set its scientific character against its revolutionary and class character. His Darwinian idea of development as adaptation, Zhuang says, led him to fatalism, technological determinism and a view of democracy as gradual expansion. From this Zhuang derives his later positions: 'ultra-imperialism', defence of the fatherland in the First World War, and 'pure democracy' set against proletarian dictatorship. A second move is that Kautsky failed to see imperialism and revisionism as products of the new epoch. Zhuang adds that he lacked theoretical courage, sought a middle path between left and right, and put the appearance of unity first. Zhuang concludes that Kautsky's case warns that theoretical innovation loses vitality once it departs from Marxism's essential attributes. The article proposes holding firmly to dialectical and historical materialism. It also calls for uniting science with revolutionary character, thorough theory with conscious practice, and class character with the people's interests. These principles are linked to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to the Two Integrations, and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Kautsky's trajectory and how it is used to argue for theoretical orthodoxy in current Chinese theory work.

The scientific content, value and means of promoting the correct view of the history of the Second World War 论正确二战史观的科学内涵、价值意蕴与弘扬路径 Ma Fuyun Zhang Bo Eighty years after the end of the Second World War, Ma and Zhang argue, some states use narratives of the war as a political tool of hegemonism, distorting the history that underlies the post-war international order. The article sets out what it calls the correct view of the history of the Second World War, a formulation it traces to Xi Jinping's statements and to the May 2024 China–Russia joint statement. Its thesis is that this view is scientifically grounded in historical materialism, has concrete political and normative value, and should be actively promoted through historical scholarship, international exchange and digital communication. The article is organised in four parts. It first sets out the scientific content of the view, built on three principles: objectivity, the people as the subject of history, and systematic or holistic method. It then lists the erroneous views it rejects: Western-centrism, historical nihilism and historical revisionism. Next it discusses the view's value for the international order and for global governance. It ends with three practical paths of promotion: a fact-based narrative system, multi-level international exchange platforms, and digital communication. The authors argue that the correct view answers each erroneous view in turn. Western-centrist accounts, they say, sideline the Chinese and Soviet theatres. The authors counter with figures such as over 35 million Chinese and over 27 million Soviet casualties, and the claim that over 77.5% of German and allied forces were consumed on the Soviet–German front. Nihilist claims, such as that the Chinese Communist Party fought only evasively, are rejected as undermining the justice of the victory and the Party's legitimacy. Revisionist claims, such as the 'Japan as victim' thesis and denial of the Nanjing Massacre, are described as dissolving responsibility for aggression. The authors further hold that the correct view supports the United Nations system and the Global Governance Initiative, which they contrast with the failed Versailles–Washington system. Ma and Zhang conclude that the view should build a historical consensus: oppose war and cherish peace, those who love war will perish while justice prevails, and seek common ground while shelving differences. They call for cross-checked archival evidence, interdisciplinary and global research paradigms, and narratives that include civilian memory. They also propose using the United Nations, UNESCO, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS, academic bodies and civil groups, plus short video, immersive technology and flagship media, to counter deepfake and algorithm-driven distortions. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars link Second World War memory to current diplomacy and global governance and to communication strategy.

Constructing the false legitimacy of ideology: how American cultural hegemony is built, and its crisis 建构意识形态的虚假正当性：美国文化霸权的建构方式及其危机 Ye Rurong Ye Rurong asks how the United States has built a "false legitimacy" for its ideology, which epistemological traps keep reproducing it, and how current "America First" policies erode it. The article argues that US cultural hegemony rests on a carefully constructed false legitimacy. In Ye's account, that legitimacy is now unravelling under the pressure of systemic capitalist crisis and a shifting global balance of power.
