The article draws on Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony, supplemented by Raymond Williams, David Harvey, John B. Thompson, Edward Said and Samuel Huntington. It begins by clarifying the concept of legitimacy and argues that the Chinese "zhengdangxing" (legitimacy in a moral sense) renders "legitimacy" better than "hefaxing" (legality). It then examines how the US constructs this legitimacy, through liberal ideology, consumer culture and asymmetric media communication. Next it turns to the cognitive traps involved, and finally to the erosion of legitimacy in the Trump era. Ye identifies three traps. The first is an illusion of "identical" interests, in which the particular interests of the hegemon and of property owners are presented as shared by subordinate groups and countries. The second is "value-neutral" discourse, produced by a new stratum of "organic intellectuals" (media, public relations and cultural workers), which hides the politics behind culture. The third is a false universality, in which "universal values" are said to be Western capitalist ideology repackaged. Ye then argues that as US material strength declines, Washington has shifted from leadership by consent to "non-legitimate" domination. It has moved from "identical interests" to "America First", from depoliticisation to "pan-politicisation" (cultural decoupling, visa limits, platform restrictions, technology blockades), and from universal values to "American exceptionalism", shown in tariffs and withdrawals from international agreements. Ye concludes that these shifts have not rescued US hegemony. In the article's view they have accelerated the collapse of its false legitimacy and produced a structural crisis of cultural hegemony. The author suggests this ends the long Western monopoly on global discourse and offers China a window to step outside Western-set frameworks and build its own autonomous discourse system. Read the original if you want a Gramscian, China-based critique of US soft power and "universal values" that ties cultural hegemony to Trump-era policy.

The history, present and future of the Danish communist movement An interview with Lotte Hørlyck Madsen, chair of the Communist Party in Denmark 丹麦共产主义运动的历史、现状与未来——访共产党(丹麦)主席洛特·于特夫特·麦德森 An De Zhao Dingqi This is an interview, conducted by An De and Zhao Dingqi for World Socialism Studies (2026, no. 1), with the chair of the Communist Party in Denmark (KPiD), named in the Chinese text as Lotte Yutefute Maideseng. The interviewee reviews a century of Danish communism and gives the party's view of present-day Denmark, Europe and China. The central message is that the movement remains fragmented and is not yet in revival, and that its prospects depend on rebuilding working-class strength and unity. The questions run chronologically. They begin with the founding of the first communist party in 1919 and its record in the 1930s and under Nazi occupation. They go on to the Cold War, the splits of the 1960s, the aftermath of the Soviet collapse and the 2006 founding of the KPiD. Later questions concern the party's current challenges, the 2023 merger of two other communist parties, the labour movement, the welfare state, the far right, and the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The interviewee argues that the Danish welfare state was won through class struggle by a strongly organised trade-union movement, not granted by the bourgeoisie. In this account, reformists read the class compromise as acceptance of capitalism, whereas communists do not regard welfare as a bridge to socialism. With the collapse of European socialism and the rise of neoliberalism, the interviewee says, the ruling class no longer needs compromise, and the welfare system is being dismantled. The interviewee also describes a neo-fascist threat nourished by neoliberal policies and calls for broad anti-fascist unity centred on social struggle. The party's strategy is an anti-monopoly alliance of the majority. Denmark is placed in the core of the Global North, whose wealth is traced partly to colonialism and slavery. The interviewee judges it too early to speak of a full communist revival in Denmark, citing anti-communism and war hysteria, though some young people are radicalising. The party's own tasks are to become a genuine vanguard, to root itself in the core of the working class and to reach the young. The interviewee describes China as a balancing force against the transatlantic alliance and says the party will counter rumours about China among Danish leftists. Read the original if you want a first-hand account of Danish communist history and factional divisions, or a European communist party's view of China and the new Cold War.

On the cultural subjectivity of the Communist Party of China 论中国共产党的文化主体性 Liu Hongchang Cultural subjectivity is described in the article as a signature concept of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Liu Hongchang asks what it means for the Communist Party of China (CPC) to hold cultural subjectivity, and how that subjectivity has taken shape over a century of Party practice. The answer is that the Party is the political agent driving the development of Chinese culture, and that its cultural subjectivity consists of four linked attributes: cultural consciousness, cultural autonomy, cultural creativity and cultural transcendence. Liu first distinguishes three nested levels of cultural subject: the Chinese nation, the Chinese people and the Party. The Party's cultural subjectivity is defined as the cultural awareness and capacity inherent in the Party itself. The article then works through the four attributes in turn, drawing on Party documents, the writings of Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and episodes from the revolutionary period, the early People's Republic and the reform era up to the present. On consciousness, Liu argues that the Party has taken up a cultural mission, deepened its understanding of culture's place (from a supporting tool to a livelihood and economic force), and grasped cultural laws in time and space. On autonomy, the Party is said to have chosen its cultural path, planned its cultural strategy (from Deng's call for socialist spiritual civilization to the 'cultural power' goal for 2035) and defended cultural security, in contrast to a Kuomintang portrayed as dependent on imperialism. On creativity, Liu points to the people-centred orientation of culture, the creation of revolutionary and socialist culture, and methods such as the Two Integrations and 'drawing the essence, discarding the dross'. On transcendence, Liu draws on Marx's remarks on Greek art and the relative independence of culture. The Party is said to have pushed culture ahead of its economic base through the 'Double Hundred' policy and literacy campaigns, and through constitutional and legal provisions on cultural leadership. Liu concludes that the Party's cultural subjectivity rests on its leadership of cultural work and on a people-centred stance, and that it underpins the Party's ability to create new culture in the new era. The article treats this subjectivity as tied to the fate of Chinese culture and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account of how Chinese scholars frame the Party's cultural role, with its historical periodisation and the official policy documents it cites.

Marx's critique of capitalist wages 马克思对资本主义工资问题的批判 Yuan Jiaxi Yuan Jiaxi asks how Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme exposes the nature of capitalist wages and, through it, the secret of capitalist exploitation. Digital-intelligence technology empowering the integrated development of ideological and political courses across universities, middle schools and primary schools 数智技术赋能大中小学思政课一体化建设 Yan Xiaofang This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2026, asks how generative AI can help integrate ideological and political courses across primary, middle and university stages. Digital discipline inspection and supervision: using technology to strengthen the penetrating power of anti-corruption work 数字纪检监察：以科技赋能提高反腐败穿透力 Shi Pengpeng Shi Pengpeng, a deputy dean and professor at the School of Discipline Inspection and Supervision of China University of Political Science and Law, takes up a call from Xi Jinping at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) to keep raising the "penetrating power" of anti-corruption work. Intelligent computing as an aid to building China's independent knowledge system 智能计算助力构建中国自主的知识体系 Tong Dezhi Tong Dezhi takes up a task the Party has set for philosophy and the social sciences: building an independent knowledge system. Resolutely getting things implemented is the ideal and conviction of Communists in action 狠抓落实是共产党人行动着的理想信念 Wang Yubo Writing in the People's Daily on 25 February 2026, Wang Yubo, Yunnan's governor, argues that implementing the Party Central Committee's major decisions is a basic requirement of upholding the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership. Providing strong public-opinion support for striving through the 15th Five-Year Plan period Marking the tenth anniversary of Xi Jinping's 19 February 2016 speech on the Party's news and public opinion work 为奋进“十五五”提供强大舆论支撑 Liu Siyang Writing in the People's Daily on the tenth anniversary of Xi Jinping's symposium speech on the Party's news and public opinion work (19 February 2016, the "2.19" speech), Liu Siyang, a senior official of the All-China Journalists Association, argues that the speech remains the fundamental guide for the media in the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030). Revolutionary music and women's work in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region 革命音乐与晋察冀边区妇女工作 Wang Tiezhu This short piece, published in Guangming Daily in February 2026, asks how the Communist Party used revolutionary music in its work among women in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region during the War of Resistance against Japan. Village governance and the remaking of the village cadre corps in the Shandong anti-Japanese base areas 山东抗日根据地的村政建设与干部群体重塑 Ma Mingchong How did the Communist Party turn village governance in Shandong, where early in the War of Resistance grassroots power was largely held by local bullies and gentry, into a working base for wartime mobilisation? New developments in the theory of state sovereignty in the digital age A roundtable on cyber sovereignty 数字时代国家主权理论的新演进 This is a written expert roundtable published in Guangming Daily on 13 February 2026, hosted by two of the paper's reporters, Ji Wenya and Wang Jin. Key focal points for teaching the course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" well 讲好“习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想概论”课的关键着力点 Liu Hongsen Liu Hongsen, writing in Guangming Daily, asks how university teachers can teach the compulsory course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" (the "Introduction" course) effectively. Making the Party's innovative theory enter minds, hearts and souls Reflections on teaching the course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" 让党的创新理论入脑入心入魂 Chen Peiyong Chen Peiyong, writing in Guangming Daily in February 2026, asks how teachers can teach the university course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" so that the theory takes root in students. Chen's answer is that the thought is broad, deep and still developing, so teachers need a full grasp of it, real insight into the age, solid theoretical training and teaching experience. The aim is a classroom that is attractive enough for the thought to enter students' minds, hearts and souls. The commentary is a short piece of pedagogical advice arranged under five headings. They cover the course's teaching philosophy and goals, the need to understand two "objects" (the thought itself and the students), the move from textbook logic to teaching logic, the support that academic research gives teaching, and the use of practical cases. Chen's central moves are as follows. First, teachers should keep asking what students gain, because Chen holds that a sense of benefit, rather than ease of material, makes a course attractive. Marx's concrete paths for developing the materialist conception of history 马克思发展唯物史观的具体路径 Peng Qifu Yan Shuang This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (3 February 2026) asks how Marx developed the materialist conception of history after founding it. In their account, while guiding the workers' movement and proletarian revolution he opened three concrete paths of development, showing a dialectical interaction between universal theory and particular practice. The article takes the three paths in turn. The first is Marx's analysis of specific French political events in The Class Struggles in France, 1848 to 1850 and The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte. The second is his exposition of the laws of the capitalist mode of production in Capital. The third is his search for a way to cross the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, drawing on the Asiatic mode of production and the Russian village commune. On France, the authors argue that Marx read the 1848 revolution and Bonaparte's restoration through class struggle rooted in the economic base. The peasants' attachment to "Napoleonic ideas" is presented as evidence that ideology has relative independence and can act back on social being. In Capital, they say, Marx applied the theory to the production process and built the doctrine of surplus value, with absolute and relative surplus value as the capitalist's two methods. On Russia, they argue that Marx saw the commune as a fulcrum of social renewal. It gained content on revolutionary strategy, state power, ideology critique, proletarian emancipation and the diversity of social formations. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented overview of how Chinese scholars present Marx's own development of historical materialism.

Marx's critique of the "German modern problem" 马克思批判“德国式的现代问题”的理路 Liu Yong This short commentary from China Social Sciences Today asks how Marx, in his 1844 "Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction", understood the "German modern problem". The article follows Marx's critique at three levels: the "anachronism" of the German system, its political-economic roots, and the state of German classes. It closes by suggesting the analysis still informs how latecomer countries' modernization is understood. Liu contends that Germany in 1843 had missed the 1789 moment yet faced a capitalism whose contradictions were already visible in Britain and France. It therefore had to take on national unification, political emancipation and human emancipation together, rather than in sequence. For Liu, this makes Germany a prototype of resolving several tasks at once through theoretical critique and revolutionary practice. Marx's critique of the historical school of law and of the practical and theoretical political parties leads to the anatomy of civil society and to the materialist conception of history. Liu describes the German bourgeoisie as late, dependent on feudal power and compromising, and the Junker landlords as having turned into a harsh capitalist class. Liu concludes that Marx moved from German particularity through its political-economic roots and class analysis to a universal path: proletarian revolution as the fundamental solution to the problems of modernization. Liu presents this as a diagnosis of nineteenth-century Germany and as a lesson for latecomer countries facing "time-space compressed modernization". Read the original if you want a brief Chinese reading of the 1844 Introduction as a theory of late-developer modernization.

The limits of "algorithmic time" from the standpoint of historical materialism 从唯物史观看“算法时间”的限度 Sun Yan This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2026, asks how "human time" can regain its meaning and practical measure as AI accelerates social life. Drawing on Marx's analysis of technology and machinery, the article moves through three steps: the technical logic of algorithmic time, the limits of its neutrality, and the return to human time. It uses examples such as traffic scheduling, medical imaging, delivery riders timed by the second and algorithmically fragmented user attention. It also refers briefly to Habermas. Sun identifies three features of algorithmic time: computability, efficiency and measurability. Sun holds that these carry no exploitation in themselves, but become institutionalised through three logics: acceleration, discipline, and quantification-cum-coercion. In this account, capital no longer only lengthens or intensifies labour. It controls the rhythm, structure and distribution of time, and hides this behind \"technical neutrality\". Practice then shrinks from purposeful activity to task execution, which Sun reads as the colonisation of the lifeworld by system logic. Sun concludes that, in line with Marx's view of free time as the measure of human development, productivity gains should enlarge disposable time. Under socialism, the people-centred approach to development points to rebuilding this measure. Sun proposes embedding values in algorithms, treating time as a negotiable and guaranteed public resource, and protecting time for meaning and social interaction. The article states that the true value of new quality productive forces lies in widening people's time boundaries rather than in general acceleration. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist reading of AI, labour platforms and time politics.

The modern course and scholarly character of Chinese classical studies 中国古典学研究的现代历程与学理特质 Li Zhen Li Zhen takes up a question raised by the recent boom in classical studies, which followed the first World Classics Congress over a year ago: what is Chinese classical studies, and what should it study? The article argues that further work needs theoretical clarification on two fronts. One is a historical account of how classical studies took shape as a modern discipline. The other is an internal understanding of the classics as the foundation of Chinese civilization. Li holds that the field's distinctive trait is its focus on canonical texts, and that the canon has repeatedly renewed itself. The piece is a short newspaper essay in three parts. The first traces the emergence of Chinese classical studies in modern scholarship in three stages. The second asks what counts as a classic, a canonical text and a statecraft text. The third surveys changes in the canonical system from the pre-Qin period to the late Qing and after, and draws a lesson from them about civilizational renewal. On history, Li says the term was used by Liang Qichao in 1923 for Qianlong–Jiaqing-era textual scholarship, but 'national learning' was then the more common label. It entered modern scholarship in the mid-1990s through comparative, literary-historical work centred on excavated texts of the pre-Qin and Han periods. Over the past fifteen years it has become more rooted in Chinese tradition, systematic, institutionalised and in dialogue with Western classics. Li notes that this breadth raises the question of what is not classical studies. On substance, Li argues that the field's core is the study of the fundamental principles, values, history and texts of classical China, with the canon as its main body. Citing the Zhuangzi, the Hanshu and Zhang Xuecheng, Li says the canon goes beyond Confucian classics to include the writings of the various schools of thought, as 'words that carry the Way'. Li then identifies three major shifts in the canon: its establishment in the Western Han, its reshaping in the Tang and Song, and its upheaval from the late Qing. Each shift coincided with a major turning point in history. Li concludes that only a spirit of the age able to lead history to a higher level can become a new classic, and that the canon keeps its classic status only through continual self-renewal. Chinese classical civilization endures, Li says, because its basic principles remain open to history, not because the texts are old. Classical studies therefore looks to the classics for resources to answer the questions of the present. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Chinese scholars currently define the scope, history and purpose of Chinese classical studies.

The historical revisionism behind Takaichi's fallacies 高市谬论背后的历史修正主义思想 Zhang Yanru This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 30 January 2026, examines the erroneous remarks on Taiwan made by Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae. It then analyses her characteristic political method and its goals, and closes by linking her Taiwan remarks to earlier Japanese justifications for expansion. Zhang also describes her 2025 visit to a Japanese military cemetery in Kuala Lumpur and her long campaign, with groups such as the New History Textbook compilation association, to change the term for wartime "comfort women" in textbooks, which the Japanese cabinet and education ministry accepted in 2021. Zhang concludes that Takaichi aims to consolidate conservatives, raise support for constitutional revision and build backing for stronger security, and that long tenure could pull Japanese politics further in this direction, which Asian countries should watch. The article likens her Taiwan arguments to Yamagata Aritomo's "line of interest" and Japan's 1933 claims over Northeast China. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic view of how Takaichi's historical positions are interpreted in the dispute over her Taiwan remarks.

Heroic narrative communication in the history of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army 东北抗联历史的英雄叙事传播 Liu Sen This short commentary asks how the history of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (Dongbei Kanglian) can be communicated effectively in the age of intelligent media. Continuous storytelling through social media and popular culture is likened to "spiritual drip irrigation" that consolidates the core value system. Narrative problems and strategies in the international communication of China's War of Resistance stories 中国抗战故事国际传播的叙事难题与策略 Meng Wei Meng Wei asks how China's stories of the War of Resistance against Japan can be made more credible and persuasive to audiences abroad. The commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 30 January 2026, holds that telling these stories well defends historical truth and promotes shared values of peace and justice. The author argues that despite real gains since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the narratives still suffer from problems that limit their reach and credibility, and that these can be addressed through six strategies. The piece has two parts. The first diagnoses four weaknesses in current narratives. The second sets out six strategies for improving international communication. Meng draws on a 2025 Donghua University survey of ten "red" venues, the National Radio and Television Administration's 2013 campaign against "anti-Japanese thunder dramas", and its July 2025 notice on short dramas about the war. On the diagnosis, Meng says that the narratives are "hard to explain, hard to spread and hard to believe". Wartime culture in China leans toward macro and collective storytelling and lacks the individual and third-party perspectives found in international memory of the Second World War. Meng recommends linking grand narrative to personal experience through small objects such as a grain of rice or an IOU. The author also calls for reducing "cultural discount" by studying target audiences and avoiding divisive expressions, and for reaching young people. The other proposals are multimodal digital and immersive formats, with technology serving content rather than spectacle, and international education and scholarly cooperation. Meng concludes that effective communication must correct distortion, context gaps and trivialisation while building a contemporary international influence for the culture of the War of Resistance. The author says that shifting foreign audiences' views is a process of layering and acculturation, not replacement. The stated aims are to counter historical revisionism and nihilism, oppose unilateralism and hegemonism, and win wider international respect and cooperation for China. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars frame the weaknesses and remedies of wartime-history communication abroad.

The philosophical connotations of "investing in people" “投资于人”的哲学内涵 Zhang Dang This commentary in Guangming Daily asks what philosophical content lies behind the economic phrase "investing in people". The occasion is the call of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) to closely combine "investing in physical assets" with "investing in people". The piece has two parts. Zhang contends that investing in people does not reject the profit-seeking nature of investment but raises its direction and priorities, moving from "seeing only things" to "seeing people too". In value terms, the author says traditional investment treats people as instruments for meeting return targets and falls into "instrumental rationality". Investing in people instead makes human life, development and dignity the aim, and builds human capital as competition shifts from capital-intensive to talent-intensive. In practice terms, education, healthcare, pension and fertility-support policies are said to develop individual capacities and relieve livelihood worries, creating a virtuous circle between individual and social progress. In systems terms, such investment is described as covering the whole life cycle and expressing equal respect for development rights. Zhang concludes that investing in people does not negate investing in physical assets. The two are dialectically unified: material investment supplies the base, while investment in people supplies the capacity to turn it into value. Each is said to fail without the other, and together they form the investment support for high-quality development. The author presents this as a scientific methodological guide for the new era and as a concrete expression of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars give a Marxist philosophical gloss to a current economic policy formula.

Continuously forming new growth points for expanding domestic demand 不断形成扩大内需的新增长点 He Lilong Writing in Guangming Daily on 9 February 2026, He Lilong takes up how China can keep generating new growth points for domestic demand during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). He presents this as the supply-and-demand expression of developing new quality productive forces. The piece is a short commentary organised in five sections. It covers a people-centred source of new demand, an innovation-driven consumption ecosystem, new investment tracks created by green transition, new market space opened by structural change, and a dynamic, time-sequenced cycle of growth. The examples range from artificial intelligence, the low-altitude economy and esports to energy storage, battery recycling, the silver economy and county-level markets. He's central claim is that new growth points arise from people's rising aspirations for a better life combined with market innovation. Structural change, He argues, opens demand through population ageing, county markets (over 38% of retail sales in 2025, per the article), urban renewal with the urbanisation of migrant workers, and import substitution for technologies subject to Western restrictions. He concludes that short-term and long-term policy must be balanced: modest counter-cyclical consumption incentives secure livelihoods and stabilise expectations, while long-term bets such as quantum technology and biomanufacturing build future competitiveness and create investment and jobs now. He calls for institutional innovation to activate market forces and for combining improvement of livelihoods and consumption with investment in both things and people. Using rigorous institutions and rigid enforcement to lock power in an institutional cage 以严密制度和刚性执行把权力关进制度笼子 Song Fufan This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily (9 February 2026) takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that the Party's self-reform centres on governing power. For implementation, Song calls for top leaders to set an example, for education that leads officials to know the rules and stand in awe of them, and for greater openness in Party and government affairs so that power operates in the sunlight. Implementing the Party Central Committee's major decisions and plans more resolutely and effectively 更加坚决有力地贯彻落实党中央重大决策部署 Wu Fulai Tan Jun Published in the People's Daily on 9 February 2026, this commentary asks why and how Party members and officials should carry out the major decisions and plans of the Party Central Committee. Pooling efforts to strengthen university counsellors' capacity for ideological and political guidance 聚力提升高校辅导员的思政引领能力 Dong Mingming This short commentary, first published by People's Daily Online, asks how universities can raise the capacity of their counsellors (fudaoyuan) to provide ideological and political guidance. On political character, Dong calls for counsellors to be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, to observe Party discipline, to safeguard ideological security by guiding student societies, classroom teaching and online speech, and to take part in a "big ideological and political" pattern working with subject teachers. A problem-oriented methodology of reform 问题导向的改革方法论 Chen Yingtao Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2026, Chen Yingtao asks how China's reform, now in what the article calls a critical stage and a deep-water zone, can deal with problems that involve many actors, factors and dimensions at once. The commentary is organised in three parts, which Chen presents as an ontology, an epistemology and an axiology. The first treats the origin of complex problems in practice, the second the scientific modes of thought needed to handle them, and the third the value basis of reform. It ends with a short note on future tasks. On the ontological side, Chen holds that complex problems arise from deepening reform and the movement of contradictions, and that they reflect the historical stage reached after the principal contradiction shifted in the new era. Solving them means changing their conditions through cultural guidance, institutional innovation and technological progress. Epistemologically, the author combines systems thinking, dialectical thinking and bottom-line thinking, illustrated by integrated reform of education, science and talent, by rural revitalisation and by financial-risk prevention. The origins, wrong turns and reassessment of neoliberalism 新自由主义的滥觞、歧路及反思 Liu Shiqiang Liu Shiqiang, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2026, takes up the growing global development deficit: widening inequality, class antagonism and ecological crisis. The article argues that these are the result of neoliberalism's over-expansion since the end of the Cold War and reveal deep flaws in it as a political idea and development model. Understanding it, Liu says, is a precondition for rebuilding the global development order. The piece is organised in three parts. It first traces neoliberalism from classical liberalism through Keynesianism to the Friedman-inspired Reagan–Thatcher turn, and sets out its core tenets. It then examines theoretical defects and present difficulties in the West, citing US data on income concentration and election spending. Finally it turns to the effects on developing countries and on global governance. Liu summarises neoliberalism's core as full privatisation and free markets, multiparty democracy with checks and balances, and multiculturalism with individual primacy. The author treats these as one interlocking whole serving the free movement and unlimited accumulation of capital. In Liu's critique, this puts capital above economy, politics and society, producing monopoly, crisis, “veto politics”, commodified social life and, in the end, crises of state governance. Exported to Latin America, Eastern Europe and Asia, it brought stagnation and unrest, and Liu describes “liberal democracy” promotion as cover for hegemony and capital expansion. Liu reads populism, protectionism and Trump's tariffs as products of its failure. Liu concludes that the world must move beyond the binary of laissez-faire and closed conservatism. The author calls for a dynamic balance between market efficiency and social fairness, checks and government capacity, and individual rights and social values, and for respect for other states' legitimate rights in building a community with a shared future for mankind. The decline of neoliberalism in the United States is irreversible 美国新自由主义式微不可逆转 Zhang Guoxi This newspaper commentary asks whether successive US administrations could rescue neoliberalism after its systemic decline. Zhang contends that Obama's rescue measures stabilised the economy briefly but left financial monopoly and unequal wealth distribution untouched, and so fed Occupy Wall Street and populism. Trump, in this account, abandoned neoliberal globalisation through tariffs and "America First" but intensified tax cuts, deregulation and privatisation, serving big capital under a populist cover. Biden's policy, marked by Jake Sullivan's 2023 Brookings speech and the "new Washington consensus", is read as a sublation of neoliberalism and a return to Keynesianism, though it keeps a "limited liberalism". Zhang concludes that neoliberalism is essentially social Darwinism and cannot resolve polarisation, social division or industrial hollowing-out. In this reading, US governments treat any "-ism" as a tool for protecting national interests, hegemony and global capital returns, and neoliberalism has completed its mission. Milei economics: the extreme alienation of neoliberalism 米莱经济学：新自由主义的极端异化 Xie Wenze Xie examines the economic programme of Argentine president Javier Milei, which the article calls "Milei economics". Xie describes Milei's creed as hostility to Marxism, social justice, the welfare state and Peronism. His theory treats the state as the "enemy of freedom", rejects market failure and dismisses Keynesianism and the developmentalism of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean. His platform of privatization, liberalization and dollarization works like "shock therapy": cuts to the federal bureaucracy, deregulation, planned sales of 41 state firms, and 30-year tax breaks for foreign investors in lithium and shale. Xie says the short-term gains rest on damage to the economy's foundations. Disputes over resource revenue have set the federal government against provinces such as Chubut. Poverty fell from 52.9% to 31.6% between mid-2024 and mid-2025, which Xie attributes mainly to lower inflation and regards as unsustainable. Xie draws three warnings: avoid ideologizing economic theory, avoid extreme policies lacking social buffers, and avoid theoretical dogmatism that ignores national conditions. Developing countries, the author concludes, should seek a balance between market and government, build their own development theory and defend economic sovereignty. Read the original if you want a short Chinese academic assessment of Milei's economics and the lessons it draws for developing countries.

Promoting the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation 推动科技创新和产业创新深度融合 Zheng Qinghua Writing in Guangming Daily, Zheng Qinghua takes up the call, made in the proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), to promote the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. Zheng argues that, given a complex domestic and international environment, this integration needs systems thinking, a global outlook and a long-term view. It should be oriented to national strategic needs and rest on an innovation system in which diverse actors share goals and build jointly. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out why integration is necessary at this time. The second proposes an implementation path across five dimensions: overall planning, institutional reform, market allocation of factors, multi-party linkage and external cooperation. The third turns to the specific role of universities, which Zheng describes as an important actor in the integration. On necessity, Zheng presents integration as a precondition for seizing the initiative in innovation, as the "only path" to developing new quality productive forces, and as the basis of new competitive advantages. Zheng holds that national strength depends less on R&D spending or patent counts than on how fast results are turned into industry and how closely the innovation chain and industrial chain are coupled. Engels's view of scientific socialism 恩格斯的科学社会主义观 Bai Bingzhuo Bai Bingzhuo, writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2026, revisits Engels's reflections on scientific socialism, the part of Marxism where Engels is said to have played a key role. The intellectual-historical context of Marx's thought on justice 马克思正义思想的思想史语境 Zhang Shoukui Since the turn of the century, Chinese scholars have disputed whether Marx rejected justice as a normative category or pursued a higher form of it. Upholding a people-centred approach to advance the modernization of social governance 坚持以人民为中心 推进社会治理现代化 Gao Weixing Wang Chong This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2026, asks how social governance can be improved and modernized in line with the Party's proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan. Institutional opening-up seen from the dimension of governance modernization 从治理现代化维度看制度型开放 Liu Jiangning Liu Jiangning takes up the call in the Party's recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan, adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), to "steadily expand institutional opening-up". Anchoring on the goals of a strong science and technology nation and a strong financial nation to develop science and technology finance 锚定科技强国与金融强国目标发展科技金融 Chen Yulu Chen Yulu, president of Nankai University, argues in this commentary (published in the People's Daily on 3 February 2026) that science and technology finance should be developed deliberately for the goals of building a strong science and technology nation and a strong financial nation. Telling the story of China's frontier governance in the new era well 讲好新时代中国边疆治理故事 Mao Zhanwen This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2026, asks how China's frontier governance in the new era should be narrated in international communication. The development code from poverty alleviation to rural revitalisation A dialogue with Wang Sangui, Dean of the China Institute for Poverty Reduction at Renmin University of China 从脱贫攻坚到乡村振兴的发展密码 This is an interview in the Economic Daily series "Dialogue with Economists" (29 January 2026), in which a reporter questions Wang Sangui, Dean of the China Institute for Poverty Reduction at Renmin University of China. Read the original if you want an official-academic account of how Chinese scholars explain the logic of poverty alleviation, the transition period and the "regular support" phase, with the figures and policy mechanisms Wang cites.

Experience and lessons of labour rule of law in the Central Soviet Area: a historical study based on Red China 中央苏区劳动法治建设的经验与启示——基于《红色中华》的历史考察 Wang Mouyin Using the Soviet government's official newspaper Red China (founded December 1931) as its source, this short commentary asks what the labour law of the Central Soviet Area shows about early Party-led rule of law. The establishment and improvement of the labour insurance system in the early years of the People's Republic of China 新中国成立初期劳动保险制度的建立与完善 Jiang Yingchun Jiang Yingchun, in a newspaper article published in Guangming Daily in January 2026, asks how the Chinese Communist Party built a labour insurance system in the early years of the People's Republic. Nurturing an upbeat and striving spirit across the whole nation 涵养全民族昂扬奋发的精神气质 Li Jinghua This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 28 January 2026, takes up a line from the proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025): to lead cultural development with the core socialist values and nurture an upbeat, striving spirit across the whole nation. Implementing the Party Central Committee's major decisions and plans more resolutely and effectively 更加坚决有力地贯彻落实党中央重大决策部署 Tang Junfeng This commentary in Guangming Daily (28 January 2026) responds to Xi Jinping's call, at the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, to implement the Central Committee's major decisions and plans "more resolutely and effectively". The scientific connotation and practical orientation of strengthening social resilience 增强社会韧性的科学内涵和实践指向 He Haigen Sun Daiyao This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 27 January 2026, takes up the call in the Proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan, adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), to "strengthen economic and social resilience". World China studies: seeing the world from China and China from the world 世界中国学：从中国看世界，从世界看中国 Li Bozhong Li Bozhong, writing in Guangming Daily, argues that the study of China has become a worldwide field, which he calls "world China studies" (Global China Studies). Grasping the rich connotations and practical requirements of combining rule of law with rule of virtue 深刻把握坚持依法治国和以德治国相结合的丰富内涵和实践要求 Zhou Youyong This commentary, published in the People's Daily in January 2026, explains what it means to combine governing the country by law (yifa zhiguo) with governing by virtue (yide zhiguo), and why and how this should be done. The strategic significance and practical requirements of vigorously boosting consumption 大力提振消费的战略意义和实践要求 Yu Weiping Writing in the People's Daily on 26 January 2026, Yu Weiping, a deputy director of the CPPCC Economic Committee, examines why the Party leadership has made boosting consumption a priority and what is required to do so. Doing more practical things for the people and raising the mass-organising capacity of primary-level Party organisations 更好为群众办实事解难题 不断提升基层党组织的群众组织力 Hou Xibao This short commentary, first published in People's Daily on 23 January 2026, asks how primary-level Party organisations can better organise, mobilise and unite ordinary people. The rich connotations and original contributions of the anti-poverty theory with Chinese characteristics 中国特色反贫困理论的丰富内涵和原创性贡献 Wang Lin Writing in the People's Daily on 23 January 2026, Wang Lin examines what the author calls the anti-poverty theory with Chinese characteristics, which Xi Jinping first named in February 2021 at the national poverty-alleviation commendation conference. The new development model underpins steady and sustained progress of China's economy 新发展模式支撑中国经济行稳致远 Guo Chunli Guo Chunli, a deputy director at the National Development and Reform Commission's macroeconomic research institute, comments on the recommendation for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) to form more economic development patterns led by domestic demand, driven by consumption and based on endogenous growth. Expanding space for development by meeting people's livelihood needs 在满足民生需求中拓展发展空间 Li Zhiming This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 22 January 2026, takes up the relationship between economic development and people's livelihood (minsheng: education, health care, elderly care, housing, social security). The Chinese narrative of ecological civilization construction from the perspective of new media 新媒体视域下生态文明建设的中国叙事 Huang Ting Huang Ting asks how the grand narrative of ecological civilization construction can reach ordinary people in a fragmented, visual and interactive media environment. Several important concepts for enhancing the international communication of Chinese civilization 提升中华文明国际传播力的几个重要观念 Hu Yu Hu Yu takes up what the author calls two mismatches facing China amid Chinese modernization: cultural soft power lags behind economic hard power, and international reputation lags behind international contribution. The first is feeling (renqing): content rooted in everyday life and sincere emotion moves audiences more than argument. The second is the people: ordinary Chinese, and ordinary foreigners friendly to China, should be the protagonists and communicators, in line with the mass line. The third is humanism: Hu proposes a "new humanism", scientific, peaceful and inclusive, built on Marxist principles, together with attention to cultural heritage and to technology for good. The South Manchuria Railway Company's responsibility for aggression cannot be concealed “满铁”的侵略罪责不容掩盖 Li Xiaochen Tian Jiacheng This newspaper commentary (China Social Sciences Today, January 2026) addresses the role of the South Manchuria Railway Company ("Mantetsu") in Japan's invasion of north-east China. Using the innovative achievements of poverty alleviation to advance agricultural and rural modernization 以脱贫攻坚创新成果促农业农村现代化 Ye Xingqing Writing in Economic Daily on 21 January 2026, the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Ye Xingqing asks what the experience of the poverty alleviation campaign offers for the next stage of agricultural and rural modernization. Accelerating high-level scientific and technological self-reliance through systems thinking 以系统思维加快高水平科技自立自强 Jiang Cheng Writing in Guangming Daily, Jiang Cheng takes up the call of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) to accelerate high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and lead the development of new quality productive forces. The theoretical content and practical orientation of adhering to the general keynote of seeking progress while maintaining stability 坚持稳中求进工作总基调的理论内涵和实践指向 Chen Hangyu Following the 2025 Central Economic Work Conference, which called for adhering to the general keynote of making progress while maintaining stability in the 2026 economic work, Chen Hangyu explains what this principle means in theory and how it should guide policy. Rectifying formalism to lighten the burden on the grassroots 整治形式主义 为基层减负 Song Ge Zhou Wenzhang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2026, takes up the campaign against formalism and for reducing burdens on grassroots officials. Building a Beautiful China to advance the modernization of harmony between humanity and nature in all respects 以美丽中国建设全面推进人与自然和谐共生的现代化 Yu Xiang This commentary, originally published in the People's Daily on 21 January 2026, is a study piece on the first volume of Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Ecological Civilization. Why Marxism retains an even more vigorous vitality 为何马克思主义能保持更加旺盛的生命力 Yang Geng Most schools of thought decline after their founders die, Yang Geng observes, yet Marxism has kept producing successors who answer new questions and absorb the best of human culture. The third turns to China and the Two Integrations, which Yang presents as the way to open up new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxism. Along the way Yang engages Lukács, Fromm, Popper, Heilbroner and Collingwood. Yang rejects two readings. One holds that Marxism has an "empty space" where a theory of the human being should be. It rests on real points of common ground and should be guided by the practice of Chinese modernization. Yang concludes that contemporary Chinese Marxism belongs to both Marxism and Chinese culture, and that it alone represents China's future direction. Be highly vigilant against Japan's reckless gamble and resolutely defend the post-war international order A perspective from international law 高度警惕日本铤而走险 坚决捍卫战后国际秩序——国际法视角的透视 Pu Ping Writing in Guangming Daily on 19 January 2026, Pu Ping argues that Japan's current leadership is challenging the post-war international order, and that international law shows why this must be resisted. Takaichi's signal of possible armed involvement is described as the product of a long-running right-wing strategy of 'using Taiwan to contain China'. The author calls on Asia-Pacific countries and peace-loving peoples to unite against Japanese right-wing forces, and to uphold a correct view of the Second World War. Guarding strictly against the revival of Japanese militarism 严防日本军国主义死灰复燃 Song Zhiyong Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2026, Song Zhiyong, a professor of Japanese studies, argues that Japan's new prime minister, Takaichi Sanae, is reviving militarism. In Song's account, Takaichi has challenged China's red line on Taiwan, pushed to revise the "peace constitution" and Japan's security policy, sought to breach the "three non-nuclear principles" and raised military spending. He calls on the international community to take this seriously and respond, to prevent a repeat of history and protect peace in East Asia and the world. Advancing Chinese modernization through the power of culture 以文化之力推动中国式现代化建设 Shi Xuezheng Chen Jiaxi Li Danzhou Taking up the statement of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) that cultural prosperity is an important mark of Chinese modernization, three Shenzhen-based authors argue that advancing Chinese modernization requires developing socialist culture under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Adhering to the close integration of investing in things and investing in people 坚持投资于物和投资于人紧密结合 Sun Cunliang Cui Huabin This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 19 January 2026, takes up the principle that investment in physical assets ("things") and investment in human beings must be closely combined. The fundamental purpose of advancing foreign-related rule of law work and the paths to achieving it 推进涉外法治工作的根本目的及其实现路径 Huo Zhengxin Writing in Guangming Daily on 16 January 2026, Huo Zhengxin, a professor of international law, asks what foreign-related rule of law work (涉外法治) is ultimately for and how it should be built. Slogans and the Communist Party's shaping of opinion in the Great Revolution: the case of Workers' Path 从标语口号看大革命时期中国共产党的舆论动员——以《工人之路》为例 Tang Juan How did the Communist Party use slogans to mobilise opinion during the Great Revolution of the 1920s? Tang concludes that slogans were an intuitive, widely reaching tool of early Party political communication and made a lasting contribution to policy propaganda, mass mobilisation and building the ranks. As evidence of reach, Tang cites a peak circulation of 10,000 copies, roughly one for every four or five strikers. It first traces the theoretical lineage and innovation of the idea, then reviews the achievements of the new era in coordinating the two, and finally sets out practical paths for the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The lineage runs from the holistic approach to national security (2014) through the 19th and 20th Party Congresses, the 2023 Central Economic Work Conference and the Recommendations adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). In the authors' account, the idea is a creative fusion of Marxist views of development and security that moves beyond treating them as opposites. They contend that it innovates on three fronts. It treats security as an internal component of development, unlike what they describe as mainstream Western economics. It shifts security thinking from defensive to "development-oriented" security. It widens social governance towards risk prevention and multi-party participation. The authors cite figures to show progress: GDP of 134.9 trillion yuan in 2024, grain output of 1.43 trillion jin in 2025, and renewable capacity of 2.17 billion kilowatts by mid-2025. They also point to a falling government debt-to-GDP ratio relative to the G20 average and lower crime and accident rates. They acknowledge remaining weaknesses: dependence on foreign high-end chips and industrial software, uneven supply-chain resilience, financial and local-debt risks, and immature rules for AI, cross-border data and biosecurity. For the 15th Five-Year Plan period the authors call for four steps: building a modern industrial system with advanced manufacturing at its core; achieving high-level scientific and technological self-reliance through the new-type whole-nation system; strengthening the national security system under centralised leadership; and building capacity in key areas. These areas include political, food, energy, supply-chain, cyber, data, AI and financial security. They stress that coordination is a dynamic, long-term task rather than a fixed balance. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party's security-and-development principle is framed, with the official statistics and policy priorities attached to it.

Raising the effectiveness of macroeconomic governance 提升宏观经济治理效能 Wang Yiming Taking its cue from the 2025 Central Economic Work Conference's call to raise the effectiveness of macroeconomic governance, this commentary (published in Guangming Daily on 13 January 2026) asks how China should move from "macro-control" to "macroeconomic governance". Wang Yiming argues that changes in the economy make this shift necessary, that it produced results during the 14th Five-Year Plan period, and that the 15th Five-Year Plan period and 2026 call for more active, better coordinated policy. The article has four parts. It first sets out the logic of the shift from macro-control to governance, then reviews the achievements of the 14th Five-Year Plan period. It then turns to priorities for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, drawing on the Recommendations adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), and ends with policy orientation for 2026, the first year of the new plan. Wang contends that the economy now shows weak demand against strong supply, weaker investment-driven growth, a technology-led divergence in economic structure and a less stable external environment. Against this background he contrasts governance with traditional macro-control on five points: the actors (government and market as joint means of resource allocation, not subject and object), the goals (aggregate balance, structural optimisation, quality and risk prevention rather than smoothing cycles), the focus (supply and demand together), the methods (coordination across fiscal, monetary, industrial and other policies, plus expectation management) and the horizon (domestic and external balance). For the next plan period he stresses counter-cyclical and cross-cyclical adjustment, policy coordination, expectation management and a growth model led by domestic demand and consumption. He ties the last to reforms: shifting the consumption tax to the point of consumption and down to local government, extending public services to migrants from rural areas where they live, and easing market entry in services. For 2026 Wang calls for a more proactive fiscal policy that keeps necessary deficit and spending levels while preserving sustainability and "investing in people", and for a moderately loose monetary policy that treats prices as an anchor and keeps liquidity ample. He credits the 14th Five-Year Plan period with GDP passing 130 trillion yuan and a contribution of around 30 per cent to world growth, figures he reports from official sources. Read the original if you want an official-leaning economist's summary of how Chinese policy thinking frames the move from macro-control to governance and the priorities for 2026.

Excavating traditional Chinese economic thought to drive paradigm innovation in economics 挖掘中国传统经济思想 推动经济学范式创新 Duan Bo Cheng Lin Duan Bo and Cheng Lin ask how Chinese economists can build an autonomous body of economic knowledge with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. In the authors' view this would yield an analytical framework and research paradigm suited to socialism with Chinese characteristics and marked by Chinese subjectivity. The article takes five core assumptions or themes of Western mainstream economics in turn: capital-centredness, the "economic man" hypothesis, resource allocation and the role of government, the focus on competition, and the treatment of ecological problems. For each, the authors set out a criticism and then name resources in classical Chinese thought. They cite the Book of Documents, Mencius, Guanzi, Sima Qian, Gu Yanwu and Zhu Xi, among others. The authors portray Western mainstream economics as a defence of capitalist reproduction that obscures surplus value. In their account, the people-centred standpoint of Chinese economics finds support in the min-ben (people-as-foundation) tradition. Against "economic man", they cite dialectical pairings in the tradition: self-interest and altruism, material and spiritual life, instrumental and value rationality. On markets, they read Guanzi's "light and heavy" doctrine and Sima Qian as showing government and market as coordinated rather than opposed. On competition and ecology, they cite Gu Yanwu's view of orderly competition, ideas of harmony and cooperation, and "unity of heaven and man". The authors also note that the min-ben tradition served monarchical rule and lacked institutional guarantees, so its class character must be removed and its ideas grounded in the rule of law. Duan and Cheng conclude that critical reflection on Western theory, together with creative use of traditional thought, can ground a distinctively Chinese economic paradigm. They say this paradigm would stress common prosperity, cooperation beyond zero-sum thinking, a community with a shared future for mankind, and harmony between humans and nature. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese economists use classical sources to argue for an alternative to Western economics, and which texts and concepts they cite.)

Innovative development of the theory and methods of investigation and research 调查研究理论与方法的创新发展 Wang Guowei This short commentary in Guangming Daily argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping's statements on investigation and research (diaoyan) have advanced the theory and methods of this Party tradition. Wang Guowei presents them as answering what such research is, why it matters and how to do it well. The article first sets out three theoretical contributions: the spiritual essence of investigation and research, its people-centred value, and its functional position drawn from Party history. Maintaining historical patience: methodological lessons from the CPC's long-term governance 保持历史耐心：中国共产党长期执政的方法论启示 Zhou Jin Zhou Jin's commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the concept of "historical patience" (lishi naixin) and asks what it shows about how the Communist Party of China (CPC) governs over the long term. Zhou argues that it is both a spiritual quality and a scientific method of thinking, forged over the Party's century-plus of struggle. The article presents it as a distinctive concept put forward by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, using a "big historical view". In Zhou's account it reflects a scientific grasp of the laws of Communist Party governance, socialist construction and human social development. The piece has three parts. The first grounds historical patience in historical materialism and traces the idea through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, including Xi's 2013 remark on urbanisation at the Central Urbanisation Work Conference. The second runs through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, the era of socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Examples include the protracted war, the household contract responsibility system, the graded opening of the economy, poverty alleviation, ecological protection and regional coordination. The third part sets out five practical requirements. Zhou's central claim is that historical patience is not passivity. Referring to the Marxist view that the succession of social formations is a long "natural historical process", Zhou holds that the Party respects objective laws while exercising historical initiative. The five requirements are: following laws together with taking initiative; linking quantitative accumulation to qualitative leaps; combining long-range strategy with flexible tactics; matching the big historical view with a problem-oriented approach; and pairing "success need not be mine" with "success must have my contribution". Zhou says the last of these means taking a long-term view while acting responsibly in the present, and that it is shown in generations of successive struggle. Zhou concludes that China's huge population, vast territory and complex conditions make development a long and arduous process. Zhou adds that the present period, with strategic opportunities alongside growing risks and uncertainties, calls for patience in particular. Goals such as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a modern socialist power and common prosperity are described as tasks achievable only through step-by-step accumulation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present long-term governance and Xi-era concepts in official discourse.

Grasping the "five musts" in depth to get the 15th Five-Year Plan period off to a good start 深刻把握“五个必须” 推动“十五五”良好开局 Zhong Caiwen This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 13 January 2026, interprets the "five musts" that Xi Jinping set out at the Central Economic Work Conference at the end of 2025. Zhong presents them as regular patterns drawn from recent practice for economic work under new conditions. The author argues that they both summarise past experience and guide future development, and that they enrich Xi Jinping's economic thought. Applying them well, Zhong says, is the way to get the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030) off to a good start. The article has five sections, one for each "must". They cover fully tapping economic potential; pursuing policy support and reform and innovation together; making sure the economy is both "liberalised effectively" and "well managed"; closely combining investment in physical assets with investment in people; and meeting external challenges by building up internal strength. Each section follows the same pattern: a rationale, supporting figures and practical tasks for 2026. Zhong's argument has three main strands. First, China's large size, huge market, complete industrial system and skilled workforce are said to supply the potential, while the socialist system gives certainty. Second, short-term macro policy is likened to treating symptoms and reform to building long-term strength, so each is said to fail without the other. "Liberalising" is defined as equal treatment for all forms of ownership, and "managing" as building a law-based economy and curbing "involution-style" competition. The author cites education and health spending below developed-country levels and insists that the two kinds of investment reinforce each other. On external challenges, Zhong describes rising tariffs, unilateralism and what the article calls Western containment of China. It contends that history shows China's strength in meeting such shocks, citing the fall in the export share of GDP from about 34 percent in 2007 to about 19 percent. The proposed response is to concentrate on one's own affairs. This means a modern industrial system, self-reliance in science and technology, a unified national market, more diverse export markets and wider opening up. Zhong concludes that China is confident of meeting outside pressure and of advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an authoritative, official-line reading of the 2025 Central Economic Work Conference and the economic priorities of the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Expanding the international science and technology innovation centres carries strategic significance 国际科技创新中心扩围具有战略意义 Qiu Rui This commentary, published in Economic Daily in January 2026, asks why the Central Economic Work Conference of 2025 decided to widen the scope of the country's international science and technology innovation centres, and what follows from that decision. Qiu argues that the move, which extends the Beijing centre to the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region and the Shanghai centre to the Yangtze River Delta, is a major strategic decision. In Qiu's account it responds to intensifying great-power rivalry in technology and is meant to make China a leading source of original innovation. The article has three parts. The first reviews the achievements of the three centres (Beijing, Shanghai and the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area) since the 18th Party Congress (2012), citing China's first place for three consecutive years in the World Intellectual Property Organization's 2025 ranking of top 100 innovation clusters. The second explains why expansion is necessary and what orientations should guide it. The third identifies each region's weaknesses and proposes region-specific measures. Qiu's central claim is that technological competition has shifted from single-point contests to competition between systems. Qiu then assigns each region a task. Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei must bridge the gap between basic research and industrialisation. The Yangtze River Delta must strengthen basic theory and the division of labour among its provinces. The Greater Bay Area must reinforce basic research and align rules across its distinct legal and customs systems, using Hong Kong's strengths. Qiu concludes that coordinated and differentiated development of the three centres should move China from "single-point breakthroughs" to "system leadership". The author expects this to produce a multipolar, tiered strategic pattern on the global innovation map. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the expansion of the innovation centres is justified and what regional tasks are proposed for it.

Guiding financial institutions to step up support for expanding domestic demand 引导金融机构加力支持扩大内需 He Dexu Zhang Xuelan This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in January 2026, asks how finance can better support the expansion of domestic demand. It takes its cue from the 2025 Central Economic Work Conference, which made 'adhering to domestic demand as the driver and building a strong domestic market' a key task for the first year of the 15th Five-Year Plan. He and Zhang argue that financial support must shift from scale-driven to quality-and-efficiency-driven, so that its fit with demand and its sustainability improve. The piece has four parts. It first explains why the shift is needed, then identifies structural problems in financial support, seen from the standpoint of households, enterprises and financial institutions. It closes with three groups of policy proposals: coordination of fiscal and monetary policy, reform of financial institutions, and a broader support ecosystem. It draws on central bank reporting, loan data for the first 11 months of 2025 and IMF and World Bank growth forecasts. The authors argue that slower growth in total financial aggregates is natural as the economy moves from high-speed to high-quality development. Easing in total volume alone, they say, cannot energise households and firms facing high savings rates, weak propensity to consume and mismatched financing. They identify gaps: consumer credit products that are homogeneous and do not reach flexible workers or those with imperfect credit records; a shortage of medium- and long-term funding for small manufacturers and specialised 'little giant' firms; and banks squeezed by narrowing interest margins and rising bad loans. The authors call for systemic reform rather than piecemeal adjustment. Their proposals include special relending tools or quotas for consumer credit, fiscal interest subsidies and tiered loss compensation through local guarantee systems, and assessment indicators that reward inclusive consumer lending. They also urge a shift from collateral-based to credit-based lending using digital credit profiles, and county-level inclusive finance outlets. Capital-market channels such as real estate investment trusts for community commercial facilities are another proposal. Fully tapping China's economic potential 充分挖掘中国经济潜能 Yuan Lei This newspaper commentary explains one of the "five musts" set out by the 2025 Central Economic Work Conference: that the country "must fully tap its economic potential". Yuan Lei argues that China's economy is large not only in volume but in latent potential, and that turning this potential into momentum for high-quality development is a strategic task for the coming Five-Year Plan period. The article has three parts. It first asks why potential deserves attention, citing achievements of the 14th Five-Year Plan period. It then identifies where the potential lies, in four "dividends". Finally it sets out how potential can be converted into growth drivers, and closes with remarks on method. Yuan holds that tapping potential is both a lesson from past experience and a guide for future work. The article cites an economy of about 140 trillion yuan in 2025, final consumption contributing close to 60% of growth in 2021–2024, and per capita GDP of 13,445 US dollars in 2024. It links potential to the goal of reaching the level of a moderately developed country by 2035 and to building the new development pattern. The four dividends are institutional (the leadership of the Communist Party and the capacity to concentrate resources), market (over 1.4 billion people and more than 400 million middle-income earners), industrial (the most complete industrial system in the world, in the author's account) and talent (about 860 million working-age people and rising education levels). To convert advantages into momentum, Yuan proposes four lines of work: build a high-level socialist market economy and a unified national market; expand domestic demand on both the consumption and investment sides; drive industrial innovation through scientific and technological innovation, including key technologies and emerging industries; and link education, science and technology, and talent in a virtuous circle. The author calls for strategic, systemic and bottom-line thinking and for coordinating short- and long-term, macro and micro policies. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists frame "economic potential" at the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan period.

Understanding the philosophical implications of the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point decision 深刻领会中央八项规定精神的哲学意蕴 Chen Chaofan This short commentary in Economic Daily asks what Marxist philosophy lies behind the Central Committee's eight-point decision on improving Party conduct, issued after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It reflects the people-first stance because conduct is, in the author's view, a question of the Party's relationship with the masses, and combining popular oversight with the Party's self-reform is presented as the way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Chen cites a 2024 National Bureau of Statistics survey in which 94.9 per cent of respondents endorsed its results. The decision also exemplifies systems thinking, since conduct and corruption are treated as intertwined and the rules are written into Party regulations, and it shows continuity from earlier Party traditions such as the 'Two Musts'. Combining theory and practice to explain the power of ideas A review of the fourth set of the Economic Daily series on Xi Jinping economic thought 理论和实践相结合诠释思想伟力 Xiao Xiao This short commentary, published in Economic Daily in January 2026, reviews the fourth set of the Economic Daily's book series on studying and applying Xi Jinping economic thought. The meaning and paths of industrial innovation during the 15th Five-Year Plan period “十五五”时期产业创新的内涵与路径 Shi Jianxun Writing in Economic Daily in January 2026, Shi Jianxun takes up the recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). The article asks how industrial innovation, the step that turns scientific and technological innovation into real productive forces, should be understood and advanced in 2026–2030. Shi argues that it is a key lever for avoiding "involution-style" competition and for responding to external suppression, and that it must be coordinated with technological innovation and regional development. The commentary is organised under five headings: the content and driving logic of industrial innovation; science and technology as its lead; its link to regional development; integration into international industrial and supply chains; and the improvement of the development environment. It draws throughout on wording from the Plan recommendations, such as implementing an "industrial innovation project", building a modern industrial system and developing new quality productive forces. Shi first sets out six forms of industrial innovation: creating new industries from scratch, upgrading traditional ones with advanced technology, restructuring through industrial transfer, new cooperation models such as clusters and ecosystems, better industrial policy and capacity governance, and innovation arising from international division of labour. Four forces drive it: market demand, technological innovation, industrial competition and policy. Shi then argues that technological innovation is the endogenous driver and industrial innovation its realisation of value. Shi acknowledges gaps in key core technologies and calls for breakthroughs in integrated circuits, industrial machine tools and high-end instruments, with enterprises as the main innovators. Regions should avoid blind duplication of projects and develop in complementary ways according to their endowments, and China should integrate more deeply into global supply chains, including through the Belt and Road Initiative. Shi concludes that, because industrial innovation demands heavy investment, long cycles and high risk, the state must set strategy, back basic research and build a favourable environment. Shi calls for a unified national market, stronger intellectual property protection, a shift of industrial policy from selective to inclusive and functional forms, and capacity governance with anti-monopoly enforcement and early-warning systems to curb disorderly expansion. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented statement of how the 15th Five-Year Plan recommendations frame industrial innovation and its links to technology, regions and global supply chains.

Building a solid foundational and strategic support for the development of new quality productive forces 筑牢新质生产力发展的基础性战略性支撑 Liu Hongda This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 6 January 2026, asks how education, science and technology, and talent can be advanced as one integrated whole to support new quality productive forces. Basic characteristics and development direction of the modern industrial system 现代化产业体系基本特征与发展方向 Zhang Hui Writing in Economic Daily in January 2026, Zhang Hui asks how China should build a modern industrial system during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The philosophical wisdom of "historical resolve" “历史定力”的哲学智慧 Xu Hengbing Xu Di This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2026, takes up "historical resolve" (lishi dingli), a category the authors describe as an original concept of Chinese communists in the new era. They define it as the steady, unshakeable strategic capacity and spiritual outlook of a historical subject that has grasped historical laws and the trend of the times. Xu and Xu argue that, seen through a "grand view of history", it unites conformity to law with purposiveness, long-term goals with stage-by-stage tasks, and national rejuvenation with human progress. The article is organised around three formulations of Xi Jinping: "stand on the right side of history", "maintain historical patience" and "stand on the side of human progress". Each section treats one as a philosophical dimension of historical resolve: direction and orientation, time, and global horizon. The authors draw on Marx, Engels, the ancient thinker Xunzi and Immanuel Wallerstein, and refer to Party history from the New Democratic Revolution to the present. In the first section, the authors argue that standing on the right side of history means uniting "conformity to law" (grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production) with "purposiveness" (the Party's fundamental aim of serving the people wholeheartedly).
