Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-aligned economic commentary links Xi Jinping's cultural thought, humanistic economics and industrial upgrading.

Steering the new journey of the 15th Five-Year Plan period with the Party's overall leadership 以党的全面领导领航“十五五”发展新征程 Dai Lixing Guo Wenjing Dai Lixing and Guo Wenjing write in response to the Recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). That document makes "upholding the Party's overall leadership" the first principle for economic and social development in 2026–2030. The authors argue that this leadership explains the achievements of the 14th Five-Year Plan period and is the fundamental guarantee for the next plan period and for Chinese modernization. The article, published in Sichuan Party Building in November 2025, has three parts. It first credits the 14th Five-Year Plan results to the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. It then explains why the Recommendations give Party leadership such prominence. Finally it sets out four sets of measures for putting that leadership into practice. For the 14th Five-Year Plan period, the authors cite GDP rising towards about 140 trillion yuan in 2025, R&D spending above 3.6 trillion yuan in 2024, and a rise in the national innovation ranking from 14th to 10th. They attribute these results to centralised, unified decision-making, for example the September 2024 Politburo package of incremental policies, and to strategic steadiness in pursuing "one blueprint to the end". For the coming period they give three reasons for the priority: a world of accelerating change and uncertainty, the socialist character and direction of Chinese modernization, and the Party's role in rallying the people around common prosperity and whole-process people's democracy. The proposed measures are: strengthening political guidance through Xi Jinping Thought and the Two Establishes and Two Upholds; deepening the Party's self-reform through supervision of "key minorities", stricter conduct and anti-corruption work; focusing on people's livelihoods in employment, education, health and elderly care; and improving institutions, including reporting and accountability systems for carrying out Central Committee decisions. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party leadership is linked to the 15th Five-Year Plan and of the measures the authors propose for it.

Creating high-quality urban living spaces 营造高品质城市生活空间 Zhao Zheng This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 6 November 2025, asks how Chinese cities can build high-quality living spaces. Zhao Zheng, a researcher at the Development Research Center of the State Council, takes the July 2025 Central Urban Work Conference and the Party and State Council opinions on high-quality urban development as his starting point. He argues that cities must become livable, comfortable and convenient homes for all residents. Zhao first explains why living-space quality matters and what it now means, then sets out three areas of work: housing, infrastructure and public services. Each area is illustrated with a local case, in Hangzhou, Chongqing and Sichuan. In Zhao's account, urbanization is shifting from rapid growth to stable development, and cities from large-scale expansion to improving the quality and efficiency of existing stock. High-quality living space therefore needs a people-centred orientation. It combines "investing in things" (housing, roads, pipelines) with "investing in people" (education, healthcare, elderly care, childcare). On housing, Zhao calls for "good houses" and complete communities, together with the renovation of urban villages and old neighbourhoods. On infrastructure, he calls for upgrading underground pipelines and transport networks and building 5G and computing networks. On public services, he wants more balanced, higher-quality provision tailored to the elderly, young families and flexible workers. Zhao concludes that these measures would turn policy aims into tangible living environments and support common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise official-policy statement of the 2025 urban agenda, with brief Chinese case examples.

The ideological superstructure: a key category for state governance under historical materialism 思想上层建筑：唯物史观下国家治理的关键范畴 Yang Hutao Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for state governance and social development to be better aligned with each other, Yang Hutao asks how the state governance system and the basic economic system actually interact within historical materialism. The article proposes the "ideological superstructure" as the missing analytical category linking the two. Yang argues that the shared ideas defining a political community are the key to the character and performance of state governance. The article first reviews Marx's uses of "superstructure", especially in The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte and the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. From these it separates a political superstructure (legal and political institutions, army, courts) from an ideological one (political and legal thought, morals, beliefs, sentiments). It then discusses the role of the latter in state building and state capacity, draws on Chinese history, compares the United States and China, and ends with the Chinese case under the heading of putting the people first. Yang's central move is to treat the ideological superstructure as the load-bearing frame beneath the visible political superstructure, comparable to informal institutions beneath formal ones. It rests on the basic economic system and fixes the source of legitimacy for political authority. The article reads China's four great historical transformations as changes in legitimacy ideas tied to productive forces, and criticises convergence and universal-values theories for ignoring differences in these ideas. Its sharpest distinction is between "sovereignty of the people", which answers whom power belongs to, and "putting the people first", which answers whom power serves. Yang contends that Western capital-led states hold only the first, and drift towards rentier and financial-capital dominance, while China unites both. Drawing on Michael Mann and others, Yang adds that the three dimensions of infrastructural capacity (penetration, extraction and negotiation) depend on shared knowledge supplied by the ideological superstructure. Yang concludes that modernizing state governance means building core values systematically, not merely improving institutions. In the author's account, "putting the people first" is the soul of China's ideological superstructure and has been turned into policy goals such as self-reliance, poverty alleviation, common prosperity and Chinese modernization. The author presents this as a path of governance combining historical tradition with the needs of the present. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars extend base–superstructure theory to state governance, or want to see a Marxist comparison of Chinese and Western legitimacy concepts.

The danger of fascism in the United States A view from the 1950s 美国法西斯主义的危险 Paul A. Baran This is a Chinese translation of an abridged essay by the Marxist economist Paul A. Baran, written in 1952 and republished in Monthly Review in April 2025. The editors' note presents it as still relevant to Trump-era America. Baran argues that the left and progressives are dangerously complacent about fascism in the United States and refuse to see it as a likely stage of American capitalist development. The essay first rebuts the common view that a regime counts as fascist only if it resembles Germany or Italy: mass movements in brown or black shirts, a single party with a leader, extreme racism and the abolition of all opposition. It then offers a definition of fascism by social function and traces how American conditions differ from the classic European cases. Baran contends that this checklist confuses political form with social content. In his account, fascism is a political system of the imperialist era, of war and of revolutionary upheaval, which strengthens the state as an instrument of capitalist rule. He holds that a ruling class resting on 100 to 200 giant corporations has built an alliance between big business and the military. Because of full employment from military spending, a weak left and organised labour allied with business, Baran says storm troopers and concentration camps are not yet needed. He describes instead an ideological regime that uses an external threat to remove communists and independent socialists from public life and punishes dissent with dismissal, ostracism and harassment. Baran concludes that, whatever form its actions take, the business–military alliance performs all the essential functions of a fascist regime. He calls it the American form of government in this era, an instrument of harsh class struggle at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a short, historically grounded Marxist argument for treating fascism as a functional rather than a formal category, and for seeing why the Chinese editors chose to republish it now.

The historical standing of the CPC's independent and autonomous mountain guerrilla warfare during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国共产党开展独立自主的山地游击战的历史地位 He Husheng How did the Communist Party of China (CPC) keep its independence while building the broadest anti-Japanese national united front? He Husheng argues that the answer lay in "independent and autonomous mountain guerrilla warfare". In the author's account, this raised guerrilla tactics to a strategic policy, freed the Party from Comintern constraints, the Kuomintang's attempt to absorb but not tolerate the Communists, and erroneous views within the Party, and marked a major theoretical and strategic advance in armed struggle. The article, published in 2025, has four sections. The first treats the background, ideological basis and theoretical innovation of the policy. The second treats its strategic significance for the united front and armed struggle, and how it fitted the military situation. The third follows its application, including the move from mountain to plain guerrilla warfare, and its contribution to victory. The fourth assesses its historical standing through a "grand view of Party history" with objective, dialectical and subjective dimensions. He contends that the policy rested on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, on Mao Zedong's analysis of the war (notably On Protracted War), and on the Party's own capacity for independent judgement. It twice surpassed earlier practice: from mobile warfare to guerrilla warfare, then from ordinary guerrilla tactics to a strategy centred on independence and Party command of the army. Its core was absolute Party leadership over the army and reliance on the people in a people's war. According to the author, it let the base areas behind enemy lines support the frontal battlefield, produced victories such as Pingxingguan, and expanded base areas that later underpinned the founding of the People's Republic. In the fourth section the author reads the policy as historically inevitable, as an expression of the unity of opposites and of continuity and discontinuity, and as evidence of the Party's historical initiative. He links it to the unity of Party spirit and the people's character, to the Party's confidence in national rejuvenation, and to the Party's dual history as social revolution and self-reform. Read the original if you study CPC military history or how contemporary Party historians apply the grand view of Party history to the War of Resistance.

A historical examination of the Communist Party of China's leadership of cultural construction during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗日战争时期中国共产党领导文化建设的历史考察 He Juan He Juan asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) led cultural construction during the War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45), and what that record offers for building a strong socialist cultural nation today. The article argues that the Party recognised victory could not be won without cultural mobilisation. In the author's account, this led it to develop New Democratic culture, build a "cultural army", pursue a Chinese philosophy and social science, orient literature and art towards the masses, and expand wartime education. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical background: Japanese militarism's cultural enslavement of occupied areas, the cultural autocracy and revivalism of the Kuomintang diehards, and the Party's growing cultural self-awareness. The second, the longest, describes five practical paths: the New Democratic cultural banner, the "cultural army" of intellectuals and organisations, the Sinicisation of Marxism in the humanities and social sciences, literature and art for the masses, and cadre, school and social education. The third part draws lessons for the present. He's central claim is that the Party defined a cultural direction as "national, scientific and mass-oriented", which answered both cultural restorationism and wholesale Westernisation. The author presents the Party as combining a united front among cultural figures with ideological leadership by Marxism. Examples include the Anti-Japanese Association of Chinese Writers and Artists, Mao Zedong's call for a "cultural army", reformed traditional opera, new yangge works, and historical scholarship by Fan Wenlan and Guo Moruo. The article also cites Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region figures on schools, literacy groups and night schools to show the reach of education. He draws five lessons: uphold Marxism's guiding position and the Party's cultural leadership; hold to a Chinese cultural standpoint, in line with the Two Integrations; value intellectuals and build the Party's cultural ranks; keep culture oriented to the people; and build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in philosophy and social science. The author links these to Xi Jinping's cultural thought and Chinese modernization, and concludes that the Party's comprehensive leadership of cultural work is the fundamental guarantee for a strong socialist cultural nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of wartime cultural policy, organisations and works, together with the lessons drawn for today.

The CPC's European organisation and its efforts to win over and struggle against anarchists, in the perspective of the international communist movement 国际共运视域下中共旅欧组织对无政府主义者的争取与斗争 Wang Qiaoshen Wang Qiaoshen asks how the Communist International's changing stance towards anarchists shaped the early Chinese communists in Europe. The article takes issue with Arif Dirlik's account of a 1922 'split' between Chinese Marxists and anarchists, which Wang says overlooks the Comintern side. Wang argues that the dispute between the CPC's European organisation and the Gongyu she (Spare-time Society), a group of Chinese anarchists in France, cannot be understood without tracing its texts back to Comintern debates, and that the Comintern first sought an alliance with anarchists and then moved to opposing them. The article follows the polemic from 1922 to 1924, using the journals Shaonian (Youth) and Gongyu. Part one covers the argument over Soviet Russia, part two the argument over organisation (trade-union autonomy versus a vanguard party), and part three the Comintern's repositioning of anarchists within the united front. Wang compares the Chinese texts with their sources, including International Press Correspondence, speeches by Lozovsky and Trotsky, and French communist and syndicalist writings. The foreign anarchist sources include Freedom, Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman. Wang shows that the Chinese anarchist Ou Shengbai drew his claims of Russian failure and 'party dictatorship' from Western anarchist writings. Zhou Enlai's reply in Shaonian, in Wang's reading, drew on Comintern reporting and played down wartime communism's faults, stressing instead the peasants' narrow class outlook. The Chinese communists then borrowed from the Comintern's polemics against the French syndicalist Robert Louzon to argue that the party is the working class's 'brain'. Wang notes that Yin Kuan and Xue Shilun at times conflated the repressive function of proletarian dictatorship with the party's vanguard role. Following Lozovsky's notion of an 'anarcho-reformist front', Chinese writers moved towards class-based criticism. Wang judges some of it exaggerated, such as Ren Zhuoxuan's charges, and notes that Zinoviev's more conciliatory line left the Comintern's own position wavering. Wang concludes that between the Comintern's first congress in 1919 and its fifth in 1924 the alliance with anarchists dissolved into opposition. The European Chinese communists criticised anarchism in order to build a common front against capitalism and the yellow trade-union international, not to eliminate it, but with little success. Anarchism then lost its revolutionary character and, after 1927, served as an ideological tool of Guomindang repression. For the Chinese communists, Wang argues, the struggle clarified the party's vanguard mission, and the CPC later found a path different from Soviet Russia's on leading the masses. Read the original if you study early CPC history, Sino-anarchist relations or the Comintern's united-front policy and want a text-by-text tracing of sources.

Motives, practice, lessons: a three-dimensional study of the Communist Party of China's political mobilisation during the War of Resistance against Japan 动因·实践·镜鉴:抗战时期中国共产党政治动员的三维探赜 Li Xianzong Tang Di This article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) turned a divided and endangered nation into a force capable of sustained resistance to Japan between 1931 and 1945. Li Xianzong and Tang Di argue that political mobilisation was the decisive mechanism: through ideological education, organisational networks and the alignment of material interests, the Party converted scattered national energies into a unified popular force. They organise their account around three dimensions: motives, practice and lessons for today. The article, published in Red Culture Journal in 2025, has three parts. The first sets out the historical motives: the national crisis created by Japanese aggression and the appeasement or inaction of Western powers and the League of Nations, popular anti-Japanese enthusiasm, and the mobilising experience the Party had accumulated in the Great Revolution and the land revolution. The second part surveys wartime practice under three headings: propaganda and education, organisation-building, and interest-linking policies. The third part draws lessons for the present. On practice, the authors describe mass cultural propaganda (slogans, drama, the Yellow River Cantata, newspapers such as Liberation Daily), literacy campaigns, and international publicity through Xinhua, overseas newspapers and visiting foreign journalists. They cite the growth of Party membership from about 40,000 to over 1.2 million, mass associations for peasants, women and youth, and an army that grew from some 50,000 to 1.2 million, with 2.6 million militia. They also treat rent and interest reduction, the production campaign (with 2 million additional mu of arable land in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region in 1942–44, per the article) and the 'three-thirds' system of government as ways of tying popular interests to the war effort. The authors draw three lessons. First, adhering to the Two Integrations, meaning the integration of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its traditional culture, is the 'golden key'; they link it to Xi Jinping Thought and to the concept of new quality productive forces. Second, the mass line is described as the Party's institutional strength in organising the people. Third, strategies must be adapted to circumstances, as in the shift from 'opposing Chiang and resisting Japan' to 'pressing Chiang to resist Japan' and in 'life as mobilisation' methods such as kang-side meetings. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of wartime mobilisation, with local examples and figures, framed to draw lessons for contemporary Party work.

The CPC's perception of and policy towards Britain during the Second KMT–CPC Cooperation, 1937–1940, and its effects 第二次国共合作背景下中共对英国的认识、政策及其影响（1937—1940） Wen Cheng Wen Cheng asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) viewed British policy between the outbreak of full-scale war in 1937 and the Tripartite Pact of September 1940, and how that view fed back into its handling of relations with the Kuomintang (KMT). The article opens with Mao Zedong's 1940 remark tracing a 'vertical line' from Neville Chamberlain to the KMT's anti-communist 'friction expert' He Shaonan. Wen argues that the CPC's attitude to Britain rested on domestic and international conditions, above all the state of KMT–CPC relations, and in turn shaped its handling of those relations. The author notes that existing scholarship concentrates on British aid after the Pacific War began in 1941, leaving the earlier period unstudied. The article follows three phases. It begins with the united-front line adopted after the Comintern's Seventh Congress (1935) and the search for a pro-British, anti-Japanese alignment. It then covers the deterioration of Anglo-Soviet relations from the Munich Conference to the Soviet–German pact of August 1939, and ends with the CPC's push for the KMT to reject Britain and ally with the Soviet Union, up to 1940. Sources are mainly CPC leaders' speeches and internal documents. Wen's central claim is that the CPC read international alignments through the lens of KMT–CPC cooperation. Early on it treated Britain as a vital but wavering ally. After Munich and the 1939 Soviet–German pact, it feared a 'Far Eastern Munich' in which Britain, Japan and Chiang Kai-shek would form an anti-Soviet, anti-communist bloc. The CPC therefore revived anti-British criticism, partly in line with Comintern instructions, to keep the KMT from joining the Anglo-French camp. Wen holds that the main aim was to preserve the anti-Japanese united front. He adds that the fear of a full Anglo-Japanese settlement proved exaggerated, though it was understandable for the weaker party, and that the criticism also harmed relations with Britain and with the KMT. In 1940 the Anglo-Japanese rift widened, Soviet standing rose and France fell. The CPC then replaced anti-British rhetoric with a drive to ally with the Soviet Union and to reconcile with the KMT. Wen reports that Mao and Zhang Wentian later acknowledged that opposing KMT entry into the Anglo-American bloc had been too sharp as policy. The author concludes that 1937–1940 CPC policy must be understood within a five-sided relationship involving Britain, the Soviet Union, Japan, the KMT and the CPC, and that this period of adjustment was made independently of Moscow. Read the original if you study CPC wartime diplomacy, the united front or Sino-British relations and want a source-based account of how foreign policy judgements shaped Party strategy.

Marx and Engels on building the political capacity of the proletarian party, and its contemporary value 马克思恩格斯无产阶级政党政治能力建设思想及其当代价值 Ma Mingchong Ma Mingchong asks what Marx and Engels thought about building the political capacity of the proletarian party, and what that thinking offers the Communist Party of China today. The article argues that political capacity is the party's most fundamental and first-ranking capacity. Although Marx and Engels never coined a formal concept of it, Ma contends that their writings and practice amount to a coherent body of thought. Ma opens by linking this to the emphasis on political capacity placed by the Party leadership around Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic content of the thought: its aim of human emancipation, and its orientation towards political leadership, political judgement, political comprehension and political execution. Ma ties these four to the "political judgement, comprehension and execution" now stressed in Party documents. The second part derives principles from three relationships: capacity and power, capacity and authority, and capacity and Party consciousness. The third part draws five contemporary implications, supported by texts from Marx, Engels and Lenin. Ma's central move is to read Marx and Engels's practical positions as components of political capacity. Examples are the Communist League's collective decision-making and annual congresses (leadership), Engels's shift to legal means in the 1870s and insistence on the party's independence (judgement), and political exposure and agitation, the party press and class struggle (execution). On the three relationships, Ma argues that capacity wins power, and that both rest on the principle of the people. Authority comes from capacity and is voluntarily accepted, and it is often embodied in leaders chosen for their ability. Capacity and consciousness advance together through self-criticism. For the present, Ma calls for placing political capacity first in Party political building and for holding firmly to political direction, which Ma treats as the guarantee of the party's proletarian character. Ma also calls for strengthening collective leadership, political mobilisation around ideals and conviction, and struggle capacity to preserve unity. The decline of the Soviet Communist Party is offered as a cautionary case, and Ma links the task to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar draws on Marx and Engels's texts to ground current Party-building doctrine.

The generative logic of data capital and its general and specific characteristics: an interpretation based on Marxist political economy 数据资本的生成逻辑及其资本一般性和特殊性——基于马克思主义政治经济学的阐释 Wang Shuixing Qiu Mengwen Wang Shuixing and Qiu Mengwen ask how data becomes capital and what distinguishes data capital from earlier forms. Starting from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) call to build national data infrastructure, they argue that data capital is a new form of capital that embodies and deepens capital's general features while having its own distinctive properties. They present a scientific view of data capital as necessary for regulating and guiding its healthy development. The article has three main parts followed by a conclusion. The first traces the sequence "raw data – data resource – data commodity – data capital". The second draws on Marx's classic texts to define capital's general character and shows how data capital manifests it. The third sets out the general features of data (immateriality, ubiquity, dependence, diverse sources) and then four specific attributes of data capital. The authors reconstruct the genesis of data capital as a process of capitalist appropriation. Platforms collect users' traces and take over ownership of the data, which the authors call a modern "data enclosure movement". Hired "data labourers" then process it into commodities and so create surplus value, and users' continued activity supplies fresh raw material for expanded accumulation. They summarise capital's general character as profit-seeking, motion and "subjection to things" (wuyixing), and argue that data capital intensifies each. It shows stronger profit-seeking, faster circulation because data is immaterial, and a harsher domination of people by reified relations. Living labour remains the only source of surplus value, and the authors describe "data colonies" built by multinational firms. The four specific attributes are sustainable usability, comprehensive reach over production, consumption, distribution and social life, value multiplication, and deeper, more concealed exploitation. The last includes algorithmic management, the "996" working pattern, gig work, and the extraction of value from users' unpaid activity and leisure time. The authors conclude that data capital has both a "civilising" side, which advances productive forces, and a "barbaric" side, namely more hidden exploitation and sharper polarisation under digital capitalism. For China they call for upholding and improving the socialist market economy, accelerating independent innovation in digital technology, building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system for the digital society, and regulating data capital so that data is "taken from the people and used for the people", in service of common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy account of data as capital, linked to Chinese policy on data governance and common prosperity.

The Central Eight-point Regulation: the "institutional blade" of the Party's self-reform 中央八项规定：党的自我革命的“制度利刃” Li Ting This newspaper commentary asks how the Central Eight-point Regulation, adopted in December 2012, has served the Party's self-reform. Li argues that the regulation used a "small incision" to bring about large change: it reshaped the Party's political ecology through institutional innovation and became a model for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's claim that self-reform is the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. It then takes in turn the regulation's response to the "four tests" and "four dangers", its problem-oriented method, the pairing of rules with technology, the link between Party and state governance, its theoretical significance, and its international meaning. Li's central claim is that rules and technology work together. The author cites a closed-loop mechanism of public complaints, discipline inspection and departmental correction, and the writing of the regulation into Party discipline rules. Li also cites digital platforms: monitoring of over a million official vehicles and budget disclosure covering 98% of county governments. The author adds that Party regulations were aligned with state law and that a "Party supervision + state supervision + mass supervision" network was built. Li argues that this moved style-building from campaign-style governance to routine practice, and joined institutional governance with ideological Party-building. Li concludes that the regulation shows strong vitality and has enriched Marxist Party-building theory. The author reports that its "institution + technology" anti-corruption model has been recognised by the United Nations and promoted in 56 countries. Li calls for continued rule-based Party governance and self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the eight-point regulation within self-reform theory.

Grasping the contemporary meaning of Party spirit and forging a firm political character 把握党性时代内涵 锻造坚定政治品格 Lu Han This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks what Party spirit (dangxing) means for Chinese Communists and how it is to be cultivated. Lu Han argues that Xi Jinping's statements on the subject answer what Party spirit is, why it must be strengthened and how, and that they enrich Marxist Party-building theory and give Party members a basic guide to self-cultivation. The article is organised as a sequence of seven requirements, each presented as a way of tempering Party spirit. It draws on Xi's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and quotes him on ideals, struggle and Party-spirit education. Lu's core claim is that Party spirit starts from political standpoint: the Party has no interests of its own and represents only the proletariat and the people, so members must put the public interest first. From this follow firm belief in communist ideals and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a clear stance on politics and discipline, and the unity of Party spirit and the people's character. Lu holds that the two are inseparable, since there is no Party spirit apart from the people's character. Work style is treated as a question of Party spirit, with Party spirit as the root, style as its expression and discipline as its safeguard. Lu also calls for the courage and skill to struggle, handling contradictions dialectically in the course of Chinese modernization. Finally, Lu proposes cultivating the Communist's "learning of the heart" through Party-spirit education, organisational life, daily self-discipline and the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-spirit cultivation is framed in official discourse under Xi.

Opening a new chapter in Chinese modernization with a spirit of historical initiative 以历史主动精神奋力开创中国式现代化建设新局面 Lü Xinbin This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today on 30 October 2025, reads the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) through the idea of "historical initiative" (lishi zhudong). Lü Xinbin argues that modernization does not fall from the sky but has to be achieved through this spirit. In Lü's account, the plenum communiqué, Xi Jinping's work report and speech, and the Party's proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan embody it. The aim is to open a new chapter in Chinese modernization. The article is organised around three kinds of initiative: theoretical, spiritual and practical. Each is tied to a pairing that Lü calls a unity: conformity to laws and purposiveness, historical consciousness and confidence in China, and strategic resolve and innovation. Lü presents these as one process of theoretical consciousness, spiritual self-strengthening and practical action, aimed at basically achieving socialist modernization. The piece ends with a short call to philosophy and social science researchers. On theory, Lü says historical initiative rests on Marxist historical materialism. Historical actors must grasp objective laws and also use their agency to make history. The plenum's judgement that the 15th Five-Year Plan period is a critical one is said to reveal the internal laws of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization. On spirit, Lü links historical initiative to the Party's courage in self-reform, its habit of learning from history, and its pioneering outlook. Lü also stresses the creativity of the people, citing Xi's call to arouse the historical initiative of all the people. On practice, Lü names three tasks. The first is shouldering the mission through continuity, holding to high-quality development and "one blueprint to the end". The second is seizing opportunity through reform, with Party leadership running through comprehensive deepening of reform. The third is guiding development with systems thinking, above all balancing development and security, so that high-quality development and high-level security reinforce each other. Lü concludes that social scientists should build historical initiative into studying and implementing the plenum's spirit. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary frames the Fourth Plenum and the 15th Five-Year Plan in the language of historical initiative.

Continuing to expand higher-level opening up 持续扩大更高水平对外开放 Jin Ruiting This newspaper commentary, published after the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), asks how China should expand high-level opening up during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Jin argues that opening up is a distinctive mark of Chinese modernization and that, over the next five years, China should focus on institutional opening up and key sectors to raise its opening to a new level. The article has two parts. The first reviews achievements of the 14th Five-Year Plan period in four areas: foreign trade, two-way investment, institutional opening up and the Belt and Road Initiative. The second sets out four strategic directions for the coming period. Jin cites figures such as goods trade ranking first globally for eight consecutive years, services trade passing 1 trillion US dollars, and over three-quarters of countries joining Belt and Road cooperation. Drawing on these, the author describes a shift from opening based on flows of goods and factors to opening based on rules, regulations, management and standards. The proposed directions are: expanding autonomous opening, from "passive adaptation" to "active design"; innovating trade by moving up value chains and expanding services and digital trade; widening two-way investment cooperation; and building the Belt and Road to higher quality, from a "bold sketch" to a "meticulous painting". Jin concludes that, despite unilateralism, protectionism and hegemonism, China's determination to expand high-level opening and share development opportunities will not change. The author calls for a higher-level open economy system. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned summary of how Chinese economists frame the opening-up agenda for 2026–2030.

Building a powerful green engine for high-quality development 为高质量发展打造强劲绿色引擎 Li Weiming This commentary, published in Economic Daily on 31 October 2025, responds to the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) and its proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan. Li Weiming argues that the goals of "new major progress" in building a Beautiful China and of a comprehensive green transformation of economic and social development show the Party leadership's consistent priority on ecological civilisation. In Li's view, green development can serve as a strong engine for high-quality development. The piece has two parts. It first reviews achievements of the 14th Five-Year Plan period, citing figures on air and water quality, ecological restoration, clean energy, the national carbon market and green factories. It then sets out five tasks for the coming period. Li draws on the 14th Five-Year Plan record to argue that environmental protection and economic growth are not opposed but dialectically unified. Good ecology is presented as both part of a better life and an internal requirement of high-quality development. The five tasks are: strengthening green growth momentum through industrial restructuring and cleaner key sectors; deepening pollution control and ecosystem protection; building a new energy system on the principle of establishing the new before breaking the old; pursuing the carbon peak steadily; and fostering green modes of production and living through social mobilisation. Li concludes that, guided by Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilisation, these measures will secure the carbon peak on schedule and lay the base for carbon neutrality. Read the original if you want a concise official-economist overview of the green transition's reported results and the policy priorities linked to the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Letting the sources of cultural innovation and creativity flow fully 推动文化创新创造源泉充分涌流 Xiao Guiqing This commentary, published in Economic Daily on 31 October 2025, asks how to stimulate cultural innovation and creativity across the whole nation as part of building a socialist cultural powerhouse. Xiao Guiqing argues that cultural flourishing is an important mark of Chinese modernization. Taking up the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), which set the goal of a markedly higher level of social etiquette and civilisation in the 15th Five-Year Plan period, Xiao contends that four tasks must be pursued together. The piece is organised under four headings: deepening reform of cultural institutions and mechanisms, raising original creative capacity, fostering a good cultural ecosystem, and strengthening digital and intelligent technology empowerment. Each section gives a set of policy-oriented measures rather than a historical or theoretical survey. The aim, in Xiao's framing, is to mobilise all sides to take part in cultural construction and provide lasting momentum for the cultural powerhouse. On institutions, Xiao insists on the Party's leadership over culture, guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and the principle that social benefits come first and are unified with economic benefits. The author also calls for a unified, open and orderly cultural market, support for state-owned and non-public cultural enterprises, and protection of property rights. On originality, Xiao proposes drawing on fine traditional Chinese culture under Marxist guidance, reinterpreting it for contemporary taste, and improving support, copyright protection and production planning for film, television and documentaries. On ecosystem, Xiao links 'upholding fundamental principles while innovating' with the Two Integrations, the policy of letting a hundred flowers bloom and a hundred schools contend, academic and artistic democracy, and serious criticism. On technology, Xiao advocates national cultural data resources, computing infrastructure, and new formats such as digital publishing, digital art and immersive spaces using artificial intelligence. Xiao concludes that these measures together can convert cultural resources into cultural development strengths and build a modern cultural industry system that is high-level, full-chain and multifunctional, integrated with tourism, education and health. The text reads as an official-style policy exposition of how the Plenum's cultural goals might be implemented. Read the original if you want a concise sample of how Party-affiliated scholars translate the 15th Five-Year Plan's cultural agenda into concrete institutional, creative and technological measures.

A historical-materialist interpretation of "major reforms must have a legal basis" “重大改革于法有据”的历史唯物主义阐释 Yang Jun Yang Jun, writing in Guangming Daily in October 2025, asks how reform and the rule of law can be coordinated, and argues that Xi Jinping's proposition that major reforms must have a legal basis can be explained from the standpoint of historical materialism. Yang presents it as an original proposition within Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law and as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out the context: Xi first stated the principle in November 2013 and it was repeated at later plenums, including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then gives the theoretical logic, and finally four practical steps for carrying the principle out. Yang identifies a tension between reform, which breaks with existing arrangements, and law, which keeps order through fixed norms. Yang also notes that some reforms have been pushed forward at the cost of legality. The theoretical argument has three moves. Reform and law share a basic value, since law expresses the will determined by the people's common interests, citing The German Ideology. Law secures the socialist direction, predictability and long-term stability of reform. Law is historical, rooted in the mode of production, so existing law must guide reform where it still fits, and law reform becomes part of reform where it lags. In practice, Yang calls for four steps: identify the legal basis in current law when a reform is planned; review whether conflicts with current law can be resolved by interpretation or require breaking with it; amend the law at the outset where conditions allow; and otherwise obtain formal legislative authorisation for pilot reforms, then codify proven experience. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Party legal theory links reform and legality, including the stages of legislative practice it proposes.

Understanding and grasping "strengthening the Party's ideological leadership" 深刻理解和把握“增强党的思想引领力” Shuang Chuanxue This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 31 October 2025, follows the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) and its proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan. Shuang Chuanxue takes up one item in the plenum's call to strengthen the Party's leadership: enhancing the Party's ideological leadership (思想引领力). The author argues that ideological work is the foundation of Party building and the basic guarantee of unity in thought and action, which is needed to advance Chinese modernization. The piece has three numbered sections. The first sets out why such leadership is necessary, from theoretical, historical and practical angles. The second analyses what ideological leadership consists of, through four sources of strength in theory. The third proposes four practical tasks: theoretical innovation, a cleaner political environment within the Party, new methods of communication, and high-quality development. In the first section, Shuang draws on Engels and Marx on the relative independence of ideology and its effect on the economic base, on the Russian Revolution, and on the Soviet and East European collapse. In the author's account, that collapse occurred partly because ruling parties did not struggle against erroneous ideas, and the author quotes Xi Jinping to this effect. In the second section, ideological leadership is said to rest on four forces: scientific truth, a people-centred emotional force, a creative force of keeping pace with the times, and a practical force of answering people's concerns. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as embodying all four, with the delivery of a moderately prosperous society cited as evidence that solving problems persuades more than explaining them. For the third section, Shuang calls for combining the upholding and the development of Marxism through the Two Integrations, and for deepening study of the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Shuang also calls for correcting the "four forms of decadence" (the 四风 work-style problems), using micro-videos, big data and AI for targeted communication, and pursuing high-quality development, including new quality productive forces and deeper reform. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party commentary now frames ideological leadership within the 15th Five-Year Plan period.

A scientific plan for opening a new phase of Chinese modernization 开创中国式现代化建设新局面的科学谋划 Huang Maoxing Zhang Jianwei This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 31 October 2025, interprets the Recommendations for formulating the 15th Five-Year Plan for national economic and social development, adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). Huang and Zhang argue that the Recommendations are a programmatic document that sets out what kind of development is to be achieved in 2026–2030 and how, and that they express the Party Central Committee's 'historical initiative' in opening a new phase of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first explains why the 15th Five-Year Plan period occupies a pivotal position, linking what came before with what follows, in the effort to substantially realise socialist modernization by 2035. The second describes the plan as a further general mobilisation and deployment, covering its historical bearings, key tasks and the consultation behind it. The third sets out the 'six upholds' principles that are to guide the period. In the first part, the authors view the period from three angles: history, the demands of the times and value orientation. Historically, it is one of three five-year periods needed to reach the 2035 goal. In terms of tasks, it is a critical period for laying foundations, with per capita GDP reaching the level of moderately developed countries as one marker. In terms of values, it is a window for making more evident progress towards common prosperity. The second part lists seven main goals and twelve fields of strategic tasks, from a modern industrial system to national defence. It reports that Xi Jinping chaired the drafting group and that an online consultation in May and June drew more than 3 million valid suggestions. The third part argues for upholding Party leadership, the people first, high-quality development, comprehensive deepening of reform, an effective market combined with an enabling government, and coordination of development and security. The authors conclude that the Plenum's guidance should be implemented with a spirit of historical initiative, concentrating on China's own affairs so as to continue the 'two miracles' of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned reading of how the 15th Five-Year Plan Recommendations are framed and justified for a Party and public audience.

On the new alienation of emotional labour in digital capitalism and its dissolution 论数字资本主义情感劳动新异化及其消解 Ma Chao This article from World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 6) asks how emotional labour is newly alienated under digital capitalism and how that alienation might be dissolved. Ma Chao argues that digital technology has not changed the essence of alienated labour under capitalist relations of production, but has made it broader, deeper and better hidden than in the industrial era. The remedy, in Ma's view, lies ultimately in abolishing capitalist private ownership, with interim measures available now. The article has four parts. It first distinguishes Hochschild's "emotional labour" from Hardt and Negri's "affective labour" and defines the digital form. It then describes four concrete manifestations, analyses three underlying logics, and finally proposes paths to dissolving the alienation. Examples come mainly from live-streaming, short video, fan labour and virtual companionship services. Drawing on Marx's theory of productive labour, Ma holds that emotional labour is non-productive because it neither yields material commodities nor can be measured in socially necessary labour time. It is nonetheless commodified and drawn into capital's valorisation, for example by lengthening hours or intensifying work. Ma maps Marx's four forms of alienation onto algorithmic recommendation ("addictive emotional commodities"), traffic competition (staged personas), panoptic emotional surveillance ("unconscious spiritual colonisation") and covert platform discipline (three layers of exploitation, including free appropriation of user trace data). These are traced to a capital–technology logic (platform capitalisation), a capital–consumption logic (commodification of private feeling) and a capital–institution logic (private ownership of emotional commodities). Ma concludes that the fundamental way out is to abolish capitalist private ownership and rebuild individual ownership on common possession of the means of production, while accepting that digital capitalism cannot be removed in the short term. Meanwhile Ma proposes three reconstructions: of the technology logic (transparent, ethically reviewed algorithms and non-profit digital infrastructure), of the consumption logic (public, non-commercial emotional services and education against consumerism), and of the institutional logic (tiered data rights and copyright for emotional data). Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical treatment of platform labour, live-streaming and data rights that applies Marx's alienation framework to emotional work and ends with policy proposals.

Marx and Engels's fourfold critique of Russian Narodism and its scientific method 马克思恩格斯对俄国民粹主义的四重批判及其科学方法 Ji Mengling Wang Yonggui How did Marx and Engels argue against the Russian Narodnik (populist) claim that Russia could bypass capitalism and move directly to socialism? Ji Mengling and Wang Yonggui argue that the critique had four parts, each aimed at a distinct Narodnik thesis and each using a distinct analytical method. In their reading, together these parts exposed the theoretical errors of Narodism and gave guidance on whether a 'non-capitalist path' was possible. The article draws on Marx and Engels's direct polemics, including 'Refugee Literature' and 'On Social Relations in Russia', Marx's letter to the editorial board of Otechestvennye Zapiski, his correspondence with Vera Zasulich, and the 1882 Russian preface to the Communist Manifesto. It treats Herzen, Lavrov, Bakunin, Tkachev and Mikhailovsky as the Narodnik interlocutors. The four sections take up the 'superiority of the village commune', the 'revolutionary advantage of Russia', the 'peasantry as revolutionary subject' and the 'non-capitalist path utopia'. On the commune, the authors say Marx and Engels used historical analysis to show that communal land ownership and the artel were forms suited to backward conditions, and that the Russian commune was being dissolved from within and by the 1861 emancipation. On revolutionary advantage, Engels used comparison to argue that socialist revolution presupposes both bourgeoisie and proletariat, and that the tsarist state served the nobility's interests. He therefore judged Tkachev's claim that Russia lacked these classes to be detached from reality. On the peasantry, class analysis showed their isolation and weakness, which made them unreliable as a leading revolutionary force. Finally, dialectical analysis rejected both a deterministic reading of Western capitalist development and the idea that Russia could leap ahead alone. Russia might cross the 'Caudine Forks' of capitalism only if a Russian revolution and a proletarian revolution in the West complemented each other. The authors conclude that Marx and Engels's critique was long-running and thorough, continuing after Marx's death, when Engels still called for struggle against Narodists everywhere. They hold that this critique displays the scientific method of Marx and Engels in dealing with rival currents of thought. They also present it as a source of methodological guidance and experience for criticising erroneous social trends today. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how Marx and Engels's analytical methods were applied to Russian Narodism, with close attention to the specific texts.

The construction logic and pathways of an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of CPC history and Party building 中共党史党建学自主知识体系的建构逻辑及路径探析 Li Jia Li Jia asks how the newly established first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building (zhonggong dangshi dangjianxue) can build its own autonomous knowledge system. The article starts from Xi Jinping's statement that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's autonomous knowledge system, and from the 2024 regulations on Party history study and education. Li argues that the discipline must achieve academic independence and standardisation while upholding Party leadership and ideological security, and that an autonomous knowledge system is the way to overcome the discipline's subordinate status and marginal discourse. The article is organised in three parts: theoretical foundations, internal structure, and practical pathways. Li names three foundations: Marxist party theory, historical materialism, and the Party-building theory of Sinicised Marxism, from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The structure is then divided into a disciplinary system, an academic system and a discourse system, and the final part gives measures for each. Li's central claim is that the three systems form one organic whole: the disciplinary system is the 'skeleton', the academic system the 'flesh and blood', and the discourse system the 'medium of expression'. The disciplinary system has four modules: Party history, Party leadership and Party building, the discipline's own metatheory, and the practical work of Party affairs. The academic system rests on theory-building, summing up experience, problem orientation and methodological innovation, including data science and social network analysis. The discourse system needs a chain of concepts, propositions, theories and categories, and must manage the tension between political and academic language. Li also sets out three relationships to handle: political and academic, theoretical and practical, national and global. For practice, Li proposes four second-level disciplines, interdisciplinary tracks such as 'Party history plus digital humanities', a course and textbook matrix, a staged training model from undergraduate to doctoral level, dual supervisors drawn from Party and government, and reform of academic evaluation. For discourse, Li calls for three communicating teams, integrated traditional and new media, accurate translation of core terms such as full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and international communication through the Belt and Road Initiative and comparative study of party systems. Li concludes that the discipline, as the foundation, the core and the bridge respectively, should develop in a systematic way to support Party building. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholars plan the curriculum, methods and international communication of this new discipline.

The tactical evolution and strategic use of the CPC's tunnel warfare in Central Hebei during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中共冀中地道战的战术演进与策略运用 Wang Guangyao Wang Guangyao asks how tunnel warfare (didao zhan) arose on the Central Hebei plain during the War of Resistance against Japan, and under what conditions it became an effective tactic. The article argues that it was an innovation in plain guerrilla warfare guided by Mao Zedong's theories of guerrilla and protracted war, and that its development depended on shifts in the balance of forces as well as on Party leadership. The article follows the tunnels in four stages. It begins with the Japanese 'cage policy' of blockhouses and strongpoints, then turns to the early, limited use of tunnels, using the 1942 Beitan massacre in Dingxian as its main case. It next examines how tunnel warfare was perfected after 1942, and closes with a short assessment. Wang draws on Japanese commanders' memoirs and reports, Chinese Communist directives, local statistics and combat accounts. Wang contends that the cage policy, with the 'May 1st sweep' of 1942 as its peak, destroyed the older mobile guerrilla methods and forced the use of tunnels. Early tunnels were scattered, unconnected and used only for hiding, and some cadres dismissed them as 'flightism'. Digging was also costly, and at Beitan the lack of armed protection, anti-gas measures and neighbouring tunnels led to the deaths of over 800 civilians. The article then credits several factors for the change: Japanese overextension and strategic contraction from 1943; Liu Shaoqi's October 1942 instruction to turn tunnels from purely defensive works into a form that could also attack; and mass mobilisation, with government-organised digging from 1944. The result, in Wang's account, was the village-tunnel tactic, which combined fortified villages, rooftop and ground passages, concealed entrances and mines. Wang presents the December 1944 defence of Shijing village as a model case. Wang concludes that tunnel warfare moved ordinary ground guerrilla fighting underground and created a three-dimensional battlefield behind enemy lines. The article attributes its success to unified leadership, organisation, mass mobilisation, independence and innovation. In this reading it spread to southern and eastern Hebei and remained in use during the Liberation War. Read the original if you study the CPC's military history, Party documents on guerrilla strategy, or Japanese counter-insurgency in North China, and want detailed local evidence.

Cognitive shaping and the construction of revolutionary discourse in Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region exhibition narratives: a textual analysis based on the CPC's main newspapers 陕甘宁边区展览叙事中的认知塑造与革命话语建构——基于中共主要报刊的文本分析 Wang Haijun Chen Yuzhen How did the Communist Party use exhibitions in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region during the Yan'an period to shape popular perceptions and build a revolutionary discourse? Wang and Chen argue that exhibitions, which were given the political purpose of 'serving the War of Resistance and production', worked as open 'narrative texts'. In their account, these texts shaped the Party's image and ordinary people's understanding of economic and cultural construction, scientific knowledge and wartime mobilisation. They also strengthened the revolutionary narrative of national unity in resisting Japan. The study draws mainly on reports in Liberation Daily and the New China Daily, which the authors say carried 168 reports, editorials and speeches on exhibitions between 1936 and 1946. The first part describes six forms of presentation: ceremonial layout and spatial arrangement, slogans and inscriptions, physical exhibits, graphic displays, newspaper coverage, and interpersonal communication such as guides, symposia and comments from foreign visitors. The second part sets out six themes: the 'most advanced party', support for resistance and construction, 'labour creates everything', improved production technology, the border region's hygiene campaign, and women's liberation. The third part assesses the significance of these exhibitions. The authors' central move is to treat the exhibition as a text that visitors 'read' from the moment they enter. Portraits of leaders and labour heroes, calligraphy by Mao Zedong and Zhu De, prizes and statistical charts conveyed Party policy in ways the authors consider hard for other propaganda forms to match. Repeated pairings of words such as production, technology, resistance and national defence are said to have linked everyday labour to the war effort. The authors also present praise from Kuomintang officers and foreign guests as an 'other-shaping' effect that strengthened the Party's image beyond the border region. Wang and Chen conclude that the exhibitions broadened people's horizons, spread scientific and hygienic knowledge, challenged feudal ideas and won support from outside the base area. They credit the exhibitions with increasing political identification with the Party and achieving what the authors call political integration. They describe the exhibitions as an important part of the Party's revolutionary cultural work in the New Democratic period and as an example of 'telling the story of the War of Resistance well'. Read the original if you study Yan'an-era propaganda, the history of Party exhibition work, or the use of press sources to analyse revolutionary discourse.

The multidimensional construction of the Chinese Communist Party's "Zhonghua minzu" discourse during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国共产党“中华民族”话语的多维构建 Zhao Chao Zhao Chao asks what the term "Zhonghua minzu" (the Chinese nation) meant in the Chinese Communist Party's wartime discourse, and why the Party used it as it did. Responding to Xi Jinping's calls in 2023 and 2024 to build an autonomous discourse system for the community of the Chinese nation, the article sets aside scholarly disputes over the concept and looks at the Party's own usage. Its thesis is that, between 1931 and 1945, the term carried three distinct meanings, those of state, citizenry and nation. It also served as a tool for mobilising people and competing for discursive authority, not only as a description of an objective entity. The article first criticises existing scholarship for treating discourse as a neutral expression of the Party's views and for reading the term mainly through domestic ethnic relations. It then sets out a semantic framework built from example sentences and their common co-occurring words. Three sections follow, one for each meaning, each tied to the Party's aims and to the historical setting. Sources include Party documents, manifestos, editorials in Jiefang Ribao and Xinhua Ribao, and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhang Wentian, Wang Ming, Zhou Enlai and others. In the "state" sense, equivalent to China, Zhao argues that after the Japanese invasion and the North China Incident of 1935 the Party moved from internationalist class language to patriotic language. Phrases such as "national liberation" and "the Party and the Zhonghua minzu" presented the Party as a defender of state interests and as "the advanced sons and daughters" of the nation. This also served in a contest with Chiang Kai-shek's China's Destiny over who represented the nation. In the "citizenry" sense, equivalent to the Chinese people, the term countered Japanese enslaving education and defeatism, using the "450 million" formula and appeals to history and national spirit. In the "nation" sense, the Party answered Japanese separatist propaganda aimed at Hui and Mongol groups by presenting a pluralistic and unified nation. It also criticised Chiang's "clan theory" as Han chauvinism. Zhao concludes that the concept's content is multidimensional and must be read in context. The Party's wartime construction of it was also constrained by its own understanding, by domestic and international politics, and by rival political actors. Zhao suggests that later research should separate meanings by context and purpose, and that this helps in understanding the value of building an autonomous discourse system for the community of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you study Chinese Communist Party history, wartime nationalism or Party ethnic-policy discourse and want a close, example-based analysis of how the term was used.

How the Communist Party promoted the formation of a sense of community of the Chinese nation during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国共产党推动中华民族共同体意识的形成 Zheng Dahua Zheng Dahua asks how the Communist Party helped bring about, during the War of Resistance against Japan (1931–45), what Xi Jinping now calls the sense of community of the Chinese nation: a community of shared weal and woe, honour and disgrace, life and death, and destiny. The article argues that the Chinese nation moved from an "in-itself" to a "self-aware" community in modern times, and that this transition was completed in the war years, especially during the period of all-nation resistance. Zheng says earlier scholarship has covered Party ethnic theory and policy but has paid little attention to this particular consciousness. The article has three parts. The first traces the Party's theoretical understanding of the "Chinese nation", from its first use of the term in 1922 through Yang Song's 1938 lectures to Mao Zedong's 1939 text The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party. The second looks at propaganda and education stressing that all ethnic groups faced the same threat of national extinction. The third examines the mobilisation of "comprehensive all-nation resistance" and the anti-Japanese national united front. Zheng draws on Party resolutions, telegrams, editorials and leaders' writings. Zheng contends that the Party first had to settle who belongs to the Chinese nation. Yang Song, following Stalin's definition, treated it as a modern nation. Mao instead described a long-established nation made up of the Han and dozens of minority peoples, which Zheng calls a major contribution and the groundwork for shared consciousness. The Party then stressed a common fate under Japanese aggression and used the figure of the Yellow Emperor as common ancestor. It also held that the nation's supreme interest outranks that of any individual, class or ethnic group. A 1940 outline on the Hui people ranked the contradiction with Japan above ethnic and class contradictions. Finally, Zheng argues, building the united front, countering Han chauvinism and mobilising minorities produced genuine all-nation resistance, which made the "live together, die together" consciousness possible. Zheng concludes that the consciousness formed under Party leadership laid the foundation for the turning point in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation that victory in the war represented. The article presents the Party as the driving force behind both the concept of the nation and the sense of common destiny. Read the original if you want a documented account, drawn from Party sources, of how wartime Party texts defined the Chinese nation and its relation to minority peoples, and of how this is now linked to the contemporary concept of the community of the Chinese nation.

Clarifying Marx's concept of productive forces: disputes, misreadings and corrections 马克思的生产力概念辨析：争议、误读与澄清 Liu Wei Huan Yingqi Liu Wei and Huan Yingqi take up a long-running problem in Marxist theory: scholars still dispute and misread what Marx meant by "productive forces". The authors argue that this blurs the concept and weakens current work on new quality productive forces. Their thesis is that Marx's mature concept is single and coherent, and that it can be recovered by reading Capital, Volume I closely. The article first sets out a method. Early texts such as the German Ideology and the letter to Annenkov, and Marx's unpublished manuscripts, are treated as secondary to Capital, Volume I, which Marx himself prepared for publication. Four sections follow: the content of the concept, the "factor productive forces" formulations, the claim that the concept has a double meaning, and the place of science and technology. Along the way the authors discuss Lefebvre, Bukharin, Stalin, Wang Xuewen and G. A. Cohen. Liu and Huan define productive force as the overall power that arises when living labour, objectified labour and natural conditions combine. Marx's references to "new" productive forces created by cooperation or the division of labour are read as the surplus gained from organisation. Expressions such as "individual" or "machine" productive forces are said to follow the usage of Marx's day and not to introduce new concepts. Hence the authors reject proliferating labels such as "data productive forces". They also deny that Marx had separate philosophical and economic meanings, arguing that the difference lies in scope (the whole of society versus a given production process). On technology, they hold that it is not an extra factor and not a "permeating element". It is instead a specification of how the existing factors are combined and of their properties and quantities. Science, they argue, becomes a productive force only when applied through technology, and Marx's remarks on why eighteenth-century British capital could exploit scientific advances are cited in support. For research on new quality productive forces, the authors call for avoiding the habit of loading every possible factor into the concept. They propose studying it through concrete labour processes at the levels of the firm, the industry and the industrial system. They also argue that treating all science as a productive force may have fed the "two skins" problem between scientific research and the economy. They conclude that science policy should focus on the application of science to industry. Read the original if you want a close, text-based argument about Marx's productive forces and its bearing on how Chinese scholars theorise new quality productive forces.

On the idea of "valuing benevolent love" in excellent traditional Chinese culture 论中华优秀传统文化中的“讲仁爱”思想 Ni Suxiang Taking up Xi Jinping's call to bring out the contemporary value of excellent traditional Chinese culture, which he summed up as valuing benevolent love (renai), putting the people first, keeping good faith, upholding justice, promoting harmony and seeking a world of great harmony, Ni Suxiang examines the first of these. The article argues that renai is the core of that tradition and the most concentrated expression of the essence of Chinese civilisation. It holds that the idea rests on a coherent philosophical foundation, evolved over time, and has acquired new content in the contemporary period. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundations: the ontology of the unity of heaven and humanity, the doctrine that human nature is originally good, and the method of extending oneself to others. The second traces the historical course of the idea. It covers pre-Qin Daoist, Confucian and Mohist positions, the Han-to-Ming elaborations by Dong Zhongshu, Han Yu, Zhang Zai, the Cheng brothers, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, and the modern reinterpretations by Gong Zizhen, Kang Youwei and Tan Sitong. The third part sets out the content of the idea at three levels: the individual, the group and the state. Ni argues that the heaven–humanity unity, developed from the Zhou through Mencius to Wang Yangming's "one body" benevolence, joined graded love with universal love. Ni treats Mencius's view of human nature as better suited to ethical demands than Xunzi's, and reads Confucian "graded love" (love radiating outward from kin) as more workable in premodern conditions than Mohist impartial love. Ni cautions against reducing it to a defence of the clan system or a tool of the ruling class. Ni also defends Yang Zhu's emphasis on self-regard as a part of the tradition. In the final section, Ni maps love of self, kin, others and all things onto individual ethics, and professional duties for officials, teachers and doctors, and state governance. Ni concludes that renai has been creatively transformed and developed into a norm regulating relations among people, between humans and nature, and between states. The article links it to the socialist core values ("friendliness"), the Party's "life first" stance, people-centred development, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind. In Ni's account, socialism goes beyond the traditional minben (people-as-root) idea by addressing democracy as well as livelihood. The author calls for further excavation of the idea to build spiritual strength for the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich survey of how Confucian, Daoist and Mohist ideas of love are presented as a resource for contemporary Party ideology and ethics education.

Lenin's fourfold critique of bourgeois ideological and political education in "The Tasks of the Youth Leagues" 列宁《青年团的任务》对资产阶级思想政治教育的四重批判 Wei Qiang He Qiuyue Wei Qiang and He Qiuyue ask what Lenin's 1920 speech "The Tasks of the Youth Leagues" reveals about the nature of bourgeois ideological and political education. Clarifying them, in their view, helps socialist ideology gain a clear advantage in that competition. The article is organised into four sections, one for each critique, and draws mainly on Lenin's speech, supported by other writings by Lenin and by Marx and Engels, notably The German Ideology. The four targets are the "class spirit" running through bourgeois education, its hypocrisy, its extreme egoism, and its use of religion to "fetter the minds of workers and peasants". Each section first sets out Lenin's diagnosis and then, in the authors' reading, the remedy he points to. On the first two points, the authors argue that, in Lenin's analysis, bourgeois education serves the ruling interests of the exploiting class, justifies its order and trains "servants useful to the bourgeoisie". Its hypocrisy lies in the gap between promised freedom, equality and democracy and the reality of wage exploitation, which the authors present as rooted in private ownership of the means of production. On the third and fourth points, they hold that egoism ("each for himself, God for all") is instilled from infancy and can only be uprooted by abolishing private ownership. Religion, they argue, is used to justify exploitation and to console the exploited with the promise of heavenly happiness. The authors conclude that, for Lenin, bourgeois education cannot be reformed within capitalism, because the bourgeoisie controls both material and intellectual means of production. They report that he locates the deepest social root of religion in the "unpredictable force" of capital, so it can be dispelled only by opposing every form of capital's rule, by proletarian unity, and by scientific socialism. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Lenin's youth-league speech is used in current Chinese ideological and political education research to frame the contest between ideologies.

Discursive narrative in the external communication of the modernization of harmony between humanity and nature 人与自然和谐共生现代化对外传播的话语叙事论析 Xiao Huanyuan Meng Xiaorui Xiao Huanyuan and Meng Xiaorui ask how China can narrate to the world its "modernization of harmony between humanity and nature", which they present as the ecological dimension of Chinese modernization. They argue that, under what they call Western green discourse hegemony, this idea must be turned into a coherent external discourse and narrative system, so that it counters Western misreadings, strengthens China's "green discourse power" and presents China as a responsible major country. The article has three parts. The first sets out the context: the need to give ecological discourse a world dimension, the "traps" in Western accounts of China's ecology, and the failure of Western ecological modernization theory. The second describes how the narrative works, through discourse production, textual form and communication. The third proposes ways to improve it. In the authors' account, Western discourse casts China as an ecological threat, as the party that should bear climate responsibility, and as an "environmental authoritarian". They hold that Western ecological modernization, which relies on technology and markets, cannot resolve capitalism's structural contradictions. The core of the article reads China's narrative as a drama. Its setting is global ecological crisis and Western unilateralism.
