Its plot is a "comedy" of ecological justice between species, within and across generations, and across borders. The authors say this narrative is carried by a matrix of official channels (leaders' speeches, forums, state media) and non-official ones (think tanks, NGOs). The authors propose three strategies. The first is a discourse framework resting on China's independent knowledge system and built around exchange and mutual learning, peaceful development and win-win cooperation. The second is narrative texts that link China's development to human progress, told through small-scale stories about the Belt and Road Initiative and common prosperity. The third is to raise communication effectiveness through metaphor and multimodal media, plural voices including foreign commentators, and varied platforms, among them non-Western outlets. Read the original if you study Chinese international communication or green discourse and want to see how Chinese scholars use narrative theory to frame ecological messaging.

How the young Marx's view of socialism sublated the thought of Moses Hess 青年马克思社会主义观对赫斯思想的扬弃 Liu Huachu Wang Bo How did socialism move from an ethical ideal to a scientific theory? Liu and Wang take up this question by tracing the relation between the young Marx and Moses Hess, whom they call the "father of German socialism". They argue that Marx critically absorbed Hess's philosophical communism between 1841 and 1845 and then sublated it, replacing Hess's subjective-idealist, ethical socialism with a socialism grounded in historical materialism and political economy. The article has four parts. It first describes the German context of the 1830s and 1840s: mass pauperization, the arrival of French socialist ideas, and the rival paths of Wilhelm Weitling and Hess. It then sets out Hess's three contributions: the "philosophy of action", the critique of communication and money as alienation, and the ideal of a free and then "organic" community. The third part shows how Marx took up Hess's ideas from the Rheinische Zeitung to the 1844 Manuscripts. The fourth part explains how Marx went beyond Hess. The authors identify three points of departure. First, Hess confined his attention to the sphere of money and exchange and rejected capitalism from outside. Marx grasped the dialectic of civil society and of labour, distinguishing objectified from alienated labour and seeing capitalism as a historically necessary, transitory form. Second, Marx added private property as the link that moves the analysis from alienated communication to alienated labour. He later made production determine the forms of intercourse, which yields the productive forces–forms of intercourse framework of historical materialism. Third, Hess retreated to "loving union" and the abstract "human race", while Marx located the agent of communism in the proletariat and its revolutionary practice, which changes relations of production. The authors conclude that the path from Hess to Marx shows socialism becoming a science. They present this as a rebuttal to current trends that reduce socialism to a value-based utopia or to social concern. They bring in Althusser's "break" but stress that scientific socialism does not reject subjective values. In their reading Marx's view of socialism is a unity of ethical value and scientific logic. Read the original if you study the young Marx, the Hess–Marx relationship or the sources of historical materialism, and want a Chinese scholarly account of the passage from Hess's ethical socialism to scientific socialism.

Reanalysing the relationship between Marx and Feuerbach in the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right 《黑格尔法哲学批判》中马克思与费尔巴哈思想关系再分析 Chen Weici Did the young Marx, when writing his 1843 manuscript Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, still work inside Feuerbach's anthropological materialism? The article, published in Theoretical Studies in 2025, contends that Marx's use of Feuerbachian vocabulary and method already served different aims. The article opens by setting out the "Feuerbach factors" in the manuscript: the subject–predicate inversion method and a humanist stance, shown in Marx's emphasis on popular sovereignty, democracy and the abolition of the estates. It then rebuts Louis Althusser's reading, drawing on MEGA2 debates over the manuscript's dating, on Charles Barber, Z. Rosen, David McLellan, Rubel-era and Soviet editors, and on Rabin. The final part presents Marx's creative use of the inversion method and his concretisation of humanism. Chen's main moves are three. First, against Althusser, Chen argues that the concept of a "problematic" is undefined and serves his thesis of a rupture, and that Marx gave borrowed terms such as alienation and species-being different meanings, emphasising sociality rather than natural attributes. Second, Chen holds that dating the manuscript by Feuerbach's influence is circular, and that Marx used the inversion method earlier in his notes on Epicurean philosophy and in his closeness to Bruno Bauer. The decisive spur to criticising Hegel, Chen says, was Marx's work on the Rheinische Zeitung, where problems such as the wood-theft debate forced him to confront private property and material interests. Third, Marx retained the negative side of Hegel's dialectic, insisting that civil society and the political state are separate extremes that cannot mediate each other. He also turned Feuerbach's abstract sensuous being into a critique of the state's internal institutions. Chen concludes that Marx replaced Feuerbach's abstract "species-essence" with the real human being living in society, and extended this to a demand for popular legislative power based on universal suffrage and, ultimately, an association of free people. Neglecting this agency, the author says, feeds readings such as the "rupture thesis" and the "two Marxes", which break the continuity of Marx's thought. Read the original if you work on the young Marx, the dating debates around the 1843 manuscript, or the Chinese reception of Althusser's reading of Feuerbach.

Marx's "inversion" of Hegel's dialectic seen through the development of historical materialism 从唯物史观发展脉络看马克思对黑格尔辩证法的“颠倒” Lu Tong Gu Dongyue Lu Tong and Gu Dongyue take up the question of what Marx actually did when he "inverted" Hegel's dialectic. They argue that the usual reading, which treats it as a switch from idealism to materialism or a transplanting of the dialectic onto a materialist foundation, is formalistic and misses Hegel's "rational kernel". In their account, historical materialism is a change of theoretical framework: from an "abstract philosophical dialectic" to a "concrete historical dialectic" grounded in people's real productive activity. The article reads Marx's works in sequence to trace the inversion as a gradual process. It first reconstructs Hegel's "one–many–one" structure, in the Phenomenology of Spirit, the Logic and the overall system. It then follows Marx through the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. A closing section draws out the implications. The authors argue that for Hegel, estrangement and its sublation are both activities of consciousness, moving from an initial concept through opposed concepts to a higher one. Marx first reversed the starting point in the Critique, making civil society rather than the idea of the state the beginning. In the 1844 Manuscripts he turned Hegelian estrangement into estranged labour, whose structure the authors regard as identical, and relocated the negation of the negation into real life. They hold that this was still unfinished, since it rested on a humanist return to human essence. Marx completed the inversion in the Theses and The German Ideology. He recast the structure as "many–one–many", with practice as its form, and found the motive force of history in the development of people's needs for production and life. On this reading the negation of the negation becomes only a phenomenal regularity of history, not its logical premise. The authors conclude that Marx inverted Hegel's dialectic in four respects: its starting point, its sphere, its structure and its driving force. The result is historical materialism, which unites the dialectic with human productive activity and makes it open rather than a closed circle. They also claim that once human needs become the premise of the dialectic, "the human being" steps out from behind thought. They add that this lays a theoretical foundation for proletarian liberation, the free and all-round development of the person and the "modernization of the human being". Read the original if you want a close, text-by-text account of how Marx's early works relate to Hegel's logic of "one" and "many".

Anti-Japanese patriotic propaganda in overseas Chinese periodicals in the Americas during the War of Resistance 抗战时期美洲侨刊的抗日爱国宣传 Yan Guangchen This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks what role periodicals run by Chinese students and overseas Chinese in North and South America played in the resistance to Japan after the Mukden Incident of 1931. Yan argues that these publications spread information, mobilised opinion and gathered donations. In the author's account, they energised Chinese communities abroad, drew echoes from opinion in the host countries and helped shape international anti-fascist forces. The article proceeds by country. It first treats the United States, where it distinguishes publications run by Chinese students, by long-settled people of Chinese descent and by Chinese cultural figures who went there. Its examples are the Chinese Students' Monthly, the English-language Chinese Digest (San Francisco, founded 1935) and the Chinese-language Free World (New York, 1942). It then turns to the Chinese-language Canadian paper Tai Han Kung Pao (Da Han Gong Bao) and, finally, to two Peruvian periodicals, Gong Yan Bao and Oriental Review (Dongfang Yuebao). Yan's central claim is that these periodicals used the languages and channels available to them. The Chinese Students' Monthly reported on Japanese aggression. Chinese Digest, in English, reached second- and third-generation Chinese Americans and reprinted pieces from the New York Times and reports of American boycotts and relief funds. Tai Han Kung Pao, the organ of the Chinese Freemasons' Zhigongtang, criticised Japan's Twenty-One Demands. After 1931 it called for an end to civil war, and after 1937 it ran war-telegram columns, urged fundraising and bond purchases and encouraged skilled overseas Chinese to return. Yan reports that in Peru, Gong Yan Bao organised donations, and that Zhou Enlai praised the Peruvian community's fundraising in an inscription. Yan concludes that overseas Chinese periodicals are an extension of China's external communication and a source of international soft power. They used Chinese, English and Spanish to expose Japan's ambitions, call for donations and promote patriotism, and Yan describes this as the American chapter of a shared national effort at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a brief survey of specific Chinese-diaspora newspapers and magazines in the Americas during the war, with their titles, editors and themes.

The Spanish International Brigades and China's anti-Japanese national united front 西班牙国际纵队与中国抗日民族统一战线 Wang Wenxian Writing for the 80th anniversary of the victory in the War of Resistance against Japan and the world anti-fascist war, Wang treats the Spanish Civil War and China's resistance as the western and eastern battlefields of a single global struggle. The commentary opens with the International Brigades: volunteers from more than 50 countries, over 30,000 people in total, including Chinese volunteers. Wang then traces how the united front took shape, from the Comintern's Seventh Congress (1935) and the August 1st Declaration to the Wayaobao meeting and the second Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. A third section looks at exchanges between the two battlefields, and a final section compares the two models and draws lessons. Wang's central claim is that the two cases differ in structure. The Brigades are described as an 'external aid internalised' model, in which outside forces fought inside the country, though the author says they failed to integrate Spain's local social forces. The Chinese front is described as 'internally generated, externally linked': it mobilised domestic forces first and then sought foreign help. The author points to interaction between the two sides, including Zhu De's and Mao Zedong's messages to the Spanish people, the song 'Defend Madrid', Chinese volunteers in Spain, and the 'Spanish doctors' such as Norman Bethune who later came to China. Effective anti-fascism, Wang argues, requires the dialectical unity of local initiative and a global outlook. Wang concludes that the Chinese Communist Party drew lessons from Spain. Mao named the united front first among the 'three magic weapons' in 1939. The author holds that victory required a strong, mature party leadership, the broadest possible domestic and international united front, and no abandonment of independence and self-reliance. Wang links the Brigades' vow to save freedom in Spain and across the world with the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, and treats the two as continuous in essence. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars connect the Spanish Civil War to the united front and to present-day internationalist rhetoric.

The important role of the Communist Party of China in the world anti-fascist united front 中国共产党在世界反法西斯统一战线中的重要作用 Hao Ping Hao Ping, a professor of history, argues that the Communist Party of China was the earliest initiator and core leader of the world anti-fascist united front. It ends by drawing links to present-day international cooperation. Hao points to the August 1st Declaration of 1935 and the Wayaobao meeting as the first calls for uniting all states opposed to Japanese imperialism. The author stresses that the Party combined alliance-building with strategic autonomy. As evidence, Hao cites Mao Zedong's refusal of Comintern requests to send troops to support the Soviet Union, on the grounds that guerrilla war behind enemy lines tied down more Japanese forces. In Hao's account, the base areas pinned down large Japanese forces, and Egyptian, Indonesian and Vietnamese movements drew on the Party's united-front ideas. Confucian doctrine of the people's hearts and the modern concept of "the people" 儒家民心论与现代“人民”概念 Chen Zhiwei Chen Zhiwei asks how the Confucian idea of minxin (the hearts of the people) relates to the modern political concept of renmin ("the people"). The commentary argues that the modern concept inherited the core content of the Confucian doctrine, which kept it from being an empty term. At the same time, Chen holds that the two differ in substance. The piece first traces the doctrine from the Zhou conquest of the Shang through the Book of Documents and Confucius to Mencius. It then examines how the word "people" was used in classical texts. Finally it follows the shift to "popular sovereignty" in modern Chinese thought, from Huang Zongxi, Wang Fuzhi and Gu Yanwu through Sun Yat-sen to Marxism in China. Chen reads the early Zhou move from an unchanging mandate of Heaven to a mandate that shifts according to a ruler's virtue as the root of the idea. Confucius ranked the people's trust above food and arms. In Chen's reading, Mencius made the mandate of Heaven depend on the people's acceptance, so that political power effectively originates with the people, and drew the conclusion that the people are most important and the ruler least. Chen argues that in classical texts "people" was a passive group, and that Confucians placed the min low in the social hierarchy. The modern concept rests on equality and popular sovereignty, drops the metaphysical basis of the mandate of Heaven, and replaces it with revolutionary-history narratives and the ruling party's aim of serving the people. Chen concludes that the question of winning or losing popular support carries over from Confucian thought, but with new meaning: the min's low rank is removed and equal subjects are stressed. In Chen's account, "the people" is thereby disenchanted and becomes a fully modern political concept. Read the original if you want a short account of how a Chinese scholar links classical Confucian political thought to the Party's language of "the people".

Understanding China and understanding the world: the two-way convergence of world China studies and area studies 读懂中国与理解世界：世界中国学与区域国别学的双向奔赴 Li Kaisheng Writing in a newspaper commentary, Li Kaisheng asks how area and country studies (regional and country studies, qū yù guóbié xué) relate to world China studies, meaning the study of China by scholars abroad. Li compares the international relations view of states to billiard balls that follow mechanical rules, and the area studies view to team sports in which each player's skill and will matter. On this basis Li calls world China studies "the area studies of other countries". Li criticises Western "democracy export" as a failure to respect other countries' conditions. The three dimensions are illustrated with cases: US tariff policy as a sign of hegemonic decline; the claim that India is the "next China", which Li says ignores a changed international environment; and Chinese innovation, which Li attributes to a combination of factors rather than to state subsidies. China's journey back to the world stage 中国重返世界舞台的历程 Hadir Said This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how China has returned to a central position in world affairs and what its global vision offers. The author, an Egyptian political scientist, argues that China's rise rests on a long historical experience and that its proposals deserve attention because they answer pressing needs of a troubled international order. The piece moves from China's image as a peaceful civilisation to its transformation from a colonised, divided country into the second-largest economy. It then turns to the period since 2013, the Belt and Road Initiative, and the Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. The last of these was put forward by Xi Jinping at the "SCO Plus" meeting in Tianjin. Said contends that China's conduct cannot be understood without the "century of humiliation" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, two themes that shape its self-image. Since 2013, the author says, China has pursued the status of a core world power on three pillars: national revival, a community with a shared future for mankind, and more Chinese wisdom in global governance. The Belt and Road Initiative is presented as a new, more open and balanced model of globalisation, open to states of any political system and tilted towards developing countries. Said adds that this vision is gaining recognition in the Global South. Historical and contemporary China in a global perspective 全球视野下的历史中国与当代中国 Martin Jacques In this short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, the British writer Martin Jacques argues that the role, nature and importance of China studies are being transformed in step with China's own rise. Jacques compares the field today with that of twenty years ago, when study of China was concentrated on China itself and pursued mainly by sinologists. He then covers the field's geographical shift towards the Global South, the effect of social media and artificial intelligence, and the Western habit of judging China by Western standards. Jacques contends that as China becomes central to global growth, climate change, governance, technology and the Global South, China studies grows more interdisciplinary and of interest to non-specialists. He argues that the field's centre of gravity is moving away from the West: countries such as Brazil, Nigeria, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia need to understand China through the Belt and Road Initiative, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and trade, and they increasingly form views from their own experience. For Jacques, most Western scholars still view China through a Western prism and measure it by its degree of 'Westernisation', so that China always 'fails'. He attributes this to two centuries of Western hegemony and a single-world-view mentality, which he says leaves Western predictions about China almost always wrong. Jacques concludes that China studies is only at the beginning of a major expansion, and that China's history, culture, governance and foreign policy remain largely misunderstood. He holds that China must be understood on its own terms, and that the demand for such understanding will be the field's chief challenge in coming decades. Read the original if you want a brief, openly polemical statement of how a prominent Western commentator on China sees the globalisation of China studies and the decline of Western interpretive authority.

Chinese modernization of the rule of law and its global significance 中国式法治现代化及其世界意义 Lin Wei Lin Wei, in a commentary for the Chinese Social Sciences Today (29 October 2025), asks what global significance the Chinese path of rule-of-law modernization holds. Lin describes it as a new path, led by the Communist Party, that combines Marxist legal theory with China's realities and with excellent traditional legal culture. The author argues that it will help reshape the world legal order and create a new form of human legal civilization. The piece sets out seven aspects of this significance. They are a self-reliant model for developing countries, an autonomous Chinese legal knowledge system, a people-centred orientation, the coordination of domestic and foreign-related rule of law, the creative transformation of Chinese legal civilization, legal support for high-quality development, and the rule of law in cyberspace. Lin's core claim is that a path based on national conditions offers developing countries a way to avoid dependence on Western models. The author presents the legal knowledge system, guided by Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law, as a new theoretical resource. For global governance, Lin cites figures: as of June 2025, 306 laws in force, 55 of them specifically foreign-related; 26,000 foreign-related civil and commercial cases concluded by courts in 2024; and 207 overseas branches of Chinese law firms. Lin also holds that property protection and a better business environment give investors stable expectations, and that laws on cybersecurity, data and algorithms offer a Chinese approach to digital governance. Lin concludes that China's practice is a milestone in the history of the rule of law and will provide experience and ideas for other countries. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how an official-aligned legal scholar presents the international relevance of China's legal development, with statistics on foreign-related legal work.

Entering China's vast contexts to expand China Studies 深入博大中国场景 拓展中国学研究 Lin Shangli Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, around the second World Conference on China Studies, Lin Shangli asks how China Studies should develop as it becomes an international field. Lin's answer is that any account of China detached from Chinese contexts risks becoming spectating from the far shore. Research should therefore be embedded in three settings: a continuous civilisation of five thousand years, a super-large-scale society, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The short commentary takes these three settings in turn, calling them the temporal, spatial and ecological scenes of China Studies. It opens by citing Xi Jinping's letter to the first World Conference on China Studies, which described the field as the study of both historical and contemporary China. It closes with a call for China Studies to move beyond studying China as an object. In Lin's account, the temporal scene means treating ancient language, philosophy and culture as continuous with contemporary development. The spatial scene rests on what Lin calls the "Chinese miracle": rapid economic growth, long-term stability and effective governance. Lin cites a population of over 1.4 billion, GDP above 130 trillion yuan, 660,000 urban and rural communities and a five-level chain of decision-making as a "large-sample laboratory" for economics, political science and policy studies. Lin links these to traditional governance logics and says they can test the limits of existing theories and yield new analytical frameworks. Lin concludes that a new form of human civilisation is the concentrated expression of Chinese civilisation, society and socialism, not an abstract concept. China Studies should move from "object study" to "joint theory-building", engaging with concepts such as whole-process people's democracy, Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Drawing a new pattern of peace and prosperity through the Global Governance Initiative: an interview with Kyrgyzstan's former prime minister Djoomart Otorbaev 以全球治理倡议绘就和平繁荣新格局——访吉尔吉斯斯坦前总理卓奥马尔特·奥托尔巴耶夫 Chu Guofei This is an interview, conducted by Chu Guofei of Chinese Social Sciences Today, with Djoomart Otorbaev, former prime minister of Kyrgyzstan. Otorbaev says the UN's membership has grown from 51 to 193 states and its "content" has changed since 1945, so ideas for improving it are urgently needed. He describes the SCO, which in his account has grown from six members to a 26-country "family", as a model because its documents rest on consensus; he praises the Tianjin summit of 2025 and says Kyrgyzstan will chair the SCO in 2026, with a summit in Bishkek. He criticises protectionism by the United States and the European Union, which he says have lost competitiveness, and presents the Global South as committed to free trade and investment. Otorbaev points to the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway as a flagship Belt and Road project, stresses trust as the precondition for cooperation (citing Confucius), and says equal dialogue requires education and knowledge. Read the original if you want a Central Asian former head of government's view of China's Global Governance Initiative, the SCO and Global South cooperation.

Advancing society-wide general education in artificial intelligence 推进人工智能全社会通识教育 Ai Zhiqiang Zhu Lingling This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 30 October 2025, asks how general education in artificial intelligence (AI) can be extended from schools to the whole of society. Starting from Xi Jinping's call to promote AI education at all school stages and general education across society, Ai and Zhu argue that it would raise national AI literacy, spread the benefits of technology and guard against risks. They contend that it should be built as a system. The article sets out five components: differentiated target groups, a tiered curriculum, varied delivery channels, a mechanism linking learning and assessment, and a multi-party support structure. Each is treated briefly and with practical examples. On content, the authors propose a principle of tiered, categorised, all-age and lifelong learning. Primary, middle and high schools, vocational and general higher education, working professionals and older people would each follow their own path. The curriculum would move from what AI is, to how to use it, to how to use it responsibly, so that the public shifts from being able to use AI to using it well. Delivery would combine online courses and question-answering systems with AR and VR exhibits in science museums, libraries, community centres and village halls. A credit-bank system would record learning outcomes, and group-specific indicators would assess results. For support, Ai and Zhu call for Party committee leadership and government direction, including standards, evaluation and dedicated funds. Enterprises would open training platforms and application sites, universities would build courses and train teachers, and science associations and the media would produce and spread popular materials. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese policy writing translates a leadership directive on AI into an implementation framework for education.

The united front as a powerful instrument for winning hearts and pooling strength 统一战线是凝聚人心汇聚力量的强大法宝 Jiang Rui This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 30 October 2025, asks how the united front can continue to rally popular support and unite forces in the new era. Jiang Rui argues that, as the Party leadership has put it, winning hearts and minds is "the greatest politics", and that the united front is a "powerful magic weapon" for this task. The article presents it as a political advantage of the Communist Party of China that matters for building a modern socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article opens with the historical record of the united front, from the National Revolutionary united front to the patriotic united front of the reform period, and with the framework developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then turns to current policy: the 2022 Central United Front Work Conference, the 20th Party Congress report, and the proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan, which call for improving the "broad united front work" pattern. The text is organised in three numbered sections: the united front's strategic position, the practice of great unity, and consensus-building. Jiang's central argument is that great unity must grow in both breadth and quality. The article links this to harmony in five sets of relations: political parties, ethnic groups, religions, social strata, and compatriots at home and overseas, including Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan. For each, the author sets out tasks, such as the new type of party system, forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, and the sinicisation of religion. On consensus, Jiang says the Party must hold the "centre of the circle" while widening inclusiveness, so that unity and diversity coexist. The author describes shared political foundations as upholding Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, and supporting national reunification. Jiang concludes that, with society more diverse and the internet changing the united front's work, ideological guidance and consensus-building must be strengthened and methods innovated, online and offline. The author gives the people's political consultative conference a role as a specialised consultative body that resolves conflicts and builds consensus. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how united front work is framed in late 2025, including its themes of unity and diversity and its five relationships.

Guiding principles for economic and social development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period “十五五”时期经济社会发展的指导方针 Li Qiang This is a programmatic article by Li Qiang, published in the People's Daily on 30 October 2025, explaining the guiding principles for economic and social development set out in the Central Committee's Recommendations for formulating the 15th Five-Year Plan. These were adopted at the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). Li argues that the 2026–2030 period is a link between past and future in the drive to basically achieve socialist modernization by 2035, and that the guidelines must be fully understood and carried out in drafting and implementing the plan. The article has three parts. The first locates the 15th Five-Year Plan period historically, within the course of Chinese modernization and within what it calls profound changes in the world unseen in a century. The second sets out the guiding ideology and the "six adherences" that together make up the guidelines. The third lists practical requirements in four areas and ends with instructions on drafting the plan outline. Li's core claim is that the period should be approached through two formulas: "consolidating the foundation" and "exerting full force". The first means strengthening resilience on matters basic to development and security; the second means coordinated breakthroughs across all fields under the "five-sphere" and "four-pronged" overall plans. Facing an uncertain international environment, Li says China should pursue certainty through high-quality development and the six adherences: Party leadership, putting the people first, high-quality development, comprehensive deepening of reform, combining an efficient market with a capable government, and coordinating development and security. The practical tasks are building the new development pattern, with a stronger domestic cycle and a unified national market; integrating scientific and industrial innovation to develop new quality productive forces according to local conditions; improving livelihoods and advancing common prosperity; and securing the new development pattern with a new security pattern. Li concludes that the State Council will draft the plan outline on the basis of the Recommendations. Drafters are to consult widely, work out major policies, reforms and projects, and ensure that special, regional, spatial and local plans reflect the guidelines. The article closes with a call to rally around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the leadership frames the priorities and official vocabulary of the 15th Five-Year Plan.

On comprehensively strengthening the Party's work style 论全面加强党的作风建设 Zhu Lingjun Shan Boya Zhu Lingjun and Shan Boya ask why the Chinese Communist Party should attend to its work style (zuofeng), what the work covers and how it should be done. Their answer is that work style is the visible form of the Party's nature and purpose, bears on its survival, and has been strengthened since the 18th Party Congress (2012) through a set of tested practices. The article is a research article aimed at providing scholarly support for Party building in the new era. The authors define work style as the way Party members, cadres and organisations show Party spirit in their conduct, covering ideology, work, leadership, daily life, study and writing, and meetings. They set out its theoretical sources in classical Chinese ideas of "wind" (feng) as custom and moral influence, in remarks by Marx, Engels and Lenin on bureaucracy and bad habits, and in statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. They then explain its significance, review historical experience, and describe innovations since 2012. The core argument is that, in the authors' account, work style shapes the Party's image, popular support and survival, and decides whether its undertakings succeed. They cite a 2024 National Bureau of Statistics survey in which 94.9 per cent of respondents approved of implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, against 75 per cent satisfaction with Party conduct and anti-corruption work before 2012. Historical experience is grouped under seeking truth from facts, linking theory with practice, staying close to the masses, integrity, hard struggle, appointing people on merit under democratic centralism, and discipline. For the period since 2012 the authors identify six practices: choosing the right entry point (the eight-point regulations), leadership setting the example, immediate correction, reform and institutional innovation, strict standards, and concentrated education campaigns. The authors conclude that work style needs constant attention because it rebounds if relaxed, and that economic achievement cannot substitute for it. They present the practices as experience for advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and link them to the Party's self-reform and to escaping the "historical cycle" of rise and fall. They call on cadres to examine themselves first during the current study and education campaign on the eight-point regulations. Read the original if you want a systematic official-academic account of how Party School scholars justify and periodise Party work-style building from Mao to Xi.

Party integration: a new type of social integration and a comparison 政党整合：一种新的社会整合类型及比较 Wang Qing Market transition has left Chinese society differentiated, atomised and weakly connected. Wang Qing asks how the state can integrate such a society at the grassroots, given that existing research offers three models: government–society coordination, administrative integration and technological integration. The article argues that each has structural limits and proposes a fourth type, "party integration", in which the ruling party works on its own organisations, administrative bodies, economic organisations and mass self-governing bodies to rebuild grassroots order. The article begins with a literature review. It runs from Durkheim's organic and mechanical solidarity, through Parsons's AGIL scheme, to Tönnies. It then follows the stages of Chinese grassroots state-building from imperial times to the present. Wang defines social integration as the state integrating society, rather than the Western focus on individuals joining society. The three existing types are then set out, and party integration is introduced and compared with them, in the author's Table 1. The analysis uses three dimensions: form of power, organisational structure and working mechanisms. Wang identifies a typical weakness in each existing model. Government–society coordination risks state involution when state capacity is weak, and societal dependence on the state when it is strong. Administrative integration is blocked by departmental self-interest. Technological integration is instrumentalist and cannot make autonomous decisions. Party integration is described as a "re-integration" of the three. It combines internal integration (leading small groups, party groups, centralised management by portfolio, and the party's own organisation-building) with external integration of society. Drawing on Michael Mann, the author says the party's power is both concentrated, through political authority, and diffuse, through "doing work with people" and emotional governance. Party organisations are embedded in state and non-party bodies, including new economic and social organisations and new employment groups. Flexible informal mechanisms such as work teams and the "Fengqiao experience" add to this. Wang concludes that party integration pursues both order and vitality, moving society from compliance towards identification. The author notes that diffuse power still depends on concentrated power as its backing. The balance between the two must therefore be managed, and formalism in some localities remains a problem for later study. Read the original if you want a political-science account, in the Chinese academic mainstream, of how the Communist Party's grassroots role is theorised as a model of social integration, and how it is set against other integration models.

"Entering the cities" and "going to the countryside": the CPC's practice of currency unification around the founding of the People's Republic “进城”与“下乡”：新中国成立前后中共的货币统一实践 Liu Mengyan How did the Communist Party of China (CPC) turn a patchwork of base-area currencies into a single national currency, and make it circulate in both city and countryside? Liu Mengyan argues that the unification ran in three stages: the "birth" of the renminbi, its "entry into the cities" and its "going to the countryside". In this account, currency unification was the key link in unifying financial and economic work and in consolidating the new state. The article is a historical study of roughly 1937 to 1952, drawing on Party directives, telegrams, conference resolutions and regional reports. It begins with the plural currencies of the War of Resistance and the Liberation War, then follows the North China financial conferences of 1947 and 1948 to the founding of the People's Bank of China on 1 December 1948. The two later sections cover urban and rural circulation, with cases including Beijing, Tianjin, Shanghai, Wuhan, Hunan and Hebei. Liu's central argument concerns how the renminbi was established in each setting. In the cities it faced local base-area notes, the Nationalist government's gold yuan and silver-dollar notes, foreign currencies and a dominant silver dollar, with speculation rampant. The Party handled these in sequence: fixed exchange rates and later withdrawal of local notes, conversion and expulsion of the gold yuan, step-by-step controls on foreign currency, and a two-sided campaign against silver. That campaign combined administrative suppression, such as the raid on the Shanghai securities building, with commodity-indexed savings deposits. In the countryside the obstacles were a traditional preference for goods over money and a lack of trust in the notes. Liu describes campaigns to reject silver and support the renminbi, together with propaganda, tax payment in renminbi, agricultural loans, remittance networks, and state and private trade, which the author says were chosen over mainly administrative means. Liu concludes that by the end of 1951 a unified renminbi market, excluding Tibet, Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, had been basically established. The author cites figures for 1952: peasants held 51.6 per cent of renminbi in circulation, and the commercialised share of agricultural output rose from 30 to 37 per cent between 1950 and 1953. Liu presents currency unification as the first link in unified financial control and as a support for later industrialisation. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the early People's Republic displaced rival currencies and built trust in its money.

Ethical risks of generative AI in ideological and political education and ways to resolve them An examination from the perspective of the subjectivity of those being educated 生成式人工智能赋能思想政治教育的伦理风险与化解路径——基于教育对象主体性视角的考察 Yan Ruifeng Yan Ruifeng asks what ethical risks arise when generative AI, especially large language models, is used to empower ideological and political education (sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu), and how they can be resolved. The article argues that the one-sided expansion of technical (instrumental) rationality erodes the value rationality on which this education rests. In Yan's account, this "colonizes" the educational process and alienates the subjectivity of those being educated. The article has three parts. The first sets out three technical logics through which subjectivity is dissolved: datafied discipline, algorithmic substitution of cognition, and technological mediation of intersubjectivity. The second derives four ethical risks from them. The third proposes four countermeasures, each matched to one risk. The analysis draws on Marx's account of alienated labour and on Habermas-style notions of intersubjectivity, and cites Xi Jinping on ideological and political work. Yan holds that datafied discipline turns learners' behaviour, emotions and thoughts into quantifiable data and so weakens value subjectivity. Algorithmic substitution is read as an extension of labour alienation into cognition, outsourcing thinking and eroding metacognition. Technological mediation turns the teacher–student relation into a three-way teacher–AI–student structure, which the author calls "pseudo-intersubjectivity". The four resulting risks are disordered value beliefs, caused partly by training data drawn mainly from Western value systems and by AI hallucination; mental inertia that hides the spirit of innovation; diluted humanistic feeling, because AI can only simulate emotion statistically; and weakened responsibility, which shows up as anonymity-driven misconduct, "data-score" moral behaviour, academic dishonesty and a diminished personality. Yan proposes four remedies, under the principle of "people-oriented, intelligence for good". The first is ideological security work: Party leadership over education-sector ideology, a corpus embedding Marxist values and the core socialist values, value alignment across the whole AI pipeline, and an ethics review committee. The second is education mechanisms built around innovation, including AI literacy and evaluation systems that weight innovation. The third is emotionally intelligent design and a teacher-led "teacher–machine–student" model. The fourth is moral-responsibility education with a distributed responsibility network and new integrity mechanisms. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how AI risks in political education are framed through subjectivity, ideology and responsibility ethics, together with concrete governance proposals.

The vitality of ideological and political education: theoretical interpretation and paths to strengthening it 思想政治教育生命力的理论阐释与提升路径 Wang Meijun Dai Rui Wang Meijun and Dai Rui take up a concept they say is still only vaguely understood in the field of ideological and political education: its "vitality" (shengmingli). Existing work, they argue, has not systematically explained how this vitality is sustained, how it shows itself, or how effective it is. The article proposes that vitality is an active, creative and driving spiritual force of the discipline itself. It sets out the concept's meaning, components and sources of momentum, and then offers four routes for strengthening it. The article first reviews three existing views: a "combined forces" view, an "active adaptation" view and an "external indicators" view, which it finds descriptive rather than conceptual. It then traces the term from biology to philosophy, psychology and pedagogy, and draws on Marx and Engels's historical materialism. Next it divides vitality into four components: discipline building, theoretical research, practical activity and the image of discourse. It then identifies three generative drivers: internal contradictions, changes in the social environment, and people's developmental needs. The last section gives the four paths. The authors define vitality as the survival capacity and development potential people show in transforming the objective world. In ideological and political education, they say, it is a subject-driven, overall resultant force with a value-guiding and spirit-shaping function, grounded in concrete practice. They locate its basic driver in contradictions between worldview and methodology and between truth and value. They add that environmental conditions, technology and norms give external momentum, while the need for personalised content, differentiated methods and varied media reinforces it. The four paths are: moving theory from "explaining" to "leading"; moving practice from "cognition" to "action", including replacing effect-oriented evaluation with efficacy-oriented evaluation; deepening the fusion of the real and the virtual through technology while guarding against algorithmic dependence and ethical risk; and combining "hard constraints" with "soft guidance" in institutions through participatory design, emotional transmission and flexible enforcement. The authors conclude that vitality shows ideological and political education is becoming a self-aware process of subject-driven construction across a person's life, not a passive one. They tie practical renewal to Chinese modernization and the Two Integrations. Read the original if you study the theory of ideological and political education in China, or want to see how the discipline conceptualises its own vitality, drivers and reform directions in the digital era.

Comprehensively improving cadres' capacity for modernization 全面提高干部现代化建设能力 Hong Xianghua Li Mengke This short commentary in the Party journal Dangjian asks how Party cadres can acquire the abilities needed to carry out Chinese modernization. Hong Xianghua and Li Mengke argue that cadre capacity must be raised across the board, and that this is a systematic and long-term task requiring several kinds of training at once. The article has two parts. The first sets out what the requirement means, drawing on Xi Jinping's call, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), for the "eight kinds of skills" and "seven abilities" and for political, leadership and work capacity suited to Chinese modernization. The second sets out practical routes to achieving it. On content, the authors treat political capacity as first in rank and as the basis for leadership and innovation. Leadership capacity means setting direction, planning the whole picture and balancing paired relationships such as top-level design and practical exploration, or efficiency and fairness. Work capacity is to be tailored to posts, with stress on economic work, digital governance and emergency response. The four routes are ideological tempering, political training, practical experience and professional training. These involve study of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, loyalty and discipline, grassroots and frontline postings under the "four down to the grassroots" system, and regular, tiered, technology-assisted training. The authors conclude that these measures will give the building of a modern socialist country a strong contingent of cadres. Read the original if you want a concise statement of current official thinking on cadre education and capacity-building under Chinese modernization.

Experience and lessons from building the responsibility system for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 全面从严治党责任体系建设的经验与启示 Liu Xianchun Zhang Can Liu Xianchun and Zhang Can ask what the Communist Party of China's history can teach about building a responsibility system for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They take as their starting point Xi Jinping's instruction at the Political Bureau study session of 27 June 2024, which for the first time put this system on the agenda and called for responsibility to be in place at three levels: responsible actors, requirements, and assessment and accountability. The authors argue that the Party's century of practice holds experience that can strengthen awareness of responsibility and make the duties of governing the Party effective. The article has three parts. The first identifies three core elements: the Party's position as the leading core, clear and tiered responsibilities, and the building and enforcement of rules. The second examines five key mechanisms: passing responsibility down the chain, supervision and accountability, assessment and incentives, education and guidance, and democratic centralism. Each is traced from the revolutionary years through the reform era to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), with citations to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. In the authors' account, Party leadership is the soul of the system because it supplies direction, motivation and safeguards. They describe the Party as moving from rough to refined definitions of duty, and from basic disciplinary bodies to a full supervision system that includes the merged Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and National Supervisory Commission, inspection tours and the "four forms" of discipline. Democratic centralism is presented as the basic mechanism that restrains power and makes decisions scientific. The third part draws seven lessons, in pairs of elements to be combined: top-level design and grassroots practice; historical wisdom and the tasks of the times; theoretical innovation and practical exploration; intra-Party supervision and external checks; accountability of organisations and of individuals; rule-making and effective enforcement; and assessment with dynamic adjustment. The authors conclude that the responsibility system must form a complete loop from concept to practice and from rules to feedback. Their proposals include a clear list of duties for each Party organisation and cadre, accountability that is precise and neither lax nor overextended, and support for officials who take initiative under the "three distinctions". They present this as a guarantee of the Party's long-term rule and the country's lasting stability. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars historicise Party responsibility mechanisms and the Third Plenum's agenda on Party-building reform.

The Communist Manifesto's scientific construction of the Marxist discourse system and its significance 《共产党宣言》对马克思主义话语体系的科学构建及其意义 Zhao Ende Han Haitao Zhao Ende and Han Haitao ask how Marx and Engels built a Marxist discourse system in The Communist Manifesto, and what that example offers for building a Marxist discourse system suited to China and to the present. They argue that the Manifesto is both the programmatic document and the theoretical model for constructing such a system. Existing scholarship, the authors say, has mostly catalogued and explained the Party's theoretical innovations, so a return to the classic text is needed. The article has four parts. It first presents the Manifesto as a theoretical programme, a party declaration and a banner for spreading Marxist discourse. It then examines the logic and style by which the text constructs that discourse, followed by its themes, main line and methods. The last part considers the Manifesto's role in the worldwide spread of Marxism and its meaning for the Communist Party of China. The authors' central claim is that discourse serves theory, and that the materialist conception of history underlies the whole discourse system. On this basis the Manifesto ties discourse to class interests, treats the proletariat and its party as the subject of discursive struggle, and rebuts bourgeois charges on private property, education, 'eternal truths' and the family. Its theme is 'human emancipation', its main line is communist revolution, and 'class' is its starting category. Four methods are drawn out: unity of logic and history, of critique and construction, of construction and dissemination, and of the general and the particular, the last shown by the prefaces to later editions. The authors also credit the text's declaration form, short paragraphs, rhythmic historical narration and first-person voice for its persuasive force. The authors conclude that the Manifesto's translation and circulation, which Plekhanov and others testified to, show how discourse wins over the masses and shapes party-building. They propose that the Party's discourse has followed the Manifesto's analysis of social contradictions, passing through the themes of revolution, construction, reform and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as the principal contradiction changed. The people-centred wording of each period is, in their account, a continuation of the Manifesto's value stance. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory reading of the Manifesto as a model of discourse construction and of how Chinese scholars link it to current discourse innovation.

Socialization of production, human development and the self-preservation of capital: an analysis based on Marx and Engels on the role of capital 生产社会化、人的发展与资本的自我保存——基于马克思恩格斯关于资本作用论述的分析 Wang Zhongru Wang Zhongru takes up the question of how Marx and Engels understood capital, arguing that popular views of it are often distorted. The author notes that the well-known passage on capital's willingness to commit any crime for 300 per cent profit is a quotation Marx took from T. J. Dunning, and that it is often wrongly treated as Marx's own judgement. Wang's thesis is that Marx and Engels saw capital as a historically necessary carrier of the socialization of production and a material precondition of all-round human development, and that its disappearance is also its 'self-preservation'. The article has five sections. It begins with the misreadings of capital, then examines capital as a carrier of socialization (of the means of production, of labour forms and of products). It next treats capital and human development, then the extinction of capital and the meaning of 'self-preservation'. It ends with the historical experience of socialist states, from Lenin's New Economic Policy to reform and opening up, and with the role of capital in the socialist market economy. The evidence is drawn mainly from Capital, the Grundrisse, Engels's Anti-Dühring and Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, and Lenin on cooperatives. Wang argues that Marx and Engels combined moral critique with scientific critique, and that capital's destruction of small production and its cooperative labour created social labour and productive forces that individuals could not reach alone. Human development shows a paradox in which social relations grow richer while the individual becomes more one-sided, a contradiction capital cannot resolve. Reading Marx's Grundrisse passage, Wang holds that capital's extinction means abolishing its character as a relation of domination while keeping the factories, machines and land. Violence plays only a secondary role, and it is capital's own contradictions and the growth of science that bring about its end. Wang claims that the Soviet and Mao-era practice of eliminating capital and small production by force failed, and that no better carrier of socialization has yet been found. Wang concludes that capital cannot be abolished until a more effective carrier exists. Under the Communist Party's leadership in China, the author says, capital serves human development and does not dominate production, so Western left critiques of capital cannot simply be applied to China. Citing Xi Jinping, the article calls for bringing out capital's positive role while controlling its negative effects. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's close reading of Marx and Engels that is used to justify private capital under socialism, including the argument about Lenin's cooperatives and Soviet history.

The political logic of techno-feudalism as an expression of the nature of capital, and its critique 技术封建主义表征资本本质的政治逻辑及其批判 Liu Yanfeng Tu Liangchuan Liu Yanfeng and Tu Liangchuan take up the thesis of "techno-feudalism", advanced by Western scholars such as Yanis Varoufakis and Cédric Durand, and ask what it reveals about the nature of capital in the digital age. They argue that big technology firms such as Amazon, Google and Facebook, by monopolising platforms, data and algorithms, have returned capitalism to a feudal-like structure of hierarchy, dependence and exploitation. The article's aim is to clarify the concept, expose its logic and take a critical stance towards it. The article opens by contrasting traditional feudalism with its "hyper-modern" form along four lines: land gives way to data as the key means of production, overt coercion to concealed exploitation, landlords to tech giants, and serfs to "cloud serfs". It then proceeds in three main sections: digital labour (gig work, "play labour" and the move from "cloud proletarians" to cloud serfs), technological monopoly power (platform capital, self-legitimation, algorithmic control), and data production at global level (cloud rent, data reproduction, data colonialism). A closing section offers reflections and policy proposals. Liu and Tu contend that platforms function as fiefs: workers and firms must obey platform rules and pay rent or share profit to gain access. Gig work offers formal flexibility but fragments labour and subjects workers to algorithmic rating and surveillance. Activities that feel like play, such as content sharing, are said to generate value for platforms, turning users into "digital tenant farmers". Platforms extract "cloud rent" from advertisers, merchants and users, and present monopoly as innovation, openness and sharing. Globally, the authors describe data colonialism, in which developed countries and tech giants exploit data from developing countries, leaving the latter in a "semi-colonial, semi-feudal" digital dependency. The authors conclude that understanding and limiting the technological power of the tech giants is key to a fairer, more open society. They propose strengthening antitrust supervision (stricter merger review, mandatory opening of platform interfaces and data), raising workers' rights (legal recognition of platform workers, algorithm transparency, working-time limits), and building a global data governance framework (data localisation, unified protection rules, regulated data circulation and trading). Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist treatment of the techno-feudalism debate, with its policy recommendations on platform monopoly, gig labour and data sovereignty.

Methodological self-awareness: building a narrative system for Chinese modernization through Marx's method of presentation 方法自觉：马克思叙述方法视域下中国式现代化的叙事体系构建 Huang Jing Bao Jin Huang Jing and Bao Jin take up a question raised by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for accelerating a Chinese discourse and narrative system: how can China's own narrative of Chinese modernization reach an international audience? The authors argue that existing scholarship studies the theory, practice and values of this narrative but neglects its methodology. They contend that Marx's method of presentation (Darstellungsmethode, 叙述方法) offers the missing guide, and that using it would also break what they call the Western monopoly on narrative methodology. After a short review of the literature, the article has three main parts. The first sets out the basic determinations of Marx's method of presentation, drawing on the Afterword to the second edition of Capital Volume I, the critique of Hegel and The German Ideology. The second applies these to diagnose three obstacles facing the narrative of Chinese modernization. The third draws three lessons from Marx for building the narrative system. On Marx, the authors distinguish the method of presentation from the method of research. Research appropriates material and traces inner connections. Presentation then reproduces the results as a concrete whole, shaped by its object and its readers, and it should take the form of a 'real' rather than an 'ideal' narration of history. On this basis, they identify three obstacles. The first is a shortage of narrative depth, with too little movement from the abstract to the concrete. The second is the one-track Western narrative of modernization, which they say is backed by capital power and used to stigmatise Chinese modernization, including in digital and algorithmic spaces. The third is a barrier of discourse between Chinese narrators and foreign readers. They locate its causes in Western-centric readings, a propaganda-oriented and one-way style of outward communication, and Western control of digital technology. The authors propose three remedies. Research and presentation should be unified, combining systematic study of Chinese modernization with a systematic account of it. Narrative discourse should pursue a 'revolution in terminology' and reader-awareness. This means new concepts that can win international recognition, a balance between universality and particularity, and reframing for foreign contexts. The narrative should follow 'real historical narration', avoiding both the imposition of Western schemas and the pursuit of speculative concepts, and it should rest on the 'big historical view'. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars use Marx's methodological texts to frame the international communication of Chinese modernization.

What Chen Yun's methods of investigation and research teach us 陈云同志的调查研究方法给予我们的启示 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu draws lessons for today from the investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) practice of Chen Yun, the Party's long-serving economic leader. The article opens with Mao Zedong's remark at the 1962 Seven Thousand Cadres Conference that Chen Yun understood socialist construction better than most and that "his method is investigation and research". Zhu argues that Chen's methods remain a valuable legacy that should be studied and applied. The piece was published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025. The article is organised around four requirements of good investigation: approaching it without preconceptions, being thorough and meticulous, listening to differing views, and having the right purpose. Each section combines Chen's own statements with episodes from his career, including the 1949 Shanghai prices mission, the 1953 grain purchase and sale policy, the 1959 coal industry symposium and his 1961 fieldwork in Qingpu. Each also cites Xi Jinping's remarks on research work, and the closing section refers to the March 2023 Central Committee work plan on investigation and research. Zhu's central claim is that Chen's "fifteen-character formula" ("not bowing to superiors, not bowing to books, only to reality; exchange, comparison, repetition") underpins his method. In Zhu's reading, "not bowing to superiors" does not mean disregarding them: Chen insisted on carrying out central directives while starting from local reality, and Zhu cites his 1961 proposal on household contracting. Zhu points to Chen's 15 days in a Qingpu village, his detailed sow-rearing observations and his arithmetic against double-cropping rice as models of depth. On listening, Chen sought out dissenting views and truth-tellers and took responsibility for the leadership's errors. On purpose, Zhu stresses that Chen treated research as a means to solve problems, and that he put people's livelihood first, as in his proposals on vegetables, soybeans and private plots. Zhu concludes that, amid what the article calls great changes unseen in a century and deep-seated contradictions in reform and development, investigation and research is a "family heirloom" to be used more fully. He calls for grasping real conditions more thoroughly and understanding objective laws more deeply, so as to carry socialism with Chinese characteristics for a new era forward. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's account of Chen Yun's working methods, with concrete episodes and the official framing of the 2023 campaign to promote investigation and research.

Grasping profoundly that problems of work style are in essence problems of Party spirit 深刻把握作风问题本质上是党性问题 Xu Mei Xu Mei takes up Xi Jinping's statement that problems of work style are in essence problems of Party spirit (dangxing). The article argues that how a Communist handles work-style problems measures their faith in Marxism, their belief in socialism and communism, and their loyalty to the Party and the people. Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, it urges Party members and officials to join the cultivation of Party spirit with work-style building, in order to consolidate the results of the study and education campaign on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. The piece has three parts. The first sets out what the formula means, drawing on Xi's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second surveys Party history from the founding through the Yan'an rectification, the early People's Republic and reform and opening up to the Xi era, to show that Party spirit has always been treated as the root of work style. The third sets out three practical requirements for the present. The core argument is that work style is the outward expression of Party spirit: inner conviction shows itself in conduct. Xu follows Xi in holding that the basic test of Party spirit is the distinction between public and private interest. Formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance are traced to wavering ideals, a distorted view of power and weak discipline, so the author says work style cannot be fixed case by case. Problems must be treated by going back to their ideological roots and by addressing Party spirit itself. The historical survey cites documents such as the Gutian Conference, Liu Shaoqi's On the Self-Cultivation of Communists and the 1941 Decision on Strengthening Party Spirit. Xu proposes three measures. Members should strengthen their ideals and convictions through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and regular self-examination. Intra-Party political life should be conducted seriously, with democratic life meetings and criticism and self-criticism. The spirit of the Party's self-reform should guide strict discipline, zero tolerance for breaches of the eight-point regulation and the "four forms" of discipline enforcement. The author presents this as a work-style guarantee for Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a clear example of how Party officials link work-style campaigns to Party spirit, with a short Party-history survey of that link.

Precision teaching in ideological and political theory courses based on knowledge graphs 基于知识图谱的思政课精准教学探析 Wang Jing Liu Dan Wang and Liu ask how knowledge graphs, a tool of educational digitalization, can make university ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke) more targeted and effective. Citing Minister of Education Huai Jinpeng's 2023 call to use learner profiles and educational knowledge graphs to teach students according to their aptitude, they argue that knowledge graphs, combined with algorithms and human–machine collaboration, empower precision teaching across three links: understanding students, supplying content and evaluating results. The article has three parts. The first explains why knowledge graphs suit precision teaching, noting that large, mixed-major classes and heavy teaching loads make traditional ways of knowing each student inadequate. The second sets out a construction framework and workflow, illustrated with the course Ethics and the Rule of Law. The third proposes three practical paths: profiling students, algorithmic resource recommendation, and real-time evaluation. The authors argue that a course graph must be built around the training objectives (the mission of cultivating moral character and talent) and organised around knowledge content (knowledge clusters, an ability bank and a question bank), relations among them, and mappings from objectives to abilities, questions and knowledge. Construction proceeds by fixing a knowledge framework with subject experts (five levels of knowledge points with prerequisite, successor and related links), developing and tagging teaching and assessment resources, and letting platform data adjust the links. In practice, multimodal analysis sorts student data into five dimensions (knowledge, emotion, ability, behaviour and thought) to generate profiles such as 'systematic consolidation', 'precise and efficient' and 'curious explorer', each paired with a teaching strategy. Entity recognition and relation extraction build the graph and drive recommendations. Online collaboration, multidimensional interaction and instant feedback, with examples from the May Fourth Movement and the War of Resistance against Japan, are said to support whole-process and whole-element evaluation. The authors conclude that knowledge graphs can renew teaching concepts and models, tailor courses to individual needs and promote students' all-round development. They call on teachers to diagnose students' knowledge and ability levels, customise learning paths, use algorithms to allocate resources and push content, and monitor online learning in real time. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-oriented account of how Chinese scholars propose to apply AI-based knowledge graphs and student profiling to political theory teaching.

Promoting high-quality development of socialist cultural-ethical advancement in the new era 推动新时代精神文明建设高质量发展 Feng Xiujun Feng Xiujun's commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts takes up the instruction Xi Jinping delivered at the national commendation conference on spiritual civilization construction held in Beijing on 23 May 2025. Xi called for high-quality development of this work so as to give strong spiritual force to building a strong country and to national rejuvenation. Feng argues that Xi's remarks have answered major theoretical and practical questions about the field and deepened the Party's understanding of its laws. The article has three parts. The first sets out why high-quality development of spiritual civilization matters. The second lists practical requirements under four headings: theoretical armament, cultural nourishment, integrated urban-rural development and fostering good social customs. The third describes a long-term mechanism built on Party leadership, coordination among agencies and society, and reform and innovation. On significance, Feng presents the coordination of material and spiritual civilization as a defining feature of Chinese modernization. In this account spiritual and cultural force works as a booster of the economy, a guide for political civilization and an adhesive for social harmony. Feng also points to problems such as lack of faith, distorted values, moral lapses and loss of good faith in some fields, and argues that only sustained effort can address them. On practice, the first task is to arm the whole Party and the public with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to build an ideology with strong cohesion. Feng also calls for cultivating core socialist values, strengthening ideals-and-convictions education, narrowing urban-rural gaps in public cultural services, and promoting moral models and family virtues. Feng concludes that the work is a long-term systemic project requiring steady effort. Feng calls for Party committees to hold leadership, management and discourse power over ideological work, for performance assessment of officials to include spiritual civilization results, and for a leadership system in which Party and government, civilization committees, departments and society each play a role. Feng also proposes using the internet, big data and artificial intelligence, and building a healthy online culture, especially for young people. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists present the aims, tasks and mechanisms of spiritual civilization work after the May 2025 conference.

Advancing the "Two Integrations" to consolidate cultural subjectivity 推进“两个结合”巩固文化主体性 Shang Zhixiao Shang Zhixiao asks how a Chinese "cultural subjectivity" was established and how it can be kept strong. The article, a commentary in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscript, answers that the Two Integrations are both the route by which the Chinese Communist Party built cultural subjectivity and the reliable guarantee for consolidating it. The Two Integrations are the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The piece has three sections. The first argues that the Two Integrations are the fundamental way of establishing cultural subjectivity. The second explains how each of the two integrations consolidates it. The third sets out three ways of deepening the Two Integrations in the present, drawing on Xi Jinping's statements and on Xi Jinping's thought on culture throughout. Shang presents cultural subjectivity as the basis on which a culture can lead and cohere. In the author's account, the Party took up the task of saving the nation in the semi-colonial, semi-feudal era and built a new "national, scientific and popular" culture on a socialist foundation. This process went together with finding the right development path. The first integration, Shang argues, secures the road and the material and institutional base on which culture rests. The second integration provides the cultural soil and the space for innovation: it makes Marxism Chinese and makes fine traditional culture modern, giving socialism with Chinese characteristics greater historical depth. Shang says the resulting culture neither cuts off tradition nor rejects foreign achievements. For the present, Shang calls for consolidating cultural subjectivity through three means. These are firm cultural confidence, which the author treats as the outward expression of cultural subjectivity; upholding fundamental principles while innovating, meaning commitment to Marxism, Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics alongside creative transformation of tradition; and openness and inclusiveness toward other civilizations' achievements. The aim is a new culture suited to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the Party's theorists link the Two Integrations to cultural subjectivity and cultural confidence in 2025.

Althusser's reconstruction of the "problematic" of Marx's epistemology and its limits 试论阿尔都塞重塑的马克思认识论“总问题”及其局限 Tan Yong Tan Yong examines Louis Althusser's attempt to reconstruct the epistemological "problematic" (总问题) of Marx's thought. Althusser formulated it as the question of which concepts and conceptual systems allow one to think the elements of a structure, their structural relations and the effects of that structure. Tan argues that this formulation is partly justified, because it fits Marx's texts and the logic of German classical philosophy, but that it cannot stand as Marx's fundamental problematic. The article has three parts. The first tests Althusser's formulation against Marx's texts, looking at the object of knowledge, the conceptual tools and the link between them. The second places it in a sequence running from Kant's "how is knowledge possible" to Hegel's "how is a scientific system of truth possible", and then to Althusser's question. The third sets out the limits. Tan draws on Adorno and Alfred Sohn-Rethel for much of the critique. In the first part, Tan argues that Marx treated capitalist society as a structured organism and built new concepts such as surplus value and the value form to analyse it. Marx's dialectical materialism and his method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete then tie these concepts to reality. In the second part, Tan reads Kant as limited by the transcendental subject and the subject–object model, and Hegel as idealist, minimising the human subject and ignoring society. On this reading, Althusser's question marks Marx's advance over both: it brings in history, society and structural thinking. In the third part, Tan names three limits. The question leaves out practice beyond "theoretical practice", meaning mental labour. It is confined to a structuralist way of thinking and so neglects the unity of the logical and the historical. And it does not address Marx's guiding principle that social being determines social consciousness. Tan holds that Sohn-Rethel's "real abstraction", with money as the bridge to abstract thought, answers this principle better. Tan concludes that Althusser's reconstruction widens the field of research on how Marx's epistemology broke with Kant and Hegel. In Tan's view, it commits the error of taking a part for the whole, and the true problematic of Marx's epistemology still needs further study. Read the original if you work on Althusser, Marx's relation to German classical philosophy, or Sohn-Rethel's real abstraction and want a Chinese critique of structuralist readings of Capital.

On Daniel Brudney's normative interpretation of alienation in the young Marx 论布鲁德尼对青年马克思异化问题的规范性阐释 Zhang Zuliao Zhang Zuliao examines Daniel Brudney's reading of alienation in the young Marx. Brudney does not deny the traditional historical-materialist view that changing the mode of production is the basic route to overcoming alienation.
