He adds a normative claim: the degree to which alienation is overcome should measure the justice of a society. Brudney justifies this claim through a Rawlsian method, reflective equilibrium. Zhang argues that the justification fails at key points. Reflective equilibrium cannot work as a self-sufficient method, and Brudney's conception of the person as "concern" is metaphysical. On this account the project ends in the foundationalism Rawls opposed. The article has four parts. The first reconstructs Brudney's reordering of the four determinations of alienated labour in the 1844 Manuscripts. The second sets out his idea of mutual concern and "structural friendship", drawing on the Comments on James Mill. The third explains how Rawls's constructivist framework, the original position joined with reflective equilibrium, is supposed to keep a conception of the person open to revision. The fourth part assesses Brudney's use of it. Zhang takes Rawls's own constructivism as the benchmark for judging whether Brudney's justification works. Zhang reports that Brudney puts alienation from labouring activity first, ahead of alienation from the product. In this reading alienation becomes a failure of relations between subjects, in which people produce "for" one another and for the species. Brudney also rejects the assumption that communism requires the overcoming of material scarcity. Zhang then argues that in Rawls reflective equilibrium operates only inside a wider structure. The conception of the person there is distilled from public political culture and stays provisional. Brudney has no original position and does not say what the "features" of time, place and culture are. His conception of concern is derived from a metaphysical notion of human nature, so it cannot be revised by reflection. Brudney himself concedes that readers "must find a given conception of the person". Zhang concludes that Brudney's scheme produces only limited "reflection" without real "equilibrium". It is a weakly constructivist foundationalism, which may explain his preference for the young Marx over the mature one. Zhang still credits the attempt with restoring a normative dimension to the young Marx that had been greatly underestimated. Zhang adds that even refined reflective equilibrium introduces historicity only to a limited degree. How a normative standard can be joined with historical materialism remains, in Zhang's view, a task for Marx studies and political philosophy. Read the original if you work on the normative reading of Marx, on alienation, or on Rawls–Marx comparisons and want a detailed internal critique of Brudney's method.

Unifying the yardstick of government conduct to advance the building of a unified national market 统一政府行为尺度推进全国统一大市场建设 Wang Tinghui In this commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, Wang Tinghui asks how to remove the obstacles that block a unified national market. Citing Xi Jinping's formula of "five unifications and one opening", Wang argues that obstacles such as impeded factor flows, local protectionism and market fragmentation largely stem from inconsistent conduct by local governments, differing policy standards and deviations in implementation. The article sets out three groups of measures: establishing institutional standards for government conduct, building cross-regional and cross-departmental coordination, and strengthening supervision along the whole chain of government action. Each group is broken into three sub-measures. On standards, Wang proposes a unified negative list for policy-making covering market access, subsidies, tax breaks and financing, with fairness and legality review of local rules. Wang also calls for national standards for public resource trading to end "local preference" and for enforcement guidelines that narrow discretion and ensure like cases receive like penalties. On coordination, Wang proposes policy coordination among provinces, starting with pilots in Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, the Yangtze River Delta and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Wang also urges departmental coordination lists and a shift in local performance evaluation away from GDP and investment attraction towards market integration, with a "one-vote veto" for regions practising market fragmentation. On supervision, Wang advocates a national big-data monitoring platform combined with reporting channels for firms, graded correction by higher authorities, and an accountability measure that reaches local leaders, balanced by policy incentives for regions that perform well. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented account of how Chinese scholars propose to discipline local government behaviour in building the unified national market.

Breaking structural barriers to curb "involutionary" competition 以打破结构性壁垒整治“内卷式”竞争 Ling Yongnhui Ling Yongnhui's commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks why "involutionary" competition (neijuan) has spread in some traditional and emerging Chinese industries, and how to remedy it. Ling defines it as excessive competition in which disorder in the market pushes competition costs far above returns. The thesis is that, in institutional-economics terms, the key cause is a structural contradiction between administrative barriers that are too high and market barriers that are too low. The piece first explains how such competition arises, then sets out remedies. Ling treats it as a problem that must be cleared away in building a unified national market, because it squeezes firm profits and, in Ling's account, can feed a vicious chain from lower profits to weaker incomes, insufficient demand and surplus capacity. Ling traces two paths. In the first, high administrative barriers, vertical (state control over factor allocation) and horizontal (local protectionism and local industrial policy), block firms from upgrading and from exiting, so they compete passively on price. In the second, low market barriers draw many firms into low-end sectors, where they imitate rather than innovate and keep industry concentration low, so competition is active but destructive. The remedy follows the principle of "establishing and breaking in parallel": subtract from administrative barriers and add to market barriers. To subtract, Ling proposes shifting industrial policy towards consumer-side subsidies and upstream innovation, extending cross-regional fair-competition review to local investment incentives, and reforming taxation so that consumption taxes become a stable local revenue source. To add, Ling proposes higher national and industry standards, tighter control of new capacity, support for mergers led by leading firms, and stronger industry self-discipline and credit systems. Read the original if you want a concise policy-oriented account of how a Chinese economist links anti-involution measures to the unified national market.

A critique of the technological positing (Gestell-like "setting-up") of digital capitalism 数字资本主义的技术摆置批判 Xie Yazhou Xie Yazhou asks how capitalism "sets up" human society through technology, and what is distinctive about this under digital capitalism. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, Xie argues that the "artificial intelligence" promoted by digital capitalism is a technological imaginary that leaves no room for the daily labour through which people build their lifeworld, and that it is an expression of capitalism's inherent technological force. The short essay begins from the commodity as Marx described it, then moves to the structure of capitalist production, and finally to the digital stage. It draws on Marx, Kant and Gilbert Simondon, and on the idea of a "real abstraction" in commodity exchange. Xie's central claim is that capitalism sustains itself not by producing ever more commodities but by maintaining a "world of things" through which its synthetic, abstract mechanism operates. Value turns relations between people into relations between things, so capitalism rests on a thing-to-thing structure (inter-objectivity) rather than a subject-to-subject one (inter-subjectivity). Digital technology, in Xie's account, turns all objects and subjects into code. It lets capitalism posit things at a higher level and become a self-planning "transcendental subject". On this basis Xie says daily life now depends more on phones and data identities than on trust or love. Xie concludes that the world planned and posited by this "transcendental subject" is a world of things, not a human one, and that the key task is to return the world to human beings. Read the original if you want a short, philosophically oriented Marxist critique of AI and digital capitalism that combines commodity theory with Kantian and Simondonian ideas.

Digital capitalism: intertwined transformation and predicament 变革与困境交织的数字资本主义 Shi Pu This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how digital capitalism should be understood and criticised with Marxist tools. Shi argues that it is the capitalism of the information age, not a rupture with capitalism's tradition. It releases productive potential while deepening economic polarisation, alienated labour and governance problems. The piece has three parts: the historical emergence of digital capitalism, a historical-materialist critique of it, and the practical predicaments it produces. It draws on Marx's remarks on historical economic forms, on production in general, and on the Rhodes passage, and gives examples from platform work. In Shi's account, data, platforms and algorithms are absorbed into capital's valorisation and accumulation. The logic of capital, the wage-labour position of workers and the tendency towards new inequality are therefore unchanged. The article claims that the digital mode of production is a historical product, that "general data" plays the role Marx assigned to production in general, and that platforms are a shell through which capital controls global industrial chains that still depend on the real economy. Shi identifies three predicaments: users produce data but cannot control it or share in its returns; the anarchy of production deepens through algorithmic opacity and weak regulation; and both wealth polarisation and worker impoverishment intensify. For the latter two, the article cites figures on the market share of the top ten technology firms and on the wealth share of the bottom half of humanity. Shi concludes that criticism must return to the material basis of production, expose "digital fetishism" and break data monopolies so that technology serves human liberation rather than capital accumulation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies classical categories to platforms, data and gig labour.

Contemporary Western digital capitalism in the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域中的当代西方数字资本主义 Lan Jiang This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how contemporary Western digital capitalism should be understood. Lan argues that it is not merely capitalism applying a new tool. In Lan's account, digital, network and intelligent technologies have produced a new mode of capitalist control, exercised through digital platforms that allocate production factors and govern the circuit of accumulation. Lan calls for a return to historical materialism and the critique of political economy. The piece moves through three headings: changes in the factors of production, the transformation of the mode of production, and platforms and the new monopoly. It sets digital capitalism against earlier industrial and finance capitalism, drawing on Marx's Capital and on the work of Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean. Lan's central claim is that data and computing power have joined land, labour-power, capital and credit as factors that decide whether firms survive. Just as banks gained control through credit rating in the late nineteenth century, platforms now do so through data, traffic and computing power, integrating individual firms into platform-run industrial chains. Lan also contends that digital capitalism leaves wage labour in place but turns stable employment into gig and outsourced work, so that firms shed the legal protections and workers bear the risks. A few giant platforms, in this reading, become monopolies above both workers and industrial capitalists, and Lan notes that Varoufakis and Dean call this 'technofeudalism', which they treat as a metaphor. Lan concludes that Marx's intellectual legacy still has analytical force and that historical materialism and the critique of political economy remain tools for analysing and criticising digital capitalism. The piece ends with Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force once it grips the masses. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist framing of platform capitalism and its link to the technofeudalism debate.

The Five-Year Plans as a relay advancing the process of Chinese modernization “五年规划”接力推进中国式现代化进程 Zhang Guanzi Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, Zhang Guanzi asks what the Five-Year Plans reveal about the Chinese Communist Party's leadership and about the institutional advantages of Chinese governance. The author argues that continuous five-year planning is a distinctive Chinese model of national governance, and that it works as the key mechanism for both driving and measuring Chinese modernization. The commentary is framed as groundwork for carrying out the coming 15th Five-Year Plan. The piece is a short commentary in four sections. It first traces the origin of the plans from the First Five-Year Plan of 1953 to the shift to the term "five-year plan" (规划) from the 11th plan. It then describes how plans are drafted and promulgated, how they embody a people-centred approach to development, and how they secure long-term strategic stability while allowing dynamic adjustment. Zhang's central claim is that the plans combine scientific and democratic procedure with Party leadership. Drafting is described as a closed loop of investigation, scientific verification, consultation and legal enactment, with top-down coordination and bottom-up participation. The author calls Party leadership the single most fundamental lesson of plan-making. Poverty alleviation serves as the main example: it ran as a priority from the 11th to the 13th plans, became a binding target in the 13th plan, and shows how a "goal guidance, resource coordination, coordinated execution" system mobilises national resources. Zhang also argues that targets link successive plans to the "three-step" strategy and the Two Centenary Goals, that approval by the National People's Congress gives plans legal force, and that mid-term evaluation, annual plans and emergency adjustments let plans adapt without abandoning long-term aims. Zhang concludes that the plans' continuity, legal backing and flexibility, a unity of "strategic resolve" and "tactical vitality", make them an important methodology for steady progress in Chinese modernization, which is presented as a dynamic process rather than a fixed blueprint. The author also holds that plans measure success by people's sense of gain, happiness and security rather than by growth rates alone. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic account of how the Five-Year Plan system is explained and justified as the 15th Five-Year Plan approaches.

Unwaveringly following the path of ecological priority and green development 坚定不移走生态优先绿色发展之路 Han Bin This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in October 2025, asks how China should handle the relationship between economic growth and environmental protection now that its economy has moved from high-speed growth to high-quality development. Han Bin argues that Xi Jinping's call to follow the path of ecological priority and green development is a theoretically grounded break with conventional growth models. The author presents it as the direction for high-quality development and long-term national competitiveness. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical logic of the path, the second reviews practical results since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and the third outlines tasks for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, following the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025). Evidence comes from policy documents issued in 2024 and 2025 and from statistics on emissions and energy. In the theoretical section, Han presents the path as a development of Marxist ideas on the dialectical unity of humans and nature and of production and ecology. The author contrasts it with a Western modernization model described as capital-centred, materialist and based on pollution first, cleanup later. Han describes the shift as one from instrumental to value rationality, with ecological protection a priority in economic decisions and well-being rather than GDP as the goal. The article cites progress such as the 'new three' export industries (new-energy vehicles, lithium batteries, photovoltaics) and the 2024 fall in carbon dioxide emissions per 10,000 yuan of GDP of 3.4 per cent. It also cites a non-fossil share of energy consumption of 19.8 per cent and coal power below 40 per cent of installed capacity. Han calls for three further steps: stronger ecological protection and restoration, with zoning-based controls and integrated management of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts; greener and lower-carbon urban and rural construction; and cautious but steady progress towards the carbon peak before 2030 and carbon neutrality before 2060. Concrete proposals include carbon-intensity targets, local assessment systems and product carbon footprint management. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary links Marxist theory, new quality productive forces and the 15th Five-Year Plan agenda to green transition policy.

An action guide for the green transformation of the development model 推动发展方式绿色转型的行动指南 Jian Xiaowen This commentary, published in Economic Daily on 29 October 2025, takes up the question of how the green development concept can guide the shift of China's development model. Jian Xiaowen argues that green development, as one element of the new development philosophy, is the 'underlying colour' of high-quality development and supplies a basic guideline and action guide for the comprehensive green transformation of economy and society. The piece takes its cue from the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), which called for accelerating that transformation and building a beautiful China. The article has three parts. The first draws lessons from home and abroad, the second looks at meeting the people's need for a fine ecological environment, and the third sets out how to move the development model towards green and low-carbon forms. It refers to China's reform-era record, to the Western 'pollute first, clean up later' path and the 'eight major pollution incidents', and to green manufacturing strategies in the United States, Japan, Europe, India and Brazil. Jian's core reasoning is that the concept answers both historical and present conditions. In the author's account, China's extensive growth model produced air, water and soil pollution and unsustainable patterns, while the Western path imposed heavy costs and shows what to avoid. Rising popular expectations have moved from 'having enough' to 'having good', so ecological quality is both a livelihood and a political matter. Jian also contends that green development drives industrial upgrading by writing ecological benefits into evaluation systems and encouraging green consumption, and that new quality productive forces are by nature green productive forces, so that greenness should be a test of them. Jian calls for applying the green concept across production, distribution, circulation and consumption. Proposed measures include pollution control, ecological compensation between protected and benefiting regions, market trading and clearer ecological rights, realising the value of ecological products, green-oriented assessment systems, fiscal, financial and pricing policy support, and public education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links green development to high-quality development, new quality productive forces and the people-centred approach after the Fourth Plenum.

Making vigorous innovation cities a priority 着力建设富有活力的创新城市 Zhou Lin This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the call, made at the Central Conference on Urban Work in Beijing in July 2025, to build "vigorous innovation cities". Zhou Lin argues that innovation is the main engine of urban modernization and that cities, as the places where innovation clusters, have become the main arena of global competition. Building such cities is presented as both an internal requirement of high-quality development and a strategic choice for national competitive advantage. The article has two parts. The first sets out the contemporary meaning of an innovation city under three headings: a people-centred stance, a systems-integration orientation, and the fusion of humanistic and technological values. The second proposes coordinated action along five dimensions: innovation resources, innovation space, innovation scenarios, innovation services and innovation culture. Zhou draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on the "people's city" and on systems thinking. In Zhou's account, the people's city idea means an innovation system in which everyone takes part and shares the results. The systems orientation calls for top-level design that lets knowledge, technology, talent and capital flow freely and links basic research to industrial application. The five dimensions carry the practical proposals. For resources, Zhou proposes innovation consortia led by leading technology firms and regional city-cluster mechanisms. For space, the proposals are stronger innovation capacity in development zones, mission-list and "open competition" models for key technologies, and land-use flexibility. For scenarios, new technologies would be applied in urban renewal. For services, Zhou offers full-lifecycle support for innovators, science-and-technology finance with "patient capital", and integrated services for talent. For culture, the author advocates tolerance of failure, science education in schools, and drawing on traditional Chinese culture. Zhou concludes that an innovation city is a multi-level, multi-actor systems project that has to be adapted to each city's circumstances. The author holds that technology should be guided by humanistic spirit, with socialist core values and traditional Chinese virtues informing frontier innovation, rather than following a logic of technological supremacy. Read the original if you want a concise outline of the policy measures that urban innovation is expected to involve after the July 2025 Central Conference on Urban Work.

Grasping in depth the thesis that "the essence of modernization is the modernization of people" 深刻把握“现代化的本质是人的现代化” Zhang Ruifen This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 29 October 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that "the essence of modernization is the modernization of people". Zhang Ruifen argues that the formulation gives people a foundational place in Chinese modernization. In the author's reading it identifies the fundamental force behind that project and sets its value direction. The article sets out the thesis's core meaning, its value and the practical routes for carrying it out. The text has three parts. The first explains the core meaning. The second sets out the theoretical, historical and practical grounds for the thesis. The third proposes ways to advance the modernization of people within Chinese modernization. It draws on Xi Jinping's speeches, Marx's Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, and examples such as poverty alleviation, rural revitalization and the common prosperity demonstration zones. Zhang's central move is to treat people as the fundamental driver, the ultimate purpose and the core yardstick of modernization. People's changing needs, skills and rights propel change in industry and institutions. The aim is their free and all-round development, not material abundance as such. Progress is judged by whether people's ideas, abilities and rights match a modern society. The author then gives three grounds. The thesis develops Marx's theory of free and all-round human development. It is said to transcend the alienation found in capital-centred Western modernization. It also responds to the principal contradiction of the new era, which the author breaks down into mismatches of supply and demand, unequal resource distribution and gaps in capabilities. For practice, Zhang calls for carrying out the strategic plans for Chinese modernization, including industrial upgrading, education and science reform, employment and public-service equalization, and household registration and social security reform. Zhang also wants rising needs and skills to feed back into growth through new consumption, lifelong learning and wider participation in grassroots governance. A third proposal is a mutual-reinforcement mechanism. It would add indicators of people's modernization to evaluation systems, monitor changing needs and keep a people-centred orientation. The author says this would form a closed loop in which strategy supports people's development and people empower the strategy. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link Xi Jinping's formulation to Marx's theory of human development and to policy proposals.

Chen Yun's thinking and contribution on "how to be a Communist Party member" during the War of Resistance 全民族抗战时期陈云对“怎样做一个共产党员”的思考和贡献 Xiong Qiuliang How should a Communist Party member behave? Xiong Qiuliang takes up this question through the work of Chen Yun, who headed the Party's Organization Department during the war against Japan. Xiong argues that Chen's essay "How to Be a Communist Party Member" (30 May 1939) gave a theoretically and practically sound answer. In Xiong's account the essay grew out of the pressures of rapid Party expansion and became a key document for building the membership. The article notes that earlier studies mainly examine the content, features and influence of Chen's six standards for members, and sets out to examine the historical background, the development of his thinking and its distinctive features. It has four parts: the background of fast membership growth after 1937; Chen's step-by-step thinking from 1938 to 1939; a reading of the essay itself; and its three main characteristics. Xiong traces how the Central Committee's 1938 decision to recruit members on a large scale (membership reportedly passed 500,000 by the end of 1938) brought problems of quantity over quality and of petty-bourgeois social composition. Chen's response developed through speeches and drafts: "How to Be a Revolutionary", the Qu Qiubai memorial talk, his proposed oath, the memo on north-west Shanxi, and the case of Liu Ligong, expelled for refusing a Party assignment. The essay covers qualifications, social composition, procedures, probationary members and six standards: lifelong struggle for communism, revolutionary interests above all, discipline and secrecy, tenacious execution of decisions, serving as a model for the masses, and study. Xiong identifies three features: a problem-oriented approach, emphasis on members' political character, and a systematic set of entry conditions and norms. Xiong concludes that Chen combined Marxist-Leninist requirements for members, Mao Zedong's ideas on Party building and the wartime situation. In this reading, the six standards enriched Mao's Party-building doctrine, were included among 22 required documents in the Yan'an rectification movement, and remain relevant. Xiong ends by calling for continued strict control of entry and attention to members' worldview, to support Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the sources, drafts and case that shaped a foundational Party-building text of the Yan'an period.

The Communist Party of China's early explorations of the peasant movement in 1924 一九二四年中国共产党对农民运动的早期探索 Cui Jing Cui Jing asks how the Communist Party of China moved, between its Third Congress in 1923 and its Fourth Congress in January 1925, from adopting a resolution on the peasant question without much follow-through to raising the worker–peasant alliance. The article argues that 1924 was the year of this "key leap" in understanding. Early exploration of the peasant movement in that year supplied both the theoretical possibility and the practical basis for the shift. Drawing largely on the Chronicle of the Communist Party of China (New-Democratic Revolution period, 1924 volume), the article first sets out the background: earlier peasant organisations at Yanqian, Haifeng and Hengshan, and the first Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. It then examines three areas: early theoretical discussion of the peasant question; the creation of institutions to train peasant-movement cadres; and early practice in Guangdong, Hunan, Hubei and Anhui. On theory, Cui reports that Zhou Enlai, Deng Zhongxia, Zhang Tailei, Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and Chen Tanqiu described the peasantry as a huge, impoverished and inherently revolutionary force. They saw the movement as still at a "budding" stage, with aims such as rent reduction, abolition of surcharges and the formation of peasant associations and armed self-defence. Cui notes that the Party still placed this force within the national revolution against imperialism and warlords, and had not yet fully stated its own leading role. On cadres, the Guangzhou Peasant Movement Training Institute, run under Kuomintang–Communist cooperation with Peng Pai as director of the first class, combined revolutionary theory, agricultural knowledge and military training. Similar schools were set up in Hunan and Hainan. On practice, Guangdong's movement grew through Party-led associations and self-defence forces, backed by armed support in the Guangning conflict. Elsewhere the Party used branches, peasant study societies and rural surveys, adapting its methods to local conditions. Cui concludes that by the end of 1924 the Party's theoretical understanding had deepened, its experience had grown and its methods had diversified, though no theoretical consensus existed and regional development was uneven. The author also credits the period with experience in cadre training. Read the original if you study early CPC history, the origins of the worker–peasant alliance, or the Kuomintang–Communist united front and peasant cadre training.

The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the nation-wide War of Resistance 中国共产党是全民族抗战的中流砥柱 Zhang Taiyuan Zhang Taiyuan takes up the question of what role the Communist Party of China played in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan, which the article calls the first completely victorious national liberation struggle in modern Chinese history. The thesis is that the victory was a victory of the whole nation and that the Party acted as its "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu), providing direction, unity, military strength and moral example. The article is organised in four sections, each ending with a lesson for the present. They cover the Party's overall resistance line and strategy of protracted war; its promotion and defence of the anti-Japanese national united front; guerrilla warfare, the battlefields behind enemy lines and the base areas; and the heroism of Party members and the spirit of resistance. Evidence comes from Party documents, Mao Zedong's writings, statements by Xi Jinping, campaign statistics and accounts of individual heroes. Zhang argues first that the Party was the earliest to call for armed resistance and set the course through the Luochuan Conference (1937) and Mao's On Protracted War (1938), which relied on mobilising the masses. Second, the Party was the initiator and firm defender of the united front, maintaining it even after the Southern Anhui Incident. Third, citing figures, Zhang says that in the stage of strategic stalemate the Party-led rear battlefields faced 58 to 62 per cent of Japanese forces in China and almost all puppet troops. The article reports that Party-led forces fought over 125,000 engagements, killed or captured about 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops and built 19 base areas. It then presents martyrs such as Yang Jingyu, the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain and Deng Yufen as embodiments of patriotism and resolve. Zhang concludes that the Party's political programme, firm will and exemplary conduct sustained the nation's hope and forged a great spirit of resistance. The lessons drawn are to uphold the Party's overall leadership, consolidate the broadest patriotic united front, rely on the people, and use the spirit of resistance to advance Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-centred account of the War of Resistance is presented in a Central Party School publication, including its figures and exemplary stories.

The War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression: the historical turning point on the road to the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 抗日战争：中华民族走向伟大复兴的历史转折点 Zhang Hao Writing in Modern Chinese History Studies (2025, no. 4), Zhang Hao asks why the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (1931–45) should be seen as the turning point from national crisis to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that the victory ended imperialist powers' free seizure of Chinese territory, established China's standing as a major country, and set the direction for the new China. Zhang presents this as the fundamental precondition for national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Japan's long-prepared plan to conquer China, in two phases: seizing the islands and territories around the mainland from 1879 to the Russo-Japanese War, then the stepwise path from the Mukden Incident to the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 1937. The second part examines why war was unavoidable and what kind of war it was. The third sets out four respects in which the victory marked a turning point. Zhang's core argument draws on Japanese official statements, Mao Zedong's wartime writings and Party documents. Japan's declared national goals and its 'peace' terms of 1935 and 1937 are read as demands that China become a colony, so that negotiation could not succeed. The war is therefore characterised, following Mao, as a national revolutionary war of survival and liberation, which even the Nationalists called a necessary stage towards national revival. The four aspects of the turning point are: the first complete victory over a foreign invader after a century of defeats; a major contribution to the world anti-fascist war, with China as the Eastern main theatre; the Communist Party's role as the 'mainstay' (zhongliu dizhu), which Zhang says made it the natural leader of rejuvenation; and the emergence of a prototype of the new China. Zhang concludes that the victory restored national self-confidence, overcame the 'fear of Japan' and prepared the ground for the People's Republic and the socialist system. The war is presented as opening a new era in the history of the Chinese revolution and in the course of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a Chinese-historiographical account of the war that links it to the Party's leadership and to the rejuvenation narrative, with many quotations from Mao and from Japanese wartime sources.

An analysis of the distinctive advantages that allow the Communist Party of China to carry out self-reform courageously 中国共产党勇于自我革命的独特优势论析 Wu Bo Xi Jinping has called the courage for self-reform the Party's most distinctive trait and greatest strength. Wu Bo asks not why or how the Party should carry out self-reform, but why it is able to do so. The article's answer is that the Party's practical experience, traditions and spirit have formed a set of advantages. Wu describes these as the rational development and use of the Party's own resources, and argues that they must keep being exploited if the Party is to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wu identifies six advantages: political (comprehensive Party leadership), value-based (selflessness), ideological (upholding fundamental principles while innovating), organisational (a tight structure and a capable cadre corps), disciplinary, and institutional (the system of governing a large party). Each is traced through four periods: the new-democratic revolution, the socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Each is illustrated with statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, and with key Party documents. Wu makes three main moves. First, the Party is said to have no special interests of its own, and this selflessness, together with its founding mission, its commitment to correcting errors and its pursuit of advanced and pure character, supplies the courage and motive for self-reform. Second, self-reform is said to rest on centralised and unified leadership by the Central Committee, democratic centralism, the Two Upholds, and a tight organisational system. It also draws on Marxism adapted to China, on traditional Chinese culture and on the Party's revolutionary spirit. For traditional culture, the author cites concern for hardship, the idea of treating illness before it appears, and the ideal of inner sageliness and outer kingliness. Third, the author argues that discipline education, the unity of Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline, and a system of Party regulations, internal supervision and inspection tours turn these advantages into practice. Wu says this system answers the difficult problem of self-supervision for a long-ruling party, and contrasts it with bourgeois parties and the Soviet party. Wu concludes that a strong Marxist party is forged through self-reform, and that pushing the Party's great self-reform through to the end requires analysing its inherent advantages as well as its necessity and methods. The author calls for continued development of these resources, so that self-reform stays "always on the road" and the Party keeps to the forefront of the times. The article is a Party-history and Party-building study that presents the Party's historical record largely in affirmative terms. Read the original if you want a systematic, period-by-period account of how Chinese Party scholarship explains the Party's capacity for self-reform and the sources it cites for each advantage.

The "xinxue" of Communists: the "inner sage" learning of Marxists' self-reform 共产党人的“心学”：马克思主义者自我革命的“内圣”之学 Wu Wenxin Xi Jinping has called Party-spirit education the "xinxue" ("learning of the mind-heart") of Communists and placed it within the Party's "self-reform". Wu Wenxin asks what this Communist xinxue is and how it differs from the Neo-Confucian tradition of Wang Yangming. The article argues that it is a Marxist-faith learning, in which cultivating an "inner sage" disposition of wholehearted devotion serves the "outer king" task of serving the people. The article is published in Taishan Journal (2025, no. 3). It has four parts. It first names the key terms of Communist xinxue and traces its cultural source to Wang Yangming. It then treats xinxue as the study of Marxist belief and sets out its content. Next it lists five ways in which it claims to surpass traditional xinxue. Finally it applies the method to Party history study and education. Wu reads Wang's "extending innate knowing" and "unity of knowing and acting" as Party-spirit self-awareness and unity of knowing and acting. On this reading, the Party's purpose of wholeheartedly serving the people is itself a Communist "inner sage and outer king": wholeheartedness is inner cultivation and self-reform, and serving the people is the outward work of social revolution. The author says Communist xinxue differs from the traditional kind in five ways. It is thoroughly materialist, since it rests on the materiality of consciousness. It is a xinxue of the people, extended to the roughly 99 million Party members. It stresses social practice over withdrawal. It is spiral rather than cyclical in its self-reform. And it is oriented to communist values rather than to personal sagehood or religious salvation. For practice, Wu takes Xi's formula of unifying study, thought and application, and of knowing, believing and acting. Learning and thinking must be combined, thought must lead to application, knowledge must turn into belief, and belief into action. Wu concludes that Party history education and other regular Party-spirit cultivation are all forms of practising this xinxue. In Wu's account, study is the means, thought the key and application the aim, while knowledge is the carrier, belief the core and action the destination. The author warns that knowledge not turned into belief leads to corruption and "two-faced" officials. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school scholar draws on Wang Yangming's thought to frame Party-spirit education and self-reform.

Human–machine collaboration under large-model production and changes in the labour process of digital capitalism 大模型生产下的人机协作与数字资本主义劳动过程变迁 Huang Zaisheng Huang Zaisheng asks whether human–machine collaboration in the era of large-model (generative AI) production, which digital capital presents as a reconciliation of humans and machines, is freeing workers from digital servitude. Drawing on labour process theory and Marx's political economy, the article argues that such collaboration is essentially the latest round of capital's \"accelerated mechanisation\" to raise labour productivity. It contends that the supposed \"re-humanisation\" of work is an ideological gloss, and that collaboration brings a distinctive form of deskilling. The article is organised in four parts. The first traces how collaboration emerged and takes three practical forms: intelligent assistants, \"digital employees\" and general-purpose AI agents, followed by its dynamic evolution. The second examines the \"re-humanisation\" narrative in three respects: work content, free time and the results of labour. The third analyses four mechanisms of deskilling: substitution of mental labour, the erosion of the skill premium, a paradox in generating complex cognitive ability, and over-reliance on AI. A short conclusion follows. Huang draws on empirical studies such as a call-centre study and creative-writing experiments. Huang's first move is to read the collaboration narrative as a new way of manufacturing consent. Digital capital promises to relieve workers of repetitive tasks, yet still needs cheap global labour for data cleaning and algorithm supervision, which the author calls \"ghost work\". Citing Marx on free time, Huang argues that capital turns freed time into surplus labour and that gains in productivity accrue to capital rather than to workers, who face \"time poverty\" and dependence on platforms. The second move concerns deskilling. AI tools level performance between novices and experts, which dissolves the skill premium. Heavy use of digital employees also cuts off the practice through which complex cognitive abilities develop. Because large models statistically recombine existing knowledge, over-reliance dulls creativity and could lead to \"model collapse\". Huang concludes that human–machine collaboration raises the productivity of digital capital and produces an unprecedented \"digital prosperity\", while knowledge workers suffer deeper deskilling beneath a surface of humanised conditions. Even if workers became \"cyborgs\", the human–machine hybrid would remain an object of extraction as long as capital controls the key means of production for large models. The author expects workers to become \"digital poor\" and the biggest losers of the AI wave. Read the original if you want a Marxist labour-process critique of generative AI that draws on recent empirical studies of workplace AI use.")

New conditions, new tactics and new developments in the US communist movement: an interview with Haz Al-Din, executive chairman of the American Communist Party (ACP) 美国共产主义运动的新形势、新策略和新发展——美国共产党(ACP)执行主席哈兹·阿尔丁访谈 Haz Al-Din Feng Jiaxin This is an interview, conducted by Feng Jiaxin, a doctoral student at Peking University's School of Marxism, with Haz Al-Din, first executive chairman of the American Communist Party (ACP). The ACP was formed in 2024 by members who left the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) around its 32nd National Convention. The interview asks how the new party understands its origins, strategy and place in the US left, and how it views China. The questions fall into three parts: the background to the ACP's founding and its differences from the CPUSA; its theory and practice, covering elections, Trump's second term, labour and welfare policy, inequality, digital organising, anti-communism, other left groups, foreign contacts and five-year goals; and its views on China's achievements. Al-Din answers at length on each topic. Al-Din says the CPUSA has become a dependent adjunct of the Democratic Party and, in his words, a revisionist body, whereas the ACP stresses practice, discipline and 'socialist patriotism'. He criticises the US left, including the Democratic Socialists of America, for sectarianism and for losing touch with working people. The ACP does not expect to win the presidency. It aims to build local authority and survive an anticipated constitutional crisis, through community service, labour support and cooperatives. Its programme includes debt cancellation, nationalised banking and key industries, and five-year-plan-style coordination. Al-Din argues that Trump is unintentionally accelerating the decline of US hegemony. On China, Al-Din calls it the most advanced socialist country and a model the ACP cites to Americans. He praises Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Chinese modernization as dialectical and long-term, in contrast with a Western modernization driven by private profit. For the next five years the ACP seeks financial self-sufficiency, local footholds and the public standing the DSA has today. Read the original if you want a first-hand account of a new US communist party's strategy and of how its leader reads China, shown in a Chinese journal.

Laying a solid cultural foundation for building a strong country and national rejuvenation 筑牢强国建设、民族复兴的文化根基 Li Yi Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 15), Li Yi takes up Xi Jinping's statement that building a culturally strong country bears on Chinese modernization as a whole, on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and on international competitiveness. Li argues that this task requires adherence to Party leadership, to the path of socialist cultural development with Chinese characteristics and to Marxism as the guiding ideology. It also requires rooting culture in Chinese civilisation, so as to strengthen the people's spiritual strength. The piece is organised around three qualities that Li says must be consolidated: the subjectivity (zhutixing) of Chinese culture, the leading role of Marxism as the "soul" that activates traditional culture as the "root", and the independence of "firmly walking our own path". Li draws on Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, passages from Marx, Engels and Li Dazhao, and examples such as the Liuchi Lane approach to grassroots governance, the listing of Beijing's Central Axis as a World Heritage Site, and the animated film Ne Zha 2. In the first section, Li presents the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, as an expression of cultural and spiritual subjectivity. Without it, Li says, a nation cannot treat its own or other cultures correctly. In the second, Li holds that Marxism and traditional culture suit each other and enrich each other, so that the Party must neither abandon Marxism nor forget its cultural roots. Li contends that this approach goes beyond the old "ti-yong" (substance–function) relationship and resolves the long dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, which Li sees in both wholesale Westernisation and cultural restorationism. In the third section, Li describes the cultural achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), lists remaining challenges, and says culture must be built for and by the people. Li concludes that cultural strength depends on self-reliant spiritual independence, a people-centred orientation and a large body of cultural talent. Li holds that this is compatible with openness and mutual learning among civilisations, and rejects what the author calls Western theories of a "clash of civilisations" and "civilisational superiority". The task, in Li's account, is to cultivate socialist culture with Chinese characteristics for a new era. Read the original if you want a senior Central Party School official's account of how the Second Integration and cultural subjectivity are framed in Party discourse on building a culturally strong country.

An important lesson of the Party's self-reform in the new era Advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party by starting with conduct 新时代党的自我革命一条重要经验 Li Neng The article takes up a statement by Xi Jinping on 30 June 2025, at a Politburo study session, that advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party by starting with conduct (zuofeng) is an important lesson of the Party's self-reform in the new era. Li Neng, an executive vice-president of the Jiangxi Provincial Party School, argues that this formulation reveals the inherent links between conduct building, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform. The author calls on readers to grasp its origins, content and practical path. The piece has three parts. The first traces where the lesson comes from, the second explains what it means, and the third sets out how to uphold and apply it. It is a Party-school commentary built around Xi's own formulations, with little outside evidence, and it focuses on the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In explaining the origins, Li names three sources: the practical innovation of implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, which the author says broke a series of long-standing bad practices; institutional innovation in building a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; and theoretical innovation in understanding self-reform, including Xi's claim that self-reform is the Party's second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. On content, Li lists Xi's "five adherences": setting iron rules, leading from the top beginning with the Politburo, targeting the "four malpractices" with campaigns and special rectifications, sustained and detailed effort, and treating Party spirit, conduct and discipline as one whole in which conduct, discipline and anti-corruption work are linked. For application, Li proposes four requirements. The first is to strengthen Party spirit through theoretical study, intra-Party political life and the Party's mass line. The second is to regulate the exercise of power, with a proper view of power, clear authorisation and checks, and a system of rules centred on democratic centralism. The third is to use strict supervision and discipline, including handling conduct problems and corruption together. The fourth is to fulfil Party-governance responsibilities through accountability. Li presents all of this as safeguarding Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present conduct building as the entry point for Party discipline and self-reform.

The origins of the "revolutionary discourse" of modern China: early explorations in adapting Marxist "revolutionary discourse" to China 现代中国“革命话语”的起源：马克思主义“革命话语”中国化的早期探索 Wang Juanjuan Wu Hanquan Scholars have studied modern China's "revolutionary discourse" with growing interest, but Wang and Wu observe that its origins are seldom examined. Taking a social-history approach, the article argues that this discourse arose from the spread of Marxism during the May Fourth period. In its account, early Chinese Marxists read revolution through classical Marxist "revolutionary discourse" and applied class-struggle theory creatively to Chinese conditions. The article covers Chinese thought between 1919 and 1927. It opens with the basic content of classical Marxist revolutionary discourse, then sets out three social-historical conditions for its Chinese formation: the discourse environment left by the bourgeois revolution, the model of the October Revolution, and the radicalisation of May Fourth "social reconstruction". The final section identifies eight themes of the early Chinese discourse, drawing on Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Qu Qiubai, Cai Hesen, Zhao Shiyan, Yun Daiying, Deng Zhongxia and Zhou Enlai. The authors summarise classical Marxist discourse in six points: revolution arises from the development of the productive forces; it changes the social system, centred on ownership; its subject is the oppressed proletariat; it is led by a proletarian party; it proceeds by armed force; and it aims at a communist society. They argue that early Marxists then adapted this framework to a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China. The eight themes they identify are the nature of Chinese society and its revolutionary history, the aims of the "national revolution", Marxism as guiding thought, Communist Party leadership, the mass character of revolution, armed struggle, the united front, and the claim that the Chinese revolution is part of the world revolution. Wang and Wu conclude that the discourse took shape in a May Fourth context, but mainly through the efforts of early Marxists and early Communists to adapt Marxist revolutionary theory to China. They hold that it rested on the Party's political practice of transforming Chinese society. In their view it supplied the logical starting point and discursive conditions for the theory of New Democratic revolution and became part of China's Marxist political science. Read the original if you study the intellectual history of the early Communist movement and want a detailed account of how its leaders framed revolution in the 1920s.

On Marx's critique and transcendence of Ricardo's political economy 论马克思对李嘉图政治经济学的批判与超越 Yuan Jinqiu Liu Jie Yuan Jinqiu and Liu Jie ask what Marx's critique of David Ricardo actually achieved and why it still matters. They answer that Marx's political economy is a revolutionary break with classical political economy, not a continuation of Ricardo. They present this against two modern challenges: Böhm-Bawerk and Samuelson, who reject the labour theory of value, and Schumpeter, who treats Marx as Ricardo's heir. In the authors' view, both fall back to Ricardo's level or below. The article has three parts. The first traces four stages in Marx's reading of Ricardo: rejection under Feuerbach's influence (Paris Notebooks), strong endorsement (The Poverty of Philosophy), initial doubt (London Notebooks), and full critique and transcendence (the manuscripts of 1857–63 and Capital). The second examines Marx's treatment of Ricardo's value theory, rent theory, international trade, accumulation and view of machinery, drawing mainly on Theories of Surplus Value. The third compares their methods. The central argument is that Marx resolved the "two difficulties" of Ricardo's system. The first is how the exchange of capital and labour fits the law of value. The authors say Marx answered it with the two-fold character of commodities and labour, and the concept of labour-power. The second is how equal capitals yield equal profits. Marx answered it by distinguishing surplus value from profit and value from price of production. Marx's absolute rent, the authors add, rests on landed monopoly and agriculture's lower organic composition of capital. They suggest that platform economies reproduce a variant of this rent. On method, they argue that Ricardo's abstraction was incomplete and ahistorical, treating bourgeois relations as natural, while Marx used historical materialism and dialectics. These include ascending from the abstract to the concrete and the unity of the logical and the historical. The authors conclude that Marx's critique of Ricardo and the formation of his own political economy were one process. They hold that it exposed the historical transience of capitalism and the conflict between socialised production and private ownership. They add that its ultimate purpose is to give scientific grounds for proletarian revolution and a path to communism and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed, stage-by-stage account of Marx's relation to Ricardo, or a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Schumpeter and of neoclassical critiques of the transformation problem.

From the philosophy of practice to practical materialism: Cieszkowski, Hess and Marx 从实践哲学到实践唯物主义：切什考夫斯基、赫斯与马克思 Lin Zhao Fan Xingxing How did the young Marx move from Hegelianism to practical materialism? Lin Zhao and Fan Xingxing take up one thread that Hiromatsu Wataru identified in this transition: the Young Hegelian critique of Hegel's philosophy of history by August von Cieszkowski and Moses Hess. Marx never discussed either in his published work, and Engels left them out of his account. The authors argue that both men developed a 'philosophy of practice' that prepared Marx's turn, but remained trapped inside idealism, so Marx's practical materialism is a real break rather than a continuation. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Cieszkowski's Prolegomena to Historiosophy (1838) and its link between philosophy of history, philosophy of the future and philosophy of practice. The second turns to Hess, from The Holy History of Mankind to The European Triarchy and On the Essence of Money, and his critique of modernity and his socialism. The third asks what it means for Marx to replace 'philosophy' with 'materialism', by asking what was wrong with the philosophy of history and what the philosophy of practice still lacked. In the authors' account, Cieszkowski made practice the 'synthesis' of Hegel's system and opened the future to knowledge and action. Hess brought the argument down to subjective spirit and the present, and added French socialism and a critique of private property. Both, the authors argue, stayed inside the 'mystical shell' of Hegel's dialectic. Cieszkowski dealt only with spiritual elements and had no historical subject. Hess kept a V-shaped narrative of paradise, suffering and a new Jerusalem, and treated bourgeois modernity as simply evil. Marx, by contrast, grounded history in civil society, the mode of production and the critique of political economy, and identified the proletariat as the subject that modern industry and property relations produce. Lin and Fan conclude that practice becomes scientific only when it is understood through its material preconditions. At that point the philosophy of practice turns into practical materialism, which they also call a theory of proletarian revolution. They suggest that Marx and Hess parted ways, on this view, because of this difference, with Marx heading toward scientific socialism and Hess toward Zionism. Read the original if you study the Young Hegelian background to Marx's thought, or want a Chinese reading that sets Cieszkowski and Hess against Marx's break with philosophy.

The westward road of educated youth to Yan'an during the War of Resistance 抗战时期知识青年奔赴延安的西行之路 Wang Xiaosi This short historical piece, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, describes the journey made by educated young people to Yan'an during the War of Resistance against Japan. Wang uses "westward journey" as a symbolic term for a generation's search for light and progress. The article argues that, despite great physical obstacles, the journey showed the pull of Yan'an as a revolutionary base and the young people's commitment to national salvation and their ideals. The article first sets out the objective constraints: distance, limited transport and cost. It then traces the routes from Shanghai to Xi'an, and finally the last stretch from Xi'an to Yan'an. Evidence comes from press reports such as Shen Bao (1939) and from the recorded experiences of individual travellers, including writers, artists and students. Wang notes that Shanghai–Xi'an travel ran along "two horizontal and one vertical" routes: the Longhai railway, the Yangtze route via Wuhan, and a southern sea route via Hong Kong, Guangzhou or Vietnam and Kunming. As Japanese advances cut each in turn, travellers shifted to the next; one artist couple took seven months. The final stretch of nearly 400 kilometres had no railway. Travellers used rough roads, mule carts and mostly walking, which Wang links to Mao Zedong's description of the Xi'an–Yan'an road as the "first lesson" at the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University. Wang concludes that the hardships could not stop the stream of young people heading to Yan'an. In the article's view, the journey confirms the attraction of the revolutionary base and the young people's firm convictions. Read the original if you want a concise, source-based account of the practical routes and hardships of reaching Yan'an in wartime.

The spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army as an enduring monument forged by the Communist Party of China 东北抗联精神是中国共产党熔铸的不朽丰碑 Li Xiaoyu This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks where the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (Kang Lian) came from. The article first sets out the historical background: the Japanese occupation after the September 18th Incident of 1931, early volunteer forces, the Party-led guerrilla units of 1932, and the formal founding of the United Army in February 1936. It then examines three foundations of the spirit, namely its historical setting, its ideological base and its organisational guarantee. On ideology, Li holds that Party cadres sent to the northeast, such as Yang Jingyu and Zhao Yiman, used Marxism to raise soldiers' understanding from simple patriotism to a grasp of national independence and the world anti-fascist cause. The author points to the journal Lenin's Banner and study classes as channels for this. On politics, Li stresses the Party's early calls for resistance and the anti-Japanese national united front line. On organisation, Li cites political departments, commissars and the principle of building Party branches at company level. The article calls on readers to understand this inner link, carry on the "red genes" and work for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how current Party-education writing links a wartime resistance narrative to the principle of Party leadership.

Deepening research on the Communist Party's war of resistance behind enemy lines in North China 深化中国共产党华北敌后抗战研究 Fu Jing Fu Jing, writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in October 2025, asks how research on the Communist Party's anti-Japanese resistance in North China can be extended. Fu argues that North China was strategically vital to Japan, and that the Party became the "mainstay" of the national war of resistance there. New Chinese and foreign archives, newspapers, diaries and memoirs, in Fu's view, make further work possible in three areas. The short commentary opens with the outbreak of full-scale war in July 1937 and the region's geography, resources and transport links. It then proposes three research directions: the anti-Japanese national united front, operations behind enemy lines, and the building of grass-roots political power. Each section sketches the historical background before listing questions that deserve study. On the united front, Fu describes a region divided among local power-holders, with a weak Nationalist government and competing British and American interests. Fu urges study of how the Party won over local forces, organised underground work in occupied cities and villages, and sought international support. On military operations, Fu cites the Pingxingguan victory, the Hundred Regiments Offensive and railway sabotage, and asks how the Party adapted tactics to terrain and linked North and Central China. On grass-roots power, Fu points to the production campaign, the "three-thirds" system and theoretical education, and calls for work on cadres, Party branches and how the centre guided local struggle. Fu concludes that deeper study would enrich the history of the war and of the Party, and would show more fully the Party's role as the mainstay of resistance. Read the original if you want a brief guide to the research agenda that Chinese historians are setting for the Party's war of resistance in North China.

The Asiatic conception of society in Marx's theory of world history 马克思世界历史理论中的亚细亚社会观 Wang Xudong This short commentary asks how Marx's view of "Asiatic" society changed and why it came to be included in his scheme of world history. Wang argues that around 1853 Marx shared the Europe-wide image of Asia as a stagnant society, but that in the Grundrisse he built a new framework and so moved Asiatic society from a regional particularity to a universal stage of history. The article first outlines the Asiatic conception current in Europe in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It then turns to Marx's 1853 articles on India in the New-York Daily Tribune, the Grundrisse chapter on pre-capitalist forms, his 1881 draft replies to Vera Zasulich, and the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. Wang says the European conception moved from state ownership of land under despotism (eighteenth century), to the absence of a bourgeoisie and civil society (early nineteenth), to the despotic state resting on patriarchal communities (late nineteenth). In 1853 Marx described India as stagnant, without private landownership or history, and as able to change only through British capitalism's \"double mission\". In the Grundrisse, Wang argues, Marx instead identified three features of Asiatic ownership: the individual's dependence on the community, communal landownership, and the union of agriculture and handicrafts within the community. His focus shifted from the despotic state to the community and its land tenure. Wang links this to Marx's effort to escape Eurocentrism by studying Asia on its own terms, which allowed the \"Asiatic mode of production\" to open the sequence of stages in the 1859 Preface. Wang concludes that the Grundrisse framework guided Marx's later work on Asiatic society, including the \"agricultural commune\" of 1881, and that the text made Asiatic society part of world history. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's treatment of the Asiatic mode of production developed from the 1853 India writings to the Grundrisse and the 1859 Preface.

The world-historical logic in Marx's theory of fetishism 马克思拜物教理论中的世界历史逻辑 Sun Jia Sun Jia asks how Marx's theory of fetishism can explain the course of world history and the fate of human subjectivity. The short newspaper essay argues that history can be read as the continual remaking of forms of dependence. In this reading, humans demystify and master natural forces while falling under social forces that they create and that become independent through reification. The article traces Marx's thinking from the 1842 Bonn Notebooks, where he excerpted de Brosses on fetish worship, through the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and the Grundrisse to Capital. It then turns to the ethnological notebooks of 1879–82 and closes with a brief note on digital technology. Sun's central distinction is between two kinds of fetish. The natural fetish of early societies is 'destructible': when it fails to satisfy desire, its worshippers smash it. The commodity, money and capital fetishes of capitalism are 'indestructible', because they are reified social relations and part of the whole system of exchange. Sun links this to the three forms of dependence in the Grundrisse: personal dependence, personal independence resting on dependence on things, and the free association of individuals. Scientific revolution ends mystified dependence on nature, but capitalism re-naturalises social relations, so demystification must now be directed at society. Sun concludes that the free association of individuals is the historical direction in which social forces return to conscious human control, at a higher level than the early blood-based community. Algorithmic authority, data worship and artificial intelligence myths are presented as new forms of modern fetishism. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-language account of how fetishism theory is being used to read world history and digital technology.

Marx on the relationship between "history" and "world history" 马克思对“历史”与“世界历史”的关联性阐述 Jiang Haibo Jiang Haibo asks how Marx, in his Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58, understood the relation between national "history" and the overall process of "world history". Jiang argues that Marx redefined both categories through the critique of political economy, escaping the Eurocentrism the author attributes to Hegel's view of world history as the unfolding of spirit. The result, in Jiang's reading, is a dialectical unity of the two. The short article first traces how the category of "history" changes with the mode of production. It then examines how history and world history are linked, and ends by assessing the contemporary value of this idea. Jiang contends that in pre-capitalist societies, natural economy, feudal landholding and guild restrictions kept history closed and local. Capital's drive for surplus value broke these limits, pulling all peoples into the world market, reorganising production factors globally and ending separate national narratives. The global division of labour created by large-scale machine industry ties the two categories together. National history becomes a partial expression of the whole, while world history supplies the conditions for overcoming local limits. Jiang adds that national differences feed the diversity of world history, and that Marx, though critical of colonial brutality, acknowledged its transformative role. Modern China's path from the Opium War to the 1911 Revolution is offered as an example. Jiang sets Marx against two opposed Western tendencies: a nationalist view of history that equates it with national history, and a globalist view that denies national particularity. Marx's approach, Jiang says, supports a historical understanding that unites nationality and universality. Jiang also holds that his idea of a "human wholeness" is consistent with a community with a shared future for mankind, which the article presents as a contemporary development of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic account of how Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts are linked to current Chinese foreign-policy language.

Accelerating the construction of an independent knowledge system for Chinese ecological economics 加快构建中国生态经济学自主知识体系 Liu Yaobin This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how China should build an independent knowledge system for ecological economics. Liu Yaobin takes Xi Jinping's call to build an independent Chinese system of knowledge as the starting point. Liu argues that such a system is a mission of the era for a modernization in which humanity and nature live in harmony, and that it also serves China's voice in global environmental governance. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the mission and the need for original concepts and theories drawn from China's own conditions. The second treats China's ecological civilization practice as the "roots" of the system. The third treats the "two mountains" idea as its "soul". Liu holds that practical results confirm the theory: the article cites a 57 per cent fall in PM2.5 in key cities, more than thirty years of simultaneous growth in forest area and stock, and energy consumption growth of 3.34 per cent a year supporting 6.11 per cent economic growth over 2013–2024. In Liu's account, institutional innovations such as the "1+N+4" legal framework, central environmental inspections and the river and lake chief system turn the principle of internalising externalities into governance practice. The "two mountains" idea, which Liu describes as a Sinicised development of Marxist ecological thought, treats nature as "natural capital" and a source of value. Liu presents this as a shift from Western environmental economics' externality theory to an "endogenisation" theory, supported by mechanisms such as GEP accounting, ecological compensation and carbon trading. Liu concludes that the system is needed for Chinese modernization and for global environmental governance. The author calls for deeper summing-up of local experience, definition of signature concepts, extraction of original theory and Chinese discourse, guided by the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic leadership frames ecological economics as part of building independent knowledge systems.

Guiding smart city construction with the concept of the people's city 以人民城市理念引领智慧城市建设 Li Zhisong Writing in China Social Sciences Today (October 2025), Li Zhisong takes up the 2025 Central Urban Work Conference's call to put the people's city concept into practice and to build convenient and efficient smart cities. Li argues that smart city construction has achieved results but is held back by practical difficulties, and that it needs the people's city concept and a multi-actor governance mechanism to move forward. The short commentary has three parts. It first reviews progress since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in policy design, coverage, intelligent infrastructure and governance performance. It then identifies problems in implementation. It ends with two proposed paths. On achievements, Li cites a 2024 guideline on citywide digital transformation, with targets for 2027 and 2030, and a 2022 white paper reporting more than 500 pilot cities. On problems, Li points to weak grassroots consultation, such as poorly designed questionnaires and inadequate explanation, and to poor data updating and system maintenance. Li also describes the tension between the traditional "departments and localities" (tiao-kuai) administrative pattern and systemic governance. Grassroots units lack authority over technology partners and depend on fiscal funds, while departments build data silos. Li attributes these failures partly to the lack of a scientific governance concept, which leads to evaluation by indicators such as GDP. Li proposes, first, that governments apply the people's city concept, summed up as "people's cities are built by the people and for the people", across the whole governance cycle. Achievements of the Party-led communications enterprise during the War of Resistance Building the wartime communications system centred on Yan'an, 1937–1945 全民族抗战时期党领导通信事业的建设成就 Yuan Jialiang This short historical commentary asks how the Chinese Communist Party built and ran its communications system during the War of Resistance against Japan. The author counts 50 central documents on the subject and describes the Military Commission's Third Bureau as the unified manager of units and personnel. Its radio networks grew from six to a Yan'an-centred system of eight stations and eight networks by 1940, alongside a local telephone network and long-distance wire lines. Trained operators rose to nearly 5,000, and radio stations from 34 in 1937 to nearly 700 in 1945. Actively building China's autonomous knowledge classification system 积极构建中国自主知识分类体系 Sun Guozhu Sun Guozhu asks how Chinese scholarship can move beyond building discipline-by-discipline autonomous knowledge systems towards a deeper layer: an autonomous knowledge classification system and a 'public framework of principles' (gongong xueli kuangjia). Writing in a newspaper commentary, Sun argues that mutual understanding between civilizations depends on aligning modes of thinking, which are embodied in the knowledge systems each civilization produces. The classification system is presented as the 'chip' or underlying logic of knowledge production. The piece first distinguishes the autonomous knowledge system from the classification system. The latter is a framework for classifying knowledge, and Sun borrows Yan Fu's phrase 'the method of all methods, the learning of all learning' to describe it. The public framework is the set of universal principles on which classification rests, so that realising one amounts to completing the other. Sun then proposes three dimensions of work: rethinking how disciplines divide and recombine, overcoming the split between the sciences and the humanities, and drawing on Chinese civilization's own intellectual resources. On the first dimension, Sun notes that existing human knowledge is built mainly on Western disciplinary frameworks and calls for integrating the classification schemes of other civilizations, since the social sciences and humanities often lack a single optimal answer. On the second, Sun treats the sciences–humanities divide, citing C. P. Snow's 'two cultures' and Marx's remark that natural science and the science of man will become one science. Sun adds that science is ultimately a 'technique' (shu) and cannot be the shared foundation of society, which should rest on a 'way' (dao). Sun adds that AI and the problem of value alignment give the humanities a practical role. On the third, Sun contends that Chinese learning historically stressed scholarship and method, producing a synthesising, 'comprehensive' character. Sun argues that this should help dispel the 'China had no science' view, which Sun attributes to civilizational misunderstanding and narrow Western disciplinary definitions. Sun concludes that forming a new form of human civilization requires an autonomous knowledge system, and that exploring classification and the public framework is an important breakthrough for reform. The system should not become a fixed standard but a living, open scheme that can be adjusted as humanity comes to know and change the world. Sun presents this as significant for reconciliation among civilizations and for a fresh arrangement of 'the sum of human knowledge'. Read the original if you want a short statement of one scholar's agenda for rethinking disciplinary classification within the Chinese debate on autonomous knowledge systems.

New quality productive forces leading the building of a modern economic system 新质生产力引领现代化经济体系建设 Yuan Lei This newspaper commentary asks how China should build a modern economic system under a new round of technological and industrial change. Yuan Lei argues that new quality productive forces are the core engine of this effort and must be matched by new production relations. Building the system, in this reading, is the process of developing productive forces and forming relations of production suited to them. The article has three parts.
