It first sets out what the modern economic system consists of, namely four linked sub-systems of production, distribution, circulation and consumption. It then reviews progress made in recent years, citing figures for each sub-system, and lists remaining problems. It closes with directions for improving each sub-system. Yuan's central move is theoretical. The author distinguishes two kinds of interaction between productive forces and production relations: gradual improvement of relations that broadly fit, and, where innovation lifts the quality of productive forces, an adaptive reconstruction of production, distribution, circulation and consumption. Economic change driven by new quality productive forces is placed in the second category. On results, the article cites GDP above 130 trillion yuan in 2024, disposable income of 41,314 yuan per head, over 170 billion parcels delivered, and retail sales of over 48.3 trillion yuan. It also names weaknesses: many industries remain in the middle and lower ends of global value chains, income gaps persist, and supply and demand are mismatched. Yuan proposes innovation-driven upgrading of production, including self-reliance in core technologies and "AI+" transformation of traditional industries. In distribution, the author calls for coordinating primary distribution, redistribution and the third distribution, with common prosperity as a goal. For circulation, Yuan urges a unified national market under the formula "five unifications and one opening". For consumption, the author recommends combining short-term stimulus with long-term institutional reform. Read the original if you want a concise official-style economic overview of how Chinese policy writers link new quality productive forces to production, distribution, circulation and consumption, with the statistics they cite.

Three dimensions for promoting high-quality development of university research 推动高校科研高质量发展的三重维度 Wu Chen Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2025, Wu Chen starts from the headline figures of the 14th Five-Year Plan period. These include total R&D spending of over 3.6 trillion yuan in 2024, 48% above 2020, and first place worldwide in research personnel, high-level journal papers and international patent applications. Wu asks what research should pursue behind such numbers. The answer is that universities need to treat research quality as the central task, practical application as the fundamental mission, and international leadership as the direction of effort. The commentary is organised in three parts, one for each dimension. The first examines the gap between publication volume and real quality. The second draws on the Ming-Qing idea of jingshi zhiyong to define what research is for. The third looks at paradigm change in science and at how China might lead rather than follow. Each part ends with proposals on university philosophy, resource allocation and evaluation. On quality, Wu argues that paper counts do not equal competitiveness. Chinese papers are on average cited less than American, British or EU papers, and China publishes fewer papers in Nature and Science and has won fewer Nobel Prizes and Fields Medals. Wu calls for an end to performance-first thinking, KPI pressure and short-cycle evaluation, and for long-term funding of basic, curiosity-driven work. Wu also wants evaluation based on value rather than journal rank, citing the 2025 Nobel laureate Shimon Sakaguchi, whose key 1995 result appeared in a mid-ranked journal. On application and leadership, Wu holds that publication is not the endpoint of research. Wu proposes a three-in-one model of basic research, technology development and applied transfer, with resources directed to core national problems and evaluation based on problems solved. Wu says this is compatible with free exploration. On leadership, Wu urges targeting the frontier in AI, quantum physics, controlled nuclear fusion and hydrogen energy, shifting research paradigms towards complex systems, simulation and data science, and taking bold steps into uncharted fields to achieve overtaking by changing lanes. Wu concludes that these shifts would give research lasting momentum and underpin China's drive to become a strong country in education, science and talent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese education scholar links research evaluation reform to national science and technology goals.

The internal mechanism by which culture supports high-quality economic development 文化支撑经济高质量发展的内在机理 Zhu Hongjun This commentary in Guangming Daily asks how culture sustains economic development. Zhu Hongjun builds on Xi Jinping's remarks in Zhijiang xinyu (Xi's collected Zhejiang-era essays) and argues that culture gives economic development three things: deep humanistic value, high organisational efficiency and stronger competitiveness. The piece follows that three-part structure, one section for each. It draws on contrasts between Western mainstream economics and Marxist political economy, on traditional Chinese ethics, on the Party's record of economic work, and on the example of Zhejiang's regional economy. It ends with proposals for the new era. On value, Zhu contrasts the "rational economic man" of Western economics, which the author ties to the logic of capital, with a Marxist stance that puts people first. Traditional ideas such as enriching the people and balancing righteousness with profit are presented as cultural resources, and the call to cultivate a financial culture with Chinese characteristics is read as an application of the Two Integrations. On organisation, Zhu credits cultural traditions of honesty, contract and cooperation with lowering transaction costs. Zhejiang's tailoring, footwear and small-commodity trades are offered as cases, as is corporate culture's role in cohesion. On competitiveness, advanced culture is said to raise workers' quality and digital skills, and the digitalisation of culture is said to raise the whole economy. Zhu calls for firm cultural confidence, for building a strong socialist cultural nation, and for balancing material and spiritual civilisation. Zhu also urges using core socialist values to build consensus, promoting entrepreneurial spirit, and cultivating new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated commentary links culture to high-quality development.

The profound meaning of "ensuring decisive progress toward basically realizing socialist modernization" “确保基本实现社会主义现代化取得决定性进展”的深刻内涵 Tao Wenzhao This commentary in Guangming Daily interprets a goal set by the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025): that the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030) must "ensure decisive progress toward basically realizing socialist modernization". Tao Wenzhao argues that the formula is more than a time-bound benchmark. In the author's reading, it expresses the Party's sense of mission and historical initiative, and its resolve to push Chinese modernization into greater depth. The article has three parts. The first sets out the "spirit and essence" of the goal. The second places it in historical context, between the close of the 14th Five-Year Plan and the longer road to 2035 and beyond. The third names three key areas for breakthroughs: scientific and technological innovation, reform and opening up, and security-oriented development. The text quotes Xi Jinping on strategic patience and on pressing ahead with urgent tasks. Tao argues that the goal rests on three foundations. These are a mission that anchors direction, continuity with earlier staged goals such as the step-by-step building of a moderately prosperous society, and an active stance that seizes the initiative. On the historical position, the author insists that "decisive progress" means a qualitative leap and systemic breakthroughs, not merely quantitative accumulation or isolated gains. It also requires seamless continuity with the 14th Five-Year Plan and early preparation for longer-term technologies, talent and governance. For the key areas, Tao calls for a shift from "following and running alongside" to "running alongside and leading" in technology. The author names fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum information and integrated circuits, and calls for new quality productive forces and a new-type whole-nation system. Tao also calls for deeper reform toward a high-standard socialist market economy and a unified national market. The Two Unwaverings are to be upheld, and security is to be treated as the precondition of development, with food, energy, supply-chain and financial risks guarded against. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of how the 15th Five-Year Plan period is framed within the 2035 modernization goal.

Re-examining the Communist Party of China's role as the mainstay in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 对中国共产党在抗日战争中发挥中流砥柱作用的再认识 Zhu Jiamu Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this article asks why the Communist Party of China's role as the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the war needs to be re-examined, and what that role consisted of. Zhu argues that the Party's leadership was decisive to the victory, and that the claim should be defended against what the author calls historical nihilism. The article opens with Xi Jinping's statements of 2014 and 2020 on the Party's mainstay role, which Zhu treats as the guiding framework. It then gives a brief historiography. Early People's Republic accounts, in Zhu's view, undervalued the Kuomintang's frontal battlefield. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) the Party corrected this. Zhu says a later wave of nihilism went to the opposite extreme. The main body sets out eight ways in which the Party played its role, and a short final section turns to present-day implications. Zhu's eight points run chronologically. The Party was first to call for armed resistance after 1931, first to propose a national united front, and first to promote Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. It framed a comprehensive-war line and the protracted-war strategy of Mao Zedong's On Protracted War. It built up guerrilla forces and made the rear-area battlefield a main battlefield. It followed a policy of resistance, unity and progress, and it checked Kuomintang anti-Communist campaigns without breaking the united front. It built 19 anti-Japanese base areas, which the author says covered over a million square kilometres and about 100 million people. It also forged a wartime spirit through heroes such as Yang Jingyu and Zhao Yiman. Zhu contends that anyone respecting the historical facts can see this role, and that without the Party the war would have lacked a correct line, mass participation and moral support. Zhu concludes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the ideological situation has changed fundamentally, but that hostile forces at home and abroad will keep belittling the Party's wartime role in order to attack its legitimacy and the socialist system. The author calls for propagating the mainstay role, upholding a "correct view" of the war and answering nihilism with historical facts. The aim is to rally the people around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a senior CASS historian presents the official case for the Party's wartime leadership and how it is tied to current ideological work.

"The Poverty of Philosophy": which philosophy, which poverty? The last metaphysics and Marx's critique “哲学的贫困”：什么哲学?什么贫困?——最后的形而上学与马克思的批判 Lin Jinlong Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy answers Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty, yet Marx never says directly what he means by "philosophy" or by "poverty". Lin Jinlong takes up this gap, which the author says scholarship has long neglected. The article proposes that Proudhon's thought is the "last metaphysics", the final effort of the metaphysical tradition after Hegel's system dissolved. On this reading, the poverty Marx names is both an original poverty and a final one. The article first reconstructs Proudhon's "economics-metaphysics" through five features. These are his idea of "science", his claim that economics is concrete metaphysics, his "natural history of labour", his series of economic categories, and his defence of small private property. It then examines the role of "God" in Proudhon's text and his ambivalent debt to Hegel. Next it sets out Marx's critique of Hegel and of Proudhon, and ends by placing Proudhon alongside the Young Hegelian "ideologists" of The German Ideology. Lin argues that Proudhon borrows Hegel's dialectic as antinomy and series, but rejects Hegel's "absolute idea" and replaces it with an "infinite" God. Marx, in Lin's account, finds that Proudhon reduces the dialectic to a bare thesis and antithesis. Proudhon also treats categories such as division of labour, machinery, monopoly and taxation as a logical sequence detached from history. His "economic evolution" therefore takes place "in the mystical embrace of the absolute idea". Lin concludes that Proudhon uses Hegel against Hegel and only swaps one "God" for another, which Lin names as the root of philosophy's poverty. He is "last" because he advanced beyond the German ideologists by seizing the dialectic and joining reason with experience. He is "original" because he remains within the idealist conception of history. Lin concludes that the "philosophy" criticised is Proudhon's attempt to unify reason and experience within Hegelian conceptual dialectics. The "poverty" is the failure of metaphysics to renew itself from within. Proudhon's "unity of experience and reason" is contrasted with Marx's "unity of the logical and the historical", which is anchored in labour as sensuous, objective activity and in real history. Historical materialism, Lin holds, ends classical metaphysics as a closed system and offers a new periodisation of the history of philosophy. Read the original if you want a close comparison of Proudhon's and Marx's texts and a reading of Proudhon as post-Hegelian metaphysician.

Advancing the building of a unified national market in depth 纵深推进全国统一大市场建设 Li Yuju Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 14), Li Yuju takes up the instructions Xi Jinping gave at the sixth meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission on 1 July 2025 on advancing the building of a unified national market. Li argues that this is a strategic deployment by the Party Central Committee. In Li's account it underpins the new development pattern and high-quality development, and it requires that the basic requirement of "five unifications and one opening" be put into practice. The article has three parts. The first traces the continuity of Party theory and practice on the unified market, from Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remark that socialism can also have a market economy to the 2022 Central Committee and State Council opinions and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The second reviews results since the 18th Party Congress (2012): top-level design, market rules and institutions, and the use of several market advantages. The third sets out concrete measures under each of the six requirements. Li's central claim is that the Party's line has been continuous: the market's role moved from "basic" to "decisive" in resource allocation, and the goal moved from a socialist unified market to a high-standard market system. Drawing on Marxist political economy, Li holds that a unified national market keeps the circuits of social reproduction open. As evidence of progress, Li cites a shorter negative list for market access (117 items in the 2022 edition, 106 in 2025), a logistics-cost ratio of 14.1% of GDP in 2024, and 63% of electricity traded through markets. For the remaining problems, Li names local government conduct rooted in a distorted view of performance, such as disorderly investment attraction and low-price competition. The remedies Li proposes include a single national negative list, fair-competition review, unified regulation and enforcement, integrated land, labour, capital, power and data markets, and appraisal systems that penalise breaches of market unity. Li concludes that the unified national market must be open to the world rather than closed. Li calls for cutting the foreign-investment negative list, giving foreign firms national treatment, implementing the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and pursuing accession to the CPTPP and DEPA. Li also calls for integrating domestic and foreign trade. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese policy-makers link market unification to local-government behaviour, regulation and opening up, with the policy documents and figures cited.

Heroes of the War of Resistance inscribed on the motherland's soil Memorials, place names and the memory of the anti-Japanese war 祖国大地铭刻抗日英雄的名字 Hu Yuhan Published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, this commemorative essay asks how the heroes of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression are remembered in the physical landscape of China. Hu Yuhan argues that monuments, mountains, counties, schools and streets named after them each fix a particular wartime memory and together form an epic of the Chinese nation. The essay presents these heroes as the basis of a spirit that should be honoured and emulated today. The essay is organised in three parts. The first covers heroic military units and the sites that commemorate them: the Hundred Regiments Offensive monument at Shinao Mountain, the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army and its eight women fighters, and the Liulaozhuang Company of the New Fourth Army. The second turns to senior commanders, among them Zuo Quan, Dai An'lan, Peng Xuefeng, Tong Linge, Zhao Dengyu and Zhang Zizhong. The third treats civilians and non-combatants, including the Yimeng "Red Sister-in-law" Ming Deying, the overseas Chinese fighter Li Lin and the writer Yu Dafu. Hu's method is narrative: each case combines a short battle account, a death in action and the way the person is now commemorated. Examples include the county renamed Zuoquan, a school renamed after Peng Xuefeng, and three Beijing streets named after Tong, Zhao and Zhang. The author credits the Communist-led Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army with holding the enemy rear, and also includes Kuomintang generals such as Dai An'lan and Zhang Zizhong. The essay quotes tributes from Zhou Enlai, Mao Zedong and Zhu De. It stresses the endurance, self-sacrifice and patriotism of soldiers and civilians alike, and describes the war as one fought by the whole nation and won by the whole nation over fourteen years. Hu concludes that a nation with hope cannot do without heroes, and that the great spirit of resistance is a precious spiritual asset and a driving force. The best way to honour heroes, the author says, is to revere, learn from and strive to become heroes, so that heroic spirit gathers strength for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commemorative writing presents war memory, with its place names, named heroes and tributes from Party leaders.

Carry forward the Yan'an style of work and cultivate a good Party conduct 弘扬延安作风 培塑优良党风 Zhao Shaojie Zhang Yu This short commentary, published in the Party journal Dangjian in June 2025, asks how the Party's wartime Yan'an style of work can serve present-day Party conduct. Zhao and Zhang argue that the Yan'an style, the outward expression of the Yan'an spirit, offers nourishment and strength for the current study and education campaign on the central Party's eight-point regulation, and that good conduct will in turn support Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. The authors open with Xi Jinping's remark that the Yan'an style defeated the 'Xi'an style', and recall that in the Yan'an period the Party stressed discipline education and fostered ties between theory and practice, close links with the masses, and criticism and self-criticism. The body is organised under four headings: firm ideological foundations, a deep commitment to the people, strict discipline, and a spirit of hard struggle. Each section pairs historical examples with a task for today. Mao Zedong's plain meal for Chen Jiageng, Zhou Enlai learning to spin during the production campaign, the 1944 speech 'Serve the People', Yan'an-era disciplinary regulations and the corruption case of Xiao Yubi, and the labour models of the production campaign all serve this purpose. The authors treat these as models for officials: to hold their position on matters of principle, to stay clean, to keep close to the people, to respect discipline and to oppose formalism and bureaucracy. The authors conclude that Party members and cadres should turn the Yan'an style into personal conviction and practical action, so that Party conduct draws together popular support and shapes social customs. Their stated aim is concrete results in serving the people and promoting development. Read the original if you want a compact example of how current Party-building writing draws on Yan'an history to support the eight-point regulation campaign.

Leadership of the Communist Party of China as the fundamental feature of China's new type of party system 中国共产党领导是中国新型政党制度的根本特征 Zuo Peng Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks to non-Party figures at the Spring Festival gathering on 20 January 2025, Zuo Peng argues that leadership of the Communist Party of China is the fundamental feature of China's new type of party system. The system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation under Party leadership is presented as a political creation that grew from Chinese soil. Zuo sees it as the product of integrating Marxist party theory with China's realities and with its fine traditional culture, and as the conclusion of comparison with Western party politics. The article is organised around three claims about what Party leadership secures. First, it ensures the system represents the fundamental interests of the broadest people in a genuine, broad and lasting way. Second, it unites the parties and non-Party figures around shared goals. Third, it enables institutionalised, standardised and procedural arrangements that gather opinions and make decisions more scientific and democratic. Zuo traces the system's history from the united front of the revolutionary period through the founding of the People's Republic, the reform era and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On representation, Zuo argues that the Party has no special interests apart from those of the nation and people, and that it integrates the specific interests of the groups the democratic parties connect with into the people's fundamental interests. Zuo describes the system as uniting governing and participating, leadership and cooperation, consultation and oversight. In this account it avoids the defects of one-party rule without supervision and of multi-party rotation with vicious competition. On decision-making, Zuo says Party leadership has built party consultation, democratic oversight and participation in the discussion of state affairs into standard procedures, so that the democratic parties are consulted before and during policy implementation. Zuo concludes that upholding and improving the system bears on the Party's long-term governance and the country's lasting stability. The article describes the system as having historical inevitability, great creativity, superiority and vitality. It also holds that the system embodies the essence of fine traditional culture and the requirements of the socialist system, and that it contributes to modernizing national governance and to human political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line case for the primacy of Party leadership within China's multi-party cooperation system.

Reflections on deepening research into the basic principles of Marxism from a knowledge-system perspective 深化马克思主义基本原理研究的知识化思考 Zhang Yunfei Responding to the new requirements the Party Central Committee set in November 2024 for the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, Zhang Yunfei asks how research on the basic principles of Marxism can be deepened by building a "knowledge system" for the field. The article, published in Ideological and Theoretical Education in 2025, argues that this system should become a Chinese-style, world-class component of China's independent knowledge system of philosophy and social sciences. Zhang's answer is that the knowledge system has to be defined by a clear object of study, a distinctive research paradigm, a balanced set of resources and a concrete disciplinary mission. The article has four parts. It first defines the object of study of Marxism, of Marxist philosophy and of the basic-principles knowledge system. It then sets out a research paradigm of holistic, integrated and comprehensive study. Third, it discusses three kinds of resources: Marxism itself, fine traditional Chinese culture, and foreign philosophy and social science, including Western social thought and world Marxist currents. The last part assigns the knowledge system three functions: strengthening scientific belief and ideals, supporting the innovation of ideological and political theory courses, and serving the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization. Zhang holds that the object of study is the universal laws of development of nature, society and thought. These laws are not the object of dialectics alone: Marxist philosophy supplies the worldview and methodology, while political economy, scientific socialism and the other branches uncover the laws. The knowledge system is then the knowledge-form expression of the basic principles, and it takes in the discipline, academic and discourse systems. For the paradigm, Zhang says Marxism's wholeness derives from the wholeness of its object. Research must also integrate Marxism with its sinicized forms, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and must bring together field-specific strands such as Xi's ecological civilization thought. On resources, Marxism is the main body, tradition is a historical-cultural source reached through the Two Integrations, and foreign thought serves as a reference, to be neither swallowed whole nor dismissed. Zhang concludes that the system must turn scientific knowledge of the "two inevitables" into firm belief and ideals. It must also reshape textbook structure and teacher competence and the methods of teaching, and it must generate a "socialism knowledge system" and a "modernization knowledge system" for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how a leading Chinese Marxist theorist links the discipline of basic principles, ideological and political teaching and the project of an independent knowledge system.

Theoretical logic and focal points for strengthening the political and organisational functions of Party organisations in the new era 新时代增强党组织政治功能和组织功能的理论逻辑与着力方向 Zheng Shipeng Zheng Shipeng takes up a goal set out in the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform: strengthening the political and organisational functions of Party organisations. The article argues that this task is a key link in the Party's new great project of Party building, a lever for following the Party's mass line, and a safeguard for Party leadership of deepened reform. Zheng's thesis is that the two functions are internally coupled, with organisation serving politics, and that strengthening them is both a theoretical requirement and a practical programme. The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic of the two functions, drawing on Marx, Engels, the 1922 Second Congress Party constitution and Xi Jinping's statements. The second explains why strengthening them matters. The third proposes four areas for action. Zheng also cites Party statistics for the end of 2023: 99.185 million members and 5.176 million primary-level organisations. Zheng defines the political function as the Party organisation's basic function: expressing the interests of the great majority, formulating and implementing policy, and mobilising society. The organisational function is the foundation of Party building and serves the political function. Their coupling means political function gives organisation a people-oriented direction, while organisation builds unity and shared political will. The article gives three reasons for strengthening them. It enriches the Marxist theory of party building, it supports the Party's self-reform in leading social revolution, and it raises the quality of Party leadership over deepened reform. The four focal points are that the organisational line should serve the political line and be led by political building. Party organisations should move from formal coverage to effective coverage, including in new economic and social organisations. The mass line should be strengthened through people-centred work and social appeal. Supervision mechanisms, including digital supervision, should be integrated to build a capable cadre corps. Zheng concludes that strengthening both functions will consolidate the Party's political and organisational foundations. They will help ensure that central decisions are carried out at every level and advance Chinese modernization alongside the new great project. The article identifies weak, hollowed-out and marginalised grassroots organisations, and trivialised organisational life, as problems that need regular rectification. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of current Party-building orthodoxy, with its concrete proposals on grassroots coverage and supervision.

Nurturing university students in the new era with the Chinese Communist Party's spirit of struggle: value dimensions and cultivation paths 以中国共产党奋斗精神涵养新时代大学生的价值向度与培育路径 Zhao Yimo Gong Weijia Zhao Yimo and Gong Weijia ask how the Chinese Communist Party's spirit of struggle can be built into the ideological and political education of university students. They treat this spirit as a core part of the Party's spiritual lineage and as a driving force of historical development. Their thesis is that integrating it into university education helps train a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and supports both social progress and the all-round development of the individual. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical content of the spirit of struggle along three dimensions. The second identifies three value orientations for students. The third proposes cultivation paths across five areas of education: moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour. The authors draw on Marx, Mao Zedong's On Contradiction and episodes from revolution, construction and reform. The authors read the spirit of struggle through three lines. Practical rationality means seeking truth from facts, grounded in the Marxist view of labour and the cycle of practice, knowledge and renewed practice. Dialectical thinking means turning contradictions and pressure into momentum, with targeted poverty alleviation as their example. Innovation means keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. For students, they argue, this spirit consolidates historical understanding and guards against historical nihilism. It also calibrates values by reconnecting the individual with the collective, a task they say capital logic has made harder. And it strengthens political identification through cognition, emotion and practice. For education, they propose concrete steps. History and current cases would serve moral education. Course-embedded problem chains would serve intellectual education, such as the 'two bombs, one satellite' spirit in artificial intelligence courses and the Xiaogang village contract in entrepreneurship teaching. Red-themed fitness training would serve physical education. Revolutionary aesthetic resources would serve art education. Model workers such as Wang Jinxi and Jiao Yulu, plus service and production work, would serve labour education. The authors conclude that weaving the spirit of struggle through all five strands of education offers value guidance and practical routes for training socialist builders and successors. The article is largely conceptual and prescriptive, with illustrative examples rather than empirical evaluation of outcomes. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-spirit themes are translated into course design and teaching activities in Chinese higher education.

On the innovative spirit of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化创新精神 Sun Tingting This article, published in Ideological and Theoretical Education (2025, no. 8), asks what the innovative spirit generated by Chinese modernization is, why it matters and how it can be fostered. Sun Tingting argues that Chinese modernization has produced an innovative spirit of 'daring to climb the heights and be the first', which is also a major spiritual driving force for advancing Chinese modernization itself and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the spirit's value for the present era. The second analyses its inner meaning. The third proposes ways of cultivating it. Sun draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements, on the history of the People's Republic from the Mao period through reform and opening up to the new era, and on US think-tank reports and statistics on China's research capacity. Sun gives three reasons for the spirit's present value: it is needed to speed up scientific and technological innovation and the development of new quality productive forces; it is needed for building a strong country, since the article presents national competition as ultimately competition in innovative spirit and capacity; and it is needed to break what Sun calls the 'extreme pressure' of US and Western technology containment. Sun contends that such pressure strengthens China's drive for self-reliance. The spirit itself has four aspects: pioneering, independent, collaborative and sustained innovation. Sun contrasts the sustained innovation of Chinese modernization, supported by Party-led strategic planning and institutional innovation, with Western modernization. Western modernization is described as capital-led, short-termist because of party rotation, and prone to Schumpeter's 'creative destruction'. For cultivation, Sun calls for nurturing innovative young people through innovation education, and for creating a social atmosphere that respects innovation and tolerates failure. Sun also calls for long-term mechanisms covering demand orientation, innovation leadership, competition and policy support, and for stronger collaboration among government, enterprises, universities and research institutes. Sun presents the new-type whole-nation system as the framework for this collaboration. Read the original if you want a Party-school-style account of how innovation is framed as a spiritual resource of Chinese modernization and of the policy measures attached to it.

A dialectical-materialist epistemological interpretation of the great founding spirit of the Party 伟大建党精神的辩证唯物主义认识论阐释 Ouyang Song Ouyang Song asks how the 'great founding spirit of the Party' can be understood through the epistemology of dialectical materialism. The spirit was first formulated by Xi Jinping on 1 July 2021, at the centenary of the Communist Party, in 32 characters: upholding truth and ideals, practising the original aspiration and shouldering the mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting heroically, and being loyal to the Party and faithful to the people. Ouyang argues that it arose from the practice of founding the Party, was tested and strengthened in a century of Party-building, and so illustrates the Marxist account of how practice and consciousness interact. The article has three parts. It first sets out the content of the founding spirit, treating the four pairs of phrases as an organic whole and as both the 'source' and one specific strand of the Party's spiritual lineage. It then examines how the founding of the Party gave rise to the spirit, using the early Party organisations, the spread of Marxism associated with Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu, and the labour movement, including the strikes in Shanghai and the work of Mao Zedong, Peng Pai and Deng Zhongxia. Finally it traces the spirit's effects over the Party's history. Ouyang's central move is to map the spirit onto the 'two leaps' of cognition. The early communists' practice carried them from perceptual to rational knowledge, which is the first leap. The second leap, from rational knowledge back into practice, is shown in the spirit's later influence on the Party's course. Ouyang argues that it is the common thread of the Party's 'spiritual lineage', from the Jinggangshan and Yan'an spirits to the poverty-alleviation spirit. It also spurs the Party's self-reform, drives the successive leaps in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and inspires the achievements Ouyang attributes to the Party across four historical periods. Ouyang concludes that the founding spirit upholds materialism, since practice is the source and driving force of knowledge, and dialectics, since consciousness acts back on practice. It is described as a 'success code' of the Party's century of struggle and an inexhaustible spiritual resource for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article ends by calling on Party members to rally around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to work toward a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an example of how Party historians use epistemological categories to frame the official narrative of the Party's founding and century of history.

Promoting positive interaction between high-quality development and high-level security 推动高质量发展和高水平安全良性互动 Ma Haiyun Zhang Yu This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how China should coordinate development and security. Ma and Zhang argue that the Party Central Committee's strategic deployment on this question rests on scientific principles. They hold that it should be pursued through a positive interaction between high-quality development and high-level security. The piece has three parts: the philosophical logic of coordinating development and security, the supply of policy, and local practice. It draws on materialist dialectics and systems thinking, then turns to policy documents on hazardous chemicals and to provincial examples from Jiangsu, Gansu, Jiangxi and Jilin. The authors read development and security as a unity of opposites. Development is dynamic and carries competition and risk, while security is relatively static and requires stability, so the two are in tension. Yet development guarantees security and security is the precondition of development. In policy terms, Ma and Zhang present "intrinsic safety" (本质安全), a preventive approach that removes risks at source without hampering development, as an effective measure. They cite documents such as the 14th Five-Year Plan for hazardous chemicals work safety (2022), and say Jiangsu, Gansu, Jiangxi and Jilin have issued intrinsic-safety measures across chemicals, mining, construction and water conservancy. The authors conclude that China is gradually building a policy supply system for coordinating development and security, and that local governments are producing rich practice, with Jiangsu reporting falling accident numbers and deaths. Read the original if you want a brief official-style account of how intrinsic safety in work-safety governance is presented as an example of coordinating development and security.

Using a systems perspective to link improving conduct, enforcing discipline and fighting corruption 以系统观念推动正风肃纪反腐相贯通 Liu Ziyi Wu Fulai Liu and Wu take up the Party's formula of 'integrating' work on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption (zhengfeng, suji, fanfu). They argue that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee has applied a systems perspective to Party building, and that this perspective should now guide efforts to deepen full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in support of Chinese modernization. This short commentary is organised in three parts: the underlying rationale for integrating the three tasks, the core meaning of the formula, and practical paths for putting it into effect. The rationale is drawn from Marxist method, the Party's historical experience and current conditions. On rationale, the authors hold that problems of conduct and corruption are two sides of one coin and share a root, while lax discipline causes both. They trace the practice from the revolutionary period through the campaign against Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan to the post-1978 period. On core meaning, they identify three focal points: wholeness, coordination and dynamism. In their account, improving conduct leads, enforcing discipline guarantees, and fighting corruption clears obstacles, together forming a closed-loop system. For practice, the authors call for integrated responsibility, with Party committees, discipline commissions, functional departments and individual cadres each fulfilling defined duties. They also call for integrated institutions, which would fix effective experience in rules, close loopholes behind the interweaving of misconduct and corruption, and apply Party discipline and state law together. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for treating conduct, discipline and corruption as one governance system.

The value of building a discourse system for ideological and political education across university, secondary and primary schools 大中小学思政教育话语体系建设的价值意蕴 Long Jixing Liu Jin This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks why a discourse system for integrated ideological and political education across universities, secondary schools and primary schools is worth building. Long and Liu argue that, with the institutional framework for integration largely in place, discourse building has deep value in three respects. The authors start from the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to promote integrated ideological and political education across all school levels, usually pursued through integrated ideological and political theory courses. They note progress on textbooks, practice bases, teaching staff, steering committees and policy documents, while acknowledging problems still to be solved. First, Long and Liu say, discourse building is a matter of theory: practice of integration has run ahead of its knowledge system, so experience must be raised into systematic, autonomous knowledge. Second, they link it to the Chinese discourse and narrative system called for by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). They describe international discourse power as a contest between Chinese and Western ideologies, in which Western discourse is dominant, and call for guarding mainstream ideological security. Third, they present it as a basis for the strong ideological and political guidance that Xi Jinping places first among the traits of a leading education power. The authors conclude that the discourse must explain integration requirements, evaluation standards and students' mechanisms of reception, and must absorb the Party's latest theoretical innovations. They call for drawing on Marxist theory and traditional Chinese culture, innovating in both content and form, and telling the story of Chinese ideological and political education to the world. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how official Chinese education discourse justifies discourse building in this field.

Contributing Chinese wisdom and proposals to UN reform 为联合国改革贡献中国智慧和方案 Mao Ruipeng Writing in the China Social Sciences Today on the UN's 80th anniversary, Mao Ruipeng argues that the United Nations must deepen reform to improve its representativeness and effectiveness amid accelerating multipolarity and complex global challenges. The article contends that China, as the largest developing country and a permanent member of the Security Council, offers wisdom and concrete proposals that show the conduct of a responsible major country. It presents Xi Jinping's Global Governance Initiative, announced in September 2025 at the "SCO Plus" meeting, as a further public good for reform. The commentary has three parts: the principles behind China's reform stance, four pairs of relationships to be handled correctly, and China's positions on specific reform areas. These areas are the Security Council, the development system and management arrangements. Mao describes China's stance as defending the UN's central role, advancing consultation and shared benefit while opposing any single power setting the agenda, protecting developing countries' interests by strengthening the development pillar, and favouring gradual, practical steps. The four relationships are reform and preservation, vision and reality, South and North, and systemic and step-by-step change. On the Security Council, Mao reports China's view that the core problems are unfair composition and insufficient representation, and that developing countries need greater voice, with intergovernmental negotiations as the main channel. Mao concludes that China's positions reflect support for the UN, for developing countries and for humanity's future. The article cites China's support for the Secretary-General's "UN80 Initiative", its development funds, and its 2025 contributions of over 20% of the regular budget and over 23% of the peacekeeping budget. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the Chinese official line on UN reform as presented by a Shanghai think-tank scholar.

Academic research on the history of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, and the transmission of its spirit 抗美援朝史的学术研究与精神传承 Liu Qiang This short commentary asks how scholarship on the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea is developing and how the war's memory should be passed on. Liu describes the war as a just war fought under extremely unequal conditions, and argues that research on it has a high academic value and an important value for transmitting the spirit of the war. Liu notes that over seven decades the field has widened to take in logistics, social mobilisation, cultural construction and war memory, drawing more on local archives and oral sources. The article has two parts: a section on small-scale perspectives, mainly material life, and a section on three levels of cultural memory. In the first part, Liu treats clothing, food, shelter and movement as windows onto the Chinese People's Volunteers' survival, the state's logistics and industrial capacity, and the Party's political work. Examples include the "fistful of fried flour, a fistful of snow" and the "glory tea". In Liu's reading, these ordinary hardships show patriotism, internationalism, revolutionary optimism and heroism. The second part divides memory into national memory (veteran care, martyrs' burials, commemoration), social memory (art, media, public education) and individual memory (veterans' recollections), which Liu says complement one another. Liu concludes that the spirit of the war continues Chinese civilisation and the national awakening of modern times. Liu calls it a strong impetus for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and urges Chinese scholars to build a discourse of material life history that can take part in international dialogue. Read the original if you want a brief sample of how current Chinese scholarship links Korean War research to patriotic memory and commemoration.

The historical significance and contemporary value of the Resist America, Aid Korea Movement 抗美援朝运动的历史意义和当代价值 Hou Songtao Hou Songtao, in a newspaper commentary from October 2025, asks what the mass political movement that accompanied the Korean War meant for China then and now. The author defines the Resist America, Aid Korea Movement, launched on 26 October 1950, as a campaign to support the war materially and morally, running alongside it throughout. Hou argues that it carries deep historical significance and continuing value. The article is organised in four parts: the movement as a pillar of victory in the war, as a driver of economic reconstruction, as a force for ideological integration, and as a source of spiritual wealth. It draws on the circumstances of 1950, the movement's organisational steps, and Xi Jinping's 2020 summary of the Resist America, Aid Korea spirit. Hou stresses the imbalance between the two sides: the United States held, in the author's figures, two-thirds of the capitalist world's national product and 70 per cent of its gold reserves, while the new China was poor and poorly armed. Mobilisation through propaganda, enlistment, support for the front and donations, equal to the cost of 3,710 fighter aircraft, is said to have secured victory. By linking patriotic pledges and production drives to the policy of fighting, stabilising and building at once, the movement is said to have completed economic recovery on schedule by 1952. Hou also argues that it ended the 'sheet of loose sand' condition of Chinese society through the removal of imperialist influence, 'three-hatred' education against pro-American, worshipful and fearful attitudes, and patriotic education. Hou concludes that the spirit forged in the war and tested in the movement drove wartime victory, reconstruction and ideological unity, and will keep inspiring the Chinese people against hardship and strong adversaries. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholarship frames the home-front campaign of the Korean War.

The Northeast industrial base's important contribution to the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea 东北工业基地在抗美援朝战争中的重要贡献 Han Han Han Han, writing in China Social Sciences Today (24 October 2025), asks how China's Northeast industrial base related to the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea. The author argues that victory would have been far harder without the Northeast as a strategic rear area, and that the war in turn spurred the region's later development. The commentary first reviews the base's wartime role in production and in transport. It then considers what the region's industrial heritage means today, and ends with proposals for how that heritage should be presented. Han describes the Northeast as the war's general logistics base. Factories in Shenyang, Anshan and Fushun produced and repaired weapons and equipment, and light industry supplied uniforms, shoes and food. The author cites Shenyang's No. 53 Factory, named a national model factory, and the railway network, including the 'Little Tiger' locomotive, the first train into Korea, and the Yalu River bridge at Tonghua. On this basis Han draws three lessons: mutual aid within the socialist camp, the dialectical unity of national construction and national security, and the shared origin of the fighting spirit and the self-reliant Daqing spirit. Han holds that the Aid Korea spirit receives too little attention in Northeast heritage work. The author proposes brand building and storytelling, such as documentaries, oral histories and social-media projects, and immersive exhibitions and cultural products. These are meant to fill a gap in the heritage narrative and to contribute to the region's full revitalisation and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese heritage and memory discourse links the Korean War to Northeast industrial history.

The great spirit of resisting US aggression and aiding Korea: timeless and ever fresh Marking the 75th anniversary of the Chinese People's Volunteers' entry into the Korean War 伟大抗美援朝精神跨越时空历久弥新——纪念中国人民志愿军抗美援朝出国作战75周年 Zhao Xuzhou Ban Xiaoyue Published in China Social Sciences Today on 24 October 2025, this commemorative press report marks the 75th anniversary of the Chinese People's Volunteers entering the Korean War. It asks how the 'great spirit of resisting US aggression and aiding Korea' can keep its force in the present. The reporters, drawing on scholars and museum staff, present the war as securing peace for the new People's Republic and the spirit as a resource to be passed on through oral history, education and further research. The piece opens with the anniversary, the crossing of the Yalu River in October 1950 and the 1,007 days of fighting. It then moves through four sections: the war's strategic results, the rescue of veterans' memories, the spirit's role in the new era, and how historical research can support transmission. Interviewees include scholars from Central China Normal University, Harbin Normal University, Liaoning University and Liaodong College, and the deputy director of the Memorial Museum of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea. In the speakers' account, the victory of 'less steel but more spirit' over a stronger enemy broke the myth of American invincibility, raised China's international standing and gave the first Five-Year Plan a peaceful environment. Nationwide mobilisation also aided economic recovery. The article describes urgent oral-history work: a major National Social Science Fund project launched in 2023, student visits to 571 veterans since 2016, and a documentary series with over 700 interviewees. Interviewees propose immersive technologies, ideological and political education, and cross-disciplinary research with foreign archives to rebut historical nihilism. One scholar sets out a 'wide, detailed, deep' research agenda and a loop of historical interpretation, value transformation and practical empowerment. The report concludes that, at a new historical starting point, the spirit remains a driving force. It calls on readers to unite around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and advance towards building a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a snapshot of how Chinese academics and official institutions currently frame the memory, teaching and research agenda of the Korean War.

The planning wisdom of Chinese Communists: a long-termist outlook on economic and social development 中国共产党人的规划智慧：一种长期主义的经济社会发展观 Qu Jing An Weifu Published in Guangming Daily on 27 October 2025, just after the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) adopted the Party's proposals for the 15th Five-Year Plan, this commentary asks what lies behind the Party's practice of drawing up and successively carrying out five-year plans. Qu Jing and An Weifu argue that the achievements of Chinese modernization are not a sudden "miracle" but the product of a distinctively Chinese long-termist outlook on economic and social development, which they call the planning wisdom of Chinese Communists. The authors organise the piece around three questions: what planning is, why it is needed, and how plans are made and implemented. They draw on the history of the plans from the first (1953–57) to the 15th, citing Mao Zedong, Engels and Xi Jinping, official documents and examples from specific plans. The text is a short newspaper commentary rather than a detailed study. On the first question, the authors say planning arose from China's conditions of scattered, small-scale production in 1949 and, after reform and opening up, became a remedy for the defects of spontaneous market adjustment. They define it along two dimensions, looking further in time and wider in space. On the second, they offer three reasons: planning is the necessary route for late-developing countries to "take off"; it addresses market failure and, in their view, forms an organic whole with the market; and it joins strategic goals to policies and concrete measures under a Party that coordinates the whole. On the third, they list three principles: a people-centred stance; research and consultation that combine top-down design with public input, citing over 3.113 million online suggestions for the 15th plan; and a clear implementation mechanism with defined responsibilities. The authors conclude that this process keeps socialist construction going "generation after generation" with "one blueprint followed to the end", and that this is what makes the outlook long-termist. They present the plans as consistent in aiming at a modern socialist country while uniting long-term goals with stage-by-stage tasks. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese commentators justify five-year planning ahead of the 15th Five-Year Plan period.

Methodological self-awareness in advancing the systematisation and academic grounding of the Party's innovative theory in the new era 新时代推进党的创新理论体系化学理化研究的方法论自觉 Duan Yan Duan Yan takes up Xi Jinping's statement that advancing the systematisation (tixihua) and academic grounding (xueli hua) of theory is an inherent requirement and important route of theoretical innovation. The article asks why this work matters for the Party's innovative theory since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and what methodology should govern it. Duan argues that the research should be guided consciously by the Two Integrations and the "Six Musts" of the 20th Party Congress report (2022), and carried out across three systems: disciplines, scholarship and discourse. The article has three parts. The first sets out the significance of the work, the second the methodological principles to follow, and the third the practical paths. Duan defines systematisation as turning concepts, principles and methods into a coherent, layered organic whole, and academic grounding as revealing the determinate content of theory through induction, deduction, analysis and abstraction. The two are described as mutually reinforcing. On significance, Duan argues that the work helps build China's autonomous knowledge system and strengthens the standing of Chinese philosophy and social science. In this account, Western countries now exercise hegemony through knowledge production, with Western modernization theory as the main example. The work also converts political and academic discourse into popular and external discourse, raising the theory's appeal and international reach. On method, the Two Integrations are said to guide the study of original and signature concepts such as Chinese modernization, the new-type party system and the Party's self-reform institutions, which are derived from practice and tested against it. The Six Musts (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, a systems approach, and a worldwide perspective) are treated as a layered whole that shapes how the theory is built. For practice, Duan calls for coordinated disciplines, with interdisciplinary study of new quality productive forces as an example. Duan also proposes links between textbooks and ideological and political courses, training for the "five armies" of theoretical talent, academic platforms and think tanks, and a discourse system that connects political, academic and popular language at home and uses targeted narratives abroad to counter what the article calls Western discourse traps. The article concludes that the whole Party should consciously adopt this methodology so that the theory is rooted in China and recognised worldwide. Read the original if you want a Party-theory view of how Chinese scholars are directed to organise research on Xi Jinping Thought and the construction of an autonomous knowledge system.

The historical evolution and reflective construction of Chinese cultural subjectivity 中华文化主体性的历史嬗变与省思建构 Chen Hongjuan How did Chinese culture lose, and then regain, its cultural subjectivity? Chen Hongjuan treats cultural subjectivity as a culture's capacity to absorb and integrate the "other" and to innovate consciously, and as the basis of cultural confidence. The article argues that this subjectivity was strong before the Opium War, collapsed in modern times, and was rebuilt, consolidated and then raised up under the leadership of the Communist Party of China. The article is organised chronologically in three parts. It first covers the display and loss of subjectivity, from the ancient "all under heaven" order to the post-1840 crisis. It then examines the Party's rebuilding of subjectivity in the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and reform and opening up. The third part addresses the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Chen's core argument rests on three tasks that the Party is said to have handled dialectically in each period. The first is to identify the "subject" of cultural innovation: the Party rejected both wholesale Westernization and restorationist cultural conservatism, sifting the "essence" of tradition from its "dross". The second is to assimilate foreign culture on the principle of "China as the main body, foreign things serving China". The third is to create new culture by combining Marxism with Chinese culture. For the new era, Chen adds that cultural subjectivity has moved from defence to assertion. The author describes the Two Integrations as ending older confusions over Marxism and tradition and turning an implicit method into a conscious one. Chen also holds that Chinese culture can offer "Chinese wisdom" for problems of Western modernity, and contrasts this with a declining Western-centrism. Chen concludes that Chinese cultural subjectivity is not nostalgia for tradition. In the author's account it is a living cultural organism, shaped by adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and confirmed through Chinese modernization. Clarifying this history, the author suggests, offers a guide for strengthening cultural subjectivity further. Read the original if you want a periodised Party-historical account of how official discourse links cultural subjectivity, the Two Integrations and Chinese modernization, with many citations of Party leaders and Republican-era debates.

Chinese modernization offers lessons for development in the Global South 中国式现代化为全球南方发展提供经验启示 Xu Xiuli Li Xiaoyun Xu Xiuli and Li Xiaoyun ask what Chinese modernization can contribute to development studies and to the Global South. They argue that it offers useful lessons for resolving three classic dilemmas in global development theory. The first is how to balance independent national development with integration into the international order. The second is how to handle relations among government, market and society so that they combine forces while keeping a productive tension. The third is how to "go out" into development cooperation while moving beyond colonial and hegemonic models toward a more equal community of development. The article presents Chinese modernization as a driver of a "third academic transformation" in China, in which researchers move beyond a dependent centre–periphery position in global knowledge. It is organised in three sections, one per dilemma, each setting China's experience against comparative cases. These include African structural adjustment, Mexican and Venezuelan import substitution and "delinking", Argentina's instability, fragmented African states with strong civil-society organisations, and the divide between "big" and "small" development. On the first dilemma, the authors argue that integration and sovereignty need not be opposed. They credit sustained reform and opening up, "selective learning" and keeping control of the development process, and they cite Deng Xiaoping's remark to the World Bank president. They contrast this with Africa, where adjustment programmes allegedly produced debt, aid dependence and unrest, and with Mexico and Venezuela, where radical delinking brought inflation and crisis. On the second, they present poverty reduction as a model in which government, market and society are embedded in one another, and they link Argentina's decline to weak political institutions. On the third, they describe China's "win-win" platforms, new institutions and global initiatives, together with "parallel experience sharing" that matches the partner's stage of development and treats partners as equals. The authors conclude that developing countries should keep independent development as the core goal, integrate into the existing international system pragmatically and step by step, and allow trial and error. They should build an "effective government, efficient market and vigorous society" around priorities fixed for each stage, and draw on South–South cooperation's principles of no political conditions and mutual benefit. They also call on Global South states to revive the tradition of "uniting for self-strengthening". Read the original if you want a Chinese development-studies account of Chinese modernization, set against African and Latin American cases and framed for Global South audiences.

Origins and discursive innovation of the concept of a "high-standard socialist market economy" A conceptual-history study “高水平社会主义市场经济体制”概念的源流考释与话语创新 Hu Rongtao Peng Yiming Hu Rongtao and Peng Yiming ask where the concept of a "high-standard socialist market economy" (高水平社会主义市场经济体制) comes from and what is new about it. They note that existing scholarship has treated its challenges, features, logic and tasks but has paid little attention to its conceptual history. The article argues that the concept, presented as a "new type of relations of production" suited to new quality productive forces, took shape over a long process of Party exploration of the government–market relationship. In their account it is an original concept produced by the Two Integrations. The article has three parts. The first traces the concept's discursive sources: the economic-system ideas of Marx, Engels and Lenin (including the New Economic Policy), late Qing and early Republican thinking on state and market (Wang Tao, Zheng Guanying, Liang Qichao, Sun Yat-sen, Zhang Jian), and early Communists such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Cai Hesen. The second follows its formation from the 1930s planned-economy debates, through Mao Zedong, Chen Yun and Zhang Wentian, to the "socialist market economy" of the reform era. The third assesses its discursive innovation. In the authors' reading, the formation runs from planning with some market elements, through a "planned commodity economy", to the socialist market economy system proposed under Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin. Party documents then moved from the market's "basic role" to its "decisive role" and from "macro-control" to "better playing the role of government". The 19th Central Committee's Fifth Plenum formally introduced the "high-standard" formulation, and the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) placed it first among the reform priorities. The authors identify three innovations. It enriches the discourse through "upholding fundamental principles while innovating", and it criticises Western neoliberal economic discourse. It extends dialectical thinking on an "efficient market and a capable government". And it contributes to a "revolution in terminology" in the discourse of Chinese modernization, covering its desired form, its actual form and its means of realisation. Hu and Peng conclude that the concept marks a more mature and settled basic economic system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They also hold that it gives Chinese modernization an institutional content and offers legitimacy resources for the Party's long-term rule. They present building such a system as a necessary path for deepening reform comprehensively. Read the original if you want a detailed genealogy of this Party formulation and a view of how Chinese scholars present its conceptual history.

Virtual simulation experiments empowering ideological and political theory courses: an innovative exploration 虚拟仿真实验赋能思政课教学的创新探索 Zhang Yu Wang Qingqing Zhang Yu and Wang Qingqing ask how virtual simulation experiments (VR-based teaching) can be built into university ideological and political theory courses so that they raise the courses' relevance and appeal. They note that current use is mostly for demonstration, for extracurricular activities and by a minority of teachers, which leaves it superficial and formalistic. Their answer, drawn from the Tsinghua University course "Ideological and Moral Cultivation and the Rule of Law", is that the technology works only when it is embedded in the classroom as a regular part of teaching, under the teacher's guidance. The article has four parts. It first sets out why such experiments are needed: the digital age, the generational traits of students described as "digital natives", and the "big ideological and political course" initiative. It then describes the Tsinghua teaching model. Next it identifies the regularities by which the experiments work, namely knowledge transmission, emotional cultivation and value guidance. Finally it proposes innovation paths. The case material is VR experiences built around the lives of Deng Jiaxian and Nan Rendong. The core of the argument is a small-class blended model. About 15 students, in five groups, choose one of six themes, such as life values, ideals and convictions, or the spirit of scientists. Each session moves from a teacher's lecture to an immersive VR experience, then group discussion, presentations, peer review and a teacher's summary. The authors insist that technology must not weaken the teacher's leading role, and they cite classroom questionnaires in which most students said the method improved engagement and sense of gain. They argue that VR supplies intuitive, multimodal knowledge, that immersion creates the emotional identification on which value formation rests, and that discussion of real-world issues turns experience into reflection and action. Values guidance is presented as the ultimate aim. The authors propose three paths. The first is a new teaching model that unites teacher leadership with student agency. The second is to integrate the experiments into the "big ideological and political course" framework as low-cost practical education, with suitable themes and carefully designed processes. The third is to build platforms and shared resources across universities and school levels, to research teaching methods, and to strengthen teachers' ability to educate online. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-based account of how a Chinese university integrates VR into Party-led ideological education, including its course design and the officially stated rationale.

Consolidating and developing the subjectivity of Chinese culture and the principles it requires 中华文化主体性的巩固发展及其原则遵循 Xu Guomin Shi Yutong Xu Guomin and Shi Yutong take up the question of how the subjectivity of Chinese culture (中华文化主体性) can be consolidated and developed. They start from Xi Jinping's 2023 remark that cultural confidence comes from cultural subjectivity. The authors argue that many scholars treat subjectivity as a static essence and remain trapped in oppositional thinking. In their view it is a dynamic "cultural complex" formed through the practice of national rejuvenation, and its philosophical basis is the theory of integration and of comprehensive innovation. The article has three parts. The first traces the century-long dispute over "ancient and modern, China and the West", from Wei Yuan, the Self-Strengthening Movement's "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application" and the Reformers Kang Youwei and Yan Fu, through Sun Yat-sen and the New Culture Movement, to Li Zehou's "Western substance, Chinese application". It then reviews Zhang Dainian's "comprehensive innovation" and Fang Keli's "Marxism as soul, Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application". The second part follows how the Party consolidated cultural subjectivity in four periods. The third derives guiding principles. The authors contend that Chinese cultural subjectivity has a Marxist "soul vein" and a traditional-culture "root vein", and that it is a product of the Two Integrations. They say this complex unifies dialectical and analytical thinking, collectivism and individualism, and "one guiding principle" with "diverse development". In their account, Marxism's guiding position is the fundamental principle. They hold that the creative transformation of fine traditional culture, above all through the second integration, is the most basic one. They add that absorbing the rational elements of Western culture, after rejecting Western-centrism, is an important third principle. The article concludes that handling the relations among Marxism, fine traditional Chinese culture and Western culture, and so building a pattern of "one dominant, many diverse", lies at the core of consolidating cultural subjectivity. All of this, the authors say, must serve Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They also hold that comprehensive-innovation theory still leaves the relative status of the three components unclear. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how debates on Chinese versus Western learning are recast around Marxism and the Two Integrations.

On the comparative research method in ideological and political education 论思想政治教育比较研究方法 Gao Di Tang Songge Comparative research has been part of the discipline of ideological and political education since the 1980s. Gao and Tang ask what the comparative method is, why it is justified and how it should be used. Their thesis is that, as the discipline builds an autonomous knowledge system, the method must be clarified and made more scientific. In their account it rests on Marxist premises and must be anchored in China's own standpoint and needs. The article has three parts. The first gives a theoretical account of the method and its value. The second builds a typology of methods. The third sets out principles for applying it. The authors survey five existing ways of classifying comparative methods, such as by social-science levels, by descriptive, analytical and explanatory comparison, or by research steps. They then propose their own scheme, organised by research purpose. Gao and Tang describe the method as a fusion of qualitative and quantitative work, combining synchronic and diachronic comparison. It holds a necessary tension between objectivity and subjectivity. They ground it in the dialectic of the universal and the particular, in Marx's theory of world history and in Marx's idea of the "other", which they read as critical borrowing measured by China's own yardstick. Their four types are comparison-description, comparison-attribution, comparison-prediction and comparison-mutual construction, and these can be combined. Three principles follow. First, Marxist views of comparison require that like be compared with like, that all the relevant facts be grasped and that the underlying essence be revealed. Second, comparison should proceed from Chinese standpoint and needs, strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence, solving practical problems and offering "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions". Third, it should serve the autonomous knowledge system through greater methodological rigour, a clearer logical architecture and more self-conscious innovation. The authors conclude that the comparative method has long borrowed tools from other disciplines, and these carry the "other's" ways of seeing. They call for methods that express the discipline's own nature and for a consistent "I"-centred perspective when judging forms of ideological and political education elsewhere. Read the original if you study the methodology of ideological and political education in China, or want to see how Chinese scholars link Marxist theory, national standpoint and the building of an autonomous knowledge system in discussing comparative research.

The methodology by which the "Second Integration" creates a new cultural organism “第二个结合”造就新的文化生命体的方法论探赜 Ma Mingchong Ma Mingchong takes up a formula from Xi Jinping's 2023 speech on cultural inheritance and development: the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture is not a "platter" or a physical mixture but a "chemical reaction" that produces an organically unified new cultural organism. The article asks what methodological foundations, components and functions lie behind this process. Ma argues that the Second Integration rests on a Marxist philosophy of practice and gives rise to five modes of thinking that serve the building of a socialist cultural power and Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the philosophical basis: Marx's critical inheritance from Kant and Hegel, and the contemporary activation of traditional Chinese philosophical resources. The second presents the methodological components, namely strategic, historical, dialectical, systems and innovative thinking. The third considers the methodological functions, first as a window on the laws governing the building of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, and then as a dialectical method for handling relations such as active and passive, tradition and modernity, and universal and particular. In the first part, Ma reads Kant's cultural theory as bound to a dualism of subject and object, and Hegel's as the self-movement of the Absolute Spirit. Marx, in Ma's account, grounds culture in the material practice of the working people and thereby gives it subjective initiative and a practical ontology. Ma then argues that Chinese ideas can be reactivated on this basis, such as "the people are most important" becoming a people-centred philosophy of governance, and the ideal of great harmony becoming a community with a shared future for mankind. The five modes of thinking are described as an organic whole that dismantles "Western centrism", the "end of history" thesis and historical nihilism. Ma also rejects Karl Popper's reading of Marxism as economic determinism, stressing culture's independence and its reaction on the economy. Ma concludes that the five dimensions of methodology form a rigorous theoretical system that supplies a philosophical coordinate for socialist cultural construction. He also presents it as offering a Chinese approach to global cultural governance and to a new form of human civilization. The article traces a historical line from Mao Zedong's "make the past serve the present" through Deng Xiaoping's cultural policy to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), which it describes as a move from "theoretical transplantation" to "independent innovation". Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholars ground the Second Integration philosophically and tie it to claims about civilization and global order.
