Innovating the scenario methods of ideological and political education in the era of large models 大模型时代思想政治教育场景方法创新 Zhao Jianchao Wen Yanfei Zhao Jianchao and Wen Yanfei ask how large AI models are changing the "scenes" (changjing) in which ideological and political education is carried out, and what methods should follow. They define an educational scenario as the deep fusion of a "field" (the web of connections mediated by educational technology) and a "scene" (the values conveyed through it). Their thesis is that large models bring a "scenario revolution": the field becomes interconnected, cross-boundary and co-created, and the educational scene becomes more personalised, integrated and emergent. Published in Ideological and Theoretical Education (2025, no. 8), the article follows a three-step line of inquiry: scenario narrative, scenario analysis and scenario evolution. Narrative is examined through four dimensions: subject, time, space and ideology. Analysis is examined through four techniques: data mining, network analysis, modelling and simulation, and computational experiments. Evolution is examined through four system properties: self-adaptation, self-organisation, self-replication and self-creation. On narrative, the authors argue that large models move subject narrative from informational to node-based forms, time narrative from real-time to user-defined, and space narrative from mass communication to "pan-audience" communication centred on each individual and to social integration. In ideological narrative, they say the models supply fuller content that meets learners' need for mainstream ideology, and use "filtering" and "selection" strategies to prompt recognition, so that concrete individuals become identified subjects of the mainstream ideological field. On analysis, they claim models can automatically extract the meaning of scenarios, assess their value, build digital twins and run parallel virtual and real experiments that complement each other. On evolution, they hold that models activate the scenario's capacity to adapt, self-organise, replicate through "genetic information" and create, ending in whole-system emergence. The authors conclude that innovating scenario methods through this narrative–analysis–evolution logic can raise the efficiency, benefit and effect of scenario-based education, and that intelligent transformation opens a new path for the field. The argument is conceptual and framework-building, with no empirical case studies and no discussion of risks. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education conceptualise AI, digital scenarios and ideological recognition, and want the detailed taxonomy of methods.

The theoretical implications, institutional innovation and practical paths of "the Eight-Point Regulation changes China" “八项规定改变中国”的理论意蕴、制度创新与实践路径 Cai Zhiqiang Xiao Ruining Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee headed by Xi Jinping has treated the Central Committee's Eight-Point Regulation on Party conduct as the opening move in governing the Party. Cai Zhiqiang and Xiao Ruining ask what theoretical meaning, institutional innovation and practical path this measure represents. They argue that, by using concrete behavioural bans as a "small entry point", it has reshaped the institutional framework of Party conduct and become a "golden calling card" of Party governance. In their view its significance goes well beyond conduct itself. The article has three parts. The first places the regulation within the adaptation of Marxist Party-building theory to Chinese conditions, under three heads: the people-centred values of a Marxist party, new routes for the Party's self-reform, and a new paradigm of Party building. The second treats it as a revolutionary creation in governing the Party and the country, covering its roots in the Party's traditions, its institutional breakthroughs and its political functions. The third sets out four paths for implementation in the new era. The authors argue that the regulation inherits the Party's fine style, from the Yan'an rectification to the "Two Musts", while changing the mode of governance. They say it moved from temporary, campaign-style requirements to a standing, closed-loop system of rule-making, inspection, accountability and improvement. It also combines inner-Party supervision with popular supervision, and joins the "first answer" (democracy) and the "second answer" (self-reform) to the Party's historical-cycle question. They describe it as a shift from guarding mainly against external threats such as "colour revolution" to a self-reforming type of Party building. They link conduct to corruption, noting that "wind and corruption" often appear together and need to be investigated together. They also credit it with restoring public trust and cutting the corrosive influence of capital on political power. For implementation, the authors call for four steps. These are regular study and education; precise special campaigns against new, disguised forms of the "Four Undesirable Work Styles", using big data and similar tools; long-term institutions, including a responsibility system, tailored local rules, supervision loops, technology-enabled oversight and a culture of integrity; and systematic, coordinated governance that links the regulation to national and grassroots governance. They conclude that the regulation should be sustained until good conduct becomes custom, and built into Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-school account of how the Eight-Point Regulation is framed theoretically and how current anti-formalism and anti-corruption work is meant to be taken forward.

The evolution of ancient Chinese supervisory legislation and its lessons for today 古代监察立法的流变与当今镜鉴 Shu Shaofu Shu Shaofu asks what the long history of supervisory (jiancha) legislation in imperial China can offer to present-day anti-corruption lawmaking. Starting from Xi Jinping's calls at the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection plenary sessions to continue national anti-corruption legislation and revise the Supervision Law, the author argues that the best of ancient supervisory law is part of fine traditional Chinese culture. Drawing on it, Shu contends, can help advance anti-corruption legislation and the effort to make officials unwilling, unable and not daring to be corrupt. The article is a historical survey that moves through three stages. It first covers the "embryonic" stage from the pre-Qin period to the Qin, with the Rites of Zhou, the Lü Xing and the Qin bamboo slips from Shuihudi. It then traces the "flourishing" of local supervisory regulations from the Han through the Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties, Sui and Tang. Finally, it examines the "maturing" of the system under the Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing, ending with the Qing Qinding taigui as the fullest supervisory code. A closing section draws lessons for today. Shu's central claim is that supervisory law developed from provisions scattered inside criminal and administrative codes into stand-alone regulations and finally into comprehensive codes. Examples include the Han Six Articles for Inquiry, the Song rules for mutual monitoring among supervisory officials, and the Yuan regulations for establishing the censorate. The author stresses that these laws bound the supervisors as well as the supervised, and formed a network covering the centre and the localities. From this the author draws three lessons: keep revising and refining law, build a complete and well-connected body of regulations, and develop a supervisory culture. Shu proposes keeping the Supervision Law up to date, especially against new and hidden forms of corruption. The author also calls for filling gaps in the law on anti-corruption procedure, oversight and remedies, and for amending the Legislation Law so that the National Supervisory Commission has equivalent legislative powers. Shu further proposes aligning the Supervision Law with the Criminal Procedure Law and the Audit Law, and cultivating a supervisory culture that draws on traditional integrity ideals. Read the original if you want a detailed dynasty-by-dynasty survey of ancient supervisory statutes, or want to see how Chinese legal scholars link historical precedent to current anti-corruption legislation.

Marx and Engels's fourfold critique of Russian populism and its scientific method 马克思恩格斯对俄国民粹主义的四重批判及其科学方法 Ji Mengling Wang Yonggui How did Marx and Engels respond to the Russian populist claim that Russia could bypass capitalism and move directly to socialism? Ji and Wang argue that their response was a sustained, four-part critique, aimed at what the authors call the theories of village-commune superiority, Russian revolutionary advantage, the peasantry as revolutionary subject, and a non-capitalist path. The authors present this critique as a model of scientific method for confronting erroneous currents of thought today. The article takes each of the four targets in turn, drawing on Marx and Engels's polemics with Herzen's successors and with the revolutionary populists Lavrov, Bakunin and Tkachev. Texts discussed include Engels's writings on Russia's social question, Marx's letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski, his correspondence with Vera Zasulich, and the 1882 Russian preface to the Communist Manifesto. Each section pairs a populist claim with the analytical method the authors see Marx and Engels using against it: historical, comparative, class and dialectical analysis. On the commune, Ji and Wang report that Marx and Engels treated communal land ownership and the labour artel as forms found at low stages of development across many peoples. In their reading, the survival of these forms showed Russian backwardness, and the commune carried an internal duality of common arable land and private plots that drove its decay, which the 1861 reform accelerated. Against Tkachev, Engels argued that socialist revolution presupposes both bourgeoisie and proletariat. He also argued that the tsarist state served the nobility and that exploitation by nobles, usurers and speculators already resembled capitalist relations. Against reliance on the peasantry, he stressed peasant isolation and weakness, citing the quickly extinguished Spanish rising organised by Bakunin. Ji and Wang conclude that Marx and Engels did not deny a non-capitalist path but analysed it dialectically. The commune could not generate anything new from itself, and communal property was disappearing. Russia's chance of skipping the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism depended on a Russian revolution complementing proletarian revolution in the West. The authors add that Engels continued after Marx's death to call for struggle against populists everywhere, and they hold that this critique offers methodological guidance for criticising mistaken social trends now. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of the Marx–Engels debate with Russian populism and of how that debate is used as a method for ideological critique.

The temporal horizon of Marx's dialectics and its historical significance 马克思辩证法的时间性视域及其历史意义 Liu Shaoming Liu Shaoming asks how temporality conditions the appearance of dialectics in Marx's philosophy, a question the author says existing scholarship has not addressed. Earlier studies, Liu notes, stress the consistency, internal unity or mutual interpretation of dialectics and history, but do not show what Marx's temporality does for dialectics. The article argues that a phenomenological 'original time' in Marx's theory is the condition under which the dialectical subject, its negativity and its basic forms become manifest. The article begins by contrasting dialectics (which privileges mediation and negation) with phenomenology (which privileges immediate givenness), and argues that the two can be combined. Drawing on Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Marcuse, Liu reads Marx as performing a transcendental reduction that returns individual, nature and society to sensuous practical activity. Three sections then take up three temporal horizons: simultaneity, futurity and the historical field. A final section compares Marx with Hegel. In Liu's account, simultaneity unites subject and object, and individual and society, in one practical activity, so that the true dialectical subject is 'individual–society–nature'. Futurity, expressed in survival and reproduction, self-confirmation and the pursuit of truth, brings out primordial difference and self-negation. The historical field, in which past, present and future are unified, is where the negation of the negation and the unity of opposites appear; Liu treats the latter as derived from the former, using the relation of productive forces and relations of production as an example. The three horizons are said to form a methodological and a real unity. Liu concludes that Marx inherits Hegel's concepts of subject, negativity and historicity, but surpasses Hegel's 'non-temporal' dialectics. Hegel's absolute spirit is, in this reading, abstract, its negativity feigned and its future already fixed, and his concept is placed above time. Marx's temporal dialectics supplies a real basis for the subject, its motive force and its forms, and so becomes a tool for criticising reality and exposing the 'eternal present'. Read the original if you work on Marx's dialectics, phenomenological readings of Marx, or the Marx–Hegel relation and want a detailed argument built on Husserl, Heidegger and Marcuse.

Synchronous advancement of ideological and political course construction and arming minds with the Party's innovative theory: its integrative meaning and practical path 坚持思政课建设与党的创新理论武装同步推进的一体化意蕴及其实践进路 Luo Hongjie In May 2024 Xi Jinping instructed that the construction of ideological and political courses in schools should proceed in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory. Luo Hongjie takes up this instruction, abbreviated as 'synchronous advancement', and asks what logic lies behind it, what problems it addresses and what goal it serves. The article argues that the formula is best read through the lens of 'integration' (yitihua), meaning orderly connection across space and effective sequencing across time, and that this reading clarifies both its theoretical basis and its practice. The article is built in three parts. The first sets out the integrative meaning of the formula along three aspects: course construction, theoretical arming, and the combination of the two, including coordination across primary, secondary and tertiary schooling. The second offers a theoretical account drawing on Marx, Lenin and Engels, and on the notions of 'ideological reality' and 'theoretical reality'. The third proposes a practical path and ends with three relationships to be handled. Luo's core argument has two moves. First, drawing on Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force once it grips the masses, Lenin's theory of 'inculcation' from outside, and the gap between students' 'ideological reality' (their actual thinking) and the 'theoretical reality' of an evolving theory, Luo contends that synchronisation must be continuous and integrated. Second, the practical path follows a 'point–plane–body' sequence. The 'point' identifies problems: fragmented and passive theoretical arming, partial and delayed integration of theory into teaching, and low enthusiasm for theoretical interpretation, with teachers and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as key subject and content. The 'plane' calls for horizontal integration through textbooks, teaching methods and content. The 'body' calls for vertical sequencing across school stages through coordinated actors, graded content and institutional mechanisms. Luo concludes that synchronisation should keep students' ideological reality, theoretical reality and practical reality consistent. The author proposes that time and space, leading and receiving subjects, and the three 'realities' be handled as paired relationships. Luo also distinguishes this formula from integration of ideological education across school stages: the former concerns bringing the Party's theory into every stage's courses, the latter concerns repetition and gaps between stages. Read the original if you study Chinese ideological and political education and want a detailed Chinese-language account of how the 2024 instruction is being theorised and operationalised.

Marx's transcendence of Feuerbach's doctrine of "sensuous intuition" and the formation of historical materialism 马克思对费尔巴哈“感性直观”学说的超越与历史唯物主义的生成 Li Chengwang Xu Ziyang Engels called Feuerbach an intermediate link between Hegel's philosophy and the Marxist standpoint. Li and Xu ask why Marx's transcendence of Feuerbach's "sensuous intuition" should be seen as a key step in the formation of historical materialism. They argue that existing scholarship oversimplifies the question: it stresses either Feuerbach's abstract "species-essence" or his reliance on sensuousness, and so obscures how the two aspects of his doctrine fit together. The article is a history-of-ideas reconstruction in three parts. The first examines how Feuerbach criticised Fichte's "intellectual intuition" and Hegel's philosophy of spirit in order to build his own doctrine. The second explains why the young Marx, from his legal studies in Berlin through the Rheinische Zeitung and the Paris Manuscripts, drew on Feuerbach. The third shows how the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology went beyond him. On the authors' reading, Feuerbach answered Fichte's split between the transcendental and empirical self by making a sensuous subject with real needs the starting point. He answered Hegel's self-moving concept by holding that sensuous objects can be grasped only through species-thinking. Marx's early difficulties were the opposition between what is and what ought to be, and Hegel's "logical, pantheistic mysticism" on material interests. Feuerbach's ideas helped Marx with both, and with his critique of alienated labour and money in the Paris Manuscripts. The authors then argue that Marx came to see sensuous intuition as merely theoretical. The Theses replace it with "objective activity", that is, practice, and define human essence as the ensemble of social relations. The German Ideology develops this into a theory of comprehensive production, with five forms of production, and into a theory of relations of production. On this account the world Feuerbach intuits is in fact a historical product, and no transcendental species-essence is needed to explain illusory ideology, which the authors trace to the naturally arising division of labour. The authors conclude that moving beyond Feuerbach was necessary for Marx to unify thought and being in practice and to create a scientific theory of history. That theory could also propose abolishing capitalist private ownership, which a moral critique of alienation could not do. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the Fichte–Hegel–Feuerbach–Marx line of development and of how the Paris Manuscripts, the Theses and The German Ideology relate to Feuerbach.

Marx's historical and class consciousness in examining the transformation of money into capital 马克思考察货币转化为资本的历史意识与阶级意识 Liu Jingdong Liu Jingdong asks how Marx's account of the transformation of money into capital, and of labour-power becoming a commodity, supplies a framework for understanding both the birth of capital and its world history. The article argues that Marx's critique of capital and of political economy rests on an organic unity of historical consciousness and class consciousness. In Liu's reading, this unity lets Marx explain the shift from traditional to modern modes of production and expose the exploitative essence behind apparently free and equal exchange. The article draws mainly on Volume 1 of Capital (Part Two, 'The Transformation of Money into Capital'), on Volume 2's chapter on the circuit of money capital, and on Marx's 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts. It has four sections. The first treats money becoming capital as the precondition of the move from traditional to modern production. The second treats the emergence of capital and the free worker. The third examines the social conditions of the circuit of money capital and the new class relations. A short conclusion follows. Liu makes three main moves. First, the author contrasts simple circulation (C–M–C, aimed at use-value) with the circulation of capital (M–C–M′, aimed at self-expanding value), and treats the capitalist as 'personified capital' driven only by surplus value. Marx's contradiction in the general formula is resolved, Liu says, only by labour-power becoming a commodity, whose use creates more value than it costs. Second, labour-power can be a commodity only where workers are free in a double sense, which is the historical result of primitive accumulation separating producers from the means of production. Marx's remark that this condition 'contains a whole world history' is read as having both a temporal and a spatial meaning. Third, in the circuit M–C…P…C′–M′ the purchase of labour-power looks like a fair contract, yet the author argues that it conceals exploitation. Bourgeois economists such as McCulloch miss this because of their class position and non-historical thinking, in Liu's account. Liu concludes that Marx identified the commodity status of labour-power as the social-historical condition for money to become capital, and so traced the mechanism of transition from traditional society to modern capitalism. By piercing the 'veil' of free and equal exchange, Marx, on this reading, reached his judgement that capitalist commodity production is an epoch-making mode of exploitation. The article also treats the way labour and the means of production are combined as a basic criterion for distinguishing social formations. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reading of Capital Volumes 1 and 2 that stresses the unity of historical method and class standpoint in Marx's critique of capital.

Foreign Marxists' critique of capitalist modernization 国外马克思主义者对资本主义现代化的批判 Ma Xinying Ma Xinying asks how Marxists outside China have criticised capitalist modernization in the twenty-first century, and what that critique shows. The article argues that, even in the digital age, capitalist modernization remains a troublemaker in world modernization because of capitalism's inherent contradictions. In Ma's account, foreign Marxists combine Marx's critical stance with new theoretical resources to produce a new critique. The article has three parts. The first surveys six strands of critique: digital capitalism, biopolitics, the modern state (including new imperialism), ecological crisis, space, and modern society (alienation and social acceleration). Thinkers discussed include Dan Schiller, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Giorgio Agamben, Roberto Esposito, Bob Jessop, Edward Soja, Rahel Jaeggi and Hartmut Rosa. The second part identifies three trends distinguishing this work from twentieth-century critique, and the third assesses its significance. Ma's central claim concerns the three shifts. Critique moves from diachronic to synchronic, borrowing Saussure's terms: it no longer traces modernization's historical origins but cuts across its present features and their internal connections. It moves from critiquing modernity to critiquing modernization itself, because, Ma says, postmodern discourse has dissolved the authority of metaphysical reason and modernity's harms are now accepted as given. And it moves from socio-cultural to political critique, with hegemony, power, justice and biopower as key concepts, reactivated by the 2008 financial crisis. Ma concludes that this critique exposes new contradictions of contemporary capitalism, which the article calls international financial monopoly capitalism. It also shows that a fragile planet cannot bear capitalist modernization, and that capitalism's private appropriation is increasingly incompatible with globalization. Ma notes that foreign Marxists such as John Bellamy Foster and David Kotz are less pessimistic than before, because socialist modernization offers a new point of reference. The article presents Chinese modernization as embodying a more progressive path of civilisation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Western and foreign Marxist theories of digital capitalism, biopolitics, space and alienation are classified and evaluated in Chinese academic discourse.

How latecomer countries can develop productive forces: starting from Marx's critique of Friedrich List's The National System of Political Economy 后发国家如何发展生产力——从马克思的《评弗里德里希·李斯特的著作〈政治经济学的国民体系〉》谈起 Chen Liangbin Marking the 180th anniversary of Marx's 1845 manuscript on Friedrich List's The National System of Political Economy, Chen Liangbin asks how latecomer countries can develop their productive forces. Chen argues that List's programme for German catch-up serves the German bourgeoisie, that Marx both criticised and surpassed it, and that Marx's own theory of productive forces gives scientific guidance to latecomers. The renewed interest in a 'neo-Listian school' in the early twenty-first century is the stated reason for revisiting the text. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs List's theory of national productive forces, which rests on a critique of Adam Smith's cosmopolitan free trade and has three components: state intervention, priority for industry and protective tariffs. The second sets out Marx's critique of each component, then traces how Marx's productive-forces theory developed from the German Ideology through the Grundrisse and Capital to the 1859 Preface, and finally his late view of Russia and the 'Caudine Forks of capitalism'. The third draws implications for developing new quality productive forces. In Chen's reading, Marx saw List's state intervention as the hypocrisy of a weak German bourgeoisie seeking state protection while dressing its interests in the language of national spirit. List's industrial priority confused the forces that industry awakens, meaning the workers, with the capitalist industrial system that will eventually be broken by them. List's protective tariffs, Chen says, are the same capital logic as free trade, binding a country to the world market. Chen holds that Marx surpassed List by adopting a proletarian standpoint and locating Germany's backwardness in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Chen distinguishes a micro level, with subjective and objective productive forces and science and technology, from a macro level, the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production. Chen concludes that new quality productive forces require science and technological innovation, reform of production relations to create what Xi Jinping calls new-type production relations, and better coordination of production factors such as data and knowledge. Once List's class standpoint is sublated, Chen adds, his emphasis on state intervention, tariff protection and national spirit still has relevance. Chen links these to the new-type whole-nation system, resistance to foreign trade protectionism and promotion of the Chinese national spirit. Read the original if you want a Chinese account that links Marx's critique of List to current debates on new quality productive forces and technological self-reliance.

The "Schulz factor" in the transformation of the young Marx's philosophical thought An examination based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 青年马克思哲学思想变革中的“舒尔茨因素”探析——基于《1844年经济学哲学手稿》考察 Shao Yu Shao Yu takes up the "Schulz factor": Marx's extended quotations from Wilhelm Schulz's Die Bewegung der Produktion in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, especially Notebook I. The question is what problem led Marx to "material production", and what role and limits Schulz had in the young Marx's philosophical change. Shao argues that Schulz supplied empirical material and a viewpoint from material production, but that Marx's concerns were already formed and he read Schulz from a Feuerbachian standpoint. The article first reviews earlier scholarship, from Cornu and Rubin to Japanese and German studies and recent Chinese work. It then goes through Marx's quotations in two places: the chapter "Wages", on workers' poverty, and the chapter "Profit of Capital", on competition between large and small capitalists. In each case Shao sets Marx's context beside the original context in Schulz. The article ends by assessing the factor's role against Marx's earlier engagement with poverty and with Feuerbach. In Shao's reading, Marx and Schulz share a target: political economy that treats the worker as a labouring animal and offers average wages as evidence of progress. Shao argues that Marx goes further, tracing poverty, alienated labour and the concentration of capital to private property. For that reason Marx judges wage increases and wage equality, as in Proudhon, to be inadequate reforms. Schulz, by contrast, looks to state-led reform and the growth of free time and spiritual life. Shao calls this an abstract "spiritual production" close to Hegel's philosophy of history, whereas Marx holds that civil society determines the political state and that private property must be abolished in social reality. Shao concludes that the Schulz factor had a direct and an indirect effect. It gave Marx an empirical angle for criticising political economy. It also pointed to a way beyond Feuerbach's intuitive materialism, towards historical materialism. Its effect was limited, however. Marx had been thinking about worker poverty and real freedom since the Rheinische Zeitung period, and Schulz mainly reinforced principles he already held. Read the original if you study the formation of Marx's historical materialism or want a close text-based comparison of Marx's excerpts with Schulz's original arguments.

The normative content of Marx's idea of human emancipation and its historical unfolding 马克思人类解放思想的规范性内涵及其历史性展开 Lin Yuchuan Lin Yuchuan takes up an open question in Chinese research on Marx's political philosophy. Is the political philosophy found in Marx's early writings the same as the one implicit in his critique of political economy and historical materialism? If it is, how should the continuity be understood? Lin's answer is that human emancipation is the core proposition of Marx's political philosophy. It is normative, and its normative content becomes more concrete and historical over time without being abandoned. The article has five parts. It first establishes human emancipation as the central proposition, tracing it from Marx's early writings through the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period to the later works. Lin then defends its normative character against the view, illustrated by Hans Kelsen, that historical materialism excludes norms. Next, the article sets out four levels of normative content across Marx's career. Finally it examines the mature period and closes with brief remarks on the present. Lin argues that Kelsen sets up a false opposition between the a priori and the empirical. Historical materialism can accommodate norms once ideas are allowed to act back on the economic base, and norms can be abstracted from empirical facts. On Lin's reading, Marx's early claim that emancipation returns the human world to human beings was derived from the alienation of civil society, not from a purely a priori premise. The four levels are: equal respect and freedom (the Rheinische Zeitung period); conditions for each person's full development, distinguishing political from social emancipation; the emancipation of labour for the proletariat; and an association of free individuals. Lin holds that the critique of exploitation and alienated labour in Capital deepens the early ideas and does not break with them. He therefore rejects readings that base Marx's mature political philosophy on a non-normative concept such as the division of labour. Lin concludes that human emancipation is an era-specific proposition. While humanity remains in the stage of 'dependence on things' and wage labour persists, it takes the form of the emancipation of labour, or the proletariat's social emancipation. In that long stage it breaks down into sub-questions such as winning power, ownership reform, democracy, equality and distributive justice, and rights protection. Lin holds that these can approach Marx's ideal only if grasped from the standpoint of labour's emancipation. Human emancipation is thus presented as a historical mission to be completed through staged tasks. Read the original if you work on Marx's political philosophy, on the normative versus historical-materialist readings of Marx, or on Chinese debates about the unity of the early and mature Marx.

The Two Integrations as a powerful driving force for the development of Chinese philosophy “两个结合”激发中国哲学发展强大动力 Han Donghui Han Donghui reviews Chinese philosophy during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021–2025) in a commentary for the Chinese Social Sciences Today. The author argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Culture has given philosophy strong momentum, and that the Two Integrations have set its direction. The piece surveys the field in broad strokes: the philosophical foundations of the Party's theoretical innovation, the cultural thought associated with Xi, the building of an autonomous knowledge system, and four relationships that Han says that effort has had to handle. It draws on work by Marxist philosophers, scholars of Chinese tradition and Chinese scholars of Western philosophy. Han presents the Two Integrations, especially the second, as the basic guide and scientific method for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In this account they have extended historical materialism and the epistemology of practice, and have informed a methodology of seven modes of thinking. Han describes an autonomous knowledge system as neither simple "de-Westernization" nor a mere return to origins. It is meant to be rooted in Chinese practice and to engage in equal dialogue abroad. Examples include the concept of "Chinese Marxist philosophy", work on "all under heaven" and "great unification", and proposals for Chinese phenomenology and Sinophone philosophy. The four relationships are core research versus real-world concerns, reinterpreting the classics versus creative transformation, technology ethics, and self-confidence versus mutual learning among civilizations. Han concludes that philosophers have strengthened cultural subjectivity and academic autonomy by linking past and present, tradition and modernity, and the local and the international. Looking to the next five years, Han expects a philosophy rooted in China yet global in outlook. Read the original if you want a brief official-academic overview of how Chinese philosophy presented its recent agenda under the Two Integrations.

Writing the early industrial history of the Republic: a field report on the "156 Projects" research team 书写共和国早期工业发展史——“156项工程调研”项目组纪实 Zhang Yixin This is a newspaper feature by a reporter for China Social Sciences Today (22 October 2025), based on interviews with the "156 Projects" research team at the Institute of Economics, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The 156 Projects were the key industrial construction projects of the First Five-Year Plan period. Zhang presents them as the foundation of New China's industrialisation and reports on how the team has studied them. The article's thesis, in the team's words, is that reform of state-owned enterprises cannot simply copy a market template. It must balance historical experience, national strategy and social responsibility. The report describes several years of fieldwork across more than ten provinces and cities, covering 30 key enterprises. It visits Yunnan Tin (Gejiu), North China Pharmaceutical, Lanzhou Petrochemical, Wuhan Iron and Steel, China First Heavy Industries, Harbin Turbine and Angang. The team is led by Zhao Xuejun, and Yu Wenhao is also quoted. Work was divided into overall, industry and regional-economy studies, and the team has gathered over a hundred types of enterprise materials. Zhang highlights two of the team's moves. The first is method: a \"three-generation interview method\" with old, middle-aged and young technical and managerial staff. It is paired with cross-checking of Russian archives, factory gazetteers and meeting minutes where company records were incomplete or restricted. Zhang reports that this comparison led the team to conclude that the share of independent innovation, set against Soviet technical aid, was very high. The second is evaluation: the team says it moved beyond a \"GDP-only\" view of state firms. It stresses their contribution to core technology, supply-chain security, worker training, environmental upgrading and social stability. Zhao is quoted as saying efficiency is only one measure of such firms. The article reports that draft manuscripts are done on topics such as the projects' construction and commissioning, their links with Luoyang and Anshan, and the steel and petrochemical industries. The team has also submitted policy recommendations. These include using state-owned enterprises' Party-history resources for education and balancing public-interest and corporate functions in reform. Zhang describes the projects' legacy as a spirit of self-reliance that still drives efforts to overcome technological chokepoints. Read the original if you want a journalistic, officially framed account of how this research project works and what conclusions it draws on state enterprise.

Grasping the "six dimensions" to advance new development of socialist culture 把握好“六个维度”推进社会主义文化新发展 Wang Hai This newspaper commentary sets out how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture can guide the further development of socialist culture. Wang Hai describes it as the cultural chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, enriching Marxist cultural theory. Wang argues that explaining it well supports propaganda and ideological work, continuity of Chinese civilisation, a strong socialist cultural nation and cultural confidence. The piece is organised around six dimensions: Party leadership of cultural work, the Second Integration, cultural confidence and traditional culture, culture for the people, the goal of a cultural nation, and cultural communication abroad. On leadership, Wang holds that culture reflects politics and economics and has a clear ideological character, so its direction requires the Party's comprehensive leadership. The longest section treats the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture. Wang says it frees thought from cultural blind imitation of the West and rests on five points: the two sides are compatible, they enrich each other, they firm up the path's foundations, they open space for innovation and they consolidate cultural subjectivity. The remaining sections call for protecting heritage, producing high-quality cultural products for the people, raising citizens' moral standards and soft power, and telling China's story well internationally. Wang concludes that culture is a driver of economic development, a tool of governance and a spiritual force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Through communication, the author says, the world will see China as committed to peaceful development. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholars present the main themes of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture.

Developing agricultural new quality productive forces requires attention to policy direction 发展农业新质生产力需关注政策方向 Zhang Jingjing This short commentary asks what institutional and policy direction should guide the development of agricultural new quality productive forces. Zhang defines them as a new form of productive force, relying on modern science and technology, innovation and new organisational forms, and oriented towards digitalisation, intelligence, greening and integration. The author argues that policy should be adapted to local conditions and focused on a few key areas. The article has two parts. The first explains why development must suit local conditions, covering regional differences, distinctive local industries and sustainability. The second sets out priority areas for policy: regional planning, agricultural technology support, fiscal, tax and financial measures, infrastructure and public services, and research and talent training. Zhang's central claim is that respecting regional differences avoids one-size-fits-all policy and makes resource use more efficient while protecting the ecology. Examples include eco-livestock farming in the fragile west, flowers in Yunnan, and cotton and fruit in Xinjiang. The author calls for differentiated support: grain-producing areas would get farmland and seed-breeding support, specialty zones would get subsidies, tax relief and tailored credit, and mountain or remote areas would get suitable machinery, roads and remote services. Zhang concludes that a sound institutional and policy framework for agricultural new quality productive forces matters greatly for implementing the rural revitalisation strategy. The author expects continued policy improvement to give rural revitalisation stronger momentum and to move agricultural and rural modernisation to a new stage. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented overview of how agricultural new quality productive forces are being framed in Chinese development discussion.

The emancipatory character of Marx and Engels's view of morality 马克思恩格斯道德观的解放性特质 Wang Rongyou Wan Yujie This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks what distinguishes Marx and Engels's view of morality. Wang and Wan argue that it has a clear emancipatory character, expressed in three ways: moral critique contains intellectual emancipation, moral practice points to institutional emancipation, and the moral ideal pursues human emancipation. The article takes the three dimensions in turn. It first examines four targets of Marx and Engels's moral critique, then their revolutionary practice, and finally their ideal of the liberation of humanity. Each dimension is defined briefly and supported with classic formulations from Marx and Engels. On critique, Wang and Wan say Marx and Engels exposed religious morality as illusory, Hegel's morality as idealist, feudal hierarchical morality as base, and bourgeois morality as hypocritical. They cite Marx's debates on the law on thefts of wood and the formally free labour contract concealing surplus-value exploitation. On practice, the authors argue that the historical materialist case against capitalism leads to the proletarian revolution. They list the means: developing productive forces, class struggle, party-led workers' movements and the "two ruptures". The proletariat is the agent, and its revolutionary moral qualities are stressed. On the ideal, emancipation has an individual side (free individuality, socialised means of production, the end of the old division of labour, shorter necessary labour time) and a species side (reconciliation with nature, society and oneself). The authors conclude that the three elements form one whole. Critique clears away ideological obstacles, practice creates material conditions, and the ideal supplies value orientation and goals for both. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style outline of how Chinese scholars present Marxist moral theory as an emancipatory framework.

Research on Marxist ethical thought must foreground the "question of standpoint" 马克思主义伦理思想研究要突出“立场问题” Li Peichao In this short commentary in Chinese Social Sciences Today, Li Peichao argues that studying Marxist ethical thought requires grasping its standpoint, viewpoint and method, and above all its standpoint. Li holds that the standpoint is a value standpoint: it concerns for whom moral criticism and defence are made and whose freedom, justice and dignity are pursued. The piece has three parts. The first defines the value standpoint as the essence of Marxist ethics. The second explains why it must be settled first, by contrasting Marxism with other currents in the history of ethics. The third draws consequences for building a Chinese Marxist ethics. Li contends that from Marx's early essay on choosing a profession through to his critique of capitalism, the standpoint stays constant: that of the proletariat and the people. It is neither that of a "minority elite" nor "value-neutral". Many Western currents, in Li's account, leave aside people's concrete historical existence and develop ethics as a refined, inward-looking intellectual exercise, such as debates over the trolley problem that ignore its causes. Li argues that such "standpoint-free" ethics covertly expresses a standpoint of withdrawal from real moral relations and conflicts of interest. For Li, viewpoint and method only embody and justify the standpoint, and separating them from it turns Marxist ethics into abstract knowledge. Li calls for a discipline system, academic system and discourse system of Marxist ethics with Chinese characteristics, built on the Two Integrations and serving Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Li rejects borrowing Western paradigms or using them as the test of whether Marxist ethics is valid. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese ethicist links the people's standpoint to the project of an indigenous Marxist ethics.

The epochal yardstick of Marxist ethics 马克思主义伦理学的时代标尺 Li Yitian Li Yitian asks what should decide whether Marxist ethics exists and what scope it should have. The short commentary argues that the test is not whether Marx and Engels wrote a dedicated ethics treatise, but whether Marxism responds to real ethical problems. Li calls this the "large yardstick" and presents Marxist ethics as an undertaking of large scale in three senses. The piece is organised under three headings: "large scale" and "large size", "large ethics" and "large theory", and "large history" and "large practice". It begins with the scattered textual basis in Marx and Engels, then turns to the normative structure of Marxism, and ends with the historical and practical setting of the field. Li notes that Marx's key moral passages sit in unpublished manuscripts, and that Engels's Anti-Dühring devotes only three sections to ethics. Even so, Li holds that Marx and Engels meet the criteria of systematic moral thought and ethical normativity. Li draws from the classics three positive themes (freedom, equality, association) and three negative ones (alienation, exploitation, division), and argues that these can be understood only by moving beyond ethics into economics, sociology and anthropology. Ethics must also engage politics, economics and religion, using historical materialism to critique them and then to construct their normative principles, especially under socialism. Li adds that Marxist ethics needs a long-term historical view, including its own "changes from ancient to modern" over two centuries. Li concludes that Marxist ethics should not be confined to speculation about good and evil or to a narrowly drawn moral domain. It should place the present within long historical time and take in social phenomena arising from great practice, which Li says will help build and refine its body of knowledge. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how the scope and legitimacy of Marxist ethics are being framed.

Building a unified national market requires both breaking and establishing 建设全国统一大市场须破立并举 Xie Lijuan Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, Xie Lijuan asks how the unified national market should be pushed deeper during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Xie argues that construction is moving from removing barriers to unifying rules and opening institutions, and that this will make the economic cycle flow more smoothly. This short commentary starts from the basic requirement of "five unifications and one opening" and the shift in official wording from "accelerating" to "advancing in depth". It then takes up four areas: the modern circulation system, fair competition and market order, coordinated improvement of the business environment, and data as a factor of production. Xie reads opening in two directions: internally, removing hidden institutional obstacles between regions; externally, using the domestic market to attract global factors and help national brands go abroad. Circulation is described as the core hub of the large market, and Xie calls for lower logistics costs, more efficient commerce and data empowerment. On competition, Xie cites the revised Anti-Monopoly Law and the Fair Competition Review Regulations, and reads the 2025 call to tackle "involution"-style competition as a calibration of corporate values. Xie also warns that regions competing alone on policy raise uncertainty for cross-regional business, and urges backward regions to close gaps faster. Xie concludes that integrating data with traditional factors will lift factor-market integration and release consumption potential. A deeper unified market, in Xie's view, will let the huge domestic market offset external uncertainty and raise the quality and resilience of the dual circulation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese economist frames current policy priorities for the unified national market.

The value of the Digital Silk Road for win-win cooperation 数字丝绸之路对合作共赢的价值 Ivan Sharafanov Ivan Sharafanov, a foreign faculty member at the University of International Business and Economics, asks what the Digital Silk Road contributes to international cooperation and how its obstacles might be overcome. This commentary, originally published in Economic Daily on 24 October 2025, argues that the initiative is a practical response to the current stage of technological change. In the author's view, it upgrades the Belt and Road Initiative's connectivity model, offers a platform for coordinating multilateral rules, and serves as a public good for global digital economic cooperation. The article begins with Xi Jinping's proposal of the concept at the first Belt and Road Forum in 2017 and his follow-up remarks in 2019. It then moves through three sections: the rationale for building the Digital Silk Road, practical cooperation in two fields, and policy responses to current problems. The author cites figures on digital economy growth, including a Chinese digital economy of 53.9 trillion yuan in 2023, and examples such as the China–Pakistan cross-border optical cable, the China–ASEAN Information Harbour, the 'Silk Road e-commerce' framework and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP). Sharafanov's central claim is that the Digital Silk Road extends 'hard connectivity' (energy, ports, railways) into 'soft connectivity' in cloud computing, big data, 5G, artificial intelligence, cross-border cables and the alignment of digital rules and standards. He contrasts rising trade protectionism in some countries with China's promotion of open cooperation, secure cross-border data flows and compatible technical standards. He identifies obstacles: fragmented global digital governance, hard multilateral coordination, new digital trade barriers, data security and privacy concerns, and limited voice for emerging economies in standard-setting. The author proposes three measures: stronger bilateral and multilateral rule coordination, using the WTO, RCEP and the G20 and creating regional digital trade demonstration zones; a dispute-settlement mechanism for digital trade, drawing on WTO experience; and closer cooperation on data security and privacy, with basic compatibility of standards while respecting national data sovereignty. He concludes that the initiative gives emerging economies more say in global digital governance and gives fresh momentum to global recovery and sustainable development. Read the original if you want an example of how a foreign academic in China presents the Digital Silk Road in the official policy framing, with the cited statistics and examples.

The logic and practice of the digital economy empowering high-quality development 数字经济赋能高质量发展的逻辑与实践 Gao Zhigang Gao Zhigang asks how the digital economy, described as a new economic form produced by the latest scientific-technological revolution and industrial transformation, drives high-quality development. The article, a newspaper commentary, argues that the digital economy embodies the internal requirements of the new development philosophy and delivers high-quality development through industrial upgrading and better allocation of production factors. It opens by citing Xi Jinping's calls to accelerate the digital economy and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision on building supporting institutions. Gao cites figures showing the digital economy growing from 11.2 trillion yuan in 2012 to 53.9 trillion yuan in 2023, with core industries accounting for about 10% of GDP in 2024. The piece has three parts. The first links the digital economy to each of the five elements of the new development philosophy: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. The second sets out two implementation paths, industrial structure upgrading and factor allocation. The third lists weaknesses and policy proposals. The core claim is that data, as a new production factor, combines with land, labour and capital and permeates production, distribution, circulation and consumption. In Gao's account, this lifts total factor productivity, lets lagging regions leapfrog, cuts energy use and emissions through industrial internet and monitoring networks, lowers barriers to cross-border trade and investment, and spreads education, healthcare and jobs more widely, contributing to common prosperity. In practice, Gao says, it raises industrial structure towards high-tech, high-value-added activity, and creates a cycle of precise matching, higher efficiency and multiplied value through platforms, algorithms and digital finance. Gao concedes that China's digital economy remains big but not strong, citing weak governance, insufficient core technology innovation and shallow integration of the digital and real economies. The author proposes stronger top-level design and data legislation, new infrastructure, self-reliant digital technology innovation with support for leading firms, and faster digital industrialization and industrial digitalization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official-media economics links the digital economy to the new development philosophy and to current policy priorities.

Empowering the high-quality development of women's causes through scientific and technological innovation 以科技创新赋能妇女事业高质量发展 Wang Xiaoli This newspaper commentary responds to Xi Jinping's keynote at the Global Leaders' Meeting on Women, held in Beijing on 13 October 2025. Wang takes up his call to use scientific and technological innovation to drive the high-quality development of women's causes. Wang argues that the call sums up Chinese practice, answers the risk of setbacks for women worldwide, and meets the need to seize the new round of technological and industrial change. The article has two parts. The first reviews how technology has strengthened women's development in China, through policy support for women in science and through digital technology. The second turns to the international dimension and to what remains to be done. Wang cites figures: 40 million women in science and technology in 2024, over 45% of the total; 2.846 million women in research and development, 1.692 million more than in 2012; and an upper age limit for a national young-scientist fund raised from 45 to 48. In the digital economy, the article reports that women make up over half of internet entrepreneurs and about a third of those in digital trade and livestreaming. Internationally, Wang points to China's Global AI Governance Initiative, a UN General Assembly resolution on AI capacity-building, a global centre for digital empowerment of women, and training courses for women from developing countries. Wang calls for stronger digital infrastructure, digital skills in national education, a gender-inclusive digital industry, and better protection of women's labour rights. Wang concludes that China aims to build an open, fair and just environment for technological development. It would let women take part in and lead digital change, and would remove bias against women at the source of digital and intelligent technologies. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links Xi Jinping's remarks on women to technology policy, with the statistics and initiatives it cites.

Promoting high-quality development of the nationwide fitness programme 推动全民健身事业高质量发展 Hu Deping Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2025, Hu Deping asks how China's national fitness programme can move to high-quality development. The commentary argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee has made nationwide fitness a national strategy, and that further progress now depends on improving the public service system behind it. Hu ties this to the aim of building China into a leading sports nation and a healthy China. The piece has three parts. The first reviews what Hu describes as the vigorous growth of mass fitness, citing popular grassroots events such as the "Village Super League", "Village BA" and "Su Super League". The second discusses how to improve public services for fitness in line with the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The third sets out directions for the coming 15th Five-Year Plan period, when a new National Fitness Plan (2026–2030) is being drafted. Hu presents growth in three respects: participation, integration and novelty. The article cites official figures for the end of 2024: 4.8417 million sports venues, 3.0 square metres of venue space per person, and national physical-fitness monitoring covering all 31 provinces. On services, Hu calls for standards at national, sector and local level, a system of rules that is adjusted to changing public needs, and a mix of "an effective government" and "an efficient market" with social forces taking part. Hu then names remaining problems: uneven development between urban and rural areas, regions, groups and sports, and resources that are scattered and lack drive. Hu proposes three lines of work: problem orientation, balanced and accessible provision, and coordinated integration. Fitness services should be equalised across groups and places, and Hu would use artificial intelligence, big data and cloud computing to match supply to demand. Fitness should also link up with health, education, tourism and other sectors under the "sports plus" idea, so that it does not circulate only within sport. Hu presents this as a contribution to Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how Chinese policy discourse frames mass fitness, public services and health in the run-up to the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Understanding the "commonness" of the common values of all humanity 深刻认识全人类共同价值的共同性特征 Wang Gonglong Writing in the People's Daily on 24 October 2025, Wang Gonglong asks what is distinctive about the common values of all humanity (peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom) advanced by Xi Jinping. Wang argues that their defining feature is "commonness", and that this commonness is concrete, respects difference and serves the shared interests of humanity, in contrast to Western "universal values". The short commentary opens by presenting the values as an original concept of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought and a product of the Two Integrations. It then has two parts: the theoretical, historical and practical logics behind the commonness, and a contrast with Western "universal values". Wang grounds the commonness in three logics. Theoretically, the six values express needs shared by people across systems, ideologies and faiths. Historically, citing Marx and Engels on world history, Wang says growing universal exchange lets values that serve common interests settle into shared ones. Practically, deepening interdependence and global challenges make the community with a shared future for mankind both a community of interests and of values. Wang says Western "universal values" rest on an abstract view of human nature, deny particularity and aim at uniformity, leading to "sameness without harmony". Wang also rejects the opposite view that values are wholly plural. Drawing on the dialectic of the general and the particular, Wang says the common values allow diverse interpretations and routes of realisation, and cites Marx and Engels to argue that Western universalism presents particular interests as general ones. Wang concludes that promoting these values requires not imposing one's own values or models, distinguishing values from their forms of realisation, and respecting each country's own paths. Wang calls for the values to be embodied in practice that benefits each country's people. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Chinese commentators distinguish the common values of all humanity from Western universalism.

Political-philosophical implications of Marx's distinction between "the property of the individual" and "private property" An examination based on the Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58 马克思区分“单个人的财产”与“私有财产”的政治哲学启示——基于《政治经济学批判（1857—1858年手稿）》的考察 Tu Liangchuan Tu Liangchuan asks what Marx's distinction between "the property of the individual" (单个人的财产) and "private property" in the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse) contributes to political philosophy. The article argues that, although Marx was analysing forms of production before capitalism, the distinction follows his method of reading earlier forms in light of the developed one. In Tu's reading it criticises capitalist "property appropriation" (财产占有) and looks forward to a communist ideal of "property ownership" (财产所有) that serves all-round individual development. The article has three main sections plus a conclusion. The first traces how individual property in the general conditions of production, mediated by the community, dissolved into private property through the Asiatic, ancient and Germanic forms of ownership. The second examines how bourgeois property rights, presented as freedom and equality, become a power of domination, drawing on Hegel's link between property and freedom and on Marx's critique. The third turns to Marx's picture of "social individual ownership". The conclusion links the distinction to common prosperity in the course of Chinese modernization. Tu's central move is to separate a right (the individual's use of the conditions of labour) from a power (capital's command over others' labour). Under capitalism, the supposedly equal exchange between capital and labour hides the separation of labour from its objective conditions. In this account, workers' surplus labour becomes capital's surplus value, so that "the product appears as the property of another". Tu argues this is a basic condition of capitalist production and not an accident. Against it, the individual's property is described as non-closed and non-exclusive: it consists in the "common social productive capacity" and in a "social individual ownership" that unites social appropriation with individual ownership. Tu concludes that abolishing capitalist private ownership and building communist social individual ownership would return property to being the material basis of human essential powers and of free individuality. The article presents common prosperity as the political restoration of this positive content and as a historical-materialist critique of capitalist appropriation. For Tu, Marx's distinction offers a theoretical reference for judging ownership questions in modern political philosophy and a guide for building the mechanism of "property enjoyment" under common prosperity. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of property in the Grundrisse or on how Chinese scholars link it to common prosperity.

Confirming the essence of artificial intelligence from the perspective of historical materialism, and its significance 唯物史观视域下人工智能本质的确证及其意义 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang asks what artificial intelligence (AI) fundamentally is, as a premise for thinking about the human–machine relationship. The article argues that AI can be understood by borrowing the way Marx analysed the essence of things, especially the human essence. On this view AI is a 'human-like' being: an externalisation of human knowledge and rational capacity, but not equal to human intelligence and not capable of fundamentally surpassing it. The article opens by tracing Western philosophical views of essence, from Plato and Aristotle to a 'universal' essence (Hobbes, Spinoza) and a 'particular' essence (Feuerbach). It then reconstructs Marx's treatment of the human essence, from the species-essence of the 1844 Manuscripts to the Theses on Feuerbach's 'ensemble of social relations'. The second section applies this method to AI through three questions: what distinguishes AI from other beings, how it came about historically, and what its real properties are. The third section draws out the significance of this determination. Liu makes three claims. First, as the 'brain' of automated machine systems, AI is the externalised, objectified form of human knowledge, which Liu links to Marx's account of machinery as the 'organs of the human brain'. Second, its emergence is a necessary stage in the development of the productive forces, extending the automation of manual labour to part of mental labour. Third, AI both exceeds and does not exceed human intelligence. It outperforms individuals in specialised, data-driven tasks, but it stores the knowledge of humanity as a whole. It also lacks the bodily needs and life experience from which human intelligence arises, and it lacks practice, in the sense of purposeful transformation of the environment to meet a subject's needs. On this basis Liu argues that AI's capacity for emancipation and its alienating effects are internally linked. Under capital's logic, AI shortens necessary labour time but deepens exploitation and produces a 'useless class'. Liu's reading is that the negative effects stem from capitalist control and use, not from AI itself. Following Marx, Liu rejects both radical progressivism and conservative romanticism and calls for neither utopian myths nor fantasies of catastrophe. AI is described as a material basis for human liberation, not a 'divine' being beyond humanity. Read the original if you want a Marxist-philosophical argument on AI's essence that draws on Marx's texts on machinery and the human essence.

Sandel's critique and reconstruction of the Rawlsian conception of the self 桑德尔对罗尔斯式自我观念的批判及重构 Zhu Huiling This research article examines Michael Sandel's critique of the conception of the self in John Rawls's A Theory of Justice, and Sandel's attempt to replace it. Zhu Huiling takes Rawls's claim that the self is prior to its ends, and so the right prior to the good, as the logical starting point of Rawls's theory and the target of Sandel's most distinctive philosophical work. Zhu concludes that Sandel's critique is incomplete and his reconstructed self probably unsuccessful, yet that the effort remains philosophically important. The article is built in three parts. The first treats the defects Sandel finds in the deontological self as a moral subject: an impoverished, 'unencumbered' self and a possessive subject that cannot support claims of desert. The second turns to the self as agent and discusses possession, choice and reflection, including the original position and the veil of ignorance. The third sets out Sandel's 'constitutive self', which Sandel links to Alasdair MacIntyre's 'narrative self' and to Confucian ideas, and then assesses it. A short conclusion draws out its significance for Sandel's later thought. In Zhu's account, Sandel argues that Rawls's self stands at a distance from its attributes and so cannot ground a thick sense of desert. Rawls's 'choice' amounts to taking inventory of existing desires, and reflection is limited to outward calculation. Behind the veil of ignorance, parties do not choose principles but recognise them, which in Sandel's reading shows a hidden reliance on an intersubjective self that Rawls officially excludes. Zhu rejects critics such as Will Kymlicka and Philip Pettit, who hold that Sandel's revisable self is no different from Rawls's, and maintains that the two differ in the nature of the subject, not only in its capacities. Zhu nonetheless finds that Sandel cannot say how far the community constitutes the self or reconcile free will with constitution. Citing Jack Crittenden, Zhu also points to a dilemma: if the self is framed by its community's ends it cannot reflect on them, and if it can reflect on them they do not constitute it. Zhu concludes that Sandel's critique has three lasting merits. It makes people reconsider the community and its values, though Zhu says it should not be read as communitarianism, since Sandel's common good is a reflectively formed one. It prepares the ground for Sandel's revival of civic republicanism and his later critiques of the market society and meritocracy. And it invites reconsideration of Confucian ideas of self, society and state, where Zhu notes that Western divisions between private and public are absent. Zhu urges readers to look at their own society's conditions and Chinese classical thought to find their own questions and solutions. Read the original if you are interested in the Sandel–Rawls debate on the self, or in how a Chinese scholar assesses it and relates it to Confucian thought.

Time and the remainder of the system: Schelling's philosophy of the "Ages of the World" 时间与体系剩余：谢林的“世界时代”哲学 Wang Ding Wang Ding asks how a post-Kantian philosophical system can unite its beginning (the "One") with its completed whole (the "All") when that beginning must be immediate. The article's thesis is that the solution of Schelling's early period and of Hegel turns the beginning into a "remainder" of the system. In Wang's reading, Schelling's later philosophy of the "Ages of the World" (Weltalter) tries to repair this through a critique of time and a rebuilt "metaphysics of time". The article has three parts. The first sets out Hegel's three requirements for a system and Schelling's objection to Fichte's "self-positing of the I". The second takes up Schelling's 1827 lectures on the system of the ages of the world and his critique of time. The third examines the distinction between "principle" and "cause", the role of God, and the problems that remain. Wang also disputes readings of Schelling by Xian Gang and Markus Gabriel. Wang argues that Schelling objected to Fichte because self-consciousness cannot ground the conditions of its own existence. After Fichte, the beginning became a law that recurs at every level of the system. That law, however, is a bare fact (Dass) which the system cannot absorb, so the "ouroboros" structure never closes. The same law also strips the system of real time, because everything becomes an ever-present "now", or eternity. Wang reads Schelling's response as a "Möbius-strip" folding back on the law itself, asking what lies before and after the "now". Wang concludes that Schelling therefore introduces "cause" (Ursache) as distinct from "principle". The cause explains why the ideal outweighs the real, a relation that is willed rather than necessary. On this reading, God appears as the cause of the "better", which restores teleology. Wang presents the "system of the ages of the world" as a historical, ontological and teleological metaphysics, not mysticism. The article ends with open questions: where the ground of a given highest ground lies, whether the world can give itself meaning, and, if not, where one could now go beyond it. Read the original if you follow German idealism, Schelling and Hegel, or debates about system, history and meaning in philosophy.

The ontological construction of sensation and its contemporary effects: a new reading of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 感觉的存在论建构及其当代效应：《1844年经济学哲学手稿》的新解读 Bao Jin Huang Jing Bao Jin and Huang Jing take up the young Marx's account of sensation in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. They argue that it is usually read as a Feuerbachian anthropological materialism and dismissed as immature. In their reading, the account is first of all ontological. Marx accepts Feuerbach's principle of sensuous objectivity but builds the practical structure of sensation on "sensuous activity", and this breaks with the basic framework of metaphysics. The article has four sections. It first contrasts Hegel's treatment of sense-certainty in the Phenomenology of Spirit with Feuerbach's critique in Principles of the Philosophy of the Future, and with earlier empiricism. It then examines the objective relations of sensation in the Manuscripts, and Marx's reworking of Feuerbach's concepts of passivity and passion. It ends by tracing contemporary effects of Marx's account, drawing on Byung-Chul Han, Eva Illouz, Bernard Stiegler and Herbert Marcuse. The authors argue that Feuerbach treated sensation as something ready-made and never asked how it comes to exist. Marx transforms Feuerbachian "passivity" into passion, a driving force that takes hold of its object, so that passivity and activity form a dialectical unity. With the help of MEGA2, the authors stress Marx's distinction between appropriation (Aneignung), possession (besitzen) and having (Haben). Real sensation is an active appropriation of objects, and "practical sensation" shows that sensation has a practical structure. This makes the sensuous world a historical product and, the authors suggest, lays a basis for historical materialism. In the final section the authors apply this reading to the present. Under private property, sensation becomes the sense of having, and capital, money and quantified, homogenised objects impoverish it. Commodified emotion and digital platforms supply "pseudo-sensations" that replace real sensuous needs. The authors close by presenting Marx's idea of the liberation of the senses as a dimension of human emancipation and of modern civilisation, with sensory needs developing in a full and profound way. Read the original if you work on the young Marx, Feuerbach or the ontology of sensuousness and want a case for linking the Manuscripts to critiques of affective and digital capitalism.

Marx's view of labour justice and its bearing on labour happiness With a discussion of the basic content of labour-concept education in universities in the new era 马克思劳动正义观及其对劳动幸福的现实观照——兼论新时代高校劳动观教育的基本内容 He Hanhun Lai Mingzhu He and Lai start from Marx's claim that labour is the species-essence of human beings and ask whether the proposition of 'labour happiness' can stand, given how often labour makes workers unhappy. They answer that it holds as a normative ('ought') judgement, and that the labour which produces happiness must be just labour. On this basis they argue that Marx's theory of labour justice explains what labour happiness is and what conditions it requires, and that it fixes the content of labour education in universities. The article has three main sections and a closing discussion. The first presents labour justice as the ground of labour happiness. The second treats justice of the labour subject and of the labour object (means of production) as the fundamental precondition. The third treats just motives and the protection of labour rights as basic conditions. The closing section turns to labour-concept education in universities since the 18th Party Congress (2012), citing Xi Jinping's 2018 call for an education system combining moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour education, and the 2020 central guidelines on labour education. The authors define just labour as labour whose usefulness exceeds its harmfulness, so that people share in happiness. They draw on Marx to argue that the labour subject must be capable and must do labour as a duty, within physical and mental limits set by age and sex. For the object, they hold that ownership of the means of production must be just, citing Marx's idea of re-establishing individual ownership on the basis of common possession. In their reading, public ownership addresses the defects of large-scale private ownership, though the authors say China's uneven development still requires unwaveringly encouraging the non-public sector. They also distinguish slave labour, labour for a living, decent labour and free associated labour, and contend that capitalist profit motives and wage labour undermine happiness for workers and for society as a whole. The authors propose that university labour education rest on Marx's view of labour as making the person, aim at labour happiness, and make labour-justice education its core task. They set out five strands: labour as moral formation, labour happiness, labour duty and the labour subject, labour process, and labour rights. These include rejecting consumerism and 'lying flat', and respecting labour models and the craftsman spirit. They also include learning to comply with labour law. Read the original if you want a Marxist ethical reading of labour, happiness and ownership linked directly to current Chinese ideological education policy.

On the oppositional logic of objectified labour: material exchange (Stoffwechsel) in Capital and its manuscripts 论对象化劳动的对立逻辑 ——基于《资本论》及手稿中的物质变换理论 Sun Lin Sun Lin asks how Marx's critique of political economy, in Capital and its manuscripts, builds on the concept of objectified labour (对象化劳动), and what logic of opposition lies inside it. The article, published in Social Sciences (Shehui kexue) in 2025, argues that objectified labour is the gravitational centre of the critique. Through Marx's theory of material exchange (Stoffwechsel, rendered here as 'material exchange'), it unfolds in three progressive layers of opposition: external, internal and essential. Sun presents this as a reversal of Hegel's logic of abstract identity between self and object, and as a break with Feuerbach. The article first sets out the philosophical background: Hegel's speculative identity, Feuerbach's critique of it as theology, and Marx's earlier remarks on objectivity in the 1844 Manuscripts and The Holy Family. Part one treats social material exchange through the metamorphoses of commodity and money. Part two argues that value, commodity and capital are each objectified labour. Part three turns to the natural conditions of 'objective activity' and to the possibility of a positive sublation of objectified labour. In Sun's reading, the commodity–money opposition in simple circulation is only an external, successive opposition. It rests on an internal opposition between use-value and exchange-value, which operates 'simultaneously' and through reversal. Capital's circulation extends this into an essential, totalising opposition between objectified labour and living labour.
