The 'apparent exchange' of labour-power for wages, and the way past labour dominates present labour, produce fetishism and the 'inverted world' of the economic trinity. Sun argues that because the contradiction is antagonistic, not pre-harmonised as in Hegel, the ideal continuity of capital breaks down in the real separation of sale and purchase. The result is world-market crises. Sun concludes that the opposition of objectified labour is only a logical opposition within a non-identical reality. The way beyond capital's totality lies in use-value and the natural conditions of living, non-objectified labour, which the author says cannot be dissolved into abstract value substance. Sun holds that recovering these conditions remains important for criticising the problems of capitalist modernity. Read the original if you work on Marx's Stoffwechsel, the Hegel–Marx relation or the Grundrisse and Capital manuscripts, and want a dense, philosophically oriented reading of objectified labour.

Amplifying the multiplier effect of the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation 放大科技创新和产业创新深度融合的乘数效应 Yan Xiangbin This commentary, first published in the Economic Daily in October 2025, asks how China can deepen the integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. Yan Xiangbin takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the two are the basic path for developing new quality productive forces. Yan argues that the integration should be pushed to produce a "multiplier effect", meaning a non-linear amplification of innovation value, which would turn research results into real productive capacity and support high-quality development. The piece has three parts. The first defines the multiplier effect and gives three reasons it matters. The second reviews evidence that science and industry already reinforce each other. The third sets out institutional measures. Yan stresses that artificial intelligence and other fast-moving technologies make the matter more urgent, and that China should draw on its super-large market and complete industrial system. Yan defines the multiplier effect as the result of coupling the innovation chain with the industrial, capital and talent chains. The author gives three reasons it matters. It supplies endogenous growth momentum, since growth driven by inputs and scale is no longer sustainable. It supports autonomous and controllable industrial chains, because "chokepoint" problems partly stem from research stranded in laboratories. It offers a route from "low-end manufacturing" to "high-end leadership". As evidence, Yan cites 2024 R&D spending above 3.6 trillion yuan (2.68% of output), an enterprise invention-patent commercialisation rate of 53.3%, and 9.5% growth in high-tech manufacturing value added in the first half of 2025. The article also describes joint "technology communities" in intelligent connected vehicles as an example of industry feeding back into research. Yan calls for institutional innovation so that "systemic coordination" replaces isolated development and two-way empowerment replaces one-way support. The proposals are enterprise-led, market-oriented evaluation of research results; diversified investment and financing for commercialisation; regular mechanisms for collecting and publishing industrial technology needs; stronger intellectual property protection and technology intermediaries; and a larger role for firms in setting research agendas, including specialised and innovative small and medium-sized enterprises. Yan also urges classified management of innovation and a culture that tolerates failure. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official economic commentary links new quality productive forces to innovation policy and the commercialisation of research.

Accelerating the cultivation of a nationally integrated data market 加快培育全国一体化数据市场 Wang Xuhui This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in October 2025, asks how China can turn its large stock of data and its wide range of application scenarios into economic momentum. Wang Xuhui argues that the answer lies in accelerating the cultivation of a nationally integrated data market. In the author's view, such a market would let data work as a multiplier on economic development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The piece has three parts. The first sets out China's advantages in data volume and use cases, citing figures for 2023 and 2024 on data production, AI-related data growth, the digital economy's share of GDP and patents. The second explains why efficient allocation of data matters. The third proposes ways to make data marketable and valuable, and mentions ten provincial-level pilot zones for data factors. Wang's central claim is that data, as a new type of production factor and a basis for new quality productive forces, can raise total factor productivity and help recombine technology, capital, labour and land. The author gives two reasons for building the market: it is needed for the new development pattern and high-quality development, and it is needed to win new advantages in international competition in the digital economy. Wang says the market should be unified, secure and open, and based on reciprocal cooperation. It should bring together public, enterprise and personal data, remove regional barriers and 'data silos', and build trusted-circulation mechanisms. The author lists four tasks: speed up basic data institutions, including a structurally separated system of data property rights and rules for circulation and cross-border flows; strengthen data infrastructure; improve the quantity and quality of data supply through classified and graded management; and design a multi-level system of data trading venues with national, regional and sectoral platforms that complement and compete with one another. Wang says the market should let the market play the decisive role in allocating resources while the government plays its role better. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of China's data-market policy priorities, with the latest figures the author cites.

The 14th Five-Year Plan period: solid steps forward for Chinese modernization A dialogue with Wang Yiming, Vice Chairman of the China Center for International Economic Exchanges “十四五”：中国式现代化迈出坚实步伐——对话中国国际经济交流中心副理事长王一鸣 Ouyang You This is an interview, published in the Economic Daily's "Dialogue with Economists" series, in which reporter Ouyang You questions Wang Yiming, Vice Chairman of the China Center for International Economic Exchanges. It takes stock of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021–2025). Wang argues that, despite a severe external environment, China kept its economy stable and took solid steps in advancing Chinese modernization through high-quality development. The conversation has four parts: achievements in scale, quality and structure; the shift in growth drivers and the upgrading of comparative advantage; the general lessons drawn from the period; and the outlook for the 15th Five-Year Plan. Wang supports the first part with figures on GDP, research spending, industrial structure, urbanisation, trade and China's contribution to world growth. He also reviews the new development philosophy under its five headings: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. Wang holds that the new development philosophy was turned into concrete projects and reforms, and that China's old low-cost-labour advantage is giving way to new ones: an ultra-large market, a complete industrial chain, technological innovation, the digital economy and new energy. He presents the main lessons as "five must-coordinate relationships": an efficient market and a capable government; aggregate supply and demand; nurturing new and updating old growth drivers; improving the incremental and revitalising the existing; and raising quality while expanding total volume. He attributes the period's results fundamentally to the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Looking ahead, Wang describes the 15th Five-Year Plan period as a critical one for laying the base for basically realising socialist modernization. He lists external pressures, including a new technological revolution, slower world growth, supply-chain restructuring and what he calls US containment. He also lists domestic ones: weaker labour and capital contributions, a maturing industrialisation and urbanisation, and tougher green transition tasks. He calls for adhering to high-quality development, developing new quality productive forces according to local conditions, and treating Chinese modernization as the greatest political task. Read the original if you want an official-leaning economist's statistical review of the 14th Five-Year Plan and a view of the policy priorities for the next plan.

Coordinating supply and demand: practical results and theoretical innovation 统筹供需的实践成效与理论创新 Chen Yanbin Writing in Economic Daily in October 2025, Chen Yanbin examines the principle that China must "coordinate the relationship between aggregate supply and aggregate demand", put forward by Xi Jinping at the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference. Chen argues that this principle sums up the practice of macroeconomic governance since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Chen's account, it also breaks through Western macroeconomic policy theory and contributes to building an autonomous Chinese system of economic knowledge. The commentary has four parts. It first traces how understanding of supply–demand coordination deepened, then compares this with Western macro-policy theory. It next sets out three features of the new understanding and ends with policy proposals for reaching a higher-level dynamic balance of supply and demand. Chen presents the Party's understanding as developing in three steps: supply-side structural reform to improve supply quality; demand-side management to expand domestic demand; and finally the combined push of both. Western theory, rooted in industrial-era economies and centred on short-term counter-cyclical demand management, is said to pay little attention to aggregate supply. Chen holds that it therefore struggles with multi-source supply shocks and with the data-driven changes of the digital economy, and that Western economies have been unable to escape weak growth since 2008. Chinese practice, by contrast, combines stabilisation, growth and structural policies ("three policies in one"), which the author says lets it handle both supply and demand shocks and lift potential growth. Chen also stresses expanding external as well as domestic demand, and keeping total supply at a reasonable level, citing the campaign against "involution-style" competition. Chen calls for deepening supply-side structural reform through innovation and data as a production factor. On the demand side, Chen urges treating domestic demand as a long-term strategy, with measures on employment, incomes, social welfare, the consumption environment and the quality, efficiency and structure of investment. Chen also calls for greater consistency among monetary, fiscal, stabilisation, growth and structural policies. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS economist presents supply–demand coordination as an official theoretical innovation and policy agenda.

How a small county became the "world's vegetable basket": an investigation of Anqiu, Weifang, Shandong 小县城如何变身“世界菜篮子”——来自山东潍坊安丘市的调查 Wang Jinhu This is a field report from the Party newspaper Economic Daily, written by reporter Wang Jinhu. It asks how Anqiu, a landlocked county-level city in Weifang, Shandong, became known as the "world's vegetable basket". According to the report, Anqiu exports more than 600,000 tonnes of vegetables a year to over 80 countries and regions, and its farm exports have led Shandong's counties for 16 years. The article answers that Anqiu has followed a path of "ecology first, brand empowerment and alignment with international standards", which it presents as high-quality development in agriculture. The report moves through three sections: the area's natural endowments, the building of an international "passport" of standards and traceability, and the spread of ecological farming. It draws on visits to farms and firms, with named farmers, managers and officials, and on figures supplied by them. Products covered include volcanic-soil millet, tomatoes, ginger, spring onions, garlic, sweet potato products and chicken skewers. The core argument has three steps. First, natural conditions such as volcanic and selenium-rich soils, abundant sunshine and 500 years of ginger breeding give the produce its quality. Second, the report credits institutional innovation: a national base for technical trade measures and a real-time platform comparing standards of 56 trading partners, which it says warned firms six months ahead of Japan's tightened onion pesticide limits in March 2024. It also describes a "dual-code" system, an electronic safety code plus an ecological origin traceability code, which it says brings price premiums of 30 to 40 per cent. Third, the report describes a shift towards ecological farming and deep processing: organic fertiliser supplied at cost through a state-run mechanism, subsidies of up to 50,000 yuan per mu for new greenhouses, 1,397 farms converted, and 2,000-plus processed products. It also describes an integrated domestic and export "dual circulation" approach, with one standard for both markets. The article concludes that Anqiu's experience rests on strict regulation to earn trust abroad, ecological transformation to create premium value, and extended value chains so that farmers gain most from the added value. It cites 60,000-plus smallholders linked to the export chain and 2.6 billion yuan in extra farmer income in 2024, and notes the local aim of moving from a major agricultural city to a strong healthy-food city. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially framed case study of a county-level export agriculture model, with local figures and named enterprises.

Building a science and technology finance system suited to scientific and technological innovation 构建同科技创新相适应的科技金融体制 Guo Tianyong Writing in Economic Daily on 10 October 2025, Guo Tianyong asks how China should build a financial system that fits its drive for technological innovation. Guo argues that science and technology finance is a key lever for strengthening national strategic scientific and technological strength and for upgrading the economy. It must be developed on the basis of China's national conditions and stage of development. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out why science and technology finance matters, then reviews recent achievements and remaining problems, and finally proposes five measures. It draws on policy documents from 2024 and 2025 and on statistics for science and technology lending and bonds. Guo argues that finance links capital to innovation and helps shift growth from factor-driven to innovation-driven. The article cites 44.1 trillion yuan in science and technology loans by June 2025, up 12.5 per cent year on year, and about 600 billion yuan in innovation bonds. Guo also lists problems: bank reluctance to lend to asset-light start-ups, weak venture capital with low private participation, and a tendency in government funds to invest heavily but manage poorly. The central claim is that China should not copy Western models. Banks, which hold about 90 per cent of financial-sector assets, should remain the main channel and adapt their products and risk assessment. Guo's five proposals are to strengthen bank-led indirect finance, improve banks' ability to serve innovation, refine investment–loan linkage, make government investment funds more market-oriented and patient, and open direct financing channels through multi-level capital markets and private capital. Guo presents these as the basis of a science and technology finance system with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy approach to science and technology finance, with recent figures and a list of proposed measures.

Making better use of fiscal policy to boost consumption 更好发挥财政促消费的作用 Ma Haitao Yao Dongmin This commentary, published in the Economic Daily in October 2025, asks how fiscal policy can do more to lift household consumption at a time of weak domestic demand and greater external uncertainty. Ma and Yao argue that public finance, as a pillar of state governance, is a key lever for stimulating consumption and sustaining economic recovery. They set this within the strategic goal of expanding domestic demand, which this year's Government Work Report placed first among the year's tasks. The article has two main parts. The first reviews what fiscal policy has done since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in four areas: income distribution and social security, structural tools for big-ticket consumption, services consumption, and green consumption. The second identifies remaining problems and sets out four sets of proposals: fiscal spending, tax structure, government investment, and fiscal-financial coordination. The authors illustrate the first part with figures from official sources. The authors credit personal income tax reform, the merging of rural and urban residents' pension schemes in 2014, and rising basic pensions with strengthening consumer expectations. They cite 2024 ultra-long special treasury bonds for equipment renewal and consumer-goods trade-ins, and say these drew in more than 1.3 trillion yuan of related sales. They also report that services rose from 39.7% to 46.1% of per capita consumption spending between 2013 and 2024. Despite this, they say consumption remains structurally narrow and confidence is lacking, with weak primary healthcare, thin community elderly-care coverage and uneven public services between regions. Their proposals include more targeted transfers to low- and middle-income and flexibly employed groups, more spending on education, childcare, primary care and elderly care, and employment support schemes. They also propose a higher share of personal income tax from high earners, moving the consumption tax collection point to the retail stage and devolving part of it to localities, using fiscal funds to draw in private capital, and interest subsidies, risk-compensation funds and guarantees for consumer credit. Ma and Yao conclude that fiscal resources should be allocated more precisely across supply and demand. They call for income security, tax optimisation, better service provision and expectation management, aiming at a mechanism in which fiscal support underpins, finance amplifies and the market responds. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of the fiscal measures China has used to stimulate consumption and the policy direction commentators close to the Party's economic policy debate propose next.

Coordinating the great task of boosting consumption 统筹做好提振消费大文章 Ji Zhengju Liu Minru Liu Chengli Wang Xiaorui This commentary, published in Economic Daily on 16 October 2025 and written by Ji Zhengju, Liu Minru, Liu Chengli and Wang Xiaorui, asks how China should consolidate and extend the gains made in boosting consumption. It holds that final consumption is the lasting driver of economic growth and that, under the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the strategy of expanding domestic demand has produced historic results, especially during the 14th Five-Year Plan period. The piece has three parts. The first describes six features of changing consumption patterns: consumption's basic role in growth, the growth of household, government and production-related consumption, rural consumption, the rising share of improvement-oriented consumption, higher-quality services, and new consumption formats and scenarios. The second sets out four priority directions for boosting consumption, and the third lists concrete measures to put in place. The authors cite figures to show progress. Consumption contributed 44.5 per cent of economic growth in 2024. From 2013 to 2024 rural consumption grew at about twice the urban rate and the Engel coefficient fell by 1.4 percentage points. Online retail sales also outpaced total retail sales growth. The authors nonetheless say that insufficient effective demand remains a prominent problem: household consumption's share of disposable income is falling and households are cautious. Their four priorities are raising consumption capacity (of households, government and enterprises), strengthening willingness to consume, promoting consumption upgrading, and improving the consumption environment. For implementation the authors call for coordinated reforms: prioritising employment, reforming income distribution, adjusting taxation, easing urban settlement for migrant workers, improving social security, and raising government consumption spending by "investing in people". They also propose refining trade-in and equipment-renewal policies and the use of ultra-long special treasury bonds. They further call for stronger consumer rights protection, removal of restrictive measures in the consumption field, and better paid-leave arrangements. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the policy agenda for domestic consumption at the close of the 14th Five-Year Plan period.

Building a new system of high-quality, efficient services 着眼优质高效构建服务业新体系 Zhang Yingxi This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 17 October 2025, asks how China should build a new system for the services sector that is both "high-quality" and "efficient". Zhang Yingxi starts from Xi Jinping's call to build such a system and to integrate modern services deeply with advanced manufacturing and modern agriculture. The author argues that this is needed to extend industrial chains and add value, and to meet people's rising demand for better and more varied services. The task should be pursued together with high-quality development. The piece has three parts. The first explains what is "new" about the new system, under three headings: innovation-driven growth, quality first, and structural coordination. The second sets out three relationships to manage: comprehensive advance versus breakthroughs in key areas, efficiency versus fairness, and domestic development versus opening up. The third proposes four practical paths: optimising supply, digital transformation, cross-sector integration and standards-building. Zhang's central claim is that the "new" system is a systemic project, not an accumulation of new business forms. It combines technological innovation, such as AI and big data, with institutional change such as simpler approvals and better standards. Quality governance should run from standard-setting to evaluation, with policy support so that "high quality, high price" becomes normal in the market. Coordination should link sectors (technology, finance, logistics), supply chains, regions and industries. On efficiency and fairness, the author holds that the two reinforce each other, citing online education for remote areas, vocational training and smart elderly care. On domestic and external development, Zhang points to the huge domestic market, more open market access, and wider reach for Chinese services standards abroad. The practical proposals include strengthening producer services such as R&D, logistics and finance, and personalising consumer services. They also include building AI-native firms and new consumption scenarios, developing integrated models such as culture-tourism and blockchain-based farm-to-table supply chains, and filling standards gaps in elderly care, childcare, domestic services and digital services. Zhang also calls for a feedback loop of implementation, evaluation and improvement, backed by sanctions for dishonesty and mechanisms for exiting the industry. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of current Chinese policy thinking on services-sector upgrading.

The connotations and path of agricultural modernization with Chinese characteristics 中国特色农业现代化的内涵和路径 Tu Shengwei This commentary, first published in the Economic Daily in October 2025, asks what distinguishes China's agricultural modernization and how it should be advanced. Tu Shengwei, a researcher at a state macroeconomic research institute, builds on Xi Jinping's statements that there can be no national modernization without agricultural and rural modernization, and that modernizing agriculture is the basic requirement for building a strong agricultural country. Tu argues that, although agricultural modernization has features common worldwide, there is no universal standard, and China has followed a path of its own. The piece has three parts. The first sets out five features of the Chinese path. The second identifies five new requirements arising from changes in the domestic and external environment for agriculture, rural areas and farmers. The third proposes four key measures. It is a short policy-oriented commentary and does not engage in extended theoretical debate. Tu's five features are reliance on the two-tier operating system (household contract operation as the base, combined with collective management), the principal position of farmers, coordination between an efficient market and a proactive government, the long-term coexistence of large and small operations, and the fusion of farming-culture heritage with green development. The new requirements are cultivating new quality productive forces in agriculture, deepening reform to strengthen endogenous momentum, smoothing circulation between industry and agriculture and between city and countryside, promoting green and low-carbon development, and safeguarding agricultural industrial security amid protectionism and geopolitical conflict. Tu holds that agricultural modernization is the foundation of Chinese modernization and determines its quality. For action, Tu calls for strengthening food security through the strategies of storing grain in the land and in technology, adapting new quality productive forces to local conditions with a focus on core technologies such as seed sources and key machinery, building a modern rural industrial system by integrating primary, secondary and tertiary industries, and improving market-based allocation of factors. On land, Tu proposes orderly pilots extending the second round of land contracts by 30 years on expiry, stabilising contract relations, and exploring voluntary compensated exit from the 'three rights'. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the current official framing of agricultural modernization in China and its policy priorities.

Using fiscal policy to serve and underpin medium- and long-term planning 发挥财政作用服务和支撑中长期规划 Lü Wei Writing in Economic Daily in October 2025, as the 14th Five-Year Plan ends and the 15th is being drafted, Lü Wei asks how public finance can best serve and support medium- and long-term planning. The commentary argues that finance is a pillar of national governance, and that the plan should set direction while fiscal policy provides the guarantee. Lü calls for macro policies to work in step with development planning so that plan decisions are carried out in practice. The article is organised around three roles that Lü assigns to fiscal policy: a foundational role, an institutional role and a guaranteeing role. Each role is tied to concrete policy areas. It opens with a statement from Xi Jinping on how the 15th Five-Year Plan period should be planned, and it proceeds as a list of policy recommendations. Under the foundational role, Lü says fiscal policy should drive high-quality development in four ways. It should build innovation momentum through more basic-research funding, tax incentives and support for new quality productive forces. It should back a comprehensive green transition through incentives and a green tax system. It should widen the domestic circulation by shifting fiscal emphasis towards people's livelihoods and consumption. And it should promote common prosperity through inclusive social security and redistribution. Under the institutional role, Lü treats deepening fiscal and tax reform as the key step: zero-based budgeting and performance management, clearer central–local fiscal relations with more local own revenue and more general transfers, and a modern tax system based on statutory taxation. Under the guaranteeing role, Lü distinguishes anticipatory from binding plan targets and calls for better management of fiscal resources. Lü also calls for closer coordination of fiscal and financial policy, and for removing institutional bottlenecks such as tax rules that hinder a unified national market and burdens on private firms. Lü concludes that deeper fiscal and tax reform, together with coordinated policy tools, will give the plan the financial and institutional backing it needs. The piece is a policy-oriented statement of how the economic establishment frames the fiscal agenda for the 15th Five-Year Plan. Read the original if you want a compact outline of the fiscal priorities that Chinese commentators link to the 15th Five-Year Plan, including budget, central–local and tax reform.

Doing economic work in accordance with the new development philosophy 遵循新发展理念做好经济工作 Zhou Wen This commentary, first published in the Economic Daily in October 2025, asks how officials should carry out economic work under the new development philosophy. Zhou argues that the philosophy, made up of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing, is the most important of the theories advanced since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Zhou's account it plays a strategic, programmatic and guiding role in the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Zhou ties the argument to a Political Bureau meeting at the end of July, which called on leading cadres to adopt a correct view of political achievements. The article has three parts. The first goes through the five concepts one by one. For each it sets out recent achievements, remaining problems and tasks ahead. The second part addresses how to turn the philosophy into practice, through systemic coordination, stronger cadre capability and institutional safeguards. The third part sets out what a correct view of political achievements means for leading cadres. Zhou's central claim is that the five concepts form one interconnected whole and cannot be pursued separately. Innovation must be balanced against regional coordination and ecological protection. Fiscal, monetary and industrial policy should work together, and the Yangtze River Delta is offered as an example of coordination. The most extended section lists the attitudes required of cadres. They should treat benefiting the people as the greatest achievement, seek progress while maintaining stability, and reject formalism and "vanity projects". They should adapt policy to local conditions, think systemically, and treat the country as "one chessboard". Zhou criticises GDP-centred thinking, excessive local debt, blind expansion into new energy vehicles and big data, and "involutionary" competition among localities over investment. Zhou calls for a unified national market and for evaluation indicators that give more weight to innovation, environment and livelihoods. Zhou concludes that a leader's view of political achievements is bound up with their view of development. Only by holding the right values, strategic composure, a practical working style and a systemic outlook, the author says, can the new development philosophy become high-quality development. Zhou presents this as a foundation for the 15th Five-Year Plan period and for socialist modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how official commentary links the new development philosophy to cadre evaluation, local-government behaviour and the economic priorities for the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Giving full play to culture's role in nurturing aspirations and cultivating sentiments 充分发挥文化养心志、育情操重要作用 Lian Ziqiang This short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 23 October 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at a Political Bureau study session to use culture to nurture aspirations (xin zhi) and cultivate sentiments (qing cao). Lian Ziqiang argues that the strength of a culturally strong socialist country shows above all in people's ideological outlook, spirit and cultural refinement. Promoting cultural education is presented as both an internal requirement of building a culturally strong country and a practical need for steadiness amid what the author calls a century of great change. The piece first defines the two functions, then gives historical examples, then turns to the sources of cultural resources and to practical measures. It draws on Party history from the revolutionary and socialist construction periods to the present era. Lian contends that healthy culture internalises values as cultural and value identification, binds people through shared symbols, rituals and beliefs, and fosters social cohesion and a positive social ethos. The author cites slogans from successive periods as examples of how culture has inspired people. The sources named are advanced socialist culture, revolutionary culture and fine traditional Chinese culture, guided by core socialist values. On the supply side, Lian says the main cultural contradiction has shifted from "whether there is" to "whether it is good", which calls for better public cultural services and products, a large and well-structured pool of cultural talent, and the use of artificial intelligence, big data and virtual reality for precise, immersive delivery. The author concludes that culture-building must start and end with people, and that stronger cultural influence will give spiritual support to Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links cultural policy, core socialist values and new technology to moral and ideological education.

The key to building a modern socialist country in all respects lies in the Party: studying Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China 全面建设社会主义现代化国家关键在党——学习《习近平谈治国理政》第五卷 National Association for Party-Building Studies (Quanguo Dangjian Yanjiuhui) This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 23 October 2025 as the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee met in Beijing, is a study piece on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. It argues that the key to building a modern socialist country in all respects, and to national rejuvenation, is the Party. In the authors' reading, Xi Jinping's statements show that a strong country presupposes a strong Party and that a strong Party in turn aims at and rests on a strong country. The text is organised around three questions. It first looks back at why the Communist Party can lead the Chinese people in building a modern country. It then identifies five major risks and challenges facing the Party on the new journey. Finally it asks what kind of 'the world's most powerful political party' is to be built and how to build it. On the historical question, the authors trace the Party's role through the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era, and describe Chinese modernization as a path that breaks the equation of 'modernization = Westernization'. They cite a Party membership of 100.271 million and a comprehensive organisational system. The five challenges are the great changes unseen in a century; the task of high-quality development, where some cadres are said to lack ability or willingness to act; the internet as the 'biggest variable' in ideological struggle; separation from the people; and corruption, which they say has become more hidden and variable despite an 'overwhelming victory' in the anti-corruption struggle. For strengthening the Party, the authors set out five pillars: resolutely achieving the Two Upholds and grasping the decisive significance of the Two Establishes; scientific theory, centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Two Integrations; a strong cadre and talent corps; firm organisation, including Party-building in new economic and social organisations and among new forms of employment; and the Party's self-reform through problem-orientation, innovation, strictness and institutions. The piece closes with a call for strategic resolve and unity around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-building establishment frames Party leadership as the precondition of Chinese modernization, and the risks it names.

The growing pains of intelligent transformation and their resolution: an analysis based on Marx's view of machinery 智能化转型阵痛及其消解 ——基于马克思机器观的分析 Sun Daiyao Hua Yuanming Why does the shift to artificial intelligence bring painful dislocations such as job loss, heavier workloads and widening inequality? Sun and Hua argue that the cause lies neither in technology as such nor in individual differences in ability. In their account it lies in the way intelligent technology is combined with labour under capital, and Marx's analysis of machinery still explains this. The article first reviews existing explanations: technology-centred (enabling versus replacing technologies), individual-centred, Robert Owen's moral critique and Schumpeter's "creative destruction". It then reconstructs Marx's diagnosis of the "machine question" and tests whether it applies to AI. The second part analyses the roots and forms of the pains; the third proposes ways to resolve them, drawing on Xi Jinping's speeches and recent Chinese policy documents. Sun and Hua's central move is to distinguish machinery as such from its capitalist form. For Marx, machines become fixed capital, dead labour set against living labour, and workers move from formal to real subsumption. The authors hold that differences between intelligent systems and machine systems (infinite copying, no wear, simulation of thought) do not change this. They argue that AI remains material and cannot become a civilisational subject, and that the shift is comparable to mechanisation. Capital monopolises data and computing power, so AI becomes an instrument of capital's discipline over labour. The authors trace three consequences: technological unemployment, hidden intensification of work (including unpaid data production on platforms) and growing inequality between capital and labour and among workers. The authors propose three ways to dissolve the pains. First, understand capital's dual character under the socialist market economy and curb its negative effects, for example through public computing and data platforms. Second, protect the rights of emerging workers, including platform workers, and cultivate a "new type of worker" who is autonomous and creative. Third, build a harmonious human–machine civilisation through ethical governance of AI, a new type of production relations suited to new quality productive forces and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Marxist, capital-centred account of AI's labour effects that links Marx's machinery theory to current Chinese policy.

Marx and Engels on the modernization path of latecomer countries and its contemporary value 马克思恩格斯关于后发国家现代化道路的思想探索及其当代价值 Yang Yushi Marx and Engels wrote on how latecomer countries might modernize, and their statements differ in tone. Yang takes up that difference and the Western readings of it. Hobsbawm, in Yang's account, thought Marx leaned towards Narodnik theory, while Levine ascribed the gap to opposed views of history. Yang rejects both as misreadings that posit a Marx–Engels opposition. The article argues the difference marks an unfinished form of the theory (Marx) and a completed form (Engels), built on shared premises. The article has four parts. It first traces how Marx built his theory of modernization, moving from belief in capitalist modernity to critique and then to transcendence. It then covers Marx's late attempt to apply that theory to Russia, in the letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski and the drafts of the reply to Vera Zasulich. A third section follows Engels's work from 1874 to the 1890s. The last two sections compare the two thinkers, then turn to Soviet and Chinese practice. Yang argues that Marx and Engels agreed on two points: latecomer countries can avoid capitalist modernization and skip the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, and this needs preconditions, above all preserving the country's own favourable factors such as communal landholding. Marx stressed the possibility, left the preconditions unresolved, and cut the Zasulich drafts down sharply. Engels, after Marx's death, specified two indispensable conditions: favourable internal factors and an external model, namely revolution in Western Europe. Seeing both fading in Russia, Engels grew pessimistic without abandoning the thesis. Yang adds that Chinese scholars explain the gap by historical context, and argues that this also reflects a theoretical movement from the universal to the particular. Yang concludes that both thinkers worked in a spirit of seeking truth from facts. Lenin's New Economic Policy is presented as an inventive answer to the missing external model. The Soviet Union is said to have later rushed towards the future society regardless of its productive forces. China, in Yang's account, combined the universal theory with its own conditions through Party leadership, the basic socialist economic system, and reform and opening up, thereby advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of the Marx–Engels debate on the Russian commune, or the textual case for linking it to Chinese modernization.

Digital capital or digitalised monopoly finance capital? Understanding the complexity of contemporary capitalism 数字资本抑或数字化垄断金融资本——基于当代资本主义的复杂性理解 Liu Zhihong What is the dominant form of capital in contemporary capitalism? Liu Zhihong takes up the claim, increasingly accepted among scholars, that digital capital has replaced finance capital as the dominant or even the general form of capital. Liu agrees that digital capital has risen sharply but argues it cannot simply be declared the dominant form. The article's answer is that the dominant form is digitalised monopoly finance capital. The article has five parts. It first tests the case for digital capital's dominance, then reconstructs the concept of finance capital from Hilferding and Lenin and distinguishes a narrow and a broad sense. It next sets out finance capital's continuing power over other capital forms, and then examines how finance and digital capital relate. A final section brings in monopoly and concludes. Liu draws on Hilferding, Lenin, Marx, Harry Magdoff, Sweezy, John Bellamy Foster, Nick Srnicek and Dan Schiller. Liu makes three main moves. First, digital capital does not control finance capital: it has not removed the blindness of industrial and financial capital, since overproduction and crises persist and digital capital has its own blindness rooted in profit-seeking. It also takes a smaller share of profit than finance capital. Second, finance capital in the broad sense merges with functioning capital. Liu argues that finance capital owns and funds the digital platforms and takes much of their profit, much as interest-bearing capital splits surplus value in Capital, Volume III. Third, digital and finance capital are classified by different criteria (digital versus non-digital, and by industrial function), so they are not true opposites. Many digital capitals are simply finance capital in digital form. Liu concludes that the choice between digital and finance capital is a false "either-or", and that monopoly is the basic logic of capitalism now. Only monopoly digital capital could be dominant, and such platforms are controlled by, or themselves become, monopoly finance capital. Following Foster's "monopoly-finance capital", Liu proposes "digital monopoly finance capital", with monopoly as its basic quality, finance as its main feature and digitalisation as its new trait. Liu frames this as a complexity-based approach, citing Edgar Morin. Read the original if you want a Marxist, philosophically framed argument against "digital capitalism" theories that keeps finance capital central.

Leaps in the quality of talent and new quality productive forces 人才质态跃升与新质生产力 Hong Yinxing Bian Yuanchao Hong Yinxing and Bian Yuanchao ask what kind of workforce new quality productive forces require and which institutions can produce it. Taking their cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for institutions supporting comprehensive innovation, they argue that innovation is the essence of new quality productive forces and that talent is its base. Labourers are the most active element, and both complex and simple labourers must undergo a leap in quality. The article has three parts. The first describes the "quality form" of talent needed, covering strategic scientists and technology entrepreneurs. The second takes up education racing against technology, including how the quality of simple labour can be raised. The third sets out institutions and incentives: support for chain leaders, venture investors, income distribution and competition for talent between regions. It draws on Marx's "collective worker", Schumpeter, Piketty, Goldin and Katz, Phelps and Knight. The authors hold, following Marx, that complex labour is a historical category: the schooling needed to perform it rises with technology, and AI now threatens to displace even complex labour. Talent chains should therefore be matched to innovation and industrial chains, with strategic scientists and technology entrepreneurs as the "chain leaders". Education must lead technology and not follow it, through forward-looking university curricula and lifelong learning. This would move simple labourers from "human–machine substitution" to "human–machine symbiosis". Training costs, they say, should be shared among workers, firms and government. On incentives, the authors call for property-rights protection, tolerance of failure, and exit channels for venture capital through STAR Market and ChiNext-type boards. They also propose differentiated pay for researchers, intellectual-property-based sharing of gains, and equity, options and salary for entrepreneurs so that human capital is converted into equity. They add that regions should compete for talent in a healthy way, based on local comparative advantage, public services and research conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy view linking new quality productive forces to labour theory, education policy and income distribution.

The accelerating evolution of changes unseen in a century and high-standard opening up 百年变局加速演进与高水平对外开放 Hong Junjie Writing in Economic Daily on 22 October 2025, Hong Junjie asks how China should respond to what official discourse calls the accelerating "changes unseen in a century". The commentary argues that closing off cannot meet these changes and that China must steadfastly pursue high-standard opening up. In Hong's account, such opening up shapes new development advantages, turns China's development into opportunities for other countries and creates a favourable external environment for Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts. The first describes four trends: a rebalancing of the international political order as Global South countries rise, a deep adjustment of the economic development paradigm under artificial intelligence and new energy, severe challenges for global governance, and more frequent clashes between civilizations. The second explains, from the standpoint of historical materialism, why opening up is the right response. The third sets out four practical directions for advancing it. Hong argues that the core of the present upheaval is a deep adjustment of the relations of production and the economic base. High-standard opening up is said to do four things: solve development problems and support high-quality development; build a strong science and technology country through open cooperation; take part in reforming global governance; and promote mutual learning among civilizations, thereby refining a "Chinese approach" to the changes. Hong presents opening up and security as one organic whole, to be handled with systems thinking and bottom-line thinking. For action, Hong calls for steadily expanding institutional opening up, aligning domestic rules with high international standards and countering Western "small yard, high fence" containment. Hong also proposes a comprehensive pattern of opening up that coordinates regions and platforms such as pilot free trade zones, and wider multilateral and bilateral cooperation, including a network of high-standard free trade areas and unilateral opening to the least developed countries. The fourth direction is to put the four global initiatives (on development, security, civilization and governance) into practice, in support of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university president links the "changes unseen in a century" to the official case for high-standard opening up.

Persistently advancing the Party's work style building 锲而不舍推进党的作风建设 Zhu Dayi This short commentary, published in the PLA Daily on 22 October 2025, argues that the Party's work style (zuofeng) bears on its image, on popular support and ultimately on its survival. Zhu Dayi, drawing on Xi Jinping, holds that bad styles are stubborn and recurrent, so good ones cannot be secured once and for all. Style building is therefore called a perennial theme of Party building and part of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece first sketches the Party's historical record on style, citing the Central Soviet Area, the Yan'an period, the "Two Musts" before entering Beijing and the reform era. It then says the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the Xi era deepened understanding of the subject, and that the current stage of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation brings unprecedented risks. Three areas for action follow: Party spirit, Party–mass relations and leading by example. Zhu's central claim is that style problems are at root problems of Party spirit, and that their core is the relationship between the Party and the people. On Party spirit, the author calls for lifelong cultivation, study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and joint handling of Party conduct, discipline and corruption. On the masses, officials are urged to feel for ordinary people, listen to them and learn from them. On leadership, "key minority" cadres should set an example by taking on hard tasks, practising integrity, opposing privilege and maintaining a sound family ethos. Zhu concludes that style building must become regular and long-term, with attention to the everyday, the detailed and the sustained. Good style is presented as a source of cohesion and a driving force for the Party's cause. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames Party conduct, discipline and leadership responsibility in 2025.

A historical examination of the law of mutual exchange and learning among civilizations: a critique of the Eurocentric unilinear view of history 文明交流互鉴发展规律的历史考察——基于对欧洲中心主义单线史观的批判 Liang Xiao Liang Xiao asks how the new-era conception of civilization, and in particular the idea that exchange and mutual learning are a law of civilizational development, can be used to read world history. The article's thesis is that the Eurocentric unilinear view of history, which presents Europe as the self-generated centre and leader of human history, ignores precisely this law. Liang treats that view as an intellectual root of historical nihilism and argues that European civilization itself developed through exchange with other civilizations. The article begins with the new-era conception of civilization, which Liang grounds in Xi Jinping's statements and in Marx and Engels's thinking on interaction between peoples. It sets out four features: civilization as the product of human labour and wisdom, as diverse, as equal, and as developing through mutual learning. It then reconstructs four tenets of Eurocentrism, drawing on Hegel, Condorcet, Ranke and J.M. Blaut. The remaining sections criticise these tenets in turn and finish with a separate critique of the theory of Oriental despotism. Liang argues that history was multilinear and that Europe was not the world's centre for most of it. Classical Greece had contemporaries in China and India, and Latin Christian Europe in the Middle Ages was a peripheral region. Greek achievements are placed within an eastern Mediterranean civilization circle, and medieval Europe's recovery is traced to the twelfth- and thirteenth-century translation movement from Arabic and to the influence of Chinese inventions. The supposed Greek-to-Renaissance continuity is called a fiction, because Arab scholars, in Liang's account, did not merely preserve Greek texts but absorbed, corrected and advanced them. Liang then rejects the Oriental despotism theory, which explains Western creativity by 'freedom' and Eastern stagnation by 'despotism'. In this account, abstract freedom is a faulty measure of state forms, and city-states were an early, weaker form. Liang contends that unified monarchical states, such as Ptolemaic Egypt with the Library and Museum of Alexandria and the Abbasid caliphate with al-Ma'mun's House of Wisdom, had the capacity to organise exchange and large scientific projects. Liang calls for deeper study of world civilization history, for developing historical materialism, and for building an autonomous knowledge system of Chinese and world civilization history. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS scholar uses the new-era conception of civilization to challenge Eurocentric historiography, with a detailed case on Greece, the Arab world and medieval Europe.

A Spaniard's observations on Chinese modernization 一个西班牙人对中国式现代化的观察 Julio Ceballos Julio Ceballos, a Spanish business consultant and writer, contributed this piece to the People's Daily to accompany his Spanish-language book Xuanji Tu (the Xuanji Diagram). The book draws on 18 years of work and life in China. Ceballos argues that China is not an unsolvable puzzle but a living jigsaw, and that its development experience offers lessons for Europe. The thesis is that there is no single fixed recipe for modernization: each civilisation can find its own path. The text is a first-person commentary built around four themes: why he wrote the book, strategic patience, education and innovation, and resilience and solidarity. It rests on anecdotes from Sichuan, Shandong, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Nanjing and Jinan, together with a few figures on research spending and talent. The book's title refers to an ancient astronomical instrument and to a palindrome poem by Su Hui, which he reads as a sign that there are many ways to meet global challenges. Ceballos's central contrast is between European political horizons, limited by election cycles and quarterly reports, and Chinese planning over decades, carried by the Five-Year Plans. In his account this continuity is sustained by a cadre promotion system based on experience, results and execution, which he calls performance-oriented governance. He also holds that China treats education, digital strategy and AI ethics governance as long-term national investments, and that social cohesion works as a ready-made resource when crises arrive. He cites figures that China leads the world in high-level scientific talent and in total research personnel, and that its 2024 R&D spending exceeded the EU average. Ceballos presents his book as an invitation and a bridge between Europe and China, not as uncritical praise or an idealised comparison. He admits that no system removes all problems. He proposes cooperation on resilience, social cohesion and community collaboration, with mutual respect for difference. His closing formula is "one equation, many solutions". Read the original if you want an example of how a foreign business observer's praise of Chinese long-term planning is presented in the Party's flagship newspaper, as one of the China Studies pieces on this site.

Making good use of the "Big Ideological and Political Course" to strengthen the leading force of ideological and political education 善用“大思政课” 增强思政引领力 Wu Qiantao Wu Qiantao's commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 9 October 2025, takes up the idea of "leading force of ideological and political education" (sizheng yinlingli), a phrase Xi Jinping introduced at the National Education Conference in September 2024. Wu argues that a key way to strengthen this force is to make good use of the "Big Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke), a approach to teaching ideology and politics that goes beyond the classroom. Wu first defines "sizheng" as shorthand for the worldview, outlook on life and values a society or party promotes. In his account, it covers ideological and political education, ideological and political work, socialist ideological education and the ideological and political courses themselves. The article then sets out three "bigs": a big sense of responsibility, a big content system and a big space for extension. Each is tied to one function: giving direction, supplying driving force, and building an education pattern involving all personnel, the whole process and every dimension. On responsibility, Wu holds that the course serves the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and cultivating "new-era people" loyal to the Party. He calls for Party leadership over its construction, better top-level design and a place for it as the highest form of school ideological work. On content, he stresses three strands: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture, and the histories of the Party, the PRC, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation. Wu says these turn theory into a teaching system and a system of belief. On extension, Wu proposes practice bases and "walking" courses in rural revitalization and grassroots governance, AI, big data and VR for teaching, and new-media matrices. He also proposes cross-department coordination, "curriculum ideology and politics" across all subjects, and integrated courses from primary school to university and between family, school and society. He concludes that this would make the leading force a systemic effect that builds the socialist direction of a strong education nation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official framework for ideological and political education under Xi Jinping's "education powerhouse" agenda.

Raising original creative capacity and communication capacity in digital culture 提高数字文化原创能力和传播能力 Sun Qianqian This newspaper commentary asks how China can strengthen both the originality and the reach of its digital culture. Sun Qianqian argues that museums' digital exhibitions, from Dunhuang mural restoration to virtual tours of the Terracotta Army pits, show rising original capacity. Raising it, Sun says, is necessary for passing on fine traditional Chinese culture, supporting high-quality development and strengthening national cultural soft power. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to improve cultural originality, then offers four sections: holding to cultural roots, technological empowerment, cross-sector integration, and international communication. Each pairs examples with policy suggestions. Cases include the Sanxingdui bronze tree model, a Yangzhou digital Classic of Mountains and Seas exhibition, the game Black Myth: Wukong and the film Ne Zha 2. Sun contends that originality must rest on cultural subjectivity, with digital technology serving as an empowering tool, not a substitute for tradition. The author calls for breakthroughs in key technologies, AI-assisted creative tools, big data and blockchain for content delivery, and ethical rules and copyright standards for AI creation. Sun also stresses integration with the economy and society, citing 2024 cultural trade of 1.4 trillion yuan, of which network audiovisual and similar digital trade exceeded 370 billion yuan (25.8%). Abroad, Sun says Chinese digital culture is moving from single-product export to whole-ecosystem expansion. Sun proposes systematic thinking: building an industrialised IP system, developing digital cultural brands, combining intangible heritage with tourism, and fostering an open, orderly digital cultural market. For overseas reach, Sun urges international fairs, cooperation with Belt and Road Initiative partners, talent recruitment and copyright cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official-line commentary links digital technology, cultural industry policy and soft power.

Providing institutional support for building a strong cultural nation 为文化强国建设提供制度支撑 Wang Zengfu Wang Zengfu, writing in Guangming Daily in October 2025, asks how institution-building can support the drive to turn China from a large cultural country into a strong cultural nation. Taking up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) principle of making institution-building the main thread of deepening reform, Wang argues that cultural institutions regulate cultural order, guide cultural governance and coordinate the elements of cultural development. Strengthening the cultural system of socialism with Chinese characteristics is presented as both a guarantee of cultural soft power and a necessary choice for national rejuvenation. The article is organised in four parts, each pairing a goal with a set of institutional measures. These are: using the strengths of the cultural system to strengthen ideological leadership; stimulating institutional vitality; improving the cultural system to raise governance capacity; and consolidating institutional safeguards to widen the paths to cultural prosperity. It is a policy-oriented commentary that draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and Party documents rather than on empirical cases. Wang's central claim is that Party leadership and Marxism's guiding position are the foundation of the cultural system. In Wang's account, public ownership, the people's democratic dictatorship and the Party's governing status determine Marxism's guiding role in ideology. The practical agenda that follows includes a public cultural service system that moves from "having" to "excellent", and top-level design guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. It also covers reform that keeps social benefits first while managing the dual ideological and market character of cultural products. Wang then lists specific systems: heritage protection with scientific and technological support, comprehensive online governance including protection of minors, cultural security against what the author calls hostile Western ideological infiltration, and an international communication system with new concepts and expressions. Wang concludes that cultural legislation, market supervision and technological support must be strengthened so that China can keep its cultural subjectivity amid global cultural competition. Proposals include multi-level cultural law and judicial protection of intellectual property, restructuring state-owned cultural enterprises, a fair and unified cultural market, and secure management of cultural data. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars frame cultural institution-building, ideological security and international communication in the context of building a cultural powerhouse.

The Grand View of History: the socio-historical outlook of contemporary Chinese Marxism 大历史观：当代中国马克思主义的社会历史观 Liu Zhuohong This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 13 October 2025, asks what the "Grand View of History" (da lishi guan) is and where it sits within Marxist theory. Liu Zhuohong argues that it is a new socio-historical outlook of contemporary Chinese Marxism. In Liu's account it grew out of the Communist Party's summing-up of its century of experience, its reading of the era, and its seizing of the historical initiative. Liu traces its articulation to Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article first places the concept on the foundation of historical materialism, which it says the Grand View both inherits and develops by linking the inner logic of the past with the practical logic of the present. It then presents the concept as a fusion of three views: a people-centred view of history, a practice-centred view and a developmental view. A final section describes the Grand View as a creative advance on historical materialism, with its own distinctive features. Liu's core argument has three parts. First, the people are the creators of material and spiritual wealth and the main force of social change, so the Grand View requires standing with the people and respecting their creativity. Second, history is a history of practice, and practice always unfolds in a particular "social field" (shehui changyu); Liu holds that grasping history through the unity of practice and social field deepens the historical-materialist concept of history. Third, the Grand View treats past, present and future as one integrated whole, which Liu analyses in ontological terms (what is present or absent as practice) and epistemological terms (completed practice can be examined as a whole to extract laws). Liu concludes that the Grand View keeps the people-first character, problem-oriented practical character and holistic character of historical materialism. It also stresses historical thinking and historical confidence: facing the Party's past problems honestly, drawing on historical laws and learning from experience. Liu says this strengthens cultural confidence and supplies a method for taking on present missions, and so advances historical materialism in the unity of theory and practice. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists currently present Xi Jinping's "Grand View of History" as a development of historical materialism.

Building on our own strengths: teaching the "Great Ideological and Political Course" well in information-technology universities 立足自身优势，上好信息科技特色高校“大思政课” Xu Mei Xu Mei, Party secretary of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, asks how universities that specialise in information technology can use their own traditions and disciplinary strengths to run the "Great Ideological and Political Course" well. Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2025, Xu argues that such universities should turn their distinctive profile into an advantage in moral education, in line with the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out the value of the course for these universities, then names four relationships to be handled, and finally proposes practical paths. These are organised around four "big" elements: classroom, platform, teaching staff and overall framework. Xu's core claim is that disciplinary and technological resources should be fused with value guidance rather than used on their own. The four relationships are disciplinary distinctiveness and the laws of education, instrumental rationality and value rationality, multiple actors and university leadership, and on-campus and off-campus resources. Xu warns against the idea that technology is all-powerful and insists that university Party committees steer the work. The practical measures include using the university's revolutionary history in teaching and ceremonies, and building AI-based student development platforms, citing Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications' "You AI" platform. Others are dual mentors from the university and industry, and a closed loop in which industry sets problems, students and teachers solve them and firms evaluate the results. Xu concludes that this approach would produce talent who combine technical skill with patriotism and a sense of mission for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and who contribute to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how a Party-led technical university describes the integration of AI and industry partnerships into ideological and political education.

The significance and pathways of raising the effectiveness of the global communication of Chinese culture 提升中华文化全球传播效能的意义和路径 Zeng Xiangmin Li Chaopeng Zhao Xijing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 14 October 2025, asks why the global communication of Chinese culture needs to become more effective and how that can be done. Zeng Xiangmin and two co-authors take as their starting point the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which call for stronger international communication capacity. They argue that raising communication effectiveness is both strategically necessary and practically feasible, and that it requires coordinated work on four fronts. The piece has two parts. The first sets out the significance of the task, and the second proposes four practical routes: drawing on cultural resources, innovating the discourse system, training versatile communication talent and building a plural set of communicators, and creating self-controlled platforms and new carriers of communication. Each route is broken into short sub-measures. On significance, the authors say that competition in cultural soft power has become a key dimension of overall national strength. They hold that ideas such as harmony in diversity and "all under heaven is for the public" match global demands for peace, development and cooperation. They also point to three conditions: the depth of Chinese civilisation, state support for international communication, and new technologies such as artificial intelligence and immersive media. On method, they urge strengthening cultural confidence and cultural subjectivity, distilling spiritual symbols, and presenting both historical and contemporary China. They also call for shifting from "display and promotion" to "interaction and participation", combining grand and micro narratives, and diversifying language, channels and settings. Communication should be a "chorus" of official bodies, think tanks, cultural enterprises, young people and overseas Chinese rather than a "solo". The authors conclude that, in the international opinion arena, "platform is channel, and channel is influence". They call for digital cultural products, everyday objects that carry cultural elements, and multilingual, algorithm-supported communication matrices that match the needs of different audiences. They also want universities to build interdisciplinary programmes in language, culture, journalism and digital technology. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy framework for the international communication of Chinese culture, as set out in a Party newspaper in late 2025.

The historical position, rich connotations and contemporary value of the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang in the new era 新时代党的治疆方略的历史方位、丰富内涵和时代价值 Su Cheng Published in Guangming Daily on 15 October 2025, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call of 24 September to implement the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang in the new era "completely, accurately and comprehensively". Su Cheng argues that this requires grasping the strategy's historical position, its rich connotations and its contemporary value. The author presents the strategy as the concentrated expression of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era on Xinjiang work. The article has three sections. The first places the strategy in the era that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012) and in Xinjiang's role in national rejuvenation. The second sets out its content, including the "eight adherences" and five guiding principles. The third assesses its value in guidance, theory and international example, and closes by pointing to the achievements of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region over its 70 years. On historical position, Su describes Xinjiang as a security barrier in the north-west, a gateway for opening to the west, an energy and agricultural base and a core area of the Silk Road Economic Belt. The author states that terrorism, separatism and religious extremism, together with Western forces that fabricate a so-called "Xinjiang issue", heighten its strategic importance. On content, Su lists the "eight adherences", including social stability and lasting peace and order as the overall goal, forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, the sinicisation of religion and high-quality development. The guiding principles are governing Xinjiang by law, stabilising it through unity, enriching it through culture, building it through prosperity and building it for the long term. Su reads the strategy as showing Marxist dialectics: balancing the two-sided and the focal, the whole and the part, and continuity and innovation. On value, Su claims the strategy offers scientific guidance, enriches border governance theory by tying frontier regions to national strategy, and gives multi-ethnic states a "Chinese solution". The author asserts that it curbs terrorism and extremism at source while protecting citizens' basic rights and freedoms. Su concludes that Xinjiang's achievements demonstrate the strategy to be entirely correct and show the strength of the Party's leadership and of China's path on ethnic questions. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative-style statement of how official Chinese commentary frames Xinjiang policy in 2025.

Correctly grasping the relationship between commonality and difference 正确把握共同性和差异性的关系 Chu Songyan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in October 2025, takes up a principle Xi Jinping set out at the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Affairs: that ethnic work must correctly handle the relationship between commonality and difference. Chu argues that the two stand in a dialectical unity. Commonality presupposes difference, and difference is oriented towards commonality, so the Party's ethnic work can be done well only if both are handled properly. The article first sketches the historical formation of a pluralistic, integrated Chinese nation. It then treats the two sides in turn: increasing commonality, and respecting and accommodating difference. It closes by drawing on historical experience and the Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On commonality, Chu holds that it is not homogenisation but the largest common denominator produced by exchange among ethnic groups. It rests on the 'four togethers' community concept and the 'five identifications' (with the motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics). On difference, Chu says customs, culture and arts should be protected and passed on, and cites a figure that over one-third of China's UNESCO intangible heritage items come from minorities. Chu adds that commonality must remain dominant: difference must not weaken it, and Han chauvinism and local ethnic nationalism are opposed. Differentiated regional support policies are proposed. Chu concludes that forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation requires upholding the Party's overall leadership and increasing commonality while respecting difference. The aim is to strengthen the ideological, social, cultural-psychological and security foundations of ethnic unity in support of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-school framing of ethnic policy and its key slogans.

Building a comprehensive, multi-level system for cultivating a culture of integrity 构建全方位多层次的廉洁文化培育体系 Zhang Xianfeng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 16 October 2025, asks how a culture of integrity (lianjie wenhua) can be built into a lasting system rather than a one-off campaign. Zhang Xianfeng argues that it is a systemic undertaking that cannot be completed in a day or by a single actor. It needs a cultivation system that is comprehensive in coverage, multi-level in penetration and wide in reach. Zhang begins from the policy background: the Party's emphasis since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the 2022 General Office guideline on integrity culture in the new era, and the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which called for a three-year action plan for 2025–2027. The article is then organised under three headings: differentiated guidance, faster innovation in methods, and integrated promotion. On differentiated guidance, Zhang sets out distinct approaches for four groups. Leading cadres are the 'key minority' and need mandatory, cautionary education, risk-point screening and the 'cage of institutions' to constrain power. Ordinary Party members need discipline awareness and public integrity pledges. Students need integrated primary-to-university education, and the general public needs cultural products and easy reporting channels with protection for whistle-blowers. On innovation, Zhang proposes digital tools such as a 'smart integrity education' cloud platform, big-data risk early warning and virtual-reality exhibition halls. Zhang also proposes integrity-themed cultural brands, cartoon figures and creative merchandise, and the placing of integrity elements in everyday settings such as parks, festivals and village life. On integrated promotion, Zhang calls for a closed-loop management system with a joint conference mechanism, task lists broken down to individuals, and inclusion of results in the Party conduct and ideological work responsibility assessments. Zhang also proposes a shared resource platform with personalised content recommendation, and an evaluation mechanism using quantified indicators and independent third-party assessors. Feedback would then drive a plan–execute–check–adjust cycle, moving integrity culture from 'visible coverage' to 'effective coverage'. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-oriented picture of how Party-school scholars and official media describe the operational design of anti-corruption cultural work.

Forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and building a modernized socialist Xinjiang 铸牢中华民族共同体意识 建设社会主义现代化新疆 Bu Lingquan Writing in Guangming Daily on 17 October 2025, shortly after Xi Jinping led a central delegation to the celebrations of the 70th anniversary of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region (September 2025), Bu Lingquan sets out how Xinjiang should carry out its work in the new journey of building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation.
