The author argues that Xinjiang must fully, accurately and comprehensively implement the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang in the new era, centred on forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, in order to build a harmonious, prosperous, civilised, secure and ecologically sound modernized socialist Xinjiang. The commentary is a Party-line policy exposition in three parts. The first deals with forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation as the main thread of work. The second covers the overall goal of social stability and lasting peace and order, and the five pillars of the governing strategy. The third deals with Xinjiang's role in the national picture and the contribution it is to make to Chinese modernization. Throughout, Bu draws on Xi Jinping's statements. In the first part, Bu calls for deepening education in ethnic unity and progress, promoting interaction, exchange and integration among ethnic groups through the embedding of communities in space, culture, economy, society and psychology, and carrying forward fine traditional Chinese culture, citing heritage sites such as Jiaohe and Niya. The second part presents the strategy as governing Xinjiang by law, ensuring stability through unity, enriching Xinjiang through culture, making the people prosperous, and long-term building of Xinjiang. In Bu's account this includes opposing ethnic separatism and religious extremism and teaching that Xinjiang has been an inseparable part of Chinese territory since ancient times. The third part calls for developing distinctive industries, new quality productive forces, cultural tourism, ecological protection, the core area of the Silk Road Economic Belt, and improved livelihoods. Bu concludes that Xinjiang should anchor itself to the "five major strategic positions" assigned by the Centre, including a gateway for opening to the west, an energy and resource base, and a barrier for national geopolitical security. The author calls for shifting from "blood transfusion" assistance to "blood-making" co-existence, so that people of all ethnic groups share in development. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how Party-aligned scholars in Xinjiang present current policy priorities, framed around the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang.

Advancing the construction of an autonomous knowledge system for CPC history and Party building studies through academic innovation 以学术创新推动中共党史党建学自主知识体系构建 Zhao Nuo Writing in Guangming Daily (17 October 2025), Zhao Nuo asks how the newly established first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building studies can build its own autonomous knowledge system. The author argues that the discipline, which studies the Party's history and the laws of its self-development, is among the most distinctively Chinese in the social sciences and should help build Chinese philosophy and social sciences with their own system. The answer offered is sustained academic innovation along three mutually dependent lines: knowledge, theory and method. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's recent remarks on the National Education Conference and on Fudan University's 120th anniversary, which Zhao treats as the fundamental guidance for this task. It then has three sections, one for each type of innovation, and closes with a short summary of how they fit together. Examples come from the author's own research, from wartime diplomacy and from digital tools. On knowledge innovation, Zhao calls for a closed loop from sources to concepts through "three connections": linking history and reality to find new materials (local archives, oral history, audiovisual records); linking the whole and the individual to reach new viewpoints (for instance, cadres' diaries showing that their perceptions of the situation drew on both Marxist classics and Neo-Confucian ideas of "form" and "momentum"); and linking Party history and Party building to create new concepts such as the Party's self-reform. On theory, the author holds that Marxism is the "soul", excellent traditional Chinese culture the "root", and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era the latest resource, with scholars expected to answer the questions of the times and the Two Integrations as the guide. On method, Zhao advocates interdisciplinary borrowing (institutional analysis, network analysis, political psychology) screened by a Marxist standpoint, plus digital humanities: text mining of cadres' writings, large databases and GIS reconstruction of revolutionary sites. Zhao concludes that knowledge innovation is the foundation, theory innovation the core "beams and pillars", and method innovation the engine, and that together they form the basic path for building the system. The task is described as significant and demanding. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Peking University scholar proposes to operationalise the "autonomous knowledge system" agenda in Party history research, including its use of digital methods.

The contemporary significance of the Communist Party of China's strategic guidance in the War of Resistance against Japan 中国共产党抗战指导谋略的当代意义 Zhao Weibo Liu Siwei Published in Guangming Daily on 19 October 2025, this short commentary follows Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration of the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Zhao Weibo and Liu Siwei ask what the Communist Party of China's wartime strategic guidance can still teach today. They argue that the Party, acting as the "mainstay" of the resistance, combined a global outlook, coordination across several domains, innovative military strategy and flexible armed struggle, and that each of these yields lessons for current national security. The article has four sections: using a global vision to coordinate national security; multi-domain coordination to build a winning combined force; continuous innovation in military strategic guidance; and resolute yet flexible military struggle. Each section first reviews the Party's wartime practice and then draws a lesson for the present. The wartime evidence includes the Party's declaration after the outbreak of the Pacific War in December 1941, the united front, base areas behind enemy lines, guerrilla tactics, the Hundred Regiments Campaign and Mao Zedong's 1938 writings on guerrilla warfare. The authors argue that the Party set China's resistance within the global anti-fascist struggle, predicted that Britain and the United States would eventually join the anti-Japanese camp, and treated the Soviet Union as a reliable external ally. At home, the Party built a national united front through concessions such as reorganising the Red Army into the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army, shifting to rent and interest reduction, and adopting the "three-thirds" system of government. Behind enemy lines it expanded base areas and turned their economic and social resources into military capacity through production campaigns and streamlined administration. Militarily, the authors credit the Party with making guerrilla warfare the main form of combat and with deliberately shaping the battlefield, in the manner of a game of go. They also credit it with shifting strategy as circumstances changed, combining guerrilla and mobile warfare, and seizing the initiative. From this history the authors derive proposals for today. China should approach security with a global vision, mutual learning among civilizations, multilateralism and self-reliant development, and should build the capacity for total people's war and an integrated national strategic system. It should develop algorithmic, unmanned and cognitive warfare, pre-position in space, the deep sea, the polar regions and cyberspace, and conduct military struggle that is "not out of control, not showing weakness, not suffering loss", so as to safeguard territorial sovereignty and maritime rights. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese military-academic writers link the history of the War of Resistance to present-day security and military-strategy thinking.

The world significance of Chinese modernization seen through time, space and civilizational narrative 从时间、空间与文明叙事看中国式现代化的世界意义 Wang Guang This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 20 October 2025, asks what Chinese modernization means for the world. Wang Guang argues that there is no single fixed model of modernization, and that Chinese modernization has opened a diverse, multidimensional path. In the author's account, its global significance lies in three dimensions: time, space and civilization. Together they allow China to move beyond time, space and civilizational narratives dominated by the Western developed countries. The article is a short essay with three sections, one for each dimension. The first deals with time, drawing on Marx's analysis of free time and on the history of standard time. The second deals with the spatial order of East and West that capital produced. The third deals with the European narrative of civilization and the alternative that Chinese modernization is said to offer. Wang draws on Marx and Engels, Vico, Norbert Elias, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On time, Wang follows Marx in treating free time as the product of others' unfree time, and says that China, like other colonised countries, once supplied free time to the Western powers. The author cites the 1884 adoption of Greenwich time and the 'coastal time' imposed on Shanghai's Bund after 1840 as examples of time made into power and ideology, placing advanced countries 'upstream' and latecomers 'downstream'. In this reading Chinese modernization has closed that gap, moving China from lagging behind its age to catching up with it and then leading it. On space, Wang cites the Communist Manifesto's line that the bourgeoisie made the East dependent on the West and argues that China's success is narrowing the East–West development gap, while capitalism's institutional failures are exposed. On civilization, Wang says Europeans built hierarchies of 'civilized' and 'barbarian' peoples that justified colonial violence. Chinese modernization, by contrast, creates a new form of human civilization based on equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness. Wang concludes that Chinese modernization has given the Chinese people control of their own time and fate. The author adds that it offers a civilizational narrative with cultural agency, which supports a community with a shared future for mankind and expresses a commitment to peace and development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese scholarship presents the global significance of Chinese modernization through Marxist ideas about time, space and civilization.

The value implications of common prosperity in spiritual life 精神生活共同富裕的价值意蕴 Liang Jiafeng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, asks what value significance attaches to "common prosperity in spiritual life", the idea that common prosperity must cover people's spiritual as well as material life. The article starts from the relation between material and spiritual life, noting that Marx never formally proposed "spiritual wealth" but did refer to the wealth and poverty of the spirit. On the value basis, Liang contends that common prosperity is a requirement of socialism and a feature of Chinese modernization, and so cannot do without spiritual prosperity. On the value goal, Liang argues that spiritual prosperity affirms the people's status as the subject of history, answers the demand for all-round social progress, and serves the free and all-round development of the human being. Liang concludes that spiritual common prosperity is an inherent requirement of meeting people's growing needs for a better life. In Liang's account, industrial modernization elsewhere produced "one-dimensional" people and a loss of humanistic spirit, whereas Chinese modernization balances material and cultural-ethical advance. The practical proposals are to put social benefit first, to enrich cultural creation, to improve public cultural services and to develop cultural undertakings and industries together. Strengthening the idea of using culture to engage in dialogue with the world 强化用文化同世界对话的理念 Lian Ziqiang This Guangming Daily commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call, in his article on accelerating the building of a cultural powerhouse, to use culture in dialogue with the world. Seizing the key links to make ideological and political work in universities more targeted 抓住关键环节，提高学校思政工作针对性 Yin Zhaohua Following the Central Committee's recent issuing of the Regulations on Ideological and Political Work of the Communist Party of China, this Guangming Daily commentary asks how universities can make their ideological and political work more targeted and effective. Making red culture a "living source" that nourishes students' minds 让红色文化成为滋养心灵的“源头活水” Dong Jie This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 21 October 2025, asks how universities can make red culture a lasting source of moral and ideological nourishment for students. Accelerating the construction of a discourse system for the Communist Party of China's self-reform 加快构建中国共产党自我革命话语体系 Liu Xianchun Writing in Guangming Daily, Liu Xianchun argues that the Party needs to build, quickly, a discourse system for its self-reform that has Chinese characteristics, style and manner. Understanding the rich meaning and practical requirements of "investing in people" 深刻理解和把握“投资于人”的丰富意蕴和实践要求 Sun Cunliang Zhang Feixue This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, takes up the policy concept of "investing in people" (投资于人). Better coordinating high-quality development and high-standard security Expert commentary on studying volume one of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping 更好统筹高质量发展和高水平安全 Li Fei Huang Jing This commentary by Li Fei and Huang Jing of Xiamen University appeared in the People's Daily on 20 October 2025, in a series on studying the first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping. Understanding the institutional advantages shown by Five-Year Plans 深刻认识五年规划彰显的制度优势 Wang Yiming Writing in the People's Daily as the 14th Five-Year Plan period nears its end, Wang Yiming asks what institutional advantages China's Five-Year Plans display. A historical examination of the law of exchange and mutual learning among civilizations: a critique of the Eurocentric unilinear view of history 文明交流互鉴发展规律的历史考察——基于对欧洲中心主义单线史观的批判 Liang Xiao Liang Xiao takes up a question set by Xi Jinping's view that exchange and mutual learning are a law of civilizational development: what happens to world history when that law is applied to Europe itself? The article argues that the Eurocentric unilinear view of history, which presents Europe as the self-generating, necessary and leading line of world history, is a fiction. In Liang's account, European civilization owed its vitality and creativity to borrowing from other civilizations, and the unilinear view is an important intellectual root of historical nihilism. The article has four main parts. It first sets out the new-era conception of civilization (civilizations as products of human labour and wisdom, diverse, equal, and developing through mutual learning) and traces its background in Marx and Engels. It then reconstructs four core claims of Eurocentrism, drawing on Hegel, Condorcet, Ranke and J. M. Blaut. The third part rebuts these claims point by point, and the fourth examines the theory of oriental despotism. Liang's examples run from ancient Greece and Rome through Han China, Byzantium and the Abbasid caliphate to the medieval Latin West. Liang makes three moves. First, civilizational development is multilinear: Greek philosophy, mathematics and medicine did not clearly surpass contemporary Chinese or Indian achievements, and for most of the period from the fifth to the fifteenth century Latin Christian Europe was a peripheral corner of Eurasia. Second, Greek brilliance came out of the wider eastern Mediterranean world, and Europe's later revival depended on the twelfth- and thirteenth-century translation of Arabic scholarship and on Chinese inventions; the claim that Arabs merely 'preserved' Greek texts is, Liang says, a distortion, since Arab scholars corrected and extended them. Third, Liang rejects the despotism-versus-freedom thesis as ahistorical. In Liang's reading, small city-states and early feudal polities represent a lower stage of state development, and unified monarchies had greater capacity to organise exchange, as the Ptolemaic Museum of Alexandria and al-Ma'mun's House of Wisdom show. Liang concludes that both the Greek golden age and the rise of European modernity followed the law of exchange and mutual learning. The author calls for research on world civilizational history and for deepening historical materialism in order to build an autonomous knowledge system for the history of Chinese and world civilization. The article also urges openness and inclusiveness in building civilization today, so as to bring Chinese civilization to new heights. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses Eurocentrism critique and the history of Greek, Arab and European science to support the official doctrine of mutual learning among civilizations.

Grasping and conducting criticism and self-criticism scientifically and accurately through dialectical thinking 以辩证思维科学准确把握与开展批评和自我批评 Chen Hexiang Chen Hexiang, a professor at the Shenzhen Party school, asks how Party members and officials can make criticism and self-criticism an effective tool rather than a blunt one. Writing in the People's Daily in October 2025, Chen argues that the answer lies in dialectical thinking, which the author presents as the basis of Xi Jinping's remarks on the subject since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The piece is framed by the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to use this "weapon" to keep the Party's political ecology clean. The article has three parts. The first sets out the multiple values of criticism and self-criticism. The second turns to methods and strategies, and the third to the "art" of turning opposition into unity. Xi's statements are quoted throughout. The text is tied to the current campaign of study and education on the central Eight-point Regulation, and to the aim of making improved work style routine and long-lasting. In the first part, Chen identifies three functions. Epistemologically, criticism works as a "corrector" that exposes hidden contradictions and corrects cognitive bias within the cycle of practice and understanding. Dialectically, it is a "negative mediator" of sublation: a constructive negation that moves from negating the status quo to raising expectations of improvement and then reconstruction, in a cycle of unity–criticism–unity. In practice, its effects are twofold. Chen lists six criteria for telling constructive from destructive criticism, among them aim, object, attitude, content, communication and consequences. The second part pairs four methods, each of which should be balanced rather than chosen once and for all: inward and outward focus, fast and slow timing, public and private settings, and direct and indirect expression. The third part calls for balancing principle with flexibility, the whole with the part, and the present with the long term. Chen concludes that the courage for self-reform is the Party's most distinctive quality and that criticism and self-criticism are central to preserving its vanguard character and purity. Chen calls on every Party member and official to use the tool often and well, until it becomes a habit, a sense of duty and a responsibility. The stated aim is to strengthen the Party's capacity for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-advancement on the path to national rejuvenation. Understanding and implementing the Global Governance Initiative from a systematic and holistic perspective Study notes on volumes one and two of Xi Jinping's "On Upholding Comprehensively Deepening Reform" 从系统和全局把握践行全球治理倡议 Sun Jisheng This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 10 October 2025, is a study piece on the Global Governance Initiative that Xi Jinping put forward at the "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Plus" meeting. Sun Jisheng, a vice president of China Foreign Affairs University, argues that the initiative is a further original contribution to Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought. The third proposes how to put it into practice, and cites support from several countries and from UN Secretary-General Guterres. Sun presents five core concepts. Sovereign equality is the first precondition. International rule of law is the fundamental safeguard, and the author criticises double standards and the imposition of a few countries' \"house rules\". As an example of delay, Sun cites the 100 billion US dollars a year in climate finance pledged at Copenhagen in 2009 for 2020, a target first met in 2022. Sun concludes that putting the initiative into practice would have a wide and lasting effect on how humanity meets global challenges. China's home-court diplomacy as an important platform for world peace and development 中国主场外交为推动世界和平与发展搭建重要平台 Zhang Li Writing in the People's Daily after the Beijing commemoration of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin, Zhang Li takes up what China's "home-court diplomacy" (zhǔchǎng wàijiāo, diplomacy hosted on Chinese soil) contributes. Filling the gap in global narratives of the Second World War Interview with Ivona Ladjevac, deputy director of the Institute of International Politics and Economics, Serbia 填补全球二战史叙事空白——访塞尔维亚国际政治经济研究所副所长伊沃娜·拉杰瓦茨 Wang Youran This is an interview, published in Chinese Social Sciences Today on 29 September 2025, with Ivona Ladjevac, deputy director of the Institute of International Politics and Economics in Serbia. The reporter, Wang Youran, spoke to her after the launch of the English edition of A New History of the Second World War, edited by the Institute of World History at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The launch and an international conference, "Rebirth from the Fire: Civilization and War", took place in Athens on 28 August. The interview has three questions: what Ladjevac took from the event, how the book differs from mainstream Western histories, and what its multilingual publication means for reflection on the war and for peace. The book is already on sale in Greece and the United States, and further language editions are being prepared. Ladjevac argues that the book draws on primary sources in Chinese, English, German, Japanese, French and Russian, including material from China and other non-Western theatres that Western accounts under-use. She stresses its position that the war began with the 18 September 1931 Incident, not with Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939, which makes China's resistance the first major front against fascism and the main Eastern theatre. In her view, placing East Asia at the centre changes readers' picture of the war and balances world historical narrative, which matters at a time when, she says, many try to alter history. Ladjevac concludes that the English edition lets Chinese scholarship reach global readers across a language barrier and encourages comparative reflection. She says this "mutual visibility" would make global memory of the war more balanced rather than uniform. She also holds that the book's account of solidarity against aggression carries lessons for a world of geopolitical tension. Read the original if you want a Serbian scholar's endorsement of the Chinese claim that the war began in 1931, or a view of how this Chinese-edited history is being received abroad.

As the pattern of international cultural trade evolves, China is becoming a powerful engine A lecture by Professor Hua Jian at Fudan University 伴随国际文化贸易格局演变 中国正在成为强力引擎 Hua Jian This text, published in Jiefang Daily on 30 September 2025, is based on a lecture given by Hua Jian at Fudan University. Hua argues that cultural consumption has become a new engine of economic growth, that digitalisation and intelligent technology are redrawing the landscape of international cultural trade, and that China has been the fastest-growing and fastest-rising force in this field over the past two decades. The lecture has three parts. It first defines international cultural trade (trade in cultural goods and cultural services) and describes it as a global 'super network chain' of investors, producers, distributors and users. It then turns to digital cultural trade as the most dynamic new track, using music, art-market and Ireland examples. Finally it sets out China's position, its proposals for the trade order and its export record. Hua's central claim is that digitalisation reshapes the rules of cultural trade around the combination of production factors. Trade competitiveness depends on high-end factors such as content, technology and capital, so countries must cultivate or import them to move up the global cultural value chain. Hua cites streaming's 69 per cent share of 2024 global music revenue and Ireland's creative-service exports of US$231.3 billion in 2022. On the order of trade, Hua contrasts the US 'free competition, efficiency first' approach and the French 'cultural exception, controls and protection' approach, which Hua says cannot satisfy all parties, with China's 'development first, inclusiveness and shared benefit' approach. Rooted in building a community with a shared future for mankind, this approach is summarised as development, inclusiveness, joint effort and linkage between domestic reform and global order. Hua reports that between 2002 and 2022 China's creative-service exports grew 39.4-fold and creative-goods exports 7.8-fold. In 2022 goods exports reached US$249.9 billion, first in the world, and services exports US$67 billion, fifth. Hua concedes that China's service exports still trail those of the United States, Ireland, the United Kingdom and Germany, so there is large room to improve in technology-, capital- and creativity-intensive services. The lecture ends by committing China to keep moving up the value chain. Read the original if you want an official-leaning scholarly account of how Chinese researchers frame China's role and proposals in global cultural trade, together with the trade statistics Hua cites.

Opening up a new realm of Party self-reform 开辟自我革命新境界 Ding Xiaoqiang Hao Aihong This newspaper commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily on 30 September 2025, reads the fifth volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China through the chapter on upholding the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership and carrying the Party's self-reform through to the end. The authors organise the chapter's material under three headings: the systematisation of Xi Jinping's ideas on self-reform, the identification of problems unique to a large party, and the building of a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They cite specific speeches and articles collected in the volume for each. On the first point, Ding and Hao describe Xi's January 2024 speech at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection as completing this systematisation. In their account it answers why the Party must, can and how it should carry out self-reform, and sets out a strategic approach of nine "takes" ("jiu ge yi"). On the second, they present the "six how-to-always" questions (Xi, January 2023) as the main factors affecting the Party's vanguard character and governing capacity, plus seven requirements for removing the soil in which corruption grows. On the third, they set out four "full" features of the approach and five systems to be improved: organisation, education, oversight, institutions and responsibility. The authors conclude that mastering this theoretical system strengthens theoretical awareness and practical motivation to open up a new realm of self-reform. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned guide to how the fifth volume of Xi's collected governance texts presents Party self-reform and its component formulas.

Bringing ideological and political elements to life in stage performance The gala "Justice Will Prevail" as a model for the "Great Ideological and Political Course" 让思政元素在文艺演出中“活起来” Ren Yanhong Wu Runfeng This commentary takes the gala "Justice Will Prevail", staged for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, as a case for ideological and political education. In the first part, the authors say the music and staging build collective memory across generations, present red classics in contemporary form to strengthen cultural confidence, and make clear the responsibility of young people in the new era. In the second part they propose three pairings. History and present-day experience would be joined in "immersive" classrooms, for example at revolutionary sites. Professional guidance would be combined with mass participation, including crowdsourced topics and modular creation. Emotional resonance would be combined with value guidance and assessed through a "whole-chain" evaluation covering process, outcomes and participation. The authors conclude that such performances can move from a single artistic display to a long-term project of moral education and cultivating people through culture. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese educators frame mass cultural events as vehicles for patriotic and ideological education.

Institution-building requirements for further deepening reform comprehensively 进一步全面深化改革的制度建设要求 Ma Yujie This newspaper commentary, drawing on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, asks what institution-building must achieve if reform is to be further deepened comprehensively. Four points of emphasis are named: firm confidence in the system, improvement of the system, institutional innovation and institutional security. The piece opens with the policy trajectory: the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The 2019 plenum introduced the tiers of fundamental, basic and important institutions. The body of the text has three sections, on confidence, innovation and security. On confidence, Ma says it rests on recognising the system's inherent values and on a balance between a stable essential nature and an adaptable form. The Party's self-reform is presented as a driver of this adaptation. On innovation, the author holds that reform is never finished, so the system must stay open. That openness is conditional on upholding Party leadership and the socialist path, combining top-level design with grassroots exploration, and keeping a people-centred approach. On security, Ma cites worsening competition between the "two systems" worldwide. The author calls for stable operation, reform and visible institutional strengths to work together. This means guarding against ossification, abandonment of the system's direction and stagnation, and keeping the fundamental and basic institutions relatively stable while important institutions are refined. Ma concludes that institutional strengths must be turned into governance effectiveness, yielding reform dividends at home and a comparative advantage in international institutional competition, which the author calls the most fundamental competition between states. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars frame institution-building as the main thread of the current reform agenda.

Defending the victory in the Second World War and moving together towards a community with a shared future for mankind 捍卫二战胜利成果 携手迈向人类命运共同体 He Husheng Guan Muyao Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, He and Guan ask how the outcome of the Second World War can be defended and global governance reformed. Starting from Xi Jinping's anniversary speech, they argue that, as the world enters a new period of turbulence and change, China must uphold a correct view of the war's history. In their account, this is the basis for a fairer global governance system and for a community with a shared future for mankind. The commentary has three parts. The first reviews China's wartime contribution and its role in building the postwar order. The second sets out how China's proposals are leading reform of global governance, centred on the Global Governance Initiative that Xi announced on 1 September 2025 at the \"SCO Plus\" meeting. The third lists three requirements for building a community with a shared future for mankind: a shared intellectual foundation, institutional reform, and common civilizational values. The authors argue that China's war of resistance opened earliest, lasted longest and tied down Japanese militarism. They cite more than 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties, and they say it frustrated Axis plans for strategic coordination. In their reading, China was a founder and designer of the United Nations and now applies sovereign equality, international rule of law and genuine multilateralism against hegemonic logic, \"decoupling\" and unilateralism. As evidence of a people-centred, action-oriented approach, they point to rice-technology experts, medical teams, poverty-reduction projects and more than 50,000 peacekeeper deployments, the largest contribution among the permanent Security Council members. The authors conclude that three things are needed. First, upholding the legal conclusions of the postwar international trials and opposing historical revisionism. Second, reforming the UN-centred system by addressing the Security Council's \"democratic deficit\" and by raising the representation of developing countries and the Global South. Third, drawing on Chinese cultural ideals such as \"harmony in diversity\" to support a multipolar world and inclusive globalization. They present China as both a permanent Council member and the largest developing country, able to act as an insider and leader in this reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics link Second World War memory to the case for global governance reform and the Global Governance Initiative.

From "irreversible" to "unstoppable": how to understand the historical process of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation Q&A interpretation published in Study Times, 29 September 2025 如何认识中华民族伟大复兴历史进程从“不可逆转”到“势不可挡”？ Dong Zhenhua This Q&A-style commentary, originally published in Study Times, responds to a question from Zhu Hongjun of Anhui University of Finance and Economics. The question concerns a shift in Xi Jinping's wording: at the centenary of the Party (2021) he called national rejuvenation an "irreversible" historical process, and at the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance (2025) he called it "unstoppable". Dong Zhenhua, head of a department at the Central Party School, argues that the shift marks a process that, on the basis of historical necessity, has gathered further irresistible strength. In Dong's reading it is both a summing-up of the past and a declaration about the future. The article is organised in four sections, each naming a source of that strength: the leadership of the Communist Party, Marxist theory, reliance on the people, and the Chinese path of modernization. A closing section places these within the international situation and China's relation to the world. Dong draws on Party resolutions, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and statements by Xi Jinping, and follows the story from the modern semi-colonial period through the revolution, socialist construction and reform to the present. Dong's central claims are that the Party is the "backbone" that turned a humiliated nation into one that has "stood up, grown rich and become strong", and that Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions gave it accurate strategic judgement. Dong adds that rejuvenation can only come through the people, by pursuing development for the people, by the people and shared by the people, and by common prosperity and whole-process people's democracy. Dong presents Chinese modernization as an independent exploration that rejects what the article calls the Western path of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization, and as avoiding the trap of the "one-dimensional man". Dong also holds that China's peaceful, cooperative approach to a community with a shared future for mankind places it on the side of historical progress. Dong concludes that, under the Party's leadership and on the path of Chinese modernization, time and momentum are on China's side and the cause will advance. The strength of truth, the people, faith, morality and practice together form what the article calls an unstoppable historical torrent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party Central School scholars explain official rhetoric on national rejuvenation, and how they link it to Party leadership, Marxism, the people and foreign policy.

Advancing military course development and raising university students' national defence literacy 推进军事课建设 提升大学生国防素养 Li Ke This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 28 September 2025, takes up the reform of the compulsory military course (junshi ke) in Chinese universities. Li Ke argues that the course is the main channel of national defence education for students and a key means of implementing the 2022 opinions on strengthening national defence education and the revised 2024 National Defence Education Law. The article contends that the course should combine political, ideological, contemporary and innovative qualities. The piece sets out eight directions for reform: content, ideological security, teaching staff, core military elements, frontier developments, new technology, a combined first- and second-classroom system, and assessment. It is a practical programme addressed to university teachers and administrators rather than a theoretical study. Li's core proposals are that Party, army and revolutionary history be built into chapters such as national defence and war, and that teaching strengthen students' political awareness and their commitment to national security, including political, institutional and ideological security under the holistic view of national security. Li also calls for joint teaching by serving soldiers, military experts and civilian staff, and for study of Xi Jinping's thought on strengthening the military, the Art of War and On War. The author wants teaching to address emerging security domains such as the deep sea, space and polar regions, and to use AI, big data, virtual simulation, war-gaming and VR battlefield training. Li proposes making national defence literacy the central goal, moving students through knowing, feeling, intending and acting, supported by field study, volunteer work, competitions and commemorations. Assessment should combine summative and process evaluation, with defence practice reports, reading reflections and a "national defence literacy growth file". Read the original if you want a concise sample of how a university military instructor presents the official agenda for defence education and its proposed teaching methods.

The four dimensions of Wang Yangming's "extending innate knowing" 王阳明“致良知”的四个维度 Li Chenggui Wang Yangming described his whole teaching as nothing more than the three characters zhi liangzhi, usually rendered 'extending innate knowing'. Li Chenggui observes that, in Wang's view, few people actually practise it, because they grasp liangzhi (innate knowing) imperfectly and treat 'extending' as too easy. The article asks what the ultimate meaning of the doctrine is and answers that it unfolds in four dimensions: cultivating the roots of goodness, removing selfishness and impurity, discerning right from wrong, and constructing order. The piece is a short exposition, first published in the Guangming Daily, that proceeds through close reading of Wang's own statements. It takes each dimension in turn, defines it, and supports it with Wang's metaphors and examples, such as planting, the sun dispelling shadows, a bright mirror and the judging of lawsuits. A closing section summarises the four and draws out features of each, then comments on the doctrine's theoretical and practical significance. In Li's account, the first dimension treats the innate good as something to be nurtured, accumulated through 'gathering righteousness' and enlarged by learning from worthy people. The second requires that extension be sincere, single-minded and impartial, so that selfish intent does not contaminate even good deeds. The third makes innate knowing a constantly awake and fully manifest standard that must be put into action: knowing good and evil without doing good and removing evil counts, for Wang, as not knowing. The fourth holds that extension gives order and value to things, to the mind and to society. Li concludes that the doctrine is not only an inward self-cultivation but also carries a strong outward concern for a good society. Li concludes that 'extending innate knowing' is a concrete and dynamic idea combining theory and practice. Theoretically, he presents it as Wang's enrichment and transcendence of Mencius's idea of innate knowing, moving it from a static to a dynamic form. Practically, he says it contains Wang's method for forming an ideal personality and his path to an ideal society, and he links it to a longing for a harmonious society. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based outline of Wang Yangming's central doctrine as presented by a Chinese philosopher in a state newspaper, along with its claimed present-day relevance.

Raising the digital competence of leading cadres 提升领导干部数字化胜任能力 Qiu Rui This short commentary, published in Study Times on 26 September 2025, asks how leading cadres can acquire the digital competence that the deepening construction of digital government requires. Qiu argues that, with big data, cloud computing, blockchain and artificial intelligence changing public expectations of government, the country needs cadres with strong digital awareness who can make digitalisation an effective tool of governance. The article begins from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls for a cadre corps able to lead modernization. It then moves through three steps: the digital mindset cadres need, the competence they must show across the digital economy, digital government and digital social governance, and the shortcomings Qiu sees at present. It ends with four proposals. Qiu describes digitalisation as an intellectual revolution as well as a technical change, and divides digital thinking into three parts: sensitivity to data, use of data and technology to solve problems, and data-based decision-making that replaces reliance on experience. The article identifies gaps in four areas. Some cadres reduce digitalisation to technical tools, depend too heavily on outside technical providers, struggle with data sharing and security across departments, or follow a technology-first approach that neglects public needs. Qiu proposes tiered, practice-oriented training; cross-departmental platforms and task forces to break down data silos; simulation platforms and training in algorithm oversight, data privacy and technical ethics, under the principle of technology as a tool and service as the foundation; and inclusion of digital competence in cadre evaluation, with measurable indicators and incentives that favour cadres combining governance thinking and technical understanding. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party media frame digital skills training and assessment for officials.

New trends and features of the international youth movement 国际青年运动的新动向新特征 Ma Jinxiang Writing in Study Times (25 September 2025), Ma Jinxiang argues that the international youth movement has grown more active and influential and now serves both as a "barometer" of global structural contradictions and as a force shaping social governance and global development. The commentary sets out to classify its types, stage features and underlying drivers, which Ma treats as a precondition for understanding young people's values and actions. The article looks at the previous five years. It identifies three types of action: political participation on governance and rights, anti-war and peace advocacy, and rights and public-interest action on ecology, technology ethics and anti-violence. It then describes four features (issues, participants, methods, organisation) and four drivers. On features, Ma argues that issues now cut across political, economic, social and ecological fields and point to deep contradictions in power structures and distribution. Participants are more diverse and divided, with generational differences emerging; Ma says some newly emerging youth groups hold more extreme demands and have less trust in governance systems. Methods combine visible protest with softer ones such as cultural works and online campaigns, and organisation is networked and fluid, with short-lived groups. On drivers, Ma points to organisational leadership, social media, triggering events and, as the "inner engine", structural contradictions: slower growth, inequality, unstable employment, identity conflict and a "capacity deficit" in global governance. Ma concludes that the movement is both a challenge to global governance and a positive force for change. Ma calls for better governance mechanisms, stronger international cooperation and guidance of rational expression, so that youth enthusiasm becomes constructive action on climate, peace and social fairness. Read the original if you want a short, official-media typology of recent youth movements and of the drivers Chinese commentary attributes to them.

The indelible historical memory of the Chinese nation On the Red Flag Canal spirit 中华民族不可磨灭的历史记忆 Chen Xiaoping This short commentary in Study Times (26 September 2025) takes up the Red Flag Canal spirit, which Xi Jinping has called an indelible historical memory of the Chinese nation. Chen opens with Xi's remarks of 2011, 2019 and 2022, including the claim that the spirit is of one lineage with the Yan'an spirit. The author argues that these remarks affirm its lasting value and offer a basic guide for drawing wisdom and strength for overcoming difficulties. The article first recounts how the spirit arose in Lin County (now Linzhou), Henan. It cites chronic drought, the 1959 crisis and the decision to draw water from the Zhang River. It then lists the construction achievements between 1960 and 1969, and the canal's foreign recognition. Four sections follow, one for each element of the spirit. Chen takes the spirit's content as self-reliance, hard struggle, solidarity and cooperation, and selfless dedication. Self-reliance is called its essence, illustrated by the author's figures that local people made 77 per cent of the cement and that the state supplied 14.94 per cent of total investment. Hard struggle is shown through scarce food, improvised tools and inventions. Solidarity is presented as an institutional advantage of concentrating efforts on major tasks, with cadres sharing the workers' conditions. Selfless dedication is illustrated by county Party secretary Yang Gui, the worker Ren Yangcheng and the technician Wu Zutai. Chen concludes that the spirit embodies the Party's nature and purpose and the people's historical agency. The piece serves as a Party-history primer on a model spirit. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writers present the Red Flag Canal as a source of spiritual heritage in the new era.

How the Party forged intellectual strength during the nationwide War of Resistance 全民族抗战时期党对知识力量的锻造 Gao Xueping This short commentary, drawing on documents held in the Central Archives, asks how the Communist Party of China treated intellectuals during the nationwide War of Resistance against Japan. Gao argues that the Party united, trusted and trained progressive youths and intellectuals who joined the revolutionary ranks, turning them into an important force in winning the war. The article is organised under four headings: recruiting intellectuals in large numbers, valuing them, training and educating them, and their contributions to victory. It relies on directives such as "Recruit Large Numbers of Intellectuals" (1939), the 1941 instruction on specialists in the army and the 1942 instruction on intellectual cadres in the troops. Gao shows how recruitment was justified by statements from Mao Zedong and Chen Yun that the war and the building of a new China required intellectuals. The Party promoted them, gave them responsibility according to their expertise, guaranteed material treatment and did not impose rigid political requirements on non-Party specialists. Local base areas issued their own measures to reward technical work. For training, Gao points to the Counter-Japanese Military and Political University and technical schools such as the Yan'an Natural Science Institute. The 1942 directive's formula of "tolerate, transform, use" is presented as an interconnected, dialectical whole. Gao concludes that these policies won intellectuals' support for the Party's resistance and laid a solid basis for victory and for building the liberated areas. Their contributions included wartime propaganda, literary work and agricultural and military science, such as crop improvement at the Guanghua Farm. Read the original if you want a brief, archive-based account of the Party's wartime policy towards intellectuals and the documents behind it.

"Intelligence for good": the rationale and path of AI innovation and development “智能向善”：人工智能创新发展的理与路 This is a published roundtable discussion, with a closing expert commentary, from Guangming Daily (26 September 2025). It asks how artificial intelligence can be steered towards "intelligence for good" (zhineng xiang shan) and why. The participants are Li Ling (Fudan University), Lin Jialin (Sun Yat-sen University) and Lu Liqiang (Zhejiang University). They argue that AI is a human-made tool that must embed human values throughout its life cycle, and that governance must balance innovation and risk. An editors' note ties the discussion to the State Council's August 2025 opinion on the "AI+" initiative and to the Tianjin Declaration of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. The discussion has three parts. The first sets out the dividends and ethical risks of AI. The second asks what principles should guide AI and clarifies the human–machine relationship. The third turns to governance paths and the coordination of government, enterprises and the public. Chen Changfeng of Tsinghua University closes with a commentary. Li lists economic, livelihood and public-governance dividends. Lin and Li catalogue risks such as information cocoons, algorithmic bias, deepfakes, structural unemployment and ideological risk. Lu reads these through historical materialism, as products of a new mode of production involving social cooperation, the \"collective worker\" and \"general intellect\". Li argues that AI is not an independent subject but an objectification of human essential powers, so \"intelligence for good\" extends human moral action. Lu and Lin stress value alignment and keeping humans \"present\". On governance, Lu proposes to escape the Collingridge dilemma by using technology to support regulation. This means life-cycle controls: admission checks, regulatory sandboxes and graded penalties. Li adds agile, graded and classified oversight, with stricter rules for high-risk uses. Li describes China's model as distinct from the EU's rule-heavy approach and the US's develop-first approach. In Li's account it rests on balancing an effective market with a capable government, producing what Li calls \"Chinese governance\" of AI. Chen endorses the discussion as a response to the State Council's call to build a theoretical system of intelligence for good. Chen criticises \"dataism\" and AI worship as inverting the relation between technology and value rationality. Chen proposes eight principles: dignity, human autonomy, fairness, transparency, personal information protection, safety, responsibility and sustainability. Chen also calls for interdisciplinary dialogue between humanities scholars and engineers. The participants conclude that AI carries human values and should serve people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars frame AI ethics and governance in official policy terms, and how they combine Marxist concepts with governance proposals.

Grasping the key points in a theoretical (xueli) elaboration of the Two Integrations What "integration" means, and how the second integration can be carried out 把握“两个结合”学理化阐释的关键点 Liu Jianjun Liu Jianjun, a professor at Renmin University of China, argues in this Guangming Daily article that any serious theoretical account of the Two Integrations must first settle a basic question: what exactly is "integration" (jiehe)? Liu holds that the term should be established as a philosophical category with a defined meaning and limits, rather than used loosely. Doing so, in Liu's view, gives later research a base and a direction. The article moves in two steps. The first part defines the concept within materialist dialectics, locates it in the Party's innovation theory, and introduces a new notion, "mode of integration". The second part applies this to the two integrations in turn. It treats the first integration briefly and then sets out four ways of advancing the second: language, scholarship, theory and practice. Liu defines integration as a state of mutual connection and unification between different things, based on real need and inner fit, that tends toward fusing into something new. On this reading it is both a category of universal connection and one of contradiction, reflecting the law of the unity of opposites. Liu says the second integration, between Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture, cannot reuse the pattern of the first, which joined theory and practice. It concerns the relation between the "soul" and the "root" of the Party's guiding ideology. Modelled on the "mode of production", the "mode of integration" is meant to show how integration happens. Liu separates mechanical, external combination from inner, organic integration, citing Xi Jinping's remark that integration is a "chemical reaction" rather than a "platter". The four ways proposed are Marxism speaking Chinese (translation, refined terminology, Chinese grammatical habits); joint scholarship by Marxist and traditional-culture researchers; the Party's theoretical innovation, culminating in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; and practice. Liu concludes that theoretical innovation and practical innovation must advance together. The great practice of Chinese modernization is described as the source and driving force of the second integration, and Liu calls on theorists to take part in construction and reform. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar tries to turn the Two Integrations into a defined concept with identifiable methods, and how the second integration is meant to proceed.

Empowering the building of modern people's cities through innovation 以创新赋能现代化人民城市建设 Feng Chujian Xu Zhuqing This commentary, published in Economic Daily in September 2025, asks how innovation can drive the building of modern people's cities. Feng and Xu take as their starting point the Central Urban Work Conference of July 2025, which listed innovation first among six dimensions of the modern people's city. They argue that innovation marks a strategic shift in urban development thinking and offers a practical path to high-quality development. The authors organise the piece around three tasks: redefining urban functions so that technology serves the people, accelerating coordination among cities, and improving urban quality so that the innovation ecosystem works better. They sketch the historical growth of urban functions and cite examples from the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei, Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta and middle Yangtze regions, as well as Shanghai. Feng and Xu contend that technology should serve three goals: resilient and secure cities, efficient smart governance through digital public services and unified city management, and green, liveable cities with technologies for an ageing population. They then argue that cities should look beyond their own boundaries, specialising and cooperating within city clusters and metropolitan areas through shared platforms, innovation enclaves and benefit-sharing mechanisms. Finally, they hold that competition between cities will become competition between innovation ecosystems, driven by new quality productive forces, and that what matters is connecting innovation actors rather than merely concentrating resources. Shanghai's large-model innovation community is offered as an example. The authors propose building connected ecosystems through diverse collaborative networks of firms, universities, government and finance, through high-quality urban renewal that creates innovation spaces, and through a culture that tolerates failure and honours scientists, craftspeople and entrepreneurs. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese policy researchers interpret the 2025 urban work agenda in terms of innovation.

Contributions of principle to enriching and developing Marxist political economy 丰富发展马克思主义政治经济学的原理性贡献 Zhang Yu Zhang Yu asks how the Chinese Communist Party's economic theory has added to the basic principles of Marxist political economy, not merely applied them. The article, published in Economic Daily in September 2025, argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought contains a series of new principle-level results. In Zhang's account, these enrich and develop Marxist political economy, especially the political economy of socialism. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the structure of the basic principles laid down by Marx and Engels. It then traces how Chinese Marxists have developed them, from Mao Zedong's explorations and Deng Xiaoping's call for a political economy combining Marxist principles with Chinese socialist practice, to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It closes with the tasks facing contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. Zhang divides the classical principles into four levels: general laws of social development, laws shared by several economic formations (commodity economy and the labour theory of value), laws specific to capitalism (surplus value), and the basic features of future socialism and communism. These principles are said to form an organic whole that must be held to firmly and also developed, not treated as dogma. Zhang lists a series of principle-level results, including the new development philosophy, high-quality development, new quality productive forces and a high-standard socialist market economy. Zhang groups them into three kinds of development. The first extends existing theory, as in the Party's comprehensive leadership over economic work. The second creates new principles, as in the economics of Chinese modernization. The third reaches new conclusions, as with the category of public capital and the call to study capital under new conditions. Zhang adds that the Sinicisation of Marxism runs from the general to the particular and back again. Socialism is not yet a dominant world form, so China's experience is cast as the most typical material for generalising socialist political economy, much as England was for Marx's Capital. Zhang concludes that Chinese scholars should systematically summarise China's experience in economic development, the socialist market economy, the socialist economic system and opening up. They should raise it into theory with both distinctive subjectivity and wide universality. Zhang holds that many new problems cannot be answered from the classics. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's account of how Chinese economists present Xi Jinping's economic thought as a contribution to Marxist principles, including its treatment of capital and the market.

Promoting open research cooperation and linking China with the world: an interview with Magdalena Skipper, Editor-in-Chief of Nature 共促科研开放合作，联结中国与世界——访《自然》总编辑玛格达莱娜·斯基珀 Yang Yifu This is an interview, published in Guangming Daily on 25 September 2025, in which reporter Yang Yifu speaks with Magdalena Skipper, Editor-in-Chief of Nature and Chief Editorial Advisor for the Nature Portfolio. It took place in Beijing as Springer Nature set up a China Academic Advisory Council and held its first forum. The article's framing is that Chinese research is advancing rapidly and that publishers are paying closer attention to cooperation with Chinese scientists. Skipper's main message is that China is making major progress across many fields and that open, trustworthy science depends on broad collaboration. The interview has four sections. The first covers why the council was created and how it is composed. The second deals with the history of Springer Nature's cooperation with China and Skipper's view of Chinese research. The third turns to open and credible science, including open data and transparent peer review. The fourth addresses the challenges and uses of artificial intelligence in research and publishing. Skipper says the council is a platform for exchange among the parts of the research ecosystem. It has 25 leaders from research, funding, policymaking and industry, rotating every three years, and it includes early-career researchers and women scientists. It follows similar councils established since 2021 in the United States, Europe, Africa and Latin America. She points to the Nature Index 2024 research leaders ranking, where China stays first, and says Chinese work is moving from internationally driven projects to independent domestic development. She attributes this to state funding and years of overseas training and joint research. On openness, she stresses data sharing with fair credit for data generators, privacy protection and the UNESCO principle of "as open as possible, as closed as necessary". She also describes Nature's decision, from 16 June 2025, to publish peer review reports with accepted original research articles. On AI, Skipper says it cannot be an author because it cannot take responsibility, that AI used as a research tool beyond simple copy-editing must be declared, and that Springer Nature uses AI tools to detect misconduct such as image manipulation. She expects China's progress to strengthen and calls for cooperation across disciplines, sectors and countries. Read the original if you want a publisher's view of China's place in global science, Nature's transparency policies and its AI rules, as presented in a Chinese state newspaper.

Strengthening day-to-day supervision by Party organizations 强化党组织日常监督 Zhang Lisi This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 25 September 2025, asks how Party organizations can make their day-to-day supervision of Party members and cadres more effective. Zhang Lisi argues that such supervision is both an institutional constraint and a means of guidance and correction. In Zhang's account it is a key tool of the Party's self-reform and of making improvements in conduct routine and lasting. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to strengthen daily supervision and increase its "penetrating power and effectiveness". It then sets out four areas of work: ideological foundations, supervisory skills, institutional safeguards and working style. The author refers throughout to the central Eight-point Regulation and the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles". Zhang argues that Party organizations stand on the front line, know their members at close range and can intervene early, so that individual lapses do not become systemic risks. The author calls for theoretical study and discipline education, case-based training, and digital platforms with data comparison and early warning. Zhang also proposes five institutional measures: vertical coordination between levels, cross-department supervision led by discipline inspection organs, wider supervisory methods, deployment of supervisory strength to the grassroots, and clear responsibility lists. Without a solid working style, the author warns, even good systems become "armchair strategy". Zhang concludes that improving supervision is a systemic task requiring coordinated effort, with the aim of full and regular coverage, a clean political environment and a good atmosphere for getting things done. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Central Party School scholar presents the practical agenda for Party supervision under full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Principles for building an independent knowledge system of Chinese philosophy and social sciences 构建中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系的原则遵循 Bai Xianliang Wang Feng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, asks what principles should guide the building of an independent knowledge system (zizhu zhishi tixi) for Chinese philosophy and social sciences. Bai and Wang start from Xi Jinping's statements that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics is ultimately about constructing China's own knowledge system, and from his November 2024 instruction on the Marxist theory research project. They argue that this instruction yields four guiding principles: uphold the Two Integrations, take root in Chinese soil, continue the Chinese cultural lineage, and strengthen the academic foundation. The article is organised as four numbered sections, one per principle. Each defines the principle and explains what it requires of scholars. It draws on Xi's formulations and on the Party's historical record in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. It also refers to Chinese modernization and to the 20th Party Congress (2022) blueprint. On the Two Integrations, the authors hold that Marxism must guide the system, but not through quoting classical texts selectively. They say it should be applied through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, combined with China's realities and its fine traditional culture. They add that this does not mean closing off foreign scholarship, which should be absorbed critically. On rooting in Chinese soil, they present Chinese modernization as the first-hand material and the testing ground of theory, which must be able to withstand practice. On cultural lineage, they stress cultural continuity, subjectivity and innovation, naming values such as benevolence, people-centredness, good faith, justice and harmony. On the academic foundation, Bai and Wang call for original, identifying concepts, citing whole-process people's democracy and new quality productive forces. They also call for coordinated development of the disciplinary, academic, discourse and textbook systems. They say the system should draw on Chinese and foreign resources and engage international scholarship, so that the world comes to know "China in scholarship". The authors conclude that these principles together make the system rigorous, persuasive and influential. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official guiding principles for China's philosophy and social science knowledge system as presented in the Party press in 2025.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating to improve the quality and effectiveness of ideological and political education 守正创新提升思政教育质效 Ge Jihong This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 25 September 2025, asks how ideological and political education can reach young students more effectively and make the Party's innovative theory take root in their minds and hearts. Ge Jihong, head of a cultural creativity institute at Zhejiang University of Media and Communications, argues that the answer lies in upholding fundamental principles while innovating. The article begins from Xi Jinping's instructions on school ideological and political courses and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Ge acknowledges that the overall environment for these courses has improved and that students' Four-sphere Confidence has grown. The author nonetheless lists persisting problems: spoon-fed instruction, dry language and empty content that ignores current concerns, and teaching geared to exams rather than to value identification. The body has three sections, on strengthening political guidance, on making the courses more targeted and appealing, and on combining theory with practice. Each draws on Zhejiang examples, mainly short videos on Xi's Zhijiang Xinyu and a portrait project for martyrs. Ge's core claim is that political guidance is the basic function of the courses, and that this does not mean simple propaganda. Theoretical rigour and political orientation must go together, and ideals should rest on rational acceptance of scientific theory. The author calls for a shift from one-way instruction to two-way interaction and from the closed classroom to society. Examples include students making short videos in the "short, fast, new, lively" style, students using their professional skills to portray martyrs, and young people lecturing peers in their own idiom. Ge also proposes a closed loop of "what is needed, taught, understood and used", with "walking" courses that move from "book-based reasoning" to "narratives of the land". A 2022 programme bringing Hong Kong students to Zhejiang is cited as moving participants from knowing to believing. Ge concludes that joining theory and practice returns ideological and political education to its essence and implements the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. In this view, a "society as classroom" approach lets students move from cognitive agreement to putting belief into practice. The goal is a new generation that the Party can rely on to take up national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official commentary describes current methods of ideological and political education in universities, with concrete Zhejiang cases.

The new development philosophy leading high-quality development in Xinjiang 新发展理念引领新疆高质量发展 Xing Guangcheng This newspaper commentary argues that Xinjiang's high-quality development should be guided by the new development philosophy. Xing presents Xinjiang work as holding a special place in the overall work of the Party and state, bearing on the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author credits Xi Jinping's guidance on border governance with enabling major breakthroughs in the region. The author cites Xinjiang's first intelligent computing centre in Karamay as an example. On green development, openness and sharing, the article lists carbon-peaking pilots, Belt and Road rail links and free trade zone reforms, and employment, social security and rural revitalisation measures. Xing treats improving livelihoods and building unity as the core of Xinjiang's development. Xing concludes that high-quality development in Xinjiang is a systemic project requiring full and accurate implementation of the Party's governance strategy for Xinjiang in the new era. The author calls for balancing development with security, deepening reform and expanding opening up, so that Chinese modernization takes firm new steps in Xinjiang. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official discourse links the new development philosophy to Xinjiang policy, with the statistics Xing cites.

Writing a new chapter of Xinjiang's practice of Chinese modernization 谱写中国式现代化新疆实践新篇章 Su Cheng Marking 70 years since the founding of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in 1955, this newspaper commentary (published in Economic Daily, 24 September 2025) argues that Xinjiang's achievements, especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), prove the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang in the new era to be "completely correct" and to be upheld in the long term. Su Cheng contends that Xinjiang work must be understood at the level of national strategy and the overall project of Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts. The first explains why Xinjiang matters to the national whole: as the author describes it, it is a security barrier on the north-western frontier, the core area of the Silk Road Economic Belt, an energy and agricultural base, and a multi-ethnic home where the Chinese nation community is being built. The second reviews economic and social results since 2012. The third sets out tasks for the new journey. In the second part Su cites figures: regional GDP rose from 749.947 billion yuan in 2012 to 2.053408 trillion yuan in 2024, and per capita GDP from 33,495 to 78,660 yuan. Imports and exports grew from 158.96 billion to 434.16 billion yuan, and the number of open ports reached 19. Su also reports that absolute poverty has been eliminated, employment has grown to 13.91 million, and incomes have risen. The third part sets out three tasks: implementing the new development philosophy in full, including technological innovation and new quality productive forces; building a modern industrial system that reflects Xinjiang's strengths in energy, agriculture, new energy, new materials, tourism and cross-border e-commerce; and fostering a new growth pole in southern Xinjiang through industrial layout, urbanisation, rural revitalisation and infrastructure. Su concludes that Xinjiang work should be planned within the whole of Chinese modernization, balancing development with security and opening up with security, and pursuing governance by law, ethnic unity, cultural enrichment, prosperity and long-term construction under the overall goal of social stability and lasting peace and order. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary presents Xinjiang policy, with statistics, on the 70th anniversary of the region.

The junzi (exemplary person) in Chinese culture 中华文化中的君子 Wang Xuedian Wang Xuedian asks what the figure of the junzi, often rendered "gentleman" or "exemplary person", contributes to Chinese culture, and argues that no other type so fully embodies the Chinese nation's moral ideals and pursuit of personality. In Wang's account, the concept moved from an aristocratic title under the kinship-based Zhou order to a personal ideal open to all. The article, a newspaper essay drawn from a longer book chapter, holds that understanding junzi culture is a way to grasp the mainstream of Chinese culture itself. The essay proceeds in five parts. It traces the term's history from the Book of Documents and Book of Songs through Confucius, Mencius and Xunzi. It then examines the junzi's image, using jade, the "four gentlemen" of plum, orchid, bamboo and chrysanthemum, and the "nine virtues". Next it considers the junzi's essence and the means of self-cultivation. It then describes how the ideal permeated society, and ends with its modern forms. Wang's central claim is that the core quality of the junzi is ren (benevolence). Figures such as Qu Yuan and Su Dongpo, whose conduct departed from the classical descriptions, were still widely called junzi because of their humane concern. On cultivation, Wang follows the Great Learning: sincerity of intent and rectifying the heart are the route of self-cultivation, ideally extending outward to family, society and the world. The ideal spread through Han-dynasty Confucian primacy and the Tang–Song examination system, which, Wang says, carried it from the court into village life and shaped national character. Wang notes Liang Qichao's 1914 Tsinghua lecture, which compared the junzi with the English gentleman and urged adapting the ideal to a new age. Contemporary junzi, in Wang's examples, include the rice scientist Yuan Longping and border guards, and the modern ideal is open equally to all. Wang calls for creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture, and for cultivating modern junzi personality as the core of an "ethics-oriented" Eastern way of life. Read the original if you want a concise, officially published overview of how a leading Chinese scholar presents the junzi tradition and its contemporary uses.

Feelings for family and country: a distinctive spiritual hallmark of Chinese civilization 家国情怀：中华文明的鲜明精神标识 Chen Yanbin Zhang Jinqiu Chen Yanbin and Zhang Jinqiu take up the question of where Chinese 'family-and-country feelings' (jiaguo qinghuai) come from and why they persist. The article, a newspaper essay in Guangming Daily, defines them as a deep emotional bond that ties individual and family fate to the destiny of the nation. The authors argue that this bond is a distinctive spiritual hallmark and cultural gene of Chinese civilization, formed over several thousand years. The essay is organised in five parts. It traces the sentiment to the agrarian roots of Chinese civilization, then to the 'family–state isomorphism' of the traditional social order, and then to the transmission of family traditions. It goes on to examine how the idea worked in moments of national crisis, from Yue Fei and Wen Tianxiang to Lin Zexu, the anti-Japanese war and the nuclear-submarine engineer Huang Xuhua. It ends with the contemporary value of the idea. The authors' central move is a chain of explanation. Attachment to the land, which they contrast with nomadic and maritime civilizations, was lifted into family-and-country feeling through a social order in which family and state were built on the same pattern. They point to the Western Zhou feudal-patriarchal system, the Qin-Han unification and the Confucian sequence from self-cultivation to 'bringing peace to all under heaven'. Family traditions and family instructions, such as Yan Zhitui's Family Instructions for the Yan Clan, then carried these values across generations. In crises, the authors say, filial duty was converted into loyalty to the nation. They present this as the reason Chinese civilization is the only one to have continued unbroken in the form of a state. The authors conclude that family-and-country feeling remains a source of spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They call for it to be passed on, especially to young people, so that individuals tie their fate to the nation's, in a period of what they call changes unseen in a century. They also propose drawing on the traditional experience of family instruction to build good family traditions, which they say would support clean Party conduct, honest government and sound social customs. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official-academic writing presents family culture and patriotism as a continuous civilizational inheritance.)
