Cultivating people, benefiting the people, nourishing cities and promoting industry through culture: doing well in the inheritance and development of culture 以文化人、以文惠民、以文润城、以文兴业 在推动文化传承发展上善作善成 Zhong Huibing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, interprets a formula Xi Jinping offered during an inspection visit to Tianjin in February 2024: using culture to cultivate people, benefit the people, nourish cities and promote industry. Zhong Huibing treats the four-part formula as an interconnected whole that gives ideological and practical guidance for the inheritance and development of culture. The author presents it as a requirement of Chinese modernization and of the Party's new-era cultural mission. The piece has three parts. The first explains each of the four components with historical illustrations, from the Duke of Zhou's rites and music and Confucian education to the Book of Songs and the popular culture of Tang–Song cities. The second sets out the formula's internal logic, its bearing on urban cultural work, and its value as a methodology. The third lists practical measures for each of the four tasks. Zhong's central claim is that the four parts form a logically tight system linking culture to human development, people's wellbeing, urban governance and economic growth. Cultivating people requires upholding the Party's leadership in cultural matters, building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power, and using the Party's innovative theory to forge people's convictions. Benefiting the people means a people-centred orientation. Nourishing the city means protecting heritage and urban cultural continuity while developing it. Promoting industry means treating culture as a pivot of high-quality development and calling for a humanistic economics. For cities, the author reads the formula as a set of principles that puts people at the core and treats culture as the city's soul. For the new journey, Zhong proposes concrete steps. These include studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and cultivating core socialist values. They also cover improving public cultural services with balanced urban–rural coverage and digital delivery, building a cultural governance mechanism under Party leadership, and reusing historic buildings and red cultural resources. The last measures are deepening the integration of culture and tourism and fostering new digital cultural industries. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-aligned scholars turn Xi's cultural directives into policy-oriented guidance for city-level cultural work.

Using the Party's innovative theory to transform the subjective and objective worlds 用党的创新理论改造主观世界和客观世界 Zang Anmin Writing in the People's Daily (24 September 2025), Zang Anmin takes up the question of how Party members should put the Party's innovative theory to work. The author's answer is that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should be treated as a weapon for changing both the objective world and one's own subjective world. Zang presents this as a long-standing Party tradition and as a requirement for advancing Chinese modernization. The piece has two main parts. The first sets out six principles for studying, grasping and applying the theory: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global outlook. The second part turns to Party members and especially leading cadres, and sets out practical requirements for political ability, discipline, competence and work style. It draws on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong's On Practice, Xi's speeches and examples from Party history and Chinese tradition. Zang's central move is to treat transformation of the subjective and objective worlds as one unified process. Citing Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, the author holds that the proletariat changes itself while changing circumstances. Cadres are therefore urged to raise their political judgement, comprehension and execution, and to remain loyal to the Party in line with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. They are also urged to follow the Party Constitution, think in terms of the whole country, and build the "eight skills" and "seven abilities". Work style is summarised as being both clean and bold in action. Cadres are to avoid corruption, dare to act within Party discipline, act promptly and do investigative research. They are also asked to hold a correct view of performance, citing Zhejiang's "Eight-Eight Strategy" and the Saihanba afforestation effort as examples. Zang concludes that the two kinds of transformation reinforce each other, and that only by grasping this can one understand the dialectical unity of the Party's self-reform and social revolution. The Party is to keep reshaping its members' ideals and Party spirit while changing the objective world, so that the whole Party keeps unified thinking, firm will and coordinated action. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party commentary links theoretical study, cadre conduct and the goals of Chinese modernization.

Traditional Chinese conceptions of leisure and the pursuit of a good life 中国传统休闲观念与生活追求 Zhao Yuqiang Zhao Yuqiang, writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, asks what traditional Chinese leisure meant and what kind of life it aimed at. Taking the view that the study of leisure is "a philosophy of life", Zhao argues that Chinese leisure folded an understanding of the Dao into everyday life. In this account it balanced humanity and nature, freedom and order, liveliness and calm, and pursued a meaning of life beyond mere rest or entertainment. The short essay has three parts. It first traces the etymology of the characters for "leisure" (xiu and xian) through oracle-bone inscriptions, bronze inscriptions and early texts such as the Book of Songs, the Analects and Zhuangzi. It then sets out three schools' models of leisure: Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist. Finally, it outlines how leisure practice changed from the Shang and Zhou to the Ming and Qing and names four distinctive features of the Chinese pursuit of a good life. Zhao reads xiu as rest after labour, linked to heaven's mandate, morality and aesthetics. In Zhao's reading, xian moves from a spatial gap to free time and from a bolt or fence to self-possessed ease, so that leisure is a free state of "becoming toward the Dao" in daily life. Confucian leisure is described as virtue-centred, built on ritual and music; Daoist leisure as naturalist and playful, which Zhao compares with Schiller and Huizinga on play; Buddhist leisure as contingent, tranquil and Chan-inflected. Zhao sees a historical shift from the sacred to the secular, from emperors and aristocrats to literati and commoners, and from martial vigour to refined gentleness. Zhao identifies four features of the Chinese pursuit of a good life: poetic dwelling in harmony between humans and nature; a coexistence of the refined and the popular; bodily and mental well-being tied to health-cultivation philosophy; and a union of effort and spiritual realm. The last involves cultivating virtue and leisure skills, subtracting desire and material burdens, and engaging the world with enthusiasm so that leisure can drive innovation. Zhao presents these as a distinctive source of insight into life and its wisdom. Read the original if you want a concise overview of the philological roots and philosophical schools behind Chinese ideas of leisure, as presented in an official-newspaper essay.

Free labour and active leisure in the age of artificial intelligence 人工智能时代的自由劳动与积极休闲 You Xilin Writing in Guangming Daily, You Xilin asks how the free time released by artificial intelligence should be used. The article argues that leisure patterned on rest, which serves the recovery of necessary labour, cannot resolve the defects of labour done for a living. In You's view, AI allows a shift towards "active leisure", in which free time is spent on free labour, understood as the full development of human capacities. The piece is a short essay in three parts, drawing mainly on Marx. The first part defines necessary labour and "passive leisure" and cites Marx on alienated labour. The second sets out Marx's idea of free labour and the realm of freedom and links it to active leisure. The third looks at how acceleration and consumerism distort leisure today, and at how AI can make the transition possible. You's core move is to treat passive leisure as dependent on necessary labour. Under the division of labour, work becomes simplified and tiring, so rest, entertainment and consumer culture function as compensation, however rich that culture becomes. Under what the author calls accelerationism, this leisure turns into consumerism and hedonism, and as AI replaces programmed work the purpose of labour weakens, which in You's account breeds nihilism. Active leisure, by contrast, covers every non-subsistence activity that matches Marx's three senses of all-round development: realising natural and cultural potential, overcoming one-sided specialisation, and richer social relations. You distinguishes it from hedonism. AI, as a proxy for necessary labour, replaces fixed tasks and divisions of labour, so that people can pursue varied free labour in human–machine cooperation. You concludes that the key to the transition is breaking the cycle between passive leisure and the externally imposed purposes of necessary labour, and developing self-directed activity with its own internal purpose. Active leisure, the author says, gives free time meaning, counters nihilism and pushes necessary labour itself to become more humane. You adds that this is a social condition, requiring technological progress and social freedom, and cannot be reached by individual self-cultivation. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist account of AI, free time and leisure, written for a general newspaper readership in China.

The contemporary value and global significance of high-level opening up 高水平对外开放的时代价值与世界意义 Wang Heng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's recently published article on steadfastly advancing high-level opening up. Wang Heng argues that high-level opening up is, internally, a route to developing new quality productive forces suited to local conditions and, externally, an extension of Chinese modernization that fits the modernization aims of developing countries. In this reading it carries contemporary value and global significance for stabilising the world economy, improving global governance and driving sustainable development. The piece is organised in three sections, each pairing an account of significance with practical measures. The first deals with building an innovative and inclusive open world economy through mutually reinforcing domestic and international circulations. The second deals with institutional opening up as a way to build a fairer and more rational global governance system. The third deals with making the fruits of opening up benefit people in all countries more widely and fairly. It closes by linking opening up to a community with a shared future for mankind. In the first section, Wang argues that the new development pattern and an open world economy support each other. The first draws on China's industrial system and market scale, and the second lowers transaction costs and widens factor flows. The article cites an average annual contribution of about 30 per cent to world economic growth during the 14th Five-Year Plan period. In the second, Wang presents institutional opening up, meaning alignment of rules, regulations, management and standards, as the basis of governance coordination. Wang says it shifts governance from Western-led to pluralist co-governance and moves China from adapting to rules to co-creating them, citing the Belt and Road Initiative and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership. In the third, Wang says opening up should aim at people's livelihoods, citing the China–Laos Railway and the Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway as examples of local benefit. Wang calls for strengthening the domestic circulation, upgrading free trade zones and ports, deepening cooperation with Global South countries, and improving the business environment and intellectual property protection. Wang also urges building platforms such as trade expos, and channelling industry, innovation, finance and talent exchange towards livelihood projects. Opening up is described as an essential road to prosperity that creates a favourable external environment for deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links high-level opening up, institutional opening up and the Global South to Chinese modernization.

Why we pay attention to humanistic economics: observations and reflections on young scholars entering the field (Part 1) A roundtable in Guangming Daily “我们为什么关注人文经济学”——关于青年学者投身人文经济学研究的观察与思考（上） This is a moderated roundtable published in Guangming Daily (23 September 2025), led by reporter Chen Heng. Three young scholars explain why they have turned to "humanistic economics" (renwen jingjixue), a field that has grown since Xi Jinping raised the idea during the 2023 Two Sessions. The participants are Zong Yacong (Central University of Finance and Economics), Su Peijun (Soochow University, philosophy) and Chai Dongdong (Hangzhou Normal University, cultural industries). They present the field as an academic trend, a value stance, a form of cultural self-awareness, a way of engaging with reality and a path for their own careers. The discussion follows five questions from the host. Why has humanistic economics become an academic hotspot? How does its people-centred stance affect research? Is it an expression of cultural self-awareness? Which real-world problems does it address? What does it mean for young scholars' careers? The participants draw on their own institutions, research institutes at Soochow, Hangzhou Normal and Central University of Finance and Economics, and on their own projects in philosophy, culture economics and cultural-industry studies. The speakers contrast the field with conventional economics, which they say centres on efficiency, rational choice and quantification and neglects questions such as "for whom is development". Zong and Chai say the people-centred stance moves research towards human dignity, well-being and the all-round development of the person. Chai says it recasts culture as an ecosystem, not only a product with exchange value. Su describes the field as a theoretical product of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and of the Two Integrations, which in Su's view lets Chinese tradition be treated as a living presence, not an object to be combined. Su cites Suzhou and Hangzhou as practical cases of culture and the economy reinforcing each other. Su also proposes a "three-dimensional governance model" that balances government and market through humanistic values. The participants conclude that young scholars' involvement is, in Zong's words, a historical necessity. They see it as a route to an independent Chinese knowledge system and discourse, to interdisciplinary skills, to policy and local-development work and to reform of teaching in fields such as cultural-industry management. Chai argues that these courses currently stress management over ethics and social responsibility. This is the first half of a two-part feature. Read the original if you want to see how early-career Chinese scholars justify entering a state-promoted research field and how they link it to Xi Jinping's economic and cultural thought.

The Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression made a major contribution to saving human civilization 中国人民抗日战争为拯救人类文明作出了重大贡献 Liu Xiaoquan Li Deman Published in Guangming Daily in September 2025, this short commentary takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the 80th anniversary commemoration of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Liu and Li argue that the Chinese people, through enormous national sacrifice, made a major contribution to saving human civilization and defending world peace, and that Xi's remark offers a new reading of the war's place in world history. The article moves from the war itself to the present. It covers the defence of Chinese civilization, China's role in the global anti-fascist war and postwar order, China's later peace and development diplomacy, and the tasks ahead. The authors first claim that victory safeguarded more than five thousand years of civilizational achievement and restored China's standing as a major country. They then argue that China's theatre, the earliest and longest of the war, was the Eastern main battlefield, tied down the bulk of Japan's forces and enabled the Soviet Union to move troops west. They cite Chinese military and civilian casualties of over 35 million. The Cairo Declaration, Yalta arrangements and China's permanent seat on the UN Security Council are presented as the legal and institutional outcomes. From this the authors derive a continuity: because Chinese civilization is peaceful by nature, China upholds the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, the Global Security Initiative and the Global Development Initiative, alongside high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. The authors conclude that remembering the war serves to shape the future. They call for building a community with a shared future for mankind, implementing the Global Civilization Initiative, and upholding a UN-centred international system. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Chinese commentary links the memory of the anti-Japanese war to current foreign-policy initiatives.

Giving full play to the positive role of artificial intelligence in raising employment quality 充分发挥人工智能在提升就业质量方面的积极作用 Li Chang'an Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, Li Chang'an asks how artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to raise the quality of employment, not just its quantity, as China pursues high-quality and full employment. Li argues that AI, which the article treats as the leading representative and core driver of new quality productive forces, offers more opportunities than challenges for employment quality in China. Realising this, in Li's view, requires deliberate policy to reduce the risks and strengthen the benefits. The commentary opens by defining high-quality full employment as a multidimensional idea. At the macro level it covers sufficient jobs, fair conditions, an improved employment structure, efficient matching of people and posts, and harmonious labour relations. At the micro level it covers stable work, reasonable pay, reliable protection and occupational safety. It then sets out five opportunities from AI, followed by five policy tasks. Li notes that technological change may lower or raise employment quality, or be neutral, depending on a country's development stage, economic structure and industrial policy. The fourth technological revolution, Li says, affects the labour market more broadly and deeply than earlier ones. The opportunities listed are new high-skill occupations (the article cites 93 new occupations released since 2019 and 36.159 million workers in core digital-economy enterprises at end-2023); higher incomes, including for remote-area residents, people lifted out of poverty and disabled people; safer and lighter work through robots and automation; fairer hiring through recommendation algorithms; and better rights protection and skills training through digital platforms. Li nonetheless warns that AI carries risks of lowering employment quality. The proposals are to build an employment-friendly development model, strengthen the employment-first policy with assessments of AI's effect on job quality and a related indicator system, narrow the digital divide through wider "AI Plus" application, and invest in people through AI-assisted vocational training, with attention to migrant workers. Li also calls for an ethics oversight system, led by government with enterprise and worker participation, to curb algorithmic discrimination in hiring, appraisal and dismissal, backed by stronger labour law. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy framing of AI and employment quality in China, with some figures from 2023–2024.

Building China's independent knowledge system of international relations: a dialogue with Zheng Yongnian 建构中国自主的国际关系知识体系——对话郑永年 This is an interview, published in the People's Daily on 22 September 2025, in which the journal People's Tribune questions Zheng Yongnian. Zheng is a chair professor and dean of the School of Public Policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and head of the Qianhai Institute for International Affairs. The interview asks how to build a Chinese independent knowledge system of international relations, guided by Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought. Zheng's answer is that Western theories reflect Western, and especially American, geopolitical experience and cannot explain Chinese practice, so Chinese theory must be built from China's own historical and contemporary experience. The conversation moves through four topics. It begins with the context and obstacles for such a system, then turns to how geopolitics shaped European and American concepts of international relations. It next examines how geography shaped traditional Chinese foreign policy, and ends with the features of diplomacy in the new era and five proposed building blocks for a Chinese theory. Zheng's central argument is that geopolitics shapes both a country's practice and its concepts. European states of roughly equal strength produced sovereign equality, alliances, balance of power and maritime expansion. Zheng presents the United States, with a simple geopolitical setting, as sustaining hegemony through market integration and by making allies bear its costs. He says (neo)realism, (neo)liberalism, hegemonic stability theory and democratic peace theory defend that practice and are not general laws. Zheng warns against studies of ancient China that merely supply "Chinese material" for Western concepts. He also describes the tributary system as a misnomer for a "tribute-and-bestowal" arrangement, akin to unilateral opening, and sees China's traditional approach as defensive and focused on frontiers and neighbours. For the present, Zheng describes new-era diplomacy as great-power diplomacy, development diplomacy toward the Global South, and open diplomacy, citing a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. He proposes five foundations for theory: rethinking traditional wisdom such as the tribute-and-bestowal system as "moral realism"; the concentric structure from frontier to neighbours to world; non-interventionism; engagement with autonomy; and openness. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account, in the officially endorsed framing, of how China's international relations theory should be grounded in history and geopolitics.

Using a law-based business environment to help the private economy develop steadily and over the long term 以法治化营商环境助推民营经济发展行稳致远 Wu Xiaoyan This commentary, published in the People's Daily in September 2025, asks how a law-based business environment can support the healthy, high-quality development of the private economy. Wu Xiaoyan, head of the NDRC's business environment centre, argues that the rule of law is an inherent requirement for private firms to grow. Citing Xi Jinping, Wu holds that a socialist market economy is in essence a law-governed economy and that the rule of law is the best business environment. The article has three parts. The first sets out why a law-based business environment matters, under four headings: protecting lawful rights, stabilising expectations, supporting innovation, and the legal basis for equal treatment. The second reviews progress in legislation, law enforcement, the judiciary and the cultivation of law-abiding awareness. The third lists four priorities for further work. It builds on the Private Economy Promotion Law, which took effect in May 2025. Wu's core argument is that equal legal protection and predictable rules reduce uncertainty for entrepreneurs and so encourage investment and innovation. Wu says that the Two Unwaverings require all forms of ownership to have equal access to production factors, fair competition and equal legal protection, with property rights as the foundation. Wu cites figures to show progress: private firms produce over 70 percent of technological innovation results, and 3,952 'no penalty for first or minor violations' items had been issued by the end of 2024. Over 6,500 improper enforcement actions were corrected through administrative review in 2024, and more than 97 percent of firms in a World Bank survey judged Chinese courts fair and reliable in commercial disputes. Wu also argues that clear limits on government power, under the principle that officials may act only where the law authorises them, stabilise expectations and let the market play the decisive role in allocating resources. Wu concedes a gap remains between current conditions and what private firms need, and calls for continued reform using rule-of-law thinking. The proposals are stronger protection of property and lawful rights, including equal liability for infringements and limits on seizing assets. They also cover more standardised enforcement against firms, faster dispute resolution and bankruptcy handling, and a government that sets an example, including clearing arrears owed to small firms and punishing official breaches of trust. Read the original if you want an official statement of how Chinese policymakers link legal reform, the private economy and innovation, with the policy measures and statistics cited.

The cultural-strategic significance of building the China Studies Literature Research Centre at the National Library of China 国家图书馆中国学文献研究中心建设的文化战略意义 · Chen Ying Chen Ying asks what role the China Studies Literature Research Centre of the National Library of China should play in the strategy of building a socialist cultural power. China studies is defined as research by overseas scholars, including ethnic Chinese abroad, who read China through the eyes of an "other". It covers traditional sinology, studies of modern China and the tracking of current political, economic and social questions. The article, published in the Chinese Journal of Library Science in 2025, argues that the Centre's collections, reference tools, policy services and exchange work all serve that strategy, and that it should be rebuilt around digital and intelligent methods. The article first sketches the history of China studies abroad and of Chinese scholars' attention to it. It then traces the National Library's collecting since the 1920s: the foundations laid under Yuan Tongli, exchange networks after 1949, and later purchases. It reports holdings as of the end of 2024 of more than 150,000 titles in over 90 languages, more than 200 foreign periodicals and six purchased databases. Next it reviews three kinds of output: bibliographies, the journal International Sinology, and other studies. It then covers policy-reference services and cultural exchange, and ends with weaknesses and proposed remedies. Chen's central claim is that the Centre should be positioned as "one repository and three centres": a general China studies repository, an academic research centre, a decision-reference centre and a cultural exchange centre. The author argues that the strategy of becoming a cultural power, set out at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) and the 20th Party Congress (2022), gives libraries their mission: preserving Chinese civilisation, supporting cultural innovation, guiding public culture and promoting exchange and mutual learning. The author lists gaps, including thin coverage of Latin America and Africa, scarce manuscripts, outdated reference works, limited AI use, shortage of translators and a lack of any joint catalogue. Proposed responses are systematic acquisition, a "smart" collecting system, faster updates of reference works, a handbook series on China studies in each country, knowledge-graph databases, machine translation, a global union catalogue and training in Chinese cataloguing. Chen concludes that the Centre, guided by the cultural-power strategy and renewed through digital technology, should become a window for the state and the public on world trends and a foundation for taking Chinese culture abroad. The author presents it as belonging to both China and the world. Read the original if you want a detailed institutional history of China studies collecting in China's national library, or want to see how a library professional ties this work to Party cultural policy and to policy-advisory functions.

The Global Development Initiative in the perspective of world Sinology: motives, impact and prospects 世界中国学视域下的全球发展倡议：动因、影响与前景 Gao Xiaosheng Du Yaning Gao Xiaosheng and Du Yaning ask how foreign governments, think tanks, media and scholars have read the Global Development Initiative, which Xi Jinping first proposed at the UN General Assembly on 21 September 2021. The authors say existing Chinese research explains the initiative mainly from China's own standpoint and rarely examines overseas perceptions with primary sources. Working from the perspective of world Sinology, they set out to analyse the initiative's 'mirror image of the other'. They conclude that international responses are broad, practical and mostly positive, though they contain some misreadings. The article is organised around three questions, each answered through overseas sources. It first reviews why, in outsiders' view, China launched the initiative. It then covers the initiative's impact at national, regional and global levels, and its prospects, including challenges and potential. The authors draw on institutions and figures such as the Asia Foundation, ISEAS, AidData, the Lowy Institute, the Atlantic Council, the European Parliament's foreign affairs committee, and scholars and officials from Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas. On motives, the authors report three overseas readings: a response to China's internal and external development pressures; a diplomatic move to widen China's influence at the UN and in global governance; and a step towards changing the international order, seen variously as raising the Global South's standing, as geopolitical rivalry, or as a push for a fairer order. On impact, they say foreign commentators see the initiative as helping to deliver the UN 2030 Agenda, as a platform for cooperation and experience-sharing, and as breaking the monopoly of a Western-centred model such as the 'Washington Consensus'. On prospects, overseas observers cite vague mechanisms, domestic pressures in China, an unclear relation to the Belt and Road Initiative, economic uncertainty, geopolitical suspicion and competition from other donors. The authors identify three features of the overseas response: comprehensive and varied perspectives, a pragmatic orientation towards implementation and national interest, and generally positive views mixed with misreadings. They attribute the misreadings to political stance, class perspective and Cold War thinking, for example politicising development or treating the initiative as a tool of rivalry with the United States. They conclude that the initiative has moved from concept to practice, and call for a measured, dialectical reading of foreign views and for steps to guide more accurate international understanding. This, they argue, would support a more inclusive Chinese discourse and the image of a responsible major power. Read the original if you want a dense, source-rich survey of how foreign think tanks and scholars have interpreted the Global Development Initiative, as reported by Chinese researchers.

The moral dilemma of the Ming loyalists 明朝忠臣的道德困境 Frederic Wakeman Jr. This piece, published in the journal Guoxue in February 2014 and credited to Wei Fedi (Frederic Wakeman), asks how the men who had served the Ming dynasty coped morally and intellectually with its fall in 1644 and with their own survival under the Qing. The author argues that guilt, scholarship and a new historical relativism shaped the loyalists' response, and that the Qing eventually absorbed their loyalty into its own legitimacy. The text moves from individual cases to intellectual history and then to state policy. It opens with the poet Wu Weiye, who served the Qing and was burdened by guilt, and goes on to the painter Chen Hongshou and the historian Zhang Dai, who changed their names or their way of life. It then turns to the philosophers Huang Zongxi and Wang Fuzhi, to the decline of Wang Yangming's idea of innate moral knowledge, and to the Kangxi, Shunzhi and Qianlong emperors' treatment of the loyalists. The author first argues that many loyalists turned to poetry and above all to history-writing, both to commemorate 1644 and to bury it. Kangxi's special examination of 1679 and the invitation to help compile the official Ming History, in the author's reading, gave them a shared stake with Chinese officials who had submitted to the Qing. Second, loyalists faced an uncomfortable question: Donglin idealism had fed factional strife, while Chinese collaborators were carrying out the fiscal, legal and economic reforms the late Ming literati had wanted. This pushed thinkers such as Wang Fuzhi towards a functionalist, historically relative view in which institutions and moral judgements depend on their particular period and set of relations. Wakeman holds that this relativism did not last. A broad reaction against Wang Yangming's school and the revival of Cheng-Zhu orthodoxy, backed by Kangxi and others, brought back absolute duties such as loyalty and filial piety. Qing rulers, ambivalent towards anti-Manchu loyalists, praised their loyalty as an abstract virtue; honours rose under Shunzhi and Kangxi and peaked under Qianlong, who was motivated largely by anger at the turncoat Qian Qianyi. By the time of the 1673 Revolt of the Three Feudatories, loyalty to the Qing had overtaken loyalty to the Ming. Read the original if you want a compact account of how early Qing intellectuals and rulers reshaped the memory of Ming loyalism.

Deepening implementation of the "AI+" action to provide strong momentum for high-quality development 深入实施“人工智能+”行动 为高质量发展提供强大动能 National Development and Reform Commission This commentary, issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and published in the People's Daily on 12 September 2025, explains why and how the "AI+" action should be implemented in depth. It takes as its starting point the State Council's recent Opinions on Deepening the Implementation of the "AI+" Action, which set a timetable and roadmap for AI applications across sectors. The article argues that integrating AI with every area of the economy and society is both an urgent task and a long-term strategic question, and that it will supply strong momentum for high-quality development. The text has three parts. The first sets out four reasons for the action's importance. The second lists China's favourable conditions: data, industrial system, application scenarios, market size and talent. The third outlines the Commission's own work plan under five headings: an innovation-driven intelligent economy, a more caring intelligent society, stronger supporting factors, a better environment for application, and security safeguards. On significance, the article presents the action as a strategic choice to seize the new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation, as an inherent requirement of cultivating new quality productive forces, as a way to meet the people's needs for a better life, and as a step to help all countries take part equally in intelligent development. It treats AI as a "lead goose" technology that raises total factor productivity and shifts growth from factor-driven to innovation-driven. For conditions, it cites figures: 41.06 ZB of data produced in 2024, or 26.67% of the global total; a full set of industrial categories; more than 1,500 industry models; about 200 million business entities; and the world's largest pools of R&D personnel. For implementation, the Commission pledges coordination among departments, between central and local levels, and with society. Measures include high-quality corpora, data property rules, the "East Data, West Computing" hubs, open-source ecosystems, pilot-test bases, financial support and demonstration roles for state enterprises. It also promises AI skills training, employment-risk assessment, and monitoring and early-warning systems to make AI applications compliant, transparent and trustworthy. Read the original if you want an official statement of the policy rationale, figures and work priorities behind the "AI+" action.

Grasping the seven vital forces of Marxism 把握马克思主义的七大生命力 Tian Peiyan This commentary, published in the People's Daily in September 2025 under the byline Tian Peiyan, asks what makes Marxism a living theory and answers that it has seven kinds of vitality. The author lists them as natural affinity with the people, far-sighted foresight, strong explanatory power, enduring creativity, thoroughgoing critical power, strong absorptive capacity and extraordinary capacity to forge those who study it. The stated purpose is to strengthen theoretical confidence and help readers study and apply Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece has seven sections, one for each quality. Each section first draws on Marx and Engels: their statements on the proletariat, their predictions, their critiques of rival currents, their reading of Morgan and Darwin, and the character of the classic texts. Each section then argues that Xi Jinping Thought carries the same quality forward. The text presents this body of thought as contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Tian argues that each quality has a Marxist source and a counterpart in current Party theory. Marxism's people's standpoint is matched by the principle of putting the people first, common prosperity and whole-process people's democracy. Marx's scientific predictions, such as the recurrence of economic crises, are matched by the Two Centenary Goals and medium- and long-term planning. On explanatory power, the author claims that today's global tensions and crises of capitalist states can be explained with Marxism. The author also lists Xi Jinping Thought's original contributions, including the "six musts", the new development philosophy and a community with a shared future for mankind. The critical and absorptive sections stress Marx's critiques of Lasalle and Bakunin, the self-revision of the Manifesto, and the Party's struggle and self-reform. They also stress the Thought's roots in Marxism, traditional Chinese culture and foreign civilizations. Tian concludes that grasping these seven forces strengthens theoretical confidence and shows the vitality of Xi Jinping Thought. The author says that Party members and officials who study it gain governing skills and Party spirit, theorists gain a route to rooting research in Chinese soil, and the public gains cultural self-confidence. The text claims that the Thought is advancing Chinese modernization and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is irreversible. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party commentary presents the continuity between Marx and Engels and Xi Jinping Thought.

Scientifically and rationally promoting the realization of the value of ecological products 科学合理推动生态产品价值实现 Meng Fan This short commentary in the People's Daily asks how the value of ecological products can be realized in a scientific and rational way. Meng Fan argues that a sound value-realization mechanism is a key route for putting into practice the idea that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. In the author's account it is also part of Xi Jinping's thinking on ecological civilization and of modernizing environmental governance. The article opens by citing Xi's call, in the Selected Works on Ecological Civilization, for protection and restoration to earn fair returns and for damage to carry a cost, and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision on the mechanism. It then proceeds in three steps: the meaning of ecological products, the institutional logic of realizing their value, and a set of practical measures. Meng defines ecological products as clean air, clean water and a pleasant climate, divided into material supply, regulating services and cultural services. The value-realization mechanism turns their ecological, economic and social value into benefits through compensation and market development, so that protectors benefit, users pay and damagers compensate. The author holds that the process converts natural resources into ecological products and then into economic returns, requiring reforms in rights registration, performance assessment, compensation, market development and green finance. A 2021 central opinion set out six mechanisms covering the whole chain. Meng calls for locally adapted policies, standardized and branded ecological products, and a refined compensation system based on the principle of 'whoever benefits compensates; whoever protects benefits', including cross-regional pilots. The author also urges diversified development models, such as rural leisure tourism, under strict protection. Read the original if you want a concise official-style statement of how ecological product value realization is framed in Chinese policy.

Carrying forward the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression: from great victory to great rejuvenation 传承和弘扬伟大抗战精神 从伟大胜利走向伟大复兴 Wang Qiang Published in the People's Daily after Xi Jinping's speech of 3 September 2025 marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary sets out how the Party should read that war's spirit. Wang Qiang argues that without grasping how the great spirit of resistance grew, and why victory was won, the war's meaning cannot become a lasting source of strength. The author's thesis is that this spirit should be carried forward to advance national strength and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has four sections. The first traces the origins of the resistance spirit. The second describes the force it released in the war itself. The third assesses its lasting significance, for the Party, for China and for the wider world. The fourth lists four ways to carry it forward today. Wang draws throughout on Xi's speech and other statements, and briefly cites Engels on the lessons of history. In Wang's account, the spirit has three roots: the long-standing spirit of the Chinese nation, the modern history of national struggle against aggression, and the Communist Party's sense of mission. The Party, the author says, rallied a divided people while other political forces wavered or capitulated. Wang presents the war as three kinds of battle. It was a turning point for the nation, a forging of the Party, and a life-and-death test in which the people's army relied on people's war. The spirit is then said to have enriched the Party's spiritual lineage, to have underpinned the nation's path from 'standing up' to 'becoming strong', and to have encouraged oppressed peoples. Wang adds that the Global South is now changing the world's map. Wang calls for four applications of the spirit. These are unity and struggle toward rejuvenation; confidence and strategic resolve during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, answered with high-quality development; resolute struggle against external pressure and containment; and win-win cooperation against Cold War thinking, hegemonism and protectionism, moving toward a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang treats the spirit as living and not as a thing of the past. Read the original if you want to see how a National Defence University researcher links wartime memory to current Party themes in the official press.

Seek unity through struggle and unity survives Revisiting Mao Zedong's "On Tactical Problems of the Present Anti-Japanese United Front" 以斗争求团结则团结存 Xiong Chengshuai This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in September 2025, rereads Mao Zedong's outline of a report given to senior Party cadres in Yan'an on 11 March 1940. Xiong argues that the text's maxim, that unity sought through struggle survives while unity sought through concession perishes, supplies a methodology of struggle for handling major risks and complex relationships. The article sets the report in the crisis of late 1939, when Nationalist military and political pressure threatened the Communist–Nationalist alliance and the anti-Japanese national united front. It then presents two sets of principles drawn from the text: how to wage struggle that is justified, advantageous and restrained, and how to win the majority while opposing a minority. It closes by linking the text to present-day China–US relations. On struggle, Xiong sets out three principles: self-defence, victory and truce. Self-defence means not attacking first, yet responding resolutely and actively to attack. Victory means keeping struggle local, preparing thoroughly and striking the most reactionary faction first. Truce means stopping after one round and seeking peace so the struggle stays temporary and controllable. On winning the majority, Xiong reports Mao's division of the Nationalists into diehards, middle and progressive groups. Mao also identified middle forces, such as the middle bourgeoisie, enlightened gentry and regional power-holders, who could be won if the Party was strong, respected their interests and showed progressive victories. Xiong concludes that the Party's wartime practice of building up its own strength while struggling flexibly with the Nationalists preserved the united front. The author says the principles of unity and struggle remain a guide for new great struggles. Xiong then contends that concession and compromise earn no respect from the United States, which the author accuses of containment, tariff, trade and technology wars, and that firm resolve and skill in struggle are needed for stable relations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentators draw on Mao's wartime united-front writings to frame present-day foreign policy.

Vigorously promoting the educator spirit distinctive to China 大力弘扬中国特有的教育家精神 Mei Bing Published in China Social Sciences Today in September 2025, this commentary takes up how the "educator spirit distinctive to China" can move from an inspiring ideal to conscious action among teachers. Mei opens with Xi Jinping's reply to representatives of the Special-Post Teachers programme, who work in rural schools, and treats these teachers as a living example of that spirit. The author argues that promotion needs a systematic mechanism built on research, cultural inheritance, dissemination and practice. The article is organised around four headings: systematic research and interpretation as the foundation, highlighting the distinctive features of Chinese civilization as the core, a comprehensive communication system as the safeguard, and improved paths of practice as the key. Each section lists specific measures. They range from research frameworks and digital databases to selecting model teachers, media campaigns, teacher training and evaluation reform. Mei argues that the educator spirit continues the Party's teacher-building line since the 18th Party Congress (2012), which the author calls both a creative transformation of Marxist educational theory and an innovative development of traditional Chinese educational wisdom. The author calls for research across history, theory and reality, and for comparison with Western educational theories in order to break the habit of "interpreting China through the West" and build an autonomous Chinese pedagogical discourse. The spirit is traced to figures such as Confucius, Wang Yangming and Cai Yuanpei, and presented as a source of cultural confidence and a link for exchange between civilizations. On practice, Mei proposes a three-part path of training, evaluation and coordination. This includes a growth ladder from special-post teacher to backbone teacher to educator-type teacher, and a shift from quantitative metrics to a developmental evaluation system. Mei concludes that the educator spirit should become part of teachers' professional makeup and improve educational governance, supporting the building of a leading education nation. The author calls on Party committees and governments to take political responsibility, and on society to give teachers priority and support. Read the original if you want to see how a university Party secretary links teacher-development policy, cultural confidence and Party leadership of education in the official discourse of 2025.

Lessons from the Party's discipline building in the Xiangshan period 香山时期党加强纪律建设的经验启示 Huang Xiaofang Huang Xiaofang asks what experience the Communist Party's discipline building in the Xiangshan period offers today. This was the roughly six months in 1949 when the Central Committee was based at Xiangshan, Beijing, and, as the article describes it, carried out the march to the whole country, preparations for the new Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and the founding of the new state. Huang argues that nationwide victory in the War of Liberation was inseparable from stronger discipline in the Party and army, and that this experience matters for full discipline building and the Party's self-reform today. This short commentary draws three or four lessons from the period and sets each beside developments since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The sources are mainly directives, speeches and regulations from 1949 by Zhu De, Mao Zedong and the Central Committee, set beside Xi Jinping's statements and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China. Huang's main points are that discipline must serve the Party's central task, rest on the people's interests, keep pace with changing conditions, and combine education with enforcement. In 1949 the central task was consolidating victory and shifting the Party's focus from countryside to cities. Rules on mass discipline, the "eight-point" proclamation protecting people's lives and property, and corrections to abuses during city takeovers, such as free entertainment for troops or seizure of capitalists' property, are presented as examples. Education before entering Shanghai and a system of rewards and punishments are also cited. Huang concludes that the Party under Xi Jinping has followed the same lines. Mass discipline became one of six disciplines, with political discipline first. The Regulations were revised three times, and regular discipline education was linked to strict punishment of every violation. In Huang's view, these measures provide disciplinary support for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-history scholarship ties the 1949 period to current discipline policy.

The logic of interaction between the Party's self-reform and social revolution 党的自我革命与社会革命的互动逻辑 Liang Haifeng Liang Haifeng asks how the Communist Party's internal renewal relates to the wider transformation of Chinese society. The article argues that the Party's self-reform and social revolution form a dialectical unity in which each strengthens the other. Self-reform supplies internal motive force and political leadership for social revolution, while the practical results of social revolution serve as the ultimate yardstick of whether self-reform is working. This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today, first treats self-reform as the engine of social revolution and then social revolution as the external test of self-reform. It then turns to Party conduct (zuofeng) as the link between the two and lists current obstacles and remedies. Liang draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, on Mao Zedong's and Deng Xiaoping's theories of Party building, and on the campaigns of the Xi Jinping era. Liang reasons from the Marxist premise that the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production drives history, and that a proletarian party's revolutionary character makes self-reform its core dynamic. Social revolution then feeds back in three ways. Its achievements, such as the economy's size and the elimination of absolute poverty, are said to confirm the Party's self-reform. The problems it exposes, such as corruption, formalism and bureaucratism, mark where self-reform must aim. Its goals, including the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, modernisation of national governance and high-quality development, set the tasks of self-reform. Conduct building is the bridge, converting the Party's purity and advanced character into practical strength, though Liang says formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance still threaten it. Liang proposes deepening conduct building through ideological education and Party-spirit training, firmer institutional constraints, regular supervision and "zero tolerance" for violations. The author concludes that persistence, summed up as making such work "regular" and "long-term", is needed to keep the Party's advanced and pure character and its role as the leadership core. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building scholars at CASS connect self-reform with social transformation through the idea of Party conduct.

Injecting innovative momentum into the dissemination of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army spirit 为东北抗联精神传播注入创新动能 Gao Shiying This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today (11 September 2025) asks how new media can strengthen the spread of the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army. Gao Shiying, an associate professor at a university school of Marxism, argues that content innovation, technological empowerment, platform linkage and audience interaction can raise the reach and influence of this spirit today. Gao treats this as a new task for passing on red culture. The article begins with the Party Central Committee's April 2022 formulation of the spirit: firm conviction of loyalty to the Party, national righteousness in going to the aid of the country, and heroic resolve to fight to the end. It then describes the technical and audience base provided by new media, citing internet penetration of 78% in China by June 2024. It goes on to the new forms and channels this offers, and ends with the mechanisms that Gao says give the spirit lasting vitality. Gao's central claim is that new media change both presentation and participation. Short video, animation, livestreaming and VR/AR make the history of the fighters vivid, while likes, reposts, comments and re-creation on platforms such as Bilibili and Douyin bring young people closer to revolutionary history. Content production shifts from professional institutions to ordinary users, as in Weibo topics where people share family stories of anti-Japanese forebears. Gao also points to big-data recommendation and AI image restoration as tools for reaching target audiences and for restoring the faces of heroes. Gao cautions that historical authenticity must be kept and that shallow or entertainment-driven content must be avoided. Gao concludes that the digital, interactive and fragmented features of new media open broad space for innovative dissemination and let the spirit take on new life in the digital age. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ideological-education writers link red culture and digital communication strategy.

The fundamental guidance for advancing urban–rural integrated development in the new era 新时代推进城乡融合发展的根本遵循 Wei Houkai Wei Houkai argues that Xi Jinping's body of statements on urban–rural integrated development is the fundamental guidance for the new era and an integral part of Xi Jinping's economic thought. In Wei's account, these statements reveal the trends and laws governing city and countryside, set out the goals and direction of integration, and develop the Marxist theory of urban–rural relations. Urban–rural integration is presented as an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization. The article, a commentary in the Party-run Economic Daily, has four parts. The first covers the trends and laws of urban–rural change; the second the goals and direction of integration; the third the practical path; the fourth the theoretical innovations. Wei traces Xi's remarks from 2013 to recent Party meetings, including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and follows the shift in policy language from coordinating urban and rural development to integrating it. Wei makes three main moves. First, citing Xi's 2018 statement, Wei holds that while the urban share rises and the rural share falls, the countryside will not disappear and the two will coexist over the long term. Wei adds that villages may vanish without the countryside doing so, and that cities and villages each follow their own laws. Second, the goals are the 'five equalizations' of basic rights, public services, incomes, factor allocation and industrial integration. Third, the path combines strategic coordination of new-type industrialization, new-type urbanization and rural revitalization with institutional reform, and takes the county as the entry point. Wei notes that counties hold about 90 per cent of national land and over 50 per cent of the population. Wei concludes that Xi advances Marxist theory in two ways. One is the theory of an urban–rural community, building on Marx and Engels, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. The other is the conception of a new type of industry–agriculture and urban–rural relationship, whose wording changed from 'comprehensive integration' in 2017 to 'coordinated development' in 2020. Wei reads this change as reflecting the new development philosophy and the aim of common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's systematic account of how official urban–rural policy language has evolved and how it is justified.

Contributing "silver-haired strength" to advancing Chinese modernization Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on work for the next generation 为推进中国式现代化贡献“银发力量” China National Committee for the Care of the Next Generation Published in the People's Daily in 2025, the 35th anniversary year of the China National Committee for the Care of the Next Generation, this commentary is written by the committee itself. It takes up how retired cadres and other elders can contribute to Chinese modernization by nurturing young people. Its answer is that the committees should study Xi Jinping's statements on the subject, gather the "silver-haired strength" of the "Five Elders", and make moral education central to their work. The text has three parts. The first sets out Xi Jinping's statements on work for the next generation under five headings: ensuring worthy successors, fostering virtue through education, treating older people as a resource, and the committees as an institutional arrangement. The second draws lessons about how the committees should work. The third lists concrete tasks for the committees. The authors give figures for the committees' reach: over 1.07 million organisations, more than 13 million "Five Elders", 70,000 "Five Elders" workrooms and 424,000 off-campus tutors. The authors argue that raising young people as "socialist builders and successors" is a strategic task on which the future of the Party and country depend. They present the committees, approved by the Party Central Committee in 1990, as an institutional innovation for using older comrades in the ideological and political education of youth. Their account of how the committees should operate has four elements: Party leadership, moral education with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, service to the Party's central tasks through local organisation, and use of elders' distinctive strengths. The proposals centre on three projects: moral education, care for the next generation, and the committees' own high-quality development. They include getting Xi's thought into textbooks and classrooms, teaching Party and national history, promoting legal awareness, supporting left-behind and migrant children, and training young rural talent and industrial workers. The committees are also to widen their organisational coverage and strengthen coordination among member units. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-led mass organisation for retired cadres describes its mission and organisation in official language.

Using rule-of-law thinking to create a healthy environment for the development of the private economy 用法治思维营造民营经济健康发展环境 Xu Hong Writing in the People's Daily (11 September 2025), Xu Hong takes up the question of how rule-of-law thinking can support the sustained, healthy and high-quality development of the private economy. Xu argues that the Private Economy Promotion Law, in force since 20 May 2025, is a milestone, and that implementing it requires, among other things, a criminal-justice environment that protects the lawful rights of private enterprises and entrepreneurs while still punishing genuine offences. The commentary begins with Xi Jinping's statements on the private economy and with figures it cites: private firms are over 92 per cent of all enterprises, contribute over half of imports and exports and tax revenue, and provide over 80 per cent of urban employment. It then traces the Party's policy line and constitutional amendments, the Civil Code and other laws. Its second half turns to criminal law and sets out three principles: no crime without explicit legal provision, the rule of applying the older law unless the newer one is more lenient, and criminal punishment that is necessary, appropriate, reasonable and fair. In Xu's account, the rule of law gives market actors a stable, predictable environment, marks the boundary between government and market, and strengthens integrity and compliance. Xu treats current difficulties as partial, temporary and surmountable, arising from structural change and from firms' weak legal awareness. On criminal justice, Xu calls for clear lines between economic disputes and crimes, administrative violations and crimes, and corporate and individual liability. Xu also calls for guarding against profit-driven enforcement and the use of criminal means in civil disputes. The older-law-or-more-lenient-law principle is meant to treat firms' past irregularities in historical context, with wrongful cases corrected. Xu concludes that criminal punishment must be assessed for its effects on employees, supply chains and industries, and be consistent with macro policy. Because private firms are credited with over 70 per cent of technological innovation results, Xu proposes a judicial tolerance-of-error mechanism and a restrained approach to criminalising innovative conduct, so that entrepreneurship and the tolerance of failure are encouraged. Read the original if you want an official-line account, by a criminal-law scholar, of how the new law is meant to shape policing and prosecution of private businesses.

Strict supervision and discipline enforcement as a sharp tool of the Party's self-reform 从严监督执纪是党的自我革命的利器 Gai Yixin Gai Yixin takes up Xi Jinping's statement that strict supervision and discipline enforcement is "a sharp tool of the Party's self-reform". The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, argues that this practice is both a means of punishing corruption and correcting conduct and a pillar for keeping the Party from changing its nature, colour or flavour. Gai presents it as a key measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. The piece has three parts. The first traces strict supervision and discipline enforcement to Marxist party theory and to more than a century of Party history. The second describes what it contributes to self-reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012): firm discipline, punishment of corruption and rectification of work style. The third sets out how to strengthen it further. In the first part Gai argues that the Party's vanguard character is not innate or permanent. Citing Marx and Lenin on party discipline, and episodes from the Jinggangshan period, Yan'an, the early People's Republic and reform and opening up, Gai holds that long-term rule exposes the Party to the erosion of power, capital and personal ties. Gai says the Party therefore needs routine, institutionalised supervision. In the second part, Gai credits the "four forms" of supervision and discipline enforcement, the revised disciplinary regulations, the anti-corruption drive of "no forbidden zones, full coverage, zero tolerance" and the campaign against the "four malpractices". Gai nonetheless describes the anti-corruption situation as still severe and complex. Gai calls for three measures: a coordinated supervision system joining intra-Party and popular supervision; stronger day-to-day supervision by Party organisations, with closed-loop management of problems found; and joint investigation and handling of unhealthy work styles and corruption, through investigation, case-based reform and prevention. Gai concludes that supervision can only be strengthened, never weakened. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party theorists in 2025 link discipline enforcement to the Party's self-reform and to the Party's own account of its history.

Regulating the exercise of power as a requirement of anti-corruption work Institutions, supervision and the ideological foundation of exercising power for the people 理论资源导航 Wang Daguang Wu Tongge Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that "anti-corruption must regulate the exercise of power", Wang Daguang and Wu Tongge argue that corruption is at root the abuse of power for private gain, and that fighting it therefore means tightening supervision and restraining power. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, presents this as guidance for the new era and for carrying the Party's self-reform through to the end. The authors organise the argument in three parts. The first concerns key links in the chain of power: authorisation, use and restraint. The second concerns building a comprehensive, multi-layered system of power supervision. The third concerns consolidating the ideological base of holding and using power for the people. Throughout, they quote Xi Jinping's remarks and cite Party documents such as the decisions of the Third and Fourth Plenums of the 19th Central Committee. In the first part the authors say that the anti-corruption situation remains "severe and complex", with existing corruption not yet cleared and new cases still arising, so rules must keep pace. They call for scientific authorisation (a division of decision-making, executive and supervisory powers, with power lists, negative lists and responsibility lists), procedural discipline for decision-making, approval and law enforcement, and transparency so that power works "in the sunshine". In the second part they stress enforcing rules rigidly, applying democratic centralism fully, with leading officials setting an example, and building two defences: early warning and precise correction, the latter using the "three distinctions" to tell error from wrongdoing while keeping officials motivated. In the third part they urge officials to hold a correct view of power and to stand in awe of the people, the organisation and Party discipline and law. The authors conclude that institutional constraint, supervision and moral-political cultivation must advance together, in line with the formula of not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt. Officials are told to treat power as service and responsibility, accept organisational supervision, observe the Eight-point Regulation and act under the law, never above it. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party-building writing in 2025 links anti-corruption institutions with the ideological education of cadres.

Advancing self-reform requires strengthening the foundation and Party spirit Five requirements for enhancing Party spirit among Party members and cadres 推进自我革命必须固本培元、增强党性 Zhang Hao Zhang Hao's commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that advancing self-reform requires strengthening the foundation and Party spirit (dangxing). Zhang argues that Party spirit plays a central role in the Party's self-reform and that its enhancement must be put into practice so that Communists keep the Party's advanced and pure character. The piece reads as a study of Xi's formulation rather than an independent theoretical inquiry. The article follows the five requirements in Xi's wording: firm ideals and convictions, loyalty to the Party, deep feeling for the people, sound moral character, and honesty and integrity. Each requirement gets its own section, and each section is divided into three practical routes or demands addressed to Party members and cadres. Zhang draws on Xi's speeches, classical Chinese sayings, Marx and examples of model Communists such as Jiao Yulu and Zhang Fuqing. On ideals, Zhang argues that conviction rests on mastering theory, above all Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, on grasping the laws of historical development, and on concrete work in one's post. On loyalty, the article treats the Two Establishes as the decisive political achievement of the new era and calls for turning that consensus into the Two Upholds. It also asks cadres to keep the "matters of national importance" in mind and to observe discipline, political discipline above all. On the people, moral character and integrity, Zhang holds that Party spirit and the people's nature are unified, and urges cadres to rely on the masses and learn from them. Zhang also urges them to draw on traditional Chinese culture and on heroic models, and to use criticism and self-criticism. Finally, they should cultivate reverence, wariness and bottom lines against corruption. Zhang concludes that Party spirit is the basis of a Communist's conduct and career, and that the Party's self-reform depends on cadres continually cultivating it in these five respects. The text is a normative, exhortatory guide rather than an analysis of cases or institutions. Read the original if you want a clear example of how Party-school-style writing in 2025 turns Xi Jinping's formula on Party spirit into concrete expectations for cadres.

The practical power and lessons of the Party's strategy for governing Tibet in the new era 新时代党的治藏方略的实践伟力和经验启示 Wang Hongxiao Marking the 60th anniversary of the Tibet Autonomous Region, this commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 16) takes up Xi Jinping's call of 20 August 2025 to implement fully the Party's strategy for governing Tibet in the new era. Wang Hongxiao argues that the strategy, formed after the 18th Party Congress (2012), has produced historic change in Tibet and yields lessons for achieving long-term stability and high-quality development there. The article has three parts. The first traces the strategy's lineage from Mao Zedong's Tibet policy through Deng Xiaoping's stress on economic development to the 1990s formulas of "long-term construction of Tibet" and handling development and stability together. It then presents the strategy's content, summarised as the "ten musts" set out at the Seventh Central Symposium on Tibet Work. The second part reviews achievements in stability, economy, livelihoods, ethnic and religious work, culture, ecology and border consolidation. The third draws seven lessons. In Wang's account, the strategy rests on the thesis that "to govern the country, one must govern the borders; to govern the borders, one must first stabilise Tibet", and on the four major tasks of stability, development, ecology and strengthening the borders. Wang cites figures: regional GDP of 276.5 billion yuan in 2024, 628,000 people lifted out of poverty, rural per capita disposable income of 21,578 yuan against 5,698 in 2012, and public cultural facilities said to cover 100% of localities. Wang describes religious freedom as fully protected and reports that the sense of security among residents is above 99%. The lessons are: uphold Party leadership; put the people at the centre; balance development and security; pursue high-quality development; forge a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation; govern Tibet by law; and treat the whole country as one chessboard, combining central support with counterpart assistance. Wang also calls for guiding Tibetan Buddhism to adapt to socialist society and for promoting the common national language. Read the original if you want an official-line overview of Tibet policy, with the Party's own statistics and its framing of governance principles, as presented in a central Party journal in 2025.

The Communist Party of China's external relations during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国共产党的对外交往工作 Li Zhongjie Li Zhongjie examines how the Communist Party of China conducted contacts with foreign countries and peoples during the War of Resistance against Japan (1937–1945). Li argues that this work, which the Party's own 1944 directive called "semi-independent diplomacy", introduced the Party and the anti-Japanese struggle to the world and promoted a world anti-fascist united front. In Li's account it marked the Party's first steps onto the international stage and laid a foundation for the diplomacy of the People's Republic. The article is a historical narrative in three parts. The first traces how the Party opened a window to the outside world, from the reception office at Yan'an and the visits of Edgar Snow, Agnes Smedley, Norman Bethune and others to the US Army Observation Group of 1944. The second covers the push for an international anti-fascist united front, including the work of the Southern Bureau in Chongqing, the 1941 Yan'an conference of Eastern peoples and intelligence cooperation with the Soviet Union and the Allies. The third deals with China's rise to great-power status and the Party's role at the founding of the United Nations. Li's central claim is that the Party combined internationalism with patriotism and independence with the pursuit of foreign support, under the line of "publicise abroad and win over". Li stresses the 1944 Directive on Diplomatic Work, which set a national standpoint, rejecting both xenophobia and deference to foreigners, and tied diplomacy to the united front. Among the evidence cited are the reception of over 7,000 guests between 1938 and 1941, the impact of Snow's Red Star Over China and the Party's warning to Moscow of the German attack in 1941. Li also recounts how Zhou Enlai and US pressure secured a Communist delegate, Dong Biwu, a place in China's delegation to the 1945 San Francisco conference. Li concludes that the Party's wartime diplomacy broke the blockade around it, won international recognition and contributed to China's first entry into the ranks of the great powers since the modern era, including a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Li reads the signing of the UN Charter with a Chinese brush as a symbol that the Chinese people's contribution to the anti-fascist war had been recognised. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of the Party's early foreign relations and the episodes the Party historiography emphasises.

Grasping theoretical and practical requirements: developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 把握理论和实践要求因地制宜发展新质生产力 Chen Yunping This short commentary from the Economic Daily takes up Xi Jinping's repeated instruction that new quality productive forces be developed "in light of local conditions" (yindi zhiyi). Chen Yunping argues that this is a scientific method which joins the Marxist theory of productive forces with the practice of Chinese modernization. In Chen's reading, it deepens understanding of how productive forces are driven and how they evolve. The article first sets out why the approach matters, internationally and domestically. It then gives four theoretical foundations and three practical requirements, all in condensed form. The author closes by describing regional differences in factor endowments, industrial bases and functional positioning, with examples drawn from coastal and inland regions. Chen makes two central moves. First, the approach is tied to the change in the principal contradiction of Chinese society and to deepening reform: uneven and inadequate development is partly regional, so letting each place pursue its own path should draw out local potential and gradually narrow gaps. Because productive forces determine relations of production, Chen adds, developing them requires adjusting those relations through further comprehensive deepening of reform. Second, the theoretical grounding is traced to dialectical materialism (the particularity of contradiction), to seeking truth from facts (no "one-size-fits-all" approach or campaign-style rushing), to comparative advantage theory (extended from labour, land and resources to new-quality factors) and to regional coordinated development theory. In practice, Chen holds that resource-rich regions can start from resource-based industries and move towards deep processing and recycling. Labour-abundant regions can upgrade labour-intensive industries towards skill-intensive ones, and large industrial clusters are better placed for breakthroughs such as battery or autonomous-driving technology. Coastal regions are said to suit electronic information, biomedicine and new energy, and inland regions specialised manufacturing, resource processing or logistics. Chen concludes that tying development to functional positioning avoids homogeneous competition and resource misallocation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary justifies regionally differentiated industrial policy in terms of Marxist theory and the Party's ideological vocabulary.

Deepening the understanding of the laws governing the development of new quality productive forces 深化发展新质生产力的规律性认识 Zhao Zhenhua Zhao Zhenhua, writing in Economic Daily in September 2025, asks how new quality productive forces should be understood and developed as the country enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period. The article argues that doing so requires a change in development thinking, respect for objective laws of development, and the guidance of dialectical and historical materialist method. It presents the concept as Xi Jinping's creative development of Marxist productive-forces theory and calls for developing these forces in ways suited to local conditions. The piece has three parts.
