The first links leaps in productive forces to the liberation of thought and the renewal of development ideas, citing the 1978 debate on the criterion of truth, Deng Xiaoping's 1992 southern tour and the 14th Party Congress. The second sets out three laws of development: revolutionary technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors, and deep industrial transformation and upgrading. The third lists four methodological principles. Zhao first holds that new quality productive forces embody the new development philosophy and must break with extensive growth, so development should not put "old wine in new bottles", even under downward economic pressure. On the three laws, the author stresses basic research as the precondition for technological breakthroughs, combining free exploration with organised research on key technologies. Zhao adds that data, knowledge, technology and management now join labour, capital and land as production factors, and that a unified national market and the market's decisive role in allocating resources are needed to release them. For industry, Zhao calls for applying technology to traditional sectors, pursuing "AI Plus" initiatives and nurturing future industries with patient capital. The methodology section calls for seeing connections across the whole system, grasping principal contradictions (above all core technology bottlenecks), and building production relations suited to the new forces through deeper reform and opening up. Zhao concludes that the "one key for one lock" principle should guide local practice: avoid rushing in and bubbles, avoid a single model, and base plans on thorough investigation of each place's resources, industrial base and research conditions. The author says this approach lets China seize the initiative in development and create new economic momentum. Read the original if you want a concise, Party School-style statement of how official discourse frames the laws, methods and local pathways of developing new quality productive forces.

How the Party identified and trained military-industrial talent in the base areas during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期党对根据地军工人才的发掘与培养 An Na Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, An Na asks how the Communist Party built a workforce for the arms industry of its anti-Japanese base areas during the War of Resistance (1937–1945). The article argues that the Party, recognising the importance of independent military production, drew in talent from many fields and so formed a technically skilled and politically reliable corps of military-industrial personnel. In An's account, this corps kept production running and laid the personnel foundation for the arms industry of the Liberation War and the People's Republic. The piece is a short historical commentary organised under three headings: combining the recruitment of highly trained specialists with the absorption of skilled craftsmen; founding military-industrial schools to train technical backbone staff; and using several measures to nurture and motivate such personnel. It draws on Party documents, including the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (1938) and a 1941 Central Military Commission directive, and on local military-history sources. Its cases come mainly from the Taihang base area of the Eighth Route Army and from the New Fourth Army's central China bases. An's central claim is that recruitment came from two directions. The Party brought in returned students from Europe and Southeast Asia and university professors and students, many of whom joined the Eighth Route Army's mobile working group, and it also drew skilled workers from arsenals in Hebei, Shanxi and Shandong. The Huangyadong arsenal is cited as a training ground, with output figures such as tens of thousands of rifles and over 580,000 hand grenades. Schools such as the Taihang Industrial School, said to have trained nearly 400 mid-level managers and technicians, and the Huaibei Industrial School of the New Fourth Army's Fourth Division supplied further staff. The article then stresses a mix of political study, including a minimum 15 per cent of class time at Taihang, technical training and incentives. These included higher grain wages, medical and family benefits, and awards for inventions and above-quota output. An concludes that these political, technical and material measures released the creativity of military-industrial personnel and strengthened the base areas' military capacity, even in the hardest years of 1942–1944. Individual designers such as Liu Guifu, creator of the 'Bayi-type' cavalry rifle, are presented as products of this system. Read the original if you want a brief, source-referenced overview of the Party's official narrative on talent policy in the wartime arms industry, with named schools, factories and incentive measures.

The historic contribution of the Communist Party of China to building the community of the Chinese nation during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国共产党推进中华民族共同体建设的历史贡献 Chen Jinlong Writing in Guangming Daily shortly after the 80th anniversary commemoration of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), Chen Jinlong asks how the Communist Party of China advanced the building of the community of the Chinese nation during the war. Chen argues that the war was an important stage in that history. Four things consolidated the community's foundations: the practice of a nationwide war of resistance, new relations among nationalities, the construction of a discourse of the Chinese nation, and emotional closeness among the nationalities. The article is organised in four numbered sections matching these four themes. It draws mainly on Party documents of 1935–1945 collected in the multi-volume compilation of key documents since the Party's founding. It also draws on Mao Zedong's wartime writings and speeches by Mao and Zhang Wentian at the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee. Examples include appeals to Hui and Mongol peoples, policy outlines on Hui and Mongol questions, and the formation of resistance forces in Daqingshan and in Hebei and Bohai. Chen's core argument is that mobilising all nationalities was both a military necessity and a means of community-building. In Chen's account, the Party's anti-Japanese national united front covered every nationality as well as every party and class, and the Party worked to raise the confidence of minority peoples and helped form armed units among them. Chen says the Party then built new nationality relations on equality in economic, political and cultural life, on unity, and on economic measures such as tax limits, protection of Mongol pastures and support for Hui production. Chen adds that Party narratives of a shared multi-ethnic history, of civilisational achievement and of revolutionary tradition gave historical and political support to the community. Chen presents emotional bonds, citing Xi Jinping's 2024 remark that emotional closeness is a 'strong bond', as resting on trust built through communication, the address of minority peoples as 'brothers', and national self-confidence and pride. Chen concludes that the war's shared struggle laid the foundations of the community of the Chinese nation, and that the Party's wartime practice contributed historically to its construction. The piece is a short commentary that links wartime policy to current official language on ethnic unity. Read the original if you want a concise account, with archival citations, of how current Chinese official historiography presents wartime Party nationality policy as the origin of the community of the Chinese nation.

Promoting innovation in urban grassroots governance through joint consultation and joint governance 以共商共治推动城市基层治理创新 Zhang Ge Zhang Ge, writing as Party secretary of Beijing's Haidian District, asks how urban grassroots governance can be renewed in a megacity. The commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2025, answers that consultation and joint governance, led by Party organisations, offer the route. It takes as its guide Xi Jinping's remarks on consultative democracy and grassroots governance, and the Central Urban Work Conference of July 2025. The piece presents Haidian's "Let's Work It Out Together" deliberation mechanism, built on the city's "respond to complaints" reform. It describes a four-part practice: Party building as leadership, consultation, work centred on the grassroots, and joint building of a better home. The author reports that after about two years of practice, complaint volumes have fallen, the resolution rate has risen and satisfaction has improved. The text has three main sections: Party leadership, institutional design, and people's satisfaction as the yardstick. First, Zhang argues that Party building gives consultation its political direction. Grassroots Party organisations set the agenda and mobilise resources, and Haidian has a five-tier organisational system running from sub-district Party committees to model Party-member households. Second, institutional design must move the focus of governance downwards: the district cut paperwork and meetings for grassroots cadres, set up a five-step procedure (collect, discuss, act, supervise, assess) and created more than 650 deliberation platforms. Zhang links the mechanism to the "Fengqiao experience", presenting consultation as a way of resolving conflicts early, and says 79 long-standing problems have been resolved since 2023. Third, Zhang treats consultation as the practical form of whole-process people's democracy. Residents, new social organisations, new forms of employment, volunteers and professionals take part in deciding what is done, who does it, how, and how it is judged. The author cites over 9,000 long-standing problems, such as property management, meals for the elderly and parking, solved since 2023, and concludes that consultation is the foundation while implementation is the key. Read the original if you want a first-hand official account of how a Beijing district presents its consultation mechanism and results.

Talent training in the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army 东北抗日联军的人才培养 Zhang Kuan This short commentary asks how the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (abbreviated as "the United Army") organised study and training under wartime conditions, and what that study achieved. Zhang Kuan argues that learning in the United Army was adapted to war. In the author's account it shaped the force's ideological cohesion and fighting strength, and produced many cadres and fighters with both military skill and firm political conviction. The article has three parts. The first surveys the forms of study: political-military schools, schools attached to units, temporary training classes, and company-level groups such as literacy classes, shooting and tactics groups, political discussion meetings and Lenin study circles. The second describes a distinctive model summed up as "rifle plus pen". The third assesses the results under three headings. The piece draws on statements by the commander Zhou Baozhong and on period documents and reports. Zhang notes that the formal schools often existed in name only. The Third Army, for example, sent its instructors and students to frontline units, and the United Army had little printing equipment. Fighters copied textbooks by hand, made their own teaching aids or used captured materials. Because attacks by Japanese and puppet forces were frequent, regular classroom teaching gave way to self-study in gaps between fighting. In the "rifle plus pen" model, the "rifle" meant weapons, guerrilla tactics and special skills such as skiing, boat handling and winter survival. The "pen" meant political education and basic literacy, together with Japanese, Russian and Korean. Zhang credits the training with three results. It produced cadres, including about 300 military-political cadres from the school in the Tangwang River area. It raised tactical ability through practice-based discussion. It raised cultural and political levels together. Zhang concludes that the United Army's study practice was a microcosm of the Chinese Communist Party's fourteen years of resistance to Japan. The author draws the lesson that fighting strength depends not only on better equipment and technology. It also depends on "using study to promote fighting", and on ideological education that builds absolute loyalty in the sense of "the Party commands the gun". Read the original if you want a brief, officially framed overview of education and training in the Northeast guerrilla forces in the 1930s and 1940s, or an example of how the history is used in Party-building discourse today.

The Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army spirit remains ever fresh 东北抗联精神历久弥新 Wang Zhuoya This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 8 September 2025, argues that the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (Dongbei Kanglian) retains lasting value today. Wang opens with Xi Jinping's 2016 remark in Heilongjiang that this spirit, with others such as the Daqing spirit, should still be used to educate Party members and cadres. The author defines the spirit as three elements: firm faith in the Party, national righteousness in answering the national crisis, and heroic determination to fight to the end. The article is organised under three headings, one for each element. Each is illustrated with episodes from the fourteen-year struggle that the Party-led force waged against a far larger enemy. Wang draws on figures such as Yang Jingyu, Zhou Baozhong, Zhao Yiman, Chen Hanzhang and the eight women fighters who drowned themselves in the Wusuli River. On Party faith, Wang cites Yang Jingyu's resistance despite starvation and Zhao Yiman's refusal to betray secrets under torture, and presents both as expressions of Marxist conviction. On national righteousness, the author points to the united-front declaration of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, which offered cooperation to all anti-Japanese forces regardless of faction. Wang says this awakened the national consciousness of people in the Northeast. On fighting to the end, Wang describes sub-zero conditions, Japanese policies of forced relocation and collective punishment, and the refusal of Chen Hanzhang and the eight women to surrender. Wang concludes that, as the world undergoes what the text calls changes unseen in a century, today's readers should draw on this spirit. The author calls for a willingness to struggle, for firm ideals and convictions as a lifelong task, and for lasting commitment to communist ideals and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commemoration of the anti-Japanese war links wartime heroism to present-day ideological education.

Outlook for the integration of artificial intelligence and consumption during the 15th Five-Year Plan period “十五五”时期人工智能与消费融合发展前瞻 Xia Jiechang Wang Wenji Writing in September 2025, Xia Jiechang and Wang Wenji ask how "AI plus consumption" can help release domestic demand during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). They tie the topic to Xi Jinping's call to "vigorously boost consumption" and to the State Council's August 2025 opinions on the "AI Plus" initiative. Their thesis is that AI will reshape supply–demand relations and consumer behaviour, moving the consumption system into a digital, intelligent and personalised stage. This short commentary has two parts. The first sets out four features of the current stage: technological evolution, supply and demand structure, inclusiveness, and the institutional environment. The second sets out four policy directions: intelligent supply, key application scenarios, underlying capabilities, and flexible institutional safeguards. The authors cite 249 million users of generative AI products in China by December 2024 and project 40 per cent compound annual growth for the AI large-model market. Xia and Wang argue that large models are moving AI consumption from isolated scenarios to full-chain, ecosystem-based penetration. They see consumers shifting from data providers to active participants, and platforms building "data + algorithms + computing power + scenarios" ecosystems. They also identify risks: an "intelligence divide" that excludes lower-income and older groups, and algorithmic recommendation that may induce irrational consumption and homogenise tastes. They also point to unclear data ownership, weak algorithm transparency, vague platform responsibility and fragmented enforcement. For supply, they urge firms to turn products such as appliances, wearables and cars into emotional carriers and platforms into intelligent ecosystem operators. The authors call for more widely accessible computing power, public high-quality data (including "data public-interest pools") and open-source model ecosystems. They also propose pilot scenarios in health care, elderly care, culture and tourism, plus ex ante risk warning against algorithmic discrimination and false interaction. They further propose tiered, classified and dynamically adjustable governance: stronger accountability and transparency duties for large platforms, and guidance with tolerant regulation for small firms. They conclude that policy should give equal weight to development and governance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy agenda for AI-driven consumption and its governance ahead of the 15th Five-Year Plan.

The mainstay of the nation's all-out resistance and the staunch leadership core of national rejuvenation 全民族抗战的中流砥柱民族复兴的坚强领导核心 Zhang Taiyuan Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), this newspaper commentary by Zhang Taiyuan takes up Xi Jinping's description of the Communist Party as the mainstay of the nation's all-out resistance. Zhang argues that this role is shown above all in the Party's initiation, advancement and defence of the Anti-Japanese National United Front. The piece follows the history chronologically. It starts with the Party's early calls for a united front, then covers the formal adoption of the policy at the Wayaobao meeting (1935), the Xi'an Incident (1936), the founding of the Kuomintang–Communist united front in 1937, and the Party's conduct during the war, including after the Southern Anhui Incident. It ends with lessons for the present. Zhang's central claim is that the Party was the first to call for, and then consistently pushed, a united front. He traces this from a January 1933 declaration and the August First Declaration through the shift from "pressing Chiang to resist Japan" to "allying with Chiang". In Zhang's account, the Party's peaceful settlement of the Xi'an Incident reflected its confidence in contending for leadership of the resistance. Zhang says the Party behind enemy lines kept to independent guerrilla warfare and avoided further military action against the Kuomintang even after the Southern Anhui Incident. He concludes that without the Party there would have been no national united front, and without that front no all-out resistance. Zhang draws the lesson that winning hearts is the greatest politics and that the united front remains a means of gathering strength. He calls for consolidating the broadest patriotic united front under Party leadership, improving the overall united front work structure, and uniting people at home and overseas to advance Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how Party historians frame the Party's role in the wartime united front.

Historical lessons on the key to victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression 中国人民抗日战争胜利关键的历史启示 Qu Qingshan Writing after Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), Qu Qingshan asks what was decisive in the Chinese people's victory. The answer is that the Communist Party of China's role as the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) was the key to victory. Qu presents this as a historical conclusion and as a lesson for upholding Party leadership in the new era. The piece first appeared in the People's Daily on 8 September 2025. The article is organised in five parts, each opening with a statement from Xi. It treats the Party as the earliest advocate and organiser of resistance; as the builder of the anti-Japanese national united front; as the source of the strategy of all-out resistance and protracted war; as the leader of the rear-area battlefield behind Japanese lines; and as the forger of the great spirit of resistance. It draws on declarations, dates, military statistics, and remarks by Mao Zedong, Ye Jianying and some Japanese and American observers. A short closing section draws lessons for the present. Qu argues that after the 1931 Mukden Incident the Nationalist government pursued non-resistance, while the Party issued declarations, led guerrilla war in the Northeast and backed the national salvation movement. It then promoted the united front, from the 1935 August 1st Declaration through the peaceful settlement of the Xi'an Incident and the second Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, and defended it against anti-Communist offensives. Qu credits Mao's On Protracted War and the guerrilla strategy with guiding the war. The article holds that the enemy-rear battlefield became the main battlefield once the war reached the stage of strategic stalemate. It cites figures for the share of Japanese forces in China that Party-led troops fought, ranging from about 58 to 75 per cent a year from 1938 to 1945, and reports that the liberated areas covered nearly 1 million square kilometres and had a population of nearly 100 million. Qu also credits Communists' vanguard role with shaping the national spirit, while mentioning Nationalist officers who died in battle. Qu concludes that the Party's mainstay role is the most fundamental point to remember when commemorating the war. In his reading, Party leadership is the foundation and lifeline of the Party and the state. He calls for a deep grasp of the Two Establishes, strengthened awareness, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. He also calls for unity under Xi Jinping to advance national strength and rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of the current official Party-history account of the war and the way it links that account to present-day political demands.

Reflections on upholding and developing the Marxist view of religion in the new era 新时代坚持发展马克思主义宗教观的思考 Gong Xuezeng Gong Xuezeng, a professor at the Central Party School, asks how the Marxist view of religion should be upheld and developed in the new era. In this short commentary, Gong argues that Marxist guidance is a consistent requirement of the Party Central Committee for religious affairs and religious studies, and that it must be both maintained and developed. The piece defines the Marxist view of religion, summarises the theory of Marx and Engels and the Leninist view, and closes with three cautions about reading the classics today. Gong calls the Marxist view of religion essentially a historical-materialist one, understood in a broad sense as an evolving outlook. Its basic content, in Gong's account, is a theory of religion as a distorted reflection of social life, with a dual social role and a long path to eventual disappearance, and a proletarian party's attitude: freedom of belief, separation of church and state, and rejection of leftist attempts to abolish religion by force. Gong then argues that these principles should be neither negated nor treated dogmatically. Religion was a marginal concern for Marx, Engels and Lenin, who studied it mainly through class analysis and could not foresee religion under socialist rule. Some specific judgements therefore no longer fully apply, though the basic principles remain valid. Gong concludes that the Soviet party left mostly historical lessons, while the Chinese Communist Party finally succeeded. Different approaches to studying religion should respect one another, but Party and state research institutions must treat Marxist guidance as a principle that cannot be shaken. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese position on how Marxist religious theory should be applied today.

On Protracted War: a strategic beacon that lit the way to victory in the War of Resistance 《论持久战》：照亮抗战胜利的战略灯塔 Ji Chunfang This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2025, assesses Mao Zedong's 1938 work On Protracted War. Ji presents it as a model of adapting Marxist military theory to China. The author argues that its scientific foresight and practical guidance shaped the course of the War of Resistance against Japan, and that it still inspires efforts toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised under three headings: how the work cleared away confusion and set the direction of resistance, how its analysis of the situation revealed the laws of the war, and how it guided practice and built national spirit. Ji argues that Mao answered two harmful positions of the early war, the 'theory of national subjugation' and the 'theory of quick victory', by comparing the two sides. Japan was strong but waged an unjust war with limited resources, while China was weak but fought a just war with large territory and population. From this Mao drew the three stages of strategic defence, stalemate and counter-offensive. Ji also highlights Mao's tactical principles of offence within defence, quick decision within protracted war, and exterior lines within interior lines. In practice, the author credits trading space for time, raising guerrilla warfare to strategic status, and mass political mobilisation through the anti-Japanese national united front. Ji concludes that the work gave the nation a firm faith in victory and turned the spirit of resistance into a wider commitment to justice. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style Chinese account of how On Protracted War is now presented in the 2025 commemoration of the war's victory.

The great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression took shape in the Changbai Mountains and Heilongjiang waters 伟大抗战精神在白山黑水间发轫 Wang Xiliang Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (3 September 2025), this short commentary asks where the "great spirit of resistance" began. Wang Xiliang argues that it took shape in China's north-east after the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, forged by Communists who fought in the front line. In the article's account, the 14 years of struggle show that the Chinese Communist Party deserved to be called the mainstay of the war. The article opens with a quotation from Xi Jinping's anniversary speech, then follows the north-east resistance in three steps: the Party's immediate call to resist, the building and sacrifice of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, and the way the "spirit" of that army fed into the national one. Wang draws on Party documents from September 1931 and on figures for troop strength, losses and named commanders. Wang stresses that the Manchurian Provincial Committee and the Central Committee issued declarations and resolutions within days of the incident. In this account they condemned Japanese imperialism and the Nationalist government's non-resistance policy, and called on the masses to fight. The author says that Communists sent over 500 members into the volunteer armies, then set up their own guerrilla units, which took up the banner alone after the volunteer armies' main force collapsed in early 1933. These units were renamed and in 1936 reorganised as the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, which reached more than 30,000 men in 11 armies across over 70 counties. Wang describes the Japanese and puppet authorities' encirclement campaigns, collective-responsibility rules and forced "collective hamlets", which cut the army to about 1,000. More than 30 senior commanders, including Yang Jingyu and Zhao Shangzhi, died, along with over 80 division-level cadres. Wang concludes that the north-east army's spirit was a "trickle" that joined the wider national spirit and enriched it. He places it alongside later heroes of the full-scale war, such as Zuo Quan, Zhang Zijing and the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, including figures from Nationalist forces. He holds that the victory shows justice, peace and the people will prevail, and that this spirit still drives the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Party's current narrative places the north-east resistance within the great spirit of resistance, with the main organisations and casualty figures it cites.

The Communist Party of China leads in forging and promoting the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression 中国共产党引领弘扬伟大抗战精神 He Husheng Xue Siqi This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2025, asks how the Communist Party of China shaped the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression. He and Xue argue that the Party was the mainstay of the nation-wide War of Resistance and, through its political programme, firm resolve and exemplary conduct, led the forging of that spirit. The article follows the war from the September 18th Incident (1931) to the later stages of the conflict. It organises the Party's role under four headings: raising the banner of national salvation, mobilising the whole people, fighting on the front line, and upholding independence and unity. In the authors' account, the Party was first to call for armed resistance and a united front, citing the August 1st Declaration, the December 9th Movement and the peaceful settlement of the Xi'an Incident. They say it put national interest above past enmity with the Kuomintang. They credit it with a line of all-out, protracted resistance and with heroes such as Yang Jingyu and Zuo Quan. They describe the victory at Pingxingguan, the Hundred Regiments Offensive and guerrilla warfare in the enemy's rear, and state that by the war's later stage Party-led forces fought about 60 per cent of Japanese troops and 95 per cent of puppet troops. They also say the Party combined alliance with struggle against Kuomintang anti-communist moves and sustained the base areas through the production campaign. The authors conclude that the Party's independence, commitment to unity and sacrifice instilled an unshakeable belief in victory, which became a shared national resolve. They quote Xi Jinping on the Party's consistent stance for resistance, unity and progress. The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the nation's war of resistance 中国共产党是全民族抗战的中流砥柱 Wang Guangyi This short commentary, published in 2025 in the China Social Sciences Today, argues that the Communist Party of China was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the whole nation's War of Resistance against Japan. After 1938, Wang says, the bases behind enemy lines became the main battlefield. The article cites the tying down of more than two thirds of Japanese forces in China and 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops killed. The far-reaching significance of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan from the perspective of civilizational history 从文明史视域看抗日战争胜利的深远意义 Yu Zuhua Writing in the China Social Sciences Today (5 September 2025), Yu Zuhua asks what the victory of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression, and of the World Anti-Fascist War, means when viewed through the history of civilization. Yu argues that the war was a life-and-death struggle at a moment when both Chinese and human civilization were under grave threat, and that the Communist Party led the Chinese people to a victory of civilization over barbarism. The short commentary is organised in two parts. The first concerns the defence of Chinese civilization, including its territory, its cultural relics and its national spirit. The second concerns the rescue of human civilization and the upgrading of civilizational forms. In the first part, Yu describes the war as the first fully victorious anti-invasion struggle of modern China. Yu cites the southward evacuation of Palace Museum treasures and the relocation of universities such as the Southwest Associated University as examples of protecting cultural memory. Yu further argues that the war preserved the continuity of Chinese civilization while launching its rebirth. In this account, Mao Zedong's New Democracy, the 1939 definition of a pluralistic and unified Chinese nation, and the call to concretise Marxism in China all emerged from the war. In the second part, Yu contends that China's resistance helped defeat fascism, secured China's place among the "Big Four" Allies and the founding of the United Nations, and fed anti-colonial movements. Yu also presents New Democracy as an early exploration of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Yu concludes that the victory will be remembered both for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and for the advance of human civilization. In Yu's view, Chinese modernization's creation of a new form of human civilization shows that China will again contribute to world peace. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars in 2025 framed the war's anniversary in civilizational terms.

The conception of civilisation in Capital 《资本论》的文明观 Bai Gang Bai Gang, writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, asks what Marx's Capital says about civilisation. The article's thesis is that, in essence, civilisation means the 'enlightenment of the human being' as opposed to barbarism, and that Capital is therefore a 'theory of civilisation' aimed at the full liberation of individuals' free personality. Bai argues that this theory culminates in a 'revolution of the highest civilisation' that cultivates 'highly civilised human beings'. This is a short newspaper piece in three parts. The first treats capital as 'another name for civilisation'. The second traces a 'civilisational turn' from the 'civilising aspect of capital' to the highly civilised person. The third presents Capital's 'dialectic of civilisation' and describes the book as a 'midwife' of a new civilisation. Bai supports each step with passages from Marx on capital, colonies and the working day. Bai holds that civilisation appears as the evolution of things (tools, machines, means of production), which Marx treated as its 'measure' and 'indicator'. Capital analyses capitalist civilisation by analysing the thing called capital, from the commodity through money to interest-bearing capital, and so exposes the secret of commodity, money and capital fetishism. Capital's civilising tendency, in Bai's reading, drives productive forces, global expansion and the subordination of East to West. Yet it yields a civilisation of things rather than persons: capital has independence and individuality while living individuals do not, and capitalist civilisation is hypocritical and, in the colonies, openly barbarous. Bai concludes that Marx did not simply negate capitalist civilisation. He recognised its 'civilising side' as the material basis for a higher social form founded on the free and all-round development of each person. On this reading, the labour theory of value concerns the status and significance of labour, not only the source of value. By revealing the law of surplus value and the secret of the capitalist mode of production, Capital would shorten the 'birth pangs' of a new civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese philosopher frames Capital as a theory of civilisation and human liberation.

Five-year plans (guihua) as an important way for the Communist Party of China to govern the country “五年规划”：中国共产党治国理政的重要方式 Tang Yalin Qian Kun Following Xi Jinping's remarks in April 2025 that the scientific formulation and successive implementation of five-year plans is an important Party experience and a political advantage of socialism with Chinese characteristics, this commentary asks how that practice should be understood. Tang and Qian argue that the five-year plan (renamed "planning" in 2006) is a mature, institutionalised way for the Party to govern, which relays China's modernisation from one period to the next and embodies the strengths of the system. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts. It first sketches the history from the First Five-Year Plan (1953) to the 14th Five-Year Plan; it then lists three institutional advantages the plans display; finally it examines how the plans coordinate government, market and society. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on examples such as the consultation for the 14th Five-Year Plan. In the authors' periodisation, the first five plans built an independent and fairly complete industrial system, including the Third Front construction. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the plan came to cover social development and became more standardised, with mid-term evaluation and central–local coordination. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi has personally led the drafting groups and pushed for a unified planning system and a national development planning law. The three advantages they name are the Party's centralised and unified leadership, which they say avoids the mutual obstruction and policy reversals of Western multiparty systems; a people-first orientation, illustrated by seven symposiums and over a million online messages for the 14th plan; and the ability to concentrate resources on major undertakings. The plan is then presented as the expression of a proactive government, an effective market and a vibrant society: it gives the market a clear direction, remedies market and social failures, and channels public participation. The authors conclude that scientifically formulating and continuously implementing five-year plans produced the "two miracles" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability and a path of modernization with universal significance. They place this in the context of the coming 15th Five-Year Plan, stressing scientific, democratic and law-based decision-making, and building a high-standard socialist market economy and a unified national market. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the five-year plan as a governance institution ahead of the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Consolidating and expanding the systemic advantages of high-quality development in the 15th Five-Year Plan period 巩固扩大“十五五”时期高质量发展体系优势 Ma Yide Taking its cue from the Political Bureau meeting of 30 July 2025, this commentary asks how the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030) should be understood and what advantages China should build on. Ma Yide argues that the period is a decisive stage on the way to basically realising socialist modernization by 2035, and that consolidating and expanding China's systemic advantages is the key to high-quality development. The article has two parts. The first locates the period historically; the second examines four advantages named by the Political Bureau: the socialist system, the super-large market, the complete industrial system and abundant talent. Ma describes the period as a link between past and future, a time of strategic breakout amid global change, and a phase of deepening high-quality development. Citing per capita GDP of 95,749 yuan in 2024, the article says reaching about US$30,000 by 2035 requires average growth above 4.5 percent. It also cites weak global growth forecasts, rising R&D intensity and a middle-income group of over 400 million. On the advantages, Ma holds that the new national system will sharpen efforts on "chokepoint" technologies. Domestic demand and industrial upgrading are said to reinforce each other. Because human-capital spending is still below the OECD average, Ma proposes treating education, science, health and training as "broad human-capital investment" with a binding indicator. Ma concludes that consolidating these advantages will lay a solid foundation for basic modernization in 2035, and that the period requires understanding change accurately and responding to it actively. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line account of how Chinese policy scholars frame the priorities of the 15th Five-Year Plan period, including the statistics and the human-capital proposal.

The dialectical logic of institution-building in the new era 新时代制度建设的辩证逻辑 Xu Bin Xu Bin, writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, asks how institution-building should proceed as the Party pursues further comprehensive deepening of reform. Taking Xi Jinping's instruction to make institution-building the main thread of reform, Xu argues that this guidance rests on materialist dialectics. Three paired relationships must be handled together: top-level design and grassroots exploration, establishing the new and abolishing the old, and systematic advance and local breakthrough. The piece is a short commentary with three numbered sections, one for each pair. Each section follows the same pattern. It cites Xi Jinping's formulation, places the pair in the history of reform and opening up and in the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then sets out what the pair requires in practice. Examples include Xiaogang village's household contract system, Shenzhen, free trade pilot zones and supervision and judicial reform pilots. In the first pair, Xu reads the interaction of top-level design and grassroots exploration as a movement from the particular to the universal and back, an instance of the cycle of practice, knowledge and practice, and an application of the Party's mass line. Because reform has reached a "deep-water zone" and institutions are more mature, Xu says top-level design should now be strengthened. In the second pair, Xu cites Marx on dialectics and distinguishes "break first, then build", which suited the revolutionary period, from "build first, then break", which Xu calls the dominant method now that social structure is stable. Examples are revising laws, adjusting industrial structure and green transition. In the third pair, Xu says reform needs comprehensive coverage and a focus on the economic system, with the 20th Central Committee's Third Plenum (2024) stressing systems integration and priorities. Xu concludes that only by combining these three pairs can institution-building meet the demands of the times and promote social development, laying an institutional foundation for Chinese modernization. Xu calls for scientific top-level planning under centralised Party leadership alongside encouragement of replicable local experiments. Xu also calls for decisive removal of entrenched institutional defects together with careful construction of new ones, and for coordinated reform that targets bottlenecks and points of public grievance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present reform strategy through dialectical categories and Xi Jinping's formulations.

Carrying forward the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression to advance national strength and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 弘扬伟大抗战精神 奋进强国建设民族复兴伟业 Yan Xiaofeng Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this commentary asks what the wartime experience offers to the present drive to build a strong country. Yan Xiaofeng argues that understanding the war as a great national awakening, and carrying forward the great spirit of resistance, supplies the unity and self-reliance needed to advance national strength and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in five parts. It covers the Communist Party's role in the war; the three truths of 'justice, peace and the people will prevail'; the components of the resistance spirit; the creativity the war elicited; and China's contribution to the anti-fascist war and to modernization in the wider developing world. Each part pairs a wartime lesson with a present-day task, drawing on Mao Zedong's wartime writings and speeches by Xi Jinping. Yan contends that the Party was the mainstay of the war and the vanguard of the nation, through the anti-Japanese national united front, the protracted-war strategy and people's war. From this the author concludes that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of the Second Centenary Goal, and calls for the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds to be put into practice. The spirit of resistance is broken into patriotism and a consolidated sense of community of the Chinese nation, unyielding integrity, self-reliance, and firm belief in victory. Yan reads each as a guide for current struggles, including the need to take the nation's fate in its own hands and avoid copying foreign models. In the author's account, the war also showed creativity: with no precedent to follow, the Party devised united-front policy, military strategy and the rectification movement, just as Chinese modernization today must open its own path. On the international side, Yan describes China's resistance as the main Eastern theatre of the anti-fascist war that tied down the bulk of Japan's forces. The author presents China today as part of the Global South, neither imitating a 'Western model' nor asking others to copy a 'Chinese model', and as pursuing a community with a shared future for mankind and a new form of human civilisation. The author also says the aim of peaceful reunification of the country will not be accompanied by any pledge to renounce force over Taiwan. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's example of how the memory of the war is tied to Party leadership, Chinese modernization and the Global South in official discourse in 2025.

The property-rights logic of technological colonialism and its critique 技术殖民主义的产权逻辑及其批判 Yu Genxiong Yu Genxiong takes up the "technology cold war" fought over intellectual property, patents and copyright, and argues that Western capitalist states are using their technological advantage to practise a new form of colonialism. The article's thesis is that this technological colonialism rests on a property-rights logic: a fusion of technology-as-property and capital power. Yu contends that exposing and criticising this logic can check hegemonic attempts to crush other countries and support equal, mutually beneficial cooperation on technology rights. The article has three parts. The first traces colonialism from old military conquest through neo-colonialism to technological colonialism, which Yu says now appears as an independent form. The second reconstructs its logical structure from the concepts of technology property rights and capital power. The third criticises technology property and the conception of rights built on it, drawing mainly on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital and the 1844 manuscripts, with references to Lenin, Marcuse and Stirner. Yu identifies three features of technological colonialism: it is deeply concealed behind "voluntary" agreements and consumerist technology fetishism; it exerts systemic control over whole societies; and it is extremely oligarchic, producing technological impoverishment elsewhere. In the logic of this system, technology property is treated as an ideal, knowledge-based form of personal property, while capital power controls its monopoly, global spread and distribution. Yu answers that technology property is both a result and a precondition of labour, is the product of social rather than purely private labour, and unites the material and the ideal. On this reading, the claimed right to own it rests on three illusions: that property is simply a relation between people and things, that property rights are purely private, and that they are the exclusive advantage of certain nations, an idea Yu links to Eurocentrism and the theory of civilizational superiority. Yu concludes that technological colonialism damages colonised countries systemically, harms the capitalist countries themselves by deepening the opposition between technology and labour, and obstructs technological progress through monopoly, citing Lenin on monopoly prices. The article argues that the fruits of human civilization should be distributed on the basis of an equal and open conception of rights. Read the original if you want a Marxist property-theory critique of Western technology monopoly and the "technology cold war" from a Chinese academic perspective.

How the "Second Integration" resolves the "dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western": its ideological implications “第二个结合”破解“古今中西之争”的思想蕴涵 Yang Zengdong Dang Jiamei Since the Opium War, Chinese thought has been caught between "tradition" and "modernity" and between the "native" and the "foreign". Yang Zengdong and Dang Jiamei take up Xi Jinping's 2023 claim that China is now better placed than ever to resolve this "dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western". They argue that the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, supplies the resolution, because it overcomes both the opposition of tradition to modernity and the tension between native and foreign cultures. The article is organised in three parts. The first addresses the temporal dimension, the "ancient–modern" question, and treats the Second Integration's handling of tradition under four heads. The second addresses the spatial dimension, the "Chinese–Western" question, and the third draws practical implications for civilizational development and for Chinese modernization. The authors draw on Gadamer, Husserl, Habermas, Huntington and Marx's and Engels's remarks on tradition and history. In the first part, Yang and Dang contend that tradition and modernity are not absolute opposites, since modernity grew out of pre-modern roots and traditions are constantly dissolved and created anew. They say the Second Integration works in three steps: it sifts out negative elements by making "fine" traditional culture, not tradition in general, one party to the integration; it safeguards cultural subjectivity; and it "discovers" tradition through creative transformation and innovative development, with Marxism as the "soul". In the second part, they argue that Chinese intellectuals who either rejected tradition or opposed modernity both fell into Eurocentrism by equating modernization with Westernization. Using the notion of "inter-culturality", they claim that Marxism and Chinese culture share compatible values and that each chooses the other. The Second Integration therefore recognises difference and achieves a "heterogeneous fit" (yigou qihe), so Marxism can no longer be regarded as foreign. The authors conclude that the dispute has been genuinely resolved. They present this as showing that openness, mutual learning among civilizations and cultural confidence are the way forward. They add that Chinese modernization, rooted in both Marxism and Chinese culture, has the universal character to offer other countries Chinese wisdom and experience, whereas they describe Western modernization as claiming civilizational superiority and prizing material over human development. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory scholar draws on Gadamer, Habermas and Huntington to argue that the Second Integration overcomes the "ancient–modern, Chinese–Western" divide.

The Two Integrations as a "chemical reaction": the meaning of a metaphor “两个结合”作为“化学反应”的思想喻义 Wu Hongzheng Zhang Yang Xi Jinping has said that "integration" is not a "platter" or a simple "physical reaction" but a "chemical reaction" that produces a new, organically unified cultural life-form. Wu and Zhang take up the question of what this metaphor means for the Two Integrations (combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture). They argue that reading it correctly is the key to the core meaning of the concept, which they call original and emblematic of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article is organised in three parts, each drawing out one implication of the metaphor. The first treats the Two Integrations as life activity, tracing the idea from the historical blending of Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist thought through the founding of the Communist Party to successive stages of Sinicised Marxism. The second treats them as creative innovation that depends on cultural subjectivity. The third holds that the "reaction" must yield something new, and it surveys theories, paths and institutions said to result. Wu and Zhang's central move is an analogy with biology. Just as chemical reactions drive an organism's metabolism and produce new cells, the Two Integrations drive the "cultural life-form" of the Chinese nation and produce new ideas, theories and culture. From this the authors draw a contrast between creative combination and mechanical juxtaposition. Applying theory to reality by "cutting" or "fitting" it is, in their reading, the dogmatism seen in Wang Ming. The second integration likewise cannot stop at comparing points of agreement between Marxism and tradition. It must reinterpret classical sources in the context of the new era. The authors then list what they say the reaction has generated: Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They also point to the primary stage of socialism and the coexistence of multiple forms of ownership with public ownership. In their account, the "Chinese characteristics" of socialism come from traditional culture, for example the "great unity" idea, which they say was transformed into democratic centralism. They conclude that grasping the metaphor helps open new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and supports Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese theorists interpret Xi's metaphor philosophically and use it to define the creative character of the Two Integrations.

Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's statements on upholding the dominant position of Marxist political economy 学习贯彻习近平总书记关于坚持马克思主义政治经济学主体地位的论述 Wu Qingjun Gu Zhengyun Wu Qingjun and Gu Zhengyun ask why Western economics came to dominate Chinese economics after reform and opening up, and what should be done about it. They argue that this dominance resulted from uncritically learning Western market-economy theory while building the socialist market economy. In their view it should be corrected, so that Marxist political economy for the new era becomes the mainstream of Chinese economics teaching and research, with useful elements of Western economics absorbed in a subordinate role. The article first reviews how the standing of Western economics changed from 1979 to the present. It then sets out the harms of Western economics occupying the mainstream, relying heavily on quotations from Xi Jinping and one from Deng Xiaoping. A third section explains why Marxist political economy should hold that place. The last and longest section makes five proposals on scholarship, curriculum, journals, doctoral training and course design. The authors describe a shift from critical study of Western economics in the early 1980s to wholesale acceptance from the mid-1990s. They cite the predominance of Western economics in course numbers, teaching hours, postgraduate entrance exams and journal articles. Drawing on Xi, they claim that Western mainstream economics ignores social relations and class and cannot explain crises under capitalist private ownership. They also hold that copying it undermines the public-ownership base of the economy. They present hostile foreign forces as using economic theory to promote privatisation, a 'colour revolution' and 'peaceful evolution'. Marxist political economy, they say, offers a scientific and dialectical method and serves the socialist system, so socialist market-economy theory must be built on it. The authors propose that the Party and government interact constructively with Marxist scholars to build new-era Marxist political economy, which they define as Xi Jinping's economic thought plus innovative work by Marxist economists. They call for total teaching hours in Marxist political economy to slightly exceed those in Western economics. They also want at least half of the articles in a journal's special columns on Xi's economic thought and Marxist political economy, and one-third in general journals and university journals. Further proposals are to prioritise doctoral training in Marxist political economy, as in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences programme, and to integrate Xi's economic thought into Western economics courses. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar translates this ideological position into concrete institutional proposals for universities and journals.

Lenin's late view of culture and its implications for the inheritance and development of culture 列宁晚年文化观及其对文化传承发展的启示 Wang Yanlong Xu Kangzhou Wang and Xu ask what Lenin's late writings on culture contribute to socialist cultural construction, and what they offer China today. They argue that Lenin treated culture as a multidimensional category and gave the "cultural revolution" a central place in building socialism. In their view this approach, read alongside Xi Jinping's call for a "cultural mission" and for building a strong socialist culture, supplies a useful reference for China's own cultural work. The article has three parts. The first sets out Lenin's multidimensional account of culture: its broad and narrow senses, its class character, its economic role, and his critique of Narodism (populism). The second reconstructs the logic of his late cultural thinking in the New Economic Policy period, covering its methods, practical grounding, theoretical depth and overall framework. The third draws lessons for China under three headings: independence and self-reliance, openness and inclusiveness, and upholding fundamental principles while innovating. The authors argue that Lenin used historical materialism and the idea of society as a living organism to place culture within the whole of socialist construction. They report his claims that illiteracy rules out communism and that cooperatives and industrialisation require a cultural revolution. They also report his warnings that changing peasant habits takes generations and that haste in cultural matters is most harmful. On this reading, Lenin's "two cultures within each national culture" thesis ties culture to class, and he held that the proletariat, through its vanguard party, must lead cultural work. The authors turn these points into proposals for China. They call for Party leadership of cultural work and for cultural subjectivity, for reform of cultural institutions in the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and for socialist core values. They also propose spreading traditional culture abroad and using AI and digital technology for innovation, with the Two Integrations as the guide to "upholding fundamental principles". Read the original if you want a Chinese academic reading of Lenin's late cultural writings, or an example of how they are linked to current Chinese cultural policy.

Reflections on promoting the intensive (connotative) development of ideological and political theory courses 关于推动思想政治理论课建设内涵式发展的思考 Zhang Leisheng Long Xiaofei Zhang Leisheng and Long Xiaofei ask how the university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) can move from expansion to quality-focused, internally driven development. Taking Xi Jinping's call to promote the courses' development "in a way that upholds fundamental principles and breaks new ground", the authors argue that such development rests on the dialectical unity of adhering to orthodoxy and innovating. They add three supports: a better-integrated curriculum, a well-run "Big Ideological and Political Course", and a stronger teaching force. The article treats course development as a systemic project and is organised in four parts. It first sets out what adhering to fundamental principles and innovating mean, then turns to the curriculum system, the "Big Ideological and Political Course", and the quality of teachers. It draws on the history of the course schemes since 1949 (the 1952, 1961, 1985, 1998 and 2005 schemes) and on specific textbook and curriculum examples from senior secondary and undergraduate levels. On the first point, the authors say that adhering to fundamental principles means keeping the courses Marxist in theory, socialist in politics, focused on cultivating people in thought, and rule-bound as courses. Innovation is presented as an attitude, a cultural trait, an accumulated experience and a way of thinking. On the curriculum, they call for integration across six stages from primary school to doctorate, with national course standards "one for each stage, one for each textbook". They identify repetition, disconnection, gaps and inverted sequencing in current content, such as the order in which basic Marxist concepts appear. The "Big Ideological and Political Course", which extends teaching into society, must stay ideologically consistent with the classroom courses. The authors want its resources improved, Schools of Marxism to coordinate it, and entertainment-style or superficial formats avoided. For teachers, they stress the "six requirements" set by Xi and the need to pass tests of politics, professional competence and professional ethics. The authors propose reforms to selecting, training, refreshing, evaluating and rewarding teachers. These include an integrated bachelor-to-doctorate training route in Marxist theory, lifelong retraining, evaluation that does not favour research over teaching, and better pay and status. They conclude that integration, unity of principle with innovation, and a stable teaching force are the keys to higher course quality. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of current policy thinking on how ideological and political courses are structured, taught and staffed, including the problems the authors identify in curriculum design and teacher evaluation.

Paths to making practical teaching in university ideological and political theory courses more precise 增强高校思政课实践教学精准性的进路探究 Yang Yuan Yang Yuan takes up a problem in Chinese higher education: practical teaching in university ideological and political theory courses has grown in importance, yet the author says it still suffers from formalism, entertainment-style activities and superficiality. Yang argues that moving from "formal coverage" to "real effectiveness" requires a "precision mindset" (jingzhun siwei) and proposes three routes to it. The article opens by citing the January 2025 outline on building China into a leading education power (2024–2035), which calls for a larger share of practical teaching. The article is organised in three parts, each following the same pattern of a practical requirement, a diagnosed shortcoming and a proposed remedy. The parts deal with precise positioning of teaching philosophy, precise matching of teaching methods, and precise layout of teaching space. Yang draws on Marx's remark that social life is essentially practical, on speeches by Xi Jinping on students' subjectivity and on precision in online ideological education, and on the 2025 education outline. On teaching philosophy, Yang criticises uniform syllabi, standardised content and rigid schedules that leave students little room for independent learning. The author calls for a shift from teacher-centred "teaching" to student-centred "learning", likening precise "drip irrigation" to indiscriminate "flood irrigation". Content would be tailored to students' majors and to year-by-year concerns, such as adaptation in the first year and life choices in the fourth. On methods, Yang urges that traditional formats such as surveys, visits and volunteering be adjusted through inquiry-based, project-based and task-driven teaching. New formats would use big data and AI to reach differentiated audiences, so that students move from "being made to practise" to "wanting to practise". On space, Yang observes that practice is too often confined to offline venues and neglects online settings. The author proposes a "reality plus virtual" field that combines local practice bases (communities, villages, factories, museums) with 5G, VR, AI and 3D simulations and "smart classrooms". Yang concludes that precision in philosophy, methods and space together can convert the knowledge system of ideological and political courses into students' system of belief. The author presents this as a way to strengthen students' faith in Marxism, their confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics and their confidence in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The discussion stays at the level of principles and examples, with no empirical data or case studies. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese education researchers currently frame practical teaching in ideological and political courses, using the language of precision, student-centredness and virtual-reality technology.

On the difficulty of ideological and political education and its innovative development 论思想政治教育的艰难性及创新发展 Xi Houjun Xi Houjun takes up a question the author says has been neglected in the field of ideological and political education: why the work is so hard. After more than 40 years of disciplinary development, Xi argues, research has produced rich findings on its value, regularity and effectiveness, but not on its distinctive difficulty (jiannanxing). The article holds that this difficulty can be treated as an independent research topic, and that naming it is meant to sharpen the work's targeting and guiding power, not to excuse it. The article is built in three parts. The first explains why the difficulty deserves attention. It draws on scholars' remarks and on Xi Jinping's comments that students' sharp questions are hard to answer thoroughly. The second sets out four dimensions of difficulty: political, theoretical, practical and the audience. The third offers a development path through three capacities, and a short conclusion places the problem in the context of social transition. In Xi Houjun's account, the difficulty follows from the nature of the discipline. Politically, the work is openly political, so overcoming prejudice such as the label of "brainwashing" is hard. Theoretically, content that is abstract and systematic must be turned into vivid, connected reasoning and tied to reality, which taxes both teachers and students. Practically, education works as a "weapon of criticism" and cannot by itself abolish the social relations that produce mistaken ideas, a point supported by quotations from Marx and Engels. As for the audience, learners look for tangible interests, which ideological education supplies mainly as knowledge and spiritual guidance. To address these, Xi proposes strengthening scholarly capacity (sizheng xueshuli), the capacity to lead (yinlingli) and attractiveness (xiyinli). These are to be pursued through better argument, a more rigorous theoretical basis, attention to learners' circumstances, new media, team confidence and institutional support under the "big ideological and political education" concept. Xi concludes that today's difficulty is a composite product of social transformation and the rebuilding of value order. The article names globalised cultural currents, the expansion of capital logic, great-power contests over ideological discourse, reification consciousness and the erosion of educators' authority as pressures. It stresses that the four dimensions and three strategies are not exhaustive. It also calls for sustained Party and state support, public understanding and better practitioner skills. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of how scholars in the field frame the obstacles facing ideological and political education, and how they link them to current policy language.

Integrating Xi Jinping Thought on Culture into the teaching of the course "Ideology, Morality and the Rule of Law" Principles, content and implementation paths 习近平文化思想融入“思想道德与法治”课教学探究 Wang Shijing This article, from the field of ideological and political education, asks how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture can be brought into the first ideological and political theory course that university students take, "Ideology, Morality and the Rule of Law". Wang Shijing argues that the integration must not be a simple "stacking" of content. It should follow set principles, be tied to specific teaching content, and use new implementation methods suited to the digital era. The article has three parts. The first sets out three general principles. The second maps the content of Xi's cultural thought onto the chapters of the 2023 edition of the textbook. The third proposes implementation paths organised around three dimensions: learning, belief and teaching. It is aimed at Generation Z university students and at the teachers who instruct them. Wang's first move is to state the principles as three paired relationships: political guidance with scholarly inquiry, knowledge transmission with value formation, and theoretical indoctrination with practical enlightenment. Each pair is described as dialectically unified and not to be separated. The second move divides Xi's cultural thought into three theories, of spiritual independence, of value pursuit and of moral cultivation. Wang assigns these to chapters one and two, chapters three and four, and chapter five respectively. The Two Integrations, especially the second, are to be explained so that students grasp cultural confidence and the Party's theoretical creativity. Socialist core values and a view of civilisations based on equality and mutual learning are to be linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. The third move concerns method. Wang calls for case comparison, historical tracing, situational teaching, flipped classrooms, online platforms and volunteer service activities. Teachers are also to offer a scholarly critique of Western social trends and of what the article calls the "de-" tendencies (de-mainstreaming, de-historicising, de-Sinicising, de-ideologising and de-valuing). Wang concludes that the integration is both knowledge transmission and the shaping of belief, and that teachers must themselves hold firm convictions in order to pass them on. The goal is for students to move from theoretical recognition to firm belief in Marxism, socialism with Chinese characteristics and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Party theory is turned into chapter-by-chapter curriculum design and teaching method in Chinese university ideological courses.

How to understand Party spirit 怎样理解党性 Zhang Zhongjun This short commentary, published in Qiushi in 2025, asks what Party spirit (dangxing) is, how it should be understood, and why it matters. Zhang defines it as the Party's inherent essential attribute as embodied in each member: the Party's ideals, stance, purpose, discipline and work style made concrete in a member's thinking, speech and conduct. Citing Xi Jinping, Zhang argues that Party spirit is what determines what kind of Party member a person is, and that it must be forged throughout one's life. The article moves in three steps. It first traces the concept from Engels and Lenin, who tied it to class standpoint, through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and other earlier leaders, who stressed common nature, unity of action and discipline. It then explains why Party spirit matters today, setting out the international situation, the demands of long-term governance and the failings Zhang sees among some members and cadres. Finally it names three relationships to be handled in cultivating Party spirit. Zhang lists the criteria of strong Party spirit: firm ideals and convictions, loyalty to the Party, a people-centred standpoint, honesty and integrity, and self-discipline. Zhang says that in the new era, with the world undergoing what the article calls changes unseen in a century and the country advancing Chinese modernization, the Party needs members of strong Party spirit. Failings such as superstition, vanity projects, putting self above the organisation and corruption are traced mainly to internal causes, namely insufficient self-cultivation, rather than to weak supervision or the social environment alone. The three relationships are these. Party spirit and the people's character are said to be unified, so upholding one means upholding the other. Public and private interest is the "ruler" of Party spirit, and legitimate personal interests are acknowledged but distinguished from selfishness. Individuality must be subordinated to Party spirit, with Mao's distinction between creative and destructive individuality used to show that creative individuality is compatible with it. Zhang concludes that Party spirit is not innate and is never secured once and for all, but needs rigorous inner-Party political life and tests in hardship. The text offers the example of a village Party secretary who died saving villagers in the Beijing floods of July 2025. It links the argument to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and to the Party's long-term ruling position. Read the original if you want a concise, official Qiushi statement of how Party spirit is currently defined and what leading cadres are expected to do about it.

The great War of Resistance forged a spirit; the Party as mainstay built the victory 伟大抗战凝精神 中流砥柱铸辉煌 Liu Yue Published for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, this newspaper report by Liu Yue gathers the views of five Chinese historians. It argues that the Communist Party's role as the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the war and the Great Spirit of Resistance should be understood through solid historical evidence and carried forward today. The report has three parts. The first covers the meaning of the Party's mainstay role, from the 1931 Mukden Incident to the 1945 surrender. The second sets out the content and legacy of the Great Spirit of Resistance. The third reviews recent research trends and future directions. The scholars quoted come from the Central Party School, Zhejiang University, Nankai University, Beijing Normal University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The scholars credit the Party with a leading role in the war. They cite its early call for resistance, Mao Zedong's three-stage theory in On Protracted War, guerrilla warfare, the battlefield behind enemy lines and 19 anti-Japanese base areas. Wang Meiping cites Japanese archives, including a 1937 Home Ministry report, as showing that Japan itself saw the Party as central to resistance. Wang Binglin describes the Spirit of Resistance as patriotism, national integrity, heroism and conviction of victory. The scholars hold that this spirit and the Party's leadership reinforce each other. Hou Zhongjun sees scholarship moving from the question of who led to who played the decisive role. The report calls for interdisciplinary work, including digital and AI methods, and for more study of the Party's institutional innovation, governance and links to the global anti-fascist war. It also urges sharing international archives and answering Japanese right-wing efforts to downplay aggression. It concludes that the spirit and the Party's mainstay role still inspire the drive to build a strong country and achieve national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a compact view of how Chinese historians and the official press frame the Party's wartime role on the 80th anniversary.

Remembering history in order to better create the future 铭记历史是为了更好地开创未来 Commentator of China Social Sciences Today This commentary from China Social Sciences Today (3 September 2025) marks the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. It argues that upholding a correct view of the history of the Second World War is necessary for respecting historical truth, defending historical justice and safeguarding the postwar international order. It frames the commemorations, including China's military parade, as a responsibility towards the future as well as respect for the past. The piece opens with a quotation from Xi Jinping and a warning that Japanese right-wing forces, in the commentator's account, deny responsibility for aggression and refuse to admit guilt. It then proceeds through three stated needs, each introduced as a reason for a correct view of the war, and closes with a short statement on the present world situation. On historical truth, the commentator describes China's battlefield as the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war, the earliest, longest and costliest in national sacrifice. The article cites Chinese military and civilian casualties above 35 million and direct and indirect economic losses of 100 billion and 500 billion US dollars at 1937 prices. It credits the Communist Party of China with a pivotal role. On justice and order, it says China's victory saved world peace and gave rise to the great spirit of resistance. The commentator presents the war as the product of hegemonism and power politics, and calls for supporting the UN-centred system and a community with a shared future for mankind. The commentary concludes that, amid accelerating global change, humanity stands at a crossroads between unity and division, dialogue and confrontation, win-win and zero-sum outcomes. It calls for firm opposition to hegemonism, power politics, historical revisionism and the revival of fascism and militarism. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Chinese narrative around the 2025 anniversary and its link to current foreign-policy language.

Fully recognising China's major contribution to victory in the world anti-fascist war Interview with Richard Overy, historian of the Second World War at the University of Exeter 充分认识中国抗战对世界反法西斯战争胜利的重大贡献 Chen Mirong This is an interview, conducted by Chen Mirong for Chinese Social Sciences Today and published in September 2025, with Richard Overy, professor of history at the University of Exeter and a specialist on the Second World War. It begins from the Western textbook date of 1 September 1939 and from Overy's view, first set out in 1987, that the war began in 1931. The occasion is the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the world anti-fascist war. Chen's questions cover three topics: why Overy moved the start of the war to 1931 and how Western historians responded; why China's theatre is underrated in global literature; and which research areas and cooperation could correct the bias. Overy argues that the war should be seen as the result of three rising empires (Japan, Italy and Germany) expanding in China, Africa and central and eastern Europe.
