In his account, the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931 was the first armed challenge to the order dominated by Britain and France since 1919, and appeasement of Japan encouraged later aggression in Ethiopia, Austria and Czechoslovakia. He attributes under-recognition of China's role to the scarcity of detailed English-language studies, language barriers and the war's vast geography. In his view, Japan never defeated Chinese forces, and China's prolonged resistance blocked Japan's planned "new order" and tied down its main army. Overy suggests further work on the social history of the war, on how China sustained resistance with scarce weaponry, and on the Communist Party's leadership and the base areas, using archives. He notes that public perceptions remain tied to national narratives, so change will be slow. He hopes that translation of Chinese scholarship and open archives will lead to joint research. Read the original if you want a short statement, by a Western historian, of the case for dating the Second World War from 1931 and of the research gaps he sees on China's wartime role.

Reconstructing the discourse on the main Eastern theatre from a global-history perspective 重构全球史视域下东方主战场话语体系 Cai Sheng This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2025, asks how the Chinese theatre of the Second World War should be placed in global history. Cai Sheng argues that mainstream Western narratives treat it as secondary, and that a global-history approach, free of Western-centrism, shows it to be the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war. The article is organised around three dimensions: time, space and value. Each is set against a Western-centric account that Cai presents as fragmenting or belittling China's war of resistance. On time, Cai rejects 1939 as the start of the war and proposes the Mukden Incident of 1931, placing Japan's invasion alongside Italy's attack on Ethiopia and Germany's annexation of Austria. Cai divides the war into three phases: containing expansion (1931–1937), resisting alone (1937–1941) and allied cooperation (1941–1945). On space, the article contends that China tied down Japan's army, disrupted Axis coordination, supported the Allied 'Europe first' strategy, cooperated with other theatres through the Burma campaign and the Party-led base areas, and served as a rear base. On value, Cai credits the Chinese theatre with undermining colonial legitimacy, enabling China's role in founding the United Nations, and offering experience, including the Three-Thirds system and On Protracted War, to later independence movements. Cai calls for fixing 1931 as the start date, rebuilding the theatre's links with other fronts, and creating a multi-dimensional value assessment covering military, political and civilizational contributions. Cai presents this as both historical restoration and a resource for new international relations and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars argue for a 1931 start date and a central place for China in global anti-fascist history.

How the Tokyo Trial reshaped understandings of the international rule of law 东京审判重塑国际法治认知 Xu Chi Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the anti-fascist war in 2025, this newspaper commentary asks what the Tokyo Trial contributed to modern international law. Xu Chi argues that, together with the Nuremberg Trial, it ended an old order in which war was a sovereign right, and that its significance is still underrated because of Western-centred narratives. The author holds that recovering its meaning matters now, amid unilateralism and hegemonic politics. The piece is organised in four sections. The first sets the Tokyo Trial against the power-politics logic of traditional international law. The second treats its dismantling of the nineteenth-century discourse of "civilization". The third examines the Asian dimension: victim states, the judges Mei Ru'ao, Jaranilla and Pal, and regional legacies. The last turns to present-day relevance and calls for a pluralistic international rule of law. Xu contends that the two trials created the crimes against peace and crimes against humanity and established that launching aggressive war is itself a crime. In reply to critics who invoke nullum crimen sine lege, the author argues that the principle exists to restrain state abuse of criminal law, and that aggressive war is the sum of serious "natural crimes" whose criminality needs no written statute. Individual criminal responsibility, applied to figures such as Tojo Hideki, is said to have broken the myth of absolute state immunity. Xu also argues that the trial reversed the roles of China, the Philippines and India, once labelled "barbarous", and Japan, which had styled itself "civilized", thereby exposing the hierarchy of civilizations as hypocritical. Xu says Asian participation gave the trial its legitimacy. Chinese suffering since 1931 widened its jurisdictional frame, and Pal's dissent is quoted as criticising colonial double standards. The author links the trial to the 1951 San Francisco Treaty, Article 9 of Japan's constitution and later victims' lawsuits. The author calls for defending a UN-centred international system and an order based on international law, and for rejecting the use of law as an instrument of power politics, in line with a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese official-academic framing of the Tokyo Trial's legacy and its use in current arguments about international law.

Interdisciplinary methods boost research on ecological civilization 跨学科方法助推生态文明研究 Cao Kangkang Cao argues that ecological civilization is an inherently cross-disciplinary field, and that studying it requires interdisciplinary methods rather than a simple stacking of disciplinary knowledge. In Cao's view, genuine exchange between disciplines allows researchers to grasp the complexity of ecological civilization construction more comprehensively and to find new solutions. The short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2025, is organised around three groups of disciplines: natural sciences, social sciences and the humanities. For each group Cao sets out three ways it contributes to the study of ecological civilization. For the natural sciences, Cao lists theoretical support from ecology, environmental science and climatology; technological innovation such as geographic information systems for real-time monitoring; and science popularisation that builds public awareness. For the social sciences, the three contributions are social surveys and data collection, qualitative analysis and case studies, and quantitative analysis and modelling for forecasting. For the humanities, Cao points to historical methods such as environmental history, literary reading of ecological writing, and philosophical reflection on ecological ethics, including environmental justice and ecological responsibility. Cao concludes that interdisciplinary methods have significant application value and prospects, and calls for more exchange and cooperation among disciplines to support more scientific and rational environmental protection and sustainable development strategies. The piece is a stage result of a National Social Science Fund project on ecological philosophy in Capital and its manuscripts. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how Chinese scholars map the disciplinary landscape of ecological civilization research.

The historical standing of the Eastern main battlefield, seen through the international order 从国际秩序看东方主战场的历史地位 Chen Haiyi Chen Haiyi, writing in a Chinese Social Sciences Today commentary of September 2025, takes up the standing of the Chinese theatre in the Second World War. Western mainstream accounts date the war's start to Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939, and Chen says foreign scholarship has long neglected or ignored China's role. The article argues that the evolution of the international order, from the League of Nations to the United Nations, offers a useful lens for understanding China as the Eastern main battlefield of the world anti-fascist war. The piece follows three stages. It covers China's appeal to the League after the Mukden Incident of 1931, the long resistance after the full-scale invasion of 1937, and China's part in building the postwar order from 1942 to 1945. Chen first holds that the Chinese theatre was the earliest anti-fascist battlefield. After 1931 the League's appeasement, led by Britain and France, and American inaction left China to bear Japanese aggression largely alone. The article credits the Chinese Communist Party with organising anti-Japanese guerrilla forces in the Northeast. Second, Chen cites the League's own journal Headway, which in 1942 called China the first victim of the aggression that set off the war. Third, Chen argues that China's resistance tied down Japan. It forced Japan to give up the "northward advance", delayed the "southward advance" and, through the expedition to Burma, helped frustrate a Japanese–German link-up. This, the author says, made China one of the "Four Powers", a signatory of the Declaration by United Nations, a founding member of the UN and a permanent member of the Security Council. Chen concludes that the shift from the weak League to the more authoritative UN carries the lessons of China's war and the strategic contribution of the Eastern main battlefield. China moved from being an object of aid to a builder of the international order. Read the original if you want a short statement of the Chinese historiographical case for the war's earlier start and China's role in founding the UN.

Patriotic fervour and fighting spirit in New Fourth Army literature 新四军文学中的爱国热情与战斗精神 Huang Xiaojuan Huang Xiaojuan, in a short newspaper essay, asks what patriotic and martial spirit is carried by the literature of the New Fourth Army, a Communist-led anti-Japanese force in central China. The author argues that this literature is an inseparable part of War of Resistance literature. It joins feelings of attachment to homeland with a determination to fight to the end for national independence. The essay first defines New Fourth Army literature as one strand of the army's wider artistic activity, which also included music, art, drama and singing. Huang identifies three sources: works by writer-soldiers such as Qiu Dongping, Wu Qiang, Nie Gannu and Chen Yi; works from occupied and Nationalist-held areas that depict the army; and memoirs written after the army's designation was abolished in 1947. It then turns to geographical perception and to poetry. Huang first reads Chen Yi's 1939 reportage Spring in Jiangnan during the War of Resistance. Soldiers who at first cursed the Maoshan rainy season later see the landscape transformed, which the author takes as a sign of changing circumstances and of the trust between army and people. Huang then argues that a "complex of attachment to the land" fuelled resistance, and reads Chen Yi's classical poems and the poet Lu Mang's verse in this light. Wu Qiang's account of the actress Li Ming, killed by Japanese fire, is paired with Chen Yi's poem on her dying words, "revolution sheds blood, not tears". Huang concludes that the New Fourth Army's sacrifice and its literature, which fuses love of home with fighting spirit, make it an outstanding representative of red culture. The unyielding drive for national independence is presented as an important component of revolutionary and red culture. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how Chinese scholars frame New Fourth Army writing within red culture and War of Resistance literature.

The Communist Party of China's escape from the historical cycle of rise and fall: an interpretation from the mass-line view of history 中国共产党跳出历史周期率的群众史观阐释 Ma Qiuli Yang Kai The article asks how the Communist Party of China can escape the 'historical cycle' of rise and fall, the question Huang Yanpei put to Mao Zedong in Yan'an. It starts from Xi Jinping's formulation of two answers: popular supervision of government, and the Party's self-reform. Ma and Yang argue that existing research has not applied historical materialism consistently here. They propose to read the problem through the 'mass view of history', which treats the people as the creators of history. On this basis they claim that the Party can escape the cycle by combining popular supervision with self-reform. The article has three parts: why the cycle arises, why the Party must escape it, and how it can. The first part covers exploitative-class states and then relatively backward socialist states, using Marx, Engels, Lenin, Chinese classical sayings and the example of the Soviet Communist Party. The second part ties escaping the cycle to the Party's historical mission. The third part reviews popular supervision and self-reform from the Central Soviet Area to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the authors' account, the cycle is a recurring overthrow of regimes. Its root cause is a ruling group whose rule seriously diverges from the people's interests. Exploiting classes, backed by the ruling group, keep intensifying exploitation. The ruling group's own corruption also erodes popular interests, so overthrow cannot be avoided. In backward socialist countries, Ma and Yang say, material motives and the need to govern through a vanguard stratum create room for Party members to degenerate. Market economy and long years in power add further tests, and they cite a Siberian newspaper poll in which 85 per cent said the Soviet party represented its apparatus. The Party can avoid this, they argue, because as a proletarian party its interests match the people's. Popular supervision is said to be authentic, broad, targeted, self-motivated and useful for governance. Self-reform is said to be thorough, conscious and guided by Marxism. The authors conclude that the Party must stay in power for a long time, to develop the productive forces, suppress reactionary forces and carry out the long process of reaching communism. They call for continued popular supervision and self-reform. Specific measures are developing whole-process people's democracy, innovating forms of mass supervision, improving the Party's rules for self-reform and maintaining full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists use classical Marxist texts to ground Xi Jinping's 'two answers' in historical materialism.

Key focal points for advancing Party building in emerging fields 推进新兴领域党的建设的着力点 Tang Yalin Tang Yalin takes up the question of how the Party should build its organisation in the new economic, social and online spaces created by private-sector growth, the socialist market economy and new technology. Tang argues that new economic organisations, new social organisations and new forms of employment are both a key platform for Chinese modernization and a focal point for Party building in the new era. Strengthening Party building there is presented as the key to keeping the private economy on the right course, and as an indicator of the modernization of national governance capacity. The article opens with the policy trajectory: the Constitution's treatment of the non-public economy, the 2012 Central Committee General Office opinion on Party building in non-public enterprises, the 18th, 19th and 20th Party Congress reports, and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It also cites Xi Jinping's February 2025 remarks to private entrepreneurs and the Private Economy Promotion Law of April 2025. Tang then describes four features of emerging fields, and ends with three sets of measures. In Tang's analysis, workers in emerging fields such as delivery riders, ride-hailing drivers and couriers are mobile, dispersed and atomised, work intensively under platform algorithms, and generate labour tensions and social spillover effects in communities. Citing a national workforce survey, Tang notes that 84 million platform-type workers make up 21 per cent of a 402 million workforce. Tang calls for fusing community-based, regional and grid-based Party building, and for an organisational system that joins offline and online. Examples include online Party-building and consultation platforms and 24-hour service channels. Tang also proposes moving from comprehensive coverage to effective coverage of Party organisations and strengthening the Party-building responsibility system, with annual agenda-setting and evaluation. Tang concludes that Party organisations should combine "organisational work" with "work on people", attending to the material, cultural and emotional needs of new workers and the financing and development needs of new organisations. Online channels would build emotional connection with this aim. The stated goal is a pattern in which the Party, government and emerging-field actors move in the same direction. Read the original if you want a concise statement of current Party-building priorities for platform workers and private-sector organisations, with its policy references.

Achievements and experience of "Chinese governance" in the new era 新时代“中国之治”的成就及经验 Tian Kaiyuan Against what the author describes as a world of turbulence and accelerating change, in which "Chinese governance" contrasts sharply with "Western disorder", this article sets out the achievements and lessons of China's governance in the new era. Tian argues that "Chinese governance" is a concentrated summary of results achieved under Communist Party leadership in modernizing the national governance system and capacity. In the author's view it answers that question for China and offers Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to reforming global governance. The article has three parts. The first reviews achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012): institutional strengths, economic and social stability, national security, defence, emergency management, social governance, and the fusion of high-quality development with governance innovation. The second draws out main lessons. The third sets out directions for further modernizing governance. Tian supports the first part with figures, including a 2024 economy of 134.9 trillion yuan, R&D spending rising from 1 trillion yuan in 2012 to 3.6 trillion in 2024, and trade with Belt and Road Initiative partners above half of China's total. Tian's core claim is that institutional advantages are being converted into governance effectiveness, with "Chinese governance" resting on "Chinese institutions" and being in essence governance by the people. The lessons offered are: Party leadership as the fundamental political guarantee; a people-centred approach, including whole-process people's democracy and grassroots governance; balancing reform and governance; renewing the Party's mass line, for example through the "Fengqiao experience"; technology and digital platforms as an engine of governance; and combining independent innovation with mutual learning among civilizations. The author presents Chinese modernization as breaking the myth that modernization equals Westernization and as a new path for developing countries. For the future, Tian calls for upholding centralised Party leadership and balancing development with security. Other proposals are consolidating the domestic economy, relying on the people to build resilience against risk, fostering new growth drivers alongside the green transition, and pursuing high-standard opening up under the new development paradigm. The author also calls for greater influence in global governance, contributing public goods and a Chinese approach to improving the global system. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how the Chinese state presents its governance record and the lessons it draws from it, with the supporting statistics.

Understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization through the "six musts" 从“六个必须坚持”深刻把握习近平生态文明思想 Liu Ruyue This short commentary, published in the Party journal Dangjian in 2025, sets out how to grasp Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization through the "six musts" (six principles to be upheld). Liu presents the thought as an important part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and as the fundamental guide for ecological civilization building. Understanding it through the six principles, Liu argues, strengthens theoretical and practical commitment to that work. The article takes the six principles in turn: a people-first value stance, self-confidence and self-reliance, adherence to fundamental principles while innovating, a problem-oriented approach, a systems perspective, and a global outlook. Each section pairs the principle with examples from policy and from China's international role. On the people-first principle, Liu argues that a good ecological environment is described as the most inclusive public benefit and that the thought enriches the Marxist view of people's livelihood. On self-reliance, the article contends that green development goes beyond the Western path of polluting first and cleaning up later, and that China's carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals are firm while their pace and methods are for China to decide. On innovation, Liu holds that the idea that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets is a creative development of Marxist productive-forces theory, combined with traditional Chinese ecological wisdom. The systems principle is illustrated by the idea of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts as a community of life. Liu concludes that the thought is widely recognised internationally and that China has become an important participant, contributor and leader in global ecological civilization building, citing the Kunming-Montreal biodiversity framework and implementation of the Paris Agreement. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Party-affiliated scholars frame the core principles of Xi's ecological thought.

Raising the capacity to govern the cultural sphere under conditions of informatization 提升信息化条件下文化领域治理能力 Ouyang Xuemei Ouyang Xuemei's commentary takes up a remark by Xi Jinping at the 17th collective study session of the Politburo of the 20th Central Committee. Xi called for raising the capacity to govern the cultural sphere under conditions of informatization, so as to consolidate the Party's governing foundation and mass base ideologically, spiritually and culturally. Ouyang presents this as guidance for propaganda, ideological and cultural work in an age of digital, networked and intelligent technology, and argues that cultural governance capacity must be raised comprehensively. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the task matters. The second identifies four key areas of cultural governance online and cites a figure of 1.108 billion Chinese internet users by December 2024, an internet penetration rate of 78.6%. The third lists the measures needed, framed as study and implementation of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Ouyang gives three reasons for the task: it is required to modernize the national governance system and capacity; it is needed to consolidate the Party's governing and mass base amid more diverse and contested ideas; and it is needed to counter what the author calls Western digital hegemony, in which Western states use algorithms and big data to manipulate public opinion. The four areas are holding the leading role in online public opinion, building an online spiritual home around core socialist values and mainstream culture, using digital and intelligent tools to widen access to cultural services, and strengthening cultural soft power and international discourse power. The measures proposed are Party leadership over propaganda, ideology, media and the internet; an online mass line; multi-party governance; stronger cultural legislation; new technology for content management; and training of talent who combine cultural and technical skills. Ouyang concludes that Party leadership is the most fundamental guarantee of cultural governance, and that technology, law, market actors and ordinary internet users must be combined in one system. The author points to gaps in current law on data security, privacy, technology ethics and algorithmic fairness, and calls for faster legislation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated scholarship frames internet and cultural governance in 2025, together with the specific policy measures it lists.

The dialectical wisdom of advancing exchange and mutual learning among human civilizations 推进人类文明交流互鉴的辩证法智慧 Pang Lisheng Gong Yifei Pang Lisheng and Gong Yifei ask how different civilizations can coexist and develop in the modern world, taking as their starting point Xi Jinping's Global Civilization Initiative and its call for exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. They argue that this idea goes beyond the West-centred view of civilization and embodies a "practical dialectics" of civilizational exchange. In their account, it overcomes the understanding-bound (intellectual, non-dialectical) thinking behind Western civilizational theories. The article has three parts. The first argues that the age of world history requires a new view of civilization and criticises three Western positions: hegemonism, isolationism and the clash-of-civilizations thesis. The second analyses three dialectical relations in civilizational development. The third sets out four practical paths for promoting exchange and mutual learning. The authors read Fukuyama's "end of history" and Daniel Bell's "end of ideology" as hegemonist, Franz Boas's historical particularism as isolationist, and Samuel Huntington's thesis as a one-sided view that treats difference as inevitable conflict. They say all three rest on a metaphysical subject–object dualism. Against this they set three dialectical pairs: universality and particularity, individuality and worldliness (self and other), and necessity and contingency. Universality, they hold, appears only through particular civilizations, and the Western "universal values" are a particularity posing as universality. Cultural subjectivity, in their view, means autonomy of path and originality of theory, and is compatible with openness to other civilizations. Exchange and mutual learning are presented as a necessary tendency that works through contingent factors. For practice, the authors propose four steps: recognise the plurality of civilizations and respect their diversity; build a community with a shared future for mankind and foster understanding between peoples; promote the common values of all humanity (peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom); and take mutual learning as the path to shared progress. They acknowledge that exchange will meet ideological prejudice and narrow national interests. They conclude that it requires rejecting both dogmatic absolutism and the "bad infinity" of relativism. Read the original if you want a Marxist-philosophical, dialectics-based reading of Xi Jinping's civilizational thought and its critique of Fukuyama, Boas and Huntington.

Writing a new chapter for the times in Party conduct building on the new journey 书写好新征程党的作风建设的时代新篇 Sun Mingzeng Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, Sun Mingzeng asks how Party members and cadres should carry forward the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) at a critical point between the 14th and 15th Five-Year Plans. The article takes as its occasion the Politburo meeting of 25 April 2025 and Xi Jinping's May 2025 remarks in Henan on the study and education campaign on implementing the eight-point regulation. Sun's thesis is that conduct building is a permanent task that bears on the Party's survival and that it should provide strong support for Chinese modernization. The commentary has three parts. The first explains why conduct matters, drawing on theoretical, historical and practical logics. The second reviews what the author presents as achievements in conduct building since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out five practical directions for the new journey. Sun draws on statements by Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping and on the Party's historical record from the revolutionary years through reform and opening up. In the first part, Sun argues that conduct is the concrete expression of a party's nature, purpose and line, so a ruling party that tolerates unhealthy tendencies risks losing popular support and power. In the author's account, the Party's history shows that the further it keeps from such tendencies, the closer it stays to the masses. The second part credits Xi Jinping's discourse with deepening understanding of conduct as a question of Party spirit and of the Party's relationship with the people. It also credits the Party Central Committee with improving political ecology, issuing Party regulations on discipline, supervision and frugality, and curbing hedonism, extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism. The final part calls for strengthening ideological foundations, targeted rectification combined with positive example-setting, leading cadres setting an example, investigating and handling unhealthy conduct and corruption together, and consistently strict management. Sun concludes that conduct building has no end point and must become regular and long-term, with responsibility assigned at every level of the Party. Big-data tools should be used to trace leads on misconduct. The aim, in Sun's words, is to ensure the Party never changes in nature, colour or flavour. Read the original if you want a representative example of how a Party-school scholar frames the 2025 campaign on the eight-point regulation within the official discourse on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Raising the quality and effectiveness of universities' service to the integrated development of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation 提升高校服务科技创新和产业创新融合发展的质效 Ma Xiaojie Ma Xiaojie, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, asks how Chinese universities can better serve the fusion of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. Citing Xi Jinping, the article treats this fusion as the basic path to developing new quality productive forces. Ma argues that universities should build a mutually supporting system of talent cultivation, scientific innovation and the transfer of research results into practice, and should use their particular strengths to deepen that fusion. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the two kinds of innovation matter for new quality productive forces and high-quality development, and why universities are a key link, citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The second sets out the "three-legged" system in detail. The third offers five sets of practical measures: talent training, discipline layout, research supply, transfer of results, and Party building together with innovation culture. In Ma's account, each leg of the system is being reshaped. Talent training moves from supply-driven knowledge transmission to demand-driven innovation, cross-disciplinary study and open, ecosystem-style training. Research moves from the linear laboratory model to networked, "organised research" that links basic research, technology transfer and industrial conversion. Transfer of results should be both "reaching for the sky" (world-class work) and "standing on the ground" (real productive use), supported by proof-of-concept, pilot-scale testing, benefit-sharing and financing, and by collaboration among government, industry, universities, research institutes and users. Ma's concrete proposals include dual mentors from academia and industry, disciplines aligned with industrial clusters, joint laboratories with leading firms, university science parks, evaluation systems that reward technology transfer, and international scientific cooperation. Ma also calls for Party branches to be set up within disciplines, major platforms and transfer projects, for "AI+" curricula, and for promotion of the spirit of scientists and educators. The aim, Ma says, is to contribute momentum to new quality productive forces and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed picture of how a university Party leader frames higher education's role in national innovation policy and which institutional measures are recommended.

Developing new forms of employment requires stronger legal safeguards 发展新就业形态须强化法治保障 Office of the Social and Legal Affairs Committee of the National Committee of the CPPCC The article, a policy commentary reprinted from Qiushi, asks how China should support and regulate platform-based \"new forms of employment\" such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and online streamers. Its answer is that the central problem is institutional: rules have lagged behind practice, so the authors call for law-based means to support and regulate this work and so promote high-quality development. The text has three parts. It first presents new-form workers as an important force for development. It then sets out the main problems that need attention, and it closes with four sets of legal and institutional measures. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks praising these workers as \"hardworking little bees\", on survey figures and on a list of recent State Council and ministerial policy documents. The authors cite the 2023 national survey of the workforce, which counted about 402 million workers, of whom 84 million (21 per cent) are in new forms of employment, mostly under 35. They credit this work with expanding job options and incomes, including for low-income and rural migrant workers. They then identify three problems: algorithmic management by platforms with monopoly power and information advantages, weak rights protection (long hours, and pension and medical insurance coverage of only about 50 per cent for flexible workers), and labour, labour-contract, employment-promotion and dispute-mediation laws that predate the digital economy. They note that over 80,000 first-instance civil cases involving new forms of employment were concluded in 2024. The authors call for four measures. First, innovative regulation: platform duties on working hours and minimum pay, more transparent and fair algorithms, and coordinated enforcement. Second, rights protection through differentiated, category-specific policies, wider occupational injury insurance after the pilots begun in 2022, and legal aid. Third, care and services through Party building, training, trade-union consultation and participation in grassroots governance. Fourth, revision of the main labour laws, when conditions are ripe, to define the nature and criteria of new-form labour relations in national legislation. Read the original if you want an official Party-journal statement of how the Chinese state frames platform labour, with its figures and its proposed legislative agenda.

Some reflections on the development of artificial intelligence 关于人工智能发展的几点思考 Gou Husheng Writing in Qiushi in 2025, Gou Husheng asks how China should steer the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, especially large models. Gou argues that a Chinese path of AI development depends on handling four dialectical relationships: innovation and openness, development and security, government and market, and industrial application and social governance. The piece is framed by Xi Jinping's remarks on AI and by the State Council's recent opinion on implementing the "AI Plus" initiative. The commentary is short and built in four parts, one for each relationship. Each part states a principle, then illustrates it with examples from China, the United States and the European Union. Cases include DeepSeek, lidar and autonomous driving, the Eastern Data, Western Computing project, ChatGPT's funding history and International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates on jobs. On innovation, Gou holds that self-reliant innovation is the "root", without which openness becomes dependent development. Openness, through open-source frameworks, talent exchange and global governance, keeps China from becoming a technological island. Gou describes the US as using technological hegemony and the EU as relying on legislation, while China promotes "technology sharing and capacity building". On security, Gou lists risks such as deepfakes, data poisoning, algorithmic bias, academic junk and data-compliance problems, and says China should neither brake out of fear nor accelerate recklessly. On the state and the market, Gou says government fills gaps in basic research and coordinates infrastructure, data and standards, while the market drives commercialisation, which is the synergy expected under the socialist market economy. On governance, Gou cites price discrimination, "information cocoons" and job displacement, and calls AI a tool that augments human capabilities. Gou concludes that AI should serve high-quality development and social fairness while strengthening China's position in global competition. The author calls for a dynamic balance between efficiency and fairness, innovation and security, and commerce and people's livelihood. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior state-enterprise official presents official AI policy thinking in a Party journal.

Strengthening Global South studies to gather the mighty strength of the Global South 加强全球南方研究 汇聚全球南方磅礴力量 Xu Yanling This short commentary argues that China needs to strengthen research on the Global South. Xu Yanling starts from the claim that the century's great changes are accelerating, that the balance of global forces is shifting, and that the collective rise of the Global South is an irreversible historical trend. In Xu's view, better scholarship would raise the Global South's voice and influence, help gather its strength, and advance building a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the strategic significance of Global South studies. The second reviews existing Chinese work and identifies gaps in its depth and breadth. The third proposes how scholarship can contribute to unity among Global South states. Xu draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements at the BRICS+ dialogue, the Beijing summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation and elsewhere. Xu says such research serves three purposes: shared prosperity and a firmer basis for cooperation, exchange of experience on modernization, and world peace and multipolarity. On existing work, Xu credits Chinese scholars with progress on the concept of the Global South, on different countries' views of it, and on discourse and communication systems. Xu then finds the research lacking in depth. It centres on changes to international order and the community with a shared future, while other dimensions of the Global South's rise, the question of who represents it, and challenges such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence receive little systematic study. Research on Global South modernization is also described as lagging. Xu's recommendations are to balance the differences among Global South countries against what they share, mainly through area studies. Xu also calls for research on China's role, responsibilities and practical paths within the Global South, and for building the field's internal momentum. That means policy guidance, project-based research, field surveys, support for small-language specialists, Global South research centres and a government–think tank–university training mechanism. Xu presents this as providing theoretical reference for China's foreign policy toward the Global South. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics frame the research agenda on the Global South in line with official foreign-policy language.

Protect, pass on and spread the treasures of Chinese culture well 把中华文化瑰宝保护好、传承好、传播好 Xu Dongtao This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up Xi Jinping's instruction, given during a May 2025 visit to the Longmen Grottoes in Luoyang, that cultural treasures be protected, passed on and spread well. Xu presents the three tasks as a sequence: protection is the precondition, transmission gives the heritage its spirit, and dissemination extends the results of both. The author describes heritage as non-renewable and credits the Party leadership with historic achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The piece is organised in three sections matching the three verbs. It draws on examples such as the Longmen Research Institute's digital archive, the Dazu district's talent recruitment in Chongqing, Shanxi University's joint graduate school for grotto culture, Dunhuang VR, the game Black Myth: Wukong, and the Sanxingdui VR exhibition. On protection, Xu proposes combining technology, talent training and legal safeguards, and notes that the revised Cultural Relics Protection Law took effect on 1 March 2025. Xu adds that open questions remain, including ownership of digital heritage and rules for private capital. On transmission, the author says digital tools and "cultural heritage +" industrial brands can bring heritage into contemporary life. On dissemination, Xu argues that short video, livestreaming and immersive exhibitions have turned one-way communication by museums into two-way cultural co-creation. Xu concludes that such work expresses and strengthens cultural confidence and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author calls for strengthening protection, deepening transmission and widening dissemination so that heritage continues across generations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links heritage policy, digital technology and cultural industries to Xi Jinping's formulations.

How to view right-wing populism in the United States 怎么看美国右翼民粹主义 Wang Dong Wang Dong, a professor at Peking University's School of International Studies, asks how American right-wing populism should be understood. Writing in Qiushi in 2025, Wang argues that it is no accident but the product of intertwined economic, political and cultural factors, deliberately stoked by right-wing politicians. Wang describes a current that has become systematised, ideological and programmatic, with the "Make America Great Again" (MAGA) movement as its core driver. The commentary has three parts: the roots of this populism, its distinguishing features, and its practical effects at home and abroad. The roots are traced along economic, political and cultural lines. The features include an anti-elite narrative, extreme nationalism, social-media mobilisation and an economic-geographic split. The effects cover democratic institutions, trade, social cohesion and foreign policy. On causes, Wang points to the losses of industrial workers under neoliberal globalisation, citing Federal Reserve data for 2025 that the richest 0.1% of households hold 13.8% of national wealth and the bottom 50% hold 2.5%. Wang also points to representative democracy's failure, with money-driven politics, party polarisation and "veto politics". Wang gives most weight to identity and culture: since 2016, dispersed grievances have been recast as a "white working class versus immigrants" opposition, making populism the latest form of the long "culture war". Wang contrasts it with left-wing populism, which the author describes as rooted in urban and low-income groups on the coasts and aimed at redistribution. Right-wing populism, in Wang's account, rests on middle-class and Rust Belt white blue-collar voters and is more xenophobic and culturally conservative. Wang judges that, although populism partly responds to the failure of traditional governance, it poses a serious challenge to America's internal and external development and to the international order. Wang cites the 6 January Capitol attack, tariffs, social division and withdrawals from multilateral bodies and agreements as evidence. Wang concludes that while structural problems remain unresolved, populism will keep resurfacing, and that studying it helps in grasping US policy and the global situation amid "changes unseen in a century". Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-journal author frames US populism and its global consequences.

Vigorously pass on and promote Lingnan culture 大力传承弘扬岭南文化 Publicity Department of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee This commentary by the Guangdong provincial Party publicity department, published in Qiushi (2025, no. 17), asks how Guangdong can protect and pass on Lingnan culture, the regional culture of south China, while the province develops rapidly. It opens with Guangdong's Yingge dance and dragon-boat racing as signs of cultural confidence. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that diverse local traditions together make up Chinese civilisation, it presents Lingnan culture as an important branch of Chinese culture. Its answer is to preserve it, display it and pass it on. The piece is organised in three parts. The first, "Why Lingnan", traces the region's history from archaeological finds of 600,000 to 800,000 years ago through the Nanyue kingdom and the living city of Chaozhou. The second describes protection work, covering heritage sites, museums, archives and research. The third sets out the "new mission" of passing the culture on and out. In the article's account, Lingnan culture was formed from three sources: Central Plains culture brought by northern migrants, maritime civilisation, and local traditions. Its core is said to be patriotism and loyalty, shown in figures such as Lady Xian, the "Three Loyalists of Lingnan", Lin Zexu and Sun Yat-sen, and in a practical, hard-working popular character. On protection, the authors cite authentic restoration of the Nanfeng ancient kiln, the suspension of a Dongguan urban-renewal project to preserve a Ming-era wall, regulations to keep old city districts, and 412 registered museums. They report that the province allocated 193 million yuan to intangible heritage in 2019–2024 and set up special research projects. Transmission, the authors say, rests on four things: integration into daily life (the micro-renovation of Yongqingfang in Guangzhou), succession through new generations of heritage bearers, shaping popular sentiment through works such as the dance drama Yingge and red-culture events, and exchange and mutual learning. In the last of these, Guangdong acts as one of the "two important windows" on reform and opening up, using its overseas Chinese ties and the Qiaopi (remittance letter) archives to spread Chinese culture abroad. The authors conclude that Guangdong will contribute to a culturally strong country. Read the original if you want an official Party-media example of how a provincial leadership frames regional heritage policy within national cultural strategy.

Continuing to stimulate strong momentum for economic recovery and improvement 《求是》杂志评论员：持续激发经济回升向好的强劲动能 This commentary, issued under the byline of Qiushi magazine's commentator (issue 17, 2025), asks how China can sustain its economic recovery as traditional growth drivers weaken. For each area it names problems: core technologies controlled by others, weak investment mechanisms and talent shortages in emerging industries; data silos, algorithmic discrimination and infrastructure gaps in the digital economy; and firms that are unwilling, afraid or unable to transform among traditional industries, which make up over 80% of manufacturing. It stresses that new drivers should not be equated with new industries, and that traditional ones must not be discarded. The remedies it proposes include the new whole-nation system, long-term and "patient" capital, the "AI+" initiative, large-scale equipment renewal and support for digital transformation of small and medium firms. It also proposes better policies for healthcare, elderly care and education services. It concludes that China stands at a new starting point for high-quality development and will create fresh achievements. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary framed the 2025 economic outlook and policy priorities.

Integrating the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression into the building of the "Great Ideological and Political Course" 将伟大抗战精神融入“大思政课”建设 Peng Qinghong Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2025, Peng Qinghong asks how the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression can be built into the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke), the effort to extend ideological and political education beyond the classroom. For lasting effect, Peng proposes cooperation between Party committees, publicity departments, ideological and political teachers and subject teachers. Other proposals are partnerships with memorial halls and cemeteries, a supply of content covering sources, teaching resources and research, incentives for teachers and students, and guarantees of organisation, funding and staffing. The aim is to make integration institutionalised, standardised and long-term. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese university leaders are told to turn wartime commemoration into concrete ideological and political education practice.

The historic contribution of China's War of Resistance in a global perspective 全球视野下中国抗战的历史性贡献 Gao Guorong Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2025, Gao Guorong asks what place China's War of Resistance against Japan (1931–45) holds in the global anti-fascist war. The article argues that China shouldered the main Eastern theatre, was the decisive force in defeating Japanese fascism, made an indispensable contribution to the Allied victory in Europe, and inspired national liberation movements in colonial and semi-colonial countries. This is a short commentary in three parts, followed by a brief conclusion. The first part treats China's role in resisting and defeating Japan. The second examines China's support for the Allied strategy of "Europe first, Asia second". The third discusses the war's effect on China's own rejuvenation and on liberation movements elsewhere. The article closes with positive assessments from wartime leaders: Mao Zedong, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill. Gao holds that China began the world's anti-fascist war with the Mukden Incident of 1931, opened the first large-scale anti-fascist battlefield in Asia after 1937, and fought largely alone for over a decade because of Western appeasement. According to the article, the Chinese theatre consumed 4.55 million Japanese troops (killed, wounded, captured or surrendered), 70 per cent of Japan's total losses. Gao argues that by pinning down Japan's main army, China let the Soviet Union avoid a two-front war, because Japan's "northward" plan failed and Japan did not attack the USSR after Germany invaded it. The article adds that China supplied airfields, harbours, materiel and intelligence, and sent an expeditionary force to Burma in 1942. Gao concludes that victory in the war was a turning point in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation: the first complete victory over a foreign invader in modern times. The article says it brought the abolition of many unequal treaties, the recovery of territory including Taiwan, a higher international standing and a stronger Communist-led revolutionary force. It also claims the war exposed the falsehood of Japan's "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere" and heralded postwar decolonisation across Asia, Africa and Latin America. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese account of the war's global significance, including the wartime leaders' statements it cites.

Awakening good people's longing for peace and commitment to it New progress in research on evidence of Japan's crimes in China and its value 唤起善良的人们对和平的向往和坚守 Zhang Lianhong Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), Zhang Lianhong surveys recent research on evidence of Japanese military crimes in China. Zhang argues that research in China and abroad has reached unprecedented breadth and depth, and that its value lies in historical justice and in safeguarding peace. The piece has three parts. The first reviews new source material: archives, oral history and online databases. The second examines interdisciplinary and big-data methods. The third sets out the contemporary significance of this work. Cases include the Nanjing Massacre, bacteriological and chemical warfare, Unit 731, the "comfort women" system, indiscriminate bombing and forced labour. On sources, Zhang notes that Japan's government destroyed core wartime files before the war ended, leaving a shortage of first-hand documents. Zhang concludes that this research counters historical nihilism and Japanese right-wing denial, strengthens national spirit and collective memory, and carries a warning for the world about extreme nationalism and militarism. The article cites Chinese casualties of over 35 million and describes victory as a turning point in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It links remembering history to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a brief official-register overview of the new sources and methods in studies of Japanese war crimes in China, and of how they are framed in the 2025 anniversary commemoration.

Qiushi commentator: Dealing more effectively with prominent problems of formalism 《求是》杂志评论员：更加有效整治形式主义突出问题 This commentary by a Qiushi commentator (Qiushi, 2025 no. 17) takes up the Party's campaign against formalism and for easing burdens on grassroots officials. The historical turning point from deep crisis to great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation Commemorating the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression 中华民族从深重危机走向伟大复兴的历史转折点 Ju Li Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), Ju argues that the war was the turning point at which the Chinese nation moved from the deep crisis of the modern era towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article presents the war as the longest, largest and costliest national liberation struggle China had fought against foreign invasion, and as the first complete victory in such a struggle since 1840. It frames this with Xi Jinping's formulation of the victory as a historical turning point. The article is organised in three parts followed by a short conclusion. The first covers the awakening and unification of the nation, from the Japanese advances of 1914–1937 to the Party's call for resistance, the student movement of 9 December 1935 and mass mobilisation at home and overseas. The second asks why China won after a century of defeats, and answers through the Party's leadership, the people's army and the spirit of resistance. The third examines China's changed international standing, the abolition of unequal treaties and the road to the founding of New China. Ju concludes that the 105 years from 1840 to 1945 were a period of decline, and that the 80 years since have seen the Party found New China, carry out socialist construction and reform and opening up, and build a moderately prosperous society in all respects. In the author's view, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has now entered an irreversible historical process. Read the original if you want an example of how the official Party narrative, as carried in the journal Qiushi, presents the War of Resistance and links it to the present.

Drawing on the history of the War of Resistance against Japan to advance political army-building 镜鉴抗战历史 推进政治建军 Research Centre for Party History and Military History of the PLA, Academy of Military Sciences Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, this commentary from the PLA Academy of Military Sciences' Party and military history research centre asks how the Party's wartime experience can guide political army-building (zhengzhi jianjun) today. The authors argue that during the war the Party deepened its understanding of how to build the army politically, and that this understanding enabled a weaker force to defeat a stronger one. They hold that it remains essential as world, national, Party and military conditions change. The article is organised around four relationships that, in the authors' account, the war revealed: military affairs and politics, the Party and the army, the army and the people, and spirit and matter. Each section first recounts wartime evidence, drawing on Mao Zedong's On Protracted War, Party documents, the Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army, and the 1944 report by Tan Zheng. It then sets out what the authors call tasks for the new journey, citing Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). First, the authors argue that war is politics by other means. They say the Party's judgement that the Sino-Japanese contradiction had become principal let it forge the united front and reorganise the Red Army, so that the army's tasks followed national tasks. Second, the authors cite the Party's insistence on its own command of the gun: the army's wartime bodies, such as military-political committees, and the stance that Communists should fight for the Party's, the people's and the nation's military power. They draw from this the need to uphold absolute Party leadership, the chairman responsibility system of the Central Military Commission and the Two Establishes. Third, they present the people as the basis of victory and call for stronger military–civilian unity, combat-readiness and integration of new quality productive forces with new quality combat capability. Fourth, they stress fighting spirit, citing about 35 million Chinese casualties and calling for ideological education, realistic training and a martial culture. The authors conclude that upholding political army-building is the fundamental reason the people's army moves from victory to victory. They call for absolute Party leadership, the army's original purpose, and a will to fight and win, so that the army becomes purer, more glorious and more reliable. In their view this will support Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's military research establishment links wartime history to current army-building doctrine and to Xi Jinping's military thought.

Drawing strength for advancing from the great spirit of resistance to Japanese aggression 从伟大抗战精神中汲取奋进力量 Liu Guopu Writing for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), Liu Guopu examines Xi Jinping's series of statements on the war. The commentary argues that these statements are more than a historical summary. In Liu's account they apply historical materialism creatively, serve as a weapon against historical nihilism, supply spiritual momentum for Chinese modernization, and offer Chinese historical wisdom for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece is organised into four sections, one for each of these claims. It moves from the theoretical and methodological character of Xi's statements to their polemical function, then to their domestic role in national rejuvenation, and finally to their international significance for global governance and the writing of Second World War history. It closes with a short call to deepen the scholarly study of these statements. Liu makes three main moves. First, working within the Two Integrations, Xi's account is said to treat the "people" as the deepest source of victory. It folds the frontline and behind-the-lines battlefields, the base-area governments, the rear-area salvation movements, and overseas Chinese and foreign friends into a framework of "people's war". It also places the war in both the long span of Chinese civilisation and the global anti-fascist struggle, which Liu says rebuts Eurocentric readings and narrow nationalism. Second, against historical nihilism, which Liu says fragments and distorts the record, the statements stress the Communist Party's role as the mainstay of resistance and China as the main Eastern theatre. Third, the great spirit of resistance (patriotism, indomitable integrity, heroism, confidence in victory) is presented as matching the values needed to face today's risks, such as technological bottlenecks and unbalanced development. Liu concludes that Xi's statements unite historical, theoretical and practical logic, and that the war's lessons ("justice, peace and the people will prevail") bear on peace and development today. As examples of putting them into practice, Liu cites the National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre victims and commemorations of victory. Liu calls for turning historical memory into drive for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary in 2025 presents Xi Jinping's war narrative as theory, as ideological defence and as international message.

Drawing wisdom and strength for the road ahead from the great victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 从中国人民抗日战争伟大胜利中汲取不断前行的智慧和力量 Party History and Literature Research Institute of the CPC Central Committee Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commemorative article asks what lessons the victory holds for the present. Gathering the strength to remember history and strive for national rejuvenation Qiushi editorial on the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan 《求是》杂志编辑部：凝聚起铭记历史、矢志复兴的强大力量 Qiushi editorial department Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression, this editorial from Qiushi (no. 17, 2025) argues that remembering the war is a basis for building the future. Improving the study system of the theoretical study groups of Party committees 完善理论学习中心组学习制度 Dou Qingshen This short commentary, published in Study Times on 29 August 2025, asks how the study system of the theoretical study groups (中心组) of Party committees and Party leadership groups can be improved. The article opens with a brief history, from the study system and the General Study Committee set up in Yan'an, through reform and opening up, to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The spirit of the War of Resistance: a powerful spiritual force enabling the Chinese nation to overcome all difficulties and obstacles 抗战精神：中华民族战胜一切艰难险阻的强大精神动力 Guo Fang This short commentary, published in Study Times on 29 August 2025, takes up the 'great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression' (the spirit of the War of Resistance). The article first sketches the war as a just struggle against Japanese fascism, from the Mukden Incident of 1931 to the full-scale invasion of 1937. Guo presents the four components as a structure: patriotism, in the sense that everyone is responsible for the nation's fate, is the core; national integrity is its expression in character; heroism that fears no violence is its outward quality; and belief in ultimate victory is its inner driving force. In the account, the Communist Party's early declarations and its call for a united front shaped national mobilisation, while both Nationalist and Communist forces fought, on the frontal and enemy-rear battlefields respectively. Examples include Yang Jingyu, the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain and the battles of Pingxingguan, Taierzhuang and the Hundred Regiments Offensive. Guo credits Mao Zedong's three-stage prediction of the war with sustaining confidence. The author concludes that this conviction let a poorly equipped people defeat a stronger enemy, which the piece calls a miracle in the history of warfare. Its framing is the continuing relevance of the spirit to national rejuvenation. The world significance of the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression Perceptions and writings from Western scholarship 中国人民抗日战争的世界意义 Liu Bensen Writing in a Chinese social science newspaper in August 2025, Liu Bensen asks how Western scholarship now assesses the world significance of China's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression. Liu argues that Western historians increasingly recognise the Chinese theatre as the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war. In this reading, China's resistance made a decisive contribution to Allied victory and to the post-war order, and offered a model for national liberation movements elsewhere. The article is a short commentary built around works by mainly American and British historians and journalists, set against Xi Jinping's statement that the war was from the start of great significance for saving human civilisation and defending world peace. It has three sections: the Chinese theatre as historical starting point and strategic fulcrum of the anti-fascist war; China's role in forming the anti-fascist alliance and reshaping the post-war order; and the war as a strategic example for national liberation movements. In the first section, Liu cites scholars such as Andrew Buchanan and Ted Uldricks, who treat the 1931 Mukden Incident as the beginning of the Second World War, and Ronald Spector and Rana Mitter, who argue that China tied down the main Japanese army forces and supported Allied operations. In the second, Liu draws on Mitter, Uldricks and Graham Peck's contemporaries such as Stilwell to present the Shanghai battle, the Yunnan–Burma campaigns and China's part in founding the United Nations as shaping the war's course and the post-war order. In the third, Liu cites Spector, Max Boot, Mark Selden and others on people's war, guerrilla warfare, protracted war, the united front and base-area building as models taken up by revolutionaries abroad. Liu concludes that the war made a decisive contribution to victory and restored China's standing as a major power. Remembering it and deepening understanding of its world significance, Liu says, serves the common values of humankind and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a quick guide to the Western-language scholarship that Chinese academics cite to support the claim of the war's global significance.

Upholding the "Two Integrations" to build a culturally strong nation 坚持“两个结合”建设文化强国 Liu Shuijing This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 29 August 2025, asks how China should build a culturally strong nation. Liu Shuijing argues that the Two Integrations are the necessary path for developing socialism with Chinese characteristics on the foundation of more than five thousand years of Chinese civilization, and an important route for shouldering the cultural mission and building a culturally strong nation. The piece draws on articles in volume five of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, which stress that the key to Chinese characteristics lies in the Two Integrations. Liu presents the Two Integrations, especially the "second integration", as the Party's summary of the experience of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as a grasp of the laws of Chinese civilization's development. In Liu's account, since 2012 they have produced theoretical innovation, a fundamental turn in the ideological sphere, creative transformation of traditional culture, the Global Civilization Initiative, and a marked rise in cultural soft power. Liu calls for two things. First, hold to the "soul" of Marxism, uphold its guiding position in ideology, and maintain the Party's cultural leadership, combining positive publicity with struggle over public opinion. Second, carry forward the roots of fine traditional culture, build cultural confidence and subjectivity, deepen cultural reform, and draw on foreign achievements to create new work. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links the Two Integrations to cultural policy.

Raising the level of social security governance in the digital age 提升数字时代社会安全治理水平 Wang Hongmei This commentary from Guangming Daily asks how China should manage the social security risks that accompany the digital economy. Wang argues that these risks are more complex and more prone to cascading effects than traditional ones. The author holds that they call for coordinated, systematic governance, in line with policy documents such as the Overall Plan for Building a Digital China and the 2025 key tasks for the digital economy. The piece is organised around four tasks: building mechanisms to identify social security problems precisely, improving the governance system, building smart management platforms, and responding better to public concerns and expectations. On identification, Wang calls for real-time monitoring and early warning around data rights, circulation and income distribution. Wang also wants attention to market volatility and to emerging gaps between groups and regions, balancing an efficient market with an effective government. On governance, Wang urges a holistic outlook of prevention first, cross-departmental coordination, and more detailed rules building on the Cybersecurity Law and Data Security Law, with stricter penalties for personal data leaks. The platform proposal envisions a closed-loop process of sensing, analysis, pushing alerts, response and linkage, with digital twins used to forecast risks such as supply-chain disruption. Finally, Wang proposes using both traditional and digital channels to gauge public opinion, providing tailored services for the elderly, and strengthening social assistance. The author also wants workers in new forms of employment brought into social insurance. Wang presents this as a way to protect workers' rights and promote social fairness and harmony. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official-leaning Chinese scholarship frames digital-era risk governance and its policy priorities.

The "fire-bearer" of Marxist truth The scholarly path of the economist Guo Dali 马克思主义真理的“播火者” Zhao Zhenhua Marking the 120th anniversary of Guo Dali's birth, Zhao Zhenhua presents the economist and translator as a "fire-bearer" of Marxist truth and a founder of Marxist political economy in China. The article, published in Study Times in August 2025, argues that Guo's significance lies in three things: the first complete Chinese translation of Capital, his work in explaining and popularising it, and his use of its stance, viewpoint and method on China's real problems. Zhao first sketches five stages in the Chinese reception of Capital, from early introductions by Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu to Chen Qixiu's partial translation of 1930, and on to the complete translation Guo made with Wang Yanan (published in 1938), Guo's later revisions, and the later revisions by the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. The article then turns to Guo's lectures at the Central Party School, published in 1978 as On Marx's Capital, and to his pre-1949 writings on industry, science and the countryside. Zhao makes four claims for the 1938 translation: it spread Marxism's light in China, it laid the basis for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, it supported the study of Western economic thought through Guo's other translations, and it left a spiritual legacy of perseverance, rigour and self-sacrifice. On Guo's exposition, Zhao stresses his concision (about 160,000 characters on three volumes), his reading of passages within the whole work (for example on why Marx's preface omits distribution relations), and his use of comparison, philological checking and links to socialist construction. On China's problems, Zhao reports Guo's arguments that China must leap past the handicraft and manufacturing stages to machine industry, that this requires socialist production relations, that science must be both applied and built up, and that consumer and defence industries cannot be separated. Zhao concludes that, on the road to a modern socialist great country, Guo's pursuit of truth, rigorous scholarship and indifference to fame should be inherited and promoted. Zhao also finds present relevance in Guo's views on agriculture and on the joint development of defence and civilian industry, which he links to today's military-civilian integration. Read the original if you want a Party School economist's tribute to Guo Dali, with details on the translation history of Capital in China and on Guo's own economic writings.

The historical contribution of the Counter-Japanese Military and Political University to the Anti-Japanese National United Front 抗大在抗日民族统一战线中的历史贡献 Gao Shiying This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks what the Counter-Japanese Military and Political University (Kangda) contributed to the Anti-Japanese National United Front. Gao argues that Kangda, the Communist Party's highest military academy, trained more than 100,000 military and political cadres and helped consolidate and develop the Front. The author also calls it a "revolutionary furnace" in modern Chinese educational history. The article opens with the background of the national crisis after the 1931 Mukden Incident and the founding of the school in 1936 as the Chinese Anti-Japanese Red Army University. It then examines three areas of contribution: spreading anti-Japanese theory, safeguarding national unity in the war of resistance, and taking part in actual combat. Examples include course content, songs, student recruitment, responses to Kuomintang actions and named battles. On theory, Gao says Kangda made the Party's united front policy and Mao Zedong's writings compulsory study, and sent students out as propaganda and work teams, including performance troupes whose shows reportedly even persuaded a garrison of puppet troops to defect. On unity, the author stresses that students came from different provinces, ethnic groups and parties, including Kuomintang members, and that the school did not require belief in communism. After the Southern Anhui Incident (1941) and the 1943 troop concentration against the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, Kangda staff and students are said to have denounced the Kuomintang and prepared defences. On combat, Gao cites the anti-"mopping-up" campaign, the Hundred Regiments Offensive and other engagements. Gao concludes that Kangda put the Party's united front line into practice, took it deep among the people, and contributed to national independence and popular liberation. The author quotes Mao Zedong's view that Kangda was the most revolutionary and progressive military school. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholarship presents Kangda's wartime role in united front work.

The Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression opened the main Eastern theatre of the World Anti-Fascist War 中国人民抗日战争开辟世界反法西斯战争东方主战场 Li Ying Cao Ziyang Yang Kai Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), the authors take up Xi Jinping's formulation that the Chinese people's resistance to Japan opened the main Eastern theatre of the anti-fascist war. They argue that China began fighting earliest, fought longest, tied down the main body of Japan's forces and played a decisive part in Japan's final defeat. The article is a commentary in a Party newspaper, organised in three parts. The first sets out the chronology and the sacrifices China suffered. The second examines how the Chinese theatre constrained Japan and supported the Allies in Europe and the Pacific. The third deals with the Communist Party's role and the distinctive character of the Chinese front. It draws on statements by Xi, Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Roosevelt, Stalin, Churchill and Japanese sources. The authors define the anti-fascist war by its nature, so any war against fascist aggression counts. On this basis, they say, the war began with the Mukden Incident of 1931, 14 years of fighting, against under six years for other Allies. They argue Japanese plans for 'northward' or 'southward' expansion both required control of China. They say China's resistance pinned down most of Japan's army and so prevented an attack on the Soviet Union and a Japanese–German link-up in the Middle East. It also bought the Allies time and supported their 'Europe first' strategy. They credit the Communist Party as the 'mainstay' of national resistance: it led the united front, opened the rear-area fronts behind enemy lines and rejected capitulation. They cite figures of over 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties and over 1.5 million Japanese troops killed. The authors warn that judging China's front by Western-theatre standards, such as the absence of decisive set-piece battles, is shallow. They say the Sino-Japanese war was a protracted war of attrition between a weak country and a strong one. They conclude that the victory raised China's international standing and helped build the postwar order centred on the United Nations. They call for a 'correct view of the history of the Second World War' and opposition to distortions of it and to hegemonism. Read the original if you want to see how Party historians present China's role in the anti-fascist war in the 80th-anniversary commemoration.

Commemorating victory is to win forever 纪念胜利是为了永远胜利 Xiang Xianbiao Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this newspaper commentary asks what the commemoration is for. Xiang's answer is that remembering the victory serves to draw confidence and strength for the future and to secure the great victory of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The piece is short and moves from the war to present-day tasks. It recalls the 14 years of resistance and its results, then takes up three themes in turn: the role of the Communist Party, the spirit of the resistance, and the war's international significance and its lessons for peace and national strength. It closes with a 1945 editorial from Liberation Daily. Xiang argues that the Party was the "mainstay" of the victory, because it raised the banner of the anti-Japanese national united front and its members stood on the front line. From this the author concludes that the Party's overall leadership must be upheld and strengthened today, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. The author also credits the war with producing a great spirit of resistance, made up of patriotism, national integrity, heroism and conviction of victory, which people are urged to carry into the present. Citing China's role as the main Eastern theatre of the anti-fascist war, Xiang draws four lessons: uphold Party leadership, remember that backwardness invites attack, strengthen national defence awareness, and keep to peaceful development. Xiang concludes that the Chinese people will defend and extend the hard-won fruits of victory and advance the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
