Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media link the memory of the War of Resistance to Party leadership and current political goals.

Advancing high-quality development and high-efficacy governance in universities in tandem 协同推进高校高质量发展与高效能治理 He Xiuchao This commentary in Guangming Daily asks how Chinese universities should handle two tasks together: high-quality development and high-efficacy governance. He argues that the two are mutually reinforcing, like the two wheels of a cart or two wings of a bird. Pursuing them jointly, in He's view, is both an internal requirement of comprehensive reform of higher education in the new era and a driving force for building a strong education nation. The piece has four sections. It first sets out what high-quality development means for universities, then the basic logic of effective governance, then the interaction between the two, and finally practical steps to promote that interaction. Throughout, He draws on Xi Jinping's statements on talent cultivation, first-class universities, systems thinking and education digitalisation. In He's account, high-quality development is a combined leap in talent training, disciplinary innovation, international competitiveness and social service, not one indicator. Talent training must join moral education with innovation. Disciplines should be built around basic, applied and interdisciplinary strengths, linked to industry and to key technologies. Governance, for He, must shift from fragmentation to integration, with cross-disciplinary platforms, joint goals for knowledge creation and training, and digital tools for decision-making. The two reinforce each other: development goals set the direction of governance, while governance supplies institutional foundations and resources. This forms what the author calls a virtuous circle. He proposes three measures. The first is to build consensus on public values through digital democratic consultation, outside advisory bodies and cultural education. The second is to improve coordinated governance by devolving some powers to second-tier colleges, setting up cross-departmental platforms and holding joint meetings. The third is to deepen digital applications through unified data platforms, digital skills training and rules on data security, privacy and algorithmic transparency. He says these should keep technology serving moral education and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse links Xi Jinping's high-quality development agenda to university management and digitalisation.

Advancing the deep integration of Party building and business in free trade port parks 推进自贸港园区党建与业务深度融合 Liu Libo Wang Famin This commentary, published in Study Times on 27 August 2025, asks how Party building and business operations can be integrated in the industrial parks of the Hainan Free Trade Port. Liu and Wang argue that three principles resolve the problem of Party work and business running as "two skins": guidance by belief, linkage of interests and integration of sentiment. They hold that the three reinforce one another and supply lasting momentum for high-quality development. The piece is organised in three sections, one per principle. Each pairs a short statement of rationale with examples of mechanisms said to be in use in the parks, and the authors present these as existing practice rather than proposals. On belief, the authors say Party organisations in the parks put political building first and make studying the Party's theory a priority. Tools include a "first agenda item" study system, "Party member shock teams" and a three-tier organisational structure, so that an "organisation chain" drives the industry, talent and innovation chains. On interests, citing Marx on the link between ideas and interests, they describe Party-run channels for firms' demands, such as service officers, government–business forums and Party-member responsibility zones, plus Party-guided benefit-sharing among government, enterprises and research bodies. On sentiment, they describe a 24-hour service hotline, pairing of Party members with foreign and skilled staff, cultural events and the parks' response to Typhoon Yagi ("Moji"), which they say turned emotional identification into practical capacity. The authors conclude that belief supplies direction, interests supply drive and sentiment supplies cohesion, so that Party leadership is built into enterprise services throughout. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party media describe grassroots Party-building practice in Hainan's free trade port parks.

"Demeanour: People and events in the Party's work-style building" published Xinhua notice of a new book from the Party History and Literature Research Institute 《风范——党的作风建设中的人与事》出版发行 This is a short Xinhua news notice, dated 26 August 2025, announcing the publication of a book titled Fengfan (roughly "Demeanour"): People and Events in the Party's Work-Style Building. The notice reports that the Central Institute of Party History and Literature compiled the volume to put into practice the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, promote the Party's glorious traditions and fine work style, and use Party history as a guide to the present. According to the notice, the book was issued by the CPC History Press. It collects 83 articles totalling 170,000 characters, and it tells short stories to convey larger principles. The stories feature veteran revolutionaries, heroes and model figures. The notice says these stories illustrate several fine habits: linking theory with practice, staying close to the masses, criticism and self-criticism, hard work and plain living, and seeking truth and being pragmatic. It presents the book's central message as the view that the Party's work style is the Party's image, that it bears on whether the people support the Party, and that it determines the success or failure of the Party's and the country's cause. The notice concludes that the book will help Party members, cadres and the public study the history of work-style building. It says the book should help carry good traditions into the new journey and promote good work style in the new era. It adds that new results in work-style building will give strong backing to the advance of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official media present Party-history publications and the way they link work-style building to current Party goals.

Upholding and promoting the correct view of the history of the Second World War 坚持和弘扬正确二战史观 Yu Pei Writing in Guangming Daily on the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, Yu Pei argues that the results of the Second World War cannot be challenged. The commentary holds that upholding a "correct view of the history of the Second World War" is an urgent task at a time of rapid global change, and that it protects historical justice. Yu sets out four components of this view, then explains why it counts as correct and what defending it requires. The piece is a short commentary that ends with a call for international cooperation. The four components are as follows. The war was a deliberate war of aggression launched by Germany, Italy and Japan, and appeasement by Britain and France hastened its arrival. Victory resulted from the joint struggle of an anti-fascist alliance of states with different social systems. China and the Soviet Union, as the main Asian and European theatres, made decisive contributions, and Yu credits the Communist Party of China with leading national resistance. Documents such as the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation, the founding of the United Nations, and the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals shaped the postwar order. Yu calls the view "correct" because it respects historical facts, laws and dialectics and reflects the interests of the great majority. The author describes historical revisionism, historical nihilism, neo-Nazism and militarist revival as betrayals of historical justice. Yu concludes that defending the historical truth means guarding the bottom line of human civilization. Citing Xi Jinping, Yu says humanity stands at a crossroads between confrontation and dialogue. The author calls on peoples to draw on this view, to uphold a fair multipolar order and to help build a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary framed Second World War memory in the 80th anniversary year.

The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the War of Resistance against Japan 中国共产党是抗日战争的中流砥柱 Liu Zhipeng This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily shortly before the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, asks what role the Communist Party of China played in that war. Liu Zhipeng argues that through political leadership, strategic planning, exemplary military action and moral integrity, the Party played an irreplaceable part and was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the war. The article moves through five areas: the Party's early call for resistance and the anti-Japanese national united front; its line of total resistance and the protracted-war strategy; the opening of the battlefield behind enemy lines; the spirit of hard struggle; and the sacrifice and national integrity of Party members. Evidence includes the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, the 1935 August First Declaration, the Wayaobao meeting, the Xi'an Incident, the reorganisation of the Red Army into the Eighth Route Army and New Fourth Army, and Mao Zedong's 1938 On Protracted War. Liu contrasts the Party's people's war, which relied on mobilising the masses, setting up democratic governments and reducing rent and interest behind enemy lines, with what the article calls the Nationalist Party's one-sided resistance that relied on government and army. Liu credits guerrilla tactics and the behind-the-lines front with forcing Japan to fight on two fronts, and says that this front became the main battlefield in the stage of strategic stalemate. Liu also cites Yan'an's production campaign and the deaths of commanders such as Zuo Quan and Yang Jingyu as proof of the Party's spirit. Liu concludes that the Chinese people and history chose the Party through this war, and that grasping this conclusion matters today for promoting the resistance spirit, uniting the nation and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party narrative of the anti-Japanese war's leading role is currently presented in the mainstream press.

Passing on and carrying forward the great spirit of the War of Resistance in the new era 在新时代传承和弘扬伟大抗战精神 Xiao Chunbai Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (2025), and prompted by the film Dead To Rights (Nanjing zhaoxiangguan), this newspaper commentary asks how the great spirit of the War of Resistance should be passed on today. Xiao argues that this spirit remains an inexhaustible source of strength for the new era and must be handed down from generation to generation. The article first explains what is "great" about the spirit: its sacrifice and character, its cultural content, its historical thinking and the leadership of the Communist Party. It then turns to practical measures, grouped under two headings: basic infrastructure for transmission and institutional safeguards. Xiao contends that the spirit combines traditional and revolutionary culture and so supports cultural confidence. It also holds historical lessons, such as that those who love war perish and those who forget war are endangered, which the author says help the country reach modernization. Xiao stresses the Party's role in uniting a fragmented society, building the anti-Japanese national united front and the "three-thirds" system of government, and coordinating fronts and forms of warfare. The practical proposals include using biotechnology and artificial intelligence to protect and reconstruct sites, building digital archives of letters and oral history, and bringing the spirit into textbooks and classrooms. They also include regulating film and literature so that history is neither deified, belittled nor stigmatised, and strengthening legal protection for martyrs and sites. Xiao concludes that, as China enters a critical period for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the Party's leading role and the spirit of resistance must be carried forward so that the country can pass the tests of the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholarship in 2025 links wartime memory to cultural confidence, Party leadership and heritage and education policy.

Research on the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression must uphold a correct view of history 深入开展中国人民抗日战争研究必须坚持正确历史观 Xu Zhimin Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this commentary from the People's Daily argues that deeper research on the war must rest on a correct view of history. Xu Zhimin takes up Xi Jinping's call to "let history speak" and contends that distortions of the war's history are still current both abroad and at home. Xu first sets out what a correct view of history means: historical materialism, a Party-led and people-centred reading, and a perspective that places the war in world history. The piece then identifies three targets of rebuttal: historical nihilism inside China, the views of Japanese right-wing figures and some politicians, and what Xu calls the political and academic bias of Western scholars. It closes with the practical tasks of future research. Xu argues that the Chinese Communist Party led the resistance as its "mainstay". As evidence against Nationalist-era rumours, Xu cites the 1932 Declaration of War on Japan and the 1933 offer of a joint-fighting agreement. Xu also states that Communist-led forces fought 58–75 per cent of Japanese troops in China during the stalemate stage and cites the Hundred Regiments Offensive. Xu criticises Japanese denial of the Nanjing Massacre and glorification of aggression, and Western accounts that treat the Chinese theatre as subordinate. Xu adds that more Western scholars are now revising these views in light of Chinese-supplied sources. Xu concludes that research remains insufficient relative to the war's significance. Xu calls for fuller overall and thematic studies, stronger collection of archives at home and abroad with critical scrutiny of selectively opened foreign records, and unified study of the 14-year war from 1931. Xu also calls for continued international exchange, citing joint Chinese–Japanese–Korean histories and the Sino-Japanese Joint History Research. Read the original if you want an official-line statement of how Chinese historians are directed to frame the war, historical nihilism and international scholarship.

Shaping a new pattern of fostering virtue and cultivating people through the "Big Ideological and Political Course" 以“大思政课”塑造立德树人新格局 Lü Chao Lü Chao, writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, asks how the "Big Ideological and Political Course" can be used to give new shape to the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating people. The article takes its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks to education-sector political advisers during the 2025 "Two Sessions", which called for joining the ideological and political "small classroom" with the "big classroom" of society. Lü's thesis is that this model is the main channel for strengthening ideological guidance and for supplying talent for Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the "Big Ideological and Political Course" matters. The second discusses regularities that should be understood more deeply: focusing on moulding minds, emphasising practical education, and strengthening systems thinking. The third proposes new paths for building the course, covering problem-solving, methods and evaluation. Lü cites the 453 national practice-teaching bases and examples from Peking University, Renmin University of China and the National University of Defense Technology. Lü argues that the course is needed for three reasons. It carries out the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating people amid complex ideological struggle, rapid advances in the internet and artificial intelligence, and young people who prefer personalised and diverse experiences. It also advances the content-based development of ideological and political courses, which the author says currently suffer from weak links between theory and reality and from narrow methods. Finally, it consolidates the ideological and political foundations of young students. In practice, Lü calls for knowledge teaching to be joined to value guidance, explicit to implicit education, and scientific to humanistic training. Lü also wants more practical teaching, online and offline integration, and overall planning of classrooms, teaching staff and platforms. Lü proposes integrating ideological and political education across primary, secondary and tertiary levels, which the author says now repeat content and work in isolation. Schools, families and society should be linked in one system. Teaching should use case-based, inquiry-based and experiential methods, practice bases and digital platforms such as "Study Power" (Xuexi Qiangguo). Lü also wants a "community of evaluation" of teachers, students and parents, with indicators of knowing, believing and acting, and with AI used to support assessment. Read the original if you want a Party-school-style account of how current policy on university ideological and political education is being operationalised, including its AI and practice-base elements.

High-quality ideological and political education leading the cultivation of top-notch innovative talent in universities: a practical path 高质量思想政治教育引领高校拔尖创新人才培养的实践进路 Qiu Yanghai Qiu Yanghai asks how universities can use high-quality ideological and political education to guide the cultivation of top-notch innovative talent. Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to raise the quality of home-grown talent training, the article argues that such talent is strategically vital: it is, in Qiu's account, the fundamental way to answer the "Needham question" and the "Qian Xuesen question", and it underpins breakthroughs in core technologies and the development of new quality productive forces. Qiu's thesis is that political and ideological quality is a cornerstone of such talent's success, so universities need a dedicated, well-resourced ideological and political education system for them. The article is a policy-oriented piece organised in three parts. The first concerns top-level design, the second the construction of an education system, and the third the safeguarding institutions. Each part sets out numbered measures, with examples such as leadership groups, joint training with schools and enterprises, differentiated curricula and individualised evaluation. Qiu cites a 2020 Ministry of Education guideline on integrating ideological and political content into courses and one survey figure on student stress. On top-level design, Qiu proposes a "special zone" for these students built on three mechanisms: a special plan embedded in the university's medium- and long-term and five-year plans, a coordination mechanism, and a feedback mechanism. The coordination mechanism includes a leadership group headed by senior university leaders, a community of universities, local governments, research bodies, enterprises and families, and integration across primary, secondary and tertiary stages. The feedback mechanism uses big data and generative AI to track students and graduates. On the system itself, Qiu calls for high-grade ideological and political theory courses with leading teachers, for ideological and political content woven into specialist courses and research training, and for daily education led by well-qualified counsellors. On safeguards, Qiu stresses resource orientation (small classes, eminent research supervisors, Party branches in research platforms led by "dual leaders"), targeted environmental and psychological support, and inclusive evaluation. That evaluation would place more weight on political assessment, process and the long term, for instance by extending review cycles from one year to two. Qiu concludes that these measures would help such students form correct political views, a sense of the larger picture and clear judgement of right and wrong, so that universities can supply strategic talent for Chinese modernization. Political evaluation is presented as the safeguard of direction, while process-based and long-cycle assessment protects exploratory research. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Chinese higher-education policy writing proposes to combine ideological and political education with elite talent training.

Digital-intelligence empowerment of Party governance modernization through the lens of complex adaptive systems theory Systemic logic and practical path 复杂适应系统理论视阈下数智赋能政党治理现代化的系统逻辑与实践进路 Tang Qingpeng Writing in a Party-affiliated journal, Tang Qingpeng asks how digital-intelligence technologies (big data, cloud computing, AI) can enable the modernization of the Communist Party's own governance, which the article treats as a precondition of Chinese modernization. Tang argues that existing research, especially abroad, concentrates on party competition and elections and misses the organisational and systemic side. The article proposes complex adaptive systems (CAS) theory as a remedy: the Party is a complex system that adapts non-linearly to its technological environment, so empowerment is neither automatic nor always beneficial. The article has four parts. It first states the problem and reviews the literature, then derives a logic of digital-intelligence empowerment from the three CAS properties of adaptability, openness and emergence. Next it identifies three practical difficulties, each tied to one property, and finally sets out four paths of response. Tang draws on Marx's remark that new productive forces change modes of production and social relations, and cites figures such as 99.185 million Party members and 5.176 million primary organisations at the end of 2023. In the first half, Tang reads empowerment as a process in which the Party actively uses technology, not merely receives it. It operates on Party governance methods, the governance system and governance capacity. Its emergent values are stronger governing capacity, a technical means of tackling the "unique problems of a large party", and greater ability to lead the modernization of national governance. The second half turns to risks, described as "empowerment" turning into "binding". Tang names a rejection effect (skills gaps, uneven digitalisation, "information islands", copycat platforms), security risks (cyberattacks, data leaks) and digital formalism, such as rigid quantitative indicators and points rankings on the Xuexi Qiangguo platform. Tang proposes four paths: an internet-minded, forward-looking outlook; digital channels that serve the Party–masses relationship under the mass line; institutional arrangements for data integration and data security; and digital literacy and talent training for Party members and cadres. The article presents CAS theory as moving beyond technological determinism toward active, systemic practice. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school scholarship applies systems theory to Party building, including its frank list of implementation problems such as formalism.

Writing a new chapter for our times in Party conduct building on the new journey 书写好新征程党的作风建设的时代新篇 Sun Mingzeng Writing in 2025, Sun Mingzeng takes up the question of why improving the Party's conduct (zuofeng) remains essential and how it should be advanced on the "new journey". The article is tied to the study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the central Eight-point Regulation, which a Politburo meeting in April 2025 and Xi Jinping's inspection in Henan in May called for. Sun argues that conduct-building is a lasting theme of Party building and a safeguard for Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why conduct matters to a Marxist party, drawing on theoretical, historical and practical logics. The second reviews achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third proposes four or five lines of work for the period spanning the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan and the drafting of the 15th. Sun's central claim is that conduct expresses a party's nature, purpose, programme and line, so neglecting it risks losing popular support and power. The article traces this through the Party's history, from wartime traditions and rectification campaigns to reform-era campaigns. It credits the post-2012 period with deeper understanding of conduct as a question of Party spirit and of the Party's relationship with the people, a better political ecology, a fuller system of Party regulations, and a purer Party style. For the future, Sun calls for stronger ideological and political foundations through study. Other measures are targeted rectification combined with the promotion of good practice, and leading cadres setting an example. Sun also urges treating unhealthy work styles and corruption together, using big data to find leads, and building a closed loop of investigation, governance, supervision and education. Sun concludes that conduct-building has no end point and calls for "genuine and strict, long-term and strict" management, with responsibility assigned at every level of Party organisation. The aim, in the article's terms, is to ensure the Party never changes in nature, colour or flavour and to secure Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official 2025 framing of the Eight-point Regulation campaign and the policy measures it emphasises.

Opening a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times through the Two Integrations 在“两个结合”中开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Tang Aijun This short commentary, a study note on Volume V of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is a major theoretical innovation produced by the Two Integrations. Tang Aijun contends that the Thought has opened a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has two parts. The first presents the Two Integrations as the fundamental route for developing Marxism in China. The second treats the Thought as the model case of applying both integrations, drawing on passages from Volume V. Tang says the first integration, with China's concrete realities, addresses theory and practice and aims to overcome dogmatism and subjectivism. The second, with excellent traditional Chinese culture, addresses the fusion of two cultures and aims to overcome cultural and historical nihilism. According to the author, the Thought answers the great questions of the new era, such as what socialism to uphold and how to build a modern socialist country. It also draws on traditional culture, and Tang gives the theory of exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations as an example. In this account, the theory combines Marxist views of civilizational exchange with the Chinese ideal of harmony without uniformity. Tang concludes that the Two Integrations sum up the Party's historical experience and deepen its understanding of how theory is innovated. The author names a key task for studying Volume V: grasping the original contributions and principled theoretical results that the Thought has made to upholding and developing Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party-school reading of the Two Integrations and of Volume V's place in it.

Hegel's "science" and Capital 黑格尔的“科学”与《资本论》 Zhang Donghui Liu Xiaolan Zhang and Liu ask what it means to call Capital a "science" and argue that, seen through Hegel's concept of Wissenschaft, disputes over which discipline the work belongs to are largely pointless. Their thesis is that Capital inherits Hegel's demand for systematic, self-grounded science but transcends his idealism through historical materialism. This short newspaper piece first sets out Hegel's concept of science, then turns to Marx's own remarks on Hegel in the Afterword to the second edition of Capital. It closes by contrasting Marx's treatment of capital with Hegel's Absolute, and by criticising the systematic dialectic school represented by Arthur. On the authors' account, Hegel's science requires two features: a systematic totality ("the truth is the whole") and grasp of the Absolute. Empirical knowledge such as Newtonian mechanics or history falls short of this, in his view. Capital's circuit, M–C–M′, and capital's ability to create the organs it lacks resemble the self-returning movement of Absolute spirit, but the authors present this as Marx's expository convenience, as in his "coquetting" with Hegelian idiom. Reading Capital through Hegel's logic alone breaks down when capital meets its limits and crises, since for Marx "the real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself". Marx therefore sublates Hegel's logical narrative into a historical one: logic becomes a retrospective summary of history, not its essence. The authors conclude that Capital meets Hegel's demands for systematicity while overcoming his idealism, making it a genuine science of the capitalist mode of production and offering methodological insight into contemporary capitalism. Read the original if you want a brief statement of the Hegel–Marx methodological relationship and a critique of systematic dialectic readings of Capital.

Strengthening the Party's overall leadership over urban work 加强党对城市工作的全面领导 Fu Gaosheng Taking its cue from the recent Central Urban Work Conference, which stated that building modern people's cities requires stronger Party leadership over urban work, this commentary argues that the Party's overall leadership is the fundamental guarantee of good urban work. Fu Gaosheng draws on Xi Jinping's statements on urban work to set out the theoretical and practical significance of this principle. The piece, published in Guangming Daily on 26 August 2025, has three parts. It first reviews how Party leadership has served urban work since 1949, then explains how leadership should be exercised, and finally turns to the capabilities required of Party members and cadres. Fu says Party leadership gives urban work its direction, notably through the "people's city" concept advanced since the 18th Party Congress (2012), its planning (five-year plans and five central urban work conferences) and its organisational base, including four-tier Party organisations from street to building. Leadership, Fu argues, must be comprehensive, systematic and holistic: it should cover the whole life cycle of a city, treat urban work as a subsystem linked to rural work and to economic, political, cultural, social and ecological construction, and build a governance community of Party committees, government, market and residents in line with whole-process people's democracy. Fu calls on cadres to study Xi's urban-work remarks, to adopt a correct view of performance that makes benefiting the people the greatest achievement rather than focusing only on GDP or large projects, and to improve their work style with patience and consistent plans across changes of leadership. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary links urban governance to Party leadership.

Strengthening the conscious commitment of Party and government organs to leading by example in living a frugal life 增强党政机关带头过紧日子的自觉性 Ruan Dongbiao This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 26 August 2025, responds to the revised Regulations on Practising Economy and Opposing Waste in Party and Government Organs, recently issued by the CPC Central Committee and the State Council. Ruan Dongbiao argues that the revision tightens the institutional bolts on Party and government organs' pledge to "live a tight life", and that officials must take up frugality as a matter of conscious commitment. The piece moves from cultural tradition to Party history, then to current practice. It cites classical sayings on thrift, recalls the Jinggangshan and Yan'an periods and figures such as Jiao Yulu and Gu Wenchang, and then turns to the revised rules on funding, travel, official receptions, vehicles, meetings, office space and resource saving. Ruan contends that thrift is a Party tradition and follows from the Party's purpose: the Party and government live frugally so that ordinary people can live well. Savings are said to free funds for innovation, rural revitalisation, ecology, education and health, and to support high-quality development; examples are Daliangshan in Sichuan and Dingxi in Gansu, where 15 rural water projects reportedly reached 1.22 million people. The author also credits an anti-waste rules system with curbing "corruption on wheels" and wasteful banqueting, and describes layered supervision and big-data platforms, including a national asset-sharing platform that, according to the article, saved over 40 million yuan. Ruan concludes that thrift must be built into the work style of Party and government organs through stricter oversight and risk control, and that the revision shows Party conduct-building is always "on the road". Party members and officials are urged to be self-disciplined and to set an example in hardship. Read the original if you want a brief example of official Party-media framing of the 2025 anti-waste regulations and the central rules on conduct.

The method of abstraction in Marx's critique of political economy 马克思政治经济学批判中的抽象法 Pan Bin This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how Marx's method of abstraction gives his critique of political economy its scientific character. Pan Bin argues that abstraction is the core of that method. It allowed Capital to see through the appearances of capitalism and to uncover its inner mechanisms and laws. The article first distinguishes Marx's method of research from his method of presentation, citing the Afterword to the second German edition of Capital (1873). It then explains the movement "from the concrete to the abstract" and "from the abstract to the concrete", and ends with a sketch of how Capital applies the two movements in sequence. Pan reads "from the concrete to the abstract" as the research method. It starts from real, complex capitalist reality and extracts the simplest categories, such as commodity, value, labour-power and "labour in general". These categories, unlike those of classical economics, are not treated as natural and eternal. The presentation method then runs "from the abstract to the concrete": categories such as money, capital, profit and rent are derived step by step, each containing the earlier determinations plus new ones. Abstraction is the mediating bridge between the "real concrete" and the "concrete in thought". The author holds that only a thought process containing both movements counts as a genuine process of abstraction. Pan concludes that Capital forms a complete "concrete–abstract–concrete" progression. It begins with the commodity as the "economic cell" and moves through value, surplus-value production, capital circulation and the tendency of the profit rate to fall. In the author's account this reconstructs the whole picture of capitalist operation and shows its inherent crisis tendencies and historical limits. Read the original if you want a compact introduction to the research/presentation distinction and the logic of abstraction in Capital as Chinese philosophy scholars present it.

The core of the problem of work style is the relationship between the Party and the people 作风问题核心是党同人民群众的关系问题 Huang Xianghuai Huang Xianghuai, a deputy director and researcher at the Central Party School, offers a study commentary on Xi Jinping's statement that "the core of the problem of work style is the relationship between the Party and the people". The author argues that this relationship is the fundamental question for a Marxist proletarian party. Serving the people wholeheartedly, in Huang's reading, must show itself in the Party's governance, its line and policies, and also in its work style. The piece appeared in the journal Dangjian (Party Building) in 2025. The article has three parts. The first looks at Party work-style building through the Party–people relationship. The second argues that building a good work style means keeping flesh-and-blood ties with the people. The third proposes that the ability to do mass work be used as a yardstick of how effective work-style building has been. In the first part, Huang says work-style building must start from and return to serving the people. The people should take part in it and judge it, and its results must be tangible to them. The Party is urged to combine "establishing" good practices with "breaking" bad ones, citing Xi's line that the people are the "examiners". In the second part Huang sets out three requirements for cadres: shed bureaucratic airs, stay grounded by going to the grass roots, and cultivate moral rectitude through Party-spirit training. Huang warns that dropping official airs without getting close to the people can leave hidden or mutated formalism and bureaucratism. In the third part, Huang calls on Party members and cadres to improve three abilities. These are investigation and research, which Huang says must not become formalistic; guiding public opinion in the internet age, where "Four Dimensions of Misconduct" problems can be amplified online; and innovation in work methods, given the more diverse interests of different social groups. Huang concludes that cadres should be seen by the public to have both a good style and strong capability. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party Building presents Xi Jinping's work-style discourse to cadres and links it to the mass line.

The concepts, interrelations and integrity of Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline 党性党风党纪的概念内涵、相互关系及整体性探析 Ding Junping Zhang Ang Ding and Zhang take up a formula from Xi Jinping: Party spirit (dangxing), Party style (dangfeng) and Party discipline (dangji) form an organic whole, in which Party spirit is the foundation, Party style the manifestation and Party discipline the safeguard. The authors argue that existing scholarship either treats only two of the three concepts or studies all three without tracing their historical evolution. They also find that the "trinity" has not been explained systematically in theoretical terms. They aim to fill both gaps and to support the requirement to "grasp all three together". The article has three parts. The first defines each concept, drawing on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping and later leaders, and on the main scholarly positions. The second traces how the Chinese Communist Party's understanding of the three evolved, from the Red Army's disciplinary rules and the Yan'an rectification campaign through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then gives a theoretical account of their relationship. The third part explains why the three form a whole. The core argument is that each element has its own role. Party spirit is the "inner basis" that determines the nature of style and discipline, and the driving force of the Party's self-reform. Party style is a "barometer" and "window" through which otherwise hard-to-measure Party spirit and the strictness of discipline become visible. It also has relative independence: good style nourishes Party spirit and discipline, while bad style erodes them. Party discipline is the "anchor" that supplies institutional constraint and educational guidance, yet it depends in turn on strong Party spirit and sound style. The authors say the whole is shown in four features: coordinated governing subjects, complementary functions, shared goals and a common method. The shared goals include solving the problems unique to a large party and keeping the Party advanced and pure. The common method rests on putting the people first, problem orientation and systems thinking. The authors conclude that the three must be tackled together, and that implementing this still faces difficulties. They name three open questions: how to coordinate the governing subjects effectively, how to cover all elements and avoid a "barrel effect", and how to build workable mechanisms. They propose integrating the three across organisation, mechanisms, process and institutions, so that the whole exceeds the sum of its parts. They also call for breakthroughs on prominent problems in each area, including strengthening the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Party-building theory in China defines and links these three concepts, with a historical survey of leaders' statements.

The narrative logic of Marx and Engels on the evolution of civilisational forms 马克思恩格斯文明形态演进的叙事逻辑探赜 Li Yanyan Wang Jie Li and Wang ask how Marx and Engels narrated the evolution of civilisational forms, and argue that their account, built on historical materialism and the theme of human emancipation, differs from earlier evolutionary schemes. They contrast it with three accounts: Spengler's life-cycle of cultures, Jaspers's four periods centred on the Axial Age, and Marcuse's three stages of repression. In the authors' reading, Marx and Engels theorise at three levels, macro, meso and micro, each marked by a dialectical unity. The article is organised accordingly. Part one treats the macro trend, the unity of antagonism and non-antagonism. Part two treats the meso level, the stages of evolution, as a unity of continuity and innovation. Part three treats the micro level, the concrete paths of different nations, as a unity of the general and the particular. The authors draw on Engels's Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, the Grundrisse, the Critique of the Gotha Programme and the Marx–Zasulich correspondence. At the macro level, the authors argue that forced division of labour and enslaved labour make the "age of civilisation" antagonistic. Wage labour is, in their words, a concealed form of slavery, and class struggle runs between those who create civilisation and those who enjoy it. This antagonism is to give way to a non-antagonistic stage of "free individuality". At the meso level, they combine the "four-form" and "three-form" readings into stages of open slave labour, concealed slave labour and autonomous labour. Productive forces, the "fruits of civilisation", are inherited from stage to stage, while the institutional "shell" of production relations is repeatedly broken through. At the micro level, they argue that Marx and Engels paired the general rise from lower to higher forms with particular paths, citing their reflections on Russia's village commune and the possibility of bypassing the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism. The authors conclude that Marx and Engels replaced abstract rational spirit with the activity of real individuals and replaced metaphysical thinking with dialectics, thereby surpassing a priori rationalist views of civilisation. They draw three practical lessons: confidence that civilisation will reach free individuality while contradictions of the present are tackled; inheritance of old civilisational elements alongside the creation of new ones; and respect for common requirements of progress while each country chooses a path suited to its conditions. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language reconstruction of Marx and Engels's theory of civilisational forms, set against Spengler, Jaspers and Marcuse.

China's "people-centred" path of governing science and technology ethics “以人民为中心”的中国科技伦理治理之路 Xiao Wei Xiao Wei asks how science and technology ethics should be governed in an age of artificial intelligence and big data, when ethical challenges cut across disciplines and touch on safety, social fairness, public interest and human dignity. The article argues that China is following a "people-centred" path, in which ethics governance is oriented to the interests and participation of the people. It first appeared in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2025. The piece has three parts. It first links the aim of "promoting human well-being" to the people-centred principle. It then explains why the people's principal position must be upheld in ethics governance. Finally it sets out how to build a governance system with broad public participation. Xiao draws on the 2022 Opinions on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance, with its five ethical principles, on Xi Jinping's April 2025 Qiushi article on building a strong science and technology nation, and on UNESCO, WHO and UN sustainable development frameworks. Xiao contends that "promoting human well-being" is a shared international value, while the people-centred principle is the Communist Party's basic political stance. The two are said to coincide in treating the human being as the foundation, in focusing on dignity, rights and all-round development, and in stressing shared benefits. Because technology is double-edged, Xiao argues, governance cannot be left to experts, institutes or firms regulating themselves. The public should be participants, supervisors and beneficiaries, with rights to information, expression and participation. Drawing on a 2021 WHO framework, Xiao names participation, inclusiveness and responsiveness as key features. Inclusiveness is divided into inclusion of groups, of viewpoints and of rights protection. Xiao proposes building the system at three levels. Institutionally, this means public hearings, social review and ethical impact assessment, with citizen forums before major biomedical applications. At the level of mechanisms, community organisations, media platforms and civil bodies would join a structure of government guidance, corporate responsibility, expert participation and shared governance by the people. Culturally, ethics education would be built into national education and public communication. Xiao concludes that public participation gives innovation social support and moral grounding, and also provides risk warning and social stability. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese official discourse links technology ethics governance to the people-centred principle and public participation.

Re-examining the Marxist view of the masses: from the dissolution of fetishism to the generation of intersubjectivity 重审马克思主义群众观：从拜物教消解到主体间性的生成 Ma Youru Historical materialism holds that the people are the true subject of history, yet Ma Youru argues that under capitalism this truth is deeply obscured by commodity fetishism. The article proposes that re-examining the Marxist view of the masses requires criticising and dissolving fetishism, then reconstructing the masses' subjectivity as a process of intersubjectivity that is generated through practice. The short commentary first describes how fetishism turns social relations between people into relations between things, then identifies the material route to overcoming it, and finally sets out the dimensions of intersubjectivity. It ends by summarising a three-step dialectical path. Ma contends that fetishism works at the levels of production, exchange and consumption. Workers come to see themselves as commodities, social ties are reified, and history appears to have no subject, only the self-unfolding of capital. Because fetishism is rooted in private ownership and generalised commodity production, Ma argues that criticism of ideas is insufficient. Only the revolutionary practice of the masses, aimed at abolishing private ownership and founding an "association of free individuals", can pierce the illusion. In such an association Ma identifies three dimensions of intersubjectivity: mutual recognition as equals, symbiotic practice, and co-generation of the community's form and goals. Ma presents this as overcoming the opposition between collectivism and individualism. Ma concludes that the Marxist view of the masses follows a path from dissolving fetishism, through the practical formation of subjectivity, to the internal construction of intersubjectivity. The "masses" are therefore a historical force that is continually generated, not a fixed concept, and Ma holds that this theoretical legacy retains critical and emancipatory force today. Read the original if you want a brief, philosophically oriented restatement of the Marxist theory of the masses through fetishism critique and intersubjectivity.

Universities should serve as the vanguard of education reform 高校要当好教育改革排头兵 Wang Xiaoru This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call for Chinese universities to lead education reform. Wang argues that universities should act as the vanguard of that reform, anchored in the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education (立德树人), and should help build a strong education nation. The article is organised around three reasons. First, reform is an inherent requirement of the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Second, universities have particular strengths that qualify them to lead. Third, reform is necessary for high-quality development of higher education. On the second point, Wang lists talent, teaching and research capacity, cultural exchange and multi-party cooperation as the sources of universities' leading role. On the third, the author calls for systemic innovation in three areas. Evaluation should move away from overemphasis on research, test scores and credentials, and should add weight to practice, innovation and moral conduct, with ideological and political content in courses counted in staff assessment. Training models should be adjusted to national strategy and industry needs through interdisciplinary courses and project-based learning. Management should give departments more autonomy, tilt resources to frontline teaching and set up a tolerance-for-error mechanism. Wang concludes that the Party's leadership must run through the whole reform process. Universities should train people for the Party and the country, and should use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to shape students' values. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-line language on university reform and moral education is presented in a Chinese academic commentary.

The Communist Party of China's role as the mainstay was the key to victory in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 中国共产党的中流砥柱作用是中国人民抗日战争胜利的关键 Lu Yi Lu Yi takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that the Communist Party's role as the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) was the key to victory in the War of Resistance against Japan. The article, a commentary published in the People's Daily in August 2025, argues that this is a scientific conclusion drawn from a full review of the 14-year war and a settled historical verdict. Lu presents the victory as the first complete victory over foreign invasion in modern Chinese history and a turning point towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised around four areas in which the Party is said to have played an irreplaceable role: political guidance through the anti-Japanese national united front, social mobilisation through the total-resistance line, strategic guidance in military affairs, and Party building. It draws on Mao Zedong's wartime writings, Party documents from 1935 to 1945, and recent remarks by Xi. It also cites observers outside the Party: Liang Shuming, Chen Jiageng, a Nationalist propagandist, the US Army Observation Group in Yan'an and Japanese military histories. Lu argues that the Party first proposed, then promoted and finally defended the united front, from the 1935 August 1st Declaration through the Xi'an Incident to the formal Nationalist–Communist cooperation of 1937. The Party is said to have kept the front intact through three anti-Communist upsurges by pursuing both unity and struggle. Lu contrasts the Party's line of mobilising the whole people with the Nationalists' government- and army-centred line, and credits the Party's guerrilla strategy, set out in On Protracted War, with moving the enemy-rear battlefield to the centre of the war. Party building, in Lu's account, supplied the capacity for this through Mao Zedong Thought, the Yan'an Rectification, a consolidated leadership and the Party's style of work, which Lu sums up in the 'three magic weapons' of united front, armed struggle and Party building. Lu concludes that the Party that saved the nation in wartime is also the core of leadership for national rejuvenation today. The author calls for firmly upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and applying the Party's historical experience and the spirit of resistance. Lu also urges the Party's self-reform and a new great project of Party building. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily account of the Party's wartime leadership, and of how that history is tied to current Party-building themes.

The fourfold logic behind the emergence of "ideological and political leadership capacity" 论思政引领力的四重出场逻辑 Bai Xianliang Wang Yichen In September 2024 Xi Jinping told the National Education Conference that a leading education country with Chinese characteristics must have, first of all, strong "ideological and political leadership capacity" (sizheng yinlingli). Bai and Wang ask why this concept appeared and why it was ranked as the first trait of such a country. They argue that its emergence is scientific, reasonable and necessary, and that this can be shown through four logics: disciplinary, theoretical, historical and practical. The article is a conceptual and historical study in ideological and political education. It first places the concept within the discipline's forty years of development and traces its precursors in Party documents. It then turns to its Marxist foundations, surveys the Party's ideological and political work from the New Democratic Revolution to the post-2012 period, and finally links the concept to current strategic tasks. The authors first present the concept as a "signature concept" for building an autonomous body of knowledge in the discipline. They trace it through phrases such as "ideological leadership capacity" in the 19th Party Congress report (2017) and earlier scholarly work on the leading force of ideological and political education. Second, they ground it in three Marxist principles: the dialectic of social being and social consciousness, the doctrine of "inculcation" (read as combining instilling with enlightening, not rote cramming), and the theories of human essence and free, all-round development. Third, they argue that the Party's record shows ideological work uniting revolutionary forces, building consensus for construction, and promoting the liberation of thinking after reform and opening up. On the practical side, Bai and Wang contend that the concept answers the needs of building a leading education country. They name the Party's overall leadership of education, the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, and education modernization by 2035. They also see it as required for socialist ideological work, which includes ideological security, leading online public opinion, and combining constructive and critical work against erroneous trends. They add that it drives Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through spiritual motivation, direction and consensus. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholars justify and theorise this new official concept, with its Party-document genealogy.

The meaning and key points of strengthening ideals and convictions in building a leading country in education 教育强国建设背景下坚定理想信念的内涵意蕴与着力要点 Liao Xiaoqin Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's September 2024 speech at the National Education Conference, this article asks why young students' ideals and convictions must be strengthened in building a leading country in education, what those ideals and convictions contain, and how to strengthen them. Liao Xiaoqin argues that firm ideals and convictions are the core of ideological and political guidance in this project and a source of strength for building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first sets out the strategic value of strengthening ideals and convictions. The second traces how their content has been formulated in Party discourse, from "two" and "three" beliefs to "four". The third proposes four key working points. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches and Party documents, including the resolution on the Party's century of struggle and the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Liao identifies three kinds of strategic value: guarding national ideological security in a setting of "two overall situations", training builders and successors of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and providing spiritual support for national rejuvenation. On content, the author says that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the formula has grown into four elements: faith in Marxism and communism, conviction in socialism with Chinese characteristics, trust in the Communist Party of China, and confidence in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Liao's reading, trust in the Party is the core that binds these into a composite spiritual system. The proposed working points are to ground the effort in Chinese modernization, to make fostering patriotism the first task, to teach differently by age group and audience while coordinating family, school and society, and to build regular institutional mechanisms, including online education and measures against online ideological risks. Liao concludes that ideals and convictions must be anchored in the practice of Chinese modernization and in daily life, and must be matched to students' stages of development, if they are to take firm hold. Education is presented as the means of ensuring that each generation of young people takes up the task of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how current Party discourse frames ideals-and-convictions education for students, including the "four beliefs" formula and the proposed institutional measures.

A cultural interpretation of making ideals-and-convictions education regular and institutionalised 理想信念教育常态化制度化的文化阐释 Han Liying The Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) called for making education in ideals and convictions regular and institutionalised. Han Liying asks what this means when read through culture rather than administration. The article argues that the aim is to turn faith in Marxism, the lofty ideal of communism and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a "spiritual atmosphere" present everywhere, and into values people hold without consciously noticing them. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the cultural context: the "great changes unseen in a century", Chinese modernization and the Two Integrations, and the Party's century of struggle. The second analyses the cultural meaning of "regularisation" and of "institutionalisation" separately. The third proposes cultural strategies, built on traditional culture, everyday life and institutional mechanisms. Han's central move is to place regularisation in three "normal states": the historical normal of reform and opening to the outside world, daily life, and the course of a human life. Ideals should be forged through history and national-condition education, applied "at all times, in all places, in all matters", and kept up through life stages, with the limited individual life given meaning by service to society. Institutionalisation is treated as a value-bearing process: citing Marx and Engels, Han argues that institutions serve and free people rather than restrict them, raise the efficiency and quality of education through supervision and accountability, and work through an institutional culture that follows the Confucian tradition of moral guidance over coercion. The strategies proposed are threefold. First, deepen the foundation of belief with fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, through cultural cognition, innovation, ritual experience and environment. Second, root the work in daily life, so that people's material and spiritual needs are met and their sense of happiness and of gain grows. Third, build three mechanisms: education and guidance (theory, history and national-condition education), practice-based cultivation, and cultural influence. Read the original if you study ideological and political education in China and want to see how Party educational policy is justified through cultural, Confucian and Marxist references.)

Ideological and political education large models: generative logic, core meaning and practical application 思政大模型：生成逻辑、内核要义与实践运用 Cui Jianxi Chen Haowen Following the global spread of ChatGPT from 2022 and the release of the Chinese model DeepSeek in January 2025, Cui and Chen ask how large-model AI can be built for, and used in, ideological and political education. They propose a specialised "ideological and political large model" (sizheng damoxing) and argue that clarifying how it is generated, what it is and how it can be applied would help move it from theoretical idea to practice. The article has three parts. The first sets out how such a model is generated, through four components: ideological and political education big data, suitable algorithms, strong computing power and a performance orientation. The second defines the model, its characteristics and its functions. The third turns to practical use in data integration, interaction and teaching methods. The authors draw on examples of educational models in other fields and on Marx's remarks on machines. A central move is that data and algorithms are not neutral. The authors argue that data carry the ideology of those who produce them, so training material must be screened to remove content at odds with the educational value orientation. Algorithms are likewise an extension of human will, so they should be designed under Marxist guidance and keep the model within the value bounds of ideological and political education. The model is defined as a specialised tool combining general and professional intelligence. Its stated characteristics are ideological character, human-like intelligence, tool character and progressive learning, and it remains dependent on people and cannot replace educators. Three functions follow: integrating data into one model-based resource base, sustained dialogue, and giving educators technical skills. For practice, the authors propose merging separate databases into an integrated intelligent resource base. They suggest discursive, heuristic, simulated and scene-based interaction, with each learner in effect having a personal tutor. They also propose three teaching methods: an "intelligent learning companion", a "virtual expert" system and multimodal teaching that converts between text, audio, video and images. The authors present these as ways to overcome the technical barriers educators face with new technologies and to advance the digital-intelligent transformation of ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a detailed conceptual framework for AI in Chinese ideological and political education, including how its ideological requirements are built into the technical design.

The connotation, essence and enhancement path of the ideological and political guiding force of education 论思政引领力的内涵、实质与提升路径 Cao Jinlong Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference in September 2024 listed six defining features of a strong education nation, with ideological and political guiding force (sizheng yinlingli) placed first. Cao Jinlong takes up what this concept means, what it is in essence, and how it can be strengthened. The article argues that it is a systemic, collective force generated across all links of education, and that it is in essence the guiding force of socialist ideology realised in education. The article is organised in three parts. The first clarifies the concept through a linguistic and conceptual analysis of "ideology and politics" and of "guiding force", borrowing the idea of force from physics. The second sets out its spiritual essence, tracing the Party's tradition of treating political work as a "lifeline", the political character of education, and the question of ideological security. The third proposes a path of improvement built on three questions: who exerts the force, on whom, and how. Cao contends that the concept should not be reduced to the force of ideological and political theory courses, or to the discipline of ideological and political education, since other courses and disciplines, and even support staff, also convey the Party's values. Drawing on the idea that force requires a source, a target and conditions, Cao defines it as the combined capacity of educators to lead learners to accept Marxist guidance and socialist institutions. In Cao's account, the proletariat openly acknowledges education's political nature, unlike the bourgeoisie, which is said to conceal it. The article describes schools as a front line of ideological work, where hostile forces compete for young people, so that winning youth requires strong guiding force. For the path forward, Cao calls for collective action by theory-course teachers (the core) and other teachers, counsellors and staff (an indispensable supporting group). Guidance should be precise, responding to students' individual intellectual puzzles and practical difficulties. Cao also calls for coordination within schools, between school, family and society, and between offline and online spaces, aiming to turn the internet from the "biggest variable" into the "biggest increment". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of ideological and political education conceptualises this new official term and translates it into concrete educational practice.

Integrating the ideological and political "small classroom" with the social "big classroom" 融合思政教育“小课堂”和“大课堂” Qiu Feng This newspaper commentary asks how ideological and political theory courses in schools can become more persuasive. Qiu argues that, following Xi Jinping's call to join the classroom "small classroom" with the social "big classroom", such courses must tie theory to social reality and practice rather than rely on explanation and logic alone. The piece has two parts. The first sets out why the integration matters. The second proposes four practical links for carrying it out, and draws on the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) initiative. In the first part, Qiu holds that integration helps teachers explain principles in a deeper, more thorough and livelier way, because students experience and reflect on them themselves. Qiu also says the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), supply content, and that local examples make courses more credible. Integration is further said to help students understand national and popular conditions, so that they become capable successors to the cause of national rejuvenation. The four links are: widening teachers' horizons, for instance through visits to archives, Party history museums and achievement exhibitions; expanding practical teaching through fieldwork and patriotic education sites; coordinating schools and society under Party committee leadership; and using information technology, such as VR tours of Party memorial halls and virtual battlefields. Qiu concludes that a course delivered across the country, and not only in lecture halls, will build firmer convictions, deepen national identity and foster patriotic feeling in students. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance on the "Great Ideological and Political Course" is translated into teaching methods.

The international dissemination and influence of On Protracted War 《论持久战》的国际传播及影响 Deng Shaogen This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how Mao Zedong's On Protracted War (1938) travelled beyond China and what effect it had. Deng Shaogen argues that the Communist Party of China gave great weight to spreading the work abroad, and that through foreign journalists and international friends it had major international influence. The article follows the text from its delivery as lectures in Yan'an (26 May–3 June 1938) through publication in the journal Jiefang and in separate editions. It then covers Soviet and Comintern endorsement, the English translations, Japanese translation and reading, and the reception among Western leaders and observers. Deng stresses that the Comintern understood and supported the protracted-war line, citing Ren Bishi's September 1938 article in Pravda and Dimitrov's praise of the work as epoch-making. Citing the researcher Zhang Shengxiang, Deng records at least four English translation efforts, including a lost Wuhan manuscript and versions serialised in Shanghai. Deng also reports that Japanese media and military staff translated the text, and that the general Okamura Yasuji called it a highly valuable strategic document, with Japanese attitudes moving from disdain to despair. Deng concludes that the work had a positive effect in the Western world and drew high praise internationally. As evidence, the article mentions reports that copies lay on the desks of Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill, Stilwell's description of it as a superb textbook, and Edgar Snow's phrase "prophecy in the cave dwelling". Read the original if you want a compact survey of the translation history and foreign reception of On Protracted War, as presented in Chinese scholarship.

Carrying forward the great founding spirit of the Party to speed up building a strong agricultural country 弘扬伟大建党精神 加快建设农业强国 Liu Wugen This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 21 August 2025, asks how the great founding spirit of the Party can inform the drive to build a strong agricultural country. Liu argues that carrying forward this spirit has real practical significance for that goal and for building a modern socialist country, on the premise that a strong country first needs strong agriculture. The piece takes the four components of the founding spirit in turn: upholding truth and ideals; staying true to the original aspiration and mission; fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely; and being loyal to the Party and faithful to the people. Each section sketches the Party's historical record on that theme, then links it to the present task. In Liu's account, each component answers a specific need. Upholding truth and ideals calls for using the Marxist stance, viewpoint and method, together with Xi Jinping's statements on agriculture, rural areas and farmers, to find a Chinese path of agricultural and rural modernization suited to a large country of small farms. The original aspiration and mission turns the Central Committee's two-step plan into responsibility: basic agricultural modernization by 2035 and a strong agricultural country by mid-century. Liu names weak agricultural foundations, low efficiency, resource constraints, weak competitiveness and the urban–rural income gap as the difficulties that require struggle. Liu concludes that loyalty to the Party and service to the people keep the effort on course. The author calls for raising farmers' incomes, treating food security as a matter of national importance, advancing rural revitalization, and achieving self-reliance in agricultural science and technology. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building discourse is tied to agricultural policy in 2025.

Bringing the Party's leadership advantages into play to promote scientific and technological innovation vigorously 发挥党的领导优势 大力推进科技创新 Wei Rong This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 21 August 2025, argues that the Communist Party's overall leadership is the precondition for high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and for building China into a leading science and technology power. Wei Rong places this in a world of accelerating great changes, in which international competition increasingly centres on high technology. The article cites the 20th Party Congress (2022) goal of becoming a science and technology power by 2035. The piece first reviews the Party's science policy from the founding of the People's Republic to the present, then explains why innovation matters to the Party's mission, and finally sets out four ways to use the Party's leadership advantages. In Wei's account, the Party has adjusted its science policy to each period's needs: the 1956 call to "march on science", the 1978 formula that science and technology are productive forces, the 1985 reform decision, the strategy of invigorating the country through science and education, and the innovation-driven development strategy of the new era. Wei argues that innovation serves the Party's founding mission and is a necessary condition for Chinese modernization. It also strengthens national security, which requires a new type of whole-nation system and solutions to "chokepoint" problems. The four proposals are centralised Party leadership with full-chain planning and stronger basic research, integrated education, science and talent under the principle that the Party manages talent, deeper reform that makes enterprises the main innovators, and self-reliance combined with open international cooperation. Wei concludes that China's own innovation path depends on turning the Party's political and institutional advantages into driving force for innovation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link Party leadership to the science and technology agenda.

Grasping in depth that problems of work style are essentially problems of Party spirit 深刻把握作风问题本质上是党性问题 Xu Mei This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that problems of work style are essentially problems of Party spirit. Xu Mei argues that whether Communists can resolve style problems is a key measure of their faith in Marxism, their belief in socialism and communism, and their loyalty to the Party and the people. The author calls on Party members and cadres to link self-cultivation of Party spirit with style building, as a way of consolidating the results of the study and education campaign on the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. The article has three parts. The first sets out what it means to say that style is a matter of Party spirit. The second reviews the Party's history of style building, from its founding through the Gutian Conference (1929), the Yan'an rectification, the 1950s campaigns, the post-1978 Party rectification and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to practical requirements for the new journey. Xu's central claim is that Party spirit is internal and style is its outward expression: wavering belief, a lost sense of purpose or discarded Party spirit will inevitably show up in conduct. The author names the distinction between public and private interest as the "fundamental yardstick" of Party spirit, and traces formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance to distorted worldviews, ideals and views of power. For this reason, Xu argues, correcting style cannot treat each incident in isolation; it must look through style to Party spirit and solve the underlying problem. The historical survey is used to show that the Party has consistently treated Party spirit as the root of style building, citing documents such as the 1941 decision on strengthening Party spirit and Liu Shaoqi's writings. For practice, Xu proposes three measures: firm ideals and convictions, sustained through regular ideological self-checks; serious intra-Party political life, including democratic life meetings, criticism and self-criticism and the "three meetings and one lesson"; and a spirit of the Party's self-reform, with zero tolerance for breaches of the eight-point regulation and use of the "four forms" of discipline. The aim, the author says, is to provide a strong style guarantee for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-building commentary links ideology, discipline and the Party's own history in the campaign on work style.

Lessons from Chen Yun's methods of investigation and research 陈云同志的调查研究方法给予我们的启示 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu asks what present-day officials can learn from the way Chen Yun, a leading economic policymaker of the first and second generations of Party leadership, carried out investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu). Opening with Xi Jinping's call to study Chen's scientific ways of thinking and working, Zhu argues that Chen made investigation the precondition of decision-making. In Zhu's account, this was a direct application of seeking truth from facts, and Mao Zedong himself said at the 1962 Seven Thousand Cadres Conference that Chen's method was investigation and research. The commentary is organised around four requirements: coming to the facts without preconceptions, being thorough and detailed, listening to dissenting views, and having the right purpose. Each is illustrated with episodes from Chen's career: his Yan'an-era formula, the 1961 fieldwork in Qingpu, the 1959 coal-industry symposium, the 1949 Shanghai prices mission, the 1953 grain purchase and supply policy, and the food-supply measures of the early 1960s. Zhu supports each point with passages from Xi Jinping's speeches and notes the March 2023 Central Committee General Office plan to promote investigation across the Party. Zhu's central claim is that reliable research begins with the principle 'not bowing to superiors, not bowing to books, only to reality', which Chen distinguished from disobedience: policies must be carried out, but adapted to local conditions. Zhu stresses Chen's thoroughness, citing his fifteen days living with farmers in Qingpu, his detailed calculations showing double-cropping rice to be less profitable than single-cropping, and Mao's praise for 'speaking with figures'. Zhu also describes Chen's deliberate search for opposing views and unwelcome truths, and his use of trusted friends and aides as a second channel of information.
