The purpose of all this, Zhu says, was to solve problems affecting people's livelihood, which Chen treated as a political matter. Zhu concludes that investigation remains a Party 'family heirloom' to be used more fully. He points to what he calls a world undergoing changes unseen in a century and to deep-seated contradictions in reform and development. Deeper research, he argues, will help officials grasp actual conditions and objective laws and carry socialism with Chinese characteristics forward in the new era. Read the original if you want a Party-history-based account of how Chen Yun's working methods are being held up as a model for the current campaign to revive investigation and research.

The Communist Party of China and the nationwide War of Resistance through the eyes of Western eyewitnesses 西方亲历者视域下的中国共产党与全民族抗战 Zhang Deming Zhang Deming asks how Western journalists, diplomats, officers and doctors who visited the anti-Japanese base areas under Communist leadership described the Communist Party of China (CPC) after the nationwide War of Resistance began in 1937. The short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2025, argues that these outside observers, through their own accounts, confirm the Party's role as the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the nationwide resistance. Zhang organises the material under three headings: the line of all-out resistance, the consolidation of the Anti-Japanese National United Front, and guerrilla warfare behind enemy lines. The witnesses quoted include Edgar Snow's contemporaries and others such as Agnes Smedley, Theodore White, Evans Carlson, John S. Service, Israel Epstein, Rewi Alley-era visitors like Anna Louise Strong, the Austrian doctor Jakob Rosenfeld, and the German journalist Hans Shippe. Their statements are set beside passages from Mao Zedong, Peng Dehuai and Party documents such as the 1937 Luochuan Conference decisions. Zhang's central move is to read these testimonies as evidence for the Party's own account. On the all-out resistance line, observers described mass mobilisation, village self-defence units and close army–people ties, in contrast with what Zhang calls the Kuomintang's one-sided reliance on government and army. On the united front, they noted the Party's persuasion of other forces, the "three-thirds" system of government and moderate rent reduction that protected landlords' interests. On guerrilla warfare, they recorded tactics such as tunnel and mine warfare, the role of militias, and the fact that Communist-led forces pinned down most Japanese and puppet troops, which Zhang says rebuts Kuomintang charges that Communist forces "roamed but did not fight". Zhang concludes that the Western eyewitnesses saw the Party's political leadership and strategy at first hand and that their writings helped present a positive international image of the CPC. Some observers, such as Epstein, expected the Party to become China's dominant force. Zhang treats the Party's account of the Southern Anhui Incident of 1941 and of Kuomintang friction as settled, relying on the quoted witnesses as external confirmation. Read the original if you want a compact sampler of Western wartime testimony on the CPC as it is used in current official Party-history narrative.

Inheriting and promoting the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army 传承与弘扬东北抗联精神 Li Shujuan Writing in Guangming Daily in the year of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance (2025), Li Shujuan, a professor at Harbin Normal University, takes up the history and meaning of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (the Northeast Anti-Japanese Allied Forces). Li argues that, under Communist Party leadership, its fourteen years of struggle from 1931 to 1945 produced a distinctive spirit. In Li's account this spirit embodies the wider spirit of the War of Resistance and forms an important part of the Chinese Communists' spiritual lineage. The short commentary has three parts. It first recounts the army's hardships: the Japanese military build-up, the forced "collective hamlets", blockades, hunger, clothing shortages and extreme cold. It then assesses the army's historical standing, and finally turns to the moral qualities of individual commanders and fighters. Li draws on Japanese and Soviet sources, letters and reports by commanders such as Zhou Baozhong and Feng Zhongyun, and recollections of veterans. Li's central claim is that the Northeast was the starting point and the longest-running theatre of the Eastern anti-fascist war. The article argues that the army tied down large Japanese forces, citing figures for Japanese military spending and Kwantung Army casualties. In this reading, it delayed both Japan's "northward" and "southward" advances and indirectly supported the Soviet Union. It also helped Soviet forces in 1945 through reconnaissance and by serving in the Soviet 88th Independent Rifle Brigade, and it prepared the ground for the Party's later takeover of the Northeast. The spirit itself is illustrated through loyalty to the Party despite long lost contact (Zhao Shangzhi, Feng Zhongyun), patriotic sacrifice (Zhao Yiman, Xu Chengshu, the twelve martyrs of Xiaogushan), and the unyielding resistance of Yang Jingyu. Li concludes that research on the army's history has important academic and practical value in 2025. The author calls for study based on a correct view of the Second World War history and on empirical historical methods. Such work would cover the army's course of struggle, its conditions, its contributions and the contemporary value of its spirit, and would offer international scholarship a further angle on China's war. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army is presented in official commemorative writing, with the sources it cites.

Laying a solid cultural foundation for ideological and political education 筑牢思想政治教育的文化之基 Feng Lihua Sun Xiguo This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how ideological and political education can be given a firmer cultural footing. Feng and Sun argue that it must be guided by Xi Jinping's cultural thought, so as to deepen its theoretical depth, cultural thickness and practical effectiveness and cultivate a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised around three requirements: upholding the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education (立德树人), adhering to the Two Integrations, and cultivating the core socialist values. Each is treated as a way of linking Party ideology with Chinese cultural tradition. On the first point, the authors say that Xi's cultural thought answers the questions of whom to train, how and for whom. They call for a shift from 'propaganda and indoctrination' towards 'value guidance' and 'cultural initiative', and for an educational system that unites political, cultural and contemporary dimensions. On the second, they hold that combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional culture makes the teaching more relevant, humane and persuasive. On the third, they see the core socialist values as drawing on traditional ethics, revolutionary culture and socialist culture, and want them to run through the whole teaching process, from understanding to habitual conduct. The authors conclude that, on the new journey, schools should build a 'big ideological and political course' pattern. It would integrate Marxist principles, traditional culture and the spirit of the Communist Party, strengthen the sense of community of the Chinese nation, and supply ideological and cultural support for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Chinese ideological education is justified in terms of Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

The traditional cultural foundations of the "Three Musts" “三个务必”的传统文化底蕴 Yang Junling This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2025, asks where the "Three Musts" announced by Xi Jinping draw on China's traditional culture. Yang Yunling's author, Yang Junling, argues that the Three Musts continue and develop Marxist theories of party and state building and also inherit and develop excellent traditional Chinese culture. Guided by the Two Integrations, Yang says, uncovering this cultural background helps to grasp the essence and practical demands of the formula. The article takes the three "musts" in turn: never forgetting the original aspiration and keeping the mission in mind; remaining modest and prudent and working hard; and daring and being good at struggle. For each, Yang pairs classical sources, such as the Book of Documents, the Book of Changes, Laozi, Confucius, Mencius and Xunzi, with passages Xi Jinping has cited since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yang argues that the first "must" combines the Marxist people's standpoint with the traditional idea that the people are the foundation of the state. The second joins the Marxist spirit of self-reform to traditional virtues of humility and vigorous striving. The third merges the Marxist spirit of struggle with an ancient wisdom of struggle, seen in myths such as Yu Gong moving the mountains and in Confucian and Daoist ethics. In each case Yang presents the Party's formula as a creative transformation and innovative development of tradition. Yang concludes that on the new journey the Party should internalise the mission of the people's happiness and national rejuvenation, guard against officials turning from public servants into masters, and sharpen its methods of struggle. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-aligned scholarship ties current Party slogans to classical Chinese sources.

Understanding the significance of "work style building is always on the road" 深刻理解“作风建设永远在路上”的重大意义 Huang Qisong Huang Qisong takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that "work style building is always on the road" and asks why it matters for a Marxist party. Writing in a Guangming Daily commentary of August 2025, Huang argues that Party conduct is not a peripheral matter but the foundation of the Party's governing position and of popular political identification with it. The thesis is that the formulation reflects an objective law of long-term rule and deepens Marxist party theory. The piece has three numbered sections. The first links work style to the Party's governing base and political identity, drawing on the Communist Manifesto, Lenin's vanguard party and Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era statements. The second presents the formulation as the "deep code" of the Party's vitality over a century. The third treats it as a deeper understanding of how parties are built, including a comparison with Western party politics. Huang first contends that the vanguard character of a proletarian party is not given in advance but must be forged through continuous self-construction, above all in work style. Bureaucratism, formalism, hedonism and extravagance are described as products of a distorted view of power that weaken the Party's close ties with the people. Second, bad work styles are said to be stubborn, recurrent and tied to their era, from the "sugar-coated bullets" of the early People's Republic to the market logic of the reform period and the "four tests" and "four dangers" today. Hence work style building must be sustained, and it is presented as the key entry point for the Party's self-reform, through the anti-corruption struggle, the eight-point rules and campaigns against the "four undesirable work styles". Third, Huang places this in a line from the Yan'an rectification and the Three-Antis and Five-Antis campaigns to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, as an answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Huang describes Western party politics as periodic "political performance" and a struggle for power whose difficulties are almost insoluble, and contrasts this with the Chinese approach. Huang concludes that continuous work style building gives long-term Party rule a political guarantee and offers a new approach to Marxist party building. In Huang's account it also underpins Chinese modernization and carries world-historical significance as a Chinese solution for party politics. Huang calls for work style building to run through the whole of the new great project of Party building. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building discourse in 2025 justifies permanent work style campaigns and frames them against Western party systems.

Studying and thoroughly grasping the latest achievements of the Party's theoretical innovation A reading of volume five of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China 学深悟透党的创新理论最新成果 Chen Zhigang This short newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, introduces volume five of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. Chen describes the volume as the authoritative and systematic record of the latest results of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author argues that it shows the Party's practice in high-quality development, deeper reform and the building of a modern socialist country, and that it should guide Party members and the public in studying the Party's theoretical innovation. The article is organised around three themes drawn from the volume. The first is advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, with the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the volume's opening. The second is the Two Integrations as the route of theoretical, institutional and cultural innovation. The third pairs new quality productive forces with the Global Civilization Initiative and the Global South as contributions to a community with a shared future for mankind. On modernization, Chen reports the volume's claim that Chinese modernization overturns the equation of modernization with Westernization, offers developing countries another path, and is a new form of human civilization. Chen says it requires the Party's overall leadership, high-quality development as the first task, and deeper reform, citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). On the Two Integrations, the author presents the first as keeping Marxism abreast of the times and the second as giving it Chinese character, and calls the second a fresh liberation of thought. On productive forces, Chen summarises Xi's January 2024 definition: innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency, high-quality advanced productive forces. The author adds Xi's caution against blind rushes and a single model, and his call to tailor development to local conditions. Chen presents the Global Civilization Initiative, proposed in March 2023, as a third pillar alongside the Global Development and Global Security Initiatives. The author also cites Xi's statements from 2023 and 2024 on the collective rise of the Global South as a major historical event. Chen concludes that the volume offers new answers to major questions of reform, governance and foreign affairs, and serves as an action guide for studying the Party's theory. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how volume five of The Governance of China is presented to Party cadres and the public.

An analysis of the event-centred view of history in foreign Marxist theory 国外马克思主义理论中的事件史观探析 Hu Yaohui How should historical change be understood when revolutions do not coincide with the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production? Hu Yaohui takes up this problem by tracing a lineage of "event-centred" views of history within Marxism outside China. These thinkers give priority to discontinuity, contingency and human agency over continuity, teleology and evolutionism. Hu argues that the lineage recovers real strengths of historical materialism but exaggerates rupture until the event becomes mystified, and that Marx's own event analysis offers the corrective. The article moves through four sections. It begins with Walter Benjamin's "now-time" (Jetztzeit) in the Theses on the Philosophy of History, then turns to Louis Althusser's theory of the conjuncture and overdetermination, and then to Alain Badiou's theory of the event, with Slavoj Žižek and Giorgio Agamben mentioned as related figures. The final section reads Marx's The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte as a model of event analysis and uses it to criticise the three thinkers. Hu treats the October Revolution as the practical backdrop, since it undermined linear evolutionary history. Hu reads Benjamin as breaking with homogeneous, empty time and with Social Democratic faith in progress. Benjamin's "real state of exception" is the event, but his appeal to messianism sits uneasily with materialism. Althusser, in Hu's reading, is better seen as a theorist of the conjuncture than a structuralist: the conjuncture contains an empty place filled only by action, though he never settled "determination in the last instance" by the economy and ended in an aleatory materialism of the encounter. Badiou pushes contingency to the absolute, so that event and being are severed, and Hu says this leaves a Kantian split and a dialectic that discards Hegel "with the bathwater". Against these, Hu reads the Brumaire as linking three levels: the economic base (long duration), class perspective (conjuncture) and the event (short duration). On this reading Marx admits contingency, even of personal character, while keeping it within class structure and the contradiction of productive forces and relations of production. Hu concludes that these thinkers each emerged when the international communist movement was blocked, and that they share a view of the world as unclosed and reject Hegelian totality. Two criticisms follow. They grasp only conjuncture and event, not the longer time span, and so confuse contingency with openness; Hu cites Badiou's treatment of May 1968 as isolated rather than part of a world-historical wave. They also dilute class, whereas the proletariat remains the fundamental subject and needs a strong party, or action falls into voluntarist decisionism or a messianic view of miracles. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese-Marxist assessment of Benjamin, Althusser and Badiou on contingency and revolution, set against Marx's Brumaire.

The four dimensions of foreign left-wing scholars' spatial critique of twenty-first-century capitalism 国外左翼学者对21世纪资本主义空间批判的四重维度 Li Shule Li Shule asks how Western left-wing scholars have reworked the critique of capitalist space for the twenty-first century. The article argues that the field has moved from Henri Lefebvre's "production of space" to the "production of spatial scale", which David Harvey and Neil Smith treat as the key to understanding contemporary capitalism. Li reconstructs this turn as four interlocking dimensions of critique: the global city, the new state space, the new world system and bodily space. The article draws on Lefebvre, Harvey, Smith, Edward Soja, Manuel Castells, Saskia Sassen, Doreen Massey, Neil Brenner, Bob Jessop, Etienne Balibar, Neil Davidson, Alex Callinicos, Ellen Meiksins Wood and Peter Sloterdijk, among others. Each dimension gets its own section with two sub-themes: global-city landscape and power-geography networks; geopolitical effects of state restructuring and the rescaling of state space; uneven geography and new imperialism; and the political-economic and ontological critiques of the body. A concluding section sets out the logical order of the four dimensions and assesses their limits. Li argues that capitalism reorganises urban scale to create global cities, then reshapes state space to stabilise accumulation, then rebuilds global scale into an asymmetric world order. Finally, it exploits workers through hierarchies of bodily scale. In Li's account Harvey's "body-scale" system measures differences in the value of workers' bodies in order to exploit dispersed, varied subjects collectively. Smith's examples include the displacement of homeless people from public space, while Sloterdijk's "crystal palace" is read as capital's interior space, which excludes those outside it. Li also defends the capital-logic/territorial-logic analysis of the new imperialism against Davidson's objection that it offers no deeper internal relations. Li concludes that the four dimensions form a closed logical whole, running from the global city as starting point to the body as the point at which exploitation lands. The scholars' contribution, in Li's view, is to reveal how capitalist spatial domination operates across macro and micro scales, and the left must respond at the level of scale to set its political demands. Li also names three weaknesses: a drift towards "scale-centrism", a weakened Marxist class analysis, and no effective link between spatial critique and revolutionary practice. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Harvey and the geography of capitalism, or want a Chinese scholar's systematic assessment of this literature.

Foreign Marxists' critique of capitalist modernization 国外马克思主义者对资本主义现代化的批判 Ma Xinying Ma Xinying asks how Marxists outside China have criticised capitalist modernization in the twenty-first century, and what distinguishes this critique from that of the twentieth century. The article argues that, in the era of digital technology, capitalist modernization remains a "troublemaker" in world modernization because of capitalism's inherent contradictions. In Ma's account, foreign Marxists have combined Marx's critical stance with new theoretical resources to produce a new critique, marked by three shifts and carrying three kinds of significance. The article has three parts. The first surveys six new lines of critique: digital capitalism, biopolitics, the modern state (including new imperialism), ecological crisis, space, and modern society. It draws on Dan Schiller, Hardt and Negri, Agamben, Esposito, Bob Jessop, Edward Soja, Rahel Jaeggi and Hartmut Rosa. The second part identifies three trends. The third part sets out what the critique reveals about contemporary capitalism, about the stage reached by modernization, and about hopes for the future. Ma's central claim is that the critique has moved from diachronic to synchronic analysis, from critique of modernity to critique of modernization itself, and from socio-cultural to political critique. Borrowing Saussure's terms, Ma argues that twentieth-century critics traced the historical origins of capitalist modernization, whereas present-day critics cut across the present and ask how it shapes people's lives. Ma also argues that, after the 2008 financial crisis, themes such as hegemony, power, justice and biopower became the core of the critique. Ma contends that this critique exposes new contradictions: between expanding productive capacity and insufficient world demand, between financial predation and the financial sovereignty of developing countries, and between technological acceleration and alienation. Globalisation, in this view, is increasingly at odds with capitalist private appropriation. Ma concludes that capitalism is not the only path of modernization and that the world is too fragile to bear its unlimited mode of development. Unlike their twentieth-century predecessors, foreign Marxists are described as less pessimistic, because socialist modernization now offers a reference point. Ma cites John Bellamy Foster on ecosocialism, David Kotz and proposals for digital socialism, and presents Chinese modernization as embodying a progressive, people-centred and green alternative. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how recent Western Marxist theory is classified and used in debates about modernization.

Latin American left-wing governing parties' exploration of national development models 拉美左翼执政党对国家发展模式的探索 Yang Jianmin Shan Chongyun After the 2022–2024 election cycle, 13 of Latin America's 19 main countries are governed by left or centre-left parties. Yang and Shan ask what alternatives to the neoliberal development model these governments are actually pursuing. They argue that all three types of left government have so far failed to build an effective alternative, and that the left–right contest over neoliberalism will therefore continue. The article defines a development model, following the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, as a country's comprehensive exploration in political, economic and external affairs. It sorts governing left parties into three types: the long-ruling radical left (Cuba, Venezuela, Nicaragua), the "ultra-left" (Mexico) and the moderate left (Chile, Colombia, Brazil). Case sections cover Venezuela under Chávez and Maduro, Mexico under López Obrador and Sheinbaum, and Boric, Petro and Lula. The authors then draw lessons and assess challenges and prospects. The authors argue that the current round is the region's second attempt at autonomous development, after the populist and import-substitution regimes of the 1930s–60s, but that it has not broken out of the capitalist framework. Venezuela nationalised on a large scale yet remains oil-dependent and has seen about 7.7 million people emigrate. Mexico nationalised energy and minerals, including lithium, but kept the basic neoliberal framework and the USMCA. Chile and Colombia began radically and drifted to pragmatism, and Brazil uses transformation mainly as a slogan. The authors credit these governments with correcting distribution and social governance, but say they neglected party theoretical and organisational development. Yang and Shan identify three challenges: slow growth (a regional average of 0.9% in 2015–2024), a resurgent right and far right, and growing splits among left governments, for example over Venezuela's 2024 election. They nonetheless expect the left to remain resilient, citing a century-old socialist tradition and terms in office running to 2026–2030. They call on left governing parties to treat theoretical and organisational building as a long-term goal. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic typology of the Latin American left, with country detail on Venezuela, Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Brazil up to early 2025.

A review of domestic scholarship on world socialism and the international communist movement over the past five years 五年来国内学界关于世界社会主义与国际共产主义运动研究状况述评 Ju Junjun This literature review surveys Chinese scholarship on world socialism and the international communist movement over roughly 2020–2024. Ju Junjun sets the period against what the article calls accelerating great changes unseen in a century: the pandemic, the Ukraine crisis, geopolitical rivalry, decoupling and the rise of the Global South. The review also notes a run of anniversaries, including Engels's 200th, Lenin's 150th, the Paris Commune's 150th and the Party's centenary. It reports that research has deepened in response, with a stronger critique of capitalism and closer attention to how socialism with Chinese characteristics relates to world socialism. The review is organised in six thematic sections. These cover the theory and practice of the existing socialist states (Vietnam, North Korea, Laos and Cuba, after their 2021 Party congresses); the condition of communist, socialist and left parties abroad; and the main currents of socialist thought. The remaining sections cover the history of the communist movement, the long course and likely trends of world socialism, and the world significance of the Chinese Communist Party's theory and practice. A short conclusion assesses the field. Ju reports that scholars treat the parties in developed capitalist countries, the post-Soviet and Eastern European parties and those of Asia, Africa and Latin America separately, and that they track the decline of social-democratic parties such as the German SPD and the French Socialist Party. On currents of thought, the review lists work on eco-socialism, Latin American 21st-century socialism, social democracy, Arab socialism, market socialism and digital socialism, with some scholars disputing the last. On history, it records commemorations of the Paris Commune, the New Economic Policy and the International organisations, and renewed debate on the Soviet collapse. Many scholars, Ju says, describe the present as a mix of overall ebb and local upsurge, or as one flourishing branch (China) alongside blossoms elsewhere. Several, in this account, hold that Chinese modernization and socialism with Chinese characteristics open a new option for world socialism. In the conclusion Ju judges that the field has grown in strength, scope and topical relevance. Ju names two weaknesses: young researchers' thin foundations and duplicated work, and a tendency to repeat stock formulas or to equate innovation with following current politics. The article calls for cross-disciplinary and cross-institutional cooperation. It also calls for more theoretical and forward-looking work, grounded in Marxist principles, to build a Chinese autonomous knowledge system and discourse system. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Chinese-language publications and scholarly positions on world socialism, foreign left parties and the communist movement's history since 2020.

The logic of survival and development of communist parties abroad today 当前国外共产党生存发展的逻辑机理透析 Hua Bin Tang Haijun Hua Bin and Tang Haijun ask what condition communist parties outside China have been in since the start of the twenty-first century, how they appear within today's world socialist movement, and how their future should be judged. They argue that most of these parties have emerged from the trough that followed the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet collapse and have steadied themselves. In their view the world socialist movement has begun a favourable recovery, though a slow and uneven one. The article has three parts. It first surveys the parties' circumstances using figures the authors attribute to the International Department of the CPC Central Committee: around 200 parties in about 90 countries, roughly 20 million members, and most parties small and politically marginal. It then identifies six shared features. Finally it draws four conclusions about prospects and about China's policy towards these parties. In the authors' account, the shared features explain how the parties survived. They held to Marxism or scientific socialism while renewing it, explored varied paths to socialism (examples include Vietnam, Cuba, Spain, India and Brazil), and criticised capitalism as historically transient and crisis-prone. Their resistance to existing politics is described as limited and 'weak-intensity', and they defend social justice, workers' interests and peace. They also strengthen Party building through leadership systems, recruitment, training and discipline. On prospects, the authors say these parties are a political force that cannot be replaced, and a natural ally of the Communist Party of China against US-led bloc confrontation. They also note sectarian divisions, for example over the Ukraine crisis, and say China can offer political guidance and coordination. The authors conclude that capitalism has been declining since the 2008 financial crisis and that socialist movements in many countries have begun to recover. They add that the pattern of strong capitalism and weak socialism, with capital on the offensive, will not change fundamentally soon. Many non-ruling parties still face small and ageing memberships, tight finances and internal disputes. Progress will therefore be a spiral rising through twists and turns. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic overview of foreign communist parties, with figures, examples and the policy view that China should treat them as allies.

A study of the positive interaction between the Party's theoretical innovation and practical innovation in the new era 新时代党的理论创新与实践创新良性互动探析 Che Zongkai Che Zongkai asks how the Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation and practical innovation have interacted in the new era, and why this matters for understanding and extending Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that this body of thought is the product of a "positive interaction" (liangxing hudong) between the two kinds of innovation under Party leadership. It also holds that the same interaction supplies a method for advancing theory on the basis of practice in the new journey ahead. The article has three parts. The first sets out the dialectical relationship between theory and practice, drawing on Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong and tracing it through the Party's history, from Mao Zedong Thought to Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The second applies this to the new era, covering the changed principal contradiction, the major questions of the era, and the Party's summaries of experience. The third looks ahead to national rejuvenation and Chinese modernization. Che's central argument is that practice is both the source and the driving force of theory, while theory guides practice and is in turn tested and developed through it. For the new era, the author reads the "Ten Clarifications" as original theoretical conclusions drawn from practice and the "Fourteen Commitments" as the basic strategy for applying theory in work. The "thirteen areas of achievement" summarised in the Party's third historical resolution are presented as practical verification of the theory. The author also holds that the "six musts" in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) contain the stance, viewpoint and method behind this interaction. They are: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, a systems approach, and a global vision. Looking forward, Che calls for continued interaction in the face of two pressures: the strategic overall picture of national rejuvenation and "changes unseen in a century" in the world. The author proposes advancing theory through the Two Integrations, combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Che also argues that the practice of Chinese modernization, including deepening reform after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), is a rich source for further theoretical innovation. Read the original if you want a systematic, official-line account of how Party theorists frame the theory–practice relationship in Xi-era ideology and the structure of its core formulations.

Mao Zedong's original contributions to constructing Chinese Marxist philosophy in the Yan'an period 延安时期毛泽东对构建中国马克思主义哲学的原创性贡献 Zhao Zihan Zhao Zihan asks what Mao Zedong originally contributed to building a Chinese Marxist philosophy, and argues that existing studies still need to answer this from the standpoint of the unity of worldview and methodology. The article holds that in the Yan'an period (1935–1948) Mao inherited the basic categories of Marxist philosophy and enriched them in light of Chinese conditions, producing the first typical result of Chinese Marxist philosophy. The article first sets out the conditions that made this possible: Mao's world outlook, which combined Chinese and Western sources, and his Chinese sensibility, which linked tradition and modernity. It then traces how Mao treated three categories in turn: practice, labour and reality. Finally it assesses his contributions under four headings: ontology, worldview, methodology and values. Zhao argues that Mao did not make 'matter' his sole starting point, as Soviet philosophical textbooks did. Mao instead moved the emphasis to practice and contradiction, in works that became On Practice and On Contradiction, and treated labour as the basic form of practice for organising the masses. Matter and practice then converge in the category of 'reality', which Zhao reads as an ontology that sidesteps the later dispute between material and practical ontology. Mao called the Marxist worldview a 'cosmology' and held that worldview and methodology are one thing, with materialist dialectics as the core. In Zhao's reading, Mao also recast the traditional Chinese relation of knowing and acting as a unity of the two, and made the people the subject of history and the point of departure and destination of value. Zhao concludes that Mao activated Marxist principles and Chinese practice in both directions and brought traditional Chinese culture into dialogue with Marxist philosophy. The article links this to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for an independent knowledge system in Chinese philosophy and social sciences. It presents the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a continuation of Mao's unified approach. Read the original if you study Mao Zedong Thought, the philosophy of the Yan'an period, or the Chinese debate over practical versus material ontology.

Research on the CPC's War of Resistance against Japan from the perspective of holistic history: a conference report Review of an academic symposium held in Shenzhen, 16 November 2024 “整体史视野下的中共抗战史研究”学术研讨会综述 Shi Yingxin Zhang Xueyao This is a report on the symposium "Research on the CPC's War of Resistance against Japan from the Perspective of Holistic History", held on 16 November 2024 at the Shenzhen campus of Harbin Institute of Technology. It was co-organised by the editorial office of Studies of CPC History and the university's School of Marxism, ahead of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance. More than 30 scholars from universities, Party schools, military academies, research institutes and journals took part. The report says the field is shifting from a single-track political and military history towards a more multidimensional holistic history. The meeting combined commentary on eight selected papers with roundtable thematic speeches. The papers covered North, Central and South China and addressed military strategy, mobilisation, social life, weaponry, Kuomintang–Communist relations and international factors. The report groups the discussion into several areas: the holistic and international framing; regional, social and cultural history; renewed work on traditional military, political and economic topics; methods; and sources. On framing, participants called for placing the CPC's resistance within the world anti-fascist war and comparing it with responses to aggression in Europe, America, Asia, Africa and Latin America. One scholar urged treating the War of Resistance and the War of Liberation as one continuous line, and others urged viewing the frontal and enemy-rear battlefields together. Participants identified gaps in work on Northeast China before August 1945, on the Central Plains, Central China and Shandong afterwards, and on the Rear Area. They proposed more attention to women, film, medical care, veterans, emotions and human relationships, and to cultural-relic protection. Proposals on traditional fields included technological history of base-area arms industries, quantitative work on base-area economies and a longer time frame for studying the councils. Methodological suggestions included global history, fieldwork, virtual-reality reconstruction, maps, interdisciplinary work and critical borrowing from Western and Japanese scholarship. On sources, participants urged collecting foreign archives, Japanese and Russian materials, grassroots diaries, local inscriptions and technicians' notebooks, and treating memoirs with caution to avoid "survivor bias". The report concludes that future research should widen its scope to topics such as war and the ecological environment, social security, education and law, integrate methods across disciplines, and pursue "heterogeneity" by looking for what is changing and distinctive. It expects deeper disciplinary integration to make the field more comprehensive and to link it to Chinese and world history. Read the original if you want a map of current research agendas, gaps and source suggestions in Chinese-language scholarship on the CPC and the anti-Japanese war.

The Anti-Japanese National United Front as the basic guarantee of victory in the War of Resistance 抗日民族统一战线是抗战胜利的基本保证 Theoretical Study Group of the Party Leadership Group, Central Institute of Socialism Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), and the 90th anniversary of the August 1st Declaration and the Wayaobao meeting, this commentary asks why the Anti-Japanese National United Front deserves to be called the basic guarantee of victory. The authors, a Party theory study group at the Central Institute of Socialism, answer that the Front, led by the Communist Party of China, turned a divided China into a united force against aggression. The piece was published in Qiushi, 2025 no. 16. The text is organised in three parts: the Front as the political foundation of victory, as its foundation of strength, and as the creator of a favourable external environment. It draws on the 1935 declaration and the Wayaobao Politburo meeting, the shift from opposing Chiang Kai-shek to pressing and then allying with him, the Xi'an Incident, the Southern Anhui Incident of 1941, and the building of an international anti-fascist front. It closes with lessons for today, citing Xi Jinping's statements on the united front. The authors argue that the Party first proposed and promoted the broadest united front, contrasting this with what they describe as the Kuomintang government's retreat and passivity. Within the Front, they say, the Party held the leadership through independence and unity in resistance and the formula of developing progressive forces, winning over the middle forces and isolating the diehards. They credit the Front with coordinating the Kuomintang's frontal battlefield and the Communist-led battlefield behind enemy lines, mobilising the national bourgeoisie, enlightened gentry, ethnic minorities, religious figures and overseas Chinese, and turning the war into a people's war. Externally, they present the Party as pushing for an international anti-fascist front, culminating in the Declaration by United Nations (1942), and as drawing support from foreign doctors, journalists and fighters. The authors sum up the history as 'without the Communist Party, no Front; without the Front, no victory'. They draw four lessons: uphold Party leadership, the theme of great unity, the correct handling of unity and diversity, and sound tactics. They call for further developing the patriotic united front of the new era to gather the strength of Chinese at home and abroad for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party's official narrative links the wartime united front to present-day united front work.

Empowering the dissemination of the Party's innovative theory with generative AI 以生成式人工智能赋能党的创新理论传播 Zhang Wenjun This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how generative AI can help spread the Party's innovative theory when communication is shifting from broad coverage to precise reach. Zhang argues that AI can build detailed audience profiles and tailor content to each group. In Zhang's account, this addresses the "last mile" problem of moving audiences from knowing a theory to endorsing and practising it. The article proceeds in five steps: building audience profiles with intelligent technology; keeping a people-centred orientation; explaining theory in language audiences know; delivering it through the right channels and at the right times; and forming a communication–feedback–iteration loop. It ends with a short assessment of what this represents. Zhang says profiles draw on explicit data, such as registration and reading time, and implicit data, such as social-media topics and sentiment, and are updated continuously. On this basis, content can be adapted: anime-style material for young people, case-based reports for entrepreneurs, and picture-and-text items on local change for older people. Scene-specific content is another example, such as short videos for teachers. Zhang adds that AI can match platforms and timing to groups, and can assess behavioural, emotional and cognitive feedback to simplify or reformat material. Zhang presents building profiles as a way of listening to the people, in line with a people-centred approach. Zhang concludes that such tailored communication is a new exploration of popularising the Party's innovative theory in the intelligent age. It does not negate traditional methods but makes them more precise and vivid. Zhang holds that adhering to communication for the people while innovating through technology will strengthen the theory's guiding and cohesive power. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-school scholars frame AI-assisted ideological communication and audience targeting.

Promoting the connotative development of ideological and political theory courses in universities 推动高校思政课建设内涵式发展 Wu Lili This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) can improve in quality rather than simply expand. Wu Lili takes Xi Jinping's instruction to explain principles "deeply, thoroughly and vividly" as methodological guidance. The author argues that each of the three requirements corresponds to a distinct goal: theoretical depth, thoroughness and liveliness. The article is organised in three parts, one for each requirement. It links them in sequence: depth is the basis of thoroughness, and both underpin liveliness. Wu draws on the integration of ideological and political education across university, secondary and primary schooling, on Marx, Lenin and Xi, and on examples from the first-year course on ideology, morality and the rule of law. On "depth", Wu argues that university teachers should go beyond the secondary-school emphasis on memorising "what" something is. They should explain "why" through the unity of the historical and the logical, and "how it is possible" through practice, drawing on Marxist theory and on other disciplines. On "thoroughness", the author calls for teaching that responds to events, to the times and to current trends, so that students come to accept that the Party's success rests on Marxism adapted to China. On "liveliness", Wu proposes taking case material from students' everyday lives, replacing textbook and academic language with ordinary speech, and integrating mainstream discourse with the online language of students born after 2000. Wu concludes that these three steps together raise the pertinence, appeal and sense of benefit of the courses and help students grow into well-rounded people. Teachers are urged to keep up with Party theory, with students' characteristics and with technological change. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese university teaching of Marxist theory is framed methodologically.

The rise of the Global South and China's role An interview with the Indian-American scholar Vijay Prashad 全球南方的崛起与中国角色 Zhao Dingqi This is an interview conducted by Zhao Dingqi, a reporter for the journal, with Vijay Prashad, an Indian-American scholar. Prashad is executive director of the Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and chief correspondent of Globetrotter. The interview asks why the Global South has risen, what that rise means, and what part China plays in it. Prashad presents China as a country that escaped dependency and now helps others do so. The interview has three parts. The first covers Prashad's path to Marxism and the social contradictions of India: caste, unequal growth and a weakened communist movement. The second covers the origins of the term Global South, neocolonialism and dependency, China's development path, the Belt and Road Initiative and the 'experimental' character of socialist construction. The third covers the implications of Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025. Prashad traces the term to the 1980 Brandt Commission and the 1989 South Commission. He argues that the South has moved from an 'era of protest' against IMF austerity to an 'era of construction', marked by BRICS and the New Development Bank. Neocolonial structures persist through debt and low wages, which he calls a reproduction of colonial structure. In his reading, China escaped this because of the 1949 revolution and Mao Zedong-era socialist construction, which made the post-1978 reforms possible. He names 1949, 1978 and 2013 as the key years for understanding Chinese modernization. In 2013 the Belt and Road Initiative marked a turn from dependence on Northern markets towards building Southern ones. Prashad says the success of China's industrialisation has encouraged Indonesia, Bangladesh and African states. He describes socialism as experimental: flexible, willing to allow restricted private enterprise, and aimed at people's welfare and harmony between humans and nature. On Trump, Prashad argues that the United States has dropped 'idealism' for a Kissinger-style right-wing realism. In his view the imperialist structure is unchanged, Trump is no ally of the Global South, and Washington will try to block China's and other Southern states' development. He calls on the South to stay vigilant and organise, strengthening South–South cooperation and regional institutions. He also asks that cooperation be harmonious, so that even the weakest states benefit. Read the original if you want a Marxist scholar's account of the Global South, as presented to a Chinese academic readership, with views on China, the Belt and Road Initiative and US policy under Trump.

Theoretical explorations and practical dilemmas of Western economic democracy amid the crisis of neoliberalism A critical analysis based on the "Mondragon myth" 新自由主义危机下西方经济民主的理论探索与实践困境 Peng Yufeng Worker cooperatives and "economic democracy" have long been a goal of the Western left, resurfacing after each crisis of capitalism as a "third way" between capitalism and Soviet socialism. Peng Yufeng asks whether the Mondragon Corporation in Spain's Basque Country, the most celebrated test case, actually bears out that hope. The article argues that the "Mondragon myth" is an ideological construct: the firm's recent record shows the limits of economic democracy under capitalism, and Western media use it to lend capitalism an inclusive face. The article first reviews left theorists of economic democracy, including John Roemer, Tom Malleson, Gar Alperovitz, Richard Wolff and David Schweickart, and the debates around them, such as Francis Fukuyama's and Roemer's doubts about efficiency and financing. It then turns to Western media coverage of Mondragon from 2020 to 2024 (Fortune, The New York Times, The New Yorker, The Guardian, The Christian Science Monitor). Finally it examines Mondragon's structure, finances and internal tensions, drawing on critical researchers such as Sharryn Kasmir. Peng's central move is to read Mondragon through Marx and Engels's twofold judgement of cooperatives. They praised cooperatives as a breach in the capitalist mode of production, since workers show they can manage production themselves. They also warned against illusions about them: under private ownership, cooperatives become collective capitalists whose particular interest conflicts with the social interest, and they risk becoming a "cloak" for bourgeois deception. Peng then applies this to Mondragon. Its economic success rests on niche manufacturing, but the departure of the Fagor, Ulma and Orona cooperatives weakened it. Peng, following Kasmir, argues that its democracy is largely formal, with managers in control, and that member solidarity owes more to Basque nationalism than to workplace democracy. Only about a third of its roughly 70,000 staff are members, while the rest are employees without comparable protection. Peng describes this as a hierarchy of a "worker aristocracy" over precarious staff. Peng concludes that Mondragon has drifted towards ordinary private capitalist firms, offering little beyond job stability for a minority, and has become a spectacle of capitalist pluralism, an "emperor's new clothes" for the Western left. Its exemplary significance is, in Peng's view, very limited. Read the original if you are interested in a Chinese Marxist critique of Western market-socialist and cooperative theory, or in how Mondragon research is used in debates on alternatives to capitalism.

Security of mainstream ideology in the digital-intelligence era: challenges and countermeasures 数智时代主流意识形态安全：挑战与对策 Li Huijuan Wan Xiaopeng Li Huijuan and Wan Xiaopeng ask how mainstream ideology can be kept secure in the "digital-intelligence era", their term for a period shaped by big data, artificial intelligence and networked platforms. Citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called national security an important foundation for Chinese modernization, they treat ideological security as part of national security. Their thesis is that digital technologies have created new conditions and pressures for mainstream ideology, and that these call for Party leadership, technological adoption, talent building and stronger internet legislation. The article has three parts. It first describes four new conditions: information sources becoming decentralised, content fragmented, media carriers diversified, and communication effects maximised. It then sets out four challenges, and finally proposes four basic strategies. It draws on statements by Xi Jinping and on the Opinions on accelerating the deep integration of media development. On conditions, the authors argue that when the public both produces and receives information, mainstream media and authoritative bodies lose their monopoly on the microphone. Shallow, entertainment-led content, multimodal tools such as voice cloning and emotion recognition, and recommendation algorithms are said to trap individuals in "information cocoons" and "echo chambers". From this the authors derive the challenges: competing currents of thought that test Marxism's guiding position; mainstream media needing livelier discourse that keeps authority; the need for new propaganda platforms using 5G, big data, AI and blockchain; and a governance system able to break cocoons and algorithmic discrimination through legislation and technical improvement. The authors' strategies start with upholding Party management of ideology, with leading cadres taking responsibility and top-level design. They also call for applying digital technology to risk monitoring, content production, dissemination and feedback, and for training specialist talent, including influential opinion leaders, given a young online population led by the post-2000 generation. Their final strategy is stronger legislation, building on the Cybersecurity Law and on specific penalties such as those for defaming heroes and martyrs, because the internet is not a place beyond the law. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholars frame ideological security and governance of digital media.

What counts as a shift in Marx's thought? A debate with Liu Enzhi's "new rupture theory" of Marx 何为马克思的思想转变 Kong Weiyu Kong Weiyu responds to a recent claim by Liu Enzhi of Tsinghua University that Marx's view of capital matured, or broke with his earlier view, in 1847. Liu holds that texts such as Wage Labour and Capital and The Poverty of Philosophy mark a new "production-relations view of capital". Kong accepts that Marx's understanding of capital changed in 1847 but denies that this was a rupture. The article's wider question is by what criteria any shift in Marx's thought should be judged. The article has three parts. The first sets out Liu's argument and Kong's objections. The second surveys Chinese debates over "one shift" and "two shifts" in Marx's development, and then international positions: Althusser's epistemological break, Hiromatsu Wataru's claim that Engels led the break, and the "continuity" view of Michael Quante and Marcello Musto. The third part proposes three criteria for a genuine shift and closes with Kong's own two-shift periodisation built on Marx's notebooks. Kong makes three main moves. First, judging Marx by his view of capital alone is partial, because a philosophy, an economics and a politics cannot be separated from one worldview. Second, Marx's "phenomenological" way of thinking predates 1847, and the new conception of capital came from his economic-history excerpts in the Gülich notebooks, which deepened the historical materialism of The German Ideology instead of breaking with it. Third, Kong criticises both Soviet textbook practice and Western "Marxology" as forms of "idea-first" method, and argues that no reading is free of ideology. The three criteria are a change in the underlying method, a theoretical crisis plus outside intellectual support, and a new worldview. Kong concludes that Marx's thought changed twice. The first shift ran from the "material interests" problem at the Rheinische Zeitung through the Paris notebooks and the 1844 Manuscripts. The second ran from the Brussels and Manchester notebooks to The German Ideology, which founded historical materialism, and then the Communist Manifesto. For Kong, Marx's later work deepens that method and is not a rupture. Read the original if you follow Chinese and international debates on periodising Marx's thought, or want a Chinese critique of Marxology and the MEGA2 editorial approach.

Shaping China's international image during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期中国国际形象的塑造 Wang Han Zhou Qian Wang and Zhou ask how China presented itself in international opinion during the War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45) and what that did for its standing. Opening with Xi Jinping's statement that victory restored China's great-power status and earned it respect and a high national reputation, they argue that China's active voice abroad helped win international sympathy, support and aid. The piece appeared in the China Social Sciences Today on 18 August 2025. The article sets out three channels of image-building. These are presenting the true picture and will of the resistance, using Chinese culture as a vehicle of influence, and using foreign media as a window for China's voice. Each is illustrated with examples of statements, exhibitions and press reports from the 1930s and 1940s. The authors cite Churchill, de Gaulle, the American officer Evans Carlson, the Japanese historian Inoue Kiyoshi and Anna Louise Strong as outside witnesses to the justice of China's cause and the discipline of the Communist-led forces. They describe cultural diplomacy: the 1935–36 London international exhibition of Chinese art, a 1940–41 exhibition in the Soviet Union, Mei Lanfang's performances and Gao Jianfu's anti-Japanese paintings in Macao and Hong Kong. On media, they point to coverage in The New York Times, The Times and Time, to Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China, and to the 1944 US Army Observation Group's report on Yan'an. The authors stress that American press attitudes shifted from "neutrality" early in the war to closer attention to the shared interests of anti-fascist states, which they say affected the US government and public. The authors conclude that the wartime experience of building a national image offers lessons for today. They propose that China should innovate its narrative mode in international communication in the new era and build an effective, powerful system for international opinion. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese academic commentary uses wartime history to frame present-day international communication.

The Marco Polo Bridge Incident as the starting point of the Chinese nation's all-out resistance to Japanese aggression 七七事变是中华民族全面抗击日本侵略者的起点 Zhao Xiuli Published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2025, this short commemorative commentary asks what the Incident of 7 July 1937 (the Marco Polo Bridge Incident) meant for China's War of Resistance. Zhao argues that it marked the start of the whole nation's resistance to Japan, and opens with Xi Jinping's warning against denying or distorting the history of aggression. The piece is organised under three headings: the Incident's role in bringing about the anti-Japanese national united front, in awakening the whole nation, and in raising the national spirit. It draws on Communist Party declarations of 1937, the reorganisation of the Red Army, a statement by Zhu De, and examples of wartime heroes. Zhao describes the Party calling for unity at once and the 15 July 1937 declaration on Guomindang–Communist cooperation. According to the author, the Red Army was renamed the Eighth Route Army and southern guerrillas became the New Fourth Army. In Zhao's account the Incident made the national contradiction between China and Japan the principal one, and Japanese bombing, the 'three alls' policy, the Nanjing atrocities and biological and chemical warfare tied each person's fate to the nation's. The Party, Zhao says, upheld the united front, opposed capitulation, put forward a line of all-out national resistance and a protracted-war strategy, and acted as the mainstay of victory. Zhao concludes that patriotism-centred national spirit was the decisive factor in victory and remains a spiritual driving force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author calls for deeper and broader academic research to refute Japanese denial of the history of aggression, and for remembering the martyrs. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Incident is presented in current Chinese commemorative writing.

The important role of "journalistic resistance" in the early War of Resistance against Japan 抗战初期“新闻抗战”发挥重要作用 Zhang Jiru This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks what part the press played in the early years of the War of Resistance against Japan. Zhang argues that Chinese journalists took up the pen as a weapon of resistance and built a "spiritual national defence front". In Zhang's account, "journalistic resistance" (xinwen kangzhan) and the related idea of "saving the nation through journalism" made a distinctive and irreplaceable contribution to the war effort. The article covers roughly 1936 to 1938, from the years before full-scale war to its first phase. It is organised in three parts: how the press community assembled in response to the national crisis; how a united front was built among journalists after full-scale war began; and the activities of the Chinese Youth Journalists' Association (known as "Qingji"), founded in Wuhan in 1938. Zhang's first move is to show journalists organising before the war: the Pingjin Journalism Society (January 1936), Yenching University's fifth and sixth journalism seminars, and a joint declaration issued on 2 October 1936 by more than twenty Shanghai and Nanjing newspapers. According to the article, news organisations in many other cities endorsed the declaration within about ten days. The second move is the wartime united front. Zhang cites 15 works on wartime journalism published in 1937–1938 and describes Wuhan as a national propaganda centre once major papers had relocated there. Qingji, with branches including Yan'an and Hong Kong, is presented as a journalists' united front operating under the anti-Japanese national united front. Zhang then lists Qingji's work: front-line reporting teams, welcome and send-off gatherings for war correspondents, and "reporters' forums" where Fan Changjiang urged that "national interest is above everything". It also published the journal Journalist, with special issues on war-time news policy and front-line newspapers. Zhang concludes that journalists did more than report the news. In the national crisis they took on the mission of saving the nation through journalism, and in doing so they helped steady public belief in eventual victory. The article treats the press as a distinct front in the war and ends by calling its contribution indelible. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned overview of how Chinese journalists organised themselves in 1936–1938 and how the Chinese Youth Journalists' Association is remembered in current Chinese historiography.

Responding to global challenges and advancing a multipolar world order 应对全球性挑战推动世界格局多极化 Feng Lin Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this newspaper commentary asks what the wartime alliance offers a postwar order now under strain. Feng argues that promoting a multipolar world, institutional equality and shared governance is a practical response to today's global challenges. The piece moves in three steps. It first recalls anti-fascist cooperation, citing the Chinese united front, the Soviet–American meeting on the Elbe in 1945 and Mexico's declaration of war on Germany. It then turns to the establishment of multilateralism through the UN Charter and the agencies that followed. Finally it surveys present-day multipolarity. Feng contends that states with different systems and cultures proved able to cooperate on the basis of shared justice, an experience the author links to the Chinese idea of harmony in diversity (hé ér bù tóng). The 1945 UN Charter, with sovereign equality and one vote per state in the General Assembly, is presented as the institutional result. The 1951 San Francisco conference, which excluded China and was boycotted by the Soviet Union, is described as a deviation that hardened into structural injustice. Today, the author says, BRICS states, the Global South, the European Union and the Belt and Road Initiative are strengthening multipolarity. Feng concludes that multipolarity does not harm any country's interests but ends unilateralism and builds a fairer order of joint governance, which the author calls tianxia gongzhi. Developing powers and traditional powers should both take part in reforming global governance. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese academic frames the anti-fascist war's legacy in support of multipolarity and multilateralism.

Inheriting and promoting the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression in the new era 在新时代继承和弘扬伟大抗战精神 Pu Duanhua Published in the China Social Sciences Today on 15 August 2025, this commentary asks where the "great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression" came from, what it consists of, and how it should be carried on today. Pu Duanhua argues that the spirit is a concentrated expression of the Chinese national spirit in the War of Resistance. In Pu's view it has lasting value that must be cherished and promoted. The piece has three parts. The first traces the spirit's origins. The second sets out its four defining qualities, using President Xi Jinping's formulation. The third draws four lessons for the present drive to build a strong country and achieve national rejuvenation. Pu supports the account with episodes from the war, such as the death of Yang Jingyu, the "Five Heroes of Langya Mountain" and the "Eight Hundred Heroes", and with the figure of more than 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties. Pu locates three sources of the spirit: the bloody struggle of the Chinese people after the 1931 Mukden Incident, the sublimation of the Chinese national spirit, and the firm leadership of the Communist Party of China. Pu stresses the Party's role as the "mainstay" of the war. In Pu's account, the Party raised the banner of armed resistance, upheld the anti-Japanese national united front and put forward the strategy of protracted war. The four qualities are patriotism ("everyone is responsible for the fate of the nation"), moral integrity in the face of death, heroism in fighting to the end, and unshakeable confidence in victory. Pu presents patriotism as the decisive factor in the victory. Pu concludes that building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization is a relay race requiring the same spirit. Pu calls for four things: stronger consciousness of following the Party; unity through patriotism, national unity and the unification of the motherland; self-reliance and self-strengthening; and a readiness to struggle against risks and challenges. Pu ties the first of these to upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee. Read the original if you want an example of how a military-academy leader links the memory of the anti-Japanese war to current Party leadership and national rejuvenation themes.

The evolving logic of Party building leading the modernization of primary-level governance in the new era 新时代党建引领基层治理现代化的逻辑演进 Sun Shaoyong Xiao Jianxun Sun Shaoyong and Xiao Jianxun ask how "Party building leading the modernization of primary-level governance" should be understood as a political concept that has developed over time. The concept entered central documents in 2021 and was repeated at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The authors argue that existing studies are mostly static and that a dynamic account is needed. They conclude that the concept is a distinctively Chinese governance paradigm and grounded in the Party's self-reform. The article first reviews three strands of earlier scholarship: a "generative" account, an "advantage" account that stresses the Party's ability to overcome bureaucratic dilemmas, and a "model" account built on local case studies. It then applies a three-part framework of logical foundation, logical mechanism and logical pathway. The foundation is traced through theory, history from the revolutionary base areas to reform-era village and residents' self-government, and the shift in discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The mechanism and pathway are developed in the later sections. Sun and Xiao treat the concept as a concrete form of "using the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution". They identify "Party suspension from grassroots society", meaning the Party's detachment in terms of actors, capacity, values and resources, as the starting problem. They also name three governance difficulties: structural imbalance, missing governance actors and weak capacity. They add that weaknesses in primary-level Party organizations are the main point of leverage. The shift from "Party leadership of primary-level governance" to "Party-building guidance" is described as a move from rigid leadership to a softer guiding role that gives more weight to local autonomy. Four practical pathways follow: political guidance (including "Party building plus" models such as building-based and business-district Party work), ideological education (including value consensus and moral governance), organizational construction (cross-organization platforms and mobilization mechanisms) and capacity building (political ability and service ability, including digital tools). The authors conclude that primary-level governance is the foundation of national governance and that Party building plays a fundamental role in late-developing modernizing countries. They contend that Western society-centred, corporatist and state-centred approaches cannot resolve government, market and social failure at the grassroots. In their view, the Chinese approach also differs from Western bureaucratic models because the Party and the government are not separate. Read the original if you want a systematic, official-line account of how Chinese scholars justify and periodise Party-led grassroots governance, including its concepts and local practices.

The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of combining political work with economic work, and its significance 中国共产党坚持政治工作与经济工作相结合的探索历程及其意义 Wang Yu Liu Libo Wang Yu and Liu Libo ask how the Chinese Communist Party has handled the relationship between political work and economic work, which they treat as the two most important practices of social governance. They argue that the Party has consistently combined the two in every period. In their account, this combination secured victory in the New Democratic Revolution and underlies the 'two miracles' of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. The article first defines the terms. 'Political work' here mainly means ideological and political work, which the authors place in the realm of the relations of production and the superstructure. It then traces the practice through the revolutionary years, the socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It closes with the theoretical significance of the practice. The authors draw on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The authors' central claim is that political work stands in a relationship of service and guarantee to economic work, not one of leadership over it. It secures the socialist direction of economic work, supplies spiritual motivation and helps create a harmonious social environment. Economic work in turn gives political work its material basis. They illustrate this with the principle of material interests in political education, the Yan'an production campaign, and Deng's call to attend to both material and spiritual civilization. They also name costs when the balance failed: neglect of economic work in some socialist-era years, and weak ideological work in the 1980s. For the new era, they list five contributions to Chinese modernization: political direction, ideological consensus, internal motivation, all-round human development and social stability. The authors present the practice as a creative development of historical materialism, building on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao. They say it offers lessons for socialist countries, which should avoid both over-politicization and a one-sided pursuit of economic interest. They conclude that proletarian parties can win popular support and strengthen confidence in socialism only by combining the two kinds of work under Party leadership. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-history account of how ideological work and economic work have been linked in official thinking, from Mao to Xi Jinping.

Deng Xiaoping's creative contribution to the world socialist movement 邓小平对世界社会主义运动的创造性贡献 Sun Jinsong Sun Jinsong asks what Deng Xiaoping's concept of the 'Chinese model' (Zhongguo de moshi) contributed to the history of the world socialist movement. The article argues that Deng was the first to use the term explicitly and that, with the successful opening of socialism with Chinese characteristics, it marks a creative contribution to scientific socialism. In Sun's view, the Soviet model and the 'Chinese model' represent two stages of socialist practice: a founding period and a new period of deeper exploration. The article has three parts. The first traces Deng's use of the term from 1980 to 1988, including his remarks to foreign leaders, and sets out six dimensions of its meaning: concept, content, lineage, time and space, frame of reference, and level of understanding. The second examines its intellectual sources in Mao Zedong Thought and in Party experience. The third places the concept within the world history of scientific socialism, including the Soviet model and the reform attempts in Eastern Europe. Sun argues that Deng treated 'the Chinese model', 'taking our own road' and 'socialism with Chinese characteristics' as equivalent expressions. According to Sun, the concept rests on Mao's principles of seeking truth from facts and independence, and is defined against two reference points: the Western model, from which it differs in essence, and the Soviet model, from which it differs only within a shared Marxist framework. Sun describes scientific socialism as passing through three stages: the founding of the theory by Marx and Engels, the Soviet model after 1917, and the Chinese path opened at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The Soviet model, in the article's account, supplied the first socialist standard and inspired anti-colonial struggles in Asia, Africa and Latin America, but became rigid and ended in collapse. Sun adds that the Eastern European reform paths failed, whereas China's path combined Marxist direction with selective use of capitalist instruments, such as a socialist market economy. Sun concludes that the 'Chinese model' moved socialist practice from the general to the particular. It freed world socialism from the constraint of a single model and opened an era in which several paths coexist. The author quotes Xi Jinping's 2013 statement that the so-called 'China model' was created by the Chinese people themselves and is not a product to be exported. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school account of how Deng's 'Chinese model' is placed in the lineage of Mao Zedong Thought and the history of world socialism.

Strengthening the ideological guiding force of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics in the new era 增强新时代中国特色社会主义文化的思想引领力 Xing Yunwen This newspaper commentary (Economic Daily, 14 August 2025) asks how culture can be made more prosperous and China made a cultural power. Xing Yunwen argues that the key is to strengthen the ideological guiding force of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, which the author treats as culture's core competitiveness. The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks at a Politburo study session on developing a culture with strong ideological guiding force, spiritual cohesion, value appeal and international influence. The article has three parts. The first explains why ideas form the core of culture. The second reads the Party's hundred-year history as a record of ideological leadership, from the New Culture Movement to the successive cultural goals set in each period. The third turns to present tasks: the Two Integrations, and arming society with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Xing contends that, on the historical-materialist view, the material basis of any culture is its mode of production while its inner core is a system of ideas; Marxism is said to be the core of socialist culture and the source of its advanced character. As cultural exchange and rivalry intensify, the author sees the contest for discursive power as a contest for ideological high ground, which requires continued theoretical innovation by the Party. The author holds that the "second integration", of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, is the premise of this innovation and that socialist culture is itself a product of the Two Integrations. Xing concludes that cultural work must uphold Marxism's guiding position and the Party's cultural leadership, deepen study of Xi Jinping Thought, and foster two-way interaction between ideas and cultural vehicles. The aim is to strengthen the people's spiritual strength and the cultural foundations of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link cultural strategy to ideological leadership.
