Carrying the building of Party conduct through to the end 将作风建设进行到底 Fang Wenhao Fang Wenhao, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, argues that the Party's conduct (zuofeng) is its calling card and bears on its image, popular support and survival. The commentary holds that the building of Party conduct must be carried on without letup, because the core of conduct problems is the relationship between the Party and the people. The piece opens with the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012), and its campaign against formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance. It then moves through historical models of good conduct, from the Central Soviet Area and the Long March to Yan'an and figures such as Gu Wenchang, Jiao Yulu and Yang Shanzhou, before turning to practical measures. Fang treats the distinction between public and private as the basic yardstick of correct conduct. In this reading, vanity projects, cliques and nepotism all come down to self-interest, and public funds and public power must never be used privately. Because conduct problems are really problems of Party spirit, the author calls for education in Party spirit, ideals and convictions, and systematic theoretical study. Fang also urges institutional rules that are targeted, enforceable and equally binding, with no exceptions or "hidden doors". The author further calls for tackling the main contradiction within each of the four undesirable work styles and watching for their new variants. Leading cadres, the "key minority", are asked to set an example in self-discipline and in family conduct. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party-building commentary in 2025 links the eight-point regulation to the public–private distinction and to institutional discipline.

Upholding political principle is a fundamental requirement of a Marxist party 讲政治是马克思主义政党的根本要求 Lu Jie Lu Jie takes up the Party's call to "talk politics" (jiang zhengzhi), meaning to stand firm on political principle. The commentary argues that this is a defining feature of Marxist parties and a consistent political strength of the Communist Party of China. Party members and officials, Lu says, should grasp it through theoretical, historical and practical logic. The short piece first sets out the theoretical basis in the nature of a Marxist party and its organisational principle. It then turns to history: the Paris Commune, Lenin and the Bolsheviks, the Soviet collapse, and the Chinese Party's stages from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. It closes with what officials should do in the new era. Lu contends that Marxism gives the proletarian party its direction, so political discipline keeps the Party on the people's side and unites its members under democratic centralism. Historically, Lu reads the Paris Commune's fall as a lack of centralisation and authority, and the Soviet collapse as a party that stopped talking politics and became a privileged stratum. For the present, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds are presented as the main political outcomes and markers of this principle. Lu lists five requirements for officials: theoretical study, the "three political capacities" of judgement, understanding and execution, a people-first stance, a sound view of performance, and self-discipline with integrity. Lu concludes that the Party's strength rests on strict organisational discipline and unified will and action. In practice, Lu says, this means upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee, carrying out its political line and observing its political discipline, so that it becomes a "truly iron-like organisation". Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present political loyalty as a Marxist requirement.

Showing the world a vibrant Red China Chinese Communists as seen by British and American journalists in China during the War of Resistance 向世界展现一个生机勃勃的红色中国 Zhong Zhouming This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2025, asks how British and American journalists who reached Yan'an and other anti-Japanese base areas during the War of Resistance (1937–1945) portrayed the Chinese Communists. Zhong argues that these reporters broke the Kuomintang's news blockade, gave the world a complete and truthful picture of the Communists, and supplied further evidence that the Communist Party was the mainstay of the nation's resistance. The article draws on the accounts of Gunther Stein, Harrison Forman, James Bertram, Agnes Smedley, Theodore White, Nym Wales, Freda Utley and Israel Epstein. It is organised in four thematic sections: whether the Communist-led armies actually fought, mass mobilisation, the democratic practices of the base areas, and comparisons between the Communists and the Kuomintang. Zhong's first move is to present the journalists' testimony as a rebuttal of Kuomintang claims that the Eighth Route and New Fourth Armies resisted without fighting. The author cites Stein's figures of 115,120 engagements between 1937 and March 1945 and Forman's remark that "we saw with our own eyes that the Eighth Route Army fights". The second move is to read the reporters' descriptions of organised and armed villagers, wall slogans, theatre and local elections as evidence of the Party's mass line and of working democracy. White, for example, saw the Party's strength in its tie to the peasantry. Finally, the author notes that many reporters had first stayed in Chongqing, so they compared the two parties. White judged that the Communists shone by contrast, and reporters described the leaders as frugal and selfless. Zhong concludes that these first-hand reports changed domestic and international opinion of the Communists. In the author's account, the observers saw the Yan'an model as showing China's direction and the Party as the leader of China's future, and history has borne out those judgments. The piece is a brief, affirmative use of foreign eyewitness sources to support the Party's wartime narrative. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Chinese Party-history writing uses Western journalists' testimony, and which names and quotations it selects.

A dialogue on the relationship between Western Marxism and imperialism 关于西方马克思主义与帝国主义之间关系的对话 John Bellamy Foster Gabriel Rockhill This is a Chinese translation of a written dialogue between the American Marxists John Bellamy Foster and Gabriel Rockhill. They ask how "Western Marxism" (a specific theoretical formation) differs from Marxism simply practised in the West, and how it relates to imperialism. Both argue that Western Marxism is rooted in the imperialist core and is better described as "Marxism of imperialism" or Eurocentric Marxism. The exchange has three parts. The first separates the two terms and draws on Domenico Losurdo's critique. The second sets out the "fourfold departure" of Western Marxism, with Foster recalling his graduate studies and Perry Anderson's Considerations on Western Marxism. The third turns to Eurocentrism, imperialist theory, and Herbert Marcuse as a test case, and ends with a 1963 letter from Paul Baran. Foster contends that the Western Marxist philosophical tradition abandoned the dialectics of nature and ontological materialism, and so broke with Marx and Engels. He lists four departures: from class analysis, from the critique of imperialism, from nature, materialism and science, and from reason. Rockhill adds a turn from political economy to cultural analysis and hostility to actually existing socialism. Drawing on Lenin's account of the "labour aristocracy", Rockhill reads these tendencies as products of the material conditions of intellectual production in imperialist states. He cites funding from capitalist foundations and state agencies, including Rockefeller money for a "Marxism-Leninism Project" involving Marcuse. Both insist the critique be dialectical. Marcuse, for example, is treated as radical in some respects even though he did not escape the fourfold departure. They conclude that Western Marxism should give way to a "global" or "universal" Marxism grounded in anti-imperialist struggles in the Global South. They call overcoming the fourfold departure an urgent task of theoretical class struggle amid a new Cold War. They describe this task as rebuilding historical materialism as revolutionary theory and practice. Read the original if you want a polemical, Marxist-internal critique of Anderson, Adorno, Marcuse, Badiou and Žižek, or want to see how Western authors framed this debate for a Chinese theoretical journal.

Subject, object and history under digital technology How contemporary Western Marxist theory has developed Marx's philosophy of technology 数字技术下的主体、物和历史 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang asks how contemporary Western Marxist and critical theorists have extended Marx's thinking about technology in the age of digital capitalism. Opening with Bernard Stiegler's retelling of the Prometheus myth, the article argues that technology is never a neutral tool but is embedded in power structures and historical processes. Lan's thesis is that Marx's historical materialism remains the guiding framework, while its concepts of subject, object and history have had to be rebuilt for data, algorithms and artificial intelligence. The article is organised in three parts, followed by a conclusion. The first treats technology and the subject, moving from the industrial subject to what Lan calls the intelligent subject. The second treats technology and the thing, tracing the machine from Marx's early manuscripts to Gilbert Simondon's technical object and its digital successors. The third treats technology and history, asking whether the crisis of capitalism leads forward or backward. Thinkers discussed include Guattari, Lazzarato, Negri, Dyer-Witheford, Deleuze, Stiegler, Yuk Hui, Žižek, McKenzie Wark, Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean. On the subject, Lan argues that Marx's subject is the worker bound to the machine, and that today's subject is successively encoded, linked into networks and controlled. On the thing, Lan contends that Marx, even in the 1861–63 manuscripts, still kept a subject–object scheme in which the machine is a mere mediator. Simondon, Stiegler, Hui and Žižek, in Lan's account, dissolve this scheme, so that the digital object and the wired brain merge human and thing in a network of information. On history, Lan notes that Marx never fully explains why capitalism's collapse must lead to socialism rather than regression. Techno-feudalism (Wark, Varoufakis) answers that cloud rent-seeking marks a backward step. Dean replies that capital is digging its own grave and that the broad direction remains progressive. Lan concludes that these theorists, despite thin historical verification, supplement Marx's view of history in step with the times and offer reference points for Chinese modernization. The article calls on Chinese scholars to draw on the "foreign voices" of these thinkers while building an independent Chinese system of knowledge. It also proposes a Chinese approach of "holding to the mean" in the wave of big data and AI, avoiding both technological radicalism and stagnation. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical reading of Simondon, Stiegler, techno-feudalism and Dean's debate with Wark as extensions of Marx on technology.

The rise of financial capitalism and the end of Western Marxism On methodological questions in the study of Western Marxism 金融资本主义的兴起与西方马克思主义的终结 Li Qiankun Li Qiankun takes up the long-running Chinese debate over the 'logical end' of Western Marxism and argues that shifts in its philosophical method reflect changes in capitalist reality. The article holds that classical Western Marxism corresponded to state monopoly capitalism, and that its decline followed capitalism's turn to financialization after the 1970s. This is an abridged version of an article from the Journal of Nanjing University (2024, no. 5). The article begins with the Chinese dispute. One side confines Western Marxism to the humanist line from Lukács to Adorno's Negative Dialectics. The other defines it broadly and treats postmodern Marxism and post-Marxism as its diversification. Li notes that both sides link Western Marxism to post-1970s capitalist change, and cites Perry Anderson, Susan Strange and David Graeber as making similar judgements abroad. It then sets out the shift to financialization and its intellectual effects, and closes with methodological lessons for Chinese research. Li's first move ties Lukács, the early Frankfurt School, and even Althusser (as read by the French regulation school) to state monopoly or state capitalism from the 1920s to the 1960s. After the Bretton Woods collapse and stagflation, neoliberalism, deregulation and financialization recomposed class relations, weakened the labour movement and gave rise to identity politics. Li argues that this undermined the subject–object identity dialectic and the critiques of reification and ideology built on commodity production, while money became a central concern. The second move is the left's discourse turn towards credit-money theory: Harvey, Graeber and the regulation school, then Deleuze and Guattari on desire, Baudrillard on symbolic exchange, and Negri, Hardt and Lazzarato on immaterial labour. Li concludes that Marxism's totalizing method, which crosses the boundaries between philosophy, political economy and social theory, is the right way to examine this history. Li reads the present 'great changes unseen in a century' as the exhaustion of the post-1970s accumulation model, while socialism with Chinese characteristics presents a different situation. Chinese scholars should therefore examine Western Marxist categories in their historical context, since applying them uncritically would be like 'marking the boat to find the sword'. Li also urges them to drop an apprentice mentality and research with confidence and equality. Read the original if you want a Chinese account that links the history of Western Marxism to the stages of capitalism, or if you follow how Chinese scholars frame Western Marxism methodologically.

Strengthening the rule-of-law foundations of the unified national market 夯实全国统一大市场的法治根基 Hu Ming Writing in the Economic Daily in August 2025, Hu Ming asks how law can help push forward the building of a unified national market, which the article presents as a major strategic decision of the Party Central Committee. Hu argues that the rule of law should lead, regulate and safeguard this effort, and that it should focus on remaining difficulties. The commentary notes recent legal and policy steps, including the Fair Competition Review Regulations and the 2025 negative list for market access. It cites the sixth meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, which set out the requirement of "five unifications and one opening". The text is organised under three headings: the boundary between government and market, basic market institutions, and reform of factor markets. Hu first argues that law should define the line between government and market. Hu says the market should handle what it can, and government should address what the market cannot manage, while local protectionism and inconsistent enforcement are corrected. Next, Hu calls for stronger property protection, a single national negative list, bankruptcy and exit rules, and social credit legislation. Finally, Hu proposes deeper market-oriented reform of factor markets: revising laws and hukou rules for a unified urban-rural labour market, and data legislation to build a nationally integrated data market. Hu concludes that unified rules, consistent enforcement and open factor flows, all anchored in law, are needed to deepen the unified national market. Hu also links this to aligning domestic rules with high international economic and trade standards. Read the original if you want a concise official-line statement of the legal measures proposed for market unification in 2025.

Economic construction in the anti-Japanese democratic base areas and its lessons 抗日民主根据地经济建设及经验启示 Wu Minchao This newspaper commentary asks how the Communist-led anti-Japanese democratic base areas, mostly behind enemy lines and short of resources, managed economic construction during the War of Resistance. Wu Minchao argues that this construction carried a double mission: supplying the armed forces for a protracted war and relieving the hardship of the local population. In Wu's account, only by balancing the two could the Party build the popular cohesion that underpinned victory. The article is organised in three parts: the policy of fighting and producing at the same time; placing the people's interests first; and unity between army and people. Its main case is the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, with references to the Jin-Sui, Jin-Cha-Ji, Shandong and Central China bases, and to Anhui. It ends with general lessons for the present. Wu traces the Great Production Movement to earlier preparation, from small-scale production by garrison troops, through Mao Zedong's 1939 call for people to rely on their own hands, to the 1940 Central Committee directive and the Nanniwan land reclamation by the 359th Brigade in 1941. The article cites Mao's claim that each soldier needed only three months of farming a year, and says the movement spread even to front-line and guerrilla areas. Wu then describes how the Party put the people first: land reclamation (97 万 mu, or 970,000 mu, against a plan of 390,000 in 1943), a dyke built by 210,000 labourers in central Anhui, and cooperatives. Wu presents Mao's instruction that officials spend ninety per cent of their effort helping peasants produce and ten per cent collecting taxes as an expression of the mass line. According to the article, this earned popular support, contrasted with corruption the author attributes to the Nationalists, and trained cadres for later economic work. Wu concludes that three conditions made the base areas' economic work succeed: emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, relying closely on the masses to develop the economy and improve livelihoods, and cadres sharing hardships with the people. These lessons are presented as relevant to building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation today, through innovation, people's livelihood and unity, together with independence and self-reliance. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how the Great Production Movement is now presented in Chinese public history and how it is tied to present-day policy themes.

Comprehensive thinking: the methodology of the Communist Party of China in the new era 全面性思维：新时代中国共产党的方法论 Wu Chaobang Ding Bangwen Wu and Ding take up a methodological question: how can thought grasp reality well enough to guide practice, and what mode of thinking does the Communist Party of China rely on to do so? They argue that "comprehensive thinking" (quanmianxing siwei) has grown from a summary of experience into a methodology with Chinese characteristics, and that it is the core thinking method of the Party in the new era. The piece appeared in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025. The article begins with the frequency of the word "comprehensive" (quanmian) in the reports to the 19th (2017) and 20th (2022) Party Congresses, which it counts at 96 and 109 occurrences. It then places comprehensive thinking within Marxist epistemology and the traditional idea of the unity of knowing and doing. Next it relates it to the specific thinking methods Xi Jinping has put forward, and it ends by assessing its practical necessity today. The authors make two main moves. First, they argue that comprehensiveness should not be treated as a mere sub-feature of dialectical thinking, as the standard triad of connection, development and comprehensiveness has it. In their view, dialectical thinking centres on principal contradictions, whereas comprehensive thinking attends to the whole system of contradictions, secondary ones included, and so avoids either-or metaphysics. Second, they hold that the "five" and then "six" thinking methods (strategic, historical, systemic, rule-of-law, bottom-line, people-centred and innovative thinking) each have limits. Comprehensive thinking, they say, integrates them through multi-angle analysis, multi-means verification and multi-party coordination, working at the cognitive, practical and value levels. They present Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a model case, citing the five-sphere integrated plan, the Four-pronged Strategy and a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors conclude that comprehensive thinking answers three needs. It offers a way to resolve the "development paradox" of unbalanced and inadequate development. It is a strategic choice for a changing world, in which they say it goes beyond zero-sum Western-centrism. It also supports building an autonomous Chinese system of knowledge. They expect it to keep guiding the drive towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars frame a thinking method as a distinct methodology within Xi Jinping's theory.

The meaning of "whole-process supervision of the exercise of power" “全过程监督权力运行”的内涵阐释 Zhao Fuhao This short commentary in Guangming Daily explains a formulation Xi Jinping put forward at the 21st collective study session of the Political Bureau of the 20th Central Committee: "whole-process supervision of the exercise of power". Zhao presents it as a summing-up of the Party's experience of supervising power, and as a result of innovation in theory, practice and institutions for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The author argues that it gives guidance for the Party's self-reform. Zhao first lists reasons for studying the formulation, including improving the rules system for self-reform, keeping close ties with the people, solving problems unique to a large party, and modernizing national governance. The article then reads the formulation through four dimensions drawn from Xi's 2023 speech: full coverage of content, of objects, of responsibility chains and of institutions. On content, Zhao holds that such supervision is essentially political supervision. It covers implementation of the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, central decisions, correct operation of power under democratic centralism, and corruption that mixes political and economic problems. On objects, it reaches Party organisations, members, cadres and all public officials, with leading cadres as the focus, through disciplinary, supervisory, resident-inspection and inspection tours. On responsibility chains, supervision runs through authorisation, use and restraint of power, or before, during and after the event, as in budget review, execution and audit. On institutions, Party regulations, state law, mass and media supervision, and the chain of responsibilities must be linked. Zhao concludes that the formulation shows the Party's deepening understanding of checking power. The author calls for stricter enforcement of rules, full democratic centralism, coordination among supervising bodies, technology to remove blind spots, and focus on key areas and the "key minority". Read the original if you want a brief official-style outline of how Party theorists frame power supervision within Party-building.

The ideological and political education functions of red literature and art 红色文艺的思想政治教育功能 Hong Weicheng This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (11 August 2025) asks what role red literature and art play in ideological and political education. Hong argues that, in the strategic context of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a world undergoing changes unseen in a century, stressing these functions is a necessary requirement for developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised around four functions: political guidance, the transmission of spirit, character formation and spiritual motivation. Each section is built on quotations from Xi Jinping on culture and the arts, supported by examples of novels, songs and films from different periods. Hong contends that red literature and art, as part of Party propaganda and ideological work, strengthen political identification and help guide social thinking, showing in works why the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics succeed. They are also presented as the vehicle for "red genes", letting younger people experience revolutionary history directly. On character, Hong cites works from the early People's Republic and the early reform and opening up period, such as the novel The Builders and the film Lushan Romance, as shaping patriotism and hard work. On motivation, the author points to the films Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy (2014) and the Battle at Lake Changjin series (2021), which reworked earlier classics and drew audiences across generations. Hong concludes that red literature and art give the era its backbone and take its temperature, and that they inspire the people to strive for the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars currently justify the educational role of revolutionary-themed culture.

The Communist Party's comprehensive construction of the rural base areas in North China 中国共产党对华北农村根据地的全面建设 Huo Hongwei This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how the Communist Party turned the rural areas behind Japanese lines in North China into a foundation for victory in the War of Resistance. Huo Hongwei argues that, by mobilising the masses and rebuilding the traditional countryside in politics, the economy and culture, the Party organised scattered human and material resources and laid a solid basis for final victory. The piece opens with the situation after the Lugouqiao (Marco Polo Bridge) Incident, when Japan's full-scale invasion and the Nationalists' rapid retreat left the nation, in Huo's words, at its most dangerous moment. It then takes the three fields in turn: the building of democratic government, the improvement of the rural economy, and cultural work. The Jin-Cha-Ji border region serves as the main example. On politics, Huo describes mass semi-governmental bodies giving way to border-region governments chosen by democratic election, down to village level. These were organised on the "three-thirds system" and, the author says, combined a united-front character with people's democracy. Turnout in the 1940 elections is given as over 70 per cent, and above 90 per cent in core areas, with women voting for the first time. On the economy, rent and interest reduction, mass mobilisation for production and mutual-aid cooperation raised productivity and moved scattered peasant households towards cooperative forms the author calls socialist in character. On culture, winter schools, night schools, literacy classes, wall newspapers and the arts were all, Huo says, tied to the single task of defeating Japan. Huo concludes that this all-round construction aroused national consciousness and patriotic enthusiasm, drew Japan's forces into a "sea" of people's war, and produced villages of a New Democratic character that served as a basis for the founding of New China. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party history presents the North China base areas' political, economic and cultural work.

Forging a high-calibre contingent of grassroots cadres 锻造高素质基层干部队伍 Xu Dongtao This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2025, asks how to build a high-calibre body of grassroots cadres at a time when grassroots tasks are heavy and demanding. Xu Dongtao argues that the Party should clearly signal that it values, cares for and protects grassroots cadres, and should work on five fronts at once. The article is organised around five "emphases": Party spirit and ideological grounding, the original aspiration and mission (closeness to the masses), practical needs, scientific and professional competence, and a results-based incentive system. Each section names a shortcoming Xu sees among some cadres and then lists measures that localities could try. On the first two fronts, Xu calls for selecting cadres by "both ability and integrity, with integrity first", for lectures on Party spirit by exemplary young cadres, and for short videos of their stories. Against superficial home visits, Xu proposes "people's-feelings diaries", regular analysis meetings at village, township and county levels, and periodic service weeks. On the third and fourth fronts, Xu criticises a "one mould for all" approach to training and proposes local surveys of development, reform and public needs, alongside annual rotational training and secondments to developed regions. The fifth front concerns incentives, with special recruitment drives for grassroots cadres, two-way secondments between grassroots and higher levels, and wider exchanges across prefectures and the province. Xu concludes that these measures together would strengthen Party spirit, mass awareness, practical orientation, professional ability and motivation among grassroots cadres. The proposals are framed as options for local trial, mentioning new quality productive forces and the modernization of governance as targets. Read the original if you want a concise inventory of the concrete cadre-training and selection measures currently proposed for grassroots governance in China.

Integrating the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community into legislation in ethnic minority areas Strengthening forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation through local legislation 推动铸牢中华民族共同体意识融入民族地区立法 Feng Zhidong Feng Zhidong's short commentary (China Social Sciences Today, 6 August 2025) asks how local legislation in ethnic minority areas can serve the task of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, which the author calls the main theme of the Party's ethnic work in the new era. Feng argues that since the 2015 revision of the Legislation Law, such areas have produced locally suited laws, but that "legislative formalism", meaning omnibus and repetitive legislation, limits their effect. The piece sets out four lines of improvement, framed by the principle of national legal unity and the guidance of the 20th Party Congress (2022) on scientific, democratic and law-based legislation. It closes with a note that it is an interim result of a Gansu provincial social science project on local legislation in the province's ethnic areas. Feng's first two proposals concern who leads. Party committees in ethnic areas should put legislative planning on their agendas and focus on gaps and conflict points in local law. People's congresses, not government departments, should lead drafting, so as to contain the risk of "departmental interests becoming law"; provincial congresses should review annual plans and refuse approval to repetitive or omnibus projects. The third and fourth proposals concern craft: precise topic selection (for example rural environmental problems), workable content that balances national legal unity with legitimate local interests, and concise texts, citing Xi Jinping's advice to enact only as many articles as needed. Coordinated legislation among neighbouring areas, through joint meetings, would reduce imitation and duplication. Feng concludes that coordination can only resolve differences between adjacent areas. The deeper problem of legislative formalism, in the author's view, requires a change in how ethnic areas understand legislative values, concepts and, above all, performance goals. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-line view of how local lawmaking in ethnic regions is meant to support national unity policy.

Engels's thought on modernization and its contemporary value 恩格斯的现代化思想及其当代价值 Liu Jun Marking the 130th anniversary of Engels's death, Liu Jun asks what his work offers for understanding modernization. Liu notes that Engels never used the term itself, but argues that his analyses of the "modern state", "modern bourgeois society" and "modern socialism" contain a rich theory of it. The article contends that this theory supplies scholarly resources and guidance for advancing Chinese modernization. The piece, a newspaper commentary, has four parts. It first reads Engels's remark on the industrial, political and philosophical revolutions in England, France and Germany as a three-dimensional account of modernization. It then turns to the dual character and internal contradictions of capitalist modernization, and to the unity of universality and particularity in modernization paths, drawing on Engels's late writings on Russia and the East. It ends with the "two reconciliations" and a new form of human civilization. Liu argues that modernization is a systemic socio-historical project. The modern mode of production is its material basis, the modern state its political guarantee, and modern subjectivity its human force, with the social revolution of industry taking foundational priority. Capitalist modernization, in Liu's reading, advances civilization yet produces conflicts between humans and nature and between classes, rooted in the logic of capital valorization and reification. From Engels's remarks on Russia, Liu draws three points: modernization joins a scientific measure with a value measure, it is not Westernization, and Eastern countries can move from a sequential to a simultaneous mode of development and "leap over" capitalism. Liu says this undermines the Western claim that its own model is unique and universal. Liu concludes that Engels's "two reconciliations", of humanity with nature and of humans with one another, point to a higher civilization in which individuals develop freely and fully. Liu presents Chinese modernization as this orientation in practice. It is described as harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature, people-centred, and opposed to the capital-centred and materialist Western path. Liu adds that it offers Chinese wisdom for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise, officially placed account of how Engels is currently mobilised in Chinese discourse on modernization.

The dialectical relationship between economic base and superstructure in Anti-Dühring 《反杜林论》中经济基础与上层建筑的辩证关系 Yang Hongyuan Yang Hongyuan notes that the dialectics of productive forces and relations of production, and of economic base and superstructure, are often applied in subjective, one-sided, dogmatic or formalistic ways. The commentary argues that a return to Engels's Anti-Dühring, and to its critique of Eugen Dühring's theory of political violence, restores the positive principles behind these categories. Yang first sets out Dühring's "theory of force", then reconstructs Engels's replies. These cover the claims that violence is the purpose of economic life, the origin of property and a harm to society. The piece then turns to what Engels concludes about the determining role of the economic base and the relative independence of politics. In Yang's account, Dühring subordinates economic life to political life and natural law, and treats all property as "property based on violence". Engels answers that violence protects exploitation but does not create it, and that economic interest is the end while violence is only a means. Property, wage labour and the bourgeoisie arose through economic development, and the means of violence, such as weapons, depend on economic resources. Yang adds that Engels also affirms the superstructure's relative independence. Public functions in early communities hardened into political rule, and slavery arose when productivity allowed surplus labour. Violent revolutions, Yang says, serve to liberate productive forces. Yang concludes that Engels's critique shows the interaction of base and superstructure, with the economic base ultimately decisive. Violent revolution, including the proletarian overthrow of the bourgeoisie, is presented as clearing the way for new productive forces. Read the original if you want a short, text-based reminder of how Anti-Dühring grounds the base–superstructure principle.

Economic globalization and developing new quality productive forces 经济全球化与发展新质生产力 Zhang Yanyan Su Jian Shao Yujia This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 5 August 2025 as a result of a National Committee of the CPPCC research project on new quality productive forces, asks how China should develop such forces under conditions of deepening economic globalization. The authors argue that no country can solve all innovation problems alone. In their view, open innovation and international scientific cooperation are therefore indispensable, and they present this as guidance from Xi Jinping's economic writings. The article opens with Xi's statements on open innovation and then proceeds in three sections. The first treats globalization as a trend that must be grasped, looking at technological change (artificial intelligence, the digital economy, green technology) and at international competition. The second addresses new challenges to globalization. The third turns to the steady expansion of institutional opening up. Each section is anchored in quotations from Xi Jinping. The core argument draws on historical materialism. The authors say the new challenges to globalization, such as the rise of anti-globalization sentiment, fragmented trade rules, protectionism and unilateralism, arise because relations of production lag behind the development of productive forces. They attribute these trends partly to some Western countries, whose hollowed-out manufacturing and domestic tensions between growth and distribution are, in the authors' account, wrongly blamed on globalization by some politicians. The answer they propose is to use innovation to adjust global relations of production: opposing unilateralism, improving the multilateral trading system, and pairing technological innovation with management innovation and industrial cooperation. Examples include digital core technologies, green and low-carbon industries, smart manufacturing and high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. The authors conclude that China should steadily expand institutional opening up, moving from opening in flows of goods, capital and people to opening in rules, regulations, management and standards. They say this would help clarify property rights over innovation gains, improve the allocation of data and technology, and attract global factors of production. They call for alignment with high-standard international economic and trade rules in areas such as intellectual property, subsidies, environmental standards, government procurement and finance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary links new quality productive forces, globalization and institutional opening up.

The young Engels's critique of the English utopian socialists 青年恩格斯对英国空想社会主义者的批判 Lin Jin Tang Zhengdong Lin Jin and Tang Zhengdong ask how the young Engels's engagement with English utopian socialists shaped his path to the materialist conception of history. They argue that his borrowing from and sublation of these thinkers moved his critique towards the poverty of the English working class and the legitimacy of private property. It then led him to a view grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and social relations. The authors present this as a necessary development, set against Western readings of Engels as a positivist. The short article follows Engels from his arrival in England in November 1842 through a series of early texts: the "Letters from London" (1843), Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, "Progress of Social Reform on the Continent", The Condition of the Working Class in England, and finally The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. The figures discussed are William Thompson, John Bray, John Watts, Robert Owen and, briefly, William Godwin. Lin and Tang say Engels admired the English socialists for starting from verifiable facts and attacking private property on economic grounds. His critique of Malthus drew on Watts's distinction between population and the means of employment. They then argue that Engels moved beyond them. He rejected Thompson's claim that workers should enjoy the full product of labour, treated Owenite communities as experiments rather than realisable ideals, and saw that their reliance on reason and moral persuasion reflected an unhistorical view in which only psychological development counted. In the authors' reading, this left them without a sense of the proletariat's historical mission and within abstract humanism. The authors conclude that Engels's joint construction of historical materialism with Marx was inevitable rather than accidental. They note that the Communist Manifesto treated the utopians' limits as fitting an undeveloped class struggle while valuing their critical elements. Read the original if you want a concise account of Engels's early debt to Watts, Thompson and Bray and of how he left them behind.

"For the Party and the people, promote the good and expose the bad, value both ear and eye": Xi Jinping on journalism and public opinion work in Zhejiang Tracing his remarks and practice on news and public opinion work during his time in Zhejiang “为党为民、激浊扬清、贵耳重目” Zhao Yu Chen Peihao Zhao Yu and Chen Peihao review what Xi Jinping said and did about news and public opinion work while he worked in Zhejiang (the speeches cited date from 2002 to 2006). They argue that these remarks produced a three-part requirement: work "for the Party and the people", work that promotes the good and exposes the bad (jiluan yangqing), and work that "values ear and eye", meaning fact-finding by listening and looking. In their view, tracing these remarks systematically helps in understanding today's changes in the media landscape, in discourse, and in the balance between offence and defence. The article first appeared in the People's Daily in August 2025. The article is organised in eight sections, each built around a phrase from Xi's Zhejiang speeches. They cover the Party principle in journalism, news work as a special ideological task, the line of "unity, stability and encouragement" with mainly positive coverage, the people's standpoint, the internet as a new front, innovation, the mass line in reporting, and the building of the journalist corps. Most evidence comes from Xi's addresses to Zhejiang media officials, to Party propaganda meetings and to central media staff based in the province. The authors argue that Xi tied journalism's political character to professional demands. Media must remain the mouthpiece of the Party and the people, with the Party managing both media and cadres. Journalism is described as a special ideological field, where "a single guiding ideology" should steer diverse social currents. The authors present positive coverage as a way to build consensus and keep the public mood steady, and they say reporting must unify promoting Party positions with reflecting popular concerns. Xi's call to make the internet a "new position, new channel and new carrier" and his remark that blocking wrong ideas is not enough, because the main theme must be sounded, are presented as early responses to the digital age. The authors also report his demands for innovation, for journalists to go to the grassroots, to avoid fake news and hype, and to build a corps that is politically strong, professionally skilled, disciplined and upright. The authors conclude that the Zhejiang experience offers lessons for the systemic reform of mainstream media in the new era. They list five: take a firm political stand and unify Party spirit with people-centredness; lead media trends through innovation; rely on investigation and the masses; build a full-media communication system; and invest in talent. They add a wider aim of a "big propaganda" pattern in which the whole Party takes part. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Xi's Zhejiang-era statements on media are now being presented as a basis for Party media policy.

Understanding the contemporary significance of Party conduct building 深刻领会党的作风建设的时代意蕴 Liu Li This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, reads Xi Jinping's statements on Party conduct building (zuofeng jianshe) as both a theory of what conduct problems are and a practical system for tackling them. Liu Li links the piece to the 2025 campaign of study and education on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. The author argues that this body of thought raises the Party's understanding of conduct work to a new level and gives it an ideological weapon for the new era. The article moves through seven of Xi's formulations, each paired with a classical Chinese saying and a call for "a high degree of consciousness". They cover conduct as a matter of the Party's survival, conduct as a question of Party spirit, the relationship with the people, the eight-point regulation, the "four undesirable work styles", the "critical few" of leading cadres, and long-term mechanisms. Liu's central claims are that conduct problems are never minor but bear on the Party's survival and on popular support. They are rooted in weak Party spirit and a fading sense of purpose, and at core they concern the Party's relationship with the people. The author presents the eight-point regulation as a rigid, long-term rule, noting that it replaced "in general" with "without exception" and carries no "trial" label. Liu adds that formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance must be treated as the principal contradiction and that leading cadres must set the example. Institutionalisation is presented as the route from treating symptoms to treating causes. Liu concludes that conduct building must advance in step with the Party's and the people's cause, and calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform to be sustained on the path of Chinese modernization. Theoretical clarity and rigid institutions are said to ensure political firmness and conscious action. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present Xi's conduct-building discourse in 2025.

Advancing the reform and innovation of ideological and political courses across universities, secondary and primary schools 推进大中小学思政课改革创新 Yang Tianmei Cao Sheng Published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2025, this commentary by Yang Tianmei and Cao Sheng takes up how ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) can be reformed as a single integrated system running from primary school to university. The authors argue that such integrated reform and innovation is a key step in carrying out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. They rely throughout on Xi Jinping's statements on the subject. The piece has two parts. The first sets out the theoretical significance of integrated reform, divided into an epistemological and an axiological dimension. The second proposes seven practical paths: leadership and communication mechanisms, cooperative working mechanisms, integrated curriculum building, integrated teaching staff development, integrated teaching and research, resource sharing, and a leading role for university schools of Marxism. On the theoretical side, the authors say integration must follow Marxist epistemology and the dialectic of practice and cognition, matching course content to students' cognitive development at each stage. They describe the sequence as moral feeling in primary school, ideological foundations in middle school, political literacy in high school and a sense of mission at university. On the value side, they link integration to answering whom education trains, how and for whom, and to producing new-era people who can shoulder national rejuvenation. They also tie it to the strong ideological and political guidance expected of a Chinese-style education powerhouse. In practice, the authors call for joint planning by education authorities, university Marxism schools and primary and secondary schools. They propose a research direction on integration within the Marxist theory discipline, and the recruitment of senior school teachers as postgraduate supervisors. They also want training from multidisciplinary university staff for schools short of teachers in areas such as law and mental health. Other proposals include collective lesson preparation, use of local red-culture resources, links between teacher promotion and participation, varied teaching methods, and shared courses and practice bases. The authors conclude that universities, with their talent, theoretical, disciplinary, curricular, teaching and resource advantages, should lead integrated construction. In their view this would make the courses more targeted and effective, and would help train people who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and ready for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the institutional measures currently proposed for linking Party-line ideological education across school levels.

Rural mutual aid and cooperation in the Central Soviet Area as a demonstration of the Party's wisdom 中央苏区农村互助合作彰显党的智慧 Zhang Liankui This short commentary examines the mutual aid and cooperation that the Communist Party of China led among peasants in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian during the Central Soviet Area period. Zhang argues that the movement was both a strategic answer to wartime economic hardship and an early experiment in changing rural relations of production. In Zhang's account it supported the revolutionary war, restored farm output and consolidated Soviet power. The article moves from causes to organisation to results. It first explains how the fragility of smallholder farming after land reform, together with the Nationalist blockade and encirclement campaigns, created demand for cooperation. It then describes the system of cooperatives, its operating principles and its regulatory documents, and ends with the movement's effects. Zhang reports that the Party worked on the principle of voluntariness and mutual benefit, opposed coercion, and measured labour exchange in work points. Cooperatives covered circulation (consumer, purchasing, marketing, grain and credit societies), agriculture (field-tilling teams, labour mutual-aid societies, plough-ox cooperatives) and handicrafts. The author cites figures such as 1,206 labour mutual-aid societies in Xingguo County by April 1934 and more than 500,000 cooperative members across the area. Zhang credits the movement with higher grain harvests, better allocation of labour and support for the preferential treatment of Red Army families. Zhang concludes that these experiments showed early Party wisdom in leading collective economy. The author names centralised, unified Party leadership, respect for peasants' wishes and interests, and gradual, realistic methods as the main lessons. The article treats the period as a source of the Party's later rural work methods. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of cooperative organisation in the Jiangxi–Fujian base areas, with local statistics and policy documents.

Historical experience of the century-old Party in rectifying formalism and bureaucratism 百年大党整治形式主义官僚主义的历史经验 Wang Maosen Wang Maosen asks what the Communist Party of China has learned over more than a century of fighting formalism and bureaucratism. The commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, argues that these experiences are important for strengthening Party conduct in the new era and for eliminating the two problems effectively. The piece follows the Party's record from the democratic revolution through the early People's Republic to the reform era. It cites Mao Zedong's condemnation of bureaucratism, the Yan'an rectification movement, the Common Programme, the early campaigns to rectify Party style and Party organisations, and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Wang organises the record into three pairs of lessons. The first combines a protracted, sustained struggle with targeted campaigns on specific problems. The second pairs the "lead goose effect" of leading cadres, who set an example, with stronger supervision by the masses. The third pairs political education, which builds ideological awareness, with institution-building, which Wang describes as tightening the "cage of rules". Wang treats the two evils as twins that both stem from subjectivism detached from reality. Looking ahead, Wang calls for using big-data supervision, "smart Party building" and "Internet plus supervision" to raise effectiveness and widen public participation. Wang also calls for improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, so that Party conduct work becomes regular, long-term and institutionalised in support of building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a short, official-style summary of how Party history is used to frame current campaigns against formalism and bureaucratism.

Understanding and grasping "upholding the Party's cultural leadership" in depth 深刻认识把握“坚持党的文化领导权” Yang Hongyuan Yang Hongyuan takes up one of the core elements of Xi Jinping's thought on culture: upholding the Party's cultural leadership. In this commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 31 July 2025, Yang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has treated the question as strategically vital to the fate of the Party and state. In Yang's account, it has answered what cultural leadership is, why it must be upheld, and how to uphold and consolidate it. The piece has three parts. The first sets out what cultural leadership means. The second explains why cultural subjectivity makes it necessary, given the tasks of national rejuvenation and the current international environment. The third lists practical requirements: theory, innovation, and concrete institutional leadership over propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Yang defines cultural leadership as, in essence, leadership over ideological work, covering the powers of leadership, management and discourse. Yang treats ideological leadership as the foundation of all Party leadership, alongside political and organisational leadership, and holds that a rising class must win cultural leadership to take the initiative in making history. The Party exercises its leading role through ideological guidance, core socialist values, international discourse power and cultural reform. Yang cites new technologies such as mobile internet and artificial intelligence, a more diverse range of ideas, and what the author calls hostile forces' ideological infiltration as reasons why this leadership matters more. Consolidating cultural subjectivity, citing Xi Jinping, is presented as the basis of cultural confidence and of any culture's capacity to lead and radiate influence. Yang calls for arming the whole Party and educating the people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and for building popular identification with it. Yang also asks for cultural innovation grounded in practice, paired with adherence to the correct direction. Leadership must be made concrete through centralised, unified Party leadership over propaganda, ideology, media and the internet, and through unifying Party spirit with the people's interests. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists explain the concept of cultural leadership and its practical implications.

Putting the requirements of the Party's self-reform in the new era more fully into effect 把新时代党的自我革命要求进一步落实到位 Hu Guoxi This commentary responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the 21st collective study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee. Xi called for the Party's self-reform to be implemented more fully in five areas: understanding, Party spirit, regulation of power, strict supervision and discipline, and responsibility for Party governance. Hu Guoxi argues that these five requirements form a closed loop of top-level design that gives strategic guidance and a practical path for carrying self-reform through to the end. The piece is short and takes the five requirements in turn, treating each as a link in one chain. It draws on Xi's formulations throughout and adds images such as power's 'revolution' and 'rotation', and the Party organisation's unsheathed blade. Hu's central claims run as follows. Self-reform is first an ideological revolution, so mistaken views must be rejected, including that it is troublesome, excessive or 'none of my business'. Party spirit must be tempered, because the author holds that weak Party spirit leads to degeneration. Hu argues that corruption is at root the use of power for private gain, so self-reform must focus on governing power by making it operate transparently and traceably under institutional constraints. Hu also notes that cases are more often dug up passively than uncovered proactively, and calls for routine supervision and joint investigation of misconduct and corruption. On responsibility, Hu calls for a performance outlook in which running Party affairs well counts as the greatest achievement, and for a complete chain of responsibilities, accountability and assessment. Hu concludes that this will build an atmosphere of strictness and integrity and advance full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary presents the Party's self-reform agenda and its rhetoric.

Making better use of the rule of law in further deepening rural reform 更好发挥法治在进一步深化农村改革中的作用 Zhang Zhenli Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2025, Zhang Zhenli takes up the question of how legal tools can support further rural reform after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhang argues that rule-of-law thinking and methods must be used to handle the major issues of rural reform, so that law "consolidates the foundation, stabilises expectations and benefits the long term". The piece is a short commentary that follows recent Party and State Council documents on rural reform and the comprehensive revitalisation of the countryside. The article is organised in three parts. The first addresses the relationship between farmers and land, which Zhang, citing Xi Jinping, calls the main line of rural reform. The second covers integrated urban–rural development, and the third covers effective rural governance. Each part lists the relevant statutes, such as the Land Management Law, the Civil Code, the Rural Land Contracting Law, the Rural Revitalisation Promotion Law and the 2024 Law on Rural Collective Economic Organisations, and then sets out tasks for the present. On land, Zhang holds that the basic rural operating system rests on four elements: collective land ownership, the foundational role of household operation, stable contracting relations, and the improved "three rights separation" arrangement. Zhang describes how legislation has strengthened the legal standing of collective owners and households, and calls for better contract management, orderly pilots extending second-round contracts by thirty years, and respect for farmers' wishes in land transfer. On urban–rural integration, Zhang urges collective economic development that benefits members, a unified urban–rural construction land market, priority fiscal support and the extension of basic public services to all permanent residents. On governance, Zhang calls for Party-led village self-governance combining self-rule, rule of law and moral governance, along with stronger grassroots Party organisations, public legal services and village rules to change social customs. Zhang concludes that law must be used to protect farmers' rights and keep reform on a legal footing, while ensuring Party leadership in rural governance. The piece is largely a policy-oriented survey of existing legislation with proposals for its application. Getting organised as the source of strength behind victory in the War of Resistance against Japan 组织起来是抗日战争胜利的力量之源 Wang Binglin Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary asks how the Chinese nation organised itself, why it could, and what this means today. Wang Binglin argues that getting organised (组织起来) was the source of strength behind victory, because the awakening of the Chinese people and the nation's cohesion against foreign aggression proved decisive. The piece first appeared in Guangming Daily on 30 July 2025. The article has three parts. The first describes how organisation was built in the political, military, economic and popular spheres. The second explains the Communist Party's role as advocate and defender of that organisation. The third draws lessons for the present. Wang's evidence includes the Three-Thirds system of government, the National Political Council, Pingxingguan, mine warfare, rent and interest reduction, and mass associations in the Jin-Cha-Ji border region and Shandong. In Wang's account, Mao Zedong's diagnosis in On Protracted War was that Japan dared to bully China mainly because the Chinese people were unorganised. The anti-Japanese national united front joined all classes, parties, ethnic groups and overseas Chinese, and fighting was organised through two coordinated battlefields. Wang credits the Communist Party with the united front line, with maintaining independence within it, and with theory such as On Protracted War and New Democracy. Wang also credits Communists' self-sacrifice and the Party's use of traditional culture, such as the 1937 rites at the Yellow Emperor's Mausoleum and works like the Yellow River Cantata, as a spiritual bond. Wang draws three lessons for the new journey. Upholding the Party's overall leadership is the fundamental guarantee of consensus, and Wang cites Xi Jinping on the Party's strength coming from organisation. Party members must act as vanguard models to bind the masses. Patriotism, as the core of the national spirit, should be promoted through the creative transformation of traditional culture. This is meant to gather strength for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship reads the War of Resistance as a lesson in organisation and Party leadership, with the historical examples Wang selects.)

Strengthening ideological and political guidance to empower university education 以强大思政引领力赋能高校育人工作 Wang Yin This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 30 July 2025, asks how universities can build what Xi Jinping at the 2024 National Education Conference listed first among the six attributes of a strong education nation: the capacity for ideological and political guidance. Wang Yin argues that universities should develop an ideological and political work system that keeps pace with the times, resonates with young people and connects with practice. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the meaning of this guiding capacity, then its role in the university education system, and finally concrete measures for running socialist universities with Chinese characteristics. Wang presents the capacity as continuing the Party's tradition of treating ideological and political work as a "lifeline", as expressing the political, popular and strategic attributes of education, and as answering the challenges of a world undergoing changes unseen in a century. In Wang's account it supports the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, secures the Party's overall leadership of universities, and widens channels of value guidance through ideological and political theory courses, "curriculum ideology and politics" and a second classroom of practice. Wang calls for university Party committees to take political responsibility and improve the "big ideological and political" pattern of work, advancing the reform of whole-staff, whole-process and all-round education. Wang also proposes teaching Party theory in depth, training teachers jointly, using student organisations and Party activities, and expanding social practice. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party official frames ideological and political education within the drive to build a strong education nation.

Building a high-calibre corps of ideological and political theory teachers for the new era 建设新时代高素质思政课教师队伍 Li Haipeng This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 30 July 2025, asks how to build a high-quality teaching force for ideological and political theory courses in schools and universities. Li argues that such teachers are central to the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The author calls the work systematic and strategic, to be pursued through four tasks: strengthening political development, raising professional ability, promoting collaborative education and improving evaluation. The piece opens by placing teachers within the three questions of education: whom to cultivate, how, and for whom. It then sets out four requirements, each framed as a "checkpoint": belief, training, the educational ecosystem and orientation. Li draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements on these courses and on his stated qualities for their teachers. Li contends that these teachers must train socialist builders and successors who support Party leadership and the socialist system, joining theoretical teaching with value guidance and conveying belief and ideals as well as knowledge. In practice, Li calls for putting political criteria first in selecting, training and employing teachers and for study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author also proposes full-cycle training from entry to career growth, research projects and teaching platforms, and clearer duties and career paths inside schools, together with school-local and inter-school cooperation. Evaluation should abandon the fixation on papers and titles, stress classroom quality and students' ideological growth, and make teachers' ethics the first criterion. Li concludes that a corps of teachers strong in politics, theory and teaching craft is the way to ensure the fundamental task of fostering virtue is carried out, and that it should lead students to align personal development with national strength and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of current Party expectations for ideological and political theory teachers in China.

Expanding ideological and political courses through walking On "walking" ideological and political courses as a route to educating new-era youth 用行走扩容思政课 Zhang Yanqing Writing in the 80th anniversary year of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), Zhang Yanqing presents the "walking" ideological and political course as an important way of forging new-era youth. In this commentary, "reading ten thousand books" meets "travelling ten thousand miles": students learn at sites such as Yan'an, the Nanjing Massacre memorial and the Marco Polo Bridge. Zhang, citing Xi Jinping, argues that such courses link the small classroom of theory to the big classroom of society. The piece is short and organised around three tasks. It first discusses red resources, then excellent traditional Chinese culture, and finally the teaching design and support structures that make these courses effective. Examples include Jinggangshan, Zunyi and Xibaipo, and Renmin University of China's course along Beijing's Central Axis. Zhang's core argument is that red sites turn patriotic education from slogans into lasting spiritual imprints, and that cultural sites and intangible heritage make tradition a living skill rather than a museum exhibit. The author insists that these visits must not be superficial sightseeing. Instead, a loop from the first classroom to the second and back should join theory, teaching topics and practice. Zhang proposes three supports: joint "big classroom" bases such as laboratories and university history museums, digital platforms, and a "big teaching force" including specialists from various fields and local experts. In the author's view it extends knowledge and cultivates a lifelong commitment to the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style example of how practice-based ideological and political education is promoted in Chinese schools.

Bringing red culture into Party-spirit education 发挥红色文化在党性教育中的作用 Wei Min Writing in a newspaper commentary of July 2025, Wei Min asks how red culture can be used in Party-spirit education for Party members and cadres. Against the background of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Wei argues that this is both an innovative application of Marxist cultural theory and an important route to strengthening members' Party-spirit cultivation. Wei holds that, on Marxist cultural theory, advanced culture shapes group values and gives spiritual guidance, so red culture's collectivism and revolutionary idealism match the aims of Party-spirit education. Heilongjiang's core symbols are the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army spirit and the Great Northern Wilderness spirit. Wei cites Zhao Shangzhi and Yang Jingyu as models of conviction, and the transformation of the wilderness into farmland of 11.38 million hectares as an illustration of serving the people and the mass line. Party building as leadership in resolving governance problems of county-level modernization 付伟、党建引领化解县域现代化的治理问题 Fu Wei This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how grassroots governance can be modernized so that it supports county-level modernization. Fu argues that Party building as leadership (党建引领) is the key lever for doing so. The piece takes its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for a grassroots governance system led by Party organizations. The article first sets out the new demands that county modernization places on grassroots governance, then draws on the experience of Jiangyin city, as seen by a Peking University research team, to propose three directions for improvement. Fu describes a rise in both the quantity and the quality of governance tasks, which leaves grassroots bodies overburdened ("a small horse pulling a big cart"). The author attributes this to fragmentation between functional lines and territorial levels, low popular participation ("cadres act, the masses watch") and weak mechanisms for involving social forces. The remedies are to strengthen Party coordination across departments and relieve village and community organizations of top-down tasks and assessments; to build precise, responsive services through grid-based management, digital platforms and "smart" government; and to mobilise residents through a new-era mass line, illustrated by Jiangyin's "1+10+N" system linking Party members with households. Fu concludes that high-quality grassroots governance, led by Party organizations, is what advances county modernization. Fu also calls for ending "one-assessment-decides-all" practices and for giving grassroots bodies more room to experiment. Striving to strengthen the explanatory power of the basic principles of Marxism 努力增强对马克思主义基本原理的解释力 Tang Zhenming Tang Zhenming asks why the explanatory power of the basic principles of Marxism needs to be strengthened and how this can be done. Opening with Xi Jinping's statement that the general principles set out by Marxism remain entirely correct 170 years after the Communist Manifesto, the author argues that a stronger account of these principles is essential. It matters for grasping Marxism's scientific character, displaying its truth and advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is a short commentary published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2025. The article is organised around three reasons. The first concerns scientific character: Tang treats philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism as the three components in which the principles' scientific nature is concentrated. The second concerns truth: Marxism's truth is said to rest on the universality of its basic principles and to be tested in practice. The third concerns strategy, linking the principles to the Two Integrations and to the task of keeping the Party's theoretical foundations sound. Tang then lists three practical requirements. Tang's central move is to distinguish between the basic principles and the specific methods and conclusions derived from them. The principles are described as the "master key" and "master switch" for understanding the world, of universal validity, whereas derived conclusions can change with the times. On this basis, Tang says Marxism is true because its basic principles are universal truths, not because every statement by Marx and Engels over a century ago fits present reality. Truth is held to be objective and practice-tested, and without practice the principles would become abstract dogma. The Two Integrations are presented as a question of what is being integrated with: without the basic principles neither integration with China's concrete realities nor with fine traditional Chinese culture could exist. Tang also says that doubts about, or demonisation of, Marxism are best answered by presenting its principles' truth. Tang proposes three tasks, framed as upholding what is correct while innovating. These are systematic study of the classic works, to grasp their essential meaning and not merely cling to every conclusion of the classical authors; interpretation tied to the present context of Chinese modernization, using historical, cultural and comparative methods; and closeness to the people's needs, so that the principles reach ordinary people. Tang's stated aim is to supply an ideological foundation for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university Party official presents the status of Marxism's basic principles and the guidelines for interpreting them.

Thoroughly implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation: polishing the Party's golden calling card of conduct building Summaries of expert presentations at the forum "Theory and Practice of Ruling-Party Building" 深入贯彻中央八项规定精神 擦亮党的作风建设金色名片 This is a report on a forum, "Theory and Practice of Ruling-Party Building", jointly held by the Academy of Marxism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Jiangxi Normal University and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. Its theme was the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation and the Party's conduct building (zuofeng jianshe). The editors present abridged remarks from several participants, held while a Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the regulation was under way.
