They include Zhu Xiaoli (Jiangxi Normal University), Deng Chundong (formerly of the Academy of Marxism), Liu Jianhui (formerly of the Central Party School), Liu Jingbei (formerly of the China Pudong Cadre College), Liu Honglin (Fudan University), Ding Junping (Wuhan University), Song Jin (East China Normal University) and Zang Xiuling (Shandong University). The speakers largely agree that the regulation is a starting point rather than an end. Deng describes conduct building as the premise of all Party building, a determinant of the Party's political advantages and the most basic factor in its long-term rule. Liu Jianhui and Song stress that the regulation is a basic requirement and a first step, linked to the claim that conduct building is never finished. Ding finds the spirit of the regulation centred on integrity and self-discipline, thrift, practical efficiency and close ties with the masses. Liu Honglin asks how to strengthen the enforcement of intra-Party regulations, and Zhu and Liu Jingbei call for systematic study of Xi Jinping's statements on conduct. Zang draws on Chen Yun's example of ideals, Party spirit, seeking truth from facts, plain service and diligent study. The participants conclude that conduct building should be made regular and long-term, and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party should be deepened. Several link the campaign to the Party's long-term rule and to Chinese modernization, and Liu Jianhui presents it as part of the Party's self-reform. Zhu proposes three research priorities: systematising Xi's discourse, theorising the results and experience since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and studying the historical experience of the Party's century. Read the original if you want a compact view of how Party-affiliated scholars frame the eight-point regulation, its theory and its place in Party discipline.

Consolidating the rule-of-law foundation of high-standard opening up 夯实高水平对外开放的法治根基 Yang Song This commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (28 July 2025) asks how high-standard opening up can proceed on a rule-of-law track. Yang Song argues that the key lies in the rule-of-law dimension of institutional opening up (制度型开放). Citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and Xi Jinping's remarks at a Politburo study session in November 2023, Yang holds that law accompanies opening, so foreign-related rule of law must advance with each step of opening. The piece has three parts. The first traces how institutional opening up entered Party documents, from the 2018 Central Economic Work Conference through the 19th Central Committee's Fourth and Sixth Plenums, the 14th Five-Year Plan and the 20th Party Congress (2022) to the 2024 Third Plenum. The second sets out a system of six "theories" of institutional opening up. The third turns to the broader consequences for China's place in the world. In the core of the argument, Yang describes institutional opening up as aligning rules, regulations, management and standards with international norms. The six components are institutional alignment, opening, inclusiveness, standards, competition and security. Alignment means actively matching high-standard trade rules such as CPTPP and DEPA. Opening refers to measures such as pre-establishment national treatment with a negative list and the new Foreign Investment Law. Inclusiveness is tied to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and to opposing unilateralism. Standards means that China's institutions should "go out", gaining rule-making power in a global order that Yang says developed countries still dominate. Competition covers institutional rivalry with the US and the West, to which Yang says China responds with the Belt and Road Initiative, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the BRICS bank. Security treats institutional security as the baseline and the cornerstone of the holistic approach to national security, with rule of law as its guarantee. Yang concludes that China should align domestic rules with international standards, raise the competitiveness of its economic legal institutions, uphold inclusiveness and an economic-security bottom line, and push its standards abroad. This calls for inclusive, open, breakthrough and innovative thinking in building a new system of an open economy. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese legal scholars frame institutional opening up and foreign-related rule of law in terms of official policy.

Using digital-intelligence technology to improve the quality and effectiveness of intra-Party supervision 以数智技术助力提升党内监督质效 Liang Ruiying This newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 28 July 2025) asks how big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence can be built into intra-Party supervision while guarding against risks. Liang argues that such "digital-intelligence" supervision can become a new engine for improving the quality and effectiveness of supervision and for strengthening efforts against misconduct and corruption. The piece is organised around three tasks: building a digital-intelligence supervision platform, improving the mechanisms that govern it, and raising the digital-intelligence skills of those who carry out supervision. On the platform, Liang proposes a chain of linked components (inspection, evaluation and feedback, risk warning, problem handling, information release). The author calls for Party committees to coordinate funding, technology and personnel, for data barriers to be broken down, and for platforms to be merged, for example by combining tax, transport, property and finance data so that discipline inspection bodies can spot problems early. On mechanisms, Liang calls for Party regulations that set the scope and limits of technology use, give discipline inspection organs lawful access to data, and guard against misuse, privacy breaches and leaks. Supervision should sit within a system led by Party committees, with discipline inspection and supervisory commissions coordinating and cooperating with audit, accounting and statistical supervision. On skills, Liang says supervisors must change traditional thinking, and that digital-intelligence competence should be assessed and linked to evaluation, promotion and appointment. Training, through Party schools and cadre education institutions with added technology courses, should address concrete problems in applying technology to supervision. Liang presents these steps as moving supervision from reliance on experience and after-the-fact response towards combining experience with technology and acting in advance. The string of self-reform must be drawn tighter Commentator's article in Qiushi 《求是》杂志评论员：自我革命这根弦必须绷得更紧 Qiushi commentator This commentary in Qiushi (2025, no. 14) takes up Xi Jinping's remarks at the 21st collective study session of the 20th Political Bureau, held before 1 July 2025, on making the eight-point regulation and the long-term mechanism against the "four undesirable work styles" more effective. It then turns to current conditions, to misunderstandings among some cadres, and to four requirements: strengthening Party spirit, regulating the exercise of power, strict supervision and discipline, and layered responsibility. The author presents the eight-point regulation as a small opening that drove a wider transformation of work style, and calls self-reform the Party's second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Because Chinese modernization and deeper reform face heavy tasks and external risks, the author holds that the Party cannot slacken, and cites officials who broke rules during the current study campaign as a warning. The author rejects the views that self-reform harms the Party's image or obstructs economic growth, and argues that it removes obstacles and restores vitality. The commentary calls on Party members to study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to temper themselves in practice. It also calls for transparent, traceable systems that put power "in the cage of institutions", joint supervision, and the investigation of work-style and corruption cases together. Leading cadres, as the "key minority", are urged to shoulder responsibility for Party governance. Starting from how the Yan'an style defeated the Xi'an style 从延安作风打败西安作风谈起 Lin Jingwei Why did the Communist Party win power in China? Lin Jingwei takes up Xi Jinping's remark that the Party prevailed in the New Democratic Revolution partly by keeping flesh-and-blood ties with the people and so "defeating the Xi'an style with the Yan'an style". Writing in Qiushi in 2025, as the Party ran a study and education campaign on the Eight-point Regulation, Lin argues that conduct and work style decided who won popular support and, with it, the country. The article first defines the Yan'an style and contrasts it with the Xi'an style, which stands for Kuomintang conduct. It then gives three reasons for the Yan'an style's success and ends by asking how it can be passed on. Lin relies on anecdotes and testimony: Mao Zedong's 1940 rebuke over an escort, Chen Jiageng's visits to Chongqing and Yan'an, the accounts of Edgar Snow, Theodore White and John Davis, and Zhu De's letter asking for a loan. Lin reads the Yan'an style as the Party's moral and personal strength, set beside its strength of truth, which Lin identifies with correct theory. It rested on three things: faith in revolutionary ideals, close ties to the masses, and self-reliance with hard struggle. Lin sets Mao's "ten absences" against the Kuomintang's corruption, which the article illustrates with the phrases "five ways to success" and "tight at the front, feasting at the rear". In Lin's account, the shift of popular sentiment by late 1947 was a turning point, and it confirms that those who win the people's hearts win the country. Lin warns that holding power tests a party's style, and cites Song Meiling's remark that the Communists had not yet tasted power. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Lin says, the Eight-point Regulation and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party have restored its vitality and are a key lesson of the Party's self-reform. Lin calls for the Yan'an style to be carried forward, with work-style building made routine and long-term, in support of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated historian uses Yan'an-era episodes to support current work-style campaigns.

The theoretical features of Marx's idea of the emancipation of labour 马克思劳动解放思想的理论特质 Yan Guohong Writing in Guangming Daily (28 July 2025), Yan Guohong asks where Marx's idea of the emancipation of labour comes from and what its core content is. Yan argues that the idea is not an isolated innovation but a dialectical sublation of ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, German classical philosophy and classical political economy. At its centre, in Yan's account, is the link between labour and human liberation, aimed at the free and all-round development of the human being. The short article has two parts. The first traces three sources: Aristotle and Cicero; Kant and Hegel; and William Petty, Adam Smith and David Ricardo. The second sets out the basic core of the idea around three questions: what labour is, how labour is emancipated, and by what path. A brief closing note ties the idea to the present. Yan argues that each source gave Marx something specific. Aristotle's distinction between the labour of free people and the toil of slaves showed that labour has a social-historical character. Cicero's remarks on hired labour pointed to an early form of alienation. Kant supplied the principle that the human being is an end in itself, and Hegel the dialectical view of labour as both transforming nature and forming the self. Classical economists supplied the labour theory of value, which Marx developed into the theory of surplus value. In the core of the idea, Yan presents labour as the species-activity that distinguishes humans from animals. Under capitalism it becomes alienated, so that it affirms the worker's self no longer. Emancipation therefore requires abolishing the capitalist system and establishing socialism, and it also depends on highly developed productive forces that cut necessary labour and let labour become life's prime need. Yan concludes that the idea retains contemporary value. Technology is reshaping forms of labour, and the sharing economy is reshaping the distribution of value. Yan states that the idea provides theoretical support and guidance for advancing Chinese modernization through high-quality development. Read the original if you want a compact survey, in the style of a Party-school commentary, of the intellectual lineage and main propositions of Marx's theory of labour emancipation.

Grasping the theoretical meaning of "measure" scientifically 科学把握“度”的理论内涵 Zhang Ziyu This newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 25 July 2025) asks what "measure" (du) means in Marxist philosophy and why it matters for practice. Zhang argues that measure is the link between quantitative and qualitative change. It is also a key yardstick for understanding how things develop, analysing social phenomena and guiding action. Zhang notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi Jinping has repeatedly stressed grasping measure, for instance in the art of struggle, in macroeconomic regulation and in resource use. The piece has three parts. The first treats measure as the critical point between quantity and quality. The second links measure to the relation between truth and error. The third turns to how the Party and state should recognise, grasp and apply measure on the new journey. Zhang draws on Marx, Engels (including Dialectics of Nature) and Lenin (Philosophical Notebooks). Zhang defines measure as the boundary beyond which accumulated quantitative change produces a qualitative leap. It marks the limit of a thing's old quality and the starting point of a new one, and it also serves as a gauge of stability and of stages of development. Citing Engels and Lenin, Zhang adds that truth holds only within certain conditions and limits. Going "one small step further" past them turns truth into error, so people must test and develop truth in practice, starting from reality. Zhang calls for accurate recognition of measure, which means keeping to bottom-line thinking and using certainty to meet uncertainty. Zhang also calls for objective grasp of measure, and for scientific application of it that draws on the Party's sense of historical initiative. Examples include differentiated ecological management, risk early-warning in science and technology, and Chinese modernization. Zhang concludes that turning the philosophy of measure into institutional effectiveness supports high-quality development. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars link dialectical categories to current policy language.

The threefold meaning of "maintaining historical patience" “保持历史耐心”的三重意蕴 Sun Laibin This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, examines Xi Jinping's repeated call to "maintain historical patience" (baochi lishi naixin). It opens with Xi's remarks in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and at the Central Urban Work Conference of 14 July 2025, where he warned against rushing urbanisation and industrialisation. Sun Laibin argues that the phrase has three layers of meaning: a dialectical character, a strategic rationale and practical requirements for pursuing Chinese modernization. The piece is organised under three headings. The first defines historical patience and explains its dialectical qualities. The second sets out why it matters strategically, drawing on Party history, the "two overall situations" and the demands of development. The third lists what the principle requires in practice. Sun draws on Xi's speeches throughout, together with examples such as the C919 airliner, the ten-year Yangtze fishing ban and the Xiong'an New Area. Sun defines historical patience as a long-term view, steady strategic planning and composed temperament, grounded in grasp of historical laws. In this reading it combines respect for objective laws with initiative, so it is not passive waiting, and it balances speed and slowness and long-term planning with present action. Strategically, Sun presents it as a lesson from the Party's successes and from mistakes such as the Great Leap Forward, which the article attributes partly to impatience. Sun also ties it to the "two overall situations" and to high-quality development, which the article treats as a long and arduous task requiring a shift from quantity to quality. For practice, Sun calls for a "grand view of history", including the balance between progress and setbacks on the path to socialism, and a correct view of performance that puts serving the people ahead of showy achievements. Sun also calls for a fighting spirit, directed at corruption through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and at external pressure on China's sovereignty and development. The article presents patience as compatible with, and supported by, firmness and sustained effort. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars interpret Xi Jinping's "historical patience" and link it to Chinese modernization, governance and anti-corruption.

Teachers of ideological and political courses should practise the spirit of educators 思政课教师要做教育家精神的践行者 Chen Juan Chen Juan, writing in Guangming Daily on 25 July 2025, asks how teachers of ideological and political courses can turn the "spirit of educators" into daily practice. Chen argues that the six dimensions of that spirit set out by Xi Jinping closely match his "six requirements" for such teachers. Because the teaching staff is the key to these courses, Chen calls for building the teacher corps as a foundational task in the new era. The short commentary has two parts. The first proposes institutional measures to strengthen teachers' conscious commitment to the spirit of educators. The second sets out how teachers should apply it in teaching, research and social service. On institutions, Chen calls for making the spirit of educators a required part of teacher training, in a regular and institutionalised way. Chen also wants it written into evaluation, including qualification, hiring, promotion and awards, with teaching outcomes and professional ethics as the main standards. Chen would end the fixation on scores, diplomas, papers and titles, and would give more weight to teaching and teaching research. Resources should include priority development of the Marxist theory discipline, policy support for teachers and publicity for model teachers. For practice, Chen urges more inspiring and interactive teaching methods, including new technologies. Research should address major problems of national rejuvenation and feed into the classroom. Teachers should also take part in whole-staff moral education, policy research and public theory outreach. Chen concludes that teachers should uphold virtue in conduct, scholarship and teaching, and become firm believers in and practitioners of the spirit of educators. Chen presents this as essential to cultivating people for the Party and the country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse links Xi Jinping's remarks on educators to concrete training, evaluation and teaching measures for ideological and political course teachers.

The theoretical contributions and contemporary value of the Seventh Party Congress 党的七大的理论贡献与时代价值 Yang Na Writing in a newspaper commentary, Yang Na takes up the Seventh Party Congress, held at Yang'jialing in Yan'an in spring 1945, when China faced the question of where it was heading. Yang argues that the Congress built a complete theoretical system covering guiding ideology, political line and Party organisation. In the author's account, this system carried through revolution and governance and still offers guidance today. The article is organised in three parts: the Congress's theoretical landmarks, its historical echoes in practice, and its relevance in the new era. It draws on the new Party constitution, Mao Zedong's report On Coalition Government, and later events from the civil war to the early People's Republic. Yang reads the Congress as doing three things. It wrote Mao Zedong Thought into the Party constitution as the guide for all work. It set a political line aimed at a New Democratic China and a coalition government. It also made serving the people wholeheartedly the Party's fundamental purpose, refined democratic centralism, and distilled the Party's three styles of work. Yang traces its later effects: the blueprint was realised within four years, its ideas on people's congresses and a mixed economy shaped the early state, and its stress on work style fed the multi-party cooperation system. For the new era, Yang links the Congress to the Two Integrations, to a people-centred development philosophy and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Yang concludes that the Congress's method, popular standpoint, historical initiative and work style continue to support Chinese modernization and the Party's self-reform. Achievements in poverty alleviation, technology and diplomacy are presented as evidence of this continuity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how current Party scholarship links the 1945 Congress to Xi Jinping-era themes.

New trends in foreign Marxist critiques of capitalist modernization 国外马克思主义开展资本主义现代化批判的新趋势 Ma Xinying This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, asks how foreign Marxism has adapted its critique of capitalist modernization to the twenty-first century. Ma Xinying argues that, although digital technology has expanded capitalist productive forces, capitalism's inherent contradictions and the problems of global capital accumulation keep capitalist modernization a source of trouble in world modernization. In response, Ma identifies three trends in the new critique. The piece sets twenty-first-century work against the twentieth-century tradition of critique. It treats each trend as a shift from one orientation to another: from diachronic to synchronic critique, from critique of modernity to critique of modernization itself, and from socio-cultural to political critique. On the first shift, Ma says twentieth-century critics, working from Marx's world-historical outlook, traced capitalist modernization from feudal and pre-modern origins. Twenty-first-century critics instead take a cross-section of modernization as a single present context and concentrate on its current features and its effects on how people live. On the second, Ma argues that because most countries are now integrated into modernization, alienation and the crisis of industrial civilisation are treated as given. Critics therefore judge negative effects from subjects' own feelings, beliefs and actions, and examine modernization's structure, path, power control, new contradictions and global consequences. On the third, Ma contends that critical theory worked mainly in sociological, psychological and epistemological terms, whereas critique now turns on politics: new imperialism, neoliberalism, spatial and biopolitics, state governance, digital capitalism and ecological justice, with hegemony, power, equality and justice as key concepts. Ma concludes that these three shifts characterise the current direction of foreign Marxist critique of capitalist modernization. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how a Chinese scholar maps recent changes in foreign Marxist thinking on modernization.

Marx's view of spiritual life and its contemporary embodiment 马克思精神生活观及其现实体现 Kulaixi Yibulayin Kulaixi Yibulayin asks what historical materialism says about spiritual life and how Marx's view should guide the enrichment of people's spiritual world today. The author argues that Marx's historical materialism is not a 'soulless materialism'. In this reading, Marx returned spiritual life from abstract speculation to material production and to the question of human emancipation. The article ties this to Xi Jinping's call at the 20th Party Congress (2022) to meet the people's growing spiritual and cultural needs, and to Chinese modernization. The article has four parts. It first sets out the essence of spiritual life in Marx: its basis in material production, its subject as the 'real social human being', its mode as universal free intercourse, and its aim of all-round human development. It then examines Marx's criticisms of four kinds of 'unscientific' spiritual life, and his constructive alternatives. The last part turns to present-day applications in China. Kulaixi presents Marx's critique as aimed at four targets. These are the 'abstract' spiritual life of Hegel and Feuerbach, the 'illusory' life of religion's other-worldly consolation, the 'reified' life under capital's logic, and the 'one-sided' life produced by the capitalist division of labour. Each critique, the author says, comes with a positive programme. It calls for a practice-based spiritual life that changes the world, a this-worldly life for real people, and a human-centred life built on social rather than capital logic. It also calls for an all-round life in a communist society of freely associated individuals. The author stresses that, for Marx, ideological forms are overcome only by overthrowing the social relations that produce them. In the final section the author draws practical conclusions. Enriching the people's spiritual world requires advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics across economic, political, cultural, social and ecological fields, and holding to a 'people-centred' value orientation. It also requires promoting mutual learning among civilizations and shared human values, and holding firm to communist ideals while rejecting bourgeois false ideology. The author connects this to creating a new form of human spiritual civilization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar draws on Marx's texts to ground current Party policy on cultural and spiritual construction.

The multiple meanings of "socialist revolution" and "socialism" in Lenin's writings after the October Revolution 十月革命后列宁著述中“社会主义革命”“社会主义”概念的多重含义 Yu Liangzao Why did Lenin call Soviet Russia's revolution "socialist" and call certain emergency measures "socialism", when he also said the country had not yet built a socialist society? Yu argues that these terms in Lenin's post-October writings are not simple descriptions of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the people's current practice. In Yu's reading they carry a long-range view of the future, a global view, praise for heroic struggle, and a resolve to keep the cause advancing. The article follows Lenin's usage from late 1917 through the civil war to the New Economic Policy of 1922. It draws on his speeches to peasant and soviet congresses, "The Immediate Tasks of the Soviet Government", his remarks at the Seventh Party Congress (1918) and a 1920 review of the revolution's first three years. It is organised in three sections, one for each of three claims, plus a conclusion that links Lenin's concepts to the Chinese Communist Party today. First, Yu holds that Lenin joined present practice to its future. Measures such as land redistribution, workers' control and bank nationalisation were compatible with capitalism, but they led towards socialism, so the revolution could be called socialist. Soviet Russia was a "socialist republic" because it had set out on that road, while it remained in a "transition period" consistent with Marx and Engels. Second, Lenin tied the Russian revolution to European and world revolution, describing Russia as one link in a world chain and insisting that victory could not be secure without it. Third, Yu says that when Lenin called accounting and control, or grain collection, "socialism" or "living socialism", he used the word loosely. Yu argues he did so to praise the masses' creativity and to mark measures on which the survival of Soviet power depended, while keeping the classical view that socialism lacks commodity production, classes and the state. Yu concludes that these concepts reflect experience gained in the revolutionary struggle and in building a new system. The author sees the same qualities in the Chinese Communist Party of the new era: the "Two Centenary Goals" show a future vision, a community with a shared future for mankind shows a global vision, and the campaign against poverty shows heroic struggle. Yu presents this as adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you study Lenin's changing use of the word "socialism", or want to see how Chinese scholars link Leninist concepts to current Party discourse.

The Western model of modernization and its contemporary predicaments 西方国家的现代化模式及当代困境 Wang Wei Wang Wei asks how Western countries modernized and why their model now faces systemic difficulties. The article argues that Western modernization was capital-centred rather than people-centred, that it produced great wealth alongside polarisation, ecological damage and colonial plunder, and that its internal flaws now surface as governance crises. Developing countries, Wang concludes, may learn from the West but should not treat it as a model. The piece has three parts. It first traces the rise of Europe from the British Industrial Revolution through the second and third industrial revolutions, the spread of industrialisation to Germany and the United States, and the formation of a world economy with a core and a periphery. It then describes the shared features of the Western model, with examples from Britain and the United States. Finally it surveys contemporary governance problems, including deindustrialisation, populism and identity anxiety. Wang's central move is to define Western modernization as capital-centred. In this account capital concentrates wealth and political power, replaces personal dependence with dependence on things (materialism, utilitarianism, fetishism), selects technology for surplus value rather than ecological reasons (illustrated by Manchester's air and water pollution), and drives colonial expansion on which Western development is said to have depended. Wang cites Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping to support this reading, and says it was the Chinese modernization path that broke the equation of modernization with Westernization. A second move links the model's flaws to its later stages: as deindustrialisation hits workers and townspeople, wage stagnation and inequality feed populism, such as Brexit, the Yellow Vests and American economic and white nationalism. Wang reads these as signs of government failure, market failure and social disorder, with governments, markets and society all revolving around capital. Wang concludes that world modernization began in the West but will not end with its flawed model. Conditions for latecomers differ sharply from earlier times, and Wang calls on developing countries to find paths suited to their own circumstances rather than copy Western experience. Wang adds that Western states which deflect attention outward instead of examining the roots of their problems risk deeper internal crises. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese academic account presents the historical development and current difficulties of Western capitalism for a general Party-journal readership.

The self-identity crisis in accelerated capitalist society and its critique from political economy 加速资本主义社会的自我认同危机及其政治经济学批判 Wang Xiaoxia Wang Xiaoxia asks why individuals in what Hartmut Rosa calls accelerated capitalist society, above all in the digital age, suffer a crisis of self-identity. The article argues that the crisis grows out of capital's logic of acceleration. This logic changes how people interact and exist, and produces a loss of meaning, a loss of trust, existential anxiety and false identification. Wang offers a critique grounded in Marxist political economy and proposes ways of sublating the crisis. The article has three parts. The first defines self-identity, drawing on Marx's view of the human essence as the ensemble of social relations, on Giddens and on Rosa, and then traces three causes of the crisis. The second sets out three manifestations and criticises each in turn: commodification, the expansion of digital platforms, and the totalising logic of acceleration. The third turns to practical paths, at the levels of the individual, platform regulation and the critique of capital itself. For the causes, Wang points to the inversion produced by money fetishism, the collusion of capital and technology in exploiting emotion, and competition that makes emotional choices a legitimate principle of distribution. The manifestations are then examined. Commodification shapes false self-identity through consumerism and narcissism. Platforms create risks of lost trust through online violence, surveillance of privacy and fraud. Acceleration turns individuals into self-exploiting 'achievement subjects' whose lives feel uncontrollable. Wang reads these as continuations of Marx's critique of machinery and of the capitalist as the 'driving wheel' of a society in which wage labourers are 'driven wheels'. Wang proposes that individuals strengthen critical reflection, adopt a rational view of consumption, resist blind involution and protect their privacy. The state should improve laws on digital platforms, regulate online communication, including real-name registration, and make platforms balance economic and social benefits. Wang adds that capital has a dual character, civilising and exploitative, and that the logic of capital can be transcended only by sublating capitalist relations of production through their own contradictions. Read the original if you are interested in how Rosa's theory of social acceleration is combined with Marxist political economy to analyse digital capitalism and subjectivity, and in the policy remedies Wang draws from it.

The logic and path of promoting all-round human development through new quality productive forces 以新质生产力推动人的全面发展的逻辑与路径 Song Ziling Qiu Gengtian Song Ziling and Qiu Gengtian ask how new quality productive forces can advance the all-round development of the human being. They note that existing scholarship has studied the concept's meaning, features and applications but has rarely linked it to human development. Their thesis is that new quality productive forces are a milestone form of productivity that supplies the material conditions for all-round development, provided that technological innovation is steered by talent and kept ethically in check. The article has three parts. The first sets out the features of all-round development under Chinese modernization, drawing on Marx's multiple determinations of human essence: the all-round development of practical activity, the enrichment of social relations, and the improvement of overall quality. The second explains the logic through which new quality productive forces enable this development, in four respects. The third turns to practical paths centred on technological innovation, covering talent, the proper use of emerging technology and its ethical risks. On the logic, the authors argue that new quality productive forces raise practical capacity by strengthening subjects' cognition, extending practice into non-material objects such as data and information, and increasing interaction between subject and object. They widen social interaction through digital media and reduce physical distance. They loosen the old division of labour through platform and gig work, cross-field technological integration and new industries such as unmanned factories. They also lengthen free time through efficiency gains, flexible work and the sharing economy. On the paths, the authors call for cultivating high-calibre talent while also developing ordinary workers, and for using technology "wisely". They analyse Industry 4.0 as an example of new quality productive forces, but also warn of its risks, including cities dominated by industry and the loss of personal data. In their account, these ethical risks stem from the excessive capitalisation of science and technology, which produces new forms of alienation. The authors conclude that promoting all-round human development through new quality productive forces is an irreversible historical trend. They propose a talent-development mechanism, humane, ecological smart cities, and a division of responsibility among government, enterprises and individuals for privacy and data security. The aim is to turn the "misuse" of technology into its "proper use" so that its benefits reach all people. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese theorists tie the concept of new quality productive forces to Marx's theory of human development, including its treatment of free time, the division of labour and technological alienation.

Advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance by starting with Party conduct 从抓作风入手推进全面从严治党 An Yufeng An Yufeng takes up Xi Jinping's statement that starting with Party conduct to advance full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is an important lesson of the Party's self-reform in the new era. Published in Guangming Daily on 24 July 2025, the commentary argues that conduct is the Party's image, bears on public support, and decides the success of the Party's and the country's undertakings. An holds that the eight-point regulation adopted after the 18th Party Congress (2012) opened up the whole field of conduct building. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why conduct building matters. The second turns to methods and requirements. The third describes practical paths for carrying it forward. It draws on the Yan'an-era contrast between the Yan'an and Xi'an styles, on Xi's remarks about the eight-point regulation, and on a list of Party education campaigns since 2012. An argues that conduct problems are in essence problems of Party spirit, and that their core is the Party's relationship with the people. The author therefore ties conduct to ideals and convictions, to serious inner-Party political life, and to the mass line. On method, An calls for linking the rectification of conduct, the enforcement of discipline and the fight against corruption, and for making these efforts routine and long-term through institutions. The author also proposes strict management systems and a framework to make officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt. On practice, An urges rigorous implementation of the eight-point regulation and sustained correction of the “four undesirable work styles” (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance). Leading officials are to set an example, including in family conduct, so that good Party conduct lifts social and popular customs. An concludes that conduct building must be sustained and pursued from the top down, with leaders acting as a “lead goose”. Local bodies are to treat public satisfaction as the measure of improvement. The author also calls for a healthy political ecology and “amicable yet clean” relations between government and business. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party-affiliated scholars present conduct building within Party self-governance.

The distinctive contributions of women delegates to the CPC's Seventh National Congress during the War of Resistance against Japan 党的七大女性党代表在抗战中的独特贡献 Zhuang Qiuju Zhuang Qiuju, in a short piece for the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2025), asks what the women delegates to the Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China (1945) contributed to the War of Resistance against Japan. The author argues that, despite differing ages, origins and schooling, these women played an important role on every front of the war. The article opens with a profile of the 52 women delegates, 18 of them alternate delegates, who made up 6.9 per cent of all delegates. Zhuang gives their average age as 33, notes that they came from 14 provinces, that about 37 per cent had peasant family backgrounds and that 52 per cent had secondary schooling. It then treats their work under two headings: strengthening the fight against the Japanese, and promoting national unity in resistance. On the first, Zhuang describes women who fought at the front, built base areas and guerrilla units, and joined anti-"mopping-up" campaigns, citing Li Zhen, Liu Yaxiong and An Jianping. Others gathered intelligence and moved funds and supplies underground, such as Wei Gongzhi, who helped bring a large sum raised by the Communist International from Shanghai to Xi'an. On the second, Zhuang says the delegates ran propaganda, mobilised workers' groups and united influential figures in the united front. They paid particular attention to women: according to the author's incomplete count, 44 of the 52 worked in women's organisations. Zhuang concludes that the women delegates acted as an independent force in the resistance, whose contributions to fighting, base-area construction and final victory are indelible. The piece is a stage result of a National Social Science Fund project on the history of the Party's marriage policy. Read the original if you want a concise, example-rich account of how Chinese scholarship presents women Party delegates' wartime roles and the biographical details behind it.

The Seventh Party Congress and the building of the Party's work style 党的七大与党的作风建设 Zhou Liangshu Zhou Liangshu, a professor at Peking University's School of Marxism, argues in this newspaper commentary that the Seventh Party Congress (1945) was a milestone in the history of the Communist Party's work style. In Zhou's account, the "three major work styles" that Mao Zedong summed up and established there laid a foundation for victory in the new-democratic revolution. They also pointed the way for building a Marxist ruling party after that victory. The piece first explains why the Congress met in 1945, 17 years after the Sixth. It traces the delay to war and then to the Yan'an rectification movement and the study of the Party's history, which produced the first "historical resolution". It then shows how the Congress combined review of the past with a forward-looking line, and finally turns to the three work styles and Mao's plain-language formulation of them. Zhou identifies three points on which the Party leadership had reached consensus about Party building: democratic centralism, unity among comrades, and leading by example, especially in self-criticism, where Mao criticised his own mistakes before the Congress. The three work styles are integrating theory with practice, maintaining close ties with the masses, and criticism and self-criticism. The Congress wrote them into the Party constitution for the first time. Mao also put them in everyday terms as telling the truth: "no stealing, no pretending, no boasting", meaning no plagiarism, no feigned knowledge and no inflated reports. Zhou concludes that Mao both summarised and practised these styles, citing his calls for modesty, prudence and wholehearted service to the people, and his Foolish Old Man story. On this basis Zhou holds that the Seventh Congress marks a boundary stone in the history of Party work style. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned account of how the 1945 Congress is presented in Party-history writing on work style.

Strengthening the guiding power of the "Great Ideological and Political Course" through a more complete system Practice at Wuhan University of Technology 以体系完善增强 “大思政课”引领力 Sun Xianyi Shen Laijin This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 24 July 2025, asks how a university can build out the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) so that ideological and political education becomes more persuasive and influential. Sun and Shen, both from the School of Marxism at Wuhan University of Technology, present their own institution's practice as an answer. They argue that the course should be run with an open door, mobilising resources beyond the classroom, and that this serves the fundamental task of fostering virtue and nurturing talent. The article is organised around three areas of work at the university, followed by a section on teaching staff. These are holding the classroom as the main front, building distinctive ideological-education brands, and using society as a large classroom. A short closing passage commits the university to continued development under the same headings. On classroom teaching, the authors describe ties between national policy and students' daily lives, rural revitalisation cases, virtual-simulation reproductions of red memorials, and classroom debates on topics such as the key to common prosperity and Chinese modernization. They also report that courses in all disciplines are being aligned with ideological education, citing a physics-based project approved by the Ministry of Education in 2023. On brands and practice, they list the "one course, one brand" activities, cultural programmes, platforms combining innovation, volunteering or the arts with ideological education, a practice base with a hospital, and a WeChat column. On society as classroom, they cite student volunteer teams, visits to factories, bridges and tunnels tied to the university's industry strengths, and the "three goings, three learnings" red-themed projects. Training sessions, collective lesson preparation and ethics lectures for teachers are also described. The authors conclude that building a high-quality "Great Ideological and Political Course" is now unavoidable for the university's reform of ideological teaching and a key means of raising a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The university plans to keep the campus as the main front, extend education into society and strengthen its brands. Read the original if you want a concrete, institution-level example of how a Chinese university reports implementing the "Great Ideological and Political Course" in classrooms, practice activities and community settings.

Making ideological and political theory courses more appealing and engaging A review of Professor Li Xia's "Research on Innovating the Teaching Discourse System of University Ideological and Political Theory Courses" 让思政课教学更有吸引力感染力 Zhang Yanguo This is a book review by Zhang Yanguo of Li Xia's Research on Innovating the Teaching Discourse System of University Ideological and Political Theory Courses (China Social Sciences Press, April 2024). Zhang holds that ideological and political theory courses touch students only if their teaching discourse is innovative and carries intellectual force. In Zhang's view, the book makes a new and useful contribution to that task. Zhang reports that the book is organised around the questions of who teaches these courses, what kind of course to teach and how to teach it well. It sets four goals for discourse innovation: ideological quality, theoretical quality, affinity and relevance. It draws on a survey of university students' expectations and on analysis of the teaching language in prize-winning demonstration lessons. According to the review, Li defines each goal and pairs it with a unifying principle. Ideological quality is the soul of teaching, theoretical quality its foundation, affinity its precondition and relevance its focus on students' real concerns. From the survey and case analysis Li distils "six musts and six haves" for teaching language, and names problems such as the pull of diverse social trends, fragmented online information, uniform discourse and over-abstraction. Li's proposed remedy is student-centred teaching, with a model of "theory + problems + cases + classroom participation" and a dialogic dual-subject classroom. The model is illustrated with the course on the basic principles of Marxism. Zhang sees the book's novelty in its clear goals, its classroom design, its student-centred stance and its systematic method. Zhang concludes that the book offers useful reference for improving the effectiveness of teaching discourse and for reform of both these courses and "course-embedded" ideological education. Zhang adds that some topics need deeper treatment, including how to realise the Two Integrations in class, how to use fine traditional Chinese culture, and how to make teaching more artful. Read the original if you want a brief overview of current Chinese thinking on teaching discourse in university ideological and political courses.

The opening-up effects of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的开放效应 Xu Xiujun Xu Xiujun takes up the place of openness in Chinese modernization and the effects that a more open China has on the world. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that reform and opening up is the key move deciding the success or failure of Chinese modernization, Xu argues that Chinese modernization is open and inclusive by nature. In this account it develops through exchange and mutual learning among civilizations, and higher-level opening will bring more positive effects for world peace and prosperity. The article is built in three parts. The first presents opening up as the distinctive mark of Chinese modernization, in three respects: a necessary condition, an important driving force, and a necessary response to economic globalization. The second sets out how Chinese modernization promotes common development worldwide. The third argues that it leads change in the global governance system and order. On the first point, Xu traces how China drew on foreign capital, technology and management experience after reform and opening up to achieve rapid growth. Xu also holds that, amid rising unilateralism and protectionism and attempts to contain China, continued opening is needed to build new international competitive advantages and the new development pattern. On the second point, Xu cites figures: average annual growth of 8.9% in 1979–2023, a 24.8% average contribution to world growth, and nearly 800 million people lifted out of poverty. Xu adds China's huge market, its trade and investment position, and the Belt and Road Initiative and three global initiatives. The article says Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers developing countries another path. On the third, Xu says it promotes equal and orderly multipolarity, inclusive economic globalization that benefits all, and fairer global governance. Xu describes the present system as built mainly by Western powers after the Second World War and as failing to meet the demands of developing countries. Xu concludes that Chinese modernization follows a path of peaceful development, rejecting war, colonialism and plunder. Xu says it advances a community with a shared future for mankind and leads towards more just and reasonable global governance. The text is a short policy-oriented essay in Party-theory language that relies on official statements and statistics. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese official scholarship links opening up, global development and global governance reform.

An outline of the factors that generate the modern strength of Chinese civilization 中华文明的现代力量生成因素论要 Yang Zengdong Huang Shize Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that Chinese modernization endows Chinese civilization with modern strength, while Chinese civilization gives Chinese modernization its deep foundations, Yang Zengdong and Huang Shize ask how this "modern strength of Chinese civilization" came into being. They argue that it is not accidental but the necessary result of historical development, and that it arises from four interacting factors. Understanding these factors, they say, matters for strengthening cultural confidence and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised around the four factors, each treated in its own section. The first is the outstanding characteristics of Chinese civilization, the second is the leadership of the Communist Party of China, the third is the Second Integration, and the fourth is the conscious action of the Chinese people. A short closing section compares China with Latin America, Africa and the West. The authors first claim that the modern strength is a historical and indigenous force, formed through continuity rather than rupture. They contrast Chinese civilization with the "fractured" civilizations of the West and say it is endogenous, active and self-aware. They tie its five characteristics (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) to the Party's leadership: through revolution, ideological guidance and mass organisation, the Party liberated the people and created a new form of human civilization. They then present the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, as the cultural main line. In their account it sublates the dross of tradition, dispels Western-centrism, consolidates cultural subjectivity and answers earlier currents of cultural restorationism and wholesale Westernisation. Finally they locate the subjective driving force in the people's historical initiative, cultural confidence, theoretical consciousness grounded in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and strong national identity. The authors conclude that the generation of this strength is both a historical and a contemporary question. In their reading, Latin America and Africa once had brilliant civilizations and faced similar outside interference but did not rise as China has. The West, though it entered modernity early, lacks later momentum because of its limitations. The strength, they say, springs from the practice of the people and will advance through it. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars link civilizational distinctiveness, Party leadership and the Second Integration within current official discourse on Chinese modernization.

Raising the quality and efficiency of producer services to support the development of new quality productive forces 以生产性服务业提质增效有力支撑新质生产力发展 Zhou Haichuan Zhou Haichuan takes up a policy question set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): how producer services, meaning R&D, design, information, consulting, logistics and after-sales services for production, can support new quality productive forces. The article argues that high-quality development of these services is a key link in cultivating such forces, but that China's producer services still have four weak points that need targeted remedies. The piece is a short policy commentary in four steps. It first explains why producer services matter, then identifies four shortcomings in China's current position, and finally sets out five lines of action. It draws on statistics for 2023 and on examples from smartphones, industrial internet platforms and AI talent supply. On the first point, Zhou assigns producer services four roles: a key link in innovation, a catalyst for new production relations, a support for high-grade production factors, and an accelerator through digital platforms. As evidence, the article says intangible services such as operating systems, software and chip-design patents account for about 55% of a smartphone's value. The four weaknesses are weak science and technology service capacity, poor transfer of research results, shallow integration with industry, and insufficient high-end professional services. Zhou cites figures: research and technical services made up only 7.2% of the revenue of large producer-service firms in 2023; subscription models were 15% of industrial internet platform revenue; and the shortfall in AI talent exceeds 5 million. Zhou calls for supporting innovation platforms and key laboratories, building full-chain transfer services centred on pilot-scale testing, and deepening the integration of advanced manufacturing with producer services. Zhou also proposes cultivating data, talent and technology-finance factors, and opening services further, including negative lists for cross-border services trade and a bigger role in international standard-setting. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-aligned economic commentary links the sectoral policy of producer services to the new quality productive forces agenda, including the figures it cites.

Deepening the understanding of the laws governing the relationship between aggregate supply and aggregate demand Reflections on studying Volume I of Selected Economic Works of Xi Jinping 深化对总供给与总需求关系的规律性认识 Qiao Xiaonan Wang Yi Zhang Wenjin Written as a study note on Volume I of Selected Economic Works of Xi Jinping (published March 2025), this article asks how Xi Jinping's economic thought treats aggregate supply and aggregate demand, which of Marxist political economy's principles it develops, and how the two should be balanced in future. The authors argue that this body of thought treats supply and demand as a unified whole within the cycle of social reproduction. They contrast this with the Western tradition, which in their account separates supply-side from demand-side analysis. The article opens by situating the topic among the five "must balance" relationships set out by the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference. It then gathers Xi's statements into three core views, derives four "laws" or regularities, and ends with policy proposals for supply, demand and the links between them. The authors, writing from Nankai University, cite scholars such as Li Xuesong, Chen Yulu and Guo Kesha as earlier work on the theme. The central move is to read supply and demand through Marx's schema of social reproduction, in which production and consumption sit at the two ends and distribution and exchange connect them. Smoothing the circulation of the national economy is therefore, the authors say, the substance of balancing supply and demand. They claim Xi's thought extends Marx's reproduction theory in four ways: it moves from a closed to an open economy by distinguishing domestic from international circulation; it refines supply and demand structures, including the need to keep non-productive sectors such as finance and real estate in proportion to productive ones; it balances short-term growth with long-term development under high-quality development; and it combines an effective market with an effective government under socialist market economy institutions. The authors propose action on three fronts. On the supply side, they call for cultivating new quality productive forces and building a modernised industrial system. On the demand side, they call for expanding consumption, investment and external demand to build the new development pattern. For linking supply and demand, they urge improving the livelihood system and building a unified national market. They conclude that this reasoning offers a method for building an independent Chinese system of economic knowledge. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Xi Jinping Thought on the economy is framed in terms of Marx's reproduction schemes, along with a full list of the policy measures the authors propose.

Coordinating aggregate supply and aggregate demand to keep the national economic cycle unobstructed 统筹好总供给和总需求的关系，畅通国民经济循环 Liu Wei Fan Xin Liu Wei and Fan Xin take up one of the "five musts" drawn from the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024: the need to coordinate the relationship between aggregate supply and aggregate demand and keep the national economic cycle unobstructed. The authors argue that this principle is a basic problem of macroeconomic theory and the underlying logic of China's macroeconomic regulation. They also hold that it is the urgent requirement for countering the current shrinkage of both supply and demand. The article has three parts. It first surveys how Western and Marxist economics have treated supply and demand: classical economics, the German historical school, Keynesianism and its offshoots, supply-side economics, national accounting, and Marx's theory of social capital reproduction. It then traces China's practice, from "comprehensive balance" under the planned economy to three phases of macro-regulation since reform and opening up. The last part diagnoses present conditions and sets out policy proposals. The authors contend that classical economics stressed supply because supply shortage and free competition defined the industrial revolution, while Keynes's demand analysis answered the Great Depression. In Liu and Fan's reading, Marx's two-department reproduction model explains the institutional roots of capitalist crises and guides analysis of socialist reproduction. They divide China's regulation into demand management (1978–2012), supply-side structural reform as the main line (2012–2021), and, since the 20th Party Congress (2022), coordination of both ends. For the present, they cite persistently negative price indices, weakening consumption and investment, corporate difficulties, industrial restructuring, rising factor costs and external pressure from US and Western tariffs, monetary shifts and technology controls. They judge that demand contraction currently hits harder than supply contraction. Liu and Fan call for expanding domestic demand and strengthening the domestic circulation, while continuing supply-side structural reform and pursuing high-quality supply that leads demand. They also propose four steps. The first is linking medium- and long-term strategic planning with annual targets. The second is coordinating fiscal, monetary and other policies through consistency assessment. The third is shifting to a "more proactive fiscal policy and moderately loose monetary policy". The fourth is deepening reform to build a high-standard socialist market economy, so that demand pulls supply and supply creates demand. Read the original if you want a systematic, official-aligned account of how Chinese economists place current macro policy within the history of supply-and-demand theory and of reform-era regulation.

Reform and innovation to drive high-quality development of state-owned enterprises 改革创新推动国企高质量发展 Fan Zhihong Chen Jin This short commentary, published in Economic Daily in July 2025, asks how deeper reform and innovation can push state-owned enterprises (SOEs) towards high-quality development. Fan and Chen argue that SOEs are a material and political foundation of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that strengthening them is necessary for serving Chinese modernization. The authors take as their basis the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which calls for stronger, better and bigger state capital and SOEs. They note that reforms since the 18th Party Congress (2012) have improved layout, innovation capacity and efficiency, but identify remaining problems: incomplete modern enterprise systems, weak asset structures and unfinished upgrading. They propose three areas of action. First, the authors call for improving the modern enterprise system: clearer powers and responsibilities among governance bodies, Party leadership built into every stage of corporate governance, flatter and more market-responsive management, reformed incentives and tolerance-of-error rules, and smarter supervision. Second, they urge SOEs to focus on their main business and to concentrate state capital in the "three concentrations": national security and the economic lifeline, public services, and forward-looking strategic emerging industries. Third, they argue SOEs should be the main force in scientific and technological innovation, acting as hubs and "chain leaders" that integrate resources, fund basic and frontier research, and act as patient capital. The authors conclude that these measures would strengthen supply-chain security, raise SOEs' core competitiveness and support a modern industrial system and a technologically strong country. They also support cooperation between SOEs and private firms through industrial alliances. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy agenda for SOE reform after the Third Plenum.

Party conduct and image-building of the Communist Party during the nationwide War of Resistance 全民族抗战时期党的作风建设与形象展示 Yue Kui Yue Kui asks how the Communist Party of China built up its own conduct and public image during the nationwide War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45), and what this achieved. The newspaper commentary argues that, faced with Japanese aggression, Nationalist die-hards' anti-communism and prejudice abroad, the Party strengthened its self-construction, especially its conduct (zuofeng). In Yue's account, this raised its cohesion, appeal and fighting capacity and produced rapid growth in its strength. The piece is organised in four sections. They cover the Party's people-centred orientation and its political and organisational character; legal and democratic construction in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region; discipline and clean governance; and the united front, military struggle and propaganda at home and abroad. It draws on Party documents, Mao Zedong's writings and episodes from Yan'an, and cites a US Army observer's remark about the Communists. Yue's central claim is that conduct and image reinforced each other. The author points to the Party's self-definition from 1935 as the vanguard of both the proletariat and the whole nation, the rectification campaign against subjectivism, sectarianism and Party formalism, and the Yan'an hospital and epidemic-prevention campaigns as evidence of serving the people wholeheartedly. Border-region legislation, universal suffrage for adults over eighteen, the "three-thirds" system and assemblies are presented as guarantees of people's democratic rights. Strict discipline is illustrated by the executions of Huang Kegong and Xiao Yubi, which Mao said served to educate the Party. Yue adds that newspapers such as Xinhua Daily and Liberation Daily, an international propaganda committee and visits by foreigners to the border region spread this image. Yue concludes that the Party became the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) of national resistance and presented itself as hardworking, resolute, united with the masses, democratic and progressive. In the author's reading, this image demonstrated strong governing capacity and vitality, gave hope for national salvation and won international support. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Party-history writing presents wartime conduct, discipline and propaganda as sources of the Party's authority.

Chen Yun's rich leadership experience in managing economic work 陈云负责经济工作的丰富领导经验 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Chen Yun's birth, to learn from Chen's rich leadership experience, especially in economic work. The article argues that Chen, a member of the first and second generations of the Party's central leadership, was one of the pioneers and founders of China's socialist economic construction. In Song's account, he put forward important views and measures and found creative ways to solve problems and open up new situations. This short newspaper article is organised in three parts. The first deals with Chen's thinking on modernization and the Four Modernizations. The second covers industrialization, economic recovery after 1949, and the handling of food, livelihood and construction. The third examines his exploration of the socialist economic system, the market and the plan, and reform, and closes with his working method. Song draws throughout on Chen's collected works and selected works. Song stresses that Chen insisted on a clear grasp of national conditions before modernizing, quoting his remark that for backward countries the issue is having something at all. He also stressed that modernization must be socialist, led by the Party, and pursue material and cultural-ethical progress together. Song presents Chen as always viewing economic law politically and from the standpoint of the whole country. Construction had to match national financial and material strength, with priorities and proper proportions among sectors, grain security and agriculture taking first place. At the Eighth Party Congress (1956) he described state and collective operation as the mainstay, with individual enterprise, free production within the plan and free markets as supplements. After reform and opening up he favoured comprehensive balance, macro-control that keeps the economy lively without disorder, and cautious, pilot-tested reform. Song concludes that Chen's methods rested on seeking truth from facts, summed up in his fifteen-character formula "not by authority, not by books, only by reality; exchange, compare, repeat", and in his view that policy-makers should spend over ninety per cent of their time on investigation. Song holds that this experience still offers important lessons. Read the original if you want a brief, official-register overview of how Chen Yun's economic thought and working method are presented in Party-affiliated scholarship on the 2025 anniversary.

Passing the Long March spirit down the generations 让长征精神代代相传 Du Fanding Du Fanding, who led the drafting of the Long March National Cultural Park plan, takes stock of the park's first six years. Writing as the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory approaches, Du argues that the project has begun to deliver results. In the author's account, it preserves the physical carriers of the Long March spirit, interprets them vividly and uses them for Party-style education. The newspaper commentary is organised in three parts: protection of resources, interpretation of the spirit, and red education. It draws on examples from provinces along the route, which the 2021 plan brought together across 15 provincial-level units. It describes the park as the only one of the five national cultural parks built around a revolutionary spirit. On protection, Du reports that the number of immovable Long March relics has grown from over 1,600 to 2,000. The newly recognised sites include historic road remains, and relics are now identified as a group around major events, as at the Xiang River battle site. Du also cites the 2022 designation of "red grasslands" to give the crossing of the grasslands a material basis. On interpretation, the article lists research publications, a museum alliance, stage dramas, digital exhibitions and documentaries. On education, it points to Party schools, cadre academies and "Great Ideological and Political Course" classes, plus study routes where students make straw sandals and carry stretchers. Du says one Yibin county project has received 220,000 visitors since 2021. Du concludes that future work should be cautious yet innovative and should seek methods that suit current needs. The aim is a protection, display and transmission system that reflects national will, standards and image and enjoys international esteem. Du presents this as the way to keep the Long March spirit a lasting source of motivation. Read the original if you want an insider's overview of how a flagship heritage and red-education project is being implemented, with concrete local examples.

The historical dialectic of the state and capitalism in Capital and its manuscripts 《资本论》及其手稿中国家与资本主义的历史辩证法 Guo Qiang Guo Qiang argues that scholarship on Capital has concentrated on its economics and neglected its theory of the state, while work on Marx's theory of the state has turned mainly to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and The Civil War in France. The article contends that Capital and its manuscripts contain a systematic account of the state's origin, essence, functions and future, derived from the state's link to the capitalist economy. Guo points to Marx's "five-part" and "six-book" plans, both of which reserve a separate section for the state. The article is organised in five parts. It treats in turn the essence of the bourgeois state, its functions, relations between states in foreign trade and the world market, the historical limits of the state form, and Marx's anticipation of the state's withering away. Guo draws on Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts, the preface and introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, the London Notebooks, and related passages from Engels. Guo's central claim is that Marx explains the state from civil society, meaning material life relations, rather than from the state itself. The bourgeois state emerged with primitive accumulation, relying on the colonial system, public debt, modern taxation and protective tariffs, and its laws (enclosure acts, labour statutes, factory acts) serve capital even when they concede to workers. Guo reads the state's dual functions as public affairs arising from the nature of all societies and specific functions arising from the opposition between government and the mass of the people. The state's dependence on capital's command over labour, hidden behind formal freedom and equality, is said to be the "most hidden secret" of the state form. The contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, Guo argues, makes the state a "collective capitalist" unable to resolve the opposition between universal and particular interests. Guo concludes that Marx foresaw replacing the "illusory community" of the state with an association of free individuals who own the means of production in common and distribute means of consumption according to labour time. In this account, society would then take back state power, and the state apparatus would be consigned to a museum of antiquities. Guo presents this as the completion of human emancipation beyond merely political emancipation. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reconstruction of the state theory in Capital and its manuscripts, drawing on Marx's planning schemes and economic categories.

The 21st century still needs Lenin On Žižek's defence and rehabilitation of Leninism 21世纪依然需要列宁 Luo Zixuan Guo Lishuang Why has Lenin returned to Western radical-left debate, and how does Slavoj Žižek defend him? Luo and Guo argue that Lenin has been misread and stigmatised as a symbol of totalitarianism because his critique of bourgeois freedom threatens the legitimacy of liberal democracy. They present Žižek's call to "repeat Lenin" as the most prominent response, while holding that it also exposes the predicament of the Western left. The article has four parts. It first describes how Lenin was labelled totalitarian and why this served capitalism. It then sets out Žižek's defence across his Lenin books, from Repeating Lenin (2001) to Lenin 2017 (2017). A third section explains why Žižek holds that the century still needs Lenin, and a conclusion assesses this Western turn from the authors' own standpoint. The authors report three moves in Žižek's defence. First, Leninism does not necessarily lead to Stalinism: Žižek reads Lenin's economic and nationality policies and his "political testament" as incompatible with Stalin's course, and ranks the October Revolution with the French Revolution as a world-historical "event". Second, Lenin opened a revolutionary path from a desperate situation after 1914, when the Second International collapsed into patriotism. Third, "repeating Lenin" means recovering what Lenin failed to do and the courage to make the impossible possible, not returning to Lenin. Žižek, in this account, uses Lacanian theory to show that liberal "freedom of choice" is a framed, forced choice, and that Western Marxism has been tamed into cultural critique. Luo and Guo conclude that the Western left's turn to Lenin reflects its difficulties: a muted working class, short-lived protests such as Occupy Wall Street, and a defanged critical theory. Whether it will help remains, they say, to be seen. They propose a more realistic option: recognising socialism with Chinese characteristics as an inheritor and developer of Leninism that is opening a new phase of world socialism. Without this, they argue, "repeating Lenin" risks becoming an empty slogan. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Žižek's Leninism and of how Chinese scholars view Western radical-left thought.

Critical strategy and methodology in the face of the production of abstract space A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space 面对抽象空间生产的批判战略与方法论 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing reads the methodological discussion in Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space, asking how a critical theory can confront an abstract space of capitalism whose relations of domination are invisible behind economic appearances. Zhang argues that Lefebvre responds with three linked proposals: a critical strategic hypothesis grounded in historical materialism, a regressive–progressive method of historical analysis, and the reconstruction of spatial codes. Zhang values these but repeatedly judges that Lefebvre cannot say how a spatial revolution would actually be carried out. The article follows three sections. The first treats the historical-materialist premises of spatial critique, the second the regressive–progressive method and its Marxian origin, and the third the rebuilding of spatial codes and the political strategy for change. Zhang draws on Lefebvre's other works, including Critique of Everyday Life and The Survival of Capitalism, and on Marx's Grundrisse, Sartre, Foucault and Lenin. In the first section, Zhang reports Lefebvre's claim that contemporary abstract space has become a technologically programmed, surveilled realm of social engineering. Lefebvre rejects idealist theories of discursive or Cartesian mental space, grounds spatial theory in the three material productions of The German Ideology, and holds that the production of space has replaced or overlain the production of things, allowing capitalism to survive. Zhang adds that Lefebvre fails to ask "whose technological utopia?" In the second section, Lefebvre takes Marx's idea that the anatomy of man is a key to the anatomy of the ape and applies it to space. Zhang explains that it also works synchronically: advanced capitalist space, such as the firms Microsoft and Apple, illuminates labour-intensive production elsewhere, and polluting industry is moved to poorer countries. In the third section, Zhang argues that recoding space through new language unifying public and private, inside and outside, work and non-work, will remain subjective unless the mode of production changes. Zhang concludes that Lefebvre's strategic hypothesis is directionally right but vague. It rejects the Russian single-centre model, allows for revolutionary subjects drawn from the margins or from the developed working class, and accepts both violent and parliamentary paths. Zhang observes that it offers no workable plan for breaking Western capital's domination of world space. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese reading of Lefebvre's spatial methodology and its limits, set against Marx's historical method and unequal capitalist development.
