Progress and prospects in building the theoretical system of humanistic economics 人文经济学理论体系建构的进展和展望 Wang Lisheng Duan Bosen This literature review surveys the scholarship that followed Xi Jinping's 2023 call, made during the national "Two Sessions" while discussing the historic cities of Suzhou and Hangzhou, to study "humanistic economics" (renwen jingjixue). Wang and Duan ask where Chinese scholars have got to in building the field's theoretical system. They find a promising start but argue that most work still treats it as a branch of economics, when it needs to be understood as a theory of civilization. The review is organised in five parts. It covers the field's basic features (object of study, disciplinary status, methods, nature), its theoretical content (the culture–economy relationship, theoretical foundations, significance), systematisation (historical genesis, discursive innovation, academic structure), and practical studies of humanistic-economy cities, Chinese modernization and new quality productive forces. A closing section assesses gaps and sets out directions. On disciplinary status, the authors sort positions into three camps: economics (Luo Weidong, Bai Yongxiu), humanities and philosophy (Sun Ruru), and civilization studies (Fan Hao). They report scholars agreeing that historical materialism is the methodological base, but differing on specific methods. Many see the field as distinct from Western "humanistic" economics because it rests on a people-centred standpoint and on Marx's critique of political economy. Foundations are drawn from Marxism and from fine traditional Chinese culture, which one scholar, Ren Ping, says must be inherited as a whole rather than reduced to Confucian fragments. In practice, studies sort cities into types, examine Hangzhou, Suzhou and Nantong, and link humanistic economy to common prosperity, rural revitalisation and high-quality development. Wang and Duan conclude that research remains tied to economics and cannot yet grasp the civilizational content of the "five-sphere" new civilizational order. They also note that some work narrows Chinese tradition to Confucianism, that case studies cluster in Suzhou, Hangzhou and developed eastern provinces, and that rural areas and corporate management get little attention. They call for work on basic categories, principles and methodology, and for linking humanistic economy to Chinese modernization, new quality productive forces and new production relations, with more attention to central and western regions. Read the original if you want a detailed map of who is arguing what in China's emerging humanistic economics debate, with many named scholars and positions.

Understanding Xi Jinping's important discourse on the modernized industrial system 深刻理解习近平总书记关于现代化产业体系的重要论述 Lin Muxi Wang Cong Lin Muxi and Wang Cong set out to explain what Xi Jinping has said since the 18th Party Congress (2012) about building a modernized industrial system. They present it as a coherent body of ideas that guides high-quality development and the building of a modern socialist country. Their thesis is that the discourse is a scientific theoretical system, rooted in China's industrial history and responsive to present conditions. The article moves through five parts. It traces the historical and practical background, from industrialisation under the Western blockade and the self-reliance line after 1949 to the shift of the industrial structure in the 2010s. It then discusses the significance of the discourse, its internal content (connotation, features, tasks), its practical requirements, and finally its value. The practical section covers the "five adherences", innovation-led development, and institutional reforms in areas such as services, infrastructure, supply-chain security and education, science and talent. The authors argue that the modernized industrial system is a distinct step beyond earlier formulas such as the "modern industrial system" of the 17th Party Congress (2007). In their reading, it places industry within the overall plan for national modernization. They define its content as an integrated system of the real economy, technological innovation, modern finance and human resources, and as one that is complete, advanced and secure. They call for new quality productive forces, led by technological innovation, and for upgrading traditional industries rather than phasing them out. They contend that the real economy, especially manufacturing, must remain the foundation. In the authors' account, the discourse sums up China's industrialisation experience and moves beyond mainstream Western theory, which treats a service share of 70 per cent or more as the mark of a modern economy and which they link to deindustrialisation. They also say it develops Marxist productive-force theory and offers developing countries a Chinese approach to modernization. They call for further systematic and theoretical study of the discourse. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists present the policy logic behind industrial upgrading, supply-chain security and technological self-reliance.

Cultivating the Communist's "learning of the mind" begins with firm ideals and convictions 修炼共产党人“心学”首在坚定理想信念 Chen Yanbo This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call for Party members to cultivate a Communist "learning of the mind" (xinxue), unifying study, thought and practice, and knowledge, belief and action. Chen Yanbo argues that this cultivation starts with firm ideals and convictions, which steady the will, temper resolve and raise fighting spirit. The piece is organised in three steps, each borrowing a concept from the Ming thinker Wang Yangming. It treats ideals as the "first-rate matter" of a Communist, firmness of conviction as "training through affairs", and fighting spirit as the "unity of knowledge and action". Chen contends that the Party differs from other parties in being organised around shared ideals rather than shared interests, so joining it means making those ideals one's own life priority. On this reading, the Party's survival of setbacks rests on its lofty aims, and the Communists who founded New China held firm to the aim of saving the nation through Marxism. Firm conviction, the author says, is never spontaneous or permanent. It must be renewed over a lifetime, and the anti-corruption cases of recent years show to Chen that political, economic, moral and lifestyle degeneration begins with loss of ideals. The author links firm conviction to loyalty and strong Party spirit, and describes it as the "special material" that resists corruption. Chen concludes that, facing growing risks, Communists with firm convictions will recognise their historical mission, stay confident in communism and in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and develop the capacity to struggle. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-building writing draws on Neo-Confucian heart-mind philosophy to discuss ideological discipline.

Grasping the distinctive features of the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 把握全面从严治党体系鲜明特征 Li Tian This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how to understand the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Li presents it as a dynamic system that is rich in content, fully equipped, scientific and efficient, and as a product of theoretical, practical and institutional innovation in Party building in the new era. The author argues that it must be read through systems thinking, by identifying the features of each of its five sub-systems. The article takes its structure from Xi Jinping's speech at the 15th collective study session of the Political Bureau of the 20th Central Committee. That speech named five components: organisational, education, oversight, institutional and responsibility systems. Li devotes one section to each and pairs each with two features. Li assigns rigour and connectedness to the organisational system, citing coverage of central, local and grassroots levels, of new economic and social organisations and of new employment groups, and the use of digital tools. Continuity and integration describe the education system, with its regular and intensive study and its mechanisms such as the "three meetings and one lesson". Guidance and coordination mark the oversight system, in which intra-Party supervision is linked to the Party's self-supervision and to supervision by the people. Wholeness and effectiveness describe the institutional system, and clarity and layering the responsibility system. Li reads the last as a closed loop of assigning, performing, questioning and pursuing responsibility, which is meant to stop pressure from weakening as it passes down the hierarchy. Li concludes that these paired features together make up the systemic character of the whole and that each sub-system must be understood through its own practical requirements. The article is a brief interpretive gloss on Xi's speech rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style outline of how Chinese Party scholars classify the components of Party-building policy.

The history of the War of Resistance as a living "great ideological and political course" 抗战史是生动的“大思政课” Shen Youhong Writing in Guangming Daily on 22 July 2025, Shen Youhong takes up Xi Jinping's recent call, made during a visit to the Hundred Regiments Offensive memorial hall in Shanxi, to tell the story of the War of Resistance well and pass the great spirit of resistance down the generations. Shen's thesis is that the history of the war is itself a living "great ideological and political course" for young people, and that this spirit should shape a new generation able to shoulder national rejuvenation. This short commentary, timed to the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, first describes the war and the spirit it produced. It then sets out three tasks in education: deepening historical understanding, elevating patriotic feeling, and turning the spirit into practice. On historical understanding, Shen cites the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, the Pingxingguan victory and the Hundred Regiments Offensive, and proposes red cultural resources and VR reconstructions to teach the Communist Party's pivotal role and the spirit's world significance. On values, Shen holds that patriotism is the core of the spirit, that it echoes the core socialist values, and that young people should move from "historical memory" to "value consciousness". On practice, Shen points to the united front and tactical innovations such as tunnel and mine warfare as examples of practical wisdom. Shen concludes that young people should carry on a practical, hard-working spirit, take initiative and innovate in reform and development, and so contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the memory of the anti-Japanese war is framed in Chinese official education discourse in 2025.

Grasping the interactive logic between the Party's self-reform and social revolution 把握党的自我革命与社会革命的互动逻辑 Liang Haifeng This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how the Party's self-reform and social revolution relate to each other. Liang Haifeng argues that the two are dialectically unified and mutually reinforcing, and that together they drive the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Liang presents a "double revolution" in dynamic balance as a strategic requirement for keeping the Party vital. The article first treats self-reform as the Party's key instrument for leading social revolution, citing Xi Jinping and the campaigns of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since 2012. It then argues that the results of social revolution are the ultimate test of self-reform. Finally it turns to Party conduct as the link between the two, and to the problems still facing it. Liang cites economic scale, manufacturing capacity and poverty alleviation, including the lifting of nearly 100 million people out of poverty, as evidence that self-reform works. In the other direction, Liang says problems in social development, such as formalism and bureaucratism, expose weaknesses in Party building that self-reform must address. Conduct building is described as a hub: it purifies the Party and turns that purity into practical strength for social revolution, including a closer bond with the people. Liang concludes that formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance still erode the Party's credibility and the popular base of social revolution. The author calls for conduct building to be pursued with persistence over the long term, supported by stronger institutions. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-building scholarship currently links internal discipline to national development goals.

Changes in the structure of legally protected interests under digital capital 数字资本的法益结构变迁 Wang Lipei Wang Lipei asks how law should respond to digital capital, which the author defines as a new capital form existing in digital shape, built by accumulating and processing data and invested in the digital economy for returns. The article argues that data combines personality elements and property elements, so the traditional split between personality rights and property rights no longer fits. Wang sees early signs of a composite "personality–property right" in China's Personal Information Protection Law and the EU's Digital Markets Act. This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (22 July 2025) moves in four steps. It first describes the distinct character of digital capital, then the limits of the traditional property-centred legal order, including the EU's GDPR. It then lists institutional bottlenecks and proposes a new framework, and ends with a general conclusion. Wang argues that digital capital is marked by a "dual alienation" of personality and property. Data carries users' behavioural traces and emotional preferences, yet platforms turn it into tradable commodities, convert unpaid user activity into monopoly assets and widen distributive injustice. In Wang's account, consent rules, weak priority rules between dignity and data utility, fragmented legal tools and the platforms' technical advantage keep existing law from responding. Wang proposes a "three-dimensional" structure. It has a layered, independent right of digital personality, a tiered model for sharing data revenue with data trusts, and coordinated rules including antitrust duties, algorithm transparency, algorithmic impact assessment and a "digital supervisor". Wang concludes that the shift is the legal projection of the move from industrial to digital civilisation. Law should move from absolute ownership to "digital symbiosis", from freedom of contract to "algorithmic justice" and from private-right protection to "digital human rights". Wang calls for balancing efficiency gains against inalienable personal dignity. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese legal-theory proposal on data rights, platform power and algorithms.

Applying and governing artificial intelligence in basic education 人工智能在基础教育领域的应用及治理 Wang Jia Wang Jia asks how artificial intelligence (AI) can serve fair, high-quality basic education while its ethical, privacy and security risks are kept in check. Opening with Xi Jinping's calls to integrate AI deeply with education and to teach AI at every school stage, the article argues that basic education, as the starting point of talent cultivation, offers real opportunities but needs early, deliberate governance. It is a short commentary from Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), 2025, no. 13. The piece has three parts. The first describes what AI changes in basic education: ideas and models of teaching, the structure and ecology of education, and the balance of resources. The second sets out three risks: over-reliance on AI, misleading values, and the dissolution of the educational community. The third proposes five governance strategies, from legislation to international exchange. On benefits, Wang says AI tools can personalise learning content, shift goals from transmitting knowledge to building overall capacities, help teachers and parents through diagnostic reports, and carry top teachers' courses to remote mountain areas. Predictive analysis of enrolment and teacher needs, and multimodal generation for deaf students, are said to advance educational equity. On risks, Wang argues that stress on AI literacy may crowd out other capacities, and that students may lose independent and critical thinking. Algorithms may carry developers' value preferences and create "information cocoons", particularly in education on national conditions and political identity. More human–machine interaction may weaken the teacher's role, and opaque algorithms may endanger minors' data and privacy. Wang calls for specific legislation on AI in basic education, building on the Interim Measures for Generative AI Services and the Regulations on the Protection of Minors Online, plus ethical guidelines. Wang also proposes multi-level content review involving platforms, third-party bodies and education authorities, AI training for teachers and age-graded AI literacy courses for pupils, and pilot demonstration zones under inclusive and prudent regulation. Finally, China should take part in setting international rules and standards and offer "Chinese solutions" to raise its influence. Throughout, the article holds that AI must serve the basic questions of whom to train, how and for whom. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Central Party School scholar frames AI in schooling in Party-policy terms, with a list of regulatory measures.

Telling the story of whole-process people's democracy in practice 讲好全过程人民民主实践故事 Zhou Siqi This short commentary argues that vivid stories of the Communist Party's democratic practice can make the breadth and effectiveness of whole-process people's democracy tangible. Zhou holds that such storytelling helps break Western dominance of democratic discourse, strengthens the international voice and image of Chinese democracy, and offers what the article calls Chinese wisdom to developing countries seeking their own democratic paths. The piece is organised around three claims: that whole-process people's democracy is the most broad, the most genuine and the most effective democracy. Each section ties one quality to a question (democracy of whom, what kind of democracy, what democracy is for) and ends with suggestions for how the story should be told in the new era. On breadth, Zhou says the model rejects elite-led democracy and covers all people regardless of ethnicity, occupation, region or class, with rights running through elections, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight. On authenticity, the article describes a closed loop from expressing demands to policy and evaluation, so that popular consent becomes continuous rather than a momentary grant at elections. On effectiveness, Zhou presents democratic centralism as converting institutional strengths into governance capacity, citing consultative decision-making, crisis mobilisation and grassroots governance. Zhou proposes legal clarification of participation rights, digital channels, blockchain-based traceability, big-data analysis of public opinion, constitutional safeguards and a theory of democratic effectiveness. The conclusion is that institutional innovation, technological empowerment and cultural cultivation should advance together. Read the original if you want a concise example of how this democratic model is framed for international communication in Chinese academic writing.

What kind of self-cultivation Communists need Revisiting Liu Shaoqi's "How to Be a Good Communist" 共产党人要有什么样的修养 Ding Junping Why should Communist Party members still read Liu Shaoqi's 1939 lecture on self-cultivation, and what does it ask of them? This short commentary, first published in Study Times in July 2025, revisits the text and argues that it remains relevant to Party members and cadres today. Ding Junping contends that it can help them keep the Party's purpose in mind and settle questions of worldview, outlook on life and values. The lecture was delivered in July 1939 at the Marx-Lenin Institute in Yan'an and is included in the first volume of Liu's Selected Works. Ding cites Xi Jinping's remark that it enriched Party-building theory and educated generation after generation of Communists. The commentary follows the lecture in three steps: why cultivation is necessary, what its content is, and how Marxism-Leninism should be studied. It closes with lessons for the present. Ding reports that Liu begins from historical materialism: people change nature and so change themselves, and Communists, as the most advanced revolutionaries, must reform themselves while reforming society. Cultivation matters most in times of success, Liu warns, since some members become arrogant, bureaucratic and corrupt after victory. Its content covers theory, political and strategic ability, moral character, discipline, work style, ties with the masses and general knowledge. It must not be abstract or detached from practice, and its only aim is to serve the people and the revolution. Ding stresses Liu's view that theoretical study and cultivation of a proletarian standpoint depend on each other. Liu criticises reciting phrases and conclusions, and calls for combining universal truth with the concrete practice of the country's revolution. Ding concludes that, under full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the new great project of Party building, every member still needs to strengthen their training and cultivation. The author calls for serious study of the Party's innovative theory, especially Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and for unity of knowing, believing and doing. Members should do their own jobs conscientiously and so contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style account of how Liu's text is presented in current Party-building discourse.

Small matters and minor details as the "touchstone" for testing Party spirit 小事小节是检验党性的“试金石” Liu Junjie Liu Junjie, in a commentary first published in Study Times in July 2025, takes up a question of Party discipline: why do so many violations of discipline and law begin with matters that officials dismiss as trivial? Citing Xi Jinping's remark that small matters reflect character and style and contain Party spirit, principle and personality, Liu argues that holding the line on discipline is both a requirement of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and a basic guarantee of the Party's vanguard character and purity. The article is organised around the functions Liu assigns to the "red line" of discipline. It is first the foundation of the Party's work style, then the first barrier against lawbreaking, then a means of cutting the chain of corruption, and finally the "guardian" of public trust. It draws heavily on Xi's statements, including his address to the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection on 6 January 2025, and ties its closing section to the current study and education campaign on implementing the central Eight-point Regulations. Liu's central claim is that decline is gradual. Neglected small matters weaken Party spirit and produce a "broken windows" effect. The author describes a three-stage path from breaking discipline to breaking the law (weak discipline awareness, then chancing a breach of the red line, then total collapse) and a parallel path from lax style to power-for-rent-seeking to systemic corruption. Against this, Liu defends the principle that discipline must be stricter than law and come before it, since Party discipline is a high standard and law a bottom line. Liu proposes combining deterrence ("dare not"), institutions such as power lists and conduct rules ("cannot"), and cultivated conviction through Party-spirit education ("do not want"). Liu also urges investigating and addressing style problems and corruption together. Liu concludes that officials should treat small matters as the touchstone of Party spirit, oppose formalism and bureaucratism, avoid extravagance and waste, and so build the first line of defence against corruption and degeneration. The stated aim is to ensure that central decisions take root at the grassroots and to secure public trust and the Party's governing base. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the link between everyday conduct, discipline inspection and anti-corruption policy in 2025.

Improving investigation and research requires attention to methods 改进调查研究应重视方式方法 Zhao Yong This newspaper commentary argues that investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) is the Party's "family heirloom" and a basic skill for all work, and that its methods and style need to be improved. Zhao Yong notes that Xi Jinping has stressed the practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and that the first of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations concerns improving it. The author holds that deepening it serves Party conduct, leadership capacity and long-term governance. The piece has three parts. The first concerns problem awareness and a problem-oriented approach. The second concerns a systematic outlook and scientific methods. The third concerns improving work style and avoiding formalism. On the first, Zhao says the task is to establish the facts, identify the real problem and put forward practicable countermeasures. Conclusions should follow investigation, the principal contradiction should be addressed first, and findings should be turned into concrete measures and then tracked and assessed. On method, the author calls for unity of "going in person" and "engaging the mind", of field and online investigation (big data, sampling surveys), and of investigation and analysis. On style, Zhao rejects showcase-style research. The author urges precise topic selection rather than following trends, and unannounced visits under the "four no's, two straight" approach so that officials hear real views. The author also urges travelling light with fewer accompanying staff and simpler reception. Zhao concludes that research done this way will produce reliable information and workable policies, and that officials should learn from the people. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party cadres are expected to conduct investigation and research in the Xi Jinping era.

The string of self-reform must be drawn tighter 自我革命这根弦必须绷得更紧 Wang Jinfen This newspaper commentary takes up Xi Jinping's remark, made at the 21st collective study session of the 20th Politburo, that the Party's tasks are heavy, its governing environment is exceptionally complex, and the string of self-reform must be drawn tighter. Wang argues that this reflects the Party leadership's historical responsibility and sense of risk, and that continuous self-reform is the Party's defining trait and greatest strength. The piece first recalls that the Party has corrected its course through self-reform at each major historical juncture. It then sets out the pressures of the present: the tasks of Chinese modernization and a turbulent international and domestic environment. It closes with four practical measures and a reference to the current campaign to study and implement the central Eight-point Regulation. Wang's central claim is that the Party's spirit, leadership and governing capacity bear directly on whether Chinese modernization succeeds. Whether the Party passes this test depends on its willingness to purify, improve, renew and strengthen itself. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the author says, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has resolved many problems, but solving the difficulties peculiar to a large party is long-term work with no room for fatigue. The proposed measures are to consolidate ideological foundations through theoretical education, perfect institutions that restrain and supervise power, keep up a high-pressure stance against corruption with zero tolerance, and motivate officials, including through tolerance of error and correction mechanisms. Wang concludes that the Party must keep the strict tone for the long term so that it remains the core of leadership for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary justifies sustained Party discipline in 2025.

Empowering the integrated development of ideological and political courses across university, secondary and primary schools with generative AI 以生成式人工智能赋能大中小学思政课一体化建设 Wang Feng Long Haoyang This short commentary from People's Daily asks how generative artificial intelligence can support the integrated development of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) across university, secondary and primary schools. Wang and Long argue that, amid rapid AI progress and educational digitalisation, the technology can strengthen resource integration, practice settings and evaluation, and so raise the quality and effectiveness of ideological and political education. The article opens by citing Xi Jinping's call to treat integrated course development as an important project. It then takes three areas in turn, each following the same pattern: current difficulties, followed by AI-based remedies. These are a resource base covering all school stages, a blended virtual-and-physical space for practical education, and a whole-process evaluation system. On resources, the authors identify repetition and weak sequencing between stages' textbooks, cases that lag behind current events, and uneven regional provision. They propose AI that analyses textbook logic, flags gaps, turns political events into stage-appropriate cases and supplies layered materials for each level. On practice, they note the lack of a stepped path from primary to university, limits of time and space for offline activities, and weak feedback. They propose simulated historical scenes and AR, VR and MR technologies, plus large-model analysis of student work. On evaluation, they criticise reliance on exam scores, the lack of tools to measure values and attitudes, and inconsistent standards across stages. They propose multimodal learning analytics, personalised diagnostic reports, a cross-stage standards converter and digital portraits of each student's development. The authors conclude that such a data-driven, intelligent, continuously improving system would support personalised and differentiated teaching and help realise the educational goals of integrated courses. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames AI applications in Chinese ideological and political education.

Party building leading the construction of modern people's cities 党建引领现代化人民城市建设 Yang Dian Responding to the 2025 Central Urban Work Conference, this newspaper commentary asks how modern people's cities should be built. Yang argues that Party building is the fundamental guarantee: only by upholding the Party's overall leadership and a performance outlook that puts the people first can urban construction keep a clear direction and draw on co-building, co-governance and sharing. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the people's-city concept as the guiding direction, then identifies current problems in urban development and governance, and finally lists measures for strengthening Party leadership over urban work. Yang names three challenges: fragmented governance and weak coordination between departments, grassroots bodies overburdened and under-resourced, and poor cooperation between government and society, with limited institutional channels for participation. In the author's view, these can be solved only through Party building, all the more so as urbanization shifts from large-scale expansion to improving existing urban stock. The proposed measures include a Party-committee-led governance system, a three-tier street–community–grid structure of Party organizations, "smart Party building plus smart city" tools, whole-process people's democracy at the grassroots, and revised cadre evaluation that rewards residents' sense of gain, happiness and security rather than growth speed. Yang concludes that Party leadership must run through every field and stage of urban planning, construction and governance so that policy is not distorted. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link urban governance reform to Party building after the 2025 conference.

Persistently strengthening the Party's work style 锲而不舍加强党的作风建设 Zhu Lingjun Shan Boya Writing in July 2025, after Xi Jinping's remarks at the 21st collective study session of the Political Bureau, Zhu Lingjun and Shan Boya ask how the Party's work style (zuofeng) should be built up and kept up. They argue that the Party's self-reform is the "second answer" to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. In their account, starting from work style is an important experience of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. The piece appeared in the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News and is a short commentary. The authors organise the discussion in three parts. The first traces the theoretical sources of the concept: classical Chinese ideas of "wind" (feng) as custom and moral influence, remarks by Marx, Engels and Lenin on the habits of proletarian parties and on bureaucratism, and the statements of Chinese Party leaders from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. The second reviews historical experience under six headings, running from ideological style to discipline. The third describes the practice of the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The core claim is that work style has been a continuous thread in the Party's history and a mark of its nature and purpose. Its historical forms, in the authors' account, include seeking truth from facts, linking theory with practice, close ties with the masses, honesty and integrity, plain living and hard struggle, appointing people on merit under democratic centralism, and discipline as a guarantee. For the new era, Zhu and Shan describe a sequence of measures that began with the eight-point regulation of the Central Committee in December 2012. The measures include leadership by example, concentrated education campaigns, immediate rectification, institutional reform, and strict standards. They say these were aimed at formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance (the "four undesirable work styles"), and that results were published monthly for 141 consecutive months up to June 2025. The authors conclude that work-style building must be made routine and long-term, so that the cycle of "tighten and it improves, relax and it rebounds" is broken. They call for continued study of Xi's statements, a persistently strict tone, and the current education campaign on the eight-point regulation. Read the original if you want a concise official account of how Party scholars link work-style rectification to Chinese tradition, Marxist classics and the post-2012 anti-formalism campaign.

Letting the Jinggangshan spirit radiate new light for our times 让井冈山精神放射出新的时代光芒 Luo Qinghong Written in the year of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), this newspaper commentary asks how the Jinggangshan spirit, formed in the revolutionary struggle of the late 1920s, should be carried forward in the present. Luo argues that it is a lasting asset in the Communist Party's "spiritual genealogy" and that it must be given new meaning under today's conditions. The piece opens by linking the Party's role in the anti-Japanese war to a lineage of spirits that begins with the great founding spirit of the Party. It then moves through three sections: how the Jinggangshan struggle produced the spirit, where the spirit sits in the genealogy, and four practical requirements for the new era. The commentary was published in the Party's discipline inspection newspaper in July 2025. In the first section Luo traces the spirit to four sources. These are firm ideals and convictions after the failures of 1927, when Party membership fell from nearly 60,000 to just over 10,000, and a seeking of truth from facts that led to a rural-centred revolutionary road despite doubts from the Comintern and Stalin. The other two are hard struggle under blockade, and reliance on the masses. In the second section Luo presents the spirit as inheriting the founding spirit and shaping the Soviet Area, Long March, Yan'an and anti-Japanese war spirits. The same section extends the line to the Dazhai, Daqing, reform and opening up and poverty-alleviation spirits. For today Luo calls for four things: holding to communist ideals and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and keeping to one's own path guided by seeking truth from facts. Luo also calls for continued Party conduct building under the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, and a people-centred approach built on the mass line. Luo says conduct building has produced marked results over more than ten years but must continue. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school and discipline-inspection commentary links revolutionary-era memory to current Party-building tasks.

Methods and pathways for strengthening the guiding power of ideological and political education 增强思政引领力的方法路径 Xie Ruijin Xie Ruijin, a researcher at a provincial theory research centre and Party secretary of Anhui University of Chinese Medicine, asks how universities can strengthen their "guiding power" in ideological and political education. The commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, starts from Xi Jinping's statement at the National Education Conference (2024) that a leading education power must have six strengths, of which ideological and political guiding power comes first. Xie argues that universities should work on several fronts at once to raise this power and to lay an ideological foundation for educating a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece sets the context as a period of accelerating global change, continuing struggle in the ideological sphere and increasingly diverse thinking among young students. It then proposes four pathways: strengthening Party leadership as an organisational guarantee, promoting the spirit of educators, making good use of the "great ideological and political course", and strengthening digital empowerment. Each is given a short section with concrete measures. On leadership, Xie calls for Party committees to oversee all school work, for the president responsibility system under Party committee leadership to be improved, and for the ideological work responsibility system to be strictly applied so that the Party holds leadership, management and discourse power over campus ideology. Xie also proposes collaboration among school, family and society. On teachers, Xie urges that political identification with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era be deepened, that professional ethics become the first criterion in evaluation, and that results in moral education carry more weight in promotion and awards. For the "great ideological and political course", Xie advocates taking classes out into society through Red education bases and rural revitalisation sites, integrating the Party's innovative theory into all ideological and political courses, and promoting "curriculum ideology and politics" across subject courses. On digital tools, Xie calls for online courses, virtual simulation and big-data platforms, while stressing that technology should raise quality and not replace teachers, and that educators should use technology without being ruled by it. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party secretary presents the practical measures linked to the "education power" agenda in ideological and political work.

A historical-materialist reading of the complex link between cultural forms and the development of an age, and its contemporary implications An analysis based on Marx's Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy 文化形态与时代发展复杂关联的唯物史观阐释及其当代启示 Wang Xiaofeng Wang Xiaofeng asks how Marx's 1857 Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy explains the relationship between an age and its culture, using ancient Greek art as the main case. The article argues that Marx treats culture as bound to the social conditions that produce it, yet not mechanically determined by material production. Wang presents this as a theoretical basis for current Chinese debates on cultural construction and the 'Second Integration'. The article has five parts. The first discusses Marx's claim that classical art can no longer be produced in its 'epoch-making' classical form. The second takes up why classical art still gives enjoyment and serves as a norm. The third covers culture's tie to 'a definite form of social development'. The fourth treats the uneven relation between material production and art. The fifth draws lessons for the study of Chinese culture. Wang draws on Engels, Mao Zedong and Marx's other works, and on examples from Greek myth, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment and Chinese history. Wang makes three main moves. First, cultural 'revivals', whether the Renaissance or the Hundred Schools of Thought in China, are said to be new cultures with new content that borrow older forms, so Marx's remark is read as affirming real, non-abstract progress through the negation of old forms. Second, classical works still move people because they express the essence of their time or shared human feeling, such as love of nature and longing for freedom. Their charm is tied to immature social conditions that cannot return, and rigid classical norms can also restrict a culture's spread, as Wang says happened with classical poetry. Third, Wang stresses the uneven relation between material and cultural development: undeveloped eras can produce major art, individual talent matters, and backward countries such as Germany and France could lead in philosophy. Wang adds, citing Engels, that economic development retains the final say. Wang concludes that Marx's text points to a path of creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture, guided by Marxism. The article warns against two errors: dismissing tradition as worthless, and exaggerating its achievements, for instance by claiming that socialist ideas could arise in an old peasant economy. Wang also says ancient concepts, such as 'the people', must be distinguished from their modern meanings rather than matched by surface analogy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar uses Marx's Introduction on art and the age to support current Party policy on integrating Marxism with traditional culture.

Critique of the logic of capital in Marx's theory of world history and its contemporary significance A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义 Wang Xinsheng Zhang Jianrong Wang Xinsheng and Zhang Jianrong ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society, and how it can be overcome. They propose reading Marx's critique in Capital and its manuscripts through his theory of world history, rather than treating it in isolation. Their thesis is that Marx's critique of capital's logic unites the critique of the "old world" with the discovery of a "new world", and that it still offers resources for understanding contemporary capitalism. The article has three main parts. The first traces how the logic of capital arose in world history: its premises, its spatial and temporal expansion through the world market, its historical limits and its effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique, including its dialectical basis and its three strands, which the authors label real, historical and value critique. The third draws out four contemporary meanings, namely digital capitalism, socialist construction in China, alternative paths to modernization, and human development. The authors argue that capital's logic, the inner law of ceaseless pursuit of surplus value, built the world market and remade human society. They hold that it is also self-contradictory: rising organic composition, falling profit rates and general overproduction mean that capital's own limits constrain it. Marx's critique is an immanent, dialectical one, unlike that of classical economists, who treated capital as eternal, or of utopian socialists, whose criticism was external. The authors say the critique exposes fetishism and abstract domination, the temporary character of capitalism, and the inversion that makes people servants of capital. They claim the same contradictions create the material base and the proletariat for a communist world history. The authors conclude that Marx's critique remains valid because digital capitalism, in their account, intensifies rather than abolishes exploitation on a private-ownership basis. For socialism with Chinese characteristics at the primary stage of socialism, they say it justifies using capital as a factor of production to develop the productive forces while regulating its negative side and preventing disorderly expansion. They also argue that capitalist modernization is not the only route to modernization, and that sublating capital means absorbing its achievements while overcoming its defects, in order to achieve people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a text-based, Capital-centred account of how Chinese scholars link Marx's critique of capital to digital capitalism and to the regulation of capital in China today.

The ownership basis of new quality productive forces: an examination based on the theory of productive forces and relations of production 新质生产力的所有制基础：基于生产力和生产关系理论的考察 Li Chunbing Chen Xuejuan Hu Huaiguo The authors ask how China's ownership structure can help turn scientific and technological innovation into new quality productive forces. They argue that the leap from innovation to real productive forces is not spontaneous. It requires keeping to the Two Unwaverings while deepening reform, so that new relations of production fit the new productive forces. Their thesis is that public and non-public ownership complement and reinforce each other, and that this gives China an ownership advantage. The article works within Marx's framework of productive forces and relations of production, with ownership of the means of production treated as the core of the latter. It has four sections. The first reviews Marx's account of productive forces, relations of production and ownership. The second defines the \"quality\" of new quality productive forces. The third traces how China's ownership structure and science policy developed from 1949 to the present. The fourth sets out how the two ownership forms should work together. In the authors' reading, drawing on the Grundrisse and Capital, science and technology are both a productive force and a means of labour, and the core element of new quality productive forces. Innovation becomes real productive force only when it joins with enterprises and industrial innovation, so enterprise ownership forms the entity-level basis. The historical section argues that the single public-ownership structure of the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution period concentrated science on military and heavy-industrial fields. It credits reform-era recognition of the primary stage of socialism, and of non-public ownership, with releasing innovation. The final section assigns distinct roles. Public ownership gives strategic direction, concentrates resources and supplies patient capital. Non-public ownership supplies flexibility and application scenarios, and the article cites figures for the private sector's contribution to taxes, GDP and innovation. Mixed-ownership reform is presented as a way to address \"bottleneck\" technologies. The authors propose an analytical logic running from technological innovation to ownership to a leap in productive forces. They conclude that advance cannot rest on a single ownership form. Collective research capacity in the state sector and market sensitivity in the private sector should both be used, within an institutional environment that encourages cooperation, to build new relations of production and release an institutional dividend. Read the original if you want a political-economy account of how Chinese economists link ownership structure to new quality productive forces, with the historical narrative of science policy and the mixed-ownership argument.

The core and distinctive features of the new round of scientific and technological revolution from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域下新一轮科技革命的核心与特质 Zhang Jianyun Zhang Jianyun asks what lies at the centre of the current round of scientific and technological revolution and how it changes the mode of production. The article's answer is that the leading force is a "digital-intelligence technology system", formed by the convergence of information technologies, and that its core is artificial intelligence freeing mental labour on the basis of massive data. Zhang argues that this pushes digital cultural production to the fore, fuses cultural and material production, and runs against capitalist logic while fitting socialism. The article has three parts. The first traces how older information technologies (computers, digitisation, AI, the internet, mobile communication) merged after 2000 with cloud computing, the Internet of Things, mobile internet and blockchain, and why data is the system's "concrete in thought". The second compares the machine system of the industrial revolution, which freed manual labour, with AI, which Zhang says frees mental labour. The third examines changes in the means of production, the form of labour and the organisation of cooperation, with reference to DeepSeek as a Chinese case. Zhang draws on Marx's account of labour as first constructed in the head, to argue that mental labour is "ideal construction" that needs abundant information and strong processing capacity. Machine learning is described as simulating this process and assisting the human brain. Zhang insists that AI-generated output is not objectified human labour and cannot meet emotional needs or replace human labour. Data, as non-physical information, is said to be non-rival, easily copied and to gain value through sharing, so private ownership loses its traditional importance. Zhang claims that capital's drive to monopolise data, its centralised wage-labour model and Western decoupling policies obstruct these tendencies. Zhang concludes that socialist public ownership, with its aim of common possession of the means of production, supports data sharing, small-scale distributed cultural production and deeper socialisation of labour. Zhang links this to Marx's "association of free men" working as "one social labour force" and to a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. The article holds that socialism will reshape human civilisation in a fair and reasonable way. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of AI and data as forces of production, in which mental labour, data ownership and the socialist–capitalist contrast are central.

Theoretical questions on the "Second Integration" in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts 学习理解马克思主义中国化“第二个结合”的若干理论问题探析 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin takes up several theoretical questions raised by the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with excellent traditional Chinese culture, which forms one half of the Two Integrations. The article argues that the proposition rests on a long evolution of Party thinking and on new archaeological and historical findings. In Liu's view, it must be applied through a dialectic of criticism and absorption, openness to other civilisations, and a view of tradition as a whole. The article has five sections. It first traces the Two Integrations from Mao Zedong's 1938 report On the New Stage, through Ai Siqi's philosophical defence, the 1945 Party constitution and the 17th Party Congress (2007), to Xi Jinping's formulation in 2021 and 2023. It then sets out the conditions that made the Second Integration possible. The remaining sections treat the handling of criticism and absorption in cultural inheritance, the relation to other civilisations, and the need to approach traditional culture as a composite. Liu first argues that the Chinese Civilization Origins Project and excavations at sites such as Erlitou show an independent origin, a "pluralistic yet unified" structure and an "endogenous dynamic" behind five thousand years of continuity. Second, drawing on the idea that the ideological superstructure has relative independence, Liu holds that the Party's attitude to tradition has been constant: in revolutionary periods the emphasis fell on criticising decadent elements, and in peaceful construction on absorbing excellent ones, with neither dropped. On this basis Liu defends the May Fourth attack on Confucianism and Lu Xun against a "re-criticism", and warns against reviving any single ancient school. Third, Liu argues that openness to foreign achievements goes together with rejecting "Western-centrism", "universal values" and Westernization, citing the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Tradition, Liu adds, is a composite of Daoist, Mohist, military, legalist and other strands, not Confucianism alone, and Liu reads Xunzi's long exclusion as the cost of narrow orthodoxy. Liu concludes that the Second Integration calls for creative transformation and innovative development under Marxist guidance. It does not call for copying the past wholesale. Liu proposes drawing every progressive, popular and useful element from the whole of the tradition in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the Second Integration is justified historically, and of how criticism of tradition is reconciled with its revival.

The capitalist production logic of digital labour and the alienation of subjectivity 数字劳动的资本主义生产逻辑及其主体性异化 Lu Yankai Zhang Liwei What counts as digital labour, and how does capital extract value from it? Lu and Zhang argue that digital labour is in essence a form of capitalist exploitation, and that the surplus of digital platforms still comes from the living labour of waged technical workers rather than from the free online activity of users. The article also holds that this logic produces the alienation of workers' and people's subjectivity. The article has three parts. It first reviews definitions of digital labour, from Dallas Smythe's audience commodity theory through Tiziana Terranova and Christian Fuchs, and criticises their breadth. It then analyses how digital platforms and algorithms arise, how platform capital valorises itself, and how algorithmic management consolidates capital's power. Finally it examines alienation at two levels: the digital worker and the human being as a social subject. The authors' first move is conceptual. Drawing on Marx's account of labour and productive labour, they distinguish labour from mere activity: labour is purposive, productive and involves toil. Ordinary users' browsing and entertainment is therefore not labour, and the data it generates has no value until waged workers sort and process it. Digital labour is defined as purposive human activity that processes data using digital technology, covering software development and web design as well as gig work such as ride-hailing and food delivery. Second, they model platform capital circulation and argue that gig platforms also take monopoly profit through commission. Third, they describe alienation: de-skilling of workers, digital fetishism that conceals algorithms and reifies labour relations, an inversion of subject and object in a 'digital prison', and estrangement between people through information cocoons. The authors conclude that criticism should target the defects of digital capitalism, not digital civilisation, so as to ease the social 'birth pangs' of digital capitalism and move towards digital socialism. They call for demystifying digital fetishism and restoring human beings as the subject of labour. For China they propose accelerating new quality productive forces, strengthening labour supervision of digital firms and protecting data engineers and gig workers. They also propose tougher anti-monopoly enforcement, in line with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Read the original if you want a Marxist-political-economy argument that separates digital labour from online activity and links platform exploitation to alienation, written from within the Chinese policy context.

Promoting the development of new quality productive forces through the new-type whole-nation system A political-economy perspective 以新型举国体制推动新质生产力发展 Zheng Yangtao Zheng Yangtao asks how China's new-type whole-nation system for tackling key core technologies can drive the development of new quality productive forces. Reading the question through political economy, Zheng argues that the system is a major theoretical innovation of Chinese political economy and an expression of the new relations of production that advanced productive forces require. The article is a research piece published in Jinyang Journal in 2025. The article has three parts. The first sets out why strengthening the system matters, citing the achievements of the planned-economy-era whole-nation model, the pressure of Western technological hegemony, and the demands of innovation-driven high-quality development. The second analyses the internal mechanism linking the system to new quality productive forces. The third lists priority reform tasks. Zheng draws on Marx's remarks on the productivity of labour and cooperation, on Xi Jinping's statements, and on the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Examples include photovoltaics, State Grid and national big-science facilities. The core argument is that the principle that relations of production must fit productive forces implies a new organisational form for allocating innovation resources. Zheng says this form works through three supports: an innovation ecosystem that speeds the conversion of results into output; efficient coordination of government and market, in which the government anticipates and guides rather than correcting afterwards; and enterprise-led innovation consortia, with leading firms linking universities, research institutes and small firms. Zheng illustrates the government role with a nationwide computing-power network that directs eastern demand to western data centres. The article treats the system as a way to move China from technology follower to leader. Zheng proposes four tasks: improve the Party's centralised and unified leadership over science and technology work; build an integrated allocation mechanism joining the innovation, industrial, capital and talent chains; build an enterprise-centred innovation system, including support for state-owned, private and small specialised firms; and expand open international cooperation while balancing openness with security. The author presents these as a way to release reform dividends and speed new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a political-economy account of how Chinese scholars link the new-type whole-nation system to productive-forces theory and to concrete institutional reform.

The impact of artificial intelligence development on the labour market An analysis from the perspective of political economy 人工智能发展对劳动力市场的影响 Xu Zheng Wu Xiaoliang Xu Zheng and Wu Xiaoliang ask what artificial intelligence (AI) will do to employment, and whether it can ease the contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production. They note that existing research is mostly quantitative and concentrates on job numbers and job structure. The authors instead use Marxist political economy and focus on alienated labour. They argue that under capitalism AI deepens alienation and labour-market inequality. Under socialism, in their account, AI can serve the people and support free and all-round human development. The article has four parts. It first reviews the dispute between a "creation" view, in which AI generates jobs, and a "deprivation" view, in which it displaces workers. It then restates Marx's account of technology and relative surplus population. Next it analyses AI-driven alienation. Finally it sets out the effects of AI under socialist conditions and a practical path, with recommendations for the state, firms and workers. The authors read Marx's claims about machinery as a duality: machines expel workers while also creating work elsewhere. They add that rising organic composition of capital reduces demand for labour. They then extend Marx's alienation categories to AI. In their account, AI deepens the separation of manual and mental labour, human subjects, workers and their products, and workers and productive activity. Algorithmic management, data labour and platform monopoly are said to fragment labour relations and widen the gap between high-skill shortage and low-skill surplus. Under public ownership and a people-centred orientation, the authors hold, the same technology can reduce labour intensity, extend free time and lay material foundations for communism. They add that over the long run technological unemployment need not mean mass unemployment. The authors propose four measures: upholding the socialist system and workers' status as主体 of production, with curbs on data monopolies; a national AI strategy and talent training; redistribution, retraining, unemployment insurance and public-benefit jobs, including higher taxes on high-skill earners; and a new, flexible division of labour that ends overwork ("involution"). They conclude that under socialism with Chinese characteristics AI can help bring the relations of production into line with the productive forces and contribute to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy argument that applies Marx's theory of alienation to AI and labour markets, with concrete policy proposals.

Promoting the integrated development of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation 推动科技创新和产业创新融合发展 Yang Yilong This commentary asks how scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation can be fused so that China develops new quality productive forces and achieves high-quality development. Yang argues that the two are mutually reinforcing and that their deep integration is a core component of national competitiveness. Citing Xi Jinping, Yang presents the pairing as "the basic path" for developing new quality productive forces and for gaining strategic initiative in international technological competition. The article has three parts. The first explains the relationship between the two kinds of innovation. The second considers how technological innovation can build a modernised industrial system. The third turns to strategic emerging industries and future industries, with separate treatments of artificial intelligence, life sciences, and new energy and new materials. It draws throughout on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference and speeches by Xi. Yang's central claim is one of two-way traction. Technological innovation is the "booster" of industry: basic research is its source, core technologies are the key to turning results into products, and universities and research bodies supply talent, with the socialist system's ability to concentrate resources invoked as an advantage. Industrial innovation is the "main battlefield" that provides market demand, application scenarios and incentives, and so drives further technological iteration. On this basis Yang calls for technology to empower the real economy, upgrade traditional industries rather than abandon them, and raise the industrial base and modernise industrial chains, with firms as the main body of innovation. For the new sectors, Yang proposes concrete priorities: mastering "root technologies", high-end chips, large models, computing power and datasets in AI; better research management and data sharing in life sciences and biomanufacturing; and market reform, price mechanisms and basic research in new energy and materials. Yang also urges making AI a focus of the 15th Five-Year Plan and expanding patient capital. Read the original if you want a Red Flag-style statement of how current policy links innovation, industrial upgrading and new quality productive forces, with sector-by-sector policy suggestions.

Classic translation and the paths of theory dissemination in the Yan'an period 延安时期的经典翻译与理论传播路径 Liu Shuo Liu Shuo asks how the translation of Marxist classics in Yan'an (the Party's wartime base) worked as a means of theory dissemination. The article argues that this was not mere linguistic conversion but a composite process joining text production, dissemination and practical guidance. In Liu's account it moved Marxism from the study to the battlefield and set the principle of linking theory with practice for the Party's news and communication work. The short piece, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, covers three mechanisms: organised translation and editing, popularised communication, and the practical conversion of theory. It then turns to localisation, to mass participation in theory study, and to the international reach of the "Yan'an experience". It closes with lessons for the present. Liu describes an institutional system: a translation and editing department at the Marxist-Leninist Institute (1938), a Military Commission translation office, and a 1939 Central Committee directive on propaganda and printing. Dissemination used Party newspapers, publishers, and also yangge operas, wall newspapers and leaflets that rendered class theory as colloquial slogans. Liu holds that converting terms such as "working class" into peasant-centred expressions, and recasting the city-centred path as "encircling the cities from the countryside", marked a shift from literal translation to problem-oriented communication. Liu concludes that Yan'an translation was a successful exploration of how the Party used communication to secure ideological leadership. For the era of all-media, Liu draws three lessons: theory should address Chinese problems, rest on popular participation and dialogue, and pursue mutual learning among civilisations. Liu also urges online and offline study, new-media lectures, and multilingual translation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era under the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line view of Yan'an translation as a model for present-day theory communication.

The theoretical implications of grasping the "critical few" 抓住“关键少数”的理论意蕴 Zhang Hao This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 16 July 2025, asks what theoretical significance lies in Xi Jinping's repeated call to "grasp the critical few" (关键少数), meaning leading cadres. Zhang argues that this body of statements is an innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that it displays the distinctive theoretical features of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece is a short theoretical commentary, not an empirical study. The article begins with the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which links the "critical few" to the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, the correction of the "four undesirable work styles" and the fight against privilege. It defines the group and then proceeds in two parts. The first part sets out five ways the idea advances Marxist theory. The second part identifies five features of Xi Jinping Thought that it displays: being of its time, people-centred, systematic, dialectical and practical. On the first part, Zhang says the idea refines the historical-materialist view of the relation between the masses and leaders, defines the group concretely (senior cadres, "top leaders" of each unit, and county Party secretaries), and extends Marxist thinking on power through power lists, accountability and supervision. It also enriches methods of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Zhang reads Xi's formula of managing "all" Party members while concentrating on senior cadres as an application of Marxist contradiction analysis, combining the "emphasis on key points" with the "two-sided view". On the second part, the author links each feature to Xi's statements, for example the "people-centred" quality to the claim that cadres come from the people and serve them. The author also says the approach draws on traditional Chinese governance ideas such as "leading from above" and "governing the state begins with governing officials", as an instance of the Two Integrations. Zhang concludes that grasping the "critical few" means grasping the key point of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and of national governance, since "the Party must govern itself, beginning with its cadres". The author calls for action on political development, strict selection and appointment, better assessment and a fuller supervision system, so that cadres set an example in advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party theory presents cadre discipline and leadership responsibility as a Marxist, Xi Jinping Thought-based method.

Marx's dialectic of labour and the limits of Western modernity With a commentary on Heidegger's account of the relation between Marx and Hegel 马克思的劳动辩证法与西方现代性的限度 Liu Guixiang Liu Guixiang takes up Heidegger's claim that Marx merely inherited and applied Hegel's dialectic of labour, so that Marxism remains inside the subject-centred metaphysics of modernity. The article argues that Heidegger correctly identifies Hegel as the source of Marx's concept of labour but mistakes this source for the nature of Marx's thought. In Liu's reading, Marx's dialectic of labour sublates Hegel's and points to a critique of modernity and the communist movement, which together answer the 'riddle of history'. The article is organised around three questions: what Heidegger actually says about Marx and Hegel (drawing on the Letter on Humanism and 'The Principle of Thinking'); how Marx inherits and goes beyond Hegel; and how Heidegger assesses the contribution and limits of each. Liu traces Marx's five critiques of Hegel, from the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right to the Paris Manuscripts, The Holy Family, The German Ideology and The Poverty of Philosophy. The article then places the Marx–Heidegger dispute within the wider field of modernity debates, citing Löwith, Marcuse, Lukács, Althusser and Habermas. Liu's central move rests on Marx's Paris Manuscripts. Marx credits Hegel with grasping labour as the self-generation of humanity, but faults him for knowing only abstract, mental labour, so that objectification stays 'a circle within thought'. Marx replaces self-consciousness with the sensuous human being and makes 'objective activity' the starting point of a new materialism. Liu presents this as an ontological revolution that predates Heidegger's Being and Time by more than eighty years. Heidegger's analysis, by contrast, is ontological and phenomenological, whereas Marx's is practical and dialectical-materialist. Liu also notes that Heidegger acknowledged communism as an experience of world-historical significance, yet still read Marx through Feuerbach's humanism. Liu concludes that Marx's dialectic of labour overcomes the opposition between humanism, which fixes on human essence, and historicism, which appeals to time, by showing history's diachronic and synchronic dimensions arising together in humanity's dealings with the world. Reunification, in this account, comes through the critique of capitalism and the communist movement rather than Hegelian triads or Heideggerian meditation on Being. Liu holds that this points to a new form of human civilisation beyond capitalism. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Heidegger's reading of Marx and Hegel, grounded in close reference to the Paris Manuscripts.

Being born from nothing: the logical beginning of Capital 有生于无：《资本论》的逻辑开端 Dai Ligang Dai Ligang takes up the question of where Capital logically begins, a problem the author ties to constructing the "rational form" of Marx's historical dialectic. Dai argues that the value-form school, which makes value and its forms the beginning, reads the relation of being and non-being the wrong way round. On Dai's account, Marx's critique reverses "non-being arises from being" into "being arises from nothing". The article opens by dismissing both the Soviet textbook reading of dialectics as an essential "law" and the Heideggerian-phenomenological existential reading. It then reviews the debate over the beginning: Rosenthal and Ilyenkov's realist reading with the commodity as starting point, Hans-Georg Backhaus's value-form dialectic, and Chris Arthur's New Dialectic, which draws on Hegel's Logic and Roy Bhaskar's account of absence. It also covers critical realist objections that put production at the core. Dai then returns to Marx's method of critique, drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno, and examines the German terms verschwindet and Verrücktheit in the Grundrisse. Dai distinguishes two moments of critique, following Adorno: Critique I shows how capitalism constructs a fetishised "second nature", and Critique II pierces its false objectivity and shows the historical, non-eternal character of the value form. Dai charges Backhaus and Arthur with keeping only Critique I. By treating use-value and value as potentiality and realisation, they make the illusion permanent, and they substitute value-form determinism for the labour theory of value. Dai holds that Marx instead uses "disappearance" as a verb, so that use-value and concrete labour become a non-being that is absent but still stands in negative, heterogeneous relation to value. Verrücktheit ("derangement") describes value's domination over use-value, which appears only as "abstract chaos". The same negativity recurs in the relation of capital and labour, and Marx's late "Notes on Wagner" is cited as showing that the commodity, not value, is the starting point. Dai concludes that the beginning of Capital is the commodity's internal contradiction, not a self-realising value form. Dai also revises Arthur's table of the relations between production and exchange. Post-structuralist readings such as Hardt and Negri's, and practice-based or phenomenological readings, are said to miss the mechanism of dialectical movement. In Dai's view, that movement is driven by absent non-being negating being, which also allows the ideological illusion to be pierced. Read the original if you work on value-form theory, the New Dialectic or the Hegel–Marx relation, and want a critical Chinese reassessment built on close reading of Marx's German terms.

Re-examining the "method of inquiry" and "method of presentation" in Marx's Capital 马克思《资本论》的“研究方法”和“叙述方法”再审视 Bai Gang Wang Xuchun How should the method of Marx's Capital be understood? Bai and Wang argue that reading it only as ascent from the concrete to the abstract (inquiry) or from the abstract to the concrete (presentation) narrows Marx's dialectic and its materialist horizon. They contend that the two methods must be grasped as a unity, and that this unity, with Marx's concept of the "power of abstraction", marks the "critical and revolutionary" character of Capital's methodology. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the "two paths" of political economy in Marx's 1857 Introduction and the distinction between inquiry and presentation. The second returns to Capital to read the unity of the two methods through Marx's reply to the Russian critic Kaufman, Engels's "logical and historical" principle, and Marx's break with Hegel and Proudhon. The third turns to the "power of abstraction", the critique of commodity fetishism and the question of how capitalism's real conditions of life are revealed. Bai and Wang hold that the method of inquiry appropriates material and traces the inner connections of its forms, while the method of presentation reproduces the "life of the material" in thought so that it looks like an a priori construction. Reading Marx's description of presentation as "scientifically correct" as a verdict against inquiry, they say, hides Capital's materialism. Against Kaufman, who saw Marx as a Hegelian idealist, they stress Marx's inversion of Hegel: the logic of things, not the "thing of logic". The order of categories is set by their place in the structure of modern bourgeois society, with capital as a "universal light", not by historical sequence. The authors present Marx's power of abstraction as a "real abstraction" arising from social practice. It differs from the intuitive abstraction of classical political economy and the speculative abstraction of Hegel. In the commodity, social relations between people appear as relations between things, and the contradiction between use-value production and value valorisation drives capital to undermine itself. The authors conclude that the methodological revolution of Capital lies in critically inheriting both classical political economy and German philosophy through the power of abstraction. They say this let Marx explain the capital–labour relation scientifically for the first time and turned dialectics into a revolutionary weapon against capitalist society. They also treat Capital as, in effect, a critique of Hegel's logic. Read the original if you work on the methodology of Capital, the Marx–Hegel relationship, or the debate over inquiry versus presentation and real abstraction, and want a densely sourced argument.

Promoting deep integration of the real economy and the digital economy 促进实体经济和数字经济深度融合 Jia Lijun Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for a system to promote deep integration of the real economy and the digital economy, this commentary asks why such integration matters, where it is most likely to stall, and how policy should address this. Jia Lijun argues that integration is the key to sustaining China's economic development and industrial upgrading, given that China is the world's largest manufacturing country. The article has three parts.
