The first sets out the practical significance of integration; the second identifies three critical "nodes" (technology, industry and enterprise); the third proposes measures for each node. It draws repeatedly on statements by Xi Jinping and is aimed at manufacturing in particular. On significance, Jia presents integration as a strategic choice in the new round of technological and industrial change, the core driving force of new-type industrialization, an inherent requirement of new quality productive forces, and a path to national competitiveness and greater influence in global value chains. On the nodes, Jia contends that digital technology is a bundle of sub-technologies (artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data, the Internet of Things, blockchain), so that no single one transforms production and their integration and compatibility are what count. Industries differ in their processes and industrial systems, so digital transformation must be tailored to each. At enterprise level, large firms have made progress, while small and medium-sized manufacturers lack internal drive, innovation capacity and the funds for initial and continuing investment. Jia's proposals follow the three nodes. For technology, build an innovation system led by enterprises, with state-owned enterprises heading industry–university–research consortia to overcome "chokepoint" bottlenecks, plus test zones, intellectual property protection and standards in smart manufacturing and data security. For industry, differentiated strategies for process and discrete manufacturing, collaboration along supply chains, and support for emerging industries. For enterprises, government-led transformation platforms offering one-stop services, new management models, and leading firms opening platforms to small and medium-sized firms. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-journal writing links the digital economy, new-type industrialization and manufacturing policy.)

The Two Integrations: the necessary path for adapting the Marxist worldview and methodology to the Chinese context and the needs of our times “两个结合”：马克思主义世界观、方法论中国化时代化的必由之路 Tang Zhengdong Tang Zhengdong asks how the Two Integrations (combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture) have adapted the Marxist worldview and methodology to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article argues that each principle of dialectical and historical materialism now appears in a concrete, distinctively Chinese theoretical form. It presents this as the work of Xi Jinping and the Party leadership around him in the new era. The article is organised in three parts. The first takes dialectical materialism: the material unity of the world, the movement of contradiction, the fundamental method of materialist dialectics, and the dialectic of cognition and practice. The second takes historical materialism: the movement of the basic contradictions of society, material production as the foundation of social life, and the people as makers of history. For each principle, Tang compares how Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping applied it. The third part examines how excellent traditional Chinese culture fits each principle. Tang's central move is to say that the classical authors applied each principle to specific tasks, such as criticising idealism and capitalism or defending the New Economic Policy. They had no occasion to work out its concrete forms under socialist construction. The Party, in Tang's account, supplied these forms: "proceeding from reality" as a restatement of material unity, with reality understood as changing; "problems" as the form contradiction takes under socialism, where "crisis" was its form under capitalism; the wholeness and continuing development of the basic social contradictions; a correct and comprehensive use of the productive-forces criterion; and the combining of top-level design with "crossing the river by feeling the stones". The second move is cultural. Tang contends that ideas such as "change is the natural way of heaven and earth" and "unity of knowing and doing" resonate with Marxist principles. In Tang's view, this gave the Party a stronger cultural subjectivity and guarded against one-sided readings that British empiricism or German idealism, he says, produced in their traditions. Tang concludes that the First Integration gives Marxism's adaptation a practical basis and the Second gives it a cultural basis, and that the two are dialectically unified. Together they have enriched the cultural life of Marxism's basic principles and given its worldview a clearer Chinese style, serving as the cultural form of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, principle-by-principle account of how Chinese Party theorists present the Two Integrations as a philosophical method, and how Xi Jinping's statements are placed in a line from Marx to Deng.

Guiding young people with Marxist scientific theory 以马克思主义科学理论引领青年 Han Xiping Han Xiping asks how the Party should guide China's young people at a time when the country is pursuing Chinese modernization. The article argues that Marxist scientific theory must lead and equip the young generation, so that youth can take up their part in building a modern socialist country and in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Han presents this as a long-standing strength of Marxist parties and as an urgent task of the present. The piece, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts, has three parts. The first explains why theoretical guidance of youth is an advantage of Marxist parties. The second explains why the drive to build a modern socialist country in a full sense requires such guidance. The third sets out practical routes for carrying it out. Han draws on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and many statements by Xi Jinping. In the first part, Han contends that Marxist parties differ from bourgeois parties because they openly lead youth with scientific theory. In Han's account, bourgeois parties claim ideological freedom while quietly transmitting bourgeois values. Marxism, Han says, gives young people a firm political stance, scientific ways of thinking (historical, dialectical, systemic and innovative) and a noble character linked to national and popular causes. In the second part, Han describes youth as the main force in the national project up to mid-century. Han also says young people are exposed to varied social trends and to ideological infiltration by hostile forces, especially online, and so need the means to tell right from wrong. The third part proposes better ideological and political courses from primary school to university, including AI-assisted evaluation and "walking" classes of fieldwork. It calls for coordinated work among Party committees, schools, Party schools, the Communist Youth League and social organisations. It also urges fresh language on platforms such as Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Bilibili and Zhihu, and participatory formats such as "red murder-mystery" games on Party history. Han concludes that the Party must keep guiding youth with Marxist theory and use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to shape their ideals and character. Han presents this as a condition for young people to answer the call of the Party and the people. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-journal author links Marxist theory, youth work and ideological security, and which concrete measures in education and online media are proposed.

"Servants of the people, not officials": the "Yan'an style" in the eyes of foreign visitors “只见公仆不见官” Sun Xin This short commentary asks what foreign visitors to Yan'an saw of Chinese Communist Party leaders, and what that record means for Party conduct today. Sun argues that journalists, officers and diplomats who went there in the Yan'an period left accounts presenting leaders as "servants of the people, not officials". In Sun's view, this image helped build the Party's reputation and support, and it carries lessons for current efforts to uphold the central Party leadership's eight-point decision on conduct. The article draws on testimony from Edgar Snow, Anna Louise Strong, Agnes Smedley, Theodore White, John S. Service, Harrison Forman and members of the 1944 US Army Observation Group, among others. It is organised under three headings: the leaders' simplicity, their contrast with the Nationalists and their service to the people, and democratic practice in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. Sun's central move is to treat these outsider accounts as evidence of a new view of power. In their reports, as Sun reads them, power served the people rather than personal privilege: the visitors noted austere living, the absence of ranks, titles and bodyguards, and leaders who talked with peasants and worked in the fields. Sun also cites visitors who judged the border region's government to be elected by the people and not authoritarian, as Nationalist propaganda claimed. The article presents this as the concrete form of the "Yan'an style": hard struggle, close ties with the masses, integrity and opposition to privilege. Sun concludes that these qualities remain a Party "family heirloom" and calls for them to be carried forward in the new era. Sun urges standing with the people, keeping close ties with them, and implementing the eight-point decision persistently so that work-style building becomes regular and long-term. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-aligned writing uses foreign eyewitness accounts of Yan'an to support current conduct campaigns.

Focusing on the cultivation of innovative talent and strengthening science–education collaboration in nurturing people 聚焦创新型人才培养 强化科教协同育人 Xi Yinglun Xi Yinglun, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, takes up the question of how universities can train a large, well-structured and high-quality corps of innovative talent. The third concerns practice-oriented paths: institutional innovation, platform building and resource integration. Each part opens with quotations from Xi Jinping and then sets out measures for universities. In the first part, Xi Yinglun contends that universities must put serving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation first. The piece is a practical policy proposal from a university administrator, written in the Party's official vocabulary. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Party-school and university administrators translate Xi Jinping's statements on education, science and talent into institutional measures.

Opening a new chapter in ideological and political education for the new era 开创新时代思政教育新局面 Wang Chengbin Wang Chengbin, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how universities can open a new chapter in ideological and political education in the new era. The commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's May 2024 instruction on school ideological and political courses and his remarks at the 2025 Two Sessions. Wang argues that the "Big Ideological and Political Course" is the answer. It joins the ideological and political "small classroom" to the "big classroom" of society, and Wang presents it as a new form of university ideological and political education. The article builds its account of "Big Ideological and Political Course" construction around four components. Ideological and political courses are the core and foundation, social practice is the extension, innovation and entrepreneurship is the upgrade, and the "second classroom" transcript is the support and guarantee. Each component gets its own section, and Xi Jinping's statements are quoted throughout as the basis for the argument. A short closing section sets out three requirements for future work. On the core courses, Wang calls on teachers to move away from one-way indoctrination towards respect for students' agency. Nanjing Normal University's practice-results transformation centre is given as an example. On innovation and entrepreneurship, Wang proposes a "reaching the sky and standing on the ground" principle. Programmes should serve national strategy and high-quality development, and should also build on each university's own disciplinary strengths. The "second classroom" transcript quantifies student performance in ideological and political activities, and Wang assigns it evaluation, resource-integration and collaborative functions. Wang concludes that "Big Ideological and Political Course" construction must achieve "three fits": with national development strategy, with the university's overall plan, and with students' growth needs. It should be built into disciplinary development, talent training and social service, and delivered in a tailored, lifelong and close-at-hand way. The stated aim is to nurture a new generation who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and equal to the task of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, practice-oriented example of how a university Party leader frames ideological and political education reform under Xi Jinping's guidance.

The historical contribution of the victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression to building a strong country and national rejuvenation 抗日战争胜利对强国建设、民族复兴的历史贡献 Chen Jinlong Writing in a Chinese newspaper in July 2025, ahead of the anniversary of the victory over Japan, Chen Jinlong asks what the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression contributed to building a strong country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chen argues that the victory was the historical turning point from deep national crisis towards rejuvenation. In this reading, the war taught the importance of national strength, strengthened national cohesion, brought the Communist Party to maturity and raised China's international standing. The commentary is organised in four parts. It treats in turn the development of productive forces, the unity of political parties, ethnic groups and the people, the Party's leadership, and China's international position after 1945. Chen supports each part mainly with statements by Mao Zedong and Zhu De, wartime editorials in Liberation Daily, and a statement by Xi Jinping on the war's global significance. Chen's first claim is that Japan could attack China in the 1930s because its productive forces were far more developed, and that the Party concluded national strength ultimately rests on developing productive forces. Industrialisation, science and technology, and the use of intellectuals followed from this, and Chen cites Mao's wartime calls to recruit intellectuals in large numbers. Second, Chen holds that the Party's united front, its ethnic equality policies and its mobilisation of the people through democracy, production and popular culture built the forces on which later national strengthening would rely. Third, Chen argues that the war established the Party's leadership position, improved its capacity to govern and mobilise, produced a central leadership around Mao, and trained cadres through theoretical study and clear selection standards. On the international side, Chen describes China as the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war, which tied down most of Japan's army and eased pressure on the Soviet Union, the United States and Britain. Chen adds that China took part in founding the United Nations and became a permanent member of the Security Council, which laid the basis for its standing as a major power. The article concludes that the victory should be viewed through a "grand historical outlook" as part of the long course of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 2025 official narrative links the wartime experience to present-day goals of strengthening the country and national rejuvenation.

A deep understanding of the value of upholding the Party's cultural leadership 深刻理解坚持党的文化领导权的价值意蕴 Zhang Beiping Writing in Guangming Daily on 15 July 2025, Zhang Beiping takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the "most essential feature" of the path of socialist cultural development with Chinese characteristics is upholding Party leadership. The article argues that upholding the Party's cultural leadership (wenhua lingdaoquan) is a core element of Xi Jinping's thinking on culture and a necessary requirement of the Party's mission in the new era. Zhang's thesis is that its strategic significance and value can be understood in four dimensions. The commentary is organised in four numbered sections: strengthening cultural confidence by safeguarding the Marxist "soul" and the "roots" of Chinese civilisation; consolidating the cultural foundation by serving people's livelihood and winning hearts; building cultural security through confrontation and defence; and displaying the value of civilisation through exchange and integration. It ends with a short summary stating that Party cultural leadership is the fundamental guarantee for building a socialist cultural power. In the first section Zhang links cultural confidence to cultural subjectivity, which the article presents as strengthened by the Two Integrations, and calls for an autonomous Chinese body of knowledge to dispel the myth that "Westernisation equals modernisation". The second section argues that no modern state or party can lead effectively without a value system that unites people. It points to public cultural provision and mass events such as "village evening galas" and the "Village Basketball Association", as well as digital technologies. The third section claims that Western powers hold "cultural hegemony" and use "colour revolutions" to undermine governments. Zhang proposes three responses: upholding fundamental principles while innovating, telling China's story well, and strengthening discursive struggle against what the article calls the "China threat" and similar narratives. The fourth section rejects ranking civilisations and presents online exchanges between Chinese and American users, and a foreign influencer's tour of China, as examples of two-way cultural empowerment. Zhang concludes that only by upholding the Party's cultural leadership can socialist culture become the shared values and ideological base of the whole nation and a force for national rejuvenation. The author presents this as enabling China to take on a new cultural mission and to contribute to a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in mid-2025 links cultural leadership to cultural confidence, ideological security and international communication.

The historical dialectic of the state and capitalism in Capital and its manuscripts 《资本论》及其手稿中国家与资本主义的历史辩证法 Guo Qiang Guo Qiang argues that scholarship on Capital has concentrated on its economic theory and neglected the theory of the state it contains. Studies of Marx's state theory, in turn, tend to rely on the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right or The Civil War in France. The article holds that Capital and its manuscripts reveal the origin, essence, functions and future trend of the state through the state's links with the capitalist economy. The article first notes that Marx's 'five-part' and 'six-book' plans both reserved a separate section for the state. It then moves through five themes: the essence of the bourgeois state, its functions, relations between states in foreign trade and the world market, the historical limits of the state form, and the prospect of the state's withering away. Evidence is drawn from the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Preface and Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, the London Notebooks, Capital, and Engels. Guo's central claim is that Marx explains the state from civil society, not from the state itself. Capital's rule over labour, rooted in private ownership of the means of production, is said to translate into political domination, so that formal freedom and equality conceal exploitation. On this reading, the state has a dual character: it performs 'public affairs' arising from the nature of all societies and 'specific functions' arising from the opposition between government and the mass of the people. Its economic role runs through the colonial system, public debt, modern taxation and protective tariffs, and factory legislation is presented as a concession won by class struggle. Guo adds that the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation cannot be cured by a state that is, in effect, the 'total capitalist'. In the world market, bourgeois society 'oversteps the bounds of the state', bringing both development and colonial oppression. Guo concludes that Marx foresaw replacing the 'illusory community' of the state with an 'association of free individuals'. In it, means of production would be socially owned, labour would be joint, and individual ownership would be re-established on the basis of cooperation. Free time, not labour time, would become the measure of wealth. The state machinery would then be placed in a museum of antiquities, and society would take back state power. Read the original if you want a source-based account of how Capital and its manuscripts treat the state, tracing the planned 'state' section through to the withering away of the state.

Critical strategy and methodology facing the production of abstract space A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space 面对抽象空间生产的批判战略与方法论 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing reads the methodological discussion in Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space, asking how a critique can confront bourgeois abstract space, which produces invisible relations of domination behind an economic surface. Zhang argues that Lefebvre responds with three moves: a strategic hypothesis grounded in historical materialism, a regressive–progressive method of historical analysis, and a revolutionary reconstruction of spatial codes. Zhang praises these as Lefebvre's most concentrated methodological reflection, but repeatedly finds his account of how revolution could be realised thin. The article has three sections. The first sets out the historical-materialist basis of spatial critique and Lefebvre's claim that production of space has replaced the production of things within space. The second treats the regressive–progressive method, which Lefebvre traces to Marx's Grundrisse remark that the anatomy of man is a key to the anatomy of the ape. The third turns to the reconstruction of spatial codes and to Lefebvre's political strategy. Zhang draws on Lefebvre's other works, including The Survival of Capitalism, and on Sartre, Foucault, Lenin and Walter Benjamin. Zhang's central claim is that Lefebvre sees contemporary abstract space as a technologically programmed realm of surveillance and social engineering, and rejects idealist theories of discursive or Cartesian mental space, insisting that technical ordering is objective spatial practice. Lefebvre holds that capitalism has survived because productive forces now develop through the production of spatial relations. Zhang reads the regressive–progressive method as a spatialised temporal structure: developed capitalist space is the key to under-developed space within the same world, shown in uneven development and the export of polluting industry. Zhang adds criticisms: Lefebvre never asks "whose technological utopia?", underrates the critical theory he attacks, and misses that planners are themselves steered by capital. On politics, Lefebvre rejects the Russian single-centre model of revolution and argues for plural subjects, including marginal groups and parts of the working class, and for varied forms, violent or quiet. His aim is differential space against the homogenising logic of abstract space. Zhang judges this dialectical in orientation but without any workable plan, and holds that changing spatial discourse is empty unless the mode of production changes. Read the original if you study Lefebvre, Western Marxist spatial theory, or Zhang Yibing's critical method of reading foreign Marxist texts.

The contemporary value of Aristotle's thought on friendship 亚里士多德友爱思想的当代价值 Wu Qiong This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks what Aristotle's account of friendship (philia) can offer a present marked by individualism, virtual and instrumental social ties. Wu argues that its core, friendship grounded in virtue and the common good, remains a valuable intellectual resource for ethics, governance and everyday life. The article first sets out Aristotle's typology in the Nicomachean Ethics. It then draws three contemporary lessons: friendship's place in human happiness, its link with justice and happiness in global moral construction, and its role in community governance. Wu reads Aristotle as dividing friendship into pleasant, useful and good friendship, with only the last being friendship in the highest sense. Virtuous friendship, Wu says, is the glue of the city-state and the greatest external good for happiness, though it grows out of the more common pleasant and useful kinds. Wu then claims that happiness, justice and friendship are dialectically interdependent: just order secures the conditions for happiness and friendship, and friendship adds emotional and social support. The author applies this to international relations, sustainable development and the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. Wu also applies it to governance of the digital economy and artificial intelligence, where states should adopt values of friendship and mutual help. Wu concludes that Aristotle's thought goes beyond personal feeling and narrow interest and spans ethics, political philosophy and metaphysics. It is presented as a spiritual coordinate for easing instrumentalised relationships, building a harmonious and happy society and promoting people's all-round development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academic commentary draws on classical Greek ethics to address contemporary governance and global moral questions.

The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the nation-wide War of Resistance 中国共产党是全民族抗战的中流砥柱 Zhang Taiyuan Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, Zhang Taiyuan asks in what sense the Communist Party of China (CPC) was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the whole nation's resistance. The article argues that the victory was a victory of the entire nation and, above all, one in which the CPC played this pivotal role. It was published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025. The piece is organised in four sections, each ending with a lesson for the present. They cover the Party's line and strategy of protracted war, its promotion and defence of the anti-Japanese national united front, its guerrilla warfare and base areas behind enemy lines, and the spirit of resistance forged by its members and fighters. Zhang draws on Party declarations from 1931 to 1937, Mao Zedong's writings, military statistics and accounts of individual martyrs and heroes. Zhang contends that the Party gave the resistance its direction through the line of all-out resistance set at the Luochuan Meeting (1937) and the strategy in Mao's On Protracted War (1938), which held that mobilising the people was the root of victory. The Party then initiated and upheld the united front with the Kuomintang, even after the Southern Anhui Incident, and so held the alliance together. On the military side, the article cites figures for the Eighth Route Army, the New Fourth Army and the Party-led base areas: the Party-led rear-area battlefields are said to have faced 58–62 per cent of Japanese forces in the stalemate stage, and over the war to have eliminated about 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops and established 19 base areas. The article presents these results as the concrete form of the Party's pivotal role. It also describes the courage of figures such as Yang Jingyu, Deng Yufen and the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, presented as expressions of patriotism, unyielding integrity and conviction of victory. Zhang concludes that history teaches the need to uphold the Party's overall leadership, to consolidate the broadest patriotic united front, to rely on and mobilise the people, and to treat the great spirit of resistance as a resource for national rejuvenation. The article links these lessons to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Central Party School historian presents the CPC's role in the War of Resistance in the official narrative of 2025, with its figures and chosen examples.

Resolving prominent problems of work style with the spirit of self-reform 以自我革命精神解决作风方面突出问题 Tang Junfeng Tang Junfeng takes up the Party-wide study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, launched in 2025. The article argues that the campaign should be carried out in the spirit of the Party's self-reform, and that tackling work-style problems, which Xi Jinping calls an important historical lesson, is a way of advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece is a commentary built in three parts and draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements. The first part explains how the eight-point regulation, issued after the 18th Party Congress (2012), enriched the means of self-reform. The second sets out how to conduct the current campaign. The third discusses how to make work-style building a regular and lasting task. In the first part, Tang identifies four features of the regulation: it is an iron rule with no "trial" label, it relies on leadership by example from the Political Bureau downwards, it combines tough enforcement with long-term persistence, and it keeps close ties with the people. According to the author, before 2012 lax Party governance allowed formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance to persist, and the regulation curbed practices once thought impossible to stop. The second part calls for tempering Party spirit, since work style is at root a matter of Party spirit. It also calls for rectifying the "four undesirable work styles", observing discipline and practising honest, pragmatic action. The third part proposes integrating study, self-examination and rectification, handling Party spirit, work style and discipline together, and combining individual self-discipline with oversight by Party organizations and the masses. Tang concludes that the campaign is time-limited but that implementing the regulation has no end point. Tang calls for turning external requirements into inner motivation and for building regular, long-term mechanisms. Work style is presented as a question of the Party's bond with the people and of its long-term rule. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-school commentary presents the eight-point regulation and the 2025 campaign in terms of self-reform.

Continuously achieving the Party's self-purification and self-renewal 不断实现党的自我净化和自我革新 Li Zhongjie Writing in Beijing Daily (14 July 2025), Li Zhongjie reflects on more than a century of Party conduct building (zuofeng jianshe) in the Communist Party of China. Starting from Xi Jinping's warning that Party style bears on the Party's image, on public support and on its very survival, Li argues that such work is a permanent task through which the Party achieves self-purification and self-renewal. The short commentary is organised as five "reflections". They deal with Party style as an expression of the Party's nature, the need to treat style as a matter of survival, the open-ended character of the work, the answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall, and the balance between purity and vitality. Li defines Party style as the Party's observable image and a "barometer" of its nature, purpose and relationship with the people. Good style signals vigour; bad style signals disease. Citing Xi that style problems are stubborn and recurrent, Li holds that work on them is always "on the road". Li presents two historic answers to the question of how to escape the historical cycle: Mao Zedong's "new path of democracy", with the people supervising government, and Xi's Party self-reform, which the 20th Party Congress (2022) tied to the claim that anti-corruption is the most thoroughgoing self-reform. Li concludes that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must purify the Party without making it lifeless. Quoting Xi, Li says the aim is a healthy political ecology in which people get things done, so that society is both orderly and vibrant. Persistent work on Party style is said to let the Party keep the initiative under any conditions. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for Party conduct building, as presented by a senior Party historian.

The world-historical significance of China's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 中国抗日战争的世界历史意义 Hu Dekun Hu Dekun, a historian at Wuhan University, asks what place China's War of Resistance against Japan holds in world history. In this commentary, published in Beijing Daily in July 2025, Hu argues that the war was both an integral part of the global anti-fascist war and a source of historic contributions to its victory. The article is organised around four claims. China opened the earliest and longest-lasting Eastern main battlefield of the anti-fascist war; Chinese resistance supported the Soviet Union, the United States and Britain in their theatres; China helped to build the postwar international order; and the war laid the foundation for the founding of New China. Hu moves chronologically from the Mukden Incident of 1931 through the full-scale invasion of 1937 to the Allied alliance of 1942. Hu dates the start of the Second World War in the East to 18 September 1931, and treats the period to 1937 as one of local resistance, with guerrilla warfare led by the Communist Party in the north-east. After 1937, Hu says, the Kuomintang-led frontal battlefield and the Communist-led battlefield behind enemy lines together tied down the bulk of Japan's army and part of its navy. In Hu's account this prevented Japan from attacking the Soviet Union, delayed and weakened its southward and westward advances, and relieved pressure on Allied forces in the Pacific, North Africa and Burma. Hu also credits China with early calls for an anti-fascist alliance, with a place among the 'Big Four' in the 1942 Declaration by United Nations, and with involvement in creating the United Nations, the World Bank and the IMF. Hu presents the war as a test that exposed Kuomintang autocracy and corruption while strengthening the Communist Party's prestige, which Hu says prepared its victory in the War of Liberation. Hu concludes that at the turning point from world war to postwar peace and development, China wrote a 'glorious chapter' in world history. The piece reflects the official narrative that stresses the Communist Party's central role. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese historians present the Eastern main battlefield thesis and the war's link to the founding of New China.

The mission and path of comprehensively deepening reform in social science work at universities 高校社科工作全面深化改革的使命与路径 Li Xiaobing This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today on 14 July 2025, asks how university social science work should respond to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which set out the direction for further comprehensively deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Li Xiaobing argues that universities must take Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as their guide and uphold the Two Integrations, so as to move philosophy and social sciences to a new level. The piece is organised under three headings: consolidating theoretical foundations and building a knowledge system; engaging in social practice to serve national development; and cultivating new-era talent while inheriting and renewing culture. Each contains several concrete tasks for university social scientists. On the first, Li holds that the Two Integrations supply the methodological guidance: researchers should keep Marxism as the "soul" while drawing on excellent traditional Chinese culture as the "root". Li also calls for building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system by balancing "upholding fundamental principles" and innovation, and for interdisciplinary work. On the second, Li urges stronger think tanks and a "government, industry, academia, research and application" collaboration mechanism, deeper use of big data and artificial intelligence (for example through humanities labs), and reformed evaluation that rewards quality, contribution and integrity. On the third, Li calls for teaching that integrates theory and practice, produces socialist builders and successors, and strengthens cultural confidence through cultural exchange. Li concludes that such work should supply intellectual support for building a community with a shared future for mankind and serve national strategy. Read the original if you want a short example of how a university Party leader frames the tasks of social science work after the Third Plenum.

The victory in the War of Resistance against Japan as a great victory of the national spirit with patriotism at its core 抗日战争胜利是以爱国主义为核心的民族精神的伟大胜利 Chinese Academy of Social Sciences Marking the 80th anniversary of the victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, this commentary in Qiushi, attributed to the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the victory was a great victory of the national spirit with patriotism at its core. It argues that this spirit was the decisive factor in the war and that the Communist Party of China turned popular patriotic feeling into a historical force. The text has three parts. The first traces how patriotism, described as the heart of the Chinese national spirit, was awakened after the Opium War of 1840 and reached a new height after the September 18th Incident of 1931. The second examines the Party's role in the war. The third sets out how the spirit should be promoted today through publicity, education, the internet and scholarship. The core argument in the second part holds that without a vanguard party, simple patriotic feeling could drift into narrow nationalism or blind xenophobia. According to the article, the Party gave patriotism a new content by making national independence and liberation its first task. It was the first to call for armed resistance in 1931 and to declare war on Japan in 1932. It also promoted the Anti-Japanese National United Front, leading to the second Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. The article further credits the Party with relying on and mobilising the people, through the idea of protracted war and guerrilla warfare, so that the conflict became a true people's war, which it calls the fundamental reason for victory. Communist-led forces are said to have fought at the front at great sacrifice, and the article cites a figure that they tied down 58–75 per cent of Japanese forces in China after the stage of strategic stalemate began. The article concludes that the spirit must be carried forward. It calls for publicity on the Party's pivotal role and on China's contribution as the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war. It urges patriotic education that focuses on young people and links the war's history with Party history, and says new media should be used. It also calls on philosophy and social science to build a Second World War discourse system and to rebut distortions of history. This effort is tied to national rejuvenation under Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-journal statement of how the war's history and spirit are framed for patriotic education and historical research in 2025.

A historical-materialist reading of the complex relation between cultural forms and the development of an era, and its contemporary implications An analysis based on Marx's Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy 文化形态与时代发展复杂关联的唯物史观阐释及其当代启示 Wang Xiaofeng Wang Xiaofeng asks how Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy explains the relation between an era and its culture. Wang argues that Marx's remarks on Greek art supply a historical-materialist framework for contemporary work on culture, and in particular for the debate on how to achieve the second of the Two Integrations, the union of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The article is organised in five parts. The first four read Marx's text closely, with supporting passages from Engels, Mao Zedong and the Eighteenth Brumaire. They take up why classical art cannot be reproduced in its classical form, why it still gives aesthetic enjoyment, how culture is bound to 'a definite form of social development', and the uneven relation between material production and art. The fifth part draws implications for Chinese cultural policy. Examples range from Greek myth, the Renaissance and the Enlightenment to the Hundred Schools of Thought, Tang and Song poetry and Yan'an-era works. Wang's central claim is that cultures arise and fade with the social conditions that produced them, so any cultural 'revival' is a new culture with new content rather than a repetition. Classical works nonetheless keep their charm because they speak to shared human feeling, natural beauty and the aspiration to freedom, as an adult can enjoy a child's naivety without becoming a child again. Wang also stresses that Marx rejected mechanical determinism. Art can flourish where production is backward, individual talent matters, and the relative independence of consciousness lets economically backward countries, such as Germany in philosophy, produce advanced culture. Wang adds, following Engels, that this cannot be made absolute. For Chinese cultural construction, Wang concludes that the real question for the Two Integrations is how to integrate, not whether. Wang warns against both dismissing tradition and idealising it beyond its era or class. The author proposes creative transformation and innovative development of tradition, a distinction between traditional culture and its enduring spirit, and critical sublation instead of surface analogies between ancient and modern concepts. Read the original if you want a close Marxist reading of the Introduction's aesthetics applied to current Chinese debates on tradition and the Two Integrations.

The ownership basis of new quality productive forces: an examination based on the theory of productive forces and relations of production 新质生产力的所有制基础：基于生产力和生产关系理论的考察 Li Chunbing Chen Xuejuan Hu Huaiguo How can China turn scientific and technological innovation into new quality productive forces, and what kind of ownership structure supports that leap? Li, Chen and Hu argue that the leap is not automatic. In their account it requires deeper reform and new relations of production in which public and non-public ownership complement and reinforce each other, while the Party's principle of the "two unwaveringlys" is maintained. The article starts from Marx's framework of productive forces and relations of production, in which ownership of the means of production is the core of the relations of production. It then defines new quality productive forces as advanced and real productive forces, with technological innovation as their core element. A historical section traces ownership and science policy from 1949 through the Mao-era single public-ownership structure to the reform period. The last part draws policy implications for public, private and mixed-ownership enterprises. The authors propose an analytical logic running from technological innovation through ownership to a leap in productive forces. Drawing on Marx's Grundrisse, they treat science both as a productive force and as a means of labour. They argue that innovation becomes real productive force only when combined with enterprises and industrial innovation, so enterprise ownership forms the material basis. They credit public ownership with directing the replacement of old productive forces by new ones, through concentrated resources, strategic planning and "patient" capital. They credit the non-public sector with turning disruptive innovation into applications, citing figures such as over 60 per cent of GDP and over 70 per cent of technological innovation results. Mixed-ownership reform, they say, can bring the two together and help overcome "chokepoint" technologies. The article concludes that China's ownership structure gives it an institutional advantage. State-owned firms contribute collective research capacity, and private firms contribute market sensitivity and flexibility. Each compensates for the other's weaknesses, and the authors call for an institutional environment that supports both. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese economists apply the productive forces and relations of production framework to the ownership question behind new quality productive forces, including a Party-historical account of science and ownership policy.

Critique of the logic of capital from the perspective of Marx's theory of world history, and its contemporary significance A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义 Wang Xinsheng Zhang Jianrong Wang and Zhang ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society, and how it can be overcome. They propose reading Marx's critique of it through his theory of world history, arguing that the two are inseparable: the logic of capital governs the formation of world history and human development, while world history supplies its origins, limits and the path to its sublation. Drawing on Capital and its manuscripts, the article has three parts. The first traces how the logic of capital arises and expands historically: its preconditions, its spread through the world market, its limits and its effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique. The third draws out four contemporary implications, which the authors tie to digital capitalism, socialism with Chinese characteristics, modernization and human development. The authors argue that Marx's critique is an immanent, dialectical one. It differs from classical economists, who treated capital as eternal, and from utopian socialists, whose criticism was external. Marx exposes the logic of capital through three linked critiques: of reality (fetishism and abstract domination), of history (capital's own limits, the 'barrier' to capitalist production being capital itself) and of values (the reduction of people to one-sided, alienated beings). Its aim is to find within the old world history the new one that sublates it. On this reading capital has a dual character: a civilising side as a factor of production and a destructive side as a relation of production. The authors say it should therefore be neither wholly negated nor justified. Wang and Zhang conclude that the critique remains a 'pathology of capital' of world-historical significance. They claim it shows that digital capitalism is a more concealed form of exploitation on a private-ownership basis. They also say it explains why capital has a place in the primary stage of socialism, where its positive side is to be used and its disorderly expansion regulated. In their account it undermines the idea that capitalist modernization is the only path and points towards the free and all-round development of the person. Read the original if you want a text-based account of how Chinese scholars link Marx's world-history theory and critique of capital to digital capitalism and the role of capital under socialism.

The core and distinctive features of the new round of scientific and technological revolution from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域下新一轮科技革命的核心与特质 Zhang Jianyun Zhang Jianyun asks what is the essence, core and distinguishing character of the current round of scientific and technological revolution, and answers from a historical-materialist standpoint. The article argues that a "digital-intelligent" technology system, formed by the convergence of older and newer information technologies, leads the revolution. Its core, in Zhang's reading, is that artificial intelligence, built on massive data, liberates mental labour, and this changes the mode of production. The article has three parts. The first traces the fusion of twentieth-century technologies (computers, digitisation, AI, the internet, mobile communications) with twenty-first-century ones (cloud computing, mobile internet, blockchain, the Internet of Things) into what the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) called the "data-intelligence" system. The second draws on Marx's account of machinery and of labour to explain how AI relieves mental labour. The third examines three changes in production: the content of the means of production, the form of labour, and the organisation of cooperation. It contrasts how capitalism and socialism relate to each. Zhang uses Marx's method of ascending from abstract determinations to the "concrete in thought" and names data as that concrete, around which all the technologies are organised. Machine learning, Zhang argues, simulates the brain's "ideal construction" of things, so AI aids mental labour much as the machine system freed manual labour. Zhang holds that AI output cannot replace human labour, because it lacks human emotion and so cannot be objectified in the way human labour is. Data is described as non-physical, easily copied, non-exclusive and gaining value when shared, which Zhang says undermines the importance of private ownership. Zhang contends that capital's logic of monopoly, mass wage-labour production and decoupling runs against these demands. Socialist public ownership, small-scale distributed cultural production and a community with a shared future for mankind are presented as compatible with them. DeepSeek is offered as an example. Zhang concludes that digital-intelligent technology makes possible Marx's "one social labour force" and that socialism, by meeting the objective demands of the new productive forces, will reshape human civilisation in a fair and reasonable way. The article links these claims to new quality productive forces and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist theoretical account of AI, data and the digital economy, with attention to the contrast it draws between capitalist and socialist institutions.

Theoretical questions on the "Second Integration" in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context Notes on studying and understanding the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture 学习理解马克思主义中国化“第二个结合”的若干理论问题探析 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin takes up several theoretical questions raised by the "Second Integration", the proposition that the basic principles of Marxism must be combined with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article argues that this proposition deepens the Party's understanding of how Marxism is adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It holds that it became possible because of new archaeological findings and a more mature theoretical understanding under Xi Jinping. It also holds that it requires a balance of critique and absorption, openness to other civilizations, and a view of tradition as a whole. The article has five parts. It first traces the history of the Two Integrations from Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation to Xi Jinping's 2021 and 2023 statements. It then lists the new historical conditions for the Second Integration, drawing on the Chinese Civilization Exploration Project and research on the Xia dynasty. The remaining parts cover how the Party has treated tradition in different periods, how the Second Integration relates to learning from other civilizations, and why tradition should be approached as a composite whole. Liu's central claim is that the Party's basic attitude to tradition has been consistent, with emphasis shifting to the main task of each period. In revolutionary periods critique of decadent elements dominated, while in peacetime construction absorption of the best elements does, and the other element is never dropped. On this basis Liu defends the May Fourth attack on Confucianism and Lu Xun's critique as historically necessary. Liu rejects any \"re-criticism\" of them today. On foreign cultures, the author urges mutual learning among civilizations while resisting \"Western-centrism\", \"universal values\" and \"Westernization\". Liu also warns against reviving any single school. Citing Chen Xianda, Ren Jiyu and Xi, Liu stresses that Chinese tradition is plural and mixed, with Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Legalism and Buddhism interacting, and gives Xunzi's marginalisation as a warning against narrow orthodoxy. Liu concludes that, under Marxist guidance, the progressive, people-oriented and useful elements of Chinese tradition should be developed through creative transformation and innovative development. The aim is to enrich contemporary Chinese Marxism and serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu presents this as consistent with the Party's long-standing method rather than a break with it. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the Second Integration is justified historically, and of how it handles critique, foreign influence and the plurality of Chinese tradition.

Evidence of Unit 731's atrocities and a rebuttal of Japanese denial of the invasion of China An interview with Jin Shicheng of the Exhibition Hall of Evidence of Crimes Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army 实证731部队残暴行径 驳斥日本否认侵华言论 Zhao Xuzhou This is an interview, conducted by a reporter for China Social Sciences Today (Zhao Xuzhou) with Jin Shicheng, a staff member of the Exhibition Hall of Evidence of Crimes Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army. It was prompted by the Hall's first domestic release of the complete 83-minute video testimony of Kurumizawa Masakuni (胡桃泽正邦), a former Unit 731 member. The video was recorded in August 1991 in Iida, Japan, and the Hall obtained it in August 2024 from the Japanese researcher Hara Fumio. The interview has three parts: what the testimony confirms about Unit 731's crimes, what value such materials have for scholarship and for rebutting denial of the invasion, and what the Hall has done and still plans to do in collecting evidence. Jin also explains why Kurumizawa's account was dropped from later editions of Morimura Seiichi's Akuma no hoshoku (The Devil's Gluttony). Jin argues that the testimony shows bacteriological warfare to have been an organised, top-down state crime. As evidence, Jin cites Kurumizawa's route into the unit through the army medical school and the puppet Manchukuo's Dalu Academy of Sciences, and his claim to have dissected 300 people. Jin adds that it corroborates earlier research on test subjects called "maruta", on a special prison holding at least 40 people, and on the production of two tonnes of germs a day. In Jin's account the testimony is first-hand, detailed and from the perpetrator's side, and it also shows the unit's strict secrecy. Jin says the US exempted Unit 731 from prosecution in exchange for its experimental data, so most members stayed hidden, and that the testimony helps international opinion face the nature of Japanese militarism. Jin outlines the Hall's work: protecting 27 sites, 23 of them national key cultural relics; recording over 400 hours of oral testimony in Japan; holding over 300,000 pages of archives; and carrying out 12 state and provincial projects, including ones funded by the National Social Science Fund of China. The Hall's stated aim is to have the site listed as World Heritage and its archives entered in the Memory of the World Register. Next steps include collecting materials held by former members' descendants and Japanese civic groups, linking research with public outreach through the Hall's role as a patriotic education demonstration base, and strengthening international communication. Read the original if you want a Chinese museum specialist's account of the Kurumizawa testimony and of how Chinese institutions plan to document and publicise Unit 731.

The positive-science character of historical materialism 唯物史观的实证科学性质 Yang Lizhen Zhao Rui Is historical materialism a positive (empirical) science? The authors identify three positions in Chinese scholarship: affirmation, flat denial, and a vague stance that neither affirms nor denies. They argue that only the first matches Marx's intention. In their view Marx called historical materialism a positive science explicitly on more than one occasion, and the claim is also built into its essential nature. This short newspaper-style piece rests mainly on Marx's formulation in The German Ideology, that real, positive science begins where speculation ends, in front of real life. It reads that passage together with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach. It then takes four attributes in turn: actuality (xianshixing), practicality, critical character and popular character (renminxing, orientation to the people). The central claim is that Marx's "positive science" is defined against Hegelian speculative philosophy, not simply modelled on natural science. The authors say it is a "positive science within positive science". It inherits the natural sciences' pursuit of truth but adds the four attributes. Actuality means that every principle derives from real history and the real individuals in it, with capitalist society as the main object of study. Practicality means that material production is the starting point and foundation, and the authors call it the most fundamental attribute. Criticism means opposing philosophies that, in the authors' account, supply theoretical justification for private property. Critique of old philosophy is a means, and the aim is a theoretical guide for working people to change the world. Popular character means that the masses create material and spiritual wealth and decide social change. The authors present this attribute as both the starting point and the destination of the theory. The authors conclude that this positive-science character made philosophy a real science for the first time. They argue that philosophy must go beyond abstract logical deduction and beyond criticism that looks sharp but leaves private ownership untouched. It must instead pass the tests of reality, practice and the people. The piece is a compact restatement of an orthodox reading of Marx's method. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese Marxist scholars defend the scientific status of historical materialism against rival views.

From fetishism to data worship: Marx's critical theory in the digital age 从拜物教到数据崇拜：数字时代的马克思批判理论 Wang Qian Wang Qian asks how Marx's critique of fetishism, ideology and alienation can still explain a world in which data, algorithms and platforms increasingly mediate social life. The article argues that reification has not ended in the digital age but continues as "data worship", deepening capital's domination over people. In Wang's reading, the supposed neutrality of data, the personalised narratives of algorithms and the platforms' precise regulation of behaviour together form a new ideological structure of digital capitalism. This short commentary, published in a Party-affiliated social science newspaper, is organised in three parts that follow three themes in Marx's critique. It moves from commodity reification to data reification, from false consciousness to algorithmic ideology, and from alienated labour to data alienation. Wang draws on Capital, The German Ideology and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and brings in Lukács on reification and Althusser on interpellation. Wang's first move is that data, being immaterial, real-time and copyable, makes the value form more abstract and more concealed. Its mystery, like that of the commodity, lies in the unseen labour and practice it extracts, while value is increasingly measured by captured attention and predicted behaviour. Second, the article argues that algorithms take over the role of Althusserian interpellation: through personalised recommendation they shape what individuals can perceive, and feedback loops produce cognitive closure and "voluntary passivity". Third, data alienation blurs the line between labour and non-labour and between production and consumption, so that clicks, attention and emotion become sources of value, and individuals lose control over both their product and their understanding of their own existence. Wang concludes that Marx's critical theory has a renewed task: to expose the social relations hidden behind data forms, to resist capital's total occupation of the subject, and to reaffirm human social essence and practical freedom. Wang calls for a view of the subject grounded in sociality, historicity and practice as the way to reopen a path to emancipation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar adapts fetishism, ideology critique and alienation theory to the study of data and algorithms.

The significance of Herder for the formation of Marx's thought 赫尔德对马克思思想形成的意义 Ma Jianqing Ma Jianqing asks whether Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803), a leader of the Sturm und Drang movement, influenced Marx, and if so which elements, to what degree and by what routes. The article argues that the link is real but fragile and thinly documented. Marx's German heritage, it holds, should not be reduced to Hegelian speculative philosophy, since it also includes wider eighteenth-century currents that Herder helped shape. After a brief review of scholars who mention the connection (Isaiah Berlin, F. M. Barnard, Allen Wood, among others), the article proceeds in three parts. It first reconstructs channels of dialogue: Marx's 1839 folk-song collection drawing on Herder's Stimmen der Völker in Liedern, his reading notes of 1844–47, and references in letters. It also traces indirect mediation through Hegel, Feuerbach, Savigny, Goethe and Gans. It then compares Herder and Marx on the human being, language and history, and finally assesses the relation between anthropology and historical materialism. Ma argues that Herder's view of human nature as self-expression through action anticipates the objectification theory of the 1844 Manuscripts. Herder's thesis that thought and language are inseparable, and his naturalistic account of language's origin, are said to resonate with Marx's remarks on language as social and as the element of thought in The German Ideology and the Grundrisse. Herder's treatment of history as natural, causal and organic is likened to Marx's idea of history as the true natural history of man and of society as an organism. Most of this influence, Ma suggests, reached Marx through Hegel and Feuerbach. Ma concludes that both thinkers faced a shared task at the secularising turn of philosophy: reconciling ideal and real, universal and particular. Herder's anthropology, however, still relied on metaphysics, on God and on an inflated role for spirit, and in the sense of Marx's critique of German ideology it remained idealist. Historical materialism, grounded in practice and material production, is presented as dissolving the tensions in Herder's thought. The author warns against both exaggerating the link and opposing the two thinkers absolutely. Read the original if you study the intellectual genealogy of Marx's early work or the German Romantic and Sturm und Drang background to historical materialism.

Marx and Engels's critique of capitalist modern civilization and its implications 马克思恩格斯对资本主义现代文明的批判及启示 Sun Xuan Sun Xuan asks how the value core of capitalist modern civilization shapes that civilization and drives it into structural difficulty, and what Marx and Engels's critique offers for exploring other paths of civilization. The article argues that, because capitalism's value core is the supremacy of material interests and the maximisation of capital, it cannot realise the free and all-round development of the human being. Sun proposes a new path of human civilization that puts that development at its centre and embodies the values of a community. The article opens by surveying Schumpeter, Gu Hongming, Rousseau and Weber on modern civilization. Sun finds that they mostly describe value deviation and dilemmas without showing systematically how the value core acts on civilization. The second part reads Marx and Engels through historical materialism across five dimensions: material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. The third part turns each dimension into a constructive counterpart. In Sun's account, Marx and Engels credit the bourgeoisie with enormous productive achievements, the overthrow of feudal authority and the opening of a world market. They also show that the same logic produces overproduction crises, a representative state that is a "illusory community" serving capital, and colonial subordination of the East to the West. Spiritual life is hollowed out by money fetishism, labour is alienated, and nature is plundered. Sun's alternative replaces the capitalist logic of "for capital, relying on labour, developing capital" with "for people, relying on people, developing people". Concretely, it calls for ownership and distribution that serve the majority, a "real community" of people's democracy, equal exchange among civilizations, and cultural production oriented to the people. It also calls for a division of labour that frees work from mechanical fragmentation, and for ecological development that reconciles using and protecting nature. Sun concludes that capitalist modern civilization is being progressively "disenchanted" and shows a tendency to decay as the world becomes more multipolar. The lesson, in the author's view, is to move from a "thing-centred" to a "people-centred" civilizational standard. Material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization would then be developed within a community of all-round development and exchange. This is presented as a way to settle disputes over civilizational values and to ease civilizational conflict. Read the original if you want a systematic, five-part Chinese philosophical reading of Marx and Engels on capitalist civilization, and the normative alternative that Sun builds from it.

The machine narrative in Marx's context and its conceptual genealogy 马克思语境中的机器叙事及其概念谱系 Zhao Zelin Existing scholarship reads Marx on machines mainly through the philosophy of science and technology or through the critique of political economy. Zhao argues that this work rarely shows how Marx's machine-related concepts are connected to one another. The article contends that Marx's machine is not an isolated object but part of a narrative with an internal generative logic and a conceptual genealogy. Working from Marx's own texts, the article traces a sequence: traditional tool, machine tool, machine, automaton and machine system; then the automatic machine system and the automatic factory; then the factory system, factory legislation and wider social institutions. It is organised in three main sections, followed by a short conclusion. Zhao also draws on Charles Babbage, Lewis Mumford and Andrew Ure to show where Marx follows or departs from them. In the first move, Zhao says Marx goes beyond Babbage's structural account by adding the 'subjective' side of the modern machine, the automaton with 'mechanical' and 'intelligent' organs. Marx treats the machine system as the bridge from the machine as a single object to the machine as a social-historical element. In the second move, Zhao argues that capitalist machine production reverses the relation between worker and machine. This is not a loss of human subjectivity in general. It is one class, the capitalists, appropriating the subjectivity of another through ownership of capital. Machines are dead labour that transfer value, while only living labour creates surplus value, and this is why capitalists build the factory system and have it codified in factory legislation. Zhao presents these as arrangements that stabilise capitalist relations and socialise the conflict, without changing the underlying relationship. Zhao concludes that, for Marx, the source of alienation is capitalist private ownership of the means of production and its capital logic, not the machine itself. Zhao reads Marx as warning that smashing machines will not free workers. Instead, the contradiction between private ownership and the socialisation of machine production points towards public ownership and the use of machines for people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based reconstruction of Marx's machine concepts and their links to the factory system and factory law, rather than a debate on contemporary technology.

The threefold limits of marginalism from the standpoint of historical materialism Revisiting the first clash between marginalism and Capital 唯物史观视域中边际主义的三重限度 Gao Jianmin In 1884 Philip Henry Wicksteed used William Stanley Jevons's marginal utility theory to attack Marx's labour theory of value in "Das Kapital: A Criticism". Gao notes that later critics, such as Rubin, Hilferding and Bukharin, mostly targeted later marginalists like Böhm-Bawerk, and that the few replies to Wicksteed were partial. The article argues that, judged by historical materialism, Wicksteed's critique fails in three dimensions: its form of thought, its methodology and its view of history. Gao takes this to confirm the scientific character of Marx's labour theory of value. The article is organised in three sections matching these dimensions. The first deals with fetishistic thinking and the misplacement of the value form. The second deals with methodological individualism and the paradox of "abstract utility". The third deals with a non-historical outlook and a "clumsy" supply-and-demand theory. Gao draws on Capital, Marx's letters, Engels, Rubin, Lukács, Postone, Sohn-Rethel, Whitrow and others, and works through Wicksteed's examples of Robinson Crusoe and a commodity-free community. Gao argues first that Wicksteed forgets the capitalist social form that gives concepts such as utility equilibrium their meaning. He projects the value form, along with a money-schema and clock-time calculation, onto societies without commodity exchange, and so treats relations between people as natural properties of things. Second, by defining value as "abstract utility", he subjectivises it and replaces Marx's real, socially situated individuals with abstract consumers. In Gao's reading this confuses value with use value, makes the explanation circular, and leaves money's role as measure of value unexplained, since money already presupposes value. Third, Gao holds that Wicksteed's theory reduces to supply and demand, takes technical change and the pursuit of surplus value as given, and ignores the M–C–M′ question of where surplus value arises, namely in the purchase of labour-power. Gao concludes that Wicksteed, like classical and vulgar economists, treats exchange, money and value as eternal categories and so cannot grasp their historical origin. Gao attributes this to his position within a reified world, to the separation of exchange from thought, and to his bourgeois standpoint. For Gao, historical materialism is the "recollection of origins", and Marx's critique of political economy ties categories to the real historical movement of capitalism. Read the original if you want a detailed Marxist rebuttal of the earliest marginalist critique of Capital, grounded in value-form theory and the critique of fetishism.

On a new model of exchange among human civilizations 论人类文明交往新模式 Tang Aijun Tang Aijun asks what view of civilizational interaction should guide a world marked by civilizational clashes and hegemony. The article argues that the Party's concept of 'exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations', put forward since the 18th Party Congress (2012), is a new model of civilizational interaction that goes beyond the Western-centric model. In Tang's account, it offers 'Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach' to handling relations between civilizations. The article has three parts. The first draws on Marx's theory of world history, and on Fei Xiaotong, to trace the move from isolated 'each to its own beauty' civilizations to universal interaction driven by capital. The second criticises the Western-centric model through four elements: the singular concept of civilization, the hierarchy of civilizations, the 'civilizing mission' and the 'end of history' thesis. The third sets out the new model and the historical conditions Tang says make it possible. Tang grants the Western-centric model a historical progressiveness: it spread productive forces and universal interaction. He nonetheless holds that it exported capital's contradictions, brought colonial disaster and licensed intervention as a main source of civilizational conflict. Against it he sets four principles. These are a plural view of civilizations, civilizational equality (equal in value, attitude and order, with 'partnerships of diverse civilizations'), mutual learning through open, reciprocal dialogue, and coexistence under the principle of 'harmony without uniformity'. Tang presents these as drawing on Marxist theories of interaction and on traditional Chinese culture, and as responding to multipolarity, shared global problems and the crisis of modernity. Tang concludes that moving beyond Western-centrism is the main trend of civilizational development. He argues that the Party has built an 'exchange–mutual learning–coexistence' model, backed by mechanisms such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Dialogue of Asian Civilizations. Tang adds that a community of diverse civilizations requires a deep change in cultural mentality. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western civilizational discourse, from Guizot to Fukuyama, and the theoretical grounding of Beijing's civilizational-exchange rhetoric.

Keeping secrets is a glorious tradition and fine work style of the Party 保守秘密是党的光荣传统和优良作风 Zhang Jianjun Zhang Jianjun's commentary, published in the Chinese Discipline Inspection and Supervision News on 10 July 2025, argues that protecting Party and state secrets is both a concrete expression of Party discipline and a glorious tradition and fine work style of the Party. It is prompted by the revised Law on Guarding State Secrets, which took effect on 1 May 2024. Zhang holds that recalling how Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and other older revolutionaries practised secrecy helps carry that tradition forward today. The piece is a short historical-exemplary essay organised under three headings, each introduced by a quotation from Xi Jinping: firm ideals and absolute loyalty to the Party; strict observance of confidentiality discipline; and leading by example so that secrets are kept safe. Each section is built from anecdotes and recollections about Mao, Deng Xiaoping, Ren Bishi, Chen Yun, Deng Yingchao, Zhou Enlai and Liu Shaoqi. A brief closing passage turns to present-day tasks. In the first section, Zhang recounts the narrow escapes of Mao and Deng during underground work in the 1920s, and Ren Bishi's refusal to reveal his identity under torture in 1929. Zhang presents these as proof that such figures valued protecting Party secrets above their own lives. The second section cites Chen Yun's writings on Party discipline, Deng Yingchao's account of Zhou Enlai telling her nothing before leaving to lead the Nanchang Uprising, and Mao's telegrams ordering secret documents burned before the Southern Anhui Incident and during the Huaihai Campaign. The third section shows leaders enforcing secrecy within their own households: Liu Shaoqi's rule of not saying, asking or reading what one should not, even in front of his children, and Chen Yun's refusal to tell his wife in advance of a price change in 1962 or 1963. Zhang concludes that, facing a broader and more complex national security environment, the Party should apply the holistic approach to national security and promote high-quality development of confidentiality work. In Zhang's view, this work bears on the Party's long-term governing position, national security, people's wellbeing and national rejuvenation, and should contribute to building a strong country through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a sample of how official Party media use revolutionary-era anecdotes to teach confidentiality discipline to cadres.

Furthering comprehensively deepening reform in the spirit of historical initiative 以历史主动精神进一步全面深化改革 He Husheng Xue Siqi He and Xue take up the question of how the Communist Party of China can carry reform further after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Their answer is that the Party must keep up what they call the spirit of historical initiative, a distinctive ideological strength of Marxist parties. They argue that this spirit is the key to deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The piece, a commentary in a Party discipline newspaper, has three parts. It first traces historical initiative through the new-democratic revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out the internal logic by which this spirit guides reform. Finally it draws practical requirements for the new journey. The central move is a three-part account of the spirit's content. Historical self-awareness, meaning accurate knowledge of laws, stages and trends, supplies theoretical initiative and answers where initiative is heading. A clearly identified historical subject, the people, supplies practical strength and answers who realises it. Historical responsibility supplies spiritual drive and answers how it is realised. The authors present reform and opening up as the Party's active "breaking of the deadlock" and the post-2013 comprehensively deepening reform as active "construction". On this reading, historical initiative reached a new height in the new era. The authors make three proposals. The Party should grasp the trend of the times, anchoring reform to the overall goal of improving socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing national governance. It should also keep its political foundation by strengthening Party leadership, fostering a fighting spirit and pursuing the Party's self-reform. Finally it should hold to the people's standpoint, uniting Party leadership with the people's principal role and combining top-level design with grassroots exploration. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary links the concept of historical initiative to the reform agenda set out in 2024.

The epistemological foundations of Lenin's theory of imperialism 列宁“帝国主义论”的认识论基础 Hu Xiaokun Hu Xiaokun asks what theory of knowledge underlay Lenin's analysis of imperialism and his judgement that socialist revolution could succeed first in a relatively backward country.
