The short article, published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, argues that Lenin made practice the criterion of a materialist epistemology and held together subjective initiative and objective law. On this basis, Hu says, he analysed the international situation and Russia's social character, and laid the Marxist epistemological groundwork for breaking the single capitalist world system and founding the first socialist state. The article begins with the early twentieth-century passage from free competition to monopoly capitalism and the division of the world among monopoly alliances. It then turns to the First World War, the collapse of the Second International and Russia's position as the weakest link in the imperialist chain. Hu draws on several Lenin texts: Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, the Philosophical Notebooks (on Hegel), Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, and The Development of Capitalism in Russia. Hu's central move is to read the dispute with the Second International's revisionists as a philosophical conflict. In Hu's account, they rested on relativism and distorted dialectics into scepticism and sophistry. They then favoured reformism and vulgar evolutionism, denied the imperialist character of the war and ignored the concrete conditions for revolution. Against them, Lenin defined dialectics as the study of contradiction within the essence of things, with transitions between opposites that are conditional, and marked by leaps and breaks in gradual development. Hu applies this to imperialism: free competition turns into its opposite, monopoly, sharpening contradictions at world scale, while the proletariat's struggle becomes international as production is increasingly socialised. Hu then shows how Lenin applied this method to Russia. In this account, Lenin saw Russian capitalism as dependent on the landlord class at home and on European and American capital abroad. He judged that the 1861 land reform deepened the contradictions in the class structure. He therefore defined the revolution as a revolutionary-democratic dictatorship of the proletariat and peasantry, led by a vanguard party and linked to national-liberation movements. Hu concludes that an active materialist epistemology, stressing purposeful human activity within objective conditions, guided socialism's leap from theory to practice and from one country to several. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese philosophical reading of how Lenin's dialectics and theory of knowledge underpin his account of imperialism and the October Revolution.

Lenin's thought on cultural leadership 列宁关于文化领导权的思想 Yan Peiyu Yan Peiyu, in a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2025), presents Lenin's writing on cultural leadership (cultural hegemony) as a distinctive feature of his philosophy. Yan argues that, after Marx and Engels decoded the logic of capital, Lenin's task was to build and consolidate proletarian power in the age of imperialism, and that this led him to study cultural leadership. The article reads Lenin's thought as inheriting the Marxist tradition of cultural critique and as having three layers. These are the Party spirit principle in cultural creation, firm Party control of cultural leadership in developing proletarian culture, and the construction of a socialist cultural subjectivity through state cultural leadership. On the first layer, Yan traces Lenin's 1905 essay on Party literature and argues that he linked Party spirit to ample room for individual creativity and warned against formulaism. On the second, Yan describes Lenin's criticism of the Proletkult, which sought a "pure" culture independent of the Party. Lenin held that proletarian culture grows from the lawful development of all human knowledge, and Yan adds his "two cultures" theory of inherited culture. On the third, Yan points to raising the people's cultural level, avoiding rashness in cultural matters, and combating bureaucratism, symbolised by Oblomov. Yan concludes that the common thread is a shift in Lenin's problematic from the logic of proletarian revolution to that of socialist construction, driven by twentieth-century world-historical change and Russia's transformation. This shift, in Yan's reading, turned Lenin from a revolutionary leader into an "architect" of socialism. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of how Lenin's views on culture, the Party and the state are framed in current Chinese scholarship.

Lenin's hidden treasury of philosophical thought Rereading the Philosophical Notebooks 列宁哲学思想的隐性宝库 Liu Jun Liu Jun argues that Lenin's Philosophical Notebooks, often undervalued beside Materialism and Empirio-Criticism because they are reading notes and excerpts, are a 'hidden treasury' of his philosophy. Whereas the earlier book mainly set out the epistemology of dialectical materialism, the Notebooks, in Liu's view, cover materialist dialectics, the history of philosophy and philosophy of nature. The commentary first reviews the text's composition and publication history, from the eight blue notebooks of 1914–15 written in Bern to the Soviet and Chinese editions. It then lists rival readings: the Soviet 'planned monograph' view of Kedrov, a practice-based dialectic reading, and Western 'Leninology' accounts that see a Hegelian turn or a break with Lenin's earlier thought. Liu holds that these positions rest on differing theoretical and ideological standpoints. Liu locates the Notebooks' innovation in their overall design, a Leninist outline of a system of materialist dialectics. Lenin compared Hegel's Logic with the logic of Capital and held that dialectics, logic and epistemology are identical, with the unity of opposites as the core. His notes on natural science, Liu says, anticipated holistic and systemic approaches and criticised absolutising laws and simple causality. Liu also argues that the dialectic of the general and the particular gave a philosophical basis for backward countries such as Russia to reach socialism without passing through capitalist development. Liu concludes that these methodological principles, originating with Marx and Engels, became a complete system in Lenin and carry theoretical and practical weight for Marxism and the socialist movement. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic overview of the Notebooks' editions, the debates about them and their significance for Leninist philosophy.

Using sinicized Marxism to excavate and elucidate China's fine traditional culture 以中国化的马克思主义挖掘和阐发中华优秀传统文化 Lin Jinping Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for inheriting China's fine traditional culture as part of Chinese modernization, the article asks which theoretical tool is suited to excavating and elucidating that culture. Lin argues that the tool can be neither rationalised modern Western culture nor a conservative, self-enclosed Chinese culture, but only Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions. The article appeared in Philosophical Trends, 2025, no. 1. The article has four sections. The first criticises the Western view of Chinese culture, using Hegel and Weber as main examples and Russell as a more appreciative counterpoint. The second examines the limits of reading Chinese culture only from within, focusing on Confucian "family-state isomorphism". The third makes the case for sinicized Marxism, drawing on Marx, Engels and Mao Zedong. The fourth sets out three methodological principles for the work. Lin contends that Hegel and Weber judged China by Western political experience, especially the separation of civil society from the political state, and so found Chinese culture wanting. In Lin's reading this view overlooks the Daoist and Buddhist pull towards non-political life and the Confucian stress on self-cultivation. A purely internal approach, by contrast, risks conservatism. Lin notes that Confucianism worked as an ideology but that rulers practised "Confucian outside, Legalist inside", and that its real force lay in village and family life, which modernisation changes. Marxism, Lin argues, has critically reflected on Western rationalism and demands adaptation to concrete conditions, so it can treat Chinese culture as part of China's reality, with respect and dialectically, following Mao's call to discard feudal dross and absorb democratic essence. On method, Lin proposes three requirements. First, respect and understand traditional culture. Second, treat "excavation and elucidation" as nurturing a living organism, not mining a resource, so that it supports creative transformation and innovative development. Third, engage in equal dialogue and keep self-reflection, avoiding a prophet-like stance, since the present is itself historically limited and judgments of what is "fine" may change. Lin warns against dogmatising Marxism or treating tradition as an outdated resource. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical account of why Marxism is presented as the proper framework for engaging traditional culture, including its readings of Hegel, Weber and Confucianism.

The low-cost development path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的低代价发展之路 Qiu Gengtian Qiu Gengtian argues that the large body of research on Chinese modernization lacks a perspective from the study of costs (daijiaxue, literally the study of 'prices paid' in development). Modernization everywhere carries costs, and a high-cost model would forfeit the historic missions assigned to Chinese modernization, including the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article's thesis is that Chinese modernization should follow a low-cost path, which requires the Party and society to cultivate a conscious 'cost awareness'. The article has three parts. The first defines cost, classifies it, and reviews how Xi Jinping, Western writers (Rachel Carson, the Club of Rome's The Limits to Growth, E. O. Wilson, Stavrianos) and Chinese scholars have described the costs of modernization. The second traces Chinese modernization from the 1950s to the present as a process of overcoming costs. The third sets out what cost awareness involves and how costs should be regulated. Qiu divides costs into cost-type, sacrifice-type and negative-consequence costs, and into 'necessary' and 'man-made' costs. In Qiu's account, modernization without cost cannot exist, so only high-cost and low-cost modernization are real options. Low-cost modernization means maximum development gain for minimum input, risk and harm. Qiu holds that modernization costs are unavoidable but controllable, and that progress and cost are interdependent, mutually constraining and mutually connected. Reducing costs raises 'modernization returns', so the best pattern is low cost, high development and high returns. Qiu presents the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as one of correcting earlier costs: Party discipline, extensive growth, ideological problems and ecological damage. Earlier mistakes such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution are counted as man-made costs. Qiu calls for cost awareness that avoids both an idealised view of modernization and a pessimistic one. Costs should be actively reduced ('cut' necessary ones, 'eliminate' unnecessary ones) and kept within what people and ecosystems can bear. Four measures are proposed: public tolerance, the degree of modernization achieved, how widely benefits are shared (linked to common prosperity), and compensation for those who bear sacrifices. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-School-style attempt to build a 'cost theory' of Chinese modernization, including its typology of costs and its account of how past errors are framed.

The philosophical logic of constructing a discourse system of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 中国特色哲学社会科学话语体系建构的哲学逻辑 Huang Hai Responding to the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to speed up building a discourse system of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, Huang Hai asks what philosophical logic should govern its construction. The article argues that the task can be understood through four pairs of dialectical categories: the one and the many, criticism and construction, the general and the particular, and the ought and the is. Each pair, in Huang's account, corresponds to a distinct problem the discourse system must face. The article opens by defining the discourse system as the outward expression of the theoretical and academic systems, built around Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It then devotes one section to each category pair, labelling them respectively the preconditional, strategic, generative and practical problems. Throughout, Huang uses discourse clusters such as Chinese modernization, a community with a shared future for mankind, shared values of all humanity and a new form of human civilization as running examples. On the one and the many, Huang holds that the single guiding principle (the "dao") is Marxism and its Chinese innovations together with fine traditional Chinese culture, from which diverse signature concepts grow. On criticism and construction, the author argues that building Chinese discourse requires dismantling the epistemology of "Western centrism", for example the equation of modernization with Westernization, while constructing independently. Huang says the Chinese modernization narrative does both by contrasting itself with Western modernization. On the general and the particular, the discourse must be commensurable with general rules of discourse production and be "understood across cultures", yet carry distinctive Chinese concepts, so that its local character gives it wider significance. Huang contrasts the shared values of all humanity with what the article calls Western "universal values". On the ought and the is, Huang treats "what to say" as the ideal content and "how to say it" as the practical expression. The author calls for unifying political, academic and popular discourse, so that the discourse has political height, theoretical depth and the warmth of everyday life. Huang concludes, citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), that building Chinese discourse and narrative systems is urgent given what the article describes as Western dominance of international discourse power. The aim is to turn institutional strengths and governance effectiveness into discursive strengths. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosophy journal frames discourse-system building through dialectical categories and the current official vocabulary of discourse power.

The historical presence of philosophy Origins and position of Hegel's theory of the history of philosophy 哲学的历史性在场 Feng Jiahui The modern idea that philosophy is inseparable from its history owes much to Hegel's Lectures on the History of Philosophy. Feng Jiahui argues that this position was not a self-evident premise for Hegel but a theoretical solution to a problem in his own development. For post-Kantian thinkers seeking a scientific, systematic philosophy, the fact that philosophy has a history was a serious challenge, and Hegel's answer is traced here through its stages. The article follows Hegel from his early Jena years to his mature system. It first examines the 1801 'Differenzschrift' and the 1801/02 lectures on logic and metaphysics, then the mid-Jena turn to the historicity of spirit and the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807). It then turns to the six lecture courses on the history of philosophy given from 1819, with discussion of Hegel's Logic, Karl Vieweg's recent reconstruction, and critics such as Fulda. Feng's central claim is that Hegel moved from asserting the supra-historical unity of philosophy to the principle of the 'agreement of history and logic'. Early on, reason was single and its system lay beyond history. Three insights then changed this: knowledge's history is constitutive of knowledge, contradiction drives thought forward dialectically, and 'spirit' covers both individual moments and the whole. The Phenomenology offered a preparatory account but, as an introduction to the system, did not settle the matter. In the mature theory, the author stresses, Hegel speaks of the 'identity' of history and logic, not their 'unity', and does not claim one-to-one correspondence. Citing Fulda, Feng reads the principle as holding at the main nodes of philosophy's history, like supporting points in a building, not at every detail. Feng concludes that Hegel founded the philosophical study of the history of philosophy, which becomes philosophy's own theoretical task, not a branch of intellectual history. The author also identifies a cost. Hegel's historicity concerns the living present, not the future, so a completed logic sits uneasily with a history of philosophy that cannot end. Either philosophy has exhausted its possibilities, or Hegel's logic is itself only a historical product. Read the original if you study Hegel's development, post-Kantian systematic philosophy or the relation between history and logic, and want a close textual account of how this principle emerged and where its limits lie.

The construction and transcendence of "moral politics": Rousseau, Hegel and Marx “道德政治”的建构与超越：卢梭、黑格尔与马克思 Zhang Dang Zhang Dang takes up the relation between morality and politics, which the article treats as a basic tension of modernity. The thesis is that Rousseau saw the separation of the two and proposed rebuilding a "moral politics", and that Hegel tried to repair the proposal with "ethical politics". On Zhang's reading, both remained trapped in the same predicament, and only Marx resolved it by moving the question from morality and will to property relations. The article, published in Philosophical Research in 2025, is organised in three parts. The first sets out why moral politics was needed, tracing Machiavelli's split between morality and politics and the positions of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau on the state of nature and the social contract. The second examines Rousseau's "general will" and his proposals on inequality, then Hegel's critique, with a side glance at Kant. The third follows Marx from his 1843 reading notes on Rousseau to the critique of political economy. Zhang argues that Rousseau located inequality and servitude in society rather than nature, but then defended property as a sacred right, which conflicts with his attack on private property. Hegel, in Zhang's account, rightly criticised Rousseau's voluntarist freedom, its link to Jacobin terror, and Kant's empty moral law. By distinguishing morality from ethical life (Sittlichkeit), Hegel made freedom concrete, but his rational state left the economic basis of the political state unexplained. Marx, Zhang says, used historical materialism to reject the premise of the individual as will, and in The German Ideology treated the state as a form through which the bourgeoisie secures its property. In Capital he separated private property based on the producer's own labour from that based on exploiting others' labour. Zhang holds that Rousseau and others blurred this distinction and so indirectly defended capitalist private property. Zhang concludes that Marx went beyond moral politics by taking the proletariat as the revolutionary subject, abolishing capitalist private property and re-establishing "individual ownership" on the basis of associated labour. In this reading Marx dissolved the split between modern morality and politics and gave a scientific guide to reducing the wealth gap and achieving real democracy and equality. Read the original if you study Marx's relation to Rousseau and Hegel, or the history of political philosophy on property, democracy and the state.

Continually dusting off the mind 不断掸去思想上的灰尘 Yue Ming This short commentary asks how Party members and cadres should deal with the ideological problems behind misconduct. Yue starts from Xi Jinping's remark that the Party's prominent problems are, at root, problems of thinking. The article argues that the current campaign of study and education on the central Eight-point Regulation is a chance for self-examination and correction, so that cadres can dust off their thinking and correct deviant behaviour. The piece is a brief exhortatory essay in a Party journal, apparently written as part of that campaign. It moves from diagnosis, which covers where ideological 'dust' comes from, to two remedies: inner steadfastness and regular criticism and self-criticism. It draws on classical Chinese sayings, an anecdote about the Yuan-dynasty scholar Xu Heng, and a passage from Mao Zedong. Yue holds that formalism, bureaucratism, shirking responsibility and the hidden, mutated forms of the 'four undesirable work styles' all come down to wavering ideals, weak awareness of the Party's purpose, distorted values and the influence of subjectivism, utilitarianism and hedonism. The first remedy is resolve of the kind Xu Heng showed in declining to pick pears from an ownerless tree: 'the pear tree has no owner, but my heart has one'. The second is criticism and self-criticism, which Yue presents, following Mao, as sweeping and washing away dust, and which calls for openness to sharp criticism. Yue concludes that style problems are at bottom problems of Party spirit. Party spirit and moral standing, in Yue's view, do not improve automatically with age, length of service or promotion, so members must keep up self-cultivation, self-restraint and self-reform. They should measure themselves against Party style, Party spirit and Party discipline to keep the political character of Communists. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party journals frame ideological self-cultivation within the Eight-point Regulation campaign.

Strategic outlook on AI empowering the transformation of higher education 人工智能赋能高等教育转型的战略前瞻 Zhang Fuqing Zhang Fuqing, writing as a university Party secretary in a newspaper commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today on 9 July 2025, asks how artificial intelligence can drive the transformation of Chinese higher education. Zhang argues that AI, the core driver of what the article calls the Fourth Industrial Revolution, is reshaping educational concepts and models. In this reading, AI-enabled higher education has become a source of competitive advantage and a key variable in moving China from a large education country to a strong one. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statements on education and AI, then proceeds through four headed sections: leading the digital transformation of higher education; reconstructing the higher education ecosystem; fostering a distinctive 'Chinese paradigm'; and steering the strategy of building China into a leading education power. It closes with role-specific recommendations for education administrators, universities, teachers and students. Zhang's central claim is that AI changes higher education at every level, and that this change should be directed by national strategy. On the ecosystem, the author points to new teaching models built on platforms such as the National Smart Education Platform for Higher Education, personalised learning, multi-dimensional and data-driven evaluation, and more refined university management. On the 'Chinese paradigm', Zhang holds that AI must serve national strategic goals, uphold the socialist orientation of education and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, and promote educational equity. The Ministry of Education's 'MOOCs in the West' programme is offered as an example of digital technology serving equity and of the advantages of the new type of whole-nation system. Zhang concludes with proposals for each actor. Administrators should draw up strategic plans, set goals and rules for research, talent training and ethical governance, and create dedicated funds. Universities should adopt an 'AI+' education system. Teachers should treat AI as a 'cognitive enhancement partner' rather than a replacement, forming an 'education triangle' with students and AI. Students should build AI literacy and data-security awareness and become 'high-level AI masters'. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university leader links AI in education to national strategy and the 2035 goal of becoming a leading education power.

Modern Japan's road to the war of aggression against China 近代日本的侵华战争之路 Zang Yunhu Published in the China Social Sciences Today on 9 July 2025, ahead of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance, this short historical commentary traces how modern Japan's aggression against China unfolded. Zang opens with Xi Jinping's description of Japan's continuous aggression as the darkest page of modern Chinese history. Zang argues that the aggression lasted more than 70 years from the 1874 invasion of Taiwan, and was most intense in the half-century of the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 and the later war of aggression. The article is a chronological survey in five stages: the twenty years before the 1894–95 war (1874–1893); the twenty years after it (1895–1914); the First World War and the years to 1930; and the period from partial to full-scale war (1931–1945). It follows Japanese actions towards Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands, Korea, Shandong and north-east China, and closes with the Chinese resistance. Zang's central claim is that the 1874 landing in Taiwan, Japan's first overseas military action, began a continuous line of aggression, even though the 1871 Sino-Japanese Treaty of Amity was an equal treaty. In this account, the annexation of Ryukyu, the 1890 "line of interest" doctrine centred on Korea, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki shaped a continental policy and reversed the relationship between the two countries. The Twenty-One Demands, the 1927 Tanaka-era policy of separating Manchuria and Mongolia, and the invasions of 1931 and 1937 are presented as stages of the same course. Zang credits the Communist Party-led national united front and the rear-area resistance with a pivotal role, and describes China as the main Eastern theatre of the Second World War. The 14-year resistance is called the first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times and a turning point towards national rejuvenation. Zang calls for renewed study of this history and its lessons. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the official Chinese periodisation of Japanese aggression, 1874–1945.

The CPC-led resistance behind enemy lines as seen in Japanese private sources 日本民间资料所见中国共产党领导的敌后抗战 Zhang Zhan This short commentary asks what privately held Japanese records reveal about the Chinese Communist Party's leadership of the war of resistance behind Japanese lines. Zhang argues that regimental and battalion histories, veterans' memoirs and wartime interviews show how Japanese officers themselves explained their failure, and that they placed the Party's mobilisation of the people at the centre. The article draws on Japanese military and private materials, including an internal army document titled The Operations of the Chinese Army, statements by staff officers such as Inomoto Kumao and Matsumura Tomokatsu, the memoir of Tokutsu Junichi, a regimental history, and a lecture by Prince Mikasa. It moves from Japanese misjudgements of Chinese resistance, to the role of the敌后 (behind-the-lines) front, to the contest for popular support. Zhang reports that Japanese officers widely believed China was a divided nation lacking national consciousness, and expected a short war. According to the sources cited, the Japanese army later conceded that events followed the Communist account of a three-stage protracted war, and that occupied land became 'Communist territory'. Zhang stresses accounts attributing Communist strength to ties with the people: a North China Area Army estimate of at least 500,000 unarmed civilians aiding the Communist forces, Tokutsu's 'fish and water' image, and Prince Mikasa's contrast between Communist discipline and Japanese plunder. Zhang concludes that these Japanese sources, read as the opponents' own testimony, show that winning popular support decided the outcome and that the Party-led resistance behind enemy lines changed the course of the war. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the Japanese-language testimony that Chinese historians now use in studying the anti-Japanese war.

The Communist Party of China's role as the mainstay was the key to victory in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression 中国共产党的中流砥柱作用是中国人民抗日战争胜利的关键 Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance) Committee Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression, this commentary from the Central Party School's governing committee takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that the Communist Party's role as the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) was the key to victory. It also treats victory as the Party's own triumph in that role. The authors present this as a settled historical conclusion and as a basis for upholding the Party's overall leadership today. The text is organised in five sections, each naming one source of the Party's decisive role. These are political leadership and sound strategy, the anti-Japanese national united front, the great spirit of resistance, standing on the side of justice and human progress, and Party building. Each section ends by drawing lessons for the present. These are tied to the Two Establishes, the Two Upholds and Chinese modernization. The authors argue that the Party first identified the contradiction with Japanese imperialism as the principal one. It then developed the strategy of protracted war and opened the battlefields behind enemy lines. They cite figures: Party-led forces fought over 125,000 engagements, wiped out 1.714 million Japanese and puppet troops, and built 19 base areas with nearly 100 million people. They say the Party promoted peaceful resolution of the Xi'an Incident and the second Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. It held to "resist, unite, progress" against three anti-Communist high tides. In their account, patriotism-centred national spirit, a "cultural army" and the Party's internationalist stance connected China's front to the global anti-fascist war. They add that the Yan'an rectification movement and the Party-building "great project" of 1939 made the Party cohesive enough to lead. The authors conclude that the Party's leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and its greatest institutional advantage. They call for the Party to keep strengthening its political leadership and the united front, to carry forward the spirit of resistance, and to reject distortions of Second World War history and hegemonism. They also call for continued full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which they say has found a "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how Party-school theorists link the memory of the anti-Japanese war to current claims about Party leadership and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

Making red resources the spiritual engine of the "great ideological and political course" 让红色资源成为“大思政课”的精神引擎 Zhang Junzheng Zhang asks how "red resources" (the material and spiritual legacy of the Communist Party's history) can be built into university ideological and political education. Citing the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference in September 2024, the author argues that doing so serves the university mission of training people for the Party and the country. It is also presented as necessary for cultivating a new generation suited to the new era. The short commentary has three parts: the logic of integrating red culture into the "great ideological and political course", the features that make the fit possible, and practical paths for universities. It is aimed at university administrators and Party committees rather than at theorists. On logic, Zhang describes four pairings: material with spiritual, theory with practice, historical moment with present events, and inner with outer. On features, the author finds that red resources and the course share a common basis in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, a common cultural root in traditional Chinese culture, and similar educational functions. The practical section proposes a sound institutional system with unified Party committee leadership, better coordination across stages of schooling and between school, family and society, fresh narratives that bring in the "four histories", and richer carriers such as ceremonies, campus-history materials and local red-culture tours. Zhang concludes that red resources, used through these institutional and educational mechanisms, can strengthen students' political sensitivity and ideological commitment and help guard against major security risks. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a university Party official frames red-resource education and its practical implementation.

Building a new pattern of collaborative education between ideological-political courses and curriculum-based ideological-political education 构建思政课程与课程思政协同育人新格局 Hu Xihua This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, asks how university ideological-political theory courses and the ideological-political content of other subjects can work together as one education effort. Hu Xihua argues that the two are close in task and aligned in goal, and that coordinating them is both a requirement of the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and a practical response to current problems in ideological and political education. The piece first defines the terms. Ideological-political courses are the main channel of ideological and political education in universities. Curriculum-based ideological-political education means weaving such elements into specialist courses so that knowledge transmission and value guidance coincide. It then sets out four lines of action, quoting Xi Jinping repeatedly in support. First, Hu calls for the Party's overall leadership: university Party committees should take principal responsibility, with Party secretaries and presidents leading in the classroom, and should link departments and institutions to share resources. Second, teachers should form diverse collaborative teams of theory teachers, specialist teachers, industry experts and model workers. Such teams would map each specialist topic to ideological elements and draw a "concentric circle" of shared goals. Third, Hu proposes a new discourse system that moves from "embedding" to "internal growth". It would translate political language into academic and everyday language and use short video and livestreaming. Fourth, Hu proposes joint platforms with industry, such as enterprise laboratories and industry colleges, working through courses, cooperation and practice. Hu concludes that this pattern would tie ideological education to regional economic and social development and form a mutually beneficial education ecosystem. The author presents it as meeting the needs of the new era and of training well-rounded talent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance on ideological-political education is turned into institutional measures for universities.

The key to socialism with Chinese characteristics lies in the "Two Integrations" 中国特色社会主义的关键在于“两个结合” Luo Wendong Lü Handong Luo Wendong and Lü Handong take up Xi Jinping's claim, made at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, that what makes Chinese socialism distinctive is its Chinese characteristics, and that the key to those characteristics is the Two Integrations. The article, published in Shandong Social Sciences in 2025, argues that the Two Integrations are the necessary path, the greatest magic weapon and the continuing requirement for opening up and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats the Two Integrations as the necessary path, setting out how they provide the theoretical cornerstone, how the first integration (Marxism with China's concrete realities) gives the system its content in each era, and how the second (Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture) deepens its cultural roots. The second part tests the claim that the Two Integrations are the greatest magic weapon against four components: path, theoretical system, institutions and culture. The third part draws forward-looking requirements for the present. The authors argue that socialism with Chinese characteristics is neither a copy of Marx's templates, of Soviet practice nor of Western modernization, but a creation produced by combining Marxism's basic tenets with Chinese conditions and culture. On the path, they cite Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping against copying foreign models. On theory, they present the Two Integrations as a weapon against dogmatism, empiricism, nihilism and restorationism. On institutions, they trace the people's congress system, political consultation and regional ethnic autonomy to traditional ideas such as people-centred governance and "great unity". They add that the integrations consolidate Chinese cultural subjectivity, which they describe as damaged in the modern semi-colonial period. For the present, the authors call for self-confidence and self-reliance in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and for building an autonomous Chinese system of knowledge. They also call for openness in pursuing Chinese modernization, whose five features they link to traditional concepts such as "harmony between humanity and nature", and for creating a new form of human civilization. In their account, this requires both keeping to fundamental principles and innovating. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Party theory connects the Two Integrations to Chinese modernization, with the leadership quotations that support it.

The historical basis of production and the logical beginning of exchange: Marx's value-form theory in the process of research and the process of presentation 生产的历史基础与交换的逻辑开端：基于马克思价值形式理论研究与叙述过程的探讨 Li Qiankun Li Qiankun takes up a dispute over whether production or exchange has priority in Marx's critique of political economy. Since the second half of the twentieth century, Li says, Western left theory has given exchange discourse logical priority and has tried to replace or reject Marxism's categories of production. The article argues that in his research Marx found production to be the historical basis of exchange, but in presenting the capitalist mode of production in Capital he made exchange the logical beginning. Together these two processes make up the distinctive method of his value-form theory. The article opens with the Western currents Li has in mind: Western Marxism and Western Marxology, the New Reading of Marx, the New Dialectic, Uno school and regulation theory, Habermas and Baudrillard. It then follows Marx's treatment of money from On the Jewish Question and the 1844 manuscripts through the Grundrisse, the 1859 Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, and the 1861–63 and 1863–65 manuscripts. A final section reads the opening of Capital Volume 1 and closes by discussing Heinrich's position. Li's central claim is that Marx's early explanations of money rested on exchange, private property and the division of labour. In the Grundrisse and the 1859 work, Li argues, he had not yet joined labour-power and surplus-value theory to value and money, and still confused exchange-value with value. Only with the theory of average profit and prices of production in 1861–63 did he explain money from the total process of capitalist production, since the commodity as a product of capital contains paid and unpaid labour whose quantity cannot be directly measured. Li holds that this is why value must take the money form. In Capital, Marx begins with exchange because the commodity form is the cell form of bourgeois society, because value and money can only be explained through value-form analysis, and because the analysis of exchange leads to labour-power as the special commodity behind money becoming capital. Li adds that this order of presentation is a 'circle' that presupposes the earlier grasp of production. Li concludes that Marx unites the logical and the historical: production brings contradiction, struggle and historical change, while exchange brings formal norms and synchronic structure. Both aspects, Li says, belong to the capitalist mode of production. Heinrich, in Li's reading, keeps the logic of presentation but drops the historical dimension and the foundational place of production. Li contends that left theories starting from exchange risk confirming capitalism's validity and dissolving history. Read the original if you work on value-form theory, the New Reading of Marx or the research/presentation distinction, and want a close textual account of how Marx's treatment of money developed.

Critique of the logic of capital in Marx's theory of world history and its contemporary significance A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义 Wang Xinsheng Zhang Jianrong Wang Xinsheng and Zhang Jianrong ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society and how it can be overcome. They propose a perspective that reads Capital and its manuscripts through Marx's theory of world history. Their thesis is that Marx's critique of the logic of capital unites the criticism of an 'old world history' with the discovery of a 'new' one, and that this critique keeps its significance for the present. The article has three main parts. The first traces how the logic of capital came to shape world history: its preconditions in primitive accumulation and the separation of labourers from the conditions of labour, its expansion through the world market, its historical limits and its historical effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique. The third draws out four contemporary implications: for understanding digital capitalism, for building socialism with Chinese characteristics, for exploring modernization paths and for the free and all-round development of the human being. The authors argue that Marx's critique is dialectical and immanent. It does not defend capital as eternal, as classical economists do, and it does not criticise it from outside, as the utopian socialists do. It has three strands: a critique of reality (the abstraction and fetishism through which relations between people appear as relations between things), a historical critique (capital's own barriers, such as the falling profit rate and crises of overproduction) and a critique of values (capital's reduction of people to one-sided, alienated beings). For the authors, the contradictions of capital also generate the material and social conditions for communism as a new world history. On this basis they hold that digital capitalism leaves the exploitative essence of capital unchanged. They also argue that capital has a civilising side as a factor of production and a destructive side as a relation of production. The authors conclude that the critique of capital's logic is a 'pathology of capital' with world-historical meaning. They call for regulating its negative aspects and making full use of its positive ones in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for recognising that capitalist modernization is not the only route to modernity. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based Chinese account of how Marx's world-history theory is used to link the critique of capital to digital capitalism, the regulation of capital in China and alternative modernization.

State-owned enterprises and the development of new quality productive forces: theoretical logic, practical difficulties and paths forward 国有企业发展新质生产力：理论逻辑、现实困境与路径选择 Tang Jijun Wang Xiaolei Tang Jijun and Wang Xiaolei ask how state-owned enterprises (SOEs) should develop new quality productive forces, a topic they say existing research has treated mainly at the macro level and not systematically at the level of the firm. Their thesis is that SOEs have strong reasons and capacities to lead this process, but they face obstacles in original innovation, institutions and the layout of the state sector that must be removed through further deepening of reform. The article has three parts. It first sets out the theoretical logic of SOE involvement from four angles: forming production relations suited to new quality productive forces, the missions assigned to SOEs, raising total factor productivity, and strengthening international competitiveness. It then identifies three practical difficulties, and finally proposes three paths, drawing on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and on Xi Jinping's remarks on new production relations. On the theory, the authors argue that frontier technologies are too costly and uncertain for small firms and often for large private ones, so SOEs, with their capital strength, reform experience and policy support, should lead the change in production relations. They link the task to national security, high-level scientific self-reliance, the role of SOEs as 'chain leaders' of modern industrial systems and regional coordination. On the difficulties, they cite weak original innovation (inadequate basic research spending, weak incentives, closed innovation models), imperfect governance, error-tolerance, evaluation and investment mechanisms, and an unreasonable layout marked by unclear core business, over-broad diversification, thin presence in emerging fields and east–west imbalance. The proposed paths are to make SOEs the 'source' of original technology through innovation consortia, higher R&D spending and better incentives; to embed Party leadership in modern corporate governance while building error-tolerance and mission-based evaluation; and to optimise the state-sector layout by focusing on core business, acting as chain leaders, investing in emerging and future industries, and promoting east–west cooperation. The authors also warn against narrowing or over-extending the concept of new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented account of how Chinese economists see the SOE role in technological upgrading and the problems they identify in SOE governance and layout.

Empowering the development of new quality productive forces through state-owned enterprises: theoretical basis, historical experience and practical paths 以国有企业赋能新质生产力发展:理论基础、历史经验与实践路径 Lin Pan Lin Pan asks how state-owned enterprises (SOEs) can drive the development of new quality productive forces, the Party's term for advanced productive forces defined by high technology, high efficiency and high quality. The article argues that SOEs, because the state owns or controls their capital, can follow political goals and take on strategic, non-routine tasks. In Lin's view they should therefore serve as the main force and the "source" and incubator of new quality productive forces. Lin contrasts this with earlier studies that stress private firms' innovative drive. The article has three main parts. The first sets out the theoretical basis in Marx and Engels on state-run economic organisation, and in Lenin's and Stalin's Soviet practice of state enterprise. The second reviews the history of technology absorption and innovation in Chinese SOEs: the "156 projects" of the 1950s, the reform-era policy of "trading market access for technology", and the later shift to indigenous innovation. The third diagnoses current problems and proposes reforms at the macro, meso and micro levels. Lin reads Marx and Engels as expecting the state eventually to take over the direction of production once productive forces outgrow joint-stock management. Lin treats the Soviet SOE system as a successful mechanism for concentrating resources and for technological innovation before the 1970s. For China, Lin cites the First Tractor Plant in Luoyang as a case of Soviet technology being localised. Lin lists three present weaknesses: the new-type whole-nation system is not fully used, industrial chains are poorly coordinated, and internal organisation is weak, including Party-building and business work running as "two skins" and shortages of skilled talent. Lin also admits monopoly and principal–agent problems. Because new quality productive forces call for new relations of production, the article proposes institutional innovation at three levels. At the macro level, it urges stronger legal and policy backing for industry–university–research cooperation, "patient capital" and "SOE+" innovation consortia. At the meso level, it wants SOEs to act as "chain leaders" in strategic emerging and future industries and to promote digitalisation and data circulation. At the micro level, it calls for integrating Party leadership with corporate governance, and for talent evaluation and income distribution that reward innovation. Lin concludes that SOEs are both the backbone for cultivating new quality productive forces and the main arena where they take effect. Lin adds that leading does not mean doing all research in-house: SOEs should be innovation platforms that coordinate other actors. Lin calls for an "effective market" and a "capable government" to work together, backed by policy across basic research, funding, talent, finance and intellectual property. Read the original if you want a state-sector-centred account of new quality productive forces, with Soviet and Chinese historical cases and a detailed list of reform measures.

The basic contradictions of society and the driving forces of social development in the intelligent era 智能时代的社会基本矛盾与社会发展动力 Sun Weiping Sun Weiping asks how historical materialism can explain the basic contradictions of a society being reshaped by artificial intelligence, and what those contradictions imply for social development. The article argues that intelligent productive forces are outgrowing capitalist relations of production inherited from the industrial age. In Sun's account, the resulting mismatch between productive forces and relations of production, and between the superstructure and the economic base, is a fetter on the intelligent society. Resolving it is presented as the fundamental driving force of development. The article has four parts. It first distinguishes 'technological social formations' (fishing and hunting, agricultural, industrial, intelligent) from economic social formations, and describes intelligent productive forces and the intelligent society. It then examines how relations of production lag behind these forces, and how the superstructure lags behind the economic base in ideology, governance, ethics, law and culture. The last part sets out measures for change, and a short conclusion follows. Sun's first move is to propose that communist society could be built on the foundation of the intelligent society. Data, algorithms and computing power are non-rivalrous and shareable, which Sun reads as favouring public ownership. Sun also points to demand-driven planning and the reduction of labour time as further links. The second move is a diagnosis of contradiction. Private ownership and the logic of capital restrict the development of intelligent productive forces through technological monopoly. Human–machine competition produces a 'new alienation'. Digital and intelligence divides produce technological unemployment and a 'useless class'. Algorithms are said to become an ideological machine, to obscure digital democracy and to risk 'machine-enforced governance'. Law and ethics also lag behind the claimed 'subject' status of intelligent robots. The third move is a programme of transformation. It would advance AI technology while keeping the principle that 'the human being is the end'. It calls for a new public ownership of digital means of production (through data shareholding, data remuneration and digital dividends) and open-source, publicly supervised algorithms. It also proposes distribution and a division of labour suited to this ownership, a decentralised participatory digital democracy, regulation of giant firms, and a tripartite system of rights and responsibilities for designers, algorithms and users. Sun concludes that productive forces should keep developing, relations of production and the superstructure should be adjusted accordingly, and the basic contradictions should be turned into momentum for building the intelligent society and laying the ground for communism. Sun stresses that this is a long, complex undertaking. Even in socialist China, with public ownership established, industrial-era relations and superstructure still need deep adjustment, and the concrete form of new public ownership of digital resources remains to be explored. Read the original if you want a Marxist, historical-materialist framework for AI, including its proposals on digital public ownership and governance, as published in a leading Chinese journal.

The historical position of China's War of Resistance in the world anti-fascist war 中国抗战在世界反法西斯战争中的历史地位 Wang Meiping Writing in a newspaper commentary of July 2025, Wang Meiping asks what place China's War of Resistance against Japan holds in the Second World War. Wang argues that it was an important part of the world anti-fascist war and, after the Pacific War began, its main Eastern theatre. In Wang's account, Cold War structures led the international community to overlook this role for a long time. The article follows three stages: the local resistance after the 18 September 1931 Incident, the full-scale resistance from 7 July 1937, and the period after Pearl Harbor in December 1941. For each stage Wang considers what China's fight cost Japan, how it constrained Japanese strategy, and how it affected the wider anti-fascist camp. Japanese official statistics on casualties and military spending are cited throughout. Wang's central claim is that total war cannot be won by military superiority alone. It also requires exhausting an opponent's strategic resources and will to fight until it has "nothing to fight with" and "no one willing to fight". On this reading, China, though weak, used its vast territory, large population, mobilisation capacity and resistance spirit to wear Japan down. Wang says China opened the earliest anti-fascist front, was the only Eastern front until December 1941, and tied down over 80 per cent of Japan's army before the Pacific War and 50 to 60 per cent afterwards. Wang adds that this fighting also deterred a Japanese attack on the Soviet Union and prompted Britain and the United States to aid China. Wang concludes that China's fourteen years of resistance, as the main Eastern theatre, made an indelible contribution to human morality and world peace, and to the postwar international order. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the current Chinese historiographical case for China's role in the Second World War, together with the Japanese statistics Wang uses.

The contribution of the Eastern main battlefield deserves fair assessment 东方主战场的贡献应获公正评价 Nadia Helmy This short commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by Nadia Helmy, an Egyptian political scientist and Asia specialist. Writing in the 80th anniversary year of victory in 2025, Helmy argues that China's role as the main battlefield of the East in the Second World War has received too little international recognition and should be assessed fairly. Helmy opens with a visit to the Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance against Japanese Aggression at the Marco Polo Bridge in Beijing. The text then summarises the course of the war: the 1931 Mukden Incident, the puppet state of Manchukuo, the full-scale war from 1937, the Nanjing Massacre and Unit 731, the Lytton Report, the Potsdam Declaration and Japan's surrender in 1945. The author's central claim is that China's contribution and sacrifice, put by the article at over 35 million military and civilian casualties over fourteen years, were in some respects greater than those of the United States and Britain. Helmy contends that Western states used the war's outcomes for their own interests and overlooked China's part, and that Japanese textbooks play down or delete the history of the invasion. Chinese scholars, and China specialists worldwide, are therefore urged to restore China's real contribution and step outside what Helmy calls a US and Western ideological narrative. Helmy cites Xi Jinping's May 2025 call in Russia to uphold a correct view of the history of the Second World War. Helmy concludes that scholars should remind the world of China's sacrifices, that Global South countries have reason to take China as a model, and that the war's spirit still inspires efforts toward the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The author calls on all countries to learn from history and to cooperate in building a peaceful, mutually beneficial world. Read the original if you want an example of how a foreign scholar's commentary on the anti-fascist war is presented in Chinese academic media.

Placing China's War of Resistance memory within global war history 构建全球战争史中的中国抗战记忆 Rana Mitter This short commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by the British historian Rana Mitter. It asks why China's War of Resistance against Japan remains one of the least understood parts of the Second World War in the West, and how that can change. Mitter argues that Western scholarship has improved markedly over the past decade, but that the war is not yet fully part of Western understanding of global conflict. Mitter first gives reasons for the neglect: the war has received too little attention in Western countries, and the sources are mainly in Chinese or Japanese, languages that are little studied in Europe and North America. He then surveys scholarly progress since the 1990s, naming Ezra Vogel, Stephen MacKinnon and Hans van de Ven, and mentions his own 2013 book Forgotten Ally: China's World War II 1937–1945. A central trend Mitter identifies is placing the war in a global-history frame, stressing its position in the world order and comparing China's experience with that of other countries. He sees two openings for future work. One is access to Chinese archive-based research, such as that in the journal Studies of the War of Resistance against Japan, which non-Chinese readers still struggle to use. The other is the post-war period: Asian reconstruction is far less studied than European, and Mitter points to growing interest in international institutions, above all the United Nations, in which Roosevelt's 'Four Policemen' idea gave China a key role. Mitter concludes that comparative social history is a promising direction. He holds that research should bring out both what is distinctive about China's wartime experience and what it shares with other regions, and that this experience should be known globally. Read the original if you want a brief, author-sketched map of Western scholarship on the Sino-Japanese War and the research gaps a leading historian sees.

The global significance of the main Eastern theatre 东方主战场的全球意义 Alpha Mohamed Jalloh This short commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by Alpha Mohamed Jalloh of Sierra Leone, written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the World Anti-Fascist War (2025). Jalloh argues that the Eastern theatre, centred on China, was a decisive front of the Second World War, even though historical attention has focused mainly on Europe. The piece first describes the Chinese theatre as the longest-running and largest in Asia, beginning with the 18 September 1931 incident. It then assesses the theatre's global significance from two angles and closes with remarks on historical memory and present-day peace. Jalloh states that Chinese forces and civilians fought almost alone against Japan until the Pacific War began in 1941. In the article's account, Japan committed over half its troops in China and used up resources meant for other Asia-Pacific areas, which bought the Allies time to deploy, re-equip and counterattack. The two angles are a long-term buffer against fascism in Asia, which forced Japan into a war of attrition, and a catalyst for Allied cooperation. On the second point, Jalloh says China's resistance laid the basis for the alliance with the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union and led to China's role as a founding UN member and permanent Security Council member. Jalloh concludes that remembering this history supports peace, mutual respect and multilateral cooperation, and calls on the international community to respect historical truth. In the article's view, belittling the contributions of China and other non-Western countries erodes collective memory and global solidarity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a scholar from Africa frames China's wartime role for a Chinese audience in the anniversary year.

Marx's endogenous money thought A comprehensive discussion based on money types and theoretical structure 马克思的内生货币思想 Wang Yao Marx praised Ricardo's value theory but repeatedly criticised his monetary theory. Wang asks what Marx's own theory of money was and why it diverged from Ricardo's quantity theory. The article argues that Marx built an endogenous money theory, in which prices determine the quantity of money, drawing on the Banking School rather than on Ricardo. It holds that Marx distinguished metallic, credit and fiat money, and that endogenous and quantity-theory logics apply to different types. The article first traces the intellectual sources: the Currency School versus Banking School dispute, the earlier bullionist controversy, and the quantity theory and endogenous theory as modern schools. It then examines the money types of Marx's time (metallic money, credit money, and the question of whether sterling was fiat money), using the pound's history from 1694. Finally it reconstructs the theoretical structure in three parts: the endogenous money equation, the real bills doctrine and the law of reflux. Wang relies on close reading of Marx's texts and on writers such as Schumpeter, Blaug, Hodgson and Shaikh. Wang's central claim is that the same currency can follow different laws under different regimes. Sterling was convertible, and so endogenous, in 1694–1797, 1821–1914 and 1925–31, but exogenous and fiat in 1797–1821, 1914–25 and after 1931. Ricardo wrote during the 1797–1821 suspension of convertibility, which explains his preference for the quantity theory. Marx wrote during the gold standard's height. Wang reads Marx's equation PQ/V = M as running from prices to money, and reads his treatment of real bills and reflux as linking money to capital movement. On this reading Marx anticipated Keynes's liquidity trap through his remark that credit-based money turns into metal-based money in crises. Wang concludes that Marx's criticism of Ricardo may be one-sided, given the different monetary regimes each faced, and that Marx did not clearly count bank deposits as money. Wang nonetheless sees Marx's endogenous framework as close to post-Keynesian thinking and relevant to China, where deposit money dominates M2 and the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference put social financing before money supply. Money is held to play a passive, secondary role in economic fluctuations. Read the original if you study Marx's monetary theory, the Currency–Banking School debate, or the historical grounding of endogenous money.

Major theoretical innovations in the basic socialist economic system since the new era 新时代以来社会主义基本经济制度的重大理论创新 Huang Kainan Huang Kainan asks what theoretical innovations lie behind the way the basic socialist economic system has been extended since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that the three-part system formulated by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) rests on three theoretical "combinations", each of which reconciles positions that earlier theory treated as opposed. Huang presents these as major results of Xi Jinping's economic thought and as building blocks for an autonomous Chinese economics. After an introduction reviewing existing research on the system's content, evolution and advantages, the article devotes one section to each combination. The first concerns a public-ownership-based ownership structure and the market economy. The second concerns the labour theory of value and the regulation and guidance of the healthy development of capital. The third concerns an efficient market and a capable government. A short conclusion lists directions for further work. On ownership, Huang contends that both traditional Marxist economics (which sees no commodity economy under public ownership) and Western mainstream economics (which makes private property a precondition of markets) are overcome. In the primary stage of socialism, public ownership has a dual character, non-commodity and commodity, and markets need only clearly defined trading rights, not private ownership. The mechanisms are state-enterprise reform, rural collective property reform and the Two Unwaverings. On capital, Huang holds that only living labour creates value, but capital may share in distribution. Returns that compensate for risk, especially "residual risk" under Knightian uncertainty, are legitimate. Returns from monopoly control of working conditions are not, which Huang takes as grounds for antitrust action, a focus on the real economy and a financing structure matched to risk. On government and market, Huang argues that markets evolve and are partly built by government. Government's role extends to industrial policy and strategic planning. The two are said to combine in addressing scarce, idle, newly created and shared resources. Huang concludes that socialist market economy, based mainly on public ownership, can avoid the disorder that private capital's pursuit of partial interests causes in capitalist market economies. It is also said to unify micro-level and macro-level efficiency. The article calls its own treatment preliminary. It proposes studying how the three innovations are logically connected and how a high-standard socialist market economy evolves. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese economists theorise the compatibility of public ownership, the labour theory of value and market mechanisms.

The role of data as a factor of production in economic growth at the stage of new quality productive forces 新质生产力阶段数据要素在经济增长中的作用 Zhang Xiaoxi Zhang Xiaoxi asks how data, now treated as a fifth factor of production after land, labour, capital and technology, drives growth under new quality productive forces. The article argues that data reshapes traditional production modes and supplies a new source of growth, as the economy shifts from resource-driven to innovation-driven expansion. The short article moves in four steps: the economic characteristics of data, the mechanisms through which data empowers growth, the main obstacles to its use, and policy recommendations. Its examples include manufacturing, agriculture, finance, medicine and retail, and the regional cases of Guizhou, Zhejiang and Shenzhen. Zhang identifies three traits of data: marginal cost close to zero, non-rivalry and non-excludability, and network effects with increasing returns to scale. Because of these traits, Zhang holds, the use value of data far exceeds its ownership value, so returns should be distributed by use rather than ownership. Growth then works through higher productive efficiency, faster innovation, upgrading towards knowledge-intensive industries, and narrower regional gaps through an integrated national data market. The obstacles listed are data silos, privacy and security risks, an immature data market with weak pricing, and a shortage of skilled personnel. Zhang recommends a unified national data market with trading and pricing rules, a dedicated data protection law and privacy-computing technologies, investment in 5G and Internet of Things infrastructure and a national big-data platform, new data-science programmes and vocational training, and digital-economy demonstration zones in central and western regions. Read the original if you want a brief policy-oriented overview of how Chinese economists link data to new quality productive forces.

Dual drivers, dual effects and dual-dimension institutions in developing new quality productive forces 发展新质生产力的双重驱动、双面效应与双维制度 Hu Lei Hu Lei takes up a gap in the growing literature on new quality productive forces: what drives their development, what effects they have, and what institutions should steer them. The article argues that their development is propelled by two forces, an internal technological one and an external institutional one. It also argues that it produces two-sided effects, creative and destructive, and therefore calls for a matching pair of institutional arrangements, one that encourages innovation and one that controls risk. The article opens with Xi Jinping's 2023–2024 statements on new quality productive forces and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then has three sections. The first sets out the technological and institutional logics of development. The second analyses creative and destructive effects. The third proposes technological and institutional innovation. Hu draws throughout on Marx's Capital and the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, as well as on Schumpeter's notion of creative destruction. On the drivers, Hu describes an internal chain of technological innovation, qualitative change in the factors of production, and industrial upgrading. An external chain runs from institutional reform to new relations of production to new quality productive forces, following the historical-materialist law that relations of production must fit the productive forces. On the effects, the creative side comprises new modes of production (data, platforms, digital capital), new industries and new jobs. The destructive side comprises investment bubbles, income polarisation by region, between capital and labour and among workers, and the displacement of jobs by machines. Hu also draws on Marx's account of machinery under capitalism to argue that China must prevent development from being trapped in the logic of capital valorisation. Hu proposes a mechanism for "dual-dimension co-evolution" of institutions. To maximise creative effects, the article calls for a new-type whole-nation system, a high-standard market system, distribution according to factors and expanded consumption. To limit destructive effects, it calls for orderly replacement of old industries (establish the new before breaking the old), "patient capital" with curbs on disorderly capital expansion, an employment-first policy, and stronger protection of workers' rights. Hu concludes that technology and institutions must advance together so that development serves the people rather than capital. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy treatment of new quality productive forces that links Xi's formulations to classical texts and to concrete policy proposals on innovation, capital and employment.

Revisiting the mercantilist and physiocratic views of wealth and their subject Starting from "Private property and labour" in Notebook III of the Paris Manuscripts 再论重商主义和重农学派的财富观及其主体之思 Huang Zhijun Huang Zhijun takes up the section "Private property and labour" in Notebook III of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. There Marx, following Adam Smith, treats the mercantilists as placing labour outside wealth, the physiocrats as moving labour into wealth as its subjective essence, and Smith as making general labour the universal essence. Huang calls this a widely accepted "strong logic" of transition and argues that it is too simplified and labelled. Going back to the mercantilist and physiocratic texts, Huang proposes a "weak logic" instead: labour is a subjective element of wealth in mercantilism, and a subjective component, not the subjective essence, in physiocracy. The article has three parts. The first re-examines mercantilism on money and wealth, on circulation and wealth, and on the forms of existence of people in the mercantilist age, drawing on Smith, Schumpeter, Marx, William Stafford, Thomas Mun and Fernand Braudel. The second turns to Quesnay and physiocracy, covering their view of the nature of wealth, the composition of wealth through the "net product", and the understanding of the subject, including the classes of the Tableau économique. A conclusion then assesses traditional histories of political economy, Marx's early and late views, and the link between views of wealth and ways of human existence. On mercantilism, Huang argues that Smith's label of "confusing money with wealth" fits only some early writers. Citing Schumpeter, Stafford and Mun, Huang holds that later mercantilists located the source of wealth in manufacture and production, so labour was already an internal element. On physiocracy, Huang follows Marx in crediting it with moving the study of surplus value into production, and sees a tension between declaring labour the essence of wealth and treating labour as an element of land. Huang's reading of Quesnay is that land remains the sole source of wealth. Agricultural labour only shapes natural products, and agricultural labour is therefore the subjective component, not the subjective essence, of wealth. Huang concludes that Marx's 1844 judgements still relied on Smith, because Marx had not yet developed his theories of value and surplus value. In Capital and its manuscripts, Marx divides mercantilism into early and late phases and credits physiocracy more accurately. Huang also criticises Rosenberg's history of economic thought for repeating Smith's picture and for reading the physiocratic view of value as labour-created. Huang adds that the mercantilist age had varied modes of human existence, while physiocracy tied the subject to land and agriculture, which modern industry would negate. Read the original if you study the history of political economy, Marx's early economic reading of his predecessors, or the Smithian framing of mercantilism and physiocracy.

Building a historical narrative of the Eastern main theatre cannot wait 建立东方主战场历史叙事刻不容缓 Zhang Sheng Writing in a newspaper commentary on the eve of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance and the world anti-fascist war (2025), Zhang Sheng argues that China urgently needs its own historical narrative of the Eastern main theatre. Zhang holds that Western narratives have long made China's war effort nearly invisible, and that this shapes how the war is remembered. The piece opens with the Orientalist tradition traced to Herodotus and then turns to the Indian–Burmese–western Yunnan campaigns after Pearl Harbor. It recounts the Chinese Expeditionary Force in Burma in 1942, British mistrust of Chinese troops, the death of Dai Anlan and the later counter-offensive of 1943–44. It then contrasts Churchill's memoirs with Japanese military postwar accounts. Zhang's central move is to show that Churchill's six-volume memoirs, begun in 1948, play down China. Zhang cites his remark about the loss of two Chinese divisions and his brief treatment of the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, Zhanggufeng and Nomonhan. Because Roosevelt had died and Stalin left no memoirs, Zhang says, Churchill controlled the narrative, and China was made to 'disappear'. Against this, Zhang cites the Japanese Defence Agency's history, which treats the Pacific and Burma campaigns as an extension of the war on China and records the strength of Chinese forces. Zhang also cites Hans van de Ven's criticism of Western-centrism. Zhang concludes, citing Xi Jinping's statements on the Eastern main theatre and China's decisive role, that building an autonomous narrative is now pressing. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese historians argue against Western accounts of the Second World War.

China's War of Resistance and its global contribution 中国抗战的世界性贡献 Gao Fujin Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (2025), this newspaper commentary asks what China's war contributed to the world anti-fascist struggle. Gao argues that China opened the main Eastern theatre, tied down Japan's army and so made a major contribution to Allied victory. The piece first sets out the military case for China's role as the main Eastern battlefield, using casualty figures and troop-deployment statistics. It then turns to assessments from abroad, citing Roosevelt, Marshal Chuikov, Russian and British scholars and the British press in 2005. Gao contends that some Western scholars, shaped by "Western-centrism", deny the Chinese theatre's significance. Against this, the author reports that China fought the longest and began the world's first anti-fascist front. By the author's figures, Japan kept up to 94 per cent of its army in China before the Pacific War and still about 70 per cent afterwards, with over 2.8 million Japanese troops committed in China. Gao credits the protracted war led by the Communist Party with wrecking Japan's plans to strike north against the Soviet Union and south into Southeast Asia, and cites a 1943 Japanese North China Area Army report on Communist-led forces as enemy corroboration. Gao concludes that China raised the banner of the world anti-fascist war first and gave strong support to the Allies. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese narrative on the Eastern theatre and the foreign testimonies it marshals.

China's War of Resistance holds an important place in the world anti-fascist war 中国抗战在世界反法西斯战争中具有重要地位 Zhu Chengshan Marking the 80th anniversary of Japan's surrender in 1945, this newspaper commentary responds to claims that still circulate about the Second World War: a "Western-determinist" view, a "European main theatre" thesis, and the idea that the United States contributed most to victory. Zhu Chengshan argues that these views deliberately downplay the Eastern main theatre, and that China's War of Resistance against Japan held an indispensable strategic place in the world anti-fascist war. The piece has three parts. It first presents China's resistance as the opening of the world anti-fascist war, beginning in north-east China in 1931. It then defines the Chinese theatre as the Eastern main theatre, and finally examines how China's war undermined the fascist powers' global strategy. Zhu's central argument rests on duration, scale and strategic effect. He says China fought for 14 years, eight years before the European theatre and ten before the Pacific, with casualties of over 35 million. The article cites figures showing that the Chinese theatre tied down 54%–94% of Japan's army, including 32 of 34 divisions in 1938, and accounted for 70% of Japanese casualties. It argues that this pressure led Japan to abandon its northward advance against the Soviet Union, giving the USSR and the Allies strategic breathing space. Zhu supports this with statements from Mao Zedong, Stalin, Roosevelt, Marshal Chuikov and Japan's own official war history.
