He credits the Communist Party with a pivotal role through protracted and guerrilla warfare. Zhu concludes that China's contribution gave the anti-fascist war "time, space and moral" support, and that it later allowed China to take part in global governance as a builder of world peace. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese case for the Eastern main theatre, with the statistics and wartime testimonies it relies on.

The Communist Party's War of Resistance on the main Eastern battlefield, as seen in Japanese historical sources 日本史料所见东方主战场的中共抗战 Wu Xiangping Song Yi Wu and Song ask what Japanese wartime documents reveal about the Chinese Communist Party's role in the War of Resistance against Japan. Their thesis is that these sources confirm the Party was the mainstay of China's resistance on the main Eastern battlefield of the world anti-fascist war. They also present the sources as an outside view that rebuts claims denying that battlefield's place and role. This short newspaper commentary, published in July 2025, is organised in two parts. The first treats the Party as the core anti-Japanese force after the 1931 Mukden Incident and the 1937 Marco Polo Bridge Incident. The second treats敌后 (behind-the-lines) resistance and the Japanese forces it tied down. The authors draw on reports by the Toho Kokusaku Doshikai, Japanese army staff, the South Manchuria Railway Company and the Domei news agency. The authors quote Japanese documents that, in their account, saw the Party's central aim as resistance and recognised its united front, political mobilisation and guerrilla warfare. A 1943 Domei survey, as cited, calls the linked North China base areas a 'red corridor' and a 'cancer' obstructing Japan's exploitation of the region. The authors read this as proof that Japan regarded the Party as its real opponent, and add that the 1940 Hundred Regiments Campaign tied down large forces and damaged transport lines. Wu and Song conclude that the Party tied down and wore out large Japanese forces in North China and opened a rear battlefield through 19 base areas. They say these areas preserved resistance when the frontal battlefield suffered setbacks. They add that the Party gained military strength, political experience and mass support that proved decisive for postwar politics. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars use Japanese sources to support the Party-centred account of the war.

China's theatre opens the main Eastern front of the world anti-fascist war 中国战场开辟世界反法西斯战争东方主战场 Zhang Yuan Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in 2025, this short commentary argues that the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression opened the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war. Zhang holds that it played a decisive part in defeating Japanese fascism and made a lasting contribution to the Allied victory. The piece follows three themes. It first traces the war from the 18 September 1931 Incident through the 1937 Marco Polo Bridge Incident to Japan's surrender in 1945. It then considers how China's theatre tied down Japanese forces and supported other fronts. Finally it examines how the war affected China's international standing. Zhang says the resistance began the world anti-fascist war and became the first large-scale anti-fascist front in the East. According to the article, 80 per cent of Japan's army divisions were in China between 1937 and 1941, and over a million Japanese troops remained there after the Pacific War began. It cites Chinese losses of 35 million military and civilian casualties. The author also points to the expeditionary force sent to Burma, to the air bases and strategic materials China supplied, and to the 1943 treaties ending British and American extraterritorial privileges. In Zhang's account, China's signing of the 1942 Declaration by United Nations and its seat as a permanent member of the Security Council confirmed its great-power status. Zhang concludes that revisiting this history defends the outcomes of the anti-fascist war and international fairness and justice. The author adds that it also actively promotes a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Chinese anniversary narrative presents China's role in the Second World War.

Young people must remember the important role of China's War of Resistance in the world anti-fascist war 青年人要牢记中国抗战在世界反法西斯战争中的重要作用 Olga Vladimirovna Dubkova This short commentary is a Chinese version of a piece by Olga Dubkova, a Russian associate professor in China. It asks how young people remember the Second World War and argues that they must keep a living memory of China's part in the world anti-fascist war. Dubkova presents the war as a shared human tragedy whose dead must not be reduced to statistics. The author draws on family stories of the war and on annual classroom discussions with students. The main evidence is a written questionnaire given to third-year students at Xi'an International Studies University. It asked which countries played the most important role, which major events took place, and who the war heroes were. According to Dubkova, 65% of respondents ranked China first, 28% the Soviet Union and 7% the United States. Students listed 46 battles and events, most of them in Europe, and few of those set on Chinese soil, which Dubkova calls a "memory gap". Of the 49 heroes named, from 12 countries, 18 were Chinese, 9 American and 7 Soviet. Dubkova reads this as a view of the war as a global catastrophe, but also as evidence of thin knowledge and little online material about wartime events and heroes in China. Writing before the 80th anniversary commemorations of September 2025, Dubkova calls for preserving humanity's shared memory of the war. The author links this to common human values, the core values of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and intercultural ties among young people. Dubkova also urges using many kinds of resources to tell stories of the Chinese resistance and its heroes. Read the original if you want a small student survey on Chinese youth memory of the war, or a Russian scholar's view of Sino-Russian wartime remembrance.

Strengthening research on the history of the War of Resistance is of great significance 加强抗战史研究意义重大 Kim Jin-hwan This short commentary is a Chinese-language text by the South Korean scholar Kim Jin-hwan, written for the 80th anniversary in 2025 of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. Kim argues that the war was a major part of the global anti-fascist struggle and that deeper historical research on it is needed. The piece first sets out what the victory meant, then recalls the sacrifices behind it, and finally turns to present-day problems of historical memory and to the need for archival research. Kim describes the victory as having three meanings. For China, it was the first complete victory over foreign aggression in modern times and kindled hopes of independence; for Asia, it gave moral encouragement and reduced losses on other fronts; for the world, China joined the anti-fascist alliance with the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union. In Kim's account, by tying down the main Japanese forces in China, Chinese soldiers and civilians prevented the spread of the war to the Soviet Union and Southeast Asia and saved millions of lives, so that without their sacrifice there would have been no world victory. Kim notes that the comfort women issue, the Nanjing Massacre and Unit 731 remain unresolved, and criticises Japanese right-wing forces and textbooks that play down war crimes, which Kim says threatens peace in East Asia. Kim calls for fuller use of archives, including Japanese-origin materials in Chinese archives that are still unpublished. Read the original if you want a brief view from a South Korean academic on how the anniversary is framed and why archival work is urged.

Carrying forward the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army and strengthening ideals and convictions 传承东北抗联精神 坚定理想信念 Zhong Haitao This newspaper commentary asks how Party members and officials today can draw on the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (Northeast Anti-Japanese Allied Army) to firm up their ideals and convictions. Zhong argues that the unit's fighters endured extreme hardship and torture because of an unshakeable loyalty to the Party. The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks on revitalising the Northeast and on using red resources as teaching material. The article is organised around three questions that Zhong treats as the logic of ideals and convictions: whether one believes, whether one acts, and for how long. Each is illustrated with episodes from the Northeast resistance, including the commanders Yang Jingyu and Zhou Baozhong, the political commissar Feng Zhongyun and the 'red capitalist' Zhu Shouyi. A short closing section links the three questions to present-day tasks. On belief, Zhong says conviction begins with grasping the dialectic of ideal and reality: ideals arise from reality but must stand above it and lead change. Yang Jingyu's final days, when he predicted that others would carry on the cause, are offered as proof that lofty ideals are a spur and not an escape. On action, Zhong holds that fighters who gave up comfortable lives showed knowledge and practice united, and warns against empty talk. On endurance, Zhong recounts Zhou Baozhong's offer in 1939 to let starving soldiers leave, after which 120 stayed, and describes tests of power in peacetime as the same test of persistence. Zhong concludes that promoting the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army spirit means first building belief, then strengthening practical commitment, and finally sustaining perseverance. Only by turning conviction into long-term struggle, the author says, can new prospects open for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-education writing uses regional revolutionary history to frame ideological discipline for cadres.

Party conduct in the new era, seen through the victory of the "Yan'an style" over the "Xi'an style" 从“延安作风”打败“西安作风”看新时代党的作风建设 Wang Yongjie Wang Yongjie takes up Xi Jinping's remark that Mao Zedong and other older revolutionaries in Yan'an defeated the "Xi'an style" with the "Yan'an style". The commentary asks what this history means for Party conduct today. Wang's thesis is that the eight-point regulations of the Central Committee (2012) continue the Yan'an style while adapting it to new conditions, and that both keep the Party's close ties with the people. The article, a newspaper commentary published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, has three parts. The first recounts Mao's 1940 conversation and sets out four features of the Yan'an style. The second presents the eight-point regulations as the new era's version of that tradition, and the third turns to institution-building and long-term practice. Wang links the piece to the current Party-wide study and education campaign on the eight-point regulations. Wang defines the Yan'an style as honest and clean government, close links with the masses, and theory tied to practice, and contrasts it with the Kuomintang's "Xi'an style" of extravagance, pleasure-seeking and detachment from the people. The four features are a firm political direction, the fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, the ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts, and self-reliance with hard struggle. For the present, Wang argues that a people-centred stance requires curbing formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance, which Xi likens to a wall between Party and people. Wang also argues that leading cadres, the "critical few", must set the example, and that unhealthy conduct and corruption share roots and must be investigated and handled together. Wang concludes that Party conduct must be made routine and lasting, because such problems recur and resist change. Wang calls for firm, long-term enforcement, rigid institutions, cultivation of Party spirit, conduct and discipline together, and good family discipline among officials so that Party style lifts social customs. Wang presents this as a safeguard for national rejuvenation and for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want an official Party-school account of how current conduct campaigns are tied to the Yan'an legacy.

Surveillance capitalism: origins, history and impact 监控资本主义：起源、历史与影响 Kenneth Lipartito This is a Chinese translation of an article by the historian Kenneth Lipartito on surveillance capitalism, the concept popularised by Shoshana Zuboff's 2019 book The Age of Surveillance Capitalism. Lipartito asks how surveillance became embedded in economic life and what it costs. The author argues that surveillance is best seen as a long-built infrastructure, and that its pursuit of certainty threatens the creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship that have driven capitalist growth. The article moves from definition to history and then to theory. It sketches how firms extract and commodify personal data, traces surveillance back to nineteenth-century credit reporting and the FICO score, and compares the regulatory approaches of the EU and the United States. It then draws on Kenneth Arrow, Jens Beckert, Keynes, Hal Varian and Claude Shannon's information theory. A closing section considers generative AI and possible alternatives. Lipartito makes three main moves. First, surveillance began in efforts to build trust among strangers in modern society and brought real benefits, such as wider access to credit. Algorithms built on historical data nonetheless risk 'automating inequality', and privacy laws that stress accuracy and consent may end up making surveillance more precise. Second, infrastructures gain momentum and become 'black boxes', and the open design of the internet allowed Google, around 2001, to discover the profit in user data. Third, drawing on Shannon, the author argues that information is the reduction of uncertainty. Varian's 'perfect contract' assumes information equality, whereas surveillance is strategic collection that deepens information asymmetry. Eliminating uncertainty replaces creative uncertainty with false certainty. Lipartito concludes that total transparency and predictability reshape selfhood and agency, and that corporate algorithms, not centralised state planning, now threaten freedom. The author warns that generative AI could 'colonise' social life and degrade its own training data. Infrastructures are not unstoppable, however, and the author points to failed technologies such as the videophone and the One Laptop per Child programme. Coordinated political effort could build a different future around other values. Read the original if you want a historically grounded, information-theoretic critique of surveillance capitalism that stresses economic stagnation and innovation more than ethics.

The historical origins, development and future prospects of the Ecuadorian left 厄瓜多尔左翼的历史缘起、发展历程与未来展望 Wang Di Wang Di asks how the Ecuadorian left arose, developed and fell back, and what this reveals about socialist movements in Ecuador and the prospects of the Latin American left. The article argues that the left, active since the mid-1920s, reached its peak with Rafael Correa's election in 2006, part of the regional "pink tide". It contends that the left now faces serious obstacles and an unclear future. The article first traces the origins of the left to the 1895 liberal revolution, the influence of the Mexican and Russian revolutions, and the domestic crisis after the collapse of cocoa exports. It then divides the left's history into five phases: emergence (1926–1933), expansion (1934–1958), crisis and split (1959–1977), reorganisation (1978–2006) and renewed development (2007 to the present). A final section sets out five difficulties and offers a short forecast. Wang's account of origins links the rise of wage labour under liberal rule to the bloody suppression of the 1922 Guayaquil strike, which showed workers the need for their own party. The Socialist Party was founded in 1926 and soon split over ties to the Comintern. In Wang's reading, later radicalisation, Cold War US intervention and fragmentation produced crisis, and the left returned through elections. Under Correa the left promoted "socialism of good living" and a "citizens' revolution", which Wang credits with state-building, higher public investment, more revenue and a more assertive foreign policy. The right returned in 2021 and 2023. Wang identifies five current difficulties: US geopolitical pressure, factionalism (especially between the Indigenous movement Pachakutik and traditional left parties), the lack of a clear political line, an incomplete theory of "good living" socialism, and growing distance from the people. The author concludes that the left should strengthen internal unity, keep close ties with the masses and continue theoretical innovation based on national conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly periodisation of Ecuador's left, from the 1920s Socialist and Communist parties to the Correa era.

The Communist Party of Argentina's exploration of the socialist path Analysis of the current situation and outlook 阿根廷共产党对社会主义道路的探索 Zhou Songfeng Zhou Miao The article examines the Communist Party of Argentina (PCA), founded in 1918, and asks how it is positioned today under President Javier Milei and whether it can expand. The authors argue that the party has limited electoral influence and faces serious internal and external constraints, but that deepening social contradictions and a regional left revival give it new openings if it adjusts its strategy. The study begins with the party's origins: the early spread of socialist ideas in Argentina, including Marx's 1872 envoy to the International Workingmen's Association, and the growth of an immigrant-fed working class. It then reviews the party's current theory and practice, including its 28th National Congress in September 2024, its online propaganda and research apparatus, and its alliances at home and abroad. The final sections set out challenges and prospects, and close with a short conclusion. On theory, the authors report that the PCA advocates state intervention, resists what it calls economic imperialism and criticises capitalism for producing dependency and weak proletarian representation. They illustrate this with the 2001 crisis after IMF-guided reforms and with Monsanto's grip on soybean farming. On practice, the PCA opposes Milei's "shock therapy", joined the January 2024 strike and backed student protests over university funding. The authors identify weaknesses: a junior role in Peronist-led coalitions, no seats in national or provincial legislatures, 130,000 members in 2022 and falling, an ageing leadership with no systematic succession, and a rightward shift in public mood. For the outlook, the authors point to a poverty rate of 52.9% in the first half of 2024, falling support for Milei, working-class protest and the election of left governments in several Latin American countries. They argue these trends could raise the appeal of the PCA's platform. The authors also note that the party sends delegations to China and studies the Communist Party of China's experience on development, poverty alleviation and Party building. They conclude that the PCA will keep seeking a socialist model suited to Argentina and the region. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of a small Latin American communist party, its recent congress and its prospects under Milei.

New trends in the communist parties of developed capitalist countries 当前发达资本主义国家共产党发展新态势 Yu Weihai Yu Weihai asks how communist parties in developed capitalist countries are faring amid what official discourse calls the "great changes unseen in a century", and what this shows about world socialism. The article argues that these parties have moved beyond the trough that followed the Soviet collapse. Some have grown and are adapting, though they remain weak and divided. Yu also presents their trajectory as support for Xi Jinping's judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics is a banner of twenty-first-century scientific socialism. The article has three parts. The first describes new developments since the 2008 financial crisis: organisational and electoral gains, theoretical innovation, and sharper conflicts between parties. The second identifies new features: networked international relations, growing reliance on online media, and persistent internal weaknesses alongside stronger external pressures. The third draws lessons for the study of world socialism. Evidence comes from membership figures, election results and party documents for the United States, Belgium, Greece, Portugal, France, Japan and others. Yu reports membership growth in the Workers' Party of Belgium and the Communist Party USA, along with local election successes in Austria, and the founding of new parties in Australia, New Zealand, Germany and the United States. Yu also notes declines in the French, Spanish, Portuguese and Japanese parties. Many parties have taken up ecology, digital capitalism and identity politics, the last of which splits them. Quarrels over the Ukraine crisis and over imperialism have fragmented the international platforms. Yu warns that heavy reliance on social media risks turning some parties into "online" or "media" parties detached from the masses. Yu lists further internal problems: ideological swings to left and right, ageing memberships and thin finances. External problems include anti-communism and competition from new radical groups. Yu concludes that these parties, despite hostile conditions, keep up anti-capitalist struggle and show world socialism entering a phase of seeking breakthroughs. The author calls for scholars to study the parties' theory and practice, and the new socialist elements inside each country. Yu cites rising support for Chinese socialism among more than twenty such parties, including a 2023 document of the German party, and treats it as evidence that Chinese socialism is a "mainstay" in revitalising world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview, with data and examples, of Western communist parties and how Chinese scholarship frames them.

Party discipline and conduct building of the Communist Party of China during the full-scale War of Resistance 全面抗战时期中国共产党的纪律和作风建设 Jin Minqing Jin Minqing, writing in the Party discipline newspaper China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News (July 2025), asks what the Communist Party of China learned about discipline and conduct (zuofeng) during the full-scale War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45). The author argues that the Party's explorations in this period helped forge it into a politically, ideologically and organisationally mature Marxist party able to lead national resistance, and that these experiences still offer lessons today. The article is built in three parts. The first treats discipline as the guarantee of the political line and of the authority of the Party Central Committee. The second treats close ties with the masses as the core of conduct building, with the Yan'an Rectification Movement as its main example. The third covers the harsh punishment of corruption and crime, and the way the Party summed up its experience in theory and institutions. Cases include the Wang Ming affair, Huang Kegong and Xiao Yubi. Jin's central claims are as follows. First, discipline serves the line: the author cites Mao Zedong's formulas that discipline is the guarantee of carrying out the line and that the line is the 'kingly way' and discipline the 'hegemonic way', both indispensable. Discipline in turn means upholding central authority and unified leadership, which the author illustrates with the removal of Wang Ming's Yangtze Bureau and with the 1942 decision on unified, 'integrated' Party leadership in the base areas. Second, conduct building combined work on a 'critical few', senior cadres who set an example, with the 'vast majority'. The author describes this through the Yan'an rectification, the 1943 decision on leadership methods (the mass line) and the 1941 decision on investigation and research. Third, the executions of Huang Kegong and Xiao Yubi, both veterans, show that no special persons were exempt, and Jin says they consolidated the bond with the people. Jin concludes that the Party turned this experience into theoretical and institutional innovation. Mao set out the content of Party conduct and the three fine styles (integrating theory with practice, close ties with the masses, self-criticism). The Sixth Plenum documents set out the 'four obediences', and the Seventh Congress (1945) Party constitution wrote discipline into its general programme as an organisational foundation. Jin presents the joint handling of conduct, discipline and anti-corruption as an enduring method of Party building. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic account of how wartime Party history is used to frame discipline and conduct building today.

Accurately grasping the scientific methods of investigation and research 准确把握调查研究的科学方法 Feng Bing Jia Yanni This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how Party members should conduct investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) in order to carry out the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and advance Chinese modernization. Feng and Jia argue that investigation is the basis of all sound decision-making and that it must follow five scientific principles. The article moves through five requirements in turn: seeking truth from facts, a systems approach, the mass line, a problem orientation, and keeping pace with the times. It draws on Marx and Engels's own investigative work, Party experience from the revolutionary period to poverty alleviation, and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). The authors present these principles as a working method. Cadres should visit both successful localities and troubled ones, and should listen to unwelcome views as well as welcome ones. Research should be "deep, practical, detailed, accurate and effective". The authors hold that its worth is judged by whether problems are actually solved and findings turned into institutions and policy, not by the scale of a survey or the quality of its report. They also call for updating methods, such as conferences, fieldwork and village-based investigation, with networked information, modern technology and several disciplines, and for combining qualitative and quantitative analysis. The authors conclude that investigation is the source of sound judgement and is needed for both policy-making and implementation. They treat Xi Jinping's speeches on the subject as the basic guide for a Party-wide drive to revive it. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official methodology of investigation and research as presented in Party-school and Party-building writing.

Opening up a better future through unity and struggle 用团结奋斗开辟美好未来 Qu Qingshan Qu Qingshan takes up Xi Jinping's 2022 statement that unity and struggle is the only way for the Chinese people to create great historic achievements. The article, a study-and-interpretation piece in Qiushi (2025 no. 13), presents this as a major thesis that answers who creates China's historic undertakings and how. Qu argues that it has both theoretical and practical weight as the country faces a changing international environment, intense great-power rivalry and demanding domestic tasks. The article has three parts. The first treats unity and struggle as the most distinctive spiritual mark of the Chinese people and the Communist Party. The second reviews four historical dimensions: the development of the Chinese nation, the history of the Party, the history of the People's Republic, and the history of reform and opening up. The third turns to the present and sets out what unity and struggle require on the new journey. In the core argument, Qu holds that the Chinese nation's spirit combines creativity, struggle, unity and dreams, with patriotism at its core. Qu links it to the Party's "spiritual lineage", which runs from the Jinggangshan spirit to the poverty-alleviation and anti-epidemic spirits. The historical survey then credits each period's achievements to unity and struggle. These include the victory of the new-democratic revolution, socialist transformation and construction, the reforms after 1978, and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the elimination of absolute poverty for nearly 100 million rural people. Qu concludes that all of the Party's and people's successes are the result of unity and struggle. Looking ahead, Qu says that unity built around a clear goal, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, is the firmest kind. The goal is to be pursued through Chinese modernization and the two-step strategy to 2035 and the middle of the century. Qu calls for four commitments: upholding Party leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; putting the people first; daring and being skilled in struggle; and maintaining the broadest patriotic united front. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how the Party leadership presents its history, national spirit and current tasks under a single slogan.

Forging the vanguard of the era, showing the strength of a great Party 锻造时代先锋 展现大党伟力 Zheng Qi This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 4 July 2025, takes up the milestone that Party membership has passed 100 million. According to the latest Organisation Department figures cited by Zheng Qi, the Communist Party of China had 100.271 million members at the end of 2024, a net rise of 1.086 million (1.1%) over 2023. Zheng argues that this scale shows the Party's attractiveness and vitality, but that quality, not number, must remain the foundation of its strength. The piece has three sections. The first traces the principle of 'quality first' through Marx and Engels in the Communist League and the First International, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. The second reads the Party's size as evidence of its appeal and of rising quality since 2013. The third sets out measures for consolidating the numerical advantage while raising quality. Zheng's central claim is that quantity is the carrier of strength and quality its soul, and that a large membership does not automatically become a quality advantage. As evidence of quality, the article cites an average of 20.627 million applicants and 2.377 million new members a year in 2013–2024, a selection ratio of 8.7 to 1. It also reports that more than 80% of new members each year since the 18th Party Congress (2012) were aged 35 or under, that members with college education or above have exceeded 50% since 2019, and that frontline workers have made up over half of new recruits for eight years. Zheng contrasts this with the 'marginalised' membership and 'hollowed-out' organisations of some Western parties. To turn scale into quality, Zheng calls for three things. Education and management should be strengthened through Party schools, the 'three meetings and one lesson', and a digital 'smart Party building' system. Discipline should be tightened through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, in the spirit of the Party's self-reform, with zero tolerance for corrupt members. Members should be tested in practice through 'dual reporting', Party responsibility zones and shock teams. Zheng presents this as the way for a Party of over 100 million to lead Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise official-line statement of how Party-building scholars link membership growth to quality control, with the recruitment statistics cited.

Grasping the original contributions of the Party's organizational line for the new era 深刻把握新时代党的组织路线的原创性贡献 Beijing Municipal Association for Party Building Research This commentary, written collectively by the Beijing Municipal Association for Party Building Research and carried in the People's Daily in July 2025, sets out what it regards as the original theoretical contributions of the Party's organizational line for the new era. The line was first put forward by Xi Jinping at the national organization work conference in July 2018 and elaborated at a Politburo study session in 2020. The authors argue that it is a landmark result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and a distinctive concept of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article is organised around five contributions: the first definition of the content of an organizational line; the first statement of a basic layout for organizational work; the joining of ideological and organizational Party building; the shift towards systematic construction; and the political criteria for selecting officials. It closes with the line's purpose of serving the political line. Historical references run from Marx, Engels and Lenin through the 1928 Sixth Party Congress, the Gutian Conference and the Yan'an rectification to the post-1978 period and the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors contend that the classics stressed organization but never named an organizational line. In their account, the Chinese Party introduced the term in 1928 yet for decades left its content undefined, and organizational work was often equated with cadre work or with grassroots branch building. The new-era formulation is said to resolve this by setting a basic layout of one focus and two emphases: building the organizational system, cultivating high-calibre cadres and attracting talent. It pairs this with Xi's image of organization as the 'form' and ideas as the 'soul', so that theoretical armament underpins organizational strength. The article also presents the stress on integrity first, with both integrity and ability, as a concrete form of the traditional principle of appointing people on merit. The authors conclude that the line serves the Party's political line and, in their words, provides a strong organizational guarantee for upholding the Party's overall leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. They call for linking ideological and organizational Party building, strengthening the organizational system, and carrying the Two Upholds through to every level of the Party. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-press statement of how the organizational line is now officially framed and periodised in Party-building theory.

Addressing Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together as an effective path to self-reform 党性党风党纪一起抓是实现自我革命的有效途径 He Jinglei This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2025, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) instruction to "address Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together". He argues that handling the three together is an effective route to the Party's self-reform, because each performs a distinct function that must be linked to the others. The article is organised around two principles. The first is systems thinking, which treats the three as an organic whole. The second is strategic thinking, which aims at a long-term mechanism. Between them the author considers the three elements both jointly and one by one. He describes Party spirit as the foundation, Party style as its outward expression and Party discipline as the guarantee. In his view the three are complementary rather than rivals, and strengthening one strengthens the others. He also gives each its own role. Breaches of style and discipline, he says, usually begin with wavering Party spirit, so cultivating it is the root-level remedy. Party style shapes the political ecology and public support. Party discipline is a rigid constraint, and he calls for combining discipline education with disciplinary punishment. For the long term, He calls for routine Party-spirit education as a lifelong task, because Party spirit does not grow automatically with seniority or rank. He also calls for a sustained educating role for Party style and for steady improvement of discipline, under the requirements that rules exist, are followed, are enforced strictly and that violations are pursued. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-building commentary in China explains the relationship between the three concepts.

How the Japanese Communist Party uses culture as a vehicle for spreading Marxism: an analysis of its practice 日本共产党以文化为载体传播马克思主义的实践探析 Pan Jin'e Xu Wennong Pan and Xu ask how the Japanese Communist Party (JCP) has spread Marxism in a country where the emperor system, the family system and Confucian ethics remained dominant after the Meiji Restoration. Their answer is that the JCP has used culture as its vehicle, adjusting Marxism to local conditions rather than transplanting it. The authors present this as an experience of wider value for the world socialist movement. The article moves from the early 20th century to the digital age in three parts. The first covers the early spread of Marxism in Japan, the clashes with Japanese tradition, and the JCP's efforts at cultural adaptation. The second examines the cultural vehicles the party has used: publishing, literature and the arts, and mass cultural activities. The third turns to the party's indigenous path of theoretical innovation, its responses to contemporary social problems, and its use of digital media. The authors argue that Marxism's revolutionary content conflicted with the religious and mystical elements of Shinto and Buddhism, with the emperor system, and with family loyalties that, in their account, blunted workers' class consciousness. The JCP is said to have responded by tying Marxism to concrete problems, such as landlord–tenant relations in the countryside and wages and conditions in the cities. It also reinterpreted Confucian "benevolence and righteousness" and the Buddhist idea of the equality of all beings alongside class equality. Cultural carriers followed: the party newspaper Akahata, new editions of Capital, proletarian literature such as Kobayashi Takiji's Kanikosen, theatre, workers' songs, festivals and workers' clubs. The authors also credit Japanese Marxists with reinterpreting classic theory in the 1920s–30s debates on Japanese capitalism. They further say Marxist ideas have been developed on exploitation, the labour theory of value and distribution, including proposals for a basic income. Since the 2000s the party has moved onto electronic newspapers, a website, social media and YouTube. The authors conclude that the JCP has combined theoretical resilience with cultural vitality, bridging Marxism's universality and Japan's cultural particularity. They hold that ideological appeal depends not only on a theory's scientific character but also on its deep coupling with local cultural traditions. Emotional resonance with the people, they say, is what turns Marxism from an "ideological weapon" into a "spiritual belief". They offer this as a methodological model for cross-cultural dissemination of theory. Read the original if you study the JCP, the localisation of Marxism outside the West, or how Chinese scholars assess the use of cultural forms in socialist propaganda.

Pursuing the appeal of theory through the long course of history On "A Study of the Historical Development of the Two Theoretical Cornerstones of Scientific Socialism" 在历史长河中追寻理论的魅力 Wang Fuxin This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily on 3 July 2025. Wang Fuxin reviews Professor Zhu Dapeng's monograph A Study of the Historical Development of the Two Theoretical Cornerstones of Scientific Socialism (People's Publishing House). Wang argues that the book shows scientific socialism to be a theory with lasting appeal, and that studying its theoretical foundations as a whole is a key to understanding that appeal. The two cornerstones are the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value. According to Wang, Zhu analyses how they relate to the overall development of scientific socialism. The book looks at its historical course, its present circumstances and its future trends, and it combines theory with practice. Wang organises the review around four qualities the book brings out: depth, sincerity, breadth and vitality. Wang gives each quality a ground. Depth comes from resting on the long course of human history. As an example, Wang cites the apparent paradox that the surplus-value theory was completed in Capital (1867), after scientific socialism was founded in the Communist Manifesto (1848). The book resolves this by pointing to a fairly complete theory of the working class already held by Marx and Engels, which linked the two cornerstones. Sincerity comes from holding the moral high ground, in the aim of human liberation. Breadth comes from addressing real problems of the age, including current disputes over the production and distribution of surplus value. Vitality comes from driving new practice. The book lists present challenges to the materialist conception of history, which Wang says can be settled fully only through new practice. Wang concludes that scientific socialism advances in stages only when it holds to the stance, viewpoint and method of the two cornerstones. The review presents socialism with characteristics of China as the current achievement of this process, one that opens space to lead the times and guide practice. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language account of how this monograph frames the two cornerstones and why a Party-affiliated scholar considers it significant.

Organisation and mobilisation in building the anti-Japanese democratic political power 抗日民主政权建设中的组织动员 He Ju Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan (2025), this short commentary asks how the Communist Party organised and mobilised the people while building democratic political power in the anti-Japanese base areas. The author argues that democracy was the primary means of mobilising the nation, and that the base areas, above all the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, drew mass support because they practised it. The piece moves in three steps. It first sets out the wartime logic linking the united front to state-building, citing Mao Zedong's 1937 formulation and the Party's ten-point programme for resisting Japan. It then describes how democratic institutions were built in practice: the "three-thirds system" and the electoral campaigns. Finally it examines the consequences of this democracy, using Xie Juezai's 1940 remarks and the testimony of visitors to Yan'an. In Hu's account, the base areas faced severe political, economic and military difficulties, especially in 1941–1942, and overcame them by mobilising the masses and relying on self-reliance. The author presents the three-thirds system (one-third Communists, one-third non-Party progressives, one-third centrists) as a way of widening participation without weakening Party leadership, which depends on exemplary conduct and persuasion. To overcome low literacy and weak democratic habits, the Party used spoken, written and artistic propaganda, and devised voting methods such as the bean ballot. The author lists four results of "the border region has democracy": wider political participation, a transformed social outlook (the "ten absences"), an influx of talent, and the winning of popular support in contrast to Guomindang-ruled areas. The author concludes that strong mass mobilisation is a distinctive strength of the Party and an important reason for the revolution's victory. In this reading, the Party turned a national crisis into an opening for national rejuvenation and earned its place as the mainstay of united resistance. The author also says that drawing out these experiences helps promote the wartime spirit and build a strong country. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned overview of how Party scholarship presents democracy and mass mobilisation in the Yan'an-era base areas.

Forging the spiritual backbone of Chinese Communists with the great founding spirit of the Party 以伟大建党精神铸牢中国共产党人精神支柱 Wang Zhongru This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks where the great founding spirit of the Party comes from and why it should anchor the spiritual backbone of Chinese Communists. Wang Zhongru argues that this spirit expresses the Party's advanced character and gives fundamental guidance for fulfilling its nature, purpose and historical mission under new conditions. The piece traces the spirit to three sources and then turns to the present. These are Marxist theory, traditional Chinese culture, and a firm stand with the people. It adds a fourth strand, the Party's historical consciousness and initiative, before linking the argument to the goals set by the 20th Party Congress (2022). Wang argues that the Party's century-long fidelity to truth and ideals rests on loyalty to Marxism, especially in its sinicised form. The author presents the willingness to sacrifice and fight as an inheritance from classical Chinese ethics, citing poetic lines on duty and martyrdom, and says the Party's mission of seeking the people's happiness and national rejuvenation is borne out by poverty alleviation, pollution control and welfare gains since the new era began. In Wang's reading, the Party's historical initiative, shown in the War of Resistance, the founding of the new China and reform and opening up, is the key support of the spirit. Wang concludes that, to meet risks on the new journey, the Party must use the great founding spirit to forge its members' spiritual backbone and gather strength for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party School scholars link founding-spirit rhetoric to Marxism, tradition and current policy goals.

Common traits of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系共同特质 Liu Ronggang This short commentary asks what the great spirits in the "spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists" share, despite their different content. Liu Ronggang argues that these spirits, which the Party formed through revolution, construction and reform, have ten common traits. The author notes that the first batch of spirits was officially published in September 2021, after approval by the Central Committee. The article is a list-based survey. It sets out ten traits in turn and gives for each a few examples drawn from named spirits, such as the spirit of founding the Party, the Long March spirit, the Jinggangshan spirit, the Yan'an spirit, the special economic zone spirit and the Silk Road spirit. It closes with an account of why the genealogy has these common features. Liu's ten traits are firm ideals and convictions, loyalty to the Party, living up to the original aspiration and mission, seeking truth from facts, serving the people, pioneering innovation, hard work, daring to struggle, dedication and sacrifice, and solidarity and cooperation. Each is tied to quoted wording from individual spirits and described as a basic requirement or strength of the Party. On causes, Liu says the genealogy comes from practice, continues the spirit of founding the Party, and carries forward the Chinese national spirit. Liu presents these traits as the shared core of the Party's spiritual wealth and as a call to keep the original aspiration and mission in a new era. Seeking truth from facts is described as the Party's ideological line, to be applied by studying Marxism and its adaptation to China. Read the original if you want a compact official-style summary of how Party historians classify the spirits in the genealogy.

Deepening research on the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 深化中国共产党人精神谱系研究 Wang Binglin Wang Binglin, writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (1 July 2025), argues that research on the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists, which takes the great founding spirit of the Party as its source, needs to be deepened. In the author's view, promoting this genealogy supplies spiritual impetus for socialism with Chinese characteristics, nourishes Party building and provides resources for training a new generation. Wang adds that such research has real academic value for the Party's innovative theory and for building the discipline of CPC history and Party building. The short commentary has three parts: the precise meaning of the concept, the need for scholarly rigour and seriousness, and directions for further research. Wang treats the concept as an innovation in discourse introduced by the Party Central Committee under Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On the concept, Wang explains the stress on 'Communists' rather than 'the Communist Party'. People create and pass on the spirits, the genealogy is a large system of many individual spirits, and some spirits were not formed by the Party alone: the great spirit of resistance was forged by the whole nation, and the Yimeng and Saihanba spirits by the people together with Communists. On rigour, Wang calls for combining history and theory, with claims resting on solid historical sources. Research should be based on the first batch approved by the Central Committee. Wang urges caution in re-defining revolutionary spirits and in raising local spirits arbitrarily. Wang also holds that general work-style requirements such as a spirit of unity or struggle should not be placed in the genealogy, lest its seriousness be diluted. Wang proposes further work on how the genealogy formed, viewed through the Two Integrations; on its contribution to Chinese modernization; on its function within the discipline of CPC history and Party building; and on its shared values in a global perspective. Read the original if you want a brief view of how a Party historian sets conceptual limits on what counts as part of the official spiritual genealogy.

Forging the cause of national rejuvenation with the great founding spirit of the Party 以伟大建党精神铸就民族复兴伟业 Mao Huabing Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, Mao asks what role the "great founding spirit" of the Communist Party of China plays in the effort to achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author argues that this spirit is the Party's winning formula over more than a century and the ideological core guiding the national cause, and calls for more scholarly study of it. The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the Party's centenary in 2021 about the Party's spiritual lineage. It then traces how successive spirits arose in each period: the Red Boat spirit at the Party's founding, the Jinggangshan, Long March and Yan'an spirits in the revolution, the Daqing and Red Flag Canal spirits after 1949, and the reform-era and post-2012 spirits such as poverty alleviation and the fight against Covid-19. Mao makes three moves. First, the founding spirit is said to embody the Party's original aspiration and mission through a people-centred historical materialism, a firm belief in lofty ideals and a readiness for "great self-reform". Second, it is said to steer national rejuvenation by keeping to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and avoiding both the "old path" and the "evil path". Third, Mao calls for distilling each era's spirit scientifically and for refuting historical nihilism, which the author says underlies attacks on these spirits and on model figures. Mao concludes that the founding spirit is never "completed" and will keep being enriched as the Party leads the people towards rejuvenation. The author urges firm rebuttal of erroneous currents of thought and deeper propaganda and education work that is integrated into the overall cause of the Party and state. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholarship presents the Party's spiritual lineage as a source of legitimacy and guidance.

Building a strong and powerful Marxist governing party 建设坚强有力的马克思主义执政党 Xiao Guiqing Published in Guangming Daily around the Party's anniversary on 1 July 2025, this short commentary asks what it takes to build a strong Marxist governing party. Xiao Guiqing argues that the Communist Party of China, born in a period of national crisis, has tied its own development to the fate of the Chinese nation. In Xiao's account this has produced a Marxist governing party that leads the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, enjoys popular support and is willing to undertake self-reform. The article has three sections. The first traces the growth of Party membership and organisation through four historical stages: the revolutionary period, the early socialist period, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second turns to building a united and disciplined membership. The third deals with the vanguard and exemplary role of individual Party members. Xiao draws repeatedly on Xi Jinping's statements. Xiao contends that growth in size matches the Party's historical position and mission. The article cites a membership of 100.271 million in 5.25 million primary-level organisations, up from a little over fifty at the founding, and presents this as evidence of the Party's appeal and cohesion. Internal strength, Xiao argues, comes from ideological Party building and theoretical education, including eight Party-wide education campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also comes from full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point regulation on conduct, strict control over admission, and the handling of unqualified members. For members themselves, Xiao sets out three requirements: firm ideals and service to the central tasks of the Party and state; excellent performance in one's own post; and service to the people, starting with their most pressing and practical concerns. Xiao concludes that the Party's strength depends on both the quality of its members and the solidity of its grassroots organisations. A Party that is large, ideologically united, strictly disciplined and rooted in the people is presented as able to meet the major tests ahead. The piece is a concise statement of the official line on Party building in the new era. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party-school scholar presents Party building in the mainstream press, or a compact summary of the stock themes and figures used in 2025 discussions of Party discipline and membership.

The mainstay: the great role of the Communist Party of China in the nationwide War of Resistance 中流砥柱：中国共产党在全民族抗战中的伟大作用 Zhang Taiyuan Zhao Jinghan Zhang Taiyuan and Zhao Jinghan, writing in Guangming Daily in July 2025, ask what role the Communist Party of China played in the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan. Their answer is that the Party was the "mainstay" (zhongliu dizhu) of the nationwide resistance and its national vanguard. In the authors' account, the Party's political line, firm will and exemplary conduct sustained the hope of national salvation and set the correct direction of the war. The short commentary is built in three parts. The first concerns the Party's determination in defending national independence, the second its line of all-out resistance and its strategy and tactics, and the third its role as the backbone of the resistance behind enemy lines. The authors rely heavily on statements by Mao Zedong, Ye Jianying and Xi Jinping. They also cite Japanese military reports and the observations of foreign journalists and a US military observer group. First, the authors contrast the Party's steadfastness with the Guomindang's wavering between fighting and negotiating. They support this with Mao's 1936 answer to Edgar Snow, the sacrifice of commanders and heroic units, and Japanese wartime statements that the "truly anti-Japanese force" was the Communist Party. Second, they credit Mao's On Protracted War and his writings on guerrilla warfare with foreseeing three stages of the war. They also credit the united front and the mobilisation of the masses, which they treat as the key to victory. Third, they argue that the base areas and the battlefield behind enemy lines grew until they became the main theatre of resistance. As evidence they cite the 1940 offensive by 105 regiments in North China, population and troop figures for the base areas, and 19 base areas covering nearly 1 million square kilometres with a population of nearly 100 million. The authors conclude that the Party's mainstay role was the key to victory. They present the Guomindang-led front and the Communist-led rear battlefield as cooperating in a shared strategic posture. They add that the Party also worked to build an international anti-fascist united front, and that China's resistance was the Eastern main theatre of the world anti-fascist war. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party-history narrative of the War of Resistance as it appeared in the 2025 commemorations, including its use of Japanese and foreign sources.

How patient capital empowers new quality productive forces: inner mechanism and paths of cultivation 耐心资本赋能新质生产力的内在机理与培育路径研究 Li Zhe Wang Chengyun Li Zhe and Wang Chengyun take up the call at the Politburo meeting of April 2024 to "develop venture capital actively and expand patient capital" as a way of developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions. They argue that patient capital is a concrete form of capital under the socialist market economy, that it develops Marxist capital theory, and that it can drive new quality productive forces through three channels, while facing real risks that call for coordinated cultivation. The article has four main parts. It first defines patient capital and its attributes, then explains how it empowers new quality productive forces. It next identifies risks and challenges, and finally proposes cultivation paths for investment firms, government, policy and the market environment. A short conclusion follows. The authors draw on Marx's definition of capital as a social relation, on Lin Yifu and Wang Yan's definition, and on Western work on long-term private-equity investment. The authors distinguish what patient capital shares with capital in general from what is specific to it. Like all capital, it is a factor of production that seeks valorisation, moves and accumulates. Its specific features are long investment horizons, counter-cyclical positioning, strategic orientation and relative safety. In the Chinese setting, they say, state capital is its main force, alongside long-term bank, insurance and social security funds. They argue that it empowers new quality productive forces by stabilising capital markets, acting as a "technological partner" that funds long-cycle research and the conversion of results into production, and supplying "financial impetus" to emerging and future industries, new-type workers and green development. The risks they identify are a complex domestic and international situation, the conflict between short-termist investment concepts, models and appraisal systems and long-term innovation, and incomplete or unstable policies and an immature venture market. To address them, they call for longer performance-evaluation cycles (five years or more), fault-tolerance and incentive mechanisms, and a guiding government role in coordination, risk control and infrastructure. They also call for better tax policy, exit channels and regulation, and a market environment that protects intellectual property. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese economists frame patient capital within Marxist political economy and the policy agenda for new quality productive forces.

Lefebvre's spatial dialectics in the context of the critique of political economy: a further examination 政治经济学批判语境下列斐伏尔的空间辩证法申论 Zhang Xiuhua Zhao Jingjing Zhang and Zhao ask how Henri Lefebvre carried Marx's critique of political economy into the dimension of space, and what that move is worth today. They argue that Lefebvre inherited Marx's tradition and joined the critique of capital with the critique of space. In their account he extended Marx's labour–production dialectic of practice into a spatial dialectic. They also hold that this dialectic has real limits, chiefly its neglect of time. The article has three parts. The first treats the production of space as the ground on which Lefebvre built his dialectic. It sets out his claim that earlier historical materialism had an 'absence of space', and traces the method of ascent from the abstract to the concrete from Hegel through Marx to Lefebvre. The second part reconstructs the 'three-dimensional' picture of abstraction, contradiction and difference. The third assesses the contemporary significance of the dialectic, its reception by Harvey, Foucault and Soja, and its shortcomings. The core move is the authors' reading of Lefebvre's triad of spatial practice, representations of space and representational (symbolic) space. Under capitalism this triad is alienated into 'abstract space' ruled by exchange value, which the authors say Lefebvre links to a 'space fetishism' modelled on Marx's commodity fetishism. Space becomes one-dimensional, human relations to space and to one another are estranged, and space turns into an instrument of state power. Contradictions inside abstract space are said to generate a 'differential space', reached through a 'spatial revolution' by the urban proletariat allied with those on the margins. The authors stress that Lefebvre's third term is an independent element resting on difference, not a synthesis of the first two as in Hegel and Marx. The authors credit Lefebvre with spatialising dialectics, enriching Marx's theories of alienation and reification, and pointing towards a just space. They then raise three criticisms. He elevates space over time, which in their view conflicts with Marx's emphasis on free time and with the unity of history and practice. His triad lacks an internal dialectical connection, so its ontological basis is left 'suspended'. His differential space is utopian and aesthetic, closer to the Western Marxist tradition of aesthetic redemption than to Marx's reliance on changes in the mode of production and social revolution. Read the original if you study Lefebvre, spatial theory or Western Marxism and want a Chinese Marxist assessment that tests his work against Marx's critique of political economy.

The dialectical method and the wisdom of the mean in exploring the path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化道路探索的辩证方法与中庸智慧 Zhang Shiwei Zhu Yao Zhang Shiwei and Zhu Yao ask how Chinese modernization came to take a path distinct from the Western and Soviet models. Taking the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its decision on deepening reform as a starting point, they argue that the key lies in a method: the Party's fusion of Marxist dialectics with the traditional Chinese wisdom of the mean (zhongyong), as part of the Two Integrations. The article has four parts. The first treats the historical conditions and theoretical premises of Chinese modernization, tracing the global wave of modernization from Britain's industrial revolution, the Opium War as the turning point for China, and the late-Qing search by reformers and revolutionaries for Western models. The second examines how a dialectical self-awareness emerged from the later New Culture Movement, through Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai, Li Da, Ai Siqi and Mao Zedong. The third analyses how the mean is applied in practice, and a short conclusion follows. The authors argue that traditional zhongyong, born of feudal society, carried eclectic and metaphysical elements and a hierarchical outlook. In their account Marxist dialectics removed these limits and gave it a scientific content, while its stress on balance, the unity of opposites and moderation proved compatible with materialist dialectics. They then claim that this transformed 'grasping the two ends and using the mean' shaped three areas of practice. In choosing a road, it avoided copying either the Western or the Soviet model. In strategy, it balanced independence and self-reliance with opening up, avoiding extremes. In policy, it sought dynamic balance through common prosperity, the five-sphere overall plan, harmony between humans and nature, and non-alignment in foreign policy. The authors conclude that the success of Chinese modernization is not accidental but the result of combining Marxist dialectics with the mean, which they describe as a mutual embedding of practical and speculative reason. They expect further development of the Two Integrations, especially the 'second integration', to bring methodological innovation and extend the strengths of this combination. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars link Marxist dialectics with traditional philosophy to explain the distinctiveness of Chinese modernization.

On the distinctive worldview contained in Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化蕴含的独特世界观 Tian Pengying Tian Pengying takes up a statement by Xi Jinping in February 2023 that Chinese modernization contains a distinctive worldview, outlook on values, history, civilization, democracy and ecology. Tian argues that the worldview is the precondition for the others, so it must be understood first, including its theoretical basis, cultural sources and global horizon. The article sets out to explain, from a philosophical angle, what this worldview is, what it contributes theoretically and what its world-historical significance is. The article is organised in five sections, each presenting a relationship through which Chinese modernization is said to view the modern world: China and the world; the general and the particular; matter and spirit; humanity and nature; and openness and independence. It draws on Marx's theory of world history, Lenin's and Mao Zedong's treatment of the dialectic of the general and the particular, and Marx's critique of capital. It also cites Xi Jinping's speeches throughout. Tian's central move is to place Chinese modernization within a world-historical process. In this account the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is irreversible and converges with world socialism and global modernization. Tian describes three "basic plates" of the modern world: Chinese, Western and Global South modernization. Modernization has common features, namely a material and technological base, similar stages, similar drivers and kindred civilizational forms, but it also shows historical diversity, so "modernization is not a multiple-choice question with a single answer". Western modernization, in Tian's account, is driven by the logic of capital. It produces materialism, alienation and the exhaustion of nature, whereas Chinese modernization seeks coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress and harmony between humanity and nature. In foreign affairs Tian rejects the "Thucydides trap" as fatalism and argues for peaceful development, win-win cooperation and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Tian concludes that Chinese modernization is not self-enclosed but in dialogue with the world. By handling these five relationships dialectically, it offers what Tian calls wisdom for humanity at a new crossroads of civilization and points towards a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party theorists present the philosophical foundations of Chinese modernization, and how they set it against Western modernization.

Critique of capitalism amid deepening technological monopoly and global fracture: responses and reconstruction A survey of foreign Marxist research in 2024 技术垄断深化与全球秩序裂变下的资本主义批判：应答与重构 Qiao Ruihua This is an annual review of Marxist scholarship outside China in 2024. Qiao Ruihua asks how foreign Marxists responded to what the article calls a structural crisis of capitalism, marked by technological monopoly, algorithmic exploitation, geopolitical conflict, ecological crisis and the rise of the Global South. Qiao's overall assessment is that the year's work kept the critical tradition alive and innovated in method, themes and practical paths. The review has three parts. The first covers work on established currents: early Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci), the Frankfurt School (including the 101st-anniversary lectures by Axel Honneth and Nancy Fraser) and post-Marxism (Laclau and Mouffe's radical democracy, biopolitics). The second covers ecological, spatial and digital critiques of capitalism. The third tracks changes in contemporary capitalism through Lenin's theory of imperialism, critiques of new imperialism and critiques of neoliberalism. Qiao reports each scholar's position and then adds a short evaluation. Post-Marxism is judged to have weakened class analysis and drifted into identity politics, so it should be assessed dialectically. Kohei Saito's "degrowth communism" is described as lacking textual basis in the late Marx, as vague in defining growth, and as utopian. In the digital section, Yanis Varoufakis, Slavoj Žižek and others argue that rent-driven "techno-feudalism" is replacing profit-driven capitalism. John Bellamy Foster is cited on the metabolic rift and on the continuing relevance of Lenin's imperialism theory. Qiao also reports Foster's rejection of the Western-left view that China and the United States are both imperialist powers. Qiao concludes that 2024 foreign Marxist research deepened the understanding of capitalism's essence and offered theoretical resources for global crises, and that the Global South received growing attention. The review also names weaknesses: academic insularity, weak explanatory and practical force, fragmentation and shifting positions. Qiao calls for strengthening wholeness and practical orientation within the framework of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a quick map of the 2024 foreign Marxist literature on digital capitalism, ecology, imperialism and neoliberalism, together with a Chinese academic evaluation of it.

Grasping the methodology for strengthening the Party's work style 把握加强党的作风建设的方法论 Wang Yanlong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2025, asks what methods underlie Xi Jinping's remarks on strengthening the Party's work style (作风建设) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang Yanlong argues that these remarks settled what to tackle and how to tackle it in work-style building under new conditions, and that they contain a coherent set of ways of thinking and working. Grasping this methodology, Wang says, would help create a clean political ecology and strengthen the Party's resolve to continue the effort. The piece is organised around four paired principles, each opened with a quotation from Xi: unifying the elimination of the "four undesirable work styles" with the establishment of new ones; unifying breadth of vision with attention to detail; unifying prevention with consolidation of foundations; and unifying clarity of direction with firm implementation. Each pair is tied to dialectical reasoning and illustrated with examples from the Party's recent practice. Wang's first move is to present each pair as dialectical. Breaking and establishing are said to be mutually dependent: positive models and the spirit of Chinese Communists are promoted so that bad habits can be removed, and clear rules replace unwritten ones. Second, the author treats the eight-point regulation of the Central Committee as an entry point that avoided piecemeal fixes, and treats "preventing illness before it arises" and "consolidating the foundations" as a way of treating both symptoms and root causes. This includes disciplinary education, the institutional drive for officials not to dare, not to be able and not to want to be corrupt, inspection systems and big-data supervision platforms. Third, clear direction is linked to contradiction analysis, and implementation to the law of quantitative change becoming qualitative change, the "nail-hammering" spirit. Wang cites 2024 figures from discipline inspection bodies: 118,000 cases of hedonism and extravagance, with 157,000 people criticised or punished, and 107,000 cases of formalism and bureaucracy, with 156,000 people. Wang concludes that work-style building is a protracted struggle with no end point. It requires precise targeting, sustained effort, and routine, institutionalised and long-term mechanisms, so that good work style becomes a permanent feature of the Party and the Party never changes in character. Work style is described as a matter of Party spirit and of popular support for the Party's governing position. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents work-style campaigns through dialectical method and recent enforcement figures.

Inheriting and carrying forward the great founding spirit of the Party to advance Chinese modernization A roundtable of four scholars, published for the Party's 104th anniversary 继承发扬伟大建党精神 推进中国式现代化建设 Wang Haokui This is a written roundtable, moderated by Guangming Daily reporter Wang Haokui and published on 1 July 2025, the Party's 104th anniversary. It asks how the great founding spirit of the Party can be carried forward in the new era, and how Chinese modernization can draw wisdom and strength from it. The four scholars treat the spirit as a continuing resource for the Party's central tasks, and the editors present it as guiding the Party's cause. The participants are Dai Yanjun (Central Party School), Yan Xiaofeng (School of Marxism, Tianjin University), Liu Jingbei (former deputy president of the China Executive Leadership Academy Pudong, East China Normal University) and Chen Jinlong (South China Normal University). The discussion has four sections, each tied to one element of the spirit: upholding truth and ideals; fulfilling the original aspiration and mission; fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely; and being loyal to the Party and living up to the people's trust. The last section is linked to the current Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. On truth and ideals, Dai argues that the Party has held to Marxism and adapted it to Chinese conditions, correcting errors through self-reform, while Yan calls for stronger ideals and convictions and counts losing them among the Party's distinctive problems as a large party. Chen and Liu read the Party's history as one of seeking the people's happiness and national rejuvenation, and Liu ties the original aspiration and mission to the Party's central task of advancing Chinese modernization, to high-quality development and to the new development philosophy. Chen traces the spirit of fighting bravely from the war of resistance to later episodes such as the Korean War, the "two bombs, one satellite" project and reform-era flood and earthquake relief, and Dai says it remains necessary for new technological, governance and national-security challenges. Liu and Yan treat conduct as a matter of Party spirit and of the Party's ties with the people, and argue that the eight-point regulation, rectifying the "four undesirable work styles" and linking work-style rectification with anti-corruption work are the means of staying loyal to the Party and the people. The participants conclude that the founding spirit should shape ideals, people-centred development, a readiness for struggle and Party conduct as China pursues the second centenary goal. They call for continued study and education, and for ending the pattern of campaigns that tighten and then relax. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the founding spirit in 2025 and tie it to Chinese modernization and Party conduct.

The great founding spirit of the Party: the wellspring of the Communist Party's spirit 伟大建党精神：中国共产党的精神之源 Qi Biao Writing in the People's Daily for the Party's anniversary in 2025, Qi Biao asks what it means to call the \"great founding spirit of the Party\" the \"wellspring of the Party's spirit\". The article treats the concept, introduced by Xi Jinping in his speech at the centenary in 2021, as an original conceptual label that deserves close study. Qi's thesis is that the founding spirit is the Party's spiritual source in three senses: it expresses the Party's essential nature, it is the origin of the Communist Party members' spiritual genealogy, and it explains why the Party stays vital. The piece has three main sections. The first traces how the Party has defined its own spirit, from Mao Zedong's and Deng Xiaoping's \"revolutionary spirit\" to Xi's work from 2005 onwards on the \"Red Boat spirit\" and the call to preserve the founders' fighting spirit. The second places the founding spirit within the \"spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists\", whose first list of 46 spirits was released in September 2021. The third links the founding spirit to the Party's vitality and to the problems facing a large, long-governing party. Qi reads the four-part formulation (upholding truth and ideals, practising the original mission, fearing no sacrifice, and being loyal to the Party and the people) as the Party's political soul, its fighting character and its purpose. The genealogy is described through four periods, from the Jinggangshan and Yan'an spirits to the poverty-alleviation and anti-epidemic spirits. In Qi's view, this genealogy records the nation's passage from \"standing up\" to \"becoming prosperous\" to \"becoming strong\", and it carries the Party's \"red genes\", which must not change. Qi argues that a party's vitality is measured by whether it keeps the striving spirit of its founding, not by how long it has existed. The article cites the Party's recoveries from setbacks, and the changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012), as products of a \"historical initiative\" spirit. Qi acknowledges that corruption and the \"four undesirable work styles\" conflict with the founding spirit and could pollute the Party's source if they spread. The article calls for the Party's self-reform, drawing on Xi's remarks on the \"unique problems of a large party\", so that the Party does not change in character and can escape the \"historical cycle of rise and fall\". It also calls for training successors to carry on the red genes. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party discourse positions the founding spirit within the Party's spiritual genealogy and its self-reform agenda.

The spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army as an important embodiment of the great founding spirit of the Party 东北抗联精神是伟大建党精神的重要体现 Liu Xinjun This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2025, asks how the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (Dongbei Kanglian) relates to the great founding spirit of the Party. Liu Xinjun argues that the former is a concrete unfolding and vivid embodiment of the latter, and a key component of the genealogy of Chinese Communists' spirit. The article first summarises the founding spirit as stated by Xi Jinping in 2021: upholding truth and ideals, staying true to the original aspiration and mission, fearing no sacrifice and fighting bravely, and being loyal to the Party and the people.
