It then sets out three features of the Northeast spirit and closes by tracing how each corresponds to the founding spirit. Liu identifies the three features as firm belief and loyalty to the Party, the national righteousness of going to the rescue of the nation, and the heroism of fighting to the death. Examples include Yang Jingyu's two westward expeditions to regain contact with the Central Committee, Zhao Shangzhi's loyalty despite two expulsions from the Party, and Zhao Yiman's conduct under torture. Liu then maps these features onto the founding spirit. Loyalty reflects upholding truth and ideals and loyalty to the Party and the people; defending the nation reflects the original aspiration and mission; and the long guerrilla struggle under harsh conditions reflects fearlessness and bravery. Liu concludes that the two spirits are in the same line of descent and that the Northeast spirit shows the depth of the founding spirit. Inheriting it is said to matter for strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence, for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party historians link a regional wartime spirit to the official genealogy of Communist spirit.

Critique of capitalism amid deepening technological monopoly and global fracture: responses and reconstruction Developments in foreign Marxism in 2024 技术垄断深化与全球秩序裂变下的资本主义批判：应答与重构 Qiao Ruihua This is an annual review of research in foreign Marxism (Marxism outside China) for 2024, published in World Socialism Studies in 2025. Qiao Ruihua asks how scholars outside China responded to what the article calls a structural crisis of capitalism, marked by technological monopoly, algorithmic exploitation, geopolitical conflict, ecological crisis and the rise of the Global South. The review concludes that foreign Marxism advanced in both theoretical critique and practical reconstruction, while remaining fragmented. The survey has three parts. The first covers traditional schools: early Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci), the Frankfurt School and post-Marxism. The second covers problem-oriented work on ecological, spatial and digital capitalism. The third tracks changes in contemporary capitalism, including Lenin's theory of imperialism, new imperialism and neoliberalism. Each section summarises individual scholars' books, lectures and conferences from 2024. Qiao highlights several positions. On the Frankfurt School, Axel Honneth called for a postcolonial rereading of critical theory, and Nancy Fraser argued that labour links gender, race and class. On post-Marxism, the review cites Clyde Barrow and others as showing a weakened focus on the working class, and Qiao judges that it drifts into identity politics. In ecological critique, John Bellamy Foster's metabolic-rift analysis is set against Kohei Saito's degrowth communism, which Qiao finds poorly grounded in Marx and utopian. In digital capitalism, Yanis Varoufakis's "technofeudalism" thesis, in which rent displaces profit, is presented alongside Žižek's similar diagnosis and warnings of a widening digital divide for the Global South. On imperialism, Foster's Monthly Review essay marking Lenin's centenary defends Lenin's theory and rejects Western-left claims that China and the US are equivalent imperial powers. Qiao concludes that 2024 research deepened the understanding of capitalism and supplied theoretical resources for addressing global crises. The review also finds weaknesses: academic insularity, fragmentation, wavering political stances and limited explanatory and practical force. It calls for greater coherence within a historical-materialist framework and a stronger practical orientation. Read the original if you want a broad, China-based survey of 2024 Western and international Marxist scholarship, with named authors and titles, and a sense of how Chinese reviewers assess it.

Review of the symposium on building a Chinese autonomous knowledge system of atheism “建构中国自主无神论知识体系”学术研讨会综述 Zhang Ge This is a report on an academic symposium, "Building a Chinese Autonomous Knowledge System of Atheism", held on 19 April 2025 by the editorial office of the journal Science and Atheism. The event took up Xi Jinping's 2022 call to build an autonomous Chinese system of knowledge in philosophy and the social sciences. The report presents atheism as the premise and foundation of Marxism, and as work that serves ideological security and the prevention of risks in the religious sphere. The meeting was chaired by Chen Zhigang, vice-president of the Academy of Marxism and editor-in-chief of the journal. More than twenty scholars and students attended, from the Central Institute of Socialism, the China Tibetology Research Center, the Ministry of Education, the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai Normal University, Beijing Technology and Business University and several CASS institutes. The report is arranged in three parts: theory and method; the disciplinary, academic, discourse and textbook systems; and the adaptation of Marxist atheism to Chinese conditions. On method, participants disagreed over emphasis. Gong Yun proposed five points, including basic conceptual research, patient specialist work and discursive innovation. Zuo Peng argued that Chinese atheism as a field must first exist as a body of knowledge before "autonomy" can be discussed, and that this requires an ontological demonstration that there are no gods and a critique of theology. On building the systems, Zhu Xiaoming proposed a four-part book series, from the classic writers' statements to an Introduction to Marxist Atheism and an Atheism Dictionary. Zhang Xinying warned that atheist teaching had been marginalised and called for a sub-discipline within religious studies and a postgraduate track. Zeng Chuanhui described the three systems as a closed loop of organisation, core and vehicle. On adapting Marxist atheism to China, Zhao Wenhong set out four academic missions: cultural, political, social and territorial security. Yao Hongyue proposed an academic path, from concepts to theory, and a practical path that analyses the social effects of Chinese theological systems. In closing, Chen Zhigang said his office would turn the goals into a roadmap and timetable, unite research teams nationwide and produce more short videos for mass audiences. Read the original if you want a record of the positions, institutions and proposed projects now shaping the official agenda for atheism research in China.

Guiding the great self-reform with the great founding spirit of the Party 以伟大建党精神引领伟大自我革命 Dai Lixing Guo Wenjing Dai Lixing and Guo Wenjing, in a commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2025), ask how the great founding spirit of the Party can guide the Party's great self-reform. They argue that the two are internally unified, and that the founding spirit supplies the moral and spiritual basis on which the Party's capacity for self-reform rests. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the mutual relationship between the founding spirit and self-reform, then explains the value the founding spirit brings to self-reform, and finally proposes practical paths tied to the "four selves". The authors read the founding spirit as four elements, each matched to a function. Seeking truth and holding to ideals gives belief and theoretical grounding; practising the original aspiration and shouldering the mission strengthens the Party's members and its people-first stance; fearlessness and heroic struggle supplies the will to turn the blade inward; loyalty to the Party and faithfulness to the people fixes political direction. Self-reform, in turn, is described as the founding spirit carried forward and put into practice, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. For practice, the authors call for stronger ideological and theoretical work, cultivation of Party spirit and a sense of responsibility, sustained discipline and anti-corruption work building on the "three no-corruptions", and people's supervision, with public satisfaction as the measure of results. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party scholars link founding-spirit rhetoric to the Party's self-reform agenda.

The scientific concept of developing green productive forces and its realisation 发展绿色生产力的科学理念及其实现 Zhang Yunfei Zhang Yunfei asks how green productive forces, understood as the driving force of building a Beautiful China, should be conceived and developed. The article argues that green productive forces are the inner character and direction of new quality productive forces, and that they can be developed only if the new development philosophy is applied as an internally unified whole and if the basic contradictions of society are transformed together. The article has three parts. The first explains why green productive forces are intrinsic to productive forces in general and to new quality productive forces in particular. The second takes the five elements of the new development philosophy (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) in turn and links each to green productive forces. The third applies the Marxist framework of the relations between productive forces, relations of production, economic base and superstructure. Zhang's central move is to define productive forces as the real capacity to realise the metabolism between humans and nature, so that harmony between the two is built into the concept. On this basis, traditional productive forces appear as "black" or "brown", and new quality productive forces as "green" in their objects of labour (information, data, knowledge), means of labour (digital tools) and labourers (combining intelligent and ecological literacy). Zhang then calls for uniting digital with green technology and economy, and for coordinating urban–rural, regional, river-basin and maritime development. The article also calls for "green" opening up to the world, and for ecological products to be supplied fairly to meet people's need for a beautiful environment. Finally, Zhang argues for a new ecological paradigm in productive forces, relations of production built on ecological compensation, public ownership of primordial natural goods with no privatisation, and a state with stronger public governance. Zhang also argues for dropping the view of productive forces as the power to conquer nature. Zhang concludes that green productive forces can become the sustainable fundamental driver and economic foundation of a Beautiful China if the new development philosophy guides them and the whole social structure changes accordingly. Zhang presents Xi Jinping's statements on the subject as the basic guide and calls for further deepening reform in line with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist-ecological account of how new quality productive forces, ecological civilisation and the basic contradictions of society are linked in policy terms.

All-round human development: the essential requirement of Chinese modernization 人的全面发展：中国式现代化的本质要求 Zhou Hang Niu Xianfeng Zhou Hang and Niu Xianfeng ask how Chinese modernization relates to Marx's idea of the all-round development of the human being. They argue that the all-round development of the person is the essential requirement and fundamental value of Chinese modernization, which they present as both an economic and social modernization and a path by which people's needs, free and conscious practice, free individuality and social relations are progressively enriched. The article begins from Marx's statement that man appropriates his all-round essence in an all-round way, as a total man. The authors read this as three levels of essence: the species essence of free conscious activity, the social essence as the ensemble of social relations, and the individual essence as free individuality. From this they derive four yardsticks, which structure the article: human needs, labour practice, social relations and free individuality. Four sections apply them in turn to Chinese modernization, drawing on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On needs, the authors hold that material and spiritual needs must be met together, and that needs and production stimulate one another. They cite the primary stage of socialism, high-quality development, new quality productive forces and cultural policy as means to this end. On free and conscious practice, they contend that the basic economic system, the people's congress system and whole-process people's democracy secure the institutional conditions, while common prosperity and technological innovation supply the material base and free time that Marx saw as necessary. On free individuality, they use Marx's three stages (dependence on persons, dependence on things, free individuality). In their account, Chinese modernization removes dependence on persons, treats material things as a means to human ends rather than following the logic of capital, and encourages creativity through educational reform. On social relations, the authors argue that public ownership as the main body, Party leadership, the political institutions and a shared sense of community for the Chinese nation prevent exploitation and class antagonism. They say these create harmonious relations among people, with nature and among ethnic groups. They conclude that the modernization of the human being is its essential requirement, and that Chinese modernization is the necessary path to all-round human development and comprehensive social progress. Read the original if you want to see how Party School scholars connect Marx's theory of human development to current official concepts of Chinese modernization.

A political-economy analysis of "techno-feudalism" “技术封建主义”的政治经济学分析 Pan Yue Cheng Enfu Pan Yue and Cheng Enfu examine the "techno-feudalism" thesis advanced by left-wing scholars such as Cédric Durand, Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean. Varoufakis claims that rent has defeated profit, that "cloudalists" rather than the proletariat will end bourgeois rule, and that techno-feudalism rather than socialism will replace capitalism. The authors answer that digital platforms have not surpassed capitalism. In their reading, "cloud rent" is a form of ground-rent-like income that ultimately derives from surplus value created by wage labour. The article first reconstructs the theory's categories: cloud capital, cloudalists, cloud fiefs, cloud rent and cloud serfs. It then defines digital space and digital platforms as the "land" on which people work and live, and sets out a classification of platforms. The next sections explain how platform monopoly generates rent and apply Marx's theory of ground rent to e-commerce platforms. The final section assesses the theory's claims about markets, profit and historical trend. The core move is an analogy with Marx's rent theory. Platform ownership, the authors argue, is ownership of virtual labour space, and platform revenue combines interest on invested capital with true "cloud rent" (which they call "platform rent"). They identify differential platform rent I and II, arising from uneven traffic and from additional investment, and absolute platform rent. The latter is illustrated with a formula showing that e-commerce shortens circulation and reduces commercial capital, yielding excess profit. Monopoly platform rent rests on monopoly prices. They also argue that data rent is only a surface phenomenon, since monopoly of digital space underlies it. The authors conclude that markets and profit have not disappeared, because exchange persists even where platforms isolate buyers from one another. Cloud rent is paid out of production, merchants' profit or workers' wages, so it derives from industrial workers' labour. They see techno-feudalism as a technological extension of capitalist relations that intensifies exploitation and monopoly and accelerates capitalism's decline. They credit the theory with exposing digital capitalism but fault its metaphor of regression and its neglect of the proletariat's historical role. Read the original if you want a Marxist rent-theory critique of Varoufakis and Durand, including the e-commerce rent model.

Structural transformation of the qualitative forms of productive forces and its practical implications An interpretation based on Capital and its manuscripts 生产力质态的结构性变革及其现实启示 Ding Xiaoqin Hou Wanyue Marking the 140th anniversary of the publication of Volume II of Capital, Ding Xiaoqin and Hou Wanyue reread Marx's theory of productive forces in Capital and its manuscripts to clarify what they call the 'qualitative form' (zhitai) of productive forces. They argue that Marx's analysis, in which transformations of this form underpin the rise of capitalism and the succession of social formations, provides the theoretical basis for understanding new quality productive forces. The authors present Xi Jinping's statements on the concept as a terminological and methodological innovation in Marxist productive-force theory. The article has four parts. It first defines the structure of productive forces through three kinds of natural force. It then traces how a new qualitative form emerged under machine-based large-scale industry, moving from simple cooperation to manufacture to the machine system. Next it turns to Marx's remarks on how productive forces would develop in a future society. The last part draws implications for developing new quality productive forces in China. The core argument distinguishes three natural forces and the productive forces that correspond to them: the labourer's own physical and mental capacities (individual productive force), the forces of nature applied through tools and machinery (social natural productive force), and the force of socially organised labour through cooperation and division of labour. The authors hold that the qualitative form of productive forces has three layers: substantive elements, science and technology, and modes of organisation. In their reading, the move from manufacture to machine industry marked a qualitative leap, because science and natural forces were incorporated into production, mental and manual labour separated, and the machine system became the material carrier of knowledge and a ruler over living labour. Under capitalism, they say, all three productive forces appear as capital's productive forces and can turn into destructive forces, including ecological ones. In a future society, they argue, machines would become the common property of associated workers, labour would become free labour, and surplus labour and free time would return to the producers. The authors conclude that new quality productive forces mark a transitional stage between the qualitative leap of capitalist productive forces and the productive forces of a future society. They call for upgrading in three areas: comprehensive optimisation of substantive elements, with science and technology innovation in the lead and attention to social factors; a harmonious reconstruction of the relation between production and ecology, with green development as the foundation; and a qualitative leap in how production factors are combined, with public ownership, self-reliance in core technologies and international scientific cooperation. Read the original if you want a close reading of Capital, Volume II and the manuscripts used to ground the theory of new quality productive forces.

"One Step Forward, Two Steps Back": Lenin's critique of the Menshevik view of organisation and its present-day lessons 《进一步，退两步》批判孟什维克关于组织的观点及其现实启示 Huang Rongsheng Liu Dongxu Huang and Liu revisit Lenin's polemical work One Step Forward, Two Steps Back (written February–May 1904) to ask what its critique of the Menshevik view of organisation says about building a proletarian party. They argue that Lenin exposed the substance and harm of Menshevik organisational ideas and set out basic principles of party-building that still apply. Writing in 2025, they present the text as guidance for the Chinese Communist Party's drive to strengthen the political and organisational functions of Party organisations, as called for by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article has five sections. Four reconstruct Lenin's rebuttals of Martov and the Mensheviks on four issues: blurred membership boundaries, the party's relation to trade unions and mass organisations, "autonomism" versus centralism, and party discipline. The fifth draws four lessons for the present: building a tightly knit organisational system, upholding the authority of the Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership, upholding and improving democratic centralism, and tightening Party discipline and rules. In the authors' reading, Lenin held that the party must be an organised whole and not a loose political alliance, and that it must be kept distinct from the class. They also report his view that the party leads unions and other mass organisations, which cannot stand outside its guidance. Centralism, he argued, must be written into party rules, because the minority must yield to the majority and the part to the whole. The authors distinguish this from bureaucratic centralism. They say Lenin traced Menshevik hostility to discipline to the psychology of bourgeois intellectuals, whereas the factory trains workers in organisation. For Lenin, discipline rests on Marxism and binds leaders as much as ordinary members. The authors conclude that Lenin's critique offers a model for the Party's full and rigorous self-governance. They call for optimised grassroots organisations, higher-quality members, strengthened Party political-building, and better mechanisms to implement central decisions. They also propose education in democratic centralism, a more developed system of Party regulations, and stronger enforcement of political discipline. They cite Xi Jinping on persistent problems such as weakened implementation of Party leadership, "deliberation without decision" and disregard of discipline. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school style reading links Lenin's 1904 organisational polemic to current Party-building doctrine.

Why the September 18 Incident was the beginning of the Second World War 九一八事变何以是第二次世界大战的开端 Lu Xiaona Lu Xiaona asks why the September 18 Incident of 1931, Japan's seizure of north-east China, should be treated as the start of both China's War of Resistance and the Second World War. The author argues that the debate is not only about a date: it bears on the global standing of China's resistance and on China's international voice in writing the history of the war. This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, is organised under four headings. They cover the collapse of the old order, the continuity of aggression and the universality of resistance, the responsibility of the great powers, and the historical agency of the world's peoples. Lu rejects the common distinction between the "world anti-fascist war" and the Second World War as having different starting points, calling them two sides of one war. In the author's account, Japan's aggression was the first fascist challenge to the Versailles–Washington system, and Western appeasement and the League of Nations' inaction let the order collapse. Lu also holds that Japan gave Germany and Italy a model and helped lay the basis of the Axis, and that anti-fascist resistance by many peoples began after 1931, not only when Britain and France entered the war. Lu blames the great powers' self-interested calculations for the League's failure. Lu concludes that dating the war from 1931 warns that no state can stand aside from aggression and that major powers should impose firm sanctions instead of appeasing. It would also acknowledge China's role as the main eastern anti-fascist theatre and challenge a "Western-centred" narrative that, in the author's view, marginalises China, Africa and Oceania. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the Chinese academic case for 1931 as the start of the Second World War.

Building Party conduct on the foundation of firm ideals and convictions 以坚定理想信念为根基推进作风建设 Zhang Yanman Writing as the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation is under way, Zhang takes up the question of how to build Party conduct on a lasting footing. Quoting Xi Jinping's call to "return to basics and strengthen the foundation", the commentary argues that firm ideals and convictions must be treated as a lifelong task. In Zhang's view they are the root of work on conduct and of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece has three parts. The first explains why firm convictions are the foundation of founding and strengthening the Party. The second surveys how the Party has pursued ideal-and-conviction education across four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third sets out five routes for strengthening convictions today. Zhang argues that convictions are a weapon for keeping the Party advanced and pure, the base of its long-term governing strength and an essential requirement for its central tasks. In the historical survey, the author lists measures such as the Party's minimum and maximum programmes, the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention, rectification campaigns, discipline inspection bodies and the series of study-and-education campaigns since the new era began. The five routes are: raising theoretical level in Marxism; remembering the founding mission and "matters of national importance"; strengthening cultural confidence and intra-Party political culture; self-reform and a readiness to struggle; and education backed by Party regulations and institutions. Zhang presents these as a path from knowing to believing to acting. Zhang concludes that convictions must be cultivated throughout life and tied to study of innovative Party theory, self-cultivation and practical work. The author calls for deeper grasp of the Two Establishes, strengthened awareness and confidence, and the Two Upholds, together with institutional rules that make conviction education routine. The goal, in this account, is to supply a firm political guarantee for building a strong country and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party-building discourse links ideological conviction, institutional discipline and conduct work in 2025.

Building an ideological and political education system that consolidates the foundation and forges the soul 构建固本铸魂的思想政治教育体系 Chen Diming Writing in a Party journal in 2025, Chen Diming takes up the call in the Outline for Building a Strong Education Nation (2024–2035), issued in January by the Central Committee and the State Council, to build an ideological and political education system that "consolidates the foundation and forges the soul". Chen argues that universities, as frontline positions of socialist ideological work, must make moral education the central task. They must also run ideological and political work through the whole of teaching, in order to train a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first explains why such a system matters, the second sets out what it means, and the third proposes practical measures. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements, including his speech at the 2024 National Education Conference, and on a Ministry of Education document on university ideological and political work. Chen gives four reasons for the system's importance. It follows from the political requirement of Party leadership over universities and from the need to raise the quality of ideological and political education amid global change and the pressure of AI and network technology. It is also needed to put moral education into practice among students who are still forming their values. On meaning, Chen describes a system that has political, popular and strategic attributes. It consists of seven linked sub-systems: theoretical armament, discipline teaching, daily education, management and services, security and stability, staffing, and evaluation and supervision. It also balances high-quality development with high-level security, so that graduates are firm supporters of the Party and the socialist system. For implementation, Chen calls for stronger top-level design under Party committees, using Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Chen also calls for better teacher training and ethics, and for following the laws governing ideological work, teaching and student growth. The proposals include making classrooms the main channel, encouraging student self-education and building converged-media platforms. Chen concludes that such a system will realise education that involves all staff, covers the whole process and reaches every dimension, and will open a new stage for higher education. In this account, it will also ensure that young people "listen to the Party and follow the Party". Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated university leaders present the policy framework and priorities of ideological and political education in the drive to build a strong education nation.

Mastering investigation and research as a basic skill 掌握调查研究这个基本功 Niu Xianfeng Niu Xianfeng takes up Xi Jinping's repeated call for cadres to master diaoyan, "investigation and research", as a basic skill of governance. The article argues that this practice is the concentrated expression of Marxist world outlook and methodology, a family heirloom of the Party, and an urgent requirement for tackling the problems met in advancing Chinese modernization. It situates the call in a sequence running from the first of the Eight-point Regulations (2012), through Xi's 2021 Central Party School speech, to the 2023 work plan on promoting investigation and research across the Party. The piece is organised in four parts. It first explains why investigation and research embodies Marxist epistemology and the mass viewpoint, tracing the practice to Mao Zedong's 1930 Xunwu investigation. It then argues that mastering the skill requires adherence to the Party's ideological line and to the mass line, and closes with the methods needed to do it well. Throughout, Niu builds the case mainly from Xi's remarks, supplemented by Mao's. Niu's core move is to tie the practice to two Party principles. On the ideological line, seeking truth from facts is split into \"facts\" (starting from reality, rejecting perfunctory or pre-scripted visits) and \"truth\" (analysing raw material to find underlying regularities), so that conclusions come after investigation rather than before it. On the mass line, investigation is presented as going to the people, listening to them and drawing on their creative practice, which the author links to meeting the principal contradiction of the new era and to high-quality development. On method, Niu calls for a solid work style and sincere motives, a problem-oriented approach, and a focus on practical results. The author treats staged, \"bonsai\" or token inspections as formalism and bureaucratism rooted in a distorted view of political achievement. Niu concludes that deep, rigorous research is a precondition for sound decisions in further comprehensively deepening reform and for moving towards national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Party-school discourse frames investigation and research within the Party's ideological line, mass line and the 2025 campaign on the Eight-point Regulations.

Improving Party conduct is always a work in progress 作风建设永远在路上 Liu Xiaoxin This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that improving Party conduct (zuofeng jianshe) is "always on the road" and must be pursued without relaxation. Liu Xiaoxin argues that conduct is tied to the Party's image, to popular support and to its survival. The piece is written to support the study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point decision on conduct. The article has three parts. The first explains why conduct matters, the second reviews the Party's record on conduct in four historical periods, and the third sets out how to win what Liu calls a "tough and protracted battle" on conduct. The historical survey runs from the New Democratic Revolution through the socialist revolution and construction and the reform era to the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu argues that conduct is required by the Party's nature and purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, that it decides the success of the Party's cause, and that it sets the tone for social customs. On this basis Liu holds that Chinese modernization will meet serious risks, which call for stricter Party governance and the Party's self-reform. The historical review stresses Mao Zedong's "three major styles", the Yan'an rectification campaigns, the post-1949 rectification drives and the 2001 and 2009 decisions on conduct. It treats the eight-point decision adopted in December 2012 as the first major Party regulation of the 18th Party Congress era, and credits Xi Jinping's personal example with a decisive role in its implementation. For the future, Liu calls for three measures. The first is to focus on the "key minority" of leading cadres and lead from the top down. The second is to turn conduct work into regular, standardised and lasting practice through institutions with clear red lines. The third is to investigate and address undesirable work styles and corruption together, since Liu says they share a root, by tracing corruption from conduct problems and conduct problems from corruption. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party commentary frames the history and current tasks of conduct building and the eight-point decision.

The strategic role of universities in integrating scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation 发挥高校在科技创新与产业创新融合发展中的战略作用 Ren Shaobo Ren Shaobo, Party Secretary of Zhejiang University, asks how universities can help integrate scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. Ren argues that technological innovation is the endogenous driving force of industrial innovation, while industrial innovation is where technological innovation realises its value. Universities, in this account, are the key link between science and technology, talent and innovation. They should build a mutually reinforcing system of talent training, technological innovation and the commercialisation of results, in support of high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, is organised in four parts, each opening with Xi Jinping's statements and Party documents, including the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and the Third Plenum decision (2024). Each part names shortcomings in current university practice and then proposes remedies. The four parts cover raising innovation capacity and the supply of original research, recruiting and developing talent, connecting the innovation chain through commercialisation and start-up incubation, and building an innovation and entrepreneurship ecosystem. Ren first holds that universities have too little strategic weight in the national innovation system, supply too little original research and lack well-organised, goal-oriented research. Remedies include strengthening basic and interdisciplinary research, building high-level platforms such as national key laboratories, and reforming collaborative mechanisms so that the innovation, industrial, talent and funding chains are joined up. On talent, Ren calls for strategic talent maps, easier flows of personnel among universities, institutes and firms, "talent special zones" and evaluation reform. The third and fourth parts propose entrepreneurship education, incubation through university science parks and proof-of-concept centres, university-run venture funds offering "patient capital", and shared-benefit arrangements with firms and alumni. Ren concludes that universities should act as the source of innovation and as drivers of industry, and so cultivate new quality productive forces. The article presents this as a way to support Chinese modernization and the building of China as a leading country in education. It treats alumni networks, regional culture and flexible intellectual-property arrangements with firms as parts of one ecosystem centred on universities. Read the original if you want a university Party leader's detailed, policy-oriented account of how Chinese universities are being steered towards technology transfer, talent mobility and industry partnership.

An interpretation of "standing on the right side of history" through historical materialism “站在历史正确的一边”的唯物史观阐释 Tang Aijun Xi Jinping has repeatedly called on China to "stand on the right side of history". This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks what the phrase means when read through historical materialism. Tang Aijun argues that historical materialism supplies the basic theoretical framework for interpreting it, and that the phrase asks historical agents to choose correctly at a historical crossroads. The article has three parts. The first sets out the context in which the formulation appears: a world history of growing interdependence, set against sluggish economic recovery, unilateralism, protectionism and what the author calls hegemonic bullying. The second gives the underlying philosophical logic in three points. The third draws out practical requirements for the historical subject. Tang's core move is to reconcile historical determinism with subjective choice. History advances in a spiral, with setbacks and "countercurrents", so that its actual course has a right and a wrong side. Because, in Marx and Engels's words in The Holy Family, it is real, living people who make history, agents can act correctly or incorrectly. Tang then names three senses of the "right side": grasping and applying historical laws; discerning the great trends of the age, by looking at the past, seeing essences behind appearances, identifying the principal contradiction and finding certainty amid uncertainty; and standing with human progress. For the last, Tang takes productive-force development as the objective measure and the free and all-round development of the individual as the subjective measure. This means serving the interests of the great majority, upholding historical justice and international morality, and promoting shared human values. Tang concludes that the right side of history demands an active historical spirit, summed up in three tasks: "observe the broad trends", "respond to changes" and "turn crises into opportunities". The author presents these as drawing on the dialectical conversion of danger into opportunity and as calling for a fighting spirit under geopolitical pressure. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists ground a leader's slogan on international affairs in historical-materialist philosophy.

Inheriting and promoting the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression in the new era 在新时代继承和弘扬伟大抗战精神 Liu Guangming Published in the People's Daily on 27 June 2025, ahead of the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary asks how the "great spirit of resistance" should be inherited and promoted today. Liu Guangming argues that this spirit, forged in the war, remains a precious moral resource for the new journey of building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Facing foreseeable and unforeseeable risks, the author holds, the country must keep advancing precisely where things are hardest and most dangerous. The article has three parts. The first sets out the spirit's content, following Xi Jinping's four-part formulation: patriotism of shared responsibility for the nation's fate, national integrity of preferring death to surrender, heroism of fighting to the end without fear of violence, and a firm belief in victory. The second explains its value for the present. The third sets out how to turn it into practice on the new journey. Each element is traced back to figures from Chinese history, such as Fan Zhongyan, Wen Tianxiang, Zheng Chenggong and Yu Gong, and then to wartime examples, including the Battle of Shanghai, Pingxingguan, Taierzhuang and the Hundred Regiments Offensive. Liu's central claim is that the spirit was forged under the leadership of the Communist Party, which Liu calls the "mainstay" of the national resistance and its chief cultivator. The author attributes to the Party the united front, the line of all-out resistance, the protracted-war strategy and guerrilla warfare. Liu also argues that the spirit turned a latent trait of courage and self-strengthening in the national character into an active one, so that the nation was spiritually reborn after repeated defeats in the modern period. For the new journey, Liu calls for converting the spirit into strategic initiative, extraordinary courage and strong strategic resolve. In practice this means studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, relying on one's own strength, pressing ahead with deepened reform, law-based governance and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including a zero-tolerance anti-corruption campaign. It also means holding steady against pressure and containment from hostile forces while advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how Party-state discourse links the memory of the anti-Japanese war to present-day political mobilisation and to the 2025 commemorations.

Memories of the War of Resistance in the archives of the Hundred Regiments Offensive 百团大战档案中的抗战记忆 Gui Tengfei Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), this short piece in Study Times reads a set of documents held in the Central Archives to recall the Hundred Regiments Offensive. Gui Tengfei presents the campaign, fought by the Eighth Route Army in North China from August 1940 to January 1941, as the largest and longest strategic offensive the Communist-led army launched in the war. The article draws on orders and telegrams signed by Zhu De, Peng Dehuai and Zuo Quan, including the preparatory order of 22 July 1940 and the campaign deployment of 8 August on breaking the Zhengtai railway. It also cites later directives on naming the campaign, the second-stage plan, anti-'mopping-up' planning, and a 1940 statistical report on mobilisation in central Shanxi. It is organised under four headings: taking the initiative, flexible adaptation, hard struggle, and unity of army and people. Gui argues that in summer 1940 Japan's 'cage policy' in North China, setbacks on the Nationalist front and talk of peace had left the country pessimistic, so a victory was needed. According to the article, the original plan of 22 regiments grew to 105 regiments and about 200,000 troops as units joined on their own initiative. The author describes three phases with shifting tactics, improvised methods of sabotage and 'home-made' weapons against fortified lines, and says the fighters endured heavily armed opponents through sheer persistence. Civilians, militia and local organisations supplied intelligence, transport and labour; Gui cites a Japanese staff officer's recollections to show Japanese forces facing a 'sea' of people's war. Gui concludes that the offensive struck the cage policy, tied down Japanese troops, raised the prestige of the Party and the Eighth Route Army, and reversed low morale nationwide, further proving the Communist-led forces' role as the 'mainstay' of resistance. The article says its patriotic spirit offers lasting inspiration for staying true to the Party's founding mission. Read the original if you want a brief, officially framed account of the Hundred Regiments Offensive that shows which archival documents are being highlighted in the 2025 anniversary commemorations.

The great founding spirit of the Party: the spiritual source of the Communist Party of China 伟大建党精神：中国共产党的精神之源 Zeng Yi Zeng Yi's commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, asks why the "great founding spirit of the Party" is described as the "source" of the Communist Party of China's spirit. The article notes that Xi Jinping first put forward the formulation in 2021 at the centenary of the Party, and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) wrote "carrying forward the great founding spirit" into its theme. Zeng argues that the spirit is both the starting point of the Party's lineage of spirit and its guiding thread, expressing the Party's political character. The piece is organised around two attributes of the founding spirit, which Zeng calls narrative and theoretical. It first traces the spirit to the founders' own intellectual paths, citing Li Dazhao, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Liu Shaoqi on how they came to Marxism. It then reads the 32-character formula in two halves, drawing on Mao's writings, Engels's graveside speech, early Party congress documents and recent statements by Xi. Zeng argues that "source" has two senses: origin ("源头") and root ("本源"). As origin, the spirit stems from the Party's creation and from a national awakening in which Marxism was combined with China's concrete realities and traditional culture. As root, its first two phrases, on upholding truth and ideals and on the original aspiration and mission, answer what the Party is to do, namely its political ideal and goal. Its last two phrases, on fearlessness in struggle and on loyalty to the Party and to the people, answer what the Party is, namely its political essence and foundation. Zeng links these to the Party's growth from about fifty members to nearly 100 million and to what the author calls the twin miracles of rapid growth and long-term stability. Zeng concludes that the founding spirit answers the fundamental question of what the Communist Party is and what it intends to do, summarises the political nature of a Marxist party, and points to the focus of Party political building. On this view it will encourage the whole Party to move forward and provide political assurance for building a strong country and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the founding spirit as the root of the Party's spiritual lineage, together with the historical quotations used to support that reading.

Fine conduct shows the Party's personality strength 优良作风彰显党的人格力量 Wang Yu Wang Yu's commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, asks how the Communist Party of China wins public trust and secures its long-term rule. The author argues that, alongside the "power of truth" embodied in correct theory, the Party has a "power of personality" that shows itself chiefly in its fine conduct, and that sustained work on conduct is therefore essential in the new era. The piece first defines "personality strength" as the outward effect of inner moral qualities, which attracts and unites followers. It then names the three fine styles in which this strength is concentrated. It ends with a historical survey of Party conduct-building from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wang's central claim is that the power of truth and the power of personality complement each other: theory without personality strength is pale and unconvincing, while personality strength gives theory its reach. The three fine styles are linking theory with practice, maintaining close ties with the masses, and criticism and self-criticism. In the author's account, these respectively guard against dogmatism, keep the Party serving the people, and let it correct itself, creating a virtuous circle between Party and people. Wang concludes that conduct-building is the key route by which the Party shows its personality strength, because ordinary people judge the Party by the behaviour of the Party members around them. The article credits the eight-point rule (2012), the campaign against the "four malpractices" and long-term institution-building with renewing Party and government conduct. It also calls for perseverance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media link conduct-building to the Party's legitimacy and public support.

Extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grass roots 推动全面从严治党向基层延伸 Qi Weiping This short commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to keep extending full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grass roots. Qi argues that the grass roots are the foundation of the Party's governing position, so Party building and grass-roots governance must be guaranteed by rigorous Party discipline. The article is organised around three tasks: making anti-corruption work in people's everyday surroundings tangible to ordinary people, fostering an atmosphere in which grass-roots cadres dare to act, and ensuring that livelihood policies are carried out locally. It opens with the 'tigers and flies' anti-corruption approach and ends with policy implementation. On corruption, Qi argues that 'petty corruption' at the grass roots must be brought within the anti-corruption campaign, since unresolved cadre corruption would impair state governance and weaken the Party's credibility. Extension downward means greater intensity, not just wider coverage, and Qi proposes linking discipline inspection and supervision with grass-roots inspection tours. On cadres, Qi notes that the country has over 5.17 million grass-roots Party organisations and that 'lying flat' and reckless action persist. Qi proposes positive incentives, fair selection and promotion, training and job rotation. On livelihood policy, Qi proposes making policy delivery a key assessment indicator, holding inactive cadres accountable and opening channels for public oversight. Qi concludes that grass-roots cadres must unite Party spirit with the people's interests, so that people feel the Party's care through concrete benefits. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the grass-roots dimension of Party discipline and anti-corruption work in 2025.

Strengthening ecological civilization education in universities 加强高校生态文明教育 Guo Yongyuan Zhang Keyan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks how universities should carry out ecological civilization education. Guo and Zhang argue that it must be built into the national education system under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization. They present this as part of training a new generation committed to a socialist ecological civilization outlook and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The authors begin from the Party's policy documents on building a Beautiful China. They then describe the content of Xi's ecological thought and set out proposals in four areas: teaching and curriculum, scientific research, international exchange, and institutional design. Guo and Zhang claim that Western models of ecological governance have achieved little against global problems such as climate change and species loss. In their account, Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization brings a revolution in discourse at the ontological, axiological and methodological levels. They therefore call for it to guide classroom teaching, textbooks, student activities and school management. They propose strengthening ideological and political courses, compiling new textbooks, and using Marxism to revive fine traditional ecological culture. They also call for a research chain running from green projects to green products, and for university think tanks. The authors conclude that universities should add ecological education to international exchange, telling China's story abroad. They also propose school-level planning, regulation and an evaluation system, so that students adopt green, low-carbon lifestyles and take part in building a Beautiful China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party discourse sets out the tasks of ecological education in higher education.

The theoretical innovation and practical power of the thesis that "humanity and nature are a community of life" “人与自然是生命共同体”重要论断的理论创新和实践伟力 Yu Hai Yu Hai takes up the thesis, put forward by Xi Jinping in the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), that humanity and nature form a community of life and that people must respect, adapt to and protect nature. The article argues that this thesis is a major theoretical innovation: it rests on Marxism, on traditional Chinese ecological culture and on long practical exploration, and it carries real weight in practice. Yu says it is central to grasping Chinese modernization and to advancing the building of a Beautiful China. The commentary, a newspaper theory piece, looks at the thesis in historical, theoretical and practical terms. It first traces its three sources. It then sets out the basic requirements for implementing it, reviews the achievements recorded since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with the international dimension of building a clean and beautiful world. On the sources, Yu reads the thesis as continuing Marx's view that humans are products of nature, and as drawing on classical Chinese texts such as the Laozi, Mencius, Xunzi and the Book of Rites. Yu also traces it to Xi's local posts in Zhengding, Xiamen, Ningde, Sanming and Shanghai, where Xi stressed both preventing pollution and the economic value of green mountains and clear waters. The requirements are to plan development from the standpoint of harmony between humanity and nature, to treat respecting, adapting to and protecting nature as a dialectical unity, and to balance high-quality development with high-level protection. Yu argues that China, with over 1.4 billion people and limited environmental capacity, cannot follow the Western path. The article cites progress in air and water quality, green and low-carbon transition, ecosystem protection, the dual carbon goals and institutional reform. Examples include average PM2.5 falling from 72 to 29.3 micrograms per cubic metre between 2013 and 2024, and 90.4% of surface-water sections rated Class I–III in 2024. Yu concludes that the thesis offers direction for international cooperation. The article calls for joint action on climate change under multilateralism and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, for biodiversity governance, and for cooperation on desertification, marine pollution and nuclear safety. It also calls for a green Belt and Road Initiative, which Yu presents as contributing Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to global ecological governance. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese ecological civilization theory is framed and which achievements it cites.

Marx's notebooks on religion in MEGA2 and their theoretical value MEGA2版中马克思的宗教笔记及其理论价值 Chen Suwen Marx's reading notebooks, collected in the fourth division of MEGA2 (the historical-critical edition of the Marx-Engels complete works), are described by Chen as the 'workshop and laboratory' of his thought. This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks what two little-studied notebooks of 1840–1842 reveal about the young Marx. Chen argues that they are Marx's only two religion-themed notebooks and that together they record his intellectual 'awakening' before historical materialism. The article first introduces the Berlin Notebooks (1840–1841), excerpts from Aristotle, Leibniz, Hume and Spinoza, and the Bonn Notebooks (1842), excerpts on art and the history of religion, including works by Rumohr, Creuzer, de Brosses and Benjamin Constant. It then clarifies what 'religiosity' means, sketches Marx's religious upbringing and Young Hegelian circle, and explains the political pressure of the Prussian state after 1840. It closes by locating the notebooks within Marx's development. Chen's central claim is that the notebooks served a double critique. Marx regarded Feuerbach's The Essence of Christianity (1841) as having settled the purely Christian question, yet the political and philosophical problems tied to religion remained. He faced the official philosophy of Schelling and the Young Hegelians, above all Bruno Bauer, whose work Chen calls theology in another form. Chen reads the Berlin Notebooks as a philosophical approach to religion, drawing on thinkers with a rudimentary materialism. The Bonn Notebooks, with their material on fetishism and natural religion, take an anthropological and sociological approach. Chen concludes that the notebooks show Marx already moving against idealism, a move Chen describes as 'leaving Germany' and a 'French turn'. The Aristotle excerpts signal a reaction against the German theoretical tradition, while the French works on fetishism and religion point towards French materialism and socialist and communist ideas. Chen stresses that this stage was still far from the maturity marked by The German Ideology. Read the original if you want a brief orientation to the Berlin and Bonn Notebooks and to how a Chinese scholar places them in the young Marx's development.

Historical experience of Party membership building during the War of Resistance The period of the nationwide war of resistance against Japan 全民族抗战时期党员队伍建设的历史经验 Wang Rui This short commentary asks how the Communist Party of China handled the tension between expanding its membership and maintaining its quality during the nationwide War of Resistance against Japan. Wang argues that the Party resolved this creatively. According to the article, membership grew from just over 40,000 at the start of the war to more than 1.2 million by 1945, while the Party's vanguard character and purity were preserved. The article is organised around three experiences: balancing breadth with vanguard quality in recruitment standards, combining theoretical education with practical training, and combining strict discipline with care for members. Wang draws on Party resolutions of 1935–1941, the 1942 rectification campaign and the Seventh Party Congress. Wang traces how recruitment standards shifted. The Wayaobao meeting (1935) made willingness to struggle for Party policy the main criterion, and a 1938 resolution called for recruiting members tenfold and a hundredfold. After rapid expansion harmed quality, a 1939 decision urged quality over quantity. Wang then describes ideological education, the rectification campaign and practical tests such as rent reduction, production drives and guerrilla warfare. Finally, Wang points to a disciplinary system applied equally to ordinary members and leaders, paired with a policy of "examination and promotion in equal measure" and the principle of curing the illness to save the patient. Wang concludes that these practices provided an organisational guarantee for victory in the war and in the New Democratic Revolution, and contributed to Marxist party-building theory. The author also holds that they offer lessons for advancing the new great project of Party building in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of wartime Party recruitment, education and discipline, with references to key Party documents.

The landmark significance of the Seventh Party Congress in the history of Party building 党的七大在党的建设史上的里程碑意义 Li Ying Marking the 80th anniversary of the Seventh Party Congress (April–June 1945), Li Ying, a researcher at the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, argues in this newspaper commentary that the congress was a landmark in the history of Party building. Li notes that Xi Jinping visited the congress site at Yangjialing in Yan'an in October 2022 and called for telling its story well. In Li's account, the congress developed Mao Zedong's thinking on Party building, substantially revised the Sixth Congress constitution, and formally formed the Party's first generation of central collective leadership with Mao Zedong at its core. The article has three main sections. The first reviews Mao's reports and speeches at the congress, including On Coalition Government, the oral political report and the concluding speech. The second examines the 1945 Party Constitution and its changes from the 1928 version. The third traces how the leadership collective took shape, from the Zunyi Meeting through the 1943 reorganisation of central bodies to the election of the Seventh Central Committee. On Mao's thinking, Li stresses the 'three work styles': integrating theory with practice, close ties with the masses, and self-criticism, which Mao presented as marks distinguishing the Party from all other parties. Li also covers Mao's treatment of Party spirit and individuality as a dialectical unity, relations among different groups of cadres, and speaking truthfully. On the constitution, Li identifies four innovations: a General Programme added for the first time; a clear definition of the Party's nature; the first statement of four duties and four rights of members, with rules on age and on leaving the Party; and a fuller formulation of democratic centralism with 'four subordinations'. On leadership, Li argues that Mao's position was reached through correct leadership and recognised by Liu Shaoqi, Ren Bishi, Chen Yi and others. Li concludes that these measures reflected the Party's ideological, political and organisational maturity, established Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology, and displayed the institutional strengths of a Marxist party. After the congress, Li says, the united Party advanced to the victory of the new-democratic revolution in 1949. Read the original if you want an official Chinese account of how the Seventh Congress is presented in Party-history writing, especially on the 1945 constitution and the formation of Mao's leadership collective.

Grasp the problem and you grasp the concrete 抓住了问题也就抓住了具体 Zhu Peilei This short commentary, published in Study Times on 25 June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's remark that grasping the problem means grasping the concrete, and applies it to improving Party conduct (作风建设). Zhu argues that ordinary people judge conduct not by the number of meetings, speeches or documents but by which problems actually get solved. The author presents problem-oriented, detail-focused work as a distinctive feature of conduct-building in the new era. The piece opens by noting that the Party's history of victories is tied to its ability to seize the key problem of each period. Zhu stresses that problems are concrete, change over time, and that yesterday's remedy may become today's new ailment. The main body then sets out four pairs of distinctions cadres need to draw, before a brief closing call. The core argument is that problems must be classified before they are solved, and that principle should not be used to answer concrete complaints from grassroots people. Zhu separates matters of principle, where there is no room for compromise (political direction, the people's interests, national security), from flexible matters that allow local experimentation. Individual problems are to be mined for general lessons, while general problems need top-level design. Problems at one link in a chain are distinguished from problems of the whole process, and simple problems, which call for quick action, from deep and complex ones, which need systemic and lasting mechanisms. Zhu concludes that internalising this approach is a basic skill for leading cadres facing new contradictions. Telling the 'genus' from the 'species' of a problem is described as the key to the concrete, and the author expects governance to improve as countless specific problems are handled by category. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-press commentary translates Xi Jinping's problem-oriented rhetoric into guidance for cadres' working methods.

Grasping Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline together 坚持党性党风党纪一起抓 Li Yu This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline form an organic whole: Party spirit is the foundation, conduct the outward expression and discipline the safeguard. Li Yu argues that handling the three together, and linking the correction of work style, the enforcement of discipline and the fight against corruption, summarises practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and deepens understanding of how a Marxist ruling party is built. In Li's account it is also a key lever for the Party's self-reform. The article has two parts. The first traces the idea from Engels's first use of "Party spirit" in 1845, through the Communist Manifesto and Marx and Engels's 1879 letter to Bebel, to Lenin's remarks on discipline at the ninth congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). It then follows the Chinese Communist Party's own experience, from the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention to the reform era. The second part sets out practical requirements. Li argues that Xi's formulation combines treating symptoms and root causes, and combines inner consciousness with outer norms. It sets up a dialectical path from cultivating Party spirit, to forming work style, to shaping discipline, and so supports tackling cases where misconduct in work style and corruption are intertwined. Li proposes three practical principles. The first is systematic thinking, with overall advance and breakthroughs on key points. The second is making the effort regular and long-term, attending to small details such as gift-giving and club hospitality. The third is leading from above, with leading cadres as the "critical few". Li concludes that grasping the three together is essential to keeping the Party advanced and pure. Li calls for integrating this work into everyday tasks, linking it to assessment systems and coordinating the organisation, propaganda and discipline-inspection bodies. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of the theoretical lineage and practical agenda behind the Party's current campaign on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption.

Origins, strategies and effects of the Communist Party of China's emotional mobilisation in the Yan'an period 延安时期中国共产党情感动员的缘起、策略及效应 Li Dan Most studies of the Communist Party of China's mass mobilisation follow a class-struggle line and focus on political and economic dimensions. Li Dan argues that this neglects emotion. The article takes emotional mobilisation, defined after Bai Shuying as the process of using emotional work in interaction to arouse, stimulate or change people's cognition, attitudes and evaluations. It asks why the Party mobilised emotions in the Yan'an period, how it turned feeling into revolutionary action, and what followed, so as to explain from the angle of emotional identification why the Party was able to succeed. The article has three parts: the origins of emotional mobilisation, its strategies and its effects. The evidence is drawn mainly from statements by Mao Zedong, Ren Bishi, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Xie Juezai, from Zhao Chaogou's reportage Yan'an Yi Yue (A Month in Yan'an), from wartime pictorial publications and from border-region education regulations. It also cites Elizabeth Perry's work on the Chinese revolution and emotion. Li identifies three emotional obstacles in the early Yan'an years: a latent national consciousness, passive revolutionary morale marked by fear and defeatism, and hesitant attitudes towards the Party after Guomindang propaganda against it. Li then sets out five strategies that, in the article's account, escalated step by step: improving material life through land distribution and relief to lay an emotional foundation; arousing national sentiment; shaping the image of the Party through Mao Zedong, the disciplined army and model figures such as Norman Bethune, Zhang Side and labour heroes; intensifying anger by publicising Japanese atrocities, including in photographs; and political education. Education also regulated emotion, for example by curbing the killing of prisoners and, through the rectification movement, by unifying feeling. Li holds that emotional mobilisation helped the revolution succeed, citing Perry's view that the Party beat the Guomindang partly by mobilising popular emotion. It also deepened popular emotional identification with the Party, including its leader, policies and character, and enriched understanding of Mao Zedong Thought, with Mao portrayed as an expert in emotional mobilisation. Li adds that emotion worked together with other forms of mobilisation, and that it is gradual and long-term but, once aroused, the most fundamental and lasting. Read the original if you study Yan'an-period mass mobilisation, Party propaganda or the role of emotion in Chinese revolutionary history, and want the primary sources the author draws on.

The roots of the Party's spirit of self-reform in fine traditional Chinese culture: an exploration 党的自我革命精神的中华优秀传统文化根脉探析 Huang Gang Zhang Jing The article asks how the Communist Party of China's spirit of self-reform is rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture. Huang and Zhang present that spirit as a concrete outcome of the Two Integrations in the field of Party building. They argue that it fits closely with four traditional ideas and has turned them from static cultural 'genes' into a dynamic political practice. The article has four main sections, each pairing a traditional value with an element of Party discourse. The first links the 'historical cycle' question, which Huang Yanpei put to Mao Zedong in 1945, to a consciousness of hardship and potential danger. The second links the 'unique problems of a large party' to the moral character of self-scrutiny in solitude. The third links the 'four selfs' (self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation) to the idea of discarding the old and establishing the new. The fourth links the 'sitting an exam' spirit to the ceaseless striving of the Chinese nation. Classical sources such as the Book of Changes, Confucius, Mencius, Mozi and Wang Yangming are set beside speeches by Xi Jinping and earlier Party leaders. The authors' central move is to read each Party practice as a modern continuation of a classical ethic. Self-reform is the Party's 'second answer' to the historical cycle, after Mao's 'new path of democracy', and the authors tie it to the maxim of preparing for danger in times of peace. Criticism and self-criticism, inspection tours and the Party's rectification and education campaigns are read as updated forms of 'being watchful over oneself when alone' and of correcting faults. Revisions of the Party Constitution and of Party regulations, the Eight-point Regulation and the emphasis on study are cast as inheritors of the reformist tradition. Xi's phrase that self-reform is 'always on the road' is read as the contemporary form of the ancient ideal of self-strengthening. Huang and Zhang conclude that the self-reform spirit has moved from fit with traditional culture to combination and then to fusion, achieving the 'creative transformation and innovative development' of that culture. They state that this cultural root gives full and rigorous self-governance of the Party a deep foundation. In their view it also supplies spiritual strength for resolving the problems unique to a large party and for building a Marxist party that stays in power long-term. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building theory is justified through Chinese classical sources, with the specific classical phrases it uses for each pairing.

The value, historical evolution and basic experience of the Communist Party of China's building of cultural leadership 中国共产党文化领导权建设的价值意蕴、历史演进及基本经验 Xiao Guangwen Ge Qiuyue Xiao and Ge take up the Party's cultural leadership (cultural hegemony in the Gramscian register, rendered in Chinese as the Party's "cultural leadership"), a proposition Xi Jinping put forward in the new era. They argue that existing scholarship concentrates on the new era, theoretical bases and practical paths, and that the topic should be examined across the Party's century-plus history. Their thesis is that building cultural leadership strengthens the Party's governing position and ideological foundation, and that its history yields lessons for propaganda and cultural work today. The article is organised in three parts: the value of cultural leadership, its historical evolution, and the basic experience drawn from it. The historical section moves through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It cites Lenin, Marx and Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. On value, the authors contend that cultural leadership is an inherent requirement of consolidating the Party's core leadership, a political guarantee for taking on a new cultural mission, and the key to holding the dominant say in ideological work. They argue that it supports cultural subjectivity through the Two Integrations, the goal of a cultural powerhouse by 2035, soft power and cultural security. Historically, they trace a line from left-wing cultural organisations and Yan'an literary policy, through control of the media and the "Double Hundred" policy, to the Three Represents and the new era's emphasis on core socialist values. From this they derive four lessons: comprehensive Party leadership over cultural work, backed by law and institutions; the guiding position of Marxism in ideology; a people-centred orientation; and resolving the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, to achieve cultural innovation. The authors conclude that the Party has built cultural leadership step by step through winning, constructing, consolidating and improving it, and that this experience offers guidance for building a cultural powerhouse. They call for firmly holding leadership, management and discourse power in ideology, countering Western non-Marxist currents and historical nihilism, and reconciling a unified guiding ideology with cultural diversity. Read the original if you want a periodised, officially aligned account of how the Party conceptualises its cultural leadership from 1921 to the present, with references to key Party documents.

The people-centred character of the Chinese Communist Party's self-reform 中国共产党自我革命的人民性意蕴阐析 Liu Dongxu Huang Rongsheng Liu Dongxu and Huang Rongsheng ask in what sense the Chinese Communist Party's "self-revolution" (rendered here as the Party's self-reform) has a "people-centred" (renminxing) character. They argue that this character is the foundational one among its several attributes. It follows from the Party's essential nature as a Marxist party, and it runs through each of the four "selfs" named in official documents: self-purification, self-improvement in the sense of perfecting itself, self-renewal and self-elevation. The article opens with a review of Chinese scholarship since Xi Jinping first used the term in 2015. That work covers the term's origins, meaning, features and experience, and a few studies treat its people-centred side. The authors say they draw on political science, Party history and Marxist philosophy, guided by Xi Jinping's thinking on Party self-reform and by the Party's practice over more than a century. They also tie the discussion to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Chinese modernization. The body has five parts: the origin, then one part for each of the four "selfs". On the origin, the authors cite Marx and Lenin to argue that genuine "people-centredness" belongs to proletarian parties, while bourgeois parties use it as a cover for class interests. The Party, in their account, has no special interests of its own, which gives it the courage to correct itself. It also aims to safeguard and develop the fundamental interests of the great majority. Self-purification is then linked to a mission of responsibility to the people: listening to their voices, dealing with fading original aspiration, lost ideals and corruption, and filtering out "impurities". Self-improvement rests on relying closely on the people, taking in their views, and repairing the Party's body, strengthening its mechanisms and broadening its functions. Self-renewal means decisions that reflect popular wishes and acceptance of popular oversight, which the authors present as the "second answer", alongside democracy, to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Self-elevation means accepting the people's judgement, protecting their interests, and building the skills to serve them. The authors conclude that self-reform and people-centredness are mutually reinforcing and that the Party's long-term governance depends on both. They present their reading as theoretical support for studying the Third Plenum's decisions, raising the Party's leadership of deepening reform and Chinese modernization, and rallying the people behind building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how official Party-building discourse links self-reform to the people, with its supporting citations from Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping.

An institutional path for leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform An analysis based on the "spillover effect" of intra-Party regulations 以党的自我革命引领社会革命的制度路径研究 Wang Shao The 20th Party Congress report (2022) calls for "leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform". Wang asks how this leadership can be given an institutional and practical form, not only an ideological one. The article argues that intra-Party regulations, through what it calls their "spillover effect" beyond the Party, are the main institutional channel linking the two revolutions. The article has three parts. It first defines "spillover effect" and sets out the relationship between that effect and the two revolutions. It then analyses the institutional logic of the leadership relationship. Finally it examines concrete institutional arrangements, using named regulations such as those on united front work, inspection tours, discipline inspection and joint Party–government documents. Wang defines spillover as an extension of the scope of a regulation's force: in space, in persons and in subject matter. Social revolution is read, following Xi Jinping, as a new movement of social construction that consolidates the existing superstructure and can only be led by the Party. Because intra-Party regulations govern both "Party building" and "Party leadership", Wang argues, they mediate between self-reform and social revolution.
