The institutional logic has two strands: effect moving from inside the Party to outside it, and from self-discipline to discipline of others. The Party restrains itself, and its regulations then guide society mainly through broad direction and only limited direct regulation. Wang insists that such spillover must not replace state law. In practice, the author says, spillover works through Party leadership, rigorous self-governance and Party–government cooperation. It also raises the Party's revolutionary leadership capacity through leadership regulations, the Party's leadership system and "hybrid" Party regulations issued jointly with state organs. Wang concludes that the spillover effect is a distinctive strength of the legal system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and operates through both authorising and prohibiting provisions. In the article's account, this dual effect strengthens the Party's capacity to lead and also sets the direction and aims of social revolution. Read the original if you study Party-building theory, intra-Party regulations or how Chinese scholars link Party discipline, the legal system and social governance.

A precious asset for Party conduct in the new era 新时代作风建设的宝贵财富 Huang Yan Qiao Yijiao This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how the revolutionary culture of the Communist Party can inform efforts to improve Party conduct today. Huang and Qiao argue that revolutionary culture holds rich ideas on conduct, and that its glorious traditions and fine style remain a spiritual asset for the new era. The authors draw on episodes from the Jinggangshan period, the Long March, the Yan'an rectification movement and the early People's Republic. They cite Mao Zedong's "single lamp wick", Zhou Enlai's "ten family rules", the "Three Rules of Discipline and Six Points for Attention" and the "six provisions" of the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee. The argument is organised around four qualities. Firm conviction and the courage to win supply the ideological foundation. Putting the people first and serving without selfishness give conduct its purpose. Seeking truth from facts and self-reform are described as the key path, with the Yan'an rectification movement presented as a model of criticism and self-criticism against subjectivism, sectarianism and "Party formalism". Hard struggle and dedication are called the essential requirement. For each, Huang and Qiao set a present-day demand, including the Two Upholds, solving people's pressing concerns, investigating conduct and corruption together, and rejecting hedonism and extravagance. The authors conclude that cadres should keep applying the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. In their view, revolutionary culture should nurture the original aspiration, strengthen resolve and give Party members a loyal, clean and responsible character, adding "red momentum" to building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link revolutionary history to current campaigns on Party conduct.

Innovating student work models to raise the level of Party building in universities 创新学生工作模式 提升高校党建水平 Cui Zhigang Wen Qin Cui Zhigang and Wen Qin argue that student Party members are the 'key minority' in universities' 'all-round education' arrangement, and that raising their quality answers the basic question of whom to train, how and for whom. Their short commentary, from the Chinese Social Sciences Today, presents the '1234' model of Party member education and training introduced at Nanchang Normal University. The article describes the model as four sets of measures: a 'Youth Candle Vanguard Corps', a 'dual-mentor linkage' mechanism, a 'three services' practice platform and training in 'four abilities'. It reports that the model addresses weak continuity and weak practical grounding in training student Party members. It is presented as the result of a Jiangxi provincial university Party-building research project. The authors describe a four-tier structure running from the university to colleges, Party branches and student residence service stations. In it, each college sends 12 student Party members a year to central training. Party-affairs staff act as one-to-one mentors, and corps members serve as class leaders in Party school courses, so that 'educators are educated first'. Practice runs through serving teachers and students, the branch and society, including rural revitalization research. Training targets political, professional, practical and employment abilities. As evidence the authors cite results over three years: 8 corps members won national scholarships, 16 entered master's programmes, one joined the Western Programme and over 20 went to basic education posts in Jiangxi. They conclude that the model moves student Party members from 'theoretically qualified' to 'fully competent'. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how a Chinese teacher-training college organises student Party member training.

The contemporary development of materialist dialectics 唯物辩证法的时代发展 Zhang Tao This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks what Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has added to materialist dialectics. Zhang Tao argues that this body of thought has made a systematic contribution, rooted in China's practice of revolution, construction, reform and governance, and that the contribution falls into five areas. The article is organised around five paired formulations, each presented as an original contribution on one dimension of dialectics: problem-oriented practical dialectics, contradiction-transformation process dialectics, strategy-centred systems dialectics, people-first subject dialectics, and historical-initiative historical dialectics. Each is defined against a rejected alternative. Zhang contrasts problem orientation with rationalism detached from practice and with utilitarian pragmatism, and names three kinds of key problems: those that are widespread, those that are paradoxical, and those that are newly emerging. Process dialectics, covering reform, bottom-line thinking, innovation and harmony, is set against either-or thinking. Systems dialectics, built on strategic significance, planning and realisation, is set against short-sighted and one-dimensional metaphysics. Putting the people first is set against atomistic individualism and defines the people as a subject led by the proletariat and its vanguard party. Historical initiative is set against a mechanical materialism that waits for laws to realise themselves. Zhang concludes that this body of thought has given materialist dialectics a distinctive form in China and shows the Chinese Communists' theoretical thinking and dialectical wisdom. Zhang calls for Marxist theorists to keep exploring these contributions, and says that historical initiative should help turn a capital-first world order into a people-first one. Read the original if you want a compact outline of how current Chinese scholarship frames the Chinese-context contribution to dialectics.

Capital's critique and transcendence of Hegel's dialectic 《资本论》对黑格尔辩证法的批判与超越 Sun Lin Sun Lin takes up the Hegelian element in the dialectic of Capital, which the author treats as an unavoidable problem for research on the materialist conception of history. The article asks how the dialectic of Capital relates to Hegel's "nous" and "logos", and in what way it goes beyond them. Sun's thesis is that Marx actively sublated Hegel's speculative dialectic, grounding it in real social-historical "metabolism" (material exchange), so that the dialectic becomes a materialist one rooted in real essential human powers. The piece is a short essay in three parts. The first reads the development of the commodity through the image of the embryo, drawing on Engels's description of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit as an "embryology of spirit". The second examines Marx's remark that in the chapter on value he "coquetted" with Hegel's characteristic modes of expression, set against the Logic's sequence of being, essence and concept. The third treats metabolism as the manifestation of force and as a "dialectic of force". In Sun's reading, the simple value form is an embryonic form that matures through changes of form into money and then capital. Metabolism has two senses: change in the material's form and exchange between use-value and exchange-value. Sun argues that Marx moves Hegel's inverted, supersensible world from speculation to the social-historical level, where the interactive relation turns into an exchange relation and a fetishistic society emerges. Hegel's force, which Sun equates with free will, becomes in Marx the unfolding of capital's drive for self-valorisation, the real ground behind the conversion of forces. Capital is thus the only thing that realises free will in ideas, yet in reality it is caught in contradiction and repeated crisis, and its "spectral objectivity" depends on the metabolism continuing. Sun concludes that breaking the blockade of objectified labour requires a dialectic with real reflective power and will. Its ground is the essential powers of sensuous human beings in sensuous activity, which restore use-value and make the dialectic one of continual self-reflection and self-revolution. The author adds that this carries foundational significance for further liberating and developing social productive forces and raising social vitality today. Read the original if you study the Hegel–Marx relationship in Capital, especially the theory of metabolism and the form of value, and can read dense philosophical Chinese.

Exploring paths of education to empower the training of young Marxists 探索育人路径 赋能青年马克思主义者培养 Ruan Yuchun This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, describes how the Guangdong Provincial Party School trains young Marxists. Ruan Yuchun presents this work as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as a way to pass the Party's cause on to the next generation. The author's thesis is that Party schools should combine theoretical education with practical education. The piece is organised in two parts. The first covers paths of theoretical education: course development and a reading culture. The second covers paths of practical education: themed activities, social surveys and new practical formats. All examples come from the school's own programmes. On theory, Ruan reports that the school uses case-based, seminar-style, simulation and on-site teaching, and holds collective lesson-preparation meetings across departments. It also works with the Central Party School, other Party schools, universities and research institutes. It promotes reading of the original works of Marxism, Chinese classics and Western classics through reading months and shared-reading events, so as to address trainees' "knowledge anxiety". On practice, the school runs salons and Party-day activities linked to Greater Bay Area quality branding and urban-rural integration. It sends survey teams to Dongguan, Zhaoqing, Qingyuan, Heyuan and Jiangmen. It has also set up a "Yue-Jing Cai" micro-salon with trainees from Beijing, which produces survey reports and policy advice. Ruan concludes that these methods help trainees strengthen their theoretical grounding, hold to principle on questions of path, direction and stance, and improve their political judgement, understanding and execution. The aim is to turn the Party's innovative theory into a "golden key" for solving development problems. Read the original if you want a concrete, officially framed example of how a provincial Party school describes its youth training methods.

Studying closely Xi Jinping's important statements on strengthening the Party's work style 深学细悟习近平总书记关于加强党的作风建设的重要论述 Song Fufan Writing in connection with the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, Song Fufan argues that Party members must study Xi Jinping's statements on the Party's work style closely. The commentary opens from the premise that the Party's style is its image and bears on its survival. Song contends that these statements give scientific guidance for making work-style building a regular and long-term practice in the new era. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the basic answers Xi's statements give on work style. The second explains why the campaign matters for building a high-calibre cadre corps, for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The third lists practical requirements for the campaign. Song's central claim, taken from Xi, is that work-style problems are at root problems of Party spirit (dangxing) and, at their core, of the Party's relationship with the people. Hence work style must be built by tempering Party spirit and by bringing Party and masses closer together. For the first, Song names firm ideals and convictions, a correct handling of public and private interests, rigorous intra-Party political life, and a thorough spirit of self-reform. For the second, Song names the mass line, genuine feeling for the people, and cadres' position as public servants. Song presents work-style building as the breakthrough point of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), starting from the eight-point regulation. Song's practical requirements are these: leading cadres, as the 'key minority', set an example; they hold correct views of power, of achievements and of career; the 'four undesirable work styles' (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance) are corrected; work-style correction, discipline and anti-corruption are pursued together; and the effort is made routine and long-term through institutional mechanisms. Song also calls for positive incentives alongside tolerance of error and correction. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Central Party School scholarship presents Xi Jinping's work-style discourse and the logic of the 2025 campaign.

Governing the Party with a reform spirit and strict standards 坚持用改革精神和严的标准管党治党 Zhao Xiuhua Zhao Xiuhua examines the requirement, set out by Xi Jinping in July 2024 at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee's Third Plenum and repeated in January 2025, to "govern the Party with a reform spirit and strict standards". The article argues that this is an essential part of Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building. In Zhao's account, a reform spirit and strict standards together keep the Party vital and sustain its full and rigorous self-governance. The article has four parts. It first presents the reform spirit as a historical lesson of Party building across the revolutionary, socialist-construction, reform-and-opening and new-era periods. It then discusses problem-oriented self-assessment, and innovation in ideas, methods and institutions. The last part sets out what it means to apply strict standards in terms of criteria, content and process. A short conclusion follows. Zhao holds that the reform spirit supplies three things to Party governance: awareness of the times, new approaches and measures, and internal motivation. The author cites examples including the Yan'an rectification movement, the campaigns against corruption and bureaucracy in the 1950s, and today's digital tools such as big-data inspection and online Party building. Self-assessment is to be made against three yardsticks: external and domestic challenges, the demands of new technologies and organisational forms, and people's rising aspirations for a better life. Strictness is then specified in five standards (political, ideological, organisational, conduct and work style). It also covers every area of Party building and every Party member, with "key minorities" singled out, and runs through the whole process from admission to accountability. Zhao concludes that the secret of the Party's lasting vitality is advancing its own building in a reform spirit, and that self-reform with strict requirements keeps its original mission fresh. The author argues that long-term governance amid what the text calls great changes unseen in a century depends on this approach, which is presented as a fundamental guarantee for Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned exposition of how Party-building theory links the reform spirit to disciplinary and institutional measures after the Third Plenum.

The problem of the "real movement" in communist theory A core issue in how the contemporary Western radical left interprets communism 共产主义理论中的“现实运动”问题 Li Jian Li Jian takes up Marx and Engels's definition of communism in The German Ideology as the "real movement which abolishes the present state of things" and asks what kind of communism deserves that name, and how it can take hold in actual history in the twenty-first century. The article examines influential Western radical-left thinkers to see how they have reconstructed communist theory around this problem. Li argues that these thinkers raise the right question and offer useful perspectives, but abandon historical materialism, so their accounts remain at the level of discourse. The article has four parts. It first sets out the radical left's double approach to communism as both "idea" and "real movement", drawing on Alain Badiou, Slavoj Žižek, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. It then traces their shift from abolishing capitalism's existing conditions to "the production of subjectivity", through three themes: preconditions, main line of development and value goal. A third part gives Li's critical assessment from a historical-materialist standpoint. The last part draws lessons for developing a new form of human civilization. In Li's account, the radical left rests the shift on changed class relations under digital capitalism, where immaterial labour is said to dominate. It sees the main line in the mutual reinforcement of heterogeneous subjects (Hardt and Negri's multitude, Jacques Rancière's "part of those without part") and community, and the goal in the recovery of human subjectivity and emancipation. Li's critique is that these thinkers do not tie the antagonism to abolishing private ownership, stress contingency and events over historical necessity, and leave the "real movement" in the realm of ideas. Their goal, Li says, is individual rather than class emancipation, and their subject concepts sit outside the proletariat. Li concludes that this theory lacks a historical-materialist foundation and has little practical effect, yet it can be critically borrowed. He argues that it clarifies the relation between capitalist and communist civilization, links the historical and value dimensions of communism, and applies the principle that thought should tend toward reality. For the new form of human civilization, Li calls for institutional innovation guided by the direction of communism and for drawing out the historical initiative of the people. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Badiou, Žižek, Hardt, Negri and Rancière on communism, and of how such work is brought into debates on Chinese civilizational theory.

Seizing the historic opportunity of AI development to build a new pattern of higher education 抢抓人工智能发展历史机遇构建高等教育发展新格局 Zhang Guangjun Zhang Guangjun, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, asks how universities should respond to artificial intelligence (AI) as a driver of the new round of scientific and technological revolution. The author argues that universities must grasp this historic opportunity with a higher political standpoint and more systematic strategy, build a new pattern of higher education, and so help a strong education nation support Chinese modernization. The piece is a Party-journal commentary that draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements. The article has four parts. It first sets out three ways AI is changing higher education: the education system, the paradigm of scientific research, and global talent competition. It then turns to reshaping how top-notch innovative talent is trained, through new educational concepts, teachers' roles and student assessment. The third part covers disciplinary crossover and industry–education integration. The last part deals with university governance, Party leadership and ideological education. Zhang's central claim is that AI's effect is a reshaping of educational paradigms, not a simple addition of technology. In teaching, the stress shifts from transmitting knowledge to higher-order thinking, personalised and precisely matched learning, and blended virtual–physical spaces. Teachers become designers of learning, and assessment moves beyond exam scores to a three-in-one system of knowledge, ability and value formation. In research, the author expects AI-driven science to become a new paradigm, citing the 2024 Nobel prizes in physics and chemistry as evidence of disciplinary convergence. Universities are urged to strengthen basic research on data, algorithms and computing power, build "AI+" crossover with the humanities as well as the sciences, and link education, talent, innovation and industry chains. Zhang concludes that higher education must combine "upholding fundamental principles" with innovation. In this account, Party leadership must steer the direction of universities in the AI era, drawing on the Two Establishes, the Two Upholds and the Four-sphere Confidence. Ideological and political education must run through AI-enabled teaching to counter risks such as algorithmic bias, "information cocoons", hidden academic misconduct and emotional alienation. The author also proposes embedding socialist core values in recommendation algorithms. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party-affiliated university leader frames AI and higher-education reform in official terms.

The connotation, characteristics and contemporary value of "life-based ideological and political education" 论“生活思政”的内涵特征和时代价值 Wang Weizhong Cao Heming The article takes up "life-based ideological and political education" (shenghuo sizheng), a concept put forward in 2018 by the Party committee of the Zhejiang Wanli Education Group and developed at Zhejiang Wanli University. Wang and Cao argue that, although the idea is not strictly new, it opens a research space and deserves systematic theoretical treatment. Their thesis is that it is best understood as an educational philosophy that roots ideological and political education in students' everyday lives. The piece has three parts. It first reviews existing definitions and then analyses the two components, "life" and "ideological and political" work or education, to reach a working definition. It then sets out three defining features, and finally assesses the concept's value for theory, for university practice and for building a strong education nation. On definition, the authors hold that life-based ideological and political education is not simply a subset of everyday ideological education, nor an all-encompassing "unified field". It is a concept that stresses the importance of "life" for such work, covering both real and online life, and combining explicit and implicit education. They identify three features: it is grounded in life and focused on nurturing people, working across individual and dormitory "small spaces" and wider "large spaces" such as classes and clubs; it draws on culture to shape people, with culture as the key to fusing life and ideological education; and it uses digital means, linking precision and digital ideological education to bridge virtual and real life. Its value, they say, lies in new research topics, including empirical research, in a model of whole-staff, "all-round" nurturing built on the "three-all" approach and the "seven nurturing" mechanisms, and in supporting the "leading force of ideological and political education" that Xi Jinping introduced at the National Education Conference in September 2024. The authors conclude that the concept gives theory a new field, gives universities a fresh way to innovate, and supplies the everyday ground on which the leading force of ideological and political education can operate. They present Zhejiang Wanli University's experience as a model of this. Read the original if you study Chinese university ideological education, or want to see how a locally coined practice concept is given theoretical form and tied to current Party discourse.

Resolutely defending the historical contribution of the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression to victory in the world anti-fascist war 坚定捍卫中国人民抗日战争对世界反法西斯战争胜利的历史贡献 PLA National Defence University Published in Qiushi in 2025, this commentary by the PLA National Defence University takes up the place of the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression in the Second World War. Following Xi Jinping's repeated statements, it argues that the Chinese theatre was the main Eastern theatre of the world anti-fascist war and that China made a major contribution to the victory. It also holds that this contribution must be remembered and defended today. The text has three parts. The first sets out the Chinese theatre's military and strategic contribution. The second presents that contribution as a collective achievement of the whole nation and draws lessons from it for the "new journey". The third turns to present-day tasks: countering distortions of China's wartime role, preventing the revival of Japanese militarism, and upholding Taiwan's status as part of China. It closes with a call on the armed forces to carry forward the spirit of resistance. In the first part, the article argues that China began resisting fascism earliest, fought longest and paid the highest price. It cites 1.5 million or more Japanese troops eliminated, over 70 per cent of Japan's Second World War casualties, and more than 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties. It says China's resistance tied down Japan, ruled out a Japanese "northward advance" against the Soviet Union, delayed the "southward advance", and supported the Allies' "Europe first" strategy. It also points to the expeditionary force sent to Burma, and to support for anti-Japanese forces in Korea and Vietnam. The second part draws on Mao Zedong's On Protracted War and attributes the victory to the Chinese people's love of peace, courage, global outlook and unity under the anti-Japanese national united front. From each of these it derives a task for the present: military preparedness, fighting spirit, the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind, and unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. In the third part the authors say some forces portray China as a passive victim, credit the Allied victory to Britain and the United States alone, or promote a narrative of Japanese victimhood. They hold that the post-war trials of Japanese militarism were incomplete, and that China will never permit militarism to return. They cite the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation as confirming Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan, and call for opposing "Taiwan independence" and upholding the one-China principle and the "1992 Consensus". Read the original if you want an example of the official Chinese military-academic account of the war's international significance, and of how it is tied to current positions on Japan, Taiwan and national security.

Advancing the broad, multi-level and institutionalised development of consultative democracy 推进协商民主广泛多层制度化发展 Zhang Shuhua Writing in the Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) in June 2025, Zhang Shuhua takes up Xi Jinping's call to advance the broad, multi-level and institutionalised development of socialist consultative democracy. Zhang argues that this form of democracy is a distinctive institutional feature and political strength of Chinese-style democracy. The article presents consultation as the practical meaning of "people's democracy" in China: matters of common concern are discussed by the people, in order to find the greatest common denominator of society's wishes. The piece has three parts. The first explains why consultative democracy matters, the second describes how it has operated across the system of national governance since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and the third sets out measures to make institutionalisation "take effect on the ground". It is a short commentary and cites no external scholarship. Its evidence is drawn from Party regulations, the work of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and local practice. Zhang gives three reasons for the system's significance. It embodies Party leadership and the Party's public-minded governing outlook, particularly through consultation between the Party and the democratic parties under the new type of party system. It promotes social integration by seeking the "greatest common denominator" of interests and uniting respect for the majority with care for minorities. It also promotes democratic oversight, which the author says helps correct errors and makes decisions more responsive to public opinion. On practice, Zhang lists seven institutional platforms: party, people's congress, government, CPPCC, people's organisation, grassroots and social-organisation consultation. Party and CPPCC consultation are described as the main channels. Zhang cites regulations on united front work and political consultation, the CPPCC's input into medium- and long-term plans including the 14th Five-Year Plan, and local forums such as democratic heart-to-heart talks and villagers' deliberation councils. Zhang concludes that the system already has a clear framework running from the centre to localities, and calls for it to be made more effective. The proposals include mechanisms for informing participants and feeding results back, treating institutionalisation as part of political structural reform, an open consultative atmosphere fostered by the ruling Party, and stronger consultative capacity among the democratic parties. Zhang ties this to the project of national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for consultative democracy and its institutional channels as presented by a leading Chinese political scientist.

Comprehensively strengthening the Party's conduct to open a new realm of leading national governance through Party governance 全面加强党的作风建设开辟以治党引领治国新境界 Deng Maosheng Writing in Study Times (23 June 2025), Deng Maosheng argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has used the improvement of Party conduct, beginning with the eight-point regulations of the Central Committee, to open a new realm in which governing the Party leads governing the country. In Deng's account, the Party must be governed well first, so that it can lead the people in governing the state. The commentary has three parts. The first describes the changes attributed to the eight-point regulations, including a transformed political climate, and notes problems that remain. The second sets out the political logic linking Party building and national governance, and the role of conduct building within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The third identifies three long-term problems that conduct building must address. Deng claims the regulations changed China's political ecology in four respects: clear politics, clean officialdom, a prosperous country and secure people. Deng contrasts this with what the article calls political polarisation and social tearing in many Western countries. Drawing on past deviations, Deng argues that politics and economic development cannot be separated, and that disorder in politics undermines growth, citing the "middle-income trap" as an example. Party conduct is presented as a key lever, with the stress on officials, especially leaders, since strict governance of the Party is above all strict governance of officials. Deng presents the anti-corruption campaign as the Party's most thorough self-reform and says its scale has no precedent in the dynastic histories. Deng also asks officials to accept tighter discipline so that ordinary people can feel at ease. Deng concludes that three problems need sustained attention: separation from the masses after taking power, corruption once in office (especially under market-economy conditions, where power can be exchanged for wealth), and spiritual complacency after a long period of peace. Deng calls for conduct building to become regular and long-term, and for the Party to keep using its self-reform to lead social revolution, in service of Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Party policy researcher presents the link between Party conduct and national governance.

Cadre education in the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army during the War of Resistance 抗战时期东北抗日联军的干部教育 Wu Yang Bai Lu This short historical article, published in a newspaper in June 2025, asks how the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army trained its cadres and what distinguished that training. Wu and Bai note that from 1933 the Party-led forces absorbed volunteer armies and other local groups, and that rapid expansion left the army short of capable cadres. They argue that cadre education became essential for carrying the Party line into the army and that it produced a stronger, more cohesive force. The article first sets out four methods: short-term training classes and training schools attached to units; training teams that moved with the army; a political-military school for senior cadres, opened in 1936 under Zhao Shangzhi; and selection of cadres for study in the Soviet Union. It then describes the content, which fell into military skills, political theory and basic literacy. Wu and Bai identify three features. The methods were flexible, for example by turning an entire company into a training team when activists could not be spared, or by training a unit on skis. Education stressed the exemplary role of cadres, shown in disciplinary rules issued in 1939 and in the conduct of those trained in the teams. It also linked theory to practice, using recent battles in tactical teaching and asking students to compare their own hardships with lessons on capitalism. The authors conclude that the army valued cadre education from its founding and that it raised the cadres' overall quality and resolve. In their view these cadres passed instructions up and down and set an example, which strengthened cohesion and advanced the northeastern resistance. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how a guerrilla force organised training under wartime conditions.

How Marxism understands "human essence" 马克思主义如何理解“人的本质” Liang Bo Liang takes the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to put the people first as a starting point and asks how Marxism arrives at a true account of the human essence. The commentary argues that, for Marxism, humans are real subjects engaged in material production within concrete social relations. On this view the essence of the human is both socially determined and historically formed, in contrast to abstract theories of human nature. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts: practice as the basis for grasping the real human essence, the class character of humans within historical development, and the free and all-round development of the person as the value goal. It draws on Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, the 1844 Manuscripts and the Communist Manifesto. It ends with the Chinese Communist Party's record and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Liang contends that Feuerbach's "species essence", Enlightenment "natural rights" and ancient Chinese debates on whether human nature is good or evil all construct an abstract human being detached from social relations. Marx instead locates the essence in practice and in production, so it changes with modes of production, from dependence on kin communities, through personal dependence, to the "dependence on things" of capitalism. In class society, Liang argues, no supra-class human essence exists, and the social attributes of people appear first as class attributes. Liang concludes that communism is the social form in which the human essence is regained on the basis of developed productive forces, and that the Party's policies from "serving the people" to reform and opening up and common prosperity pursue this aim. The piece presents Chinese modernization as centred on human development and calls for adherence to the principle of putting the people first. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-press commentary links Marx's theory of human essence to current policy language.

Learning from history: upholding the correct view of the Second World War 以史为鉴 坚持正确二战史观 Li Chunfeng This short commentary, written after Xi Jinping's May 2025 state visit to Russia for the 80th anniversary of the Soviet Union's victory in the Great Patriotic War, asks what it means to uphold a "correct view of the Second World War". Li argues that doing so, and resisting incorrect views, helps to criticise historical nihilism and to draw lessons from history. The piece opens with Xi's pledge that China and Russia will jointly defend the outcomes of the war's victory. It then sets out three requirements: adopting a grand historical outlook, adhering to historical materialism, and criticising historical nihilism. Li uses casualty figures, battlefield episodes and examples of foreign aid to China. Li first holds that a grand historical outlook means judging the war in the span of human civilisation. On this basis the author cites over 100 million casualties worldwide, 35 million Chinese casualties and 300,000 deaths in the Nanjing Massacre, and presents China as committed to peaceful development and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Second, historical materialism requires recognising the people as the principal force of the anti-fascist victory. Li points to the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, Yang Jingyu and the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, as well as the Hump air route and Norman Bethune. Third, Li says historical nihilism, rooted in "Western-centrism" and the political right, spreads a "Japan as victim" narrative. It denies the contributions of China and the USSR and the Communist Party's leading role. Li concludes that the correct view of the war must be upheld and nihilist distortions rejected, so that the results of China's War of Resistance are defended. The author stresses the Communist Party's role as the "mainstay" of national resistance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary frames the Second World War and historical nihilism after Xi's 2025 Moscow visit.

Forging the heart and soul: opening a new phase in cultural education in universities 立心铸魂 开创高校文化育人工作新局面 Yan Longzhong Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (23 June 2025), Yan Longzhong asks how universities can carry out cultural education in line with Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The author argues that cultural education and moral cultivation are integral to ideological and political work in higher education and to ensuring the Party's cause is passed on. Universities, Yan holds, should draw on excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture to "forge the heart and soul" of a "new generation for the new era". The commentary opens by describing Xi Jinping's thought on culture as the cultural part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and as a result of the Two Integrations. It then sets out three tasks: forging the soul through culture, educating people through culture, and nourishing the mind through culture. Each task is tied to a metaphor (the "steering wheel" of values, the "backbone" of commitment, and the "spirit" of striving) and broken into practical measures. On soul-forging, Yan says students should be guided to hold firm faith in Marxism, conviction in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and confidence in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author proposes using the "four histories" and comparisons between China and the West to counter what is described as denigration of socialism and erroneous trends of thought. On educating through culture, Yan argues that each of the three cultural strands has a distinct role: traditional culture lays the spiritual foundation, revolutionary culture strengthens the spiritual lifeline through Party, revolutionary and martyr stories, and advanced socialist culture, centred on core socialist values, enriches students' inner world. On nourishing the mind, the author proposes three channels: campus environments that carry cultural elements, locally distinctive cultural courses, and themed activities such as reading campaigns combining online and offline formats. Yan concludes that universities should combine explicit and implicit education so that culture works quietly and continuously on students, and should build a cultural space that is deep-rooted, harmonious and inclusive. The piece is a practice-oriented statement of how Xi Jinping's cultural thought is to be applied in university student work. Read the original if you want an example of how a university student-affairs official frames cultural education and the tasks of ideological and political work in Chinese higher education in 2025.

Attending to military–political relations in the war zones during the War of Resistance against Japan 关注抗战时期的战地军政关系 Chen Mo Chen Mo argues that the relationship between stationed armies and local governments in the war zones is an important but under-studied topic in research on the War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45). Defining 'war-zone military–political relations' as the interaction between garrison forces and provincial, district and county governments, excluding the central-level Nationalist–Communist relationship, the author sees it as a Chinese case of civil–military relations. The article is a research agenda rather than a finished study: it maps what scholars have found and what remains unresolved. The article is organised around four questions: the position of military power in the war-zone power structure; the role of military commanders in local administration; military–political friction; and the separate efforts of the Nationalists (Guomindang) and the Chinese Communist Party (CPC) to manage these relations. For each, Chen sets out existing scholarship and then lists cases, mechanisms and comparisons that still need study, on both the Nationalist front and the CPC-led base areas behind Japanese lines. Chen holds that both parties raised the status of armies and officers in rebuilding local power. On the Nationalist side, the author cites figures showing that of 67 wartime provincial chairmen, 77.6 per cent had military backgrounds (70 per cent in war-zone provinces), a pattern linked to Chiang Kai-shek's preference for the army over the Party. In the base areas, armies founded governments and, from 1938, military leaders often headed joint military–political committees. Friction arose over personnel, finance and especially grain requisition, as in the Eastern Hubei incident, and also inside the base areas, where Mao Zedong and He Long criticised overbearing army cadres. Chen contends that Chiang usually sided with the military, leaving the underlying tensions unresolved. The CPC, by contrast, is said to have eased the problem through unified leadership from September 1942, rectification, the campaign against warlordism and the 'support the government and cherish the people, support the army and give preferential treatment to military families' campaign, a far more successful approach in Chen's account. Chen concludes that all four areas leave room for further work, including year-by-year and regional quantitative studies of power shifts, commanders' practical solutions (for example Chen Cheng's grain rationing in Hubei and Luo Ronghuan's sea-salt trade in Shandong), the reasons some armies and governments cooperated under shared hardship, and the long-term effect of the two parties' divergent approaches, to be analysed with political science and sociology. Read the original if you work on wartime Chinese history, Nationalist or CPC institutions, or civil–military relations and want a detailed list of sources, cases and open questions.

An analysis of the Communist Party of China's military leadership in the period of the New Democratic Revolution 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党的军事领导力探析 Ma Kangmei Yi Ming Ma and Yi ask how the Communist Party of China forged, and kept strengthening, the military leadership that let a weak revolutionary army defeat much better-equipped opponents between 1927 and the Korean War. Their thesis is that this leadership rested on three principles: the Party commanding the gun, unity between officers and soldiers, and people's war. All three, they argue, depended on valuing and cultivating people. The article opens with an introduction that uses Mao Zedong's analysis of the balance of forces to explain how strength and weakness can be reversed in war. Three substantive sections follow, one for each principle, and a conclusion closes the piece. The evidence is drawn from the failed Nanchang, Autumn Harvest and Guangzhou uprisings, the Sanwan reorganisation, the Gutian Conference, the War of Resistance against Japan, and comparisons with the Kuomintang army. On the first principle, the authors argue that early Red Army units kept the habits of old mercenary armies and often collapsed. Mao's response was to place Party committees at battalion level and above, branches in companies, and groups in squads and platoons, which in the authors' account turned military command into collective Party decision-making. They add that the company is the basic unit of combat and daily life, and so the right place for a Party branch. On the second principle, officer–soldier equality and the "three major democracies" (political, military, economic) are said to have produced class feeling, self-management and initiative, in contrast with the Kuomintang's reliance on money and coercion. On the third, the authors describe a three-tier armed system of main forces, local guerrillas and militia, rooted in land reform and discipline toward civilians, which they credit with large-scale guerrilla war behind Japanese lines and with five specific effects on Japan's war effort. Ma and Yi conclude that Party organisation at the grass roots, military democracy and fusion with the masses together made up the Party's military leadership, and that each rested on a Marxist concern with the human being. They cite the peasant origins of most of the 1,614 founding-era generals, and the remoulding of former Kuomintang units, as evidence that Party leadership can turn ordinary people into capable soldiers. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated scholarly account of how Chinese military leadership principles are explained and justified, including its use of leadership-science and psychological arguments.

Lessons from building a Chinese autonomous knowledge system of Xinhai Revolution history 建构中国自主的辛亥革命史知识体系的启示 Ma Min Ma Min takes up a task he describes as pressing for Chinese historians: accelerating the construction of an autonomous Chinese knowledge system of historical studies. He argues that research on the 1911 (Xinhai) Revolution, and the way its own autonomous knowledge system took shape, is a model case that offers several lessons for that wider project. The article has three parts. It first traces more than 70 years of Xinhai Revolution scholarship in the People's Republic in three stages: emergence (1949–1966), flourishing (1978–1989) and deepening (1990 to the present). It then identifies five defining features of the resulting knowledge system. Finally it looks ahead to how the field might be extended. For the historical account, Ma holds that the early stage, guided by historical materialism, established the 'bourgeois revolution' thesis through class analysis and a mass-centred view of history. In the 1980s, he says, mainland scholars refined this thesis in debate with Taiwan scholars' 'revolution of the whole people' view and overseas scholars' 'gentry movement' view. Since the 1990s, social history, the modernization paradigm and postmodern approaches have broadened the field. The five features are: historical materialism as the 'soul'; historical sources as the 'foundation'; academic-system building, meaning concepts, theories and findings, as the 'core'; major monographs as the visible 'form'; and institutions and journals as the 'network'. Ma stresses that the system is open: it drew on Western, Japanese and Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan scholarship, so 'autonomy' must not exclude sensible borrowing. Ma proposes widening the field's horizons in time, space and society. In time, he follows Zhang Kaiyuan's 'three hundred years' idea and urges study of links between the Hundred Days' Reform, the late-Qing New Policies, the Xinhai Revolution, the May Fourth Movement and the founding of the Communist Party, within the larger frame of national rejuvenation and Chinese modernization. In space, he calls for Asian and global perspectives and for regional studies. In society, he advocates combining revolutionary and social history, with finer empirical work such as local, visual and individual-experience studies. Ma sees this as a 'new revolutionary history' of renewal. Read the original if you want a Chinese historian's account of how the field's paradigms developed and of the research directions he proposes for it.

The spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists in the perspective of historical progress: theoretical picture and practical significance 历史进步视野中的中国共产党人精神谱系：理论图景与现实意义 Xing Yunwen Yan Manqing Xing Yunwen and Yan Manqing ask how the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists should be located within the long course of human history, and what its significance is today. They argue that the question comes down to a prior one, how spirit takes part in historical progress, and that Marx and Engels's historical materialism gives the theoretical route for answering it. On this basis, the authors present the genealogy as an important spiritual driving force of historical progress. The article has three parts. The first reviews how Marxist views of historical progress reconsidered the place of spirit, from Hegel's teleological account to Marx and Engels's reinterpretation. The second examines how the genealogy was formed and developed, along three lines: the value of putting the people first, the complex movement of social contradictions in different periods, and the dialectic between objective historical laws and the subjective spirit of historical agents. The third sets out the genealogy's significance for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, world socialism, human civilization and the free and all-round development of every person. In the authors' reading, Hegel treated history as the self-development of Absolute Spirit, which left spirit without a real subject. Marx and Engels, citing The German Ideology and Engels's late letters, located history in the practice of real individuals and rejected the reduction of historical materialism to economic determinism. Progress, on this view, results from the combined force of economic base and superstructure, practice and spirit. The authors apply this to the Party. They hold that the great spirit of Party founding is the source of a genealogy whose branches include the Jinggangshan, Xibaipo and Yan'an spirits. Its inner core is the value of putting the people first, and its growth comes from respecting historical laws while exercising historical initiative. The authors conclude that the genealogy supplies lasting spiritual momentum for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and strengthens the Chinese nation's sense of community. They also hold that it leaves a distinctive mark on the world socialist movement, offering other socialist countries a spiritual example, and that it is a resource for civilizational progress that draws on both traditional Chinese culture and Marxism and challenges Western-centric notions of civilizational superiority. They further argue that its "sublime" value orientation enriches the human-liberation perspective of all-round human development. Read the original if you want to see how Party-history spirit studies are grounded in Marxist philosophy of history and tied to claims about Chinese modernization and world socialism.

Making the Party's innovative theory take root among the people in the digital age 数字时代推动党的创新理论深入人心 Zhang Weizhou Writing in the China Social Sciences Today (25 June 2025 posting of a 20 June article), Zhang Weizhou takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee's (2024) call to build a system that arms the whole Party, educates the people and guides practice with the Party's innovative theory. Zhang argues that digitalisation has reshaped communication and created three tensions: depth of content against breadth of reach, theoretical height against audience reception, and system completeness against innovation in carriers. The proposed answer is a "three-dimensional architecture" of systematic research, scenario-based communication and coordinated advancement. The commentary is built around three practical pathways, each illustrated with examples from Xi'an, where the author works in the municipal publicity department. These are a people-centred communication model, technological innovation in the delivery system, and a collaborative communication ecosystem. Zhang cites Xi Jinping's remarks on news communication, on systematising theory and on integrated media development as support for each section. On the first pathway, Zhang holds that one-way indoctrination yields diminishing returns online, so theory must be adapted to audiences through cognitive fit, scenario embedding and emotional resonance. Xi'an's "Runli Xi'an" project, with live-streamed Q&A, online volunteer communicators and a points system, is presented as moving learning from "I speak, you listen" to co-creation. On the second, Zhang describes a converged network of smart platforms (such as the Learning Powerhouse app), social media and offline VR/AR or holographic exhibitions, while warning of information cocoons, privacy disputes and over-personalisation. Zhang proposes a framework of "values as substance, technology as function", with safeguards such as weighting mainstream values, data desensitisation and human review. On the third, Zhang outlines a feedback loop of communication, feedback, assessment and optimisation, and a three-tier city, district and community network. Zhang concludes that bringing the theory into ordinary homes consolidates the Party's governing foundation and gathers strength for national rejuvenation. This requires correct political, opinion and value orientations and innovation in concepts, content, forms and mechanisms, so as to open the "last kilometre" of theoretical arming. Xi'an's practice is offered as a model of three shifts: from content supply to shared meaning-making, from technology as tool to ecosystem, and from one-way governance to multi-party cooperation. Read the original if you want a concrete local example of how Party propaganda departments plan digital theory communication, including Xi'an's platforms and mechanisms.

The logical evolution of the core meaning of the Chinese Communist Party's original aspiration and mission 中国共产党初心使命核心意蕴的逻辑演进 Li Jing Yue Ziqi The article asks what the Chinese Communist Party's founding aspiration and mission (chuxin shiming) – to seek happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation – actually contain, and how that content has developed. Li Jing and Yue Ziqi argue that its core meaning is best grasped through three connected logics: theoretical, historical and practical. In their account, the aspiration and mission unite theory with practice, history with the present, and knowing with doing. The piece is organised in three sections. The first sets out the theoretical meaning by answering three questions: what the mission is, why the Party adopted it, and how it is to be carried out, drawing on Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. The second traces the historical meaning through four periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third turns to practice since the 20th Party Congress (2022), covering Chinese modernization, common prosperity, the building of a modern socialist country and a new cultural mission. The authors' central claim is that the mission expresses the proletarian vanguard character of the Party in specifically Chinese form. They hold that the Chinese working class, oppressed by imperialism, the bourgeoisie and feudal forces, was especially resolute, and that the Party therefore joined class mission, national destiny and popular wellbeing. Historically, they say, the Party has always linked its maximum programme (communism) with the common ideals of each period, so that the mission rose to new levels at each stage. In the new era, they list achievements in Party building, whole-process people's democracy, the new development philosophy, the elimination of absolute poverty and ecological civilization, which they present as giving the mission firmer institutional, material and spiritual support. The authors conclude that pursuing the mission today means upholding Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, putting the people at the centre of development, and pursuing common prosperity through a coordinated system of primary, secondary and third distribution. They also call for accelerating new quality productive forces, and for adapting Marxism to Chinese culture through the Two Integrations, with the aim of creating a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Party-theory scholarship frames the Party's founding mission across its history and into the present.

The Bandung spirit today and China's contribution 万隆精神的时代回响与中国贡献 Ren Hongyan Marking the 70th anniversary of the 1955 Bandung Conference, Ren Hongyan asks what the "Bandung spirit" of solidarity, friendship and cooperation means for a turbulent present. The article argues that the spirit remains vital, and that the Global South should carry it forward and give it new content through the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Ren presents China as an indispensable contributor both in 1955 and since. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, has three parts. The first assesses the conference's historical impact. The second explains why the Bandung spirit is still relevant, covering the rise of the Global South, the growth of South-South cooperation, cooperation mechanisms, and China's role. The third sets out four areas in which the spirit matters under current conditions. In the first part, Ren credits Bandung with accelerating decolonisation, citing a rise in independent Asian and African states from 29 to 73 between 1955 and 1969. Ren also calls it the formal start of South-South cooperation, a declaration for peace and justice whose ten principles were absorbed into UN documents, and a milestone for the new China, whose Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence fed into those principles. For the present, Ren cites figures that the Global South accounts for over two-thirds of the world's countries and population, over 40% of world output and about 80% of growth. Ren credits the Belt and Road Initiative, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the New Development Bank, BRICS and the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives with advancing cooperation, and treats Xi Jinping's 2015 call to give the spirit new content as the guide. Ren sees unilateralism, protectionism and great-power bullying, with no state named in the argument beyond "certain major powers", as threatening the world. The article calls on the Global South to defend international fairness and the UN-centred order, keep economic cooperation open, resist bloc confrontation in the name of peace, and promote civilizational diversity. It ends by citing Zhou Enlai's 1955 "seek common ground" statement and Xi's pledge that China will remain a reliable friend of developing countries. Read the original if you want an official Chinese account of how Bandung is being invoked in current Global South diplomacy.

Accelerating the formation of source-material, discourse and theoretical systems for the community of the Chinese nation 加快形成中华民族共同体史料体系、话语体系和理论体系 Mao Huabing Mao Huabing takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the ninth collective study session of the 20th Politburo, to speed up a self-reliant Chinese system of historical sources, discourse and theory on the community of the Chinese nation. Mao argues that these "three systems" are an innovation in ethnic theory that applies the basic principles of Marxist ethnic theory to China's conditions and fine traditional culture. In this reading they support one another and form the scholarly and practical basis for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The article begins with current ethnic work. It cites uneven development in some regions and the rise abroad of separatism and religious extremism as threats to unity. It then devotes one section to each system: the source-material system, the discourse system and the theoretical system. A short conclusion describes how the three fit together. On sources, Mao calls for wider and better-organised collection: a thematic database that combines documents, archaeology, inscriptions and oral tradition, uses digital and AI tools, and verifies authenticity. Research should move from elite to popular perspectives, use cross-cultural and interdisciplinary methods, and follow historical materialism by reading fragments within the whole. On discourse, Mao says Western ethnic theory has dominated, so the concept of "nation" (minzu) has been stressed more than that of the "Chinese nation" (Zhonghua minzu). The proposed remedy is original concepts, plain-language communication, and the Party's leadership of discourse, with political, academic, everyday and international registers converting into one another. On theory, Mao advocates "de-familiarisation" and "re-problematisation" of existing concepts under Marxist guidance, a people-centred principle and unity of theory and practice. Mao also calls for more research on basic and practical problems, and for stronger disciplines and training of specialists. Mao concludes that the sources are the foundation, discourse is the bridge and theory is the soul of one organic whole. This whole is said to develop the Party's ethnic theory and policy, add substance to China's self-reliant knowledge system, and strengthen ethnic identity and cultural confidence. Mao also suggests that it can offer a Chinese approach to ethnic problems and civilisational conflict worldwide. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned account of how Chinese scholars are expected to build the research agenda behind the "community of the Chinese nation" concept.

Building the enforcement capacity of intra-Party regulations as the concrete form of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 党内法规执行力建设是全面从严治党的具体化 Huang Tianhong This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how the Party's self-reform can be secured institutionally. Huang Tianhong argues that strengthening the enforcement capacity of intra-Party regulations is the concrete form of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and that such regulations are indispensable to a long-term mechanism of self-reform. The piece first explains why institutional guarantees matter: they turn good working styles formed in self-reform into norms, support mechanisms for finding and solving problems, and help restrain power. It then sets out the roles of intra-Party regulations, headed by the Party Constitution, as a basis, a code of conduct, a standard for supervision and a source of values. The second half proposes four routes to better enforcement. Huang's core argument is that enforcement itself should embody the spirit of self-reform. The four routes are: improving the scientific quality and consistency of drafting (clear wording, no overlap or conflict between rules, alignment with the Constitution and law, timely revision with Party and public input); raising the integrity and professional competence of those who enforce; fostering rule-consciousness among all Party members and cadres; and strengthening supervision. On supervision, Huang calls for accountability mechanisms, links between Party and state, democratic, judicial, public and media oversight, performance assessment, and a mechanism that tolerates honest error while separating it from deliberate wrongdoing. Huang concludes that periodic campaigns of cleansing are necessary, but that long-term purity and vanguard status depend on reform and institutions. Pursuing self-reform scientifically and systematically is presented as a distinctive advantage of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and policy measures for improving the implementation of Party regulations.)

Making the "walking ideological and political course" take root in minds and hearts 让“行走的思政课”入心入脑 Lü Qimei Li Shuning This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how the "walking ideological and political course" (practice-based teaching outside the classroom) can truly persuade university students. The authors argue that the "big ideological and political course" initiative is not mere expansion in scale. In their view it restructures the elements of teaching through a dialectic of "seeing the large in the small". Taking the 2025 work plan issued by the Ministry of Education and nine other departments as its starting point, the piece is organised around three "bigs": a "big teaching force", a "big classroom" and a "big platform". Each section pairs a broad aim with concrete, small-scale methods. On teachers, the authors call for "great teachers" who combine disciplinary mastery with moral example, and for student-centred design. This includes menu-style activity choices, a "compulsory core plus elective" practice chain, problem-based guidance and mixed evaluation. On the classroom, they propose drawing on local revolutionary sites, traditional culture and the Party's founding spirit. They also propose immersive settings, including AR, visits to families, factories and fields, and ritual activities on meaningful dates. On the platform, they propose online-offline systems for showcasing student work, flipped classrooms, and cooperation among family, school, government and society. Volunteering and the "three going to the countryside" campaigns would serve as practice. The authors frame all this as the Marxist cycle of practice, knowledge and renewed practice. The authors conclude that the "big teaching force" is realised in each teacher's classroom craft, the "big classroom" in small observations in the field, and the "big platform" in cooperation among many actors. They present this unity of broad vision and fine detail as the basic guide for making the course reach minds and hearts. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese university ideological and political education is framed and what practical measures are proposed for it.

Resolutely fighting the anti-corruption struggle as a tough battle, a protracted war and an all-round campaign 坚决打好反腐败斗争攻坚战持久战总体战 Zhou Xinqun Zhou Xinqun's commentary, first published in the Party discipline newspaper China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News in June 2025, explains Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to fight corruption as a tough battle (gongjianzhan), a protracted war (chijiuzhan) and an all-round campaign (zongtizhan). Zhou argues that the formulation reflects a scientific reading of the situation and the laws of anti-corruption work. The author treats it as a political struggle the Party cannot afford to lose. The article is organised around three questions: why the three-part fight is needed, why the Party can win it, and how to advance it. The first section analyses the current situation. The second lists the Party's advantages. The third sets out five practical tasks. On the first question, Zhou holds that corruption remains serious, stubborn and recurrent. The author points to stock not yet cleared, new cases still emerging, collusion between officials and business, corruption among top leaders and in sectors such as finance, state enterprises and energy, and more concealed forms. The tough battle answers the difficulty of the task. The protracted war answers its long-term nature, which Zhou illustrates with dynastic decline and with lingering feudal and capitalist-influenced cultures of privilege. The all-round campaign answers its complexity, requiring the Party to advance the three-sphere approach of not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt, and to draw in the whole society. On the second question, Zhou cites a firm leadership core, scientific theory, popular support, an improved system of rules and supervision, and a rich set of preventive tools. For the third question Zhou proposes five tasks: strengthening the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership, keeping up high-pressure punishment, tightening checks on power, investigating and tackling unhealthy work styles and corruption together, and continuously cleaning up the political ecology through Party life and a culture of integrity. The three battles are presented as one integrated whole, not a sequence. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-press account of how the post-2012 anti-corruption campaign is framed, including its current priorities and policy vocabulary.

Carrying forward the Red Boat Spirit and keeping all undertakings in the front rank 传承红船精神 推动各项事业走在前列 Hu Jian Marking the 20th anniversary of the Red Boat Spirit (proposed in 2005), this commentary from Study Times (18 June 2025) asks how the spirit has driven the development of Jiaxing, the Zhejiang city where the Party's founding congress ended on a boat. Hu argues that the three components of the spirit have turned spiritual strength into material strength, and that the same spirit must guide Jiaxing's future path towards Chinese modernization. The piece opens by defining the spirit's three elements: pioneering initiative, firm ideals and perseverance, and selfless dedication to the Party and the people. It then reviews Jiaxing's record over two decades in five areas: economic growth, integrated urban-rural development, technological innovation, reform, and green and harmonious development. The final sections set out plans and requirements for the coming period, including economic, reform, innovation and Party-building tasks. Hu's central evidence is a set of statistics, which the author attributes to the Red Boat Spirit. Regional GDP is reported to have risen from 116.6 billion yuan in 2005 to 756.95 billion in 2024, and the urban-rural income ratio to have fallen from 2.02 to 1.51. Jiaxing is also said to rank first or second in Zhejiang on several innovation and digitalisation indicators. Looking ahead, Hu says the city will follow the "Eight-Eight Strategy", make high-quality development its first task, and aim at narrowing the "three major gaps". It will also deepen reform and opening up, build a manufacturing-innovation city, develop new quality productive forces, and pursue green and low-carbon transition. Hu also calls for strengthening Party building, with a cadre corps that is loyal, pragmatic and clean, and for continued anti-corruption work and study of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. Hu concludes that Jiaxing got where it is through spirit and must rely on spirit to move forward, and that the Red Boat Spirit remains its main source of inner motivation. The city is to become an important centre of the Yangtze River Delta urban cluster and to write a new Jiaxing chapter of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a local example of how Party commentary links the Red Boat Spirit to economic indicators, development plans and Party-building tasks.

Treating both symptoms and root causes: sustaining Party work-style building 标本兼治持之以恒推进作风建设 Liu Zhiming This newspaper commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 19 June 2025, asks how the Communist Party of China can make improvement of its work style (zuofeng) a lasting, routine undertaking. Liu Zhiming argues that building a good work style is a decisive source of the Party's strength, that the problem is stubborn and recurrent, and that only an approach treating both symptoms and root causes (biaoben jianzhi) can consolidate results. The piece is built in three parts. It first reviews the Party's history of work-style building, from Mao Zedong's rectification campaigns and the Yan'an style through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then argues that the work remains unfinished, citing current problems. Finally it sets out three practical lines of effort. Liu's core argument is that work-style problems are at root questions of Party spirit and of the Party's relationship with the people. The author lists persisting problems: wavering ideals, breaches of the eight-point regulation, formalism and bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, and disguised variants of these. Liu cites a 2024 National Bureau of Statistics survey in which 97.4 per cent were satisfied with the Party Central Committee's implementation of the eight-point regulation, but warns that old habits could rebound. The three remedies are to keep reinforcing the eight-point regulation, to strengthen Party-spirit cultivation (using the image of a pathogen that can relapse if the 'master switch' of worldview is wrong), and to build comprehensive institutions, because many apparent style problems are in fact institutional ones. Liu concludes that work-style building has a starting point but no end point, and that it must advance in step with the stage reached by the Party's and the people's cause, including further comprehensive deepening of reform and Chinese modernization. Proposed institutional measures include long-term mechanisms to reduce burdens on grassroots officials, revised performance appraisal, incentive and error-tolerance mechanisms, and checks on the allocation and exercise of power. Read the original if you want a concise official-style statement of how Party theorists frame the continuity and institutionalisation of work-style campaigns in the Xi Jinping era.

"The enemy advances, we advance": how the Eighth Route Army prevailed in North China “敌进我进”：八路军在华北的制胜之道 Deng Zhengyun Deng Zhengyun examines how the Eighth Route Army answered Japanese "cage" policies and "three-all" sweeps in North China during the War of Resistance against Japan. The short commentary argues that the strategy of "the enemy advances, we advance", which Deng presents as a creative stroke of Mao Zedong's military thought, was no passive evasion. In Deng's account it turned the Japanese rear into the front line. The piece rests on Mao's guerrilla concepts: turning defence into offence, fighting quick battles within a protracted war, and making enemy bases into guerrilla bases. Deng then works through three cases: the "three-three system" combat groups, the armed work teams (wugongdui), and the "red and black accounts" system. On the combat groups, Deng describes small units that cut telephone lines, blew up railway bridges and ambushed supply columns, which allegedly forced Japan to commit over 70 per cent of its troops to rear-area defence. The work teams, proposed by Nie Rongzhen in 1942, infiltrated occupied areas. Deng cites figures such as a 40 per cent monthly disruption of rail transport and the Ranzhuang tunnel defence. The red and black accounts recorded the conduct of collaborators and tied their survival to it. Deng cites a 400 per cent rise in puppet-troop desertion in 1943. Deng concludes that the approach traded space for time and built small victories into large ones. In this reading, strategic success depends on breaking conventional thinking. Read the original if you want a brief, celebratory account of Eighth Route Army guerrilla tactics, and of how they are presented in current Chinese popular historiography.

Grasping the root and foundation of work-style building 抓住作风建设的根与本 Li Kunpeng This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how the Communist Party of China should deepen its campaign to improve the conduct of its members, known as work-style building. Li Kunpeng argues, following Xi Jinping, that work-style problems are at root problems of Party spirit. Weak Party spirit produces distorted conduct, such as formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. The article proposes three lines of effort: building an ideological foundation, holding firm to ideals and the Party's purpose, and enforcing rules and moral self-cultivation. It draws on Xi's statements, the Party's history (including the "two musts" of the Xibaipo period) and the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. Li holds that cadres should arm themselves with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era through study that is systematic, prompt, reflective and tied to practice. The author says the "four undesirable work styles" are only surface symptoms, and that the real cause is departure from the Party's purpose of serving the people. The commentary links firm ideals to a people-centred approach and to the mass line. It also calls for updating Party regulations to cover hidden variants of the four work styles, naming "electronic red envelopes" and gifts sent by courier, and for strict implementation. Li concludes that combined ideological education, institutional constraint and moral cultivation will carry work-style building further and help build a Marxist governing party. The author calls on senior cadres to lead by example, drawing on traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary family traditions and discipline over relatives and staff. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-building view that work style is rooted in Party spirit.

The dialectical logic of building the Party's cultural leadership in the new era 新时代党的文化领导权建设的辩证逻辑 Wang Yan Liu Yang Wang Yan and Liu Yang take up the concept of "the Communist Party of China's cultural leadership" (cultural hegemony in Gramsci's vocabulary), which Xi Jinping put forward in June 2023.
