The article asks why building it is necessary, what it consists of, how it should be carried out and what it is for. Its thesis is that cultural leadership building in the new era rests on a set of dialectical relations, which the authors say show the Party acting with initiative and practical rationality. The article has four parts. The first treats the "ought" of this work as drawn from history, driven by present needs and oriented to the future. The second sets out its core meaning. The third turns to the practical layout. The fourth discusses its value. The authors trace Party practice from the new-democratic revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the present, and they draw on Gramsci, Marx and Engels, and Xi's speeches. In the authors' account, cultural leadership has three core dimensions: building a power system aimed at ideological leadership, a political practice that fosters national identity, and a governance strategy covering cultural production, management and communication. These are said to be mutually supporting. The practical layout rests on three unities: Party spirit with people-centredness, systematic design with targeted measures, and innovation with critique. The authors argue that creation opens cultural space while struggle against capital-driven alienation, Western-centrism and historical nihilism protects cultural security. They cast Western cultural influence, including "universal values" and consumerist commercial products, as a threat to cultural security that this leadership must counter. The authors conclude that the work brings value on three levels. It consolidates cultural subjectivity, notably through the Second Integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. It supports spiritual independence for the Chinese nation's modernization. It offers developing countries a "Chinese wisdom" for resisting Western cultural hegemony. They call for effectiveness to be judged by whether Party aims fit popular needs, whether overall planning is matched by precise measures, and whether cultural progress is matched by cleaning up cultural disorder. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how cultural hegemony is conceptualised in current Chinese ideological work.

On the Communist Party of China's capacity for modernization in the new era: components, logic of formation and integrated pathway 论新时代中国共产党的现代化建设能力：构成要素、生成逻辑与集成路径 Hu Hongbin Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for comprehensively raising cadres' capacity for modernization, and Xi Jinping's later demand to raise the whole Party's Marxist level and modernization capacity, Hu Hongbin asks what this capacity actually is, how it forms in practice and how it can be fully raised. Using systems thinking, the article argues that the Party's modernization capacity is an organic whole made up of several types of element. Hu contends it can be raised only by integrating those elements through a systematic pathway. The article has four parts. It first defines the capacity and its functions in the deepening of Chinese modernization. It then sets out the capacity's components, explains the mechanism and modes by which it forms, and ends with a three-stage pathway for improvement. Hu draws on Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping to ground systems thinking as a method. Hu sorts the components into three groups. Foundational elements are theoretical (Marxist modernization theory and the theoretical system of Chinese modernization) and historical (the Party's long exploration from Mao Zedong to Deng Xiaoping and after). Operational elements are executive (strategic, policy and reform execution) and social (the public's recognition of and participation in the Party's agenda). Safeguarding elements are organisational, institutional and personnel-related, with a high-quality cadre corps as the key. Because these elements come from different actors, Hu identifies three generative modes: "endogenous" construction by the Party, "exogenous" assistance from social actors, and collaborative "symbiosis" between the two. The proposed integrated pathway improves the elements at three points: construction and input, integration and adjustment, and output after practical conversion. At the centre is a comprehensive, digital "one-stop" Party-building platform that breaks down administrative and information barriers. It would be paired with dynamic coordination and practice-conversion mechanisms, followed by feedback and evaluation mechanisms. Hu also calls for stronger cadre training, wider channels for social participation and a summary of the people's experience of modernization. Read the original if you want a systems-theory account of how Party-building scholarship frames capacity-building for Chinese modernization, including its proposals for platform design and evaluation mechanisms.

Methodology for advancing the systematization and academic grounding of the Party's innovative theory 推进党的创新理论体系化学理化的方法论 Chen Jinlong Chen Jinlong takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the sixth group study session of the 20th Politburo, to "vigorously advance the systematization and academic grounding" of the Party's innovative theory. The article defines that theory as Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Systematization means starting from the texts and revealing their structure and internal relations. Academic grounding means using the theories and methods of different disciplines to bring out their underlying reasoning. Chen argues that this work follows a methodology with three parts: a holistic perspective, academic expression and the recognition of laws. The article is organised in three sections, one for each part. The first treats the theory as a whole: its formation, content, features and historical standing. The second works through levels of academic expression: signature concepts, original concepts, basic categories, propositions, principles, and worldview and methodology. The third identifies the laws of Communist Party governance, socialist construction, human social development and the Party's own theoretical innovation. On the holistic perspective, Chen lists five conditions behind the theory's formation: theoretical sources, practical foundation, cultural heritage, the conditions of the age, and subjective conditions. Chen proposes organising its content under fifteen headings, from the Party's overall leadership to Chinese modernization, and assesses its standing across long historical spans. On academic expression, Chen names four signature concepts (socialism with Chinese characteristics, Chinese modernization, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation). Chen also names original concepts such as whole-process people's democracy, new quality productive forces and a community with a shared future for mankind. Chen says these should be explained with disciplinary tools, for example political science for democracy and Marxist political economy for productive forces. On laws, Chen holds that the theory has deepened understanding in four areas, citing the Two Integrations and the Party's self-reform as principle-level results. Chen concludes that systematization and academic grounding are distinct but mutually supporting: grounding rests on systematization, and systematization relies on grounding. Chen calls the task practical as well as theoretical, one that requires the whole Party and especially scholars, who must master the concepts and methods of their disciplines. Chen also links it to building an independent system of Chinese philosophy and social science knowledge, which the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) placed within cultural reform. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese academics are told to frame, categorise and explain Xi Jinping Thought as a scholarly system.

Understanding that the core of the style-of-work problem is the Party's relationship with the people 深刻理解作风问题核心是党同人民群众的关系问题 Chen Li Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 7), Chen Li takes up the Party-wide study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. Chen's thesis, drawn from Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), is that the core of the problem of work style (zuofeng) is the relationship between the Party and the people. On this reading, work-style building must centre on keeping the Party's flesh-and-blood ties with the masses, upholding the Marxist mass viewpoint and applying the Party's mass line. The article has four parts, each arguing that focusing on this relationship has a different kind of basis: theoretical, practical, realistic and policy-based. The first part goes through Marx and Lenin. The second covers the Party's history from 1919 to the present. The third turns to current conditions and tasks. The fourth sets out the deployment of the campaign and five practical requirements. Chen's central move is to derive the point from historical materialism. Marx's view that the masses make history, and the Communist Manifesto's description of the proletarian movement as that of the immense majority, are presented as the basis for how a Marxist party must treat the people. Chen reads Lenin as adding that a party's strength comes from the masses and that bureaucracy is a major source of popular discontent, so improving work style is necessary. Chen then argues that Chinese Communist experience confirms this, citing Mao Zedong's "bastion of iron" remark, the Central Soviet Area ditty on cadres, and the "half a quilt" story. Under present conditions, the author says, Chinese modernization and a turbulent international environment require reliance on the people. Chen adds that problems of impure thinking, organisation and work style persist and that the Party faces the "four tests" and "four dangers". Chen calls for five things: strengthening ideals and convictions through Marxist historical materialism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; practising the mass line and addressing people's pressing concerns; targeted action against formalism, bureaucracy and disguised variants of the "four undesirable work styles", with joint investigation of misconduct and corruption; enforcing discipline, including mass discipline; and persistence, since work-style problems recur. The aim is to make work-style building regular and long-term and to maintain the Party's vanguard character. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party historian presents the theoretical lineage and official rationale for the 2025 campaign on the eight-point regulation.

A new account of the process of ideological and political education from the perspective of social operation 基于社会运行视角的思想政治教育过程新论 Dai Yuqi Yu Xiaochun Dai Yuqi and Yu Xiaochun ask how the process of ideological and political education should be understood once it is placed within the wider operation of society rather than treated as an isolated teaching activity. They argue that the process has a pronounced social character, and that viewing it through 'social operation' (society as a living organic whole in motion and change) gives a fuller grasp of its meaning and logic. The authors present this as both a critique of traditional educational models and an exploration of models suited to the new era. The article proposes three layers of the process, running from core to periphery: self-organising operation inside the ideological and political education system, interactive operation between that system and other social subsystems, and 'ubiquitous' operation in which such education is embedded in society as a whole. Each layer gets its own section, which sets out the process's elements (educators, educatees, content, methods and context), describes how it unfolds, and proposes ways to optimise it. The self-organisation concept is traced to Kant. In the authors' account, the three layers differ in how widely the five elements are defined. In self-organising operation, educators are professional theory and propaganda staff, educatees are highly organised groups such as Party members, soldiers and students, and methods are explicit ones such as theoretical indoctrination. In interactive operation, the categories widen to all who work in culture, media and education, and to loosely organised groups such as flexible workers. Methods become implicit ones such as exemplars, motivation and influence, and the system exchanges resources with the political, economic, cultural and technological subsystems. In ubiquitous operation, implicit political, ideological, economic and cultural factors run through the process. The authors distinguish benign, neutral and malign social operation and argue that a well-functioning society itself acts as an 'invisible' form of such education. For optimisation, the authors call for broadening the field beyond schools and teachers, ensuring all elements are present and linked, and coordinating mechanisms, personnel (full-time and part-time) and resources across social subsystems. They also call for closer ties to practice, responsiveness to social concerns and greater continuity across time and space, including online. They state that Chinese society is currently in a benign, stable and improving state, which they say strengthens the effects of such education. Read the original if you want a systems-theoretical framework for studying ideological and political education as part of society, and how Chinese scholars conceptualise its explicit and implicit forms.

Constructing a value-added evaluation system for teaching ideological and political theory courses in universities 高校思政课教学增值评价体系构建探赜 Chang Qing Chang Qing asks how the teaching effect of university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng courses) can be evaluated effectively as these courses move towards high-quality development. The author borrows the economic notion of "value-added" evaluation, which looks at the "added value" created between input and output and so measures process as well as result. The article argues that such a system goes beyond traditional outcome-based evaluation, records the whole teaching process and separates out the effects of unfair background factors. The article is published in School Party Building and Ideological Education (2025, no. 8) and has three parts. The first sets out the design orientation of the system around three goals: knowledge, ability and emotional identification. The second builds the indicators, weights them with the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) and describes how the system is applied. The third discusses the difficulties of construction and proposes countermeasures. Chang derives the indicators from official documents and speeches by Xi Jinping. The three first-level indicators are acquisition of Marxist theoretical knowledge, students' ability to analyse and solve problems, and loyalty to the Party and state. Second-level indicators include knowledge of Marxist theory and of the Party's innovative theory, practical and complex problem-solving ability, and political literacy, moral feeling and self-identification. AHP is used to build a three-tier hierarchy, a 1–9 scale pairwise comparison matrix and a consistency test. Application is to centre on students' learning outcomes and a dynamic feedback mechanism of data collection, analysis, feedback generation and adjustment. Chang names three difficulties: emotional and political goals resist quantification, teachers of large classes struggle to track students' changing behaviour, and evaluation is affected by uncertain external and individual factors. The proposed responses are to fuse multi-source data (text and behaviour logs, with teachers and supervisors as evaluators), to track students with online platforms, for instance attention curves and interest in theoretical and social issues, and to reduce uncertainty through what the author calls the "common base-point principle", which seeks the core link between students and Marxist theory. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholars try to turn the goals of political-theory teaching into measurable indicators and weighted evaluation models.

The logic and mechanisms of integrating revolutionary cultural relics into the "Big Ideological and Political Course" 革命文物融入“大思政课”建设的逻辑与机制 Wu Xiaowei Wu Xiaowei takes up a practical question in Chinese ideological and political education: how revolutionary cultural relics can be built into the "Big Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke), a concept Xi Jinping stressed in 2021 when he said it must be used well and tied to reality. The article argues that the relics are a high-quality teaching resource and that integration needs a clear rationale, guiding principles and working mechanisms. Wu sets out these three layers in turn. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out why integration is possible and valuable. The second lists six principles tied to six elements of the construction work: subjects, objects, purpose, content, method and context. The third describes two forms of integration and the mechanisms each requires. Wu cites figures that China has registered 36,000 immovable revolutionary relics, over one million state-held movable items and more than 1,600 revolutionary museums and memorial halls. On value, Wu argues that the relics embody revolutionary history and spirit, enrich the content of teaching, and link the classroom with society at large. They also open the way to "inter-subjective" education, in which teachers and students explore the relics together. The six principles are collaborative education, teaching according to aptitude across school stages, moral cultivation (lide shuren), adaptation to local conditions, keeping pace with the times through digital technology, and building immersive settings. In the third part, Wu distinguishes two forms. In the first, relics enter the classroom indirectly, through teachers' retelling, and need a screening mechanism and an embedding mechanism. In the second, museums and memorial sites themselves become courses, and need a collaboration mechanism and a transformation mechanism that turn social actors into participants in a community of educators. Wu says that in each pair the first mechanism is a precondition of the second, and that feedback runs between them. Wu concludes that integration works only if multiple actors are coordinated, the resources are screened and fitted to specific courses, and sites are converted into learning environments, all in service of the fundamental task of moral education. The relics are presented as helping to strengthen emotional identification with the Party's revolutionary history. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese education scholars design practical frameworks for using museums and red heritage in ideological and political teaching.

Japanese archives corroborate the Communist Party of China's role as the mainstay of the War of Resistance against Japan 日方档案佐证中国共产党在抗日战争中的中流砥柱作用 Wu Xiangping Writing in Guangming Daily in 2025, Wu Xiangping asks what Japanese wartime records reveal about the Communist Party of China's (CPC) part in the War of Resistance against Japan. Wu argues that these records, seen from the enemy's side, confirm the Party's role as the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) of the resistance. In Wu's view they also refute claims that glorify the Kuomintang's war effort while denying the CPC's position and role. The article draws on documents produced by Japanese bodies from 1929 to 1944. These include South Manchuria Railway (Mantetsu) survey reports, Foreign Ministry intelligence compilations, army staff papers, and publications by Japanese policy and foreign-affairs associations. It also cites remarks by Prime Ministers Konoe Fumimaro and Abe Nobuyuki and by Prince Mikasa. It is organised in three parts: how Japanese observers rated the CPC as a political force, how the Japanese army made the CPC its main military target, and how Japanese sources judged the strength of CPC forces. Wu's core argument rests on quoted Japanese assessments. Before and after the Mukden Incident (1931), Japanese reports called the CPC the most potential political force in China and the centre of an emerging anti-Japanese united front. After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of 1937, Japanese army documents, in Wu's account, named the Communists as the key target of military 'suppression'. They record that the Eighth Route Army and local guerrillas filled the 'vacuum' left in North China when most Kuomintang main forces withdrew, and set up base areas. Japanese officials described the CPC-led bases as a 'cancer' and the Party as the real enemy of Japan's 'new order'. Wu also cites Prince Mikasa's 1944 remark that the Japanese army could not match the Communist forces. Wu concludes that the Japanese records show the CPC organising resistance immediately after 1931 and promoting the anti-Japanese national united front and Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. They also show it leading resistance behind enemy lines, building 19 base areas, and tying down Japanese forces. In Wu's reading, this changed the balance of forces and laid the foundation for final victory. Read the original if you want to see which Japanese-side documents are cited in support of the CPC's wartime role as presented in current Chinese historiography.

A cultural banner raised high in the fires of the War of Resistance against Japan The cultural resistance led by the Communist Party of China and its great significance 抗日烽火中高擎的文化旗帜 Wang Jiping Writing in Guangming Daily on 18 June 2025, Wang Jiping argues that the cultural resistance led by the Communist Party of China was an integral part of the Chinese people's War of Resistance against Japan, alongside its military, political and economic dimensions. In Wang's account, it repelled Japanese imperialism's cultural aggression and enslavement, defended Chinese national culture, lifted morale and gathered the spirit of the nation. The article is organised in three parts. The first presents cultural resistance as a struggle to defend Chinese culture against Japanese policies in occupied areas. The second sets out the Party's role as the mainstay of that effort, covering united-front organisations, the press, literature and art, music, academic work, science and education. The third turns to the significance of cultural resistance for national spirit and for the development of Chinese culture. Wang describes Japanese cultural policy as destruction of institutions and books, persecution of intellectuals, slogans such as the "New Order in East Asia", and enslaving education. Against this, the article says, Party-led patriotic cultural workers built a broad cultural united front, from the 1936 declaration signed by Lu Xun, Guo Moruo and Mao Dun to the 1938 founding of the All-China Anti-Aggression Association of Literary and Art Circles in Wuhan. Wang cites works such as the Yellow River Cantata and the March of the Volunteers, the founding of Marxist history, philosophy and economics, and cadre-training schools in the base areas. Drawing on Mao Zedong, Wang holds that because the new culture after the May Fourth Movement was proletarian-led New Democratic culture, cultural resistance had to be led by the Party. Wang concludes that the Party's leadership carried forward the great spirit of resistance, opposed Kuomintang cultural dictatorship and feudal or capitulationist currents, and advanced the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. In this reading, it moved Chinese culture from bourgeois new culture to New Democratic culture and opened a new stage in cultural development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state scholarship frames wartime culture as Party-led and as a foundation for later Marxist scholarship in China.

Deepening the joint investigation and joint handling of unhealthy work styles and corruption 深入推进风腐同查同治 Tao Yuanhao This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 18 June 2025, takes up the instruction that the Party should deepen the joint investigation and joint handling of unhealthy work styles and corruption. Tao Yuanhao notes that Xi Jinping raised the point at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, and that the session's communiqué called for a mechanism to push the correction of work styles and the fight against corruption forward as one. Tao argues that this approach reflects a higher level of understanding of the regularities of Party conduct and anti-corruption work in the new era. The article has three sections. The first sets out why the approach is a major strategic consideration for keeping the Party healthy. The second explains why work-style problems and corruption share one root, and describes two directions of inquiry. The third sets out practical measures for building a clean political ecosystem. On the theory, Tao draws on the formula that Party spirit, Party conduct and Party discipline form an organic whole, with Party spirit as the foundation, conduct as its expression and discipline as its safeguard. The article presents the approach as a summary of practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and as a requirement of the Party's self-reform. In Tao's account, bad work styles and corruption are two faces of one problem: both stem from wavering ideals and convictions, and corruption often begins with a dinner, a gift or a red envelope. "Investigating corruption through work style" follows such clues to hidden bribery and power-for-money deals. "Correcting work style through corruption cases" examines the extravagance and indulgence behind corrupt officials. Tao proposes that joint investigation should punish cases where the two problems intertwine, by enforcing the eight-point regulation, pursuing new and hidden forms of corruption, and investigating bribe-givers together with bribe-takers. Joint handling should remove common roots through Party-spirit education, institutional improvements such as multi-department supervision of the "four unhealthy tendencies", and strict discipline. Tao also calls for stopping small problems early and for using big data to find leads. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the rationale and the working methods behind current Party discipline campaigns.

Accelerating the transformation of scientific and technological achievements in the new era 加快新时代科技成果转化 Qu Dacheng Qu Dacheng takes up the problem of getting scientific and technological achievements out of the laboratory and into production, a step the article treats as the link between science and application. Qu argues that accelerating this transformation is a priority for China as states compete for the commanding heights of a new technological and industrial revolution. The piece is a policy commentary that follows the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for deepening reform of the mechanisms for transforming scientific and technological achievements and strengthening the national technology transfer system. The article has three parts. The first sets out why transformation matters: for high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, for forming new quality productive forces, and for industrial innovation. The second names four key elements, namely technology, people, finance and markets, and discusses the science base, education and talent, and financial backing. The third proposes new pathways, drawing on quotations from Xi Jinping and on the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference. In Qu's account, transformation is the point where innovation chains meet industrial chains, and its weakness is the so-called "valley of death", where many results remain idle in laboratories. Qu holds that the new-type whole-nation system should be used to strengthen enterprises as the main body of innovation, speed up work on key core technologies and deepen industry–university–research integration. The concrete measures cover government guidance and top-level design, shared pilot-scale testing platforms, and institutional reform such as granting researchers rights over职务 service-related results through an "empowerment + transfer + agreed income" model. They also include training professional technology managers and building a science-and-technology finance system with insurance, risk-compensation funds and long-term government guidance funds. Qu concludes that a combination of state guidance, enterprise leadership, talent development, supportive law and policy, and finance suited to innovation can turn more original and frontier technologies into real productive forces. The article presents this as raising China's position in global industrial and value chains and supporting high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy agenda on technology transfer and its reform measures as presented in a Party theoretical journal.

Shaping a new pattern of fostering virtue through the "Great Ideological and Political Course" 以“大思政课”塑造立德树人新格局 Lü Chao Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 11), Lü Chao takes up Xi Jinping's remarks to education-sector political advisers at the 2025 national "two sessions". Xi called for merging the ideological and political "small classroom" with the social "big classroom". Lü argues that the "Great Ideological and Political Course" is the main channel for fostering virtue and cultivating talent, and for supplying the personnel that Chinese modernization requires. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out why the Great Course matters. The second sets out the regularities that should guide it. The third proposes new paths for building it. Lü draws on Xi's speeches and on official documents, including the Education Power Construction Plan (2024–2035) and a Ministry of Education opinion on digitalising education. Lü also cites examples: 453 national practice teaching bases, and university brands at Peking University, Renmin University and the National University of Defense Technology. Lü gives three reasons for the Great Course. It is needed to carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent amid ideological struggle, rapid growth in the internet and artificial intelligence, and changes in how young people think. It is needed to develop ideological and political courses in depth. And it is needed to consolidate students' ideological foundations. On method, Lü highlights three principles: focusing on forging souls, emphasising practice-based education, and strengthening systems thinking. Under these principles, knowledge transmission goes with value guidance, explicit teaching with implicit teaching, and scientific literacy with humanistic grounding. Teaching, faculty and platforms are planned as a whole, and schools, families and society are linked. Lü's proposals concern three areas. The first is problem-solving, through integrated ideological and political education across primary, secondary and tertiary levels, with shared content, rituals and teacher training, plus a school–family–society framework. The second is innovation in method: case-based and interactive teaching, practice bases, and online "smart teaching" via platforms such as Xuexi Qiangguo. The third is results-oriented evaluation, with teachers, students and parents forming an "evaluation community" that assesses students' knowing, believing and acting and uses AI-assisted tools. Read the original if you want a Party-journal account of how ideological and political education is being extended beyond the classroom, including its institutional examples and policy references.

Strengthening the protection and use of revolutionary cultural relics 加强革命文物保护利用 Gao Yifan Gao Yifan takes up how revolutionary cultural relics should be protected and put to use in the new era. Opening with Xi Jinping's statements that such relics carry the Party's and the people's history and that protecting them is a shared responsibility of the whole Party and society, Gao argues for a combined programme. It rests on scientific protection, activation of the relics' contemporary value, wider social reach and durable institutional mechanisms. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscript, is organised in four parts. The first deals with building a scientific protection system; the second with activating the relics' value today; the third with expanding their social influence; and the fourth with long-term mechanisms. Gao cites figures from the National Cultural Heritage Administration: over 36,000 registered immovable revolutionary relics and more than one million movable items or sets. Many sites, Gao notes, still suffer from disrepair and inadequate protection. Gao's core argument is that protection and use must move together under the principle of 'upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground' (shouzheng chuangxin). On protection, Gao calls for grading by historical value, degree of endangerment and difficulty of conservation, not only by administrative level. Gao also wants detailed classification, stronger technology such as 3D scanning, virtual reconstruction and AI, and dedicated regulations following the revised Cultural Relics Protection Law of 2024. On use, Gao proposes integration with cultural tourism and rural revitalisation, while warning that this must not become mere 'sightseeing with a plaque'. Gao also proposes adding relics to the national education system, including the 'large-scale ideological and political course', and building a short-video and new-media communication matrix. Social coordination and international exhibitions are meant to raise cultural soft power and international discourse power. Gao concludes by proposing long-term mechanisms. These include a national coordinating body, giving revolutionary relics more weight in the 15th Five-Year Plan for cultural heritage, a special central fund with local budget lines and social capital, and performance supervision of spending. Gao also calls for interdisciplinary training that combines conservation skills with Party history, Marxist theory and communication studies, and for a professional qualification system. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated researcher sets out current policy priorities for 'red heritage' work, from legal and technological protection to education, tourism and overseas outreach.

From "civilization through technology" to "technology through civilization" New China's path to modernization and the character of its civilization in the long durée “由技术而文明”到“由文明而技术” Hu Tianjiao Hu Tianjiao asks how to understand what is distinctive about the path of Chinese modernization and about the new form of human civilization built on it. The article argues that Western modernity operates on a logic of "civilization through technology", under which technological and productive power decides who counts as civilized. New China, in Hu's account, first worked within this logic and then moved beyond it towards "technology through civilization". Taking a long historical view and a China–West comparison, the article begins with the nineteenth-century Western "intrusion" into China and the civilized/barbarous/savage hierarchy that legitimised colonialism. It then examines two strands of New China's technological effort: building an independent and complete industrial system, and pursuing cutting-edge science alongside mass mobilisation of local knowledge. A third part sets out how China is said to have transcended the logic through three steps. Hu contends that late-Qing and later Chinese thinkers followed the same sequence from technology to civilization, and that New China needed a modernization that was both self-directed and progressive. Examples include the 1956 long-range science plan, the Chinese malaria drug artemisinin and hybrid rice. Yet the article holds that China did not simply assimilate this logic. It recognised it "negatively" as a historical reality, for example in the Sino-Soviet dispute over whether Western "position of strength" policy had ended. It then separated civilization from technology by defining civilization relationally, by a state's commitment to equal international order and respect for other nations' paths. Finally it re-anchored technology in the people: developed for the people and relying on them. Hu points to the 1950s combination of advanced weaponry and the "mass line", with its flat project teams and cooperation among cadres, experts and workers. The author says this model influenced Toyotism and post-Fordist practice and avoided the deskilling of workers under capitalism. The conclusion is that China's path corrects the defects of modern civilization rather than overturning it, and that it remains unfinished and open to the future. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language argument linking technology, civilizational discourse and Chinese modernization, with historical cases from the 1950s onward.

Social spatial practice, representations of space and representational spaces A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space 社会空间实践与空间表象和表征 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing reads the core of Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space (1974): how social space is produced through the "triad" of spatial practice, representations of space and representational spaces. Zhang argues that Lefebvre's critique of everyday life moved from a time-based view of history to a logic of spatial production. Zhang calls this shift a "Lutheran revolution" in the understanding of space, and also identifies logical blind spots in Lefebvre's account. The article is a close, concept-by-concept commentary on Lefebvre's French text. It moves through four sections: spatial practice as the reproduction of modes of production and social relations; the role of representations; the three-part dialectic itself; and the "micro-texture" of social space (the human subject, historicity and the primacy of practice). Zhang draws on Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and Capital, and on Husserl and Heidegger. Zhang repeatedly uses Lefebvre's earlier works, Metaphilosophy and The Urban Revolution, as a comparison. Zhang's central claim is that for Lefebvre social space is not a physical container but a field of relations that arises and vanishes in everyday practice. Buildings and roads serve only as tools that reactivate those relations. In capitalism Lefebvre identifies three levels of reproduction: of life, of labour-power and of the social relations of production. Representations of space (plans, knowledge, codes) and representational spaces (lived, imagined experience) can mask real relations, for instance by presenting market exchange as natural. Zhang's own critical addition is that Lefebvre overlooks how, in class societies, only rulers hold the power to conceive space, so the conceiving-doing distinction is historically specific rather than universal. Zhang ties this to Marx and Engels's account of the separation of self-activity from material production. Zhang also notes that Lefebvre holds practice to be primary while allowing mutual interaction among the three moments, and that Lefebvre rejects the primacy of ideas over practice as an illusion. Zhang concludes that Lefebvre's spatial theory enriches historical materialism by showing in detail how ideas, symbols and lived experience take part in producing social relations. It keeps a materialist base in practice, and it locates people's own existence as the substance of social space. Zhang adds that its strengths are limited by Lefebvre's neglect of the development of productive forces and of class inequalities in who shapes space. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Western Marxism or spatial theory and want a Chinese Marxist critical reading, which uses Zhang's own interpretive vocabulary, of the three-part spatial dialectic.

The historical creation and practical achievements of "combining education with productive labour" “教育与生产劳动相结合”的历史创建和实践成就 Xu Xiyuan Liang Yanbing Xu Xiyuan and Liang Yanbing take up the Marxist principle of combining education with productive labour, which they describe as both part of Marxist educational theory and a long-standing tradition of the Chinese Communist Party. They note that artificial intelligence has prompted worries about labour education being outdated, the deskilling of labour and technological unemployment. The article argues that the Party's practice, from the revolutionary years to the present, shows the principle to be historically necessary and productive, and that it remains a guide for education in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the principle arose and developed, under four headings: the needs of economic production, the need to overcome the separation of knowledge from practice, the need to overcome the split between mental and manual labour, and the aim of all-round human development. The second reviews achievements in three fields: transforming society, promoting production, and cultivating people. The third draws lessons for the present and uses Xi Jinping's 2024 speech at the National Education Conference as its reference point. Xu and Liang tie each historical stage to a distinct need. In the base areas of the Yan'an period, schools and students took part in the production campaigns in order to survive the blockade. After 1949, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping presented the principle as a remedy for schooling cut off from society and for the gap between mental and manual workers. The authors credit the Party's practice with giving working people access to education, with bringing intellectuals and workers and peasants together, with raising the status of women, with supporting economic growth and innovation, and with producing people developed in moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour terms. They distinguish this from capitalist combinations of education and labour, which they say serve the extraction of surplus value and short-term employment. The authors conclude that the history confirms the classical Marxist view of the principle as the fundamental route to transforming society, raising labour productivity and forming well-rounded people. They propose upholding Party leadership, adopting a people-centred approach, and innovating in practice: compulsory labour education at every school level, family–school–society cooperation, and vocational education that integrates industry and education. They present this as a distinctive contribution of socialism with Chinese characteristics to global education. Read the original if you want a Party-historical account of how the education–labour principle has been justified and applied from the revolutionary bases to current labour education policy.

Mao Zedong on the Zunyi Conference 毛泽东论遵义会议 Lin Xuwu The Zunyi Conference, an enlarged Politburo meeting held during the Long March in January 1935, is widely treated as a historic turning point for the Chinese Communist Party and for Mao Zedong's own career. Lin Xuwu observes that existing scholarship has paid little attention to what Mao himself wrote and said about it. The article sets out to identify Mao's relevant texts, his core views and the historical value of those views. Lin first counts the sources. Searching Mao's Selected Works, Collected Works and selected letters, the author finds 20 writings that mention the conference 40 times in all, 36 before 1949 and four after. The first is from December 1936 and the last from September 1963. The main part then sets out four strands in Mao's assessment, and a final section assesses their value. In Lin's reading, Mao consistently held that Zunyi corrected the serious "Left" errors of 1931–34, which he variously called opportunist, dogmatist and subjectivist. Mao also credited the conference with promoting unity in the Party and the Red Army. Lin points to Mao's decision to confine the meeting mainly to military questions and to avoid labelling the earlier line a full line error, and to his insistence on thanking those comrades who had erred. The third strand is independence and self-reliance. Lin argues that the Party corrected its course without Comintern direction and criticised a Comintern adviser in a Central document for the first time. Mao is quoted as saying that real understanding of independence began at Zunyi. The fourth strand treats Zunyi as a turning point in line and in ideological work. Lin concludes that Mao's views shaped the 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in Party History and fed into the later historical resolutions, including the 2021 resolution on the Party's century of struggle. Lin also holds that Mao's insistence on analysing both sides of the earlier period, rather than rejecting everything, exemplifies dialectical and historical materialism. Independence and self-reliance, in the author's account, runs from Zunyi through Mao, Deng Xiaoping and later leaders to the Party's ten historical lessons. Read the original if you want a source-based account of how Mao characterised Zunyi and how that characterisation entered official Party historiography.

Establishing and improving a long-term mechanism for building socialist cultural and ethical progress 建立健全精神文明建设长效机制 Sun Cunliang This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in June 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction on spiritual civilization work. The instruction calls for stronger organisational leadership, deeper reform and innovation, and broad social mobilisation, so as to form a long-term mechanism in which all parties share responsibility. Sun Cunliang argues that this requirement both distils historical experience and answers present-day conditions, and that it points the way to high-quality development of spiritual civilization work. The article opens with the Dragon Boat Festival activities run through New Era Civilization Practice Centres, then proceeds in three parts. The first reviews the Party's experience from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) onwards, citing resolutions of the Sixth Plenum of the 12th Central Committee and the Sixth Plenum of the 14th Central Committee, the later leadership system, and measures since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second explains why such a mechanism fits the era. The third sets out three practical directions. Sun's central claim is that spiritual civilization is a systemic, long-term task that cannot be left to cultural departments or to campaign-style governance. The author gives three grounds: the people's expectations have shifted with the change in the principal contradiction, the work cuts across every field and requires coordination among Party committees, government, enterprises, social organisations and citizens, and shaping people's thinking is gradual and faces the long-term, complex influence of Western ideology. Institutional mechanisms are presented as the way to overcome the 'gust of wind' effect of campaigns. Sun then proposes strengthening Party leadership through a 'single chessboard' approach and performance assessment, deepening innovation through the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) reforms and digital technologies, and mobilising enterprises, charities and volunteers. Sun concludes that institutional innovation, coordination among actors and pooling of resources will let civilization practice endure and supply ideological guarantees and moral nourishment for national rejuvenation. Spiritual and cultural needs are linked to common prosperity in the realm of spiritual life. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present the institutional logic behind spiritual civilization work and its link to Xi Jinping Thought on Culture.

Fundamental guidelines and practical paths for building a strong education nation in the new era 新时代教育强国建设的根本遵循与实践路径 Chen Junjing This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, asks how China should build a strong education nation (jiaoyu qiangguo) and answers by interpreting Xi Jinping's September 2024 speech at the National Education Conference, his Qiushi article "Accelerating the Building of a Strong Education Nation" and the 2024–2035 outline for the goal. Chen Junjing argues that these texts provide the fundamental guidelines and the practical path for the task. The article has three parts: the political direction and value coordinates of the effort; the practical path to a high-quality education system; and the supporting systems needed to sustain it. On direction, Chen stresses the Party's overall leadership, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Chen also calls for a people-centred approach that narrows urban–rural gaps, and for a global outlook that contributes Chinese educational wisdom to a community with a shared future for mankind. On the path, Chen proposes integrating education, science and technology, and talent, with universities reforming disciplines, training models and evaluation. Chen also proposes strengthening original innovation, and opening education to the outside world through a cycle of input, integration and output. For support, Chen calls for institutional reform, deeper integration of AI and digital tools, a stronger teaching force guided by the spirit of educators, and industry–education integration across the education, talent, industry and innovation chains. Chen concludes that educational strength should become talent, scientific and development strength, underpinning Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics are presenting official education policy in 2025.

Economic practice and theoretical exploration in the period of socialist revolution and construction Reflections on compiling "Economic History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1978)" 社会主义革命和建设时期的经济实践与理论探索 He Yaomin He Yaomin, who led the team of authors, introduces a new national textbook, Economic History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1978), published by Renmin University of China Press. He describes it as the first systematic, centrally compiled textbook on the economic history from 1949 to the start of reform and opening up, and a core course text for university economics. The article, a reflective commentary from Guangming Daily (17 June 2025), argues that studying this period's economic practice and theory will help build an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese economics. He first sets out the contemporary value of this research. He then defines the object of study at three levels and names the key themes of the period. The last part deals with method. He lists concrete topics that he says deserve further study, including the general line for the transition period, land reform and agricultural cooperation, the planned economy, heavy-industry priority and the Angang Constitution. He argues that the period of less than thirty years, despite serious setbacks, established the socialist economic system and an independent, relatively complete industrial and national economic system. In his account it also formed the path of socialist economic construction, which laid the political, institutional and material foundations for later development. Some experiences can be distilled into core concepts of Chinese economics, such as self-reliance, concentrating resources on major undertakings and respecting objective economic laws. On method, He calls for dialectical and historical materialism, guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. He also calls for a correct view of Party history, which neither hides mistakes because of achievements nor denies achievements because of mistakes. He insists that the periods before and after reform and opening up must not be used to negate each other. He concludes that the theme of the period is the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, its main thread is exploring the path of economic construction and modernization, and its essence is achievement and valuable experience. He presents this as a basis for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Chinese economic historian frames the official approach to the 1949–1978 period and the principles behind a state-sanctioned textbook.

Improving the comprehensive internet governance system 健全网络综合治理体系 Zeng Runxi This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to improve the comprehensive internet governance system. Zeng Runxi argues that this system is now an important part of China's national governance system and that building it is a complex systems project. It requires, the author says, grasping the laws of internet development and applying systems thinking so that governance becomes more effective and the online environment "clearer and more orderly". The article is organised under four headings: upholding the Party's overall leadership; deepening reform of the internet management system; maintaining a healthy online ecosystem; and coordinating development and security. Each section draws heavily on statements by Xi Jinping on cyberspace work and turns them into practical tasks for Party committees, officials, government departments, companies and users. On leadership, Zeng argues that the Party must keep control of the internet and that responsibility for online ideological work must be fully enforced. The author also calls for Party building to be integrated with business operations in internet firms and online social organisations, and for better online skills among leading cadres. On management, Zeng proposes integrating governance actors, levels, institutions and tools, and covering the whole process from prevention to feedback. A pattern of Party leadership, government management, corporate responsibility, social oversight and netizen self-discipline is to be built, with the cyberspace administration coordinating across departments. On content and security, Zeng calls for strengthening mainstream ideas and opinion, building the Party's innovative theory into the common ideological foundation, countering mistaken trends and harmful information, and improving the supply of online content. The author also urges legal safeguards, continued "Clear and Bright" campaigns and protection of minors. On generative artificial intelligence, Zeng proposes tiered and classified management, a regulatory sandbox, traceability rules and domestic core technologies. The article ends by urging international cooperation and a community with a shared future in cyberspace, offering "Chinese wisdom and Chinese solutions". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the Party's current policy line on internet governance is being explained in the official press.

Making good use of the "grand ideological and political course" to cultivate new-era youth 善用“大思政课”培育时代新人 Zhou Jing This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 17 June 2025, asks how schools can make better use of the "grand ideological and political course" (da sizheng ke). Zhou Jing, drawing on Xi Jinping's remarks, argues that it is a necessary part of reforming ideological and political courses in the new era. Zhou contends that coordination mechanisms, a stronger teaching force and use of society as a classroom will raise the courses' guiding power and produce "new-era people" loyal to the Party and committed to national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first deals with top-level design and coordination across school levels and departments. The second concerns teachers. The third concerns taking teaching out of the classroom into society. On coordination, Zhou calls for stronger Party leadership over the courses, with school Party secretaries and principals personally involved. Zhou also wants Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era built into teaching, and the aim of educating through all staff, all stages and all aspects pursued. Universities should form joint teaching bodies with urban and rural schools, share resources on cloud platforms and send teachers to rural areas, to narrow uneven development. On teachers, Zhou proposes refined full-time staff, a wider pool of part-time lecturers, a social lecturer database, training, and speaking teams drawing on veterans and model figures. On practice, courses should move to red-education sites, fields, factories and volunteer activities, using local resources and formats such as "mobile red classrooms". Zhou concludes that combining the "small classroom" of the course with the "big classroom" of society will let students understand basic principles in real situations and deepen their belief. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state educators describe the practical implementation of ideological and political education in schools.

Doing ideological and political work and united front work well, and keeping absolute loyalty to the Party as a political hallmark The CASS Party Leadership Group's theoretical study centre group studies Xi Jinping's important statements on strengthening and improving ideological and political work and on the Party's united front work in the new era 认真做好思想政治工作和统战工作 永葆对党绝对忠诚的政治本色 This is a news report from China Social Sciences Net on the fifth (enlarged) study session of 2025 held by the theoretical study centre group of the Party Leadership Group of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) on 19 June. The session studied Xi Jinping's important statements on strengthening and improving ideological and political work, and his important thinking on the Party's united front work in the new era. Its stated aim was to push CASS units to carry out the responsibility systems for both kinds of work. CASS President and Party Leadership Group Secretary Gao Xiang chaired the meeting and spoke. Vice-presidents Peng Jinhui, Zhao Rui and Li Xuesong attended, as did Hang Yuanxiang of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection team stationed at CASS. Zhao Rui gave the keynote speech, and Xin Xiangyang, head of the Institute of Marxism, gave an exchange speech. Heads of Party organisations in CASS units also took part. According to the report, the meeting described ideological and political work as the Party's fine tradition and political advantage, and as the "lifeline" of all work. It said that Xi's thinking on the united front is part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the meeting's account, this thinking answers why a united front is needed, what kind, and how to consolidate it. The meeting called CASS a political organ centred on research. It said the first task is to study and explain Xi Jinping Thought and to build a disciplinary theoretical system guided by it. The meeting called on CASS units to strengthen political and ideological guidance, build up their talent teams and improve work style. It also demanded rigorous implementation of the central inspection rectification requirements, with focus on societies, associations, foundations, non-entity research centres and enterprises under CASS. Read the original if you want a short record of how CASS leadership frames its political-work priorities and inspection rectification in mid-2025.

Continuing to make work-style building regular and long-term 持续推进作风建设常态化长效化 Wang Xiangming Wang Shifeng This short commentary, published in Beijing Daily in June 2025, asks how work-style building (zuofeng jianshe) should be pursued so that it becomes a regular and lasting feature of Party life. Wang and Wang argue that work style is a decisive entry point for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and that it must be sustained through the eight-point regulation of the Central Committee rather than treated as a passing campaign. The authors link the issue to the Party's survival in power. The piece opens with the March 2025 notice calling for a Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the eight-point regulation, and with Xi Jinping's remarks in Henan on that campaign. It then has three parts: the essential requirement and core problem of work-style building; why work style is the key entry point for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; and three directions for opening up new prospects. Historical examples from the revolutionary period are used as illustrations. Wang and Wang contend that work-style problems are at root problems of Party spirit (dangxing), and that the core issue is maintaining close ties between the Party and the people. Departing from the masses is, in their words, the greatest danger for a Marxist party in power. They argue that the eight-point regulation works as a small opening that can set the whole effort in motion: tackling the "four malpractices", especially formalism and bureaucratism and their covert variants, while exposing linked corruption. Their three directions are to trace problems to their root by strengthening ideals and convictions; to lead from the top, with senior leaders setting the example, citing Mao Zedong and Zhu De; and to keep work style tied to the Party's central tasks, handled constantly and in detail. The authors conclude that using the eight-point regulation as the entry point, and letting work-style building drive full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, is an important response to the great changes unseen in a century. They call for perseverance in rectifying Party conduct and enforcing discipline, so that the effort supports Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2025 frame the eight-point regulation campaign and its links to Party spirit and mass-line ideas.

The moral content of the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系的道德内涵 Wei Jianguo Wei Jianguo asks what moral content lies inside the "spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists", the series of revolutionary spirits that begins with the great founding spirit of the Party. The article argues that this lineage and the lofty morality of Chinese Communists are essentially the same thing. It therefore treats the lineage as a direct source for moral construction in the new era, and says that distilling its moral values is an important task for contemporary Marxist ethics in China. The piece is a short commentary first published in Guangming Daily in June 2025. It has three parts: the lineage as bearer of a high moral spirit; the lineage as a "textbook" of moral cultivation across the Party's history; and its role in supporting citizens' moral construction today. Wei draws on remarks by Xi Jinping and discusses the Lei Feng spirit and the Jiao Yulu spirit as examples. Wei first lists over twenty values in the lineage, such as seeking truth, self-sacrifice, hard struggle, selflessness, collectivism and integrity. Wei then condenses them into ten moral requirements: holding to ideals, seeking truth from facts, fearing no sacrifice, serving the people, hard struggle, daring to blaze new trails, selfless dedication, collectivism, patriotism, and self-reliance. These are said to have stayed constant from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, even as their expression changes. Patriotism, for example, once meant resisting foreign invasion and now means striving for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Wei argues that named spirits such as Lei Feng and Jiao Yulu serve as moral exemplars, in line with the Party's long reliance on model-setting. Wei adds that the lineage's moral spirit matches "advanced socialist morality" in content and so feeds citizen moral education. Wei concludes that Marxist ethics should systematically uncover the moral genes, spirit and requirements in the lineage and summarise Communists' virtues. This would enrich the socialist moral value system and guide moral practice, so as to build a moral system that matches Chinese modernization. Party members and cadres are urged to honour loyalty to the Party, public virtue that benefits the people, and self-discipline. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ethics scholars link Party spirit to moral education and citizen morality.

Promoting understanding through action: making Party members' pledges and their fulfilment real 以行促知做实党员承诺践诺 Liu Qiangjin This short commentary, published in Study Times on 16 June 2025, argues that grassroots Party building should stress not only learning in order to act but also acting in order to know, so that practice deepens understanding. Liu Qiangjin, writing from the Suzhou Municipal Tobacco Monopoly Bureau (Company) in Anhui, presents the bureau's practice of Party members' pledges and their fulfilment as a vehicle for this. The author claims that such practice unifies study, reflection and application, and makes ideological and political education reach members' minds and hearts. The article sets out a management scheme the bureau calls the 'seven haves': specific items, a certain weight, an environment and atmosphere, actual action, process supervision, application of results, and safeguard mechanisms. Each element is described with concrete requirements, ending with a note on the Party's share of the workforce and the regulations on Party work in state-owned enterprises. Liu's core argument is that pledges must avoid empty, formalistic declarations. Pledges should be tied to the unit's development goals, to the member's own weaknesses and to social responsibility. They should be challenging, targeted, feasible and measurable, with quantified targets and deadlines rather than vague words such as 'improve'. They are to be declared publicly at Party meetings, displayed on notice boards, desk plates and short videos, and reported monthly. Each is overseen by a supervisor, normally the branch secretary or a committee member, who vets quality, checks progress at least quarterly and assesses completion, with roughly 10 and at most 20 members each. Results feed into democratic life meetings, 'two excellents and one pioneer' selection, cadre assessment and talks with members, but are not used directly for annual performance appraisal, so that members are encouraged to set demanding pledges. Liu concludes that the scheme, with a single A4 page per pledge, flat supervision and closed-loop management, helps integrate Party building with business operations. The article states that Party members make up about 50 per cent of the bureau's staff. The author claims the practice has deepened members' ties with the public, strengthened their political, ideological, theoretical and emotional identification with the Party, and raised their sense of achievement, mission and ability. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-level example of how a grassroots Party organisation in a state-owned enterprise operationalises member pledges and their supervision.

Easing burdens, empowering cadres, encouraging responsible action 减负赋能激励担当作为 Yang Wenjia This short commentary, first published in the Party's discipline-inspection newspaper in June 2025, asks how the campaign against formalism and bureaucracy can lighten the load on grassroots cadres without weakening their sense of responsibility. Yang argues that relief from burdens must be built into the Party-wide study and education drive on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, so that cadres can act with fewer encumbrances. The piece opens by recalling Xi Jinping's instructions on easing grassroots burdens: clarify powers and duties, set no unrealistic targets, and avoid meetings and documents without substance. It credits local authorities with trimming documents and meetings and standardising inspections and assessments. It then notes that problems persist, and ends with measures on mechanisms and incentives. Yang's central claim is that formalism and bureaucracy are stubborn and recurrent and keep reappearing in new forms. Examples include vanity projects, padded reports, mechanical process management and digital tools that become a "fingertip burden". Yang urges targeted investigation, moving from solving single problems to solving whole categories of them, and standing mechanisms such as meeting-free weeks, merged meetings and shared research data. Yang adds that burdens that show up at the grassroots often originate higher up, so Party organisations at every level must take responsibility. Burden reduction, in this account, does not mean reducing responsibility. Yang proposes better cadre appraisal that rewards practical results and commitment to the grassroots. Discipline inspection organs should keep up routine supervision and apply the "four forms" of accountability precisely, combining strict management with care. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party media frame the link between combating formalism and motivating grassroots cadres.

Giving full play to the key role of the "Situation and Policy" course 发挥好“形势与政策”课的关键作用 Hong Bo This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks what role the "Situation and Policy" course should play in the development of ideological and political theory courses in Chinese universities. Hong Bo argues that it is a special and indispensable course because it responds quickly to what the Party, society and students themselves want to know, and that it therefore has an irreplaceable part in the high-quality, content-focused development of such courses. The piece begins from Xi Jinping's call to improve the relevance and appeal of ideological and political courses. It then organises its case around three features of the course: timeliness, pertinence (targeting) and comprehensiveness. It ends with practical suggestions for teaching resources and practice-based teaching. On timeliness, Hong holds that the course should use the achievements of Chinese modernization as its vehicle. It should combine the classroom with "the big classroom of society" so that students grasp Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and develop patriotism and an international outlook. On pertinence, the author describes the course as a front line of ideological struggle. It should explain policy and hot-button issues, strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence and help students resist arguments such as the "China collapse" and "overcapacity" theories. On comprehensiveness, Hong says the course can link topics such as a community with a shared future for mankind or cultural strength to other courses, complementing them rather than duplicating them. Hong concludes that the course should be linked more effectively with other courses and supported by a combined package of teaching points, dedicated textbooks, lecture materials, collective lesson preparation and research. The author also proposes on-site formats such as "ideological and political classes in museums and venues" and "walking" classes. Read the original if you want a short, official-style statement of how Party-aligned educators define the purposes and teaching methods of the Situation and Policy course.

The most important thing in building a good work style is to "be serious" 抓作风建设最重要的是“讲认真” Lin Xueqi Lin Xueqi takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the most important thing in building a Party work style (zuofeng) is to "be serious" (jiang renzhen). Without seriousness, Lin argues, cadres drift into perfunctory work, overlook problems in front of them, and fall back on formalism. The commentary, published in Guangming Daily, presents this principle as the basic guide for the current study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the central Party's eight-point regulation and for making that regulation take root. The piece has three parts. It first traces "being serious" as a long-standing tradition of Party governance, citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and then Xi Jinping. It then explains why seriousness is intrinsic to deepening work-style building. Finally it sets out four areas of practice: political clarity, deepening rectification, handling work style and corruption together, and cultural cultivation. Lin's core claim is that work-style building is long-term and prone to relapse. Good style is, in Lin's words, hard to repair once damaged, and bad practices regrow "like leeks after cutting", as Xi put it, because their stubbornness and recurrence were underestimated. Seriousness therefore means persistence, attention to detail and institutional arrangements that tackle problems at source, in the "nail-driving" spirit. Lin also argues that corruption among cadres often begins with style problems and that each feeds the other. Investigating corruption through style problems and correcting style through corruption cases should therefore proceed together, to reduce existing corruption and curb new cases. Lin concludes that the Party must keep to the conviction that seriousness matters most, and must treat work-style building as always "on the road". Concrete proposals include combining concentrated campaigns with routine governance, field research into hidden variants of the "four undesirable work styles", and stronger integrity-culture education that draws on classical sources about upright officials. Lin says a sound Party style will lift government, social and popular conduct and gather strength for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school commentary presents the eight-point regulation campaign and the rhetoric of work-style discipline.

A fluid-dynamics perspective on the relational field of social space A reading of Lefebvre's The Production of Space 社会空间关系场境的流体动力学透视 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing reads Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space (1974) as the point where Lefebvre moves from a temporal to a spatial line of historical-materialist analysis. Lefebvre's critique of everyday life had already shifted alienation theory from macro political economy to micro social life. Zhang argues that the book's social space is not a container of objects but a field of relations produced by human activity, and that Lefebvre describes it through an analogy with fluid dynamics. The article has three parts. The first sets out the complexity of social-spatial relations, the second the fluid-dynamics image and the market networks of the information age, and the third the principles Lefebvre proposes for studying social space. Zhang follows Lefebvre's text closely, quoting French terms, and adds contemporary illustrations such as Alipay, PayPal, online book purchases and the localisation of Coca-Cola and KFC products in China. Zhang identifies three features of social space: its relations interpenetrate and overlap beyond the physical fabric of buildings and squares, they can conceal one another (capital's exploitation of wage labour is hidden behind commodity, money and financial forms), and they work at several levels, local, national and global, where the global does not abolish the local. Lefebvre's fluid-dynamics image is, in Zhang's reading, only a metaphor for non-substantial relations and flowing force relations, and Lefebvre himself warns against overusing it. Zhang then reports Lefebvre's principles: move from the old problematic of things to relations; focus on human practical activity; unmask the hidden production and reproduction of social relations, including class relations, so as to avoid 'space fetishism'; and expel the ideology that fragments space into passive containers. Zhang also notes that Lefebvre moves from industrialisation to urbanisation, and the author calls Lefebvre's line between broad and narrow historical materialism muddled. Zhang concludes that Lefebvre's social-space research aims to see through the fetishised appearance of space to the hidden social relations, above all the contradiction between private ownership of the means of production and the socialisation of productive forces. Such research must be both retrospective and prospective, looking towards an 'other' space and time in a different society. Zhang presents this as a method derived from Marx's Capital. Read the original if you want a close, term-by-term guide to Lefebvre's spatial method, with the French originals, by a leading Chinese scholar of Western Marxism.

Leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform: internal logic, spiritual strength and practical orientation 以党的自我革命引领社会革命：内生逻辑、精神伟力与实践指向 Zhang Li Taking up the formulation advanced by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Zhang Li asks why the Communist Party of China can lead profound social change by reforming itself. The article argues that leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform is a distinctive dynamic of Chinese modernization, rooted in historical materialism. It is presented as the Party's key historical experience and a precondition for further comprehensively deepening reform. The article has three main sections, followed by a short conclusion. The first examines the internal logic of the idea in terms of value, history and practice. The second turns to the spiritual strength that sustains it, organised around historical consciousness, initiative and creativity. The third sets out the practical orientation in five areas: theoretical innovation, political stance, spiritual will, institutional norms, and reform and innovation. Zhang draws on Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto, on Xi Jinping's statements, and on the Party's history from the 1920s to the present. In the first section, Zhang argues that historical materialism gives the Party a people-centred value stance, the goal of the free and all-round development of the individual, and a method of advancing in stages. The Party's social revolution is therefore said to share the same subject, direction and process as its self-reform. The second section holds that the Party's historical awareness is shown in its three historical resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021), and that it awakens the people's initiative through the Party's own pioneering and fighting spirit. The third section presents the Party's self-reform and the social revolution as reinforcing each other. Self-reform aims to lead the revolution, and the revolution is judged by whether it succeeds. In turn, the revolution depends on self-reform as its fundamental guarantee. Zhang concludes that willingness to reform itself is what distinguishes the Party from other parties. The author calls it a "mission-driven" party, set apart from what the article describes as the self-interested, power-seeking and task-oriented parties of the West, and sees this as a major development of modern party theory and practice. The proposals include adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, keeping a people-centred stance and strengthening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.
