Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party-building scholarship in China links the Party's self-reform to historical materialism and to the project of national rejuvenation.

Strengthening Party building in the "three new" sectors in the new era: logic and optimised paths 新时代加强“三新”党建的逻辑理路与优化路径 Liu Zhenxin Wang Jinzhu The 20th Party Congress report (2022) was the first to speak of Party building in the "three new" sectors: new economic organizations, new social organizations and new employment groups such as couriers, food-delivery riders, ride-hailing and truck drivers, and livestreamers. Liu and Wang ask why such Party building is needed, what it is, and how it should proceed. They argue that it follows from a theoretical, a historical and a practical logic, and they propose three paths to strengthen it. After a literature review that finds existing studies too propagandistic, too macro-level and too short on historical comparison, the article sets out its three logics in turn. It then traces the evolution from "one new" to "two new" to "three new" Party building in four stages from 1978 to the present. The final section turns to practice. It draws on official statistics, Party documents and speeches by Xi Jinping, and cites Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong. The theoretical logic rests on the principle that "where there are masses, there is the Party", which the authors trace from Marx, Engels and Lenin through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The historical logic describes a shift from simply founding Party organizations, to making them effective, to strengthening their political and organizational functions. The practical logic holds that the "three new" sectors are a weak link in grassroots Party building. The article cites 174 million new economic entities in 2023, 881,000 social organizations and 84 million platform workers. In the authors' account, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party requires comprehensive coverage in content, targets, responsibility and institutions, so it requires strengthening Party building in these sectors. The authors propose three paths. First, secure the Party's leadership through a coordinated management system, writing Party building into company and organization charters, and cross-appointment of Party members and management. Second, integrate Party building with business development through "Party building plus" activities and service centres for workers. Third, build the "three new" Party organizations themselves with a reformist spirit and strict standards, across political, ideological, organizational, disciplinary, institutional and anti-corruption work. Read the original if you want a systematic official-academic account of how Party building in the private, social-organization and platform-labour sectors is justified and organized, with statistics and a chronology of Party documents.

Knowledge, ideas and values in the discipline of CPC history and Party building 论中共党史党建学中的知识、理念与价值观 Shang Zhixiao Writing about the newly designated first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building, Shang asks what its content should consist of as China builds an autonomous knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences. The article's thesis is that the discipline needs three interlocking components: knowledge, ideas and values. Shang presents these as dialectically united and as the basis on which the discipline performs its functions. The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to build an autonomous knowledge system, and argues that the discipline should be understood as self-directed, as marked by Chinese characteristics, and as strongly political and ideological. It then takes each component in turn: knowledge, then ideas and values together. It ends by examining how the three relate and by illustrating the relationship with the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea, before offering practical requirements. Shang defines knowledge as the discipline's foundation, with two tasks: establishing facts and explaining underlying principles. Such knowledge is said to be objective, truthful, systematically complete and publicly credible. Ideas express the subject's opinions and attitudes, since people can disagree about the same facts. The Party's leadership is the example of an idea. Values are the guiding stance the discipline instils in its audience. They are not stated separately in textbooks but are embedded in the ideas and knowledge. The three differ in the subject–object relation: in presenting knowledge the subject respects the object, in forming ideas both count, and in guiding values the subject leads. Shang uses the Korean War to illustrate: troop numbers and campaigns are knowledge, judgements on why the war began and its justice are ideas, and the Great Anti-US Aggression Spirit is the value orientation. The aim is to avoid both mechanical materialism and subjective idealism. Shang concludes that the discipline can secure its place only if knowledge, ideas and values are developed together. The author proposes four practical requirements: study Party history seriously, grasp the Party's practice within Chinese modernization, understand Party building and the Party's self-reform, and firmly trust the Party's leadership. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar defines the content and ideological function of this new discipline and how the discipline links its scholarly claims to political guidance.

The "-isms" disputes in economics and their social-philosophical foundations 经济学的“主义”之争及其社会哲学基础 Zhu Fuqiang Why do disputes between economic schools persist even though every school builds mathematical models and cites econometric evidence? Zhu Fuqiang argues that each school rests on a social philosophy, above all a view of how individual and collective interests relate. In this account, models and statistics have become rhetoric that supports prior convictions, so the "-isms" disputes cannot be settled by claims to scientific method. The article first sets out four social-philosophical outlooks in Western thought: the optimistic (natural harmony), the pragmatic (harmony achieved by human effort), the fatalist (innate conflict) and the radical (conflict rooted in ownership). It links each to thinkers and schools, from Smith, Bentham, Malthus and Marx to Keynes, Veblen and Pareto. It then explains how the first three outlooks merged into a mainstream, and compares how Marxist and neoclassical economics treat exploitation. It closes with the roots of the dispute and ways to ease it. Zhu contends that from the late nineteenth century, and decisively in the 1970s and 1980s, classical liberalism, conservatism and Keynesian pragmatism converged into neoclassical liberalism. Neoclassical economics was thereby turned from Marshall's gradualist, evolutionary version into a doctrine of laissez-faire. The present contest is therefore between this mainstream and Marxist economics, in the shorthand of "preserving Marx" versus "non-Marx". The author says the two branches each capture one dimension of exploitation: Marxism stresses concentrated private, money power in production, while neoclassical thought attends to public power and to unequal exchange. Both are said to share a naturalist "affirmative rationality", which pushes policy to swing between extremes. Zhu concludes that all schools carry ideology and none is simply progressive or backward, because their social philosophies are incommensurable. The author calls for recognising each school's one-sidedness and seeking complementarity, so that economic theory can integrate and develop. This is also meant to help readers avoid being misled by mainstream textbooks. The author also judges neoclassical liberalism to be closer to business studies than to an economics of enriching nation and people. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's typology of economic schools by social philosophy and an account of why Marxist and mainstream economics clash.

Marx's writings on the East and Chinese modernization 马克思的东方社会论述与中国式现代化 Wang Xiaozhang Wang Xiaozhang asks what Marx's scattered writings on China and Eastern societies contribute to the theoretical self-awareness expressed in the concept of Chinese modernization. The article argues that Marx's account explains why Chinese modernization is both necessary and desirable: Western-style modernization is "impossible" for China because of its traditional social structure and its position in the world order, and "undesirable" because of its capitalist form. The article first sets out Marx's general view of history, the three stages from personal dependence through material dependence to free individuality, and the tension between historical progress and moral cost. It then turns to Marx's journalism on the Opium Wars and the Taiping movement, his remarks on the "Asiatic mode of production", and his 1848 free-trade speech. Wang also draws on dependency theory, Qin Hui's contrast between "small-community" and "large-community" societies, and Immanuel Wallerstein's distinction between technological and emancipatory modernity. Wang argues that Marx separates modernization from its "narrow bourgeois form". Old China's dissolution under British guns was brutal and hypocritical, yet in Marx's view it was inevitable once large-scale industry created world history. On the Asiatic mode, Wang reads Marx as holding that land belongs to a despotic centre above self-sufficient village communities, which blocked exchange and kept the economy static. From this Wang concludes that China had to reform the centralised state first, and that the state must be a stronger, development-oriented actor, not a weaker one. Because China began modernizing from a subordinate position, the "underdeveloped" condition of dependency theory, Wang holds that Western colonial routes cannot be copied. Wang concludes that the features of Chinese modernization, including common prosperity, the coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development, strip away the bourgeois form and return to Marx's goal of human emancipation. In this reading, Chinese modernization is not merely a particular case set against a universal one, but a socialist alternative to the Western-style type. It could open the way for what Wallerstein calls emancipatory modernity and enrich Marxism in turn. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical justification of Chinese modernization built on Marx's Eastern-society texts, and on how Marx's views on state, land and world order are used in that argument.

The theoretical path of Marx's ecological thought and ecological revolution An examination based on the relations-of-production paradigm 马克思生态思想的理论路径与生态革命 Xu Hengbing Xu Di Many Western scholars hold that Marx's thought lacks an ecological dimension, or that he ended up in a pro-technology 'Prometheanism'. Xu Hengbing and Xu Di dispute this. They argue that Marx's analysis of the human–nature relationship underwent a paradigm shift, from a single subject–object paradigm to a paradigm of relations of production. In their reading, this shift gives lasting guidance for analysing ecological problems and for building socialist ecological civilization. The article has three parts. The first traces Marx's path from the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, through the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, to Wage Labour and Capital, the 1857 Introduction and Capital. The second examines the roots of ecological problems under capitalist relations of production. It also criticises rival explanations from Leiss, Agger, Giddens and others, and draws on Moishe Postone and David Pepper. The third discusses how changing relations of production leads to ecological revolution, and briefly turns to China's own experience. The authors argue that the 1844 Manuscripts remained within an abstract subject–object scheme and ended in circular reasoning about alienation. They claim that from The German Ideology onward Marx placed the human–nature relationship on the basis of human–human relations in production. On this basis, under capital nature becomes a pure instrument of self-valorisation, and capital's boundless pursuit of surplus value drives ecological damage such as the loss of soil fertility. The authors therefore reject Leiss's idea that a mindset of 'controlling nature' is the root cause, and Agger's emphasis on high consumption. In their view both are secondary effects of the relations of production. Marx's target is also a specific form of capitalist labour, not human mastery of nature as such, which answers the charges of Prometheanism and anthropocentrism. The authors conclude that Marx's ecological programme is a thoroughgoing revolution aimed at overthrowing capitalist relations of production. They hold that ecological problems are at root social problems. Socialism does not automatically bring harmony with nature, they add, but lays the foundation for it. They state that China's ecological problems since reform and opening up stem from an unreasonable mode of development and mistaken ideas, not from the socialist system. They see the Party's drive for high-quality development and ecological education since the new era as addressing the key issue. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical rebuttal of the 'anti-ecological Marx' thesis, set against Western ecological Marxism and linked to Chinese ecological civilization discourse.

Putting the people's city concept into practice in urban development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period 在“十五五”城市发展中践行人民城市理念 Deng Zhituan This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks how Chinese cities should carry out the people's city concept when drawing up their plans for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). Deng Zhituan argues that the principle that the people's city is built by the people and for the people, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), gives the basic direction. Cities should become more liveable, innovative, smart, green, humane and resilient, giving residents a greater sense of gain, happiness and security. The article has two parts. The first reviews what cities achieved during the 14th Five-Year Plan period in five areas: economic momentum, cultural heritage and digitalisation, livelihood provision, governance, and ecological transition. It then names pressures at home and abroad, including technological competition, the climate crisis, population concentration alongside hollowing-out in some cities, and commercial pressure on historic preservation. The second part sets out several relationships to be balanced in the coming period. Deng's core argument is that these relationships must be handled with dialectical thinking, and the article gives each a set of practical measures. They include serving national strategy while fixing a city's own position; balancing long-term goals against short-term growth; combining high-quality development with a high quality of life; and pairing digital with green and low-carbon transformation. Deng also covers organic urban renewal with cultural continuity, deeper reform with higher-level opening up, and high-quality development with high-level security. Proposals include a three-tier transmission mechanism from national strategy to local implementation, a 'green GDP' accounting system, '15-minute living circles', small-scale 'embroidery-style' renewal of historic districts, institutional opening-up pilot zones, and a broad security governance system with early-warning mechanisms. The article presents Xi Jinping's work in Xiamen in the 1980s as an example of the people-centred, forward-looking planning it recommends. Deng concludes that, in the 15th Five-Year Plan period, cities should seize the historical initiative and uphold a people-centred approach, so that the people's city concept is embedded in the key fields of urban construction. The article is a programmatic piece that mixes a review of recent achievements with policy proposals, and it gives little supporting evidence or data. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary on urban planning in 2025 links the people's city concept to concrete planning tools and to the framing of the 15th Five-Year Plan.

Leading high-quality development with high-quality planning Experience and lessons from drafting and implementing the "Xiamen Economic and Social Development Strategy, 1985–2000" 以高质量规划引领高质量发展 Jin Min Jin Min asks what a 1985 local plan can teach those now drafting the 15th Five-Year Plan (the "15th Five-Year Plan" for 2026–2030). The commentary takes up the "Xiamen Economic and Social Development Strategy, 1985–2000", drawn up under Xi Jinping, then Xiamen's executive vice-mayor. Jin presents it as the earliest development plan among China's special economic zones and the first 15-year local strategy. The author argues that its methods remain a practical model for planning in an era of high-quality development. The article has two parts. The first draws five lessons from the Xiamen strategy: a people-centred orientation, foresight, a systemic approach, a practical work style and historical patience. The second turns each lesson into a recommendation for the current planning cycle. The author closes by linking the lessons to Chinese modernization and to the 2035 long-range goals. In Jin's account, the Xiamen strategy set income targets for workers and farmers, covered social and ecological goals, and consulted citizens. It proposed a "harbour city" and a three-step plan for a free port, and it had a three-tier structure of overall concept, 21 special studies and priority projects. Jin adds that Xi led research trips to Beijing and Singapore, and that the plan was built to outlast changes in personnel and terms of office. Jin presents these features as proof that systematic, practical planning drives high-quality development. Jin proposes that the 15th Five-Year Plan should track people's needs through a dynamic mechanism, plan early in fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology and green transition, and build multi-level policy frameworks and regional cooperation. It should also set measurable, auditable targets and give long-term, graduated goals in key areas. The author concludes that Chinese modernization depends on combining respect for the people's primary role, systemic coordination, foresight, effectiveness and strategic stability. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-state commentary uses Xi Jinping's early local work as a template for current national planning.

Making the cultivation of Party spirit a lifelong task for Communists 把锤炼党性作为共产党人的终身课题 Xu Jian This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks how Party members and cadres can build a sound work style. Xu Jian argues that style problems are at root problems of Party spirit (dangxing), so cultivating it must be treated as a lifelong task. The author turns to the Marxist classics to support this and ties the argument to the Central Committee's eight-point regulations. The article draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin in three sections. The first treats Party spirit as the distinguishing mark of proletarian parties. The second links firm Party spirit to firmness in theory. The third presents practice as the test of Party spirit. In Xu's reading, Lenin held that "non-partisanship" is a bourgeois product that obscures class contradictions, while strict Party spirit turns class struggle into a conscious, principled one. Engels's criticism of German "absolute socialism" and Lenin's claim that philosophy is partisan lead Xu to argue that theory must align with the proletariat's fundamental interests. Study of theory therefore trains Party spirit, and Xu names Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the first thing to study. Citing Marx on the Blanquists and Lenin on active participation in Party work, Xu holds that Party spirit shows in conduct, not only in attitude. Xu concludes that Party spirit is not innate but forged through study and practice. Cadres should keep correcting their political direction, strengthen their commitment to the masses and take responsibility, helped by strict inner-Party life, discipline and the Party's self-reform. Xu says this is how the eight-point regulations can curb the "four undesirable work styles" and problems such as hedonism and inaction. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-building writing in 2025 draws on Marxist classics to justify work-style campaigns.

The meaning of "people-centredness" for deputies to the people's congresses 人大代表的“人民性”意涵 Liu Xiaomei This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 13 June 2025, asks what the "people-oriented character" (renminxing) of deputies to the people's congresses means and how law secures it. Liu Xiaomei argues that it has two components: putting the people at the centre, and the "Two Linkages". The occasion is the fourth revision of the Deputies Law, adopted by the National People's Congress on 11 March 2025, the first revision made by the full NPC. The article moves in four steps. It first sets out the value goal of people-centredness, then the principle that deputies keep close ties with the people, with a historical sketch from Mao Zedong through the 1979, 1982 and 1992 laws to documents of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then discusses how voters' interests relate to the interests of the people as a whole, and ends with the institutional guarantees. Liu's central claim is that the revised law now requires deputies to be people-centred, to practise whole-process people's democracy, to stay in close touch with the public, to represent the people's interests and will faithfully and to accept supervision. The "Two Linkages" are ties between state organs and deputies and between deputies and the public. Citing Marx, Liu holds that deputies depend on voters' trust and can be recalled, so faithfully reflecting voters' interests is a deputy's first duty. Because the people's interest is not the simple sum of voters' interests, Liu says deputies must reconcile the two. They do so by looking beyond their own constituency to broader and longer-term interests, and by ensuring that the full body of deputies, including every ethnic group, represents the whole people. Liu identifies three institutional guarantees: elections together with the part-time deputy system, which keeps deputies in their own workplaces and communities; the liaison system, including "deputy liaison stations" and grassroots legislative contact points; and supervision, with recall as the last and strictest means. In Liu's account, moving from elections to recall closes the loop of safeguards for deputies' people-oriented character. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of the 2025 revision of the Deputies Law and of how Chinese scholars link deputy representation to whole-process people's democracy.

Writing a new chapter for our times in Party conduct building on the new journey 书写好新征程党的作风建设的时代新篇 Sun Mingzeng Writing in mid-2025, Sun Mingzeng asks what Party members and cadres must understand and do to strengthen the Party's conduct (zuofeng) at a critical juncture between the 14th and 15th Five-Year Plans. The commentary was written in the context of the campaign of study and education on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, called for by the Politburo in April 2025. Sun's thesis is that Party conduct bears on the survival of a Marxist party, that the new era has produced significant results, and that further work is needed to guarantee Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out why conduct matters, on theoretical, historical and practical grounds. The second surveys achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third proposes five lines of action for the new journey. Sun draws on statements by Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and on the Party's history from the revolutionary years through the reform era. Sun argues that conduct is the concrete expression of a party's nature, purpose, programme and line, and that a ruling party which tolerates unhealthy tendencies risks losing popular support and power. Citing the Party's history of rectification campaigns, Sun presents attention to conduct as a 'family heirloom' that sustains the Party's vitality. The achievements listed are a deeper understanding of how conduct work operates (drawing on Xi's remarks), an improved political ecology within the Party, a more complete system of Party regulations, and a purified Party image. For the future Sun proposes strengthening ideological foundations through study, targeted correction of problems that anger the public alongside the cultivation of good examples, and leading by example from senior cadres. Sun also calls for tackling unhealthy practices and corruption together, using big data to detect leads, and a strict, sustained system of responsibility at every level. Sun concludes that conduct building is never a stopgap and has no end point. It must be pursued with the 'Four Malpractices' (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance) held in check and with 'real and long-lasting strictness'. The result, in Sun's account, would be to ensure the Party never changes its nature. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party-school writing frames conduct building, the eight-point regulation campaign and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in 2025.

Promoting the great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression and advancing the cause of building a strong country and national rejuvenation 弘扬伟大抗战精神 奋进强国建设民族复兴伟业 Yan Xiaofeng Marking the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War (2025), Yan Xiaofeng asks how the war's legacy can serve present national goals. The article argues that understanding the war as a moment of national awakening, and promoting the great spirit of resistance, supplies the unity and self-strengthening drive needed to advance the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in five parts. It treats the Communist Party's role as the mainstay of the war, the truths the war revealed, the content of the resistance spirit, the creativity the war called forth, and China's contribution to the world anti-fascist war and to modernization in the Global South. Each part links a historical point to a present-day task, drawing heavily on Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. Yan's central move is a parallel between the war and the current project. Under the Party's leadership, the author says, the united front, the strategy of protracted war and people's war, and the Rectification Movement from 1942 produced victory. Likewise, adherence to Party leadership, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds is presented as the guarantee for the second centenary goal. The article reads Xi's formula "justice, peace and the people will prevail" as guidance for today: the cause is just, it pursues peace by building a strong military and a community with a shared future for mankind, and it relies on the people. Yan also states that peaceful reunification with Taiwan will be sought with utmost sincerity but without renouncing the use of force. The resistance spirit is broken down into patriotism and a strengthened sense of community of the Chinese nation, unyielding integrity, self-reliance, and unshakeable confidence in victory, each tied to present struggles. Yan concludes that the Chinese path to modernization has no ready template, so it needs historical initiative, a readiness to struggle and innovation. It must also keep to Party leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics, high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy and common prosperity. The author describes China as neither urging others to copy a "Western model" nor exporting a "Chinese model", but as offering the Global South new options. Read the original if you want an example of how Party theorists in 2025 link the war memory to Chinese modernization and Party leadership.

CPC leadership as the fundamental feature of China's new-type party system 中国共产党领导是中国新型政党制度的根本特征 Zuo Peng Zuo Peng takes up Xi Jinping's call, made on 20 January 2025 at a Spring Festival gathering with non-Party figures, to firmly grasp CPC leadership as the fundamental feature of China's new-type party system. The article argues that this leadership is what lets the system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation under the CPC function as a basic political institution. In Zuo's account, it is a political creation that grew from Chinese soil and compares favourably with Western party-political models. The commentary, from a journal of the Party's theoretical press, is organised in three parts. Each part names one thing that CPC leadership "ensures": representation of the fundamental interests of the people, unity around shared goals, and institutionalised, procedural collection of opinions for decision-making. Zuo supports these points with a historical sketch running from the united front of the revolutionary period and the founding of the People's Republic through the post-1978 period to the present. Zuo's core claim is that the system combines ruling and participating, leadership and cooperation, consultation and supervision. The CPC is presented as having no special interests apart from those of the nation and people. It is said to integrate the specific interests of the groups the democratic parties represent into the people's fundamental interests, seeking the "greatest common denominator". Zuo contends that this avoids two defects: a single party lacking supervision, and competing parties taking turns in office with vicious rivalry. Leadership is also said to make the system's three channels work. These are party consultation, participation in political affairs and democratic supervision, which Zuo describes as ways of improving the scientific and democratic quality of decisions and of correcting errors. Zuo concludes that the system has historical inevitability, creativity, superiority and vitality. It is said to embody the essence of fine traditional Chinese culture and the requirements of socialism, to play an irreplaceable part in modernising national governance, and to contribute to human political civilisation. Maintaining and improving it is described as bearing on the Party's long-term rule and the country's lasting stability. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line justification for the party system, including its historical narrative and its stress on the Party's leading role.

The "ontology," analytical paradigm and basic map of the concept system of CPC Party-building studies 中共党建学概念体系的“本体论”、分析范式与基本图谱 Liu Honglin With the History and Party Building of the CPC newly established as a first-level discipline under law, Liu Honglin asks how its concept system should be built. The article argues that Party-building studies must start from concepts: they must take the Communist Party of China as their object, treat the advanced nature of Marxist parties as the foundation, and draw core concepts from Marxist party theory and the Sinicised theory of Party building, while also using a comparative view of world parties. The article has three parts. The first treats the "ontology" of the field (its object of study) and sets out four principles for building the concept system. The second discusses the essential attributes of Marxist parties, drawing on the Communist Manifesto, Lenin and Party leaders' statements, and compares rival analytical paradigms. The third sets out a hierarchy of basic, core, theory-identifying, important and general concepts, and lists examples of each. Liu holds that the object of study should be understood through a "big Party-building outlook" rather than a narrow one: Party leadership, Party building, Party affairs work and intra-Party regulations together. The four principles are seeking truth from facts, combining policy language with scholarly language, layered and systematic structure, and stability combined with openness. Liu argues that advanced nature, a unity of political, practical and theoretical advancement, is the essential attribute of Marxist parties and the "meta-concept" and basic analytical paradigm. Liu judges the "mission-oriented party" and "party-centrism" paradigms less comprehensive, since the Party's mass character, representativeness, responsibility and mission all derive from its advanced nature. Basic concepts, such as party organisation, discipline and party politics, are treated as neutral and comparable across countries, so Liu says they should not count as core concepts. Core concepts are anchored in advanced nature and fall into three levels: the overall level (full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Party's self-reform, democratic centralism), the institutional level (such as the Party congress system and inspection tours), and the middle level (such as the mass line and rectification campaigns). Negative phenomena such as formalism and bureaucratism are excluded from the core. Liu calls for three urgent tasks: set scientific criteria for classifying concepts, so that basic concepts are not mistaken for core ones; adopt a world vision and the big Party-building outlook to fix basic concepts and the framework; and keep ontology, epistemology, methodology and axiology united while extracting core and identifying concepts from Party theory according to advanced nature. Read the original if you want a detailed taxonomy of concepts in the emerging discipline of Party-building studies and the author's reasoning for placing advanced nature at its centre.

Shaping the image of the Communist Party of China as a major party in the new era 新时代中国共产党大党形象的塑造 Hu Guosheng Guo Qian Hu Guosheng and Guo Qian ask how the image of the Communist Party of China (CPC) has been built in the new era, and what that image consists of. Starting from the Central Committee's call to "tell the story of the Party's governance well", they argue that the Party's "big party" image rests on four positioned identities: a centenarian party, the largest party, a ruling party and a world party. They contend that these identities show historical self-confidence, courage in self-reform, a people-first stance and a global outlook, and that shaping them helps the state secure control over how the Party and country are portrayed abroad. The article is organised in four sections, each matching one dimension of image-building: historical accumulation, Party building, governing philosophy and international contribution. Each section breaks the dimension into three or four sub-images, drawing mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches, Party Congress reports and the 2021 historical resolution. A short conclusion places the argument in the context of great changes unseen in a century and the need to build international communication capacity. In the first two sections the authors link historical self-confidence to historical consciousness (summing up achievements, the Party's spirit and traditional culture, including the Two Integrations) and to historical initiative (grasping laws of history, shouldering missions, opening new horizons). As the largest Marxist ruling party, they say, the CPC faces problems peculiar to its size, which it answers through self-reform: purifying the political ecology through the Central Committee's eight-point rules and the anti-corruption campaign, tightening Party rules and discipline, updating outdated ideas, and raising the quality of cadres through education campaigns. The later sections present a people-first ruling party that applies the mass line, reduces poverty and pursues common prosperity, and a world party that proposes a new form of human civilization and a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors cite peacekeeping, pandemic assistance and climate commitments as evidence. They conclude that this image makes China's international profile fuller and more accurate and helps foreign audiences hold a "correct view" of the CPC and China. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese scholarship frames the Party's image-building and its official rationale.

An intellectual-history study of how the concept of the "Communist Party" spread in China “共产党”概念在中国传播的思想史考察 Xiao Chunbai Xiao Chunbai asks how the term and idea of the "Communist Party" entered China, and how history came to "choose" one party out of many that used the name. The article argues that this was a gradual and winding process: Marxism was accepted first, then various organisations called themselves communist parties, and only later did the party led by Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao prevail. Xiao presents the study as useful for developing Party-building discourse with Chinese characteristics and for understanding the laws governing Communist Party rule. The article has four sections. The first traces early circulation of the Communist Manifesto, from partial translations by Chinese students in Japan (1907–08) to Chen Wangdao's full Chinese translation of 1920, and notes the 1912 newspaper notices announcing a "Chinese Communist Party". The second explains why early Party groups were called "socialist" rather than "communist". The third reconstructs how the name "Communist Party of China" was fixed, including the rival groups claiming it. The fourth draws lessons. Xiao argues that the name "Communist Party" became universal only gradually: German, Russian, French and other parties began as social-democratic or socialist parties, and the Russian party renamed itself in 1918. In China, Xiao says, the socialist label was more influential, and early organisers used "socialist party" and "communist party" almost interchangeably. The reasons given include the large anarchist presence among early members, nationalists seeking national revival, doubts that China's small working class was ready, and the founders' own earlier democratic or reformist backgrounds. Xiao reports that Chen Duxiu consulted Zhang Shenfu and Li Dazhao, and that after Voitinsky's advice the name Chinese Communist Party was chosen. Xiao adds that at the Third Comintern Congress in 1921 five groups claimed to represent Chinese communism. The article concludes that a party's fate depends on its turning points, not its starting point. Xiao concludes that the naming process shows the Party's goals were tiered from lower to higher, while its highest ideal never wavered, citing Xi Jinping on communism as the Party's founding ideal. The short naming period meant limited theoretical preparation and mixed membership, so the author treats ideological Party-building as a lasting tradition. The early spread of Marxism is read as a scattered form of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which became conscious only after the First Congress in 1921. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich account of the early Chinese communist groups and the debate over "socialist" versus "communist" naming, written from an official Party-history perspective.

A century of debate on the relationship between Marxism and traditional Chinese culture A review and outlook of the scholarship 马克思主义与中国传统文化关系的百年论争 Zhang Yingkui Wang Meilin Zhang and Wang review a hundred years of Chinese scholarship on how Marxism relates to traditional Chinese culture. They begin from Xi Jinping's call at the centenary of the Communist Party (2021) to integrate Marxism both with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional culture. The authors argue that the question, which they link to 'which road China takes' and to ideological security, has never been settled, and that the scholarship falls into four schools of thought. The article covers the period from Marxism's arrival in China (dated to 1899) to the present. It traces four positions in turn: the 'heterogeneous conflict' theory, the 'limited symbiosis' theory, the 'absorption and fusion' theory and the 'two-dimensional development' theory. It names representative figures for each, among them Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, Liang Shuming and Mou Zongsan, Mao Zedong, Feng Youlan, Fang Keli and Jiang Hui. It also cites foreign commentators such as Joseph Levenson, Max Weber and Joseph Needham. On the authors' reading, the first school treats the two as mutually exclusive orthodoxies, whether in the form of Marxists who reject Confucianism or Confucians, including the mainland New Confucians Jiang Qing and Kang Xiaoguang, who want to replace Marxism. The second admits traditional culture only as a resource that Marxism may critically draw on. The third, which the authors call the current mainstream, seeks mutual absorption under Marxist guidance. The fourth treats the two as relatively independent, with Marxism as the 'soul' and traditional culture as the 'root', each developing in its own field. The authors judge the first school's 'Confucianising China' project to be utopian. They fault the third and fourth for not explaining the mechanisms of integration or the division of functions in practice. The authors observe that research stays mostly at the level of what ought to be, with little on practical policy. They propose four directions: advancing the Two Integrations within Chinese modernization, building a more tolerant and dialogic atmosphere, making ideological security a basic aim of promoting traditional culture, and designing institutions and policies for both. They also insist that the two systems differ in essence and cannot replace one another. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Chinese-language scholarship on Marxism and Confucian tradition, and a view of how mainland scholars frame the issue today.

The historical-materialist road to "universal world history" 通向“普遍的世界历史”的唯物史观之路 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng asks what Marx meant by "universal world history" (universal history), a concept first formulated by Kant and then filled with different content by Hegel. The article argues that for Marx the concept refers to the unified world-historical whole, communism, that emerges once "universal intercourse" has sublated the particular interests of single nation-states and overcome civilisational barriers. Wu presents this reading as a theoretical support for the new categories of 21st-century Marxist world-history theory in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has three parts. The first compares how Kant, Hegel and Marx pursued the concept: Kant through a contractual "league of nations" and perpetual peace, Hegel through the theodicy of Absolute Spirit moving from the Oriental to the Germanic world, and Marx through historical materialism. The second part sets out Marx's critique of idealist versions, drawing mainly on The German Ideology. The third part states the principles of universal world history under three headings: a "universal class", highly developed productive forces, and the breaking of "domination–subordination" relations of production. Wu argues that Kant's scheme never started from real human beings and Hegel offered only a "thought in the form of universality" that gave no real freedom. Following Marx, Wu holds that the true ruler of world history is not nature's hidden plan or Absolute Spirit but the relations of production built on capitalist private property, whose expansion began with commercial capital and manufacture. Wu applies Marx's critique of false communities and ideology to the present. In this reading, "universal values" are the modern form of an abstract universality that masks the pursuit of national interest through zero-sum thinking, unilateralism and de-globalisation. Wu concludes that Marx's road runs through the proletariat as the "universal class" and through productive forces developed enough to create universal intercourse. It also requires overcoming the domination–subordination structure, such as the city–country opposition and the opposition between developed and late-developing nations. Wu proposes that building a community with a shared future for mankind is the 21st-century Marxist content of "universal world history". Nations that sublate narrow interests on the basis of common values of all humanity could partly escape capital's logic and move towards communism. Read the original if you want a close textual account of Marx's critique of Kant and Hegel on world history, and of how a Chinese theorist links it to current world-history concepts.

Deconstructive practice, methodological path and significance of cultural materialism Centred on Raymond Williams's The Country and the City 文化唯物主义的解构实践、方法论路径及意义 Feng Hao Shao Hong Feng Hao and Shao Hong ask how Raymond Williams's cultural materialism, usually discussed at the level of theory, works as a method in practice. They argue that The Country and the City (1973) is a key worked example of the theory. In their reading it shows cultural materialism deconstructing the pastoral tradition and, in doing so, supplies a methodological path that deepens Marxist literary criticism. The article first sets out the theory's origins. Williams presents it in Marxism and Literature as a critique of the orthodox base–superstructure model. It then identifies three links between the theory and the book: the book as an instance of the theory, a shared revolt against orthodox Marxism and Cambridge's official English culture, and a shared stress on historical analysis. Next it examines the book's deconstructive practice through language, structure of feeling and perspective. A final section draws out the method's theoretical and practical significance. The authors argue that Williams moves from literature as 'reflection' of reality to literature as 'representation' and as a form of production. In their account, the green language of pastoral verse removes labour, poverty and exploitation, and the poems conceal the agrarian capitalism behind the country estate. Different structures of feeling, from pastoral innocence to the city in Blake and Wordsworth to social mobility in Hardy, mediate between local experience and dominant narratives. The progression 'perspective–form–social relations' ties a writer's vantage point, as in Ben Jonson's patron's house, to a social order. The authors read Williams's method as uniting theoretical, textual and historical analysis, and they reject Terry Eagleton's charge that cultural materialism abandons historical materialism. In their view Williams questions one-way, exclusive economic determination without denying the importance of economic practice. The authors conclude that cultural materialism makes the base a dynamic historical process. It adds sensitivity to concrete experience in Marxist literary criticism, and it shifts criticism from aesthetic to social value while widening literary history. They suggest that future work should move towards local experience and lived practice, and should reread the theory against new literary and artistic forms. Read the original if you study Raymond Williams, Marxist literary theory or cultural studies and want a detailed case-based account of how cultural materialism operates as method.

The generative logic and practical principles of Chinese modernization An examination based on Marx's theory of the social organism 中国式现代化的生成逻辑与实践遵循 Liu Dong Liu Dong asks why Chinese modernization can offer other countries a new option for achieving modernization. The author's answer is that its generative logic can be explained through Marx's theory of the social organism, a component of historical materialism. Read this way, Chinese modernization is a creative application of that theory in China, and the theory in turn yields practical principles for advancing it. The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2025, has three parts. The first sets out the theory: the holistic development of the organism's elements, its all-round production and reproduction, and its open, integrating tendency. The second maps five features of Chinese modernization onto the theory and traces each through the Party's history from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. The third draws four lessons from the theory. Liu's central move is to treat modernization as the outcome of the social organism's economic, political, cultural, social and ecological elements developing together, driven by the production of material goods, ideas, human life itself, social relations and the human–nature relationship. On this basis Liu links each feature to a part of the theory. A huge population corresponds to the reproduction of human beings. Common prosperity corresponds to the people as the subject of practice. Material and cultural-ethical advancement corresponds to resolving the principal contradiction. Harmony between humanity and nature corresponds to the reproduction of that relationship. Peaceful development corresponds to the ideal of a society without exploitation. The author contrasts this with Western modernization, which in the article's account is dominated by the logic of capital and has relied on pollution before clean-up, war, colonialism and plunder. The four lessons are that the organism's capacity for self-directed choice requires Party leadership. Its wholeness calls for a systems approach. Its changeability calls for reform and innovation. Its openness calls for expanding opening up. Liu concludes that Marx's theory shows modernization to be neither a single path nor identical with Westernization. In the article's view, Chinese modernization is a form of conscious, Party-led remodelling of the social organism that both follows general laws and reflects China's own conditions. The author calls for upholding Party leadership in every field, coordinating development systematically, deepening reform, and widening opening up at a time of mounting risks. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese theorist grounds the official account of Chinese modernization in Marx's organism concept and in a Party-history narrative.

Guiding the building of people's cities with the people's city concept 以人民城市理念引领人民城市建设 Lin Chen Li Jing This commentary, first published in People's Daily in June 2025, takes up how cities should be built and developed in the course of Chinese modernization. Lin and Li argue that the "people's city" concept, summed up in Xi Jinping's formula "people's cities built by the people and for the people", is the essence of a Chinese path of urban development. In their reading, it answers the basic question of for whom and by whom cities are built. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statements on urban work, drawing on the first volume of his selected economic writings. It then sets out urbanisation data: global urban population shares from a 2023 UN-Habitat report, and China's rise from a 10.64% urbanisation rate in 1949 to 66.16% at the end of 2023. The middle section presents four features of people's cities, each with a city example. The final section lists four relationships that must be handled. The authors contend that the concept follows from the principle of putting the people first and from the Party's leadership, which they call the fundamental guarantee of urban work. The four features are a people-centred approach (illustrated by Shanghai and Xiamen), serious protection of historical and cultural heritage (Beijing), urban modernization that supports new quality productive forces (Hangzhou), and protection of the urban ecological environment (Fuzhou, Chengdu). They stress that modernization means the modernization of people, not just industrial expansion or population concentration, and that it must not come at the countryside's expense. To advance people's city construction, the authors call for balance between top-level design and grassroots exploration, between modernization and cultural preservation, between concentrated and dispersed development, and between urban high-quality development and rural revitalization. They hold that cities and countryside should become mutually dependent, with two-way flows of resources. The goal is cities that are liveable, resilient and smart, and that give residents a sense of belonging. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official urban-policy line in 2025, with its statistics and city examples.

Developing whole-process people's democracy is a systematic undertaking 发展全过程人民民主是一项系统工程 Yang Xuedong Yang Xuedong, writing in the Party School newspaper Study Times, asks how whole-process people's democracy, a concept still new as a theoretical category, can be developed further. The commentary argues that it is a systematic undertaking. In Yang's account, it needs deeper theory, better summing-up of practice, stronger international explanation and closer coordination among all actors in state governance. The piece first traces the concept from Xi Jinping's 2019 visit to a legislative liaison point in Shanghai through its 2021 entry into law and Party documents. It ends with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called whole-process people's democracy an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. Yang then names three shortcomings and sets out five tasks. The three shortcomings are limited academic definition and comparison with other democratic types, insufficiently refined practical experience, and far more domestic publicity than external explanation, including inconsistent foreign-language renderings. Yang's tasks include building a theory that turns political discourse into academic discourse. Western-led democratic theory, centred on competitive elections, is described as facing serious challenge. Others include applying the concept within existing institutions, above all the people's congress system, and mobilising every level and department of governance. Yang also proposes an index system for measuring democratic governance that differs from Western-led measures and can be operationalised and compared. The author concludes that this would help to explain China's approach to the world and strengthen confidence in Chinese-style democracy. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese political scientist sets out the research and institutional agenda for this official concept.

Advancing the "dual integration, dual creation" drive to do well in Party building in emerging fields 深入推进“双融双创”做好新兴领域党建文章 Tian Hongjian Tian Hongjian, head of the Binzhou (Shandong) municipal Party committee's social work department, reports on how the city has carried out the "dual integration, dual creation" campaign in Party building. The "Great Ideological and Political Course" and the building of a "three-wide education" pattern in universities “大思政课”助推高校构建“三全育人”格局 Wang Wenjie Writing in the Study Times (11 June 2025), Wang argues that the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) can help universities build and deepen the "three-wide education" pattern. Generative AI empowering propaganda, ideological and cultural work: transformation, risks and responses 生成式人工智能赋能宣传思想文化工作：嬗变、风险与应对 Wu Yalin Wu Yalin asks how generative AI, represented by ChatGPT and DeepSeek, is changing China's propaganda, ideological and cultural work, and how that work should respond. The article argues that the technology brings new capacities but also risks to ideological security, the information environment, communication effectiveness and cultural content. It holds that the work must adopt digital-intelligence thinking so as to turn these 'variables' into 'increments'. The article has three parts. The first identifies four new features: richer and faster content supply, more precise and intelligent distribution, a shift from interpersonal to human–machine communication, and the integration of subjects, objects, media and environments. The second sets out four risks, which Wu labels the 'whirlpool', the 'swamp', diluted effectiveness and 'hollowing out'. The third proposes four innovation paths. Wu draws on Kittler, Baudrillard and post-truth theory, and cites regulations from 2023 and 2025 as well as examples such as CGTN's AI-assisted animated series. On risks, Wu contends that models trained largely on English-language data carry Western bias and 'digital hegemony'. Their conversational, 'zero-distance' style is said to make ideological influence implicit, and young people (Generation Z) are described as especially exposed. 'Disembedded' human–machine dialogue is said to weaken trust in official media, and Western-led AI is said to squeeze out Chinese traditional culture. Wu's responses are demystifying the technology while strengthening value guidance and political resolve, reducing information noise through AI-literacy education and rule-of-law governance, building a Chinese cultural database and large language models, and upgrading discourse and the work force. Wu concludes that this work is a systemic undertaking that must move forward in step with the technology, coordinating public opinion, culture, domestic and foreign communication, and online and offline work. The author recommends that propaganda and cultural departments use AI to help traditional Chinese culture 'come alive' and spread abroad, while keeping the Party's leadership over the technology. Building an ideological and political education system that consolidates the foundation and forges the soul 构建固本铸魂的思想政治教育体系 Peng Qinghong Yuan Zhengchen The article takes up the first of the "eight systems" listed in the Outline of the Plan for Building a Leading Country in Education (2024–2035), issued by the Central Committee and State Council: an ideological and political education system that "consolidates the foundation and forges the soul" (gùběn zhùhún). Peng and Yuan argue that this system is a necessary requirement for keeping to a socialist orientation in schooling and for carrying out the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent. They present it as the direction that building a leading education country must be anchored to. The text has three parts: the significance of the system, its core meaning, and the paths for building it. It draws mainly on the Outline and on statements by Xi Jinping, and it is a policy-interpretive piece rather than an empirical study. Its target is ideological and political education from primary school to university, together with the families, society and government bodies that surround schools. They stress four features: unity of goals, plurality of actors, richness of resources, and continuity across stages, including integrated courses for primary, secondary and tertiary levels and the use of artificial intelligence and big data for tailored teaching. For construction, the authors propose four paths. These are raising political standing under unified Party committee leadership, adopting a systems perspective, concentrating on key tasks, and integrating resources. The key tasks are ideological and political theory courses, with textbooks centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and teacher training. Resource integration draws on Party and national history, museums, digital platforms and social practice. The authors conclude that this is a long-term systems project requiring forward-looking, innovative research, with the aim of producing successors who are reliable for the Party. Firmly establishing a correct view of the history of the Chinese nation 牢固树立正确的中华民族历史观 Wang Dong Wang Yonggui Wang Dong and Wang Yonggui take up the question of what a correct view of the history of the Chinese nation is and why it should be firmly established. Their starting point is Xi Jinping's speech of September 2024 at the national conference commending ethnic unity and progress. In it, Xi said that all ethnic groups jointly opened up the country's vast territory, founded a unified multiethnic state, wrote its history, created its culture and fostered its national spirit (the "five commons"). The authors treat this as the theoretical statement of the correct view, and argue that holding it is required both by Xi's thinking on ethnic work and by building the Chinese national community in order to advance Chinese modernization. The article is a short commentary in Red Flag Manuscript, organised in three parts. The first sets out the meaning and significance of a history view based on the "five commons". The second sets out the principles and methods for establishing it. The third proposes practical routes for doing so, covering research, education and cultural identity, and storytelling at home and abroad. In the first part, the authors argue that this history view enriches the adaptation of Marxist ethnic theory to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They present it as an application of the Two Integrations, especially the second, since it draws on ideas such as "all under heaven as one family" and "harmony and coexistence". They also say it strengthens the ideological basis for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and deepens understanding of how nations develop. On method, they call for historical materialism, a long-range view linking past, present and future, and defence of the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. They also call for firm criticism of mistaken views of history that, in their account, dismember, distort or fabricate history under the cover of scholarship. For practice, the authors propose three things. The first is to strengthen historical research, through the project to trace the origins of Chinese civilization and studies of the history of exchange and integration among ethnic groups. The second is to build a shared spiritual home. They list ethnic-unity education within national and social education, promotion of the standard national language and nationally compiled textbooks, and shared cultural symbols. The third is to tell the story of the Chinese nation effectively at home and to the world. Marx's thought on the city in the perspective of social reproduction and its contemporary development 马克思社会再生产视域中的城市思想及其当代发展 Lin Mi Western urban Marxists such as Henri Lefebvre, David Harvey and Manuel Castells are often said to have made the city a Marxist theme. In their view, Marx and Engels treated it only as a site of production. Lin Mi disputes this. The article argues that in Marx and Engels the city expresses definite social relations, is an inner mechanism of a given mode of production, and externalises the contradictions of those relations. It therefore has to be studied from the standpoint of social reproduction as a totality. The article has three parts. The first treats the city as a historical totality, tracing it from ancient society through medieval society to modern capitalism. The second treats the city as a social totality, in which capitalist social relations are continually reproduced. The third turns to Lefebvre, Harvey, Castells and Neil Smith, and asks how they developed Marx's approach. Lin also uses Peter Saunders's three methodological types (Durkheimian, Weberian, dialectical) and Lukács's critique of reification. Lin's central move is methodological. Empiricist and Weberian approaches are called formal-rational "external reflection", which defines the city by population or size and turns it into a fixed natural entity. Marx's "ascent from the abstract to the concrete" instead traces how the city arises historically, as city and countryside move from an "undifferentiated unity" to opposition and then to the "urbanisation of the countryside". Lin then argues that the capitalist city reproduces capital relations economically, through urbanisation as a way of absorbing surplus capital. It does so politically and ideologically as well, through an unequal urban–rural order of morality, law and ideas of freedom and equality. This order hides the contradiction between capital and labour and amounts to what Lefebvre and Harvey call the fetishism of space. In Lin's reading, the Western urban Marxists show that capital now reproduces its relations through the production of space itself. Examples are urban planning and gentrification across the Fordist and post-Fordist stages, Castells's "collective consumption", and Harvey's "urban lifestyle". The city is also the setting in which the proletariat grows and may achieve liberation, so that the right to the city and spatial justice become issues. Lin concludes that Marx's critique of political economy is an open system that must keep moving towards historical specificity, and that the city is one concrete expression of this. Lin suggests that this line of inquiry could underpin a Chinese autonomous knowledge system on the modernization of urban–rural relations, and could ground the study of urban questions in the context of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese Marxist scholar reconstructs Marx's urban thought from the method of the critique of political economy and reads Lefebvre, Harvey and Castells as extensions of it.

An analysis of research on the political roots of contemporary European and American populism 当代欧美民粹主义政治根源研究探析 Ma Jinyi Wang Puqu This review article surveys Western political-science scholarship on why populism has risen in Europe and the United States, with a focus on the third wave of populism. The authors argue that Western research, while it has made some progress in tracing populism to tensions inside liberal democracy, is marked by idealism, metaphysical thinking and a failure to identify any fundamental way out of the capitalist democratic predicament. Only socialism, they conclude, can resolve the crisis. The article first sets out the field. It contrasts the older "normal pathology" view of radical-right populism with Cas Mudde's "pathological normalcy" thesis and his definition of populism as a thin-centred ideology, and notes that economic-insecurity and cultural-backlash explanations have dominated. It then reviews three clusters of work on political roots: the conflict between two faces or pillars of democracy (Margaret Canovan, Yves Mény and Yves Surel, Rudy Andeweg and Tom Louwerse, Peter Mair); deeper paradoxes of democracy (Canovan, Yannis Papadopoulos, Cesare Pinelli); and a representation-crisis reading using principal–agent logic (Herbert Kitschelt, Kenneth Roberts, Paul Taggart, Oliver Schmidtke). The authors credit this literature with three advances: a shared working definition built around ideology, the pure people, the corrupt elite and popular sovereignty; a first treatment of populism as internal to democracy; and a recognition of the contradictions between democratic principles and institutions, such as empowerment undermining transparency. Their critique is Marxist. They say the scholars treat ideas as the main driver and so invert the relation between material conditions and consciousness; that they split elites and the people into a metaphysical opposition, sharing the elitist tradition they study; and that they trust Western democracy's capacity for self-correction. Citing Levitsky and Ziblatt on polarisation, the authors argue that this trust is misplaced, and they present Lee Drutman's proposed electoral reforms as an example of reform that does not escape Canovan's paradox. The authors conclude, from historical materialism, that patching the capitalist political and economic system cannot stop populism's challenge or capitalist democracy's decline. In their view, only a socialist revolution that replaces capitalism with socialism addresses the underlying contradictions and overcomes populist tendencies. They also say the 2024 European Parliament elections and Donald Trump's re-election show the relevance of the topic. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Western theories of populism's political origins and a Chinese Marxist critique of them.

Towards a positive philosophy: Marx and the philosophical transformation of modern civilization 走向实定哲学：马克思与现代文明的哲学转型 Liu Senlin Liu Senlin asks how Marx's philosophy responds to a modern world in which, in the words of the Communist Manifesto, all that is solid melts into air and all that is holy is profaned. The article argues that the loss of old certainties demands a new grounding of certainty, which Liu terms 'positivity' (shiding xing, from the German 'positiv'). Building a world that is grounded, open to the future and meaningful is, in Liu's view, the core of Marx's philosophical change and of his reflection on modernity. The article has four parts. It first traces the shifting meaning of 'positiv' from officially or traditionally 'posited' authority, through Hegel, late Schelling, Feuerbach and the empiricist 'culture of fact', to experience-based verification. It then examines Marx and Engels's call in The German Ideology for a 'genuine positive science'. The third part treats reification as a second modern source of positivity, and the fourth turns to positivity in the spiritual sphere and the problem of nihilism, drawing on Nietzsche, Weber and William McGaughey. Liu argues that positivity reached Marx from several channels: the humanities (Schelling, the early Romantics), the natural sciences, and above all the social sciences, especially political economy. Only after engaging political economy did Marx stop subordinating empirical reality to reason and begin to rebuild theory on a positive foundation, which for Liu marks the turn to the critique of political economy. Liu reads reification dialectically: as a progressive stage of the 'dependence on things' that raises productivity and fairness over personal dependence, yet as a limit when judged from the stage of free individuality. The article also criticises Max Stirner's 'Unique One' as a petty-bourgeois fantasy. Liu concludes that Marx sought more than fair distribution of wealth and rights. Capital dissolves every sacred value into the calculable and exchangeable, which paves the way for modern cynicism, the 'last man' and a flattened civilization. Liu holds that material productive forces are the foundation of positivity but not all of it, and that a transcendent, spiritual dimension is also required. Liu also proposes that ontology and the split between theoretical and practical philosophy be rethought, and leaves open how Marx's anti-metaphysics relates to twentieth-century philosophy. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's relation to German classical philosophy, Schelling and Feuerbach, or in philosophical readings of reification and nihilism.

Marx and Engels's theory of civilization and its contemporary value 马克思恩格斯的文明理论及其当代价值 Zhang Sanyuan Zhang Sanyuan starts from the recent prominence of "civilization" in Chinese scholarship, following the claim that Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilization. The author argues that a "return to Marx" is the necessary route for addressing it. Marx and Engels wrote no dedicated treatise on civilization, Zhang says, yet historical materialism is itself a scientific theory of civilization, and recovering it gives Chinese modernization its "soul-vein" (hún mài, the deep lineage that sustains it). On that basis Zhang presents Chinese modernization as a creative application of the theory. It is said to surpass Western modernization through a self-reliant, holistic and global view of civilization, with the Second Integration of Marxism and traditional Chinese culture as the key to a modern Chinese civilization. A community with a shared future for mankind is described as a real step towards the communist ideal. Fully recognising the real harms of the hedonistic and extravagant outlook on values 充分认识享乐奢靡价值观的现实危害 Ren Jie Ren Jie, a researcher at the Academy of Marxism, argues that hedonism and extravagance remain a live danger for the Chinese Communist Party and must be treated as a problem of values and Party spirit, not merely of conduct. The commentary starts from the proverb that extravagance marks the beginning of decline. It notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has listed these tendencies among the "four undesirable work styles" and that Party and public conduct have improved. In Ren's account, such problems are recurrent and stubborn, so they must be cured at the source by strengthening ideals and convictions. The piece, published in China Discipline Inspection and Supervision (2025, no. 10), has two main sections. The first sets out three ways in which a hedonistic and extravagant outlook corrodes Party spirit: it departs from the Party's nature and purpose, it conflicts with Party discipline, and it departs from the Party's goals. The second section argues that the spirit of hard struggle never goes out of date, and answers doubts about whether thrift is still needed. Ren draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on examples of revolutionary martyrs and contemporary "model figures". Ren contends that, as Xi Jinping has said, style problems are fundamentally problems of Party spirit, rooted in incorrect views of the world, of life and of values. Left unchecked, extravagance damages the Party's image, turns the "fish-and-water" bond with the people into one of "oil and water" (a pun on perks), weakens cohesion and fighting capacity through disregard for discipline, and saps inner drive once ideals fade. Ren sets the austere lives of Peng Pai and Fang Zhimin, and of Liao Junbo and Huang Wenxiu in the new era, against officials who indulge in luxury. On consumption, Ren says that pursuing a better life is not the same as extravagance, and that encouraging consumption should be distinguished from waste, given the emphasis on green, low-carbon living within Chinese modernization. Ren concludes that at a critical stage of building a strong country through Chinese modernization, with greater risks and challenges, cadres must reject hedonism, keep up hard struggle and thrift, and keep public and private interests clearly separate. They should clear their minds of stray thoughts, correct deviations in conduct and strengthen their defences against corruption. A new interpretation of Marx's dialectics in the algorithmic society 马克思辩证法在算法社会的新诠释 Qin Zehua Qin Zehua asks how Marx's dialectics can be reactivated to read the algorithmic society. The article argues that this is no simple transplant of theory but an epistemological revolution that looks past the surface of digital alienation to the relations of production. In Qin's account, dialectics must pierce the ideological illusion of technological neutrality and expose the antagonistic logic inside algorithmic society. The short essay has three parts. It first restates the method of the "concrete totality" and argues that it remains valid in the digital age. It then describes a "leap" in how contradictions move, in form, content and space. Finally it shows how dialectics can "solve" the contradictions of the digital age, drawing on Capital, the Theses on Feuerbach, Theories of Surplus Value and The Poverty of Philosophy, with a reference to David Harvey's "spatial fix". Qin's central move is to carry Marx's categories into the digital sphere. The dual nature of the commodity becomes a duality of data: data is a product of human interaction and so should be a "digital commons", yet under capital it becomes exclusive "digital private property". This split is said to generate a new class antagonism between an "algorithmic bourgeoisie" and a "digital proletariat". Alienation is described as threefold: in products, in the labour process and in species-being. Clicks and likes are treated as "micro-labour", through which dead labour, in the form of data, exploits living labour and blurs the line between productive and unproductive labour. Spatially, cloud infrastructure is said to bring developing countries into a "data colonial" system that reproduces the centre–periphery structure. Qin concludes that the aim is not to reject algorithms but to free them from the logic of capital. The article points to data-commons arrangements, experiments in algorithmic democracy, blockchain-based data rights, open-source communities and transnational digital labour solidarity as practical forms of dialectics. It calls for a threefold synthesis: revolutionary restructuring of production relations, institutional practice of technological democratization, and the emancipatory return of human subjectivity. New understandings and driving forces in building an ecological civilization 生态文明建设的新认知与发展动力 Zhang Yunfei Zhang Yunfei asks what is new in the Party's thinking on ecological civilization since the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article argues that the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has deepened its answers, producing great achievements and enriching Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization. In Zhang's view, this amounts to an innovative development of contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism on ecological civilization. The article is organised in four parts: new understanding of the laws governing ecological civilization construction; a broadened path of construction; the new focus of ecological civilization institutional reform; and new driving forces for future development. It draws mainly on Xi's 2023 speech at the national conference on eco-environmental protection, the 19th and 20th Party Congress reports, and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). First, Zhang presents the "five major relationships" from the 2023 speech: high-quality development and high-level protection, key-problem tackling and coordinated governance, natural recovery and artificial restoration, external constraints and internal drivers, and the "dual carbon" commitments and autonomous action. Zhang reads them as an organic whole embodying an "ecological dialectics". Second, Zhang holds that Chinese modernization is a modernization of harmony between humanity and nature, which builds ecological civilization into modernization from the start. This, the author says, distinguishes it from the Western pattern of "pollute first, clean up later", from Western ecological modernization, and from eco-capitalism and eco-imperialism, and offers the Global South a new option. Zhang concludes that the Party has clarified the direction of reform and improved its top-level design, enriching the ecological theory of the new era. Accelerating the deep integration of culture, science and technology, and industry during the 15th Five-Year Plan period “十五五”时期应加快推动文化、科技和产业深度融合 Hou Yanquan Hou Yanquan, deputy director of a strategic planning institute at the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology's Industrial Culture Development Center, argues in this commentary (Guangming Daily, 11 June 2025) that the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030) should see faster deep integration of culture, science and technology, and industry. The piece claims that great-power competition is shifting from "technology plus industry" to "technology plus industry plus culture". The article has two parts.
