The second diagnoses present obstacles, namely an incomplete policy system, a shortage of composite talent and slow growth of new business forms, and then offers four recommendations. Hou's central claim is that technology and industry already form a two-dimensional system, and that culture adds a "software" upgrade that turns it into a three-dimensional structure supporting high-quality development. Starting from culture, the article sees value guidance, talent support and creative vitality flowing into innovation; starting from technology, it sees the cultural sector becoming a main arena for developing new quality productive forces through digital, networked and intelligent change, including artificial intelligence; starting from industry, it sees culture and technology jointly upgrading traditional industries and nurturing emerging and future ones. Hou presents this as laying a foundation for Chinese modernization. The well-deserved mainstay: the status and role of the Communist Party of China in the War of Resistance against Japan, revisited Revisiting the Communist Party of China's status and role in the War of Resistance against Japan 当之无愧的中流砥柱 Xu Zhimin Writing for the 80th anniversary of victory in 2025, Xu Zhimin takes up historical nihilism in the study of the War of Resistance against Japan. Xu says this tendency repeats Kuomintang diehard slanders, such as that the Communist Party "fought guerrilla war but not the enemy" or put "seven parts into expansion, two into coping, one into resisting Japan". Xu argues that the Party was the mainstay of the war (zhongliu dizhu), and that scholars should uphold a correct view of the war's history. The article is a short newspaper commentary built around several headed sections. They cover the Party as vanguard of resistance, its leading role in the national united front, the line of all-out resistance and protracted war, the rear-area battlefield, the mobilisation of international anti-fascist forces, and the forging of the spirit of resistance. It ends with three requirements for research on the war in the new era. Xu's central move is a chronological record of Party initiatives. These include its declarations after the 18 September 1931 Incident, the 1932 declaration of war on Japan, the call for a united front, and its role in forming the Second United Front after 1937. Xu says the Party held the "leading core" even after the Southern Anhui Incident of January 1941, when it chose to struggle without breaking the alliance. Xu also presents Mao Zedong's On Protracted War as the guide to strategy, with guerrilla warfare dominant in the stalemate phase. Citing the Hundred Regiments Offensive of 1940 and Japanese shifts of effort towards the base areas, Xu holds that the rear-area battlefield became the main battlefield, working with the frontal one. Xu adds that the Party built links with anti-fascist forces abroad, such as the 1941 Yan'an conference of Eastern nations. Xu concludes that denying the Party's contribution distorts memory and obstructs the transmission of the spirit of resistance. Xu proposes three principles for research: guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, a correct view of the war's history, and drawing on history to build the future and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese historiography currently defends the Party's wartime role against revisionist claims.

British archives and the historical writing of the Eighth Route Army's War of Resistance 英国档案与八路军抗战的历史书写 Xiao Ruping Xiao Ruping asks what the holdings of the British National Archives can add to the study and writing of the Eighth Route Army's resistance behind Japanese lines during the War of Resistance against Japan. Xiao argues that Foreign Office and War Office files contain extensive material on the Chinese Communist Party and the Eighth Route Army. In the author's view, these records give an outside, Allied view that supports the army's significance and offers new reference points for historians. The piece is a short commentary in a national newspaper. The article sorts the British sources into three groups. The first is the reports of the British embassy in China, sent to the Foreign Office. The second is military intelligence from attachés and intelligence officers, held by the War Office. The third is the accounts of British journalists and resident expatriates who visited or lived in the North China base areas. Xiao draws on ambassadors Archibald Clark Kerr and Horace Seymour, as well as Bertram, Günther Stein, Michael Lindsay and William Band. Xiao reads the embassy reports as showing a growing British appreciation of the Communist-led forces, especially after the Pacific War began. Military intelligence is presented as praising guerrilla warfare for tying down large numbers of Japanese troops. It is also said to record the army's growth, its shortages of weapons and medicine, and the hardships of anti-'mopping-up' campaigns. The author cites a 1944 report that at least 22 divisions, 64 per cent of Japanese forces in China, were engaged by the Eighth Route Army. The same report is said to describe Nationalist troops behind the lines as heavily defeated. The journalists' and expatriates' accounts are used to illustrate tunnel and mine warfare, peasant support, and the part played by militia and self-defence units. Xiao treats these as showing why the army succeeded, summed up as 'people's war'. Xiao concludes that the archives cannot show the whole picture of the Eighth Route Army's war. Even so, the author holds that they show its historical position, its basic forms and characteristics, and part of the reason for its victory. Xiao acknowledges that British collectors had varied motives, but argues that the materials still confirm the army's significance from another's point of view. Read the original if you want a short overview of what British diplomatic, military and press sources say about the Eighth Route Army, and how a Chinese historian uses them.

From classical theories of imperialism to new theories of imperialism: concepts and paradigms On foreign left-wing scholars' "return to historical materialism" 从经典帝国主义论到新帝国主义论：概念与范式 Qin Shiya Qin Shiya takes up a debate among foreign left-wing scholars since the early twenty-first century: how the classical theory of imperialism (Hilferding, Luxemburg, Bukharin, Lenin) relates to the new theory of imperialism (Harvey, Wood, Callinicos). The article sorts the positions into a "continuity" view (Callinicos), a "rupture" view (Harvey) and a "transcendence" view (Panitch and Gindin). Qin argues that the disagreements come down to two questions, what imperialism is and how it should be studied, and that all sides end up by "returning to historical materialism". The article has five parts. It first examines imperialism as a specific policy in Hobson, Hilferding, Luxemburg and Kautsky. It then follows the move to imperialism as a historical stage in Bukharin and Lenin, and describes how Harvey and Callinicos periodise a new stage after 1970 or 1991. It next compares economic–political paradigms, then turns to the theoretical reconstruction that the "return" involves, and ends with a conclusion. Qin's central move is to reject the charge, made by the "transcendence" camp, that classical theory is economically reductionist and ahistorical. In Qin's reading, classical theorists historicised imperialism as a stage of capitalism. Luxemburg treated accumulation as a mix of economic exchange and political violence, and Bukharin set capital's expansion against the limits of the nation-state. Lenin's definition was economic but, Qin argues, covered political manifestations as well. The new theorists use dual frameworks: Harvey's capitalist and territorial logics of power, Callinicos's economic and geopolitical competition, and Wood's economic and extra-economic power. Robinson, a transnational-state theorist, criticises such dualism. Qin traces the dispute to differing understandings of the economic base and of the state, and notes Engels's 1890 letter to Conrad Schmidt on the state's reaction on the economy. Qin concludes that these paths share one aim, the innovative development of historical materialism in the context of globalisation. The article says this requires a new theory of the capitalist state, which Harvey also calls for, and a re-conceptualisation of accumulation such as Harvey's "accumulation by dispossession", which Qin notes critics find too broad. Qin presents continuity and innovation together as supplying an indispensable framework for judging contemporary capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of the Callinicos–Harvey–Panitch–Gindin–Robinson debate and its roots in the classical theorists.

Four dimensions of foreign left-wing scholars' critique of twenty-first-century capitalist space 国外左翼学者对21世纪资本主义空间批判的四重维度 Li Shule Li Shule asks how left-wing scholars outside China have updated the critique of capitalist space for the twenty-first century. The article argues that the field has moved from Henri Lefebvre's "production of space" to the "production of spatial scale", which Li presents as the key to understanding capitalism today. This shift is said to produce four linked dimensions of critique: the global city, new state space, the new world system and bodily space. The article surveys Lefebvre, David Harvey, Neil Smith, Edward Soja, Doreen Massey, Saskia Sassen, Neil Brenner, Bob Jessop, Etienne Balibar, Neil Davidson, Alex Callinicos, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Peter Sloterdijk and others. Each of the four dimensions is divided into two sub-themes. For the global city these are urban landscape and the power-geographic network. For state space they are geopolitical critique and the scale of the new state space. For the world system they are uneven geography and new imperialism. For the body they are political-economic critique and ontological critique of life. Li's central claim is that capitalism reorganises space at successive scales to sustain accumulation: the city, then the state, then the globe, and finally the body. Global cities are read as command points of unequal exchange, where gentrification and slums express capital's seizure of spatial rights. Brenner and Jessop treat the state as a re-scaled, path-dependent space rather than a fixed container. Harvey and Smith treat uneven geography, dispossession and "new imperialism" as the core of the new world system. Li defends the capital-logic/territorial-logic approach against Davidson's objection that it misses deeper relations. At the bodily scale, Harvey and Smith describe a "body-scale" system of value differentials that lets capital exploit dispersed workers in common, while Sloterdijk's "crystal palace" image shows how those outside capital's interior space are exposed to risk. Li concludes that the four dimensions form a chain from logical starting point to extension, deepening and final target. The article credits this body of work with showing the unity of capitalist spatial domination across macro and micro scales, and says the left must answer these dilemmas at the level of scale. Li also names three limits: a tendency toward "scale-centrism", a weakened class analysis, and no effective link between spatial critique and revolutionary practice. Read the original if you want a systematic map of Anglophone and European spatial theory since Lefebvre, together with a Chinese Marxist assessment of its limits.

Analytical political economy: the revival of Analytical Marxism in economics 分析政治经济学：分析的马克思主义在经济学领域的复兴 Chen Weikai Chen Weikai asks how Analytical Marxism, which declined after 1990, has re-emerged in economics as a community called Analytical Political Economy (APE), and what Chinese scholars can learn from it. The author argues that APE critically inherits the methodology of Analytical Marxism, avoids its narrowness, and has become one of the most active schools of Marxist economics outside China. Chen also holds that it has three shortcomings that need correcting. The article has three parts. The first traces APE's development. It begins with the roots of Analytical Marxism in economics: Morishima Michio's mathematical Marxian economics, Sraffa's Production of Commodities by Means of Commodities, and John Roemer's reconstruction of Marxian theory. It then follows APE from the 1991 Notre Dame workshop to the 2007 revival at Queen Mary, London, and to the 2018 volume Analytical Political Economy. The second part sets out APE's methodological features and the third offers a critical assessment. Chen's central distinction is between a broad and a narrow conception of the analytical method. The narrow one is Rational Choice Marxism, which insists on methodological individualism and reductionism and which, in Chen's view, caused the decline of Analytical Marxism's economics. The broad one, following Erik Olin Wright, stresses scientific norms, precise concepts and rigorous argument. APE adopts the broad conception and has three traits. It uses precision tools such as the axiomatic method. It seeks microfoundations while stressing the dialectical interaction of micro and macro, including structural constraints and the social formation of individuals. It is also pluralist about tools and paradigms, and Chen cites Roemer's class–exploitation correspondence principle as a valid result despite its neoclassical setting. Chen identifies three weaknesses. APE lacks a distinctly Marxist research programme and should study the laws of motion of the contemporary mode of production, including platform-based forms of organisation. It also neglects dialectics, which Chen treats as complementary to analytical methods rather than a rival to them. And it concentrates on foundational problems such as the transformation problem and the falling rate of profit, so it should engage more with empirical questions. Those include monopoly power, digital labour relations, climate change, automation and AI, using tools like big data and causal inference. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of APE's origins, key figures and methodological debates, together with an assessment from the standpoint of Marxist political economy.

New trends in the Philippine left-wing movement in the twenty-first century 21世纪菲律宾左翼运动的新态势 Hei Ran Hei Ran asks how the Philippine left has developed since the early twentieth century and what shape it has taken in the twenty-first. The article argues that, although the left has gained theoretical and practical ground since 2000, it remains fragmented and politically weak, and its prospects are not optimistic. The article is organised in four parts. It first traces the movement from the anti-colonial struggles and early labour unions, through the founding of the Communist Party of the Philippines in 1930 (PKP-1930), to the split of 1968 and the post-Marcos divisions. It then surveys the main parties of the present: the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and the Revolutionary Workers' Party of Mindanao (RPM-M) on one side, and the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party and the Partido Lakas ng Masa (PLM) on the other. Hei goes on to identify three new features and ends with an assessment of prospects. On theory, Hei reports that the parties sharpened their critique of capitalism after the 2008 financial crisis and sketched socialist futures, including the CPP's 2014 outline and the PLM's emphasis on communal solidarity ("Bayanihan") and ecological repair. On practice, the article describes party-building and wider international contacts. Its core argument is that the movement shows three features. Left politics is fragmented, because of ideological splits and the dominance of political dynasties. Tactics are flexible, with armed struggle combined with peace talks or electoral participation. Strategic aims are broader, extending from class struggle and land reform to labour rights, gender equality and the environment. Hei concludes that the left's prospects depend on its adaptability. The author points to the CPP's leadership vacuum after the deaths of its founder Jose Maria Sison and other leaders, to doubts about the party's internal democracy, and to the weak electoral showing of the left in 2022. The article holds that only left unity could shift the position of the dynastic families and open a path towards socialism, while noting that the movement's future is still to be observed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Philippine left parties, their doctrines and their divisions, from their origins to the mid-2020s.

New trends in the Philippine left movement in the twenty-first century 21世纪菲律宾左翼运动的新态势 Hei Ran Hei Ran surveys the Philippine left from its origins to the present and asks what is new about it in the twenty-first century. The article argues that the movement has made theoretical and practical progress since 2000, including a new critique of capitalism and more flexible tactics. It also argues that the left is increasingly fragmented, and that its prospects remain unpromising unless it unites. The article opens with a history. It runs from the early labour organisations under American colonial rule and the founding of the Communist Party of the Philippines in 1930, through the repression of 1948 and the split of 1968, to the second rectification campaign of the early 1990s. It then profiles the main parties in two groups: communist (the Maoist CPP and the Revolutionary Workers' Party of Mindanao) and social-democratic (the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party and the Partido Lakas ng Masa). It then covers each party's recent theory, party-building and inter-party relations, before assessing future prospects. Hei draws three new features from the post-2000 period. First, fragmentation: ideological and strategic splits widened after the 1990s, and the failed 2005 Laban ng Masa alliance is the example given. The author adds that powerful political clans, who hold over 60 per cent of House district seats, push divided left parties to join centrist coalitions. Second, tactics shifted from reliance on armed struggle to a dual track of armed struggle plus negotiation and electoral participation, as in the talks between the Duterte government and the National Democratic Front. Third, goals broadened after the 2008 financial crisis from class struggle and land reform to labour rights, gender equality, ecology and public services. Hei concludes that the left has not formed a united camp and so cannot dislodge clan power. The author lists the weaknesses of each party: the CPP's leadership vacuum after the deaths of Sison and the Tiamzons and its subjectivism and sectarianism, the regional limits of the Mindanao party, and the Democratic Socialist Party's loss of cadres and the weak 2022 election showing of the left. The author calls for left unity as the precondition for any transition towards socialism, while leaving the future open to further observation. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of Philippine left parties, their factions and recent programmes, for comparison with other Southeast Asian left movements.

New trends in the Eurocentric Left's denial of the theory of imperialism 欧洲中心主义左翼否认帝国主义论的新动向 John Bellamy Foster This is a Chinese translation of an article by John Bellamy Foster. It asks why large parts of the Western Left now deny or abandon the Marxist theory of imperialism, and what is at stake. Foster argues that the split between the Western Left and revolutionaries in the Global South is wider than at any time since the Second International collapsed in 1914. He traces it to the relative decline of US hegemony and the economic rise of former colonies and semi-colonies. The article has three parts. The first re-reads Lenin's theory through all his writings on imperialism from 1916 to 1920, not only Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, together with early Comintern texts and Mao Zedong's class analysis. The second follows the theory after 1945 through Paul Baran, Samir Amin, Arghiri Emmanuel, world-systems theory and research on global value chains. The third surveys denials of imperialism, from Bill Warren and Giovanni Arrighi through Hardt and Negri and David Harvey to Vivek Chibber, William I. Robinson and Gilbert Achcar. Foster's central claim is that critics wrongly present Lenin as a theorist only of rivalry among great powers. He contends that Lenin also made the exploitation of oppressed nations the economic root of imperialism, tied to monopoly capital and to a "labour aristocracy" in the core. Empirical work on labour-cost differences and global value chains is said to show that the Global South suffers super-exploitation. Foster reads the Eurocentric positions as a way of avoiding that evidence: Chibber's "Kautskyan world", Robinson's transnational capitalist class, Harvey's "accumulation by dispossession" and the labelling of China and Russia as imperialist or sub-imperialist. He describes China's foreign policy as non-interventionist, in contrast to US military interventions and bases. Foster concludes that anti-imperialism does not mean abandoning class struggle in the core. He argues that revolution has for a century centred on the periphery, and that anti-racist traditions such as Du Bois's and the Black Alliance for Peace are central to it. In his view, Left thinkers who treat anti-imperialism as the enemy end up supporting imperialism amid ecological crisis and the risk of nuclear war. Read the original if you want a polemical, Marxist account of the Western Left's debates on imperialism, with a detailed bibliography and Foster's reading of Lenin, Baran and Amin.

Making education in ideals and convictions regular and institutionalised 推动理想信念教育常态化制度化 Liu Jianjun Te Nige'er This article takes up the call, in the Decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), to "promote the regularisation and institutionalisation of education in ideals and convictions". Liu and Te argue that this is a complex, strategic and systematic undertaking, essential for leading people to hold the lofty communist ideal and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for gathering spiritual strength behind further deepening reform and Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first clarifies the core meaning of the formula, moving from the concepts of ideal and conviction to the necessity of such education and then to what regularisation and institutionalisation each involve. The second reviews the history of the demand, citing its repeated appearance in Party documents from 2019 to 2024, and sets out its significance. The third proposes five mechanisms for putting it into practice. In the authors' conceptual analysis, ideal points to the future and conviction to the present; each depends on the other, and "ideals and convictions" is an integrated concept that goes beyond both. Regularisation means making such education familiar, habitual and part of daily life, in contrast to campaign-style efforts. Institutionalisation means giving it rule-governed, systematic, normative and dynamic safeguards. The authors present the two as mutually reinforcing, in a spiral of regularisation, institutionalisation, new regularisation and new institutionalisation. They hold that it supplies spiritual impetus for modernization and cultural reform, upholds Marxism's guiding position in ideology against what they describe as Western ideological infiltration, supports the Party's self-reform, and shapes young people's worldview and values. For practice, Liu and Te call for mechanisms for ideals-and-convictions education itself, for cultivating civilisation, for cultural nourishment, for motivating talent, and for education in core socialist values. Their specific proposals include coordinating schools, families and communities, targeting different groups, promoting model figures and new-era civilisation practice centres, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture, and supporting educators. Read the original if you want to see how Party-aligned ideological and political education scholarship defines and justifies this official formula and the institutional measures it proposes.

The original contributions of General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on ideological and political theory courses 习近平总书记关于思想政治理论课重要论述的原创性贡献 Qi Ruqiang Zhu Xiaonan This article from Ideological and Political Education Research (2025, no. 1) asks what is original in Xi Jinping's statements on ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke), the compulsory Marxist theory and moral-education courses taught from primary school to university. Qi and Zhu argue that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi has answered three basic questions: what kind of course this is, why it must be run well, and how to run it well. In their account the result is a body of theory and practice that contributes to Marxist pedagogy and to the courses themselves. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats Xi's new understanding of the courses' nature, covering their status and their essence. The second covers teaching theory, namely the "eight unifications" as a methodology and the "six requirements" for teachers. The third turns to practice and examines how Xi has reshaped the way the courses are organised. It draws on Xi's speeches, including the 2019 symposium for teachers of these courses, his visit to Renmin University of China, and the National Education Conference of September 2024. On the courses' nature, the authors argue that Xi defines them as the key course for fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. They are not ordinary knowledge courses but courses in mainstream ideology and values. His formula that their essence is "to explain principles" (jiang daoli) uses reasoning as the link between political and academic content and between knowledge and values. The authors say this corrects the earlier tendency to lean towards either politics or knowledge. They read the eight unifications as eight pairs of contradictions, and the six requirements as a refinement of teacher-quality theory. In practice they credit Xi with three advances. The first is coordination between ideological-political courses and "ideological and political education across the curriculum" (kecheng sizheng). The second is integration of these courses across primary, secondary and tertiary stages. The third is the "great ideological and political course" (da sizhengke), which extends teachers, curricula, classrooms and teaching materials into society. Qi and Zhu conclude that Xi's statements form a rigorous and wide-ranging system whose value has not been fully drawn out, and that it is still developing. They note that the 2024 National Education Conference listed "ideological and political leadership" first among the qualities of a strong education nation, and they call for continued study of Xi's contributions. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Xi's discourse on Marxist education is framed and how the policy documents and practices behind it are described.

Firmly grasping the distinctive orientation of improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 牢牢把握健全全面从严治党体系的鲜明指向 Liu Yiran This short commentary asks what orientation should guide efforts to improve the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, a requirement set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Liu argues that the system rests on four linked features: strengthening Party leadership, comprehensive coverage, strictness in everything, and governance in the sense of treating problems. The author presents these as the system's defining direction and as evidence of the central leadership's resolve to deepen Party building. The article is organised in four sections, one for each feature, and closes with a brief summary. Liu draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements and on the record of campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the mass line education campaign, the "Three Stricts and Three Honests" education and the "Two Studies, One Action" learning drive. It is an exposition of official positions rather than a comparative or empirical study. Liu's central claim is that Party leadership is both the purpose and the guarantee of rigorous self-governance. Hence Party committees must bear primary responsibility, discipline inspection commissions must carry out supervision, and the authority of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core must be upheld. Coverage must be "comprehensive" in three senses: everyone in the Party is both agent and object of governance, the campaigns have moved from the "critical few" leading cadres towards ordinary members, and political, ideological, organisational, conduct, anti-corruption and institutional work must be treated as one systematic project. Strictness must be real, courageous and lasting, so that it does not become a passing campaign. Governance, in the author's reading, means both managing and curing: it is problem-oriented, driven by a sense of vigilance about future risks, and marked by a willingness to take responsibility. Liu concludes that the system is a dynamic whole, rich in content, complete in function and efficient in operation. Improving it requires implementing the general requirements for Party building in the new era and sustaining overall Party leadership. The "comprehensive" requirement, the "strict" tone and the "governance" concept should be built into the system, with greater institutionalisation, standardisation and scientific rigour. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars present the official logic of Party discipline and self-governance.

Critique of communicative capitalism and the emancipation of the subject 交往资本主义批判与主体解放 Hu Jiandong Hu Jiandong takes up the "critique of communicative capitalism" raised by Western left scholars such as Jodi Dean. The short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2025, argues that technological change has not ended alienation. In Hu's account, capital now invades everyday communication, and emancipation requires abolishing private ownership of technological means of production, not simply developing technology. The piece first traces the historical emergence of communicative capitalism, linking the expansion of communication to successive forms of civilisation and to the fourth technological revolution of big data, cloud computing, 5G and artificial intelligence. It then analyses how this stage exploits people, and closes by setting out a social order based on technology sharing and universal communication, drawing on Marx. Hu holds that communicative capitalism results from the interaction of \"capital becoming technological\" and \"technology becoming capital\". Its core logic remains exploitation and expansion, but the target shifts from factory labour to the social relations at the centre of the commodity. Every browsing, following or forwarding act produces data that is appropriated without payment, and capital also controls the supply of information in order to profit from unequal attention. Hu cites Dean's claim that the imbalance between information supply and demand for attention is the system's basic contradiction. Hu concludes that private ownership still fetters new technologies, whose potential for governance, education and health is used only selectively and often destructively. Technology alone does not liberate, and revolutionary theory and struggle are needed. Hu calls for removing private ownership of technological means of production and for full technology sharing, so as to approach the universal intercourse Marx envisaged. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist reading of Jodi Dean's concept and its link to Marx's theory of intercourse.

Coordinating integrated reform of the systems and mechanisms for education, science and technology, and talent 统筹推进教育科技人才体制机制一体改革 Qiu Rui Qiu Rui, a professor at the Beijing Municipal Party School, takes up a policy question set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): how to reform education, science and technology, and talent as one system. This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, argues that the three are inseparable parts of the national innovation system. Integrated reform, Qiu contends, should raise the system's overall effectiveness and underpin new quality productive forces. The article first explains why integration matters, then examines three strands of reform in turn. These are comprehensive reform of higher education, reform of the science and technology system, and reform of talent development mechanisms. It draws on the Plenum decision and the Outline Plan for Building a Leading Education Country (2024–2035). Qiu holds that science and technology innovation depends on talent, talent on education, and education in turn supplies talent for scientific progress. Universities are described as the key meeting point of the three. Qiu calls for subject planning driven by national strategic needs, an independent system for training top innovative talent, and closer ties between universities, national laboratories and leading firms. For science and technology, Qiu proposes a collaborative platform in which the government guides, high-tech industry leads, and universities, research institutes and financial bodies support. Government is urged to respect market rules and tolerate failure. For talent, Qiu stresses evaluation reform, "breaking the five onlys" and setting new standards, and long-cycle support for young researchers. Qiu concludes that integrated reform is a complex, long-term task requiring systems thinking and joint research, decision-making and implementation. It should remove blockages across the education, talent, innovation, technology and industry chains. Read the original if you want a concise Party-school statement of how current policy links education, science and talent reform.

Research progress among foreign left-wing scholars on the digital economy 国外左翼学者关于数字经济的研究进展 Ma Shenxiao Zhang Yuanxuezhan This is a literature review, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2025, no. 1), of recent work by left-wing scholars outside China on the digital economy. Ma and Zhang trace the field back to 1970s contributions such as Dallas Smythe's "audience commodity", Maurizio Lazzarato's "immaterial labour", Tiziana Terranova's "digital labour" and Dan Schiller's Digital Capitalism. Their aim is to describe the trajectory of this research and offer leads for theoretical work on the digital economy. The review is organised around four clusters of problems. These are algorithmic labour control and the upgrading of "manufacturing consent"; changes in workers' conditions, including the gig economy and prosumers; the varied forms of platform organisation and their monopolistic tendencies; and the critique of digital capitalism, with proposals for governing it and visions of digital socialism. On labour control, Ma and Zhang report scholars describing algorithmic management as a digital "panopticon" (Rabih Jamil's "algopticon"), in which surveillance deepens information asymmetry between capital and labour. They present Michael Burawoy's "making out" game as extended into digital tournaments and gamified platforms, while workers resist through platform loopholes, social media organising and legal action. On the gig economy, some scholars see greater inclusion, but most stress precarity, and recent work attends to the heterogeneity of gig workers. The prosumer concept is contested: Christian Fuchs's "organic composition of labour" treats unpaid user activity as value-producing, whereas Nick Srnicek and Bartosz Mika deny that such activity is labour in the value-theoretic sense. On platforms, the review sets out Steven Vallas and Juliet Schor's five metaphors and explains monopoly by natural factors (scale, network effects, data) and by governance and financialisation, citing Cecilia Rikap on intellectual property rents. On digital capitalism, the authors report the view that it remains governed by capitalist accumulation and exploitation, producing a "digital proletariat". Proposed responses include platform cooperativism, labour-law and antitrust reform, and data-privacy regulation such as the GDPR. Some thinkers, among them Evgeny Morozov and Kees van der Pijl, see big data as opening new possibilities for socialist planning, while others, such as Silvia Rief, warn that technology alone is no solution. Read the original if you want a map of Western left debates on algorithmic control, platform monopoly and digital socialism, with names and concepts to follow up.

Inheriting and carrying forward the fine tradition of the Xunwu Investigation 继承和弘扬《寻乌调查》的优良传统 Wang Junwei Marking the 95th anniversary of Mao Zedong's investigation in Xunwu, Wang Junwei argues that the Xunwu Investigation remains a model for how Party members should conduct investigation and research, which the article calls the Party's family treasure. Wang links the text to the revolutionary road of "encircling the cities from the countryside", to adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions and to the "living soul" of Mao Zedong Thought. The piece appears amid the Party-wide study and education campaign on the eight-point regulations, in which improving investigation and research is one task. The article opens with the background: in 1930 Mao produced a cluster of rural investigations and the essay Oppose Book Worship, after the Red Fourth Army was criticised by superiors for "circling around" instead of expanding towards central cities. Wang then describes the May 1930 investigation in Xunwu, with its meetings lasting over ten days, visits to shops and markets, and the later 80,000-character report. The remainder draws lessons under two headings: what makes an investigation "correct", and what the Party style it embodies requires today. Wang identifies several features of a "correct investigation": a clear problem and purpose, a representative "sparrow" to dissect, informants who speak truthfully, a focus on the principal contradiction (urban commerce and old land relations), and the ability to draw general conclusions from raw material. Wang says the report's detailed figures, such as the 23 forms of exploitation in three categories, supplied evidence for the land-revolution line and for urban policy. The second theme is style: Wang quotes Mao on becoming a pupil of the people and quotes Xi Jinping's examples of the Bazhazhan strategy in Zhejiang and cycling in Zhengding. Wang also repeats Xi's warnings against formalist research, such as "dragonfly-skimming" visits, "imperial envoy" tours, staged visits and visiting only successful places. Wang concludes that the Party's work has advanced when investigation was valued and has suffered when it was neglected. Leading cadres are urged to go to difficult and complicated places, hear the truth, avoid snap decisions on arrival, and use the Party's innovative theory to study new problems. Wang presents this as serving scientific decision-making and the Party's governing capacity in the new era. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how Mao's Xunwu method is being used to frame current campaigns against formalism in research.

High-quality Party building must lead high-quality development 必须坚持以高质量党建引领高质量发展 Sui Guorong This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, takes up a point Xi Jinping made when joining the Jiangsu delegation at the third session of the 14th National People's Congress: economically large provinces must "shoulder the main load" and should use high-quality Party building to lead high-quality development. Sui Guorong argues that high-quality development is the first task of building a modern socialist country in all respects, and that Party building is its fundamental political guarantee. Sui stresses that high-quality development covers all areas of Party and state work, not only the economy, and is required of every region, not just developed ones. The article is organised around six dimensions of Party building, each introduced as a way of supporting development: political, ideological, organisational, conduct (work style), disciplinary and institutional building. A short closing paragraph draws the strands together. The central move is to link each dimension of Party building to a specific contribution to development. Political building supplies direction: Sui calls the Party's overall leadership the "sea-calming needle" of the cause, citing the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and credits the Party with enabling China to complete in decades an industrialisation that took Western countries centuries. Ideological building provides theoretical armament through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Organisational building, in Sui's account, embeds Party organisations in new economic and social organisations and among new groups of workers, selects cadres willing to take responsibility, and attracts talent so that organisational strength becomes productive strength. Conduct, discipline and institutions are treated as conditions: opposing formalism and bureaucratism, promoting investigation and research, advancing the three-part aim of not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt, fostering a "clean and amicable" relationship between government and business, and revising Party regulations so they are simple, workable and enforced. Sui concludes that Party members should rally around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, strengthen the political and organisational functions of Party organisations, and find the point where improved Party building meets development, "focusing on development when doing Party building and doing Party building to promote development". Cadres are urged to take on heavy responsibilities with a pragmatic and clean image. Read the original if you want a compact example of how current Party-building discourse in China ties the Party's internal construction to economic development goals.

Promoting the all-round development of workers 促进职工全面发展 Ma Yuna This newspaper commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the meeting marking the 100th anniversary of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, for a worker-centred orientation of work and for promoting workers' all-round development. Ma Yuna argues that, amid a new round of technological revolution and industrial change, such development is needed to produce high-quality employment and to feed high-quality development. The piece has three parts. It first sets out why the task matters, then names the requirements of the present period, and finally lists conditions that would favour it. Ma writes in the register of Party commentary and draws throughout on Xi's speeches. On significance, Ma presents workers' all-round development as the labour-sphere expression of Marx's theory of human development, as a requirement of further comprehensively deepening reform, and as part of the people-centred approach to development. Ma holds that workers' demands are shifting from survival needs to development needs, such as pay, skills, rights protection and participation in management. The requirements include integration into Chinese modernization, adaptation to a modern industrial system through lifelong learning and innovation incentives, and recognition of workers' own agency, supported by the model-worker, labour and craftsman spirits. Ma's proposed conditions are the Party's overall leadership, with Party building and ideological work among workers; guiding workers to serve national strategies; a worker-centred orientation covering employment support, aid to workers in difficulty and democratic management in enterprises; and coordinated action among government, industry, enterprises and society, supported by digital service platforms. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links trade-union work to Chinese modernization and high-quality development.

Historical materialism as a transcendence of Feuerbach's philosophy An inquiry into foundational questions in the discipline of the history of Marxism's development 历史唯物主义是对费尔巴哈哲学的超越 Heng Lin Heng Lin asks how historical materialism emerged in the specific conditions of nineteenth-century Germany, and what part Feuerbach's philosophy played in that process. The article argues that Feuerbach's anthropological materialism was an indispensable transitional link and a direct theoretical precondition. Marx and Engels, in this account, criticised and surpassed it by placing practice and social-economic relations at the centre of their thinking. The article has five parts. It first sets out the German background: industrialisation in the Ruhr and Saxony, the crisis of 1847, feudal political fragmentation, and the intellectual currents of Hegelianism, the Young Hegelians and utopian socialism. It then traces Marx's and Engels's changing relationship to Feuerbach, from enthusiasm to rupture. Two textual comparisons follow: the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 against Feuerbach, and the Theses on Feuerbach against the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology. A conclusion draws the threads together. Heng's central claim is that Marx took three things from Feuerbach: the primacy of matter, the idea of religious alienation, and a focus on the human being. Marx then transformed each of them. In the 1844 Manuscripts, alienation is carried from religion into wages, profit and rent, so that it is explained through political economy. The Theses of 1845 are read as the decisive break. They criticise old materialism for grasping reality only as an object of contemplation and not as practice, and they define the human essence as the ensemble of social relations. The Feuerbach chapter then develops the full system: social being determines social consciousness, and the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production drives social change. Heng treats the Theses as a qualitative leap that still lacked a developed theory, and the Feuerbach chapter as a mature one. Heng concludes that historical materialism arose from several interacting factors. These were German classical philosophy, including the rational kernel of Hegel's dialectic; Feuerbach's materialism; the contradictions of German capitalism; and Marx's and Engels's own theoretical and practical work. The author presents the result as critical inheritance, not wholesale rejection, and cites Xi Jinping on practice and on Marxism as a guide to action. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the Marx–Feuerbach relationship, traced through the 1844 Manuscripts, the Theses and The German Ideology.

The Zhaojin spirit: the spiritual driving force behind the existence and growth of the Northwest revolutionary base area 照金精神：西北革命根据地存在和发展的精神动力 Ding Deke This short commentary, published in Study Times in June 2025, asks what sustained the Northwest revolutionary base area, the one that Ding Deke calls the only complete base area to survive late in the Agrarian Revolutionary War. Ding argues that the Zhaojin spirit, formed in the struggles of the early Northwest and especially in the Shaanxi–Gansu border base centred on Zhaojin, was the spiritual driving force behind that survival. The article presents it as a precious cultural resource for the Party's revolution, construction and reform. The article opens with Xi Jinping's 2015 remarks in Shaanxi on the mass base at Zhaojin. It then sketches the armed struggle from the Qingjian Uprising (1927) and Weihua Uprising (1928) through Liu Zhidan's guerrilla forces to the Zhaojin base of 1933 and the Nanliang-centred base that followed. Ding then sets out the spirit's three-part content as part of the Chinese Communists' spiritual genealogy. Ding defines the spirit as "firm belief in loyalty to the Party, heroic courage in tenacious struggle, and a work style rooted in the masses." For each element the article gives examples. Liu Zhidan, Xie Zichang and Xi Zhongxun kept faith despite failed uprisings, imprisonment and the damage done by a "Left" line. Heroism and revolutionary optimism appear in Wang Taiji's last poem, Zhou Enlai's remark that the Chenjiapo decisions were "Marxism of northern Shaanxi", and the defence of Xuejiazhai, where women fighters died. Mass-rooted work meant village-by-village mobilisation and a united front with local militias, one of whom sheltered sick soldiers in 1933. Ding concludes that these three qualities embody the Communists' original aspiration and mission and the character they sought to show. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how the Zhaojin spirit is defined and illustrated, for example in Party-history education.

Historical materialism as a transcendence of Feuerbach's philosophy An inquiry into foundational questions for the discipline of the history of Marxism 历史唯物主义是对费尔巴哈哲学的超越 Heng Lin Heng Lin asks how Feuerbach's philosophy related to the emergence of historical materialism in the particular conditions of nineteenth-century Germany. The article argues that Feuerbach's anthropological materialism supplied a direct theoretical premise and a transitional link for Marx and Engels. Historical materialism, in this reading, then criticised and transcended Feuerbach by bringing practice and social-economic relations into materialism. The article is arranged in five parts. It first sets out the German background: industrialisation and the 1847 crisis, political fragmentation under feudal power, Hegel and the Young Hegelians, and utopian socialism. It then traces Marx's changing relation to Feuerbach, from the Rheinische Zeitung period and the 1843–44 correspondence to the break marked by the Theses on Feuerbach. Two textual comparisons follow: the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 against Feuerbach, and the Theses against the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology. A conclusion draws these threads together. Heng's central claim is that Marx took over Feuerbach's materialist starting point, his view of humans as natural, sensuous beings, and his theory of religious alienation. Marx then recast these through political economy. In the Manuscripts, alienated labour is analysed through wages, profit and rent, so that Feuerbach's critique of religion becomes a critique of capitalist relations. The article says the Theses mark a qualitative leap: Feuerbach's materialism is faulted as merely contemplative, and the human essence is redefined as the ensemble of social relations. The Feuerbach chapter, Heng argues, then develops the full system: social being determines consciousness, and the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production drives social change. Heng presents the Theses as an initial statement and the German Ideology chapter as a mature, systematic theory. Heng concludes that historical materialism arose from several interacting factors: German classical philosophy, Feuerbach's materialism, Germany's social contradictions, and Marx's and Engels's own theoretical work and practical activity. Feuerbach was indispensable but limited, and those limits pushed Marx and Engels on. The article presents historical materialism as critical, inheriting and innovative, not a wholesale rejection of earlier thought. Heng also cites Xi Jinping on practice and on Marxism as a guide to action. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-by-text account of the Marx–Feuerbach relationship, as presented in Chinese scholarship on the history of Marxism.

Building digital oral-history archives for the discipline of CPC history and Party building 中共党史党建学口述历史数字档案建设论略 Lü Xiaoying Lü Xiaoying asks how digital oral-history archives can be built as a new documentary foundation for the discipline of CPC history and Party building, a new first-level discipline. Writing against the background of the national strategy of cultural digitization, the author argues that combining digital technology with oral history changes the form of historical sources. Such archives, Lü contends, support the construction of an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline. The article has three parts. The first sets out the value of building such archives. The second defines the concept and its scope: essential attributes, features, forms and classification. The third lays out an operating procedure for collecting and processing the material, organised by a "whole life cycle" approach in three stages: preparation, execution and post-collection care. Lü defines a digital oral-history archive as a record of the discipline's development, narrated by those who took part in or heard of events, collected by standard methods, and generated and stored in digital form. The author claims it complements official archives, which are often notices, summaries and reports. It also draws on history, film and media studies, archival science and sociology, and it supports Party history study and education. The archive keeps the primary-record character of traditional archives, takes multimodal forms (text, audio, video, virtual reality, holograms), and is classified into personal, event and composite types. These can be subdivided by generation of interviewee, institution, discipline and region. The operating rules cover interview lists and outlines, authorisation documents, a cataloguing scheme for describing each record, a mutually respectful interview in which the interviewee speaks freely, and transcription that combines AI with manual checking. They also cover editing by people with Party-history expertise and encrypted storage of sensitive data. Lü concludes that following this procedure can produce scientific, institutionalised and standardised technical norms for the archives. In the author's view, digital technologies are a "double-edged sword" that needs methodological guidance, and collecting and studying these archives is integral to building the discipline's autonomous knowledge system. Read the original if you want a practical, discipline-specific framework for oral-history archiving in Chinese Party history research, including the author's typology and its references to technical standards.

On the distinctiveness of the theoretical development of the Communist Party of China 论中国共产党理论发展的独特性 Cao Fengqi Cao Fengqi asks what is distinctive about the way the Communist Party of China (CPC) has developed its theory. The author argues that this theoretical development is dynamic, historically conscious and self-initiated, and that it combines upholding fundamental principles with innovation. Cao also contends that the Party's innovative theories are underrated in the West, because of ideological constraints and deliberate efforts to discredit them. The article examines the Party's theoretical development through four philosophical dimensions: ontology, axiology (value theory), epistemology and methodology. Each dimension is illustrated by tracing the main theoretical achievements in turn: Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The evidence is mainly quotation from Party leaders and from their key texts. Cao assigns one distinctive feature to each dimension. Ontologically, the Party's theory is a development of Marxism and not of any other doctrine, so that upholding fundamental principles while innovating (shouzheng chuangxin) is its first principle. In terms of value, it is defined by the people-centred stance (renminxing), including respect for the people's initiative. Epistemologically, it is defined by seeking truth from facts (shishi qiushi), which Cao treats as the thread running through Marxism's practical theory of knowledge in China. Methodologically, it is defined by the Two Integrations, which the author presents as the fundamental method of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Cao notes that epistemology and methodology are easily confused, and distinguishes them by treating the former as the guiding insight and the latter as the principle for putting theory into practice. Cao concludes that the Party's theoretical development is a continuing process of opening new horizons for Marxism in China, and of pursuing and practising truth. Cao holds that understanding this helps grasp the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought, and calls for applying the "Six Upholds" in advancing Party theory. The author also presents the approach as useful for systematic and scholarly study of the Party's theory and for telling China's story well. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists frame the continuity from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping.

A powerful ideological weapon for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on the Party's self-reform 新时代全面从严治党的强大思想武器 Qu Qingshan Qu Qingshan presents Xi Jinping's thinking on the Party's self-reform as a theoretical resource for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article contends that this body of thought distils the Party's century-plus of experience and answers why the Party must, can and how it should carry out self-reform. Qu treats self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decline, and as an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece, which appeared in Qiushi in late 2024, has three parts. The first assesses the theoretical significance of the thinking for Marxist party-building doctrine. The second reviews how it has guided Party governance in the new era. The third sets out how the "nine uses" (jiu ge yi), the practical requirements Xi has laid down, should drive further work on the new journey. In the first part, Qu argues that the thinking results from the Two Integrations. It draws on the critical and revolutionary nature of dialectical materialism, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, and on classical Chinese ideas of renewal and self-examination. Qu also claims it offers a path to the problem of self-supervision by a ruling party, and says it refutes the notion that multi-party rotation or separation of powers is needed to correct a governing party. In the second part Qu describes rigour in ideology, Party management, discipline, cadre management, conduct (including the eight-point regulations) and anti-corruption. Qu reports an "overwhelming victory" against corruption and says the Party has found the second answer to the historical cycle. The third part elaborates the nine requirements: centralised leadership as the fundamental guarantee, leading the great social revolution as the purpose, Xi's thought as the guide, escaping the historical cycle as the strategic goal, and solving problems unique to a large party as the main focus. The remaining requirements are a full system of Party governance, strong organisation and cadre ranks, improved conduct, discipline and anti-corruption work, and combining self-supervision with supervision by the people. Qu concludes that the nine requirements form a coherent whole, combining strategy and deployment, epistemology and method. Qu calls on the Party to study the thinking thoroughly and implement it so that the Party remains the leading core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party's leadership presents its self-reform doctrine, its theoretical sources and its practical agenda for the new journey.

The core meaning of building a high-standard socialist market economy 构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制的核心要义 Zhao Feng Duan Yuchen Zhao Feng and Duan Yuchen ask what a high-standard socialist market economy system means in theory and how it should be built. They argue that, with the principal contradiction in society changed and socialism with Chinese characteristics in a new stage of development, it is a key goal of economic reform for further liberating productive forces and achieving high-quality development. The short article, published in Chinese Social Sciences Digest (2025, no. 3), identifies four interdependent components: strong market entities, a unified and efficient large domestic market, a dialectical unity of an efficient market and a capable government, and smooth flows of factors between domestic and foreign markets. It then treats four tasks in turn. First, the authors call for the Two Unwaverings: consolidating public ownership, deepening state-enterprise reform, and widening space for private firms after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Second, the market must play the decisive role in allocating resources, which requires modern property rights, fair competition, a credit system and factor-market reform. Third, government must do better, through the Party's comprehensive leadership, a stronger macroeconomic governance system and greater governance capacity. Fourth, they urge high-standard opening up: institutional opening, a focus on western and north-eastern regions and free trade zones, and high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. The authors conclude that the task is to combine the socialist system with the market economy more closely. They describe it as a complex systemic project that needs coordination among institutions, and as an ongoing exploration whose content will change with practice. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy framework for market-economy reform as presented in 2025.

Taking institution-building as the main thread to lead further comprehensively deepening reform 以制度建设为主线挈领进一步全面深化改革 Wang Puqu Wang Puqu takes up one of the basic principles set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further comprehensively deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization: that institution-building should be the main thread of reform. Wang argues that this principle both sums up the historical experience of reform in the new era and serves as a guide to action for the new journey. The article is a research article published in Political Science Research. The article has two main parts. The first sets out what institution-building means for comprehensively deepening reform. The second turns to the implementation paths for leading further reform through institution-building. Between them, Wang lists the functions institution-building performs, from the Two Integrations to risk prevention. In the first part, Wang argues that institution-building is driven by the development of the basic and principal contradictions of society. It adjusts interest relations and the relations between power and rights, and it amounts to supply-side structural reform of institutions in the building of a modern state. Wang describes it as embodying a philosophy of "breaking and establishing" together, with establishing first. Its leading functions include realising the Two Integrations, further liberating productive forces (including new quality productive forces), and serving as an authoritative lever for regulating interests. It is also described as the main track of modern state-building, a vehicle for core socialist values, and a safeguard against major risks in a period of great global change. On implementation, Wang calls for stronger Party leadership over institution-building, including full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for a people-centred approach: institutions built for the people, reformed in their service and innovated with their support. Wang adds that institution-building should be organised around the overall goal of reform, led by economic restructuring and pursued through rule-of-law thinking. It should uphold fundamental principles while innovating, favour systematic integration, key priorities and practical effect, and be assessed by its effectiveness in advancing Chinese modernization. Wang holds that the basic criterion for assessment is for whom institutions are built, whom they serve and on whom they rely. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic exposition of how institution-building is framed as the organising logic of the post-2024 reform agenda.

Advancing the Party's governing capacity through new results in improving conduct 以作风建设新成效推进党的执政能力建设 Zheng Haixiang Zheng Haixiang's commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2025, takes up the Party-wide study and education campaign on the central Eight-point Regulation, which the Central Committee ordered from the 2025 National People's Congress and Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference sessions until July. Zheng argues that better Party conduct should be tied to building a strong governing capacity, as a guarantee for further comprehensively deepening reform and for Chinese modernization. The piece first defines "strong governing capacity", then sets out three tasks: developing the Party's governing theory, improving its leadership and governing institutions, and raising its overall capabilities through institution-building and cadre work. Zheng describes governing capacity as the Party's ability, grounded in full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, to run state power and manage public affairs in an institutionalised way. In this account leadership is the political precondition of governing, and effective governing is the basis of effective leadership. Governing theory should rest on the question of for whom, by whom and how the Party governs, with a people-centred outlook and the Two Integrations. Institutionally, Zheng calls for refining leadership systems, optimising relations between Party and state, mass, inter-party and intra-Party structures, and strengthening whole-process people's democracy and the socialist legal system. Zheng calls for a stronger system of Party regulations built around the Party Constitution and democratic centralism, along with reform of cadre selection and regular training. The aim is to combine governing-capacity building with the modernization of national governance. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-building scholarship links the conduct campaign to governing capacity and Chinese modernization.

Teaching the "Great Ideological and Political Course" through social practice A summer volunteer teaching project in rural northern Shaanxi 在社会实践中上好“大思政课” Zheng Jinlong Wang Tianqiang This short commentary reports on how a teacher-training college puts the "Great Ideological and Political Course" into practice. Zheng and Wang describe a ten-day "Three Going to the Countryside" summer programme run by Suide Normal College of Yulin University from 21 July 2024 in Changjiagou village, Suide, Shaanxi. Under the theme of shouldering responsibility for Chinese modernization, the authors present it as a way for students to be educated, develop their abilities and contribute to society. The article is organised as a descriptive account of the volunteers' work. It covers their daily classroom teaching, a set of specialist courses (paper-cutting, dance, calligraphy, origami, music, sport and writing) and two psychological team-building activities held with partner university teams. It closes with a reflection on what the experience means for the student volunteers. The authors' main claim is that teaching in villages turns practical service into ideological and political education. They describe volunteers drawing on their teacher-training backgrounds, using varied methods and multimedia, and tailoring lessons to individual children. The specialist courses are said to pass on fine traditional Chinese culture, for example the paper-cut "zhuaji doll" and calligraphy. The team-building games are said to raise the children's mental health, teamwork and time management. Zheng and Wang conclude that the programme helped students understand rural education and their future responsibilities as educators. They express confidence that the students will follow the school motto and grow into "striving youth" in step with the country and the people. Read the original if you want a concrete, institution-level example of how Chinese universities describe summer practice as ideological and political education.

The value concepts of China's diplomacy in the new era 新时代中国外交的价值理念 Gao Xiaolin Gao Xiaolin takes up a phrase from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): the Communist Party of China seeks "progress for humanity and a world of great harmony". The article argues that this aim is the distinctive value concept of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thinking and an integral part of promoting lasting peace, prosperity and progress worldwide. Gao presents it as grounded in Marxism, rooted in Chinese tradition, drawn from the Party's historical experience and suited to a changing world. This short commentary, published in a Party-affiliated newspaper, is organised in four sections. The first covers the Marxist Party's value pursuit, the second the inheritance of fine traditional Chinese culture, the third the historical experience of "keeping the whole world in mind", and the fourth the Party's conscious response to global change. The historical section runs from the New Democratic Revolution through the founding of the People's Republic and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gao argues first that Marx's theories of human emancipation and world history supply the foundation: communism means the free and all-round development of the individual, and growing global interdependence lets the Party treat humanity as an organic whole and move beyond narrow nationalism. Second, Gao finds cultural sources in the traditional ideals of "great harmony" under heaven, peaceful coexistence, and "harmony in diversity", which are said to explain why China seeks mutual learning among civilizations rather than cultural hegemony and does not impose its values. Third, Gao reads the "great changes unseen in a century" as both opportunity and risk, citing the collective rise of emerging economies, scientific breakthroughs, unilateralism, protectionism and hegemonism, and presents the Party's value pursuit as its Chinese approach to these changes. Gao concludes that the Party stands on the side of historical progress and human civilization, and contributes Chinese wisdom and solutions to global problems and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece is a statement of the official framing of Chinese diplomacy and does not engage rival interpretations. Read the original if you want a concise sample of how a Chinese Marxist academic links Marx's world-history theory, traditional culture and Party history in explaining foreign-policy values.

The conceptual logic of "the critique of capital" The core of the "doctrine of the concept" in Marx's political economy “资本批判”的概念逻辑 Liu Daoyi Liu Daoyi asks how Marx's critique of capitalism is organised as a system of concepts, and what the "logic of Capital" requires of later critiques of capital. The article argues that Capital is built as a body of concepts moving around one core concept that defines the essence of the capitalist economic system. It holds that this "concept-movement" reflects the real "contradiction-movement" of capitalism and so gives later theory a model of "logical normativity". The article first traces the idea of concept-movement to Hegel's speculative logic and Marx's inversion of it. It then sets out four basic forms of conceptual movement in Capital: critique of old concepts, definition of new ones, remodelling of concepts and conversion between concepts. A second section follows the genesis of this logic across the 1844 Manuscripts, the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts and Volume I. A third section works through the logic of Capital's three volumes: the production process, the circulation process and the total process of capitalist production. Liu's central claim is that Marx's research ran through repeated cycles from the concrete to the abstract and back to the concrete. The first cycle fixed "alienated labour" as the core concept. After the later manuscripts, "surplus value" replaced it as the core. Abstract and concrete are relative: commodity is abstract relative to money, money relative to capital, and surplus value relative to profit. Liu reads Volume I as the full definition of surplus value, Volume II as the mediating forms of capital's circulation, and Volume III as its concrete forms (profit, average profit, price of production, commercial profit, interest, rent). The final part, "Revenues and their sources", is likened to the "absolute idea" in Hegel's logic and is read as a critique of vulgar economics and its "trinity formula". Liu concludes that this conceptual system, centred on surplus value, rejects the "factor theory" and other defences of capitalism, and differs from Hegel's reconciled "absolute spirit". The author argues that it therefore drives practical change through critique of unjust, unequal economic orders and a scientific vision of a good life. Liu presents it as necessary for any critical study of present-day global capitalism and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Hegel-informed account of how Capital's categories are derived and related, drawing on the manuscripts as well as the published volumes.

The "Locke factor" in the construction of Marx's thought The critique of the "theory of innate ideas" as an example 马克思思想建构中的“洛克因素” Nie Jinfang Nie Jinfang asks how far John Locke shaped the philosophy Marx called the "new materialism" or "modern materialism". The article contends that Marx's thought contains many "Locke factors" that earlier scholarship has treated only in broad, abstract terms. Nie takes one case: Locke's critique of the theory of innate ideas in Book I of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding. The argument is that Marx inherited Locke's line of attack and then surpassed it by grounding it in the history of capitalist society. Using a textual ("文本学") method, Nie reads the Essay against Marx's doctoral dissertation, the Rheinische Zeitung and Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher writings, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the 1844 Manuscripts, The Holy Family and The German Ideology, with Engels's Anti-Dühring as a supplement. The article has four sections. They cover the "innate principle" as a groundless hypothesis, the absence of universal consent, reason and its link to reality, and the testing of particular ideas (identity, mathematical axioms, substance) against social history. Nie notes that Locke's labour theory of property and his liberal politics are left for separate studies. Nie's central claim is that Locke's rebuttals are largely abstract and logical, while Marx's are placed in time, place and class. Locke argued that religious ideas vary across peoples and that no principle commands universal consent. Marx, in Nie's reading, reduces religion to the self-consciousness of an alienated world and shifts criticism from heaven to earth. He also shows through the "Jewish question" that there is no consensus on "emancipation", and builds a ladder from political to social to human emancipation. On reason, Nie points to the Paris Manuscripts, where Marx sets wages, profit and rent side by side and so treats them as parts of a social whole governed by capital. On identity, mathematics and substance, Nie argues that Marx and Engels treat identity as grounded in difference and mathematical axioms as drawn from reality. They also contrast speculative "substance" (the "Fruit" of The Holy Family) with a materialist one, tracing the latter through Locke's influence on French materialism. Nie concludes that Marx replaced the "innate principle" of ideas with a "real principle" and located the origin of ideas in practice. He did so by moving from critique of religion and the state to the political economy of civil society. Nie adds that the Locke case shows Marxism's inseparable link with the Western intellectual tradition, and it also shows how Marx's changes of thought tracked social change. Read the original if you work on the intellectual sources of Marx's materialism, or want a close, text-by-text comparison of Locke and Marx on ideas, religion and reason.

Nature, labour and capital in Capital and its manuscripts: a deductive reading With a note on the practical wisdom of the ecological outlook of Chinese modernization 《资本论》及其手稿中的自然、劳动与资本关系演绎 Wang Weiping Gao Yuqian Wang and Gao ask how Marx's Capital and its manuscripts treat the relationship among nature, labour and capital, and what that treatment means for ecological thinking today. They argue that Marx presents history as a dynamic interplay of the three, moving from fundamental opposition under capitalism towards coordinated unity under socialism. In their view, this unity is both historically necessary and the value orientation of the ecological outlook of Chinese modernization. The article first sets out the three concepts: nature as the "prior" foundation, labour as the mediating activity, and capital as a social force. It then follows three stages: separation turning into combination, unity turning into opposition, and enslavement giving way to transcendence. A final section turns to the ecological outlook of Chinese modernization and draws three practical implications. The authors rely mainly on close reading of Marx's texts, including the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, supplemented by references to Xi Jinping's statements. The central analysis holds that capital's drive to self-valorisation, which the authors describe as its "effect principle" and "valorisation law", intensifies the exploitation of labour and the impoverishment of nature. Nature "costs capital nothing", and technology serves as capital's ally in dominating both workers and the natural world. The authors then read Marx as locating capital's limits in itself, in natural boundaries and in workers' bodily limits. On this reading, crises, proletarian association and the negation of private property lead to free labour and the "revival" of nature. Turning to the present, the authors argue that Chinese modernization, defined as modernization in which humanity and nature coexist in harmony, rests on three points. These are treating humans and nature as a community of life, developing socialist ecological labour with ecological aims, workers and tools, and using institutional strengths to steer capital. Because capital still operates in the primary stage of socialism, the authors call for regulating it through Party leadership, the basic economic system, the rule of law and administrative oversight, so that it serves ecological construction. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Capital's ecological content and its link to current Chinese environmental policy discourse.
