The philosophical logic of constructing a discourse system of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 中国特色哲学社会科学话语体系建构的哲学逻辑 Huang Hai Following the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to accelerate the building of disciplinary, academic and discourse systems of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, Huang asks what philosophical logic should govern the construction of the discourse system. The article argues that four paired categories (the one and the many, critique and construction, the general and the particular, the ought and the actual) frame the basic problems, and that Marxist guidance and Chinese practice together make the resulting discourse autonomous. Huang opens by defining the discourse system as the outward expression of the theoretical and academic systems. It is built around the question of what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold and develop in the new era, and it has already produced discourses such as Chinese modernization, the shared values of all mankind, a community with a shared future for mankind and a new form of human civilization. Four sections then treat each pair as a distinct problem: a precondition, a strategy, a question of generation and a practical question. On the first two pairs, Huang holds that the "one" is the guiding "Dao", meaning Marxism and its Sinicized theories plus fine traditional Chinese culture, while the "many" is the cluster of distinctive concepts and expressions. Critique and construction must be unified. Huang says the "modernization equals Westernization" frame reflects Western-centrism and treats Western discourse as "local knowledge" rather than universal truth. On the third pair, the discourse must be commensurable with others, so as to avoid "talking to itself", while keeping its own core categories. Huang presents the shared values of all mankind as an example of generality, and the Western "universal values" discourse as a counter-example. On the fourth pair, the "ought" is what to say and the "actual" is how to say it. Huang asks for political, academic and popular discourse to be fused, with theoretical depth and rich practice as the foundation. Huang concludes that the Chinese discourse system must rest on thoroughgoing theory and on the practice of Chinese modernization. Citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Huang stresses the need to build Chinese discourse and narrative and to raise the effectiveness of international communication, given what the article describes as Western dominance of global discourse power. The aim is to turn institutional strengths and governance effectiveness into discursive strength. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher uses dialectical categories to justify and structure official discourse-building, and how Chinese modernization serves as the main case.

High-quality development as a major innovation in the categories of Marxist political economy 高质量发展是马克思主义政治经济学范畴的重大创新 Qiu Haiping Qiu Haiping argues that high-quality development is an original and signature concept of Xi Jinping's economic thought and a major innovation in the categories of Marxist political economy. The commentary, first published in the People's Daily in June 2025, holds that the concept both applies and extends the Marxist tradition. Qiu presents it as the "hard truth" of the new era and the first task of building a modern socialist country. The piece sets out four ways in which the concept develops Marxist political economy. These are the theory of stages of economic development, the thinking on the quality of economic development, the thinking on the mode of development, and the theory of productive forces. For each, Qiu first recalls what Marx, Engels and Lenin said, drawing on Capital and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. Qiu then sets out Xi Jinping's statements from 2012 to 2024. On stages, Qiu traces Xi's successive judgements from the "three-phase superposition" and the "new normal" to the 2017 claim that China had moved from high-speed growth to a stage of high-quality development. Qiu says all of these point to high-quality development. On quality, Qiu holds that Xi's definition, which covers meeting people's needs for a better life and embodying the new development philosophy, goes beyond a GDP-centred accounting system. On the mode of development, Qiu links Marx's distinction between extensive and intensive reproduction to Xi's 2017 criteria for supply, demand, input-output, distribution and macroeconomic circulation. On productive forces, Qiu argues that new quality productive forces carry forward high-quality development and give productive forces a distinction of "qualitative forms" that Marx never made. Qiu concludes that Xi's expositions on high-quality development are scientific theory that has been borne out in practice. Qiu cites growing innovation capacity and the upgrading of traditional industries since the new era began. Qiu calls for continued study of Xi Jinping economic thought and for treating high-quality development as the priority, so as to offer "the greatest certainty" to an uncertain world. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary presents Xi Jinping's economic concepts as continuous with, and innovations upon, classical Marxist political economy.

Running high-quality affiliated schools to serve the high-quality and balanced development of basic education 办好高质量附校 服务基础教育优质均衡发展 Yan Shuai This short commentary from Guangming Daily asks how teacher-training universities can use their affiliated primary and secondary schools to serve high-quality, balanced development of basic education. Yan Shuai argues that such schools are the universities' "experimental fields" and a key strategy for building a leading education nation. The author holds that universities should run them in an organised way, since basic education is in a critical period of change. The piece is built around three requirements for "organised" high-quality schooling: Party leadership and the right direction, an organisational advantage that raises quality and standards, and the effective mobilisation of both universities and schools as models for others. Each is developed in three concrete points. On leadership, Yan calls for a clear political, popular and strategic orientation, schools sited in regions of national strategic priority, and reform of the leadership system in primary and secondary schools so that Party organisations play their leading role. The author also proposes integrated ideological and political education across university, middle and primary levels, with university Marxism schools guiding teaching and textbooks. On quality, Yan urges group-based, intensive school management; subject and talent support that helps schools interpret curriculum standards and use new textbooks; and teacher training that treats affiliated schools as a "second campus" for student teachers. Yan concludes that universities should build communities for shared development, such as the university alliance for basic education led by Beijing Normal University. They should also develop products such as artificial intelligence, brain science, assessment and smart-campus tools, and spread the benefits of each good school to its wider region through shared resources, results and teacher training. Read the original if you want a brief official-style statement of how teacher-training universities are expected to link affiliated schools, Party building and regional basic education.

Secret communications in the Hubei–Henan–Anhui Soviet area during the Agrarian Revolutionary War and their historical role 土地革命战争时期鄂豫皖苏区的秘密交通与历史作用 Chen Dongfang Chen Dongfang, writing in Guangming Daily (4 June 2025), takes up the clandestine front of the Chinese Communist Party's struggle in the New Democratic revolution, a subject the author says has drawn growing scholarly attention. The article asks how the secret communications network of the Hubei–Henan–Anhui Soviet area was built and what it contributed. Chen argues that, under Guomindang blockade, building this network was an urgent task, and that it played a positive role in the founding, development and growth of the base area. The piece is a short historical commentary in two parts. The first describes how the network was set up, with reference to the Party Central Committee's early statements on the importance of secret communications and the instructions of the 7 August Conference (1927). The second sets out the network's historical significance. The evidence consists mainly of memoirs, Party history compilations and local histories, with examples of named couriers, stations and operations. In the first part Chen distinguishes two types of line. One was established by the Central Committee and ran from outside into the base area: an eastern line from Shanghai, centred on a central station at Dianbu town in Hefei with four sub-stations, and a western line through Wuhan or, later, Zhengzhou, Xinyang, Luoshan and Guangshui. The other was built by the base area's own Party organisations and ran outwards, as in Liu'an, Xinyang and northwest Anhui. The second part credits the network with three functions. It secured the Centre's political leadership by carrying documents and escorting cadres such as Xu Xiangqian and Shen Zemin. It broke the economic blockade by smuggling medicine, salt, arms and cloth through shops, inns and clinics used as cover, and by passing on intelligence, including a tip that led to the capture of Zhengyangguan. It also drove social mobilisation, by helping to organise grain distribution, recruit soldiers and rebuild Party organisations. Chen concludes that the secret lines and their couriers were also an efficient "seeding machine" that scattered revolutionary seeds across the base area and its surroundings, forming an important part of the Party's social mobilisation. The article presents secret communications as a key but little-noticed support for the Soviet area's survival. Read the original if you want a concise, source-based account of Party underground logistics in the Hubei–Henan–Anhui base area, with named routes, stations and couriers.

Inheriting and innovating excellent traditional Chinese culture from the perspective of "education by all, throughout the process and in all respects" “三全育人”视角下中华优秀传统文化的传承与创新 Zhang Wei Yang Haiping Zhang Wei and Yang Haiping ask how excellent traditional Chinese culture can be passed on and renewed within higher education. They take as their framework the concept of "education by all, throughout the process and in all respects" (sān quán yùrén). Their thesis is that inheritance should not be a simple replication of historical knowledge: core cultural values must be turned into educational resources that shape young people's values and support social and spiritual development. The article is organised in three parts: holistic inheritance, innovation suited to the times, and multi-dimensional collaborative education. The first deals with how to build a systematic understanding of cultural roots. The second takes up digital technology, points of contact between tradition and modern society, and new forms of expression. The third sets out how schools, families, society and government can cooperate across the stages of a student's education. A short concluding section draws these together, and the authors note that the work is supported by national and Xinjiang-level research projects. On inheritance, the authors call for a "whole–part–whole" logic and an attitude of sublation: outdated elements, such as the hierarchy of the culture of ritual (li), should be separated from still-useful ethical norms like respect for others and self-restraint. They warn against reducing tradition to fragmentary labels. On innovation, they argue that digital tools such as virtual scenes, short videos, AI-based learning applications and big-data analysis should reshape how culture is interpreted, but must stay oriented to cultural substance rather than "technology for technology's sake". Ideas like "harmony without uniformity" and "the Way follows nature" are said to speak to alienation and ecological problems. On collaboration, they propose staged teaching (cognition, critical reflection, innovative practice), informal settings such as campus design and student clubs, and pluralistic evaluation through projects and service feedback. The authors conclude that transmitting this culture amounts to continuing and rebuilding cultural vitality, and to reproducing cultural subjectivity. They call on schools to make traditional culture a core aim of talent cultivation, on families to lead by example, and on society to respect tradition and encourage innovation. They propose a linked mechanism of "core positioning, innovative methods, system rebuilding" to move learners from cultural consciousness to cultural confidence. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese ideological and political education scholars link traditional culture to the "three-whole" education framework and to practical curriculum and evaluation design.

Exploring Party building at the CPC's Seventh National Congress and its historical lessons 中共七大加强党的建设的探索及其历史启示 Xue Lin Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2025, Xue Lin asks what the Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in Yan'an from April to June 1945, can teach the Party about strengthening itself today. The author's thesis is that the Congress marked the Party's maturity politically, ideologically and organisationally, and that its work on Party building offers wisdom for resolving the "unique problems of a large party". The piece is a short newspaper commentary, a stage result of a National Social Science Fund project on Yan'an's exploration of those problems. Xue opens with the Congress's context: more than 1.2 million members, nearly a million troops and leadership over almost 100 million people. The article then moves through five themes, each closing with a lesson for the present: the Party's nature and purpose, the leading core, ideological unity, the capacity to govern, and the Party's "three styles of work". Evidence is drawn from the 1945 Party Constitution, speeches by Mao Zedong and Liu Shaoqi, and a Liberation Daily editorial, with Xi Jinping's 2022 assessment of the Congress as a milestone. Xue's central claim is that the Congress answered "what the Party is and what it is for" by defining it as the vanguard of the working class that represents the interests of the nation and people, with serving the people wholeheartedly as its fundamental purpose. Mao Zedong Thought was established as the guiding ideology, summarised in nine aspects, and written into the Constitution. The Congress also elected a new Central Committee under Mao and, in Xue's account, achieved unity through intra-Party democracy and the discipline of "keeping in line with the Centre". Finally, Xue stresses the three styles of work: integrating theory with practice, close ties with the masses, and self-criticism, which Mao treated as a mark distinguishing the Party from others. Xue concludes that today's Party members must strengthen their awareness of the Party's purpose, oppose privilege, accept supervision by the people, and uphold the authority of the Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership. The author also calls on members to study the Party's innovative theory, raise their ability to govern and to struggle, and use criticism and self-criticism to keep the Party's political life clean and vital. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party scholarship draws present-day Party-building lessons from the 1945 Yan'an Congress.

Methodological guidance for ideological and political education of children and teenagers 做好少年儿童思想政治教育的方法论指引 Li Yongzhi This commentary asks how ideological and political education for children and teenagers can be done well. Li argues that Xi Jinping's "sixteen-character" requirement, first set out in 2014 at a Children's Day event in Beijing, offers a methodological guide: remember the requirements, have role models in mind, start from an early age, and accept help. The piece is a short People's Daily article. It reads each of the four phrases against educational principles and links them to Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2025 "two sessions" on coordinating classroom teaching with society as a "big classroom". It ends with a brief assessment of results over the past decade or so and of new challenges. Li makes three main moves. First, the four phrases embody the unity of knowing and doing: remembering the requirements is the base of knowledge, role models turn knowing into doing, starting small shapes conduct, and help from teachers and parents bridges the two. Second, the phrases follow the cycle of practice, understanding, renewed practice and deeper understanding, and Li says this addresses the gap between theory and practice in traditional education. Third, they call for teaching suited to the pupil, using stories and analogies to explain demanding ideas to young children, and for timely answers to current problems such as competing over possessions or ignoring advice. Li cites Xi's remarks on these. Li concludes that the education system has made clear progress under this guidance, citing stronger curriculum channels, role-model teachers and practice-based education. Li notes that the information age brings new demands, and calls for the Party's leadership and broad mobilisation of social forces. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary draws a method for moral and political education of the young from Xi Jinping's remarks.

How labour ownership was alienated into capital ownership From Locke and Hegel to Marx 劳动所有权何以异化为资本所有权？ Hu Shun Scholars have recently disputed whether Locke's theory of labour ownership justifies capitalist exploitation and whether Marx seriously criticised Locke. Hu Shun sets this dispute aside and traces an internal line of development from Locke through Hegel to Marx. The article argues that Locke established the identity of labour and property, Hegel grounded it metaphysically and noticed its negative effects, and Marx showed labour and ownership coming apart, so that labour ownership turned into capital ownership. Hu concludes that it is better to criticise views that confuse capital ownership with labour ownership than to argue over whether Locke or Hegel defended exploitation. The article has four sections: the identity of labour and ownership in Locke, the negative effects of that identity in Hegel, the separation of labour and ownership in Marx, and a short conclusion. Hu reconstructs Locke's argument against Filmer, his limits on accumulation and his treatment of money. Hu then follows Hegel's route from will and personality to possession of the body and of things, and his analysis of poverty in civil society. The Marx section runs from the 1842 debate on gathering fallen wood to the 1844 Manuscripts and the 1857–58 manuscripts. Hu reads Locke's argument as a descending sequence from God to person (body), then labour, then thing. In this reading, Locke's money is a means of exchange and hoarding, not self-expanding capital, so his theory stays monistic, with labour as the only ground of property. Hegel's sequence runs from person, as the unity of will and body, to possession and then to the thing. Hegel sees that the labour-ownership principle produces the paradox of poverty amid excess wealth and the rabble, which his proposed remedies cannot solve. Marx, in Hu's account, moves from treating ownership as a legal relation to treating it as a historical relation of production. He then shows that capitalists exchange surplus value from earlier rounds of production for labour-power, so that ownership means appropriating others' products for the capitalist and, for the worker, treating one's own product as another's property. Hu concludes that the line from Locke and Hegel to Marx runs "labour, property, poverty, exploitation", and that Marx's work lifts modern political philosophy to the level of the critique of political economy. Neither Locke nor Hegel discussed exploitation, and Marx did not label their theories apologetics. In Hu's view, apologists nonetheless use them to present capital ownership as naturally just labour ownership, and Hu holds that Marx's critique targets private ownership of the means of production, with public ownership as the principle of scientific socialism. Read the original if you study the relation between Marx and early modern political philosophy, or want a close account of how Marx's view of ownership changed between 1842 and 1857.

"Antagonism" and "harmony" in economic and social development, and their transcendence A reading of Marx's "Bastiat and Carey" 经济社会发展中的“对抗”“和谐”及其超越 Nie Jinfang Nie Jinfang offers a close reading of "Bastiat and Carey", the opening section of Marx's 1857–1858 manuscripts (the Grundrisse), which he says scholars have largely neglected. Drawing on the MEGA2 edition, Nie criticises existing studies for extracting fragments to fit external frameworks rather than reconstructing Marx's own reasoning. The article argues that the text, written in response to the 1857 crisis, shows Marx treating "antagonism" and "harmony" as relative, coexisting conditions, and that it still bears on present-day problems. The article first sets out the crisis of 1857–1858 and Marx's survey of the political economy of his day, which he divided into four unproductive types: eclectic compendia, mere accumulation of material, repetition of old policy disputes, and careerist extension of classical authors. It then examines Marx's account of Henry Carey and Frédéric Bastiat as the two exceptions. Nie goes through the American context of Carey's thought, the contrasting national settings of the two men, and Marx's remarks on Bastiat's chapter on wages. A final section draws four lessons for the present. Nie argues that Marx credits the two men only for rejecting the classical economists' theoretical expression of bourgeois society. Carey, shaped by a bourgeois society that began "from itself" in North America, blames the state for disturbing harmony, yet ends up demanding protective tariffs. Bastiat, writing from backward France, places harmony in an imagined, ideal form found only in England and America and favours free trade. Marx judges both to be unhistorical and bound by a single national outlook. Nie then follows Marx's rebuttal of Bastiat's claim that wages are a "fixed income": it takes one side of a relation as the whole, and it ignores the instability and the risk that wage labour brings. Nie also reads the later five-part plan of the Introduction as evidence that Marx gave the state's economic functions a place in political economy. Nie draws four lessons. Antagonism and harmony coexist, and antagonism should be a means to sublate itself, neither concealed by talk of harmony nor made an end in itself. State functions are shifting from political coercion towards economic roles, and they should respect economic laws and avoid "statism". Thinkers must combine a national standpoint with historical awareness and a global outlook. Lasting theory also grows out of major events and hard intellectual labour, as the Grundrisse did. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based commentary on a little-studied opening of the Grundrisse and its link to the 1857 crisis.

New quality productive forces empowering Chinese modernization: a literature review and outlook 新质生产力赋能中国式现代化：文献述评与展望 Kang Jinxia Zhang Xu This literature review surveys Chinese scholarship on how new quality productive forces "empower" Chinese modernization. Written after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), it treats the concept as a strong driver of Chinese modernization and high-quality development. Kang and Zhang aim to consolidate recent findings and identify where further research is possible. The review is organised around four questions: the analytical frameworks scholars use, the operating mechanisms of empowerment, the proposed implementation paths, and an overall assessment with an outlook. Frameworks are grouped by their basis: Marx's thought on modernization, the theory and practice of Chinese modernization, and the theory of new quality productive forces itself. The mechanisms section distinguishes theoretical from empirical methods. It then sorts substantive claims into three schools: industry empowerment, factor empowerment and civilisation empowerment. The paths section covers principles, institutional guarantees and practical routes. The authors report that scholars largely work from historical materialism: qualitative change in productive forces transforms relations of production and drives modernization. In their account, the literature has not yet specified concrete empowerment mechanisms, and it tends to neglect relations of production. They illustrate this with driverless vehicles, where the issue is not only job displacement but a restructuring of production relations. They add that frameworks should include national institutional factors, namely a dual path of institutional advantage developing productive forces and productive-force growth prompting institutional reform. Education, they argue, is the decisive link, since people are both the goal and the active force. Kang and Zhang conclude that the literature has begun to build a research paradigm for a Chinese autonomous economics knowledge system, has formed a basic analytical framework, and is moving from theory towards empirical indicators for measuring effects. They propose two directions: situating Chinese modernization and new quality productive forces in the world history of modernization, with comparison to Western modernization and a return to Marx's analysis; and studying the distinctive mechanisms through which Chinese modernization fosters new productive forces, including comparison with other countries' modernization models. Read the original if you want a map of the 2024–25 Chinese debate, with the scholars and frameworks named, and a view of the gaps the authors identify.

Promoting the development of new quality productive forces through high-standard opening up 以高水平开放推动新质生产力发展 Huang Qunhui Huang Qunhui asks how high-standard opening up can drive the development of new quality productive forces, a concept Xi Jinping first put forward in September 2023. The author argues that new quality productive forces, as an advanced form of productive forces in line with the new development philosophy, must also accord with the principle of open development. Expanding high-standard opening up, in Huang's view, creates a favourable international environment for them. The article has three parts. The first reads productive forces as a system with three dimensions: elements, structure and function. The second uses statistics and a composite index to identify weak points in China's development of new quality productive forces. The third sets out three priority areas for using opening up to advance them. Huang holds that the core marker of new quality productive forces is a large rise in total factor productivity. On the elements side, the author cites shortfalls in high-level talent, basic research spending (6.65% of R&D in 2023) and computing infrastructure, noting that chip imports were 72% of the global total in 2022. On structure, a six-dimension index of the modernized industrial system gave China 0.54 in 2019, behind the United States, Japan and Germany. Completeness is China's strength, while advancement, openness and security are weaker. On function, total factor productivity growth has hovered around 1% since the 2008 crisis, and Huang links its earlier surges to the gains from reform and opening up. Huang proposes three priorities. The first is a world-class international business environment, including a "tech immigration" scheme for foreign talent, new markets for technology factors, and alignment with high-standard trade rules such as CPTPP and DEPA. The second is to build the modernized industrial system through open cooperation in global industrial and supply chains, easing foreign investment access and encouraging foreign R&D centres in China. The third is to make free trade zones platforms for testing high-standard rules, such as cross-border data flows, and to use Hainan, the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong and Macao as demonstration sites. Huang presents these steps as a way to raise total factor productivity and support the goal of basically achieving modernization by 2035. Read the original if you want an economist's policy-oriented account linking new quality productive forces to institutional opening up, with the index and productivity figures it cites.

The materialist dialectics in further deepening reform comprehensively: an exploration 进一步全面深化改革的唯物辩证法意蕴探赜 Jia Limin This article asks how the Chinese Communist Party has drawn on materialist dialectics in the policy of further deepening reform comprehensively. Jia Limin argues that the Party's grasp of three laws of dialectics (the transformation of quantity into quality, the unity of opposites, and the negation of the negation) has let it fix the historical position, the concrete tasks and the overall goal of this round of reform. The author presents this as a creative application of Marxist method that can help improve the quality and efficiency of reform in the new era. The article has three main sections, one for each law. The first treats reform and opening up as a process in which gradual change and qualitative leaps interweave, and places further deepening within it. The second applies the law of the unity of opposites to identify the starting point, the focal point and the key point of reform. The third uses the negation of the negation to set out the role, the path and the forward-moving character of the reform. Jia draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong's "On Contradiction" and Xi Jinping's statements, and refers to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and that of the 20th (2024). Jia's central moves assign each stage of reform a dialectical position. Comprehensive deepening of reform after 2013 is read as a qualitative leap, in its starting problems, its process and its results. Further deepening is then read as a new quantitative phase built on that leap, with greater breadth, depth and effectiveness. For the unity of opposites, the author names the starting point as the contradiction between the overall goal of reform and the reality of reform, citing formalism and weak coordination among departments. The key point is the principal contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Reform should therefore focus on liberating and developing the productive forces, with economic reform in the lead, while combining the "two-point" and "emphasis" approaches. Finally, further deepening is treated as the stage of negation of the negation. It sublates earlier reform by keeping its positive elements, for example by moving from the "six focuses" of 2013 to the "seven focuses" of 2024, and adds new ones. Jia concludes that further deepening is a higher-level reform that is dynamic and continuing, not a stopping point, and that it will advance with irresistible momentum. Reform should uphold the Party's leadership and other major principles, link itself to Chinese modernization, combine emancipating the mind with seeking truth from facts, and show a fighting spirit and historical initiative. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic maps the Party's reform agenda onto the three laws of dialectics.

Integrating volunteer service education into ideological and political theory courses 将志愿服务教育融入思政课 Li Zhishui This short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 3 June 2025, asks how volunteer service education can be built into the ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) taught in Chinese schools and universities. Li Zhishui argues that these courses carry an important mission in guiding students to uphold the volunteer spirit and contribute their youthful strength. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's May Fourth reply to a volunteer teaching team in the western border region and a April 2024 General Office guideline on improving the volunteer service system for the new era. That guideline calls for volunteer service to be made part of moral education for minors and ideological and political education for university students. Li then sets out three principles. The first is to combine serving the people with a global outlook. Li proposes drawing on cases such as student volunteers at China Agricultural University's science and technology courtyards and environmental volunteers in the Danjiangkou reservoir area, and encouraging participation in international volunteer projects where feasible. The second is to combine classroom teaching with practice: Marxist principles and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should explain volunteering's significance for Chinese modernization, supported by "walking" ideological and political classes in the community. The third is to link focused goals with continuity across school stages. On the third principle, Li calls for integrated planning from primary school to university: storytelling for primary pupils, responsibility education through practice in middle school, and theoretical explanation at university that turns emotional experience into value conviction. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official guidance on volunteering is being translated into teaching recommendations for ideological and political courses.

Lenin's thought on the international union of the proletariat and its contemporary significance 列宁无产阶级国际联合思想及其当代意义 Wang Zifeng Wang Zifeng asks what Lenin's thought on the international union of the proletariat consisted of and what it offers today. The article argues that Lenin, building on Marx and Engels, adapted the idea to the imperialist era and so extended it from workers alone to the proletariat together with oppressed nations. In Wang's view this thought, realised through the Communist International, still has practical value for the international communist movement and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The article has four parts. It first sets out the background: the shift from free-competition capitalism to imperialism and the division of the world into oppressing and oppressed nations. It then presents Lenin's basic ideas under five heads: the necessity of union, its leading force, its leading organisation, its objects and its goals. A third part reviews practice, namely support for proletarian struggles in imperialist countries and for national liberation in colonies and semi-colonies. The last part turns to present-day implications. Wang's central move is to show that Lenin tied the socialist revolution to the national and colonial question, so that the slogan became "proletarians of all countries and oppressed nations, unite". Union is presented as a condition of world revolution, a path to liberation and a precondition of communism, led by national communist parties and the Communist International. Its partners include peasants, non-proletarian classes and oppressed nations, brought together in a broad united front that exploits divisions among enemies. Its goals are a world federation of soviet republics and ultimately communism. Wang credits the Comintern with helping found communist parties in Europe and America and, in China, with helping form the first Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. Turning to today, Wang describes a "new Cold War" in which Western states use sanctions, technology blockades and ideological infiltration against socialist countries, while left forces in capitalist states are marginalised. Wang calls for communist parties to resist this jointly, to set aside disagreements and use the current great changes unseen in a century to revive the world socialist movement. Wang also urges the Communist Party of China to uphold the idea of proletarian international union, strengthen socialism with Chinese characteristics and expand inter-party exchanges. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS researcher draws on Lenin and the Comintern to frame the Party's present approach to inter-party relations and international communist solidarity.

Winning the people's trust and support through new results in improving Party conduct 以作风建设新成效不断赢得人民群众信任拥护 Pan Xihua Writing during the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, Pan Xihua asks what Party conduct work should focus on and how it should proceed under current conditions. The commentary argues that Party members and officials must hold a stance rooted in the people, keep a presence anchored in the heart, and treat their conduct as an examination ground, so that Party conduct yields new results and the Party keeps its advanced and pure character. The piece is organised in three numbered sections. The first treats the people's stance as the Party's fundamental political position. The second concerns the mindset of officials, namely reverence for the people and identification as their servants. The third sets out internal discipline and external popular supervision as complementary requirements. Pan argues that the question of whom a party serves and relies on is the test of its nature, citing the Communist Manifesto and Xi Jinping to say that Party conduct is a barometer of public support. Left uncorrected, bad conduct becomes an invisible wall between the Party and the people. Officials should therefore revere the people, take popular opinion as the best yardstick, and exercise power for the people, fairly, lawfully and honestly. The author adds that conduct outside working hours is also an examination, calling for self-discipline in private life, and that the people should be the final judge of results, through open channels for suggestions, criticism and supervision. Pan concludes that conduct building is a protracted effort that cannot be completed in one stroke. The eight-point regulation should become an internalised habit, in order to consolidate the Party's popular base, keep it the leading core of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short example of how official commentary links Party conduct, the mass line and the current eight-point regulation campaign.

The Communist Party of China's historical exploration of its cultural mission in the New Democratic Revolution and its contemporary implications 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党对文化使命的历史探索与当代启示 Li Qunqun Li Qunqun asks how the Communist Party of China understood and carried out its cultural mission during the New Democratic Revolution, and what that experience offers for taking on a new cultural mission today. The article argues that the Party saw itself as a 'mission-driven party' guided by a logic of responsibility. In Li's account, its clear grasp of the cultural mission and its willingness to act on it greatly promoted the flourishing of New Democratic culture. The article has three parts. The first treats the modern crisis of traditional Chinese culture. It covers the disputes over 'substance and function' among wholesale Westernizers, restorationist Confucian conservatives and New Confucians, and then the Party's growing cultural self-awareness. The second part examines how the Party understood and practised its cultural mission, under four headings: the leading force, the tasks, the development path and the guiding principle. The third part draws four lessons for the present, with frequent reference to Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. Li holds that the Party's rise as a cultural subject came with its correction of dogmatism towards Marxism and of blanket rejection of tradition. Mao's call for a 'national, scientific and mass' new culture of the Chinese nation expressed this. Li presents the wartime cultural path as combining Marxism with fine traditional culture. This meant defining culture through historical materialism, inheriting it critically ('discarding the dross, absorbing the essence') and serving the revolution. The Party's cultural leadership, its orientation towards the people after the Yan'an Forum, and its mass cultural campaigns are said to have won popular support and identification. From this, Li draws four principles for the present. They are upholding the Party's cultural leadership while innovating (including digital cultural transformation and online cultural governance), promoting fine traditional culture to strengthen cultural confidence, respecting the people's principal position, and keeping a Chinese cultural standpoint while drawing on the best of other civilizations. Li links these to Xi Jinping's formulations and to the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads Yan'an-era cultural policy as a precedent for current cultural leadership and cultural confidence.

Teaching the deeper logic of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics 讲好坚持和发展中国特色社会主义的深层次逻辑 Li Guoquan This teaching-oriented article takes up Chapter 1 of the university textbook Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, whose theme is socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li Guoquan argues that the chapter's core and most difficult teaching task is to explain the deeper logic of upholding and developing this socialism. In Li's account, its distinctive features rest on four logics: historical, cultural, theoretical and practical. The article is organised in four sections, one per logic. Each identifies the key points to be conveyed to students, flags the "difficult" teaching problems, and suggests examples or quotations from Xi Jinping to use in class. It covers the 500-year history of socialism, the relation between the periods before and after reform and opening up, the role of traditional Chinese culture, the doctrine of scientific socialism, and the features of the new era. On the historical logic, Li says teachers must show socialism with Chinese characteristics as the outcome of world socialism's development and of the Party's long search for its own path. The two historical periods before and after reform and opening up should be presented as continuous, and Li warns that separating them amounts to historical nihilism aimed at discrediting the Party's path. On the cultural logic, Li holds that the continuity of Chinese civilisation determines that China must follow its own path, and that the Two Integrations, especially the "second integration" with traditional culture, supply cultural subjectivity and governance resources. On the theoretical logic, Li argues that this socialism fits scientific socialism through Party leadership, public ownership, distribution according to work and a socialist market economy, and that it accords with Marxist laws of social development and the view that the people make history. On the practical logic, Li lists five ways in which the new era is new: the changed principal contradiction in society, a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, new strategic goals, a changed relationship between China and the world, and a renewed Party shaped by the Party's self-reform. Li describes the endeavour as a great social revolution and as the necessary road to national rejuvenation and Chinese modernization. Teachers should reinforce students' confidence in the path through historical and international comparison. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style syllabus for this textbook chapter frames its key arguments, difficult points and teaching examples.

Conditions for applying artificial intelligence in ideological and political education 思想政治教育应用人工智能的实现条件 Chang Yanhui Chang Yanhui takes up a gap in work on ideological and political education (sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu) and artificial intelligence. Existing studies, the author says, infer from AI's technical features how it might empower the field, but they seldom consider what conditions are needed for real-world adoption. The article argues that a discussion of prospects should be both imaginative and realistic. It therefore sets out the likely uses of AI and then the technical conditions and the norms that would make those uses possible. The article has three parts. The first explains the principles of current generative AI (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Doubao and similar products), which Chang describes as specialised, weak AI built on data, algorithms and computing power, and then lists application scenarios. The second discusses the technical conditions: national policy support, energy and computing costs, the data to be used in training, and the role of educators in development. The third proposes rules for standards, data collection, market access, content review and legal compliance. Chang argues that AI can support academic research by gathering literature and public-opinion data and generating new forms of presentation. It can also act as a teaching assistant, producing text-to-video scenes for abstract value concepts and supporting differentiated, targeted outreach, as the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) urged. For these uses Chang calls for three kinds of data to be fed into models: published research, the Party's accumulated teaching experience, and longitudinal data on students and teachers. Ideological and political educators, Chang says, should help build industry-specific models by advising on parameters, vetting data quality and giving feedback. Because the field bears on national ideological security and students' wellbeing, the author proposes authoritative third-party assessment of 'intelligent' products, schools keeping control of data collection instead of leaving it to internet firms, and entry rules for products. Chang notes that the opacity of AI results conflicts with the transparency that the field requires, so important decisions must stay with human educators. Chang further proposes review of AI-generated content under the principle of political standards first, upholding Marxism's guiding position and guiding algorithm design with core socialist values. In Chang's account, domestic AI products tend to hold the correct political stance, while some foreign products conceal liberal values behind a show of neutrality. The article also calls for rules grounded in the Data Security Law and the Personal Information Protection Law, with data classified into four types: ideological security, students' political views, physical and mental health, and diverse lifestyles. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of ideological and political education sets out the practical, regulatory and ideological conditions for adopting AI in that field.

Advancing Asian economic integration from the new starting point of Asia's overall revitalisation 站在亚洲整体振兴新起点上推进亚洲经济一体化 Ouyang Yao This newspaper commentary, written against the background of US protectionism, asks how China should use its ties with its Asian neighbours to respond to an uncertain world economy. Ouyang Yao argues that speeding up Asian economic integration is both a necessary answer to unilateralism and protectionism and the route to building a community with a shared future with neighbouring countries and to Asia's overall revitalisation. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's description of Asia as standing at a new starting point. The article has three parts. The first sets out why good-neighbour relations matter, drawing on a cyclical account of hegemonic rise and decline and on three trends in Asia's economy. The second discusses how to deepen integration through the ASEAN way, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and a China–Japan–South Korea free trade area. The third lists four advantages China can contribute: market size, technological innovation, industrial leadership and infrastructure capacity. Ouyang contends that rising hegemons favour free trade and multilateralism, while declining ones turn to protectionism and trade barriers. Against this, the author cites Asia's 49 per cent share of global GDP in 2024, its growing manufacturing base and complete industrial chains, and rising intra-Asian trade dependence. Asia's stability can therefore counter global uncertainty. The author presents the ASEAN model of consultation, with no fixed leading country, as suited to Asia's diversity, and cites RCEP's effects: intra-regional trade up about 3 per cent in 2024, and intermediate goods at roughly 66 per cent of trade in 2023. Ouyang proposes that RCEP members shorten zero-tariff transition periods, remove non-tariff barriers, move towards negative-list commitments, make rules of origin easier to use, and add operational detail on digital trade and intellectual property, together with dispute-settlement channels. The author also urges China to import more from ASEAN, export high-tech goods and invest abroad to spread technology, lead a multipolar "flying geese" production network, and build railways and ports, citing the Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. The goal is for the fruits of Chinese modernization to benefit Asian countries. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese economist links Asian regional integration, RCEP and Belt and Road-style infrastructure to China's response to US trade policy.

The logical path to consolidating the Party's cultural leadership in the new era 新时代筑牢党的文化领导权的逻辑进路 Wang Fei Zhang Wen This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (29 May 2025) asks how the Party can consolidate its cultural leadership in the new era. The authors argue that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee has put forward "upholding the Party's cultural leadership" as a defining task. They hold that it must be strengthened along four logical lines. The piece is organised as four "logics": theoretical, historical, realistic and practical. Each is tied to a concrete requirement, ranging from Marxist guidance and the people's standing as the main body of culture to international discourse power and the Two Integrations. On the theoretical line, the authors say Marx and Engels grounded culture in practice and stressed spreading socialist ideas among the working class. They present the Party's cultural leadership as an innovative development of that theory. On the historical line, they review the Party's record from the New Democratic Revolution to reform and opening up. They conclude that the people's standpoint and the unity of Party spirit and people's character are the basic principles. On the realistic line, they describe Western states as trying to infiltrate culture with hegemonism and weaken the Party's ruling base. They therefore call for stronger international communication, telling China's stories well, and export of film, animation and games. The practical line rests on the Two Integrations within Chinese modernization. The authors propose surveying local cultural needs, building rural cultural brands and urban cultural venues, putting classics into curricula, and using modern technology for cultural platforms. Their conclusion is that these steps will strengthen cultural leadership and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated scholars frame cultural leadership in current official terms.

Deepening Party conduct building in the new era 纵深推进新时代党的作风建设 Kan Daoyuan This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, asks how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) should be pushed further. Kan Daoyuan argues that the Party's conduct is its image, bears on popular support and decides the success of its cause. In Kan's view, the effort must be made routine and long-lasting through a firm grounding in Party spirit. The article opens by defining conduct, which covers ideological, work, leadership and lifestyle styles as well as styles of study, writing and meetings. It then turns to the continuing correction of the "four undesirable work styles", the role of leading cadres as the "critical few", the base in Party spirit, and the institutional and mass mechanisms needed for lasting results. Kan holds that ideological conduct is the fundamental layer, since solving it resolves the others, and that Party conduct sits at the core of social and popular customs while also being shaped by them. The eight-point rule of the Central Committee is presented as the "first cut" of the Party's self-reform, used to tackle formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. Kan warns that these problems are stubborn and may return in hidden forms. Leading cadres must set an example, because problems often show up below but originate above. Conduct is ultimately a matter of Party spirit, measured by the distinction between public and private interest. Kan calls for stronger ideals and convictions, a correct view of public and private, and a combined approach to Party spirit, conduct and discipline, with joint investigation and joint treatment of conduct and corruption problems. Kan also proposes institutional supervision, performance appraisal and cadre selection tied to conduct, and a dense supervision network that relies on the masses. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present conduct building and the eight-point rule in 2025.

Efforts to unite the international Maoist movement and its latest developments 国际毛主义运动联合化探索及最新动态 Yu Weihai Shu Huiqian Yu and Shu ask how Maoist parties around the world have tried to form international organisations since the 1980s, and what the founding of the International Communist League (ICL) on 26 December 2022 means for them. They treat the ICL as the latest result of decades of effort, and as an event that merits tracking in order to judge the role of Maoist parties in today's international communist movement. Their assessment is mixed: the ICL has real significance, but it also carries long-standing weaknesses. The article first sorts Maoist parties into three types: those waging armed struggle (the Philippines, India, Turkey, Peru), those not yet doing so (mostly in Europe and Latin America), and those that moved to parliamentary politics (Nepal). It then traces earlier umbrella bodies: the Revolutionary Internationalist Movement (1984–2006), the International Conference of Marxist-Leninist Parties and Organizations (International Newsletter) (1998–2017), and the International Coordination of Revolutionary Parties and Organizations (2010). Joint May Day statements, commemorations, regional conferences and open debate in 2022 over a draft proposal are presented as the main forms of cooperation. The second half sets out the ICL's doctrine and activities, followed by an evaluation. On the authors' account, the ICL holds that imperialism is in a general crisis driven by three contradictions: imperialism versus oppressed nations, bourgeoisie versus proletariat, and rivalry among imperialist powers. It sees a new wave of proletarian revolution and takes Marxism-Leninism-Maoism as its guide, promoting people's war and a 'unity–struggle–unity' method against fragmentation. Yu and Shu credit it with anti-imperialist activity, stronger unity among small parties and a distinct revolutionary path unlike the parliamentary road of most Western communist parties. They also criticise it on three counts: it denies that any socialist states exist, which they call a mistaken view of China and others; it shows sectarian tendencies; and its programme is idealised and abstract. As evidence of sectarianism, the authors note that no new members have joined in two years, and that the Communist Party of India (Maoist) and the Communist Party of the Philippines stayed out. They add that a split in Sweden followed the ICL's founding. They quote the Indian and Philippine parties' objection that a universal people's war line and a central international body would override national conditions. They conclude that the road to broad Maoist unity remains difficult. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the organisational history of world Maoism, the ICL's founding documents and the objections raised against it.

Techno-feudalism and the problem of the "general intellect" in the digital economy 技术封建主义与数字经济时代的“一般智力”问题 Huang Dan Huang Dan takes up the concept of techno-feudalism, which foreign scholars have recently used to describe an economy dominated by digital oligarchs, and asks whether it explains the exploitation and power structures of the digital economy. The article's answer is double. The concept is flawed as a historical analogy and as an account of platforms, yet it points to a real phenomenon: the private enclosure of Marx's "general intellect". The article first sets out the concept as developed by Cédric Durand and Yanis Varoufakis, who describe rent extraction by platforms, "cloud rent", cloud landlords, vassal capitalists and cloud serfs. It then criticises the concept on two counts, its reading of feudalism and its neglect of platforms' productive side. A third section turns to the preconditions of digital rent-seeking and then to the privatisation of the general intellect. It draws on Marx's "Fragment on Machines", Hardt and Negri, Žižek, Yann Moulier-Boutang and Carlo Vercellone. A short closing section discusses generative AI. Huang argues that feudalism, as Ganshof, Bloch and Perry Anderson understand it, rests on extra-economic coercion and political-legal ties, not on the mere existence of rent. Digital rent is a purely economic, commercial form of capitalist rent. Platforms such as Amazon also produce and innovate, so their income combines profit and rent, and concepts like platform capitalism or cognitive capitalism fit better. Rent-seeking still depends on scarcity, and Huang argues that this scarcity is artificially created. Big data, open-source libraries and publicly funded patents are collectively produced but enclosed through intellectual property, algorithmic control and monopoly, which the article calls a "second enclosure". Following Moulier-Boutang and Vercellone, Huang holds that the capital logic of closure clashes with a cognitive-labour logic of open circulation and cooperation. Huang concludes that this contradiction is both a deepening of exploitation and a source of emancipatory potential. Large language models trained on public data are cited as a new instance of the general intellect being absorbed by capital. The article calls for rediscovering its public character through institutions and technology, and points to platform cooperativism, democratic platforms and the redistribution and sharing of public data as early steps. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of the techno-feudalism debate that turns it into a question about knowledge enclosure and the general intellect.

Technofeudalism examined: a new form of monopoly capitalism 技术封建主义思潮辨析：垄断资本主义的新形态 Zheng Han Zheng Han takes up the technofeudalism thesis advanced by Western left scholars, chiefly Cédric Durand and Yanis Varoufakis, who hold that digital capitalism has regressed into something resembling feudalism. The article grants that this current captures many features of the digital age. It argues, however, that its main concepts stay within Marx's own categories and that many of its judgements run against his analysis. Zheng's answer is that Big Tech is a new form of monopoly capitalism, not a feudal order. The article first reconstructs technofeudalism through three claimed 'discoveries': profit has given way to 'cloud rent', class relations have turned into lord–serf dependence (Varoufakis's 'cloud proletarians' and 'cloud serfs'), and markets and profit are being eroded. It then tests these claims against Marxist theory in three steps: the circuit of capital, labour and users, and global monopoly. It closes with the question of emancipation, drawing on company data on cloud market shares, R&D spending, lobbying and staffing. Zheng argues that the tech giants remain functioning capitalists. They pass through the full industrial-capital circuit, buy labour-power and appropriate surplus value, and also act as commercial capital by matching supply and demand. In the article's account they remain subject to competition and innovation, and they maintain infrastructure, unlike rentier landlords. Platform workers are wage-labourers under real subordination, and algorithmic management deepens that control. Users, by contrast, are said to take part in the reproduction of labour-power, so the claim that they perform unpaid 'serf' labour is judged a misreading of Marx's concept of labour. Finally, the concentration of cloud services, political lobbying and the 'revolving door' are presented as confirmation of Lenin's account of monopoly capitalism. Zheng concludes that technofeudalism is a supra-historical philosophy that cannot grasp capitalism's developmental dynamic. The tech giants, the author says, redistribute power within the bourgeoisie but leave the capital–labour antagonism intact. Varoufakis's 'cloud uprising', which would include some vassal capitalists, is judged a bourgeois-style coalition that overestimates online mobilisation. The article calls for analysis in the Marxist tradition and for struggle strategies aimed at digital capitalism's weaknesses. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Durand and Varoufakis, backed by detailed data on Big Tech's market power.

Algorithmic hegemony and ideological manipulation: how Western states discipline intelligent algorithms 算法霸权与意识形态操控：西方国家规训智能算法的路径探赜 Zhang Xuesen Zhang Xuesen asks how Western states, drawing on their early lead in technology, have shaped intelligent algorithms into a system of "algorithmic hegemony" that serves their ideology, and how other countries can respond. The article argues that laws, industry standards and policy guidance in the West steer how algorithms are developed, used and supervised, so that algorithms become a hidden instrument for spreading Western ideology. It presents this as a global contest over algorithmic sovereignty and ideological security. The article has four parts. The first describes mechanisms of control: algorithmic surveillance, recommendation systems and "data colonialism". The second treats the embedding of Western values in algorithm design, through bias, agenda-setting and information filtering. The third analyses monopoly in three forms, technological, data and capital. The fourth proposes strategies for breaking Western algorithmic dominance. Zhang draws on Foucault, Deleuze, Bauman, Zuboff, Sunstein, Couldry and Mejias, O'Neil, Pasquale, Harari and Samir Amin. Zhang's central claim is that algorithms have moved society from Foucault's disciplinary society to a Deleuzian "society of control", in which a "post-panopticon" of fluid surveillance makes people's behaviour and emotions transparent. In the author's account, the PRISM programme and Meta's behavioural analysis illustrate this. Recommendation systems create "filter bubbles" and group polarisation, and Western media filter content about China. Cases such as Amazon's recruitment algorithm, a US criminal-risk tool and Meta's housing adverts illustrate algorithmic bias. Zhang then reads the whole system through Amin's centre–periphery model. Mathematical foundations, "black box" opacity, control of global data flows and a "global digital monopoly alliance" tie technology, data and capital together. In this reading, algorithms execute the logic of capital and entrench dependence in latecomer states. Zhang calls for China and other developing countries to reduce dependence on Western algorithms. Proposals include special research funds, a "core algorithm" programme and closer links between universities, institutes and firms. Zhang also urges unified legislation and supervision, with algorithm registration, assessment and accountability, and training and recruitment of talent, including from overseas. Internationally, Zhang advocates joint standards, transparency and fairness assessments, and a fair, open and inclusive global algorithm order that reflects developing countries' interests. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship frames Western platform power as hegemony and what policy remedies it proposes.

World socialism in the face of changes unseen in a century A review of the 14th World Socialism Forum 应对百年未有之大变局的世界社会主义 Ren Jiasi This is a report on the 14th World Socialism Forum, held in Beijing on 9–10 September 2024. The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences hosted it, and its World Socialism Research Centre, Academy of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought research centre co-organised it. Over 60 foreign Communist Party leaders and left-wing scholars from more than 30 countries attended, together with Chinese specialists. The theme was the current changes in the world, the era and history. Ren groups the speeches into five themes: the great changes unseen in a century and China's responsibility; the "East rising, West declining" shift in the global political order; socialism with Chinese characteristics and the development of world socialism; the difficulties and prospects of Western capitalism; and the world significance of further deepening reform and Chinese modernization. Speakers included CASS vice-president Zhen Zhanmin, International Department official Chen Zhou, Spanish Communist Party leader José Luis Centella and Li Shenming (in writing). Many Communist Party representatives and scholars from Latin America, Africa, Europe and Asia also spoke. As Ren reports it, participants broadly agreed that the Global South is rising, that unilateralism and protectionism are growing, and that the contest between capitalism and socialism is shifting in socialism's favour. Several foreign speakers described China's peace diplomacy, the Belt and Road Initiative and the three global initiatives as reshaping the world order. Other speakers argued that capitalism is in deep crisis and cannot overcome its inherent contradictions, naming inequality, ecological damage, digital hegemony and debt. Left parties in Europe, the United States and Brazil were described as fragmented or marginalised, and some speakers urged them to draw on China's experience. Chinese speakers presented Chinese modernization as an alternative to "modernization equals Westernization". Some warned of Western anti-socialist propaganda and cognitive warfare and called for stronger international communication. The report concludes that attendees were confident in socialism's vitality and willing to cooperate. Several saw world socialism as entering an upswing, with socialism with Chinese characteristics as its mainstay. Speakers also treated the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as China's answer to global change. Read the original if you want a detailed record of who said what at the forum, particularly the views of foreign Communist parties and scholars on China, capitalism and the future of socialism.

Grasping the distinctive advantages of whole-process people's democracy from the dimension of practice 从实践维度把握全过程人民民主的显著优势 Zhang Chunzhao Feng Yinghong This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily, asks how the distinctive advantages of whole-process people's democracy can be understood through practice. Zhang and Feng argue that it is the most broad, genuine and effective form of socialist democracy. In their account it supplies momentum and institutional guarantees for deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. It first traces the Party's century of democratic exploration, from the border-region councils of the revolutionary period through the 1954 constitution and the reform era to the new era. It then describes the system's institutional procedures and participatory practice. Finally it assesses the practical value of the model. The authors identify the institutional supports as the Party's leadership system, the people's congress system, the new type of party system, and grassroots self-governance. They say that democratic election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight form a complete closed loop of practice. They also argue that the model extends democracy beyond politics into the economy, culture, society and ecological civilization. In their view it surpasses Western-style democracy by attending to both process and result, procedure and substance, and representation and participation. Zhang and Feng conclude that whole-process people's democracy has distinct Chinese features while reflecting a shared human pursuit of democracy. They present it as a contribution of Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to democratic development worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the history, institutions and comparative claims of whole-process people's democracy in 2025.

The Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the nation's War of Resistance 中国共产党是全民族抗战的中流砥柱 Cao Ziyang Writing in Economic Daily in May 2025, ahead of the 80th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, Cao Ziyang argues that the Communist Party of China (CPC) was the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) of the whole nation's resistance. In Cao's account, the Party's leadership was decisive in four areas: political and ideological guidance, organisation and mobilisation, strategy and tactics, and military struggle. The commentary is organised chronologically and thematically in four sections. It first traces the CPC's early armed resistance from the Mukden Incident (1931) through the Xi'an Incident (1936) to the outbreak of full-scale war in 1937. It then turns to the Party's role in building and defending the anti-Japanese national united front, its general line and strategy for protracted war, and the rise of the rear-area battlefield behind Japanese lines. Cao's central claims run as follows. The Party issued the earliest calls for armed resistance, led guerrilla forces in the north-east, dropped the slogan of opposing Chiang Kai-shek in favour of pressing him to resist Japan, and helped bring about the peaceful resolution of the Xi'an Incident and the second Kuomintang–CPC cooperation. When the Kuomintang turned to passive resistance and anti-communism after the stalemate stage began, the Party adopted a policy of both uniting with and struggling against it, and a line of developing progressive forces, winning over the middle and opposing the diehards. On strategy, Cao credits the Luochuan Conference (1937) and Mao Zedong's 1938 works, including On Protracted War, with setting out a comprehensive people's war line and the three stages of the war. Cao concludes that the Party-led rear-area battlefield became the main battlefield, citing about 1.32 million regular troops, over 2.6 million militia and 19 liberated areas by war's end. Cao concludes that without the CPC and the base-area forces and people it led, complete victory could not have been won, and presents the victory as the turning point from national crisis towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The Party, Cao says, will remember this history and lead the people toward building a strong country and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party-history narrative of the CPC's leading role in the War of Resistance is currently presented, with its chronology and key documents.

Raising the "new quality combat power" of state security organs through new results in Party conduct 以作风建设新成效提升国家安全机关新质战斗力 Chen Yixin Writing in Study Times (28 May 2025), Chen Yixin, identified as Party secretary and minister of the Ministry of State Security, asks how work on Party conduct can strengthen the fighting capacity of China's state security organs. He argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee's campaign on conduct, which began with the eight-point regulations, has changed Party, government and social ethos. In his account, the security organs are now applying this through the current study and education campaign on the spirit of those regulations, in order to raise what he calls "new quality combat power". The article is a programmatic report organised under eight headings: political leadership and loyalty; investigation and research; innovation; practical combat readiness; cutting paperwork and meetings; thrift; Party self-reform and supervision; and a fighting spirit. Each section opens with a statement by Xi Jinping and then lists measures the ministry's Party committee says it has taken. Chen gives some concrete details, such as weekly, monthly and quarterly follow-up on Xi's directives, a first batch of 10 observation points for reducing burdens on grassroots units, and falls in several categories of spending in 2024. Chen's central claim is that the security organs' political character comes first, since he calls them the "knife handle" of the Party and people, so their conduct and their operational strength cannot be separated. He describes institutional measures: a revised set of detailed rules on the eight-point regulations, a supervision system to promote the Three Forms of Non-corruption, tighter accountability, and a ban on disguised or mutated violations. He pairs these with operational reforms: "virtual institutions, substantive operation and integrated mechanisms" without changing organisations or staffing, technology-driven methods, and combat teams. Read the original if you want a first-hand view of how the security leadership links Party conduct campaigns to institutional reform and operational goals, and of the vocabulary it uses.

Understanding the methodology of strengthening Party conduct in the new era 深刻理解新时代加强党的作风建设的方法论 Cai Wencheng Writing as the Party-wide study and education campaign on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation gets under way, Cai Wencheng, a professor and dean at Lanzhou University, asks how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng) in the new era should be understood methodologically. Cai argues that firm ideals and convictions are the root of good conduct, so formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance are traced to a loosened ideological "master switch". The eight-point regulation is described as a small entry point, seemingly about a mooncake or a meal, that drives the larger strategy of Party discipline. Strict self-cultivation must go with practical action, and leading cadres, the "critical minority", set the example while ordinary members push upward. Institutions must be tightened and enforced through law-based means, so that improvement is standardised and lasting. Cai concludes that conduct-building has a starting point but no end, and that Party committees and their top officials must bear responsibility consistently and over the long term. The eight-point regulation is described as a lasting iron rule, and Cai holds that good Party conduct should in turn lead social and popular customs. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official discourse frames Party conduct campaigns as a set of dialectical working methods.

Promoting high-quality development of trade union work in the new era and on the new journey 推动新时代新征程工会工作高质量发展 Wang Dongming Wang Dongming, chairman of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions (ACFTU), offers a study-and-implementation commentary on Xi Jinping's speech of 28 April 2025. They should also build a knowledgeable, skilled and innovative industrial workforce, improve a "universal plus special" system of rights protection and services, and reform to strengthen their political, advanced and mass character. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the ACFTU leadership frames the union's tasks after its centenary, and of the official vocabulary used for them.

Upholding the dialectical unity of breaking and establishing to make further comprehensive deepening of reform take root 坚持破和立的辩证统一 推动进一步全面深化改革走深走实 Zheng Shanjie Zheng Shanjie, writing as head of the National Development and Reform Commission, takes up Xi Jinping's instruction that further comprehensively deepening reform should centre on institution-building and should stress "breaking and establishing together, establishing before breaking". Zheng argues that the principle draws on the Two Integrations: Marxism combined with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, citing ideas such as "getting rid of the old to bring in the new". The article presents these as the Commission's way of carrying out the Third Plenum's reform agenda. Read the original if you want an official statement of how this reform method is turned into planned economic policy tasks.

China–Russia High-level Think Tank Forum (2025) opens in Beijing Report on the opening session, 30 May 2025 中俄智库高端论坛（2025）在北京召开 This news report, originally from People's Daily Online, covers the opening on 30 May 2025 of the China–Russia High-level Think Tank Forum in Beijing. Building a strong education nation around the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education 围绕立德树人根本任务建设教育强国 Huang Jing'ou This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks on education since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Understanding the rich meaning of "turning good conduct into custom" 深入理解“化风成俗”的丰富意蕴 Su Shengli Guo Guangyin This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, appears while the Party is running a study and education campaign on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations on conduct. The first defines the term, drawing on classical Chinese ideas of feng (prevailing ethos, imposed from above by example) and su (custom, habit widely accepted and practised by ordinary people). The second sets out three shifts the concept requires. The third discusses how to sustain the effort, citing Xi's remarks, including those from his March 2025 inspection in Guizhou and Yunnan. The authors argue that work-style problems are stubborn and prone to rebound, citing Xi's remark that "tighten up and it improves, relax and it bounces back". They say hedonism, extravagance, formalism and bureaucratism persist, and that undesirable practices take new, concealed forms because the root causes of the "four undesirable work styles" have not been removed. For the last, they cite Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era claim that the people would learn from a Party with a fully upright style. On how to persevere, the authors call for three measures. The first is strengthening ideals and Party spirit, since work-style problems are at root problems of Party spirit. The second is a problem-oriented approach that watches for rebound and for hidden variants of misconduct.
