They conclude that only this will break the cycle of improvement and relapse and make good conduct a lasting custom. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary explains the Party's work-style campaign and Xi's phrase "turning good conduct into custom".

Mao Zedong's thinking and practice on "never becoming a Li Zicheng", and its lessons 毛泽东对“决不当李自成”的思考、实践及其启示 Liu Haifei Chen Lian'nian Mao Zedong repeatedly warned the Communist Party to learn from the failure of Li Zicheng, the peasant rebel leader who took Beijing in 1644 but whose regime collapsed within a short time. As the Party prepared to take power nationwide, Mao stressed that it was going to Beijing to take an examination and must "never become a Li Zicheng". Liu and Chen argue that earlier scholarship mostly introduced Mao's thinking on the subject, while his concrete practice after 1949 and the deeper lessons drawn from it have received less attention. Their article tries to fill that gap. The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's attention to Li Zicheng from his youth through the revolutionary period: the Great Revolution and land revolution years, the War of Resistance against Japan, and the late civil war. The second sets out six areas of practice after the Party entered Beijing. The third draws six lessons for the present, linking them to Xi Jinping's statements on the Mao-era warning. In the authors' account, Mao located Li's failure in the lack of a leading class or party, the absence of a secure base, arrogance and underestimation of the enemy, corruption within the leadership, and the lack of institutions representing the majority. The wartime reading of Guo Moruo's essay on the 300th anniversary of the 1644 events and the 1945 "cave dialogue" with Huang Yanpei fed into the "Two Musts" and the rules adopted at the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949). The six areas of practice are Mao's personal self-discipline; eliminating threats, including the decision to intervene in Korea; the united front; ties with the masses and opposition to bureaucracy; the Three-Antis campaign and the execution of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan; and institutional safeguards such as people's democratic dictatorship, public ownership and the handling of letters from the public. Liu and Chen conclude that Mao's reflections are a political legacy whose inheritance bears on long-term Party rule. Their six lessons are drawing wisdom from history, staying alert to danger in times of peace, upholding the Party's glorious traditions, keeping up work on Party conduct and discipline, treating anti-corruption as a permanent task, and using two answers together to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. These two answers are supervision by the people and the Party's self-reform. An analysis of "historical initiative" from the perspective of Marxism 马克思主义视阈下“历史主动”问题探析 Mei Lan Mei Lan asks what "historical initiative" (lishi zhudong) means in Marxism and why it matters. Earlier studies, the author says, drew on Marx and Engels's judgements of the proletariat and discussed the present-day significance of the "spirit of historical initiative" from the standpoint of the socialist movement, but could not explain how the problem arises or what it means philosophically. Mei argues that historical initiative is not mere subjective agency. It is a practice-based process of making history, and the concept of practice reveals its essence. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the problem's "logic of formation" from Marx's concept of practice, especially the Theses on Feuerbach. The second examines the concrete grounds on which Marx and Engels judged historical initiative, drawing on the Communist Manifesto's critique of utopian socialism and Marx's assessment of the Paris Commune. The third derives three general forms of historical initiative from their reflections on proletarian revolution. In Mei's reading, practice is the activity of changing the world, so history is made by people and becomes "their own" only when they act to change it. Initiative therefore means "going to practise", not waiting for history to unfold. Because the changed world is a social formation, the standard for judging initiative is concrete. Marx and Engels faulted the utopian socialists for the "absence of action", since they gave the proletariat no distinctive political movement. They praised the Commune for smashing the old state machine. Mei restricts the bearer of initiative to the working class, whereas the petty bourgeoisie, in the article's account, lacks autonomy. The three general forms are: stimulating initiative by creating material, class and ideological conditions; exercising it through organised, political direct action and class struggle; and keeping it through flexible strategy, illustrated by Marx's analysis of the failure of the 1848 revolution in France and by the long-term nature of socialist construction after seizing power. Mei concludes that elucidating historical initiative frees Marxism from historical determinism and makes people the subject and creator of history. The author adds that this deepens the understanding of the relation between initiative and practice. In the "new era" and on the "new journey", Mei calls for a more conscious strengthening of the spirit of historical initiative, and of the determination, courage and perseverance to change the world, in order to advance socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a close philosophical reading of how Marx and Engels's texts on practice, the Commune and revolutionary strategy can be organised into a theory of historical initiative.

Techno-feudalism: meaning, controversies and responses An interview with the French economist Cédric Durand 技术封建主义：内涵、争议与应对 Zhao Dingqi This is an interview conducted, translated and edited by Zhao Dingqi of the journal World Socialism Studies. The interviewee is the French economist Cédric Durand, professor at Paris 13 University and author of Techno-féodalisme (2020), described as the first systematic political-economy study of the topic. The interview asks why the internet's early promise of liberation gave way to monopoly power, and what 'techno-feudalism' means as a description of capitalism under digital technology. The conversation has three parts. The first traces the 'Californian ideology', fictitious capital and the origins of the concept. The second covers the features of techno-feudalism and three kinds of criticism. The third asks whether techno-feudalism has replaced capitalism and how resistance might be organised. Durand also places his book in relation to earlier work: cyberpunk-era uses of the term, McKenzie Wark, Yanis Varoufakis's 2024 book, Marx's 'industrial feudalism' and Habermas on the refeudalisation of the public sphere. Durand argues that control of data and of the tools of social coordination now takes priority over production, much as control of land did under feudalism. In his account, platform owners extract 'rents' from users' data and set rules for social life, which blurs the line between economic and political power. He answers three criticisms. First, techno-feudalism differs from feudalism: production is not small-scale and labour is more socially interdependent than ever, but the monopolised asset is appropriated predatorily. Second, the concept does not flatter capitalism, because anti-capitalist critique stays valid whether or not the hypothesis proves right. Third, on the depth of change in production relations, he treats it as an open historical question. He says the trend is towards control investment with zero-sum returns. On resistance, Durand backs digital commons and free software but considers them insufficient. He does not favour restoring full competition. He proposes revived digital public utilities under the UN or other international cooperation, modelled on the Universal Postal Union. He adds two caveats: the ecological footprint of AI, and the fact that digital collaboration cannot alone secure emancipation, which also depends on people's collective agency. Read the original if you want a first-hand statement of Durand's techno-feudalism thesis, his replies to critics and his policy proposals, as presented to a Chinese Marxist audience.

Lukács's Ontology of Social Being as a misplaced reading of Marx 卢卡奇《关于社会存在的本体论》对马克思的错位阅读 Yang Haifeng Yang Haifeng examines Georg Lukács's late work The Ontology of Social Being, which rebuilds Marx's philosophy on the basis of labour. Yang argues that this reconstruction rests on a "misplaced reading" (cuowei yuedu) of Marx, and that earlier discussions of Lukács have not identified the problem. The misplacement is said to be twofold: logical, because it explains Marx through a Hegelian ontology of labour, and textual, because it reads Capital through the Grundrisse. The article opens by noting three shifts from History and Class Consciousness: Lukács accepts the priority of nature, criticises Hegel's subject–object identity, and replaces practice with labour as the ontological basis. Yang concentrates on the third. The first section reconsiders Marx's development from The German Ideology to Capital, set against the humanist (Fromm), Althusserian, Soviet-textbook and Chinese-textbook views. The second section sets out Lukács's labour ontology, and the third compares the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Grundrisse and Capital. It also counts Lukács's citations in the second volume of the Ontology. Yang's central claim is that the shared consensus on the continuity of Marx's thought after 1845 is mistaken. In Yang's account, Marx moved from a "production logic", concerned with satisfying needs and close to classical political economy, to a "capital logic", in which the drive for surplus value governs material production and turns needs into carriers of insatiable desire. Lukács's labour ontology, with its unity of teleology and causality, its "second nature" and its account of freedom, extends the production logic. Yang traces it to Hegel's treatment of labour and to the 1844 and 1857–58 manuscripts. Yang adds that the Grundrisse already holds both logics, and that Marx there warns that capital cannot be understood from material production or from objectification and alienation. According to Yang, Lukács cites Capital about 81 times but follows the Grundrisse's labour-ontological line. Yang also criticises Postone and Arthur for explaining capital through value, since Marx held that value is determined by capital. Yang concludes that Lukács reconstructed Marx creatively but missed the major shift from The German Ideology to Capital, and so could not resolve the difficulties of labour ontology. Yang says the same limit affects Christine Gould's reading and, in part, Postone's. Properly understanding Lukács and other Western scholars therefore requires re-reading Marx, in order to gain a theoretical reference point. Read the original if you study Lukács, Western Marxism or the relation between the Grundrisse and Capital, and want a Chinese scholar's argument about labour ontology versus capital logic.

The problem of the "real movement" in communist theory A core issue in how the contemporary Western radical left interprets communism 共产主义理论中的“现实运动”问题 Li Jian Marx and Engels wrote in The German Ideology that communism is 'the real movement which abolishes the present state of things'. Li asks what kind of communism deserves to be called a 'real movement' and how it can take root in actual history in the twenty-first century. The article reads the answers of influential Western radical-left thinkers, and argues that, lacking a historical-materialist foundation, their theory differs fundamentally from Marx's and has little practical effect. Li nonetheless holds that it offers useful points of reference for developing a new form of human civilization. The article has four parts. It first sets out the radical left's double approach to communism as both 'idea' and 'real movement', drawing on Alain Badiou, Slavoj Žižek, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri. It then traces their shift from abolishing capitalism's present state to the 'real movement' of producing subjectivity, treating its preconditions, main line of development and value goal. A third part assesses these views from a historical-materialist standpoint, and a fourth draws lessons for the new form of human civilization. In Li's account, these thinkers rest the shift on changed class relations in digital capitalism, on mutual reinforcement between heterogeneous subjects (Hardt and Negri's 'multitude', Jacques Rancière's 'part of those without part') and communities, and on restoring human subjectivity. Li's critique has three main strands. The thinkers do not tie the antagonism between labour and capital to abolishing private ownership, and 'common' ownership is not Marxian public ownership of the means of production. They stress contingency and event over the 'iron necessity' of historical laws, and lose sight of the proletariat as the revolutionary class. They also keep the 'becoming' of communism in the realm of ideas rather than its 'empirical birth', and reduce emancipation to the individual's. Li concludes that, despite these flaws, the radical left's work clarifies the relation between capitalism and communism, restates Marx's original aim of criticising the old world while discovering a new one, and applies the principle that thought should tend toward reality. For the new form of human civilization, Li calls for continued institutional innovation, for socialist reform guided by the direction of communism, and for drawing out the people's historical initiative. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Badiou, Žižek, Negri, Hardt and Rancière on communism, together with an account of how such work is made useful to Chinese theory.

Building broad consensus for further deepening reform comprehensively 广泛凝聚进一步全面深化改革共识 He Husheng Fang Liang This short commentary, published in Beijing Daily in May 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's remark that building broad consensus and mobilising all positive factors is very important for the smooth advance of reform. He Husheng and Fang Liang argue that, at a critical period for advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, consensus is both a safeguard and a necessary path for further deepening reform comprehensively. The article is organised in three parts. The first explains why consensus matters, the second sets out what the consensus must contain, and the third proposes how to build it. It draws on Xi's speeches and on the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform. The authors say consensus does three things for reform. It lays an ideological foundation by turning perceptual understanding into rational conviction. It resolves practical problems, since reform has reached a stage in which, in Xi's words, only hard bones remain to be gnawed, and these involve complex interests. It also gathers a strong joint force, which the authors describe as a political strength of the Party. They then divide the content of consensus into three dimensions. Leadership consensus rests on the Party's leading role. Ideological consensus rests on the theoretical innovations of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, notably Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Interest consensus requires cadres and citizens to develop a sense of the overall situation and to treat adjustments of interests and personal gains and losses correctly. For practice, the authors call for three measures. The first is upholding the Party's overall leadership and the authority of the Central Committee, so that reform decisions are carried out. The second is deepening institutional reform to coordinate social interests, balance fairness and efficiency, handle distribution and address the concerns people feel most directly. The third is strengthening ideological work, guiding public opinion on reform, promoting positive publicity and keeping Marxism in its guiding position. Bringing into play universities' role as a vanguard force in scientific and technological innovation 发挥高校科技创新生力军作用 Ren Xiaolong This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, asks how Chinese universities can serve as a vanguard force in scientific and technological innovation. The first concerns inheriting and promoting the spirit of scientists as a source of motivation. The second concerns improving research systems and mechanisms. The third concerns building a virtuous cycle among education, science and technology, and talent. Ren draws throughout on speeches by Xi Jinping, the 2021 Central Talent Work Conference and the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on deepening reform. On the first point, Ren presents the spirit of scientists as part of the Chinese Communists' spiritual lineage. On the second, Ren calls for universities to align basic research with national strategic needs and to target 'bottleneck' technologies. They should also move from 'papers to papers' topic selection towards organised research, use the new type of whole-nation system, and strengthen links with enterprises and local governments so that results are converted into industry applications. On the third, Ren proposes adjusting disciplines dynamically to national needs, advancing the 'new engineering, new medicine, new agriculture and new liberal arts' initiatives, and combining science education with the humanities. Universities should also build up strategic scientific talent, focus policy on young talent, and continue reforms that end the 'five onlys' in evaluation. They should create management based on trust, respect and tolerance. Ren concludes that these measures would let universities contribute more to building a leading scientific and technological power and advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese university leader translates central policy language on science, talent and education into institutional tasks.

A deep understanding of the theoretical meaning and innovative contribution of building a new development pattern 深刻理解构建新发展格局的理论内涵与创新贡献 Zhang Yan Wang Chen Zhang Yan and Wang Chen write in the People's Daily in 2025 about the "new development pattern" that Xi Jinping first proposed in 2020. This pattern takes the domestic circulation as the mainstay, with domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. The authors describe it as an original, signature concept of Xi Jinping's economic thought. They argue that it unites strategy, theory and practice, and that it innovatively develops Marxist political economy. The piece first sets out the strategic, theoretical and practical sides of the concept. It then reads the concept through four areas of Marxist political economy: the laws of economic circulation, the world market, social reproduction, and the contradictions of capitalist economic operation. Each section pairs Marx or Engels, or a statement by Xi, with the authors' account of how the new pattern extends that framework. The authors also contrast the new pattern with what they call the limits of Western economics. On circulation, the authors say the pattern adds to the production–distribution–exchange–consumption cycle. It asks for supply to adapt to demand, for fairer distribution, and for a wider exchange sphere that includes the unified national market, logistics and finance. On the world market, they present it as an open dual circulation, not a closed one, and cite rising outward direct investment and high-level opening. They also name the Belt and Road Initiative. On reproduction, they stress scientific and technological self-reliance, new production factors such as data, and a modern industrial system. On capitalism, they say it distinguishes capital from capitalism: capital's drive for profit must be regulated, while its role as a production factor is used under the socialist market economy. They also call for balancing opening with security. The authors conclude that the pattern rests on Marxist worldview and methodology and reveals the objective path from economic power to economic strength. They call for understanding it in terms of historical necessity, long-term development and the whole of modernization, and for relying on the nation's own strength. The text links this to planning for the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary ties a current economic policy concept to Marx's theories of circulation, the world market and reproduction.

Value theory, crisis theory and the contemporary world from a Marxist perspective An interview with the British Marxist economist Michael Roberts 马克思主义视角下的价值理论、危机理论与当代世界 Qin Shiya This is an interview, conducted by Qin Shiya for World Socialism Studies (2025, no. 4), with the British Marxist economist Michael Roberts (born 1946), author of The Great Recession and The Long Depression and a long-time blogger on the world economy. Asked what is central to Marxism, Roberts names class struggle as the driver of history and the law of value, under which capitalism is a system of production for the profit of owners of the means of production. From this he derives his main thesis: crises are inherent to capitalism and stem from a falling rate of profit, so they cannot be cured by reform. The interview has four parts: Marxist value and crisis theory; financialization; digital capitalism and 'technofeudalism'; and Trump and economic imperialism. Along the way Roberts discusses Engels's editing of Capital, volume 3, cryptocurrencies, artificial intelligence, the North–South gap, public debt and prospects for the global economy. He closes by describing his blog, aimed at activists rather than academics, and a forthcoming sequel to The Long Depression. Roberts argues that the tendency of the profit rate to fall (Capital, vol. 3, chs 13–15) is Marx's core crisis theory, and rejects underconsumptionist and overproduction accounts as secondary to profitability. He dismisses Michael Heinrich's claim that Engels distorted Marx's text as 'nonsense'. He holds that Keynes, Minsky and monopoly-capital theorists all wrongly suggest capitalism can be stabilised. In his view financialization has not turned capitalism into a money-making system detached from exploitation, because most profit still comes from workers' production. Likewise, big-tech firms are for him thoroughly capitalist, so he rejects 'technofeudalism'. He also rejects 'multitude' as a replacement for the proletariat, treating mental labour as value-creating. Roberts expects another recession before the end of the decade, possibly triggered by corporate debt and 'zombie' firms, and describes the post-2009 period as a long depression. He argues China has avoided capitalist crises through its large state sector and planning, and should expand both. He predicts Trump's tariffs and tax cuts will raise tensions and inequality, and calls for developing countries to cooperate under governments representing labour and common ownership. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist's profit-rate view of crisis, finance, AI and US–China rivalry, presented to a Chinese Marxist readership.

Mastering investigation and research as a basic skill 掌握好调查研究这个基本功 Li Xiuduo This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 26 May 2025, asks how Party members and cadres can master investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) as a basic work skill. Li Xiuduo, an associate professor at a university school of Marxism, argues that it is the foundation of sound decisions and a 'family heirloom' of the Party that must be carried forward. The piece opens by citing the emphasis placed on it since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the first of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, and Xi Jinping's statements that research must be regular and go to the masses and into practice. It then sets out four requirements: seeking truth, putting findings into practice, using scientific methods, and learning from the people. Li argues that research must establish real problems and real facts, guided by seeking truth from facts, and avoid staged or perfunctory visits. It must be done in person through the 'four withouts and two directs' approach, including in places with many complaints and complicated contradictions, rather than by demanding forms and data from grassroots units. Li also calls for varied methods, combining micro and macro, qualitative and quantitative analysis, and for hearing minority and opposing views. Finally, research is presented as the mass line in action, drawing on Mao Zedong and the Third Plenum decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Li concludes that good research findings should be turned promptly into decisions and concrete measures, so as to solve problems and support the further comprehensively deepening of reform. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents research methods and the mass line to cadres.

The revolutionary character of Marx's thought An analysis based on the Theses on Feuerbach 马克思思想的革命性特质 Li Yang Li Yang asks what the Theses on Feuerbach reveal about the revolutionary character of Marx's thought. Engels called the Theses the first document containing the germ of a new world outlook. Li argues that this short text concentrates Marx's revolutionary quality, both as a philosophical revolution and as a philosophy of revolution. The commentary has two parts. The first traces revolutionary character through Marx's life and work: his critique of reality, his theoretical critique, and his practical activity. The second turns to the Theses themselves, covering their view of human essence, their new conception of practice and the new materialism. Li holds that Marx's critique was not moral indignation but a thorough theoretical critique grounded in the laws of social development. It led from the criticism of Hegel and of Feuerbach to political economy and scientific socialism. In the Theses, Li reads human essence as the ensemble of social relations. Practice becomes the core category, overcoming the opposition of subject and object and of individual and society. Li stresses that this is not a new practice-based ontology or metaphysics. Practice points concretely to revolution: changing circumstances and self-change coincide only as revolutionary practice, and the truth of thinking is a practical question. This active theory of reflection gives communism a revolutionary philosophical basis. Li concludes that we still live in the historical era Marxism identified, so the Theses' revolutionary quality remains the spiritual essence of the age. Citing Xi Jinping, Li calls on contemporary Marxists to let the Party's self-reform lead social revolution, and to combine Marxism with present conditions. Read the original if you want a short, Party-aligned introduction to how Chinese scholars currently read the Theses on Feuerbach.

Re-examining Marx's social theory and its contemporary relevance 重审马克思社会理论及其当代性 Lü Jingmei Lü Jingmei takes up Marx's proposition of the "self-criticism of bourgeois society", from the Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, as a way to reread Marx's social theory and show why it still matters. The article argues that this reading does not replace other interpretations but enriches the description and understanding of bourgeois society. It treats Marx's social theory as an anatomy of bourgeois society as a whole, as well as an account of real individuals and their reified condition. This is a short commentary published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, and it is a stage result of a National Social Science Fund project on Marx and Engels's idea of social self-criticism. It first sets out how Marx conceives bourgeois society, then compares two routes to understanding it, and finally turns to three kinds of contemporary "power" in Marx's theory: to explain, to criticise and to shape social reality. Lü argues that Marx treats bourgeois society as a constantly moving "real subject", composed by individuals yet structurally determining them. Two routes lead into this society. The political-economy route takes the relation of capital and labour as its axis, and the social-political-philosophy route takes the relation of individual and society. Lü proposes refining the latter into individual, society and state, inserting a middle level of economic society, which they call Weberian ideal types. This gives the abstract contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and the antagonism between bourgeoisie and proletariat, more concrete bearers. In Lü's view it also balances structure and agency, so the two routes complement each other. On contemporary relevance, Lü argues that Marx's method can explain changes such as immaterial labour, globalisation, financialisation and digital technology, if they are seen as expressions of society's self-movement. It can also criticise a capitalism that has learned self-repair through the reproduction of social relations, a point Lü draws from Althusser and Lefebvre. Lü adds that Marxism informs feminist, ecological and anti-colonial movements, and that China should keep reflecting on social-relations reproduction and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a compact, theory-oriented statement of how Chinese scholars link Marx's social theory to contemporary capitalism and to China.

Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee for further comprehensively deepening reform 党的领导是进一步全面深化改革的根本保证 Wang Yonghao Taking its cue from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this article argues that Communist Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee for further comprehensively deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Wang presents this as a study of the Plenum's guiding principle, drawing heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches. The author holds that the principle sums up the experience of reform and opening up and explains why it has succeeded. The article is a short Party-theory piece in three parts. The first treats Party leadership as historically inevitable, running through the periods of new democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second presents Party leadership as the root cause of the achievements of comprehensively deepening reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third presents it as the "sea-calming needle" that lets reform withstand risks and challenges. Wang's first move is historical. After the Opium War China became semi-colonial and semi-feudal, and in the author's account no class or political force, from peasants to bourgeois reformers and revolutionaries, could change this. The Communist Party emerged from the union of Marxism-Leninism and the workers' movement, and Wang credits it with national independence, the socialist system, the shift to a socialist market economy and the nation's rise. Second, the author points to new institutions such as the Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform, led by Xi, as the means by which the Party drove reform from local experiments to systematic integration, with mature institutions and modernised governance. Third, citing the 20th Party Congress (2022) warning about "black swan" and "grey rhino" events, Wang contends that deep reform will touch entrenched interests and meet unpredictable risks. Only the Party's overall leadership, in this view, keeps reform's stance and direction secure. Wang calls for the Party to uphold its overall leadership without wavering, and for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including the Party's self-reform, anti-corruption work and selection of reform-minded cadres. The author also urges study of the Two Establishes and practice of the Two Upholds, together with awareness of risk, a fighting spirit and bottom-line thinking. The article concludes that these will let reform consolidate its gains and open new prospects amid crisis. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-theory journals present the link between Party leadership and the reform agenda after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee.

Digital empowerment of integrated reform and innovation in ideological and political courses across university, secondary and primary schools 数字化赋能大中小学思政课一体化改革创新 Pan Jingang Pan Jingang takes up how digital technology can advance the integrated development of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) across primary, secondary and tertiary education. Pan frames the question with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for integrated reform of these courses, and with the 2025 National Education Work Conference, which called for continuing the national education digitalization strategy. The article's thesis is that digital technology can break down barriers between school stages, reform teaching models and innovate institutions, producing a pattern of collaborative education that raises teaching quality. This is a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (23 May 2025), and it is a stage result of a National Social Science Fund project on Xi Jinping's statements on school ideological and political courses. It is organised in three parts: building integrated shared platforms, integrating teaching, learning and evaluation, and promoting collaborative education. Each part is supported by quotations from Xi Jinping. Pan's first argument concerns platforms. Digital resource libraries, unified data standards and a big-data monitoring centre are presented as a remedy for scattered teaching materials and "data islands". Pan adds that natural language processing and knowledge graphs can link moral cultivation in primary school, political understanding in secondary school and theoretical deepening at university into a progressive sequence. The second argument is about teaching and teachers. Big-data analysis and machine learning are said to build individual learning profiles, which allow more precise teaching and richer evaluation than exam scores. Pan also proposes training courses in digital skills for teachers and incentives that count digital teaching results in promotion and appraisal. Pan concludes that digital empowerment is a complex systemic project needing work on top-level design, institutional mechanisms and platform building. Pan proposes a leadership mechanism of Party committee unified leadership, joint management by Party and government, and divisions of labour among departments. Pan also proposes a unified evaluation system across all stages, digital training platforms and pairing of schools in developed and less developed regions to narrow the digital divide, and links between schools, families and society, so that the classroom and the "big classroom" of society work together. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese education officials and scholars connect digitalization policy with ideological and political education.

Advancing the building of a community with a shared future with neighbouring countries 深入推进周边命运共同体建设 Zhai Kun Writing after Xi Jinping's state visits to Vietnam, Malaysia and Cambodia on 14–18 April 2025, Zhai Kun, a professor of international relations at Peking University, argues that China's work with its neighbours should be organised around building a community with a shared future with neighbouring countries. The commentary, published in the People's Daily theory section, presents this as the guiding line set by the Central Conference on Neighbourhood Work in April 2025. Zhai holds that the aim serves regional stability and, in turn, the broader goal of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article has three parts. The first sets out the long-term strategic positioning of neighbourhood work and the "historic achievements" since the 18th Party Congress (2012), comparing the 2013 symposium on neighbourhood diplomacy with the 2025 conference. The second examines the working framework that supports the project. The third describes the system of values behind it: a shared vision, guiding principles and an "Asian values" foundation. Zhai makes three main moves. First, he reads the change in name from "neighbourhood diplomacy work" to "neighbourhood work", and from "symposium" to "work conference", as showing that neighbourhood affairs now span domestic and foreign, economic, political and diplomatic fields and receive fuller Party attention. He describes development and security as the "two wheels" of this work, with the Belt and Road Initiative as the main platform (the article cites agreements with 25 neighbours and China as largest trading partner of 18) and an "Asian security model" as strategic support, which he contrasts with Western great-power hegemony. Second, he traces the evolution of the values system: the "five homes" vision (peace, tranquillity, prosperity, beauty, friendship), the addition of "a shared destiny" to the principle of amity, sincerity, mutual benefit and inclusiveness, and the affirmation of peace, cooperation, openness and inclusiveness as Asian values. Zhai concludes that relations with neighbours are at their best since modern times, but that regional and global change are now closely linked and bring serious challenges. He says China has reached a consensus on a shared-future community with 17 neighbours, forming two "clusters" in the Indochina Peninsula and Central Asia. Continuity of policy, he argues, gives China the confidence and strategic resolve to deepen the project. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese commentators frame the 2025 neighbourhood policy line and its value language.

Assessment of Japanese scholarship on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 日本学界习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想研究状况评析 Zhuo Mingliang Zhou Yaru This is a review article on how Japanese academia has studied Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era since the 19th Party Congress (2017). Zhuo and Zhou argue that Japanese scholars' attention to the Thought has grown steadily. In their account, the Japanese view offers a useful "neighbour's perspective" for building an international system of interpretation and for strengthening China's international communication. The article opens with library and database indicators of Japanese interest. It then surveys four main topics: Chinese modernization, common prosperity, the Belt and Road Initiative, and a community with a shared future for mankind. It closes with four features of the Japanese literature, concerning content, stance, researchers and institutions, and a short set of recommendations. The authors first cite figures from CiNii, Japan's largest academic database. As of 2 November 2024 it listed 397 books and 2,651 papers under the keyword "Xi Jinping Thought", up from 249 books and 1,786 papers in April 2021. Under each topic they then group Japanese views. On Chinese modernization, scholars such as Muratada Tadayoshi, Nakagane Katsuji and Takahara Akio are reported to offer explanatory theories: large-country scale, external stimulus, political stability, late-development advantage and traditional inheritance. On common prosperity, scholars discuss expanding the middle-income group and the policy's relevance to Japan's own inequality. On the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind, they report praise from former prime ministers Fukuda Yasuo and Hatoyama Yukio, alongside analysis of effects on Japan's economy. Zhuo and Zhou conclude that Japanese researchers focus on policy, economics and Sino-US and Sino-Japanese relations, and analyse the theoretical system itself less. They describe most scholars as objective and note that many are Japanese specialists with experience of China. They add that government and corporate think tanks also advise firms on trade with China. The authors call for tracking overseas research and for reforming international communication mechanisms, so as to "tell China's story well". Read the original if you want a Chinese-side overview of Japanese scholars, institutions and views on Xi Jinping Thought, or want to see how Chinese researchers present and use foreign reception of it.

Upholding the correct view of the history of the Second World War 坚持正确二战史观 Liu Bensen Writing eighty years after the end of the Second World War, Liu argues that unilateralism and geopolitical conflict are eroding the international consensus on the war, so a "correct view of the history of the Second World War" must be upheld. The short commentary holds that this requires respect for historical fact, opposition to historical nihilism, defence of the order built on the UN Charter, and a complete collective memory of the war. The piece is organised in five steps: respect for facts as the premise, opposition to historical nihilism as an urgent task, defence of the postwar order as a practical requirement, shaping and spreading collective memory as a strategic path, and drawing on history to shape the future as the aim. On facts, Liu cites foreign scholars to support three claims: the 18 September 1931 Incident opened the world anti-fascist war, China and the Soviet Union were the main Asian and European theatres, and the war was also a revolutionary and independence struggle. Liu says current nihilism works through selective memory rather than outright denial. Its Western forms, in the author's account, are Eurocentrism, marginalisation of the Eastern theatre, and a "liberator narrative" that downplays Soviet and Chinese contributions. Liu also claims that some Western powers are diluting the Nuremberg and Tokyo verdicts in order to reshape rules in their own favour. Liu calls for defending the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and the "enemy state clauses" of Article 107 of the UN Charter. Liu also calls for stronger history education for young people and for building China's own discourse on the war, so that its contribution is better understood abroad. The author closes by citing Xi Jinping on jointly safeguarding the victory and international fairness and justice. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship frames the war's history and its present-day uses.

Key points for building a knowledge system of online ideological and political education 构建网络思想政治教育知识体系的着力点 Xie Yujin Li Jun This short commentary asks how to build an autonomous knowledge system for online ideological and political education, a field that emerged after China's full internet connection in 1994. The authors say the field has produced many studies and trained many specialists. They also say it still fits new conditions imperfectly, lacks completeness and systematic order, and needs greater practical effect. They propose three priorities: grounding the system in Chinese reality, enriching its content, and organising it systematically. The piece opens by citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), whose Decision calls for differentiated and targeted mechanisms for online moral and ideological education. It then takes the three priorities in turn. The first is autonomy, which the authors treat in terms of theory and practice. The second is the breadth of knowledge. The third is systematisation through principles, methods, and evaluation and governance. On autonomy, the authors argue that the system should be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and rooted in China's online practice, citing the scale of China's internet users and digital economy. They describe a basic logic running from network information technology to people's thought and behaviour to online education. Within it they distinguish three kinds of knowledge: preparatory technical knowledge, composite analytical knowledge drawn from several disciplines, and practical professional knowledge. To remedy fragmentation, they call for an integrated system. It would have a principles system that responds to artificial intelligence, a methods system combining adapted classic methods with big-data, algorithmic-push and human–machine approaches, and an evaluation and governance system. The authors conclude that evaluation and governance let the knowledge system assess, absorb feedback and renew itself. They call for evaluation indicators, behavioural data analysis, intelligent platforms, and ethical, legal and self-regulatory rules. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese ideological education scholars frame the digital-age agenda of this field.

Pushing the international order towards greater fairness and rationality 推动国际秩序朝着更加公正合理的方向发展 Gao Zugui Writing in a Guangming Daily commentary on the eve of the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, Gao Zugui asks how the postwar international order should be sustained and improved. The author argues that the UN-centred framework has survived repeated tests and still underpins peace, development and security, and that China is working to make it fairer and more rational. The piece first traces the order's origins in the UN Charter of 1945 and its value to developing and smaller states. It then identifies two pressures: United States unilateralism and a turbulent world of overlapping security, economic and environmental crises. The second half sets out China's positions on Security Council reform, human rights, regional and international organisations, and global governance. Gao contends that the greatest challenge to the order is the United States, which, after the Soviet collapse, tried to make it an instrument of its own hegemony and has more recently left international mechanisms and breached international law. Gao also notes that US power to dominate alone has weakened, while other centres of power and non-state actors have grown in influence. Against this background, the author presents China as standing on the side of fairness and justice, defending the UN system, international law and the multilateral trading system. Gao describes China's support for Security Council reform that gives more weight to the Global South and Africa, for human rights suited to national conditions, and for bodies such as the BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the New Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which are said to complement existing institutions. Gao concludes that China's advocacy of equality among states, opposition to hegemony, a multipolar world, the Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind and the global initiatives on development, security and civilisation is guiding the improvement of the current order. Read the original if you want a concise, official-leaning statement of how a Central Party School scholar presents China's role in UN-centred global governance in 2025.

Building and applying the knowledge system of the Marxist theory discipline 马克思主义理论学科知识体系的构建和应用 Zhang Leisheng Twenty years after Marxist theory was established as a first-level discipline (at the end of 2005), Zhang Leisheng argues that its high-quality development now depends on constructing and applying its own knowledge system. The commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, treats this as part of the wider task of building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences with Chinese characteristics. The piece has two parts. The first deals with construction: the discipline's leading position among the Chinese social sciences, why it needs its own knowledge system, and what that system consists of. The second deals with application, moving from the knowledge system to the course system, the textbook system and the teaching system in graduate education. On construction, Zhang holds that two decades of debate about the discipline's connotation, structure, research objects and personnel training show that, to differ from Marxist philosophy, Marxist political economy and scientific socialism, it must study Marxism as a whole. In Zhang's account, the knowledge system is the condensed expression of three further systems. The disciplinary system has three elements: object, features and research directions. The academic system is the body of theory that reveals the object's essence and laws. The discourse system is its form of expression and must combine scholarly and ideological character. On application, Zhang argues that the knowledge system determines the modular master's and doctoral curricula, which in turn determine the textbook system. Textbooks then have to be turned into a teaching system that students can understand and enjoy. Zhang concludes that existing textbook types cannot meet the needs of training high-quality talent. The commentary calls for stronger textbook construction with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. It also calls for digital and audiovisual materials and a teaching resource base at both first- and second-level discipline scope, containing basic materials, documents, guiding questions and theoretical discussion. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Chinese Marxist theorist links discipline-building to curriculum, textbooks and teaching in Marxist theory education.

Comprehensively advancing digital-intelligence technologies to empower educational transformation 全面推进数智技术赋能教育变革 Luo Jing Tian Xiaowei This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily after the 2025 World Digital Education Conference in Wuhan, asks how digital and AI technologies should be used to transform education. Luo and Tian argue that advancing digital-intelligence empowerment across the whole education system is a shared choice of countries worldwide, and that China must pursue it while keeping a correct value orientation. The article opens with examples from the conference's exhibition, such as virtual simulation platforms and AI calligraphy analysis. It then sketches how education and technology have shaped each other, from oral-era apprenticeship to print-era classroom teaching. It cites international moves (UNESCO's 2023 guidance on generative AI, South Korea's AI education plans, the UK's 2024 document) and China's policy documents, including the Education Power Construction Plan (2024–2035). The authors report that, three years into the national education digitalization strategy, China's overall level of education modernization has entered the ranks of upper-middle-income countries. They also cite the world's largest education resource base, more than 60.8 billion views on the national smart education platform, and 590 million person-times of benefit from MOOCs in western regions. They also name remaining gaps: a low share of high-skilled talent, uneven coverage of quality resources, and insufficient digital literacy among teachers and students. Their answer is to hold to fostering virtue through education and a people-centred orientation, to integrate AI into all elements of teaching and talent training, and to deepen international exchange. Luo and Tian call for lifelong learning, including AI ethics and the ability to judge digital information. They also call for stronger digital leadership among administrators, digital teaching ability among teachers, and higher-order thinking among students. They present this as support for high-quality development, for building China into a leading education country with Chinese characteristics, and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style account of China's education digitalization policy and the figures used to promote it.

Leading social customs and popular mores with a good Party style 以优良党风引领社风民风 Zhang Tai This short commentary, originally published in Guangming Daily on 22 May 2025, responds to Xi Jinping's article in issue 10 of Qiushi on persistently implementing the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. Zhang Tai, an associate research fellow at Shandong University, argues that a good Party style is a force that unites Party and people and sets the tone for wider social customs. Zhang presents Xi's call to persist for twenty or thirty years as a mark of the Party's determination. The piece moves from the value of a good Party style, through a historical sketch from the Party's founding, the early People's Republic and reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), to current tasks. It cites one local example and closes with recommendations for continued work. Zhang contends that when Party members and cadres work for the people and practise thrift and hard work, they set an example that improves society and raises cohesion. As evidence, Zhang describes Haikou's enterprise service officers, in which local heads act as one-to-one service staff to counter formalism and bureaucratism, and notes that the clean-plate habit and green consumption are spreading. Zhang sees these as a positive interaction between Party style and social style. Zhang calls for leading cadres, the "key minority", to lead by example and for Party members to cultivate Party spirit and accept popular supervision. Zhang also urges organisations to improve cadre selection and to build on documents such as the opinions on integrity culture. Because style problems recur and persist, Zhang says, the effort must be sustained with a nail-driving spirit. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary frames the eight-point regulation and the current Party study campaign on it.

Grasping the historical, theoretical and practical logic of the Party's work style building Studying Xi Jinping's important statements on strengthening the Party's work style 深刻把握党的作风建设的历史逻辑、理论逻辑和实践逻辑 Ouyang Song Ouyang Song's commentary, first printed in the Party's discipline-inspection newspaper in May 2025, takes up the study and education campaign on thoroughly implementing the central Party's eight-point rules, then under way across the Party. Ouyang argues that Xi Jinping's statements on work style (zuofeng) can be understood through three connected logics, historical, theoretical and practical. Grasping them, the author says, will help the campaign take root and give work style building new results. The piece is organised around those three logics. The historical section traces work style from the Party's founding through the Yan'an period, the early People's Republic, the opening of reform and opening up, and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The theoretical section sets out why style is at bottom a question of Party spirit. The practical section lists concrete tasks for the present. On the historical side, Ouyang presents a continuous line from the Yan'an style that defeated the Xi'an style, through Mao Zedong's warnings against bureaucratism, to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 view that correcting the Party's style was decisive. The eight-point rules of 2012 are cast as the opening move that revitalised the whole effort. Theoretically, the author argues that style is the personal force of a Marxist ruling party, determines the success of its cause, centres on relations with the people, and drives the Party's self-reform. The author therefore says the remedy is to address Party spirit so that officials do not dare, cannot and do not want to deviate. Practically, Ouyang calls for handling Party spirit, style and discipline together, and for leading by example from the top. The author also urges persistent correction of formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance. Further calls are to investigate misconduct and corruption jointly, to build lasting rules and institutions, and to let the Party's style lift social customs. Ouyang concludes that work style building bears on Chinese modernization and on leading a great social revolution through a great self-reform, so it must be "always on the road". The author asks for sustained effort in being constant and long-lasting, strict and practical, and deep and detailed. Read the original if you want an official-line account, by a former head of the Party history office, of how the eight-point rules are placed in Party history and theory.

Advancing the effective empowerment of consultative democracy by digital technology 推进数字技术有效赋能协商民主 Sun Jun This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, asks how digital technologies such as big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence can strengthen consultative democracy in China. Sun argues that digital technology opens broad space for consultative practice, but only if its risks are managed and it is treated as a tool rather than an end. The piece first describes consultative democracy as an important component of whole-process people's democracy, with cultural, theoretical, practical and institutional foundations. It then sets out three areas of action: bridging the digital divide, breaking out of information cocoons, and safeguarding data security. Sun contends that digital technology fits the practical stages of consultative democracy more closely than it fits electoral democracy. In the author's view it can lower the cost of building consensus and turn institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. Digital empowerment must rest on a people-centred approach that joins humanistic orientation with technological governance. On the digital divide, Sun calls for more investment in infrastructure, extension of resources to grassroots and less developed areas, and better digital literacy among participants. On information cocoons, platforms should improve recommendation algorithms, and consultative actors such as members of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) should use e-mail, WeChat and Weibo to be reachable. On data security, Sun proposes full-process data management, anonymisation of personal data, stricter platform rules and a fuller legal framework. Sun concludes that these measures would better realise the principle of consultation "with the people and for the people" while keeping digital empowerment safe and reliable. Read the original if you want a brief statement of official-academic thinking on digital governance and consultative democracy in China.

The historical dimension in the Theses on Feuerbach 《关于费尔巴哈的提纲》中的历史维度 Lin Qing Writing in a newspaper commentary, Lin Qing asks whether and how a historical dimension appears in Marx's Theses on Feuerbach (1845), a text whose wording centres on materialism and 'practice'. Lin argues that the Theses complete a socio-historical turn in materialism. Marx takes over Feuerbach's materialist 'inversion' of Hegel but restores the social and historical dimension that Feuerbach discarded. The result, in Lin's account, is the new materialism, or historical materialism. The article moves through three steps. It first shows how the socio-historical dimension comes to the fore in the Theses' account of being and of knowledge. It then turns to Marx's critique of the idea of an 'end of history'. Finally it considers what the historical dimension means for Marx's philosophical revolution, drawing on The German Ideology. Lin reads Thesis 1 as showing that contemplation and the purely objective view of the object are both unhistorical, since history appears only in the relation between subject and object. Theses 3 and 6 then make human social being the unity of changing circumstances and self-change, 'the ensemble of the social relations'. On knowledge (Thesis 2), Lin holds that Marx places cognition within historical change and requires a critique of ideology before the real object can be known. On Thesis 9, Lin argues that contemplating civil society is not enough, because Hegel in effect treats it as the end of history. Marx's standpoint is 'human society or social humanity', which calls for transforming civil society through revolutionary practice. Lin concludes that Marx turns philosophical questions into socio-historical ones. Traditional philosophy, especially Hegel's, put society and history inside the framework of philosophy, whereas Marx puts philosophy inside the framework of society and history. In Lin's view the Theses mark the start of this philosophical revolution. Read the original if you want a concise reading of the Theses on Feuerbach as the starting point of historical materialism's socio-historical turn.

The dialectics of practice and the spirit of historical initiative 实践辩证法与历史主动精神 Wang Yicheng This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, rereads Marx's Theses on Feuerbach as the founding document of Marxist philosophy. Wang Yicheng argues that Marx's concept of practice, understood as the dialectical unity of subject and object, supplies the philosophical basis for what is now called the spirit of historical initiative (历史主动精神). The article has three parts. It first treats the Theses as a paradigm revolution centred on practice, then asks how changing the world is possible, and finally draws out a contemporary reading. Wang follows the concept of practice from the Theses through The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto to Capital. Wang says Marx surpassed Feuerbach and sublated Hegel. Feuerbach's inversion of subject and predicate, in this reading, left sensuous objects abstract and intuitive, while Hegel grasped the activity of practice only as the self-development of absolute spirit. Marx kept Hegel's dialectical principle of activity and rooted it in material production. Wang rejects two misreadings of practice: as pure subjectivity detached from objective conditions, and as an objective process without a subject. Practice is both conditioned by existing historical circumstances and able to transform its objects. The laws of history, like the economic laws analysed in Capital, exist within people's own activity. Wang concludes that the spirit of historical initiative needs two things together. It must rest on a scientific grasp of objective laws, to avoid voluntarism, and it must reject mechanical determinism and fatalism. Wang presents changing the world as the historical mission of the proletariat, and the joining of Marxism with the workers' movement as the realisation of that task. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-school-style account of how the Theses on Feuerbach is linked to the current slogan of historical initiative.

The new-materialist implications of practice 实践的新唯物主义意蕴 Ma Junhai Ma Junhai returns to Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, which the article calls the manifesto of Marx's new materialism. The question is what new materialism is and how it goes beyond both old materialism and idealism. Ma's answer is that Marx makes practice a way of thinking and a theoretical principle, which at once criticises and creatively synthesises the two earlier positions. The article presents this return to the source as a way of disclosing the 'secret' of Marx's philosophical revolution, not as idle repetition. The short piece, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, has three parts. The first traces how the concept of practice changed from Aristotle through Kant, Fichte and Hegel. The second examines the metaphysical thinking of old materialism, represented by Feuerbach, and of idealism, represented by Hegel. The third sets out how new materialism changes the mode of thinking. Ma argues that grasping new materialism depends on understanding practice as a mode of thinking. Treating practice vulgarly pulls new materialism back into natural thinking, and treating it as absolute returns it to metaphysics. Marx, on this account, absorbed the purposiveness, freedom, creativity and mediation found in earlier thinkers, but extended practice to economic and all other real activity and made it humanity's originary way of being. Idealism, in Ma's reading, develops the active side abstractly and reaches only a concreteness of thought. Old materialism offers mere static intuition of the sensuous world and lacks the dimensions of history and activity. Both, Ma says, rest on the principle of identity. New materialism restores the primacy of the object while understanding the sensuous world as the product of human negating, creative activity, and so as 'the history of industry'. Ma concludes that new materialism has a revolutionary character and an orientation towards the future. It goes beyond merely verbal intellectual activity, reshapes people's values and calls them to revolutionary practice. Humanity, Ma holds, can leave consciousness behind through practice and change the world. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style account of how Chinese scholars read the Theses on Feuerbach through the idea of practice as a way of thinking.

Practising true multilateralism 践行真正的多边主义 Chen Dongxiao Written for the 80th anniversary of the United Nations (2025), this commentary asks what multilateralism genuinely requires and why it is under strain. Chen argues that the UN-centred international system and multilateralism built on coordination and cooperation remain the best way to solve global problems. In Chen's account, a few Western countries pursue hegemonism and unilateralism while using a "rules-based international order" to dress up "pseudo-multilateralism". The article opens with a short history of multilateralism, from the Peace of Westphalia (1648) and the Concert of Europe after 1814–1815, through the International Telecommunication Union and Universal Postal Union and the League of Nations, to the UN. It then sets out three defining features of true multilateralism, lists the current challenges, and ends with three proposals. Chen treats the rise of the Global South and of forums such as the G20, BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation as new momentum for the system. Chen defines true multilateralism by three features: interdependent interests and indivisible security, so that decisions start from collective rather than individual interests; equal rights for all states regardless of size or wealth, with sovereign equality as the first principle of the UN Charter; and universal rules reached by consultation and applied without exceptionalism or double standards. Against this, Chen charges that a few Western states launch tariff and trade wars, build exclusive "small-circle multilateralism" such as an "Asia-Pacific NATO" and a "chip alliance", impose sanctions and decoupling, place domestic law above international law, and block IMF quota reform. Chen concludes that today's troubles arise because the Charter's principles have not been implemented, not because they are outdated. Chen calls for rallying consensus under the banner of a community with a shared future for mankind, practising the principle of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, and upholding international rule of law without exceptionalism or double standards. Chen frames the choice as one between a unipolar hegemony and an equal, orderly multipolar world, and cites Xi Jinping's call to practise true multilateralism. Read the original if you want an authoritative Chinese official statement of how Beijing defines "true" multilateralism and contrasts it with the policies of the United States and its allies.

Experience and lessons from the Communist Party of China's work on improving its conduct 中国共产党作风建设的经验和启示 Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee This Qiushi article, written by the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, asks what the Party's long record of work on its conduct (zuofeng jianshe) teaches for the present. Opening with Xi Jinping's statement that Party conduct bears on the Party's image, popular support and survival, it argues that four historical lessons should guide the continuing campaign to study and implement the Central Committee's eight-point regulations. The text moves chronologically through each of four lessons, citing episodes from the 1921 founding programme, the Jiangxi Soviet and Yan'an periods, the early People's Republic and reform and opening up, and then the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Each section pairs quotations from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Zhou Enlai, Chen Yun and Xi with examples. Each ends with a paragraph of lessons for the "new journey". The first lesson is that Party spirit (dangxing) is the root of conduct problems, resting on ideals and convictions. The second is that conduct centres on the Party's flesh-and-blood ties with the people, kept up through the mass line. The third is that improvement must come from the top down, starting with the "critical few" of leading cadres, and the article presents the eight-point regulations as the Politburo setting that example. The fourth is that conduct work must combine establishing and eliminating: promoting exemplary models and fostering healthy norms, while correcting the "four undesirable work styles" and fighting corruption. The author treats unhealthy practices and corruption as sharing one root. The article concludes that, amid what it calls great changes unseen in a century and the critical period for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the Party must keep implementing the eight-point regulations without relaxation. It calls for a strong conduct guarantee for Chinese modernization. Specific proposals include treating Party-spirit cultivation as a lifelong task, advancing "not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt" together, and having leaders fight privilege. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party leadership currently summarises its conduct-building history and the historical examples it uses to support it.

The inherent logic and practical requirements of deepening reform of the Party-building system 深化党的建设制度改革的内在逻辑与实践要求 Ni Mingsheng This commentary asks why the Party's institutional arrangements for its own building need further reform and what that reform should involve. Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Ni argues that deepening reform of the Party-building system is both a component of and a guarantee for further comprehensively deepening reform. In Ni's account, it provides firm support for advancing Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out why the reform matters, drawing on the classics and on the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second identifies the key priorities and the points of leverage for reform. The third lists six practical measures for making the reform effective. Ni's central argument is that institutions must change with the times. Citing Marx on institutional change as an interaction between productive forces and relations of production, Ni treats Party-building institutions as part of the superstructure, which must adapt as the economic base is reformed. The reform is also presented as the way to solve the "six 'how to always' problems", the difficulties said to be unique to a large party, through the principle of using institutions within the Party to govern the Party. On priorities, Ni calls for motivating Party members and officials to drive reform, building long-term mechanisms for study and discipline education, and reforming cadre personnel management so that officials can be promoted or demoted, and mistakes tolerated and corrected. Ni also stresses strengthening the political and organisational functions of Party organisations. Ni concludes that the reform should convert the Party's political, organisational and institutional strengths into governance effectiveness, so that "Party governance" leads "China's governance". The six measures include improving the Party's leadership system, integrating Party building across its different dimensions with the fight against corruption, making the organisational system effective from top to bottom, normalising the promotion and demotion of cadres, and regular training. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-building reform agenda after the Third Plenum is framed in official-academic discourse.

Solving development problems through reform 以改革的办法破解发展难题 Zheng Xinli Zheng Xinli, a former deputy director of the Central Policy Research Office, argues in this People's Daily commentary that reform remains the means of resolving China's development difficulties. As reform deepens it touches sharper conflicts of interest, so Zheng holds that it must combine systematic design with continued bold experiment. The piece first credits the past four decades of reform with economic, poverty-reduction, social and ecological achievements, citing figures such as GDP passing 130 trillion yuan in 2024 and manufacturing at about 30 per cent of global value added. It then turns to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its roadmap for Chinese modernization, and ends with three problem areas for reform. Zheng's central claim is that "top-level design" and "crossing the river by feeling the stones" must be used together, a principle he presents as an application of historical materialism. Top-level design supplies coordinated goals that are adjusted over time, while stone-feeling means pilot projects whose lessons are generalised once proven. He sets out three areas for reform. Insufficient effective demand calls for better macroeconomic coordination. Agricultural and rural modernization lags behind industry and cities, and Zheng sees the countryside as the greatest source of future growth. Technological innovation requires integrated reform of education, science and talent systems and use of the new whole-nation system. Zheng concludes that the plenum's more than 300 reform measures will only take effect with clear responsibilities, tracking of results and policies pointing the same way. He ties this to the goal of basically realising socialist modernization by 2035. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior policy figure presents the reform agenda after the 2024 plenum.

Strengthening the Party's overall leadership: multi-dimensional exploration and practice in Yunnan 加强党的全面领导立体化探索与实践 Zhang Changshan Zhao Ziyao This newspaper commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, asks how the Party's leadership and Party building can be strengthened in Yunnan, a border province with many ethnic minorities. Zhang and Zhao take Xi Jinping's instructions during his inspection tour of Yunnan as their starting point. They argue that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of development and that the quality of a locality's "political ecology" is a key test of its Party building. The article is organised as a five-part programme: political leadership at the core, the purification of political ecology, long-term mechanisms for improving work style, organisational innovation in building the cadre corps, and grassroots Party organisations as fortresses for border governance. Under each heading the authors set out what Yunnan should do and cite local practices already tried, including the "first-line work method", the "project work method" for rural revitalisation and a "political health checklist". Zhang and Zhao's central move is to treat political construction as the guiding thread that is then turned into concrete mechanisms. They call for tracking systems and supervision to ensure central decisions are carried out locally, loyalty education drawing on Yunnan's revolutionary sites, and a regular, quantified assessment of political ecology with an "assessment–rectification–improvement" loop. They also propose a cadre system that rewards actual performance and tolerates and corrects mistakes, training for fields such as the digital economy and green transition, and Party-building models differentiated by sector. The authors conclude that Yunnan's experience shows the Party's leadership must be merged with local conditions and pursued systematically, so that a healthier political ecology and high-quality development reinforce each other. They urge Yunnan to keep a systems mindset, address new problems and convert the strengths of Party building into governance effectiveness in support of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building doctrine is translated into provincial-level policy measures in a border region.

Adhering to bottom-line thinking to prevent and defuse risks and challenges 坚持底线思维 有效防范和化解风险挑战 Han Yu Han Yu's article, a Party-theory commentary published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2025, asks how Party members and officials should apply Xi Jinping's statements on "bottom-line thinking" (底线思维) to prevent and defuse risks. Han argues that bottom-line thinking is a scientific concept, a mode of thought and a working attitude that rests on dialectical materialism. The author holds that it should guide efforts to balance development and security and so support high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first sets out the meaning of bottom-line thinking and its philosophical logic. The second explains its present-day value, tracing it to traditional Chinese culture, the Party's historical experience and current strategic needs. The third lists practical requirements for putting it into practice. Han defines the bottom line as the lowest limit and the critical point at which a thing changes in quality. Bottom-line thinking means setting minimum goals, starting from the worst case, preparing fully and aiming for the best outcome. Han describes it as risk-preventive, problem-oriented and proactive, and reads it as an application of dialectical pairs: favourable and unfavourable factors, quantitative and qualitative change, and subjective initiative and objective law. The author cites Mao Zedong's call to "base estimates on the most difficult conditions", Deng Xiaoping's remarks on preparing for major risks and Xi Jinping's repeated instructions. Han also argues that the Party faces both strategic opportunities and risks, citing "great changes unseen in a century", external suppression and "black swan" and "grey rhino" events. The author says the ability to use bottom-line thinking is a standard for judging leading cadres. Han proposes four practical steps. These are to raise awareness of hardship and build risk monitoring and early warning; to improve institutions for risk research, assessment, coordination and accountability, with emergency plans and training; to strengthen responsibility so that officials guard their own areas and act at each stage of a risk; and to cultivate a fighting spirit that confronts problems directly. The aim, in Han's account, is to keep affairs above the bottom line while reaching for higher goals. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party writing presents the philosophy and cadre-training uses of risk prevention.
