The contemporary significance of defending the victory in the Second World War and the post-war international order 深刻理解维护二战胜利成果和战后国际秩序的时代意义 Zhao Long Writing in the People's Daily on 21 May 2025, in the 80th anniversary year of the end of the Second World War and the founding of the United Nations, Zhao Long asks why defending the war's outcomes and the post-war order matters now. The commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's visit to Russia on 7–10 May and the China–Russia joint statement issued there. Zhao argues that this defence is not abstract commemoration but a dynamic practice that depends on three things: great powers sharing responsibility, adapting to multipolarity, and answering the demands of the Global South. The piece has three sections, one for each requirement. The first deals with the UN-centred international system as the core product of the 1945 victory and with the challenges to its authority. The second treats the post-war order as something historically changing, and sets out China's position on multipolarity. The third turns to the rise of the Global South and the question of fairness and justice in global governance. In the first section Zhao says unilateralism and bullying are weakening the system. Zhao's examples are 'country first' policies, unilateral and secondary sanctions imposed under domestic law, and Cold War 'small circles' and 'value alliances'. Zhao presents China as a founding UN member that supports the Security Council and contributes to peacekeeping, and presents China and Russia as models of non-aligned, non-confrontational cooperation. In the second section, from a historical-materialist standpoint, Zhao holds that the Yalta system and bipolarity have long since ended. Zhao criticises 'rules-based international order' rhetoric, NATO expansion and tariff, trade and technology wars, and endorses 'equal and orderly world multipolarity', in which states of every size take part equally and new mechanisms supplement rather than replace the existing order. In the third section Zhao cites IMF figures: the Global South accounted for over 40% of the world economy in 2024 and contributed 80% of growth. Zhao argues that governance structures have not caught up with this shift, and that powers who label BRICS or the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation 'anti-Western' are the main source of instability. Zhao concludes that states should reform and improve the post-war order and its multilateral mechanisms on the basis of genuine multilateralism, so that Global South countries can join global industrial and supply chains and develop through industrialisation and modernisation. Stability of institutions, Zhao says, rests on shared values, and justice in the order rests on historical awareness. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese international-affairs scholar presents the UN system, multipolarity and the Global South in the 2025 anniversary context, in a People's Daily commentary.

Never relaxing the strict tone 始终坚持严的基调不放松 Li Juan This short commentary, published in the Party's discipline-inspection newspaper in May 2025, responds to Xi Jinping's article in Qiushi on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation (中央八项规定). Li Juan argues that, with the new journey bringing heavy tasks of reform, development and stability, the Party must keep a strict tone on conduct without relaxation, so that improved work style opens a new phase of high-quality development. The piece describes the eight-point regulation as a landmark measure of Party governance in the new era and a move to build credibility. It reviews more than a decade of enforcement, cites recent figures and a recent case, and then sets out what must be done going forward. Li's central reasoning is that strictness has been the regulation's guiding principle from the start, citing Xi's remarks that the rule is rigid and carries no "trial" label. The author points to monthly published data on violations, now in its 139th consecutive month, and to the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles", with no exceptions for anyone. Asked whether enforcement can pause, Li answers with 16,994 cases and 22,547 people criticised or punished in March 2025, and with ten officials in Luoshan County, Xinyang, Henan, who broke the rules during a study-and-education campaign. Because bad practices can revive, Li calls for resisting arguments such as "minor matters" or "harm to development", and for severe punishment of disguised violations. Li concludes that the regulation is a long-term hard rule and that persistent, strict implementation will gradually produce clean conduct and a clean political environment. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media frame continuing work-style discipline in 2025.

Upholding the correct view of the Second World War and resolutely defending historical justice 坚持正确二战史观 坚定捍卫历史正义 Liu Jun This commentary, originally published in People's Daily on 21 May 2025, was written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression, the Soviet Great Patriotic War and the World Anti-Fascist War. It takes as its occasion Xi Jinping's state visit to Russia and his attendance at the Victory Day commemoration. Liu Jun argues that defending "historical justice" requires protecting the results of victory in the Second World War, holding to a correct view of that war, and upholding the United Nations and international fairness. The piece is organised under three headings. The first defines historical justice and lists what China and the Soviet Union gained from the war. The second sets out the elements of the "correct view of the Second World War" and describes Chinese-Russian cooperation on it. The third links this view to the authority of the UN and the postwar international order. Liu draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements and on the Sino-Russian Joint Statement signed during the visit. Liu begins from a Marxist conception in which history is the foundation of justice and a correct view of history guides a just history. On this basis the author lists the war's results for China and the USSR: defeat of Japanese militarism and German fascism, the return of Taiwan and the Penghu Islands to China, a key role in founding the UN with permanent Security Council seats, and the collapse of the colonial system. The correct view, in Liu's account, holds that China and the USSR were the main Asian and European theatres and made decisive contributions. It also holds that China's war began earliest and lasted longest, that the Chinese Communist Party led the resistance, and that the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals are beyond challenge. Liu accuses some Western countries of using historical nihilism, double standards and discursive reconstruction to downplay the two countries' contributions and shake the postwar order in order to preserve hegemony. The author also criticises those who deny or glorify aggression. Liu concludes that China and Russia, by making the correct view a matter of institutionalised bilateral cooperation, are taking a stand for international justice. The Joint Statement commits them to joint education and commemorations, research into Nazi and Japanese war crimes, and cooperation on searching for the remains of the fallen. The author expresses confidence that peoples worldwide will side with historical correctness and fairness. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary framed the 80th anniversary, Sino-Russian historical memory politics and the postwar order in 2025.

The practical value of strengthening integrity culture in the new era 新时代加强廉洁文化建设的实践价值 Lin Guoqing Lin Guoqing's commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Journal in May 2025, asks what practical value the Party's drive to build an "integrity culture" (lianjie wenhua) has in the new era. It starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report and the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which called for a three-year action plan for 2025–2027. Lin argues that grasping the significance of this work is a precondition for understanding its place in a comprehensive "all-out war" against corruption. The piece is organised under four headings. Each names one area of value: carrying forward fine traditional Chinese integrity culture, building a clean political ecosystem, stimulating the people's pursuit of truth, goodness and beauty, and displaying the political character of a Marxist party. Lin draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks, and on Confucian, Daoist and Legalist sources. Lin first presents the current effort as a "creative transformation and innovative development" of a long tradition. As examples, Lin cites the writing of "integrity in the family" into the Party's integrity and self-discipline code, the inclusion of opposition to privilege in intra-Party regulations, and local research centres and campaigns that take integrity education into enterprises, schools and families. Lin then links integrity culture to the goal of cultivating a "do not want to be corrupt" consciousness, tied to shame and value rejection, and to popular support. Leading cadres' family conduct is said to set a model for Party and government style. Finally, Lin places the effort in a Marxist lineage running from the Communist Manifesto and the Paris Commune to Lenin's campaign against bureaucracy and the CPC's own record. The author claims that international comparison shows other developing countries falling into the "middle-income trap" through party corruption, while the CPC's integrity culture secures political, cultural and spiritual guarantees for Chinese modernization. Lin concludes that integrity culture cannot be built in one campaign. It must be sustained over the long term, like the eight-point regulations the Party has said it will keep in force. Lin holds that the work has no end point and no shortcut, and that it should become a spiritual pillar of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present integrity culture as a link between tradition, Marxist party-building and anti-corruption policy.

Opening a new phase of high-quality development through new results in improving Party conduct 以作风建设新成效开创高质量发展新局面 Chen Peng This short commentary in Study Times (21 May 2025) takes up the link between Party conduct and economic development. Chen Peng argues that the Party's conduct is its image, bears on popular support and decides the success of Party and state undertakings. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks at a Politburo meeting, the author holds that the study and education campaign on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulation should produce results that open a new phase of high-quality development. The piece is built in two parts. The first reviews the Party's history to show that good conduct is both fighting strength and productive force: the Yan'an period, the early People's Republic, the reform era and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out practical measures for making conduct-building serve development. Chen's central claim is that good conduct builds cohesion, morale and creativity, and so converts into productivity. The author cites the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region's "ten nots" and the saying that "Yan'an conduct defeated Xi'an conduct" as evidence from the revolutionary period. For the present, Chen says conduct-building has become a variable affecting the depth of reform and the quality of development. It should therefore be embedded in solving development problems, target formalism and bureaucratism, and promote practical work and willingness to take responsibility. Chen calls for perseverance and for institutional safeguards: closing loopholes that breed unhealthy tendencies, writing gains into rules and enforcing them strictly. Party members and cadres should use good conduct to lift social customs and public morale. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party media link Party discipline campaigns to economic work in 2025.

Learning from history, committed to rejuvenation 镜鉴历史 矢志复兴 Institute of Military Political Work Research, Academy of Military Sciences Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary by a research institute of the Academy of Military Sciences asks what that war should teach China today. It opens with Xi Jinping's article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta during his May 2025 visit to Russia. The authors argue that the lessons of the war must be absorbed to keep the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on course. The piece has three parts. The first describes the suffering inflicted by Japan's invasion, citing figures on casualties, destroyed industry, economic loss and cultural plunder. The second sets out how the victory, in the authors' account, opened the way to national rejuvenation. The third draws four present-day lessons on Party leadership, the people, national security and world peace. In the second part the authors present five legacies of the war. It tempered the Communist Party into a mature leading force, with Mao Zedong Thought established and the Yan'an rectification campaign strengthening Party building. It awakened the whole nation, and it forged a people's army rooted in the masses through guerrilla warfare. It also produced the great spirit of resistance and restored China's standing as a major power, including its role in founding the United Nations. The authors cite casualties of more than 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians and direct economic losses of 100 billion US dollars. The lessons for today follow from this. The authors call for stronger Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for a people-centred approach, since the people are described as the creators of history. They urge stronger strategic capacity to defend sovereignty and security, summed up as 'only those able to fight can stop war', and say the military must be ready to win when called on. They also call for upholding a correct view of the Second World War, the postwar order and the UN Charter, and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Remembering history, they say, is meant to cherish peace and not to perpetuate hatred. Read the original if you want an example of how a military-affiliated body in Qiushi ties the war's memory to Party building, defence preparedness and foreign-policy themes.

Promoting the Long March spirit and advancing the construction of the Long March National Cultural Park 弘扬长征精神 推进国家文化公园建设 Chen Shifa Han Xueyan This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (19 May 2025) takes up the Long March National Cultural Park, one component of China's system of national cultural parks. The authors argue that summing up the experience of building the park and planning its future direction is both the core of raising construction effectiveness and a precondition for making better use of what has already been built. Their thesis is that construction is now shifting from 'building well' to 'using well' and 'developing well'. The piece has three parts. It first lists achievements, drawing on provincial examples from Jiangxi, Fujian, Guizhou, Gansu and Shaanxi. It then sets out four guiding principles for construction and development. It closes with five concrete proposals for the 'living utilisation' (活化利用) of the park. The authors describe the park as an outcome of implementing Xi Jinping's thought on culture and upholding the Party's cultural leadership. On achievements, the authors report that key projects have largely been completed and have produced a spatial layout linking a core exhibition park, distinctive exhibition sites and concentrated exhibition belts. They cite provincial frameworks such as Fujian's 'three parks, six belts and many sites' and Guizhou's '1+3+8' project system. They also say the park has boosted red tourism and serves as a means of promoting rural revitalisation. The four principles are: coordinating construction with development; unifying theory and practice; matching capital input with returns, including market-based operation; and combining scientific protection with living utilisation, in which digital protection and a database of Long March red cultural resources play a part. The authors propose an efficient coordination mechanism, supported by relevant laws and regulations and by cross-disciplinary approaches. They also call for a unified Long March brand built on a 'history-based' design concept, and for 'Long March+' cultural-tourism products supported by price-compensation for red study tours. Further proposals are to integrate park resources into universities' 'big ideological and political course' and to use metaverse and immersive digital experiences that, in their words, foster positive political identification among the public. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how Chinese scholars frame the policy goals, market logic and ideological-education uses of the Long March National Cultural Park.

China's War of Resistance changed the course of the world anti-fascist war 中国抗战改变世界反法西斯战争走向 Wang Fengqing This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, argues that the 14-year Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression was not only a part of the world anti-fascist war but altered its course. Wang Fengqing contends that China's resistance changed the fate of the Chinese nation and made an immeasurable contribution to final victory. The article is organised in three parts. It first treats China as the earliest and longest-fighting anti-fascist country, then China's role in advocating and promoting a world anti-fascist alliance, and finally China's support for the Soviet–German and Pacific theatres. Four long-term mechanisms are needed to keep reducing burdens on the grassroots 持续为基层减负应健全四项长效机制 Su Yongxiang Su Yongxiang takes up the problem of formalism and bureaucratism that weigh on grassroots cadres in China. A new layout: fresh thinking on improving the institutional system of whole-process people's democracy 新布局：健全全过程人民民主制度体系新思路 Xu Yaotong This short commentary reads the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as setting out a "new layout" for improving the institutional system of whole-process people's democracy. The spirit of resisting US aggression and aiding Korea: daring to struggle and skilled in struggle 抗美援朝精神：既敢于斗争又善于斗争 Yan Hui This short commentary, published in Study Times on 16 May 2025, takes up the spirit forged in the war to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea (1950–53). Empowering teaching innovation in university ideological and political courses with digital-intelligence technology 以数智技术赋能高校思政课教学创新 Ke Meng This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, asks how big data, intelligent algorithms and virtual reality can improve university ideological and political courses (sizheng ke). Resolutely upholding the post-war international order 坚决维护战后国际秩序 Wu Zhicheng Writing in the year of the 80th anniversary of victory in the World Anti-Fascist War and of the founding of the United Nations, Wu Zhicheng argues that the post-war international order must be firmly defended against unilateralism and hegemonic bullying. Consolidating the civilizational foundations for building China's independent knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences 夯实构建中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系的文明根基 Zhang Liwen Zang Fengyu This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, asks how China's independent knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences can be given a firm civilizational base. Promoting the correct view of the history of the Second World War 弘扬正确二战史观 Liu Guangming Peng Chunlin Writing in Guangming Daily on 15 May 2025, Liu Guangming and Peng Chunlin respond to Xi Jinping's call, made during his state visit to Russia for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Soviet Great Patriotic War, to "uphold" and "jointly promote" a correct view of the history of the Second World War. Implementing the spirit of the eight-point regulation: what comes next? 落实八项规定精神接下来怎么干? The great spirit of resistance against Japanese aggression as a precious asset for national rejuvenation 伟大抗战精神是砥砺复兴的宝贵财富 Zhou Junjie Zhou Junjie asks how the spirit forged in the War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression (1931–1945) can serve China today. Zhou presents revolutionary heroism as a creative fusion of the Marxist view of heroes and the Chinese tradition of sacrificing life for righteousness. The author also says the victory spread values of freedom, justice and peace and shook the colonial system. Zhou then calls for the spirit to be used in three ways. First, it should consolidate unity, so that people remember the Party's role as the "mainstay" of the war, trust it, and channel patriotism into Chinese modernization. Second, it should help overcome difficulties, which means vigilance against risks, bottom-line thinking and a readiness to struggle in a world of great changes. Third, it should defend peace, which Zhou argues must be won through struggle and strength, including readiness to act when core national interests are harmed and the building of a world-class military. Read the original if you want an example of how a military-affiliated Party theorist ties war memory to current themes of national rejuvenation, struggle and national defence.

Promoting the deep integration of moral education and running it through the whole process of nurturing students 推动德育深度融入 有效贯穿育人全过程 Meng Xianli Han Yanfang This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, responds to Xi Jinping's remarks during the 2025 Two Sessions that moral education should run through intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour education. They say this requires systems thinking and an all-staff, whole-process, all-round pattern of nurturing students. The article takes the four pairings in turn: moral and intellectual education, moral and physical education, moral and aesthetic education, and moral and labour education. Each section describes a current shortcoming, traces its cause and proposes remedies. The authors cite the Plan for Building a Strong Education Country (2024–2035) as policy background. In the authors' account, each pairing is held back by treating moral education as an add-on. Schools favour knowledge over values, rely on slogans in sport, teach art technique without value guidance, and reduce labour education to simple manual tasks. They attribute these problems to exam-oriented habits and to evaluation systems that count fitness scores, competition results or skills but not moral value. The authors propose dual teaching goals and a two-dimensional evaluation of knowledge mastery and value internalisation. They also call for sport and art courses that embed rule-following, teamwork, resilience and patriotic feeling, and for labour projects with ethical content backed by cooperation among families, schools and society. The aim is to cultivate well-rounded builders and successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official education policy on moral education is explained to teachers and school administrators.

Guiding young people with Marxist scientific theory 以马克思主义科学理论引领青年 Han Xiping Han Xiping asks how Marxist scientific theory should be used to guide young people as China builds a modernised socialist country. Writing in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, Han argues that such guidance is a distinctive strength of Marxist parties, is required by the task of Chinese modernization, and needs new practical methods. The commentary has three parts. The first explains why theoretical guidance of youth is an advantage of Marxist parties. The second links it to the current stage of building a modern socialist country. The third sets out practical routes: ideological and political courses, institutional arrangements, and new forms of discourse. In the first part, Han contrasts Marxist parties with bourgeois parties. In Han's account, bourgeois parties proclaim freedom of thought yet covertly convey bourgeois values, whereas Marxist parties openly arm youth with a scientific worldview and method. Han says this theory gives young people a firm political position, scientific modes of thinking (historical, dialectical, systemic and innovative) and lofty character. In the second part, Han presents young people as the main force in national rejuvenation who face ideological infiltration online from what the article calls hostile forces and from Western capitalist ideology. They therefore need Marxism to tell right from wrong and to reconcile personal aims with the national cause. Han's practical proposals begin with integrated ideological and political courses from primary school to university. These would use artificial intelligence and big data for feedback, and "walking" courses based on fieldwork and volunteering. Han also calls for Party committees, schools, Party schools, the Communist Youth League and social organisations to share responsibility under Party leadership. Finally, Han proposes a new-media matrix on platforms such as Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Bilibili and Zhihu, regulation of traffic-driven algorithms to counter "information cocoons", and participatory formats such as Party-history "murder mystery" role-play games. Han concludes that the Party must keep arming youth with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want to see how a university Party official sets out the ideological, institutional and media methods of youth work in the Chinese modernization era.

Promoting the innovative development of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy 推动当代中国马克思主义政治经济学创新发展 Li Zheng Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (13 May 2025), Li Zheng takes Volume I of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping as the occasion for asking how contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy is being advanced. Li argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought turns practical experience into a systematic economic doctrine. The article presents it as both the latest result of the Party's innovative theory and a Chinese contribution to Marxist political economy. The commentary is organised under four headings. It covers adherence to Marxism's guiding role, the Two Integrations, guidance for building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, and the guidance this thought offers for economic practice at home and in other developing countries. Li first claims that Xi's thought keeps Marxism's basic stance and method: a people-centred position, dialectical and historical materialism, and the basic principles of political economy. Examples include the dominant place of public ownership alongside the Two Unwaverings, and the idea of data as a factor of production that earns income. Li then argues that the thought combines Marxism with China's realities and with traditional culture. Innovation as the first driving force and new quality productive forces draw on Marx's productivity theory. The notion of "harmony between humanity and nature" and the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind draw on traditional ideas. Li adds that concepts such as high-quality development, the new development philosophy and Chinese modernization, together with the "six musts" and "five balances", form the core of an autonomous Chinese economics. Li concludes that the thought is a fundamental guide for Chinese modernization, including high-quality development, the market's decisive role alongside a better-performing government, and resilient industrial and supply chains. Li also contends it offers lessons to the Global South on people-centred development, high-quality growth and balancing development with security. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists frame Xi Jinping's economic thought as Marxist political economy.

The core of the problem of work style is the Party's relationship with the people 作风问题核心是党同人民群众的关系问题 Hong Xianghua Yang Jiahui This commentary, first carried in the Party discipline newspaper China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News in May 2025, argues that the core of Party work style building is keeping flesh-and-blood ties between the Party and the people. Hong and Yang contend that the Party's greatest political strength is its close connection with the masses and that its greatest danger in office is becoming divorced from them. The piece moves in three steps. It first restates the people's role as the source of the Party's strength, with examples from the revolutionary years. It then turns to the Party's tradition of serving the people, citing exemplary cadres such as Jiao Yulu and Kong Fansen. Finally it sets out measures for the long term. The authors draw on the Marxist view that the people are the creators of history and argue that good work style has been vital to the Party's growth. They say that under reform and opening up, a market economy and long-term rule, the risk of detachment has grown. They name formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance, the "four undesirable work styles", as an invisible wall between Party and people. In their account the eight-point rules have reshaped the Party's image, but work style problems recur and need sustained effort. Hong and Yang propose theoretical education, a revival of the spirit of hard struggle, and long-term mechanisms: practical services for the people, regular investigation and research, and continuous work style building. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party School scholars link work style, the mass line and institutional measures in official discourse.

Raising the quality and effectiveness of universities' service to the integrated development of scientific and industrial innovation 提升高校服务科技创新和产业创新融合发展的质效 Ma Xiaojie Ma Xiaojie, Party Secretary of Lanzhou University, asks how universities can better serve the integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. Opening with Xi Jinping's statement that the two are the basic path to developing new quality productive forces, Ma argues that universities should build a mutually supporting system of talent training, scientific innovation and the transfer of results into practice. The article has three parts. The first explains why the integration of the two kinds of innovation matters for new quality productive forces and high-quality development, and why universities are a key link. The second sets out the three-part university system, describing changes in each of its legs. The third offers five practical directions: talent training, discipline layout, the supply of research, the transfer of results, and Party-building and innovation culture. Ma supports the argument throughout with quotations from Xi Jinping and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Ma's central claim is that the three functions of universities must develop together rather than separately. In talent training, Ma sees a shift from supply-driven to demand-driven education, from disciplinary silos to interdisciplinary work, and from a closed campus to an open ecosystem. In research, Ma calls for organised research, a chain running from knowledge creation through technology transfer to industrial application, and a new national system for pooling major resources. On transfer, Ma urges concept-verification systems, pilot-scale platforms, reformed rights-sharing and evaluation that counts industrial service. The aim is research that is both 'reaching the sky' and 'standing on the ground'. Ma concludes that universities should use their strengths to co-define problems with firms, train talent jointly, tackle research challenges together and share in turning results into products. Ma calls for ideological and political education in the spirit of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, dual mentors from academia and industry, discipline 'special zones', AI-enabled curricula and Party branches built on research platforms and transfer projects. These steps are said to feed Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated university leader's concrete policy agenda for linking higher education, research commercialisation and industrial policy.

Beware of old problems of formalism in new guises 警惕形式主义老问题新表现 Xu Xiaoming This short commentary, published in Study Times in May 2025, argues that formalism remains a stubborn problem in the Party's conduct despite a decade of campaigning. Xu holds that formalism is incompatible with the Party's nature and purpose and is an enemy of its original mission. Although the "four forms of decadence" have been largely tackled since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xu says they have not been eradicated, and formalism keeps mutating like a stubborn skin complaint. Xu first recalls the Party's long opposition to formalism: Mao Zedong's remark that formalism is deadly, his use of rectification campaigns, and Deng Xiaoping's treatment of it as an issue for reforming Party and state leadership institutions. The piece then examines three new variants, named after parts of the body: formalism "at the fingertips", "at the toes" and "at the pen tip". It closes with a general call for sustained effort. For each variant Xu names the symptom and then a remedy. Fingertip formalism means app check-ins and instant replies in work chats that tie grassroots cadres to their screens; Xu says its root lies in the head, in a distorted view of performance, and calls for cutting such tasks so cadres can go among the people. Toe formalism means staged inspection tours that show only highlights; Xu calls for going deep, being practical and judging research by results. Pen-tip formalism means reports that inflate achievements, play down shortcomings and pad data; Xu traces it to lazy governance and wants cadres to stop treating "traces" as achievements. Xu concludes, citing Xi Jinping, that improving Party conduct is never finished and must be pursued relentlessly, with constant pressure and deterrence. The author argues that lasting results require turning persistence into routine and building long-term institutions. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party media frame the current campaign against formalism and bureaucratism at the grassroots level.

The question that determines the Party's survival and development Xi Jinping's emphasis on "political direction" 关系党生存发展第一位的问题 Yao Chong This short commentary, originally in Study Times (12 May 2025), takes up the question of why "political direction" matters for the Communist Party of China. Yao defines it as a party's basic stance, goals and trajectory on core questions such as the state system and social structure. The article contends that whether it is correct bears directly on the Party's future and on the success or failure of its cause. The piece works through five statements by Xi Jinping on keeping to the correct political direction since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They date from 2012, 2013, 2018, 2020 and 2024, and each is tied to a different setting: the constitution anniversary, propaganda and ideological work, Party discipline, Politburo democratic life meetings, and reform. Yao's central move is to treat political direction as something rooted in history and practice rather than subjectively set. It is said to be embodied in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in the Party Constitution as its institutionalised form, and in Party leadership over ideology and reform. For officials, the author calls for political acuity, systemic thinking and dialectical method, so that political problems are spotted early. On reform, the article argues that comprehensive Party leadership keeps reform serving the people and aimed at common prosperity. Yao concludes that firmness on political direction underpins Chinese modernization and keeps Party members aligned with the Central Committee with Xi at its core. The text is a study-guide style exposition of Xi's remarks rather than an independent analysis. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how Party media present Xi's statements on political direction across 2012–2024.

The great significance of strengthening Party conduct in the new era 新时代加强党的作风建设的重大意义 Jin Minqing Jin Minqing asks why strengthening the Party's conduct (dang de zuofeng jianshe) matters so much in the new era. The article argues that it is a decisive guarantee for the Party's task of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. In Jin's account, the Party faces unprecedented risks, so it must govern itself with a spirit of reform and strict standards and sustain work on conduct. The article is built around three claims, each developed in its own section. Conduct-building is described as a weapon for preserving the Party's advanced and pure character, as a key measure for consolidating the foundation of long-term governance, and as an important guarantee for achieving the Party's central task. Jin draws throughout on Mao Zedong's writings and on Xi Jinping's statements on conduct, the Party's self-reform and the mass line, and traces the historical record from the Jinggangshan base area and the Yan'an period to the post-1949 rectification campaigns. First, Jin follows Xi in treating problems of conduct as fundamentally problems of Party spirit. Conduct expresses the Party's nature and purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and it also drives the Party's self-reform. In the new era, Jin says, formalism and bureaucratism have become entangled with corruption, which makes conduct a political problem. Second, popular support is presented as the Party's ultimate legitimacy. Jin argues that conduct-building helps the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and decline. Mao's answer was letting the people supervise government, and Xi's second answer is self-reform. Jin adds that conduct-building addresses the problems unique to a large party. Third, Jin argues that Party leadership is the defining feature of Chinese modernization. Cadres' conduct is therefore how that leadership is made concrete, and it is how the mass line is applied and how common prosperity is advanced. Jin concludes that the Party's conduct and image are part of its strength, its moral force alongside the force of truth, and that they partly determine the success or failure of Chinese modernization. The author calls on Party committees, especially at city and county level, to treat unhealthy tendencies and corruption near ordinary people as a regular task. Cadres are urged to keep a people-centred stance. Read the original if you want a representative Party-theory account of how current official discourse links conduct, legitimacy, self-reform and modernization.

Accelerating the construction of an independent knowledge system for the discipline of Marxist theory 加快构建马克思主义理论学科自主知识体系 Liu Jianjun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2025, no. 8) in the 20th anniversary year of the first-level discipline of Marxist theory, Liu Jianjun asks what it means to build an "independent knowledge system" (zizhu zhishi tixi) for that discipline. Taking up the goal set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Liu argues that the task must be understood carefully and carried out through the discipline's six second-level sub-fields. Liu first defines the terms. "Independent" means rooted in China rather than copied from the West; "knowledge system" means turning practical experience into general knowledge that is logically systematic rather than scattered. The article then sets out the discipline's origin in 2005 and its scope, and goes through the six sub-fields in turn: basic principles of Marxism, history of Marxism's development, the adaptation of Marxism to China, foreign Marxism, ideological and political education, and basic problems in modern Chinese history. The central distinction in Liu's argument is between Marxism as guiding ideology and Marxism as an academic discipline. Liu holds that the two operate at different levels and should not be conflated, and that Marx and Engels hold the "intellectual property" of Marxism itself, so one cannot call Marxism as such a Chinese independent knowledge system. What China can build independently is the discipline's knowledge system. For basic principles, Liu stresses upholding the principles ("keeping to the right path") over innovation. Liu distinguishes the principles from their textbook systematisation, a task Liu assigns to Chinese Party members and scholars, who must move beyond the system originally imported from the Soviet Union. For foreign Marxism, Liu proposes absorbing its critiques of capitalism while criticising its "misreadings and reconstructions" of Marxism from a Marxist standpoint. Liu concludes that each sub-field needs its own knowledge system. Liu calls for a narrative of Marxism's development in China and for work on classic texts and editions. Liu also proposes more study of the theoretical results of adapting Marxism to China, and turning Party experience in ideological education into systematic knowledge. Liu further wants a scientific answer to why history and the people chose Marxism, the Communist Party and socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Renmin University professor defines the scope of the Marxist theory discipline and its six sub-fields in official terms.

Promoting the spirit of educators and nurturing outstanding teachers for a great country in the new era 弘扬教育家精神 培育新时代大国良师 Zhu Fengjuan This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, asks how the "spirit of educators" can guide the building of a high-quality teaching force. Zhu argues that this spirit supplies core value guidance for teachers and should shape what a good teacher in the new era is expected to be. The piece opens with the national commendation of model workers, which included teachers in western universities, rural schools and special education. It then links the theme to the Outline for Building a Leading Education Country (2024–2035), which calls for an action to "forge the soul and strengthen teachers" through the spirit of educators. This is to run through teacher training, teaching, research and social practice. Zhu organises the argument around three qualities of a good teacher for a great country. The first is great virtue: teachers should hold firm ideals, serve the people and the Party's governance, and act as moral exemplars in fostering virtue and cultivating people. The second is great wisdom: teachers should unite professional skill with moral cultivation, being both teachers of classics and teachers of character, and should respect the laws of education. The third is great vision, built on benevolent love, with the Guangming Daily's example of the headmaster Zhang Guimei, and on a sense of mission that extends to promoting the common values of all humanity. Zhu concludes that carrying out the action to forge the soul and strengthen teachers will root this spirit in teachers' hearts and help gather strength for building a leading education country. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official discourse describes the ideal teacher and links teacher ethics to the education-power agenda.

Strengthening Party-building leadership to support innovation in community governance 强化党建引领 助力社区治理创新 Wang Caizhang This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 9 May 2025, asks how Party building can lead innovation in urban community governance. Wang argues that grassroots governance is the foundation of national governance and that the community is its basic unit, the "last mile" linking the Party and government to residents. The author's answer is three mutually supporting paths: organisational leadership, resource-guarantee leadership and service leadership. The piece opens with the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which call for Party-building leadership of grassroots governance. It draws on the author's field investigations of communities in various places, and moves through the three paths in turn before presenting them as one system. On organisation, Wang observes that grassroots Party organisations are weakening and need better structures: Party general branches and branches set by Party-member numbers, clear divisions of labour with residents' committees and supervisory committees, deliberation rules, and a weighing of the pros and cons of concurrent posts. On resources, Wang describes community foundations, charity supermarkets and public-interest markets that pool internal and external resources, with Party building supplying mobilising power. On services, the author calls for needs-oriented work, assessing residents' needs through observation, home visits, focus groups and joint community meetings. Wang concludes that the three paths form a systematic project running from building organisations to delivering services. The stated aims are better governance mechanisms, mobilised resources, improved services and residents' greater sense of gain, which would modernize grassroots governance systems and capacity. Read the original if you want a brief, practice-oriented account of how Chinese scholars frame Party-led community governance.

Keeping firmly to the right direction in research on the War of Resistance against Japan 牢牢把稳抗战史研究方向 Xu Zhimin Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, shortly after Xi Jinping's article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta on the 80th anniversary of victory in the Soviet Great Patriotic War, Xu Zhimin asks how research on the War of Resistance against Japan should be oriented. The commentary argues that scholars must resist two errors: denying the Communist Party's role in the resistance, and ignoring China's contribution to the world anti-fascist war while exaggerating that of the United States and Britain. The piece is built around four themes drawn from Xi Jinping's statements on the war: the significance of the 18 September 1931 Incident, the Party as the 'mainstay' of the resistance, China as the main Eastern theatre, and defence of the postwar order. It closes with proposals for the discipline. Xu argues that the 1931 Incident opened the world anti-fascist war, and notes that a growing number of Chinese and foreign scholars date the Second World War from it rather than from 1939. The author describes the Party as the political guarantee of final victory through its united front and its war behind enemy lines. Citing casualty and economic-loss figures, Xu holds that the Chinese theatre pinned down the main Japanese army, thereby supporting the Soviet Union and the Allied strategy. Historical nihilism and revisionism in Germany, Japan and in resistance-war studies are presented as threats to the postwar order. Xu calls for building the discipline's 'three systems' (disciplinary, academic and discourse), developing an autonomous body of knowledge with original concepts, using big data and artificial intelligence on sources, and spreading a correct view of the war. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on wartime historiography is framed for Chinese historians in 2025.

A full review of how Western discourse positions China's War of Resistance against Japan 全面检视西方话语下的中国抗战定位 Liu Benson Writing in a Chinese Social Sciences Today piece of May 2025, Liu argues that Western scholarship still systematically misplaces China's War of Resistance against Japan, despite recent shifts such as Rana Mitter's China's Forgotten Ally and Hans van de Ven's call to put China's experience into the concept of the Second World War. Liu holds that Chinese scholars should critically review this literature and build their own theoretical system for the war, one that can win global recognition. The commentary has three parts. It first lists four biases in Western accounts, then explains their political and academic causes, and finally proposes a shift from being defined by others to defining oneself. Liu identifies the biases as the marginalisation of the Eastern theatre, the reduction of China's war to attrition or a mere "tripwire", a failure to grasp the war as a whole and the nature of the "people's war", and the exaggeration of foreign aid. Cited authors include William Hill, Gerhard Weinberg, Anthony Kubek and Rana Mitter. Liu traces these biases to Cold War thinking and ideological prejudice, to Western-centrism (including John Keegan's "peripheral theatre" and the Fairbank "impact–response" model), and to selective use of archives, though newly opened Chinese sources such as the Chiang Kai-shek diaries have helped. Liu calls for digital document platforms, transnational research communities and an independent body of knowledge on the war. As a first step Liu proposes a "rejuvenation paradigm", guided by historical materialism, rooted in Chinese historiography and centred on the Communist Party's leadership of national rejuvenation. Liu also wants China's war placed within global anti-fascist, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial narratives. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic critique of Western historiography on the Sino-Japanese war and the case for a self-defined research paradigm.

Advancing Party conduct building from the standpoint of serving the Party's overall work 从服务党的工作大局的高度推进作风建设 Zhu Peilei This short commentary, published in Study Times in May 2025, asks how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) should be understood and pursued. Zhu Peilei argues, following Xi Jinping, that such work serves the Party's overall work and is not an isolated task. Improving conduct, in this reading, should be the same process as carrying out the Party's theory, line and policies and advancing reform and opening up and socialist modernization. The article first sets out the historical record, from the Yan'an rectification movement, which established standards such as linking theory with practice, to the correction of the "four undesirable work styles" in the new era. It then turns to the present, when the Party's size, time in power and environment make conduct problems more complex. It closes with practical directions for 2025, the final year of the 14th Five-Year Plan. Zhu contends that conduct building has gone beyond disciplinary tidying-up and become a key variable in the depth of reform, the quality of development and governance effectiveness. The author traces a continuing line from the "two musts" to the "three musts" and from the Eight-point Regulation to the current study and education campaign on it, and describes a system covering thinking, study, work, leadership and cadres' private life. Two tasks are stressed. One is to improve conduct through close ties with the people, curbing formalism and bureaucratism and exposing "lying-flat" cadres. The other is to temper conduct in complex conditions, citing China–US trade friction, technology blockades and geopolitical conflict, so that cadres become more pragmatic and efficient. Zhu calls on the whole Party to use the study and education campaign on the Eight-point Regulation, and to link it with implementing central decisions and with the work on Party integrity and anti-corruption. The aim is to produce new results in conduct building and a new phase of high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media in 2025 link conduct building to economic and national tasks.

Conduct building should aim to turn good practice into lasting custom 作风建设重在化风成俗 Liu Ziyi Wu Fulai Writing in the People's Daily in May 2025, Liu Ziyi and Wu Fulai ask how the Party's work on conduct (zuofeng jianshe) can be made durable. Their answer is the idea of "turning conduct into custom" (huafeng chengsu): improved practice should settle into habit and conscious commitment rather than remain a campaign result. They present it as a key phrase in Xi Jinping's remarks on the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, including his March 2025 inspection tour of Guizhou and Yunnan, where he spoke of loosening in some places and a rebound of bad habits. The article is a short commentary tied to the Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the spirit of the eight-point regulation. It is organised in three parts: the idea as an expression of the Party's self-awareness as a Marxist party; its roots in the Party's history from the revolutionary years to the new era; and three practical requirements for the present. On the first point, the authors read the Han Shu line on rulers shaping "wind" and the people's "custom". They define "wind" as phased results of top-down education and correction, and "custom" as a lasting good climate in which cadres' norms and values are internalised. They describe this as a dialectical shift from quantity to quality, which opens a new stage rather than ending the work. For the present, they set out three requirements. The first is to combine targeted correction with treatment of root causes, since the "four undesirable work styles" (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism, extravagance) reappear in disguised forms, such as "digital traces" replacing meeting overload; corruption and misconduct should be investigated and addressed together. The second is to join external constraint, through Party regulations, with inner conviction, through ideological education. The third is to align Party and government conduct with social and popular customs, with leading cadres setting the example. The authors conclude that conduct building has no end point and must be kept up consistently until good conduct becomes habitual. In their account, this supports the Party's long-term governance and provides a safeguard for further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building discourse in 2025 frames the long-term institutionalisation of the eight-point regulation and its historical lineage.

University functional league organisations should strengthen the "three attributes" and raise the "three capacities" 高校功能型团组织要增强“三性”提升“三力” Xu Xiaoqiang Gu Zhaoliang This short commentary asks how functional league organisations in universities should define their identity and make their education of students effective. Xu and Gu argue that these units must hold to three attributes, namely political character, mass character and precision, and that doing so raises three corresponding capacities: ideological guidance, organisational cohesion and service. The authors begin with the revised regulations on grassroots Communist Youth League work in regular universities, issued jointly by the League's Central Committee and the Ministry of Education. These call for functional league organisations built on student self-governing bodies such as student unions and clubs, or on groups formed around a task. The article then takes each attribute and capacity in turn. On political character, Xu and Gu hold that it is the essential attribute of the League. Functional organisations sit mostly in informal, interest-based groups, which have strong cohesion but must not trade away political character to win participation. The authors link mass character to advanced character as a dialectical unity: the vanguard role needs a mass base, and mass activity needs political direction. They call for managing student self-governing bodies, promoting role models and building online communities, so that students can find the League. On precision, they cite Xi Jinping's call to solve practical problems for young people, and propose campus culture, festival-themed activities and innovation and entrepreneurship competitions as the vehicles. The authors conclude that functional organisations can extend League coverage, strengthen the grassroots and join the first and second classrooms. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-youth work in Chinese universities frames organisational reform.

Making a concerted effort to strengthen the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 着力加强全面从严治党体系建设 Du Shuting This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today on 8 May 2025, responds to the 15th collective study session of the Political Bureau of the 20th Central Committee, which discussed improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Du argues that such a system is the key to preserving the Party's vanguard character and purity within the Party's self-reform, and sets out how it should be strengthened. The article is organised around five tasks: consolidating the foundations through ideological and Party-spirit education; building a tightly organised structure; raising the effectiveness of supervision; improving the system of intra-Party regulations; and pooling the efforts of Party organisations and members through clear responsibilities. Du proposes concrete measures under each heading. On organisation, the author calls for a closed-loop mechanism of decision, execution, supervision and feedback, tracking platforms for implementing central decisions, and Party organisations in new fields such as internet and logistics firms. On supervision, Du stresses political supervision centred on the Two Upholds, power and responsibility lists for top leaders, and the combination of intra-Party supervision with public reporting, supported by big-data analysis. On responsibility, Party committees, discipline inspection commissions, committee secretaries and individual members are each assigned defined duties. Du concludes that the task is long and arduous and requires sustained effort across the Party, providing a political and organisational guarantee for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned summary of the practical measures commentators link to the 2025 Politburo study session on Party self-governance.

Pushing Marxist political economy to a new stage 将马克思主义政治经济学推向新境界 Li Qiankun Writing in a newspaper commentary on the first volume of Selected Economic Works of Xi Jinping (published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, May 2025), Li Qiankun presents the volume as the authoritative text of Xi Jinping's economic thought. Li argues that this thought inherits the philosophical methodology and basic standpoint of Marxist political economy and, from the standpoint of a new historical era, carries that discipline to a new stage. The piece is organised in three steps. It first traces the origins of Marxist political economy, from classical political economy to Marx and Engels's critique. It then sets out what Xi's economic thought preserves (the article's "upholding the fundamentals"). Finally it lists the innovations Li credits to it. In Li's account, Marx and Engels's critique of classical political economy helped produce historical materialism, which in turn allowed them to treat economic categories as expressions of social relations rather than relations among things. Li holds that Xi's thought keeps four inheritances: the people-centred standpoint, the historical-materialist method, centralised and unified Party leadership over economic work, and a global outlook. Li then names the innovations: judgments that the world is undergoing great changes unseen in a century and that China has moved to high-quality development; the new development philosophy and the new development pattern; the upholding and improvement of the basic socialist economic system, including the Two Unwaverings; and a deeper understanding of capital's characteristics and laws, especially finance. Li concludes that these elements make Xi's economic thought both continuous with Marx and Engels and a response to present conditions. Li notes that Engels described a broad political economy as still "to be created", and presents Xi's thought as the latest theoretical answer to that task in socialist construction. Li claims that the institutional measures offer a Chinese approach to economic-system innovation for the world. Read the original if you want a short, official-line overview of how Chinese scholars link Xi Jinping's economic thought to the Marxist political-economic tradition.

Building a culturally strong nation requires upholding Marxism as the fundamental guiding thought Interview with Sun Laibin, Party secretary of the School of Marxism at Peking University and special supervisor of the National Supervisory Commission 建设文化强国必须坚持马克思主义这一根本指导思想 Sun Laibin This is an interview with Sun Laibin, Party secretary of Peking University's School of Marxism and a special supervisor of the National Supervisory Commission, conducted by a reporter from the discipline-inspection newspaper. It follows Xi Jinping's remarks at the 17th collective study session of the Political Bureau, which called for building a culturally strong nation by 2035 while upholding Marxism as the fundamental guiding thought. Sun argues that Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere is the precondition for that goal. The interview has three questions. The first asks how to understand Marxism's guiding position in ideology; the second, where the theoretical advancement of the Chinese Communist Party lies in the new era; the third, what new demands the system of ideological work responsibility now faces. Sun first argues that ideological security indicates the stability of state power, citing Marx's remark on the dissolution of forms of consciousness and the Soviet collapse and 'colour revolutions' as confirmation. Diversity of ideas, he says, is an objective result of diverse ownership forms and distribution methods, but it does not mean diversity of guiding thought, because the dominant ideology depends on the dominant ownership relations: the primary position of public ownership, the people's democratic dictatorship and Communist Party leadership. Sun then holds that a Marxist party's advancement lies first in its theory, and that upholding and developing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is, in contemporary China, genuinely upholding Marxism. On implementation, Sun calls for stronger responsibility for ideological positions, especially universities and the internet, and for combining 'establishing' (raising the Marxist banner) with 'refuting' erroneous trends. Problems should be sorted into political-principle, ideological-understanding and academic questions, handled respectively by firm opposition, persuasion and scholarly debate. Sun concludes that Party members and cadres must deepen their study of Xi Jinping Thought and that ideological workers should both reason persuasively and be willing to confront statements that challenge the political bottom line. The text presents the basic system of Marxism's guiding role as a major institutional innovation first stated in 2019. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official ideological and cultural policy is explained to Party and supervisory audiences, including the handling of universities and online space.

Practising whole-process people's democracy: implementing and improving the people's supervisor system 践行全过程人民民主落实和完善人民监督员制度 Ying Yong Writing in Study Times in May 2025, Ying Yong, head of the Supreme People's Procuratorate, argues that implementing and improving the people's supervisor system is an important way for procuratorates to put whole-process people's democracy into practice. Under this system, citizens drawn from many walks of life oversee how procuratorates handle cases. Ying presents it as a means of ensuring that prosecutorial power is exercised for the people, subject to the people's supervision and satisfactory to the people. The article has three parts. The first explains why the system matters, noting that the Supreme People's Procuratorate began exploring it in 2003 and that Party documents from the 18th Party Congress (2012) onward ordered its deepening, including a 2015 reform plan. The second reviews progress in selection, supervisory effectiveness and support for supervisors, with figures. The third sets out four requirements for further work. Ying's core reasoning is that the system serves three purposes. It widens orderly citizen participation, in line with the constitutional principle that all power belongs to the people. It adds external oversight to internal procuratorial controls, so that those who supervise others also accept supervision. It also helps test cases against public perceptions of fairness. As evidence, Ying cites the 'separation of management and use' mechanism, under which judicial administrative bodies select and manage supervisors while procuratorates organise their work. The article reports 25,000 supervisors nationwide, 740,000 case-handling activities supervised since 2015, 470,000 opinions offered and an 89.3 per cent adoption rate. Ying calls for upholding Party leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and for accepting supervision more consciously by inviting supervisors to take part wherever possible. Ying also urges closer cooperation between procuratorates and judicial administrative bodies, and for the supporting mechanisms to be completed. The article names gaps in linking the system with other external checks and in guaranteeing supervisors' ability to perform their duties. Read the original if you want an official procuratorial account of how citizen oversight of prosecutors is institutionalised in China, with statistics and the rules governing it.

The journal The Communist and the building of the Party's mobilisation capacity during the War of Resistance 《共产党人》杂志与抗战时期党的动员能力建设 Wang Fengqing Wang Fengqing, writing in Guangming Daily (7 May 2025), asks how the Party journal The Communist (Gongchandang ren) helped the Chinese Communist Party build its capacity to mobilise the population during the War of Resistance against Japan. The journal was an internal theoretical publication of the Central Committee. It ran from October 1939 to August 1941, for 19 issues, a period of Guomindang anti-communist policy and a serious setback for the anti-Japanese united front. Wang argues that the journal gave timely, practical guidance to Party organisations and members, and so played a historical role in gathering strength for national victory. The short article treats the war as a contest for popular support as well as a military one. It is organised around three themes in the journal's content: the vanguard and exemplary role of Party members, the flexible use of mobilisation methods, and the timely summing up of useful experience. Wang draws on articles by Yang Shangkun, Zhang Wentian, Li Weihan and Yang Song, on field reports from villages and army units, and on directives of the Central Propaganda Department. On the first theme, Wang reports that the journal's authors insisted that Party members set an example, whether by keeping the Party distinct from ordinary masses and expelling opportunists, or by befriending even die-hard and middle elements in the united front. Under the "three-thirds" system of government, Party members were to win over non-Party people by exemplary work. Local reports described branches that made leading by example part of Party education. On the second theme, the journal advised tailoring propaganda to its audience: enemy troops, the army's own soldiers, international opinion and young people. Youth work, it said, should be lively and sincere rather than recite resolutions. Central directives on writers, on propaganda against the enemy and puppet regimes, and on agitation among the masses asked for vivid, popular language tied to people's immediate concerns. Wang concludes that the journal's guidance was both theoretical and practical, and that its habit of summarising experience, a tradition he describes as a political strength of the Party, helped spread successful practice. Examples include women's work in Wan County, Hebei, and a grain-collection committee in Yan'an in which 18 of 27 representatives were non-Party and the grain quota was exceeded. Wang judges that this had a positive effect on mobilisation work. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how a wartime Party journal is presented in current official historiography as a tool for training and mobilising cadres.

The "Chinese National Liberation Vanguard" before and after the outbreak of the all-out War of Resistance 全民族抗战爆发前后的“中华民族解放先锋队” Wang Jianwei This short historical piece, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, examines the Chinese National Liberation Vanguard (known by its Chinese abbreviation, Minxian dui), a youth organisation born in the December Ninth Movement of 1935. Wang Jianwei argues that the Communist Party used it as its basic organisational form to reverse its unfavourable position in youth work after the failure of the Great Revolution. In the author's account, it mobilised young people as a vanguard force, helped the Party organisation grow and drew youth into the national War of Resistance. The article follows the organisation in three stages. It first covers the formation of the vanguard from the southward propaganda corps of early 1936 and its training, publicity and recruitment work through that year. It then turns to the Party's leadership and the organisation's expansion into a national body in 1937. Finally it traces its role after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of July 1937 and its dissolution in 1938. Wang's central claims concern the vanguard's dual character. Outwardly it presented itself as a non-partisan national salvation group, while in practice the Beiping Party committee ran a Party group inside it and Party members held leading posts. Wang cites 1936 directives from the Central Secretariat and Zhang Wentian urging the use of open or semi-open youth names, which the author says let the vanguard take over much of the function of the damaged Communist Youth League. The author also stresses its military and ideological training: drills in the Western Hills, summer camps, reading circles and periodicals. By Wang's figures, membership rose from about 300 to over 2,300 in Beiping by the end of 1936, and about 6,000 members nationally by February 1937. After the fall of Beiping and Tianjin, members joined guerrilla units and base areas, and registered numbers reached over 30,000 by April 1938. Wang concludes that the vanguard preserved the gains of the December Ninth Movement in a more fixed organisational form and corrected the looseness of earlier student movements. Its members, in the author's phrase, moved from "taking up the pen" to "taking up the gun", forming a high-quality cadre corps that supplied the Party and the war behind enemy lines. The Central Committee decided in November 1938 to dissolve it in favour of local youth national salvation associations, as youth work shifted to the base areas. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-historiography account of how the Communist Party organised student youth in North China in 1935–38.

A major milestone in the history of the Party Commemorating the 80th anniversary of the Seventh Party Congress 在党的历史上具有重要里程碑意义 Li Rong Marking the 80th anniversary of the Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in Yan'an from April to June 1945, Li Rong argues that the congress was a landmark in Party history. In Li's account it summed up more than two decades of the new-democratic revolution, set the line, programme and tactics, and wrote Mao Zedong Thought into the Party constitution as the guiding ideology. The congress went down as a "congress of unity and victory", and Li draws five lessons from it for the present. The article has three parts. The first describes the long preparation: the 17-year gap since the Sixth Congress (1928), the repeated postponements, the election of delegates, their dangerous journeys to Yan'an, and their participation in the Yan'an rectification movement. The second narrates the congress itself, including Mao's opening speech, his political report "On Coalition Government", the reports by Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai, the new constitution, the first secret-ballot election in a Party congress, and the First Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee. The third part moves from the victory of 1949 to the five lessons. Li presents the rectification movement and the 1945 resolution on questions of Party history as what produced ideological unity among delegates, who were examined on dogmatism and empiricism and asked to criticise themselves. From the congress, Li draws five requirements. The Party must maintain unity and its position as the leading core, which Li links to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. It must innovate in theory, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It must follow the mass line and serve the people wholeheartedly. It must carry out criticism and the Party's self-reform. And it must stay alert to danger and be ready to struggle, as Mao listed 17 difficulties in 1945. Li concludes that the congress showed the Party's political, ideological and organisational maturity, and that its lessons bear directly on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and on building a strong modern socialist country. Li calls for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation to be pursued through Chinese modernization with heightened vigilance. Read the original if you want an official Party-history reading of the Seventh Congress and of how it is used today to support Party unity, leadership and self-reform.

Taking up the mission the Party has assigned to the Communist Youth League in the new era and on the new journey 担起新时代新征程党赋予共青团的使命任务 Secretariat of the Central Committee of the Communist Youth League of China Written by the Secretariat of the Communist Youth League (CYL) Central Committee and published in Qiushi in 2025, this programmatic commentary asks how the League should carry out the tasks the Party has set for it. It takes as its basis Xi Jinping's speech at the League's 19th National Congress and his talk with the new League leadership in June 2023. The authors argue that the League must remain the Party's assistant and reserve force, and that its work should follow the Party's central tasks. The text is organised around six "how" questions: how to hold to the League's fundamental position, how to nurture new-era youth, how to serve the overall agenda, how to be a bridge to young people, how to energise League organisations, and how to govern the League strictly. Each section first reviews achievements since 2023 and then sets out tasks for the new journey. The authors give figures and examples, including the 390,000-plus League branches in the theme education campaign, "Youth Post Houses" for graduates, and the Western China volunteer programme. The core claim is that political character is the League's first attribute, so that "where the Party's flag points, the League's flag follows". The authors say the League must become a political school guiding young people's thinking, a vanguard force for long-term struggle, a firm bridge between the Party and youth, and an advanced organisation. They report that League organisations in new fields grew from under 100,000 five years earlier to over 700,000. They also describe efforts on youth employment, mental-health services and grassroots reform. Alongside this, the authors stress that young people are exposed to varied social currents and to hostile forces, which makes ideological guidance harder. The authors conclude that the League should deepen reform at the grassroots, expand organisational coverage, and apply full and rigorous self-governance of the Party's logic to League cadres and members through discipline, training and tighter admission. They call for mobilising young people to contribute to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an official account of how the League's leadership frames its priorities, achievements and tasks under Xi Jinping.

Opening up a new realm for Marxist political economy 开拓马克思主义政治经济学新境界 Ding Renzhong This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today (7 May 2025) reads the first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping as a new body of theory for political economy with Chinese characteristics. The volume collects Xi's main writings on economic construction from November 2012 to December 2024. Ding Renzhong argues that it reflects the Party Central Committee's reflection on, and theoretical summary of, economic practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Ding's view it shows the core content and distinctive qualities of Xi Jinping's economic thought. The article is organised around four qualities: Party spirit (dangxing), people-centredness, epoch-making relevance (shidaixing) and innovation. Each section pairs statements by Xi with Ding's own reasoning. The last section places the volume in a lineage from Mao Zedong's economic ideas, through the post-1978 reform period, to the present. On Party spirit, Ding argues that strengthening Party leadership of economic work expresses three advantages: the political system, the economic management system and the continuity of policy. On people-centredness, Ding says it follows from the Party's purpose, from historical materialism and from the nature of socialism, and links it to common prosperity. On the epoch-making quality, Ding names three tasks: deepening reform, expanding opening up and advancing scientific and technological innovation. Ding cites the 22 pilot free trade zones and the Hainan free trade port, membership of regional trade agreements, the Belt and Road Initiative, and the innovation-driven development strategy. On innovation, Ding lists theoretical results of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. They include the theory of the essence of socialism, the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism, the new development philosophy, the socialist market economy, the economic "new normal" and the three rights in rural land contracting. Ding endorses Xi's statement that these were not addressed by the Marxist classics and open up a new realm for Marxist political economy. Ding expects further theoretical results under Xi Jinping's economic thought, and a contribution to an autonomous Chinese system of economic knowledge. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned overview of how Chinese economists frame Xi's economic writings and their place in Marxist political economy.

Making great efforts to improve political capability 着力提高政治能力 Central Party School (National Academy of Governance) Committee This article, issued in the name of the Central Party School (National Academy of Governance) committee and published in Qiushi in 2025, takes up the question of how Party members and officials should raise their political capability.
