It argues that, at a critical period for building a strong country and advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, political capability is the first among the abilities cadres need. It presents this as a response to Xi Jinping's repeated calls to speak plainly about politics and to place political cultivation first in Party-spirit cultivation. The text is organised as eight tasks, each introduced by a short heading: strengthening political loyalty; keeping to the correct political direction; serving the political big picture; strictly observing political discipline and rules; strengthening political responsibility; preventing and defusing political risks; continually purifying the political ecosystem; and cultivating sound political ethics. Each section combines statements by Xi Jinping, references to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and model cadres such as Jiao Yulu, and practical demands on officials. The argument rests on a few moves. First, loyalty to the Party is treated as the primary political quality, and the article says it must be anchored in the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, including upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee. Second, direction, the overall interest and discipline are linked: officials are told to put local and sectional interests beneath the national whole, to treat political discipline as the foremost of the Party's six disciplines, and to report major matters as required. Third, the article stresses risk and conduct: it calls for vigilance against political risks, including those it attributes to hostile Western forces, for resistance to cliques and 'one-man rule', and for the cultivation of personal and official virtue. The article concludes that officials should turn political requirements from external demands into inner conviction, so that they become politically firmer and more mature. It calls on them to take up responsibility in priority areas such as high-quality development, to practise full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and to build a clean political ecosystem. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of the Party-school line on what 'political capability' demands of cadres in the Xi Jinping era.

How the Communist Party of China won the "two historical initiatives" 中国共产党何以赢得“两个历史主动” Chen Li This commentary, published in Study Times on 5 May 2025, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Chen Li asks how the Party has won what the speech calls two "historical initiatives": keeping the Party from changing in quality, colour or flavour, and uniting the people behind the building of a strong country and national rejuvenation. Chen's answer is that the Party has led social revolution through self-reform and has pursued the fight against corruption on a sustained, systematic basis. The article is organised in four parts. It first treats the anti-corruption struggle as a long-term political task of the Party's self-reform. It then sets out three strands of the approach: deterrence through high-pressure punishment, restraint through institutions and supervision, and moral and ideological cultivation. Throughout, Chen draws on Xi's formulations and on the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Chen's account, the Party leadership has repeatedly judged the situation to be "still severe and complex", moving from the "three persistents" of 2013 to the "two stills" of the latest plenum, which note that existing corruption has not been cleared and new cases keep emerging. The central method is to advance in an integrated way the aims that officials should not dare, not be able and not want to be corrupt. Chen describes zero tolerance, no "restricted zones" and no quotas for investigations, and cites 2024 figures: 2.175 million leads handled, 877,000 cases filed and 889,000 people disciplined, including 58 centrally managed cadres. The article presents institutional measures as the root remedy: power lists, tighter procedures, Party regulations, discipline placed ahead of law, inspection tours with full coverage, and a full and rigorous self-governance of the Party system. It adds ideological education, a correct view of power, and a healthier political culture within the Party. Chen concludes that the struggle must continue, with the Party fighting a decisive, protracted and all-round battle against corruption. The article presents this as essential to Chinese modernization and to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party commentary explains the anti-corruption campaign and its link to the Party's self-reform.

Adhering to the path of cultural development with Chinese characteristics 坚持中国特色社会主义文化发展道路 Li Yuanyuan This short commentary, published in Economic Daily on 30 April 2025, asks how China should keep to the path of cultural development with Chinese characteristics. Li Yuanyuan argues that Party leadership is the most essential feature of this path and the organisational and ideological guarantee for building a culture-strong country. The piece first recalls the principle that the Party manages propaganda and ideology, and says the Party has led cultural work through the revolutionary, construction and reform periods. It then credits the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with a fundamental turn in the ideological field and stronger cultural confidence. Li sets out three tasks for the present. The first is to uphold Marxism's guiding position in ideology. Li holds that Marxism is a guide to action, not dogma, and that it fits Chinese civilisation closely. Li calls for the Two Integrations to be applied so that theoretical, institutional and cultural innovation continues. The second is to improve cultural governance in the information age: strengthen internet management according to law, guard against online ideological risks, reform mainstream media and build a multi-level communication matrix. The third is to let the core socialist values guide cultural work. Li lists their incorporation into law, textbooks, the "two benefits" standard for cultural output and citizen moral-building programmes. Li concludes that only by making the core socialist values everyday, concrete and lived can they become the people's shared pursuit and secure the cultural foundation for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party-school scholarship frames Party leadership, ideology, media governance and values education in cultural policy.

Putting political cultivation first in Party-spirit cultivation 把政治修养摆在党性修养的首位 Shi Xu Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2025, this commentary takes up a directive Xi Jinping gave at a Politburo democratic life meeting in December 2024: that political cultivation (zhengzhi xiuyang) must come first in the cultivation of Party spirit (dangxing). Shi Xu places the directive within the current Party-wide study and education campaign on implementing the central Eight-point Regulation. The author's thesis is that forging Party spirit and raising ideological awareness requires putting political cultivation first, so that cadres steadily improve their political judgement, political understanding and political execution. The article has three sections. The first sets out why the priority is necessary, the second argues that political cultivation is the most fundamental form of cultivation for Party members and cadres, and the third describes how cadres should pursue it as a lifelong task. Shi draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on the reports to the 19th Party Congress (2017) and the 20th Party Congress (2022). On necessity, Shi gives three reasons. Political development is said to lead the Party's overall building, so cultivation must follow that order. Fulfilling the tasks of Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is said to require politically reliable cadres. And the "unique challenges of a large party" can be met only by looking at problems politically. On primacy, Shi contends that political attributes are a party's first attribute, that political cultivation underpins the Party's vanguard character and purity, and that it sets the direction and effect of theoretical, moral, cultural, professional and disciplinary cultivation alike. If political cultivation goes astray, the author says, the other kinds lose their meaning. For practice, Shi proposes three tasks: tempering political character through loyalty to the Party, which the author describes as unconditional and tied to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; building political ability through political experience; and strengthening political responsibility, including a correct view of performance that values both visible and long-term achievements. The author concludes that cultivation never ends and must continue "to the end of one's life". Read the original if you want to see how current Party-building commentary links Party spirit, political loyalty and cadre conduct to Xi Jinping's recent directives.

The contemporary value of promoting the Bandung Spirit 弘扬万隆精神的时代价值 Luo Jianbo Marking the 70th anniversary of the 1955 Bandung Conference, this newspaper commentary asks what the Bandung Spirit offers the world today. Luo Jianbo argues that, as the "Global South" rises collectively while unilateralism, protectionism and bullying grow, the spirit's core elements of independence, solidarity and cooperation, and seeking common ground while shelving differences have a new value. In Luo's account, China contributed decisively to the conference and will make new and greater contributions to the common interests of the Global South. The piece opens with a reference to Xi Jinping's recent signed article in Malaysian newspapers, which called for promoting the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and the Bandung Spirit. It is then organised in three sections, each pairing one element of the spirit with a present-day task: independence and international fairness, solidarity and Global South development, and seeking common ground and exchange among civilizations. On independence, Luo recalls that the 29 Asian and African participants opposed colonialism and imperialism and adopted ten principles of international relations, and that China's delegation helped make anti-imperialism a core part of the spirit. Today, the author says, hegemonic and zero-sum thinking persist, so states should uphold equality, mutually beneficial cooperation and consultation, oppose "decoupling" and defend the World Trade Organization-centred trading system. On solidarity, Luo cites UN-agency figures that about 35.4 per cent of the world's population, and 64.8 per cent in Africa, cannot afford a healthy diet. The author describes the Global South as a collective identity and says South-South cooperation has shifted from national liberation to mutual benefit in pursuit of modernization. China's zero-tariff treatment for the least developed countries and the Belt and Road Initiative are presented as examples. On seeking common ground, Luo credits Zhou Enlai's delegation with bridging divisions at Bandung and treats the approach as a Chinese contribution to international relations that rejects bloc division by ideology. The author links it to the common values of all mankind, a community with a shared future for mankind, and partnership without alliance. Luo concludes that greater Chinese influence in building international consensus and in civilizational exchange is an inherent requirement of that community. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official scholarship presents Bandung as a basis for China's Global South diplomacy.

Grasping the distinctive features of the Party's cultural leadership 深刻把握党的文化领导权的鲜明特质 Wang Yan This short commentary takes up Xi Jinping's proposition, advanced at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, of the "cultural leadership" of the Communist Party of China. Wang Yan argues that understanding its distinctive features is required for studying Xi Jinping's thought on culture and is a precondition for giving the building of a strong cultural nation a firm political guarantee. The article identifies five features: advancement, political character, contemporary relevance, popular character and systemic character. Writing in the framework of the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Wang devotes one short section to each feature. The sections move from the Party's grasp of the laws of cultural development, through ideological work, responses to new conditions at home and abroad, and service to the people, to the Party's overall coordination of cultural work. On advancement, Wang says the Party has summarised three sets of laws: those of socialist cultural construction, which proceed from the interaction of economic base and superstructure; those of traditional Chinese culture, guided by the Two Integrations; and those of human civilisation, involving exchange and mutual learning. On political character, Wang holds that cultural leadership is in essence leadership over ideological work, since a regime's collapse often begins in the realm of ideas. Wang points to the system of Marxism's guiding role, ideological responsibility systems and Party study mechanisms. On contemporary relevance, the article describes opposition to cultural hegemonism, historical nihilism and "universal values", and the Party's self-reform. Wang adds that the people-centred character appears in meeting diverse spiritual needs and equalising basic public cultural services. Systemic character is said to cover leadership over propaganda and public opinion, cultural innovation, and the management of cultural organisations. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party theorists currently define the Party's cultural leadership.

The significance and practical requirements of establishing a mechanism for delivering high-quality cultural resources directly to the grassroots 科学把握建立优质文化资源直达基层机制的重大意义和实践要求 Zhou Qin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2025 no. 7), Zhou Qin takes up a reform measure set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and repeated in the 2025 government work report: establishing a mechanism that delivers high-quality cultural resources directly to the grassroots. Zhou argues that the mechanism matters for meeting the people's cultural needs and for building a culture-strong nation. The article also sets out what must be done to put it into practice. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the mechanism is significant. The second identifies its key tasks around three questions: whether the resources are good, whether they reach the grassroots, and whether the supply mechanism is flexible. The third proposes practical paths. Zhou draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on Party documents from the 19th and 20th Party Congresses and the 14th Five-Year cultural development plan. Zhou's core argument is that the main tension in cultural supply has moved from whether there is enough to whether it is good and refined. In Zhou's account, uneven allocation between town and country and between regions still leaves gaps in high-quality supply. Zhou proposes defining quality by the depth, breadth and influence of a cultural resource. The author links the mechanism to common prosperity in spiritual life and to strengthening grassroots cultural confidence as a foundation of the culture-strong nation. On practice, Zhou calls for three things. The first is better content, through a people-centred orientation in creative work, talent incentives, grassroots amateur arts teams and the participation of non-public cultural enterprises. The second is moving resources downward, through urban support for rural culture, tilting resources towards old revolutionary areas, ethnic minority and border regions, and services for older people, minors, disabled people and migrant workers. The third is service innovation, through digital platforms offering order-based, menu-based and appointment-based services, and a main-branch library and cultural centre structure. Zhou presents these as parts of a systematic reform. Read the original if you want to see how a Party theoretical journal turns the Third Plenum's cultural-service reform into concrete policy tasks.

Studying and implementing the spirit of the Central Economic Work Conference and putting the Party Central Committee's decisions into effect 深入学习贯彻中央经济工作会议精神 扎实推动党中央决策部署落地落实 Party Leadership Group of the National Development and Reform Commission This article, a study-and-implementation piece by the Party leadership group of the National Development and Reform Commission, takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024. The authors argue that the speech reviews 2024, assesses the current situation and sets out the work for 2025. They call on officials to unify thinking and action around it, put work first, and use high-quality development to advance the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text has four parts. It begins with an account of the progress made in 2024. It then weighs the challenges and opportunities facing the economy, followed by an explanation of the "regular patterns" of economic work that Xi's speech distils. It ends with a list of tasks for putting the Central Committee's decisions into effect in 2025. The first part cites figures on growth, industry, consumption, employment, innovation, trade, grain output, debt and incomes. On the outlook, the authors apply a "two-sided" method. They set external pressures against favourable factors, and weak domestic demand against what they call a stable base, many advantages, strong resilience and great potential. They cite political guarantees such as the Two Establishes, institutional strengths, supply and demand potential, and stronger macro policy. In the third part they present Xi's guidance as five relationships to be balanced: an effective market and an enabling government, total supply and total demand, new and old growth drivers, increments and existing stock, and quality and total volume. They place the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership as the fundamental guarantee of economic work. The final part lists tasks for 2025. These are more proactive fiscal policy and moderately loose monetary policy, measures to boost consumption and investment, and faster development of new quality productive forces with a modern industrial system. They also include a unified national market, further opening up, containing risks in property, local debt and small financial institutions, coordinated urban–rural development and better livelihoods. The authors conclude that these steps will keep the economy recovering and lay the groundwork for the 15th Five-Year Plan period. Read the original if you want an official summary of the economic priorities, policy language and data the Party leadership used to frame 2025.

Drawing the strength of cultural confidence from red culture 从红色文化中汲取文化自信的力量 Zhao Yongfu Zhao Yongfu asks how red culture, the culture created under Communist Party leadership, can serve as a source of cultural confidence. Opening with Xi Jinping's March 2025 remarks in Guizhou on using regional red and ethnic cultures to strengthen cultural confidence, the author argues that red culture both underpins that confidence and should be actively transmitted and renewed. The context is the drive for national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out why red culture gives cultural confidence its foundation. The second discusses how to draw strength from it through inheritance and dissemination, in Party training, school ideological education and public storytelling. The third turns to innovation: technology, red tourism and international communication. Examples come mainly from Guangxi, where the author works. Zhao defines red culture as advanced culture created by the Party and the people in revolution, construction and reform. In this account it results from combining Marxism with China's circumstances and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article says it carries forward traditional ideals such as benevolence, people-centredness and national integrity, and that the Party's "spiritual lineage" runs from the Jinggangshan and Long March spirit to the poverty-alleviation and lunar-exploration spirits. For transmission, Zhao points to Party history study rules, integrated ideological education from primary school to university, and storytelling, with the Xiang River battle and Guangxi's memorials as the example. For innovation, the author proposes AI presenters, VR and AR exhibitions, immersive live performances, themed red-tourism routes, and international storytelling with trained communicators and a discourse system foreigners can understand. The author also says new quality productive forces should empower the cultural industries. Zhao concludes that protecting and using red resources, passing on the red gene and telling red stories are the way to firm cultural confidence, in line with Xi Jinping's directives. The author presents international dissemination as a way to help the world understand the Party and China and to raise national soft power. Read the original if you want to see how Party-history officials frame red culture, and what practical measures they propose, from cadre education to digital media and tourism.

Decoding the "One Core, Two Wings, Three Cultures, Four Histories" model of ideological and political education 解码“一核二翼三文四史”思政育人模式 Jiang Feng This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2025, describes the "One Core, Two Wings, Three Cultures, Four Histories" model of ideological and political education that Beijing has piloted. Jiang presents it as a successful local experience that offers lessons for building ideological and political courses in schools and universities nationwide. The model is tied to the "big ideological and political course" and to integrating such education across primary, secondary and tertiary levels. The article first explains the model's four components. It then reports a May 2024 Beijing call for course-based ideological and political education results, and lists four measures taken to promote integration across school stages. Jiang defines the "core" as Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The "two wings" are dedicated ideological and political courses and ideological content built into other subjects. The "three cultures" are fine traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture, and the "four histories" are the histories of the Party, New China, reform and opening up, and socialism. On results, the author reports 261 submissions from the city's 17 districts, about four-fifths of them teaching case designs, for example literature lessons drawing on classical works and physics lessons recounting Chinese scientists' stories. The measures are a provincial-level guideline on integration, five pilot zones, a digital map of over 200 practice-teaching bases, and a 34-member expert committee. Jiang concludes that the model systematically integrates ideological and political content and brings it closer to students' lives and level of understanding. The author calls it a meaningful attempt and exploration, not a finished solution. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how Beijing structures ideological and political education across school stages, and of the policy measures behind it.

The political and revolutionary character of Marx and Engels's thought and its contemporary relevance An interview with Professor Terrell Carver of the University of Bristol 马克思恩格斯思想的政治性、革命性及其当代启示 Liu Zixu This is an interview, conducted by Liu Zixu of the Institute of Marxism, CASS, with Terrell Carver, a Marx and Engels scholar at the University of Bristol. It asks how the intellectual relationship between Marx and Engels should be understood and what their work offers today. Carver's main answer is that both men saw themselves as political activists from youth, and that later readers have anachronistically recast their subversive journalism and pamphlets as philosophy or economics. The conversation moves through four areas: the Marx–Engels partnership, including the 'young' and 'later' Engels; the question 'which Marx?'; Marx's contributions on profit, historical materialism and the base and superstructure; and Marx in historical context, covering colonialism, national liberation, Eurocentrism, gender and the prospects for human emancipation. It closes with Carver's view of what Marx, Engels and Marxism research should do next. Carver rejects the binaries commentators impose, such as young/mature Marx, break/continuity, and philosophy/economics, as projections that make biographical drama. In his reading, Marx's writing from the outset responded to changing political circumstances, readerships and censorship rather than reflecting a closed theoretical journey. He adds that Engels presented 'a Marx' for political purposes after 1883, and he describes his own approach as post-structuralist: meaning is constructed by readers, so there are 'many Marxes'. On economics, he reads Marx as locating profit in production, in the special surplus-producing property of human labour, and the opening theoretical chapters of Capital as a prelude to a political critique. He therefore regards claims that capital is neutral and creates value as vulgar economics that blunts class struggle. Carver judges that Marx remains the most comprehensive analyst and critic of capitalism and that Marxism has been a progressive force for emancipation. He calls 'Eurocentrism' a poorly framed charge, and he sees the present as a bind in which identity-based and national struggles are weakly linked to anti-capitalism. He urges researchers to drop worn-out framing concepts and to give less priority to theory over practice, to canonical books over journalism and letters, and to MEGA's separation of 'economic' works. Read the original if you want a Western specialist's anti-anachronistic account of Marx and Engels as political actors, as presented to a Chinese Marxist readership.

The core and distinctive features of the new round of scientific and technological revolution from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视域下新一轮科技革命的核心与特质 Zhang Jianyun Zhang Jianyun asks what lies at the centre of the current round of scientific and technological revolution and what it means for the mode of production. The article's thesis is that the leading force is a digital-intelligence technology system, formed by the convergence of information technologies. Its core, in Zhang's reading, is artificial intelligence that builds models from massive data and so liberates mental labour. This in turn merges cultural and material production, and Zhang argues that capitalism's logic runs against these new productive forces while socialism complements them. The article has three sections. The first traces the technological convergence: twentieth-century computers, digitisation, AI, the internet and mobile communications, joined from the 2000s by cloud computing, the Internet of Things and blockchain. The second examines how AI assists the human brain and why this is the revolution's key content. The third turns to changes in the means of production, forms of labour and the organisation of cooperation, and contrasts capitalist and socialist institutions. Zhang draws on Marx's Capital, the 1844 Manuscripts and statements by Xi Jinping, and refers to DeepSeek as a recent case. Zhang uses Marx's method of ascending from abstract determinations to the 'concrete in thought' and names data as that concrete: the individual technologies are all organised around producing, circulating and using data. Following Marx's account of labour as ideal construction before material transformation, Zhang says machine learning simulates this process of 'conceptual construction'. Just as the machine system freed manual labour in the nineteenth century, AI frees mental labour today. Zhang holds that AI-generated content cannot objectify human emotion or serve as a final product, so it cannot replace human labour. Data, being easily copied, non-exclusive and gaining value when shared, undermines private ownership. Digital cultural production, small-scale and distributed, fits socialist public ownership better than capitalist mass hiring. Blockchain-based internet cooperation, Zhang suggests, makes Marx's 'one social labour force' conceivable. Zhang concludes that capitalist private ownership and the logic of capital, together with the hegemonic thinking of Western states, obstruct digital-intelligence productive forces, while socialism is suited to them and will reshape human civilisation in a fair and reasonable way. The article presents new quality productive forces and a community with a shared future for mankind as outcomes of this alignment. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical account, from within Chinese Party scholarship, of AI, data as a factor of production and mental labour.

The Communist Party of Argentina's exploration of the socialist road Analysis of the current situation and outlook 阿根廷共产党对社会主义道路的探索 Zhou Songfeng Zhou Miao The authors ask where the Communist Party of Argentina (PCA), founded in 1918, stands today and what its prospects are under the presidency of Javier Milei. They argue that the party's influence is limited by a hostile political climate and by weaknesses in its own organisation. They also contend that social crisis, working-class discontent and the resurgence of the Latin American left offer it new room for growth. The article first traces the party's origins: the early spread of socialist ideas in Argentina, including Marx's 1872 envoy to the International Workingmen's Association, and the growth of an immigrant-fed working class. It then reviews the party's present theory and practice, covering its economic nationalism, its critique of capitalism, its defence of workers and students, its 28th National Congress (September 2024), its websites and journal, and its alliances at home and abroad. Two sections follow on current challenges and future trends. In the authors' account, the PCA sees dependency on foreign capital and international financial institutions as the root of Argentina's problems. They cite the 2001 crisis and Monsanto's role in the soy sector as examples, and the party calls for state control of key industries and a socialist alternative. The authors then set out the party's difficulties. Milei's election and his alignment with Trump squeeze its space. Its reliance on larger left coalitions leaves it without seats in the legislature. It has about 130,000 members (2022) and an ageing leadership, and public sympathy for the left has fallen. Against this they set Milei's austerity, with a poverty rate of 52.9 per cent in the first half of 2024, the anger of workers and students, and the return of left governments across the region. The authors conclude that the PCA, though constrained, still has potential to promote social justice and regional unity among progressive forces. They expect it to keep seeking a socialist model suited to Argentine and regional conditions while defending workers' rights and pushing for anti-capitalist change. The article also notes that the party's delegations have visited China to study its experience. Read the original if you want a China-based overview of a small Latin American communist party, its recent congress and the reasons Chinese scholars give for its weakness and prospects.

From critique to reconstruction: the theoretical path of Yun Daiying's atheist thought 从批判到重构：恽代英无神论思想的理论进路 Li Yong Deng Ying This research article examines the atheist thought of Yun Daiying, an early Chinese Communist leader and May Fourth-era figure. Li and Deng argue that Yun moved from criticising theism to building a positive moral and life-value system without gods. In their account, this makes him a pioneer in adapting Marxist atheism to the Chinese context, although his thought has real limits. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical background: the "old superstition" of folk belief, the "foreign superstition" of spiritualism, the religionisation of Confucianism, and Christianity as cultural aggression. It also traces Yun's passage from anarchism, reformism and utopian socialism to Marxism, completed around 1921. The second part analyses his thought as "demolition" (po) and "construction" (li). The third assesses its value and limitations. Li and Deng argue that Yun first criticised the "old atheism", which denied gods simply because they were unknown. In their reading, Yun showed that ignorance can equally lead to belief, as it did for Kant and Spencer. He therefore rebuilt atheism on material realism, a dialectical epistemology that joins doubt with the knowability of truth, and historical materialism. On that basis he denied the existence and nature of gods, traced belief to "instinctive emotion" and "hazy knowledge", and condemned theism as a numbing consolation, a brake on science and a tool of class oppression and imperialist aggression. For the "construction" side, the authors report that Yun rejected faith as the main moral driver, proposing "wisdom and love" instead. He also derived goodness from experience and sympathy and denied that human life has a divine purpose. The authors credit Yun with breaking feudal ideological constraints, opposing imperialist cultural aggression in the anti-Christian movement, and laying a foundation for Chinese Marxist atheism. They also identify limits. His early thinking was inconsistent and showed the influence of empiricism and Kant, and his scepticism sometimes allowed that gods might not be absolutely ruled out. His attacks on Christianity lacked dialectical balance, and his class-struggle framing needs updating now that exploiting classes are said to have disappeared. Read the original if you study the history of Marxist atheism in China, or Yun Daiying's intellectual development and his anti-Christian writings.

Lenin's approach to resolving problems within the Party and the Chinese Communist Party's self-reform A textual study based on What Is to Be Done? 列宁解决党内问题的思路与中国共产党的自我革命 Guo Chao Yu Haiqing Guo and Yu ask what Lenin's What Is to Be Done? (1902) offers the Chinese Communist Party as it pursues the Party's self-reform. They argue that the book sets out a systematic method for dealing with internal problems that starts from members' ideas, and that the method still applies to the Party in the new era. The article opens with Xi Jinping's citation of Lenin on openly admitting mistakes. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Lenin's critical analysis of the Russian Social-Democratic Party's "confusion, disintegration and vacillation", including the roots and harms of "worship of spontaneity" and his rebuttal of the Economists' slogans. The second draws out Lenin's "scientific approach" in four elements: whom to win over, the form of struggle, the groundwork, and the channel. The third turns to five lessons for the Chinese Party. On the authors' reading, Lenin traced the crisis to Economist ideology, which they describe as trade-unionist and bourgeois in class character. Lenin treated the Economists' "demagogues" as opponents, while winning over the young members they misled and training workers as professional revolutionaries. The struggle was to be theoretical rather than merely organisational, grounded in materialist analysis of major real-life problems, and carried out through an all-Russia political newspaper. The authors say the paper would give scattered local groups a common "plumb line" and real ties among them. They hold that today's world remains in the historical era Marx identified, so ideological erosion and temptation still threaten Party members. They link the "four dangers" and "seven haves" to weak theoretical grounding. The authors draw five proposals. The Party should unify "curing the illness to save the patient" with high-pressure anti-corruption work. It should make criticism and self-criticism routine through discipline and leadership example. It should select a small number of readable, theoretically rigorous interpretive works as required reading, using central leadership, anonymous expert review and anonymous sampling of cadres' views. Finally, it should build a dedicated online platform for theoretical study and discussion among Party members, in the manner of Lenin's all-Russia newspaper. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-building study uses Lenin's text to justify ideological work and concrete study and discussion measures in the Party's self-reform.

Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao in the early Republican Confucian religion debate: theoretical exploration and leadership role 陈独秀、李大钊在民初孔教论争中的理论探索及其领导作用 Gu Mingshu Hu Xiaohong This article revisits the debate over Confucianism as a state religion in the early Republic of China. After the 1911 Revolution, Kang Youwei, Chen Huanzhang and others petitioned parliament to make Confucianism the state religion and write it into the constitution. Gu and Hu argue that Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, as leaders of the New Culture Movement, took a leading part in opposing this. In the authors' account, they also began to examine theoretical questions about religion, which makes the episode an early point of contact between Marxism and the study of religion in China. The article concentrates on the two state-religion campaigns of 1913–1914 and 1916–1917. It begins with the pre-debate period (1915–1916), when Chen and Li touched on religion in broader essays. It then covers Chen's rebuttal of Kang in New Youth (October 1916) and his exchange with the reader Yu Songhua. The remaining sections treat religion's essence and the nature of Confucianism, whether religion can be abolished, and the separation of religion and politics. A concluding section assesses the significance of the debate. Gu and Hu argue that Chen judged religion by the standard of science and democracy. He held that religion is an otherworldly faith resting on divine command and imagination, whereas Confucianism is a worldly ethical system and so not a religion. He therefore called for science to replace religion and expected all religions to be abandoned. Li, by contrast, explained religion through economic life and social development. The authors see in his work elements of the materialist conception of history, especially after the October Revolution, and read the debate as a shift from Western scientific and democratic thought to Marxism. On politics, the authors report that Chen opposed writing Confucianism into the constitution on grounds of separation of religion and state and freedom of belief. He accepted a Confucian association only as a private body. The authors conclude that the debate deepened the critique of religion and theism and advanced the New Culture Movement. They also see it as an initial union of Marxist views of religion with the study of Chinese religion, and as a first attempt at the Two Integrations in this field. They add that it left lessons for the Party's leadership of ideological debate: face problems directly, build theory, build a publishing platform such as New Youth, and guide young people. Read the original if you study the early Chinese Marxist view of religion, the New Culture Movement, or how contemporary scholars draw on this debate for ideological and political education.

Understanding the true meaning of "upholding a worldwide vision" What it means, why it is held, and how it is put into practice 深刻理解和把握“坚持胸怀天下”的思想真谛 Xu Yanling Xu Yanling takes up the principle of "upholding a worldwide vision" (jianchi xiongHuai tianxia), which the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) listed among the Party's historical experiences. The 20th Party Congress (2022) report presented it as part of the stance, viewpoint and method of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Xu argues that it should be grasped on three levels: what it means, why the Party holds it, and how it is carried out. The article follows this three-part structure. The first part sets out four components of the principle's meaning. The second traces its sources in Marxism, in traditional Chinese culture, in the Party's history from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, and in present-day global conditions. The third describes the practical path, summed up in four phrases: clarifying the great principle, creating great harmony, acting with great righteousness and taking the great way. In Xu's account, the principle means broadening the world outlook and developing global thinking, and it means pursuing shared destiny and common development. It also means responding to widespread concerns through global governance and deepening exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. Xu argues that it rests on the Marxist aim of human emancipation and on the Chinese idea of "all under heaven as one family". It is also confirmed by the Party's record of supporting other peoples' struggles, opposing hegemonism and pursuing peaceful development. For the present, Xu says the principle is a correct choice for a turbulent world marked by Cold War thinking, because China's certainty can offset the world's uncertainty. Xu holds that the practical path begins with shared human values: peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom. It continues with a community with a shared future for mankind, built at bilateral, regional and global levels. It also includes the Global Development, Global Security and Global Civilization Initiatives, the high-quality Belt and Road Initiative and a stronger voice for the Global South. Xu concludes that this is how the Party contributes Chinese wisdom, solutions and strength to human peace and development. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party theorists link the Party's global outlook to Marxism, Chinese tradition and current foreign-policy initiatives.

Promoting the great spirit of the Chinese nation and building a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation 弘扬中华民族伟大精神 构筑中华民族共有精神家园 Qiu Chunyan Fu Yanyan This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call to build a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation as cultural support for building the Chinese nation as a community. The authors argue that grasping the internal link between the great spirit of the Chinese nation and this shared spiritual home is the core route to forging a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation. The piece has two parts. The first sets out how the great spirit underpins the shared spiritual home. The second takes four components of that spirit in turn: creativity, struggle, unity and dream. In the first part, Qiu and Fu present the great spirit as the core of the shared home and identify four links between them: shared spiritual content, the transmission of history and culture, the strengthening of national identity, and resonance of values. They name patriotism, collectivism and the core socialist values as the value basis that unites the ethnic groups within a pattern of "diversity in unity". In the second part they assign each component a role. Creativity energises innovation and cultural confidence. Struggle mobilises all ethnic groups for the Chinese Dream. Unity strengthens cohesion and is called the lifeline of the Chinese people. The dream spirit integrates personal and national aspirations and is described as the soul of the shared home. The authors conclude that promoting these four aspects in the new era will strengthen identification with the Chinese nation and culture, and will keep the shared spiritual home vital. They also link this to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official ethnic-unity discourse ties the great spirit of the Chinese nation to nation-community building.

Grasping scientifically the stance and direction of the great struggle 科学把握伟大斗争的立场和方向 Chen Long This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2025, takes up a passage in which Xi Jinping says that risks and challenges threatening the Party's leadership, the socialist system, national sovereignty and security, core interests, the people's fundamental interests or the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation must be met with resolute struggle and victory. Chen Long argues that this passage settles the question of stance and direction in the "great struggle", and also sets basic requirements and methods for it. The piece is short and has three sections. The first concerns the need for a clear understanding of the "fundamental questions" of struggle. The second deals with holding firmly to the people's stance. The third deals with upholding Party leadership and the socialist direction. Chen draws on Xi Jinping, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, and on the Party's history from the revolutionary period to reform. Chen's first move is that leaders need clear heads about what banner to raise and what road to take, since in Xi's words a large country cannot make "subversive errors" on fundamental questions. Chen says this clarity comes from understanding the "new historical characteristics" of the struggle, namely a world of great change and the demands of national rejuvenation at home, and from a firm grasp of Marxism and the Party's innovative theory. Second, Chen presents the people's stance as the Party's fundamental political stance, rooted in Marxism's aim of human liberation and in the Party's purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly; the people are described as the Party's greatest support against risks. Third, Chen holds that reform and innovation must have a direction, neither rigid and closed nor a change of banner. The direction is the self-improvement of the socialist system, which Chen says depends on the Party's comprehensive leadership and, at its core, on upholding the authority of the Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership. Chen concludes that Chinese modernization requires standing firm on the people's stance, adhering to the socialist direction and maintaining Party leadership without wavering. Chen calls on Party members to grasp the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, hold to the Four-sphere Confidence and carry out the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the ideological basis of "struggle" in the Xi Jinping era, for study of official discourse.

Raising university teachers' ideological and political leadership through the "four guides" 以“四个引路人”提升高校教师的思政引领力 Wang Gang Wang Gang takes up a concept Xi Jinping first used at the National Education Conference in September 2024: "ideological and political leadership" (sizheng yinlingli), placed first among the six strengths of a strong education nation. Wang argues that for university teachers of ideological and political courses, Xi's call to be "guides" in four respects offers the fundamental guideline for raising this capacity. The four are shaping character, acquiring knowledge, innovative thinking and dedication to the motherland. This short commentary in a newspaper devotes one section to each of the four guides. Each section sets out three tasks for teachers. A closing section treats the four as a single system. In Wang's account, character is built through teachers' own ethics, value guidance and a sense of rules. Knowledge rests on solid scholarship, effective teaching methods and taking students out into society through "walking" classes. Innovative thinking is cultivated through heuristic teaching, free expression and intelligent technology such as VR and AI. Dedication to the country is nurtured through family-and-country feeling, a sense of mission and digital tools, including a proposed assessment system for students' patriotic sentiment. Wang presents the four as a closed loop of values, knowledge, methodology and attachment to family and country. Wang concludes that teachers who consistently take the "four guides" as their guideline will raise ideological and political leadership and train a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a prescriptive statement of Party-line pedagogy, with examples from classroom practice. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Xi's educational directives are being turned into teaching guidance for university ideological and political courses.

Continuously strengthening the targeting of ideological and political theory courses 不断增强思政课的针对性 Ren Peng This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2025, takes up one of the four qualities Xi Jinping has asked of university ideological and political theory courses (sixiang zheng zhi ke): ideological depth, theoretical rigour, affinity and targeting. Ren Peng argues that targeting (zhenduixing) is the most basic precondition, because depth, rigour and approachable language all depend on it to reach, guide and win over students. The article first explains why targeting matters and then diagnoses present shortcomings. It ends with practical proposals. Ren defines targeting as a precise fit between what is taught and what students need, with the student at the centre and content and methods adjusted to different learners. On the case for targeting, Ren offers three reasons: it determines teaching effectiveness, since the courses differ in whether they stress principles, history or values and should not be taught uniformly; it answers students' confusions, such as those over "involution" and "lying flat"; and it serves the fundamental task of cultivating successors to the socialist cause. On the problems, Ren points to three: teachers' limited grasp of students' varied thinking, teachers' own capacity and thin practical experience, and teaching methods that lag behind, including superficial use of AI and VR and a gap between textbook and online language. Ren proposes that teachers adopt a "user mindset", carry out first-hand research among students and tailor courses to different majors. They should also draw fresh material from reform and development practice. On method, Ren calls for genuine use of big data and AI in "digital integration" of courses, and for recasting academic, policy and textbook language into the idiom of young people. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-school scholar frames the aims and practical problems of ideological and political course reform in 2025.

Multidimensional innovation in building ideological and political courses in the new era 新时代思政课建设的多维创新 Deng Yan This short commentary asks how practical teaching in university ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) can overcome the problem of 'stressing theoretical indoctrination while neglecting practical cultivation'. Deng argues that the answer is to build practice teaching around General Secretary Xi Jinping's inspection tours of localities, guided by the principle of unifying theory and practice within the 'Eight Unifications'. The aim is to let students move between the 'small classroom' of the course and the 'big classroom' of society. The article is organised around one main line, two driving forces, a three-dimensional content system and four types of teaching vehicle. It cites Xi's remarks on the 'great ideological and political course', on teacher guidance and student-centred teaching, and on content drawn from socialism with Chinese characteristics. It closes by linking the model to the Outline for Building a Strong Education Nation (2024–2035). Deng's central moves are as follows. First, local inspection sites supply concrete cases that tie general policy to familiar places and people, which the author says counters fragmented resources, abstract theory and shallow emotion. Second, teachers' leading role and students' initiative are combined through learning-profile modelling with intelligent technology, interdisciplinary work and government–enterprise–university cooperation. Third, content is organised under four themes: rural revitalisation, cultural heritage, science and technology, and ecology. It is delivered through mobile classrooms, short films, online writing in Gen-Z idiom and think-tank-style reports. Deng concludes that turning inspection routes into teaching routes is a creative application of the unity of theory and practice and a contemporary practice of the Marxist view of practice. In Deng's account it moves students from 'ideological awakening' to 'awakening to mission'. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars propose to build leader-centred local case studies into university political-course teaching.

The anti-corruption struggle in the new era has won the Party the historical initiative 新时代反腐败斗争为党赢得历史主动 Tian Peiyan This commentary, first published in the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News on 24 April 2025, interprets a judgement Xi Jinping made at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Xi held that the new era's anti-corruption struggle has won the Party two forms of "historical initiative". The first is keeping the Party from degenerating in nature, colour or flavour. The second is uniting and leading the people in building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. Tian Peiyan argues that grasping this judgement strengthens confidence and clarity for pressing the struggle further, so that the Party's great self-reform can lead the great social revolution. The article has three parts. The first sets the anti-corruption record in a lineage running from Marx, Engels and Lenin through the Party's early history. That history includes the 1926 notice on purging corrupt elements, the harsh Soviet-period and Shaan-Gan-Ning regulations, and the post-1949 campaigns, among them the execution of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan. The second part sets out what the struggle has achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to how the struggle should continue. In Tian's account, the new-era campaign carried forward the Party's tradition of resisting corruption and has raised its capacity to do so. The author credits Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building and on the Party's self-reform, and a mechanism that advances "not daring, not being able and not wanting to be corrupt" together. It has also created a deterrent momentum in which, the author says, there are no untouchable people or forbidden zones. The second initiative is shown through stronger Party leadership and political supervision, with 12,000 people disciplined for political violations in 2024. Tian also cites cleaner finance, state enterprises and livelihood sectors, a better business environment, and stronger public cohesion. Tian warns that the situation remains "severe and complex", pointing to unremoved stock and new increments of corruption, collusion between officials and business, hidden new-type corruption, and incomplete supervision. The author rejects both complacent optimism and the view that anti-corruption harms growth. The article calls for strategic resolve, deeper work on the three "nots" through punishment, institutional reform and education, and combined effort by Party committees, discipline bodies, departments and the public, with Party-building work linked to the struggle. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-discipline media present anti-corruption as a source of political legitimacy and a framework for next steps.

Strengthening conduct building to energise a sound Party organisational system 加强作风建设为健全组织体系注入动力 Ming Yang Peng Zhaolong This short commentary, published in Study Times on 23 April 2025, asks how the Party's organisational system can be improved in quality and function as well as in coverage. Ming and Peng argue that work-style (conduct) building is the "soul-like bond" running through that system and an important guarantee of the vitality of Party organisations at every level. The piece has two parts. The first sets out three effects of good conduct: greater cohesion and fighting strength, stronger leadership and execution, and greater appeal and influence in emerging fields. The second proposes three ways of building conduct into organisational development. Throughout, the authors illustrate their points with the work of the Henan Jiao Yulu Cadre College, where they appear to work, as the campaign to study and implement the central Eight-point Regulation is under way. The authors argue that top-down, tier-by-tier conduct practice gives the system vertical reach, and that conduct building helps remove "paper implementation" so that central decisions are carried out in full. They note that 84 million workers in new forms of employment, 21% of the workforce, make Party building in emerging fields necessary, and they present flexible Party organisation and online branches as examples. Their practical proposals are three-tier theoretical study with dual assessment of study results and conduct; stricter requirements for the "key minority" of leaders, including a "top leader" project, negative lists and dynamic conduct files; and grassroots institutional measures such as star ratings for branches. The authors conclude that conduct building and a sound organisational system reinforce each other, and that the current campaign should use conduct as a breakthrough point to optimise structure and upgrade function. They present the college's courses, case teaching and its teaching site in Lankao County as practical models. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-school practice is linked to the official discourse on conduct building and organisational development.

Upholding the mass line: key historical lessons from rule-of-law building in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region 坚持群众路线：陕甘宁边区法治建设的重要历史经验 Xu Shi Writing in Guangming Daily (23 April 2025), Xu Shi argues that the mass line, described as the Party's lifeline and fundamental working line, has consistently guided the Party's leadership of legal construction. The commentary takes the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region of the Yan'an period as its case. Xu contends that its legal system always put the people's needs and interests at the centre, and that this earned popular support and laid foundations for victory in the War of Resistance and the Liberation War and for legal construction in the People's Republic. The piece is a short historical commentary that follows the legal process from legislation through adjudication and mediation to legal education and cadre discipline. Xu notes that in 13 years the Border Region government issued more than 1,000 laws, regulations and normative or programmatic documents. Evidence includes the Border Region's governing programmes, its regulations on human rights and property rights and on elections, and the judicial practice of Ma Xiwu and Xi Zhongxun's instructions to judicial personnel. Xu's core argument is that the mass line was built into each stage. In legislation, Party policy set the direction, the Three-Thirds system and general elections broadened participation, and laws were issued only after investigation, consultation and majority agreement in the Border Council. In the courts, on-the-spot and circuit trials, oral complaints, waived fees and the 'Ma Xiwu method' of trial, illustrated by the 1943 Feng Pen'er marriage case, are presented as making justice accessible. Xu adds people's mediation committees, which drew on local custom, and legal education delivered through literacy classes, newspapers, drama and songs. Xu stresses that the mass line also requires leading cadres to set an example and requires full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Examples cited include the 1937 death sentence on Huang Kegong, anti-corruption regulations, the rule that Communists who break the law are punished more severely, cadre training, and a right of citizens to accuse officials. Xu also cites the execution of the trade official Xiao Yubi after villagers reported him, and Lin Boqu's personal replies to more than a hundred complaint letters. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how Yan'an-era legal practice is presented today as a model of the mass line in law.

A historical examination of the Party's organisational strength building during the War of Resistance against Japan 抗战时期党的组织力建设的历史考察 Xiong Qiuliang Xiong Qiuliang asks how the Communist Party of China built up its organisational strength (zuzhili) during the War of Resistance against Japan, and what that experience offers today. Defining organisational strength as the Party's capacity to mobilise, organise and unite cadres and the masses to carry out its line, Xiong argues that the Party grew from small and weak to large and strong in this period and served as the mainstay of national resistance. This is a short commentary in Guangming Daily, supported by a major National Social Science Fund project on Party membership building. The article is organised around four components of organisational strength, each linked to a wartime practice: a lofty organisational goal (leading capacity), a tight organisational system (cohesion), a well-built Party membership (combat effectiveness) and close ties with the people (power to call on the masses). Xiong draws on speeches and documents by Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun and Peng Zhen, on Party resolutions, and on examples from the Yan'an centre and the base areas. On leadership, Xiong stresses theoretical study and ideological education at Yan'an, together with Mao's On Protracted War and his theory of New Democracy, which are said to have given the Party and the people a clear sense of the revolution's course. On cohesion, Xiong cites the 1942 decision unifying leadership in the base areas under Party committees, democratic centralism, and the 'four subordinations' adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (1938), enforced through Party regulations and expulsions. On membership, Xiong describes the rapid expansion from 1938, reaching 800,000 members by 1940, and then the 1939 decision on consolidating the Party after 'sudden expansion' and campaign-style recruitment let in unqualified people. On mass work, Xiong argues that Party branches won support by meeting practical needs: rent and interest reduction, the production campaign, the 'three-thirds' system, elections and winter schools. Xiong concludes that wartime experience shows organisational strength rests on firm ideals, strict structure and discipline, quality membership, and a livelihood-based bond with the people, and that it offers lessons for advancing the Party's 'great new project' of Party building in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of how Party historians present wartime Party building, with references to the primary sources it cites.

Grasping the inherent unity of Party discipline and getting things done 把握党的纪律和干事创业的内在统一性 Wu Yating Tang Xiaoqin This newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 23 April 2025) takes up Xi Jinping's statement at a Politburo democratic life meeting in December 2024 that Party discipline both educates and constrains, and also protects and motivates, so that discipline and getting things done are inherently unified. Wu and Tang argue that the remark summarises experience from full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era and gives guidance for strengthening discipline while encouraging officials to take initiative. The authors first trace the Party's emphasis on discipline from the first programme of 1921 through Mao Zedong, the early People's Republic and Deng Xiaoping to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). They then set out the relationship between discipline and enterprise, and close with two practical directions for the new journey. Wu and Tang contend that discipline works in two ways. It marks bottom lines and boundaries, acting as a safety barrier that keeps officials honest and on the right track. It also gives them freedom and space to act, since clear rules and a clean political ecology protect officials who want to and can get things done. Because the Party has long been in power, they say, officials without experience of severe trials may drift into comfort-seeking or confusion. They therefore propose centring discipline education on the Party's central tasks, with struggle and responsibility education to lift officials' sense of mission. They also call for accurate use of the "four forms" of supervision and discipline enforcement and strict application of the "three distinctions", to address officials who act recklessly, fail to act, dare not act or act poorly. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line statement of how current Party discipline work is linked to calls for officials' initiative.

Understanding the centenary course, achievements and basic experience of Chinese trade unions under Party leadership 深刻领悟党领导的中国工会百年历程、成就和基本经验 Liu Xiangbing Marking the centenary of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions (ACFTU), founded at the Second National Labour Congress in Guangzhou on 1 May 1925, this commentary reviews what a century of Party-led trade unionism has meant. Liu Xiangbing, writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2025, argues that Chinese unions have always rallied around the Communist Party and mobilised workers around its programme and the central tasks of each period. The author presents the history as a resource for carrying forward the workers' movement in a new era. The article has three parts: the course of the unions' history, their achievements, and the experience drawn from them. The historical section follows the unions through the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It opens with the Party's First Congress resolution of 1921 and the Secretariat of the Chinese Labour Union. In Liu's account, the achievements include contributing to the founding of New China, consolidating the Party's governing base and state power, acting as the main force in economic development and modernization, supporting harmonious and stable labour relations, and promoting the spirit of model workers, labour and craftsmanship. The core argument lies in five lessons. Liu holds that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of union work, and that unions must serve the Party's central tasks, which in the new era means striving for the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Unions must act as a bridge and link between Party and workers and as an important social pillar of state power. They must also protect workers' legitimate rights and serve them wholeheartedly. Finally, they must keep reforming and innovating. Throughout, the author relies heavily on statements by Xi Jinping. Liu concludes that these experiences are of lasting importance for union work and for developing a trade union path with Chinese characteristics. The author stresses that unions should safeguard workers' rights while also representing the overall interests of the people, and that their greatest danger is losing contact with workers. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party narrative on the role and history of the Chinese trade union movement.

The current state of ideological and political short videos and paths to improving their reach 思政短视频传播的现实镜像与优化路径 Liu Chao Short videos have become a new platform for ideological and political education in universities, but Liu argues that their communication effect is held back by weak production teams and distorting platform algorithms. Writing in April 2025, the author links the question to the Education Power Plan Outline (2024–2035), which calls for deeper integration of ideological and political work with information technology. Liu holds that raising the quality of such videos is the best way to build a distinctive online ideological and political education brand. This short newspaper commentary has two parts. It first describes three problems: formulaic content, weakly professional operating teams, and value drift under recommendation algorithms. It then proposes four remedies covering content, teams, algorithms and an intelligent communication ecosystem. On content, Liu criticises the "teacher on camera plus slideshow" format and calls for micro-narratives, timely responses to young people's anxieties, and a move from transmitting knowledge to generating meaning. On teams and platforms, the author urges incentives, "ideological and political education plus communication" graduates, regular exchange between ideological and political experts and new-media staff, and algorithms that move from traffic first to value first, with ideological-education weighting, AI content screening and a feedback loop. Liu also proposes shared resource libraries, matrix distribution across platforms and tiered communication for students and the wider public. Liu concludes that these videos are both an innovation in digital-age education and a strategic need for mainstream ideology to hold online ground. The author calls for balance between technological instrumentality and value-led agency, and for a systemic approach of content first, technology as enabler and mechanisms as safeguard. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese university lecturer frames the practical problems and policy options of online ideological and political education.

Key issues in a century of philological study of The German Ideology 《德意志意识形态》百年文献学焦点问题探析 Zhao Yulan The German Ideology, written by Marx and Engels in 1845–47 and never published in their lifetime, is widely regarded as the work marking the birth of the materialist conception of history. Zhao Yulan reviews a century of philological work on the manuscript, which has produced more than ten editions, and identifies three questions that have dominated scholarly attention: how the text should be presented, what form of writing it represents, and which chapter is its core. In each case Zhao defends the established view against the position taken in the latest historical-critical edition. The short article first traces the editions: Riazanov's 1924 and 1926 publications of the "Feuerbach" chapter, the complete MEGA1 text of 1932, the new Feuerbach editions after Barna's 1962 discovery in Amsterdam, and the MEGA2 pre-edition (2004) and full volume (2017). It also notes a 2018 chronological edition by Hubmann and Pagel and a 2019 online Feuerbach edition produced by Chinese and Japanese scholars. It then takes the three disputed questions in turn. On presentation, Zhao sets out the shift from logical ordering (Riazanov, MEGA1, the 1960s editions) to Taubert's chronological ordering in 2004, and then the MEGA2 editors' rejection of it in 2017, which Zhao calls a "negation of the negation". On form, Zhao argues that the MEGA2 "quarterly journal" thesis, first proposed by Galina Golovina in 1980, explains only the project's origin. After the break with the Westphalian backers in 1846, Zhao says, Marx and Engels withdrew other contributors' texts, and Marx's 1860 letter refers to "a work" in two volumes, so the text remains a work. On the core chapter, Zhao rejects the MEGA2 editors' preference for the "Saint Max" chapter, because its bulk comes largely from line-by-line quotation of Stirner. Pages 1–29 of the Feuerbach manuscript, Zhao adds, were written first and do not derive from it. Zhao concludes that the "Feuerbach" chapter keeps its unique status, and that the choice of ordering depends on whether the manuscripts are treated as unfinished texts or as parts of a work. The article closes by saying that thorough philological study can deepen understanding of the text and support independent Chinese research on Marxist texts, contributing to an autonomous system of knowledge in Chinese philosophy and social sciences. Read the original if you want a compact overview of the editorial history of The German Ideology and a Chinese scholar's response to the MEGA2 editors' positions.

Making deepened theoretical armament run through every aspect of university ideological and political courses 将深化理论武装贯穿高校思政课建设全过程各方面 Xu Tao This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 23 April 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's instruction that the building of ideological and political courses in schools should advance in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory. The instruction is also written into the Outline of the Plan for Building a Strong Education Country (2024–2035). Xu Tao argues that deepening this theoretical armament is of the utmost importance for university ideological and political courses, and that the courses should be used to train a new generation who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and ready to shoulder national rejuvenation. The piece is organised under three headings: securing the political direction of the courses, consolidating their content, and stimulating innovative thinking in how they are run. Xu writes from the standpoint of a university Party secretary and gives practical measures at each level, from curriculum design and teacher training to student practice and campus culture. Examples are drawn mainly from university practice, such as finance and economics institutions. On political direction, Xu holds that Marxism must be the fundamental guide and that students should be taught through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author also calls for integrating the courses with course-embedded ideological education across all subjects, and for a stronger sense of universities as ideological front lines that resist erroneous trends of thought and monitor student attitudes. On content, Xu urges rigorous, scholarly exposition of Party theory with critical-thinking training, attention to its historical and traditional-cultural roots, and new modules such as an introductory course on Xi Jinping Thought on economics, developed jointly by Marxism and economics schools. On innovation, Xu proposes organised research platforms across disciplines, stronger teacher training and collective lesson preparation, "micro-innovations" such as a first-day class given by model figures, and practice bases, rural visits and entrepreneurship projects so that students apply theory. Xu concludes that high-quality development of these courses requires sustained effort and ever more thorough theoretical armament, together with new approaches and plans. The text is a policy-oriented statement of how a university leadership frames the task, and it offers concrete examples of implementation. Read the original if you want a short, official-register account of how university leaders translate the directive on theoretical armament into curriculum, teaching and campus-management measures.

Linking up the correction of work styles, the enforcement of discipline and the fight against corruption 把正风肃纪反腐贯通起来 Xin Xiangli This short commentary, published in 2025, takes up the Party's current campaign on conduct and discipline. Xin argues that correcting work styles (zhengfeng), enforcing discipline (suji) and fighting corruption must be treated as one connected task rather than three separate ones. The piece follows the launch of a Party-wide study and education drive on the spirit of the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and Xi Jinping's call, made during inspections in Guizhou and Yunnan, to link the three together. The commentary is built in four steps. It first sets out why work style matters to popular support, then explains the internal link between improper work styles and corruption. It next reviews the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally turns to the Party's present responsibilities and what Party organisations at all levels should do. Xin's central claim is that improper work styles and corruption share the same root and feed each other. In this reading the "four undesirable work styles" run counter to the Party's nature and purpose, while corruption erodes its governing foundation. Handling them together, by investigating corruption through work-style problems and correcting work style through corruption cases, is said to cut the chains of interest that bind the two. Xin acknowledges that in some places the problems have rebounded and that blind spots remain, so the effort must be sustained. Xin concludes that a Marxist governing party of more than 99 million members and over 5 million primary-level organisations needs systems thinking to advance Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The proposals include mechanisms for jointly investigating and handling work-style and corruption cases, attention to Party spirit, work style and discipline together, and a focused, practical study and education drive. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media currently frame the link between work style, discipline and anti-corruption.

The people's congress system as an important institutional vehicle for realising whole-process people's democracy in China 人民代表大会制度是实现我国全过程人民民主的重要制度载体 Wang Haifeng Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech marking the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress (NPC), this article from Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2025 no. 6) argues that the people's congress system is an important institutional vehicle for realising whole-process people's democracy. Wang Haifeng holds that the system must be upheld under Communist Party leadership and that an institutional framework must secure the people's position as masters of the country. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical and practical significance of whole-process people's democracy. The second explains why the fundamental political system carries it. The third lists measures to uphold, improve and operate the people's congress system so that it performs this role. Wang presents whole-process people's democracy as an original concept of Xi Jinping that enriches the Marxist theory of the state, and as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. In the article's account, it links democratic election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight into one chain, and unites process and outcome, procedural and substantive democracy, direct and indirect democracy, and the people's democracy and the will of the state. The people's congress system carries this, Wang argues, in three ways. Its design embodies the constitutional principle that all power belongs to the people, and the executive, supervisory, judicial and procuratorial organs are created by, answerable to and supervised by the congresses.
