Its election, consultation, decision-making and oversight mechanisms operate the chain. The system also turns Party proposals into state will through legal procedure. Wang cites the 2021 revision of the NPC Organic Law and the 2022 revision of the Local Organic Law, which wrote whole-process democracy into law. Wang calls for upholding the organic unity of Party leadership, the people's position as masters of the country and law-based governance. Further proposals include improving the socialist legal system with Chinese characteristics centred on the Constitution, and strengthening congress oversight of the executive, supervisory, judicial and procuratorial organs. Wang also urges supporting deputies in performing their duties under Party leadership, with grassroots legislative liaison points and better contact with constituents, and building up the congresses and their standing committees themselves. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official Party-school account of how the people's congress system is tied to whole-process people's democracy, including the specific institutional measures it recommends.

Achieving positive interaction between high-quality development and high-standard security 实现高质量发展和高水平安全良性互动 Tang Junfeng Writing in Guangming Daily in April 2025, Tang Junfeng takes up the Party's call, repeated at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), to coordinate development and security. Tang argues that high-quality development and high-level security support each other and form a dialectical unity. National security is presented as the foundation on which Chinese modernization can proceed steadily. The short commentary has three parts. The first explains why national security underpins Chinese modernization, citing China's historical experience of foreign bullying and war and a present international environment the author describes as marked by unilateralism, protectionism and uncertainty. The second sets out how high-quality development and high-level security relate to each other. The third turns to practical measures for the new journey. In the central section, Tang describes development as the Party's first priority, to be pursued through the new development philosophy, with innovation, coordination, green, open and shared development each answering a particular problem. Security, in turn, is both a condition for development and a yardstick of its results. The author holds that higher-quality development changes what security requires. Protection must move from single fields to systemic, multi-dimensional coverage: economic security stresses industrial resilience and autonomy, data and network security face contests between attack and defence, and military security faces intelligent technologies. Security boundaries must therefore be adjusted dynamically to find the best balance between efficiency and stability, openness and self-reliance, and innovation and risk. Neither side should be stressed at the other's expense. Tang proposes three lines of action: resolutely applying the holistic approach to national security, including absolute Party leadership and the "ten adherences"; modernizing the national security system and capacity, with the aim of a higher-level "Peaceful China" and a new security architecture to safeguard the new development pattern; and treating security as a shared responsibility of the whole of society. The last includes breaking down departmental and local barriers, clarifying chains of responsibility, and expanding national security education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-state commentary links the development–security agenda to Chinese modernization and the holistic approach to national security.

Mastering the lifelong task of the Communist: Xi Jinping on Party spirit cultivation Xi Jinping's emphasis on "Party spirit cultivation" 修好共产党人的终身课题 Ma Xiaomei This commentary, published in Study Times in April 2025, sets out what General Secretary Xi Jinping has said about Party spirit cultivation (dangxing xiuyang) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Ma defines the practice as Party members' self-education, self-reform and self-improvement, and presents Xi's statements as the fundamental guide for training the "study of the heart" of Communists in the new era. The piece proceeds chronologically through six Xi texts or speeches: on the Party Constitution (2012), the national organisation work conference (2013), the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection plenary (2016), an inspection in Tibet (2021), the closing session of the 20th Party Congress (2022), and the Politburo democratic life meeting (December 2024). Ma's reading is that Xi treats Party spirit as something never finished: it is not innate, does not grow automatically with seniority or rank, and requires lifelong effort, like a room that must be cleaned regularly. The Party Constitution is the basic standard, and leading cadres must set the example. Xi also draws on fine traditional Chinese culture and the Two Integrations, and on the founding spirit of the Party. Ma reports that the later texts put political cultivation first, tie it to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and require that Party spirit keep pace with theoretical innovation. Ma concludes that Party members should study and observe the Party Constitution, draw on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and keep loyalty to the Party Central Committee as their basic political responsibility. Read the original if you want a compact, dated chronology of Xi's main statements on Party member self-cultivation as the official press presents them.

Problems of work style are essentially problems of Party spirit 作风问题本质上是党性问题 Hong Xianghua Zhang Guangze This commentary, published in the Party's discipline-inspection newspaper in April 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's formula that problems of work style are essentially problems of Party spirit. Hong and Zhang argue that Party spirit is the inner foundation of work style and work style its outward expression: a pure Party spirit yields correct conduct, an impure one does not. The piece is organised in four short sections. It treats cadres' conduct as a barometer of public judgement of the Party, political life within the Party as a purifier, firm ideals and convictions as the root of good work style, and the cultivation of Party spirit as a lifelong task. It draws on Yan'an-era and revolutionary examples and on conduct since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors contend that cadres' attitudes and conduct directly shape popular trust, and that neglecting work style erects an invisible wall between Party and people. They describe serious, rigorous inner-Party political life as a means of filtering out harmful elements and as the soil in which good style grows. Conviction, in their account, is the root: they cite Jinggangshan frugality, the Huaihai campaign, Huang Wenxiu and Zhang Fuqing as cases where ideals became practical conduct, with loyalty to the Party as the key test. Hong and Zhang call on Party members to place political training first, draw on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, treat Party rules as a constant mirror, and strengthen inner-Party supervision. Work style building, they say, is never finished. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building commentary links discipline, ideology and public trust.

Promoting a new type of relationship between the Communist Party of China and political parties of the world 推动构建新型的中国共产党与世界政党关系 Liu Jianchao Writing in Qiushi in 2025, Liu Jianchao, identified as head of the CPC's International Department, asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) should build a new type of relationship with political parties worldwide. Liu argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the CPC has moved from friendly exchanges to a leading role among the world's parties. The task now, Liu says, is to consolidate a global network of party partnerships under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece has three parts. The first describes four ways in which the CPC has become a pioneer, leader, promoter and supporter among world parties. The second sets out the new situation, tasks and opportunities. The third lists four lines of work for the Party's external work. Liu cites figures such as contacts with more than 700 parties and political organisations in over 170 countries by the end of 2024, and a June 2024 briefing in Xiong'an attended by representatives of about 40 countries. In Liu's account, the CPC explores the laws of governing for ruling parties, shares governance experience, widens exchanges without ideological dividing lines, and supplies global public goods such as the community with a shared future for mankind, the three global initiatives and the Belt and Road Initiative. Liu reports that foreign party figures value this experience and that some parties wish to build their own versions of "socialism with distinctive features". Liu presents three drivers for a new relationship: parties' heavier responsibility in a turbulent world, governance challenges from social change and artificial intelligence, and global divisions and realignments that no party can handle alone. Liu proposes four tasks: strengthen the global party partnership network through political dialogue, the high-level dialogue between the CPC and world political parties, and BRICS and Shanghai Cooperation Organisation channels; promote mutual learning on governance; deepen development cooperation, including a "party plus" platform and support for each ruling party's own path to modernization; and bring peoples closer through cultural exchange, Belt and Road livelihood projects and think-tank alliances. Liu says this will create a favourable external environment for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an official statement from the Party's foreign-liaison leadership on how the CPC frames its inter-party diplomacy in 2025.

The historical-analytical method of the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》的历史分析方法 Shan Chuanyou Shan Chuanyou asks by what method Marx and Engels reached the Communist Manifesto's two central conclusions: the inevitable downfall of capitalism and the inevitable victory of the proletariat. The article answers that this was the historical analysis method. Applied from the standpoint of world history and through the basic laws of historical development, it underlies the Manifesto's account of capitalism, the proletariat and rival socialisms. This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Journal in April 2025, is organised in five parts. These cover the world-historical perspective, the historical position of capitalism, the mission of the proletariat and its party, the historical errors of competing socialist currents, and the dependence of revolutionary practice on concrete historical conditions. Shan draws mainly on the Manifesto, with a reference to The German Ideology and to the prefaces of 1872 and 1882. Shan makes three main moves. First, capitalism and world history form one process: the bourgeoisie opened the world market and subordinated backward nations and the East to the West, which also extends class antagonism worldwide and creates the conditions for international proletarian unity. Second, capitalism is assessed dialectically. It brought formal personal freedom and an unprecedented growth of productive forces, but private appropriation, periodic crises and overproduction mean it will be sublated, and it produces its own gravediggers in the proletariat. Third, the author reads the Manifesto's critique of reactionary, conservative and utopian socialisms as a charge of historical error. In Shan's reading, these currents try to turn back history, to stay fixed in the present, or to leap beyond history. Shan stresses that the Manifesto's guidance for Communists in France, Switzerland, Poland and Germany varies with national circumstances. The 1872 and 1882 prefaces likewise hold that the basic principles are correct but their application depends on concrete conditions. The author concludes that, under new historical conditions, researchers should still use a world-historical perspective and the basic laws of history to study the new features of capitalism and to develop Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-academic reading of the Manifesto's method, framed for current work on Marxist theory in China.

Accurately understanding the basic tenets of Marxism in the "Two Integrations" 准确理解“两个结合”中的马克思主义基本原理 Tao Wenzhao Tao Wenzhao takes up a term that, in his view, is neglected in current discussion of the Two Integrations: "the basic tenets of Marxism" (Marxist basic principles), which holds the leading position in the formula. The Two Integrations join Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. Tao argues that grasping the formula correctly first requires grasping this term correctly. This short commentary appeared in Beijing Daily in April 2025. The article has four parts. It traces how the wording has changed in Party usage; it distinguishes broad and narrow senses of "Marxism"; it explains why "basic tenets" replaced "universal truth"; and it indicates what the basic tenets contain. Tao draws on the Selected Works of Mao Zedong, later volumes of Mao's writings, and statements by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On wording, Tao reports that before 1949 the Party spoke almost entirely of "universal truth", and that "basic tenets" became the prevailing usage only after reform and opening up. Tao treats the older and current phrasings as substantively identical, but sees the current one as more precise. On scope, Tao reasons that because the other terms in the formula already carry "China", Marxism there must mean classical Marxism from outside China. Yet Tao adds that later "integrations" should reasonably take in the existing results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, Mao Zedong Thought above all. The phrase "basic tenets" also screens out scattered individual judgements, dogmatic readings and tacked-on erroneous views, which Tao says helps prevent copying texts mechanically. Tao says the tenets consist first of a worldview and methodology, namely the stance, viewpoint and method that Xi Jinping calls the living soul of Marxism, including seeking truth from facts. Tao also lists major propositions from philosophy (the material world; productive forces and relations of production; base and superstructure), political economy (labour as the source of value; surplus value) and scientific socialism (the historical tendency towards socialism and the free and all-round development of each person). The author stresses that no such list is exhaustive or fixed, and that the tenets should be viewed developmentally. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Party terminology around the Two Integrations has evolved and how a Chinese Marxist scholar defines the term "basic tenets".

Winning the historical initiative through the Party's self-purification of its conduct 在党风的自我净化中赢得历史主动 Li Zhongjie Li Zhongjie, a Party historian, takes up Xi Jinping's warning that the Party's conduct (zuofeng) bears on its image, public support and ultimate survival. He argues that, across more than a century, improving conduct has been a continuous process of self-purification through which the Party has won the historical initiative. In his account, this process must continue if the Party is to escape the "historical cycle" of rise and decline. The piece, published in Qiushi in 2025, is a Party-historical commentary in two parts. The first surveys conduct-building from the founding through the revolutionary years, the early People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the eight-point rule. The second draws five reflections from this record. Li's historical narrative links conduct to survival at each stage: the Rectification Movement in Yan'an, the Two Musts before the Party took power, and the successive anti-corruption measures under reform. For the present era he presents the eight-point rule against the "four undesirable work styles" (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance) as the entry point of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. His five reflections hold that conduct expresses the Party's nature and vitality, that it must always be viewed as a matter of life and death, and that it is never finished. He also says the Party's two answers to the historical cycle are Mao Zedong's "new path of democracy" and Xi's self-reform. Finally, he says the Party must be purified yet remain full of vitality. Li concludes that, in a more complex international and domestic setting, only thorough self-reform and a sound system of full and rigorous self-governance can keep the Party self-purifying and self-improving. He says this should not produce a lifeless organisation but a healthy political ecology in which cadres take initiative and society stays dynamic as well as orderly. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party presents the history of its conduct-building and the reasoning behind the eight-point rule and the self-reform campaign.

Habermas's revision of the consensus theory of truth and its contemporary implications 哈贝马斯对真理共识论的修正及其当代启示 Huang Meidi Huang Meidi examines how Jürgen Habermas revised his consensus theory of truth in Truth and Justification (1999). The author argues that Habermas abandoned truth as an epistemological concept and recast it as a norm of action rooted in everyday practice. Huang holds that Chinese scholarship has mostly studied the earlier phases of his truth theory and neglected this third one. The article also asks how the revision can help meet the regression of intersubjective communicative action in the digital age. The article has four sections. The first reconstructs the consensus theory and its self-negation, after Habermas's criticism of correspondence, coherence and pragmatist theories of truth. The second looks at the lifeworld, its 'non-thematized' and 'situational' sides, and at the dialogue (discourse) that clears doubts. The third presents the resulting 'truth of action'. The fourth applies the theory to information overload, algorithmic recommendation and false consensus. Huang's core claim is that the early theory merged the performative attitude with the reflexive attitude, which made truth equivalent to justification and left the theory without a realist basis. Habermas's remedy was to treat the lifeworld as a quasi-transcendental background in which truth is unconditionally taken for granted. When doubts arise, participants step into discourse, adopt a reflexive attitude and test validity claims, then return to the lifeworld as actors. In Huang's reading, this 'actor–discussant–actor' shift reconciles the unconditionality of truth with the rational acceptability of justification. Huang also notes that Habermas's division of lifeworld situations is crude, because he borrows selectively from Husserl and Schütz. Huang concludes that the 'truth of action' ties Habermas's epistemology to his critical social theory, discourse ethics and political philosophy. For the digital age, Huang argues that moving from the lifeworld into dialogue helps people assess false information. The reflexive attitude counters algorithmic filter bubbles, and an 'cognition–action' view means users can test platform-generated consensus through practice and cooperation. The author adds that Wellmer's criticism of the ideal speech situation shows why formally open platforms may still produce false consensus. Read the original if you want a close account of the Truth and Justification phase of Habermas, or a Chinese attempt to apply it to digital communication.

The basic logic and strategic paths for raising the Party's leadership level in comprehensively deepening reform 提高党对全面深化改革领导水平的基本逻辑与战略路径 Tang Huangfeng Liu Linfeng Tang Huangfeng and Liu Linfeng ask why the Communist Party's level of leadership matters for the further comprehensive deepening of reform and how it can be raised. Taking up the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which names the Party's leadership level as a core aim and its overall leadership as the first principle of reform, the authors argue that this level directly determines whether reform succeeds or fails. They propose a three-part account: the underlying logic, the internal mechanism, and the strategic path. The article is organised in three sections. The first sets out the logic under three heads: fidelity to scientific socialism's principle of Marxist party leadership, the Party's accumulated experience of leading reform and opening up, and the Party's mission and responsibility in the new era. The second examines the mechanism through which leadership acts on reform, in four dimensions: direction and path, strategy and tactics, policy and institutions, and organisational and personnel support. The third turns to practical paths. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and cites figures on the Party's organisation and on the Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform. In the authors' reading, the Party sets direction by holding the line on fundamentals and the people-centred stance, sharpens strategy through sound judgement of complex conditions and national planning, and supplies policy and institutional frameworks. They cite the central reform leading body, set up in 2013, which they say has held 72 meetings and approved over 600 documents, together with decision-making, coordination and supervision mechanisms. They also point to a Party organisation of more than 99 million members and to cadre and talent management. Under the Party's leadership, they argue, reform moved from local experiments to systematic integration. For the new journey, the authors call for four improvements. These are the central leadership's overall design, coordination and integrated advancement of reform; the ability of Party committees at each level to produce replicable, extendable experience, including through the mass line and pilot schemes; the mobilisation of cadres and members; and supervision, inspection and follow-up of implementation. They conclude that institution-building should be the main thread and that the whole Party must keep a strategic and historical initiative in raising its leadership level. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party-building scholarship links leadership capacity to reform implementation.

Re-examining Marx's materialist conception of history: an investigation based on The German Ideology 重审马克思的唯物史观：基于《德意志意识形态》的考察 Ma Canlin Is the materialist conception of history that Marx and Engels developed in The German Ideology a genuine historical science, or does it fall back into an ideology of productivism? Ma Canlin takes up this question, prompted by critics such as Jean Baudrillard, who argued that Marx's analytical tools were themselves a sophisticated ideological illusion of capital. Writing from the standpoint of the history of ideas, including Marx's own development, Ma argues that the text founds a real science of history and that its difference from productivism can be shown. The article has three main parts plus a conclusion. The first part treats the materialist conception of history as a practical materialism and distinguishes Marx from Feuerbach. The second part addresses the charge of productivism, drawing on Baudrillard, Hannah Arendt, Max Weber, Antonio Negri and Herbert Marcuse. The third part asks what the object of historical materialism is. Ma draws on Marx's Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts, Engels's late letters and the readings of Lukács and Althusser. Ma makes three moves. First, the "inversion" of thought and being does not separate Marx from Feuerbach. For Marx, matter is the product of human sensuous activity (praxis), and nature is historicised nature. Ma warns, however, against reading this as a subjectivist philosophy of practice, because practice always unfolds under inherited conditions, so the text holds subject and object together dialectically. Second, answering the critics, Ma says Marx distinguishes three senses of freedom: non-interference, non-domination, and the realm of freedom beyond necessary labour. Marx also holds that this last realm can flourish only on the basis of the realm of necessity, so material production is not the opposite of freedom. Third, the object of historical materialism is not the economy but a social whole of economic, political and ideological elements. Ma calls this whole structured and uneven rather than Hegelian and expressive, and says political economy is a branch of the science that studies the economy as part of that whole. Ma concludes that The German Ideology rebuilt the meaning of matter on the basis of practice and sketched the structure of the social whole, even though it first gave an impression of economic determinism. That challenged the legitimacy of the philosophy of history and announced a genuine positive science of history. The theoretical revolution was neither instant nor smooth, Ma says, and it involved a long process of reversals and struggle. Read the original if you work on Marx's early texts, the debates over productivism and economic determinism, or how Western critics of Marx are answered from within the Chinese Marxist tradition.

The historical-materialist content of innovation phenomena, innovation practice and innovative thinking 创新现象、创新实践和创新思维的历史唯物主义内涵 Bao Dawei Bao Dawei asks what innovation means when it is understood through historical materialism, covering both material production and social institutions. The article argues that human civilization is driven forward by innovation practice, marked off in stages by innovation phenomena, and guided by effective innovative thinking. Bao holds that the concept of innovation must be grasped from a "big history" standpoint and according to the general laws of social development. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats innovation as a phenomenon and its distinctly human character. It sets out three levels: the development of productive forces, the adjustment of relations of production, and the dynamic between economic base and superstructure. The second analyses the "object-structure" of innovation practice, covering subject, intermediary and object. The third examines innovative thinking as the forerunner of practice. Bao draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping, and contrasts historical materialism with rationalism, mechanical materialism and constructivism. Bao argues that innovation is a human activity that depends on human cognition and carries human intentions. It is nonetheless objective, because motives and conditions are shaped by history and by contradictions between subject and object. Innovation practice has a structure: a self-sublating subject, intermediaries such as labour tools and ideology, and ever-renewed objects. Innovative thinking is described as a "rehearsal" in thought of the negation of the negation, and Bao says it is effective when objective and systematic. Under class society and capitalism, Bao claims, it suffers a double deficiency, because particular interests limit objectivity and the division of labour and the culture industry limit systematic vision. Bao concludes that the double deficiency can be overcome at two levels. Micro-level ideological critique through Marxism, both dialectical and historical materialism, frees thinking from old concepts. At the macro level, social conditions must no longer be dominated by particular interests. The people, and within them the proletariat led by Marxist parties, are presented as the creators and testers of innovation. Bao points to the institutional strengths of socialism with Chinese characteristics, such as concentrating resources on major undertakings, long-term strategic planning and an innovation-driven ecosystem. Read the original if you want a systematic Marxist-philosophical account of innovation, with extensive use of the classics, as it appears in current Chinese theoretical writing.

Continuing to extend full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grassroots 持续推动全面从严治党向基层延伸 Li Junwei This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to "continuously extend full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the grassroots". Li Junwei argues that grassroots Party organisations underpin all Party work and its combat effectiveness, and that closing the "last mile" of Party discipline requires clear responsibilities, stronger grassroots supervision and lighter burdens on local cadres. The article has three parts. The first describes extension to the grassroots as a distinctive feature of Party governance in the new era. The second sets out priority tasks. The third explains how such governance consolidates the Party's long-term rule. In the first part, Li holds that the Party has combined a focus on the "critical few" (senior cadres) with discipline over the "vast majority", passing responsibility down level by level. Li says that the Party has built up branches and made grassroots organisations "fortresses", and that campaigns against corruption in poverty relief, land requisition and similar areas won public trust. The priority tasks are to make Party committees bear primary responsibility, in line with the responsibilities of functional departments and discipline inspection bodies, and to deal routinely with misconduct and corruption close to ordinary people, such as school meals, village collective assets and funeral-sector abuses. Li also calls for integrating supervision (discipline inspection, inspection tours, auditing, big-data tools), extending inspections to villages and communities, and implementing the 2024 regulations on curbing formalism to reduce burdens on the grassroots. Li concludes that Party requirements must reach every link of grassroots governance, every branch and every member, through stricter education, management and Party life. Li also holds that results must benefit the public, since "the people's hearts are the greatest politics", with cadres' conduct serving as the barometer of Party conduct. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the Central Party School frames grassroots Party discipline, supervision and burden reduction in 2025.

The Party's leadership of urban work: historical review and lessons 党领导城市工作的历史回顾与经验启示 Xue Zelin Xue Zelin starts from the fact that China's urbanization rate passed 60% in 2019, which the author takes to mark a middle-to-late stage of urbanization. The article asks how the Party's historical experience of urban work can be summed up so that the idea of the "people's city" runs through all urban work and points to a modernized path of urban governance. Xue's answer is that two keywords, "the people" and "development", run through seventy-five years of practice, and that four lessons follow. After a short survey of existing studies, organised around the Party's centenary and the seventy years of the People's Republic, the article builds a three-dimensional analytical framework. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on the people's city, his call for systems thinking and the policy cycle of formulation, implementation and evaluation. Xue then reviews key urban-work meetings and documents in three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. A final section sets out a path for people's-city building under Chinese modernization. In the framework, formulating the policy of building a people's city is the policy-making stage. The principle that the people's city is built by the people is the implementing tool, and the principle that it is built for the people is the evaluation standard. Xue reads the three periods through this lens, from the shift from consumer to producer cities, through the focus on urban economic growth, to the new-era aim of urban governance modernization. From this Xue draws four lessons: upholding the Party's leadership, putting the people first, seeking truth from facts, and building consensus and unity of purpose. The author also links urban governance models to successive industrial revolutions and argues that the fourth, digital one gives China a chance to explore its own urban path. Xue concludes that urban work must follow the Party's leadership and a people-centred stance. Policy formulation should meet the era's mission, given what the author calls unprecedented urbanization, ageing and digitalization. Implementation should operate at the macro, meso and micro levels, from functional positioning to "people's livelihood projects". Evaluation should treat residents as the principal body, with rights to be informed, to participate and to supervise. Read the original if you study Chinese urban policy, the Party's official account of its urban work, or how the people's city concept is being turned into an analytical framework.

Chinese Communists' understanding and critique of capitalist modernization 中国共产党人对资本主义现代化的认识与批判 Liu Mingming How should a latecomer country relate to the modernization that the capitalist West pioneered? Liu Mingming argues that Chinese Communists have never worshipped or copied capitalist modernization. Instead, the article says, they have insisted on 'surpassing through critique'. Liu holds that copying it would only make a relatively backward country a dependency, and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation therefore requires a new road of modernization that sublates the capitalist one. The article begins with the failure of the late Qing and republican-era schemes (from 'Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for use' to wholesale Westernization) advanced by the landlord class and the bourgeoisie. It then sets out four features of the Communists' critique: its proletarian standpoint, its comprehensive scope, its dialectical method and its aim of transcendence. It draws on the Communist Manifesto, Mao Zedong's 1944 remarks on industrialization and several statements by Xi Jinping. In Liu's account, the critique is comprehensive because capitalist modernization is characterised as expansionist and predatory, materialist, destructive of the balance between humans and nature, and polarising in wealth. Liu adds that it rests on a 'centre–periphery' structure of exploitation that can enrich a few but not deliver common prosperity. The method is dialectical: Communists separate what is specific to the capitalist system (colonial expansion, materialism, polarisation, ecological imbalance) from the shared achievements of human civilization (advanced science and technology, scientific management, cultural accomplishments), which they say should be learned from. Liu argues that Chinese modernization surpasses the capitalist model by keeping a socialist direction, competing openly in the capitalist world market, and correcting capitalism's distortions, without implying that other countries must follow China's path. Liu concludes from the standpoint of historical materialism that this transcendence is objectively necessary. Chinese modernization grew out of the critical inheritance of capitalist achievements, so Liu warns that wholesale negation of Western modernization would harm it. Capitalist modernization cannot resolve the contradiction between socialized production and private ownership. Liu says Chinese modernization removes this obstacle by keeping public ownership dominant and pursuing common prosperity, and that Party leadership and Marxism supply its political and cultural guidance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-aligned scholarship frames the critique of Western modernization and the case for Chinese modernization as its successor.

Further deepening reform comprehensively and adhering to institution-building as the main thread 进一步全面深化改革与坚持以制度建设为主线阐论 Xu Yaotong Xu Yaotong takes up a principle in the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization: that further comprehensive deepening of reform must "adhere to institution-building as the main thread". Xu treats this as a new formulation and the core idea of the Decision. The article argues that the two are dialectically linked: reform needs institution-building as its main line, and institution-building depends on further deepening reform. The article has three parts. The first traces a historical lineage from Marx and Engels, through the Paris Commune, to the Chinese Communists from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. The second analyses the six components of "further comprehensively deepening reform" in the Decision: historical position, requirements of the times, guiding thought, overall goal, principles and tasks. The third parses the phrase "adhere to institution-building as the main thread" and what it implies for method. Xu reads Marx and Engels as holding that socialism is a developing, constantly reforming society with no ready-made blueprint, so that reform and institution-building are ordinary, permanent tasks. Xu argues that each of the Decision's six components ties back to institutions, with the seven areas of focus essentially being institutional systems. Xu also glosses "main thread" as three things: main purpose, main axis and leading role. The article counts 187 uses of "institution" in the Decision. For method, it follows the Decision's formula: strengthen top-level design, advance breaking and establishing together, and establish the new before breaking the old. It also separates three tiers of institutions. Fundamental institutions are to be consolidated, basic institutions improved, and important institutions innovated through new supply. Xu concludes that reform must carry institution-building through its whole process, across all fields and mechanisms, and into every step and procedure, under the rule of law. Officials are urged to build institutional awareness and act by the rules. Xu presents this as continuing a long line of Party practice, from Deng Xiaoping's call for a more mature and fixed set of institutions to Xi Jinping's stress on institution-building. Read the original if you want a Party-theory exposition of the Third Plenum's institutional logic, with its historical genealogy and its textual breakdown of the Decision.

Extending Marx's theory of world money With a discussion of strategic choices for the current internationalisation of the renminbi 马克思世界货币理论的再拓展 Liu Haoyan Liu Haoyan starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to advance renminbi internationalisation in an orderly way. The article argues that this task cannot rest on inherited Western theory and needs Marx's theory of world money. Marx mainly analysed metallic money, and later Marxists did not build a full doctrine for the age of sovereign credit money. Liu proposes to extend Marx's insights on money, credit, social power and international relations into such a doctrine, and to use it to guide China's currency strategy. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's scattered remarks on world money (its origin, form, functions and contradictions) and reviews later left-wing scholars such as Lapavitsas, de Brunhoff, Duncan Foley, Samir Amin, David Harvey and Michael Hudson. The second sets out how world money is generated under sovereign credit money, and what it does to issuing and using countries. The third assesses the renminbi's position, its obstacles and recommended policies. Liu's central claim is that a 'dual power structure' of economic and political power determines which currency becomes world money. The economic factors are trade scale, financial markets, transaction costs, monetary credit and the power to settle scarce commodities. The political ones are political stability, international institutions, strategic alliances and military strength. World money works in two directions: issuers gain policy independence, seigniorage and financial leverage over others, but also face a stronger currency, industrial hollowing-out, the Triffin dilemma and financial risk. Liu cites the pound and Germany and Japan after 1945 to show why users may hesitate to challenge the incumbent currency. On this basis Liu identifies obstacles for the renminbi: the quality of trade, immature financial markets, late cross-border infrastructure, the exchange-rate dilemma, geopolitical pressure, imbalance in international financial bodies and security risks. Liu calls for a steady, gradual approach with four elements: high-quality development and technological upgrading, a bond-market-centred financial system, digital legal tender and fintech, and tools to defend monetary sovereignty alongside reform of international monetary institutions. Liu warns against internationalisation for its own sake. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy framework for currency competition and renminbi strategy, with detailed data and policy proposals.

A Chinese scholar (Prof. Pan Jin'e) on the significance of Xi Jinping's first foreign visit of the year, to Vietnam 中国学者（潘金娥教授）谈习近平总书记、国家主席今年首访的意义 This is a short interview, first published by the Vietnamese outlet Nhân Dân (People's Daily online) on 14 April 2025. Its Beijing correspondent interviews Pan Jin'e, a professor at the Academy of Marxism, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and a specialist on Vietnam, during Xi Jinping's state visit. Pan argues that making Vietnam the first destination of the year shows how highly China values Vietnam and bilateral relations. The interview moves through four topics: Xi's repeated visits and the priority given to neighbourhood diplomacy; economic and trade cooperation; people-to-people exchanges; and cooperation between the two ruling parties. Pan notes that this is Xi's fourth visit to Vietnam as both Party General Secretary and state president since 2015. In Pan's account, neighbourhood diplomacy is a priority for China, and Vietnam is a priority within it, because both countries are socialist states led by communist parties. Pan expects progress under the "six more" framework, especially in practical cooperation. Pan cites 2024 trade figures above US$260 billion by Chinese statistics and above US$200 billion by Vietnamese ones, and points to potential in supply chains, border roads, railways and ports. On the party side, Pan holds that party relations have long set the direction of state relations. Pan concludes that cooperation should deepen in each area. Pan proposes using shared revolutionary heritage sites and new media to reach young people, strengthening exchanges between party leaders on the international situation and development paths, and translating each side's leaders' works. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of how China's Vietnam policy was framed during the April 2025 visit.

The conception of history in the Communist Manifesto and the development of modern society 《共产党宣言》的历史观与现代社会发展 Liu Jianjiang This short commentary asks what conception of history the Communist Manifesto sets out and why it still matters. Liu argues that the Manifesto, besides fixing communism as a goal, gives a scientific statement of the materialist conception of history, which explains both how modern society came into being and where it is heading. The article first draws on the Manifesto's account of the origin of modern bourgeois society. It then turns to the Manifesto's forecast of future society. It closes by pointing to the 1872 German preface, which says that the general principles remain correct while their application depends on historical conditions. Liu reads the Manifesto as tracing the bourgeoisie to the growth of productive forces and relations of production within feudal society. The Manifesto credits the bourgeoisie with a "very revolutionary part": it created enormous productive forces and opened up world history through the world market. The article then identifies three signs of crisis. These are the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, the opposition of capital and wage labour with its periodic overproduction crises, and the creation of the proletariat as the bourgeoisie's "gravediggers". From this Liu draws the Manifesto's conclusion that the bourgeoisie can no longer rule. Only proletarian revolution can end exploitation, and it leads to an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. Liu concludes that the Manifesto's conception of history shows the scientific character and truth of Marxist theory. Rereading it after more than 170 years is said to help strengthen historical self-confidence, historical consciousness, historical mission and historical initiative. Read the original if you want a concise, orthodox summary of the Manifesto's historical materialism as presented in a Chinese Party-theory outlet.

The essence–appearance method of penetrating insight: the fundamental method of Marx's critique of political economy 本质－现象透视法：马克思政治经济学批判的根本方法 Liu Zhihong Which method is basic to Marx's critique of political economy? Liu Zhihong argues that it is neither the ascent from the abstract to the concrete nor any other familiar procedure, but what Liu calls the essence–appearance method of penetrating insight (本质－现象透视法). Liu holds that this method has been widely known but never adequately recognised or developed, and that recent scholarship has treated the ascent from the abstract to the concrete as the main method of Capital without discussing it. The article was published in Studies on Marxism, 2025, no. 3. The article has three parts. The first re-reads the ascent from the abstract to the concrete, using the 1857 Introduction, as a movement from essence to appearance. The second sets out the content and logic of the essence–appearance method in five steps: the distinction between essence and appearance, essence producing illusory appearances, appearances posing as essence, penetrating appearances to grasp essence, and criticising appearances on the basis of essence. The third shows the method at work in Capital and its manuscripts, including the analysis of interest-bearing capital and the theories of surplus value, and explains why it is fundamental. Liu's central claim is that the 'abstract' at the starting point is the decisive essence, above all value, and that the ascent to the concrete is the dialectical concretisation of that essence into ever more complex appearances. In Liu's account, Marx stresses that capitalism necessarily generates a system of inverted appearances, whose core is the illusion that capitalism is rational and eternal. Only by seeing through these appearances, and then criticising them from the standpoint of essence, can the historical and transitory character of capitalism be shown. Liu argues that this method governs the use of the ascent from the abstract to the concrete and also of typical analysis and scientific abstraction. It is fundamental because it serves Marx's overall aim of criticising and surpassing capitalism, his overall problem of why capitalism must give way to communism, and the critical and revolutionary substance of materialist dialectics. Without it, Liu contends, the ascent could slide into vulgar economics. Liu concludes that Hegel's dialectic is concretised directly as the ascent from the abstract to the concrete, whereas Marx's dialectic is concretised first as the essence–appearance method and only then as the ascent. Liu adds that criticism of illusions must move from ideas to practice, because only changing the capitalist mode of production removes their basis. Liu uses the image of a tree: the ascent is a 'branch', and the essence–appearance method is the 'root'. Read the original if you work on Marx's methodology, the philosophy of Capital, or current Chinese debates on the dialectical structure of the critique of political economy.

Marx's historical consciousness and class consciousness in examining the transformation of money into capital 马克思考察货币转化为资本的历史意识与阶级意识 Liu Jingdong Liu Jingdong asks how Marx's account of the transformation of money into capital, and of labour-power becoming a commodity, supports a reading of the birth of capital and the world history of capital. The article argues that Marx's analysis rests on an organic unity of historical consciousness and class consciousness, which together let him do two things: criticise capital and criticise bourgeois political economy. The article draws mainly on Volume I of Capital (Part Two, "The Transformation of Money into Capital") and on Volume II's chapter on the circuit of money capital. It also refers to Marx's 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts. It is organised in three parts: money becoming capital as the precondition for the shift from traditional to modern modes of production; the emergence of capital and the free worker as the secret of capital's birth and world history; and the social conditions of the money-capital circuit and the new class relations. A short conclusion follows. Liu first contrasts simple circulation C–M–C, aimed at use-value and consumption, with the circulation of capital M–C–M′, aimed at self-expanding value. For Liu, this contrast marks two different social-economic epochs, and the capitalist appears as personified capital driven by surplus value. Liu then follows Marx through the contradiction in the general formula of capital. Surplus value cannot arise from circulation, whether exchange is equivalent or not, yet it cannot arise outside it, and Marx resolves this through labour-power as a commodity. Labour-power can be a commodity only once workers are free in the double sense and the separation of producers from the means of production has occurred through primitive accumulation. Liu holds that this condition "contains a whole world history". In Volume II, Liu argues, Marx revisits the point to show that the formula M–C…P…C′–M′ presupposes a wage-labouring class on a social scale, and that the wage form conceals exploitation behind formal equality, which bourgeois economists treat in ahistorical terms. Liu concludes that Marx's unity of historical and class consciousness exposes the claimed freedom and equality of exchange as a veil. Behind it, in Liu's reading, lie capital's exploitation, domination and enslavement of labour, which is why Marx calls capitalist commodity production an "epoch-making" mode of exploitation. The article also presents the combination of labourers and means of production as Marx's criterion for distinguishing economic epochs. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reading of Capital Volumes I and II on the origin of capital, and an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars frame Marx's historical method and class analysis.

Activating China's fine traditional culture with Marxism: objectives, principles and approaches 马克思主义激活中华优秀传统文化：目标、原则与进路 Yan Lianfu Yang Jinfu Yan Lianfu and Yang Jinfu ask how Marxism can "activate" the fine elements of China's traditional culture, and to what end. Taking up Xi Jinping's 2023 and 2024 remarks on the high degree of fit between Marxism and fine traditional culture, they argue that activation should drive the creative transformation and innovative development of that culture. The new culture formed through the Second Integration, they say, would become the cultural form of Chinese modernization and support the building of a strong socialist cultural nation. After a literature review that finds existing work strong on feasibility, methods and significance but weak on systematic planning and long-term mechanisms, the article is organised in three parts. It sets out four objectives, seven principles and seven concrete approaches. The approaches each pair a traditional idea with a Marxist counterpart, such as "harmony between heaven and humanity" with the Marxist ecological view. The four objectives rest on a set of pairings. Marxism's advanced character is said to activate the tradition's values and adaptability. Its worldwide character is said to activate the national character and universal value of Chinese culture. Its critical and revolutionary spirit is said to reshape the tradition's harmonious core, which the authors link to the Party's self-reform. Its developmental outlook is said to activate the tradition's capacity for adaptation. The seven principles are named guidance, excavation, endowing with new meaning, infusion, interpenetration, fusion and climbing. The authors present them as a two-way process in which Marxism becomes Chinese and traditional culture becomes modern, with the combination a "chemical reaction" rather than a mere assemblage. The seven approaches link traditional ideas to ecological civilisation, a community with a shared future for mankind, people-centred livelihood policy, moral construction, high-quality development, the unity of knowing and doing, and individual striving. The authors conclude that the work is a historic mission for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They call for deeper research on the mechanisms of integration and wider application in the economy, politics, society, culture and ecology. They also call for cultural products with Chinese characteristics and for training people versed in both Marxist theory and traditional culture. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Party theorists frame the Second Integration in terms of goals, principles and policy areas.

The salient themes, inherent characteristics and construction priorities of the discourse system of ideological and political education in the new era 新时代思想政治教育话语体系的鲜明主题、内在特质与建构重点 Gu Chao Wang Xuejian Taking up Xi Jinping's call to build disciplinary, academic and discourse systems with Chinese characteristics, Gu Chao and Wang Xuejian ask what the discourse system of ideological and political education should look like in the new era. They argue that it is shaped both by the themes of the age and by the nature of ideological and political education itself. On that basis they set out its themes, its inherent characteristics and the priorities for building it. The article has three parts. The first identifies four themes: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, moral and political education with answers to students' doubts, contention over discourse power in international communication, and digital-intelligent transformation. The second describes three sets of inherent characteristics: how the discourse is generated, its constituent elements, and the ways it is converted for audiences. The third proposes four construction priorities. On the characteristics, the authors argue the discourse is generated through realism, subjectivity (anchored in national language, culture and a stance of "putting ourselves first") and knowledge content. It has three layers: political discourse at the core, academic discourse in the middle and everyday discourse on the outside. These layers are linked by conversion: political discourse becomes more scholarly, academic discourse more accessible, and everyday discourse more engaging, through storytelling, metaphor and popular buzzwords. The authors also warn of risks from digital transformation, including digital colonialism, instrumental rationality and algorithmic "echo chambers". On construction, they call for four things. The first is to uphold Marxism and the mainstream ideology and to adopt a people-centred stance. The second is to build an autonomous knowledge system with distinctive concepts, including on Chinese modernization, and to move away from Eurocentric knowledge. The third is to ground the discourse in China's achievements since reform and opening up, explaining the reasoning behind them. The fourth is to draw on Chinese civilisation and cultural confidence. The authors conclude that the discourse system should combine value guidance with knowledge content, and political stance with accessible expression. They propose that it should convert China's development experience into general concepts and paradigms. They present this as a way both to counter Western discourse hegemony and to extend the influence of Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education conceptualise the layers, themes and tasks of their field's discourse.

The Party-admission oath ceremony over a hundred years: theoretical interpretation, forms of practice and functional value 百年历程中的入党宣誓仪式：理论阐释、践行方式、功能价值 Gao Fujin Lu Yuanyi This article examines the oath-taking ceremony through which new members join the Communist Party of China (CPC). Gao and Lu treat it as a mandatory step in recruiting members and as a solemn pledge to the Party, the country and the people. They argue that, across more than a century, the ceremony has moved from a rough early form to a settled one and then to continuing refinement. They present it as a basis for the "major honours system" of a large Party and country, and for telling the CPC's story to the world. The article has three parts. The first sets out the ceremony's theoretical sources and basic attributes. The second surveys four forms of practice: the regular ceremony, joining at the front line, secret admission and posthumous recognition of membership. The third assesses the ceremony's functions at the level of the individual, the group and the Party as a whole. Cases range from the Anyuan miners' club in 1922 to Zou Taofen (1944), Qiu Shaoyun (1952) and a pandemic-era recognition in 2021. A short closing section links the ceremony to Xi Jinping's 2021 renewal of the oath. Gao and Lu trace the ceremony directly to the Statutes of the Communist League drafted by Marx and Engels in 1847, which set out a question-and-answer admission procedure. In their account, it reached the CPC partly through the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party and Lenin. They identify three stable attributes: class character, shown in portraits, the singing of the Internationale and oath wording; popular character, shown in oath content and the growing number of non-members attending; and advanced character, shown in adaptable forms and Marxist guidance. Procedures varied by period, for example in the object of salute, until the 12th Party Congress (1982) made the Party flag the national standard. The clenched-fist gesture is described as the constant element. On function, the authors argue that the oath strengthens each member's political belief and sense of duty, builds a collective organisational culture and ideological identity through its symbols, and gives the Party a fuller public image. They conclude that the ceremony is an important result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They call for further work on its meaning and on members' understanding and observance of the oath. Read the original if you study Party building, political ritual or the history of CPC admission practices and want a Chinese-language account with many historical examples.

Zhu De's understanding of and reflections on talent work in the early years of the People's Republic 新中国成立初期朱德对人才工作的认识与思考 Zhang Feng How did the early People's Republic try to solve its shortage of skilled people, and what did Zhu De contribute? Zhang Feng, an associate researcher at Yangzhou University, argues that Zhu De, a leading member of the Party's first generation of central leadership, gave sustained attention to talent work after 1949. Zhang holds that his many statements and proposals helped launch and develop the new state's talent enterprise and still offer historical lessons for today. The article draws on Zhu De's speeches, inscriptions, telegrams and letters from roughly 1949 to 1956. It is organised in four parts: the urgency and importance of talent work; the use of former professional and technical personnel; the training of the country's own modernised talent; and the principles of talent cultivation. Cases range from engineers and scientists to air force, navy and military-academy personnel, young people and women. Zhang's first move is to show why talent mattered. The author cites a figure of fewer than 50,000 science and technology personnel with university education in 1949, and reads Zhu De's repeated calls for technical skill as tied to three needs: industrialisation, scientific development and a modernised national defence army. Second, Zhang reports Zhu De's view that former Guomindang-era experts, including air force and navy technicians, should be used after a process of 'unity, education and remoulding', and that this was a political task. Third, Zhu De is said to have insisted on self-reliant training: running regular schools, especially military academies, and encouraging youth and women to become specialists, even while Soviet help was welcomed. Two principles run through this: political and professional competence must be united ('politics plus technology'), and theory must be combined with practice. Zhang concludes that Zhu De, moved by hopes for national strength and popular wellbeing, laid out guiding ideas and a blueprint for the sustained development of talent work. In the author's assessment, this shows the foresight of the older generation of proletarian revolutionaries on a question bearing on the fate of the Party and state. Read the original if you study early PRC cadre and technical-personnel policy, Zhu De's thought, or the history of military modernisation and education, and want a documented account from Party sources.

Goals and tasks in constructing a system of methods for ideological and political education 思想政治教育方法体系建构的目标任务 Wang Xisheng Wang Xisheng takes up a premise question that he says has been neglected in the study of ideological and political education: what goals and tasks a system of methods for the field should serve. Since the first treatise on methods appeared in 1985, the author counts more than 150 related works, over twenty of them systematic. Wang argues that these systems differ so much in aim because their builders look at methods differently, and proposes that the goals and tasks be reset along three lines: theoretical depth and precision, practical validity and reliability, and an inclusive disciplinary identity. The article has four parts. It first reviews representative systems: Wang Xuanwu's Ideological and Political Education Methodology (1985, revised 1992), Zheng Yongting's work with its historical and contemporary dimensions, and Zu Jiahe's textbook centred on educator and educatee, with brief notes on others. It then sets out four expectations for the new era, followed by a critique of how systems are built, and finally the proposed resetting of goals. In Wang's account the main existing systems share a narrow scope and mostly follow the process of educational work. The author contends that Marxism, the Marxism of the twenty-first century, and Xi Jinping's writings on ideological work should not be only a "theoretical basis" but the top-level method of the system. Wang ties this to the analysis of people's ideas through productive forces and relations of production, extending it to new quality productive forces and the digital economy. The author also calls for a "strong ideological and political guiding force", the wider "big ideological and political education" pattern, and technology-enabled methods such as large-model teaching. Three terms organise the critique: scope (which methods are included), angle (the dimension of construction) and focal point (where effort concentrates). Wang notes that the field has no consensus on focal point, so additional systems struggle to add up. Wang concludes that systems should supply an insightful theoretical schema, refined into a genealogy of methods whose internal relations are explained. They should also offer an operational map tested for validity and reliability, and show a distinctive, value-laden disciplinary character that rejects Weberian value neutrality while absorbing methods from pedagogy, psychology, sociology and management. Read the original if you work on the theory of ideological and political education, or want to see how Chinese scholars survey and critique the field's methodology texts and link them to Party priorities.

Goals and strategies of institution-building in the context of further comprehensively deepening reform 进一步全面深化改革视域下制度建设的目标体系与策略方法 Li Xiaoyu Li Xiaoyu takes up institution-building as the main thread of the reform agenda set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article asks what problems current institution-building faces, what goals it should be anchored to, and which strategies and methods can achieve them. Li argues that institution-building is the central line of further comprehensively deepening reform, and that it should rest on six goals and be pursued through a set of differentiated methods. The article has three parts. The first sets out why institution-building is necessary. The second builds a framework of goals and checks it against current conditions in China. The third discusses strategies and methods: who supplies institutions, what drives institutional innovation, which principles apply and which concrete paths exist. Li draws on Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping, Lenin, Weber, Huntington, Douglass North, and Acemoglu and Robinson, and illustrates the argument with cases such as the Zhejiang reforms and market segmentation. Li gives three reasons for necessity: bringing the strengths of the socialist system into play, building a modern socialist great power, and meeting great-power competition, which the author describes as ultimately competition between institutions. Criticising indicators such as the World Bank's governance index for ignoring national conditions, Li holds that governance has general, national and task-specific attributes. From these Li derives six goals: completeness, unity, hierarchy, systematicness, coordination and adaptability. On methods, Li argues that the centre should lead on fundamental, top-level institutions, while local governments, enterprises and individuals innovate in concrete ones. Innovation is driven by crisis, development needs and opening up. Li also classifies paths into six types: filling gaps, consolidating, strengthening implementation, regulating and adjusting, improving, and abolishing. Li concludes that a new form of reform is emerging, guided by Party leadership, problem orientation, top-level design, systems integration, institutional and mechanism reform, and a focus on reshaping relationships. The author maintains that continuous institutional innovation will provide the impetus and institutional guarantee for Chinese modernization. The author also stresses that reform is never finished and must be carried through. Read the original if you want a Chinese-journal account of how institution-building is theorised and classified under the 2024 reform decision, with a detailed typology of reform measures.

Paths for advancing the Party's self-reform through ideological building 以思想建设推进党的自我革命的路径考察 Chen Si Li Zhiyong Chen Si and Li Zhiyong ask how ideological building (sixiang jianshe) can drive the Communist Party of China's self-reform. They start from the 20th Party Congress (2022) claim that self-reform is the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Their thesis is that the problems self-reform must address share a root in ideals and convictions, so ideological building is both a key lesson of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era and a necessary measure for the future. The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic linking ideological building to self-reform. The second surveys four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third proposes five directions for further work. On the theoretical side, the authors argue that ideological building gives self-reform three things: theoretical guidance, because practice and theory advance in a cycle; value orientation, because self-reform is meant to lead the "great social revolution"; and a method, because corruption, the "four winds" and disloyalty are all traced to weakened ideals. Self-reform is therefore described as first of all an ideological revolution. The historical survey presents a continuous practice: rectifying erroneous lines (the 1935 Zunyi Meeting), Mao Zedong's principle of building the Party ideologically, the Yan'an Rectification Movement, the 1950s rectification campaigns including the Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan case, the full Party rectification of 1983, and the centralised education campaigns of the new era. The authors credit the new-era emphasis on making officials unwilling to be corrupt for laying an ideological basis for the anti-corruption campaign's "overwhelming victory". For the future the authors call for firmer ideals and convictions, adherence to the Two Integrations so that practical innovation drives theoretical innovation, theoretical armament that combines concentrated and routine education, and attention to the "critical few" leading cadres, including family conduct. They also call for learning, practice and assessment mechanisms that make the work regular and long-term, combining ideological building with institutional governance. Read the original if you want a systematic official-academic account of how Party theorists link ideological education to anti-corruption and Party discipline, with a historical periodisation from 1921 to 2024.

An analysis of the historical starting point of the modern transformation of Chinese civilization 中华文明现代转型的历史起点析论 Chen Dianlin Liu Ming When did the modern transformation of Chinese civilization begin? Chen Dianlin and Liu Ming take up this question, which they describe as a foundational problem for tracing the evolution of Chinese civilization since the modern era, and on which they say scholars have reached no consensus. Using the perspective of the Second Integration, they argue that the starting point cannot be a single event. It is a historical period running from the May Fourth Movement to the founding of the Communist Party of China. The article first surveys six existing views. Three tie the starting point to the old-democratic revolution: the Opium War, the 1911 Revolution and the First World War. Three tie it to the new-democratic revolution: the spread of Marxism, the founding of the Party and the founding of the People's Republic. The authors criticise each in turn. They then examine the question through three lenses: its time and space, its concrete cultural form, and its agent. A further section looks at the historical, cultural and practical circumstances, drawing on early Party figures such as Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai, Li Da and Zhou Enlai. The authors argue that the Opium War brought national crisis but did not yet reach Chinese values and ethics. They hold that the 1911 Revolution was undone by Yuan Shikai's restoration, and that the Party's founding aimed first at class struggle. They also hold that the founding of the People's Republic marks a later stage rather than a beginning. Drawing on Marx and Engels, they present transformation as driven by the shift from a smallholder agrarian mode of production to industrial modernity. In their account, traditional culture has a dual character, as national spirit and as feudal ideology. They see its critical sublation as the way forward, with Marxism supplying the key and sharing common values with Chinese tradition. The Party, as the vanguard of the proletariat, is the agent, and early Party writers identified the proletariat as the leading force. The authors conclude that three dimensions converge in the period from the May Fourth Movement to the Party's founding. These are intensifying national crisis and modernizing pressure, the linking of Marxism with Chinese cultural elements, and the Chinese working class's emergence as a political actor whose cultural mission the Party affirmed. They present this as a historical basis for building a modern Chinese civilization today and for adapting Marxism to Chinese tradition. Read the original if you want a systematic review of Chinese scholarly positions on periodising Chinese civilization's modernization, and an example of how the Second Integration is used as an analytical framework.

The "Two Integrations": rationale and path for building a Party-building discourse system “两个结合”：党建话语体系构建的理与路 Sun Zhaohong Sun Zhaohong asks how the Chinese Communist Party should build and refine its discourse on Party building (the concepts, phrases and narratives used to describe and guide its own construction). The article argues that the discourse system has grown through the Two Integrations, meaning the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. In the new era, Sun contends, the system must continue to rest on this method so that it has a "soul" of truth, "roots" in culture and "strength" in practice. The article is organised in three parts, one for each of these three dimensions: theory, culture and practice. Each part first sets out why that dimension is the foundation of Party-building discourse and then explains how the Two Integrations should be applied to it. Sun draws on Party history from the Marxist-Leninist doctrine of party building and Mao Zedong's sinification of Marxism, through Deng Xiaoping's institutional reforms, to Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the first part, Sun treats Marxism as the "soul" of the discourse, carried forward through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and now guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the second part, traditional culture is the "root". Sun's example is "seeking truth from facts", an old phrase whose meaning the Party has enriched, and Sun stresses that the two sources must "fit" each other and form a new "cultural living organism", not a mere assembly. The "two vanguards" formulation (the Party as vanguard of both the working class and the Chinese people and nation) is offered as an instance of this synthesis. Sun adds that traditional culture must be screened, since feudal clan-based networks are said to feed corruption. In the third part, practice is the source of the discourse. Sun traces the progression from "ideological party building" to institutional governance and the "new great project", and treats the Party's self-reform as the latest innovation. Sun says discourse must summarise historical experience and address current problems, such as the "six how-to-always" challenges facing a large party. Sun concludes that a Chinese Party-building discourse needs Marxist theory, cultural subjectivity and practical problem-solving together, since Western party theories cannot explain the Party's experience. The Two Integrations, Sun argues, should produce a distinctive discourse that answers how a long-governing Marxist party is to be built and offers the Party's answer to corruption as a global problem. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal links discourse construction to the Two Integrations, with examples of specific Party-building terms.

Contemporary interpretations of Marx's theory of alienation and their significance David Harvey's "universal alienation" and Hartmut Rosa's "new alienation" 马克思异化理论的当代阐释及其意义 Zhou Ke Since the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 appeared, Marx's theory of alienation has been continuously disputed. Zhou Ke divides recent foreign interpretations into a textual-interpretation school (Allen Wood, Bertell Ollman, Robert Tucker, Allen Buchanan, Andrew Sayers and others) and an "application and development" school (Erich Fromm, Herbert Marcuse, Henri Lefebvre). The article argues that David Harvey's "universal alienation" and Hartmut Rosa's "new alienation" continue the second path and offer useful lessons for understanding contemporary capitalism and exploring alternatives to it. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Harvey's account, drawn mainly from Seventeen Contradictions and the End of Capitalism and a 2018 essay for Marx's bicentenary. The second sets out Rosa's social-acceleration theory and his notion of resonance, from Social Acceleration (2005) and Resonance (2016). The third assesses what both contribute to the critique of capitalism. On Zhou's reading, Harvey takes alienation to run through all capitalist contradictions, from production to consumption, debt, politics and ecology. He traces its intensification to deindustrialisation, technology and consumerism, and to the circulation of capital through production, realisation and distribution. He therefore proposes a "revolutionary humanism", opposed to Althusser's expulsion of alienation from Marxism. Rosa locates alienation in the time structure of late modern society. Technological acceleration, acceleration of social change and acceleration of the pace of life are driven by competition, a cultural promise and a self-propelling feedback loop. He identifies five forms of alienation (spatial, of the world of things, of action, of time, and of self and society), and proposes "resonance" as a non-alienated relation between subject and world. Zhou concludes that both thinkers carry on Marx's scholarly tradition, extend his total critique of capitalism to wider domains, and explore alternatives to capitalism. The author also judges that Harvey's proposals and Rosa's resonance projects remain content with local reforms and normative principles, avoid deeper questions of institutions and the revolutionary subject, and so carry a utopian and reformist character. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Harvey and Rosa as heirs of Marx's alienation concept, including its critical verdict.

Marx's critique of Eurocentrism and its implications 马克思对西方中心论的批判及其启示 Yang Shengping Some Western scholars, especially on the left, now describe Marxism as a typical case of Eurocentrism. Yang Shengping cites Andre Gunder Frank's ReOrient (published in Chinese as 'Silver capital'), which charges Marx and Weber with seeking the origins of capitalism in European particularity. Yang argues the opposite: historical materialism and the theory of world history are the most thorough critique of Eurocentrism, though Marx's own break with it developed over time. The article draws lessons for cultural development in China today. The article has three parts. The first shows that the founding of historical materialism was itself a critique of Eurocentrism, and distinguishes a historical 'centre' from 'centrism'.
