The second traces how Marx's critique developed in stages, from the 1840s to his death, and tests it on the late writings on Russia and the 'Kafkaesque' passage, the 'Caudine Forks of capitalism' (Marx's own phrase). The third turns to present-day implications for China, chiefly the building of 'cultural subjectivity'. Yang contends that, because Marx grounds history in material production, he avoids Hegel's spirit-based Eurocentrism, and that a leading country at a given stage is only a temporary centre, not a permanent one. Yang divides Marx's later work into phases and argues that his earlier remarks on India and the Asiatic mode of production still bore the mark of Western sources, while his work from the 1870s, with first-hand material on Russia, rejects both 'European uniqueness' and 'Eastern stagnation'. Yang rejects readings that treat the Western path and the Russian 'leapfrog' path as unrelated, saying this risks an 'anti-Eurocentric Eurocentrism'. In Yang's account the two paths are linked within a world history dominated by capitalism. A leap is possible only given external conditions, such as Western example and support, and productive forces cannot be skipped. Yang concludes that criticism of Eurocentrism is a means, not an end, and that the aim is theory that can guide China's development. Cultural subjectivity should be judged first by cultural advancement, not nationality, and should absorb the best achievements of all peoples, including developed capitalist countries. Eurocentrism as a view of history and as a political and value stance should be rejected, while Eurocentric modes of thinking and discourse can be selectively transformed and used. Yang adds that national character should be open and combined with advancement in a new organic cultural whole. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's late writings on Russia and non-Western paths, and its link to current debates on cultural subjectivity and an independent knowledge system.

The discursive resolve of Marx's critique of capitalism 马克思资本主义批判思想的话语定力研究 Jiang Linteng Qiao Ruijin What gives Marx's critique of capitalism its lasting power? Jiang Linteng and Qiao Ruijin argue that it lies in an internally unified body of discourse, which they call its "holistic discursive resolve" (zhengtixing huayu dingli). The article sets out to show how Marx articulated his theory, in order to deepen understanding of the essence of Marxism and to advance its development. The authors analyse this discourse in three dimensions, each organised around a question Marx kept asking: the form of the discourse (what is the root of social alienation?), its content (how can the world be changed?) and its significance (how is human emancipation possible?). Each section follows Marx's path from the Rheinische Zeitung period and the 1844 manuscripts through the German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, Capital and the 1857–58 manuscripts to his late anthropological and historical studies. A short conclusion draws the three together. In the authors' reading, Marx moved from philosophical and political critique to the critique of political economy, tracing alienation from alienated labour through the theory of surplus value and commodity fetishism to capital's domination. This opens onto the question of change, where Marx's starting point of "real individuals" and "revolutionary practice" makes people the subjects who transform the world. Finally the authors present human emancipation as the aim of Marx's whole discourse: communist revolution by the proletariat, the sublation of private property, wage labour, the division of labour and classes, and the "three forms" of social development. They stress that communism is an ongoing movement and not a panacea. The authors conclude that the three questions correspond to "explaining the world", "changing the world" and unifying the two. This lets Marx combine grand and micro narratives, avoiding both relativism and absolutism, and makes his writings a coherent "artistic whole". They add that studying this resolve helps in understanding Marxism's essence, in developing Marxism in the new era and in building a discourse system with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a systematic, Chinese-language reading of Marx's thought as one discursive whole organised around alienation, practice and emancipation.

The necessity and the ought of green development after escaping the "Malthusian trap" 超越“马尔萨斯陷阱”之后绿色发展的必然与应然 Lu Feng Lu Feng asks which direction human civilisation should take now that modern development has escaped the "Malthusian trap". The article argues that the "black development" of early modernity, which was built on fossil fuels, pollution and the conquest of nature, was historically necessary but is unsustainable. Lu contends that civilisation must turn to green development, meaning ecological civilisation, if it is to avoid destruction. The article has three sections. The first reinterprets Deng Xiaoping's dictum "development is the absolute principle" through the economic historians Gregory Clark and Oded Galor, and treats China's reform-era growth as an escape from the trap. The second characterises "black development" and the early modern worldview behind it, then sets out the scientific and philosophical challenges to that worldview. The third describes green development and what it requires of production, distribution, consumption and innovation. Lu argues that before 1800 the living standards of labouring people were no better than those of other animals, and that rapid innovation in modernization lifted them above that level. The early modern ideology, he says, rested on a physicalist view of nature, a dogmatic rationalism that held nature to be fully knowable and conquerable, and a human-centred value theory. Drawing on Prigogine, cosmology and complexity science, Lu proposes a creative, "vitalist" view of nature and a humble rationalism, and concludes that nature cannot be conquered. He then argues that the economy is a subsystem of the biosphere. On this basis he holds that the "trickle-down" pattern of distribution is not sustainable, because material wealth has ecological limits and rich-led consumerism cannot be generalised. He proposes progressive taxation within democratic and legal frameworks, a circular economy, renewable energy and green consumption, all driven by green innovation in technology, ideas and institutions. Lu concludes that civilisation can keep developing without limit through innovation, but only if it abandons the conquest of nature. He adds that this conquering drive is tied to war between humans and war against nature. He cites China's "dual carbon" commitments (peak emissions before 2030, carbon neutrality before 2060) and its stress on respecting nature as signs that Chinese civilisation is turning green. Read the original if you want a philosophical argument from a Chinese ecological-civilisation scholar that links economic history, critiques of anthropocentrism and distributional justice to green development.

Making good use of the "Great Ideological and Political Course" to raise the ideological and political leadership of universities 善用“大思政课”提升高校思政引领力 Jiang Jiaping Writing in April 2025, Jiang Jiaping, Party secretary of Anhui Normal University, takes up the concept of "ideological and political leadership" (sizheng yinlingli). Xi Jinping introduced it at the National Education Conference in September 2024, and the January 2025 Outline for Building a Leading Education Country lists it first among the traits of a strong education system. Jiang argues that universities should use the "Great Ideological and Political Course" as the main lever to strengthen this capacity, together with a broad working philosophy, structure and system of "great" ideological and political work. This newspaper commentary is organised around four "great" elements. They are "great education of people" (organisational, curricular, practical and cultural education), the "great classroom" of society, the "great front" of ideological positions, and the "great teaching force". Each section turns Xi's statements, including his March 2025 call to merge the ideological and political "small classroom" with the social "great classroom", into measures for university Party committees. Jiang defines ideological and political leadership as the combined strength of intellectual, moral, spiritual, cultural and practical forces that leads society's members into the effort to build an education powerhouse and achieve national rejuvenation. On this basis, the author calls for Party committees to coordinate the "Three-wide Education" reform and integrate schools, families and society. Courses should be built around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and every subject should carry ideological content. Teaching should use museums, memorials, fieldwork and volunteering to show the Party's achievements. Jiang also stresses the ideological struggle in cyberspace, where "if we do not occupy it, others will". The author proposes using big data, blockchain and DeepSeek in online teaching, and building a teaching force from full-time and part-time instructors with four-level training. Jiang concludes that universities must act proactively on all four fronts so that ideological and political leadership grows through history education, education about national conditions and life education. The author's recommendations are practical: organisational leadership, curriculum reform, practice-based teaching, digital methods and teacher recruitment and training. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how a university Party leader translates current Party education policy into institutional measures.

Marx's critique of Hegel's philosophy of right 马克思对黑格尔的法哲学批判 Cheng Guangyun Cheng Guangyun asks how Marx's early critique of Hegel's philosophy of right should be understood, and what it settled. The article argues that Marx still worked inside Hegel's speculative philosophy, yet used it to expose a contradiction between Hegel's political doctrine and his own logic. In doing so, Cheng contends, Marx took the decisive step away from Hegel by founding popular sovereignty on the labouring, propertyless estate. The article is a compact reading of Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, built around Hegel's three political powers: the monarchy, the executive and the legislature. Cheng first sets out Hegel's method, in which the philosophy of right is the visible front stage and the Logic is the hidden back-stage programme. The text then takes each power in turn, setting Hegel's account against Marx's objections, and closes with the question of who can represent the universal interest of the state. Cheng's central claim is that Hegel repeatedly breaks his own logic when it conflicts with the Prussian political reality he wants to defend. Examples include making the monarch the subject of the state rather than its predicate, placing the executive between crown and legislature, and reducing the legislature to an advisory body. Cheng reports that Marx reversed Hegel's inversion: the monarch depends on the people, and sovereignty belongs to the people. Marx also called Hegel's bureaucracy 'state formalism' that treats the state as private property, and he rejected the estates as private interests posing as universal ones. Against this, Marx demanded direct democracy, a single chamber and universal, unrestricted elections. Cheng adds that Marx's argument remained entangled in speculative concepts and bore the mark of Feuerbach and the Young Hegelians. Cheng concludes that Marx and Hegel shared one problem, namely who represents the universal and public interest of the state. Hegel answered with the monarch, bureaucracy and estates. Marx answered with the labouring estate, which at this stage was still a speculative category and not yet the historical and practical proletariat. Cheng suggests that once popular sovereignty rests on that estate as the people's subject, the principle of the dictatorship of the proletariat is close at hand. Read the original if you want a short, text-based account of how the early Marx's break with Hegel's theory of the state is reconstructed from the Logic–philosophy of right relationship.

The construction and transcendence of "moral politics": Rousseau, Hegel and Marx “道德政治”的建构与超越：卢梭、黑格尔与马克思 Zhang Dang Zhang Dang asks how modern political philosophy has dealt with the separation of morality from politics, and how Marx's thought resolves the difficulty. The article argues that Rousseau diagnosed this separation and proposed rebuilding "moral politics". It holds that Hegel refined the project through his distinction between "ethical life" and "morality", and that Marx went beyond both by tracing the problem to property relations. The article follows a genealogy in three parts. It begins with Hobbes's and Locke's accounts of the state of nature and of property, and with Rousseau's critique of them. It then covers Rousseau's "general will" and his programme against inequality, followed by Kant's shift after the French Revolution and Hegel's assessment of Rousseau. The final part takes up Marx's 1843 Rousseau notes, his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, his historical-materialist method and his critique of political economy. Zhang's central claim is that Rousseau and Hegel both work from will and reason and both accept the legitimacy of private property. For that reason, the author says, Rousseau ends up defending property as "sacred" while attacking inequality. Hegel's "ethical politics" in turn leaves unresolved how the ethical state becomes real, and risks formalism. Marx, in this reading, borrows Rousseau's democratic ideas to criticise Hegel's "state formalism" and calls for a "true democracy". He treats individuals and communities as products of material production and forms of intercourse. The author gives special weight to Marx's distinction between private property based on the producer's own labour and private property based on exploiting others' labour, which is said to expose the confusion behind Rousseau's position. Zhang concludes that Marx dissolved the gap between morality and politics by locating its root in private ownership and the state that protects it. The route beyond it, in the article's account, is for the proletariat to act as the revolutionary subject. It would rebuild economic forms and social institutions, and restore "individual ownership" on the basis of associated labour. The author presents this as a scientific practical guide towards reducing the wealth gap and achieving real democracy and equality. Read the original if you are interested in the Rousseau–Hegel–Marx lineage in political philosophy, or in how Marx's property theory is used to answer the moral-political question.

The formation and main content of Lenin's thought on the Communist Party's long-term leadership of all undertakings of the workers' and peasants' state 列宁关于共产党长时期领导工农国家各项事业思想的形成及其重要内容 Yu Min Marx and Engels held that the proletarian state and the proletarian party would wither away once the transition period ended and the first stage of communist society began. Yu Min argues that Lenin, drawing on practice after the October Revolution, departed from this view. In Lenin's reading, both state and party must persist for a long time, through the transition period and the first stage of communist society, and the Communist Party must lead every undertaking of the workers' and peasants' state. The article presents this as having contemporary significance. The article is in three parts. The first traces how Lenin arrived at the idea, from The State and Revolution (1917) through the civil war and the 1920 pamphlet "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder. The second sets out five areas of Party leadership that Lenin discussed: the state and its organs; economic work; culture and education, including ideology and the social sciences; diplomacy and foreign trade; and the Red Army. The third draws lessons for the present. Yu argues that Lenin's experience of fierce class struggle, with armed rebellion, assassinations and foreign intervention, led him to see the dictatorship of the proletariat as a prolonged and desperate war. He also placed Russia only at the "initial stage" of the transition, which Yu reads as meaning that the transition itself has stages and is very long. On this basis Lenin rejected the German "Left" denial of the party as a leap to the highest stage of communism. Yu then reports Lenin's positions against the Trotskyist, Workers' Opposition and Democratic Centralist proposals on trade unions and economic management, where the Party was to lead as the vanguard. Yu cites Lenin's handling of the Brest-Litovsk peace, the Genoa Conference instructions, and the political commissar system as examples of Party leadership in practice. Yu concludes that Lenin enriched Marx and Engels's thinking on the withering away of state and party. The article links this to the Chinese Communist Party's consolidation of its long-term governing position and to "upholding the Party's overall leadership", citing Xi Jinping's reports to the 19th and 20th Party Congresses. In Yu's account, Lenin lacked time to state the principle of comprehensive Party leadership explicitly, and the CCP has since summarised its own and Soviet experience and developed it. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Lenin's post-1917 practice is used to ground the doctrine of long-term Party leadership, with detailed citations of Lenin's texts.

The historical characteristics of the CPC's promotion of the spirit of historical initiative in the new era, and their practical implications 新时代中国共产党发扬历史主动精神的历史特点及其现实启示 Ding Junping Yang Yating Ding Junping and Yang Yating ask how the Communist Party of China has put the "spirit of historical initiative" into practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what that practice implies today. They argue that the Party has taken the initiative in four ways: in achieving major results, in shouldering its historical mission, in drawing lessons from history and in opening up bright prospects. In their account this is a correct choice for national development and Party building, and it supports the Party's new tasks in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The article first traces how Xi Jinping has used the concept of "historical initiative". It dates his first new-era use to 2013 and counts 13 mentions in nine speeches in 2021–2022. It also cites a mention in the explanation of the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The authors then review the existing literature, which they say mostly follows a "formation–promotion" pattern and pays little attention to new-era practice. The main body sets out four historical characteristics, and a closing section draws four implications. In the authors' reading, the four characteristics are as follows. First, the Party leads great change with a strong sense of political responsibility, sustained by ideals and convictions and by its mission. Second, it follows a people-centred development philosophy, treating the people's aspiration for a better life as its goal. Third, it summarises history using scientific methods, linking different periods, balancing success and failure, and applying the lessons creatively, as in the third historical resolution and its "ten affirmations". Fourth, it opens up prospects by judging the trend of the times, through the "two overall situations", the three major questions of the era, and timed goals such as the Two Centenary Goals. The authors present these as showing the Party's strategic and theoretical initiative. The authors draw four implications. The Party should hold to Marxist belief and use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to strengthen conviction. It should lead the great social revolution through the Party's self-reform. It should draw strength from the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists that begins with the founding spirit of the Party. And it should respect the people's principal position and learn from their wisdom. They conclude that the spirit of historical initiative will continue to be promoted and will help the Party answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party theorists frame "historical initiative" in Xi-era documents and of the research literature on it.

Establishing a correct view of the history of the Chinese nation 树立正确的中华民族历史观 Wang Dong Wang Yonggui Wang Dong and Wang Yonggui take up what they call the correct view of the history of the Chinese nation (Zhonghua minzu), and argue that it should be firmly established. Their starting point is Xi Jinping's speech of September 2024 at the national commendation conference on ethnic unity and progress. There Xi said that China's peoples have jointly opened up the country's vast territory, founded a unified multi-ethnic state, written its history, created its culture and fostered its national spirit. The authors read this as the theoretical statement of the correct historical view and as a basis for historical confidence and for building the Chinese nation as a community. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out the meaning of a historical view built on the "five commonalities" (the five "jointly" formulations above). The second gives the principles and methods for establishing it. The third lists practical paths. It is a short Party-journal piece that relies mainly on Xi's statements and does not discuss specific historical cases. In the first part, the authors argue that this historical view advances the adaptation of Marxist ethnic theory to Chinese conditions, drawing on the Two Integrations, especially the integration with traditional Chinese culture through ideas such as "all under heaven as one family". They also claim it supplies the ideological basis for forging a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation. In their account it shows the formation of a "pluralistic yet unified" nation as a historical necessity and supports the case for a community with a shared future for mankind. The second part names three principles: the historical-materialist method, which treats national unity as a historical inevitability; holding to the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity; and firm criticism of erroneous historical views. The authors say some people, under the banner of scholarship, dismember, distort and fabricate history. For practice, the authors propose deeper historical research, including continuing the project to trace the origins of Chinese civilization and studying exchanges among ethnic groups. They also call for building a shared spiritual home through education, the national common language and standard national textbooks, and shared cultural symbols. A third proposal is to tell the story of the Chinese nation through media at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party's official line on ethnic work and national history is framed and what practical measures it names.

Grasping the core meaning and practical requirements of developing new quality productive forces 深刻领悟发展新质生产力的核心要义和实践要求 Zhong Ying This article in Red Flag Manuscript sets out to explain what new quality productive forces are, why they matter and how to develop them, following Xi Jinping's speeches and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhong argues that Xi's discussion of the concept systematically answers these three questions and represents an innovation in, and development of, the Marxist theory of productive forces. The article is a Party-theory commentary. The text has three parts. The first defines new quality productive forces as an advanced form of productive forces consistent with the new development philosophy. The second presents their development as an intrinsic requirement of, and key lever for, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The third gives practical requirements: innovation, industrial upgrading, local adaptation and reform of the relations of production. In the first part, Zhong relies on Xi's definition: innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality, with a sharp rise in total factor productivity as the core marker. Zhong reads the "new quality" through the three elements of productive forces. These are new types of workers, new means of labour such as artificial intelligence and digital technologies, and new objects of labour such as new materials, new energy and data. Zhong holds that Chinese modernization and high-quality development need a solid material and technological base, which these forces supply. In the practical part, Zhong stresses original and disruptive innovation and says core technologies cannot be begged or bought. Technology must be turned into industry ("from 0 to 1" and "from 1 to infinity"), with strategic emerging and future industries as the main arena. Traditional industries should be upgraded rather than discarded: the article cites their share at about 80% of industrial value added above designated size. Zhong calls for adapting to local conditions, avoiding a rush into the same sectors and bubbles, and building the new before breaking the old. Zhong concludes that production relations must be adjusted to suit new quality productive forces. The proposals include deepening economic and science-and-technology reforms, removing bottlenecks, building a high-standard market system, letting advanced factors of production flow smoothly, expanding high-level opening up and linking education, science and talent policy. Institutional innovation is presented as the way to remove obstacles and release innovative energy. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theorists link new quality productive forces to high-quality development, local policy and the reform agenda of the Third Plenum.

Forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation 铸牢中华民族共同体意识 Pan Yue Pan Yue sets out the official case for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation (铸牢中华民族共同体意识), the principle that Pan says is now the main thread of the Party's ethnic work. The article, which first appeared in Qiushi, presents the principle as a major original judgement of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Pan argues that it enriches Marxist ethnic theory and consolidates the path of resolving ethnic issues with Chinese characteristics. The text has four parts. It traces how the formulation developed between 2014 and 2024 through Xi Jinping's speeches and explains its meaning and importance. It then sets out the principle's theoretical sources in Marxism, Chinese civilisation and a century of Party ethnic work. Finally, it lists practical requirements in theory-building, education, narrative and ideology. Pan's core argument is that the principle responds to specific present conditions. These include uneven development in ethnic regions, growing population movement and mixing among ethnic groups, and what Pan calls sharp ideological struggle in the ethnic sphere. Pan describes the shared consciousness as a reflection of an objectively existing historical community. Four relationships are to be handled correctly: commonality takes the lead over difference, and the shared national consciousness takes precedence over the consciousness of individual ethnic groups. Chinese culture is the trunk and ethnic cultures the branches, and material development does not automatically produce unity. Pan grounds all this in the Two Integrations, especially the integration of Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. Pan also cites the ideas of great unification and 'harmony without uniformity' as part of that heritage. Pan's practical proposals include building an autonomous Chinese ethnic-theory knowledge system, distinct from Western ethnic theory, and a discipline of Chinese national community studies. They also include making the principle part of Party-building and performance assessment, and promoting the national common language and nationally compiled textbooks. Pan further calls for telling the story of the Chinese national community, rebutting foreign criticism of ethnic policy, and opposing historical nihilism, extreme nationalism, religious extremism, Han chauvinism and local nationalism. Pan concludes that only a firmly forged sense of community can gather the strength for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of current Party doctrine on ethnic policy, with its stated rationale and policy agenda.

China's proposal for promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations 推动文明交流互鉴的中国方案 Zhai Maiyun This short commentary presents the Global Civilization Initiative, which Xi Jinping first put forward on 15 March 2023 in a keynote speech at the CPC in Dialogue with World Political Parties High-level Meeting. Zhai argues that the initiative offers a Chinese answer to how different civilizations can coexist, and that it breaks with the Western narrative of civilizational conflict. Together with the Global Development Initiative and the Global Security Initiative, it forms what the author calls a logically tight system of global initiatives. The article first criticises two Western paradigms of civilizational interaction, then explains how the initiative goes beyond them, and finally sets out how it might be put into practice. The first paradigm is Samuel Huntington's "clash of civilizations"; the second is a "civilizational superiority" view that the author describes as a hierarchy of civilizations. Zhai contends that Huntington's 1993 thesis presupposed conflict, exaggerated the danger of cultural difference, divided the world crudely into seven civilizations, and served to give the United States a new enemy for sustaining hegemony. The "superiority" view, in the author's reading, treats Western political and economic models as universal standards and exports them one way, which invites confrontation. Against these, the initiative follows Xi's formula of exchange over estrangement, mutual learning over conflict, and inclusiveness over superiority. It "unbinds" relations between civilizations from relations between states, denies that civilizations can be ranked, and offers the common values of all humanity in place of "universal values". The author cites the UN General Assembly's designation of 10 June as International Day of Dialogue among Civilizations. Zhai calls on governments to reject exclusive, values-based diplomacy and to support cultural exchange. The author also asks international organisations to practise genuine multilateralism, and says China will provide institutional and financial support. The author presents the creative transformation of traditional cultures as the route to a shared spiritual homeland for humanity. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese official commentary frames the Global Civilization Initiative against Huntington and Western claims of civilizational superiority.

Super digital platforms and new trends in new-imperialist monopoly 超级数字平台与新帝国主义垄断新趋势 Xu Zhixiang Responding to Xi Jinping's call to study contemporary capitalism and its changes, Xu Zhixiang asks what "super digital platforms" are, how they reshape monopoly under "new imperialism", what the essence and consequences of this change are, and how China should respond. The article argues that these platforms (Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Facebook) are a new organisational form of finance capital, and that they drive imperialist monopoly towards new forms, means, scope and functions. The article has four parts. It first defines super digital platforms and their three-dimensional operating system of "algorithm control + data concentration + cross-domain integration". It then defines new imperialism as the post-Cold War stage of monopoly capitalism and sets out four new trends. The third part analyses their essence and effects, and the last proposes responses for China. Xu argues that monopoly shifts in four ways: from local, fragmentary monopoly to global aggregated monopoly; from a mix of production and capital concentration to mainly capital concentration, driven by speculation; from monopoly bounded by time and space to "beyond time and space" monopoly, including the "platformisation of everyday life"; and from economic to "extra-economic" monopoly, resting on control of discourse and on Western cultural and ideological hegemony. In essence, the author holds, this is a collusion between "technofeudalism" and "digital imperialism". It reshapes global accumulation by dispossession through creative destruction, deepened inequality and a "全时域+全方位" (all-time, all-round) system of exploitation. By Marx's logic of underconsumption it is said to end in a "super digital platform crisis" of relative overproduction. Xu holds that the capitalist system is the root of these problems and that China's public-ownership-based system allows it to curb the harms of capital logic. The proposals are: classify platforms by ownership, function and degree of competition; strengthen public ownership of platforms and place a state-led "digital central enterprise" at the core of a national big-data platform; enact laws such as a Digital Labour Law and revise the Anti-Monopoly Law; accelerate indigenous innovation in core digital technologies; and build a community with a shared future for mankind in the digital field, through the Belt and Road Initiative and joint global governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist political economist combines Lenin's theory of imperialism with debates on platform capitalism and technofeudalism to derive concrete policy proposals.

Mao Zedong's exploration of and contribution to the path of modernization after the founding of the People's Republic 新中国成立后毛泽东对现代化道路的探索与贡献 Zhang Guozuo Yang Ruonan Zhang Guozuo and Yang Ruonan ask how Mao Zedong approached the modernization of a poor, populous country after 1949, and what that exploration left for later generations. Taking up Xi Jinping's description of Mao as the 'great founder' of China's socialist modernization, they argue that Mao's work gave Chinese modernization its ideological, material and institutional preconditions. They also contend that it anticipated the five features that Xi now attributes to Chinese modernization. The article is organised around those five features, each treated as an area of Mao's post-1949 thought and practice. It covers the country's huge population, the orientation towards fairness, equality and common prosperity, the joint improvement of material and cultural life, and the pairing of economic growth with the protection of nature. It ends with the creation of a peaceful international environment. The authors draw on Mao's speeches, annotations and letters and on statistics from the Mao period, and close by linking Mao's exploration to Xi's formulations. On population, the authors argue that Mao saw a large population as both a heavy responsibility and a source of strength. They credit his leadership with the patriotic health campaigns, rural barefoot doctors and cooperative medical care, which raised life expectancy, and with literacy drives, which cut illiteracy. On equality, they say Mao opposed both egalitarianism and excessive disparity, and pursued a staged, balanced route to common prosperity, set out in 'On the Ten Major Relationships'. On the environment and foreign policy, they cite Mao's calls to 'green the motherland' and to integrate farming, forestry and herding. They also cite his policy of fighting to stop war, advocating peaceful coexistence and 'never seeking hegemony'. The authors state that China under Mao launched no war of aggression for its own modernization. The authors conclude that Mao's practice, in their words, gave a first answer, in theory and practice, to how a poor China could modernize. They present this as a process of repeated practice and understanding, in line with Mao's 'On Practice'. They add that Xi has inherited, enriched and systematized this legacy as Chinese modernization, with its essential requirements, strategic timetable to the middle of the century and guiding principles, and that studying Xi's statements reveals both continuity with Mao and further innovation. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars trace Xi-era Chinese modernization back to Mao-era policies and sources.

Advancing the integrated development of ideological and political education across universities, secondary and primary schools through a systems perspective 以系统观念推进大中小学思想政治教育一体化建设 Chang Qing Chang Qing, a university Party official, takes up how the integration of ideological and political education across universities, secondary schools and primary schools should be advanced. The newspaper commentary argues that this integration must be treated as an organic whole and a systems project, guided by what it calls the systems perspective, a core element of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Chang's view, it bears directly on whom education serves, what kind of people it cultivates and how, and is a key step in the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out why integration is necessary. The second identifies three dimensions for it: sequence, effectiveness and depth. The third outlines a practical route, covering institutional coordination, continuity of student development and a multi-actor pattern of education. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Chang gives three reasons for integration: it ensures the Party's cause has successors, it reflects the political, popular and strategic attributes of education, and it serves the building of a strong education nation, whose first listed trait is the capacity for ideological guidance. The core argument pairs concepts in three relations. Wholeness and progression concern coordinating courses, course-embedded ideological education and everyday ideological work, while stages from primary school to university move from easy to difficult. Direction and effectiveness require the guidance of Marxism and Party leadership, with results measured first by the cultivation of virtue. Value and knowledge hold that values are conveyed through knowledge, with new Party theory, core socialist values and traditional culture as key content. On implementation, Chang calls for stronger top-level design and coordination among Party committees, education authorities, research bodies and schools, with support for staff, resources and artificial intelligence. Chang also calls for spiral progression across stages, from goals to textbooks and teacher training, and for cooperation among schools, government, local communities and museums. The article presents this as raising the efficiency of integration. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official discourse links systems thinking, the 'big ideological and political course' and the building of a strong education nation in Chinese schooling policy.

Reinterpreting Heidegger's practical philosophy A supplement to Volpi 重解海德格尔实践哲学 Liu Mingfeng Franco Volpi's reading of Heidegger's relation to Aristotle became a model for studying Heidegger's practical philosophy, yet Liu Mingfeng argues that Chinese scholarship has mostly introduced it without critical reflection. The article sets out Volpi's work, identifies its gaps, and offers a supplement. Liu's thesis is that Heidegger's practical philosophy begins not in the analysis of Dasein in Being and Time but in the early Freiburg 'hermeneutics of facticity', which the author holds to be a practical philosophy in its own right. The article places Volpi within the 1960s revival of practical philosophy in Germany and follows his main works, from Heidegger e Aristotele (1984) to the 1989 essay on the homology between Being and Time and the Nicomachean Ethics. It then turns to Heidegger's 1922 'Natorp Report', the early Freiburg lectures and the 1923 course on the hermeneutics of facticity. Liu also discusses Jacques Taminiaux, Gadamer, Jean-Luc Nancy and Adorno as comparison points. Liu credits Volpi with showing that Dasein exists first as praxis and production rather than theory, and that Heidegger 'ontologizes' Aristotle. Volpi's focus, however, falls on the Marburg period after 1923, and Volpi never takes up the hermeneutics of facticity, even after the early lectures were published. The author reads that hermeneutics as the appropriation of one's present situation through interpretation, which draws in Aristotle as a historical source. Following Gadamer's and Volpi's method of analogy, Liu compares this appropriation with Aristotelian phronesis, the choice of right action in a concrete situation. Liu adds an 'internal' argument: in the 1921–22 lectures Heidegger unites philosophy and hermeneutics as the self-interpretation of factical life, which makes philosophy itself a lived practice. Liu concludes that the hermeneutics of facticity is a practical philosophy, but a formal one. Because it is a circle of life interpreting itself, it can offer no external guidance or norms. Its significance, in Liu's view, lies in grounding the primacy of the concrete situation and in giving ethical action an authentic orientation. Liu defends Heidegger's refusal to prescribe norms by comparing it with Adorno's view that no standard of the good life is possible in a wholly corrupt society. Read the original if you work on Heidegger, Aristotle or Gadamer and want a critique of Volpi that draws on the early Freiburg lectures.

Decoding the mechanism of cultural confidence and strength through the lens of the Two Integrations 解码“两个结合”视域下的文化自信自强机制 Sun Shaoyong Chen Zhongbin Sun Shaoyong and Chen Zhongbin ask how the Two Integrations (integrating Marxism with China's specific realities and with its fine traditional culture) relate to the task of building cultural confidence and strength. They argue that the two are closely linked and reinforce each other: advancing cultural confidence and strength is both an inherent requirement and the goal of the Two Integrations. The article sets out the logic of this relationship, explains its internal mechanism and proposes practical paths. The article has three parts. The first treats the logical relationship, claiming that the two share a common goal (building a culturally strong country), compatible values and the same principal force, the people. The second explains the "endogenous mechanism" under three headings: understanding of laws, creative thinking and grasp of the times. The third sets out four practical paths. In the central section, the authors argue that the Two Integrations deepen understanding of how fine traditional culture is created, spread and integrated. For example, they say culture tends to spread from high to low positions of value and, as it matures, differences give way to shared elements, which they link to the ideals of harmony in diversity and a common spiritual home for all ethnic groups. They also claim that the Two Integrations widen creative thinking by joining revolutionary culture with the great founding spirit of the Party, traditional moral ideas with the core socialist values, and cultural renewal with modern science and technology. On the grasp of the times, they hold that the Two Integrations answer the demand to strengthen national cultural soft power and bring out the contemporary governing value of traditional culture. For practice, the authors call for Marxist guidance across cultural work, including cultural undertakings and industries, reform of the cultural system and public cultural services. They also call for deeper interpretation and more innovative expression of fine traditional culture. They want the core socialist values to guide cultural production, social consensus and individual conduct. Finally, they urge exchange and mutual learning among civilizations while upholding a Chinese cultural standpoint, drawing on the Global Civilization Initiative. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship links the Two Integrations to cultural policy and the project of cultural strength.

Party leadership and the rule-of-law character of the "Fengqiao Experience" in the new era 党的领导与新时代“枫桥经验”的法治属性 Zhao Yang Liu Yongyan The "Fengqiao Experience" began in Fengqiao township, Zhuji, Zhejiang, in the 1960s as a method of resolving disputes locally through mass mobilisation. Zhao Yang and Liu Yongyan ask in what sense its new-era form, shaped since the 18th Party Congress (2012), has a rule-of-law character. They argue that this character grows out of Party leadership: under the Party, the experience applies rule-of-law thinking and methods, inherits traditional Chinese legal culture, and advances the modernization of grassroots governance. The article has three parts. The first sets out what the rule-of-law character means, both the general features of modern rule of law (supremacy of law, equal protection, checks on power, procedural justice, protection of rights) and its Chinese features. The second examines the conditions that formed it: Party documents from the 18th Party Congress to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Xi Jinping's statements on the experience since 2003, and links to traditional legal culture. The third turns to practice, using cases from Zhejiang and Shandong and the court system. The authors identify four Chinese features: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, a pluralistic dispute-resolution mechanism that combines rigid legal norms with flexible mediation, and the linking of governance theory to local legal practice. They trace its roots to the traditional ideas of \"fairness, forgiveness and trust in the people\", to \"village-law autonomy\" and to combining virtue with law, which they present as an instance of the Two Integrations. Their cases are the \"three ups and three downs\" decision-making mechanism in Fengyuan village, digital tools such as Wenshang County's online petition system, and one-stop dispute resolution and litigation services in Zhejiang courts. They credit these with shifting governance from ending litigation towards having little litigation at all. The authors conclude that the new-era Fengqiao Experience is a component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a practical expression of Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law. They present it as a workable approach to grassroots governance on the rule-of-law track, and call for continuing to uphold and develop it so as to form a pattern of shared contribution, governance and benefits. Read the original if you want a Party-line account of how Chinese legal scholarship ties grassroots mediation to Party leadership, official documents and traditional legal culture, with Zhejiang and Shandong cases.

Marx and Engels's theory of civilization and its contemporary value 马克思恩格斯的文明理论及其当代价值 Zhang Sanyuan As civilization has become a high-frequency term and a scholarly hotspot, Zhang Sanyuan argues that clarifying it requires "returning to Marx". Marx and Engels never wrote a dedicated treatise on civilization, but Zhang contends that historical materialism is itself a genuine, scientific theory of civilization. The article sets out to reconstruct that theory and show its guiding role in the civilizational logic of Chinese modernization. The article has four parts. It first outlines four periods in the formation of the theory (from the early 1840s to Engels's late writings) and then presents five principles for interpreting it. It then sets out the theory's core content, its distinguishing features, and finally its contemporary value, drawing mainly on The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, Capital and Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Zhang holds that the five interpretive principles are the people-centred, critical, thoroughgoing, processual and holistic. The core claim is that civilization originates in "the production of the immediate means of life", develops as an open process, follows the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and has human emancipation and all-round development as its theme. Zhang argues that the theory unites the ideal with the practical, class character with humanity as a whole, criticism with construction, and system with development. In this reading it exposes capitalist civilization as a unity of civilization and barbarism, and rejects idealist, "hero" and single-line views of history in favour of multiple paths. Zhang concludes that the theory is not outdated. In the article's account, it grounds the communist ideal, points toward a universal happy life, and supports building a community with a shared future for mankind. It also underpins confidence in civilizational self-awareness under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhang presents Chinese modernization, through the Two Integrations, as a creative application that surpasses the capital-centred Western civilizational outlook. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese interpretation of Marx and Engels on civilization and its link to the official idea of a new form of human civilization.

A historical examination from launching reform to further deepening reform comprehensively 从实行改革到进一步全面深化改革的历史考察 Chen Jinlong Chen Jinlong asks how China's reform has evolved from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that this path involved both a changing conceptual content of 'reform' and shifting practical priorities. Tracing it, Chen holds, helps clarify the internal logic of reform history. The article is a Party-history study in four stages. It begins with reform centred on economic restructuring and early talk of comprehensive reform in the 1980s. It then covers comprehensive and deepening reform aimed at a socialist market economy and the Scientific Outlook on Development (1992–2012). Next it treats comprehensive deepening of reform from the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally further comprehensive deepening under the banner of Chinese modernization. Chen relies mainly on speeches and documents by Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao, Xi Jinping and Party plenums. Chen's central move is to show that each stage's reform concept was justified by a different driver. Early reform was tied to the Four Modernizations, opening up and the improvement of socialism; later stages were tied to the market-economy goal, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and then to modernizing national governance, demonstrating institutional advantages, solving prominent problems and the movement of basic social contradictions. Further comprehensive deepening is presented as a two-way relation with Chinese modernization, and as driven by institutional innovation, the principal social contradiction and the development of new quality productive forces. Chen lists the 14 key tasks and 'seven focuses' of the 2024 plenum as expressing this link. Chen concludes that reform has been gradual, with stage-specific priorities and economic reform always the leading element. In Chen's account, the trajectory shows the Party's historical initiative as a 'mission-driven' party that leads reform and relies on the people. The family of reform concepts that results is said to lay a foundation for an autonomous Chinese body of knowledge about reform. Read the original if you want a documented, quotation-rich account of how official reform terminology developed from 1978 to the 2024 plenum.

The four perspectives in the construction of Marx's theory of mental production 马克思精神生产理论建构的四重视域述论 Bi Tianliang Deng Chunyu Bi Tianliang and Deng Chunyu take up Marx's category of "mental production" (精神生产), which he developed while building his theory of communist society and the all-round development of the human being. Existing scholarship has studied its meaning, formation, features and contemporary value; the authors argue that the theory is best grasped as a whole through the several perspectives from which Marx constructed it. Their thesis is that four perspectives together make up the theory: the division of labour, the critique of political economy, the totality of social production, and the all-round development of the person. The article is a research essay with four numbered sections, one per perspective. It moves from a historical account of mental production under successive forms of ownership, through Marx's typology of productive and unproductive mental production against Smith, Say and List, to the place of mental production within the system of social production, and finally to its value for individual development. It closes with a short statement of the theory's present significance. In the authors' reading, Marx grounded mental production in historical materialism by tying it to the division of labour: it became a distinct sphere once mental and material labour separated, and under capitalism it is industrialised and subordinated to capital. Drawing on the Marxian distinction, Bi and Deng present "productive" mental production as that which creates surplus value for the owner of the conditions of production (Milton's writing of Paradise Lost is the example), whereas free, "unproductive" mental production is outside capital's logic and requires disposable free time. They then argue that Marx placed mental production in a system of four kinds of production: of human beings, material goods, ideas and social relations. Material production fundamentally determines it, yet it reacts back and has relative independence and uneven development, as with art. Finally, drawing on the Grundrisse, the authors link mental production to the stages of human dependence, in which capital turns it into an instrument of surplus-value creation and of money-worship and hedonism, and to its free form as a basis for all-round human development. The authors conclude that these four perspectives amount to the outline of Marx's theory of mental production and a weapon in establishing historical materialism. They contend that clarifying them rebuts Western scholars who reduce Marx to "economic determinism" or linear productive-force determinism. They also hold that the theory helps diagnose the "spiritual pathology" behind contemporary economic and social problems, helps people overcome spiritual crises and promotes common prosperity in spiritual life. Read the original if you want a concise systematic overview of how Marx's mental production theory is organised, and of how Chinese scholars link it to current ideological and cultural work.

A review of research on major foundational theoretical questions since the founding of the People's Republic 新中国成立以来重大基础理论问题研究述评 Research Group on Major Foundational Theoretical and Practical Issues, Institute of Historical Theory This review, by a research group at the Institute of Historical Theory, surveys the major foundational theoretical questions that Chinese historians debated from 1949 to the present. It argues that these debates, though limited by their historical moment, answered the theoretical needs of the Party and people in revolution, construction and reform. In the authors' account, they enriched Chinese Marxist historiography and still offer intellectual resources for national rejuvenation. The review covers six clusters of questions: the Marxist theory of social formations; the periodisation of ancient Chinese history; land-ownership systems; the sprouts of capitalism; the formation of the Han nation; and the evaluation of historical figures. It places most of them within the "five golden flowers" of the 1950s and 60s, tracing roots to the social-history debates of the 1920s and 30s. It follows each through early reform-era revival, later decline of attention, and renewed relevance. Related topics, such as the long continuity of Chinese feudal society and the Asiatic mode of production, are mentioned only briefly. The authors treat the social-formation theory as the base of the others. Once the "five-stage" scheme was accepted, they argue, disputes arose over where slavery ended and feudalism began (the "three schools, five views"), what land system dominated feudal China, when capitalist sprouts appeared, and when the Han nation formed. They record the many competing positions, including single-line versus multi-line development and three-stage versus five-stage schemes. On historical figures, they endorse class analysis combined with historicism and concrete analysis. They say reform-era challenges to class analysis, under banners such as "multiple values", fed historical nihilism, which they describe as an attempt to undermine Party leadership. The authors conclude that the debates delivered theoretical guidance for revolution and construction and many high-quality studies. In their view, the debates also created new subfields such as socio-economic history and ethnic history, and fostered a society-wide "theory fever" of open argument tied to practical needs. They call for a systematic review of this research to help build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in history, and to support Chinese modernization and the work of forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact map of mid-century Chinese Marxist historiographical debates and how Party-aligned scholars now frame their legacy.)

The "three distinctions" and the internal logic of further deepening reform comprehensively “三个区分开来”与进一步全面深化改革的内在逻辑 Xu Yulu Xu Yulu asks how the "three distinctions" (sange qufen kailai), first put forward by Xi Jinping in January 2016, relate to the programme of further deepening reform comprehensively set out at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that the distinctions, which separate honest errors in reform from deliberate or self-interested violations of discipline and law, are an internal part of what that reform needs. They encourage and protect officials who must take risks, so applying them effectively is presented as a precondition for carrying out the plenum's reform agenda. The article has three sections. The first sets out the meaning and current value of the three distinctions as a form of combining strict management with care for cadres. The second analyses their logical link to the reform agenda. The third discusses how to implement them. Xu draws on Xi Jinping's statements, the 2018 General Office guideline on motivating cadres, the Party's accountability regulations, disciplinary rules, local measures in Jinan, Shenzhen and Beijing, and a 2022 model case from the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Xu argues that the distinctions serve three aims. They underpin a precise mechanism for tolerating and correcting errors, so officials dare to act on "breakthrough" tasks. They rest on a developing system of responsibility, so officials can act skilfully on "complex" tasks. They help build a political ecology that supports getting things done, which serves the "clear" tasks. The author then links them to three reform challenges: venturing into "uncharted territory", gnawing at "hard bones", and dissolving "mental and policy shackles". Officials are said to fear conflicting policies, unclear limits and malicious reports. Xu holds that errors from inexperience, uncertain outcomes and changing environments in first-time trials should be tolerated under conditions of motive, circumstances and procedure. Xu identifies gaps in practice: weak awareness, limited ability to judge motives, vague regulations and a cautious atmosphere. The proposals are to strengthen political consciousness and Party leadership, use systematic thinking, lawful procedure and coordination between departments, build mechanisms for advance risk reporting, clearing officials' names and follow-up visits, and make more use of guiding cases. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-school account of how tolerance for officials' errors is being tied to the post-2024 reform agenda and to concrete disciplinary practice.

The historical logic and contemporary mission of building an autonomous knowledge system for CPC history and Party building studies 建构中共党史党建学自主知识体系的历史逻辑与时代使命 Yang Lanjie This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in April 2025, asks how the discipline of CPC history and Party building studies should construct its own autonomous knowledge system. Yang Lanjie argues that the task follows from China's modern history and from the Party's record of governance, and that it is a duty of scholars in the field. The author also holds that reforming how the discipline is evaluated is a necessary condition for success. The article opens with Xi Jinping's April 2022 instructions to philosophy and social science scholars at Renmin University. It then has three parts: the historical logic behind building an autonomous knowledge system, the contemporary mission of the discipline, and the role of new evaluation standards. It refers to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to the 2024 degree guidelines that set out four second-level disciplines under the first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building studies. Yang's historical argument is that modern China was pushed into a "catch-up" mentality that applied Western analytical models to Chinese experience and lost subjectivity. In Yang's account, cultural subjectivity has since revived, and the Party's achievements since reform and opening up require a locally grounded explanation. Yang presents the discipline, which centres on "the governance of the Communist Party" and "the governance of China", as one of the most distinctively autonomous fields. For its mission, Yang says it must uphold Party leadership and the people-centred stance, combine historical and political thinking, and offer Party-building experience for a new form of human political civilization. The author says some concepts, such as "political party" and "state governance", are shared with other traditions, while others, such as "the Yan'an experience", are distinctive. Yang concludes that evaluation of the discipline should stress autonomy and practice. It should not rest on counting talent titles, honours and papers, and should instead integrate moral education, social contribution, and the fit and effectiveness of training, including for Party organisation cadres. The author expects this to join professional development with social application and theory with practice. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Party-school-affiliated scholar frames disciplinary autonomy, evaluation reform and the Party-building field.

A political-philosophical project on war and peace: Marx's sublation of Rousseau 战争与和平的政治哲学筹划:马克思对卢梭的扬弃 Lan Yang Lan Yang asks how Marx's historical-materialist account of war and peace was formed through a sustained dialogue with Rousseau, and what this means for a world the author describes as undergoing deep change. The article argues that Marx sublated Rousseau's contract-theory framework: he kept its dialectical insight but moved the analysis from human nature and the state to the capital logic of modern society. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Rousseau's treatment of war and peace in four steps: the roots of war in human nature, the paradoxical condition of the state, possible routes to peace, and the evaluation of wars. The second sets out four ways in which Marx criticised and went beyond this model. The third draws out the contemporary implications of that sublation, ending with a reference to Xi Jinping's call for a community with a shared future for mankind. In Lan's reading, Rousseau traced war to private property rather than to human greed and proposed peace through republics, ultimately small ones, and defensive alliances. Lan calls this a state-centred approach resting on an abstract view of human nature. Marx replaced the abstract natural individual with the real individual in material production, so that war becomes the intensified form of power relations arising from modes of production and distribution. Marx also treated the state paradox as an expression of civil society's divisions and located the antagonisms of the modern world in the logic of capital. Lan identifies three forms: class opposition, a hierarchical international structure, and recurrent struggles for hegemony. They correspond to class wars, colonial wars and wars of hegemony. Political emancipation alone cannot end the cycle of war and peace, so Marx pointed to abolishing private ownership of the means of production and a free association of individuals, with socialist forces as the practical route. He also replaced general moral condemnation with criteria for distinguishing just from unjust wars. Lan draws three lessons. Conflicts need historical, totalising analysis rather than abstract concepts such as human nature, the state or "universal values". Hegemonism remains the main obstacle to peace, and Lan cites protectionism and trade wars used by a few countries against emerging ones. A new international political and economic order that breaks the "centre–periphery" pattern is urgently needed. Lan presents building a community with a shared future for mankind as the practical outcome and as the world-historical significance of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Rousseau and Marx on international relations, and an example of how such theory is tied to current Chinese foreign-policy language.

Establishing a seeking-truth-from-facts style of study throughout the Party Revisiting Mao Zedong's "Reform Our Study" 在全党树立实事求是的学风 Li Youxin This short commentary in Study Times revisits Mao Zedong's 1941 report "Reform Our Study" (改造我们的学习), delivered to cadres in Yan'an on 19 May 1941 and later included in volume three of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. Li Youxin argues that Mao's criticism of subjectivism, and his call for a style of study based on seeking truth from facts and linking theory with practice, still offers guidance for making improvement of Party conduct regular and long-term. The article has three parts. It first sets out the wartime background in which Mao proposed reforming study, then summarises Mao's contrast between the subjectivist attitude and the Marxist-Leninist attitude, and finally treats investigation and research as the base for changing Party conduct. It closes by linking this to current Party campaigns. Li explains that by the War of Resistance the Party had become a large mass party with many new members and cadres of uneven theoretical training. Mao's 1938 call for a Party-wide study competition improved theoretical levels but exposed a separation of theory from practice. Li reports Mao's charge that subjectivists neglect present conditions and Chinese history and study theory for its own sake. Against this stands the Marxist-Leninist attitude, in which one starts from objective reality and seeks its internal laws. Li stresses Mao's reinterpretation of the traditional phrase "seeking truth from facts" (实事求是), and his judgement that subjectivism is an enemy of the Party, the working class, the people and the nation. Li presents investigation as the basic skill that makes this attitude concrete, citing Mao's line that without investigation there is no right to speak. Li concludes that Mao's text was a key step in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, and that its emphasis on investigation remains a "family heirloom" for Party members. The article ties this to the current study and education campaign on the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, whose first item is improving investigation and research, and to Xi Jinping's remarks that style problems are at root problems of Party spirit. Li calls on cadres to go to the grassroots, keep close ties with the people, and so secure a sound style of work for Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press uses a Yan'an-era text to support present-day campaigns on Party conduct.

The historical-materialist road to "universal world history" 通向“普遍的世界历史”的唯物史观之路 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng asks what "universal world history" (universal history) means in Kant, Hegel and Marx, and what the concept offers for Marxist world-history theory in the twenty-first century. The article argues that Marx broke with the idealist versions of the concept. In Marx's historical materialism, universal world history is communism, reached through "universal intercourse" that sublates the particular interests of single nation-states and the barriers between civilizations. Wu presents this as a theoretical basis for the new categories of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, namely a community with a shared future for mankind, a new form of human civilization and common values of all humanity. The article has three parts. The first compares the three thinkers' answers to the question of where the world and humanity are heading. Kant's answer is contractarian: a cosmopolitan constitution and a league of nations for perpetual peace. Hegel's is theodicy: the absolute spirit moves from the Oriental to the Germanic world. Marx's answer is materialist and aims at human liberation. The second part sets out Marx's critique of idealism, drawing mainly on The German Ideology. The third part gives the principles of universal world history as Marx understood it. Wu's central claim is that idealist universal history has only the form of universality, not its substance. For Wu, the "thought in the form of universality" is the ruling ideology of a class or nation that presents its particular interests as common ones. Wu argues that today "universal values" play this role: unilateralism, zero-sum thinking and de-globalization are pursued under their cover. Marx located the real ruler of world history in capital and in the "domination–subordination" relations of production it creates, which grew out of manufacture and merchant capital. Wu draws three conditions from Marx. First, a "universal class", the proletariat, must form, and this is how the cyclical pattern of one particular class replacing another can be escaped. Second, the productive forces must develop to a high level, so that universal intercourse becomes possible. Third, the domination–subordination relations must be broken, as with the town–country opposition, and private ownership must disappear. Wu concludes that Marx's path shows how humanity can sublate national particular interests and build cooperative, win-win relations of intercourse. In Wu's view, "building a community with a shared future for mankind" is the new content that twenty-first-century Marxism gives to universal world history. If states build win-win relations of production on the basis of common values of all humanity, Wu argues, humanity can partly escape the capital-dominated order and move towards communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist philosophy-of-history reading of Kant, Hegel and Marx that links "universal values" and the community with a shared future for mankind to Marx's critique of ideology.

Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and two opposed conceptions of rights 马克思的《黑格尔法哲学批判》与两种对立的权利观 Wang Xueqiao Wang Xueqiao asks what Marx's unfinished and unpublished manuscript Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right shows when read through the question of rights. The article argues that the manuscript is organised around two opposed conceptions: a state-based conception of rights, represented by Hegel, and a civil-society-based conception, which Marx establishes by overturning Hegel. Although the critique appears to concern rights at the level of the state, Wang holds that its direct purpose is to ground rights in civil society. On this reading it opens the construction of Marx's historical-materialist conception of rights. The article has four parts. The first distinguishes the two conceptions and notes that the German Recht, rendered in Chinese as law, right, rights and statute, should not be reduced to law, since many economic rights in civil society do not take legal form. The second examines Marx's critique of Hegel on monarchical, executive and legislative power. The third traces how this critique led to the historical-materialist conception of rights, drawing on the 1859 Preface, The German Ideology and Critique of the Gotha Programme. A short conclusion follows. Wang's central claim is that the separation of civil society from the state makes the two conceptions possible, and that the key question is which kind of right is more fundamental. Hegel, in Wang's account, starts from the logical Idea and treats the state as the actuality of the ethical Idea. Marx reverses this: family and civil society are the presuppositions of the state, and rights arise from the 'material relations of life' rather than from the state or from a social contract, which Wang says distinguishes him from Rousseau. Wang then draws three consequences. Rights are legitimate only through their basis in civil society. The gap between rights that ought to exist and rights actually held can only be understood from civil society and property relations. The historical development of rights follows the forms of the division of labour and of ownership. Wang concludes that Marx's reading directs inquiry into the basis of rights to civil society, and that establishing the civil-society-based conception was the theoretical precondition for his historical-materialist theory of rights. Wang adds that Marx's notion of civil society widened from the narrow sense of bourgeois society to the whole of human history, so that his view of rights is not confined to the bourgeois case. Read the original if you study Marx's early critique of Hegel, the philosophy of rights, or how Chinese legal scholars link the 1843 manuscript to historical materialism.

Anti-capitalism as a form of organisation: a psychoanalytic approach 作为组织形式的反资本主义：以精神分析为切入点 Nick Malherbe This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Nick Malherbe, first published in Theory, Culture & Society. It asks whether 'anti-capitalism' is too vague a term to guide left politics, since liberal reformists and fascist nationalists have also used it. Malherbe argues that the term is best read as a 'loose signifier' for a form of organisation: collectives assemble in whatever shape current struggles require, and psychoanalysis helps explain how this works for the people involved. The article moves from the term's history, from the 1999 Seattle protests onward, to the psychoanalytic tradition's own political record. Malherbe cites Erik Olin Wright's typology of anti-capitalist strategies and Slavoj Žižek's warning that the word has lost its subversive edge. He then surveys psychoanalytic engagements with the left, from Freud and the Frankfurt School through Fanon, Deleuze and Guattari, Althusser, Mitchell, the Ljubljana school, the Essex School and Judith Butler to present-day scholars. The central sections discuss anti-capitalism's 'radical negativity' and then three dimensions of organisation: knowledge, action and being. Malherbe's core move uses Lacan's notion of enjoyment (jouissance). When liberals and anti-capitalists share the word, it offers no enjoyment and the right wins over that enjoyment through racism and nationalism. Anti-capitalism, by contrast, can offer enjoyment in lack, because it refuses a fixed organisational form and is reshaped by whoever capitalism excludes. On knowledge, the author says organisations should accept contradiction and use fantasy strategically. On action, Malherbe favours many small, everyday acts of change, such as work refusal, union building and worker cooperatives, over reliance on single heroic acts, with Rosa Parks and the 2015 South African student protests as examples. On being, solidarity rests on a shared sense of otherness rather than identical identities, though groups such as the Black Panthers sometimes need to organise around subjective coherence. Malherbe concludes that anti-capitalism, whether centralised or grassroots, local or international, depends on how people organised under a negative symbolic order understand their specific struggles. Naming it 'anti-capitalism' brings out its psychological and political value. The author calls for building organisational capacity in diverse forms to challenge capitalism's totality. Read the original if you work on psychoanalytic or Lacanian approaches to left organising, or want a survey of how psychoanalysis has been used in anti-capitalist theory.

Analytical political economy: the revival of Analytical Marxism in economics 分析政治经济学：分析的马克思主义在经济学领域的复兴 Chen Weikai Chen Weikai asks how Analytical Marxism, which declined after 1990, has revived in economics since the early 21st century, and what Chinese scholars can learn from it. The article argues that, especially after the 2008 financial crisis, a scholarly community called Analytical Political Economy has emerged. In Chen's account it critically inherits the methodology of Analytical Marxism and has become one of the most active schools of Marxist economics outside China, but it has weaknesses that need correcting. The article has three parts. The first traces the school's development: the economic roots of Analytical Marxism in Japanese mathematical Marxian economics (Michio Morishima), Piero Sraffa's work and the September Group of 1981; its decline; and the Analytical Political Economy workshops from 1991, the 2007 relaunch in London, and the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a base. The second part sets out the school's methodological features. The third offers Chen's own critique. Chen's central move is a distinction between a broad and a narrow conception of the analytical method. The broad version, drawing on Erik Olin Wright, stresses scientific norms, systematic concepts, careful argument and purposive individual action. The narrow version, 'rational choice Marxism', insists on methodological individualism and reductionism. Chen holds that this narrow approach exhausted Analytical Marxism's reconstruction of Marx's economics. Analytical Political Economy, by contrast, accepts the broad method and uses axiomatic approaches. It treats micro and macro levels as dialectically interacting, with structural constraints on individuals and the social formation of preferences. It is also pluralist about tools and paradigms, including neoclassical models, game theory and post-Keynesian economics. Chen identifies three shortcomings. The school contains much non-Marxist work and lacks a Marxist research programme; Chen calls for returning to Marx's analysis of modes of production, including platform-based forms of organisation. It neglects materialist dialectics, which Chen sees as complementary to analytical methods.
