It is too focused on basic theory (value, the transformation problem, the falling rate of profit) and should address monopoly power, digital labour relations, climate change, automation and artificial intelligence, using big data and causal inference. Read the original if you want a Chinese economist's survey of Analytical Marxism's economic lineage and a critique of its methods from within a Marxist research programme.

The event-based view of history in foreign Marxist theory 国外马克思主义理论中的事件史观探析 Hu Yaohui Hu Yaohui asks how historical materialism should understand revolutionary change when the moment of revolution does not coincide with the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. The article traces a lineage of 'event-based' views of history in Marxism outside China. These thinkers stress discontinuity, contingency and human agency, and reject teleology and evolutionism. Hu argues that this lineage recovers valuable elements of historical materialism but exaggerates rupture until the event becomes mystified, and that Marx's own analysis of events offers a corrective. The article has four parts. It first examines Walter Benjamin's 'now-time' (Jetztzeit) and his Theses on the Philosophy of History. It then turns to Louis Althusser's theory of the conjuncture, overdetermination and late 'materialism of the encounter'. The third part covers Alain Badiou's event theory, with references to Žižek and Agamben. The last part returns to Marx's The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte as a model of event analysis. Hu links the rise of each view to periods when the international communist movement was blocked. Hu reads Benjamin as breaking with linear progress: revolution can arise in any present, history is built from the standpoint of the oppressed, and a 'real state of exception' must be produced. Hu sees Althusser shifting to the conjuncture, where the 'empty place' is filled only by action, and Badiou pushing contingency to an absolute in which the event is a 'non-being' with no link to necessity. Hu argues that all three share an anti-Hegelian refusal of totality and negation of the negation, and that Benjamin's messianism, Althusser's 'determination in the last instance' and Badiou's Kantian split show the unresolved problem. Marx, by contrast, links three levels: the economic base (long duration), class analysis (the conjuncture) and the event (short duration). In this reading, contingency such as the February Revolution's unexpected turn is absorbed into class structure and the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Hu offers two criticisms of the event theorists. They grasp only the conjuncture and the event, and so confuse contingency with openness; Badiou's treatment of May 1968 as an isolated event ignores its place in world history. They also blur the proletariat as the fundamental revolutionary subject, and without a strong party, resistance stays at 'single-point blasting' and falls into decisionism or a miracle-centred view of history. Hu calls for stripping the event of metaphysics and returning to Marx's analysis of how people make history within given structures. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese scholar assesses Benjamin, Althusser and Badiou against Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire.

How foreign Marxist parties study and interpret Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 国外马克思主义政党对习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的研究阐释 Zhuo Mingliang Zhuo Mingliang asks how Marxist and communist parties outside China have studied Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that these parties, of which the author says roughly 130 in over 100 countries still keep a communist name or Marxist character, are one of the main overseas forces interpreting the Thought. According to Zhuo, they have treated it as a systematic body of theory and have assessed its world significance. The article first sets out the context: the shift of power from West to East amid "changes unseen in a century", and the growing international reach of the Thought, shown by the circulation of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China among politicians, scholars and ordinary readers. It then surveys the parties' work under four headings: the systematisation of the Thought, its core content, its worldview and methodology, and its value for world socialism and for humanity. It draws on statements by leaders of the Russian, Iraqi, Nepali, Italian, Brazilian, Czech and other parties, as well as by figures such as Hans Modrow. A closing section assesses the field. Zhuo reports that these parties trace the Thought to Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. They see it as a product of the Two Integrations, and read its core content as the fourteen basic policies. They also discuss its worldview and methodology through the "six musts": putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking and a global perspective. On world value, they regard China's results as vindicating Marxism after the Soviet collapse and offering a method for adapting Marxism to national conditions. They also read the community with a shared future for mankind and the three global initiatives as contributions to humanity. Zhuo presents these views as evidence of the Thought's influence. Zhuo distinguishes two strands of overseas research. One is practical and policy-oriented, done by foreign scholars, think tanks and journalists, who say little about the Thought itself. The other is theoretical, done mainly by Marxist parties and some left scholars, which is small in volume but valued by the author. Zhuo says these parties act as a main force in explaining the Party and rebutting Western criticism, and that their work rests on shared political identification. The author lists three shortcomings: too little work on specific fields, weak influence because many parties are small or stigmatised, and some views that need discussion or correction as misreadings. Read the original if you want a catalogue of foreign communist leaders' comments on Xi Jinping Thought, and the official Chinese academic framing of them, with sources in the notes.

New trends in the Philippine left movement in the twenty-first century 21世纪菲律宾左翼运动的新态势 Hei Ran Hei Ran surveys the Philippine left from its origins to the present and asks what is new about it in the twenty-first century. The article argues that the left has gained theoretical and practical ground since 2000 but has also become fragmented, more flexible in tactics and broader in aims, and that its prospects remain uncertain. The article is organised in four parts. It first traces the movement's history: late-colonial labour organising under US rule, the founding of the Communist Party of the Philippines in 1930, repression in 1948, the 1968 split led by Jose Maria Sison, and the splits that followed the 1986 People Power uprising and the 1990s rectification campaign. It then profiles the main parties, grouping them as communist (the CPP, the Revolutionary Workers' Party of Mindanao) and social-democratic (the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party, the Workers' and Peasants' mass-power party Partido Lakas ng Masa). It then analyses three new features and ends with prospects. On theory, Hei reports that after the 2008 financial crisis these parties sharpened their critique of capitalism and put forward socialist visions: public ownership of strategic sectors, an ecological basis for socialism and the communal ethic of Bayanihan. On the three new features, Hei argues, first, that fragmentation comes from ideological splits, the failure of the 2005 Laban ng Masa alliance and the dominance of political dynasties. Second, tactics have shifted from a single reliance on armed struggle to a dual track of armed struggle and legal participation, shown in peace talks under Duterte and Arroyo. Third, goals have widened from class struggle and land reform to labour rights, gender equality, environment and health. Hei concludes that the outlook is not optimistic. The Communist Party of the Philippines faces subjectivism, sectarianism and a leadership vacuum after the deaths of Sison and the Tiamzons. The social democrats suffer from weak cohesion, cadre loss and poor 2022 election results. Hei holds that only left unity can shake dynastic dominance and move towards socialism, while leaving the future an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of Philippine left parties, their factional genealogy and recent programmes, with citations to party documents.

Generative AI and a new field of inquiry into the value movement of digital capitalism 生成式人工智能和数字资本主义价值运动新论域 Huang Zaisheng Huang Zaisheng asks how generative AI, of which ChatGPT is the best-known example, reshapes the value movement of digital capitalism: its production, realisation and distribution of value. Working in a Marxist political-economy framework, the article argues that a form of "AI capitalism" is beginning to emerge. In Huang's account, generative AI produces abundant digital wealth, but under what the author calls "Silicon Valley private ownership" it also sharpens the inherent contradictions of the system. The article is organised around four sets of questions. It examines commodity production and consumption, the labour process under human–machine collaboration, capital accumulation under competition among large models, and threats to the capitalist order of production. It draws on Marx's discussions of machinery, the relative surplus population and accumulation, and on examples including GPT-3, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Midjourney and crowdsourcing platforms. Huang makes three main moves. First, generative AI opens a new stage of digital production: synthetic data eases data scarcity, pre-trained large models generalise machine productivity, and AI-generated content automates content creation. Digital capital thereby gains what the author calls exclusive ownership of "means of cognition". Second, human–machine collaboration changes digital labour unevenly. Unpaid user labour gains in value, crowdsourcing splits into a threatened micro-labour segment and a better-rewarded creative one, and platform workers gain somewhat better conditions. Meanwhile large models are said to create "surplus proletarians" and entrench oligopoly through a "computing-power monopoly". Third, accelerating AI undermines the conditions of capitalist order. It erodes digital capital's "spatio-temporal fix" and the absorption of living labour, and it strains the copyright regime that secures the value of knowledge commodities. It also intensifies conflict between platform firms and bourgeois states over power and ideology. Huang concludes that smart machines do not end digital labour, since collaboration frees people for more creative work. Yet the author holds that the contradictions of digital capitalism are becoming harder to reconcile. Only by going beyond the logic of capital, fundamentally changing the platform system and exploring the construction of "digital socialism" can AI benefit all and digital labour be liberated. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy reading of large models that covers commodities, labour, accumulation and state–capital power, together with a Chinese academic view of AI capitalism.

The proactive logic of "upholding the Party's cultural leadership" in the new era 新时代“坚持党的文化领导权”的主动逻辑 Liu Shuijing Zhang Pan Liu Shuijing and Zhang Pan take up the idea of "upholding the Party's cultural leadership", which Xi Jinping put forward as a formal category at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development on 2 June 2023. The authors treat it as a question bearing on ideological security, cultural sovereignty and the fate of the Party and state. Their thesis is that the proposition is the product of the Communist Party's own initiative, and that it carries a historical, a value-based and a practical "proactive logic" (zhudong luoji). The article is organised in three parts, one for each logic. The first traces the Party's handling of cultural leadership through four periods: the New Democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second sets out the value of cultural leadership in four dimensions: Party building, national development, cultural innovation and mutual learning among civilizations. The third lists five practical lines of work. On the historical logic, the authors present each period as a stage in winning, consolidating and extending leadership over culture. They cite Mao Zedong's call for a "national, scientific and mass" culture led by proletarian thought, the "Double Hundred" policy, the reform-era principle of "grasping both hands", and the new-era concepts of cultural confidence and the Two Integrations. On the value logic, they argue that cultural leadership strengthens the Party's authority and the moral legitimacy of its rule. They add that, through the "second integration", it supports the cultural form of Chinese modernization and a more equal, open world civilizational order. On the practical logic, they identify five pairings: Party spirit with the people's standpoint, positive publicity with struggle in public opinion, mainstream with diverse cultures, offline with online positions, and Party committee responsibility with the participation of many actors. The authors conclude that only by understanding this proactive logic and upholding the Party's overall leadership of propaganda, ideological and cultural work can the Party consolidate its governing position more deeply. They add that this will strengthen the cohesion of the Chinese nation and produce new achievements in Chinese culture. The article follows official discourse closely and gives a systematic account of how Party theorists frame cultural leadership. Read the original if you want a compact survey of the Party's current framing of cultural leadership, with its periodisation and the policy measures it names.

The Party's historical experience in combating formalism and bureaucratism 我们党力戒形式主义、官僚主义的历史经验 Liu Yan Wang Peng Liu Yan and Wang Peng ask what the Communist Party of China's century-plus struggle against formalism and bureaucratism can teach the present. Citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), they call both practices major enemies of the Party's mission in the new era. They argue that the Party has stayed vigilant and adapted its response to each new form of the problem. The article reviews the Party's record from the New Democratic Revolution through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and organises the experience under four headings: building an ideological defence, perfecting the institutional system, cultivating a good work style, and emphasising supervision by the masses. On ideology, the authors trace formalism and bureaucratism to wavering ideals and convictions, and cite Mao's view that formalism comes from idealism and a weak grasp of Marxism. They point to Yan'an rectification, Deng's ideological struggle and Xi's stress on Party spirit. On institutions, they follow Deng's claim that style problems cannot be solved without fixing institutions, and describe a system of Party regulations and laws covering education, regulation, restraint and punishment. On style and supervision, they note that the core problem is detachment from reality and the masses. They list the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles", and efforts to ease burdens on the grassroots. They also stress public supervision and the use of public satisfaction in assessing cadres. The authors conclude that these four measures together form the historical experience that is relevant to opposing formalism and bureaucratism today and to advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of how Party discourse links anti-bureaucratism to ideology, institution-building, work style and mass supervision.

Multidisciplinary perspectives on research into CPC Party building and their integration 中共党建研究的多学科视角及其融合 Wang Keyuan Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), scholars from many disciplines have studied the Communist Party's own construction, yet they rarely talk to one another. Wang Keyuan reviews how political science, sociology and management studies each approach Party building, sets out their strengths and weaknesses, and argues that the field has become fragmented. The article proposes ways to integrate the disciplines, prompted by Xi Jinping's January 2022 call to improve the discipline, academic and discourse systems of Party building research. The article has four sections. The first three survey one discipline each. Political science works with concepts such as the "mission-driven party", with arguments for why Party leadership is necessary in modernization, and with empirical study of leadership and governing methods. Sociology examines organisational embedding in new economic and social organisations, the co-optation of new social strata such as private entrepreneurs, and a "spatial turn" in grassroots Party building. Management studies covers Party self-governance, Party-led grassroots governance and digital tools in Party work. The fourth section assesses all three and proposes integration. Wang's critique is specific to each field. Political science, in this account, relies on grand narratives and selective historical evidence, and its concepts are not distinctive: "mission-driven party" echoes Nanni's missionary/broker distinction, and every ruling party "governs". Management studies coins labels such as "integrated governance" while neglecting historical precedents like the Yan'an-era unified leadership system. Sociology is richer and more finely grained, but borrows Western spatial theories uncritically. Wang adds that traditional Party history scholars work mainly from texts and leaders' speeches, while other disciplines favour institutional analysis or surveys, and the two groups seldom read each other's work or attend each other's meetings. Wang concludes that integrating the disciplines would produce a three-level framework of discourse, institutions and practice. Discourse means what leaders say and demand, institutions means the designs that follow, and practice means how those designs actually operate. Wang treats all three as indispensable and links the integration to the aim of "using scholarship to speak about politics", which balances academic depth with political character. Read the original if you want a map of how Chinese political scientists, sociologists and management scholars frame Party building, and where a Chinese author finds that work weak.

The "Two Integrations": historical context, theoretical logic, practical power and path of development “两个结合”：历史脉络、理论逻辑、实践伟力与发展进路 Wang Fei This article asks how the Party's principle of combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture, now formulated as the Two Integrations, arose and why it matters. Wang argues that the Two Integrations are the key to what distinguishes socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that they form the regular pattern by which Marxism is adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang presents the principle as a source of both theoretical innovation and national rejuvenation. The article has four parts. The first traces the history of the "first integration" and the "second integration" from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping, and links each to a historic leap in theory: Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second part sets out the theoretical logic. The third examines practical effects, and the fourth proposes directions for further development. On theoretical logic, Wang gives four grounds. Marxism develops by being combined with each nation's conditions and by taking national form. China's revolution, construction and reform required a solution to the problem of how to apply Marxism, after dogmatism and copying Russian experience had caused setbacks. Marxism and fine traditional culture are held to be inherently compatible, illustrated by Guo Moruo's 1925 dialogue between Marx and Confucius and by Xi's list of shared values such as "the world belongs to all". Finally, Party members' cultural consciousness and confidence turned these needs into reality. Wang distinguishes the two integrations: the first joins theory with practice, while the second joins a body of thought with a national cultural form and supplies the cultural conditions for the first. On practical power, Wang says the principle carried the Party's central tasks in each period, opened and developed socialism with Chinese characteristics, and consolidated cultural subjectivity against cultural nihilism and "Westernization". Wang concludes with three requirements. The Party must hold to Marxism as its "soul" and fine traditional culture as its "roots". It must fuse the essence of Marxism with the best of traditional culture, with Marxism remaining the guiding position and with opposition to both cultural nihilism and cultural restorationism. And it must draw fresh experience from the people's practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how the Two Integrations are traced historically and justified theoretically, with extensive citation of Mao and Xi.

Multidimensional reflections on constructing the theoretical system of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化理论体系构建的多维审思 Wang Zengfu Wang Zengfu asks how the theoretical system of Chinese modernization, described as only preliminarily built since the 18th Party Congress (2012), can be systematically constructed and innovated. The article argues that this requires a combined view of history and reality, theory and practice, and China and the world. Wang presents the task as a requirement of summarising the Party's experience, a practical need for extending the path, and an academic mission for Chinese philosophy and social science in developing world modernization theory. The article is organised in four parts. The first deals with the philosophical support and modes of thinking behind the system, beginning with a critique of Western modernization theory. The second traces the discourse and inner logic of the system, from earlier concepts such as the Four Modernizations to the formal concept of Chinese modernization. The third examines its cultural dimension and the claim that it creates a new form of human civilisation. The fourth considers its global outlook and world narrative, ending with a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang first characterises Western modernization theory as a post-1945 ideological apparatus that rests on a tradition/modernity binary, a single-line model equating modernization with Westernisation, and an overemphasis on internal causes that ignores colonial expansion. Against this, the Chinese system rests on dialectical and historical materialism, critically absorbs virtue-based thought from traditional Chinese culture and the rationalism of Western philosophy, and replaces zero-sum, self-centred, one-sided and static thinking with symbiotic, perspective-switching, holistic and developmental thinking. Wang argues that its internal logic runs through the Two Integrations, historical materialism and a people-first orientation, in contrast with capital-first Western models. Wang also holds that cultural subjectivity lets the system escape imitation and dependence, while Chinese modernization turns the general idea of modernization into a Chinese proposition and, by adhering to and innovating on scientific socialism, adds to that body of theory. Wang concludes that the system is both a product of Chinese practice and a contribution to world modernization. In Wang's account it supplies values and discursive resources for a community with a shared future for mankind, and it opens a different route for latecomer countries. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars frame the theoretical system of Chinese modernization against Western modernization theory.

Accelerating the formation of relations of production better suited to new quality productive forces 加快形成同新质生产力更相适应的生产关系 Wang Shengxiao Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this article asks what institutional changes are needed to form relations of production that fit new quality productive forces more closely. Wang argues that better-adapted relations of production are the fundamental driving force of productive-force development. On that basis, the author holds that developing new quality productive forces requires further comprehensive deepening of reform, clearing institutional blockages, and so supplying strong momentum and institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization. The article is organised around four areas of reform. These are the new-type whole-nation system for science and technology, mechanisms for industrial transformation and upgrading, institutions supporting comprehensive innovation across education, science and talent, and the rules of factor markets. Each section follows a similar pattern: why the area matters, what has been achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012), what problems remain, and what measures should follow. In the first two sections, Wang treats scientific and technological innovation as the core element of new quality productive forces. The author calls for a new-type whole-nation system under socialist market conditions, with centralised Party leadership of science and technology, a stronger role for enterprises as innovation actors, and a shift from "follower" to "leader". Industrial policy is to join technological and industrial innovation, upgrade traditional industries, and cultivate strategic emerging and future industries. The third and fourth sections argue that education, science and talent reforms must proceed together, including more autonomy for scientists and better conversion of research results. Wang also urges that factor markets, including data as a new factor, steer resources towards new quality productive forces. Proposals include patient capital, venture investment, a unified national market, anti-monopoly measures and curbs on "involution-style" competition. Wang concludes that adapting relations of production to productive forces, the superstructure to the economic base, and national governance to social development is the task of deepening reform. The article sets out the policy mechanisms it considers necessary, while acknowledging problems such as weak original innovation, scattered research resources, shortages of top talent, local protectionism and market fragmentation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how the policy agenda of the Third Plenum is linked to the theory of new quality productive forces.

Leading the development of new quality productive forces with scientific and technological innovation to build a modern industrial system 以科技创新引领新质生产力发展 建设现代化产业体系 Qu Yongyi Qu Yongyi takes up one of the key tasks set by the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: using scientific and technological innovation to lead the development of new quality productive forces and to build a modern industrial system. The article argues that this task deepens the Party's understanding of the laws of economic work and sets a direction for high-quality development. Qu holds that it requires breakthroughs in technology, innovative allocation of production factors and deep industrial upgrading. The article is organised in three parts. The first deals with innovation: basic research, key core technologies, major science and technology projects and national strategic science and technology forces. The second covers industry: transforming traditional industries, developing emerging industries and nurturing future industries. The third turns to the institutional and policy system, including finance, market competition and opening up. On innovation, Qu cites figures showing that China ranked 11th in the 2024 Global Innovation Index but that basic research accounts for under 7 per cent of R&D spending, against more than 15 per cent in the United States and Europe. The author links this gap and Western technological containment to a call for stronger state investment, a new-type whole-nation system for core technologies, and clearly defined roles for national laboratories, research institutes, universities and leading firms. On industry, Qu stresses that traditional industries, over 80 per cent of manufacturing, can also generate new quality productive forces through digital and green retrofitting. The author also proposes large-scale demonstration of mature new technologies, and strategic patience for future industries such as artificial intelligence, quantum computing and the metaverse, whose paths are uncertain. For institutions, Qu proposes multi-level financial services built around patient capital, tolerance of failure for state-backed venture funds, and legal and self-regulatory measures against involution-style competition by firms and local governments. The author also calls for deeper opening up, both through cooperation with developed countries and through joint building of industrial chains and governance rules with emerging and developing countries. Read the original if you want a compact policy-oriented reading of how the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference links innovation, industrial upgrading and institutional reform.

Chinese modernization's answer to the "world history" problem and its world-historical significance 中国式现代化对“世界历史”难题的解答及其世界历史意义 Liu Xingang Against a backdrop of protectionism, unilateralism and a backlash against economic globalization, Liu Xingang asks how Marx's theory of "world history" can inform the present. The article argues that Marx identified a set of problems produced by Western-led modernization, and that Chinese modernization, by moving beyond that model, offers a scientific answer to them. In Liu's account, this answer is a Chinese contribution to the global problems of an era of great changes unseen in a century. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's critique of Western modernization's "world history" process, drawing on The Communist Manifesto, The German Ideology and Capital, and setting it against Ricardo, Adam Smith and Bastiat. The second sets out how Chinese modernization responds, citing Xi Jinping's speeches and initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative, the BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. The third assesses the world-historical significance of this response. Liu says Marx found three problems. Formally equal exchange produced subordination, dependence and colonial relations; the world market widened development gaps and allowed the exploitation of poorer countries; and the transfer of capitalism's contradictions onto others bred trade friction, economic crisis and military conflict. Liu holds that the root error of Western modernization is to ignore differences of national conditions and culture, treating modernization as Westernization. Chinese modernization, which Liu says breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization, answers with a community with a shared future for mankind, equal and orderly multipolarity, inclusive economic globalization, genuine multilateralism and a people-centred stance. It also calls for reform of global governance that gives more weight to developing countries. Liu concludes that Chinese modernization changes the way modernization is thought about. It affirms the diversity of national paths and gives developing countries confidence to look for their own. It also offers practical platforms for cooperation, and Liu presents these as "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" to unilateralism, protectionism and de-globalization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar links Marx's world-history theory to current Chinese foreign-policy concepts and global governance proposals.

Using scientific methods to further deepen reform comprehensively and advance Chinese modernization 以科学方法进一步全面深化改革、推进中国式现代化 Lin Jianhua Lin Jianhua asks how the strategic plan to further deepen reform comprehensively can be turned into real momentum for Chinese modernization. The author's answer is that mastering and applying scientific method is an essential guarantee and a basic skill for Party members and cadres. Lin presents Xi Jinping's methodology of reform, developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012) from dialectical and historical materialism, as the guide for this task. The article is a commentary on Xi Jinping's speech at the study session for provincial and ministerial leading cadres on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It opens with a short discussion of what "method" means philosophically. It then works through four relationships that Xi identifies, one section each: reform and the rule of law, breaking and establishing, reform and opening up, and deployment and implementation. On the first two pairs, Lin argues that reform and law are like "two wings" and must move together. Reform should perfect the legal system, and major reforms should have a legal basis and proceed on legal tracks. Drawing on materialist dialectics and the Chinese tradition, Lin treats "breaking" and "establishing" as a dialectical unity: establish first, then break, and never break before establishing, so as to avoid an institutional vacuum. Lin cites past practice such as establishing the new development philosophy while breaking with GDP-centrism. On the third pair, Lin holds that deeper reform and high-level opening up reinforce each other, and calls for institutional opening up, meaning alignment with international rules and standards, while relying on self-reliance. On the fourth, Lin stresses that "one part deployment, nine parts implementation". The article calls for focus on key points, systematic integration, clear responsibilities, a correct view of performance and perseverance. Lin concludes that these methods help cadres carry the Third Plenum's reforms through to practical results. The article insists that the Party's overall leadership, Marxism, socialism with Chinese characteristics and people's democratic dictatorship must never be shaken, whatever is reformed. It is a Party-line exposition of Xi Jinping's reform methodology rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how current Chinese leadership frames the "scientific methods" behind its reform agenda.

Marx's thought on proletarian poverty as institutional poverty 马克思关于作为制度性贫困的无产阶级贫困思想 Mou Chengwen Wang Weijun The article asks where Marx located the cause of proletarian poverty. Mou and Wang define institutional poverty as poverty produced by the injustice of a society's or state's institutions. They contrast Marx with Hegel, who held that a rabble arises 'naturally' from individual differences. In their reading, Marx held that proletarian poverty is overwhelmingly caused by the institutional injustice of capitalist society, not by individual differences among workers. Marx did not rule out individual poverty, but it was not his focus. The authors build the argument around three roots of this poverty: alienated labour as the social root, class rule as the political root, and surplus value as the economic root. They draw mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Class Struggles in France 1848 to 1850, Capital and the Communist Manifesto. They also clarify concepts, such as alienation, externalisation and reification, and the Marxian categories of labour, labour-power and capital. On alienated labour, the authors set out four features. It strips labour itself of its essence, it strips the worker of theirs, it does the same to the idle appropriator, and it distorts all human relations. They treat private property, wages, capital, profit and rent as consequences of alienated labour. On class rule, they analyse the properties of ruling power and use Marx's account of French classes to show an asymmetrical structure in which the proletariat sits at the bottom. On surplus value, they follow Marx from the commodity to the free wage-worker, who is formally equal but sells labour-power. Surplus value is then accumulated and divided among industrial, commercial and loan capitalists and landowners as profit, interest and rent. The authors conclude that, because all three roots rest on the capitalist system, that system is the ultimate source of proletarian poverty. They hold that the proletariat must therefore abolish bourgeois ownership, rise to become the ruling class and win democracy. It must then take over capital step by step and centralise the instruments of production in the hands of the state, while increasing productive forces. They present this as the theoretical basis of Marx's idea of the fundamental emancipation of the proletariat and of all humanity. Read the original if you want a systematic account of Marx's early and mature critique of capitalism read through the concept of institutional poverty.

Lenin's exploration of the role of politics in the social development of backward countries 列宁关于发挥政治在落后国家社会发展进程中的作用的探索 Wang Heng Wang Shilong The article asks how Lenin, after the October Revolution, tried to use politics to drive economic and social development in a country with a backward economy and culture. Wang and Wang argue that this was a consistent thread in his thinking, which they call the "political-axis model". Under this model politics is the pivot that pulls the other elements of society along with it. They say the model passed through two stages, and that its lessons bear on China's present modernization. After a literature review, the authors say existing Chinese scholarship concentrates on political structures, the Party and the state. In their view it neglects how political functions act on the economy, culture and society during socialist construction. They then set out the general laws of social development and trace Lenin's practice in two periods: 1917–1920, when political power was used to remake the economic base directly, and 1921–1924, when he turned to political reform and cultural work. The article closes with lessons for contemporary China. The central argument starts from the Marxist claim that productive forces and the economic base decide in the long run, while the superstructure, and politics above all, can play a decisive role under particular historical conditions. Wang and Wang set Lenin against Plekhanov and Kautsky, whom they accuse of "vulgar determinism". During war communism, they say, Lenin used state power to remould ownership, distribution and resource allocation through nationalization, requisitioning and the abolition of money. This brought some successes but also peasant unrest and economic decline, and Lenin admitted the error. The authors then say the New Economic Policy shifted the focus to the superstructure: clearer division of powers between Party and soviets, stronger oversight, less bureaucracy, and investment in education and rural culture. They stress that the aim of this reform remained the liberation and development of productive forces. The authors draw two lessons. Using politics as the axis must conform to economic laws, which for China means respecting the market's decisive role in allocating resources alongside government regulation and the development of new quality productive forces. It must also keep improving the superstructure, through Chinese modernization, the modernization of the system and capacity for governance, and whole-process people's democracy. They add that China's conditions differ greatly from those of Soviet Russia and call for combining Marxism with China's circumstances. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Lenin's war communism and NEP as an account of the part politics plays in modernizing backward countries, and of how that reading is tied to current Party discourse.

Marx's Manchester Notebooks and his study of socialist doctrine 马克思《曼彻斯特笔记》对社会主义学说的研究 Kong Weiyu Kong Weiyu takes up Marx's Manchester Notebooks, which the author presents as his first systematic study of socialist doctrine. The article asks what Marx took from English socialist writers and how that work bears on the formation of historical materialism and scientific socialism. Kong's thesis is that two logics were at work: a utopian logic in the English socialists and a realist logic in Marx, who in criticising the former also sublated the residue of his own humanist logic. The article is prompted by the 2015 publication of the notebooks' second half in MEGA2, which revived international scholarship (Matthias Bohlender, Lucia Pradella, David Leopold). The article has four parts. It begins with Marx's picture of the proletariat's misery in Manchester, drawn from excerpts of Eden, Wade, Thompson, Bray and Parkinson. It then examines socialism's practical conditions, its means of realisation and its envisaged future, mainly through William Thompson and John Francis Bray. A third part treats Robert Owen on the relation between people and environment. The last part sets out the two logics and reads Bray's "two voices" through Bohlender's analysis. In Kong's reading, the excerpts on child labour, slavery and unequal exchange convinced Marx that the worker has become a literal "thing" rather than a philosophical "alienated" being. They also convinced him that hope cannot rest on the rich, so liberation must come from the proletariat itself. Kong traces to Bray the roots of later ideas: the producing class as the revolutionary subject, the worldwide character of the proletariat, machine production as the basis of social change, and the base–superstructure metaphor. Kong also sees in Bray's joint-stock scheme a possible spur to Marx's later attention to joint-stock companies. Marx rejects Bray's gradualism, his reliance on reason and his rejection of revolution, as well as Thompson's "ought" and Owen's external determinism. Kong notes that Marx's "Umstände" and "Umwelt" differ from Owen's environment, because Marx makes people and circumstances shape each other through practice. Kong concludes that Marx's "changing the world" was no mere slogan but a programme grounded in social laws, marking the birth of a new worldview. The utopians "interpret" a better future, whereas Marx studies the real movement that abolishes the existing state of things. The notebooks, Kong argues, show Marx learning from the utopians in order to break with them. Read the original if you study the genesis of historical materialism and want a close, text-based account of Marx's reading of Bray, Thompson and Owen in the Manchester Notebooks.

Advancing Chinese modernization requires vigorously cultivating an innovation culture 推进中国式现代化必须大力培育创新文化 Yan Xiaofeng Yan Xiaofeng, writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, asks how China can build the cultural conditions for innovation. The article argues that Chinese modernization is an innovation-driven modernization and that an innovation culture, meaning a culture that honours, encourages and dares to innovate, must therefore be placed in a prominent position in developing socialist culture for a new era. Yan frames this as a response to Xi Jinping's call to cultivate innovation culture and to make respect for science and the pursuit of innovation a social norm. The commentary has three parts. The first treats innovation culture as a driving force for the central tasks of the new era and the new journey. The second sets out how to create a cultural atmosphere that values and encourages innovation. The third places the cultivation of innovation culture within the development of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics for a new era. Yan cites the success of DeepSeek and the animated film Ne Zha 2 during the 2025 Spring Festival as products of long-term cultural cultivation. Yan's core argument starts from the Marxist claim that culture reflects and is determined by the economic base, yet acts back on it as a soft power. Yan reads Chinese modernization as itself an innovation, achieved through the Two Integrations and without ready-made models. Yan lists obstacles in practice: risk aversion, conformism and evasion of responsibility. The remedy comes in four steps: strengthen innovation confidence and initiative; develop innovative thinking that follows laws and starts from problems; raise innovation capacity and train talent; and build a patient environment with tolerance of failure and talent evaluation based on contribution. In the third part Yan calls for guidance by Xi Jinping's thought on culture, strengthened Party leadership over cultural work, and a balance of "upholding fundamental principles" and innovation, in which the former secures direction and the latter renews it. The Second Integration, joining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, is presented as a further liberation of thought that supplies the cultural root of innovation. Yan concludes that transforming traditional culture creatively will strengthen the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school-style commentary links innovation policy, cultural confidence and Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

In the new era and on the new journey, the Party's cultural leadership must be upheld 新时代新征程必须坚持党的文化领导权 Zhang Shihai Wang Tong Writing in the Party journal Dangjian (2025, no. 2), Zhang Shihai and Wang Tong ask why the Communist Party's cultural leadership must be upheld in the new era and how this should be done. They take as their starting point Xi Jinping's June 2023 remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, which named the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity as things that must be preserved. The authors argue that, amid accelerating global change and coexisting opportunities and risks, upholding this leadership is needed to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. The short commentary has two parts. The first sets out why cultural leadership matters. The second identifies four main points of focus for putting it into practice. The authors draw throughout on Xi Jinping's statements on publicity, ideological and cultural work, and tie the argument to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which they say requires a flourishing Chinese culture. On significance, Zhang and Wang present cultural leadership as an inherent requirement for a Marxist ruling party doing ideological work, and as a safeguard for building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. They credit it with strengthening ideological defences, shaping mainstream opinion and uniting the people spiritually. On practice, they call for four things: maintaining Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere as a fundamental system; being guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; innovating in concepts, methods (including artificial intelligence and other digital technologies) and grassroots work; and uniting Party spirit with the people's character. On the last point, they hold that the two are consistent. Party principles must be stated openly and confidently. Party theory must also be made accessible to ordinary people and respond to their concerns. The authors conclude that upholding the Party's cultural leadership is a systematic project requiring coordinated effort, and that it is the basis for unity of thought, politics and action. They hold that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, together with innovation grounded in practice, will sustain its force. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's current official line on cultural and ideological leadership is explained in a Party-oriented journal for cadres and academics.

Leading and safeguarding the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics through full and rigorous Party and university governance 以全面从严管党治校引领保障中国特色世界一流大学建设 Zhang Jun Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, Zhang Jun, Party secretary of Beijing Institute of Technology and a member of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, asks how full and rigorous self-governance of the Party can lead and safeguard the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics. Zhang argues that the Party's self-reform and stricter Party management in universities are consistent with, and necessary for, better performance in education, science and talent work. The article takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the Party's self-reform must continue, drawing on the Party's history, the demands of Chinese modernization and the idea of escaping the 'historical cycle' of rise and decline. The second examines the political considerations behind tightening Party governance in universities, looking at their mission, their internal and external situation and the problems Zhang identifies. The third proposes concrete measures. Zhang's central claim is that self-reform is the Party's distinctive strength, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to the anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In universities, Zhang says, Party governance matters more because of the 'Two Great Situations', international rivalry over science and talent, and growing resources and integrity risks. Zhang names shortcomings in supervision: weak political development, thin ideological and political education, insufficient transmission of responsibility, and corruption in research, construction and admissions. The proposed remedy has three strands: making the Party's overall leadership effective, including the president responsibility system under the Party committee and ideological education; institutionalising the fusion of Party-building with academic work through comprehensive, specialised and deeper inspection tours, extended to secondary-level Party organisations; and making rigorous governance long-term through discipline education, institutional constraints and the 'Three不 [not daring, not able, not wanting] to be corrupt' approach. Zhang concludes that a systematic approach to Party governance, covering all content, personnel, responsibilities and institutions, should turn the Party's leadership advantage into an advantage in building world-class universities. The article is a Party-internal programmatic statement from a university leader and discipline official rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want to see how Party discipline and inspection work are linked to higher-education policy in current official discourse, including the specific mechanisms proposed for universities.

On the content dimensions of building an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of ideological and political education 论思想政治教育学自主知识体系构建的内容向度 Hou Yong Ke Zengjin Hou Yong and Ke Zengjin take up the call to build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences and ask what this means for the discipline of ideological and political education. Their thesis is that the system should be built along the lines of the "three systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse systems), following a logic of knowledge organisation, knowledge production and knowledge dissemination. The article opens by clarifying what an autonomous knowledge system is. It reviews views on its function, process, structure and elements, then offers the authors' own definition: a functional, procedural, systemic integration of concepts, categories, laws, methods, discourse and supporting structures. Three sections then treat the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems in turn. A fourth section sets out systems-thinking requirements, and the piece ends with six "must" principles. The central move is to link each of the three systems to a stage of knowledge work. The disciplinary system (core and branch discipline clusters, cooperation within and across disciplines, talent training and textbooks) organises knowledge. The academic system (Marxist theory and traditional Chinese culture as foundations, basic theory and interdisciplinary borrowing) produces it. The discourse system (a "terminological revolution" around original concepts, narrative and international communication) disseminates it. The authors say the three are interdependent: the disciplinary system is the foundation, the academic system the driving force and the discourse system the key. They also stress that interdisciplinary borrowing must avoid mechanical copying. A second move places the whole project within Chinese modernization, with the aim of the modernization of the human being, and calls for top-level design and methodological innovation at macro, meso and micro levels. The authors conclude that the project is long-term and systematic. They list principles: the Two Integrations, putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, preserving fundamental principles while innovating, problem orientation, systems thinking and a global outlook. They add that dimensions beyond the three systems still need study. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education frame disciplinary construction, its sub-fields, methods and discourse strategy.

A reading of the final part of Capital: "Revenues and their sources" 《资本论》终篇“各种收入及其源泉”读解 Gu Hailiang Marking the 130th anniversary of the publication of Volume III of Capital and of Engels's death (1895), Gu Hailiang offers a close reading of Part VII of Volume III, "Revenues and their sources". Gu argues that this part is the closing part not only of Volume III but of all three theoretical volumes of Capital, and that it gathers the logic of the whole work. The article traces the theme chronologically and then by topic. It begins with Marx's first treatment in the 1861–63 manuscripts and his shift of Volume III's theme from "capital and profit" to the configurations of the process as a whole. It then follows Part VII chapter by chapter: the trinity formula, the analysis of the production process, the "semblance of competition", production and distribution relations, and the classes. It ends with three general points on the significance of Part VII as a conclusion. Gu's central reasoning is that wages, profit, interest and rent appear to spring from labour, capital and land, but that ownership of these factors only entitles owners to shares in a value already created. In Gu's account, all such revenues are transformed shares of surplus-value, which is the product of unpaid labour by wage-workers. Total surplus-value sets the limit on the sum of profit, interest and rent. Distribution relations, Gu stresses, are the reverse side of production relations and share their historical and transitory character. The classes of wage-workers, capitalists and landowners are defined by what they own. Gu also reads Part VII as completing the move from the abstraction of the "direct production process" to the concrete forms of capital in the process as a whole, and as extending the labour theory of value and the theory of surplus-value: the dual character of labour, the organic composition of capital, realisation in reproduction, and the transformation of value into prices of production. Gu concludes that Part VII reveals how the mystified forms of revenue conceal the real source of value and surplus-value, and that it brings Capital's theoretical logic to completion. The reading also credits Engels's editorial work on the unfinished manuscripts, including the short opening of the final chapter on classes. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx's manuscripts of 1861–65 lead into Part VII and how a Chinese Marxist economist interprets its place in Capital.

The value and practical path of empowering university ideological and political theory courses with the "Two Integrations" “两个结合”赋能高校思政课的价值意蕴与实践理路 Zhang Rongjun Zhang Xi Zhang Rongjun and Zhang Xi ask how the Two Integrations (combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) can be used as an intellectual resource in university ideological and political theory courses. They argue that this is both necessary and feasible, and that it can make the courses more theoretically grounded and persuasive. In their view it also meets the courses' basic tasks of Marxist theoretical education and the transmission of traditional culture. The article opens with a short review of existing scholarship. The authors note that studies have focused either on integrating traditional culture, or on integrating Marxist principles, into these courses, and that the Two Integrations as a whole have been less examined. The body then has three parts: the value of the Two Integrations for the courses; the scholarly grounds on which the two fit together; and a practical path of implementation. On value, the authors hold that the Two Integrations supply resources for fostering virtue and cultivating people (lide shuren). They also help to produce a new generation capable of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, by addressing what the authors call students' lack of faith, wavering conviction and insufficient confidence, and strengthen students' cultural confidence. On fit, they identify three shared features: both rest on Marxism and fine traditional culture, both are guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and both aim to serve socialist modernization. The practical path has four strands. The Two Integrations should be built into students' overall qualities and into teachers' political and theoretical competence. They should also shape teaching content, covering Marxist theory, the achievements of the Sinification of Marxism, and history and moral education. Finally, they should inform evaluation, where the authors propose assessing teachers' teaching and research and replacing grade-only assessment of students with one based on knowing, feeling, will and action. The authors conclude that integrating the Two Integrations into students, teachers, content and assessment together can make the courses more targeted and effective. The argument is largely prescriptive and works within official policy documents and Party-congress texts rather than empirical testing. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese education scholars translate Party theoretical formulations into teaching content, teacher requirements and assessment criteria for university political courses.

The Third Plenum of the 20th Party Congress shows firm resolve to see reform through to the end 党的二十届三中全会彰显将改革进行到底的坚强决心 Li Junru Li Junru takes up Xi Jinping's description of the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as showing 'firm resolve and strong sense of mission' to carry reform through to the end. The article argues that the plenum, the tenth Third Plenum since reform and opening up began, marks a new stage in China's reform, and that 2024 was distinguished by the Party's determination in preparing, adopting and implementing its Decision. The piece has three parts. It first distinguishes 'reform', 'comprehensively deepening reform' and 'further comprehensively deepening reform'. It then considers why this distinction matters, through a brief historical comparison of Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. Finally it reviews 2024: the drafting process, Xi's May inspection in Shandong, the plenum of 15–18 July, and the follow-up in Politburo meetings, policy documents and legislation. Li's central argument is that 'comprehensively deepening reform' is not merely 'reform' with adjectives added. Drawing on Deng's 1992 southern tour remarks and Xi's 2013 statements, Li reads it as reform aimed at 'governance', that is, modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. The 2024 phase keeps that overall goal but adds a new theme, Chinese modernization. Li periodises the shift: Mao 'organised' the people, Deng made them 'lively', and Xi's 2013 phase stressed 'lively yet orderly'. The 2024 plenum, in Li's account, begins a stage in which national governance and social development are better matched. Li illustrates this with the planned Private Economy Promotion Law, which protects private firms' rights while setting legal and ethical obligations. Li concludes that the 300-plus reform measures, the dense flow of documents, laws such as the decision to raise the statutory retirement age gradually, and opening-up steps such as visa-free transit and the removal of foreign-investment restrictions all show the Party means to follow through. Li reports that the measures improved confidence and economic recovery after the Politburo meeting of 26 September, and that some foreign firms expanded investment in China. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-school reading of how the 2024 plenum relates to earlier reform stages, together with a chronological record of its implementation.

Platform capitalism and the industrial reserve army 平台资本主义与产业后备军 Ildeli Colombini This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Brazilian scholar Ildeli Colombini (the Chinese name is a transliteration; the original spelling is uncertain). It asks how work organised through digital platforms should be understood in Marx's terms. The author argues that existing research is largely descriptive or too broad, and so misses new concrete forms of the subsumption of labour and of the formation of the industrial reserve army. The article has four parts. It first surveys the literature on platform work, from the uncritical "sharing economy" to critical notions such as uberization, on-demand work and platform capitalism. Two theoretical sections follow, on formal and real subsumption and on the reserve army, drawing on Capital and Marx's unpublished sixth chapter. A conclusion closes the piece. Examples range from ride-hailing and delivery (Uber, Ifood, Loggi) to engineering, design and care platforms (Turing, Upwork, Care.com). Colombini makes two central moves. First, platforms produce surplus value rather than a feudal-style rent, as the "digital feudalism" thesis holds. Formal subsumption arises because self-employed drivers, designers and programmers are separated from the conditions of their work. Real subsumption arises through algorithmic management, which extends and intensifies work, individualises tasks and pay, hides its rules from workers, and uses user ratings to push competition and "subordinate self-management". Second, because workers return to the market after each task, platforms fold the reserve army into active work itself. The author calls this a new sub-category of Marx's floating reserve army, with competitive pressure constant rather than cyclical. This also internalises the struggles of the unemployed, which may unite employed and reserve workers and explain the rise in platform-worker organising. Colombini stresses this is only a possible new fissure, as platform owners seek new ways to split the two groups. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of platform labour built on subsumption and the reserve army, set against "digital feudalism" and precarity theories.

A sharp ideological weapon for strengthening Party conduct in the new era Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions on strengthening Party conduct 新时代加强党的作风建设的锐利思想武器 Qu Qingshan Writing as the Party's official historian, Qu Qingshan takes up Xi Jinping's body of statements on Party conduct (作风建设). Qu presents them as a theoretical resource for the 2025 campaign of study and education on implementing the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, which runs from the spring session of the National People's Congress to July. The article's thesis is that these statements form a coherent theory, part of Xi's thinking on Party building and on the Party's self-reform, that guides the campaign. The article is organised in three parts. The first covers why conduct matters, what kind of problem it is and what its core is. The second covers the main measures, the key tasks and the 'critical minority' of leading cadres. The third covers effective methods, purposes and institutional guarantees. Qu quotes Xi extensively throughout, including his March 2025 remarks in Guizhou and Yunnan, and cites the monthly publication of data on violations of the eight-point regulations, which had reached its 137th consecutive month. In Qu's reading, Xi holds that Party conduct determines whether the people support the Party and whether its cause succeeds. Conduct problems are at bottom problems of Party spirit (党性), measured by the distinction between public and private interest, and at their core they concern the Party's relationship with the people. The eight-point regulations are described as a long-term, strict starting point. The campaign against the 'four undesirable work styles' (formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance) is a continuing task, to be pursued without 'fatigue syndrome' and against new covert variants. Leading cadres must set an example from the top down, and Qu stresses that Xi's own conduct is held up as a model. For the longer term, Qu reports Xi's call to link correcting conduct, enforcing discipline and fighting corruption, and to investigate and handle conduct problems and corruption together. Conduct work should extend to study, writing and meeting styles, and should shape social customs through a combination of moral advocacy and a 'negative list' of prohibitions. Party committees and discipline commissions bear defined responsibilities, supported by regularised institutions and technological supervision. Qu concludes that conduct building is never finished and urges Party members to study these texts and carry out the campaign thoroughly. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-history reading of how Xi's conduct theory is organised and presented at the start of the 2025 campaign.

Improving the system of intra-Party regulations from the perspective of the Marxist systems view 马克思主义系统观视角下的党内法规制度体系完善 Meng Hui Wang Yafei The article asks how the system of intra-Party regulations can be further improved now that the Party has declared it "relatively complete". Meng and Wang argue that this system should be treated as a genuine "system" in the sense of the Marxist systems view. On that basis, they say, its problems can be diagnosed and fixed as a whole rather than regulation by regulation. The authors first review the official definition of the system, from the 2017 Opinions on strengthening intra-Party regulation to the 2021 additions, and note that existing scholarship has seldom applied systems thinking to it. They then describe the system through four features: wholeness, structure, function and openness. For each feature they set out current difficulties, and then propose remedies. Engels on nature as an interconnected totality is their main classical reference. In their account, the system has a vertical hierarchy (the Party constitution, central regulations, ministerial regulations, local regulations) and a horizontal "1+4" framework of four blocks: organisation, leadership, self-development and supervision. The authors identify several problems. Some regulations are dormant or conflict with newer rules. The concepts "intra-Party regulation system" and "intra-Party regulation institutional system" are used interchangeably. Substantive rules lack procedural counterparts. The blocks overlap, and the self-development and supervision blocks far outnumber the leadership and organisation blocks. The system's "value rationality" is neglected. Drafting is insufficiently democratic and lacks technical standards. The proposed remedies are to plan the whole system and clarify its concepts. The authors also call for filling gaps, for example with regulations on ideological and political work, and for supporting rules for the United Front regulations. They would reclassify overlapping provisions, shifting the focus from "no rules to follow" to good rules and good governance, and open drafting to rank-and-file members. They also propose a technical drafting standard, piloted locally. They conclude that only by abandoning "fragmented" thinking can the system be optimised. Read the original if you study Party-building, intra-Party regulation or how Chinese legal scholarship applies systems theory to the Party's own institutions.

Between substance and function: source problems from the perspective of a "policy history of reform and opening up" 体用之间：“改革开放政策史”视野下的史料学问题 Zhao Nuo Zhao Nuo takes up a methodological problem in the emerging study of the history of reform and opening up: how to find direction in a mass of sources when core archives are limited and peripheral materials are abundant. The article argues that researchers should choose research questions first, so that the questions guide where to look. Zhao proposes the "policy history of reform and opening up" as the point where sources and questions meet, and holds that sources and questions are mutually constitutive ("substance and function") rather than separate. The article first justifies policy history. Zhao says policy is the link between theory and practice and a baseline in the sources, and describes the decades since 1978 as an "era of policy". Zhao then sets out three working strategies, each with examples drawn from the author's own research: extending the time frame, moving down to local archives, and connecting policy history with neighbouring fields. The examples are price reform, the household contract responsibility system in the provinces, and the 1982–1988 institutional reform of the State Council. Zhao's core claim is that policy history has been dismissed as a dull account of meetings and documents, but can be made productive. Treating policy as "policy chains" and "policy networks" lets researchers reuse already published materials such as leaders' works, document collections and periodicals. For price reform, this reveals a "triangular balance" among price stability, social stability and growth. Local archives, in Zhao's account, show that the usual "breakthrough, central approval, full roll-out" narrative and the reform/conservative divide are too crude. Provincial decisions came in three waves with uneven timing, and Shandong's leaders promoted reformers while avoiding open controversy. Finally, "peripheral sources" such as reference books, diaries, letters, periodicals, film and poetry can be combined with institutional, intellectual, cultural and social history, and some may become core sources. Zhao concludes that the history of reform and opening up needs source work organised around a sense of direction chosen through research questions. The article recommends policy history as the way to do this and warns against anxieties about fragmentation, arguing that a few focused topics are what the field needs now. The aim, Zhao says, is to join theoretical and practical lines of history and to trace the historical logic of governance. Read the original if you work on the sources and methods of Party history or reform-era history and want concrete guidance on archives, document collections and local materials.

The Seventh Party Congress and the establishment of Mao Zedong Thought as the Party's guiding ideology 党的七大与毛泽东思想指导地位的确立 Han Zhenfeng Marking the 80th anniversary of the Seventh National Congress of the Communist Party of China (held in Yan'an, April–June 1945), Han Zhenfeng asks why that congress matters and how it came to establish Mao Zedong Thought as the Party's guiding ideology. Han argues that the congress summed up more than twenty years of the new-democratic revolution, set a correct line, programme and tactics, overcame erroneous ideas within the Party and wrote Mao Zedong Thought into the Party constitution. In this account, the result was unprecedented unity on the basis of Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. The piece is a short commemorative commentary from the Guangming Daily. The article has four parts. It first recounts the long preparation and the proceedings of the congress, including the reports by Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai. It then traces the formation of Mao Zedong Thought in stages: germination (1921–1927), formation (1927–1935), maturity (1935–1945) and later development. A third part follows the emergence of the term "Mao Zedong Thought" itself, and a final part assesses the congress's significance. Han contends that the congress had been repeatedly postponed since 1931 partly because of war conditions and partly because the Party was not ideologically united on major questions. In Han's reading, the Yan'an rectification movement removed dogmatism, subjectivism and sectarianism, and the Sixth Plenum's resolution on historical questions prepared the ground by affirming Mao's leadership. Han then follows the concept from Zhang Ruxin (1941) and Deng Tuo (1942) to Wang Jiaxiang's 1943 article, which first used the term "Mao Zedong Thought". The Seventh Congress constitution defined it as the thought unifying Marxist-Leninist theory with Chinese revolutionary practice, and Liu Shaoqi's report on the constitution summarised its content in areas such as new democracy, the peasantry, the united front, revolutionary war and Party building. Han concludes that establishing Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology scientifically summed up the revolution's experience and expressed the Party's ideological, political and organisational maturity. The author presents it as the start of independent theoretical creation and as the guide that led to the founding of the People's Republic and to the foundations of socialist institutions. The piece uses the framing of the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how Party historiography presents the Seventh Congress and the genealogy of the term "Mao Zedong Thought".

Why China won the War of Resistance against Japan Reading the "cave dialogue" between Mao Zedong and Edgar Snow 抗战为什么赢 Chen Hongmin Discussions of Mao Zedong's contribution to strategy in the War of Resistance against Japan usually turn to On Protracted War (1938). Chen Hongmin looks instead at an earlier text: Mao's July 1936 conversations with the American journalist Edgar Snow in a Yan'an cave dwelling. Chen argues that Mao's prediction there, that China would win under three conditions, broadly matched the actual course of the war and explains why China prevailed. The article first sets out the Mao–Snow exchange, drawing on the three related topics recorded in Selected Works of Mao Zedong and on Snow's Red Star over China. It then examines two of Mao's three conditions in turn: the formation of the Chinese anti-Japanese united front, and the formation of an international anti-Japanese united front. The third condition, revolutionary movements among the Japanese people and in Japan's colonies, receives only a brief assessment. Chen stresses that Mao made his confident call, "Japan must lose, China must win", when only partial resistance was under way, the Nationalists and Communists were still at war and foreign support was negligible. In Chen's reading, the judgement rested on Mao's method of contradiction analysis, which treats internal causes as the basis of change and external causes as conditions. On this basis the national united front was the internal and principal condition, and the international front and Japanese revolution were external ones. Chen traces the national front from the Communists' calls after 1931, through the Xi'an Incident and the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (1937), to the Nationalist–Communist cooperation declared that September. He credits the front with mobilising ethnic minorities, overseas Chinese and relocated industry and universities, and says it fostered a consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community. For the international front, Chen follows Soviet aid, Western hesitation, the Pearl Harbor attack (1941), the creation of the China Theatre and the American volunteer air force (the "Flying Tigers"). Chen concludes that the Chinese and international fronts, the latter widened into the anti-fascist united front, were strong enough to defeat Japan, even though anti-war movements in Japan and its colonies never reached the level needed to halt the aggression. In Chen's view, history confirms the correctness of Mao's 1936 prediction. The article also cites Xi Jinping's statements on the people's war and on foreign assistance. Read the original if you study the historiography of the Anti-Japanese War, the Communist Party's united front theory, or how Chinese scholars present wartime Sino-American and international cooperation.

Mao Zedong's thinking and practice on the "Second Integration" in the Yan'an period 延安时期毛泽东关于“第二个结合”的思考与实践 Zhu Wei Zhu Wei asks how Mao Zedong, in the Yan'an years (1936–1947), combined Marxism with Chinese history and culture, which today's Party theory calls the Second Integration. Zhu argues that Mao never formulated it as a separate concept, but that it was already embedded in his proposition of the sinification of Marxism. In Zhu's reading, it shows the theoretical awareness and practical initiative behind the "Second Integration" later set out under Xi Jinping. The article has five parts. It traces how Mao raised the sinification proposition in 1938 and how his wording developed up to 1943. It then explains why Mao studied Chinese history and culture, and sets out his attitude, principles, methods and routes for treating the cultural heritage. It ends by showing how Mao drew on traditional culture to enrich Marxism. The evidence is Mao's speeches, letters and comments on the work of Fan Wenlan, Chen Boda and Ai Siqi, and on Peking-opera adaptations. Zhu's central claim is that Mao read the heritage through historical materialism, not as simple inheritance. His attitude was to respect history and not sever it. His principles were "making the past serve the present" and "weeding through the old to bring forth the new". His method was critical sifting of "democratic essence" from "feudal dross", as in his support for a Marxist history of Confucian classics and for a general history of China. Zhu adds that Mao reworked old terms such as "seeking truth from facts", gave them Marxist content, and made them part of the Party's ideological line.
