In the other direction, Zhu says Mao drew on the national spirit (the Foolish Old Man story, hard struggle), on Sunzi's military thought, on cadre standards such as "appointing people on their merits", and on popular idioms and operas to give Marxism a national form. Zhu presents this as part of Mao's struggle against Wang Ming's dogmatism and of his response to the national crisis. Zhu concludes that Mao treated integration with Chinese culture as subordinate to, and serving, integration with the concrete practice of the revolution, in order to make Marxism take root in China. Only after the 18th Party Congress (2012), Zhu says, did the Party need to separate out the Second Integration and give it explicit content. Zhu calls for continuing to link the essence of Marxism with the best of traditional culture and with the shared values of ordinary people. Read the original if you want a source-based account of the Yan'an roots of the Second Integration, with many of Mao's remarks on culture, history and philosophy.

The functional positioning of intra-Party regulations in relation to intra-Party power 论党内法规之于党内权力的功能定位 Liu Changqiu Liu Changqiu asks what function intra-Party regulations (dangnei fagui) should serve in relation to power inside the Chinese Communist Party. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), governing the Party according to regulations has been heavily stressed, and the author notes that many scholars treat the regulations mainly as a means of restraining intra-Party power in order to protect Party members' rights. Liu argues that this view is one-sided. The article's thesis is that the regulations have two dimensions: they must both declare and safeguard intra-Party power and regulate and restrain it, and the two functions are unified in serving the Party's political needs. The article has four parts. It first reviews the existing scholarship and traces the rights-centred habit of thought in modern jurisprudence that Liu holds responsible for the one-sided emphasis. It then sets out the two-dimensional positioning, treating declaring and safeguarding power as the primary function and regulating and restraining it as an important one. The third part argues that both functions serve the Party's political needs, using Party history from 1921 to the post-2012 period. A short conclusion draws out implications for institution-building. Liu draws on political science and jurisprudence to argue that law gives power its authority and so sustains order, and that restraint of power rests on this. Unlike state law, which is rights-based, intra-Party regulations are said to give priority to members' obligations, strengthening discipline, the authority of the Party Central Committee and unified action. Liu also holds that unchecked intra-Party power invites abuse, corruption and policy errors, so the regulations must set conditions, procedures and responsibilities, which Liu presents as an expression of the Party's self-discipline and self-reform. Historical examples include Mao Zedong's 1938 call for detailed intra-Party rules against factionalism, the 1955 supervisory commissions and Deng Xiaoping's remarks on Party rules. Liu concludes that the apparent conflict between the two functions is a dialectical unity. Regulation design should seek a "golden mean" between safeguarding and restraining power, rebalancing the intra-Party power structure by dividing and allocating powers sensibly. Liu credits the regulatory system built since 2012 with strengthening centralised leadership while curbing corruption. Read the original if you study Party-building theory or intra-Party law and want to see how a Chinese legal scholar justifies a power-strengthening function for Party rules alongside the rights-protection view.

Japanese scholarship on the history of the Anti-Japanese National United Front: a review Postwar studies from the late 1940s to the present 日本学界的抗日民族统一战线史研究回顾 Ma Siyu This review surveys how Japanese scholars have studied the history of the Anti-Japanese National United Front since 1945. Ma argues that the research tracks developments in Japan's modern Chinese history field and shows changing Japanese perceptions of China. The article also asks what frameworks Japan relies on when discussing China, and what such research means for Japan today. The article is organised in three periods. The first runs from the early postwar years to the 1960s, the second covers the 1970s to the 1990s, and the third covers the twenty-first century. It discusses a long list of Japanese historians, among them Nakanishi Tsutomu, Eto Shinkichi, Ishikawa Tadao, Nozawa Yutaka, Nishimura Shigeo, Tanaka Hitoshi, Hirano Tadashi, Mizuba Nobuo and Takahashi Nobuo. It ends with a concluding assessment of the trend as a whole. In Ma's account, early postwar scholars treated the United Front as a revolutionary experience and a model for Japan's democratisation. They stressed the Chinese Communist Party's correctness and autonomy from the Comintern, and the 1960s anti-security-treaty struggle strengthened this concern. From the 1970s, doubts about a "revolution-centred view of history" and the rise of a "Republican-era view of history" moved attention elsewhere. Scholars turned to nationalism, democracy and state-building, to the Nationalist government, regional power-holders and intellectuals, and to mass movements beyond party relations. Since 2000 the topic has been folded into the study of contemporary China. Some work traces the origins of present-day political institutions, including "one country, two systems", to the United Front. Other work examines rural society and the Comintern's influence. Ma concludes that Japanese interest has shifted from looking for a revolutionary model to understanding China's political and society, so that China moves from being a "subject" to being an "object" of study. Ma says the open challenges are how to understand contemporary China more accurately through history and how to use that study to rethink Japan's own problems. Ma also says Chinese scholars can use the survey to follow overseas research and deepen their own. Read the original if you want a detailed, name-by-name guide to postwar Japanese historiography of the United Front and the shifting frameworks behind it.

The "Two Integrations" and the creation of a new cultural organism “两个结合”与新的文化生命体的造就 Liu Jianwu Liu Jianwu takes up Xi Jinping's statement that integration is "not a platter" but a "chemical reaction" producing an organically unified new cultural organism. The article asks what this organism is, how it is formed, and what its outcomes and wider influence are. Liu's thesis is that the Two Integrations (of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) are a process of mutual fit, fusion, interaction, respect and mutual fulfilment, and that this process has produced a new cultural form, adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out five features of the formation mechanism. The second describes the product in three forms: a new theory, a new culture and a new civilisation. The third discusses the lasting effects of the concept. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches, with some reference to Mao Zedong and the Party's history from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the mechanism, Liu argues that Marxism and traditional culture are compatible in four respects: ideals ("a world of great harmony" and communism), the people-centred standpoint, the spirit of striving, and the collectivist view of the person. Integration is achieved by solving China's concrete problems, not by moving from book to book. Marxism "activates" the genes of Chinese civilisation, while traditional culture "enriches" Marxism's cultural life. Liu rejects both "using Confucianism to transform Marxism" and the reverse, insisting on mutual respect. On outcomes, Liu holds that the new theory is Marxism adapted to China, which is the "soul" of the organism. The new culture is socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, joining the "soul vein" (Marxism) and the "root vein" (tradition). The new civilisation is Chinese modernization, which the article presents as surpassing Western modernization and breaking the equation of modernization with Westernization. Liu concludes that the concept consolidates China's cultural subjectivity and spiritual independence, and helps resolve the "ancient–modern, Chinese–Western dispute". It also clarifies the Second Integration against the claims that one side must replace the other or that Marxism is simply foreign. In Liu's account, Marxism adapted to China is now Chinese culture that has grown from Chinese soil. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the "new cultural organism" is conceptualised and what it is said to imply for culture, modernization and civilisation.

The historical basis of production and the logical starting point of exchange: on the research and presentation processes in Marx's theory of the value-form 生产的历史基础与交换的逻辑开端：基于马克思价值形式理论研究与叙述过程的探讨 Li Qiankun Li Qiankun takes up a dispute over whether production or exchange has priority in Marx's critique of political economy. Since the second half of the twentieth century, the author notes, Western left theory has given exchange discourse logical priority and has tried to replace Marxism's categories of production with it. This is most visible in the New Reading of Marx and the New Dialectics school. Li argues that in the process of research Marx uncovered production as the historical basis of exchange, but in the process of presentation of the capitalist mode of production he made exchange the logical starting point. Together, Li holds, these two processes make up the distinctive method of Marx's theory of the value-form. The article has three parts. The first surveys the turn from production to exchange in Western Marxism and Marxology (Lukács, Gramsci, Korsch, the Frankfurt School), in value-form schools (Backhaus, Reichelt, the Uno school, the Regulation school, Rancière, Arthur), and in Habermas and Baudrillard. The second traces Marx's treatment of money from On the Jewish Question through the 1844 manuscripts, the Grundrisse, the 1859 Contribution and the 1861–63 manuscripts. The third reads the opening of Capital, and the conclusion discusses Heinrich and Foucault. Li argues that the early and middle Marx still explained money through exchange, private property and the division of labour, and left the theory of the dual character of labour and surplus value separate from the theory of value and money. In Li's account, the theories of average profit and prices of production in the 1861–63 manuscripts joined these lines. The commodity that results from capitalist production contains paid and unpaid labour, so its value cannot be measured directly and must take the money form. Li then argues that Capital still begins with exchange for three reasons: the commodity form is the cell form of bourgeois society, value can appear only through exchange relations, and the analysis of money becoming capital requires exchange, because exchange creates no value and so points to labour-power as the special commodity. Marx himself, Li notes, called this a 'circle' in the presentation. Li concludes that the historical priority of production and the logical priority of exchange express Marx's unity of the logical and the historical, and reflect the character of capitalism itself. Production carries contradiction and antagonism, while exchange supplies a formal, normative appearance. Li says that Western approaches that start from exchange, with Heinrich as the typical case, keep the logic of presentation but lose history, and risk ending up confirming capitalism's validity. Read the original if you work on the New Reading of Marx, value-form theory or the relation between Marx's research method and his method of presentation, and want a Chinese philosophical rejoinder with close textual reference to Marx's manuscripts.

Opening up a new realm for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 开拓中国特色社会主义政治经济学新境界 Zhang Yu Writing in the People's Daily on 3 April 2025, Zhang Yu, a professor at Renmin University of China, takes up the newly published first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping. The article argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought is the latest achievement of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Zhang's reading, it opens a new realm for that discipline and marks a new leap in adapting Marxist political economy to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece first traces the Party's handling of Marxist political economy from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out Xi's requirements for developing a contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, lists the concepts Zhang counts as original contributions, and describes the theory as a systematic whole. It closes by presenting the thought as having universal and global significance. Zhang's central claim is that Xi's thought answers a new question of the era: how to uphold and develop a socialist economy so as to achieve more efficient, fairer, more sustainable and safer development. He lists as original contributions the Party's overall leadership of economic work, the people-centred development philosophy, the new development philosophy, high-quality development, new quality productive forces, the basic socialist economic system, the new development pattern, and balancing development with security. Zhang says the system has a clear structure: high-quality development is its theme, and the people-centred philosophy is its main thread. He also contends that Xi's guidance on drawing on Western economics only selectively, and not copying its ideological content, lays the basis for an autonomous Chinese body of economic knowledge. Zhang concludes that Xi's economic thought is both the Marxist political economy of contemporary China and that of the twenty-first-century world. As examples of principles with general validity, he cites the people-centred philosophy, Chinese modernization, and a community with a shared future for mankind. He adds that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. He calls on Chinese Communists to answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and so to keep enriching Marxist political economy. Read the original if you want an official-line account, from a leading Renmin University economist, of how Xi's economic thought is placed within Marxist political economy and presented as a Chinese contribution to it.

Building an anti-corruption institutional system with Chinese characteristics for the new era An interview with Lu Pinyue, senior professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics 构建新时代中国特色反腐败制度体系 Lu Pinyue This is an interview with Lu Pinyue, senior professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, who has researched the topic. It was published in Marxist Studies (2025, no. 3). Lu takes up why corruption has been an unsolved problem throughout history and why, in Lu's account, only socialism under the Communist Party's leadership can build an anti-corruption system that treats both symptoms and root causes. The interview has four parts. It first explains why anti-corruption matters and why old systems failed, then analyses the causes and types of corruption under the socialist market economy. It next sets out the essential features and basic architecture of the new-era system, and finally examines the "three-no" mechanism (not daring, not being able, not wanting to be corrupt). The interviewer's questions follow this order, and Lu quotes Xi Jinping extensively throughout. Lu argues that the essence of an institution is set by its principal contradiction. In exploiting-class systems, whether imperial China, the Kuomintang or capitalism, anti-corruption responds to popular pressure while protecting the rulers' fundamental interests. Lu cites "skinning and stuffing" under the Ming and, for capitalism, political donations, lobbying, the "revolving door" and asset-declaration schemes. Under socialism, by contrast, the Party's anti-corruption will, which represents the people, is said to dominate absolutely over a small minority seeking illegal gain. Lu describes the architecture as "one foundation" (full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Party leadership and the people first), "two answers" (popular supervision of power and the Party's self-reform), the "three-no" mechanisms, and correcting the "four undesirable work styles". The "three-no" system is the central link. Lu pairs strict supervision with protection of officials who err in good faith, and rejects "high salaries to nurture honesty", locating the real cause of corruption in lost conviction. Lu concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has made a major contribution to this age-old problem. Lu holds that the system will keep developing alongside the building of a modern socialist country and that high-pressure anti-corruption must continue, since power always carries the risk of corruption. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars explain the logic, types and institutional design of the current anti-corruption campaign.

Efforts to unite the international Maoist movement and the latest developments 国际毛主义运动联合化探索及最新动态 Yu Weihai Shu Huiqian Yu Weihai and Shu Huiqian ask how Maoist parties around the world have tried to unite since the 1980s, and what the founding of a new international body in December 2022 means. They argue that the International Communist League, formed on the 129th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, is the latest result of these efforts and an important event for the international Maoist movement. In their assessment, it has real significance but also serious flaws. The article first surveys Maoist parties since the 1980s. It sorts them into those waging armed struggle (the Philippines, India, Turkey, Peru), those not yet doing so, and those that moved to parliamentary politics (Nepal). It then traces earlier international bodies: the Revolutionary Internationalist Movement (1984–2006), the International Conference of Marxist-Leninist Parties and Organizations (International Newsletter, 1998–2017) and the International Coordination of Revolutionary Parties and Organizations (ICOR, founded 2010). It next sets out the League's theory and practice, and ends with an evaluation. The authors report the League's own case. It holds that imperialism is in a general crisis driven by three contradictions: imperialist powers against oppressed nations, bourgeoisie against proletariat, and rivalry among imperialist states. It also holds that a new wave of proletarian revolution is rising, that Marxism-Leninism-Maoism is the guide to action, and that people's war is the path forward. In their evaluation, the authors credit the League with anti-imperialist and anti-hegemonic activity, with strengthening unity through debate and joint statements, and with offering an alternative to the parliamentary road taken by many Western communist parties. They also identify three problems. In their view the League wrongly denies that socialist countries exist today, including China. They also see sectarian tendencies: the League has recruited no new members, and the large Indian and Philippine parties have stayed out. Finally, they call its claim that people's war is the only road idealised and empty, citing objections from the Communist Party of India (Maoist) and the Communist Party of the Philippines. The authors conclude that Maoist unity remains difficult. They see the League's weaknesses as long-standing ailments of the movement whose negative effects deserve vigilance. The article supplies a chronology of Maoist organisations, joint statements and debates, with figures on party strength. Read the original if you study the international communist movement, Maoist parties outside China, or how Chinese scholars assess them.

Mao Zedong's threefold reshaping of the traditional Chinese doctrine of contradiction 毛泽东对我国传统矛盾学说的三维重塑 Wang Xiangqing Yang Xue Wang Xiangqing and Yang Xue ask how Mao Zedong related to the doctrine of contradiction in traditional Chinese philosophy, which earlier thinkers expressed through the terms yin-yang, "two ends" and similar notions. They argue that Mao's engagement with it took three forms: sublation, innovative development and creative transformation. Because Mao treated the law of the unity of opposites as the fundamental law of materialist dialectics, the authors take his reading of this doctrine as the core of his encounter with traditional Chinese dialectics. The article first traces the doctrine from the Book of Changes through Han Feizi, Liu Yuxi, Laozi, Dong Zhongshu, Ban Gu, Zhang Zai, Zhu Xi and Wang Fuzhi. It then sets Mao's On Contradiction (1937), his reading notes, his 1958 Chengdu talk and his leadership writings against this background. The three parts follow the three modes of reshaping, each illustrated with textual evidence. On sublation, the authors say Mao kept the idea that opposites transform into each other but rejected the unconditional version found in Laozi and Wang Fuzhi, noting his marginal comment "under certain conditions" on Li Zhi's preface. Mao also reversed the tradition's tilt towards identity over struggle: in his account identity is relative and struggle absolute, and he added the category of antagonism. On innovative development, the authors credit Mao with first using the paired concepts of universality and particularity and of principal and non-principal aspects, with the latter prompted by his annotations to a Soviet dialectics textbook. He is also credited with holding that a thing's nature is fixed by the principal aspect of its principal contradiction, and that this aspect can change. On creative transformation, the authors show Mao turning contradiction into leadership methods. These pair a broad survey with close study, general calls with individual guidance, leaders with the masses, and the doctrine of two points with the doctrine of the key point, the last illustrated by the image of "playing the piano". The authors conclude that Mao neither simply inherited nor simply discarded the traditional doctrine. He kept its rational elements, extended them with new concepts and arguments, and turned them into practical methods of work. The article presents this as a case of dialectical continuity between traditional Chinese thought and Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you study Mao Zedong Thought, the intellectual sources of On Contradiction, or the link between traditional Chinese philosophy and Party leadership methods.

The roots of the Party's spirit of self-reform in fine traditional Chinese culture 党的自我革命精神的中华优秀传统文化根脉探析 Huang Gang Zhang Jing Huang Gang and Zhang Jing ask how the Communist Party's spirit of self-reform relates to fine traditional Chinese culture. They argue that this spirit is a concrete result of the Two Integrations in the field of Party building. In their account, it is rooted in traditional ideas and moral norms that the Party has inherited and carried forward. They present this as theoretically and practically significant for the full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. The article is organised around four traditional cultural qualities, each paired with a contemporary Party concept. The first is a consciousness of hardship and danger, linked to the "historical cycle" question. The second is moral self-scrutiny in solitude, linked to the "difficulties unique to a large party". The third is renewal by discarding the old, linked to the "four selves". The fourth is ceaseless self-strengthening, linked to the "examination" spirit. Each section draws on classical sources such as the Book of Changes, the Analects, the Zuo Commentary and the Daodejing, alongside speeches by Xi Jinping and Mao Zedong. The authors present self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of dynastic rise and fall, after the "new path of democracy" that Mao gave in 1945. Concepts such as bottom-line thinking, risk prevention, criticism and self-criticism, and the inspection system are read as modern versions of old ideas about vigilance, self-examination and mending one's faults. The four "selves" (self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation) are tied to the Book of Changes idea of renewal, with the Party's institution-building, repeated revisions of the Party Constitution, the Central Committee's eight-point regulations and its emphasis on study cited as evidence. The authors claim that the Party's self-reform gives these culturally inherited traits a dynamic form. The authors conclude that the Party's self-reform spirit fits closely with the traditional values of preparedness against danger, self-reflection, renewal and perseverance. They describe a progression from fit to integration to fusion, which they say achieves the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture. In their view, this cultural foundation supplies spiritual strength for resolving the difficulties unique to a large party and for building a Marxist party that stays in power over the long term. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building theory is tied to classical Chinese sources and to Xi Jinping's formulations.

New features of the left–right contest in Latin America and their impact on the political ecology of parties 拉美左右翼博弈的新特点及其对政党政治生态的影响 Yuan Dongzhen Yuan Dongzhen asks how the long-running competition between left and right parties in Latin America has changed in recent years, and what this means for party politics. The article argues that the clear alternation cycles of earlier decades have blurred. Left and right are now evenly matched, and neither holds a lasting advantage. The article first traces the shift from the left-wing "pink tide" (from about 2000 to 2014) to a right-wing rebound and then to a mixed picture after 2018. It reviews the 18 elections of the 2021–2024 "super election cycle" year by year, noting that the left won 11, the right 6 and a centrist party 1. It then examines how the contest spills across borders, what economic and social changes lie behind it, and what consequences follow for the region's political ecology. Yuan makes three main moves. The first is that the contest has become regional. The author cites links between right-wing forces and Spain's Vox, the Madrid Forum and the Conservative Political Action Conference, and left-wing networks such as the Puebla Group and the São Paulo Forum. The author also cites diplomatic ruptures over Peru's Castillo and the Ecuadorian police raid on Mexico's embassy, personal insults between leaders, and divided regional responses to Venezuela's 2024 election. The second is that the main causes are economic and social. Yuan points to a second "lost decade" in 2015–2024 with average growth of 0.9 per cent, rising poverty, voters with an anti-establishment mood, and a more independent, impoverished middle class. In this account, voters switch between left and right out of dissatisfaction rather than ideology. The third is that the effects are damaging. Winners often have weak mandates, with low first-round vote shares and few legislative seats, so governments are weak. Left–right divisions have also harmed regional bodies such as UNASUR and Mercosur. Yuan concludes that these changes are tied to the economic and social cycle and will not alter the "normal state" of Latin American party politics. The left's appeal rests on deep inequality, and the right's elitist influence stays entrenched because few countries have undergone profound social change. The author expects left–right competition and alternation in office to continue. Read the original if you want a detailed, election-by-election account of Latin America's left–right balance since 2021, written from a Chinese academic perspective, together with the author's explanation of it.

Evolution, current state and future of Spain's left-wing political forces since the financial crisis 金融危机以来西班牙左翼政治力量的演变、现状与未来 Jia Zhonghai Wang Zhiwei How have Spain's left-wing political forces developed since the 2008 financial crisis, and where are they heading? Jia and Wang argue that the left has moved from a dominant Socialist Party (PSOE), through a brief rivalry with the new party Podemos, back to a pattern of one strong party and many weak ones, now operating through coalition government. They hold that its prospects remain unpromising. Using general elections as the main thread, the article divides the period into four phases: PSOE struggling in government (2008–2011), Podemos's rise (2011–2016), a PSOE–Podemos stand-off and the first left coalition (2016–2023), and PSOE's narrow re-election with the Sumar movement (2023 onwards). It then identifies five features of the period and closes by assessing the left's outlook. The authors characterise the pattern as "one strong, many weak", with "two strong" appearing only briefly around 2016. They attribute Podemos's peak to the crisis, fertile populist ground and disillusion with traditional parties, and expect these conditions not to recur. They argue that Spain's trajectory tracks the radicalisation of the European left (Syriza, the Five Star Movement, Portugal's Left Bloc), and that Spain lags slightly behind. They also say right-wing parties (the Popular Party, Ciudadanos, Vox) have taken much of the space opened by populism. Coalition government brings left cooperation but also the loss of PSOE's dominance and friction between partners. Traditional parties are recasting their identity: PSOE's "we are left" slogan and the Communist Party's return to Leninism in 2017. Podemos, in their account, must balance its online grassroots model with functional party organisation. Looking ahead, the authors point to three problems. The Sánchez government's concessions to Catalan and Basque parties have provoked mass protests and economic risk. The left cannot offer a real alternative to neoliberalism: PSOE is constrained by the EU, the right and regional forces, while the radical left criticises more than it constructs. Internal division, fragmentation, an ageing membership and the distance between the labour movement and the socialist movement also persist. They conclude that the left must strengthen itself internally if it is to help revolutionary conditions mature as capitalism's general crisis nears. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Spanish left politics, with election data and a periodisation since 2008.

Marx's critique of Western-centrism and its implications 马克思对西方中心论的批判及其启示 Yang Shengping Some Western scholars, especially on the left, now claim that Marxism is itself a typical case of Western-centrism. Andre Gunder Frank, in ReOrient, is the example Yang Shengping gives. Yang argues the opposite: historical materialism and Marx's theory of world history are the most fundamental and thorough critique of Western-centrism, though Marx's own thinking took time to free itself from its traces. Yang also draws lessons for cultural construction in China today. The article has three parts. The first defines Western-centrism and shows why historical materialism undermines it. The second traces how Marx's critique developed, dividing his work after historical materialism into stages: before the 1850s, the 1850s and 1860s, and the 1870s until his death. The third turns to present-day implications, covering cultural subjectivity, cultural advancement and cultural national character. Long endnotes add textual evidence and conceptual clarifications. Yang separates Western-centrism as a view of history, as political and value stance, and as a mode of thinking and discourse. Marx's materialist basis in modes of production, the author says, removes the first two, but the third persists. Yang reads Marx's early writings on India and China, which relied on Western sources, as bearing some such traces, for example the 'stagnant East' and the absence of private property. Yang holds that Marx's later work on the dual nature of the Russian village commune corrected these. Against readings that make Marx's late Russian path 'unrelated' to the West, Yang argues that this risks an 'anti-Western-centric Western-centrism'. In Yang's account the two paths, capitalist and leapfrogging, are linked. A leap past capitalism depends on Western capitalist development and on absorbing its advanced achievements, and the 'central' position of advanced countries shifts over time. Yang concludes that criticising Western-centrism is a means, not an end, and that the aim is theory able to guide China's development. Social institutions can be leapt over, Yang says, but productive forces cannot, so learning from advanced capitalist countries is indispensable. Cultural subjectivity should be built first on cultural advancement rather than national character. It should avoid narrow nationalism and take selectively from all excellent cultures, since Western modes of thinking and discourse partly reflect real regularities. Yang describes the aim as fusing advanced culture with national character, with Marxism as scientific theory in the lead, in line with the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the claim that Marx was Eurocentric, or want to see how that rebuttal is tied to current debates on cultural subjectivity and an autonomous knowledge system.

The split and transformation of Europe's radical left parties: the case of Germany 欧洲激进左翼政党的分裂与蜕变：以德国为例 Wu Huiping Wu Huiping asks what the January 2024 split of Germany's Left Party (Die Linke) reveals about the European radical left. Sahra Wagenknecht left the party and founded the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW). Wu argues that the split is a case of radical-left parties adjusting under political pressure, and that BSW's programme marks a sharp turn away from the Left Party's democratic socialism towards what the article calls left conservatism. The article first traces the Left Party's origins in the PDS (the successor to East Germany's ruling party) and in the WASG, a split from the Social Democrats (SPD). It then describes its factional divisions between conservative and pragmatic-reformist camps. It sets out its democratic socialist programme, the 2011 Erfurt Programme and its policy demands, followed by BSW's programme, the effects of the split on the Left Party, and similar parties in France, Italy and Slovakia. A closing section considers the radical left's prospects. Wu's central claim is that both parties are left-populist, but they differ sharply. The Left Party criticises capitalism and is liberal on migration. BSW avoids capitalism critique and is anti-establishment rather than anti-system. It keeps radical left positions on welfare, taxation and peace but takes restrictive, culturally conservative positions on migration. Drawing on Niedermayer's theory of party competition, Wu explains BSW's success by a shift to the right in society and by the Left Party's failure to answer new challenges. According to the article, BSW drew most of its 2024 votes from the SPD and the Left Party, and the Left Party lost its parliamentary group and its position in eastern Germany. Wu sees comparable mixes of left economics and nationalism in La France Insoumise, the Five Star Movement and Slovakia's Smer. Wu concludes that this is a pragmatic response to real political pressures rather than a general 'conservative turn'. The radical left can recover only by working with other left parties, as in France's New Popular Front and the Dutch left alliance. Wu notes that the Left Party's pacifist foreign policy obstructs this. Wu also calls on the radical left to seize the opening created by capitalist crisis and put forward practical alternatives on ownership, distribution, growth and democracy. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of the Left Party–BSW split, with poll and voter-flow data and comparisons across Europe.

Three ways contemporary Western scholars interpret the Marxist concept of productive forces 当代西方学者对马克思主义生产力概念的三种解读方式 Yu Weidong Wang Nan Yu Weidong and Wang Nan ask how contemporary Western scholars read the Marxist concept of productive forces, which Marx never defined in a final form. The article argues that the three most influential readings, technological determinism, nature conservation and wealth creation, each hold some rationality but all fall into the same error of seeing things and not people. The authors link this to the current Chinese strategy of developing new quality productive forces. The article takes each reading in turn. Technological determinism is traced through William Shaw, Marvin Harris, James O'Connor, Slavoj Žižek and above all Jürgen Habermas. The nature-conservation reading is traced through Theodor Adorno, O'Connor, William Leiss and Alfred Schmidt. The wealth-creation reading is traced through Jean Baudrillard and Joseph Schumpeter, with roots in Petty, Quesnay, Smith and Ricardo. A fourth section assesses all three, and a conclusion draws out implications for new quality productive forces. For each reading the authors identify two features and a Marxist counter-argument. They hold that technological determinism reduces Marx's three elements (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour) to technology alone and thereby defends capitalism by sidelining labour and surplus-value theory. In their account, the nature-conservation reading wrongly equates productive forces with the domination of nature and misses Marx's idea of the 'humanised nature' produced through labour, so that nature and human emancipation are not opposed. The wealth-creation reading, they say, repeats classical political economy and ignores the 'Copernican revolution' of Marx's analysis of relations of production. Against all three, Yu and Wang insist that productive forces are a generative resultant of real individuals' labour, with the human element primary, and are neither a purely scientific nor a purely economic category. The authors conclude that the concept carries a value orientation toward human emancipation, and they draw three implications for new quality productive forces. First, development should combine the logic of capital with a people-centred logic. Second, ecological civilisation is inherent in productive-force development, citing Xi Jinping's remark that new quality productive forces are green productive forces. Third, socialist relations of production provide an institutional advantage, whereas the authors say Western scholars use distorted readings to defend capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical account of Habermas, Baudrillard, O'Connor and others on productive forces, and of how that critique is used to ground the policy concept of new quality productive forces.

An assessment of the impact of identity politics on contemporary Western left-wing movements 身份政治对当代西方左翼运动的影响评析 Chen Yuntao Why have Western left movements lost ground to right-wing populism, even as identity politics has become a major force within them? Chen argues from a Marxist standpoint that identity politics, adopted in the post-industrial era as a way out of the left's predicament, has damaged the left's political ideals. In the article's account, it weakened the left itself and helped create a cultural and social structure favourable to the expansion of finance capital. The article has three parts. The first sets out three features of identity politics in Western left movements: it replaces the working class with plural identities as the subject of struggle, it pursues cultural and everyday liberation instead of changing relations of production, and it favours decentralised individual action over parties and class organisation. Examples include Occupy Wall Street, the Global Climate Strikes, Black Lives Matter and Me Too. The second part sets out four practical dilemmas, and the third reflects on their causes. Chen's core claim is that dropping the category of class turns the left into an "unconscious instrument" of capitalist rule. The four dilemmas are these: stressing cultural equality tacitly accepts capitalism's legitimacy, and the left ends up allied with financial and tech elites and the US Democratic Party; "victim politics" and the differentiation of identities fragment potential unity and put narrow group interests ahead of the common interest; and after the 2008 financial crisis, lower- and middle-class white people were pushed towards right-wing populism. Chen contends that identity politics misreads economic and class conflict as identity conflict, neglects material interests, and abandons the class unity and party organisation needed to confront finance capital. Chen concedes that identity politics exposed new problems and mobilised marginal groups, giving it some historical significance. The article still concludes that it cannot change economic inequality, and that Western left theorists who criticise it without aiming to transform capitalist relations of production remain absorbed by capitalism. It ends by contrasting this with socialism with Chinese characteristics under the Communist Party, which Chen presents as the key force for reviving world socialism in the 21st century. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of identity politics, with its case examples from the United States and its account of the left's decline.

Constructing a systematic doctrine of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy 构建了当代中国马克思主义政治经济学系统学说 Pang Jinju Writing in the People's Daily on the publication of the first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping, Pang Jinju argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party leadership has built a systematic doctrine of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, which took shape as Xi Jinping Thought on the economy. The commentary presents the 74-item volume as an authoritative textbook and as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has three parts. It first frames the opening up of new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, a call first made in November 2015, as a revolution in twenty-first-century economics. It then turns to guiding economic research with Xi's economic thought in order to build an independent Chinese system of economic knowledge. Finally it reports on two new textbooks, on political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics, compiled by teams at Renmin University and Nankai University. Pang contends that Western economics has long held a monopoly, that Marxist political economy has at times been marginalised or emptied of content even in China, and that Chinese economics still struggles to make its case heard. Against this background and the new round of technological revolution, the author holds that an independent knowledge system is required. It must combine Marxist principles with Chinese realities and traditional culture, avoid empty or label-like exposition, and rest on core categories such as the basic socialist economic system, the new development philosophy and high-quality development. From the textbook work Pang draws two lessons: keep pace with the Party's theoretical innovation, and stay grounded in the practice of socialist economic construction. Pang concludes that economists should keep studying Xi's economic thought, use the Selected Economic Writings well and speed up building the independent system of knowledge. Read the original if you want a brief example of how an academic economist presents the official programme for Chinese economics and its textbooks.

Promoting the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilization 推动物质文明和精神文明协调发展 Liu Zhiming This newspaper commentary asks how material and spiritual civilization should be related in Chinese modernization. Liu takes recent examples, including the DeepSeek AI model and the success of the animated film Ne Zha 2, as signs of vitality in both spheres. Citing Xi Jinping, Liu argues that the two must be handled through "two hands, both firm" so that they coordinate and reinforce each other. The piece sets out three requirements for handling the relationship: a dialectical, a comprehensive and a balanced viewpoint. Each is explained briefly and tied to practical tasks such as building a high-standard socialist market economy and deepening cultural reform. On the dialectical view, Liu holds that material civilization is the foundation, supplying conditions and practical experience, while spiritual civilization supplies spiritual impetus and intellectual support. Ethical guidance should help people handle competition and cooperation, efficiency and fairness, and reject profiteering. The comprehensive view treats the two as each other's condition and aim, and calls for the unity of abundant material goods and all-round human development, with the core socialist values leading. The balanced view warns against being firm on one side and soft on the other. It joins high-quality development and new quality productive forces on the economic side with cultural confidence and a stronger socialist ideology on the cultural side. Liu concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics is neither materially impoverished nor spiritually barren. Chinese modernization, in this account, is not one of accumulated wealth alongside lost belief and rampant materialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists frame the material–spiritual relationship in official cultural policy.

Mao Zedong's historic contribution to the China-Africa community with a shared future 毛泽东对中非命运共同体的历史性贡献 Zhu Bin Xi Jinping first used the phrase "China-Africa community with a shared future" in 2013 and said that China and Africa had "always" been such a community. Zhu Bin asks what historical roots lie behind that claim and answers that Mao Zedong made a decisive contribution. In Zhu's account, Mao's support for African struggles against colonialism and imperialism laid an emotional foundation, shaped shared values and supplied basic guiding principles for the community. The article is a historical-ideological study in four parts: three substantive sections, one for each contribution, and a conclusion. It draws on Mao's talks with African leaders and delegations, telegrams, Chinese aid records and statements by African figures such as Nyerere, Kaunda and Keita. The cases include South Africa's anti-apartheid struggle, Algeria, the Suez Canal crisis, Mali and the Tanzania–Zambia (Tazara) railway. Zhu argues first that Mao built three kinds of feeling: political solidarity born of shared experience of Western aggression, friendly exchange through meetings with more than twenty African leaders, and selfless mutual help through arms, loans and training. Second, Mao promoted values of sincerity and equality, including criticism of "great-power chauvinism" among Chinese personnel in Africa. He also promoted a balance of righteousness and profit, with aid that carried no conditions or privileges, and a commitment to justice, as in his support for Egypt. Third, Mao's guiding principles were "Africa belongs to the Africans", the refusal to export revolution, service to shared strategic interests, and the improvement of ordinary people's welfare. Zhu uses the Tazara railway and well-drilling, textile and farming projects as illustrations. The article cites 2.476 billion US dollars in aid between 1956 and 1977 as 58 per cent of China's total foreign aid. Zhu concludes that Mao never visited Africa yet shaped China–Africa relations from nothing to a firm partnership. The article draws three lessons for the present. China should keep its emotional foundation and the "correct view of righteousness and interests", keep the shared values in order to support modernization across the Global South, and follow the guiding principles so that China–Africa ties become a model for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based Chinese account of how Mao-era Africa policy is being used to ground current China–Africa rhetoric.

The Communist Party of China's leadership of rural moral development: historical achievements and experience 中国共产党领导乡村道德建设的历史成就与经验 Zhang Zhitao Zhang Zhitao asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has led moral development in the countryside over more than a century, and why it has succeeded. The article argues that rural moral development has been an important and distinctive part of the Party's work in the countryside. Its theoretical roots lie in the Marxist classics, and its historical changes follow a consistent logic. Zhang presents this as a reference for the current drive for rural revitalization. After a short review of existing studies, the article has three parts. The first draws on Marx and Engels to trace the theoretical origins of the Party's approach. The second follows four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out the logic behind these changes. In the first part, Zhang reads Marx and Engels as treating morality as a "practical-spiritual" mode of grasping the world, with a normative character that can push society forward or hold it back. Marx and Engels, Zhang says, criticised peasant consciousness as selfish, narrow, scattered and conservative, and held that it can only change when socialised large-scale production replaces small-peasant production. They also made the free and all-round development of the human being the final aim. For the historical part, Zhang lists measures in each period. These include women's emancipation, campaigns against opium and gambling, literacy drives, collectivist education, the Dazhai campaign, the rural civilisation drives, the core socialist values, the protection of traditional villages, and the integration of self-governance, rule of law and rule by virtue. Zhang identifies four constant principles in the Party's approach: Marxist guidance, the Party's leading role, a people-centred position, and keeping pace with the times. On the last, the Party adjusted rural moral work to each period's principal contradiction and historical task. Zhang concludes that the century of experience has moved rural morality from traditional to modern forms and has adapted Marxist rural moral theory to Chinese conditions. The author calls for adherence to Marxist guidance, the goal of agricultural and rural modernization, and innovation in both practice and theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-by-document account of CPC rural moral policy from the 1920s to the 2020s, as the Party's own scholars present it.

The inner logic of Marx's view of civilisation and its Chinese context 马克思文明观的内在逻辑与中国语境 Zang Fengyu Zang asks how Marx understood "civilisation" and what this understanding offers for creating a new form of human civilisation today. The article argues that Marx grounded the emergence and development of culture and civilisation in material production and the basic contradictions of society. From this, Zang says, one can reconstruct a coherent inner logic of civilisation that bears on Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first surveys Marx's uses of the term from his early journalism and the 1843 critique of Hegel's philosophy of right through the 1844 manuscripts, The German Ideology, The Poverty of Philosophy, the Communist Manifesto, the economic manuscripts of 1857–63, Capital and the Morgan excerpts. The second organises these remarks into four dimensions. The third turns to Marx's writings on China, notably the Opium Wars, and then to China's present. Zang's core claim is that, for Marx, civilisation is a historically relative stage of development resting on the level of the productive forces and forms of ownership. Its progress is driven by material production, and it carries an antagonistic structure: the free time of some rests on the surplus labour of others. The article stresses a double aspect of capital's civilising role. Capital greatly advances productive forces, yet it estranges people from their own essence, so that the more civilised the workers' product, the more barbarous the workers. Marx therefore measures civilisation by human development and looks to an "association of free individuals". On China, Zang reads Marx as condemning Western aggression, as treating a closed, stagnant "semi-civilised" empire as vulnerable, and as expecting revolution to renew Chinese civilisation along a path distinct from Europe's. Zang concludes that, in the Chinese context, Marxism combined with the country's own conditions and its fine traditional culture has revived Chinese civilisation. Chinese modernization, the author argues, creates a cultural form unlike one dominated by the logic of capital and rejects both civilisational superiority and clash-of-civilisations theories. Zang cites the Global Civilization Initiative and the 2024 UN resolution on an international day of dialogue among civilizations. The author presents these as steps towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a new form of human civilisation and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a text-based survey of Marx's remarks on civilisation and of how Chinese theorists link them to current civilisational discourse.

How the young Mao Zedong understood and practised "seeking truth from facts" 毛泽东早年是怎样认识和践行“实事求是”的 Liu Jianwu Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remark at the Yuelu Academy in September 2020 that Mao Zedong was 'nurtured here' and that seeking truth from facts 'originates from here', Liu Jianwu asks how the young Mao came to understand and practise the principle before he became a committed Marxist in the summer of 1920. Liu argues that the Party's ideological line of seeking truth from facts rests on this early formation. In Liu's account, the idea ran through Mao's thought and conduct as a continuous thread, even though no early text of Mao's is known to use the phrase itself. The article follows Mao's path chronologically and by setting. It begins with his reading of Zheng Guanying's Words of Warning to a Prosperous Age in Shaoshan from 1907. It then covers his half-year at the Dongshan school, and his nine years in Changsha, at the Hunan First Normal School, under teachers such as Yang Changji and Xu Teli, and in the Yuelu Academy. It ends with Mao's own habits of reading, investigation and problem-posing, and a closing section on the character of the process. Liu's central claim is that outside influences and Mao's own inquiry together explain the result. On the first, Liu reads Zheng as treating the phrase as practical, learning applied to use, and decisive for national strength, going beyond philological scholarship. Liu finds the same ethos in the Dongshan founding documents, in Zeng Guofan's fusion of seeking truth from facts with investigating things to reach principles, in the First Normal School's tradition of practical statecraft, and in the Yuelu plaque. On the second, Liu points to Mao's refusal to follow books uncritically, shown in his marginal comments on Paulsen's ethics text, and to his 'study tours' and factory and village investigations. Liu adds Mao's view that he should understand China before studying abroad, and his 1919 plan for a Problem Study Society listing 144 problems, together with his insistence on a guiding 'ism'. Liu concludes that the young Mao's grasp of seeking truth from facts was continuous, multi-directional and concrete. It drew on late-Ming and early-Qing practical learning, reformist thought, Hunan statecraft culture and Western ideas. Liu holds that it prepared the ground for Mao's later Marxist transformation of the principle and for Xi's remarks at Yuelu. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account, written from within the Party's historiography, of the intellectual origins of Mao's seeking-truth-from-facts principle.

On the programme for transforming Chinese society in "The Great Union of the Popular Masses" 论《民众的大联合》改造中国社会的方案 Chen Zaisheng Yang Liang This article rereads "The Great Union of the Popular Masses", which the young Mao Zedong wrote in 1919 for the Xiang River Review. It asks what programme for remaking China the essay set out, and what it shows about the thinking of young intellectuals at the time. Chen and Yang argue that the essay proposed a reformist route to transformation, shaped by the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. In their reading, it also reflects Mao's own path before he became a Marxist. The article first examines why the essay was written. It points to warlord fragmentation and the misrule of Zhang Jingyao in Hunan, and to the impact of the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. It then sets out the essay's content under three headings: why China had to be transformed, which force could do it, and by what method. A final section reads the text as showing Mao's sense of historical responsibility and his contradictory state of mind. On necessity, Chen and Yang say Mao concluded that the union of the powerful, the aristocrats and the capitalists had pushed the country to an extreme, so thorough change was needed. On the force to rely on, they say Mao held that popular unions are historically inevitable and have practical grounds. Groups with shared interests form small unions, and these join into a great union that can match the unions of the powerful. The method is the "revolution of the voice", which has three strands: the voice of bread, of freedom and of equality. In the authors' account, bread is the precondition of the other two, and the other two secure it. The authors argue that the essay shows Mao's ambition to save the nation, but also his attraction to anarchism. They cite his preference for provincial self-determination and a mild course over violent revolution, since force used against force would only bring more force. The authors note that this view was shared by many progressive intellectuals of the time. In their conclusion, the proposals did not meet their aims in practice but were valuable training, and they hastened Mao's choice of Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you study Mao's early thought, the intellectual transition from reformism and anarchism to Marxism, or how Chinese scholarship now frames this text.

Moving by the "stars": the spiritual predicament of university students' online astrology and ways to relieve it A survey of the horoscope and tarot divination behaviour of 2,100 university students ​观“星”而动：大学生网络占星的精神困境与纾解之策 Wang Fei Tai Heyu Wang and Tai ask why horoscope and tarot divination have become popular among Chinese university students through online platforms, and what this means for students' ideals and convictions. They argue that online astrology, which they describe as a product of Western ideology fused with internet culture and as a form of Western cultural infiltration, carries nihilist and transcendental features. In their view it erodes students' self-reliance and Marxist belief. At the same time, they say most students are "hooked but not believing", using divination mainly as emotional relief. The study is based on a questionnaire of 25 items completed by 2,100 students (full-time undergraduates and master's students) at several universities in Dalian. It is supplemented by in-depth interviews with 20 students between October 2022 and September 2023. The article first sets out the survey method, then examines the effects of online astrology on cognition, emotion and behaviour. It then analyses the causes of its appeal and ends with four sets of countermeasures. The authors argue that divination shapes students through labelled symbols that fragment self-understanding, through enchantment that weakens the scientific spirit, and through a fatalism that undermines practical agency. They report, for example, that 7.75% of respondents say divination affects their decisions and 50.78% say it sometimes does. On causes, they point to Generation Z's need for identity construction, the use of astrology as a social symbol and "online pass", and pressure from involution, achievement-oriented competition and time anxiety. They cite Byung-Chul Han and Katz's uses-and-gratifications theory. They treat astrology as a substitute for missing stress-relief mechanisms, and also as an expression of neoliberalism, nihilism and cynicism. The authors propose a full-chain programme of atheism education built into the ideological and political theory courses. They also call for strengthening students' own agency in ideals and convictions, for universities to build a community for education in ideals and convictions that treats students with care rather than blame, and for a healthy online environment led by core socialist values that counters algorithmic information cocoons. They conclude that students, universities and society must act together to firm up Marxist belief and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want survey data and interview material on student divination in China, and an example of how ideological education scholars frame such youth subcultures.

Research on foreign Marxism from the perspective of China's independent knowledge system 中国自主知识体系视角下的国外马克思主义研究 Lan Jiang After more than forty years of rapid growth in foreign Marxism studies in China, Lan Jiang asks why Chinese scholars should study foreign Marxism, how they should do so, and what kind of research the country now needs. The author argues that translation and introduction alone no longer suffice, and that the field should be rebuilt within China's independent knowledge system on three footings: Chinese problems, Chinese discourse and China's future. The article first traces the field's origins. It notes that in the 1950s and 1960s Lukács and Lefebvre were presented as revisionists or 'progressive writers' rather than as a distinct current, and that the field took shape in the 1980s with Perry Anderson's Considerations on Western Marxism and Xu Chongwen's work on 'Western Marxism'. It then sets out the three sections of its argument, which Lan labels ontology, methodology and teleology, and closes with a proposed coordinate system for the field. Lan holds that the early generation of scholars, including Xu Chongwen and Chen Xueming, studied Western Marxism to understand contemporary capitalism at the start of reform and opening up, and that later work has often lost this problem-orientation. Methodologically, the author describes three stages: 'following' (translation), 'continuing' (genealogies such as Zhang Yibing's History of the Understanding of Capitalism) and 'speaking back' in Chinese discourse. As an example of the last, Lan criticises Kohei Saito's 'degrowth communism' as shaped by Western ideology and unsuited to China. On purpose, the author maintains that foreign Marxists' visions of the future remain partly utopian, and that their work should serve Chinese socialism: distribution and welfare at home, and the community with a shared future for mankind abroad. Lan proposes a Cartesian-style coordinate system. Its vertical axis is the historical-materialist analysis of each thinker, school and country in its own era, and its horizontal axis is Chinese problems and Chinese discourse, such as ecology and carbon reduction. The conclusion borrows Lacan's triad: Chinese problems are the Real, Chinese discourse the Symbolic and the Chinese dream of the future the Imaginary. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism redefines the field's purpose, history and method, including a critical Chinese reading of Saito.

The "Locke factor" in the construction of Marx's thought The critique of the "theory of innate ideas" as an example 马克思思想建构中的“洛克因素” Nie Jinfang Nie Jinfang asks how John Locke shaped the formation of Marx's philosophy, which Marx called the "new materialism", "modern materialism" or "new philosophy". Nie argues that Locke "took part" in Marx's intellectual development, so that Marx's thought contains many "Locke factors". Existing scholarship, in the author's view, has treated the topic only in abstract, general terms, without systematic work on specific texts. The article is one part of a larger comparison of Locke and Marx. Other parts would cover labour ownership and the labour theory of value, and liberal political theory and the "association of free individuals". Using a "textology" method, it takes only Book I of Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the critique of innate ideas, and traces its "traces" through Marx's doctoral dissertation, the Rheinische Zeitung and Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher writings, the 1844 manuscripts, The Holy Family and The German Ideology. Its four sections deal with innate principles, universal assent, the appeal to reason, and the testing of particular ideas against social history. Nie's central claim is one of inheritance and surpassing. Locke denies that principles are innate through largely logical argument, and Marx accepts the conclusion but grounds it in the real conditions of capitalist society. Marx reduces religion to worldly conditions and replaces Locke's abstract rebuttal of universal assent with historical analysis of the Jewish question. That analysis yields a ladder of "political emancipation", "social emancipation" and "human emancipation". Marx also applies "reason" to the structure of capital in the Paris manuscripts, and treats identity, mathematical axioms and "substance" (the Holy Family critique of the speculative "Fruit") as products of practice and history. The article also stresses Locke's influence on French materialism, as Marx describes it. Nie concludes that Marx replaced the "innate principle" of ideas with a "principle of reality", removed idealist accounts of where ideas come from, and found practical routes by which ideas arise and develop. In this reading, Marx's development was not just a succession of idealism, materialism and new materialism, but a gradual search within the frameworks of subject and object, spirit and matter, and idea and reality. The Locke case shows, for Nie, the inseparable link between Marxism and the Western intellectual tradition. Read the original if you study Marx's relationship to British empiricism and the Enlightenment, or want a text-based example of Chinese Marxist documentary scholarship.

The New Hunan Daily's organisation of the "Li Sixi thought" discussion 《新湖南报》组织“李四喜思想”讨论研究 Han Xiaoqing Han Xiaoqing examines a propaganda campaign run by the New Hunan Daily, the Hunan provincial Party organ, between July 1951 and January 1952. The paper invented a fictional village cadre, Li Sixi, who stopped working for the revolution once land reform had given him land, a wife, a child and Youth League membership. Han argues that the discussion was a successful case of Party propaganda and ideological guidance. In Han's account, it overcame complacency among rural cadres after land reform and was then promoted nationwide by the Central Committee. Han notes that existing scholarship mostly treats it as peasant education, and instead reads it as propaganda and thought work. The article has four parts. It first sets out the background and the occasion: cadre slackness after the 1950 Land Reform Law, the first national propaganda work conference of 1951, and the experience of the editor Zhang Yulin, whose fieldwork in Changsha county produced the prototype, the cadre Zhu Zhongli. It then analyses three methods of steering the discussion. A third part assesses results in Hunan and elsewhere, including the Central Committee's circular of 19 September 1951 and coverage in the People's Daily. A short conclusion draws lessons for present propaganda work. Han's central argument is that the paper kept control of a discussion open to readers with differing views. First, it published summary articles after one month, two months and five months, assessing progress and setting the next direction. Second, it printed dissenting letters, for example that cadres should rotate in office or that their pay should rise, alongside many rebuttals. Han argues that readers thereby reached the intended conclusion unprompted. Third, it ran testimony from Zhu Zhongli himself, revealed as the prototype only on 7 January 1952, so readers could see that holding such views was not fatal. Han adds that the final review called for combining ideological education with solving cadres' practical difficulties. Han concludes that the campaign succeeded because it chose a real and widespread problem, was carefully organised, and received backing from the Party centre and national media. The article cites over 2,300 submissions and similar campaigns in other provinces, including a "Wang Xiuzhen thought" discussion among Tianjin workers. Han suggests that, in a period of great change and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, this experience still offers lessons for ideological work and public-opinion guidance. Read the original if you study early People's Republic propaganda methods, Party press practice or the history of rural cadre education, and want the detailed documentary record.

The internal logic of Xi Jinping's important discourse on discipline inspection and supervision work 习近平关于纪检监察工作重要论述的内在逻辑 Shi Wei He Youying Shi Wei and He Youying ask what logic runs through Xi Jinping's statements on the work of the Party's discipline inspection and supervision organs. They argue that these statements form the "discipline inspection and supervision chapter" of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and are held together by a consistent line of materialist dialectics. The central task they identify is advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through Chinese modernization. The article is organised around four pairs of dialectical unities, each tied to one aspect of the work: goals and problems (objectives and tasks), overall synergy and key priorities (direction and content), self-supervision and supervision by the people (principles and attitude), and strict management and loving care (building the supervisory force). The authors draw on Xi's speeches at plenary sessions of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and on earlier remarks about "who supervises the discipline commissions". In the first move, the authors read Xi's goal orientation as keeping the organs focused on upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership. His problem orientation rests on the "four tests", the "four dangers" and the "problems unique to a large party", and the authors present it as a matter of identifying principal contradictions. Second, they say a systemic view calls for coordinating Party, supervisory, inspection and other forms of supervision and for "jointly investigating and addressing" misconduct and corruption. A focus on key points means watching "top leaders" and key issues, including sectors with concentrated power and funds and the "micro-corruption" that affects farmers. Third, they contend that because supervisors must themselves be supervised, the organs must show "thoroughly self-reforming" spirit, in a force that is "strict yet caring". The authors conclude that the discourse shows the wisdom of materialist dialectics and gives theoretical guidance and a guide to action for the organs. They add that it should help cadres strengthen their dialectical thinking and their ability to handle complex situations. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how current Party theory frames the logic of anti-corruption and supervision work, and which Xi texts it draws on.

Standardising the Party's leadership of legislative work: theoretical explanation, practical challenges and paths for improvement 党领导立法工作规范化：理论阐释、实践挑战与优化路径 Zeng Qinghui Xia Kunlun Zeng and Xia ask how the Party's leadership of legislation can move from general principle to concrete, operable rules. Their thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party's leading role in lawmaking has been firmly affirmed, but procedures for exercising it remain underdeveloped. They argue that building explicit procedural norms is both a requirement of the rule of law and an internal requirement of the Party's overall leadership. The article has four parts. It first offers a theoretical account of why such standardisation is needed, drawing on Peng Zhen's views on turning Party policy into state law. It then examines practice, using the 2023 Criminal Law Amendment (XII) as an example. Next it identifies problems in the preparatory stage, in coordination with legislatures and in protecting legislative powers. It closes with proposals for improvement. In the authors' account, Party policy is the guide and basis of legislation: mature, tested policies are raised to law through statutory procedure. They present the Party's role as macro-level leadership, setting direction and approving major legislative matters, not managing details. They identify three gaps. Party rules say little about the form of legislative proposals or the review of legislative plans, which vary across localities. The roles of Party committees, Party groups in people's congress standing committees and the congresses themselves are poorly defined, as are the rules for requesting instructions and reporting. Finally, there is no systematic procedural guarantee of the legislature's leading role. The authors say that joint Party-government documents, and Party committees deciding matters that belong to people's congresses, weaken congress authority. Zeng and Xia propose collective, documented and carefully considered legislative proposals instead of individual leaders' remarks, and a regulated process for reviewing legislative plans. They call for clearer duties for congress Party groups and a standard system of requesting instructions and reporting, with registration, supervision and accountability, and defined categories of major matters. They also want stronger support for congress deputies and for the review of draft laws, and wider use of grassroots legislative liaison points as part of whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a Chinese legal-scholarly view of the procedural gaps in Party–legislature relations and the reforms proposed.)

How Mao Zedong told the story of the Long March 毛泽东如何讲长征故事 Gao Xiaobo Gong Naixin Taking its cue from the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to tell China's story well, this article asks how Mao Zedong, a participant in and witness of the Central Red Army's Long March, narrated it. Gao and Gong argue that his storytelling can be explained through three questions: why it was needed (historical context), what it contained (core content) and how it was done (method). They present it as a resource for building a Long March discourse and a Chinese narrative system today. The study draws on Party documents, memoirs of historical figures and local gazetteers. It follows Mao's Long March narratives across three settings: the New Democratic revolution, Party building, and socialist construction. It then turns to content (experience, theory, spirit) and to method, organised by who tells, to whom, and in what form. In the authors' account, Mao used the Long March in each setting for a different purpose. In the revolutionary period he declared it a victory against talk of failure and tied it to the anti-Japanese united front. After 1949 he invoked it to warn cadres against complacency, in the "Two Musts" and elsewhere, and to encourage confidence in socialist construction. The authors identify three core themes: Party leadership and the mass line, the integration of Marxism's universal truth with China's concrete conditions (traced to the Zunyi Meeting), and a revolutionary optimism. On method, they stress that Mao combined his own telling with that of others such as Edgar Snow and Red Army soldiers' diaries. He also adapted content to students, officers, ordinary people and foreign audiences, and he blended poetry with theoretical writing, calligraphy, vivid scenes, and the unity of knowing and doing. Gao and Gong conclude that Mao's main contributions were the political judgement that the Long March was a victory, the summing-up of its lessons to establish the seek-truth-from-facts line, and the affirmation of Party leadership and the strength of the people. They also credit him with explaining the principle of adapting Marxism to China's conditions through Long March examples. They call on everyone in the new era to tell Long March stories, innovate in communication and promote the Long March spirit for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Mao's Long March rhetoric and its use in later Party narrative-building.

The full philosophical picture and theoretical significance of Feuerbach's atheism ​费尔巴哈无神论的哲学全貌与理论意义探析 Zhang Qinmin Scholarship on Feuerbach's atheism, Zhang Qinmin argues, concentrates almost entirely on religious alienation, the claim that God is an alienation of human essence. This narrows a much richer position and leaves open two questions: what form Feuerbach's materialist atheism takes in his philosophy of nature, and why his anthropology, which he himself called 'idealist', counts as atheism that Marx could accept. The article contends that only the whole of Feuerbach's 'anthropological materialism' answers these questions, and that his atheism runs consistently through worldview, epistemology and view of religion. The article has three parts. The first treats atheism in Feuerbach's 'natural science' (the external critique of God in the material world). The second treats atheism in his anthropology (the internal critique of religious consciousness). The third assesses theoretical significance by comparing Feuerbach with eighteenth-century French atheism and by tracing his role in Marx's development, then draws lessons for atheist scholarship and education in the new era. In the first part, Zhang reconstructs Feuerbach's account of theology moving from theism to pantheism to speculative idealism, culminating in Hegel, and his argument that speculative philosophy is disguised theology. Because the Idea needs sensuousness to realise itself, sensuousness is the truth, and Feuerbach thereby grounds a materialist worldview and an epistemology in which thought and being are already united in the human being. In the second part, Zhang separates religious objectification, which confirms human essence, from religious alienation, which strips it away.
