Feuerbach thus rejects the God of theology yet keeps a 'religion of man' and of love, and Zhang reads his self-description as idealist, following Engels, as a conceptual confusion rather than a difference of standpoint. Zhang concludes that Feuerbach's atheism is more thorough, broader and more dialectical than the French atheism of the eighteenth century, which dismissed religion wholesale. It was adopted by the young Marx in On the Jewish Question, The Holy Family and the 1844 Manuscripts, extended into political and economic critique, and finally 'settled accounts with' in The German Ideology on the way to historical materialism. For practice, Zhang draws three lessons: sustained atheist propaganda and education, a scientific and dialectical attitude to theism, and demonstrating human power through developing the productive forces. Read the original if you are interested in Feuerbach's place in Marxist atheism, or in how Chinese atheist scholarship draws on him.

On the disciplinary system, academic system and discourse system of Marxist theory and their interrelations 论马克思主义理论学科体系、学术体系、话语体系及其相互关系 Yuan Yinchuan Yu Fang Yuan Yinchuan and Yu Fang ask how the three systems that the 20th Party Congress (2022) told scholars to build for philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics (disciplinary, academic and discourse) should be understood in the field of Marxist theory, and how they relate. Their thesis is that the three form an integrated whole in an "one body, two wings" pattern: the disciplinary system is the fundamental support, the academic system the core and bridge, and the discourse system the basic carrier. The article opens by citing Xi Jinping's speeches and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on building an autonomous knowledge system. It then takes each system in turn. The disciplinary system is traced from Marxist theory education to the creation of the first-level discipline of Marxist theory in 2005, with its sub-disciplines and supports (courses, textbooks, teaching staff, scholarly style). The academic system is analysed through its epistemology, axiology and methodology. The discourse system is analysed through its subjects, objects, themes and methods. In the authors' account, the academic system rests on knowledge about the nature, origins and content of Marxism, on a value orientation of "for the people", and on dialectical and historical materialist methods. The discourse system asks who speaks, to whom, what is said and how, and the authors argue that good discourse unites political, academic and popular language. On the relations, they say the discipline is a "fundamental support" but not an "absolute precondition". They hold that Marx's "revolution in terminology" before the formal discipline existed shows academic and discourse systems can precede it. Without academic substance, discourse is empty symbols and the discipline is rootless. Yet discourse is the final outlet, and academic ideas can run ahead of their matching vocabulary. The authors conclude that the three systems are mutually dependent, interpenetrating and convertible, and together aim to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. They call for stronger leadership by the Marxist theory discipline, and for internationalising its discourse so that the world knows "academic China" as well as popular images of China. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how Marxist theory scholars conceptualise the "three systems" and the sub-disciplines and institutional supports of the Marxist theory discipline.

A pioneering model of guiding the study of religious history with historical materialism Engels's late research on early Christianity: contributions and lessons 以唯物史观指导宗教史研究的开山典范 Liu Xuchen Liu Xuchen takes issue with scholars who reduce Marx's view of religion to the "opium" formula or to "ideology", and who therefore claim that the Marxist classics offer only abstract judgements without empirical analysis of concrete religious questions. Liu argues that Engels's late writings on early Christianity refute this view. In Liu's account they are a pioneering model of applying historical materialism to the history of religious thought, going beyond bourgeois idealist scholarship and the incomplete critique of the Young Hegelians. After noting that Chinese scholarship has mostly folded Engels's work into general studies of the Marxist view of religion, Liu examines it as a whole under three questions: who created early Christianity, whether its visions are real, and why it won dominance. A final section draws three lessons for the discipline of Marxist religious studies and for research on scientific atheism in China. On the first question, Liu sets Engels's thesis that Christianity, like any great revolutionary movement, was created by the masses against the doctrine of divine creation. Liu lists four supports: borrowings from Greek and Roman writers such as Seneca and Philo, Jewish cultural traces in the texts, the derivation of core ideas from Stoic philosophy, and doctrines that develop gradually and contradict one another. On the second, Engels reads the visions of the Book of Revelation as invented and largely copied from Old Testament prophets, yet tied to real conditions. Examples are the number 666 as "Nero Caesar" and Rome as the great city, which Liu presents as a distorted reflection of the Christians' situation under persecution. On the third, Liu reports Engels's view that Christianity prevailed because it suited conditions in the Roman Empire. Its universalist equality matched the "levelling" effect of Roman rule, its doctrines of sin and salvation consoled a population without rights, and its simplified rites suited the slaves who made up most of the population. Liu concludes that Engels's work deserves more attention than it has received, and calls for study of Engels's method and of recent overseas scholarship on early Christianity. Liu also urges that historical materialism continue to guide religious history, criticising trends since the 1990s that favour "value neutrality" and downplay religion's ideological and political dimensions. Finally, Liu proposes, from the standpoint of the Two Integrations, deeper study of atheist thought in traditional Chinese culture, citing Wang Chong and Fan Zhen. Read the original if you want a Chinese account of how Engels's Christianity essays are used to support Marxist religious studies and scientific atheism today.

How Marxist political economy surpasses Robbins's economic philosophy 马克思主义政治经济学对罗宾斯经济哲学思想的超越 Zhu Chengquan Guo Zhijuan Marx defined the object of Capital as the capitalist mode of production and its attendant relations of production and exchange. The British economist Lionel Robbins rejected this kind of definition and formally proposed the 'scarcity' definition of economics. Zhu and Guo ask how Robbins's economic philosophy compares with Marx's, and argue that Marxist political economy surpasses it on two counts: the dialectic of matter and consciousness, and the dialectic of ends and means. The article first criticises Robbins's reading of historical materialism as an 'economic view of history', then examines his treatment of ends and means. It draws mainly on Robbins's Lectures on the History of Economic Thought from the London School of Economics, on his remarks about the 'rational economic man', and on Marx and Engels's account of social being and social consciousness. It closes with lessons for contemporary Chinese economics. On the first count, the authors say Robbins calls Marx's materialism 'crude' because it supposedly ignores human needs and purposes. In their reading, Robbins is attacking old, metaphysical materialism, so he misreads Marx, whose dialectical materialism sublated old materialism and idealism. They add that Marx, and Engels's 'parallelogram of forces', rejected economic determinism, since class struggle and ideology also shape history. On the second count, they argue that Robbins treats ends as given and economics as neutral about them. In their view, those ends rest on the assumption of private ownership and the pursuit of surplus value. Marxist political economy instead aims at common prosperity and the free and all-round development of the human being. They also hold that Marxism studies the mode of production, while Western economics studies resource allocation, which is subordinate to that mode. The authors conclude that Robbins grasped some links between matter and consciousness and between ends and means but stayed at a naive dialectic, which shows some common ground with Marxism. They propose that his scarcity definition be dialectically sublated and absorbed into Marxist political economy. This would serve the building of an autonomous Chinese system of economic knowledge, guided by Xi Jinping's economic thought and the Two Integrations. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese Marxist economists engage Western economic methodology and the definition of economics.

Hadapu and related questions on the Red Army's Long March 哈达铺与红军长征相关问题研究 Mao Lihong Mao Lihong examines what happened at Hadapu (in present-day Gansu) when the Central Red Army reached it on 18 September 1935, and why it mattered for the Long March. On 22 September Mao Zedong told a meeting of regimental-level and higher cadres that the army must complete the original plan of going north to resist Japan, and "first of all go to northern Shaanxi". The article argues that, although there is already considerable scholarship, several details need clarifying, and that Hadapu was a pivotal link in the Party's decision to settle in northern Shaanxi. The article is organised in four parts. It first sorts the competing accounts of the newspapers read at Hadapu. It then considers Hadapu as a "refuelling station" for the Red Army. Next it relates the Hadapu meeting to the Eljie (Eqiu/Eryu) and Bangluozhen meetings. It ends with the strategic significance of fixing the destination. Sources include memoirs by Ye Jianying, Li Weihan, Yang Chengwu, Geng Biao, Liu Ying and Nie Rongzhen, Zhang Wentian's reading notes, and chronologies and Party histories. On newspapers, Mao Lihong finds that sources variously name Tianjin's Ta Kung Pao, the Shanxi Daily and other Kuomintang papers. The author concludes only that learning from newspapers is widely accepted, and that so large a decision could not rest on press reports alone. Jia Tuofu's briefing at Bangluozhen supplied further intelligence, and the "newspapers decide direction" story reflects the army's longing for a stable base. On the meetings, Mao Lihong holds that Eljie set out the idea, Hadapu clarified the direction and Bangluozhen made the formal decision, so Hadapu was the hinge. As a "refuelling station" it gave supplies, medical care, recruits, reorganisation into the Shaanxi–Gansu Detachment, and morale, helped by the army's discipline and ethnic policy. It was also the only such station visited by all three front armies. Mao Lihong concludes that settling in northern Shaanxi advanced the Long March's success. It also kept to the northward anti-Japanese line and helped shift the revolution's centre of gravity from south to north. The author presents Hadapu as an important choice that carried the Chinese revolution through its lowest point and toward a major turning point. Read the original if you want a source-based account of the Hadapu newspaper accounts and of the Eljie–Hadapu–Bangluozhen sequence in Chinese Party history writing.

Mao Zedong's anti-superstition thought in the May Fourth period: an analysis 五四时期毛泽东的反迷信思想探析 Zeng Jinghan Zeng Jinghan examines how Mao Zedong's critique of superstition took shape during the May Fourth period. Existing scholarship, the author says, mostly treats these years as a single embryonic phase and neglects the process by which Mao, under the influence of 'science' and 'democracy', reflected on superstition and innovated theoretically. Zeng argues that Mao's anti-superstition discourse grew out of his participation in public life and was framed by the May Fourth narrative of 'opposing ignorance with science' and 'opposing authority with democracy'. The article has four parts. It first traces Mao's early formation through schooling, reading of the new press and membership of study societies, from his village school and the Dongshan school to the Hunan First Normal School, where Yang Changji shaped his ethics. It then sets out the two paths of science and democracy. The third part examines the historical mission of the discourse, namely 'remaking the self' and 'reforming the people'. A short conclusion assesses the limits of Mao's position at the time. Sources include his essays in Xiangjiang Review and Dagong Bao, his letters and his marginal notes on Friedrich Paulsen's System of Ethics. Zeng identifies four targets of Mao's critique: inherited folk superstition, belief in old morality, blind faith in intellectual authority, and obedience to monarchical despotism. Under 'science', Mao attributed superstition to ignorance and a lack of critical spirit, as in his 1919 comment on deaths from lightning in Changsha. Under 'democracy', he treated Confucian ethics as 'intellectual coercion' allied with political power, a view the author illustrates with his essays on the suicide of Miss Zhao. Zeng then sets out four practical prescriptions: expanding education, a revolution in philosophy and ethics, affirming individual value and free will, and the 'great union of the popular masses'. The last marks, in Zeng's reading, a shift from elite enlightenment to mass association. Zeng concludes that Mao's thinking at this stage remained a 'hodgepodge' of liberalism, democratic reformism and utopian socialism, and had not yet reached a Marxist scientific understanding of superstition. His analysis of the social roots of superstition was real but limited. Only after he encountered Marxist works in late 1919 and 1920, and by summer 1920 regarded himself as a Marxist, did his critique reach what Zeng calls a more scientific stage. Read the original if you study the intellectual formation of the young Mao, the May Fourth discourse on religion and superstition, or the roots of Chinese Marxist atheism, and want a source-rich account of his Hunan writings.

A historical study of the evolution of Mao Zedong's thought on spiritual initiative 毛泽东关于精神主动思想演进的历史考察 Wang Guanzhong Deng Jiaojiao Wang Guanzhong and Deng Jiaojiao take up Mao Zedong's idea of "spiritual initiative" (jingshen zhudong): the active, forward-looking mental state that people bring to understanding and changing the world. They treat it as part of subjective initiative and as an indispensable subjective condition for reaching a goal in practice. The article argues that Mao's thinking on the subject developed in three stages: it emerged in his student years, matured during the New Democratic Revolution, and developed unevenly after 1949. The authors link the topic to Xi Jinping's call to stimulate the people's "historical initiative" in advancing Chinese modernization. The article is organised chronologically. It begins with Mao's student decade (from 1910 to 1920), then covers the period from his conversion to Marxism in 1920 to the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. It closes with the years from 1949 to Mao's death in 1976. Evidence comes from Mao's early essays and reading notes, his letters, Party resolutions and his wartime and postwar writings. The authors also draw on his marginal comments on a Soviet political economy textbook. In the first stage, the authors argue, the young Mao combined Wang Yangming's "philosophy of the mind" with Western ideas. He prized the "power of the mind", the tempering of will and a "life of upward striving", though still on idealist and dualist foundations. In the second stage, Mao criticised passivity and the "hired-hand" mentality within the Party, and tied initiative to seizing the initiative in practice. Wang and Deng reconstruct the sequence "spiritual initiative, practical initiative, attainment of the goal". They also set out four paths to spiritual initiative: mastering Marxism-Leninism, improving cadres' ability to mobilise the masses, mental preparation, and democratic centralism as an institutional guarantee. After 1949, the authors say, Mao tied initiative more firmly to seeking truth from facts, added economic development as a path, and stressed institutions. From 1957, however, leftist errors and an inflated view of subjective effort, most visibly in the Great Leap Forward, led him to leave "blind enthusiasm" uncorrected. The authors conclude that the core of the idea is winning the initiative in practice through spiritual initiative, with respect for objective laws and seeking truth from facts as its basic constraint. They present it as a resource for overcoming pessimism, slackness and "lying flat" in the new era and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They call for building institutions, theoretical study and habits of thought that turn passivity into initiative. They also call for strict observance of democratic centralism, so as to avoid "exaggerating the role of subjective will and subjective effort". Read the original if you want a source-based chronology of how Mao's views on subjective initiative developed, including his early writings and his own errors after 1957.

Digital commodities, digital labour and digital capital in the view of contemporary Western left-wing scholars An analysis based on Marxist political economy 当代西方左翼学者视域中的数字商品、数字劳动和数字资本 Xu Yanru Western left-wing scholars treat digital commodities, digital labour and digital capital as the core elements of digital capitalism, yet Xu Yanru argues that they use these categories loosely and without consensus. The article returns to Marx's critique of political economy to ask whether data is a commodity, whether non-wage digital labour is productive labour, and why digital capital counts as capital. Xu's thesis is that these phenomena amount to a digital "reform" of capital's movement, not a "revolution" in value movement. The article surveys three schools: communication political economy (Mosco, Christian Fuchs, Dan Schiller), Italian autonomism (Hardt, Negri) and left accelerationism (Srnicek, Williams). Alongside them it discusses Smythe's audience commodity, Terranova's free labour, Ritzer's prosumption, Zuboff and Varoufakis. It has three parts, each setting out how the concept was introduced and then criticising it from Marx's value theory. On commodities, Xu holds that Mosco and Fuchs conflate raw user data, which is a means of production or consumption, with the digital commodity. Only data processed by living labour, such as that of full-time digital workers, acquires value. On labour, Xu classes full-time digital work and flexible work (gig, crowdsourcing, outsourcing) as productive wage labour, since the latter involves concealed employment and produces absolute and relative surplus value. Users' unpaid prosumption is not productive labour, because it creates no surplus value and aims at use-value. On capital, Xu argues that Schiller, Fuchs, Srnicek and Varoufakis start from digital capital as a given. They ignore the historical premise of the relation between dead and living labour, and so separate the form of capital's movement from its content. They also treat digital capital as independent of functioning capital and interest-bearing capital. In Xu's account, platform, cloud and advertising platforms fall under commercial, industrial or interest-bearing capital, and are largely controlled by financial capital. Digital capital is therefore a digital stage of capital's total movement, not a separate form, and Xu sees analyses that reify categories as still caught in metaphysics. Read the original if you want a Marxist-orthodox critique of Fuchs, Srnicek and the autonomists on the value status of data and platform labour.

Deepening understanding of the laws governing the Party's theoretical innovation 深化对党的理论创新的规律性认识 Zhao Fuke This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025, asks what regularities govern the Communist Party of China's theoretical innovation. Zhao Fuke starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) task of opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author also cites the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which stressed advancing theoretical innovation "on a new starting point". Zhao argues that richer results in the new era require a deeper grasp of five regularities. The article is organised under five headings: the fundamental method of the Two Integrations; a people-first value orientation; systematisation and scholarly grounding of theory; answering practical questions and guiding practice; and the unity of being rooted in China with having the world in view. Zhao draws on Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of the "sinification of Marxism", Xi Jinping's speeches since 2021, and the Party's recent theoretical documents. Zhao presents the Two Integrations (combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) as the fundamental method, with Marxism as the "soul" and traditional culture as the "root". Theory is said to come from the people's creative practice, so innovation must go among the masses and be followed by theoretical study and education. On systematisation, Zhao says innovation shows itself in "identifying concepts" and linking them into judgements and principles. The example given is the Party's self-reform, which Zhao says advanced Marxist party-building theory. Theory must also answer the questions of the era, such as what kind of socialism to uphold and how to build a long-governing Marxist party, and so guide practice. Zhao concludes that the Party's innovation both solves China's problems and contributes to humanity's. Starting from "what we are doing" is said to have produced the judgement that socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era and the path of Chinese modernization. Concern for the world is said to have produced the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and the three global initiatives. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the logic of theoretical innovation under Xi Jinping.

Translation, dissemination and initial application of Marxism in Tianyi and Hengbao 《天义•衡报》对马克思主义的译介传播与初步运用 Li Yingrui Marxism and anarchism both reached China in the early twentieth century as socialist doctrines, and anarchist journals played a real part in Marxism's early spread. Li Yingrui examines the anarchist periodicals Tianyi and Hengbao, which Liu Shipei and He Zhen ran in Japan in 1907–1908. The article argues that, although the papers served anarchist propaganda, they objectively advanced the early dissemination of Marxism in China, while also showing clear limits in how its editors understood it. The article has three parts. The first reviews what the journals published and how the editors glossed it: He Zhen's excerpts from the Communist Manifesto and from Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Min Ming's translations of the Manifesto and its 1888 English preface, and Liu Shipei's excerpt from Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific. The second part looks at how Liu and others applied class struggle theory and a theory of surplus value to Chinese questions. The third assesses the journals' significance and limitations. Li makes several claims about the translations. The journals began full-text translation of Marxist works into Chinese. Liu's preface to the Manifesto is described as the first Chinese preface to a Marxist work, and the Hengbao excerpt is said to be the earliest known Chinese rendering of part of Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, earlier than the 1912 version scholars usually cite. Li also argues that a full Chinese Manifesto was probably completed, though no copy has been found. On application, Liu and others criticised the capitalist state and the 'false civilisation' of capitalism, attacked imperialism, and rejected both anti-Manchu revolution and constitutional monarchy as capitalist paths. They analysed Chinese classes, including a first call for a worker–peasant alliance. Li also credits their effort to explain Marxism in Chinese idiom and to find precedents for communism in Chinese tradition, but calls Liu's equation of ancient well-field and shared-property practices with communism a mistake. Li concludes that Tianyi and Hengbao helped prepare Chinese revolutionaries to accept Marxism and contributed to its adaptation to Chinese conditions. Subjectively, though, the editors treated Marxism only as a 'supplement' or footnote to anarchism. In Li's account, they read class mainly in political and power terms. They also misread the Manifesto's 'communism' as democratic rather than anarchist, and they overlooked the role of productive forces and the historical conditions for the state's necessary existence and withering away. Li holds that this explains why they failed to find a correct revolutionary path. Read the original if you study the early translation history of Marxist texts in China, or the relation between anarchism and Marxism in late Qing thought.

Frontier report on the discipline of scientific atheism (2023) 科学无神论学科前沿报告（2023） Research Centre for Science and Atheism, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences This annual report, issued by the Research Centre for Science and Atheism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, surveys the state of the discipline of scientific atheism in 2023. It describes the year as one of difficult progress: the report says a rebound of the "religious fever" strengthened theistic currents in the ideological sphere and worsened the discipline's environment. It also notes that the discipline won second-round funding under the Academy's "Peak Strategy" and is assigned to the Academy of Marxism. The report first reviews academic events and the development of the journal Science and Atheism, including the sixth congress of the China Atheism Society (June 2023, theme: atheist propaganda and education in rural areas) and the 11th CASS Scientific Atheism Forum in Wuhan. It then summarises research in seven areas: Xi Jinping's statements on religious work and the Party's theory of religious work in the new era; the Two Integrations and atheism; Marxist religious studies; Marxist atheism and its propaganda and education; Chinese and foreign atheist thought; religious governance; and natural science and atheism. Across these areas the report reviews the positions of named scholars. Some treat the sinicisation of religion as a theoretical innovation; one cited author says it does not mean eliminating religion or politicising it. Others argue that Chinese traditional culture carries "atheist genes" that the Second Integration can link to Marxist atheism. Further work covers Marxist religious studies, the thought of Engels and Li Dazhao, and religious governance, including extremism and cults. One scholar proposes eight measures for Party atheist education, among them courses in Party schools and treating participation in religious or superstitious activities as a criterion in Party members' evaluations. In its reflections and recommendations, the report states that the discipline faces external pressure from the religious upsurge and from foreign hostile forces, and internal unresolved institutional problems. It proposes five steps: widening research links with other Marxist theory disciplines; defining scientific atheism as a branch of Marxist theory and seeking second-level discipline status; strengthening the journal's role as a theoretical organ; supporting atheism as an "unpopular discipline" through training and journal development; and expanding international influence, including a world atheists' forum. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially framed overview of who works on atheism and religious policy in China, and on which topics, as of 2023.

The building of the political discipline "Party members must not believe in religion" since the 18th Party Congress: process, enforcement and basic experience 十八大以来 “党员不得信教” 政治纪律的建设历程、执行情况和基本经验 Qu Chengji Qu Chengji examines how the rule that Communist Party members may not hold religious belief has been built up as a political discipline since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Qu opens with cases of officials who, in the article's words, "believe in ghosts and spirits rather than Marx and Lenin", often alongside corruption, and attributes this to motives such as obsession with promotion, greed, guilty conscience and hopes of karmic reward. The article argues that the rule is a key link in Party discipline, and that its experience points to two lessons: sustained ideological education and standardised disciplinary punishment. The article has three main parts. The first traces the rule's development in two stages: the period from the 18th to the 19th Congress (2012–2017), and the period after the 19th Congress (2017), including revisions to the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions in 2015, 2018 and 2024. The second part reviews enforcement through inspections and special investigations, education and training, handling of violators, and publicity. The third part draws out the basic experience and ends with a short conclusion. Qu's account of the rules lists central documents that bar members from religion, superstition and cults, including the 2016 guidelines on intra-Party political life and rules on members' online conduct (2017, 2024). The 2018 and 2024 versions of the disciplinary regulations specify a ladder of treatment: education, persuasion to leave the Party, removal from the rolls, and expulsion for those who incite through religion or organise superstition. Enforcement examples include local sweeps that identified believers and expelled some, supervision of religious sites during festivals, themed Party classes, and the expulsion of a member who made the pilgrimage to Mecca. Qu stresses that the 2024 regulations newly punish individual superstitious practice. Qu concludes that these measures have strengthened Party members' political awareness and given the rule firmer institutional backing. On education, Qu calls for Party-spirit training, themed campaigns, and long-term mechanisms such as monitors, assessments and care for members inclined to believe. On discipline, Qu calls for graded and consistent punishment so that the rule restrains both thought and conduct. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of the regulations, enforcement cases and educational methods behind the Party's ban on religious belief among its members.

The construction of an aesthetic community in Yan'an theatre production 论延安戏剧生产的审美共同体建构 Yang Funing Li Youjun How did theatre workers and ordinary people in the Yan'an period come to form a shared aesthetic world? Yang Funing and Li Youjun argue that Yan'an theatre production built a new "aesthetic community" (shenmei gongtongti). Its ideals were national liberation and equality for all, its goal was the unity of politics and aesthetics, and its main route was mass participation in artistic production. The authors present this as a new model that tied intellectuals to workers, peasants and soldiers. The article is a historical-aesthetic study of theatre in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, roughly 1938 to 1947. It is organised in four parts: aesthetic equality as the foundation, then a community of emotion, a community of national destiny, and a community of education. The cases include the new opera The White-Haired Girl, the yangge play Brother and Sister Reclaim the Wasteland, Qin opera plays such as Blood and Tears Hatred, the Mei-hu play Everyone Is Happy, and the folk artist Li Bu in the Shaan-Gan-Ning People's Theatre Troupe. The authors draw on Mao Zedong's Yan'an Talks, press reports, letters and a 2022 interview. The authors first argue that early Yan'an theatre was hampered by an unequal relationship between elite culture and folk culture. Intellectuals overrode popular taste, and the 1940–41 vogue for "big plays" showed this. Equality emerged after the 1942 Talks, through the new yangge movement, the reform of old drama and collective creation. On that basis, the authors say, shared feeling developed: creators empathised with peasants' suffering, and audiences responded with criticism and revisions that fed back into the plays. National destiny was then articulated through characters such as Wang Renhou, who encouraged audiences to see their own fate in a common struggle. Education worked through plays that reformed idlers (erliuzi), and through intellectuals learning from folk artists as well as teaching them. The authors conclude that the Yan'an aesthetic community was successful and made a major contribution to resistance to Japan and class liberation, and that classics such as The White-Haired Girl remain vital. They hold that equal aesthetic relations are what separates socialist art from earlier art. Citing Xi Jinping's 2014 speech on literature and art, they say contemporary theatre, challenged by digital media, should again write about the people's shared destiny, feelings and ideals. They add that this experience could offer a literary-theoretical interpretation of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you are interested in Yan'an cultural history, the Party's mass-line approach to the arts, or how Chinese scholars link that heritage to current cultural policy.

Conditions for applying artificial intelligence in ideological and political education 思想政治教育应用人工智能的实现条件 Chang Yanhui Chang Yanhui takes up a gap in work on ideological and political education and artificial intelligence. In the author's view, existing studies infer from the technical features of AI how it might empower the field, but rarely ask what is needed for it to work in practice. The article argues that prospects for AI in ideological and political education are credible only if three core elements (data, computing power and algorithms) are secured and if usage norms suited to both the discipline and the technology are put in place. The article has three parts. The first reviews scenarios of use, starting from the principles of generative AI such as ChatGPT, Doubao and DeepSeek, which Chang classes as specialised, weak AI. The second sets out technical conditions: national policy support, data resources and the involvement of educators in development. The third proposes regulatory norms, covering standards for what counts as an intelligent product, data collection rules, admission conditions, content review and legal compliance. On scenarios, Chang argues that AI can speed up literature searches and empirical analysis of public opinion, act as a teaching assistant, generate video scenes that make abstract values concrete, and support audience-segmented, targeted online education. On conditions, the author says costs in energy and computing power should ease through national plans, and that three kinds of data should enter model training: published research, the Party's accumulated teaching experience, and teacher and student behaviour data. Ideological and political educators, Chang holds, should help tune models, judge training-data quality and feed back on use, so that general models become specialised ones. On norms, Chang calls for independent third-party evaluation of products, schools that keep control over data collected by internet firms, and a ban on handing important decisions to AI because its opaque "black box" conflicts with the transparency the field requires. The author claims domestic AI products hold the correct political stance, whereas some foreign products hide liberal values in their algorithms. Products must therefore be guided by core socialist values, with training data screened ideologically. Chang proposes four data categories under existing data-security law: national ideological security, students' political views, their physical and mental health, and their varied lifestyles. Read the original if you want a Chinese pedagogical-ideological perspective on AI governance in universities, including its data and content-review proposals.

Identification and resonance: the communication and promotion of the spirit of the 1935 Zunyi Conference 认同与共鸣：1935年遵义会议精神的传达与宣介 Zhang Xudong Writing for the 90th anniversary of the Zunyi Conference (January 1935), Zhang Xudong asks how a decision reached by the top leadership in three days became a shared conviction across the whole Red Army. The article argues that the turning point was completed only when the conference's spirit was conveyed to every officer and soldier, consolidated through promotion, and finally accepted as a unified consensus. Zhang's thesis is that effective communication of major decisions depends on timeliness and accuracy, but above all on winning ideological identification and emotional resonance. The article has three parts. The first examines how the conference's spirit was 'conveyed' (chuanda) at the central level and at the unit level. At the central level these means were attendance at the conference, oral briefings, telegrams and documents, and assemblies held from Zhaxi to Gouba and Huili. The second part examines 'promotion' (xuanjie) through proclamations, the Red Army newspaper Hongxing, and propaganda teams. The third part analyses the identification and resonance this produced, drawing mainly on memoirs and diaries of commanders and soldiers. Zhang's central distinction is that conveying was largely passive reception, while promotion invited active participation. Conveying relied on cadre reports, study of the Resolution, its Outline and the 'Letter to All Red Commanders and Fighters', and layered discussion in which cadres criticised the 'Left' line from their own experience. Promotion used concise, mobilising proclamations, editorials and reports of victories in Hongxing, and propaganda teams with 'agitation sheds', slogans and shouted appeals. Drawing on recollections by figures such as Liu Bocheng, Xiao Ke, Nie Rongzhen and Fang Qiang, Zhang then argues that soldiers identified with the new ideological line, the new military line of active defence and mobile warfare, and the new organisational line centred on Mao Zedong. In Zhang's account, this endorsement was a rational choice as well as an emotional response, in contrast with the 'Left' line's harsh struggles and punishments. Zhang concludes that the Zunyi Conference achieved its turn from top to bottom only through this process of conveying and promotion, and that its internal implementation deserves study at the meso and micro levels as well as in general assessments. The lesson drawn is that major decisions require attention to timely, accurate and well-chosen means of communication, with a focus on ideological identification and emotional resonance. The author cites Xi Jinping's 2015 call to make good use of the conference's historical experience. Read the original if you want a source-based account, drawn from Long March memoirs and diaries, of how the Zunyi decisions were passed down through the Red Army and how official Party history interprets that process.

The emergence, interaction and transformation of the concept of "modernization" in the New Democratic Revolution period 新民主主义革命时期“现代化”概念的出场、互动与嬗变 Xu Cenchen Xu Cenchen takes up a question about the intellectual history of modernization in China. A common view holds that the Communist Party's modernization thinking began with Mao Zedong's post-1949 formula of a socialist country with modern industry, agriculture, science and culture. Xu argues that debate on the concept was already lively in the New Democratic Revolution period (roughly 1919–1949). The article contends that the concept emerged from earlier discussions of "modern civilization", fused with the idea of national rejuvenation, and was reinterpreted by Communists and left-wing intellectuals from a historical-materialist standpoint. The article is organised chronologically and thematically in three parts. The first traces the concept's appearance in the 1920s and its spread in 1930s journals, including the 1933 special issue of Shenbao Monthly on China's modernization. The second examines how "modernization" and "national rejuvenation" (minzu fuxing) converged after 1931, with debates centred on culture and the countryside. The third turns to Communist figures and left-wing writers such as Qu Qiubai, Ai Siqi, Yang Xingzhi, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Dong Biwu. Xu's central claim is that the two concepts complemented each other. According to Xu, national rejuvenation gave modernization a national perspective and helped dispel its identification with "Westernization", as thinkers such as Zhang Xiruo, Chen Gaoyong and Feng Youlan distinguished the two. In turn, modernization gave the emotionally charged call for rejuvenation a more analytical framework covering culture, economy and science. Xu then argues that Communists differed from other intellectuals in three ways. They treated revolution against imperialism and feudal forces as the precondition of modernization, drawing on Mao's "On Contradiction". They used the concept sparingly, mainly for military and technical matters, owing to their constrained political position. And from 1944–45 onwards they placed industrialization first, a line that Xu traces through Mao's "On Coalition Government", the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949) and the Common Programme. Xu concludes that the debates freed Chinese thought from the narrow East–West cultural contest and gave it a world-historical view. Xu holds that the Party's combination of Marxist theory with Chinese revolutionary and construction practice, and its choice of industrialization as the starting point, localised the concept in China and prepared later formulations such as "socialist industrialization" and the "four modernizations". Read the original if you study the conceptual history of modernization in modern China, or want the Chinese scholarly case for tracing Party thinking on modernization back before 1949.

The basic course and experience of ruling-party building since the founding of the People's Republic of China 新中国成立以来执政党建设的基本历程与经验 Liu Honglin Liu Honglin asks what a Marxist ruling party is and how one should be built, which the article treats as the basic question of Party building. Liu argues that over more than 75 years the Communist Party of China has deepened its grasp of the laws governing its own construction, and has found in self-reform a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and decline. The article sets out to draw lessons from this course for the Party's self-reform, for solving the problems unique to a large party, and for advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. The article is a historical survey in three periods: the period of socialist revolution and construction, the era of reform and opening up and socialist modernization, and the new era. Liu frames each period around the problems Party building faced. These include power alienation and corruption, separation from the masses, the 'fear of incompetence' and ideological or institutional rigidity. A short conclusion draws out general lessons. For the first period, Liu describes open Party-building, the setting up of Party committees and groups in state organs, rectification campaigns, the Three-Anti campaign (the first concentrated anti-corruption drive), cadre training and discipline inspection bodies. The Eighth Party Congress (1956) is presented as a systematic plan for ruling-party building. For the reform era, Liu stresses reform of Party and state leadership systems, the creation of intra-Party regulations, improved Party style, anti-corruption work, ruling-capacity and ruling-theory building, and themed education campaigns. For the new era, Liu stresses top-level design, the Central Eight-point Regulation, a stricter approach to cadres, responsibility systems and about forty intra-Party regulations. Liu describes these as moving Party governance from 'lax and soft' to 'strict and firm' and as forming a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Liu concludes that popular support decides the rise and fall of a party, and that winning it depends on the Party's own condition and on what it delivers for the people. Party leadership, Party building and the Party's cause are said to be mutually reinforcing, so Party building must change with the times while keeping to problem-orientation, goals and mission. Its results are ultimately to be tested by the masses' approval, through progress in Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a periodised, document-by-document account of how Party building is presented in official Chinese Party historiography from 1949 to the present.

Marx's critique and transcendence of Spinoza's rational theology 马克思对斯宾诺莎理性神学的批判与超越探析 Cai Jiangfan Chai Qianyu The article asks how Marx related to Spinoza's critique of religion, at a time when the Western radical left, from Althusser to Negri, has produced a 'Spinozist Marxism' and Althusser called Spinoza Marx's only philosophical 'ancestor'. Cai and Chai argue that Spinoza's religious critique is in essence a rational theology, and that Marx first drew on it and then criticised and surpassed it. The aim is to stop Marx being confined within Spinozism. The authors begin with the reception of Spinoza: the charge of atheism from Christians and French materialists, the German pantheism dispute, and the readings of Schelling, Hegel and Feuerbach. They then set out Spinoza's system and its critique of 'superstition'. The central section traces Marx's engagement in three stages, from his doctoral-period Berlin notes (1839–1841) through the Feuerbachian phase to the practical worldview after 1845. Cai and Chai read Spinoza's identification of God, nature and substance as a 'trinitarian' conceptual system that replaces the personal God with a necessary, self-caused substance. Spinoza treats revealed religion as superstition born of fear and ignorance, and separates philosophy (truth) from theology (piety and obedience) while still combining them in a 'true religion'. In the authors' account, Marx at first admired Spinoza's rationalism and political critique but went beyond him by adopting open atheism. He then dismissed Spinoza's substance as 'metaphysically disguised nature' separated from man. After 1845, Marx located the inversion of subject and object in commodity, money and capital fetishism, so that abstract reason's rule over reality mirrors capitalism's inverted world and cannot be removed by criticism of ideas alone. The authors conclude that Spinoza's idea of freedom as 'intellectual love of God' and his hopes for a bourgeois democratic state reflected a rising bourgeoisie's need to free philosophy from theology. By Marx's time political emancipation had proved incomplete, and Marx looked for freedom in economic and social relations instead. On the authors' reading, Marx's historical materialism defines emancipation as the free and all-round development of the person and the abolition of exploitation. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Marx's changing stance towards Spinoza, grounded in Marx's early writings and notebooks.

Retrospect and prospect: thirty years of theory and practice in online ideological and political education 回顾与展望：网络思想政治教育理论研究与实践推进30年 Wu Manyi Yang Rongsuo Marking thirty years of online ideological and political education (wangluo sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu) within a discipline that is itself forty years old, Wu Manyi and Yang Rongsuo ask what the field has accumulated and where it is stuck. They present it as the history of technology entering ideological and political education and also of Party and state will being carried out in cyberspace. Their thesis is that the field has matured in practice but still lacks settled concepts, boundaries and paradigms. They argue that both theory and practice must therefore be reorientated. The article has three parts. The first periodises the field in three stages: the rise of the internet (1994–2002), social media (2003–2012) and the mobile internet (2012–2024). Each stage is tied to technological change, to official documents, and to keyword-co-occurrence analyses of CNKI papers made with CiteSpace. The second part diagnoses theoretical and practical problems. The third sets out prospects for theory and practice. On theory, the authors identify three unresolved matters. The first is the concept, which scholars have variously defined as a tool, a way of life, a virtual world or an ecology. The second is the boundaries, which are blurred against traditional ideological and political education, offline education and other disciplines, and are eroded by uncritical cross-disciplinary borrowing. The third is the paradigm, since research stays at the level of surface operational issues, neglects ontology and epistemology, and rarely uses empirical or comparative methods. On practice, they report weak and unsustained drivers (formalism in implementing documents, thin funding, unstandardised evaluation, unmaintained platforms), generic and homogeneous content, and a technicist tendency that favours spectacle over substance. In their account, this tendency produces a fetishised appearance that hides the real relations of education. For theory, the authors call for clarifying the concept from a totalising perspective, drawing firm but open boundaries that balance guarding the discipline's own ground with crossing disciplines, and reconstructing the paradigm so that online ideological and political education is studied as a subject in its own right. For practice, they propose a sounder driving mechanism, guarantees of policy, funding and personnel, and attention to three functions: guiding values, guiding behaviour and building consensus. They conclude that the discipline, as a practical humanities field, must keep reviewing its history to answer the questions of the human–machine era. Read the original if you want a detailed periodisation and critical overview of Chinese scholarship and practice in online ideological and political education.)

Between philosophy and Capital: the internal evolution of Marx's theory of ideology 在哲学与《资本论》之间：马克思意识形态理论的内在嬗变 Zhou Luping Wu Ting Zhou Luping and Wu Ting take up a long-running dispute in Western Marxist scholarship: whether Marx's theory of ideology breaks between the early and the mature Marx, as Althusser's "epistemological break" implies. They respond to Lalande-style and Balibar-style readings that see fetishism critique replacing ideology critique after 1850. Their thesis is that Marx's theory of ideology is continuous and systematic, running from the early philosophical critiques through historical materialism to Capital and its manuscripts, where the concept is present in a "hidden" form. The article is organised in three parts. The first reconstructs the problem-field of ideology critique in the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The second treats the historical-materialist character of ideology critique in the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, The Poverty of Philosophy, Wage-Labour and Capital and the Communist Manifesto. The third locates ideology critique within Capital, discussing the generation, operation and destruction of capitalist ideology, with side-arguments against Max Weber, Horkheimer and Adorno. The authors argue first that the 1844 Manuscripts already contain a "trinity" of economic, philosophical and social critique of alienated labour, with ideology critique subordinate to all three. The German Ideology then explains ideology through the spontaneous division of labour and the split between material and mental labour. Later texts treat economic categories as the "copy" of the "original" of capital's real movement. Third, they read Capital as exposing capitalist ideology through the fetishism of commodities, money and capital, which legitimise wage labour and surplus-value extraction. Weber is said to stay at the level of the Protestant ethic, and Horkheimer and Adorno at the surface of the culture industry. The authors conclude that fetishism critique does not replace ideology critique but is its mature form inside the critique of political economy. They also take this to answer claims that Marx's ideology theory is outdated. For Marx, they say, capitalist ideology disappears only by abolishing capital and wage labour, re-establishing individual ownership and moving to socially shared production. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of ideology, the Althusser debate, or the link between the early texts and Capital.

Strengthening the livelihood foundation of building a leading education country 厚植教育强国建设的民生根基 Duan Meijuan Duan Meijuan, writing in the People's Daily in March 2025, takes up one of the six attributes that Xi Jinping assigned to a "leading education country" at the National Education Conference: the capacity to safeguard people's livelihood. The article argues that this capacity expresses the people-oriented character of education. Building a leading education country, Duan contends, requires making public education services more inclusive, accessible and convenient, and resolving the pressing educational concerns of ordinary families. This is a short Party-press commentary, organised in three steps: the meaning of livelihood-protection capacity, the weak links that hold it back, and the practical requirements for strengthening it. It draws on Xi's statements on education and on the record of the Party Central Committee since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It closes with a short passage on the author's own institution, Hunan Women's University. On meaning, Duan reads livelihood-protection capacity as embodying a people-centred philosophy of development, the idea that educational fairness underpins social fairness and justice, and a higher quality of educational supply. Duan then names three weaknesses: high-quality resources are still insufficient and unevenly distributed, notably between city and countryside; special groups, including left-behind children, children with disabilities and migrant workers' children, are inadequately served; and evaluation still leans on exam scores, so that private tutoring persists despite the "double reduction" policy. The proposed remedies follow these gaps: rebalance resources through fiscal transfers, paired cooperation and teacher rotation; reform evaluation and integrate vocational and general education; and strengthen funding, legal and digital support. Duan concludes that the work must be guided by Xi Jinping's statements on education and carried out with strict implementation, so that the results of education reform reach all people more fairly. Universities are urged to take on livelihood responsibilities, and Hunan Women's University is offered as an example. It says it links its disciplines to social needs through cooperation with industry and serves women's development. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary frames education policy in terms of livelihood and fairness, and of the policy measures it lists.

Marx and Engels's critique of modern capitalist civilization and its implications 马克思恩格斯对资本主义现代文明的批判及启示 Sun Xuan Sun Xuan asks how the value core of capitalist modern civilization shapes that civilization and drives it into crisis, a question the author says Weber, Schumpeter, Rousseau and other thinkers left unanswered. Their critiques, in Sun's reading, describe value deviation and dilemmas without systematically explaining how the core works. Sun argues that Marx and Engels, working from historical materialism, supply this explanation, and that it points to a new path of human civilization built on the free and all-round development of the human being and on community values. The article has three parts. The first defines modern civilization and reviews Western and Chinese views of its Protestant and Enlightenment roots. The second sets out Marx and Engels's critique along five dimensions: material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. The third turns each dimension into a positive alternative. For Sun, the value core of capitalist civilization is the supremacy of material interest and the maximization of capital's interests. Marx and Engels credit the bourgeoisie with huge productive achievements and with sweeping away feudal political and ideological fetters. The same core, Sun argues, produces overproduction crises, a representative state that is an illusory community serving capital, colonial and world-market domination, commodity and money fetishism, alienated and competitive social relations, and ecological plunder. Against the logic of 'for capital, relying on working people, developing capital', Sun proposes 'for people, relying on people, developing people'. In practice this means ownership and distribution systems that favour the majority, substantive people's democracy, plural and equal exchange among civilizations, non-commercialized cultural production, a division of labour that frees people from mechanical work, and harmony between humans and nature. Sun concludes that capitalist civilization is being 'disenchanted', exposing structural dilemmas and signs of decline. The lesson drawn is a return from a 'material-centred' to a 'human-centred' civilizational standard. On this basis the five forms of civilization would develop together in a community of all-round development, easing disputes over civilizational values and conflicts between civilizations. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese Marxist reading of Marx and Engels on civilization, organized by the five dimensions of civilization and linked to the current Chinese debate on a new path of human civilization.

On the logic of opposition in objectified labour Based on the theory of metabolism in Capital and its manuscripts 论对象化劳动的对立逻辑 Sun Lin Sun Lin takes up "objectified labour" (duixianghua laodong), which the article treats as the core concept of Marx's critique of political economy. The author asks how Marx, working through the theory of metabolism (Stoffwechsel) in Capital and its manuscripts, develops a dialectic of opposition that differs from Hegel's and Feuerbach's accounts of objectivity. The thesis is that objectified labour is the "centre of gravity" of the critique, and that its logic of opposition unlocks the secret of formal change (form transformation) in capitalist metabolism. The article has three parts. The first follows social metabolism from the external opposition of commodity and money to the internal opposition of use-value and exchange-value, and then to an essential opposition. The second argues that value, commodity and capital are each objectified labour. The third turns to the "positive sublation" of objectified labour through the natural conditions of objective activity. Sun reads these steps against Hegel's speculative logic, Feuerbach's critique of theology, and Marx's 1844 Manuscripts and Grundrisse-era texts. Sun's central move is to say that simple circulation yields only successive external oppositions. Money circulation, and then capital circulation, introduces "simultaneity" and "identity", through which past, accumulated labour inverts and dominates living labour. Capital is thereby described as the inversion and transposition of forces, a self-valorising "fetish" that sublates both external and internal opposition. Sun adds that this identity is only ideal. In reality the sale of labour-power is an "apparent exchange", and the gap between buying and selling makes realisation contingent, which Sun links to "modern crisis" and the world-market crisis. Sun contends that Hegel's pre-established harmony becomes antagonistic contradiction under capitalism. Sun concludes that opposition within objectified labour is a logical opposition within a non-identical reality, and that the real cause and ground is living labour and the worker who carries it. The way beyond capital's totality is to start from use-value, natural conditions, and the non-objectified labour of the human–nature metabolism, which cannot be fully dissolved into abstract value. Sun holds that recovering these conditions still matters for critiquing capitalist modernity today. Read the original if you want a close, Hegel-informed reading of Marx's metabolism, objectified labour and fetishism in Capital and its manuscripts.

Upholding the people-centred governing philosophy 坚持以人民为中心的执政理念 Zhang Fuwen This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (25 March 2025) asks what the people-centred governing philosophy of the Communist Party of China means and why it matters. Zhang Fuwen argues that it answers the questions of whom the Party governs for, whom it relies on, why it governs and how. In Zhang's account, it is both an innovative development of Marxist party-building theory and a contemporary form of the Party's fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly. The article first places the philosophy in the Marxist tradition and in the Party's history. It then shows how it appears in the Party's governing practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends by linking it to the Party's founding mission, leadership and Party discipline. Zhang argues that Marxism treats the proletarian party as an instrument of the people's interests and state organs as "public servants", not masters. On this basis the author says the Party represents no interest group or privileged stratum, and takes bringing benefit to the people as the essence of governing. The author cites the poverty-alleviation campaign as evidence, and describes governing as "for the people" and "reliant on the people", a dialectical unity realised through the mass line, now extended online in the age of artificial intelligence. Zhang assigns three roles: the founding mission is the value thread, strengthening Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is an important support. Zhang concludes that the Party's purity, advanced character and governing capacity are not innate. They must be maintained through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, so that the people-centred philosophy can be upheld. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists link the people-centred philosophy to Party building and discipline.

The Zunyi Conference: from historical event to historical landmark 遵义会议：从历史事件到历史标志 Huang Yibing Marking the 90th anniversary of the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, Huang asks why this meeting, unlike many historical events, became a lasting landmark in the history of the Communist Party of China. The author's answer is that it saved the Party, the Red Army and the revolution at a critical moment. In Huang's account, it did so by effectively establishing Mao Zedong's leadership and the leading position of a correct Marxist line, which opened a stage of independent and self-reliant problem-solving. The article has four sections. It first examines why the Party leadership before Zunyi was neither stable nor mature. It then treats the conference's organisational result, Mao's leading position, and its political result, the correct line. A final section draws out the conference's historical standing and its lessons for the present. Huang draws on Party resolutions, speeches by Mao, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, Comintern documents and Xi Jinping's remarks. Huang contends that before Zunyi the Party lost independence organisationally, because the Comintern repeatedly reshaped its leadership. It also lost independence ideologically, because Comintern resolutions and Soviet experience were turned into a dogmatic "international line" detached from Chinese conditions. Zunyi, the author argues, ended this rule in fact, building on the Tongdao, Liping and Houchang meetings. The Comintern later endorsed Mao's leadership, and the Party defeated Zhang Guotao's splittism. Huang stresses that the conference corrected the military line, and that Mao's later writings, including On Practice and On Contradiction, and the Yan'an rectification movement deepened the political and theoretical reckoning. Huang draws four lessons. The Party needs a strong and mature central leadership core; the author links this directly to the Two Establishes and to Xi Jinping's position today. It must keep to independent and self-reliant development, which the author connects to Chinese modernization. It must integrate Marxism with China's concrete realities and with traditional Chinese culture, avoiding dogmatism. It must hold to a correct political line, namely the Party's basic theory, line and strategy. Read the original if you want an official Party-history interpretation of Zunyi and how it is tied to present-day leadership doctrine.

Rethinking the adaptation of Marx's labour theory of value to our times under the challenge of artificial intelligence 人工智能挑战背景下马克思劳动价值论时代化审思 Yu Tianyu Does the arrival of ChatGPT and Sora make Marx's labour theory of value obsolete? Yu Tianyu takes up the view that artificial intelligence (AI) is an unprecedented qualitative leap in machinery, one that expels human labour from production and so undermines the principle that labour is the only source of value. Yu argues that this view rests on a mistaken picture of AI. In Yu's account, AI has not removed human labour from production, labour remains the sole source of value, and the theory still needs to be developed for the present. The article first traces how machines have displaced labour in three stages: manufacture, where workers become partial organs of the "collective worker"; large-scale machine industry, where they become "conscious limbs" of the machine; and the AI era, where Yu says they risk becoming a "useless class". It then reconstructs the challenge as two linked arguments, about the value-formation process and about exploitation. Next comes a rebuttal from Marx's own categories, followed by proposals for updating the theory and a discussion of its contemporary significance. Yu reconstructs the challenge in Marx's terms. If variable capital disappears, new value must arise in circulation, which breaks equivalent exchange, or AI must create surplus value, which would turn "labour creates value" into "machines create value" and leave capitalists with income that involves no exploitation. Against this, Yu makes three points. Physical labour is turning into mental labour. Concrete and abstract labour are being confused, since the disappearance of concrete labour in one process does not abolish abstract labour in society. And AI is a means of production, capital and a commodity, so it is itself a product of human labour and cannot be an independent producer. Yu adds that AI as fixed capital speeds up value formation and intensifies exploitation. In the hypothetical case of a society with no human labour, capital would lose the external source of its self-expansion. Yu calls for extending Marx's categories: redefining productive labour to cover hidden "free labour" on digital platforms, recognising the labour of scientific and technical staff, clarifying value creation around "intelligent commodities", and grasping the capitalist use of machines. Yu holds that the theory remains relevant for understanding contemporary capitalism, for guiding the socialist market economy and for building a harmonious human–machine relationship under Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, Capital-based Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the claim that AI refutes the labour theory of value, with its proposals for updating the theory.

Big economic provinces shouldering the main burden: setting an example in promoting common prosperity for all the people 经济大省挑大梁，要在促进全体人民共同富裕上“作示范” Gong Yun Zhu Ying This commentary, published in New Xiangjiang Review in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's instruction at the Jiangsu delegation to the National People's Congress on 5 March 2025 that big economic provinces must 'shoulder the main burden' (挑大梁) to achieve the goals of the 14th Five-Year Plan. Gong and Zhu argue that these provinces are pivotal to national development and must contribute more to high-quality development and the overall national picture. The authors first set out the national strategic significance of the requirement, tracing Xi's repeated statements since July 2022. They then turn to its practical paths, following the four points Xi gave to Jiangsu: take the lead in integrating scientific and industrial innovation, strive to be first in deeper reform and higher-level opening up, move ahead in implementing major national strategies, and set an example in promoting common prosperity. On significance, the authors invoke the Marxist dialectic of part and whole: the big provinces are the 'ballast' of the national economy and an 'engine' for surrounding regions. They cite figures that these provinces hold under a fifth of the national territory, over half the population and more than 60 per cent of GDP, and that Guangdong and Jiangsu each approached 14 trillion yuan in 2024. On common prosperity, they recall Deng Xiaoping's idea of some regions getting rich first and leading others. Given uneven regional, urban–rural and income development, they say the big provinces should help less developed areas, advance rural revitalisation, reform income distribution and equalise public services. On practice, the authors call for more research investment, firms as the main innovators, market-oriented factor reform, equal treatment of all ownership types and a better business environment. They also want provinces to link up with strategies such as Yangtze River Delta integration and the Greater Bay Area, with a 'national chessboard' mindset. For common prosperity they propose industrial transfer, paired assistance, vocational training bases in central and western regions, and replicable models, citing Zhejiang's demonstration zone for common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary translates Xi's 2025 instructions on regional leadership and common prosperity into tasks for individual provinces.

Basic issues in building the disciplinary subjectivity of ideological and political education over forty years 论析40年来思想政治教育学科主体性建设的基本议题 Yu Wenli Marking forty years since ideological and political education was set up as an undergraduate programme in 1984, Yu Wenli asks how the field can build its own disciplinary subjectivity (xueke zhutixing), meaning the independent character that makes it a discipline rather than a borrower of other fields' concepts. Yu argues that this subjectivity is the discipline's foundation and source of vitality. It has to be built through five paired relationships, which the article treats in turn. The article first separates the programme (zhuanye) from the discipline (xueke), noting that the field began as a programme in 1984 and only later became a discipline. It describes how the discipline's classification moved from education to political science and then, in 2006, to the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. It then examines in sequence: cross-disciplinary borrowing and integration; politics and scholarship; knowledge and values; and facts and norms. Yu draws on Kant, Bertrand Russell and Jürgen Habermas for supporting distinctions. Yu holds that the discipline grew out of the Party's political work in the revolutionary years and out of attempts to make the ideological work of state-enterprise staff more scientific. It has therefore drawn heavily on Marxist philosophy, pedagogy, sociology and psychology. The task now is to turn borrowing into independent knowledge, theory and method. Yu sees politics as the discipline's defining character, since it exists to uphold Marxism as the Party's guiding ideology. Yet research often stops at explaining policy, which leaves its scholarly side weak. The proposed way forward is to move from common sense to theory, to policy reasoning and then to philosophy, without setting politics and scholarship against each other. On knowledge and values, Yu describes the discipline's knowledge as experiential, or "soft", and inseparable from value formation. Yu also says that its conceptual base is still too dependent on Western concepts. The tension is between theory and practice, and between foreign and native concepts. Finally, Yu locates subjectivity in the interplay of facts (practice, problems, solutions) and norms (policies, institutions, plans). Yu concludes that an autonomous knowledge system should be built on the principle of creating Chinese knowledge from Chinese values, with Chinese knowledge carrying those values. Future efforts should balance facts and norms and avoid both pure factualism and voluntarism. The aim is a modern discipline that combines scientific and revolutionary character, politics and scholarship, and theory and practice. Read the original if you want to see how a leading scholar of the field frames its identity problems, and how it relates the Party's ideological mission to academic discipline-building.

A methodological reflection on the theoretical turn in the critique of use-value From the critique of political economy to the critique of alienated power 使用价值批判之理论转向的方法论反思 Weng Hanbing Contemporary Western Left social critique, the article observes, has concentrated on exchange-value and the logic of 'abstraction becoming domination', while the critical force of use-value has been little studied. Weng argues that Marx's use-value is not merely the natural 'usefulness' of a commodity but a category with its own social-critical content. Western Left thinkers such as Debord, Baudrillard and Agamben have converted it into a critique of alienated power. In Weng's view this marks a methodological retreat from Marx's critique of political economy towards a purely philosophical critique. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's critique of use-value along two dimensions: fetishism (the commodity chapter of Capital, Volume 1) and economic crisis (the Grundrisse's 'fragment on machines', Capital and the 1861–63 manuscripts). The second sets out three strands of the alienated-power approach: Debord's society of the spectacle, Baudrillard's The Mirror of Production and Agamben's Profanations. The third offers a methodological assessment, including the claim that digital capitalism intensifies these power mechanisms. Weng argues that, for Marx, use-value covers a commodity's natural usefulness only at the level of 'production in general'. Its social meaning appears in the value-form, where a commodity's material shell makes a social relation look like a natural property of things. Crises, in Marx's account, come from the opposition between use-value and value, as in the gap between producing and realising surplus value and in the imbalance between production sectors. Weng rejects readings that locate capital's collapse in the self-negation of capital logic. The Western Left thinkers, by contrast, detach use-value from value and productive forces from relations of production. Weng says this produces three shifts: scientific theory of contradiction gives way to a critique of power, class analysis gives way to 'subject identification', and a romantic 'reality versus what ought to be' alienation critique returns, with imagined escape through Lefebvre's 'appropriation', Agamben's 'inoperativity' and Baudrillard's 'symbolic exchange'. Weng adds that this may amount to a new form of bourgeois ideology. Weng grants that these thinkers capture real changes in capitalism since the 1960s, but holds that consumer-society power relations belong to the surface of everyday life. Citing a view that profit-seeking has shifted to financial speculation and debt-fuelled consumption, Weng locates the deeper contradiction in the imbalance between production and consumption. When crisis breaks out, the author predicts, class relations will replace the alienated relation between subject and apparatus. Weng calls for a theory of contemporary capitalist power built on Marxism's overall logic, which the author sees as especially important for critiques of digital capitalism. Read the original if you work on Western Marxism, value-form theory or critiques of the consumer society and want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Debord, Baudrillard and Agamben.

The operating logic and optimisation paths of rural grassroots Party building in leading rural revitalisation 农村基层党建引领乡村振兴的运作逻辑与优化路径 Liu Xiaoli Liu Xiaoli asks how rural grassroots Party building can effectively lead rural revitalisation, a strategy launched at the 19th Party Congress (2017) and reinforced by the 20th Party Congress (2022) emphasis on strengthening the grassroots. The article argues that Party leadership works through three linked logics (structure, process and function), and that current weaknesses in each can be remedied by targeted reforms. The article opens with a survey of existing scholarship, grouped into four perspectives: organisational embedding, authorisation and empowerment, structure and institutions, and structure–function–organisational capacity. Liu finds that most studies summarise local experience or discuss methods, and that the overall logic and a systematic path are underdeveloped. The author then builds a "structure–process–function" framework. The article moves through the operating logic, the problems found in practice and proposed paths of improvement. On operating logic, Liu holds that Party leadership builds a "one core, many actors" community of revitalisation, with the Party playing a "meta-governance" role across levels and sectors. It re-engineers mechanisms of value, interest and power to integrate social forces, and it exercises five capacities: political leadership, ideological guidance, development promotion, mass cohesion and social service. Political leadership is said to be the core and to determine the others. Liu identifies three problems: imbalance in structure (strong Party and government, weak enterprises and society), weak adaptability in process (poor coordination, rigid institutions, tensions among culture, economy and politics), and insufficient fit in function, where Party building "floats above" revitalisation as "two skins". Liu proposes widening and diversifying Party-organisation coverage, for example in industrial bases, associations and among migrant members. The author also proposes organisational linkage mechanisms, "Party–mass roundtables" and shared-interest communities, and a shift from rigid "embedding" to "integration". Further proposals are to strengthen political functions, ideological guidance under socialist core values, farmers' initiative through the mass line, incentive and mediation systems, and service provision. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-school account of how grassroots Party building is conceptualised and prescribed in rural revitalisation policy.
