What counts as important research on CPC history? Rethinking the problem of "fragmentation" 究竟何为重要的中共党史研究? Ying Xing Ying Xing asks what makes research on the history of the Communist Party of China (CPC) important, at a time when the field is flooded with submissions and publications that the author finds heavy on process and detail but light on problems, structure and weight. Ying argues that fragmentation will not be cured by gathering more sources: the field needs historical insight (shishi) of the kind valued by Chinese historiography, not merely the accumulation of archival material. The article presents its answer as five questions. Ying opens with a survey of Chinese historiographical criticism from Liu Zhiji to Chen Yinke, Qian Mu and Liu Xianxin. The survey is meant to show that many historians rejected the claim that history is simply the study of sources. The five questions then ask what the most important Party-history sources are, why political history matters, why comparison matters, which theory to borrow, and why the study of "wind and momentum" is needed. Examples come from Chen Yinke, Foucault, Weber, Fei Xiaotong and Wang Fansen, along with Red Army history. Ying makes three main moves. First, important sources are those with overall significance for the Party's thought and line, such as congress resolutions, Party constitutions and records of cadres trained in the Soviet Union, rather than whatever is convenient. The author criticises "hometown Party history", which picks subjects by ease of access. Second, political history, with organisational and intellectual history, is the centre of Party history, and Ying reads even Foucault's work on marginal groups as political history. Comparison is what lets a study move from a case to general conclusions instead of "seeing the small through the small". The author illustrates this with the Red Army's first honorary titles for combat units, awarded in the Sichuan–Shaanxi base area in 1934. Third, Ying warns against "middle-range theory" and urges sustained work on classical thinkers such as Marx, Tocqueville, Weber and Foucault. The author adds that theory can "discover" concepts in the sources as well as invent them, and that historians should combine the "solid" study of facts with the "hollow" study of climate and trends. Ying concludes that fragmentary studies with reliable sources and clear interpretation still have scholarly value, but that research differs in quality. Those who want to go beyond fragmentation must ask whether their topics carry enough weight, and should not rely on convenient sources or rapid output. Important research, the author says, "blows the wind" and does not merely receive it. Read the original if you want to understand a leading sociologist's critique of current Party-history scholarship, or the way Chinese historiographical and Western theoretical traditions are used to set methodological standards for the field.

A semiotic reading of how the Chinese Communist Party's Red newspapers shaped the revolutionary spirit 中国共产党红色报刊塑造革命精神的符号学解读 Su Jie Wang Fei Su Jie and Wang Fei ask how the Party's Red newspapers of the New Democratic Revolution period used signs to shape and spread the revolutionary spirit, a mechanism they say existing research has treated only thinly. They argue that linguistic and visual signs, combined in layered structures, conveyed revolutionary ideas, stirred popular feeling and built consensus. The study is framed by the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to build socialist ideology with strong cohesion and leadership. The authors take the Soviet-area newspaper Red China (Hongse Zhonghua) as their case. Section one identifies its linguistic signs (keywords, slogans, editorials) and visual signs (illustrations, mastheads, typefaces, layout), then examines how they combine within and across categories. Section two applies Peirce's tripartite account of the interpretant to issue 242, and section three draws historical values and present-day lessons. Saussure, Eagleton and Geertz are used as theoretical support. The central argument is that meaning is produced through relations between signs. The authors report that the paper's 172 illustrations broadly follow a conflict frame of enemy, us and friend, and that mastheads fuse fonts, a map of China, a five-pointed star and the Party emblem into a single visual narrative. Using Peirce, they treat the intentional interpretant as the Party's mobilising intent, set out in headline, body text and calls to action in issue 242. The effective interpretant is the audience's emotional resonance and cognitive reading, and the communal interpretant is the shared consensus and collective action that embed the spirit in group memory. The authors credit Red newspapers with three historical values: spreading revolutionary theory in concrete cultural symbols, strengthening identity through hero and martyr imagery, and passing revolutionary culture across generations. For the present they draw two lessons for Party media: keep a concise, forceful vernacular style, and stay close to people's livelihood, now extended through the "online mass line". They tie the latter to the Marxist principle of the people's character and to Mao Zedong's idea of newspapers run for the masses. Read the original if you want a worked example of applying Peirce-style semiotics to Party press history, with close description of Red China's mastheads and front pages.

Practical pathways for strengthening ideological and political leadership in building a strong education nation 教育强国建设背景下提升思政引领力的实践理路 Wu Yandong Yang Siqing Wu Yandong and Yang Siqing take up Xi Jinping's call, made at the National Education Conference, for a socialist education powerhouse with six strengths, the first of which is "ideological and political leadership" (siheng yinlingli). The article asks what value this capacity holds and how it can be raised. Its thesis is that ideological and political work is the "lifeline" of the project, and that stronger leadership requires a systematic, multi-dimensional practical path. The article has two parts. The first sets out the value of ideological and political leadership in building a strong education nation. The second proposes five ways of strengthening it: political leadership, value leadership, institutional leadership, curriculum leadership and leadership through the ideological and political workforce. Each is broken into three sub-measures, drawing on Xi Jinping's statements on education and ideological work. In the first part the authors argue that ideological and political leadership shows the political character of education, fixes the direction of talent cultivation, and helps build the strategic layout that integrates education, science and technology, and talent. In the second part, the authors argue that political leadership means upholding the Party's overall leadership of education, guiding it with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and strengthening Party ideological work. Value leadership means turning core socialist values into students' aims, countering what the authors call erroneous trends such as historical nihilism, and developing education with a people-centred approach. Institutional leadership means keeping Marxism's guiding position, improving the mechanism of fostering virtue through education, and running ideological work through every part of the talent-training system. Curriculum leadership covers ideological and political courses, "curriculum ideology and politics" in other subjects, and a "big ideological and political course" linking classroom and society. The authors conclude that a strong education nation needs strong ideological and political leadership. They propose steps for the workforce: building awareness, raising its organising, value-shaping and coordinating abilities, and making use of model examples, publicity and evaluation. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented account of how ideological and political education is being linked to the education-power agenda in Chinese universities and schools.

Mao Zedong's exploration of and contribution to the path of modernization after the founding of the People's Republic 新中国成立后毛泽东对现代化道路的探索与贡献 Zhang Guozuo Yang Ruonan Zhang Guozuo and Yang Ruonan ask how Mao Zedong approached modernizing a poor, populous country after 1949. Taking Xi Jinping's description of Mao as the "great founder" of China's socialist modernization as their starting point, they argue that Mao's explorations laid ideological, material and institutional foundations for Chinese modernization. In their account, these explorations already showed five features that Xi later codified as distinctive of Chinese modernization. The article is organised around those five features, each treated as a field of Mao-era practice. These are a huge population, the pursuit of fairness, equality and common prosperity, the joint improvement of material and cultural life, the parallel development of the economy and protection of nature, and the creation of a peaceful international environment. Evidence comes from Mao's speeches, comments and directives, together with statistics on health, literacy, schooling and forestry policy, and the 1971 UN vote on China's seat. A short conclusion links the Mao period to Xi's formulations. The authors argue that Mao took a dialectical view of population: a large population meant heavy burdens but also great strength. They credit the new political order, patriotic health campaigns, barefoot doctors, rural cooperative medicine and literacy drives with raising life expectancy and educational levels. On values, they say Mao rejected both egalitarianism and excessive disparity, and pursued common prosperity step by step, citing the Ten Great Relationships and Mao's 1954 remarks on a phased path to a modern socialist country. They present his calls to afforest the country and balance farming, forestry and herding as early ecological thinking. In foreign policy they stress fighting to stop war, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and a pledge never to seek hegemony. The authors conclude that Mao, working through repeated practice and reflection, gave a pioneering answer to how a poor and backward China could modernize. They argue that Xi Jinping creatively inherited and developed these explorations into the theory of Chinese modernization, with its stated features, essential requirements and strategic timetable to 2035 and mid-century. Studying Xi's discourse, they say, reveals both continuity with Mao and further innovation. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link Mao-era policy to the official genealogy of Chinese modernization, with the statistics and Mao quotations used to support it.

Strengthening "Three New" Party building to raise the effectiveness of primary-level governance 以加强“三新”党建提升基层治理效能 Wang Yang Wang Yang, a deputy dean at a university school of Marxism, takes up a practical problem in a short commentary in Guangming Daily. China's new economic organisations, new social organisations and new employment groups (the "Three New") are growing quickly, and the author asks how Party building in these areas can raise the effectiveness of primary-level governance. The thesis is that strengthening "Three New" Party building turns the Party's leadership advantages into concrete results in governance. In Wang's account, this also consolidates the Party's governing foundation and the base of national governance. The piece cites Xi Jinping's call to give priority to Party building in these three areas, and the 2025 Government Work Report's pledge to improve urban and rural primary-level governance. It is organised in three parts. The first concerns institutions and mechanisms for "Three New" Party building. The second concerns extending Party organisation and work into these fields. The third concerns widening the ways in which "Three New" Party organisations and members can play a role. On institutions, Wang calls for a chain of "overall leadership, systematic advancement, coordinated operation, and responsibility". Party committees at each level would oversee the work, supported by task forces, joint meetings, assigned contacts and performance assessment. Regional and sector-based coordination would be built around parks, business districts and buildings, and mechanisms such as "blow the whistle and report in" would be extended to these fields. On coverage, Wang proposes embedding Party organisations in grid-based management, using a "whole life cycle" model of registration, entry, empowerment and exit. For delivery drivers and similar workers, the author proposes function-based Party organisations, and uses trade unions, the Communist Youth League and women's federations, together with online one-stop platforms, to mobilise people. On roles, Wang urges flexible education such as livestreamed courses, finer-grained services that protect labour rights, industry-chain and association Party building, and consultation platforms. These platforms would carry demands upward and policy and resources downward, and they would support a governance community in which everyone has responsibility. Wang concludes that Party leadership can be put into practice at the grassroots through better coordination, wider organisational coverage and fuller use of Party members in emerging sectors. The article presents these as measures for building a governance community in which "everyone has responsibility, does their part and shares in the benefits". Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented statement of how Party-building language is applied to platform workers, private firms and social organisations at the neighbourhood level.

Deepening the joint investigation and joint treatment of unhealthy work styles and corruption 深入推进风腐同查同治 Tang Huangfeng Tang Huangfeng takes up a problem he describes as prominent in current Party discipline work: unhealthy work styles (the "four undesirable work styles") and corruption are increasingly intertwined. The article argues that investigating and treating the two together ("fengfu tongcha tongzhi") is a necessary strategic response. Tang links it to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The article, published in 2025 in a Party cadre journal, has three parts. The first sets out the basis for joint treatment. The second describes how the fusion of work-style and corruption problems appears in practice and why it arises. The third lists practical requirements for deepening the approach, grouped under joint investigation, joint treatment, and institutional and mechanism innovation. Tang's central claim is that the two problems share one root, the alienation of power. Small lapses such as accepting gifts or banquets are said to erode a cadre's defences until quantitative change becomes qualitative change, while uncorrected corruption in turn encourages bad styles. Tang identifies three forms of fusion: improper banquets masking benefit transfers, formalism and bureaucratism shielding graft, and personal enrichment alongside extravagant living. Four causes are named: wavering ideals, weak checks on power, poor enforcement of rules and unhealthy social attitudes. For remedies Tang proposes severe punishment for intertwined cases, better clue-handling, and cross-border asset recovery. The article also calls for tighter supervision of top officials, big-data supervision platforms, ideological and integrity education, and a "one case, four examinations" mechanism covering work style, institutional loopholes, responsibility gaps and the political ecosystem. Tang concludes that joint investigation and treatment is a long and arduous political task that safeguards the Party's vanguard character and its ties with the people. Its operating principle is that every work-style investigation should dig for corruption, and every corruption case should examine work style. Tang presents this as protection for Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party discipline inspection bodies are asked to link work-style rectification and anti-corruption enforcement, including its typology of cases and proposed mechanisms.

Giving full play to the role of grassroots Party organisations in government organs as fighting bastions: providing solid support for Jiangsu's new practice of Chinese modernization 充分发挥机关基层党组织战斗堡垒作用 为推进中国式现代化江苏新实践提供坚实支撑 Chu Yonghong Writing in 2025, Chu Yonghong, who heads the Working Committee of Jiangsu's provincial government organs, asks how Party building in government organs can support high-quality development in the province. The article is a practical, official-style statement that takes Xi Jinping's July 2024 instruction on Party building in central and state organs as its starting point. Chu's thesis is that the quality of organ-level Party building depends on the quality of its grassroots organisations, and that their role as "fighting bastions" should be strengthened to serve Chinese modernization in Jiangsu. The article is organised in four parts, each opening with a claim that one outcome depends on grassroots organisations: the quality of Party building, service to high-quality development, the work style and image of provincial organs, and the implementation of Party-building responsibility. Each part pairs a summary of what Jiangsu has done in recent years with a list of tasks for the future. Chu draws on named local programmes, regulations and mechanisms, such as the model-organ upgrading plan, "four-strong" Party branches and the "service for high-quality development vanguard teams". Chu's first argument concerns capacity. Political guidance, the selection and training of branch secretaries, and the enforcement of standardised rules are meant to strengthen the political and organisational functions of branches. Chu also calls for monitoring the thinking of younger officials and for stronger practical training for officials born in the 1980s and 1990s, whom Chu describes as well educated but short of experience. The second argument concerns output and conduct. Party organisations are to act on key provincial tasks, keep their platforms effective rather than showy, and encourage officials to take responsibility by dealing with reluctance and lack of skill. Discipline education following the 2024 Party discipline campaign is to continue, and measures against formalism should begin with provincial organs. Chu holds that formalism is often visible at the grassroots but rooted higher up. Chu argues that responsibility must be carried down the chain, from Party committees and groups in each department, through their organ Party committees, to the Working Committee itself. Proposals include at least one Party committee meeting every half-year on organ Party building, contact points for leading cadres, coordination mechanisms, and regular reviews of branch secretaries' reports. These are meant to close the "last mile" of accountability. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how a provincial Party working committee presents its organ Party-building agenda, its named mechanisms and its responsibility system.

How digital industry clusters empower new quality productive forces: pathways and optimisation strategies 数字产业集群赋能新质生产力的作用路径和优化策略 Wang Feng Tian Maomin Wang Feng and Tian Maomin ask how digital industry clusters help form new quality productive forces, a concept Xi Jinping introduced and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) took up. They argue that existing studies of digital technology and the digital economy stay on the side of the productive forces and neglect relations of production. In their view the digital industry cluster is the organisational form that unites both, and so a key carrier for cultivating new quality productive forces. After surveying the literature, which they group into schools on technological breakthroughs, factor allocation, labour quality, data, the digital economy, green production and the optimisation of production relations, the authors set out three reasons clusters matter. These are a transformative technology ecosystem, new production relations and a testing ground for practice. They cite Silicon Valley, Bangalore, Tsukuba and Zhongguancun, and give figures for 2023: a digital industry scale of 10.09 trillion yuan, 8.01 per cent of GDP. The article then examines five channels of empowerment and five strategies. The core claim is that clusters work through five channels. They build multi-dimensional innovation networks and speed up the conversion of research into products. They change how production factors, especially data, are allocated. They gather and train skilled people, open green development paths, and offer new ways to integrate industries. Drawing on Marx on cooperation and division of labour and on Engels on planned distribution of productive forces, the authors say clusters create a networked division of labour and new economic relations among firms and institutions. The strategies proposed are to put building before breaking, so that regions do not abandon traditional industries hastily. They also call for self-reliance in science and technology, a society-wide risk-prevention mechanism, and balanced development of traditional, emerging and future industries. The authors further want clusters to be used to incubate cross-regional digital industry belts. They give public ownership a leading role in governance and risk resistance, and conclude that internationally competitive clusters will help form production relations better suited to new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of industrial clusters that links Marxist productive-forces theory to current policy on the digital economy and regional development.

The cultural programme of the Russian Narodniks and its historical echoes 俄国民粹派的文化纲领及其历史回响 Zhou Laishun Zhou Laishun examines the cultural programme of the Russian Narodniks (populists), the movement that shaped Russian social thought and practice from the mid-nineteenth century to the early twentieth. The article argues that this programme, which rested on the people, the village commune and cultural enlightenment, supplied the theoretical core of the movement's practical goals. Zhou holds that it combined a real critique of autocracy and capitalism with romantic, class-limited illusions, and that Marxists such as Marx, Engels and Lenin criticised it for this. The article has four parts. It first treats the "going to the people" movement as an awakening of consciousness, then the commune as the programme's foundation of belief, then its moral and political critique of tsarism and capital. It ends by tracing the programme's historical echoes in the Marxist reaction. Zhou draws on Narodnik writers such as Mikhailovsky, Lavrov, Tkachev, Zaichnevsky and Eliseev. He also draws on Silver Age philosophers and on Marx's reply to Vera Zasulich, Engels's postscript to "On Social Relations in Russia" and Lenin's polemics. In Zhou's account, the Narodniks idealised peasants and the commune as a base for bypassing capitalism. Zhou describes this as a utopian, petty-bourgeois outlook close to Sismondi's romanticism, with a moral rather than economic basis, and as a heroic view of history. Zhou stresses that the commune was not uniquely Russian, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin. Marx treated it as a possible "fulcrum" of social regeneration only if a revolution protected it. The Narodniks attacked the tsar himself and Tkachev demanded immediate revolution, but Zhou argues that the movement failed. It lacked a vanguard party armed with advanced theory, swung between elite terror and one-way enlightenment, and was cut off from the masses. Zhou concludes that the movement still had positive significance. It valued the masses' historical role, criticised the feudal nobility, and began organised revolutionary agitation. Its long polemic with Marxists in the 1890s, which Lenin completed, led Russian intellectuals to Marxism and turned it from theory into practice. Zhou presents this as opening a path to modernity different from the Western one. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Narodnik thought, drawn largely from Russian sources and from the classical Marxist critique of the movement.

The new form of human civilization from the perspective of the Marxist view of civilization 马克思主义文明观视域下的人类文明新形态 Luo Yun This short commentary asks how the Marxist view of civilization, grounded in historical materialism, can guide the construction of a "new form of human civilization". Luo Yun argues that Marx and Engels, though they gave no unified definition of civilization, supplied a scientific framework for understanding its nature, development and succession. On this basis Luo presents the new form of human civilization as emerging from socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. It first discusses the concept of civilization and its diversity, citing Spengler, Toynbee, Jaspers and Xi Jinping. It then sketches the historical evolution of civilization through Marx and Engels's works, including Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Finally it turns to the new form of human civilization created under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Luo reads Marx and Engels as treating civilization as the result of human practice in transforming nature and society, tied to the growth of productive forces. Civilization, in this account, passes through three stages: its emergence (the "savage" and "barbarian" eras), the age of civilization (slave, feudal and capitalist societies), and its high development in communism, of which socialism is the initial form. Luo contends that the new form of human civilization transcends Western capitalist civilization, which the article describes as marked by contradiction, hegemony and the sacrifice of the majority. It is also said to break the equation of modernization with Westernization and to absorb the useful achievements of world civilization through Chinese modernization. Luo concludes that the new form of civilization upholds the basic principles of socialist civilization while offering a pattern for developing and late-developing countries. The article also calls on progressive forces to promote exchange among civilizations and a unity in diversity, and to counter the "clash of civilizations" thesis with the inclusiveness of Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists derive the "new form of human civilization" from Marx and Engels's view of civilization.

An assessment of the impact of identity politics on the contemporary Western left 身份政治对当代西方左翼运动的影响评析 Chen Yuntao Chen Yuntao asks why the Western left, once identified with critique and progress, has come to be seen by many ordinary people as a conservative obstacle to equality while right-wing populists such as Trump pose as anti-establishment. The article argues that identity politics, adopted in the post-industrial era to escape the exhaustion of working-class revolutionary energy, has undermined the left's own aims. In Chen's account, it has weakened the left and produced a cultural and social structure that suits financial capital. The article has three parts. The first sets out three typical features of identity-led left movements: they replace the working class with plural identities as the subject of struggle; they pursue cultural and everyday-life liberation instead of changing relations of production; and they favour decentralised, individual action over party politics and unified class action. Examples include Occupy Wall Street, the Global Climate Strikes, Black Lives Matter and Me Too. The second part sets out four practical dilemmas, and the third reflects on why identity politics has become what Chen calls an "unconscious instrument" of capitalist rule. Chen contends that identity politics tacitly accepts capitalist legitimacy by ignoring class inequality, and that the left has formed an alliance with Wall Street, Silicon Valley and Hollywood elites. In this reading, "victim politics" and differentiated identity mechanisms deepen divisions among ordinary people and replace the common goal of opposing injustice with narrow group interests. After the 2008 financial crisis, the article says, lower- and middle-class whites came to see the left as favouring minorities and were pushed towards right-wing populism. Chen's central Marxist claim is that identity conflicts derive from economic inequality, that material interests outweigh cultural identification, and that only a united class of labourers can confront financial capital. Identity politics, the author says, therefore misidentifies friends and enemies, and is "left in form, right in essence". Chen concedes that identity politics exposed new contradictions and briefly advanced social equality. The article nonetheless concludes that it leads the Western left away from socialist ideals and working-class interests, and that Western left theorists who criticise it without aiming to transform capitalist relations of production remain co-opted. Chen contrasts this with socialism with Chinese characteristics under Communist Party leadership, which the author presents as the key force for reviving world socialism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western identity politics, set within debates on the fate of the Western left and world socialism.

The new "networked" pattern of relations among communist parties abroad in the twenty-first century 21世纪国外共产党政党关系的“网络化”新态势 Yu Weihai Li Yuwei Yu Weihai and Li Yuwei ask how relations among communist parties outside China should be characterised since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Existing Chinese studies, they say, are scattered and mostly describe either cooperation or splits. The authors argue that the dominant pattern in the twenty-first century is "networked" (wangluohua): parties of many types interact densely, link in varied ways, cooperate loosely and quarrel constantly. They frame the topic through Xi Jinping's 2017 call for a new type of inter-party relations. The article first proposes the concept, then sets out five manifestations of networking. It then identifies four new structural features and ends with three reflections for the Communist Party of China. Evidence comes from party statements, the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties (IMCWP), regional forums such as the São Paulo Forum, the Party of the European Left and European Communist Action, and recent joint statements on the Middle East and Ukraine. The authors' core claim is that the network combines opposed tendencies. The five manifestations are typified actors, intensive exchange, diversified linkage, loose internationalism and routine disputes. The authors count over 400 parties, classed by their guiding ideology (Marxism-Leninism, Marxism, Mao Zedong Thought, Trotskyism, Hoxhaism and others). These parties explore separate national paths yet share a consensus after the 2008 financial crisis. Their unity is "weak", because organisations such as the IMCWP have no leadership, programme or binding decisions. The IMCWP produced two conflicting resolutions in 2022, and the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties of Europe dissolved in 2023. The authors present the structure as flat and decentralised, replacing the Soviet-led centre–periphery model. Internationalism is set against a sectarianism that claims orthodoxy and seeks "one centre". Yu and Li conclude that the international communist movement has not disappeared but has taken a new form. They also judge that networking reflects an immature stage of international unity. They argue that only "limited unity" is feasible now and that analysis must go beyond older frameworks. They call on the Communist Party of China to guide inter-party relations through the new type of party relations. They propose using the Dialogue with World Political Parties and the World Socialism Forum to build a Chinese discourse and to promote solidarity among communist parties. Read the original if you study contemporary communist parties abroad, or want to see how Chinese scholars frame them in relation to Party diplomacy.

The rich connotations of Chinese civilization and their significance for our times 中华文明的丰富内涵及其时代意蕴 Ji Mingming This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025, asks what Chinese civilization contains and why it matters today. Ji Mingming argues that it is the only great civilization that has continued unbroken to the present in the form of a state. In Ji's account, five outstanding features (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) shape its overall character, and a full grasp of them helps advance socialist cultural development and national cultural soft power. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the content of Chinese civilization: fine traditional culture, historical and cultural heritage, ethical values, and a record of exchange with other civilizations. The second takes the five features in turn, with examples from philosophy, technology and institutions. The third turns to the contemporary value of the civilization and what should be done with it. Ji leans throughout on statements by Xi Jinping and on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). On content, Ji lists values such as benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and trustworthiness, harmony between humans and nature, and attention to human development beyond material wealth. Ji adds that the civilization has always drawn on outside sources, from Buddhism to Western learning, and that Marxism was chosen in the modern period while China's distinctive path and the independence of its civilization were kept. On the five features, Ji cites the classical canon and continuous historical records for continuity; the Hundred Schools of thought, Neo-Confucianism, the Four Great Inventions and the imperial examination system for innovation; a pluralistic and unified pattern, supported by shared political, cultural and psychological identification, for unity; and an openness to foreign cultures, religions and schools of thought, together with a long-standing preference for harmony, for inclusiveness and peacefulness. Ji concludes that Chinese civilization has gathered strength in times of national crisis and led the way in times of national revival, and that its stress on harmony, balance and sustainability can offer ideas for global environmental, social and economic problems. Ji calls for inheriting the essence of tradition, absorbing contemporary achievements, and promoting exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary currently presents the five features of Chinese civilization and their present-day relevance.

Using high-quality investigation and research to generate strong momentum for comprehensively deepening reform 以高质量调研形成全面深化改革的强大动力 Zhan Yong This newspaper commentary, published in March 2025, asks how Party members and cadres can use investigation and research, which the author calls the Party's "family heirloom", to support the further deepening of reform. Zhan argues that research must be "deep, solid, meticulous, accurate and effective" if it is to locate the starting points, focal points and breakthrough points of reform and strengthen its systematic and coordinated character. The article draws on Xi Jinping's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is organised under five headings: cultivating a people-centred outlook, upholding a pragmatic work style, focusing on development practice, facing difficulties and challenges, and moving from points to the whole. Zhan's core claims are that research must follow the mass line and seek out critical voices from the grassroots, and that it must rest on seeking truth from facts, with no staged or showcase visits. It must be problem-oriented, meaning problems are faced, analysed and solved rather than shelved, and cadres should visit difficult places rather than only successful ones. Drawing on Xi's endorsement of "dissecting the sparrow", the author also ties research to a systems approach that balances the macro and micro, the whole and the part, and the particular and the general. Zhan concludes that cadres should study and apply Xi's statements on research, and treat research as practice of the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, as a way of changing work style, and as a way to resolve reform problems and drive Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school and university leaders present investigation and research as a method of governance and Party building in the current reform agenda.

Understanding in depth how the leading force of ideological and political education works 深刻把握思政引领力的作用机制 Dai Yuqi Tian Yu Dai Yuqi and Tian Yu take up a concept introduced in September 2024, when Xi Jinping told the National Education Conference that a leading education nation must have strong "leading force of ideological and political education" (sizheng yinlingli), placed first among six capacities. The authors argue that although the term is new, the function it names has run through the Party's history. Their thesis is that this force operates through distinct mechanisms in three fields: education, culture and society. The article, published in Ideological and Political Education Research (2025, no. 2), notes that most existing work approaches the concept from the angle of building a leading education nation, and says it instead concentrates on mechanisms of action. Each of its three main sections sets out functions of the leading force, then identifies shortcomings in current practice. A short conclusion describes vertical deepening and horizontal interaction across the fields. In education, the authors identify three functions: forging the soul (political and value guidance, opposing "value neutrality"), stimulating intellect (integrating ideological education with subject knowledge) and cultivating virtue (moral and emotional guidance of young people). In culture, they treat it as upholding cultural leadership, consolidating cultural subjectivity through the Two Integrations, and raising national soft power. They describe Western cultural infiltration, commercial distortion of cultural products and weak overseas communication as challenges. In society, it is said to build consensus, sustain orderly operation through self-restraint and conflict mediation, and support innovative governance. Here Dai and Tian stress balancing unity with plurality, "managing well without managing rigidly". The conclusion holds that the leading force starts in education, runs through culture and society, and that the three fields reinforce each other through shared values, integrated goals and feedback loops. The authors add that it does not belong automatically to those who do ideological work but sets higher demands on each of them, and that it requires sustained effort. They call for continuously improving ideological and political education, fitting it to mainstream values and to socio-economic development, and combining direct and indirect, explicit and implicit guidance. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholars conceptualise the functions and weak points of ideological and political work in the new "six forces" framework.

The epistemological essence of investigation and research in the Communist Party of China 中国共产党调查研究的认识论本质 Yang Ruwei Yang Ruwei examines investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu), which Xi Jinping calls a family heirloom of the Party, from the standpoint of Marxist epistemology. The short commentary argues that its essence lies in uniting a value orientation with cognition of objective laws. Yang links this to the current drive to advance Chinese modernization and to implement the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The piece has three parts: the essence of investigation and research, its process, and its features. It draws on Mao Zedong's On Practice, a passage from Marx on research, and Mao's rural surveys of 1928–1933, including the Xunwu and Mukou village investigations. Yang holds that the Party's value orientation is goal-directed, revolutionary and people-centred, while its cognition of laws is objective, systematic and developmental. Without a correct value orientation, in Yang's reading, rational knowledge and sound policy cannot be reached. The process has two steps: moving from the concrete to the abstract by gathering material, then from the abstract to the "ideal concrete" by reconstructing it in thought to produce policies. Mao's eleven rural surveys serve as the example. Yang identifies four features: objectivity, dynamism, purposefulness and timeliness. Methods must change as tasks, investigators and conditions change, and older cadres' experience cannot replace that of new ones. Read the original if you want a brief Party-building account that frames investigation and research as an epistemological process, with Mao's rural surveys as illustration.

Deng Xiaoping's summing-up of the historical experience of the international communist movement and its contemporary lessons 邓小平对国际共产主义运动的历史经验总结及当代启示 Yuan Xiuli How did Deng Xiaoping draw lessons from the rise and setbacks of the international communist movement, and what do they offer today? Yuan Xiuli argues that Deng affirmed the movement's achievements while learning from the Soviet collapse, the Eastern European upheavals and the split in the socialist camp. In Yuan's reading, these lessons remain valuable for China and world socialism at a time of what Xi Jinping calls changes unseen in a century. The article first sets out five strands of Deng's summing-up: upholding scientific socialism, seeking truth from facts, combining self-reliance with opening up, handling relations between socialist states and between parties correctly, and bringing out the superiority of socialism. A final section draws three present-day lessons. Yuan relies mainly on Deng's remarks from 1956 to 1989, framed by statements from Xi Jinping. Yuan's central claim is that Deng opposed both "Left" and Right deviations. He rejected wholesale Westernization and bourgeois liberalization, but also dogmatic attempts to leap ahead to communism. Deng also criticised copying the Soviet model, Soviet "big-power" and "big-party" chauvinism, and China's own past habit of judging other parties by Chinese experience. Yuan presents the reform-era principles as drawn from these lessons: equality and independence between parties, with no "father party", and self-reliance that does not exclude learning from abroad. Poverty, Deng held, is not socialism, so socialism must prove itself by developing the productive forces and improving living standards. Yuan draws three lessons. History should be summed up scientifically, looking forward and avoiding fruitless polemics. Whether the Party's leadership is upheld decides the fate of the movement, which Yuan links to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. And the Party should show historical initiative in the face of great changes. Yuan concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics, upheld in line with Deng's insights, is the mainstay of twenty-first-century world socialism. Read the original if you want a compact, official-line account of how Deng's remarks on communist movement history are used to support present Party-building and foreign-policy positions.

Strengthening Party conduct and discipline to clear obstacles and safeguard reform 强化正风肃纪为改革清障护航 Lü Man Writing in the Party journal Dangjian (2025, no. 2), Lü Man argues that sustained efforts to rectify Party conduct and enforce discipline are a necessary guarantee for the further deepening of reform. The article takes as its starting point the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and Xi Jinping's call at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to link work on conduct, discipline and anti-corruption. Lü's thesis is that, given the unprecedented scope and depth of reform, such work must run through every aspect of Party building to create a healthy political ecology. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out why strengthening conduct and discipline matters, drawing on three grounds: the basic principles of Marxist party-building theory, the Chinese Communist Party's historical experience, and the task of leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform. The second explains how this work protects reform in terms of breadth, depth, and force and effectiveness. The third offers methods for putting it into practice. In Lü's account, reform is both a profound social revolution and a deep-level self-reform of the Party. Lü reasons that discipline and conduct serve different functions: discipline restrains, educates and motivates throughout Party governance, while conduct displays the Party's image and sets the tone. Lü argues that, as reform tackles its hardest problems, rectifying conduct helps break 'unwritten rules', correct distorted views of power and achievements, and create a fair environment for market actors, while firmness is also needed on what must not be changed. The methods proposed are four: stress the political nature of the work, keep a strict tone, adopt precise thinking by focusing on key tasks, key people (leading officials) and key measures, and promote coordinated action across Party committees, functional departments and discipline bodies. Lü concludes that officials should act as 'promoters and doers' of reform, balancing personal and collective, local and overall, and short-term and long-term interests. The article calls for combining strict management with care for cadres, handling conduct and corruption problems together, and keeping Party discipline education regular. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school commentary links the Party's disciplinary campaign to the Third Plenum's reform agenda and to Xi Jinping's thought on Party building.

Strengthening the educational ecology of ideological and political education for university students: several reflections 加强大学生思想政治教育育人生态建设的几点思考 Bai Xianliang Peng Jun Bai and Peng ask how Chinese universities can improve the "educational ecology" of ideological and political education for undergraduates. They argue that, despite visible progress since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the work still suffers from fragmented and superficial practices. Their remedy is to build a coherent "ecological forest" and a "scenic landscape" of ideological and political education, one that carries out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The article has three parts. The first sets out why strengthening this ecology is necessary: it serves the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, it is required to build a university system of ideological and political work, and it is needed to raise the effectiveness of education amid a more complex online and ideological environment. The second diagnoses four typical problems. The third proposes four practical strategies. Throughout, the authors draw heavily on Xi Jinping's statements on education and on the 2020 guideline issued by eight central departments on accelerating that system. The core move is the diagnosis, which uses landscape metaphors. The authors describe a "bonsai" type that polishes a few exemplary showpieces while neglecting the ordinary field. A "stage-set" type arranges scenes and performers to hide real problems. A "framing" type changes packaging and angle while the content stays the same, "old wine in new bottles". A "timely" type chases hot topics for attention without explaining their substance. Against these the authors propose four remedies. The first is systems thinking applied to the whole, the elements and the process, led by the university Party committee. The second is a reform of evaluation that takes fostering virtue as the basic standard, adds humanistic care, and combines process and outcome assessment. The third is innovation that follows the laws of the field and adapts to each institution's circumstances. The fourth is long-term mechanisms. The authors conclude that effective ideological and political education cannot be quick or campaign-style. It requires routine practice, durable mechanisms and institutionalisation within university governance, so that it can release what they call the "guiding force" of ideological and political work in building a leading country in education. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education classify formalistic practice and frame the official policy language on this work in Party-line terms.

"New quality productive forces": a signature concept of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics “新质生产力”：中国特色社会主义政治经济学的标识性概念 Liu Mingsong Wang Qian Liu Mingsong and Wang Qian ask what the recently introduced term "new quality productive forces" means and why it can be called a signature concept (biaoshixing gainian) of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Their thesis is that the concept is semantically a specific kind of "productive forces", that it has three signature traits, and that its theory still has to be built up through practice, theoretical innovation and links to other concepts. The article has three parts. The first analyses the concept's meaning from three angles: its prior context, its genus–species relation to "productive forces", and its word structure. The second sets out three signature traits: autonomy of creation, centrality of structural position, and strategic character in use. The third proposes three ways to keep constructing the theoretical system. The text appeared in Socialism Studies (Shehuizhuyi yanjiu), 2024, no. 6. On meaning, the authors argue that the concept grew out of Chinese modernization, which gives it a value presupposition centred on people's development, harmony with nature and high-quality development. As a species of the genus "productive forces", it remains within Marx's framework of labourers, means of labour and objects of labour, but represents a systemic qualitative change in these elements and their combination, not a rupture. They read "new" as both temporal and evaluative, and "quality" as the leap that follows quantitative accumulation. They distinguish a science-and-technology-led aspect ("new modifying quality") from an innovation-driven one ("new promoting quality"). On signature traits, they cite Lenin's point that social relations reduce to production relations and these to the level of productive forces. In their reading, the concept gives the discipline a firmer basis in productive forces and ties together concepts such as the new development philosophy. The authors conclude that, as a new concept, it needs further theoretical development. They call for analysing representative local practices, such as digital and intelligent transformation, and for generalising from them. They also call for letting concept-building and theory-building reinforce each other. They further propose a concept cluster including "future industries" and "disruptive technologies", linked to supply-side structural reform and the modern industrial system, and extended to green transition. Read the original if you want a conceptual-analytic account, in the Chinese academic debate, of how new quality productive forces is positioned within the discipline's concept system.

Historical materialism and the Marxist conception of civilization 唯物史观与马克思主义文明观 Wang Weiguang Wang Weiguang asks what 'civilization' means in Marxism and why the question matters for the 'cultural mission of the new era' put forward by Xi Jinping. The article argues that this mission cannot be properly understood without the standpoint, viewpoint and method of historical materialism and a grasp of the Marxist conception of civilization. Wang notes that the classics never wrote a dedicated work on civilization. The article therefore reconstructs their view from scattered passages and holds that this conception is a component of historical materialism. The article is organised in four parts. The first surveys how Marx, Engels and Lenin use 'civilization' and related phrases ('civilized nations', 'civilized society') for capitalist society. The second turns to their argument that capitalist civilization produces the proletariat and will be replaced by communist civilization. The third examines Engels's periodisation, borrowed in part from Morgan, and his criticism of idealist views of civilization. The fourth distils six main tenets of the Marxist conception of civilization, drawing on texts from the Communist Manifesto to Lenin's late writings, and on Mao Zedong. Wang argues that in the classics 'civilization' usually means bourgeois or capitalist civilization, whose progressive role ('the great civilizing influence of capital') they acknowledge while exposing its basis in class exploitation. Engels, in Wang's reading, divides the 'age of civilization' into 'ancient civilization' (slave and feudal society, and the origins in primitive society) and 'modern civilization' (capitalism), marked by the division of labour, private property, class and the state. From this Wang draws six tenets. These are that productive forces are the fundamental measure of civilization; that a civilization is judged first by its social formation; that civilization is historical, so there is no abstract, 'universal' civilization; that class analysis is required; that each civilization is progressive relative to its predecessor yet is replaced; and that idealist views of civilization must be criticised. Wang concludes that although the classics gave no explicit definition, civilization can be understood as the mark and summary of the state, nature and degree of social progress. The text calls for historical, concrete, dialectical and class analysis of civilization. It treats Samuel Huntington's 'clash of civilizations' as a contemporary variant of the idealist conception, and 'Western-centrism' as a bourgeois idealist view. Read the original if you want a dense, citation-rich reconstruction of the classical Marxist texts on civilization and the theoretical grounding the author offers for current Chinese discussions of civilization.

Lenin's exploration of preventing and curbing bureaucratism and formalism 列宁对防治官僚主义形式主义的探索 Lü Weizhou Liao Bin Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article notes, the Party has made improving its work style a pivot of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, targeting bureaucratism and formalism, which Xi Jinping says "kill". Lü Weizhou and Liao Bin ask what Lenin's thinking and practice on these two ills offer today. They argue that Lenin analysed their manifestations, harms and roots in Soviet state and Party organs, and devised measures whose lessons help the Chinese Communist Party raise its leadership capacity. The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The first part reconstructs Lenin's exposure of bureaucratism and formalism and their dangers. The second part treats their political, economic and cultural roots. The third part sets out Lenin's countermeasures: socialist democracy, a sound socialist legal system, improvement of state organs, and purification of the ranks of Party members and cadres. It draws on Lenin's speeches and writings and on Soviet examples from 1918 to 1922. On manifestations, the authors say Lenin identified three forms of formalism: endless meetings, paper-shuffling, and procrastination. They report that he saw the greatest harms as damage to the Party's image and its ties with the masses, harm to popular interests, delay to socialist construction, and, as the authors put it, ultimately the survival of Party and state; the article attributes the Soviet collapse partly to these ills after Lenin's death. On roots, Lenin is said to have traced them to tsarist autocratic survivals, a fragmented small-producer economy, and low cultural and educational levels, which limited mass participation and supervision. On remedies, the authors describe elections and recall of officials, pay not exceeding a skilled worker's wage, supervisory bodies, prosecution of exemplary cases, slimmed-down institutions, personal responsibility, fewer meetings, strict admission and the 1921 purge, and cadre training, assessment and rewards. The authors conclude that Lenin left valuable experience, that the Party has drawn on and developed it since the 18th Party Congress, and that bureaucratism and formalism are stubborn and recurrent, requiring sustained effort. They call for further study of where they grow in the new era and of ways to curb new and hidden forms, so as to provide institutional safeguards for the Party's leadership of deepening reform and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Lenin's anti-bureaucracy measures are presented in current Chinese Party-building scholarship.

The spread of Marxism and Marxism-Leninism in China before the founding of the Communist Party 中国共产党成立之前马克思主义与马克思列宁主义在中国的传播 Lin Jianhua Lin Jianhua traces how Marxism, and later Marxism-Leninism, reached China before the Communist Party was founded in 1921. Written to mark the centenary of Lenin's death and of the term "Marxism-Leninism" (first used by the Comintern in 1924), the article argues that before the October Revolution Marxism was only sporadically introduced in China. After 1917, it contends, a Russian-mediated Marxism-Leninism was spread widely and deliberately, and this prepared the ground for the Party. The article has three parts. The first surveys the period from the 1870s to the 1910s, when Marxism arrived by two routes: European diplomats, students and missionaries, and Japan, through reformists, revolutionaries (Sun Yat-sen's circle, Zhu Zhixin, Song Jiaoren) and anarchists. The second covers the post-1917 route through Soviet Russia, centred on Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Chen Wangdao's 1920 translation of the Communist Manifesto, Mao Zedong's conversion, and the communist groups formed in 1920–21. The third examines why Marxism-Leninism took root and what was emphasised. Lin's central claim is a "two-way meeting" between Marxism-Leninism and China. In Lin's account, Marxism's mission of human liberation matched modern China's tasks of national independence and liberation. Pre-revolutionary Russia's conditions resembled China's, Soviet Russia pursued an equal policy toward China, and imperialist aggression ended illusions about the West. Lin argues that early Chinese Marxists, driven by the aim of national salvation, selectively stressed historical materialism and class struggle, drawing on the October Revolution's lessons. Lin discusses Lenin's continuation and development of Marx and Engels, and notes that early Party documents wrote in proletarian dictatorship, class struggle and violent revolution. Lin concludes that Marxism is not a dogma but requires concrete analysis of concrete conditions, so Marxism-Leninism in China had to adapt to local conditions while innovating. Lin links this to Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and holds that upholding the last means upholding Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-historiography account of early translations, journals and figures, with many Chinese transliterations of Marx's name.

Engels studies abroad: latest developments and hot issues 国外恩格斯研究：最新进展与热点问题 Weng Qianlin This review surveys recent scholarship on Friedrich Engels outside China. Weng notes that foreign Marxism has long carried an anti-Engels tendency, which blamed him for distorting Marx and for Marxism's crises. Weng argues that since the late twentieth century, foreign scholars have rethought this tradition, producing a revival of Engels studies that takes a 'one source, many streams' form and largely rehabilitates his standing as Marx's lifelong collaborator and co-founder of Marxism. The article has four parts. The first traces the revival, covering new texts from the second Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe (MEGA2), the 'new reading' movement, interdisciplinary methods, key monographs, journals and conferences from 1995 to 2023. The second reviews reassessments of Engels's status. The third maps the multidimensional fields in which his thought is being reactivated. The fourth draws lessons for domestic research. In the central section, Weng reports four lines of defence against older charges. Scholars such as Paul Blackledge and John Bellamy Foster reject the 'Marx–Engels opposition' thesis, including Norman Levine's 'Engelsism' and Kohei Saito's claim of an ecological divergence. Others rebut the portrait of Engels as positivist, mechanist or fatalist, and answer accusations of misreading or falsifying Capital. Here the Sendai group's catalogue of about 5,000 changes to the Capital Volume 2 manuscript is cited, and most changes are judged semantically minor. Weng then shows Engels being applied to digital capitalism, natural science and ecology, pandemics and women's conditions, war and the state, and geography and urbanisation. Weng concludes that foreign work has re-evaluated and defended Engels and confirmed the present-day explanatory power of his thought. For Chinese research, Weng proposes a systematic Engels studies that combines detailed period-specific work with holistic study. It should be problem-oriented, address modernity problems in contemporary development, and join an ideological stance with academic standards. Foreign findings should be analysed and discriminated, not accepted wholesale, as Xi Jinping has urged. Read the original if you want a map of recent foreign Engels scholarship, with its authors, debates and conferences, and a view of how a Chinese scholar assesses it for domestic research.

A century after Lenin's death: new developments in Lenin studies abroad 列宁逝世百年：国外列宁研究新进展 Wang Enming Yang Shouming This review surveys how overseas scholars, left-wing parties and media marked the centenary of Lenin's death on 21 January 2024, and what the wave of commemoration shows about current Lenin studies abroad. Wang and Yang argue that the foreign literature confirms Lenin's standing as a political theorist and fuels calls to 'return to Lenin', but that Chinese readers must assess these views critically and take a firm position. The article first lists the commemorative output: special issues and articles in Monthly Review, Jacobin, Platypus Review and similar outlets; conferences in London, Abuja, Berlin and online; a Cuban television programme; and new editions, biographies and studies. It then groups the scholarship into four themes: the philosophical sources of Lenin's thought, his theory of imperialism, his theory of socialist revolution and construction, and the contemporary meaning of Leninism. A concluding section gives the authors' own evaluation. On philosophy, the review reports Kevin Anderson, Carlos Garrido, Michael Löwy and the Russian researcher Petr Kondrashov on Lenin's reading of Hegel, his Philosophical Notebooks and his development of dialectics. On imperialism, it cites Prakash Karat and Prabhat Patnaik on how Lenin extended Marxism into a theory of world revolution, and Sunanda Sen on contemporary financialised imperialism. On revolution and construction, it covers the worker–peasant alliance, the vanguard party and democratic centralism, national self-determination, socialism in one country, the transition after 1921, and strategic and tactical flexibility. Several authors, including Atilio Boron, Paul Le Blanc and Luca Cangemi, present Leninism as a resource for empowering the people, rebuilding mass socialist movements and linking anti-imperialism to the Global South. In their closing section Wang and Yang draw three lessons. They call for a firm stance against Western scholars and politicians who, in their account, demonise Lenin under the influence of 'de-Sovietisation' and historical nihilism. They distinguish three groups behind the commemorations: Leninist communist parties, Trotskyist organisations, and independent left intellectuals. They also urge a scientific judgement of the many new theories of imperialism, using the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method. Read the original if you want a detailed map of the foreign authors, journals and events that shaped the 2024 Lenin centenary, together with a Chinese academic assessment of them.

The "Global South" and its modernization in the view of foreign left-wing scholars 国外左翼学者视域中的“全球南方”及其现代化问题探析 Zhou Miao Zhou Miao asks how left-wing scholars outside China have explained the emergence of the "Global South" and the obstacles to its modernization. The article argues that these scholars trace the South's backwardness to the capitalist world system rather than to internal traditions. It presents their work as useful for understanding the roots of the North–South gap and for confirming China's place as a member of the Global South. The article opens by noting that many Global South states declined to condemn or sanction Russia after the Ukraine conflict began. The article has three parts. The first traces how the Global South arose with the capitalist world system and compares related labels: "Third World", "developing countries" and "North/South". The second sets out four constraints on Southern modernization identified by Samir Amin, Andre Gunder Frank, Theotonio dos Santos, Immanuel-style dependency writers, Michael Hudson, Stavrianos and others. The third turns to remedies and to the role of socialism, including Chinese modernization. Zhou reports that these scholars reject the term "developing countries" because it implies a linear path and hides the historical cause of underdevelopment. In Frank's and Stavrianos's reading, development and underdevelopment are two sides of one coin, and the "Third World" names a relationship of domination, not a group of states. The four constraints are monetary and financial hegemony (Hudson's account of the dollar-debt cycle), a neo-colonial system, an unequal international division of labour (dos Santos's "industrial-technological dependence"), and dependent accumulation. The remedy these scholars propose is autonomous, self-centred development. Zhou stresses that the "delinking" proposed by Amin and others means reforming unequal relations, not closing off, and notes that Cardoso and others revised dependency theory after the "East Asian miracle". Zhou further argues that, on these scholars' accounts, socialism helped the South by inspiring independence movements, widening international room for manoeuvre and offering an alternative model. The article presents Chinese modernization as extending that alternative, citing loans without political conditions, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. It concludes that drawing on this scholarship can enrich China's proposals on global governance and help unite Southern countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese-published survey of dependency theory, world-systems and anti-imperialist writing on the Global South, or want to see how such work is used to support China's self-positioning.

Deng Xiaoping's summing-up of the historical experience of the international communist movement and its contemporary implications 邓小平对国际共产主义运动的历史经验总结及当代启示 Yuan Xiuli Yuan Xiuli asks what lessons Deng Xiaoping drew from the rise and setbacks of the international communist movement, including the split in the socialist camp, the Soviet collapse and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and what those lessons offer today. The article argues that Deng's assessment, which affirmed the movement's achievements while absorbing its failures, remains of real value for contemporary China and for world socialism. It frames this against Xi Jinping's description of a world undergoing 'changes unseen in a century'. The article is built around five sets of lessons attributed to Deng, drawn from his speeches and talks between 1956 and 1989. These are: holding to scientific socialism; seeking truth from facts; combining self-reliance with opening up; handling relations between socialist states and between parties correctly; and bringing out the superiority of socialism. A final section sets out three present-day implications, each tied to statements by Xi Jinping. Yuan's central claim is that Deng fought on two fronts, opposing both 'Left' errors (trying to enter communism too early) and Rightist tendencies such as wholesale Westernisation and bourgeois liberalisation. On inter-party relations, Yuan reports Deng's principles of equality and independence, his rejection of any 'father party', and his admission that the Chinese Communist Party itself made the error of pointing fingers during the polemics of the 1960s. Deng is also presented as tracing Soviet decline to rigid thinking and closure, so that reform and opening up is read as a decision built on lessons from both Soviet and Chinese experience. On superiority, Yuan cites Deng's position that poverty is not socialism: socialism must develop the productive forces and improve living standards, and Party leadership is itself part of its superiority. Yuan draws three implications. History should be summed up scientifically, with an eye to the future. Whether Party leadership is maintained decides the fate of a communist movement. And the Party should take historical initiative amid the 'changes unseen in a century'. The article concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics, advancing under Xi Jinping, has become the mainstay of world socialism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a source-based account of how Deng's remarks on the communist movement are used in current Party theory and in the framing of China's role in world socialism.

South Asian communist parties' exploration of the socialist road amid changes unseen in a century 百年变局背景下南亚共产党对社会主义道路的探索 Hei Ran Hei Ran asks how communist parties in South Asia have responded to what Chinese official discourse calls the changes unseen in a century, with the East rising and the West declining and the international system in transition. The article argues that these parties hold to Marxism, produce new theoretical positions and seek socialist paths suited to their national conditions. In Hei's view they have made progress but still face serious obstacles. The article surveys parties in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, including several Maoist and Marxist-Leninist groups. It has four parts: new theoretical views, struggle and governing practice, main problems, and prospects. The first part covers the parties' readings of the international situation, their critiques of capitalism and their definitions of socialism. The second covers shifts in strategy, governing experience and inter-party exchanges. Hei reports that the parties see a multipolar world in which capitalism's contradictions sharpen, citing US-led "unipolarity", NATO expansion and a "new Cold War" against China. They trace economic crises, such as Sri Lanka's external debt of US$52 billion, to capitalism and neoliberalism. Their socialist models are labelled "socialism with Indian characteristics", "socialism with Nepali characteristics" and "socialism with modern features". Hei also credits the rise of China and socialism with Chinese characteristics with strengthening confidence in socialism. On governing practice, Hei cites the Left Democratic Front in Kerala, whose leader Pinarayi Vijayan reported falling unemployment, and Prachanda's government in Nepal. The obstacles Hei lists are weak party-building, sectarian divisions, the Hindu-nationalist BJP, religious forces and interference by India and the United States, notably through the Millennium Challenge Compact. Hei concludes that the parties will strengthen party-building, build left unity (the Progressive Left Alliance in Pakistan, the Socialist Front in Nepal), counter right-wing and religious pressure and resist outside interference. The article presents the movement as developing in a winding, long-term and varied way, while world socialism remains at a low ebb overall. Read the original if you want a country-by-country account of South Asian communist parties' positions and strategies, as presented in a Chinese academic journal.

The new "networked" pattern of relations among communist parties abroad in the 21st century 21世纪国外共产党政党关系的“网络化”新态势 Yu Weihai Li Yuwei Yu Weihai and Li Yuwei ask how relations among communist parties outside China have changed since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and argue that the best description is "networking" (wangluohua). In their view, existing Chinese scholarship treats these relations only as a matter of unity versus division. They hold that 21st-century relations are better captured as a network, and they link this to Xi Jinping's call in 2017 for a new type of party relations. The article first reviews domestic literature, then sets out five manifestations of networking: differentiated party types, dense exchanges, varied forms of connection, loose internationalism and routinised disputes. It then identifies four features of the network: parallel yet interwoven paths, unity alongside conflict, a flat and grid-like structure, and internationalism set against sectarianism. It closes with three reflections for the Chinese Communist Party. The authors report, citing incomplete statistics, more than 400 communist parties, which differ in guiding ideology (Marxism-Leninism, Maoism, Hoxhaism, Trotskyism and others). These parties meet through annual international meetings, regional forums, joint statements and online platforms, but have no central leadership, common programme or binding charter. They cite the 2022 international meeting, which produced two conflicting resolutions on Ukraine, and the 2023 dissolution of the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe, as evidence of persistent dispute. The authors argue that the Soviet-centred "centre–periphery" model has given way to a decentred, flat network. In their reading this network reduces the risk of fragmentation but is held back by sectarian parties that claim Marxist orthodoxy and attack others' national explorations. Yu and Li conclude that the international communist movement has not disappeared but has taken a new form, which requires a new discourse and disciplinary system in scientific socialism. They judge networking a sign of immature international unity and consider that only "limited unity" is feasible now. They urge the Chinese Communist Party to adopt an outlook centred on itself, to apply the new type of party relations through channels such as the Dialogue with World Political Parties and the World Socialism Forum, and to promote cohesion among communist parties. Read the original if you study contemporary communist parties, the typology of their ideologies, or how Chinese scholars frame the international communist movement and the Party's role in it.

Offering "Introduction to Marxist Atheism" as a general education course in universities 高校开设《马克思主义无神论概论》通识课程探究 Chen Huiming Chen Huiming asks how Chinese universities can best bring Marxist atheism "into textbooks, into classrooms and into minds". The article argues that the best way is a general education elective, "Introduction to Marxist Atheism", run by each university's School of Marxism. Drawing on the author's own experience of teaching and researching such a course, Chen presents it as an ideological and political theory course first, not merely a specialist course in Marxist theory or religious studies. The article has three parts. The first sets out the course's significance through three teaching goals: consolidating students' Marxist ideals and convictions, fostering a correct view of religion, and forging a sense of community of the Chinese nation. The second compares forms of teaching and explains why an elective suits the current curriculum. The third gives an implementation path covering lecture notes, course content, classroom teaching and quality control. On the goals, Chen holds that the course should show that "ghosts and gods do not exist" and so protect campus ideology from theism. In Chen's account, students should learn three attitudes: not to believe in religion, to respect believers' freedom of belief, and to counter theism with tact. Party members and Communist Youth League members must not be religious. The course should also teach that Chinese history was made by the peoples of China without supernatural agency. On form, Chen finds that "integrated" and "thematic" teaching are only transitional and that specialist courses reach too few students. An elective needs no changes to departmental training plans, and the School of Marxism can supply political oversight and teachers. On implementation, Chen notes that no authoritative textbook exists, since two earlier textbooks from 2000 and 2002 are dated. Universities should therefore compile their own lecture notes, preferably by revising an existing book. Chen proposes a theory module (history of atheism and the basics of Marxist atheism) and a practice module (Communist attitudes and policy toward religion, and practising atheism). Emphasis should vary by region, from border ethnic areas, where religious extremism is the main target, to the south-east coast, where folk belief must be distinguished from feudal superstition. Teachers should also address family religious influence, and supervisors should stop any speech contrary to Marxist ideology. Chen concludes that the elective should run alongside the other two forms of teaching. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese university ideological-education staff propose to institutionalise atheism teaching, including curriculum design and classroom oversight.

Mao Zedong on "genuine internationalism" 毛泽东论“真正的国际主义” Wu Bo Wu Bo asks what Mao Zedong meant by "genuine internationalism" and how it guided the Chinese Communists in linking China's own cause to the liberation of other peoples. Taking up Xi Jinping's description of Mao as a "great internationalist" (made at the symposium marking the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth), the article argues that Mao's statements correctly handled a series of paired relationships: patriotism and internationalism, self-reliance and foreign aid, struggle and its skilful conduct, independent development and mutual learning, national liberation and world progress. The article is organised in five sections, each built around a quotation from Mao.
