It moves through the anti-Japanese war and the founding years of the People's Republic, with material from the 1950s and 1960s. It draws on Mao's talks, speeches and telegrams, and sets them against statements by Marx, Engels and Lenin on proletarian internationalism. Wu's core argument is that, for Mao, patriotism is the foundation of internationalism rather than its rival. Wu cites the 1938 report \"On the New Stage\", in which Mao argued that patriotism is internationalism applied in a war of national liberation, and contrasts this with the mistaken priority given to internationalism by the Party leadership after 1931. Wu then sets out Mao's conditions for international solidarity: self-reliance as the main basis with foreign aid as a supplement, equality among nations and opposition to great-power chauvinism, and the united front as the practical form of cooperation. The article presents the \"intermediate zones\" and the \"three worlds\" as extensions of this approach. Wu also stresses humility in learning from other countries and peoples, and Mao's call for aid to anti-colonial struggles and to newly independent states without political conditions. The examples cited include the Korean War, support for Vietnam, Algeria and Cuba, and assistance to Asia, Africa and Latin America. Wu concludes that Mao's thought offers guidance for taking a world perspective, bearing the responsibilities of a large Party and country, and offering new opportunities to the world through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of Mao's internationalism as the Party's historians present it today, with many dated quotations from his speeches.

Overseas research on the Communist Party of China's anti-corruption campaign in the new era: an analysis 新时代中国共产党反腐败问题海外研究论析 Liu Yangke Gao Xiaolin This literature review surveys how scholars outside China have studied the Communist Party of China's anti-corruption campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu and Gao argue that overseas scholarship has increasingly taken the campaign seriously and in places revised older explanatory paradigms. They also contend that some of this work remains marked by biases that Chinese researchers should answer, while its sound points deserve critical absorption. The review first sets out overseas views that the campaign opened a new stage of corruption governance, citing its resilience, institutionalisation and shift from campaign-style control to routine prevention. It then organises the literature by perspective: motives, effects (political, economic, international), institutional reforms (discipline inspection, the supervision system, inspection tours) and policy proposals. Authors discussed include Andrew Wedeman, Melanie Manion, Andrew Walder, Kerry Brown, Yuen Yuen Ang and Jamie P. Horsley. On motives, Liu and Gao report a "multi-layered dynamic system": removing the threat corruption poses to Party rule, reshaping political culture and morality, and breaking vested interests that block reform. On effects, the review finds that most studies see gains in public trust, though some judge the effect limited. Other studies report officials' passivity and a weakened pipeline of young talent. Firm-level evidence is mixed, and some sectors, such as luxury goods and hospitality, were hit. Overseas scholars also suggest more legalisation, wider social participation, and moral and cultural cultivation. The authors then criticise four tendencies: a functionalist reading that overlooks the principle of "putting the people first"; Western-centrism that takes Western experience as the benchmark; a theory-driven approach that produces a "China paradox"; and weaknesses in sources and methods, including reliance on secondary materials and fragmentary case data. Liu and Gao conclude that overseas research offers a useful international perspective for developing a distinctively Chinese path against corruption and for shaping China's clean image abroad. They call for a problem-consciousness rooted in practice rather than imported frameworks. Read the original if you want a structured map of English-language and other foreign scholarship on the campaign, together with a Chinese academic response to it.

Layers and truth-seeking: an examination of how Mao Zedong's status at the Zunyi Conference has been written in history 层累与求真：关于遵义会议毛泽东地位历史书写的考察 You Haihua Tu Guodong Did the Zunyi Conference of 1935 establish Mao Zedong's leadership of the Party and the Red Army? The authors treat this as the most contested question about the conference. They take it up from the angle of academic history and social-cultural history, tracing how mainland official and scholarly accounts have described Mao's status since 1949. They argue that official wording was built up in layers and was in turn shaped by scholars' truth-seeking research, and that the two have usefully influenced each other. The article has two main parts. The first follows the official narrative through the Party's three historical resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021), speeches by Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, and Party-history works from Liao Gailong and Hu Qiaomu in the 1950s to the 2021 Short History of the Communist Party of China. The second follows scholarship: textbooks by Hu Hua, He Ganzhi and Li Xin up to 1978, then the mainstream and dissenting views after reform and opening up. On the official side, the authors identify a steady accumulation of formulations. "Established" replaces the 1945 "began". The leadership's scope is specified as the Party and the Red Army. Deng Xiaoping's 1965 concept of a "core" is added, then Mao's correct line, and finally, under Hu and Xi, the qualifier "Marxist". The 2021 resolution largely reproduces Xi's 2016 wording and restores the phrase "in fact", which Deng had had cut from a draft of the 1981 resolution. The authors read this as a response to scholarly debate. On the scholarly side, most writers followed the official line. Since the 1980s, seven dissenting positions have appeared, including that Mao was one member of a collective led by Zhang Wentian, and that his position was secured only after the Goubadi meeting, in August or November 1935, in 1943 or at the Seventh Congress (1945). The authors say these supplement the traditional view rather than reject it. The authors conclude that official narrative has strongly standardised scholarship without replacing it, and that absorbing research findings has made the 2021 formulation more precise. They reject the idea that Party-history research should never go beyond the resolutions. They call on officials to separate research from propaganda and to uphold the principle of "no forbidden zones in academic research". They also ask Party-history scholars for self-discipline: original work, no duplicate publication, and no adulatory language. Read the original if you study the historiography of the Zunyi Conference or want a detailed comparison of official wordings on Mao's status over seven decades.

Value, fundamental guidelines and implementation paths for religion-related courses in universities from the perspective of ideological and political education in courses 课程思政视域下高校涉宗教类课程的价值内涵、根本遵循与实现路径 Xu Xiao Many humanities and social science subjects touch on religion, so universities teach what Xu Xiao calls "religion-related courses". The article asks whether such courses should and can be taught, what they should teach and how. Xu argues that they are scientific, necessary and reasonable, and that they can serve ideological and political education in courses (kèchéng sīzhèng) as well as atheist education. Xu also holds that this requires a Marxist view of religion as their guide. Xu first traces the courses' history since reform and opening up, which the article describes as swinging between "big release and big tightening". Expansion came with a "religious culture fever", and cuts came with concern over foreign religious infiltration and campus proselytising. The article then sets out four task objectives, the stance, method and principles of teaching, and concrete paths for each task. It ends by assigning duties to universities, teachers and students. Xu names four tasks: preserving the completeness of disciplinary knowledge (the disciplinary task), strengthening Marxist atheist education (the ideological-political task), resisting infiltration and campus proselytising (the security task), and passing on traditional culture (the cultural task). In the article's account, banning such courses outright would give up discursive power over religion and leave students to learn about it from believers. Teaching must adopt a dialectical and historical materialist stance, "explain religion through history" and not the reverse, keep classroom teaching distinct from preaching, and uphold the legal principle of separating education from religion. For traditional culture, Xu proposes teaching Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism by "de-sanctifying" figures, "de-scripturalising" texts and "de-sectarianising" schools. Xu also proposes opening some course content to campus security and United Front offices. Xu concludes that religion-related courses both transmit knowledge and help students form a scientific worldview. Xu calls for building the Marxist view of religion, Party religious policy and state law into them, so that ideological and political education in courses is actually put into practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese religious studies scholar links teaching about religion to atheist education, campus security and the handling of Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist heritage.

A political-economy critique of contemporary Western theories of cognitive-capitalist exploitation 当代西方认知资本主义剥削理论的政治经济学批判 Sun Liang Sun Liang takes up Western theories of "cognitive capitalism", which hold that knowledge, information, emotion and creativity now drive capital accumulation. The article asks what these theories identify as the objects and mechanisms of exploitation, and what they miss. Sun argues that they describe new forms of exploitation well but remain at the level of subjective experience. In Sun's reading, they do not question the capitalist mode of production that makes cognition available to capital, so resistance is reduced to individual self-liberation. The article distinguishes three strands of theory. The first is French (Yann Moulier Boutang, Carlo Vercellone), the second Italian autonomist (Andrea Fumagalli, Hardt and Negri), and the third associated with Franco Berardi and Maurizio Lazzarato, on AI and the brain. Section one treats the objects of exploitation: general intellect, life itself (the "social factory") and the brain and nervous system. Section two treats three forms of power: "technological feudalisation" and rent extraction, psychopolitics, and machinic enslavement. Section three offers a critique drawing on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital, followed by a short conclusion. Sun makes two central moves. First, cognitive exploitation falls within the category Marx criticised. Intellect, life and nerve activity become means of production only inside capitalist relations, under wage labour and the separation of producers from the means of production. For Sun, Marx's remark that capital does not create science but appropriates it shows that knowledge is not productive in itself. Cognitive workers are integrated into collective production and lose their products to capital. Sun reads the theorists as treating cognition directly as a factor of production, and holds that cognitive capitalism changes the form of capitalist relations but not their content. Second, Sun places cognitive capitalism within global capitalism and what the article calls new imperialism. In Sun's account, high-value cognitive work in developed countries depends on low-end labour elsewhere, on control of global value chains, intellectual property and data. Platforms also spread consumerist and individualist values. The conclusion calls for a return to Marx's critique of political economy. Sun says such an analysis helps in grasping new quality productive forces, in guarding against capital's absorption of cognitive labour, and in balancing technological development with social fairness while pursuing independent innovation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of autonomist and post-operaist theories of cognitive, digital and platform capitalism, grounded in Marx's texts.

Letting the building of a strong S&T nation lead the integrated development of education, science and technology, and talent 以科技强国建设牵引教育科技人才一体化发展 Shao Xueqing Lu Yangxu This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025 under the heading of studying the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), asks how education, science and technology, and talent can be developed as one system. Shao and Lu argue that the building of a strong nation in science and technology should be the leading force that pulls the other two together. The piece has three parts. It first explains why Chinese modernization depends on the modernization of science and technology. It then discusses the leading role of technological innovation among the three systems. Finally it sets out reform measures in evaluation, training, the innovation environment and enterprises. The authors place the argument in a period of intensifying great-power rivalry and a new round of technological revolution, in which, they say, only high-level scientific and technological self-reliance lets China stand firm. They describe education and talent cultivation as "slow variables" with many goals and complex evaluation, and technological innovation as a "fast variable" with a narrower focus. In their account, major national S&T tasks should gather and train talent, and real scientific results should test how well education and talent work succeeds. Innovation-driven reform of institutions would then pull education and talent systems along. Shao and Lu call for reform of how researchers and institutions are evaluated, including continued efforts to break the "four onlys", and for stronger self-reliant training of innovative talent, with emphasis on young people. They also propose a better environment for innovation, easier talent movement between universities, institutes and firms, and a leading role for enterprises backed by venture capital. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy logic linking science, education and talent reform in 2025.

Reconsidering some basic questions in the Marxist theory of productive forces Reflections based on labour subjectivity 马克思主义生产力理论若干基本问题再认识 Zhang Yu Zhang Yu takes up a set of long-debated basic questions in the Marxist theory of productive forces, prompted by the current technological revolution and the rise of new quality productive forces. The article argues that the essence of this theory lies in labour and its subjectivity: productive forces must be understood from the standpoint of the active human subject, not as a collection of things, as bourgeois political economy treated them. The article is organised in eight parts, each a question. It covers the core place of labour; the elements of productive forces, including the two-, three- and multi-element debates; whether their social character belongs to productive forces or to relations of production; the primacy of productive forces against the active role of relations of production; the productive-forces criterion and the value criterion; the ultimate driving force of productive-force development; how to measure productive-force levels; and the qualitative forms of productive forces. Zhang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Chinese and foreign scholars such as Wu Yifeng, Wei Xinghua and G. A. Cohen. Zhang makes three main moves. First, the social side of productive forces, meaning division of labour, cooperation and the organisation of production, is distinguished from relations of production and treated as the mediating link in a chain running from productive forces to mode of production to relations of production. Second, Zhang holds that productive forces take primacy because they supply the standard by which relations of production count as progressive, while relations of production can act decisively back and may even precede new productive forces historically. The productive-forces criterion is fundamental but not the only one, and it is joined to a value criterion through the purposefulness of labour. Third, Zhang rejects Cohen's individualist model and the Western premise of scarcity. In Zhang's reading, the saving of labour time is Marx's primary economic law and the source of productive-force growth, taking the form of the law of value, the law of surplus value and the basic economic law of socialism. On the current period, Zhang argues that productive forces are undergoing a third revolutionary leap, after agriculture and industry, centred on informatisation, digitalisation and intelligent production. New quality productive forces are in essence intelligent productive forces, and the matching relations of production are socialism's basic economic system and a high-standard socialist market economy. Zhang sees digital capitalism as sharpening capitalist contradictions while enlarging the material basis for human freedom, and expresses confidence in the Party-led achievement of high-quality development. Read the original if you want a systematic, theory-driven account of how Chinese Marxist economists are rethinking productive forces, relations of production and new quality productive forces.

Theoretical foundations and construction logic of a high-standard socialist market economy 高水平社会主义市场经济体制的理论基础和构建逻辑 Zhang Xu Zhang Xu asks what theoretical basis should guide the building of a "high-standard socialist market economy", a goal set out in the 2020 Party and State Council opinions and in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that the core issue is the relationship between government and market, and that existing research on it leans largely on Western political theory and Western economics while neglecting Marx. Zhang contends that the theoretical foundation must rest on Marx's understanding of this relationship, absorb useful elements of modern Western economics, and be tied to the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Marx's views on civil society, the state and its economic functions, drawing on Marx's early critique of Hegel, the Grundrisse, Capital and Engels's Anti-Dühring. It then extracts the basic logic of those views and turns to the Chinese Party's evolving understanding of government and market since reform and opening up. It closes by placing the high-standard market economy within the Party's overall logic of comprehensively deepening reform, running through congress and plenum documents from 1978 to 2024. In Zhang's reading, Marx had no standalone theory of government and market, but his analysis of the state as the form in which the bourgeoisie secures its property and interests contains one. Zhang points to the state's role in creating the conditions for capital, such as the coercive legislation accompanying primitive accumulation, and to the dual character of government functions: directing labour required by large-scale socialised production, and supervisory labour arising from the opposition between producers and owners. From this Zhang draws four principles: government functions rest on civil society, the relationship develops as a natural historical process, restraining government power matters as much as restraining market power, and state power must be used properly, which makes ongoing reform necessary. Zhang traces the Party's shift from the market playing a "basic" role in resource allocation to the "decisive" role announced at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), alongside "better" government. The author presents this as a major theoretical innovation and the foundation for the high-standard market economy, which is described as an enhanced and innovative version of the existing system and an important safeguard for Chinese modernization. Zhang calls for combining Marx's views on government, market and economic systems with deepened reform, so as to open new horizons for Marxist political economy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar grounds current market-economy policy in Marx's writings on the state and traces the Party's documentary lineage on government and market.

Western perceptions of new quality productive forces: main views and an assessment 西方关于新质生产力的主要认知与评析 Zhang Lisi Since Xi Jinping put forward the concept of new quality productive forces, Western media, think tanks, politicians and scholars have followed it closely. Zhang Lisi asks how the West understands the concept and why. The article argues that most Western commentary is positive or relatively objective, while a minority of views misread it out of anxiety and strategic interest. Zhang presents the survey as a way to understand the shape of Western opinion contests and to improve China's external communication. The article has four parts. It first sorts Western definitions of the concept under four headings: development strategy, development philosophy, form of productive forces, and essential character. It then reviews Western explanations of why the concept emerged, and Western judgements of its significance, including some cautions. The longest section assesses these views, covering the reasons for Western attention, four general features and four features of what Zhang calls distorted readings. Sources include the BBC, Reuters, The Economist, the Wall Street Journal, Deutsche Welle, US ambassador Nicholas Burns and academics such as Robert Kuhn and Barry Naughton. Zhang reports that many Western commentators link the concept to high-quality development, to a new stage of productive forces and to the new development philosophy. Some call it a Chinese-context development of Marxist productive-forces theory. Zhang identifies two reasons for Western attention: China's achievements in frontier fields, and anxiety in some Western states that China's rise in new energy vehicles, chips and photovoltaics will erode their technological dominance. On this reading, the unfavourable views share four traits: theoretical traps such as the 'overcapacity' thesis, tying the concept to national security, ideological labelling, and zero-sum thinking. Zhang rejects the overcapacity thesis as a false proposition and as a pretext for protectionism. Zhang concludes that Western interpretations are broadly positive and growing, and that US allies are diverging from Washington. The author calls for objective, historical and comprehensive study of Western views and for stronger external publicity on high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Zhang also advises a calm search for the roots of misreadings, firm rebuttal of what the article calls smears, and the pursuit of shared interests to build a favourable international environment. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of how Western media and experts have framed new quality productive forces, and how Chinese analysts interpret those framings.

Cultivating and expanding patient capital to empower the development of new quality productive forces 以培育壮大耐心资本赋能新质生产力发展 Zhang Yang Zhang Yang takes up a policy question raised by recent Party documents: how to build up "patient capital" (naixin ziben) so that it supports new quality productive forces. The article starts from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, both of which call for developing patient capital. Zhang's thesis is that patient capital suits the long, risky and costly path of new quality productive forces, and that the state should deliberately foster it through policy, institutions and financial innovation. The commentary has three parts. The first defines patient capital. The second explains why new quality productive forces need it. The third sets out measures to cultivate and expand it. Zhang draws throughout on the Plenum's decision and on statements by Xi Jinping, and the piece reads as a Party-theory explainer rather than an empirical study. In the definition, Zhang names three features. Patient capital is long-term, since it values long-run returns over short-term ones. It is value investing, focused on a firm's intrinsic value, business model and technology path rather than price swings. It is risk-tolerant, able to accept long periods without returns, or even losses, and to invest counter-cyclically. Zhang argues that new quality productive forces need such capital for three tasks: breaking through key core technologies and achieving high-level scientific and technological self-reliance; deeply upgrading industry and building a modern industrial system, including digital and intelligent transformation of traditional industries; and speeding the allocation of advanced production factors so as to raise total factor productivity. On measures, Zhang calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership and combining an efficient market with a capable government. Specific proposals are a package of policies, closer fiscal–financial coordination, government guidance funds and credit risk-sharing for tech firms. Zhang also wants a long-term capital ecosystem, with household savings channelled through enterprise and occupational annuities and easier exit routes for venture funds. Finally, the author proposes innovative products and relay-style financing across a firm's life cycle: angel investment at the incubation stage, convertible bonds and intellectual-property pledges during industrial transition, and smooth exit and reinvestment at maturity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary links patient capital, venture finance and new quality productive forces in policy terms.

Bringing the roles of government and market into play to promote new quality productive forces 发挥政府和市场作用促进新质生产力发展 Yin Qingshuang Xiao Lei Yin Qingshuang and Xiao Lei ask how the relationship between government and market should be arranged so that new quality productive forces can develop. They argue that the blockages in developing them are closely tied to how well government and market are coordinated in technological innovation, factor allocation and industrial upgrading. Their answer is a division of labour in which the 'visible hand' and the 'invisible hand' work together, differently at each stage of the process. The article builds on Xi Jinping's statement that new quality productive forces arise from revolutionary technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors and deep industrial transformation. It first sets out this three-stage 'generative logic', drawing on Marx, Schumpeter and the history of industrial revolutions. It then analyses government and market roles stage by stage, citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Next it diagnoses current obstacles under five headings of 'innovation': science and technology, industry, development mode, institutions and talent. It ends with six practical priorities. The core move is stage-specific allocation. In basic research, disruptive technologies and 'chokepoint' technologies, the authors hold that markets under-invest, so government should lead through planning, funding, institutions and public infrastructure, using the new whole-nation system. In crossing the 'valley of death' from laboratory to commercial use, the authors hold that the market is decisive, with entrepreneurs, enterprises and patient capital in the lead. In industrial transformation, markets drive the replacement of old industries by new ones, while government manages the social costs of 'creative destruction' and adjusts production relations. Citing Marx on science, technology and industrial change, the authors present this as theoretical grounding. They cite patent-commercialisation rates of 36.7% and 39.6% for valid invention patents (2022 and 2023) as evidence of weak conversion outside enterprises, and cite the Silicon Valley model as an example of state–market complementarity. The authors conclude that government should provide forward-looking guidance, correct market failures and supply institutions. Enterprises should lead innovation, regions should be coordinated according to local conditions, and a unified national market should be built. They also call for policy coordination, an upgraded innovation ecosystem and an orderly exit for declining industries. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-economics account of how the state–market division of labour is applied to innovation policy, with extensive reference to the Third Plenum's measures.

New forms of capital in the digital society and their distributional characteristics 数字社会的新型资本及其分配特征 Zhao Yizhang Zhao Yizhang asks how the digital transformation is creating new kinds of capital and how their distribution reshapes social stratification. The article argues that three new capital types (data capital, digital skill capital and attention capital) are distributed in different ways, and that these differences produce new advantaged and disadvantaged groups. It is written in the context of the 2023 plan for building a Digital China and the goal of common prosperity. The article starts from the sociological framework of David Grusky and Katherine Weisshaar, who identify eight types of key social resource or capital. It then explains why digitalisation of information and the emergence of a virtual space make new capital forms possible. It sets out how each of the three is acquired, analyses each along three dimensions (inequality, rigidity and crystallisation), identifies the resulting social groups, and closes with policy proposals. Zhao holds that each capital follows a distinct acquisition path: data capital through paid and unpaid digital labour gathered by firms, digital skill capital mainly through formal education and training, and attention capital through individual content creation. Data capital scores high on inequality, rigidity and crystallisation. Zhao attributes this to network effects, platform monopoly and ready convertibility into economic and even political capital. Skill and attention capital are also unequally distributed but are less rigid and less crystallised, because technology turns over quickly, attention shifts easily and algorithms are opaque. On this basis, platform owners and top executives, highly skilled specialists and influential content creators emerge as new advantaged groups. People who are disadvantaged in the traditional hierarchy and also lack digital skills or attention face a double disadvantage. Zhao proposes three measures for an inclusive digital society: redistributing the wealth created by data capital, since it rests on the digital labour of many parties; providing multi-channel digital skill training, including in basic education; and building a social security system that covers flexible workers, with adjustable contributions. Zhao presents skill and attention capital as new channels of upward mobility, while calling for attention to the doubly disadvantaged. Read the original if you want a sociological, empirically illustrated account of data, skills and attention as capital in China's digital economy, together with the policy proposals that follow from it.

A contemporary interpretation of the identity of Marx's primitive accumulation of capital and capital accumulation 马克思的资本原始积累与资本积累同一性的当代阐释 Tai Lihua Zhang Ruiqi Does primitive accumulation belong to the finished prehistory of capitalism, or does it continue? Tai Lihua and Zhang Ruiqi side with the 'continuity' position and argue that, for Marx, primitive accumulation and capital accumulation are essentially identical. They hold that primitive accumulation runs through the emergence, development and demise of the capitalist mode of production, and that this has present-day relevance. The article opens with the foreign debate. The 'termination' view (Robert Brenner, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Massimo De Angelis, Paul Zarembka) treats primitive accumulation as a completed precondition. The 'continuity' view is associated with David Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession', which the authors criticise as reformist and as focused on distribution. They then take three steps. The first is a theoretical critique of Adam Smith's 'previous accumulation'. The second is an analysis of the shared task of the two forms of accumulation. The third is a look at the historical trend, using contemporary capitalism as illustration. The authors make three main moves. First, they argue that Marx's term 'so-called primitive accumulation' answers Smith's idyllic story of thrift and diligence by stressing violence, the social history of wage labour, and capital as a social relation rather than a thing. Second, they argue that the shared aim of both forms is to separate labourers from the means of production. Primitive accumulation does this through direct and indirect violence, such as enclosures and the Corn Laws. Capital accumulation entrenches the separation through the relative surplus population. The authors argue that digital technology, platform work, migration and what they call 'war capitalism' reinforce this today. Third, they argue that conflicts between labour and capital, among capitals (monopoly tech firms, CDO and CDS speculation, the 2008 crisis) and between states sharpen the contradiction between socialised production and private ownership. They cite protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests as signs of growing class consciousness. The authors conclude that primitive accumulation is not a closed chapter. They hold that the contradictions it generates make replacement of capitalist private ownership by socialist public ownership both theoretically necessary and practically feasible. They draw three implications for China's basic socialist economic system. The first is to uphold the dominant position of public ownership unwaveringly. The second is to protect the leading role of the state-owned economy. The third is to keep the system coherent, with a role for the non-public economy, in order to support high-quality development. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of primitive accumulation, on the debate with Harvey and the 'termination' school, or on how Chinese Marxists link Capital to digital capitalism and China's economic system.

The evolution of modern Western idealist views of history and the methodological revolution of historical materialism 近代西方唯心史观的演进逻辑与历史唯物主义方法论变革 Li Chengwang Li Chengwang asks how Marx and Engels moved beyond the tradition of modern Western idealism to answer what the article calls the history–freedom riddle: how human history can realise the free and all-round development of each person. The article argues that this became possible only when they exposed the real, material source of the premises of idealist thinking, and so founded a new method for understanding history in productive labour. The article is built in three parts. The first traces the path of Western idealist views of history from Greek philosophy and Christianity through Vico, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant to Hegel, and sets out the contradictions in Hegel's philosophy of history. The second examines how the Young Hegelians, namely Bauer, Feuerbach and Stirner, tried to answer the riddle through a philosophy of self-consciousness. The third presents the methodological revolution of historical materialism, as developed mainly in The German Ideology. Li says earlier scholarship has paid less attention to the intellectual genealogy that explains why German idealism dissolved and why the Young Hegelians fell back into idealism. Li contends that Hegel treats history as the development of spirit, so that finite human beings become a stage in an infinite spirit's movement. In this reading, universality and necessity dominate particularity and individual freedom. The Young Hegelians, in Li's account, replace Hegel's absolute spirit with self-consciousness (Bauer), sensuous human essence and love (Feuerbach) or the egoistic 'unique one' (Stirner). They stay on speculative ground and oppose phrases with phrases. Marx and Engels respond in four steps. They start from the 'pure empirical' premise of the production of material life. They develop a theory of comprehensive production, comprising means of subsistence, new needs, human reproduction, social relations and mental production. They hold that individual freedom depends on social relations and can be fully realised only in a real community that abolishes capitalist private ownership. They identify the proletariat as the historical subject of that transformation. Li concludes that Marx and Engels replaced the substance-thinking and conceptual dialectic of idealism with a dialectic of concrete production, so that history appears as the history of material production. This, the article says, brought the materialist principle fully into the study of historical laws and made the philosophy 'realistic'. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the Chinese journal Studies on Marxism frames the move from Hegel and the Young Hegelians to historical materialism.

Re-examining the relationship between "alienated labour" and "private property" in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》中“异化劳动”与“私有财产”关系的再审视 Wang Yue Wang Yue takes up a long-running dispute over the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844: whether Marx argues in a circle when he relates alienated labour to private property, running from private property to alienated labour and back to private property. The article argues that the charge of "circular reasoning" rests on a prior claim that Marx's thought broke decisively after the Manuscripts, and that this claim does not hold. Read in the light of the continuity of Marx's development, Wang contends, the relation between the two concepts can be answered scientifically and the Manuscripts' significance reassessed. The article first sets out the debate. Those who see circularity attribute it to Marx's thin knowledge of political economy, to defects in alienation theory, or to a humanist presupposition about the human species-essence. Those who deny it work mostly within the text and rarely address the underlying assumption of a rupture, so the two sides talk past each other. Wang then examines three propositions behind the rupture thesis: the Manuscripts' method, their concept of the human being, and the nature of alienated labour. A final section places the Manuscripts between Marx's earlier work (the Rheinische Zeitung period, the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question) and his later work. Wang's central argument is that the Manuscripts apply, in an early form, the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete that Marx later formulated in the 1857–58 manuscripts. In this reading, "alienated labour → private property" describes the internal structure of modern capitalist society at the level of essence, whereas private property appears as the cause only at the level of appearance. The order of economic categories within capitalism is therefore not their historical order. Wang adds that Marx's "human being" is a real, sensuous, social being, different from Hegel's and Feuerbach's, and that alienated labour is a description of existing economic facts, not a moral postulate. The logical chain is thus resolved by distinguishing private property as the real starting point from the human being engaged in alienated labour as the theoretical starting point. Wang concludes that the Manuscripts supply the premise of historical materialism, a first attempt at the laws of capitalist society that leads toward Marxist political economy, and the first systematic statement of Marx's views on communism, containing seeds of scientific socialism. Wang traces this line through the Comments on James Mill, The Holy Family, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Read the original if you work on the young Marx, on the "rupture" versus continuity debate, or on Chinese scholarship on the Manuscripts, and want a detailed textual argument against the circular-reasoning charge.

Two critiques of Proudhon and the formation of Marx's labour theory of value 对蒲鲁东的两次批判与马克思劳动价值论的形成 Chen Zheng Studies of how Marx's scientific theory of value took shape have concentrated on classical political economy. Chen Zheng argues that a Proudhon factor has been neglected. The article holds that Marx's two critiques of Proudhon's view of money, in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) and in the 'Reflection' of 1851, played distinct and important roles in building Marx's labour theory of value. The article covers the late 1840s and early 1850s. It begins with Proudhon's 'constituted value' and his labour-money scheme, and with his People's Bank of 1849. It then examines the first critique in The Poverty of Philosophy and the second in the 'Reflection', written in March 1851 and included in the London Notebooks of Marx's third period of economic study. A short conclusion draws out four points. Chen argues that the first critique pushed Marx to adopt Ricardo's position openly. Proudhon's attempt to equate labour time with the 'value of labour' exposed Smith's confusion of two measures of value. Marx therefore came to see Ricardo's theory as a scientific account of bourgeois society and as the critical starting point for his own theory. Chen adds that Marx still took over Ricardo's quantity theory of money to refute Proudhon, so this critique remained flawed. In the second critique, drawing on the Currency School–Banking School dispute, Marx broke with that quantity theory. He located the root of crises in the whole system of production resting on capital, not in the monetary system. Proudhon and the bourgeois economists, in Marx's words, wanted to keep money without its properties. Chen reads this as a shift of perspective from exchange and circulation to relations of production. Chen concludes that Marx's struggle with Proudhon's view of money laid the methodological basis for his theory of value. It later underpinned his analysis of capitalist production and exploitation, and served as a bridge to his mature historical materialism and political economy. Chen also calls for the theory to confront the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to the labour theory of value, on the basis of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual history of Marx's economics, his relation to Ricardo and the London Notebooks, or the Proudhon–Marx dispute over money.

The inner mechanism by which the guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China leads self-reform and social revolution 中国共产党指导思想引领自我革命和社会革命的内在机理 Zhang Guoyu Zhang Guoyu asks how the guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China generates lasting attraction and leadership over Party members, cadres and the people. Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) claim that Marxism, adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, explains the Party's success, the author argues that existing studies concentrate on the objects and methods of ideological leadership. Zhang instead looks at how the ideology produces influence from within. The thesis is that three core elements of Marxism account for this force, both in the Party's self-reform and in leading social revolution. The article has five parts. It first identifies the three cores of the Party's guiding ideology: the inevitability of communism and the mission of each person's free and all-round development, a political standpoint of serving the great majority, and a scientific worldview and methodology. It then traces how Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era have each kept and renewed these cores. Two parts then explain the mechanism for self-reform and for social revolution, and a short conclusion follows. Zhang's central move is to treat the Party as an organisation answering three questions: why it exists, what it ultimately aims at, and how it builds its capacity. These correspond to relations of space (organisation and society), time (short-term tasks and long-term mission) and self (intention and ability). In the author's account, the Party's founding idea, its communist mission and its scientific methodology answer these questions and so drive the Party's self-reform. Because the Party claims no interests apart from the people's, Zhang argues, it can correct errors and win voluntary support. Zhang adds that the three cores operate along relational, task and pathway dimensions, none of which can be dropped. The author contrasts this with firms, governments and bourgeois parties, which the article says rest on contract, coercion or the exchange of votes for benefits. Zhang describes a reversed leadership relation in which the Party serves the people while raising their consciousness. Zhang concludes that the Party must keep building itself ideologically and theoretically, and must use self-reform to drive social revolution and move towards the 'final goal' of communism. Solving the problems unique to a large party, the author says, requires clear and firm adherence to its guiding ideology. The article gives a normative, organisation-theory account of Party ideology as an internal source of authority. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar frames ideological leadership as a link between Party-building and mass leadership, or if you study official Chinese theorising on the Party's guiding ideology.

The implications for values education of consolidating cultural subjectivity 巩固文化主体性的价值观教育意蕴 Li Yifei Li Yifei takes up a question raised by Xi Jinping's remark that any culture needs its own subjectivity to have leading, cohesive, shaping and radiating power. The article asks what mission values education carries in consolidating cultural subjectivity, and how it should carry it out. Li argues that, because core values form the hard core of any culture, values education is a central means of strengthening a distinctive, self-determining cultural self in China. The article has three parts. The first defines culture and cultural subjectivity, drawing on anthropology, psychology (William James, Carl Rogers), Marx and Fei Xiaotong. The second sets out three demands that consolidating cultural subjectivity places on values education. The third proposes three practical paths: the Two Integrations, theoretical innovation under a grand view of history and a new view of civilization, and the cultivation of a public character open to exchange. Li divides culture into a hard core (core values), a middle layer (emotions, language, institutions, specific cultural forms) and an outer ring (visible forms, emerging cultures and subcultures). Cultural subjectivity is then read in three dimensions: as identity (knowing who 'we' are), as social (confirmed through exchange with others) and as value-based (independent value judgement and choice). From these follow three tasks. Values education should build value confidence and promote the wide practice of socialist core values. It should strengthen emotional identification and love of Chinese civilization. It should also convey public spirit and the common values of all humanity, while keeping a constructive-yet-critical stance towards foreign and emerging cultures. For the three paths, Li calls on values education to explain the significance of the Two Integrations, which the article says created a new cultural form and resolved the long-running dispute over 'ancient and modern, Chinese and Western'. Li also wants it to build its own knowledge and discourse system from traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture, and to cultivate openness and a public character. The article ties these tasks to upholding the Party's cultural leadership and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese ideological-education scholar links a layered theory of culture to concrete tasks for values education.

On the "grand ecology" outlook of new quality productive forces 论新质生产力的大生态观 Lang Huihui Since September 2023, Xi Jinping has repeatedly stated that new quality productive forces are themselves green productive forces. Lang Huihui takes up this claim and argues that existing scholarship has studied the ecological elements and structure of such forces but has neglected their external environment. The article proposes a "grand ecology outlook" (da shengtai guan), which it presents not as a narrow method of environmental protection but as a world-view and methodology that unites natural and social ecology. The article follows a line from theoretical genesis to basic content to practical path. It first traces four sources of the outlook: Marx's ecological thought on productive forces, the Communist Party's historical exploration of ecological productive forces, the practical demands of the green and low-carbon transition, and systems thinking. It then sets out three sub-systems and closes with five practical measures and a short conclusion. Lang's central move is to treat new quality productive forces as a complex system of three interacting sub-systems. The internal element system comprises ecologically aware workers, digital and green means of labour, and new objects of labour. The structural-carrier system covers the greening of the industrial structure chain, the industrial chain and the supporting chain. The external environment system covers policy and institutions, rule of law and ethics, the technological innovation ecosystem, and openness. Drawing on Marx's metabolism between humans and nature and on systems theory, Lang argues that these sub-systems must exchange information, energy and elements for the system to leap forward in ecological terms. For practice, Lang identifies weak coordination among sub-systems and insufficient internal development. The article proposes five measures: coordinated action by government, enterprises and universities; stronger green technological innovation; integration of industrial clusters with green development; improved ecological standards and feedback; and a better external environment through top-level design and platforms. Lang concludes that the outlook develops Marxist theory of productive forces and offers a model for other countries facing the supposed trade-off between growth and ecology. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese scholars link Xi Jinping's "green productive forces" thesis to Marx's ecological thought and to systems theory.

Striving to be the vanguard in innovating the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project 勇当创新马克思主义理论研究和建设工程的排头兵 Huang Taiyan Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2025, Huang Taiyan asks what role Schools of Marxism should play in the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project, now in its twentieth year. The author's answer is that these schools should be the "vanguard" (paixingbing) of its renewal, with studying, researching and propagating Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the project's fundamental task. The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's instruction on the project. The instruction calls for the Two Integrations, building an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and training theoretical talent. Huang then sets out three tasks for the Schools of Marxism: systematic and scholarly interpretation of Xi Jinping Thought, more effective study and dissemination of it, and the training of high-calibre theoretical talent. On research, Huang urges schools to improve their disciplinary layout and pool resources. They should organise interdisciplinary, collaborative work, with "collective attack on key problems" rather than "fighting alone". On dissemination, Huang says winning over young people is decisive. Teaching the university course introducing Xi Jinping Thought, now offered in all universities, is described as the best form of propaganda. Teachers should combine teaching and research, "open the door" to outside teaching expertise, and use collective lesson preparation to make it a flagship ideological and political course. Huang adds that Schools of Marxism and the related disciplines have a clearer responsibility for talent training, citing a 2021 General Office document on strengthening the schools. The author proposes adjusting programmes, curricula and student intake to give integrated undergraduate-to-doctoral training, and concludes that the schools have achieved much and can do more. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a senior university Party official frames the mission of Marxism schools and the teaching of Xi Jinping Thought.

The construction logic of the order of spectacle under digital capitalism and its cognitive control 数字资本主义景观秩序的建构逻辑及其认知控制 Xie Lixia Drawing on Guy Debord's idea of the spectacle, Xie Lixia asks how digital capitalism builds an "order of spectacle" and how that order controls individuals. The article argues that digital technology turns direct social existence into images and, through three layers of control, produces "data believers" whose knowledge is standardised, whose emotions are uniform and whose behaviour is docile. The article is organised as three sections that move from cognition to emotion to behaviour, followed by a short conclusion. Each section has three sub-parts. The first covers filtering, hidden coding and preference-driven production of knowledge. The second covers emotional saturation through data, simulated intimacy and disciplinary power. The third covers the exploitation of time, the confinement of space and the governing power of discipline. Xie draws on Marx, Foucault, Marcuse, Debord and Mike Crang, among others. Xie's central move is to treat knowledge, emotion and behaviour as successive sites where capital extracts value and secures ideological control. Platforms filter knowledge at its source and during production, then bind fragments into image chains and "tacit knowledge" attached to wearable devices. Emotion is then commodified: data "painting" spreads collective feeling, platform "walled gardens" simulate closeness, and digital labour becomes "play labour". Finally, digital devices blur work and leisure, turn every place into a workstation, and embed discipline in the individual until subjectivity dissolves. Xie also introduces "data fetishism" as a successor to the fetishism of commodities, money and capital. In the conclusion Xie holds that nostalgia for a pre-digital age is not an option, and that digital capital also contains openings for liberation. The author calls for going beyond the order set by the logic of capital, regulating the capitalisation and privatisation of data, promoting digital sharing, and building a community with a shared future for mankind in which humans and the digital coexist. Read the original if you want a Marxist-Foucauldian critique of platform power that follows Debord's spectacle from cognition to emotion to bodily discipline.

The logic and path of the great founding spirit of the Party in leading the "two great revolutions" 伟大建党精神引领“两个伟大革命”的逻辑理据与路径选择 Xu Fengzhen Xu Fengzhen asks how the great founding spirit of the Party can lead and sustain what official texts call the "two great revolutions": the Party's great self-reform, which Xu describes as remaking the subjective world and answering "what the Party is", and the great social revolution, which remakes the objective world and answers "what the Party does". The article argues that this spirit is the spiritual source of the "high degree of consciousness" in "leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform", a requirement set out in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It is written in the language of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article proceeds through five grounds: discursive, historical, practical, value-based, and a final section on choice of path. It opens with the genesis of three expressions, "founding spirit", "self-revolution" and "social revolution", and then sets out five relations between the founding spirit and the two revolutions. It then reads the four components of the founding spirit against the question of where Chinese modernization comes from, where it is going, how it proceeds and for whom. Its sources run from the 1921 first Party programme and Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping's speeches. Xu's first move is conceptual. In Xu's account, "social revolution" fell out of regular use during the socialist-construction and reform eras, and Xi's 2018 speech reconnected it, so its usage traces a "V" shape. Xu also finds a "hidden" social-revolution spirit inside the "spirit of reform and innovation", alongside the explicit "self-revolution spirit". The second move is historical: the founding spirit and the two revolutions appeared together, overlap in roles, advance in step, complement each other and share traits. Without the spirit the revolutions are "blind", and without the revolutions the spirit is "empty". Third, each of the four components is tied to a question about Chinese modernization. Seeking truth and ideals concern direction and the unity of the maximum, minimum and basic programmes. Original aspiration and mission concern the starting point and national rejuvenation. Fearlessness in sacrifice concerns method. Loyalty to the Party and the people concerns purpose, as a dialectical unity of Party spirit and the people's character. Xu concludes that the spirit must be inherited (the "source") and developed (the "stream"). It is to be turned into theoretical, political, behavioural and value strengths by studying Marxism, taking the people's standpoint, cultivating revolutionary character and putting Party and people first. Xu holds that only then can Party members keep a "thoroughly revolutionary spirit" and carry Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation forward. Read the original if you want to see how Party-history scholarship ties the Party's spiritual lineage to the current formula of self-reform leading social revolution, including its account of how these terms developed.

Marx's thought on proletarian poverty as institutional poverty 马克思关于作为制度性贫困的无产阶级贫困思想 Mou Chengwen Wang Weijun Mou Chengwen and Wang Weijun ask what Marx held to be the cause of proletarian poverty, and argue that he treated it as institutional poverty, produced by the injustice of social or state institutions. They contrast this with Hegel, for whom a 'rabble' arises 'naturally' from individual differences. In Marx's view, as the authors read him, the proletariat is an artificially created mass of poor people, produced by the sudden dissolution of society, above all of the middle estate. The article is organised around three roots of this poverty: alienated labour as the social root, class rule as the political root, and surplus value as the economic root. It draws mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Class Struggles in France 1848 to 1850, Capital and the Communist Manifesto. Before turning to Marx, the authors clarify the concepts involved, such as alienation, externalisation, reification and labour. On alienated labour, the authors argue that it strips the labour process, the worker and even the idle appropriator of their essence as free activity. Its direct result is private property, whose forms (wages, capital, profit, rent) are all treated as outcomes of alienation. On class rule, they describe ruling power as scarce, hidden, monopolistic and dominating, and say it entrenches the position of the ruling class and fixes that of the ruled. They use Marx's analysis of the French classes to show an asymmetric structure in which the proletariat sits at the bottom. On surplus value, they follow the purchase of labour-power, the production and accumulation of surplus value, and its division into industrial and commercial profit, interest and rent. This process, they say, makes capitalists richer and wage workers poorer. The authors conclude that alienated labour, class rule and surplus value all rest on the capitalist system, which is therefore the ultimate root of proletarian poverty. They state that proletarians can end it only by abolishing bourgeois ownership, rising to become the ruling class, winning democracy, taking over capital step by step and intervening forcibly in property relations. They present this analysis as the theoretical basis of Marx's idea of the fundamental emancipation of the proletariat and of all humanity. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how Marx's early and mature works are linked in explaining poverty as a product of institutions.

Research on Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work: progress, hot topics and outlook 习近平总书记关于宗教工作重要论述的 研究进展、热点论域与态势展望 Zhao Jinying Wang Yongyou This is a literature review, using CiteSpace bibliometric software, of a decade of Chinese scholarship on General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work (the 'important expositions'). The authors ask how this research has developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), which topics have become central, and where it should go next. They argue that the field has produced substantial results and now needs more systematic, theoretically grounded study. The sample is 171 articles drawn from CNKI and the National Social Science Documentation Centre, searched in November 2024. The review first charts publication trends and three phases of research fronts, then maps keyword clusters. It sorts the literature into four hot topics: how the expositions came about, what they contain, what value they have, and how to put them into practice. It closes with three directions for future work. On trends, the authors find that output peaked in three periods: 2016, 2018 and 2021 (31 articles that year, the highest). In their reading, each peak followed a major Party event or speech, so scholarly attention tracks theoretical and practical developments in the Party's religious work. The research fronts moved from handling religious work in a new situation (2014–2016), to theoretical and practical innovation (2017–2019), to building Marxist religious studies as a discipline (2020–2024). On content, the authors note that scholars see the expositions as a complete system within Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They report scholarly claims of international significance for global religious governance and for a community with a shared future for mankind. The review also reports that studies of implementation are still weakly linked to practice. The authors call for three advances. First, joint study of the whole and its parts, including the expositions' relation to Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law and on culture, and deeper work on themes such as the Sinicization of religion. Second, closer integration of theory and practice, covering practical requirements, accumulated experience and concrete problems. Third, wider horizons and methods: pre-2012 history, international comparison, comparison with earlier leaders' views, empirical fieldwork and interdisciplinary approaches. Read the original if you want a map of how Chinese scholars frame and research Party religious policy, with its quantitative trend and keyword analysis.

The place of New China's 75 years in modern world history 新中国的75年在世界现代史中的地位 Zhu Jiamu Zhu Jiamu asks what position the People's Republic's first 75 years occupy in modern world history. The answer is that China's size, long history and socialist system gave it an exceptional role. Zhu describes the PRC as a force for peace, justice, democracy and progress that has consistently stood on 'the right side of history'. In this account, the PRC's influence has grown through its economic success and its role in initiating and organising international bodies and initiatives. Zhu says China's influence works through five channels: diplomacy, public appeals and global initiatives, aid, trade and economic cooperation, and demonstration through its own development. The article claims China has used force only to repel aggression and armed provocation. It then proceeds chronologically and thematically through three fields: opposing hegemonism and defending peace, opposing old and new colonialism and supporting the Global South, and resisting unilateralism and protectionism in trade, technology and ecology. On peace, Zhu traces a line from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, the Bandung spirit and the Korean War to Mao Zedong's 'three worlds' theory, which Zhu credits with enabling the thaw in US relations and China's return to the United Nations. Zhu then covers reform-era diplomacy and the new era's community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. On the Global South, Zhu presents Africa as the representative case, from the Tanzania–Zambia railway to the 2024 summit pledges. Zhu contrasts China's aid, described as unconditional, with US aid, which Zhu says carries conditions. China's poverty reduction and development experience are offered as models. On ecology, Zhu presents China as a country that, unlike capitalism, avoids the Western path of environmental plunder. The article lists environmental legislation, carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality targets, and renewable-energy figures. Zhu concludes that at each historical crossroads China has sided with peace, developing countries and humanity's common interests. Zhu expects it to keep doing so and to contribute more to building a community with a shared future for mankind. The article ends with Mao's remark that China, as a large country, should make a greater contribution to humanity. Read the original if you want an official-leaning Chinese scholarly account of how the PRC's foreign policy, Global South ties and environmental record are framed as a contribution to world history.

The cultural logic of Communists keeping the "Three Musts" in mind in the new era 新时代共产党人牢记“三个务必”的文化理路 Wang Cheng Wang Cheng takes up the "Three Musts" announced in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): all Party members must remain true to the original aspiration and founding mission, must remain modest, prudent and hardworking, and must dare to fight and be good at fighting. The article treats them as an innovative development of Mao Zedong's "Two Musts" of 1949. Wang notes that existing research clusters around their significance, historical background, meaning and practical requirements, and argues that their cultural logic has been little studied. The thesis is that the Three Musts draw on three layers of culture and that Communists can keep them in mind through the Second Integration. The article has three parts. The first traces the cultural sources of the Three Musts in excellent traditional Chinese culture, in revolutionary culture from the new-democratic and socialist revolution and construction periods, and in advanced socialist culture from reform and opening up and the new era. The second sets out their cultural significance in four respects. The third proposes three paths for putting them into practice. In Wang's account, each of the three Musts matches a strand of tradition. The first corresponds to the ideas of putting the people first, of governing the world and relieving the people's hardship, and of a world of great harmony. The second corresponds to the Book of Changes' "modesty" hexagram and to the classical stress on self-strengthening and frugality. The third corresponds to the Confucian value of courage and to the unity of knowing and doing. Revolutionary culture then carries these into Party practice, through Mao's warnings in 1949, the spirit of the Party and the Long March, and the Yan'an-era study of the fall of Li Zicheng. Wang argues that the Three Musts help to firm up Communists' ideals and convictions, to solve the problems unique to a large party, to improve Party conduct, government conduct and popular customs, and to advance the goal of building a modern socialist country. Wang proposes three paths. The first is theoretical innovation, meaning study of the Party's innovative theory, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and ideological education. The second is stronger Party spirit and moral cultivation, backed by the Eight-point Regulation and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The third is a fighting spirit that builds the capacity to meet complex situations. Wang concludes that the Three Musts safeguard the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory scholar links a current Party slogan to classical Chinese texts, revolutionary history and the Second Integration.

On the generative mechanism of the leading force of ideological and political education 论思政引领力的生成机理 Ye Fangxing Ye Fangxing takes up a concept that entered official language only recently: "ideological and political leading force" (sizheng yinlingli), listed in Xi Jinping's September 2024 speech at the National Education Conference, and again in the January 2025 Outline for Building a Strong Education Country (2024–2035), as the first attribute of a strong education country. The article asks how this force is generated. Ye argues that it arises from a practical process with five dimensions: real-world context, value direction, practical foundation, key link and supporting conditions. The article is organised in five sections that follow these dimensions. It first places the concept in the policy context of building a strong education country, citing documents from 2010, 2019, the 20th Party Congress (2022) and 2024–25. It then discusses moral education as the value direction, the school ideological and political education system as the practical base, students' inner needs as the key link, and a healthy educational ecology as the guarantee. Ye first distinguishes two senses of the term: a force as outcome, an indicator of how strong an education system is, and a force as means, the effect achieved through guiding practice. In Ye's account the force is directed by the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent (lide shuren), with moral education given priority and ideals and convictions at its core. It is realised mainly in schools through a vertical "chain" across school stages and a horizontal "network" of channels. Three parts of this system are stressed: ideological and political theory courses, ideological and political education across all curricula, and everyday ideological and political education. Ye then argues that guidance must meet students' spiritual needs through targeted, differentiated approaches, must include reflection on and criticism of negative ideas rather than simply catering to students, and must draw on students' own initiative. Ye concludes that the force depends on a good educational ecology at three levels. The macro level is a society-wide pattern of ideological and political work, the meso level is school governance, institutions and campus culture, and the micro level is the classroom as a space of meaning and emotion. Ye holds that these levels are conditional, intermediary and foundational respectively, and that they must interlock. Read the original if you want a systematic, policy-oriented account of how Chinese education scholars conceptualise ideological and political guidance within the drive to build a strong education country.

Seen through the history of theoretical innovation, the "Second Integration" is another emancipation of the mind 从理论创新史看“第二个结合”是又一次的思想解放 Feng Jun Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2025, Feng Jun argues that each step in the Chinese Communist Party's theoretical innovation has been the product of an emancipation of the mind (jiefang sixiang). The article's thesis is that the Two Integrations, in particular the "Second Integration" of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, mark the latest such emancipation. The piece is a short commentary organised in three historical stages. It first treats the revolutionary period, from the fight against dogmatism to the Yan'an rectification and the Seventh Party Congress. It then covers socialist construction and the reform era, from the 1956 exploration after the Soviet model through the truth-criterion debate and the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Finally it turns to the Second Integration under Xi Jinping. Feng's central move is to separate two lines. The "First Integration", of Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities, is said to have required breaking with book-worship and Soviet copying. It produced Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The Second Integration, in Feng's account, had been practised implicitly but was first stated explicitly in the new era, giving socialism with Chinese characteristics deeper historical roots. Feng lists five ways it frees thinking: it rejects both historical nihilism and cultural conservatism; it strengthens cultural confidence and cultural subjectivity; it deepens understanding of Chinese modernization as the continuation of an ancient civilization; it widens the space for innovation by joining Marxism as the "soul" to traditional culture as the "root"; and it points the way to a culturally strong country. Feng concludes that adhering to the Two Integrations is the necessary path for developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. He calls for creative transformation of traditional culture under Marxist guidance, guided by core socialist values. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party theorists place the Second Integration within the Party's own history of theoretical innovation.

Systems integration and the creative construction of an autonomous knowledge system How the Third Plenum Decision's systems integration of Chinese modernization elevates a "systematised economic theory" with Chinese characteristics 系统集成对自主知识体系的创造性构建 Gu Hailiang Gu Hailiang takes up the Decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. He asks what its stress on "systems integration" and a "systems perspective" means for building China's autonomous knowledge system. Gu argues that this integration is both a key to the Decision's spirit and a step that lifts China's "systematised economic theory" to a new level. The short piece, published in Beijing Daily in March 2025, sets out six features of systems integration as an autonomous knowledge system. It relies mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches on philosophy and social sciences, on the 20th Party Congress (2022) report and on the Decision itself. It also draws on Engels's remark on a "revolution in terminology", on postcolonial critiques of dependent knowledge, and on Peter Burke's history of knowledge. Gu's core claim is that the integration rests on Chinese conditions and a problem-oriented method, and that it is marked by a "revolution in terminology". He lists new concepts such as the new development philosophy, high-quality development and new quality productive forces, and presents them as signs of intellectual autonomy. He adds that the system is politically and intellectually committed to the Four-sphere Confidence while also being academic, and that it counters a "dependent" knowledge tradition tied to Western-centrism. Drawing on Burke's examples of conflict between "practical" and "theoretical" knowledge, Gu says Chinese modernization's integration joins theory-driven and practice-driven knowledge into one type. He ties this to Xi's call for a "systematised economic theory" that answers real problems and is rooted in Chinese practice. Gu concludes that systems integration offers a systematic exploration of how to build a knowledge system that combines theoretical and practical orientations. He says it has important implications for the innovative development of China's autonomous knowledge system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics link the Third Plenum Decision to the project of an autonomous knowledge system in economics and the social sciences.

The people's congress system has a distinctive advantage in safeguarding the rule of law 人民代表大会制度具有法治保障的显著优势 Lü Zhongmei Taking Xi Jinping's speech marking the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress as its starting point, this article by Lü Zhongmei, a senior NPC and legal-association official, takes up one of the system's stated advantages: that it safeguards law-based governance in all fields. Lü argues that the people's congress system is the institutional cornerstone of comprehensive law-based governance and that this advantage should be turned more fully into governance effectiveness. The article has three parts. The first sets out the constitutional and institutional foundations, tracing the system from the 1949 Common Program through the 1954 and 1982 constitutions and describing the legislative and supervisory powers of people's congresses. The second discusses the essential character of the Chinese path of rule of law. The third sets out tasks for the new journey, including legislation, the democratic work of congresses and supervision. Lü's central claim is that the system joins three things: Party leadership, the people as masters of the country, and law-based governance. In this account the Party turns its proposals into state will through statutory procedures, and the 2018 constitutional amendment writing Party leadership into Article 1 reinforces this. The article says the system pairs formal and substantive justice, draws on world legal civilisation without copying Western models, and keeps law responsive to change, citing foreign investment law, digital economy regulation and ecological legislation. Lü adds that the rule-of-law advantage supports the system's other advantages: Party leadership, whole-process people's democracy, democratic centralism, and national unity and long-term stability. For the new era, Lü calls for higher-quality legislation under a pattern of Party leadership, congress primacy, government support and broad participation. Lü also calls for better congress procedures, deputy liaison stations and grassroots legislative contact points, and for supervision that is correct, effective and lawful. The article concludes that the system's rule-of-law capacity is a benchmark of modernised state governance and a contribution to political civilisation. Read the original if you want an official-insider account of how Party-state legal scholarship presents the NPC system's constitutional, legislative and supervisory functions in the Xi era.
