Reflections on two important questions in the Critique of the Gotha Programme 关于《哥达纲领批判》中两个重要问题的思考 Yang Jianyi Marx wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme in 1875 to combat Lassallean claims that the state is a community of the whole people and that its mission is to develop freedom. Yang Jianyi argues that two questions in the text still carry theoretical and practical weight: the necessity of the dictatorship of the proletariat, and the staged character of communism. Both, the author says, must be rethought as circumstances change. The article has two main sections. The first reads Marx on the class nature of the state, on the transitional period, and on proletarian dictatorship, then follows how Mao Zedong adapted the doctrine into the people's democratic dictatorship and into the handling of contradictions among the people. It then moves through the Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao periods to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second section sets out Marx's account of communism's lower and higher phases and applies it to contemporary China. On the state, Yang argues that no supra-class state or freedom exists. The proletariat therefore cannot be emancipated through the bourgeois state and needs its own state power for the revolutionary transition. In Yang's account, Mao's people's democratic dictatorship joins democracy among the people with dictatorship over reactionaries. Under Xi Jinping, the author says, this theory has gained new content through whole-process people's democracy, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the anti-corruption campaign. On communism, Yang reads the first phase as a contradictory unity of past and future. Distribution according to labour there remains "bourgeois right", and the higher phase requires highly developed productive forces, abundant collective wealth and all-round human development. Yang warns against letting capitalist elements spread in the first phase and against importing higher-phase features into it. The move to the higher phase, Yang adds, is not automatic. Yang concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era fits Marx's description of the first phase while adding Chinese features. The primary stage of socialism, the author says, has not changed. Studying the Critique, Yang argues, strengthens the Four-sphere Confidence, supports the Two Upholds and aids the modernization of national governance, and Marxist classics need continual study. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school scholar links Marx's 1875 text to Mao's theory of people's democratic dictatorship and to current Party doctrine.

Foucault's resonant reception of Mao Zedong's thought on investigation and research 论福柯对毛泽东调查研究思想的共鸣式接受 Wang Yichen Michel Foucault led the Prisons Information Group (GIP) in the early 1970s, and Western scholarship has noted its links to Maoism. Wang Yichen argues that this literature tells a vague, linear story in which Mao's investigation thought simply reached France and Foucault adopted it. The article proposes the concept of 'resonant reception': Foucault was moved by the slogan and spirit of investigation, but understood it within his own intellectual horizon, so his investigations differ fundamentally from Mao's. The article has three parts. The first traces how Foucault met Mao's investigation thought, through the French Maoist organisations UJCM-L and the Gauche Prolétarienne, through his partner Daniel Defert, and through colleagues at the University of Paris VIII (Vincennes), including Badiou, Rancière and others. It also lists the Mao texts available in French. The second part reviews the GIP's prison inquiries: their object, purpose, method and outcomes, including the 'Intolérable' pamphlets and Discipline and Punish. The third part sets out the limits of Foucault's reception and criticises earlier scholarship. Wang makes three main moves. First, the transmission was mediated and altered: Defert was trained as a sociologist, so Foucault received a hybrid of sociological and Maoist investigation. Second, Wang contrasts the two practices. Foucault investigated mostly ordinary prisoners, not revolutionary masses. He gave investigation an ideological role of awakening opinion and passing on information, but rejected direct intellectual intervention in struggle and never entered prisons himself. Mao treated investigation as a unity of understanding, mobilising and solving problems, grounded in 'On Practice' and 'On Contradiction'. Third, Wang finds a partial convergence on investigation as knowledge production, but holds that Foucault lacked Mao's Marxist character and rootedness in Chinese history. Wang rejects both the Nietzsche-only reading and over-attributing influence to 'Maoism', which is not the same as Mao's own thought. Wang concludes that Foucault's silence about Mao reflects a free intellectual exchange of the kind he valued, and that the gap is one between the revolutionary's investigation and the scholar's. The article reads the 1968 generation's reception as a misunderstanding that took Mao's thought only as a theory of critique. In Wang's view, its constructive side, shown in On New Democracy, matters more and has been neglected by Western left-wing scholars, which Wang says should be addressed in telling China's story abroad. Read the original if you study the French reception of Maoism, Foucault's prison activism, or how Chinese scholars assess Western uses of Mao's thought.

On the guiding power of ideological and political education 论思政引领力 Xiang Jiuyu Xiang Jiuyu takes up the concept of "guiding power of ideological and political education" (sizheng yinlingli), which Xi Jinping introduced at the National Education Conference in September 2024. The 2025 Outline for Building a Strong Education Nation (2024–2035) repeated that a strong education nation with Chinese characteristics must possess it. Xiang argues that the concept is a theoretical distillation of the Party's historical experience in ideological and political education, and that it can be understood at three connected levels: macro, meso and micro. The article is organised around these levels. The macro level places the concept within the construction of a strong education nation. The meso level treats it within the ideological and political education system, including ideological and political courses (sizheng ke), the "big ideological and political course" and "ideological and political education across the curriculum". The micro level examines it as a force of mainstream ideology. Xiang also traces the concept's lineage to Xi's earlier notion of "ideological guiding power" in Party building. At the macro level, Xiang notes that guiding power comes first among the six powers Xi lists for a strong education nation. The others are talent competitiveness, scientific and technological support, livelihood security, social coordination and international influence. In Xiang's account it is the "lifeline" that shapes the other five, and it reflects national will and the value orientation of educational modernization. At the meso level, it is a unity of six forms of guidance: intellectual, political, cultural, value-based, faith-based and moral. These cannot be separated, and together they yield long-cycle, foundation-strengthening and wide-ranging advantages in moulding people. At the micro level, Xiang calls it essentially an ideological force that maintains Marxism's guiding position, orienting students towards history, the present and the future and countering views such as that communism is "remote" or "outdated". Xiang names three supports: the Party's innovative theory, the core socialist values, and the creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture. Xiang concludes that the three levels together give the concept its theoretical content and practical force. At the macro level it answers the questions of whom to train, how and for whom. At the meso level it forms a "matrix" of guidance whose strength determines the effectiveness of ideological and political education. At the micro level it shows the Party's deepening grasp of how mainstream ideology is built. Xiang calls for further scholarly elaboration of the concept and for developing a disciplinary, academic and discourse system for the field with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you study ideological and political education, Party ideology work or the official discourse on education in China, and want a systematic account of this newly coined concept.

How further deepening reform comprehensively reshapes five relationships 论进一步全面深化改革对五大关系的重塑 Chen Yongsheng Chen Yongsheng examines how the Decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization seeks to "reshape" five relationships. These are centre–locality, regional development, grassroots society, humanity and nature, and urban–rural relations. The author argues that this strand of the Decision has real cognitive and practical value and deserves systematic study. The article is built as five parallel sections. Each one first records achievements since reform and opening up (or since 1949), then lists new problems, then explains how the Decision responds and what further steps Chen proposes. It draws on official statistics, such as regional GDP figures, Gini coefficients, urbanisation rates and urban–rural income ratios, and on quotations from Xi Jinping. It closes with a note that the work is a stage result of a national social science fund project on whole-process people's democracy. On centre–local relations, Chen identifies a fiscal gap, oversized transfer payments that reduce efficiency, and uncertainty in the allocation of fiscal powers and spending responsibilities. The Decision's answer is to raise local autonomous revenue, reform transfers and move spending responsibilities upward, so that "the top orders and the bottom pays" becomes less common. On regions, the author cites a widening north–south gap and the polarising pull of megacities, and calls for complementary regional advantages and locally tailored new quality productive forces. For grassroots society, Chen points to a Gini coefficient persistently above 0.4, diversifying interests and rising risks, and endorses income-distribution reform, stronger township and street capacity and a firmer national security system. For humanity and nature, Chen notes progress in air and water quality but problems of low-quality growth, cadres fixated on growth rates, and weak ecological-product valuation. Chen urges property-rights, compensation, governance and green-finance reforms. For urban and rural areas, relative income gaps are narrowing while absolute gaps are widening, and the household-registration urbanisation rate lags the resident rate by nearly 18 points. Chen calls for supporting agriculture, enabling migrants to receive public services where they live, and integrated planning. Read the original if you want a detailed, statistics-backed Chinese official-academic reading of the Third Plenum Decision's institutional agenda across fiscal, regional, social, ecological and rural–urban fields.

An analysis of the atheist thought in Wang Fuzhi's cosmology 王夫之宇宙论中的无神论思想探析 Gao Guipeng Song-Ming Neo-Confucian cosmology, shaped by Buddhism and Daoism, tended to treat the cosmic substance as a mysterious entity beyond experience. Gao Guipeng asks how the late Ming–early Qing thinker Wang Fuzhi reworked this cosmology. The article argues that Wang stripped the Neo-Confucian cosmic substance of its divine character and built a materialist cosmos, which Gao reads as a systematic form of atheist thought. The article follows the three parts of Wang's cosmology: ontology (the cosmic substance), cosmogony (how the world arises and changes) and cosmic order (motion, change and progress). Gao sets Wang against Zhang Zai, Zhu Xi and the Cheng brothers, against Daoist and Buddhist accounts of generation, against the doctrine of heaven-human resonance, and against the Italian missionary Matteo Ricci's theological cosmos. Needham, Chen Meidong and Xiang Shiling are cited as supporting readings. On ontology, Gao argues that Wang made "supreme harmony" (taihe), a unity of material qi and its principle (li), the sole cosmic substance. It is drawn from the experienced world rather than posited beyond it, and qi is prior to li. Wang therefore rejects Ricci's "prime mover heaven" as a snake's extra feet. On cosmogony, Wang denies any beginning or end and replaces the Daoist "being from non-being" and the Buddhist "arising and perishing" with a cycle of the hidden and the manifest. Qi never disappears, so birth and death are transformations and not the work of spirits. On order, Wang holds that motion is absolute and rest relative, that "the transformations of heaven and earth renew daily", and that humanity and human nature evolve. Gao says this undermines the Neo-Confucian nostalgia for the Three Dynasties and the theological claim that human nature is innately given. Gao concludes that Wang built the origin and development of the world on materialism and removed mystical elements from Confucianism. In Gao's account, this freed people from theological constraint, focused thought on the empirical world and real life, and carried enlightenment significance. Gao concedes that Wang's evolutionary ideas remain crude and overlook the role of labour. The article notes that Marxist scholars Hou Wailu, Zhang Dainian and Xiao Qifu interpreted Wang's cosmology materialistically and promoted its modern transformation. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Wang Fuzhi is presented as a materialist and atheist thinker in the Chinese Marxist reading of the Confucian tradition.

Deepening the Party's institutions of Party building to advance the Party's self-reform 深化党的建设制度推进党的自我革命 Bao Xinjian Bao Xinjian, in a commentary published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025, argues that institution-building is the core and key element of Party building. The article holds that, in the new era, reform of the Party's institutions must be deepened to meet the internal requirements of the Party's self-reform. It asks that attention go first to three systems: the Party's leadership system, the cadre and personnel system, and the system of power supervision. The piece is organised around these three areas. Each is treated in its own section: the leadership system and democratic centralism, the selection and appointment of cadres, and the combination of intra-Party supervision with supervision by the people. Bao draws on Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto and on Marxist theories of the state to ground the discussion, and refers to the Party's existing body of internal regulations. Bao's central claim is that strict governance of the Party through institutions rests on a basic political logic: developing people's democracy and intra-Party democracy. Without the former, the Party's governing position is hard to consolidate; without the latter, institution-building cannot go deep. Democratic centralism must guard against both excessive dispersal and excessive centralisation, with tighter checks on the top leader ("yibashou") of each unit. On cadres, Bao argues that power is "granted by the people", so selection must unite Party management of cadres with democratic mechanisms, avoiding both pure vote-counting and neglect of public opinion. On supervision, Bao holds that public power always risks monopolisation and corruption. The article therefore proposes a system with intra-Party supervision at its core and supervision by the people as its driving force, drawing on the people's congresses, the CPPCC, social organisations and the media. Bao concludes that combining the two forms of supervision gives a lasting mechanism for escaping the historical cycle of rise and decline, relying on supervision by the people and the Party's self-reform as the "two magic weapons". The article credits the Party's recent discipline and anti-corruption efforts with changing a past situation of lax and soft Party governance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists link democratic centralism, cadre selection and supervision to the Party's self-reform in the Xi Jinping era.

The threefold global impact of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化的三重世界影响 Ji Qiwei Tian Zhijian Ji Qiwei and Tian Zhijian ask what influence Chinese modernization has on the world, and answer that its impact is threefold. In their account it changes the global map of modernization, contributes Chinese wisdom to building a better world, and offers experience to developing countries. They frame it as a modernization that is not self-interested but seeks happiness for the Chinese people, rejuvenation of the nation, and progress for humanity. The framing draws on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its Decision on deepening reform. The article has three main sections. The first treats Chinese modernization as redrawing the world map of modernization in terms of population, shared benefits and the place of socialist states. The second covers its contribution to economic recovery, to the questions of the times, and to opportunities for other countries. The third draws lessons for developing countries. It relies on Xi Jinping's statements, official economic figures, and examples such as high-speed rail exports and the Beidou navigation system. The authors argue that only some twenty countries with about one billion people have modernized, all of them capitalist, so that the existing modernization is a partial and 'private' one. Bringing more than 1.4 billion Chinese into modernity would, in their view, more than double the modernized population and break the equation of 'modernization = Westernization', including Fukuyama's end-of-history thesis. They also cite the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives and a community with a shared future for mankind as Chinese contributions. For developing countries, they draw three lessons: build a strong leadership core, with the Party's full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and self-reform as the model; promote all-round development rather than one-sided growth; and rely on independence and self-reliance while learning selectively from others. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization, enriches Marxist modernization theory and raises the global influence of scientific socialism. They stress that China does not export a 'China model' but offers developing countries options for independent paths. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Chinese academic writing presents the international significance of Chinese modernization, including its claims about leadership, development and the Global South.

The philosophical implications of the Party's self-reform in the new era 新时代党的自我革命的哲学意蕴 Yin Tieyan Yin Tieyan asks what philosophical foundations underlie the Communist Party of China's self-reform in the new era. The article argues that the Party's self-reform rests on the Marxist worldview and methodology, namely the basic positions of historical materialism and dialectical materialism, and that it should be understood through three sets of philosophical perspectives. The article is organised in three sections. The first deals with a holistic view and a view of tortuous development; the second with the views of connection and practice; the third with the views of contradiction and development. Yin draws on the Party's history from the New Democratic Revolution to the present, on Xi Jinping's statements, and on quotations from other Chinese scholars. First, Yin holds that self-reform must be treated as a continuous historical whole, set within world socialist revolution and the Party's century-plus history. Because new things develop along a winding, spiral path, risks and challenges are to be resolved within self-reform itself. Second, Yin presents self-reform and social revolution as a dialectical unity: social revolution is the practical basis and direction of self-reform, while self-reform is the driving force that leads social revolution. Self-reform is also tied to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a community with a shared future for mankind, and the Party's response to crises of political parties worldwide. Third, Yin argues that self-reform arises from contradictions within the Party and society, and that the "two-point theory" and the "emphasis on the key point" must be combined to grasp the principal contradiction and its principal aspect. Yin cites the 19th Party Congress (2017) judgement that the principal contradiction is now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. Yin concludes that self-reform in the new era should adhere to seeking truth from facts, investigation and research, and a scientific method for resolving contradictions. In the article's account, this strengthens the Party's long-term governing capacity and reflects its responsibility as the world's largest Marxist governing party. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese Party-building scholarship maps Marxist dialectics onto the doctrine of the Party's self-reform.

The inner mechanism and realisation path of the Communist Party of China's leadership in building the Chinese national community 中国共产党领导中华民族共同体建设的内在机理与实现路径 Wang Chuanfa Why, and how, does the Communist Party of China lead the building of the Chinese national community (Zhonghua minzu gongtongti)? Wang Chuanfa argues that existing scholarship describes the history, discourse and achievements of this project but gives only a weak theoretical answer to the question of why the Party leads it. The article's thesis is that Party leadership results from a coupling between the project's internal needs and the Party's accumulated "political potential energy". The article was published in the journal Tansuo in 2025 and opens with a short review of work on the history, discourse and experience of Party-led community building. It then proceeds in three steps: demand (why leadership is necessary), supply (why it is possible) and mechanisms (how it is realised). It draws on Tönnies, Rousseau and Marx for general theories of community and interest, and on Xi Jinping's statements on ethnic work. It also cites Party documents, constitutional and legal changes, and Party membership statistics. On the demand side, Wang holds that community-building needs emotional bonding, shared values, continuing common interests, and collective action toward shared goals. In each case, the author argues, differences of region, resources and development create tensions that only Party organisation, ideological guidance, integration and its founding mission can resolve. On the supply side, borrowing the concept of "political potential energy" from He Donghang and Kong Fanbin, Wang identifies four kinds: value-based, institutional, organisational and identity-based. Examples include the central ethnic work conferences from 1992, the addition of the phrase "forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation" to the Party Constitution (2017), the insertion of "Chinese nation" into the state constitution (2018), and a Party base of 5.065 million grassroots organisations at the end of 2022. The author names four realisation mechanisms: shaping ideas, embedding organisation, integrating resources and delivering public services. Wang concludes that the Party's "presence of leadership" (dang de lingdao zaichang) in ethnic work is both an internal requirement of community building and a necessary choice for staying on the correct path of resolving ethnic issues with Chinese characteristics. Strengthening the Party's overall leadership is described as the fundamental political guarantee of ethnic work in the new era and of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar builds a theoretical case, drawing on the idea of political potential energy, for Party leadership in ethnic affairs and in the building of national identity.

Coordinating an effective market and a capable government: forming an economic order that is both "lively" and "well-regulated" 必须统筹好有效市场和有为政府的关系 形成既“放得活”又“管得住”的经济秩序 Zhang Xu Zhang Xu's short commentary, published in Qiqi (Banner) in early 2025, takes up the Central Economic Work Conference's formula that an effective market and a capable government must be coordinated, so as to form an economic order that is both "fang de huo" (liberated and lively) and "guan de zhu" (properly regulated). Zhang argues that the formula reflects the Party Central Committee's grasp of economic laws and guides the improvement of the socialist market economy. The piece has three parts. It first explains why the market–government relationship matters, tracing it to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). It then sets out the dialectical, "two-sided" approach to market and state roles. Finally it breaks the formula into its two halves, drawing on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhang holds that market and government have different functions. The market, under the law of value, should play the decisive role in allocating resources, while government should change its functions, strengthen macroeconomic governance and regulation, and improve public services. Zhang stresses that the market economy develops under Party leadership and the socialist system, so the qualifier "socialist" must never be forgotten. "Liberating" means removing barriers: building a unified national market, strengthening competition policy, improving factor markets and property protection. "Regulating" means correcting market failure, countering monopoly and smoothing economic fluctuations, which Zhang says a market left alone cannot do. Zhang concludes that both the "invisible hand" and the "visible hand" should be used, forming a pattern in which they complement each other. The author cites early results in building the unified national market and presents capable government as an institutional advantage of concentrating efforts on major tasks. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how the market–government relationship is framed in current Chinese economic policy.

Historic transformation of the mode of production: the practical precondition of Chinese-style cultural modernization 生产方式的历史性变革：中国式文化现代化的实践前提 Liu Tongfang Zhang Qian Liu Tongfang and Zhang Qian ask what the practical, material precondition of Chinese-style cultural modernization is. They note that existing scholarship follows a cultural-history approach and explains only its intellectual preconditions: cultural exchange, the contemporary value of traditional culture, and the advanced character of socialist culture. The authors argue that these accounts leave open what drives cultural exchange, how "contemporary" is defined and where the nature of socialist culture comes from. Their answer, from the standpoint of historical materialism, is that the historic transformation of the mode of production is the practical precondition of cultural modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the dialectical relation between mode of production and cultural form, criticising economic determinism and cultural determinism. The second examines the leap in productive forces as the material basis of cultural modernization, treating the form and the content of culture separately. The third turns to changes in the relations of production and the way they gave the people a subjective consciousness of cultural modernization. Its cases include Kautsky, Bernstein and Marvin Harris on the economic side, and Max Weber, Gramsci and Toynbee on the cultural side. The Chinese material runs from the May Fourth Movement to the present. The authors hold that the mode of production drives change in cultural form, while mature culture gains relative independence and reacts back on production. Weber, Gramsci and Toynbee are described as idealist because they treat culture as the starting point of society. On productive forces, the authors argue that new media (newspapers, radio and film, television, the internet) modernised the forms of Chinese culture. They add that machine systems and artificial intelligence changed its content, with themes of industrialisation, reflection on machines and the human predicament in the AI age. Material change alone does not bring cultural change, however, so the human subject must be explained. The authors argue that two historic changes in the relations of production did this: the move from feudal to socialist public ownership, and the later move to public ownership as the mainstay alongside several forms of ownership. These changes reshaped the people's interests and led them to criticise feudal and capitalist culture and to build socialist culture. The authors conclude that cultural modernization is a long process led by the Communist Party in which both Chinese cultural form and cultural subjects become modern. They suggest that this approach helps identify new growth points for culture amid new quality productive forces. It also helps guard against the damaging influence of the logic of capital valorisation in a booming market economy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal grounds cultural modernization in the mode of production and sets itself against both economic and cultural determinism.

Upholding a systems approach: a basic principle and methodology for further deepening reform comprehensively 坚持系统观念：进一步全面深化改革的基本原则和方法论 Xiao Guiqing Lu Yang Xiao Guiqing and Lu Yang take up the principle of the systems approach (xitong guannian) set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. They argue that this approach is both a basic principle and a methodology, and that reform must be made more systematic, integrated and coordinated if it is to go further. The article has three parts. The first traces the systems approach to Marxist fundamental principles and to traditional Chinese thought, and reviews its role in reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second examines how the 2024 decision applies it: through institutional building across all fields, through the leading role of economic reform, and through balancing development and security. The third sets out three conditions for putting the approach into practice. The authors present the approach as running from Engels's account of universal connection, through Mao Zedong's "playing the piano" method and Deng Xiaoping's call for balance, to Xi Jinping's formulations. They hold that reform has moved from local experiments to systems integration, with institution-building as the main thread. On their account the decision proposes over 300 reform measures, with economic reform pulling the others along. Measures in politics, culture, society, ecology and national security are said to interlock, producing a multiplier effect of "1+1>2". Systemic reform is said to carry systemic risk, so national security reform is described as a safeguard for the whole. For implementation the authors name three requirements. First, the Party's overall leadership must be upheld unwaveringly, since it is said to coordinate interests and keep reform on the right political course. Second, the advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics should be used, including the ability to act as "one nation, one chessboard" and to meet risks with institutional strength. Third, strategy should rest on the "two overall situations": the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the systems approach is tied to the 2024 reform decision.

Historical materialism and the Marxist view of civilization 唯物史观与马克思主义文明观 Wang Weiguang Wang Weiguang starts from Xi Jinping's call to 'shoulder the cultural mission of the new era'. The article argues that this call cannot be properly understood without answering what civilization is, and that the answer requires historical materialism and a Marxist view of civilization. Wang holds that the founders of Marxism wrote no dedicated treatise on civilization, but that their scattered statements allow a coherent view to be reconstructed, and that this view is part of historical materialism. The article is a close reading of the classics. It surveys how Marx, Engels and Lenin use terms such as 'civilization', 'civilized nations', 'civilized society', 'ancient civilization' and 'modern civilization', with page-referenced citations from works including the Communist Manifesto, the Grundrisse, Capital, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State and Lenin's speeches. It is organised in four parts: civilization as capitalist civilization; the revolutionary supersession of that civilization; Engels's periodisation of the 'age of civilization'; and a closing list of the main tenets of the Marxist view. Wang's central claim is that, in the classics, 'civilization' in contexts about capitalism usually denotes bourgeois or capitalist civilization, which they praise for its historical role yet expose as resting on class exploitation. Engels's 'age of civilization' is read as running from slave society through feudalism to capitalism, marked by division of labour, commodity production, private property, classes and the state. Wang adds that tool-making in primitive society marks the origin of civilization, which he distinguishes from the beginning of the 'age of civilization'. From these readings Wang derives six tenets: the productive forces are the basic standard; the social formation determines a civilization's character; civilization is a historical category, so no abstract 'universal' civilization exists; class analysis is required; each civilization is progressive relative to its predecessor yet will be replaced; and idealist views must be criticised. Wang concludes that Marxism treats civilization as a marker of the nature, condition and degree of social progress, to be analysed historically, concretely, dialectically and in class terms. Wang presents Huntington's 'clash of civilizations' as a contemporary variant of the idealist view criticised by the classics, which in Wang's account obscures class struggle. Read the original if you want a densely documented, Chinese-language account of how a leading Party theorist extracts a theory of civilization from Marx, Engels and Lenin and uses it to frame current cultural policy.

The principled meaning of "promoting a better fit between state governance and social development" “推动国家治理和社会发展更好相适应”的原理性内涵 Xi Ge Fu Tianrui This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 14 March 2025, studies a formula from the decision adopted by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization: promoting a better fit between state governance and social development. Xi Ge and Fu Tianrui argue that this formula, added to the established pairs of productive forces and relations of production and of economic base and superstructure, is a contemporary development of the basic principles of historical materialism. They present it as a worldview and methodological guide for implementing the new development philosophy. The article has four parts. It first defines state governance and social development and the unity between them. It then links the governance–development contradiction to the basic contradictions of society, takes up the word "better" as a sign of dynamic change, and ends by reading the formula through the Two Integrations. The authors define both terms broadly. State governance is the whole system of institutions and the capacity to run them, spanning all five spheres of the overall plan. Social development is the development of society as an organic whole, so it already contains state governance as its active, leading element. On this basis Xi and Fu hold that the two are internally unified, and they say this overcomes the Western "dualism" of state versus society. They also argue that the relationship is mediated by the basic social contradictions: social development determines the governance system and policy direction, while governance acts back on the superstructure, then on the economic base, then on the productive forces. The authors treat the degree of fit as an indicator of Chinese modernization that moves through exploration and uneven progress, tied to the Party's century-long record. In their reading, the Two Integrations appear twice: in practice, such as building a high-standard socialist market economy and developing new quality productive forces, and in roots in socialism with Chinese characteristics and traditional Chinese political culture. They contend that, unlike in the West, neither state nor society has been alienated by capital expansion in China. They conclude that the formula scientifically sums up the driving force and institutional guarantee of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how Party theorists place governance within the historical-materialist scheme of basic contradictions.

The content dimensions of building an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of ideological and political education 论思想政治教育学自主知识体系构建的内容向度 Hou Yong Ke Zengjin Responding to Xi Jinping's call (2022) to build an "autonomous knowledge system" for Chinese philosophy and social sciences, Hou and Ke ask what such a system should contain for the discipline of ideological and political education. Their thesis is that it should be built through the "three systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse systems), following a logic of knowledge organisation, knowledge production and knowledge dissemination. They present this as an internal requirement of the discipline and a contribution to Chinese modernization. The article first clarifies what the autonomous knowledge system is, surveying existing views by function, process, structure and elements, and then offers the authors' own definition: an integrated whole comprising conceptual, categorical, academic, rule-based, discourse, method and supporting systems. Three sections follow, one for each of the three systems. A fourth section turns to systems thinking: strategic orientation, overall planning, structural coupling and methodological innovation. Hou and Ke argue that the disciplinary system organises knowledge: its core and branch discipline clusters, internal and cross-disciplinary coordination, and talent training and textbooks need strengthening. The academic system produces knowledge. It rests on Marxism as the "soul", excellent traditional Chinese culture as the "roots", and borrowing from related disciplines, together with basic-theory research and interdisciplinary work that avoids "mechanical borrowing". The discourse system disseminates knowledge. The authors call for a "terminological revolution" built around original, identifying concepts and for coordinated political, academic and everyday registers, along with narrative innovation. They also stress overseas communication that resists Western discourse dominance. They hold that the three systems are interdependent: the disciplinary system is the foundation, the academic system the driving force and the discourse system the key. The authors conclude that the project is long-term and systematic. It requires the Two Integrations, the principle of putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, and innovation within fundamental principles. It also requires problem orientation, systems thinking and a global outlook tied to a community with a shared future for mankind. They add that the content dimensions go beyond the three systems and need further study. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education frame disciplinary, academic and discourse construction in the language of Chinese modernization.

The Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Council: a successful exploration of building a New Democratic regime 陕甘宁边区参议会：新民主主义政权建设的成功探索 Zhang Xuemei Liu Ruiru This short commentary, published in Study Times in March 2025, asks what the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Council (canshenghui) contributed to building a New Democratic regime during the War of Resistance against Japan. Zhang and Liu argue that it was the earliest, most fully developed and most typical democratic institution in the anti-Japanese base areas, and that it was a model for other bases. The article draws on four council sessions held between 1939 and 1946. It first describes the basic framework of the regime that the council explored, then its effects on governance in the border region, and finally four lessons drawn from the experience. On structure, the authors point to a three-tier system of border-region, county and township councils, and to the 1946 Principles of the Constitution of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. They also stress the "three-thirds system", under which Communists, non-Party left-progressives and centrists each held one third of seats, and they cite the 1941 session's 219 delegates and more than 380 proposals. In Zhang and Liu's account, the council united social strata, including enlightened gentry and ethnic minority figures. It improved decision-making, for example through Li Dingming's proposal for "crack troops and simple administration". It also laid a foundation for the people's congress system and for the system of multiparty cooperation and political consultation led by the Communist Party. The authors list four lessons: upholding Party leadership, ensuring the people are masters of the country, maintaining criticism and self-criticism, and seeking truth from facts. They present these as historical experience for whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how the Party presents its wartime base-area councils as precursors of present-day political institutions.

Mao Zedong's exploration of opposing neo-colonialism and its implications 毛泽东反对新殖民主义的探索与启示 Xia Shaoguang Xia Shaoguang asks how the People's Republic avoided the fate of many newly independent states, which escaped old colonialism only to meet neo-colonialism. The article argues that this owed much to Mao Zedong's foresight and to the struggle he led. Seen through opposition to neo-colonialism, Xia contends, China's socialist modernization breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization and clarifies Mao's contribution to Chinese modernization. The article opens with the shift from old to new colonialism. It draws on the 1960s polemic against the Soviet leadership and on Mao's 1949 editorials on the US White Paper on China. It then sets out six areas of Mao-era policy: defending sovereignty, clearing away colonial remnants, economic strategy, selective opening to the outside world, new principles of international relations, and theoretical and cultural critique. A comparative section follows, covering the whole history of the PRC, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, early US and German capitalist development, and the wider developing world. The conclusion draws three lessons. Xia defines neo-colonialism as indirect control of formally independent states through economic, ideological and proxy means. In Xia's account, Mao's answer combined the Korean War, the policy of 'cleaning the house before inviting guests', socialist transformation, and building an independent and relatively complete industrial and national economic system. It also combined self-reliance, with foreign aid secondary, and aid to Asia, Africa and Latin America without political conditions. In the comparative section, Xia argues that Japan, South Korea and Taiwan modernized in dependence on the United States, and that Japan's long stagnation is a result of neo-colonialism. Xia also argues that the United States and Germany won autonomy through class oppression at home and later imperial expansion, whereas China, in Xia's telling, did neither and so shows the superiority of socialism. Xia concludes that Mao's anti-neo-colonial exploration laid the foundation for the period of reform and opening up, and that the two periods form a continuous whole. Xia criticises tendencies that downplay or deny the pre-reform era, idealise the 'Four Little Dragons' or beautify colonialism, and calls for continued criticism of comprador culture. Xia also calls for drawing on this experience in the current 'great struggle' against US pressure and against Western claims of Chinese 'neo-colonialism'. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Mao-era policy to Chinese modernization and to present-day debates on dependency and the Global South.

A historical examination of the Shenzhen Special Zone currency in the early reform and opening-up period 改革开放初期深圳特区货币的历史考察 Xiao Anmiao Between 1979 and 1985 the central government planned to issue a freely convertible local currency in the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone, but in the end decided not to. Xiao Anmiao notes that existing studies of this "special zone currency" mostly stress the effects of opening to the outside world. The article instead reads the episode as a case of central–local relations. Xiao argues that the plan was dropped because it could not be reconciled with managing the relationship between the zone and the rest of the planned economy, and with the shift of reform from the local to the national level. Drawing on leaders' speeches, State Council and People's Bank of China documents, and local statistics, the article follows the plan through three rounds of deliberation. The first began in 1979, when Guangdong raised the issue, and ended in suspension in 1982. The second was driven by the Hong Kong negotiations from 1982 to 1983. The third began in 1984 around Deng Xiaoping's inspection tour and ended with rejection in 1985. Before these, the article sketches the pressures of the planned economy, the dual-track price system and the Bretton Woods background. Xiao's central claim is that the currency question followed from the policy of "relaxing the first line and controlling the second line". Freer use of Hong Kong dollars in Shenzhen brought a "three-currency" situation of renminbi, foreign exchange certificates and Hong Kong dollars. According to the author's data, the renminbi's share of circulation fell sharply, and reverse flows of goods and certificates into the interior drew criticism in 1982. Central figures such as Chen Yun feared that the second line could not be held and that the zone would harm the non-special-zone economy. Others, including Deng Xiaoping, worried about the impact on the renminbi, but also saw a currency as needed to attract foreign capital and to prepare for Hong Kong's return. Xiao treats the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress's 1985 rejection, on the ground that "one country should not have two currencies", as the point where the argument settled. Xiao concludes that China then had three kinds of economic region (planned, experimental, highly marketised), with Shenzhen as the pivot between them. As reform spread from points to the whole country, local currency reform became comprehensive currency reform, and the special zone currency was abandoned. The author warns against treating reform and opening up as a simple linear process, since this case shows its complexity. Read the original if you are interested in the history of Shenzhen, monetary policy and the Party's internal decision-making during reform and opening up, or in a documented case of central–local bargaining.

A brief discussion of Shao Yong's atheist thought ​邵雍无神论思想略论 Cao Dong Scholarship on Northern Song atheism has centred on Zhang Zai, and Shao Yong (1011–1077), one of the "Five Masters" of the period and a forerunner of Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism, has often been classed as a theist. Cao Dong takes up this neglect and argues that Shao was in substance an atheist. The article says that his qi-based cosmology, his account of the human "spirit", his critique of ghosts and immortals, and his stress on human agency together opposed popular belief in spirits. The article first sets out the background: Neo-Confucianism arose as a revival of Confucianism against Buddhism and Daoism and against the theologised Confucianism of the Han, while Northern Song natural science, including Shen Kuo's work and the notion of investigating the "principle" (li) of things, supplied intellectual resources. It then analyses four aspects of Shao's thought. A final section assesses his contribution and limitations. Cao's central moves are as follows. Shao treated the primordial "one qi", divided into yin and yang, as the source of all things. His "spirit" (shen) is the marvellous transformative function of this qi, and things follow a cycle of qi, number, image, vessel and back to qi, governed by regularities of "twofold" and "fourfold" division rather than by a personal god. His "human spirit" is read as mind or consciousness that arises from bodily essence-qi, as the purging of selfish thoughts, and as the source of intentions, none of which implies a deity. Ghosts and spirits are held to be yin-yang qi gathering and dispersing, and Shao is said to have rejected ghosts, immortals and "improper sacrifices", stressing that fortune and misfortune come from human beings and not from heaven. He is also said to have valued human knowing ("observing things through principle") and upheld Confucian ethics against Buddhist renunciation. Cao concludes that Shao's system, like Zhang Zai's, used qi theory against religious theology, and that it did so with more speculative depth, closer ties to natural science, and a higher estimate of human value. Cao also grants limits: his number-image cosmology can slide toward theism, his denial of traditional spirits is incomplete, and his "shen" has pantheist or deist colouring. Cao closes by calling for the removal of religious-theological elements from traditional culture and the excavation of its atheist elements. Read the original if you study Chinese atheism, Song Neo-Confucianism or Shao Yong's cosmology and want a case for reading him as an atheist thinker.

Party Leadership Group of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences conveys and studies the spirit of the national Two Sessions 中共中国社会科学院党组传达学习全国两会精神 This is a short news report from Chinese Social Sciences Net on an enlarged meeting of the Party Leadership Group of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), held on 12 March 2025. The meeting conveyed and studied General Secretary Xi Jinping's speeches during the national Two Sessions and the spirit of the sessions, and planned how to put them into practice. The meeting was chaired by CASS President and Party Leadership Group Secretary Gao Xiang, who also spoke. Vice-presidents Peng Jinhui, Zhen Zhanmin and Zhao Rui, discipline inspection team head Hang Yuanxiang and Secretary-General Zhao Zhimin attended, along with the deputy secretary-general and heads of CASS units. According to the report, the meeting judged this year's Two Sessions especially significant because they fall at the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan and the start of planning for the 15th. It said they bear on implementing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Gao stressed that CASS is a political organ centred on research. He called for deeper understanding of the Two Establishes, support for the Two Upholds and the Four-sphere Confidence, and a lead role in studying Xi's speeches. He also asked for better research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, reform of institutions, training of talent, and stronger conversion of research results into practice. The meeting concluded that studying the Two Sessions is a major political task for CASS now and for some time ahead. It called for consolidating the Academy's political-development framework of "three consensuses, three commitments and three measures", and for a wave of study and publicity, so as to drive high-quality development at CASS. Read the original if you want a brief record of how CASS leadership formally frames its political tasks and institutional priorities after the 2025 Two Sessions.

Advancing the Party's self-reform through the building of intra-Party regulations 以党内法规制度建设推进党的自我革命 Jiang Xueyi Chen Jinzhao Jiang Xueyi and Chen Jinzhao, writing in a Chinese Social Sciences Today commentary of March 2025, ask what role intra-Party regulations play in the Communist Party's self-reform. They argue that building such regulations is both a support and a guarantee for deepening the Party's self-reform. They treat it as an important measure for achieving that goal. The piece has two parts. The first sets out why regulation-building is a key link. The second sets out specific measures. It draws on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), the 20th Party Congress report, and recent documents such as the 2023–2027 planning outline for central Party regulations. On the first part, the authors say intra-Party regulations form the core of the institutional system for self-reform. They contend that these regulations underpin full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and anti-corruption work, and that they improve the quality and effectiveness of the Party's self-supervision. As evidence they cite the revised disciplinary punishment regulations (January 2024), the Party discipline study campaign (April–July 2024) and the revised inspection regulations (February 2024). On measures, they call for continuous improvement of the regulatory system, better quality in rule-making, abolition of outdated rules, and fewer declaratory or merely guiding rules. They also want regulations to make Party leadership more scientific and standardised. Finally, they urge linking correction of the "four undesirable work styles" with discipline and anti-corruption, since corruption often hides in such problems and early-stage work relies on Party rules rather than state law. The authors conclude that self-reform has run through the Party's history and is the basis of its historical initiative. They call for governing the Party by institutions and regulations, and for a virtuous cycle in which the Party uses its own strength to find problems, correct deviations and raise governing capacity. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how Chinese legal scholars link intra-Party regulations to self-reform and anti-corruption.

Understanding the two dimensions of the anti-corruption struggle Historical vision and strategic height 认识反腐败斗争的双重维度 Zhu Jie Zhu Jie's commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in March 2025, asks how the significance of the anti-corruption struggle should be understood as the Party pursues further comprehensively deepening reform and Chinese modernization. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2025), Zhu argues that the struggle must be viewed with a "historical vision" and from a "strategic height", tied to the Party's mission and tasks. On this reading, such a view strengthens the Party's resolve to see the struggle through to the end. The article has three parts. The first treats historical vision and strategic height as two methods for judging the "time" and the "trend" of the struggle. The second examines Xi's formulation of the "two historical initiatives" won through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The third sets out the dialectical relationship between anti-corruption work and further comprehensively deepening reform, and ends with practical implications. Zhu says that questions have arisen about how long the struggle will last and whether it will cool down, and that these call for a scientific method. A historical vision places the struggle within the history of the Party, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the rise and fall of socialist states. The "two historical initiatives" are, in Xi's words, keeping the Party from changing in nature, colour or flavour, and uniting the people behind national rejuvenation. Zhu links them to lessons from the ruling parties of some socialist states, citing Marx and Lenin on discipline and corruption. A strategic height, in turn, treats anti-corruption work and reform as aligned in goals and coherent in logic: stricter standards empower reform, while reform spirit and institution-building raise governance capacity. Zhu stresses that the two are not in a zero-sum or opposing relationship. Zhu concludes that the struggle is neither temporary nor static, and must be upgraded as reform proceeds. The article calls for clearing existing corruption while curbing new cases, removing the soil in which corruption grows, making political supervision concrete and routine, reducing formalism at the grassroots, improving Party regulations and national anti-corruption legislation, and building a disciplined and law-governed discipline inspection and supervision force. Read the original if you want an example of how a legal scholar in the Party-building field presents the official rationale for continuing the anti-corruption campaign alongside the reform agenda.

Exploring the essence and laws of ideological and political theory courses 探求思想政治理论课的本质和规律 Tian Xinming How should one understand what China's school courses in ideological and political theory (sizheng courses) fundamentally are, and what regularities govern teaching them well? Tian Xinming takes up this question as an attempt to give the construction of these courses a more systematic, theoretically grounded form, drawing on Xi Jinping's remarks on the subject. The article's thesis is that the essence of the courses is "reasoning" (jiang daoli), that this demands explaining principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly, and that good teaching follows identifiable laws. The article has four parts. It first defines the essence of the courses; it then explains what "deeply, thoroughly and vividly" means; it then treats the eight "unities" that Xi set out in 2019 as the laws of classroom teaching; and it finally turns to the laws of teacher development. Tian draws throughout on Xi, Mao Zedong, Lenin, Marx and Engels, and uses the method of contradiction analysis. Tian argues that the "reasoning" in question is theory, and fundamentally Marxist theory. This follows from Marxism's guiding position in the Party and state, from its distinctive character as scientific and people-centred, and from the courses' particular role within the curriculum. Explaining "deeply" means moving from phenomena to essence and answering "why". Explaining "thoroughly" means tracing arguments to two root principles: that the world is unified in matter, and that the people are the creators of history. Tian adds that these principles are finally verified by social practice, not by logic. Explaining "vividly" means teaching a living Marxism, avoiding dogmatism and pragmatism, and presenting it as a system. The eight unities are read as eight contradictions to be handled, for example between political and academic character, values and knowledge, indoctrination and heuristic teaching, and explicit and implicit education. For teachers, Tian proposes three laws. They should aim at the six qualities Xi listed: strong politics, deep feeling, fresh thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline and upright character. They should master Marxism as their "home-grown skill" by reading the original works systematically. They should also unite reading, teaching and research around the same teaching priorities. The author presents these as the practical regularities behind well-run courses. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese theorists justify the content, method and teacher training of the ideological and political courses.

On the determination and attribution of Party discipline responsibility 论党纪责任的认定与归结 Zhu Linfang Between a disciplinary violation and a punishment lies the question of responsibility. Zhu Linfang argues that, as Party disciplinary practice has matured, "Party discipline responsibility" has separated out from "violation" and "sanction" to become an independent normative element, which makes its determination and attribution the key step in handling disciplinary cases. The article notes that no systematic theory yet exists on this, and that arbitrary enforcement and over-broad accountability are linked to the lack of a unified mechanism for attributing responsibility. Working from a normative-science perspective, Zhu traces the revisions of the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China (1997 trial version, 2003, 2015, 2018 and the current text) and draws on enforcement experience. The article has three parts: the place of responsibility within the constitution of a violation; the basic elements by which responsibility is determined; and proposals for improving the mechanism. Zhu's central move is to show that the older "four-element theory", modelled on criminal law, has given way to a "two-tier system" of "objective rule-breaking plus subjective culpability", in which culpability is judged only after a violation is found. The Regulations now contain four elements: capacity for responsibility as the basis, subjective fault (intent or negligence, via Article 19) as the content, force majeure and similar grounds as exclusions, and proportionality between fault and punishment. Zhu reads this as Party discipline's acceptance of the "principle of responsibility" already found in criminal and administrative sanctions. Zhu then proposes presuming fault, so that a Party member whose conduct caused loss must show absence of fault. Zhu also calls for defined standards and types of duty of care, set through guiding cases. Proportionality should be applied systematically, citing cases of over-punishment of trivial conduct and a drink-driving inconsistency. The "etc." in "force majeure and other causes" should be read as open-ended, with caution. "No Party discipline responsibility" should be read narrowly as excluding formal sanctions but not non-sanction measures such as warning education or organisational adjustment. Zhu concludes that the Regulations have established the basic elements of responsibility, but that how fault is determined, how duty of care is set, how proportionality is applied, what other exclusions exist and what the exemption clause covers all remain without settled rules. Zhu calls for further clarification through interpretation, guiding cases and typology, so as to build a more scientific mechanism. Read the original if you study Party discipline regulation, or the borrowing of criminal-law doctrines such as culpability and duty of care into intra-Party rules, and want the detailed argument and cited cases.

The "Two Integrations": historical context, theoretical logic, practical power and path of development “两个结合”：历史脉络、理论逻辑、实践伟力与发展进路 Wang Fei Wang Fei takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the Two Integrations are the Party's "greatest magic weapon" for success. These are the integration of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The article argues that grasping their history, theory, practical force and future course deepens the Party's understanding of how to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It holds that theoretical innovation should keep resting on practical innovation. The article has four parts. The first traces the history of the "first integration" and the "second integration" and the "historic leaps" each produced. The second sets out the theoretical logic. The third examines the practical power of the Two Integrations in achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The fourth sets out the path ahead. The author draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and above all Xi Jinping, together with Engels and Lenin. Wang reads Party history as a continuous effort. It runs from Mao's 1938 call to "Sinify" Marxism and his 1956 idea of a "second integration" to Xi's formulation of the Two Integrations in 2021. The "second integration" is presented as the logical extension of the first. The first joins theory to practice, while the second joins a theoretical system to a national cultural form. The theoretical logic rests on four points: the law of Marxism's development, the needs of revolution, construction and reform, the inner compatibility of Marxism with fine traditional culture, and the Party's own subjective consciousness. Wang cites Guo Moruo's 1925 dialogue between Marx and Confucius as an image of that compatibility. The practical power is illustrated by the Party's central tasks in each period and by the opening of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author also links the Two Integrations to strengthening cultural subjectivity and to guarding against cultural nihilism and "Westernization". Wang proposes three directions. The first is to hold both the "soul" (Marxism) and the "roots" (fine traditional culture), so that Marxism becomes "Chinese" and tradition becomes "modern". The second is to fuse the essence of each, with Marxism keeping its guiding role while opposing both cultural nihilism and cultural restorationism. The third is to draw fresh experience from the people's practice, so that theory gathers popular wisdom and benefits the people. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-orthodox account of how the Two Integrations are historically framed and justified in current Chinese theoretical writing.

How the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind extends and elevates Marx's theory of world history 论人类命运共同体理念对马克思世界历史理论的拓展与升华 Fu Xiaonan Yan Yuxuan Fu and Yan start from what they call a period of great changes unseen in a century, in which the questions "What is wrong with the world?" and "Where is humanity heading?" press on policymakers. They argue that Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind answers these questions. In their reading it is both a continuation and an extension of Marx's theory of world history, and in some respects a step beyond it. The article has two main sections. The first, on "logical coupling", compares the two bodies of thought on three points: their philosophical foundation, their value orientation and their ideal destination. The second, on "practical path", sets out three innovations the authors attribute to the idea: of agent, of thinking and of practice. It closes by describing five features of the world the idea aims at. On continuity, the authors say both rest on historical materialism, which Marx set against Hegel's "absolute spirit". Both aim at the free and all-round development of the human being, and both look to communism as the final goal. On innovation, they claim Marx's theory made the proletariat the agent of world history, whereas the shared-future idea widens the agent to the peoples of all countries. They also say Marx's theory pointed to class struggle against the bourgeoisie, while today's coexistence of capitalism and socialism calls for cooperation and win-win outcomes. In this account Marx criticised capitalist exploitation without denying capitalism's historical contribution, so the idea draws on the Chinese tradition of harmony to release capitalism's productive potential. It also favours dialogue over confrontation and partnership over alliance. The authors conclude that the idea offers a practical route to a new international order based on mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation. They describe it as a world of lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and inclusiveness, and a clean and beautiful environment. They present this as Chinese wisdom for global problems and as a development of Marxism's own goal. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars justify the shared-future idea as a theoretical extension of Marx's world-history theory, especially its shift from class struggle to cooperation.

The leading role of universities in integrating ideological and political theory courses across university, secondary and primary schools 论高校在大中小学思政课一体化建设中的引领作用 Xu Ruifang Wu Yutong Xu Ruifang and Wu Yutong ask how universities can best lead the integrated construction of ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) across university, secondary and primary schools. Their answer is that universities should act on the strategic importance the Party Central Committee attaches to this work, including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and use their strengths in disciplines, theory, teachers and resources to guide high-quality, content-based development of integration. The article has three parts. The first defines four roles for universities: interpreter of policy and theory, solver of teaching-research problems, trainer of teachers, and developer of high-quality resources. The second identifies three difficulties: weak links between curriculum standards and textbooks, insufficient conversion of theoretical findings into classroom practice, and limited exchange between school stages. The third sets out a path of leadership through ideas, personnel, content and methods. On the diagnosis, the authors report that university courses have no curriculum standards of their own, that primary-school goals are more detailed than those of later stages, and that textbooks repeat material or invert the order of difficulty. They give examples, such as a high-school textbook on the new development philosophy that is more detailed than its university counterpart. They also say that some research stays at the level of theoretical frameworks and that university teachers know little about what is taught in schools below them. In response, the authors call for a unified curriculum standard across all stages that still respects the differences between them, with universities taking part in drafting it. They propose that universities support the move from disciplinary theory to textbooks and then to teaching, and that they train teachers through both pre-service and in-service programmes, with teacher-training universities in the lead. They also advocate practice-based teaching using local red-culture resources, together with digital platforms and regional databases shared among universities and schools. Throughout, they frame Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the core content of the courses. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how education researchers describe the policy problems and proposed institutional measures for integrating ideological and political courses across school stages.

Carrying forward the spirit of the Zunyi Conference and continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 弘扬遵义会议精神 不断推进马克思主义中国化时代化 Xin Xiangyang Xin Xiangyang takes the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, held during the Long March, as a turning point in the Party's history. The article asks what lessons its spirit offers for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Xin argues that the conference's experience points to five requirements: a strong leadership core, the Two Integrations, seeking truth from facts, independence and self-reliance, and Party unity. This is a commentary in a Party theory journal, framed by Xi Jinping's 2015 and 2021 remarks at Zunyi and in Guizhou. Xin first recounts the background: the failure of the fifth encirclement campaign under the "Left" dogmatist line, the fall in Central Red Army strength from over 86,000 to just over 30,000, and the formation of a new three-person military group in March 1935. Each of the five sections then pairs a historical episode with quotations from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Party resolutions, and ends with a task for the new era. Xin's central claim is that the conference dealt with more than military and organisational errors. In this account it settled the question of independence and self-reliance: whether the Chinese revolution would follow the Comintern and dogmatism or find its own path under Marxism-Leninism. Xin presents the Zunyi leaders' open and inclusive conduct as evidence of both Marxist truth and the wisdom of fine traditional Chinese culture, and describes the meeting's broad participation and criticism and self-criticism as a model of democratic centralism. Xin also treats the conference as the start of Mao's leadership of the first-generation central leadership, and links this to the present by calling Xi Jinping the main founder of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and by invoking the Two Establishes. Xin concludes that, on the new journey, Party members should study Xi's directives, uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and continue the Two Integrations. They should also address China's own problems from its national conditions, and maintain unity around the Central Committee with Xi at its core, so as to advance Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Party theorist presents the Zunyi Conference as a source of current doctrine on leadership, theoretical innovation and Party discipline.

On the deep integration of artificial intelligence and ideological and political education 人工智能与思想政治教育的深度融合论要 Ren Zhifeng Liu Yang Ren Zhifeng and Liu Yang take up a problem they see in the current "AI+" research boom in education: an application-driven approach must decide which side leads. If education leads and AI is only an external tool, its potential is wasted; if AI leads, education risks technological domination and loss of its political and humanistic character. Following Xi Jinping's call to promote the deep integration of AI and education, the authors argue for moving from an "application orientation" to "deep integration", which they describe as a chemical rather than a physical reaction, and apply this to ideological and political education. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the preconditions for integration; the second analyses its complex effects on ideological and political education; the third proposes possible paths. The authors draw on Marx's remarks on machinery, instruments of labour and technology, and on Horkheimer and Marcuse for the ideological character of technology. On preconditions, the authors treat AI in three roles: as a technical means, as an infrastructure comparable to the steam engine, electricity and the internet, and as a marker of a new "intelligent civilisation". Each, they argue, matches a feature of ideological and political education: its technical logic, its changing forms, and its innovative development. On effects, they claim integration sharpens its essential ideological attribute, since AI carries implicit ideological functions and risks. It also brings out the meaning of human life, because the field must counter feelings of being replaced by machines. It makes practice more flexible through simulated and ubiquitous scenes, "strong interaction" between educator and learner, and quantified, precise evaluation. For paths, the authors propose complementing strengths: big data to digitise, deep learning to make the field more intelligent, and computing power to make it more scientific. They propose linking functions across "what machines can do", "what humans and machines can do together" and "what humans can do". They also call for coordinated development that addresses legitimacy, effectiveness and innovation, keeping the cultivation of virtue and the human subject's leading role as the fixed value coordinates. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education justify and structure AI integration, and how they combine Marxist technology theory with practical proposals.

The Zunyi Conference: turning a new page 遵义会议：翻开了新的一页 Yang Mingwei This short historical commentary, published in the Party journal Dangjian in 2025, revisits the Zunyi Conference of 15–17 January 1935. Yang Mingwei argues that the meeting was a life-and-death turning point in Party history. In Yang's account, it in effect established Mao Zedong's leadership in the Party Central Committee and the Red Army, began the formation of a first-generation central leadership collective with Mao at its core, and opened a new stage in which the Party solved China's revolutionary problems independently. The article follows events in three stages. It first traces the run-up: the heavy losses at the Xiang River at the end of 1934, the dispute over where the Central Red Army should go, and the successive meetings at Tongdao, Liping and Houchang, ending with the capture of Zunyi on 7 January 1935. It then describes the conference itself and Mao's role in it. Finally it follows the weeks after the conference, including the battle at Tucheng, the Four Crossings of the Chishui River, and the Gougba meeting. Yang's central argument is that the conference's substance was a verdict on the military line. Mao criticised Bo Gu's explanation that enemy strength caused the defeat of the fifth anti-encirclement campaign, and attributed it to errors in command, strategy and tactics. In Yang's account, Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De) had replaced mobile warfare with positional and blockhouse warfare. The meeting, according to the article, added Mao to the Politburo Standing Committee, abolished the "three-person group" and stripped Bo Gu and Li De of supreme military command. Yang adds that Zhang Wentian then took over general responsibility from Bo Gu, with Mao's agreement, and that a new three-man military group of Zhou Enlai, Mao and Wang Jiaxiang was formed after Gougba. Yang concludes that Zunyi ended the rule of Wang Ming's "Left" adventurism in the Central Committee. The article credits it with saving the Party, the Red Army and the revolution, and with laying the foundation for completing the Long March. After it, Yang writes, the Party began to apply the basic principles of Marxism-Leninism independently and became politically mature. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed narrative of the Zunyi Conference and the weeks around it, as presented in a Party publication.

General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on Party building: current state of research and outlook “习近平总书记关于党的建设的重要思想”研究现状分析与展望 Chen Jinlong This article is a literature review of Chinese scholarship on "General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on Party building". The concept was formally put forward at the National Organization Work Conference in Beijing in June 2023, which summarised its core content in the "thirteen upholds". Chen Jinlong surveys the research produced since then and argues that it has advanced considerably but still has substantial room to grow.
