The review covers five clusters of work: the grounds on which the thinking took shape, its content system, its theoretical characteristics, its value and significance, and its practical requirements. It then identifies three features of the scholarship and closes with three directions for future research. The article appeared in the journal Party Building in 2025. On the grounds of formation, Chen reports that scholars point to four dimensions: history (traditional Chinese culture and the Party's tradition of strict self-governance), reality, theory (the inheritance and development of Marxist Party-building theory) and practice. Some add a subjective condition, namely Xi's own experience and abilities. On content, researchers describe an organic whole built around full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, with its methodology and original contributions. Its characteristics are said to be originality, systematic coherence, scientific character, a people-centred orientation and practicality. Practical requirements discussed include upholding the Party's overall leadership, using the Party's self-reform to guide social revolution, and building a high-quality cadre force. Chen finds the scholarship marked by a union of political and scholarly approaches, of historical and contemporary study, and of theoretical exposition and practical pathways. The author nonetheless sees gaps: research mostly elaborates the "thirteen upholds" and pays too little attention to the underlying texts, uses fairly traditional methods, and has not linked the thinking enough to other parts of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Chen calls for a return to the texts, multidisciplinary work including big-data methods, and a wider global view of the thinking's meaning for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a brief map of how Chinese academics currently frame and study Xi's Party-building thought, and of where the author thinks research should go next.

Developing new quality productive forces with patient capital: Chinese and Western variants, dual attributes and practical paths 以耐心资本发展新质生产力：中西分野、二重属性与实践探索 He Cheng Gao Hepeng Lin Peng He Cheng, Gao Hepeng and Lin Peng ask how "patient capital" (long-term, steady investment capital) can be built up to develop new quality productive forces. They take up the policy call in the Third Plenum decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to develop patient capital. Their thesis is that Chinese patient capital differs in kind from its Western counterpart, carries both the general attributes of capital and a special long-term, steady character, and can drive technological innovation, total factor productivity and industrial upgrading, provided current obstacles are removed. The article has six parts. It first compares Western and Chinese patient capital through the history of economic thought. It then analyses the dual attributes of patient capital in a Marxist framework, sets out its value for new quality productive forces, and identifies constraints in China's capital market. It ends with practical paths and a short conclusion. Sources include Marx's Capital, Mariana Mazzucato's work, Keynesian investment theory, and Chinese statistics on turnover, basic research spending and patent commercialisation. The authors argue that Western patient capital rests on the factor-value theory and on Western investment theory. In their account this reduces capital to a production factor, drifts toward finance and speculation, and makes patience hard to sustain. Chinese patient capital, they say, rests on the labour theory of value and on a long-termist investment tradition. It is led by the Party, centred on state capital, and meant to serve the people. Drawing on Marx, they hold that patient capital shares capital's drive to self-valorisation, but chooses long holding periods and prudent management as a strategy. They attribute its usefulness to its role as a "fund stabiliser" for innovation and its pull of capital away from M–M′ speculation toward industrial capital. The authors identify four obstacles: short-termism in the capital market, citing an annual stock turnover of 273% against 102% in the United States; weak long-term investment appetite among both state and private capital; blockages in the technology–industry–finance cycle, such as a 3.9% industrialisation rate for university invention patents; and incomplete exit mechanisms. They propose responsible (ESG) investment, a guiding role for state capital, broader sources of funds (government funds, pension funds, insurance capital, regulated international capital), and a better market environment. They conclude that only under the Party's centralised leadership can patient capital become a driver of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese economic-policy argument on patient capital, with its Marxist justification and the statistics it cites.

Using sinicised Marxism to excavate and elucidate China's fine traditional culture 以中国化的马克思主义挖掘和阐发中华优秀传统文化 Lin Jinping Starting from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its call to carry forward fine traditional Chinese culture within Chinese modernization, Lin asks which theoretical tool is suited to "excavating and elucidating" that culture. The answer is that neither rationalised modern Western culture nor a conservative, self-enclosed Chinese tradition will do. Only adapted or sinicised Marxism (Marxism in its Chinese form) can serve. The article is in four parts. It first examines Western readings of Chinese culture, mainly Hegel and Weber, with Russell as a contrast. It then assesses a purely tradition-internal approach, discussing Confucianism's "family-state isomorphism", the gap between official Confucianism and practical Legalism, and the role of rural society. The third part argues for sinicised Marxism, drawing on Marx, Engels and Mao Zedong. The last part sets out three methodological requirements. Lin argues that Hegel and Weber judged China by Western political experience, notably the split between civil society and the political state, and by a faith in reason. In the author's view, this made them see Chinese culture as lacking subjectivity and a civil-society spirit, and it hid the Daoist and Buddhist longing for life outside politics. A purely internal approach, by contrast, understands the tradition but cannot lead it into modernity. Lin holds that Confucian ethics often functioned as an ideal or ideology in politics and took effect mainly in villages and families, which have since changed. Marxism, in Lin's account, disenchants Western rationalism and insists on concrete historical conditions. It must be adapted to China, treating Chinese culture as part of China's "actual conditions" and handling it dialectically, as Mao urged: discarding feudal dross and absorbing democratic essence. Lin proposes three requirements. First, respect and understand the tradition and keep close to it. Second, treat excavation as nurturing a living organism rather than mining a resource, achieving creative transformation and innovative development. Third, enter into equal, subject-to-subject dialogue with tradition, avoiding any prophet-like posture (the Zhuangzi fable of Hundun is the warning). Lin adds that what counts as "fine" is historically conditioned, so present judgements need self-reflection and humility. Read the original if you want a philosophical account of how Party theory justifies using Marxism to engage China's cultural heritage, including its readings of Hegel, Weber and Confucianism.

Methodological guide and key directions for developing new quality productive forces through further comprehensively deepening reform 以进一步全面深化改革发展新质生产力的方法指南和着力方向 Xia Wenbin Zhang Chuqiao Xia Wenbin and Zhang Chuqiao ask how new quality productive forces can be developed on a sustainable basis. Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that this requires further comprehensively deepening reform and forming new relations of production suited to it, as well as the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), they argue that reform must target the institutional blockages that hold these forces back. Their thesis is that further comprehensive reform is both the necessary route and a source of method and direction. The article, published in Shandong Social Sciences in 2025, has three parts. The first sets out the significance of the approach: for Marxist productive-force theory, for the practice of reform and opening up, and for world modernization. The second draws a methodological guide from the "three greater emphases" in the Third Plenum's Decision: systems integration, priority on key points, and practical results. The third names two main directions for effort: integrated reform of education, science and technology, and talent, and a higher-level system of opening up. In the authors' account, new quality productive forces carry forward Marx's view of the dynamics of social development, which covers the internal structure of the productive forces, their contradiction with the relations of production, and the combined force of economic, political and cultural factors. They also see it as a continuation of reform-era thinking from Deng Xiaoping to Xi. Under systems integration, they list five relationships to handle: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, development and security. They argue that capitalism cannot institutionally unite efficiency and fairness, and that socialism can. Under key points, they stress innovation, inclusiveness of ownership forms, a unified national market, fair competition and resilient supply chains. Under results, they call for target-setting, local adaptation, coordinated factor inputs and scientific evaluation, including an index of new quality productive forces. On the directions for effort, the authors call for strategic linkage of education, science and technology, and talent. They also call for stronger original, integrated and open innovation, and for joint training and operating mechanisms linking universities, firms and research bodies. They further propose institutional opening up, alignment with high international standards, and participation in reforming global economic governance. They present this as a way to bring about a different paradigm of world modernization built on common prosperity and cooperation. Read the original if you want a policy-oriented account of how Chinese scholars connect the Third Plenum's reform agenda to new quality productive forces, including concrete institutional recommendations.

Twenty-first-century Marxism in the perspective of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动视域中的21世纪马克思主义 Tao Wenzhao Tao Wenzhao takes up a formula from the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which called Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era "contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism". The article asks what "twenty-first-century Marxism" means and why the label fits this body of thought. Tao answers that the label marks an epoch-making theoretical innovation, grounded in the history of Marxism and of the international communist movement, and that China is its natural centre. The article is organised in five parts. It analyses in turn the time dimension ("twenty-first century"), the geographical dimension ("world"), the historical tasks that the concept implies, China's responsibility for fulfilling them, and the theoretical standing of the concept within the lineage of Marxism. Tao compares earlier theoretical landmarks, such as Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, with the way each was named and assessed in Party documents. Tao argues first that a theory's "era" is not mere calendar time: it is defined by changes in the epoch's themes, revolutionary subjects, contradictions and tasks. Twenty-first-century Marxism should therefore address new themes and contradictions of the century, and Tao notes that the era still needs a precise substantive characterisation. Second, the unstated geographical default is the world, because Marxism is inherently global. Tao points to irreversible globalisation and to a changing contest between the two systems, which the author describes as "the East rising, the West declining" as a trend, while the United States remains stronger than China in the present. Third, Tao holds that the concept must solve problems left open: revolution in developed countries, socialist construction, and coexistence and competition with capitalism. Because the world socialist movement's centre has shifted to China, Tao argues, China's Marxism is the principal form of twenty-first-century Marxism, and some foreign Marxist currents are described as largely confined to the study. Tao concludes that Xi Jinping Thought, by advancing Marxist theory in many fields and by proposing a community with a shared future for mankind, forms the mainstream of world Marxism in this century. Tao distinguishes "twenty-first-century Marxism" (a proper name for this thought) from "Marxism of the twenty-first century" (the plural Marxisms existing in the period), and says other countries' explorations also have value. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of the international communist movement justifies the claim that Chinese Marxism leads the world Marxist tradition in this century.

Lenin's critique of erroneous currents of thought in the period of the New Economic Policy 新经济政策时期列宁对错误思潮的批判 Wang Jianing After the New Economic Policy (NEP) was launched in spring 1921, Russian intellectual life became increasingly lively and a range of mistaken currents of thought, the article argues, disturbed public opinion and undermined the ideological basis on which the Party led the people. Wang Jianing examines how Lenin criticised the main currents and what ideas he developed in doing so. The author holds that revisiting this critique still has practical significance today. The article is organised around four targets of Lenin's criticism. These are: petty-bourgeois reformism and petty-bourgeois revolutionism over the NEP; the mechanical economic determinism of Sukhanov and others on Russia's road of development; the anarcho-syndicalism of the Trotskyists, the Workers' Opposition and the Democratic Centralists in the trade-union debate; and the Proletkult's narrow and impatient view of culture. Wang draws on Lenin's texts such as 'On the Tax in Kind', 'Our Revolution' and 'Better Fewer, But Better', and on the positions of Plekhanov, Kautsky, Bogdanov and Pletnev. Wang reports that Lenin read the NEP debate as a question of where Russia was heading. He answered the Change-of-Landmarks group, who expected degeneration into capitalism, by insisting that capitalism be developed under a socialist orientation, and he answered the 'revolutionary phrase-mongers' by arguing that capitalism, compared with small-scale production, was a step forward. For Lenin, in Wang's account, the Party had to learn to use and master capital, directing it into state capitalism. Against Sukhanov's economic determinism, Lenin held that the general laws of history presuppose particular forms of development, so Russia could first seize power and then create the conditions for socialism. Against anarcho-syndicalism, he insisted on the Party's centralised, unified leadership and on trade unions as schools and transmission belts rather than state organs. Against the Proletkult, he stressed Party leadership of culture, reliance on the broad masses and specialists, and raising the people's cultural level, starting with literacy and the status of teachers. Wang concludes that Lenin's critiques defended the socialist direction of the NEP, the political legitimacy of the October Revolution, the Party's leadership and a realistic approach to cultural construction. Wang presents them as ideas of lasting relevance for socialist construction. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of Lenin's late polemics, from the NEP to the trade-union and Proletkult debates, as presented in the Chinese Marxist literature.

Two key focal points for improving the Party's institutions and mechanisms of Party building 深刻把握完善党的建设制度机制的两个着力点 Kang Xiaoqiang Tang Yinxiao This short commentary, excerpted from a longer piece in Qianxian (2025, no. 3), asks how the Party should deepen reform of its Party-building system. Kang and Tang argue that the decisive focal point is mobilising the enthusiasm, initiative and creativity of the whole Party to drive reform and development. They present this as the basic purpose of institutional reform: upholding and strengthening Party leadership. The authors start from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. They read its Party-building provisions as continuous with the general requirements for Party building in the new era. The article then develops the point in two directions: the morale of Party members and cadres, and the social environment for reform. First, Kang and Tang hold that, with the world undergoing changes unseen in a century and reform in a critical stage, cadres must show courage and reject passivity, evasion and slackness. Second, they argue that mobilising the Party's more than 99 million members will let the Party unite over 1.4 billion people, so reform must rely on the people. In their account, this requires respecting the people's principal position and creativity, listening to the public, and collecting and summing up fresh popular experience. The authors conclude that cadres and the public should understand the complexity and difficulty of reform and handle adjustments of interests correctly, creating an atmosphere of understanding, support and participation. They describe Party building as a way to keep the Party vital, with the Party's self-reform leading social revolution. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party School scholars explain the Third Plenum's Party-building provisions.

The realisation path of the self-improvement of the socialist system An analytical framework based on the "institutional process" 社会主义制度自我完善的实现路径 Zhao Lingyun Zhao Lingyun starts from two claims by Deng Xiaoping: that reform is the "self-improvement of the socialist system", and that Chinese socialism may become "the best system in the world". The article asks how this self-improvement actually happens, and proposes the concept of the "institutional process" (zhidu guocheng) as a framework for answering. Zhao defines it as a closed cycle of five links: institutional design, institutional construction, institutional operation, conversion of institutional advantages, and institutional evaluation. The article has three parts. The first sets out the framework and grounds it in Marxist institutional theory, Deng Xiaoping's thinking on institutions, Xi Jinping's institutional discourse and the political-science literature on "process" approaches. The second applies it to three stages of the People's Republic: founding the socialist system (to 1978), establishing the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics (1978 to the 18th Party Congress, 2012), and improving and developing that system (2012 to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee, 2024). The third draws out the framework's theoretical, historical and practical implications. Zhao argues that each stage contains a complete cycle in which the evaluation stage opens the next round, so that the cycles form a spiral. On this reading, Xi Jinping's formulas of "two historical periods" and "two half-courses" describe one continuous history of building socialism. Zhao answers why the system can improve itself by pointing to its public-ownership basis and to its capacity to accommodate different economic arrangements, which Zhao contrasts with János Kornai's view that Soviet-type socialism could not be reformed. The "self" in self-improvement is identified as the system itself, with the Communist Party's leadership and the people it leads as the subject. Party leadership is therefore the internal driver of the process. Looking ahead, Zhao calls for continuing the institutional process through repeated cycles, treating the second half-course as a long, step-by-step stage. Zhao further urges a focus on institutional integration, building and converting institutional advantages, and strengthening the Party's historical initiative. Self-improvement, in this view, is not automatic, and the Party's self-reform and the system's self-improvement are described as closely unified. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory account of how Chinese scholars periodise and conceptualise institution-building since 1949.

Using "investing in people" to unblock the circulation of the national economy 以“投资于人”畅通国民经济循环 Wang Zanxin Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2025, Wang Zanxin takes up "investing in people", a phrase that drew wide attention during that year's National People's Congress and Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference sessions. Wang argues that the main macroeconomic problem is poor circulation of the national economy, and that investment in people should become the strategic fulcrum for unblocking it. This is to be done by combining it closely with "investing in things", not by replacing the latter. The commentary has three parts. It first sets out why investment in people matters for consumption, investment efficiency and the supply structure. It then argues that investment in physical capital and in people has so far been poorly coordinated, and cites Hangzhou and Changsha as local examples. It ends with proposals for rebuilding the investment pattern. Wang's central claim is that investment in physical capital shows diminishing marginal returns, while investment in people has multiplier and spillover effects. In Wang's account, consumption is shifting from subsistence to development-oriented spending on education, health care, culture, housing and insurance, which depends on public services and social investment. Wang cites a shortfall of more than 20 million skilled workers and a claim that each new start-up creates five to eight jobs. Wang describes a closed loop of rising human capital, consumption upgrading and industrial upgrading. Over-investment in things, in this reading, leads to resource misallocation, debt risk and unreleased consumption potential. Wang calls for three measures. The first is to shift investment from scale to effectiveness: cut high-energy-consuming and polluting projects, expand inclusive education, and draw private capital into elderly care and childcare. The second is to put investment in people into the macroeconomic policy toolbox, with indicators such as the share of skilled workers and the medical insurance reimbursement rate in local government assessments, and a lifelong vocational training system. The third is to integrate physical and human investment in urbanisation, rural revitalisation and large-scale equipment and consumer-goods renewal programmes. Wang presents this as a shift from a demographic dividend to a talent dividend and as an application of people-centred development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official economic commentary in 2025 frames human-capital investment as a response to weak domestic circulation.

Deng Xiaoping's lofty intellectual character as seen in the Collected Works of Deng Xiaoping (1925–1949) 从《邓小平文集（1925—1949年）》看邓小平的崇高思想风范 Gao Yi Jiang Shuping Marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee compiled the Collected Works of Deng Xiaoping (1925–1949), published in three volumes by People's Publishing House in August 2024. Gao and Jiang use the collection to ask what it reveals about Deng's intellectual character, and argue that it shows three defining qualities: firm conviction, seeking truth from facts, and strong political thinking. The article first introduces the collection: 207 items including speeches, reports, telegrams, orders, letters and inscriptions, most published for the first time. The authors present it as an authoritative supplement to the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping and a basic source for Party history research. Its three sections follow the three qualities, each illustrated with texts from the revolutionary period and framed by remarks of Xi Jinping on Deng. On conviction, the authors cite Deng's 1926 autobiography written at Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow and a questionnaire in which he said he had always been fairly communist. They also cite his later wartime and 1949 calls to educate Party members and young people in Marxism-Leninism. On seeking truth from facts, they point to Deng's insistence that central directives be applied to local conditions, and to his correction of over-hasty land reform in newly liberated areas in 1947–48. They trace this trait to his grasp of the living soul of Marxism, his experience abroad and in the field, and his study of Mao Zedong. On political thinking, they show Deng backing Mao's leadership and the Party's independence within the united front against Wang Ming's line. They also describe his strategic vision in the advance into the Dabie Mountains, and his insistence on discipline and regular written reports to the Central Committee. Gao and Jiang conclude that the collection adds a valuable body of sources for studying Deng's thought and life, the Party's history and its theory, and deserves further study. Their reading is affirmative throughout and relies on the official assessments of Deng by Mao and Xi. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's guide to newly published Deng Xiaoping documents from 1925–1949 and to how they are used to illustrate his official portrait.

The theoretical logic and pathways by which education digitalization promotes the development of new quality productive forces 教育数字化促进新质生产力发展的理论逻辑与路径探析 Wang Tianping Pan Qinqing Why, and how, can the digitalization of education advance new quality productive forces? Wang Tianping and Pan Qinqing argue that education digitalization is both a constituent part and an effective means of developing these forces, and that its main point of leverage is the training of "new quality talents". Writing in the context of Chinese modernization and high-quality development, they set out the internal logic of the link and propose practical paths. The article has three parts. The first explains why education digitalization can promote new quality productive forces, drawing on the Marxist theory of productive forces, philosophy of technology and human-capital theory. The second describes four functions: promoting the turnover of emerging technologies, cultivating cutting-edge talent, creating a digital environment, and generating digital education industry clusters. The third identifies bottlenecks and proposes five paths, ending with a short conclusion. The authors treat new quality productive forces as the third systemic revolution in productive forces, after the agricultural and industrial eras, marked by intelligent labour, digitalized factors of production and data as a new factor. Education belongs to the superstructure but also reproduces labour capacity and turns latent knowledge into actual productive power. Education digitalization therefore enlarges individuals' intellectual capital and spurs technological breakthroughs, through personalised learning, immersive environments, supportive policy and new industries such as online learning platforms. They also note risks: digital technology is a double-edged sword that may produce new inequalities, shallow thinking and privacy leaks. The authors list current obstacles: weak technological foundations, unclear mechanisms linking technology and education, low digital literacy and an incomplete institutional framework. They propose five paths: advancing digital technology innovation, raising the level of digital education services, strengthening the educational function of digital education, building collaborative industry formats such as industry–university–research cooperation, and improving top-level design through strategic action plans, coordination mechanisms and ethical and privacy rules. They conclude that integrating education, science and technology, and talent is essential for developing new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese education scholars connect digitalization policy to new quality productive forces, with detailed policy suggestions.

The "Second Integration" in historical perspective 从历史维度看“第二个结合” Ouyang Junxi Writing in Qiushi (2025, no. 5), Ouyang Junxi asks why the Communist Party of China has come to stress combining Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, and what the "Second Integration" adds to the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article argues that the Second Integration has deep historical roots, because Marxism and traditional Chinese culture are mutually compatible and the Party has inherited that culture since its founding. It opens with Guo Moruo's 1925 story "Marx Enters the Confucian Temple", in which Marx and Confucius find their ideals of society alike. The article is organised in three historical and conceptual steps. It first examines the points of fit between Marxism and traditional culture. It then traces the Party's treatment of that culture through the Yan'an period, the early People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally it presents "the Two Integrations" as the Party's greatest asset for success. Ouyang's first move is to explain Marxism's rapid spread in China partly by cultural affinity. The article finds proto-socialist elements in ideas such as "all under heaven is for the common good" and the Great Harmony, political values such as people-as-the-root and governing by virtue, and plain materialist and dialectical traditions. It cites Sun Yat-sen, Wu Yuzhang, Ai Siqi and Zhang Dainian in support. Its second move is to show continuity in Party leaders: Mao Zedong's 1938 call for Marxism to take a national form, his reuse of Chinese idioms and fables, and later formulations by Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. The article claims that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era draws on traditional concepts such as people-centredness, harmony between humanity and nature, and a community with a shared future for mankind. Ouyang concludes that the Two Integrations are the fundamental route for adapting Marxism to China and the necessary path for developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. In this account, Chinese modernization continues an ancient civilisation rather than breaking with it. The Second Integration is described as a "chemical reaction" that produces an organic new cultural entity and strengthens cultural subjectivity, confidence and initiative. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party theorists trace the Second Integration back through Chinese Marxist history and quote the leadership's key formulations on it.

Did Mao Zedong really reject the "law of the negation of the negation"? 毛泽东真的否定“否定之否定规律”吗 Fu Zhiwei Some scholars hold that Mao Zedong rejected the law of the negation of the negation, citing his remark that he did not believe quantity–quality transformation and the negation of the negation stand parallel to the unity of opposites, since that would be "three-ism, not monism". Fu Zhiwei takes up this claim, noting that Slavoj Žižek and Wang Nanshi use the passage in this way and that Stalin and Althusser offer a precedent. Fu argues that Mao did not reject the law itself. What he denied was its foundational status alongside the law of the unity of opposites. The article has four parts. It first traces the law to Hegel and sets out how Marx and Engels inverted and demystified it. It then clarifies the concept of "negation". Next it compares Mao's remarks, drawn mainly from his philosophical annotations and the Chronology of Mao Zedong, with Marx and Engels. Finally it answers three opposing positions: Stalin and Althusser, Žižek, and a more elaborate argument that the law cannot be separated from Hegelian idealism. Fu defines dialectical negation as self-negation, a moment of development, a moment of connection and, in essence, sublation. It is neither the "either/or" of formal logic nor a subjective evaluative category. Fu finds that Mao's statements match each of these points: negation arises within the thing itself, it is continuous, and it preserves what is rational in the old. Mao's wish to treat the unity of opposites as the single core law explains his remarks, because the other categories are explained through it. Fu reads "there is no negation of the negation" as a point about theoretical economy, not a denial. Against Žižek, Fu cites Mao's endorsement of "analysis and synthesis". Against the idealism argument, Fu contends that Engels and Marx treated the law as necessary even when it describes a linear process, such as communism, and not a return to its starting point. Fu concludes that Mao affirmed the law while denying it foundational status, and that this clarified the relation among the three laws of materialist dialectics. Fu presents this as consistent with Marxism and as a development of it. Fu leaves the final judgement to readers. Read the original if you want a close, text-based argument on Mao's dialectics, Hegel's logic and the Marx–Engels reworking of the negation of the negation, or if you want to see how this reading answers Žižek and Althusser.

The Chinese narrative logic of the question of modernization and its world-historical significance 现代化之问的中国叙事逻辑和世界历史意义 Wang Yonggui Wang Yonggui asks how Chinese modernization answers what the author calls the question of modernization, which he treats as the key to the larger question facing the world. The article argues that Chinese modernization shares features with other countries' modernizations but is not a 'special case' outside world trends. In Wang's account it is an original theoretical and practical achievement that points to a new form of human civilization and widens the range of paths to modernity. The article is organised around five principles that Xi Jinping has set for modernization: putting the people first, independence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, helping others while pursuing one's own development, and an enterprising attitude. Each principle forms one section, presented as a 'new concept', 'new path', 'new chapter', 'new picture' and 'new realm' of modernization. Wang draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin on Eastern societies, and on Xi's speeches throughout. Wang first contrasts a Western modernization driven by the 'logic of capital' with one in which the 'logic of the people' governs capital. Capital is treated as a production factor to be regulated, and Wang says public ownership turns the 'logic of capital' into a 'logic of labour'. He then argues that Chinese modernization dissolves the equation of 'modernization' with 'Westernization', escapes the 'centre–periphery' dependency trap and offers developing countries a model without exporting it. In the later sections, the author says a philosophy of 'unity of subject and object' and 'common values of all humanity' surpass hegemony and 'universal values'. The leadership of the Communist Party and its self-reform are credited with direction, stability and continuity. Wang concludes that Chinese modernization enriches scientific socialism by making its goals concrete, developing its principles and offering a systematic practical programme. He holds that it reverses the post-Cold War low point of the socialist movement, supplies a model for building socialism in an 'Eastern society', and gives world history a socialist civilizational benchmark. He presents the community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative as expressions of this outlook. Read the original if you want a full, systematic statement of how Chinese academic writing in 2024 frames the world-historical significance of Chinese modernization against Western modernization theory.

The historical preconditions, main features and Party-building traditions of the great beginning of Party building 党的建设伟大开端的历史前提、主要特征与党建传统探析 Liu Zhili Cui Jihan How did the Communist Party of China's earliest Party-building practice shape the habits that it now calls its Party-building traditions? Liu and Cui argue that the Party's founding and early construction, rooted in the upheavals of modern Chinese society, supplied the starting point and the formative influences for those traditions. They present this as important for understanding the self-construction of Marxist parties, especially under long-term governing conditions. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical preconditions: the disorder of social foundations, the disorientation of ideas, and the failure of party politics in the early Republic. The second identifies five features of the beginning of Party building. The third defines the essence of Party-building traditions and describes how they appear in practice, drawing on Mao Zedong, Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao and Xi Jinping. On the preconditions, the authors argue that a society likened to "a sheet of loose sand" needed a new organisational form to "awaken the masses". They add that new scientific theory was needed, and that the loose, elite-based parties of the early Republic left room for a new political force. The five features are: moving from criticising old classics to building a new "doctrine"; moving from the maximum programme to a clearly distinguished minimum programme; moving from organising "new youth" to leading "new comrades" among workers and peasants; becoming a revolutionary vanguard through belief and discipline; and moving from refusing ties with other parties to the "democratic united front". From these the authors derive the essence of the traditions: keeping to the original aspiration and mission, innovating scientific theory through the Two Integrations, and using practice as the standard. The authors conclude that these essentials appear today as three pairings: the people first together with a world-embracing outlook, Party leadership together with Party building, and spiritual shaping together with value guidance. They present these as the deeper reasons for the Party's growth from about fifty members to nearly 100 million. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from within official Party-history scholarship, of how early Party documents and congresses are linked to the Party's current account of its own traditions.

Rethinking the forms in which the "new world outlook" has been interpreted An examination based on the history of the development of Marxist philosophy 重思“新世界观”阐释形式问题 Zhang Dingxin Marx never used the term "Marxist philosophy". Zhang Dingxin asks how the "new world outlook", which Marx and Engels used for their philosophical revolution, should be understood and why its later interpretive forms matter today. The article argues that this outlook is, at root, a proletarian world outlook. Its core is the critique of political economy, not speculative philosophy alone. The successive interpretive forms (Engels's, Lenin's, Western Marxism's and Chinese Marxism's) each made real contributions. The article first traces how Marx built the outlook, from his 1842 letter to Ruge through the 1844 Manuscripts, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, the 1859 Preface and Capital. It then surveys how others presented it. Engels used historical materialism and materialist dialectics. Lenin and Stalin developed dialectical and historical materialism. Gramsci and Lukács formulated a philosophy of practice. Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping adapted it in China. A fourth section draws out principles for Marxist philosophy now. Zhang holds that Marxist philosophy has three layers: a new theory of practice, a dialectic of social history, and the critique of political economy, with the first two serving as the philosophical basis of the third. On this reading, Engels's forms were not "pre-Marxist" but registered the shift of focus from nature to human society and "real human beings". Zhang also identifies a tension between practical subjectivity and material objective reality, and argues that Marx's texts treat the two as intertwined and unified, not antinomic. Marxism is thus neither a hostile materialism nor a "practice-only" doctrine. Zhang draws three principles for developing Marxist philosophy today. It must keep its proletarian world-outlook identity. It must retain the dual dimension of philosophical critique and critique of political economy. It must combine responsiveness to the times with universal necessity. Zhang cites Xi Jinping's statements on common prosperity, on capital, on Chinese modernization and on a community with a shared future for mankind as embodying these principles. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Chinese philosophers trace the lineage from Marx through Engels, Lenin and Western Marxism to Chinese Marxism.

Chinese modernization theory and practice continually enrich and develop Marxist principles An interview with Cheng Enfu, Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences 中国式现代化理论和实践不断丰富发展马克思主义原理 Cheng Enfu This is an interview with Cheng Enfu, Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, conducted by the journal Studies on Marxism. It asks how the theory and practice of Chinese modernization enrich and develop basic Marxist principles. Cheng answers that they do so in six areas: the people as the subject of history, the two civilizations, the driving forces of social development, ecological civilization, the community, and the leadership of the proletarian party. The interview moves through six headed sections, each pairing a classical Marxist principle with the Chinese Communist Party's historical practice. Cheng draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, then follows Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the leaders who followed them. He gives most space to Xi Jinping's formulations since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Cheng presents each area as continuity plus innovation. He contrasts the Marxist "people as subject" with Rousseau's bourgeois popular sovereignty, which in his reading ignores the economic sphere. He argues that Chinese practice coordinates material and spiritual civilization where capitalist modernization produced a split. He reads comprehensive reform as the Party's handling of the contradiction between relations of production and productive forces. Marx's idea of a "true community", set against the illusory communities of class society, is for Cheng carried forward by a community with a shared future for mankind, together with the global initiatives on development, security, civilization and AI governance. Cheng also says the "three unwaverings" must not be split into preserving fundamentals and innovating, and that Party leadership decides the direction and fate of modernization. Cheng concludes that Chinese modernization, led by the Party, has added new content to Marxist theories of the people, civilization, social dynamics, ecology, the community and party leadership, and offers humanity "a new choice" of modernization. He treats Xi Jinping's statements as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed official-scholarly account of how Chinese modernization is theorised as a development of Marxist principles, with extensive citation of Party leaders.

Scientifically grasping the dialectical relationship among Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline 科学把握党性党风党纪的辩证关系 Zhang Hao Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2025, no. 4), Zhang Hao takes up Xi Jinping's formula that Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline form an organic whole: Party spirit is the foundation, Party style the outward expression, and Party discipline the safeguard. Zhang argues that the three must be handled together rather than separately, so that the Party never degenerates and remains the firm leading core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is a theoretical and policy commentary in four sections. The first three take each element in turn: Party spirit as the inner root, Party style as the visible manifestation, and Party discipline as the institutional guarantee. The fourth section explains why the three should be pursued as one, citing the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) on handling them together. Zhang's core argument is that each element reinforces the others. Party spirit, defined through Xi as a question of standpoint, determines the nature of style and discipline; without it, officials lack reverence for discipline, and problems of conduct are traced to impure Party spirit and self-interest. Style is the Party's image and a gauge of loyalty, and neglect of it invites corruption. Discipline, with its rigid constraints, turns external restraint into self-discipline and makes Party spirit and style durable. Zhang proposes that the three be pursued simultaneously, in the same direction and in combination. Each has its own emphasis: education and guidance for Party spirit, correction and restraint for style, and punishment and deterrence for discipline. The shared aim is to address the "unique problems of a large party" through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Zhang calls for concrete measures. These include theoretical study and Party-spirit education, enforcing the Central Committee's eight-point regulation, curbing formalism and bureaucratism, running Party discipline study and education, and applying discipline strictly while encouraging officials to take responsibility. The aim, in Zhang's account, is to prevent the rebound of bad practices and to sustain a clean political ecosystem within the Party. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Party-building discourse links ideological cultivation, conduct rules and disciplinary enforcement.

Mao Zedong's strategic thinking in responding to the "anti-China chorus" 毛泽东应对“反华大合唱”的战略思想 Hu Tianjiao This article asks how Mao Zedong dealt with what he called the "anti-China chorus", the wave of external hostility that confronted the new People's Republic in the Cold War, and what that experience offers today. Hu Tianjiao argues that Mao distinguished between hostile forces of different kinds, assessed their overall character from a global perspective, and held that negative factors could turn into positive ones. In Hu's account, Mao saw the fundamental answer in unity and in independent, self-reliant socialist construction. The article first describes the late-1950s pressure in three "voices": the United States (embargo, bases, obstruction of UN membership, the "two Chinas" issue), India (the Tibet revolt and the border dispute) and the Soviet Union (disputes over control, withdrawal of technical aid, differences with Khrushchev). It then examines Mao's separate approaches to each, his dialectical reading of the chorus itself, and his emphasis on domestic construction. It closes with lessons for the present, citing Xi Jinping on the "great struggle" and the "great changes unseen in a century". Hu presents Mao's approach as differentiated. Towards the US he combined struggle and diplomacy, using the 1958 shelling of Quemoy and his "noose" image of American overextension. Towards India and the Soviet Union he combined firm principle with efforts to preserve unity, for example the proposed 20-kilometre demilitarised zone on the border and the suggestion that the two parties keep their own views and await the facts. Mao also judged the chorus to be "great support for China, small opposition", with only perhaps five to ten per cent of humanity truly hostile. In Hu's reading he held that hostility exposed the reactionaries, stirred the Chinese people and sharpened awareness of imperialism's two faces. Hu reports that Mao's fundamental remedy was an independent, complete national economic system, rejection of a "slave mentality" and dogmatic copying, and vigilance against "peaceful evolution". Hu concludes with three lessons for the present. China should analyse principal and secondary contradictions, answer firmly and keep seeking unity. It should make many friends and unite most countries, as in the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. It should rely on independent construction: the Four-sphere Confidence, Chinese modernization, technological self-reliance, and guarding against "peaceful evolution" through the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Mao's Cold War foreign-policy reasoning is being used to frame China's current strategic outlook.

How the modern age can speak of the Absolute: Hegel's interpretation of Spinoza as a case 现代如何言说绝对者：以黑格尔的斯宾诺莎阐释为例 Zhuang Zhenhua Zhuang Zhenhua asks how modern thought can speak of the Absolute without lapsing into dogmatic assertion. Taking Hegel's reading of Spinoza as the test case, the article argues that Hegel's real objection is not that Spinoza's substance is static or that his geometrical method is flawed. In Zhuang's reading, the objection is that Spinoza's Absolute cannot pass the 'test' of modern life, because it is posited directly rather than shown to be necessary from within actual things. The article begins with the Absolute as a question that runs through modern philosophy, from Leibniz's 'why is there something rather than nothing?' to present-day speculative realism and new realism. Section one reviews Hegel's remarks on Spinoza in the Lectures on the History of Philosophy and in the two Logics, the Science of Logic and the Encyclopaedia Logic. Section two follows three chapters of the Doctrine of Essence, 'The Absolute', 'Actuality' and 'The Absolute Relation'. A closing section considers the contemporary relevance of Hegel's route. Zhuang's central claim is that, for Hegel, an Absolute that stands beyond finite determinations must pass two further 'gates'. The first is to discern absolute necessity in actual things, moving from contingency through relative necessity to absolute necessity. The second is to see how that necessity presents itself as freedom, through the substantial relation, causality and reciprocity. Zhuang reads the chapter on 'The Absolute' as Hegel's 'rewriting' of Spinoza's substance, attribute and mode. It remains an abstract, external reflection that never examines its own dualistic positing. The next two chapters 'complete' Spinoza, producing a new kind of substance that, on Zhuang's account, fulfils Spinoza's original intention. Zhuang concludes that Hegel 'revises' rather than 'overthrows' Spinoza, which strips the substance doctrine of its dogmatic character and offers a model for modern engagement with the Absolute. The article suggests that Meillassoux's 'necessity of contingency' echoes Hegel's move, though it says it remains to be seen whether recent realisms avoid Spinoza's predicament. Zhuang adds that Hegel's Absolute does not strengthen subjective reason or confer a 'God's-eye view'. Freedom must be preserved through renunciation of what one immediately is and has. Read the original if you work on Hegel's Logic, Spinoza reception or German idealism and want a close, text-based account of the Absolute in the Doctrine of Essence.)

Lenin's exploration of preventing and curbing bureaucratism and formalism 列宁对防治官僚主义形式主义的探索 Lü Weizhou Liao Bin Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party has treated improving its work style as an entry point for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and Xi Jinping has repeatedly said that formalism and bureaucratism "kill". Lü Weizhou and Liao Bin ask what Lenin's theory and practice against these two ills can offer the Party today. They argue that Lenin, leading the first socialist state, identified their forms, harms and roots and devised practical remedies that remain instructive. The article is organised in three parts followed by a short conclusion. The first part covers Lenin's exposure of bureaucratism and formalism in Soviet state and Party organs and the harms he ascribed to them. The second analyses their political, economic and cultural roots. The third sets out the measures Lenin proposed and carried out, drawing on his speeches, telegrams, decrees and organisational initiatives. The authors report Lenin as listing three forms of formalism: endless meetings, a paper-bound "document culture" and dilatory procedure. They present him as tracing the roots to the Tsarist legacy, to a small-producer economy (backed by figures on Soviet output in 1920 and on collectivisation) and to mass illiteracy that left administration without effective supervision. They also cite the later Soviet record, from privilege under Stalin to life tenure under Brezhnev, as showing that neglecting the problem helped bring down the Party and state. Lenin's remedies fall into four groups: socialist democracy (contact with the masses, elections and recall, pay no higher than a skilled worker's, supervisory bodies); socialist legality (prosecuting negligent officials); slimmer state organs, individual responsibility and shorter meetings; and a purer Party membership, including strict admission, the 1921 purge of some 170,000 members, cadre training and assessment, and rewards. The authors conclude that the Chinese Communist Party has drawn on Lenin's approach and developed it in the new era. They stress that the two ills are stubborn and recurrent, so the struggle must be sustained, long-term and meticulous. They call for further study of the conditions that breed them, and of new and hidden forms, in order to provide an institutional guarantee for the Party's leadership of deeper reform and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Lenin's anti-bureaucracy measures as presented in current Party-theory writing on work style.

The harm of foreign religious infiltration to the ideological security of socialist countries and its contemporary lessons 境外宗教渗透对社会主义国家意识形态安全的危害与当代启示 Zhang Kai Wang Hongsheng Zhang Kai and Wang Hongsheng ask how religion has been used by Western capitalist powers against socialist states, and what socialist countries should do about it. They argue that religion is an ideology and that, since the Cold War, foreign religious infiltration has been a major threat to socialist ideological security. In their account it contributed to the fall of Poland's socialist government and still targets China, Vietnam, Cuba and others. The article has four parts. It first sets out the Marxist view of religion as an ideological form. It then reviews the 1980s alliance between the United States and the Vatican in Eastern Europe. Next it turns to present-day cases, with most attention to Vietnam and Cuba, and to the digital sphere. It ends with proposals for defence. The authors draw on Marx and Engels to argue that religion is an ideological tool that ruling classes use to dominate others. On this basis they read the 1980s "Holy Alliance" between Washington and Rome as a deliberate strategy. They cite funding and supplies for Solidarity, papal appointment of hostile bishops, and John Paul II's visits to Poland. For the present day they point to the US International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 and annual religious-freedom reports. They also cite episcopal appointments and church-run universities in Vietnam, papal visits to Cuba, and illegal religious groups among ethnic minorities. Finally they describe online risks: foreign platforms, algorithmic recommendation, virtual churches and ChatGPT's alleged ideological bias. The authors call for religious work guided by the Marxist view of religion and Marxist atheism. This would protect normal religious activity while guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. They propose a standing mechanism with regular risk assessment, monitoring and a specialist workforce, plus coordination between government, society and individuals. They also call for strengthening ideological positions under the Party principle, through atheist propaganda, network governance and technological capacity, and university education in Marxist atheism and religious law. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholarly journal on science and atheism frames religion as a security issue, and what countermeasures it recommends.

Strengthening the position of enterprises as the main body of scientific and technological innovation 强化企业科技创新主体地位 Wu Aiqun Writing in the People's Daily on 7 March 2025, Wu Aiqun, a member of the National Committee of the CPPCC, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks to the Jiangsu delegation at the National People's Congress. Xi had described scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation as the basic path to developing new quality productive forces. Wu argues that the key to integrating the two is to strengthen enterprises' position as the main body of scientific and technological innovation, so that the innovation chain and the industrial chain connect seamlessly. The commentary first sets out the policy basis, citing the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then reviews achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including enterprises' share of more than 75 per cent of national R&D spending, and identifies remaining weaknesses. It closes with three groups of proposals: building up leading technology enterprises, having them drive whole-process and whole-chain innovation, and strengthening institutional guarantees. On problems, Wu says Chinese enterprises do little basic research "from 0 to 1", have relatively weak independent innovation and lack high-end researchers. Talent and major facilities sit mainly in universities and research institutes, and firms have little say over qualification recognition and professional titles. Wu adds that leading firms are reluctant to head industry–university–research alliances. According to the article's survey findings, they fear technology leaks and exposing their bottlenecks, and disputes over ownership of results and fears of state asset loss add to the difficulty. Wu's remedies include treating R&D spending as profit when assessing state-owned enterprises, R&D reserve funds, tax deductions and accelerated depreciation, and new titling and dual-appointment schemes for researchers. Wu also proposes enterprise-led innovation consortia, support for small and medium-sized technology firms through the "specialised, refined, distinctive and innovative" programme, and a model in which leading firms pose problems, research bodies answer them and financial institutions serve throughout. Wu concludes that deeper reform of the science and technology system, opening major national research facilities to private firms and a technology-finance system that supports patient capital and shares risk will let innovation factors gather in enterprises. This, Wu says, will serve the "four orientations", build China into a science and technology power and advance Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-affiliated adviser presents enterprise-centred innovation policy and its institutional measures in the official press.

Upholding, improving and operating the people's congress system well Studying Xi Jinping's "On Upholding and Improving the System of People's Congresses" 坚持好、完善好、运行好人民代表大会制度 Guo Rucai Li Zhaojie Published as the National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference opened their annual sessions in March 2025, this commentary is a study guide to the newly published Xi Jinping collection "On Upholding and Improving the System of People's Congresses". Guo and Li argue that the volume gives a fundamental guide for upholding, improving and operating the people's congress system well. In their account the system is China's fundamental political institution and should be turned into effective national governance as the country approaches 2035. The piece is organised under three headings. The first treats the system as a great creation in the history of political institutions and calls for confidence in China's political system. The second sets out the content of Xi's thought on the system. The third concerns democracy as an enduring idea of the Party and the people, and the need to research and publicise it. On the first point, the authors describe the system as the result of the Party's long struggle after earlier forms (constitutional monarchy, parliamentary and presidential systems, multi-party competition) failed to solve China's problems. They also hold that it is rooted in Chinese cultural tradition and that it keeps the country on the socialist path. They list the five distinctive political advantages that Xi set out in September 2024, at the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress. On the second, they trace the progression from the "Four Musts" (2014) to the "Six Musts" (2021) and the "Eight Musts" (2024). They present this as a body of thought that is both Marxist and rooted in Chinese tradition, a product of the Two Integrations. On the third, they say democracy is a common value of humanity but is realised in diverse ways. They hold that treating Western electoral models as the sole standard is itself undemocratic, and that real democracy should be judged by whether it solves the people's problems. They present whole-process people's democracy as a democracy of the full process, and the people's congresses as its main institutional vehicle. The authors conclude that practice has proved the system suited to China's conditions and capable of uniting the people behind Chinese modernization, so it must be upheld unwaveringly and developed with the times. They call for deeper research and better communication of its features and advantages, so that institutional strengths become governing capacity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the people's congress system and Xi's thought on it for study and propaganda purposes.

An analysis of the operating mechanisms of "Great Ideological and Political Course" practical teaching bases from an integrated perspective 一体化视域下“大思政课”实践教学基地运行机制探析 Yu Yongjun Chen Xi How should the practical teaching bases of the "Great Ideological and Political Course" be run so that they work across primary school, secondary school and university? Yu and Chen treat these bases as venues and education platforms serving students of all three stages. They argue that the bases link the stages, join theory to practice, pool resources and support the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Their answer is a set of five operating mechanisms. The article is a policy-oriented analysis of what it calls the integrated (一体化) approach to ideological and political courses across school stages. It is organised in five sections: a linked, coordinated mechanism; a regular interaction and communication mechanism; a stepped mechanism for education goals; a holistic evaluation and feedback mechanism; and a systematic support mechanism. Each section is broken into numbered sub-measures with concrete examples. On coordination, the authors propose a joint leadership body of education authorities, schools and base managers. It would draw up shared plans, allocate resources, set common themes such as patriotism and red culture, and make content progress from intuitive experience in primary school to social investigation in secondary school and research-based practice at university. They also propose set communication rhythms: monthly online exchanges, a joint meeting each term and a site visit each year. Goals are tiered by age, moving from moral awareness to critical thinking to analysis of social hot-button issues, with teacher training and facilities tailored to each stage. Evaluation rests on five principles: political orientation, innovation, demonstration value, replicability and effectiveness. It also uses concrete checklists covering content, venue, staff, activities, rules and funding, and it combines process with outcome, quantitative with qualitative, and self with third-party assessment. For support, the authors call for a special policy document, tax relief and subsidies for participating museums and enterprises, and coordination among education, finance and culture departments. They also propose awards for teachers, practice credits for students, honours for partner institutions and earmarked government funds supplemented by donations, with audit and public disclosure. In their view, these measures together can make the bases a lasting carrier of continuous, progressive ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-level blueprint of how Chinese education officials and scholars envisage organising, evaluating and funding cross-stage practical teaching bases.

Mao Zedong's philosophical reflections on the discipline of the Communist Party of China 毛泽东关于中国共产党纪律问题的哲学思考 Li Weiwu Li Weiwu asks how Mao Zedong grounded Party discipline in Marxist philosophy rather than treating it only as a set of rules. The article argues that Mao's reflections, running from the Party's founding to the 1960s, gave discipline a Marxist philosophical foundation. In Li's account, this explains why discipline won broad acceptance among members and was observed in practice. The article follows Mao's thinking in three stages. It begins with his 1920–21 correspondence with Cai Hesen on founding the Party and separating it from anarchism. It then turns to the late 1930s and the Seventh Party Congress (1945), where Mao worked out the dialectic of Party spirit and individuality using his philosophical writings. It ends with the principle of conscious (self-aware) discipline, which Li traces to Lenin, and with the significance of all this for today. Li makes three main moves. First, Mao drew on historical materialism to argue that factories and states alike need authority, so anarchism's immediate rejection of parties and authority ignores historical conditions. Second, in On Contradiction Mao treated differences as contradictions. Li reads the Party as a whole and its individual members as a contradiction of universality and particularity: Party spirit is the universal, individuality the particular, and each presupposes the other. Mao therefore urged members' 'creative individuality' and opposed 'destructive individuality'. Third, Li argues that Mao, following Lenin's 'free, conscious discipline', held that iron discipline rests on members' voluntary commitment to the revolution. Mao's example was soldiers leaving the apples of Jinzhou untouched, and he repeated Lenin's three conditions for discipline: vanguard consciousness, ties to the masses and a correct political line. Li concludes that Mao's reflections were tested over a century of Party struggle and advanced the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to Chinese conditions. The article links them to the full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Li notes that Xi Jinping stresses worldview, outlook on life and values as the basis of members' self-aware discipline. Li calls Mao's thought a legacy still relevant to Party discipline. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao's discipline thinking drew on Lenin, Cai Hesen and Mao's own dialectics, and how it is tied to current Party-building discourse.

Western perceptions of new quality productive forces: main views and assessment 西方关于新质生产力的主要认知与评析 Zhang Lisi Since Xi Jinping put forward the concept of new quality productive forces, Western media, think tanks, politicians and scholars have followed it closely. Zhang Lisi sets out to map how the West understands and judges the concept. The article argues that most Western commentary is positive, while a minority of views misread it and are driven by anxiety and interest. Zhang presents the survey as useful for understanding Western opinion contests and for deepening research on high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The article draws on statements by outlets such as Reuters, the BBC, CNN, the Wall Street Journal, the Economist, Deutsche Welle and Bloomberg, and by scholars and officials from Europe, the United States, Australia, Japan and South Korea. It has four parts. The first sorts Western readings of the concept's meaning into four angles: development strategy, development philosophy, form of productive forces, and essential attribute. The second covers Western accounts of why the concept emerged. The third covers Western affirmations of its significance, plus a few cautions. The fourth is Zhang's own assessment. Zhang reports that Western commentators see the concept as a response to China's need for economic revitalisation, a step to a new stage of productive forces, a continuation of the new development philosophy, a key to building a modernized socialist country, and a support for international competitiveness. Many are said to expect new momentum for China and the world and to treat the concept as a development of Marxist productive-force theory. Zhang then explains the attention by China's achievements and by Western anxiety over technological rivalry. Zhang characterises the minority of critical views as four moves: the "overcapacity" theory as a theoretical trap, linking the concept to national security, attaching ideological labels, and zero-sum thinking. Zhang concludes that Western opinion is mostly objective and favourable, and that this is based on China's economic record. Zhang calls for better external communication to tell the story of new quality productive forces, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The article also calls for a calm analysis of the roots of bias, a readiness to rebut smears, and a search for shared interests with other countries. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school scholar's classification of Western commentary on the concept, and the official framing of foreign criticism as ideological and zero-sum.

A deeper understanding of Xi Jinping's important statements on upholding a problem-oriented approach 深刻理解习近平关于坚持问题导向的重要论述 Xu Hengbing Xu Di The authors examine Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on 坚持问题导向, upholding a problem-oriented approach. The 20th Party Congress (2022) listed this as one of the "six musts" for advancing the Party's theoretical innovation. The article argues that the principle is part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and that Xi's remarks answer three questions: where the approach comes from, what it targets and what it requires. The article has three parts. The first sets out the principle's "generative logic" in theory, history and present-day need. The second identifies five main targets: new problems arising in practice, deep-seated problems of reform, development and stability, urgent concerns of the people, major issues in a changing international landscape, and prominent problems in Party building. The third lists basic requirements. It draws heavily on Xi's speeches and Party documents from 2013 to 2024. On theory, the authors argue that the approach follows from the Marxist view of practice, since problems arise from and are resolved in practice, and from the Marxist view of contradiction, since a problem is the form in which a contradiction appears. They conclude that one should identify the principal contradiction and its principal aspect. On history, they present the Party's revolution, construction and reform as a succession of major questions answered in turn. On present need, they cite Xi's list of difficulties in the economy, politics, culture, society, ecology, security and Party conduct. They treat full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform as problem-oriented work, because self-reform means confronting problems rather than avoiding them. For practice, the authors call for a stronger problem awareness, backed by political responsibility, field investigation and a view that joins history with the present, the international with the domestic, and theory with reality. They also call for a systems perspective that looks past surface phenomena and rejects treating symptoms in isolation, and they cite Xi on ecological governance and the Yangtze River Economic Belt. Finally they urge uniting problem orientation with goal orientation, so that goals give direction and problems make strategy concrete. They present this as a methodological support for advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic, source-rich account of how Party theorists present problem orientation as a method of governance and Party building.

The shift of axial research paradigms in the emergence of Marx's philosophical revolution 马克思哲学革命出场的轴心研究范式转换 Ren Ping Fan Yun Ren Ping and Fan Yun ask whether Marx's philosophical revolution and the founding of a new worldview were accompanied by a conscious change of research method, and whether that change drove the revolution. They argue that earlier scholarship studied the results, process and content of the revolution but overlooked the "axial paradigm" that structured each phase. In their account, shifts of axial paradigm were an internal methodological link in the change from old to new worldview. The article divides Marx's path into three periods, each led by a different axial paradigm: the text-and-literature interpretation paradigm, the dialogue paradigm, and the paradigm of reflective problematics. It follows Marx from his move from law to philosophy and from Kant and Schelling to Hegel, through his break with the Young Hegelians and engagement with Feuerbach and Engels. It then follows his turn to the study of political economy, ending with Capital, the Paris Commune and the Russian question. A final section draws lessons for Marxist philosophy in China. The authors hold that every paradigm has a limited range, and that Marx met a "methodological predicament" whenever his questions outgrew his method. Interpretation of texts, as in his doctoral dissertation, was in their view monological and stayed inside the history of ideas. Dialogue with contemporaries such as Bauer, Feuerbach and Engels gave two-way exchange and helped him leave Hegel behind. The paradigm of reflective problematics, shown in the Rheinische Zeitung's "material interest" problem, Engels's critique of political economy and the Manchester visit, moved him from criticising "copies" to criticising the historical "original". The three paradigms ended up as "one body, two wings", with problematics as the body and the other two as wings. The authors conclude that methodological self-awareness and the founding of the new worldview advanced together. They add that paradigms alternate synchronically as well as diachronically, and that no paradigm is permanently present. Finally, they propose that the "one body, two wings" pattern can be a breakthrough point in building an autonomous knowledge system of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you want a methodological periodisation of the young Marx's development, with detailed attention to the Rheinische Zeitung, the Manchester notes and the influence of Engels.

The epistemological presuppositions of Marx's critique of political economy 马克思政治经济学批判的认识论前提 Luo Jiu This short commentary asks what epistemological presuppositions underlie Marx's critique of political economy. Luo argues that, although epistemology was not central to Marx's thinking, his critique rests on premises quite different from those of mainstream natural and social science, and that Marx was fully aware of this. Marx continues the tradition of German critical philosophy and refuses to treat capitalist economic activity as a natural, eternal fact. The article first places Marx after Kant and Hegel, then turns to his objections to classical political economy. It closes with Marx's own method of abstraction, drawing on his discussion of the concept of production. Luo contends that Marx should not be separated from epistemology or read only ontologically. Instead, Marx's thought needs an epistemology that moves beyond the paradigm of subjectivity philosophy and grasps things themselves, so that changing the world becomes possible. Following Hegel's critique of Kant, Marx inherits the post-Kantian demand to "know things themselves". On this reading, political economy treats atomised individuals, private property and the division of labour as universal presuppositions, and capitalist reproduction then reinforces them. Its abstractions yield empty "abstract identity", while Marx's abstraction keeps what it abstracts tied to the whole and to historically specific social relations. Luo concludes that classical economists therefore miss surplus value, the dual character of labour and commodities, and the relations of domination hidden in capital and wage labour. Marx's critique, in the article's account, grasps identity within difference and so understands capitalism more fully. It also shows the practical necessity of changing the capitalist facts it exposes. Read the original if you want a compact philosophical account of Marx's epistemology and its Kantian and Hegelian background.

Expanding the content of ideological and political education in the new era and building an autonomous knowledge system 新时代思想政治教育内容的拓展及自主知识体系建构 Dong Yahua Dong Yahua asks how the content of ideological and political education should be innovated in the new era, on what basis, and what theoretical foundations the resulting expansion offers for an autonomous knowledge system of the discipline. The article, marking forty years since the discipline was founded, argues that content must develop in response to practice and under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It holds that the expanded content can be organised into ten "conceptions" and supported by a four-layer knowledge structure. The article has three parts. The first sets out the grounds for innovation: social practice, illustrated by the shift from "legal system education" to "rule-of-law education" after the 15th Party Congress, and the guiding theory of the Party's latest Marxism. The second classifies the new content into six dimensions (ideals and convictions, core values, the Chinese spirit, cultural thought, ecological thinking, all-round human development) and ten conceptions, placed within the established five blocks of ideological, political, moral, cultural and psychological education. The third part builds the knowledge system.
