Dong's core argument is that the ten conceptions, from worldview and ecology to political, national, ethnic, reform-and-innovation, moral, cultural and mental-health outlooks, extend the discipline's original framework in line with the principle of keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. For each, the article lists teaching priorities, such as whole-process people's democracy, rule-of-law education, common prosperity and forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation. The knowledge system then has four layers: Marxist fundamentals; Xi Jinping Thought as the core; Chinese and foreign disciplinary theories, including Western democratic theory, as a critical reference; and social practice and fine traditional Chinese culture. Drawing on Lakatos, Dong calls the first two the theoretical "hard core" and the last the "protective belt". Dong concludes that these four layers should work together so that the aim of forging souls and nurturing people with Xi Jinping Thought takes root. The article is a programmatic outline of curriculum content rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education classify new-era teaching content and justify an autonomous disciplinary knowledge system.

"Construction" (jianshe): a preliminary study of political engineering in the CPC's governance of the Party and the country “建设”：中国共产党治党治国的政治工程学初探 Zhu Guowei Zhu Guowei starts from the observation that "construction" (jianshe) is everyday vocabulary in the Communist Party of China, yet scholars treat it only as a set of topics (Party building, state building) and not as a concept in its own right. The article argues that jianshe is the general theoretical category best suited to capture what the Party is doing when it governs itself and the country. On this basis the author proposes a "political engineering" framework centred on the Party, as an attempt at a new research paradigm for studying the CPC. The article moves through five steps. It first looks for a general category centred on the Party, tracing the late Qing and early Republican turn from reform to "building a party", and contrasting this with Goodnow, Schattschneider and Huntington on parties. It then shows how jianshe became the Party's practical theme after 1949 and links it to Marxist ideas of a proletariat that consciously builds a new society. A critical survey of "social engineering" follows, covering Weber, Pound, Qian Xuesen, Popper, Hayek and Scott. The last section reviews work on political and constitutional engineering before setting out the author's own framework. Zhu's central claim is that in China the party precedes the state, so the usual state–society model hides the most important political variable. Governing the Party and governing the country are, in this account, two sides of one practice, which appears as Party building and national construction. Revolution aims at construction, and the Party's own building is both a dependent variable, organised around economic and social tasks, and an independent variable that drives social change through self-reform. Zhu argues that existing social and constitutional engineering research stays on the level of methodology or Western institutional design. It never identifies the Party as the core agent or jianshe as the way the engineering is carried out. The author answers Popper's charge of utopianism by pointing to policy experiments and by holding that top-level design and "crossing the river by feeling the stones" can be combined. Citing Lenin, Zhu adds that construction is political, because the direction set by the leadership decides the direction of the work. Zhu concludes that jianshe has historical continuity and present-day integrating power, and so can bring together findings that disciplinary divisions have fragmented. Guided by historical materialism, it stresses the interaction of subject and object, which the author says corrects one-sided engineering thinking. Zhu admits that most of the material is familiar and suggests alternative labels such as "politics of construction" or "party engineering" for further discussion. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars try to build an indigenous conceptual vocabulary for Party studies and want to see how they position it against Western social and constitutional engineering theory.

The spirit of the Zunyi Meeting: ever more genuine, ever more new 遵义会议精神历久弥真历久弥新 Lin Jianhua Lin Jianhua asks what the Zunyi Meeting of January 1935, held during the Long March, still offers the Party today. The article argues that the meeting's spirit gives lasting guidance for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Lin treats it as a decisive turning point in Party history and builds the argument on Xi Jinping's 2015 and 2021 remarks in Guizhou, which call for drawing on the meeting's experience. The piece is a short commentary, published in the journal Dangdai Guizhou in 2025. It first recalls the background: the failure of the fifth anti-encirclement campaign in 1934, the Central Red Army's losses early in the Long March (from over 86,000 to just over 30,000, in the author's figures), and the enlarged Politburo meeting at Zunyi. It then sets out five requirements for advancing the adaptation of Marxism, each tied to a lesson from Zunyi and to a present-day task. Lin's core claim is that Zunyi settled a question of line and leadership as well as military errors. In the article's account, it ended the rule of leftist dogmatism, effectively established Mao Zedong's leadership, and began the first-generation central leadership collective. Lin then draws five lessons: a strong leadership core; the Two Integrations (Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture); seeking truth from facts, since the defeat is attributed to detachment from reality; independence and self-reliance, in contrast to obeying the Comintern; and Party unity, upheld through democratic centralism, open debate and criticism and self-criticism. For each, Lin cites statements by Mao, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Party resolutions. Lin concludes that the Party must apply these lessons in the new era. That means grasping the Two Establishes, strengthening the Two Upholds, rallying around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and being guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in pursuing Chinese modernization. The article is a commemorative Party-history piece, not an archival study. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-school commentary links the Zunyi Meeting to current slogans on leadership, theory and unity.

Foundational questions in constructing Marx's view of morality An analysis based on The German Ideology 马克思道德观构建的基础问题 Zhang Yonggang Zhang Yonggang takes up the long dispute between "Marxist moralism" and "Marxist immoralism", associated with Allen Wood, who calls Marx a critic of all morality, and with Rodney Peffer and Ziyade Hussami, who find moral values in Marx's thought. The article argues that neither side can be settled by quarrelling over the word "morality". In Zhang's view, Marx's moral outlook has to be read from its foundations in historical materialism, in the life of real people and in concrete social life, as set out in The German Ideology. The article is organised in three parts. The first asks how morality can legitimately exist within historical materialism and how its normative content is formed. The second turns to the concern with human existence: the "real individual" as the practical subject of morality and the free and all-round development of the human being as its ultimate aim. The third treats morality oriented to social life, including its role as an ideological "tool of thought" in the working of society. Zhang draws on Engels, Kai Nielsen, David McLellan, Alasdair MacIntyre and Paul Blackledge. Zhang argues first that morality is a form of social consciousness determined "in the last instance" by the economic base, but not by it alone. Fatalist and mechanical readings of historical materialism are rejected, as is moral absolutism. The apparent contradiction between Marx's condemnation of bourgeois morality and his moral language against exploitation is said to dissolve: he rejects bourgeois moral content while holding a normative vision of a communist society of human self-realisation. Humans are both "actors" and "authors" of moral norms, which resolves the tension between agency and structural determination. Second, Zhang disputes Wood's split between "moral" and "non-moral" goods. On a broad sense of morality, freedom and self-realisation are moral values, and history's direction and morality's core demand coincide. Zhang concludes that Marx's morality is a distinct "other construction" set against traditional moral philosophy. It does not slide into moral nihilism or moral determinism, and it moves from maintaining social order to pursuing human emancipation. Clarifying these foundations, the author says, answers the objections to Marx's view and supports a Marxist moral theory grounded in the texts. Read the original if you work on Marxist ethics or the Wood debate and want a Chinese scholar's systematic reading of The German Ideology on morality.

From climate ethics to climate justice: themes and trends in Western climate ethics research 从气候伦理到气候正义：西方气候伦理学研究的主题与趋势 Yang Tongjin Gu Yueming This review surveys Western scholarship on climate ethics from 1992 to the present. Yang and Gu argue that the field has moved from clarifying the ethical principles of the climate regime towards climate justice as its central theme, while steadily widening its scope. The text appeared in the journal Foreign Theoretical Trends (2024, no. 5). The authors divide the literature into three stages tied to global climate governance: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change stage (1992–2003), the post-Kyoto Protocol stage (2004–2014) and the Paris Agreement stage (2015 onwards). They then examine four major themes: general theory of climate ethics, climate justice, the ethics of geoengineering, and the ethics of climate responsibility. A final section identifies three emerging directions: non-anthropocentric climate ethics, climate migrants and refugees, and population ethics. Yang and Gu report that early scholars such as Dale Jamieson and Stephen Gardiner presented climate change as an ethical rather than purely scientific or economic problem, one that cost–benefit models cannot capture. On climate justice, the review sets out relational and non-relational foundations, the main distributive principles, and the dispute over historical responsibility, where supporters and sceptics offer competing grounds. On responsibility, it contrasts collectivists, who hold that individuals' main duty is to build just institutions because single emissions are inconsequential, with individualists, who reject the tragedy-of-the-commons model and defend personal duties to cut emissions. In geoengineering, the authors summarise doubts about moral hazard, the slippery slope and unequal procedures. On the new directions, the article describes proposals for multi-species climate justice, debates over who should compensate climate migrants and how, and disputes over population policy, including Simon Caney's critique of restrictive proposals and the argument that developed countries should bear more responsibility for reducing birth rates. The authors conclude that climate ethics is increasingly interdisciplinary and tied to implementation of the Paris Agreement, and that designing population policy acceptable to many interest groups remains an open task. Read the original if you want a structured map of Anglophone climate ethics debates, with names, titles and positions, from a Chinese academic perspective.

Forty years of change in the undergraduate programme and academic discipline of ideological and political education: a multi-perspective reflection 40年来思想政治教育专业与学科变革实践的多域审思 Huang Rongsheng Marking the 40th anniversary of the establishment of the ideological and political education programme (zhuanye) in 2024, Huang Rongsheng asks what the programme and the academic discipline (xueke) of ideological and political education are, where they came from and where they should go. The author notes that scholars agree on the relation between practice and theory but disagree on how programme and discipline relate: which belongs to which, which came first, and which guides the other. Huang's answer is that the two are distinct but bound by a shared purpose and have developed in mutual support, and that their next stage should shift from scale to quality. The article is organised in three perspectives. The first, conceptual, defines the programme as a category of study set up in universities to train specialists in ideological and political work, and the discipline as an academic classification that studies how people's ideological and political qualities form and how education shapes them. The second, historical, periodises each track using official catalogues and policy documents. The third looks ahead to goals and measures for the new journey. Huang argues that the two share three commitments: training people for the Party and the country, training specialists in ideological and political work, and teaching through courses. On history, the programme is traced from 1984 through setting-up, stabilisation and improvement phases. The discipline is traced from 1987 through inception, initial establishment, merger and renewal, ending in its place as a second-level discipline under the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. Huang stresses that this path was unusual, since the programme came first and the discipline later. The author describes the programme as catalysing the discipline, the discipline then supporting the programme with textbooks, degree programmes and teaching staff, and both serving university courses in ideological and political theory. For the programme, Huang proposes optimising training plans, building a systematic curriculum and compiling key textbooks. For the discipline, the proposals are building an autonomous knowledge system, raising the quality of its academic workforce and strengthening research. Three general measures follow: holding to the "lifeline" and "central link" role of ideological and political work, advancing reform and innovation, and strengthening bases and platforms. Read the original if you study how Chinese higher education institutionalised ideological and political education, or want a detailed chronology of the relevant catalogues, policies and textbooks.

Leading and safeguarding the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics through full and rigorous Party and university governance 以全面从严管党治校引领保障中国特色世界一流大学建设 Zhang Jun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao, 2025 no. 4), Zhang Jun takes up the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and Xi Jinping's call to govern the Party with a reforming spirit and strict standards. The author argues that universities in the "Double First-Class" initiative must make full and rigorous self-governance of the Party the guiding and protective force for building world-class universities with Chinese characteristics. In Zhang's account, this serves Chinese modernization and the wider aim of building China into a leading country in education. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out why the Party's self-reform matters, drawing on history, present needs and long-term considerations. The second examines why universities in particular need to deepen full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, looking at their missions, their internal and external circumstances, and their existing weaknesses. The third proposes measures. Zhang is writing from inside the system, as a Central Commission member and a university Party secretary. Zhang contends that self-reform is a proven lesson of the Party's history, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to the post-2012 anti-corruption drive. For universities, the author says, the stakes are higher because they carry political, popular, strategic and international responsibilities, and because they face intense competition in science and talent amid external containment. Zhang acknowledges problems: weak ideological work, uneven transmission of responsibility, and corruption in research, construction and admissions. The proposed remedy is a systematic approach in three strands: making the Party's overall leadership effective, including the president-responsibility system under Party committee leadership and ideological and political education; integrating Party-building with university work through inspections that go deeper, are more specialised and reach lower levels; and making discipline education, institutional constraints and strict governance long-term, with "first-form" early intervention and stronger oversight of top leaders. Zhang concludes that universities must keep a strict tone over the long term, treat problems and their root causes together, and link anti-corruption work with reform, institution-building and development. The aim is to turn the Party's leadership advantage into an advantage in building world-class universities. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior university Party official presents the link between Party discipline and higher-education policy in 2025.

Report on the 2025 symposium on the development of the discipline of scientific atheism 2025年科学无神论学科发展研讨会综述 Zhang Ge This is a report on a symposium on the development of the discipline of scientific atheism, held in Beijing on 30 November 2024 to plan work for 2025. It was organised by the CASS Centre for Science and Atheism and the China Atheism Society, with the journal Science and Atheism as co-organiser. The report notes that the discipline is a 'special discipline' funded under the CASS 'Pinnacle Strategy'. Over thirty scholars and students attended, in person and online. Participants came from the Central Party School, the Central Institute of Socialism, the China Tibetology Research Center, several universities and several CASS institutes. The report is organised in three parts: ten priority research themes for 2025, key tasks in building the discipline, and proposals for the discipline's platforms. It ends with a summing-up by He Xinyuan, head of the special discipline, after remarks by Luo Wendong, Party secretary of the Academy of Marxism, and others. On research, speakers called for systematic study of the classic writers on atheism, for work on the four systems (disciplinary, academic, discourse and textbook) of Marxist atheism, and for criticism of theology. Li Shen argued that atheism is the soul of Marxist religious studies and that the spread of theism is linked to non-Marxist religious studies. On building the discipline, Zhu Xiaoming proposed a 'four-piece set': an anthology of the classics' writings on atheism, interpretive studies, a textbook on Marxist atheism and an atheism dictionary. Others urged making atheism a compulsory subject for cadres and young students, and a stable university discipline, starting with a second-level discipline within Marxist theory. On platforms, speakers urged the China Atheism Society to recruit young scholars and the journal to seek CSSCI listing. Some also urged the research centre to work as a think tank. He Xinyuan pledged to consolidate the four platforms, start textbook writing and press for inclusion in cadre training. The spread and transformation of the concept of "nihilism" “虚无主义”概念的传播与衍变 Zhang Shunyue This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (27 February 2025) asks how the term "nihilism" (xuwu zhuyi) entered Chinese and why its meaning has remained so unclear. Zhang notes that "nihilist party", "nihilism", "Narodnik", "anarchist party" and "anarchism" were often used interchangeably, so that the sense of each shifted with the speaker's stance. The article's thesis is that in early twentieth-century Chinese usage "nihilism" meant Western Nihilism, anarchism and Daoist "emptiness and non-action" all at once. The piece follows the term in three stages. It begins with the ancient Chinese word xuwu, found in Daoist texts such as the Laozi commentaries, the Zhuangzi and the Guanzi. It then traces the Western Nihilist/Nihilism from its Russian origins through late Qing transliterations and the Japanese translation "nihilist party". Finally it looks at dictionaries and at attempts by Liao Zhongkai and Zhou Zuoren to clarify the concept. Zhang's central reasoning is that the term arrived through two channels that blurred it. Drawing on Jiang Lu, the article says Nihilism was used in Russia from 1829 as a term of abuse, then attached to the democrats and assassins of the Narodnik movement. Late Qing writers mostly transliterated it. The translation "nihilist party" came via Japan, where Kayama Sentaro's book on modern anarchism was repeatedly introduced to China under "nihilist party" titles. This led, in Zhang's account, to nihilism, populism and anarchism sharing one label. The article shows the confusion in the dictionaries of Yan Huiqing (1908) and Hemeling (1916), which separated a philosophical sense from a political one. Zhang reports that Liao Zhongkai (1906) listed socialism, anarchism and nihilism as three separate doctrines but later translated a book on anarchism under a "nihilist party" title. Zhou Zuoren (1907) argued that assassination was a political tactic and that nihilism was a philosophical doctrine rooted in materialism. Zhang judges that these efforts had little effect, because intellectuals of the period used many new terms without studying them systematically. Read the original if you want a compact, source-based account of the term's early Chinese history, from Daoist usage to the translations of the late Qing and early Republic.

Distinguishing the origins of overseas studies of the Communist Party of China 海外中国共产党研究的起源辨析 Han Qiang Feng Ziyan Where did overseas research on the Communist Party of China begin? Han Qiang and Feng Ziyan note that scholars in China have not reached consensus on this, and argue that the answer lies less in fixing one date or place than in comparing the motives, methods and priorities behind each candidate origin. They hold that the field's early history is bound up with the Party's changing international standing. The article first sets out three views found in Chinese scholarship: a Japanese origin, a Soviet and Comintern origin, and a US origin. For Japan it cites intelligence reports and early studies from 1921 to 1926. For the Soviet Union it points to Comintern-era reports and a 1926 history by the adviser Naumov. For the United States it cites journalists and diplomats, Edgar Snow, and John King Fairbank's Harvard East Asian Center. It then compares the three on motive, method and focus, and closes with lessons for Chinese research. On motive, the authors describe Japanese work as driven by anti-communism and the needs of the invasion of China, Soviet work as driven by ideology and strategy, and American work as serving foreign policy and later shifting from journalism to academic area studies. On method, they credit Japan with document collection, oral history and fieldwork, the Soviet Union with archives and Marxist methodology, and the United States with interdisciplinary and comparative approaches and mentor-based training. They argue that each country's research priorities followed its national interests. In their account, Japanese research now faces decline, Russian research is expanding as archives open, and American research concentrates on the contemporary Party and informs government policy. Han and Feng draw four lessons. Chinese scholars should use overseas archives and methods, and judge overseas findings critically, given their ideological leanings and the dual role of scholars as policy advisers. They should also support domestic re-research and train talent. Finally, they should address the asymmetry between extensive foreign study of the Chinese Communist Party and weaker Chinese study of foreign parties, especially in the United States. They call for an independent body of knowledge on political parties. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the history of overseas research on the Party is framed, and which sources and debates it cites.

Leading and safeguarding the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics through full and rigorous Party self-governance in running universities 以全面从严管党治校引领保障中国特色世界一流大学建设 Zhang Jun Writing after the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2025), Zhang Jun, a university Party secretary, asks how full and rigorous Party self-governance can lead and safeguard the building of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics. The author's answer is that the Party's self-reform and the advance of higher education are internally unified. In this account, strict Party discipline in universities is a precondition for them to serve Chinese modernization. The article is a commentary in three parts, framed by Xi Jinping's speeches. It first sets out why the Party's self-reform matters, then examines why universities must pursue full and rigorous Party self-governance, and finally proposes concrete measures. It draws on Party history, from the Yan'an rectification campaign to the post-2012 anti-corruption drive, and on supervisory work in universities such as inspection tours and discipline-inspection reform. Zhang argues that self-reform is the Party's proven method, a necessity for Chinese modernization and the fundamental way to escape the "historical cycle" of rise and decline. The author says universities face heavier tasks, which are political, popular, strategic and international in character. The proposed remedies are threefold: put the Party's overall leadership into practice, embed Party building in university operations through deeper, more specialised and more grassroots-level inspection, and make governance durable through discipline education, institutional constraints and sustained anti-corruption work. A study of the spread of "micro-superstition" among young people 青少年群体“微迷信”行为蔓延态势研究 Zhuo Mingliang Yuan Tao Zhuo Mingliang and Yuan Tao examine "micro-superstition" (wei mixin), a term they use for lightly held, everyday beliefs and practices that lack scientific basis but are widely followed, such as praying for exam luck or consulting online fortune-telling. The authors argue that, although these practices involve a lower degree of belief than traditional superstition, they remain superstitious in nature. In their view, if left unchecked among young people, they erode scientific outlook, the spirit of striving and collectivism, and pose an ideological security risk. The article opens with a short history of the modern, anti-scientific meaning of "superstition" in China. It then proceeds in four parts: five main manifestations, four potential harms, four causes, and four policy recommendations. The manifestations include temple incense-burning, worship of statues on school campuses before exams, online divination such as "cyber merit" and "AI Buddha", imported practices such as tarot, astrology and Japanese shrine charms, and a market in superstition-themed products. The authors cite figures on temple ticket bookings, social media topics and the fees charged by tarot bloggers. On harms, the authors claim that micro-superstition damages young people's inner world, invites fraud, spreads negative values, and opens a channel for Western ideological infiltration. They also warn that shared group identities could serve political mobilisation, citing the "Arab Spring" as an analogy. On causes, they stress anxiety arising from developmental pressures (the sense of being unable to "lie flat" yet unable to win the "rat race"), the spread of individualism, utilitarianism and pan-entertainment trends online, venture capital that has turned fortune-telling into a profitable industry, and weakened anti-superstition education that leaves young people tolerant of it. The authors propose that youth organisations and government departments study and respond to young people's real difficulties, especially in employment and marriage. They also call for stricter supervision of self-media, with sensitive-word databases, penalties and blocking of overseas sites, tighter regulation and investment screening of the cultural and entertainment market, and stronger education in scientific atheism and Marxist materialism through schools, the Communist Youth League and central media. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese academics frame youth folk-belief practices as an ideological and governance issue, with concrete survey-style examples and policy proposals.

Developments among foreign communist parties in 2024: new openings amid a trough, seeking unity amid diversity 2024年外国共产党发展动态：低谷中蕴新机 多样中求团结 Yu Haiqing Yu Haiqing's annual survey asks how communist parties outside China fared in 2024, a year the author describes as marked by an increasingly complex international situation and by the accelerating "great changes unseen in a century". The article's answer is that the parties kept up extra-parliamentary struggle and recorded mixed electoral results. Some achieved real revivals, but internal divisions in the international communist movement grew and held back the advance of world socialism. The review has four parts. It first covers activity outside parliament: commemorations of Lenin on the 120th anniversary of his death, campaigns against NATO on its 75th anniversary, and struggles against anti-communism, right-wing governments and imperialism. It then compares election results in what the author calls the "super election year", from the European Parliament elections to votes in Turkey, Sri Lanka, Uruguay, India, Japan, Brazil, Chile and South Africa. Next it reports party congresses and strategies in socialist-ruled states (Vietnam, Laos, the DPRK, Cuba) and in the Japanese, US, Turkish and Argentine parties. It ends with splits and new party formations. On elections, Yu sorts the European parties into three groups: stable (the Communist Party of Greece, AKEL of Cyprus), long-declining (the French, Portuguese and Spanish parties), and visibly reviving (the Czech-Moravian alliance, the Communist Party of Austria, the Workers' Party of Belgium). Elsewhere results diverge as sharply. Yu cites the victory of the Marxist Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Sri Lanka and gains in Turkey and Uruguay, against sharp losses in Brazil and Chile and the Japanese party's own admission of weakening strength. On division, Yu points to the new parties founded in Germany, the United States and Austria, to the sharpening rivalry between the World Anti-Imperialist Platform and European Communist Action, and to the repeated breakups of Nepal's communist coalitions. Yu reads these as signs both of diversification and of fragmentation. Yu concludes that the turbulent global situation offers room for growth above all to parties that combine adherence to principle with flexibility, allowing them to revive after setbacks. The year, in Yu's view, again showed the importance of unity: world socialism can advance only through cooperation among socialist forces, by narrowing differences and building consensus on common goals. Read the original if you want a detailed, country-by-country account of 2024 election results, party congresses and factional disputes among foreign communist parties, as reported from a Chinese state-academic perspective.

Marx on the "retribution" of colonialism and its contemporary lessons A close reading of "The Indian Revolt" and related texts 马克思论殖民主义的“报应”及其现实启示 Xu Qin Xu Qin asks what Marx meant by "retribution" (baoying) in his 1850s writings on British rule in India, and what that idea says to the present. The article argues that Marx used the word in a materialist-dialectical sense: colonialism's own crimes produce the opposition that undoes it. Xu opens with Xi Jinping's 2018 warning that trade wars and economic hegemony will end up like "lifting a rock only to drop it on one's own feet", and presents Marx's concept as an earlier warning to the colonial powers. The study rests on Marx's New-York Daily Tribune articles on the 1857 Indian uprising, including "The Revolt in the Indian Army", "The Indian Revolt", "The Indian Question" and "Investigation of Tortures in India", together with his writings on the East India Company. After separating Marxist "retribution" from religious karma, Xu identifies three forms of it: the sepoy army that Britain built and that then rebelled; the sepoys' "atrocities" as a concentrated reflection of British conduct; and the cost of holding India, which could exceed any revenue. A final section draws conclusions for today. Xu contrasts religious retribution, which is run by an alien supernatural power and rests on idealism, with the Marxist version, in which people themselves are the agents and cause and effect are objective. In this account Marx treated the revolt as retribution because it came from the British-trained, British-fed sepoys, not from the plundered peasantry. Xu says Marx tied the sepoys' violence to British annexations, tax torture and officers' cruelty, and criticised The Times for inflating it. On cost, Xu cites Marx's point that India's revenue never reached the British treasury, while Parliament lent the Company over £50 million. Only a small group of shareholders, officials and traders profited. Xu concludes that colonialism's end as a system, which the author dates to Namibia's independence in 1990, did not end colonial thinking. The author charges the United States and the West with neo-colonial hegemony, citing domestic disorder and the Gaza vetoes as self-inflicted costs, and calls on them to abandon colonial thinking and follow the trend of peace, development, cooperation and win-win outcomes. The article also urges a new type of international relations built on mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation, and links this to the Global Security Initiative, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Marx's India articles, or an example of how Chinese scholarship ties them to current foreign-policy language.

The second leap over the "Caudine Forks" “卡夫丁峡谷”的第二重跨越 Yu Bin Yu Bin asks why the Soviet Union, having apparently crossed the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism that Marx discussed in his late writings on Russia, fell back into them, and what this means for China. The article argues that the Soviet Union and China completed only a first leap, which abolished the capitalist system. A second leap remains: workers must fully master the achievements capitalism created. Yu reads the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) call to raise the whole Party's "Marxist level and capacity for modernization" as the path to this second leap. The article has four parts. It first traces the incomplete crossing, from Marx's 1881 reply to Vera Zasulich through the October Revolution, the Soviet collapse and China's reform and opening up. It then defends the claim that the first leap was completed, against two views in the scholarly literature. A third section examines the first leap's shortcomings, covering Lenin's New Economic Policy, the Soviet model, the Party's treatment of intellectuals in China and Deng Xiaoping's response. The last section names three new problems of the second leap and proposes measures for Party members. Yu's central move is to separate two leaps. The first is the abolition of capitalist relations of production and the "two ruptures" of the Communist Manifesto, with traditional property relations and traditional ideas. The second is the real appropriation of capitalism's positive results, above all knowledge. Yu holds that the Soviet Union fell not through backwardness but because Party members' Marxist level was too low to break fully with feudal and bourgeois ideas, which left it open to Gorbachev's turn to democratic socialism and to "peaceful evolution". Yu then names three requirements. Science and labour must be directly united, so that production is not left under the control of capital. The people led by the Party must be the subject of the leap, since development must rely on and benefit them. Marxist level and modernization capacity must rise together, since either alone leads to failure. Yu proposes theoretical study, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and practice of whole-process people's democracy. Party members are given tasks by workplace: civil servants, state-owned enterprises, private firms, individual traders and mixed-ownership companies. Yu concludes that once members have these capacities, the goal of a modernized socialist power will be reached, and other countries may then look to China as a model. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Marx's Russia writings to Party-building and Chinese modernization.

Activating the outstanding elements of China's excellent traditional culture 激活中华优秀传统文化中的优秀因子 Han Qingxiang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 3 March 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's instruction to use Marxism to activate the vital elements of China's excellent traditional culture and give them new meaning for the era. Han Qingxiang reads the instruction as setting out the agent, object, purpose and method of activation, and as a basic guide to building a strong socialist cultural power. Han argues that Marxism and traditional culture are highly compatible, so activation can bring out the contemporary value of tradition and serve national rejuvenation. The piece has three parts. The first identifies which "outstanding elements" are to be activated; the second sets out how activation should proceed; the third lists the new contemporary meanings to be given to them. For the first part, Han draws on Chinese philosophy, ethics and morality, and the shared everyday values of ordinary people. The core argument concerns method. Han says activation means making traditional culture "modern" and giving Chinese civilization modern strength, and it must resolve four questions: cognition, agent, method and purpose. On agent, Han holds that Marxism is inclusive, opposes dogmatism and shares with tradition the goals of national rejuvenation and peaceful development. The method is mutual empowerment through the Two Integrations: tradition supplies soil for adapting Marxism, and Marxism renews tradition. The purpose is to consolidate the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation, move beyond Western-centred narratives of modernity, and build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system. Han also proposes new contemporary meanings. Harmony between humans and nature is linked to ecological civilization, "the world belongs to all" to a community with a shared future for mankind, and "the people as the foundation" to putting the people first. Traditional ethics is linked to Party-building, loyalty to the Party, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and official integrity, while everyday values are linked to family ethics, honest labour and the rule of law. Han concludes that activation should release creative vitality in Chinese culture, assert its subjectivity, build an autonomous knowledge system and raise the global influence of Chinese civilization. It would also enrich people's spiritual world and strengthen Party leadership over culture. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the relation between Marxism and traditional culture, and which concepts they select for reinterpretation.

Clarifying the materialist foundation of Marxist epistemology 马克思主义认识论的唯物主义基础辨析 Wang Xiaosheng This short theoretical piece, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025, asks how Marxist epistemology can keep its materialist foundation while recognising the subject's activity in cognition. Wang Xiaosheng argues that stressing subjectivity can undermine materialism, while the theory of reflection, though materialist in stance, has not explained why reflection is objectively valid. The article's answer is that the objective validity of reflection must be shown through a bodily, material basis that remains present inside sensation, reason and concepts. The article moves in three steps under three headings: the objectivity of sensation and experience; the spiritualisation of sensation and experience; and the non-conceptual element within concepts. Wang engages Husserl's phenomenology, Adorno's critique of it, Kant's idea of the manifold of sensibility, and Hegel's concept of actuality. Examples include the bent stick in water, the pain of the body, a blind person's grasp of 'red', and a mother's 'love'. Wang observes that both defenders and critics of reflection treat sensory experience as unreliable, yet cognition depends on it, so it must contain something objective. Husserl locates this in the indubitable fact of having an experience, which Wang calls a subjectivised objectivity. Following Adorno, Wang locates it instead in the body: objectivity in sensation comes from material interaction, not from reflection. Cognition nonetheless spiritualises sensation, making it neutral and expressible in language, and the objective content survives as a 'trace' of bodily activity. Reason is likewise both opposed to nature and an extension of it, and logic rests on a pre-logical base. Concepts therefore contain non-conceptual elements; without them they are empty words, and scientific innovation often comes when such elements break through existing concepts. Wang concludes that Marx's concept of actuality, unlike Hegel's, contains the bodily element and connects with external reality, so that a concept 'contains' reality rather than merely referring to it. Marxist epistemology, in this reading, is dialectical materialism that sees both the objective basis of cognition and the interaction of body and mind, offering a key to the problems of traditional subject–object dualism. Read the original if you want a compact attempt to ground the Marxist theory of reflection in the body through Adorno and phenomenology.

Using red resources to strengthen the fighting spirit of young cadres 运用红色资源增强年轻干部的斗争精神 Wang Yan This commentary asks how "red resources" can be used to build the fighting spirit (douzheng jingshen) of young cadres. Wang takes up Xi Jinping's call to use such resources to strengthen ideals and convictions and raise the capacity to struggle. The article argues that the historical, cultural and contemporary value of these resources should be tapped so that young cadres learn to shoulder heavy responsibilities, work hard and confront problems. Wang organises the piece around four types of red resource: historical events, revolutionary heroes, revolutionary spirit and revolutionary cultural relics. Each is linked to a distinct quality to be cultivated: struggle consciousness, will, strength and wisdom. Xi Jinping's statements are cited throughout as the guiding framework. On historical events, Wang says they show that struggle is tied to individual survival and national strength. They should be studied through a connected view, on the basis of reliable sources, so that political education works through events. On heroes and spirit, Wang calls for learning loyalty, persistence and plainness, and for the Party's self-reform, a people-centred approach and tempering in strict inner-Party political life. On relics, Wang proposes a shift from rescue to preventive protection, protecting objects together with their surroundings, and using modern technology and immersive display. Wang also proposes linking revolutionary culture education to anti-corruption education, including integrity education bases at red sites, and deeper research into the history behind relics. The aim is for Party members and cadres to take up the task of national rejuvenation through concrete action. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school writing links heritage protection to cadre training.

Grasping the inherent unity of upholding the Party's overall leadership and putting the people at the centre 深刻把握坚持党的全面领导与坚持以人民为中心的内在统一性 Du Feijin This Guangming Daily commentary by Du Feijin takes up two principles that the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization says must be upheld: the Party's overall leadership and putting the people at the centre. Du argues that the two are inherently unified. In this reading, only Party leadership keeps reform people-centred, and only a people-centred approach keeps the Party close to the masses and preserves its advanced and pure character. The article has three parts. The first treats Party leadership as the primary principle of reform, examined through theoretical, historical and practical logics. The second sets out why reform must be people-centred. The third explains the unity of the two principles and ends with practical requirements for Party committees, officials and Party members. On leadership, Du cites the Communist Manifesto to claim that a proletarian party has no interests apart from those of the proletariat as a whole. The author holds that reform and opening up has been led by the Party from the start, from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The article credits Xi Jinping's personal leadership and Party institutions, including the Party's leadership system as the fundamental leadership system, with enabling reform to break through entrenched interests. On the people, Du presents them as four subjects of reform: the value subject, the driving subject, the evaluating subject and the sharing subject. As examples, Du cites social security expansion, income-distribution reform and the 221 revisions made to the draft Decision after consultation. The unity is said to show in three ways. The Party's nature and purpose match the people-oriented character of reform. Centralised, unified leadership by the Party Central Committee is the most reliable guarantee of the people being masters of the country. The Party's goals match the people's aspirations, as in the plenum's "seven focuses". Du calls for deeper understanding of the Two Establishes and for the Two Upholds, with no selective implementation of central decisions. Local reform plans should fit local conditions. Du also calls for a renewed mass line, extensive investigation and research, and the development of whole-process people's democracy, so that the people's wisdom shapes reform design. Read the original if you want an example of how the official Party-building discourse links Party leadership, the people-centred principle and the 2024 reform Decision, with the Decision's own examples and formulations.

Research on building ideological positions: course, main achievements and future trends 意识形态阵地建设研究的历程回顾、主要成就与趋势展望 Li Liaoning Yu Jingyuan This literature review surveys more than twenty years of Chinese scholarship on "ideological position building" (yishi xingtai zhendi jianshe), the effort to hold and expand the physical and virtual spaces where Marxist ideology is transmitted. The authors argue that the research has tracked national economic conditions, policy priorities and technological change. They conclude that it still lacks overall coherence, theoretical grounding and historical depth. The article was published in a 2024 journal on Party building and ideological education. The review divides the research into four phases. The first, after reform and opening up, drew little attention. Attention then rose after Xi Jinping's 2014 holistic approach to national security, with universities as the main focus. The 19th Party Congress (2017) called for strengthening position building and management, and publications peaked in 2019. After the Party's third historical resolution (2021), output declined, with universities and the internet remaining central. The main body then sorts the literature into four themes: why position building is necessary, the key concepts, the main arenas, and response strategies. On necessity, the authors report that scholars point to the Soviet collapse, which they attribute partly to the loss of control over public opinion. They also report the view that ideology has no vacuum, that socialist and capitalist ideologies are in irreconcilable contest, and that Western pressure on China persists. On concepts, scholars treat a "position" as both real and virtual space, and read "position consciousness" as both cognition and responsibility. The authors note that no clear definition of position building exists. The strategies they summarise are strengthening position consciousness, occupying positions with Marxism, upholding Party leadership, combining position building with the rule of law, and taking the initiative in struggle. The authors identify three gaps. Research should treat position building as a system, covering its features, current problems, goals and evaluation mechanisms. It should draw more on Marxist theory, such as the views of contradiction and of time and space, rather than on Western theories of hegemony. It should also offer a systematic account of the Chinese Communist Party's century of experience in this field. Read the original if you want a map of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship is organised, including its main themes, representative studies and recommended directions.

Lenin's idea of the ruling party's "general leadership" and its contemporary value 列宁执政党“总的领导”思想及其当代价值 Shi Weilei After the October Revolution the Bolsheviks became a ruling party and had to decide how it should lead a state without simply running it. Shi Weilei argues that Lenin, combining Marx and Engels's theory of party leadership with the practice of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks), developed an idea of the ruling party's "general leadership" (总的领导). In Shi's reading, this is overall, supreme leadership of the whole of national life, exercised through state power rather than in place of it. The article has four parts. It traces the idea through three phases: an embryonic stage (1917 to spring 1919), a preliminary formation (1919 to early 1921) and a final formation (from 1921). It then sets out the idea's content, the means of implementing it, and its value today. Shi draws mainly on Lenin's writings and on resolutions of the Party congresses of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). Shi's central claim is that "general leadership" combines several features. It is supreme and comprehensive, covering state power, the economy, culture and the military. It is the unity of political, ideological and organisational leadership, including the principle that the Party manages cadres. It includes general supervision through independent Party control commissions. Lenin first used the term in 1920, in criticism of the Proletkult. In 1922 he used it against the confusion of Party and soviet functions, which Shi says weakened both. Shi lists the means of exercising it: guiding legislation without replacing law, Party groups and exemplary Communists inside other bodies, cadre selection, leadership of trade unions and the youth league, democratic centralism, a ban on factions, and better capacity to oversee the whole and coordinate the parts. Shi concedes that the Russian party failed to resolve the problem in practice, but holds that Lenin set out the right path in theory. Shi concludes that the idea is a theoretical source for the Chinese Communist Party's "comprehensive leadership" in the new era. Shi claims that "general", "everything" and "comprehensive" mean full coverage and indirect, overall leadership, not meddling in detail. The article calls for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership, and for leadership over all work. It also calls for a tight organisational system from central to grassroots level, and for stronger leadership capacity, above all political leadership. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory account of how Lenin's writings on the party and the state are used to ground the current doctrine of the Party's comprehensive leadership.

The generative logic, connotations and transmission paths of the Communist Party of China's "red genes" 中国共产党红色基因的生成逻辑、内涵解析及传承路径探赜 Yin Yan Meng Zishuo Yin Yan and Meng Zishuo take up the concept of the "red gene" (hongse jiyin), which Xi Jinping first used in 2013, and ask how it arose, what it contains and how it can be passed on. Borrowing the biological metaphor, the authors treat the red gene as the core structure that sustains the Party's vitality as a "political organism" and distinguishes it from every other party. They argue that it is not an innate property but the product of historical, practical and dialectical conditions, and that understanding it helps explain "why the Party can". The article has three main parts. The first examines the generative logic along three lines: a theoretical logic rooted in Marxism, a historical logic rooted in Chinese traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture, and a practical logic formed over more than a century of Party history. The second analyses the connotations of the red gene. The third sets out four paths of transmission, followed by a short conclusion. On connotations, the authors identify four features, each tied to a source. The gene is scientific, grounded in faith in Marxism and communism; people-centred, rooted in the principle of putting the people first; combative, forged in revolutionary struggle and shown in the Party's self-reform; and innovative, visible in the successive adaptations of Marxism to Chinese conditions. On transmission, they propose passing on and extending the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists (jingshen puxi), protecting and using material red resources such as sites and memorials (with digital display technologies), deepening Party-history study and education, and building a red-education system. The last of these would link schools with local sites, link schools with each other, and integrate the content into ideological and political theory courses. Yin and Meng conclude that a party can keep its vanguard character and vitality only with spiritual nourishment, and that the four paths should be pursued together so that the "red land" passes to later generations. They note shortcomings in current practice, including neglect or damage of some red heritage sites and gaps in the spiritual lineage. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party-building scholarship frames political-cultural inheritance, with its sources, content and educational measures set out in one place.

The Communist Party of China's practice of strengthening discipline during the New Democratic Revolution and its lessons 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党加强纪律建设的实践与启示 Zhang Deming Zhang Deming asks how the Communist Party of China built up discipline between its founding in 1921 and 1949, and what that record offers for discipline-building today. The article argues that the Party steadily refined its rules on political, organisational, integrity, mass-line, work and lifestyle discipline, and that this raised discipline awareness across the Party and laid a solid foundation for revolutionary victory and the founding of New China. The article has three parts. The first traces the development of discipline through successive Party constitutions, from the First Congress (1921) to the Seventh Congress (1945), and through the Great Revolution, Agrarian Revolutionary War, War of Resistance against Japan and War of Liberation. The second identifies three features of the period. The third draws three lessons for the present. In Zhang's account, the first feature is the building of supervisory bodies: the Central Supervisory Commission after the Fifth Congress, inspection regulations, the Soviet-era workers' and peasants' inspection organs, and later supervisory commissions. The second is an ever fuller body of rules, including early anti-corruption notices, the 1933 directive on punishing corruption, secrecy regulations, and the 'Four Subordinations' (individual to organisation, minority to majority, lower level to higher level, whole Party to the Central Committee). The third is warning education through exemplary cases: Xie Busheng, Huang Kegong and Xiao Yubi were executed, and Zhang Guotao was disciplined and eventually expelled. Zhang cites Mao Zedong's view that Party and Red Army members must follow stricter discipline than ordinary civilians. The article also covers military discipline, namely the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention, and the Two Musts of 1949. Zhang concludes that today's Party should keep up anti-corruption work and make it routine and long-term, drawing on Xi Jinping's call to advance the 'dare not, unable, unwilling' approach together. The article also calls for improving discipline rules and institutions, citing the revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions that took effect in January 2024. It further urges stronger discipline education, with emphasis on political and organisational discipline, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line overview of the Party's early disciplinary institutions and cases, and of how they are linked to current campaigns.

Marx and Engels's thought on modernization and its contemporary implications 马克思恩格斯的现代化思想及其当代启示 Zhou Dan This article asks what Marx and Engels contributed to the theory of modernization, a topic that postwar Western modernization studies took up only later. Zhou Dan argues that their theory of social development is above all a theory of modern society, and that it therefore amounts to a body of thought on modernization. In the author's reading, that thought supplies a theoretical foundation and a direction for Chinese modernization. The article is organised in five parts. It begins with three preconditions of modernization, drawn from Engels's remark on the English industrial revolution, French political revolution and German philosophical revolution. It then treats the assertion of human agency, the value goal of the free and all-round development of the individual, the logic by which Marx and Engels confront the problems of their age, and their vision of a future communist civilisation. Each part ends by linking the classical position to Chinese modernization. Zhou's central move is to read modernization as having three dimensions: modern persons (philosophical revolution), the modern state (political revolution, illustrated by the French Declaration of the Rights of Man) and the modern material mode of production (industrial revolution). Marx and Engels, the author notes, rarely used the word itself, and mostly in connection with modern production. Zhou then argues that they gave modernization a dialectical analysis. They credited capitalism with advancing the productive forces while criticising capitalist modernity as a process in which the valorisation of capital devalues the human being. They also held that modernization has no single prescribed pattern, since historical conditions differ between countries. Engels's theory of the resultant of historical forces and Marx's theory of world history are used to ground the claim that people, as the practical subject, drive modernization. Zhou concludes that Marx and Engels made the free and all-round development of the individual the core value of modernization, and that this points to a 'community of free individuals' and a shared human future beyond Western centrism and 'universal values'. In the author's account, Chinese modernization is the contemporary practice of this thought and has overcome the inherent dilemmas of capitalist modernity, through a socialist market economy and a people-centred approach. Zhou calls for pursuing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese reading of how Marx and Engels's classical texts are used to legitimise Chinese modernization.

Marx's thought on productive forces and its implications for developing new quality productive forces 马克思生产力思想及其对发展新质生产力的启示 Sun Shaoyong Sun Shaoyong asks how new quality productive forces, a concept prominent in Party policy since 2023, can be grounded in Marx's own account of productive forces. The article argues that new quality productive forces belong to Marx's category of productive forces but give it new content in technological form, historical meaning, internal requirements and strategic value. In Sun's reading, the concept amounts to a terminological and paradigm shift in Marxist productive-force theory for the twenty-first century. The article has four parts. It first sets out three core determinations of productive forces in Marx: the creative power of 'real individuals', a combined force formed in actual production, and the capacity for metabolic exchange between humans and nature. It then interprets new quality productive forces through historical materialism, political economy and modernization. A third part draws practical implications, and a short conclusion follows. Sun cites Marx's German Ideology, Capital and his critique of List, alongside Xi Jinping's statements and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Sun's central move is to read new quality productive forces through Marx's three elements of productive forces: labourers, means of labour and objects of labour. New technologies such as artificial intelligence and data replace some manual labour, push workers towards mental labour, and create new use-values and new value. Sun treats division of labour and cooperation as the 'social labour' dimension and links the concept to Chinese modernization through technological, factor and industrial modernization. Because Marx treats productive forces as historically specific and as unity of natural and social productive forces, Sun holds that new quality productive forces are necessarily 'green productive forces'. Sun draws four proposals. These are to train high-quality 'new quality labourers' by linking education, science and talent; to develop green technology and new energy; to adjust relations of production, including the basic socialist economic system, the Two Unwaverings, distribution by labour combined with distribution by factors, and a new nationwide system for major innovation; and to integrate the digital and real economies. Sun concludes that labourers play the leading role and that tracing the concept to Marx clarifies its features and requirements. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese scholars derive new quality productive forces from Marx's texts and what policy measures they attach to it.

Raising the quality of people's lives in building Chinese modernization: inherent requirements and practical dimensions 在中国式现代化建设中提高人民生活品质：内在要求与实践向度 Ding Yuanzhu Ding Yuanzhu takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's call to "promote people's wellbeing and raise the quality of their lives" and asks what "quality of life" (shenghuo pinzhi) means and why it is central to Chinese modernization. The article argues that the features of Chinese modernization named in the report, including common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress and harmony between humanity and nature, all find concentrated expression in the quality of people's lives. Understanding the concept, Ding contends, is therefore important for grasping the essential requirements of Chinese modernization. The article opens with a conceptual section defining life quality as a composite of economic, social, cultural and spiritual elements, with objective and subjective dimensions and individual and group levels. It then draws on Marx and Engels's theory of all-round human development, Walt Rostow's stages of growth, and Amartya Sen. Later sections discuss how to combine objective measurement with subjective assessment, including happiness, and then turn to policy priorities in the new development stage: social resilience, ageing, employment, artificial intelligence, education, incomes and consumption, with Japan's consumption experience as a cautionary case. Ding's core argument is that life quality is the necessary outcome of development at a certain stage. Following Rostow's added stage of "the pursuit of quality of life", Ding holds that economic growth should be judged by what it brings to all the people. Objective conditions and subjective satisfaction are each necessary but not sufficient, so the two must be assessed together. Placing "the all-round enrichment of material things and all-round human development" side by side is presented as a continuation of Marx's theory of human development, with free time and free choice as markers. Ding adds that government should look beyond individual happiness to the long-term wellbeing of society as a whole, because market-driven individual desires can foster greed. On policy, Ding calls for attention to the effects of epidemics, ageing, digitalisation and climate on wellbeing. Ding also calls for the employment-first strategy, education reform in response to AI, attention to young people and avoidance of "involution", and a rise in incomes, with a more balanced distribution, to support consumption. The conclusion invokes the 20th Party Congress's five major principles, including Party leadership and a people-centred approach, as guiding the effort to raise life quality. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated scholar's account of how "quality of life" is conceptualised in the discourse of Chinese modernization and linked to employment, ageing and consumption policy.

Marx's conception of revolution and its significance for the new era 马克思革命观及其新时代意蕴 Gao Junhua Gao Junhua takes up Hannah Arendt's claim that Marx, though the greatest theorist of revolution, almost wholly ignored the revolutionaries' real intention, the founding of freedom. The article treats this as a representative misreading: it denies freedom a place in Marx's theory and then pits the mature Marx against the young Marx. Gao argues that Marx's conception of revolution can be understood only through the close link between political and social revolution and through its relation to freedom. On that basis, Gao explains in what sense China in the new era speaks of continuing revolution. The article has four parts. The first sets out the scientific content of Marx's conception, drawing on On the Jewish Question, the Communist Manifesto and Hal Draper's Karl Marx's Theory of Revolution. The second examines its value orientation, distinguishing political freedom from social freedom. The third discusses the revolutionary subject, the proletariat. The fourth turns to the new era, taking up the Party's self-reform and common prosperity. Gao holds that for Marx political revolution is the struggle between classes over state power, and that it need not be violent: Marx allowed some countries to win power through universal suffrage. Bourgeois revolutions, in this reading, produced only formal freedom, because the split between state and civil society and private ownership left real freedom unrealised. Social revolution therefore means developing the productive forces, replacing private ownership of the means of production and so overcoming alienated labour, and it serves as the basis of political revolution. Against Arendt, Gao argues that Marx never abandoned freedom: it appears in the Paris Commune, in the later notion of the 'free individuality', and in the realm of freedom beyond the realm of necessity. The proletariat, as a universal class, moves from a class in itself to a class for itself through revolutionary practice, uniting consciousness with reality and the universal with the particular. Gao concludes that two themes of the new era extend Marx's conception. The Party's self-reform is presented as political revolution, expressing Marx's stress on the proletarian party and his dialectic of the subject remaking itself. Common prosperity is presented as social revolution, resting on developed productive forces, adjusted relations of production with public ownership in the leading position, and the material basis for individual freedom. Gao links these in the Party's formula of leading a great social revolution through a great self-reform. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar defends a freedom-centred reading of Marx against Arendt and ties it to current Party doctrine.

Reflections on the presuppositions of paradigm construction in Chinese Marxist philosophy From the perspective of the "self-justification of philosophical paradigms" 中国马克思主义哲学范式建设的前提意识之思 Cao Dianshun Cao Dianshun asks what presuppositions must be examined before a distinctive paradigm of Chinese Marxist philosophy can be built. Reading paradigm construction as a process of the paradigm's "self-justification", the author argues that four preliminary questions come first: its theoretical premises, its problem-consciousness, its theoretical grounds and its academic discourse. The thesis is that Chinese Marxist philosophy needs a paradigm that fuses "realistic practicality" with "scientific academic quality" and moves beyond a derivative "apprentice" stage. The article, published in Theoretical Investigation (2024, no. 5), has four sections matching these four questions. The first treats "practicality" and "academic quality" as the twin theoretical premises and their inner unity. The second takes "concern for reality" and "genuine philosophy" as the problem-consciousness behind paradigm construction. The third reflects critically on the field's theoretical grounds, and the fourth defines the academic discourse of the new paradigm. Cao's central move is a set of contrasts. Practicality is the guiding principle, logical starting point and test of any paradigm, while academic quality is its basic requirement. The author criticises "apprentice academic quality", Chinese scholarship that reads Marx through Hegel, Kant or Heidegger, copies Soviet textbooks (the author cites Ai Siqi's generation) or simply adopts Marxism outside China. In Cao's view this mimicry and dogmatism limits originality and delays the arrival of the paradigm-construction stage. In the final section Cao separates "realistic practicality" from idealist "rational practicality" and from dogmatic "theoretical practicality", and "scientific academic quality" from "abstract rational" and "apprentice" scholarship. Cao holds that only a paradigm combining the first of each pair can guide Chinese modernization, by stressing the particular side of historical materialism while Marx already set out its general logic. The author concludes that this fusion is both a historical task set by social development and the academic discourse of paradigm construction. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher frames the shift from importing Western and Soviet theory to building an original, self-assertive Marxist philosophy.

The "comprehensive innovation" theory of culture and the "Second Integration" 文化“综合创新”论与“第二个结合” Zhang Yunyi Can the twentieth-century philosopher brothers Zhang Shenfu and Zhang Dainian be compared with the Song-dynasty Cheng brothers? Taking up a suggestion by Fang Keli, Zhang Yunyi argues that they can: both pairs lived in epochs of cultural turning point, and the Cheng brothers' synthesis of Buddhism, Daoism and Confucianism finds its modern counterpart in the Zhangs' synthesis of Marxism, Chinese tradition and Western thought. The article's thesis is that a single thread, the "Second Integration" of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture, runs from the Zhangs' "comprehensive innovation" theory to Fang's later formula "Marxism as soul, Chinese culture as substance, Western learning for application". The article has four sections. The first traces the intellectual sources of "comprehensive innovation" over four centuries of Sino-Western encounter, from Xu Guangqi's "Chinese mould, Western material" through the debates on substance and function, on the origins of Chinese and Western learning, and on their relative merits. The second sets out the contributions of Zhang Shenfu (the 1930s "merging of three streams": Confucius, Russell, Lenin) and Zhang Dainian (the "synthesis of materialism, ideals and analysis"). The third examines Fang Keli's "Marxism as soul" formula and the criticisms it drew. The fourth presents the Second Integration as the unifying line of Fang's career. Zhang Yunyi's central move is to distinguish synthesis from eclecticism. Drawing on the Zhangs, the author holds that a true synthesis needs a backbone, which for them was Marxist dialectical materialism, so that Marxism leads while Chinese and Western learning are absorbed. Fang's formula, in this account, adds a third term to the old two-term substance–function framework and answers the question of how Marxism, Chinese culture and Western culture relate. It is presented as a scholarly paradigm superior to wholesale Westernisation, Confucian revival, and the older formulas of Chinese substance with Western function or the reverse. Zhang cites Fang's replies to critics who call the three-part model a patchwork: each element has its own "function", with Marxism guiding, Chinese culture as the main subject, and Western learning as a "stone from another hill". Zhang concludes that Fang, Zhang Dainian, Zhang Shenfu and Feng Qi belong to a "comprehensive innovation school" or "Second Integration school", which the author identifies with the Marxist school in Chinese philosophy. The article points out that Fang described the integration of Marxism with Chinese culture as his lifelong commitment, and that Xi Jinping's statements on the Two Integrations, on Marxism as the "soul" and traditional culture as the "root", echo elements of Fang's formula. Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual genealogy of the Second Integration in Chinese philosophy, with extensive quotation from the Zhangs and Fang Keli.

"The masses" and "spirit" Based on Marx and Engels's arguments in The Holy Family “群众”和“精神” Yang Ke Li Zhongjun Yang Ke and Li Zhongjun treat the relation between "the masses" and "spirit" as a basic question of historical materialism. They also present it as a precondition for advancing common prosperity in the spiritual life of the people. Their thesis is that Marx and Engels, in The Holy Family, rejected the speculative opposition of spirit to the masses and set out a dialectical unity of the two. The authors say this unity underpins the current policy goal that common prosperity cover both material and spiritual life. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Marx and Engels's critique of Hegel and the Young Hegelians, in particular Bruno Bauer's "critical criticism". It then sets out their positive account of how masses and spirit are unified. The third part draws out the contemporary significance of this unity, and the fourth derives practical requirements from it. It cites Xi Jinping's remarks and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) alongside the classical texts. In the authors' reading, the speculative philosophers made three moves. They separated spirit from the masses and made the masses mere bearers of spirit. They cast the masses as spirit's "true enemy". They then excluded the masses from history, so that history became that of a few outstanding individuals. Marx and Engels, Yang and Li argue, traced this inverted worldview back to an inverted world of minority oppression and bourgeois exploitation. Against it they held that the masses are the subjects of historical activity and thought, and that ideas which part from interests disgrace themselves. Ideas also achieve nothing unless "people who can use practical force" internalise them in the masses' thinking and carry them out in the masses' activity. From this the authors derive three footholds for spiritual common prosperity. These are the unity of material and spiritual life, coordination between spiritual production and spiritual needs, and mutual promotion of cultural undertakings and the cultural industry. The latter requires breaking capital's grip on spiritual production while still using capital's positive role. They propose three requirements: putting the people at the centre, arming the masses with advanced theory (specifically Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), and advancing material abundance and spiritual richness together as part of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a close reading of The Holy Family is used to justify current Chinese policy on cultural and spiritual life.

A powerful ideological weapon for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on the Party's self-reform 新时代全面从严治党的强大思想武器 Qu Qingshan Qu Qingshan presents Xi Jinping's thinking on the Party's self-reform as a body of theory that has emerged from the practice of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that this thinking answers why the Party must reform itself, why it can, and how it should proceed. It treats self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of order and chaos, rise and fall, and as an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article, published in Qiushi in late 2024, has three sections. The first assesses the theoretical significance of the thinking for Marxist party-building doctrine. The second reviews what the Party's practice in the new era has achieved. The third sets out how the "nine requirements" (the "nine yi") are to guide the next stage of the work. Qu's first argument is that the thinking is a result of the Two Integrations. It rests on Marxism, whose dialectics is "critical and revolutionary", and on Chinese traditions of renewal and self-examination. Qu also claims that it offers a way to solve the problem of self-supervision for ruling parties, and that it rejects the view that multi-party rotation or separation of powers is needed to correct a governing party. The second argument is practical. Qu lists the measures taken to tighten ideology, political discipline, cadre management, work style and anti-corruption work, including the eight-point regulations. Qu reports that the anti-corruption struggle has won an "overwhelming victory" and says this shows that strictness and substance are what make governance of the Party effective. The third argument is that the nine requirements form one systematic whole.
