They are: centralised and unified leadership by the Central Committee as the fundamental guarantee, leading the great social revolution as the fundamental purpose, and escaping the historical cycle as the strategic goal. The remaining six are: solving the unique problems of a large party, perfecting the system of self-governance, building strong organisations, correcting work style and discipline, and combining self-supervision with supervision by the people. Qu concludes that the Party must study this thinking thoroughly and put the nine requirements into practice. This, Qu says, will make sure the Party remains the strong leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The text is an authoritative Party-theoretical exposition that follows the official line closely. Read the original if you want a representative account of how Party theorists in 2024 framed self-reform, its sources and its operational requirements.

Scientifically grasping the major significance and practical requirements of deepening institutional reform in Party building 科学把握深化党的建设制度改革的重大意义和实践要求 Liu Zhiming Liu Zhiming interprets the section on Party building in the decision adopted by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. The article asks what institutional reform in Party building should change, how, and with what results. Its answer is that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of reform, so the Party's own institutions must be reformed with a reformist spirit and strict standards. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why deepening this reform matters. The second states the basic requirements for carrying it out. The third lists concrete tasks for the current period, which the author calls a critical phase for implementing the Plenum's decision. On significance, Liu gives three reasons. Party-building reform is part of modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. It is needed to motivate Party members and cadres to drive reform and development. It is also required by the 'great new project of Party building' and by the Party's long-term tests and dangers, including slackness, inadequate ability, detachment from the masses and corruption. On requirements, Liu says reform must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It must hold to three things that 'cannot change': centralized and unified Party leadership of reform, the overall goal of improving socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a people-centred orientation. Its starting point is to energise cadres. For the practical agenda, Liu proposes long-term mechanisms for study and education, continued reform of cadre personnel systems, and stronger political and organisational functions of Party organisations, including in new economic and social organisations and among new employment groups. Liu also calls for better education and management of members and for greater authority and enforcement of intra-Party regulations, with a clear chain of responsibility. Liu presents these steps as ways to improve the Party's leadership and long-term governing capacity. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's reading of the Third Plenum's Party-building measures and the official vocabulary of Party discipline and cadre management.

Historical experience and operating logic of the Party's self-reform 党的自我革命的历史经验与行动逻辑 Dong Zhenhua Dong Zhenhua takes up the Party's self-reform, which the 2021 Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience (adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee) lists among the lessons of its century of struggle. The article asks how the Communist Party of China has sustained this practice and how it should be carried further in the new era. Dong argues that self-reform is the Party's distinguishing mark and its source of vitality, and that it must be deepened to keep the Party the strong leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece is a short theoretical commentary organised around four requirements, each opened with a quotation from the Resolution. These are a problem-oriented political consciousness, an emphasis on political building and theoretical armament, the courage to cut inward against corruption, and the cherishing of historical experience. Dong draws on episodes such as the Zunyi Meeting, the Yan'an rectification, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Dong first contends that the Party reforms itself because it keeps a sense of crisis and a habit of self-examination. In this account, only the Party itself can defeat it, so it must face problems such as the dangers of slackness, insufficient capacity, detachment from the people and corruption. Second, Dong holds that a party is by nature a political organisation representing class interests, so political building and theory must keep pace with each other to turn theoretical identification into conviction. Third, Dong treats anti-corruption as the most serious test, tracing a line from revolutionary-era discipline and the Three-Anti and Five-Anti campaigns to the post-2012 campaign against both "tigers" and "flies" and the aim of making officials unable, unwilling and afraid to be corrupt. Dong proposes building a theoretical system of Party self-reform, applying the mass line so that ordinary people take part, and accepting supervision while practising criticism and self-criticism. Dong also calls for focusing on the principal contradiction, naming corruption, formalism, bureaucracy and detachment from the masses as the main problems. The conclusion is that a Party able to lead social revolution can also carry out self-reform, and that full and rigorous self-governance must never pause. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists frame self-reform as historical experience and as a programme of action.

Advancing whole-process people's democracy through the Party's mass line 以党的群众路线推动全过程人民民主发展 Li Feng Song Xiongwei Li Feng and Song Xiongwei ask how whole-process people's democracy, written into the title of the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), can be grounded in the Communist Party's own historical practice. They note that existing scholarship stresses how this democracy differs from Western democracy and how the Party leads it, while the mass line is usually treated as a political requirement or work style. The authors argue that the mass line is the historical root and fundamental line of whole-process people's democracy, and that the two should be analysed together. The article has three main parts. The first sets out why whole-process people's democracy cannot do without the mass line, moving from state-building before and after 1949 to the unity of Party leadership and popular democracy, and then to the enrichment of democratic values. The second reviews practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) across the "five democratic links": elections and consultation, decision-making, and grassroots management and supervision. The third makes proposals on Party leadership, people's aspirations for a better life, and an online mass line. Each practice section ends by naming remaining problems. The central claim is that the mass line, as the Party understands it, is a leadership method that avoids both bureaucratism and "tailism", and so differs from what the authors call Western populism and elitism. They tie it to democratic centralism, described as the mass line applied within the Party and as the organisational principle of the state, so that "democracy" and "centralisation" are linked. The authors argue that embedding the mass line in elections, consultation, policy cycles, grassroots self-governance and online petition channels makes democracy more responsive and effective, citing the 2013 mass-line education campaign, the People's Congress system, village consultation rules and online consultation for the 14th Five-Year Plan. They also cite a study using list experiments, which reportedly shows that local officials weigh netizens' views when setting welfare policy. The authors acknowledge shortcomings: low enthusiasm for participation, formalised consultation, decisions taken by a single leader, token expert involvement, weak supervision and incomplete "social coordination". They conclude that the mass line must be upheld unwaveringly and made more institutional, so that its values and stance run through all governance. The aim is to realise citizens' democratic rights and raise the Party's capacity to lead and govern. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school account that frames whole-process people's democracy as a continuation of the mass line, with examples from consultation, policy-making and online governance.

The genesis and operating logic of "the Party is the supreme political leadership force" “党是最高政治领导力量”的生成与运行逻辑 Liu Jingbei Lu Jingcheng Liu Jingbei and Lu Jingcheng examine the formula "the Party is the supreme political leadership force", written into the Party Constitution at the 20th Party Congress (2022). They ask where it comes from, how it has been confirmed in Party rules and state law, and how it operates in practice. The article's thesis is that the principle rests on classical Marxist theory and on the Party's century of experience, and that it is now given institutional form and carried out through the Party's system of leadership institutions. The authors present this as a basic requirement of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first traces the principle's genesis: its theoretical sources in Marx, Engels and Lenin, its historical testing since the 1920s, and its formal statement under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second examines how the principle is confirmed, first in Party regulations centred on the Party Constitution, then in law, from the Constitution down to ordinary statutes. The third treats the Party's leadership institutional system as the vehicle through which the principle operates. The authors argue that the political character of a proletarian party and its vanguard role make Party leadership essentially political leadership. In their account, \"supreme\" signals that the Party represents the highest interests of the people, and that Party will is the conscious conversion of popular will. They trace the vocabulary of \"centre\", \"core\" and \"supreme\" through Party documents to the formulation that emerged after the 18th Party Congress (2012). They describe a progression from Party Constitution to state Constitution to ordinary law, citing the 2018 amendment placing Party leadership in Article 1, and the revised organic laws of the National People's Congress and the State Council. On operation, the authors point to mechanisms such as the Two Upholds, Party groups and leading small groups, systems for implementing central decisions and for requesting instructions and reporting, cadre capacity-building, and institutionalised Party self-reform through inspection tours. They also stress a people-centred standard, citing public satisfaction as a test of reform. They conclude that the principle must be upheld and the leadership system further improved, so that Party leadership runs through all of national governance and supports the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory account of how the leadership principle is anchored in Party regulations and state law.

Origins and discursive construction of the CPC's concept of "exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations" A conceptual-history study 中国共产党“文明交流互鉴”概念的源流考释与话语建构 Wang Yuqi Qi Weiping Shan Shilian The article takes up the concept of "exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations" (文明交流互鉴), which the authors call a signature concept of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Using a conceptual-history approach, they ask how the term was formed and filled with meaning in key Party documents. Their thesis is that it took shape in four stages and that its newer meanings have been layered on its earlier ones rather than replacing them. The study begins with the historical semantics of the three component words in classical Chinese texts, then with the views of Marx, Engels and Lenin on civilizational contact under capitalism. It then follows the concept through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The sources are mainly Party resolutions, directives and leaders' speeches. The authors argue that no unified concept existed in traditional China, though "civilization", "exchange" and "mutual reflection" each had usable senses. They report that the Party's early stance combined openness to foreign progressive culture with opposition to cultural conservatism, to imperialist "cultural aggression" and to wholesale Westernization. After 1949 the idea appeared as foreign cultural liaison and cultural diplomacy, mostly with the Soviet Union. After 1978 the vocabulary moved from "culture" to "civilization", and in their account Hu Jintao's 2001 speech in France was the term's formal debut. For the era of Xi Jinping, the authors describe added historical, practical, theoretical and contemporary meanings. Civilizations are said to be colourful, equal and inclusive. The concept is tied to Chinese modernization, a community with a shared future for mankind, common values of humanity, a civilizational outlook and the Global Civilization Initiative. The authors conclude that the concept grew out of China's traditional culture and the Marxist-Leninist view of civilization, and that it forms part of building a Chinese discourse and narrative system. They expect the Party to link discourse and practice more closely and to offer more global public goods. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-by-document chronology of how this Party term was built, or if you study Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and Chinese foreign-policy discourse.

The threefold logic of the Communist Party of China's self-reform 中国共产党自我革命的三重逻辑 He Mengyi Why does the Communist Party of China show a distinctive capacity for self-reform? Writing after Xi Jinping's speech at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, which set out "nine requirements" for advancing the Party's self-reform, He argues that this capacity rests on three mutually supporting logics: theoretical, historical and practical. The short commentary takes each logic in turn. The theoretical section looks to Marxist doctrine on party building, the historical section to episodes from 1921 onwards, and the practical section to the challenges and measures of the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On theory, He holds that although the Marxist classics never used the term, the idea is embedded in their work. The author points to Marx's call for ruthless criticism of everything existing, to the Communist Manifesto's account of communists as having no interests apart from the proletariat as a whole, and to communism as a long revolutionary movement needing successive generations. On history, He cites the August 7th Meeting of 1927, the Zunyi Meeting of 1935, the Yan'an-era rectification campaign and the 1978 debate on practice as the criterion of truth as moments of self-correction. On practice, the author names problems of unbalanced development, state governance and impurities within the Party, and credits the eight-point rules, intra-Party education campaigns, revised Party regulations and the "three no-corruptions" approach. He concludes that self-reform is an internally grounded and conscious choice, and that the demands of building a strong country and national rejuvenation require the Party to continue it in the spirit of serving the people. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party theorists present the roots of self-reform in Marxist theory, Party history and current practice.

The innovative role of the Third Party Congress in the development of the National Congress system of the Communist Party of China 党的三大对全国党代会制度发展的创新作用 Yang Kai Yang Kai asks what the Third National Congress of the Communist Party of China (1923, held in Guangzhou) contributed to the development of the Party's national congress system. The author argues that, although scholarship has mostly stressed the Third Congress's role in the united front, its institutional innovations were equally significant. Yang identifies three: a transition in delegate selection from appointment to democratic election, the practice of unifying thinking before the congress, and new features of the agenda. The article places the Third Congress within the sequence of congresses from the First to the Seventh. It opens with a survey showing that research on the Third Congress is thin. By the author's account, a search of the National Social Science Fund database found no funded project on it, and a CNKI search returned only 186, 3 and 1 results for different keyword formulations. The three main sections draw on delegates' memoirs (Luo Zhanglong, Xu Meikun, Zhang Guotao, Liu Renjing and others), Maring's reports and the text of the Party constitution. On delegates, Yang shows that the First and Second Congresses relied on regional dispatch or designation. For the Third Congress, regional committees held nomination and discussion procedures, although practice varied. Some delegates were elected and others designated, so Yang calls it a transitional case. On preparation, the Third Congress was the first to hold a preparatory meeting and to draft its main resolutions and reports beforehand after consulting Party organisations. Yang says later congresses continued both practices. On the agenda, it was the first to amend the Party constitution, adding provisions on probationary membership, two sponsors for each applicant and lower-level approval of admissions. It also elected a new Central Executive Committee after canvassing delegates. Yang cites the earliest surviving vote tally, a younger leadership and the first industrial workers among its members. Yang concludes that the Third Congress set precedents that later congresses inherited. The author argues that research should look at causes and at process, and at both larger and smaller processes. Larger processes would place a single congress in the whole sequence leading to the Seventh Congress, the most mature by Yang's account. Smaller ones would examine how a single congress was convened, drafted and decided. Read the original if you study early Party institutions and want a source-based account of delegate selection, pre-congress preparation and constitutional revision in 1923.

The generative logic of the Communist Party of China's conception of civilization 中国共产党文明观的生成逻辑 Zhang Bo Zhang Bo asks how the Communist Party of China's conception of civilization came about and what it consists of. The article argues that this conception, guided by Marxism and rooted in Chinese tradition, goes beyond Western theories of civilizational superiority and of a clash of civilizations. In Zhang's account, it offers a theoretical guide for building a modern Chinese civilization and a new form of human civilization. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the conception's core meaning in six features: it is people-centred, socialist, scientific, constantly innovating, "harmony in diversity", and world-minded. The second identifies four formative conditions: Marxist theory, traditional Chinese thought, over a century of Party practice from the new-democratic revolution to the new era, and the Party's sense of cultural mission. The third describes the system's four dimensions: civilizational critique, values, construction and governance. Zhang's central move is to trace the conception to two sources. From Marx and Engels it draws theories of the nature, forms, structure, driving forces and subjects of civilization. From Chinese tradition it draws harmony between humanity and nature, the idea of "all under heaven", "harmony in diversity" and a benevolent moral outlook. Zhang then argues that the Party fused these in practice. It criticised both wholesale Westernisation and wholesale restoration of the past, and it developed the "five-sphere" model of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. It also asserts that civilizations are equal in value and puts the people before capital. Zhang concludes that the conception is theoretically deep, practically grounded and marked by the Party's initiative, and that it benefits the world as well as China. It is presented as a response to the question of where human civilization is heading. It is said to point towards inclusive thinking, dialogue between civilizations and a vision of "each appreciating the beauty of others". Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-theoretical account of how Chinese official discourse on civilization is derived from Marxism, tradition and Party history, with extensive references to Xi Jinping's statements.

New progress in research on the methodology of ideological and political education in the new era 新时代思想政治教育方法论研究的新进展 Liu Tao This is a literature review of scholarship on the methodology of ideological and political education (the body of theory about the methods used in such education) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu treats this methodology as an important part of the discipline's knowledge system. The review argues that research has advanced by following three methodological principles: upholding fundamental principles while innovating, being problem-oriented, and thinking systemically. The review is organised in three sections that match those principles. The first covers basic theory: core concepts, "meta-theory", theoretical sources and historical development. The second covers new problems: big-data methods, the teaching methods of ideological and political theory courses, and the use of specific methods. The third covers the construction of a knowledge system, meaning the structure of methodological systems and research methods. Liu names many scholars and works under each heading, including Luo Yuting, Xiang Jiuyu, Lou Shuhua, Zou Shaoqing and Zhang Yaocan. On basic theory, Liu reports that definitions have come to stress interaction between educators and the people they educate, and that scholars separate "method" from "methodology", the latter being a systematic abstraction of methods. Theoretical support is drawn from Marxist classics, traditional Chinese culture, the educational practice of Chinese Communists such as Mao Zedong, and Xi Jinping's discussions. On new problems, the review describes work on integrating big data with the discipline, on diversified and technology-enabled teaching, and on borrowing from sociology, psychology, linguistics and cognitive neuroscience. On system-building, it traces successive frameworks (activity-process, epistemological, contradiction-based, strategic-guidance) and recent debates, such as whether the system can be made scientific or only disciplinary. It also covers research paradigms and methods, including theoretical, textual, historical, interest-analysis and oral-history approaches. Liu presents the field as marked by growing methodological self-awareness, with a rich output of books and papers. Anniversaries such as the discipline's 30th and 40th have prompted retrospective summaries. The review does not set out a separate list of gaps, but it points to the continuing task of deepening theory, digital transformation and system-building. Read the original if you want a map of the main Chinese scholars, titles and subtopics in this subfield, for example when tracing how the discipline's teaching and research methods are being theorised.

The value orientation of Marx's view of life and its contemporary significance 马克思生活观的价值旨趣及其当代意义 Sun Min Sun Min takes up the question of how Marx's view of life (shenghuo guan) relates to his philosophical revolution. The article argues that the two are inherently unified: Marx's philosophical innovation lies in the historical-materialist dimension of his view of life. Sun contends that scholars have neglected this link, which leaves Marx's philosophical revolution understood abstractly and obscures the value orientation of his view of life. The article has three parts. It first contrasts Marx's view with the rationalist view of life of traditional philosophy, using Marx's critique of Hegel, and describes the existential reading of sensuous activity and the critique of capital. It then sets out four aspects of the value orientation of Marx's view of life. The last part names three kinds of contemporary significance, covering the development of Marxist philosophy, a new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy, and the grasp of present-day human practice. Sun's central claim is that Marx moved from abstract life to real life, from interpreting life to changing it, from the world of language to the lifeworld, and from dogmatic life to living life. In Sun's account, traditional philosophy treated life as spirit or idea and so could only explain it. Marx grounded life in practice and in the contradictions between productive forces and relations of production and between economic base and superstructure, so changing life requires changing social relations of production. Sun also criticises Husserl and Heidegger for bracketing material production, and reads Wittgenstein's return of words to everyday use as partly congruent with Marx. Sun adds that a people's life must be grasped through its own history, culture and traditions, and that otherwise historical materialism becomes dogma. Tradition itself is described as a living thing renewed through present practice. Sun concludes that the four aspects together make up Marx's philosophical revolution and open a path to a better life for humanity. In Sun's view, grasping them helps recover the authentic spirit of Marx's philosophy and supports a new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy that links China's fate with the world's. It also helps address the crises of virtual practice and of nature, society and spirit. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical account that ties Marx's view of everyday life to historical materialism and to current debates on Marxist philosophy.

Re-examining Marx's proposition on uneven development between art and material production, and its cultural implications 马克思不平衡关系命题的再辨析及其文化启示 Bao Jin Bao Jin returns to a passage in Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, where Marx says that the flourishing of art is by no means proportionate to the general development of society or its material basis. The author notes that scholars still disagree. Some treat the imbalance as local and accidental, with rough proportion as the long-run rule. Others treat imbalance as absolute and balance as accidental. Bao seeks to clarify the proposition's real meaning so as to grasp the objective laws of cultural production and to inform China's new cultural mission. The article has three parts. The first separates two forms in which the imbalance appears, synchronic and diachronic, using Greek epic and tragedy as the example. The second links the Introduction to Marx's 1861–63 manuscripts, where capitalist production is described as hostile to certain branches of spiritual production such as art and poetry. The third draws cultural lessons, discussing how Marx used the concept of culture and then connecting the proposition to Xi Jinping's statements on culture. Bao argues that the imbalance is both synchronic (art against material production and against other civilisations of the same era) and diachronic (early art against later art and later material production). Greek art arose from an underdeveloped social stage and still serves as a model. The hostility thesis supplies the proposition's internal tension. Commodity art production follows capital's logic and is marked by capital, scale and popularity. Free spiritual production, by contrast, is self-regulating, unique and rich in ideas, so Milton writes Paradise Lost as a silkworm spins silk. Bao adds that free spiritual production is not wholly outside commodity production. It draws its means and nourishment from its own era, so its autonomy has historical limits, as Adorno also observed. Bao draws three implications. First, culture's comparative advantage supports inheriting excellent traditional Chinese culture and shaping a cultural form of Chinese modernization, one that seeks balance within dynamic imbalance and opposes unilateralism and hegemony. Second, Marx's open appreciation of Greek culture supports mutual learning among civilisations over claims of civilisational superiority. Third, the transcendence of free spiritual production means spiritual abundance is a basic requirement of socialist modernization, and it cannot be measured in economic terms. Read the original if you want to see how a Marxist aesthetics debate is connected to current Party cultural policy and to Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

A systematic analysis of integrating the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture 马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合的系统分析 Hong Xiaonan Hong Xiaonan takes up the Party's formula, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. The article asks why this combination is necessary, possible and real. Using the method of unity of the logical and the historical, Hong concludes that Marxism has not failed China and China has not failed Marxism. The relationship must be guided by Marxism and by a scientific attitude to tradition, rejecting both cultural and historical nihilism and cultural restorationism or conservatism. The article opens with a semantic analysis of the proposition. It asks why the text says "basic principles" rather than Marxism as a whole, "fine" traditional culture rather than traditional culture in general, and "tong" (with) rather than "he" or "yu" (and). Hong distinguishes traditional culture, cultural tradition, Chinese culture and Chinese traditional culture, and traces how Mao Zedong's wording of the "second integration" of 1956 developed. Sections then deal with necessity, possibility, the two directions of benefit, and the conditions for healthy interaction. On necessity, Hong reviews how early Chinese Marxists, above all Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, chose Marxism through emotional and intellectual needs, and follows Chen's 1921 and 1923 lectures favouring communism over other socialisms. On possibility, citing Zhang Dainian, Xi Jinping and the 20th Congress report, Hong argues that fine traditional culture is highly compatible with the values of scientific socialism in four areas: cosmology ("unity of heaven and humanity"), views of the world order ("the world belongs to all"), views of society ("harmony without uniformity") and morality. Hong adds that the two are not identical. Confucian materialism, dialectics and utopianism differ from their Marxist counterparts. Hong argues that the benefit runs both ways. Marxism gave tradition new vitality, as with the Party's reworking of "seeking truth from facts", "a moderately prosperous society", "keeping pace with the times" and "a community with a shared future for mankind". Tradition in turn gives Chinese Marxism its distinctive style and lifts its own simple materialism and dialectics to a higher level. The integration is not between equals but an organic one led by Marxism. Hong calls for creative transformation and innovative development of tradition, and presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the model. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholarship justifies the second of the Two Integrations, with its conceptual analysis and its historical cases from Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao.

The three historical dimensions of the normativity of intra-Party regulations 党内法规规范性历史渊源的三重维度 Li Jinheng Where does the normativity of intra-Party regulations come from? Li Jinheng takes up what the article calls one of the "meta-questions" of research on these rules: why they can legitimately guide, evaluate, constrain and even discipline Party members. Li argues that existing work, which approaches the question through legal studies and political party research, does not cover the whole field. The article proposes three historical dimensions: the history of ideas, the history of practice and the history of civilization. This short commentary appeared in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) on 27 February 2025. It places intra-Party regulations within the Marxist theory of the political party, the Chinese Communist Party's own record of institution-building across revolution, construction and reform, and the long Chinese tradition of good law and good governance. Each dimension has its own section, followed by a brief closing paragraph. On the history of ideas, Li holds that intra-Party regulations are the product of a stage in the development of Marxist party theory and of the proletarian revolution. This explains why they exist relatively independently of state law: a revolutionary organisation needs no state "permission" for its internal rules. It also explains why they are stricter than state law, since members carry higher duties than ordinary citizens and need binding external discipline as well as self-conscious Party spirit. On the history of practice, Li says that regulations, whether imported through the Comintern or originating in China, must pass through a process of "canonisation" that turns responses to specific problems into lasting norms. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party's self-reform has driven the systematic construction of the regulations. On the history of civilization, Li draws four lessons from traditional governance: the blending of ritual and law, "clear virtue and cautious punishment", "inner sageliness and outer kingliness", and "the people as the root of the state". Li concludes that the normativity of intra-Party regulations must be explained historically, by showing how the rules were generated and standardised in the Party's own construction and practice. Li also locates their foundation in the transition of Chinese political civilization from tradition to modernity. The article adds that the Party's self-reform in the new era requires understanding the complex changes affecting full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese Party-law scholars frame the sources of intra-Party regulations beyond a purely legal analysis.

Providing legal safeguards for implementing the Global Development Initiative 为落实全球发展倡议提供法治保障 Cao Junjin This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how law can support the Global Development Initiative that Xi Jinping first proposed at the UN General Assembly in September 2021. Cao Junjin argues that the rule of law is an important safeguard for the Initiative's implementation, and that China's legal framework for it is still incomplete. The piece has three parts. It first sets out what law contributes, then proposes how to build a legal system for the Initiative, and finally outlines supporting institutional measures. Cao notes that Article 18 of the Foreign Relations Law mentions the Initiative but, in Cao's reading, remains declaratory and principled. Two trial working documents from the International Development Cooperation Agency, on a fund pool and a project pool, also exist. Cao says law makes implementation forceful, orderly and effective by pooling scattered resources, regulating project approval, procurement, monitoring and evaluation, and creating financing and cooperation rules. Cao proposes either a unified "Global Development Promotion Law" or separate laws on international development cooperation or foreign aid, linked to sectoral laws. Cao adds that regulations should cover private-sector participation, and that treaties and tripartite projects with developed countries and international organisations could create "contractual international law". Cao calls for more legal research on the Initiative, a clearly designated lead agency, stronger funding and training of international development law specialists. On funding, Cao notes the 2022 upgrade of the South-South cooperation fund to the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund, with an extra US$1 billion on top of US$3 billion. Cao suggests further capital increases and sector funds, such as a global education fund. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese legal-policy view of how the Initiative might be institutionalised.

The political-economy logic of developing service-oriented manufacturing 发展服务型制造的政治经济学逻辑 Qi Hao This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what service-oriented manufacturing means for Marxist political economy. Qi Hao defines it as manufacturers providing services across a product's whole life cycle, from design and financing to maintenance and recycling. The author argues that it is a new mode of production that carries new quality productive forces and that it calls for new relations of production. The article has three parts. The first treats service-oriented manufacturing as a vehicle for new quality productive forces. The second examines how it raises the degree of socialisation of production. The third sets out the new production relations it requires, in data, in technology firms and in finance. Qi holds that in Marxist terms a qualitative change in productive forces depends on a new mode of production. Smart products and the Internet of Things create a "data–service" cycle, which the author says integrates the real and digital economies, improves equipment use through leasing and pay-per-use, and eases overcapacity in durable goods. Every firm becomes a node in a denser network of data and service flows, and user data lets local innovation spread across industries. Qi therefore reads it as a leap in socialisation. Following the principle that productive forces determine relations of production, Qi calls for three measures. These are laws that settle data ownership, cooperation between technology and manufacturing firms with curbs on monopoly over data and computing power, and "patient capital" against short-term returns. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-political-economy framing of digital-era manufacturing within the discourse on new quality productive forces.

Viewing the cultural industry of the new era through Marx's theory of division of labour and cooperation 从马克思的分工协作理论看新时代文化产业 Xu Zhuoshun Wang Tianxin Prompted by the success of the domestic game Black Myth: Wukong and the animated film Ne Zha 2, this newspaper commentary asks how China's cultural industry can develop further in the new era. Xu and Wang argue that the idea of coordinated development (xietong fazhan), which they present as a deepening and extension of Marx's theory of division of labour and cooperation, explains these successes and should guide the industry. The piece has three parts. It first traces the move from Marx's division of labour and cooperation to coordinated development. It then identifies three kinds of coordination behind industrial growth. It closes with three practical recommendations. Drawing on Marx's Economic Manuscript of 1861–63, the authors describe division of labour as the totality of particular productive activities and cooperation as the basis of social combinations aimed at higher productivity. Coordination, in their reading, combines high specialisation with close cooperation, capturing efficiency gains while limiting the costs of excessive division. The three coordinations are cultural innovation with dissemination, internal enterprise systems with the external environment, and multiple business formats. The authors cite the game's developer, Game Science (Youke Hudong), as an example of the second, and online literature, film and games as examples of the third. The authors call for coordinated innovation in culture and technology, including high-precision digitisation of relics and heritage. They urge stronger support for small and medium cultural-technology firms and for innovation ecosystems, and joint creation of high-quality original content for global audiences, with promotion on overseas social media. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars apply Marx's cooperation theory to cultural-industry policy.

Grasping the people-centred character of further deepening reform comprehensively 深刻把握进一步全面深化改革的人民性品格 Deng Yilin This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what gives the drive to further deepen reform comprehensively its people-centred character (renminxing). Deng argues that this character is the essential attribute of Marxism and a distinguishing feature of the reform agenda adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). In the author's reading, it expresses the Party's founding mission and underpins innovation in Chinese modernization. The article takes the Plenum's principle of 'putting the people first' and breaks it into four aspects. These are the value orientation of the people above all, respect for the people's principal role and creativity, the goal of bringing benefit to the people, and people's livelihood as the basic thread running through reform. It draws on Party documents and a 2024 remark by Xi Jinping in Chongqing. Deng contends that reform starts from the people's overall, fundamental and long-term interests, and that it has moved from solving the problem of 'having enough' to solving that of 'being good enough'. The people are presented as the practical agents and the source of strength of reform, and their satisfaction as the final test of its results, so that reform becomes a way of pursuing the Party's mass line. The author describes human development as the end of social development, treats modernization as at bottom the modernization of people, and calls for both making the 'cake' bigger and dividing it fairly. On livelihood, Deng lists remaining weaknesses: uneven urban–rural development, income gaps, unequal educational resources, scarce quality healthcare, employment pressure and incomplete social security. The author calls for reforms in income distribution, employment, social security, housing, medical care and childcare and elderly care, so that people's sense of gain, happiness and security grows. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the people-centred principle of the Third Plenum reform agenda.

Fully grasping the requirements of our times for Party discipline building 全面把握党的纪律建设时代要求 Wang Jianqin This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how Party discipline building should keep pace with the tasks set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Wang argues that keeping discipline abreast of the times is a requirement for deepening institutional reform of Party building and keeping reform on the right political course. The article describes discipline building as a prominent feature of the overall plan for Party building in the new era. It then sets out four areas of emphasis: political discipline, the Party's central tasks,主体 responsibility for Party governance, and consolidating the results of the Party discipline study and education campaign. Wang contends that political discipline is the core of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the mark distinguishing Marxist parties from others. Its core content is the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and it should lead the other disciplines: organisational, integrity, mass, work and lifestyle. The author presents the new Central Committee implementing measures on the "four forms" of supervision and discipline as an institutional achievement. Wang also says some officials still misjudge the long-term nature of the task. In the author's account, "key minority" corruption and the "four undesirable work styles" persist, so Party committees and their secretaries must carry primary responsibility. Wang calls for stronger supervision of leading cadres, especially top officials, with no privileges or exceptions in applying discipline. The author also proposes turning the results of the discipline education campaign into regular, lasting study mechanisms, and into officials' everyday habits. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of current priorities in Party discipline building.

The theoretical characteristics of the Party's propaganda, ideological and cultural work 党的宣传思想文化工作的理论特质 Zhao Shumei Zhao Yunheng This short commentary asks what distinguishes the Communist Party of China's propaganda, ideological and cultural work as a body of theory and practice. The authors argue that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping has systematically set out why the work matters, where it is headed, who does it and how. They contend that it displays three paired characteristics: unity of Party spirit and people's character, of principle and innovation, and of the national and the global. The article is organised around these pairs, with a short framing introduction. It treats each pair in turn, first describing the two sides and then stating what the resulting characteristic enables. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements on leadership, the goals of the work, new media, historical nihilism and cultural confidence. The authors present the work as a response to fundamental questions that Xi is said to have answered. On the first pair, the authors say that upholding Party leadership over ideology and the principle of Party spirit goes together with a people-centred orientation that serves and educates the masses. They hold that the Party's aims coincide with the people's fundamental interests, so the pairing consolidates the Party's governing base and gathers strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. On the second pair, principle means firm adherence to Marxism's guiding position and treating ideological security as part of national political security. Innovation means new ideas, methods and grassroots practice, a "big propaganda" concept, and new formulations such as "cultural identity is the deepest level of identity". Together these amount to "upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground". The authors add that the third pair, timeliness and practicality, is shown in the response to new media and to historical nihilism. The fourth, the national and the global, combines emphasis on Chinese cultural subjectivity and an autonomous knowledge system with learning from other civilizations, international communication and a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors conclude that these characteristics let the Party keep its direction while moving with the times, turn grassroots experience into working principles, and build national cultural confidence. They also say the characteristics help China withstand the clash of ideas and culture and present itself as a self-reliant civilizational power. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists summarise the logic of Xi-era ideological work.

The trajectory and direction of the development of political economy with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义政治经济学发展的脉络与方向 Han Wenlong This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today asks how the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics has developed and where it should go next. Han Wenlong argues that this body of theory grew out of China's economic practice alongside reform and opening up, and that amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century it must keep widening its scope and depth. In Han's account, it should supply theoretical support for an autonomous Chinese system of economic knowledge and guidance for economic practice in the new development stage. The article has two parts. The first divides the field's history into three periods: 1949–1978, 1978–2012, and 2012 to the present. The second sets out three directions for further development: stronger problem-oriented research, a more systematic and open theoretical system, and a wider international outlook. On the historical side, Han describes the first period as one of exploration, producing theories of the basic contradictions of socialism, public ownership and comprehensive balance of the national economy, despite what the article calls a tortuous course. The second period, opened by the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and Deng Xiaoping's proposal at the 12th Party Congress (1982) to build socialism with Chinese characteristics, deepened work on ownership, distribution and the socialist market economy. For the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Han presents Xi Jinping's economic thought as the latest result, and lists ten research areas. These include the Party's overall leadership of economic work, high-quality development, common prosperity, new quality productive forces, the basic socialist economic system and the balance of development and security. For the future, Han calls for a 'problem–theory–practice' paradigm applied to issues such as local government debt, demographic change and artificial intelligence. Han also asks for clearer core concepts and foundations, given differing views on the starting category and main logical thread, together with new methods such as big data and causal inference and selective use of Western economics, and for explaining China's experience in accessible language. Han concludes that the discipline is both a summary of past experience and a forward-looking project. Its tasks are to answer practical problems, build a rigorous and open system, and offer a Chinese approach to global economic governance. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic overview of how Chinese scholars periodise their political economy and what research agenda one economist proposes for it.

Building Chinese economics under the guidance of Marxist political economy 以马克思主义政治经济学为指导建设中国经济学 He Zili This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 27 February 2025, asks how China should build its own autonomous system of economic knowledge. He Zili argues that the system must be guided by Marxist political economy, which he treats as the only possible foundation for the country's political economy, rather than by any other body of economic theory. Its task, in his account, is to answer new questions arising from economic construction under socialism with Chinese characteristics and to reveal the laws governing its relations of production. The piece is organised around four requirements for building this knowledge system. These concern the object of study, the value standpoint, the starting point of research, and the elaboration of Xi Jinping's economic thought. He draws contrasts with Adam Smith, Say, Robbins and Samuelson, and with what he calls Western economics, and ends with four practical tasks. In the core argument, He contrasts Western definitions of economics, which centre on scarce resources, wealth production and distribution, with the Marxist definition. Marxist political economy takes the mode of production and its corresponding relations of production, distribution and exchange as its object, and He says Chinese economics should take the socialist mode of production with Chinese characteristics as its object. He holds that Western economics claims to be value-free but has itself become part of bourgeois ideology, whereas Marxist political economy openly states its class standpoint and its people-centred orientation. He also calls for starting from the "new historical juncture" of the new era, in which the principal contradiction is between people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, and for high-quality development to be the main task. He concludes that the central task is now to raise the scholarly interpretation and systematic construction of Xi Jinping economic thought, which he lists as a series of original contributions, from Party leadership of economic work to new quality productive forces. He proposes four tasks: studying its formation and development, extracting its categories and logic, building textbooks around it, and strengthening the "three systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse). The aim is to end the practice of copying Western economics to tell China's story. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official line on how China's economics discipline should be constructed under Xi Jinping Thought.

Using Party building to lead the protection and transmission of rural intangible cultural heritage 以党建引领乡村非物质文化遗产保护传承工作 Han Pengyun This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Journal in February 2025, asks how rural intangible cultural heritage can be protected and passed on under present conditions. Han argues that Party building should lead the work, with Party organisations at county, township and village levels providing motivation, organisation and a means of action. Han first defines rural intangible heritage as cultural forms handed down by villagers over generations, together with related tools, objects and sites. The author names two features: strong regional markers and a reflection of peasants' aesthetic tastes. Han then lists the pressures it faces, including urbanisation, the outflow of young labour, weak awareness, a gap in successors and falling peasant participation. The remainder is organised around three kinds of leadership: ideological, organisational and action-based. On ideology, Han calls for Party organisations to study Xi Jinping's thought on culture, treat heritage as a political responsibility, and train cadres and members to act as exemplars. On organisation, Han proposes cultivating successors, including returning graduates and outside specialists, and building village cultural councils and associations based on new-era civilisation practice stations. On action, Han suggests converting heritage into products and brands to form cultural new quality productive forces, integrating it with rural tourism and cultural IP, and buying heritage performances as free public cultural services. Han concludes that Party-building leadership is the engine of high-quality development for rural heritage. The author presents the process as the Party putting the people at the centre, upholding its cultural leadership and promoting common prosperity in peasants' spiritual life. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building language is applied to rural cultural policy.

Consolidating the scientific foundations of building a leading country in science and technology 夯实科技强国建设的科学根基 Wan Jinbo Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, after the national science and technology work conference of 13 January stressed "organised basic research", Wan Jinbo argues that basic research is the source of the whole scientific system. The commentary holds that China needs to strengthen organised basic research and technological science to achieve high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. Wan first reviews recent progress, citing the rise in basic research spending from 49.88 billion yuan in 2012 to 249.7 billion yuan in 2024, and the building of national laboratories and key laboratories. The author then cites international rankings, including the Global Innovation Index, the Nature Index and a list of top scientists, as evidence of growing strength. The final sections set out measures for the coming decade. Wan's central claim is that strong international influence in basic research marks a leading science and technology country and shapes the shifting of global centres of science, talent and education. The author describes China's innovation as moving from "tracking and learning" to "original leadership", while acknowledging weak original innovation, dependence on foreign key technologies and a shortage of top talent. Wan proposes three linked types of research: strategy-oriented systematic, frontier-oriented exploratory and market-oriented applied basic research, supplying new quality productive forces at source. Wan calls for coordinating major tasks, institutions, platforms, funding and international cooperation, combining competitive and stable funding, and deepening enterprise-led links between industry, universities and research. The author also urges an innovation-friendly culture with property protection, so that the goal of a leading science and technology country, ten years away, can be met. Read the original if you want a short official-style overview of how a Chinese Academy of Sciences researcher frames basic research policy and its statistical case.

Further unleashing the private economy's role in driving high-quality development 进一步发挥民营经济对高质量发展的推动力 Guo Chunli This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily (27 February 2025) asks how the private economy can contribute more to high-quality development. Guo Chunli argues that the private economy is an important achievement of the socialist market economy and a key foundation of high-quality development in the new era. The author calls for a better environment for its healthy growth. The piece first reviews private firms' contribution under five headings of the new development philosophy: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. It then turns to four sets of measures on finance, market institutions, property rights and public opinion. Guo cites figures to show the sector's weight. Private firms are said to contribute 70% of technological innovation outputs, over 50% of tax revenue and 80% of urban jobs. They are also said to account for over 50% of foreign trade and almost 80% of charitable donations. The author presents these as evidence that private enterprises already drive high-quality development in each area, and that the new round of technological revolution and industrial change opens new space for them. Guo proposes easing financing difficulties, tackling late payments to private firms, and opening major research infrastructure and national technology projects to them. The author also calls for stronger basic market institutions covering property rights, market access and fair competition, along with action against arbitrary fees, fines and inspections. Finally, Guo urges a supportive social climate that promotes entrepreneurship and rebuts slander against private entrepreneurs. Read the original if you want a concise, statistics-backed statement of the official case for supporting the private economy in early 2025.

Marx's resolution of Rousseau's "paradox of freedom" 马克思对卢梭“自由悖论”的解决 Yang He Rousseau opens The Social Contract with the claim that man is born free yet is everywhere in chains. Yang He argues that this "paradox of freedom" exposes a tension between liberty and equality inside classical liberalism, and that Marx resolved it, not by refuting Rousseau but by transforming it critically through historical materialism and the theory of surplus value. The article appeared in the Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025, no. 1. The piece has three parts. The first reconstructs the liberal tradition (Locke, Grotius, Hobbes, Adam Smith) on natural rights, property and labour, and shows where Rousseau departed from it and why his proposed "moral and collective" community remained utopian. The second follows Marx's engagement with Rousseau, from the Kreuznach notebooks through the 1844 Manuscripts, and Hegel's influence on him. The third turns to the present: liberal adjustments (Keynesianism, neoliberalism, Hayek, Rawls) and the Chinese Communist Party's practice. Yang's core claim is that Rousseau failed because his view of history was moralised and rooted in human nature. In the author's reading, Marx replaced this with a materialist account in four steps. Freedom is grasped through labour and the saving of labour time, and so is historical. Equality is a product of commodity exchange and cannot be an innate right, since formal equality in the market conceals exploitation in production. True community is not the political state, which Marx treated as a "false community", but arises when the means of production are socially owned. And the alienation narrative of subject, estrangement and return is replaced by the development of productive forces through class antagonism. Yang concludes that liberal remedies remain trapped in Rousseau's paradox because they serve capital's logic. The author argues that public ownership and common prosperity are Marx's two basic requirements for resolving it, and that the Party has developed them through the basic socialist economic system, the elimination of absolute poverty and Chinese modernization. The author adds that regulating capital under the socialist market economy, while using its productive role, remains an open theoretical task. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Rousseau, Hegel and liberalism that links classical texts to the current common prosperity agenda.

Methodological shifts in the young Marx's exploration of the philosophy of law 青年马克思法哲学探索中的方法论转换 Sun Meitang Why did the young Marx, starting from legal questions, have to take a "detour" through the critique of political economy, and how did his materialism and dialectics combine to bring about that change? Sun Meitang argues that the common explanation, which holds that the Rheinische Zeitung debates on material interests moved Marx from "copy" to "original", is not wrong but is too simple. In Sun's reading, the change in Marx's legal thought was complex, and it was accompanied by a change in method. The article, first published in 2014, follows Marx from his university years and the Rheinische Zeitung commentaries (on press censorship and the law on wood theft), through the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right written at Kreuznach, to the critique of political economy. It sets this path against Marx's wider reading in history, politics and economics, and against the rise of capitalism in Western Europe. At each stage Sun identifies a different form of dialectics: the dialectic of the understanding, negative dialectics, and finally historical or practical dialectics. Sun argues that in the Rheinische Zeitung period Marx measured actual Prussian law against an ideal of law, shaped by Hegel and the Enlightenment, as it "ought" to be. This opposition of ought and is remained abstract, but it exposed the economic interests behind legal relations. In the critique of Hegel, Marx then turned Hegel's own negative dialectics against him in two ways. He reversed the relation between concept and reality, so that civil society and the family become the basis of the state. He also replaced a dialectic serving monarchical absolutism with one oriented to the people and to democracy. Sun holds that this critique still worked within Hegel's logic. Only the critique of political economy, which Sun calls practical dialectics, could treat law as a product of material life. On this view, justice and legality become historical results of rising productive forces and of human liberation, and every legal form is both legitimate and illegitimate in its time. Sun concludes that for Marx the question of law is finally the question of human emancipation. It cannot be settled by conceptual deduction, only by social transformation. The article adds that today's context differs from Marx's, so his words cannot simply be applied to the rule of law under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Sun says his guidance can be realised only by grasping that justice and legality mean human emancipation and that legal problems are solved through real social change. Read the original if you are interested in how Marx's method developed from legal criticism to political economy, or in a Chinese reading of Marx's philosophy of law in relation to Hegel and Althusser.

Treating reification within the dialectical relation of spirit and body 在精神与肉体的辩证关系中对待物化 Huang Xiaofeng Wang Xiaosheng Since Lukács, Western Marxist critiques of capitalism have increasingly targeted reification rather than the system's internal contradictions. Huang and Wang argue that most thinkers have not found the right way to deal with it. Their thesis is that reification cannot be abolished but must be both accepted within limits and continually resisted, using Marx's materialist dialectic of body and spirit and of subject and object. The article has four sections. It first criticises Lukács's theory of reification as idealist, then looks for the roots of reification in the opposition of spirit and body. It next compares three ways of overcoming the subject–object opposition: Lukács's Hegelian route, Heidegger's phenomenological route and Marx's route. A final section discusses the theoretical and social significance of reification, drawing on Adorno and Horkheimer, Honneth, Kant, Descartes and Baudrillard. The authors contend that Lukács turned Marx's analysis of the economic base into a question of ideology and, through the category of totality, rebuilt Marx along Hegelian lines. They trace reification to the way humans must control external nature and so also their own bodily nature, which leaves spirit purely rationalised. Spirit that excludes the body is then avenged by nature and ends up following natural laws. On this view Lukács's strategy of subject conquering object cannot truly overcome reification, since a rationally run system stays reified. Heidegger's attempt to leap beyond the dichotomy turns Being into a thing and risks negating civilisation. For Marx the subject is a living, self-contradictory human being, and the use-value of commodities, which cannot be calculated, is the non-identical element that resists reification. Huang and Wang conclude that reification is partly rational, because survival requires separating subject from object, but becomes harmful when it is unconditionally rationalised. They ascribe the difficulty of seeing through it to commodity fetishism, to existential and epistemological factors, and to the blending of true and false, as in Baudrillard's hyperreality. They call for reviving passions suppressed in daily life and reconciling them with spirit, without Lukács's excessive stress on the subject or Heidegger's abandonment of it. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Lukács and Heidegger on reification that rests on materialist dialectics.

Debates over the logical starting point of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and reflections on them 中国特色社会主义政治经济学逻辑起点的争论与反思 Chen Long Wu Xuzhong Chen Long and Wu Xuzhong take up a question that, in their account, remains unsettled: what should be the logical starting point (the first category) of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics? Scholars have proposed commodity, the socialist economic system, public ownership, the state, the people, surplus product and more. The authors argue that the starting point cannot be chosen in isolation from the discipline's object of study and its whole theoretical system, and that Marx's Capital is the necessary reference. They conclude that the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism is the most defensible starting point, while accepting that no single starting point is uniquely correct. The article first sorts the existing positions into three camps. The "imitators" (for example Liu Mingyuan, Duan Xuehui and Cheng Enfu, Yan Pengfei, Zhou Shaodong and Wang Song) take commodity, in modified forms, as the starting point. The "opponents" propose the state (Qiu Haiping), the people as subject, labour productivity, particular interest relations or surplus product. The "eclectics" (Wei Xinghua, Liu Qian and Pei Xiaoge) propose the basic economic system, which the authors say leading recent textbooks also adopt. The authors then compare the approaches in three respects: methodology, object of study and level of research. On method, the authors hold that the disagreement arises from differing readings of how Marx fixed Capital's starting point. They argue that the "ascent from the abstract to the concrete" demands a simple, cell-like category, but that this is feasible only for a mature social formation, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is still developing. They reject the state as a starting point because the principle of unity of the logical and the historical, in their reading, was not Marx's method but originated with Engels. They favour Marx's "universal light" method, which begins from the relation that determines all others. On the object of study, they contend that Capital examined mature, purely private capitalism with capital as its single thread. The socialist market economy, by contrast, has heterogeneous production relations and two regulating mechanisms, state and market. On levels, the authors say Capital is pure theory, whereas the Chinese discipline also covers historical-institutional and policy analysis, which are more concrete. The authors conclude that the discipline's practical, problem-oriented character allows several concrete starting points and a "block-type structure" of parallel theoretical systems. They concede this is less tightly logical than Capital's "artistic whole" but call it a pragmatic route. They urge a more tolerant attitude to the debate and faster construction of the theoretical system along different starting points. Read the original if you want a structured survey of Chinese proposals on the starting point of socialist political economy, and an argument for the basic economic system drawn from Marx's methodology.

New quality productive forces empowering the high-quality development of the real economy 新质生产力赋能实体经济高质量发展研究 Chen Jian Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for institutions that deepen the integration of the real and digital economies, this article asks how new quality productive forces can drive the high-quality development of the real economy. Chen argues that they hold strategic value, but that three sets of difficulties must be overcome through policies aimed at factor allocation, technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrading. The piece appeared in Theoretical Horizon in December 2024. The article has three parts. The first sets out the strategic value of new quality productive forces for consolidating the foundations of the national economy, building a modern industrial system and raising China's position in global value chains. The second identifies problems that need solving: shocks to the traditional real economy, gaps in key core technologies, and obstacles to upgrading traditional industries. The third proposes countermeasures under three headings: innovative allocation of production factors, revolutionary technological breakthroughs and deep industrial transformation. Chen's core claim is that new quality productive forces are advanced productive forces whose carrier is industry. In the author's account, they drive innovation, raise efficiency and quality, spread from emerging sectors to traditional ones, and serve digitalisation, high-end upgrading and low-carbon development. They also supply data as a new factor, which the author says supports a unified national market and digital trade. On the problem side, Chen names global economic volatility, technological change, shifting consumer demand and the rise of new business forms. The article also cites insufficient R&D spending, foreign technology blockades and intellectual property barriers, and a gap between universities, research and industry. It notes that traditional industries account for over 80 per cent of manufacturing and face problems of efficiency, quality, pollution and energy use. Chen cites examples such as AI use in coal mining and a building-materials firm said to have raised labour productivity by over 50 per cent. Chen proposes stronger innovation-driven policy and R&D funding, support for basic research and talent training, and closer cooperation among industry, universities and research institutes. Further proposals are international scientific cooperation, stronger intellectual property protection, and world-class advanced manufacturing clusters. For industry, the author calls for high-end, intelligent and green upgrading, including strict environmental accountability for officials and tax and loan incentives for firms. Read the original if you want an overview of how a Chinese economics article links new quality productive forces to real-economy policy, with its list of problems and proposed measures.

An outline of the theoretical themes of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 中国化时代化马克思主义理论主题论纲 Zhang Ronghua Liang Chao Zhang Ronghua and Liang Chao ask what central questions the Party's Marxist theory, adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, has set out to answer. They argue that this body of theory has a continuous "theoretical theme", which they call a "red thread" running through the stages the article labels saving the nation, building the country, enriching it and strengthening it. The authors note that few scholars have studied this theme directly, since most work treats the three major theoretical achievements separately. The article appeared in 2025, after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article first defines the theme, describes its structure and sets out why it is worth studying. It then takes in turn Mao Zedong Thought, the system of theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics (Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development), and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For each, it lists how the theme was expressed: revolution, the building of socialism, and Party building, then development and national strengthening. A final section condenses these into one overall formula. The core claim is that the theme has a "1+3" structure. The "1" is the question of what Marxism is and how to uphold and develop it. The "3" are the questions of what kind of socialism, what kind of socialist modern great country, and what kind of long-governing Marxist party to build, and how. The authors treat these three as extensions of the first. They say the three achievements share a common source (the Two Integrations and shifts in the principal contradiction), a common direction (national prosperity, rejuvenation and the people's happiness) and a common purpose (a mass-line view of history). They also distinguish the theoretical theme from the themes of the times, of practice and of Party congresses, and from major research questions, treating the theoretical theme as a distillation of the last. The authors conclude that theoretical themes are layered and progressive, and that studying them clarifies the main line of the adaptation of Marxism and the content of twenty-first-century Marxism. They call for fully implementing Xi Jinping Thought and the spirit of the Third Plenum, so that this theory drives Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how Party theorists periodise the Party's theoretical innovation through a single set of recurring questions.

An analysis of the subject dimensions of comprehensively deepening reform 全面深化改革的主体向度解析 Li Gang Cheng Xinlin Li Gang and Cheng Xinlin take up a question raised by the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization: who is the 'subject' of reform when the Decision commits to 'putting the people first'? The authors argue that the people are the subject of comprehensive reform in four distinct senses, and that this reflects a new level of understanding of 'the people' in the Party's reform experience since 1978. The article was published in Theoretical Horizon in 2024. The article is organised in four sections, each treating the people as one kind of subject: practical subject, value subject, interest subject and evaluation subject. Each section opens with a classical Marxist premise, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and then relates it to reform practice from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the present. Examples include the household contract responsibility system at Xiaogang village, market-oriented economic reform, and the Party's 2017 judgement on the principal contradiction in society. In the authors' account, the people are the practical subject because history is made by the masses, but the masses can act effectively only if organised under Party leadership, which the authors treat as the guarantee of reform. As value subject, the people make reform a means of creating conditions for each person's free and all-round development, both by raising productive forces and by cultivating capable people. As interest subject, the people raise the problem of balancing individual and collective interests. The authors, following Marx and Engels, read these as dialectically united and cite whole-process people's democracy and the socialist market economy as ways of handling the relation. As evaluation subject, the people judge whether reform has delivered. The authors ground this in their practical experience, their value orientation and their direct interests. On evaluation, the authors propose three measures: respect the people's capacity to judge and follow the mass line, build positive incentives by responding promptly to public feedback, and remove institutional obstacles to evaluation. For the last, they call for smoother channels, with more online and offline platforms and simpler procedures for passing opinions to the relevant departments. They conclude that, given the greater complexity and risks facing reform, reliance on the people's participation matters even more. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of the 'people as subject' principle in current Party reform theory, linked to Marxist classics and reform history.

Fully and accurately grasping the principles of further deepening reform comprehensively 全面准确领会和把握进一步全面深化改革的原则 Qu Qingshan This article, published in Qizhi (Banner) in early 2025, is an interpretive study of the "six adherences" that the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) set out as principles for further deepening reform comprehensively.
