Qu argues that these principles condense Xi Jinping's new thinking on comprehensive reform, and that they must be understood fully and accurately and upheld unwaveringly in practice. The text has three parts. The first explains the significance of the six principles from four angles: historical, practical, theoretical and methodological. The second sets out the content of each principle and the question it answers. The third turns to practical requirements for regions, departments and Party organisations implementing the Plenum's decisions. Qu presents the six principles as one organic whole, each answering a distinct question about reform. Party leadership answers who leads; a people-centred approach answers for whom; upholding fundamental principles while innovating answers the question of stance and direction; institution-building as the main thread answers the question of goals; law-based governance answers the question of path; and a systems approach answers the question of method. On "upholding fundamental principles", Qu states that Party leadership, Marxism, the socialist path with Chinese characteristics and the people's democratic dictatorship cannot be shaken, or reform would be led onto "the wrong path". Qu also stresses the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and calls for balancing relationships such as government and market, efficiency and fairness, and development and security. In conclusion, Qu asks that each principle be turned into a working requirement. These include safeguarding the authority of the Party Centre, starting from the people's fundamental interests, building institutions that are practical and effective, using law to consolidate reform results, and coordinating measures through clear task lists, timetables and priorities. The article closes by calling for unity around the Party Centre with Xi Jinping at its core and for pressing on with reform. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line exposition of the six principles of the Third Plenum's reform agenda, as presented by a senior Party theorist.

An analysis of the practical positioning of the new development stage 新发展阶段的实践定位探析 Sun Yingshuai Zhao Shiyu Sun Yingshuai and Zhao Shiyu ask where the "new development stage", which China formally entered after the completion of a moderately prosperous society and the first centenary goal, sits in the Party's periodisation of Chinese society. They answer, following Xi Jinping's formulations, that it is a sub-stage within the primary stage of socialism, the stage of comprehensively building a modern socialist country and advancing towards the second centenary goal, and a great leap in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article appeared in Guancha yu sikao (Observation and Thinking), 2025, no. 1. The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these three formulations. The first treats the relation between the new stage and the primary stage of socialism. The second discusses modernization, the new development philosophy, the new development pattern and high-quality development. The third covers national rejuvenation, common prosperity and a new form of civilisation suited to Chinese modernization. The authors draw on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, together with economic data such as IMF figures and 2023 per-capita GDP. In the first part the authors argue that scholars have studied what is "new" and "changed" in the stage more than what is unchanged. They list five points of continuity: time span, the basic contradiction, people's all-round development still resting on dependence on things, China's developing-country status, and the goals of modernization. They hold that the stage is a "leap stage" rather than a "transitional stage", belonging to the theory of social stages and not of social formations. It is, in their account, a partial qualitative change inside a continuing quantitative accumulation, and a preparation for a higher stage, for which they call for an evaluation system. Later sections link the new stage to new quality productive forces, common prosperity and a Marxism-based civilisational renewal. The authors conclude that in the new stage the Party will lead the people towards a strong modern socialist country by applying the new development philosophy, building the new development pattern, pursuing high-quality development and common prosperity, and so achieving national rejuvenation. They stress the risks they identify, including great-power rivalry, containment by the United States, domestic imbalances and the demands of Party self-governance. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Party theory defines the new development stage and its relation to the primary stage of socialism.

Capitalism and the grand narrative of early modern world history 资本主义与近代早期世界史宏大叙事 Yu Jinyao Yu Jinyao asks why capitalism, once the organising concept of modern world history, has largely disappeared from accounts of the early modern period. Yu argues that this marginalisation is a mistake. Capitalism, in the article's view, is a basic fact of the past five centuries, and dropping the concept leaves historians without an effective tool for analysis and critique. The article has four main parts. It first traces the decline of capitalism as a historical category, blaming postmodern attacks on grand narratives and anti-Eurocentric global history. It examines the California School, taking in Gunder Frank, Kenneth Pomeranz, R. Bin Wong and Li Bozhong. It then sets out seven elements of Marx's concept of the capitalist mode of production and discusses capitalism's creative and destructive sides. Finally, it applies these to early modern debates. Yu reads Marx as defining capitalism by wage labour, commodity production in which labour-power itself is a commodity, ceaseless accumulation, and a world market, with the capitalist era beginning in the sixteenth century. On this basis Yu argues that commercial growth alone does not produce capitalism. Applying "Smithian growth" to Ming–Qing Jiangnan, Yu says, treats a largely domestic commodity economy as equivalent to Europe's world-market-based commercial capitalism, when Jiangnan stayed at the stage of capitalist sprouts. Coal and colonies, the article contends, mattered in Britain only because capitalism had developed there, which is why Spain and Portugal gained less from their empires. Yu adds that "interaction" cannot explain colonial plunder or ecological damage, which the concept of capitalism and Marx's primitive accumulation can. Yu concludes that any divergence between East and West happened early, when capitalism grew in Europe while elsewhere it remained in sprout form. Yu presents this as a matter of fact, not Eurocentrism, and says that Frank's call to abandon the concept only courts attention. The article proposes capitalism as the framework for a new grand narrative of early modern world history, built on Marx's theory of the capitalist mode of production. Read the original if you want a Marxist historian's critique of the California School and of "Smithian growth" in Chinese debates on Jiangnan and the Great Divergence.

Engels's influence on Marx's turn to political economy: a textual study based on Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy 恩格斯对马克思转向政治经济学研究的影响——基于《国民经济学批判大纲》的文本考察 Guo Jinlong How far did Engels's early essay, Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy (1843–44), shape Marx's move into political economy? Guo Jinlong argues that the essay was the first work of Engels's economic studies and an opening piece of Marxist critique of political economy, and that Engels was both a forerunner and a guide for Marx. The article nonetheless concludes that the influence was real but external: it was not the internal, decisive factor in Marx's turn. The article examines the Outlines against Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, which acknowledged the essay as an original and rich work. It is organised under four kinds of influence: orientation (the path of analysing real social problems economically), method, specific theses, and the communist goal. Guo draws on Engels's biography from Bremen through Berlin to Manchester, on Marx's Rheinische Zeitung and Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher years, and on commentators such as Terrell Carver, David McLellan, Cornu and Ilyichev. Guo's central claims are as follows. On orientation, Engels had reached the economic critique of society before Marx, but Marx was already pushed towards it by his Rheinische Zeitung encounters with material interests and by his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, which located the anatomy of civil society in political economy. Guo therefore rejects McLellan's view that Engels redirected Marx's attention. On method, Engels's historical, materialist and dialectical analysis of the basic categories of political economy, ending in the abolition of private property, surpassed Proudhon, Hess and the economists. Marx's Manuscripts, still governed by a humanist logic of alienation, took over Engels's starting point in private property and his category-based analysis of wages, profit and rent. Guo lists six shared theses, including the premise of private property, labour as free activity, wages at subsistence level, concentration of capital, and communism as reconciliation. On the communist goal, Guo holds that what drew Marx to the Outlines was its economic argument for communism, which matched his own aim of human emancipation. Guo concludes that grasping the Outlines' influence in this limited and balanced way is key to understanding the link between Marx's and Engels's early economic thought. Read the original if you study the formation of Marx's political economy, the Marx–Engels intellectual relationship, or the 1844 Manuscripts, and want a close textual comparison that disputes the idea of Engels as the decisive influence.

Centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee as the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well 党中央集中统一领导是做好经济工作的根本保证 Yang Ming This commentary takes its starting point from Xi Jinping's speech at the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, which called centralised and unified leadership by the Party Central Committee "the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well". Yang Ming argues that this is a law-like insight drawn from economic practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and that it points the way to completing the targets of the 14th Five-Year Plan and making a good start on the 15th. The article has three parts. The first explains why the principle holds, drawing on the experience of the new era, the need to secure the right direction of economic development, and the role of the Party in resisting risks and challenges. The second sets out how the Party's capacity to lead economic work can be strengthened. The third turns to practical requirements for the coming year. Yang's core argument is that the Party leads economic work as its central task, so the Central Committee must bear overall responsibility. In the author's account, the 2019 to 2023 economic work conferences repeatedly reaffirmed this principle. Yang describes the economy as a huge ship that needs steering as it grows, and says the authority of the Central Committee is what lets the whole country act as "one chessboard" and follow one blueprint. The second part urges leading cadres to work with political awareness, scientific method, rule-of-law thinking and professional skill. It also presents the five "must balance" relationships from the 2024 conference: an efficient market and a capable government, aggregate supply and demand, nurturing new and updating old growth drivers, improving the incremental and revitalising the existing, and raising quality while expanding quantity. The author also points to institutional arrangements such as the Politburo Standing Committee, the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission and the Central Commission for Deepening Overall Reform. For the year ahead, Yang calls for keeping to the general principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability, concentrating on key tasks (placing boosting consumption and expanding domestic demand first), and uniting efforts for high-quality development. Yang also calls for guarding against Central Committee decisions being emptied out through documents and meetings, and for judging officials by real results. Read the original if you want to see how Party-theoretical commentary links Xi Jinping's economic thought, the 2024 economic work conference and the Party's leadership system into one argument for centralised leadership.

Leading the development of new quality productive forces through scientific and technological innovation 以科技创新引领新质生产力发展 Zhao Zhenhua Zhao Zhenhua takes up the instruction of the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference to "lead the development of new quality productive forces through scientific and technological innovation" and asks what these forces are, how innovation produces them and what path should be followed. The article, published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscript in 2025, argues that innovation is the leading factor in new quality productive forces. In Zhao's account this makes it central to building a modern industrial system, winning strategic initiative in international competition and meeting people's aspirations for a better life. The article has three parts. The first sets out the features of new quality productive forces in the present era. The second explains the internal logic by which technological innovation drives their development, drawing on Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping's statements. The third proposes a path in four steps: reform of production relations, original innovation, the conversion of research results into output, and development adapted to local conditions. Zhao's core argument is that productive forces advance through science and technology, now at an accelerating pace and across ever wider fields, with converging disciplines and globalised innovation. Innovation raises industries to higher levels and lifts the three elements of productive forces (labourers, means of labour and objects of labour) and the way they combine. Technological innovation also induces managerial, institutional and cultural innovation. Citing Engels's "parallelogram of forces", Zhao presents these as a joint resultant that is mutually conditioning. Because production relations must adapt to productive forces, the author says, further comprehensive deepening of reform is needed. Zhao calls for a better division of roles between market and government. Enterprises should be the main actors in innovation, state capital should move toward forward-looking strategic emerging industries, and private firms should be able to lead major technological projects. The author also urges stronger basic research and a new national system for pooling resources on key technologies, along with markets for trading research results. Eastern regions should lead original innovation and western regions should focus on application, without abandoning traditional industries, and the "Internet Plus" and "AI Plus" initiatives should be accelerated. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy reasoning that links innovation, reform of production relations and regional industrial strategy.

Three dimensions of upholding harmony between humanity and nature 坚持人与自然和谐共生的三重维度 Huan Qingzhi Huan Qingzhi examines "upholding harmony between humanity and nature", which the article calls the theoretical cornerstone of Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization. The author argues that it answers, at the level of Marxist ecological philosophy, why China builds an ecological civilization, what kind it builds, and how. The thesis is that the principle has three connected dimensions: a material-ontological premise, a philosophical-ethical outlook, and a national development strategy. The article follows these dimensions in turn. The first is the premise that "humanity and nature are a community of life". The second is the ethic of respecting, adapting to and protecting nature. The third is the strategic choice to build a Chinese modernization in which humanity and nature live in harmony. Huan draws on Engels's Dialectics of Nature, Marx's account of labour as metabolism with nature, Xi Jinping's speeches, and Party congress documents. Examples include the Saihanba forest farm, the national parks system, functional zoning and Yellow River policy. In the first part, Huan holds that nature is the material origin of human life. Even digital labour depends on natural inputs, and the relation between humanity and nature is the most basic social relation, interacting with relations between people. The author contrasts capitalist and socialist institutional frameworks as giving modernization different ecological outcomes. In the second part, "respecting" nature means obeying ecological laws, "adapting" means adjusting to nature's rhythms (for example through land-use zoning, ecological red lines and climate adaptation), and "protecting" nature means integrated care of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grasslands and deserts. In the third part, Huan treats harmony with nature as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. The author says it responds to the people's demand for a better life, offers an alternative to the Western model, and suits a large developing country that cannot copy Western consumption patterns. Material and ecological civilization must advance together, since neither can exist without the other. Huan notes that the foundations of improvement remain fragile and endorses the "five major relationships" Xi set out at the 2023 national ecological conference. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars derive the ecological civilization doctrine from Marxist texts and policy practice.

On the new quality mode of production 论新质生产方式 Lu Baolin Xie Hui Lu Baolin and Xie Hui take up a gap in the literature on new quality productive forces. In their view, existing studies tend either to reduce the concept to technological progress or to treat it in isolation as a matter of changing production relations. The authors argue that, in Marxist political economy, the mode of production is the missing link between productive forces and relations of production. Whether productive forces have undergone a qualitative change, they contend, depends on whether the associated mode of production has changed fundamentally, so cultivating new quality productive forces requires remaking the basic form of the mode of production. The article has four parts. It first clarifies, from Marx's texts, what the mode of production means and how it relates to productive forces and relations of production. It then traces the capitalist mode of production from simple cooperation through manufacture to large-scale machine industry. Next it analyses how breakthrough changes in the mode of production come about under capitalism. Finally it discusses how China, in the new stage of development, can move from a traditional mode of production to a new quality one. Lu and Xie define the mode of production as a unity of a material substance (how labourers and means of labour combine) and a social form that carries the relations of production. They read Marx's account of machine industry as showing mutual shaping: capital relations drive the mode of production, which in turn produces a leap in productive forces. They draw five mechanisms from Capital: changes in the means of labour as the foundation; the chase for extra surplus value as the driving force; competition as the means of diffusion; state intervention, such as factory legislation, as a catalyst; and deepening specialisation spreading the new mode across the whole system. They apply this to China's large-scale, standardised, export-oriented mode, which they say rested on cheap factors, open supply chains and rising overseas demand, supports that have weakened since 2008. For the transition, the authors propose five measures: iterating and upgrading the means of labour through a new system for mobilising national resources; embedding Party leadership in corporate governance; being guided by the new development philosophy; developing mixed-ownership economy; and building a high-standard socialist market economy. In a closing note they describe great-power competition as at bottom a competition between modes of production. They argue that only an original, high-quality material mode of production, under the basic socialist economic system, can let China catch up with developed countries. Read the original if you want a Marxist, production-mode reading of new quality productive forces that stays close to Capital and ends in concrete policy proposals.

The philosophical foundations of the theory of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化理论的哲学根基 Feng Yanli Feng Yanli asks what lies beneath the theory of Chinese modernization, beyond surface-level exposition of its positions. The article argues that the "six outlooks" embedded in Chinese modernization (worldview, values, view of history, view of civilization, view of democracy and view of ecology) form the theory's philosophical foundation. Feng takes as the starting point Xi Jinping's remark after the 20th Party Congress (2022) that the theory is a major theoretical innovation and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the philosophical foundation matters: it deepens research into the regularities of China's distinctive path, and it widens the practical scope of the theory by handling the relations between tradition and modernity, part and whole, and present and long-term development. The second part defines the foundation's core meaning through three principles ("the people first", independence and self-reliance, and "having the world in mind") and then describes each of the six outlooks in turn. The third part examines how the six outlooks cohere. Feng's central claim is that the foundation is an organic whole with a vertical and a horizontal structure. Vertically, the worldview, grounded in dialectical and historical materialism, plays the leading role and determines the other five outlooks; Feng supports this with Marxist claims that history, civilization and democracy are rooted in practice and the people's role. Horizontally, the six outlooks interact at the same level, which Feng illustrates through the mutual shaping of the view of history and the view of civilization, while each keeps its own emphasis. Feng contrasts each outlook with Western counterparts, presenting the Chinese ones as surpassing zero-sum thinking, capital-centred values, the "clash of civilizations" and an approach to development that neglects the environment. Feng concludes that the six outlooks together constitute the theory's philosophical foundation and develop dynamically as practice resolves real contradictions. Understanding them is said to give theoretical guidance for advancing Chinese modernization and to offer "Chinese wisdom" for world modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic account, in official Party-theory terms, of how Chinese scholars derive the "six outlooks" from Marxist philosophy and relate them to one another.

The innovative development of the Marxist theory of ownership in the age of the digital economy 数字经济时代马克思主义所有制理论的创新发展 Bao Weijie Bao Weijie asks in what sense the Marxist theory of ownership can be developed further under the digital economy. The article argues that the theory should be read as an organic whole rather than as a question about the title to means of production alone. On that reading, it both changes and stays the same in the digital age. Its classical core remains fully applicable to the critique of digital capitalism, and Bao also proposes new research agendas. The article first sets out three theoretical questions: whether to take a structural or an element-based view, which principle to start from, and what practical purpose the research serves. It then divides the argument into the "change" of ownership theory and its "constancy", examined through historical materialism. A final section reviews the literature on the digital economy and on ownership theory. It closes with three directions for further work. On "change", Bao uses three core propositions: who owns the means of production, how labourers are combined with them, and how products are distributed and appropriated. Data now appears as a new, non-material means of production with several possible owners (platforms, the public). Platform work, such as ride-hailing, produces a "semi-combined state" in which workers own part of the means of production. Data revenue is being recalculated. On "constancy", Bao holds that capital's employment of wage labour is unchanged, and that digital productive forces are social labour's productive forces, not "platform capital's" productive forces. Platforms gain "original" and "derived" data ownership, extract rents and lobby against antitrust rules, and Bao cites a 2020 US House Judiciary Committee report on Google and Facebook. In Bao's reading this confirms the limits of labour's liberation under digital capitalism. Bao proposes three research directions. The first is the impact of the digital economy on traditional ownership relations, including platform capital as a new type of owner and the subjectivity and rights of digital workers. The second is the applicability of ownership theory to building socialist ownership, to anti-monopoly work and to preventing the disorderly expansion of capital, with attention to public capital combined with digital technology and to whether "social ownership" might be realised. The third is data ownership, including data rights confirmation, tiered public, enterprise and individual rights, and the ownership of AI-generated products. Bao ties this work to the aim that all the people share the dividends of the digital economy. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy account of platform capitalism and data ownership, with a map of the domestic literature.

Deng Xiaoping's contribution to exploring the "Two Integrations" and its profound lessons 邓小平对“两个结合”探索的贡献及其深刻启示 Liu Zhiming Liu Zhiming asks how Deng Xiaoping contributed to what the Party now calls the Two Integrations, and what that record offers for the present. The article argues that after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), Deng led the Party in exploring both integrations around the building of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Liu's account this produced a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is published in Marxism Studies (2024, no. 11). It has four parts: why socialist modernization requires the Two Integrations; how Deng developed them; the achievements that resulted; and the lessons for today. Liu concedes that Deng mostly spoke of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete reality and never explicitly proposed the integration with fine traditional Chinese culture. Liu nonetheless holds that the second integration is implicit in his work, because Chinese culture and history form part of China's "concrete reality". Liu gives four reasons from Deng for the Two Integrations: the lessons of the revolution, the need to keep solving concrete problems, the novelty of modernization as an undertaking, and the failures of copying the Soviet model. Deng's exploration, Liu argues, rested on upholding Marxism's universal truth and basic principles, including seeking truth from facts, the Four Cardinal Principles and the principles of socialism. It also rested on grasping China's conditions: a weak economic base, a large population with little arable land, and the primary stage of socialism. On culture, Liu reports that Deng called for critical appraisal of tradition under Marxist guidance, while opposing both "Left" and Right errors and feudal and bourgeois influences. Liu lists five achievements: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Party's basic line, a new path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a distinctive socialist system, and a renewed ethical-cultural life. Liu draws three lessons. Marxism must be upheld fully and as a whole, including the successive theories of adaptation and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and Chinese modernization must be advanced. Policy must start from the primary stage of socialism, including the "new development stage" within it. China must keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, avoiding both ossification and abandoning socialism, while continuing to innovate. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of Deng Xiaoping's Marxism, and of how current official discourse links his thought to the Two Integrations.

Treating reification within the dialectical relation between spirit and body 在精神与肉体的辩证关系中对待物化 Huang Xiaofeng Wang Xiaosheng Since Lukács introduced the critique of reification, the authors observe, Western Marxism has often criticised capitalism for the reification it produces rather than for its internal contradictions. Huang and Wang argue that most thinkers have not found the right way of dealing with reification. They propose a materialist-dialectical approach: reification is to be both acknowledged as rationally necessary to a degree and continually resisted. The article has four sections. It first argues that Lukács's theory is idealist in nature, then traces the roots of reification to the opposition of spirit and body. It next compares three ways of overcoming the subject–object dichotomy: Hegelian idealism (Lukács), Heidegger's phenomenology, and Marx's dialectical materialism. A final section considers the theoretical and social significance of reification, drawing on Adorno and Horkheimer, Honneth, Kant and Baudrillard. The authors contend that Lukács shifted Marx's analysis from the economic base to ideology and took over Hegel's notion of totality, so that the 'reified totality' repeats the Hegelian claim of a society governed by spirit. Following Adorno and Horkheimer, they trace reification to a civilisational necessity: to survive, humans must master external nature and also their own bodily nature. This divides spirit from body and subject from object. Heidegger tries to leap over the opposition and so negates civilisation, while Lukács's proletarian subject-object, even if it took control, would still run a rationalised system. For the authors, Marx's subject is a living, self-contradictory person, and the incalculable use-value of commodities is the non-identical element that resists reification. The authors conclude that reification cannot be abolished, because human survival requires it, but that it can be resisted by reviving suppressed passion and reconciling it with spirit. They hold that the problem of modern capitalist civilisation is that reification is unconditionally treated as rational. Under commodity fetishism and in Baudrillard's 'hyperreality', true and false needs become hard to tell apart, and excessive competition between states and individuals becomes self-harming. They call for a Marxist materialist dialectic that avoids both Lukács's idealism and Heidegger's contemplation of Being. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical reading of Lukács, Heidegger and Marx on reification, with particular attention to the body–spirit relation.

The alternating law of nationalisation and privatisation in advanced Western capitalist countries: logic, reality and trends 西方发达资本主义国家“国有化-私有化”迭变律：逻辑、现实与趋势 Qin Meng Why do advanced capitalist countries swing between nationalisation and privatisation? Qin Meng argues that existing Chinese scholarship has described these waves and assessed their motives and results, but has lacked a theoretical framework. The article offers one, combining Marxist political economy with Karl Polanyi's "double movement", and treats the alternation as a regular law (diébiàn lǜ) of capitalist development. Published in Contemporary Economic Research in 2025, it also draws lessons for China's state sector. The article first sets out the framework. It reviews Marx, Engels and Lenin on the basic contradiction of capitalism and the growing socialisation of ownership, then Polanyi's account of market "disembedding" and the protective counter-movement in The Great Transformation. Qin then surveys three waves in the United States, Britain, France and West Germany: large-scale nationalisation from the 1930s to the late 1970s, privatisation from 1979 to 2008 beginning with Thatcherism, and a brief renationalisation after the 2008 financial crisis. A final section turns to the twenty-first century and what the author calls a crisis of state governance. The central move is to treat the two forces as complementary. Following Meng Jie's reconstruction of historical materialism, Qin holds that relations of production have a dual function, so that politics and ideology can themselves act as production relations. Nationalisation therefore has two drivers: the pressure of socialising productive forces and crisis (path A), and the dominant ideology, such as Keynesian interventionism or neoliberalism (path C). Qin argues that after 2008 bank rescues and part-nationalisations mainly benefited monopoly finance capital and burdened public finances. Rising inequality and populism, including Trump and Brexit, then combined with neoliberalism to bring a new round of privatisation. Nationalisation under capitalism, the author concludes, always serves to defend private ownership and so reverses once it erodes private profit. Qin draws four lessons: nationalisation and markets are not simply opposed; neoliberal hegemony keeps privatisation dominant and deepens contradictions; China's socialist market economy rests on the organic combination of public ownership and the market; and neoliberal privatisation must be resisted. The author calls for stronger, better and larger state-owned enterprises, further reform of their governance, and a better combination of an effective market with a capable government, so as to escape the Western cycle. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Western state ownership, with country data and the explicit link to policy on China's state sector.

Upholding the five "must coordinate" principles in economic work 坚持以五个“必须统筹”做好经济工作 Li Yuju Gu Yan This article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2025, interprets the five "must coordinate" principles set out at the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024. Li and Gu argue that these pairs of relationships are regularities distilled from China's economic practice, apply dialectical and historical materialism to current economic contradictions, and further enrich Xi Jinping's economic thought. They present the principles both as rules for economic work and as a scientific methodology for high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The article devotes one section to each of the five relationships: an effective market and a capable government; aggregate supply and aggregate demand; fostering new drivers of growth and updating old ones; improving the incremental and reviving the stock; and raising quality and expanding total quantity. Each section follows a similar pattern. It cites Xi Jinping and recent Party documents, including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), gives illustrative data, and then lists the measures announced at the 2024 conference. The central claim is that each pair is a unity of opposites that must be handled dialectically rather than by choosing one side. On market and government, the authors say the market allocates resources most efficiently but cannot do everything, so the state must correct market failure, under Party leadership and the socialist system. On supply and demand, they say policy emphasis should follow shifts in the principal contradiction and its main aspect. They cite the stimulus package of September 2024 as a response to weak domestic demand. On new and old drivers, they reject treating new quality productive forces as a replacement for traditional industry. For quality and quantity, they invoke the law of the transformation of quantity into quality. They cite figures such as 18.9 million registered business entities in 2024 and new-energy vehicle output rising from 18,000 in 2013 to over 13 million in 2024. The authors conclude that the five relationships reveal the basic law of using a systems approach in economic work. They also supply tools for what they call a well-sung "economic chorus", offer guidance for macroeconomic governance, and form an innovation in contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. They call for long-term adherence to the principles and stress the Party's overall leadership, especially the centralised and unified leadership of the Central Committee, amid greater external pressure and domestic difficulty. Read the original if you want a close view of how official commentary explains and justifies the economic policy framework adopted at the end of 2024.

Accelerating the formation of distribution relations suited to the development of new quality productive forces 加快形成与新质生产力发展相适应的分配关系 Xu Ji Liu Xueliang Xu Ji and Liu Xueliang take up Xi Jinping's call to build new relations of production suited to new quality productive forces, and ask what distribution relations that would require. Their thesis is that distribution relations and new quality productive forces can reinforce each other, but only if the distributional risks of the new round of scientific-technological revolution and industrial transformation are managed. The article, published in Caijing Zhiku in 2024, treats distribution as a core component of the relations of production. The article first sets out the two-way interaction. Fair incentives for talent, knowledge and technology are said to support new quality productive forces, while these forces create conditions for reforming distribution and for common prosperity. It then reviews Chinese and international literature on four channels of disruption: employment structure, income polarisation and skills, labour–capital conflict and equality of opportunity, and falling labour income share with unbalanced development. It next identifies four potential paths by which new quality productive forces could improve distribution, and closes with policy proposals. On the risks, the authors draw on studies of automation. These include estimates of jobs at high risk of replacement, from Frey and Osborne's 47% for the United States to more moderate task-based estimates of 6–12%. They also cite research on the polarisation of middle-skill workers, platform-based flexible employment, algorithmic discrimination, and capital-biased technical change and "superstar" firms. The authors then argue the effect is not necessarily negative. In their account, a people-centred employment ecology, new rules for factors such as knowledge, technology and data to share in distribution, a high-standard market system that curbs monopoly, and innovation-driven integration of town and country and of regions (for example the "East Data, West Computing" project) can narrow gaps. The authors conclude that suitable distribution relations should centre on rewarding innovation and respecting labour, knowledge, talent and creativity. They propose better protection for workers in new forms of employment, incentives that reward innovation and tolerate failure, technology-enabled targeted poverty relief and public services, and digital social governance. The governance measures include algorithm audits, "precision taxation" and a data-income scheme that favours data creators in primary distribution and uses data taxes in redistribution. Read the original if you want a literature-rich account of how Chinese economists link new quality productive forces, technological unemployment and common prosperity.

Major institutional achievements of comprehensively deepening reform in the new era 新时代全面深化改革的重大制度成果 Chen Jinlong Wu Zhinan Chen Jinlong and Wu Zhinan ask what institutional results the Party's drive to comprehensively deepen reform has produced since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what these results suggest for the next stage. Their thesis is that the main outcome is institutional: a more mature and settled system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, whose advantages should now be converted into governance effectiveness. The article first appeared in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), 2025, no. 1. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remark that institution-building now carries greater weight in reform. It then sets out four headings: the steady improvement of the institutional system, the full display of institutional advantages, the rising authority of institutions, and the accumulated experience of institution-building. The first section follows the three tiers of the system: fundamental, basic and important institutions. The authors argue that reform has consolidated the fundamental institutions, such as the Party's overall leadership and the people's congress system. It has also improved the basic institutions, including multiparty cooperation, regional ethnic autonomy, public ownership as the mainstay and the socialist market economy. Finally, it has innovated in the important institutions, including the legal system, administration, social security, ecological protection and supervision. They identify three advantages: Party leadership, the primacy of the people and centralised unity. They also say institutional authority has risen through stronger institutional awareness, supervision of implementation and better governance results. As evidence they cite the Central Commission for Comprehensively Deepening Reform, recurring Party education campaigns, the supervision regulations, poverty alleviation and the response to COVID-19. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as the channel for popular participation. The authors draw four lessons for further reform. These are to keep institution-building as the main thread, to unite upholding fundamental principles with innovation, to combine top-level design with grassroots exploration, and to treat breaking down and building up as a dialectical unity, building first and breaking afterwards. They call for reform to proceed steadily and firmly toward the goals set by the Party Central Committee. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party scholars classify China's institutional system and describe the lessons of a decade of reform.

On the humanistic-economy attribute of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化的人文经济属性 Luo Weidong Luo Weidong asks what most basically defines Chinese modernization as distinct from the Western model. The article argues that its fundamental attribute is its people-centred character, and that in economic terms this means a "humanistic economy" (renwen jingji), an economy that takes the human being as its starting point, purpose and standard. Luo holds that, in this sense, the humanistic economy coincides with a socialist economy and can only be realised under socialism. The article first traces the move from the "four modernizations" to Chinese modernization, as formulated at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then reflects on capitalist modernization and sets out three senses of "humanistic economy": a cultural economy, an economy attentive to workers' human traits, and a human-centred economy. It surveys intellectual sources from Confucian thought, Aristotle and Aquinas through Sismondi and the utopian socialists to Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, the Communist Manifesto and Capital. It closes with institutional practice, including Zhejiang province, and a research agenda. Luo contends that capitalist modernization is driven by the logic of capital and profit maximisation, which inverts means and ends and produces polarisation, ecological damage and conflict. The first two senses of humanistic economy still treat people as instruments of wealth creation. Sismondi is credited as a founder of humanistic economics but lacked a scientific method, while Marx's critique of political economy gave it a scientific form. Under Chinese modernization, Luo describes the humanistic economy as seven things: a people's economy, an economy of common prosperity, a market economy, a moral economy, a cultural economy, an aesthetic economy and a green economy. Luo concludes that the humanistic economy is the basic attribute of Chinese modernization and that Chinese modernization, so defined, is modernization as it should be. Luo judges that conceptual innovation is largely done but theoretical work lags behind. The article proposes research on reconciling capital's profit-seeking with humanistic goals, on common prosperity and high-quality growth, on the threat AI poses to employment and human character, on the place of human modernization, and on building an autonomous Chinese economics. Read the original if you want a Chinese economist's account of how humanistic economics is linked to Marx, Confucianism and Party policy, and of its proposed research agenda.

Postone and Adorno: two materialist orientations of dialectics 普殊同与阿多诺对辩证法的两重唯物主义定向 Lu Kaihua Moishe Postone argued in Time, Labor, and Social Domination that Marx's mature concept of labour is not Hegel's alienation of a conscious subject but a historically specific form of labour under capitalism. Lu Kaihua reads this as continuing Lukács's aim of giving Hegelian dialectics a materialist turn, echoing Lukács's 1967 self-criticism that History and Class Consciousness was 'more Hegelian than Hegel'. The article's thesis is that Postone's 'positive' dialectic of capital and Adorno's negative dialectics are not truly opposed. Lu proposes an 'alliance' between them. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Postone's critical inheritance from Lukács, covering his account of capital as a quasi-independent social subject-substance, the historical development from manufacture to machine industry, and where he departs from Lukács. The second argues that Postone's criticism of Adorno, as a pessimistic heir of Lukács trapped in the philosophy of consciousness, is too simple. The third sets Adorno's Negative Dialectics beside Lukács's 1967 preface and draws on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Logic, Fichte and secondary commentators. In Lu's reading, Postone locates materiality in the social effects of the value form, not in the class consciousness of the proletariat. His 'treadmill' dialectic holds that productivity gains raise material wealth but not value created per unit of time, which forces ever-greater productivity and produces ecological and social crises. Lu argues that Postone's ideal-typical analysis leaves out concrete labour, social organisation and ideology, as Postone himself admits. Adorno's primacy of the object, Lu argues, already treats value as a 'quasi-independent' entity and traces domination historically. Lu concludes that Postone's capital dialectic gives critical theory a useful account of structural contradiction, but it risks a Fichte-like conceptual compulsion by turning capital into an 'absolute self'. Adorno's negative dialectics, Lu argues, warns against this risk and against the closure of Lukács's totality. Lu paraphrases Kant: without positive dialectics, negative dialectics becomes empty, and without negation, positive dialectics goes blind. Read the original if you work on Postone, Lukács or the Frankfurt School and want a Chinese-language case for reconciling value-form theory with Adorno.

Theoretical sources and features of the heterogeneity dimension in New Historicist criticism 新历史主义批评异质性维度的理论渊源及其特征探析 Cheng Xiangzhan Fan Jing This article asks where the concept of 'heterogeneity' in New Historicism comes from and what features it gives the school. Cheng and Fan argue that, unlike traditional historicism, which pairs the 'universal' with the 'particular' or 'different', New Historicism prefers 'heterogeneity'. They trace this mainly to Michel Foucault and Michel de Certeau, whose shared influence they say produces a distinctive 'heterology' in New Historicist practice. The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. It examines in turn a heterogeneous view of history, a heterogeneous view of power and discourse, and a constructivist method centred on the 'Other'. Its main New Historicist figures are Stephen Greenblatt, Louis Montrose, Hayden White and Catherine Gallagher. It also draws on commentators such as Jürgen Pieters, Ian Buchanan and Frank Ankersmit. The authors make three main moves. First, Foucault's discontinuity and Certeau's idea of history as writing about the Other move New Historicism from a singular History to plural 'small histories'. White's tropology replaces deductive logic with figurative logic, and Greenblatt's wish to 'speak with the dead' is read as a Certeauvian struggle against death. Second, New Historicism takes up Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity, for instance in Greenblatt's self-fashioning and Gallagher's work on marginal women writers. It also takes up Certeau's strategy–tactics opposition, which Montrose uses to ask how subjects keep some autonomy. Third, the authors argue that Certeau's 'New World' writing and Foucault's marginal anecdotes together shape the school's characteristic methods, namely thick description, anecdotalism and interdisciplinarity. The authors conclude that heterogeneity runs through New Historicist theory and practice, which they call a literary-critical version of postmodern historiography. They credit it with directing attention to marginal materials and plural histories, and with promoting practice-orientation and cross-disciplinary work, which they say is useful for building Chinese literary theory. They also warn of risks: attention to particulars may become an escape from theory, and uncritical copying in China may end in 'theory-less homogenisation'. They add, following Tao Dongfeng, that China's 'new liberal arts' should aim to advance modernity, not return to the medieval. Read the original if you study New Historicism, Foucault and Certeau's reception in literary criticism, or debates over how Chinese literary theory should use Western critical schools.

Marx and Engels on the global time lag in capitalist development 马克思恩格斯论资本主义发展的全球时差 Xu Changfu Xu Changfu takes up a neglected part of historical materialism, its geographical dimension, and asks how Marx and Engels understood the uneven timing of capitalist development between countries. The article argues that the two thinkers held a systematic view of a global 'time lag' (shicha) in capitalism's development. Xu says they never set this out in a dedicated text, so the article reconstructs it from their writings and links the scattered arguments together. It was published in Marxism and Reality in 2024. The article has three main parts. The first follows Engels from 1842 to his last years: his first judgement that England lagged behind the Continent, his reversal by 1844, and his later comparison of England with France, Germany and the United States. The second turns to Marx, in three stages: the 1843 introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the 1848 writings on the English, French and Prussian revolutions, and the preface to Capital, Volume I (1867). The third part draws these together into a map of the world and a short conclusion. Xu argues that Engels worked by observation, while Marx built a theory. In Xu's reading, Marx moved from lags between elements of one society (German philosophy ahead of German politics), to lags between whole societies (the 1648 and 1789 revolutions, and Prussia's March revolution as 'more than half a century' behind), to an economic essence: England as the classic site of the capitalist mode of production, showing other countries 'the image of their own future'. From these texts Xu derives six descending 'gradients', from England down to India and China. They fall into three tiers of lag, measured in decades, centuries and millennia respectively. Xu concludes that Marx and Engels stressed capitalism's global reach and world-historical significance, while still noting differences between countries. On Xu's reading, the guiding principle is that communist revolution has its objective material conditions only once the first three gradients have made the whole world capitalist. Russia's possible leap over capitalism's 'Caudine Forks' and the collapse of China's traditional economy after the 1894–95 war are treated as external triggers for European proletarian revolution. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reconstruction of the geographical and temporal logic in Marx's and Engels's view of uneven capitalist development.

Methodological shifts in the young Marx's exploration of the philosophy of law 青年马克思法哲学探索中的方法论转换 Sun Meitang Why did the young Marx, who began with legal commentary, end up addressing questions of law through the critique of political economy rather than through law itself? Sun Meitang takes up this familiar trajectory, from the Rheinische Zeitung to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of law to political economy. Sun argues that the popular explanation, that Marx met the problem of material interests and moved from the 'copy' to the 'original', is not wrong but oversimplified, and overlooks a change of dialectical method. The article follows Marx's path in four stages. It first treats the Rheinische Zeitung commentaries on press censorship and the wood-theft law, then the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, then the reasons for the turn to political economy, and finally how Marx's practical dialectic works out legal questions in economic analysis. Sun also places the shift in its wider setting: the rise of capitalism in Western Europe, Marx's reading in history, economics and politics, and his contacts with Engels. Sun's central claim is that Marx's dialectic passed through three forms. In the Rheinische Zeitung period it was an 'understanding' dialectic (zhixing bianzhengfa) that measured actual Prussian law against an ideal law that 'ought to be', with traces of Hegel. In the critique of Hegel it became a negative dialectic that turned Hegel's conceptual method against him: civil society and the family are the basis of the state, not the reverse, and democracy is the genuine unity of universal and particular. Because law and state arise from material life, they cannot be understood from themselves, so Marx moved to a historical, practical dialectic. Sun, drawing on Althusser, reads Marx's 'inversion' of Hegel as a change in the structure of dialectic, not a mere reversal of its content. Sun concludes that Marx converted legitimacy from a question of legal doctrine into one of historical process and human emancipation, so that justice, equality and legality are results of developing productive forces and not moral postulates. Every historical legal form is both legitimate and illegitimate, and even socialist distribution according to work retains traces of 'bourgeois right'. Sun adds that Marx's context cannot simply be transplanted onto the rule of law under socialism with Chinese characteristics, but that its essence, emancipation and social transformation over speculation, can guide it. Read the original if you want a close account of how Marx's methods in the philosophy of law developed from the Rheinische Zeitung to political economy.

Three perspectives on the spatial critique theory of foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义空间批判理论的三重视域 Wang Yuchen Gao Xiaoxi Wang Yuchen and Gao Xiaoxi ask how spatial critique, a major strand of left theory since the late twentieth century, developed across different currents of Marxism outside China, and what it gained and lost. They argue that it appears in classical Western Marxism, neo-Marxism and post-Marxism, with shared features but divergent stances on modernity versus postmodernity. Their verdict is that it enriches the critique of capital but ends in a radical retreat from class politics. The article takes three thinkers as representatives of the three traditions. Henri Lefebvre stands for classical Western Marxism, David Harvey for neo-Marxism, and Edward Soja for post-Marxism and the Los Angeles school. The authors read each through his theory of space, then draw wider comparisons with Foucault, Deleuze, Massey, Negri and world-systems theorists. On Lefebvre, the authors say that his humanist totality, reached through the production of space, the dialectic of space and the right to the city, replaces class emancipation with individual freedom and differences. Harvey, in their account, turns Lefebvre's meta-philosophy into a historical-geographical materialism: accumulation by dispossession, "creative destruction" of cities and uneven geographical development explain how capital displaces its crises. His process dialectic and "dialectical utopianism of space and time" are credited with keeping a class standpoint. Soja is portrayed as the weakest case. His thirdspace and spatial justice rest on a loosely defined idea of production relations and on marginal narratives, and so, the authors say, cannot reach private ownership as the root of injustice. For the authors, all three recast the contradiction between labour and capital as oppositions such as totality/fragment, global/local and centre/periphery. The authors conclude that spatial critique reflects the weakness of foreign Marxism in forming a collective subject. It exchanges class narrative for marginal positions and micro-politics, and amplifies the utopianism they see as inherent in foreign Marxism. They still credit it with prompting a clarification of space within historical materialism and with widening the empirical perspective on capital. They single out Harvey as the most valuable, although they judge that he also wavers on the priority of time and space and does not escape postmodernism. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese assessment of Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja that places spatial theory within debates over Western Marxism, post-Marxism and the fate of class politics.

The ecological implications of developing new quality productive forces 论发展新质生产力的生态意蕴 Li Yongsheng Xu Xialin Li Yongsheng and Xu Xialin take up Xi Jinping's statement that new quality productive forces are "themselves green productive forces" and ask what ecological meaning the concept carries. They argue that new quality productive forces are inherently ecological. In their reading, the shift from "natural productive forces" to "social productive forces" and then to new quality productive forces marks a deeper Party understanding of how economic and ecological construction relate. The article opens with Xi's remarks from September 2023 to mid-2024 that link the concept to green development. It then has three parts: the ecological connotation of new quality productive forces, the ecological thinking needed to develop them, and their ecological orientation. The first part covers the optimised combination of productive elements, digital and green technology, harmony between humanity and nature as a value goal, and an ecological innovation system. The later parts draw on Marx, Engels, Xi Jinping Thought on Civilization and ecology, and economic theory such as the environmental Kuznets curve. The authors' central move is to read productive forces, following Marx, as a metabolic relation between humans and nature. On this basis they say new quality productive forces overcome the opposition between economy and environment. They reason that protecting the environment is protecting productive forces. They recommend three modes of thought: materialist dialectics, green development and ecosystem thinking. Ecosystem thinking is to be applied through innovative allocation of elements for protection, technological breakthroughs for pollution control, and deep industrial upgrading for restoration. The orientation is then set out under three headings. The first is respecting natural law, including the "mountains, waters, forests, farmlands, lakes, grasslands, deserts and ice" as a community of life and global ecological governance. The second is coordinating green technology innovation, upgrading the three productive elements, and fostering strategic emerging and future industries. The third is meeting people's ecological and living needs through platform, low-carbon circular and smart-industry economies. The authors conclude that high-quality development is the primary task of building a modern socialist country and that developing new quality productive forces means developing green productive forces. They present the concept as a "balance beam" between ecological construction and economic growth. In their view, grasping its ecological implications helps connect Xi Jinping's economic thought with his thought on ecological civilization and advances Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated scholars tie new quality productive forces to Marxist ecological ideas and to ecological civilization policy.

The centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee is the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well 党中央集中统一领导是做好经济工作的根本保证 Zhu Ying Gong Yun Taking its cue from the Central Economic Work Conference of 11–12 December 2024, this commentary examines Xi Jinping's statement that the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee is the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well. Zhu Ying and Gong Yun argue that this is the first of the thirteen basic components of Xi Jinping's economic thought and has a guiding role within it. Their thesis is that Party leadership over economic work is both a historical lesson and a theoretical necessity. The article has two analytical parts and a practical one. The first sets out why centralised leadership matters, through a survey of the Party's record from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, and through the claims that it keeps the economy on a socialist course and is the main defence against major risks. The second explains the theoretical meaning of the principle by drawing on historical materialism, Lenin and the Communist Manifesto. The third lists concrete paths for implementation. The authors' central move is to derive Party leadership from the dialectic of economic base and superstructure. Citing Lenin, they hold that classes are led by parties and can act with a unified will only under their own party. The Communist Party, as a proletarian vanguard representing the great majority, must therefore lead the economy to serve its economic base. They add that public ownership as the mainstay and common prosperity define the socialist market economy, and that only Party leadership keeps it on course. They present the external setting as a world undergoing great changes unseen in a century, with domestic demand weak and protectionism, unilateralism and de-globalisation rising. For practice, the authors call for three things. Party members must uphold the Central Committee's authority through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Cadres must raise their capacity by studying Marxist political economy and Xi Jinping's economic thought, by investigating conditions, by punishing corruption and formalism, and by making decisions scientific and law-based. Institutions must also be improved, including the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, the annual economic work conference, local implementation of central policy, and the Third Plenum's reforms. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale linking Party leadership to economic governance in the Xi era.

New quality productive forces: a major innovation and development of the Marxist theory of productive forces 新质生产力：马克思主义生产力理论的重大创新与发展 Lu Guoqi Chen Xinjian Lu Guoqi and Chen Xinjian ask how the concept of new quality productive forces, first put forward by Xi Jinping during an inspection tour of Heilongjiang in September 2023, relates to the Marxist theory of productive forces. They argue that it is a scientific, complete and systematic theoretical system and a major innovation and development of that theory, offering guidance for high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The authors define it as a leap in labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimal combination, marked by high technology, high efficiency and high quality. The article was published in Theoretical Exploration (2024, no. 6). After a short introduction it is organised into six sections. Each pairs one element of the Xi-era formulation with a strand of Marxist theory that it is said to develop: quality–quantity unity, the composition of productive forces, productive-force progress, the ecological theory of productive forces, the dialectic of productive forces and relations of production, and the methodology of productive-force development. Each section opens with Marx and Engels, drawing mainly on Capital, and then turns to Xi's remarks and the policies they imply. The central move is to show continuity and innovation together. Marx held that new productive forces cannot rest on quantitative expansion alone, and the authors read “high quality” (zhiyou) as the contemporary form of this quality–quantity unity. Marx treated science as a “spiritual productive force” that shortens labour time, and in the authors' reading this becomes technological innovation as the core driver, with digital means of labour and data as a new object of labour. Marx's critique of the “productive force of capital” becomes the claim that new quality productive forces are by nature green productive forces, uniting social and natural productive forces. On the relations of production, the authors draw on the unity and struggle of opposites to call for new relations of production through deepened reform, including market-based reform of factor allocation, a new whole-nation system and closer coordination of education, talent and technology. Their methodological formula is to establish the new before breaking the old, adapt to local conditions, and give classified guidance. The authors conclude that new quality productive forces extend Marxism in the Chinese context and the needs of the times, and they attach concrete proposals to each section. These include upgrading traditional industries and fostering emerging and future industries, strengthening basic research and work on core technologies, and promoting a green transition in development. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link this concept to Marx's texts and to specific industrial, technological and reform policies.

Bringing into play the leading role of state-owned enterprises in China's digital economy Based on an understanding of the characteristics of digital capital 发挥国有企业在我国数字经济发展中的引领作用 Liu Haoyan Liu asks how digital capital can be regulated and guided so that China's digital economy develops in a high-quality way. The article argues that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) must play the leading role, as the "lead goose" with private firms as the "main force". Liu bases this claim on both the nature of digital capital and China's practical experience, and presents it as integral to a Chinese-style path of digital modernization under a socialist market economy. The article opens by separating the general and the specific features of digital capital. It then builds its case in three steps: SOEs as the "ballast" of the digital economy (security, guiding capital, shared benefits); SOEs as the "lead goose" in innovation, industrial chains and international competition; and four policy recommendations. Liu draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital, Xi Jinping's remarks and Chinese data and cases, and compares these with the United States and Europe. In Liu's account, digital capital shares the general traits of capital: profit-seeking, mobility and a dual character. It also has three specific traits. It has pan-accumulation, drawing unpaid user labour and data beyond the wage relationship. It has super-expansiveness, through winner-takes-all dynamics and cross-sector spread. It is composite, combining productive, commercial and financial functions in whole ecosystems. From this Liu argues that private capital alone tends to diverge from national goals, for example by favouring platforms over basic technology, which the author links to "choke-point" problems. SOEs can resist transnational digital monopolies, take on high-risk basic research and infrastructure, narrow income and regional gaps, and anchor domestic innovation systems. They can also help to fill, strengthen and extend industrial chains, and help private firms "go global" and compete for international standards. Liu proposes four measures: using Party building to speed SOE digital transformation and key-technology breakthroughs; using capital operation to drive innovation; building a "state and private advance together" model of division of labour with private firms; and drawing on international innovation resources and talent. The author concludes that SOEs under Party leadership are a major advantage of socialist China over Western capitalist states. Liu holds that they secure the socialist character of the digital economy. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist political-economy case for state-owned enterprises in the digital sector, with specific examples such as TD-SCDMA and China Mobile's orders to Huawei.

On the ontological character of Marx's method of critique of political economy: the category of labour as an example 论马克思政治经济学批判方法的存在论属性——以劳动范畴为例 Xia Ying Xia Ying asks what Marx's "method of political economy" in the 1857 Introduction to the Grundrisse actually is. The article argues that it should not be read as a general methodology or epistemology of capitalist society. In Xia's reading, the passage mostly describes the path of classical political economy and of Kant and Hegel. Marx's own critique instead performs an "ontological deduction" of economic categories, one that probes the real conditions and limits of those categories. The article has three parts. The first separates Marx's description of classical political economy's "two paths" (from the concrete whole to abstract determinations, and back up to the concrete) from Marx's own advance. It reads the "scientifically correct method" through Kant's theory of knowledge and Hegel's idealism. The second part sets out how Marx moves beyond this standpoint, using the Introduction's remarks on the thinking head, the real subject and the "dual tension" between categories and historical reality. The third part tests the approach on the category of labour, tracing it through monetarism, mercantilism, physiocracy and Adam Smith. Xia's central claim is that Marx changes the core problem. Classical economists, Kant and Hegel all aim to secure the "purity" of category deduction within thought. Marx instead posits a real subject, society or material life, that stays independent of the head and always has to be presupposed. Categories therefore take their content from the historically specific social reality and not from speculative dialectic. Xia stresses that this yields a break between history and logic, not their unity. Using the German terms Allgemein and überhaupt, Xia argues that Marx replaces Hegel's triad of universal, particular and individual with a standoff between the "general" and the "determinate". On this reading, "labour in general" is "practically true" only in developed capitalism, where labour has become indifferent to its particular kinds. Xia concludes that Marx offers no free-standing methodology; the method is "presented" in the course of a historical exposition and is not stated as a separate doctrine. The ontological, materialist character of the critique, Xia argues, lets Marx use classical categories to expose the limits of capital's logic, for example through crisis and surplus value. This also supplies the starting point for his later study of capital. Read the original if you work on the Grundrisse Introduction, on Marx's relation to Kant and Hegel, or on the philosophical status of economic categories, and want a close German-term reading of the labour category.

Marx and Engels's theory of the relations of production and its sinicization 马克思恩格斯生产关系理论及其中国化的发展 Tian Keqin Tian Keqin asks how Marx and Engels's theory of the relations of production has been carried forward in China, and what it implies for present reform. Published in 2024 after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee, the article argues that the Chinese Communist Party has applied the theory's basic standpoint and method to Chinese conditions. In Tian's account, this has been done in revolution, construction and reform, and has produced specific forms of socialist production relations suited to China's level of productive forces. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theory's content: the general law linking relations of production to productive forces, the essence and structure of production relations, and their forms. The second traces the Chinese development in three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third draws lessons for today, centred on new quality productive forces, new production relations suited to them, and further comprehensively deepening reform. On the classical theory, Tian stresses that productive forces generally play the determining role, while relations of production can react back on them. Tian holds that a one-way reading, either "productive forces only" or "production relations only", distorts historical materialism. On the Chinese side, Tian describes a sequence: new-democratic relations of production and the socialist transformation; Mao Zedong's exploration of the contradictions of socialist society and of commodity production; and the shift under reform from single public ownership to a basic economic system. That system combines public ownership as the mainstay with several ownership forms, distribution according to work alongside other methods, and a socialist market economy. For the new era, Tian cites the stress on letting the market play the decisive role in allocating resources while the government plays its role better, and the dual-circulation development pattern. Tian concludes that continuing to adapt the theory to Chinese conditions is both a requirement of Marxism's development and the route to liberating productive forces. The author calls for new production relations that fit new quality productive forces, and for deeper reform guided by the "six adherences" of the Third Plenum, including Party leadership and a people-centred approach. Tian presents the socialist system's advantage as its ability to adjust production relations to advanced productive forces. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars link the classical theory of production relations to the policy line of the 2024 Third Plenum.

Cultivating and expanding patient capital to advance new quality productive forces 培育和壮大耐心资本 推动新质生产力发展 Hong Yinxing Jiang Jichuang Hong Yinxing and Jiang Jichuang ask how China can grow "patient capital", a term that entered official documents in 2024, so that it supports new quality productive forces. They argue that technological breakthroughs of the kind these forces need involve heavy investment, long cycles and high risk. In their view short-term capital cannot meet these conditions, and patient capital is therefore an important support and driver of the new forces. The article opens with the April 2024 Politburo meeting and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for developing patient capital. It then reviews the sparse literature, which it describes as mostly theoretical or empirical studies of listed firms, and says this literature has not examined the concept's content or mechanisms. The authors define patient capital, explain how it promotes new quality productive forces, examine three forms (technology credit, venture capital and the stock market), and end with five policy recommendations. The authors define patient capital as strategic, socially responsible, proactive, rational and scarce risk capital that takes part in the management of the firms it funds. Not all long-term capital qualifies, since they require strategic vision and active involvement. They propose a broad scope covering bank credit, venture capital, primary-market equity, bonds, industrial funds and government guidance funds, but limited to the real economy rather than virtual economy. Citing Marx on the costly equipment needed to exploit science, they argue that innovation needs both funding and risk-sharing, and cite the steam engine, canals and railways, and Silicon Valley as historical examples. On technology credit, they note that such loans were 1.01% (small and medium technology firms) and 5.63% (high-tech firms) of total loans at the end of 2023. They propose larger supply, lower rates, longer terms and stricter screening against loans diverted to property. For venture capital and stocks, they stress longer fund lives and tighter entry and delisting rules. The policy proposals are to develop venture capital and the stock market together; to build multi-level capital markets; and to make state capital the main "ballast" of patient capital through reformed evaluation, incentives and fault-tolerance. They also propose bringing in international patient capital, which they say invests earlier, and building a supporting system of legislation, coordinated fiscal and monetary policy, and differentiated conduct regulation. Capital that stays long in loss-making state enterprises is, they say, not patient capital but "helpless" or "problem" capital that must be restructured. Read the original if you want a Chinese economists' policy framework linking finance, state capital and new quality productive forces, with figures on technology lending and venture investment stages.

The fundamental guidance for further deepening reform comprehensively 进一步全面深化改革的根本遵循 Li Zhiyong Zhang Wanying This article, published in Qiushi's sister Party journal Qianxian (Frontline) in early 2025, asks what should guide the next stage of reform in China. Li and Zhang argue that the new ideas, viewpoints and judgements on comprehensively deepening reform put forward since the 18th Party Congress (2012) by the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core answer why and how reform must be deepened in the new era. In their account, these ideas supply the fundamental guidance for further comprehensively deepening reform. The article has three parts. The first sets out the practical basis: reform has entered a stage of tackling hard problems, and the authors trace the sequence of plenums from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The second presents the theoretical guidance, centred on the "six adherences" set out in 2024. The third turns to implementation through "three greater emphases". For the authors, the practical record shows reform moving from local experiments to systematic integration.
