They cite 72 meetings of the central reform commission or leading group over 11 years, more than 600 reform documents and over 3,000 reform plans. The "six adherences" are the Party's overall leadership, a people-centred approach, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, institution-building as the main thread, law-based governance in every field, and a systems approach. The authors present these as a summary of experience since reform and opening up and as a guide to the rule-governed nature of reform. On method, they call for greater emphasis on systematic integration, on key priorities (with economic reform as the lead) and on practical results, pursued with a "nail-driving spirit". Li and Zhang conclude that further deepening reform requires studying and applying Xi's ideas on the subject, mastering these methods and building broad consensus. They state that the aim is to mobilise every positive factor for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is an authoritative-style exposition of current Party doctrine rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a compact, official-register account of how Chinese Party theorists link the 2024 reform decision to Xi Jinping's earlier statements on reform principles and method.

The impact of artificial intelligence on the economy and society 人工智能对经济社会的影响 Zhu Xufeng Zhu Xufeng asks how artificial intelligence (AI), as a fusion of modern information technology with the socio-economic system, is changing production, daily life and governance, and what risks come with it. The article argues that AI empowers industries and restructures the economy, but also deepens social differentiation and creates ethical and governance problems. These, Zhu holds, call for agile governance and international cooperation. Published in Qiushi's sister journal Qianxian in early 2025, it frames the topic as important for building a strong science and technology nation, for new quality productive forces and high-quality development, and for Chinese modernization. The article has four parts. It first outlines AI technology and industry: three levels of intelligence (perceptual, cognitive, creative), three layers of the industrial chain (foundation, technology, application), and China's position, including the world's largest industrial robot market. It then examines how AI empowers sectors and adjusts industrial structure, then how it reshapes social structure, and finally the ethical and governance challenges and responses. Zhu cites figures such as a projected 7 per cent boost to global GDP over ten years from generative AI and International Federation of Robotics data on robot stock. Zhu argues that AI is upgrading industry, services, smart cities, energy and information technology, while redistributing value between capital and labour. The article lists four distributional changes: polarisation of returns to capital and labour, a wider income gap between high-skilled and ordinary workers, polarisation of profits between large intelligent firms and ordinary firms, and a deeper intelligence divide between core and peripheral countries, producing a technology-driven globalisation. In society, routine jobs are automated and demand for high-skilled workers rises, unequal educational resources entrench inequality, and personalised information feeds create filter bubbles that polarise politics. On governance, Zhu points to algorithmic bias, privacy and data security, and lagging, fragmented global rules. Zhu notes responses such as the EU's 2018 ethics guidelines, UNESCO's 2019 recommendation and China's 2019 governance principles for responsible AI. The article calls for data-protection laws, stronger state supervision, agile governance with rapid response and continuous adjustment, and international standard-setting, and it urges individuals to keep learning new skills. Zhu concludes that coordinated development of technology and governance could bring a more intelligent, efficient, fair and inclusive era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of how a Chinese scholar links AI's economic effects, social stratification and governance questions.

Implementing reform with a nail-driving spirit 以钉钉子精神抓好改革落实 Wu Gangping Written in the wake of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024, this commentary asks how the Party's plan for further deepening reform can be turned into results. Wu answers that the "nail-driving spirit" (钉钉子精神), a style of work stressing hard-nosed, persistent implementation, must guide every stage of carrying out reform. The piece first appeared in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), 2024, no. 24. The article has three parts. The first explains why the spirit is needed: it is presented as a fine Party tradition, a key to the achievements of the new era, and a practical necessity for the current round of reform. The second sets out its core meaning under three headings: a correct view of political achievements, a correct methodology, and the handling of several major relationships. The third turns to practice and names three requirements: serving the people wholeheartedly, being truth-seeking and pragmatic, and having the courage to take responsibility. Wu leans heavily on Xi Jinping's image of hammering a nail: one or two blows leave it loose, and only seven or eight make it firm. On this basis Wu argues that implementation matters as much as design, citing the saying "one part planning, nine parts implementation". The Plenum set more than 300 major reform measures, to be completed by 2029, and the article treats this tight schedule as grounds for stronger follow-through. Wu calls for a correct view of political achievements, in which benefiting the people counts for most, and for guarding against formalism and vanity projects. Wu also calls for responsibility chains with accountability, field investigation, and balance between reform and the rule of law, breaking down and building up, reform and opening up, and deployment and implementation. Wu concludes that cadres, above all leading ones as the "key minority", must carry reform through step by step, test it by tangible results and public satisfaction, and reject "lying-flat" attitudes. Wu presents this as essential to advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party-aligned writers frame cadre responsibility and implementation after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee.

Coordinating aggregate supply and aggregate demand to further unblock the circulation of the national economy 统筹好总供给和总需求关系 进一步畅通国民经济循环 Xie Di Xie Di's commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts, takes up the instruction of the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024 to "coordinate the relationship between aggregate supply and aggregate demand and keep the national economy's circulation unobstructed". Xie presents this as Xi Jinping's summary of the laws of China's economic development in the new era. The article argues that planning supply and demand together is more than top-level design for one year's economic work: it also marks a refinement of the concept of macroeconomic governance, and matters for high-quality development. The piece has four numbered sections. The first sets out the theory of aggregate supply and demand, covering aggregate and structural balance, the dialectic of supply and demand, and Xi's theories since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second deals with short-term and long-term macroeconomic regulation. The third discusses expanding domestic demand and unblocking the economic cycle, with consumption and investment data for 2023 and 2024. The fourth sets out the demand-side and supply-side policy tools, tying them to the 2024 Conference's measures. Xie argues that under the socialist market economy the contradiction between private and social labour persists, so balance between aggregate supply and demand is occasional and temporary, while imbalance is normal. Citing Xi, Xie holds that China has cyclical and aggregate problems but that structural problems are the most prominent, so supply-side structural reform remains the main line. Xie also insists there is no way to "bypass the short term and go straight to the long term". Supply-side reform and the strategy of expanding domestic demand are therefore complementary, not substitutes, and should reach a higher-level dynamic equilibrium in which demand pulls supply and supply creates demand. Xie classes fiscal and monetary measures as demand-quantity management, income distribution as demand-structure management, and supply-side structural reform as supply-structure management. Xie cites figures to show that room for expanding consumption and investment remains large. They include retail sales of consumer goods of over 47 trillion yuan in 2023, and a 16.1 per cent rise in equipment purchase investment in the first ten months of 2024. Xie concludes that a more proactive fiscal policy, moderately loose monetary policy, consumption-boosting measures and the supply-quality tasks set by the Conference together serve stable growth, employment and prices, and income growth in step with the economy. Read the original if you want an official-line economist's account of how Chinese policy framing links Marxist supply-demand balance with the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference agenda.

Digital technology as a booster of common prosperity in spiritual life 数字技术助推精神生活共同富裕 Tang Renwu Shi Xiaowen This short commentary from Beijing Daily asks how digital technology can help realise common prosperity in spiritual life, which the authors treat as an integral part of Chinese modernization. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that common prosperity means abundance in both material and spiritual life, Tang and Shi argue that generative AI and related technologies are accelerating this goal. They also acknowledge that the same technologies carry risks that could widen spiritual inequality. The article has three parts. The first sets out why digital technology has an inherent capacity to enrich spiritual life. The second traces the Chinese Communist Party's commitment to spiritual abundance from the revolutionary base areas through the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third lists challenges and offers five policy recommendations. On the first point, the authors take the practical logic of spiritual common prosperity to be "spiritual need, spiritual production, spiritual enjoyment", drawing on Marxist views of spiritual life and on Maslow's hierarchy of needs. They contend that digital technology is efficient, interconnected and decentralised, breaks down household-registration, regional and work-unit boundaries, and gives different groups more equal access to knowledge. Immersive technologies, in their account, extend the human body and mind ("the extension of humans" and "extended humans") and bring new spiritual satisfaction. They also name risks: imbalance between supply and demand of spiritual products, widening divisions, information overload, algorithmic bias and privacy leaks. The authors propose that governments should: expand digital infrastructure and digital literacy training in less developed areas; set legal and ethical rules for algorithms, privacy and automated decisions; build occupational safety nets and retraining for workers displaced by automation; regulate recommendation algorithms to curb information overload and homogenised content; and strengthen safeguards in critical sectors such as health, finance and transport. They present this as a way to raise people's sense of fulfilment, happiness and security and support free and all-round human development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link AI and digital technology to the discourse of common prosperity and spiritual life, and a list of their policy suggestions.

Turning the long-term positive fundamentals into high-quality development outcomes 将长期向好基本面化为高质量发展成果 Hu Zhihao Hu Zhihao's newspaper commentary asks how China can convert the economy's long-term positive fundamentals into concrete high-quality development, given entrenched problems and short-term shocks. Hu argues that the underlying conditions have not changed, and that policymakers should set priorities, treat symptoms and causes together, and guide expectations sensibly. The piece is organised under three headings: attention to nominal growth, effective use of policy tools, and reviving consumption as the lead driver. It draws on the 14th Five-Year Plan and the 2035 goals, official policy language on fiscal and monetary stance, and data on consumption shares and household wealth. Hu contends that sustained nominal growth, meaning real growth plus mild inflation, steadies expectations and supports the renminbi exchange rate. Cost-push or runaway inflation would not be sustainable, so demand stimulus must go with high-quality supply and new quality productive forces. Hu says loose monetary policy alone cannot lift weak aggregate demand, so fiscal spending must create demand directly, with the financial sector helping through bond issuance and central bank purchases of government bonds. On consumption, Hu notes that household consumption is close to 40% of GDP, well below the US, Japan and South Korea. Hu calls for stable income expectations, better income distribution, a fuller social security net, steadier asset prices (given household wealth of 482 trillion yuan net) and a larger household share of national income. Read the original if you want a brief, official-leaning economist's reading of China's 2025 macroeconomic policy mix and its consumption rationale.

Building China's international image in the new era 建构新时代中国国际形象 Wang Zhen This short newspaper commentary asks how China's international image should be measured and built, and who should hold the authority to define it. Wang Zhen starts from the global attention drawn by DeepSeek and the film Ne Zha 2, and from the Global Times' report on China's international image, a survey of 51,000 people in 46 countries. The author argues that the survey marks a shift from an image shaped by others to one shaped by China itself, and that China must build its own discursive power. The piece has three parts. The first reads the survey results and the significance of the report. The second sets out three academic approaches to assessing a national image and questions the claimed neutrality of Western polling bodies. The third makes proposals for building China's own discourse power, under two headings: strengthening self-awareness and confidence, and strengthening design and guidance. Wang reads the survey as showing that 77 per cent of respondents see China's economy as strong, that over 90 per cent expect growth over the next decade, and that 69 per cent want China to take a larger part in international affairs. The author says this refutes Western claims of a Chinese economic collapse or a peak in China's rise. Wang also stresses that developing-country respondents, including those in the Global South, were given particular weight and were more favourable. The three approaches to assessment are communication studies (opinion polling), marketing (national brand indices) and international politics (soft power). Wang argues that Western pollsters present themselves as scientific but can shape results through agenda-setting, assumed positions and sampling. As evidence the author cites funding of US think tanks and media organisations by government bodies, including the US Agency for International Development. Wang concludes that questions about China's image cannot be settled by a few Western institutions or politicians, nor by Western standards alone. The author calls for resisting what the piece describes as Western slander in international opinion contests, and for original theoretical frameworks acceptable abroad. Wang also urges adherence to the Four-sphere Confidence, support for Chinese media to "go global", and narratives that overseas audiences can understand and respond to. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar frames image-building as a contest over discursive power and cites the Global Times survey in support of that view.

Holding great assemblies in the Yan'an period 延安时期开大会 Yang Zhangwen Zhang Yongqian This short commentary, published in Jiefang Daily, looks at the large assemblies held in the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region during the Yan'an period. The authors argue that these meetings, each focused on a distinct theme, fixed work priorities, allowed policy to be made soundly, mobilised people and resources, unified thinking and advanced the revolution. The article covers three kinds of gathering: the border region's councils and its production-mobilisation meetings; the 1944 culture and education conference; and the 1942 Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art. It ends with a short statement of what these assemblies offer later revolution and construction. On the councils, the authors describe the three-tier system of border region, county and township and the powers set out in the 1939 organisational regulations. They note that the 1941 revision added powers, such as removing senior officials, and enlarged the county council's powers from eight items to eleven. They present production mobilisation as Mao Zedong's answer to fiscal strain after 1939: 'starve, disband, or do it ourselves?' On culture and education, they summarise the 1944 resolution on wall newspapers, literacy for ancillary staff and mass entertainment. For the Yan'an Forum, they set out Mao's three points: literature and art are part of the revolutionary cause, writers must take the standpoint of the people, and popularisation guides the direction of art. The authors conclude that the assemblies yield lessons for later practice. These include uniting Party leadership with a people-centred approach, consulting the people, protecting democratic rights through institutions and law, and embedding consultative democracy in elections, decision-making, management and oversight. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed overview of Yan'an-era councils, conferences and the Yan'an Forum and how they are used in current Party history writing.

The historical contribution of the Fourth Party Congress of the CPC to Party organisational building 中共四大对党的组织建设的历史贡献 Li Chuanbing Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, Li Chuanbing asks what the Fourth National Congress of the Communist Party of China, held in Shanghai on 11–22 January 1925, contributed to the Party's organisational building. Li's answer is that the congress, besides raising the questions of proletarian leadership in the democratic revolution and the worker-peasant alliance, revised the Party constitution and adopted a resolution on organisational questions. In Li's account, these steps made organisational work more institutionalised and standardised and supported the continuing advance of the Great Revolution (1924–27). The article first sets the background: after the First United Front of 1924, Party membership rose from 420 at the Third Congress to 994 at the Fourth, yet Li says the size and the organisational and leadership standards of Party bodies lagged behind the rising revolution. It then examines the Resolution on the Organisational Question and the Second Revised Party Constitution under three headings: improving the organisational system, improving the leadership system and upholding central authority, and refining organisational procedures. On the organisational system, Li highlights the establishment of the branch (zhibu) as the basic unit, formed wherever three or more members were present, with set meeting schedules and duties beyond recruitment, such as running clubs, labour schools and mutual-aid societies. Committees and Party fractions in the Kuomintang and other bodies, including Whampoa Military Academy, extended Party influence. On leadership, the congress elected a new Central Executive Committee with Chen Duxiu as general secretary, created a Central Organisation Department and cut the structure from five levels to four. Li also reads its call for "democratic centralism" as an early form of democratic centralism. On procedures, admission was simplified from three approval stages to two, withdrawal decisions were moved to the local committee, probationary members gained the right to attend branch meetings, and rules for transferring organisational affiliation were added. Li concludes that the congress holds an important place in Party-building history. He cites the Central Committee's contemporary judgment that recognising the importance of organisation was one of its major advances, and Cai Hesen's view that organisational work began to take the right path afterwards. Li notes that membership reached 3,470 ten months later and 57,967 by the Fifth Congress in April 1927. Read the original if you want a concise, document-based account of how the 1925 congress shaped Party branches, admission rules and central leadership structures, as presented in official Party historiography.

Explaining principles, infusing love, putting into practice: continuously strengthening the guiding power of ideological and political work in universities 讲理、融爱、力行，不断提升高校思政引领力 Liu Jiamei This short commentary starts from Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2024 National Education Conference. Xi listed six capacities of a leading education country, and Liu notes that the guiding power of ideological and political work comes first. Liu argues that universities can raise this guiding power along three paths: explaining principles (讲理), infusing love (融爱) and putting ideas into practice (力行). The article is organised under three short headings, each unpacked into three sub-points. "Principles" covers Marxist fundamentals, the theory behind Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and everyday guidance on how to live, study and act. "Love" covers care, passion and a larger patriotic love. "Practice" covers hands-on activity, learning that follows industry trends, and volunteering. On principles, Liu calls for teaching why Marxism is scientific and suits China, and for guiding students to read original works and to "truly study, understand, believe and apply" it. Teaching must also reach students through the internet and forms they like. On love, Liu says educators should first understand students' needs, for example through "one-stop" community centres combining tutoring, counselling and talks. They should also awaken intrinsic motivation and nurture patriotic feeling through immersive experiences, alumni visits and red culture on campus. On practice, Liu proposes a broad ideological and political education system in which classes extend into society, internships, research placements and volunteering. Liu concludes that students should unite knowledge and action, so that what they learn is applied, their capacity to innovate grows and their ideals come alive. The piece is a practical outline for university ideological and political educators. Read the original if you want a concise example of how current Party language on education is turned into suggestions for campus ideological and political work.

Accelerating an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese philosophy and social sciences as a strategic force for building a leading education nation 加快构建中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系 打造教育强国战略引领力量 Chen Yulu Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, Chen Yulu takes up the newly issued Outline of the Plan for Building a Leading Education Nation (2024–2035). The Outline names the construction of an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese philosophy and social sciences as a strategic force for strengthening higher education. Chen argues that universities should take the lead in this task, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. This short commentary has three parts. It first sets out why an autonomous knowledge system matters, then explains the advantages universities hold, and finally proposes five routes for building the system. Chen contends that new phenomena arising on the path of Chinese modernization require systematic explanation from the social sciences. The article also links the project to international discourse power, cultural confidence and the training of talent. Universities are said to have three advantages: strength in basic research, a broad and interdisciplinary range of disciplines, and their role as a window for exchange with the outside world. The five routes are to strengthen moral education and the cultivation of talent, autonomous training of personnel through "new liberal arts" and AI-enabled programmes, theoretical innovation rooted in Chinese practice, policy advice through university think tanks, and strategic communication abroad. Chen concludes that Chinese philosophy and social sciences should move from solving Chinese problems to contributing to global ones, offering "Chinese wisdom" and "Chinese solutions" within global education governance. Read the original if you want a university president's official-line account of how higher education is expected to carry out the Party's agenda for philosophy and social sciences.

Coordinating the advance of new urbanization and comprehensive rural revitalization 统筹推进新型城镇化和乡村全面振兴 Gao Fan This newspaper commentary from Guangming Daily asks what it means in practice to "coordinate the advance" of new urbanization and comprehensive rural revitalization. Gao Fan argues that urban-rural integration is an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization, and that the pace of change in urban-rural structure determines how far modernization as a whole advances. The article takes its cue from the Central Economic Work Conference of 2024 and the No. 1 Central Document of 2025. Gao sets out six dimensions of coordination: industrial layout, factor allocation, spatial planning, the provision of public goods, the way development is evaluated, and the reform of institutions and mechanisms. Each is presented as a separate task, with specific policy measures attached. On industry, Gao argues that the old split, with farming in the countryside and manufacturing and services in cities, must give way to joint planning. Agriculture should draw in urban factors and technology, and rural resources should become new industries and markets. On factors, land, labour and capital should move in both directions through market-oriented reform, including the "three rights separation" of rural land, and through digital tools. On space, Gao calls for a shift from a sharp urban-rural divide to a blended pattern, with county seats and central towns as the "continuum" linking city and village. For public goods, Gao urges more fiscal support for rural education, healthcare and old-age care, and faster citizenship for migrants from the countryside. Evaluation should give more weight to rural and integration indicators in local government appraisal, and the article ties this to protecting farmland and grain farmers. Gao concludes that single reforms have limited effect and that household registration, land and social security reforms must work together. Read the original if you want a concise outline of the policy agenda behind urban-rural integration as presented by an economist writing in the Party press.

Leading with innovation to promote high-quality development of the private economy 以创新为引领促进民营经济高质量发展 Zhang Jin This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the symposium on private enterprises for private firms to pursue high-quality development, focus on their main business and strengthen independent innovation. Zhang Jin argues that the private economy has been an important innovative force since reform and opening up. The author holds that improved policy, market and talent conditions, together with further policy implementation, will let it contribute more to new quality productive forces. The piece has three parts. The first reviews private enterprises' achievements in innovation. The second sets out the favourable conditions for their innovative development. The third lists the policy measures that Zhang says should be carried out. On achievements, Zhang cites private firms becoming China's largest foreign-trade players from 2019, with exports of electric vehicles, 3D printers and industrial robots rising 13.1%, 32.8% and 45.2% year on year. The author also says these firms are moving China from innovation "follower" to "leader" and are a key force in artificial intelligence, big data, new energy and biomedicine. As favourable conditions, Zhang names policy support since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the 2023 Central Committee and State Council opinion on private-economy growth. Further conditions are a domestic market with over 400 million middle-income people, a talent pool in which the "demographic dividend" is turning into a "talent dividend", and entrepreneurial spirit. Zhang calls for removing barriers to market access and factor use, and for supporting private firms in taking on major national science and technology projects. The author also urges easing financing difficulties through market-based risk-sharing and credit systems, and strengthening the application of results and intellectual property protection. Zhang presents these steps as helping private enterprises contribute to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise official-line statement of how Party-aligned economists frame private-sector innovation policy in early 2025.

Combining the boosting of consumption with higher investment returns 实现提振消费与提高投资效益的有效结合 Huang Kainan Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, Huang Kainan takes up the first task set by the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: vigorously boosting consumption, improving investment returns and expanding domestic demand across the board. Huang argues that insufficient domestic demand is the main current difficulty of the economy, and that consumption and investment should be pursued together. Doing so would, in this account, create a virtuous circle and a high-level dynamic balance between supply and demand. The short commentary begins with a technical clarification of how consumption and investment are credited with contributing to GDP. It then has two main sections: how consumption depends on investment returns, and how investment returns should be guided by consumption. It closes on the roles of market and government. Huang notes that the expenditure method, behind the 'three engines' of growth, overstates the contribution of consumption and investment and understates that of exports. Imported goods are deducted only under net exports, and exports now carry more domestic value added, with general trade above 64%. Hence Huang calls for both stronger exports and greater efforts on domestic demand. Boosting consumption, whether by raising income or by borrowing, needs investment returns as its support; in Huang's phrase, consumption is past investment and investment is future consumption. Raising wage income means raising the 'cooperative surplus' of labour and capital and the labour share in primary distribution. In turn, investment should avoid blind, duplicated and low-efficiency projects, which Huang links to curbing 'involutionary' competition. It should target infrastructure, upgrading consumption and equipment renewal, with reforms to investment evaluation and fiscal-financial coordination. Huang concludes that the market should play the decisive role in allocating resources while an 'effective government' uses fiscal and monetary policy. Fiscal, monetary, industrial and competition policies should work together to expand demand and improve the supply structure. Read the original if you want a concise official-economist account of the 2025 domestic demand agenda and its reasoning on the consumption–investment link.

The idea of "harmony and union" (hehe) in the Book of Changes as part of China's fine traditional culture 中华优秀传统文化中的《周易》“和合”思想 Shi Shaobo Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (26 February 2025), Shi Shaobo argues that the Zhouyi (Book of Changes), first of the Confucian Five Classics, takes "harmony and union" (hehe) as its core value. Shi holds that the idea, especially in the themes of heaven–earth union and water–fire complementarity, has shaped Chinese thought for millennia and deserves deeper study. The short commentary opens with the terminology of the Yijing and Yizhuan, then traces the characters he and he and the compound hehe through early texts such as the Guoyu, Mozi and Shiji. It then follows the Zhouyi's treatment of harmony at four levels: humans and nature, between people (extended to society and states), and within the self. Shi reads the hexagram structure as a model of hehe: the 64 hexagrams contain 192 yang and 192 yin lines, whose mutual opposition and interdependence drive constant change. On this basis the author finds in the text a call to cherish nature while using human initiative in accord with natural law. Harmony between people rests on benevolence, righteousness and good faith, as in the Tongren and Zhongfu hexagrams, and personal harmony on yin–yang balance, moral cultivation, prudent speech and the mean. Change, Shi stresses, leads to flourishing only when it is orderly and upright. Shi concludes that if every person and country develops uprightly, the Zhouyi's ideal of \"preserving supreme harmony\" and peace for all states can be reached. The piece presents the text as a resource for harmony with nature, society and oneself. Read the original if you want a brief introduction to how a contemporary Chinese scholar presents the Book of Changes' hehe idea as a traditional cultural value.

The spread and transformation of the concept of "nihilism" in China “虚无主义”概念的传播与衍变 Zhang Shunyue This short piece, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 26 February 2025, asks how the concept of "nihilism" (xuwu zhuyi) entered Chinese and why its meaning has been so unclear. Zhang argues that the term's introduction and evolution were highly complex: in the early twentieth century it referred at once to Western Nihilism, to anarchism, and to the Daoist ideas of "emptiness and non-action". The article proceeds chronologically and by sources. It begins with the classical meaning of xuwu in Daoist texts, then traces the transliteration of Nihilist in late nineteenth-century Chinese newspapers and diplomats' diaries. It next follows the Japanese route through which "nihilist party" became the standard rendering, examines early English–Chinese dictionaries of 1908, 1913 and 1916, and ends with attempts by Liao Zhongkai and Zhou Zuoren to clarify the concept. Zhang's central argument is that Chinese usage became confused as the term passed through Japan. In the 1880s Japanese translators rendered Nihilist as "nihilist party", and after 1903 Liang Qichao's essay and translations of Kayama Sentarō's work on modern anarchism, often retitled with "nihilist party", made nihilism, populism and anarchism "share one hat". The dictionaries reflect this: the 1916 dictionary Guanhua gave separate philosophical and political senses, the latter equated with anarchism. Zhang reports that Zhou Zuoren in 1907 tried to separate nihilism as a philosophical doctrine from terrorism, but that such efforts had little effect, and that Liao Zhongkai himself used the terms inconsistently. Zhang concludes that in early twentieth-century Chinese, many intellectuals used such "new terms" in polemics without systematic understanding, leaving the meaning of "nihilism" ambiguous. The piece offers a conceptual history rather than a contemporary political argument. Read the original if you are interested in the translation history of Nihilism in China and the early dictionary and periodical sources behind it.

The CPC's practice of reforming rural bad customs in the Yan'an period 延安时期中国共产党治理乡村陋习的实践 Zhao Junpeng Chen Xu Zhao and Chen ask how the Communist Party, during the Yan'an period, could reform customs that villagers had followed for generations without damaging popular enthusiasm or weakening the revolution. Their answer is that the Party adjusted its reform policies and used traditional art forms creatively. In their account, this removed popular resistance, rebuilt rural order, strengthened the revolutionary base and advanced cultural change in the countryside. This short newspaper piece first sets out why the authors regard "bad customs" as obstacles, then draws out the lessons of reform. It draws on examples from the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region: spirit-medium superstition, opium use and the oppression of women. The authors argue that these customs held back revolutionary consciousness, limited the growth of revolutionary forces and harmed the government's image, citing corrupt anti-opium officials. Early coercive measures, such as the 1939 ban on foot-binding and prison sentences for spirit mediums, are said to have provoked resistance and rumours. The Party then adapted. It tolerated old customs to some degree, shifted its approach to religion towards education, and tied reform to production by giving mediums, idlers and opium users land, tools and grain. It also recast folk forms such as yangge, drama and "Western pictures" as vehicles for science, hygiene and free marriage, following Mao Zedong's call to transform old forms. Zhao and Chen conclude that this reform loosened the hold of inherited habits and renewed the social foundations of the countryside, changing rural attitudes and creating a new rural order. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Chinese official-academic framing of Yan'an-era social policy, with examples from the Border Region.

Valuable experience of deepening institutional reform of Party building in the new era 新时代深化党的建设制度改革的宝贵经验 Liu Qiang This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what lessons can be drawn from the institutional reform of Party building since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu Qiang argues that the reform, first proposed at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and given a prominent place at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), has produced a body of experience that matters for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and for Chinese modernization. The article sets out five principles in turn, each presented as a requirement of the reform, and closes with a brief summary. It draws examples from Party regulations, cadre management and the Party's leadership system. Liu argues that guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the fundamental guide, and that the Party's overall leadership is the fundamental guarantee. A problem-oriented approach is the focus: Liu names cadres who act improperly or fail to act, weakened Party members' vanguard role, and weak grassroots organisations. Keeping to fundamental principles while innovating is the essential requirement, illustrated by new regulations and a revised disciplinary code. A systems approach is the methodology, as Party leadership reform is said to lead reform in other fields, supported by the 2023–2027 plan for central Party regulations. Liu concludes that these five principles together form the experience of more than ten years, reflecting shared ideological understanding within the Party and offering direction for broader and deeper reform that keeps Chinese modernization on course. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party theorists summarise the logic of Party-building institutional reform.

Forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation as the guide to high-quality development in ethnic minority areas 中华民族共同体意识引领民族地区高质量发展 Li Junjie Li Junjie, writing in the China Social Sciences Today on 26 February 2025, asks how high-quality development can be achieved in ethnic minority areas. The answer given is that development there should be guided by forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, oriented towards increasing commonalities, and driven by new quality productive forces. Li presents this as both a necessary road to building a modern socialist country and an important task of building the Chinese national community. The article has four parts. It first sets out why forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation is the main line of ethnic work. It then explains why high-quality development in ethnic areas needs new quality productive forces. Next it examines how the two innovations relate in theory and logic. Finally it proposes four paths for promoting development in ethnic areas. Li's central move is to treat the two concepts as complementary. In Li's account, new quality productive forces are the material base and basic support for forging the community consciousness, while that consciousness supplies the spiritual impetus and value orientation for those forces. Li frames this as a relationship between matter and consciousness and between economic base and superstructure. Technological, organisational, industrial and cultural innovation are said to narrow regional gaps, widen channels of exchange and strengthen identification with the Chinese nation. Li lists problems in ethnic areas, including narrow industrial structures, weak innovation capacity and uneven development, and argues that new quality productive forces can serve as a new engine for addressing them. The two are also said to share the aim of national rejuvenation and the realisation of Chinese modernization in ethnic areas. Li proposes four paths: upholding Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee; pursuing common prosperity as the goal, through rural revitalisation, infrastructure, fiscal transfers and targeted programmes; promoting exchanges, interaction and integration among ethnic groups, including mixed residential and community structures; and making Chinese modernization the central task. Li calls for linking improvements in people's livelihoods with building cohesion. Read the original if you want an official-line statement of how ethnic policy and economic development goals are being tied together, including the list of specific policy programmes.

Leveraging the advantages of a super-large market to strengthen industrial and supply chain resilience 发挥超大规模市场优势 提升产业链供应链韧性 Yang Ligao Li Yushuang Yang and Li take up how China can use the scale of its domestic market to make its industrial and supply chains more resilient. They note that, despite growing competitiveness, China still faces anti-globalisation sentiment, geopolitical conflict and technology blockades, and that dependence on others for key technologies has not fundamentally changed. Their answer is that the super-large market is a structural advantage that can be turned into resilience through targeted policy. The short commentary first sets out three channels through which market scale supports resilience, then offers three sets of policy measures. It opens with a statement by Xi Jinping on China's complete industrial system and its large domestic demand, and it closes with a note that the work is part of a National Social Science Fund project. On the mechanisms, the authors argue that scale raises the expected returns of innovation, widens application scenarios and spreads R&D costs, which helps fill gaps in chains. Scale economies lower costs and encourage industrial clusters, which strengthens chains. A large market can also sustain a full industrial system; the authors say China is the only country with every industrial category in the UN classification, which they describe as an internal stabiliser in emergencies. To exploit these effects they call for expanding domestic demand through income distribution reform, a larger middle-income group and better investment quality. They also urge a modern circulation system of logistics and rural delivery networks, and a unified national market with fewer regional barriers, market-based factor allocation, stronger property rights and a better business environment. The authors conclude that the super-large market already plays a prominent supporting role but needs these further measures to be fully effective. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the policy logic linking domestic market scale, innovation and supply chain security in Chinese economic discourse in early 2025.

Accelerating the construction of China's industrial chain policy system 加快构建我国产业链政策体系 Yu Rongjian Cen Jie Yu Rongjian and Cen Jie take up a gap in Chinese economic policy: policies exist for industries and for individual firms, but there is no policy category aimed specifically at the industrial chain. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (25 February 2025), they argue that building the new development pattern, securing industrial and supply chains and gaining new advantages in international competition all require a complete, forward-looking and precisely implemented industrial chain policy system. They propose building it around five aims: safeguarding security, promoting innovation, raising efficiency, expanding openness and improving governance. The commentary first sets out two background conditions, then the five focal points, then three supporting mechanisms. The background covers weaknesses in China's own chains and the measures taken by developed countries. The five focal points each receive a short list of concrete tasks. The closing section turns to institutional safeguards for the policy system itself. On the background, the authors say China's chains show bottleneck ("chokehold") technologies, weak lead firms, poor upstream–downstream links and no backups for key links, while existing policies are fragmented across departments ("nine dragons controlling the water"). They point to US measures such as Section 301, Section 337, the 2018 export control law and the Wassenaar Arrangement, and to US and Japanese reshoring subsidies from 2020. Their five-part programme includes security measures (strengthening strengths, filling gaps, firming links, building resilience and barriers), innovation policy aimed at domestic demand, self-reliance in technology and digital-intelligent upgrading, and efficiency, openness and governance measures. On governance, they call for a three-tier "chain leader system" (链长制) under national, regional and grassroots leaders, extended to cover innovation chains, and for AI-based platforms for chain management. For implementation the authors call for a national industrial chain leading group and pilot programmes in sectors such as chips and high-end equipment. They also want wider participation by firms, associations and think tanks in policy-making, performance management with dynamic adjustment, and a monitoring centre producing security, innovation, credit and governance indices. Their stated aim is an autonomous, controllable and secure industrial chain and the modernization of China's industrial chains. Read the original if you want a compact checklist of the policy measures that two Chinese business-school scholars propose for industrial chain security, innovation and governance.

Cultural prosperity as an important hallmark of Chinese modernization 文化繁荣是中国式现代化的重要标识 Luo Sihai Writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in February 2025, Luo Sihai takes up the Party's 2024 decision on further deepening reform, which names the building of a strong socialist culture and the promotion of cultural prosperity as key reform goals. Luo argues that cultural prosperity is an important hallmark of Chinese modernization. In Luo's view, achieving it requires guidance from Xi Jinping's thought on culture, and it must keep to the distinctively 'Chinese' line of modernization. The commentary is organised in four parts. The first sets out the guiding role of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The remaining three discuss practical tasks: strengthening cultural confidence, strengthening cultural innovation and expanding cultural influence. Luo draws on the Decision and on Xi Jinping's remarks throughout, and cites Marx's 1845 notion of 'mental production' from The Holy Family. Luo argues that Chinese modernization pursues material and cultural-ethical advancement together, so that without socialist cultural prosperity there can be no socialist modernization. Cultural confidence, in Luo's account, calls for embedding core socialist values in law, institutions and everyday moral norms, and for building an independent Chinese system of philosophy and social science under Party leadership. Cultural innovation rests on cultivating innovative talent and on meeting the public's varied spiritual and cultural needs, which Luo describes as lagging behind material development. Expanding influence means raising national soft power by summarising 'Chinese experience' with 'Chinese reasoning', and strengthening international discourse power through vivid storytelling and digital and intelligent communication. Luo cites TikTok travel content as an example of how overseas audiences form images of China. Luo concludes that the Chinese modernization process should fuse modernization with socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, through these combined efforts. Culture is presented as the spiritual support for national rejuvenation and for a world facing great changes. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated academics link cultural policy, ideology and international communication to the post-2024 reform agenda.

Always making the Party's innovative theory the primary task of forging souls and educating people 始终把党的创新理论武装作为铸魂育人的首要任务 Pu Duanhua This commentary by Pu Duanhua, first published in the PLA Daily on 24 February 2024, takes up a requirement in a recent notice from the Political Work Department of the Central Military Commission on the army's annual education campaign. The notice calls for always making arming people with the Party's innovative theory the primary task of "forging souls and educating people" (铸魂育人) in the armed forces. Pu argues that this requirement correctly identifies the status and function of theoretical armament and gives the military a clear direction for this foundational work. The piece has three numbered sections. The first explains why theoretical armament deserves priority, the second what role it plays in forging souls, and the third how to carry it out in practice. Pu draws on Lenin, early Party documents, Mao Zedong's principles for the Red Army and Xi Jinping's statements on talent and ideological unity. In the first section, Pu gives three grounds for the priority. It follows a regularity of proletarian parties, which need to "instil" advanced theory from outside to produce successors for a long-term cause. It continues a tradition the Party and army have kept since the first Party Congress and the Red Army's early days. It is also required to train high-quality officers for building a strong military and a world-class army by the centenary goal of 2027. The second section assigns theory three functions: political guidance, value shaping and goal orientation. Under political guidance, officers and soldiers should grasp the Two Establishes, strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence, carry out the Two Upholds and implement the chairman responsibility system of the Central Military Commission. Under value shaping, theory should counter the effects of competing social currents. Under goal orientation, it should unite the force around the centenary goal. In the third section Pu proposes three measures. The first is to study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Xi Jinping Thought on Strengthening the Military in depth and persistently, with attention to original texts. The second is to promote a Marxist style of study that links theory to practice and opposes empty talk and a split between theory and practice. The third is to make leading cadres, the "critical few", set an example as the "lead geese", studying first and more deeply. Read the original if you want a concise example of how PLA political-work writing justifies and operationalises ideological education.

The "historical consciousness" of the Chinese nation 中华民族的“历史意识” Lin Guobiao Lin Guobiao asks what historical consciousness is, what distinguishes the one found in the Chinese nation, and what practical use it has. The article, a newspaper essay in Guangming Daily (February 2025), argues that Chinese historical consciousness stresses continuity and the transmission of historical culture, and that cultivating it can strengthen several modes of thinking used in present-day governance. Lin presents understanding it as important for the continuation and renewal of Chinese civilisation. The essay has three parts. The first defines historical consciousness as people's memory, reflection and evaluation of their own development, drawing on Nietzsche, Jörn Rüsen, the Japanese scholar Kawakatsu Yoshio and the Australian historian Greg Dening. The second sets out the features of the Chinese variant, citing Xi Jinping's remark that valuing, studying and drawing on history is a fine tradition of the Chinese nation. The third lists eight kinds of thinking capacity that historical consciousness is said to improve. In Lin's account, historical consciousness always has a contemporary orientation: it interprets the past from present concerns and gives actions meaning and direction. Chinese historical consciousness is described as deep, connecting past, present and future, and practical. Lin finds three distinguishing commitments: combining "historical reason" with historical experience (including the tradition of taking the ancient kings as models); a seek-truth-from-facts view that presents history as it was; and an "organic" view that stresses the interconnection and continuity of events. These traits are then said to turn into methods of thought. Lin links the traits to strategic, historical, dialectical, systems, innovative, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. For example, the organic view is tied to systems thinking, the tradition of "learning from Yin's downfall" (yinjian) to bottom-line thinking, and the pursuit of "the way of governance" to rule-of-law thinking. Lin concludes that cultivating historical consciousness helps people judge things within the continuity of history and solve current problems. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar ties a nation-specific concept of historical consciousness to official discourse on thinking methods.

Cleaning up the online environment requires breaking the "information cocoon" 净化网络环境亟须破除“信息茧房” He Shuxuan This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 24 February 2025, takes up the "information cocoon" (xinxi canfang), the condition in which algorithms surround users with customised content. It was prompted by a joint notice from the Cyberspace Administration of China and other ministries launching a special "Qinglang" campaign against typical algorithm problems, including homogeneous content pushing. He argues that strict, law-based enforcement is needed to build a healthy, orderly and diverse information environment. The piece first defines the phenomenon and lists its harms to individuals, society and the state. It then sets out five lines of action: government supervision and legislation, platform responsibility and transparency, cooperation between regulators and research institutions, public education, and punishment of false information. He argues that cocoons narrow users' horizons, produce cognitive bias, stifle innovation, hinder communication between groups and may damage social harmony. The author also says wrongdoers exploit algorithmic recommendation for false advertising, traffic fraud and telecom scams, citing recruitment platforms that stoke job anxiety to sell expensive memberships. On the remedies, He proposes dedicated algorithm regulators, periodic algorithm audits and specific algorithm laws built on principles such as fairness and explainability. Platforms should disclose how their algorithms work and diversify recommendations. Regulators should use AI to monitor algorithms, "fighting magic with magic", and blockchain and digital watermarks should secure the traceability of content. He concludes that law-based enforcement is a necessary step towards an open, inclusive and truthful digital society, and that it also needs the joint effort of all sectors. Public critical thinking and rumour punishment are treated as part of the same effort. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese legal scholars and official media frame algorithm governance and the "information cocoon" in policy terms.

Strengthening expectation management to raise the overall effectiveness of policy 加强预期管理 提高政策整体效能 Lin Muxi Wang Cong This newspaper commentary takes up the instruction of the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference to strengthen expectation management and to advance policy implementation and expectation guidance together. Lin and Wang argue that managing expectations, mainly through information dissemination that acts on the psychology of economic actors, reduces expectation bias and turns favourable social expectations into orderly, rational economic behaviour. In their view this is important for improving the macroeconomic governance system and raising its capacity. The article has three parts. The first sets out why expectation management matters more and more. The second describes its main content and requirements. The third proposes how to improve the mechanisms for expectation management, a task the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) named when it called for improving macroeconomic governance. On importance, the authors give three reasons. Expectation management helps to create policy synergy for high-quality development, because broader goals and a wider range of policy tools risk what they call fallacies of composition or decomposition. It is a precondition for deepening reform, since reform adjusts interests and needs guidance of public opinion. It is also a key measure against the difficulties the economy faces, and the authors trace how successive Central Economic Work Conferences from 2021 to 2024 put stabilising expectations first. On content, they stress government credibility, stable consumption and investment expectations, and better expectations among firms, especially private and small and micro enterprises, alongside deepening state-owned enterprise reform. On mechanisms, they propose four improvements. These are a policy system linked to development plans, with a richer toolbox and better coordination between departments. They also want more quantified and composite indicators, such as confidence indices. They add regular tracking and communication, with transparent policy explanation and use of mainstream media, and early-warning and risk-identification mechanisms covering inflation and deflation expectations and financial markets. The authors conclude that building these mechanisms is the central task if expectations are to move towards policy goals and if macroeconomic policy is to support high-quality development. They treat expectation management as part of the modernisation of national governance. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists frame expectation management as a macroeconomic governance tool and what institutional measures they propose.

How 5G technology can strengthen the guidance of mainstream ideology and public opinion 5G技术助力提升主流思想舆论引导力 Lin Minjian Writing in China Social Sciences Today (21 February 2025), Lin Minjian takes up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to integrate the management of news publicity and online opinion. The commentary argues that applying 5G technology to strengthen the guidance of mainstream ideology and public opinion is both a necessary response to new challenges and an unavoidable result of new technologies spreading through society. Lin organises the proposals under four headings: "5G+content" production, "5G+public opinion" governance, "5G+media" communication scenarios, and a "5G+talent" workforce. Each is tied to an image of mainstream opinion work: an "gravitational field", a "firewall", an "adhesive" and "concentric circles". On content, Lin argues that robot writing, digital anchors and platforms such as Xinhua's "central kitchen" raise output, while CCTV's "5G+8K" and "5G+VR" broadcasts make mainstream content more attractive. On governance, Lin warns that 5G speeds the spread of negative opinion and false information. The author calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and core socialist values, together with joint government–media prevention and control mechanisms and routine big-data monitoring of opinion. On communication, Lin urges wearables, smart homes, holographic formats and precise algorithmic delivery. Lin concludes that mainstream media need a workforce with political awareness, media literacy and technical skill. Proposed measures include reformed incentive systems, training in new technologies, and cultivating politically firm, popular scholars as online opinion leaders. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship frames 5G and big data as tools for opinion guidance.

The turn in media convergence from the perspective of Marx's theory of spiritual interaction 马克思精神交往理论视域下媒介融合的转向 Guo Jing Guo Jing asks why more than a decade of media convergence in traditional media has produced disappointing market returns and communication effects. The commentary argues that Marx's theory of spiritual interaction (精神交往) offers a way forward. Its thesis is that convergence should shift its focus from building platforms to fostering equal, mutually understanding interaction between people. The piece has three parts. It first defines journalism as a form of spiritual interaction, then turns to the Party's newspaper history in the New Democratic Revolution period, and finally sets out two practical paths for convergence. It is a short newspaper commentary rather than a full study. Guo reads Marx as treating interaction as the starting point of social relations and spiritual interaction as an expression of free human life. On that reading, journalism involves emotional resonance and an exchange of values, and there is no fixed split between 'communicator' and 'audience'. Technical platforms, the author says, only achieve delivery at the level of material production, not genuine exchange. The author cites worker-peasant correspondents and grassroots newspaper-reading groups as models of this kind of interaction. The two paths are, first, to grasp people's living conditions and urgent concerns, moving from building an 'internet of connections' to building a 'network of popular hearts'. Second, interaction should be rooted in grassroots social networks. Guo argues that in an age of node-based communication, other nodes such as self-media have a natural 'interactive qualification' that converged media products lack. Guo concludes that traditional media must treat themselves as one node among many and embed journalism in social relationship networks, or they cannot join the social communication system or achieve high-quality development. The author ties this to the development of the Party's propaganda and cultural work. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese media scholars apply Marx's concept of interaction to journalism practice and convergence policy.

Methods for building an international communication strategy system with Chinese characteristics 中国特色国际传播战略体系构建方法 Chen Hong Responding to the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to build a "more effective international communication system", Chen Hong asks how an international communication strategy system with Chinese characteristics should be built. The author argues that it must rest on a value system, a structural system and an operating system, and that the aim is to strengthen global strategic cooperation against shared conflicts and challenges. The piece is a short newspaper commentary. It is organised in three parts. The first concerns communication practice grounded in a community with a shared future for mankind. The second concerns deepening all-media, multidimensional discourse among government, media, enterprises and individuals. The third concerns an operating system for multiple audiences, with a focus on Generation Z. Chen argues that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind supplies the guiding value, and that the Belt and Road Initiative gives it a practical platform. Emotional resonance, in this account, can cross cultural and language barriers. The author assigns distinct roles to each actor: government as communicator and gatekeeper, media as guarantor of accurate reporting, enterprises as carriers of brand values, and individuals as spontaneous disseminators. These actors need a professional deliberative mechanism, and messages should fit local cultural contexts to avoid "communication without understanding". Chen cites the overseas spread of Chinese 5G technology as an example. Generation Z, described as the first "digital natives", is presented as key to building a communication system for all. The author notes that TikTok has over 1.1 billion daily active users worldwide, yet only seven central state-owned enterprises have official accounts. Chen calls for a combined system in which government leads, media cooperate and enterprises support, so that young people can take part in cross-cultural exchange. The aim is shared cultural understanding worldwide and a higher-quality stage of international communication. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Chinese communication scholars frame audience strategy, especially towards Generation Z.

Playing a "quartet" to continue the historical cultural lineage and spread Chinese culture 弹好赓续历史文脉传播中华文化的“四重奏” Zhang Xiaofeng Zhu Xiangfeng This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the 17th collective study session of the Political Bureau (28 October 2024) on building a cultural powerhouse. Zhang and Zhu argue that two tasks must be pursued together: protecting and passing on cultural heritage so that the historical cultural lineage continues, and using that heritage as a vehicle for communicating Chinese culture abroad. They present the work as a four-part "quartet". The piece is organised into four sections, each with a musical metaphor: a "song blending past and present" on integrating heritage into daily life, research and management; a "digital empowerment" section on protection, exhibition and storytelling; a "link between China and abroad" section on translation and self-presentation; and an "external communication symphony" on inclusiveness and integration. Examples include the Great Wall village of Shixia, the digital Dunhuang, Palace Museum, Great Wall and Sanxingdui projects, and a China–France exhibition on the Forbidden City and Versailles. On the domestic side, the authors call for linking tradition to everyday life and tourism, for coordinated research on archaeology, intangible heritage and minority histories (in order to strengthen a sense of community of the Chinese nation), and for a management system built on censuses, a national database and a "protection first" principle. They argue that digital tools can restore damaged texts, create immersive virtual exhibitions that also reduce visitor damage, and renew narrative by combining grand and individual stories. On the international side, they propose a national translation capacity, key shared concepts and expressions that carry a Chinese style, and communication that starts from shared historical memory with other countries. Zhang and Zhu also call for a multi-channel communication pattern: inviting foreign journalists to sites such as Liangzhu, Erlitou and Yinxu, dialogue with Western media and scholars, a focus on social media platforms, and tailored strategies for each country. They state that this should present Chinese modernization, the Chinese path and Chinese ideas, and promote understanding of them abroad. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned academics translate the cultural-powerhouse agenda into concrete policies on heritage, digital technology and international communication.

Opening a new realm of contemporary Chinese development 开辟中国当代发展新境界 Gohi Bi Foua Claude Alain This commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by Gohi Bi Foua Claude Alain, an Ivorian associate professor at Panzhihua University, published in Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025. Writing as a foreign observer who has visited China several times, the author argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), under Xi Jinping's leadership, China has opened a new realm of development. The author presents this as a record of achievement that is also a source of lessons for other developing countries, Africa in particular. The article is organised under five headings. It first surveys China's changes in the new era in social, economic, cultural and diplomatic fields, drawing on the author's own impressions. It then takes up whole-process people's democracy, Chinese modernization, the relevance of China's model for African states, and Xi's global ideas, notably a community with a shared future for mankind. It closes with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the further deepening of reform. Alain argues that no democratic model is universally valid and that whole-process people's democracy, rooted in Chinese conditions, produces social cohesion that the author contrasts with polarisation in Western societies. The author cites criticism of Francis Fukuyama's end-of-history thesis to claim that Western democracy is far from the best option. Chinese modernization is described as led by the Communist Party, people-centred, ecologically minded and peaceful, in contrast with Western expansionism and the policy shifts the author attributes to multiparty systems. For Africa, the author contends that China offers a feasible path, respects independence, and gives aid without political conditions, whereas US policy is said to focus on economic and military interests; Kenya is cited as a case of Belt and Road investment benefiting infrastructure and manufacturing. The author concludes that China supports genuine multilateralism, contributes to tackling climate change and other global problems, and that its opening to the world will widen after the Third Plenum. Alain predicts that more partner countries will benefit and that Western attempts to contain China's rise will fail. Read the original if you want an example of how an African academic's favourable view of China is presented in Chinese official academic media, or if you are interested in the China–Africa comparisons it draws with US policy.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating to promote the intension-based development of ideological and political courses in universities 守正创新推动高校思政课建设内涵式发展 Mei Zhengli This newspaper commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how university ideological and political courses (sizheng courses) can improve their quality and appeal. Mei argues that the answer lies in balancing two requirements, upholding fundamental principles (shouzheng) and innovating (chuangxin). Taking Xi Jinping's instruction on the subject as its starting point, the article treats this balance as the basis of what it calls intension-based development, meaning growth driven by internal elements and quality rather than expansion in scale. The piece is organised in three parts. The first explains why both principles and innovation are needed. The second covers fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education (lide shuren) through three internal elements: teaching content, teaching channels and teacher quality. The third sets out three innovative measures: integrating ideological and political courses across primary, secondary and university stages, aligning dedicated courses with ideological content in other subjects, and using digital and intelligent technology. In Mei's account, upholding principles means keeping to Party leadership, Marxism as the guiding ideology, socialist conviction and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture. Innovation means moving from rote instruction to student-centred teaching that links theory to current events and to students' majors. Mei proposes building high-quality classes through lively language and varied pacing, and extending learning through rural-revitalisation fieldwork, volunteer teaching and visits to red heritage sites. Teachers should be both scholars of classics and moral exemplars, which the author ties to study of Marxist classics, teaching competitions and professional ethics. On innovation, Mei describes stage-by-stage curricula, model courses with design guidelines, and smart platforms with VR and AR for "precise drip irrigation" of ideas. Mei concludes that combining steadfastness on direction with innovation in methods will produce a new generation capable of carrying the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and socialist modernization. The article is a practical, policy-oriented statement rather than a theoretical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party official frames current guidance on ideological and political education, including its practical recommendations for classrooms, teachers and technology.

Improving the price mechanism for green and low-carbon development 完善绿色低碳发展价格机制 Liu Yaobin Writing in a newspaper commentary in February 2025, Liu Yaobin asks how prices can be made to carry the costs and value of green and low-carbon development. Liu defines green and low-carbon development pricing as a market mechanism through which prices reflect supply and demand, resource scarcity and the cost of green and low-carbon development. The author argues that it has two main components, ecological product prices and carbon pricing, and that improving it is a basic requirement of high-quality development and of building a modernization in which humanity and nature coexist in harmony. The article first traces the policy lineage of the idea, from the resource and environmental price formation language of the 17th Party Congress (2007), through the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee and the 2018 and 2023 national ecological and environmental protection conferences, to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then gives three reasons for the mechanism, sets out five measures for improving it, and closes with four relationships that must be handled correctly. Liu argues that the mechanism deepens ecological civilization reform, is a key route for putting into practice the idea that “lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets”, and fits the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Pricing ecological products is presented as a way to make their non-monetary value explicit, while the national carbon market is described as sending price signals and steering funds towards high-potential emitters. The proposed measures include market-based allocation of resource and environmental factors, clearer carbon asset property rights, a unified green certificate system, government-guided prices for ecological products affecting people's livelihood, multi-party price supervision, and revised price laws and monitoring systems. The four relationships Liu names are: high-quality development and high-level protection; an efficient market and an effective government; unified openness and orderly competition; and external constraints and endogenous motivation. Liu concludes that handling each of these in a complementary, dialectical way is the practical premise, cognitive core, governing principle and objective requirement of a sound pricing mechanism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese policy scholarship links carbon markets, ecological product value realisation and price reform.

Working wholeheartedly in the interests of the people Written for the 80th anniversary of "Serve the People" 彻底地为人民的利益工作 Li Wei Marking eighty years since Mao Zedong's 1944 speech "Serve the People", Li Wei argues that the slogan is far more than propaganda. In Li's account, it is a theoretical and moral creation that turned Marxism into everyday practice and changed the moral outlook of the Chinese nation. Li laments that scholars have given it little dedicated study and calls for it to be treated as a permanent task for the Party and for Chinese thought. The article opens with Li's personal route to the theme, from reading about Marx's choice of a profession and learning from Lei Feng in the 1960s to reflecting on the Soviet collapse. It then traces the idea's origins in Marx, Engels and Lenin, and its development in the Red Army's discipline and in Mao's work in the Jiangxi Soviet and at the Seventh Party Congress (1945). The later sections take up the meaning of "the people" and of "serve", and Mao's policies in education, health and Party conduct. Li ends with present-day corruption. Li makes three main moves. First, the idea has Marxist roots, but Mao's distinctive step was to build a code of honour from the bottom up: the Three Main Rules of Discipline and Eight Points for Attention first told soldiers what harm not to do, and only then asked for selfless service. Second, Li reads "the people" as a class and political concept, with workers and peasants as its main body. For this reason Mao said "serve the people" rather than "serve people", and Li accuses Gorbachev of using abstract talk of "the person" to disguise anti-people content. Third, the principle has to be specific: Mao attended to salt, rice, bridges and teachers' pay, and ran a frugal, clean government. Li concludes that "Serve the People" is the Party's sole purpose, its lifeline and the bond between Party and people, and a landmark in the intellectual history of the Chinese nation. Citing cases of officials' corruption and press headlines on abuses against peasants, Li contends that the Party today often falls short of its own standard. Li therefore calls for a new chapter of "Serve the People" under reform and opening up and the socialist market economy. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic Chinese reading of Mao's service ethic, and of how it is used to criticise present-day cadres' conduct.
