How Northeast China can accelerate the development of new quality productive forces 东北地区如何加快发展新质生产力 Chang Qinglin This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, asks how China's northeast can speed up the development of new quality productive forces. Chang Qinglin argues that doing so is a necessary step in carrying out the strategy of comprehensively revitalising the northeast in the new era and in advancing Chinese modernization. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's 2023 and 2025 remarks in Harbin, Liaoning and Jilin, which it treats as a guide to action. The article has three parts. The first sets out the region's foundations: Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang and five eastern Inner Mongolia league-level cities, with about 110 million people. The second lists the obstacles. The third proposes five sets of measures. On foundations, Chang points to the digital and intelligent upgrading of traditional industry and agriculture, growth in new energy, biomedicine and artificial intelligence, and strong universities and research bodies. On challenges, the author cites figures: the three provinces' 2023 R&D spending of 111.59 billion yuan equals 26.5 per cent of Jiangsu's, and R&D intensity of about 1.74 per cent is 65 per cent of the national average. Other problems named are a university patent conversion rate of around 10 per cent in Liaoning, local sourcing of only about 40 per cent of parts by central-government automotive firms, under 5 per cent of national high-tech enterprises, talent loss, and weak coordination. The proposed responses are to build innovation platforms and technology-transfer and science-finance systems, to offer special talent policies, and to reform ownership of職務 scientific results by giving researchers partial or full rights. They also include strengthening the "chain leader" role of central state-owned enterprises such as FAW and Harbin Electric, and building a regional investment coordination system. That system would rest on a Harbin–Changchun–Shenyang–Dalian axis, with a specialised role for each city. Chang concludes that, by integrating technological and industrial innovation and improving policy supply, the northeast can turn scientific innovation from a "key variable" into a "strong increment" for revitalisation. The aim is a shift from scientific strength to industrial and economic strength. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented account of how a Party-school scholar translates the new quality productive forces agenda into regional measures, with the author's statistics on northeastern R&D.

Accelerating a complete domestic demand system and expanding domestic demand in all respects 加快培育完整内需体系 全方位扩大国内需求 Huang Maoxing Xue Jianhan This newspaper commentary asks how China should put into practice the strategic requirement, set out at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), to "accelerate the cultivation of a complete domestic demand system". Huang and Xue argue that expanding domestic demand in all respects is the necessary choice for sustaining the economic recovery. They point to the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, which placed boosting consumption, raising investment returns and expanding domestic demand first among its nine tasks for 2025. The article has three parts. The first sets out why expanding domestic demand matters. The second argues that there is wide room for it, drawing on 2024 statistics for GDP, retail sales, consumer spending and fixed-asset investment. The third lists policy measures centred on consumption and people's livelihood. On the reasons, the authors contend that expanding demand underpins the new development pattern by smoothing the domestic economic cycle and reducing dependence on external markets. They also describe it as a long-term means of changing the development model, from factor-driven to innovation-driven, from investment-led to coordinated consumption and investment, and from reliance on external demand to domestic-demand leadership. It would also speed industrial upgrading. On room for growth, they cite four sources: a very large market (GDP of 134.9 trillion yuan in 2024, up 5%), a complete industrial system, a population of over 1.4 billion including more than 400 million middle-income earners, and coordinated urban–rural and regional development. The proposed measures are to widen the "two news" policies (large-scale equipment renewal and trade-in of consumer goods) and expand service consumption. The authors also call for investment in priority areas with stronger assessment of returns, high-quality supply that creates new demand, coordinated fiscal and monetary policy, and higher household incomes backed by a stronger social security system. They present these as the way to turn the strategy into practice and promote high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the rationale and policy toolkit for boosting domestic demand in China's 2025 economic agenda.

Technological and institutional innovation as twin drivers of the shift from old to new growth drivers 科技创新和制度创新双轮驱动新旧动能转换 Wang Yiming Writing in People's Daily in February 2025, Wang Yiming takes up a line from the Central Economic Work Conference: that China must coordinate the cultivation of new growth drivers with the renewal of old ones, and develop new quality productive forces in light of local conditions. Wang argues that the transition from old to new drivers can be made smooth and sequential only if technological innovation and institutional innovation work together as 'two wheels' turning at once. The piece presents this as guidance for high-quality development. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out how new and old drivers relate, using the property sector, the 'new three' exports (new-energy vehicles, lithium batteries, photovoltaics), heavy industry and shipbuilding as examples. The second argues that technological innovation is the key to the transition. The third argues that institutional innovation is the fundamental condition, covering the innovation ecosystem, science-and-technology finance and further reforms. Wang contends that new and old drivers are dialectically linked and change over time, so old industries can be upgraded into new ones. The author cites figures: traditional industries account for about 80 per cent of industrial value added above designated size, while strategic emerging industries make up only about 13 per cent of GDP. The principle is therefore to build the new before breaking the old. On technology, Wang stresses original and disruptive innovation and the full chain from basic research to large-scale industrialisation, and names weak original capacity and poor commercialisation as shortcomings. On institutions, Wang says government should act selectively, shifting from direct allocation of resources to supplying rules and services. Strict intellectual property protection, fair competition and the decisive role of the market are described as the core of a good ecosystem. The author also criticises finance geared to short-term, collateral-based lending that does not suit technology firms. Wang calls for patient and long-term capital, venture and angel funds, and a science-and-technology finance system. Wang also proposes reforms to the ownership of职务 research results, data and technology markets, research funding, enterprise-led innovation and talent evaluation. The overall aim is to let traditional industries, emerging industries and future industries each open new room for growth under high-quality development. Read the original if you want an official-economist view, published in the Party's main newspaper, of how the Central Economic Work Conference line on new and old growth drivers is being turned into policy priorities.

China's economy leads the world to rethink the essence of development Interview with Carles Brasó Broggi, professor of arts and humanities at the Open University of Catalonia, Spain 中国经济引导世界反思发展要义 This is an interview, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, in which a reporter questions Carles Brasó Broggi, a professor in the Department of Arts and Humanities at the Open University of Catalonia in Spain. The topic is China's economic history, from antiquity to reform and opening up. Brasó Broggi argues that China has contributed to world development and continues to prompt others to reconsider how development should proceed. The interview has three questions. The first asks when China's economy stood out globally. The second asks how ancient China's development model, and the link between its political system and its economy, compares with the West's. The third asks about the main factors behind growth since reform and opening up. On history, Brasó Broggi, citing Angus Maddison, holds that China ranked among the leading economies in most periods, the exception being 1840 to the 1970s. He urges looking beyond the Four Great Inventions to a wider global history of technology. As an example, he notes that Wang Zhen's Nongshu described a spinning machine about 500 years before Britain's Industrial Revolution, and that Wang warned of mechanization's social and natural costs. In comparing models, he says both China and Europe were agrarian. In his account, China invested heavily in canals and irrigation and was mostly unified, unlike Europe. He sees market laws, state intervention and class relations as broadly similar in both. On the reform era, he lists open-minded borrowing from many schools of economists, pragmatic and gradual experimentation (such as special economic zones) unlike the Soviet Union's radical reform, and a favourable demographic structure. He says no comprehensive theory of China's development yet exists. Brasó Broggi concludes that China combined internal and external drivers to sustain decades of growth while raising living standards, which he describes as unprecedented in world economic history. Read the original if you want a short, accessible view from a Spanish scholar on how China's long-run economic history and reform-era success are presented in Chinese media.

What the classical dispute over rhetoric and dialectic still teaches us 古典思想争论的当代启示 Michael Trapp This is a Chinese translation, by Yang Xue, of a speech given by the classicist Michael Trapp at the first World Congress of Classics. Trapp takes up the second-century orations of Aelius Aristides, which answer Plato's critique of rhetoric in the Gorgias. He rejects the common view that these texts are stale pedantry and argues that they remain worth reading. The talk reviews Aristides' attack on Plato in three parts: his defence of rhetoric against the charge of being non-scientific, his rebuttal of Plato's criticism of four great Athenian statesman-orators, and his portrayal of Plato's school as an aberration in Greek tradition. Trapp then looks at Aristides' own positive account of rhetoric, including his revised Prometheus myth. Trapp concedes Aristides' exaggeration and uncritical assumption, inherited from Isocrates, that a true orator is virtuous. He nonetheless finds real force in the rebuttal. Plato calls rhetoric mere guesswork (stochastikê), and Aristides answers that aiming is a rational act. He adds that archery, navigation and medicine are genuine crafts despite relying on conjecture. In Trapp's reading, this challenges Plato's rationalism and his sharp opposition of reason and unreason. Trapp also notes that dialectic alone struggles to found a political community: the Republic confines dialectical exchange to an elite and leaves room for deception and coercion. Trapp declines to name a winner, saying both sides have blind spots, and he does not endorse Aristides' idea that rhetoricians are automatically defenders of civilisation. He concludes that the quarrel keeps alive the question of how we communicate and engage with others, and that classical works supply models of both rhetoric and dialectic and make debate over them necessary. Read the original if you want a short classicist's defence of an ancient anti-Platonic text and its present-day relevance.

The distinctive qualities of the Party's leadership in further deepening reform comprehensively 进一步全面深化改革的鲜明特质 Liu Sifang Writing in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, Liu Sifang asks why and how the Communist Party of China can guarantee the success of reform. The commentary argues that the Party's comprehensive leadership is the fundamental guarantee for further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization, as set out at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Liu holds that this guarantee rests on six capacities, which the article calls the Party's "six distinctive qualities". The piece first sets out the framing: leadership by the Party is described as the key lesson of reform and opening up and of the reform work of the new era. It then takes the six capacities in turn: political leadership, ideological guidance, strategic planning, mass organisation, social appeal and spiritual drive. Each is defined, and each is linked to concrete requirements for the current round of reform. A final section turns to the Party's self-reform. Liu defines political leadership as the ability to grasp direction and the overall situation. In Liu's account it keeps reform on course, secures the Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and keeps reform tied to Chinese modernization. Ideological guidance rests on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Two Integrations. Strategic planning combines top-level design with local experimentation, pairs breakthroughs in key areas with overall advance, and builds systems of goals, policies, work and evaluation. Mass organisation means relying on the people and the mass line. Social appeal means uniting different groups around a shared vision of national rejuvenation. Spiritual drive means drawing on the Party's lineage of spirit, encouraging bold innovation and protecting reformers. Liu concludes that further reform is a profound change in theory, organisation, institutions and popular participation. To keep it on course, the Party must keep up the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution, and the author says the harder the social revolution, the more thorough the self-reform must be. The author calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and for stronger institutional norms for self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise statement, in official Party-theory language, of how Chinese scholars frame Party leadership as the guarantee of reform after the Third Plenum.

Taking Xi Jinping Thought on Culture as guidance to strengthen the leading power of ideological and political education 坚持习近平文化思想为指导提升思政引领力 Liu Yongxiang Sun Xinran This short commentary, published in early 2025, takes up the concept of "leading power of ideological and political education" (sizheng yinlingli), which Xi Jinping first put forward at the National Education Conference and presented as the primary feature of a strong education nation with Chinese characteristics. Liu and Sun argue that this capacity must be built by integrating the Party's innovative theory into ideological and political courses, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Culture should serve as the guiding framework. The authors tie their argument to the Outline Plan for Building a Strong Education Nation (2024–2035) and to the Study Outline of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, which they say offers systematic guidance. The piece is organised around four tasks: upholding Marxism's guiding position in ideology, advancing the Two Integrations, forging a sense of community for the Chinese nation, and using revolutionary cultural relics in teaching. On the first two tasks, Liu and Sun hold that Marxism-is-outdated claims and the idea that "modernization means Westernization" still reach young people through the internet. They call for popularising theory, listening to students' difficulties, and explaining Marxism's contemporary explanatory power. They present the "second integration" as having resolved the modern "dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western", and urge building a Chinese independent knowledge system, coordinating textbooks across courses and developing a "great ideological and political education" paradigm. On the third and fourth, they call for refuting mistaken ethnic theories, teaching the course on the Chinese national community well, and making core socialist values part of daily life. They list weaknesses in red-culture practice, including student-centred visits with little teacher guidance, content detached from textbooks, perfunctory tours and museum displays lacking theoretical coherence. Their remedies are a Party-history narrative built around revolutionary relics, a bridging role for teachers, and oral-history methods that turn students into interpreters. The authors conclude that ideological and political courses address students' ideals and convictions, which rest on cultural values. They describe strengthening this leading power as a task bearing on the Party's long-term rule and national stability, to be pursued persistently. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school educators link Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to concrete teaching reforms in ideological and political courses.

Advancing with the times: raising governance capacity in the cultural sphere 与时俱进提升文化领域治理能力 Wen Zhizhong Lu Yanchen This short commentary, written after a Politburo collective study session, asks how governance capacity in the cultural sphere can be raised under conditions of informatization. Wen and Lu argue that this capacity is a necessary requirement for building a socialist cultural powerhouse by the 2035 target set by Xi Jinping, and an important guarantee of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article proceeds through five principles, each introduced by a heading: upholding Party leadership, keeping to fundamental principles while innovating, integrating culture with technology, maintaining cultural confidence, and fostering the core socialist values. It draws throughout on Xi's statements and on the Third Plenum decision (2024) on deepening reform. The authors argue that Party leadership gives cultural governance a consistent direction, protects ideological security and shields cultural work from market uncertainty. They hold that Marxism's guiding role, Xi Jinping's cultural thought and the Two Integrations underpin the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. They call for big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence, described as new quality productive forces, to make governance more intelligent and precise, and for better governance of cyberspace. They add that cultural reform, scholarly and artistic democracy and a larger body of cultural talent would release creativity. Wen and Lu present the core socialist values as the basis for guarding cultural sovereignty and security against what they call foreign cultural infiltration. They conclude that a healthy, open and dynamic governance ecosystem would deepen Chinese modernization and offer Chinese wisdom to global cultural diversity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse links cultural governance, ideological security and digital technology.

Upholding and consolidating the Party's cultural leadership from three dimensions 从三个维度坚持和巩固党的文化领导权 Lin Xianming Zhuang Ruoyu Lin and Zhuang ask how the Communist Party of China can uphold and consolidate its cultural leadership (cultural hegemony) at a time when, in the authors' words, the world is undergoing changes unseen in a century and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered a critical period. They argue that cultural leadership bears on ideological security, cultural security and the realisation of cultural modernisation, and propose three dimensions for strengthening it. The short commentary treats cultural leadership as a question of a class's or party's discursive power in ideology, not only of culture. It moves through three headings: upholding and strengthening Party leadership, putting the people at the centre, and consolidating the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. On Party leadership, the authors say it keeps culture on the right course, resists foreign cultural erosion, secures Marxism's guiding position and lets the Party concentrate resources on cultural undertakings. They call for the Two Upholds, stronger strategic planning (citing the 14th Five-Year Plan for cultural development) and firm Party control of propaganda and ideological work. On the people-centred dimension, they hold that Party spirit and the people's character must be unified, and cite the television dramas Minning Town and The Age of Awakening as examples. On cultural subjectivity, they call for adherence to Marxism, creative transformation of traditional culture, socialist core values and an independent Chinese knowledge system. The authors conclude that these three measures together provide the political, popular and cultural foundations of the Party's cultural leadership in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated scholars frame cultural leadership in current ideological education.

Starting from "knowing, feeling, willing, acting": guiding university students towards a stronger identification with Chinese civilization 从“知情意行”入手，引导大学生更好认同中华文明 Ji Mingming Ji Rong This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, asks how universities can lead students to recognise and identify with Chinese civilization. Opening with Xi Jinping's call to strengthen young people's "ambition, backbone and confidence" as Chinese, the authors argue that education should follow the laws of students' thinking and of teaching, and work through four links: knowing, feeling, willing and acting. The text takes each link in turn and gives two practical measures for each. Knowledge is addressed through courses and academic events; emotion through campus culture and festivals; will through role models and online outreach; action through cultural social practice and cultural entrepreneurship. The authors treat identification as a progression from cognition to commitment. They propose integrating civilization education into the curriculum, with lectures, debates and expert dialogues, so that students understand its origins and contribution to human civilization. They suggest campus sculptures, murals and traditional festivals, opera and dance as ways of building emotional resonance. To build will, they call for carefully chosen exemplars, new-media content and AI-based monitoring of online opinion to help students resist harmful online culture. Finally, they propose site visits, intangible heritage work, craft learning and creative products as practice. The authors conclude that this approach will lead students to take up responsibility for promoting excellent traditional Chinese culture and building a modern Chinese civilization, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how university leaders frame civilization education and ideological work with students.

Giving full play to the leading role of higher education in supporting high-level scientific and technological self-reliance 发挥高等教育龙头作用 支撑高水平科技自立自强 Gong Qihuang Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, Gong Qihuang, president of Peking University, takes up how universities can serve high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. Drawing on the Outline of the Plan for Building a Strong Education Country (2024–2035), Gong argues that high-level research universities, as part of the national strategic science and technology force, should act as the vanguard in the battle over key core technologies. The commentary is organised around four tasks. These are adjusting the disciplinary structure to national needs, assembling strategic talent, producing frontier science and technology, and working with other strategic science and technology forces. Gong supports each with passages from Xi Jinping and with the Outline's call to integrate education, science and technology, and talent. On disciplines and talent, Gong calls for rapid, even extraordinary, placement of urgently needed fields and for unconventional selection of strong students in basic disciplines, with integrated undergraduate-to-doctoral training. Universities should recruit globally through fast-track channels, develop strategic scientists and young talent, and use trust-based evaluation with long, stable support for basic fields. On research, Gong urges combining goal-oriented and free exploration, strengthening organised research and the "open competition" mechanism (jiebang guashuai). Universities should also link with national laboratories, leading firms and local governments, drawing on the whole-nation system for concentrating resources. Gong concludes that universities should reform research paradigms and organisational models and build the whole chain from basic research to industrial application. The author presents this as a way for universities to act as a vanguard in developing new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from a leading university president, of how Chinese higher education is expected to support the national science and technology strategy.

Several foundational questions for theoretical innovation in the digital economy 数字经济理论创新的几个基础问题 Hong Yongmiao Shi Jiuling Published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, this commentary asks which basic questions must be settled before economic theory can be renewed for the digital economy. Hong and Shi argue that three issues come first: the nature of data as a factor of production, the measurement of data's value and of its contribution to growth, and the changes that data and artificial intelligence bring to relations of production. They treat recognising data as a new factor as only the starting point of theoretical innovation. The authors first set out the properties of data: it is non-consumable, non-exclusive and highly mobile, and it takes effect only when combined with labour, capital, technology and management. They then turn to valuation and pricing, to the measurement of data's contribution to growth, and finally to four shifts in production relations: AI replacing labour, asymmetries on platforms, the digital divide and cross-border data competition. On value, Hong and Shi apply Marx's labour theory of value. Data's value is condensed human labour: labour in forming raw data, transferred objectified labour in collection and processing, and the living labour of data workers. Because data combines with other factors in non-linear, context-dependent and time-sensitive ways, they say its value creation extends the labour theory of value. They note that non-exclusivity challenges the scarcity assumption of conventional theory, and that free digital services are hard to explain with it. Fully competitive market prices could in principle reveal data's value, but such markets do not yet exist. The authors point instead to market design theory, experimental economics and simulation, and they warn that hasty recognition of data assets on balance sheets could produce a 'data asset bubble'. Drawing an analogy with the 'productivity paradox', they say that better measurement of intangible capital is needed to capture data's role in growth, which calls for a production function suited to the digital economy. The authors conclude that economic growth theory, measurement and statistics all need innovation, and that production relations deserve equal study alongside the growth of productive forces. They call for evidence-based research tied to digital practice. They also call for scientific grounds for a fairer and more inclusive model of growth, since without good governance gig workers, small firms and consumers are weak against platform capital. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language agenda linking Marx's labour theory of value to data pricing, growth measurement and platform labour relations.

Building a higher-standard new system for an open economy through institutional opening-up 以制度型开放建设更高水平开放型经济新体制 Yang Jijun This short commentary in Guangming Daily (February 2025) asks how China can build a higher-level open economy now that tariff-based "border opening" is largely settled. Yang Jijun argues that the answer is institutional opening-up: moving from the cross-border flow of goods and factors to alignment with high-standard international economic and trade rules. Yang first traces the shift, noting that the 2018 Central Economic Work Conference first called for moving from opening based on flows of goods and factors to opening based on rules and other institutions. The article then defines four components of institutional opening-up: rules, regulation, management and standards. It closes with the challenges China faces and a set of responses. Yang describes rules opening as the foundation, covering both compliance with WTO and regional trade agreement rules and participation in writing new ones. Regulatory opening is illustrated by the removal of foreign-ownership caps in finance and the "zeroing out" of foreign-access restrictions in manufacturing. Management opening means streamlining administration, and standards opening means aligning with ISO and other standards. Yang says developed countries are competing to control the next generation of trade rules. Upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership over publicity, ideological and cultural work 坚持和加强党对宣传思想文化工作的全面领导 Zhang Shihai This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, takes up how the Communist Party of China should secure its cultural leadership. Vigorously promoting high-quality development of China's new energy 大力推动我国新能源高质量发展 Cheng Zhiqiang Writing in the People's Daily on 19 February 2025, Cheng Zhiqiang, a cooperation director at the Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization, takes up how China can sustain high-quality development of its new energy sector. Cultivating high-level talent independently to help develop new quality productive forces 自主培养高层次人才 助力发展新质生产力 Han Qingsong Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (17 February 2025), Han Qingsong asks how China's postgraduate education can supply the high-level talent needed for new quality productive forces. Cultivating talent for new quality productive forces is the key to sustainable development 培养新质生产力人才是实现可持续发展的关键 Zhai Tingting This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, argues that training large numbers of people with innovative thinking, interdisciplinary knowledge and practical ability is the key to sustainable development. The threefold logic of building an independent knowledge system for Chinese philosophy and social sciences 构建中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系的三重逻辑 He Xiying Taking up Xi Jinping's remark during a visit to Renmin University of China that building Chinese philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's own independent knowledge system, He Xiying asks what logic underlies that project. Vigorously promoting the mutual fit and interaction of new quality productive forces and new industrialization 大力推动新质生产力与新型工业化契合互动 Qu Yongyi Writing in Study Times in February 2025, Qu Yongyi asks how new quality productive forces and new industrialization can be made to fit and reinforce each other. People first: the core value orientation of Marxist social governance 人民至上：马克思主义社会治理的核心价值向度 Zhang Zonglan Liang Dawei This short commentary asks how the principle of putting the people first shapes social governance in China. A good ecological environment is the most inclusive public benefit for people's well-being 良好生态环境是最普惠的民生福祉 Hu Jun Hu Jun, writing in Study Times in February 2025, takes up the thesis that a good ecological environment is the most inclusive public benefit for people's well-being. Identifying the key levers for high-level scientific and technological self-reliance 找准高水平科技自立自强关键抓手 Sheng Chaoxun This newspaper commentary, first published in Economic Daily in February 2025, asks how China can achieve high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. Popularising the Party's innovative theory in the new era: communication practice and future paths 新时代党的创新理论大众化的传播实践与未来进路 Zhang Sen This short commentary, published on Guangming Net in February 2025, asks how the Party's innovative theory can be made accessible to ordinary people in the internet age. The value implications of building a socialist cultural powerhouse 建设社会主义文化强国的价值意蕴 Qin Xuan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, asks what is at stake in building a socialist cultural powerhouse, the cultural goal set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Upholding a Chinese modernization of harmony between humanity and nature 坚持人与自然和谐共生的中国式现代化 Zhao Zhonghua Chen Zongbo This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, takes up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and its claim that Chinese modernization is a modernization of harmony between humanity and nature. Marxist research as the foundational project of ideological and theoretical construction 马克思主义研究是思想理论建设的基础工程 Gao Guoxi This newspaper commentary (Chinese Social Sciences Today, 12 February 2025) takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project is the "foundational" and "strategic" project of the Party's ideological and theoretical work. Systematically grasping the value connotations of building a strong education country 系统把握建设教育强国的价值内涵 Sun Xiuling Sun Xiuling's commentary in Guangming Daily (February 2025) interprets the Outline for Building a Strong Education Country (2024–2035), recently issued by the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and the State Council. Building a new pattern of fostering virtue through education and cultivating new-era talents who can shoulder major responsibilities 构建立德树人新格局 培养堪当重任的时代新人 Li Zhongjun This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, responds to the Central Committee and State Council's Outline Plan for Building a Leading Education Country (2024–2035). The relationship between raising quality and expanding total output must be well coordinated 必须统筹好提升质量和做大总量的关系 Lai Desheng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, interprets one of the "five must-coordinate" relationships set out at the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: the relationship between raising quality and expanding total output. The essential meaning of making political supervision concrete, precise and routine 政治监督具体化精准化常态化的精髓要义 Bai Xianliang Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2025, Bai Xianliang takes up the Party's call to make political supervision concrete (具体化), precise (精准化) and routine (常态化). Understanding the historical-materialist implications of digital civilization 深刻理解数字文明的唯物史观意蕴 Liu Yan This short commentary asks how "digital civilization", a term Xi Jinping used in a 2021 message to the World Internet Conference, should be understood through historical materialism. In the author's account, digital technology marks a new technological social formation, following hunting-gathering, agrarian and industrial civilizations, and a digital form of social interaction, moving from closed toward open civilization. Under socialism, Liu contends, digital civilization restores human essence and sublates the control logic of digital capitalism, where capital becomes a "special ether" colluding with technology. Tools such as blockchain, cloud computing and ChatGPT are presented as objectifications of human agency that raise labour productivity and free time. Liu concludes that digital civilization follows the universal logic of human freedom and liberation, and, through connectivity, sharing and joint governance and the Digital Silk Road, supports a community with a shared future for mankind and resolves civilizational conflicts caused by digital capitalism. The unity of Chinese civilisation and the Chinese nation's pursuit of national unification 从中华文明统一性看中华民族对国家统一的追求 Wang Qiangan This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how the unity of Chinese civilisation explains the Chinese nation's persistent pursuit of national unification. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, which set out the "five prominent characteristics" of Chinese civilisation, Wang argues that the tradition of "great unification" has been a main thread of China's political order and thought and culture throughout its history. Wang's central claims are that ideas of a unified realm, a central "China" and shared Yan and Huang ancestry developed early, and that cultural identification came to outweigh blood descent. In this account the idea of "Hua and Yi as one family" gradually became the mainstream. Nourishing the core socialist values with excellent traditional Chinese culture 以中华优秀传统文化涵养社会主义核心价值观 Li Nan This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how excellent traditional Chinese culture can nourish the core socialist values. The central move is to pair traditional concepts with Marxist and Party-theoretical ones. Marx's philosophical critique needs no epistemological justification 马克思的哲学批判无需“认识论”证成 Xia Ying Xia Ying takes issue with a recent trend in Marx studies that treats epistemology as the necessary guarantee of the "rigour" of Marx's philosophy. This reading rests on the 1857–58 manuscripts' section on the method of political economy and extends to general reflection on dialectics. Xia argues that Marx's philosophy needs no such justification, and that an epistemology of "the cognition of cognition" would turn it into a form of idealism. The commentary is a polemical newspaper piece that engages directly with Professor Wu Meng's account of the three layers of meaning in Marx's epistemology. It first sets out two presuppositions Xia finds hidden in that account. It then offers a positive alternative, an ontological reading of Marx's method, and ends by drawing out what follows for how Marx's concepts should be understood. Xia's first move is that the epistemological reading assumes the object of knowledge must be built theoretically before inquiry begins, and that its "form of givenness" must be fixed. In Xia's view, the first assumption strips categories such as labour of their concrete historical setting and returns Marx to the abstractions of the classical political economists. The second, which Xia says has a Husserlian transcendental-phenomenological flavour, confines the object within consciousness. It also reduces the relations of production and the productive forces to ahistorical "social structures", so that philosophy slips back from "changing the world" to "interpreting the world". Xia's second move is that Marx's object, human society, is the product of human practice and is not a ready-made thing set against the knower. Society is therefore something continually being generated, and the knowledge of it shapes its development. Understanding it is an ontological question from the start, and this dissolves the subject–object dualism and the tension between freedom and necessity. Marx's "abstract power" needs no mediating form, because any such mediation could stifle the generative character of the concrete and the abstract. Xia concludes that Marx cared less about accurately representing the existing world than about the conditions under which it can be transformed. Logical and historical unity is, in Xia's words, only an expedient of his method. There should be no Marxist epistemology of "the cognition of cognition" detached from the study of concrete social reality, and its legitimate concerns can be better expressed within an ontological horizon. Read the original if you follow debates on Marx's method and the status of epistemology in Marxist philosophy, or want a short, pointed Chinese critique of the epistemological reading of Marx's economic manuscripts.

What is "Marx's epistemology"? “马克思认识论”何谓？ Wu Meng Wu Meng takes up a question that he treats as neglected in current research on Marx's philosophy: what "Marx's epistemology" means. In this short commentary the author notes that "epistemology" now tends to suggest either modern subject–object epistemology or the "textbook system" built on it. Wu argues that if epistemology is read broadly, as "knowledge of knowledge", Marx's epistemology is an important field that cannot be ignored, and defines it as Marx's self-aware understanding of his own cognition of historical, real movement. The article is organised around three layers of meaning, which together form its answer. The first concerns Marx's theoretical self-awareness about the object of his knowledge. The second concerns his awareness of the rigour of his own theoretical practice, discussed through historical materialism and the critique of political economy. The third concerns how this epistemology establishes thoroughgoing materialism. A closing sentence combines the three into a definition. On the first layer, Wu reads the first Feuerbach thesis to mean that an object cannot become an object by itself. It appears together with a historical ground, namely the practice that makes its "appearance of universality" possible. Marx's critiques of Feuerbach, Hegel, the Young Hegelians and classical political economy aimed to fix this object. On the second layer, Wu holds that historical materialism arose from repeatedly questioning the historical presuppositions of capitalism's universal appearance, and that the critique of political economy traces the form-determinations of classical economists' "eternal" categories back to their historical conditions. Marx's ascent "from the abstract to the concrete" in Capital and its manuscripts, in Wu's reading, rests on explicit and implicit arguments for its own rigour. On the third layer, Wu argues that sensuous life is historical and concrete and is directly tied to the objective dimension (mode of production and productive forces). It therefore does not need abstract thought to secure its link to "essence". Marx's reflection on his own practice is described as the "embodied" presence of a historical "appearance–guidance" structure, which lets him question the preconditions of universality and avoid the "content trap" of idealism. Wu concludes that Marx's epistemology is itself the justification of thoroughgoing materialism. Read the original if you want a compact, philosophically dense statement of why Marx's thought contains an epistemological dimension beyond the modern subject–object model.

We must keep in mind that high-quality development is the hard truth of the new era 必须牢记高质量发展是新时代的硬道理 Fan Peng Fan Peng's commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (11 February 2025) takes up Xi Jinping's statement that high-quality development is the "hard truth" (硬道理) of the new era. Fan argues that the statement is a new development of Xi Jinping's economic thought and a fresh expression of Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism in contemporary China. Around 1939 the hard truth was revolution against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism; in 1992 Deng Xiaoping's "development is the hard truth" answered the contradiction between material needs and backward production. The present formula answers the new principal contradiction and the shift from high-speed growth to high-quality development. Fan presents it as continuing Deng Xiaoping Theory while adding new demands. For implementation Fan calls for understanding the Two Establishes, strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence as the subjective force behind development, and fully applying the new development philosophy in practice. It is described as sustaining social stability, adding diversity to human civilization and supporting a shared future. Upholding and applying the systems view to promote high-quality employment 坚持和运用系统观促进高质量就业 Han Wei This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how universities should handle graduate employment. Creating a new form of human civilization through the coordinated development of the "five civilizations" 以“五大文明”协调发展创造人类文明新形态 Wei Xin Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that coordinated development of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization has created a new path of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization, this newspaper commentary asks what the "five civilizations" contribute. Wei argues that their harmonious advance gives Chinese modernization its comprehensive, coordinated, developmental and people-centred character. In the author's account, this marks a new height for Chinese civilization and enriches human civilizational progress. The article is organised into five sections, one for each civilization, followed by a short closing statement. Each section defines the civilization concerned as a foundation for the others, then describes what the author sees as China's distinctive path in that field. The sections cover the material base, political institutions, culture and values, livelihoods and social governance, and ecology. On material civilization, Wei points to Xi Jinping's economic thought and to new quality productive forces, which the author says reshape labour, the government–market relationship and capital allocation. On political civilization, the author contends that Chinese modernization surpasses the "endogenous difficulties" of the Western path, listing capital exploitation, alienated labour, polarization, environmental damage and expansionist plunder. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as going beyond Western "liberal democracy", which Wei says treats elections as the sole standard. On spiritual civilization, the author stresses the Two Integrations, which combine Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. On social and ecological civilization, Wei cites poverty alleviation, public services, grassroots governance, green development and participation in global environmental governance. Wei concludes that Chinese modernization unites economic prosperity, political democracy, cultural flourishing, social fairness and good ecology. In the author's view, it has overcome the internal predicaments of conventional modernization and offers the world a distinctive route, contributing to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars present Chinese modernization as a civilizational alternative to Western modernization.

Cultural identity: Huayan studies from the perspective of the Chinese national community 文化认同：中华民族共同体视野下的华严学 Wang Jing This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks how Huayan (Avatamsaka) Buddhist learning helped bind China's peoples together over a thousand years. Wang Jing argues that Huayan thought, moving from the western frontier to the interior and then to the northern frontier, became a spiritual resource for fostering a sense of the Chinese national community and for the integrated historical process of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the westward origins of the Huayan Sutra, from translations by Central Asian and Dunhuang-born translators in the Han to Jin periods to the full sutras obtained from Khotan. The second follows the spread of Huayan northwards under the Liao, Western Xia, Jin and Yuan. The third examines Huayan's philosophy of perfect interfusion and its influence on later Chinese thought. Wang's central claim is that Huayan served as a cultural bond between the interior and the frontiers. The author notes that the sixty-fascicle translation of 418 and the eighty-fascicle version of 699, produced under Empress Wu Zetian with the Khotanese monk Siksananda, linked Khotan and the Central Plains and moved Huayan from sutra study to a formal school. In the Liao, Western Xia, Jin and Yuan, rulers and monks adopted and translated Huayan texts, which Wang reads as direct inheritance of interior Huayan during periods of division. Philosophically, the doctrine of the 'four dharma realms', the 'six characteristics' and the 'ten mysteries', summed up in 'one is all, all is one', is said to dissolve oppositions and justify the coexistence of different peoples. Wang adds that Cheng Hao, Zhu Xi, Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming drew on Huayan ideas. Wang concludes that Huayan's perfect interfusion promoted exchange and blending among peoples, contributed to the pattern of diversity within unity of the Chinese nation, and underpinned a Neo-Confucian cultural system that supported the Chinese national community in the Song to Qing periods. The piece calls Huayan an important intellectual resource for forging a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Buddhist history is being linked to the contemporary discourse on national unity and ethnic integration.

Understanding common prosperity in step with the times 与时俱进地理解共同富裕 Ma Junfeng Wang Xinwei This short commentary argues that common prosperity must be understood in both content and form in step with the times. Ma and Wang hold that, now that the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects is complete, the concept differs qualitatively from what it meant three or four decades ago. The article has three sections. They take up common prosperity as a response to the aspiration for a better life in the new era, its basis in the socialist market economy, and the need to broaden and raise the richness of what is shared. The authors contend that once material scarcity has been overcome, the core issue is no longer opposition between rich and poor but differences in degrees of affluence. They cite per capita disposable income rising from 171 yuan in 1978 to 35,189 yuan in 2021, and Engel coefficients of 28.6 per cent (urban) and 32.7 per cent (rural). They argue that common prosperity rests on the socialist market economy and the Two Unwaverings, and that this economy is not simply "socialism plus a market economy". They also urge that shared public goods, such as transport, security, culture and ecological benefits, be counted alongside private wealth, and that digital sharing and less sensitivity to wealth gaps would help attract and develop talent. Ma and Wang conclude that the goal is reached through high-quality development, with all positive forces united. They link this to the strategies of rejuvenating the country through science and education and of strengthening it through talent. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Party-aligned scholars recast common prosperity around public goods, market institutions and talent.

Common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism 共同富裕是社会主义的本质要求 Qi Yanhong Qi Yanhong, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, argues that common prosperity is the fundamental principle and essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a defining feature of Chinese modernization. The author proposes building on the idealist dimension of Marx's political philosophy while drawing on China's practice of socialist modernization, in order to develop a more realistic political philosophy. The short commentary has three parts. It first sets out common prosperity as a goal of socialism, contrasting Marx and Engels's critique of capitalism with the Party's record from Mao Zedong to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then traces the shift in China's basic social structure from an egalitarian orientation to one oriented to fairness. Finally, it considers how common prosperity should be advanced in the new stage. Qi contends that capitalism, by its nature, produces polarisation between rich and poor, and that even Western welfare states serve to preserve the rule of capital. Socialist public ownership removes structural inequality and so provides the institutional precondition for common prosperity. Qi reads Deng Xiaoping's idea of letting some get rich first as grounding common prosperity in the development of productive forces. Marketisation has also brought social problems that, in Qi's account, now centre on how fairness and justice can promote common prosperity. For the new stage Qi proposes three measures: stronger state regulation of the market through taxation, social security and redistribution; stronger democracy and rule of law, including whole-process people's democracy; and socialist values of fairness, equality and community in place of Western individualism. Qi concludes that common prosperity ultimately depends on the people acting as builders, governors and evaluators together, on sound institutional design and legal rules, and on a social ethos of fairness and solidarity. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar links common prosperity to the contrast between socialist and capitalist modernization.

A political-philosophical interpretation of common prosperity 共同富裕的政治哲学诠释 Wang Lü This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what common prosperity means within Marxist political philosophy. Wang argues that common prosperity is a political project that goes beyond the difficulties of capitalist modernization. In the author's account it is a distinguishing mark of socialist political civilization, carrying the values of putting the people first and realising the people's longing for a better life. The article sets Marx's view against the tradition of modern Western political philosophy, drawing on Locke, Hobbes and Charles Taylor. It is organised in three sections: common prosperity as the basic precondition for people's free and all-round development, as a value narrative of fair sharing, and as an ideal social vision that unfolds step by step. Wang contends that Western political philosophy rests on an atomised individual driven by bodily wants, so that modernization becomes an arena of competing interests. Contractual procedural justice, built on the 'rational economic man', is said to weaken concern for concrete persons and the sense of community. Wang reads Marx's observation of paradoxical poverty amid growing wealth, and his statement that future production will aim at the prosperity of all, as the basis for common prosperity. On this reading it sublates procedural justice and capitalist poverty, and expresses a socialist justice of 'everyone participates, everyone benefits'. Wang concludes that Marx's common prosperity is not mere material accumulation or levelling. It is directed against the 'absolute poverty of the human essence' under the logic of capital and fetishism, and values active individuals with individuality and independence. It will be realised through historical practice, ending in each person's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese philosopher grounds the policy of common prosperity in Marx's critique of liberal individualism.

Common prosperity: China's "solution" for realising fairness and justice 共同富裕：实现公平正义的“中国方案” Wang Li Wang Li asks how China's experience of fairness and justice should be understood and theorised. The commentary argues that common prosperity is both a practice of fairness and justice and the "signature concept" and core category of a Chinese theory of it, and so offers a "Chinese solution" to the world. The piece has two parts. The first presents common prosperity as a great practice of socialist fairness and justice. The second turns to its theoretical elevation, arguing that this practice needs its own theory of justice. In the first part, Wang describes four steps: eliminating absolute poverty through the poverty-alleviation campaign; giving common prosperity broader content, covering material abundance, cultural and spiritual wealth, democracy, rule of law and the environment; relying on the advantages of the socialist system, including multi-level distribution through primary distribution, redistribution and third distribution; and following a two-stage road map from 2020 to 2035 and then to the middle of the century. Wang contends that only socialism can realise common prosperity, and that capitalist approaches to justice can amount only to reform and patching under private ownership. In the second part, Wang holds that China's achievements cannot be explained by any Western school of political philosophy or theory of justice. Common prosperity, in this account, draws on elements of Chinese philosophy and supplies the concepts for a systematic Chinese theory. Wang concludes that practice, achievements and theoretical summary together give common prosperity a solid scholarly basis as China's contribution on fairness and justice. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese academics present common prosperity as a theoretical category that stands apart from Western theories of justice.

Marx's critique of List from the perspective of common prosperity 共同富裕视角中马克思对李斯特的批判 Lin Zhao This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what happens to a nation whose modernization plan lacks common prosperity. Lin Zhao argues that Germany met this problem first, and that Marx's critique of Friedrich List shows how socialist modernization differs from capitalist modernization. The author presents this as a lesson for Chinese modernization. Lin first sets out List's national economics: it shifts economics from the growth of wealth to the growth of productive forces, and it proposes stage-based trade policy, including a customs union and protective tariffs for German industry. Lin then turns to Marx's reading notes on List and his remarks in The German Ideology. Lin's central claim is that List's national economics contains no 'nation'. List examined industry but not people, class relations or the relations of production. In Lin's account, protection benefited German capitalists while workers bore alienation as an unmentioned cost. Marx therefore saw List's 'mythical' harmonious nation as doomed under private property, much as Smith's mythical individual was. Lin adds that List's nationalism undermines itself, because workers' nationality, in Marx's words, is labour and self-sale. For this reason Marx refused to choose between free trade and tariff protection. Lin concludes that neither classical political economy nor List's theory can produce a nation that combines flourishing productive forces with internal unity. Marx's socialism offers the theoretical possibility, and Lin says its practice falls to Chinese modernization, which takes common prosperity as its basic requirement. Read the original if you want a brief account of how Marx's critique of List is used to support the Party's common prosperity agenda.

Common prosperity and shared coexistence 共同富裕与共同生存 Li Yitian In this short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (6 February 2025), Li Yitian asks how common prosperity relates to the broader human condition of living together. Li argues that common prosperity is a special and ideal form of "shared coexistence" (gongtong shengcun), one that requires material wealth, political will and a strong ethical commitment to equality, universal sufficiency and harmony. The piece has three parts. The first treats common prosperity as a vision. The second examines shared coexistence as the ordinary human condition. The third presents common prosperity as a high-quality form of coexistence. Li first holds that, as a vision, common prosperity remains a long-term goal, given the long duration of the primary stage of socialism. Citing Marx on civil society, Li argues that free markets grant individual rights but cannot deliver collective prosperity, and may even dissolve coexistence through competition. Collective prosperity therefore needs a force beyond market logic. Li then distinguishes three ordinary forms of coexistence: a stress response to external pressure, which is passive and temporary; a limited internal balance of interests, in which wealth gaps are tolerated; and an overall pattern of survival. None of these takes common prosperity as its aim. Li concludes that common prosperity demands prosperity for every individual, not just groups or society in aggregate. It rejects any hardening of social mobility channels and any evasion of the duty of the first-enriched to help the rest. It turns competitive coexistence into symbiotic coexistence, which Li reads as a sign of socialist China's persistence in seeking better paths for human society. Read the original if you want a brief philosophical framing of common prosperity as a quality of social existence rather than an economic indicator.

Vigorously enhancing national cultural soft power and the influence of Chinese culture 大力提升国家文化软实力和中华文化影响力 Liu Runan This newspaper commentary asks how China should raise its national cultural soft power and the influence of Chinese culture. Liu argues that this task, set out in Xi Jinping's October 2023 instruction and in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), is a basis for building a socialist cultural power and for Chinese modernization. The piece is organised around five requirements, each introduced with the word "must" and supported by statements from Xi Jinping from 2013, 2018, 2023 and 2024. They concern ideological guidance, traditional culture, international communication, China's image and civilisational exchange. Liu first holds that the work must be guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture and must draw on fine traditional culture, whose spiritual markers and creative energy should be distilled and renewed. Second, the author calls for rebuilding the international communication landscape. This means constructing Chinese discourse and narratives, using 5G, artificial intelligence and VR/AR, and building media clusters and an all-media matrix. Messages would be tailored to regions and audiences, with the Belt and Road Initiative as one setting. Third, China should promote its proposals and present itself as a credible, lovable and respectable country. In Liu's account, Xi's statements abroad already portray China as a civilised, Eastern, responsible and socialist major country. Liu concludes that China should deepen exchange and mutual learning among civilisations. Examples include translating foreign classics, hosting academic conferences and holding international film festivals. The aim is new cultural achievements that join past and present and link China and the West, adding value to Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the current official framework for cultural soft power and international communication.

Grasping the ecological-civilisation value and logic of Chinese modernization 准确把握中国式现代化的生态文明价值意蕴及逻辑理路 Wang Qing Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (February 2025), Wang Qing takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) formula that Chinese modernization is "a modernization of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature". Wang argues that this makes ecological civilisation a defining feature of Chinese modernization. In the article's account, it is neither the traditional industrial model of "civilisation without ecology" nor a copy of the Western path of "pollute first, clean up later", and it therefore has values and comparative advantages the Western model cannot match. The commentary is organised in four sections. The first deals with "lucid waters and lush mountains" and green productive forces; the second with institutions and mechanisms as the basic guarantee of green development; the third with the people-centred stance expressed in the pairing of ecology and livelihood; and the fourth with the joint development of digitalisation and ecologisation. Wang draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements on ecological civilisation. Wang's central move is to treat the ecological environment as an internal element of productive forces, so that protecting it is protecting productive forces. On this basis Wang identifies green productive forces with new quality productive forces, driven by green, low-carbon and circular technologies. Wang proposes intensive, innovation-led growth in place of extensive growth, a unified national market for carbon, water, energy and emission rights, regulated capital, and green skills among workers. A second move concerns institutions: the strictest rules and enforcement, clearly defined natural-resource property rights, and mechanisms for realising the value of ecological products. Wang further argues that ecological goods belong within livelihood and social justice, to be expanded through green productive forces and shared through the "three distributions". Finally, digital technologies such as AI, big data and digital twins are said to make ecological governance more precise, systematic and open. Wang concludes that Chinese modernization, by combining green productive forces, suitable production relations, ecological livelihood and digital-ecological transformation, offers a distinctive and superior model of human–nature harmony. The piece is a short programmatic commentary that sets out the current official line rather than engaging in debate. Read the original if you want a compact view of how Chinese scholars link green development, new quality productive forces, common prosperity and digitalisation within the discourse of ecological civilisation.

Firmly holding the main front of online ideology 牢牢守住网络意识形态主阵地 Zhao Yuanyuan Ye Benqian Zhao Yuanyuan and Ye Benqian take up how China should secure ideological work in cyberspace, which they call the main battlefield, main front and forefront of ideological struggle in the new era. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statements that there is no national security without cybersecurity and that control of online ideological leadership means safeguarding state sovereignty and political power, they argue that the Party must keep firm leadership, identify core problems, and build up mainstream ideas, culture, values, opinion and technology platforms. The piece is a short commentary first published by China Theory Net (Zhongguo lilun wang). After an opening on the strategic importance of online ideology, it is organised around seven imperatives, each beginning with the phrase 'must': steady the core of leadership, pinpoint the main problems, sing the main theme, cultivate mainstream culture, promote mainstream values, strengthen mainstream opinion, and build main platforms. A short closing section calls for study of Xi Jinping's thought on cultural work and on building a strong cyber power. The authors present online ideology as an extension of ideology into cyberspace, marked by virtuality, anonymity, hard-to-control spread, fragmentation and pan-entertainment. For them this calls for the principle of 'the Party manages the internet', with the Party coordinating government, enterprises, society and netizens, resisting capital's manipulation of technological innovation, and upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. They credit campaigns such as 'Qinglang' with improving the online environment but say the ideological struggle has not been decisively won. They warn of Western capitalist infiltration, information cocoons and opinion storms. Marxism, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the core socialist values are to lead online content, using party media and popular formats. Mainstream culture is to draw on traditional and revolutionary heritage and oppose historical nihilism. Authoritative information should crowd out rumours, and breakthroughs in core technologies such as chips, operating systems and quantum communication are needed, since the authors hold that whoever controls advanced network technology controls ideological leadership. The authors conclude that online ideological work is a 'war without gunsmoke' and that, in a line they quote, failing the internet test means failing the test of long-term rule. They propose persistent study of Xi Jinping Thought, firm Party leadership, Marxism's guiding position, and a technologically advanced security barrier, which they say will supply ideological backing for building a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese theoretical discourse frames internet governance as ideological security.

Using Xi Jinping's Fujian experience to build a "grand ideological and political course" Drawing on Fujian's distinctive strengths in teaching young students 发挥独特优势，善用习近平总书记在福建的探索实践成果建设“大思政课” Sun Qiaozhen This commentary, published on China Theory Net in February 2025, asks how the exploratory practice of General Secretary Xi Jinping during his years of work in Fujian can be used in the "grand ideological and political course" (da sizheng ke) for young students. Sun Qiaozhen argues that Fujian is an important place where Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era was nurtured and put into practice, and that telling these stories well helps students follow the leader's path and grasp the formation of the Thought. The article is organised in five parts, each presenting one aspect of Xi's Fujian record and then drawing a lesson for students. These are his style of leadership, his working style, his methods of thinking, his sincere devotion to the people, and his concrete practical achievements. Each part moves from Xi's work in Xiamen, Ningde and Fuzhou to what Sun describes as the continuation of the same qualities after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In Sun's account, Fujian examples show foresight, openness and innovation: lifting Ningde out of poverty, the Fuzhou "3820" strategic project, the Xiamen free-port-type special zone, and later the Belt and Road Initiative. They also show a pragmatic style of fieldwork, such as visiting all nine counties and cities of Ningde, and a systematic, dialectical way of thinking, including the idea that a "weak bird can fly first". Sun adds Xi's declared commitment to serve the people, the "Four Ten-Thousand Households" approach, and achievements such as "Digital Fujian", the ecological province concept and collective forest tenure reform. Sun concludes that these results show a great leader's growth and give students material for sensing the power of the Thought. Students are urged to adopt Xi as a model: to link personal prospects with the nation's fate, practise investigation and perseverance, master scientific thinking methods, stand with the people, and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how Fujian-based material is framed for Party-led ideological and political education of university students.

Telling the story of the peaceful character of Chinese modernization well 讲好中国式现代化的和平性故事 Wei Junquan Wei Junquan takes up the claim, set out in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), that Chinese modernization is a modernization that follows the path of peaceful development. The article links this to Xi Jinping's description of peacefulness as one of the "outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilization. Wei argues that this peaceful quality is a core cultural marker and a key point of support for building China's national image in international communication. The article has three parts. The first traces the intellectual sources of peacefulness in Confucian, Mohist and Daoist thought and in the history of China's external exchanges. The second looks at how peacefulness is enacted in communication practice, covering relations between humans and nature and relations between people and between states. The third sets out its contemporary value through a comparison between Chinese and Western civilizations. Wei draws on the Chinese-language literature on communication studies and Chinese modernization. Wei argues that the idea of harmony (he) runs through Chinese thought, from "harmonizing all nations" and the ideal of great harmony to the Tang, Ming and Qing formulations of ethnic and international relations. Examples such as Zhang Qian, Jianzhen and Zheng He are presented as reciprocal, peaceful exchange. In the second part, Wei contrasts a Western capitalist logic that treats nature as a resource to be dominated and so produces alienation with a Chinese view of nature as a medium and a subject, expressed in "harmony between humanity and nature". In international relations, Wei sets peaceful development against the "clash of civilizations" thesis, the law of the jungle, zero-sum games and hegemonism, and contrasts Western atomistic individualism with a Chinese holistic way of thinking. Wei cites other scholars to argue that Western capital accumulation involved colonial plunder and a hegemonic logic. Wei concludes that peacefulness draws on China's own historical development and on traditional culture, and also responds to survival and communication problems common to humankind. The article presents the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives, a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative as practices that show China's concern for world peace and offer a model different from Western modernization. Wei suggests that stressing peacefulness can strengthen the reach of Chinese civilization and help build a cooperative international environment. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese communication scholars link traditional ideas of harmony to current foreign-policy discourse and national-image building.

Raising urban safety and resilience through new-type urban infrastructure construction 以新型城市基础设施建设提升城市安全韧性 Li Zhao Writing in the People's Daily on 7 February 2025, Li Zhao asks how cities can become safer and more resilient as the risks they face grow more complex. The commentary argues that building new-type urban infrastructure, which combines new-generation information technology with urban construction and governance, is the route to resilient cities. It takes as its basis the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and a November 2024 central opinion that sets a goal of notable results by 2030. The piece first explains what new-type urban infrastructure does: it makes city operations safer, more orderly, smarter and more efficient, and it supports new quality productive forces and high-quality development. It then sets out four areas of work: government guidance, institutional mechanisms, scientific and technological innovation, and social participation. Party leadership is to run through all of them. On government guidance, Li calls for top-level design, integrated use of infrastructure to avoid duplicated construction, a standards and evaluation system, and risk-prevention and data-security mechanisms. On institutions, Li proposes breaking down data barriers, a diversified financing system with government investment as guide and enterprises as the main body, and life-cycle management that moves from one-way regulation toward collaborative governance. On innovation, Li urges breakthroughs in key technologies and multidisciplinary talent training. On participation, state-owned enterprises should lead, private firms should get fairer market access, and experts and residents should take part. Li concludes that these actors should each contribute their strengths so as to form a strong joint force for building resilient cities. The article is a policy-oriented explanation of official guidance, not an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy agenda for urban digital infrastructure and resilience in early 2025.

Building an open environment for scientific and technological innovation with global competitiveness 打造具有全球竞争力的科技创新开放环境 Wu Yulong Writing in Guangming Daily, Wu argues that Chinese modernization depends on the modernization of science and technology, and that high-quality development needs innovation to create new momentum. Citing the Central Commission for Deepening Overall Reform (June 2024) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), the commentary holds that building an open innovation environment with global competitiveness is essential to self-reliant innovation and is an inherent requirement of developing new quality productive forces. The short piece sets out three areas of work: deepening reform of the science and technology system, gathering innovation talent, and integrating into global innovation networks. Each is presented as a list of policy measures. On institutional reform, Wu treats major technological innovation as the core of new quality productive forces. The author calls for better planning and management of science and technology programmes, more investment in basic research, and a stronger position for enterprises as the main innovators. On talent, Wu calls the workforce of researchers the first resource of innovation and proposes training domestic talent through closer links between education, industry and research, while recruiting top overseas talent under more open policies. On openness, Wu cites Xi Jinping on taking the initiative to join global innovation networks. The author proposes wider institutional opening, cross-border innovation programmes, joint science and technology cooperation zones under the Belt and Road Initiative, and stronger intellectual property management and technology security. Wu concludes that these measures together would build a more coordinated, open and efficient innovation system that supports high-quality development. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary links science and technology policy, talent policy and international openness to new quality productive forces.

Ideological and political courses told in four narratives: teaching comprehensively deepening reform in depth, thoroughly and vividly 四重叙事的思政课：讲深讲透讲活全面深化改革 Liu Xingyun This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, asks how university ideological and political courses can teach the policy of comprehensively deepening reform more effectively. Liu Xingyun proposes the narrative teaching method, which the author describes as combining knowledge, emotion, will and action, and which is said to work through lived situations, carried meaning and multi-way interaction. The thesis is that teachers should use four kinds of narrative (image, emotion, history and innovation) to tell the reform story in depth, thoroughly and vividly, and so raise the practical effect of moulding students' ideals and character. The piece has four numbered sections, one for each narrative.
