Image narrative covers the achievements of reform and opening up; emotional narrative covers the great spirit of reform and opening up; historical narrative covers the basic laws of comprehensively deepening reform; and innovation narrative covers the blueprint for further reform. Each section gives concrete classroom suggestions, drawing on the decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and on remarks by Xi Jinping. On image narrative, Liu urges using charts, paintings, documentaries, films and generative-AI animations so that reform results show "principle in the picture", beauty and moral character. For emotional narrative, the author draws on Xi's call for teachers to have feelings for family and country, for transmitting the Way, and for benevolence. Liu proposes telling stories of reformers, using role-play, and turning the reform spirit into both moral qualities and action. For historical narrative, the author asks teachers to adopt developmental, systemic and dialectical thinking: comparing reforms across history, linking course content in Marxist principles and Chinese modern history, and explaining both achievements and unresolved problems. For innovation narrative, Liu recommends telling stories of scientific teams, adopting the online and humorous speech style of young people, and using VR, AR and XR. Liu concludes that these four narratives together can build an approach to education that moves from knowledge to practice and from emotion to deeper commitment. The author expects this to strengthen students' identification with reform, their confidence in theory, and their patriotism and innovative spirit. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Chinese university teachers are being advised to turn Party policy on reform into classroom practice.

Deepening national defence education for all in the new era and gathering positive energy for loving the country and strengthening the military 深化新时代全民国防教育 汇聚爱国强军正能量 Lu Xiaoqing Writing in the People's Daily on 6 February 2025, Lu Xiaoqing, head of the Jiangxi Provincial Party Committee's Publicity Department, asks how the province should put the newly revised National Defence Education Law into practice. The law was adopted by the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress. Lu starts from Xi Jinping's statements that national defence belongs to the whole people and that education in it is a foundation for a strong defence and army. The article argues that Jiangxi should use its revolutionary heritage to apply the law and "gather positive energy" for loving the country and strengthening the military. This is a short commentary by a provincial official, organised under three headings. The first covers a multi-level education system; the second, wider channels and vehicles for education; the third, a work structure with institutional guarantees. Each section opens by citing what the revised law now requires, then lists measures for Jiangxi, with references to local programmes, planning documents and sites. On the education system, Lu calls for targeting three groups. These are leading cadres, who would be trained through Party study groups, Party schools and a graded training system that extends to state-enterprise executives, school principals and media heads. Young people, the group Lu calls the top priority, would be reached through the "big ideological and political course" reform, model defence schools, "red study tours" and military-skills experiences. The whole population would be reached through legal publicity and the integration of defence education into cultural and civilised-practice activities. On channels, Lu proposes telling defence stories through converged media, new films and television series and model figures. Lu also proposes immersive digital exhibitions at the province's roughly 2,900 revolutionary sites, and a red-heritage brand built on research into the Jinggangshan and Soviet-area spirit. On organisation, Lu stresses Party leadership. Under the revised law, defence education duties formerly shared among the military and local governments are unified under the Party Central Committee and local Party committees. Lu proposes revising the Jiangxi Defence Education Regulations, strengthening military–civilian coordination through joint meetings and open-barracks events, and building an expert pool. Lu also proposes budget lines and donations for funding, and putting defence education into the 15th Five-Year Plan, performance assessments and ideological inspections. Lu's stated aim is for caring about, loving, building and defending national defence to become a common social practice in Jiangxi. Read the original if you want a worked example of how a provincial Party leader turns a national law on defence education into concrete local measures and institutional targets.

Empowering the study of Chinese civilization with digital-intelligence methods 以数智方法赋能中华文明研究 Chen Yunsong Writing in People's Daily, Chen Yunsong asks how big data and artificial intelligence can be used to deepen research on Chinese civilization and the fine traditional culture it carries. Citing Xi Jinping's calls for deeper study of Chinese civilization and for the creative transformation of traditional culture, Chen argues that 'digital-intelligence' methods should complement, not replace, traditional humanistic scholarship. The piece is a short commentary, not a research article. The article is organised in four parts: scientific measurement of culture and civilization; revealing the deep structure of civilizational texts; capturing the beauty of cultural heritage; and strengthening civilization studies through the principle of upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground. Chen's examples include book-corpus word frequencies, topic modelling of Tang and Qing poetry, joint image–text analysis of literati painting, and Nanjing University's digital atlas of Chinese ancient cities. Chen's central claim is that soft indicators such as cultural influence and renown are hard to measure with questionnaires because of researcher bias, whereas large-scale book, internet, media and academic data allow multidimensional indices of cultural symbols. Topic models and deep learning can survey corpora no individual scholar could read, for example the roughly 50,000 surviving Tang poems, and make deep structures visible. For heritage, historical satellite images, lidar, drones and GIS can rebuild old city fabric and move protection from static records to dynamic monitoring. Chen calls this approach 'distant reading of culture' and likens its relation to traditional scholarship to that of telescope and microscope. Chen concludes that the method can help correct bias in Western databases and large language models, speed the building of China's independent knowledge system in philosophy and social sciences, and raise the discourse power of Chinese civilization globally. The author also notes limits, namely high technical thresholds and dependence on massive data and complex algorithms, so it must be combined with traditional methods. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how computational humanities is being framed within China's cultural-confidence and cultural-subjectivity agenda.

Deepening the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project in the new era 深入推进新时代马克思主义理论研究和建设工程 Huang Zhaoquan Marking the 20th anniversary of the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project, Huang Zhaoquan takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction on the project's new-era direction. The commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2025, argues that universities should use their strengths to promote the project's high-quality development while adhering to fundamental principles and innovating. Huang sets out three areas of work for universities: building the discipline, training teachers, and serving society. Universities are described as key sites of the project, with advantages in translating classic works, theoretical interpretation, textbook and discipline systems, and talent training. On discipline building, Huang calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position, strengthening the first-level discipline of Marxist theory, and combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and traditional culture. Research should focus on major theoretical and practical questions around deepening reform and Chinese modernization, and on building an independent Chinese system of knowledge. On teachers, Huang calls for a corps that is politically strong, theoretically capable and morally sound, with faith in Marxism rooted in teachers before students. On social service, Huang proposes problem-oriented research, popularising the Party's innovative theory in plain language, and teacher participation in Party and government decision consultation. Huang concludes that these measures would turn the discipline's strengths into practical contributions to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, backed by funding and evaluation reforms. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party leader translates Xi Jinping's instruction into institutional tasks for Marxist theory programmes.

The world significance of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的世界意义 Yang Guangbin This commentary, published in the People's Daily in February 2025, asks what Chinese modernization means beyond China. Yang Guangbin argues that it has changed China itself, rewritten the paradigm of world modernization and created a new form of human civilization. The piece has three sections. The first compares Chinese modernization with Western modernization and traces China's own 'relay race' from the founding of the People's Republic through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second discusses benefits to the Global South. The third turns to civilizational questions. Yang characterises Western modernization as monopoly-based: it spread the capitalist 'modern world system' through force and industrialization, and, citing Thomas Piketty, channelled large flows of income from the Global South to wealthy countries. In Yang's reading, US containment of Chinese technology reflects an effort to keep a monopoly on advanced productive forces. By contrast, the article credits China's market, industrial base and independent R&D with breaking such monopolies. It cites low-cost smartphones and photovoltaics, Chinese firms' role in mobile broadband (Mexican internet use rising from 44% to 75%, 2014–2023) and aid projects that it says strengthen governance in recipient states. Yang concludes that Chinese modernization, rooted in traditional culture and the essence of scientific socialism, offers a model of shared development, common security and mutual learning among civilizations rather than conflict. It is presented as an example for Global South countries seeking independent modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily framing of Chinese modernization as an alternative to the Western path.

China explores a new model of global development 中国探索全球发展新模式 Li Xiaoyun Xu Xiuli This commentary, published in the People's Daily, asks what path of development can replace the Western model, which the authors say has lost its capacity to guide sustainable global development. Li and Xu argue that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers the world a new development model and path. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statement that no single modernization model or standard exists. It then moves through three sections: the three global initiatives and the Belt and Road Initiative as practical expressions of a plural development model; a critique of the Western model's single, one-dimensional modernity; and an account of how Chinese modernization surpasses it, with the China–Africa partnership as the main example. The authors trace the Western model to the age of exploration and describe it as producing North–South domination, dependence, widening inequality and ecological damage. Against this, they present Chinese modernization as marked by strong leadership and long-term planning, common prosperity, balanced material and cultural progress, harmony between humanity and nature, peaceful development and strategic resolve. They cite the China–Laos railway, Central Asian energy cooperation, and wind and solar equipment exports as evidence. They also point to the basic socialist economic system, in which public ownership underpins fairness and the non-public sector drives vitality. Li and Xu conclude that Chinese modernization is leading Global South countries toward a fairer, more sustainable and more inclusive path, and that it supports a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary contrasts Chinese modernization with the Western model for an international development audience.

Building a higher-level rule-of-law China 建设更高水平的法治中国 Zhang Wenxian Zhang Wenxian, a senior jurist, asks what is meant by the call to build a "higher-level rule-of-law China". The phrase first appeared as a task in the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and was restated by Xi Jinping in August 2024. Zhang argues that it amounts to building a higher-level socialist rule-of-law state, and that its aim is a modernized "country strong through law". The piece was published in Beijing Daily in January 2025. Zhang says the "higher level" has three progressive aspects: making all areas of state work subject to law, building a China of "good law and good governance", and implementing a strategy of becoming a country strong through law (fazhi qiangguo). The article then describes six features of such a country and ends with an assessment of China's present position. On the first aspect, Zhang lists four tasks: placing national work, state governance, specialised legal work and domestic and foreign-related rule of law all on a legal track. On the second, Zhang contrasts instrumentalist legal culture in ancient China and formalist Western legal culture with a model of "good law and good governance". Good law is scientific, embodies good values, is well drafted and is well implemented. Zhang presents China's shift from "legal system" to "rule of law" as a move from formal rule of law to a combination of formal and substantive rule of law. On the third aspect, Zhang traces the idea to the Legalist thinker Han Feizi and the "strengthening the state by upholding law" tradition, which Xi has cited. Zhang adds that the Central Committee has not yet formally proposed "strong through law", though Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law already contains it. The six features include law as a core social value, the authority of the Constitution, protection of rights and restraint of power, strong voice in global governance, and integration of law with digital technology. Zhang concludes that China is already a "big country in law", having built a legal system in 45 years from the "seven laws in one day" of 1979, but is not yet strong through law. The shift from the first to the second is described as a historic strategic transformation that demands great effort. Only then, Zhang argues, can the "rule-of-law dream" and the "strong-country dream" flourish together. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Chinese legal theorist interprets the official goal of a higher-level rule-of-law China.

Promoting new results in the Party's discipline building 推动党的纪律建设不断取得新成效 Deng Yifei Zhang Licheng Zhang Xiaobing This commentary, published in the PLA Daily on 27 January 2025, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Deng, Zhang and Zhang argue that discipline building must occupy a prominent place within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and must be pursued persistently, strictly and regularly in order to produce new results. The piece is organised in three parts. The first explains why discipline building matters at present, the second sets out the main ideas Xi Jinping has put forward since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and the third lists practical measures for the new journey. The authors give three reasons for the importance of discipline. It is, they say, necessary to solve the problems unique to a large party, such as keeping unity of thought and will and a healthy political ecology. It is also needed to preserve the Party's vanguard character and purity under long-term rule, and to let the Party's self-reform lead the social revolution of Chinese modernization. They then summarise Xi's ideas: discipline as the fundamental means of governing the Party, political discipline and political rules as the first priority, a strict tone with no leniency and no exemption for the many or the minor, and a balance of strict management with care and encouragement. Here they cite the Two Establishes, the Two Upholds and the "four forms" of supervision and discipline enforcement. On practice, the authors call for continuous discipline education so that members know the Party constitution and regulations and respect boundaries. They also call for firm enforcement, so that rules become a rigid constraint, and for a chain of responsibility in which Party secretaries bear primary responsibility and leaders, the "key minority", set an example. They present discipline building as a long and arduous task, because full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is "always on the road". Read the original if you want a concise example of how military-affiliated Party writers present the official line on discipline building after the 2025 plenum.

A theoretical examination of building an original academic system for Chinese philosophy 构建中国哲学原创性学术体系的学理审视 Wu Xiangdong Wu Xiangdong takes up the task of building an independent body of knowledge in Chinese philosophy and social science, which he treats as resting on an original academic system for Chinese philosophy. Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Wu argues that the task can only be advanced by first clarifying three concepts in the formulation: "academic system", "originality of Chinese philosophy" and "construction". The article proceeds through these three keywords in turn. It first separates the academic system from the discipline system and the discourse system. It then grounds the originality of Chinese philosophy in the question of autonomy and subjectivity, drawing on Xi Jinping's remarks on the matter. Finally, it asks who should do the building and by what method. Wu defines the discipline system as the institutional platform, the academic system as the core content (an organic whole of concepts, categories, propositions and methods) and the discourse system as its form of expression, which also carries discourse power. Philosophy, in Wu's account, is the theoretical self-awareness of a nation's practice, so China's own path of Chinese modernization requires a philosophy of its own. Wu cites Fairbank's later revision of his "impact–response" model as support for the view that China's modernization has internal sources. On method, Wu names the Two Integrations as the main route and applies them to three relations. In the relation of past and present, Wu calls for critical inheritance of traditional philosophy so that Marxism becomes Chinese and tradition becomes modern. In the relation of China and the West, Wu calls for openness and mutual learning. In the relation of theory and practice, Wu holds that China's philosophy must come from the practice of Chinese modernization, be tested in it, and be expressed in language the people understand. Wu concludes that Chinese philosophers, as the agents of construction, must be encouraged to develop their own subjectivity. Wu notes that philosophy and social science in China still have numbers but lack top-level masters, and calls for more effort to cultivate them. The piece is a programmatic statement of how the official goal of an autonomous knowledge system could be understood in philosophy. Read the original if you want a concise Party-aligned account of how Chinese philosophers conceive the relation between academic system, discourse and the Two Integrations.

Advancing new quality productive forces faster through deep industrial transformation and upgrading 以产业深度转型升级推动新质生产力加快发展 Cao Wenhong In this commentary for Guangming Daily (27 January 2025), Cao Wenhong argues that deep industrial transformation and upgrading is one of the key forms through which new quality productive forces develop. Cao holds that it must be the main direction of effort if new quality productive forces are to be developed faster. The piece opens with a definition of deep transformation and upgrading and a statement of the problems facing China's industrial structure. It then has two numbered sections. The first covers how industry itself should change: upgrading traditional industries and promoting coordination among industries. The second treats the institutional and policy side, arguing that the task is also a reform question. Cao notes that traditional industries remain the base of the economy but suffer from distorted factor prices, low-end lock-in in value chains and pollution. The author calls for applying artificial intelligence and big data, green and low-carbon transition, closer cooperation along industrial chains and stronger links between enterprises. Cao stresses, citing Xi Jinping, that developing new quality productive forces does not mean abandoning traditional industry, and that local conditions and one-size-fits-all models must be considered. On institutions, Cao distinguishes strategic emerging industries from future industries and proposes different policy support for each, including pilot zones for the latter. The article also calls for stronger top-level design. Cao concludes that the Party's unified leadership, a new whole-nation system, a unified national market and stable, transparent, law-based policy should make deep industrial upgrading and new quality productive forces reinforce each other. Read the original if you want a short official-style statement of how industrial policy is linked to the new quality productive forces agenda in early 2025.

Building a Chinese discourse system of logic Lessons from Western research on ancient Chinese logical thought 构建中国逻辑话语体系 Li Dubai Wang Kexi Li Dubai and Wang Kexi ask how contemporary China can build its own discourse system of logic, and argue that tracing Western scholarship on ancient Chinese logic offers useful guidance. They treat Chinese logic as one of the three source traditions of world logic, alongside Greek logic and Indian hetuvidya (yinming), and as basic to Chinese philosophy. Their thesis is that Chinese logicians should draw on Western research while grounding their work in Chinese cultural and historical context and avoiding uncritical "interpreting China through the West". The piece, a commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (25 January 2025), surveys Western research in broad phases. It begins with missionary sinology and James Legge's translations, then the early twentieth century, when Hu Shi and Feng Youlan mediated Chinese thought to the West. It moves on to the 1950s–60s, when professional philosophers took over and the "China has no logic" view prevailed, and then to the 1970s onward, when scholars such as A. C. Graham, Chad Hansen, Chung-Ying Cheng and Christoph Harbsmeier advanced the field. It ends with twenty-first-century work. The authors make three main moves. First, they say early Western and Chinese-émigré scholarship either overlooked logic or, as with Hu Shi, explained Mohist ideas by analogy with Western deduction and inductive methods, which they judge did not bring out Chinese logic's distinctiveness. They quote Bochenski and others to show that the 1960s denial of Chinese logic rested on a narrow, Aristotelian idea of logic. Second, they credit later scholars with recognising its richness: the 1973 New Encyclopaedia Britannica entry, Cheng's three levels of study, Ian Johnston's 2009 complete translation of the Mozi, and interdisciplinary and culturally situated approaches. Third, they criticise formalising studies that presuppose a rigorous two-valued extensional system, ignoring the language and cultural setting, and note the concentration on the pre-Qin period at the expense of later developments, including the reception of Indian and Western logic in China. The authors conclude that Western studies give Chinese logic a reference frame and an "other" perspective, and that China's growing international standing offers a chance to spread Chinese logical thought globally. They call for research that pursues modern transformation vertically and mutual learning between China and the West horizontally, producing a three-dimensional model linking past and present, China and the West. They also urge cultural confidence and a base in local history. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-scholarly overview of Western sinological work on Chinese logic and of how Chinese logicians propose to respond to it.

Deepening reform to promote the deep integration of the real and digital economies 持续深化改革促进“实数”深度融合发展 Xiang Xiaomei This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how institutional reform can promote the deep integration of the real (physical) economy and the digital economy, abbreviated in Chinese as "shi-shu" integration. Xiang Xiaomei argues that such integration should be the main line for developing new quality productive forces and will supply lasting momentum for Chinese modernization. The piece takes its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which made high-quality development the first task of building a modern socialist country. The article has three parts. It first explains what integration means and why it matters globally and domestically. It then sets out three ways integration serves new quality productive forces: breakthrough innovation, the upgrading of traditional industries, and cross-sector cooperation. It closes with four policy areas that need strengthening. Xiang stresses that the real economy is the foundation of the national economy and that digital technology must strengthen it ("以数强实") rather than drift away from it. Integration is not blind or superficial digitisation, the author says, but the use of digital knowledge and information as key production factors, driven by cloud computing, AI, blockchain and the Internet of Things. Xiang holds that integration shortens R&D cycles and lowers uncertainty, helps traditional industries raise total factor productivity on both supply and demand sides, and gives rise to platform economy, smart agriculture, humanoid robots, quantum information and the low-altitude economy. The author acknowledges remaining weak points and says integration needs managerial and institutional change as well as technological innovation. Xiang proposes four sets of policies. The first is a policy system for digital technology innovation, drawing on the new whole-nation system and integrated reform of education, science and talent. The second covers digital industrialisation and industrial digitalisation, including support for manufacturers and small firms and an "AI Plus" initiative. The third is the marketisation of data factors, through national computing infrastructure, data trading rules and solutions to problems of data ownership and sharing. The fourth is a supportive framework of financial reform, a unified national market, high-level opening up and data security, because new productive forces require matching new relations of production. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a provincial Chinese academic presents the policy agenda linking the digital economy to new quality productive forces.

Upholding the dialectical unity of breaking down and establishing in reform 在改革中坚持破和立的辩证统一 Qin Long Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Qin Long examines the reform methodology that Xi Jinping has summarised as upholding the dialectical unity of 'breaking down' (po) and 'establishing' (li). The formula calls for doing both together, establishing before breaking, and breaking what must go only once its replacement is in place. Qin argues that this approach is an important expression of Marxist materialist dialectics and a guide for deepening reform as part of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first explains the po–li relation through three dialectical laws. The second traces the idea through Marx and Engels, Lenin, and the Chinese Communist Party's history from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi. The third turns to the present stage of 'further deepening reform comprehensively', which Qin describes as a tough phase of reform. Qin argues that po and li are opposed, since strengthening one weakens the other, yet also unified: breaking without establishing is blind destruction, and establishing without breaking leaves no room for the new. In terms of quantitative and qualitative change, the new germinates inside the old, and old habits persist after the new appears, so the two alternate in cycles. Under the negation of the negation, breaking is sublation, discarding what is ossified while keeping what is useful. Qin reads the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse in Marx and Engels as a po–li process. Lenin's insistence on smashing the old state machine, and his adoption of the New Economic Policy, are presented as the same logic applied in practice. The Party's history is read as a continuous application of this logic. Qin concludes that reform today must be systemic and integrated rather than piecemeal. Its sequencing and timing should seek a balance between removing old ills and setting up new institutions, and the formula should be applied through the principle 'establish first, break later'. Establishing first means setting out the main direction and framework so as to stabilise expectations, growth and employment. Breaking later means screening out old systems and policies that no longer fit the aims of transforming the growth model and improving quality and efficiency. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how the Party presents this reform method as rooted in Marxist dialectics and in its own history.

Using the deep integration of the digital and real economies to speed up new quality productive forces 以数实深度融合为抓手加快发展新质生产力 He Jianfeng Chen Xiruo This newspaper commentary asks how new quality productive forces can be developed faster. He and Chen answer that the deep integration of the digital economy and the real economy, which they call 'digital-real integration', should be the main lever. They describe it as a typical form of new quality productive forces, resting on digital technology and the use of data as a factor of production. They cite Xi Jinping's Politburo study session and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as the policy basis. The article is organised around four dimensions of integration: technology, factors of production, industry and institutions. Each section explains how integration drives new quality productive forces and then lists measures to advance it. On technology, the authors say digital tools shorten R&D cycles and create a closed loop of research, production and feedback. They call for breakthroughs in core technologies through the new-type whole-nation system and for faster conversion of results into production. On factors, they argue that data-centred recombination of factors needs clear data property rights, a unified market, and the smart upgrading of labour, capital and land. On industry, they call for digital transformation of traditional sectors, cross-sector integration of business forms, and a modern industrial system. On institutions, they argue that new production relations must suit the new forces. They assign roles to government (standards and infrastructure), the market (supply and demand for digital goods) and enterprises (integrated business processes). The authors conclude that integration across all four dimensions would produce a unified and efficient ecosystem for developing new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a short, policy-oriented example of how Chinese economists link the digital economy to the official agenda of new quality productive forces.

Exploring a new path for coordinated urban–rural and regional development in Guangdong 探索广东城乡区域协调发展新路径 Yue Sheng Yue Sheng's commentary, first published in the People's Daily in January 2025, asks how Guangdong can tackle uneven urban–rural and regional development, which Xi Jinping has called the province's biggest obstacle to high-quality development. The author argues that the "Hundred-County, Thousand-Town, Ten-Thousand-Village High-Quality Development Project" (the "Hundred-Thousand-Ten Thousand Project") is a provincial-level innovation in Chinese modernization. In Yue's account, after several years of practice it has produced results and experience that can be drawn on elsewhere. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the project matters, the second reports results under four headings, and the third sets out lessons. Yue presents the project as modelled on the earlier "Ten Million Project" and centred on the county as the point of leverage. The four headings are county economies, town renewal, village revitalisation and urban–rural integration. In the first part, Yue describes the project as key to regional coordination, county vitality, rural revitalisation and grassroots governance. Guangdong is said to promote strong counties, which in turn lift towns and villages, under the Party's overall leadership. The results come mostly as figures the author reports. They include 32 counties growing faster than the provincial average in the first half of 2024, 15 industrial transfer platforms and 124 towns among China's top thousand. They also include 22 national modern agricultural industrial parks and a 11.4 billion yuan provincial special fund for 2024. Yue distils five lessons. These are combining an effective market with an effective government under Party leadership, following the new development philosophy and building new urban–rural relations, and putting people first and mobilising society. The last two are using reform to remove the urban–rural dual structure, and persistence through the "one-three-five-ten" timetable of goals. Yue concludes that Guangdong will keep pursuing the project to offer its experience to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an official-style overview of Guangdong's county-centred rural strategy, with the provincial statistics and policy mechanisms it cites.

The "state" perspective on building Chinese modernization 中国式现代化建设的“国家”视角 Wang Jiangcheng This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (24 January 2025) asks what role the state plays in building Chinese modernization. Wang Jiangcheng argues that the state's capacity to set development goals, govern effectively and safeguard security is central to realising the Party's task of building a modern socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised under three headings: national development goals, state governance effectiveness, and national security capacity. Each is tied to Party documents, including the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). On development, Wang says the "Five-sphere Integrated Plan" gives development a growing holistic character, with the countryside and ethnic border regions named as the two areas that must be broken through. Urban–rural integration is presented as the basic strategy for rural modernization. In border regions, the Party's line of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation is said to give all reform and development its meaning. On governance, Wang describes a "developmental governance" model and argues that institutional strengths must be converted into governance effectiveness, with Party leadership as the fundamental political guarantee and the rule of law as the path. On security, Wang holds that without national security there can be no modernization, and singles out non-traditional threats such as information security, national identity in ethnic and religious fields, and international public opinion. Wang concludes that the three capacities together underpin Chinese modernization, and that security work needs stronger core competitiveness in the fields mentioned. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line overview of how Party scholars frame the state's developmental, governance and security roles, including its emphasis on rural and ethnic border regions.

Telling the story of the Chinese national community to the world 对外讲好中华民族共同体故事 Li Tao Li Tao takes up how China should communicate abroad the idea of forging a sense of community for the Chinese nation, which the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has made the main thread of ethnic work. Li argues that some Western states and media use the language of human rights to weaken the cohesion of this community, and that China must build an external discourse system to answer what the author calls Western media's "discourse hegemony" on ethnic issues. This short commentary has two parts. The first sets out three dimensions of external discourse: Chinese civilization, the Chinese political system, and human development. The second proposes practical routes: diversifying communicators, selecting discourse texts, and technological change. On the three dimensions, Li calls for stories of exchanges and integration among peoples, from Zhao Wuling's adoption of nomad dress to Emperor Xiaowen's reforms of the Northern Wei. Li also calls for stories of ethnic unity and progress under China's institutions, to escape the "Western-centrism" trap, and for promoting a community with a shared future for mankind in terms foreign audiences can accept. On practice, Li finds that communication now relies mainly on official actors using declaratory, policy and combative language, which lacks warmth and depth. The author urges a larger role for civil and academic voices, agenda-setting on human rights instead of merely appealing to facts, and a shift from "borrowing a boat" to "building a boat" through Chinese-owned international platforms. Li concludes that these measures would raise the effectiveness of external communication and help build a fairer global communication order. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-education writing frames international communication on ethnic issues.

The Belt and Road Initiative reconstructs international communication capacity “一带一路”重构国际传播力 Wang Min Wang Min, writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how China can overcome its difficulty in making its voice heard internationally. The author argues that since the Second World War the international communication order has been dominated by Western developed states, leaving developing countries in economic dependence and what the article calls cultural colonisation. Wang contends that the Belt and Road Initiative offers China a new opening to rebuild its communication capacity and to change that order, in the context of building a community with a shared future for mankind. This short commentary is organised around three headings: economic foundation, cultural guidance and media reinforcement. Each is presented as a source of a different strength in China's international communication. On the economic side, Wang argues that infrastructure and investment projects reshape city structures and trade links, weaken existing dependency relations and give China concrete, visible achievements to point to. The author cites National Bureau of Statistics data on rising trade with partner countries and says these results undermine the Western "power expansion" reporting frame. On culture, Wang points to the digital Silk Road, the Sino-Saudi animated film Kong Xiaoxi and Hakim, and regular Belt and Road festivals and expos, arguing that communication shifts from government-led to multi-actor, so that storytellers become the world rather than China alone. On media, Wang calls for more multilingual reporting and says themes such as the green Belt and Road widen the content of Chinese media. Wang concludes that the initiative is an international communication practice under the community with a shared future for mankind, expressing both hard and soft power. The author holds that it gives developing countries visibility as concrete economies and cultures rather than a vague group. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars link the Belt and Road Initiative to discourse power and international communication.

Understanding and advancing the development of new quality productive forces through systems thinking 以系统思维理解和推进新质生产力发展 Yan Guohua Yan Guohua, writing in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, argues that new quality productive forces should be understood and promoted through systems thinking. In Yan's account, they are not a simple combination of advanced productive forces and industrial structure but a complex systematic undertaking. It depends on iterating new technologies and industries and on a coordinated leap in the related elements, so it calls for overall planning and a macro perspective. The short commentary is organised in three parts. It first sets out the systemic features of new quality productive forces, then their systemic value and goals, and finally a path for advancing them. Throughout, it builds on Xi Jinping's statements on the subject and on the idea of the systems approach as a basic way of thinking and working. Yan reads the concept through three lenses: its internal elements, its form of development and its conditions of formation. Internally, it follows an "elements–structure–function" logic built on labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimised combination. In form, it is a deep transformation that couples economic, cultural, social and ecological dimensions rather than a local upgrade of traditional productive forces. On goals, Yan holds that its underlying logic is the new development philosophy, high-quality development, Chinese modernization and the people's needs for a better life. Productive forces are also described as the "key" to historical materialism. Yan presents five paths: renewing ideas, including avoiding a rush into the field and the creation of bubbles; reforming institutions and mechanisms to remove blockages; applying digital and intelligent technologies; raising the quality of talent; and improving the wider social atmosphere. Yan concludes that the whole of society and many actors must act together, since a change in one element affects the whole. The social atmosphere should encourage innovation, openness and tolerance of failure, and should support sound evaluation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary on new quality productive forces is framed through Xi Jinping's statements and the systems approach.

Public space as the fullest expression of the core meaning of the "people's city" concept 公共空间充分彰显人民城市理念的核心要义 Li Jun Li Jun asks how urban sociology can study the "people's city" concept through public space. The author argues that public space is its most direct and fullest expression, and that studying it can link practice to theory and build a Chinese-style urban sociology able to talk with Western urban space research. The commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, first reviews Western work from the Chicago School to Lefebvre, Harvey and the "new urban sociology". It then turns to Chinese research on public space and to Shanghai's public-space system since Xi Jinping put forward the people's city idea in 2019. It ends with fieldwork-based problems and proposed reforms. Li reads Western urban space as chiefly dominated by capital, with public space threatened by commodification and privatisation. Chinese studies, in Li's account, stress power and capital logics and call for more weight on "life logic". Li proposes that public space should embody four aspects of the people's character: publicness, diversity, participation and perceived experience. The author lists problems such as wasted space, excessive self-run provision and rigid functions. Li proposes supply-side reform in four areas: guiding public spirit, with Party-building leadership visible in more community spaces; stressing public governance and deliberation; finer planning around the 15-minute community life circle; and integrated, professional, socialised and "Internet Plus" operation. Li concludes that public space should be run so that services, deliberation and community governance operate together, and so that people's sense of gain and belonging serves as the test of success. Li ties this to common prosperity and whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a Shanghai sociologist's short account of how the people's city concept is turned into public-space policy and research agendas.

Accelerating the construction of a financial system for Chinese modernization 加快构建中国式现代化金融体系 Chen Yao Chen argues that building a financial system suited to Chinese modernization is both the direction of China's financial development and a new requirement for finance to support the drive to build a strong country. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, the author notes persistent problems: low quality and efficiency in serving the real economy, financial risks, weak regulation and governance, and a low level of financial opening. The commentary sets out seven main areas of effort. These are Party leadership of financial work, legislation, regulatory reform, the supply of finance to the real economy, modern institutions and markets, institutional opening, and inclusive finance. Chen presents Party leadership as the essential requirement, tracing it from the 1998 Party notice to the creation of the Central Financial Commission and Central Financial Work Commission in 2023. The author treats financial security as part of national security and says it depends on handling the dialectic between credit, leverage and risk. Serving the real economy is called the fundamental purpose, with more resources for infrastructure, advanced technology, strategic emerging industries and rural revitalisation. Chen contrasts Western finance, said to pursue self-expansion and profit maximisation, with a Chinese finance whose basis is serving the people. Chen concludes that, as China now has the world's largest banking system, credit market and foreign-exchange reserves, a financial system of this kind is inevitable. The author also calls for moving from opening in capital and goods to opening in rules and standards, and for advancing renminbi internationalisation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the policy priorities that Party-affiliated scholars link to Chinese modernization in finance.

Attitudes and principles for promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations 推动文明交流互鉴的态度和原则 Shao Sheng This commentary, published in Study Times in January 2025, takes up the recent publication of the Outline for Studying Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Shao Sheng argues that Xi Jinping's three statements of 2014 on civilizations (that they are colourful, equal and inclusive) set out the correct attitude and principles for exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations, and that they help in addressing a complex international situation and global challenges. The piece first summarises the Outline's account of the Party's position since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then takes the three principles in turn. Each is illustrated with historical cases: ancient river-valley civilizations and the spread of bronze metallurgy, the Arab synthesis of knowledge from several civilizations, the Silk Road and the monk Xuanzang, and the cultural meeting point of Dunhuang. On diversity, Shao holds that civilizational variety arises from differences in natural environment and is a dialectical unity of diversity and identity, so progress lies in many civilizations flourishing and influencing one another rather than in one dominating. On equality, the author presents every civilization as a treasure of humanity and says that exchange requires discarding arrogance and prejudice, citing Xuanzang's two-way transmission of Buddhist and Chinese texts between China and India. On inclusiveness, Shao argues that closed civilizations decline and that Chinese civilization has endured because it has kept absorbing outside influences, as at Dunhuang. Shao concludes that global problems such as environmental crisis, economic inequality and social unrest cannot be met by any single civilization. The author calls for respecting diversity, promoting equal dialogue and fostering inclusive development, and describes this as both a historical responsibility of the Chinese nation and a shared aspiration of the world's peoples. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party media present Xi Jinping's civilizational principles with historical illustrations.

Building a sound policy and institutional system requires upholding "people's wellbeing comes first" 构建合理的政策制度体系要坚持“民生为大” Guan Xinping This commentary, first published in Study Times in January 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that under Chinese modernization "people's wellbeing comes first". Guan Xinping asks how a sound system of social policy can be built to deliver it. The author argues that economic growth must be matched by better social policy, and that the central task is a policy system organised around three types of livelihood provision: universal, foundational and safety-net. The piece has four parts. It first explains why the principle matters for Chinese modernization, then defines the three types of provision. It then assesses current shortcomings and closes with four proposals for strengthening and optimising social policy. Guan writes as director of a Nankai University institute for social construction and management. Guan gives four reasons why the principle matters. It is an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization and of common prosperity, because markets alone are said to be unable to handle income gaps, unemployment, illness or care needs. It also supports high-quality development by raising human capital and domestic consumption, and it creates stable social conditions. On the three types, universal provision covers all members of a group (social insurance, education, health). Foundational provision guarantees basic income and services, and is not low-level provision but is set "to the best of our ability" according to economic conditions. Safety-net provision targets groups in hardship through social assistance and welfare services. Guan finds universal and safety-net coverage still insufficient, basic public services uneven, and links between programmes weak, risking gaps or duplication. Guan makes four proposals. These are stronger top-level design, including national standards for basic public services; a better funding mechanism; fairer distribution, with urban–rural integration, transfer payments and support for low-income groups; and better management and service delivery through professional social work and integrated grassroots services. The author cites budget spending on livelihood areas at close to 10% of GDP, or about 17% with social insurance, and calls this still inadequate. Guan wants a larger livelihood share under more proactive fiscal policy. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese social-policy scholar frames welfare reform within Chinese modernization, common prosperity and high-quality development.

Forming a powerful joint force: the "twin-wheel drive" stressed by General Secretary Xi Jinping 形成协同发力共同推进的强大合力—习近平总书记强调的“双轮驱动” Liu Li This commentary from Study Times reviews how Xi Jinping has used the image of a "twin-wheel drive" (shuanglun qudong): two wheels turning together to give strong momentum, meaning two aspects that are coordinated, pushed forward jointly and planned as a whole. Liu argues that studying these remarks supports dialectical thinking and a systems approach to building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised chronologically around six speeches given since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They cover cyber security and informatisation (2014), new-type urbanisation and rural development (2015), science-and-technology and institutional innovation (2018), practical cooperation and civilisational dialogue with Greece (2019), science and reform in agriculture (2023), and the carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals (2023). Liu presents each pairing as a dialectical unity rather than a choice between opposites. Security safeguards development and development is the purpose of security. Technological innovation opens new fields while institutional innovation removes obstacles to it. Under the "dual carbon" goals, a "capable government" and an "effective market" are to work together through a new-type whole-nation system and through the market's decisive role in allocating resources. The article restates Xi's policy detail in each area, such as integrating urban and rural planning, equalising basic public services and strengthening agricultural science and technology. Liu concludes that the twin-wheel approach expresses the "two-point theory" (liangdian lun) and the systems concept, and should guide coordinated action in the new era. Read the original if you want a compact survey of where Xi has used this formula and how Party media present its logic.

Education, science and technology, and talent as the foundational and strategic support for Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的基础性战略性支撑 He Yiting He Yiting explains a thesis from the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): that education, science and technology, and talent are the foundational and strategic support for Chinese modernization. In He's reading, education is the foundation, science and technology the key, and talent the root. Because innovation depends on talent and talent on education, He argues that advancing the three together is the key path to Chinese modernization. This short commentary, published in the Party newspaper Study Times, has four sections. The first three take education, science and technology, and talent in turn, each combining a statement of its role with an account of achievements, remaining weaknesses and the reforms the Decision calls for. The fourth section deals with integrated reform of the systems and mechanisms governing all three. The goals it cites are a leading education system by 2035 and a leading science and technology power by 2035. He argues that education is both a content of modernization and a driver of it, and that the shift from a large education country to a strong one requires deeper comprehensive reform. For science and technology, He sketches successive industrial revolutions to argue that each technological leap has raised productive forces and shaped national fortunes. He says China still has weak original innovation, key technologies controlled by others and too few top scientists. Talent is described as the most active production factor, so that innovation-driven development is in essence talent-driven. He lists structural contradictions in China's talent pool and calls for removing institutional barriers, ending the "four onlys" in evaluation and building evaluation based on innovation and contribution. He concludes that the three must be planned, decided and deployed as one, with systems thinking and a problem-oriented approach. This means using the new whole-nation system to raise the overall efficiency of the national innovation system, and cultivating an innovation culture that tolerates failure. He presents this as the way to supply the talent, intellectual support and innovation momentum that Chinese modernization needs. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed statement of how Party theorists link education, science and talent policy to Chinese modernization after the Third Plenum.

Unwaveringly advancing high-quality Belt and Road cooperation 坚定不移推进高质量共建“一带一路” Zhao Lei This newspaper commentary argues that the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has moved from a proposal to practice and has entered a stage of high-quality development, which China should pursue unwaveringly. Zhao Lei opens with the December 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, which called for making high-quality BRI cooperation "deeper and more solid" and for improving overseas comprehensive services. Zhao also cites Xi Jinping's view that opportunities for BRI development outweigh the challenges. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the global and strategic significance of high-quality BRI cooperation. The second weighs opportunities and challenges. The third turns to institutional mechanisms and overall planning. Zhao draws on figures, such as the number of Chinese overseas enterprises, and on projects including the Chancay port in Peru, the Jakarta–Bandung high-speed railway and the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway. Zhao presents high-quality BRI cooperation as the main route to high-level opening up, which supports Chinese modernization, and as a strategic support for major-country diplomacy and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. On risks, Zhao points to unilateralism, protectionism and geopolitical conflict. The author proposes early-warning platforms for overseas projects, compliance with local law and anti-corruption measures. The core of the argument is three kinds of coordination: "hard", "soft" and "heart" connectivity; major landmark projects alongside "small and beautiful" livelihood projects, such as the Luban Workshops for vocational training; and consolidating traditional fields while expanding digital, green, AI and health cooperation. Zhao concludes that openness is a defining mark of Chinese modernization and that persistent high-quality BRI cooperation will create more development opportunities and momentum for Chinese modernization and for shared global development. Zhao also calls for better mechanisms, including for investment and financing, risk control and a "clean" Silk Road. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Central Party School researcher frames BRI priorities, risks and project examples in official terms.

Better realising the role of enterprises as the main body of innovation 更好发挥企业创新主体作用 Pan Jiadong Xiao Suping This short commentary in Guangming Daily (January 2025) asks how enterprises can better serve as the main body of innovation. Pan and Xiao argue that firms sit at the key point where science, technology and the economy meet. Strengthening their position, they contend, helps turn scientific results into real productive forces and cultivates new quality productive forces. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision to strengthen enterprises' status in scientific and technological innovation. It then has two parts: the mechanisms through which enterprises drive innovation, and practical paths for improving their role. Examples come from artificial intelligence, synthetic biology and brain science. On mechanisms, the authors identify three. Scenario-driven demand and technological iteration advance together, with leading firms building technical foundations and small and medium-sized firms building applications. Enterprises link scientific discovery to commercial conversion, because they respond fastest to market demand. They also push technologies into patents and patents into standards, which the authors treat as a 'soft' source of competitiveness. For paths, they propose backing enterprises in major research projects, including private firms in national laboratories. They also propose enterprise-led innovation consortia supported by government funds and 'patient capital', and encouraging firms to lead in setting domestic and international standards. The authors conclude that coordinating the innovation, industrial, capital and talent chains depends on strengthening enterprises' role. They call for greater basic research spending by firms, fault-tolerance and incentive mechanisms, and fuller incubation systems. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy reasoning on enterprise-led innovation in China in early 2025.

Building the "greatest consensus" and balancing five relationships: striving to do economic work well An interpretation of the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference 凝聚一个“最大共识” 把握五个“必须统筹” 奋发有为做好经济工作 Zhong Caiwen This article, published in the People's Daily on 23 January 2025, interprets the formula that Xi Jinping presented at the Central Economic Work Conference at the end of 2024: "one greatest consensus and five must-balance relationships". Zhong argues that the formula further enriches and develops Xi Jinping's economic thought and gives guidance for economic work in the coming period. The "greatest consensus" is that the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership is the fundamental guarantee of good economic work. The article devotes one section to each of five relationships that must be balanced in promoting high-quality development. These are: an efficient market and a capable government; aggregate supply and aggregate demand; nurturing new growth drivers and updating old ones; improving the incremental and revitalising the existing stock; and raising quality and expanding total volume. Across the sections, Zhong repeatedly frames each pair as a dialectical unity rather than an either/or choice. On government and market, Zhong says that better use of government does not mean more government. It means avoiding both absence and overreach, building a unified national market and regulating enforcement. On supply and demand, the article calls expanding domestic demand a long-term strategy and not a short-term expedient, and it pairs this with deepening supply-side structural reform. On new and old drivers, it holds that new quality productive forces are a matter of "quality" rather than of which industry is involved. Traditional industries are described as the base of emerging ones and should be upgraded, not discarded, and each region should develop its own approach. On stock and increment, it urges reviving idle land, housing and other assets and exploring a national macro balance sheet. On quality and quantity, it says that high-quality development is the primary task of Chinese modernization, and that quality leads quantity while scale in turn gives quality room to grow. Zhong concludes that Party members should arm themselves with this innovative theory and work energetically to build the economic foundation for Chinese modernization. The text is an authoritative Party-press reading of the conference, and it presents the policy line as it was officially framed in early 2025. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how official commentary explains the priorities of China's 2025 economic work and the conceptual vocabulary behind them.

The Annales School nourished by Marx's theory of history 马克思历史理论沾溉下的年鉴学派 Zhang Jingmei Zhang Jingmei asks how far the French Annales School, which Peter Burke called a "French historical revolution" (1929–1989), drew on Marx's thought. The author argues that the school's central idea of "total history" was nourished by Marx's theory of world history. Marxism served as a "source of living water" for several generations of Annales historians, who produced a school both thoroughly French and thoroughly global. Published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, the piece follows the school in three stages. It begins with its founding context: the positivist political history of Seignobos and Langlois, the First World War, the October Revolution and the 1929 crisis. It then turns to Fernand Braudel's leadership after 1946, and finally to the third generation after 1968, including Jacques Le Goff. It closes with a short assessment of the school's weaknesses. Zhang's main move is to claim a shared outlook. Marx's German Ideology set out the concept of world history and the thesis that history becomes world history, which Zhang reads as treating human society as an organic whole. This, the author says, matches the Annales demand to study society as a totality. Zhang cites Lucien Febvre urging readers to read Marx and Lenin, and Burke's view that Braudel owed more to Marx than Febvre or Bloch did. Braudel is quoted calling Marx the first to build true social models on the long term. The author treats this closeness as partly tactical, since Marxists were allies against political history, and partly methodological, in the shared stress on structure, the long term and totality. Under the third generation, Zhang says, the relationship became "ambiguous": Le Goff acknowledged Marx as a master of the new history but rejected what he saw as a crude economic determinism. Braudel criticised his successors for abandoning total history. Zhang concludes that the Annales School is both an heir to French historiographical tradition and part of a wider world current, with Marxism as one source. The author also names an inborn flaw: the school neglects human subjective agency, favouring collective phenomena, static structures and the environment over individuals and the people's role in making history. On this point, Zhang says, it differs considerably from Marx's world-history theory. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist account of how the Annales School relates to Marx and where it falls short.

Seizing the opportunity to strengthen original and disruptive scientific and technological innovation 把握机遇加强原创性颠覆性科技创新 Xiong Hongru Writing in the Economic Daily in January 2024, Xiong Hongru asks how China can move from following existing technologies to leading them. The article opens by saying that a country's ability to produce major original and disruptive scientific results is the first measure of world-leading strength. Xiong argues that, in a harsher external environment, China must shift from tracking and incremental innovation towards pioneering, leading innovation, in order to raise the overall performance of the national innovation system. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts. It first sets out the opportunity created by rapid technological and market iteration. It then lists China's favourable conditions, using figures on research input, output, talent, infrastructure, firms and scale. It ends with four policy directions for building new advantages in science, technology and industry. Xiong's central claim is that major breakthroughs are usually discontinuous: transistors replacing vacuum tubes, digital communication replacing analogue, power batteries replacing combustion engines. Such innovation brings technological uncertainty and "creative destruction", and, in Xiong's view, matters especially for latecomer countries facing faster technical change and rising protectionism. It is needed to end dependence on foreign core technologies, build "asymmetric advantages" and safeguard economic and national security. Xiong cites figures to show that China is well placed: R&D intensity above the OECD average, 30.3% of papers in the most influential journals in 2022, rising basic research spending (from 49.88 billion to 225.91 billion yuan, 2012–2023), 77 national major science and technology facilities, and 679 firms among the global top 2,500 R&D investors. Xiong adds the advantage of scale, citing the most complete industrial system and a very large market that lowers the cost of trial and error. Xiong concedes that original innovation remains weak, some key technologies are still controlled by others, and top talent is scarce. The proposals are to strengthen basic research and forward-looking planning, with reform of evaluation away from quantified metrics; to coordinate national strategic science and technology forces with market-based innovators, with firms as the main innovators; to build matching talent, long-term finance and industrial systems; and to raise China's global innovation position through institutional opening. Read the original if you want a concise, data-supported statement of the official policy case for original and disruptive innovation, written by a State Council research official.

Coordinating the cultivation of new growth drivers and the renewal of old ones 统筹好培育新动能和更新旧动能的关系 Zhang Qizai Writing in Economic Daily in January 2024, Zhang Qizai takes up the instruction of the Central Economic Work Conference to coordinate the cultivation of new growth drivers with the renewal of old ones, and to develop new quality productive forces in line with local conditions. Zhang argues that China is at a critical stage of economic transformation and upgrading, and that handling the relationship between new and old drivers correctly is essential for both a real improvement in quality and a reasonable increase in quantity. The commentary has two parts. The first clarifies what new and old drivers mean and why the two should be pursued together. The second sets out four priority tasks: innovation, market-based mechanisms, new types of production factors, and locally tailored development of new quality productive forces. Zhang illustrates the argument with policy measures on strategic emerging industries and with a steel-sector example of digital upgrading. Zhang defines new drivers as innovation-led advanced productive forces and the production relations suited to them, and contends that growth driven by expanding factor inputs is weakening as demand, not supply, becomes the main constraint. Cultivating new drivers means building strategic emerging industries and future industries; renewing old ones means upgrading traditional industries, not simply eliminating them. Of three possible transition modes, namely keeping old drivers while growing new ones, replacing old with new, or doing both at once, Zhang holds that the first two leave the drivers unintegrated and risk large economic swings or a gap in drivers. The third needs a relatively complete industrial system, and since Chinese industries range from followers to leaders, leading industries should focus on new drivers and following industries on renewing old ones. Zhang calls for AI-assisted innovation, stronger basic research and national innovation platforms; better investment and financing, a leading role for state capital, equal protection of private enterprises and a unified national market; digital and AI-enabled upgrading of traditional industries; and regional choices based on resource endowments, avoiding blind imitation. Zhang concludes that this two-wheel drive will build new advantages for economic development. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how an economist at a Chinese state think tank links the new/old driver transition to new quality productive forces and industrial policy.

The shifting spirit of the age and the changing image of China 时代精神的流转与中国形象的变迁 Fang Weigui Fang Weigui asks why Western images of China have swung between admiration and contempt. Opening with the German sinologist Wolfgang Franke's remark that these images reveal the observers' standpoints more than the object observed, the author argues that each image reflects the spirit of its age, Western needs of the moment and the values of its makers. The piece, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, extends this claim to the present day. The article surveys Western views of China from antiquity to the early twentieth century. It begins with the vague Roman 'Seres' and Marco Polo, then treats the Jesuit-driven enthusiasm of roughly 1250–1750 and the hostile image that followed the Jesuits' dissolution around 1775. It ends with the early twentieth-century 'Orient fever', stressing the shift from Confucian to Daoist texts and the place of Chinese poetry in Western literary reception. Fang's central device is two 'cross-century blocs': a positive image running from the Jesuits through Leibniz, Wolff, Voltaire and Diderot, and a negative one from Anson, the Macartney mission, Montesquieu, Rousseau, Herder and Hegel. The author attributes the swing to Enlightenment needs, later Eurocentrism, Christian and imperialist missionary consciousness, and ignorance of Chinese history, noting that Western knowledge relied on Jesuit works. Fang adds that popular and elite images of China differ. After the First World War, the author says, a Western spiritual crisis and Nietzschean cultural pessimism fed a Daoist craze, seen in Klabund's call to 'become Chinese Europeans', in Li Bai's rise as the emblem of Chinese culture, and in Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde. Fang concludes that European affirmation or denial of China since the eighteenth century has come from Europe's own needs. The author contends that contemporary Western views remain largely the same, expressing Western positions on a changed situation and sometimes carrying Cold War thinking. Recent Western reception of Chinese literature is described as utilitarian, with selection driven by critical content or topical interest more than literary quality. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese scholarly account of how Western images of China have been historically constructed, especially in literary reception.

Strengthening the theoretical system of the Chinese nation as a community 加强中华民族共同体理论体系建设 Sun Beibei This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily takes up Xi Jinping's call to build a theoretical system for the Chinese nation as a community (Zhonghua minzu gongtongti). Sun Beibei argues that forging a sense of community for the Chinese nation requires a scientific and complete theory. In the author's account, this is part of building an independent Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge and of shaking off the influence of Western theories of nationality and their discourse. The piece has three parts. The first concerns method, the second the research agenda, and the third disciplinary development and personnel. On method, Sun holds that the Two Integrations must run through the whole project: combining Marxist nationality theory with China's concrete realities, and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The first calls for study of the classical Marxist writers and of Xi Jinping's thinking on ethnic work. The second calls for deeper research on the history of the Chinese nation and on the 'four commons' view of history, in which territory, history, culture and spirit are all said to be jointly created by all ethnic groups. The aim is to secure the power to narrate history and set discourse. On content, Sun proposes three lines of research. These are a systematic study of Xi's thought on ethnic work, clarification of basic concepts and relationships (nation, commonality and difference, pluralistic unity), and major practical questions, including shared spiritual homeland, governance modernization and preventing risks in the ethnic sphere. Sun calls for interdisciplinary cooperation among Marxist theory, ethnology, history, anthropology, archaeology and other fields. The author also proposes better research platforms, incentives, core expert teams, support for niche fields and training of young scholars. The aim is a Chinese-led body of sources, discourse and theory. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official research agenda for ethnic theory and its institutional implications.

Making better use of the educational function of museums 更好发挥博物馆的教育功能 Wang Xiaowen Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Wang Xiaowen, director of the Liaoning Provincial Museum, asks how museums can better perform their educational function and meet the public's spiritual and cultural needs. The commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's call to strengthen museum building and to make full use of museums' educational role, and from the Party's goal of building a culturally strong country. Wang argues that education is a core mission of museums and that it should be advanced by upholding fundamental principles while innovating. The piece opens with figures the author cites for 2023: 6,833 museums in China, more than 40,000 exhibitions, more than 380,000 educational activities and 1.29 billion visits. It has three parts. The first sets out why education is central to museums. The second reviews results achieved, through policy documents since the 2008 free-admission notice and through three practices: study tours, museum–school cooperation and technology-enabled experiences. The third offers four directions for the future. In Wang's reading, museums teach through objects rather than texts, support self-directed and lifelong learning, and help turn fine traditional Chinese culture into forms the public can understand and identify with. The author illustrates this with examples: the Hebei Museum's study-tour programme, the Nanjing Museum's summer courses, Liaoning's cooperation with Shenyang education authorities on a 'museum–school–family–society' education community, and digital projects such as the Digital Library Cave and Dunhuang immersive exhibitions. Wang then argues that future work should be rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture and a people-centred approach, with digital tools used to match content to audience needs. The author also calls for wider partnerships with schools, research bodies and regions, for staff who understand both museums and education, and for digital transformation. Wang concludes that museums should cultivate patriotism, public morality and 'new people of the era', build on socialist core values, and deliver inclusive, high-quality education both on site and online. The text is a short practitioner's commentary rather than a theoretical study, and it mainly reflects how a museum director frames the sector's tasks under current cultural policy. Read the original if you want a concise account of official priorities for museum education in China, together with examples from Chinese museums.

Centralized and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee is the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well 党中央集中统一领导是做好经济工作的根本保证 Liu Wei Writing in People's Daily after the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2024, Liu Wei takes up the claim that centralized and unified leadership by the Party Central Committee is the fundamental guarantee for doing economic work well. Liu presents this as a regular pattern drawn from China's economic practice and as an important part of Xi Jinping's economic thought.
