The commentary argues that the pattern is confirmed by experience and should be understood through the demands of high-quality development. The piece has three parts. The first cites two cases from the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012): the response to Covid-19 in 2020 and the policy turn of September 2024. It also traces how Central Economic Work Conferences in 2019, 2020 and 2023 stated the same conclusion. The second part explains the claim in terms of high-quality development. The third sets out practical requirements for implementation. Liu's core argument rests on three links between Party leadership and high-quality development. First, leadership sustains and improves the basic socialist economic system. Liu grounds this in the dialectic of productive forces and relations of production and of economic base and superstructure, which calls for the superstructure's active role. Second, leadership makes scientific governance and overall coordination possible, bringing consistent policy orientation in macroeconomic governance and balance in urban–rural and regional development. Third, leadership is said to enable the correct handling of the government–market relationship, with the digital economy and new quality productive forces as examples. In the evidence, Liu notes that China's GDP grew 2.2% in 2020, which the article calls the only positive growth among major economies, and that the September 2024 package of incremental policies lifted confidence and brought a clear recovery. Liu calls for action under the principle of 'putting work first' so that Central Committee decisions are carried out. Leaders should build their capacity for economic work and judge economic questions with political insight. They should also use rule-of-law thinking, treating the socialist market economy as essentially a law-based economy, and speed up building a high-level socialist market economic system, following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Read the original if you want an authoritative People's Daily statement of how Chinese economic discourse links Party leadership to high-quality development and the socialist market economy.

Bringing the promotion of the educator's spirit into the international communication discourse system 将弘扬教育家精神纳入国际传播话语体系 Song Qiang This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, takes up the call of the 2024 National Education Conference to raise the international influence and discourse power of Chinese education. Song argues that the distinctively Chinese 'educator's spirit' should be built into international communication, so that Chinese education stories and the stories of Chinese educators are told abroad. The piece has three parts. It first explains why the educator's spirit matters for international communication, then discusses how to distil its content for foreign audiences, and finally sets out strategies for telling the stories systematically and continuously. Song contends that education can act as a shared global language and that, according to 2024 data cited in the article, China's soft power index ranked third worldwide. Foreign interest in how China builds its teaching force is therefore expected. On content, the author proposes improving the system of honours for teachers, planning communication around positive messaging with comparison and borrowing, and sorting educators into types. The stated aim is to turn institutional, organisational, human, developmental and cultural advantages into communication advantages, supporting a strong education nation and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese education authorities frame international communication and discourse power.

Understanding Xi Jinping's thought on culture to promote the integrated development of moral and aesthetic education in universities 深刻领会习近平文化思想 推动高校德育美育融合发展 Chen Xiaohong This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how Chinese universities should combine moral education (deyu) with aesthetic education (meiyu). Making the "Great Ideological and Political Course" knowledgeable, high-quality and smart 让“大思政课”有知、有质、更有智 Liu Zikang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, takes up the question of how to build the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke). Developing agricultural new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 因地制宜发展农业新质生产力 Zhang Haipeng Zhang Yanlong This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily (21 January 2025) takes up the call of the 2024 Central Rural Work Conference to develop agricultural new quality productive forces in line with local conditions. Forming an economic order that is both "lively" and "well-regulated" 形成既“放得活”又“管得住”的经济秩序 Liu Wei Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Liu Wei comments on the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, which listed "five must-balance relationships". First among them is the relationship between an effective market and a capable government, with the aim of an order that is both "lively" (fangde huo) and "well-regulated" (guande zhu). Liu treats this as guidance on the government–market relationship, which the article calls the core question of economic reform. The thesis is that the two are complementary, and that each needs its own institutional foundation. The article has four parts. It first traces how the Party's understanding of the government–market relationship deepened, from the 1992 goal of a socialist market economy through the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then sets out the institutions an effective market requires and those a capable government requires. It closes with two principles for combining the two. Liu's core argument is that an effective market rests on a high-level socialist market economy system. That system has two layers. Competition institutions cover market-entity rules, meaning modern enterprise institutions and the Two Unwaverings, and transaction rules, meaning market-determined prices, anti-monopoly rules and a unified national market. Basic institutions cover the rule of law and a credit system. A capable government, in Liu's account, mainly means active and systematic macroeconomic governance by the central government, which also corrects market failure. Liu says China's governance system rests on the socialist system and has five features: reform measures are part of governance; policy covers structural and development policy as well as monetary and fiscal policy; it uses both counter-cyclical and cross-cycle adjustment; state-owned enterprises give macro governance a micro-level base; and regulation can shift between demand-side and supply-side approaches. Liu concludes that government and market are not opposed but mutually reinforcing, since more competition strengthens the micro-foundations of macro governance. Their functions should be defined by the problems they address, not by a mechanical division of fields. The market works directly through competition among micro-level actors where property rights are clear and rules fair. Government works indirectly, guiding actors from the macro level where markets fail. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned economist's reading of the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference formula and of how it fits the Party's evolving doctrine on the state and the market.

Accelerating the development of the new rural collective economy 加快发展新型农村集体经济 Kang Jiaojiao Wu Fangwei This short commentary by Kang Jiaojiao and Wu Fangwei takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) call to develop a new rural collective economy. The authors link the new collective economy to three goals. It strengthens the "unified" side of the two-tier management system, helping to meet food security and technology needs. It raises public services, social security and the rural living environment. It also raises incomes and cuts the risk of individual farming, which they present as a main lever for common prosperity. They say development remains insufficient and propose that Party leadership, described as the "compass", underpin it through stronger grassroots organisations, better personnel and professional managers. Improving the support system for strengthening agriculture, benefiting farmers and enriching farmers 完善强农惠农富农支持制度 Zhou Qisen Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Zhou Qisen takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee's (2024) call to improve the support system for strengthening agriculture, benefiting farmers and enriching farmers. Understanding the holistic approach to national security through scientific thinking 以科学思维领悟总体国家安全观 Zhang Rui Marking the tenth anniversary in 2024 of Xi Jinping's holistic approach to national security, this newspaper commentary argues that the concept contains a rich set of scientific modes of thinking. Dialectical thinking appears in the "five coordinations", for instance internal and external security, or traditional and non-traditional security. Zhang adds that historical thinking draws on the Party's century of experience while rejecting historical nihilism. Zhang concludes that applying the holistic approach requires combining these methods, linking theory with practice, and continually updating methods in science and technology, talent and international cooperation. Answering questions and guiding their resolution is the fundamental task of theory 回答并指导解决问题是理论的根本任务 Yao Hongzhi Writing after Xi Jinping's instruction marking the twentieth anniversary of the Marxist Theory Research and Development Project, Yao asks how scholars should carry out their central task: studying and promoting Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Scholars should criticise erroneous ideological trends and identify what the thought adds to Marxism, not only what it inherits. A wholly new political system grown from Chinese soil Understanding the universal, particular and distinctive attributes of China's people's congress system 从中国土壤中生长起来的全新政治制度 Li Lin Writing in Beijing Daily in January 2025, Li Lin takes up Xi Jinping's description of the people's congress system as a "wholly new political system grown from Chinese soil". Li asks how this system should be understood in comparative political-philosophical terms. The commentary argues that it has three attributes at once: universality, particularity and difference. Together, Li says, these mark its historical position and its Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each attribute. The first treats universality, drawing on Mao Zedong's 1954 speech on the draft constitution, on common human values, on the conceptual vocabulary of representative government, and on the National People's Congress's work in the Inter-Parliamentary Union since 1984. The second sets the system against Western capitalist democracies, citing Mao and Deng Xiaoping. The third compares it with other socialist states such as Vietnam, North Korea and Cuba. On universality, Li argues that the system shares with world political civilisation concepts such as the constitution, elections, the rule of law, human rights and checks on power, and that Chinese institutions give these a "Chinese-style" content. Li holds that the system promotes shared human values and so serves as a fundamental political institution for building a community with a shared future for mankind. On particularity, Li states that China rejects presidential, parliamentary, constitutional-monarchy, "separation of three powers" and multiparty systems. In Li's account, the difference in state character and form of government sets it apart from Western capitalist systems. On difference, Li says the primary stage of socialism gives the system distinct features. These include Party leadership combined with people's mastery and law-based governance, whole-process people's democracy, regional ethnic autonomy and multiparty cooperation under Party leadership. Li concludes, in the Marxist terms of the particular containing the general, that the three attributes exist together in dialectical unity. Universality, Li says, supplies a shared cultural basis for exchange with other countries. Particularity shows the socialist nature of the system and its claimed advantages. Difference shows its Chinese, contemporary and practical features. Li adds that this highlights the world significance of Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a senior CASS scholar frames the people's congress system's relation to Western and other socialist models.

A new view of civilizations: opening a threefold transcendence in global civilizational development 新文明观：开启全球文明发展的三重超越 Shao Sheng This commentary, published in Beijing Daily in January 2025, draws on the newly issued Study Outline of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. The piece takes each transcendence in turn: exchange over estrangement, mutual learning over conflict, and inclusiveness over claims of superiority. It combines a historical account of Western expansion since the age of exploration with critiques of Samuel Huntington's "clash of civilizations" and of the idea of civilizational superiority. Shao contends that Western colonial expansion built a West-centred world system, destroyed or remade other civilizations and made exchange coercive and one-way. In the author's account, this laid the seeds of racism, nationalism and terrorism, and today some Western leaders sustain estrangement through trade, technology and information wars. Huntington's thesis is described as a misreading of history that mistakes conflicts of interest for civilizational difference and serves hegemony. The author calls the doctrine of civilizational superiority a colonialist construct behind "universal values" and "the end of history", and argues that Western modernization itself depended on Mesopotamian, Chinese and Arab achievements. Accelerating the intelligent transformation of political work in the armed forces 加快推进军队政治工作智能化建设 Wang Yongchang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how political work in the Chinese armed forces can be made "intelligent" through artificial intelligence, big data and cloud computing. Wang Yongchang argues that the process must follow the basic principles of military political work while adapting to the technical features of AI, so that "intelligence plus political work" develops through mutual shaping rather than technology simply replacing human work. The article is organised in four sections: moving from informatization to intelligent political work; revitalising political work as the "lifeline" of the army; consolidating the distinctive advantages of the people's army under intelligent conditions; and making AI a trustworthy assistant. It covers technical building blocks (data, computing power, models, algorithms, infrastructure), organisational questions such as military–civilian coordination, and governance questions of ideology, ethics and regulation. Wang's first central move is that intelligent political work is not unmanned political work and does not weaken the human subject. It combines revolutionary and humanistic spirit with technological rationality, inheriting the Party's command over the army, the mass line and leading by example, while building on the data and systems created by informatization. Second, Wang stresses demand-led application scenarios in ideological education, public opinion work and personnel management, and argues that political-work data, being data about people, requires specially designed datasets and algorithms and a "cloud–edge–end" computing layout. Third, the author calls for self-reliance in core technologies such as algorithms and domestic high-performance chips, and for governance of AI risks. Wang concludes that the military should draw on late-mover advantages to turn technological strengths into soldiers' spiritual strength, Party committees' decision-making strength and units' operational strength. The author calls for vigilance against algorithmic ideological risks at the stages of training data, content production, recommendation and decision support, for human dominance in human–machine cooperation, explainable algorithms, and clear rules on rights, duties and oversight. Empowering the modernization of rural governance with digital-intelligence technology 数智技术赋能乡村治理现代化 Zhang Yunping This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how digital-intelligence (shuzhi) technologies can advance the modernization of rural governance, which Zhang Yunping treats as part of modernizing the national governance system and as a requirement of building a modern socialist country. On skills, Zhang proposes training for farmers and especially for village cadres, plus incentives to attract information-technology talent. On effectiveness, Zhang calls for more precise public services, such as 'internet plus' grassroots governance, simple apps and elderly-friendly services. Zhang also urges reducing digital burdens by avoiding digital formalism and idle platforms, and securing data through legal rules, tiered protection and risk assessment. Zhang concludes that the aim is good rural governance that maximises public interest, so that technology 'empowers' rather than burdens villages. "Walking" ideological and political courses: innovative and heartfelt Yunnan Province's practical exploration of reform and innovation in ideological and political education “行走”的思政课，“走新”又“走心” Guangming Daily research team This field report from Guangming Daily (20 January 2025) asks how ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) can move students rather than merely instruct them. Its research team visited schools and universities across Yunnan and argues that the province has made these courses more attractive and influential by taking them out of the classroom, in what it calls "walking" courses. The report presents Yunnan's practice as a model worth drawing lessons from. It recalls Xi Jinping's 2020 visit to the Southwest Associated University site, where he stressed training builders and successors of socialism. Three sections follow: unity of knowledge and action, teaching through multiple channels on ethnic unity, and coverage of all school stages. A closing section sets out "experience and implications" in four points. The team describes several examples. Visits to historic sites, the "Zhang Guimei Ideological and Political Lecture Hall" (15 recorded lectures and over 300 local sessions, according to the report) and the Puer oath-tablet site on ethnic unity are said to make the courses "visible" and "memorable". Yunnan is also said to be integrating teaching across primary, middle, secondary and university levels through a steering committee, local teaching materials, shared online resources and more than 25,000 full-time teachers. The report concludes that Yunnan has grasped the needs of the times and acted on Xi Jinping's instructions, so that these courses become "golden courses" that students like and benefit from for life. It credits the gains to institutionalised Party leadership, links between classroom and social practice, and a stronger teaching force. Computing power as the new infrastructure for high-quality economic development 算力是经济高质量发展的新基建 Wei Jieyu Cai Yuezhou This short commentary, published in Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, argues that computing power (suanli) is the foundation of the digital economy and a new form of infrastructure for high-quality development. Wei Jieyu and Cai Yuezhou open with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for building and operating national data infrastructure and promoting data sharing. They present faster construction of computing infrastructure as necessary for releasing the value of data as a production factor and for integrating the real and digital economies. The article has three parts. It first explains why computing power underpins the digital economy, then reviews progress and remaining problems in China's computing infrastructure, and finally sets out four groups of policy recommendations. The authors draw on official policy documents, national statistics up to mid-2024 and an international computing power index report. Wei and Cai argue that computing power is both the base for applying digital technologies and a constraint on industrial change, since the digital transformation of traditional industries depends on supply of computing power. They cite the 2022–2023 Global Computing Power Index report: each one-point rise in the index is said to raise digital-economy value added by 3.6‰ and GDP by 1.7‰. On progress, they report total capacity of 246 EFLOPS by June 2024, second in the world, with annual growth near 30% and intelligent computing growing over 70% in 2023. They also describe the eight national hubs under the East Data, West Computing project, with eastern hubs serving latency-sensitive work and western hubs handling back-end processing. They name three problems: dependence on imported high-end chips, electricity supply and cost, and incomplete technical standards. The authors recommend concentrating research on chip technology through the new-type whole-nation system (xin xing juguo tizhi), with diversified funding. They also call for top-level design and moderately advance deployment of capacity, and for siting computing centres where green power is plentiful and cheap, with joint scheduling of electricity and computing. They further urge application scenarios in industrial internet, intelligent transport and digital government, and a coordinated hardware and software ecosystem. Algorithmic recommendation empowering core values education 算法推荐赋能核心价值观教育 Peng Xiaolan Peng Xiaolan asks how algorithmic recommendation, a technology that profiles users' data and pushes content to match their inferred interests, can be used in education in the core socialist values. The commentary argues that, in the context of digital education, the technology can identify and track new ideological and behavioural trends and supply new methods for the models, settings and momentum of such education. It also holds that the technology produces specific tensions that must be managed through guiding principles. The piece is built in three parts. The first describes three ways algorithmic recommendation empowers core values education: personalised, data-based and dynamic recommendation. The second sets out three contradictions between the technology and the aims of the education. The third offers three sets of measures, built around value orientation, ethics and law, and the laws of education. On the benefits, Peng argues that personalised recommendation returns education to a one-to-one mode, big-data decision-making lets educators monitor learning and shape policy, and dynamic recommendation lets learners plan their own paths. Each is said to generate a "new quality" of teacher–student relations, learning materials and learners. The contradictions are algorithmic customisation versus all-round development, which risks distorted cognition and closed information circles. Algorithmic substitution versus creativity is the second, because black-box opacity and dependence weaken dialogue and human agency. Algorithmic bias versus educational fairness is the third, since small errors in data labelling, unclear accountability among designers and platforms, and privacy risks may distort outcomes. Peng proposes that algorithms be guided by values. This means improving recommended content, building safeguards against "information cocoons", embedding Marxist theory and uplifting values, and following the national guidance on algorithm governance, with lawful training data and regular security assessments. Algorithms should also be bound by ethics and law, through data security, privacy and appropriate public disclosure of their purposes and workings. Finally, they should be developed in line with educational laws, through personalised yet selectable teaching plans and efficient feedback channels that track learners' creativity and curiosity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-education scholarship frames AI and recommender systems as both tools and risks for teaching core values.

Experience and lessons from the popularisation of Marxism in the Yan'an period 延安时期马克思主义大众化传播的经验与启示 Xi Haisha This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks what the Communist Party's work of spreading Marxism among ordinary people in Yan'an (the Party's wartime base) can teach the present. The article is organised around three headings: innovation in the discourse used to spread Marxism, a wider reach for its dissemination, and greater effectiveness of its communication. It draws on Party documents of 1941 and on Mao Zedong's 1942 speech "Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing". Xi's core account is that Marxism had to be explained in the language of the Chinese people and of the masses, and that Party newspapers did this by taking up vivid popular speech. Dissemination ran through cadre schools, newspapers and radio, and also through folk forms such as yangge opera, New Year pictures, woodblock prints and drama. Xi stresses targeted communication: cadres, peasants and intellectuals were reached by different means, from cadre education and literacy campaigns to the Yan'an Rectification Movement and the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art. Xi credits this with party unity, close Party–mass ties and national political mobilisation. Xi concludes that practice-based innovation in discourse, targeted communication mechanisms and shared values pursued through persistent struggle underpinned the effectiveness of Yan'an-era communication. For today, Xi calls on mainstream media to uphold the Two Integrations, innovate their discourse and strategies, and use online media to draw "concentric circles" online and offline. Creating an effective form of grassroots communication Blackboard newspapers and worker-peasant correspondents in the War of Liberation period 创造基层传播的有效样态 Tian Zhongchu This short commentary from China Social Sciences Today asks how the Communist Party built effective grassroots communication during the War of Liberation (1945–49). Tian argues that the organic fusion of the village blackboard newspaper with worker-peasant correspondents was an effective form of grassroots communication in that period. Tian opens by noting that the Party is often described as the party that values the grassroots most, a commitment the author sees in its insistence on grassroots newspaper work. The article first traces the background: wall newspapers and bulletins in the Soviet areas, the 1939 call for wall newspapers or 'mass blackboards', and the 1940s slogan of 'the whole Party and the masses run newspapers'. It then describes what a blackboard newspaper was: a chalk-written board carrying national news, local news, criticism, praise and cartoons, laid out like a paper. It draws on local examples from Shandong, the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region, Hebei-Shanxi and the Huai-Hai and Yanfu areas. Tian's central argument is a two-way relationship. Correspondents were the main contributors, and in many villages the management of correspondents merged with that of the blackboard. For the professional press they were 'amateur reporters', but for the blackboard they were its 'professional reporters'. In turn the blackboard was the 'main position' for developing correspondents. It offered illiterate or semi-literate villagers ways to take part, such as dictated 'messages'. It also gave far more chances to see their writing published, and it taught editing, organising and newspaper-reading. Tian cites figures such as 1,024 of 1,416 submissions published in one Funing village, and 10,038 of 17,541 items posted in Lianshui county during a two-month contest. Contemporary sources, quoted by the author, call the blackboard the peasants' own 'mouthpiece', the correspondent movement the 'crops' and the blackboard the 'soil'. Tian concludes that peasants moved from 'silent' to 'speaking' subjects, and that the blackboard's reach, though limited, fostered their cultural agency. The author regrets that blackboards left almost no records, so later readers must rely on fragments. The historical lesson drawn is that, even as media change, new media should be built from grassroots conditions. Workers and peasants should get guidance, protection and new roles, so that people and media grow together and strengthen socialist ideology and culture. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Communist Party grassroots journalism in the late 1940s and the examples it cites.

Methodological consciousness in consolidating cultural subjectivity 巩固文化主体性的方法论自觉 Gu Chengmin Song Guo This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how cultural subjectivity (wenhua zhutixing) can be consolidated. Gu and Song take the concept from Xi Jinping's remarks that any culture must have its own subjectivity if it is to stand firm, travel far and have the power to lead, unite, shape and radiate. They argue that consolidating it is an original proposition of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and requires a high degree of methodological consciousness. The piece is organised in three parts. The first deals with the methodological premises: the context in which the concept appeared, its essential determinations and its cognitive structure. The second sets out three methodological standpoints. The third presents three methodological principles. Each part is built around passages from Xi Jinping's speeches. On the premises, the authors place the concept in three contexts. In the intellectual context it is a 'terminological revolution' within Marxist cultural thought. In the historical context it condenses the Party's experience of leading cultural development. In the contemporary context it answers the new cultural mission. They hold that its essence lies in practice, since it originates in the subjectivity of real people, and in an objective independence that distinguishes one culture from others. On standpoints, they require upholding the Party's overall leadership as the political guarantee and direction. They also require a people-centred value standpoint, in which the people are both the practical and the value subject. The third standpoint is resolving the 'dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western'. On principles, they name the Two Integrations, which they say consolidate cultural subjectivity. They also name upholding fundamental principles while innovating, which they cast as thesis and synthesis, and self-confidence and self-reliance. The last of these means avoiding a 'master copy', 'template', 'reprint' or 'replica' of other models. The authors conclude that clarifying these premises, standpoints and principles gives consolidating cultural subjectivity its intellectual foundation and its practical direction. In their account this lets Chinese culture keep strategic composure amid global change and assert itself in cultural contestation. Read the original if you want a concise outline of how Chinese scholars systematise Xi Jinping's concept of cultural subjectivity in methodological terms.

The inner meaning of the new form of human civilization 人类文明新形态的内在意蕴 Chen Zhigang Chen Zhigang takes up a formulation of Xi Jinping: that Chinese modernization is "a new form of human civilization". The article asks in what sense this form is new and answers that Chinese modernization offers a new model of modernization, goes beyond Western-style modernization in theory and practice, and gives developing countries a fresh option. Chen presents this as evidence of the Communist Party's civilizational consciousness and cultural confidence. The piece is a commentary in Red Flag Manuscript, organised in three parts that follow the three clauses of Xi's formulation. Each part defines one aspect of the new civilizational form: continuing an ancient civilization, innovating socialism with Chinese characteristics, and surpassing capitalist civilization. Chen draws on classical Chinese sources (the Book of Documents, Guan Zhong, Confucius, the Book of Changes, Laozi) and on Party policy language. In the first part, Chen argues that the modernization path is rooted in traditional culture through "creative transformation and innovative development". Ideas of enriching the people, "people as the root of the state", "small prosperity" and "harmony between heaven and humanity" are said to reappear as common prosperity, whole-process people's democracy and harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. In the second, Chen holds that the path embodies the essence of scientific socialism without copying the classical writers' blueprint or other countries' practice: it combines public ownership with a socialist market economy and adds distinctive political institutions. The third part claims that the path draws on all outstanding achievements of human civilization while rejecting what Chen calls the old Western road of capital-centred, polarising and expansionist modernization. Chen says it breaks the equation of "modernization = Westernization", reshapes the world's modernization map through a population of over 1.4 billion, and advances a view of civilizations based on equality, mutual learning and a community with a shared future for mankind. Chen concludes that Chinese modernization and the new form of human civilization are two sides of one process: modernization is the driving force and path, and the civilizational form is its crystallisation. The new form is described as uniting continuity with innovation, independence with openness, and the national with the global. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists in early 2025 explain the "new form of human civilization" and link it to tradition, socialism and a critique of Western modernization.

The theoretical meaning of "the Chinese spirit is the soul of socialist literature and art" “中国精神是社会主义文艺的灵魂”的理论意涵 Liu Zhuo This commentary takes up a formulation from Xi Jinping's speech at the Forum on Literature and Art (15 October 2014): "the Chinese spirit is the soul of socialist literature and art". Liu Zhuo argues that its meaning can be grasped only within the overall development of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On this reading, the formulation places demands on literary theory that go well beyond the content of individual works. The piece moves from history to cultural policy. It begins with the Chinese spirit as a national spirit forged in modern struggle, then turns to the inscription on the Monument to the People's Heroes and to the tension between "revolutionary-history" and "modernization" narratives of modern China. It goes on to the Party's "original aspiration", the core socialist values, and the earlier guideline that literature and art should serve the people and socialism. Liu makes three main moves. First, the Chinese spirit is both the result and a cause of the success of the socialist road, and it points to the Chinese people as historical subject rather than only to traditional civilization. Liu holds that the clash between the two historical narratives is resolved in the Party's account built around the Two Centenary Goals, and that patriotism, the core of the Chinese spirit, is not exclusive nationalism. Second, Liu sees a shift in wording from defining "China" through "socialism" to defining "socialism" through "China". Third, the core socialist values, called the concentrated expression of the Chinese spirit at the 19th Party Congress (2017), must "land" in people's lives. The author compares the earlier guideline that literature serves the people and socialism with the new formulation, which stresses the creator's own consciousness and treats the socialist character of literature as intrinsic rather than imposed from outside. Liu concludes that "soul" should be read as the soul that rejuvenates and strengthens the nation. The commentary links this to the Party Central Committee's goal of a socialist cultural superpower by 2035 and to cultural confidence, which it says must lead the way. Writers are asked to fuse ancient and modern and to bridge China and the West. Literary theorists, Liu argues, must study socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping's thought on culture to build a theory rooted in tradition, grounded in the present and open to the world. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences literary scholar ties official cultural-policy language to debates over historical narrative and core socialist values.

Digital finance empowering the development of new quality productive forces 数字金融赋能新质生产力发展 Tian Kan Writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in January 2025, Tian Kan asks how digital finance can support the development of new quality productive forces. The author starts from the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, which stressed technological innovation as the lead for new quality productive forces and the building of a modern industrial system. Tian argues that digital finance, by combining digital technology with traditional financial services, can optimise factor allocation, drive technological innovation and promote industrial upgrading. The short commentary sets out five mechanisms through which digital finance is said to work. They are a full-process service mechanism, an ecosystem-chain integration mechanism, a data-value release mechanism, a financing credit-enhancement mechanism and an inclusive service mechanism. Each is illustrated with practical measures for finance institutions, enterprises, universities and government. In the full-process mechanism, Tian says big data and AI models can help firms identify promising research directions, while seed funding, venture capital and credit support carry projects through early research. Pledging data assets and intangible assets such as patents, together with digital matching platforms, is presented as a way to ease commercialisation and market entry. The ecosystem mechanism uses blockchain and cloud computing to break up 'information silos', steer capital toward fields such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, and link firms, universities and research institutes in joint technical work. The remaining mechanisms rely on integrated data to improve technology, production, talent and market factors, on multidimensional credit profiles, risk-sharing tools and regulatory technology to improve the financing climate, and on mobile services, rural outlets and tailored products to draw small firms and individual entrepreneurs into the effort. Tian concludes that digital finance, by activating market participants in all these ways, gives new quality productive forces strong momentum. The article also calls for government, finance institutions and firms to build risk-sharing and policy-support arrangements, with feedback channels to adjust services, while holding the line against systemic risk. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented Chinese account of how digital finance is expected to serve the new quality productive forces agenda, including the specific instruments proposed.

A historical and dialectical view of the development of digital capitalism 历史辩证地看待数字资本主义的发展 Bai Jing This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today asks whether digital capitalism has moved beyond Marx's account of capitalism. Bai Jing notes that some scholars hold that digital capital accumulation exceeds Marx's definition of capitalism and call the labour theory of value into doubt. Bai argues the opposite: only Marxist theory can scientifically explain the development logic of digital capitalism and guide practice. The piece first clarifies the concept, tracing the term to Dan Schiller's 1999 book Digital Capitalism. It then turns to primitive accumulation, labour forms and alienation, and closes with a brief note on China's own digital development. Bai distinguishes digital capital, which may appear in both socialist and capitalist modernization, from digital capitalism, which exists only under capitalist private ownership. Digital products that enter circulation are commodities embodying abstract human labour. Drawing on Marx's account of primitive accumulation as the separation of producers from the means of production, Bai argues that leisure time becomes production and consumption time. Capital controls reproduction through waged and non-waged labour, and exploitation extends into all areas of social life. Private appropriation of data deepens alienation, as described in the 1844 Manuscripts. The forms of accumulation are new, Bai says, but the underlying logic is unchanged. Bai concludes that revealing the essential logic of digital capitalism and making good use of digital capital is an important task for contemporary Marxist research. Bai calls on China, building a digital China within Chinese modernization, to guard against digital alienation, stress fairness and sharing, and make digital capital serve new quality productive forces and high-quality development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party-school scholar defends the continuing explanatory power of Marx's theory against claims that digital capitalism has superseded it.

Digital capitalism from a Marxist perspective 马克思主义视域下的数字资本主义 Liu Xinyu This short commentary from China Social Sciences Today asks how digital capitalism, which Liu Xinyu describes as the latest form of capitalist development, should be understood, and how it can be overcome. Liu reads it through historical materialism combined with the critique of political economy. The thesis is that digital capitalism is a historical product of capital relations, that it still rests on exploitation and profit-seeking in a more hidden form, and that it extends alienation to the whole of human life. The piece has three parts. The first traces the turn from industrial and financial capital to digital capital, which Liu presents as a response to overaccumulation and the 2008 financial crisis. The second offers a political-economy critique of data, platforms and user activity, drawing on Marx, Adorno and Christian Fuchs. A short closing section turns to Chinese modernization and the digital economy. Liu argues that capital's drive to maximise surplus value stays constant across industrial, financial and digital stages. Digital capital opens a new space of exploitation in the virtual world, while big data and cloud computing steer production and investment. Only data taken up by platform algorithms counts as valuable, and its value includes the mental and physical activity of both developers and ordinary users. Users have no direct wage relation with platforms, so, in a phrase Liu quotes, exploitation is hidden "in the structure of play". Platforms sell user data, target advertising and so speed circulation and indirectly reproduce the wage relation. Liu also says this immaterial labour reaches into life time and extends exploitation beyond working hours, which Liu calls biopower. Liu adds that criticising digital capitalism does not mean rejecting digital tools, since it is a historical stage, much as money as general equivalent was an advance. Liu concludes that digital capitalism does not bring free and all-round human development. In Liu's account it brings subjection to technology and capital, loss of subjectivity, a weaker real economy, more unemployment and a wider wealth gap. The critique should aim to break data monopoly and make platform data truly shared. Liu holds that modernization is not Westernization or capitalization, and cites the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to integrate the digital and real economies deeply as the direction for China. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist account of platform labour, data value and alienation, ending in the official policy line on the digital economy.

Artificial intelligence and the opinion-guiding capacity of mainstream media 人工智能助力主流媒体舆论引导力 Gong He Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for integrated management of news and publicity and online public opinion, Gong asks how mainstream media can strengthen their capacity to guide opinion. The commentary argues that artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, offers new means of doing so, though it carries risks. The piece first lists three difficulties: a more plural and open set of opinion actors, with algorithmic "information cocoons" and platform-controlled visibility; online discourse that shifts quickly and is emotional, leaving official responses lagging in time and space; and cross-media and global opinion fields that overlap and sharpen confrontation. It then sets out three ways AI can be embedded in the work of mainstream media. Gong's first point is that AI can build the scenario for news and opinion guidance: it can personalise delivery, help set the tone early in an event, filter rumours and vulgar content, and support international cooperation. Second, it can rebuild the discourse ecology by analysing public emotion and generating empathetic language, and by producing interactive content and cross-language texts for international communication. Third, it can run through the whole process of opinion monitoring: scanning sources, flagging crises, predicting trends, grading incidents and producing multimodal content. Gong concludes that AI supports role change, new styles of expression and process re-engineering in news and publicity. The author also warns of homogenised content, path dependence, and challenges of technological ethics and transparency, and says that keeping information truthful and credible is a priority. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned view of how AI is expected to serve opinion guidance in Chinese state media.

The problem of poverty in American society in the 1960s 20世纪60年代美国社会中的贫困问题 Li Yun This short newspaper commentary asks why poverty persisted in the United States in the 1960s, despite its postwar economic strength. Li Yun argues that behind the apparent prosperity lay a serious social crisis, and that federal anti-poverty policy could not remove poverty because its institutional roots in inequality were left untouched. The article proceeds in three parts: poverty as a chronic ailment of American society, the failure to eradicate it fundamentally, and the continuing widening of the wealth gap into the 1970s and later. It draws on Michael Harrington's The Other America, the sociologist Diana Pearce, Lyndon Johnson's reforms and Robert Putnam's Our Kids. Li identifies Black poverty and the 'feminization of poverty' among single-mother households as the two most visible cases, citing figures on female-headed households among poor families (23% in 1959, 28.5% in 1965). Johnson's 'war on poverty' and 'Great Society', including the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act, education laws, medical aid and aid for families with dependent children, are said to have cut the poverty rate from 22% to 13%. Li nonetheless calls such reforms 'scratching an itch through the boot', leaving many Black Americans in worsening poverty amid racial conflict and urban unrest. Li concludes that widening inequality, class stratification and the decline of the white blue-collar class have undermined the American Dream and public belief in 'equality of opportunity'. The article contrasts the founding ideals of the Declaration of Independence with this reality. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese academic commentary characterises American poverty and inequality.

Applying the labour aristocracy theory to the analysis of British society 运用工人贵族理论分析英国社会 Liu Yaohui This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today, asks how the concept of the "labour aristocracy" helps explain class relations in Britain from the mid-nineteenth century to the early twentieth. Liu Yaohui argues that Marxist classical writers and left-wing scholars made it one of the core concepts for understanding Victorian and Edwardian class relations, the labour movement and imperialism. The article first traces the concept's origins in 1830s British observers' description of the highest stratum of skilled workers. It then reviews Marx's implicit usage, Engels's explicit formulations, Lenin's wartime writings and, in the mid-twentieth century, Eric Hobsbawm's work, and closes with an assessment of the theory's value. Liu reports that Engels, in 1871 and in his 1885 essay on England in 1845 and 1885, tied the labour aristocracy (factory workers and skilled trade unionists) to Britain's monopoly position in the world economy, which he expected to erode. Lenin, in Liu's account, located the decisive mechanism in the bourgeoisie's deliberate bribing of part of the working class with colonial super-profits, which Lenin held responsible for the failure of international solidarity. Hobsbawm's 1954 essay proposed six criteria, above all income level and stability, and argued that the old labour aristocracy dissolved after 1914. Liu notes that his economistic reading drew criticism. Liu concludes that, despite its vagueness and the lack of a single definition, the theory clarifies the formation, structure and stratification of the British working class and its differences from other industrial countries. Debates around it have prompted wide research, and Marxist historians and left-wing figures still use it. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how Engels, Lenin and Hobsbawm treated the labour aristocracy.

The "Second Integration" consolidates the cultural foundations of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era “第二个结合”筑牢新时代中国特色社会主义文化根基 Zhang Ruitao Zhang Ruitao asks how the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, supports the development of socialist culture in the new era. Drawing on Xi Jinping's description of it as a further "emancipation of the mind", Zhang argues that it is the "only path" for developing the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Zhang's account it strengthens cultural confidence, advances cultural consciousness and opens a way forward. The piece is a newspaper commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today. The article is organised under four headings. The first deals with continuing the "roots" of fine traditional culture, the second with the modern transformation of that culture, the third with holding to Marxism as the "soul", and the fourth with building a new form of human civilization. Zhang draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches, including the symposium on cultural inheritance and development and its "five salient features" of Chinese civilization, and on classical Chinese sources such as the Discourses of the States (Guoyu). Zhang's central move is to present culture as a unity of two lines of descent. Fine traditional culture is the "root", and Marxism is the "soul". Cultural confidence, as Zhang defines it, means critically inheriting the best of tradition and correcting its dross, which Zhang calls a dialectical "cultural consciousness". The Party is cast as the inheritor of tradition rather than a nihilist about history or culture. The "creative transformation and innovative development" of tradition means reinterpreting it for the present and, under core socialist values, joining it to Marxist principles in a new cultural form. Zhang also argues that institutions such as the people's congress system, political consultation, a unitary state and regional ethnic autonomy are deeply linked to Chinese ideas of people-centred governance and unity in diversity. Zhang concludes that the Second Integration lets Marxism take root in China with Chinese-style discourse and makes socialist culture a reality rather than a possibility. The traditional ideal of "harmony and integration" (hehe) is said to have produced the "common values of all mankind", which Zhang traces to older values such as benevolence, "all under heaven for the common good" and "harmony without uniformity". Zhang presents these values as China's contribution to a community with a shared future for mankind, respecting civilizational diversity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary links the Second Integration to cultural confidence, traditional concepts and the idea of a new form of human civilization.

The "object" logic of communication in systematising Chinese stories 中国故事体系化的“物”理传播逻辑 Wang Feng'e This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, asks how to tell China's story well, as Xi Jinping has called for, when technology is changing the relation between people and things. Wang argues that things (wu) are gaining agency and that "everything is media", so China's international communication should build a system of communication through objects alongside narration by people. The author frames four practical questions: what to tell, with what, where, and how. The piece is organised around those four questions. Wang first sets out the content of the stories, then classifies the objects that can carry them, then identifies the settings where they can be told, and finally proposes methods. Objects are grouped by the three kinds of story: Chinese stories, stories of the Communist Party, and stories of the new era. On content, Wang says a story consists of teller, story, setting and audience, and that the core "principle" to convey is why the Communist Party "can", Marxism "works" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good". Drawing on Schramm's formula of selection probability, Wang holds that audiences need stories of use to them. On objects, Wang lists cultural heritage, revolutionary relics, and new-era items such as films, e-commerce and payment platforms, high-speed rail and artificial intelligence. Such objects are told in media platforms, everyday consumption and overseas tourism, where visitors' own experience lets objects speak. On method, Wang proposes "observing things through things", citing Shao Yong and contrasting phenomenology's suspension of presuppositions, so that objective regularities show through objects. Wang also urges attention to objects' mobilising power (even idols and fans are described as reified media), giving each object a focused function, and building object-centred narrative platforms, which the author says do not yet exist. The aim is presented not as cultural domination but as mutual learning among civilisations and a communicable world. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese communication scholars link the "object turn" in narrative theory to the official task of telling China's story well.

Leading the accelerated formation of new quality productive forces with the new development philosophy 以新发展理念引领新质生产力加快形成 Su Yubo This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today argues that the new development philosophy should guide the accelerated formation of new quality productive forces. Su Yubo takes Xi Jinping's statement that these forces are an inherent requirement and key focus of high-quality development as the starting point. Su contends that the approach matters for economic quality, international competitiveness and the initiative in building a modernized country. The article is organised around the five components of the new development philosophy: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. Each section names the problem the component addresses and links it to the formation of new quality productive forces. Su argues that innovation supplies the driving force, citing high-speed rail, 5G and space exploration, while also listing weak points such as low basic-research spending, a low rate of converting research results, and dependence on foreign core technologies. Coordination is tied to regional balance, with Xi's launch of the concept during an inspection of the Northeast offered as significant. Green development is presented as the ecological form of these productive forces, linked to the carbon peak and carbon neutrality pledges. Openness draws on Marx's remark about world-historical inventions to argue that technology is global. Sharing is framed as the "make the cake bigger" and "divide the cake well" contradiction, which new quality productive forces are said to ease by converting into improved livelihoods. Su concludes that matching an advanced supply side to people's growing and diversified needs is required if the fruits of modernization are to reach all people more fairly. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-school-style commentary maps the five elements of the new development philosophy onto new quality productive forces.

Similarities and differences: Merleau-Ponty's and Marx's theories of the "object" 相同与差异：梅洛-庞蒂与马克思的“对象”理论 Liu Shaoming Liu Shaoming compares how Marx and Maurice Merleau-Ponty conceive the "object". Starting from Merleau-Ponty's remark that Marx introduced the concept of the human object, later taken up and developed by phenomenology, Liu argues that both thinkers share a form of transcendental reduction: objects appear only on the basis of human activity. They nonetheless differ over how objects appear and over whether relations of production ground an object's basic meaning. The article has three parts. The first sets out four points of agreement on how objects appear. The second sets out differences, divided into produced versus perceived objects and relations of production versus a general environment that confers meaning. The third draws out the significance of the comparison for the history of ideas, for the complementarity of the two theories and for the strengths of Marx's position. On agreement, Liu says both treat sensuous or perceptual activity as the original meeting of person and thing, and see the object as both immanent and transcendent. Both treat tools as extensions of human capacity, and both hold that human beings, unlike animals, can relate to objects in many ways. On difference, Marx's objects are shaped through labour, have a transparent history in industry, and are grounded in social relations of production. Merleau-Ponty's objects are brought into view by the bodily schema, have a semi-opaque history of sedimentation, and depend on a bodily environment with no single priority. Liu reads this as the reason why Merleau-Ponty sees no general reification of persons by objects and treats freedom as always partial, whereas Marx ties reification to private property and liberation to the development of productive forces. Liu concludes that the comparison shows phenomenology inheriting and transforming Marx's theory of the object, along a line from German classical philosophy through Marx to phenomenology. The two accounts complement each other in how objects exist, in historicity and in the grounding of natural science. Liu argues that Marx's approach has three advantages: Merleau-Ponty underestimates relations of production, neglects the mechanisms of reification, and treats freedom in a less developed way. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language comparison of Marx and phenomenology on objecthood, and a view of how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends Marx's priority.

Phenomenology and Marx's philosophy: grounding and critique 现象学与马克思哲学：建基与批判 Ma Yinghui Can phenomenology and Marx's philosophy be set side by side? Ma Yinghui, in a short piece for the Chinese Social Sciences Today, concedes that they differ in object and aim: phenomenology starts from consciousness and aims to re-found Western civilisation, while Marx's critique of political economy demonstrates capitalism's eventual demise. Ma nonetheless argues that the differences do not form a gulf and that the two work as complementary perspectives. The article first notes the mutual borrowing between Western Marxism and the phenomenological movement, citing Lukács, Marcuse, Adorno, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty and the 1960s attempts at fusion. It then turns to their shared historical background and compares them on ontology and on method. Ma holds that both arose from the interlinked scientific, industrial and social revolutions that followed non-Euclidean geometry, which gives them a common root. Ontologically, Husserl's pure consciousness, Heidegger's Dasein and Marx's social-historical existence are said to form a "three-dimensional prism". Husserl supplies a cognitive model, Heidegger the mode of existence of subjects within large-scale capitalist production, and Marx the source of Husserl's objects and the social-historical basis of Heidegger's analysis. Methodologically, Ma argues that Marx's analysis of value-form had already treated form as real being. Phenomenology builds meaning on formal relations, whereas Marx examines how those relations are generated and asks whether new relations of production are possible. Ma concludes that the cross-view of the two philosophies lets us understand the scientific and revolutionary character of Marx's philosophy more deeply, and see more clearly the origins, features and future of modern existence. Read the original if you want a brief, programmatic Chinese argument for reading Husserl and Heidegger together with Marx.

Further comprehensively deepening reform must always uphold the people's principal position 进一步全面深化改革要始终坚持人民主体地位 Ren Pengcheng This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today takes up one of the "six adherences" set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): putting the people first in further comprehensively deepening reform. Ren Pengcheng argues that upholding the people's principal position gives scientific guidance and a value orientation for advancing Chinese modernization and creating a higher-quality, happier life. The article moves from theory to practice and then to tasks. It first grounds the principle in the Marxist view of the people as makers of history and in the Party's fundamental political stance. It then reviews achievements since reform and opening up and since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with measures for the current round of reform. Ren's central claim is that the people are both the beneficiaries and the source of strength of reform. The article presents the Party's century of struggle, the elimination of absolute poverty and the build-out of education, social security and health systems as proof that reform aims at the people's wellbeing. It also treats the Party's theoretical innovations as products of the people's wisdom, and cites Xi Jinping: reform is meaningful when done for the people and has momentum when it relies on them. For the next stage, Ren calls for strengthening Party leadership through the Party's self-reform, and for sustaining ideals and convictions through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Ren also calls for testing reform by actual results and public satisfaction, drawing on investigation and research, the mass line and whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official discourse links the people's principal position to the Third Plenum's reform agenda.

The narrative code of "inspiring understanding of the Way" in ideological and political courses in the new era and new journey 新时代新征程思政课“启人悟道”的叙事密码 Chen Bo This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how teachers of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in universities can make their teaching more persuasive. Chen Bo argues that they should build a habit of narrative thinking and teach through stories. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that deep truths must move and convince people through storytelling, the author holds that stories connect events to students' own situations and so carry value guidance indirectly. The article sets out four kinds of story that teachers should draw on, each tied to a "way" (dao): Chinese history and culture, the Party's revolutionary success, reform and development, and human civilisation. It rests the approach on the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics and on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture. On culture, Chen recommends using the structure of Chinese characters, ancient artefacts, the sayings of ancient thinkers and classical poetry to convey ideas such as benevolence, people-centredness and harmony. On revolution, teachers should tell the stories behind the Long March, Yan'an and Jinggangshan spirits, using local and campus resources and varied media such as images, museum visits, interviews and virtual experiences. On reform, Chen lists examples including the restoration of the college entrance examination, Xiaogang village's contract system, Zhongguancun, the "lucid waters and lush mountains" idea and the poverty reduction of nearly 100 million people. The author adds that teachers should present the Party's strategic wisdom in Chinese modernization. The fourth strand asks teachers to promote exchange among civilisations through Dunhuang and Silk Road culture and cooperation stories from the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese pedagogical writing links storytelling methods to Party history and official political themes.

How new media can empower the building of red culture brands 新媒体赋能红色文化品牌建设 Liu Li This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today asks how new media can be used to build brands around red culture, the spiritual legacy formed by the Party and the people in revolution, construction and reform. Building a theoretical system of the Chinese nation as a community 构建中华民族共同体理论体系 Peng Fengwen This short commentary in China Social Sciences Today takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at a Political Bureau collective study session, to build a scientific and complete theoretical system of the Chinese nation as a community (zhonghua minzu gongtongti). Advancing the great practice of common prosperity with a spirit of historical initiative 以历史主动精神推进共同富裕伟大实践 Pan Xuefeng This commentary from a Party-theory research base asks how the Communist Party's "spirit of historical initiative" can guide the work of advancing common prosperity as China moves from building a moderately prosperous society to building a modern socialist country. The author calls for the path to be adjusted in good time to national and international conditions, and for the Party to keep its historical consciousness and sense of responsibility. Pan claims that this will offer "Chinese wisdom" and a Chinese approach to the shared cause of peace and development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link common prosperity to Marxist classics and official doctrine.

Using new quality productive forces to drive the building of a modern industrial system 以新质生产力牵引现代化产业体系建设 Tao Feng Xu Yang This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how new quality productive forces can drive the construction of a modern industrial system. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Chinese economists link new quality productive forces to industrial policy, with regional case examples.

Creating a relaxed policy environment for developing new quality productive forces 为发展新质生产力营造宽松政策环境 Zhang Chengsi Writing after the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, Zhang Chengsi asks how macroeconomic policy can best support new quality productive forces in 2025. Monetary policy, by contrast, is to improve the financial ecosystem. Zhang stresses that "moderately loose" does not mean aimless liquidity injection. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese economist links fiscal and monetary policy to new quality productive forces after the December 2024 policy conference.

The Two Integrations are thoroughly dialectical An interview with Roland Boer “两个结合”具有彻底的辩证性 This is an interview, published in China Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), with Roland Boer (薄国强), a professor of philosophy at Renmin University of China who has moved from work on Western Marxism to research on Marxism adapted to China and on socialism with Chinese characteristics. Boer argues that the Two Integrations are "thoroughly dialectical" and uses that reading to discuss the Party's vitality, Western crisis and Chinese modernization. It ends with cultural exchange and an etymological reading of Chinese modernization. On the Two Integrations, Boer reads the method through three formulations: "weeding through the old to bring forth the new", "dialectical selection and rejection" and "upholding fundamentals while innovating". Boer concludes that Chinese modernization contributes to the "universality" or commonality of modernization through its distinctive features. He also says the Party's experience of combining Marxism with national conditions offers other communist parties a methodological lesson rather than a template to copy. He attributes differences between Western and Chinese scholarship on China to language barriers, differing academic discourse and differing ideological backgrounds, and calls for "academic bridges". Read the original if you want a Western Marxist's account of the Two Integrations, Chinese modernization and Western decline as presented in a Chinese state-affiliated outlet.

Providing legal safeguards for ecological civilization in the new era 为新时代生态文明建设提供法律保障 Zhang Ruiping This short commentary asks what the drafting of an Ecological Environment Code signifies for China's new era. Zhang describes the code as organised in five parts: general provisions, pollution control, natural ecological protection, green and low-carbon development, and ecological and environmental liability. In Zhang's account, it would integrate a body of more than 30 laws, over 100 administrative regulations and over 1,000 local regulations. The author says these now overlap, and that codification can remove conflicts, fill gaps and improve enforceability. Zhang also cites the 2018 constitutional amendment and the 2022 UN General Assembly resolution on a clean, healthy and sustainable environment as supports for writing environmental rights into the code. Zhang concludes that codification is more than a consolidation of existing rules. In the author's view, it reflects a change in the idea of rule of law in the new era and public consensus on environmental protection. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the rationale for China's environmental code and the policy documents behind it.

How legal research can serve the building of a higher-level socialist country under the rule of law 法学研究如何服务建设更高水平的社会主义法治国家 Wang Xu Responding to Xi Jinping's letter to the ninth national congress of the China Law Society, this short commentary asks how Chinese legal scholarship can serve the building of a "higher-level socialist country under the rule of law". Wang argues that legal research must first read the current practical situation correctly. Otherwise it risks "spatio-temporal misplacement", either reviving problems from earlier stages or importing foreign problems as its own agenda. The article first grounds the demand in the nature of law as a theory-driven practice, citing Max Weber's view of jurisprudence as a social science. It then identifies five practical features of the present stage, which Wang treats as the basic framework, problem list and theoretical premise for research. For each feature, Wang names a shortfall that scholars need to address. The five features are: a settled intellectual climate favouring comprehensive law-based governance, grounded in Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law; an institutional climate of modernizing state governance through law; a practical climate of protecting citizens' rights; an innovative climate of legal reform; and an external climate of coordinating domestic and foreign-related rule of law. Against each, Wang points to uneven and insufficient legal supply, local and departmental protectionism, "trusting petitions, not law" and weak rule-consciousness, the need to assess different reform methods, and weak theory on foreign-related law. Wang gives particular weight to a "defence mechanism against shocks to shared social psychology", which the article calls a new and major topic and the basis of the "great unity" system under Party leadership. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese legal scholar translates the Party's rule-of-law agenda into a research programme.

Building a higher-level socialist rule-of-law country 建设更高水平的社会主义法治国家 Zhou Shangjun This commentary in the China Social Sciences Today takes its cue from Xi Jinping's letter of 10 January 2025 to the ninth national congress of the China Law Society. In the first part, Zhou lists leadership of the Party over law-based governance, law for and by the people, unity of reform and law, integration of core socialist values into law, and a professional legal workforce. As evidence Zhou cites the Supervision Law (2018, revised 2024), the Civil Code (2020) and the revised Organic Law of the State Council (2024). Zhou also gives workforce figures: over 95 per cent of judges and procurators have law degrees or higher, and the number of lawyers has grown from 300,000 to 725,000. Zhou claims that Party leadership has opened a new 'autonomous' path of legal modernization, distinct from the 'self-generated' and 'transplanted' types, and a new form of human legal civilization. For the next stage Zhou proposes four aims: more scientific rule-of-law construction, through systematic planning and performance indicators; more standardized, through higher-quality legislation in new and foreign-related fields; more socialized, through public participation, social fairness and better public legal services; and more intelligent, through digital transformation, big data and AI in litigation and legal services. Guiding the development of ethnology with a sense of community for the Chinese nation 用中华民族共同体意识引领民族学学科建设 Yang Zhengquan Writing in the China Social Sciences Today after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Yang Zhengquan asks how ethnology, as a discipline, should respond to the call to build an autonomous Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge. The answer is that the discipline must be led by forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Yang calls this the primary political task of ethnology today and argues that the field must not drift from it. The commentary is organised around three sources of guidance, each tied to a sub-discipline of ethnology. The first is contemporary Chinese Marxist theory of nationalities, linked to Marxist nationality theory and policy. The second is the idea of the 'Four-way Togetherness', linked to a discipline Yang calls Chinese nationality studies. The third is the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, linked to anthropology and world ethnology. Yang draws on the Plenum's Decision and on statements by Xi Jinping. Yang presents Xi Jinping's important thinking on strengthening and improving ethnic work as the contemporary Chinese Marxist theory of nationalities, and lists its twelve 'musts' from the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work. The 'Four-way Togetherness' means sharing weal and woe, honour and disgrace, life and death, and destiny. Yang says it requires balancing commonality and diversity, and the Chinese national community consciousness and the consciousness of each ethnic group. The author repeatedly names Western theoretical and discursive influence as a problem in Chinese ethnology. Yang also calls for textbooks such as the Introduction to the Chinese Nation Community, general histories of the Chinese nation, work on ancient texts and artefacts, and support for younger scholars. The aim is to train specialists who command this theory and have fieldwork skills. Read the original if you want to see how a senior academic administrator links Party nationality policy to the reorganisation of ethnology's sub-fields and training.

Empowering the development of new quality productive forces through intelligent decision-making 以智慧决策赋能新质生产力发展 Zhang Shuhui Wang Zhenyu Zhang Runze This newspaper commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today, asks how national decision-making capacity can support the growth of new quality productive forces. Zhang, Wang and Zhang argue that high-quality, intelligent decision-making is an important foundation for such forces, and that digital and intelligent national decision-making infrastructure is the public technical base needed to lift that capacity. The piece has three parts. It first explains why new quality productive forces need high-quality decisions at the level of government, enterprises, and universities and research institutes. It then defines national decision-making infrastructure and describes its functions. Finally, it assesses the technical conditions and existing foundations in China for building it. The authors contend that decision-making is shifting from human-intelligence-led models towards "hybrid intelligence", in which algorithmic models perform situational awareness, forecasting and scenario simulation alongside experts. They define decision-making infrastructure as the technical facilities and organisations used to gather information, design responses and evaluate options. These include knowledge databases, algorithm model libraries, computing centres, think tanks and universities. In their metaphor, databases make it a "searchlight" and algorithm models make it an "engine". They hold that large language models, multi-agent systems and big data now make intelligent decision-making technically feasible. The authors judge that China already has a basis in managed government data and models, high-end think tanks, and open research platforms. They propose a national-conditions information platform for real-time data collection, an algorithm model platform with clear decision variables, and intelligent application systems built from scenario problems and response cases. How to present the "original theoretical image" of ideological and political education 怎样呈现思想政治教育的“理论原相” Wu Hongzheng Marking forty years since ideological and political education was established as an academic discipline in 2024, this book review by Wu Hongzheng assesses a four-volume work by Li Zhongjun (Northeast Normal University) and colleagues, Research on the Ideological and Political Education Thought of Marx and Engels (the Research). Wu argues that the work presents the "original theoretical image" (lilun yuanxiang) of the field in a distinctive way, grounded closely in the classic texts. The review also contends that the work leaves the logical links among its parts underdeveloped. The Research collects Marx's and Engels's direct and indirect remarks on the subject and organises them along four dimensions: concepts, categories, content and methods.
