Wu describes 11 concepts, nine pairs of categories (such as individual and society, thought and interest, theory and practice), ten kinds of educational content, and ten methods, including theoretical inculcation, critique and exposure, and self-reform. The review goes through each dimension and notes what the book contributes and what it omits. Wu's main criticisms are logical. The book does not explain why these 11 concepts matter and others, such as freedom or species-essence, do not. It also does not state the dialectical principle that categories come in pairs, as in Hegel's logic, nor does it move from paired opposites to their synthesis. Its textual fidelity, Wu says, risks losing the "living soul" running through the texts. It also leaves open what "all-round" means in the all-round development of the person. On methods, Wu asks whether the defence of inculcation takes account of Marx's views on the people's subjecthood, and whether the stress on critique overlooks Marx's positive inheritance from German classical philosophy. Wu concludes that the Research respects the classics, avoids forced interpretation, and offers a necessary "anatomical" analysis. Its four dimensions form a chain: analysis runs from front to back, and construction from back to front. Wu argues this supports the scientific and theoretical development of a young discipline whose concepts, categories and principles are still vague, and helps build an independent Chinese knowledge system of ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a short critical assessment of how Chinese scholars are recovering Marx and Engels as a foundation for the discipline of ideological and political education.

Inheriting and disseminating red culture in classic ethnic-minority literature 红色文化在民族文学经典中传承与传播 Huang Xiaojuan This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, asks how red culture embedded in the classics of ethnic-minority literature can be passed on within China and communicated abroad. Huang Xiaojuan argues that these classics carry red culture in distinctly ethnic forms while also giving it a universal, world-facing dimension. In the author's view, rereading them strengthens national identity and helps present the image of the Chinese nation as a single community to the world. The piece opens by defining literary classics and red culture, which the author describes as a product of integrating Marxism with Chinese realities, formed from the New Democratic Revolution through reform and opening up. It then has two main sections: the ethnicized character of red culture and its contemporary inheritance, and its worldwide character and overseas dissemination. Examples include Manchu writers such as Shu Qun and Duanmu Hongliang in anti-Japanese war literature, and the Yan'an-trained arts troupe that went to Shenyang in 1945. Huang contends that patriotism, ethnic unity and the Party's leadership recur as themes in minority literature, and that these works express red culture through ethnic lifeways, folk epic traditions, proverbs, songs and storytelling. The author then turns outward, citing the film script Sons and Daughters of China, which won an international festival prize, and Chinese troupes at the 1949 World Festival of Youth in Budapest. A lineage of heroes across revolution, construction and reform is presented as uniting ethnic and temporal character. Telling China's story well, Huang argues, lets these works evoke empathy across cultures and build Chinese cultural subjectivity. Huang concludes that carrying forward red culture in minority classics is a mission of the new era, helping to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The author proposes linking dissemination to international Chinese-language education through a "Chinese+" teaching model, and says such work can also help build a discipline system for literary studies with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars link ethnic literature, red culture and external cultural communication.

Empowering the building of the Chinese national community with new quality productive forces 以新质生产力赋能中华民族共同体建设 Kong Ting This newspaper commentary asks how new quality productive forces can support the building of the Chinese national community (Zhonghua minzu gongtongti), a task Xi Jinping stressed at a Politburo study session. Kong argues that developing such forces in ethnic minority regions can promote high-quality development there. In the author's view it also deepens cultural and psychological identification and supplies the material and cultural support for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. After defining new quality productive forces as innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality, in contrast to factor-driven traditional productive forces, the article takes three fields in turn: economic, social and ecological construction in ethnic regions. Each section follows the same pattern. It states the field's role in the community, lists current difficulties, sets out four measures, and describes the expected outcome. Kong links each field to a type of community: an economic community of shared prosperity, a socially interembedded community, and an ecological community of harmony between humans and nature. In the economic field the proposals include innovation systems with ethnic characteristics, digital upgrading of ethnic industries, talent systems and paired assistance from developed regions. In the social field they cover digital governance, smarter public services and digital preservation of ethnic cultures. In the ecological field they cover green technology, eco-industries and regional ecological compensation. The author concludes that these measures would strengthen endogenous growth, promote exchanges among ethnic groups, improve governance and safeguard the ecological security of ethnic regions. All of this is presented as laying a material, social and ecological foundation for forging a strong sense of community. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse links the economic agenda of new quality productive forces to ethnic-affairs policy.

Strengthening new quality productive forces requires the craftsman spirit of the new era 壮大新质生产力需要新时代工匠精神 Shang Wenjie Shang Wenjie asks how the craftsman spirit (gongjiang jingshen) can help build up new quality productive forces. The commentary argues that contemporary China's craftsman spirit rests on the Marxist principle of serving the people, and that combining it with new quality productive forces is a spiritual driving force for their growth. The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts. It covers the humanistic content of new quality productive forces, the mass support they need, and the production relations that must match them. It draws on the Mozi, on Mao Zedong's writings on industrialization, and on statements by Xi Jinping. Shang says today's craftsman spirit sublates earlier forms. It keeps the tradition of fine workmanship but adds "pursuit of excellence", meaning products that are also useful and widely affordable. This, the author argues, strengthens the "sharing" element of the new development philosophy. Citing Mao's accounts of balancing heavy industry, agriculture and light industry, Shang contends that the Party won popular support for industrialization by serving the masses, and that visible shared benefits would do the same now. Shang also holds that ancient craftsmen were exploited and alienated. By contrast, the present-day spirit supports reform of distribution and better relations between people in production, helping to form new production relations. Shang calls for labour policies that give the craftsman spirit a prominent place, raise workers' pay and social standing, and revise policies that conflict with its values. Shang also urges education that combines labour with schooling, joining cultural, skills and moral training, to set off a new surge of the workers' movement. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars link the craftsman spirit, new quality productive forces and the Marxist theory of production relations.

Talent cultivation and the development of new quality productive forces With a critique of the Western concept of "human capital" 人才培养与新质生产力发展 Huang Weijie Huang Weijie asks how China should design talent-cultivation models that serve new quality productive forces, and argues that doing so requires resisting the Western discourse of "human capital". Starting from Xi Jinping's call to adjust university disciplines and training models, the author contends that treating training as "investment in oneself" misleads thinking about education. This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today, first outlines the features of human capital theory, citing Gary Becker and Theodore Schultz. It then links the discourse to contemporary capitalist accumulation, and finally draws conclusions for talent policy in China. Huang argues that the theory casts wages as the "return" on a worker's skills and assumes individuals are responsible for funding their own education and health. In the author's reading, this discourse arose when over-accumulated capital moved into privatised public fields such as education and medicine, while a relative surplus population intensified competition among workers. Workers are thus forced to spend wages on skills, and the cost of reproducing labour-power is shifted away from capital, sometimes through debt. Using Marx's historical materialism, Huang claims the "self-investing" subject is an abstract presupposition that ignores ownership of the means of production and hides capital–labour exploitation. Huang concludes that education, health and similar public undertakings should receive public investment and be shared socially, easing workers' burdens and improving the combination of labourers, means of labour and objects of labour. The author calls for guarding against excessive privatisation of these fields and for implementing the strategy of strengthening the country through talent, so that gains from reproducing labour are not captured by developed capitalist countries. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-philosophical critique of human capital theory tied to current Chinese talent policy.

The natural-force sources of productive forces and new quality productive forces 生产力的自然力来源与新质生产力 Yuan Jinqiu Yuan Jinqiu asks how new quality productive forces should be defined in light of the theory of productive forces founded by Marx and Engels. The article argues that the theory of new quality productive forces inherits and develops that tradition. In Yuan's account, new quality productive forces are the sublation of the "productive force of capital" achieved through socialist construction. The short commentary has four parts. It criticises the long-dominant "constituent elements" reading of productive forces and sets out three natural-force sources. It then explains how capital generates its own productive force and what contradiction this contains. Finally it links the new development philosophy to the essential definition of new quality productive forces. Yuan holds that the elements model (means of labour, objects of labour, labourers, plus science and technology) does not explain where productive forces come from as an objective material power. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Yuan locates three sources: human beings' own natural powers, the natural power of social labour (cooperation and division of labour), and natural forces in nature. Under capitalism all three are capitalised, so the resulting power appears as capital's productive force. Its drive to exploit these sources to the limit damages them, through labour-power decline and ecological destruction, and so becomes a fetter. Under socialism, Yuan argues, production serves people's needs and all-round human development. A productive force formed by applying the new development philosophy to exploiting the three sources is a "people's productive force", and this is the fundamental criterion for new quality productive forces. Yuan concludes that new quality productive forces are a new chapter in Marxist productive-force theory, written by Chinese communists in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact theoretical argument that grounds new quality productive forces in Marx's account of natural forces and capital.

New quality productive forces empowering common prosperity 新质生产力赋能共同富裕 Liu Yiwen Liu Yiwen asks how new quality productive forces can serve common prosperity in contemporary China. In this short commentary for China Social Sciences Today, the author argues that eliminating poverty and achieving a prosperous society was Marx's consistent theoretical aim, and that developing new quality productive forces is now the necessary path to common prosperity. The piece begins with Marx's analysis of poverty, from the Rheinische Zeitung through the Paris manuscripts to Capital. It then distinguishes absolute poverty from relative poverty and treats, in turn, how new quality productive forces help eliminate each. On Marx, Liu reads absolute poverty as rooted in the separation of labour from property, and relative poverty as a matter of unjust distribution and spiritual hardship grounded in the theory of surplus value. For absolute poverty, Liu points to three channels: scientific and technological innovation, whose results are said to flow into poor areas; industrial upgrading, where socialist modernization treats capital as a neutral economic instrument; and higher-quality workers. For relative poverty, the author argues that new quality productive forces reshape the model of economic development and of economic governance. Digital technology is said to help coordinate market and government so that gains reach the people in an orderly way. Liu concludes that China, recognising poverty as a comprehensive social problem, is developing new quality productive forces to eliminate both kinds of poverty and build a society of free and all-round human development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary links Marx's theory of poverty to current policy on new quality productive forces and common prosperity.

The concept of "new quality productive forces" from the perspective of innovation 创新视角下的“新质生产力”概念 Zhou Ke Zhou Ke, a philosopher at Wuhan University, offers a short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on how the concept of new quality productive forces can be read through innovation. Zhou argues that innovation leads the formation of these forces, defines their character and is a basic requirement of the new development philosophy. Reading the concept this way, Zhou holds, shows how it enriches Marx's theory of productive forces under present-day conditions. The piece has three sections: the subject dimension of advanced productive forces, the optimisation of their structure of elements, and institutional innovation. Zhou draws mainly on Marx's critique of Friedrich List, the analysis of the labour process in Capital, and Xi Jinping's statements on the topic. First, Zhou says Marx's concept of productive forces stands out by stressing the worker as subject. Marx criticised List for separating wealth from its causes and so reducing people to things. Zhou reads Xi's statement that new quality productive forces are advanced productive forces led by innovation as stressing innovative activity and talent. Second, the labour process involves labour, objects of labour and means of labour. Zhou argues that today's shift to digital and intelligent means of labour and to data as an object of labour calls for a move from a "demographic dividend" to a "talent dividend". Third, relations of production can promote or hinder productive forces, so Zhou says new quality productive forces need new relations of production through deeper reform. Zhou concludes that institutional and mechanism innovation, especially in the economic and scientific systems, must combine government planning with market regulation. It must also link the innovation, industrial and capital chains, and pair a high-standard domestic market with high-level opening up. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-theoretical framing of new quality productive forces that links Marx's texts to current policy language.

The Marxist evaluation system: current challenges and a path to construction 马克思主义评价体系：境遇分析与建构理路 Zhang Li Xu Guofeng Zhang Li and Xu Guofeng, in a short piece for the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, ask how a Marxist evaluation system can be built when it faces rival systems. They define it as a system internal to Marxist theory, running through the productive forces, relations of production and superstructure, and guiding all-round human development and social progress. They argue that it is now seriously challenged and must be rebuilt around a people-centred orientation. The authors distinguish three components: systems for evaluating Marxist theory itself, systems of a Marxist character, and systems that give Marxist evaluations of social practice. The first half diagnoses three challenges. The second half sets out three principles of construction, each tied to a level of logic and a set of indicators. The authors trace the capital-based evaluation system to the emergence of surplus product, which in their account shifted family evaluation from inner qualities to external, symbolic ones. They then criticise metric-driven assessment in schools, where pupils' scores are tied to teachers' pay and promotion, and the over-development of individual consciousness, seen in "refined egoism" and "lying flat". For construction, they propose indicators grouped under the people-centred orientation, historical materialism and dialectical materialism. Examples include children's family companionship, labour productivity, the urban–rural income gap and trade with Belt and Road partners. They warn against making any indicator absolute, citing the urbanisation rate and population mobility. The authors conclude that indicators should steer reform, opening up and the image of an open and approachable China, while securing peace and stability for all-round human development. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese Marxist scholars link evaluation theory to concrete social indicators.

Raising the discursive power of Marxist ideology in the new era 提升新时代马克思主义意识形态话语权 Luo Yuting Writing in a newspaper commentary after Xi Jinping's recent instruction on the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project (the "Marxism Project", launched by the Central Committee in 2004), Luo Yuting asks how the Project has strengthened the discursive power of Marxist ideology in the new era. Luo argues that over 21 years, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Project has largely overcome a situation in which China's ideology "had reasons but could not state them, stated them but could not spread them, spread them but could not resonate". It is described as the key project for raising Marxist ideological discourse power. The article is organised around three functions of the Project: promoting theoretical innovation, theoretical dissemination and the putting of theory into practice. Each is tied to one of the three problems in the formula above. The author draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on figures about the Project's research centres, textbooks, popular readings and digital outreach. On innovation, Luo says the Project applies the Two Integrations and the "six musts", sets up research centres on socialist democracy, contemporary thought trends, international communication and Chinese civilisation, funds more than 700 key topics, and has set up 19 research centres on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On dissemination, it has produced unified textbooks for ideological and political theory courses and over 110 key textbooks for humanities disciplines. It also issues the popular series Theory Hotspots Face to Face, with total circulation in the tens of millions, uses digital platforms, and runs a Marxist literature collection project for international audiences. On practice, Luo contends that the Project turns theoretical, academic and ideological language into policy, popular and everyday language, and studies concepts such as people-centredness, Chinese modernization, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Luo concludes that through these three channels the Project has reversed Marxism's earlier "absence" in some disciplines, textbooks and forums. In the author's assessment, the ideological situation has undergone a fundamental, overall change, the guiding position of Marxism is consolidated, and the Project supplies strength for national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the Marxism Project's work is presented as building ideological discourse power.

Universities should advance ideological and political theory courses in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory 高校要坚持思政课建设与党的创新理论武装同步推进 Han Xu This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2025, responds to Xi Jinping's instruction that the building of ideological and political theory courses in schools should advance in step with arming teachers and students with the Party's innovative theory. Han Xu, a university Party secretary, argues that universities should treat high-quality, distinctive courses of this kind as the lever for raising the overall effectiveness of theoretical education and for the content-based development of ideological and political education. The piece is organised in five sections. It sets out the theoretical basis for the dual task, the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the practical effects required in the classroom, the need to raise the level of systematic and scholarly interpretation, and the building of a "big ideological and political course" framework. A final section on safeguards deals with the teaching staff. Han first places the task in the Party's tradition of theoretical education, citing the Gutian Conference and the Yan'an rectification movement as precedents. In this account, the courses are the main venue for Marxist and ideological education, and their essence, following Xi, is "explaining principles". Han then argues that the courses must be targeted and probing: content detached from students' needs, such as employment, entrepreneurship and technological innovation, will not win their conviction. Teachers should therefore use lively cases, group discussion and simulation, and should work together to build a systematic, well-structured curriculum on Xi Jinping Thought so that they can teach theory rather than only tell stories. Han calls for a "big ideological and political course" in which ideological content is carried by specialist teachers, counsellors and administrators, and in which classroom teaching is linked to visits to patriotic education bases and high-tech firms. The author also proposes stricter entry standards for ideological and political course teachers, training, incentives and an exit mechanism. The aim is a teaching force described as politically strong and broad in vision. Han concludes that advancing the two tasks together is a duty of the era and that universities should keep innovating their models in order to train socialist builders and successors. Read the original if you want an example of how a university Party leader translates a central directive into concrete institutional measures for ideological and political education.

Developing new quality productive forces requires an interest-coupling mechanism 发展新质生产力需要建立利益耦合机制 Meng Hui This short commentary, first published on Guangming Online's theory channel, asks how institutional reform can get the many actors in innovation to pull in the same direction. Meng Hui argues that new quality productive forces cannot advance without an "interest-coupling mechanism" (liyi ouhe jizhi) that aligns parties whose interests are not fully identical. Meng presents building such a mechanism as the starting and ending point of current reform of the science and technology system. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statements that innovation, including institutional and managerial innovation, is the distinctive feature of new quality productive forces. It then identifies five stakeholders in scientific and technological innovation: scientists, their research institutions, technology-based enterprises, innovation service providers, and governments at all levels. For each, Meng sets out the core interests that drive decisions. The last part turns to how these parties relate to one another and to the principles and measures of reform. Meng's central diagnosis is that each party decides according to its own core interest. Scientists prioritise frontier questions, top journals and honours. Institutions seek to attract funding, projects and talent. Firms seek revenue and profit, service providers add reputation and credibility to that, and local governments focus on output, jobs and tax. Meng says this divergence explains the weak link between industry, universities and research, and the "two skins" separation of science and industry. Meng proposes five principles: application orientation, seeking consensus, freeing constraints, each taking what it needs, and government concession of interests. Government should act as the "coupler", preferably working through service providers by market means. When any party loses out, the mechanism should first readjust shares and weights. If that fails, government should mediate without raising its own short-term gains, and should cede current direct benefits or even some powers while keeping its regulatory bottom line. Meng also proposes incentives outside the distribution mechanism itself. Scientists who contribute to applied fields would receive academic status and pay equal to that of leading basic researchers. Research institutions would be assessed partly on how far they advance new quality productive forces. Firms would be compensated through policy, fiscal and market tools for losses incurred in advancing their whole sector. Intermediaries would be given coupling tasks as a way into the market. Meng concludes that new quality productive forces must rest on a community of shared interests in innovation and on a reworked distribution mechanism, and that departing from this principle brings resistance or failure. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese policy-oriented account of how stakeholder interests in innovation are analysed and how government's role as mediator is framed.

Talent cultivation amid global digital economy competition 全球数字经济竞争下的人才培养 Lin Jing Cheng Molei This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how countries are training digital talent as digital technologies reshape industries and international competition. Lin and Cheng argue that skilled, responsible digital talent bears directly on how fast and how well new technologies, business forms and models emerge, and so supports high-quality development. They present education reform for digital talent as a priority that governments around the world have taken up. The article opens with UNESCO's September 2024 framework on the digital transformation of education, which has an outer layer of priorities, goals and principles and an inner layer of six pillars. It then surveys national practice under three headings: policy guarantees, hardware support, and curriculum and teaching reform. The cases come from the United States, the European Union, Australia (including New South Wales), Japan, the United Kingdom and Singapore. On policy, the authors describe the US National Educational Technology Plans, issued since 1996 and renewed in 2024 around three divides (digital use, design and access). They also describe the EU Digital Education Action Plan 2021–2027 and Australia's Digital Economy Strategy 2030. On hardware, they cite US broadband and digital-equity programmes, EU strategies funded through channels such as Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe, and Japan's GIGA School initiative to give every student a device. On curriculum, they point to successive US STEM strategies, the UK's integration of information technology into core subjects and blended teaching, and Singapore's student learning platform and graded coding and digital courses. The authors conclude that countries are pursuing digital talent cultivation through a combination of planning, infrastructure investment and curricular change, each adapted to national conditions. They offer no explicit recommendations for China in the text; the article works as an overview of foreign practice set against global digital competition. Read the original if you want a compact list of the named policy documents and programmes that Chinese education researchers cite when describing digital education abroad.

Grasping the value content of the modernization of the human being in full 全面把握人的现代化的价值内涵 Zeng Hanjun This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how the degree of a society's modernization should be judged. Zeng Hanjun argues that it depends not only on the development of objects but also on the advancement of the human subject. On this basis the author holds that the essence of Chinese modernization is the modernization of the human being. The piece draws on Xi Jinping's statements that the people's yearning for a better life is the starting and end point of modernization, and that its success depends on a people-centred approach. It then moves from the people as the driving force of modernization, to what the modernization of the human being means, to the role of the Party's mass line, and closes with a call to unite. Zeng argues that people are both the creative subject and the value subject of Chinese modernization, and that its ultimate goal is the free and all-round development of the human being. The author defines the modernization of the human being as a shift in values, behaviour, thinking and emotions from the traditional to the modern. Because Chinese modernization covers more than 1.4 billion people, Zeng calls it the largest and hardest modernization in history. Individuals must therefore take its realisation as their own task, reflecting on and creating themselves through practice. The Party, for its part, relies on the people, follows the mass line, and cites poverty alleviation and the building of a moderately prosperous society as results. Zeng concludes that advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization ultimately means deepening the expansion of human essential powers, towards free and conscious practical activity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary links Chinese modernization to the Marxist theme of human development.

Using the newly revised National Defence Education Law to build strong patriotic and military-strengthening forces Shanghai's approach to implementing whole-people national defence education 以落实新修订国防教育法为契机 凝聚爱国强军的磅礴力量 Zhao Jiaming Zhao Jiaming, a senior Shanghai Party official, writes in the People's Daily on how to put the newly revised National Defence Education Law of the People's Republic of China into practice. The author argues that national defence is the foundation of national survival, and that a strong defence requires national defence education to reach the whole population. Zhao holds that the revised law, by clarifying the content, guiding ideology, coverage, methods and support mechanisms of such education, matters greatly for promoting patriotism and strengthening the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece opens by citing a changing international environment, in which traditional and non-traditional security threats are said to intertwine. It gives Shanghai a special responsibility as an international metropolis and a front line of reform and opening up. It is then organised in three parts, each pairing what the revised law requires with what Shanghai has already done and what it will do next: ideological guidance, extending education from key groups to society as a whole, and coordination of institutions and resources. On the first point, Zhao stresses that national defence education has a distinctly political character and must follow the Party's line. The revised law names Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its guiding ideology, and Zhao presents Xi Jinping's thinking on strengthening the armed forces as decisive for the work. On coverage, the author calls for combining universal education with attention to leading cadres, described as the key group, and young people, described as the foundation, so that progress with these groups pulls the rest of society along. Shanghai's measures include a curriculum system for cadres, youth brand activities, mass events, new-media channels, and the use of the city's red-heritage sites. On coordination, Zhao points to strengthened Party leadership, a dedicated working mechanism under the municipal publicity leadership group, designated education bases, and the involvement of social organisations, universities, veterans and volunteers. Zhao concludes that these steps will make national defence education a genuinely society-wide undertaking, in which military and civilian sectors cooperate and the whole population takes part. The article offers a view of how a leading Party official describes local implementation of the law under the Party's guidance. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Shanghai's leadership translates national defence legislation into institutions, programmes and propaganda work.

Adapting to profound changes in social structure to innovate social governance 顺应社会结构深刻变化创新社会治理 Li Peizhi Writing in the People's Daily in January 2025, Li Peizhi, director of the Institute of Sociology at the Tianjin Academy of Social Sciences, takes up the relationship between social structure and social governance. Li argues that China's social structure is changing profoundly, and that governance must be innovated in step with these changes to advance Chinese modernization. The commentary defines social structure as covering employment, population, family and income structure. It then reviews three of these dimensions with statistics: employment, population and income. It closes with proposals drawn from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Li holds that structure and governance reinforce each other: structure shapes how governance actors cooperate, while governance innovation can improve structure. On employment, the author cites about 200 million flexible workers in 2023 and about 300 million migrant workers in 2024, and says platform workers need rights protection. On population, Li describes a shift to population decline, with falling birth rates, ageing and regional divergence, and endorses fertility-support policies. On income, Li cites faster rural than urban income growth and narrowing regional gaps since 2012 and 2013, and calls for further progress towards common prosperity. Li concludes that structural change brings both benefits and challenges, and that social and economic structure must develop in step. The proposals are: Party leadership of governance, livelihood protection within development, and a social governance community in which everyone has responsibility, does their duty and shares in the benefits. Li also calls for tracking structural change through social surveys and adjusting policy with a systemic perspective. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line overview of how Chinese sociologists link demographic, employment and income data to governance policy.

Forming an economic order that is both "lively" and "well-regulated" Balancing an efficient market and an enabling government 形成既“放得活”又“管得住”的经济秩序 Zhang Laiming Zhang Laiming, a deputy director of the Development Research Center of the State Council, comments in the People's Daily (16 January 2025) on a principle from the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2024. Xi Jinping listed five areas that must be coordinated. The first is the relationship between an efficient market and an enabling government, with the aim of an economic order that is both "放得活" (lively, freed up) and "管得住" (well controlled). Zhang presents this as a necessary requirement for improving the socialist market economy and advancing high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first places the principle within the history of China's market-economy exploration, from the planned economy to the socialist market economy. The second argues that this order is the starting point and goal of balancing market and government. The third turns to current problems and concrete measures, citing the draft Private Economy Promotion Law and a State Council General Office opinion on regulating administrative inspections of enterprises. Zhang argues that the government–market relationship has been the core question throughout China's reform path. The author cites 1979–2023 average growth of 8.9% and a 24.8% average contribution to world growth as evidence of success, while calling the socialist market economy a still-new system. Zhang describes the target order as one based on the rule of law, since the socialist market economy is "in essence a law-based economy". The author also holds that the boundary between market and government is not fixed but shifts with the stage of development, the principal contradiction, technology and the international environment. It therefore needs continual adjustment guided by dialectical and historical materialism. Zhang names problems on both sides. On the government side are improper intervention, local protectionism and weak safety enforcement, as well as overreach and absence. On the market side are abuse of dominant position and false advertising. The proposed remedy is institution-building and stricter enforcement. The measures include equal treatment of all forms of ownership, anti-monopoly enforcement, a unified national market, market-determined factor prices and protection of property rights. The author's formula is that the more standardised government conduct is, the more effective the market. Read the original if you want a concise official-economist statement of how the "effective market and enabling government" formula is being explained after the Third Plenum.

Henry's phenomenology of life reading of Marx 亨利对马克思的生命现象学解读 Cui Weifeng This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today presents Michel Henry's phenomenological interpretation of Marx. Cui explains that Henry set himself against Althusser's "symptomatic reading" and against the thesis of an epistemological break in Marx. Henry instead treats Marx's whole thought as a self-evident philosophical system built on one foundational concept: the reality of the living individual. The article first sets out Henry's method, which draws on Husserlian phenomenological reduction, and the claimed relation of essential grounding among Marx's concepts. It then discusses reality as the transcendental origin of history, using The German Ideology and Capital. A final section links reality to historicity and compares Marx with Husserl and Heidegger. In Cui's account, Henry holds that class struggle and economic production cannot ground history, because they depend on a more basic productive principle, the living individual. Marx's famous starting point in "living individuals" is read as an unconscious use of reduction, and for that reason Hegel's dialectic is replaced by a new ontology rather than simply inverted. Henry therefore reads the sequence of Marx's concepts as a history of transcendental origins, not a linear chronology. Cui reports that Henry sees Husserl's inner time-consciousness as lacking historical genesis, and Heidegger's historicity as dissolving into Dasein's existential structure. Cui concludes that, for Marx, history is an open possibility, and that individual experience gains real historical meaning only in the sense of historical genesis. Cui also remarks that Henry's purely phenomenological notion of history risks abstraction. From the standpoint of historical materialism, Cui adds, freedom is reached in a true community that overcomes the contingency of class-society division of labour. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language orientation to Henry's anti-Althusserian reading of Marx.

Why Marx was not an egalitarian 马克思为什么不是平等主义者 Bao Dawei Was Marx an egalitarian of some kind, or a political philosopher of equality? Bao Dawei argues that he was not. Read as egalitarian political philosophy, Marx's texts cannot account for his position, and the author holds that only the "grand historical view" of historical materialism can separate Marx's thought from the various egalitarianisms. This is a short newspaper-style essay in the history of Marxism. The essay first explains why Marxism so often looks like egalitarianism. Equality is an everyday experience and a basic norm of modern political ethics. Marxism also draws on egalitarian sources, namely French and English utopian socialism and left Hegelianism. Early workers' movements, including Weitling's, pursued egalitarian aims, and Western Marxist readings have sometimes fused Marxism with egalitarianism. It then sets out three reasons why inequality is, for Marx, only a phenomenon, and ends with how equality can actually be achieved. Bao's three reasons are as follows. By the measure of historical progress, inequality does not mark backward productive relations, and Marx and Engels criticised Proudhon's teleological moralising about equality. By the logic of capitalist relations of production, equality is the bourgeoisie's own ideology, under which "equal exploitation of labour-power" is capital's first human right, and Enlightenment thinkers also attacked inequality. By theoretical radicalism, moral judgement stays at the level of appearances, whereas Marx sought to grasp "the root of the matter". In Bao's reading, Marx's early critique in On the Jewish Question and the Communist Manifesto shows that legal equality makes people isolated monads and legitimises new class exploitation. Real equality depends on a revolutionary reconstruction of the superstructure and on the abolition of classes, which lies beyond egalitarian political philosophy. Bao concludes that Marxist theoretical radicalism must stay "on the road", because egalitarianism cannot escape what Rancière calls the "embarrassment" of modern politics: what the shifting mix of equality and inequality actually consists of. The author notes that scholars disagree, citing Kai Nielsen, who stresses Marx's concern with equality, and Allen Wood, who denies that Marx treated social equality as good in itself. Bao sides with separating Marx from egalitarianism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language statement of the case against reading Marx as an egalitarian, and a map of the scholars it engages, including Cohen, Wood, Nielsen and Rancière.

Seizing the initiative in high-quality economic development 把握经济高质量发展主动权 Li Zhenghua Ding Xiaoshan Following the Politburo meeting and the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2024, this commentary in China Social Sciences Today examines the phrase "promoting stability through progress" (yi jin cu wen). Li and Ding argue that the phrase is a key to guiding economic work in the coming period. In their reading, it shows how the Party leadership is seeking to seize the initiative in high-quality development. The authors first trace how the policy keynote of seeking progress while maintaining stability, used since the 18th Party Congress (2012), grew into a 24-character formulation in 2024. They then explain the roles of "stability" and "progress" and their dialectical relation. The second half sets out four requirements for putting the principle into practice. Li and Ding treat stability as the goal and progress as the driving force. They argue that pursuing stability without progress lets problems accumulate, so that stability becomes empty talk. Progress, through changing the growth model, adjusting structure and technological innovation, is therefore the route to stability. They cite 2023 exports of the "new three" (electric vehicles, solar panels, lithium batteries), which they say reached a trillion yuan, up 29.9%. The four requirements are an active attitude, a correct direction, a scientific method and systematic top-level design. Direction means progress that keeps to the socialist system, while method means "establish before breaking", for example building a new-energy supply system before cutting coal. Top-level design means "systematic integration and coordination", which the authors link to the systems approach stressed by Xi Jinping. The authors conclude that "promoting stability through progress" is an important guideline for economic work in the new era. They call for a more active attitude, clear direction, scientific method and systematic design so that reform and development reinforce each other. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference's wording is being interpreted in Party-affiliated scholarship.

Striving for a high-quality, positive interaction between development and security 努力实现发展和安全的高质量良性互动 Guo Chao Wang Shengyu This commentary from China Social Sciences Today takes up the call in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to achieve a positive interaction between high-quality development and a high level of security. Guo and Wang argue that coordinating development and security is a core governing principle of the Party and a requirement for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts: the significance of the principle, its core meaning, and strategic measures. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and the Plenum decision. On significance, the authors hold that the "two miracles" of rapid growth and long-term stability owed much to coordinating development and security, and that whether the two can be integrated will decide whether these achievements continue. They define "positive interaction" as mutual reinforcement. In their account, high-quality development is the greatest security, because it supplies the material base, strategic support and popular backing for security. High-level security is the best development, because the overall national security outlook, a modernized national security system and security for high-level opening up protect growth from systemic risk. For practice, Guo and Wang propose three measures: uphold Party leadership in planning and deploying both tasks together; apply systems thinking to keep the two in dynamic balance, like a bird's two wings; and deepen reform so that development and security concepts, systems and mechanisms are integrated. The aim is a new development pattern matched by a new security pattern. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary frames the development–security relationship.

Finding the right focal points for building ideological and political theory courses in universities in the new era 找准新时代高校思政课建设着力点 Zhang Yuguang This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today, asks how universities should build their ideological and political theory courses (sixheng ke) in the new era. Zhang Yuguang, a university Party official, argues that universities must study and implement Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference (2024) and his May 2024 instructions on school ideological and political courses, and must identify the right points of leverage. The stated goal is to cultivate people of the new era who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and ready to shoulder national rejuvenation. The article is organised around four areas of work: reforming and innovating the teaching of these key courses; planning a \"big ideological and political course\" with systems thinking; using digital technology to extend the courses' reach; and raising the professional level of the teachers. Each section opens with Xi Jinping's remarks and then sets out what universities should do. On teaching reform, Zhang calls for a problem-oriented approach, which the author presents as a basic Marxist standpoint. Teachers should address the handful of questions that students are actually puzzled by and explain facts and principles one by one. The author asks for more student participation, content drawn from the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and language students find easy to accept. On systems thinking, Zhang urges coordination among many actors, collaborative mechanisms with funding and facilities, use of local red resources, and integrated courses across university, middle and primary schools. On digital technology, the article proposes immersive classrooms using generative AI, XR and VR, and a curriculum built around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On teachers, Zhang proposes building a team that is politically strong and broad in outlook. This means fostering professional pride, promoting the spirit of educators, and reforming evaluation and promotion so that teaching comes first. It also means that teachers should hold firm Marxist belief, give rigorous theoretical answers to students, and improve through recruitment, training, incentives and teaching competitions. Zhang concludes that these four measures together will push the courses to a new stage of high-quality, connotation-based development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university Party official translates central directives on ideological and political education into practical measures.

Cultural development must follow the Party's mass line in the new era 文化建设必须走好新时代党的群众路线 Yu Guoshi Wu Yonghan This newspaper commentary asks how China can build a socialist cultural power and achieve a new cultural brilliance. Yu and Wu answer that cultural work must rest on the historical-materialist view that the masses make history, on a people-centred value orientation, and on the practice of going 'from the masses, to the masses'. In short, they argue that culture must follow the Party's mass line in the new era. The article is organised in three parts. The first holds that cultural development originates in the people's practice. The second takes 'cultivating the mind through culture' as the goal. The third makes the masses' evaluation the highest standard. Each part is anchored in quotations from Xi Jinping and ends in practical tasks. In the authors' account, culture is a superstructure rooted in social practice, which the people create. Cultural workers should therefore grasp the pulse of the era, respect the masses' creativity, learn from the people, and go to fields, workshops and markets for fieldwork. As the goal, culture should meet the people's growing and more diverse cultural needs, with provision tilted toward rural areas. It should also promote the core socialist values and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, strengthen patriotism, and foster a sense of community of the Chinese nation. As the standard, whether the people are satisfied is the test of a work. The authors therefore call for raising public cultural literacy, bringing culture to grassroots audiences through performances and mobile technology, and innovating to claim the online cultural sphere. The authors conclude that a flourishing socialist culture depends on the Party keeping close to the people, treating them as the source, the beneficiary and the judge of culture. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the mass line to cultural policy, public cultural services and ideological work.

In what sense is Marx an egalitarian? 马克思在何种意义上是平等主义者？ Xu Feng Xu Feng takes up a debate in contemporary political philosophy: whether Marx was an egalitarian. Some scholars, such as Kai Nielsen, read his critique of capitalist exploitation as resting on a firm commitment to equality. Others, such as Richard Miller and Allen Wood, hold that Marx valued equality only instrumentally, as a means to freedom and self-realisation. Xu argues that Marx is best understood as a relational egalitarian, not a distributive one, and that his relational egalitarianism differs from the contemporary version in three respects. The piece, published in the China Social Sciences Journal, has four parts. It first notes that the dispute depends on what counts as egalitarianism, since the Rawlsian tradition treats equality as an independent, intrinsic value. It then covers Marx's critique of equality as bourgeois ideology and the places where he points to a more real equality. It ends with the move from distributive to relational equality and the features that set Marx apart. Xu reads Marx's historical materialism as treating moral principles, equality included, as ideological products of particular conditions. Formal equality in contract and exchange, in this reading, masks real class inequality, and the myth of meritocracy legitimises exploitation by presenting unequal ownership of the means of production as personal merit. Yet Marx also points to something more substantive: his critique of the division of labour, and his two stages of communist society, in which distribution by labour still carries the 'birthmarks' of the old society. Xu argues that Marx treats distribution as derived from relations of production and criticises a fixation on distribution as 'vulgar socialism', so what he seeks is the dissolution of class domination, in line with relational egalitarians. The three differences are these. Marx offers an empirical analysis of capitalism instead of an abstract normative theory. He treats relational equality as the necessary outcome of changed production relations, not as an a priori norm. And he looks to class struggle and revolution, not top-down policy, charity or civic education. Xu concludes that Marx is an egalitarian only in a particular sense. Equality for him is a factual state that follows from collective control of the means of production, not an independently justified moral goal pursued through redistribution. Marx's path, Xu says, is more direct and more radical than that of present-day relational egalitarians. Read the original if you want a concise account of how the analytic debate over Marx and equality can be recast through the distributive/relational distinction.

Improving the market access system to underpin a high-standard socialist market economy 完善支撑高水平社会主义市场经济体制的的市场准入制度 Liu Tao This commentary, published in Study Times in January 2025, asks why market access matters and how it should be improved. Liu Tao argues that the market access system is a basic institution reflecting the relationship between government and market, and that improving it is a reform task for building a high-standard socialist market economy. The piece is anchored in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the August 2024 Opinions on improving the market access system. The article has three parts. It first explains why market access is a foundational market-economy institution. It then sets out three reasons why improvement matters. It ends by describing a five-part target system. Liu argues that open, transparent access lets prices form effectively and supports the basic economic system, including the Two Unwaverings. Improvement is presented as key to combining an effective market with a capable government, as a requirement for new quality productive forces, and as a need for aligning with international rules. The five goals are openness and transparency, orderliness, equal competition, clear powers and responsibilities, and strong supervision. In practice this means one national negative list, matching treatment of domestic and foreign capital, and wider access in services. It also means a ban on unauthorised extra access barriers outside the list, assessment before measures are changed, and tighter oversight of monopolistic segments and finance. Liu concludes that these measures would give solid support to a high-standard socialist market economy. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of the policy logic and the main requirements of China's 2024 market access reforms.

Vigorously cultivating and promoting heroic culture 大力培育和弘扬英雄文化 Chen Zhen This commentary, first published in the PLA Daily on 15 January 2024, asks why and how the People's Liberation Army should cultivate heroic culture. Chen Zhen argues that heroic culture is an important part of the military's strong-army culture, a driver of morale and fighting spirit, and a support for the army's cohesion and combat capability. Preserving the army's heroic character, the author says, requires sustained effort to promote it. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out three reasons why heroic culture is needed. The second describes its distinctive features and spiritual content. The third proposes concrete ways to cultivate and promote it. Chen draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks on heroes and heroic spirit, and on examples from Chinese history and the history of the Party and army. On the reasons, Chen contends that heroic culture strengthens political loyalty, because it carries faith in Marxism, confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics and in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It also raises moral standards and serves the goal of building a world-class military. On its features, the author argues that it combines an enduring core with change over time, affirms the people as makers of history while recognising the role of outstanding individuals, and values both great deeds and ordinary people doing ordinary work well. In this account, heroes include scientists and astronauts as well as ordinary workers and rank-and-file soldiers. For practice, Chen proposes three lines of work. The first is better education and publicity: classroom teaching, ceremonies, and less abstract, formulaic and exaggerated portrayals of heroes. The second is more varied carriers, including original literary, film and music works, heroes' former residences and martyrs' cemeteries, and new technologies such as 5G and artificial intelligence. The third is stronger institutions: legal protection under the Heroes and Martyrs Protection Law, regular rather than episodic activity, and support for the families of those who died. Read the original if you want a short example of how PLA ideological work frames heroic culture and its practical measures.

Aligning with high-standard international economic and trade rules to promote high-level opening up 对接国际高标准经贸规则促高水平开放 Wang Xiaohong This newspaper commentary asks how China should treat high-standard international economic and trade rules, such as the CPTPP and the DEPA. Wang argues that aligning with them would help create a market-oriented, law-based and internationalised first-class business environment and would support high-level opening up. The first half explains why alignment matters. Wang notes that these rules go beyond border liberalisation to cover competitive neutrality, state-owned enterprises, intellectual property, labour and environmental protection, subsidies, government procurement, transparency and anti-corruption. The second half lists six areas for reform. In Wang's reading, the rules offer institutional support for opening China's goods, services, capital and labour markets, and for both "bringing in" and "going global". Wang also links alignment to the new development paradigm of domestic circulation as the mainstay with domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. The article says that smoother cross-border flows of data, capital and personnel would raise the quality of domestic circulation and help secure supply chains against onshoring, nearshoring and friend-shoring. The author adds that alignment would foster inclusive cooperation with developing economies and mutually beneficial cooperation with developed ones. Wang calls for reforms in six areas: services trade opening through negative lists; digital trade and cross-border data governance; lower tariffs and easier customs for goods; a shorter foreign-investment negative list with stronger investor protection; fair competition, including transparency and national treatment for foreign firms; and deeper state-owned enterprise reform, including mixed ownership. Read the original if you want a concise official-media statement of the policy rationale and reform agenda for rule alignment in early 2024.

Coordinating the optimisation of incremental resources and the revitalisation of existing stock 统筹好做优增量和盘活存量的关系 Zeng Zheng This commentary, first published in Economic Daily in January 2024, asks how China should handle the relationship between increments (new resources, investment and borrowing capacity) and stock (what already exists). Zeng Zheng argues that the two are dialectically united: stock is the basis of increment, and increment transforms stock. The author presents this as a rule drawn from the Party's use of dialectics and systems thinking, and as an element of macroeconomic governance. The guiding policy is to let increment drive stock and stock promote increment. The article takes its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision, which called for optimising the allocation of incremental resources and adjusting the stock structure, and from the Central Economic Work Conference. It then works through three fields: market-based allocation of factors of production, management of social assets, and the handling of debt across the macroeconomy. In each field Zeng takes several paired cases, each with a stock side and an increment side, and cites figures such as 2023 manufacturing assets above 150 trillion yuan and government debt of 85 trillion yuan. Zeng's core move is to turn the abstract pairing into specific policy pairs. For factors of production, these include idle urban land against new construction-land quotas, existing human capital against the three-child policy, existing patents against key core technologies, and existing data against data-scale expansion. For assets, they include upgrading traditional industry alongside investing in emerging industries, using PPP and REITs for existing infrastructure alongside new infrastructure, and absorbing unsold housing while stabilising property investment. For debt, the author pairs treating existing government, corporate and household debt with raising each sector's capacity to borrow and invest or consume. The article reports 2023 debt ratios of 67.5% for government, 168.4% for non-financial firms and 72.4% for households. Zeng concludes that stock optimisation and the release of increment must advance together, with the aim of raising resource-allocation efficiency across the economy. Each pair comes with a proposal, such as a unified urban–rural construction-land market, technology-sharing platforms, data-trading rules, a package of local-debt swaps, and lower mortgage rates with more consumer-credit support. Read the original if you want a compact, policy-oriented account of how Chinese economic commentary links the stock–increment framework to land, technology, data, infrastructure, property and debt measures.

Strengthening the "six capacities" of a leading education country to support the building of a Healthy China 增强教育强国“六力” 支撑健康中国建设 Li Xiaoming Huang Hefeng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how medical education can serve the goal of building a leading education country with Chinese characteristics. Li and Huang take Xi Jinping's formulation at the second national education conference of the new era, which names six capacities, and argue that building national medical strength around them underpins both medical education quality and the Healthy China project. The article goes through the six capacities in turn, each with a short list of tasks for medical schools: ideological and political guidance, talent competitiveness, scientific and technological support, capacity to safeguard people's wellbeing, social coordination, and international influence. It closes with a general statement on how medical schools should orient themselves. Li and Huang call for moral education to be the first content of training, with ideals and professional ethics running through the whole process. They propose integrated curricula, "medicine plus X" and clinical medicine plus public health programmes, and AI in teaching. They want medical schools to target frontier science and national needs, with strategic fields such as precision and digital medicine, and to tackle "bottleneck" problems in translating basic research. On wellbeing, they urge new programmes in specialisms in short supply, standards and guidelines suited to China, and wider and more balanced distribution of quality medical resources. They also propose partnerships among schools, hospitals, firms and government, and international joint programmes and laboratories offering a "Chinese approach" to global medical education. The authors conclude that medical schools must uphold the socialist orientation of education and put people's health first. They also call for balance between supporting national strategy and meeting livelihood needs, and between rooting in China and drawing on international experience. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a leading Zhejiang University medical school leadership translates Xi Jinping's education-power agenda into concrete tasks for medical education.

The rich connotations of the unity of Chinese civilization 中华文明统一性的丰富内涵 Yang Yue This short newspaper commentary takes up unity as one of the salient characteristics of Chinese civilization. Starting from Xi Jinping's statements on the subject, Yang argues that this unity grew from the shared experience of the peoples' ancestors and rests on a great unification of a vast territory and large population. In Yang's account it covers territory, politics, ethnicity and culture. The article is organised around four formulations drawn from Xi Jinping: the nation's territory cannot be divided, the state cannot be thrown into chaos, the nation cannot be scattered, and civilization cannot be broken. Each is treated as a separate dimension, with historical examples from the pre-Qin period through the Qin, Han and later dynasties to the Qing. Yang argues that each dimension has its own foundation: a sense of belonging to the land, cohesion around a political ideal of great unification, a centripetal force among ethnic groups, and cultural identity as the deepest form of identification. The author cites the Gongyang commentary, Qin standardisation of script, axle widths and weights, and Qing-era examples of ethnic integration. Yang concludes that cultural identity and political unification together explain why China is, in the author's words, the only ancient civilization to keep continuous history, distinct culture and stable territory. Yang concludes that this unity distinguishes Chinese civilization from others and ensures that the Chinese people will pursue national unification. The author calls for grasping it in order to strengthen ethnic groups' sense of belonging and to build national strength and rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official discourse links historical continuity to national unity and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

Continuously raising the level of modernization of social governance 不断提升社会治理现代化水平 Hu Ming Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Hu Ming asks how social governance can be modernized further and argues that the answer lies in staying on the path of social governance with Chinese characteristics. The author presents this path as the product of the Communist Party's combination of Marxist governance theory with China's concrete practice and with governance ideas in excellent traditional Chinese culture. The piece is a short commentary that takes its cue from Xi Jinping's important instructions on social work. The article has three parts. The first explains why modernizing social governance is integral to Chinese modernization. The second sets out several key relationships that, in Hu's view, must be handled to understand the regularities of social governance. The third lists four practical requirements for following the path of social governance with Chinese characteristics in the new stage. In the first part, Hu gives three reasons: meeting the people's rising expectations for a better life amid more complex social conditions in the information age; creating a stable social environment for high-quality development; and supporting the modernization of the national governance system and capacity through a pattern of joint contribution, joint governance and shared benefits. The second part identifies four pairs of relationships: Party leadership and diverse participation, which Hu calls the fundamental difference from Western social governance; the central, city and grassroots levels; order and vitality, summed up as being lively without disorder; and rule of law, rule of virtue and self-governance, which should work together under Party leadership. Hu concludes with four requirements. These are upholding the Party's overall leadership, including Party building in new economic organizations, new social organizations and new forms of employment; putting the people first, through the Party's mass line, the "Fengqiao experience" and grid-based grassroots platforms; building sound institutions and mechanisms, including relief of burdens on the grassroots, professional social workers and volunteer services; and applying systems thinking. The author sees these as supporting long-term national stability. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of how Party-affiliated scholars frame social governance and the tasks of social work under Chinese modernization.

Understanding accurately and comprehensively the global significance of China's poverty alleviation campaign 准确全面理解中国脱贫攻坚的世界意义 Han Jun Writing in the People's Daily on 15 January 2025, Han Jun, Minister of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, takes up the question of what China's victory in its campaign against poverty means for the rest of the world. The commentary starts from Xi Jinping's remarks at the 19th G20 summit that poverty in developing countries can be solved and that "China can succeed, and other developing countries can succeed too". Han argues that China's experience is a resource for the Global South and for the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece has three parts. The first sets out three ways in which the campaign matters internationally: it reshaped the global map of poverty, it raised confidence in the Global South, and its results have stood up to testing. The second part presents five principles of the Chinese approach as a new path for poverty reduction. The third looks ahead to consolidating the results at home and deepening international cooperation. Han cites figures, foreign leaders' remarks and UN statements as supporting evidence. Han reports that more than 800 million people have been lifted out of poverty since reform and opening up, which he says amounts to over 70 per cent of global poverty reduction. In his account, the 2030 Agenda poverty target was met ten years early, and the Party has prevented large-scale relapse into poverty during the five-year transition period. The core of the argument is the five principles. These are putting the people first, targeted poverty alleviation, poverty reduction through economic development, poverty reduction through local distinctive industries, and poverty reduction through promoting common prosperity. Han contends that aid alone harms efficiency, while growth alone widens gaps. He says industry-based support moves from "blood transfusion" to "blood-making", and that mobilising government, society and market produces a broad anti-poverty pattern. He quotes UN Secretary-General Guterres as praising targeted poverty alleviation. Han calls for continued consolidation of the results through 2025, the last transition year, and afterwards for a permanent mechanism to prevent relapse. He also calls for deeper South–South cooperation, sharing poverty-reduction stories, and exporting agricultural technologies such as Juncao and hybrid rice under the Belt and Road Initiative. He closes by linking this to Chinese modernization and a just world of common development. Read the original if you want an official statement from the agriculture ministry of how China presents its poverty experience as a model for the Global South, with the supporting statistics it cites.

Building a system for transmitting traditional Chinese virtues 构建中华传统美德传承体系 Zhang Hongxia This newspaper commentary in Guangming Daily takes up a task set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): building a system for transmitting traditional Chinese virtues. Zhang Hongxia describes these virtues as the essence of Chinese culture and an inexhaustible source for moral construction. The author argues that such a system requires sustained work in four areas: excavation and interpretation, communication, education, and institutional guarantees. The article is organised under four numbered headings. It first deals with content, then with a three-dimensional communication matrix, then with joint educational effort by schools, families and society, and finally with institutional support. Each section lists concrete measures rather than historical or philosophical analysis of particular virtues. On content, Zhang calls for using both traditional methods and digital and intelligent technologies to uncover virtues such as patriotic dedication, diligence and thrift, and filial piety. These should be explained accurately, comprehensively and in scholarly terms. Guided by Marxism, they should be given new meanings through creative transformation and innovative development, and be expressed in modern discourse. On communication, the author wants traditional and new media to work together, and domestic and overseas publicity to reinforce each other, for example through translating classics and holding international seminars. On education, Zhang proposes integrating virtue education across primary, secondary and university stages and treating the family as the first classroom. The author also proposes targeted approaches for officials, enterprises, communities and villages, with officials described as the "key minority". Zhang's institutional proposals rest on Party leadership, a mix of "soft" social norms such as village and citizen codes and "hard" legal rules, and support in personnel, technology and funding. Incentives would include selecting moral models, local "traditional virtue lecture halls" and a system for evaluating citizens' moral quality. The stated aim is to make transmission routine and long-lasting. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented account of how official discourse envisages operationalising the transmission of traditional virtue through media, schooling and governance.

Helping Global South modernization through the development of Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化发展助力全球南方现代化 Wang Bo Zhai Dayu This commentary, published in the People's Daily in January 2025, asks how China's path can support modernization across the Global South. Wang and Zhai argue that modernization is the shared task of Global South countries, and that Chinese modernization offers them new momentum and an alternative to the Western model. The authors begin with the obstacles they see in the Western-led international order: hegemonism, economic sanctions and "human rights" standards. They then review China's contributions: the Belt and Road Initiative, the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives, reform of global governance, development finance and civilizational exchange. Wang and Zhai make two central moves. First, they cite figures to show China's role: development aid to over 160 countries, Belt and Road cooperation with over 150 countries and 30 international organizations, and, three years after the Global Development Initiative was launched, nearly 20 billion US dollars mobilised for over 1,100 projects. They also point to the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the BRICS New Development Bank and the upgraded Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund. Second, they contrast the Western pursuit of power, which they describe as a jungle law and zero-sum thinking, with a peaceful path in which China pledges never to seek hegemony, expansion or spheres of influence. They add that, because Southern countries differ in history and conditions, China respects diverse routes to modernization and does not impose a single model. The authors conclude that China, as a member of the Global South, seeks shared flourishing rather than sole success. They expect it to keep learning from and helping Global South countries, and to contribute to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary presents China's role in the Global South and the link between Chinese modernization and Global South modernization.

"AI Plus" empowering the development of new quality productive forces “人工智能+”赋能新质生产力发展（人民要论） Dong Zhiyong Writing in the People's Daily column "People's Forum" on 13 January 2025, Dong Zhiyong takes up the "AI Plus" initiative, which the Central Economic Work Conference at the end of 2024 named a key task for the year. Dong argues that artificial intelligence, as a general-purpose technology that can serve as a tool in almost every economic activity, can foster new quality productive forces. In the article's account, this would raise both the quality and the quantity of economic growth and strengthen China's strategic position in global competition. The piece is a short commentary in three parts. It first reviews what the author presents as China's achievements in AI. It then sets out how AI opens new space for new quality productive forces. Finally it proposes measures for seizing what it calls a major historical opportunity. The author acknowledges that China's overall AI level still lags behind developed countries. The core argument runs through the two middle sections. Dong credits China's progress to new information infrastructure (419.1 million 5G base stations by November 2024), a supportive policy environment with local action plans in Beijing, Shenzhen and Shanghai, and rich application scenarios.
