Dong cites more than 38,000 generative-AI patent applications in 2014–2023 and a smart-manufacturing sector of 2,884.16 billion yuan in 2023. Dong then claims three benefits from AI Plus: driving economic transformation and upgrading, supporting economic and data security amid global technological competition, and making development more inclusive through rural revitalisation, personalised education and more efficient public services. Dong calls for four steps: building a healthy industrial ecosystem with market-oriented innovation and differentiated regional clusters; creating an effective data-factor market, including data property rights and wider opening of public data; building a multi-level talent training system and attracting global talent; and improving regulation through legal frameworks on privacy, algorithmic transparency and ethics, plus international coordination. These measures, the author says, would serve high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary links AI policy to new quality productive forces and economic security.

Rooting theoretical innovation in China's economic construction practice 将理论创新扎根于我国经济建设实践 Zhang Zhuoyuan Writing in People's Daily, the veteran economist Zhang Zhuoyuan reflects on his career to argue that economic theory must grow out of practice. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks that theory arises from real life and lives by innovation, Zhang contends that Chinese economists should tie their research to national development needs and root theoretical innovation in China's economic construction. The piece is a personal reflection rather than a formal study. Zhang recounts how an early interest in political economy led to the Institute of Economics, where mentors such as Sun Yefang shaped a method of linking theory to practice. Zhang then describes research on price reform in the 1980s and participation in drafting more than ten central documents between 1993 and 2013. Zhang's central claim is that economics is a practical discipline whose innovation depends on starting from reality and being problem-oriented. The Marxist-Leninist classics, in this account, offer principles, standpoint and method but no ready-made answers, so economists must work out answers themselves. Zhang says field investigation and contact with price departments led to the idea of advancing price reform through marketization, and that engagement with reform and opening up supplies theoretical support for policy. Zhang calls on economists to seize the opportunity of the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012) and to build economic theory with distinct Chinese characteristics. Zhang, now over ninety, says they still follow new questions such as the development of new quality productive forces, and urges adherence to a practice-first spirit. Read the original if you want a short, first-person statement of how a leading Chinese reform-era economist describes the relationship between theory, fieldwork and policy drafting.

Three new forms of historical nihilism 历史虚无主义的三种新样态 Chen Tian This short commentary in Study Times asks how historical nihilism is changing in the current environment. Chen argues that the trend will not leave the stage on its own. Instead it is shifting from open, blunt expression to oblique and concealed forms, and its themes are becoming more "academic". The author calls for attention to three new forms. The article takes the forms in turn: networked, intelligent (AI-driven) and "academicised". It is a brief survey with a few examples, not a systematic study. On the first, Chen says that since the 1990s, and especially after 2010, historical nihilism has moved onto social platforms, livestreaming and game apps. Open denials of historical materialism and attacks on heroes have, the author notes, decreased online. Chen reads this as concealment through fragmented narratives and everyday infiltration, not retreat, and cites a blogger whose account name "73I" is said to encourage forgetting Japanese wartime atrocities. On the second, Chen describes generative content tools producing material in bulk, deepfakes and "bot armies" posting and liking it, and recommendation algorithms targeting users with such content. On the third, the author says nihilists dress idealist history in scholarly language, citing partial sources. The leading example is the "New Qing History", which Chen says denies Manchu–Han integration, claims the Qing was not China and now extends to maritime claims, and which Chen calls false. Chen concludes that these forms increase concealment and deception and that AI will create further room for spread, which needs high vigilance. Historians are urged to oppose "New Qing History" openly and to restore a true picture on the basis of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writers characterise current forms of historical nihilism and the "New Qing History" debate.

Advancing the building of a leading country in education with strong ideological and political guidance 以强大的思政引领力推进教育强国建设 Huang Siguang Published in Study Times in January 2025, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the National Education Conference that a leading country in education should have six strengths. Huang Siguang focuses on the first of them, the capacity for ideological and political guidance. The author argues that it is a continuation of the Party's tradition of ideological and political work and a basis for building an education system with Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised in three parts. It first explains how this capacity defines the political character of the education drive, then how it steers the direction of that drive, and finally what universities can do to strengthen it in practice. Huang contends that ideological and political guidance gives education its socialist foundation, reflects the Party's overall leadership of education, and expresses the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. In the author's account, it builds cohesion around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, stimulates creativity among staff and students, and links universities to the strategies for science, technology and talent. The proposed measures are to develop ideological and political courses in depth, using digital technology and red resources, to build a high-calibre teaching and counselling workforce, and to create a pattern of coordination across courses, research, practice, culture, online work and management. Huang concludes that guidance should be turned into concrete results for high-quality development in higher education, so that all staff, throughout the whole process and in every respect, take part in fostering students. Read the original if you want to see how a university Party secretary presents the role of ideological and political education within the education-power agenda.

Raising the capacity to convert and disseminate social science knowledge: contributing social science strength to Chinese modernization 提升社科知识转化和传播能力 为推进中国式现代化贡献社科力量 Zhang Xinke This short commentary, originally published on Guangming Online, asks how the popularisation of social science (社科普及) can meet the public's more varied cultural needs and the networked, digital turn in communication. Zhang argues that popularisation only works if people can understand, remember, accept and use the knowledge. The key, in Zhang's view, is to strengthen the capacity to convert and disseminate social science knowledge, so that "popularising" and "reaching" the public are truly joined, in service of Chinese modernization. The article is organised as a sequence of eight "conversions", each tied to a specific capacity: rational to perceptual, theoretical to everyday, meaningful to interesting, written to spoken, flat to three-dimensional, static to dynamic, traditional to digital, and valuable to heartfelt. Examples come from Jiangsu Province, where the author works, and from books, television programmes, museums and video platforms. Zhang's central claim is that abstract knowledge must be linked to lived experience, ordinary language and engaging forms. Cited cases include Silent Spring, a popular history series, a law professor's comic fictional character, Jiangsu storytelling contests, and VR and AR in museums. Zhang also points to the television programme Classics in China and to short videos on Bilibili, where the author reports that knowledge-related content exceeds 45% of plays. Digitalisation, big data and AI are presented as the breakthrough point, enabling precise audience profiling, feedback and a combined online and offline service pattern. The last conversion stresses commitment: Zhang describes Jiangsu's joint provincial–city meeting system, volunteer writers and broadcasters, entrepreneur sponsorship and grassroots performance teams as examples of shared social responsibility. Zhang concludes that popularisation should become a public cultural service close to ordinary people. Read the original if you want a practitioner's view of how a provincial social science federation frames popularisation work and Jiangsu's practical examples.

Grasping the inner connection between Chinese modernization and common prosperity for all the people 深刻把握中国式现代化与全体人民共同富裕的内在关联 Jia Ruoxiang This commentary, first published on Guangming Online's theory channel, asks how Chinese modernization and common prosperity for all the people are internally linked. Jia Ruoxiang argues that Chinese modernization is by definition a modernization of common prosperity for all the people, and that the link can be understood from three angles: the Communist Party's original aspiration and mission, the essence of socialism, and the basic socialist economic system. The piece opens by recalling that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has given common prosperity growing weight, citing poverty alleviation and the building of a moderately prosperous society. It also cites the 20th Party Congress (2022) report and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and says China has now reached a stage of steadily advancing common prosperity. Three main sections follow, one for each angle. On the Party's mission, Jia reasons that a modernization led by a Party whose purpose is to serve the people must start from and return to people's aspirations for a better life. This requires two things together: making the social wealth "cake" bigger through high-quality development and new quality productive forces, and cutting and sharing it more fairly by preventing polarization and equalizing basic public services. On the essence of socialism, Jia maps the two words of common prosperity onto the classic formula: "common" corresponds to eliminating exploitation and polarization and addresses unbalanced development, which reflects advanced relations of production; "prosperity" corresponds to liberating and developing the productive forces and addresses insufficient development. On the economic system, Jia sets out public ownership as the mainstay alongside other forms of ownership, and distribution according to work alongside other methods. The author also discusses coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, and the socialist market economy with a "promising government" and an "efficient market". Jia concludes that common prosperity must fit China's stage of economic development and advance in step with modernization, producing milestone results at each stage. It covers spiritual, cultural, ecological and social wellbeing as well as material wealth, and aims at the all-round development of the person. Read the original if you want a concise example of how an official policy researcher ties common prosperity to the Party's mission, the essence of socialism and the economic system.

Expanding domestic demand through the mutual reinforcement of consumption and investment 以消费和投资的相互促进扩大国内需求 Fang Honglin Wang Pengfei This commentary in Guangming Daily (January 2025) takes up the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference's call to boost consumption, raise investment returns and expand domestic demand in all respects, listed as the first of nine priority tasks for 2025. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the policy logic behind the 2025 domestic-demand agenda.

Coordinating the cultivation of new growth drivers and the renewal of old ones 必须统筹好培育新动能和更新旧动能的关系 Li Xuesong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, takes up one of the "five must-coordinate" relationships set out at the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: the relationship between cultivating new growth drivers and renewing old ones. The first explains why the coordination matters for high-quality development, for developing new quality productive forces locally, and for optimising the economic structure. The second sets out how to push both tasks together through policy support and industrial upgrading. The third lists four types of new driver whose share of the economy should keep rising. In the first part Li holds that the two processes reinforce each other, and that where old drivers face shrinking demand or outdated technology, the principle of establishing the new before breaking the old should apply. The third part sorts new drivers into four types: "new-quality-led" (digital economy, new energy, biomedicine, high-end equipment), "demand-upgrading" (higher household income, public services, new infrastructure), "structure-optimising" (factor-market reform, urban–rural integration, a unified national market) and "opening-up" (services opening, institutional opening, international capacity cooperation, the Belt and Road Initiative). Li concludes that sustained growth of new drivers is the core force behind high-quality development, and that it must proceed alongside the orderly transformation of old ones to avoid a prolonged period of painful adjustment. The article is a policy-oriented exposition of the 2024 conference line rather than a theoretical study. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how a leading Chinese economist classifies new growth drivers and the policy measures linked to them.

Taking multiple measures to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation 多措并举铸牢中华民族共同体意识 Chu Feng This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation (the Chinese-language term is zhulao Zhonghua minzu gongtongti yishi). Opening up broader prospects for Chinese modernization through reform and opening up 在改革开放中开辟中国式现代化更加广阔的前景 Yan Lianfu This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 10 January 2025, takes its cue from Xi Jinping's 2025 New Year address. The author describes China as the main trading partner of more than 150 countries and regions, and presents its opening up as win-win cooperation that offers the world new opportunities and contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in early 2025 links the New Year address and the Third Plenum to cadre incentives, regional development, green growth and institutional opening up.

Correctly handling the "five major relationships" to build China into a leading country in education 正确处理“五个重大关系”，扎实推进教育强国建设 Zou Qingchao This short commentary takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference in September 2024, which set out a systematic plan for building a leading country in education. The pairs are: supporting national strategy and meeting people's livelihood needs; knowledge learning and all-round development; training talent and meeting social needs; orderliness and vitality; and taking root in China while drawing on international experience. In Zou's account, each pair is complementary rather than opposed. Education must supply talent for national strategy while giving people fairer access to quality schooling. Knowledge learning should not be narrowed to exam scores but integrated with moral, physical, aesthetic and labour education. Education should serve high-quality development and new quality productive forces, and combine Chinese cultural roots with selective foreign learning. Zou concludes that building a leading country in education is a long-term, systematic undertaking centred on the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent. Promoting the development of new quality productive forces through high-quality work on young talent 以高质量青年人才工作推动新质生产力发展 Wei Ziping Ding Ning This commentary, first published on People's Forum Network (Renmin Luntan Wang), asks how work on young talent can support the development of new quality productive forces. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to keep up innovation and with a January 2024 measure from the Ministry of Natural Resources on training and using young science and technology talent. On policy, the authors cite the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which treat education, science and technology, and talent as foundational support for Chinese modernization. They argue that China's talent pool is large but still falls short of what new quality productive forces require. Their proposals are to encourage innovation through projects and competitions and by grounding it in practice; to promote cross-disciplinary cooperation and industry–university–research platforms; to give ideological and political education; and to allow orderly talent flows while guarding against talent loss and waste. Opening a new phase in Marxist theoretical research and construction through upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground 在守正创新中开创马克思主义理论研究和建设新局面 Tang Dengyun Liu Zongling This commentary, first published on People's Forum Online, responds to Xi Jinping's recent instruction on the Project for Marxist Theoretical Research and Development in the New Era. Xi called the Project a foundational and strategic undertaking for the Party's ideological and theoretical work. Tang and Liu argue that, after twenty years of the Project and a large body of research results, it should now be pursued by upholding fundamental principles while innovating, so as to open a new phase of Marxist theoretical research and construction. The authors organise the piece around three tasks. The first is studying and propagating Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second is deepening research on the Two Integrations. The third is building an independent system of knowledge in philosophy and the social sciences. Tang and Liu contend that Xi Jinping Thought is contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism, and that it marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They say it should be studied in a systematic, theoretically grounded way, tied to the achievements of Chinese modernization, and brought into textbooks, classrooms and young people's minds. The Two Integrations, combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, are described as the fundamental path of theoretical innovation, joining the "soul" and the "roots". The authors call for turning Chinese experience into Chinese theory, with particular attention to the "second integration" and to Chinese modernization as a new form of human civilization. On the knowledge system, they hold that Marxist guidance is the basic mark distinguishing contemporary Chinese philosophy and social science. They also hold that distilling Chinese modernization's original contribution to world modernization theory is the main line of this effort. The authors conclude that Marxist theory work should refine signature concepts and original theories, strengthen disciplinary and textbook systems, and study major problems of China's development and Party governance on a regular basis. They also call for attracting and training theoretical talent and strengthening ideological institutions and positions, including to address the imbalance between people's cultural needs and supply. The stated aim is to consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere and move towards common prosperity in both material and cultural life. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars frame the tasks of the Marxist theory project after Xi's instruction.

Making the Party's innovative theory take deeper root among the people 让党的创新理论更加深入人心 Yang Tao Zhang Yueping This short commentary, published in January 2025, responds to a recent instruction from Xi Jinping on the Project for Marxist Theoretical Research and Development in the New Era. The instruction calls for systematic, scholarly study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for more targeted, effective propaganda. Yang and Zhang argue that the Party's theoretical innovation contains new experience and wisdom whose full understanding strengthens theoretical consciousness and confidence and helps the theory reach ordinary people. The article is organised around three tasks: publicising the historical experience of a century of struggle, upholding the original aspiration of putting the people first, and answering the latest demands of the era's questions. On history, the authors say that Marxism gave China's people a direction after earlier searches for national salvation failed. In their account the nation moved from saving the country to building, enriching and strengthening it, guided by adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On the people, they hold that people-centredness is Marxism's most distinctive character and that the Party's purpose is to serve the people wholeheartedly. On the era's demands, they argue that new risks make theoretical confidence more important, and that it requires deeper study of the Party's theory and a clear line against erroneous trends of thought. The authors conclude that Party members should use Marxism to address China's concrete realities, act as doers in building Chinese modernization, and press on towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-school commentary frames the task of popularising official theory after Xi's instruction.

Chinese modernization: a new paradigm and new opportunities for modernization in the Global South 中国式现代化：“全球南方”现代化的新范式与新机遇 Ye Benqian Fu Zhen This short commentary asks how Chinese modernization can serve countries of the Global South as they pursue their own modernization. Ye and Fu argue that Chinese modernization, through its distinctive path, practical results and international influence, offers these countries a new path and a model to learn from. They open with Xi Jinping's statement that the collective rise of the Global South is a defining mark of great global change. The article has three parts. The first describes the mixed situation of the Global South, in which opportunities and difficulties exist side by side. The second sets out what Chinese modernization demonstrates to other developing countries. The third turns to practical channels through which China is said to assist the modernization of these states. On opportunities, the authors cite a rise in the Global South's share of world GDP from 24% to over 40%, deeper South–South cooperation and a more favourable multilateral setting. On difficulties, they list dependence on primary-product exports, weak industry and technology, poor infrastructure, unequal education and health provision, and wide wealth gaps. They then draw five lessons from China's experience: independent exploration of a path suited to national conditions rather than copying the West; a people-centred approach, illustrated by poverty alleviation, education and medical insurance; gradual and coordinated reform; and reliance on scientific and technological innovation backed by talent training. In practice, they point to the Belt and Road Initiative (the China–Laos and China–Thailand railways, the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor), trade and investment that move industrial links to partner countries, and technology transfer such as agricultural projects in Tanzania and the China–Belarus industrial park. The authors conclude that China remains a member of the Global South and a reliable long-term partner for developing countries. In their view, deeper cooperation will give Global South modernization lasting momentum and help build a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary presents Chinese modernization as a reference point for the Global South.

Strengthening research on China's frontier history and building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system of frontier studies 加强中国边疆史研究 建构中国自主的边疆学知识体系 Lü Wenli Huang Fengfu This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's call at a Politburo study session to strengthen multidisciplinary research on frontier history and frontier governance and to speed up an autonomous Chinese knowledge system of frontier studies. Lü and Huang argue that research on China's frontier history should play the foundational role in building that system. The article first sketches the development of frontier research since the late Qing, following the historian Ma Dazheng's three peaks: the Northwest historical geography school, the 1930s–40s "frontier administration studies", and the period after the 1983 founding of the CASS frontier history and geography research centre. It then sets out how theory and discipline-building should advance, and finally what frontier history must contribute to the new knowledge system. On method, the authors call for Marxism as guidance and for the "five commons" view of the Chinese nation's history, which holds that all ethnic groups jointly developed the territory, the state, the history, the culture and the national spirit. They also urge drawing on ideas such as "great unity", reliable and varied sources (including overseas archives, missionary records and artificial intelligence tools), and the integration of archaeology, anthropology, sociology, politics, linguistics and geography. On substance, they say frontier history should explain the laws of how China's territory formed, summarise governance experience, and treat the shift from "governing according to local custom" to "unifying governance and cultivating education" as the general trend. Lü and Huang propose a national frontier studies society, dedicated research funds, university courses and master's and doctoral programmes, and "identifying concepts" that make the work accessible to the public. In their account, this would support forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and the modernization of frontier governance. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned outline of how Chinese scholars frame frontier history and the institutional agenda for frontier studies as a discipline.

Western Marxism on subject production in the age of intelligent media and its theoretical critique 西方马克思主义关于智媒时代的主体生产及其理论批判 Li Xinyue Dai Xuehong Li Xinyue and Dai Xuehong ask whether media still carry an ideological character once generative AI produces content (AIGC) and non-human actors join human ones in the media world. Their answer is that intelligent media remain a modern ideological state apparatus. They also hold that Western Marxist theories of media ideology still describe how subjects are produced, although each has limits that only historical materialism can address. The article sorts Western Marxist media-ideology theory into three strands and applies each to the present. The first is the humanist line of alienation running from Lukács to Horkheimer and Adorno. The second is the hegemony line from Gramsci to the Birmingham School (Stuart Hall). The third is the structuralist and post-structuralist line from Althusser to Foucault. Each section pairs the classical theory with a contemporary critique: technological fetishism, cultural inequality, and biopolitics. In the first strand, reification and the culture industry standardise media products and produce homogenised subjects. The authors apply this to AIGC, where they see a technological fetishism that treats technology as autonomous, citing Postman and Ellul. In the second strand, Gramsci's idea that ideology is a material force, and the Birmingham School's emphasis on audiences decoding from below, lead to a critique of inequality. The authors cite Herbert Schiller on the global digital divide and cultural dumping, and Nick Couldry on fragmented audiences. They add that machines do not alter the underlying relations of production, giving the example of a Microsoft chatbot that produced racist output within 24 hours. In the third strand, Althusser's interpellation of individuals as subjects and Foucault's decentred power and biopolitics are applied to AI. The authors argue that truth matters less than process and metrics such as click rates, and that people are reduced to abstract populations and to identities dependent on virtual relations (with Byung-Chul Han on transparency). The authors conclude that all three strands remain traceable today but share a class limitation. In their view, humanism replaces a historical standpoint with monism, hegemonic resistance risks being absorbed by capital, and structuralist discipline turns people into undifferentiated elements of the capital market. Real subject emancipation, they argue, requires the free and all-round development of each person. That means going beyond capitalist alienation and the limited division of labour, and changing the relations of production so that people fully appropriate their products. Read the original if you want a structured survey of how Lukács, Gramsci, Althusser, Foucault and others are used to critique AI-era media, written from a Chinese historical-materialist standpoint.

Adhering to a problem orientation as the theoretical hallmark of Deng Xiaoping's philosophical thought 坚持问题导向是邓小平哲学思想的理论特色 Ouyang Ying Ouyang Ying asks what distinguishes Deng Xiaoping's philosophical thought and answers that its defining feature is a consistent problem orientation. Opening with Xi Jinping's assessment of Deng Xiaoping Theory at the commemoration of Deng's 120th birthday, the article presents attention to problems as a distinctively Marxist trait. The article, published in Qianxian in 2024, is organised as a three-stage sequence: identifying problems, studying them, and solving them. Each stage is tied to a role in the development of Deng's thought and supported by quotations from Deng's reform-era speeches and by remarks from Xi. Ouyang argues that grasping problems is the logical starting point: Deng focused on major issues such as economic growth and living standards, urged daring to admit backwardness, and applied the materialist dialectic's principle of the principal contradiction, for instance by singling out the reorganisation of leadership bodies. Studying problems is the source of innovation: Deng added "emancipating the mind" to "seeking truth from facts", treated the two as internally united, and looked behind surface difficulties to the essential question of what socialism is and how to build it. Solving problems is the driving force, giving Deng's thought the character of an "applied philosophy" that combines problem-focus, practical application and philosophical depth. The author concludes that Deng's thought took real-life problems as its source and the practical need to resolve social contradictions as its motive power, matching Xi's account of how theories arise. Read the original if you want a short, Party-journal presentation of how Deng's philosophy is framed today as problem-driven and applied.

The formation, construction and predicament of Western countries' global technological monopoly power 西方国家全球科技垄断权力的形成背景、构建方式及其困境 Li Yan Li Yan asks how Western countries came to hold a technological monopoly within the global economy, how that monopoly operates as a form of power, and why it is now in difficulty. The article argues that this monopoly is a defining feature of contemporary capitalism. In Li's account it arose from the contradiction between the globalisation of productive forces and international monopoly capital's pursuit of excess profit. It deepens capitalism's basic contradictions, and Western attempts to defend it are producing a predicament. The article has four parts. The first traces the formation of the monopoly during economic globalisation, drawing on Marx's analysis in Capital of science becoming separated from labour and serving capital, and on Arrighi, Dicken and Mandel. The second analyses how monopoly power is built, using Gereffi's distinction between buyer-driven and producer-driven global commodity chains. The third examines the challenge from developing countries' industrial upgrading and the US response, with semiconductors and Sino-US technology cooperation as cases. The fourth sets out policy proposals for China. Li argues that as industrialisation spread and manufacturing competition intensified, multinationals withdrew from low-profit production and concentrated on research, design and standards. They monopolised knowledge resources, protected them through an intellectual property regime and sanctions pushed by developed countries, and controlled subordinate suppliers through bargaining power and technical standards. Developing-country firms are described as locked into low-end links. Li then points to firms such as Huawei and South Korean semiconductor makers as evidence that catching up is possible. According to Li, US measures against Chinese semiconductors and research cooperation damage supply chains and international innovation, and they intensify the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation. Li concludes that the monopoly is entering a predicament, and that Western containment will push developing countries to seek technological self-reliance. For China, Li proposes four measures. First, a stronger state role through the new-type whole-nation system and state-owned enterprises. Second, a sound intellectual property regime that avoids an "intellectual property trap". Third, reciprocal countermeasures and antitrust action against abuse of intellectual property. Fourth, a more active lead in international science and technology cooperation, including through the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy account of the technology rivalry with the United States, together with the policy proposals Li draws from it.

Marx's theory of the social power of capital and its contemporary value 马克思资本社会权力理论及其当代价值 Duan Xuehui Duan Xuehui takes up Marx's claim that capital "is a social power", a theme the author says has received little systematic study. Existing work, in Duan's view, treats the forms of capital power only in fragments, looks at "capital power" without its social character, and explains its origin only through capital's profit-seeking nature. Drawing on Capital and its manuscripts, the article argues that capital power is a ramified power rooted in ownership, that it derives historically from the social power of commodities and money, and that it is transient. It then draws lessons for regulating capital in China. The article has four parts. It begins with the research background, including the Party Central Committee's calls since December 2020 to strengthen anti-monopoly work and prevent the "disorderly expansion of capital". It then sets out the content of capital's social power in its economic, political and cultural forms, and the genesis and tendency of that power. The final part turns to present-day value, with five proposals for the primary stage of socialism. Duan's core move is to treat ownership as the basic power from which the others derive. Economic power covers ownership of means of production and, in substance, of labour-power, the appropriation of surplus labour, command and supervision, compulsion, and the freedom to use and dismiss workers. Political power appears in capital's use of and entanglement with state power, class rule, and cultural power appears in control of ideology, where "freedom, equality and human rights" are said to serve capital valorisation. Capital's power is traced from commodity to money to capital, and its social root is the relations of production. Duan reads capital's contradictions with the proletariat, and between its general social power and capitalists' private power, as showing that the power is historical and temporary. For China, Duan argues that capital remains necessary for developing the productive forces in the primary stage of socialism, and that all forms of capital, public and private, tend to expand their power. The author calls for drawing on the socialist system, the Two Unwaverings, Party leadership and legal "traffic lights" to govern capital, and for restraining power as well as capital, so as to cut the link between "capital becoming power" and "power becoming capital". Duan also urges differentiated handling of public, private and foreign capital, vigilance towards international financial monopoly capital, and state control over digital capital. Read the original if you want a close textual reading of Capital on capital's power and an example of how this theory is applied to current Chinese policy on regulating capital.

Grasping the dialectical relationship between economic development and cultural construction from the perspective of humanistic economics 在人文经济学视域中把握经济发展与文化建设的辩证关系 Wang Shengsheng Liu Huihui Wang Shengsheng and Liu Huihui ask how economic development and cultural construction relate to each other, and why this matters for Chinese modernization, which the article describes as a modernization in which material and cultural-ethical progress are coordinated. Their answer is that humanistic economics, a research theme prompted by a remark of Xi Jinping in 2023, offers a framework for linking people's needs, the economy and culture, and for explaining the Chinese state's role in making the two reinforce each other. The article appeared in Economic Perspectives (Jingji zongheng), no. 12, 2024. The authors begin by arguing that both mainstream Western economics and most Marxist political economy neglect culture when explaining China's rapid growth. The former centres on the rational "economic man"; the latter centres on production relations and the Party's political leadership. The article then proceeds in four steps: the "real person" and the dual needs, material and spiritual, in which economy and culture are united; the economy's determination of culture; culture's reaction on the economy; and the socialist state as the agent that connects the two. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Gramsci and Althusser, and on cultural-industry data. Wang and Liu hold that, in the historical-materialist order, the level of productive forces and the dominant relations of production determine the content and form of culture. In their account, capitalist relations produce a culture of individualism and consumerism, while public ownership and people-centred development produce one of collectivism and common prosperity. In the other direction, culture raises workers' skills, binds people to a given mode of production, and shapes government economic governance. They cite Soviet and East European failure and Chinese success as showing that cultural outcomes decide political and economic systems. The authors treat the state as the key link. Capitalist states, they say, present class interests as public interest and cannot both promote the economy and sustain a cohesive culture. The socialist state is a distinct case: it is simultaneously part of the economic base, the political superstructure and the ideological superstructure, and guided by Marxism it uses economic laws consciously. They reject Western "authoritarian development" and "China collapse" readings as ideologically limited. They conclude that the state's active role must be exercised and that national governance be modernized. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese political economists extend the base–superstructure relation to culture and the state through humanistic economics.

The theoretical logic and practical path of the transformation of the mode of production in the digital age 数字时代生产方式变革的理论逻辑与实践路径 Xiao Lei Xiao Lei asks how big-data and artificial-intelligence technologies are transforming the mode of production, understood in Marxist terms as the unity of productive forces and relations of production. The article argues that the rise of "digital productive forces" is changing how the elements of production combine technically and socially. In Xiao's account, this produces new relations of production and new contradictions, which China must manage through institutional reform. The aim is to build what the article calls a new form of socialist digital civilization within Chinese modernization. The article has four parts. The first treats digital productive forces as the material basis of the change: their elements, their place among new quality productive forces, and their effects on labour productivity, the division of labour, innovation, and the space and time of capital movement. The second examines the new relations of production: data ownership, platform-based coordination of the national economy cycle, algorithmic regulation, and systemic change in the economic structure and superstructure. The third identifies four internal contradictions. The fourth sets out policy paths for high-quality development of digital productive forces. Xiao's central move is to argue that data, as a core means of production, is socially generated by users but its use is privately monopolised by platforms. The resulting income is described as a "data rent", comparable to monopoly over free natural forces in Marx's analysis. A second contradiction is between platforms' public-infrastructure character and their private ownership. Further contradictions are between digital monopoly power and state power, and between states over the internationalisation of digital productive forces. The article also draws on Varoufakis's "technofeudalism" thesis and on the claim that algorithms are not neutral but define relations among workers, platforms and consumers. Xiao proposes strengthening state protection of digital productive forces, building a national innovation system and data-property institutions, and training digital workers. The article also calls for a new ownership structure with public ownership predominant in key digital sectors, algorithm supervision, regulation of digital capital, and a new social safety net. It further calls for Party leadership of digital-economy development, "digital common prosperity" and a cyberspace community with a shared future. The conclusion links these steps to Lenin's electrification formula and to the material conditions of a higher stage of communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy framing of platforms, data and algorithms, as it appears in Chinese policy-oriented scholarship.

Accelerating the construction of new-type relations of production suited to new quality productive forces 加快构建与新质生产力相适应的新型生产关系 Han Wenlong Tang Xiang Han Wenlong and Tang Xiang take up Xi Jinping's statement that developing new quality productive forces requires further comprehensively deepening reform to form new-type relations of production that fit them. Writing in the Party journal Qianxian (2024), they argue that a new round of technological revolution and industrial change creates new demands on the relations of production. They set out to clarify what the new-type relations of production are and what they require, and to offer a theoretical guide for building them. The article has three parts. The first defines the new-type relations of production through three components of the techno-economic-social paradigm: new factors, new technologies and new industries. The second presents these relations as the institutional foundation of new quality productive forces. The third lays out an institutional framework, divided into reform paths and implementation mechanisms. The authors' core move is to match each element of the new productive forces with a corresponding institutional arrangement. On factors, new-type workers, means of labour and objects of labour call for talent-training and education systems, an intelligent technology-innovation system, and a data-factor system of ownership and markets. On technology and industry, they call for mechanisms that steer breakthroughs in key technologies and upgrade traditional industries while fostering emerging and future ones. They then propose six reform paths: economic reform built on property rights, including data rights of ownership, use and income; science and technology reform; talent reform; reform of the ecological civilisation system; a high-standard socialist market economy built around a unified national market; and wider institutional opening up. Reform is to proceed under the Party's unified leadership. The authors also call for the rule of law and stronger enforcement, including protection of property rights, market supervision, workers' rights and data privacy. The authors conclude that relations of production act back on the productive forces, so building new-type relations is a key lever and practical driving force for their development. They say reform should aim at the organic unity of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. They also propose supporting policy systems for production, distribution, exchange and consumption. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars link new quality productive forces to institutional reform, including the treatment of data as a factor of production.

The generation and driving forces of the category "new quality productive forces": an interactive perspective on policy discourse and academic discourse “新质生产力”范畴的生成与动因：一个政策话语-学术话语互动的视角 Wang Shouyi Chi Yaoxian Wang Shouyi and Chi Yaoxian ask how the category "new quality productive forces" came about and why. They argue that existing research either reads the term from policy documents or traces the history of productive-force theory, and neglects the link between policy discourse and academic discourse. Treating policy language as academic language without scrutiny, in their view, produces conceptual confusion and superficial scholarship. They propose a framework of "practical challenge – policy response – theoretical construction". The article first sets out the theoretical base in Marxist productive-force theory, distinguishing a general level (productive forces as historical, continuous, interacting with relations of production, and social) from a specific level (the shift from individual natural power to social natural power in science, technology, division of labour and cooperation). It then traces policy discourse on productive forces from 1949 through land reform, the 1956 priority on heavy industry, reform and opening up, and the post-18th Party Congress (2012) period. Political economy textbooks serve as markers of academic discourse. The last sections review policy and scholarly accounts of the new category, covering connotation, extension and measurement. Wang and Chi argue that, since the founding of the People's Republic, policy discourse has led academic discourse in Chinese political economy, and that academic textbooks have tended to follow policy passively. In their account, the shift in the principal contradiction (1981 versus the 19th Party Congress in 2017) and digital technology changed workers, objects and instruments of labour, prompting the category's first use in September 2023. They read the policy side as answering three questions: what kind of productive force, how to develop it under the new development philosophy, and for whom, namely the people. They read the academic side as dividing into work on connotation, extension and four measurement approaches, whose differing results the authors say cause confusion. They also stress that the category covers both ideal form ("new") and the relations of production in which it grows ("quality"). The authors conclude that the category carries a people-centred value orientation, reflects a particular stage of high-quality development, is practice-oriented, and shows policy discourse leading theoretical innovation. They call for economic analysis that goes beyond natural-science approaches to reform organisation, exchange and distribution and build new relations of production. They also call for reading policy documents and theoretical logic together, and for turning policy discourse into academic discourse, which they say strengthens confidence and counters neoliberal discourse. Read the original if you study how Chinese policy concepts become academic categories, or want a survey of early scholarship on new quality productive forces.

Correctly grasping the connotation and practical paths of new quality productive forces 正确把握新质生产力的内涵和实践途径 Zhang Xu Zhang Xu asks how new quality productive forces should be understood theoretically, now that they have emerged in China's modernization drive and are driving high-quality development. The article argues that they are best understood as the modernization of the labour process (the production process). On that reading, they follow the general laws of productive-force development and are also a new, Chinese-characteristic form within Chinese modernization. The article is a short theoretical piece in Qianxian (2024, no. 9). It begins from Marx's account of production, productive capacity and productive forces, drawing on the Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, the 1846 letter to Annenkov and the 1857–58 manuscripts. It then reviews successive scientific-technological and industrial revolutions, and ends with three practical requirements. Zhang's core move is to apply Marx's simple elements of the labour process to the new concept. These elements are purposeful activity, the object of labour and the means of labour. Zhang reads Marx's remark that economic epochs differ by how and with what means of labour things are made as grounding the claim that technology reshapes both the labour process and the structure of productive forces. In this account, successive revolutions moved from machine systems to electrification, automation, information technology and artificial intelligence. They shifted the workforce towards mental, intelligent labour and added control machines to the machine system. Scientific and technological innovation is therefore the core element of new quality productive forces, which appear in the digital economy and AI. Zhang cites Xi Jinping's definition, centred on a leap in labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimal combination, with a marked rise in total factor productivity as the core indicator. The article presents this as a continuation and creative development of Marx's view of productive forces. Zhang proposes three tasks. First, labourers must be valued, trained and protected, linking education, science and technology, and talent policy, and avoiding a focus on technology that ignores people; high-tech and traditional talent should be developed in parallel. Second, new relations of production must form through deeper reform of the economic, scientific-technological and management systems, redefining the position of each labour-process element through new distribution relations under a high-level socialist market economy. Third, society's initiative should be unleashed by improving income distribution for factors including labour, knowledge, technology, management, capital and data, and by tolerating failure in innovation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-journal theory ties new quality productive forces to Marx's labour-process categories and to reform of production relations.

Ethical dilemmas of digital labour and how to respond to them 数字劳动的伦理困境及其应对 Hao Yun Li Wenjing Hao Yun and Li Wenjing ask what ethical problems arise from digital labour in the digital economy and how they can be addressed. They argue that digital labour has reshaped the mode of production and can support the development of new quality productive forces. In their account, it also produces three ethical problems, which require measures covering workers' status, labour relations and the wider institutional environment. The article, published in the Party journal Qianxian in 2024, has three parts. The first describes how digital labour has given rise to a new mode of production. The second identifies the ethical problems that accompany it. The third sets out solutions. The authors open with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and Xi Jinping's call to digitalise manufacturing, services and agriculture. On the benefits, the authors define digital labour as productive and non-productive labour in which workers use digital tools to produce and process data. They credit it with raising productivity, creating flexible employment, improving the allocation of production factors and spreading the dividends of the digital economy. They cite a report that China's digital economy reached 50.2 trillion yuan in 2022, 41.5 per cent of GDP. On the problems, they invoke Marx's notions of species-being and free activity. First, digital capital instrumentalises workers through algorithmic management, which they call digital Taylorism, and so damages workers' subjectivity. Second, labour time and space expand without limit and the line between work and leisure blurs, which erodes workers' freedom. Third, the digital divide, data monopolies and unequal computing power distribute the fruits of digital labour unfairly. The authors propose three responses. Workers should be given training and ethical support so that they become leaders of digital labour's development rather than mere executors. Labour relations should be coordinated through platform oversight, algorithmic transparency and updated rules on data protection, fair competition and social insurance. Finally, a dynamic labour environment should be built through infrastructure, welfare mechanisms, public education and international policy dialogue, so that relations of production suit new quality productive forces and the digital economy achieves high-quality development. Read the original if you want an overview of how a Party-journal article applies Marxist concepts such as alienation and free activity to platform and gig work, and of the policy remedies it proposes.

A scientific and comprehensive understanding of the labour theory of value in the age of artificial intelligence 科学全面认识人工智能时代的劳动价值论 Tu Liangchuan Does Marx's labour theory of value still apply when artificial intelligence reorganises production and appears to remove the worker from it? Tu Liangchuan argues that it does. In the article, which appeared in Qianxian in 2024, AI is said to change how labour is organised and how it works, but not to overturn the theory's core claims. Tu holds that apparent refutations rest on an inaccurate or partial grasp of what the theory says. The article has three main sections. The first takes up the challenge AI poses to the theory from the standpoint of dialectical and historical materialism. The second turns to the practical logic by which AI changes production and everyday life. The third, under the heading of upholding fundamental principles while innovating, sets out directions for developing the theory further, in line with the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to open up new realms of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Tu's central move is to restate that living human labour is the only source of value and that value is fixed by socially necessary labour time. AI, as an objectified product of human labour, only imitates and amplifies human capacities. Its algorithmic self-growth is described as a semblance of living labour, and the value it yields belongs to those who develop and use it. In Tu's account, its value passes into fixed capital, so unmanned production creates no new value or surplus value, and the supposed contradiction between automation and the theory is a false proposition produced by empiricists. Tu also argues that non-material labour remains inside capitalist relations of production, so Marx's abstract-labour theory still applies. Capitalist use of AI is said to produce a paradox: it frees people from dangerous work, yet it also extends hidden exploitation and control into daily life, turning life into a factory. Tu concludes that the AI age is still the historical epoch Marxism identified, and that AI labour enriches and confirms the labour theory of value. Tu calls for further study of surplus-value theory and the theory of capital turnover. They also call for confronting problems such as the independence of abstract labour, the ubiquity of surplus labour and the absolutisation of class separation, so that workers keep the leading role in production and the gains of the AI era are distributed rationally. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Marxist theorists defend the labour theory of value against claims that AI creates value.

Patient capital empowering the development of new quality productive forces: internal logic and paths of realisation 耐心资本赋能新质生产力发展：内在逻辑与实现路径 Qi Yudong Luan Jing Qi Yudong and Luan Jing take up a policy phrase from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for developing "patient capital". They argue that this link in the cultivation of new quality productive forces is increasingly neglected and misunderstood. Their thesis is that patient capital is long-term, quality-oriented, innovation-oriented and tied to the real economy, and that these traits fit what new quality productive forces need at the level of the firm, the industry and the macro-economy. The article first reviews definitions from Deeg, Ivashina and Lerner, and the impact-investing fund Acumen, and contrasts them with Chinese work that starts from capital heterogeneity. It then sorts patient capital into government-guided funds and market-led funds (angel, venture and private equity). Next it draws on economic history, from Watt's steam engine and Edison's lighting to Fairchild and Silicon Valley, and on cases such as Nvidia and Hillhouse's restructuring of Belle. The last part sets out policy paths for China. The core argument is that technological revolutions repeatedly follow a cycle in which venture capital drives early innovation, speculative bubbles then form, and finance finally returns to real production. Drawing on Marx's distinction between industrial capital (M–C…P…C′–M′) and fictitious capital, the authors hold that only capital anchored in production yields productive forces. They cite the Solow paradox to claim that the payoff from general-purpose technologies comes late, so patient capital is needed. At the micro level it helps firms to grow large, strong, excellent and durable. At the meso level it backs 0-to-1 breakthroughs, commercialisation and diffusion. At the macro level it supports new production functions and higher total factor productivity. For China the authors propose three measures. The first is to improve the capital market through the full fundraising–investment–management–exit chain and wider long-term sources such as insurance, banks, state capital and government funds. The second is to reform evaluation, fault-tolerance and incentive systems, including longer assessment cycles and less focus on preserving and increasing the value of state assets. The third is to build multi-tier markets and "green channels" so that technologies reach the market and give patient capital a profitable basis. Read the original if you want a Chinese economic-theory account of patient capital that mixes Marxian categories, Western economic history and concrete financial-policy recommendations.

Further comprehensively deepening reform must adhere to a systems perspective 进一步全面深化改革必须坚持系统观念 Zhang Zhidan Zhang Zhidan takes up one of the "six musts" in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further comprehensively deepening reform: the requirement to adhere to a systems perspective. The article argues that the systems perspective is a basic Marxist epistemology and method, and that reform should now be planned as a whole, with integrated design and mutually reinforcing measures, if it is to reach a higher level. The piece is a theoretical commentary in three parts. The first explains why the systems perspective is a foundational way of thinking and working. The second discusses five major relationships that must be handled correctly. The third sets out three requirements for reform: systematicness, integrity and coordination. It draws throughout on speeches by Xi Jinping and on the plenum decision. Zhang first places the systems perspective within Marxist dialectical materialism and within Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the author's account, Deng Xiaoping already treated reform as a systematic project, and since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has moved reform from local experiments to "systems integration". The second part then treats five pairs of relationships: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. For each, Zhang argues that the two sides condition and reinforce each other, so neither should be pursued at the other's expense; the government–market pair, for example, calls for the market to play the decisive role in allocating resources while government makes better use of its own role. The third part says reform must be systematic, integral and coordinated. It must also be centrally led by the Party, give priority to principal contradictions, and match the pace and policy direction of reform across fields from the market economy to national security. Zhang concludes that only a systems perspective can avoid piecemeal, fragmented adjustment and the working at cross-purposes of different reforms. It would thereby supply the momentum and institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization. The author calls for stronger systems thinking, unified Party leadership and a "combination of punches" across the listed institutional fields. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official reform agenda after the Third Plenum is framed in Marxist methodological terms, and which relationships it singles out.

Getting the relationship between government and market right 处理好政府和市场关系 Yin Qingshuang Xiao Lei Published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in late 2024, this article takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the Third Plenum decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024) centres on handling the relationship between government and market, with a high-standard socialist market economy at its core. Yin and Xiao argue that getting this relationship right is the core question of economic reform and the guide for building such an economy and advancing Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the issue matters; the second traces how the Party's understanding of the relationship has developed since reform and opening up and what the relationship involves; the third lists priority tasks for the next stage of reform. It relies heavily on Xi Jinping's formulations and on Party documents from the 14th Party Congress to the Third Plenum. The authors present four reasons for the issue's importance: it follows from a people-centred approach to development, from upholding the basic socialist economic system, from building a high-standard socialist market economy, and from the shift to high-quality development. They describe the relationship as complementary rather than opposed, so that the market plays a decisive role without playing every role. Yin and Xiao say this breaks with the Western dualism of state versus market and applies dialectical thinking. They also describe the relationship as dynamic and strategically oriented, with no single model, and as needing adjustment to each country's basic economic system and stage of development. The authors propose tasks including upholding the Two Unwaverings, with state capital concentrated in strategic sectors and private firms supported in leading major technology projects. They also call for freer movement of production factors and a unified national market, clearer roles for government and private investment, and a fair market environment for new quality productive forces. Their last proposal is to align macro policies with national strategic plans. The overall aim is a balance that is both "lively" and "well-managed". Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the state–market relationship and the reform agenda after the Third Plenum.

New quality productive forces unleash powerful momentum for economic growth 新质生产力激发经济增长澎湃动力 Liu Ying Liu Ying asks how China can move off its traditional growth path at a time when global industrial and supply chains are being reshaped. The commentary argues that accelerating the development of new quality productive forces, with innovation in the leading role, is the way to drive high-quality development. It links this to Xi Jinping's strategic plan, the 2024 Government Work Report and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The piece is organised in three parts. The first treats a large rise in total factor productivity as the core marker of new quality productive forces. The second looks at the carriers of these forces: upgrading traditional industries and developing strategic emerging and future industries. The third covers deepening reform in the economic, science and technology, talent, financial and fiscal systems. Liu defines total factor productivity as the residual in growth after labour and capital inputs are removed, and says it can rise through technological progress or better resource allocation. On this basis the author describes new quality productive forces as advanced and green productive forces that cannot form spontaneously. They require technology-led industrial innovation, new ideas, and management and institutional change. The author cites data as a core factor, giving a digital economy of 50.2 trillion yuan in 2022. The author also cites China's leading position in solar and wind power and new-energy vehicles, and Beijing's plans for 20 future industries. Liu holds that reform is the necessary path. The author calls for a unified national market and factor-market reform, and for science and technology reform that turns patents into productivity, backed by R&D spending of 2.64% of GDP in 2023. Further proposals are talent reform to turn the demographic dividend into a talent dividend, financial reform that raises direct financing and supports innovation, and fiscal reform that realigns central and local powers and uses 1 trillion yuan in ultra-long-term bonds to draw in patient capital. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy case linking new quality productive forces to total factor productivity and structural reform.

Three important engines leading high-quality development 引领高质量发展的三大重要动力源 Feng Xiaoxu Xia Jiechang Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called on the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta and the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area to play a better role as engines of high-quality development, Feng Xiaoxu and Xia Jiechang ask how these "power sources" can be built up. They argue that the three regions should lead national high-quality development by developing new quality productive forces in ways suited to local conditions. The article first reviews the record of each region. It then explains why developing new quality productive forces is an inherent requirement and key focus of high-quality development, and closes with policy proposals for the three regions and for cross-regional cooperation. It was published in Qiushi's sister journal Qianxian (Frontline) in 2024. In the authors' account, the three regions have achieved strong results. They cite Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei GDP of 10.4 trillion yuan in 2023, 1.9 times the 2013 figure. They give Yangtze River Delta GDP as above 30 trillion yuan, 24.4 per cent of the national total, and the Greater Bay Area's output as above 14 trillion yuan, about one-ninth of the national economy on under 0.6 per cent of its land. Drawing on Xi Jinping's January 2024 remarks, the authors then link new quality productive forces to four pillars: scientific and technological innovation as the core element, a modern industrial system as the form high-quality development takes, institutional and mechanism innovation as its safeguard, and green development as its "background colour". They say the regions' strengths in innovation, industry, reform conditions and green practice differ, and that tailoring development to each helps address unbalanced and inadequate development. The authors conclude that deep-seated problems remain and propose region-specific tasks: relieving Beijing of non-capital functions, deepening Yangtze integration, and strengthening the Hengqin, Qianhai and Nansha platforms in the Bay Area. They add four general measures: high-level collaborative innovation networks and talent centres; better-linked industrial and supply chains; improved cross-administrative coordination mechanisms; and joint ecological protection and green transition. Read the original if you want an official-line overview of how regional strategy is tied to new quality productive forces, with the 2023 regional statistics and policy proposals set out in one place.

Implementing the "Two Unwaverings" to promote the common development of economies under all forms of ownership 落实“两个毫不动摇”促进各种所有制经济共同发展 Zheng Hongliang Zheng Hongliang takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively to advance Chinese modernization, which spells out the Two Unwaverings more concretely than before and stresses their implementation. Zheng argues that the Two Unwaverings are a basic strategy and major Party policy, and that realising them requires continuous improvement of institutions and mechanisms so that public and non-public ownership can develop together. The commentary has three parts. It first traces the policy's history from the 1984 reform decision through the 15th Party Congress (1997), which made public ownership as the mainstay with diverse ownership forms the basic economic system, and the 16th Congress (2002), which formulated the Two Unwaverings, to their inclusion in the basic strategy at the 19th Congress (2017). It then sets out the complementary strengths of state-owned and private firms. Finally it proposes institutional reforms in three areas: the market system, multi-level institutional innovation and opening up. Zheng's central claim is that the two sectors complement each other in several ways. State firms are concentrated in key sectors, including natural monopolies and public goods, while private firms operate mainly in competitive fields and are called the "people's economy". Zheng also contrasts the longer principal–agent chains and soft budget constraints of state firms with the clearer property rights of private ones, and cites empirical work in support of mixed ownership. Zheng cites figures crediting the private sector with over 50 per cent of tax revenue, over 60 per cent of GDP and over 80 per cent of urban employment. Zheng treats calls to privatise state firms and talk of eliminating private ownership or of the private economy "leaving the stage" as dogmatic or mistaken challenges to the basic economic system. Zheng says the second tendency has recently grown. Zheng calls for a high-level socialist market economy and a unified national market. Zheng also calls for four layers of institutions (foundational, targeted, principal-body and specialised) that guarantee equal use of production factors, fair competition and equal legal protection. A third call is for deeper opening up, including reforms that would help China join the CPTPP, such as reducing administrative monopoly, hardening budget constraints and strengthening corporate governance in state firms. Read the original if you want a concise official-line academic account of how the 2024 Decision frames state and private ownership and what institutional reforms it implies.

The articulation of modes of production and the common development of multiple forms of ownership 生产方式连接理论与多种所有制经济共同发展 Hu Leming Liu Mengyuan Hu and Liu ask how the principle of keeping public ownership dominant while developing multiple forms of ownership side by side can be explained as a unified whole. They argue that existing studies usually treat the public and non-public sectors separately, in terms of their roles and efficiency, which invites one-sided views such as the claims that the state advances while the private sector retreats, or the reverse. They propose borrowing the theory of the articulation of modes of production, developed by John G. Taylor and others, to supply a comprehensive account of how ownership forms relate to one another. The article has four parts after the introduction. It first reconstructs the theory, from dependency theorists such as Paul Baran and Andre Gunder Frank through Ernesto Laclau, Pierre-Philippe Rey and Taylor. It then extends the framework through a reading of Marx and Samir Amin, and sets out a typology of ways in which modes of production connect. Finally, it traces the history of ownership policy in China from 1978 to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), and draws policy proposals from the typology. The authors reject Taylor's claim that Marx assumed a single mode of production per society, citing Marx's remarks that every social formation contains remnants of the old and seeds of the new. They credit Taylor with making "articulation" a concept for the relations among coexisting modes, and they widen it. They define articulation as an institutional arrangement or practice that eases latent opposition among differing modes. They distinguish three types: master–subordinate, block-type (plate-like), and fusion-type, the last divided into integrated (such as mixed-ownership enterprises) and contractual forms. In their account, political power and ideological structure determine which type prevails. On this reading, the relation between public and non-public ownership in China moved from master–subordinate in the early reform years, through block-type in the 1990s, to mostly fusion-type in the new era. The authors conclude that policy should foster fusion-type articulation. They call for deeper mixed-ownership reform, including cross-shareholding in both directions and reform of governance as well as of capital structure. They also call for better relational contracts within industrial clusters, so that small and medium-sized firms do not become an exploited periphery of leading firms, and for foreign-invested firms to serve as a link between domestic and international circulation. They reject both decoupling and dependent development, and they present these steps as support for the Two Unwaverings and the new development philosophy. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy argument that applies Western Marxist theories of articulation, with a typology and a periodisation, to ownership policy under reform and opening up.

Understanding and grasping the methodology of further comprehensively deepening reform 深刻认识和把握进一步全面深化改革方法论 Zhu Heng Wang Weiguo This commentary from Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 22) takes up the methodological guidance Xi Jinping gave on 29 October 2024 at the opening of a study seminar for provincial and ministerial leading cadres on the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhu and Wang argue that reform is a systematic project requiring scientific method, and that grasping this methodology is essential for turning the plenum's strategic plans into a force for advancing Chinese modernization. The article is organised around four principles drawn from Xi's speech, each given its own section: uniting reform with the rule of law; the dialectical unity of breaking and establishing; uniting reform with opening up; and handling the relationship between planning and implementation. Each section quotes Xi, explains the principle, and then lists practical requirements for the current stage of reform. On law, the authors say reform and the rule of law are like two wings or wheels: legislation should anticipate and guide major reforms, while law is improved through reform. They stress that this requires the Party's overall leadership, a problem-oriented approach and a people-centred stance. On breaking and establishing, they read Xi's formula "establish first, break afterwards" as making establishing the aim and breaking the means. Establishing first allows reform to move swiftly, and breaking in due time keeps it steady. They give the examples of ending the fixation on test scores, diplomas and papers in education evaluation, and the fixation on GDP in economic reform. On opening up, the authors hold that opening brings in advanced ideas and technology while reform builds the foundation for higher-level opening. They call for aligning with high-standard international trade rules, defending the multilateral trading system, building a community with a shared future for mankind and promoting high-quality Belt and Road Initiative development. On implementation, they stress that "one part planning, nine parts implementation". They call for workable reform plans, accountability systems tied to a correct view of performance, and a systematic approach that combines top-level design with grassroots exploration and the initiative of both central and local levels. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line summary of how Party theorists present the methodological principles of the current reform agenda.

Promoting high-quality development requires guarding against "old wine in new bottles" 推动高质量发展要防止“新瓶装旧酒” Wang Bin This short commentary, published in Study Times in January 2025, takes up a warning Xi Jinping gave in January 2024: some officials, while claiming to promote high-quality development, are in practice pouring "old wine into new bottles". Wang argues that real high-quality development requires "new wine in new bottles", meaning new content as well as new forms. The piece first explains the metaphor and the practices it describes. It then sets out what high-quality development means, drawing on its positioning, mode, goals and results. It goes on to discuss new quality productive forces and the deepening of reform, and closes with a call for fresh thinking, methods and practice.
