Wang says the "old wine" problem appears when localities announce new policies, projects, technologies or models while keeping the traditional development mode, habitual thinking and outdated management. In Wang's view this is contrary to materialist dialectics, to the nature of high-quality development and to China's actual conditions. Developing new quality productive forces is presented as the "new wine", since they are marked by high technology, high efficiency and high quality and so guard against innovation for its own sake. Wang also stresses building production relations suited to the productive forces. The commentary applies the same logic to reform: renamed measures with unchanged substance fail to build the needed institutions. As an example, it cites localities that set up large government-guided funds to build "patient capital" without grasping its dual policy and market character, which wastes resources. Wang concludes that the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) shows the leadership's resolve to remove institutional obstacles, and that economic reform is the "ox's nose" leading further comprehensive deepening of reform. Officials are urged to read changing conditions accurately, adapt scientifically and seek change actively. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-press commentary turns a leader's metaphor into guidance for officials on high-quality development.

Using investigation and research to break through problems and open new horizons Rereading Mao Zedong's "Oppose Book Worship" 以调查研究推动破难题开新局 Wang Ying Writing in the Party school newspaper Study Times, Wang Ying asks how the Communist Party can effectively solve hard problems and open new horizons. The commentary answers with the formula Mao Zedong gave in May 1930 in "Oppose Book Worship": "investigate actual conditions". Wang argues that the essay remains a source of Marxist thinking and working methods for the new journey of deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The piece is a short commentary on a classic text. It first recounts the essay's history: originally titled "Investigation Work", it circulated in lithograph form in the Central Soviet Area and was lost. It was rediscovered in the early 1960s, retitled by Mao in 1964, and added in 1991 to the second edition of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong, volume one. Three sections then follow, on investigation as problem-solving, on opposing two kinds of book worship, and on the need for continual investigation. Wang's central argument is that investigation is a question of ideological line as well as method. Citing Mao, Wang says that without investigation one has no right to speak, and that solutions can only come from studying a problem's present state and history. Mao targeted two tendencies: blindly and formally carrying out superior instructions, and copying Marxist texts and the Soviet model. Wang notes that Mao himself added in 1964 the line that Marxist books must be studied but combined with China's actual conditions. Wang also links continual investigation to the Marxist law of the unity of opposites, and cites Mao's 1961 remark that investigation must continue "for ten thousand years". Wang concludes that investigation and research are a Party tradition and a matter of success or failure for its cause. The commentary calls for making full use of this "family heirloom" in carrying out the tasks set by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It urges a problem-oriented focus on key reform tasks, so that leaders have a clear grasp of conditions, firm resolve and the right methods, and so advance Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present Mao's investigation doctrine as guidance for current reform.

Upholding ideological and cultural foundation-building to consolidate absolute loyalty to the Party 坚持思想文化固本培元筑牢对党绝对忠诚 Nie Fuya This commentary, published in Study Times in January 2025, asks how ideological and cultural work can strengthen the absolute loyalty of state security personnel to the Party. Its author, identified as a Party committee member and head of the political department at the Ministry of State Security, argues that holding ideological leadership is the basis of all leadership. On that basis, Nie contends, the Party's absolute leadership over state security organs requires building a staff that is firm, pure and dedicated. The piece is organised under three headings. The first says why ideological and cultural work must take a clear political stance. The second sets out how political guidance can forge loyalty. The third explains how the work should innovate with the times. On the first point, Nie gives three reasons: the requirement of the Party's absolute leadership, the study and implementation of Xi Jinping's thought on culture, and the continuation of the 'red bloodline'. Nie asks state security organs to take political loyalty as the first task and to deepen Party history education, drawing on the history of the covert front. On the second, the author proposes four measures: consolidating the theoretical foundation through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the holistic approach to national security; promoting the historical tradition of loyalty; holding up exemplary figures, including ordinary ones; and creating a cultural atmosphere through ceremonies such as flag-raising, oath-taking and awards, and through literary and artistic works on national security themes. On the third, Nie lists five kinds of awareness to be fostered: political, front-line (positions for propaganda and education), audience, quality-product and technological awareness. Audience awareness means tailoring content to leading cadres, young officers and the public. Technological awareness means using new technologies to empower ideological and cultural work. Nie concludes that ideological and cultural work should be anchored in the Party's cultural leadership and be adjusted to changing conditions. It should also produce what the author calls an 'iron army' of state security personnel with reliable political loyalty. The text is a statement of institutional priorities and working methods rather than an analytical study. Read the original if you want a primary example of how a senior state security official describes ideological education, the 'red' tradition and cultural programmes inside China's security apparatus.

Understanding the buzzwords of China's economic development 读懂中国经济发展热词 Xu Xiaoming This short explanatory piece, first published in the Party discipline newspaper China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News, sets out to help readers understand the key terms in current discussion of China's economy. Writing at the start of 2025, Xu presents 2024 as a year in which the economy, despite greater external pressure and domestic difficulties, remained generally stable while making progress, and shows the new terms as expressions of that development. After an opening overview of 2024, the article defines seven terms in turn: new quality productive forces, patient capital, future industries, the package of incremental policies, the silver economy, the debut economy and the low-altitude economy. Each entry follows a similar pattern of definition, characteristics, significance and prospects. The author's overview credits ultra-long special government bonds and the policy package with expanding domestic demand and lifting consumption. Xu defines new quality productive forces as an advanced form of productivity led by innovation, marked by a major rise in total factor productivity and described as an inherent requirement of high-quality development. Patient capital, which comes mainly from government funds, pension funds and insurance capital, is presented as a necessary condition for developing these forces. Future industries are described as frontier-technology sectors still at an early stage, needing sustained investment and cooperation among government, firms and universities. The incremental policy package is portrayed as comprehensive and coordinated, covering fiscal, monetary, employment, industrial and consumption policy, with the aim of long-term high-quality development. The silver economy, debut economy and low-altitude economy are treated as growth areas in which Xu notes opportunities and, for the last, obstacles such as weak airspace management, thin infrastructure and low technical standardisation. Xu concludes that these concepts show an economy displaying resilience and potential, which the article calls an important engine of world economic growth. For the newer sectors, the author calls for better policy frameworks, infrastructure, technology research and safety supervision, with government, firms and society working together. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned glossary of the economic vocabulary used in Chinese policy discourse at the end of 2024.

Upholding the "Two Integrations" to advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 坚持“两个结合”推进马克思主义中国化时代化 Feng Bo This short commentary, first published on the Xuanjiangjia website, asks how the Two Integrations can be upheld in order to advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Feng argues that this task is long and arduous and depends on four requirements: theoretical confidence, a problem-oriented approach, systematic integration and strong talent support. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to put down roots in China, continue the Chinese cultural lineage and build an autonomous system of knowledge in Chinese philosophy and social sciences. It then reviews the Party's practice of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities, and its combination with fine traditional Chinese culture. Four short sections follow, one for each requirement. On theoretical confidence, Feng presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a new leap in adapting Marxism, and calls on readers to be firm believers in it and faithful practitioners of it. On problem orientation, Feng starts from the principal contradiction of the new era and argues that theory must address major practical problems and listen to ordinary people. Systematic integration means combining basic Marxist research with applied research and spreading good local experience. Talent support means training politically reliable theorists, using both senior experts and younger scholars, and building incentive and evaluation systems, while guiding theoretical work so that it stays on the right course. Feng concludes that theoretical and practical awareness must be sustained, and that research on Marxism and innovation in theory and practice must keep deepening. The stated aim is to contribute to building a modern socialist country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a local Party school presents the practical requirements of the Two Integrations.

Advancing high-quality development of the Yangtze River Economic Belt through regional coordination and integration 以区域协同融通推进长江经济带高质量发展 Li Xuesong Li Xuesong asks how the Yangtze River Economic Belt can move from cost-driven, scale-based expansion to innovation-driven high-quality development. The article argues that the Belt is one interdependent system whose public problems cannot be handled by any single administrative unit. In Li's view, regional coordination and integration must therefore be the main lever, replacing a mindset of competition with one of cooperation and shared benefit. The article opens by quoting Xi Jinping's call for provinces along the river to deliberate jointly, govern the ecology together, build jointly and share development. It then diagnoses four shortfalls in coordination: industry, cities, the ecological environment, and scientific and technological innovation. Each shortfall is matched with a set of remedies, and the article closes with proposals on innovation networks and 'innovation enclaves'. On the diagnosis, Li describes a clear east–west gradient. The Yangtze River Delta leads in output, city coordination and innovation, while the middle and upper reaches suffer from weak industrial foundations, 'core–periphery' city structures and fragmented innovation. Li also points to administrative barriers, local protectionism and weak cross-boundary governance. For industry, Li proposes orderly gradient transfer: Jiangsu and Zhejiang as a 'dual core' for labour-intensive manufacturing, Jiangsu as the anchor for capital-intensive sectors, and technology transfer from the lower reaches to Anhui, Hubei, Sichuan and others. For cities, Li calls for integrated markets, fiscal and tax revenue-sharing for cross-regional projects and enclaves, and the Chengdu–Chongqing urban agglomeration as a breakthrough linking the three major agglomerations. Li also proposes linking the Belt with the Belt and Road Initiative. For ecology, Li urges legally backed ecological red lines, a law on ecological compensation, vertical and horizontal compensation, and unified monitoring networks. For innovation, Li recommends corridors modelled on the G60 Science and Technology Innovation Corridor, shared major scientific facilities, university alliances and two-way enclaves, with the aim of world-class advanced manufacturing clusters. Li concludes that these measures would build ecological and interest communities along the river. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented regional economics account of Yangtze coordination, with sector-by-sector and province-by-province proposals.

Empowering the development of new quality productive forces in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area through digital transformation 以数字化转型赋能粤港澳大湾区新质生产力发展 Liu Sheng Chen Xiuying Taking up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to develop new quality productive forces in line with local conditions and to integrate the real and digital economies, Liu and Chen ask how digital transformation can drive such development in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area. They argue that digital transformation is becoming the key path for the region's high-quality development. This short commentary is organised in three parts: achievements, challenges and measures. It draws on regional statistics and examples from Guangdong, including industrial, service-sector and governance initiatives. On achievements, the authors cite the China Digital Economy Development Index Report (2024): Guangdong's digital economy reached 6.9 trillion yuan in 2023, first in the country for eight years, with Shenzhen's core digital industries adding over 1 trillion yuan. They also report that 29,000 large industrial enterprises had been digitalised and over 650,000 small and medium-sized firms connected to cloud services. They identify four challenges: uneven infrastructure across cities, weak digital innovation in chips, operating systems and key AI algorithms, inadequate regulation of cross-border data flows and privacy, and the difficulties small and medium-sized enterprises face with funding, technology and talent. The authors propose four responses: strengthen infrastructure and use regional support schemes to narrow gaps, raise innovation capacity through closer ties among government, industry, universities and research, improve regulation and cross-border data governance, and support small firms through training, funding and leadership from large enterprises. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented overview of Guangdong's digital economy data and the official agenda for linking digitalisation with new quality productive forces.

Scientific methods for developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 因地制宜发展新质生产力的科学方法 Liu Qirui Luan Yongyu Liu Qirui and Luan Yongyu take up a methodological question: how should new quality productive forces be developed in line with local conditions? Starting from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which made this a measure for improving the institutions of high-quality development, they argue that the approach gathers the methodological wisdom of Xi Jinping's economic thought. In their view it must be grasped fully, accurately and comprehensively if further reform is to advance Chinese modernization. The article is organised around seven modes of thinking, each presented as a method drawn from Xi Jinping's statements: strategic, historical, dialectical, systems, innovation, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. Each section pairs the method with a concrete task, ranging from national coordination and the Party's historical role to regional differentiation, education and talent, the legal environment, and economic security. Most claims are supported by quotations from Xi's speeches and Party documents. Three moves carry the argument. First, the authors read the 'new' and the 'quality' of new quality productive forces as a dialectical pair: 'new' means technological, industrial and other innovation, and 'quality' means high-quality development under the new development philosophy. They contend that, with resource and environmental constraints and a shift from factor inputs to total factor productivity, technology-led industrial innovation is the only new path. Second, they argue that localities should build on their own resource endowments, industrial base and research conditions, while staying within one national plan and a unified national market. The authors stress that there is more than one model, and that finance must serve the real economy. Third, they claim that education, science and talent must be advanced together, and that the rule of law protects innovation, intellectual property and both leading and specialised small firms. They also hold that high-quality development and high-level security reinforce each other. The authors conclude that new quality productive forces can form faster, and new production relations be shaped faster, only under the Party's comprehensive leadership and the centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. They present the seven methods as a practical toolkit for local officials and policymakers. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party theorists frame local-conditions-based development of new quality productive forces and the methods they link to it.

Upholding the path of integrated development of education, science and technology, and talent with Chinese characteristics 坚持中国特色教育科技人才一体化发展道路 Guo Hailong Guo Hailong asks what historical experience the Communist Party has accumulated in promoting education, science and technology, and talent as one integrated undertaking, and how that work should be coordinated going forward. The article's answer is that over a century of exploration the Party has produced a distinctive path of coordinated development, which it says combines Marxist views of education, science and talent with China's concrete conditions and with traditional Chinese culture. Guo describes this path as the result of the Party's hard exploration and as showing the strengths of China's state system and governance. The article treats the path as comprising the education development path, the independent innovation path and the path of self-reliant talent training, all with Chinese characteristics. It organises the path around "eight upholds": Party leadership, the "four orientations", a development orientation, goal guidance, reform and innovation, institution building, rule-of-law thinking, and openness and cooperation. Each section gives a short historical sketch, from the Party's early period through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and then sets out three requirements for the present. Guo's central claim is that Party leadership is the most essential feature, and that errors on this point would have catastrophic consequences. Guo requires centralised and unified leadership, carried through every field and stage, while the Party sets direction, plans and policy rather than managing every detail. Other sections tie the path to Xi Jinping's concepts: the new development philosophy, high-quality development and new quality productive forces. They also tie it to the goal of building a strong education, science and technology, and talent nation by 2035, and to a reform that Guo describes as neither closed and rigid nor a change of banner. Guo also stresses systematic institution building, lawmaking that is precise and timely, and global innovation cooperation under a community with a shared future for mankind. Guo concludes that these eight features answer both why and how education, science and technology, and talent should be coordinated. The article presents them as guidance for the "new journey" of building a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It is a statement of official interpretation, not a critical or empirical study.

Read the original if you want a compact account of how Party-state discourse frames the integration of education, science and technology, and talent policy, including its main slogans and their historical lineage.

How to make capital more patient 怎样让资本更有耐心 Meng Fanxin This short commentary asks what "patient capital" is, why capital can be patient and why China needs more of it now. Meng defines it as capital focused on long-term investment, with high risk tolerance and endurance of short-term market swings. The article argues that patience is compatible with capital's profit-seeking nature and is essential to technological innovation. The piece begins with the term's recent prominence in Party and economic-work meetings. It then distinguishes patient capital from merely long-term capital, explains where patience comes from, and links it to innovation and to new quality productive forces. It closes with four policy directions. Meng rejects the view that capital's drive for quick profit rules out patience. In the author's account, patience arises from understanding the lengthy, risky path from scientific discovery to industrial change, and from building a "community" between investors and innovative firms. Because innovation must cross a "valley of death" between research and market, Meng argues that patient capital matches its internal rhythm and is needed to address the lack of long-term funding for new quality productive forces. Meng proposes a predictable, law-based investment environment; high-quality investment targets and ways to connect venture capital to innovators; a virtuous cycle of science and technology, industry and finance; and a leading role for state capital. State capital and government funds should serve as the "ballast" of patient capital, with assessment over the full life cycle and reasonable tolerance of failure. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register account of why Chinese policy circles promote patient capital and what measures they link to it.

Coordinating an effective market and a capable government 统筹好有效市场和有为政府关系 Zhang Xiaojing Dong Yun This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 8 January 2024, takes up the instruction of the Central Economic Work Conference that the relationship between an effective market and a capable government must be coordinated, so as to form an economic order that is both "lively" and "well managed". Zhang and Dong present this as a hard-won lesson about the laws of economic work and as an epistemological and methodological basis for current economic policy. The article first traces how the government–market relationship has evolved since reform and opening up, from the planned economy through the 14th Party Congress (1992), the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It then sets out the theoretical logic of the two "hands", the tasks of government in high-quality development, and concrete reform measures. The authors argue that Western economics has swung between laissez-faire and state control, whereas Chinese practice has gone beyond both neoclassical doctrine and traditional political economy. In their account, the market's strength lies in efficiency, and government's in compensating for market failure, macroeconomic regulation, and shaping and supporting markets. They hold that the balance shifts with the stage of development: government mobilisation was central when China was backward, but excessive intervention now obstructs high-quality development. They therefore locate the centre of gravity in government and call for correcting misplaced, overreaching and absent government functions, in the dimensions of resource allocation, rule of law, fairness and national security. On reform, Zhang and Dong propose that building a high-standard socialist market economy should make markets "lively" through freer movement of labour and capital, citing household registration reform and financial supply-side reform. Government should keep things "well managed" through counter-cyclical macro policy, an expanded government balance sheet when private balance sheets contract, and the containment of risks such as local government debt and small financial institutions. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party economists framed government–market relations at the start of 2024.

Intellectual threads and two-way interpretation in the "dispute between ancient and modern, China and the West" “古今中西之争”的思想线索和双向阐释 Yang Huilin Yang Huilin, a professor at Renmin University of China, asks how the long-running "dispute between ancient and modern, China and the West" can be resolved. Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Yang takes up Xi Jinping's remark that the present era is better placed than any before it to resolve this dispute. Yang's thesis is that the world's texts should be read as "intertexts" and that scholarship should take the form of dialogue. Such dialogue can recover the distinct texture of Chinese civilisation and also give access to Western systems of knowledge. The piece has three parts. The first looks at Chinese resources in Western reflection on metaphysics, drawing on Graham, Kristeva, Heidegger, Levinas, Badiou and Western theologians. The second traces a dialogical tradition in modern Chinese scholarship: Lü Simian, Qian Mu, Zhang Guangzhi, Liang Shuming, Feng Youlan, Zhang Dongsun and Zhou Zuoren. The third sets out the method of "mutual reference" and "mutual interpretation" between China and the West. Yang is a chief expert on a major National Social Science Fund project on conceptual tools for dialogue between Chinese and Western civilisations. Yang's central contrast is linguistic. In Indo-European subject–predicate syntax, Being is explained through the predicate "is". Yang says classical Chinese lacked this use, so that A. C. Graham found the small word "is" vital to Western philosophy but meaningless in Chinese. Chinese thought instead rests on polar relations, yin and yang. Yang links this to Western concepts of relationality and "correlation", and to the "correlative thinking" described by Sinologists. Yang's case study is Zhang Dongsun's 1938 essay on thought, language and culture. It was translated in 1939 and summarised by Mazumdar in 1956, but entered the core of Western debate only when Kristeva read it. Effective conceptual tools, Yang argues, are "productive" rather than merely "descriptive", and translation works in both directions. Yang's examples are Heidegger's "Es gibt" and Derrida's Donner la mort. Yang concludes that mutual reference and interpretation seek neither agreed conclusions nor a single governing logic. They reactivate the resources of both sides and bring new self-understanding along with understanding of others. Such deep dialogue, Yang says, can counter talk of civilisational superiority and conflict, and should lead to exchange over estrangement, mutual learning over conflict and inclusiveness over superiority. Yang proposes tracing back and restoring each side's theoretical tools and sources of problems as the basic task. Read the original if you are interested in comparative philosophy, translation and Chinese–Western intellectual exchange, or in how a Chinese scholar frames this project.

Cultivating high-calibre talent suited to green and low-carbon development 培育与绿色低碳发展相适应的高素质人才 Xu Huajun Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Xu Huajun asks how China can train the large body of skilled people needed to meet its carbon peak and carbon neutrality commitments. Xu argues that green and low-carbon development depends on mobilising universities, enterprises and society as a whole to produce talent that practises, adapts to and leads low-carbon change. The article is a short newspaper commentary that takes its policy cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The piece is organised around three actors: universities, enterprises and the wider public. Each section gives a short list of practical measures. Xu refers to the Ministry of Education's implementation plan for building a national education system for green and low-carbon development, and cites Xi Jinping's call for a simple, moderate, green and low-carbon way of life. For universities, Xu proposes faster building of disciplines and majors such as energy storage, hydrogen, carbon capture and carbon trading, together with interdisciplinary training and new textbooks. Xu also proposes innovation and entrepreneurship education, competitions, and integrating the Party's carbon decisions into ideological and political education and campus culture. Enterprises, Xu says, must first green their own operations, then act as a bridge by co-training students with universities, co-building research platforms and developing professional evaluation standards. For society, Xu calls for family, community and social-organisation campaigns, continuing education for working people, and online courses and new-media outreach. Xu concludes that combining these channels would create a multi-level learning system that raises public awareness and produces innovative people with practical ability. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary links carbon-neutrality goals to education, workforce training and ideological work.

Modernization is not an ideology but a development experience Lecture by Professor Zheng Yongnian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's "Wenzhi Lecture Hall" 现代化不是意识形态而是发展经验 Zheng Yongnian This is the text of a lecture given by Zheng Yongnian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and posted in January 2025. Zheng asks where China's opening up should go next and what China can contribute to a more open world. The answer is that China should deepen high-level opening, including unilateral opening to less developed countries, and treat Chinese modernization as a development experience for the Global South rather than as an ideology. Zheng begins with his years working in the United States and Britain during the Thatcher and Reagan revolutions. He then compares three historical modernization models: the Latin American, the US-allied and the isolated. Next he reads China's two waves of opening, the forced opening after the Opium Wars and the opening after 1978. He then assesses the current international situation, covering Western decline, multipolarity and the Global South. The final part turns to development, artificial intelligence, regulation and unilateral opening. In Zheng's account, Chinese modernization is unusual because it has achieved both development and independence, whereas the other models bring dependence or isolation. He says the second wave of opening depended on specific conditions, including Cold War geopolitics, Western capital seeking a "new frontier" and Western hopes that China would become more like the West. Those conditions have changed, because the United States now favours protectionism and economic nationalism. Zheng argues that great-power competition is mainly a contest of development models. He notes that the US leads in AI, that Europe over-regulates, and that China produces strong research but weak application, with talent leaving for Silicon Valley. He argues that regulation should follow development, as in Singapore. Zheng also holds that unilateral opening, which he says Britain and the US practised, would reshape trade patterns and reduce confrontational thinking. Zheng concludes that China should keep a peaceful, win-win mindset, avoid pessimism about the "great changes unseen in a century", and avoid big mistakes. He asks whether China can sum up its experience of developing while staying independent and offer it to the Global South as a reference. He also says Chinese modernization needs strategic thinking beyond economics, for example by opening to foreign-owned hospitals and building mutual interdependence. Read the original if you want to see how a prominent Chinese scholar links openness, the Global South, US–China technology competition and Chinese modernization in a single public lecture.

Strengthening the ability to grasp and apply laws 增强把握运用规律能力 Zhang Xu This short newspaper commentary interprets the Central Economic Work Conference's call for five relationships to be "properly coordinated". Zhang Xu starts from the view that external conditions are worsening and the economy faces difficulties. Zhang also holds that China's economic foundation is sound, and that the basic trend of long-term improvement is unchanged. The article argues that handling these five relationships well is how positive factors become real development results. The piece takes the five pairs in turn: an effective market and an enterprising government; aggregate supply and aggregate demand; fostering new growth drivers and updating old ones; improving the increment and revitalising the stock; and raising quality and expanding total volume. Each gets a brief explanation tied to the Conference's policy language. The piece ends with a point about Party leadership and the capabilities required of officials. Zhang presents the market–government pairing as a law that a high-level socialist market economy must follow. It combines the general law that the market plays the decisive role in allocating resources with the avoidance of the defects of capitalist market economies, through a stronger role for the Party and government. On supply and demand, Zhang names weak investment, insufficient consumption and sluggish exports as demand-side problems, and capacity surplus as a supply-side one. Zhang reads the Conference's priority on boosting consumption as a way to raise total demand. The remaining pairs are linked to high-quality development, new quality productive forces driven by technological and institutional innovation, better resource allocation, and the material basis of Chinese modernization. Zhang concludes that whether China can manage the world's second-largest economy depends fundamentally on how well the Party plays its leading role. Leaders at all levels are urged to study, investigate and gain practical experience. The aim is to strengthen their ability to grasp and apply the laws of the market economy, of social development and of nature. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-affiliated economist presents the Central Economic Work Conference's priorities in official terms.

Grasping the five "must-balance" relationships to keep the economy on a steady and lasting course 把握五个“必须统筹好” 确保经济航船行稳致远 Li Yongjian Li Yongjian's commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily in January 2025, interprets five relationships that the Central Economic Work Conference said must be properly balanced. They are: an effective market and a capable government; total supply and total demand; cultivating new drivers of growth and renewing old ones; improving incremental quality and revitalising existing stock; and raising quality while expanding total output. Li presents these as a programmatic requirement of the Party Central Committee. In Li's reading, they summarise past practice, guide future development and further enrich Xi Jinping's economic thought. The article takes the five relationships in turn under separate headings. For each, Li explains what balancing means and gives policy examples and statistics on the housing market, employment, new energy vehicles and consumption. The commentary closes by treating the five as one method for economic work. On markets and government, Li argues that the market should play the decisive role in allocating resources, and that the government must correct market failures through macroeconomic policy, long-term investment in basic research, a unified national market and basic social safety nets. On supply and demand, Li cites the new energy vehicle industry as evidence that high-quality supply can generate new consumption. Li also identifies weak consumption as the core variable and calls for expanding service consumption and keeping domestic and external demand in balance. For new and old drivers, Li holds that new quality productive forces require building the new before dismantling the old, and that old industries, including agriculture, can be upgraded digitally. On stock and increment, Li points to unsold housing and local hidden debt, and to the 8 trillion yuan debt-swap arrangement. On quality and quantity, Li holds that growth remains necessary to pass through the middle-income stage and sustain employment, while "speed worship" should be abandoned. Li concludes that the five relationships are a regular pattern drawn from the Central Committee's assessment of the situation and a scientific method for overcoming difficulties. Li calls for applying them while seeking progress within stability, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, building before breaking, and coordinating policy as a system. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference's guidelines were explained to a domestic audience, with the supporting statistics Li cites.

Expanding development advantages through capability building 以能力提升扩大发展优势 Cao Dongbo This newspaper commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily in January 2024, asks what abilities Shanghai's officials need if the city is to play a leading and exemplary role in advancing Chinese modernization. Cao Dongbo argues that Shanghai must build three capabilities: strategic agility and initiative, focusing on critical junctures and overcoming difficulties, and grasping laws of development while allocating resources scientifically. The piece follows these three capabilities in turn. Each is defined conceptually, tied to remarks by Xi Jinping, and then applied to Shanghai's industrial and urban agenda. Cao draws on the book Xi Jinping in Shanghai, on Xi's 2007 visit to Baoshan District, and on the Central Economic Work Conference's call for major economic provinces to "shoulder the main burden". Cao presents strategic agility (flexible adjustment) and strategic initiative (seizing opportunities) as complementary. As examples he cites Xi's earlier push for balanced development of the three industrial sectors, with manufacturing not neglected, and Shanghai's aim of becoming a national AI hub. On critical junctures, he reads the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and of the 18th Central Committee (2013) as epoch-making turning points. He describes tackling "hard bones" and "choke-point" problems as concentrating resources on bottlenecks. On laws of development, he invokes Marxist philosophy and calls for tailored policies for producer services, knowledge-intensive services and consumer services. Cao concludes that these three capabilities are the core of urban development and the foundation of high-quality development. He calls for a consistent, persistent style of work, likened to hammering in a nail with repeated blows. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-school-style leadership discourse is applied to Shanghai's industrial policy.

Opening up broader prospects for Chinese modernization 开辟中国式现代化更加广阔的前景 Feng Jun This newspaper commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily in January 2025 and reposted on the Academy of Marxism site, takes up Xi Jinping's New Year message that the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) sounded the call for further comprehensive deepening of reform. Feng Jun argues that Chinese modernization will open up still broader prospects through reform and opening up, and that further reform must be organised around it as its central theme. The piece is organised under three headings: the historical shift from "modernization in China" to "Chinese modernization"; the rejection of the equation of modernization with Westernization; and the status of Chinese modernization theory within Marxist theory. On the first point, Feng traces the path from the Opium War and the Self-Strengthening Movement through the founding of the People's Republic to reform and opening up. The author insists that the periods before and after 1978 are stages of one exploration and must not be set against each other. On the second, Feng argues that no single modernization model or universal standard exists, that the Western process coincided with capitalism but this does not make modernization Westernization, and that China's experience widens the options open to developing countries. Feng concludes that the theory of Chinese modernization, with its defining features, essential requirements and major principles, is a major achievement of scientific socialism and part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative links Chinese modernization to reform and opening up, to civilisational claims and to Party theory.

Doing a good job of assessing the consistency of macro-policy orientation 做好宏观政策取向一致性评估 Jiang Fuwei This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily, takes up the call of the Central Economic Work Conference held at the end of 2024 to bring economic and non-economic policies together in a single assessment of macro-policy orientation consistency. Jiang argues that such assessment is the precondition for making policies work as a coordinated 'combination of punches' and for raising their overall effectiveness in support of high-quality development. The piece first explains why non-economic policies such as environmental protection and education belong in the assessment, then sets out three practical measures. It is a compact policy argument rather than a survey of literature or cases. Jiang contends that non-economic policies shape resource allocation, market expectations and social wellbeing. Environmental policy, for example, restrains high-emission industries while fostering green industries; education raises human capital and innovative capacity. Joint assessment, the author says, avoids a 'fallacy of composition' in which policy goals cancel or contradict one another, and balances short-term, local gains against long-term, overall goals. The proposed measures are a cross-departmental coordination mechanism with regular meetings and shared data; digital-intelligent assessment using big data, artificial intelligence and digital-twin simulation; and greater disclosure of assessment standards and results. Jiang concludes that consistency assessment, backed by cross-department cooperation and feedback, would improve policy transparency and public trust, stabilise market expectations and encourage corporate investment and innovation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese economist interprets the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference's emphasis on policy coordination.

Deepening understanding of the "five balances" 深化对“五个统筹”的认识 Zhao Zhenhua This commentary, first published in the Economic Daily in January 2025 (the site gives 2024 for the print date), interprets the "five balances" (五个统筹) set out at the Central Economic Work Conference held at the end of 2024. Zhao Zhenhua argues that they are a body of regularities distilled from the Party's economic work. In Zhao's account they apply dialectical and historical materialist method to current economic contradictions, serve as principles for economic work and as a method for high-quality development and Chinese modernization, and further enrich Xi Jinping's economic thought. The article opens by defining "balancing" as taking the whole picture into account and coordinating policies, against a background of what Zhao calls great changes unseen in a century, pressure from the United States-led West, weak global recovery and insufficient domestic demand. It then takes the five pairs in turn: an efficient market and a capable government; aggregate supply and aggregate demand; nurturing new drivers of growth and renewing old ones; improving the increment and revitalising the stock; and raising quality and expanding total volume. On the market and the state, Zhao holds that neither unregulated competitive capitalism nor a highly centralised planned economy has proved viable, and that the two should complement each other rather than stand as separate blocks. The cycle of "loosening leads to chaos, tightening leads to stagnation" is attributed to misplaced or absent government functions. On supply and demand, Zhao calls for deepening supply-side structural reform while expanding effective investment (housing, urban renewal, rural infrastructure) and consumption (income growth, social security, vouchers for low earners). On new and old drivers, Zhao says traditional industries are a base for new quality productive forces and should be upgraded with digital technology, with each region choosing its own path. Zhao treats increment and stock as mutually reinforcing, and defines quality through continuity, balance, sustainability, fairness and security. Zhao concludes that quality should be raised within the expansion of total output and total output expanded through higher quality, since this lays the material foundation for Chinese modernization. Proposed measures include a unified, open and orderly market, breaking regional blockades and monopolies, integrating the real and digital economies, and higher-level opening up. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference's guiding principles and the policy measures attached to each.

Adhering to a problem-oriented approach and coordinating integrated reform of the education, science and technology, and talent systems and mechanisms 坚持问题导向，统筹推进教育科技人才体制机制一体改革 Sun Xiaolei This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how the integrated reform of the education, science and technology, and talent systems and mechanisms should be advanced. Sun Xiaolei argues that it is a global, holistic and forward-looking strategic arrangement, and the practical path for implementing the strategies of invigorating China through science and education, strengthening the country through talent, and innovation-driven development. Sun holds that it must rest on three principles: a problem-oriented approach, a people-centred stance and systems thinking. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each principle. The first deals with identifying the main line of reform, the second with its direction, and the third with how it is carried out. Under the first principle, Sun argues that closer links between research and application, shorter conversion cycles and industries built on innovation make traditional mechanisms ill-suited to high-quality development. Sun calls for breakthroughs in management and service, resource allocation, talent evaluation and income distribution, including distribution by contribution of factors such as knowledge, technology and data. Under the second, Sun says reform must serve the all-round development of the person, with high-calibre talent as its core. Under the third, Sun calls for foresight, overall planning and holistic implementation, citing a remaining gap with developed countries in key technologies and global top talent. Sun concludes that reform should move from local experiments to systems integration, supported by Party leadership, national coordination mechanisms, supporting legislation, and assessment and accountability. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated academics present this reform agenda in official language.

Improving institutions and mechanisms for cultivating and practising core socialist values 完善制度机制，培育和践行社会主义核心价值观 Ma Xuejiao Zhang Xiuhong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily, takes up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to improve the institutions and mechanisms for cultivating and practising core socialist values. Ma and Zhang argue that such values are indispensable to building a strong education nation and to advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Their thesis is that the institutional advantage should be turned into a guarantee of value confidence and a driver of high-quality development in education. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the values matter for building a strong education nation. The second sets out how to embed them in law, social development and daily life. The third proposes mechanisms to make the institutions work over the long term. It is a short policy-oriented essay, not a scholarly study, and draws on Party documents rather than empirical evidence. On significance, the authors tie the values to three attributes of education. Its political attribute requires the Party's education policy and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, so as to produce capable successors. Its people-oriented attribute means education that satisfies the people and serves common prosperity, supported by the spirit of educators and by teachers' ethics. Its strategic attribute links education to science, technology and talent. On institutions, they trace the path from writing the values into the Constitution to the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and the Third Plenum, and call for them to move from soft moral constraint to hard institutional provision. They also call for integration into public policy, social governance and moral systems, and for education that is lived and daily. For long-term operation, the authors propose five mechanisms: Party-led organisation and accountability; coordination across departments, with integrated ideological and political education from primary school to university, and cooperation among family, school and society; incentives and sanctions, including negative lists; and an evaluation-and-feedback cycle. They present these as the means of making the institutions effective in practice. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link value education, law and educational governance in the official discourse after the Third Plenum.

Advancing the fundamental task of fostering virtue through moral education in the new era with the guiding power of ideological and political education 以思政引领力推进新时代立德树人工程 Xia Zhilun Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Xia Zhilun, director of the Hunan Provincial Department of Education, takes up the idea of the "guiding power of ideological and political education" that Xi Jinping put forward at the national education conference in September 2024. Xia argues that this power heads the "six powers" of a strong education nation with Chinese characteristics, expresses its political character, and gives the basic guidance for the project of fostering virtue through moral education. The short commentary has three parts. They treat the guiding power of ideological and political education as setting the direction, strengthening the intellectual engine, and clarifying the value pursuit of that project. Xia illustrates each part with measures taken in Hunan Province. On direction, Xia holds that the education nation must keep to the socialist orientation of schooling and use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to shape students' beliefs. Universities are described as a front line in the ideological sphere, and talent training must produce people who support Party leadership and the socialist system. On ideas, Xia calls for integrating the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times into the whole training process, so that young people clear away confusion amid competing currents of thought. On values, Xia calls for promoting core socialist values and helping students balance personal and social value. Xia cites Hunan's upgraded university ideological work programme, provincial leaders teaching ideological and political courses, eight innovation centres, an online "I Am a Successor" classroom, and integrated university-to-primary-school course communities in 14 cities and prefectures. Xia presents these as ways to strengthen young people's ambition, integrity and confidence. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a provincial education official applies the "guiding power" formula to moral education in practice.

The "AI Plus" initiative and the cultivation of future industries “人工智能+”行动引领未来产业培育 Jiao Hao Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2025, Jiao Hao asks how the "AI Plus" initiative can lead the cultivation of future industries. The initiative was announced at the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference. Jiao argues that, by integrating AI with sector-specific knowledge and technical resources, it speeds up technological breakthroughs and helps identify and nurture high-potential future industries. The commentary takes the six future-industry fields named in the official implementation opinions: future manufacturing, information, materials, energy, space and health. It then examines four channels through which the initiative works: building a technological base, reshaping business models, empowering industrial and supply chains, and promoting a digital innovation ecosystem. Each channel is illustrated with examples such as quantum information, humanoid robots, brain-computer interfaces, the metaverse, biomanufacturing and new energy storage. Jiao holds that AI supplies core technologies (machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision) and, combined with other frontier technologies such as quantum computing, speeds up iteration. In business models, the author describes a shift towards platform-based operation, precise response to individual user needs, and a logic of integrating the digital and the real economy. For supply chains, AI is said to make them more open, predictable and traceable and to deepen human–machine collaboration. In the innovation ecosystem, AI helps stakeholders (firms, laboratories, universities, government) predict technology trajectories and combine innovation factors. It also supports innovation consortia in the Yangtze River Delta biomedical sector and lets the public help correct industries that stray from a proper path. Jiao notes that future industries are still at a gestation stage and lack mature risk-identification and regulatory systems. The author calls for risk assessment systems for AI applications, a review system for technology ethics, and faster AI legislation, so that innovation and social and economic benefits interact well and future industries move towards high-quality development. Read the original if you want a short, example-led official-style account of how AI policy is linked to future-industry planning in China.

Coordinating the relationship between an efficient market and a capable government 统筹好有效市场和有为政府的关系 Hong Junjie This commentary in Guangming Daily takes up a formulation from the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: the need to coordinate an "efficient market" and a "capable government" so as to create an economic order that is both "lively" and "well managed". Hong Junjie, a university president and professor, argues that the formulation explains how government and market can be combined more effectively. In Hong's reading, it is a theoretical innovation that enriches Marxist political economy's account of the market economy and points the way to a high-standard socialist market economy. The article has three parts. The first explains why the coordination matters, both for a high-standard socialist market economy, as stressed in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and for high-quality development. The second names three relationships to be handled: vitality and order, efficiency and fairness, and development and security. The third applies the market–government pairing to the four links of social reproduction: production, distribution, circulation and consumption. Hong's central claim is that markets and governments are complementary. Markets allocate resources through price signals and competition and drive innovation. They also produce information asymmetries, under-supplied public goods and disorderly capital expansion, which government must correct through policy design, regulation and public services. Hong therefore says that to make the market more effective, government must be more capable. In production, Hong calls for supply-side structural reform and new quality productive forces, which are to be fostered jointly by government planning and market competition. In distribution, the market is said to dominate primary distribution, while government handles redistribution through taxes, social security and transfers, and both encourage a "third distribution" through charity. Hong grounds this in historical materialism: distribution relations are part of the relations of production and are determined by the state of the productive forces. Hong concludes that the "visible hand" and the "invisible hand" should run through every link of the national economic cycle. In circulation, Hong urges a unified national market, institutional opening up and logistics infrastructure. In consumption, Hong urges a long-term mechanism for expanding demand: more jobs, higher pensions and medical insurance subsidies, the "two news" policies and new consumption areas such as the silver economy. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 2024 economic policy line links market–government theory to concrete measures in each part of the economic cycle.

Three relationships to get right in building a high-standard socialist market economy 构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制需要把握好几个关系 Li Chungen This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how the goal of a high-standard socialist market economy should be pursued. Li Chungen takes as his starting point the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called such a system an important safeguard of Chinese modernization and set the aim of building it fully by 2035. Li argues that the task depends on handling three pairs of relationships correctly: government and market, top-level design and practical exploration, and high-quality development and high-standard security. The piece is organised in three numbered sections, one for each relationship, after a short introduction. It places the 2024 Plenum decision in the line of the 14th Five-Year Plan and the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, and cites Xi Jinping on the establishment of a socialist market economy as a major theoretical and practical innovation of the Party. Li then turns to the current stage of reform, which he describes as a period of tackling hard problems in uncharted territory. On government and market, Li holds that the market's decisive role in resource allocation is a general law of market economies, but that unrestrained markets produce insufficient demand, unfair distribution and widening gaps. Government must therefore regulate, correct market failures and protect fair competition, while avoiding excessive intervention and fixing clear boundaries between the two so that the combined effect exceeds the sum of its parts. On top-level design and exploration, Li calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership, reforming state-owned enterprises, directing capital to emerging industries and developing new quality productive forces, while respecting popular initiative, opening more to private firms and following a sequence of experiment, summing up and then wider rollout. On development and security, Li treats them as two wheels of one cart, calling for a unified national market, the Two Unwaverings, equal property protection, compliance, risk prevention and curbs on local protectionism and involutionary competition. Li concludes that integrating these relationships will lay a solid foundation for a modern socialist country by the middle of the century. Li's proposals are framed as tasks for the reform period ahead rather than as an assessment of past results. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of how the 2024 Plenum's market-economy reform agenda is explained to a general Chinese readership.

Cultivating new quality productive forces and shaping new drivers and new advantages 培育新质生产力 塑造新动能新优势 Shao Fangqiang Zhang Jie This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2025, asks how new quality productive forces can be cultivated so as to generate new drivers and advantages of growth. Shao and Zhang argue that, in the age of the internet and what they call intelligent interconnection, high-quality development requires productive forces marked by high technology, high efficiency and high quality. The article is organised around four sources of a 'leap' in productive forces: breakthrough technological innovation, structural industrial upgrading, open business-model innovation, and a well-developed supply of institutions. It illustrates the middle two with examples from Changle district in Fuzhou, Fujian, and a national modern agriculture park in Yongqiao district, Suzhou, Anhui. On technology, the authors hold that intelligent interconnection breaks down technical barriers, links innovation resources and spreads into production networks, so digital technology should be used to integrate resources and promote cross-sector innovation. On industry, they cite nearly a thousand lace factories in Changle that used digital technology from design to delivery, and call for linking upstream and downstream firms and lengthening the industrial chain. On models, they point to 5G, internet-of-things and AI applications in agriculture, and urge shared-economy, customised and flexible management models that suit new relations of production. On institutions, Shao and Zhang call for upholding the Party's overall leadership over productive-force development, local policies adapted to local conditions, and rules that bring relations of production into line with new quality productive forces and raise total factor productivity. They conclude that deeper reform in key areas will provide the institutional guarantee for the leap. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academic commentary links digital technology, industrial policy and Party leadership under the new quality productive forces framework.

Understanding and grasping the methodology for further comprehensively deepening reform 深刻认识和把握进一步全面深化改革方法论 Zhu Heng Wang Weiguo This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscript (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, explains the methodology of reform set out by Xi Jinping on 29 October 2024. Xi spoke at the opening of a study session for provincial and ministerial-level leading cadres on the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhu and Wang argue that reform is a systematic project requiring scientific methods, and that these methods give guidance for turning the plenum's strategic plans into strength for advancing Chinese modernization. The article is organised around four principles drawn from Xi's speech: uphold the unity of reform and the rule of law; uphold the dialectical unity of breaking the old and establishing the new; uphold the unity of reform and opening up; and handle correctly the relationship between deployment and implementation. Each section quotes Xi, restates the principle and then lists practical requirements. The text is a short Party-theory commentary, not an empirical study. On reform and the rule of law, the authors describe the two as the wings of a bird, with legislation adapting to reform and law securing its results. They tie this to Party leadership, problem orientation and a people-centred stance. On "breaking and establishing", they stress "establish first, break afterwards": establishing makes reform swift, while breaking on that foundation keeps it steady. Their examples are ending the fixation on test scores, diplomas and papers in education evaluation, and on GDP in economic reform. On opening up, they hold that opening brings in advanced ideas and technology while reform builds the basis for higher-level opening, and they link this to the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. On implementation, Zhu and Wang write that reform is hard to carry out as well as to plan. They call for workable plans, a complete chain of responsibility, accountability systems linked to assessment, and a systemic approach that joins top-level design with grassroots exploration and the initiative of both central and local governments. They conclude that these four methods give a scientific guide for the new stage of deepening reform. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line reading of how Xi's reform methodology was presented to cadres after the Third Plenum.

Marx and Engels's thought on modernization and its contemporary implications 马克思恩格斯的现代化思想及其当代启示 Zhou Dan Modernization theory emerged in the West after the Second World War, but Zhou Dan argues that Marx and Engels had already developed a thought on modernization through their analysis of modern society and capitalist industry. The article reconstructs this thought and contends that it supplies the theoretical foundation and orientation for Chinese modernization. Its main claim is that Marx and Engels treated modernization as a process centred on real human beings, aimed at their free and all-round development, and open to a plurality of national paths. The article has five sections. The first draws on Engels's remark about the industrial revolution in England, the political revolution in France and the philosophical revolution in Germany to identify three preconditions: the modern individual, the modern state and the modern material mode of production. The next sections treat the human subject as the force of modernization, free and all-round development as its value goal, and the critique of capitalist modernity as its way of thinking. The last turns to the communist future and the "association of free individuals". Zhou's central move is to read Marx and Engels as both affirming and criticising capitalist modernity. Capitalism, in this account, advanced productive forces and opened the world-historical stage, yet subordinated human development to the valorisation of capital and produced alienation, crises and a "fictitious community". Zhou holds that Marx and Engels therefore rejected any single formula for modernization. They pointed to diverse paths shaped by history, culture and geography, and to a socialist "new modernity" that supersedes capital's logic. Zhou also cites Engels's "parallelogram of forces" as a theory of how individual wills combine into historical force, and stresses the unity of material and intellectual production. Zhou concludes that Chinese modernization is the contemporary practice of this thought. In the article's account, it is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, combining an effective market with an active government and a people-centred approach, and so has substantively surpassed Western modernization and its claims to "universal values". The author calls for building a community with a shared future for mankind and for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic account of how Marx and Engels's texts are mobilised to ground Chinese modernization theoretically.

Accelerating the construction of a discourse system for the Chinese national community 加快构建中华民族共同体话语体系 Wang Yanzhong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 20), Wang Yanzhong takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at a Politburo study session, to correct the tendency of Chinese ethnology to be swayed by Western theories of nationality and to build China's own systems of historical sources, discourse and theory on the Chinese national community. Wang argues that building this discourse system quickly is theoretically and practically important for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first explains why the task is urgent after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second presents cultural confidence as the basic precondition. The third sets out methods and concrete measures: historical research, a body of source materials, disciplinary development, training of researchers and fieldwork. In Wang's account, a self-reliant discourse is needed to advance ethnic work with the aim of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation as its main line. It is also presented as a theoretical weapon against what the author describes as Western interference through ethnic, religious and human rights discourse. Wang holds that cultural confidence rests on more than 5,000 years of civilisation and on the nation's cultural subjectivity, and that only a holistic view of history, summed up in the "five commonalities", can ground an autonomous discourse. Wang then calls for research that follows the historical, theoretical and practical logics of the nation's formation, stresses the growing commonality among peoples, and compares China's path with other countries' handling of ethnic questions. Wang calls for fuller use of historical and archaeological sources, multidisciplinary research led by the research bases for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, and support for young scholars. Wang also calls for more fieldwork, with theory drawn from the Party's practice of revolution, construction and reform and developed through the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and the practical agenda for building the Chinese national community discourse in ethnic studies.

Using economic system reform as the lead in further deepening reform comprehensively 经济体制改革为牵引进一步全面深化改革 Jiang Chuanhai This article, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in late 2024, explains why economic system reform should "lead" the further comprehensive deepening of reform set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Jiang Chuanhai argues that deepening economic reform remains the focus of reform as a whole and that it drives and conditions reform in other fields. The piece is an interpretive commentary on Xi Jinping's statements at the study seminar for provincial and ministerial leaders on the Plenum. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the lead role matters; the second lists four "inherent requirements" for carrying it out; the third sets out concrete tasks for economic reform. These tasks are the mechanisms for high-quality development, new drivers and advantages of development, the Two Unwaverings, a unified national market, and the basic institutions of the market economy. Jiang's reasoning begins from the Marxist premise that the economic base determines the superstructure. On this view the pace of major economic reforms sets the pace of many others, so economic reform is the "ox's nose" that moves the whole. The author gives three grounds: the internal logic of comprehensive reform, the need for high-quality development, and the modernization of the system and capacity of national governance. Jiang says the market system is still incomplete and that government–market relations are not fully settled. The four requirements are to be both "lively" and "well-regulated" in handling government and market; to combine key breakthroughs with systematic planning; to build up (li) and break down (po) together, building first; and to rely on national conditions while drawing on the best of other civilizations. On tasks, Jiang calls for institutions favouring innovation, coordinated regional development, green development, opening up and shared development. The article also urges building production relations suited to new quality productive forces, together with deeper integration of the real and digital economies. It calls for consolidating public ownership while supporting the non-public sector, removing local protectionism to form a unified national market, and strengthening property protection, fair competition, anti-monopoly enforcement and the social credit system. Jiang concludes that this approach reflects the Party's grasp of the laws of reform and that officials must act as implementers and doers. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary justifies the primacy of economic reform within the post-2024 reform agenda.

The "great changes unseen in a century" from the perspective of long economic waves 经济长波视角下的“百年变局” Huang Wenyi Hu Leming Huang Wenyi and Hu Leming ask how the official judgement that the world is undergoing "great changes unseen in a century" can be understood in economic terms. Drawing on Xi Jinping's call to study economic conditions through long cycles, they argue that long-wave theory (Kondratieff cycles) gives an effective tool for locating the present moment and for reading the paradigm of global economic development. Their thesis is that the world is in a turbulent restructuring phase that will give way around 2030 to a new upswing, and that China is positioned to benefit if it responds correctly. The article has three main parts. The first builds a framework of long waves and industrial revolutions, tracing three industrial revolutions from the 1760s to the present, each made up of two Kondratieff waves. The second examines trends in the current "techno-economic paradigm" in three areas: energy and technology, institutions and organisation, and the global economic order. The third considers China's opportunities and challenges and sets out a Chinese response, followed by a short conclusion. The authors divide each industrial revolution into four stages (introduction, expansion, synergy, maturity), and place the present in the synergy stage of the third revolution and the downswing of the sixth Kondratieff wave, which began with the 2008 financial crisis. They expect a maturity stage and upswing from about 2030. In their reading, connectivity, renewable-energy and intelligent-manufacturing technologies will favour flatter, networked, cooperative organisation, while the "rise of the East and decline of the West" and the stronger weight of emerging economies reshape the global order. For China they see opportunities in multi-point technological breakthroughs and an institutional "soil" suited to the new revolution. They also see risks: Western pressure and technology controls, weak standard-setting, structural unemployment and a worsening external environment. The authors propose three national strategies: a precisely implemented innovation-driven development strategy, modernisation of state governance and its capacity, and a new pattern of comprehensive opening up with active participation in global governance. They conclude that China is on the "right track" and prepared for the coming upswing, and that, if the first-step goal for 2035 is met, the second step of building a modern socialist country will fall within the upswing. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese economic journal uses long-wave theory to give the official "great changes" thesis an economic-historical basis and a policy agenda.

Coordinating high-quality development and high-standard protection 统筹推进高质量发展和高水平保护 Wang Congxia Wang Congxia takes up the first of five relationships that Xi Jinping named at the National Conference on Eco-environmental Protection: that between high-quality development and high-standard protection. The article argues that ecological protection and economic growth are not an either/or choice. In Wang's account, the two are mutually reinforcing and must be advanced together on the basis of the idea that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. The piece has three parts. The first sets out how high-quality development and high-standard protection relate to each other. The second presents their joint pursuit as an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization, under three headings: harmony between humanity and nature, the logic of building ecological civilization, and the development of new quality productive forces. The third turns to practical measures, drawing on the July 2024 Third Plenum Decision on further deepening reform. On the relationship itself, Wang argues that high-quality development is the precondition of protection because it supplies the financial, technological and market support for it. High-standard protection, in turn, underpins development: it sets bottom lines through eco-environmental zoning and spatial planning, drives industrial and energy restructuring, and supplies ecological products. Wang quotes Xi's view that protecting the environment is protecting productive forces, and that green development is the 'underlying colour' of high-quality development. On this basis the article presents Western modernization, with its 'pollute first, clean up later' path, as the contrast to a Chinese modernization of harmony between humanity and nature. For policy, Wang calls for three things. The first is to establish the new development philosophy firmly and plan modernization with foresight, at the level of the whole and at the strategic level. The second is to shift the development model towards green and low-carbon forms, through a protection system, a governance system based on source prevention and precise pollution control, and a system of market incentives and technology. The third is to build a green, low-carbon, circular economy by greening industry, converting green technologies into products, and encouraging green lifestyles. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writing presents ecological policy as part of Chinese modernization and new quality productive forces after the 2024 Third Plenum.

Accelerating the development of new quality productive forces and steadily advancing high-quality economic development 加快发展新质生产力 扎实推进经济高质量发展 Zhang Xu Taking its cue from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform to advance Chinese modernization, this article asks how the new development philosophy, high-quality development and new quality productive forces fit together. Zhang argues that they form one system.
