The new development philosophy supplies the guiding principles, high-quality development is the first task of socialist modernization and the test of whether the philosophy is being carried out, and new quality productive forces are the intermediate link that connects the two. The article has three parts. The first sets out how to understand and apply the five elements of the new development philosophy (innovation, coordination, green, open and shared development), stressing a problem-oriented and systemic approach. The second discusses how to coordinate the philosophy with high-quality development, covering institutional design, regional coordination, the real economy, the division of tasks between central and local governments, and performance evaluation. The third turns to new quality productive forces, drawing on Marx's writings on productive forces and the labour process, and on Xi Jinping's statements. Zhang's central move is to read each element of the philosophy broadly: innovation as integrated innovation rather than technology alone, green development as a re-engineering of social production rather than environmental protection, and shared development as a step towards common prosperity rather than distribution alone. High-quality development is then presented as a shift from speed and scale to quality and efficiency, and as the standard by which the philosophy is judged. The author cites dependence on imported chips, lithography machines and machine tools as evidence of the need to innovate. New quality productive forces are described as both a new state of productive forces and an ongoing process. Zhang places them within a modernized economic system and argues that they need new relations of production. Zhang concludes that high-quality development has to rest on deeper reform. Specific proposals include removing institutional obstacles to technological innovation, allowing room for failure, turning research results into industry, and funding future industries. Traditional industries should be upgraded, not abandoned, and policy should vary by region. Zhang also calls for a performance evaluation that adds ecological, livelihood and social indicators and rewards innovation rather than growth alone. The article ties all of this to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the new development philosophy, high-quality development and new quality productive forces are linked, and how it draws on Marx's concept of productive forces.

The "tianxia worldview" and the traditional legal-cultural origins of the sense of community for the Chinese nation “天下观”与中华民族共同体意识的传统法文化渊源 Zhang Yan Ke Lan Zhang Yan and Ke Lan ask where the sense of community for the Chinese nation (the Chinese term is zhonghua minzu gongtongti yishi) comes from in China's traditional legal culture. They argue that the ancient tianxia ("all under heaven") worldview is its cultural root. On their account, this worldview treated the order of the world as cultural and ethical rather than as a matter of blood, territory or a single dynasty. They also distinguish it from the Western concept of empire. The article has four parts. It first traces the concept of tianxia and its links to "China" (zhongguo), the "five zones" (wufu) model and the unity of family, state and tianxia. It then looks at the "great unification" (dayitong) ideal and the fluid Hua–Yi distinction (Chinese versus "barbarian"). The third part follows the shift from "the Chinese nation" to the "community of the Chinese nation" and sets out the legal content of the sense of community. A short conclusion looks ahead. The authors make three moves. First, they argue that in the Confucian tradition the Hua–Yi distinction rested on adherence to ritual (li) and not on descent. Outsiders who accepted ritual could become Hua, and Hua who abandoned it could become Yi. Together with dayitong, which turned the ideal into centralised, legal and administrative practice, this is said to have produced the idea of "Hua and Yi as one". Second, they say the defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 pushed China out of the tianxia order and into the nation-state order. Liang Qichao introduced "Zhonghua minzu" in 1902, and Fei Xiaotong's 1988 "pluriform and unitary" formulation completed the concept. Third, they describe the community as a political entity formed through national identity, identity with the Chinese nation and cultural identity. They support this with legal instruments: the 2018 constitutional amendment, the system of regional ethnic autonomy, the National Common Language Law of 2000, and the proposed law on promoting ethnic unity and progress. The authors conclude that tianxia thinking carried the inclusive idea of "Hua and Yi as one family" and became a pillar of Chinese civilisation. It later developed into modern nation-state theory. They call for fuller implementation of the constitution's principle of ethnic unity, a more complete body of specialised laws, and faster legislation on ethnic unity and progress. They also call for stronger cultural and national identity, to lay the ideological and cultural foundations for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a legal-cultural account of how Chinese official discourse on ethnic policy traces its roots to classical sources such as tianxia, dayitong and the Hua–Yi distinction.

The foremost characteristic of a education powerhouse with Chinese characteristics: ideological and political guiding force 中国特色社会主义教育强国的首要特质 Li Hui Li Hui takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference (9–10 September 2024), which listed six capacities that a socialist education powerhouse with Chinese characteristics should have and placed "ideological and political guiding force" (sizheng yinlingli) first. The article argues that this ordering is a new contribution both to Xi's discourse on education and to the theory and practice of ideological and political education. Its thesis is that this guiding force is what gives the education powerhouse its Chinese character. The article has three parts. The first explains why the guiding force is the distinctive Chinese feature of an education powerhouse, tracing Xi's statements from 2014 to 2024. The second defines the guiding force and breaks it into components. The third sets out practical routes for strengthening it. In the first part, Li follows Xi's remarks from the 2014 Peking University symposium through the 2016 and 2018 conferences to 2024. In Li's reading they move from "Chinese characteristics" to socialist universities with Chinese characteristics and then to an education powerhouse with Chinese characteristics. Li treats the guiding force as the same thing as the guiding power of socialist ideology, with university ideological work as a part of it. The second part says the force is made up of three elements: the guidance of Marxist thought, the value guidance of core socialist values, and the goal guidance of fostering virtue and cultivating talent (lide shuren). Li argues they produce a combined force only when they act in the same direction. The third part names four routes: goal, discipline, curriculum and evaluation. Li lists the Marxist theory research and construction project (launched 2004), the first-level discipline of Marxist theory (2005), and the pairing of ideological and political theory courses with "curriculum ideology and politics". Li also lists the 2020 Overall Plan for Deepening Education Evaluation Reform in the New Era, aimed at the "five onlys" (scores, further study, diplomas, papers, titles). Li concludes that the guiding force expresses the Chinese character of the education powerhouse. Li adds that strengthening it in turn shows the superiority of socialism with Chinese characteristics in theory and institutions. Both rest on the basic task of education: whom to train, how to train them and for whom. Li says that how to improve the supporting systems and mechanisms, and how Marxist theory can lead other social science disciplines, still need study. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Party-line scholarship interprets the first of the "six capacities" in Xi's 2024 education speech and the policy instruments linked to it.

Four basic questions about adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化的四个基本问题 Han Jianxin Han Jianxin sets out a primer on a core concept of Party theory: what it means to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, why this is necessary, what it has produced, and how it should continue. The article argues that Marxism is a method rather than a dogma. In Han's account, it must be fused with China's concrete conditions and traditional culture, and each stage of this process has yielded a historic theoretical advance. The text, which first appeared on the Xuanjiangjia website in November 2024, is organised into four numbered sections that follow the four questions of the title. It draws heavily on Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of the "Sinification of Marxism", Engels's remarks on method, the 2021 Party history resolution, and speeches by Xi Jinping. The third section reviews a century of Party history from the October Revolution and the founding of the Party in 1921 to the present. On the "why", Han argues that Marxism's own nature requires adaptation: citing Engels, Han holds that its worldview is a method and a starting point for research, and that its basic principles must be combined with each country's actual situation to solve real problems. On the "results", Han identifies three achievements: Mao Zedong Thought, the system of theories of socialism with Chinese characteristics (Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development), and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Each is presented as a "leap" that answered the main tasks of its period. Han adds that using plain Chinese idiom matters because truth only has force once the people grasp it. For the future, Han calls for the Two Integrations and the "six musts" of the 20th Party Congress (2022) to guide theoretical innovation. Han also calls for innovation grounded in practice and in the creativity of the people through the mass line. Theory should be made systematic and academically rigorous, and the Marxist "soul" and Chinese cultural "roots" should not be abandoned. Han presents continuing this work as the historical responsibility of today's Communists. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Party theorists periodise and justify the adaptation of Marxism in China.

The high degree of fit between the moral outlook of fine traditional Chinese culture and the value propositions of scientific socialism 中华优秀传统文化中的道德观同科学社会主义价值观主张高度契合性研究 Chen Hongjuan Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which says that the moral outlook embodied in fine traditional Chinese culture is highly compatible with the value propositions of scientific socialism, Chen Hongjuan asks in what respects that fit holds. The article argues that, on the question of how individuals should relate to themselves, to others and to the group, traditional Chinese morality and Marxist scientific socialism converge at four levels: value concept, goal of individual moral development, principles of social morality, and the value logic of political morality. The article is organised in four sections matching these levels. It pairs the Confucian-centred ideal of cultivating oneself to bring peace to others and taking the world as one's responsibility with Marx's "truly human morality". It then pairs the unity of knowing, feeling and willing with the all-round development of the human being, "delighting in the group and valuing harmony" with developing one's true nature in society, and "the world as one's own task" with liberating humankind. Throughout, Chen cites classical Chinese sources extensively alongside Marx, Engels and Xi Jinping, and contrasts both traditions with Western morality. Chen's central move is a contrast. Traditional Chinese morality, Chen argues, starts from the distinction between humans and animals, treats morality as internally generated and self-disciplined, and is society-centred. Western traditional morality is described as starting from the human–god relation and as externally imposed, and as shifting after the Renaissance to individual-centred rationalism and utilitarianism. Scientific socialism, in Chen's account, criticises the individualism and hypocrisy of capitalist morality, grounds morality in autonomy and in humanity's "species-being", and subordinates private interest to common interest. Chen reads the traditional priority of righteousness over profit, the golden rule of reciprocity and the path from self-cultivation to governing the realm as parallel to this. A second move links the fit to economic base: Chen says traditional culture arose under what Marx called the Asiatic form of ownership, in which the individual is not independent of the community, which favoured collective morality. Chen also notes that early Chinese introducers of Marx stressed his perseverance in terms of the Confucian ideal person. Chen concludes that both traditions refuse to see people as isolated individuals and look towards a return of values to the collective and society, citing Xi Jinping's remark to this effect. The article presents the fit as grounded in shared value logic rather than coincidence, and so as support for combining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source comparison of Confucian, Daoist and Neo-Confucian moral concepts with Marx's and Engels's writings on morality, as framed by official Party discourse.

Reflecting on the premises of paradigm construction in Chinese Marxist philosophy From the perspective of the "self-justification of a philosophical paradigm" 中国马克思主义哲学范式建设的前提意识之思 Cao Dianshun Cao Dianshun asks what premises must be examined before Chinese Marxist philosophy can build a distinctive research paradigm of its own. Treating paradigm construction as the process by which the paradigm justifies itself, Cao argues that four "premise-reflections" come first: on the theoretical premise, on problem-consciousness, on theoretical grounds, and on academic discourse. The thesis is that paradigm construction must unite "practicality" and "academic character", and must leave behind a stage of "apprentice scholarship". The article opens by placing paradigm construction as a third stage of research, after studies of Marxist philosophy paradigms and of Chinese Marxist philosophy paradigms. Its four sections follow the four premise-reflections in turn. Each is built around paired concepts, such as practicality and academic character, "realistic concern" and "genuine philosophy", and "theoretical practicality" and "apprentice academic character". The text draws on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong, Gadamer and Xi Jinping's formulations about philosophy and social science. Cao first holds that practicality supplies the method, starting point and test of paradigm construction, while academic character supplies its standards and guiding principle, so the two are internally unified. Second, Cao diagnoses an earlier phase of "apprentice academic character" in Chinese Marxist philosophy. Examples include textbook-paradigm work shaped by limited sources and Soviet influence, and readings that explain Marx through Hegel, Kant or Heidegger. In Cao's view this imitation and dogmatism limits originality and delays the arrival of paradigm construction. Third, Cao proposes a new discourse. "Realistic practicality" is set against idealist "rational practicality" and dogmatic "theoretical practicality", and "scientific academic character" against "abstract rational" and "apprentice" scholarship. Cao treats these two as complementary features of a paradigm guided by historical materialism. Cao concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy should stress the particular logic of historical materialism, since Marx already set out its general logic. It should keep reflecting on social practice and keep up original theoretical research. Cao presents this as a mission set by social development and as a way to serve Chinese modernization theoretically and practically. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher sets out the conceptual preconditions for an autonomous Chinese Marxist philosophical paradigm and criticises earlier Chinese scholarship.

On the necessity, possibility and innovative contribution of the "Second Integration" 论“第二个结合”的必要性可能性及其创新性贡献 Mei Rongzheng This article takes up the "Second Integration", the principle, announced by Xi Jinping in July 2021, of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. Mei Rongzheng argues that it is necessary, possible and innovative, and that it is a "further ideological emancipation". The article is a response to the lively discussion that followed Xi's 2023 speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. It singles out three questions that Mei thinks need deeper study. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the Second Integration is necessary, in three respects: understanding the socialist road, building a culturally strong country, and building a modern Chinese civilization. The second asks why Marxism and traditional culture can be combined, and gives four grounds. The third sets out the innovative contributions of the Second Integration. Mei draws on Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, and cites passages by Marx and Engels on China. On necessity, Mei argues that China's path cannot be understood without its five thousand years of civilization. He treats the "five outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) as the basis of the Second Integration. On possibility, Mei argues that Marxism is the general and Chinese culture the particular. He adds that Marx and Engels wrote extensively on China, and that the Marxist classics therefore already contain elements abstracted from Chinese history. He also argues that the "First Integration" already included traditional culture, citing Mao's use of classical idioms. On innovation, Mei contends that the Second Integration raises traditional culture from one element of "China's concrete reality" to an equal partner of Marxist principles, as one of the two sides of the "universal truth" Deng Xiaoping described. It also clarifies the route to the "new cultural mission", by promoting classical scholarship, strengthening Marxist guidance of cultural research and raising national cohesion. Mei casts this as a defence against Western ideological infiltration and historical nihilism. He concludes that it deepens the cultural roots of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical defence of the Second Integration, including its use of Marx's and Engels's remarks on China.

Cultural confidence and the logical dimensions of Chinese modernization 文化自信与中国式现代化的逻辑向度 Liu Jianhua Li Tingyan Liu Jianhua and Li Tingyan take up the relationship between cultural confidence and Chinese modernization, which they say scholars have not yet treated systematically. They argue that the two have developed together over a century of Party history and that each supplies something the other lacks. In their formula, cultural confidence gives Chinese modernization spiritual strength, while Chinese modernization gives cultural confidence modern strength. The article has three parts. The first traces a historical logic in which cultural confidence moves through cultural awakening, independence, innovation and rejuvenation, while the path of modernization moves through choice, exploration, practice and definition. The second sets out how the two are theoretically embedded in each other. The third turns to practice, covering how cultural confidence supports modernization and how modernization shapes cultural confidence. In the historical section, the authors run from the reformers and Sun Yat-sen after the Opium War, through the New Culture Movement, Mao Zedong's insistence on independence, the cultural theories of Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Their theoretical section argues that traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture each feed Chinese modernization. Traditional ideas such as grand unification, common wealth and the unity of heaven and humanity are said to underpin its features: a huge population, common prosperity and harmony between humanity and nature. In the other direction, the authors say modernization updates cultural confidence through digital media, wider horizons and a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. This, they write, moves cultural confidence towards civilizational confidence and a new form of human civilization. On practice, the authors call for persistence on the path of socialist cultural development with Chinese characteristics and for the promotion of core socialist values. They also call for firm Party leadership in ideological work, a people-first cultural outlook, and cultural exchange and mutual learning that keeps cultural independence. They further propose using technology to bring cultural resources into everyday life. They conclude that the Party's pursuit of modernization reflects deep cultural self-awareness and a commitment to a modernization with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact example of how current Chinese scholarship links cultural confidence, Party history and Chinese modernization.

A comprehensive understanding of the basic approach to constructing the subjectivity of Chinese culture 全面理解中华文化主体性建构的基本进路 Han Sheng Han Sheng takes up the question of how Chinese cultural subjectivity (wenhua zhutixing) is built and why it matters for a country's modernization. The article argues that cultural subjectivity is an organic unity of "not forgetting one's origins", "absorbing the foreign" and "facing the future". In Han's account, China has since reform and opening up, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), developed a clear approach to this task, achieving spiritual independence and setting the goal of a strong cultural nation. The article presents Xi Jinping's thought on culture as the fullest expression of this approach and as a guide to action for building a socialist cultural power with Chinese characteristics. It is organised around three themes, each introduced by a four-character slogan: the Second Integration as the inner thread, creative continuation of tradition as the basic proposition, and exchange and mutual learning among civilizations as the key arena. First, Han argues that the combination of Marxism's basic principles with excellent traditional Chinese culture, the "Second Integration", has run through the Party's cultural work for over a century. Han calls it "another ideological emancipation" that moved China from absence to presence in the world's civilizational map, and that grounds Chinese modernization culturally. Second, drawing on historical materialism, Han holds that cultural subjectivity requires "upholding fundamental principles while innovating". Modernization should reactivate and renew tradition, not break with it, in the sense of Feng Youlan's "speaking on from" the past, while rejecting cultural conservatism and revivalism. Third, openness is said to be a precondition of a growing civilization. Han introduces the idea of the "meaningful other", whom a culture treats as a constitutive condition of its own growth, and urges a move from conflictual to constructive relational rationality. Han concludes that this construction of cultural subjectivity gives Chinese modernization a deep cultural justification and breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization. In the article's view it models a way to resist Western hegemonic thinking and the homogenising logic of colonialism in a new type of globalization. Understanding this approach is said to help Xi Jinping's thought on culture guide Chinese modernization towards national rejuvenation and the progress of world civilization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how current Chinese theory links the Second Integration, tradition and civilizational dialogue under the heading of cultural subjectivity.

Marx's conception of revolution and its significance for the new era 马克思革命观及其新时代意蕴 Gao Junhua Gao Junhua takes up Hannah Arendt's claim that Marx, despite being the greatest theorist of revolution, almost wholly neglected the revolutionaries' true aim, the founding of freedom. Gao treats this as a representative misreading: it denies the idea of freedom in Marx and so his theory of revolution, and it pits the mature Marx against the young one. The article argues that political and social revolution are closely linked in Marx, and that freedom is central to his conception of revolution. On that basis it explains in what sense China in the new era speaks of continuing revolution. The article has four parts. The first sets out the scientific content of Marx's conception of revolution, drawing on On the Jewish Question, the 1844 articles against Arnold Ruge and the Communist Manifesto, and on Hal Draper's study of Marx's revolutionary theory. The second examines the value orientation of that conception, namely political and social freedom, and answers Arendt. The third takes up the revolutionary subject, the proletariat. The fourth applies the framework to China since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gao's central move is that bourgeois political revolution delivered only formal freedom, because the state was separated from civil society and private ownership remained. Social revolution is therefore needed: developing the productive forces, replacing private ownership of the means of production with public ownership, and supplying the basis for political revolution. Against Arendt, Gao holds that she mistakes Marx's concern with abolishing alienated labour for neglect of freedom, and that the mature Marx kept the ideal of free individuality. Gao also argues that the proletariat moves from a class in itself to a class for itself through revolutionary practice, uniting ideas with reality and the particular with the universal. Gao reads the new era through this lens. The Party's self-reform is presented as political revolution, and common prosperity as the core content of social revolution. Gao calls the formula of leading a great social revolution through a great self-reform (the 'two great revolutions') a theoretical innovation that develops Marx's theory. Common prosperity rests on developing the productive forces, keeping public ownership dominant while supporting the non-public sector, and creating conditions for free time and all-round human development. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic defence of Marx's theory of revolution against Arendt, or an example of how it is tied to the Party's self-reform and common prosperity today.

The cultural theory of "comprehensive innovation" and the Second Integration 文化“综合创新”论与“第二个结合” Zhang Yunyi Zhang Yunyi asks how the twentieth-century Chinese theory of cultural "comprehensive innovation" (zonghe chuangxin) relates to the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's fine traditional culture. The article argues that this combination is the guiding thread running from the "comprehensive innovation" theory of Zhang Shenfu and Zhang Dainian to Fang Keli's later formula "Marxism as soul, Chinese culture as substance, Western culture as function". Zhang opens by comparing the two Zhang brothers with the Song Neo-Confucians Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, as Fang Keli had suggested. The article is built in four parts. It first traces the intellectual sources of comprehensive innovation over roughly four centuries of Sino-Western encounter, from Xu Guangqi's "Chinese mould, Western material" through the "substance and function" debates of the late Qing. It then examines the contributions of Zhang Shenfu and Zhang Dainian. Next it follows the move from comprehensive innovation to Fang Keli's formula, and finally it shows how Fang's career-long commitment links these ideas to the Second Integration. Zhang Yunyi's central claim is that "synthesis" in the two Zhangs' thought is not eclecticism. Zhang Shenfu's 1932 "three streams into one" (Lenin, Russell, Confucius) and Zhang Dainian's later formulation both place Marxist dialectical materialism as the backbone, and the article defends them against orthodox critics who called them idealist compromise. Fang's formula, the article argues, adds a "soul" to the traditional substance–function pair. It defends the formula against charges of redundancy and replies to critics by distinguishing the different senses of "function" for each element. Zhang cites Fang's statements that Marxism-Chinese tradition integration was his lifelong commitment, dating a 1984 formulation of the "two integrations" to Fang. Zhang concludes that scholars such as the two Zhangs, Feng Qi and Fang Keli form a Marxist school that could be called the "comprehensive innovation school" or the "Second Integration school". The article notes that Xi Jinping's statements on the Two Integrations, such as Marxism as the "soul" and fine traditional culture as the "root", contain elements of Fang's formula. Read the original if you are interested in the intellectual genealogy of the Second Integration within Chinese philosophy and in debates over how Marxism, Chinese tradition and Western thought should be related.

Understanding and following the laws of building socialist culture with Chinese characteristics 论对中国特色社会主义文化建设规律的认识与遵循 Jiang Yingchun Jiang Yingchun reads the cultural provisions of the Decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) as a deepening of the Party's understanding of the laws governing cultural work. The article asks what these laws are and what they demand in practice. Its answer is that Marxist guidance, a holistic view of socialist culture and the strengthening of national cultural soft power are the three core requirements, and that together they enrich Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article has three main parts. The first deals with Marxist guidance: the system of Marxism's guiding position in the ideological field, resistance to liberalism, and mastery of Marxist theory. The second treats socialist culture with Chinese characteristics as an organic whole of fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, and sets out the continuity, contemporaneity and global dimension of cultural development. The third concerns soft power: culture's social functions, institutional culture, a culture of "peaceful development", and the cultural industries. A short conclusion follows. Jiang argues that Marxism is the soul and the defining mark of socialist culture, and that without it culture would lose direction. Liberalism is presented as the most persistent and widespread challenge, backed by the political and economic systems of capitalist states. Jiang draws on Deng Xiaoping's criticism of abstract humanism and of the theory of alienation under socialism, and on Althusser's warning, to link such tendencies to the Soviet collapse. Traditional culture must be transformed creatively, with no cultural restorationism, and revolutionary culture must be defended against historical nihilism that rejects revolution in favour of reform. Culture is also said to act back on the economic base, so historical materialism is not economic determinism. In the soft-power section Jiang calls for communicating China's institutional culture, above all whole-process people's democracy, against Western "constitutional democracy", and for countering what the article calls Western cultural hegemony with a culture of peaceful development linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. Jiang concludes that culture's role in national rejuvenation is prominent but that problems remain: the Party's leadership and discourse power in culture have weakened in some respects, Marxism is still marginalised in some fields, and the international reach of Chinese cultural products is weak. Citing Lenin, Jiang says cultural tasks need long, persistent effort. The article calls for implementing Xi Jinping's thought on culture to build cultural strength for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned reading of the Third Plenum's cultural agenda, including its ideological argument against liberalism and historical nihilism.

Improving people's quality of life in building Chinese modernization: inherent requirements and practical dimensions 在中国式现代化建设中提高人民生活品质：内在要求与实践向度 Ding Yuanzhu Ding Yuanzhu takes up the phrase "improving people's quality of life" (生活品质), which the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) placed alongside "promoting the people's wellbeing". The article asks what the concept means and why it is an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization. Ding argues that the Congress's stress on common prosperity, the coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement, and harmony between humanity and nature all converge in quality of life, and that grasping the concept deepens understanding of what Chinese modernization requires. The article is organised in three parts. The first defines quality of life as a composite of economic, social, cultural and spiritual elements, with objective and subjective sides, individual and group levels, and a link to all-round human development. The second discusses how to combine objective measurement with subjective evaluation, including happiness as an indicator. The third turns to practical priorities in the new development stage: social resilience, quality employment, incomes and consumption. Ding draws on Amartya Sen, W. W. Rostow, the Finnish sociologist Erik Allardt, and Japanese experience with weak consumption. In Ding's reading, the Congress's pairing of the "all-round enrichment of material things" with "all-round human development" continues Marxist theory, which Ding divides into three levels: bodily and mental development, the capacity for activity, and free development, including free time and free choice of occupation. Citing Rostow's later addition of a stage of \"pursuing quality of life\", Ding presents the concept as a natural product of economic maturity. Ding adds that wealth growth does not automatically raise wellbeing, so a government representing society as a whole should look beyond individual satisfaction and the market. This is said to explain why Chinese modernization must follow the five-sphere integrated plan. On practice, Ding calls for strengthening resilience to epidemics, ageing, digital change and climate; the employment-first strategy, with attention to the effects of artificial intelligence, education reform and young people, including avoiding \"involution\"; and rising incomes, better distribution and stronger consumption. Ding concludes that the Party's five major principles from the 20th Congress show the way to raising quality of life. Read the original if you want a Chinese policy scholar's account of how \"quality of life\" is being conceptualised within Party discourse on people's wellbeing.

Three major issues in building Marxist parties from the perspective of the historical course of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动历史进程视域下马克思主义政党建设的三个重大问题 Lin Jianhua Why has the international communist movement alternated between triumphant advances and severe setbacks? Lin Jianhua answers that the decisive factor is the Party, and that the quality of Marxist party-building can be measured by three things: scientific theory, outstanding leaders and iron discipline. The article, published in 2024, treats these as the three major issues running through more than 170 years of the movement since the Communist League (1847) and the Communist Manifesto (1848). The article is organised in three sections, one for each issue. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and moves through the Communist League, the First, Second and Third Internationals, the October Revolution, the dissolution of the Soviet Communist Party and the history of the Communist Party of China. Each section ends by linking the historical lessons to the Party's present situation. On theory, Lin argues that Marxism guides the Party and must develop with its era. Each theoretical breakthrough answered the questions of its time, and the Party prospers when it upholds Marxism's guiding role. In this reading, the Chinese Party's growth and the Soviet Party's dissolution show the contrast. On leaders, Lin grounds the argument in historical materialism: the people make history, but outstanding leaders give direction and cohesion, and upholding their authority is a vital principle. Lin cites the Paris Commune's failure, attributed by Marx and Engels to a lack of centralisation and authority, and the praise given to successive leaders. On discipline, Lin holds that unity of thought underpins organisational unity. Lin attributes the Soviet Party's collapse to abandoning centralised leadership and allowing Party organisations to become autonomous. Lin concludes that Marxist parties succeed when guided by scientific theory, steered by outstanding leaders and forged by iron discipline. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Lin writes, Xi Jinping has been the Party's core and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era its guide. The article presents the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as the logical outcome of this history, together with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform as the Chinese answer to the problem of historical cycles of rise and decline. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese scholars frame Party theory, leadership authority and discipline within the history of the communist movement.

The idea of self-reform in the perspective of the history of the international communist movement 国际共运史视域中的自我革命观 Chai Shangjin An Yaqin Chai and An ask what the 170-year history of the international communist movement shows about the link between a Marxist party's own transformation and the success of social revolution. Taking Xi Jinping's statement that the Party must be bold in carrying out self-reform as their starting point, they argue that Marxist parties have led social revolution through self-reform, and that winning socialism and holding power over the long term require keeping the founding mission and applying full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the end. The article moves chronologically through four stages. It begins with Marx and Engels, the Communist League and the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to Lenin's ideas on party building, to the Soviet and East European experience, and finally to the Communist Party of China from its founding to the present. It also surveys the Communist Parties of Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, Russia, Brazil and South Africa, and the Workers' Party of Korea. The authors note that Marx and Engels never used the term "self-reform" (自我革命). They argue, however, that the "two ruptures" in the Manifesto, with traditional property relations and traditional ideas, imply that communists must remould themselves while transforming the world. In their reading, Lenin supplied the substance: theoretical guidance, a vanguard that stays advanced, pure and tied to the masses, democratic centralism with criticism and self-criticism, vigilance against bureaucracy, and strict discipline. The Soviet case is treated as the negative lesson. Stalin's extreme centralisation and personality cult are said to have cut the party off from the people. Gorbachev's "democratisation" and pluralism then replaced self-reform and led to the party's dissolution in 1991. On the Chinese side, the authors trace Mao Zedong's rectification campaigns, Deng Xiaoping's "the Party must govern itself" and the post-2012 answer to the "historical cycle" problem, which they call self-reform as the second answer after supervision by the people. The authors conclude that a strong Marxist party is the decisive condition for the proletarian cause. They argue that the Chinese Party's self-reform offers a reference for other communist parties, several of which they say have drawn on it. They call for treating full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as a permanent task for solving the problems unique to a large party. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theoretical account of how the history of the communist movement is used to justify self-reform, including its reading of the Soviet collapse and of other parties' experience.

Political lessons from the Communist Party of Argentina's failure to grow from a century-old party into a great century-old party 阿根廷共产党未能从百年老党成为百年大党的政治教训 Tan Daoming Tan Daoming asks why the Communist Party of Argentina (PCA), founded in 1918 and the first communist party in Latin America to pass its hundredth year, never became a great party. According to the article, membership rose from 766 to nearly 200,000 by the early 1980s but fell to 17,000 in 2021. The party never governed, never held a sizeable bloc of seats in Congress, and ended as a junior partner in a left coalition led by the Peronist Justicialist Party. Tan's thesis is that three failings explain this: dogmatism, sectarianism and a lack of initiative, with dogmatism the fundamental one. The article is organised around these three lessons, followed by a short conclusion. It traces the PCA's history from its split with the Socialist Party and its subordination to the Comintern and later the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, through successive splits in 1922, 1925, 1928, 1963 and the 1990s. It then reviews four periods of missed opportunity: the labour-movement years of the 1920s and 1930s, the nationalist 1940s and 1950s, the revolutionary 1960s and 1970s, and the democratic era since the 1980s. Comparisons with the Chinese and Cuban revolutions are used as contrasts. Tan argues that the PCA followed each turn in Comintern and Soviet policy without adapting it to Argentine conditions. These turns were the ultra-left 'Third Period', the Popular Front, and Khrushchev's 'peaceful coexistence'. Tan holds that this cost the party leadership of the labour movement, which Perón and the Justicialists took, and left it opposed to the nationalist current Perón used against it. It also kept the party out of the armed struggle of the revolutionary years and led it to appease the 1976 military regime. In Tan's account, dogmatism fed bureaucratism in the leadership, so that the party grew distant from its own members and from the lower classes. Almost every split is linked to external issues such as Trotskyism, the Sino-Soviet dispute and the collapse of the USSR. Tan concludes that deference to outside directives prevented the localisation of Marxist theory and the discovery of a path to socialism suited to Argentina. The labels 'Creole communism' and 'extroverted party' stuck to the PCA, and it never moved from left internationalism to a national socialist party. Citing Eric Hobsbawm's remark that every communist party is the product of a marriage between the national left and the October Revolution, Tan calls the PCA's a failed marriage. Tan nonetheless regards the century as offering both achievements and lessons. Read the original if you study Latin American communist parties, Comintern influence on parties in the Global South, or the Argentine left's relationship with Peronism, as seen from a Chinese academic perspective.

Digest of theoretical and academic viewpoints in 2024: Marxist philosophy 2024年理论学术观点要览——马克思主义哲学篇 Sun Shoutao This short review, published in Beijing Daily on 6 January 2025, surveys Chinese scholarship in Marxist philosophy during 2024. Sun Shoutao, deputy dean of the School of Marxism at Nankai University, groups the year's work around three themes: Xi Jinping's thought on culture, the theoretical system of the Chinese nation as a community, and a Chinese Marxist ecology. The first section covers studies of Xi Jinping's cultural thought, which the review calls the cultural component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second covers efforts to build a theoretical system of the Chinese nation as a community, presented as a showcase of China's independent knowledge system. The third covers attempts to define "Chinese Marxist ecology". On culture, one scholar holds that the core theory is cultural subjectivity. This scholar says it resolves the relationship between the "soul" (Marxism) and the "root" (traditional culture) through the Two Integrations. Another scholar stresses that "integration" is universal, arduous and creative. On the national community, scholars propose frameworks built on background, change, content and traits, or on an "ontology–consciousness–practice" cycle. A third scholar locates community consciousness in complementary interests, shared memory and cultural cohesion. On ecology, one study treats "Chinese Marxist ecology" as a root concept with reflective, normative and constructive derived concepts, forming a three-part logical framework. The review reports these positions without criticism and does not name further gaps. It presents the year's research as consolidating Xi's cultural thought, the independent knowledge system and a Marxist ecology with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact map of the main 2024 themes and framings in officially oriented Chinese Marxist philosophy.

Overview of theoretical and academic viewpoints in 2024: economics 2024年理论学术观点要览——经济学篇 Fang Mingyue Nie Huihua This short review, first published in Beijing Daily on 6 January 2025, surveys the main themes in Chinese economics in 2024. Fang Mingyue and Nie Huihua report that new quality productive forces drew the most attention, followed by supply-chain resilience and climate policy. The review is organised around three clusters of research. The first covers new quality productive forces under four dimensions: theoretical meaning, basic features, paths of realisation and measurement indicators. The second covers supply-chain resilience, digital technology and institutional opening-up. The third covers climate policy, climate risk and ESG (environmental, social and governance). On new quality productive forces, the authors report that scholars see them as a new, high-level modern productive force, consistent with the new development philosophy and high-quality development, and as an innovation in Marxist economics. Proposed paths stress innovation, the socialist market economy, a modern industrial system and the Two Unwaverings. Measurement studies mostly use the entropy method and find fast growth but large regional gaps. In the supply-chain work, scholars find that digitalisation, especially artificial intelligence and cloud computing, and deeper trade agreements such as RCEP and CPTPP strengthen resilience. In the climate work, scholars find that policy uncertainty suppresses firms' productivity and investment, and that customers' ESG strengths encourage upstream green innovation. The review draws no overall conclusion beyond the reported findings. It notes that many scholars place new quality productive forces within Chinese modernization, as the key to building a modern industrial system during a shift between old and new growth drivers. Read the original if you want a brief guide to the main topics and empirical findings in Chinese economics in 2024.

Giving full play to the guiding role of military theory modernization 充分发挥军事理论现代化的先导作用 Tang Junfeng Peng Chunlin Published in Guangming Daily on 5 January 2025, this commentary responds to Xi Jinping's recent instruction to an all-army conference on military theory work. Xi stressed that military theory modernization is an important part of national defence and military modernization and plays a leading role in strengthening the armed forces. Tang and Peng argue that the military must therefore accelerate theoretical innovation to build a modern military theory system with Chinese characteristics that supports the centenary goal of the armed forces in 2027 and the aim of a world-class military. The article has three parts. The first explains why military theory should lead practice, citing technological change, the security environment and the military's own goals. The second sets out how theory secures a winning edge and strategic initiative, including the place of theory among the four modernizations of national defence and the armed forces. The third turns to the principles and methods for raising the quality and efficiency of theoretical innovation. Tang and Peng contend that scientific military theory works as combat power, because it reveals the laws of war and of military building and thereby shapes force development and use. They point to networked information systems, intelligent warfare in the Russia–Ukraine and Israel–Palestine conflicts, and intensifying great-power rivalry as reasons why theory must move first. Theory, they say, should concentrate on war and operations, directing training and force building towards preparing for and fighting wars, and should lead the deepening of defence and military reform. The authors insist that innovation must keep the political character of war in view, uphold the Party's absolute leadership over the military and apply Xi Jinping's thought on strengthening the military. They also call for emancipating the mind, integrating disciplines and military-civilian cooperation, and attention to artificial intelligence, quantum information and unmanned systems. The authors add that methods must be modernized as well: research should move from reviewing past wars to "designing wars", using big data, cloud computing, AI tools, combat laboratories, modern wargaming and net assessment, and borrowing models from leading firms and think tanks. They call for stronger organisation, policy support and research capacity. Read the original if you want an official-academic view from China's National Defence University of how military theory is being tied to Xi's directives, technology trends and reform goals.

An ethical path to building a responsible AI governance system 构建负责任人工智能治理体系的伦理路径 Liu Jing Liu Jing, an associate professor of philosophy, takes up the ethical challenges raised by rapidly advancing artificial intelligence, especially generative AI. The article argues that "developing responsible AI", the idea set out in the 2019 governance principles issued by China's national specialised committee on new-generation AI governance, offers a workable ethical path. In Liu's view, the key is that humans remain the responsible agents for the AI they create. This is a short newspaper commentary in applied ethics. It first describes how AI blurs the boundary between humans and machines and extends ethical relations to a new pair, "human and AI". It then sets out a human-centred ethical stance with three principles, and ends with three requirements for building a responsible governance system: global cooperation, a shared responsibility mechanism, and the cultivation of AI literacy and a sense of responsibility. Liu identifies three moral dilemmas in the human–AI relationship. The dilemma of good and evil arises because AI is no longer a simple tool and can bring benefit or harm. The dilemma of dignity arises because over-reliance on AI may weaken human subjectivity. The dilemma of responsibility arises because AI's partial autonomous behaviour leaves a "responsibility gap" in traditional ethics. Liu answers with a human-centred stance, citing Xi Jinping's idea of "people-centred, AI for good", and with three principles: intelligence for good, dignity, and responsibility. Liu stresses that responsible AI does not mean building moral machines. It means humans taking responsibility, and that this stance is not strong anthropocentrism but treats the human being as an end. Governance, Liu adds, needs a responsibility mechanism that spreads accountability across governments, firms, industry and users. Liu describes the responsible agent as a joint human–machine unit and says everyone should see themselves as a responsible agent. Liu concludes that institutions and mechanisms are not enough and that moral cultivation of the "heart" is needed, since this is what AI cannot replace. The article presents China's Global AI Governance Initiative as a Chinese approach grounded in a community with a shared future for mankind, and urges narrowing the "intelligence divide" between countries. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese philosophy scholar links Party-endorsed AI governance language to ethical concepts such as dignity, responsibility and human-as-end.

Reform requires a "nationwide chessboard" mindset People's Daily "Thought and Perspective" commentary, 6 January 2025 改革要树立全国一盘棋思想（思想纵横） Wang Yunsong This short commentary in the People's Daily takes up a directive from Xi Jinping at the second plenary session of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): all regions and departments should adopt a "nationwide chessboard" mindset when carrying out reform. Wang Yunsong argues that further comprehensively deepening reform cannot be confined to one's own "plot of land" and must be planned within the overall interests of the Party and the country. The piece moves in four steps. It first grounds the principle in the Marxist dialectic of whole and part, then points to practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then presents the principle as a method of thinking and working, and finally addresses how local conditions fit within it. Wang argues that the whole governs the parts and the parts serve the whole, citing Mao Zedong's 1936 remark that grasping the overall situation makes it easier to use its parts. Because reform is large in scale, wide in scope and touches deep interests, the author says it needs coordination to avoid going it alone or each acting separately. As an example, Wang cites the building of a unified national market, which is said to have removed local protectionism and market segmentation. Leading cadres, in Wang's account, should calculate "big accounts", reject watered-down implementation, and coordinate across departments and regions, especially in education, healthcare, elderly care and housing. Wang concludes that the principle does not ignore local realities. Regions should locate their role in national strategy and develop distinctive strengths and comparative advantages, so that reform proceeds steadily. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary links Marxist dialectics, Xi Jinping's directives and the practical coordination of reform.

The key to building a modern socialist country in all respects lies in the Communist Party of China An important perspective for understanding the spirit of the 20th Party Congress 全面建设社会主义现代化国家关键在中国共产党 Zhang Hefu This text is an edited version of Zhang Hefu's remarks at the Red Hall Forum seminar on understanding the 20th Party Congress (2022). Zhang takes up Xi Jinping's statement in the congress report that building a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 'depend on the Party'. Zhang presents this as a key to the congress's spirit and reads it in three ways. The remarks are short and organised around those three points: the achievements of the previous decade, the pursuit of the modernization goals, and the need for a strong Party built through strict self-governance. Zhang then lists the seven arrangements the congress report makes for Party building. On the first point, Zhang attributes the decade's achievements, including the poverty-alleviation campaign and the building of a moderately prosperous society, to the Party's leadership, to Xi Jinping as the 'core', and to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the second, Zhang argues that Chinese modernization is by definition modernization led by the Party. In this account the Party has no special interests of its own and represents no interest group, which is why it can rally the people. Third, Zhang summarises the report's seven tasks: centralised leadership, theoretical study, institutional rules for the Party's self-reform, a capable cadre corps, stronger Party organisations, stricter discipline and conduct, and a long-term anti-corruption struggle. Zhang concludes that these arrangements respond to problems within the Party and are essential if it is to keep its vanguard character, purity and governing capacity while leading modernization. Read the original if you want a brief official-affiliated summary of how the 20th Party Congress's emphasis on Party leadership is explained.

Core socialist values as a strong value support for advancing Chinese modernization 社会主义核心价值观为推进中国式现代化提供有力价值支撑 Wang Haijian Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which described Chinese modernization as one that coordinates material and spiritual civilization, this commentary asks what role the core socialist values play in reaching the goal of basically realising socialist modernization by 2035. Wang argues that the values provide strong value support for Chinese modernization: they guide it, unite society behind it and express its distinctive value orientation to the world. The piece is organised in three sections. The first treats the core values as both a product of and a guide for modernization. The second examines how they build consensus among individuals, in social life and in the legal system. The third considers how they reflect the value orientation of Chinese modernization and its claim to universal human significance. Wang first contends that the values emerged from the Party's practice of modernization, guided by Marxist values and rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture, from the Party's first programme through reform and opening up. Since the new era, Wang says, they have been set as the fundamental value guide at the national, social and individual levels, and they keep modernization on a socialist course. Second, the author proposes that the values be internalised by individuals, embedded in digital space and cultural products, and written into law, citing the 2016 guideline on integrating them into the rule of law, their inclusion in the Constitution and the Civil Code, and Supreme People's Court documents on judicial reasoning. Wang concludes that the core values are the value core of Chinese modernization and extend scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China. Citing Xi Jinping, the author argues that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers a path that does not rely on exploiting or oppressing other nations. On this view both the path and its values surpass Western models and offer a new value direction for humankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party theory links the core socialist values to the Third Plenum's modernization agenda.”

Solidly advancing common prosperity through integrated urban–rural development 在城乡融合发展中扎实推进共同富裕 Zheng Huixia This commentary in Guangming Daily asks how integrated urban–rural development can serve the goal of common prosperity. Zheng Huixia starts from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which lists improving the institutions and mechanisms for urban–rural integration as a major reform task and calls it a necessary requirement of Chinese modernization. Zheng argues that this gives direction and a path for realising common prosperity. The article is organised around five dimensions of integration: space, industry, factors of production, ecology and institutions. Each section is presented as a way of building a particular aspect of common prosperity, and each lists practical measures. Zheng treats the ideal urban–rural relationship as one of equal status, mutual dependence, complementary functions and mutual promotion. On spatial integration, Zheng calls for unified multi-plan urban–rural planning, better rural infrastructure including 5G and gigabit fibre networks, and a new type of urbanisation centred on county towns. On industry, the author proposes that cities specialise in technology- and capital-intensive sectors while the countryside develops specialised agriculture, deep processing and rural tourism, with science and technology, e-commerce and fiscal, tax and financial policy as supports. On factors of production, Zheng urges freer two-way flows of land, talent, capital and technology, including orderly transfer of land management rights and a technology-information sharing platform. The last two sections cover ecology and institutions. Zheng proposes green development, ecological compensation, green finance and wider public environmental participation. Institutional integration would mean household registration reform, reform of rural homestead and collective construction land, a further 30-year extension of land contracts in pilot areas, greater fiscal support for agriculture, rural areas and farmers, and equalised basic public services in education, health care, culture and community governance. Zheng concludes that these combined measures would build an equitable, inclusive and sustainable urban–rural system and generate the joint force needed for common prosperity. Read the original if you want a compact, policy-oriented overview of how official discourse links urban–rural integration to common prosperity after the 2024 plenum.

The people's city concept and its humanist radiance Speech by Researcher Xu Jinjiang at the "Sihai Forum" 人民城市理念彰显人文主义光辉 Xu Jinjiang This is a speech by Xu Jinjiang, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, delivered at the "Sihai Forum" and published in Jiefang Daily (reposted December 2024). Xu argues that the concept of the "people's city" expresses the essential character of Chinese cities and answers the question of for whom, by whom and to whom a city belongs. In Xu's reading, it also carries a humanist outlook that can offer lessons for urban development worldwide. Xu begins with the "right to the city" as formulated by Western progressive scholars such as Lefebvre and Harvey, and with a personal anecdote about a "ruin" that Shanghai residents would call a "heritage site". The speech then sets out two competing urban ideas, "physicalism" (xingtizhuyi) and humanism, and lists problems in Chinese urban construction. It closes with seven paired urban types, three dimensions of the people's city in the Chinese context, and three coming transitions. Xu's central distinction is between physicalism, which prizes order, geometry and the aerial view (Haussmann, Le Corbusier, Brasília, Moses), and humanism, which prizes the street-level view, historical continuity and everyday life (Jane Jacobs, Ebenezer Howard, Lewis Mumford, Sharon Zukin, Doug Saunders, Qian Xuesen's "shan-shui city"). Xu holds that early reform-era enthusiasm for physicalism was understandable and produced real achievements, but led to uniform cities, fake heritage, developer dominance and the neglect of residents' dignity and belonging. Xu proposes that humanism be the main concern now, as the flesh and blood within the physical frame, with the two ideas ultimately fused. The paired types include tourist city versus resident city, "luminous city" versus "arrival city", and internet-celebrity city versus ordinary city. Xu cites Shanghai's 2024 government work report on affordable rental housing as an example of progress. In the Chinese context Xu gives the people's city three meanings: creatively drawing on Chinese civilisational resources, combining urban renewal with whole-process people's democracy through co-construction, co-governance and sharing, and building evaluation indicators around residents' sense of presence, security, happiness, gain and belonging rather than only benchmarking against global cities. Xu foresees three transitions: from capital-driven to people's cities, from physical to humanist cities, and from physical to digital cities. Read the original if you want a Shanghai scholar's account of how Western urban theory (Jacobs, Le Corbusier, Lefebvre) is used to interpret the official people's city concept.

Improving the basic institutions of ecological civilization and strengthening the eco-environmental governance system 完善生态文明基础体制 健全生态环境治理体系 Wang Xiangrong This short commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily, responds to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The plenum described Chinese modernization as modernization in harmony between humanity and nature and called for speeding up the institutions that put into practice the idea that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. Wang argues that doing so means improving the basic institutions of ecological civilization and the eco-environmental governance system, not merely adding green space. The piece has two parts. The first deals with national institutional design around the "three lines and one list". The second applies the regional-governance logic to the Yangtze River Delta, with concrete proposals for cooperation zones. Wang presents the "three lines and one list" (ecological protection red lines, environmental quality bottom lines, resource utilisation ceilings and a negative list for environmental access) as a foundational tool. It should integrate ecological protection, environmental management, spatial planning and environmental assessment. It should also build spatial controls on environmental management units and set differentiated entry requirements. For the Yangtze River Delta, Wang calls for joint construction, governance and sharing of the environment. Proposals include demonstration zones around the Yangtze estuary and Hangzhou Bay, a Shanghai–Xuancheng–Huangshan carbon-trading cooperation zone, and a cross-regional compensation scheme for freshwater supply along the Taipu River and surrounding areas. Wang also proposes shared urban parks with equal access across cities. Wang concludes that systematic, differentiated and precise environmental management, backed by ecological compensation and cross-boundary cooperation, can ease the structural pressures that still weigh on environmental protection. The commentary suggests that the delta can serve as a model of regional coordination. Read the original if you want concrete, place-specific policy proposals for Yangtze River Delta ecological cooperation, set within the 2024 plenum's language on ecological civilization.

Spiritual construction, cultural power, philosophical thinking 精神建设—文化力量—哲学思维 Han Qingxiang Writing at the turn of 2025, Han Qingxiang describes the present as an age of rapid change, "time-space compression" and spiritual anxiety. The commentary argues that reflection on such an age should start from each individual's inner spiritual world. Han holds that cultural power speaks directly to that inner world and that philosophical thinking helps people resolve doubts, so both are urgent. The piece raises four questions in turn. These are the relation between Chinese modernization and the individual's spiritual world; the link between consolidating the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation and the individual's own subjectivity; the balance between "liberating people" and "restraining people"; and the relative distinction between culture and civilization. First, Han proposes a rule of construction "from the outside in". China's response to Western modernization moved from material objects to institutions to culture, and reform and opening up first stressed material wealth. Han argues that the new era turns to the inner emotional and spiritual world, citing Xi Jinping's statement that modernization is at root the modernization of human beings. Second, Han presents Chinese modernization as a move beyond Western-centrism, in which the contest between China and the West is a "contest of subjectivity". Han also notes the tension between national strength and individual pressure, and calls for stronger inner drive. Third, on governance, Han calls for unifying drive, balance and governance, and for reforms that people can actually feel. Fourth, Han defines culture as the premise of civilization, which sublimates it. Culture stresses "humanizing" externally, while civilization stresses inner cultivation and virtue. Knowledge without virtue, Han warns, leads to refined egoism. Han concludes that one aim of Xi Jinping's cultural thought is to move from culture to civilization. It would build a cultural form of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization, and produce people who combine inner drive and innovative vitality with rule-abiding virtue. Han says that uniting these qualities requires philosophical thinking. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Central Party School scholar links Xi Jinping's cultural thought to individual psychology and governance.

Building China's autonomous system of pedagogical knowledge requires the "Two Integrations" as its methodology 构建中国自主的教育学知识体系要以“两个结合”为方法论 Gu Mingyuan Gu Mingyuan, writing in Guangming Daily on 31 December 2024, argues that an autonomous Chinese system of pedagogical knowledge is an important part of the modernization of Chinese education. Drawing on the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, Gu contends that this system must take the Two Integrations as its methodology: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The short piece sketches the history of Chinese pedagogy, which Gu says was imported from the West via Japan about 120 years ago. It then discusses the Party's educational policy, traditional educational ideas, and a tentative framework for organising the resulting concepts. Gu argues that education has both an individual, developmental side and a social side. Western pedagogy from Comenius and Herbart, in Gu's account, dealt mainly with the former. Marxist-inspired Chinese educators such as Yang Xianjiang stressed education's social character, and Party statements from Mao Zedong's 1957 formulation to Xi Jinping's 2018 addition of labour education kept this unity. Gu treats the Party's educational policy as the "big concept" of the Chinese system, from which ideas such as "fostering virtue through education" and quality-oriented education derive. Traditional ideas such as teaching according to aptitude and "education without discrimination" are described as universal principles that should be reinterpreted through dialectical and historical materialism. Gu proposes a provisional structure headed by the Party's educational policy, divided into macro-level knowledge (education as a foundation of national prosperity, balanced development, urban–rural integration) and micro-level knowledge (the "five educations", home–school–community cooperation, student-centredness). Concepts would be classified by nature, type and level, then used to form propositions with Chinese cultural and social features. Gu calls the idea rough and offers it for discussion. Read the original if you want a brief statement by a leading Chinese educationist on how the Two Integrations apply to pedagogy.

Consolidating the foundations of belief, conviction and confidence to strengthen the guiding power of ideological and political education 铸牢信仰信念信心根基 增强思政引领力 Lan Ting Li Yufei This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 31 December 2024, asks how ideological and political education can build a strong guiding power as part of making China a leading country in education. Lan and Li argue that this power is an integral part of that goal and a requirement of Party leadership over it. They propose consolidating three foundations among young students: belief, conviction and confidence. The piece is organised in three sections, each tied to one of these foundations. They are belief in Marxism, described as the soul of guiding power; conviction in socialism with Chinese characteristics, its basis; and confidence in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which keeps it on the right course. Each section describes the foundation and then sets out measures for education. On belief, the authors call for Marxist theory education and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to shape students. They also want integrated ideological and political teaching from primary school to university and a "big ideological and political course" pattern. On conviction, they call for sound views of history, nation, state and culture, education in traditional Chinese culture, and stronger theoretical grounding. On confidence, they cite the scale and quality of China's education system. They urge integrated reform of education, science and technology, and talent, and the training of top talent at home, to support Chinese modernization. Lan and Li conclude that China should keep to its own path of socialist education development. They want this path to deliver strong ideological, political and value guidance to students under the Party's overall leadership. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-aligned academics frame ideological and political education within the education-power agenda.

Empowering gains in production quality and efficiency with the new development philosophy 以新发展理念赋能生产质效提升 Shen Jie This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how the new development philosophy should guide the formation of new quality productive forces and high-quality development. Shen argues that innovative practice needs guiding ideas as well as material conditions, so the new development philosophy must run through any understanding of how the two are related. The piece first sets out the theoretical link between the philosophy and new quality productive forces. It then offers three practical requirements: breakthroughs in core technologies, steady progress, and region-specific development. Shen contends that scientific theory is an important condition for productive forces to develop. Under capitalism, in the author's account, production stays disorderly and spontaneous, whereas only socialism can produce theory serving large-scale socialised production and people's all-round development. New quality productive forces are presented as advanced productive forces that conform to the new development philosophy. They are said to arise from technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors and industrial upgrading, not from a mere partial optimisation of traditional productive forces. Shen treats their formation as confirming the philosophy's scientific validity. On practice, Shen calls for winning the battle over key core technologies, since innovation is the first necessary condition. The author also calls for maintaining stability while seeking progress, protecting industrial and supply-chain security, and avoiding bubbles and neglect of traditional industries. Finally, regions should act according to local conditions, with Beijing supporting other regions through its role as an international science and technology innovation centre. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school commentary links new quality productive forces to the new development philosophy.

The reasoning and routes for telling China's story well in the era of "everything as media" “万物皆媒”时代讲好中国故事的理与路 Wang Feng'e Wang Feng'e takes up a question raised by the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): how to build Chinese discourse and narrative systems and tell China's story well. The commentary argues that in an era of deep digitalisation, networking and intelligence, when "everything is media", objects have acquired subjectivity, media function and narrative capacity. Wang proposes "object narrative", that is, using things as media to convey reasons, as a more scientific way to tell China's story. The piece has three parts. The first sets out what should be told: the Chinese path, China's fine traditional culture and Chinese modernization. The second identifies which objects to use: those embodying Chinese civilisation, the Communist Party's spirit of struggle, and the outlook of the Chinese people. The third considers where to tell: on media platforms, in everyday life, and in the experience of foreign visitors. Wang argues that telling the story of the Chinese path means explaining who development relies on and serves, and how it proceeds, through themes such as the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Cultural relics, intangible heritage, revolutionary relics, and newer objects such as high-speed rail, mobile payment and shared bicycles are presented as carriers of narrative, valued for their objectivity, immediacy and acceptability. Large models, consumer goods and inbound tourism are described as settings where objects act with people as narrators, so that the story is conveyed almost unnoticed. Wang concludes that building platforms for object narrative would open routes for exchange between civilisations and create a shared context of mutual understanding. Read the original if you want a short example of how official discourse on international communication is being extended to media theory and material objects.

Grasping several questions about the "Second Integration" fully 完整把握“第二个结合”的几个问题 Tao Wenzhao This short commentary, published in Beijing Daily and written as study notes on the Outline for Studying Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, asks how the Party's formula of the Two Integrations should be understood, with emphasis on the "Second Integration": combining the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Tao Wenzhao argues that it must be grasped as a whole. This means keeping four points in balance: the relation between the two integrations, the primacy of Marxism, the criterion of "fine" culture, and the orientation towards adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article proceeds through four headed sections. It first sets out how the Second Integration relates to the First, then examines the grammatical "subject" of the formula, which is the basic tenets of Marxism. It then discusses what counts as "fine" traditional culture, and finally explains the purposes of the integration. Tao cites Xi Jinping's speeches of July 2021 and June 2023 and Mao Zedong's remarks on not severing history. Tao argues that the Two Integrations have operated objectively since the Party's founding, but that the traditional-culture side was previously treated as subordinate to the First Integration. Singling it out is, in Tao's view, a deepening of understanding and practice. The First Integration remains the foundation, since "concrete Chinese realities" already include traditional culture.
