Tao stresses that Marxism is the "soul" and traditional culture the "roots": over-praising tradition while neglecting or belittling Marxism is wrong. The formula refers to basic tenets, meaning stance, viewpoint and method, not every individual claim, which guards against dogmatism. Only the "fine" part of tradition qualifies, to be judged by historical materialism through its political stance (democratic and progressive versus feudal) and its fitness for social development. Tao rejects cultural revivalism and the "Confucianisation" of theory. Tao concludes that the Second Integration serves two ends. One is adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, so that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era carries the best of Chinese culture. The other is building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, with traditional culture creatively transformed to serve that practice. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of how the Second Integration is to be understood and what limits are placed on the use of tradition.

Offering the best spiritual nourishment to the people 把最好的精神食粮奉献给人民 Li Yi Li Yi, Party secretary and vice-chairman of the China Federation of Literary and Art Circles (CFLAC), writes in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) that "putting the people first" runs through Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. The article argues that socialist literature and art are in essence the people's literature and art. Literary and art work, and the work of the federation, should therefore take a people-centred orientation and give the people the best spiritual nourishment. The piece is organised under four headings, each opening with remarks by Xi Jinping. They concern strengthening the people's spiritual strength for national rejuvenation, writing about real life, using the people's evaluation as the highest standard, and cultivating artists who love the people. Li draws on recent works, including television dramas, films and dance dramas, as well as classical literature and world masterpieces. Li also describes CFLAC programmes and plans. Li argues that culture and art are essential to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to Chinese modernization, which Li describes as the coordination of material and spiritual civilisation. Artists are urged to tell the story of the Party and of the people's struggle. Li holds that good works come from deep immersion in the people's lives, citing CFLAC field trips to Tibetan, Inner Mongolian and Xinjiang areas. Li also holds that lasting classics are those that care about the people's fate. Li says the main contradiction in cultural supply has shifted from "whether there is any" to "whether it is excellent", so quality must be the lifeline of art. The standard is whether the people support, approve and are pleased by a work, with social benefit placed first and united with economic benefit. Artists must be of both moral and artistic merit, sharing the people's joys and worries, and the poet Ai Qing is offered as a model. Li announces that the CFLAC will carry out the New Era Literary and Art Peak-building Action and the New Era Literary and Art Masterpiece Creation Project. It will also continue the "going deep into life, rooting among the people" practice, and improve talent mechanisms, with attention to young, grassroots and "new" arts workers. Li concludes that all innovation in literature and art ultimately comes from the people, and that artists should celebrate the era and build cultural peaks under Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Read the original if you want to see how a senior official of the national arts federation presents the Party's people-centred cultural policy and the federation's planned measures.

Building a bridge from theory to the masses 架起理论通向群众的桥梁 Hu Xiaolan This commentary, first published in Study Times, asks how grassroots theory lectures can help ordinary people understand and master the Party's innovative theory and policies. Hu argues that, in the new era, such work must stay close to what the people need and concentrate on mass work. Opening with Xi Jinping's call to popularise and simplify the spread of Marxism, the article treats the people's standpoint as the key to propaganda and ideological work. The article is organised around four practical areas: content, method, venues and personnel. It closes by urging story-telling about reform and development, linked to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). On content, Hu calls for a "user mindset" and "demand orientation". Big theory should be presented through small topics and local stories, and skills-based talks should be tied to people's livelihoods and production. On method, political language should be turned into everyday speech, using forms such as poetry recitation and clapper talk. Lectures should be tailored to different groups, including farmers, workers, officials and young people, and audiences should take part instead of listening passively. On venues, Hu proposes using the New Era Civilization Practice Centres, streets and squares, Party newspapers and broadcasting, and platforms such as Weibo, WeChat and Douyin. On personnel, the author proposes recruiting ordinary people as lecturers, training them, and building local lecture brands under a "one place, one brand" scheme. Hu concludes that lively stories from people's own lives make theory persuasive. The author wants lecturers to link such stories to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, so that popular strength and wisdom gather behind the Third Plenum's strategic plans. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media describe practical methods for taking official theory to local communities.

Ideological and political work with university students amid digital transformation 数字化转型中的高校学生思政工作 Zhao Xin This short commentary, published in Jiefang Daily on 30 December 2024, describes how Shanghai Jiao Tong University combines its traditional strengths in ideological and political work with information technology. Zhao Xin, the university's director of student affairs, argues that digital tools can make ideological and political education more targeted, more efficient and more attractive to students who grew up online. The article is organised in four parts: understanding students as "internet natives", building the online skills of the teaching and counselling staff, equipping student work with a "digital toolbox", and returning to real-world campus settings. Each part is illustrated with initiatives at the university. Zhao reports that the university monitors student opinion through key-stage surveys and analysis of online posts, and runs a studio that decodes internet slang ("meme guide"), which produced over 180 entries in 2024. A student development research institute founded in 2018 and a six-year counsellor training programme reaching over 1,200 trainees are presented as ways to strengthen online education skills. The university has also built self-developed systems, including a "student portrait" data warehouse, a digital "second classroom transcript" and an online service platform. Zhao stresses that digital work is complemented by a new student centre, a 24-hour service hotline, student-led think-tank projects and campus cultural events. Zhao concludes that "digital ideological and political work" is part of the digital transformation of education and of fostering virtue through education (lì dé shù rén). The university will, in the author's account, apply the new development philosophy and new technologies to raise the Party's guiding capacity in the internet era. Read the original if you want a concrete, practitioner's account of how a leading Chinese university is operationalising digital ideological and political education.

A global source of AI innovation: Shanghai's path to empowering the building of a cyber power 全球AI创新策源地 赋能网络强国建设的上海路径 Song Haitao Writing in Jiefang Daily on 30 December 2024, Song Haitao, who heads the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, presents the institute as a model of how artificial intelligence can serve the building of a cyber power (wangluo qiangguo). Song argues that AI is central to breaking technological blockades and strengthening network security. The institute, jointly established by the Shanghai municipality and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, is described as the first municipal-level new-type R&D body in AI. The piece is organised under three headings: consolidating the core technology base, cultivating an innovation ecosystem, and strengthening the talent pillar. It reports the institute's research areas, including humanoid robots, virtual power plants, DNA storage and AIGC network governance. It also covers its start-up incubation record, its partnerships with companies such as Huawei and SenseTime, and its international links. Song's central claim is that the institute links the talent chain, innovation chain and industrial chain, so that universities and firms reinforce each other. As evidence, the article cites a 2024 World Internet Conference award for a social-governance visual-understanding project and more than 20 incubated firms. Of these firms, 70% have received fund backing and 15% are unicorns or near-unicorns, with a combined valuation above 200 billion yuan. Song also points to a UNIDO global AI centre of excellence hosted by the institute, to an AI-focused MBA, and to cooperation with universities abroad. Song concludes that new quality productive forces are taking shape at the institute through the integration of frontier AI, computing power and network infrastructure. The article presents this as a distinctive Shanghai path for AI-enabled cyber power building. Read the original if you want an institutional insider's account of how a Chinese AI research body describes its role in national technology policy.

Bringing the value of the "Two Roads" spirit to bear on forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation 发挥“两路”精神在铸牢中华民族共同体意识中的价值 Zhou Yulan Chen Guangjun This short commentary asks how the "Two Roads" spirit, which arose in building the Sichuan–Tibet and Qinghai–Tibet highways, can serve the effort to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Zhou and Chen argue that the spirit, formed through the shared struggle of People's Liberation Army soldiers and people of all ethnic groups, is a high-quality spiritual resource. The authors first present the "Two Roads" spirit as a historical witness to the Party, the people and the army holding firm to revolutionary faith and revolutionary optimism under harsh conditions. They then set out three ways of putting it to use: spiritual guidance, education through cases, and widening the carriers and channels of dissemination. On spiritual guidance, the article cites Xi Jinping's summary of the spirit and the figures it gives for the road-building: 110,000 Tibetan and Han builders, over 30 million cubic metres of earth and rock, more than 400 bridges and some 3,000 deaths. It argues that these deeds can deepen the content of ethnic unity. On cases, it points to sites left by the 18th Army along the Sichuan–Tibet route, such as cave dwellings, martyrs' tombs, slogans and songs, as teaching material. For wider channels, it proposes a case library, staged "Two Roads" stories, art and music, paper-cuts, pottery, songs and cultural-tourism products. The authors conclude that fitting the spirit into this work strengthens ethnic identity, reinforces shared red memories and unites people of all ethnic groups. Their proposals are practical: collect and systematise case material, then spread it through varied cultural forms so that it takes hold in people's minds and hearts. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ethnic-unity education draws on revolutionary-era heritage and local historical sites.

Improving the Party's capacity and level in leading the building of a leading country in education 提高党领导教育强国建设的能力和水平 Zhang Haishui Guo Guoxiang Zhang Haishui and Guo Guoxiang take up the question of how Party members and officials can lead the building of a leading country in education more effectively. The short commentary, which opens with remarks by Xi Jinping on officials respecting and studying education, is organised around six requirements for cadres. These are holding the ideological and political guidance position, putting the people at the centre, grasping the laws of education, coordinating education with science and technology and talent strategies, applying systems thinking, and adapting measures to local conditions. Each section pairs a directive from Xi Jinping with practical tasks for officials. The authors give first place to ideological and political guidance, the first of the "six forces" Xi Jinping set out at the national education conference. They present it as the political attribute of education and as the force that strengthens the other five: talent competitiveness, scientific support, livelihood security, social coordination and international influence. On the people-centred requirement, they call for a mass-line approach, for policy attention tilted towards disadvantaged groups, and for narrowing gaps between urban and rural areas and between schools. They also hold that the more accurately the Party understands educational laws, the more education prospers, and they say officials should learn through dialogue with teachers. The three-in-one layout of education, science and technology, and talent from the 20th Party Congress (2022) is described as resting on talent cultivation and serving new quality productive forces. Higher, vocational and basic education are each assigned specific tasks. The authors call for systems thinking that combines school funding, teaching staff and facilities with the cooperation of families, communities and government departments. They also call for local adaptation, citing the large population scale of Chinese modernization as a reason to avoid uniform targets and to set separate paths for provinces, cities and counties. They further urge evaluation systems and law-based school governance, and policy that turns "public consensus" into public benefit. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-theory writing links Xi Jinping's education directives to concrete expectations of cadres.

Integrating integrity culture and teachers' ideological and political work in universities in the new era: significance, principles and methods 新时代高校廉洁文化与教师思想政治工作一体化建设的意义、原则与方法 Wan Hua Zhao Yonggang Wang Chao Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for strengthening integrity culture in the new era, this short commentary asks how universities can fold ideological and political work with teachers into campus integrity-culture building. The authors argue that the two should be developed as one integrated effort, starting from teachers' own conduct, so that Party conduct, teachers' ethics and the study atmosphere reinforce one another. The piece has three parts. It first sets out why teachers' ideological and political work matters for integrity culture, then states four principles for the integrated approach, and finally lists four working methods. It opens by citing Xi Jinping on putting teachers' ethics first and by invoking Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as guidance. On significance, the authors list five contributions: correct value orientation and firm communist ideals, better professional ethics, teachers as role models of academic integrity, stronger belonging to the university and its Party committee, and more exchange among teachers about integrity. The four principles are adherence to Party spirit, tailoring work to the individual, equal care, and thoroughness, with the last drawing on the Party's self-reform. The four methods are teaching by example, being serious yet patient, combining outside guidance with self-education, and uniting firmness with warmth. The authors conclude that teachers are the foundation of education and so must be the starting point for integrity culture. They call for organic fusion of the two fields, which would enrich theory and practice and support high-quality development of university integrity culture. Read the original if you want a concise example of how university discipline-inspection and Party-education staff frame integrity education as part of teachers' ideological work.

Viewing the world through the distinctive worldview embedded in Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化蕴含的独特世界观看天下 Tian Pengying Tian Pengying, writing at the end of 2024, asks how Chinese modernization can answer what the author calls the "questions of world modernization". These include polarisation versus common prosperity, zero-sum games versus win-win cooperation, and copying foreign models versus independent development. Tian argues that the distinctive worldview embedded in Chinese modernization offers a methodological option for developing countries and an innovation in modernization theory and practice. The short commentary draws on a major National Social Science Fund project on the worldview contained in Chinese modernization. It looks at that worldview through three relationships: China and the world, China and the South, and China and a new form of human civilisation. It opens by describing a world of intertwined crises, a widening development gap and environmental deterioration. Tian contends that this worldview combines the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with concern for all humanity, and treats building a community with a shared future for mankind as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. Tian describes China as a natural member of the Global South, supporting other developing countries in choosing their own paths and helping latecomers avoid the "paradox of modernization" and the "afflictions of modernity". On civilisation, Tian says the twenty-first century has three basic blocs: Chinese, Western and developing-country modernization. The author holds that Chinese modernization dissolves the discursive hegemony of Western modernization and breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. Tian concludes that Chinese modernization widens the paths open to developing countries and offers a Chinese approach to protecting and passing on human civilisation. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese scholar leading a national research project frames the worldview of Chinese modernization in relation to the world, the Global South and civilisation.

From digital "fission" to global "symbiosis": a new philosophical situation and economic outlook in cyberspace 从数字“裂变”到全球“共生”：网络空间下的哲学新局与经济展望 Gao Ying This short commentary, published on Guangming Online in late 2024, asks how rapid digital technological change and the difficulties of global digital governance can be reconciled. Gao Ying argues that the rapid "fission" of digital technology makes a global "symbiosis" urgent, and that building a community with a shared future in cyberspace is the way to balance the international digital order and protect fairness and justice. The piece has three parts. It first surveys advances in artificial intelligence, big data, blockchain, 5G and edge computing and their effect on industry. It then turns to the idea of a community with a shared future in cyberspace, citing Xi Jinping's statements, the 2024 World Internet Conference in Wuzhen and China's assistance to African countries. A final part offers a dialectical reading and an economic outlook. Gao describes the world's cyberspace as marked by cyberattacks, data leaks and what the author calls hegemonic states wielding a "digital big stick", while less developed regions face a digital divide. The community concept, in the author's account, rests on equality, mutual trust and win-win cooperation, and promises multilateral rule-making, resource sharing and joint security. Gao also reads the relationship between technology and governance through the Marxist principle that productive forces determine relations of production: digital productive forces call for new governance rules and new international relations. For the economy, Gao calls for more basic research, closer ties between universities and enterprises, work on \"chokepoint\" technologies, and the export of digital payment, e-commerce, 5G and cloud technologies through the Belt and Road Initiative. The author concludes that countries can develop sustainably only through joint consultation and mutual learning. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official discourse links digital technology, Marxist theory and the cyberspace community idea.

A heart devoted to the nation: Wu Yuzhang's life in education 才为国寸心丹——吴玉章的教育人生 Geng Huamin Liu Gaoyuan This biographical essay, published in Guangming Daily on 30 December 2024, portrays Wu Yuzhang (1878–1966) as a revolutionary who treated education as part of revolution and national construction rather than as an abstract route to national salvation. The authors, Geng Huamin and Liu Gaoyuan, present him as a "red educator" whose work ran from the work-study movement in France to Yan'an and then to the founding of new higher education in the People's Republic. The article follows Wu's career chronologically and thematically under four headings. It covers his role as a practical organiser of education, his ideas on training all-round new people, his insistence on linking teaching with practice, and his views on teachers and on family education. Evidence comes from his speeches, essays and school policies at Chengdu Higher Normal School, Yan'an University, North China University, Renmin University of China, the Chinese script reform committee and the Central Institute of Socialism. The authors argue that Wu's educational thought rested on historical materialism and a people's standpoint. He backed study abroad, literacy campaigns and script reform, and, as the first president of Renmin University of China, aimed to train "tens of thousands of construction cadres". He required political theory courses to take 20–30 per cent of teaching hours, and held that political and professional training must go together. He opposed teaching cut off from practice and demanded that "educators must first be educated". He also supported free academic debate under the Hundred Flowers policy, citing his invitation to historians with differing views on periodizing ancient Chinese history. In family education he advocated "strictness combined with love", drawing on his grandmother's and father's example and on letters to his grandchildren. The authors conclude that nurturing red educational traditions and training people for the Party and the country was Wu's greatest achievement, citing Mao Zedong's 1940 tribute to his lifelong service. They state that his educational ideas and his experience in building new higher education remain a valuable asset for the Party's leadership of education in the new era. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially framed account of Wu Yuzhang's educational practice, from Yan'an schooling to early Renmin University, and of how it is presented today.

How new quality productive forces grow in practice 新质生产力，如何在实践中成长 Wang Yiming In this commentary in the People's Daily, Wang Yiming asks what new quality productive forces are, why China should develop them and how. Wang argues that they should be understood against the current wave of scientific and technological revolution and China's shift to high-quality development. In this account they are innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality, and in essence advanced productive forces. The piece first sets out the technological and economic background, then names three sources of new quality productive forces: breakthroughs in technology, innovative allocation of production factors, and deep industrial transformation and upgrading. It then lists six relationships to be handled, and ends by placing the concept within Xi Jinping's theoretical contribution since 2023. Wang contends that the old growth model of factor inputs cannot continue and that China must rely on innovation and total factor productivity. The author's examples include artificial intelligence replacing mental as well as manual labour, data as a new production factor, and China's new-energy vehicle output passing 10 million in 2024. The six relationships are: innovation and the commercialisation of results; emerging and traditional industries (the latter said to exceed 80 per cent of manufacturing); government guidance and market mechanisms; finance and innovation; productive forces and relations of production; and top innovative talent and the wider quality of workers. Wang warns against rushing in, bubbles and one-size-fits-all approaches, and says the government should cultivate an innovation ecosystem rather than allocate resources administratively. Wang concludes that new quality productive forces are an internal requirement of high-quality development. The author presents Xi Jinping's concept as a major development of Marxist productivity theory and calls for study of it and for putting it into practice. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the practical policy balances behind the new quality productive forces agenda.

Building a new ecosystem for fostering virtue and cultivating talent in the digital-intelligence era 打造数智时代立德树人新生态 Zhu Minglun Wang Junhua This newspaper commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily in December 2024, asks how education can be rebuilt around the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent now that artificial intelligence and big data have entered schooling. Zhu and Wang argue that digitalisation of education is more than a technical upgrade. In their view it requires deeper change in educational ideas and models, and a new educational ecosystem suited to the era. The piece begins from Xi Jinping's statement that educational digitalisation is a key breakthrough for opening a new track in education. It then sets out three parts: the basic principles of the new ecosystem, the paths for implementing it, and the safeguards needed to sustain it. On principles, the authors call for correct value orientation, since intelligent technology is a double-edged sword that can bring privacy leaks and ethical problems. They also call for the all-round development of students, with teaching shifting from a teacher–student pair to a teacher–machine–student pattern. Finally, they stress education's strategic character in supporting national competitiveness. On implementation, they propose smart learning environments, integrated digital resources, personalised teaching through learning analytics and adaptive systems, and evaluation that covers creativity, cooperation and moral qualities through peer, self and process-based assessment. For safeguards, Zhu and Wang urge improved institutions, including quality monitoring and teacher development, and a high-calibre teaching force with ongoing training in digital and intelligent technologies. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese education officials frame AI-enabled teaching within the goal of fostering virtue and cultivating talent.

Practical exploration of an all-round online education system 全方位网络育人体系的实践探索 Zhang Yinshuang Writing in Jiefang Daily on 27 December 2024, Zhang Yinshuang, a deputy head of the Party Committee's student affairs department at Shanghai Lixin University of Accounting and Finance, asks how universities can use digital technology for ideological and political education. Zhang argues that integrating digital tools with this work is both a task of the times and a key lever for building a new ecosystem of ideological and political education. The article presents the university's Yiban platform as a practical example. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to raise online education capacity and with the Minister of Education's January 2024 pledge to promote AI-enabled education. It then describes Yiban, a national online community for Chinese universities, and the Lixin Yiban development centre set up in 2012. The case is organised under three headings: top-level design and institutions, content and brands, and personnel and organisational support. Zhang reports that the university adopted a "1+X" institutional framework and a school-and-college co-building model. A leading group chaired by the Party secretary includes 18 units, and Yiban work is part of the assessment of colleges and counsellors. On content, Zhang cites nine Yiban spaces, an online pre-enrolment space for new students and an annual class competition. According to Zhang, new-student registration exceeds 98%, and the competition has run for 12 years and now draws about 800 classes from nearly 30 Shanghai universities. A four-tier management system, training programmes, 22 Yiban teacher studios and 56 online culture projects are said to involve nearly 10,000 teachers and students. Zhang concludes that sustained institution-building and team development have produced an all-round online education system that has improved the relevance and effectiveness of ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a short, official-style example of how a Chinese university reports on implementing the "three-wide education" approach through an online platform.

Grasping the key links in using digital-intelligence technology to empower ideological and political theory courses in universities 把握数智技术赋能高校思政课建设的关键环节 Liu Jingwei This short commentary, first published in Jiefang Daily on 27 December 2024, asks how universities should use digital-intelligence technology (big data, cloud computing, artificial intelligence) in their ideological and political theory courses. Liu Jingwei argues that the technology brings both opportunities and challenges, and that course development must seize four key links to raise quality. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's call to fuse the traditional strengths of ideological and political work with information technology. It then sets out four numbered points: grasping the direction of technological development, guarding against technology-centrism, innovating the carriers of course delivery, and promoting collaborative education through the "big ideological and political course". Liu holds that teachers should learn and apply new technologies, since algorithms, computing power and data analysis can support every stage of teaching. The author also warns against "technology-centrism": some students rely on AI to obtain answers, plagiarise or cheat, which Liu says turns AI into a stumbling block for independent thinking and leaves students in an "information cocoon". Over-reliance, Liu argues, neglects value formation, humanistic care and ethics. On the positive side, Liu proposes online resource libraries, micro-courses, MOOCs, blended teaching, virtual teaching assistants and smart classrooms, and says these make teacher–student relations more equal. Liu concludes that the big ideological and political course should link real and virtual settings, classroom and extracurricular activity, and school and society, for example through online venues and bases. Students should use digital tools to record and share their practical experience, so that self-education extends the courses' social effect. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party-school-style university Marxism dean frames AI in political education.

Integrating digital and intelligent technology to open new paths for Communist Youth League online ideological and political work in universities 数智融合助推高校共青团网络思政新作为 Luan Mengmeng Writing in Jiefang Daily in December 2024, Luan asks how university Communist Youth League organisations can use digital and intelligent technologies in online ideological and political education. The commentary argues that integrating big data, cloud computing and AI lets the League profile young people accurately, target its education and services, and evaluate results more scientifically. The piece opens by noting that cyberspace is now students' main channel for information and expression, and cites Xi Jinping's call at the National Education Conference to expand spaces for online education and to implement the national education digitalization strategy. It then sets out three areas of benefit: accurate profiling, service innovation and improved evaluation. On profiling, Luan says analysis of students' behaviour, interests and social-media sentiment moves education from "flood irrigation" to "precision drip irrigation". It supports targeted activities, immersive VR and AR experiences and personalised content push. On services, the author describes "digital-intelligent" platforms that use machine learning to recommend career guidance and AI-based counselling offering 24-hour support. On evaluation, algorithms mine interaction records and feedback texts to monitor activities in real time and show which content works. Luan concludes that these technologies make the League's work more precise, better matched to youth needs and more forward-looking. The article stays at the level of general examples and gives no data or case evidence. Read the original if you want a short example of how Youth League cadres frame AI and big data in university ideological education.

How ideological and political large models innovate on traditional ideological and political education 思政大模型对传统思政教育的创新突破 Meng Wei This short commentary, published in Jiefang Daily in December 2024, asks how large AI models built for ideological and political education can move beyond traditional methods. Rebuilding the system of Marxist philosophy through contemporary practice and scholarly proposals A dialogue between Yang Geng and Zhang Liang on "rereading Marx" and the Collected Works of Yang Geng 以当代实践和学术主张，重建马克思主义哲学体系 Yang Geng Zhang Liang This is a dialogue between Nanjing University philosopher Zhang Liang and Beijing Normal University professor Yang Geng, prompted by the publication of the ten-volume Collected Works of Yang Geng. Its subject is Yang's long-running programme of "rereading Marx" and what it implies for rebuilding a system of Marxist philosophy. Yang's answer is that rereading must be driven by contemporary practice, remain anchored in a single objective Marx, and lead to a system unified around practice. The conversation moves through Yang's motives after the Soviet collapse, his method, the relation between "Marx's philosophy" and "Marxist philosophy", and his main works. These include In Defence of Marx, Reconstruction in Crisis, and The Rise of the East, on Chinese modernization. It ends with Yang's work on the system of Marxist philosophy, collected in Volume 6, and with Yang's own account of what the Collected Works contains. Zhang summarises Yang's method as reading Marx within "three wholes": the full history of modern Western philosophy, the full history of Marxist philosophy, and the full theoretical framework of Marxism, including political economy. Yang rejects the idea that "a thousand readers have a thousand Marxes". In Yang's view, Marx was a real historical figure whose thought rests on objective historical laws, so interpretations have a limit, like readings of Hamlet. Yang defines Marx's philosophy as the thought of Marx himself, and Marxist philosophy as that thought as developed by successors. He treats it as political philosophy, tied to practical critique and to the question of human life. He says Marx shifted philosophy's theme from "how is the world possible" to "how is human emancipation possible", with practice as its ontological basis. Yang says his aim is a Marxist philosophical system, grounded in practice, in which practical materialism, dialectical materialism and historical materialism are integrated. He presents it as a response to contemporary practice, science and philosophy. He treats Chinese modernization as the central reality for Chinese philosophers, describing it as modernization, marketization and socialist reform compressed into one time and space. He admits that his own understanding is limited by his pre-understanding, and does not claim to have recovered Marx's "original face". Read the original if you want a first-hand account, from a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher, of how he understands rereading Marx, the objectivity of interpretation and the reconstruction of the philosophical system.

Understanding the distinctive features of comprehensively deepening reform through the "seven focuses" 从“七个聚焦”洞悉全面深化改革的鲜明特质 Liu Zongling Jiang Ruibing Liu Zongling and Jiang Ruibing take up the "seven focuses" set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively to advance Chinese modernization. On values, they write that reform is carried out for the people and relies on them, and that people should judge its results. On method, they describe reform as forced by problems and deepened by solving them. They add that reform has moved step by step from points to lines to whole areas and now needs coordination across fields, levels and regions. The authors conclude that further reform should keep the Party's leadership, strengthen confidence in the chosen path, respond to new domestic and international conditions and new technological revolutions, and be planned within the \"five-sphere integrated plan\" and the \"four-pronged comprehensive strategy\". They call for greater systemic, integrated and coordinated reform. Empowering the development of new quality productive forces through an innovation culture 以创新文化赋能新质生产力发展 Zhang Yaxuan Taking up Xi Jinping's call, in a June 2024 Qiushi article, to "do a good job on the big article of innovation", Zhang argues that the formation of new quality productive forces is a process of cultural reshaping as well as an economic and technological one. On values, Zhang finds three features in traditional culture that suit the new quality productive forces: active reform, dialectical "upholding fundamental principles while innovating", and open, integrative borrowing. On institutions, the author draws on Marxist political economy, in which institutional and technological innovation are two sides of one process. Zhang lists obstacles such as uneven allocation of research resources and weak coordination, and proposes measures on investment, research platforms linking industry, universities and institutes, market rules and top-level design. Zhang concludes that cultivating an innovation culture is a key lever for advancing innovation and new quality productive forces. A social climate in which innovation becomes the norm would, in the author's view, generate internal momentum for high-quality development and the goal of building a strong country. Cultivating young people with a "Chinese heart" through education in ideals and convictions 以理想信念教育培养有“中国心”的时代青年 Shan Jingze Ye Zipeng Opening with Zhang Boling's three questions to Nankai University students in 1935 (are you Chinese, do you love China, do you want China to do well), the authors ask what it means for young people to have a "Chinese heart" today. This short commentary rests on Xi Jinping's statement that patriotism must be united with love for the Party and socialism. It sets out three tasks of ideals-and-convictions education, each tied to one dimension of the "Chinese heart": identity, pride and action. First, the authors call for systematic education in the "five histories" to pass on historical memory and the Party's revolutionary heritage. Deeply understanding "Upholding the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation" 深刻理解“高扬中华民族的文化主体性” Hao Shucui This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in December 2024, sets out how to understand the call to "uphold the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation". Hao defines cultural subjectivity as a culture's capacity, when it meets foreign cultures, to be both self-reflective and self-respecting, and on that basis to adapt and create. The author argues that this subjectivity is a precondition for national rejuvenation and for a new form of human civilisation, and that the Two Integrations supply the method for strengthening it. The piece is organised in three sections. The first links the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation to cultural subjectivity. The second ties cultural subjectivity to the creation of a "new form of human civilisation" through Chinese modernization. The third reads the Two Integrations as both an expression of and a route to cultural subjectivity. Throughout, Hao draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements, including his remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, and on the 2021 Party resolution on history. Hao's first move is to treat attitude toward cultural tradition as the main test of whether cultural subjectivity exists. In this reading, without it the basis on which the Chinese nation is itself a nation would disappear, and rejuvenation could not be discussed. Second, the author describes Chinese modernization as one that continues an ancient civilisation rather than destroying it, grows from Chinese soil rather than copying others, and is renewal rather than rupture. It is contrasted with a "universal" modern civilisation that abandons cultural subjectivity. Third, the Two Integrations are said to be Chinese-centred ("putting ourselves first and drawing on others for our own use"). Hao holds that subjectivity and the Two Integrations reinforce each other, and that paths of rigidity or of abandoning the banner fail because they suffocate or give up subjectivity. Hao concludes that "keeping to fundamental principles" and "innovating" must go together, and that building China's own knowledge system is the practical form this takes. The author calls for scholars to work under contemporary Chinese Marxism, address the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and promote the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. Hao also says that explaining the new form of civilisation abroad requires stressing "harmony without uniformity". Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship links cultural subjectivity, Chinese modernization and the Two Integrations.

Scientific legislation as a key link in handling the relationship between reform and the rule of law 科学立法是处理改革和法治关系的重要环节 Zhou Longjie This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 27 December 2024, asks how legislation can keep pace with deepening reform. Zhou Longjie argues that, of all the dimensions of rule-of-law building, scientific legislation is the key link in handling the relationship between reform and the rule of law. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping on earlier reform eras in Chinese history and on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for deepening reform "on the track of the rule of law" and for advancing Chinese modernization. It then sets out five practical requirements, followed by a note on institutional obstacles. Zhou's central claim is that reform stresses change while law stresses stability, so law tends to lag behind practice. The rule of law is therefore both a guarantee of reform and an object of reform. The five requirements are: consider legislation while designing reform measures; elevate proven experience into law, as with the 2018 Supervision Law and the Foreign Investment Law; grant authorisation under legal procedure for pilot reforms where legislation is premature, such as the rural land pilots authorised by the NPC Standing Committee; and amend or repeal laws that no longer fit reform, citing the 2023 State Council order revising 14 administrative regulations. Zhou rejects both "beneficial law-breaking reform" and the use of missing legal basis as a reason to hold reform back. Zhou concludes that overcoming local and departmental interests, and improving the quality and efficiency of legislation, is also necessary. The author calls for clearer limits on legislative power and institutional safeguards against the legalisation of departmental interests and local protectionism. Safeguarding and improving people's wellbeing through development 在发展中保障和改善民生 Lin Jinping Writing in Guangming Daily on 27 December 2024, Lin Jinping takes up a line from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): that safeguarding and improving people's wellbeing (minsheng) through development is a major task of Chinese modernization. Lin argues that Marxist thinking on wellbeing rests on three elements: material production, human needs and the distribution of interests. Production is the foundation, meeting needs and all-round human development is the goal, and fair distribution is the key. Development alone is not enough, since Marx and Engels' analysis of capitalism shows that a people-centred social system is also required. Lin calls for better income distribution, employment-first policies, social security, healthcare reform and population support, to advance common prosperity. Strengthening the consistency of macro-policy orientation to release the combined effect of multiple overlapping strategies 增强宏观政策取向一致性 释放多重战略叠加效能 Hao Zheng Ni Liangxin This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 27 December 2024, takes up a question raised by the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference: how to make the overlapping regional strategies work together. The authors begin from the fact that regional strategies now routinely overlap. The rest of the piece sets out three goals, each paired with a mechanism. In the authors' account, consistency has three dimensions. The first is overall layout, which calls for a deep-integration mechanism. Anhui, for example, should treat its three strategies as one whole, led by Yangtze River Delta integration. The second is the institutional system, which calls for a coordination mechanism. Here the authors stress balancing the whole and its parts, unity and difference, and long-term and phased policies, and they propose assessing economic and non-economic policies together. After they take effect, policies that diverge from governance goals should be adjusted or suspended. They present this as a way to bring out the distinctive strengths of socialism with Chinese characteristics and to modernise national governance. Accelerating the construction of Chinese discourse and Chinese narrative systems 加快构建中国话语和中国叙事体系 Zeng Xiangmin Tang Xuan Weng Xudong This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 November 2024, responds to the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to build Chinese discourse and narrative systems and raise the effectiveness of international communication. On narrative, they propose four dimensions: "development" (national-level stories, framed by a community with a shared future for mankind), "voicing" (authoritative responses to contested issues, moving from one-way output to interactive dialogue), "promotion" (traditional and regional culture, with strategies adapted to high- and low-context cultures) and "discovery" (everyday human stories that join individual and national narratives and, in their view, let emotion cross ideological divides). Several relationships that research on Chinese economic history should handle well 中国经济史研究应把握好几个关系 Wang Jue Writing in Guangming Daily in December 2024, Wang Jue asks how the study of Chinese economic history should be conducted so that it serves the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The four relationships are: economic theory and historical practice, where economic history should be the source of economics rather than its offshoot; national and world history, which Wang says explains why Chinese modernization is both universal and distinctive; the Chinese Communist Party and Chinese modernization; and scholarship and future development. On the third, Wang holds that research on modern and contemporary periods should show why only Marxism and the Party could lead China's rise, and that this is the main thread through the sources and data. Wang concludes that the field should adopt the Two Integrations, a global historical perspective and a contemporary Chinese standpoint, so that it shows its present value and tells China's part of the story of human civilisation. Turning the educator's spirit into conscious thought and conscious action 将教育家精神转化为思想自觉、行动自觉 Shi Xu Writing in Guangming Daily in December 2024, Shi Xu asks how teachers can make the "educator's spirit" (jiaoyujia jingshen) their own. Upholding fundamental principles and innovating to promote the content-based development of ideological and political theory courses 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Wang Haiwei This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks how ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) in Chinese universities can develop in depth while keeping to fundamental principles and innovating. Wang Haiwei, Dean of the School of Marxism at Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, takes Xi Jinping's formula as the framework: course construction must advance in step with the Party's innovative theory, draw its content from the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and rest on three cultural sources. The third section holds that excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture give the courses cultural depth, a 'red' lineage and vitality. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance on ideological and political courses is presented to the university teachers who deliver them.

Adhering to a people-centred approach and continuing to improve and develop the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics 坚持以人民为中心 继续完善和发展中国特色社会主义制度 Wan Guangxia Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Wan Guangxia asks how the plenum's overall goal of reform should be pursued: continuing to improve and develop the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernising national governance. Wan draws throughout on Marx and Engels's conception of the "real individual" and the historical materialist view of the masses, and on statements by Xi Jinping. First, Wan argues that meeting the people's needs for a better life is the basic starting point. Drawing on Marx and Engels, the author treats the needs of real individuals as the value origin of historical development. The author presents this as helping production relations fit the productive forces and as supplying momentum and institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization. The piece restates the official framing without introducing new empirical material. Always ensure that cultural development focuses on people and ends with people 始终坚持文化建设着眼于人、落脚于人 Zhang Jun This Guangming Daily commentary, published in December 2024, explains a directive from Xi Jinping that cultural development should always focus on people and end with people. In Zhang's reading, it gives guidance for developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, strengthening the people's spiritual strength and building the cultural foundation for national rejuvenation. The piece has four parts. It first sets out the value orientation of the directive through a Marxist view of culture, then discusses respecting and relying on the people's practice. It next turns to the educational function of culture and ends with institutional mechanisms in four areas: cultural production, governance, communication and talent. Zhang's core move is to argue that culture is both created by people and shapes people, so that cultural development is a unified process of humans transforming culture and culture transforming humans. From the Marxist view that the masses make history, Zhang concludes that the people decide cultural development. This requires three commitments: subjectivity (the people as creators, judges and beneficiaries of culture), historicity (inheriting and innovating the Chinese cultural tradition, with Marxism activating its best elements) and openness (learning from other civilisations). Culture's role in educating people, Zhang adds, means strengthening ideals and convictions and nurturing a new generation of all-round socialist builders. The stated aims are to raise the people's sense of cultural gain and happiness and to strengthen national cultural soft power. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links Marxist theory to current cultural policy.

The value implications of whole-process people's democracy and the guarantees of its effectiveness 全过程人民民主的价值意蕴与效能保障 Luo Feng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks what values whole-process people's democracy carries and what secures its effectiveness. Luo Feng argues that the concept inherits the core value of the Marxist view of democracy and that China's institutional system supplies several guarantees for it. Luo takes up the proposal of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to improve the institutional system of whole-process people's democracy. The piece is short and has five parts. The first places the concept in the Marxist tradition of democracy. The other four each treat one guarantee: the breadth of participants, the completeness of the process, the comprehensiveness of coverage, and the effectiveness of institutional operation. Throughout, Luo contrasts the Chinese institutions with Western representative democracy. Luo reads "people's democracy" as expressing the people's subjectivity and "whole-process" as describing democracy that is full-chain, all-round and all-covering. Drawing on the classics, Luo holds that the people's "self-determination" requires broad participants and procedures that run through the whole operation of public power. Luo then argues that Western democracy confines participation to a narrow elite game and reduces democracy to choosing rulers, citing Schumpeter. In Luo's account, China's system instead links elections, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and rests on the people's congress system, the new type of party system, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-governance. Luo adds that democracy must be tied to everyday needs in the economic, political, cultural and social fields. On effectiveness, Luo argues that Party leadership, the people being masters of the country and law-based governance must be organically unified. In Luo's view, the Party's people-centred nature makes its guidance and institutional design a key guarantee of whole-process people's democracy. The Party in turn gains influence and recognition by realising the people's democratic rights, so the two institutional systems support each other. Luo concludes that the Third Plenum's call to follow the Party's mass line in the new era points to this mutual reinforcement. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party-affiliated scholars present whole-process people's democracy against Western electoral democracy.

Focusing on the "six attributes" to advance high-quality development of education 聚焦“六大特质”推进教育事业高质量发展 Liu Yanbing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the National Education Conference that a leading country in education with Chinese characteristics should have six strengths: ideological and political guidance, talent competitiveness, scientific and technological support, capacity to safeguard people's wellbeing, social coordination and international influence. Liu Yanbing, who heads Chongqing's Party education committee and municipal education commission, argues that focusing on these six attributes will speed the high-quality development of education and support national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. The article is organised as six short sections, one for each attribute. Each opens with a quotation from Xi and then lists practical measures, mostly for schools, universities and local education authorities. On ideological and political guidance, Liu calls for the course on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to be taught well, for integrated Party-ideology courses across school stages, and for digital tools in this work. For talent and technology, the author proposes adjusting subject offerings to new industries, training top talent in basic disciplines, reforming vocational education and promoting the conversion of research results into new quality productive forces. On people's wellbeing, Liu stresses fairer access, rural schools, group-based school models and the "double reduction" policy. Social coordination is to rest on government, schools, families and enterprises sharing responsibility, while international influence is to come through opening-up, a "Study in China" brand and vocational cooperation with Belt and Road Initiative countries. Liu concludes that pursuing these six attributes together will give strong support to building China into an education powerhouse. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a local education official translates Xi's national education strategy into concrete policy measures.

Grasping the inner logic of building a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation 深刻把握构筑中华民族共有精神家园的内在逻辑 Li Junjie Writing in Guangming Daily in December 2024, Li Junjie asks how a shared spiritual home for the Chinese nation can be built, and answers by setting out seven interlocking principles that he calls its inner logic. Li presents the task as both a demand of the new era for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and a deeper aim of building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. The piece is a short commentary on Xi Jinping's recent statements on ethnic work. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2024 national conference commending ethnic unity and progress. Li treats these remarks as part of Xi Jinping's important thinking on strengthening and improving ethnic work. Seven sections follow, each starting with "persisting in" a principle and each tied to a quotation from Xi: Party leadership, cultural identity, the forging of a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, people's wellbeing, a correct view of Chinese national history, core socialist values, and broad interaction among ethnic groups. Li argues that the Party's overall leadership is the fundamental political guarantee, and that cultural identity is the root, because Chinese culture is the synthesis of all ethnic cultures. Forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation is called the main thread of ethnic work and of all work in ethnic minority areas. On the material side, Li holds that common modernization needs shared development, and that improving livelihoods and winning hearts should be the starting and end points of development in those areas. The remaining principles concern a correct view of history, with a call to refute mistaken historical views and promote the textbook and history projects on the Chinese nation. They also concern core socialist values, with stronger national common language education, and ethnic interaction, exchange and integration. Li concludes that these principles together bind the peoples of China through shared hearts and spirit and give the building of the community of the Chinese nation a strong cultural and spiritual base. Practical proposals include ethnic unity campaigns, work on ethnic affairs in cities, mutually embedded social structures and communities, and exchange programmes for young people and tourism. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese academic and Party-school writers currently frame ethnic work and the shared spiritual home.

Handling the "five major relationships" correctly: systematically reforming the system of fostering talent 正确处理“五个重大关系” 系统性改革育人体系 Li Jinchang Li Jinchang, a university Party secretary, writing in Guangming Daily in December 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the National Education Conference (September 2024) to handle five major relationships when building a leading country in education. It then lists four shortcomings that Li sees in current university talent training, and closes with four groups of reform measures. Li pairs each relationship with a task: supporting national strategy and meeting people's livelihood needs; knowledge learning and all-round development; training talent and meeting social needs; orderly regulation and vitality; and rooting in China while drawing on international experience. The shortcomings Li names are weak ideological and political education, an incomplete admissions–training–employment chain, gaps in building a high-level teaching force, and weak links between disciplines and talent training. The remedies are Party leadership throughout school governance, integration of the whole admissions-to-employment process, comprehensive reform linking disciplines to specialties and teaching, and faster building of the faculty. Li concludes that universities should apply systems thinking so that their strengths converge on raising the quality of home-grown talent and on producing top-notch innovative talent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university leader turns Xi Jinping's education directives into concrete institutional measures.

Building on the overall "Big Ideological and Political Work" framework to advance supply-side reform of ideological and political education 立足“大思政”工作整体 推动思政教育供给侧改革 Lin Wei This short commentary in Guangming Daily takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the second national education conference of the new era, for China to become a leading education power with strong "ideological and political guidance". Lin first distinguishes the broader \"Big Ideological and Political Work\" framework, which coordinates resources inside and outside the university, from the \"Big Ideological and Political Course\", which focuses on improving the quality of ideological and political courses. Lin stresses that the Big Course is not a new subject: its course character and goal of cultivating socialist builders and successors stay unchanged, so it should be managed within the ideological and political course system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party official frames the practical agenda for ideological and political teaching after the 2024 education conference.

Empowering the "Great Ideological and Political Course" through red study tours 以红色研学赋能“大思政课”建设 Guo Runkui This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily, responds to Xi Jinping's September 2024 speech at the national education conference, which called for the "ideological and political leadership" of a strong education nation. Guo contends that study tours enrich teaching forms, make content more vivid and complement the classroom, linking teaching "in the classroom" with teaching "in social life". The author lists four features: value guidance and spiritual influence, immersive learning in historical settings, integration of varied resources, and teacher–student interaction. These are said to help students form correct values and a sense of national pride. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated educators present red tourism resources as a tool of ideological and political education.

Innovating the allocation of production factors to promote new quality productive forces 创新配置生产要素 推动新质生产力发展 Yan Jiao Zhou Bo This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks how innovative allocation of production factors can drive new quality productive forces. The authors begin with a definition of new quality productive forces: advanced productive forces generated by technological breakthroughs, innovative factor allocation and deep industrial upgrading, with a large rise in total factor productivity as the core marker. They then name four weaknesses despite pilot reforms in market-based factor allocation: uneven quality of scientific and technical talent, low efficiency in allocating resources, insufficiently concentrated capital, and under-used new factors such as data. The rest of the piece is organised around remedies for each. On talent, Yan and Zhou call for an internationally competitive talent system, stronger basic and interdisciplinary disciplines, and high-level innovation platforms. They also urge industry–university–research cooperation on core technology bottlenecks and better conversion of research results. On resources and capital, they urge a green transition in energy and the use of tax incentives, subsidies and special funds to steer capital towards high-technology and strategic emerging industries. They also call for financial reform, including multi-level capital markets and wider financing for small and micro enterprises. On data, they propose standardised collection and processing, secure cross-border flows, and data sharing across regions and departments. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the factor-allocation approach to new quality productive forces as presented in the Party-state press.

Advancing the "big ideological and political course" to strengthen ideological and political guidance in universities A case report on Changshu Institute of Technology 推进“大思政课”建设 增强高校思政引领力 Yuan Man This short piece, published in Guangming Daily on 13 December 2024, is a case report on how Changshu Institute of Technology, a university in Jiangsu, builds what it calls the "big ideological and political course" (da sizheng ke). Yuan presents the university's work as an effort to carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, and to make students both professionally competent and committed to family and country. The article is organised around three areas of work. These are the classroom as the "main channel", the Party-led teaching staff (the "big teaching force"), and the wider "big classroom" of student communities, local red resources, practice teaching and online platforms. Each is illustrated with the university's own measures, programmes and figures. On the classroom side, Yuan describes the Party committee's study scheme, leaders' participation in collective lesson preparation, and a publicity effort built around a network ideological and political centre. On staffing, the article lists four teams: ideological and political teachers, counsellors, full-time and part-time Party and ideological workers, and mental-health teachers. It reports that such staff make up 1.06 per cent of teachers and students and cites teaching awards and research projects. On the wider "big classroom", it describes a "one-stop" student community with a "1+12+N" Party-building model, red-culture resources tied to the local Shajiabang story, practice bases run with governments and enterprises, and online courses and immersive teaching. It will further integrate classroom, community and practice teaching, and train more builders and successors of socialism. Read the original if you want a concrete, institution-level example of how Chinese universities describe the organisation of ideological and political education, including its staffing figures and programme names.

Combining top-level design with crossing the river by feeling the stones 把顶层设计和摸着石头过河相结合 Che Zongkai This newspaper commentary asks how further deepening reform comprehensively should be steered. Che argues that combining top-level design with "crossing the river by feeling the stones" is a reform method rich in Chinese wisdom and consistent with the Marxist theory of knowledge and practice. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at a study session on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), rejecting the claim that feeling the stones is timid or conservative. The article is organised in three parts: why reform needs top-level design, why feeling the stones means seeking truth and laws through practice, and how the two are to be held together. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and refers to the Party's revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform experience. Che holds that scientific top-level design is knowledge that comes from practice and is repeatedly tested by it, as with Mao's "blueprints" for the revolution. Feeling the stones is likewise not blind: it means trial, summing up and wider rollout, as in reform and opening up, so as to find laws through practice. The author stresses that this is not drifting, since it follows laws already understood while deepening that understanding. The two are dialectically unified: local, staged reforms proceed under top-level design, and design is drawn up on the basis of such reforms. Che calls for an overall reform plan, roadmap and timetable aimed at improving socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernising national governance, while avoiding piecemeal measures and constant reversals. In unexplored areas of Chinese modernization, the author urges bold experiments that respect grassroots initiative and yield replicable experience. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary justifies reform methodology through Marxist epistemology.

Actively building China's autonomous knowledge system of pedagogy 积极构建中国自主的教育学知识体系 Jia Yuchao This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks how China can build an autonomous knowledge system of pedagogy (educational studies). It follows Xi Jinping's 2022 remark that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's autonomous knowledge system, and the call in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to do so. Jia Yuchao argues that the route runs from distinctive pedagogical concepts, to "recognised" pedagogical theories, to a high-quality theoretical system. Jia first names three reasons for scholars' lingering uncertainty. Modern Chinese pedagogy is barely a century old and many core concepts were imported. Its knowledge production is insufficiently specialised and relies on other disciplines' methods. It also faces the pressing task of handling the relation between tradition and future. The article then defines "autonomy" through the relation between "self" and "other", and sets out three steps. On Jia's account, a distinctive pedagogical concept must be original, more explanatory and capable of wide uptake. Examples offered are "natural-disposition education" (率性教育), "educational meritocracy" (教育优绩主义), which goes beyond the merely descriptive "utilitarian education", and "inspired teaching" (兴发教学). Such concepts must build on existing Chinese and foreign ideas. A theory becomes "recognised" when its explanatory power makes it a framework that domestic and foreign peers adopt. Jia cites the question of education and new quality productive forces as an example of a theoretical issue, and says China's educational development and its part in global governance support this. Jia concludes that autonomy lies in attending to Chinese educational problems and standpoints and in being recognised as a prevailing analytical paradigm at home and abroad. This would underpin a Chinese educational discourse and the telling of China's education story. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese education scholars interpret the policy call for autonomous knowledge systems.

Making philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics truly stand among the world's academic community Interview with Zhang Donggang, Party Secretary of Renmin University of China 使中国特色哲学社会科学真正屹立于世界学术之林 Zhang Yaxiong This is an interview, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, in which reporter Zhang Yaxiong questions Zhang Donggang, Party Secretary of Renmin University of China. It follows an editors' note that recalls Xi Jinping's call to speed up the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics and an autonomous Chinese knowledge system. Zhang Donggang's answer is that such a system is required by national rejuvenation and Chinese modernization, and that universities must build it deliberately. The interview has three parts. The first explains why the task matters now. The second sets out how to build it and how to judge success. The third turns to the role of universities and the training of a new type of talent, including measures taken at Renmin University. Zhang Donggang gives three reasons for the task. Strength, in this account, is cultural, ideological and civilizational as well as economic. The system is also said to be needed to create a new form of human civilization by shedding conceptual and paradigmatic dependence on Western knowledge systems. It must also support Chinese modernization. He pictures the system as a tower. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era forms the spire. The systematic, theoretical study of the Party's innovative theory is the foundation. The tower's body is the abstraction and explanation of the practice of Chinese modernization, pursued through organised research. International communication of Chinese ideas completes the structure. Success would be judged on five criteria: originality, international influence, discursive evaluative power, capacity to support and serve national needs, and systematic theoretical coherence that overcomes excessive disciplinary fragmentation. For universities, Zhang Donggang proposes six lines of action. They are research on the Party's innovative theory, building the autonomous knowledge system, reshaping the disciplinary layout, strengthening organised research, developing new-type think tanks, and raising global influence by translating concepts such as whole-process people's democracy into accessible language. He says Renmin University has set up six new-type residential colleges, offers continuous undergraduate-to-doctoral training, designs courses around Chinese modernization, has opened more than ten new liberal-arts programmes, and runs practice projects. He calls for breaking the "superstition" of Western models. Read the original if you want an official university leader's account of how the autonomous knowledge system is to be organised, evaluated and taught in practice.

Accelerating the formation of relations of production better suited to new quality productive forces 加快形成同新质生产力更相适应的生产关系 Zhao Chunling Zhao Chunling, writing in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks how relations of production should change to fit new quality productive forces. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statement that developing them requires deepening reform and forming new-type relations of production, Zhao argues that China must speed up building relations of production better matched to them. The author presents this as a continuation and development of the Marxist principle on productive forces and relations of production. The short commentary has two parts. The first sets out why new quality productive forces make new demands on relations of production. The second lists reform measures in four areas: the economic system, science and technology, the allocation of production factors, and opening up. Zhao starts from the basic contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Relations of production are said to act as the link that turns scientific and technological results into a modern industrial system. Without that link, technology remains only a potential productive force. Zhao names five demands: more dynamic innovators, coordinated reform of education, science, technology and talent systems, a fuller market system, more rational factor allocation, and a first-class business environment. On this basis Zhao proposes that the market play the decisive role in resource allocation while government plays its role better, and that the Two Unwaverings be upheld. Zhao also calls for stronger Party leadership of science and technology and a new national system for key technology breakthroughs. Further proposals are a unified national market and wider institutional opening up. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how official theory links new quality productive forces to reform of production relations.

The standing meetings of the People's Committee of the Chinese Soviet Republic and their historical functions An examination based on Red China (Hongse Zhonghua) 中华苏维埃共和国人民委员会常务会议及其历史功能 Lin Xuwu How did the central government of the Chinese Soviet Republic actually handle day-to-day governance? Lin Xuwu takes up this question through the standing meetings (changhui) of the People's Committee, the republic's central executive organ. Lin argues that these meetings were a continuous, regular and stable institution through which the provisional central government debated policy, made collective decisions, supervised localities and managed personnel, and that they offer a concrete view of how the Party governed in the Central Soviet Area. The article rests on reports in Red China, the provisional central government's official newspaper founded in December 1931. According to Lin, the paper carried reports on 39 standing meetings between December 1931 and 15 September 1933. The analysis is organised into three functions: deciding major matters, conducting inspection tours and checks, and issuing decrees and making appointments. On major matters, Lin shows that the meetings dealt with epidemic prevention, education (notably the Lenin Normal School) and above all spring ploughing, which the author links to the priority given to agriculture in Soviet economic construction. The meetings stressed implementation as well as policy: they reviewed provincial decisions, ordered corrections and sent inspectors. Lin identifies a workflow of promoting inspection, hearing reports, collective review and issuing instructions, combined with top-down checks and bottom-up reporting. On decrees and personnel, the author counts 46 decrees and regulations, over 85 per cent of them on economic, political and cultural-educational construction, often drafted at one meeting and passed at a later one and then published in the newspaper. Twenty meetings dealt with appointments, including those of Zhu De and Zhou Enlai to top military posts in May 1933. Lin concludes that the standing meetings strengthened the central government's leadership, let it learn how local governments carried out central policy, and improved local administrative capacity. In the author's reading they also show scientific and democratic decision-making, administration according to law, openness in government affairs and the allocation of Party, government and military cadres. Read the original if you study the institutional history of the Jiangxi Soviet period or want an account of early Communist state administration drawn from the primary source Red China.

Empowering the building of ideological and political courses through culture 以文化赋能思政课建设 Fang Hongli This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, asks how culture can strengthen university and school ideological and political courses (sizheng courses).
