Fang argues that Xi Jinping's thought on culture should shape these courses, making them more persuasive and appealing and supporting their high-quality development. The piece opens with a Beijing 'big ideological and political course' staged at Renmin University for first-year students. The article cites Xi Jinping's May 2024 instruction on these courses, which names Marxism, the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture as their foundations. It then sets out three pairings of approach: political guidance with knowledge teaching, value guidance with cultural transmission, and innovative teaching methods with practical experience. In Fang's account, the courses should explain the standpoint, viewpoint and method of Xi Jinping's thought on culture, so that young people can answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. They should also draw on Marxist cultural theory and on the fit between Marxism and traditional Chinese culture, extending teaching beyond the classroom. Fang cites a scenic, role-playing class at a memorial site for the 1923 railway workers' movement as an example. Teachers are urged to use generative AI, virtual simulation and holographic imaging to build immersive scenes. Fang concludes that culture-based teaching will help the courses fulfil the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, and produce a new generation willing to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official guidance on cultural confidence is translated into proposals for ideological and political teaching.

Integrating labour education into the whole process of talent cultivation in universities 将劳动教育贯穿高校人才培养全过程 Yang Rong Yan Mengqi This short commentary in Guangming Daily asks how universities can carry out labour education across the whole of student training. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's 2020 and 2024 remarks on cultivating well-rounded builders and successors of socialism, Yang and Yan argue that universities should explore concrete implementation paths. Their thesis is that labour education should run through every stage of higher education, every part of the curriculum and every aspect of student life. The article is organised into three sections. The first deals with integrating undergraduate and postgraduate stages. The second covers embedding labour education in the full curriculum under ideological and political guidance. The third addresses weaving it into daily campus life. On staged training, the authors call for separate goals for each level: undergraduates should develop interest and habits, while postgraduates should link labour practice to research and innovation. They propose a joined-up curriculum that combines traditional crafts and farming with new forms of labour such as intelligent manufacturing, together with assessment that mixes process and outcome and quantitative and qualitative criteria. For the curriculum, Yang and Yan want specialist teachers trained to bring labour elements into their courses, and ideological and political courses to draw on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture and Marxist views of labour. Extracurricular practice should be supported through internships, university–enterprise bases and interdisciplinary projects. For campus life, the authors recommend including housekeeping and cleaning in behavioural norms, running labour-themed lectures, competitions and volunteer service, and setting up labour weeks or months. They present these measures as a way to build the labour values and abilities of a new generation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official guidance on labour education is turned into university practice.

Upholding the "Two Integrations" to build a self-reliant Chinese system of economic knowledge 坚持“两个结合” 建构中国自主的经济学知识体系 Chen Xudong This newspaper commentary, published after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) called for a self-reliant Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge, asks how to build a self-reliant Chinese system of economic knowledge. Chen Xudong answers that the Two Integrations (combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture) supply the methodological guide. The piece has three parts: the fundamental principles behind the project, the three systems (disciplines, scholarship, discourse) that must be built, and the coordination of forces needed to support it, namely personnel, textbooks and international communication. Chen argues, citing Engels, that political economy is a historical science, so economic theory must grow from practice. Integrating Marxism with Chinese realities is the logical starting point, because reform and development practice raises new questions requiring original concepts and theories. Integrating it with traditional culture means keeping Marxism as the "soul" and traditional culture as the "root". Chen cites the concept of a moderately prosperous society as a model of creative transformation of traditional economic thought into language ordinary people understand. The author calls for strengthening political economy, the history of economic thought and economic history, and developing fields such as the digital economy and humanistic economics. Chen proposes mobilising the "five armies" of researchers, with universities as the main force, and building a textbook system that reflects Marxism adapted to China and Xi Jinping Thought-guided priorities. Chen also calls for international journals, platforms and conferences to present Chinese concepts and proposals. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official discourse frames the task of building Chinese economics.

Pathways for building an autonomous knowledge system in area studies 区域国别学自主知识体系的建构路径 Zhai Xiufeng Zhai Xiufeng, writing in Guangming Daily, takes up how China's area studies (regional and country studies, quyu guobie xue) can build a knowledge system of its own. The starting point is the "dialectical unity" of representing China and representing the world. Zhai argues that an autonomous system must rest on a Chinese standpoint and Chinese practice, while also consciously rebuilding global concepts and global discourse. The route is a holistic understanding of research objects together with stronger global collaboration in knowledge production. The article has three parts. The first sets out the value basis of knowledge autonomy, including a short account of colonial-era Orientalism and Cold War area studies in the United States. The second concerns coordinating domestic construction with international dissemination, and the third asks how area studies can drive paradigm innovation in the social sciences more broadly. Africa studies serves as the main illustration. Zhai identifies two epistemological problems: fragmented, partial research, and the difficulty of uniting China and other countries in seeking independent international expression. Zhai holds that Western knowledge systems carried hierarchical or dualist worldviews that reinforced geopolitical hegemony, so these worldviews must be "disenchanted". Researchers should begin with basic questions, such as how to understand Africa and the Global South, rather than "stamp-collecting" or hastily produced policy-driven studies. Zhai also argues that autonomy depends on openness: scholars should cooperate with those from the countries studied, whose subject perspective outsiders cannot replace, and should critically reuse Western fieldwork records. Zhai further calls for platforms for knowledge production in the Global South. Zhai proposes that the newly established discipline serve as a testing ground for reform of philosophy and social sciences. Specific proposals include original problem-awareness, on-the-ground fieldwork, multidisciplinary teams, a more diverse research workforce, and evaluation systems that go beyond quantitative metrics. Zhai also calls for curricula that add global history and plural civilizations, and for original concepts rather than copied or undigested foreign ones. The aim is deep dialogue among countries' cultural traditions, development paths and ideas of modernization, leading to mutual learning among civilizations. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from within China's academic establishment, of how area studies is expected to contribute to an autonomous knowledge system.

In what respects the idea of self-reform inherits and develops Mao Zedong's thought on Party building 自我革命思想在哪些方面继承和发展了毛泽东党的建设思想 Li Jie Li Jie asks how the idea of the Party's self-reform, formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), relates to Mao Zedong's thought on Party building. The author argues that self-reform is an original contribution of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Li's account, it moves the Party's long search for a way out of the historical cycle of rise and decline from a "first answer" to a "second answer", and it inherits and develops Mao's thought in four respects. The article is a short theoretical essay in four parts, each pairing a Maoist principle with its post-2012 development. The four topics are the view of the people, the view of discipline, building the Party ideologically, and the "Two Musts". Each part quotes Mao's texts and Xi Jinping's statements, and each names the relationship that the new thought is said to handle better under present conditions. On the people, Li treats serving the people wholeheartedly and the mass line as Mao's red thread, which Xi extends by putting "putting the people first" at the head of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On discipline, Li links Mao's 1938 restatement of Party discipline to the present stress on intra-Party regulations, on placing discipline ahead of law, and on the "four forms" of supervision, which is said to improve the handling of Party discipline and state law. On ideology, Mao's rectification campaigns and the Yan'an model of education lead to the concentrated study campaigns of recent years, with Party political building leading all other areas. On the "Two Musts", Li presents Mao's Yan'an "first answer", that the people must supervise the government, as completed by the "second answer" of self-reform. Li cites the anti-corruption campaign as evidence, and sets it against those who praise Western multiparty rotation and the separation of powers. Li concludes that the Party must not lose itself amid praise, and must keep to the spirit of self-reform. Quoting Xi, Li calls for a "great self-reform" to lead a "great social revolution", and the reverse, so that the Party remains the core of leadership. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how current Party-building doctrine is tied to Mao's thought, and of how Party media frame the claim of a "second answer".

Mao Zedong's historic contribution to cultural development in China and its significance for today 毛泽东对中国文化建设的历史性贡献及其时代意义 Li Nan Li Nan asks what Mao Zedong and the Communists around him contributed to building Chinese culture, and why that contribution still matters. The article argues that their exploration and practice gave Chinese cultural development a clear direction, a practical path and a basis for confidence. In Li's account, this work is an important source of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and of the Party's new cultural mission in the new era. The article opens by recalling Xi Jinping's remarks at the meeting marking the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth. It is then organised in four parts: Marxism as the guide to the direction of cultural development; the historical mission Mao took up in response to his times; the "three adherences" that opened a practical path; and the combination of theory and practice that built cultural confidence. Li draws on Mao's writings from the New Democratic period and the early People's Republic, including On New Democracy and the 1956 speech launching the "Hundred Flowers" policy. Li's central claim is that Mao held Marxism to be the guiding thought of new culture, while not wanting it to replace Chinese culture. Mao treated imperialist and semi-feudal culture as enemies to be overthrown, and in the 1950s warned against non-Marxist influences. Li presents Marxism, in Mao's view, as guiding the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, and as needing to take a national form. The practical path rests on three adherences: serving the people and socialism; "letting a hundred flowers bloom and a hundred schools of thought contend"; and creative transformation and innovative development. Li adds that Mao took in foreign culture selectively and opposed wholesale Westernisation, while also refusing to cut off the nation's own history. Li concludes that Mao's cultural theory and practice enriched Marxist cultural theory with a distinctively Chinese style. In the author's reading, it also laid the foundation for the Party's cultural confidence, which Xi Jinping Thought on culture has since raised to a new level. Li holds that this inheritance supplies ideological resources and spiritual momentum for Chinese modernization, for building a strong cultural nation and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Mao's cultural policy is presented as a source of the current Party line on culture.

From Mao Zedong to Deng Xiaoping: historical lessons from the establishment and re-establishment of the Party's ideological line of seeking truth from facts 从毛泽东到邓小平：党的实事求是思想路线确立与重新确立的历史启示 Hu Zhenrong How was the Communist Party's ideological line of seeking truth from facts first established, lost and recovered, and what does that history teach the Party today? Hu Zhenrong argues that Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping form two peaks in this history: Mao as its founder, Deng as its defender who restored and re-established it. Despite different eras, tasks and forms, Hu holds that the line's essential meaning and basic principles stayed the same. The article traces the line from Mao's first use of the term "ideological line" in 1929 and his adoption of "seeking truth from facts" at the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (1938), through the Yan'an rectification movement, to its deviation after 1957 and its restoration at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Hu organises the account into seven lessons, each ending with a call for "the new era and new journey". These cover the line's fragility, its philosophical basis, subjectivism, investigation and emancipating the mind, the role of great figures, democratic centralism, and the line's evolving content. Hu's central claim is that the line is at root a philosophical proposition, so its establishment and re-establishment both depended on raising the Party's Marxist theoretical level. Mao supplied the philosophical argument in On Practice and On Contradiction, while Deng used the debate on practice as the sole criterion of truth, and criticism of the "two whatevers", to break dogmatism. Hu names subjectivism, grounded in dogmatic readings of the classics, as the line's opposite. He says it is overcome by understanding China's national conditions and by a Marxist style of study: Mao's investigation and research, Deng's emancipation of the mind. Hu also credits the personal integrity of both leaders and the strengthening of democratic centralism. Hu concludes that the line is the Party's lifeline and that guarding it against deviation requires Marxist education, Party-spirit training, institutional safeguards such as democratic centralism, and continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. He ties this to the primary stage of socialism as the "general basis" for Chinese modernization, and to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how official scholarship presents the continuity between Mao's and Deng's ideological lines and draws lessons for current Party building.

Learning from Mao Zedong's spirit of independent exploration and practice 学习毛泽东同志独立自主的探索和实践精神 Qu Qingshan Written for the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth (2024) and first published in Study Times, this commentary asks what the Party should draw from Mao's principle of independence and self-reliance (独立自主). Qu Qingshan argues that this principle is one of the three basic aspects of the "living soul" of Mao Zedong Thought, and that it remains a guide for the Party's work in the new era. The article is organised chronologically in four parts. It first treats the Party's early subordination to the Communist International and the turning point of the Zunyi Conference (1935). It then traces how the principle was set out and applied from the 1930s to the 1960s, using the Yangtze crossing decision, Mao's rejection of Khrushchev's proposals and the "two bombs, one satellite" programme. It closes with the principle's development under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. Qu's central claim is that the Party only truly understood independence from Zunyi onwards, after years of following Comintern directives that, in Qu's account, produced serious losses and allowed Wang Ming's leftist dogmatism to dominate. Qu presents the 1949 decision to cross the Yangtze, despite the advice carried by Anastas Mikoyan on behalf of Stalin, and the 1958 refusal of a joint submarine fleet and a long-wave radio station, as classic cases of independence. Qu also holds that the Soviet withdrawal of experts strengthened self-reliance, and that without independence there would have been no revolutionary victory and no socialist construction. Qu says Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping carried the principle forward, citing Deng's statements that foreign models cannot be copied and Xi's calls for self-confidence and self-reliance, and for refusing lectures from abroad. Qu calls for independence in the development path, theoretical innovation, the economy, science and technology, defence and diplomacy, in order to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how Party commentary uses the Comintern period and Sino-Soviet disputes to support the case for self-reliance today.

Mao Zedong's method of "persuasion and education" and its lessons for today 毛泽东同志“说服教育”方法及现实启示 Fan Yingyuan Ma Hongling This article asks how Mao Zedong's method of "persuasion and education" (shuofu jiaoyu) arose and what it offers ideological and political work today. Fan and Ma argue that the method, systematised in Mao's talk "On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People", rests on a historical-materialist outlook and gives the Party's ideological and political work a distinctive character. They treat that work as the Party's lifeline and a core political strength. The article has three parts. The first traces the method's formation from the 1927 Sanwan reorganisation and the Gutian Conference resolution, through Mao's 1944 addition on revolutionary political work as the lifeline of the army, to the post-1949 extension of political work to economic and social construction. The second sets out three principles of the method: its human-centred character, its thoroughness and its practical orientation. The third draws out lessons for the present. The authors build on Mao's distinction between antagonistic contradictions with enemies and non-antagonistic contradictions among the people, which they say are matters of right and wrong. Ideological questions among the people, they report Mao as saying, can be settled only by democratic methods of discussion, criticism and persuasion, not coercion, along the path of "unity–criticism–unity". The authors read persuasion as the "self-education of the people". They hold that administrative orders should be accompanied by persuasion and that everyone needs remoulding, exploiters and labourers alike. They also argue that remoulding comes through long practice as well as books, and that theory must be thorough to persuade thoroughly. From these principles the authors derive three recommendations for the new era. Ideological work should strengthen its people-centred orientation and its guiding power, using language close to ordinary people and responding to their aspirations for a better life. It should deepen theoretical research so that workers in the field understand Party theory thoroughly and give it scholarly grounding. It should also innovate in practice, through practical teaching, cultural resources and media convergence, using "drip irrigation" and immersive experience. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language statement of how Mao's persuasion method is presented in current ideological and political education scholarship.

How Marxism understands "productive forces" 马克思主义如何理解“生产力” Zhao Yujie This short commentary in Study Times asks what Marxism means by "productive forces" and how the concept develops over time. Zhao argues that Marx defines productive forces as humanity's capacity to transform and use nature, and that the Communist Party of China has deepened this understanding through successive stages of liberating and developing them. The article first sets out Marx's and Engels's definition, drawing mainly on The German Ideology and Capital. It then covers the social role of productive forces and traces the Party's treatment of the concept from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping through the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping. Zhao presents productive forces as both a natural and a social relation, with objective and historical features. The author holds that Marx's three elements (labourers, means of labour and objects of labour) go beyond Western theory's capital, labour and land. In Zhao's account, productive forces are the basic driving force of social contradictions and the final determinant of historical development, in line with historical materialism. The article then reads new quality productive forces as an innovation within this tradition, describing new demands on workers, technology-driven means of labour and emerging industries as objects of labour. Zhao concludes that, guided by Marx's theory, the Party has proceeded from the fundamental interests of the people and kept deepening Marxist understanding of productive forces. The article presents new quality productive forces as important for self-reliance in science and technology, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Party writers link Marx's concept of productive forces to current policy.

How does Marxism understand "heroes"? 马克思主义如何理解“英雄” Li Junshi This short commentary from the Study Times asks how Marxism understands the "hero". Li Junshi argues that the Marxist view of the masses as makers of history does not deny the achievements of heroic figures. In Li's account, the Marxist conception rests on a dialectical grasp of the relation between the people and outstanding individuals. The piece first looks at how Marx and Engels use the word "hero", then at the basic principles of historical materialism behind that usage. It then turns to Lenin and Plekhanov on the role of the individual. It ends with the heroic culture of the Communist Party of China. Li distinguishes two usages in Marx and Engels. In The Civil War in France, praise for the Communards' "heroism" (Heldenmut) is praise for courage and willingness to sacrifice. In The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Engels uses "heroic age" neutrally for a stage of Greek social development. Li argues that Marxism opposes the "heroic" view of history because it severs heroes from the masses and attributes their deeds to personal talent alone. Outstanding individuals can have great influence, in Li's reading, but only by drawing on the wisdom and strength of the people. Li cites Lenin and Plekhanov for the point that social conditions set the scope of individual influence. Li concludes that Chinese Communist heroic culture joins this historical-materialist outlook with the traditional Chinese esteem for moral character. Li gives Liu Hulan and Zhang Side as ordinary people who became model heroes, and cites Xi Jinping's remark that the new era is one that makes heroes. Read the original if you want a brief, official-register account of how Party theory reconciles the people-centred view of history with the celebration of heroes.

How does Marxism understand "happiness"? 马克思主义如何理解“幸福” Jin Jiaojiao Zhang Lili Prompted by Xi Jinping's remark that the people's happy life is "earned through work" and by the 20th Party Congress (2022) report on improving people's wellbeing, this short commentary from Study Times asks how Marxism understands happiness. Jin and Zhang answer that Marxism sees happiness as a unity of three pairs: subjective pursuit and objective creation, material abundance and spiritual richness, and individual development and social progress. The authors first contrast Marx with earlier sensualist and rationalist views of happiness. They then take each of the three unities in turn and name the corresponding outlook: a practice-based, a comprehensive and a people's view of happiness. The final section applies these to the tasks set out by the 20th Party Congress. Jin and Zhang argue that Marx starts from the \"real person\", who has needs and aims but acts under inherited conditions. Practice joins subjective pursuit to objective creation, so happiness is built up through creative activity. Material abundance is a basic condition, but in the authors' reading Marx held that capital fetishism and alienated labour turn people into slaves of money and produce unhappiness. Happiness therefore requires both material and spiritual fullness. Finally, because human essence is the ensemble of social relations, personal happiness cannot be separated from that of the people. The authors cite Marx's youthful essay on choosing a profession and his answer \"struggle\" when asked what happiness is, and they point to communism as the point where individual and social development coincide. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization should rest on these three views. They call for a spirit of struggle and innovation, for material conditions together with advanced socialist culture, and for fulfilling the people's aspiration for a better life through common prosperity. They add that China's modernization will bring benefits to the wider world. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-press statement of how Marx's idea of happiness is linked to current policy language.

How theoretical outreach can be "reasoned, engaging and useful" 理论宣讲如何做到“有理有趣有用” Wen Lihua This short commentary, first published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao), asks how theoretical outreach (lilun xuanjiang) can reach ordinary people effectively. Wen Lihua calls such outreach a key link in arming the whole Party with theory. The author's thesis is that it must be "reasoned" (youli), "engaging" (youqu) and "useful" (youyong) in order to cover the "last kilometre" and bring the Party's innovative theory into ordinary households. The piece takes these three requirements in turn, each with three practical points. It frames them within the principles of political orientation as the soul, content as the king and innovation as the key. On being "reasoned", Wen urges lecturers to master the Marxist stance, viewpoint and method behind a topic, to bring out its links with fine traditional Chinese culture, and to extend it with frontier knowledge and current issues. On being "engaging", Wen stresses clear priorities and genuine questions, real emotion conveyed through small stories about people nearby, and internal coherence through devices such as a single running case or chains of questions. Wen also calls for interaction with audiences through online and offline formats. On being "useful", the author proposes skills-based sessions tied to local production, "order-from-the-menu" sessions in which people choose topics, and tailor-made sessions on urgent public concerns. Wen concludes that lecturers should answer people's doubts with sound theory and with examples from the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The aim, in the author's account, is to strengthen the people's historical initiative and build strength for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media frame practical guidance for propaganda and education work.

How Marxism understands "true philosophy" 马克思主义如何理解“真正的哲学” Xu Hengbing Zhang Xiaoxu Writing in Study Times, Xu Hengbing and Zhang Xiaoxu ask how Marxism understands "true philosophy". They argue that Marx, while founding dialectical and historical materialism through a sustained critique of older philosophy, especially German philosophy, repeatedly set out what a true philosophy is, and that his view can be read along three dimensions. The short commentary draws on Marx's early editorial on the Kölnische Zeitung, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, with a supporting reference to Engels. It then turns to the present, linking the discussion to the Party's current theoretical work. The authors say that, first, a true philosophy belongs to its time: it responds to the era's "pressing questions" and, by grasping the general laws of social development, becomes real knowledge rather than empty speculation. For Marx and Engels these questions were where capitalism and human history were heading and how human emancipation could be achieved. Second, a true philosophy is a philosophy of the people. It serves the great majority rather than the ruling class, and Marx's starting point of "real individuals" and his goal of a "community of free individuals" express its commitment to universal emancipation. Third, it is tied to practice: it aims not only to interpret the world but to change it, and becomes a material force only when it grips the masses. The authors conclude that Marxist philosophy lasts because it opens a path to truth, not because it exhausts truth. They state that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has used this worldview and methodology to form the "six musts", part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They urge readers to study these in continuity with Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-press account of Marx's conception of philosophy and how it is linked to current official theory.

The four purposes of emancipating the mind 解放思想的四重旨归 Xiao Yingsheng This short commentary, published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao), asks what emancipating the mind (解放思想) is for at a time when comprehensive deepening of reform is under way. Xiao argues that it is the master switch for liberating productive forces and social vitality, and that it has four purposes, which the article sets out in turn. The piece is organised as four short sections, each beginning "emancipating the mind aims to…". It draws on Lenin, Mao Zedong and repeated quotations from Xi Jinping, and places the argument in the context of reform and the "great changes unseen in a century". The first two purposes are negative. Xiao says emancipating the mind breaks the grip of habit and subjective bias, which Xiao links to ossified thinking and dogmatism, citing Lenin on the power of habit among millions. It also breaks through ideological obstacles and entrenched interests, so that people are freed from path dependence, departmentalism, vicious "involution" competition and fear of difficulty. The other two are constructive. Emancipating the mind unifies thinking around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which Xiao describes as the Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. It also serves to seek truth from facts more fully, which Xiao ties to a problem-oriented approach. Xiao concludes that practice, theoretical innovation and emancipation of the mind are all without end. The author calls for answering four kinds of questions: those of China, the world, the people and the times. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party media frame emancipating the mind in the current reform period.

Cultivating a new generation for the era who keep "the nation's top priorities" in mind 培养心怀“国之大者”的时代新人 Song Yang This commentary, first published in Study Times, asks how university educators can cultivate young people who keep "the nation's top priorities" (guo zhi da zhe) in mind. Song argues that ideological and political education must make youth believers, dedicated contributors and strivers who tie personal aims to national rejuvenation. Writing from the standpoint of a university teacher, Song starts from the 20th Party Congress (2022) hopes for youth and from the "great changes unseen in a century". The piece is organised in three parts, each naming a type of person to be cultivated: believers, dedicated contributors and strivers. On belief, Song calls for guiding students to hold firm faith in Marxism and in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Song urges them to reject "involution" and "lying flat" and to fold the "small self" into the "greater self" of the Chinese Dream, using Party history, practical service and traditional culture. On dedication, teachers are asked to embody the spirit of educators, truly study and believe Party theory, bring it into classrooms and become "great teachers" who unite scholarly and moral instruction. On striving, Song asks teachers to break out of mental habits and comfort zones and to encourage innovation, research and ambitious life goals in students. Song concludes that educators should carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and become ideological and political "great teachers". The aim is a new generation who are patriotic, dedicated, able to bear heavy responsibility and trusted by the Party. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school educators frame youth cultivation in ideological and political education.

Integrating discourse into the course: method innovation in university ideological and political theory courses 话语融课：高校思政课的方法创新 Dai Yuqi Dai Yuqi, writing in Study Times, asks how university ideological and political theory courses can become more appealing and effective. The author argues that renewing the discourse system should lead the renewal of teaching methods. Dai names four classroom problems: grand talk, hard talk, stale talk and the teacher's solo monologue. The commentary asks teachers first to settle "whom to teach, what to teach and how to teach", and to keep to fundamental principles while innovating. It then sets out four paired shifts in how teachers speak: big talk told small, hard talk told softly, old talk told anew, and talk shared by many voices. On the first pair, Dai holds that teachers must keep a correct political orientation and explain the "big" principles. They should also open themes through everyday cases and local resources, linking the "small classroom of ideological and political education" to the "big classroom of society". On the second, Dai relies on Xi Jinping's call to unite indoctrination with inspiration. Firm language suits stating political positions and criticism, while softer language suits building rapport, and teachers should switch between them. For the third, Dai proposes fresh cases and vocabulary, teaching differentiated by audience, integrated teaching across school stages, and online language. For the fourth, Dai calls for a "big ideological and political course" in which schools, families and society cooperate and in which policymakers, grassroots workers, beneficiaries and students also speak. Dai concludes that discourse innovation helps the courses keep pace with the times and become more targeted, approachable and effective. The author's stated aim is to unify students' knowledge, emotion, will and action, and to produce new-era people who take up the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Marxism school dean frames pedagogical method in official terms.

A four-dimensional path to building a high-quality "Great Ideological and Political Course" 高质量构建“大思政课”的四维路径 Lu Mingchuan Writing in Study Times, Lu Mingchuan asks how universities can build a high-quality "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) in the new era. Lu argues that the key is the irreplaceable role of the school of Marxism, which should construct a "great curriculum", a "great teaching force", a "great classroom" and a "great mechanism". The short commentary opens by noting that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee has given ideological and political courses an important place in education. It defines the "Great Course" as one whose essence is the course, whose core is ideology and politics, and whose distinctive feature is scale. It then takes the four dimensions in turn. On curriculum, Lu calls for a graded sequence of required courses, a wider platform of electives, and coordination between ideological-political courses and "ideological and political elements in all courses", with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as core content. On teachers, Lu proposes strengthening full-time staff while adding visiting professors, part-time teachers, counsellors and student peer mentors. On classrooms, the author wants classroom teaching joined to social practice, with students "going out" and practitioners "invited in". On mechanisms, Lu urges integrating ideological education across primary, secondary and university levels and drawing in schools, families and society, with the school of Marxism taking the lead. The aim, in the author's words, is a social "grand chorus" of ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school theorists frame the organisational design of university ideological and political education.

How to do interactive communication of the Party's innovative theory well 怎样做好党的创新理论互动式传播 Zhang Liwei Writing in Study Times, Zhang Liwei asks how the Party's innovative theory can move from reaching audiences' eyes and ears to winning their minds and hearts in the digital media environment. The author argues that one-way, didactic communication is increasingly limited as information flows become decentralised, layered and fragmented. Interactive communication, marked by two-way exchange, instant feedback and social sharing, is presented as the key route to better reach and uptake. The commentary first argues that interactive communication must be treated as a compulsory course rather than an elective. It then sets out three practical areas: building a team of theory communicators skilled across all media, creating a communication chain in which audiences feel known and involved, and acting on several fronts in cyberspace. Zhang says news media and platforms already develop comment, bullet-screen and sharing functions, while communication of the Party's theory lags because its necessity is underestimated. The author calls for retraining communicators to shift from a communicator-centred to an audience-centred outlook, while keeping to the political task of arming the whole Party and educating the people. Agenda-setting should address audiences' real concerns through differentiated messaging. Participation should be built in through likes, quizzes, voting and rewards, with opinion leaders, Party school and Marxism school teachers, and online speaking teams. Young people are singled out as the key audience and as agents of secondary dissemination. Zhang concludes that short video, livestreaming, big data, VR and AR should be used to create hit interactive products. Interaction is described as one dimension of communication, to be combined with lightweight, immersive and targeted communication in an integrated system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writers frame the communication of official theory for social media and young audiences.

Understanding the distinctive features of the Chinese nation's modern civilization from the perspective of the "Second Integration" 从“第二个结合”角度理解中华民族现代文明的特质 Zang Fengyu Zang Fengyu, writing in the Study Times, asks what defines the modern civilization of the Chinese nation when seen through the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The author argues that this integration gave Marxism a Chinese cultural character, strengthened the cultural foundations of the Party's theory and consolidated the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. On this basis, Zang says, Chinese modernization has produced a modern civilization with a distinct historical depth and contemporary character. The piece is a short theoretical commentary organised around three claims. Modern civilization of the Chinese nation is said to concretise the Marxist view of civilization in China, to realise the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, and to accomplish a transition in modern civilization that creates a new form of human civilization. It closes with practical tasks for cultural work. Zang reads Marx and Engels as treating civilization dialectically: capital's civilizing role created vast productive forces while resting on class antagonism, and a future society was to inherit these gains while sublating capitalist civilization. In Zang's account, Chinese modernization is the practical setting where this view is applied, and Marxism and five thousand years of Chinese civilization mutually fulfil each other. Zang further contends that a people-centred path, rather than one driven by capital, materialism and external expansion, shows that capital-led civilization is not the only form of modernity. Xi Jinping Thought on Culture is presented as an open system that enriches Marxist cultural theory. Zang concludes that Chinese, socialist and modern civilization have been unified in a historically specific way, offering what the author calls a Chinese approach to humanity's search for better social systems. The author calls for building a disciplinary, academic and discourse system for civilization studies, improving mechanisms for fostering civilization, and strengthening China's cultural soft power. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Second Integration is used in official-academic discourse to frame Chinese modernization as a new form of civilization.

How does Marxism understand "cooperation"? 马克思主义如何理解“协作” Zhang Bin This short commentary in Study Times asks how Marxism understands "cooperation" (xiezuo), which Marx defines as many people working together according to plan in the same or in connected production processes. Zhang argues that cooperation creates a collective productive force greater than the sum of individual labours, and that Marx's theory still guides practice today. The article first traces cooperation through history: the Great Wall and the pyramids, integrated manufactures, and factory production under large-scale machine industry. It then sets out why cooperation raises productivity and discusses management in capitalist cooperation. Zhang explains the productivity gain through three features drawn from Marx and Engels. Cooperation has identity, shortening necessary labour time through joint action. It has systemic character, extending or concentrating the space of work and saving costs. It has a social character, stimulating competition and allowing complementary roles. Zhang adds that large-scale cooperation needs direction, like an orchestra conductor, but that capitalist management is dual: it organises social labour and also serves the valorisation of capital. Because capitalists pay for independent labour-power rather than cooperative labour-power, the extra productive force costs them nothing, which Zhang reads as deepening exploitation. Zhang concludes that, as socialised production deepens, cooperation matters more, and calls for better cooperation between sectors, organisations and countries. For the development of new quality productive forces, Zhang proposes deeper integration of industries, of the digital and real economies, and of industry, universities and research, under the Party's leadership. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-press account of Marx's theory of cooperation and its link to current policy language.

How Marxism understands the "conception of history" 马克思主义如何理解“历史观” Zhang Hong Zhang Hong's short commentary asks what the Marxist conception of history is. The author argues that it is a practical materialist view of history, starting from "real human beings" and objective laws of history. In Zhang's account, it surpasses humanist conceptions of history and shifts inquiry from "how is the world possible" to "how is human emancipation possible". The article first traces how Marx's view took shape, from the Rheinische Zeitung and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher through the 1844 manuscripts, The Holy Family and the Theses on Feuerbach. It then follows the view to The German Ideology, which Zhang says marks the formation of historical materialism, and on to the Communist Manifesto, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and Capital. It then sets out five features of the conception. The five features are as follows. Its premise is real, living individuals. Its cornerstone is practice. Its basic theory is the relation of social being to social consciousness, with the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production as the motor of history. Its subject is the people, who make history under inherited conditions. Its direction is towards communism, a free association of individuals in which, Zhang says, capitalism is ultimately replaced by socialism and communism. Zhang concludes that this is the "only scientific conception of history". The author calls for opposing historical nihilism, drawing on a "grand view of history" to understand a century of Party history, and strengthening the discipline, academic and discourse systems of research on national, Party and military history. Zhang also urges tighter guidance of propaganda and media to protect the dominance of historical materialism in ideology. Read the original if you want a compact, officially oriented outline of the Marxist conception of history and its link to the campaign against historical nihilism.

Advancing the integration of ideological and political courses across primary, secondary and university levels through reform 在改革中推进大中小学思政课一体化建设 Li Baogeng This commentary, originally published in Study Times, asks how the integrated construction of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) across primary school, middle school and university can be advanced through further reform. Li Baogeng argues that integration serves the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and marks the direction of reform in these courses. Despite steady progress, Li holds that challenges remain in teaching content, teaching methods and coordination among teachers. Li opens with Xi Jinping's 2019 call to treat integration as an important project and with the Third Plenum Decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which endorses integrated reform and innovation. The article then takes three problem areas in turn: content, teaching methods and the teaching force. On content, Li says textbooks for different stages are written by different departments and experts, producing repetition and weak links. The author proposes re-sequencing material to match students' cognitive development, with difficulty rising in a spiral, and drawing on both education experts and frontline teachers. On method, Li notes that lecturing dominates and practice is scarce, and recommends differentiated approaches by stage, from vivid, intuitive teaching in primary school to theoretical lectures at university. Li also proposes practical elements such as VR, museum partnerships and cooperation with communities and enterprises. On teachers, Li describes each stage's teachers working in isolation and calls for cross-stage teaching-research communities, regular joint sessions with peer commentary from adjacent stages, and national and local digital resource banks. Li concludes that effective integration requires stronger top-level design, better mechanisms for educating students, a stronger teaching force, innovative methods and better allocation of resources. These measures, Li says, will lay a solid foundation for training a new generation capable of shouldering national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the practical reform measures proposed for integrating ideological and political courses across school stages.

Upholding the scientific methodology of proceeding from reality in everything Xi Jinping's emphasis on "adapting measures to local conditions" 坚持一切从实际出发的科学方法论 Huang Xu This short commentary in Study Times takes up the principle of "adapting measures to local conditions" (yindi zhiyi), which Huang Xu defines as adopting measures suited to the actual circumstances of each environment. Huang argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping has applied this principle across many policy areas, and that studying these statements matters for dialectical thinking and a systems approach in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The article proceeds chronologically through seven areas, each anchored in dated remarks by Xi: poverty alleviation, new-type urbanization, agriculture, rural areas and farmers, ideological and political theory courses, ecological civilization, and new quality productive forces. Each section pairs Xi's remarks, delivered between 2012 and 2024, with a short account of current tasks. Huang's core move is to present the principle as a single scientific method running through very different fields. In poverty work it meant targeting measures to households and villages, which Huang says historically resolved absolute poverty. In urbanization, rural policy and ecology it meant respecting natural conditions, resource limits and local features. In education it meant applying uniform national requirements flexibly by time, place and student, and in technology policy it means developing new quality productive forces according to local conditions. Huang concludes that each field needs further reform: higher-quality urbanization, food security and rural revitalization, closer links between school courses and young people's needs, deeper ecological reform, and stronger scientific innovation and opening up. The piece is a compact overview of how official discourse frames this method. Read the original if you want a quick, dated inventory of Xi Jinping's statements on local adaptation across policy areas.

How Marxism understands "belief" 马克思主义如何理解“信仰” Yao Chong Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that faith in Marxism is the political soul of Communists, Yao Chong asks what Marxism itself means by "belief" (xinyang). The commentary, published in Study Times, argues that belief in Marxism is the internalisation of a scientific theory in people's inner world. Yao holds that this internalisation must begin with Marx's own conception of belief. The piece first traces how Marx rebuilt the concept through value critiques of earlier beliefs: religion and Hegelian philosophy, bourgeois political ideals, and the fetishism of commodities, money and capital. It then turns to why humans need belief and what separates Marx's version from blind worship of existing powers. It closes by linking belief to the communist ideal of human freedom and liberation. Yao contends that Marx exposed religion and speculative philosophy as ideological tools of ruling classes. He also exposed bourgeois ideals of right, freedom and democracy as protecting a minority, and showed how fetishism leaves workers ruled by their own creations. Real freedom, in this reading, requires changing social relations and modes of production. Marxist belief is therefore tied to practice: scientific truth is internalised as a guide to action and tested in social practice. Yao says it joins ultimate concern with practical concern. Communism is presented as a "real movement" rather than an abstract ideal, and human liberation as an open possibility, not a predetermined outcome. Yao concludes that grasping Marx's view of belief allows Party members and cadres to build communist belief. The author presents this as a source of spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, amid what is called great changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a short Party-press account of how Marx's critique of religion and fetishism is used to ground communist belief.

Using Marxism to activate the fine elements of traditional Chinese culture 用马克思主义激活中华传统文化中的优秀因子 Yang Hongyuan This short commentary in Study Times asks how Marxism can "activate" the fine elements of traditional Chinese culture, and what makes that possible. Yang Hongyuan argues that activation is an important route for developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics in the new era, and that it can be understood through four aspects: its agent, its preconditions, its process and its result. Yang treats activation as a core content of the Two Integrations, drawing throughout on Xi Jinping's statements. The piece moves from Marxism's leading role, to two preconditions, to the Communist Party as agent, and finally to the outcome of the combination. Yang contends that the "with" in combining Marxism and fine traditional culture implies a primary and a secondary partner, with Marxism leading as both worldview and methodology. Only the fine elements, not the whole of tradition, are to be activated. The author lists benevolence, people-based governance, good faith, justice, harmony and great unity, and holds that these fit Marxism's view of the individual as socially situated, its goal of free and全面 human development, and its socialist values. The Party is the agent: Yang says it links more than a century of Party history with five thousand years of civilisation, giving that civilisation a modern form and grounding a shared cultural subjectivity. Yang concludes that the fit leads to an organic combination, which Xi calls a "chemical reaction" rather than a "platter", producing a new cultural life-form. In Yang's account this created a cultural form of Chinese modernization, opened the treasury of fine traditional elements, strengthened cultural confidence and subjectivity, and prepared exchange with other civilisations. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style statement of how the Two Integrations is framed in Party cultural theory.

Giving full play to universities' distinctive role in building China's independent knowledge system 发挥高校在建构中国自主知识体系中的独特作用 Ren Youqun Writing in the Party newspaper Study Times (Xuexi Shibao), Ren Youqun, identified as Party secretary of Shandong University, asks how universities should contribute to building China's independent knowledge system. The commentary starts from Xi Jinping's call to build such a system and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which stressed an innovation project in philosophy and social sciences. Ren argues that universities, with their full range of disciplines, cultural accumulation and talent, have a distinctive mission in basic theoretical innovation, system-building and external communication. The piece is organised in four sections, each tied to a task for universities. These are serving the drive to become a leading education country through philosophy and social science innovation; producing original knowledge by means of theoretical innovation; strengthening Party leadership and comprehensive reform of higher education; and building organised, collaborative research while raising China's international discourse power. A closing section sets out how to balance "bringing in" and "going global". Ren's central claim is that an independent knowledge system must be rooted in Chinese practice and in the "two-way engagement" (the "two observations") with China's fine traditional culture and with the practice of Chinese modernization. Teachers should be encouraged to drop what Ren calls blind faith in Western scholarship, testing Western theories, values and concepts against Chinese practice, culture and methods. Ren also holds that Party leadership, with Marxism as the guiding position, is the political guarantee of the project. Single-scholar, free-exploration research is judged insufficient, so Ren proposes interdisciplinary teams, major cultural projects and platforms, and reform of evaluation and incentives. Shandong University's planned research clusters on China's institutional system and on traditional cultural wisdom serve as an example. On the international side, Ren rejects both closed-door construction and wholesale Westernisation, calling for critical borrowing and selective absorption while keeping China's own standpoint central. Universities should use academic dialogue, exchanges, journals and international conferences to present China's distinctive concepts and scholarship abroad, so that the world knows "China in academia" and "China in theory". Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party leader frames the institutional tasks of building an independent knowledge system in Chinese higher education.

Promoting high-quality development of publicity, ideological and cultural work 推动宣传思想文化工作高质量发展 Qian Sanxiong Writing in the Study Times, Qian Sanxiong, Anhui's provincial publicity chief, sets out how the province intends to carry out publicity, ideological and cultural work. Qian presents Xi Jinping's thought on culture as the fundamental guide for opening a new phase in this field. The article's thesis is that Anhui will pursue high-quality development of this work under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), driven by cultural institutional reform and the deep integration of publicity, culture, arts and tourism. The piece is organised around five commitments, each with three sub-tasks. They cover theoretical study, serving the Party's central tasks, integrated development of culture and tourism, ideological risk prevention, and reform and implementation. Qian draws on concrete Anhui examples: the Liu Chi Alley (Six-Foot Lane) heritage site, the Huizhou and Huangmei opera traditions, archaeological sites such as Wuwangdun, and local industries. On study, Qian calls for deeper theoretical armament through Party study groups, grassroots lecture programmes and short-video products. Qian links loyalty to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and cites cases from Party-discipline education, which in Qian's reading show that officials fail when their ideals and convictions slip. On development, Qian describes culture, cultural industries and tourism as natural new quality productive forces and calls for cultural products, new digital formats, heritage-based industries and "culture plus tourism" consumption scenes. On security, Qian says the ideological front is a frontline: the article calls for tighter ideological responsibility, control of positions and channels of communication, and risk anticipation so that erroneous ideas find no outlet. In the final section Qian calls for new thinking, concrete mechanisms such as task lists, competitive project funds and a "five-element" accountability system, and a hard-working style of implementation. Qian says these steps should make Anhui a stronger cultural province and promote the Chinese modernization effort locally. Read the original if you want a provincial Party official's practical account of how national cultural and ideological directives are turned into local programmes, tasks and accountability measures.

The spirit of educators: a yardstick for the professional competence of university ideological and political theory course teachers in the new era 教育家精神：新时代高校思政课教师职业素养的标尺 Chen Hongyuan Chen Huanhong Following the 2024 National Education Conference, which called for an action to forge the soul and strengthen teachers through the spirit of educators, the authors ask how this spirit can guide the professional competence (zhiye suyang) of teachers of university ideological and political theory courses. They argue that the spirit of educators is the proper standard and driving force for that competence, and that teachers should cultivate their beliefs, morals and character under its guidance. The article has three parts. The first shows that the content of teachers' professional competence, and the 'six requirements' for such teachers, match the six dimensions of the spirit of educators. The second breaks professional competence into four components: professional belief, method, ethics and ideal. The third proposes a practical path built on 'belief, competence and ability'. The authors map each of the six dimensions onto a component. 'Having a greater self and devotion to the country' corresponds to professional belief and to the requirement of strong politics. Teaching wisdom and a diligent, innovative attitude correspond to professional method and to the requirement of new thinking. Exemplary conduct and loving devotion to students correspond to professional ethics, self-discipline and upright character. A worldview of 'all under heaven' and 'transforming people through culture' corresponds to the professional ideal of fostering a community with a shared future for mankind. In practice, the authors call for teachers to hold firm to belief by deepening patriotic feeling and international vision, using Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to educate students. They also call for teachers to build broad knowledge and skills guided by the 'eight unifications', and to form a 'teacher–student community' marked by honest language and spiritual resonance. The authors also urge teachers to raise their development capacity in the digital economy era. This means aligning research and teaching, so that teachers move from 'teaching craftsmen' to 'educator-type teachers', and using information technology, including micro-courses and 'Internet+' classrooms. It also means using personal social media to extend ideological guidance beyond the classroom. The authors conclude that the spirit of educators supplies both the ethical orientation and the working method for teachers' professional growth. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link the official 'spirit of educators' to the training and conduct of ideological and political theory teachers.

The Communist Party of China's innovative reconstruction of the cultural subjectivity of Chinese civilization 中国共产党对中华文明文化主体性的创新重构 Liu Mengnan Liu Mengnan asks how the Communist Party of China has dealt with the "cultural subjectivity" of Chinese civilization, which the article treats as the basic mark of national self-reliance and a key factor in a civilization's future. Liu's thesis is that the Two Integrations, and in particular the "second integration" of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, sublimated this subjectivity and amounted to an innovative reconstruction of it. The article first describes a long-standing tradition of subjectivity within Chinese civilization, then turns to the Party's role from its founding to the present. It draws on Confucian thought, the historian Fan Wenlan on the changing meaning of "China", Fei Xiaotong on the Chinese nation, Stavrianos, Mao Zedong, Xi Jinping and Engels. It is a short theoretical piece rather than a case study. Liu argues that agrarian foundations, Confucian unity of family and state, and a capacity to absorb outsiders gave Chinese civilization great cohesion and continuity. On this basis Liu holds that China cannot be measured by Western paradigms such as the "nation-state" or "imagined community" and is better called a civilizational state. The Party's reconstruction of subjectivity is then set out in three parts. The Party is described as confident in the historic undertakings carried out by the people, confident in its unprecedented achievements, and, through the second integration, as having reached a new height of historical and cultural confidence. Liu presents the second integration as a further emancipation of thought, in line with Engels's view of theory as a developing guide rather than dogma. In this account it counters the loss of confidence that followed the Opium War, when Western capitalist civilization challenged China. Liu concludes that the Party reactivates the cultural subjectivity of Chinese civilization and the Chinese nation by pursuing new historical undertakings with firm ideals. It also trusts that the history it leads is on the right course and affirms the value of what it has achieved. The article offers a Party-theoretical account of how cultural confidence is linked to the Party's historical role. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Marxist theorists frame the Two Integrations through the idea of civilizational subjectivity and the notion of a civilizational state.

Three dimensions of how young people in the new era can put the Patriotic Education Law into practice 新时代青年践行爱国主义教育法的三重维度 Xiao Yu This short commentary asks how young people should respond to the Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China, adopted by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress and in force from 1 January 2024. Xiao argues that young people are both a key audience and a key agent of the law. They should put it into practice along three dimensions: knowing it, studying it and acting on it. The piece is organised around three headings: respecting and knowing the law, studying and understanding it, and observing and applying it. Xiao places the law within the legal system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and ties it to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and an international situation the author describes as marked by great changes unseen in a century. In Xiao's account, patriotism in contemporary China means the unity of loving the country, the Party and socialism, and the law is meant to reinforce this. Young people are urged to study it under Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law and to link it with the Two Integrations. They are also asked to connect patriotic education with forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation, traditional culture, core socialist values, and national defence and security education. The author adds that the law covers a wide range of content and gives particular weight to youth, and that young people should measure their own words and deeds against it. Xiao concludes that young people should follow the Party, strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence and firmly oppose historical nihilism and populism. They should also stay rational, open and inclusive toward other civilisations. The aim is to become a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official discourse presents youth patriotic education and the new law.

Consolidating the foundations of primary-level Party building requires improving three capacities 筑牢基层党建根基亟需提升三种能力 Dong Tianmei This short commentary, published on Guangming Online in late 2024, asks how Party building at the grassroots can be tied to effective social governance. Dong argues that primary-level Party organizations must raise three capacities: leadership, organizational capacity and execution. The author presents these as the means of making them the 'backbone' of governance and of strengthening the Party's governing capacity. Dong opens from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), whose decision calls for improving grassroots self-governance under the leadership of primary-level Party organizations. The piece then takes the three capacities in turn, each under its own heading, and closes with a brief remark on the overall governance system. On leadership, Dong calls for standardised organizations, including in new economic and social organizations, the rectification of weak and lax branches, better branch secretaries, and higher-quality Party members. Party leadership should neither take over everything nor leave matters alone nor issue orders. On organizational capacity, Dong argues that social mobility and fragmentation have produced a 'suspended' tendency in grassroots Party work. The remedy is a linked four-tier structure, from network units to community, street and city or county levels, and the ability to mobilise people. On execution, Dong stresses work style, opposition to formalism and bureaucratism, rapid risk response, and resident self-governance and consultation rather than government doing everything. Dong concludes that Party building and governance are united within the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity. The author calls for an organizational system that runs 'vertically to the bottom' and a governance system that extends 'horizontally to the edge', so as to end the 'two skins' problem of Party building and governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary links grassroots Party organization to the Party's governing capacity.

Making greater theoretical contributions to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 为推进马克思主义中国化时代化作出更大理论贡献 Wang Ruolei This short commentary, published in People's Daily in December 2024, asks how theorists can contribute more to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang responds to Xi Jinping's instruction on the project for Marxist theoretical research and development in the new era. The author argues that theorists should deepen their academic roots, continue the Chinese cultural lineage and shoulder a cultural mission, so as to enrich contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. The article is organised around four requirements, each introduced by 'must': uphold fundamental principles while innovating, take root in China's soil, firm up academic subjectivity, and take on a cultural mission. The last section lists five concrete expectations for theorists. Wang's central claim is that theoretical innovation rests on the Two Integrations, with Marxism as the 'soul' and excellent traditional Chinese culture as the 'root'. The 'second integration' is presented as both a major innovation and a source of further ones. The author also calls for an autonomous Chinese system of philosophy and social science. Its task is to give scholarly explanation to distinctive concepts such as whole-process people's democracy and new quality productive forces. It should also study Chinese history and culture, since Wang holds that the logic of China lies within its history. Wang warns that applying foreign theories mechanically undermines China's own legitimacy and system of meaning. Wang's five expectations for theorists are lofty ambition, broad learning across ancient and modern, Chinese and Western; understanding practice; patient, sustained research; and service to the national interest. These are tied to advancing national strength and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, official-press example of how Party-school scholars frame the tasks of theorists and the role of tradition in theory-building.

Being good at observing and handling problems politically "Political consciousness" as stressed by General Secretary Xi Jinping 善于从政治上观察和处理问题 Liang Chaowei This commentary in Study Times explains what Xi Jinping means by "political consciousness" (zhengzhi zijue). Liang defines it as a high degree of self-awareness in thinking about problems and planning measures from the standpoint of the Party's and the country's future and fundamental interests. Liang argues that studying Xi's remarks on the subject helps Party members and cadres strengthen their ideals and convictions, grasp the overall direction and take responsibility. The article is organised chronologically as a survey of Xi's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It takes six occasions between December 2018 and November 2021: the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, a 2019 meeting on deepening reform, the 2020 discipline commission plenary, the Party history education campaign of February 2021, the Party's centenary in July 2021, and the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). On each occasion, Liang links political consciousness to a specific task. These include upholding Party leadership, deepening reform comprehensively, carrying out the Two Upholds, arming the whole Party with its innovative theory, pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and drawing on the laws of history. Liang presents Party leadership as the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Authority and centralised leadership of the Central Committee are described as an historical political advantage of the Party. Liang adds that summing up a century of struggle shows the Party's skill in applying historical laws. Liang concludes that cadres should treat theoretical study as a political responsibility, keep to the Party's "examination" mindset, and carry the Party's self-reform through to the end. The article is a digest of Xi's formulations, with little independent analysis. Read the original if you want a compact, dated guide to the occasions on which Xi has invoked "political consciousness" and to how Party media present its meaning.

Strengthening the relevance and effectiveness of propaganda on the Party's innovative theory 增强党的创新理论宣传的针对性实效性 Ruan Dongbiao This short commentary, originally published in Study Times, asks how the Party's innovative theory can be made to "take root in people's minds and hearts". Taking Xi Jinping's instruction on the Marxist theory research and development project as its starting point, Ruan argues that propaganda must apply the principle of linking theory with practice. It should be problem-oriented and aimed at the actual thinking and understanding of its audience. The article sets out three requirements. The first is to explain clearly how the theory guides each field of Party and state work. The second is to hold to a problem orientation and explain the theory's content while answering practical questions. The third is to grasp the ideological state of cadres and the public so that explanation is better targeted. Ruan holds that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era sums up the laws of Party governance and of socialist construction. In the author's view it should not be presented abstractly, but tied to the concrete work requirements of reform, development and stability, of domestic and foreign affairs, and of governing the Party, state and military. Ruan acknowledges that some localities and departments apply the theory incompletely or inaccurately and show formalism and bureaucratism. The author maintains that the theory itself supplies ways to deal with these problems, and that investigation and research are needed to find them. Under socialist market conditions, interests and values are diverse and outside ideas spread online, so Ruan calls for propaganda that identifies the audience's doubts and misunderstandings and answers them directly. Ruan concludes that explanation of this kind turns study into a process that arms the mind and guides practice. It would also build political, ideological, theoretical and emotional identification with the theory, and strengthen confidence in it. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-school and propaganda circles frame the method of popularising Party theory in late 2024.

Strengthening consciousness and thoroughness in ideological remoulding 增强思想改造的自觉性和彻底性 Han Liqiang Writing in Study Times, Han Liqiang, a political commissar at the Armed Police Engineering University, takes up the first of six priorities that Xi Jinping set out for political army-building at the Central Military Commission political work conference in June 2024: strengthening consciousness and thoroughness in ideological remoulding. Han argues that the deep-seated problems Xi identified, which Xi traced to ideals and convictions, Party spirit and official integrity, can be solved only by a thorough 'ideological clean-up'. The short commentary is addressed to Party members and officials. It moves through three requirements: deepening theoretical armament, sharpening right-wrong discrimination through criticism and self-criticism, and testing results by loyalty and unity of knowledge and action. It closes with a call to treat remoulding as lifelong. Han argues that theory must be studied systematically, through original texts, training and discussion, and linked to practice, so that faith and loyalty are firmly established. Citing Marx on the communist revolution's radical break with traditional ideas, Han points to the Gutian Conference, the Yan'an rectification movement and later Party education campaigns as precedents for correcting deviations. Party members should examine themselves against the Central Committee's requirements, the Party constitution and revolutionary forerunners, and accept outside criticism. Han holds that loyalty is shown in action rather than eloquence: obeying the Central Committee, and behaving the same in public and in private, with or without supervision. Han concludes that remoulding is hard to sustain and must continue 'to the end of one's life', especially for those in senior positions. Cultivating integrity, ability, courage, vigour and harmony among cadres is said to supply the strength for Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a senior military political officer presents ideological remoulding in the Party's current army-building discourse.

Innovative exploration of an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese economics 中国经济学自主知识体系的创新性探索 Gu Hailiang Gu Hailiang, writing in the Economic Daily and reposted in December 2024, asks how Xi Jinping's economic thought supplies the basis for an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese economics. Gu's answer is that this body of thought, presented as the latest theoretical achievement of Marxist political economy in contemporary China, provides both guidance for Chinese modernization and the scholarly norms and academic foundations for such a system.
