The piece is organised under five headings: rooting theory in China's practice in the new era; refining signature concepts to bring about a "revolution in terminology"; drawing on China's fine traditional culture; adopting an international outlook; and keeping a problem orientation that integrates academic and practical concerns. Gu draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches from 2015 to 2024, including those on the Two Integrations, the 20th Party Congress report and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Gu argues that the system must grow out of China's own development practice, and cites Engels's remark that every new scientific insight brings a revolution in terminology. In Gu's account, concepts such as the new development philosophy, high-quality development, supply-side structural reform, new quality productive forces and Chinese modernization are such terminological innovations, and the last is called the most notable result of knowledge, theory and method innovation. Gu holds that the system is guided by Marxist political economy yet should say "new things" the classic authors did not say, and that it can absorb reasonable elements of Western economics on a "China first" basis. Classical-Chinese economic ideas, such as enriching the people and moderation in resource use, are said to give it cultural depth, while a community with a shared future for mankind and "Global South modernization" extend it internationally. Gu also distinguishes academic and practical problem orientations and says the system must integrate the two. Gu concludes that scholars should take Xi Jinping's economic thought as their guide, study major strategic and overall questions in economic work, and produce high-quality theoretical results. The aim is to speed up building the autonomous system and to tell the story of China's economic development in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Chinese academics are asked to frame the project of an autonomous Chinese economics.

A new height in understanding the laws of socialist cultural construction 对社会主义文化建设规律的认识新高度 Sun Daiyao This commentary, first published in Economic Daily and reposted by the Academy of Marxism in December 2024, studies Xi Jinping's thought on culture, which was formally put forward and systematically set out at the national conference on publicity, ideological and cultural work in October 2023. Sun Daiyao argues that this body of thought is the cultural part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Sun's account it marks a new height in the Party's understanding of the laws governing cultural construction under socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has two parts. The first presents the scientific method behind Xi's thought on culture: historical materialism, a problem-oriented approach drawn from materialist dialectics, and the integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second sets out four "foundational and original" ideas: the Party's cultural leadership, a people-centred value orientation, cultural confidence together with a new cultural mission, and exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. Sun draws on the Outline for Studying Xi Jinping's Thought on Culture, compiled by the Central Publicity Department. Sun argues that Xi's thought builds on Marx and Engels's view that culture rests on the economy but also acts back upon it. It places economic work and ideological work in relation: economic construction is the Party's central task, yet ideological work is "extremely important" and must not be neglected. Sun holds that culture is cast as a supporting force for high-quality development and for meeting the people's needs for a better life. On the problem-oriented side, Sun points to the "great changes unseen in a century", sharp ideological struggle and rising risks to cultural security. Xi's thought is said to answer these by answering what kind of socialist culture to uphold and how to develop it. On the four ideas, Sun stresses that leadership, management and discourse power in ideology must stay in the Party's hands. Culture should serve the people as creators of spiritual wealth. Cultural confidence, including the "second integration" of Marxism with traditional culture, is described as the basis of national rejuvenation. Civilizations should be seen as open and equal rather than ranked. Sun concludes that Xi's thought on culture is an open system that grows through the interaction of practice and theory, and it should guide Chinese modernization. Sun calls on readers to study and apply it so that learning, thinking and doing are unified. The article also proposes building Chinese discourse and strengthening international communication. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theorists frame the Xi-era doctrine on culture, ideology and civilizational exchange.

Working on curriculum-system building in universities: upholding fundamental principles and innovating for the intensive development of ideological and political courses 在高校课程体系建设上下功夫 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Cheng Shiping Responding to Xi Jinping's recent instruction that ideological and political courses should be developed in depth through upholding fundamental principles while innovating, this commentary asks how universities can build a better curriculum system for ideological and political education. Cheng Shiping argues that the answer lies in treating the whole curriculum, not only the dedicated ideological and political theory courses, as the vehicle for this education. The piece was published on the Chinese Social Sciences Net's digital ideological-and-political channel in December 2024. The article has three parts. It first identifies problems in current university practice, then sets out why a systematic curriculum is necessary, and finally proposes practical paths. Throughout, Cheng divides the system into three types of course: the required ideological and political theory courses, general education courses, and specialist professional courses. On problems, Cheng contends that some universities equate curriculum-system building with the ideological and political theory courses alone, rely on one-way indoctrination that stresses theory over practice, ignore individual differences among students, and assess mainly through written exams and papers. The three course types also tend to work separately: theory courses stay detached from other disciplines, general education neglects Marxist theory, and specialist courses neglect ideological and political content. Cheng argues that a unified system is needed to meet the demands of a globalised, informatised society, to draw on the educational function of every course, and to put into practice a comprehensive, whole-process approach to nurturing people. The proposed paths are to integrate the three course types and update content with current events and student concerns; to link a first classroom (theory teaching), second classroom (lectures and social practice) and third classroom (field study in museums and research bases); and to combine online platforms and data analysis with offline teaching. Cheng concludes that building such a system should follow changing circumstances, move towards teaching that is modern, of its time and varied, and rest on systematic thinking that organically fuses the three course types. The aim, in the author's account, is to cultivate talent of high moral character. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university lecturer in China frames curriculum reform for ideological and political education in response to Xi Jinping's directive.

The history of reform and opening up: the key logic of education in common ideals and convictions 改革开放史：共同理想信念教育的关键逻辑理路 Wan Jun This short piece asks why education in the common ideals and convictions of socialism with Chinese characteristics should be embedded in the history of reform and opening up. Wan Jun argues that doing so rests on a philosophical rationale and follows the first methodological principle of ideological and political theory courses. The author presents this as methodological guidance for university teachers who want students to hold these convictions firmly. The article has two parts. The first sets out two philosophical grounds drawn from Marxist epistemology and dialectics. The second shows how the approach applies the principle that political orientation and academic rigour must be unified in teaching. On the philosophical side, Wan holds that logic must follow history. The abstract, law-like understanding of socialism with Chinese characteristics should therefore be returned to the winding history of reform and opening up. Likewise, essence appears through phenomena, so dry laws become persuasive only when illustrated by historical figures, events and facts. On the methodological side, Wan treats academic rigour as the foundation and political orientation as the soul. The author credits the Party's leadership, a people-centred stance and a political commitment to socialism with helping China avoid the "subversive errors" of Eastern European socialist states. Convictions without theoretical support lose vitality, while those without politics lose direction. Wan concludes that teachers who grasp this logic can answer students with thorough theoretical analysis rather than empty indoctrination, which raises the appeal and effectiveness of their courses. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ideological and political education justifies teaching ideals through the history of reform and opening up.

The evolutionary logic of ecological civilization from the perspective of epistemology 认识论视野下的生态文明演进逻辑 Zhou Guangxun Chen Xuancheng Zhou Guangxun and Chen Xuancheng ask how Marxist epistemology can guide human understanding of the relationship between people and nature, at a time when the rapid development of artificial intelligence has produced new accounts of how knowledge arises and what it is. They argue that Marxist epistemology keeps its scientific vitality and remains the theoretical guide for understanding and transforming the world and for achieving harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. On this basis they present ecological civilization as the culmination of an evolution in human cognition and in forms of civilization. The article has three parts. It first sets out the two features of Marx's theory of knowledge as the authors read it: a practice-based epistemology and a theory of "reproduction" (zaixian). It then proposes surveying the history of civilization through a "grand historical materialism", drawing on Engels, Freud and Oswald Spengler. Finally it compares three ecological currents: deep green, light green and red-green. The authors hold that the process of knowing runs from practice to knowledge and back to practice, and that it moves "concrete–abstract–concrete". In their account, Marx's epistemology is not mere mirroring but a creative reworking of reflections in the mind. They argue that Western scholars have wrongly portrayed Marx as anti-ecological, Promethean and anthropocentric. In their reading, a grand historical materialism examines changes in the human–nature relation as well as in human–human relations. They map Marx's sequences of social forms, of human interdependence and of economic forms onto fishing-and-hunting, industrial and ecological civilization. The three green currents are assessed against this frame. The authors say deep green, centred on ecocentrism, ignores human relations and so misses capitalism as the source of ecological crisis. Light green, centred on modern anthropocentrism, relies on technology and economic accounting but overlooks the logic of capital. Red-green, with ecological Marxism as its mainstream, is said to sublate both by criticising the capitalist system. The authors conclude that ecological civilization is neither a return to a pre-modern society nor a postmodern rejection of growth and technology. In their view it is a civilization in which science and technology are used to transform nature in line with real human needs. Economic growth, ecological protection, social progress and free and all-round human development would advance together, and the "two reconciliations" (of humanity with nature and of humanity with itself) would be realised. Read the original if you want a short Chinese Marxist statement of how epistemology, historical materialism and the typology of Western green thought are linked to the concept of ecological civilization.

Seeking multidisciplinary theoretical support for the ideological and political education of university students Interview with Jiang Feng on using Dabie Mountains red oral culture resources 【社科专访】为大学生思想政治教育寻求多学科的学理支撑 Ming Haiying This is an interview by Ming Haiying of Chinese Social Sciences Net with Jiang Feng, professor at the School of Marxism, Hubei Normal University. Jiang is the author of a study on using the red oral culture resources of the Dabie Mountains to strengthen the ideological and political education of university students. The interview presents these resources as a legacy of China's revolutionary war period with both historical and educational value. The conversation has three parts. It first asks why the research matters, then which research methods it uses, and finally how the study of red culture can be extended through several philosophical perspectives. The oral resources Jiang names include red poems and ballads, explanations given in red-heritage venues, and folk revolutionary stories. Jiang argues that studying how these resources connect with ideological and political education can deepen students' psychological identification and emotional engagement. Jiang also holds that it can show how Marxism was adapted to the Chinese context in the Dabie Mountains area. The research draws on philosophy, ethics, history, phenomenology and educational technology, and uses five methods: social survey with resource analysis, historical logic combined with socio-economic reality, linguistic and cognitive analysis, interactive cultural study, and multi-directional comparison. Jiang then proposes widening red culture's horizons through four Marxist lenses: existence, epistemology, methodology and value theory. The last of these is tied to the core socialist values. Jiang concludes that multidisciplinary, cross-field research can give ideological and political education for students firmer theoretical grounding and uncover how the red gene is transmitted and evolves. Read the original if you want a concise account of the methods and philosophical framing behind a regional red-culture research project in Chinese university ideological education.

Continuously integrating the Party's innovative theory into ideological and political theory courses Bringing the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee into university teaching 将党的创新理论持续融入思政课建设 Cao Sheng Yan Xinqi How should the decisions of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) be brought into university ideological and political theory courses? Cao and Yan argue that integrating the plenum's spirit into these courses is both a necessity and an opportunity. In their view, it helps young people understand the plenum's new ideas and take them to heart and into practice. The short commentary is organised in three parts. It first sets out why integration matters, then identifies the content to be taught, following the seven "focuses" of the plenum's formulation. It ends with four practical routes for classroom implementation. On value, the authors say the plenum report is not only a political text but also an ideological and political education text. They hold that it strengthens students' political identification and faith, and builds their ability to analyse complex social phenomena with theory. On content, they go through the seven focuses: a high-standard socialist market economy, whole-process people's democracy, a socialist cultural powerhouse, better living standards and a higher-level safe China, a beautiful China, and stronger Party leadership and governing capacity. Each is tied to a guiding body of thought, such as Xi Jinping's economic thought or his thought on culture, and to the aim of building students' confidence in China's path. On method, the authors propose four orientations: problem-oriented, hot-topic-oriented, discipline-oriented and technology-oriented integration. They suggest starting from students' doubts about China and the world, using current events, linking the plenum to students' majors, and using virtual practice platforms and digital teaching resources. The authors conclude that sustained, targeted and innovative integration will let students grasp the plenum's theoretical and practical significance for Chinese modernization. They present this as part of raising the quality of ideological and political courses and of cultivating a generation able to build a strong country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's latest documents are translated into teaching content and methods in Chinese universities.

Understanding the scientific content of the "two mountains" concept 深刻领会“两山”理念的科学内涵 Xiang Chi Yang Ning This short commentary, published in December 2024, takes up the "two mountains" concept ("lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets"). Xiang Chi and Yang Ning start from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for better mechanisms to put the concept into practice. They argue that it innovates on Marxist productive-forces theory, is necessary for combining high-quality development with high-level protection, and is inherent in Chinese modernization as a modernization of harmony between humanity and nature. The piece has three sections, one for each claim. It moves from theory, to the relation between growth and environmental protection, to the requirements of Chinese modernization during the 14th Five-Year Plan period. In the authors' account, productive forces include protecting and improving the natural environment, so that a good ecology is a source of productive development and carries economic value in itself. They say this means developing local specialty industries, making industry ecological and ecology industrial, and spreading green technology. They present economic development and environmental protection as mutually dependent, and credit the concept with shifting ecological work from end-of-pipe clean-up to tackling problems at source through changes to industrial, energy and transport structures. Mountain, health-resort and summer-retreat tourism are offered as examples. On the practical side, the authors call for ecological red lines, spatial planning and a mechanism to realise the value of ecological products. They also want stronger governance capacity and a multi-party environmental governance system, so that building a beautiful China becomes the conscious action of all the people. They conclude that holding to the concept will support sustainable development and care for the shared planet. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how the concept is framed in official-style discourse after the Third Plenum.

Marx's epistemology of time 马克思的时间认识论 Yu Shugui This short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2024) asks how Marx understood time and why that understanding matters for his ethical thought. Yu Shugui argues that Marx opened a third path between Newton's absolute time and Kant's subjective time. On this path time is placed within the dialectical unity of subject and object, which Yu presents as both scientific and as pointing to the ethical character of time. The article moves through three themes. It first sets Marx against Newton, Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, then discusses free time as a central concept in Marx's analysis of capitalism, and finally treats time as the measure of human life. It closes with a brief remark on the acceleration of modern society and intelligent machines. Yu's core claim is that time is the 'positive existence' of human beings. Following Engels' proposition that labour created humanity, Yu concludes that social labour creates time: nature offers only the motion of matter, and people build time out of its rhythms, with the 'year' as a public rhythm. Newton, in this reading, mistook natural rhythms for time itself, while Kant swung to the other extreme. Marx sublated both by treating time as a product of social practice. Yu then reads free time as leisure time, as time of rights (escape from capital's claim on the worker's surplus labour time) and, essentially, as ethical time. Full free time is attainable only after capitalism and private ownership are overthrown, when labour becomes life's prime need. Yu distinguishes natural, social and logical (abstract) time, and argues that human beings still have biological limits, the 'biological clock'. As time units shrink to milliseconds and nanoseconds, human rhythms fall behind the pace of an intelligent society. The 'tyranny of time' that Marx criticised under capitalism is therefore turning into one dominated by intelligent machines. Yu suggests that Marx offers valuable methodological guidance for addressing this, but does not develop concrete proposals. Read the original if you want a brief, accessible Chinese reading of Marx's views on time, free time and labour as a starting point for a Marxist ethics of time.

Advancing "green education" practice in universities through the ecological civilization concepts of the new era 新时代生态文明理念推进高校绿色育人实践 Nie Xiaoyan This short commentary in the China Social Sciences Today argues that universities should build the concepts of ecological civilization drawn from Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization into their "green education" (lüse yuren) practice. Nie holds that this is both a core part of the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and a practical requirement of Chinese modernization, understood as the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. The article first sets out four concepts it finds in Xi Jinping's ecological thought, then gives two reasons why green education matters, and ends with three institutional measures. It draws on official formulations such as the new development philosophy and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee's call for coordinated education by schools, families and society. Nie reads the concepts as a unity of four kinds of outlook: harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature as a value; \"lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets\" as a mode of thinking that rejects opposing economic growth to ecological protection; respecting, accommodating and protecting nature as a view of nature; and green development as a view of development. Green education is presented as a strategic task of ecological civilization and as a response to the changed principal contradiction, in which people's needs now include a good ecological environment. University students are described as audience, communicators and practitioners of these ideas. The proposed mechanisms are an ecological civilization education system, a systematic working mechanism and a collaborative operating mechanism. The working mechanism covers teaching staff, a new curriculum and closer integration with ideological and political theory courses. The cited example is a student social practice project on ecological conditions led by college Youth League committees. Nie concludes that Xi Jinping Thought should guide the whole process of green education, so that students internalise ecological values and act on them, and so that their sense of historic mission grows. Read the original if you want a brief example of how ideological and political education in Chinese universities is being linked to ecological civilization policy.

The fundamental guidance for making ideological and political courses "explain principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly" 思政课“把道理讲深讲透讲活”的根本遵循 Wang Rangxin Wang Rangxin takes up Xi Jinping's instruction that ideological and political theory courses ("sizheng ke") in schools must "explain principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly" in the new era and on the new journey. The article asks how this can be done and answers that Xi's own instruction supplies the fundamental guidance. This has three parts: keep Marxism as the guiding ideology, use the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the substance of teaching, and use fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture as the foundation of strength. The piece is organised around these three requirements. Wang opens by arguing that the political character and ideological function of the courses are their essence. The article then treats the content of teaching: which achievements to cover, and how to teach them. The last section takes the three cultural sources in turn, with suggestions for classroom and extracurricular practice. On Marxism, Wang argues that teachers need firm belief, so that conviction and affection reach students. Teachers must also apply the Marxist worldview and methodology, which Wang says lifts a \"principle\" to theory, philosophy and fundamental principle. The courses should show Marxism's scientific, popular, practical and developing character. On content, Wang says teachers must set out the Party's history of more than a century. This includes the successive \"great leaps\", the four solemn declarations to the world, and the historic achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Methods proposed are using society as a \"big classroom\", immersive and technology-assisted experience, and inviting ordinary people, model Party members and descendants of martyrs into the classroom. On culture, Wang says fine traditional culture is the root, with its fit with Marxism. Revolutionary culture, carried by the Great Spirit of Party founding and later revolutionary spirits, is the \"source of strength\". Advanced socialist culture, centred on core socialist values, is said to be inclusive and forward-leading. Wang concludes that grounding the courses in practice, as material force, and in culture, as spiritual force, will make their principles credible, respected and lovable. The article proposes teaching bases, supplementary materials, film archives, touring talks by model figures and exhibitions of achievements. It also proposes both explicit and subtle (\"moistening things silently\") ways of shaping students' emotional belief. Read the original if you want a Party-line account of how Xi's guidance on ideological and political courses is turned into teaching content and methods.

Advancing the development of ideological and political courses in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory 坚持思政课建设与党的创新理论武装同步推进 Luo Xianyu Liu Yuan Luo Xianyu and Liu Yuan take up Xi Jinping's instruction that the development of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in schools must advance in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory. They argue that this instruction shows why such courses need to unite political orientation with scholarly rigour. In their view it supplies theoretical guidance and a method for opening a new phase of ideological and political education in the new era. The short commentary begins by noting what has changed since the 18th Party Congress (2012): the courses' higher standing in the Party's overall strategy, a larger teaching corps, new teaching methods and the use of information technology. It then points to new pressures, namely the impact of diverse social currents of thought and new problematic behaviour among young students in class. The main body is organised around five "connections": textbooks, curriculum, teaching, teaching staff and digital resources. The authors' central move is to treat political and scholarly strength as inseparable. On textbooks, they call for a system centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, with the latest theory brought in promptly and integrated across primary, secondary and university levels, plus supporting teaching guides and curriculum standards. On curriculum and teaching, they urge staged content that avoids "disconnection and inversion", closer alignment between ideological-political courses and "ideological and political education across all courses", and a shift from academic to teaching language. Teaching should answer the questions of whom to train, how and for whom, combining the teacher's leading role with the student's initiative. On staff and technology, Luo and Liu propose a well-trained corps combining full-time and part-time teachers, including Party and university leaders, and a mechanism linking school, family and society into a "grand ideological and political education" pattern. They also call for digital resource platforms, online channels and immersive VR and AR teaching built on red cultural resources. The authors conclude that these five connections, advanced together, would raise the effectiveness of the courses and fulfil the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars translate Xi Jinping's directives on ideological and political courses into practical measures for textbooks, curriculum, staffing and digital teaching.

Empowering the construction of the "Big Ideological and Political Course" in universities through digitalisation 以数字化赋能高校“大思政课”建设 Yang Xiaoxia Lai Hairong This short commentary asks how digital technology can strengthen the "Big Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) in Chinese universities. The authors, Yang Xiaoxia and Lai Hairong, take as their starting point the 2022 work plan issued by the Ministry of Education and nine other departments. They argue that artificial intelligence, big data and VR/AR will become an important route to high-quality development of the course, provided that obstacles in teacher outlook, skills, governance and infrastructure are addressed. The article has two main parts. The first sets out three aspects of the "value logic" of digital empowerment. The second names the difficulties encountered and proposes three lines of action: raising digital literacy, reforming the "supply side" of the course, and building digital infrastructure. It closes with a brief appeal to university teachers to act on Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses. On the value of digitalisation, the authors argue that data profiling of students makes teaching content more precise. They also hold that digital tools break down barriers between school stages and between spaces. VR/AR and online platforms extend teaching from the small classroom to the wider social classroom, and shared platforms ease the uneven distribution of teaching resources and permit more scientific evaluation. On the problems, they point to lagging attitudes or resistance among some teachers, insufficient digital literacy, limited application and governance shortcomings. They also see a risk of conflict between instrumental rationality and value rationality. The authors call for systematic training of teachers and students in digital skills, including the ability to recognise erroneous trends and false information online. They also want reform of teaching subjects, content, space and resources using student data and platforms, and new networks and shared resource platforms. They further call for technical defences against what they describe as Western capitalist ideological intrusion, data theft and digital viruses. Their stated aim is a high-level course that cultivates the "four-have" new generation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education frame digital technology as a tool for ideological teaching.

Continuing to advance the integrated development of ideological and political courses so that it takes deep root 持续推进思政课一体化建设走深走实 Yao Guojian Yao Guojian takes up Xi Jinping's May 2024 instruction on school ideological and political courses, which calls for deepening integrated ideological and political education across universities, secondary and primary schools. Yao argues that such integration is a systematic project, organised through theory, content and culture, for fostering a new generation able to shoulder the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first concerns the theoretical grounding of an integrated course system, the second the substance and practical content of teaching, and the third the transmission of three cultural sources: fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. On theory, Yao says each stage of schooling should seek a common denominator in the truth of Marxism and use reasoned argument suited to the students' level, so as to build a graded, spiral-rising teaching system. On content, the author proposes moving from the near to the grand: from everyday progress around students, to national achievements such as high-speed rail, the C919 airliner and the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge, to a resolve to serve the country. On culture, Yao assigns each stage a task: primary pupils cultivate virtues, middle schoolers learn to reason, high schoolers set aspirations, and university students engage with the Two Integrations. Revolutionary culture moves from enlightenment to knowledge to ideas, while students are asked to become creators of advanced socialist culture. Yao concludes that, if teaching follows the pattern of student development and links personal ideals with the cause of the Party and state, integration will open a new phase of ideological and political education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics translate Xi Jinping's directives on course integration into stage-by-stage teaching principles.

The livelihood attribute of ideological and political course teaching 思政课教育教学的民生属性 Li Hui This short commentary argues that teaching ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in schools and universities has a "livelihood attribute" (minsheng shuxing), because education is a livelihood project. Li Hui contends that grasping this attribute helps explain why building these courses is a top priority in the Party's leadership of education. The piece has three sections. The first defines livelihood as the unity of material and spiritual life. The second treats fostering virtue and nurturing talent (lide shuren) as a unity of public opinion and popular support. The third describes the kind of teacher the courses require. Li starts from historical materialism: people must first be able to live before they can make history, so material needs are the premise of any livelihood orientation. Citing the 19th Party Congress report (2017) on the principal contradiction, Li adds that growing spiritual needs must be treated as a unity with material ones. On fostering virtue, Li says the task has a political and strategic side, producing successors to socialism, and also a livelihood side. Moral and political quality is, in Li's account, the core of an individual's growth, bears on family happiness, and supports public order. On teachers, Li calls for patriotic commitment and a caring attitude towards students. Drawing on Marx's concept of alienated labour, Li contrasts capitalist education, which in this reading trains labour-power for production, with socialist education aimed at all-round human development. Li concludes that the courses have political and strategic attributes and also a livelihood attribute. Students' growth, parents' hopes and the Party and state's need for successors are said to rest on the same questions of whom to train, how and for whom. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese Marxism-school scholars link ideological education to livelihood and moral formation.

Making the building of ideological and political theory courses the top priority of Party leadership over education 把思政课建设作为党领导教育工作的重中之重 Xue Weijiang Writing in December 2024, Xue Weijiang takes up the place of school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) within the Party's leadership of education. The commentary argues that these courses are the lifeline for implementing the Party's educational policy and must be treated as the top priority of educational work. Its thesis is that Party leadership is the defining feature and advantage of such courses, that experience of building them is an important lesson in leading education, and that handling a set of key relationships in reform is the route to strengthening that leadership. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out how Party leadership shapes the courses in terms of educational direction, goals and methods. The second lists five regular patterns the author draws from experience since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to reform and innovation through the "eight unities" methodology associated with Xi Jinping. In the first part, Xue says the courses serve the people and the modernization drive, aim at the all-round development of the person, and combine education with productive labour and social practice. The second part names five lessons: upholding Marxism as the guiding ideology and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, upholding the socialist orientation and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, building a strong teaching force, rooting education in Chinese soil, and maintaining a work pattern of unified Party committee leadership with wide coordination. The third part walks through eight pairings, such as political and academic character, value and knowledge, constructive and critical approaches, theory and practice, indoctrination and inspiration, and explicit and implicit education. Xue presents these as ways to increase the courses' ideological quality, relevance and appeal. Xue concludes that firmly grasping ideological and political education ensures the Party's banner flies in every sector of education, and that reform of the courses lays the ideological and political foundation for Party leadership of education. The text is a programmatic statement of official positions rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Party-school scholars frame the leadership, teaching staff and methodology of ideological and political courses in the new era.

Practical exploration of an education system for ideological and political education in courses 课程思政育人体系的实践探索 Huang Nansong Writing in late 2024, Huang Nansong, executive vice-president of Guangzhou Institute of Technology, asks how "ideological and political education in courses" (kecheng sizheng) can be made effective in Chinese universities. Citing Xi Jinping's remarks at the National Education Conference that building a strong education nation must centre on fostering virtue and cultivating people, Huang argues that the answer lies in a system with a sound theoretical basis, coordinated delivery and progressive stages, aimed at making the content take root in students' minds and be put into practice. The short commentary has four parts. It first names three challenges facing universities: weak theoretical understanding, poor coordination, and a lack of progression in teaching content. It then offers a theoretical account of how such education works, a framework of five coordinated "actions" corresponding to the five educations, and a four-year staged path for student development. The examples come from practice that Huang presents as a model for other institutions. Huang's central move is to ground the approach in two cycles. The "cognitive cycle" runs from perceptual to rational understanding; the "practice cycle" runs from first-classroom teaching through second-classroom activities such as clubs, speeches and volunteering, to social practice. Huang sums up the underlying principle as "seeking truth from facts, taking root in the mind and putting into practice". The five actions (moral education to forge the soul, intellectual education to strengthen the foundation, physical education, aesthetic education and labour education) combine in-class and out-of-class work and, in Huang's phrase, produce a "fifth-power effect". For progression, Huang proposes a ladder with five stages: initiation in the first year, accumulation in the second, practical transformation in the third, integration and career preparation in the fourth, and a final stage of aesthetic outlook at graduation. Huang concludes that universities should carry out the national strategy on strengthening this form of education by building a system that is theoretically grounded, coordinated across processes and graded by level. The stated aim is the all-round development of students and the training of socialist builders and successors. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how a Chinese university frames and operationalises course-based ideological and political education, including its terminology and programme design.

The original contributions of the theory of new quality productive forces 新质生产力理论的原创性贡献 Sun Leqiang Sun Leqiang asks what is theoretically new in Xi Jinping's concept of new quality productive forces, which was set out at a Politburo collective study session. The article argues that the concept is more than a new term. In Sun's reading it marks an innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces and deepens understanding of how productive forces develop. The article starts from Xi's definition: innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality productive forces, consistent with the new development philosophy. It then draws out four shifts: in the driving mechanism, the ecological standard, the systemic configuration of labourers, means of labour and objects of labour, and the standard for labourers and talent. Each shift is read against Marx's remarks on productive forces and against Xi's statements. On the driving mechanism, Sun notes that Marx used the sixteenth century to separate traditional from emerging productive forces, with experience and tools giving way to science and machine systems. Sun argues that new quality productive forces rest on original, even disruptive, 'zero to one' technology and integrated innovation, not on repetitive or low-level science. On ecology, Sun holds that capital turned nature into an instrument of valorisation and caused ecological crisis. New quality productive forces are presented as green productive forces that sublate capitalist ones. On the internal system, Sun draws on Marx's idea of general intellect, which capitalism separates from labour. Sun argues that new quality productive forces need highly skilled workers who master it, data as a production factor, and new production relations. Sun concludes that developing these forces requires coordinated progress in education, science and technology, and talent. Education produces talent, talent produces original knowledge and technology, and these feed back into society's collective intelligence through the education system. Sun also calls for deeper reform of production relations and of income distribution by factor contribution. Read the original if you want a short, Party-theory account of how Marx's categories are used to ground Xi's concept of new quality productive forces.

The two dimensions of Marx's thought on democracy and their practical embodiment 马克思民主思想的二维向度及实践体现 Liu Lin Liu Lin asks how Marx's thought on democracy can be understood as a complete system, and answers that it has two complementary dimensions. The first is a 'substantive' dimension, concerning the philosophical grounds and inner value of democracy as rule by the majority. The second is an 'authenticity' dimension, concerning how that majority rule is realised in practice. The author argues that Xi Jinping's whole-process people's democracy fuses the two. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the substantive dimension through democracy's essence (a state system), its ontological basis (people's democracy) and its true aim (human emancipation), drawing mainly on Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and The Civil War in France. The second sets out the authenticity dimension as a critique of bourgeois democracy, a summary of the Paris Commune, and a set of general principles for realisation. The third applies the framework to contemporary China at three levels: the state, the people and society. Liu argues that for Marx the state is not independent of its economic base, so the extent of democracy depends on economic liberation. Political emancipation remains formal and partial, and only human emancipation goes further. On this basis the author reads Marx as demystifying representative government, universal suffrage and the separation of powers as forms that mask class rule. From the Commune the author draws four lessons: economic emancipation of labour, breaking the old state machine, self-government by the people, and public servants who can be recalled. Realisation requires the unity of new democracy with new dictatorship, of Communist Party leadership with the proletariat as the main force, and of institutional procedure with popular supervision. In the final section Liu presents whole-process people's democracy as a creative application of these principles. It must suit Chinese modernization and the primary stage of socialism. It must widen participation beyond elections and build people's political capacity. It must also advance in step with the 'five-sphere integrated plan' under the unity of Party leadership, people's mastery of the country and law-based governance. Liu adds that this institutional system needs continued refinement in the face of globalisation and informatisation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's democratic theory that links it to current Party doctrine on whole-process people's democracy.

Mao Zedong's profound exposition of a firm and correct political direction in the Yan'an period 延安时期毛泽东同志对坚定正确政治方向的深刻阐释 Luo Pinghan Gao An'yi Luo Pinghan and Gao An'yi ask why the Chinese Communist Party grew from small and weak to large and strong during the thirteen years its Central Committee spent in Yan'an. They argue that a key reason was its constant adherence to a correct political direction and its scientific handling of the relationship between lofty ideals and immediate tasks. In their account, a firm and correct political direction is the core and essence of the Yan'an spirit, and Mao Zedong's wartime statements on it remain significant for the Party today. The article reviews Mao's talks and writings from 1937 to 1939. It starts from his 1938 remarks at the Counter-Japanese Military and Political University and Shaanbei Public School, where the phrase first appeared as an educational requirement. It then follows later speeches to graduates and to young model workers, and his reports to the 1937 Party conference and the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee (1938). It closes by linking these texts to the present. The authors make three moves. First, they report Mao's view that political direction is 'like a person's head', setting the course for everything else and for the link between individual effort and national destiny. Second, they stress that choosing the right direction is easier than holding to it. They cite those who left the Party or yielded to temptation, and Mao's use of the characters of Journey to the West to illustrate firmness of direction, hardship and flexibility. Third, they argue that firmness requires uniting the Party's maximum programme (socialism and communism) with its minimum programme. Mao's 'two essays' formula, democratic revolution first and socialism second, and his statement that a Marxist bears 'both the practical tasks of the present and the lofty ideals of the future', are presented as the basis of this unity. For the authors, the concrete direction in Yan'an was anti-imperialist, anti-feudal revolution and national liberation in the War of Resistance and later the war of liberation. The authors conclude that the direction to uphold today is the lofty ideal of communism and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, together with advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. They cite Xi Jinping's call on cadres not to stray in political direction. Cadres, they say, must tie all their efforts and sacrifices to this direction. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-historical account of how Mao's Yan'an formulations on political direction are now used in official discourse on Party discipline and ideals.

Systematising and theorising the Party's innovative theory, and building China's independent knowledge system 党的创新理论体系化学理化与中国自主知识体系的构建 Pang Lisheng Sun Anmin Pang Lisheng and Sun Anmin ask how China's independent knowledge system (zhongguo zizhu zhishi tixi) can be built, and what part the Party's innovative theory plays in that task. They argue that the theory both guides the project and supplies its substance. Building the system therefore requires pushing the theory towards systematisation and theorisation, with special attention to its principle-level content (yuanli xing neirong). The article draws on Xi Jinping's 2016, 2022 and 2023 statements on philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first defines the independent knowledge system and names its three features: subjectivity, originality and systematicity. It then shows how the Party's theoretical achievements, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, guide and fill out that system. The second part treats systematisation and theorisation as methods of thought, and the third turns to excavating the theory's foundational principles. The authors say the Party's theory expresses Chinese practice and experience and applies Marxist standpoint and method. They list concepts such as whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind as original contributions that belong in the knowledge system. In their view systematisation and theorisation reinforce each other and require thoroughgoing theoretical thinking. They take Marx's Capital, with its ascent from abstract categories to the concrete, as the model, and ground the work in the questions raised by Chinese modernization. The Two Integrations and the "six musts" are named as the guiding methods. The authors call principle-level results the "foundation and base" of the theoretical edifice, and take the Two Integrations as their example of a principle needing fuller explanation. The authors call for research that goes back to the leaders' original writings, such as Xi Jinping: The Governance of China and the Selected Readings, to extract the principles, show how they connect and avoid fragmentation. They also want these principles read in a contemporary light, raised to the philosophical level, and placed within a "grand historical view". The aim is to show the stronger persuasive force of contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal links knowledge-system construction to the systematisation of Xi Jinping Thought.

Constructing the Party's ideological discourse system in the new era 新时代党的意识形态话语体系建构 Wang Peizhou Wang Peizhou asks how the Chinese Communist Party's ideological discourse should be built in an era that combines profound global change, the national rejuvenation mission and Chinese modernization. The article argues that a "one-dimensional" approach is no longer adequate. Ideological discourse, in Wang's view, must be constructed as a system along three interlinked dimensions: politics, narrative and power. The article is organised in three sections, one for each dimension, each with three sub-points. The political dimension covers value discourse, theoretical discourse and institutional discourse. The narrative dimension covers the narratives of goals, of development and of governance. The power dimension examines the power logic of discourse, hard power as the basis of soft power, and the interaction of the two. Wang draws on Party congress reports, Xi Jinping's statements and examples such as the "eight-point regulations", the Fengqiao experience and the word "taikonaut". In the political dimension, Wang argues that discourse should turn "the discourse of politics" into "the politics of discourse", mobilising people through the founding mission, through theory that gives direction, and through Party regulations that secure execution. Wang adds that Western neoliberalism, "constitutional democracy" and historical nihilism set "either-or" traps that theory must clarify. In the narrative dimension, the rejuvenation story, the people-centred story of Chinese modernization and the community-based story of governance are said to generate attraction, because they rest on real achievements. In the power dimension, Wang holds that soft power becomes discourse power only because hard power underpins it. Hard power without soft power loses cohesion, and Wang cites the Soviet collapse as the example. Wang concludes that building the ideological discourse system requires hard and soft power to interact and strengthen each other. The Party must also manage the pace and timing of propaganda and guard against ideological risk at key moments. Discourse gains force when values are matched by developmental facts. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory scholar frames ideological work through the three lenses of politics, narrative and power, and how Party-state discourse and its priorities are justified.

Adhering to a systems approach as the scientific methodology for further deepening reform comprehensively 坚持系统观念是进一步全面深化改革的科学方法论 Xin Xiangyang Xin Xiangyang takes up the call in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to 'adhere to a systems approach' (xitong guannian) in further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The article argues that this approach is both a theoretical and a practical requirement of comprehensively deepening reform, and that the Decision not only applies it but also enriches and develops it. The article has three parts. The first grounds the systems approach in Marxist dialectics and in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and in the experience of reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second places the Decision's 'five major relationships' in a line of earlier Party formulations, from Mao Zedong's ten relationships to the twelve of Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao's overall planning. The third turns to methods for hard problems: balanced coordination (tongchou jiangu) and consistency assessment of macro policy. In Xin's reading, the systems approach means analysing problems developmentally, as a whole, in their connections, comprehensively and dialectically. In practice, it requires coordination of reform plans, implementation and results across fields. The core of the second part is the five relationships: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. For each, Xin sets out how the Decision's measures try to hold both sides together, citing market-oriented reform of natural monopolies, the 'two increases' in income distribution, opening up alongside the goal of stable expectations, and risk-prevention mechanisms. In the third part, Xin presents the Decision's requirement to include non-economic policies in macro-policy consistency assessment as a safeguard. It is meant to catch policies that decay over the medium and long term, and to prevent the 'fallacy of composition', in which individually sound departmental policies work against each other. Xin concludes that the systems approach matters greatly for a cause that has no completed state, and that it is needed to build coherent, mutually reinforcing reform measures as new dilemmas multiply. The article is an official-line exposition of the Plenum Decision's methodology rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how Party theorists link the Decision's five relationships to earlier leaders' formulations and to Xi Jinping's methodology.

Grasping the multiple implications of the Two Integrations 深刻把握“两个结合”的多重意蕴 Wu Manyi Yang Rongsuo This article by Wu Manyi and Yang Rongsuo asks what the Two Integrations (combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture) mean and why they matter. The authors argue that the two integrations carry ontological, historical-subjective, logical and value implications, and that together they are the Party's most important means of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They open from the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and Xi Jinping's remarks on cultural inheritance. The article has four parts. The first treats the "first integration" as ontological; the second treats the "second integration" as expressing historical subjectivity. The third sets out the inner logic linking the two. The fourth examines their value in three dimensions, history, reality and civilisation, which the authors tie to Xi Jinping's "grand view of history", "grand view of practice" and "grand view of civilisation". Throughout, the authors trace a line from Mao Zedong Thought through to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the authors' account, the first integration is ontological because Marxism's universal worldview and method fit China's particular conditions. They hold that the integration forms a continuous historical whole and is an independent act of creation, not mere application or "external reflection". The second integration, they argue, roots Marxism in the cultural psychology and everyday values of the people, so that Marxism "speaks Chinese" and traditional culture is modernised. The first is the premise and foundation of the second, and the second deepens the first. Together they are characterised by four features: a truth-bearing origin, a practical basis, a law-like direction and a purposive aim. The authors conclude that the Two Integrations are the Party's greatest asset. They credit them with deepening understanding of the laws of Party governance, socialist construction and human social development. They present the Two Integrations as a mark of the historical and cultural subjectivity of Xi Jinping and the Party, and as the basis of Chinese modernization and a "new form of human civilisation". They call for studying Xi's statements on the Two Integrations to grasp the core of his Thought and advance high-quality development. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned philosophical reading of the Two Integrations as presented in a Chinese Marxist-theory teaching journal.

On the microfoundations of Marxist macroeconomics 论马克思主义宏观经济学的微观基础 Wang Zhongbao Wang Zhongbao asks whether efficiency at the level of the firm is consistent with efficiency at the level of the whole economy, a question the author treats as basic to both Western economics and Marxist political economy. Wang argues that Western economics cannot ground macroeconomic analysis in microeconomic analysis, because under private ownership the two kinds of efficiency come apart. Marxist political economy, in this reading, can explain why and so builds macroeconomics on a microeconomic base. The article has three parts. The first contrasts privately owned and publicly owned firms, using a reductio argument and citing Thomas Piketty, Joseph Stiglitz and David Harvey on inequality and weak demand. The second analyses sustainable macroeconomic development through ownership, income distribution, market regulation and government intervention. The third proposes a new framework for Marxist economics, listing the topics that microeconomics and macroeconomics would each cover. Wang's central claim is that ownership of the means of production determines distribution, and distribution determines whether total supply and total demand can match. Under private ownership, a firm raises its profit rate by squeezing wages and shifting costs onto workers, nature and society. Wang argues that competition and capital accumulation then polarise wealth and income, producing insufficient effective demand and recurring crises. Wang holds that Keynesian policy, neoliberalism, progressive taxation and welfare measures only soften or delay this outcome. Under public ownership with distribution according to labour, the owners of capital and of labour-power are the same people. Wang says this removes the antagonism between profit and wages and keeps income gaps small, so that micro-level and macro-level efficiency coincide. Wang calls for replacing the textbook split between a capitalist part and a socialist part with a unified "modern Marxist economics" centred on the producing firm. The aim is a shift from the "needs of revolution" to the "needs of development", to serve the socialist market economy. Its shared core would be the labour theory of value, ownership theory and the theory of distribution between capital and labour. Wang adds that where private ownership exists within a socialist market economy, it should be guided and regulated, and the public sector should keep its absolute and relative advantage. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist argument linking ownership, distribution and demand to a proposed restructuring of Marxist economics textbooks.

Five points of fit between the new development philosophy and the holistic approach to national security 把握新发展理念与总体国家安全观的五个“契合点” Xie Bo Xie Bo takes up the relationship between two components of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era: the new development philosophy, presented as the guide for economic work, and the holistic approach to national security, presented as the guide for security work. Xie argues that the five elements of the first (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) correspond closely to the substance of the second. Grasping these points of fit, the author says, is necessary for advancing high-quality development and a high level of security together, so that a new security pattern safeguards the new development pattern. The piece is a short theoretical commentary of five sections, one for each element of the new development philosophy. Each pairs the element with a security counterpart and a shared orientation: innovation with institutional change, coordination with scientific overall planning, green development with ecological security, openness with common security, and sharing with the people's security. Xie draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements, the 20th Party Congress report (2022), and the Party's decisions on security and development. Xie's central move is to show that each pair rests on a common orientation. Innovation and security reform both seek "change for the new". Coordination ("balanced, whole-system thinking") and the "holistic" in the security approach share a systems logic. The author traces how the Party has moved from stressing security (the "stand up" stage), to development ("grow rich"), to coordinating both ("grow strong"). Green development and ecological security both aim at harmony between humanity and nature. Openness is set against what Xie calls Western "zero-sum" thinking in trade, technology and security, contrasted with common security and the Global Security Initiative. Sharing and the people's security both put the people at the centre, as a stance Xie says is fundamental to the Party's governance. Xie concludes that security is the precondition of development and development the guarantee of security, and that this dialectic explains the points of fit. As the country moves toward building a modernized socialist country and the second centenary goal, the author expects the two to become more closely bound. Xie calls for mastering this dialectic, giving equal weight to development and security, and deepening their integration, in order to support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link economic and security doctrines in official discourse.

The contemporary meaning of upholding the organic unity of political security, the people's security and the supremacy of national interests 坚持政治安全、人民安全、国家利益至上有机统一的时代意涵 Xie Bo Xie Bo examines a formula that recurs in the national security discourse of the new era: upholding the organic unity of political security, the people's security and the supremacy of national interests. The article argues that this triad is a core element of the holistic view of national security. Political security is its foundation, the people's security its purpose and the supremacy of national interests its standard. Xie holds that the three are distinct in meaning yet inseparable, and must be understood together in order to modernize the national security system and capacity. The article is organised in four sections. The first three take each element in turn, tracing how Xi Jinping and Party documents have framed it: the 2014 first meeting of the Central National Security Commission, the 2018 and 2020 formulations, the 19th Party Congress report (2017), the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and laws such as the 2015 National Security Law. The fourth section turns to method, setting out how the three should be coordinated in practice. Xie's central move concerns the two ways each element is described, and the reordering of the triad. Up to 2019 the formula placed the people's security before political security; from 2020 it puts political security first. Xie reads this as showing political security to be the basic condition of the state's survival, especially the security of political power and the political system, but not as lowering the people's security. The people's security is described as the central value, since national security ultimately protects the people's interests. The supremacy of national interests is presented as governing the other two, because in the author's account China's state system makes national interests the 'greatest common divisor' of the people's interests. On method, Xie calls for coordination guided by the holistic view of national security, for each element's function to be fully used, and for the three to be integrated in the modernization of the national security system and capacity. For political security this means upholding Party leadership and the Two Upholds; for the people's security, relying on and mobilising the people; for national interests, firmly defending core interests. Read the original if you want a close textual account of how official phrasing on political security, the people's security and national interests has evolved, and how a Chinese security scholar justifies their ordering.

Promoting the integration of the spirit of the 20th Party Congress into ideological and political courses from primary school to university, with high quality 高质量推进党的二十大精神融入大中小学思政课 Yang Qicai Xu Yuehui Yang Qicai and Xu Yuehui take up a practical question in Party-led education: how the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022) can be built into ideological and political theory courses ('ideological and political courses') at primary, secondary and tertiary level. They hold that studying and implementing the Congress's spirit is the Party's primary political task and the top priority of these courses. Their answer is to teach eight defined topics and to introduce them in graduated stages. The article, first published on China Theory Net, has two parts. The first sets out what to teach: eight areas drawn from the Congress report, Xi Jinping's statements and central requirements. The second sets out how to teach it, in three steps that the authors summarise as moving 'from low to high', 'from little to much' and 'from shallow to deep'. The eight topics include the Congress's significance, its main outcomes and theme, its summing-up of a decade of change in the new era, and its account of a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They also cover the Party's mission on the new journey, which centres on Chinese modernization, the twelve areas of strategic deployment, and the expectations placed on youth. On method, the authors assign each stage a task. Primary school plants seeds through stories, pictures and video ('enlightenment'). Junior secondary school relies on cases and lived experience ('experience'). Senior secondary school stresses 'common knowledge' through observation, analysis and reflection. University stresses systematic theory that links theory with practice and history with reality. Content likewise deepens from a first grasp of the Congress's significance to a thorough understanding of its framework and the mission it assigns. Yang and Xu conclude that teachers should not simply wait, rely on documents or read them out, and should not copy mechanically. They call for goal-oriented teaching adapted to textbooks, students and available resources, with richer forms and innovative methods. The aim is for the Congress's spirit to be vivid, comprehensive and layered, so that it reaches students' minds and hearts. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Party doctrine is mapped onto a staged curriculum from primary school to university in China's ideological and political education.

Why "the influence of culture is first of all the influence of values" 为何“文化的影响力首先是价值观的影响力” Chen Na Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that the influence of culture is first of all the influence of values, Chen asks how the core socialist values (prosperity, democracy, civility, harmony, freedom, equality, justice, rule of law, patriotism, dedication, integrity and friendship) shape cultural influence. The author's answer is that these values play a pivotal role in every aspect of cultural life. The short commentary examines four common states of culture: creation, charm, exchange and infiltration. Each is paired with a metaphor for the role of the core socialist values: a banner, a fixed star, a central axis and a line of defence. Chen argues that the values answer the question of whom culture serves and which road it takes, so creators should uphold the people's standpoint and the socialist direction. Works such as the television drama The Age of Awakening and the film The Battle at Lake Changjin are cited as carrying such values, while cultural products that yield to capital logic are said to lose their way. In exchange, the values are presented as the standard for separating mainstream from tributary and essence from dross. The author portrays Western capitalist countries as using a vast cultural arsenal for infiltration and value dumping, which Chen calls a threat to China's cultural security. Chen concludes that cultural construction begins with forging its soul, and that the soul of socialist culture is the core socialist values. Cultivating them is said to bear on national security, regime survival and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars link cultural influence, soft power and cultural security to core socialist values.

Making good use of the textbook and preparing lessons well: advancing teaching of the Marxist view of journalism Teaching experience based on "Twelve Lectures on the Marxist View of Journalism" 用好教材备好课 深入推进马克思主义新闻观教学 Zheng Baowei This is the edited text of a keynote talk by Zheng Baowei, chief editor of the national textbook Twelve Lectures on the Marxist View of Journalism, given at a collective lesson-preparation event on teaching the Marxist view of journalism at Xiamen University's School of Journalism and Communication. Zheng praises the school's collective approach and offers advice, drawn from the author's own editing and teaching experience, on how to use the textbook well. The central claim is that good teaching requires understanding why the subject matters, what the textbook is for, and how it is built. Zheng's talk has six parts: the importance of Marxist journalism education; the textbook's positioning; its guiding principles of compilation; how it handles problems in teaching; its framework of twelve lectures; and the use of Xi Jinping's journalism work in Fujian as a teaching resource. Zheng traces the history of such education from 2000, through the Central Publicity Department's campaigns in 2001 and 2003, to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zheng argues that Xi Jinping's speeches of 19 August 2013 and 19 February 2016 turned this education into what the author calls a "golden period". The 2016 speech called the view of journalism the "soul" of news and public-opinion work and demanded that Marxism run through journalism research and teaching. The textbook, compiled under a project commissioned by the Central Publicity Department and the Ministry of Education, is described as the first official standard text on the subject. Zheng lists five compilation principles, including applying the Marxist standpoint, summing up the Party's journalistic tradition, reflecting the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and showing that the theory accords with the laws of journalism. The twelve lectures are grouped as introduction, basic principles, guiding principles (such as unifying Party spirit and people's character), professional norms and two practical topics. Zheng proposes that Xiamen University draw on Xi Jinping's seventeen years in Fujian, including the revival of the Mindong Daily and a 1989 Ningde speech on journalism, as a distinctive teaching resource. Zheng also repeats a 2018 call to make the Marxist view of journalism the core of journalism education, covering all staff, the whole process and every student. Read the original if you want to see how the textbook's editor describes its design, its official rationale and the way it is meant to be taught in Chinese journalism schools.

A community with a shared future for mankind from the perspective of Marxist humanistic theory 马克思主义人学视域下的人类命运共同体 Lü Hongxia Li Luming Lü Hongxia and Li Luming ask how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind can be understood through Marxist theory of the human being (renxue). Their thesis is that the idea rests on Marx's concepts of the human as a "species being", of human essence, and of human emancipation. They present it as a contemporary interpretation of Marx's "philosophy of the species" and as a Chinese answer to the problems facing a closely connected world. The article opens with the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's commitment to building such a community, and then proceeds in three sections. The first treats the idea as a contemporary reading of Marx's species philosophy. The second argues that the human mode of practical existence supplies the idea's practical principles. The third links it to Marx's theory of human liberation. Throughout, the authors cite Marx, the Communist Manifesto and Xi Jinping. The authors draw on Marx's three social forms (dependence on persons, independence based on dependence on things, and free individuality) to argue that today's world remains in the second. In their account, capital is the material root of division and conflict, and it produces a "thing-centred way of thinking" that loses sight of human species essence. They hold that a shift to "species thinking" is needed, and that the community idea follows this logic. Citing Chinese initiatives in economic, political, ecological and nuclear-security fields, and a series of "community" concepts, they say China acts on the human capacity for practice and sociality. They also argue that bourgeois political emancipation left "illusory communities" intact, whereas this idea develops Marx's theory of human liberation in a Chinese form. The authors conclude that building the community is a necessary stage on the road to human emancipation. In their view, guided by the common values of all humanity, it is a new exploration of the path of liberation and will go beyond "illusory communities" bound by interests. They describe it as a practice of great significance for turning the communist ideal into reality. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars root Xi-era foreign-policy language in Marx's humanistic and emancipation theory.

A theoretical exposition of the Marxist view of literature and art in the new era 新时代马克思主义文艺观的学理阐释 Liu Qirui Luan Yongyu Liu Qirui and Luan Yongyu set out the main elements of the Marxist view of literature and art as it has developed in the new era. They argue that the Party's literary theory, from Marx and Engels through Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping, has been renewed by combining Marxism with China's creative practice and its fine traditional culture. In their account this forms the literature-and-art chapter of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and offers fundamental guidance for the Party's cultural work. The short article is organised in five sections. They treat literature and art as part of Chinese modernization, the Party's overall leadership, the people-centred orientation, the demand for outstanding works in building a culture-strong country, and the Chinese national spirit as a source of subject matter. Each section is supported mainly by quotations from Party leaders and the Party constitution. The authors argue that modernization must coordinate material and spiritual civilization, so that literature and art nourish people's spiritual lives and help build a modern Chinese civilization. They hold that Party leadership is the basic political guarantee because contemporary Chinese art is both Marxist and socialist, and so must resist what they call bourgeois liberalization and decadent values. On the question "for whom", they follow Mao and Xi in treating the people as the source and beneficiary of art. As examples of work that combines depth of ideas, artistic craft and fine production, they cite television dramas such as The Age of Awakening and In the World. The authors conclude that works should carry the Chinese spirit, rooted in patriotism and reform, through creative transformation of traditional culture and by telling China's story abroad. They present this as practising core socialist values and building an inclusive Chinese cultural landscape. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how current Party discourse links cultural policy to Chinese modernization and Party leadership.
