Expanding and deepening the living use of red resources in the education of Party members and cadres in the new era 加大和深化红色资源在新时代党员干部教育中的活化利用 Zhang Xingliang Zhang Xingliang takes up how "red resources" can be put to more active use in educating Party members and cadres in the new era. The author argues that deeper use of these resources helps cadres perform their duties and carry out their mission. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call to make good use of red resources and notes the regulations on Party history study and education issued on 5 February 2024. Zhang defines red resources as the legacy formed as the Communist Party led revolution, construction and reform. They include revolutionary sites, memorial halls, relics and documents, and the deeds and spirit of martyrs and models. The commentary is organised around three functions: ideological and political education, practical training, and cultural transmission. On the first function, Zhang holds that studying red resources lets cadres grasp the Party's lines and history, and understand why the Party "can", Marxism "works" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good". It is also said to temper Party spirit, reinforce the Party's purpose of serving the people and shape core socialist values. On practice, the author proposes site visits, scenario simulations, online courses and media, volunteer guiding, and red tourism routes and cultural brands, so that cadres learn by doing. On culture, Zhang argues that red resources enrich cadres' historical and cultural grounding, stimulate cultural innovation, and strengthen cultural confidence and China's international influence. Zhang concludes that protecting, using and researching red resources will supply varied educational material for cadres and encourage them to model good conduct for society. The text is a short programmatic commentary, not an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-education scholarship in China frames red culture, tourism and volunteering as tools for cadre training.

Grasping the dialectics of Xi Jinping's thought on strengthening the military 深刻领悟习近平强军思想的辩证法 Li Honglang This article asks what dialectical method underlies Xi Jinping's thought on strengthening the military and argues that it forms a contemporary Chinese Marxist outlook and methodology on military affairs. Li Honglang contends that the thought rests on Marxist military dialectics, draws on traditional Chinese military culture and grows out of practice in building a strong military in the new era. In Li's account it deepens the Party's understanding of the laws of army-building and opens a new stage in the development of Marxist military thought. The article is organised around five "adherences" attributed to Xi: political guidance, stopping war through the use of force, active initiative, overall coordination, and the courage to fight and win. Each is paired with a dialectical unity: combat-power building and political work; preparing for war and being able to win; bottom-line thinking and proactive progress; breakthroughs at key points and all-round advance; and material conditions and fighting spirit. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi, then explains the mutual reinforcement of the two sides and links it to current conditions. Li's central claim is that each pair interacts and promotes the other. Politics directs the military and political work is itself a form of spiritual combat power, so the Party's absolute leadership is the soul of the army; Li ties this to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and rejects calls to depoliticise or "nationalise" the armed forces. Readiness for war is said to deter war, so the military must train for real combat amid an uncertain world, while bottom-line thinking must be combined with innovation and reform. Drawing on materialist dialectics, Li says material conditions come first but fighting spirit can offset material shortfalls, citing the Korean War formula of "less steel, more spirit" and Xi's remark that now there is more steel, there must be even more spirit. Li concludes that the five pairings should be pursued together to achieve the goal of a world-class military and to defend national sovereignty, security and development interests. The article calls for coordinated work on political army-building, reform, science and technology, talent and rule by law, and for cultivating the fighting spirit of the armed forces. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how Chinese military-theory writing frames Xi's strong-military thought in dialectical terms.

Rethinking the totality of Marx's concept of "history" 重新理解马克思“历史”概念的总体性特征 Wu Meng Wu Meng asks how the totality of Marx's concept of "history" should be understood. The author argues that the influential reading by Georg Lukács, which ties totality to a Hegelian dialectic of part and whole, is internally inconsistent. In Wu's alternative account, totality in Marx is a historical feature tied to the capitalist mode of production, not an all-encompassing whole that contains and determines its parts. The short article, published in the China Social Sciences Today, has three parts. It first sets out Lukács's exposition in History and Class Consciousness. It then identifies three weaknesses in that exposition. It ends by proposing a different reading of Marx's dialectic and of totality in his critique of political economy. Wu summarises Lukács as treating Marx's method as a dialectic of part and totality and of subject and object. Phenomena such as commodity relations and reification appear as parts, and the proletariat grasps the social totality through class consciousness. Wu objects on three grounds. First, grafting Hegel's part–whole dialectic onto Marx's analysis of capitalism is logically unsound: Hegel's concept-dialectic works because the Absolute Idea unites particularity and totality, whereas the social structure is not a particular phenomenon alongside commodity or capital relations. Second, reading Marx's ascent from the abstract to the concrete as an ascent from part to whole leaves the "mediating" concepts vague. It also cannot explain why Marx's analysis of relations between things is always combined with analysis of relations between people. Third, Lukács turns Marx's historically specific concept into an abstract logic applicable to any epoch. Wu holds that the root error is equating Marx's dialectic with Hegel's. For Marx, totality is the precondition of the historical movement of capitalist objects, namely the capitalist mode of production. It is a functional whole that cannot be objectified, the "complicity" of human and material factors, and it appears as the way phenomena are given. Wu concludes that Marx starts from historical "universality", not from "objectivity", and so avoids abstracting his concept of history. On this reading, Marx's critique of political economy asks about the historical preconditions of the universality that classical economists took to be eternal. Read the original if you want a compact, critical re-reading of Lukács on totality and the Hegel–Marx relation in the philosophy of history.

The three-dimensional historical foundations of historical materialism 历史唯物主义的三维历史底蕴 Jin Xingyu This short commentary asks what makes historical materialism a "total" conception of history rather than a mere method of historiography. Jin argues that Marx and Engels inherited and transcended the totalizing tradition of "general philosophy of history" represented by Hegel. By "returning the content of history to history", grounding it in the productive practice of "real individuals", they produced a scientific answer to the question of history in general. Jin contends that this total view rests on three dimensions. The article is organised around three paired relations: natural history and human history (the dimension of content), past and future (time), and national history and world history (space). Each section draws on Marx and Engels, chiefly The German Ideology, Engels's account of nature's evolution, the late writings on Russia and the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, and a brief citation of E. H. Carr. Jin describes the pieces as forming a single, unified, diverse and open whole. On the first dimension, Jin argues that natural and human history are structurally parallel both externally (both display diverse, mutually conditioned forms) and internally (both are governed by laws grounded in the material exchange between humans and nature). Under capitalism, Jin says, human history seems to move blindly like natural history, and this is the "alienation" that must be overcome through the active practice of historical subjects. On the second, the author holds that historical materialism links "interpretation–critique–prediction" through a "practical reflection" that works backwards from developed forms, and ties history's direction to the real movement of communism and the contradictions between productive forces and relations of production. On the third, Jin reads Marx and Engels as moving beyond a Eurocentric view of history: the diversity of national paths, including Russia's, does not negate the laws of world history, since everything depends on concrete historical conditions. Jin concludes that this practice-based "grand view of history" is an important intellectual resource for the Communist Party of China in governing the country. It is said to fit the theme of the Party's century of history and to help Marxism guide Chinese modernization and the building of a new form of human civilization. The author also links it to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style statement of how contemporary Chinese scholars present the historical, temporal and spatial structure of historical materialism.

From quantitative accumulation to qualitative leap: the generative logic of "new quality productive forces" 量变到质变：“新质生产力”的生成性逻辑 Sun Nailong Ma Yanling Taking as its starting point Xi Jinping's remarks in Heilongjiang in September 2023, this short commentary asks how the concept of new quality productive forces came about. Sun and Ma define the term as a new type of productive force that differs from traditional ones, is led by scientific and technological innovation, breaks with traditional growth paths and meets the requirements of high-quality development. They argue that the concept has a "generative logic" that can be read through the dialectic of quantitative accumulation and qualitative leap. The article is organised in three parts: the feasibility of the concept (quantitative accumulation), its inevitability (qualitative leap) and its reality (the unity of gradual change and leaps). It begins with the Marxist three-element account of productive forces and traces Party thinking on them from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping through Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. It then draws on statistics on education, agricultural mechanisation and industrial output. In the authors' account, reform and opening up expanded all three elements of productive forces: labour, means of labour and objects of labour. They cite figures such as 99 million graduates from higher education since 1978, a higher-education system with more than 44.3 million students, and China ranking first in 220 of more than 500 major industrial products. The authors present the successive industrial revolutions and the current digital and information revolution as the source of a qualitative leap, with innovation as the key to moving from "quantity" to "quality". They treat the new development philosophy and the 20th Party Congress (2022) emphasis on technological self-reliance as the policy conditions for this shift. The authors conclude that developing new quality productive forces requires three things. These are growth of the real economy, with technology converted into actual productive capacity; a leading role for innovation, which means fostering strategic emerging and future industries such as quantum information, gene technology and hydrogen energy; and the upgrading of traditional industries, which they say make up over 80 per cent of manufacturing, through deep integration of digital technology and the real economy. They claim the concept enriches and develops the Marxist theory of productive forces. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars link the Party's productive-forces tradition to the new quality productive forces concept using the quantity–quality dialectic.

Grasping the inner unity of the dialectical view of contradiction and the systems concept 深刻领悟矛盾观与系统观念的内在统一性 Leng Shuqing Guo Wangshu This short article, published in December 2024, asks how the Marxist view of contradiction and the systems concept (系统观念) relate. The authors argue that the two are not different ideas but possess an inner unity. They hold that the dialectical view of contradiction stresses the unity of opposites in the world, while the systems concept, which they trace to natural philosophy, stresses wholeness, structure, levels, openness and self-organisation. The article builds its case in two parts. The first examines the systematicity of contradiction and the contradictoriness of systems, drawing on Mao Zedong's writings and on Xi Jinping's statements about the systems concept. The second traces how each concept has been inherited and developed, from Marx, Engels and Lenin through Mao's On Contradiction to Xi Jinping in the new era. The authors also cite some scholarly literature in support. The central move is a two-way relation. Contradiction is systemic: following Mao, a large entity contains many interlinked contradictions, among which one principal contradiction plays the leading role, so the authors read Mao's principal-contradiction thesis as a foundational and original contribution to the systems concept. Systems are contradictory: Xi's formulation requires attention to principal and secondary contradictions and combines the "two-point" and "focal" approaches, which the authors read as showing the systems concept to be dialectical. The authors add that the systems concept is the unity of a worldview and a methodology. On inheritance, the authors say Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao held rich systemic ideas but never named the systems concept. They credit Xi Jinping with first stating it explicitly and building it into a theoretical system. They interpret its worldview as three unified levels: an ecological-civilisation systems concept for the human–nature contradiction, a community-with-a-shared-future systems concept for human society, and a people-centred systems concept for the principal social contradiction of the new era. The authors caution against clinging to textbook versions of contradiction or copying natural-philosophy systems thinking. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars tie Xi Jinping's systems concept to Mao's theory of contradiction and to the new-era principal contradiction.

Deepening understanding of the theoretical innovation in upholding a systems approach 深化认识坚持系统观念的理论创新 Leng Shuqing Responding to Xi Jinping's call to study the foundational theoretical results contained in the Party's new concepts and judgements, Leng Shuqing examines the injunction to uphold a systems approach (系统观念), one of the "six musts" of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that this principle amounts to a basic and original theoretical innovation across all three component parts of Marxism, and that it is a major marker of the Thought's systematic and theoretical character. The article has three sections. The first traces the inheritance and innovation of the Marxist view of contradiction and its methodology, from Marx through Mao Zedong to Xi. The second extends the claim to Marxist political economy and scientific socialism. The third presents the systems approach as a major principled theoretical achievement of Xi Jinping Thought and as a paradigm innovation in Marxist philosophy. Leng's central move is to argue that, although Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao's accounts of contradiction already carry systems-related meaning (Mao's analysis of layered contradictions and of socialist society as a system of relations, for example), only Xi explicitly urges viewing and resolving social contradictions from a systems standpoint and abstracts the systems approach into a worldview and methodology. Leng proposes the concept of a "contradiction-systems view" and treats the principal contradiction of the new era as the logical starting point of both Xi Thought and the systems approach. On this basis the author reads the new development philosophy and the turn in political economy towards "becoming strong" as expressions of systems thinking, and sees the systems approach as renewing the socialist theory of the principal contradiction. A further claim is that the approach fuses Marxist dialectics with systems science, producing categories such as systems thinking, bottom-line thinking and holistic advancement. Leng concludes that the contradiction-systems view is a major result of Xi Jinping Thought, which is described as contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. It is said to provide the worldview and methodology for building a disciplinary, academic and discourse system with Chinese characteristics. The author calls for deeper study of Xi's statements on the systems approach. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of the systems approach places this concept within the Party's official theoretical framework and within the Marxist tradition of the doctrine of contradiction.

Does the "production" of artificial intelligence create value? 人工智能的“生产”创造价值吗 Li Yaogeng Li Yaogeng asks whether artificial intelligence (AI) can create value, and what this means for Marx's labour theory of value. The commentary argues that the theory still supplies the basic framework for understanding labour's role in value creation, even as AI challenges traditional assumptions. The piece sorts AI into three types, weak, strong and super AI, and considers how each intervenes in production, labour and social relations. It also notes legal, political and ethical questions raised by each type. Li holds that weak AI, found in automated production lines and smart tools, is an extension of human labour and a new instrument of production. It raises efficiency but leaves labour as the core of value creation and workers as its subject. Strong AI, which Li treats as hypothetical, could think, learn and innovate, and might prompt a reassessment of labour's contribution. Li still sees it as working toward human-set goals under human leadership. Super AI, by contrast, is imagined as surpassing human intelligence and acting beyond human control. In Li's account it could take over resource allocation, upend existing relations of production and leave humans as passive recipients rather than subjects, challenging Marx's ideal of free and all-round human development. Li concludes that Marx's labour theory of value remains an important basis for understanding labour change in the AI era, but must be explored anew in changed conditions. The author calls for balancing technological progress with social interests and for vigilance about the risks of super AI. Read the original if you want a brief, schematic Marxist classification of AI types and their implications for labour and value.

The labour theory of value in the age of artificial intelligence 人工智能时代的劳动价值论 Qin Zizhong Does the spread of unmanned factories and the rise of general artificial intelligence make Marx's labour theory of value obsolete? Qin Zizhong, writing in a newspaper commentary, rejects the claim that the core thesis that labour is the only source of value has been broken. In Qin's view, this reading both misunderstands Marx and lacks a careful look at how AI is developing. The piece first uses Marx's dual character of commodities and labour, and his category of the collective worker, to explain unmanned production. It then turns to new questions for the theory: the dominance of mental and digital labour, Sakaiya Taichi's knowledge-value theory, and the redefinition of the working day. Finally it separates two stages of AI, before and after a threshold of autonomous consciousness. Qin argues that AI has moved from automated machines needing on-site workers, through remote control over the internet, to a stage where programmers, data engineers and internet users together form an integrated collective worker. Below the threshold, AI is a tool and its work extends human labour, so humans still create the value. Because leisure is also digitised, Qin proposes a working day with a third segment, leisure labour time, whose value is ignored or partly appropriated free by data and platform companies. Above the threshold, an autonomous AI subject would become another source of value, which would challenge Marx's thesis. Qin sees two possible responses: abandoning the thesis, which Qin says is not necessarily Marxist, or reading labour as performed by multiple subjects, including AI, which Qin calls Marxist or compatible with Marxism. The author calls for inheriting and developing the theory under new historical conditions rather than accepting it dogmatically. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist argument on how digital labour and possible AI subjects bear on the labour theory of value.

The generalisation of artificial intelligence and new questions for the labour theory of value 人工智能的通用化与劳动价值论的新论题 Tu Liangchuan Tu Liangchuan asks what the generalisation of artificial intelligence (AI) means for the Marxist labour theory of value. Writing in a Chinese social science newspaper in late 2024, the author starts from Xi Jinping's remark that AI is a major driver of the new round of technological and industrial revolution. Tu argues that general-purpose AI has moved from replacing labour with machines to replacing the labour subject itself, and that this raises new questions about value, ownership of output and the distribution of wealth. The article's answer is that general AI does not negate labour as the source of value, but that it forces a rethinking of how value, ownership and wealth are organised. The piece is built in three sections. The first treats generalisation as a 'replacement technology' that changes how labour creates value. The second considers AI's 'human-like labour' and the problem of establishing ownership (确权) of social products. The third examines AI as a 'quasi-subject' and the question of who enjoys the wealth it produces. Tu lists social problems the author associates with general AI, including 'unmanned factories', a 'useless class', digitised forms of labour and a new alienation. Tu's central claim is that general AI is an accumulation of past human labour and technical knowledge, not a new source of value. Its human-like labour carries use-value into products and may increase use-value, but it does not originate purposes or develop genuinely new use-values. For this reason AI cannot be the subject that holds rights over products, and owning AI is not a sufficient ground for claiming them, because only labourers who realise real innovation are the basis of innovative use-value. As a 'quasi-subject', AI makes means of labour into autonomous machines and removes workers from production. In Tu's reading, 'technological unemployment' and the 'useless class' stem from the capitalist logic of valorisation and of fixed capital displacing people, not from any inevitability of technology. Tu concludes that AI, as an objectified product of human essential powers, should return to humanity and become 'common wealth' under socialism. Only in this way, the author holds, can its development be economically just, politically reasonable and serving of free human development. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher defends the labour theory of value against claims that AI creates value or deserves ownership.

Giving full play to the "four major platforms" role of Schools of Marxism 充分发挥马克思主义学院的“四大平台”作用 Hu Daping Hu Daping, dean of the School of Marxism at Nanjing University, asks how Schools of Marxism can best serve as one of the "four major platforms" of ideological and theoretical work named by Xi Jinping at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences. The commentary argues that this platform function cannot be separated from the schools' core tasks of moral education and discipline building, and that it depends above all on the quality of teaching in ideological and political courses. The piece first sets out what makes a School of Marxism distinctive: it differs from government departments, general academic bodies, Party schools, the Marxist theory research and construction project, and the media. It then lists the pressures the schools face and proposes several lines of work: organised research, coordination among the sub-disciplines, interdisciplinary expertise, institutional character, and a sustainable teaching force. Hu contends that the schools' primary function is to educate people for the Party and the country, so theoretical research and propaganda must be integrated into the process of education. A research agenda that becomes "two layers of skin" with teaching would, in Hu's view, damage the main task. The schools must be strong in themselves, centring organised research on twenty-first-century Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and turning results into teaching. Hu also stresses the unity of the six second-level disciplines in Marxist theory, and the need for theorists to build real expertise in other fields to earn the respect of peers. Hu concludes that the most important task is a sustainable corps of Marxist theorists, backed by institutions and material support. Hu also asks teachers to take Marx as a model of dedication despite scarce resources. Read the original if you want a short statement from a school dean of how a School of Marxism understands its roles and pressures.

Grasping the core meaning of "let those with faith teach faith" 把握“要让有信仰的人讲信仰”的核心要义 Li Hui Li Hui, a professor at the School of Marxism at Sun Yat-sen University, comments on Xi Jinping's remark at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses that such courses must resolve students' ideals and convictions, and that "those with faith should teach faith". Li reads the remark as defining what "strong politics" means for these teachers, as addressing a long-standing problem in building the teaching force, and as supplying a value orientation for that work. The piece has three parts. The first argues that instilling scientific ideals and convictions is the core task of such courses. The second explains why conviction must take root in teachers before it can bear fruit in students. The third traces teachers' faith to self-confidence, which Li divides into the Four-sphere Confidence, confidence in the discipline, and confidence in students' need to grow and succeed. Li argues that ideals and convictions are the fundamental task of ideological and political education, and that young people are at a critical stage because they form their self-awareness while facing a gap between ideal and reality. In Li's account, the United States and the West use ideological infiltration and talent strategies aimed at young people to contain the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which makes the task more urgent. Teachers, Li says, are role models and guardians of social conscience, and political quality ranks first among their qualities. Marxist faith is described as scientific, because it rests on knowledge of laws of social development, and as morally grounded, because it rests on putting the people first. Only teachers who hold it can teach it convincingly. Li holds that teachers' confidence rests on the Four-sphere Confidence, on a Marxist theory discipline that has made historic progress since reform and opening up, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and on the conviction that socialism with Chinese characteristics gives young people chances to succeed. Li concludes that having those with faith teach faith is a requirement of both ideological and political course building and education generally, and that it is the key to the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the Party's political education literature links teachers' personal belief to the aims of ideological and political courses.

The lofty mission of ideological and political theory courses: guiding students to firmly believe in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times “思政课”的崇高使命——引导学生牢固树立对马克思主义中国化时代化的坚定信仰 Chen Binggong Chen Binggong takes up the report of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and Xi Jinping's article on opening up new realms for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Chen argues that this is also a historic task for China's ideological and political theory courses ("sizheng ke"). The thesis is that these courses have the lofty mission of leading students to hold a firm, unshakeable belief in the latest results of that adaptation. The commentary has two parts. The first explains why the mission is lofty, in three steps: the adaptation of Marxism is the living soul of a "new form of human civilisation", it is the "spiritual fulcrum" of China's future, and it is an important spiritual fulcrum for university students. The second part proposes five routes for carrying out the mission, covering teachers, teaching style, a new lecture course, the teacher corps and the training of Marxist theory students. In the first part, Chen holds that the socialist market economy, which the author calls unprecedented in Chinese civilisation, underpins Chinese modernization and the new form of civilisation. Chen describes the latest theoretical results as a "spiritual steel" that unites socialism with the market economy and humanistic spirit with commodity consciousness. Chen defines a civilisation as a community held together by value belief, and argues that people build their inner world on a single spiritual fulcrum. For university students, whose worldview, outlook on life and values are still forming, a sound fulcrum shapes their choices and futures. In the second part, Chen asks teachers to take this belief as a lifelong goal and to develop four kinds of teaching appeal: theoretical, knowledge-based, artistic and personal. Chen also proposes a systematic lecture course on the new realms, taught by leading experts, and a "two-expert" model in which teachers are both Marxist theorists and education specialists. Chen concludes that Marxist theory programmes should train their students on the "two-expert" model, since future teachers come from them. Chen attributes weak spots in current teaching, such as "failing to speak on hot topics" and low effectiveness, to a shortfall in these two kinds of competence. The text is a short programmatic statement on the aims and staffing of political theory teaching. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-school theorist frames belief, curriculum design and teacher training in ideological and political education.

Making practical teaching in university ideological and political theory courses take root and deliver results 推动高校思政课实践教学落地见效 Wang Yongbin Wang Yongbin, a professor at Lanzhou Jiaotong University's School of Marxism, asks how practical teaching in university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng courses) can be made effective. The commentary argues that, although universities have developed varied models, the practical teaching system still needs improvement and should be built more systematically. Drawing on surveys of several universities, the article first describes four models: a separate stand-alone practice course run by the School of Marxism; practice spread across individual courses; joint development with other schools and departments; and teaching bases on and off campus, described as 'walking' ideological and political courses. It then identifies common problems and sets out four proposals, citing the 2019 Opinions on deepening reform of these courses and the Ministry of Education's plan for the 'Great Ideological and Political Course'. Wang finds three shared weaknesses. Goals are unclear, so universities lack a common understanding of what content to offer; the educational value is thin, with formalism, uniform action and a few students' practice standing in for all; and implementation is loose, marked by entertainment-style activities, 'forced' or superficial fusion with professional internships, and substitution of internships for course practice. In response, Wang calls for a university-wide system led by the Party committee and the School of Marxism with other departments, detailed implementation plans offering students menus of options by discipline, fuller use of campus and external resources, and a supervision and evaluation mechanism. Wang concludes that practical teaching must unify knowing and doing and be run as a long-term systematic project, with clear responsibilities and assessment. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Chinese universities currently organise practice components of ideological and political courses and what official guidance expects of them.

The mission and responsibility of universities in building a cyber power in the new era 高校在新时代网络强国建设中的使命担当 Chen Wei Wu Manyi Marking ten years since Xi Jinping put forward the strategic goal of building a cyber power (2024), this short commentary asks what universities should contribute to it. Chen and Wu argue that higher education should treat advancing the cyber power as a major political responsibility and a glorious mission, and that it can do so in three ways. They describe these as building a "talent pool", a "technology bank" and a store of "positive energy". The authors begin by noting that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), China has built the world's largest higher education system, which they say provides a solid base. The article then takes the three tasks in turn: self-reliant training of talent, self-reliance in science and technology, and guidance by core values. It closes with a short call to study Xi Jinping's thinking on the cyber power. On talent, Chen and Wu hold that competition in cyberspace is ultimately competition for talent. They call for integrated training from primary school to university, closer ties between universities and network enterprises, and cooperation with cyberspace and public security authorities. On technology, they cite Xi's description of core internet technology as China's greatest "lifeline". They say core technologies and standards remain in developed countries' hands, and urge breakthroughs in AI, big data, 5G/6G and quantum communication. On values, they cite 1.099 billion internet users as of June 2024, nearly 50 million of them university students, and argue that socialist core values should shape online culture so that "positive energy" leads online traffic. The authors conclude that talent training is the key, technological self-reliance the core and value guidance the goal of building a cyber power. They also call for high-quality development of higher education that produces well-rounded builders and successors of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated university scholars link internet governance, science policy and ideological education.

Returning to fundamentals and breaking new ground while keeping to principle: understanding the regularities of cultural construction with Chinese characteristics 正本清源、守正创新——中国特色社会主义文化建设规律性认识 Tao Wenzhao Yang Jianyu This newspaper commentary, first published in Beijing Daily, asks how the Party's understanding of cultural construction under socialism with Chinese characteristics developed after 2012. Tao and Yang argue that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has worked through "returning to fundamentals and keeping to principle while innovating", and that this practice reached a new level of understanding and was summed up in Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article follows three stages. The first covers the period around the 18th Party Congress, when the authors say ideological problems and online disorder required correction. The second runs from the 19th Party Congress (2017) and its goal of building a socialist cultural power. The third begins with the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the systematic formulation of Xi Jinping's thought on culture in 2023. In the first stage, the authors describe a situation marked by money worship, hedonism, extreme individualism and historical nihilism, and by officials with unclear political positions. They present Xi's August 2013 speech on propaganda and ideological work as setting direction, and list four measures: cultural confidence, firm leadership over ideological work, the core socialist values, and flourishing socialist literature and art. In the second stage they cite the "nine upholds" of 2018, the institutional arrangements of the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), the 2035 goal of a cultural power set by the Fifth Plenum (2020), and the Two Integrations. In the third stage they point to the June 2023 symposium on cultural heritage and the October 2023 national work conference, which formally set out Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Tao and Yang conclude that this thought sums up the Party's practical experience of leading cultural construction, enriches Marxist cultural theory and forms the cultural component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They describe it as an open system that will keep developing with practice and as a roadmap and guide to action for the new cultural mission. Read the original if you want a concise official-style chronology of how Party discourse on culture is presented as moving from 2012 to 2023.

Forming a governance pattern of government, market and society: giving full play to the strengths of the socialist market economy Approaches from multiple directions 从多个方面入手，形成政府、市场、社会共同参与的治理格局——充分发挥社会主义市场经济体制优势 Huang Yanfen Yang Yiyong This newspaper commentary, published in Beijing Daily, takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its demand that the government's role be better exercised. Huang Yanfen and Yang Yiyong argue that the strengths of the socialist market economy lie in the organic unity of an effective market and a capable government. They conclude that this requires a governance pattern in which government, market and society all take part. The piece first explains the plenum's guidance on improving the macroeconomic regulation system, exercising government functions fully and correctly, and optimising government structure. It then sets out eight areas of action, each following a duty the plenum assigns to government: macroeconomic stability, public services, fair competition, market regulation, market order, sustainable development, common prosperity and remedying market failure. In the authors' account, scientific macroeconomic regulation uses fiscal, monetary and industrial policy to secure growth, stable prices, full employment and balance of payments. Government should handle economic regulation, market supervision, social management and public services, neither over-intervening nor leaving the market disordered. The authors also call for slimmer, better-coordinated government bodies and for a pattern of government leadership, social participation and shared governance. For each of the eight areas the authors list concrete measures. These include prudent monetary policy and supply-side structural reform, equalised public services, fair competition review, anti-monopoly enforcement, big-data supervision, consumer protection, clean energy, income distribution reform and a rural–urban social security system. Their closing point is that such multi-sided work can advance high-quality development and all-round social progress. Read the original if you want a short, official-line checklist of how Chinese economists translate the plenum's government-role guidance into policy tasks.

Upholding and implementing the "Two Unwaverings" to pool strong forces for development 坚持和落实“两个毫不动摇”汇聚强大发展合力 Yang Ming This theory-page commentary in Economic Daily (6 December 2024) asks how the Party's long-standing line on ownership should be carried out in the current period of strategic opportunity and risk. Yang Ming argues that the Two Unwaverings must be upheld and put into practice: consolidating and developing the public sector while encouraging, supporting and guiding the non-public sector. In Yang's account, both are important foundations of the socialist market economy and of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first presents the Two Unwaverings as a major Party and state policy, drawing on Xi Jinping's statements and on the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to build a high-standard socialist market economy. The second sets out how state-owned capital and enterprises should strengthen their core functions. The third turns to the private economy and proposes measures in law, reform and confidence-building. Yang's central move is to reject the view, which the author says has circulated in society, that the public and non-public sectors are opposed. The two are described as an organic unity that should complement each other, with equal access to production factors, fair competition and equal legal protection. For state-owned enterprises, Yang lists three functions: leading industry by concentrating state capital in national security, public services and emerging strategic industries; driving original innovation under the new system for mobilizing national resources; and strategic investment through patient capital that supports new quality productive forces. For the private economy, Yang calls for a law promoting it, lower market-entry barriers, and support for capable private firms to lead major technology projects. Yang also urges easier financing, regulation of fees and payment arrears, and restraint in administrative inspections. Yang concludes that deepening reform should let the two forms of ownership develop together and open up wider prospects for Chinese modernization. The author stresses that the Two Unwaverings must show up in concrete reform measures that private firms can perceive, so as to strengthen their expectations and confidence. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Party theorists frame the relationship between state-owned and private capital after the Third Plenum of 2024.

A deeper understanding of developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 深刻认识因地制宜发展新质生产力 Fan Hengshan Fan Hengshan, writing in the theory pages of Economic Daily (6 December 2024), asks how regions should develop new quality productive forces. The article starts from Xi Jinping's instruction to hold to high-quality development as the primary task and to develop these forces "in line with local conditions". Fan argues that this principle reflects an inherent link between productive-force development and regional territorial space. In Fan's account, each locality should choose which new industries, models and growth drivers to promote according to its own resource endowments, industrial base and research capacity. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out the meaning and features of new quality productive forces. The second lists five pairs of relationships that localities must handle. The third proposes five practical principles for local implementation. It is a policy-oriented piece that gives general guidance and does not discuss particular regions or cases. In the first part, Fan defines new quality productive forces as an advanced form of productive forces led by innovation, with high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality features. Their core marker is a large rise in total factor productivity, and their main driver is scientific and technological innovation. Fan stresses that "new" is never settled for good, that traditional industries can become carriers of new quality productive forces once technology is applied to them, and that no single industry has an exclusive claim. From this Fan draws two regional conclusions. Every region has reason and capacity to pursue them, but localities must avoid herd behaviour, bubbles and a single model. The five relationships are new and old, taking and forgoing, inheriting and borrowing, point and area, and speed and stability. A sixth pairing, hard and soft conditions, covers infrastructure and talent alongside the business environment. The five principles are perseverance, building the new before breaking the old, seeking the lead through distinctive strengths, committed innovation, and integrated regional coordination. Fan concludes that localities should pursue differentiated development. Each should concentrate on its own strengths, transform traditional industries instead of discarding them, and advance steadily without building "on sand". Regions should also cooperate through industrial parks, "enclave economies" and the flow of resources across the country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official economic commentary turns the concept of new quality productive forces into guidance for local governments.

Understanding the basic connotation of new quality productive forces 深入理解把握新质生产力的基本内涵 Huang Zhibin This short theory-page commentary, published in Economic Daily in December 2024, asks how to grasp the basic connotation of new quality productive forces. Huang Zhibin starts from Xi Jinping's formulation and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision. In that wording, the basic connotation is the leap in labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimised combination. Huang argues that developing these forces requires both upgrading each element and improving how the elements are combined. The article has two parts. The first sets out the new, higher demands placed on labourers, means of labour and objects of labour. The second turns to the institutional guarantees and driving forces for optimal combination and renewal, ending with a note on developing the forces in line with local conditions. Huang describes new quality productive forces as an advanced form of productive forces, led by innovation and in line with the new development philosophy, and as inherently green. Labourers therefore need knowledge of intelligent and green technology, to be cultivated through education and talent-system reform. Means of labour, mainly tools, should be upgraded or redesigned with intelligent technology. Objects of labour call for ecological protection, resource conservation and big-data use. Huang adds that mismatches between elements, such as surplus or scarce labourers, idle tools or hoarded materials, waste resources and lower efficiency. Because ownership, labour and distribution relations act back on productive forces, the author links combination to institutional reform. Huang calls for deeper economic reform and for improving the basic socialist economic system, with stronger state and private firms. The article also urges better cooperation in science and technology, a unified national market, a modern enterprise system with the Chinese characteristics the author names, and income distribution that rewards factors including data. Regions should develop new industries selectively according to their resources and industrial base. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style statement of how the three labour elements and reform measures are tied together in new quality productive forces.

Scientific answers to major economic questions of theory and practice in the new era 新时代重大经济理论实践问题的科学回答 Liu Shouying This theory-page commentary, published in Economic Daily on 5 December 2024, asks how Xi Jinping's economic thought answers the major questions of the new era: for whom development is pursued, what kind of development is pursued, and how. Liu Shouying argues that this body of thought, grounded in practice and problem-orientation, supplies scientific answers while advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu also claims that it innovates on and goes beyond traditional development economics. The article has four parts. It first sets out the fundamental guarantee and standpoint of economic development: the Party's overall leadership and a people-centred approach. It then treats high-quality development as the primary task, covering the new development philosophy, the new development pattern and new quality productive forces. A third part addresses strategic planning, and a final part compares Xi's economic thought with post-war development economics. Liu's core argument is that China's main social contradiction has shifted, so growth must move from "having enough" to "being good". High-quality development, in this account, means quality-first and efficiency-first growth, driven by reforms in quality, efficiency and momentum. It requires applying the five elements of the new development philosophy together and building a pattern centred on domestic circulation. New quality productive forces are presented as the engine, defined by innovation and a marked rise in total factor productivity. On strategy, Liu points to further comprehensive deepening of reform after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), to rural revitalization, coordinated regional development and people-centred urbanization, to a modern industrial system, and to balancing development with security. Liu concludes that, unlike traditional development economics, which drew its prescriptions mainly from the experience of successful countries, Xi's economic thought generalises from China's concrete practice. It is said to answer both how a country escapes poverty and how it then builds a modern, strong state. Liu presents it as Chinese wisdom for humanity's path to modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars frame Xi Jinping's economic thought and its claimed break with development economics.

Paths to improving the supply capacity of university ideological and political theory course teachers 提升高校思政课教师供给能力的路径 Yu Haibo Yu Haibo takes up a gap he sees in university ideological and political theory courses (sixheng ke): teachers' capacity to supply what the courses need does not match the drive to make these courses stronger. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that the key to running such courses well lies with teachers, Yu argues for a systematic approach that advances teaching, research and practice together. The short commentary, published on Guangming Online, sets out four lines of action: goals, evaluation and support, theoretical content, and teaching method. Each is tied to a slogan about what teachers need: the will, the strength, the scholarship and the technique to become a "great teacher". Yu first calls for stimulating teachers' inner motivation, countering burnout through career plans and "development communities" of senior, middle-aged and young teachers. Second, Yu proposes reforming evaluation: weighting teaching performance in promotion, avoiding counts of papers and projects, creating separate promotion tracks (teaching-research, teaching-focused, research-focused), and matching courses to teachers' academic backgrounds. Third, Yu argues that research should start from and return to teaching, so that teachers can "talk politics through scholarship" by reading original works and joining reading groups and seminars. Fourth, Yu observes that new teachers are highly qualified academically but lack systematic pedagogical training, and that short, often online certification courses have limited effect. Yu urges practical training in teaching internships, courses and competitions. Yu concludes that improving teacher supply capacity will improve the content and methods of teaching and move these courses towards high-quality development in the new era. The text is a project output funded by the Ministry of Education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese university scholars frame teacher development, evaluation reform and training for ideological and political courses.

Grasping the specific content and deep grounds of the "people's need for a better life" 把握“人民美好生活需要”的具体内涵和深刻依据 Han Xiping Du Du Han Xiping and Du Du take up the shift in China's principal social contradiction in the new era. It has moved from one between growing material and cultural needs and backward production to one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. The authors argue that understanding what this "need for a better life" contains is essential to tackling that imbalance, and that the concept rests on firm theoretical and practical grounds. The short piece has two parts. The first sets out the concept's specific content, covering material needs and spiritual needs. The second gives the grounds for meeting these needs: Marxism's value aims, the essence of socialism, and the original aspiration of the Communist Party of China. On content, the authors say material needs form the base and must be richer and of higher quality, fairer in distribution, and reasonable. By reasonable they mean guarded against the false and luxury needs Marx criticised, and against hedonism and consumerism. Spiritual needs, they add, lift the whole and follow from human nature as both material and social. On grounds, they hold that meeting these needs is the stage-specific form of Marxism's goal of human emancipation and all-round development. They link it to Deng Xiaoping's and Xi Jinping's accounts of socialism's essence and common prosperity. They also say the Party's history is one of meeting the people's needs, now moving from \"having or not\" to \"how good\". The authors conclude that satisfying the people's need for a better life runs through the whole cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics and unites lawful development with purposeful aims. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists justify this reformulation of the principal contradiction.

Optimising the paths to emotional identification in political values education 政治价值观教育情感认同的路径优化 Huang Jin Huang Jin takes up the question of how political values education for university students can win genuine emotional identification, meaning that students accept, endorse and are willing to put these values into practice. The short commentary, first published on Guangming Online's theory channel, argues that such identification is the necessary route to the goal of political values education and an urgent requirement of fostering virtue through education. Huang holds that current practice falls short and needs improved paths. Huang defines students' political values as their overall views, evaluations, attitudes and behavioural tendencies towards the political world. The author describes universities as the main front for training reliable successors to the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article then names three shortcomings: educators lacking the competence to awaken emotion, incomplete content that fails to imprint emotion, and unscientific methods that prevent emotional interaction. Three groups of remedies follow, aimed at educators, content and methods. On educators, Huang calls for stronger political literacy and theoretical grounding, together with positive emotions and emotional capacity, so that teachers can move students through real feeling. On content, the author argues that identification rests on meeting students' legitimate interests: reasonable needs should be recognised and met, unreasonable ones firmly stopped and guided. Scientific content should also be combined with humanistic content on relations between people, politics and society, and on emotion, will and belief. On methods, Huang proposes political rituals, which the author says shape national, political and emotional identification through shared emotional experience, and a blend of online and offline carriers. Huang concludes that improving educators' abilities, content and methods together will let political values education reach students emotionally and not only cognitively. Students would then understand, take part in and practise these values. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ideological and political education scholarship frames emotional identification as a task for university teaching.

The philosophical meaning and contemporary demands of emancipating the mind 解放思想的哲学意蕴和时代要求 Gao Haitao Writing in December 2024, Gao Haitao asks what "emancipating the mind" (jiefang sixiang) means philosophically and what it requires in the present. Gao argues that it is an essential demand of Marxist epistemology and that it must be pursued consciously to advance Chinese modernization and further comprehensively deepen reform. The commentary has three parts. It first grounds the concept in dialectical materialism, then reviews the direction and principles of emancipating the mind during reform and opening up, and finally turns to the tasks of the new journey. Gao defines emancipating the mind as shaking off outdated ideas and thinking patterns so that thought matches reality, which in essence means theoretical innovation. Drawing on the cycle of practice, cognition, renewed practice and renewed cognition, Gao says ideas lag behind a changing reality and become fetters unless adjusted. The obstacles are of two kinds: empiricism and dogmatism produce rigidity, while voluntarism and intuitionism produce thought that ignores objective laws. Gao says emancipation also demands the courage for self-criticism and the Party's self-reform. For the reform era, Gao stresses two principles: keeping to the right direction, meaning the Four Cardinal Principles together with reform, and putting the people at the centre, since the masses are the subject of practice. Gao calls for following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), breaking down ideological and institutional obstacles, and turning the Party's innovative theory into concrete practice at every level. Emancipating the mind, Gao concludes, serves to unify thought and action under that theory. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated writers link the Marxist concept of emancipating the mind to the current reform agenda.

Building strong ideological and political leadership for a fully built education powerhouse 为全面建成教育强国凝聚强大的思政引领力 Han Shangfeng Han Shangfeng takes up one of the "six strengths" that Xi Jinping says a socialist education powerhouse with Chinese characteristics must possess: strong ideological and political leadership. Han notes that it is listed first, and argues that it expresses the Central Committee's requirement that ideological and political work run through Party building, state governance and the whole of education. The article's thesis is that this leadership is built by strengthening Party leadership over ideological and political courses, by raising the quality of teachers, and by reforming how ideological and political education is organised. Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, the piece is a commentary by a university Party secretary, in three numbered sections. The first deals with Party leadership and the content of theory teaching. The second concerns the teaching force of ideological and political courses. The third covers institutional reform, integration of such education across university, middle and primary schools, and the "big ideological and political course". It draws heavily on Xi's remarks and on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). In the first section, Han calls for firm political orientation, with Party leadership as the basic guarantee of the direction of education. Han also wants Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to enter textbooks, classrooms and minds, and wants a framework of education involving all staff, the whole process and every aspect. The second section holds that teachers must be both teachers of knowledge and models of character, embodying the "spirit of educators". It also asks them to keep learning, including about digital technologies, so they can answer young people's questions. The third section calls for coordinated reform of educational methods, school-running models, management systems and support mechanisms. It also calls for integrated ideological and political education across school stages, and for extending the classroom into society using digital platforms, success stories of the new era and "red resources". Han concludes that these measures would turn Party leadership and theory into practical educational strength. The measures would also bind individual growth to national development and cultivate young people who take the building of a modern socialist country as their mission. The article proposes accountability mechanisms, such as placing ideological work under Party responsibility systems and assessing teachers' political conduct. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-university leader translates Xi's "six strengths" formula into concrete tasks for ideological and political education.

The crisis of neoliberal capitalism 新自由主义的资本主义的危机 Prabhat Patnaik This is a Chinese translation (abridged) of an article by the Indian Marxist economist Prabhat Patnaik. It asks why neoliberal capitalism has produced stagnation, falling incomes for working people and the rise of fascist tendencies. Patnaik argues that the crisis is inherent in the neoliberal order and cannot be resolved within it, so that overcoming it requires a break with neoliberalism, above all through controls on financial flows. The article first places neoliberalism in the longer history of capitalism, in which labour from the Global South was never free to move North and Northern capital seldom invested in Southern manufacturing. It then describes four phenomena of present globalization, sets out two basic tendencies of neoliberal capitalism, and explains why state action cannot counter them. It closes with a section on the emergence of neo-fascism and a conclusion about the prospects of the Global South. Patnaik contends that the earlier "segmentation" of the world economy has broken down, because capital now relocates to low-wage Southern economies while labour stays confined. Northern real wages stagnate and Southern labour reserves grow relatively, even where GDP growth is high. India is his main case: employment growth halved while GDP growth nearly doubled, so unemployment is hidden in discouraged workers and shared-out work. Globalized finance also removes national policy autonomy, and the state withdraws support from peasant agriculture and small producers. As a result, per capita real income of the working population falls, the surplus share rises and overproduction follows. Fiscal stimulus is blocked by coordination problems and by financial capital's opposition to taxing the rich and to deficits, so only asset-price bubbles had delayed the stagnation. Patnaik adds that today's neo-fascism, an alliance of domestic corporate oligarchy tied to globalized capital with fascist organizations, serves to divert attention and divide workers. Unlike 1930s fascism, he argues, it cannot spend its way out of crisis, because finance is now global. Patnaik concludes that neoliberalism has reached a dead end and that the Global South should recognise this soon. He argues that recent Northern trade controls do not amount to a real exit, since they leave capital controls aside and the South cannot retaliate or expand fiscally. He adds that Southern countries are burdened with unsustainable external debt and conditional bailouts, so the crisis that forces them to leave neoliberalism also makes leaving harder. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of neoliberal stagnation, labour reserves and neo-fascism from the standpoint of the Global South, with India as the key example.

The demise of capitalism: ultimate crisis and the substance of value 资本主义的消亡：终极危机与价值实质 David Janzen This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Canadian scholar David Janzen. It asks whether capitalism can be shown to be heading for a final crisis, and whether that crisis has arrived. Janzen argues that the answer depends on how value is understood, as a material substance or as a social relation. He also argues that the 'ultimate crisis' thesis has limits as a theory of history. The article compares Robert Kurz, a founder of value-critique (Wertkritik), with Michael Heinrich. It also draws on Norbert Trenkle, Alfred Sohn-Rethel, Isaac Rubin and others. It has three parts: value and crisis, the politics of crisis, and the historicity of the concept of crisis. It closes by testing Kurz's framework against the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 crisis. Janzen first sets out the substantialist view, in which value is condensed labour in commodities. On this view, automation that expels labour from production destroys capitalism's material basis. Heinrich's relational view holds that value only expresses the relation between individual and total social labour, so labour-saving technology need not end value. Janzen defends Heinrich against Trenkle's charge that he isolates exchange from production, using Aristotle's notion of potentiality. He argues that just-in-time logistics and platform capitalism blur production and circulation, yet Kurz and Heinrich draw opposite conclusions from the same facts. He then traces how Marx turned 'crisis' from a normative concept into a concept of historical science. In his reading, Marx never clearly tied crisis to permanent collapse, and Marx himself treated the 1873 crisis as unprecedented. Janzen concludes that Kurz's approach has real strengths. It explains why the 2008 crisis grew into a global catastrophe, attributing it to a lack of real capital valorisation, and it shows why stimulus and bailouts could not fix the underlying problem. It is weaker on Covid-19, a crisis that combined ecological, social, political and economic dimensions. Rejecting the 'ultimate crisis hypothesis', he says, neither endorses the 'end of history' nor implies that social development cannot be predicted. Read the original if you work on crisis theory, value-form debates or Wertkritik and want a critical comparison of Kurz and Heinrich.

A luminous text interpreting the fundamental purpose of the Communist Party of China: marking the 80th anniversary of "Serve the People" 诠释中国共产党根本宗旨的光辉文献——纪念《为人民服务》发表80周年 Wang Chuanli Tang Mengxin Marking the 80th anniversary of Mao Zedong's speech "Serve the People" (1944), Wang Chuanli and Tang Mengxin argue that this text of under 800 characters remains the fullest statement of the Communist Party of China's fundamental purpose. Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, the commentary holds that the phrase "serve the people" has become the motto of Chinese communists and a guide to their work for the people's happiness and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has four parts. It first traces the Marxist foundations of the text, then sets out how the purpose of wholeheartedly serving the people is to be put into practice. It next surveys generations of Party members presented as exemplars, from the revolutionary war years through socialist construction to the reform era. It ends with the policies of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The central argument is that the text embodies three Marxist positions: a view of history in which the masses create history, a conception of the Party as a vanguard with no interests of its own, and the idea of officials as public servants and "attendants" of the people, drawn from Marx and Engels on the Paris Commune. From this the authors derive three practical requirements: selfless sacrifice, including of life; readiness to correct mistakes when criticised, illustrated by the acceptance of proposals from non-Party figures Li Dingming and Huang Yanpei; and tireless work. Exemplars cited include Zhang Side, Lei Feng, Wang Jinxi, Jiao Yulu, Li Suli and Kong Fansen. For the present, the authors say the purpose appears in the people-centred approach, in "the people first, life first" during disasters and epidemics, in poverty reduction, and in sharing the fruits of reform through investment in education, health care, employment and social security. The authors conclude that serving the people has "a starting point but no end point" and has become the Party's spiritual gene, which will continue to guide the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Their account is commemorative and presents the Party's record largely in positive terms. Read the original if you want to see how Party theorists link Mao's 1944 speech to Marxist theory, to model figures from each period and to current policy language on people-centred development.

Basic dimensions of building China's autonomous philosophical knowledge system 建构中国自主的哲学知识体系的基本维度 Cheng Biao Cheng Biao takes up the task of building an autonomous Chinese philosophical knowledge system, which the author treats as both a major theoretical question for philosophy and a practical question bearing on China's social development and the future of Chinese civilization. The short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2024, argues that the task can be understood only through three dimensions: theory, practice and civilization. The piece takes each dimension in turn. The theoretical dimension concerns the course of Chinese philosophical research since reform and opening up. The practical dimension concerns the experience of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The civilizational dimension concerns the continuous development of Chinese civilization. On theory, Cheng says Chinese philosophy broke free of dogmatism in Marxist philosophy research, put the concept of practice at the centre, and posed the question of integrating Chinese, Western and Marxist philosophy within the effort to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author concludes that the conditions for a subjective and original system are now in place. On practice, Cheng holds that the "two miracles" and Chinese modernization supply an empirical basis, and that this experience must be raised into theory. On civilization, the author describes Chinese civilization as continuous, innovative, unified, inclusive and peaceful, contrasts it with Western modern civilization led by capitalism, and says the system's core task is to distil the "living soul" of a new form of human civilization. Cheng concludes that only by grasping all three dimensions can a subjective and original contemporary Chinese philosophy be built, laying a theoretical foundation for national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese academic and official discourse frames the project of an autonomous philosophical knowledge system.

New orientations in Western critiques of philanthrocapitalism and a theoretical assessment 西方慈善资本主义批判的新取向及理论评析 Tao Zhuorui Tao examines philanthrocapitalism, the idea first formulated in The Economist in 2006 that private philanthropy should operate like profit-seeking capital markets. Since the 2008 financial crisis it has been promoted as a remedy for capitalism's social ills. The article argues that Western left-wing scholars have criticised it comprehensively but remain limited by their class standpoint, and that a Marxist view of charity is needed to grasp its contradictions. The article has three parts. The first traces the economic and social background: the rise of a new generation of wealthy elites in the information-technology era, the spread of neoliberal values into charity, and doubts about traditional charity under the welfare state. The second surveys critiques by Western left-wing and critical scholars, including Slavoj Žižek, Robert Reich, Linsey McGoey and Wilson Japhy. The third assesses those critiques from a Marxist standpoint. Tao groups the newer critiques into three lines. They attack market-oriented commercialisation of charity as wasteful and exclusionary of citizens. They argue that philanthropic capital deepens inequality between people and sustains a 'colonial–dependency' order globally. And they hold that the logic of capital is opposed to the charitable ideal, citing tax avoidance through foundations and the claim that donors give back only a fraction of what they accumulate. Tao then identifies four weaknesses in these critiques. They stay with exchange and distribution rather than tracing charitable funds back to surplus value produced by labour. They hold the consequences to account without reaching private ownership of the means of production. They weaken the class character of charity through pluralist class views. And they neglect socialist public welfare and offer no workable proposals for citizens' philanthropy. Tao concludes that Western left scholarship is reactive, slow to respond and tends to demolish without building, with a markedly academic style. Tao calls for research to rest on the labour theory of value, the ownership of the means of production and Marxist class analysis. It should also take up the philanthropic role of working people and Marx and Engels's ideas about socialist public welfare. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western left critiques of billionaire philanthropy, with many references to English-language scholarship.

Signature concepts of China's independent knowledge system of ecological civilization and their effects 中国自主的生态文明知识体系的标识性概念及其效应 Cai Huajie This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in November 2024, asks how China's practice of ecological civilization construction can be turned into an independent knowledge system. Cai Huajie argues that the task begins with extracting "signature concepts" (标识性概念), which the author treats as the cornerstone of such a system. In Cai's account, these concepts can be organised around one root concept, "Chinese Marxist ecology", and will have lasting methodological effects. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's call to distil signature concepts and the achievements said to follow the 18th Party Congress (2012), when ecological civilization was placed within the "five-sphere integrated plan". It then has two parts: the first on how the concepts are extracted and analysed, the second on three effects they produce. Its examples include "Lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets", "a community of life on Earth" and "Beautiful China". Cai describes conceptualization as a way of grasping the relationship between humans and the world, which yields reflective, normative and constructive concepts. From the root concept "Chinese Marxist ecology", the author derives three groups. Reflective concepts respond to Western environmental disasters and mechanistic views of nature. Normative concepts include socialist ecological civilization and modernization in which humanity and nature coexist in harmony. Constructive concepts concern institutions and systems, such as integrated governance of mountains, rivers, forests, farmland, lakes, grassland and desert. Together they form a "reflection–norm–construction" framework. The three effects are adjustment and regulation of ways of production and life, revolution and innovation (a "revolution in terminology", in Engels's phrase), and communication and selection. On the last, Cai claims that Western approaches to climate change have institutional defects, which gives Chinese concepts a real chance of wider uptake. Cai concludes that these concepts give China's ecological civilization knowledge system a firm foundation and a vehicle for narration. The author also holds that they offer countries wanting both development and environmental protection a new option, and that their spread demonstrates the scientific character and vitality of Marxism. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars frame the building of an "independent knowledge system" in ecological thought, and which official slogans they treat as its core concepts.

Grasping the theoretical foundations of the "leading capacity of ideological and political education" 把握“思政引领力”的理论基础 Xiong Weina Xiong takes up a phrase from Xi Jinping's description of a strong education country: the capacity of ideological and political education to provide guidance (sizheng yinlingli). The article argues that this capacity expresses the socialist character of a "strong education country" with Chinese characteristics, and that strengthening it rests on a deep theoretical foundation in the Marxist classics. The short commentary has three parts. It first reviews what Marx, Engels and Lenin said about the political character of education. It then sets out why the classics treated ideological and political guidance as a task of the proletarian party. It ends with practical proposals for the present. Xiong draws on Lenin's 1920 rejection of "apolitical" education and on the Communist Manifesto to argue that politics shapes education, and that education in turn acts on politics, including in the Bolsheviks' mass education before the October Revolution. From this the author derives three requirements: consolidating socialist ideology, upholding Party leadership with a loyal teaching force, and encouraging learners' self-education, citing Engels's remarks on self-improvement among Russian revolutionary youth. For practice, Xiong calls for improving the institutions through which the Party leads ideological and political work, and for building ideological and political theory courses around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author also urges stronger teacher ethics and better incentives for teachers. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars ground education policy in Lenin's writings on political education.

Digital socialism: problem field and theoretical lineages 数字社会主义：问题域与理论流脉 Pan Na Pan Na asks how "digital socialism" arose as a concept, how Western left scholars took it over, and what Marxists should make of it. The article argues that the term began as a Silicon Valley ideological device and was later reclaimed by the Western left as a proposed alternative to capitalism. In Pan's assessment, this left version is valuable as a constructive and cross-disciplinary body of work, but remains a twenty-first-century utopian socialism that cannot replace capitalism.
