It was published in Open Times in 2024. The article first traces the term from Kevin Kelly's 2009 Wired essay "The New Socialism" to his later "protopia" narrative and the 2016 "techlash". It then follows the left debate over "technofeudalism", involving Kotkin, Varoufakis, Durand, Dean, Morozov, Ström and Brenner. The central part sets out three left routes: reviving the socialist calculation debate (Morozov, Benanav, Rief on Polanyi); returning to Marx's "fragment on machines" (Virno, Peters, Fuchs, Fischli, Muldoon); and "blockchain socialism", which either redesigns cryptocurrency or tries to abolish money. Pan then assesses their value, limits and lessons. Pan reads Kelly's "socialism without a state" as an anti-statist cover for tech oligarchs' interests, and finds the left models marked by the same neglect of the state. In Pan's view they omit the question of establishing proletarian state power, citing Lenin on the dictatorship of the proletariat. They also ignore Marx's "two never's" (the conditions for a new social formation must mature within the old), because they rely on digital technology alone and are designed for single countries or regions. Pan sees the Fuchs-style approach as continuing Italian autonomist readings of the "fragment on machines" and as sliding into an "ethicist politics of the subject". Pan nonetheless credits the left with linking critique to construction, theory to practice, and with drawing on many disciplines. Pan concludes that Western left digital socialism cannot transform capitalism and is confined to marginal social experiments. Pan still draws three lessons for non-Western countries: it supports the search for a new form of human civilisation, it offers meso- and micro-level ideas on technology and governance for China's digital construction, and it gives an internal view of capitalism's digital crisis. Pan calls for China to build an autonomous body of knowledge on how digital technology and scientific socialism can empower each other. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese Marxist map of the Western left's digital-socialism debates and their reception in China.

On the "resurrection" of the subject: from Lukács and Althusser to Badiou 论主体的“复活”——从卢卡奇、阿尔都塞到巴迪欧 Fan Chunyan Fan Chunyan asks how the "resurrection" of the subject in Alain Badiou should be understood against the "death" of the subject in Louis Althusser and the earlier project of Georg Lukács. The article argues that resurrection is an "Althusser–Badiou" thesis, or over a longer span a "Lukács–Althusser–Badiou" one. Badiou's revived subject stays anti-humanist and presupposes a structural "place" and contingent events, so it continues Althusser's late subject as bearer of contingent practice. Yet Badiou goes further, drawing universality out of contingency and rebuilding the subject as a "body" of truth. The article has three parts. The first traces the subject's "death" from Lukács through the early Frankfurt School (Adorno, Horkheimer) to Althusser's interpellated subject. The second examines Althusser's late "materialism of the encounter", in which the subject shifts from bearer of structure to bearer of practice. The third turns to Badiou's Theory of the Subject, Being and Event and Logics of Worlds. Fan rejects a simple humanism-versus-structuralism split and reads the subject's death as a long process. For Lukács, the active subject must be recovered from reified ideology through repeated critique and practice. Adorno and Horkheimer treat ideology as objectively necessary and the subject as heading towards self-sacrifice. Althusser rejects "false consciousness", locates ideology in the unconscious and makes the subject a "submissive" occupant of a structural place, though an indispensable one. His late encounter-materialism restores practice but leaves it without purposiveness or lawfulness. Badiou keeps the "place" but adds "outplace" (force) and makes the subject faithful to an event. Through naming, investigation and "forcing", the subject builds truth as a generic subset. In Logics of Worlds this subject acquires a body, with faithful, reactionary and obscure subjects as variants. Fan concludes that Badiou restores the creativity and agency of the practical subject while keeping Althusser's anti-humanism, which in effect answers Lukács's early search for revolutionary subjectivity. The faithful subject is presented as the worldly body of truth, pointing towards a new future. Fan also notes that, even for Badiou, practice has no room for purposiveness or lawfulness. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, Althusser or Badiou and want an account of how their theories of ideology and the subject connect.

The end of politics and "post-democracy": Rancière's philosophical critique of contemporary Western politics 政治的终结与“后民主”——朗西埃对当代西方政治的哲学批判 Zhao Dingqi This article examines how Jacques Rancière, a prominent radical left thinker and former member of Althusser's Reading Capital group, diagnoses contemporary Western politics. Zhao argues that Rancière, by distinguishing "politics" from "police", shows a depoliticising tendency in which policing displaces politics. The result, in Zhao's account, is a "consensus democracy" or "post-democracy" that has lost substantive content. Zhao presents these concepts as useful for understanding the Western political crisis and the rise of populism. The article has five parts. It first traces Rancière's break with Althusser and his turn to "history from below", then his reading of Aristotle and the notions of "dissensus" (the French 'mésentente', rendered as 'ambiguity' or 'disagreement') and the "part of those who have no part". It then sets out the two logics of police and politics. The third part covers two forms of the "end of politics", and the fourth covers post-democracy and populism. A short conclusion assesses Rancière's significance and limits. Zhao reports that Rancière treats inequality as a matter of who is allowed to speak and be seen, rather than as Marx's class inequality rooted in relations of production. Police is an invisible order that distributes bodies, roles and speech, and it turns the rules of government into natural law; Zhao cites technocratic rule as its best contemporary example. Politics arises when the "part of those who have no part", the proletarian as an excluded figure, disrupts this order in the name of equality. The "end of politics" takes two forms: the end of promises, as in Mitterrand's abandoned pledges, and the end of division, as class conflict gives way to racism and xenophobia. For Rancière, representative democracy is in essence oligarchic, and "populism" is a label that lets elites dismiss dissent from the consensus. Zhao concludes that Rancière exposes the hypocrisy of capitalist rule and the illusion of "consensus politics" shared by left and right parties. His concepts influenced Mouffe and Žižek and anticipated "post-politics". Zhao also holds that Rancière lacks a historical-materialist perspective: class inequality becomes an inequality of discourse, and his critique is not grounded in the critique of political economy, so that he is "no longer a Marxist". Even so, Zhao sees value in his call for a return of politics for analysing right-wing populism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Rancière's political philosophy and its bearing on Western populism.

Re-examining the idea of "labour ownership" in the context of the critique of political economy 重审政治经济学批判语境中的“劳动所有权”观念 Sun Liang Sun Liang takes up Locke's proposition that labour grounds property, which the article calls "labour ownership", and asks how Marx's critique of political economy dismantles it. The thesis is that Marx separates two meanings of the idea: the identity of labour and ownership, and labour appearing as negated ownership. This distinction, the author argues, takes Marx beyond both Lockean liberal political philosophy and the classical political economy of Adam Smith. The article is built in four parts, drawing on Marx's 1861–63 manuscripts, the Grundrisse and Capital. It starts with the Physiocrats and Smith and the contradiction between two determinations of exchange-value. It then turns to the way ownership becomes the appropriation of others' labour, and to the critique of fetishism as Marx's method. A short conclusion follows. Rubin and Locke are the main secondary points of reference. Sun reads Smith's wavering between the two determinations of value as an intuition of the contradiction that appears once labour and capital exchange. Smith could not resolve it, the author says, because he took the worker to sell labour rather than labour-power and did not grasp the historicity of the capitalist mode of production. For Marx, once labour-power is a commodity its owner no longer controls its use. Equivalent exchange in the market is then only a form, and the real process is the appropriation of unpaid labour. Sun holds that apologists confuse two kinds of private property, one resting on the producer's own labour and one on exploiting others'. They also conflate abstract and concrete labour and so blur social and natural relations. The author treats this as fetishism, which naturalises a historical social form, and cites Marx's account of primitive accumulation as a refutation. Sun concludes that Marx's critique keeps categories and reality in contradiction, whereas political economists close the gap and make categories into defences of the existing order. The author claims that showing how labour ownership turns into its opposite under capitalism undermines the foundations of classical political economy and Western political philosophy. The article also presents this as a way into Marx's political philosophy and its contemporary value. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Marx's critique of political economy engages Locke's and Smith's theories of property.

"The disappearance of the Other" and the "dialectics of violence": the Other and its critical dimensions in Byung-Chul Han “他者的消失”与“暴力辩证法”——论韩炳哲视野中的“他者”及其批判向度 Li Chunmin How does Byung-Chul Han use the category of the "Other" to criticise digital capitalism? Li argues that Han's account of the "disappearance of the Other" and the "dialectics of violence" opens an insightful critical path. In it, both "Other" and "dialectics" are reconceptualised and turned into a critical practice with a social-pathological dimension. Li places this against a long philosophical lineage, from Hegel, Husserl and Heidegger to Levinas, Adorno and Lyotard. The article reconstructs five critical dimensions of the Other in Han's work: the Other as "authentic object", as the opposite of "the Same" (der Gleiche), as the correlate of the "authentic self", as "authentic Eros", and as a rebellion against the logic of capital. A sixth section draws out the theoretical lessons of Han's account and then sets out three limitations. Li draws throughout on Han's own formulations on transparency, positivity, achievement society and neoliberalism. In Li's reading, authentic dialectics requires an internal negativity, which the Other supplies. Where the Other vanishes, commodities become pliant "objects of consumption", digital quantification homogenises everything, and "the Same" spreads. This produces a "dialectics of violence", a violence of positivity that removes negation. Li reports that Han traces its effects in self-exploitation experienced as freedom, shallow digital communication that lacks "listening", impoverished experience, and the alienation of vision, hearing and the body into a "depressive" or narcissistic self. Han also finds it in globalisation's homogenisation, in the neoliberal reduction of time to performance time, and in the marketing of the "true self". Li credits Han with three contributions: a multidimensional use of the Other that Li finds compatible with Marx's concept of practice, a renewed task for dialectics as both diagnosis and critique, and a critique of digital capitalism that starts from sensibility. Li also names three limits. Han neglects labour and its opposition to capital, so he never reaches the depth of Marx's critique. Han underrates the positive potential of digital technology. His theory lacks original concepts and, being essayistic, becomes fragmentary and verges on aesthetic nostalgia. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Han's philosophy and of his critique of digital capitalism.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating in ideological and political courses in the new era 新时代思政课坚持守正创新 Yin Hui This short commentary asks how ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in schools should combine continuity with change in the new era. Yin argues that "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" means holding to the courses' basic task, educational essence and fundamental nature while innovating continually to open a new phase of political education. The author notes that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee has given these courses an important place in education work. The piece is organised as seven prescriptions. The first three concern what must be kept: the task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, the courses' essence as reasoned exposition of Marxist theory, and their political and educational nature. The remaining four concern a "big ideological and political course" framework, teaching methods, evaluation, and the teaching force. Yin contends that the courses must be synchronised with the Party's innovative theory and must lead students to conclude that only socialism can save China and only Chinese modernization can develop it. Teachers are to explain Marxist theory in plain language, link it to everyday life, and draw on China's achievements and on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture. On innovation, Yin calls for a "big ideological and political course" that joins classroom, course-embedded political education and social practice, and for varied methods, including lecture, discussion and game-based teaching, that meet the challenge of digital technology. Yin also proposes multi-party evaluation of teachers and process-based assessment of students. The author calls for teachers who are "politically strong, deeply committed, innovative in thinking, broad in vision, strictly self-disciplined and upright in character", so that the courses develop in depth. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of how a university Marxism-school scholar frames the principles and practical priorities of ideological and political teaching.

Teaching well the value orientation of putting the people first 讲好坚持以人民为中心的价值取向 Shi Wenrui Shi Wenrui takes up how ideological and political theory courses in universities should teach the principle of 'putting the people first' (adhering to a people-centred approach). The author notes that the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) listed this principle among the major principles for further deepening reform comprehensively. Shi argues that teaching it systematically helps students merge personal aspirations with those of the country and people and commit themselves to Chinese modernization. This short commentary is organised around three justifications for the principle, followed by a section on teaching method. The justifications are theoretical (Marxism's people-oriented character), historical (the experience of reform and opening up) and practical (answering what Shi calls the 'people's questions' in the current period). The final part turns to pedagogy. Shi argues that the people-centred orientation reflects the historical-materialist view that the people are the fundamental force creating history, and that students should learn from reform achievements across many fields how the masses create material and spiritual wealth. The author presents the orientation as an innovative development of Marxism and as a practical application of the mass line. Shi then argues that the Party's record since the 18th Party Congress (2012) shows reform serving and relying on the people. As people's demands now extend beyond material life to democracy, rule of law, fairness, justice, security and environment, courses should use successful cases to show how reform answers these needs. Shi calls for 'Great Ideological and Political Courses' that link the classroom with society, bringing in exemplary figures and sending students out into practice, so the principle is felt as concrete rather than abstract. The aim is for students to serve the country and people in the cause of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state theory on people-centredness is translated into guidance for university ideological and political teaching.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating to promote the intensive development of ideological and political courses 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Lin Xiaofang Lin Xiaofang, writing in December 2024 in the theory channel of People's Daily Online, asks how ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in Chinese schools can develop in depth rather than merely expand. The commentary answers that this requires "upholding fundamental principles and innovating" (shouzheng chuangxin). In practice, Lin argues, that means adhering to Marxist truth, reforming teaching, and building a wider, collaborative educational pattern. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out the political foundations of the courses: political direction, Party leadership and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The second concerns reform and innovation in content, teaching methods, the teacher–student relationship and the academic discipline. The third proposes a "big ideological and political course" that draws in many actors and settings. On the first point, Lin holds that the courses must keep Marxism in its guiding position and use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to shape students' values. Party committees at all levels should treat the courses as a political responsibility. On reform, Lin calls for guidance by the "Eight Unifications", for fresh Party theory, including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), to be integrated into teaching, and for AR, VR and MR technologies to create immersive classrooms. Teaching should move from one-way instruction to a model combining teacher guidance with student agency. The "big" course is to combine traditional classrooms, online classes and society as a classroom, integrate teaching from primary school through university, and draw on local history, other subjects and daily life as resources. Lin concludes that teachers are the key. They should hold firm Marxist belief, be both "scholars of the classics" and moral exemplars, and be supported by evaluation systems that put teaching first, by training and by project funding. The aim is to cultivate a new generation who are loyal to the Party, patriotic and ready to take on national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy framework for ideological and political courses in Chinese schools and universities, and the measures now being promoted.

Integrating the spirit of labour into ideological and political education in universities 推动劳动精神融入高校思想政治教育 Gao Jianwei This short commentary asks how universities can bring the spirit of labour into ideological and political education. Gao argues that the spirit of labour is an important part of the Chinese Communists' spiritual lineage and that embedding it is a key route to fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The article proposes three practical channels: ideological and political theory courses, a labour education curriculum and practice system, and social practice activities. It closes with a general call on universities to treat the relationship between knowledge learning and all-round development correctly. Gao urges teachers of ideological and political courses to find points of fit between labour and course content, use modern information technology, run practice teaching on the theme, and invite model workers to speak in class. For labour education, universities should write it into training plans with compulsory credits, build teaching staff and materials, and set up practice bases with agricultural institutions so that students work in rural settings. For social practice, Gao points to summer study trips to revolutionary sites such as Yan'an, Jinggangshan and Xibaipo and to rural volunteer and survey programmes, through which students are meant to experience the value of labour directly. Gao concludes that universities should make the ideas that labour is most glorious, noble, great and beautiful take root in teachers and students, so that labour cultivates virtue, intellect, physique and aesthetic sense and produces capable talent. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a university Party official describes concrete steps for linking labour education to ideological and political work.

Building the "Great Ideological and Political Course" to improve the results of ideological and political education 以“大思政课”建设提升思政育人成效 Zhou Zifeng This short commentary, first published on People's Daily Online's theory channel, asks how universities can raise the effectiveness of ideological and political education through the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke). Zhou Zifeng argues that building it is a key lever for fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and for training a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article rests on Xi Jinping's repeated emphasis on ideological and political education since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It is organised in four parts: Party leadership over ideological and political courses, the role of teachers, the integration of classroom teaching with wider social practice, and the use of digital technology. Zhou first holds that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee, so courses must serve the Party and the country and be grounded in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On teachers, the author proposes regular political study, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Zhou also proposes evaluation reform, more recruitment, and part-time teachers such as model workers, heroes and master craftsmen. The author then calls for linking the \"first classroom\" (course groups, interactive methods) to a \"second classroom\" of practice bases, surveys, labour and volunteering. Finally, Zhou calls for digital means: big-data \"profiles\" of students' concerns, generative AI and recommendation tools for \"precise\" delivery of content, and virtual simulation, holographic imaging and the metaverse to recreate historical scenes. The author concludes that these measures together would widen the pattern of all-round education. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary on ideological and political teaching sets out Party leadership, teacher management, practice teaching and digital tools.

Guiding a new custom of respecting teachers and valuing education with the educator spirit 以教育家精神引领尊师重教新风尚 Zheng Shipeng This commentary, first published on the People's Daily Online theory channel, asks how the "educator spirit" (jiaoyujia jingshen) can be used to build a renewed social custom of respecting teachers and valuing education. Zheng Shipeng argues that such guidance would create a fair, respectful and harmonious environment for training high-quality teachers. In the author's view this would raise teachers' sense of professional honour, happiness and mission, and so supply the talent needed to build a strong education nation and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece takes its cue from the Central Committee and State Council Opinions on promoting the educator spirit and strengthening the teaching force in the new era. The article has three parts. The first treats the traditional Chinese roots of respect for teachers, citing Xunzi and the Book of Rites, and the need for wider social recognition of the educator spirit. The second sets out three kinds of guidance the spirit provides: value-based, emotional and practical. The third proposes three ways of creating a good social atmosphere for educators. It includes one example, a Tibetan middle-school principal in Nyingchi, to illustrate emotional commitment. Zheng contends that the educator spirit condenses the older tradition of honouring teachers into a modern form, covering ideals of serving the country, moral example, teaching according to aptitude, and a devotion to learning and innovation. Value guidance means putting the people first and treating education as a public-interest undertaking judged by popular satisfaction. Emotional guidance rests on the claim that education is essentially emotional labour. Practical guidance means unity of knowing and doing, with theory tested and revised in teaching practice, so that teachers become "great teachers" who combine skill in teaching with moral formation. The author calls for three measures: running education that satisfies the people and meets demands for diverse, personalised schooling; strengthening teachers' ethics and conduct, including ethics assessment in qualification, recruitment and awards, model teachers as exemplars and practice bases for ethics education; and building platforms where teachers can display their abilities, with open talent policies and teachers volunteering in remote, border and rural areas. Zheng presents these as ways to restore the dignity of the teaching profession and build a strong education nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state education policy links the educator spirit, teacher ethics and social respect for teachers.

Does artificial intelligence challenge the labour theory of value? 人工智能挑战了劳动价值论吗 Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin takes up a question that has followed recent advances in artificial intelligence: whether Marx's labour theory of value still holds when machines appear to replace people and when scholars speak of "immaterial labour" and "digital labour". The author's answer is that AI poses no challenge to the theory. In the digital economy, Zhou argues, the theory is not outdated but remains the scientific tool for analysing the social and historical effects of AI. This short commentary, published in a Chinese social science newspaper, has two parts. The first clarifies what the labour theory of value is, and the second applies it to labour under AI. Zhou notes that Marx himself hardly used the term. It took shape in the later nineteenth century, after the marginal revolution, in opposition to utility theories of value. Zhou also separates Marx's theory from Ricardo's and from Western economics, citing Samuelson as an example. Zhou's central claim is that the theory has to be read through historical materialism and the dual character of labour, not as the bare claim that labour creates value. In this reading, value is a historically specific proportion of exchange determined by the mode of production, and commodity relations express relations of production. Applied to AI, this yields three points. AI is essentially a complex and efficient machine, so questions about it become questions about changes in the mode of material production. Labels such as "immaterial labour" and "digital labour" should be treated with caution, because coding, designing machines and using AI are all labour, differing in socially necessary labour time. The relation between mental and manual labour, "productive consumption" and "play labour", and the data-annotation and hardware labour behind AI should be analysed through concrete social and economic relations. Zhou treats strong AI and machine consciousness as closer to science fiction. Control by data and algorithms is, in Zhou's view, a new version of the "abstract forces dominating people" that Marx already analysed. The problem of machines replacing workers dates from the Industrial Revolution and cannot be solved by Luddite machine-breaking. Zhou concludes that AI is not a "myth" but a machine system, and that Marx's theory grasps real modes of production and social formations rather than starting from anthropological premises or abstract concepts. Instead of dwelling on replacement and control, Zhou urges more active exploration of how to develop the digital economy and form new quality productive forces, where Marxist political economy will show its theoretical appeal. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the claim that AI and digital labour undermine the labour theory of value.

The innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces in contemporary China 马克思主义生产力理论在当代中国的创新发展 Zhang Yu Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Zhang Yu asks how the Marxist theory of productive forces has been developed in contemporary China. The article argues that Xi Jinping's discourse on productive forces, and above all his concept of new quality productive forces, has raised the Party's understanding of the laws of productive-force development to a new level. Zhang presents it as an original theoretical result of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is a theoretical commentary organised in nine thematic sections. Each pairs classical positions from Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping with Xi's statements and a closing judgement on what the statements add. The topics are the productive-force criterion of social progress, the socialist purpose of development, the elements of productive forces, the technological and industrial revolution, scientific and technological innovation, ecology, industrial innovation, reform of production relations, and the advanced character of new quality productive forces. Zhang's central claim is that each element of Xi's discourse develops a corresponding Marxist principle. Productive forces remain the decisive standard of social development, and their aim is to meet the people's growing needs for a better life, in contrast to capitalist monopoly of their fruits. New quality productive forces are defined as a leap in workers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimal combination, with data counted as a new factor of production. Scientific and technological innovation is described as their core element, and ecological protection is said to be protection of productive forces, so that they are inherently green productive forces. Zhang adds that technological innovation must be integrated with industrial innovation, supported by a complete industrial system and a very large market. He also argues that continued reform must make production relations fit new productive forces, drawing on socialism's institutional strengths such as the new type of whole-nation system. The article concludes that new quality productive forces are essentially advanced productive forces, characterised by the new technological revolution and by informatisation, digitalisation and intelligence. In Zhang's account they form the material and technological basis of Chinese modernization and high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise official-line overview of how Party theorists link Xi's new quality productive forces to the classical Marxist theory of productive forces.

On the actualisation of historical materialism 论历史唯物主义的现实化 Zhou Luping Zhou Luping asks how historical materialism acquires its vitality as a practical philosophy for changing the old world. The article, a short piece in Guangming Daily (28 October 2024), argues that this "actualisation" (xianshihua) runs through the whole of Marx and Engels's thought and should be grasped as a whole. Historical materialism, in Zhou's account, goes beyond the rational constraints of idealist philosophy by engaging with and criticising the capitalist world. The article is organised around three dimensions of actualisation: philosophical transformation, political reflection and economic critique. Zhou draws on texts from the mid-1840s, including the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, then on Marx and Engels's political writings on France, Germany and the United States. The article closes with Capital and its manuscripts. It also contrasts Marx with Proudhon as a thinker whose critique of capital stayed ethical. On the philosophical side, Zhou argues that the 1845 philosophical revolution dismantled speculative metaphysics and put practice and sensuous activity in its place. It also shifted the study of history to productive forces and forms of intercourse, property forms and the history of industry and commerce, which points towards communist emancipation. On the political side, Zhou reads works such as The Class Struggles in France and The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte as showing that bourgeois revolutions were driven by material interests, that class struggle was the bourgeoisie's means of establishing rule, and that political movements remained subordinate to the movement of capital. On the economic side, Zhou contends that Capital turns historical materialism into a theoretical weapon against capitalism's internal contradictions, undermines the claim that private property is rational, and points to the free and all-round development of the human being. Zhou concludes that Marx set himself apart from other thinkers by continually externalising his ideas, so that historical materialism criticises the modern world in practical terms. In this reading, philosophical change, political reflection and economic critique together lead to the real destination of human emancipation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language statement of how a Guangming Daily author frames historical materialism as a unified, practice-oriented critique of capital.

The theoretical value of the "small bundle" manuscripts in the "Feuerbach" chapter of The German Ideology 《德意志意识形态》“费尔巴哈”章 小束手稿的理论价值 Wang Guoqin Wang Daiyue This short article, first published in Guangming Daily on 28 October 2024, asks what theoretical weight should be given to the "small bundle" manuscripts of the "Feuerbach" chapter of The German Ideology. Wang Guoqin and Wang Daiyue argue that these manuscripts, though unfinished and repeatedly revised, were written later than the rest of the chapter and therefore show Marx and Engels's thinking at a more mature point. They claim the manuscripts bring out the subjective dimension of historical materialism, develop its "realistic" spirit, and help settle philological disputes over the text. The authors begin with the structure of the chapter in the new historical-critical edition (MEGA2, vol. I/5, 2017). It contains the "large bundle" of paginated main manuscripts and a "small bundle", a term the authors attribute to the Japanese scholar Hiromatsu Wataru. The small bundle comprises three chapter openings and two fragments, which the editors date to roughly May–July 1846. The authors then take three themes in turn: the subjective dimension, the realistic spirit of historical materialism, and the philological controversies. The central claim is that earlier scholarship read historical materialism mainly through its objective side, namely productive forces, forms of intercourse and civil society. The small bundle adds the concept of "real individuals". The authors say Marx and Engels, unlike Feuerbach, separate humans from animals by material production rather than by consciousness, and distinguish individuals from one another by the material conditions of production they inherit. On this reading, productive forces are the objectified powers of real individuals, so without them neither productive forces nor relations of production exist. The authors add that the fragments use "definite" five times and trace the development of ownership forms, which they take to show that historical materialism starts from empirical reality and not from abstract dogma. They cite Marx's resistance to universalising his account of capitalism's origins and his cautious reply to Vera Zasulich as examples. On the philological questions, the authors argue that the sequence of the three chapter openings shows Marx and Engels's thought clarifying. The "real individual" appears in the second opening, which they read as a response to Stirner. The deletion of a passage naming Feuerbach as the main target in the third opening suggests, in their view, that Feuerbach lost his central place as the object of critique. They conclude that the small bundle summarises the results of work on the text and deepens its account of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language account of how MEGA2's dating of these manuscripts is used to argue for a subject-centred reading of historical materialism.

Better balancing, promoting and unifying efficiency and fairness 更好实现效率与公平相兼顾、相促进、相统一 Chen Dongfang This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 25 October 2024, takes up the relationship between efficiency and fairness (equity). Chen Dongfang argues that, in order to deepen reform comprehensively and advance Chinese modernization, the two must be handled so that they are balanced, mutually reinforcing and unified, which in turn raises the balance, coordination and inclusiveness of development. The piece begins from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and a statement by Xi Jinping that Chinese modernization must create higher efficiency than capitalism while also safeguarding social fairness more effectively. It then proceeds through three headed sections: institutional reform, high-quality development, and common prosperity. Chen reads the three terms "balancing", "promoting" and "unifying" as follows: neither economic growth nor fairness may be sacrificed to the other; fairness rests on efficiency while efficiency takes fairness as its purpose and driving force; and the two must be organically combined. High-quality development is presented as the material base, since it joins "making the cake bigger" with "dividing it well", through higher total factor productivity and a more equal distribution of income. Common prosperity is the route to seeking the best balance point, through better public services, a larger share of labour income, employment and social security measures, and coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, alongside innovation, anti-monopoly measures and the orderly development of capital. Chen concludes that efficiency is the material precondition of fairness and fairness is the guarantee of efficiency. The author calls for balanced handling of both so that the fruits of modernization reach all people more fairly, which the article describes as a distinctive strength of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party commentary in late 2024 interprets Xi Jinping's formula on efficiency and fairness and links it to reform policy.

Further deepening reform comprehensively must follow the "six adherences" principles 全面深化改革必须遵循“六个坚持”重大原则 Hong Xiaonan Zhang Linlin This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 29 October 2024, interprets the six principles set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) for further deepening reform comprehensively. Hong and Zhang argue that the "six adherences" are both a scientific summary of experience since reform and opening up, especially in the new era, and a major result of the Party's deepening grasp of the laws governing reform. In their view, the principles strengthen the scientific character, foresight, initiative and creativity of reform and help it advance steadily over the long term. The article is organised as a sequence of short sections, one for each principle: the Party's overall leadership; a people-centred approach; upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground; institution-building as the main thread; law-based governance in all respects; and a systems perspective. Each section restates the principle, mostly in the language of Party documents, and draws on statements by Xi Jinping. On leadership, the authors state that Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the fundamental guarantee of reform. They tie this to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and link it to the direction of Chinese modernization. On the people-centred principle, they say the people are the starting point and value aim of reform, which must serve fairness, justice and common prosperity. On institutions, they hold that institutional advantage is a country's greatest advantage, and that reform should strengthen fundamental, basic and important institutions so that "Chinese institutions" produce better "Chinese governance". They also argue that reform and the rule of law must be unified: major reforms should have a legal basis, and proven reform experience should be turned into law. On the systems perspective, they say reform has reached a stage in which piecemeal adjustment will not work, and they name five relationships to balance: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. The authors conclude that the six principles together give guidance for pushing reform forward in a stable and lasting way. They treat the principles as interlocking: fundamentals such as Party leadership, Marxism and the socialist path must not waver, while reform proceeds boldly elsewhere. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the Third Plenum's guiding principles for reform and how they link them to Chinese modernization.

Using the systems perspective to keep further comprehensively deepening reform steady and far-reaching 以系统观念推动进一步全面深化改革行稳致远 Shuang Chuanxue Shuang Chuanxue's commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 25 October 2024, takes up one of the six major principles for further comprehensively deepening reform set out by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): adhering to a systems perspective. Shuang argues that reform has entered deep waters, and that the more complex the situation, the more reform must be made systematic, integrated and coordinated. The article has four parts. It first sets out the meaning of the systems perspective, then explains why further reform urgently needs it. It next lists five pairs of relationships that must be handled correctly, and closes with practical ways to strengthen conscious application of the principle. In the first part, Shuang presents the systems perspective as an enrichment of the Marxist view of systems, grounded in materialist dialectics. Shuang also reads it as a lesson from the Party's long experience, from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist construction to reform and opening up, and as a basic thought and work method for the new journey. The case for urgency rests on three points: the general goal of improving the socialist system and modernizing national governance, the large list of risks and difficulties still to be resolved, and the growing interdependence of reforms across fields. The five relationships are economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. Shuang treats each as a dialectical unity in which the two sides condition one another and neither should be set against the other. Shuang calls for stronger theoretical study of dialectical materialism, against mechanistic and dogmatic thinking. Shuang also calls for forward-looking thinking, planning for the whole, strategic layout and integrated advancement in practice. The systems perspective should run through the whole reform process, from policy formulation through implementation to evaluation and adjustment of results. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists present the systems perspective as a methodological principle of the current reform agenda.

A high-standard socialist market economy as an important guarantee for Chinese modernization 高水平社会主义市场经济体制是中国式现代化的重要保障 Hu Xiaopeng Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Hu Xiaopeng takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its call to build a "high-standard socialist market economy" by 2035. The article argues that this economic system is an important guarantee for Chinese modernization. In Hu's account it also develops and deepens the Party's theory of the market economy. The commentary has three parts. The first places the concept in the Party's changing understanding of the market economy, from the post-1978 position that planning and market are both economic means to the 19th Central Committee's Fourth Plenum, which listed the socialist market economy among the basic economic systems. The second treats the government–market relationship as the core problem. The third ties the project to high-quality development as the first task of building a modern socialist country. Hu's central claim is that "high standard" is a criterion both for how well the market works and for whether the system fits the basic socialist economic system. Citing Xi Jinping, Hu holds that the market's "invisible hand" cannot solve long-term underinvestment in basic research or negative externalities such as environmental damage. A high-standard system therefore asks more of the government's "visible hand", which should keep markets fair and orderly, be "lively but not chaotic", and be "free to flourish yet firmly managed". Hu adds that the system must be built on the rule of law, since the socialist market economy is "essentially a law-based economy". For high-quality development, Hu proposes institution-building as the main thread. This includes the Two Unwaverings, a unified national market, better property rights, market access, exit and social credit systems, and further reform of state-owned enterprises. It also covers a better environment for private firms, high-level self-reliance in science and technology, and institutional opening-up that aligns with international high-standard trade rules and promotes a new development pattern of dual circulation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists link the Third Plenum's market-economy goals to Chinese modernization.

On building a high-standard socialist market economy 论构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Li Yiping Li Yiping's commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 29 October 2024, takes up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to "build a high-standard socialist market economy". Li argues that the meaning of "high-standard" can only be grasped by understanding how the socialist market economy developed and what its essential features are. The piece has three parts. It first traces the history: Deng Xiaoping's affirmation that socialism and markets can be combined, the 14th Party Congress (1992) goal of letting the market play a basic role in resource allocation under state macro-control, and the Third Plenum of the 14th Central Committee's decision that made this concrete. It then defines a high-standard system, and finally lists four priorities drawn from the 2024 plenum. In Li's account, such a system allocates resources more effectively. This requires improving the price mechanism so that prices reflect scarcity, and improving competition, which Li says drives innovation and the elimination of backward producers. It also requires a correct relationship between government and market: the government's "visible hand" must obey market laws, so that markets are both "lively" and "well regulated", with scientific, standardised oversight to prevent market failure. Li names four tasks: protecting market entities through the Two Unwaverings, building a unified national market, improving basic market institutions (property rights, information disclosure, market access, bankruptcy and exit, credit systems), and forming a higher-level government–market relationship in which the market plays the decisive role. Read the original if you want a short, official-line outline of how the 2024 plenum's market-economy agenda is explained to a general Chinese readership.

Paths to building an autonomous knowledge system of Chinese humanistic economics 中国人文经济学自主知识体系的建构路径 Han Xiping Han Xiping asks how China's theorists should build an autonomous knowledge system of "Chinese humanistic economics", a field prompted by Xi Jinping's remark that economies often thrive where culture is highly developed. The article, first published in Guangming Daily in October 2024, argues that this is an important responsibility for theorists in the new era. Its thesis is that culture and the economy are tightly linked, and that a theory grounded in Chinese culture and practice should make this link explicit. The piece is a short commentary organised around five tasks. They are to clarify the people-centred purpose of economic development, to uncover cultural elements in growth, to summarise classic cases of humanistic support for the economy, to strengthen the economic force of Chinese culture, and to show the cultural function within the mode of production. Han draws on Marx, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping's remarks from his time in Zhejiang, on the history of economic thought, and on examples from several regions. Han first sketches a history of economics. In this account it began as part of moral philosophy, narrowed into mathematical formalism and instrumental rationality after the marginal revolution, and is now returning to concern with human beings. Marxist economics, Han says, redirected the field towards relations between people, and the Party's aim of meeting the people's need for a better life requires a theory that reflects this. Han then treats culture as a production factor that shapes motivation, market behaviour and innovation, which matters for cultivating new quality productive forces. Regional cases are offered as raw material for theory: ice-and-snow culture in the northeast, Wu-Yue culture in Jiangsu and Zhejiang, Confucian culture in Shandong, and film and television that draw on classical literature. Han argues for moving from practice to experience to theory, and for drawing on history, philosophy and sociology. Han also cites traditional ethics of righteousness and benefit, and values such as good faith and respect for contracts, which are said to lower transaction costs and stabilise expectations. Han concludes that humanistic economics would reveal the cultural factors behind China's development. It would also show how cultural advantages can support high-quality development and the building of a modern socialist country. Building the field means combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's realities and its fine traditional culture, and producing an economic theory with wide international influence. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Chinese economists are being encouraged to link culture, Marxist political economy and development theory.

Setting reform goals and tasks in step with the times to provide institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization 与时俱进确定改革目标任务 为中国式现代化提供制度保障 Jiang Xiaojuan Writing in the People's Daily on 30 October 2024, Jiang Xiaojuan interprets the Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively to advance Chinese modernization, adopted by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article asks how the Decision's goals and tasks update earlier reform agendas. Jiang argues that the Decision continues two epoch-making plenums while adding new requirements, and that it supplies the institutional guarantees Chinese modernization needs. The piece has two parts. The first traces the shift from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) through later "third plenums" to that of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The second examines the Decision's guiding principle of making three pairs of relations "better suited to each other" and illustrates it with specific reform measures. Jiang's central claim is that the early reform era aimed chiefly at liberating and developing the productive forces, through steps from household contracting to a socialist market economy. Since 2013, the aim has also been to improve socialist institutions and modernize the system and capacity of national governance. The Decision's three pairings are relations of production and productive forces, the superstructure and the economic base, and national governance and social development. The last is a new formulation. On the first two, Jiang says reform must "break" and "build" together. Examples include equal and long-term protection of property rights across ownership types, better market exit mechanisms such as bankruptcy rules, and institutional rules on taxation and local investment promotion. The pairing of governance and social development responds to a different problem. Jiang argues that modernization raises social vitality and instability together, as rising education and migration lift expectations. The remedy is to balance vitality with order. The Decision's measures include equal access to public services for migrants and sealing records of minor offences. Jiang concludes that the Decision contains major theoretical innovations. They rest on an accurate reading of the historical stage, of the relation between Chinese modernization's distinctive features and the general laws of modernization, and of new opportunities and challenges. Jiang calls it another landmark document in the history of reform and opening up. Full implementation, the author says, will give Chinese modernization strong momentum and solid institutional guarantees. Read the original if you want an official-line scholarly account of how the 2024 Decision is positioned against earlier reform plenums and why its governance language matters.

The critique of fetishism in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》中的拜物教批判思想 Cheng Gang Cheng Gang asks how Marx understood fetishism in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and where this stands between his earlier and later treatments. The article, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2024, argues that the Manuscripts' notion differs from the 1842 'idol fetishism' of the Cologne Gazette articles, a natural-religion idea. It also differs from the systematic fetishism of Capital, which Cheng presents as a social ontology of objective forms. Cheng places the 1844 notion between the two: it draws on religious and philosophical critique and opens the way to the critique of political economy. Cheng's central claim is that fetishism appears to be a mystical power attributed to material wealth under private property but is in substance a separation of subjectivity from objectivity. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats the political-economic dimension, the worship of private property in classical political economy. The second treats the philosophical dimension, the alienation of 'self-consciousness' in Hegel. The third sets out sensuous practice as the route to overcoming fetishism. On political economy, Cheng reads Marx as saying that Adam Smith and the Enlightenment economists, though they called the mercantilists 'fetishists', were fetishists themselves. The earlier school worshipped the product of labour as an object, while Smith's school made labour, and so the human being, the pure subjective essence of private property. In Cheng's reading, this wholly negates human objectivity and sets up a non-objective entity, so the growth of the world of things stands in direct proportion to the devaluation of the human world. In Hegel, Cheng argues, 'man' is equated with self-consciousness, so subjectivity detached from objectivity becomes an abstract 'subject' and objectivity becomes mere 'thingness'. Cheng calls Marx's critique of 'absolute knowledge' a philosophical form of fetishism critique. Cheng concludes that for Marx fetishism is a historical product of practice and a 'temporary necessity' that will be superseded. Human senses are historically formed, depend on their objects and are created only by sensuous, objective labour. Practice, which Cheng ties to Marx's 'objective activity', unites subjectivity and objectivity and leads to a return of the human being to himself. Marx's aim, Cheng says, is to expose the roots of fetishism in private property and in thought, negate private property and enable all-round human self-emancipation. Read the original if you want a compact account of how the 1844 Manuscripts link fetishism critique to alienated labour, Hegel and the later critique of political economy.

Creating history: a social-mechanism perspective 历史创造：一个社会机制的视角 Wang Dan The Marxist principle that the people are the creators of history is usually stated as a conclusion about who makes history. Wang argues that, under present conditions, it needs a further analytical tool: the category of "mechanisms of creating history", drawn from the analysis of social mechanisms. The article contends that this lens explains how the people's historical activity proceeds. On this view it is neither arbitrary nor chaotic, and it keeps its direction, continuity and stability. The article identifies six mechanisms in the process of creating history: practice, interests, orientation toward the good, organization, combined force and mutual learning among civilizations. Each section defines one mechanism and grounds it in passages from Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The sections also draw on examples from Chinese revolutionary history and on references to Western scholarship. The article closes by arranging the six into a single system. The author gives each mechanism a distinct function. Practice answers the question of means and is the basic mechanism. The interest mechanism supplies motive force, both for "maintaining" creation in ordinary production and for "transformative" creation in revolution and reform. The mechanism of orientation toward the good sets direction. It requires that conformity to law and conformity to purpose be united, and it favours common interest over polarisation, citing Why Nations Fail on inclusive institutions. Organization and combined force are linked as cause and result: mobilised masses must form a force with shared consensus and interests, which Wang reads through Engels's parallelogram of forces. The author claims that this force can be undermined by what the article calls Western "colour revolution" tactics. Mutual learning rests on the nation-state as the unit of creation and on the shift toward world history. Wang concludes that practice is the foundational mechanism, interests the core, orientation toward the good the regulator, and the other three "technical" mechanisms that sustain history-making. Together they form a unity that can move historical creation from the spontaneous to the conscious and from high cost to low. The methodological implications are listed: concrete hard work, attention to the people's immediate interests, the mass line, the united front, and openness to other civilizations. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese statement of how Party theory reads "the people as creators of history" through a mechanism-based framework, with its textual sources.

The critique of Hegel and of political economy in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》对黑格尔与政治经济学的批判 Dai Shengpeng Dai Shengpeng asks how Marx's critique of political economy in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (the Manuscripts) stands in relation to Hegel's earlier philosophical critique and reworking of the same discipline. The article argues that Marx's critique extends and deepens Hegel's logic of critique but reverses its purpose. Hegel reworked political economy to ground his theory of the state, whereas Marx criticised it to ground a new worldview and communism. The piece first reconstructs Hegel's treatment of political economy, then explains why Marx turned to a direct critique of it, and finally reads the Manuscripts as a double critique of political economy and of Hegelian philosophy. It closes by noting differences among the Manuscripts' notebooks I, II and III, and by pointing forward to The German Ideology. Dai sets out two lines of logic. For Hegel it runs: need, ownership, activity and labour, division of labour, wealth, estates, state. For Marx in the Manuscripts it runs: need, labour, division of labour, private property, class, state, communism. In Hegel's account, political economy seeks the reason at work in things, and starting from reality means starting from necessity, which he equates with freedom. Ownership is the outward form of the free will, property is freedom's first existence, and value and money give property its quantitative determination. Estates arising from diversified needs become a basis of the state. Dai holds that Hegel thus brought political economy into the perspective of human species-essence, which opened a new dimension for Marx. In Dai's reading, however, Hegel criticised from heaven rather than from the human world, so he could not explain civil society or help real human emancipation. Dai also links Marx's motives to the difficulty he met in 1842–43 in commenting on material interests and to his early misjudgements of communism. Dai concludes that in the Manuscripts communism, not the state, sublates private property and civil society. Notebooks I and II still use Hegelian terms, so Marx there remains in some sense a young Marx still within the Young Hegelian orbit. Notebook III begins a systematic critique of Hegel's dialectic and philosophy, and the two critiques together produced the new worldview and new materialism of The German Ideology. Read the original if you want a concise account, in a Chinese scholarly perspective, of how Hegel's reworking of political economy relates to the Manuscripts' critique.

Deng Xiaoping's financial thought: theoretical contributions to the path of financial development with Chinese characteristics and its practical implications 邓小平金融思想对中国特色金融发展之路的理论贡献及现实启示 Li Bin Li Bin asks what Deng Xiaoping's views on finance contributed to what official discourse now calls the path of financial development with Chinese characteristics. The article, published in 2024 after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee and the Central Financial Work Conference of October 2023, argues that Deng's financial thought is an integral part of Deng Xiaoping Theory. In Li's account it supplied the theoretical basis for China's financial reform and anticipates central themes in Xi Jinping's statements on financial work. The article opens with a short review of existing scholarship, grouped into three strands: the formation and stages of Deng's financial thought, its core content, and its practical influence. Li notes that the literature has paid little attention to how Deng developed Marxist financial theory. The body then has two main parts, on the pioneering significance of Deng's thought and on its specific theoretical contributions, followed by a section on its present-day value. Li identifies three features of Deng's thought: applying Marxist principles to Chinese conditions, requiring finance to serve economic construction and the people's interests, and pursuing reform in a spirit of innovation marked by political, holistic and open characteristics. The article then draws out three contributions. The first is the idea that finance is "the core of the modern economy", which Li reads as defining the function of finance and its link to fiscal policy. The second is the call to "run banks truly as banks", which Li credits with moving China from a highly centralised, People's Bank-dominated system towards a modern financial system through the reforms from 1979 and the 1993 programme. The third is Deng's stress on macroeconomic regulation, price stability, controlling inflation and guarding against financial risk, which Li says enriched the theory of financial governance. Li concludes that studying Deng's thought helps explain the lineage of Xi Jinping's statements on financial work. Four implications follow: grasping the political and people-oriented nature of finance, including the Party Central Committee's centralised leadership; having finance serve the real economy and preventing speculation and disorderly capital expansion; deepening financial reform to build a financial powerhouse; and strengthening macroeconomic regulation and risk prevention to avoid systemic financial risk. Read the original if you want to see how Deng's remarks on banking, money and inflation are assembled into a genealogy for current Party financial policy.

Western civilisation as seen through Western economics 从西方经济学看西方文明 Yu Bin Yu Bin takes up a description of Western economics in China's official guide to postgraduate disciplines: a field that aims at efficient resource allocation under scarcity and studies market-economy theory and policy. Yu argues that the field is seriously flawed. In this reading it does not scientifically reflect the laws of capitalism, as Marx's economics does, but turns capitalists' vulgar notions into academic doctrine. For that reason, Yu holds, it reveals the one-sided traits of the mainstream ideology and of Western civilisation. The article is organised in four parts, each reading a feature of Western economics as a trait of Western civilisation: its research goals, its content (individual agents, firms, fluctuations, growth, incentives, government policy), its schools, and its methods. Yu draws on Marx, Engels, Coase, Pigou, Pareto, Keynes, Samuelson and Zhang Wuchang, and on Xi Jinping's remarks on supply-side economics. Each section attaches a label to Western civilisation, among them absurdity, capital-centredness, plunder, deception of the people, self-contradiction and fabrication. In Yu's account, scarcity theory exists to discredit the labour theory of value, and 'efficient allocation' means giving resources, and rights such as the right to pollute, to large capital. Marginal utility theory, with its claim that utilities cannot be compared between persons, is presented as a device for blocking redistribution from rich to poor. The article says the 'rational economic man', the production function, growth models and incentive design all ignore commerce, finance and exploitation. Yu attributes the field's many schools to rival interest groups, such as industrial versus financial capital, rather than to scientific disagreement. On method, Yu separates legitimate mathematical analysis, citing Marx's reproduction schemes, from what the author calls the 'Pythagorean complex' and formalism. Examples include utility functions, the Keynesian multiplier and methodological individualism, which Yu likens to Marx's 'sack of potatoes'. Yu concludes that the proliferation of schools shows confusion, not scholarly prosperity, and that Marxist political economy is the only true economic science. Yu calls for critical study of Western economics in light of political economy and historical materialism, and rejects both direct borrowing and the 'Sinicisation' of Western economics. Chinese economics should instead be a product of Xi Jinping's economic thought and the Two Integrations. Yu also urges that individualism not be taught to Chinese graduate students. Read the original if you want to see an uncompromising Marxist critique of Western economics and of how it is taught in Chinese universities.

On money as a special general commodity 论货币是特殊的一般商品 Yu Bin Is money a "special commodity" or a "general commodity"? Yu Bin takes up this long-running dispute in Chinese Marxist economics and argues that it is badly framed. Competing definitions (money as a special commodity serving as general equivalent, as a general commodity serving as general equivalent, or simply as a commodity serving as general equivalent) all differ from the definition Marx himself gave. Yu's own answer is that money is a "special general commodity". The article, published in Guangxi Social Sciences in 2024, opens with an overview and then reviews three camps in turn: the "general commodity" view, the "special commodity" view, and the compromise view that money is both. It closes with a section setting out Yu's own position and several peculiarities of gold as money. Yu engages many unnamed scholars' arguments, tests them against passages of Capital and the Grundrisse, and uses historical cases such as Tang-dynasty silk, Xue Muqiao's commodity-reserve paper currency in the liberated areas, and cigarettes in US prisons. Yu argues that in Marx's usage only the other commodities are "special" relative to money, which is their general equivalent, so the qualifier "of all other commodities" must accompany "general equivalent". Money is also not "fixed" in the role but holds it exclusively. Against the special-commodity camp, Yu holds that gold's suitability rests less on its physical properties than on the relative stability of the socially necessary labour time needed to produce it; aluminium and silk are offered as counter-examples. The view that money is more special than general, Yu says, falls into the illusion Marx described, that a commodity seems to be money because the others express their value in it. Marx's remark that money is both general and special arose in discussing speculative price rises, when supply and demand outweigh the law of value. Yu takes Marx's actual definition (the commodity that serves as measure of value and, directly or through representatives, as means of circulation) to qualify a commodity by social function alone, which makes money a general commodity. Yu concludes that the most accurate formulation is: money is a special general commodity, or a general commodity holding a social monopoly, though even this is not a definition. Textbooks that do not start from Marx's own definition, Yu says, need to be rewritten. Yu lists further peculiarities of gold: the rivalry of gold and silver standards, the effect of plunder on its value, shifts in its labour time, its uselessness elsewhere, its role as a reserve, and its easy conversion between forms. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of money, or want to see how Chinese scholars argue over Capital's wording and its application to gold and paper currency.

On the transmission mechanism from productive forces to way of life and its implications 论生产力—生活方式的传导机制及其启示 Yu Bin Yu Bin takes up a passage in Capital in which Marx endorses a factory inspectors' report linking machine inventions to changes in the workers' way of life. From it Yu derives a chain of transmission: productive forces, mode of production, relations of production, social relations, way of life. Yu argues that this chain is the core of historical materialism, and that Marxist scholarship has attended mainly to its first three links while neglecting social relations and, above all, the way of life of the people. The article, published in 2024, has four sections. The first defends 'productive-forces determinism' against critics: Tang Changli, advocates of economic determinism, Engels's 'resultant of forces' reading of history, and Althusser's overdetermination. The second argues that the mode of production is a mediating link rather than, as Stalin held, the unity of productive forces and relations, and takes issue with Guo Guanqing's classification. The third distinguishes relations of production from social relations. The fourth turns to the people's way of life and to common prosperity. Yu's central move is to read 'determination' as ultimate and dialectical rather than one-to-one: the same productive forces may correspond to different relations of production, and each link also reacts back on the one before. On this basis Yu reads the Russian and Chinese revolutions as consistent with the theory, and says that disregarding the theory led to the earlier belief that communism could be reached quickly at a low level of productive forces. Yu then argues that social relations contain relations of production and have them as their core. Transforming social relations suits revolutionary periods, whereas in construction the task is to reproduce socialist relations of production. Yu attributes the Soviet collapse to neglect of this task and the limits of the Mao-era approach to excessive focus on social relations outside production. Yu concludes that public ownership must remain the mainstay of the economy so that socialist production relations can sustain the people's social relations. Citing Marx's accounts of working hours, child labour and the workers' living conditions, Yu argues that social relations shape way of life, and that a better way of life in turn raises workers' quality and frees productive forces. Yu calls for better working conditions, shorter working days and enforcement of labour law as part of common prosperity, and for balanced attention to every link in the chain in pursuing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist's systematic defence of productive-forces determinism and of the distinction between relations of production and social relations.

Telling China's story well requires following historical materialism 讲好中国故事需要遵循唯物史观 Yu Bin Taking up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to build China's own discourse and narrative system and present a credible, lovable and respectable image of China, Yu Bin asks why telling China's story to foreigners is so hard and how it can be done. The article argues that historical materialism, and especially the principle that social being determines consciousness, both explains the difficulty and points to the solutions. The article has three parts. The first sets out the difficulties, drawing on Zhuangzi's image of the summer insect that cannot talk of ice, on the Communist Manifesto's 'world literature', and on Engels's letters. The second sets out why the task is possible, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin. The third gives four groups of practical recommendations. Yu also criticises other authors' views, such as the claim that historical anecdotes or 'empathetic communication' will carry China's story abroad. Yu argues that foreign audiences live in a different social being, so they cannot readily grasp Chinese consciousness. In class-divided societies, Yu adds, no story pleases everyone, and Western media are hostile to socialism. Yu holds that the story can still be told in several ways. One is to reach audiences with similar social conditions, such as ordinary people in developing and developed countries who want a better life. Another is to present China's new form of human civilization as a preview of other countries' future, as Marx did with England in Capital. A third is to use China's weight as a customer, the import expo and new media, which Yu says weaken Western narrative control. Yu also says Chinese stories told as exotic 'national allegories', or films such as Dying to Survive that expose shortcomings, do not present a respectable image. Yu's proposals are: openly acknowledge China's strengths, for instance by classing China as a 'high developing country' and promoting its digital life; abandon the policy of hiding one's capabilities and be more assertive, including by exporting books and films about China's anti-hegemonic past; tell the story of the new era and of the Two Integrations; and explain socialism's difference from capitalism. Yu also proposes teaching Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to foreign students in China and creating language exams based on Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies historical materialism to international communication, along with its concrete policy suggestions.

Understanding the value implications of building a community with a shared future for mankind 深刻理解构建人类命运共同体的价值意蕴 Zhang Xiaobo Qin Hui This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2024, asks what values lie behind the idea of building a community with a shared future for mankind. Zhang Xiaobo and Qin Hui present the idea as an important part of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought and as one of the essential requirements of Chinese modernization. They argue that it should be understood as a scientific theoretical system whose values can move from recognition to consensus, and from vision to reality. The authors analyse the concept along five dimensions: its value subject, value basis, value criterion, value goal and value realisation. Each dimension is set against a contrasting position, either an abstract, Western-centred or conflict-oriented one. The authors draw on Marx's concept of the real human being, on Xi's 2015 United Nations speech on common values, on the Global Civilization Initiative of 2023, and on traditional Chinese ideals of harmony. Zhang and Qin contend that the subject of the community is the real, concrete "humanity" facing a turbulent world and a strained system of global governance, not an abstract humanity. Its value basis is the "common values of all humanity" (peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom), which the authors distinguish from the "universal values" that they say the United States and other Western states use to pursue hegemony. Its criterion is the equality and mutual learning of civilizations, in contrast to theories of civilizational superiority or clash, which they describe as grounded in prejudice. Its goal is the ideal of "each appreciating its own beauty and that of others, and the world in harmony", which they say does not mean replacing one system or civilization with another. In the authors' account, realisation of these values lies in a modernization that follows the path of peaceful development, which they say differs from a Western model built on capital, aggression and colonial plunder. They claim that China has not started a war since 1949 and has written peaceful development into its constitution and Party charter. The authors conclude that China will join other countries in a world modernization of mutual benefit and common prosperity. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Chinese commentary presents the philosophical and civilizational grounding of this concept.

The theoretical significance and practical requirements of being both "lively" and "well-regulated" Letting the market "come alive" while keeping it "under control" 既“放得活”又“管得住”的理论意义和实践要求 Lü Wei Liu Xinqi The Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) called for a high-standard socialist market economy that is both "fang de huo" (loosened enough to be lively) and "guan de zhu" (regulated enough to be controlled). This commentary by Lü Wei and Liu Xinqi takes up the formulation as a new way of framing the relationship between government and market.
