The authors argue that handling "loosening" and "managing" together expresses both the socialist character and the market-economy content of the system, and that it serves as an important safeguard for Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in three parts: deepening theoretical understanding, summarising regular patterns, and identifying practical directions. The first part places the formulation within the theory of the socialist market economy and the history of economic thought. The second links it to pairs of values: vitality and order, development and security. The third sets out concrete reform tasks. Lü and Liu define "loosening" as the government's "subtraction": reducing direct resource allocation, intervention and approvals to release market vitality. "Managing" is the government's "addition": correcting market failure, improving public services and safeguarding fairness and stability. They argue that the debate over "small" versus "big" government should give way to the criterion of an "effective" government, one that is a service-oriented government and a government under the rule of law. In their account China, unlike Western developed countries that let markets expand freely, relies on national planning, policy commitments and macro-regulation, and this explains its steady growth. They also tie the formulation to the development of new quality productive forces, which they say require new relations of production and a larger market role. On practice, the authors name three levels. The precondition is clarifying responsibilities under the Two Unwaverings, through state-enterprise reform, credit evaluation systems and support for private firms. The foundation is fair competition: removing market-access barriers, antitrust enforcement, equal property protection and financing support for small and medium-sized enterprises. The key is smooth circulation: market-determined factor prices, a unified national market, and an integrated domestic-demand system of investment and consumption. Read the original if you want a concise official-line academic gloss on how the "loosen and manage" formula is being turned into Third Plenum reform priorities.

On the complexity of the world modernization movement 论世界现代化运动的复杂性 Dai Mucai Dai Mucai asks why modernization, as a world historical process, is so complex, and what follows for how Chinese modernization should be understood. The article argues that modernization is both universal and particular: no single model or standard exists, and the complexity of the process also makes modernization theory complex. Against this background, Dai presents Chinese modernization as a path without precedent in the history of the world modernization movement. The article has six sections. It begins with the bloody origins of modernization, then examines the contested meanings of "modern", "modernity" and "modernization". It goes on to the complexity of the historical process, using Kondratiev's long-wave theory, and to the diversity of models, drawing on Cyril Black's comparative typology of more than 170 countries. It then discusses the difficulty of evaluating modernization, including the criticisms it has drawn, and ends with Chinese modernization compared with the wider movement. Dai makes three central moves. First, citing Marx on primitive accumulation, colonialism and the slave trade, the author characterises Western-style modernization as a "path of evil" built on invasion, plunder, colonization, enslavement and war, and contrasts it with a "path of good" of openness, mutual benefit, peace and cooperation. Second, Dai argues that even Western modernization varied (the Anglo-Saxon, Rhine, Nordic and East Asian models), so modernization cannot be equated with "Westernization"; the claim that Western theories present their own model as universal is called a case of taking the part for the whole. Third, modernization is both fact and value, and capitalist modernization has been criticised by utopian socialism, Marxism, Western Marxism, Western thinkers themselves and dependency theory. Dai holds that Chinese modernization shares the common features of world modernization but also rests on Chinese conditions, on 5,000 years of civilization and on the Two Integrations. Dai calls for a theoretical system open to existing modernization theories, able to speak to Western theory and to claim international discourse power. In closing, the author says the "next volume" of Chinese modernization, towards 2035 and the mid-century goal, will bring both crises and opportunities. Dai calls for Party leadership, reform and opening up, and a spirit of struggle. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of modernization theory that links Kondratiev, Cyril Black and dependency theory to the case for Chinese modernization as a non-Western path.

Building China's autonomous knowledge system of regional economics 建构中国自主的区域经济学知识体系 Wei Houkai Wei Houkai asks how China can build an autonomous knowledge system of regional economics, and argues that this rests on the distinctive features of Chinese regional economics itself. In his view, Western regional economic theory is built on assumptions drawn from developed market economies and cannot fully explain China. The piece, first published in Guangming Daily in October 2024, calls for stronger originality, innovation that builds on inheritance, and critical borrowing from abroad. The article has three parts. It first sets out what makes Chinese regional economics distinctive, then explains what an autonomous knowledge system requires, and finally proposes routes for building it. Wei points to features of China's regional economy that he says are rooted in national conditions: the Party's overall leadership, the leading role of governments at all levels, the weight given to regional strategies, plans and policies, competition and cooperation between regions, and the influence of administrative divisions and informal institutions such as cultural tradition. Wei names three defining features: guidance by Marxism, including the classical writers' ideas on balanced distribution of productive forces and urban–rural integration; conformity with the requirements of the socialist market economy; and fit with China's basic national conditions, including the primary stage of socialism. He holds that autonomy means using Chinese theory to answer Chinese questions, explain Chinese phenomena and guide Chinese practice. He says China has many original regional economic ideas, but they remain fused with practice and insufficiently theorised, which explains why no systematic, widely recognised system exists. Research should therefore start from current regional problems, explain phenomena such as rapid urbanization, city clusters and the dual-residence status of migrant workers, and guide future practice. Wei proposes a structure in which original knowledge forms the core, with inheritance-based innovation and critical borrowing as two wings. He lists concepts that he sees as originating in Chinese practice, such as targeted poverty alleviation, rural revitalization, paired-up assistance and main functional zones, and urges that they be theorised. He also urges mining ancient thought, citing the economic zoning in the Records of the Grand Historian, and adapting Western methods such as econometric techniques. Read the original if you want a short statement of how a leading Chinese rural and regional economist frames the 'autonomous knowledge system' agenda for this discipline.

On building a high-standard socialist market economy system 论构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Li Yiping Li Yiping, writing in Guangming Daily after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), asks what the plenum's call to build a "high-standard" socialist market economy system means. The commentary argues that the phrase can be grasped only by tracing how the socialist market economy developed and by understanding its essential features. The piece has three parts. The first reviews the history: Deng Xiaoping's affirmation that socialism and a market economy can be combined, the 14th Party Congress's goal of letting the market play a basic role in allocating resources under state macro-control, and the 14th Central Committee's third plenum decision. It then links the new task to high-quality development, Chinese modernization and new quality productive forces. The second part defines the "high standard", and the third lists four priorities. Li argues that a high-standard system allocates resources more effectively. This requires better price and competition mechanisms, so that prices reflect scarcity and competition, including the elimination of backward producers, drives innovation. It also requires a correct handling of the government–market relationship, in which the government's "visible hand" obeys market laws and the system is both "lively" and "well-managed". Li holds that an unruly market leads to market failure, so regulation must be scientific and standardised. Li names four priorities: protecting market actors through the Two Unwaverings; building a unified national market; improving basic market institutions such as property rights, information disclosure, market access, bankruptcy and the social credit system; and forming a higher-level government–market relationship in which the market plays the decisive role. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line account of how the 2024 plenum's market-economy goals are framed for a general readership.

Mao Zedong's contribution to creating a new form of human civilization and its contemporary implications 毛泽东对创造人类文明新形态的贡献及其当代启示 He Xinyuan Zuo Yujie He Xinyuan and Zuo Yujie ask what Mao Zedong contributed to the "new form of human civilization" that the Party's 2021 historical resolution says the Communist Party created through Chinese modernization. They argue that Mao's leadership supplied the theoretical, practical and value foundations for this civilization. In their account, it differs from traditional Chinese civilization, from capitalist civilization and from the Soviet socialist experience. The article has three parts. The first describes the historic shift of Chinese civilization from "dust-covered" to "dust-removed" civilization. The second examines the foundations laid under Mao in five fields: the economy, democratic politics, culture, society and ecology. The third draws four lessons for the present and closes by citing Xi Jinping's remark that the best way to commemorate Mao is to carry his cause forward. The authors argue that the founding of the Party, the founding of the People's Republic and the establishment of the socialist system together reversed the decline of Chinese civilization. They say each of the five fields corresponds to one component of the present "five-fold" coordinated development (material, political, cultural, social and ecological civilization). For the economy they cite socialist industrialization and give growth figures for 1952–78. For politics they point to people's democracy and the people's congress system, which they contrast with bourgeois democracy. They also discuss the culture policy of serving the people, welfare and social governance, and Mao's thinking on nature, which they present as a source of Xi Jinping's ecological thought. From this history the authors draw four lessons. First, Party leadership and the socialist road are the root cause of the new civilization. Second, its novelty lies in its people-centred character, which they set against feudal, capitalist and late Soviet civilizations. Third, the Two Integrations, which they trace back to Mao's Sinification of Marxism and his "second integration", are the basic method. Fourth, the civilization points towards communism and the free and all-round development of every person. They conclude that the new civilization will need continuing Party-led exploration. Read the original if you want to see how Mao's era is being recast in current Party theory as a foundation for the new form of human civilization.

The socialist outlook of Nepali communists 尼泊尔共产党人的社会主义观 Yuan Qun Teng Yan Yuan and Teng ask how Nepali communists have understood socialism since the Communist Party of Nepal was founded in 1949, and what that understanding implies for the country's future. They argue that the communists' outlook belongs to scientific socialism. In their account, it rests on Marxism, Party leadership, a socialist-oriented transformation and the ultimate goal of communism, while the movement is still at an early and immature stage. The article is organised around four questions: why build socialism in Nepal, what kind of socialism, how to build it, and what prospects it has. It follows the main parties through successive splits and mergers. These include the early Communist Party of Nepal, the CPN (Maoist Centre), the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the unified Nepal Communist Party formed in 2018. It draws mainly on party programmes, congress reports and leaders' statements, from the struggle against Rana family rule to the 2024 alliance. Yuan and Teng report that the parties see Nepal as a society of feudal remnants, bureaucratic-comprador capitalism and foreign interference, and that they reject both the Soviet model and 'democratic socialism'. They describe the parties' routes as peaceful, multiparty competition under the constitution (the UML's 'people's multiparty democracy') or, for the Maoists, a people's war later converted into 'twenty-first century democracy'. The authors stress the parties' own assessment that productive forces are too weak for a socialist programme now. The immediate task is therefore to complete the capitalist democratic revolution, industrialise and lay foundations. The article adds four means: Party-building, ideological work including learning from the Communist Party of China and socialism with Chinese characteristics, reliance on national conditions, and scientific and technological progress. The authors conclude that Nepali communists played a decisive part in ending the monarchy and building a democratic republic, and they present this as a sign of regional revival of world socialism. They also note that obstacles remain: feudal and bureaucratic-capitalist forces, outside interference, underdevelopment, and repeated communist fragmentation, including the 2021 split and shifting coalitions in 2024. Building socialism under capitalist multiparty competition is described as a long and difficult road. Read the original if you want a detailed, China-based account of how Nepal's communist parties have framed their strategy, doctrine and unity, drawing on their own documents.

The innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces in contemporary China 马克思主义生产力理论在当代中国的创新发展 Zhang Yu Zhang Yu asks how the Marxist theory of productive forces has been developed in contemporary China and where Xi Jinping's concept of new quality productive forces fits within it. The author argues that Xi's discussions of productive forces, culminating in this concept, raise the Party's understanding of how productive forces develop to a new level. Zhang calls it an original and foundational result of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece first appeared in Guangming Daily in October 2024. The article opens with Lenin's view that social relations reduce to relations of production and these to the level of productive forces. It then moves through nine themes, each pairing classical statements by Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping with Xi's remarks. The themes are the productive-forces standard, the purpose of production, the components of productive forces, technological revolutions, scientific and technological innovation, ecology, industrial innovation, reform of production relations, and the nature of new quality productive forces. Each section ends with a statement of what Xi is said to have deepened. Zhang's core move is to read Xi's statements as creative extensions of historical materialism. Productive forces remain the basic yardstick of social progress, and in socialism their purpose is people's growing need for a better life. In Zhang's account, new quality productive forces are defined by a leap in labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their optimal combination. They are driven by the information revolution, digital technology and artificial intelligence, with scientific and technological innovation as the core element. Zhang also presents the slogan that protecting the environment is protecting productive forces as the systematic form of Marx's idea of regulating the metabolism between humans and nature. In this reading, the socialist system and market economy together, along with deeper reform, must produce production relations suited to the new productive forces. Zhang concludes that new quality productive forces are essentially advanced productive forces. The author gives four features: they arise from the new round of technological and industrial change; they are the advanced productive forces of the information, digital and intelligent era; they rest on a leap in the combination of production factors; and they are the material and technological basis of Chinese modernization and high-quality development. In Zhang's view, the Party's vanguard character depends on representing advanced productive forces. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line overview of how Chinese theorists trace new quality productive forces back to Marx, Lenin, Mao and Deng.

The conceptual logic of "the critique of capital" The core meaning of the "doctrine of the concept" in Marx's political economy “资本批判”的概念逻辑 Liu Daoyi Liu Daoyi asks how the concepts of Marx's political economy are built and how they move, and argues that the "conceptual logic" of Capital is the methodological model for any later critique of capital. In Liu's reading, the capitalist economic system is a system of contradictions, so the concepts that define it must form an organised group centred on one core concept. The movement of the concepts, Liu argues, mirrors the real "movement of contradictions", which turns Hegel's dialectic from standing on its head to standing on its feet. The article first traces the idea of "concept-movement" to Hegel's speculative logic and then to Marx's materialist inversion of it. It next sets out four basic forms of conceptual movement in Capital and its manuscripts: critique of old concepts, definition of new ones, reworking of concepts, and transformation between concrete and abstract. It then follows the genesis of this logic through the 1844 Manuscripts, the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts, and the three volumes of Capital. Liu's central claim is that Marx moved "from the concrete to the abstract and back up to the concrete" through three theoretical cycles over some twenty years. The core concept first defined was "alienated labour" in the 1844 Manuscripts. Marx then replaced it with "surplus value", first in the 1857–58 manuscripts and then in the 1861–63 manuscripts, before fully defining it in Volume I. Liu stresses that abstract and concrete are relative: commodity is abstract relative to money, and surplus value is abstract relative to profit but concrete relative to value. From surplus value Marx derives relative surplus value, wages and accumulation (Volume I), capital circulation and reproduction (Volume II), and profit, average profit, production price, commercial profit, interest and rent (Volume III). Liu reads the closing part on revenues and their sources as the counterpart of Hegel's "absolute idea", aimed at vulgar economics and its "trinity formula". Liu concludes that this systematic argument built on surplus value rejects the "factor theory" and other apologetics for capitalism. It also differs from Hegel's harmonious final picture of absolute spirit. According to the author, the conceptual doctrine remains necessary for critical study of today's global capitalism and for thinking about "human emancipation", since it drives practical change and a scientific vision of a good life. Read the original if you study the methodology of Capital, Marx's relation to Hegel's Logic, or how Marx's core concept shifted from alienated labour to surplus value.

Grasping the reform spirit of further deepening reform comprehensively Reflections on integrating the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee into ideological and political theory courses 深入领悟进一步全面深化改革的改革精神 Hou Huiqin Hou Huiqin asks how the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively should be understood and brought into university ideological and political theory courses. The article argues that the Plenum is, like the Third Plenums of the 11th and 18th Central Committees, an epoch-making event, and that its distinctive character is "systems integration". Hou holds that this spirit must be grasped through the era, through the mission of the courses, and through worldview and method. The article has three parts. The first compares the three Third Plenums and sets out the features of the present era and of the current round of reform. The second turns to the courses themselves: their role in arming the Party and the people with theory, in the Marxist theory research and development project, and in building an independent Chinese system of philosophy and social-science knowledge. The third examines the "systems concept" as the philosophical foundation of the reform spirit. On the era, Hou argues that the world has entered a new age of peace and development, a smaller epoch within Marx's larger epoch of transition from capitalism to communism. Hou grounds this in economic globalisation, in development as the pivot of world problems, and in the collective rise of developing countries, which Hou says is ending capitalist unipolarity. Because the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics have largely taken shape, reform now has a clearer aim of perfecting institutions and requires integrated goals, comprehensive evaluation beyond GDP, and fairness in sharing results through common prosperity. For the courses, Hou calls for turning ideals and convictions into a body of knowledge centred on communism, expounding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era through worldview, historical narrative and rebuttal of erroneous trends, and contrasting Marxist knowledge systems with Western ones, which Hou says rest on fixed assumptions about human nature. Hou also treats the systems concept as a method that grasps the "general" as a real entity, and as the basis for a community with a shared future for mankind. Hou concludes that the courses have a pioneering duty in Party theory, in building an autonomous knowledge system and in applying a scientific worldview across all disciplines. Hou presents the systems concept as the key to understanding Chinese modernization, the change in the principal contradiction, and the "two overall situations" of China and the world. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist theorist links the 2024 reform agenda to the teaching of ideological and political theory and to debates over an independent knowledge system.

Grand theft capital: the increasing exploitation and robbery of the US working class 资本大劫掠：美国工人阶级面临日益严重的剥削和洗劫 Fred Magdoff John Bellamy Foster This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the American scholars Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster, first published in Monthly Review in 2023. The authors ask why the US working class has grown steadily worse off over roughly half a century. They argue that the cause is a class war waged by capital against labour, which began as a response to a structural crisis of monopoly-finance capitalism and has intensified both ordinary exploitation and outright appropriation of workers' income. The article opens with capitalism's long history of plundering land, resources and human life, then sets out the postwar 'golden age' and its end. It moves through the neoliberal turn, the assault on trade unions, and the conditions of US workers in the first two decades of the twenty-first century. It closes with estimates of income redistributed upward and a brief note on renewed labour organising. Following Baran and Sweezy's Monopoly Capital, the authors treat stagnation as the normal condition of monopoly capitalism and the postwar boom as the exception that needs explaining. In their account, capital met stagnation by raising interest rates, financialising the economy, concentrating firms, cutting taxes for the rich, offshoring production and weakening unions. They describe wage theft, misclassification of workers as contractors, non-compete clauses, understaffing, global labour arbitrage and a regressive tax system. They cite figures showing that real pay for production and non-supervisory workers rose only 15 per cent in forty years while productivity rose 75 per cent. A RAND study they cite puts the income 'lost' by the bottom 90 per cent between 1975 and 2018 at more than 47 trillion dollars. The authors conclude that the real class struggle is the one capital has waged against labour, and they quote Warren Buffett's remark that his class is winning it. They suggest that higher taxes on the rich and lower military spending could fund jobs and social programmes. Citing Bernie Sanders, they note that workers are now reorganising, and they hold that only a mass uprising from below, like that of the 1930s, can build the power needed for a fairer society. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of US inequality, financialisation and union decline, with a dense set of statistics, in a version that Chinese journals chose to translate.

A critique of American war capitalism 美国战争资本主义批判 Yang Ningcong Yang Ningcong takes up Sven Beckert's concept of 'war capitalism' (from Empire of Cotton, 2014) and applies it to the contemporary United States. The article asks what drives American decision-makers to wage war and what the consequences are. Its answer is that US war capitalism is a form of imperialism: a mechanism by which the military-industrial complex delays capitalist crisis, secures monopoly profit and sustains hegemony, while in the long run damaging the US economy, society and world peace. The article has three parts. The first traces the history in four stages: military Keynesianism around the Second World War, the 'permanent war economy' after 1945, 'Pentagon capitalism', and the transformation of the state into a 'war corporation' through the 'revolving door' between government, military, industry and think tanks. The second part analyses the essence and operating logic of war capitalism. The third examines six consequences, from blocked economic conversion and a 'parasitic' economy to manufacturing decline, social conflict, damage to world peace and the erosion of US hegemony. Yang draws chiefly on Lenin. In the author's reading, war capitalism serves the military-industrial complex in staving off capitalist collapse, continues imperialism by other means, and extracts excess war profit for monopoly capital. It runs on three practices: glorifying foreign wars, keeping up a Cold War mindset to justify arms races and budgets, and profiting from arms sales and plunder. Yang argues that this military spending crowds out civilian investment and infrastructure, and that the Pentagon and defence firms act as parasites on the civilian economy. The article cites figures such as the 2024 defence budget request of 842 billion dollars and the fall in manufacturing's GDP share from 28.12% in 1953 to 12.03% in 2015. Yang concludes, following Lenin, that war will end only when capitalism is overthrown, but that this is a long historical process. For China, the author proposes strategic composure, a path of peaceful development and support for multilateral dialogue. Yang also argues that China must neither seek nor fear war, and must build up its military strength, since preparing for war is described as the most effective means of preventing it. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies Lenin's theory of imperialism to the US military-industrial complex and draws policy conclusions for China.

The 75 years since the founding of the People's Republic as a glorious chapter in the history of socialism 新中国成立以来的75年是社会主义发展史上的光辉篇章 Zhu Jiamu Writing in 2024 for the 75th anniversary of the People's Republic, Zhu Jiamu asks why these seven and a half decades should be seen as the most brilliant chapter in the history of world socialism. The author answers that, whether in periods of correct policy or of deviation, the whole history has revolved around what socialism is and how to build it, and has produced major achievements and regularities of experience. The article opens with a short account of socialism from Marx and Lenin to the post-war socialist states and the Soviet and East European collapse. It then reviews achievements and lessons in five fields: the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology. Each is traced through the pre-reform period, the era of reform and opening up, and the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012), with frequent quotation from Xi Jinping and from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhu's central claims are that socialism with Chinese characteristics remains socialism and that errors were part of exploration. On ownership, Zhu holds that although private firms supply most tax revenue, output and jobs, public ownership remains dominant because it keeps control over the commanding heights of the economy. On the Cultural Revolution, Zhu follows the 1981 Resolution in calling it wholly wrong while insisting that the period's socialist character and construction work cannot be denied. In culture, Zhu endorses tight Party leadership of ideology and the primacy of social over economic benefit. In politics, Zhu contrasts a Party whose officials may not hold private capital with capitalist systems in which money openly shapes policy. Zhu concludes that the record shows socialism's superiority over capitalism, citing industrial output, poverty reduction, health, education and environmental figures, and that the Party's direction has been consistently firm and serious. The author admits that tasks remain, including gaps in social security and in advanced technology, but expects the cause to withstand any test under Xi Jinping's leadership. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned overview of how a senior Party historian assesses the PRC's record across economy, politics, culture, society and ecology, including its handling of the Cultural Revolution.

Mao Zedong's practical exploration of China's rural land question (1924–1949) 毛泽东关于中国农村土地问题的实践探索（1924—1949） Zhang Yong Zhang Yong asks how Mao Zedong worked out policies on the peasant land question during the democratic revolution, when neither the classics of Marxism nor Lenin's writings offered a ready answer for a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country. The article argues that Mao combined the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete conditions. In Zhang's account, this produced a coherent set of lines, policies and principles that carried the revolution to victory and opened a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article follows Mao's work in four periods: the Great Revolution (1924–27), the Second Revolutionary Civil War, the War of Resistance against Japan, and the War of Liberation. It then draws four lessons from the whole record. For each period Zhang examines the key texts and legislation, including the Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, the Jinggangshan and Xingguo land laws, rent and interest reduction, the May Fourth Directive (1946) and the Outline Land Law of China (1947). Zhang presents the land policy as a series of adjustments to changing class relations. Mao first made the peasantry, and especially poor peasants, central to the revolution. He then moved from confiscating landlords' land to rent and interest reduction in order to build the anti-Japanese united front. After 1945 he returned to land distribution, and corrected leftist excesses by relying on poor peasants, uniting with middle peasants and treating rich peasants and landlords differently. Zhang also covers Mao's investigations of rural conditions, such as the Xunwu survey, and his criticism of ultra-leftist Party leaders who attacked his approach as a "rich-peasant line". Zhang draws four lessons: independence and self-reliance, the mass line, land legislation, and seeking truth from facts through investigation. The author maintains that the policies enriched Marxist theory on the peasant question and laid the foundation for land reform after 1949. Zhang adds that the history still offers a reference for today's issues concerning agriculture, rural areas and farmers. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-historiography account of how Mao's land policy developed from 1924 to 1949 and how Chinese scholars now frame its lessons.

Deng Xiaoping's thought on historical self-confidence: formative conditions, content and contemporary value 邓小平历史自信思想的形成条件、丰富内涵与时代价值 Zhang Yanguo Zhang Yanguo asks what Deng Xiaoping meant by "historical self-confidence" and why it still matters. The article defines the term as a conviction a nation forms about its own history, resting on trust in, belonging to and pride in that history. It argues that Deng developed a coherent body of thought on the subject over a long revolutionary career. In Zhang's account, this body of thought is a distinctive part of Deng Xiaoping Theory and an original contribution to historical materialism. The article has three parts. The first sets out the sources of Deng's thinking: historical materialism and the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; the 5,000-year history of Chinese civilisation and its traditional culture; and Deng's own experience, including his classical schooling and his lifelong reading of historical works. The second part sets out the content of the thought. The third discusses its value in the new era. Zhang's central claim is that Deng answered four linked questions: why historical self-confidence is needed, what to be confident about, how to sustain it, and what it is for. It is needed because China must follow its own path and rely on its own strength, and Zhang quotes Deng as saying that copying foreign models never succeeds. It has five objects: love of Chinese history and patriotism; excellent traditional culture; openness to the achievements of other civilisations; the hard-won results of the revolution and the Party's history; and a historicist, \"seeking truth from facts\" attitude to historical figures and errors, including the 1981 Resolution on Party history and the distinction between Mao Zedong's late mistakes and Mao Zedong Thought. Zhang also presents Deng as opposing historical nihilism and as insisting that history be taught to young people. Zhang says the thought contributes to historical materialism on stages of development, paths of development, and the link between China and world history. Zhang concludes that Deng's thought supplies empirical grounds for further adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It also supplies spiritual resources for Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Zhang's view, the Four-sphere Confidence rests on historical self-confidence, which is why Deng's thought remains a source of renewal in the new era. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how Deng's views on history are used to ground present-day confidence in the socialist path.

The principles and direction of the "Two Integrations" in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, seen through Mao Zedong's philosophy 从毛泽东哲学透视马克思主义中国化“两个结合”的原则与走向 Xue Guangzhou Xue Guangzhou asks how the Two Integrations, the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, should be understood, applied and developed. Drawing on Mao Zedong's philosophy, the article argues that the Two Integrations are practical principles, not slogans. It holds that the combination must be led by Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method, and that it points towards a new Chinese philosophy. The article opens by tracing the history of the phrase "adapting Marxism to the Chinese context" from Mao's 1938 report. It then proceeds in three parts. The first interprets the two sides of the combination: "China's concrete realities" and "fine traditional Chinese culture". The second sets out principles for each integration, together with tendencies to avoid. The third outlines the developmental path of Marxist philosophy in China. Xue defines China's concrete realities by the principal contradiction and the nature of Chinese society at a given stage, and criticises neoliberal economics for rejecting China's existing economic base. On culture, the author follows Mao's formula of discarding dross and absorbing essence. Xue distinguishes traditional culture's "quintessence" (jinsui, a factual judgement of its core spirit) from its "essence" (jinghua, a value judgement), and proposes "zhong" (the mean or centre) as the quintessence. Five principles are given: take the essence and discard the dross; critical inheritance; make the past serve the present; let a hundred flowers bloom and a hundred schools contend; and, above all, hold to Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method. Xue warns against treating the Second Integration as a fusion of equals, against reducing cultural rejuvenation to a Confucian revival, and against reading Xi Jinping's thought on culture only as inheritance of tradition or of a Confucian orthodoxy. Xue sets out a three-stage path: from the Sinification of Marxist philosophy, to a Sinified Marxist philosophy, to a Chinese Marxist philosophy, and finally to a "new Chinese philosophy". Such a philosophy would absorb the best of traditional Chinese thought and of human intellectual achievement while keeping Marxism's core. Xue credits Mao's philosophical thought with a pioneering contribution and says Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has opened a new era for the process. Read the original if you want a Mao-centred, philosophical account of how the Two Integrations should be understood, including its warnings against cultural revivalism and neoliberalism.

The theoretical content and contemporary value of the "Speech at the Forum on Literature and Art" 《在文艺工作座谈会上的讲话》的理论内涵与时代价值 Hong Jun Marking a decade since Xi Jinping delivered his speech at the Forum on Literature and Art on 15 October 2014, Hong Jun asks what the text contributes theoretically and how it has shaped practice. The article argues that the speech is a major Marxist document on literature and art, comparable in standing to Mao Zedong's 1942 Yan'an Talks. In Hong's reading it consolidated Marxism's guiding position in the field, steered the development of literature and art, set out their mission in national rejuvenation, and was an early, important component of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article is organised in four sections followed by a conclusion. It covers the speech's theoretical innovation within Marxist literary theory, its problem-oriented guidance of literary and artistic work, its account of the mission of literature and art in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and Chinese modernization, and its place in the formation of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Hong draws on works of recent fiction and television, Party policy documents issued after 2014, and classical Chinese literary theory. Hong makes three main moves. First, the speech is said to ground its call for realism, a people-centred orientation and a critical stance towards Western modernist and postmodernist theory in historical materialism, and to treat 'the people' as concrete individuals, not an abstraction, by combining Engels with the Chinese min-ben tradition. Second, it diagnoses a lack of masterpieces, a decline in artists' morality, and works promoting historical nihilism, and the author credits it with prompting a revival of realist writing and stricter industry regulation. Third, Hong traces continuities with Xi's later cultural thought: the speech's demand that art be combined with excellent traditional culture is described as logically consistent with the 'second integration', and its stress on telling China's stories anticipates later statements on international communication. Hong also links the speech's view of art's social function to the Confucian 'esteem for culture' (shang wen) tradition. Hong concludes that the speech marks an epoch-making stage in adapting Marxist literary theory to the Chinese context, and that it supplied Chinese thought and approaches to new problems such as the effects of technological revolution on artistic creation and the role of art in exchanges between civilizations. The author adds that it strengthened scholars' confidence and theoretical agency in international dialogue. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese Marxist literary theory presents Xi's 2014 speech and its relation to the Yan'an Talks and to Xi Jinping Thought on Culture.

An analysis of Deng Xiaoping's thought on exercising historical initiative 邓小平发挥历史主动思想探析 Chen Dacai Chen Dacai takes up the concept of "historical initiative" (fahui lishi zhudong), which the Party has stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022), and asks how Deng Xiaoping understood and practised it. Written ahead of the 120th anniversary of Deng's birth, the article argues that Deng developed a systematic body of thought on the subject. In Chen's account, this thought laid the groundwork for the Party's call to strengthen historical initiative in the new era. The article opens by tracing the idea from Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong to Deng. It then arranges Deng's thought in three parts: the meaning of initiative, the qualities required of the historical agent, and the practical path of action. Chen draws on Deng's speeches and conversations from the revolutionary years through the reform period, including his 1978 speeches, the 1981 historical resolution and his talks with foreign visitors. Chen first argues that Deng read initiative as subjective activity, as strategic initiative (the power to shape the situation), and as something that must be continually fought for. Second, the author holds that Deng's own conduct showed historical consciousness, historical thinking (holistic, process-based and objective) and historical resolve. The last is expressed in the Four Cardinal Principles. Third, Chen presents Deng's practical path as three steps: focusing on the central question of the age ("what is socialism and how to build it"), respecting historical laws, and opening new horizons. Chen links these to the primary stage of socialism, Chinese-style modernization, a moderately prosperous society, the "three-step" strategy, and the policies of reform and opening up. Chen concludes that Deng combined a static account of initiative (subjective activity and initiative as power) with a dynamic one (striving for it in practice). In Chen's view this gave the Party an intellectual, subjective and experiential basis for the new era. Chen ends by citing Xi Jinping's remark that Deng succeeded because he grasped the trends of the age and the laws of China's development, and by urging the Party to keep drawing on that wisdom. Read the original if you study Deng Xiaoping Theory, or want to see how Party scholars now trace the concept of historical initiative back to Deng and the classical Marxist writers.

The US "Summit for Democracy" and new challenges to China's ideological security 美国“民主峰会”与我国意识形态安全的新挑战 Wang Jianfeng Wang Jianfeng asks what the Biden administration's global "Summit for Democracy" is for and what it means for China. The article argues that the summits, three of which had been held by March 2024, are a tool of ideological war against China and other states, and that they create a series of new external challenges for China's ideological security. Wang presents them as part of a wider "new Cold War" strategy aimed at preserving declining US hegemony. The article has four parts. It first explains the background to the summits: the role of "democracy" in sustaining US global leadership, and the need to restore America's "beacon of democracy" image after political polarisation and the Capitol riot. It then analyses the summits' "normative" and "functional" aspects, and identifies three inherent flaws. It ends with the pressure on China's ideological security and proposed responses at macro, meso and micro levels. Wang argues that the summits are mainly about values promotion, with practical functions subordinate to that aim. The article describes the "generalisation of democracy": technology controls, supply-chain restructuring and the Ukraine crisis are framed as democracy-versus-autocracy issues so that allies share costs. It also describes funding schemes under the Presidential Initiative for Democratic Renewal, which Wang says target trade unionists, labour groups and NGOs as potential agents of "colour revolutions". The three flaws are a single "American-style" model of democracy, vague and interest-driven criteria for invitations (Wang cites Freedom House ratings to show inconsistencies), and a false democracy–autocracy narrative that ignores the internal causes of democratic decline. On China, Wang says the summits challenge its ideological security through a contest over core values, set against the "common values of all humanity", and through a contest over development models, aimed at Chinese modernization. Wang calls for a holistic ideological security outlook under the overall national security concept, stronger international communication combining official and civil channels, and tighter online supervision and vigilance against foreign NGOs. The article also warns against being drawn into a full-scale ideological competition as the Soviet Union was. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist-institution scholar frames US democracy promotion as ideological confrontation and what countermeasures are proposed.

The basic meaning, major impact and multidimensional evaluation of the Bolshevization of the Communist International 共产国际布尔什维克化的基本内涵、重大影响与多维评价 Gong Yutao Gong Yutao asks how the Comintern's slogan of "Bolshevization" should be understood and assessed. Writing in Contemporary World and Socialism (2024), Gong argues that it was a reflection of a major strategic turn by the Communist International, that it became a movement affecting every section, and that its positive effects were the mainstream, although its negative effects must be seriously reflected upon. The article has three parts. The first traces how the Fifth Comintern Congress (1924) launched the slogan and how the Fifth Enlarged Plenum of the Executive Committee (1925) systematised it. The second examines the impact on Western communist parties (Germany, France, Italy, Britain) and then on the Communist Party of China, from the early 1920s through the Zunyi Meeting and the 1942 Rectification Movement. The third offers an evaluation of the slogan's origins, its positive effects and its negative effects. Gong shows that the 1924 congress defined Bolshevization as transplanting the internationally valid elements of Russian Bolshevism, not copying Russian experience mechanically. The 1925 plenum added eight requirements, including combating right and ultra-left deviations, theoretical training in Marxism-Leninism, winning the masses and allies, factory cells, discipline, and loyalty to the Comintern's leadership. Gong's account of Germany describes Comintern pressure that removed Arkadi Maslow's leadership, and of Italy describes Gramsci replacing Amadeo Bordiga with Comintern backing. For the Chinese party, Gong notes that Bolshevization became central after the Sixth Congress (1928) and brought leftism and dogmatism. After Zunyi, Mao Zedong's calls and the sinification of Marxism gave it a Chinese form. In evaluation, Gong holds that the slogan met the Comintern's needs as a "revolutionary international" and a "unified world party", and that it helped young parties mature and strengthened unity. Gong also criticises an inflated reading of right-wing danger, hostility towards social democrats, weakened independence of sections, the sanctification of Russian experience, and the replacement of leaders (50 parties' main leaders in the late 1920s and early 1930s, according to the article). These problems are said to be products of their circumstances and should be neither ignored nor exaggerated. Read the original if you study the Comintern, the history of the Chinese Communist Party's organisational development, or how Chinese scholars currently evaluate this history.

New explorations of the Communist Party of Belgium on the road to socialism in the 21st century 21世纪比利时共产党对社会主义道路的新探索 Guo Taiying Guo Taiying asks how the Communist Party of Belgium (founded 1921) has sought a path to socialism suited to national conditions since 2000, and what its experience shows about communist parties in Western capitalist states. The author argues that the party has revised its theory and adjusted its practice, but that results have been limited and its prospects are not promising. The article has three parts. It first divides the party's history into three stages: early exploration from 1921 to 1945, a period of zigzag and drift in the Cold War from the 1950s to the 1980s, and adjustment and transition from the 1990s onwards. It then examines new theoretical positions, and finally the party's political practice in elections, mass work and inter-party relations. Guo draws on party congress decisions and statements, including the 36th Congress of 2018. On theory, Guo reports that the party describes capitalism as in systemic crisis (economic, technological, ecological and military) and demands that Belgium leave NATO and the EU, which it calls an imperialist bloc serving monopoly capital. The party remains committed to Marxism-Leninism but reinterprets core concepts: it replaces "dictatorship of the proletariat" with "workers' power" and "class struggle" with "class solidarity". It envisions a gradual, democratic, multi-party, federal and self-managed socialism, rejects Belgian-style federalism as a drift towards confederalism, and treats religion dialectically. In practice, Guo shows, the party stays on the peaceful parliamentary road. It runs in electoral alliances with the Workers' Party of Belgium, supports strikes and trade unions, and joins the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties and the World Anti-Imperialist Platform. It also issues statements on Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Palestine. Guo concludes that the party's search for goals fitting the times, its self-transformation, its parliamentary struggle, its mass line and its inter-party contacts have somewhat improved its position. The party has held no parliamentary seats since 1985, and the author judges its achievements unremarkable. Its future depends on seizing opportunities and strengthening itself. Read the original if you study European communist parties, the revision of core Marxist-Leninist concepts in Western Europe, or the Chinese scholarly reading of foreign communist parties.

African left-wing ruling parties' joint self-strengthening in a multidimensional perspective The case of the "six sister parties" of Southern Africa 多维视阈下的非洲左翼执政党联合自强 Deng Yanting Against the backdrop of a wave of de-Westernising transformation in Africa, Deng Yanting asks how six left-wing ruling parties in Southern Africa have built a joint, transnational political bloc and what it means for African development. The six are the Revolutionary Party of Tanzania (CCM), the ANC (South Africa), the MPLA (Angola), FRELIMO (Mozambique), SWAPO (Namibia) and ZANU-PF (Zimbabwe), known as the "six sister parties". Deng argues that their joint self-strengthening grew out of shared history, now underpins Africa's autonomous development, and still faces internal and external risks. The article has three parts. The first traces the bloc through three stages: revolutionary friendship during the liberation struggles, collective resistance to neoliberalism after the Cold War, and collective reflection on governance problems since the early 2000s. The second part sets out the bloc's present significance for regional integration, for China–Africa ties and for a revival of socialism in Africa. The third part examines internal differences among the parties and pressure from the United States and the West. Deng's central claim is that Nyerere's Pan-Africanist idea of "Ujamaa", shared socialist convictions and armed struggle against colonialism, racism and imperialism created a bond that later shaped resistance to "Washington Consensus" reforms. Deng cites Zambia's United National Independence Party, which lost power after the 1991 turn to multiparty politics, as a warning. The six parties kept their ideology, party organisation and public ownership, and Deng credits this with making Southern Africa the continent's most stable sub-region. Deng presents the Southern African Development Community as party-based integration, and describes China's support, from the Tanzania–Zambia Railway to the Julius Nyerere Leadership School, as strengthening the bloc. Deng also names risks: South Africa's heavier governing burden and the ANC's loss of its parliamentary majority in 2024, Angola's oil-driven governance strains, and Western "cognitive warfare", opposition backing and selective economic incentives and sanctions. Deng concludes that ideological and institutional advantages, together with the parties' self-reform centred on their peoples, will let them overcome these constraints. In Deng's view the bloc will keep acting as a model for African unity and a base for Chinese modernization to support African revival and the Global South. Read the original if you study the Chinese academic view of African left-wing parties, party-to-party ties between China and Africa, or Southern African politics from a socialist perspective.

Challenges and strategic adjustments of the Communist Party of the Netherlands in pursuing socialism 荷兰共产党追求社会主义过程中面临的挑战及策略调整 Wang Yanlong Wang Yanlong asks how the Communist Party of the Netherlands (CPN) shaped its political position, defended socialist values and balanced socialism with democratic ideas across the twentieth century. The article argues that the party's history shows a political organisation adapting to changing international and domestic conditions. Wang holds that the party survived as long as it adjusted its policies, organisation and ideas, and that its legacy outlived its dissolution. The article follows the party chronologically in four stages. It begins with the CPN's emergence from the left wing of the Social Democratic Workers' Party and its early aims. It then treats the Second World War, when the party moved underground and led resistance. A third section covers the Cold War, from postwar peak through de-Stalinisation and the Prague Spring to decline and merger. The last section examines the party's legacy in GroenLinks (the Green Left) and in Dutch politics, followed by a brief conclusion. Wang's central claim is that the party repeatedly redefined its socialism under external pressure. In its early years it stressed class struggle, the dictatorship of the proletariat and the Comintern line. Under Nazi occupation it joined socialism to anti-fascism and democracy, set up underground networks, helped hide Jews, and organised the February 1941 Amsterdam strike. After the Hungarian events of 1956 and especially the Prague Spring of 1968, Wang says, the party questioned the Soviet model, turned to a more democratic and plural socialism, and allied with trade unions, students, feminists and peace and environmental movements. Wang attributes the party's decline in the 1980s to the collapse of Soviet-bloc socialism, a shrinking working class, a rising middle class and internal splits between reformers and traditionalists. The article cites a fall in membership from 150,000 to 6,000 and a vote of 0.6 per cent in 1986. Wang concludes that parties must respond to their environment and also renew themselves in organisation and ideas. The article credits the CPN, dissolved in 1991, with lasting influence through GroenLinks, which Wang says carried on its commitments to social justice, environmental protection and intra-party democracy. Wang also links the party to Dutch welfare, housing, education and employment policy and to popular participation. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic Chinese account of a small Western European communist party and its Cold War transformation.

Marx's theory of civilization and building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 马克思的文明理论与建设中华民族现代文明 Duan Yan Duan Yan asks what theoretical basis Marx's writings on civilization provide for the new cultural mission of building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, a task Xi Jinping set out in 2023. The article argues that Marx's theory supplies the foundation and that the Chinese project develops it further. It does so by combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, which the article calls the Two Integrations. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's theory under three headings: civilization as the unity of social formation and state form; the free and all-round development of each person as the goal of civilization; and world history as the driving force of modern civilization. The second part presents the modern civilization of the Chinese nation as an innovative development of that theory. The third sets out five practical paths for building it. In Duan's reading, Marx treats civilization as a historical category: material and spiritual progress develop together, and the state is its "summary". Marx also criticises capitalist civilization, which opened world history yet combined progress with barbarism, and he looks to a successor civilization that abolishes private ownership. Duan argues that the Chinese civilization fits this pattern in three ways. It is socialist in both social and state form, coordinating five civilizations (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological). It takes a people-centred orientation, linked to traditional minben (people-as-foundation) thought and to common prosperity. It stresses openness, mutual learning and a community with a shared future for mankind, which Duan says goes beyond the "clash of civilizations" and Western-centrism. Duan proposes five paths: advance Chinese modernization while taking China's own road; draw selectively on the achievements of other civilizations, with Chinese needs as the principle; promote the flourishing of socialist culture under core socialist values; carry out the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, with heritage protection; and spread Chinese civilization abroad through a community with a shared future for mankind. The article presents these as contributions to human progress and as a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar ties Marx's remarks on civilization, the state and world history to current Party cultural policy.

Marx's twofold critique of modern science and technology and its inheritance and development 马克思对现代科学技术的双重批判及其继承发展 Li Le Li Le examines Marx's speech of 14 April 1856 at the fourth anniversary dinner of the Chartist People's Paper, a short text the author says has received little scholarly attention. The article argues that two metaphors in the speech, modern science and technology as a "most dangerous revolutionary" and as a "shrewd spirit", ground a twofold critique: one of the facts of science and technology under capitalism, and one of the attitudes different parties take towards it. Li presents this as a basis for understanding Xi Jinping's statements on science and technology in the new era. The article has three parts. The first reads the "revolutionary" metaphor against Blanqui, Barbès and Raspail, and then sets out how science and technology work as a new social force and stand opposed to modern poverty. The second turns to the "spirit" metaphor, surveying how petty-bourgeois democrats such as Kinkel, Christian Socialists, Tories and David Urquhart's circle responded, and then Marx's view of the proletariat as the "new men". The third moves to the present and discusses Xi Jinping's remarks on science and technology. In Li's reading of the first metaphor, science and technology advance the productive forces, create revolutionary pressure and reshape the social structure. Under capitalist relations, however, they become a tool of capital: nature is conquered for profit, science is separated from workers, and machinery lengthens and intensifies labour, deskills workers and subordinates their life rhythm to the machine. Li stresses that the cause of poverty is the capitalist relations of production that distort technology, not technology itself. On the second metaphor, Li holds that only workers can master this force, through a social revolution that is comprehensive, broad in scope and historical, ending wage labour and the monopoly over technology. In the final part Li presents Xi Jinping's discourse as continuing this tradition. It treats science and technology as the primary productive force and as a foundation for Chinese modernization. Li also describes an original idea of "initiative" in science and technology, which includes judging trends, self-confidence in innovation and strategic initiative. Li lists socialist requirements: meeting people's needs, self-reliance in core technologies, a new whole-nation system to regulate capital's logic, and opposing the politicization of technology. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese doctoral researcher links a little-studied Marx speech to current Party science and technology policy.

Marx's investigation of the essence of the state through the interplay of history and political economy, and its implications 马克思在历史与政治经济学交互视域中对国家本质的考察及其启示 Wang Guang What is the state, and by what route did Marx determine its essence? Wang Guang argues that Marx's approach differs from both empirical political science and normative political philosophy. In Wang's account, Marx combined two perspectives: he went into real history to trace how states develop and change, and he went beyond the political sphere into political economy to define the state's content. Wang holds that this research path, and not only Marx's conclusions, is what present-day scholars should study. The article follows Marx's thought in four steps. It begins with the Kreuznach Notebooks of 1843 and the break with Hegel's "rational state". It then traces the state's essence through the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Holy Family, The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. Next it turns to The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, The Civil War in France and Engels's remarks on the Paris Commune and the United States. It ends with a discussion of how Marx's political philosophy should be defined today. Wang's central claim is that the Kreuznach excerpts on French, English and German history taught Marx to see property relations behind political rule, so that he reversed Hegel's order of explanation. After 1844 he tied the state to production, and in The German Ideology the modern state appears as the form that matches modern private property and serves the bourgeoisie's common interests. Wang reads the Commune as the practical answer: the working class cannot simply take over the ready-made state machine but must smash it, and the Commune returns to society the powers a "parasitic excrescence" had taken from it. In the final section Wang argues that applying Western political philosophy's standards to Marx concentrates attention on justice, equality and freedom, and neglects the state, class and revolution. Wang proposes a "broad-spectrum" Marxist political philosophy, with wider topics and a normativity grounded in scientific necessity, in which what ought to be rests on what is and what must be. Wang concludes that Marx's political philosophy differs in kind from that of Plato, Hobbes, Rawls and others, because it derives values from the laws of history and not from reason or moral principle. The article calls for widening the themes of Marx's political philosophy and for rebuilding its normativity along these lines. Wang presents this as part of building China's own independent knowledge system. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese Marxist philosophers define Marx's political philosophy against Western political philosophy, or in a close reading of Marx's early texts on the state.

Principle-level achievements of the Party's theoretical innovation in the perspective of scientific socialism 科学社会主义视阈中党的理论创新的原理性成果 Wang Conglong Wang Conglong takes up a task that Xi Jinping set in June 2023: to clarify the "principle-level theoretical achievements" (yuanlixing lilun chengguo) within the Party's innovative theory and to show how they connect. The article argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has put forward a series of original achievements of this kind, which in Wang's account have opened a new realm for scientific socialism in contemporary China. The article has three parts. The first defines principle-level achievements as major judgements that are foundational in origin, in supporting function and in essential character, and explains why proposing them is required to uphold and develop scientific socialism. The second sets out nine such achievements, each paired with a question the classics left open. The third assesses what they accomplish for scientific socialism. Wang argues that the classical writers stated only the most general principles, whose application must change with historical conditions, so new principle-level achievements are needed both to keep to the classics and to renew them. The nine achievements are: Party leadership as the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics; the general task of socialist modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; a people-centred stance; the new development philosophy; modernizing national governance; humanity and nature as a community of life; the Party's self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall; a community with a shared future for mankind; and Chinese modernization. Wang reads these as meeting four kinds of question: foundational, core, guarantee-related and forward-looking. Wang concludes that these achievements strengthen the theoretical roots of scientific socialism in China and show it in a new form. They also set a new height for its twenty-first-century development and open a new prospect for it in the contemporary world, including long-term coexistence between socialist states and the capitalist world. Wang calls Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era the scientific socialism of contemporary China. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how the Xi-era formulations are presented as extending scientific socialism.

The place and role of "needs" in the framework of historical materialism “需要”在历史唯物主义框架中的地位及其作用 Wang Wei Wang Wei asks where "needs" belong within historical materialism. Chinese scholarship since the 1980s has mostly treated need as a basic category of historical materialism, often comparing its weight with that of the productive forces. Wang argues that need is better understood as a mechanism than as a fixed category. On this view, need is not the driving force of history but the content determination of social production and social life, and it is rooted in both nature and society. The article has four sections. The first lists the problems with classing need only as a historical-materialist category. The second sets out how need determines the content of the framework. The third examines its formal determination and its limits. The fourth turns to the theory of the principal social contradiction in China, which Wang presents as a development of Marx's theory of needs. Wang draws on Marx and Engels throughout, including the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Engels's essay on the role of labour in the transition from ape to man. Wang's central claim is that need belongs to the dialectics of nature as well as to historical materialism. Natural needs form the biological precondition of society, so need cannot simply be ranked against the productive forces. In content, need defines who the historical subject is, what practice is carried out and how, the unity of natural history and human history, and the ideological forms of class society. Its form is tied to subjectivity and has limits. Needs can become distorted under exploitative relations of production, and they are constrained by natural and social conditions and by cultural tradition. Morality and law can discipline them only within limits set by the relations of production, and the development of the productive forces ultimately drives them. Need therefore does not replace the productive forces' decisive role. In the final section Wang reads the Party's formulations of the principal contradiction as putting need at the centre of socialist development. These are the 1981 formulation (growing material and cultural needs against backward production) and the 19th Party Congress (2017) formulation (needs for a better life against unbalanced and inadequate development). Wang presents this as a creative advance on Marx's theory, linked to Chinese modernization, common prosperity and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a philosophical treatment of need in Marxist theory that ends in a Party-line account of the principal contradiction.

New quality productive forces as an integration of practical and theoretical innovation in the new era 新质生产力是新时代实践和理论创新的集成 Gu Hailiang Writing in Theory Guide (Lilun daobao) in 2024, Gu Hailiang asks how the concept of new quality productive forces relates to China's economic practice and to its economics since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gu argues that the concept is an integration of that practice and of theoretical innovation, and that it achieves what Engels called a 'revolution in the terminology' of a science, here Chinese economics. For Gu it also marks the theoretical level reached by Xi Jinping's economic thought. The article opens with Engels on scientific terminology and Lenin on reducing production relations to the level of the productive forces. It then has three main sections. The first traces the concept to Xi Jinping's formulations on productive forces after 2012. The second places it within the new development philosophy, the new development stage and the new development pattern. The third links it to the modern economic system, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Gu identifies two 'theoretical cornerstones' in Xi's statements of 2014: 'unleashing and stimulating to the greatest extent the enormous potential of science and technology as the primary productive force', and achieving an 'overall leap' in the level of China's social productive forces. In Gu's account, the first deepens the thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force, and the second expresses a shift from quantitative growth to qualitative change. Gu argues that the five elements of the new development philosophy (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) give the new productive forces their basic features. The new development stage and pattern, Gu says, describe a partial qualitative change under way within rapid quantitative growth. Gu holds that the modern economic system and high-quality development require qualitative improvement in the productive forces themselves, and that the new productive forces are their precondition and driving force. Gu adds that the 2035 goals set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022) are tied to this development. In Gu's account, change is visible in the three elements of the labour process: labourers, means of labour and objects of labour. Examples include digitally skilled workers, artificial intelligence and automated equipment, new materials and energy, and data as a new production factor. Gu concludes that the sequence of concepts since 2012 runs from the new normal in the economy and supply-side structural reform to the new development philosophy, pattern and stage, the modern economic system, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. In Gu's reading, this sequence both describes the practice of the new era and constitutes theoretical innovation in China's autonomous knowledge system of economics. The concept of new quality productive forces integrates the two and shows 'Chinese wisdom and Chinese strength'. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Party-line economist places the concept within the sequence of Xi-era economic concepts and Marxist classics.

Several issues in the study of China's fine traditional culture that call for deeper reflection 中华优秀传统文化研究中需再深化思考的若干问题 Mei Rongzheng Since the Two Integrations were put forward, Chinese scholars have produced a wave of work on China's fine traditional culture, and Mei Rongzheng notes that disagreements have accompanied it. This 2024 article offers the author's own views on three contested areas: how the concept is defined, how the good is to be separated from the bad in ancient culture, and how traditional culture can be given 'creative transformation and innovative development'. Mei argues that all three need sharper Marxist methodology. The article has three parts. The first sets out five 'is and is not' propositions on the concept of fine traditional culture. The second addresses scholars who reject using ancient culture, arguing for scientific discrimination between dross and essence, and draws on the experience of the Communist Party and Mao Zedong's method of analysis. The third turns to creative transformation and innovative development (the 'two creations') and proposes a method for achieving them. On the concept, Mei holds that fine traditional culture is narrower than 'ancient Chinese culture'. It is the part with scientific, democratic, revolutionary and popular qualities, and it is a vast, integrative and historical concept. Mei rejects both historical nihilism and reactionary restorationism, such as the idea of 'Confucianising' China or the Party. On discrimination, Mei says the Party has used the people's standpoint and the practical standard of the new cultural mission, together with Mao's distinctions between slave-era, feudal-era and feudalist culture and between thinkers and the later accretions attached to them. On the 'two creations', Mei says they apply to fine traditional culture as much as to ancient culture generally, because grafting a non-Marxist heritage onto Marxism would produce eclecticism. Mei proposes Marx's method of scientific abstraction, which moves from the sensuous concrete to rational abstraction and back to the rational concrete. In this reading, Confucian concepts are stripped of their feudal social basis and then filled with the content of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Mei concludes that scientific abstraction is the effective route to the 'two creations', and that it should be combined with other methods, including the logical-historical method, critical inheritance and class analysis. Mei adds that applying it to traditional culture is a new task needing careful study and not simplification. Read the original if you want a detailed Marxist-methodological account, from a Wuhan University Marxist theorist, of how Chinese scholars debate the Second Integration of Marxism with traditional culture.

Integrating the "Two Establishes" into the soul and turning them into action 把“两个确立”融入灵魂化为行动 Qu Qingshan This piece, published in the discipline-inspection newspaper in October 2024, is a review and study guide for a training textbook, Deeply Grasping the Decisive Significance of the "Two Establishes". The book is one of the sixth batch of national cadre training textbooks. Qu Qingshan argues that it explains systematically how to understand the Two Establishes and helps Party members and cadres turn this political consensus into practical action in support of the Two Upholds. Qu first summarises the book's account of the Two Establishes through three logics: theoretical, historical and practical. He then lists four features of the book: political character, intellectual depth, practical guidance and readability. The last part draws on the book's fourth chapter and conclusion to set out what cadres should do in practice. Qu reports that the book treats the Two Establishes as a basic political principle of Marxist parties, drawing on historical materialism and Marxist party-building doctrine. It presents them as the distilled core of the Party's century of experience, in which the Party's cause advanced when the authority of the Central Committee and a guiding theory were upheld, and suffered when they weakened. It also presents them as the most important political outcome of the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Qu praises the book for tying these claims to the Party's current tasks and for using plain language, illustrations and QR-code links to reach cadres. Qu concludes that, amid what he calls great changes unseen in a century, cadres should study the book in order to take their practical lessons. He calls for reinforcing ideals and convictions through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and for improving political capacity so that the Two Upholds are carried out. He also calls for a stronger fighting spirit, broad unity, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including sustained anti-corruption work. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian presents the Two Establishes in official cadre-education literature, and how the textbook is promoted to its audience.

Grasping the "Second Integration" by systematising and theorising Xi Jinping's thought on culture 以体系化学理化为着力点深刻把握“第二个结合” Wang Weiguang Wang Weiguang, writing in the People's Daily in October 2024, asks how students of Xi Jinping's thought on culture can best grasp its central innovation, the "Second Integration": combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. Wang argues that this should be done by treating the thought as a systematic, logically tight theoretical system and by handling three relationships correctly: upholding fundamental principles and innovating, the "soul-line" and the "root-line", and "substance" and "application".
