The commentary opens by presenting the Second Integration as the necessary path for upholding and developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics. It then has three main sections, each taking one of the three relationships. A short closing passage returns to the practical side of the thought, in which Wang says theory and implementation are linked. In the first section Wang claims that the Second Integration enriches Marxist cultural theory, meets a requirement of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and is internally required for cultural flourishing. The core argument concerns the three relationships. Upholding fundamental principles is the premise and innovation the driving force. Wang holds that the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity must be kept, while Marxism is used to revitalise living elements of tradition and give them new meaning. Marxism is the "soul-line" and traditional culture the "root-line", and neither may be abandoned. Marxism is the standard for separating the essence of tradition from its dross, and Wang presents this as the way to resolve the old dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, and so consolidate cultural subjectivity. Finally, Wang says the thought joins "substance" (epistemology, what the Second Integration is) with "application" (methodology, how to carry it out), which Wang describes as a clear blueprint for building a country strong in socialist culture. Wang concludes that deepening the Second Integration on the new journey requires being guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture and combining learning with thinking, application and action. The aim, in Wang's account, is a better fit between Marxism's basic principles and traditional culture and a new phase in propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official line presents the Second Integration and the logic linking it to cultural subjectivity, in the words of a senior scholar writing in the Party's main newspaper.

Methods for interpreting the further comprehensively deepening of reform 进一步全面深化改革的阐释方法 Chen Jinlong Chen Jinlong asks how the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) narrates and explains the task of further comprehensively deepening reform, and which interpretive methods its Decision uses. The article argues that the Decision builds its account on four bases: the achievements and experience of reform, a problem-oriented stance, the theme of Chinese modernization, and dialectical and historical materialism. Together, Chen says, these give the reform agenda historical, practical and philosophical support and strengthen its explanatory and persuasive force. The article has four main sections, one for each method. It first traces reform from partial reform to comprehensive deepening and reads the Decision against that history. It then links the Decision's fourteen task areas to the "three confrontations": a complex international and domestic situation, a new round of technological and industrial revolution, and the people's new expectations. A third section follows the idea of modernization from the Four Modernizations of the 1950s and 1960s to the present. The last section examines the philosophical content of the document. Chen holds that the "six adherences" distilled from reform experience (the Party's overall leadership, a people-centred approach, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, institution-building as the main thread, law-based governance, and systems thinking) are both principles and methods. In Chen's reading, the Decision's specific institutional proposals, from data property rights to AI safety supervision, put these principles into practice. The article presents the relation between reform and Chinese modernization as reciprocal: reform supplies momentum and institutional guarantees, while modernization determines reform's content. It finds dialectics in the handling of paired relations such as government and market or efficiency and fairness, and in the formula of "establishing before breaking". It also finds historical materialism in the stress on economic reform as the lead, on the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and on the people as the main force of history. Chen concludes that the Plenum's method of interpretation has wider methodological value. Explaining a present problem should start from history and experience, keep a clear problem orientation, state its goals, and rest on dialectical and historical materialism. The article is a supportive reading of an official document, not a critical assessment. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the Third Plenum's Decision is framed and justified, and of how its official narrative logic is explained.

Deng Xiaoping: a model of seeking truth from facts 邓小平：实事求是的典范 Yang Chungui Written for the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, this article argues that seeking truth from facts (shishi qiushi) is the thread running through Deng's two great historical contributions. Yang Chungui identifies these as leading the Party's assessment of its history and of Mao Zedong's place and Mao Zedong Thought, and creating Deng Xiaoping Theory and opening the path of building socialism with Chinese characteristics through reform and opening up. Yang holds that revisiting Deng's scientific attitude, creative spirit and courage is of major practical relevance for the new journey. The article is organised in six parts. It covers Deng's role in re-establishing the ideological line after 1976, his guidance of the 1981 Resolution on Party history, and his grounding of socialism with Chinese characteristics in national conditions. It then treats his stress on practice and the masses in reform and opening up, his insistence on dialectics and on "grasping with both hands", and his preference for practical results over formalism. Yang draws throughout on Deng's speeches from 1977 to the 1992 southern tour. Yang first presents Deng as the first leading figure to oppose the "Two Whatevers" before his return to work, and as a supporter of the discussion on practice as the sole criterion of truth. The same principle, Yang argues, shaped the Resolution's verdict that Mao's merits were primary and his errors secondary, and its rejection of both wholesale repudiation and dogmatic worship. Yang then argues that Deng rejected a fixed Soviet-style model and derived policy from the primary stage of socialism. On reform, Deng is shown relying on practice and popular initiative: the "three benefits" test replaced abstract arguments over whether something was capitalist or socialist, and rural reforms are credited to peasants and grassroots innovation. Yang adds that Deng's method combined "two-point" dialectical thinking with practical, anti-formalist habits, citing his criticism of excessive meetings and long speeches in 1992. Yang concludes that Deng regarded seeking truth from facts as the basis of Marxism and the key to past and future success. The article calls on readers to study this quality and to uphold emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times and being pragmatic in advancing Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how Deng's key sayings and speeches are used to frame his legacy and the 1981 Resolution.

Firm cultural confidence and the new mission of social science workers in the new era 坚定文化自信与社会科学工作者的时代新命 Gao Dongxin Gao Dongxin, writing in China Social Sciences Today, takes up Xi Jinping's 2016 statement that confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rests on cultural confidence. The commentary argues that eight years of practice show this judgment has enriched the theory of socialist culture, laid a scholarly foundation for Xi Jinping's thought on culture, and given momentum to Chinese modernization. Its answer to what social scientists should now do is that they must take on the task of strengthening cultural confidence. The piece is organised in four parts. It first explains why firm cultural confidence matters in historical, practical and material terms. It then sets out what cultural confidence means, along horizontal and vertical dimensions. The third part builds its theoretical foundation on the "five outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilisation and on traditional humanistic values. The last part lists five duties for social science workers. Gao argues that cultural confidence helps the nation recover from the cultural inferiority of the modern period and break with "Western-centrism". In Gao's account it is also an inner force for renewing tradition, and a defence against the "erosion" of Western culture and values. At its core is confidence in core values. Gao draws on Xi's formulation of the five characteristics: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Gao holds that Chinese culture has repeatedly absorbed foreign influences without losing its roots, and that ideas such as harmony between humanity and nature, benevolence, and valuing righteousness over profit can help address global problems. For social scientists, Gao proposes five tasks: hold to a firm political direction guided by Marxism; strengthen theoretical consciousness and problem orientation; lead with innovation, following the Two Integrations; adopt a people-centred stance; and tell China's story well as interpreters and communicators of excellent traditional culture. Gao presents these as obligations flowing from Xi's directives. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a local Party-affiliated academy head restates official cultural-confidence discourse and the duties it assigns to social scientists.

Building an independent knowledge system of Chinese philosophy and social sciences through adhering to the Two Integrations 在坚持“两个结合”中构建中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系 Zhang Zhengwen Writing in the People's Daily in October 2024, Zhang Zhengwen takes up the call in the Third Plenum Decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to build an independent knowledge system of Chinese philosophy and social sciences. Zhang argues that adhering to the Two Integrations (combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) provides the methodological guidance and the fundamental route for this task. The commentary has three parts. The first explains why the Two Integrations are the fundamental route, the second identifies where to apply effort, and the third lists the supports needed. It draws throughout on statements by Xi Jinping and on the Party's century-long record of theoretical innovation. Zhang reads the two integrations as two anchors. Integration with concrete realities supplies the logical starting point: knowledge should be drawn from the practice of reform and development and answer China's problems. Integration with traditional culture is described as keeping the "soul" and the "root". Marxism, above all Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is the soul; the scholarly traditions from pre-Qin philosophers to Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism are the root. The author then names three practical levers: the discipline system (including support for fields such as oracle-bone studies and Dunhuang studies), the academic system, and the discourse system. On discourse, Zhang calls for popularising academic language, internationalising Chinese discourse and shedding reliance on Western discourse. Zhang concludes that the knowledge system must unite the three systems and be consolidated in textbook development, which is to be treated as a matter of state authority and political direction. It is described as a systemic project requiring stronger Party leadership, ideological platforms, integration of Marxist, traditional and useful foreign resources, and cultivation of talent and cross-disciplinary work. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official line links the Two Integrations to disciplinary, academic and discourse construction and to textbook policy.

The evolutionary logic, value implications and basic principles of comprehensively deepening reform in the new era 新时代全面深化改革的演进逻辑、价值意蕴及基本原则 Chen Mingfan Xiao Yao Written in the wake of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this article asks why comprehensively deepening reform should be given greater prominence and how it should be pursued around Chinese modernization. Chen Mingfan and Xiao Yao argue that reform in the new era is a continuation of the reform agenda set at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and a new chapter in advancing Chinese modernization. They present reform as a "key move" and an important instrument for that project. The article has three parts. The first traces the evolutionary logic of reform through theoretical inheritance (Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping), historical change from the modern period to reform and opening up, and shifting tasks. The second sets out four value implications. The third lists six basic principles for further deepening reform. On evolutionary logic, the authors claim that theoretical, historical and practical logic are unified. They stress the shift in the principal contradiction of Chinese society, the theme of Chinese modernization, and the overall goal of improving socialist institutions and modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. On value, they argue that reform has deepened the Party's reform record, hardened its resilience (citing growth figures and China's contribution to the world economy), extended the range of socialist reform for countries such as Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and the DPRK, and raised the effectiveness of reform for human civilization. In this last point they say reform undermines the pattern of the East's subordination to the West and encourages late-developing countries to choose their own paths. The six principles are: upholding the Party's overall leadership; putting the people first; staying true to fundamental principles while innovating; making institution-building the main thread; ruling the country by law in all respects; and applying systems thinking. The authors conclude that reform must be planned as a whole and advanced with a strong sense of historical initiative. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-scholar exposition of how the Third Plenum's reform agenda is justified historically, theoretically and internationally.”

Understanding the contributions of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era at the level of principle 深刻理解习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的原理性贡献 Li Haiqing Li Haiqing asks in what sense Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era can be said to have made "principle-level" (yuanlixing) contributions to Marxism. The article's answer is that the Thought has enriched Marxism's basic principles at the more specific levels of its hierarchy of principles. It does so by deepening knowledge of three laws: those governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. The article has three parts. The first sets out what counts as a basic principle of Marxism and argues that principles are layered, using historical materialism and its sub-principles as the example. The second defines what a principle-level contribution is, separates it from policy or method innovation and from mere originality, and gives three criteria. The third identifies eight areas of contribution. Li argues that principle-level contributions concern understanding the world, not policies and methods for changing it. Such contributions take three forms: extending principles Marxism has already developed, filling gaps the classics left, and making breakthroughs where a classical principle clashes with Chinese reality. The three criteria are a deeper account of the laws, broad guiding significance beyond China, and a key place within the Thought itself. Applying them, Li lists the following contributions. They are new quality productive forces and ecological productive forces; the socialist market economy as a basic economic system; whole-process people's democracy; the modernization of state governance; treating security as intrinsic to development; a community with a shared future for mankind; the Party's self-reform; and the claim that Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For Li, the market-economy case is a "subversive" innovation relative to the classical expectation of a product economy. Li presents the governance, security and self-reform theories as pioneering ones that fill gaps the classical authors left. Li concludes that the Thought, shaped by new historical conditions and practical demands, has made specific and profound principle-level innovations. In this account these are pioneering, comprehensive and historic contributions to Marxism in contemporary China and the twenty-first century, opening a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar defines and classifies the theoretical contributions of Xi Jinping Thought and what criteria the author proposes for judging them.

An important meeting for further comprehensively deepening reform 进一步全面深化改革的重要会议 Li Zhenghua This commentary interprets the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, held on 15–18 July 2024. Li Zhenghua argues that the meeting was a very important gathering held at a critical period for advancing national strength and rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. In Li's account, the plenum scientifically summarised experience since reform and opening up, continued the practice begun at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), and opened a new chapter of further comprehensively deepening reform. The article has three sections. The first presents the plenum as a summary of reform-era experience, citing the ten third plenums held in 46 years and economic figures such as average growth of 9.9% in 1979–2012 and GDP rising from 53.9 trillion yuan in 2012 to 126.1 trillion in 2023. The second treats it as the practical sequel to the 2013 plenum, and the third sets out the new content of the plenum's Decision, including its targets, priorities and 300-plus reform measures. Li's central claim is that reform has to be planned around the Party's central task, and that the Decision does this by linking reform to Chinese modernization and the goal of basically realising socialist modernization by 2035. Li lists six principles drawn from experience: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, institution-building as the main thread, law-based governance and a systems approach. Li also stresses continuity: the general goal of improving socialist institutions and modernising national governance repeats that of 2013, now with a deadline of 2029 and a stress on a high-standard socialist market economy and the Two Unwaverings. The plenum's "seven focuses" and three "greater emphases" (systemic integration, key priorities, practical results) are presented as the method for this stage. Li concludes that the plenum further clarified the general goal of comprehensively deepening reform and tied reform and opening up to the nation's future, the course of Chinese modernization and individual destinies. Li ranks it as another milestone in the history of reform and opening up, after the Third Plenums of the 11th and 18th Central Committees. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's official-line reading of how the 2024 plenum is positioned within the sequence of reform-era plenums.

Freedom and democracy: a preliminary theoretical construction of the common values of all humanity beyond Western "universal values" 自由与民主：超越西方“普世价值”的全人类共同价值理论建构初探 Lin Xiuneng Lin Xiuneng takes up a problem raised by the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls on all countries to uphold the common values of all humanity, including democracy and freedom. Lin observes that the right to interpret these two values has long been held by a few Western states, which bind them together as the core of their "universal values" discourse and use them to attack China's system. The article argues that freedom and democracy must be rebuilt as common values of all humanity that go beyond Western "universal values" in both content and form. The article has two main parts. The first traces how freedom, democracy and finally "liberal democracy" became Western "universal values", drawing on Constant, Berlin, Schumpeter, Hayek and Fukuyama, and then critiques that discourse. The second builds the alternative: freedom reconstructed around relations, especially relations of production, and democracy reconstructed around the people as its basis. A short conclusion draws these together. Lin contends that Western liberalism creates "universal values" by first emptying concepts of any limits on their application and then filling them with a liberal, individualist and capital-serving content. In Lin's reading, this equates modernization with Westernization and serves capital's global expansion, producing economic dependence and political disorder in countries that copy it. Against this, Lin argues that common values must address problems shared by humanity while respecting different countries' paths, so that they unite the universal and the particular. Freedom is then understood, following Engels, as understanding and consciously ordering relations between people and nature, between people, and within the self. Its limits are set by the framework of relations at each stage of development and can be widened only by collective action that changes those relations. Democracy is understood as a balance between individual and state in which the people, not an aggregate of individuals, are the subject. Lin calls for "solidarity democracy" in place of "adversarial democracy". Lin concludes that freedom and democracy belong to no single civilization or doctrine and that their meaning develops over time. They should not let the individual override the collective but should coordinate the two, and they require respect for the diversity of civilizations and paths to modernization. Lin presents this as a way for China to contest Western discursive dominance. Read the original if you want a Marxist-informed, China-based critique of liberal universalism and an attempt to rework freedom and democracy in terms of production relations and people-centred democracy.

"Attach importance to solving water security problems" Studying Xi Jinping's important statements on water management “重视解决好水安全问题” Liu Zhihui Liu Zhihui sets out to systematise Xi Jinping's statements on water management since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article asks why water work matters in the new era and how it should be done. Liu's answer is that Xi treats water security as a strategic question for the lasting development of the Chinese nation, requiring a change in thinking, large-scale ecological and engineering measures, and a stronger system of flood and drought control. The article is a study of Xi's speeches and instructions, organised in five parts. It begins with the current water-security situation, then covers the policy line on water management and the national "river strategy" for the Yangtze, the Yellow River and major lakes and wetlands. It goes on to the national water network and the South-to-North Water Diversion project, and ends with flood and drought prevention. Liu supports the account with figures on rainfall, shortages, pollution and engineering capacity. Liu's first move is to divide water-security problems into old and new. The old ones are uneven distribution of water in time and space and the resulting disasters. The new ones are water shortage, ecological damage and pollution. Second, Liu presents Xi's approach of "prioritising water conservation, balancing spatial distribution, systematic governance, and applying both the government and market hands". In this reading, population and economic scale must be fitted to water carrying capacity, and water must be managed together with mountains, forests, fields, lakes, grassland and desert. The government sets strict management and taxes, while the market handles water-rights trading. Third, Liu reports Xi's guidance on rivers and engineering. For the Yangtze this is "joint protection, no large-scale development", and for the Yellow River "protection and coordinated governance". The national water network is to be built on lessons from earlier diversion projects. Flood control is to combine structural works with non-structural measures such as responsibility systems, early warning and joint reservoir operation, always putting people's lives first. Liu concludes that Xi's statements capture the regularities of water management and provide fundamental guidance for the new era. The author calls for water resources, ecology, environment and disasters to be handled together, and for the Party to raise its capacity in saving water, allocating it, protecting rivers and lakes, and defending against floods and droughts. Liu presents this as securing water for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history-institute account of how Xi's water policy is framed, with the figures and Xi's own formulations organised by theme.

The distinctive value of the Chronicle of the Communist Party of China (New-Democratic Revolution period) 《中国共产党编年史》（新民主主义革命时期）的独特价值 Qu Qingshan Marking the 75th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic, this commentary introduces the newly published Chronicle of the Communist Party of China (New-Democratic Revolution period), compiled by the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee and issued by the CPC History Publishing House. Qu Qingshan, who heads the Institute, argues that the work is highly significant. In Qu's account it answers new demands on Party history work, enlarges the body of core Party histories, fills a gap in research and serves as an authoritative textbook. The piece is organised around four claims about the Chronicle's value. Qu first recounts its origins: a 2010 Central Committee document called for a chronicle to be compiled, and work was restarted in February 2023 after the Chinese and English editions of The Communist Party of China's Hundred Years were finished. The text then covers the work's structure, the question of historical genres, and the guidance Xi Jinping has given on how to treat Party history. Qu's central argument is that existing core Party histories are all general histories, concise and limited in scale, so they give only the trunk and outline of a great tree and not its branches and leaves. The Chronicle runs to 29 volumes, one per year from 1921 to 1949, with more than nine million characters. According to Qu, it is the richest and largest chronological core history so far, and it covers politics, military affairs, economy, culture, society, foreign relations and Party building. Qu says the compilers broke with the habits of general-history writing. They organised the work by year, month and day, supplemented it with event-based narration, and so created a new method of Party history research. Qu also stresses the word 'zheng' (correct, orthodox) in Xi's remarks on history. The compilers say they applied Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, opposed historical nihilism and relied on the Party's three historical resolutions, so as to produce an orthodox and reliable history. Qu concludes that the Chronicle is an authoritative textbook and basic reader. It is meant to help make Party history study and education a regular, long-term practice, and to help the whole Party and society learn and use Party history. Read the original if you want an official account, from the Institute's head, of why this multi-volume chronicle was compiled and how its compilers describe its method and political guidance.

Key relationships to grasp in strengthening Party discipline in the new era and on the new journey 新时代新征程加强党的纪律建设需要把握的若干关系 Lü Huidong Ding Junping How should the Chinese Communist Party strengthen its discipline in the new era? Lü Huidong and Ding Junping argue that discipline building is the fundamental, root-cause measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and that it works only if five relationships are handled correctly. Drawing on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), they present discipline as a safeguard for the Party's self-reform and for solving the problems unique to a large party. The article is a policy-theoretical essay in five numbered sections, each taking one relationship: Party leadership and discipline building; discipline and the Party's other forms of building; strict discipline and officials' personal freedom; strict discipline and care for Party members and officials; and Party discipline and state law. It relies heavily on Xi Jinping's statements and on Party documents, with a short citation of Mao Zedong on conscious discipline, and it gives a brief historical account of discipline building over more than a century. The authors argue first that Party leadership determines the direction, tasks and methods of discipline building, so discipline must be built under unified central leadership and led by political building, with political discipline as the most important kind. Discipline is tied to ideological, organizational, conduct and institutional building and to the anti-corruption struggle. Second, they hold that members' personal freedom is relative while Party discipline is absolute. They add, citing Mao, that discipline must be conscious, tied to the masses and guided by a correct political line, and that it must not become a tool for retaliation. Third, they treat strictness and care as compatible, citing the 'Four Forms' of supervision and discipline enforcement, the 'three distinctions' and mechanisms that tolerate and correct errors. Fourth, they defend the principle that discipline is stricter than law and comes before it, with discipline and law kept separate. In their account, this ends an older confusion that lowered the standard for members. The authors conclude that the Party, now pushing forward a new great project of Party building, places discipline building in a more prominent position and runs it through the whole of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They present this as the disciplinary guarantee for a stronger, long-governing Marxist party and for the Party's role as the core of leadership. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party scholars frame discipline, internal regulations and the relationship between Party rules and state law in the Xi Jinping era.

Paying more attention to systematic integration to further deepen reform comprehensively 更加注重系统集成 进一步全面深化改革 Wang Aiyun Wang Aiyun examines why the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), in deploying further comprehensive deepening of reform to advance Chinese modernization, calls for "paying more attention to systematic integration". The article argues that the requirement rests on a systems approach developed since 2012 and now acquires richer content through five major relationships that reform must handle. The piece has three parts. It first describes comprehensive deepening of reform as a complex systems project. It then traces how Xi Jinping's statements built up the systems concept as a basic way of thinking and working. Finally it takes up the five relationships named in the Plenum's Decision. Wang draws mainly on Xi's speeches and Party documents from 2012 to 2024, with illustrations from urbanisation, state-owned enterprise reform, ecological governance, and science and technology reform. Wang argues that post-2012 reform differs from earlier reform in being comprehensive. In breadth, it spans every field and both the economic base and the superstructure, so that each measure depends on the others. In depth, it has reached the "deep waters", where interests are intertwined. The author traces the progression from calls for systematic, holistic and coordinated reform (2012–13) to "systematic integration", and notes that Xi in 2020 for the first time called the systems concept a "basic" way of thinking and working. The Decision's sixth principle, upholding the systems concept, names five relationships to be handled: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. For each, Wang holds that the two sides are mutually conditioning, and that neither should be pursued one-sidedly. Wang concludes that handling these five relationships will strengthen the systematic, holistic and coordinated character of reform over the next five years. In this account, it will give Chinese modernization strong momentum and institutional guarantees. The article is an official-line exposition, citing the leadership's statements closely and offering no critical assessment. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source account of how the Party's "systems concept" and the "five relationships" were assembled into the reform guidance of the Third Plenum.

The threefold logic of the development of the supervision system of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 新时代中国特色社会主义监督制度发展演进的三重逻辑 Xiao Ruining Hong Xianghua Supervision of power, and especially self-supervision by a ruling party, is described by Xiao Ruining and Hong Xianghua as a worldwide problem and the 'Goldbach conjecture' of state governance. The article asks how the supervision system of socialism with Chinese characteristics emerged and what marks it out in the new era. Its thesis is that the system, which began in the New Democratic revolution and matured after the 18th Party Congress (2012), can be understood through three dimensions: theory, history and practice. The article has three main sections. The first traces the theory, from Marx and Engels on the Paris Commune and 'public servants', and Lenin on workers' control and the Control Commission and Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate, through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. The second follows the institutions through four stages: germination (1921–49), foundation-laying after 1949, basic formation in the reform era, and maturation since 2012. The third sets out the system's present-day characteristics. The authors argue that the system is an institutional arrangement uniting the 'two answers' to the problem of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. The first answer, attributed to Mao in his exchange with Huang Yanpei, is letting the people supervise the government. The second, put forward by Xi, is the Party's self-reform. In the authors' account the system is led by intra-Party supervision, with four forms (discipline, supervisory commission, dispatched-agency and inspection supervision) coordinated with nine others in a '1+9' pattern. It also serves the Party's overall leadership, the people's principal position, and the unity of rule by Party regulations and rule of law. The authors add that the system draws on traditional Chinese supervisory culture, such as imperial inspection and impeachment, and offers what they call a 'Chinese solution' to problems they attribute to Western separation-of-powers models. They conclude that supervision must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, aimed at modernizing national governance, and rooted in domestic conditions, since copying foreign systems will not work. They also call for better coordination among the different forms of supervision. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how official discourse periodises Chinese supervision institutions, from the 1925 Guangdong supervisory committee to the 2018 supervisory commissions.

Further study of the Marxist thought on power and the supervision of power 进一步深入研究马克思主义权力和权力监督思想 Yan Shuhan Yan Shuhan starts from Xi Jinping's remark that self-supervision is a worldwide problem and "the Goldbach conjecture of state governance". Yan argues that a ruling party can only tackle this problem by returning to the theoretical origins of Marxism and studying the classical writers' thought on power and its supervision. The article claims that this thought is a neglected resource, and that it explains both why supervision is so difficult and how the Chinese Communist Party should now approach it. The article moves from Marx and Engels to Lenin and then to the present. It first sets out two basic points in Marx and Engels: power as a general product of the state, and corruption as a product of private ownership and exploitation. It then turns to the Paris Commune and Engels's 1891 introduction to The Civil War in France. Next it covers Lenin's development of the theme: democratic centralism, party and state supervisory bodies, and the purges and anti-corruption struggle of the early Soviet years. The final section applies these ideas to the Party today. Yan's central move is to read the Commune's two measures, election with recall and workers' wages for officials, as "democratic election" and "equal wages". The aim of both is to stop officials turning from "servants" into "masters". Yan warns against taking them literally. Engels himself, Yan notes, blamed the Commune's fall partly on a lack of centralisation and authority, so recall "at any time" should not be over-stressed. Equal wages, in turn, express equality between leaders and masses as a historical-materialist category, not identical pay. Yan presents Lenin as turning this into democratic centralism, independent control commissions with authority parallel to the Central Committee, and purges that removed large parts of the membership. Yan concludes that supervision of power is a problem unique to a large party, and lists the six "how to always" problems Xi Jinping named. Yan reports reluctance to supervise, fear of supervising superiors, and weak intra-Party supervision. Confidence in solving them rests, in Yan's account, on three things: Marxist Party-building theory, the "second answer" of self-reform to the question of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall, and a Party and state supervision system. Yan stresses that giving the second answer does not mean the task is finished. Read the original if you want a Party-school scholar's account of how classical Marxist texts are used to ground current Party discipline and anti-corruption policy.

Development and innovation in the party diplomacy of socialist countries: experience and lessons 社会主义国家政党外交的发展创新及其经验启示 Yang Xiuwen Chen Haiyan Yang Xiuwen and Chen Haiyan ask how the external activity of ruling parties in socialist states, which they call party diplomacy, has developed over more than a century, and what lessons it offers today. They define it as the external affairs that ruling Marxist parties conduct around their own development and the realisation of their values. They argue that it has moved from a narrow, bloc-bound practice to a plural, institutionalised one, and that this record guides efforts to revive the world socialist movement and build a community with a shared future for mankind. The article opens by building a three-level concept of party diplomacy, from the general, to socialist parties not yet in power, to the specific case of ruling socialist parties. It then follows the history in three phases: the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Comintern; the Cold War period, including the Yugoslav split, the Sino-Soviet dispute and setbacks for the Chinese party in the 1960s and 1970s; and the period since the Soviet collapse. The post-1991 section draws mainly on China, Vietnam, Laos, the DPRK and Cuba, and also covers the São Paulo Forum and the international meetings of communist and workers' parties. In the authors' account, Cold War party diplomacy was narrow and often subordinated to Soviet leadership. Reflection on the resulting conflicts produced the principle of independence and autonomy, which they treat as a basic norm. Since the 1990s, they argue, ruling parties have served central national tasks, built multilevel networks and, in China's case, developed new forms of exchange with other parties. From this history they draw five lessons: keep innovating theory; align "a new type of party relations" with new international relations on the basis of seeking common ground while respecting differences and mutual learning; make methods coordinated, scientific and effective; diversify institutional platforms through specialised bodies and trained personnel; and treat the building of a community with a shared future for mankind as the value orientation. The authors conclude that socialist-state party diplomacy serves both the interests of its own peoples and world peace, development and the progress of civilisations. They present it as rooted in the First International and the October Revolution, and as likely to widen the international space for ruling socialist parties. Read the original if you study the history of communist party relations, the Chinese Communist Party's external work, or how Chinese scholars frame party diplomacy conceptually.

Capitalist civilisation in decline and the new form of human civilisation: an ecological perspective 从生态视角看资本主义文明没落与人类文明新形态构建 Zhang Jian Zhang Jian asks what the ecological crisis reveals about the condition of Western capitalist civilisation, and what is replacing it. The article argues that, from the standpoint of an antagonism between the logic of capital and the logic of life, Western capitalist civilisation has reached its end. In Zhang's account it will be superseded by the new form of human civilisation, represented by China and created through Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first treats neoliberalism's loss of legitimacy through its anti-ecological character, covering the commodification of nature, "green capitalism" and the export of polluting industry. The second turns to the crises of the twenty-first century and to Marx's analysis of capital's self-imposed limits. The third surveys China's ecological civilisation achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), set against Western experience. Zhang draws on Marx, on Xi Jinping's statements, and on Carlos Martinez and John Molyneux. Zhang holds that capital must break through every boundary, while the biosphere and the worker's vitality are finite. Capital is therefore self-devouring, and the article reads Marx's remark that the limit of capital is capital itself as having ecological implications. Zhang rejects blaming consumerism or treating workers as automatic bearers of species interest. In this account the underlying conflict is between capital and life, and solving the climate crisis requires a revolution in ownership of the means of production, led by a Marxist party. Zhang credits China's public ownership, Party leadership and planning with the progress made. The author lists four ways Chinese modernization goes beyond capitalism: balancing equity and efficiency, coordinated development, simultaneous growth and ecological repair, and the Belt and Road Initiative. The article cites figures on forest cover, clean energy and international cooperation. Zhang concludes that capitalism's anti-ecological character is one expression of its sharpening basic contradiction. Economic, social, political and ecological crises are deepening under accelerating technological change. In the article's view, Western capitalist civilisation is at its end while the new form of human civilisation is rising. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links ecological Marxism, critique of neoliberalism and the official narrative of ecological civilisation.

Upholding the principal position of the people in cultural development 坚持文化建设中的人民主体地位 Jiang Shuzhuo Taking its cue from the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform to advance Chinese modernization, this newspaper commentary asks how the people's principal position should be upheld in cultural development. Jiang argues that reform of the cultural system should be guided by the principle of putting the people first, so that it supports the building of a culturally strong country and Chinese modernization. The piece is organised under three headings: guaranteeing cultural rights as part of building a culturally strong country; stimulating the people's sense of agency as the central link; and promoting well-rounded human development as the core task. It draws on examples such as dragon-boat races, the village football league, book fairs, square dancing, short video, drone shows and rural art projects. Jiang contends that China has already built up practice in protecting cultural rights, with the state providing conditions and the public taking part actively. Further institutional reform is needed, for instance for disabled and elderly people in a digital setting. Citing Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, the author holds that popular creativity and the initiative of cultural workers drive innovation, and that science and technology should lead cultural change, including the cultivation of new quality productive forces in culture. Drawing on Marx's remarks on free time and on 'environment shapes people', Jiang adds that public cultural activity and cultural volunteer mechanisms should foster well-rounded development. Jiang concludes that upholding the people's principal position means protecting cultural rights, respecting popular initiative and awakening agency. It also means raising social civility and cultivating 'modern new people' alongside common prosperity, giving spiritual support to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-aligned scholars link cultural policy to the Third Plenum's reform agenda.

Xi Jinping's thought on culture and its original contribution to the Marxist theory of culture 习近平文化思想对马克思主义文化理论的原创性贡献 Gao Ren Gao Ren asks how Xi Jinping's thought on culture has added to the Marxist theory of culture. The article argues that this body of thought, presented as a theoretical summary of the Party's cultural work in the new era, makes an original Chinese contribution. In Gao's account it forms the cultural component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and opens a new stage in Marxist cultural theory. This is a short commentary first published in the Guangming Daily in June 2024. It is organised in three parts. Each part names one dimension of the contribution: the Party's cultural leadership, a strong sense of cultural subjectivity, and a sense of cultural mission. Each is tied to a deeper understanding of, respectively, the principles of Marxist cultural theory, the laws of socialist cultural development, and the paths to building a modern Chinese civilization. In the first part, Gao argues that a rising class must hold cultural leadership to establish its position, so the Party must keep full leadership over propaganda, ideology and the media. Marxism must remain the guiding ideology, and a people-centred orientation must govern creative and research work. The second part credits Xi with proposing cultural confidence as one of the Four-sphere Confidence, with building the core socialist values into the basic policy of upholding socialism, and with the Two Integrations of Marxism with China's realities and with its fine traditional culture. Gao presents these as safeguarding both the "soul" of Marxism and the "roots" of Chinese culture. The third part says that building a modern Chinese civilization requires cultural confidence and an independent path, openness to the achievements of other civilizations, and a balance of upholding fundamental principles with innovation. Gao concludes that Xi's cultural thought is an open, evolving system that will keep developing with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Gao's view it helps create a new culture for the era and promotes the free and all-round development of the human being. Gao adds that building a modern Chinese civilization also contributes to human civilization more broadly. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists present Xi's cultural thought as an advance in Marxist theory.

Deepening reform to inject vitality into building a cultural powerhouse 深化改革为文化强国建设注入活力 Xiao Guiqing This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in September 2024, reads the cultural section of the Decision of the Central Committee on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization (the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee, 2024). Xiao Guiqing argues that the Decision sets out major reforms of cultural institutions and mechanisms for building a socialist cultural powerhouse. In Xiao's account, these reforms provide ideological guarantees, spiritual strength and favourable cultural conditions for national rejuvenation. The commentary is organised under four headings: improving the responsibility system for ideological work; optimising the supply of cultural services and products; strengthening the comprehensive governance of cyberspace; and building a more effective international communication system. Each section paraphrases the Decision's measures and adds the author's explanation of why they are needed. On ideology, Xiao describes ideological work as extremely important to the Party and says that, although the situation has changed fundamentally since the 18th Party Congress (2012), struggle in this field remains sharp. The author calls for the Party to keep firm leadership, management and discourse power, to maintain Marxism's guiding position, to arm Party members with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and to cultivate core socialist values. On culture and the internet, Xiao stresses equal access to public cultural services, putting social benefits first in cultural production, protecting historical heritage, and regarding the internet as the main ideological battleground. This requires the principle of Party management of the internet, law-based governance and a multi-actor governance pattern. On external communication, the author identifies gaps between China's real image and Western perceptions, and between soft and hard power, and calls for Chinese discourse and narrative systems alongside civilizational exchange and mutual learning. Xiao concludes that deepening cultural reform will strengthen the Party's ideological leadership, spiritual prosperity for all the people and China's international voice, presenting a trustworthy, lovable and respectable image of China. The piece is a policy explanation rather than an academic analysis. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the Third Plenum's cultural-reform agenda, including its approach to ideology, internet governance and international communication.

Whole-process people's democracy: opening a new realm of human political civilization 全过程人民民主：开辟人类政治文明新境界 Bao Xinjian Bao Xinjian asks what kind of political civilization the world needs and argues that China's whole-process people's democracy answers the question. In the article's account, Xi Jinping's statements on the subject have raised socialist political civilization to a new level, opened a new realm of human political civilization and created a new form of it. Bao presents this as a response to problems that Western political models have left unresolved. The article is organised in four parts, each describing one orientation of whole-process people's democracy and what it adds to human political civilization. These are: the people as the main body of democracy; institutional guarantees and institutional reform; governance as a mission; and a commitment to the common values of all humanity. Bao draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin on democracy, the state and the Paris Commune. Bao also cites Xi Jinping, the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and recent plenums, and contrasts the approach with American-style democracy. Bao's central claim is that the decisive question in democracy is who its main body is. In Bao's reading, party and interest-group manipulation has turned American democracy into a tool of privileged minorities, causing political polarisation and social division. By contrast, the Communist Party of China is said to represent no special interest, so the people remain the main body. Bao describes a full 'chain' of democratic institutions: electoral democracy through the people's congresses, consultative democracy through the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, and grassroots self-government. Bao says these link election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight. Bao argues that this design joins democracy to governance, turning institutional strengths into governance effectiveness through broad consultation ('matters for everyone are discussed by everyone') and the building of consensus. Bao also traces the idea to the Party's century of struggle for people's democracy and to the inclusiveness of Chinese civilization. Bao concludes that whole-process people's democracy, as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization, is not democracy for a minority or a formality but the most extensive, genuine and effective kind. Bao holds that it offers a Chinese approach to the shared problem of how popular democratic power can drive state governance. It also fits the view of civilizations as diverse, equal and inclusive, set against the 'clash of civilizations' and Western-centrism. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how whole-process people's democracy is framed as a contribution to world political civilization.

Broadening the development path of the rural collective economy Improving the system of rural collective economic organisations 农村集体经济发展路径的拓展 Zheng Youguiv Zheng Youguiv asks how China can consolidate and improve its basic rural operation system and strengthen the rural collective economy. The article draws on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the Law on Rural Collective Economic Organisations, passed in June 2024. Its thesis is that the collective economy has lagged behind household contract farming, and that the remedy lies in a fuller system of collective organisations built on a systems approach. The article has three parts. The first argues that the dual-layer system, with household contracting as its base and a combination of unified and separate operation, requires the collective and household levels to develop together. The second reviews the long evolution of collective organisation, from agricultural producers' cooperatives through the people's communes to household contracting and shareholding reform, to draw out directions and principles. The third sets out concrete measures for improving the organisational system. Zheng holds that the constant is collective ownership of rural land, while the forms of collective economy change with the stage of development. Weakened collective economies, in Zheng's reading, stem from historical conditions such as tax-and-fee reform and the loss of managerial talent, not from household contracting itself. Reforms such as the separation of the three land rights and the "three changes" (resources into shares, funds into stock, farmers into shareholders) show that collective ownership can be innovative. For the organisational system, Zheng proposes making township, village and group levels substantive, with special attention to the neglected group level, and protecting original collectives' assets when administrative units merge. Zheng also urges collectives to move from "boarding someone else's boat" (joining companies or cooperatives) to "building their own boat", and to form leading organisations, as shareholding cooperatives, that work across townships. Zheng concludes that the new law gives collective economies stronger policy and legal support, but that development must follow economic laws and avoid crude administrative pressure. Party leadership should integrate resources through shareholding cooperation, not by command. Read the original if you want a policy-oriented account of how Chinese scholars link the 2024 collective economy law to the history of rural cooperation and to practical organisational design.

Another milestone meeting in the history of China's reform and opening up 我国改革开放史上又一次里程碑式重要会议 Jin Minqing Writing in Qiyi (Banner) in 2024, Jin Minqing asks where the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) stands in the history of reform and opening up. Jin argues that it is a landmark meeting comparable to two earlier plenums, and that it produced a major leap in the history of reform and opening up. The commentary presents the 2024 meeting as the third in a series of historic turning points, each responding to the demands of its own period. The article is organised around the three Third Plenums. It first treats the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), then the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), and then the 2024 meeting. For each, Jin describes the historical situation, the decisions taken and the opening of a new stage. The last section sets out the "leaps" that Jin finds in the 2024 Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. Jin contends that the Party has consistently made major reform decisions suited to each critical period. In 1978, it corrected "Left" errors, shifted the focus to economic construction and launched reform and opening up. In 2013, facing a stage of difficult reforms and entrenched interests, it moved reform from local exploration to systematic integration. For 2024, Jin identifies leaps in several areas. These are content (the "seven focuses"), principles (the "six adherences"), the planning of reform around Chinese modernization, and the main task, which Jin says shifts from liberating productive forces to developing new quality productive forces. Jin concludes that the 2024 plenum, led by Xi Jinping, expresses the Party's resolve to carry reform through to the end. Jin also says it reaffirms the banner to be held and the path to be followed in the new era. The text mainly summarises and interprets the Decision and offers little independent analysis. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how Party scholars place the 2024 plenum alongside the 1978 and 2013 plenums.

Taking institution-building as the main thread in further deepening reform comprehensively 以制度建设为主线挈领进一步全面深化改革 Wang Puqu Wang Puqu takes up a principle in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization: that institution-building should be the main thread (主线) of reform. The article argues that this principle sums up the experience of reform in the new era and guides the next stage. Its aim is to set out the basic theory of institution-building and the regularities it follows in deepening reform. The article has three parts. The first explains what institution-building means for reform. The second sets out its guiding functions. The third proposes practical paths for implementation. Wang draws on historical materialism, on statements by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, on the Plenum decision, and on economic, political, sociological and cultural accounts of what institutions do. In the first part, Wang defines institution-building as the process by which a state regulates behaviour through rules, thereby building its governance system and capacity. Wang presents it as driven by the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, as an adjustment of interests and of the relations between power and rights, and as supply-side structural reform of institutions. It combines top-level design with grassroots experience, and Wang describes it as a dynamic, long-term process. The second part credits institution-building with a series of functions: realising the Two Integrations, freeing productive forces, adjusting interests, resolving the paradox of reforming institutions through legal procedure, carrying core socialist values, and guarding against major risks. The third part sets out implementation: strengthening Party leadership, putting the people at the centre, keeping to the central task of Chinese modernization, and taking economic reform as the lead. It adds rule-of-law methods, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, 'establishing before breaking', and a problem-oriented approach that integrates systems and evaluates results. Wang concludes that the sequence runs from institution-building to deeper reform, then to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that this is the Party's roadmap for the new journey. Institutions should be judged by whether they suit national conditions, work effectively and win popular support, and by their conversion into governance effectiveness. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese political scientists frame institution-building as the logic of the 2024 reform agenda.

Improving the institutions and mechanisms for integrated urban–rural development: forming a new pattern 完善城乡融合发展体制机制：形成城乡融合发展新格局 Shangguan Zijian This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in October 2024, takes up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to improve the institutions and mechanisms for integrated urban–rural development. Shangguan argues that handling urban–rural relations well is a necessary requirement of Chinese modernization and that a new pattern of integration should be formed to narrow urban–rural differences. The article opens with Xi Jinping's and Marx's remarks on urban–rural relations, then reviews the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It next explains why improvement is needed, and ends with practical measures. Shangguan reports that the urban–rural income ratio fell from 2.81:1 in 2013 to 2.39:1 in 2023, after poverty alleviation and rural revitalization. The author nonetheless stresses that agriculture's foundation is still unstable and that gaps persist, which the article treats as a concentrated expression of the principal contradiction in society. Improvement is justified on three grounds: it fills agriculture's weak points and builds a strong agricultural country; it releases the demand of a huge market and supports high-quality development; and it meets the people's aspirations and promotes common prosperity. For practice, Shangguan proposes integrated provision of public services at county level and registering household residence where people live so that migrants share local social insurance, housing and schooling rights. The author also proposes strengthening county-level industries that enrich residents and encouraging talent, land, capital, industry and information to flow into the countryside. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of the policy rationale and measures for urban–rural integration after the Third Plenum.

The system of people's congresses as a great creation in the history of China's political development 人民代表大会制度是中国政治发展史上的伟大创造 Zhang Yuan Zhang Yuan, an associate professor at the Central Party School, argues that the system of people's congresses is not only a great creation in China's political history but also in the history of human political institutions. Written after Xi Jinping's speech marking the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress (NPC), the article presents the system as China's fundamental political system and as the main institutional vehicle of whole-process people's democracy. Its claim is that the system suits Chinese conditions, secures popular sovereignty and offers an alternative to Western democratic models. The article has four sections. The first traces the system's growth from the workers' and peasants' bodies of the 1920s through the Jinggangshan congresses, the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia border-region councils and the liberated-area representative conferences, to the 1953 elections and the 1954 Constitution. The second turns to popular sovereignty, elections and grassroots participation. The third examines governance capacity. The fourth considers the system's wider significance for democratic politics. Zhang's core argument is that the system integrates Party leadership, the people being masters of the country and law-based governance. Because administrative, supervisory, judicial and procuratorial organs are all created by, and answerable to, the people's congresses, and because democratic centralism governs state power, the author says the state acts coherently and avoids the mutual obstruction attributed to the separation of powers in some Western countries. The article credits the system with electoral safeguards (state-funded elections, said to prevent 'money politics'), with 45 grassroots legislative liaison points set up by the NPC Standing Committee, and with coordinating policies such as drug-price reform. Zhang also contrasts whole-process people's democracy, which spans decisions before, during and after, with Western 'electoral democracy', which the author describes as granting formal rights and little real power. Zhang concludes that democracy must be concrete and rooted in national history, and that the system offers a reference for other countries seeking models suited to their own conditions. It is judged, in the author's words, by objective national conditions, practical results and the people's own sense of it. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's official-line account of the people's congress system's origins, claimed advantages and its comparison with Western democracy.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground: the core logic and practical guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture 守正创新：习近平文化思想的核心逻辑与实践遵循 Cao Jinsong Writing in Jiangsu Social Sciences (2024, no. 5), Cao Jinsong examines Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and argues that its core logic and practical guide is "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" (shouzheng chuangxin). In Cao's account, this method expresses the inner logic that cultural and ideological work must follow. It is also the foundation for building a modern Chinese civilization and creating a new form of human civilization through Chinese modernization. The article has four main sections. The first unpacks the meaning of the concept from three angles: individual consciousness, creative practice, and the dialectic of historical development. The second argues that the guiding value of "upholding principles" should keep enriching theoretical innovation, through truth, practice, the people and core values. The third turns to culture-centred development, grouped under four formulas: using culture to educate people, benefit the people, nourish cities and boost industry. The fourth sets out four "lineages" to strengthen: the soul, the roots, scholarship and the cultural thread. Cao's central move is to read the formula through Xi Jinping's statement that upholding principles means safeguarding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, the Two Integrations, and the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. Innovation means new ideas, discourse, mechanisms and forms. Cao holds that the two are internally unified: upholding principles serves better innovation, and innovation serves firmer adherence. Cao then reads the thought as uniting truth with value, so that Marxist principles are joined with the value of excellent traditional culture. Cao's practical proposals include arming minds with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, protecting cultural heritage, building a philosophy and social science system with Chinese characteristics, and pursuing the national cultural digitalization strategy. The conclusion calls for more scholarly interpretation of the thought's system, closer study of its internal logic, and summing up its practical experience. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory exposition of how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture frames its method and its links to cities, public services, the humanistic economy and digital culture.

A pioneer of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy A study of Chen Xianda's philosophical thought 当代中国马克思主义哲学研究的开拓者 Hao Lixin Written shortly after the death of the Marxist philosopher and educator Chen Xianda (1930–2024) on 10 October 2024, this commemorative appraisal presents Chen as a pioneer and leading figure of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy. Hao Lixin argues that Chen's work combined philosophical depth with practical concern, and that he carried on Marxism's practical character and critical spirit under the maxim that "philosophers are not onlookers of society". The article opens with a biographical summary of Chen's posts, honours, textbooks and collected works, then proceeds through four thematic sections. These cover Chen's insistence on practice and engagement with reality, his research on the history of Marxist thought, his problem-oriented approach to Marxism and Chinese traditional culture, and his philosophical essays written for general readers. Hao's central claims are as follows. On the history of Marxist philosophy, Hao credits Chen with pioneering systematic studies, including The History of Marx and Engels's Thought, Studies on Marx's Early Thought and Towards the Depths of History. Chen's method, in Hao's account, joins history with logic, treats Marxism as an integrated whole, and rejects attempts to set the "young Marx" against mature Marxism, so as to avoid dogmatism. On culture, Hao reports that Chen saw adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and modernising traditional culture as two sides of one process. Chen used the phrase "an old country with a new mission" to argue that Marxism and traditional culture must not be treated as opposites, and he grounded cultural confidence in traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture alike. Hao also stresses Chen's opposition to historical nihilism and to cultural conservatism. Hao concludes that Chen was a model for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and for popularising it. Chen did this through essay collections such as Strolling and Musing, in which he explained abstract principles in everyday language, and through a conviction that Marxist teaching is both a profession and a belief. Hao ends with the line that the philosopher has died but his thought endures. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic assessment of Chen Xianda's career and of the methodological principles that shaped a generation of Chinese Marxist philosophy, historical materialism and the debate on Marxism and traditional culture.)

A historical-materialist critique of the capitalization of games 唯物史观对游戏资本化的批判 Liu Yuzhou Liu Yuzhou takes up the question of how games should be studied and criticised in the age of digital capitalism. The article, a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that the cultural-sociological tradition of Huizinga and Schiller, and even the Situationists' romantic view of play, treat games as a cultural phenomenon and so miss the capitalist relations of production behind them. Liu likewise rejects explanations of internet addiction that blame games themselves, and calls for a turn from cultural sociology to a critique of the capitalization of games. The piece has two parts. The first uses historical materialism to trace how game capitalization arose, dividing the modern history of games into four overlapping eras: the stand-alone era, the rent era, the consumption era and the present era of game capitalism. The second turns to political economy and names three categories of critique: the absorption of social capital, the invisible exploitation carried out through artificial intelligence, and the reproduction of bourgeois ideology. In Liu's account, each era brings the player into a closer relation with capital. Stand-alone games such as the FC console resemble simple commodity circulation, ending once money changes hands. In the rent era, players buy time cards, which Liu likens to Marx's ground rent, with the player acting as both tenant farmer and labourer. In the consumption era, nominally free games rest on what Liu calls an illusion, because makers manufacture false needs that players then pay to meet. Liu holds that capital is thereby absorbing the sphere of reproduction into production. Liu then argues that game events harvest players' social networks through sharing and vote-gathering, that AI-controlled opponents covertly gather data which can be monetised, and that game worlds such as Minecraft teach players to think only within bourgeois limits. Liu concludes that game capitalization is a historically and practically real concept, and that the game world is not purely virtual, since it derives from reality and acts back on it. Games are becoming a way of life for young people, Liu writes, and it is mistaken to say that games themselves cause addiction; the problem should be understood at the deeper level of capital's logic of self-expansion. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese Marxist scholars apply Marx's concepts, such as simple commodity circulation and ground rent, to video games and digital capitalism.

The self and the subject in the perspective of the materialist conception of history 唯物史观视域中的自我与主体 Sun Lin Sun Lin takes up a problem that idealist philosophy could never settle: how the self and the subject can be internally consistent. The article, a newspaper-length piece in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (August 2024), argues that only Marx, through the materialist conception of history, unified the two on real ground, both historically and logically. The text first traces the idealist path to this unity through four thinkers: Descartes, Kant, Fichte and Hegel. It then turns to Marx's critique, which Sun presents as inseparable from his critique of the modernity of capital. The article ends with the materialist account of the real subject's self-activity. In Sun's reading, each idealist step achieves only a partial or illusory unity. Descartes resolves the mind–body problem by appeal to a spiritual substance, which splits self from subject. Kant separates self-consciousness from free will, placing them at the poles of theory and practice. Fichte unites them through the self's action but cannot explain concrete, varied reality. Hegel gives the unity a social and historical form through the externalisation and retrieval of self-consciousness, but makes it "absolute", which for Sun turns the unity into illusion. Sun's central move is to argue that Hegel's logic of objectification mirrors the logic of capital under private ownership, which externalises itself to capture profit and surplus value and then returns to itself as expanded capital. Hegel's consistency of self and subject is therefore, in this account, a false unity grounded in fetishism, in which relations between people become relations between things. The materialist conception of history instead raises the speculative subject to a real subject whose self-activity achieves a historically conditioned consistency. Sun calls for overcoming fetishism by raising productive forces and labour capacity, and moving towards a society of the free and all-round development of every individual. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese Marxist reading of the Descartes–Kant–Fichte–Hegel sequence on selfhood and subjectivity, and its link to the critique of capital.

Cultivating the real-economy soil for Chinese modernization 厚植中国式现代化的实体经济沃土 Xia Jiechang Xia Jiechang asks why the real economy matters for Chinese modernization and how it should be strengthened. Writing in the Economic Daily in October 2024, Xia argues that a strong real economy is the material and technological foundation of Chinese modernization and of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Xia holds that the sector must be made solid, strong and excellent, and that this is the basis for high-quality development. The piece is built in three parts. It first sets out the real economy's position, drawing on Xi Jinping's statements from 2020 to 2023, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the Third Plenum decision of 2024. It then applies the new development philosophy (innovation, coordination, green, openness, sharing) to the real economy. It ends with four practical areas of work: modern agriculture, new industrialization, a new services system, and institutional support. Xia's core move is to treat each element of the new development philosophy as a feature of high-quality real-economy development. Innovation is the first driving force, resting on technology, institutional reform and talent. Coordination means the real economy and the virtual economy exist side by side, but the virtual economy must serve the real one, and manufacturing, agriculture and producer services must advance together. Green growth is an inherent requirement, openness is the necessary path, and sharing is the fundamental aim, tied to employment and common prosperity. In the policy section, Xia calls for a broad view of agriculture, better rural infrastructure and digital agriculture. Xia also calls for stronger indigenous innovation and supply-chain resilience, and deeper integration of the real and digital economies. Further proposals are to merge manufacturing and services and to integrate urban and rural development. Xia concludes that finance should serve the real economy, with tighter supervision of funds circulating idly or drifting away from the real economy. Fiscal policy should become more forceful and efficient to support the real–digital integration, and industrial policy should mainly give direction. Xia notes that the real economy is evolving into a "new real economy" fused with digital technology, and that a matching fiscal framework remains a new research question. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official economic discourse in late 2024 links the real economy, the new development philosophy and Chinese modernization.

Grasping the rich connotations of the new form of human civilization 深刻把握人类文明新形态的丰富内涵 Ma Min Ma Min takes up Xi Jinping's claim that Chinese modernization has created a "new form of human civilization" and asks in what sense it is new. The article argues that the two concepts are internally linked: Chinese modernization supplies the path and method, while the new civilizational form is its direction, goal and essential requirement.
