In Ma's account, the novelty lies in a socialist civilization that transcends Western capitalist modernity while drawing on Chinese tradition. The commentary has three parts. It first places the concept in the history of the idea of "civilization" and the current decline of Western civilization. It then sets out four ways in which the new form is said to surpass capitalist modern civilization. Finally it treats the form's Chinese cultural roots and its world significance. Ma argues that industrial civilization arose with Western capitalism and has a dual character: historically progressive against agrarian society, yet marked by exploitation through wage labour, extreme individualism and colonial expansion. Modernization, in this view, is not the same as Westernization, and the author sees an "East rising, West declining" pattern in the present world. Socialist civilization is said to surpass the West in four relationships: balanced material and spiritual progress, replacing "capital-centred" with "people-centred" development, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful coexistence rather than power politics. Ma also traces its Chinese character to ideas such as renewal, "the people as the foundation of the state", "all under heaven is shared", unity of heaven and humanity, and harmony among nations, and presents it as the outcome of the Two Integrations and of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Ma concludes that this civilization is both Chinese and global, offering a "Chinese approach" and "Chinese wisdom" that reflect common human values. The author concedes that its creation is a long process with many practical and theoretical problems still unresolved, and calls for exploration that is rooted in China while looking to the world. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official concept of a new form of human civilization is tied to Chinese modernization, a critique of Western capitalist modernity and appeals to traditional Chinese thought.

An important innovation in the Marxist theory of productive forces 马克思主义生产力理论的重要创新 Ji Zhengju This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily in June 2024, asks what the concept of new quality productive forces adds to Marxist theory. Ji Zhengju argues that Xi Jinping's call to develop new quality productive forces answers the question of what kind of productive forces the new era needs and how to develop them. In Ji's reading, it is a major theoretical result of Xi Jinping's economic thought and gives the Marxist theory of productive forces new content. The article is organised around five aspects of the Marxist theory of productive forces: its driving force, its principles, its process, its purpose and its laws of development. For each, Ji sets a classical Marxist proposition beside the corresponding feature of new quality productive forces. On the driving force, Ji notes that Marx and Engels stressed the revolutionary role of science and technology, while new quality productive forces are marked by innovation and superior quality, treating science and technology as the primary productive force and innovation as the primary driver. On the process, they are defined by a leap (yuesheng) in labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their combination, which Ji says stresses qualitative change more than "development" does. On the laws of development, Ji holds that productive forces determine relations of production. New quality productive forces therefore require new relations of production, deeper economic and science-and-technology reforms, and the removal of institutional bottlenecks. Ji concludes that each of these points enriches Marxism, and that high-quality development meets the people's growing need for a better life, which Ji presents as a new application of the Marxist view that production serves human free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official case that new quality productive forces develop Marxist theory.

Guiding high-quality development with a new theory of productive forces 以新的生产力理论指导高质量发展 Han Zhenfeng This short newspaper commentary, originally published in Economic Daily, argues that developing new quality productive forces is an inherent requirement of, and a key lever for, high-quality development. Han draws on Xi Jinping's statements that high-quality development needs guidance from a new theory of productive forces, and presents these remarks as an innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces. The piece first links productive forces to Chinese modernization and the 20th Party Congress (2022) report. It then shows how new quality productive forces fit the requirements of high-quality development, and closes with three practical areas: scientific and technological innovation, deepening reform and opening up, and talent. Han starts from the Marxist claim that productive forces are the most active and revolutionary factor and the ultimate determining force in social development. In Han's account, high-quality development is development that embodies the new development philosophy, and new quality productive forces match it in three ways. They are innovation-led, high-tech, high-efficiency and high-quality; they raise total factor productivity and spread digital technology, which supports common prosperity; and they are inherently green and low-carbon. Drawing on historical materialism, Han adds that relations of production must adapt to productive forces, so deeper reform is needed to remove obstacles and form new relations of production suited to them. Han calls for faster breakthroughs in core technologies, especially original and disruptive innovation, applied through China's huge market and complete industrial system. Han also urges higher-level opening up and better mechanisms for cultivating talent, including a climate that encourages innovation and tolerates failure. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary ties new quality productive forces to Marxist theory and to high-quality development.

Letting economic structural reform play its leading role 发挥经济体制改革牵引作用 Han Wenxiu Writing in Qiushi (2024, no. 18), Han Wenxiu interprets the decision adopted at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. Han argues that the decision's emphasis on letting economic structural reform play a leading role (牵引作用) is of major significance, and that deepening economic reform remains the focus of comprehensive reform. The piece is an official commentary on the document rather than an independent research article. The article has three parts. The first explains why economic reform should lead. The second, the longest, goes through the decision's main economic tasks under eight headings: a high-standard socialist market economy, high-quality development, comprehensive innovation, macroeconomic governance, urban-rural integration, high-level opening up, livelihoods, and ecological civilization. The third part sets out how these tasks are to be carried out. Han gives three reasons for economic reform's leading role. It accords with the Marxist principles that the productive forces determine the relations of production and the economic base determines the superstructure, so that economic reform affects the pace of reform elsewhere. It is the basic experience of reform and opening up, from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee onward, centred on the relationship between government and market. And it is required by high-quality development: Han cites per capita GDP rising from 156 US dollars to 12,700 in 2023 against a middle-developed-country average above 20,000, and says China remains a developing country facing unbalanced and inadequate development. The listed tasks include the Two Unwaverings, a unified national market, new quality productive forces, fiscal and tax reform, institutional opening up, and a distribution structure with a large middle. On implementation, Han calls for strengthening Party leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and for assigning clear responsibility for each reform task. Han also calls for stronger supervision, respect for local and popular initiative, and a firm stand against formalism and bureaucratism, with reforms judged by results and public satisfaction. The article closes by urging unity around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, so that reform can drive high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an authoritative official reading of the Third Plenum's economic reform agenda and its stated rationale.

Grasping the "Second Integration" through systematization and theoretical grounding 以体系化学理化为着力点深刻把握“第二个结合” Wang Weiguang This commentary, first published in People's Daily in October 2024, asks how to study Xi Jinping Thought on Culture in depth. Wang Weiguang argues that a key route is to grasp the "Second Integration" (combining Marxism's basic tenets with excellent traditional Chinese culture) in a systematic, theory-based way. In Wang's account, this means handling three relationships correctly: preserving fundamental principles and innovating, the "soul" and "root" lines of culture, and "substance" and "application". The piece opens by presenting Xi Jinping's cultural thought as a complete theoretical system that has developed Marxist cultural theory. It then has three main sections. The first explains why the Second Integration is the necessary path for socialist culture with Chinese characteristics. The second and third take up the relationships above, and a closing section links theory and practice through "substance" and "application". Wang gives three reasons for the Second Integration's importance. It enriches Marxist cultural theory, it is required for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and it is inherent in the flourishing of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics. On method, Wang treats "preserving fundamental principles" as the precondition and innovation as the driving force. Marxism must remain the guiding ideology and the Party must keep its cultural leadership, while traditional ideas are reactivated and given contemporary meaning. Wang's second move uses Xi's image of the Marxist "soul line" and the traditional-culture "root line", which must not be abandoned. Marxism is the standard for separating the essence of tradition from its dross, and Wang says this is how the Second Integration resolves the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, and consolidates the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. Wang's third move reads Xi's thought as unifying epistemology (what the Second Integration is) with methodology (how to carry it out). Wang concludes that advancing the Second Integration requires following Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and uniting study with thought, application and practice. This is meant to deepen the integration of Marxism and traditional culture and open a new phase of work on propaganda, ideology and culture. The piece is a statement of the official interpretation, useful for seeing how the Party's cultural-theory line is framed. Read the original if you want a concise authoritative statement of how the Second Integration is theorised within Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

Studying Deng Xiaoping's educational theory to open a new phase in building a leading education country 学习邓小平教育理论开拓教育强国建设新局面 Huai Jinpeng Writing after Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, Huai Jinpeng asks what Deng's educational theory offers for building a leading education country (jiaoyu qiangguo) today. Huai argues that the theory, formed from Deng's 1977 decision to restore the college entrance examination and his wider handling of education within socialism with Chinese characteristics, is a new development of Marxist educational theory. The task now, Huai says, is to study, inherit and carry it forward. The short commentary takes five themes from Deng's thinking. They are Party leadership and the socialist orientation of schooling, the strategic priority of education, the "Three Orientations", the central role of teachers, and the present-day tasks that follow. Each theme pairs Deng's statements with Xi Jinping's more recent formulations. Huai's central claim is that Deng's positions underpin current policy. Deng held that schools must put a firm political direction first, that all-round moral, intellectual and physical development is the standard for training talent, and that education must "face modernization, the world and the future". Huai presents this last principle as the essence of the theory. Huai links these ideas to Xi's view that who to train, how to train them and for whom is the fundamental question, and to the goal of a leading education country by 2035. Huai also stresses integrated planning of education, science and technology, and talent, and says teachers are the key to training qualified people. Huai concludes that the guiding principle must be Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, together with a firm grasp of the Two Establishes. Huai calls for education to support Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and for a corps of high-calibre, professional teachers. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state education officials link Deng Xiaoping's legacy to current education policy.

The fourfold meaning of Marx and Engels's thought on civilization With implications for developing a new form of human civilization 马克思恩格斯文明思想的四重意蕴 Huang Wenyan Song Youwen Huang Wenyan and Song Youwen ask what Marx and Engels's thought on civilization contains and what it offers for understanding the "new form of human civilization" that Xi Jinping put forward in his speech marking the Party's centenary (2021). They argue that the thought has four layers, which they label practice–civilization, history–civilization, dialectics–civilization and revolution–civilization. These layers build on one another. The authors claim that the thought goes beyond earlier Western theories of civilization and is the theoretical root of the Chinese Communist Party's creation of a new form of human civilization. The article has an introduction, four main sections and a short conclusion. Each section sets out one layer of Marx and Engels's thought. Each then draws practical lessons for China's current efforts to develop the new form of human civilization. The history section sets Marx and Engels against Toynbee, Jaspers and Huntington. In the first two layers, the authors read civilization through historical materialism. Civilization arises from the material production practice of real individuals and has practical and social attributes, with the people as its main agent. Marx and Engels divide civilization forms by economic social formation, from slave-society to feudal, capitalist and communist civilization. In the authors' view, Toynbee, Jaspers and Huntington describe features of civilizations but miss their decisive cause. The third layer treats capitalist civilization as dual, both progressive and barbaric. It then sketches communist civilization, built on social ownership, planned production, distribution according to need, the withering away of the state and free and all-round individual development. The fourth layer holds that the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production makes revolution the basic means of change, and that the proletarian party is the organising force. The authors conclude that the new form of human civilization sublates capitalist modern civilization and unites national and world character. In practice they call for the Two Unwaverings, guidance and regulation of capital so that it serves civilization, continued Party leadership and comprehensive deepening of reform. They also call for the new development philosophy, high-quality development and a people-centred stance. They add that this civilization draws on the ancient Chinese ideal of harmony among nations and can offer other countries a path to diverse modernities. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Chinese theorists derive the concept of a new form of human civilization from Marx and Engels's texts.

The principles and direction of the "Two Integrations" in adapting Marxism to China, seen through Mao Zedong's philosophy 从毛泽东哲学透视马克思主义中国化“两个结合”的原则与走向 Xue Guangzhou Xue Guangzhou asks how the "Two Integrations" (combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture) should be understood, applied and developed, and answers from the standpoint of Mao Zedong's philosophy. The article argues that both integrations must rest on seeking truth from facts, on the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method, and on a critical, selective treatment of tradition. It also maintains that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context points towards a "new Chinese philosophy". The article has three parts. The first clarifies the terms: what counts as "China's concrete realities" and as "fine traditional culture". The second sets out basic principles for each of the two integrations and warns against several tendencies. The third traces the future path of the adaptation of Marxist philosophy. Xue draws on Mao's formulations, Marx and Engels's 1872 preface to the Communist Manifesto, and Xi Jinping's statements on culture. Xue holds that "concrete realities" means above all the principal contradiction of Chinese society at each stage, and that neoliberal economics is detached from them. Xue distinguishes the "quintessence" (jingsui) of traditional culture, a factual judgement about its core, from its "essence" or best elements (jinghua), a value judgement made from the present. Xue proposes "zhong" (the mean, or centrality) as the quintessence, carrying harmony, unity, rectitude and greatness. Following Mao, Xue sets out five principles: take the best and discard the dross, critical inheritance, serving the present, a hundred schools contending, and holding to the Marxist standpoint. Xue warns against treating Marxism and Chinese culture as equal partners in a cultural fusion, against equating revival with a Confucian restoration, and against reading Xi Jinping's thought on culture as merely continuing tradition or an orthodox lineage (daotong). Xue sees a logical sequence: the adaptation of Marxist philosophy, then adapted Marxist philosophy, then Chinese Marxist philosophy, then a new Chinese philosophy. The last would absorb the best of traditional Chinese philosophy and of human thought, while keeping the Marxist soul. Xue credits Mao with pioneering work and says Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era opens a new stage, tied to building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system. Read the original if you want a Marxist-philosophical, Mao-centred account of how the Two Integrations should be applied and what they are said to lead to.

Keeping the tree of theory evergreen 让理论之树常青 Huang Yibing This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 10 September 2024, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth. Huang argues that Deng Xiaoping Theory is an important milestone in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author also holds that it must be studied and applied creatively rather than dogmatically, so that "the tree of theory" stays evergreen. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why Deng Xiaoping Theory is a milestone. The second explains how to study and use it today. The third links it to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to the continuing task of theoretical innovation. Throughout, Huang relies heavily on quotations from Xi, Deng and Mao Zedong. On the first point, Huang says the theory emerged while socialism with Chinese characteristics was being opened up after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It laid the foundation for the Party's system of theory. It addressed the question of what socialism is and how to build it, and it located the essence of socialism in liberating and developing the productive forces, eliminating exploitation and polarization, and reaching common prosperity. On the second point, Huang calls for a complete and accurate grasp of the theory as an interconnected whole, read in its historical context. Huang insists that what guides practice over the long term is its basic principles and the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method, not particular phrases. Emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts are called its essence. Creative application means upholding Deng's major conclusions while adjusting to changing circumstances. Huang presents Xi Jinping Thought as a new leap in adapting Marxism, calling it contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. It builds on Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The author names the Two Integrations as the fundamental path of adaptation and the "six musts" as its method. The commentary calls on Party members to take Chinese modernization as the soil for further innovation and to answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames Deng Xiaoping Theory's place in the Party's theoretical lineage.

Giving full play to higher education as the leading force Building a leading country in education 发挥高等教育龙头引领作用 Hao Ping Writing in the People's Daily on 23 October 2024, Hao Ping, identified as Party Secretary of Peking University, takes up the question of how universities should serve the drive to build a leading country in education. The commentary follows Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference. Hao argues that higher education is the "leading force" of this effort and must be strengthened so that it supports Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised under three headings. The first concerns fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, covering ideological and political education, discipline and talent-training reform, digital and intelligent education, and teacher development. The second concerns raising innovation capacity to serve national strategy and economic and social development. The third concerns deepening comprehensive reform of higher education in order to build world-class universities with Chinese characteristics. Hao's core claim is that universities must combine political orientation with scientific and talent functions. They should teach with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, expand the "大思政课" (broad ideological and political course) model, and adjust disciplines and training to the needs of new quality productive forces. Hao calls on research universities to join the new whole-nation system, link basic research to industry, and build an independent Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge. On reform, Hao stresses upholding the Party's overall leadership over universities, including the president responsibility system under Party committee leadership. Hao also calls for evaluation reform that ends the "five onlys" and puts the results of fostering virtue first, and for higher-level opening up in education. Hao concludes that universities should aim for six strengths: ideological and political guidance, talent competitiveness, scientific and technological support, support for people's wellbeing, social coordination and international influence. The piece reads as a programmatic statement from a university leader on how to implement central policy. Read the original if you want to see how a senior university Party official translates the national education-strengthening agenda into concrete tasks for Chinese universities.

Accelerating the building of a socialist cultural powerhouse 加快建设社会主义文化强国 Liu Tongfang Writing in the People's Daily on 27 September 2024, Liu Tongfang interprets the culture-related part of the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which lists "building a socialist cultural powerhouse" among its seven areas of focus for further deepening reform. Liu argues that accelerating this task and reforming cultural institutions and mechanisms are essential to advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a short newspaper commentary. The article has three parts. The first sets out why a cultural powerhouse matters strategically. The second explains why cultural institutions and mechanisms must be reformed. The third lists practical measures under the guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on culture: ideological leadership, cultural undertakings and industries, cultural flourishing, the people's cultural life, and cultural soft power and international influence. Liu's central claim is that national strength depends on cultural prosperity, citing Xi Jinping's line that without the flourishing of socialist culture there can be no socialist modernization. Chinese modernization, in this account, coordinates material and spiritual civilisation, and culture supports the market economy, high-quality development, people's livelihood and the Party's governing capacity. Reform is said to be necessary for three reasons: to strengthen cultural confidence through the Two Integrations, to foster a reformist and innovative spirit, and to liberate cultural productive forces in the face of market development and information technology. On implementation, Liu calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position in ideology, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era at its core, along with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and a firm grip on ideological leadership. Liu also proposes balancing the ideological and industrial attributes of culture, putting social benefits first, expanding digital and public cultural services (especially in rural areas), and building Chinese discourse and international communication in support of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary presents the cultural agenda of the 2024 Third Plenum and its main policy vocabulary.

Firmly holding the Party's leadership over ideological work and improving the ideological work responsibility system 牢牢掌握党对意识形态工作领导权 完善意识形态工作责任制 Liu Ronggang This commentary, first published in People's Daily on 22 October 2024, argues that ideological work is of extreme importance to the Party, and that the Party must keep leadership, management and discourse power over it firmly in its own hands. Liu Ronggang takes as his starting point the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), whose Decision lists "improving the ideological work responsibility system" as part of reforming cultural institutions and building a socialist cultural power. The piece begins by stressing that ideological work bears on the Party's fate, long-term national stability and national cohesion. Liu says the ideological situation has changed fundamentally since the 18th Party Congress (2012) but remains complex and severe. He then sets out four areas for improvement, each introduced by a short heading. First, Marxism must remain the guiding ideology, which Liu equates in the new era with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Xi's thought on culture. He calls for regular theory study in Party committees and for building an independent Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge. Second, he calls for better mechanisms for cultivating core socialist values, through Party history education, patriotic education, moral and online ethics work, and opposition to money worship, hedonism and historical nihilism. Third, he proposes improved public-opinion guidance and response, including spokesperson systems, risk monitoring and all-media communication. Fourth, he urges open opposition to erroneous views, with Party committees taking political responsibility, managing media outlets closely and distinguishing political questions from academic ones. Liu concludes that, as Chinese modernization advances, there is no room for compromise or retreat in ideological struggle, and that Party committees at every level must bear leadership responsibility. He calls for firm action against statements he describes as maliciously attacking Party leadership or the socialist system, distorting Party and national history or spreading rumours. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how Party ideological responsibility is framed after the 2024 Third Plenum.

Firmly grasping the political, popular and strategic attributes of education 牢牢把握教育的政治属性人民属性战略属性 Zhang Donggang Lin Shangli This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 14 October 2024, interprets Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference. The authors, the Party Secretary and the President of Renmin University of China, argue that the speech reveals three attributes of education: political, popular and strategic. They contend that building a leading country in education requires grasping all three. The piece is organised in four sections. Three sections take each attribute in turn, first explaining its meaning and then setting out what it requires in the new era. A final section turns to practice, with higher education as the "leading force" and Renmin University as the example. On the political attribute, the authors hold that education reflects its social base and ideology, and that in class society it serves the ruling class's will. They say this attribute settles the question of whom to train, how and for whom. It must be turned into a socialist direction of schooling, a role for ideological and political guidance, and the fostering of moral character and cultivation of talent, so that students are loyal to the Party, the country, the people and socialism. On the popular attribute, they stress a people-centred approach, equity and public benefit. This means fuller development of the individual, quality-oriented education, adjusting resources to demographic change, and a national digital education strategy. On the strategic attribute, they present education as the foundation of national rejuvenation. It is forward-looking, foundational and supportive of science, talent and innovation, and should be planned within Chinese modernization. The authors conclude that the "three attributes" are guiding principles for running schools and teaching. For Renmin University they pledge Party leadership, the training of "pillars of rejuvenation and pioneers of a strong nation", and an autonomous Chinese system of philosophy and social science knowledge. Read the original if you want an official university-leadership reading of the National Education Conference and of how Party ideology is tied to education policy.

Giving full play to the leading role of higher education 充分发挥高等教育龙头作用 Qiu Yong Writing in the People's Daily on 9 September 2024, Qiu Yong, Party Secretary of Tsinghua University, argues that higher education is the "leading force" (longtou) in building China into a leading country in education. Drawing on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and on remarks by Xi Jinping, Qiu holds that the Party's and the state's need for scientific knowledge and talent is more urgent than ever. The article is a short commentary setting out what universities should do. Qiu begins with the claim that every strong education country is a strong higher-education country. As evidence, the author cites the rise of Britain, France, Germany and the United States since the 15th century, which is attributed in part to leading education. The article then names four areas where higher education should lead: moral education and ideological and political courses; building world-class universities and disciplines; serving high-quality development; and international influence. On moral education, Qiu calls for a curriculum and textbook system centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, an independent evaluation system for ideological and political course teachers, online ideological education, and the "three-in-one" combination of value shaping, ability building and knowledge transmission. On university building, the author stresses Party leadership, converting the Four-sphere Confidence into confidence in education, and a shift to quality-focused, innovation-led development. On service to the nation, Qiu urges strengthening basic, emerging and interdisciplinary fields, tackling "bottleneck" technologies, expanding the Strong Foundation Plan, and deepening integration of science, education and industry. On internationalisation, Qiu proposes both "bringing in" top talent and international students and "going out" through global education governance, university alliances, cooperation with Belt and Road Initiative countries and overseas campuses. The author also calls for building a China-centred independent knowledge system and telling China's story, contributing to a community with a shared future for mankind. The article ends by calling for the flourishing of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics to drive the wider building of an education powerhouse. Read the original if you want to see how a leading university Party secretary presents official priorities for higher education after the 2024 Third Plenum.

Several issues in the study of China's fine traditional culture that call for deeper reflection 中华优秀传统文化研究中需再深化思考的若干问题 Mei Rongzheng Since Xi Jinping put forward the Two Integrations, Chinese scholarship on "fine traditional Chinese culture" has grown rapidly, but Mei Rongzheng notes that disagreements remain. The article offers the author's own views on three of them, for discussion with colleagues. Mei's thesis is that the concept must be defined precisely, that old culture must be sifted into dross and essence before it is used, and that Marxist scientific abstraction is the proper route to its creative transformation and innovative development. The article has three parts. The first sets out five "is" and "is not" propositions about the concept. The second defends full use of ancient culture against scholars who take a negative view, drawing on Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi. The third turns to method and to the Marxist way of moving from the concrete to the abstract and back again, illustrated with Capital, Mao's reinterpretations of classical phrases and Xi's concepts. Mei argues first that the fine tradition is not the same as all of ancient culture. It is a narrower, integrative, historical set of elements marked by scientific, democratic, revolutionary and popular qualities. Mei rejects both historical nihilism and reactionary revivalism, including calls to "Confucianise" China or the Party. Second, citing Mao, Mei holds that essence and dross often cannot be cleanly separated, so they must be judged by the people's standpoint and the test of practice. Mei lists six distinctions Mao drew, for example between feudal-era culture and feudalism, and between a thinker's ideas and later accretions. Third, Mei rejects the view that fine tradition needs no transformation, since simply grafting non-Marxist material onto Marxism would produce eclecticism. Concepts such as Confucian benevolence should be stripped of their feudal basis and then filled with the content of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Mei concludes that these steps, which the article calls scientific abstraction, give a method for combining Marxism with fine traditional culture and for turning old concepts into those of a modern Chinese civilization. Mei adds that applying the method to traditional culture is a new field with many open problems and must not be oversimplified. Read the original if you want to see how a Marxist scholar tries to justify and discipline the Second Integration, with Mao's methods of analysis and Marx's method of abstraction as the guide.

Scientifically grasping the methods of comprehensively deepening reform 科学把握全面深化改革方式方法 Song Jianxiao Song Jianxiao's commentary, first published in Economic Daily in July 2024, asks how the drive to comprehensively deepen reform should be carried out. It starts from Xi Jinping's remarks at a symposium with entrepreneurs and experts in Jinan in May 2024. There Xi said that deepening reform must centre on Chinese modernization, highlight key points, hold to the right value orientation and attend to method. Song's answer is that reform should rest on three methods: upholding fundamental principles while innovating, stressing systems integration, and ensuring implementation. The piece is organised under three headings that correspond to these methods. The first covers "keeping to the right path and innovating" and links it to Xi's description of this approach as an important way of thinking for the Party's governance in the new era. The second treats systems integration as both a feature and a methodology of reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third deals with making reform measures take effect on the ground. Each section ends in three or four concrete requirements. On the first method, Song argues that keeping to the right path and innovating form a dialectical unity of change and constancy, continuity and development, principle and creativity. Holding to the right path means upholding the Party's leadership, Marxism, socialism with Chinese characteristics and whole-process people's democracy. Innovation means breaking institutional obstacles and escaping path dependence. On the second, Song calls for top-level design that keeps policy orientations consistent and links overall planning with local conditions. Reforms in the market economy, high-quality development and new quality productive forces should be coordinated as a "combination of punches". On the third, Song says reform is hard to implement as well as important, and calls for a "nail-driving spirit", clear priorities, and results that people feel. Reform should be pursued with urgency and also with attention to timing, degree and effect, doing what is within capacity and persevering over the long term. Song concludes that grasping these methods lets reform keep its direction and momentum, with coordination across fields and measures that deliver. Reform is presented as a complex systemic undertaking that needs steady effort and no slackening. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary frames the methodology of reform in the Xi era, in terms of the Party's leadership, dialectics and implementation.

Adhering to reform and innovation to promote the development of new quality productive forces 坚持改革创新推动新质生产力发展 Ding Jinqing This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 17 July 2024, treats the development of new quality productive forces as both a development task and a reform task. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that developing them requires deepening reform comprehensively and forming new types of relations of production suited to them, Ding argues that bottlenecks must be cleared so that these forces supply steady new momentum for high-quality development. The article is organised in three parts. The first concerns deepening reform to release innovative vitality in science and technology. The second concerns building a modern industrial system. The third concerns shaping new relations of production through economic reform and reform of the education, science and technology, and talent systems. On innovation, Ding holds that it is the defining feature of new quality productive forces and covers technology, business models, management and institutions. The author sees weak original innovation, dependence on foreign key technologies and low conversion of results, and calls for a improved new-type whole-nation system, with centralised Party leadership of science and technology work, and for reform of science management, funding and evaluation, together with greater openness in international cooperation. On industry, Ding calls for making industries more intelligent, greener and more integrated, through supply-side structural reform, digital infrastructure, market-based green policy tools and closer linkage among sectors, regions and firms of different sizes. On relations of production, the author applies the principle that productive forces determine relations of production, and proposes a high-standard socialist market economy, a unified national market, and the Two Unwaverings. Ding concludes that talent is the primary resource and that innovation-driven development is in essence talent-driven. The author proposes integrating education, science and technology, and talent strategies, cultivating innovative talent independently, and reforming evaluation and incentive systems to give value to knowledge, technology and data as production factors. Read the original if you want a compact example of how an official Chinese economic newspaper links new quality productive forces to reform of science policy, industrial upgrading and market institutions.

Promoting further comprehensively deepening reform in the spirit of self-reform 以自我革命精神推动进一步全面深化改革 Gao Liwei Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Gao Liwei takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its blueprint for further comprehensively deepening reform. The commentary argues that the Party must keep leading social revolution through its own self-reform, and that this spirit is the precondition for carrying reform through and for supplying Chinese modernization with momentum and institutional guarantees. The piece has three parts. It first presents courage in self-reform as the Party's defining character and greatest strength. It then explains why further deepening reform requires thoroughgoing self-reform. Finally it sets out four practical directions: leadership capacity, Party rules and supervision, the political and organisational functions of Party organisations, and conduct and anti-corruption work. Gao grounds the first claim in Marx and Engels and in Mao Zedong. On this reading, the proletarian revolution is distinctive because it constantly criticises itself, and self-criticism is a form of dialectical negation. Because the Party, in the author's account, has no interests apart from those of the great majority, it can accept supervision by the people and escape the "historical cycle of rise and fall". Gao then argues that reform has entered deep waters, with unprecedented breadth, sharpness and complexity. Emancipating the mind, which the author calls the fundamental driver of reform, is impossible without turning the blade inward. Gao calls for improving the Party's leadership methods, strengthening Party regulations, combining self-supervision with supervision by the people, and persisting with the Central Committee's eight-point regulation. The author also calls for tackling formalism, bureaucratism and new or hidden forms of corruption, so that the strategic plans for reform become real strength. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links the Party's self-reform to the current reform agenda.

Comprehensively deepening economic structural reform in the new era 全面深化新时代经济体制改革 Zhao Xiaolei Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2024, Zhao Xiaolei takes up the July 2024 Decision of the Party's Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The article asks what the goal of a "high-standard socialist market economy" means and why economic reform is to lead the wider reform agenda. Zhao argues that the goal is the latest stage of a consistent line whose purpose is to liberate and develop the productive forces. The piece is a short commentary in four parts. It first traces how the reform goal has matured from the 14th Party Congress (1992) to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then sets out a Marxist theory of productive forces against Western growth theory. It next reviews how successive Party meetings tied reform to productive forces, and it ends by discussing reform together with opening up. Zhao's central move is theoretical. Western classical and neoclassical economics, including endogenous growth theory, treat production as resource allocation and technological progress, measured through factor productivity. Marxist political economy, in Zhao's account, adds that production is a social process. Productive forces therefore have a social as well as a material and technical attribute, and developing them means adjusting relations of production, not merely increasing output. On this basis Zhao reads the reform record, from 1978 through the Scientific Outlook on Development to the new development philosophy, as one thread. The change in the principal contradiction in the new era shifts the emphasis to balanced, higher-quality growth. Here Zhao presents high-quality development and new quality productive forces as the theory and form of advanced productive forces suited to a high-standard market economy. Zhao concludes that reform must proceed together with opening up. Drawing on the logic of exchange, specialisation and international trade, Zhao says a market economy is by nature open. The article calls for steady institutional opening in rules, regulations, management and standards. It also calls for a role in reforming global economic governance and for opening that supports the real economy. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Chinese economists link the 2024 reform decision to Marxist productive-forces theory and the Party's reform chronology.

Adhering to a people-centred approach in comprehensively deepening reform 坚持以人民为中心推进全面深化改革 An Haonan Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this commentary asks what it means to keep a people-centred orientation while comprehensively deepening reform. An argues that such an orientation is the fundamental driving force of Chinese modernization as it advances the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In the article's account, the people-centred approach shapes the problem focus, strategic layout and value standards of reform and opening up. Published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2024, the piece is built around four themes. It covers the liberation and development of new quality productive forces, the people's principal role and creative initiative, the pooling of the broadest public wisdom and strength, and the promotion of the people's well-being as the highest criterion of reform results. It draws repeatedly on Xi Jinping's remarks and the Plenum's conclusions. An's first move rests on the Marxist view that the fundamental task of socialism is to liberate and develop the productive forces. The author traces reform from building a market economy to deepening market mechanisms to innovation-driven development, and says that removing obstacles to new quality productive forces is now a key breakthrough point for improving living standards. The second move holds that reform is in essence a readjustment of existing interests and institutions, so it needs the people's creativity. The author says experience from the people's practice should be generalised from single 'points' of breakthrough to wider 'surfaces', and that reform has entered a stage of 'tackling tough problems' and holistic design. Reform therefore spans the economic, political, social, cultural and ecological fields and calls for systematic integration, ideological emancipation and the Two Integrations. For An, popular satisfaction is the test of reform. The author contrasts the present approach with the early strategy of letting some people and regions get rich first, and says reform now aims at common prosperity. An calls for concrete measures on income distribution, education, employment, social security, elderly and child care, healthcare, housing and environmental governance, so that people's sense of gain, happiness and security keeps growing. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the Third Plenum's reform agenda to people-centred and productive-forces arguments.

Improving the institutions and mechanisms for developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions 健全因地制宜发展新质生产力体制机制 Liu Quanhong Liu Fang This commentary by Liu Quanhong and Liu Fang, first published in Economic Daily on 15 October 2024, takes up the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee's call (2024) to improve the institutions and mechanisms for developing new quality productive forces in light of local conditions. The authors argue that this task is not only a question of development but also one of reform. In their account, deepening reform must produce production relations that fit the new productive forces. The piece has three parts. The first explains why developing new quality productive forces is a reform issue, taking in turn technological innovation, the allocation of production factors and industrial upgrading. The second sets out the methodology of "adapting measures to local conditions" (yīn dì zhì yí). The third lists systemic reforms in science and technology, traditional industries, emerging industries, future industries and factor allocation. Liu and Liu rest the argument on the Marxist premise that productive forces determine production relations. They say that new quality productive forces arise from technological breakthroughs, innovative factor allocation and deep industrial transformation, and that each of these is held back by institutional obstacles, such as weak basic research, mismatched factors and a hostile external environment. On local conditions, the authors warn against three errors: rushing in en masse, hurrying for quick results, and favouring the new while abandoning the old. They say some localities chase hot sectors such as AI and hydrogen without regard to their own endowments. This, they argue, produces homogenised industrial plans, "involutionary" investment-attraction policies and fiscal strain. They hold that traditional and emerging industries support each other, and that traditional industries should be upgraded rather than discarded. The authors propose strengthening the new whole-nation system for science and technology, and building interdisciplinary research centres. They also propose standards and exit channels for inefficient, high-emission capacity, and clearing out improper investment-attraction policies. For future industries they propose mechanisms for commercialising results, application scenarios and flexible regulation. They further call for a unified national market, "patient capital", better talent systems and income distribution that reflects the market value of knowledge, technology and data. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the policy agenda that official commentary linked to the 2024 Plenum's reform decisions on new quality productive forces.

Accelerating the building of a high-standard socialist market economy 加快构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Guan Xueling Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2024, Guan Xueling interprets the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (July 2024) on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The article asks what it means to build a high-standard socialist market economy and how this should be done. Guan argues that such a system is an important safeguard of Chinese modernization and that it rests on three tasks: implementing the Two Unwaverings, building a unified national market, and improving institutions for high-standard opening up. The commentary opens with the historical sequence from reform and opening up in 1978 to the 18th Party Congress's call for comprehensive deepening of reform in 2013. It then traces how the Party's formulation developed: "establishing" a socialist market economy at the 14th Congress, "improving" it at the 16th, and "building a high-standard" one at the 20th. Three thematic sections follow, on business entities, the national market and opening up. Guan presents the socialist market economy as a major innovation grounded in Chinese practice and as the most effective route to Chinese modernization. In this reading, the move from the market's "basic" to its "decisive" role in allocating resources shows the historical logic of the system. On enterprises, the author argues that both public and non-public sectors are essential. State-owned enterprises should deepen reform, strengthen their core functions and lead in breaking through technological bottlenecks. Private firms, which Guan says face real difficulties, need reassurance through the Two Unwaverings. On the national market, Guan says commodity and service markets are fairly well integrated, but factor and resource markets lag. The author proposes four steps, including a better institutional framework, removal of barriers to factor flows, and fuller use of idle resources. These would serve new quality productive forces. On opening up, Guan describes a shift to institutional opening, meaning alignment of "behind-the-border" rules, with free trade pilot zones and the Belt and Road Initiative as its vehicles, and calls for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the 2024 Plenum's market-economy agenda and the figures it cites.

Handling well the relationship between government and market, the core issue 处理好政府和市场关系这个核心问题 Zhou Wen Writing in the Economic Daily after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Zhou Wen argues that handling the relationship between government and market is the core issue of economic reform. The article presents the Plenum's Decision as the latest theoretical advance on this question and as part of Xi Jinping's economic thought. Zhou's answer is that a "high-level socialist market economy" requires the market to play the decisive role in allocating resources while the government plays its role better. The commentary has four parts. It first treats the government–market relationship as a worldwide problem in economics and traces the Party's evolving formulations from 1984 to 2013. It then links the issue to Chinese modernization, sets out three priorities for building the high-level market system, and finally applies the argument to new quality productive forces and the new-type whole-nation system. Zhou rejects the Western economic view of government and market as opposites, and says that applying that framework in China leads to wrong policy choices. Citing Xi Jinping, the article holds that the two are organically unified and neither may replace the other. "Better" government, in Zhou's account, does not mean more government: it means handling what markets cannot or do not handle well, without overstepping or neglecting duties. The three priorities are a fairer and more dynamic market environment (a unified national market, fair competition, market-determined factor prices), a more complete and mature system with the government–market relationship as its "ox's nose", and systematic, coordinated reform within the basic socialist economic system. On new quality productive forces, Zhou contends that scholars wrongly assume innovation comes only from markets. In Zhou's reading, the history of industrial and information revolutions shows governments leading technological change. The government should fund and coordinate high-risk basic and key technologies, while markets and private firms turn results into products. The new-type whole-nation system is presented as combining both, using national laboratories, research institutions, universities and leading firms. Zhou concludes that China has offered its own answer to a global problem. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the 2024 reform Decision frames the government–market relationship and its link to technology policy.

Deepening the understanding of the laws governing good economic work 深化做好经济工作的规律性认识 He Zili Writing in Economic Daily in March 2024, He Zili takes up the "five musts" put forward at the 2023 Central Economic Work Conference. He argues that they uphold fundamental principles while innovating, add to Xi Jinping's economic thought, and deepen the Party's understanding of the laws that govern economic work in the new era. In He's view, grasping their content matters both theoretically and practically for advancing Chinese modernization through high-quality development. This short commentary takes the five musts in turn, each under its own heading. They are: pursuing high-quality development as the "hard truth" of the new era; deepening supply-side structural reform while expanding effective demand; relying on reform and opening up to strengthen internal momentum; achieving a positive interaction between high-quality development and high-level security; and treating the advancement of Chinese modernization as the greatest political task. On high-quality development, He says it reflects the need to shift from extensive expansion to intensive growth driven by innovation, and to meet a changed principal contradiction, in which people's aspirations have moved from "having enough" to "having better". It must be guided by the new development philosophy. On supply and demand, He holds that the main constraint is now structural, so large-scale stimulus is no longer adequate. The author points to China's very large market and complete industrial system as the basis for a new development pattern centred on the domestic cycle. On the last must, He lists six relationships to handle, including top-level design and practical exploration, strategy and tactics, fundamental principles and innovation, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and self-reliance and opening up. He concludes that reform and opening up is the key to the success of Chinese modernization, and that development and security are like two wheels of a cart or two wings of a bird. He calls for an economic focus on high-quality development so that the blueprint of Chinese modernization is realised step by step. Read the original if you want a compact, official-line exposition of the 2023 Central Economic Work Conference's "five musts" and how Chinese economists frame them.

Excavating and drawing sensibly on China's fine traditional economic thought 挖掘并合理借鉴中华优秀传统经济思想 Zhao Mairu Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Zhao Mairu asks what traditional Chinese economic thought can offer to present-day economic practice and theory. The article argues that this thought holds considerable wisdom, and that excavating it and drawing on it sensibly will help further the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in practice and in theory. The piece is organised around the four moments of social reproduction in Marxist political economy: production, distribution, exchange and consumption. Each section takes one traditional idea or cluster of ideas, such as Li Kui's "exhausting the potential of the land", "storing wealth among the people", the "Ji Ran strategies" of trade, and spending "for the people". Each is then linked to a contemporary policy position. On production, Zhao presents Li Kui's Warring States reforms as intensive, careful farming that joined land and labour, and cites yield ratios that the author says were far higher in China than in Western Europe. On distribution, the people-as-foundation tradition (Mencius, Xunzi, Guanzi, Tang Zhen) is said to favour national wealth built on popular wealth, which the author connects to common prosperity and to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on income distribution. On exchange, Zhao reads the Ji Ran strategies, Bai Gui, Sima Qian's view that one should follow market tendencies, and Guanzi's counter-cyclical "heavy and light" intervention as early grasp of price laws and macro-regulation. On consumption, the author notes the dominant ethic of thrift. Zhao stresses that Xunzi, Sima Qian, Guanzi and Lu Ji, a Ming thinker, saw government spending on water works, relief and public goods as strengthening the economic base. Zhao concludes that each of these strands has "reference value" for today. They bear on liberating and developing the productive forces, on common prosperity, on building a high-standard socialist market economy, and on strengthening consumption's basic role in economic development, as the 20th Party Congress (2022) put it. The piece is brief and programmatic, and it offers no critical assessment of the traditional ideas. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese scholarship links classical Chinese economic thinking to current policy language.

Immaterial labour and digital labour: an examination from the standpoint of the materialist conception of history 非物质劳动与数字劳动的唯物史观考察 Mo Lei Contemporary capitalism is changing its forms of labour, production organisation and exploitation. Mo Lei compares two much-discussed accounts of these changes: Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's "immaterial labour" and Christian Fuchs's "digital labour". The article, a short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, argues that the two share a "family resemblance" but diverge on information, subjectivity, the measurement of exploitation and the realisation of the common. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the resemblances in background, concept and theoretical aim. Hardt and Negri start from Empire and the global biopolitical order, while Fuchs starts from financial capitalism and the rise of the internet and platforms; both work within "transnational informational capitalism". It then lists five differences, and finally asks what theoretical logic lies behind them. On resemblances, Mo notes that both approaches stress the production of knowledge, information and affect, the feminisation of work, and free communication and cooperation. Both hold that the appropriation of workers' activity and creativity is the main form of exploitation. On differences, Fuchs objects that "immaterial" implies a split between mind and matter, since information work is still brain-based material work. Mo replies that Hardt and Negri's "immaterial" refers mainly to the product. Fuchs extends Marx's rate of surplus value to include users' unpaid time, concluding that it tends towards infinity and calling users "internet slaves". Hardt and Negri reject quantification, treating exploitation as a qualitative matter of life and social relations. Fuchs also seeks platforms owned in common and a "working-class social media". Hardt and Negri focus on producing common subjectivity and on the multitude. Mo traces these differences to two sources. Hardt and Negri start from living labour and subjectivity, offering an immanent critique of how subjects produce themselves. Fuchs studies the internal mechanism of value formation through the relation between audience commodity, media and advertising. On the law of value, Fuchs extends Marx to fill the "labour blind spot" in the political economy of communication, whereas Hardt and Negri hold that unified labour time has dissolved and value cannot be fixed in time units. Mo judges that "immaterial labour" is the broader concept, while digital labour faces the difficulty of explaining how the digital generates labour. The two approaches represent the objective and subjective dimensions of Marxism's development. Mo calls for drawing on and criticising both to analyse new labour forms, exploitation, resistance and the possibilities of sharing. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language comparison of Fuchs with Hardt and Negri on labour and value.

Digital labour from the perspective of Marx's view of labour 马克思劳动观视域下的数字劳动 Li Suiyue Li Suiyue takes up a dispute in the study of digital labour: what the concept includes and excludes, and whether such labour is productive. The article argues that Marx's view of labour, applied through dialectical and historical materialism, can fix the concept's boundaries. Without this, Li warns, digital labour is stretched, trivialised or treated as play, and the common features of labour and its essence are lost. This short commentary, first published in a Chinese newspaper, has three parts. It begins by criticising two Western approaches to defining digital labour. It then sets out four general features of labour that any digital activity must meet. Finally it describes what is distinctively digital about this form of labour and offers a typology of real digital workers. Li identifies two errors in Western scholarship. Tiziana Terranova's line of thought, which Li links to terms such as audience labour and play labour, treats internet users' online consumption as labour and so produces the error of "going online is labour". Christian Fuchs's approach counts everything tied to the digital value chain, including mining and hardware manufacture, and drifts towards "all labour is digital labour". Against both, Li draws on Marx to say that an activity is labour only if it is purposeful, productive, work-like and creative. Users' browsing traces are, in Li's account, a "behavioural surplus" outside any purpose, whereas annotators and programmers labour purposefully. On the digital side, the means of labour must be substantively digital rather than merely related to digital technology. Gig workers such as delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers therefore remain traditional labourers. Li concludes that real digital labour falls into two types. The first is the work of software engineers, algorithm designers, game developers, web designers and system maintainers. The second is cultural creation by digital means, such as an online novelist writing and uploading a novel. Only by grasping both the labour character and the digital character of this work, Li argues, can scholarship avoid the theoretical and practical confusion of a "pan-digital labour". Read the original if you want a compact Chinese Marxist argument for narrowing the definition of digital labour, set against Terranova and Fuchs.

Focusing on directional, overall and strategic issues to further deepen reform comprehensively 聚焦方向性全局性战略性问题进一步全面深化改革 Xu Xiaoming Yin Jianjun Chen Shuangfei This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 30 September 2024, interprets the document adopted by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. The authors take up Xi Jinping's summary of how the document is organised, the "five emphases". They argue that these must be properly understood so that reform keeps to directional, overall and strategic issues and that its different parts work together efficiently. The article is a short interpretive piece with an introduction and five numbered sections, one for each emphasis. The emphases are the leading role of economic reform, building mechanisms that support comprehensive innovation, comprehensive reform, coordinating development and security, and strengthening Party leadership over reform. Each section gives a rationale, refers to experience since reform and opening up began, and sets out tasks for the coming five years, with the 2035 goal of basically realising socialist modernization as the anchor. On the economy, the authors invoke the Marxist contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. They hold that the economic system underlies all other systems, so economic reform can pull other reforms along. They tie this to the primary stage of socialism, which they call China's greatest national condition, and to the need to handle the government–market relationship and build a high-standard socialist market economy. On innovation, they argue that education, science and technology, and talent reinforce one another and should be reformed together. Comprehensive reform, they say, must be planned within the five-sphere overall plan and the Four Comprehensives, with attention to short and long-term goals and to local and overall interests. On security, the authors present development and security as mutually supporting and call for a new security architecture to protect the new development pattern. On leadership, they treat Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee of reform and divide it into political, ideological and organisational leadership. Political leadership is anchored in the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee. Ideological leadership rests on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Organisational leadership means better implementation mechanisms and cadre system reform. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the Third Plenum's reform agenda is framed and justified in Party media.

Steadily advancing all the people towards common prosperity 推动全体人民稳步迈向共同富裕 Jiang Yongmu Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Jiang Yongmu asks how common prosperity can be advanced further through deepening reform. The commentary, first published in the Economic Daily, argues that common prosperity for all the people is the essential feature of Chinese modernization and a goal that can only be reached by pressing ahead with reform and opening up. It presents Xi Jinping's statements on the subject as the guide for action. The piece has three parts. The first treats Chinese modernization as a modernization of common prosperity, tracing the goal from the "Great Harmony" ideal of the Book of Rites through the Party's successive historical periods. The second links reform and opening up to common prosperity, using figures on poverty and regional and income gaps. The third sets out four priority tasks: improving people's quality of life, income distribution and employment, social security, and basic public services. Jiang contrasts Western modernization, described as capital-centred and marked by polarisation, materialism and external expansion, with Chinese modernization, which is said to be people-centred and therefore to go beyond it. The author argues that reform opening-up lifted the rural poor, citing a 1978 rural poverty rate of 97.5% and the 2020 elimination of absolute poverty among 98.99 million people. Jiang also names remaining obstacles, citing 2023 figures: an urban–rural income ratio of 2.39, an eastern share of 52.1% of national output, and a gap of 85,840 yuan between the top and bottom income quintiles. In Jiang's account, deeper reform must both "make the cake bigger", through a high-standard socialist market economy and innovation, and "divide it well", through support for agriculture, coordinated regional development and better income distribution. The author presents the "six musts" of the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the worldview and method for this task. Jiang concludes that common prosperity is a long, arduous and complex historical process that demands historical patience. The author calls for coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, high-quality employment, a multi-tiered social security system, and public services that are both more balanced and more accessible. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-aligned economic commentary links common prosperity, reform and the Third Plenum agenda.

Building a high-standard socialist market economy that is "lively yet well regulated" 构建“放得活、管得住”的高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Han Baojiang Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which set the task of building a high-standard socialist market economy, Han Baojiang asks what it means for that system to be both "放得活" and "管得住" (roughly, free enough to be lively and regulated enough to stay in order). The article, a commentary first published in Guangming Daily on 3 October 2024, argues that this pairing is the inherent requirement of such a system and calls for further reform of the relevant institutions. The piece has three parts. It first traces how Party thinking on plan and market developed, from Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remarks and Chen Yun's "bird and cage" image through the 12th, 13th and 14th Party Congresses to the 18th Central Committee's Third Plenum (2013). It then sets out institutional tasks under each half of the formula. Finally it turns to the micro-level ownership base, meaning public and non-public enterprises. Han's central move is to equate "放得活" with letting the market play the decisive role in resource allocation, and "管得住" with improving government's role through macroeconomic governance. For the first, the author lists respect for the principle of material interest, better basic market institutions (property rights, fair competition, market access, bankruptcy and credit systems) and a sound factor-market system. For the second, Han lists a national strategic planning and policy-coordination system, fiscal and tax reform, and financial reform. Han also argues that consolidating the public sector supports "管得住" while encouraging the non-public sector supports "放得活". The two are presented as complementary, not opposed, and mixed-ownership economy is promoted to link them. Han leans heavily on quotations from Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and Marx. Han concludes that a high-standard system must combine an "efficient market" with an "effective government" and keep the word "socialist" in view throughout. Proposals include the Two Unwaverings, a law to promote the private economy, opening competitive infrastructure fields to private firms, reform of state-owned capital and enterprises, and easing private-sector financing. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theory frames the government–market relationship and the reform agenda of the Third Plenum.

Further deepening reform comprehensively must uphold a systems perspective 进一步全面深化改革必须坚持系统观念 Feng Jikang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 24 September 2024, takes up one of the "six adherences" set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024): that further deepening reform comprehensively must uphold a systems perspective. Feng Jikang argues that reform is a complex systemic undertaking. The systems perspective, which the author calls an important category of Marxist epistemology and methodology, should make reform more systematic, integrated and coordinated. The article is organised around five major relationships that the author says must be handled with this perspective: economy and society, government and market, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and development and security. Each receives one paragraph, with a short statement of why the two sides depend on one another and what is required in practice. Feng's central move is to treat each pair as mutually conditioning rather than opposed. Economic development is the basis of social development, and social investment in education and talent feeds back into growth. On government and market, the author calls for an effective market combined with a capable government, with the market playing the decisive role in resource allocation while the government remedies market failure. Efficiency and fairness are to be pursued together under Chinese modernization, described as modernization for the common prosperity of all. Vitality and order, and development and security, are likewise presented as reinforcing each other, with high-quality development and high-level security serving as the pairing. Feng concludes that handling these relationships through a systems perspective will give reform a stable, orderly and dynamic social setting. The text is a brief, programmatic exposition of official policy language. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party commentary frames the Third Plenum's methodology for reform.

Upholding and improving the basic socialist economic system to promote high-quality economic development 坚持和完善社会主义基本经济制度 推动经济高质量发展 Sun Libing Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Sun Libing argues that high-quality development depends on unwaveringly upholding and improving the basic socialist economic system. That system is public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse ownership forms, distribution according to work alongside other modes of distribution, and the socialist market economy. Sun presents it as showing the superiority of socialism while suiting the primary stage of socialism. The article is a Party-theory commentary in four parts. It first traces how the economic system evolved from the 1950s to the present, citing successive Party congresses from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee onwards. It then takes ownership, distribution and the market economy in turn, each tied to the aim of high-quality development and common prosperity. Sun first reads the system's development as continuous self-improvement of socialism: the Party moved from a planned economy on a public base to a market system, adding the Two Unwaverings and, in 2019, a three-dimensional formulation covering ownership, distribution and economic operation. On ownership, Sun calls for deepening state-asset and state-enterprise reform, concentrating state capital in security, public-service and emerging strategic sectors, and supporting private firms through a fairer business environment, financing and digital transformation. On distribution, citing Marx that the structure of distribution is determined by the structure of production, Sun argues that public-led ownership requires distribution according to work as the mainstay, with factor-based distribution (including data) alongside it, and coordinated primary, secondary and third distribution. On the market, Sun treats the goal of a high-level socialist market economy by 2035 as a new stage of reform. Sun calls for a decisive role for the market and a better-functioning government, a unified national market, and basic market institutions such as property-rights protection, market access, fair competition and social credit. Sun concludes that all this is needed to advance Chinese modernization and common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise official-style summary of how Party discourse links ownership, distribution and market reform to high-quality development after the 2024 plenum.

Anchoring on high technology, high efficiency and high quality in developing new quality productive forces 锚定高技术高效能高质量发展新质生产力 Fang Xiaoxia This commentary, first published in Economic Daily in September 2024, takes up the demand in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to develop productive forces marked by high technology, high efficiency and high quality.
