Fang argues that building the material and technological base of Chinese modernization requires grasping these three features, accelerating new quality productive forces and forming production relations suited to them. The piece has three sections, one for each feature, followed by a section on institutional reform. Each section pairs a historical or conceptual point with figures on China's recent performance. On high technology, Fang holds that every leap in productive forces has rested on original, disruptive technologies, and that AI, the Internet of Things, biotechnology, advanced manufacturing and new energy now form a green, intelligent and ubiquitous wave of technological revolution. The author cites R&D spending above 3.3 trillion yuan in 2023, an intensity of 2.64%. On high efficiency, Fang defines new quality productive forces through the improved combination of labourers, means of labour and objects of labour, with data as a key new factor. Labour productivity per worker is said to have risen from 72,817 to 161,615 yuan between 2012 and 2023. On high quality, Fang argues that digital technology, as a general-purpose technology, upgrades traditional industries and that new quality productive forces are inherently green. Fang concludes that new production relations must be formed through deeper reform. The author proposes mechanisms to support original and disruptive innovation, a better system for turning research into products, and institutions that help traditional industries upgrade digitally, greenly and through services. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official economic commentary links new quality productive forces to technology, productivity data and reform priorities.

Theoretical achievements on new quality productive forces highlight an original contribution 新质生产力理论成果彰显原创性贡献 Qiu Haiping Writing in Economic Daily in September 2024, Qiu Haiping asks what is original in Xi Jinping's discussion of new quality productive forces, which Xi has set out since 2023. Qiu argues that the concept is a new "revolution in terminology" within Xi Jinping's economic thought. In Qiu's account, it is the first explicit attempt to characterise productive forces by their qualitative state, and it develops Marxist political economy and historical materialism. The piece is organised in three parts. The first treats the concept as a terminological innovation and sets out the practical sources of the idea. The second places the concept within Xi Jinping's economic thought as a whole and summarises Xi's statements on it. The third turns to the Marxist category of productive forces and says what the new concept adds. It opens with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), whose decision calls for mechanisms to develop new quality productive forces according to local conditions. Qiu begins from Engels's remark that every new insight in a science brings a revolution in its terminology. Xi's economic thought has innovated either by redefining existing terms or by coining new ones, such as the new development philosophy, high-quality development and the new development pattern. New quality productive forces, Qiu says, follow this path. Qiu traces their rationale to the new stage of development, the new development philosophy, the new development pattern, high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Qiu then reviews Marx's treatment of productive forces: the human and material elements, labour productivity, and the relation between productive forces and relations of production. Qiu argues that the classics speak of new productive forces and revolutions in them but never define or classify productive forces by qualitative state. The new category does so, defined by technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors and deep industrial upgrading. Its core marker is a marked rise in total factor productivity. Qiu concludes that the concept lets historical materialism describe the productive forces of different social formations more precisely, and so deepens understanding of the laws of historical development. Qiu also stresses the call to build new relations of production suited to the new forces, through deeper reform and opening up. Qiu adds that local conditions should guide development, and that a rush into bubbles or a single template should be avoided. Read the original if you want an official-line theoretical account of why new quality productive forces are presented as an original contribution to Marxist political economy.

The innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces in contemporary China 马克思主义生产力理论在当代中国的创新发展 Zhang Yu Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Zhang Yu asks how the Marxist theory of productive forces has been developed in contemporary China. The article argues that Xi Jinping's discussions of productive forces, and above all his proposal to develop new quality productive forces, raise the Party's understanding of how productive forces develop to a new level. Zhang describes this as an original theoretical result of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is organised as a sequence of themes. Each takes a classical Marxist proposition, traces how Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping handled it, and then sets out Xi's statements on the same point. The themes are: productive forces as the standard of social progress; the purpose of socialist production; the elements of productive forces; the scientific and industrial revolutions; scientific and technological innovation; ecology; industrial innovation; and reform of the relations of production. Zhang's core move is to present each of Xi's statements as a creative development of historical materialism. Technological innovation is called the core element of new quality productive forces. Data is treated as a new factor of production. Protecting the ecological environment is described as protecting productive forces, and new quality productive forces are said to be green productive forces by nature. Zhang also argues that the relations of production must be reformed to fit new productive forces, and that the socialist system combined with the market economy has distinct advantages in liberating and developing them. The article closes by defining new quality productive forces as advanced productive forces and gives four reasons. They arise from the new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial change. They are the advanced productive forces of the information, digital and intelligent era. They raise the quality of workers, means of labour, objects of labour and their combination. They are the material and technological basis of Chinese modernization and high-quality development. Zhang concludes that the theory of new quality productive forces deepens understanding of the decisive role of productive forces, the essence of socialism, the elements of productive forces, their driving force and their relationship to the relations of production. The purpose of development, in this account, remains meeting the people's growing needs for a better life. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese theorists link Marx, Mao, Deng and Xi on productive forces and justify the concept of new quality productive forces.

The two dimensions of Marx's thought on democracy and their practical embodiment 马克思民主思想的二维向度及实践体现 Liu Lin Liu Lin asks how Marx's thinking on democracy can be organised into a coherent system and what it means for democratic practice in China today. The article proposes two dimensions: a substantive dimension, concerned with the philosophical grounds and inner value of democracy, and an authenticity (or reality) dimension, concerned with how rule by the majority is actually realised. Liu argues that the two complement each other and that whole-process people's democracy joins them in contemporary China. Part one reconstructs the substantive dimension through three headings: the essence of democracy as the form of the state, its ontological basis in the people, and its authentic aim in human emancipation. This draws on Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question and The Civil War in France. Part two treats the authenticity dimension as a demystification of bourgeois democracy and a distillation of proletarian practice, followed by Marx's general principles for realisation. Part three applies the framework to China at the level of the state, the people and society. The central move is that Marx locates democracy in the economic base and in the people's self-determination, not in abstract liberty and equality. On this basis Liu reads his critique of representative government, universal suffrage and the separation of powers as showing that they leave exploitation intact. From the Paris Commune, Liu draws four lessons: economic emancipation as the precondition, breaking the old state machine, self-government by the people, and public servants who can be recalled. For realisation Liu identifies three pairings: new democracy with new dictatorship, Communist Party leadership with the proletariat as the active force, and institutional procedure with popular supervision. Liu concludes that whole-process people's democracy fuses the substantive and authentic dimensions and is a new creation of Marx's thought in China. In the article's account, it must fit Chinese modernization and the primary stage of socialism, broaden and strengthen popular participation, and advance through the five-sphere integrated plan. It must also keep the three-way unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language case for reading Marx's democratic thought as grounding the official concept of whole-process people's democracy.

Main historical lessons of modernization since the founding of the People's Republic 新中国成立以来现代化建设的主要历史经验 Yang Deshan Guo Wei Writing in 2024, on the 75th anniversary of the People's Republic, Yang Deshan and Guo Wei ask what lessons can be drawn from the Communist Party's record of modernization. They argue that the Party's success rests on continually summing up experience, and that the record yields three main lessons: one political, one ideological and one methodological. They present this as relevant to studying Xi Jinping's statements on Chinese modernization, to implementing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), and to building a Chinese-style body of knowledge on modernization. The article is organised around these three lessons. The first concerns political direction. The second traces how the Party's understanding and strategic targets changed across four stages: building an industrial base, the "Four Modernizations", "modernization of the Chinese type" under reform and opening up, and Chinese modernization since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third examines two pairs of relationships: upholding fundamental principles versus innovation and reform, and self-reliance versus cooperation and opening up. On the political side, the authors argue that Party leadership, the socialist road and a people-centred approach were treated as the premise of modernization from the New Democratic period onward, and that the three form an organic unity. On the ideological side, they hold that the Party adjusted its goals as it learned more about modernization and about China's conditions, citing the shift from the "Four Modernizations" to the three-step strategy, a moderately prosperous society, and the two-step plan to 2035 and mid-century. On method, they claim that economic reform (from the planned commodity economy to a socialist market economy) and the strengthening of Party leadership show dialectical handling of continuity and change. Self-reliance is described as the inner basis, with opening up, including WTO entry in 2001, as an external condition turned into internal momentum. The authors conclude that the Party has consistently kept its original mission while innovating, and has combined independence with openness, neither overrating nor underrating itself, and that this has kept modernization on course. They stress that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and the world's largest developing country. Read the original if you want a Party-centred periodisation of China's modernization strategy, from the Four Modernizations to Chinese modernization, and how Chinese scholars derive official lessons from it.

Achievements and lessons of economic development in New China 新中国经济发展的成就与启示 Wu Li Marking the 75th anniversary of the People's Republic in 2024, Wu Li reviews the country's economic record and asks what it shows. The article argues that the 75 years of economic development and institutional change demonstrate the distinctive strengths of Communist Party leadership and of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics. In Wu's account, China moved from a backward agrarian country to an advanced industrial one despite scarce per capita resources and fierce international competition. The piece is a historical overview organised around three periods that Wu presents as continuous: the era of socialist revolution and construction, the era of reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Each section pairs a policy logic with statistics, such as reservoirs and irrigated land up to 1978, GDP rankings from 1978 to 2010, and GDP, social insurance and infrastructure figures for 2012–2023. A closing section lists current problems and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Wu's central claim is that each period's strategy fitted its conditions. Heavy-industry priority, planning and socialist transformation secured high accumulation at low income, and produced a complete industrial system and defence capacity. Reform introduced a socialist market economy in which the market and the government work as a "dual-wheel drive", and growth averaged nearly 10% a year from 1978 to 2012. After 2012 Wu describes the "three overlapping periods" of slower growth, structural adjustment and digesting earlier stimulus, which called for a shift to high-quality development. Wu names four continuing advantages: Party leadership, the government–market combination, the size of the economy, and abundant human capital. Wu acknowledges that unbalanced and inadequate development persists. The listed problems include an incomplete market system, weak innovation, dependence on foreign core technologies, and gaps in urban–rural development and income distribution. The article concludes that deepening reform, centred on a high-standard socialist market economy, will carry the country towards the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned narrative of China's economic history in three periods, with the statistics it cites, as an example of how Chinese scholarship presents this record.

Deng Xiaoping and strengthening the Party's leadership over propaganda, ideological and cultural work 邓小平与加强党对宣传思想文化工作的领导 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong asks how Deng Xiaoping guided the Party's propaganda, ideological and cultural work during reform and opening up, and why this mattered for the Party's fate. The article argues that Deng set the correct direction for this work by re-establishing the Marxist ideological line, holding to the Four Cardinal Principles, and drawing lessons from the Party's history, thereby upholding and strengthening Party leadership over the ideological field. The article is a historical-political study built on Deng's speeches and talks from 1975 to 1992. It has three main sections: the debate on the criterion of truth and the restoration of the ideological line; the Four Cardinal Principles as the precondition for the four modernizations; and the 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party since the Founding of the People's Republic of China. A short closing section links these to socialism with Chinese characteristics and to material and spiritual civilization. Song first presents Deng as opposing the "Two Whatevers" from 1977 on, supporting the 1978 discussion that "practice is the sole criterion of truth" and treating it as a question of whether to liberate thought. In Song's account, this restored "emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts" as the Party's line and prepared the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Song then reports Deng's 1979 insistence that the four modernizations required adherence to the socialist road, the dictatorship of the proletariat, Party leadership and Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought. Deng is shown calling Party leadership the core of the four, criticising bourgeois liberalization, and urging stronger propaganda and education on these principles. Finally, Song describes Deng drafting the Resolution, assessing Mao Zedong's merits as primary and his errors as secondary, and defending Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology. Song concludes that, under Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Party combined the Four Cardinal Principles with economic construction as the central task and with reform and opening up. In this account, that produced the basic line of the primary stage of socialism and the three-step development strategy, and opened the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Song adds that Deng called for paying equal attention to material and spiritual civilization and for firm action against "spiritual pollution". Read the original if you want a source-rich account, in Deng's own words, of how the official Party narrative links the truth-criterion debate, the Four Cardinal Principles and the 1981 Resolution to ideological leadership.

The innovative development of the Marxist theory of productive forces in contemporary China 马克思主义生产力理论在当代中国的创新发展 Zhang Yu Published in Guangming Daily in October 2024, this article asks how the Marxist theory of productive forces has been developed in contemporary China. Zhang Yu argues that Xi Jinping's series of statements on productive forces, culminating in the concept of new quality productive forces, raises the Party's understanding of the laws of productive-force development to a new level. Zhang presents it as an original theoretical achievement of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is organised as a sequence of themes. Each opens with Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong or Deng Xiaoping and then sets out Xi's corresponding formulations. The themes are: productive forces as the fundamental criterion of social development; the purpose of production as meeting people's needs; the components of productive forces; the new round of technological and industrial revolution; scientific and technological innovation; ecology; industrial innovation; reform of production relations; and the nature of new quality productive forces. Zhang's core move is to show continuity and extension. Marx's elements of the labour process (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour) are said to underpin Xi's definition of new quality productive forces as a leap in these elements and their optimised combination. Data is treated as a new production factor. Marx's view that science is a productive force becomes the claim that technological innovation is the core element. His view of metabolism between humans and nature becomes the idea that protecting the environment is protecting productive forces, so that new quality productive forces are "green productive forces". Zhang also holds that socialist institutions, combining the market economy with the socialist system, must be reformed so that production relations fit new productive forces. Zhang concludes that new quality productive forces are in essence advanced productive forces. They are described through four features: they arise from the new technological and industrial revolution, they belong to the information, digital and intelligent era, they involve a leap in factors and their combination (platform economy is one example), and they are the material and technological basis of Chinese modernization and high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party theorists link Xi Jinping's economic thought to the Marxist classics on productive forces.

Marx's thesis of "revolutionary practice" as an answer to the relation between environment and human beings 马克思“革命的实践”论断对环境与人关系的回答 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang revisits the third of Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, which holds that the coincidence of the changing of circumstances and of human activity or self-change can only be conceived and rationally understood as revolutionary practice. Liu argues that three basic questions remain disputed: what "environment" refers to, how changed activity relates to self-change, and why the relation can "only" be understood as revolutionary practice. Answering them, in Liu's view, shows how Marx's new materialism of "practice" surpasses all earlier materialism and leads towards the communist movement. The article is organised around these three questions and returns to the intellectual-historical context of the Theses. It draws on Marx's engagement with eighteenth-century French materialism (especially Helvétius) in The Holy Family, on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology, the Grundrisse and Capital, and on Hegel's master–slave dialectic. It also compares Marx's original wording with Engels's edited version, which dropped "self-change". On the first question, Liu rejects both the view that "environment" means social environment and the view that it means natural plus social environment. Liu holds that it means the "human environment": social environment together with humanised nature, excluding nature-in-itself. On the second, Liu proposes reading the relation through a "practice–education" logic derived from Marx's critical inheritance of Hegel's "labour–formation" idea. In Liu's account, changed activity is the practical precondition and aim of self-change, while awakened self-consciousness drives conscious revolutionary action, giving the proletariat a double subjectivity. On the third, Liu argues that only relational practice, dialectically uniting the human environment and humans, overcomes the subject–object dualism of mechanical and French materialism. This yields the historicity, mediating character and revolutionary character of the new materialism. Liu concludes that understanding the human environment and humans as revolutionary practice is the only way to escape the utopian trap of earlier materialisms and open the revolutionary possibility of the communist movement. The Theses, Liu notes, remain a philosophical outline that does not yet grasp the concrete forms of capitalist production relations. Even so, Liu sees in them the unity of social, natural and human history that underlies historical materialism. Read the original if you work on the early Marx, the Theses on Feuerbach or the concept of practice, and want a detailed Chinese reading of the Marx–Engels textual difference and the Hegelian background.

The profound significance of General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on Party building 深刻领悟习近平总书记关于党的建设的重要思想的重大意义 Gong Yun Gong Yun takes up the significance of what the article calls General Secretary Xi Jinping's important thinking on Party building, which it describes as formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that this body of thought answers the question of what kind of long-ruling Marxist party to build and how to build it, and that it has historical, theoretical and practical significance of a major and lasting kind. The article is organised in three parts that correspond to these three kinds of significance. The first treats the thinking as a response to the times: a world undergoing great changes, the task of national rejuvenation, and the need to solve problems in Party governance. The second sets it within the history of Marxist party-building theory, from the Soviet experience through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. The third turns to its effects in practice. In its first part, Gong contends that the thinking keeps the Party at the forefront of the times and enables it to deal with problems that had arisen earlier, including weakened Party leadership, formalism, bureaucracy, privilege and corruption. In the second, Gong argues that it answers a question open since the October Revolution, noting that the Soviet party explored it for 74 years before the party and state collapsed. Gong presents the thinking as the 'Party building chapter' of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, organised as 'thirteen adherences' and offered as a Chinese approach for party governance worldwide. In the third, Gong holds that it has reversed the weakening of Party leadership, strengthened the Party through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and secured what the article calls an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle. Gong concludes that this thinking provides the fundamental guide for advancing the 'new great project' of Party building and a firm political guarantee for Chinese modernization. The article stresses the decisive role of Party leadership and the Party's self-reform in the course of national rejuvenation and calls for continued, unwavering full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Party theorists frame the importance of Xi's Party-building thought for domestic governance, Marxist party theory and the Party's international claims.

Striving to write a new chapter in building a strong education nation in the new era and on the new journey 奋力书写新时代新征程教育强国建设崭新篇章 Party Leadership Group of the Ministry of Education This commentary, issued by the Party Leadership Group of the Ministry of Education and carried in the People's Daily on 16 October 2024, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the National Education Conference. The authors present the speech as a systematic plan and a call to the whole Party and society to build a strong education nation (教育强国). They state that the education system will carry it out firmly, and they treat the task as a new mission for strengthening education. The text has three parts. The first explains why the education system should raise its ideological and practical awareness of the task. The second sets out the strategic picture, described as the "four pillars and eight beams" of the project. The third lists priority tasks to be carried out in a spirit of reform and innovation, and a short closing stresses implementation. In the first part, the authors argue that education's status, the system's responsibilities and the grounds for confidence are all "unprecedented". They cite the 20th Party Congress (2022) goal of a strong education nation by 2035 and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) decision on integrated reform of education, science and technology, and talent. They name challenges: a falling birth rate, an ageing population, and imbalances between people's wish for better education and its uneven development. The second part says construction must follow education's political, popular and strategic attributes and aim at six capacities: ideological and political guidance, talent competitiveness, scientific and technological support, livelihood security, social coordination and international influence. It also calls for a high-quality education system that links basic, higher, vocational and lifelong education. The third part covers fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in textbooks and classrooms. It also covers supporting science, technology and talent, improving public education services, building a high-level teaching force, and making China an education centre with global influence. The authors conclude that the blueprint must become concrete work plans and responsibilities, carried out with a "nail-driving spirit" and a long-term view. They present this as turning the speech into support for Chinese modernization. The text is an official statement of the ministry's priorities and agenda, with little independent argument. Read the original if you want the education authorities' own account of the goals, vocabulary and policy priorities that followed the 2024 National Education Conference.

The milestone significance and innovative achievements of further comprehensively deepening reform 进一步全面深化改革的里程碑意义和创新性成果 Jiang Hui Writing in the Study Times in September 2024, Jiang Hui interprets the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (July 2024) and its decision on further comprehensively deepening reform. The article argues that the plenum is a landmark in the history of reform and opening up and of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Jiang's account, it opened a new stage in which further comprehensive reform is used to advance Chinese modernization, and it produced practical, theoretical and institutional results. The commentary is organised under three headings: a new stage of reform and its milestone significance; a new reform layout and its pioneering practical meaning; and new ideological development and its innovative theoretical meaning. It places the plenum alongside the Third Plenums of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the 18th Central Committee (2013). A closing section briefly describes how Chongqing is implementing the plenum's spirit. Jiang's central move is to present reform as continuous yet staged. The line from "reform" to "comprehensively deepening reform" to "further comprehensively deepening reform" is described as a response to changed conditions, with direction, theme and overall goal unchanged. Jiang contends that the 2024 plenum "upgraded" objectives, development tasks and reform deployment around the central task of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The plenum is said to address high-quality development, new quality productive forces and structural obstacles, led by economic reform and grounded in social fairness and people's wellbeing. On theory, Jiang holds that the plenum's decision condenses over forty years of experience. It also systematises Xi Jinping's new ideas on comprehensively deepening reform, which Jiang calls the "reform chapter" of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Jiang lists its main principles. They include Party leadership, a people-centred approach, problem orientation, systems thinking, institution-building as the main thread, the rule of law, and opening up. Jiang concludes that this enriches Marxist reform theory and guides the new journey. Read the original if you want an official Party-school account of how the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee is framed historically and theoretically, including a local Party leader's application in Chongqing.

The historical roots, value foundations and practical basis of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的历史根源、价值根柢与实践根基 Xiang Jiuyu Xiang Jiuyu takes up the concept of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation (中华民族现代文明), a term in current Party theory. The article asks where this new civilizational form comes from, what values underlie it and what practice sustains it. Xiang's thesis is that it is the product of civilizational renewal rather than rupture, distinct from Western modern civilization, and that it answers the long-standing doubt over whether China could create its own modern civilization and pursue modernization independently. The article is organised in three parts: historical roots, value foundations and practical basis. The roots are examined on three levels: culture, Chinese civilization as a living organism, and world history. The value part discusses national rejuvenation and civilizational flourishing, people-centredness, and the vision of a world of great harmony. The practical part names four supports: Party leadership, coordinated material and spiritual development, innovation, and building a community with a shared future for mankind. On roots, Xiang argues that the civilization results from the Two Integrations, in which Marxism as the "soul" and fine traditional culture as the "roots" combine. It is also the modern form of Chinese civilization, which Xiang says has outstanding continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Xiang adds that it is both national and world-historical. In Xiang's account, it breaks with the idea that the West is a "universal civilization" and that modernity develops linearly, since modernization is not Westernization. On values, Xiang says the civilization's people-centred stance is not a simple continuation of ancient minben (people-as-root) thought. It places the people at the centre on a Marxist basis and, Xiang claims, thereby surpasses the capital-first path of Western modernity, which Xiang describes through Marx's critique of bourgeois civilization's hypocrisy in the colonies. On practice, Xiang calls for the Party's overall leadership to be applied through its political leadership, ideological guidance, mass organisation and social mobilisation. Xiang also calls for new quality productive forces and cultural construction to advance together, for innovation in theory, institutions and culture, and for the civilization to develop within the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Xiang stresses that the civilization is still "in progress" and needs greater civilizational consciousness and confidence. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Party scholarship derives the concept of a Chinese modern civilization from the Two Integrations and from claims about Chinese civilization's distinctive features.

The profound connotations, distinctive features and value implications of the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的深刻内涵、鲜明特征与价值意蕴 Tian Zhijian Wang Xue Tian Zhijian and Wang Xue take up the concept of building a "modern civilisation of the Chinese nation", first put forward by Xi Jinping in 2022 and treated as part of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article asks what this civilisation means, what distinguishes it and what value it holds. It argues that this civilisation grows from the Two Integrations, with Marxism as its "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture as its "root", and that it is the cultural form of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out Xi's statements on the topic and reviews eight scholarly angles on the concept: the five-sphere layout, culture, civilisation in a broad sense, Chinese modernization, the new form of human civilisation, genesis, methodology and an integrated view. The second reviews three scholarly lists of features and then compares the civilisation with human civilisation in general, with ancient Chinese civilisation and with other civilisations. The third discusses its value implications. On features, the authors identify three pairings: nationhood and worldliness, epochal character and development, and subjectivity and inclusiveness. They argue that the civilisation follows the general laws of modern development and draws on Western experience, yet rejects the equation of modernization with Westernisation. They also claim theoretical and practical advantages from the Marxist and traditional sources it joins. On value, they present the "Marxism transforms China" and "China transforms Marxism" processes as mutually reinforcing, and read Xi's two "must nots" (never abandon Marxism or the traditional root) as a guide to the Two Integrations. The authors tie the civilisation to Chinese modernization, which they describe as rejecting capital-driven, polarising and expansionist paths, and to new quality productive forces as a driver of innovation. Internationally, they criticise the "clash of civilisations" thesis and claims of civilisational superiority, and call for exchange and mutual learning in building a community with a shared future for mankind. They conclude that the civilisation should be built by remaining true to its origins, absorbing foreign achievements and facing the future. Read the original if you want a systematic survey of Chinese scholarship on this concept and its official framing.

A theoretical analysis of the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的理论探析 Shang Zhixiao Shang Zhixiao takes up a new formulation in Xi Jinping's cultural agenda: "the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation" (中华民族现代文明). Xi presented the building of this civilisation as part of a new cultural mission at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023. Shang argues that the concept and the task of building it need to be understood theoretically: what it means, what form it takes, and how it relates to Chinese modernization. The aim, Shang says, is to combine the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture and to cultivate a new socialist culture. The article has four parts. It first distinguishes civilisation from culture and describes Chinese civilisation. It then traces how the concept was introduced, from Xi's 2022 visit to the Yin Ruins to the 2023 symposium. It next sets out the concept's meaning and structure, and last the historical process by which the civilisation has developed since 1949. Along the way Shang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Hegel, Russell and Voltaire. Shang defines the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation as a socialist civilisation created under Party leadership through Chinese modernization. It is rooted in Chinese civilisation, and Shang describes it as surpassing both traditional Chinese civilisation and capitalist civilisation. The author gives it a three-part cognitive structure: the Chinese nation as subject, the "modern" as historical position, and culture as form. In practice it has a leading core (the Communist Party), a base of support (the people) and a guiding direction (socialism with Chinese characteristics and advanced socialist culture). Shang holds that civilisation is the inner essence and advanced socialist culture its outward form. On that basis, building the civilisation amounts to the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture, the integration of Marxism with that culture, and the formation of a new organic cultural entity. Shang locates the civilisation's historical starting point in the founding of the People's Republic and the entry into modern society. Shang then describes more than seventy years of development through socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The article concludes that the civilisation grows within Chinese modernization, and quotes the formula that Chinese modernization gives Chinese civilisation modern force while Chinese civilisation gives Chinese modernization its depth. It calls for building the civilisation in step with that process. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese philosophers are conceptualising this newly announced term and its links to Chinese modernization.

Anchoring on the goal of building a modern socialist great power and striving forward 锚定全面建成社会主义现代化强国目标奋发进取 Ren Lixuan Marking the 75th anniversary of the People's Republic of China, this commentary asks what the goal of fully building a modern socialist great power means and how the Party should pursue it in what it calls a critical period. Ren argues that China is closer to the goal than ever, but that the remaining stretch will bring unprecedented pressure. The author holds that success depends on persevering under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, on the Party's leadership and on the people. The piece opens with a historical survey. It traces the aspiration for national strength from the humiliations of the modern era through the founding of the PRC, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out five defining features of the intended great power: socialist in nature, built through Chinese modernization, strong in all dimensions, committed to peace and a community with a shared future for mankind, and delivered through the two-step timetable to 2035 and the mid-century. The second and third parts address current challenges and the means of meeting them. Ren's central argument is that the external environment is worsening, but that internal factors are decisive. The author describes the Ukraine crisis, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, unilateralism, protectionism and containment by outside powers as sources of pressure, and says the 'Thucydides trap' is avoidable. The commentary points to record trade volumes in the first seven months of 2024 as evidence of resilience. It names high-quality development as the primary task and the 'decisive internal cause', citing the fact that only a dozen or so of over 100 middle-income economies since the 1960s reached high-income status. It links this to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its more than 300 reform measures. The closing section calls for three supports for the national project: scientific theory, a firm leadership core and the people's strength. Ren urges Party members and officials to study Xi Jinping Thought thoroughly, to uphold Xi's position as core of the Party, to implement reforms without formalism and to work closely with the masses on livelihood issues. The author presents the great-power goal as both a historical opportunity and a responsibility. Read the original if you want an authoritative People's Daily statement of how the Party framed national strength and the 2035 and mid-century goals at the 75th anniversary of the PRC.

The ideological force of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture 习近平文化思想的意识形态力量 Liang Dawei Wang Zhuo Liang and Wang ask what ideological force is contained in Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and how it strengthens the Chinese Communist Party's ideological theory in the new era. They take the term from Engels's remark that the state appears as the first ideological power over man. They argue that the Thought is a major theoretical innovation, and that its ideological force works in three dimensions: intellectual, spiritual and civilizational. The article first places Xi Jinping Thought on Culture within the body of Party ideological theory, alongside Xi's thought on the economy, rule of law, ecological civilization, military strengthening and diplomacy. Its three main sections each take one dimension in turn. The first concerns advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, the second lifting the spiritual outlook of the Chinese people, and the third building a modern Chinese civilization. It ends with a short conclusion on the international ideological environment. On the intellectual side, the authors argue that the Thought adds a cultural chapter to the adaptation of Marxism. They point to its strategic positioning of propaganda and cultural work and to the Two Integrations, in which the "second integration" joins Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. They trace this idea back to Mao Zedong and to reform-era concepts, and present it as a law-like understanding. On the spiritual side, they describe theoretical education, a people-centred orientation and the construction of values as ways of shaping public spirit. These include the Chinese Dream, core socialist values and the lineage of the Communist spirit. On the civilizational side, they name three "magic weapons": cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. The authors conclude that, amid what they call great changes unseen in a century, rivalry between states now includes culture and ideology. They claim that Western countries slander communist ideals and Marxism and discredit the Party, which creates serious risks for China's ideological field. They call for guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to consolidate the ideological foundation of national rejuvenation and accelerate the building of a modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-aligned scholars present the ideological functions of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, in the official vocabulary of the time.

Upholding the principal role of the people in cultural development 坚持文化建设中的人民主体地位 Jiang Shuzhuo Jiang Shuzhuo takes up the principle of "putting the people first" in the Decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The commentary argues that reform of cultural institutions and mechanisms must rest on the people's principal role, and that this will supply spiritual support for building a cultural powerhouse and for Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in three parts: protecting the people's cultural rights, stimulating the people's sense of agency, and promoting all-round human development. It draws on examples such as village football ("Village Super League"), dragon-boat races, square dancing, short video and art-based rural revitalisation. It also cites Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Marx. Jiang presents cultural rights as a marker of people sharing the fruits of reform and opening up. In Jiang's account, the state provides conditions for these rights while the public takes part in shaping cultural life. Jiang calls for better facilities for disabled and elderly people and for evaluation mechanisms that support cultural-technological talent. The author also stresses encouraging cultural workers to innovate and produce "peaks" of quality, and holds that grassroots creativity drives cultural trends. The final aim is cultivating "new people" suited to modernization, through public cultural environments, dialogue between experts and the public, and cultural volunteer schemes. Jiang concludes that cultural work must protect cultural rights, respect popular initiative and awaken the people's creative consciousness. In this way it would raise social civility alongside common prosperity and support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short, official-line example of how the people-centred principle is applied to cultural policy and institutional reform.

The integration logic of collective memory from the perspective of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation 铸牢中华民族共同体意识视域下集体记忆的整合逻辑 Zhang Shujuan Wang Shuo Zhang Shujuan and Wang Shuo ask how collective memory can be used to forge a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, which the 20th Party Congress (2022) made the main thread of the Party's ethnic work. They treat collective memory as an explanatory framework and argue that integrating it is a continuing process with a "before, during and after" structure. In their account, the sense of community and collective memory support each other, and memory can in turn be used to consolidate that sense. The article first draws on Maurice Halbwachs, Pierre Nora and Chinese scholars such as Wang Mingke and Ma Guoqing to define collective memory. It lists the features the authors attribute to it: uniqueness, sociality, spatio-temporal anchoring and reconstructibility. It then treats the three stages in turn: the conditions that make integration possible, the integration itself, and its continuation. Examples include the Great Wall, Yellow Emperor ceremonies, ancestral myths of minority peoples, restored historic sites and television programmes. On the "before" stage, the authors argue that memory and the sense of community share the same "site of memory", the Chinese land. They also embed each other in the sediment of Chinese civilisation and jointly shape the national spirit. In the "during" stage, the sense of community, in their reading, writes memory in two directions. It traces a shared historical memory of both national suffering (such as the War of Resistance against Japan) and lasting glory, and it deepens a shared cultural memory through the Confucian tradition, ancestral culture, oral epics and relics. In the "after" stage, the authors propose three tasks: strengthening the memory framework (its national character, stability and contemporary relevance), correcting the direction of memory, and enriching its carriers. Correcting direction means criticising "deviant memory" from erroneous trends of thought such as historical nihilism and ordering the "chaotic memory" of fragmented online space. Carriers include symbols, commemorative rituals and digital media. The authors conclude that integrating collective memory is always in progress and never finished. They hold that the call to forge a strong sense of community gives a historical opportunity to select, reproduce and reshape memory according to present needs. The aim is a memory with strong cohesion and internal continuity that gives cultural strength for moving forward. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholarship applies memory theory to ethnic policy and national identity, or want its catalogue of memory carriers and commemorative practices.

Comrade Deng Xiaoping and reform and opening up 邓小平同志与改革开放 Li Junru Marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth in 2024, Li Junru asks why Deng was able to launch and sustain reform and opening up, and what lessons his approach still offers. Li argues that Deng's historic contribution rested on a long, persistent process of exploration, on firm convictions and a lofty outlook, and on a distinctive "wisdom of reform" that remains worth studying. The piece opens by quoting Xi Jinping's judgement that today's achievements would be unimaginable without Deng's decision. The article has three parts. The first traces Deng's exploration from 1962, when he defended household output contracting in agriculture, through the 1975 rectification, the 1978 debate on the criterion of truth, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the 1982 formulation of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the 1992 Southern Tour talks. The second part examines his convictions. The third distils four features of his method, summed up as practicality, daring, flexibility and steadiness. On convictions, Li contends that Deng pursued reform to uphold and develop socialism, to revitalize China and catch up with the times, and to bring prosperity to the people. Li reports Deng saying that reform is the self-improvement of the socialist system and that poverty is not socialism, and presents his support for letting some get rich first as aimed at common prosperity. Li says critics' charges of "productive-forces-only" thinking were refuted by history. On method, Li reads "practicality" as seeking truth from facts, "daring" as bold experimentation tied to observing and summing up experience, "flexibility" as freeing thought and energising the economy under Party leadership, and "steadiness" as both prudence and stability, which Li calls dialectically unified. Li concludes that reform and opening up opened a new path of wholehearted construction and that Deng's blueprint of socialist modernization is gradually becoming reality. He calls on readers to rally around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to carry reform and opening up through, as a source of momentum for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an official Party-school account of Deng's reform thinking, with many of his quoted remarks, as presented for the 2024 anniversary.

Creative practice in opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times An analysis centred on Xi Jinping's important speeches and instructions to localities and fields of work 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界的创造性实践 He Shaohui Writing in 2024, He Shaohui asks what status Xi Jinping's many speeches, inspection remarks and written instructions to particular provinces, regions and sectors hold in the Party's theoretical innovation. The article's thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), these texts have been an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a new, practical way of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, one that opens up a new realm for that project. The article has three parts. The first treats the speeches and instructions as a component of Xi Jinping Thought: Xi's work experience as a sent-down youth and as a local leader (Zhengding, Ningde, Fuzhou, Zhejiang, Shanghai) is presented as a source of the thought, the texts as its concrete unfolding (for example in Xi Jinping economic thought and Xi Jinping thought on ecological civilization), and as enriching it further. The second part reads them as expressing the philosophical character of Marxism. The third argues that they open a new realm of adaptation. In the second part He identifies three dialectical pairings. The texts are specific yet holistic, uniting the part and the whole: the 'four centres' for Beijing or targeted poverty alleviation announced in Hunan are said to be addressed to a locality but valid nationwide. They are historical and evolving, uniting change and development: Xi's four visits to Hunan, or the move from targeted poverty alleviation to rural revitalization, show continuity with refinement, so they must not be treated dogmatically. They are strategic and long-term, uniting strategy and tactics, as in the positioning of Beijing, Shanghai and Chongqing and the new development philosophy. In the third part He argues that the texts are a model of the Two Integrations, an application of 'seeking truth from facts' (Xi's visits to 14 contiguous poor areas are cited), and a living use of dialectical and historical materialism. He concludes that they are original, principle-level theoretical results of the Party's innovative theory and will keep developing with practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-journal scholar frames Xi's regional inspection tours and sectoral instructions as theory, and how the argument is built from official formulations.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground in ideological and political courses in the new era 新时代思政课坚持守正创新 Yin Hui This short commentary, originally published by People's Daily Online, asks how school ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) should combine fidelity to principle with innovation. Yin defines the Chinese formula "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" as respecting correct direction, principles and laws while breaking through constraints to open new approaches. Applied to these courses, it means holding to their basic task, educational essence and fundamental character while innovating continuously. The article moves through seven areas. The first three concern what must be upheld: the task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, the courses' essence as reasoned argument, and their political and educational character. The remaining four concern innovation: a "big ideological and political course" pattern of education, teaching methods, evaluation systems and the teaching force. Yin argues that the courses must keep pace with the Party's innovative theory and lead students to the conclusion that only socialism can save China and only Chinese modernization can develop it. Teachers should explain Marxist theory in plain language, tie it to everyday life, and draw on the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics and on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture. Yin also calls for linking classroom teaching, course-based ideological education and social practice, for varied methods that respond to digital technology, and for multi-dimensional evaluation of teachers and students. Yin concludes that teachers are the key actors and proposes building a corps that is politically strong, deeply committed, innovative in thinking, broad in outlook, self-disciplined and upright. This, Yin holds, would achieve the high-quality, content-focused development of these courses in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Chinese academics frame the aims and methods of ideological and political education.

A pioneer of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy A study of Chen Xianda's philosophical thought 当代中国马克思主义哲学研究的开拓者 Hao Lixin Published in Guangming Daily on 18 October 2024, a week after the death of Chen Xianda (1930–2024), this tribute and appraisal by Hao Lixin presents Chen as a pioneer of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy. Hao describes Chen, an honorary first-grade professor at Renmin University of China, as a philosopher and educator who held that "philosophers are not spectators of society". The piece argues that his work combined historical depth, problem-oriented engagement with reality and a popular style. The article is organised under four headings. It first covers Chen's insistence on the practical and critical character of philosophy. It then turns to his history-of-thought research, including the first systematic Chinese study of Marx and Engels's intellectual development, a study of Marx's early thought, and the monograph Towards the Depths of History. The third section deals with his "problem-oriented" work on traditional Chinese culture and cultural confidence. The last discusses his philosophical essays written for general readers. Hao highlights three moves. First, in method, Chen held that history and logic must be studied together, that Marxism must be seen as an integrated whole, and that the sources of historical materialism are multiple and not purely philosophical. In Hao's account, this approach guards against dogmatism and rebuts attempts to set a "young Marx" against mature Marxism, and Chen also defended historical materialism against historical nihilism. Second, Chen argued that adapting Marxism to China means solving China's problems. He proposed that Marxism and traditional culture be seen as two aspects of one process, using the phrase "an old country with a new mission" (旧邦新命) and the idea of creative transformation. Third, Chen wrote plain-language essays, such as the "walking towards" image for active reflection theory, and treated Marxist teaching as a matter of belief as well as a profession. Hao concludes that Chen carried forward the practical and critical spirit of Marxist philosophy and set an example for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and for making it accessible to the public. The text is a commemorative appraisal, not a critical assessment. Read the original if you want an overview of Chen Xianda's major works and methodological ideas, or a sense of how Chinese Marxist philosophers present a leading figure of their field after his death.

Nurturing young people's patriotic sentiment through fine traditional Chinese culture 以中华优秀传统文化涵育青少年爱国情怀 Lan Xiaoxia Lan Xiaoxia asks how fine traditional Chinese culture can be used to cultivate patriotic sentiment among young people. Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Lan takes as a starting point Xi Jinping's remarks in Baoji that Chinese civilisation should be studied and explained further, and the Patriotic Education Law, in force since 1 January 2024. Lan's thesis is that, in the new era, combining traditional culture with patriotic education matters both theoretically and practically, and that this requires a systematic training framework. The short commentary has three parts. The first argues why traditional culture is the soil for patriotic feeling. The second sets out four core strands of content. The third proposes a three-part framework covering the education system, its content and its methods. Lan argues that patriotism is the "bloodline gene" of Chinese civilisation and the essence of its fine traditional culture. Cultural identity, in this reading, underlies national and ethnic identity and cultural confidence, and the Party's stress on moral education is said to make traditional culture a means of raising a new generation for national rejuvenation and Chinese modernization. The four strands are: devotion to family and country (citing Mencius and the Book of Rites); unity and a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation, traced to the ancient idea of "great unification"; self-strengthening and innovation (citing the Book of Changes and the Doctrine of the Mean); and harmony, openness and inclusiveness, which Lan links to core socialist values. Lan proposes improving the education system by building a "big ideological and political course" that joins classroom and extracurricular, school and society, and online and offline work. Patriotic content should be graded across primary, secondary and university stages, with supervision and evaluation. Content should stress history education, especially the "four histories", and bring heroes and model workers into schools. Methods should use museums and heritage sites, and also animation, musicals, short videos and other new-media forms that young people favour. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link traditional culture, the Patriotic Education Law and youth ideological education in practice.

How does Marxism understand "education"? 马克思主义如何理解“教育” Gong Keju Published in Study Times in October 2024, this short commentary asks how Marxism understands and approaches education. Gong Keju answers by drawing on Marx and Engels, arguing that proletarian education has defined tasks, methodological requirements and a political character, and that its essence is the all-round development of the human being. The piece moves through three perspectives. It begins with the demands that large-scale socialised production places on the training of labour. It then turns to the three dimensions of educational method that arise from practice as a relationship between subject and object. Finally it considers education historically, in terms of its political character and its essential purpose. Gong, building on Capital, identifies three tasks: changing "general human nature", imparting skills in a particular branch of labour, and producing developed and specialised labour-power together with firm ideals and fighting spirit. The three methodological dimensions are that educators must themselves be educated, that learners should stress self-improvement and self-education, and that the Communist Party must lead the education of workers. Gong adds that, citing Engels, education must be free of bourgeois influence and serve proletarian interests. Citing Marx, Gong holds that only proletarian education unites raising social production with the all-round development of people. Gong closes by describing education as a cornerstone of national rejuvenation. Xi Jinping's statements on education since the 18th Party Congress (2012) are presented as continuing and developing Marxist educational thought. They are said to answer the questions of whom to train, how to train them and for whom. Read the original if you want a brief Party-press overview of how Marx and Engels's remarks on education are being marshalled for current policy.

The logical path of common prosperity from the perspective of systems thinking 系统观念视阈下共同富裕的逻辑进路 Zhu Fengming Wang Ziyu Zhu Fengming and Wang Ziyu ask how common prosperity, which they describe as a complex, long-term systemic undertaking, can be understood and advanced through systems thinking. They note that systems thinking was raised to the level of a principle at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) and listed among the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Their thesis is that common prosperity can be driven forward only if its inner laws are grasped through this approach. The article has three parts, which the authors call the logical starting point, the logical support and the logical destination. The first defines systems thinking and its four features: foresight, a global view, strategic character and wholeness. The second reviews what the Party has done since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under each feature, citing figures on the Gini coefficient, regional GDP shares, poverty alleviation, social insurance, charitable trusts, culture and trade. The third turns to remaining problems and proposals. The authors argue that, since 2012, the Party has applied each feature in turn. For foresight, they cite the shared-development concept, the Zhejiang demonstration zone and the three staged targets for 2025, 2035 and the mid-century. For the global view, they cite the poverty-alleviation campaign, the treatment of common prosperity as integral to Chinese modernization, and regional coordination. For strategy, they cite its definition as a major political question bearing on the Party's governance base and the coordinated arrangement of primary, secondary and tertiary distribution. For wholeness, they cite the unity of efficiency and fairness, of material and cultural wealth, and of internal and external factors. They admit that the gap between urban and rural incomes remains large and that the Gini coefficient is still above 0.40. To carry systems thinking through the whole process, the authors call for a broad historical perspective and a global outlook, citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. They also call for balanced planning that gives priority to top-level design, high-quality development, rural revitalisation and prosperity achieved through hard work, while avoiding welfarism. Finally, they propose efficient coordination: macro-level policy coherence, and the pairing of an effective market with a capable government, urban–rural integration, state and private sectors, domestic and international circulation, and material and cultural progress. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how systems thinking is used to frame common prosperity policy, with the statistics the authors cite.

On the "dao", "xue" and "shu" of teaching ideological and political theory courses 论思政课教学的“道”“学”“术” Liu Jianjun Yin Li Liu Jianjun and Yin Li take up a formulation from Xi Jinping's speech of 18 March 2019 to teachers of ideological and political theory courses: that teaching these courses well involves not only technique (shu) but also scholarship (xue) and, above all, the Way (dao). The authors note that scholarly interpretation of this line is thin and inconsistent. They argue that it amounts to a theory of levels of teaching attainment, with technique as the lowest, scholarship as the middle and the Way as the highest. The article opens by defining the three elements and their relations, then discusses the theoretical and practical value of Xi's formulation and the question of word order. Three main sections follow, one on each level: acquiring technique, building scholarly foundations, and raising one's intellectual and ideological standing. The authors draw on Xi's speeches of 2019, 2022 and 2024, on Ministry of Education regulations for these courses, and on Lenin and Dewey. The authors read the three terms as a hierarchy that is also integrated: technique is the outward expression, scholarship the knowledge that supports it, and the Way its soul. They say this triad develops the traditional two-part Chinese notion of dao and shu into a new theory of teaching attainment. They also distinguish two orderings. Dao–xue–shu describes the overall logic of the theory and is used in the title, while shu–xue–dao describes the real process by which a teacher advances. Technique means observing teaching regulations, practising skills, learning from outstanding teachers and developing teaching artistry. Scholarship means systematic study of Marxist classics and of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, plus broad knowledge, research that supports teaching, and linking theory to practice. The Way means the political height and strategic thinking of a teacher who sees themselves as a political figure and spokesperson of the Party and state. It also means mastering Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, firm belief in Marxism, deep personal commitment, and following the laws of teaching, whose essence the authors, citing Xi, call "reasoning" (jiang daoli). The authors conclude that a teacher who grasps the essence of these courses and follows their laws, applying the "eight unities" from Xi's 2019 speech, unites dao, xue and shu and reaches the highest level of teaching. They propose further theoretical research on the levels of attainment and call for teachers to treat self-improvement as a lifelong pursuit. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars systematise Xi's remarks on ideological and political course teaching into a framework for training teachers, or if you study the language of Party-directed pedagogy.

How university ideological and political theory courses can teach the Party's innovative theory of the new era well 高校思政课如何讲好新时代党的创新理论 Xiao Guiqing Xiao Guiqing asks how university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) can teach the Party's innovative theory of the new era effectively to young students. The article, published in Marxism and Reality in 2024, argues that this is a historic responsibility of higher education. In Xiao's view it follows from the need to train a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and the task must be done by making the theory taught in depth, thoroughly and in a lively way. The article has three parts. The first sets out why teaching this theory matters. The second sets out what the courses must convey: the theory's development, its scientific system, and its worldview and methodology. The third proposes methods under three headings: making the theory 'deep' (jiang shen), 'thorough' (jiang tou) and 'lively' (jiang huo). Xiao draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements about ideological and political courses. Xiao gives three reasons for the importance of the task. The theory is the latest result of the Two Integrations, especially integration with fine traditional Chinese culture. It is the guiding thought for building a modern socialist country and for Chinese modernization. And teaching it carries out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education (lide shuren). On content, Xiao says teachers must present the theory as continuous with Mao Zedong Thought and later Party theories, and must combat erroneous views, notably on the relationship between the periods before and after reform and opening up. They must also explain the 'Ten Clarifications', 'Fourteen Commitments' and 'Thirteen Areas of Achievement', and the 'Six Musts' as a unified worldview and methodology. On method, Xiao calls for reading primary texts and building a coordinated matrix of courses from undergraduate to doctoral level, and for answering students' sharp questions through problem analysis. Xiao also calls for theoretical analysis that balances political and scholarly aims, and for everyday language. Xiao further favours student-centred teaching, new media, practical teaching outside the classroom and case studies. Xiao concludes that students should not only learn the theory but also apply its standpoint and methods to real problems, since this is how the courses achieve their purpose of fostering virtue. The article warns against reciting documents, against replacing reasoning with preaching, and against reducing teaching to a pile of stories. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned account of how Chinese university theory courses are expected to teach Xi Jinping Thought, including course structure and teaching methods.

The US "Summit for Democracy" and new challenges to China's ideological security 美国“民主峰会”与我国意识形态安全的新挑战 The article asks what the Biden administration's "Summit for Democracy" is for and what it means for China. Writing after the third summit (March 2024, hosted by South Korea), the author argues that the summits are an instrument of ideological war against China and other states labelled "authoritarian". In the author's account they pose a set of new challenges to China's ideological security. The text has four parts. It first explains why Washington revived the "democracy card", then analyses the summits' "normative" and "functional" attributes. It then identifies three inherent flaws, and finally turns to the threat to China and Chinese responses. The evidence comes from US strategy documents, summit declarations and initiatives, Freedom House reports and American scholars such as Fukuyama, Hal Brands and Robert Manning. The author contends that the summits serve to shore up a relatively declining US hegemony and to repair the image of American democracy damaged by political polarisation and the Capitol riot of 2021. Their ideological aim, the author says, takes priority over their practical functions, which include technology export controls, a coalition over Ukraine and Taiwan, and funding for "democratic reformers" in ways the author compares to Cold War and "colour revolution" tactics. The author finds three flaws: a monolithic "American-style democracy" presented as plural, vague and instrumental criteria for invitations, and a false "democracy versus authoritarianism" story that ignores domestic causes of democratic decline. For China, the author sees pressure on core values, set against the "common values of all mankind", and on the development model of Chinese modernization. The author proposes three responses. At the macro level, a holistic ideological security outlook under the overall national security concept. At the meso level, stronger international communication through combined official and non-official channels. At the micro level, tighter control of online platforms and foreign NGOs. The author also warns against being drawn into a comprehensive ideological contest like the one that exhausted the Soviet Union. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar frames the US democracy summits as an ideological security problem and what countermeasures are proposed.

A critique of historical nihilism from the perspective of the "big historical view" 大历史观视阈中历史虚无主义批判 Gao Bingliang Gao Bingliang asks how the "big historical view" (da lishiguan), which Xi Jinping has stressed repeatedly since the 18th Party Congress (2012), can be used to criticise historical nihilism. The article argues that this view is a Marxist historical outlook that grasps history across long time spans, in its connections and in its inseparable objective conditions and subjective creativity. On this basis, Gao holds that historical nihilism is an idealist trend that rejects Marxism's guiding role, the historical necessity of China's turn to socialism and the leadership of the Communist Party of China. The article is organised in three parts. The first identifies the idealist essence of historical nihilism, surveying its Western forms from god-centred myth, through reason- and will-centred philosophy (Plato, Hegel, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche), to postmodern historiography, and tracing Marxist struggles against it from Marx to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the period since 2012. The second examines its value standpoint. The third treats opposition to it as a political struggle, drawing on the Soviet collapse, the "Arab Spring" and current policy measures. Gao's core argument is that historical materialism is the decisive weapon: it returns attention to real life and the study of productive forces and relations, it relies on full and accurate historical materials, and it treats the Party's own errors by acknowledging, analysing and correcting them. Gao then argues that nihilism stands against the people, denying their role as historical subject, serving the logic of capital through commodified and falsified history, and weakening class consciousness and aspirations for a better life, including through online entertainment. Politically, Gao claims it assisted Western "peaceful evolution" in the USSR and Eastern Europe, citing Xi's account of the Soviet collapse, and that it attacks Marxism, promotes a "Western-centric" model of modernization and magnifies the Party's setbacks. Gao concludes that the struggle is in essence one against Westernisation, division, infiltration and subversion, and must be won through a comprehensive effort. The proposals are: strengthen Party leadership over ideological work, guide and manage media and monitor online opinion, and use legal means. The article lists the 2016 Party guidelines, the 2018 Heroes and Martyrs Protection Law and the 2020 Criminal Law amendment. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how current Party-ideological writing links the big historical view to the campaign against historical nihilism and to the policy and legal instruments used in it.

Chinese modernization as a wholly new form of human civilization 中国式现代化是全新的人类文明形态 Tian Pengying Zhang Xiaopeng Tian Pengying and Zhang Xiaopeng take up Xi Jinping's description of Chinese modernization as "a wholly new form of human civilization". They treat it as an evaluative proposition about civilizational value and ask what lies behind it. Their answer is that Chinese modernization combines several civilizational sources in a new synthesis, differs from Western modernization, and points to the future of human civilization. The article is organised in three parts. The first examines how Chinese modernization came to be, as an integrated creation. The second compares it with Western modernization. The third considers its orientation towards the future. The authors draw on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Aristotle, Hegel and Fukuyama. In the first part, the authors argue that Chinese modernization is an integration of three elements: a "本我" (original self) in fine traditional Chinese culture, a "真我" (true self) in the advanced essence of scientific socialism, and a "自我" (self) formed by dialectically learning from the "other", chiefly the West. They hold that this is guided by the Two Integrations. In the second part they argue that the formula "modernization equals Westernization" mystifies capitalist modernization, which is only a particular form of "modernization in general". Western modernization has a dialectical character, but its negative side recurs: polarisation, materialism, ecological conflict and violent expansion. Against this, the authors set the five features of Chinese modernization named at the 20th Party Congress (2022): a huge population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. The authors present these as socialist in essence. In the third part they argue that Chinese modernization is historically isomorphic with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and guides it, setting targets for 2035 and the mid-century.
