The "way of becoming a person" in Fang Keli's educational thought 方克立教育思想中的“成人之道” Zhang Xiaoping Liu Zihan Zhang Xiaoping and Liu Zihan present the educational thought of Fang Keli, the philosopher and educator who died more than four years before the piece was posted in 2024. They argue that Fang's principles for training graduate students form a coherent "way of becoming a person" (chengren zhi dao), meant to produce first-rate philosophy and social-science talent for the twenty-first century. The authors treat this as a legacy for later teachers and students. The article, a short newspaper-style tribute, first introduces Fang: a member of the Academy's Divisions, former president of the CASS Graduate School and former chief expert of the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project. He graduated from Renmin University in 1962 and taught for 58 years at Renmin, Nankai and CASS. It then sets out three clusters of ideas under separate headings: balancing learning and conduct, rigorous scholarship and noble character, and careful cultivation with strict management. In the authors' account, Fang's first principle, put forward in 1982 at Nankai, was "balance learning and conduct, cultivate both virtue and vocation". It unites knowing with doing and scholarship with moral character, summed up in his remark "three parts learning, seven parts being a person". The second, announced in 1998 at the Graduate School's twentieth anniversary, was "rigorous scholarship, noble character". It calls for diligence, evidence-based work, study of historical materialism and a plain, unpretentious style. The third, "careful cultivation, strict management", rests on Fang's view that a strict teacher produces outstanding students. It requires teachers to lead by example and to teach according to each student's aptitude. It also encourages the "six first-rates" that students themselves proposed: character, cultivation, knowledge, vision, ability and physique. The authors conclude that strengthening education requires strengthening teachers. They call for a highly skilled teaching corps with high ethical standards, for promoting the "spirit of educators" and for carrying out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education (lide shuren). They propose that today's educators inherit Fang's approach to scholarship and conduct. Read the original if you want a concise, admiring portrait of a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher's views on graduate training and teacher ethics, as presented in an official Chinese academic setting.

Comrade Deng Xiaoping as a shining example of upholding emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts 邓小平同志是坚持解放思想、实事求是的光辉典范 Gao Xiang This is the opening speech by Gao Xiang, President of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, at a national academic symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, later published in Studies of CPC History (2024, no. 4). Gao argues that Deng's most important intellectual trait and most distinctive style of leadership was adherence to emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts. The speech has three parts. It first treats Deng's role in re-establishing this ideological line after the Cultural Revolution. It then follows the principle through reform and opening up and socialist modernization. Finally it turns to his judgement of the character of the era and his foreign policy, and closes with a short reference to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gao presents the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) as the turning point. Under Deng's guidance, in Gao's account, the Party ended "class struggle as the key link" and shifted its focus to economic construction. Gao then lists the "leftist" and dogmatic ideas Deng is said to have countered: the Soviet model, skipping stages of development, and the preference for poor socialism over prosperous capitalism. Deng's answers were socialism with Chinese characteristics, the primary stage of socialism, and a definition of socialism's essence. Gao adds that Deng admitted and corrected errors in reform. On international affairs, Gao says Deng dropped the thesis that war is inevitable and named peace and development as the themes of the age, which underpinned opening up and the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. Gao calls this ideological line the fundamental weapon for winning advantage, initiative and the future, and credits Xi Jinping with taking it to a new level. He urges unity around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, defending the Two Establishes and achieving the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a brief, authoritative statement of how the Party leadership presents Deng's legacy in 2024.

Carrying forward the great cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics that Comrade Deng Xiaoping pioneered 把邓小平同志开创的中国特色社会主义伟大事业不断推向前进 Party History and Literature Research Institute of the CPC Central Committee Marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, this commemorative article from the Party History and Literature Research Institute of the CPC Central Committee appeared in Qiushi, the Party's theoretical journal. It argues that Deng's achievements were both historic and global, and that the best way to honour him is to follow his path. In the authors' framing, that means advancing the building of a strong country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, in line with the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The text has three parts. The first reviews Deng's career from the Baise Uprising and the civil-war campaigns, through socialist construction, to his role as core of the second generation of leadership after 1978, and then lists the personal qualities the authors attribute to him. The second assesses Deng Xiaoping Theory and its place in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The third derives six requirements for Chinese modernization from Deng's statements. The authors present Deng Xiaoping Theory as the first relatively systematic answer to how socialism can be built in a economically and culturally backward country. They name emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts as its essence. They cite his formulations on the primary stage of socialism, productive forces, the "three benefits" test and "one country, two systems". They place the theory as the opening work of the system of theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics, followed by the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which they call the "new language" of the present era. Each requirement for Chinese modernization is tied to Deng quotations and then to current policy. These are Party leadership, development as the "hard truth" now recast as high-quality development, continued reform and opening up, common prosperity and all-round human development, peaceful development, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article concludes that Deng's path has broadened and that his blueprint is becoming reality. It also reminds readers of his warning that the decades to the middle of the century would be a critical period requiring hard work. It calls on Party members to rally around Xi Jinping, to implement the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and to pursue Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party's research institute links Deng's legacy to Xi-era policy and vocabulary in 2024.

Deng Xiaoping's thought on reform and its value for our times 邓小平改革思想及其时代价值 Qu Qingshan Published in Qiushi in 2024, this article by Qu Qingshan takes up Xi Jinping's speech marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth. It asks what Deng's thinking on reform consisted of and why it still matters. Qu argues that Deng's reform thought forms a complete system within Deng Xiaoping Theory, and that it continues to guide efforts to deepen reform further and advance Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical conditions behind Deng's reform thought, summed up as four foundations. The second lists its main components and credits it with the results of reform and opening up. The third links it to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and to Xi Jinping's thinking on reform. On the origins, Qu names four foundations: the fate of the Party and country after the Cultural Revolution, lessons from socialist revolution and construction, the trends of the age, and the people's hopes for a better life. The core of the article then presents eight themes, each tied to Deng's words: Communist Party leadership, reliance on the masses, reform as the self-improvement of the socialist system, reform as liberating the productive forces, comprehensive reform, a method of being bold but steady, the criteria of the 'three favourables', and opening up as part of reform. Qu then maps the 'six adherences' of the 2024 plenum onto Deng's ideas: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, institution-building, the rule of law, and a systematic outlook. Qu concludes that more than 40 years of reform and opening up have produced what the author calls two miracles, rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. In Qu's account, they have also opened a Chinese modernization path and a new form of human civilisation. Quoting Deng's 1985 remark that reform must be judged over decades, Qu calls for upholding the banner of reform and opening up and putting the Central Committee's reform plans into effect. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how Deng's reform ideas are being linked to the 2024 plenum's reform agenda.

Achieving spiritual independence and self-reliance: historical process, theoretical implications and practical paths 实现精神上的独立自主：历史进程、理论意蕴与实践进路 Liu Mingsong The article takes up the idea of 'spiritual independence and self-reliance', which Xi Jinping put forward at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development (2023). Liu Mingsong argues that it is an important part of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. In Liu's account it is required by the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilization, and it supplies spiritual strength for Chinese modernization. Liu also holds that it strengthens the Party's fighting capacity and demonstrates the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first traces the historical process under successive Party leaderships, from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to the new era. The second sets out the theoretical implications, under three headings: Marxist belief, socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese civilization. The third proposes six practical paths. Liu's central claim is that spiritual independence underlies every other kind of independence, quoting Xi's warning that without it political, intellectual, cultural and institutional independence would be undermined. In the historical section Liu reads the Zunyi Conference (1935), the search for a Chinese path to socialism, Deng's call to 'go our own way' and the 2021 historical resolution as stages of this process. Liu argues that material and spiritual self-reliance depend on each other and that independence is not isolation. Liu concludes that spiritual independence is a necessary route to national rejuvenation and to a new form of human civilization that goes beyond the equation of modernization with Westernization. The article calls for upholding Marxism, strengthening ideological work, and drawing on traditional culture while engaging openly with the world. It is a Party-line exposition that draws mainly on leaders' speeches and official documents. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how current Party scholarship places 'spiritual independence' within Xi Jinping's thought on culture and Party history.

Continuously improving the relevance and appeal of ideological and political theory courses 不断提高思政课的针对性和吸引力 Xu Chuan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2024, asks how ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) in Chinese schools and universities can become more relevant to students and more attractive to them. Xu Chuan argues that the answer lies in closing the gap between what is taught and what students need, and in using better teaching methods to win their interest and emotional identification. The author treats these courses as the key means of carrying out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's repeated calls between 2016 and 2024 to raise the relevance and appeal of these courses. It defines the two key terms, then sets out two main sections: three relationships that should guide reform, and three practical routes for improvement. Xu lists current difficulties, including clashing currents of thought, teaching that is disconnected from students' lives, and methods that have not kept pace with the times. On the three relationships, Xu calls for unity of purposiveness and lawfulness, meaning the aim of training successors to the cause of national rejuvenation must be pursued in line with the laws of ideological work, teaching and student development. Xu also wants grand narrative and micro-narrative linked, so that large themes are carried by examples close to students' lives. The third is multi-dimensional coordination, combining online and offline, theory and practice, to move from piecemeal "indoctrination" to an intelligent, "multi-coupled" model. The routes proposed are: a problem-oriented approach that matches supply to demand at each stage, with enlightenment in primary school, experiential learning in middle school, and theoretical, exploratory learning at university; teaching language that is substantive, reasoned, emotionally engaged, measured, interesting and flavourful; and practice-based learning through the "Big Ideological and Political Course". Xu concludes that the courses should combine the classroom with the wider society, using resources such as revolutionary museums and memorial halls, so that students move from passive listening to active observation and sharing. The author calls for integrating open "Big Ideological and Political Course" resources, building a coordinated mechanism and pooling forces across society. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and recommended teaching methods for ideological and political education in China's schools as of 2024.

Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of biocapitalism in the twenty-first century 21世纪国外左翼学者对生物资本主义的批判 Liu Pengfei Gu Yongchun This review surveys how Western left-wing scholars since the early 2000s have analysed biocapitalism, the form of capitalism that extracts profit and capital accumulation from the life sciences and biotechnology. Liu and Gu take as their starting point Kaushik Sunder Rajan's Biocapital: The Constitution of Postgenomic Life (2006), which blends Marxist political economy with Foucauldian biopolitics. Their central claim is that these scholars describe the phenomenon well, but that their critique stays at the level of appearances and needs Marxist political economy to go deeper. The review is organised in three parts followed by a concluding discussion. The first part treats biocapitalism as the latest form of capitalist domination, with both continuities and new features. The second looks at the 'instrumentality' and 'redemptive' character of biocapitalism through the interplay of the logic of capital and the logic of power. The third examines biocapitalism as a biological expression of neoliberalism and new imperialism. The authors draw on Rajan, Nikolas Rose, Clayton Pierce, Melinda Cooper, Joseph Dumit and others. Liu and Gu report that, in these scholars' accounts, biocapitalism leaves private ownership and the exploitation of the proletariat intact. Biotechnology is financed by venture capital and stock markets and protected by patents, which the review describes as a 'legitimate monopoly'. Exploitation, however, shifts from the person as labour-power to the person as a living organism: value is sought in 'future' products, and working time and leisure blur as life itself becomes a source of value. Capital and state power jointly fund the life sciences, as in the Icelandic deCODE genetics database, and cloak them in a 'pseudo-religious ideology' of national salvation, as Rajan found in Indian laboratories. The review cites cases such as the Guaymi patent and the trade in kidneys as 'bio-imperialism' and 'biocolonialism'. The authors conclude that most of these scholars, constrained by their standpoint, offer only reformist or utopian solutions. They argue that the whole process of biocapitalism stays within the horizon of Marxism, and that Marxist critique of political economy is needed for a scientific response. Turning to practice, they stress the importance of biosecurity and biotechnology development for China, and they ask whether biocapitalism might eventually shift towards 'biosocialism'. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist overview of Western critical literature on biocapital, with its sources and cases, and its assessment of that literature's limits.

The self and the subject in the perspective of the materialist conception of history 唯物史观视域中的自我与主体 Sun Lin Sun Lin takes up a problem that has run through idealist philosophy: how the self and the subject can be brought into inner consistency. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that only Marx, through the materialist conception of history, unified the two historically and logically on real ground. Idealism, in Sun's account, began the path to unity, but its versions all stayed within consciousness or the Absolute. The piece is a compact critical history in four steps. It first takes Descartes and Kant, then Fichte, then Hegel, and finally sets out the materialist alternative. At each stage Sun describes how the thinker linked self-consciousness (the self) with the acting or willing subject, and then gives the verdict of the materialist conception of history. Sun presents Marx's critique of idealism as at the same time a critique of the modernity of capital. Sun reads Descartes as resolving mind–body dualism through a spiritual substance, which leaves the self and the subject split. Kant's self-consciousness and free will remain apart, on the sides of theory and practice. Fichte unites them through the self's deduction of the categories, but cannot explain concrete, varied reality. Hegel reaches unity through the externalisation and retrieval of self-consciousness in social interaction, yet the result is crowned as "absolute" and so becomes illusory. Sun then argues that Hegel's logic of externalisation and return mirrors the logic of capital, which captures profit and surplus value and returns to itself as self-valorising capital. On this reading, Hegel's consistency is the false unity of fetishism, in which relations between people have become relations between things. For Sun, the materialist conception of history turns the speculative subject into a real subject that stays beyond mere appearance. Through its own objectifying activity, this subject achieves an inner consistency of self and subject under definite historical conditions. Sun calls for raising productive forces to break through fetishism, and for raising labour capacity to overcome objectified labour, so as to move toward a society of free and all-round development for everyone. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how the self–subject problem from Descartes to Hegel is recast through Marx's critique of capital and fetishism.

Hegel's thought on labour examined from the standpoint of historical materialism 黑格尔劳动思想的唯物史观考察 Zhang Donghui Li Chunxiao Hegel's account of labour is idealist in essence, yet Zhang Donghui and Li Chunxiao argue that it contains clear tendencies towards historical materialism. Starting from Marx's remark that Hegel grasped the essence of labour from the standpoint of modern political economy, the article asks what Hegel saw in modern industrial society and where he stopped short of Marx. Their answer is that Hegel's work laid a foundation for Marx's social critique and political economy but never left objective idealism. The text first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2024). The article is organised in three sections. The first treats labour and the division of labour, the second labour and machines, and the third value as abstract labour. The authors draw on Hegel's early Jena writings (System of Ethical Life, the first Jena system draft) and the Elements of the Philosophy of Right. They also bring in Adam Smith, Adam Ferguson, Lenin and Georg Lukács as reference points, and compare Hegel repeatedly with Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The authors report that Hegel, following Smith, saw the division of labour as a system of social cooperation. In their reading, it turns purposive labour into abstract, simplified and repetitive labour. This raises skill and output but makes individuals mutually dependent and separates labour from its purpose. On machines, they argue that Hegel treated tools as mediation between humans and nature and machines as the point where labour becomes "lifeless". He saw the worker reduced to an appendage of the machine system, and he saw impoverishment and the emergence of a rabble, a picture the authors find strikingly close to Marx's early account of alienation. On value, they say Hegel distinguished use-value from value, treated value as abstract labour and as a social relation among private labours, and saw in money a social relation that anticipated what Marx called fetishism, though in a mystified idealist form. Hegel's proposed remedy was state regulation of civil society, for example through taxation. The authors conclude that Hegel's limits are plain. He never entered the language of political economy properly, never worked out the relation between concrete and abstract labour, and described alienated labour only empirically. He did not see all labour under commodity production as alienated, did not distinguish machinery in general from its capitalist application, and did not grasp capital's domination over labour. Nor did he understand labour as a mode of production through which social formations and historical laws can be understood. They cite Lenin's judgment that historical materialism applies and develops a germ of genius found in Hegel. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese Marxist assessment of Hegel as a precursor of Marx's critique of political economy.

François Furet on the materialist conception of history and the French Revolution 傅勒论唯物史观与法国大革命 Zhu Xueping This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (8 August 2024) presents François Furet's book Marx et la Révolution française (Marx and the French Revolution). Furet wrote it to counter the simplified, dogmatic and teleological work of the mainstream French school of Revolution historiography associated with Soboul and Mazauric. Zhu reports that Furet collected Marx's main statements on the Revolution from 1842 to 1871 in order to show how Marx differs from his twentieth-century French followers. Zhu follows Furet's analysis around two questions: how Marx understood the relation between the French Revolution and social revolution (the problem of a "second revolution"), and the autonomy of politics. The article moves through three stages: the young Marx, Marx after the formation of the materialist conception of history, and Marx's analyses of 1848 and the Second Empire. In Zhu's account of Furet, the young Marx arrived at social revolution from the backwardness of Germany and from his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. He saw the Revolution as the "matrix" of social revolution and recognised the state's autonomy only as "alienation" or "illusion". After the materialist turn, Furet argues, class interest becomes an all-purpose explanation. Marx then infers French bourgeois maturity from the outbreak of revolution instead of proving the necessity of revolution from that maturity. Furet concludes that revolutionary action, rather than economic development, decides in Marx's practice, so that Marx derives economic and social change "from political history". Zhu adds that Marx's early and later views are not contradictory, and that he grounds the second revolution in revolutionary practice. The author concludes that the materialist conception of history cannot be applied mechanically but must be used according to concrete historical circumstances. Zhu also calls for treating socio-economic and productive-force development as the basic starting point of all undertakings. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language introduction to Furet's critique of Marx's account of the Revolution.

Grasping the scientific connotations of the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee 深刻把握党的二十届三中全会精神的科学内涵 Shi Baoguo This newspaper commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, sets out how Shi Baoguo reads the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. Shi argues that the Decision opens a new chapter for reform and is of major significance for implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece has three parts: the significance of implementing the Plenum's spirit, its core essentials, and the scientific methods for putting it into practice. On significance, Shi claims the Decision enriches Marxist theory on social contradictions and stages of social development, serves as an action guide for Chinese modernization, and extends the Party's theoretical achievements. On core essentials, Shi names four: goal orientation, with the overall aim of improving socialist institutions and modernizing national governance by 2035; systematic integration of reform, led by economic reform; a people-centred approach, illustrated by social security, housing, childbirth support and gradual retirement-age reform; and political assurance through the Party's self-reform. On method, Shi lists "seven focuses": a high-standard socialist market economy, whole-process people's democracy, a culturally strong country, better living standards, a beautiful China, a higher level of national security, and stronger Party leadership. Shi concludes that these focuses apply the unity of the universal and particular in contradictions, and that under Party leadership the country will keep strong political cohesion and confidence in development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official reading of the 2024 Third Plenum was presented to Chinese academic and general readers.

Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as guide to building the "five social sciences" 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想指引“五大社科”建设 Zhang Xinke This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 8 August 2024, asks how philosophy and the social sciences in China should develop under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhang argues that the work should aim at five goals: theoretical, applied, popular, open and digital social science. Together these are meant to let the social sciences fulfil their functions of understanding the world, passing on civilisation, innovating theory, advising government, educating people and serving society. The article opens by noting the importance the Party Central Committee has attached to philosophy and the social sciences since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then takes the five goals in turn, each given a short section. Zhang closes by describing how the five fit together. Examples of practice come from Jiangsu province, and the article's final lines express the hope that Jiangsu's social science work will flourish. For each goal Zhang names one defining trait and one key word. Theoretical social science rests on "innovation": it should systematise theory and make it more scholarly, citing Engels on theoretical thinking and Xi's call for systematised, academically grounded theory. Applied social science rests on "practice": it should serve Party and government decision-making through think tanks, consultancy reports and institutional reform. Popular social science rests on "popularisation": it should reach minors, farmers, urban workers and civil servants. Open social science rests on "inclusiveness": it should link regions, institutions and disciplines, with social science federations as bridges. Digital social science rests on digitisation: it should use the internet, big data and AI, of which Zhang cites ChatGPT as an example. Zhang concludes that the five form an organic whole. Theoretical social science plays the role of reaching the sky, while the other four plant the work on the ground, turning results into practice that serves the people and socialism. Applied work stands at the level of practice, popular work at the level of people, open work at the level of fields, and digital work at the level of information. Zhang presents this as support for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance on the social sciences is framed in provincial academic administration, with Jiangsu as the case.

Solidly advancing high-quality development through economic structural reform 以经济体制改革扎实推动高质量发展 Niu Yaqian Tian Chaowei Published in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2024, this commentary follows the Third Plenum decision on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. Niu and Tian ask how economic structural reform relates to high-quality development. They argue that high-quality development inherently requires deepening economic structural reform, because production relations must be brought into line with the productive forces. The piece has three parts. The first explains why high-quality development calls for reform. The second reviews how adjusting production relations has driven growth since reform and opening up. The third sets out three directions for further reform. It draws on Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, on Deng Xiaoping, and on Xi Jinping's statements about new quality productive forces. The central argument rests on the historical-materialist claim that productive forces ultimately determine production relations. In the authors' reading, China has moved from high-speed growth to high-quality development, and new quality productive forces are taking shape. The authors cite figures for 2012–2023: GDP rising from 53.9 trillion to over 126 trillion yuan, per capita GDP from 6,301 to 12,681 US dollars, R&D spending from 1.91% to 2.64% of GDP, and a rise in the Global Innovation Index ranking from 34th to 12th. They say such forces need new production relations and a high-standard socialist market economy. They list remaining obstacles: administrative monopoly and market segmentation, weak institutional support for innovation, and unsmooth urban–rural integration. They also credit reform of ownership, of the market mechanism and of distribution for past success. The authors propose three steps. The first is to improve the mechanisms that put the Two Unwaverings into practice: strengthening state-owned enterprises and protecting private property rights and entrepreneurs. The second is to build a unified national market and a high-standard market system, ending local protectionism. The third is to establish a new system of high-standard opening up, including rule-based opening, free trade pilot zones and the Belt and Road Initiative. They hold that reform favouring innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development will keep high-quality development moving forward. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link Marxist theory of production relations to the Third Plenum's economic reform agenda.

Grasping the core meaning of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 科学把握构建中国特色哲学社会科学主旨要义 Feng Yanping This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how the Party's understanding of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics should be correctly grasped. Feng argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and especially since Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium speech on philosophy and social sciences, the Party has deepened its understanding of three attributes: the people-centred character (renminxing), the character of the times (shidaixing) and subjectivity (zhutixing). Together these are said to give the direction and basic guidance for building these disciplines. The article is organised in three sections, one for each attribute. The first treats the people-centred character as the essential attribute of the field. The second treats the character of the times as defining its mission and tasks. The third treats subjectivity as the basis for building an autonomous system of knowledge. Each section draws mainly on Xi Jinping's statements and on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). On the people-centred character, Feng holds that Marxism is a theory for the people, so upholding its guiding role and the Party's overall leadership in the field follows from the unity of Party spirit and the people's character. Research should be oriented to the people's major concerns, and the work should follow Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the character of the times, Feng points to the "two irreplaceables" (the irreplaceable position of the discipline and the irreplaceable role of its scholars). The article says scholars must answer the questions raised by great changes and by the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. On subjectivity, Feng sets out six requirements: continuity and national character, originality and timeliness, and systematic and specialised character. The author criticises areas where Western ideas are treated as canonical and says this reflects the lack of an autonomous knowledge system. The Two Integrations are presented as the epistemology and methodology for building such a system, with Chinese modernization, civilisation studies and the theory of the Chinese nation as a community given as examples. Feng concludes that integrating Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture should make Marxism "Chinese" and traditional culture "modern". This is said to supply internal strength for an autonomous knowledge system with Chinese style and Chinese features, and to widen the cultural roots of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames the aims and principles of building Chinese philosophy and social sciences.

Three dimensions for developing philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 发展中国特色哲学社会科学的三重向度 Hong Xianghua Marking the eighth anniversary of Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences (17 May 2016), this commentary asks how the accelerated building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics should be understood and advanced. Hong argues that the task has to be examined along three dimensions: the perspective of development, its driving force and its mode of thinking. The stated aim is a field strong in disciplinary layout, scholarly foundations, research level, service capacity and international influence, supplying intellectual support for building a modern socialist country. The piece was first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024 and is organised under three headings. The first concerns drawing on ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign resources; the second concerns theoretical innovation guided by problems; the third concerns building a systematic project across several fields. It treats Xi Jinping's speeches as top-level design and as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Hong first calls for a proactive historical spirit that looks in four directions. Inward, the field should address practical questions that concern the nation and the people. Outward, it should offer ideas on questions of humanity's future. Forward, it should address the trajectory of socialism with Chinese characteristics and of the long-governing Marxist party. Backward, it should revive fine traditional Chinese culture through creative transformation. Second, Hong holds that subjectivity, originality and responsiveness to the times come from a problem orientation, in which problems are the source of truth and innovation, and cites concepts such as a harmonious society and a community with a shared future for mankind as original products of the reform era. Third, Hong sets out a systematic project with three pillars. The disciplinary system should strengthen Marxist theory, basic disciplines, emerging and neglected fields. The academic system should cover autonomous knowledge production, research organisation, digital platforms and evaluation. The discourse system should produce distinctive concepts that international audiences can understand. Hong concludes that the field must be built on Chinese tradition, practice and problems, so that Chinese theory explains Chinese practice and practice in turn builds theory. The goal is academic discourse matching China's overall national strength and international standing, and Chinese scholarship that goes global. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official programme for Chinese philosophy and social science and of the vocabulary used to present it.

On the historical formation of ownership and the limits of the concept A twofold explanation of the multiple character of ownership from the standpoint of historical materialism 论所有制的历史形成及概念局限性——历史唯物主义视域中所有制多重性质的双重解释 Chen Guangsi Why do many forms of ownership in history appear to combine public and private features at once? Chen Guangsi takes up this question, starting from Marx's 1858 description of land ownership in British-ruled India, where it was unclear whether land belonged to the state or to private owners. Chen gives a twofold answer: such forms were shaped by several intertwined historical factors, and the concept of "ownership" itself carries a hidden private-property bias that makes them look mixed. The article moves from the historical to the linguistic level. It first looks at pre-capitalist cases: primitive clan society, classical Athens and feudal Western Europe. It then analyses the German term Eigentum (with property and propriété), and finally turns to Marx's "revolution in terminology", drawing on the Grundrisse, A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and Marx's letters. A short conclusion applies the argument to ownership under socialism with Chinese characteristics. In the first, "preliminary" explanation, Chen argues that ownership forms are more composite the more varied and interlocked the factors behind them are. Clan ownership was shaped by kinship and natural geography. Athenian land ownership was shaped by political citizenship and natural conditions. Feudal land ownership was shaped by kinship, jurisdiction, military, religious and customary factors. The second, deeper explanation is that Eigentum etymologically means what is "one's own". Marx was the first to give it the sense of an ownership system (suǒyǒuzhì). Chen argues that using the word therefore makes capitalist private ownership the implicit prototype, and every other form is read as a variant of it. On this reading, pre-capitalist societies look confused or backward, which Chen says implicitly defends capitalism. Chen explains that Marx countered this with a "revolution in terminology", treating communal ownership as the original form and private ownership as a product of its dissolution. Chen cites Marx's remarks on Indian communal property and Roman and Germanic private property, and his later work on anthropology. In closing, Chen suggests that asking how to understand the "mixed ownership" of socialism with Chinese characteristics shows that the question has not yet been posed in the right terms. Chen calls for developing an up-to-date concept of ownership and a discourse suited to Chinese socialism, and describes this as a long task. Read the original if you are interested in Marxist theory of ownership, in the conceptual history of Eigentum, or in how Chinese scholars approach the concept of mixed ownership.

The world-historical significance of a high-standard socialist market economy 高水平社会主义市场经济体制的世界历史意义 Sun Laibin Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which put the building of a high-standard socialist market economy at the forefront and set the goal of completing it by 2035, Sun Laibin asks what this project means beyond China. Sun argues that it has world-historical significance in three respects: the history of economic thought, the history of world modernization, and Chinese modernization. The article traces the line from the 1993 decision on establishing a socialist market economy, through the 18th Party Congress (2012) emphasis on the decisive role of the market in allocating resources, to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the 2024 plenum. It is organised in three parts. The first sets the Chinese approach against Western mainstream economics, certain Marxist traditions and market socialism. The second treats modernization dilemmas, and the third treats the institutional role of this economic system in Chinese modernization. Sun's core claim is that combining the basic socialist system with a market economy goes beyond neoclassical and Keynesian economics, which both treat capitalism as the suitable system. It also goes beyond Marxists such as Bertell Ollman and Hillel Ticktin, who see market and socialism as incompatible, and beyond Western market socialism, which Sun says drifted away from public ownership. Sun reads Marx's late thinking on Russia and Lenin's New Economic Policy as leaving room for this combination, and credits Deng Xiaoping with separating market and plan from the basic social system. The system is also said to address two problems of world modernization, vitality versus order and efficiency versus fairness, by combining an effective market with an enabling government. Sun concludes that the system is a key safeguard of Chinese modernization. Economic reform is the "ox's nose" that leads wider reform, reform must target specific problems such as an incomplete market system and an unresolved government–market relationship, and the 2035 target gives a clear goal. Sun cautions against both "plan worship" and the belief that the market can settle everything. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar presents the socialist market economy in Party-theory terms, set against Western economics, Marxist debates and market socialism.

A political manifesto opening China's modernization drive: rereading Mao Zedong's report to the Second Plenum of the Seventh Party Central Committee 开启中国现代化征程的政治宣言——重读毛泽东在中国共产党七届二中全会上的报告 Guo Chunsheng Guo Chunsheng rereads Mao Zedong's March 1949 report to the Second Plenum of the Seventh Party Central Committee, held at Xibaipo, through the lens of Chinese modernization as set out in the 20th Party Congress report (2022). The article argues that the report is a political manifesto that opened China's socialist modernization drive. In Guo's reading, it contains an original theory of modernization that fixed the nature and direction of the project before the People's Republic was founded. The article has four sections. The first traces the emergence of Mao's modernization thinking from his 1945 report On Coalition Government, his planned 1947 trip to Moscow, and his January 1949 talks with Anastas Mikoyan on economic and transport assistance. The second shows that the report's sixth section, on the economy, uses the terms "modernity" and "modernization", and places this alongside the postwar rise of Western modernization theory and Nehru's The Discovery of India. The third sets out four layers of Mao's theory. The fourth covers the concrete measures the report assigns to Party leadership. Guo identifies the four layers as the move from tradition to modernity, from countryside to city, the consolidation of urban leadership and recovery of production, and the Party's mastery of technology and management. In this account, Mao treats industrialization as the core of modernization and describes the roughly 90 per cent of dispersed agriculture and handicrafts as "ancient". Mao proposes guiding these sectors cautiously and step by step towards modernization and collectivization. Guo adds that the report puts state industry first, restricts private capital, plans foreign trade under state control, and names improved living standards for workers and the people as the aim of production. Guo contrasts all this with early Western theory, which Guo describes as equating modernization with Westernization. Guo concludes that Mao's report fixed the socialist character of China's modernization: leadership by the Communist Party, a leading state economy, and the transformation of an agrarian country into an industrial one. Guo links its "stood up" declaration to Xi Jinping's sequence of standing up, becoming prosperous and becoming strong. Read the original if you want a close Chinese reading of this 1949 report as a source for the Party's own account of the roots of Chinese modernization.

Enriching China's independent knowledge system of economics with the experience of Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化经验丰富中国自主的经济学知识体系 Chang Qingxin Chang Qingxin takes up a question set by Xi Jinping's June 2023 speech on cultural inheritance: how to turn Chinese experience into Chinese theory and achieve "independence and self-reliance in spirit". The article applies this to economics. It argues that systematically distilling the economic experience of Chinese modernization into systematic economic doctrine is the key to enriching and improving an independent Chinese knowledge system of economics. This is a short commentary originally published on the Guangming Online theory channel. It is organised around five tasks, each linking an aspect of practice to the knowledge system: identifying its main content, expanding its specific content, building its distinctive advantages, bringing out its independent character, and giving it cultural depth. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's formulations and on the record of the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Chang's first move is to make Xi Jinping Thought on the economy the core of the system. In the article's account, this body of thought is a systematic theoretical summary of new-era practice and has opened a new realm for Marxist political economy. Its principles should therefore supply the system's main content and structure. The second move is to ground the system in outcomes: rapid industrialisation, the elimination of absolute poverty and the Party's upholding of the basic socialist economic system. The article also presents Chinese modernization as breaking the equation of "modernization = Westernization". Chang contrasts its people-centred orientation with capital-centred Western modernization, which is said to bring stagnation, polarisation and social conflict. Economics should explain this advantage in Marxist concepts and draw lessons for developing countries. On autonomy, Chang says the system should be built around "what we are doing", citing new quality productive forces as an example. It should also tell China's story in international language, and may borrow reasonable elements of Western economics, such as finance, pricing and quantitative modelling, while keeping China's own needs first. Chang adds that traditional ideas, such as common good, enriching the people, and harmony between humans and nature, are compatible with Marxist political economy. Marxism should revive them through creative transformation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official theory discourse frames the project of an independent Chinese economics.

Xi Jinping Thought on Culture points the direction and path for resolving the problems of cultural inheritance and development 习近平文化思想为解决文化传承与发展问题指明了方向和路径 Sun Xiguo Sun Xiguo, in a commentary first published in Beijing Daily and posted in September 2024, asks how contemporary Chinese culture can be inherited and developed. The answer, Sun argues, lies in Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, which the author presents as a theoretical summing-up of the Party's cultural work in the new era and as an enrichment of Marxist cultural theory. The piece opens by listing the questions this body of thought is said to resolve: upholding the Party's cultural leadership, building China's own knowledge system, achieving the Two Integrations (especially the second), promoting cultural prosperity, building a culturally strong country, and constructing a modern Chinese civilization. It then sets out five requirements for inheriting and developing culture, each introduced by its own heading and supported by quotations from Xi Jinping. Sun's core argument runs through these requirements. Cultural confidence and problem-orientation mean turning Chinese experience into Chinese theory, because a theory is innovative only if it answers the problems of its age. Marxism is the 'soul' and fine traditional Chinese culture the 'root'. Sun holds that Marxism and traditional culture must be combined so that each fulfils the other, with Marxism becoming Chinese and traditional culture becoming modern; the result is described as the cultural form of Chinese modernization. Foreign culture should be absorbed openly but made local, with the Chinese-centred principle illustrated by the saying that a tangerine tree north of the Huai turns bitter. Finally, Sun takes up 'integrated innovation', a method first proposed by the philosopher Zhang Dainian, arguing that scholars never fully solved how to carry it out and that Xi Jinping Thought on Culture now supplies the guidance. Upholding fundamental principles while innovating means defending Marxism's guiding position, the Two Integrations, the Party's cultural leadership and the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation, and on that basis uncovering new materials, problems, views and theories. Sun concludes that this thought provides ideological assurance and cultural conditions for building a modern socialist country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the main principles of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture as applied to cultural inheritance.

Mao Zedong's strategic guidance in the great War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea 毛泽东在伟大抗美援朝战争中的战略指导 Mao Xinyu Marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, this commentary from Beijing Daily asks how Mao and the Party Central Committee won the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea against a far stronger opponent. Mao Xinyu argues that the victory rested on Mao's art of strategic direction, which let a weaker force defeat a superior one. The author holds that this experience still offers practical lessons for meeting complex risks and challenges today. The article is organised in four sections: the decision to fight abroad; control over the war's course from preparation to ending; new strategy and tactics suited to the opponent; and a people's war that combined many forms of struggle. Each section describes Mao's decisions and closes with a short lesson for the present. On the decision, Mao Xinyu says Mao weighed fighting against building the new state and judged that fighting would protect long-term interests. He is said to have limited the war by sending "volunteers" rather than the People's Liberation Army, confining it to the Korean peninsula, and restricting its aims to restoring the pre-war situation. Fighting beyond the border is presented as a way to achieve strategic defence. On the conduct of the war, the author stresses preparing for the worst case, switching between counter-offensive and positional defence, and ending through negotiation backed by military strength. On tactics, Mao is credited with recognising the enemy's strengths ("much steel, little spirit") and weaknesses and his own side's opposite profile. Mao Xinyu lists the resulting methods: small annihilation battles, rotation of troops, tunnel-based defence, night fighting, flanking manoeuvres and a "steel transport line". The final section stresses mobilising the people, the alliance with the Soviet Union and Korea, political, economic and diplomatic struggle, and fighting while negotiating. Mao Xinyu concludes that war decisions must follow the strategic overall situation, with military action subordinate to politics and immediate gains to long-term interests. Uncertainty is described as a defining feature of modern war, to be countered by deliberate, scientific leadership. The author also calls for relying on the people, combining military struggle with political, economic and diplomatic struggle, and strengthening an integrated national strategic system amid intensifying great-power rivalry. Read the original if you want an official-leaning, Mao-centred account of how Chinese military thinking frames the Korean War and its lessons today.

From "the bright moon in the heart" to "the world of practice": decoding the textual codes of Mao Zedong 从“胸中明月”到“实践天地”：破译毛泽东的文本密码 Chen Jin Chen Jin, in a short piece first published in Beijing Daily, explains why he wrote a book on the history of Mao Zedong's texts. He argues that much commentary on Mao stops at what Mao said and reduces it to a few dry concepts. In Chen's view, readers who do not know why Mao said it grasp only the outline and miss the "surplus value of thought". The article presents the book's approach in three parts: the history of how the texts were written, how they were circulated, and how they were received. Chen's aim is to "decode" Mao's textual codes and trace the link between what he calls Mao's inner "bright moon" and his "world of practice". On writing, Chen holds that Mao wrote to answer the problems of his time, citing the Gutian Conference resolution, which grew out of a dispute within the Fourth Red Army, and On Protracted War, written against the "subjugation" and "quick victory" theories. On circulation, he points to the 1925 essay on China's social classes, the "paper tiger" remark carried abroad through an interview with Anna Louise Strong in 1947, and disguised editions printed under the covers of martial-arts novels or Buddhist sutras. On reception, he notes that many texts were accepted only after setbacks, and concludes that the Chinese Communist Party's history of success is the history of how Mao's thought was accepted. Chen adds that Mao's writing has literary quality, and that the book uses a narrative style, with restored details and scenes, to ease the dryness of theoretical reading. He presents returning to the "textual scene" as a way to appreciate the force of Mao's ideas. Read the original if you want a brief authorial statement of how a leading Chinese Party-history scholar approaches Mao's writings through their composition, circulation and reception.

Marx's view of machines in the perspective of the history of philosophy 哲学史视域中的马克思机器观 Deng Pan Deng Pan asks where Marx's view of machines came from and what it added to earlier philosophy. The article, originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that this view was both a product and a scientific summing-up of nineteenth-century technological development. It also contends that the view is closely tied to Aristotle, Descartes and Hegel, and that Marx ultimately went beyond all three. The piece has two main parts. The first traces the philosophical history of tools and machines. It runs from Aristotle's treatment of the hand, stage machinery and mechanics, through medieval and early modern clock metaphors (Nicholas of Cusa, Ficino, Comenius, Descartes, La Mettrie, Christian Wolff), to Hegel's natural philosophy and his early and late social writings. The second part turns to Marx's treatment of tools and machines in Capital, his reading of contemporary engineering literature, and his Notebooks on Machinery and Technology. Deng argues that Aristotle did not clearly separate tool from machine, that Descartes turned the body into an automaton, and that Hegel distinguished the two. On Deng's reading, Hegel's Jena manuscripts criticise machines for making labour abstract and devalued, whereas the Philosophy of Right credits them with raising productivity. For Marx, by contrast, tools and machines are first of all means of producing surplus value, so their analysis rests on the social and historical conditions of their use. Deng reports that Marx divided developed machinery into motive machine, transmission mechanism and tool machine, and compared this scheme with Moritz Rühlmann's 1862 textbook. For Marx a true machine system exists where a series of complementary tool machines is driven by a central automaton, and Deng calls this the most developed form of machine production. Unlike manufacture, such a system fixes the production process by the machine rather than by the worker's habits, and runs continuously and automatically. Deng concludes that Marx drew on Aristotle and Hegel but surpassed them. Marx moved from Aristotle's technical analysis based on the circle to a view grounded in relations of production, and his conditions for building machines are said to have prepared the ground for later modular, geometric-constraint design associated with Reuleaux. The article adds that Capital set out these ideas systematically and went on to influence German philosophy of technology in the second half of the nineteenth century. Read the original if you want a compact account of the philosophical lineage behind Marx's concepts of the tool machine and the machine system.

The self and the subject from the perspective of the materialist conception of history 唯物史观视域中的自我与主体 Sun Lin Since the beginning of idealist philosophy, the question of the self and the riddle of the subject, especially the problem of their inner consistency, have remained a persistent difficulty. In this short piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, Sun Lin argues that only Marx, through the materialist conception of history, unified self and subject on real ground, both historically and logically. In Sun's reading, Marx's critique of idealism is at the same time a critique of the modernity of capital. The article traces a sequence of idealist attempts to join self and subject: Descartes, Kant, Fichte and Hegel. Each section sets out the thinker's position and then gives the verdict of the materialist conception of history. The final section turns to Marx's own solution, built around the self-activity of the real subject. Sun's account runs as follows. Descartes places self and subject together in a spiritual substance, but his dualism of mind and body leaves them split. Kant separates self-consciousness (theory) from free will (practice), so the subject can encompass the self but not the reverse. Fichte derives the categories from the self's own positing and so merges the two principles, but his self cannot explain concrete, varied reality. Hegel makes the externalisation and reclaiming of self-consciousness in social interaction the basis of subjectivity. For Sun, however, this unity is wrapped in the 'absolute' and so turns illusory. Sun's central move is to read Hegel's logic of objectification as homologous to the logic of capital: capital goes outwards, captures profit and surplus value, and returns to itself as self-valorising capital, which is the subjectivity of things. The consistency of self and subject in Hegel is therefore, Sun argues, a false unity produced by fetishism, in which relations between people become relations between things. The materialist conception of history instead raises the speculative subject to a real subject whose self-activity achieves historically conditioned consistency. Sun concludes that under capitalist private ownership this requires raising productive forces to break through fetishism and raising labour capacity to overcome objectified labour, moving towards a society of the free and all-round development of every person. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist account of how the materialist conception of history positions itself against Descartes, Kant, Fichte and Hegel on selfhood and subjectivity.

Hegel's thought on labour examined from the standpoint of historical materialism 黑格尔劳动思想的唯物史观考察 Zhang Donghui Li Chunxiao Zhang Donghui and Li Chunxiao ask what Hegel's account of labour contributed to the later materialist critique of political economy, even though his philosophy remained objective idealism. Their answer is that, in analysing modern civil society through labour, Hegel grasped the essence of labour from the standpoint of modern political economists. The authors argue that his treatment of the division of labour, tools and machines, and value and money shows clear tendencies towards historical materialism. They note that Lenin and Lukács also saw it as laying groundwork for Marx's social critique. The article, a short piece first published in a Chinese newspaper in 2024, proceeds in four sections: labour and the division of labour; labour and machines; value as abstract labour; and a closing assessment of Hegel's limits. It draws on Hegel's Jena writings (the System of Ethical Life and the First Philosophy of Spirit) and the Philosophy of Right. It also reads him alongside Adam Smith, Adam Ferguson and Marx's 1844 manuscripts. The authors argue that Hegel, following Smith, saw the division of labour making labour and needs increasingly abstract. In their account he saw that it separated labour from its purpose, simplified work into mechanical routines and shaped human subjectivity. Hegel also held that tools mediate between humans and nature and that machines make labour 'lifeless', turning workers into appendages and producing alienation and extreme poverty. The authors say he optimistically expected machines to free up time. On value, they report that Hegel distinguished use-value from value, treated value as abstract labour and as a social relation among private labours, and saw money as a social relation, which Lukács read as anticipating fetishism. They add that he proposed state regulation of civil society, for example through taxation, to counter the pursuit of wealth. The authors conclude that Hegel's limits are plain next to Marx. In their reading, he never entered the terrain of political economy or distinguished concrete from abstract labour. He therefore described alienated labour only empirically, did not see all labour under commodity production as alienated, and did not grasp capital's domination over labour. They add that he did not understand labour as a mode of production through which social formations and historical laws can be grasped. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Hegel's views on labour, machinery and value are read as precursors to Marx's critique of political economy.

François Furet on historical materialism and the French Revolution 傅勒论唯物史观与法国大革命 Zhu Xueping This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, introduces François Furet's book Marx et la Révolution française (Marx and the French Revolution). Zhu explains that Furet, a leading twentieth-century French historian, wrote it to rebut the simplified, dogmatic and teleological historiography of the dominant French school of Albert Soboul, Claude Mazauric and others. Zhu's account is that Furet sought to show a basic difference between Marx and his later French followers. The article follows Furet's collection and analysis of Marx's main statements on the Revolution from 1842 to 1871. It is organised around two questions: how Marx understood the relation between the French Revolution and social revolution (the problem of the 'second revolution'), and the autonomy of politics. It takes in the young Marx, the period after the formation of historical materialism, and the years of Capital. In Zhu's reading of Furet, the young Marx derived the idea of the Revolution as the 'matrix' of social revolution from his own reading and from German backwardness. He did not revere Jacobin dictatorship, and he recognised the state's independence only in the form of 'alienation' or 'illusion'. After his turn to historical materialism, Furet finds a tension: in theory the Revolution was the necessary product of social production, but in practice revolutionary action itself becomes decisive. Furet also finds that Marx reduced the many regimes of France to different bourgeois class fractions, and that his analysis of the Second Empire deduced economic and social evolution from political history. Zhu concludes that the young Marx's views and his later ones do not contradict each other, and that Marx grounded the 'second revolution' in revolutionary practice. Historical materialism, Zhu argues, cannot be applied mechanically but must be tied to concrete historical situations. Zhu also calls for keeping socio-economic development and the productive forces as the starting point of all undertakings. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language introduction to Furet's critique of Marx's account of the French Revolution.

Marx's view of machines in the perspective of the history of philosophy 哲学史视域中的马克思机器观 Deng Pan Deng Pan asks how Marx's account of machines relates to earlier philosophical thinking about tools and machines. The article, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that Marx's view of machines was both a product and a scientific summing-up of nineteenth-century technological development. It also contends that Marx drew on Aristotle, Descartes and Hegel and ultimately surpassed them. The first half traces the philosophical background. It covers Aristotle's treatment of the hand, stage machinery and mechanics, medieval and early modern clock analogies (Nicholas of Cusa, Ficino, Comenius, Descartes, La Mettrie, Christian Wolff), and Hegel's discussion of the steam engine, tools and machines. The second half turns to Marx, mainly Capital (the chapters on the labour process and on machinery and large-scale industry), his notebooks on machines and technology, and the engineering textbook by Moritz Rühlmann. Deng argues that Aristotle did not clearly separate tools from machines and that Descartes made the body an automaton. In the Jena manuscripts, Hegel distinguished tools from machines and criticised machines for making labour abstract and devalued. In the Philosophy of Right, by contrast, Hegel credited machines with raising productivity. For Marx, in Deng's reading, tools and machines are first of all means of producing surplus value, so the question is the social and historical conditions of their use and the class function they serve. Marx divided developed machinery into motor, transmission mechanism and tool-machine, and held that the tool-machine began the eighteenth-century industrial revolution. Deng notes that Rühlmann's 1862 textbook gives a similar classification by order of power transmission. A true machine system, in Marx's sense, links different machines in successive stages under a central automaton. Deng adds that this system reshapes the labour process and goes beyond Aristotle's circle-based mechanics. Deng concludes that Marx built on Aristotle and Hegel while going beyond them. Marx drew on his wide reading in Britain of Babbage, Ure and other writers on machinery and manufacture, set out the results systematically in Capital, and in Deng's account went on to influence German philosophy of technology in the later nineteenth century. Read the original if you want a compact survey of the philosophical genealogy of Marx's concepts of tool, tool-machine and machine system.

The self and the subject from the standpoint of the materialist conception of history 唯物史观视域中的自我与主体 Sun Lin Sun Lin takes up a long-standing problem of idealist philosophy: how the self and the subject can be brought into inner consistency. The article, a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that only Marx, through the materialist conception of history, unified the two on real ground, in both a historical and a logical sense. Sun treats Marx's critique of idealism as at the same time a critique of the modernity of capital. The article reads the idealist tradition as a sequence of attempts at this unification. It treats Descartes, Kant, Fichte and Hegel in turn, then sets out the materialist alternative in a final section. For each thinker Sun describes how the self (self-consciousness) and the subject (the acting, willing agent) are related, and then gives the verdict of the materialist conception of history. Sun's account runs as follows. Descartes unites self and subject in a spiritual substance, but resolves the mind–body split by appeal to God, which leaves them divided. Kant separates self-consciousness from free will, placing them at the theoretical and practical poles, so unity is only partial. Fichte joins them through the self's activity, but his philosophy of action cannot explain concrete, varied reality. Hegel reaches inner consistency through the externalisation and retrieval of self-consciousness in universal social interaction, yet places it in the 'absolute', which Sun says turns it into illusion. For Sun, Hegel's logic of objectification mirrors the logic of capital, which captures profit and surplus value and then returns them to itself as expanded capital. Hegel's unity is therefore a false, fetishistic one, grounded in social relations between things. Sun concludes that the materialist conception of history turns the speculative subject into a real subject that stays outside appearances. Through its own objectifying activity, this subject achieves a historically conditioned unity of subject and self. Under capitalist private ownership, Sun calls for raising productive forces to break through fetishism, and raising labour capacity to overcome objectified labour. The aim is a society of the free and all-round development of every person. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese Marxist scholar reconstructs the path from Descartes to Hegel and ties the problem of subjectivity to the critique of capital.

Hegel's thought on labour examined from the standpoint of historical materialism 黑格尔劳动思想的唯物史观考察 Zhang Donghui Li Chunxiao Zhang Donghui and Li Chunxiao ask what Hegel's account of labour contributed to the later materialist critique of political economy, and where it fell short. Their short article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that Hegel's labour thought is idealist in essence but shows clear historical-materialist tendencies. In the authors' reading, this is why Lenin and Lukács could treat it as groundwork for Marx's social critique and political economy. The authors work from Hegel's examination of modern civil society, drawing on Adam Smith and on conditions in nineteenth-century France and Britain. They take up three themes in turn: labour and the division of labour, labour and machines, and value as abstract labour. Their sources include Hegel's System of Ethical Life, the Jena manuscripts and the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, and they compare his views repeatedly with Marx, notably the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. On the division of labour, the authors say Hegel saw labour turning from purposive activity into simple, monotonous and abstract work. Needs became abstract and the means of satisfying them were separated from labour's purposes. On machines, they say Hegel treated alienated labour as an essential feature of modern society: workers became appendages of machinery, and mental and manual labour were split apart. On value, they say Hegel distinguished use-value from value, treated value as abstract labour and as a social relation among private labours, and saw money as a social relation, which Lukács read as an anticipation of fetishism. They also note his proposal that the state regulate civil society, for example through taxation. The authors conclude that Hegel's limits are plain beside Marx. In their account, he never entered the terrain of political economy or analysed concrete versus abstract labour in depth, so he only described alienation empirically. He did not regard all labour under commodity production as alienated, grasp capital's domination over labour, or understand labour as a mode of production through which social formations and historical laws can be understood. François Furet on the materialist conception of history and the French Revolution 傅勒论唯物史观与法国大革命 Zhu Xueping Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2024, Zhu Xueping presents the French historian François Furet's book Marx and the French Revolution. Zhu reports Furet's claim that Marx's own view differs in essence from that of his twentieth-century French followers. It centres on two questions: how revolution relates to social revolution (the problem of a "second revolution"), and the autonomy of politics. In Zhu's account, Furet finds that the young Marx took the Revolution to be the "matrix" of social revolution and did not revere the Jacobin dictatorship. He also granted the state some autonomy, though only in the form of alienation or illusion. After the materialist conception of history took shape, Furet argues, Marx reduced political forms to bourgeois class interest. He also could not explain the continuity and rupture of 1789–1793, and he inferred the bourgeoisie's maturity from the Revolution's outbreak. Furet concludes that revolutionary action, not social production, was decisive for Marx, and that Marx derived economic evolution from political history. This is why the Second Empire produced the paradox of a bourgeoisie that reigned without governing. Zhu's own view is that these positions do not contradict one another, because Marx grounded the second revolution in revolutionary practice. Zhu holds that the materialist conception of history cannot be applied mechanically and must be adapted to specific historical contexts. Zhu also calls for keeping socioeconomic and productive-force development as the fundamental starting point. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language introduction to Furet's critical reading of Marx on the French Revolution.

Grasping the scientific connotations of the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Party Central Committee 深刻把握党的二十届三中全会精神的科学内涵 Shi Baoguo This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 6 August 2024, interprets the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era guides the building of the "five major social sciences" 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想指引“五大社科”建设 Zhang Xinke This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how philosophy and the social sciences can be built up in the new era under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Solidly promoting high-quality development through economic structural reform 以经济体制改革扎实推动高质量发展 Niu Yaqian Tian Chaowei This newspaper commentary, published in 2024 after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee, asks why and how economic structural reform should drive high-quality development. The core reasoning is drawn from historical materialism: productive forces are the ultimate determinant of social change, and production relations must fit their level and needs. The authors say China's economy has moved from high-speed growth to high-quality development. They cite GDP rising from 53.9 trillion to over 126 trillion yuan, per capita GDP from 6,301 to 12,681 US dollars, and the Global Innovation Index rank from 34th to 12th. They also name remaining obstacles: administrative monopoly, market fragmentation, weak support for technological innovation, and insufficient demand. First, improve the mechanisms for the Two Unwaverings: strengthen state-owned enterprises and protect private property and entrepreneurs' rights. Third, establish a new system of a high-standard open economy, including institutional opening, free trade pilot zones and high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. Grasping scientifically the main thrust of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 科学把握构建中国特色哲学社会科学主旨要义 Feng Yanping This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how the Party's understanding of the philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics should be grasped. Feng Yanping argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and especially since Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium speech on philosophy and social sciences, the Party has deepened its understanding of three attributes: their people-centred character, their orientation to the times, and their subjectivity (autonomy). It must rest on six qualities, including continuity and national character, originality and timeliness, and systematic and specialised character. Feng criticises fields that treat foreign ideas as canonical, and attributes this to the lack of an autonomous knowledge system. Feng concludes that the Two Integrations, of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, are both the epistemology and the methodology for this task. Feng cites Chinese modernization, research on civilization and the theory of the Chinese nation as a community as examples. The aim is to make Marxism Chinese and traditional culture modern, and so to supply endogenous strength to an autonomous knowledge system. Three dimensions in developing philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 发展中国特色哲学社会科学的三重向度 Hong Xianghua Marking eight years since Xi Jinping's 17 May 2016 symposium speech on philosophy and the social sciences, this commentary asks how the task of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics should be advanced. Hong argues that it should be examined along three dimensions: the perspective of development, its driving force and its mode of thinking. On perspective, Hong argues that the field must exercise historical initiative by drawing on three resources Xi stresses: the Marxist theoretical system, fine traditional Chinese culture and foreign social sciences. These should match China's overall strength and international standing.
