The theory of new quality productive forces and the construction of China's independent knowledge system 新质生产力理论与中国自主知识体系建构 Wei Chuanguang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, Wei Chuanguang takes the theory of new quality productive forces as a model case of how China's independent knowledge system is being built. The article holds that the theory, associated with Xi Jinping, is an exemplar of an independent Chinese economics and offers methodological guidance for the wider project. The piece starts from Xi's 17 May 2016 speech on philosophy and social sciences and his April 2022 call at Renmin University to build an independent Chinese knowledge system. It then works through the theory under three headings: coining a distinctive Chinese term, keeping a problem orientation, and innovating theory in response to new practice. Wei argues first that new quality productive forces is a distinctive Chinese term which recasts the Marxist category of productive forces for the present era. In Wei's account, it stresses disruptive technological breakthroughs, innovation-driven development and the innovative allocation of production factors, and it is easily understood abroad. Second, the theory answers problems that "foreign theories" cannot, such as the shift to high-quality development, the digital economy and carbon peaking and neutrality. Engels's late-life guidance of the British workers' movement 恩格斯晚年指导英国工人运动的实践历程 Liu Jian This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how Engels, who led no national or international organisation in his last years, still shaped the British workers' movement. Liu argues that he acted as an intellectual and practical mentor to its most advanced figures, chiefly in two areas: the New Unionism and the founding of an independent working-class party. The article opens with Britain's place in the history of socialism and the decline of Chartist radicalism into trade unionism. It then treats two cases in turn: Engels's 1881 articles and the Marxist-led New Unionism of the late 1880s, and his advice on party-building to figures such as Mahon, Burns, Mann, Hardie and Aveling. Liu argues that Engels identified the limits of trade unionism, which sought only a "fair day's wage" and favoured a labour aristocracy. In his Labour Standard articles he named wage labour itself as the root of the problem and called for workers' ownership of the means of labour and for independent political organisation. Liu credits Marxists with leading the 1889 London dock strike, after which union membership is said to have risen from 860,000 to nearly two million. On party-building, Liu holds that British labour's dependence on the Liberals was the main obstacle. The Independent Labour Party (1893) later drifted into reformism, which Liu reads as proof that a workers' party cannot succeed without scientific socialism. Liu concludes that Engels guided British workers by indirect means: letters, newspaper articles and programmatic advice. He thereby carried on the work he and Marx had begun, and Liu says he deserves the title of the modern proletariat's most outstanding scholar and teacher. The scholarly logic of Engels's research on scientific socialism 恩格斯科学社会主义研究的学理逻辑 Zhang Fan This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how Engels studied scientific socialism and what that method offers present-day research. Zhang argues that Engels upheld Marxism's basic method while building specific methodological principles suited to scientific socialism, and so carried Marxism a considerable step forward. The article distinguishes two levels of Engels's method. One concerns scientific socialism as theory, including its place within the whole of Marxism. The other concerns it as practical movement and institutional form, including the general laws, principles and paths of social development. Zhang adds a third element, the personal qualities Engels demanded of researchers. On the theoretical side, Zhang says Engels treated dialectics, epistemology and logic as identical, required full command of concrete material, and warned against quoting out of context. Each principle of scientific socialism, in this reading, must be linked historically to other principles and to concrete experience, so that dogmatism is avoided. On the practical side, Engels made historical materialism the foundation and dialectics the mediation for grasping capitalism's tendency towards self-negation. Zhang adds that class analysis, with class struggle as the main thread, stayed central for Engels even late in life. Engels also asked that researchers be diligent learners rather than hunters of new phrases. Zhang draws five lessons for research on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They are to start from the changed principal contradiction in Chinese society, to keep a people-centred stance, to study the logical starting point of Chinese Marxism, to document its methodology, and to adopt a rigorous, truth-seeking attitude. Engels's critique of erroneous currents of thought 恩格斯对错误思潮的批判 Zhang Lin Zhou Yang This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that the history of Marxism is also a history of struggle against erroneous theories. Zhang and Zhou contend that many of Marxism's classic ideas took shape through polemics, and that Engels was not only a founder and developer of Marxism but also its loyal defender. The article reviews four of Engels's critiques in turn: Proudhonism, Bakuninism (anarchism), Dühringism and dogmatism about economic determination. It follows them from the 1840s to the late nineteenth century. On Proudhon, the authors say Engels exposed reformist schemes that left capitalism intact and prepared the ground for Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy and for Marxism's guiding role in the First International. Against Bakunin, Engels held that the state would fall once capital was abolished and the whole mode of production transformed, and that urging workers to abandon politics was mistaken. The Hague Congress of 1872 expelled Bakunin. In Anti-Dühring, the authors write, Engels attacked Dühring's philosophy, economics and socialism, and thereby set out Marxism's three component parts as one organic whole. Against the dogmatists, Engels held that the economic factor is decisive only "in the last instance", and he affirmed the relative independence of ideology. The authors conclude that Engels defended and developed Marxism after Marx's death by taking on non-Marxist currents. They hold that surveying these critiques helps consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere and is the best way to commemorate Engels. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-oriented overview of Engels's polemics and the lessons Chinese scholars draw from them.

A scientific understanding and grasp of Engels's view of authority 科学理解与把握恩格斯权威观 Li Houdong This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks what Engels's view of authority offers for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee. Li argues that Engels, in struggles against erroneous ideas inside and outside the working class, set out why authority matters for production and revolution, what it scientifically means, and how it relates to obedience and autonomy. Li holds that this has direct significance for the current stage of building a modern socialist country. The article draws mainly on Engels's Anti-Dühring and "On Authority". It is organised in three sections: why upholding the Central Committee's authority is the basic guarantee of building a modern socialist country; why the key lies in the leader's core position; and why the root lies in combining institutional authority with the authority of the rule of law. Li reads Engels as showing that authority is an objective necessity of social development, illustrated by cotton mills and railways, and as criticising anarchists who reject all authority. Li links this to the 14th Five-Year Plan period, when a complex environment calls for the Central Committee to supply guidance, leadership and mobilisation. Li treats "core" and "leader" as closely related, quoting Engels's ship-in-danger example, and argues that a party gains cohesion only by establishing and defending its leading core, namely Xi Jinping. Li adds that obedience increasingly rests on consent, with democratic and consultative elements. Li concludes that Central Committee authority depends on the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and above all on institutions and law. Perfecting the basic political system and the constitution-centred legal system would embed legal authority in political authority. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Engels's "On Authority" is used in Party-theoretical argument for upholding central leadership.

Three important documents in "Engels on China" and their theoretical value “恩格斯论中国”的三篇重要文献及其理论价值 Wang Donghong Wang Donghong, in a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2024, argues that research on what Marx and Engels wrote about China needs a full inventory of the texts. Wang counts at least 80 works by Engels on China between 1839 and 1894, and presents three that are absent from the 2015 edition of Marx and Engels on China and have not been studied. The article is organised around three texts. These are the early political essay Letters from the Wuppertal (1839), the dictionary entry "Burmah" (1858) written for The New American Cyclopaedia, and "A Newly Discovered Case of Group Marriage" (1892). Wang also notes Engels's passing references to China in letters of 1840 and in the 1842 work on Schelling. Wang reads the 1839 essay's mention of Chinese script as the earliest sign of Engels's interest in China, earlier than the 1845 Elberfeld speech that scholars usually cite. On "Burmah", Wang summarises its account of the China–Burma border, trade goods and religious differences. Wang adds that Engels's letters to Marx show how laborious the short entry was, which Wang takes as evidence of a scientific and rigorous approach. In the 1892 piece, Engels translated a Russian report that described the Giliak people as long subject to "China-ised" Manchus. Wang suggests this anthropological use of "China-ised" may help trace the origin of the concept of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Wang concludes that these texts enrich research on Engels's life and work and on the Marx–Engels relationship. The author also draws from the 1892 translation, with its more than ten alterations for German readers, an image of Engels as a translator. Wang presents the "Burmah" entry as relevant to the history and prospects of the Southwest Silk Road. Read the original if you want a bibliographic pointer to little-studied Engels texts that mention China.

On Engels's "three greats" 论恩格斯的“三个伟大” Wang Yonghe Marking the 200th anniversary of Friedrich Engels's birth, this commentary (first published in China Social Sciences Today, 18 August 2024) proposes three headings for understanding him: a great life, a great character and great contributions. Wang Yonghe argues that Engels, together with Marx, supplied the proletariat and humanity with Marxism as their strongest intellectual weapon. The piece is short and organised under the three headings. It first outlines Engels's biography (1820–1895) and his path from a bourgeois family in the Rhine Province to the workers' movement. It then turns to his friendship with Marx and his modesty, and finally lists his theoretical contributions. On life, Wang stresses his two years living among workers in Manchester, which produced The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). On character, Wang points to his financial support for Marx, his postponement of work on Dialectics of Nature to edit Marx's manuscripts, and his remark that he played "second violin". Wang cites Lenin on the friendship. On contributions, Wang names five: co-founding Marxism's basic theory; editing volumes two and three of Capital; systematising Marxism by integrating historical and dialectical materialism and naming "scientific socialism"; original work in philosophy, political economy and socialist theory; and defending Marxism against dogmatic readings and economic determinism. Wang concludes that Engels's life, character and contributions deserve remembrance, study and respect. Read the original if you want a brief, Lenin-based overview of how Chinese commentary presents Engels's role beside Marx on his bicentenary.

Rethinking the Marxist view of progress 重新认识马克思主义进步观 Zhao Song Zhao Song takes up the charge, made by some Western scholars, that Marx was a "progressivist" whose view of history is metaphysical. The article, a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today, argues that this reading misrepresents Marxism. Zhao contends that the Marxist view of progress is neither an eschatological "end of history" thesis nor a linear theory, because it is built on real human beings and their activity. The article first sets out two Western readings. Fukuyama is presented as equating Marx with Hegel in positing a final historical goal, with communism as Marx's endpoint. Sean Sayers is cited as treating Marx's theory as linear, a succession of stages each replaced by a higher one. Zhao then answers each reading in turn, drawing on passages from Marx and on Fredric Jameson. On the first point, Zhao concedes that Marx's images of a "free association" and a "realm of freedom" suggest a goal. Even so, Zhao argues that history has no preset purpose of its own: purposes belong to human activity, so history cannot end while people exist. Communism is therefore a new beginning, the end of "prehistory", as Jameson puts it. On the second point, Zhao holds that Marx's late study of "Eastern societies" and his reply to Mikhailovsky rejected a single path for all nations. The article also argues that linear progress presupposes a super-historical subject such as Hegel's spirit, whereas Marx made real, living people the agents of history. Zhao describes the Marxist view as a spiral that unites the diversity of historical paths with general laws. Zhao concludes that equating Marxism with these forms of progressivism betrays its human-centred starting point. A correct understanding, Zhao argues, has to begin from the human dimension and recognise the irreplaceable position of real people in historical progress. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language rebuttal of Fukuyama-style and linear readings of Marx, along with the passages from Marx it relies on.

The dual logic of Marx's theory of social progress 马克思社会进步理论的双重逻辑 Zhang Wen This short piece in China Social Sciences Today asks how Marx's theory of social progress relates to the Enlightenment philosophy of history from which it grew. Zhang argues that the theory contains a dual logic. The first is the grounding of history in "material relations of life". The second is the understanding of social progress as a "natural history". Together, the author contends, the two logics turn the philosophy of history into a science of history. The article first sketches the Enlightenment background, taking Kant and Hegel as its examples. It then sets out the shared premises and the decisive break with that tradition. The two main sections are headed "Understanding history through 'material relations of life'" and "Social progress as 'natural history'". The piece closes by drawing the two logics together. Zhang reads Kant's "hidden plan of nature" and Hegel's "absolute spirit" as cases where history becomes a footnote to reason. Marx, in this account, replaces reason with practice, meaning the material production of life by real human beings, as the measure of history. The constant element that makes a science of history possible is the contradictory movement of the productive forces and the relations of production, which Zhang presents as the "driving force" of social progress. The second logic draws on Marx's remark in Capital about the development of the economic formation of society as a process of natural history. Zhang uses it to show that society shares the materiality of nature, so that progress follows laws independent of human will. Yet society also transforms nature into a "humanized nature", which gives progress a subjective dimension. Human initiative can grasp the laws and speed up progress, as in the "Caudine Forks" leap, without negating the priority of nature. Zhang concludes that the two logics are not split apart but unified in material production and in the core theme of practice. On this reading, Marx's theory is a rigorously logical system. It breaks with idealist approaches to history and offers what the author calls the best account of the laws of social progress, in which progress unfolds as the working-out of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Read the original if you want a concise, Chinese-language statement of how Marx's break with Enlightenment philosophy of history is currently presented in Chinese academic commentary.

Engels's late-life guidance of the British workers' movement in practice 恩格斯晚年指导英国工人运动的实践历程 Liu Jian This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks how Engels, in his last years and without leading any organisation, shaped the British workers' movement. Liu Jian argues that he became an intellectual and practical mentor to the international workers' movement. In Britain he guided it in two ways: through the New Unionism and through the founding of an independent working-class party. The article opens by noting Britain's place as the home of utopian socialism and the birthplace of scientific socialism. It says that after Chartism the British working class lost its revolutionary edge and trade unionism took hold. Liu then takes two cases in turn: the New Unionism of the late 1880s, and Engels's advice on party-building, including the Independent Labour Party founded in 1893. Liu contends that Engels criticised trade unionism for settling for "a fair day's wage for a fair day's work" and for creating a labour aristocracy. In his 1881 articles for the Labour Standard, Engels pointed to wage labour itself as the root problem, called for workers' ownership of the means of labour and urged workers to organise and send their own representatives to parliament. Marxist-influenced leaders such as Tom Mann and John Burns led the movement, and the 1889 London dock strike was its climax. On party-building, Liu says Engels urged a break with dependence on the Liberal Party. The later reformist turn of the Independent Labour Party is presented as proof that a workers' party cannot succeed without scientific socialism as its theory. Liu concludes that Engels's indirect guidance, through letters, articles and advice to leaders such as Mahon and Hardie, marked each stage of British party-building. Liu holds that his work was inseparable from Marx's and that he deserves the title of outstanding scholar and teacher of the modern proletariat. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Engels's practical influence on late nineteenth-century British labour politics.

The logic of Engels's research on scientific socialism 恩格斯科学社会主义研究的学理逻辑 Zhang Fan This short commentary asks how Engels studied scientific socialism and what his methods mean for research today. Zhang argues that Engels upheld Marxism's basic method while building more specific methodological principles suited to scientific socialism's object and content, thereby carrying Marxism a step further. The article distinguishes two levels in Engels's work. One concerns scientific socialism as theory, including its content, relations and place within the whole of Marxism. The other concerns socialism as a practical movement and institutional form, including general laws, basic principles and paths of development. It closes with proposals for research on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On theory, Zhang reports that Engels treated dialectics, epistemology and logic as identical, called for analysis based on full command of concrete material, and warned against quoting out of context and against dogmatism. On practice, Engels is said to have made historical materialism the methodological base, mediated by materialist dialectics, to show how capitalist private ownership cannot accommodate the productive forces and moves towards self-negation. Zhang adds that Engels kept class analysis central to the end of his life, calling violent seizure of political power the "only door to the new society". Engels also stressed researchers' diligence and a sound scholarly attitude. Zhang draws five tasks for research on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They are to start from the changed principal contradiction in Chinese society, to keep a people-centred position, and to study the logical starting point of Sinicized Marxism through dialectics, epistemology and logic. They also include drawing out its methodology and keeping a rigorous, truth-seeking attitude. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how Engels's methodological writings are being tied to current Party-theory research.

Engels's critique of erroneous currents of thought 恩格斯对错误思潮的批判 Zhang Lin Zhou Yang This short commentary starts from the claim that the history of Marxism is also a history of struggle against erroneous theories. Zhang and Zhou argue that Engels was not only a founder and developer of Marxism but also its loyal defender. In their account, he criticised harmful currents in the workers' movement without mercy, and these critiques helped Marxist theory mature. The article takes four targets in turn: Proudhonism (together with Grün's \"true socialism\"), Bakuninism, Dühringism and dogmatism in late nineteenth-century Germany. Each section links Engels's critique to a stage in the consolidation of Marxism, from the First International to the Hague Congress of 1872 and the later defence of historical materialism. Zhang and Zhou report that Engels rejected Proudhon's reformism and his scheme of buying up France with workers' savings, which they say showed the necessity of violent revolution. Against Bakunin, Engels held that abolishing capital, not the state, must come first, and that telling workers to abandon politics pushes them towards priests or bourgeois republicans. Against Dühring, he set out Marxism's three components: philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. Against dogmatists who reduced Marx to economic determinism, he held that the economy decides only \"in the last instance\" and that ideology has relative independence. The authors conclude that Engels, who played \"second fiddle\" while Marx lived, took up Marx's unfinished work after his death. They hold that tracing his critiques helps consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, and they call this the best way to commemorate him. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-oriented overview of Engels's polemics and how they are presented today.

A scientific understanding of Engels's view of authority 科学理解与把握恩格斯权威观 Li Houdong Li Houdong asks what Engels's writings on authority offer for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee in the present period. The commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, argues that Engels's view of authority gives direct theoretical grounds for upholding that authority as China moves to build a modern socialist country in all respects. The piece draws mainly on Engels's Anti-Dühring and On Authority, and links them to the 14th Five-Year Plan and the 2035 long-range objectives. It is organised in three parts: why Central Committee authority is the basic guarantee of modernization, why the leader's core status is the key, and why institutional and rule-of-law authority is the foundation. Li reads Engels as treating authority as an objective necessity that accompanies social development, citing his examples of cotton mills and railways and his critique of anarchist rejection of all authority. In Li's account, Engels's stress on a core and leader means that upholding Central Committee authority includes upholding the core position of the leader, here identified as Xi Jinping. Li adds that authority now carries non-coercive meanings such as democracy, consultation and participation, and must combine political, institutional and rule-of-law authority. Li concludes that Party organisations should put political development first, unite around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and turn the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds into political commitment. Li also calls for improving the legal system centred on the Constitution, so that rule-of-law authority is embedded in political authority. Read the original if you want a short example of how Engels's On Authority is used in current Party-building discourse.

Three important documents in "Engels on China" and their theoretical value “恩格斯论中国”的三篇重要文献及其理论价值 Wang Donghong Wang Donghong, in a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks what Engels actually wrote about China. The author notes that existing compilations of Marx and Engels on China are selections rather than complete collections, yet research relies heavily on them. Wang counts at least 80 works by Engels touching on China between 1839 and 1894 and presents three texts absent from the 2015 edition of Marx and Engels on China and, the author says, not yet studied. The article takes the texts in turn: the 1839 journalistic piece Letters from the Wuppertal, with related early writings on religion; the dictionary entry Burma (1858), written for The New American Cyclopaedia; and the 1892 translation-and-commentary A Newly Discovered Case of Group Marriage. Wang argues that the first group shows Engels's interest in China from the age of eighteen, earlier than the 1845 speech usually cited, with Chinese writing and religion serving as markers of a distinct civilisation. The Burma entry, in the author's reading, gives detailed information on China–Burma geography, trade and cultural differences, and reflects Engels's careful, scientific method despite the entry's brevity; Wang cites his letters to Marx complaining about the labour it cost. The 1892 text uses the expression "China-ised" in an anthropological sense, which Wang suggests may offer a pointer for tracing the concept of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang concludes that these texts enrich the study of Engels's life, his ideas and his relationship with Marx, and that the groundwork of "Marx and Engels on China" requires a full inventory of sources. Read the original if you work on Marx and Engels's writings on China, source compilation, or the genealogy of the term "Sinicisation" in Marxism.

On Engels's "three greats" 论恩格斯的“三个伟大” Wang Yonghe Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this newspaper commentary (China Social Sciences Today, 18 August 2024) proposes three headings for understanding him: a great life, a great character and great contributions. Wang Yonghe argues that together they show why Engels deserves to be remembered, studied and revered alongside Marx. The piece is organised under those three headings. It first sketches Engels's life from his birth in 1820 to his death in London in 1895. It then turns to his friendship with Marx, and finally lists his theoretical contributions, drawing throughout on Lenin's assessments and on a few other commentators. On life, Wang stresses that Engels came from a bourgeois family yet took the revolutionary road, and that his work in Manchester led to The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845). On character, Wang points to the 40-year friendship, his financial support for Marx and his remark that he played "second violin". The contributions are set out in five points. Engels co-founded Marxism with Marx. He edited volumes two and three of Capital after Marx's death. He systematised Marxism, including the dialectics of nature and the name "scientific socialism". He made pioneering contributions in philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. He also defended Marxism against dogmatic readings and economic determinism. Wang concludes that Engels's lifelong struggle for proletarian and human emancipation, his selfless help to Marx and his modesty are all worth remembering and learning from. Read the original if you want a brief, officially oriented overview of how Chinese commentary frames Engels's life and legacy for his bicentenary.

Rethinking the Marxist view of progress 重新认识马克思主义进步观 Zhao Song Zhao Song, in a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (11 May 2024), takes up Western readings that label Marx a "progressivist". The author argues that the Marxist view of progress is neither an eschatological theory of the "end of history" nor a linear theory of progress. Both readings, Zhao holds, misread it by ignoring that it is built on real human beings. The piece first sets out the two Western claims: Francis Fukuyama's view that Marx, like Hegel, posited a final goal of history, and the reading of Sean Sayers and others that Marx's account is a linear sequence of ever higher stages. It then answers each in turn, drawing on Marx's own texts and on Fredric Jameson. On the end of history, Zhao concedes that images such as the "association of free individuals" and the "realm of freedom" suggest a goal. The author denies that this amounts to historical teleology: for Marx, history has no preset purpose, and the only purposes are those of acting human beings. Communism therefore opens a new history rather than closing history, a point Zhao supports with Jameson's formulation of the end of "prehistory". On linearity, Zhao argues that Marx's late study of "Eastern society" and his reply to Mikhailovsky rejected a universal path for all nations, and that Marxism sees history as spiral. Linear progress also implies a supra-historical subject such as spirit or self-consciousness, which Marx criticised in Hegel. In Zhao's reading, history moves through the contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production, driven by human practice, which unites diversity with general laws. Zhao concludes that equating Marxism with the "end of history" or linear progress betrays its human-centred approach. A correct understanding, the author says, must start from the irreplaceable position of real people in historical progress. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language rebuttal of Fukuyama-style and linear readings of Marx's theory of progress.

The dual logic of Marx's theory of social progress 马克思社会进步理论的双重逻辑 Zhang Wen This short commentary asks how Marx's theory of social progress differs from the Enlightenment philosophy of history from which it emerged. Zhang argues that the theory rests on a dual logic. The first is the 'material relations of life' as the source of historical motion. The second is the understanding of social progress as a 'natural history'. Both are said to be unified in human material production, that is, practice. The article first sets Marx against Kant and Hegel. Zhang says that for them history is the movement of an a priori consciousness, whether a hidden plan of nature or the self-realisation of 'absolute spirit'. It then turns to the shared premises that Marx kept: the idea of progress, humanity's capacity to advance society by perfecting itself, and the defence of human subjectivity through humanism. Finally it examines Marx's remark in Capital that the development of the economic formation of society is a natural-historical process. In Zhang's reading, Marx replaces 'reason' with 'practice' as the measure of history. Enlightenment thinkers, the author says, leave history split between empirical reality and transcendental reason and turn it into a footnote to reason. Marx instead locates a constant element in the material relations of life, the totality of production relations that form an economic structure. The contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production is what makes a science of history possible and drives progress. The 'natural history' logic then has two sides. Society shares the materiality of nature, so its laws operate independently of human will. Humans also transform nature into a 'humanised nature', treating nature as an 'inorganic body' and society as an 'organic body' in which lawfulness and purposiveness coincide. Human initiative can therefore speed progress, even to the point of a 'Caudine Forks'-style leap, but it cannot create matter itself. Zhang concludes that Marx's theory forms a rigorously logical system. It moves historical study from philosophy of history to a science of history and gives the fullest account of the laws of social progress. Progress is presented as the 'deduction' of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, unfolding in empirical time and space. Read the original if you want a concise, introductory statement of how Chinese scholarship distinguishes Marx's historical materialism from Kantian and Hegelian philosophy of history.

The value orientation of further deepening reform comprehensively 进一步全面深化改革的价值取向 Chen Jinlong Writing in Guangming Daily after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Chen Jinlong asks what value orientation should guide the further comprehensive deepening of reform. The answer is that a people-centred approach, which the author calls the Party's value stance, governs the policy-making, planning and practice of reform and so has an overarching significance for it. Chen reads the Plenum's Decision on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization as applying this principle throughout. The commentary is organised in three parts, each tied to the Decision and to statements by Xi Jinping. The first deals with respecting the principal position of the people and their creativity. The second deals with planning and advancing reform from the standpoint of the people's interests. The third deals with the people's judgement as the final test of reform results. A short conclusion draws these together. In the first part, Chen presents the people as the main force of reform: their support is needed because reform now touches deep-seated contradictions and entrenched interests. The Decision's reference to "the people's new expectations" among the "three confrontations" is read as a sign that reform responds to popular demands. The second part argues that the people's interests are concrete, and that the Decision picks entry points in distribution, employment, social security, healthcare and public services. Chen adds that Chinese modernization, which the author describes as the greatest interest of all the people, is the ultimate aim of reform. The third part says reform should be judged by how far people's interests are met, and that the people are the most authoritative evaluators. Their assessment, Chen contends, marks a starting point for the next stage of reform. Chen concludes that a people-centred orientation helps secure the direction of reform, mobilise support, build consensus and gather strength for Chinese modernization. The author adds that putting this orientation into practice depends on upholding the Party's overall leadership throughout the whole process of reform, so that the Party remains its strong leadership core. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the 2024 reform Decision is framed in terms of the people-centred principle.

How to tell the story of Chinese modernization well in the digital age 数字时代如何讲好中国式现代化故事 Zhang Honglu Zhang Honglu, in a short commentary for Guangming Daily (3 September 2024), asks how digital technology can be used to tell the story of Chinese modernization to international audiences. Starting from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and its call to rebuild the international communication landscape, the author argues that telling this story well shapes China's national image, raises its international discourse power and strengthens the influence of Chinese culture. The piece holds that big data, cloud computing and artificial intelligence have transformed the media ecosystem, and that communication is becoming mobile, social and visual. It then sets out four practical directions: new narrative methods, a communication matrix, differentiated targeting of audiences, and better feedback mechanisms. Zhang calls for stepping outside Western narrative frameworks and using Chinese discourse and Chinese narratives, with interactive, visual, multimodal and AI-generated storytelling, including short web dramas. The author proposes a matrix of many voices, among them foreign bloggers, experts and virtual "digital humans", together with integrated all-media channels. Big-data audience profiles and algorithmic distribution would tailor content to different groups. Real-time monitoring, a communication-power index and sentiment analysis would measure effects and adjust strategy. Zhang concludes that digital tools can make the story more attractive, more coordinated, more approachable and more widely spread, and so raise the effectiveness of international communication. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary translates the Third Plenum's external-communication goals into concrete digital-media practices.

Understanding Mao Zedong's "seeking truth from facts" from multiple dimensions 多维度认识毛泽东同志的实事求是思想 Peng Xiaohui This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 28 February 2024, asks how Mao Zedong's exploration of the ideological line of "seeking truth from facts" can be understood and put to use today. Peng Xiaohui argues that the principle, which Mao and other Chinese Communists formulated in Chinese terms as a summary of the Marxist worldview and methodology, can be examined through five perspectives, each carrying a lesson for present practice. The piece opens by quoting Xi Jinping's 2023 remarks on the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth, which name seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence as the three basic aspects of Mao Zedong Thought and its "living soul". Peng then takes five "views" in turn: the view of history as made by the masses, the view of the people as the main force, the view of contradiction, the view of development and the systemic view. Each section gives examples from Mao's revolutionary career and ends with a statement of what "implementing the Party's ideological line" requires now. In Peng's account, Mao's starting point was service to the people, and the masses were both the creators of history and the people best placed to understand China. This explains his insistence that Chinese problems be answered from Chinese conditions, his critique of Wang Ming's dogmatism and his path of encircling the cities from the countryside. On contradiction, Peng stresses social investigation (the Xunwu, Xingguo and other surveys; "no investigation, no right to speak") as the precondition for finding the essence of problems. On development and systems, Peng points to the changing united front policies as the revolution's tasks shifted, and to Mao's holistic planning in On Protracted War and the Liaoshen, Huai-Hai and Pinjin campaigns. Peng concludes that today's Party should follow each lesson: put the people first in advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; be self-confident and self-reliant, avoiding both rigid conservatism and uncritical copying of foreign models; be problem-oriented; uphold fundamental principles while innovating and rejecting dogmatism and empiricism; and plan the work of Party and state with foresight and a view of the whole. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary uses Mao's revolutionary experience to frame current Party methodology.

Three important dimensions of building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 建设中华民族现代文明的三个重要维度 Chu Xinyu Cui Wenlong This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's call to build a "modern civilization of the Chinese nation", presented as part of the new cultural mission set out at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Chu and Cui argue that the task is an inherent requirement of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and of Chinese modernization, and that it rests on three dimensions. The piece opens by situating the concept in Xi Jinping's cultural thought and then proceeds in three numbered sections. Each section takes one dimension: the Two Integrations, the practice of Chinese modernization, and mutual learning among civilizations. Each is developed with extensive quotation from Xi Jinping and from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). In the first dimension, the authors hold that the Marxist "soul" and the "root" of fine traditional Chinese culture must both be kept. They describe the first integration, with China's concrete realities, as aimed at solving practical problems, and the second, with traditional culture, as aimed at cultural fusion and strengthening the subjectivity of Chinese culture. The two form an organic whole. In the second dimension, they argue that the new civilization must draw on and serve Chinese modernization: it must rely on the practice led by the people, whom the authors call its creators, and in turn supply spiritual support, national identity and what they term discursive advantage. In the third, they stress openness and inclusiveness, rejecting "clash of civilizations" and civilizational superiority, and call for cultural confidence and active outreach through telling China's story well. The authors conclude that building this civilization requires combining Marxism with China's realities and culture, grounding itself in practice, and deepening exchange with other civilizations, so as to give people spiritual richness alongside material wealth. They also present it as a contribution of Chinese wisdom and solutions to human civilizational progress. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official line links the Two Integrations, Chinese modernization and civilizational exchange in the project of a modern Chinese civilization.

Advancing human civilisation through exchanges and mutual learning 在交流互鉴中推动人类文明进步 Wang Bo This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 5 February 2024, takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's congratulatory letter to the World Chinese Studies Conference (Shanghai Forum). Wang Bo reads the letter's three claims as a guide for understanding history and reality, China and the world: trace history to understand the present world, follow cultural roots to recognise present-day China, and practise mutual learning among civilisations to achieve common progress. The piece is organised in three sections, one for each claim. The first deals with the dialectic of history and reality, the second with China's cultural foundations and how to cultivate them, and the third with the attitude toward other civilisations and its practical implications. In the first section, Wang argues that the unity of logic and history is the methodological basis of Marxist philosophy, citing Marx and Engels's use of world-historical material. Against the backdrop of what the article calls great changes unseen in a century, it calls for historical thinking in assessing the world economy, international politics and ecological protection. The second section holds that the continuity of Chinese civilisation means China can only be understood through its history. It treats fine traditional Chinese culture as a basis for building a modern Chinese civilisation, and proposes family, school and social education to transmit it. The third section claims that the inclusiveness and peacefulness of Chinese civilisation mean China pursues exchange without cultural hegemony and does not impose its values or political system on others. Wang adds that civilisations should seek "harmony in diversity", not copy one another's development paths, and treat each other as co-agents of progress. Wang concludes that, given what the article describes as growing deficits in peace, development, security and governance, correct handling of civilisational differences is a precondition for international cooperation. Mutual learning, in this view, helps turn the Global Civilization Initiative from an idea into action. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese official commentary links Xi Jinping's statements on civilisation to Marxist historical method and cultural policy.

Understanding Mao Zedong's idea of seeking truth from facts from multiple dimensions 多维度认识毛泽东同志的实事求是思想 Peng Xiaohui This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 28 February 2024, asks how Mao Zedong's idea of "seeking truth from facts" (shishi qiushi) can be understood and put to use today. Peng treats it as the fundamental viewpoint of Marxism and as the Party's basic ideological, working and leadership method. The article argues that Mao and the Chinese communists distilled Marxist world outlook and methodology into this phrase in Chinese idiom, drawing on revolutionary practice. Examining it from several angles, Peng says, helps the Party use it as an effective intellectual weapon. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remark at the symposium marking the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth (2023). Xi named seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence as the three basic aspects of the "living soul" of Mao Zedong Thought. Peng then takes five "views" in turn: the mass view of history, the view of the subject, the view of contradiction, the view of development and the systems view. Each section cites episodes from Mao's career and ends with a requirement for carrying out the Party's ideological line now. Peng's core move is to read each phase of Mao's revolutionary practice as an application of a Marxist principle. Mao's stress on serving the people grounds the mass view of history. His investigation reports, such as the Hunan peasant report and the Xunwu and Xingguo surveys, and his maxim "no investigation, no right to speak", illustrate the view of contradiction. His shifting united-front policies across the revolutionary stages illustrate the view of development. On the view of the subject, Peng points to Mao's critique of Wang Ming's dogmatism and his rural-encirclement road, which rested on China's own conditions. For the systems view, Peng cites On Protracted War and the planning of the three great campaigns of the civil war. Peng concludes that each view carries a present-day demand. These are to put the people first, to be self-confident and self-reliant while avoiding both rigid closure and uncritical copying of foreign models, and to stay problem-oriented. They also include upholding fundamental Marxist principles while innovating and breaking with dogmatism and empiricism, and planning forward-looking, holistic work. The author ties this to Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how current Party commentary organises Mao's methodology into themes for contemporary governance.

A systematic grasp of the rich connotations of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 系统把握中华民族现代文明的丰富内涵 Wang Guang This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 1 April 2024, asks how to understand the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, the new task of building which has been set out by Xi Jinping. Wang Guang argues that it is the modern form of Chinese civilization and the new form of human civilization created by Chinese modernization. In Wang's account it must be grasped through dialectical thinking. The article is organised around three pairs of relations: the blending of tradition and modernity, the unity of critique and construction, and the meeting of national character and worldwide significance. Each section draws mainly on statements by Xi Jinping, with additional citations from Marx and Engels on colonialism and civilization. On tradition, Wang holds that modernity does not mean abandoning the past: a modernity that discards tradition lacks a foundation. The author cites the five salient features of Chinese civilization and presents Marxism as the soul of the new civilization, with the blending achieved through the Two Integrations, above all integrating Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. On critique, Wang describes Western capitalist civilization as built on slavery, colonialism, plunder and war behind a façade of civilization, while Chinese modernization is said to reject this logic of capital and put the people first. On the global dimension, Wang rejects civilizational superiority and calls for exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. Wang concludes that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation expresses cultural agency and cultural confidence, and that it belongs to the world as well as to China. The author presents it as embodying the ideal of harmony among all nations and a world of great harmony, and as confirming that the path chosen by socialist China is correct. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames this concept for a general readership.

Several theoretical issues that need attention in developing new quality productive forces 发展新质生产力需要重视的几个理论问题 Zeng Zheng Following Xi Jinping's remarks of 31 January 2024 that high-quality development needs a new theory of productive forces, Zeng Zheng asks which macro-level theoretical questions must be understood when developing new quality productive forces. The article, a commentary first carried in Guangming Daily on 2 April 2024, argues that beyond micro-level questions of technology, industry and markets, the topic needs to be seen through historical laws, technological trends and the adaptation of relations of production. The piece is organised in three parts. The first examines the historical conditions and practical basis for new quality productive forces. The second deals with the gradual and repetitive character of innovation and with competition between technological routes. The third addresses the mutual adaptation of productive forces and relations of production. On the first point, Zeng holds that scientific revolutions lead to industrial revolutions only under suitable economic conditions and social systems, citing a gap of about a century in the first industrial revolution. The author describes a fourth industrial revolution under way, with major countries launching national strategies, and lists China's advantages (talent, market scale, a full industrial chain, and numerical-control and digital R&D tool rates of 55.3% and 74.7%) alongside shortfalls in top talent, factor-market rules and digitalisation. On the second, Zeng uses breech-loading guns and electric vehicles to show that technologies advance in spirals, and contrasts national routes in new energy vehicles, artificial intelligence and 'green power plus computing power'. On the third, Zeng says new productive forces produce new relations such as the sharing economy and platform organisations, but also constraints such as data monopolies and widening income gaps. Zeng proposes using the new whole-nation system to pick technological tracks and concentrate on core technologies, letting the market play the decisive role in allocating resources while avoiding duplicated construction across localities, and expanding international cooperation to avoid standards gaps. In the sphere of production relations, the author calls for promoting the digital economy and strengthening regulation together, preventing digital capital and platform data monopolies from over-appropriating surplus labour. Read the original if you want a short, official-line example of how Chinese commentators connect new quality productive forces to the classical thesis on productive forces and relations of production.

Accelerating the construction of Chinese discourse and Chinese narrative systems 加快构建中国话语和中国叙事体系 Tang Aijun Writing in Guangming Daily on 1 March 2024, Tang Aijun asks how China can build a discourse and narrative system that matches its comprehensive national strength and international standing. Tang argues that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation must be accompanied by cultural revival and greater appeal of its discourse. On this view, building Chinese discourse and narrative reflects the Party's strategy of raising national cultural soft power and occupying the international moral high ground. It requires new concepts, categories and formulations that connect China with the world. The piece is a short commentary guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture and organised in three parts. The first concerns holding to a Chinese cultural standpoint and rejecting the abstract opposition between tradition and modernity. The second concerns breaking Western discourse hegemony while establishing a Chinese discourse system, above all on modernization. The third concerns combining a firm Chinese standpoint with a global outlook, through agenda-setting, signature concepts and national image. Tang contends that treating tradition as backward and modernity as progress leads to the view that modernization requires negating tradition. Rejecting this opens the way to drawing on China's fine traditional culture, whose spiritual markers should be distilled with three qualities: distinctiveness, contemporary relevance and universal significance. Tang then argues that Chinese scholarship has long been in an apprenticeship to Western theory, and that Western narratives equate modernization with Westernization and cast China as a backward 'other'. Success in practice does not turn automatically into success in discourse, so Tang calls for a Chinese modernization discourse and a plural narrative of modernization. This would present Chinese modernization as sharing common features of modernization while offering a new option for developing countries. Tang also holds that China should move from 'China's story' to 'the world's story'. Concepts such as a community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives are cited as examples that have gained international recognition. Tang concludes that China should set global agendas on governance, development, security and civilisational exchange. It should also present its views on peace, development, global governance, the correct approach to justice and interests, and civilisation. Tang says this would build an image of China as credible, lovable and respectable: a peace builder, a contributor to development and a reliable friend of developing countries. Read the original if you want a concise statement, from within the official discourse, of how Chinese commentators link cultural confidence, critique of Western narratives and international communication.

The significance of the "Second Integration" seen through the meaning of emancipating the mind 从思想解放的内涵看“第二个结合”的重大意义 Yang Hongyuan This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's description of the "Second Integration" (combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture) as "another emancipation of the mind". Yang Hongyuan argues that, by clarifying what emancipating the mind involves, one can see why the Second Integration matters and why it creates better conditions for resolving the long-running dispute over "ancient and modern, Chinese and Western". Yang builds the article around three elements that, in the author's account, make up emancipating the mind: being guided by correct theory, criticising dogmatism and subjective prejudice, and studying new circumstances to solve new problems. Each element is used as a lens on the Second Integration. The text draws on Deng Xiaoping's definition of the term, on Xi's remarks, and on the Party's earlier episodes of ideological renewal, from the Yan'an rectification to the debate on the criterion of truth. On the first element, Yang reads the Chinese word "tong" (with) in the formulation as showing that Marxism keeps the leading, guiding position, and holds that only Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times can ensure the right direction. The second element carries the most polemical weight. Yang rejects views that the Second Integration is already contained in the First, or that it elevates traditional culture too much. Yang also rejects the claim that traditional culture has replaced Marxism as the core of modern Chinese civilisation, and cultural revivalism that would "Confucianise" or "Daoify" Marxism. In Yang's reading, the move from the First to the Second Integration is a shift from spontaneous to self-aware grasp of the relation between Marxism and tradition. It also links Chinese civilisation with the socialist path and fully emancipates the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. On the third element, Yang says the Second Integration answers the central task of building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. It gives the Chinese path deeper historical roots and offers developing countries a model, according to the author. Yang calls for continuing to develop traditional culture, localising foreign culture, and producing achievements that join past and present, China and the West. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists frame the Second Integration against both dogmatist and traditionalist readings.

Advancing Chinese modernization through building a country strong in quality 以质量强国建设推进中国式现代化 Liu Huchen This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 3 April 2024, asks how the drive to build China into a country strong in quality (质量强国) can advance Chinese modernization. Liu takes the Outline for Building a Country Strong in Quality, issued by the Central Committee and State Council in February 2023, as the basic guide. The author argues that quality-focused development lays the foundation for Chinese modernization, and that five practical paths are needed to deliver it. The article has three parts. The first explains why quality building underpins Chinese modernization. The second describes the new situation and tasks, setting China's advantages against domestic and international challenges. The third sets out five practical paths: innovation and new quality productive forces, modernized quality governance, regionally coordinated quality development, quality improvements that benefit the people, and a green, low-carbon orientation. Liu's core claim is that quality is both a livelihood issue and a development issue, so high-quality development, which the author calls an essential requirement of Chinese modernization, depends on it. The author sees China's advantages in the socialist market economy and an ultra-large market, whose varied demand encourages quality innovation. The challenges listed include population ageing, a supply system that lags behind consumer demand, uneven regional quality, an industrial chain still in the middle and low end of the international division of labour, and the tight timetable for carbon peaking and carbon neutrality. The paths respond to these: basic research "from 0 to 1" and the commercialization of results "from 1 to N"; stronger laws, digital supervision and shared governance by firms, industry, society and government; joint regional brands; quality grading in food, medicine, elderly care and education; and unified green product standards and carbon-reduction measurement. Liu concludes that quality building should run through every stage of Chinese modernization, and that these five measures, planned together, can turn quality gains into material strength, better livelihoods and harmony between humans and nature. The piece is a policy-oriented commentary in official language rather than a scholarly study. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-state discourse links quality policy, high-quality development and Chinese modernization.

Grasping the true meaning of the "common values of all humanity" 深刻把握“全人类共同价值”的思想真谛 Xu Yanling Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2024, Xu Yanling takes up the concept of the "common values of all humanity", which the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) linked to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Xu presents the concept as a Chinese proposal, and as an original contribution of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, offered in response to what the article calls changes unseen in a century. The thesis is that one should understand what the values are, why they should be promoted and how. The commentary is organised in three parts, each tied to a formula of \"knowing\": knowing the meaning, knowing the reasoning, and putting it into practice. The first part defines the six values named by Xi: peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom. The second gives three reasons for promoting them. The third sets out three routes for doing so. In the first part, Xu groups the six values into three pairs: peace and development as a common cause, fairness and justice as a common ideal, and democracy and freedom as a common pursuit. Xu reads fairness as equality among states large and small, and justice as upholding the UN-centred international system together with a \"correct view of justice and interests\". Democracy has no single model: the article holds that only democracy suited to a country's conditions is real and effective, and it extends the term to the democratisation of international relations. The second part argues that the values accord with the trend of world history, answer the \"deficits\" in peace, development, security and governance, and give a value foundation for the community with a shared future for mankind. On how to promote the values, Xu calls for three things. The first is deeper theoretical elaboration, including a systematic theory covering their background, content, features, discourse and paths. The second is better international communication: unobstructed economic globalisation, use of the Belt and Road Initiative, and coordinated mainstream media, scholarly and popular channels, with audiences segmented. The third is reform of global governance: opposing unilateralism, protectionism and hegemonism, and raising the representation of emerging and developing countries. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Chinese commentary defines and justifies this concept and what practical steps it proposes.

Understanding and grasping the theme of further deepening reform comprehensively 深刻理解和把握进一步全面深化改革的主题 Wang Changlin Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this commentary asks why further deepening reform comprehensively must be organised around Chinese modernization. Wang takes the Plenum's Decision as the starting point. The article argues that this theme is a successful experience and strategic choice of the Party's leadership of reform and opening up, and that it rests on historical, theoretical, practical, developmental and reform logics. The piece is built in three numbered steps. It first sets out what modernization is and how it has unfolded worldwide. It then traces how Chinese modernization has advanced through reform and opening up, from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally it lists seven areas on which further reform should focus. Wang defines modernization as a historical process in which advances in productive forces transform modes of production and ways of life. The author identifies three waves, the steam, electrical and information-technology revolutions. Countries that became developed, in this account, built relations of production suited to the productive forces of their time, while others stagnated or fell into the "middle-income trap", and developing countries that simply copied the Western model failed. From this Wang concludes that technological and industrial revolution is the basic driver of modernization, and that institutional and cultural renewal secures it. China's own record is presented as proof that reform and opening up is the means by which modernization advances. The seven focal areas are a high-standard socialist market economy, whole-process people's democracy, a strong socialist culture, better living standards, a beautiful China, a higher-level safe China, and the Party's leadership and capacity to govern over the long term. Wang concludes that opening a new chapter of Chinese modernization still depends on reform. It must proceed from China's conditions while following the general laws of modernization, so that relations of production and productive forces, and the superstructure and the economic base, fit each other better. The author compares Chinese modernization to a ship, with reform and innovation as the engine, rule of law and social security as stabilisers, and Party leadership as the anchor. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the Plenum's reform agenda is linked to Chinese modernization.

Opening a new path of emancipating the mind through the "Two Integrations" 以“两个结合”开辟思想解放的新路径 Wang Zhiwei This commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today on 20 August 2024, asks how ideological emancipation can support the decision to "further deepen reform comprehensively" taken at the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Wang Zhiwei argues that the Two Integrations, the Party's theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, supply the guiding thought for this emancipation and give it a scientific, non-arbitrary direction. The article opens by presenting thought as the precursor of action and of social change, citing Marx on the "lightning of thought" and Xi Jinping on advanced values and emancipated thinking as sources of social vitality. It then sets out three tasks: showing that the Two Integrations are the ideological precursor of deeper reform, deepening understanding of reform through the first integration, and strengthening intellectual initiative through the second. Wang holds that the Two Integrations give reform a scientific worldview and methodology, loosen the hold of traditional habits of thought, and root reform in cultural confidence. Through the first integration, Marxism combined with China's concrete reality, Wang draws on Engels's view that socialist society is one of constant change to argue that reform is necessary and long-term, "always in progress and never completed". Drawing on Marx's account of the basic contradiction of society and Engels's account of the interaction of base and superstructure, Wang also argues that reform is arduous and complex. Through the second integration, Marxism combined with fine traditional Chinese culture, the author sees culture as an internal force that builds intellectual initiative. Wang cites sayings such as "when things reach an extreme they change" and "benefit the people by what benefits them" as ideas that support reform and its people-centred governance. Wang concludes that the second integration "opens up space for innovation" and secures cultural confidence, which the author links to the Plenum's goal of building a strong socialist culture. The article calls for consolidating cultural subjectivity and strengthening the inheritance and renewal of culture, so that the right path, scientific theory, effective institutions and advanced culture develop together as a spiritual support for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the Two Integrations to the reform agenda set at the 2024 Third Plenum.

Chinese modernization will open broad prospects through reform and opening up Understanding the major significance of the Third Plenum of the 20th Party Central Committee 中国式现代化必将在改革开放中开辟广阔前景 Li Yi Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Li Yi offers a study-and-interpretation commentary on why the plenum matters. The article argues that advancing Chinese modernization requires further comprehensively deepening reform, and that such reform must in turn be focused on Chinese modernization; the two are presented as closely linked and internally unified. The plenum's Decision is described as the continuation of the reform agenda begun at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and as a new chapter for the new era. The piece is organised in three parts. The first treats further reform as a practical necessity for realising the blueprint of the 20th Party Congress (2022), looking at domestic problems, the international environment and the need for unity. The second presents the Decision as an act of historical initiative to improve socialist institutions and modernize state governance. The third reviews the achievements since 2012 and sets out the Decision's tasks as a mobilisation order and a roadmap. Li's core reasoning is that reform is the means by which the Party has repeatedly overcome obstacles, and that it remains so. Domestically, the author lists uneven and inadequate development, an incomplete market system, a large but not strong industrial base, dependence on foreign core technologies, and urban–rural and income gaps. Internationally, Li points to accelerating global change and escalating external pressure, requiring institutions that can prevent and defuse risks. Institution-building is treated as a dynamic process that must stay on the socialism with Chinese characteristics path, avoiding both a closed, rigid road and one that changes banners. Li then outlines priority areas: economic reform led by the Two Unwaverings, the market economy and new quality productive forces; integrated reform of education, science and talent; democracy, law, culture, livelihood and ecology; the balance of development and security; and Party leadership over reform. Li concludes that the Decision's more than 300 measures should be carried out so as to complete its reform tasks by 2029 and to build a high-standard socialist market economy and basically realise modernization by 2035. The author expresses confidence that Chinese modernization will produce new and greater achievements. The text works as an authoritative-line exposition of the plenum's priorities, with strong emphasis on Party leadership. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how the Third Plenum's Decision was framed and justified in Party-theoretical media in 2024.

Understanding the scientific meaning and practical requirements of "We Must Put the People First" 深刻理解“必须坚持人民至上”的科学内涵和实践要求 Wang Ming Qing Yulin Wang Ming and Qing Yulin write in response to Xi Jinping's article "We Must Put the People First", published in Qiushi on 1 April 2024. The commentary, which first appeared in China Social Sciences Today on 25 June 2024, argues that the principle expresses the Party's unchanged ideals, nature, purpose and founding mission. The authors hold that understanding it matters for reading the "two overall situations" and for sustaining strategic resolve in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The piece is organised in three parts. The first identifies the Marxist philosophical content of the principle. The second sets out the political logic of the Communist Party's long-term governance. The third lists four practical requirements for building a modern socialist country through Chinese modernization. On philosophy, the authors find three dialectical unities in the principle. These are subject and object (the people as both the driving force of history and the beneficiary of development), theory and practice, and the historical and the contemporary. For the third, they trace the idea from Mao Zedong's "serve the people", through Deng Xiaoping's mass line, Jiang Zemin's Three Represents and Hu Jintao's Scientific Outlook on Development, to Xi's formulations. On political logic, they argue that the principle reflects a grasp of three kinds of law: the laws of social development, the traditional Chinese idea of the people as the root of the state, and the laws of socialist modernization. In their account, the Party combines the Marxist view of the people with this traditional thought, and its policies win broad support because they improve livelihoods and share results fairly. The four practical requirements are these: Party members and officials should firmly hold to a political stance rooted in the people and accept their supervision; whole-process people's democracy should be developed; popular wisdom and energy should be gathered through united struggle, including developing new quality productive forces and high-quality development to achieve common prosperity; and the people should be treated as the examiners of the Party's work. On the last point, the authors cite Xi's view that the Party's performance can be judged only by the people, and they call for officials to treat the people's concerns as questions they must answer. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the people-first principle as continuous with earlier leaders' theory and with Chinese tradition.

Improving institutions and mechanisms for developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 健全因地制宜发展新质生产力体制机制 Yin Jun Taking up the call of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to improve the institutions and mechanisms for developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions, Yin argues that deepening reform must produce relations of production better suited to these forces. The commentary, published in the Guangming Daily, presents this as the way to secure high-quality development. The piece has two parts. The first explains why local adaptation is required, drawing on basic Marxist political economy. The second sets out three areas where institutions and mechanisms need strengthening: comprehensive innovation, the allocation of production factors, and the modern industrial system. Yin reasons that new quality productive forces arise from technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of factors and industrial upgrading. Regions differ in innovation capacity, resource endowment and industrial base, so their paths must differ rather than follow one model. Because relations of production tend to lag behind productive forces, the author says the state can adjust them, across production, exchange, distribution and consumption, in line with a high-standard socialist market economy. Yin calls for a new-type whole-nation system for innovation, reform of talent evaluation and of industry–university–research cooperation, and reform of the allocation of land, labour, capital, technology and data. The market should play the decisive role while government guides factors towards promising fields and supervises factor markets. Regions should build up the new before dismantling the old, upgrade traditional industries, guide emerging industries away from bubbles and invest in future industries. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how local adaptation is linked to the Marxist theory of productive forces and relations of production.

Understanding the philosophical grounds of the people-centred approach 深刻领会以人民为中心的哲学理据 Lu Yanqin Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, Lu Yanqin takes up the principle of putting the people first, listed among the six principles of the Third Plenum decision on further deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization. The author argues that it needs to be understood philosophically, as a value stance. In Lu's account it answers the basic Marxist question of "for whom and relying on whom". The short piece is organised around three logics: the generation of a value relationship, the manifestation of the value subject, and the verification of values in practice. It draws on the history of the philosophical concepts of subject and object, and on Marx's three historical stages of human development. Lu holds that the people-centred approach treats people as both end and means, with development aimed at people and achieved through them, so that purpose-value and instrumental value are unified. Using Marx's stages (dependence on persons, dependence on things, free individuality), Lu says people become true subjects only in social relations, and that capitalism alienates and reifies them. Socialism, in this reading, supplies the material base and institutions for the all-round development of individuals. In practice, Lu points to the people's creativity in culture and to an ecological ethic expressed in phrases such as "protecting nature is protecting humanity". Lu concludes that the approach corrects both the neglect of people and the neglect of things, escapes the logic of capital, and runs through high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Studying it is said to deepen understanding of the essence of socialism and to surpass the "reified" and "abstract" person of Western civilization. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-theory writing grounds the people-centred principle in Marxist value theory.

Accelerating the building of a high-standard socialist market economy 加快构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Li Yuju This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 23 August 2024, asks why a high-standard socialist market economy matters and how to build it. Li Yuju argues that, as the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) put it, such a system is an important guarantee of Chinese modernization, and that its construction must be accelerated. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statement that markets deciding resource allocation is the general law of a market economy. It then traces reform from the 14th Party Congress (1992) to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), reviews achievements since 2013, and sets out remaining problems and tasks. Li credits the 2013 formula that the market should play the decisive role in allocating resources, with a better-functioning government, with guiding later reform. Since then, the author says, reforms have improved basic market institutions, implemented the new development philosophy, strengthened macroeconomic governance and institutionalised security in areas such as food and energy. Li then notes that an incomplete market system, underdeveloped markets and an unsettled government–market relationship still constrain high-quality development. Li concludes that the 2035 target of fully establishing the system requires markets that are both lively and well regulated.
