The tasks listed are the Two Unwaverings, a unified national market, better factor-market rules, and stronger basic institutions such as property rights, information disclosure and market access. Read the original if you want a brief, official-register summary of how the 2024 Third Plenum framed market-economy reform.

Mao Zedong's exploration of and contribution to modern Chinese civilization: from the perspective of the "Second Integration" 毛泽东对中国现代文明的探索与贡献——以“第二个结合”为视角 Huang Xianzhong Tang Yun Huang Xianzhong and Tang Yun take up a gap in scholarship on Mao Zedong. Studies, especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022), have concentrated on his exploration of Chinese modernization, while his thinking on modern Chinese civilization, which began in his youth, has received little attention. The article argues that Mao pursued this exploration consistently through the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. In the authors' account, this rooted modern civilization in traditional soil and carried forward the tradition of "all under heaven belongs to all". The article is organised in five parts. Four sections trace Mao's contribution along a sequence: direction (the ideal of a modern civilization), basis (emancipation of thought as the source of strength), steps (opening a path through historical initiative) and concept (building a form of modern civilization in practice). Each section has four sub-points, running from Mao's early writings and the New Culture Movement through the Yan'an period to the socialist construction of the 1950s and 1960s. A short conclusion links the argument to the call for building a modern Chinese civilization in the new era. The authors argue that Mao united the universality of modernization with China's particularity. In their reading, the young Mao rejected both wholesale Westernization and cultural conservatism, and understood socialism through the traditional ideal of great unity (datong). In the revolutionary years, he proposed the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions, which the authors treat as already containing the Second Integration. They cite his critique of dogmatism, his "revolutionary utilitarianism", his use of capitalism within New Democracy and his rejection of both the "two-revolution" and "one-revolution" theories. In the authors' view, these steps let China bypass the capitalist system. After 1949, they say, Mao's institutional transformation, industrialization and Four Modernizations, service to the people with collectivist ethics, and support for oppressed nations gave concrete form to a civilization based on the idea that all under heaven belongs to all. The authors conclude that Mao's exploration gave modern Chinese civilization both a distinct national character and a contemporary value orientation. They say it also opened space for a new form of human civilization through Chinese modernization. Citing Xi Jinping's 2023 remarks on the cultural mission, they urge drawing on Mao's wisdom through the Second Integration and advancing high-quality development to complete his unfinished work. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-scholarly account of how Mao's thought is now being reinterpreted through the Second Integration and the idea of modern civilization.

Comrade Deng Xiaoping and the founding of socialism with Chinese characteristics 邓小平同志与中国特色社会主义的开创 Xie Chuntao This short commemorative commentary by Xie Chuntao presents Deng Xiaoping as the figure who led the Party and people in founding socialism with Chinese characteristics. Xie describes him as chief architect of reform and opening up and modernization, founder of the path, and principal creator of Deng Xiaoping Theory. The piece argues that remembering these achievements will inspire a new chapter of the cause. The article is organised around three "new" contributions: a new path, a new theory and a new historical period. It closes by linking Deng's legacy to the Party's present tasks under Xi Jinping. On the path, Xie argues that when Deng returned to work in the late 1970s he began by correcting the ideological line and pushing the Party to reconsider what socialism is and how to build it. Drawing on Mao Zedong's explorations, the Party's setbacks and world socialist experience, he proposed "taking our own road", which combines the basic principles of scientific socialism with China's actual conditions. On theory, Xie says Deng Xiaoping Theory marked a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. He lists its ideas: the essence of socialism, the primary stage of socialism, the market economy under socialism, and the Party's basic line of "one central task, two basic points". Xie calls these an original contribution to scientific socialism. Xie credits Deng with guiding the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), which began reform and opening up, and with his 1992 southern tour. He says these changed the country and benefited world socialism. Citing Xi Jinping, Xie ends by calling for the cause to be carried forward and for reform to be deepened in pursuit of Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the official narrative of Deng's legacy is presented.

Mao Zedong and the five salient characteristics of Chinese civilization 毛泽东与中华文明突出特性 Shao Yong This article, published in Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping Theory Studies in 2024, asks how Mao Zedong's writings and remarks relate to the five salient characteristics of Chinese civilization that Xi Jinping has distilled. Shao Yong argues that Chinese modernization continues Chinese civilization, and that Mao, drawing on wide historical knowledge and classical learning, made many incisive observations on each of the five features. These, the author holds, merit renewed reflection. The article is organised in five sections, one for each characteristic: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Each section assembles dated quotations, letters, poems, marginal annotations, conversations with foreign visitors and Party documents from the 1930s to the 1970s. The material ranges from Mao's early reading of the Three Character Classic to his comments on Qin Shihuang, Cao Cao, the Records of the Grand Historian and the standard histories. On continuity, Shao stresses Mao's 1938 call for Marxist historicism that does not sever history, his 1937 sacrificial address at the Yellow Emperor's tomb, and his use of Li Zicheng's defeat as a warning against complacency after victory. On innovation, the author cites Mao's praise of the four great inventions, his formula of making the past serve the present and foreign things serve China, and his distinction between underdeveloped and more developed socialism. Shao argues that this distinction supplied an intellectual basis for the later theory of the primary stage of socialism. On unity, Shao shows Mao repeatedly defending Qin Shihuang and Cao Cao as unifiers and praising historians who favoured unification. The author also links this to Mao's rejection of a 1949 proposal to divide the country at the Yangtze, and to his view that the Party leads everything. The sections on inclusiveness and peacefulness are shorter. Shao presents Mao as favouring a critical, selective absorption of Chinese and foreign culture, including Western science and management methods, and as supporting the Common Program, the policy of letting a hundred flowers bloom and academic debate. Mao's repeated calls for peace and peaceful coexistence, alongside firm resistance to aggression, are read as expressions of the "dialectics of war". Shao concludes that we should uphold fundamental principles while innovating, continue the historical lineage and write a contemporary chapter. Read the original if you want a dense, dated collection of Mao's statements on history and culture, organised to fit the official framework of five civilizational characteristics.

Lenin's merits and historical contributions are indelible 列宁的功勋和历史贡献是不可磨灭的！ Cheng Enfu Marking the centenary of Lenin's death in 2024, Cheng Enfu argues that Lenin's achievements and historical contributions are indelible and that Leninism remains relevant in the twenty-first century. The short commentary first appeared in Guizhou Daily under the title "Commemorating the 100th anniversary of Lenin's death". Cheng moves from Lenin's analysis of imperialism, through the October Revolution and Soviet construction, to the Communist International. He then turns to the present world situation and to the relation between "war and revolution" and "peace and development". Cheng recalls Lenin's account of imperialism as monopoly, parasitic and moribund capitalism, and his law of uneven economic and political development, which Cheng links to the First World War. Cheng credits Lenin with leading the revolution in backward Russia and, afterwards, with building socialism in one country amid capitalist encirclement. Citing Deng Xiaoping's remarks of 1984 and 1990, Cheng holds that "peace and development" does not negate Lenin's "war and revolution" but is dialectically united with it. In Cheng's account, today's "new imperialism" is an international-monopoly stage of capitalism and a hegemonic system, yet the twenty-first century is an era of workers defending peace, of rapid socialist development and of building a community with a shared future for mankind. Cheng concludes that Leninism guided revolution and construction in Soviet Russia and internationally, and ranks as international Marxist theory alongside Marxism. Cheng calls on all Marxist-Leninists to re-examine the value of Lenin's Communist International amid "changes unseen in a century". Read the original if you want a brief example of how a leading Chinese Marxist economist commemorates Lenin and links him to Deng Xiaoping's thesis on the era.

Deng Xiaoping's major contribution to the methodology of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 邓小平对马克思主义中国化方法论的重大贡献 Tian Keqin Tian Keqin asks what Deng Xiaoping added to the methods by which Marxism has been adapted to China. The article argues that Deng upheld, developed and creatively applied this methodology with a high degree of methodological self-awareness. In Tian's account, Deng's constant method was to proceed from reality, from world trends and from national conditions, relying on seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance. Tian presents this as a historic contribution to the methodology of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first covers the years from Deng's return to office (1977) to the 12th Party Congress (1982). It deals with the restoration of the Party's ideological line and the assessment of Mao Zedong Thought. The second part examines the theme of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the founding of Deng Xiaoping Theory. The third part sets out how Deng applied the methodology to Chinese modernization, through four methods: seeking truth from facts, the mass line, independence and self-reliance, and dialectical thinking. Tian argues that Deng first restored the authority of practice as the test of truth, against the "two whatevers". Deng then protected Mao Zedong Thought as a coherent system and identified its "living soul" in seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. Tian then reads Deng's key concepts as methodological applications. The primary stage of socialism is presented as the basis grounded in seeking truth from facts. Common prosperity and reliance on the people are traced to the mass line. Deng's "Chinese-style modernization", framed in terms of xiaokang (a moderately well-off household), is linked to independence and self-reliance. The "one central task, two basic points" layout and the "two-handed" approach are credited to dialectical thinking. Tian also stresses Deng's view that the Four Cardinal Principles are the political precondition of modernization. Tian concludes that Deng combined Marxist fundamentals with China's conditions and the features of the era, and so gave the Party's later theory its methodological foundation. The article calls on the Party today to build on this methodology. It names the "six musts" of the new era as the Party's shared language, and calls for advancing the theory of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times together with Chinese modernization in practice. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Deng's thought is placed within the sequence from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping's new era.

On the value outlook of Mao Zedong's thought of "serving the people" 论毛泽东“为人民服务”思想的价值观 Niu Baoliang Niu Baoliang asks why Mao Zedong's thought of "serving the people" could become the political purpose of the whole Chinese Communist Party. The article's answer is that it rests on a Marxist view of class, of life and of practice, and that the three are unified in one value outlook. Niu limits the discussion to the period of the New Democratic Revolution. The article is organised in three numbered sections. The first links the value outlook to the class outlook, the second to the outlook on life, and the third to the outlook on practice. Niu draws on Mao's texts from 1925 to 1945, including "Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society", the 1944 speech "Serve the People", "On Coalition Government" and the 1945 Party Constitution. The article also cites Lenin, the Communist Manifesto and early Party programmes. Niu argues first that a party's character follows the class it represents. As a Marxist party recognising the people as creators of history, the Party represents the fundamental interests of the proletariat and the broad masses. Mao's class analysis separated enemies from the people, and Niu presents this as the basis for the claim that the Party and its armies serve the people. Second, Niu reads Mao's speech at Zhang Side's memorial, with its image of a death "heavier than Mount Tai", as defining the life value of Communists. Mao's call for "wholehearted" service was written into the 1945 Party Constitution, which demanded close ties with the masses and warned against tailism, commandism, bureaucratism and warlordism. Third, the article sets out how value became practice, from the 1921 programme and the minimum and maximum programmes of 1922 to the united fronts and the land revolution. Niu explains the alliance with the national bourgeoisie by China's small working class and weak capitalism. Niu concludes that the thought is the Party's unified value outlook and, logically and objectively, its outlook on class, life and practice, in line with historical materialism. For Niu, the divide between Communists and bourgeois parties lies in a people-centred view of history as against a view centred on heroes. Niu also warns against tailism, meaning doing whatever the masses demand, which would deny the leader's role and weaken the Party's core and its correct leadership. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the New Democratic Revolution-era texts on serving the people are tied to Marxist class theory.

Mao Zedong's leadership of the "Second Integration" during the War of Liberation: a great achievement 毛泽东领导解放战争时期开创“第二个结合”的伟大成就 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin asks how Mao Zedong, between June 1946 and September 1949, combined Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, and argues that this period opened a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. In Liu's account, the Chinese Communists faced a civil war launched by the Kuomintang with US backing. Mao responded by repeatedly drawing on, and transforming, China's cultural heritage, which Liu presents as the practice of what is now called the Second Integration. The article is organised in six thematic sections, each pairing a traditional idea with Mao's reworking of it. These are the "Great Harmony" ideal and the pursuit of communism; the old "people as the root" tradition and the scientific concept of "the people"; popular dignity and backbone against imperialism; the classical phrase "self-reliance" and its modern political meaning; the military history of Nanyang, invoked in a 1948 news dispatch; and Sunzi's maxim against pursuing a cornered enemy. Liu draws on Mao's speeches, telegrams, poems and editorial writing from 1946 to 1949. Liu's central claim is that Mao did not simply revive tradition but changed its class content. The ancient Great Harmony ideal, Liu says, was a recollection of primitive communism, and only Marxism and the Party could turn it into a real path. Likewise, ancient min-ben ("people-rooted") thought did not mean "the people" in the modern sense. Liu traces how Mao defined the people as a united front of workers, peasants, urban petty bourgeoisie and national bourgeoisie under working-class leadership, culminating in "people's democratic dictatorship" in 1949. Liu also reads Mao's rewriting of "do not pursue a cornered enemy" as "pursue the enemy with our remaining courage" as a shift from tactics to grand strategy and social transformation. Liu adds that Mao used the story of Wen Yiduo and Zhu Ziqing to turn traditional moral backbone into anti-imperialist resolve, and presented self-reliance as the basis for securing peace. Liu concludes that these cases show Mao fusing Marxism-Leninism with fine traditional culture, and links them to later ideas such as "putting the people at the centre" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Liu's view, the establishment of the new China turned the Great Harmony ideal from utopia into practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-heavy account of how Mao's wartime texts used classical Chinese references, and how Chinese scholars now frame them as an early form of the Second Integration.

Accelerating the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics from a new starting point 在新的起点上加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学 Xu Yanguo Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 8 August 2024, Xu Yanguo takes up the question of how to speed up the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, eight years after Xi Jinping's symposium on the subject (2016). Xu argues that the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) has again called for an innovation project in the field and for an independent Chinese knowledge system. The commentary holds that the field should review the past eight years and act from a new starting point. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the value of this work in the new era. The second lists four tasks for accelerating it. The third discusses how to pool the forces involved. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks on the field, including that the task is a systematic project needing top-level design. Xu offers three reasons for the work's importance: it provides theoretical support for Chinese modernization, it gives scholarly backing to the Party's theoretical innovation, and it is a lofty mission for the field. On the last point, Xu argues that Chinese philosophy and social sciences largely came from the West and carry the imprint of Western social systems. In Xu's account, such theories struggle to explain Chinese practice, especially in strongly ideological disciplines. The four tasks are research oriented to practice, summing up the laws behind China's successful practice, scholarly interpretation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and building an independent knowledge system, starting from signature concepts. On coordination, Xu calls for stronger planning across the 'five armies' of researchers: universities, Party schools, military academies, research institutes and Party and government research bodies. Xu also proposes guiding research topics, adjusting course design and giving more weight in academic evaluation to work that builds the field. Each institution type should play to its strengths, and disciplines should merge, including with the natural sciences and artificial intelligence. Read the original if you want a short, official-line outline of the priorities and institutional measures proposed for building Chinese philosophy and social sciences after the Third Plenum.

The originality requirements for building China's independent knowledge system 建构中国自主知识体系的原创性要求 Huang Yujing Xiang Jihang This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2024, asks what originality means for building China's independent knowledge system (自主知识体系). Huang and Xiang define that system as one composed of original concepts, theories and methods, and present its construction as the fundamental task of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. Their thesis is that originality must be built on materialist-dialectical methodology, following four standpoints Xi Jinping has named: practice, history, dialectics and development. The article is organised in four sections, each pairing one standpoint with a requirement. These are: drawing original results from the practice of Chinese modernization; a people-centred orientation; an open, inclusive attitude towards other bodies of knowledge; and continuing to write a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Xi Jinping's speeches are quoted throughout as the guiding framework. In the first section, the authors argue that knowledge comes from practice. Scholars should therefore find original questions in the practice of Chinese modernization, distil regularities from it, and test their theories against it. Huang and Xiang describe the relationship between theory and practice as a "double helix". On the people-centred orientation, they say the system should express the people's will, serve their spiritual needs, and be judged by their satisfaction, and they call on scholars to leave the "ivory tower". On openness, they say Marxism, fine traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship must be unified through the Two Integrations. Foreign ideas are to be sifted critically and never applied wholesale as a "sole standard". The authors say this ends the "apprentice" status of Chinese scholarship. The authors conclude that theoretical innovation never ends, because practice keeps raising new questions. They hold that contemporary China is undergoing an unusually grand practical innovation that poses many unanswered problems. They call for a system that shows subjectivity, originality and scholarly rigour, centred on "what we are doing", and that answers questions of China, the world, the people and the times. In their account, this will open new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official methodological criteria now applied to knowledge-system building in Chinese social science.

Upholding cultural subjectivity to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 坚持文化主体性 构建中国特色哲学社会科学 Lin Yahua Writing in China Social Sciences Today (7 August 2024), Lin Yahua asks how China should build a philosophy and social sciences system of its own. The author argues that this requires cultural subjectivity. Without it, Lin holds, a country cannot achieve intellectual independence or maturity, nor gain discursive power and initiative in international dialogue. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium speech on philosophy and social sciences. The commentary is organised around three requirements. The first is to take root in fine traditional Chinese culture. The second is to rest on the great practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third is to face the prospect of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and strengthen the reach and influence of Chinese culture. A short closing paragraph ties the three together under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On tradition, Lin presents the continuity of Chinese civilization as the basis of the project. Lin cites the 20th Party Congress (2022) list of traditional ideas and Xi's claim that they connect with communist and socialist ideals. Lin's examples are the moves from minben (the people as the root of the state) to democracy and from enriching the people to common prosperity. On practice, Lin argues that China's transformation is not a copy of its past, of Marxist blueprints, of other socialist states or of Western modernization, so scholars cannot analyse it with Western theoretical systems or value-laden discourse. Lin points to the socialist market economy, whole-process people's democracy and socialist ecological civilization as innovations that research should explain. On communication, Lin calls for new concepts and categories that connect Chinese and foreign audiences. Lin also calls for research on translating political discourse, and for approaching ordinary people's lives in a confident, calm and inclusive spirit. Lin concludes that only by doing so can China break the cultural hegemony of "Western centrism" and hold the power to interpret its own development. The new system should explain the sources of China's peaceful development in tradition, refine Chinese experience through practice, and set out the historical significance of the Chinese path and the comparative strengths of its institutions. It should also offer ideas and solutions for problems humanity shares. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official case for cultural subjectivity as the basis of China's philosophy and social sciences.

Developing new quality productive forces urgently requires winning five innovation campaigns 发展新质生产力亟待打好五大创新战役 Fan Jida Fan Jida, a professor and vice-dean at the Central Party School's graduate school, asks how China should put innovation at the centre of developing new quality productive forces. Writing in a Party journal after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), the author argues that innovation must be pursued through five "campaigns". These are a battle over key core technologies, a protracted war in basic research, a contest for innovative talent, a breakthrough battle for enterprises, and a positional battle in regional innovation. The article opens with Xi Jinping's description of new quality productive forces as an inherent requirement of high-quality development. It then takes each campaign in turn and ties it to the Plenum's reform decisions. Fan draws on national figures, such as R&D spending, the share of basic research and manufacturing R&D intensity. Historical examples include Britain's lead in the first industrial revolution and Germany's in the second. In the author's account, key core technologies are still often controlled by others, so China needs a new whole-nation system. Fan stresses that this system is not a return to the planned economy and does not replace private-enterprise innovation. It would work under unified Party leadership, with market, government and society acting together. Basic research is called the root of many "bottleneck" problems. The author notes that it received only 6.65% of the 2023 R&D budget of 3,327.8 billion yuan, and calls for stable funding, fewer non-research burdens for scientists and new evaluation standards. On talent, Fan proposes prioritising education, nurturing young scientists and engineers, attracting overseas experts, possibly through a high-skilled immigration system, and judging people by contribution. Enterprises are described as hindered by an inability, unwillingness or reluctance to innovate. Fan proposes wider roles for firms in setting national research agendas, R&D reserve funds, "patient capital" and stronger intellectual property protection. Regionally, the author proposes a networked pattern led by Beijing, Shanghai and the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area. It would use technology to upgrade traditional industries and develop future ones, and stay open to international cooperation. Fan concludes that new quality productive forces need matching production relations. That means reforming the science and technology system, improving incentives, and building a stronger environment for talent and enterprises. The article is a policy-oriented interpretation of Party decisions, not a theoretical study. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how a Central Party School scholar translates the Third Plenum's innovation agenda into concrete priorities, with statistics on R&D, basic research and talent.

Studying Deng Xiaoping's educational theory to open a new phase in building a leading country in education 学习邓小平教育理论开拓教育强国建设新局面 Huai Jinpeng This is a speech by Huai Jinpeng, Minister of Education, given at the opening of the national academic symposium marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth (published in 2024). Huai argues that Deng's educational theory, a new development of Marxist educational theory with distinct Chinese features, should guide efforts to build a leading country in education. Huai begins with Deng's 1977 decision to restore the national college entrance examination, which he describes as a breakthrough in setting right the errors of the previous period. The speech then takes five themes in turn: Party leadership and the socialist orientation of schooling, the priority of education, the "Three Orientations", the role of teachers, and the tasks for today. Each theme pairs Deng's statements with remarks by Xi Jinping. In Huai's account, Deng held that schools must put a firm and correct political direction first, and that "cultivating new socialist people is itself politics". Deng also placed education in a position of strategic priority and called for respect for knowledge and talent. His call for education to face modernization, the world and the future is called the essence of the theory. Huai links each point to current policy: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, moral education, the integrated advancement of education, science and technology, and talent, and the goal of a leading education country by 2035. He calls teachers the key to producing qualified talent. Huai concludes that studying Deng's theory means above all following Xi Jinping Thought, applying Xi's discourse on education and grasping the decisive significance of the Two Establishes. He calls for planning ahead, meeting change and opening new ground, so that education supports the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a short, official example of how the Education Ministry ties Deng-era theory to current education policy.

Mao Zedong's work method of having a firm grasp of the "numbers" 毛泽东胸中有“数”的工作方法 Lü Zhen Lü Zhen examines the work method that Mao Zedong summarised in 1949 as having a firm grasp of the "numbers" (胸中有“数”). The article argues that Mao creatively applied the materialist-dialectical law of the mutual transformation of quantity and quality to leading the Chinese revolution and construction. In Lü's reading, the quotation marks around "numbers" mark the word's literal sense of figures and quantities, not the everyday sense of "having a good idea" of a situation. The article is organised in five parts: the demand for scientific and meticulous work; how this grasp comes from investigation and study; the need to "see the big picture, reckon the big accounts and plan the big numbers"; attention to "degree" (度); and the move from having the "numbers" to effective action. Lü draws on Mao's 1949 speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 7th Central Committee, his notes on philosophical works, the 1930 Xunwu investigation, "On Protracted War", and military and land-reform documents from 1947–48. Lü's central claim is that quantitative analysis serves, and does not replace, judgement about essentials. Investigation must be done properly, as in the Xunwu report with its detailed class percentages and trade figures, which the author says supplied the basis for policy on rich peasants and land distribution. Numbers must also be selected from the standpoint of the whole situation: Lü reads Mao's reckoning in "On Protracted War" and his stress on uniting the great majority as examples of reckoning big accounts, citing Lenin against picking isolated facts. Finally, "degree", the quantitative limit that determines quality, let Mao periodise the civil war and set policy lines. Lü cites his troop-strength calculations in 1947–48 and his differentiated land-reform tactics for old and newer liberated areas. Lü concludes that Mao both proposed and exemplified this method, which has long helped Party cadres improve their leadership. The article presents it as relevant to the new tasks of advancing national strengthening and national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, where precision is said to be both a work requirement and an expression of Marxist epistemology. Lü ties this to seeking truth from facts and the dialectical unity of quality and quantity. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of how Mao's quantitative and investigative methods are presented in Party-history scholarship, and how they are linked to present-day cadre training.

The 2024 European Parliament elections and the development challenges facing left-wing parties 2024年欧洲议会选举与左翼政党发展挑战 Wu Yunxi Wu Yunxi asks what the June 2024 European Parliament elections reveal about the condition of Europe's left-wing parties. The article's answer is that, while centre-right parties stabilised and the far right kept rising, the left's decline slowed but split sharply, leaving it in a phase of deep adjustment. Wu attributes this to unresolved economic and social problems, an unstable electoral base and sustained pressure from populism. The article opens with the results. It reviews the three main party families (social democrats, Greens and radical left) and their groups in the Parliament, then moves through regions: Western and Central-Eastern Europe, the Nordic countries and Southern Europe. It also considers the knock-on effect on French politics, including the early National Assembly election. Wu then turns to three structural explanations, covering economic and policy constraints, the voter base of each party type, and the populist challenge. The article draws on figures for growth, debt, inflation and migration. Wu's first argument is that stagnant growth, high public debt and a cost-of-living squeeze have narrowed the room for left-wing policy. Large tax rises are said to invite attacks on fiscal sustainability, while austerity betrays the left's own principles and loses voters, which leaves a dilemma. Second, each party family is described as having a fragile base. Social democrats have become less class-oriented and more elite-led. Greens have lost their issue advantage as other parties adopt green policies. The radical left is said to lack workable alternatives and to suffer from ageing voters and dependence on charismatic leaders, and Wu adds that left parties often compete more than they cooperate. Third, Wu argues that left and populist parties draw on overlapping voters, and that migration and refugee pressures, together with right-wing populists' de-radicalising strategies, erode the left's support. Wu concludes that the elections confirm a polarised, fragmented and populist party politics, in which weakened centre-left and centre-right forces contend with a mainstreamed far right. Some social democrats are described as moving left on economic and social issues while turning conservative on culture and foreign policy, and Wu warns that the choices of Greens and radical-left parties could deepen the left's long-term difficulties. Wu calls on left parties to find new paths of party reform and governance, with stronger political leadership and organisational mobilisation. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's country-by-country account of the 2024 results and of why European left parties are struggling.

Mao Zedong's historical contribution to the "Two Integrations" and its lessons 毛泽东对“两个结合”的历史贡献及其经验启示 Ding Junping Chen Cheng Xi Jinping's formulation of the Two Integrations (2021) joins the basic tenets of Marxism to China's concrete realities and to its fine traditional culture. Ding and Chen argue that this is not a new problem. In their account, Mao Zedong, as pioneer and founder of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, made foundational contributions to both integrations, and these offer lessons for the present. The article has three parts. It first asks why Mao was able to advance the Two Integrations, citing objective needs (China's historic tasks, the failure of earlier ideologies, and the tension between a Western-born theory and Chinese conditions) and subjective conditions (his classical learning, his study of Marxist texts, and independent practical exploration). It then sets out his contributions to each integration. Finally it draws lessons for the new era. On the first integration, the authors credit Mao with proposing, in 1938, the proposition of the "sinification of Marxism". They read it as having two sides: Marxism taking Chinese form, and Chinese practice being raised into Marxist theory. They cite his methods of investigation, contradiction analysis and the mass line, and treat Mao Zedong Thought as the first historic leap. On the second integration, they argue that Mao transformed traditional culture through Marxism (for example reinterpreting "seeking truth from facts"). He also set principles for treating heritage, namely keeping the essence and discarding the dross, critical inheritance, and "letting a hundred flowers bloom". In addition, he expressed Marxism in national forms and a new literary style, helping to create a new national culture. The authors draw three lessons. The Party should arm itself with its innovative theory and keep a practice-based style of study. It should ground itself in China's national conditions amid the "changes unseen in a century". It should pursue the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, so that Marxism becomes "Chinese". They present Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as continuing Mao's project. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of Mao as precursor of the Two Integrations, or the genealogy behind current official discourse on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

Four relationships to grasp in building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 建设中华民族现代文明要把握好的几个关系 Liu Cang Liu Cang takes up what building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation requires, calling it a systemic project that spans the economy and society, domestic affairs, foreign affairs and defence. The article, a commentary in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts, argues that the task depends on handling four dialectical relationships correctly. Liu presents these as reflecting the development laws of subject and object, past and future, content and form, source and stream. The text is organised in four sections: tradition and modernity; culture and civilization; unity and plurality; and Chinese civilization and world civilization. Each section ends by claiming that getting the relationship right lets the modern civilization stand at a particular 'commanding height': historical, ideological and cultural, that of national righteousness, and that of human civilization. On tradition and modernity, Liu holds that modern China continues and develops historical China, and that modern civilization is an innovative sublimation of ancient civilization. Without the ancient, the modern becomes 'water without a source'; without the modern, the ancient becomes 'a river that runs dry'. The author calls for protection and transmission, and for creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture. On culture and civilization, Liu treats civilization as the overall state of a social formation, with socialism with Chinese characteristics as its social basis. The cultural form of Chinese modernization is described as its discursive expression. Liu links this to the cultural mission of the new era, to the Four-sphere Confidence, the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping's cultural thought. On unity and plurality, Liu argues that Chinese civilization was created jointly by all ethnic groups and that the modern civilization is a 'plural yet unified' picture. Liu cites the Party's work on forging a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation as its foundation. On China and the world, Liu says Chinese modernization, as a new form of human civilization, offers solutions to global problems and supports a community with a shared future for mankind. This rests on exchange and mutual learning among civilizations rather than one replacing another. Liu concludes by calling for China's concepts of development, civilization, security, human rights and global governance to be explained abroad, so that the world understands China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-journal author sets out the conceptual structure of the 'modern civilization of the Chinese nation' under Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

Upholding the Party's cultural leadership and the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation 坚守党的文化领导权和中华民族的文化主体性 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong's commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development that "keeping to the fundamental principles" (守正) means upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, the Two Integrations, and the Communist Party's cultural leadership and the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. Song presents this as a major innovative idea that gives the whole Party and people political assurance and spiritual strength for building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first argues that upholding the Party's cultural leadership bears on the fate of the Party and state. The second sets out how to sustain the Party's full leadership over propaganda, ideological and cultural work. The third lists concrete tasks for carrying out the "new cultural mission" of advancing cultural prosperity, building a strong socialist culture and building a modern Chinese civilisation. In the first part, Song contends that cultural leadership is a political advantage of the Party. Citing Marx and Engels, the 1921 Party resolution on publications, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, Song says the Party has always treated it as strategic. Song also holds that it is required to protect Marxism as the "soul" and traditional Chinese culture as the "root", since the Two Integrations let Marxism renew Chinese civilisation while Chinese culture gives Marxism a Chinese style. In the second part Song argues that cultural subjectivity is consolidated through cultural confidence, core socialist values written into law and policy, and the principle that the Party manages propaganda and ideology. Song adds that the Party must keep firm control of positions in public opinion, including traditional and new media, and online ideological work. Song's practical proposals include a fuller system of ideological responsibility, a Chinese autonomous knowledge system, stronger international communication, and a trained propaganda workforce. Further proposals are integrated management of traditional and new media, a "big propaganda" pattern under Party committees, and reform of cultural institutions and public cultural services. Song concludes that these steps will secure the Party's leadership and carry out the new cultural mission. Read the original if you want a compact, authoritative statement of the official line on cultural leadership and ideological work after Xi Jinping's 2023 cultural speech, including its institutional and media-management measures.

Advancing Chinese modernization through further comprehensively deepening reform 在进一步全面深化改革中推进中国式现代化 Wang Weiguang This is a study-and-interpretation commentary on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), published in Red Flag Manuscripts. Wang Weiguang asks how the plenum's Decision on further comprehensively deepening reform should be understood and applied. The author's thesis is that deepening reform is the fundamental driving force of Chinese modernization, and that the new development philosophy and high-quality development supply its content and direction. The article has three parts. The first sets out why reform must be placed at the centre of Chinese modernization and what characterises the new round of reform. The second explains the "Six Adherences" principles that the plenum laid down for reform. The third turns to high-quality development as the primary task, led by the new development philosophy. Wang draws throughout on the plenum Decision and on Xi Jinping's report and speech to it. In the first part, Wang argues that reform now sits in a "deep-water zone" and must pay more attention to systems integration, to key priorities and to practical results, driven by problems. The "Six Adherences" are: the Party's overall leadership; a people-centred approach; upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground; institution-building as the main thread; law-based governance; and a systems approach. Wang links the need for reform to shifts in the basic contradictions of society, which require continual adjustment of the relations of production and the superstructure. The third part presents new quality productive forces as an innovation-led advanced productivity, to be developed according to local conditions and not by uniform, bubble-prone campaigns. It also calls for innovation-driven development, with the state playing the leading role in key technology breakthroughs, and for institutional mechanisms that balance development with security. Wang concludes that the path runs from the new development philosophy to high-quality development, then to Chinese modernization, and finally to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author calls for unified thinking, firm resolve and thorough implementation of the plenum's measures. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-theorist's reading of the Third Plenum's principles and of how reform, high-quality development and new quality productive forces are linked.

Upholding, developing and improving China's new type of political party system 坚持好、发展好、完善好中国新型政党制度 Ji Chunfang Li Zhenghua Ji Chunfang and Li Zhenghua present the multi-party cooperation and political consultation system led by the Communist Party of China as a "new type of political party system" and ask how it should be sustained and strengthened. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), they argue that the system is a great political creation with distinctive advantages, and that the task now is to uphold, develop and improve it and to raise its effectiveness. The article has three parts. The first traces the system's origins: the failure of constitutional monarchy and Western-style multi-party models after the Opium War, the Party's united front in the revolutionary period, the 1948 May Day call and the 1949 first plenary session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. It then follows later milestones, including the 1989 Central Committee document, the 1993 constitutional amendment, the 2021 white paper and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). The second part sets out the system's advantages, and the third its requirements for the present. The core argument contrasts the new system with what the authors call "old-style" party systems. In their account, it represents the fundamental interests of the broadest public, because the Communist Party has no special interests of its own, and it channels the demands of different strata through consultation and democratic centralism. It avoids both the lack of oversight under single-party rule and the vicious competition of party rotation, since the democratic parties exercise consultative, cooperative supervision. It also promotes whole-process people's democracy by building consultation into decisions before and during implementation, which the authors say prevents social division. The authors name three requirements: uphold the leadership of the Communist Party, which they call the prerequisite and fundamental guarantee; let the democratic parties and non-party figures play their role in democratic supervision and in building state power; and consolidate a common ideological and political foundation, now defined as socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They conclude that the system suits China's conditions and will gain vitality on the path to national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party narrative on the multi-party cooperation system, with its historical milestones and stated rationale.

Turning iron discipline into conscious action 把铁的纪律转化为自觉行动 Hu Yang Writing in Red Flag Manuscript (2024, no. 13), Hu Yang asks how the Chinese Communist Party should understand and combine the coercive and the voluntary sides of Party discipline. The article argues that Party discipline is an inner unity of "iron discipline" and "conscious discipline": the first is the guarantee, the second the foundation. Hu presents this understanding as important for consolidating the effects of the Party discipline study and education campaign and for deepening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article has three parts. The first sets out why iron discipline is a defining trait of proletarian parties, citing Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping on unity, victory over risks and challenges, and discipline as a "ruler" for cadres. The second explains why Party discipline must rest on conscious acceptance. The third turns to practical paths for strengthening discipline building. In the second part Hu grounds conscious discipline in three bases: lofty ideals and convictions, given the Party's vanguard character; broad freedom and democracy, with discipline and freedom treated as a unity of opposites under democratic centralism; and a high degree of Party spirit. Hu uses Lenin's contrast between socialist discipline and the "discipline of the stick" and the "discipline of hunger". In the third part Hu proposes four measures: combining ideological Party-building with institutional governance, so that the "dare not, unable to, and not want to be corrupt" aims advance together; strictness across the whole chain, all levels, all elements and the whole cycle; handling Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline jointly, so as to cut the link from bad work style to corruption; and pairing incentives with constraints, strict management with care. Hu concludes that discipline building should move officials from fear of punishment, to being unable to break rules, to not wanting to, until discipline becomes habit that is "used daily without being noticed". Hu also calls for protecting officials who take responsibility, so that strictness does not produce passivity. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Commission for Discipline Inspection researcher links Party discipline to the Marxist-Leninist canon and to current anti-corruption practice.

Rereading Marx's aesthetic notebook 重读马克思的美学笔记 Li Suogui Li Suogui, writing in Guangming Daily (29 July 2024), revisits Marx's excerpt notes on Friedrich Theodor Vischer's multi-volume Aesthetics, or the Science of the Beautiful, prompted by a new Chinese translation published in 2023. Li argues that the notes, written in June 1857, show Marx's real command of philosophical aesthetics and that they fed into his later writing. The piece first describes the notes' fate. Li says they went unpublished in full until a Russian version appeared in 1990, and that the new translation corrects earlier mistranslations and omissions. It then follows the notes' order: definitions of aesthetics, Kant's aesthetic judgement, the "elements of the beautiful", natural beauty, fantasy and myth, and the classification of the arts. Li ends with how the notes were used. Li identifies three purposes for the notes: an invited encyclopedia entry on aesthetics, material for the 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, and a theoretical basis for judging Lassalle's drama Franz von Sickingen. Li reads Marx's selections as deliberate. Marx recorded the sublime in detail, the tragic and comic more briefly, and fantasy and myth in full, but skipped the volumes on sculpture, painting, music and poetry. The entry was declined, yet the material on myth reappears in the Introduction's question about Greek art and modern machinery. It also shaped Marx's view of Lassalle's play as tragedy, following Vischer's idea that revolution is tragedy's true theme. Li concludes that the notes were not wasted, and that Marx's closing classification table shows how far he accepted Hegelian-school aesthetics. Read the original if you want a brief account of how Marx's 1857 aesthetic notes are structured and how they connect to his later writings.

The traditional "contractual order" gradually fails: social roots of the rise of Europe's right-wing populist parties 传统“契约秩序”逐步失效：欧洲右翼民粹政党崛起的社会根源 Zhang Jinling Why have right-wing populist parties, long stigmatised in public opinion, made historic gains across Europe in the past decade? Zhang Jinling argues that their rise results from a broad rightward turn in European opinion with deep and complex social roots. In the author's reading, it reflects the gradual failure of Europe's traditional "contractual order" and, at the same time, the populists' attempt to rewrite the "social contract". The article opens with the 2024 European Parliament elections, in which the author counts 187 seats for right-wing populist groups, against 188 for the centre-right European People's Party group and 136 for the Socialists. It surveys national results in France, Italy, Austria, Hungary, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, and traces the trend from 2015, through Covid-19, to the post-2022 comeback marked by Giorgia Meloni's victory in Italy. It then examines three sets of causes: economic and social difficulties, migration and security, and deficits in representative democracy. It draws on a May 2024 BVA Xsight poll and Eurostat data. On the economy, Zhang holds that financial, euro-area and refugee crises, together with neoliberal policies that failed, produced stagnation, inequality and a weakened industrial working class and middle class. The author sees this as undermining the social base of traditional parties and as expressing discomfort with post-industrial capitalism. Populists exploit nostalgia and anxiety, and have moderated and "mainstreamed" their image. On migration, Zhang describes an "open society" split between pluralism and a wish to return to a closed one, with populists exploiting the issue and pushing established parties to harder lines. On democracy, the author argues that voters distrust elites seen as serving big capital, that low turnout among other camps helps populists, and that resentment of EU encroachment on sovereignty drives support, citing France's National Rally proposals to curb the Commission. Zhang concludes that populists cannot yet dominate the European Parliament but can obstruct decisions on migration and the green transition, with effects at national level. The author notes the populist camp is not united, since nationalism makes its parties both cooperate and check one another. Zhang calls populism a "mirror" of Western democracy that will recur, challenge the existing order and may help drive its rebuilding. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the European populist surge, with 2024 election and polling figures and a framework that links it to the failure of the post-war social contract.

The deep logic of how ideological and political education promotes the modernization of the human being 思想政治教育促进人的现代化的深层逻辑 Wu Qiong Lin Dongfang Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that the essence of modernization is the modernization of the human being, Wu Qiong and Lin Dongfang ask how ideological and political education can advance "the modernization of people". They treat this modernization as both the ultimate goal and a driving force of Chinese modernization. The authors argue that the education's essential attributes are closely tied to this process, and they organise the answer around three questions: why it can promote it (logical premise), by what means (logical unfolding), and how (logical aim). The article has three sections. The first sets out the premise: the two are said to coincide in goal, share the same value content and interlock in practice. The second turns to four functions of ideological and political education: guiding direction, shaping the spirit, cultivating new people and coordinating relations. The third lists four paths that correspond to four dimensions of people's modernization: ideas, way of life, abilities and qualities, and social relations. Wu and Lin argue that the education and human modernization point to the same end, the free and all-round development of the individual. They also hold that it serves Chinese modernization by passing on mainstream ideas and values, and that human modernization in turn pushes the education to modernize itself. In the unfolding section, the education guides people politically and in values with scientific theory and socialist core values. It builds the spiritual world, fosters hardiness, enterprise and responsibility, and promotes civilised interaction through conflict resolution, norms and consensus on shared human values. In the third section, theoretical armament is to be scientific, current and practical. Civilised social customs, including green living and a balance of material and spiritual life, are to modernize ways of life. Thinking, intellectual and labour potential are to be developed, and schools, social governance and individuals are to cooperate to modernize social relations. The authors conclude that ideological and political education raises people's thinking, forms their character, builds their abilities and guides their behaviour, and that this is how it advances human modernization within Chinese modernization. They call for stronger theoretical education built around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They also call for attention to individual needs, and for the active involvement of schools, social bodies and individuals. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education link their discipline to Chinese modernization and to Marx's idea of all-round human development.

The value implications, logical path and development principles of the "Second Integration" “第二个结合”的价值意蕴、逻辑理路和发展原则 Zhang Haifang Zhang Haifang asks what the "Second Integration", the combination of the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, means, how it works and what principles should guide it. The article argues that the two traditions share many affinities, that Marxism has gradually become the dominant ideology in China through this combination, and that the process is a two-way "mutual transformation" in which each side is changed and each fulfils the other. The article is organised in three parts. The first examines value implications: the Communist Party as the driving agent, Marxism "transforming" traditional culture, and traditional culture "transforming" Marxism. The second sets out a logical path in three registers: theoretical, historical and value logic. The third derives development principles from the "six musts" that the article presents as the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Zhang's core move is to treat the integration as a dialectical process with stages. Theoretically, it moves from mutual fit (for example, ideas of "all under heaven for the public" and the Great Harmony set beside Marxist ideas of human emancipation and communism), through mutual selection, to mutual fulfilment. Historically, it moves from formal analogy in concepts and language around the May Fourth period (Guo Moruo's "Marx Enters the Confucian Temple"), to creative development of content (Mao Zedong's reading of "seeking truth from facts", On Practice and On Contradiction), to a higher level that joins the "soul" (Marxism) with the "root" (traditional culture). The author adds that this higher level does not negate the earlier ones. In terms of value, the integration is said to reveal a general law of how Marxism takes national forms and to offer a lesson on treating tradition in modernization. The article concludes that the Second Integration should be guided by six principles: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systemic thinking, and a global outlook. Zhang says these require resisting dogmatism, historical nihilism, cultural revivalism and "Western-centrism", and that they would allow Marxism's adaptation to the Chinese context and the needs of our times to advance further. Read the original if you want a systematic statement, in current Party-theory language, of how Chinese scholars justify and structure the Second Integration.

"Act in accordance with dialectics": Deng Xiaoping's far-sighted strategic thinking “照辩证法办事”：邓小平同志高瞻远瞩的战略思维 Li Qinggang Marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, Li Qinggang takes up one of the qualities Xi Jinping singled out in Deng: far-sighted strategic thinking. Li argues that its philosophical foundation is the phrase Deng himself used and Mao Zedong endorsed, "act in accordance with dialectics". In Li's reading, many of Deng's major ideas and judgements are shot through with materialist dialectics and show a global outlook and strategic vision. The article is a short commentary published in the Party Central Committee's theoretical journal. It is organised in five parts, each pairing a Deng formula with a dialectical principle and illustrating it from the War of Resistance against Japan, the civil war, the early People's Republic, the 1975 rectification and the reform era. Li draws on Deng's wartime reports, his remarks on reform and his 1992 southern tour talks. Li's core argument runs through five pairs. First, Deng held fast to the principal contradiction: expanding the Sino-Japanese contradiction in wartime, and economic construction as the centre once the principal contradiction was defined as that between growing material and cultural needs and backward production. Second, the "emphasis on the key point" is joined to the "two-sided approach", as in Deng's insistence on "grasping with both hands, both firmly" for material and spiritual civilization, or for reform and the fight against corruption. Third, the part must serve the whole, illustrated by the Huai-Hai Campaign and by Deng's view that coastal development should first lead and later be repaid by support for the interior. Fourth, opportunities must be seized and decisions made in good time, with "crossing the river by feeling the stones" as a method of pilot testing. Fifth, "be bold, but steady" unites subjective initiative with respect for objective laws. Li concludes that the founding of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the achievements of reform and opening up are inseparable from Deng's strategic thinking and Deng Xiaoping Theory. Party members and officials are urged to study the theory completely and accurately, and not one-sidedly, and to learn Deng's world outlook and his habit of grasping the key link. They are also urged to place the cause of the Party and people in a historical and global perspective. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Party School historian presents Deng's method as dialectics, with the key quotations from Deng arranged by theme.

On the momentum of modernization in a super-large-scale country 论超大规模国家现代化发展之势 Luo Yuting Liu Hongchang Luo Yuting and Liu Hongchang ask what is distinctive about Chinese modernization as the modernization of a country with over 1.4 billion people, a population the 20th Party Congress (2022) report said exceeds that of all existing developed countries combined. They argue that this scale produces a characteristic "momentum" (shi), in which potential and kinetic energy are converted into a trend and an overall tendency of development. The article identifies five forms of this momentum: catching up, release of latent potential, scale effects, graded advance and inertial development. The article takes each form in turn. The catching-up section traces China's path from a backward agrarian state in 1949 through the Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping periods to the present, and compares it with the United States. The potential section examines institutional, human and spiritual potential. The scale section covers market size, economic resilience and room for manoeuvre. The last two sections deal with the staged, regionally sequenced character of China's modernization and with its inertia, including how that inertia should be steered. In the authors' account, China learned from the experience of earlier developers and avoided what they call the "maladies of modernity" of Western capitalist modernization, such as ecological damage, alienation, polarization, war and colonial expansion. They contend that Party leadership and the socialist system, combined with the socialist market economy, allow resources to be concentrated on major tasks. The article cites figures on manufacturing, GDP, consumption and education to support the claim that China is narrowing the gap with the United States. The authors also argue that a very large country cannot advance evenly, so reform must be staged and paced to what society can bear. Once set in motion, they say, such a country builds up great inertia, so its strategic direction should not be changed lightly. The authors conclude that modernization should proceed in graded steps while urban–rural and regional gaps are narrowed and rural revitalization pursued. They call for steering inertial momentum through economic restructuring, innovation-driven development, new quality productive forces and the pursuit of common prosperity. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how scale is used to explain the dynamics and advantages of Chinese modernization, with the supporting statistics and historical periodization.

Upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership over the reform and innovation of ideological and political theory courses 坚持和加强党对思政课改革创新的全面领导 Xu Tao Following the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for integrated reform of education and for the joint reform and innovation of ideological and political theory courses across universities, secondary and primary schools, Xu Tao asks how Party leadership should be maintained and strengthened in this work. The commentary argues that such courses are the top priority of the Party's leadership of education. It holds that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has changed their environment and ecology fundamentally, and that political, ideological and organisational leadership must now be strengthened further. The piece is organised in three parts, one for each form of leadership. The first covers political leadership and the correct direction of reform. The second covers ideological leadership and the "connotative" development of the courses. The third covers organisational leadership and a broad pattern of joint education. Xu draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2019 symposium for teachers of these courses and on other directives. On political leadership, Xu argues that the Party's leadership is the fundamental experience and greatest advantage of these courses. It must keep them tied to the socialist orientation of schooling, build political identification among teachers and students, and supply institutional safeguards, with Party organisations ensuring that institutional strengths become governance effectiveness. On ideological leadership, the author calls for fostering virtue and cultivating people, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era at the core. This means a core course and a series of related courses, updated textbooks, and practical teaching that uses the achievements of Chinese modernization, including VR and AR technology and the "great ideological and political course". On organisational leadership, Xu proposes that university Party secretaries and presidents personally take charge, and that university, faculty and branch Party bodies work together and are supervised through Party-building assessments. Xu also calls for strict standards in selecting, managing and assessing course teachers, and for evaluation reform and better status and pay. Finally, Xu urges coordination across school stages, between these courses and the integration of ethics education into other subjects, among staff, and with families, enterprises and society, all under unified Party leadership. The piece concludes that this will allow high-quality development of the courses within Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a university Party secretary presents Party leadership of ideological education in official Party discourse in 2024.

Several questions in the study of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times in the new era 新时代马克思主义中国化时代化研究的几个问题 Xiao Guiqing How has the meaning of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times developed, what is new about the "new leap" of the new era, and what links the Party's successive theoretical achievements? Xiao Guiqing takes up these three questions. The author argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era marks a new leap, and that Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi's thought form one developing whole. The article has three parts. The first traces the concept from Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation through the Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao periods to the Two Integrations after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second examines three respects in which the new era is said to bring a leap. The third sets out the internal logic that unites the theoretical achievements, under historical, theoretical and value headings. In Xiao's account, earlier theory stressed combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with the features of the age. Xi adds a combination with fine traditional Chinese culture, which Xiao calls a new theoretical proposition. Xiao holds that traditional culture was the cultural soil, not the theoretical basis, of Mao Zedong Thought and the earlier theoretical system. The leap also lies in a new theoretical system, set out in the 19th and 20th Party Congresses and the sixth plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), and in answers to major questions of the era: the direction of socialism with Chinese characteristics, Chinese modernization, and building a long-governing Marxist party. Xiao presents the Party's self-reform as a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. On unity, Xiao argues that all the achievements serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, rest on Marxism and seeking truth from facts, and put the people first. Xiao concludes that the three achievements are successive and logically connected, forming one continuously innovating theoretical system. The text is written to support further theoretical innovation as the Party pursues its second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a mainstream Party-theory account of how the concept of adapting Marxism to China has been periodised and how the Two Integrations are presented as the basis of a new leap.

The "Fengqiao experience": Mao Zedong's governance philosophy and wisdom and its contemporary development “枫桥经验”：毛泽东治国理政的理念与智慧及其当代发展 Zhou Zhongzhi Zhou Zhongzhi asks what the "Fengqiao experience", endorsed by Mao Zedong in 1963–64, reveals about Mao's approach to governing China and why it still matters. The article argues that the experience embodies Mao's governance ideas and wisdom, and that its continued development under Xi Jinping has theoretical and practical value for realising Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's thinking from "On the Ten Major Relationships" (1956) and "On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People" (1957) to the Fengqiao case in Zhejiang, where cadres and villagers reformed "four-category elements" locally. The second links the experience to traditional Chinese culture, namely joint rule by virtue and law and the people-as-foundation tradition. The third follows its development from Mao to Xi Jinping, including its adoption in the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Zhou's central claim is that Mao joined a "grand pattern" of top-level design with a "downward shift of the centre of gravity" to grassroots governance. The slogan "contradictions are not passed upward but resolved on the spot" rests on three elements: dialectical analysis of contradictions and their transformation, a historical-materialist mass line, and roots in Chinese tradition, including village rules and mediation. Zhou also treats governance culture as an "implicit institution" that supports formal rules. For the present, the author sees growing domestic and international risks as making grassroots governance urgent, and says the new-era experience has grown into a system combining self-governance, rule of law and rule of virtue. Zhou concludes that the experience should be upheld and developed by combining human effort with technology. Digital tools bring efficiency and fine-grained management, which Zhou links to Xi's image of governing "like embroidery". Zhou warns that they cannot replace face-to-face work with the masses, since reliance on online contact could breed bureaucratism and formalism. The author also says Chinese governance must rest on Chinese culture and cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how the Fengqiao experience is tied to Mao's texts, traditional culture and Xi-era grassroots governance.

Deng Xiaoping's major contribution to the methodology of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 邓小平对马克思主义中国化方法论的重大贡献 Tian Keqin Tian Keqin asks what Deng Xiaoping contributed to the methodology by which Marxism is adapted to Chinese conditions. The article argues that Deng held a strong methodological self-awareness. In Tian's account, he upheld and developed Mao Zedong's method, and he applied the methodology of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context in new ways. This opened up socialism with Chinese characteristics and moved Marxism's Chinese development into a new stage. Tian takes as his starting point Xi Jinping's remark that seeking truth from facts was Deng's most important intellectual trait. The article, published in 2024 in Marxist Studies, has three parts. The first covers the period from Deng's return to office (1977) to the 12th Party Congress (1982). It deals with his restoration of the Party's ideological line and his assessment of Mao Zedong Thought. The second part examines how he set the theme of socialism with Chinese characteristics and founded Deng Xiaoping Theory. The third part examines his creative use of four methods: seeking truth from facts, the mass line, independence and self-reliance, and dialectical thinking. Tian's central claim is that Deng tied the universal principles of Marxism to the concrete practice of modernization and to the features of the era. Tian presents the formula of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the result of that tie. Deng Xiaoping Theory, Tian argues, rests on three linked emphases: practice, productive forces and the creativity of the masses. In the third part, each method is matched to a problem. Seeking truth from facts grounds the primary stage of socialism as the basis of policy. The mass line explains the driving force of modernization, including common prosperity. Independence and self-reliance mark out a distinct path, with Deng's 'Chinese-style modernization' defined as 'xiaokang' (a moderately comfortable standard). Dialectical thinking underlies the 'one centre, two basic points' layout and the 'grasp with both hands' policies. Tian concludes that Deng combined Chinese conditions with a world outlook, and that his methods guide later development. The article calls on the Party in the new era to carry forward and apply this methodology, linking it to the 'six musts' and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Deng's thought is placed in the lineage of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, and of how it is tied to current official discourse.

Deng Xiaoping's thought on reform and its value for our times 邓小平改革思想及其时代价值 Qu Qingshan Writing after Xi Jinping's speech marking the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth, Qu Qingshan asks what Deng's thought on reform contained and why it still matters. Qu argues that it forms a complete system within Deng Xiaoping Theory and that the Party's current drive for further comprehensively deepening reform continues it. In Qu's account, the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) upheld, enriched and developed it. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical conditions in which Deng's reform thinking arose, which Qu summarises as four "bases": the future of the Party and country at the end of the Cultural Revolution, lessons from socialist revolution and construction, the trends of the age, and the aspirations of the people. The second sets out eight themes in the thought itself and the results of reform. The third draws lessons for today from the "six adherences" of the 2024 plenum. Qu presents Deng's thought as answering the question of what socialist reform is and how to carry it out. The themes are Party leadership, reliance on the masses, reform as the self-improvement of the socialist system, reform as liberating the productive forces, comprehensive reform, and "bold but steady" method. They also include the "three favourables" as criteria for judging reform, and opening up as part of reform. Qu then links each of the plenum's six principles to Deng: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, institution-building, law-based governance and a systematic outlook. Qu holds that the shift from a highly centralised planned economy to a socialist market economy, and the rise of the economy to second in the world, vindicate Deng's decision. Qu concludes that reform and opening up has "no completion, only a present tense", and that the continuity of its historical, theoretical and practical logic links Deng's era with the new era. Qu calls for unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and for implementation of the 2024 reform decisions.
