Qu describes Chinese modernization as drawing its momentum from reform and its vitality from opening up. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how Deng's reform thinking is being tied to the 2024 reform agenda.

The threefold dimensions of ideological and political education from the perspective of the modernization of the human being 人的现代化视域下思想政治教育的三重向度 Cao Qingyan Zhang Bei Cao and Zhang start from the claim that the essence of modernization is the modernization of the human being, meaning a shift in people's ideas, ways of thinking and ways of living from the traditional to the modern. They ask what this implies for ideological and political education. Their answer is that, seen from this angle, such education has three dimensions: individual, social and species-wide (the article's 'human' or 'generic' dimension), all oriented to the free and all-round development of the person. The article first sets out the logical link between the two. It argues that ideological and political education carries the modernization of the human being within its values, supplies a method for achieving it through spiritual production, and must itself be modernized in response. Three sections then take each dimension in turn, drawing on Marx's three social formations, his account of world history and the 'real community', and Xi Jinping's statements on Chinese modernization. In the individual dimension, the authors use Marx's contrast between dependence on persons and dependence on things to argue that modernization must move from an imbalance to a balance of material and spiritual life. Ideological and political education should therefore guide people towards spiritual richness, raising their spiritual needs and widening and deepening their spiritual interaction. In the social dimension, they contrast capital-driven Western modernization with Chinese modernization, which they describe as people-centred, and call on education to lead people to merge the 'small self' into the 'greater self' of nation and era. In the species dimension, they hold that individual liberation depends on the liberation of humanity, and they urge education to build global awareness and a community with a shared future for mankind on top of loyalty to the state. The authors conclude that ideological and political education is always bound up with human activity and should keep renewing itself in order to advance the modernization of the human being. Their practical proposals include cross-cultural competence, participation in global governance and in the Belt and Road Initiative, and ecological ethics. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link Marx's theory of human development to the aims and curriculum of ideological and political education under Chinese modernization.

Comprehensively deepening reform provides institutional guarantees for developing new quality productive forces in line with local conditions 全面深化改革为因地制宜发展新质生产力提供体制保障 Zhou Wen Writing after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Zhou Wen asks what institutional mechanisms are needed to develop new quality productive forces in line with local conditions. The article takes the Plenum's Decision on further deepening reform to advance Chinese modernization as its starting point, in particular its call for a mechanism that adapts new quality productive forces to each locality. Zhou argues that three sets of reforms supply the necessary guarantees: a high-standard socialist market economy, a system supporting comprehensive innovation, and high-level opening up. The article is organised in three parts, each opening with a passage from the Decision and then setting out specific measures. The first deals with the market economy system, covering basic market institutions and a unified national market. The second deals with the coordination of education, science and technology, and talent. The third deals with regional opening-up patterns, investment and trade mechanisms, and institutional opening-up. In the first part, Zhou holds that localities, especially less developed ones, need outside resources to unlock their own. This requires protecting property and intellectual property rights, improving market access, safeguarding fair competition and building a social credit system, together with a unified national market in which factors of production flow freely. The second part argues that education, science and technology, and talent must be planned together. Zhou proposes discipline-building and evaluation reforms, science and technology planning that combines national direction with local initiative, and leading technology firms that draw in small and medium-sized enterprises. Talent policy covers training, recruitment, use and orderly mobility, including movement towards poorer regions that take on national projects. The third part assigns different roles to the eastern, central, western and northeastern regions, and calls for investment and trade liberalisation. It also calls for alignment with high-standard international trade rules and support for the multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization. Zhou concludes that these reforms together would channel advanced production factors towards new quality productive forces, raise total factor productivity and create production relations better suited to them. The measures are presented as concrete tasks for implementing the Plenum's decisions. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented account of how the Third Plenum's reform agenda is linked to regional development of new quality productive forces.

The political pathology of the "economic resource curse": evolution of research and intellectual genealogy “经济资源诅咒”的政治病理学：研究演进与知识谱系 Song Yiming This literature review surveys research on why resource-rich countries often experience slow or stagnant growth, the phenomenon labelled the "economic resource curse". Song notes that scholars now broadly agree the phenomenon is real and are still debating its conditions, while its generating mechanisms, which the article calls its "pathology", remain fiercely contested. The author argues that taking stock of existing work is more urgent than adding to it, because empirical studies that refute one another have fragmented the field without advancing understanding. The article is built in six parts. It traces the history of the research in three stages, from the 1950s–70s structuralist critique (Prebisch, Singer) through the 1970–early 1990s conceptual innovations ("rentier state", "Dutch disease", Richard Auty's "resource curse") to the post-1995 phase of mechanism-hunting and empirical testing that began with Sachs and Warner. It then maps the disciplines involved, separating micro-level fields (regional economics, public administration, human geography, environmental sociology) from macro-level ones (development economics, international economics, comparative and international political economy). Its main section sets out the political-science explanations, and a final section discusses difficulties and a research agenda. In the core section Song identifies six political mechanisms: resource sectors encourage rent-seeking and corruption; they invite armed conflict, including civil war, interstate war and terrorism; they weaken domestic institutions, including property rights; they erode the state's capacity to extract resources through the "rentier effect"; and they produce an "intertemporal dilemma" in which governments cannot credibly commit to foreign investors, raising transaction costs. The author then diagnoses two problems. Empirically, the field has become a "statistical game" of mutual falsification that yields no cumulative knowledge. Theoretically, mechanisms, institutional weakness above all, are stretched beyond their explanatory boundaries, so that none can serve as a "universal acid". Song proposes returning to descriptive, country-focused case analysis that traces each exporter's particular path into the curse, in place of endless testing of existing variables. The author also calls for specifying the boundaries and conditions of each mechanism and for more attention to conditional explanations, in which resources cause the curse only together with other factors, since most work favours unconditional ones. Song presents the review as a starting point, leaving meta-analysis and further empirical work to later studies. Read the original if you want a systematic map of the political-science literature on the resource curse, with its main authors and an argument for shifting from statistical falsification to case-based research.

Mao Zedong's philosophy and practice of struggle: "neither believing in evil nor fearing ghosts" 毛泽东“不信邪、不怕鬼”的斗争哲学和实践 Xin Ping Zou Wulong Xin Ping and Zou Wulong take up the injunction to be "unbelieving in evil and unafraid of ghosts", which the Party's third historical resolution (adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, 2021) wrote into a historical resolution for the first time. They argue that Mao Zedong was its chief proponent and practitioner, and that guided by historical materialism he gradually built a systematic philosophy of struggle that is now a fine tradition and valuable experience of the Communist Party of China. The article has three parts. It first sets out the philosophical foundations of the idea, then traces three stages in its practical development from the 1910s to the socialist construction period, and finally identifies three features of the philosophy. The evidence is drawn from Mao's speeches and writings, the New Youth debate on spiritualism, the revolutionary war years and the compilation of the 1961 book Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts. On the foundations, the authors hold that "ghosts and evil" stand for superstition and illusion, and that Marxist views of truth, the analysis of contradiction and the mass line supply the philosophical basis. Mao, they say, extended the term to everything that must be fought: imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism before 1949, then reactionary forces worldwide, natural disasters, setbacks in construction, and even timidity among Party members. On the practical stages, the idea first appeared in Mao's 1919 call "do not fear ghosts" after the New Youth attack on the Shanghai Spiritualist Society. It developed through armed struggle, the Jinggangshan base, opposition to "Left" lines and the War of Resistance, and was refined after 1949, when Mao urged contempt for the enemy strategically and seriousness tactically. The three features are: starting from the principal contradiction and the main task of each period; daring to struggle; and protecting national security and social stability. The authors conclude that the philosophy proved successful and is a spiritual asset that changed the fate of the Chinese nation and contributed to the liberation of oppressed peoples. They call for studying and carrying it forward amid what they term "changes unseen in a century", so as to be "daring and good at struggle" in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese historian's account links Mao's revolutionary-era language and texts to current Party discourse on struggle.

Accelerating the construction of a self-reliant Chinese atheism knowledge system An interview with Tian Xinming of the Higher Education Science Research Development Centre, Ministry of Education 《马克思主义研究》记者：加快建构中国自主无神论知识体系 Marxist Studies reporter This is an interview, conducted by a reporter for the journal Marxist Studies (issue 7, 2024), with Tian Xinming, a researcher formerly at the Ministry of Education's higher-education social science research centre. It asks how atheism, described as an indispensable but weak discipline within philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, can be built up under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Tian answers that, following Xi's remark that the task is ultimately to build a self-reliant Chinese knowledge system, the discipline should now build a self-reliant atheism knowledge system. The interview has three parts: why, what kind of system, and how. Tian first defines "knowledge system" as the umbrella term for the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems, then reviews the discipline's history. He then sets out four dimensions of "Chinese self-reliance": guiding ideology, object of study, academic resources, and subjectivity and originality. The last part proposes a structure and method, and closes on the Two Integrations. Tian argues that the discipline started late and developed slowly, producing the saying "atheism has no one to speak for it, theism does". He nonetheless sees enough accumulated work since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to allow "integration" and "final assembly". For Tian, the guiding ideology must be Marxism as a whole, not isolated quotations. The object of study is the contradiction between a godless material world and the presence of belief in gods in social consciousness, together with the opposition of atheism and theism. Marxism serves both as guide and as primary academic resource, whereas traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship are resources only. Tian calls for a unified, theoretically grounded ("systematic and学理") discipline cluster covering theory, history and practice. An introductory textbook on atheism would condense the whole system around three questions: whether gods exist, what role atheism and theism play, and how to uphold atheism and treat religion in practice. Tian concludes that the Two Integrations are the fundamental route to building the system, and that Marxist guidance, blending of resources, subjectivity and originality, and systematisation all apply them. In practice, he says, the work must support the Party's religious policy, which combines firm atheism as a worldview with unity between believers and non-believers. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-academic blueprint for establishing atheism as a discipline, including its proposed structure and its link to religious policy.

Mao Zedong and the construction of the New Democratic system 毛泽东与新民主主义制度的建构 Zhang Jianzhou Zhang Jianzhou asks how Mao Zedong built the New Democratic system, which the author calls the "preface" and "first part" of the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that Mao was its chief architect: he set its historical preconditions, designed its "four beams and eight pillars" in politics, economy and culture, and charted its transformation into a socialist system. Zhang presents this as a solution to the institutional crisis of semi-colonial, semi-feudal China, with lessons for other formerly colonised countries. The article has three parts. The first covers the preconditions: the adaptation of Marxist state theory to Chinese conditions and the lessons of political-power building under the Soviet, anti-Japanese and liberation-war periods. The second sets out the political, economic and cultural institutions. The third examines the "timetable" and "road map" for the shift to socialism after 1949. A short conclusion places the New Democratic system within Marxist theory and in today's institutional development. Zhang's central argument is that Mao departed from a dogmatic reading of the classics and from the "one-revolution" and "two-revolution" theories. Politically, the system combined a joint dictatorship of several revolutionary classes with democratic centralism, under the Communist Party's unified leadership. Economically, it combined a state-led "one dominant, several coexisting" ownership structure with both planning and market mechanisms. Culturally, it sought a national, scientific and mass culture while seeking a "greatest common divisor" among classes' ideologies. Zhang explains Mao's 1952 decision to begin the transition at once by two factors: recovery data showing a material base, and the system's limits in financing industrialisation and checking capitalist tendencies. The transition then ran through ownership change, a political shift to a people's democratic dictatorship that is in essence proletarian dictatorship, and a longer cultural transformation. Zhang concludes that the New Democratic system was an inevitable choice and a creative answer to how socialism could be built in a backward semi-colonial country. In this reading it supplied what Marx's account of the "transition period" left unspecified. Although it became a historical concept once socialist transformation was complete, the author urges today's China to draw on Mao's legacy in improving its system of fundamental, basic and important institutions and in pursuing the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of Mao's institutional design, with the economic data and Mao quotations used to justify the 1952 shift to the transition to socialism.

Comrade Deng Xiaoping and the pioneering of socialism with Chinese characteristics 邓小平同志与中国特色社会主义的开创 Xie Chuntao This short commemorative commentary asks what Deng Xiaoping contributed to opening up socialism with Chinese characteristics. Xie Chuntao presents Deng as a figure of the century and as chief architect of reform and opening up and modernization. Xie also calls him the founder of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and principal creator of Deng Xiaoping Theory. The piece is organised around three contributions: a new path, a new theory and a new historical period. It ends by linking Deng's legacy to the work of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping. On the path, Xie says that when Deng returned to work in the late 1970s he started from correcting the ideological line and pushed the Party to rethink what socialism is. Deng drew on Mao Zedong's explorations, the Party's own setbacks and world socialist experience, and combined socialism with Chinese characteristics. On theory, Xie credits Deng with the first fairly systematic answers on building socialism in a economically and culturally backward country. Xie cites the essence of socialism, the primary stage of socialism, the socialist market economy and the Party's basic line of "one central task, two basic points". Xie holds that these made an original contribution to scientific socialism and marked a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. On the period, Xie points to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee, rural contracting, special economic zones, and Deng's 1992 southern tour. Xie concludes that Deng's work is best honoured by carrying forward the cause he began, as Xi Jinping has said. Xie calls for closer unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and for deepening reform and opening up in pursuit of Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Central Party School leader presents Deng's legacy in official Party history.

Deng Xiaoping's acceptance of Marxism as a young man: historical conditions and intellectual trajectory, seen through sources on his years in Europe 从留欧史料透视青年邓小平接受马克思主义的历史条件与思想脉络 Liu Sisi Why did the young Deng Xiaoping, who went to France on a work-study programme at 16 and later studied in the Soviet Union, come to adopt Marxism? Liu argues that existing studies divide his time abroad into separate periods and rarely set it against modern China's wider history or treat the French and Soviet years as one whole. The article contends that his turn to Marxism was historically necessary, shaped by the political climate, by earlier Chinese communists in Europe and by his own experience. The article has two main parts. The first examines four historical conditions: the May Fourth Movement of 1919, the Chinese work-study movement in France, the founding of Chinese Communist Party and Youth League organisations in Europe, and the movement to study in the Soviet Union. The second traces four stages in Deng's thinking. The evidence includes his own later recollections, his 1985 talks with foreign visitors, French police reports, Soviet-period questionnaires and self-assessments, and his articles in the Europe-based Party and Youth League periodicals. Liu argues that Deng began with a patriotic, reformist ideal of "saving the nation through industry". Hard factory labour in France then showed him the nature of capitalist society, and he abandoned that ideal. Comrades such as Zhou Enlai, Cai Hesen and Zhao Shiyan introduced him to socialist literature, and Deng later described the combination of study, persuasion and personal suffering as leading him to seek a revolutionary organisation. Liu reads his articles in the periodical Chiguang, which attack the nationalist "statist" Youth Party and denounce imperialism through an analogy with the Dawes Plan, as his first Marxist theoretical work. In Moscow, at Sun Yat-sen University, Liu says he studied a systematic curriculum, including political economy centred on Capital, and received Party discipline training, which gave him "a considerable understanding of communism". Liu concludes that Deng's early development reflected the historical setting, his hardships abroad, his exposure to capitalism and European Marxism, and the influence of a cohort of early Chinese communists who studied abroad. Liu proposes further individual, comparative and overall studies of that cohort and its contribution to the Party's founding. Read the original if you want a source-based account of Deng Xiaoping's ideological formation in France and the USSR, or of the early Chinese communists' European networks, as Chinese Party historians present them.

On the construction and consolidation of the subjectivity of Chinese culture 论中华文化主体性的建构与巩固 Zhao Jianying Zhao Jianying takes up a concept that Xi Jinping put forward in 2023: the "subjectivity" (zhutixing) of Chinese culture, which Zhao presents as a hallmark concept of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article asks what the concept means, why it must be consolidated, and how. Its thesis is that building and strengthening cultural subjectivity is necessary for cultural prosperity, for a strong cultural nation and for the modern Chinese civilization that the Party seeks to build. Zhao also presents it as an advance in the Party's cultural self-awareness and in Marxist cultural theory. The article has three parts. The first traces "subjectivity" from Protagoras, Socrates and Aristotle through Descartes, Kant and neo-Kantianism to Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, then derives cultural subjectivity from it. The second sets out four reasons why consolidation is required. The third proposes six routes: guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Party's cultural leadership, the Two Integrations, an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, openness to other civilizations, and cultural subjectivity in cyberspace. Zhao defines cultural subjectivity through four capacities named by Xi: guiding, cohesive, shaping and radiating power. In Zhao's account, Chinese cultural subjectivity has four features: originality, a leading culture within a plural whole, autonomy in exchange with other civilizations, and a conscious tradition of cultivating people through culture. Zhao says the article concerns the subjectivity of contemporary socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, guided by Marxism. The article links this subjectivity to cultural confidence, to the Party's capacity to lead its era and to national cohesion, and to cultural security. It describes Western ideological infiltration and a "Western strong, China weak" pattern in international opinion. The Two Integrations, especially integration with traditional culture, are called a "chemical reaction" in which Marxism supplies the "soul" and traditional culture the "roots". Zhao argues that Chinese theory and the social sciences need originality and must not follow foreign models. Zhao concludes that Chinese civilization has endured because of its cultural subjectivity. The article says this subjectivity was shaken after 1840 and rebuilt after Marxism arrived and the Party was founded. Zhao credits the Party leadership since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with reversing the marginalisation of Marxism in ideology. The proposals include stronger Party leadership over cultural work, management of online content, and the promotion of distinctive Chinese concepts abroad. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese Marxist scholars ground Xi Jinping's cultural thought in the history of philosophy and in the cultural security and ideological agenda of the Party-state.

Mutual learning among civilizations and the building of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 文明互鉴与中华民族现代文明建设 Qian Chengdan Qian Chengdan, a historian at Peking University, asks how mutual learning among civilizations bears on the building of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. He argues that modernization is a profound civilizational transformation and, for China, another great fusion of civilizations, larger and deeper than earlier ones. Through it, Qian says, Chinese civilization has both absorbed the world and entered it. The article is organised around three questions: the two carriers of a civilization and the "inner core" of Chinese civilization; the fusing nature of that civilization, or its capacity for "outward integration"; and the construction of a modern civilization during modernization. Qian compares China with ancient Greece, Rome, medieval Western Europe, South Asia and West Asia–North Africa. He then reviews three great fusions in Chinese history and the crisis that began in the mid-nineteenth century. Qian's central claim is that every civilization has a spiritual carrier (a religion or non-religious doctrine, its ideology) and a political carrier (state power, its institutional guarantee). Civilizations last when the two support each other. Chinese civilization, in his account, joined Confucian doctrine to a unified state more than two thousand years ago, and this pairing formed an unchanging core. The other cases, he argues, lacked such a match: Greece had no unified state, Rome had no unified ideology until it was declining, medieval Europe had faith without a state, India had ideology without a strong state, and West Asia achieved both only with Islam in the seventh century. Alongside this core, Qian presents fusion as a constant trait: the Wei-Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties period, the Song-Liao-Jin-Yuan era, and the Qing each enlarged Chinese civilization while preserving its core. He rejects as a Western fabrication the "Inner Asia" thesis about the Qing, and links Chinese openness to an early shift from a single-god cosmology to rationalism. On the modern period, Qian describes the mid-nineteenth-century crisis, in which industrial power broke open China, as a civilizational crisis as well as a political one. He concludes that China answered by pursuing modernization. It holds to its core, its core values and the cooperation of spiritual and state power, and it learns with great openness from the West and humility from non-Western experience. Chinese modernization is thus, in his words, another great civilizational fusion, at once inheritance and innovation. Read the original if you want a historian's civilizational framework, built on the "two carriers" and "core plus fusion", for the official idea of a modern Chinese civilization.

Technological drivers of the rise of Western populism in the digital age 数字时代西方民粹主义崛起的技术动因 Yang Chunlin Yang Chunlin asks why populism has risen in Western societies since the mid-1990s, a period of rapid digitalisation, and offers a technological explanation. The article argues that digital technology reshapes political and economic equality in contradictory ways, and that this both supplies populism with a favourable external environment and gives populist forces internal tools to grow. Populism's rise is read as a concentrated expression of capitalism's inherent contradictions. The article opens with the dialectic of equality in the digital age. It sets the early "digital democracy utopia" against a later drift towards monopoly and what Yang calls a "technological Leviathan". It then examines external support in three areas: economic inequality, the new media revolution in culture, and digital space's anti-establishment tendencies. A third section looks at internal empowerment through leaders, parties, discourse and elections. Cases include Brexit, Trump, Italy's Five Star Movement, Germany's AfD and the Yellow Vests. Yang's central moves are as follows. First, digital capitalism widens inequality, producing losers among blue-collar workers and the middle class who become populist supporters, and the author cites wage and productivity data. Second, new media weaken public judgement, replace elite culture with popular culture, and use algorithms to deepen polarisation. Social platforms also enable leaderless protest and weaken parties' roles in selecting elites and aggregating opinion, which Yang says leaves the West with both "insufficient democratic supply" and "excessive democratic participation". Third, populists exploit this directly: charismatic online leaders, parties run largely online, emotive and fragmentary rhetoric, and algorithmic targeted advertising, for which Yang cites Cambridge Analytica-type operations in 2016 and the AfD's 2017 campaign. Yang concludes that populism signals a rupture in Western democracy under new technological conditions: a collapsed public sphere, challenged political elites, and surveillance-capitalist governance that lacks moral appeal. Citing Habermas, Yang holds that technology is neutral but that the absence of "the human" in its development is the root of populism's rise. The article calls for a new humanist movement for the digital age. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how digital platforms, algorithms and inequality are linked to Western populism, with detailed European and American cases.

Deepening cultural system and institutional reform to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 深化文化体制机制改革 建设中华民族现代文明 Liu Lyuhong Yue Heng Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today shortly after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), Liu Lyuhong and Yue Heng ask how deepening reform of the cultural system and its mechanisms can advance the Party's cultural mission of building a "modern civilization of the Chinese nation". They argue that such reform is both the means and the guarantee of that project, and that it drives the modern transformation of Chinese civilization. The article is organised in three parts. It first sets out the logic of the link between cultural reform and civilization-building, with a historical survey running from Deng Xiaoping's era through successive Party congresses and plenums to the present. It then explains the internal pathway by which reform supplies momentum, institutional guarantees and spiritual strength. Finally it outlines the tasks of the new era, guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The authors present cultural reform as a "magic weapon", a basic principle and an unavoidable road. Historically, they trace the "two serves" and "double hundred" policies, the concept of spiritual civilization, the inclusion of the cultural industry in the national economy and the 2011 decision on cultural reform, up to the Second Integration. They argue that the modern civilization is a product of the Two Integrations and that reform must balance national character, modernity and global reach, so that Chinese culture neither reverts to the past nor becomes a Western appendage. Reform supplies momentum by activating traditional and revolutionary culture, guarantees by upholding Marxism's guiding role in ideology, core socialist values and a people-centred orientation, and spiritual strength by building cultural self-reliance, confidence and strength. For action, the authors call for guidance from Xi Jinping's thought on culture, stressing cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. They urge joining the "root" of traditional culture with the "soul" of Marxism, and building a more effective international communication system, with discourse, narrative and knowledge systems based on Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link cultural system reform to the civilizational goals set after the 2024 Third Plenum.

On the practical principles of Deng Xiaoping's theory of building socialist ideology In commemoration of the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth 论邓小平社会主义意识形态建设理论的实践原则 Jiang Yingchun Jiang Yingchun asks how Deng Xiaoping's thinking on building socialist ideology can guide ideological work today, when the coordinated development of material and cultural-ethical civilization is, in the article's words, an important feature of Chinese modernization. Jiang argues that this coordination is a process of contradiction, marked by clashes between the advanced and the backward, so that ideological struggle remains necessary. The article's thesis is that Deng's theory rests on three practical principles: grasping the fundamentals, staying vigilant in times of peace, and holding firm to conviction. Written to mark the 120th anniversary of Deng's birth, the article is organised in three sections, one for each principle. It draws mainly on Deng's speeches and interviews from the early reform period, set alongside statements by Xi Jinping, the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2014) and the resolution of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). It also refers to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe as a negative lesson. On the first principle, Jiang reads Deng's Four Cardinal Principles as the political foundation of reform and modernization, a "complete set of equipment" that must not be split up. They are presented as the basis for correcting both "Left" and Right errors, since without them correcting the Left would become "correcting" Marxism-Leninism. On the second, Jiang argues that a small minority can damage the cause, that attacks on Party leadership, multi-party systems and Western-style "constitutionalism" aim at socialism itself, and that ideological collapse brought down the Soviet Communist Party. Jiang endorses Deng's call for ideological workers to carry out criticism and self-criticism with confidence, rather than avoid struggle. On the third, Jiang holds that shared ideals unite the people and are the Party's "real advantage". Developing the productive forces is described as the material basis for showing socialism's superiority, consolidating the system and eventually reaching communism. Conviction, Jiang adds, must survive a long historical process, mistakes in work and major setbacks. Jiang concludes that these three principles remain practically important for building a socialist ideology with strong guiding and unifying power and for coordinating the two civilizations. The article presents the shift in ideological work under Xi Jinping's leadership as a result of this continuing struggle. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Deng's ideological writings are mobilised in current debates on Party leadership, "Western" political ideas and the lessons of the Soviet collapse.

Is populism a thin ideology? Reflections on and criticisms of the Mudde thesis 民粹主义是一种薄意识形态吗？ He Tao Cas Mudde's definition of populism as a "thin-centered ideology", known as the Mudde thesis, is widely accepted in comparative politics and has been cited in more than 50 Chinese articles in three years. He asks whether this definition holds up. While acknowledging Mudde's aim of a workable minimal definition, He argues that populism is not suited to being defined as a thin ideology and that the thesis is flawed both methodologically and in its core elements. The article first traces the concept to Michael Freeden's morphological theory of ideology, where key, adjacent and peripheral concepts structure "thick" ideologies such as liberalism and "thin" ones such as feminism, green thought and nationalism. It then sets out Mudde's motives and the four advantages he claims: distinguishability, categorizability, travelability and versatility. Two critical sections follow, one on methodology and one on the three core elements: the people, the elite and the general will. On method, He argues that treating populism as an ideology is only one position among several, and that Mudde's early work on European far-right parties shaped it. Figures such as Perón and Chávez shifted policy positions and seem to lack even a thin ideology. The concept of thinness is also vague, and Freeden himself now rejects its application to populism, calling it "emaciatedly thin". On the core elements, He argues that Mudde's idea of "the people" is too general and slides back into the "empty signifier" he rejects. His moral opposition between pure people and corrupt elite fits Western European right-wing populism poorly: Trump, Berlusconi and Fujimori were wealthy elites with moral flaws yet were seen as representatives of the people. His reading of the general will also departs from Rousseau. In He's account, populism instead substitutes a part of the people for the whole. He concludes that populism is a complex phenomenon with ideological, strategic, discursive and movement dimensions, and that researchers should avoid the pull of minimalism. Ideological analysis should engage seriously with ideology theory. Future work should also examine populism's quasi-religious view of politics as redemption, its preference for leaders' discretion over legal checks, and its idea of direct representation between leader and voters. In He's phrase, the problem is not that populist ideology is too "thin" but that the Mudde thesis touches only its thin outer layer. Read the original if you work on populism theory or comparative politics and want a detailed critique of the Mudde thesis drawn from the recent Western debate.

The historical development and basic experience of building the discipline of ideological and political education 思想政治教育学科建设的历史发展与基本经验 Wu Qiantao Du Sirui Marking the 40th anniversary of the undergraduate major in ideological and political education (established in 1984), Wu Qiantao and Du Sirui review how the discipline of the same name emerged and what its construction has taught. They argue that the discipline, which they describe as a key field positioned as the "lifeline" and "central link" of Party work, has moved from a major without a discipline to a mature discipline aligned with its major. They hold that its experience offers guidance for its "connotative development" in the new era. The article has three parts. The first periodises the discipline's history: germination and cultivation (1984–1995), a start and exploration phase (1996–2004), and establishment and development (2005 to the present). The second sets out four areas of achievement: the core content of research, the teaching force, the training of students from bachelor's to doctoral level, and support for the university ideological and political theory courses ("Ideological and political theory courses"). The third distils three basic lessons. The authors trace dated Party and state documents, such as the 1984 Ministry of Education notice, the 1996 doctoral programme, the 1997 listing as a second-level discipline, and the 2005 creation of Marxist theory as a first-level discipline. They then show content evolving in four strands: ideals and convictions, values, morality and the rule of law. Evidence includes staffing figures (5,650 full-time teachers in 2021, 28% of the Marxist theory total), degree-point numbers and graduate outcomes at selected institutions. The lessons are Party leadership with top-level design; building an autonomous knowledge system, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture and distinguishing its treatment of ideals, values, morals and law from politics, philosophy, ethics and law; and joining theory to practice, by supporting the courses, talent training and practical work. The authors conclude that the discipline's growth has depended on Party leadership, Party innovative theory and state policy support, and that its future lies in an autonomous knowledge system and in feeding research back into teaching and practice. They present this as an answer to the new tasks posed by the "two overall situations" and the goal of training new-era successors. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-document-based institutional history of this discipline, with data on staffing and degree programmes, and the official account of its lessons.

The principles and direction of the "Two Integrations" in adapting Marxism to China, seen through Mao Zedong's philosophy 从毛泽东哲学透视马克思主义中国化“两个结合”的原则与走向 Xue Guangzhou Xue Guangzhou asks how the Two Integrations (combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture) should be understood and carried out, and where the adaptation of Marxism to China is heading. Reading the question through Mao Zedong's philosophy, the author argues that the Two Integrations are not slogans. They need clear principles. Marxism must remain the standard by which tradition is judged, and the process should end in a new Chinese philosophy. The article has three parts. The first clarifies the two objects of integration, "China's concrete realities" and "excellent traditional Chinese culture". The second sets out the principles for each integration and warns against several tendencies. The third traces the path from the sinicisation of Marxist philosophy to Marxist philosophy in sinicised form, then to a Chinese Marxist philosophy, and finally to a Chinese "new philosophy". Mao's discussions of practice, contradiction and cultural inheritance, together with Xi Jinping's statements, supply the reference points. Xue defines China's concrete realities by the principal contradiction and the social character of each stage. The author criticises neoliberal economics for rejecting China's existing economic base, and criticises online claims that equality of starting point is enough. On tradition, Xue separates its "essence" (jīngsuǐ, a factual judgement about its basic spirit) from its "best elements" (jīnghuá, a value judgement made from the present). Xue proposes the concept of "zhōng" (the mean, rendered as harmony, unity, rectitude and greatness) as the essence of Chinese philosophy. For the integration, the author lists Mao-derived principles: take the essence and discard the dross, inherit critically, make the past serve the present, let a hundred flowers bloom, and above all keep Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method. Xue rejects treating Marxism and Chinese tradition as equal partners, and rejects reading cultural revival as a revival of Confucianism. Xue also rejects reading Xi Jinping's thought on culture only as inheritance of tradition or as a lineage of orthodoxy (dàotǒng). Xue concludes that Marxism and Chinese philosophy will eventually converge in a Chinese new philosophy. That philosophy would absorb the best of Chinese tradition and of humanity's intellectual achievements, and would be accepted by most Chinese people. The author credits Mao's thought with a pioneering contribution and says Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era opens a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, linked to building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system. Read the original if you want a Mao-centred, philosophically oriented account of how Chinese scholars debate the limits of the "Second Integration" with tradition.

Advancing the building of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation through the continuity of Chinese civilization 以中华文明的连续性推进中华民族现代文明建设 Li Zheng Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remark at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development that Chinese civilization has a "outstanding continuity", Li Zheng asks how that continuity can be used to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. The article argues that continuity gives the country cultural subjectivity and a model of "keeping to fundamental principles while innovating". Li presents it as the spiritual and methodological resource for a new form of human civilization. The article has three parts. The first sets out what continuity means: the deep origins of Chinese civilization, its uninterrupted transmission, and its habit of innovating within tradition. Li draws on archaeology, from early hominid finds through Neolithic cultures to the sequence of early states, kingdoms and empires, and on classical texts. The second part gives the "internal logic" linking past and present, and the third draws practical lessons. Li's core argument is that three features of the historical record explain why continuity can drive modern civilization-building. These are a stable and distinctive geographical environment, the value of "zhonghe" (balance and harmony), and a pattern of unity in diversity among peoples. The author reads the geography as offering strategic depth and room for development in the west, the deserts and the south, and links it to the Belt and Road Initiative. Zhonghe is read as the basis for moderate development, peaceful cooperation and a community with a shared future for mankind. Unity in diversity is traced through Xi's "four commonalities" and the Sui–Tang period. From this Li derives four relationships to manage: harmony between humans and nature, coordination of material and spiritual civilization, unity of tradition and modern wisdom, and mutual learning with other civilizations. Li concludes that building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation is a new cultural mission of the new era. The author says it must proceed along the path of Chinese modernization, through the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture. Li presents this as enriching the "new form of human civilization", which is said to go beyond Western capital logic. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic links archaeology, classical philosophy and official cultural-policy language into a continuity-based account of Chinese modernization.

The "Second Integration" and the rebuilding of cultural subjectivity “第二个结合”与文化主体性重建 Li Wentang Li Wentang takes up the question of cultural subjectivity, which the author says has run through more than a century of Chinese debates over the relation between ancient and modern, China and the West. Li reads Xi Jinping's remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development as an answer to this question, framed through the Two Integrations and especially the "Second Integration" of Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. The thesis is that this integration has revitalised Chinese civilisation and is rebuilding its cultural subjectivity. The article defines cultural subjectivity as a self-aware, creative and transcendent cultural life-consciousness, marked by historicity, creativity and transcendence. It surveys Chinese cultural history, from the Yin-Zhou transition and Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism to the late Qing, the May Fourth movement and Yan'an. It ends by assessing current scholarship. Li argues that rebuilding means renewal rather than starting over. "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application" and wholesale Westernisation both failed, in Li's account, because they ignored how cultural life develops. Marxism succeeded for three reasons: it critiques Western modernity and cultural colonialism, it points the direction by affirming science and democracy, and it is a new humanism. Li holds that this humanism fits Chinese ideals of moral self-cultivation and the unity of heaven and humanity better than liberalism does, which explains why early communists fused political and moral idealism. Li concludes that the Second Integration is another act of intellectual emancipation by the Party, to be pursued under three principles: cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and upholding fundamental principles while innovating. Li also says that scholars who command both Chinese and Western learning are in short supply and that an autonomous knowledge system is still far off. Read the original if you want a concise statement, in the Central Party School's idiom, of how the Second Integration is justified through Chinese cultural history.

Western populism and the dynamics of restructuring world politics 西方民粹主义思潮与世界政治重构的动力 Lin Hong Lin Hong asks how Western populism, a domestic political current, links national politics to international politics and so begins to restructure world politics. The article opens with three crises of the 21st century: the 9/11 attacks, the 2008 financial crisis and the 2015 European refugee crisis. Lin argues that populism, increasingly merged with nationalism, is a powerful ideational force that has moved from domestic arenas into the international system, and that world politics should be studied from the inside out, with attention to ideas and values. The article has four main sections plus a conclusion. It first traces populism's turn to the right, then examines how it reshapes domestic political processes (state–society relations, party systems, policy-making). It next analyses how populism spills over into a worldwide political current, and finally considers how it drives the reconstruction of the world political system. Lin draws throughout on Western international-relations and political-science scholarship (Rodrik, Lasswell, Milner, Gourevitch, Tsebelis, Keohane) and on Chinese scholars such as Yang Guangbin and Wang Zhengyi. In Lin's account, globalisation under neoliberalism produced inequality and identity crises, which bred a collective sense of insecurity. Populism fused with nationalism around three demands: stressing external threats, putting national interests first, and giving weight to values. Entering party competition and legislatures, populists act as veto players and push foreign policy towards decoupling, non-cooperation and hostility to international norms. Lin identifies three mechanisms of spillover: the export of domestic contradictions, the demonstration effect of core states such as the United States under Trump, and the erosion of state autonomy by globalisation. The result, the article argues, is weaker trust between states, weaker international institutions and weaker global value consensus. Lin concludes that domestic politics, ideas and anti-systemic movements have become key drivers of world political change, and that populism has replaced liberalism and socialism as the motor of change in the West. Whether right-wing populism will overturn the liberal order is, the author says, still unknown, but its ideational power is already evident. The article expects world politics to become more fragmented and uncertain, and calls for a concept of 'world politics' that goes beyond the Westphalian international-politics framework. Read the original if you want a Chinese international-relations scholar's framework linking populism, domestic politics and global order, with extensive citations of Western theory.

Building a modern Chinese civilization: profound connotations, guiding thought and practical orientation 建设中华民族现代文明：深刻内涵、思想遵循与实践旨趣 Liu Lina Liu Lina takes up the proposition of 'building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation', first put forward by Xi Jinping in October 2022 and restated in June 2023 as part of the Party's new cultural mission. The article asks what this civilization is and how it should be built. Liu's answer is that it is the cultural form of Chinese modernization and, in substance, a new form of human civilization. It must be understood through the relations among culture, civilization and modernization. After a brief review of existing scholarship, the article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the 'profound connotations' of the concept, in historical and contemporary terms. The second treats Xi Jinping's thought on culture as the 'guiding thought'. The third turns to the 'practical orientation', which Liu divides into four requirements for construction. In the first part, Liu argues that a civilizational view of modernization differs from the older, Western-derived account in three ways. It balances the universal and the particular, drawing on the late Marx's view that different civilizations cannot simply follow the Western European path. It stresses culture as an endogenous driving force. It also attends to people's conditions of existence, where it contrasts Marx's critique of bourgeois civilization with an approach that treats industrialization and urbanization as the main indicators. The second part draws on Xi Jinping Thought on culture. It names three sources of strength: consolidating the subjectivity of Chinese culture, the unity of 'substance and function' as an expression of the Second Integration, and a cultural mission that answers the value crisis Liu attributes to capitalist modernity. Liu presents capital's logic as the root of that crisis. Liu concludes that construction requires firm cultural confidence grounded in the Two Integrations, rootedness in Chinese modernization, and a proper relation between the Party's historical mission and its cultural mission. It also requires deeper exchange and mutual learning among civilizations, in opposition to theories of civilizational clash or superiority. The author links this to a community with a shared future for mankind. Liu holds that people-centredness replaces the logic of capital accumulation. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how current Party discourse connects culture, civilization and Chinese modernization, or an example of how Xi Jinping's cultural thought is expounded in Chinese academic writing.

Teaching ideological and political theory courses well on the basis of the world-acclaimed achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics 以举世瞩目成就为内容支撑讲好思政课 Yan Lianfu Responding to Xi Jinping's recent instruction on school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke), Yan Lianfu asks how these courses can be taught well. The article argues that they must be anchored in the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, which Yan says offer concrete evidence for the courses' claims. Doing so is presented as a way to strengthen students' faith, conviction and confidence and to encourage them to contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to Chinese modernization. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why achievements should be the content support of these courses. The second identifies four kinds of achievement to teach: theoretical, material and technological, spiritual and cultural, and institutional. The third proposes practical paths. It was published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscript (Hongqi Wengao), 2024 no. 13, and Yan is dean of the School of Marxism at Xi'an Jiaotong University. Yan argues that using achievements helps the courses explain principles in a deep, thorough and lively way. Achievements supply facts, data and cases to back theory. They enrich teaching content, widen teaching venues, and answer students' confusions about current events, including those arising online. Each type of achievement is linked to one form of confidence: theoretical achievements to theoretical confidence, material and technological ones to confidence in the path, cultural ones to cultural confidence, and institutional ones to institutional confidence. For institutions, Yan calls for explaining the 'institutional logic' behind the achievements. For practice, Yan proposes four emphases: all courses at every level should teach achievements; teaching should keep up with new achievements; new technologies such as AI, VR and AR should be used; and teachers and students should present achievements together, with teachers leading and students acting as active participants. Yan concludes that this approach will raise the courses' relevance and appeal and ensure that the Party's cause has successors. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Marxist-college academic turns Xi Jinping's guidance into a method for teaching political theory in Chinese schools and universities.

Consciously shouldering the principal responsibility for building ideological and political theory courses 自觉担起思政课建设的主体责任 Ma Fuyun This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 29 July 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's May 2024 instruction that schools of all levels must consciously assume the principal responsibility for ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke). Ma argues that the changes in these courses since the 18th Party Congress (2012) owe much to schools carrying out that responsibility, and that it must be strengthened further. The piece first explains why the responsibility is repeatedly stressed, citing Xi's March 2019 remarks and a joint General Office document of August 2019 naming Party secretaries and presidents as the "first responsible persons". It then sets out what the school's responsibility consists of, and closes with three practical measures. Ma contends that the courses cannot be advanced by teaching departments and teachers alone. At the macro level they serve the fundamental task of fostering virtue and nurturing talent; at the micro level they demand much of teachers and so need institutional support for training, evaluation and promotion. Ma divides the duty into leadership, institution-building, and guarantee and supervision, and also into building the School of Marxism, the Marxist theory discipline, teaching quality and the teaching force. Ma's three measures are: Party secretaries and presidents personally attend classes and direct the work; central policies are broken into indicators, responsibility lists, timetables and roadmaps; and a full system of assessment, accountability and sanctions is built. The aim is courses that students sincerely like and benefit from for life. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official line assigns duties for these courses to university leaders.

Upholding the Party's cultural leadership and the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation 坚守党的文化领导权和中华民族的文化主体性 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong's commentary expounds Xi Jinping's statement at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development that "keeping to the fundamental principles" in cultural work means upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, the requirements of the Two Integrations, and the Communist Party's cultural leadership and the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. Song presents this as a major innovative point drawn from the Party's historical experience, and argues that holding to it provides political assurance and spiritual strength for building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece has three parts. The first argues that upholding the Party's cultural leadership bears on the fate of the Party and country. The second sets out how to maintain the Party's overall leadership over propaganda, ideological and cultural work. The third turns to concrete steps for carrying out the new cultural mission. In the first part, Song traces the Party's attention to cultural leadership from Marx and Engels through the first Party congress resolution, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. The author says this leadership is a political strength of the Party and a requirement for safeguarding Marxism as the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". It is also described as a guarantee for the new cultural mission of building a strong cultural country and a modern Chinese civilization. The second part calls for confidence in culture, the cultivation of core socialist values through law and policy, the principle that the Party manages propaganda and ideology, and firm control of media positions, including the internet, with media placed under Party leadership and run by people loyal to it. Song concludes with proposals. These include fully implementing the ideological work responsibility system, building an independent Chinese knowledge system, strengthening international communication, and training a capable propaganda workforce. They also include reforming media and cultural institutions and perfecting the institutions through which the Party leads cultural development, such as a "big propaganda" pattern, integrated management of old and new media, and public cultural services. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line understanding of cultural leadership and its institutional and media-management implications under Xi Jinping Thought on Culture.

Green development empowers the leap of new quality productive forces 绿色发展赋能新质生产力跃升 Jin Xiaochun Taking as its starting point Xi Jinping's statement that green development is the foundation of high-quality development and that new quality productive forces are by nature green productive forces, this Red Flag Manuscripts article asks how green development and new quality productive forces are linked. Jin argues that green development is a basic requirement of new quality productive forces, and that it has to be realised through a green transition in both the mode of development and the way of life. The article has three parts. The first sets out why green development is required of new quality productive forces, drawing on Marx and Engels on natural conditions and on the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second turns to the green transition of the mode of development, covering the production system, the energy system and institutions. The third deals with green lifestyles and consumption, which Jin treats as the demand-side force behind new quality productive forces. Jin reasons from Marx's view that natural conditions, as objects and means of labour, are a source of use-values. On this basis, protecting the ecological environment is said to protect productive forces, and improving it to raise natural productive capacity, so that green mountains become mountains of gold and silver. The author cites figures: average annual energy consumption growth of 3% alongside economic growth above 6%, and world-leading capacity in hydro, wind, solar and biomass power. Jin nonetheless judges the overall level of green development to be still low, with growing resource and environmental pressure. The proposed remedies are digital and intelligent green production, a clean, low-carbon, safe and efficient energy system built on smart grids, and an institutional order combining an effective market with a proactive government. That order would include property rights in natural resources, ecological compensation and market trading of carbon, energy-use, water and emission rights. Jin also argues that green production technologies such as 3D printing, repair economies and sharing platforms make low-carbon consumption possible. Platform data collection that stimulates unnecessary consumption is flagged as a problem, to be met through ecological education and greener public services. Jin concludes that new quality productive forces must be green productive forces, and that development must stay within the carrying capacity of resources and the environment. The article calls for deeper integration of digitalisation and greening, a new energy system supporting the carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals, and thrifty, low-carbon habits in daily and public life. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school commentary connects Marx's account of natural conditions with the policy agenda of new quality productive forces and the green transition.

The development, basic features and trends of American Trotskyism 论美国托洛茨基主义的发展历程、基本特征及趋势 Liu Shanshan Huang Qihong Liu Shanshan and Huang Qihong ask how American Trotskyism arose, how it developed, and why it is now marginal. They argue that it is, in essence, a utopian radical current detached from American political reality. In their account its rise and decline both result from built-in flaws in its theory, organisation and practice. The authors note that existing scholarship largely stops at the 1990s and neglects the groups still active in the last two decades. The article first sets out the conditions for Trotskyism's emergence in the United States: support from the Fourth International, the Great Depression, James Cannon's turn away from the Communist Party, and the radical labour movement. It then divides the history into five stages: 1928–1938, 1938–1949, 1950–1970, 1970–1985, and the period since 1985. Each stage is tied to the Socialist Workers Party (SWP) and its theory and practice. A further section analyses current trends, and a final section offers a critical reflection and lessons for socialism. The authors present a pattern of rise and decline. Early Trotskyists built a theory of 'political revolution' against bureaucratism and organised through trade unions. Their 'end-times of capitalism' thesis was then undermined by postwar prosperity, McCarthyism, the 'vanguard of the vanguard' party model and repeated splits. From the 1960s the SWP turned to identity politics, and in the 1970s–80s, under Jack Barnes, it adopted a Cuba-centred outlook and broke with the Fourth International. The article names four current trends: ideological pluralisation and a fading Trotskyist character; marginalisation; fragmentation (over ten rival groups, and SWP membership falling to about 500); and 'de-proletarianisation', as youth and middle-class members replaced workers. The authors conclude that American Trotskyism's dogmatism, its neglect of capitalism's capacity to adapt, its abstract internationalism and its sectarianism made decline inevitable. They propose that today's Trotskyists drop dogma, end organisational fragmentation, strengthen democratic centralism and follow the mass line. They draw three lessons for socialism: unite the various left currents into a 'greater left'; keep a class-based socialist direction while engaging new social movements and identity politics; and learn from Chinese modernization, which they describe as superior to Western paths, including Party-building principles. Read the original if you want a stage-by-stage account of the SWP and smaller American Trotskyist groups, as seen by Chinese scholars of Western Marxism.

Mao Zedong's contribution to building the Chinese nation as a community, and its lessons, from the perspective of the "grand historical outlook" 历史观视域下毛泽东对推进中华民族共同体建设的贡献与启示 Yang Xiaojun Li Yinyan Yang Xiaojun and Li Yinyan ask how Mao Zedong's work on ethnic affairs should be assessed when seen through the "grand historical outlook" (大历史观) that Xi Jinping has stressed. They argue that earlier studies examined Mao's ethnic policy in narrow, specific dimensions and lacked a long-term, holistic view. Their thesis is that Mao made foundational and pioneering contributions to building the Chinese nation as a community (中华民族共同体建设), and that these contributions offer lessons for today. The article has three parts. The first defines the grand historical outlook: a long time span, wide spatial vision and holistic treatment of history, which the authors contrast with Huang Renyu's and Braudel's long-duration history. The second sets out Mao's three contributions. The third draws three present-day lessons. The authors also place the Party's current ethnic work in a line of continuity from the Mao era through reform and opening up to the new era. On the authors' account, Mao first led the peoples of all ethnic groups to found the new China, creating the basic political precondition for community-building. He reinterpreted "Chinese nation" to include the Han and dozens of minorities, and used the image of a "big family". Second, he led the establishment of the system of regional ethnic autonomy, which the authors present as moving from early ideas of self-determination and federalism to autonomy within national unity; they stress the training of minority cadres. Third, he set the principles of ethnic equality, unity and common development. The authors present reform-era and later policies such as targeted poverty alleviation as inheriting these principles, and they defend the autonomy system against calls to abolish it. The three lessons are to combine upholding and innovating Marxist ethnic theory, to unite Party leadership with a people-centred approach, and to match the nation's historical position to the goals of community-building. The authors treat the Cultural Revolution's damage to ethnic relations as a deviation in Mao's late years that should not erase his wider record. They argue that studying Mao in this way serves the Party's current ethnic work and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link Mao-era ethnic policy to the current official line on forging a shared national community, or to follow the argument against historical nihilism in ethnic affairs.

The evolution, construction and development of the functions of ideological and political education over forty years 40年来思想政治教育功能的演进、建构与发展论析 Huang Rongsheng Liu Yunbin Marking forty years since ideological and political education was established as a university specialism in 1984, Huang Rongsheng and Liu Yunbin ask how its functions have evolved, how a functional system should now be built, and where it should go next. They argue that research moved from asking whether such education is needed to asking whether it is done well, and that the field now needs a systematic, structure-based account of its functions oriented towards high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first traces three stages from 1984: early preparation, when the functions were discussed mainly as the "status and role" of ideological work; the proposal and creation of concepts as master's and doctoral programmes were set up from 1990 to 2004; and classification after the 2005 creation of Marxist theory as a first-level discipline. The second part builds a theoretical framework. The third sets out four orientations for the new era. At the core, the authors criticise existing function lists, such as service, guarantee, coordination and education functions, as drawn from experience and leaving the origin of functions unclear. Drawing on systems science, they hold that structure determines function, following the logic of "elements–structure–function" and "system–whole–comprehensiveness". They sort functions into three kinds: those from a single structure (for example, the orientation function from the structure of educators, and the cognitive function from the structure of content), those from composite structures (education, shaping, regulation, motivation), and those from the whole system's place within society. For the new era, they call for four things: serving the Party and state's central tasks by explaining, rallying and securing support for Chinese modernization; optimising goals, educators and content to empower it; raising standards to promote all-round human development; and widening the field through international comparison. The authors conclude that functions should be analysed through structure rather than listed case by case, and that the field should adopt this systemic approach while aligning its aims with the 20th Party Congress (2022) emphasis on high-quality development. They propose building international elements into curricula and improving the global communication of China's experience. Read the original if you study the disciplinary history of ideological and political education in China, or want to see how Chinese scholars apply systems theory to the field's core concepts.

The synthesis of reality in Marxist philosophy 马克思主义哲学的现实综合 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang asks what it takes to understand Marxist philosophy beyond its familiar concepts such as materialism, contradiction, productive forces and practice. The commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Journal in July 2024, argues that Marxism must be read as a comprehensive truth and placed within the real world. Theory and practice are to be brought together there, which the author calls the "synthesis of reality". The piece moves from Marx's break with German idealism to the demands placed on Marxist philosophers today. It draws on the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, then turns to Chinese modernization, big data, artificial intelligence and automated production. Lan contends that Marx's notion of practice is a real force for changing the world, not an abstract category. Citing The German Ideology on the steam engine and the spinning jenny, the author stresses that liberation depends on industrial, commercial and agricultural conditions. Marx studied the science and technology of his day, the article says, and this knowledge underpinned historical materialism and Capital, so Marxist philosophy was interdisciplinary from the start. For today's researchers this implies learning mathematics, physics, economics, law, communication studies and more. Lan adds that autonomous agents such as coordinating warehouse robots should be counted as subjects within social relations, which challenges politics, sociology and law. Lan concludes that Marxist philosophy today must break disciplinary barriers and follow changes in industry, agriculture, commerce and communication. It should also be combined with China's concrete realities and with traditional Chinese culture, as the Two Integrations require. The aim is a more humane, flexible, orderly and ecological community with a shared future for mankind under intelligent technology. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese philosophers link Marx's practice to AI and interdisciplinary research.

The inherent unity of the integrity of Marxism and the disciplinary character of political economy 马克思主义整体性与政治经济学学科性的内在统一 Zheng Jiwei Zheng Jiwei takes up a tendency in Chinese scholarship to stress the integrity (整体性) of Marxism while neglecting political economy as a distinct academic discipline. The article, a short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today of July 2024, argues that the two are inherently unified and that, in the new era, achieving this unity is an objective need for systematising and giving scholarly grounding to the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece first recalls Marx's turn to political economy from late 1843 and the emergence of political economy as an independent discipline. It then turns to the present, discussing the establishment of Marxist theory as a first-level discipline and Xi Jinping's 2023 call to make theory systematic and rooted in scholarly principle. Zheng reads Marx's forty-year turn to political economy as compatible with the wholeness of Marxism, citing Marx's description of his works as an artistic whole. Zheng objects to the view that each discipline generates its own Marxism and so dissolves the whole, calling it open to question. Systematisation, in Zheng's account, requires understanding Marxism as an integrated whole, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Giving the theory a scholarly basis requires the disciplinary character of its parts. For political economy, this aids popularisation and deeper research, and Zheng holds that Xi Jinping's economic thought can be understood in its logic only from a political-economy perspective. Zheng concludes that systematisation and scholarly grounding reinforce each other, and that integrity and disciplinarity are not opposed. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academic commentary links Marxist disciplinary debates to the Party's theoretical-innovation agenda.

Marxist philosophy's interpretation of "the human being" and its contemporary implications 马克思主义哲学对“人”的阐释及其当代启示 Yang Qiaorong Yang Qiaorong asks what Marxist philosophy means by "the human being" and what that understanding offers today. The article, a newspaper commentary first published in Guangming Daily in July 2024, argues that Marxism treats the human being not as an isolated abstraction but as a practical subject embedded in social relations and historical development. On this view, the concept gives people a way to see the deeper forces behind social change and to act consciously to push society towards greater justice. The piece has three parts. The first traces how Marx and Engels built the concept through critical engagement with German classical philosophy (Hegel and Feuerbach), British classical political economy and French utopian socialism. The second sets out three dimensions of the Marxist account: the web of social relations, the human being as a dynamic subject of history, and the ideal of complete human emancipation. The third draws three contemporary lessons, with reference to economic globalization and rapid information technology. In Yang's account, Marx replaced a transcendent, ahistorical human nature with the thesis that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. Through the theory of alienated labour, developed in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and in Capital, Marx showed how workers lose their subjectivity under capitalism. Yang then links this to the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Emancipation, in this reading, requires abolishing private ownership and class oppression, so that labour becomes a means of all-round self-realization. For the present, Yang calls for attention to how social structures shape individuals, for deepening reform, fairer distribution of wealth and more equal educational opportunity. Citing Xi Jinping, the author says socialism with Chinese characteristics, led by the Communist Party, has put a "logic of the people" above a "logic of capital". Yang also urges debate on technology ethics in the digital age, so that artificial intelligence and data technologies do not become new tools of oppression and alienation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-aligned newspaper commentary links Marx's theory of the human being to current policy themes.

A philosophical interpretation of high-quality development 高质量发展的哲学解读 Qiu Gengtian Qiu Gengtian takes up high-quality development, which Xi Jinping has called the theme of China's economic and social development during the 14th Five-Year Plan period and beyond. The article, a short newspaper piece, argues that Marxist philosophy lets readers grasp it as a whole and see its essence and laws. Qiu holds that this grasp has three logical dimensions: epistemological, axiological and methodological. The article takes the three dimensions in turn. The epistemological one asks what kind of development China should pursue. The axiological one asks why high-quality development is needed. The methodological one asks how it can be achieved.
