The second part takes each element of the guideline in turn, describing its content and possible organizational forms. Zhang draws on examples such as the "Four Stay Behinds" measures of Bijie in Guizhou province. Zhang contends that capitalist urban–rural relations mean the city dominating and dispossessing the countryside, whereas under socialism the relationship should be a worker–peasant alliance. On this view, urbanization rates should give way to rural revitalization indicators, and "local urbanization" should be built on township enterprises. The author holds that family contracting alone leaves farmers in a small-peasant trap and exposes key links in industrial chains to private or foreign capital. The remedy is a restored collective economy that unites village and commune, federates at township level, and is planned by city and county governments. Zhang names two preconditions: state guidance and planning, and eventual fusion of the collective economy with the state sector. Without them, the author warns, collectives would meet the fate Engels described for Dühring's "economic commune" under financial oligarchs. Zhang also sees attempts to dissolve village communities through shareholding reform and capital buying up land as the main threat to collective ownership. Zhang concludes that rural revitalization must be grasped through urban–rural relations and integration. That means moving productive capacity and urban talent, technology and finance down to townships and villages, and joining rural collective organizations with urban state-owned and collective enterprises. Only then, in the author's view, can the "three rural issues" be resolved and common prosperity achieved. Read the original if you want a Marxist-inflected argument for collective ownership and state coordination in rural policy, as it appeared in a Chinese policy journal in 2022.

The intellectual characteristics of the peaceful nature of Chinese civilization and its contemporary expression 中华文明和平性的思想特点及其当代呈现 Liu Feng Liu Feng takes up one of the "five outstanding characteristics" that Xi Jinping drew from Chinese civilization in his 2023 speech on cultural inheritance and development: its peaceful nature. The article argues that this peacefulness is rooted in Chinese philosophy and traditional culture. It holds that the peaceful nature is both an inner source of the civilization's continuity and a reason why building a modern Chinese civilization must follow a path of peaceful development and continue the fine traditional culture. The article has four sections. It first presents the ontological basis of peacefulness in the Chinese view of the cosmos as a harmonious whole. It then examines the idea of the unity of heaven and humanity as its intellectual foundation. Next it sets out three characteristics of the Chinese idea of "harmony". A final section turns to contemporary expression. Liu draws on a wide range of classical sources, including the Laozi, the Book of Changes, Zhang Zai, Dong Zhongshu, the Cheng brothers, Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming. Liu argues that for Laozi, the Book of Changes and Zhang Zai the universe is a harmony of yin and yang. Zhang's "taihe" (supreme harmony) and his line that opposites are resolved through reconciliation are read as expressions of a harmony-oriented philosophy, not just of dialectics. The unity of heaven and humanity takes several forms: following the seasons, correspondence between heaven and humans, and the union of human virtue with heaven. Liu holds that this makes humans and nature one whole, which supports a peaceful attitude to society and nature. Liu identifies three features of "harmony". It is many-sided, running from the individual through family, state and nature to "all under heaven". It presupposes order and difference, as in the distinction between harmony (he) and sameness (tong). It is also generative, in the maxim "harmony gives birth to things". On the contemporary side, Liu presents the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind as the highest present-day expression of this peacefulness. It is linked to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and the vision of a harmonious world. Citing Xi Jinping and Deng Xiaoping, the article says China's development has relied on peace, not expansion or colonial plunder, and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) declared Chinese modernization to be modernization by peaceful development. Liu says this research answers doubts raised by the "clash of civilizations" thesis and the claim that strong powers inevitably seek hegemony. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Chinese scholars ground the claim of a peaceful civilization in classical philosophy and connect it to current foreign-policy concepts.

Chinese Communists as the most faithful defenders, inheritors and innovators of Leninism Commemorating the 100th anniversary of Lenin's death 中国共产党人是列宁主义最忠实的捍卫者、传承者和创新者 Wang Weiguang Written for the centenary of Lenin's death in 2024, this article asks in what sense the Communist Party of China stands in continuity with Leninism. Wang Weiguang argues that Leninism is the second stage of Marxism's development and that Chinese Communists have defended, inherited and innovated it. In Wang's account, socialism with Chinese characteristics is the successful continuation of the October Revolution and Soviet construction, and a victorious practice of Marxism-Leninism in China. The article has three parts. The first sets out Lenin's contributions in practice (the October Revolution, the Bolshevik party, the Red Army, the New Economic Policy) and in theory: imperialism and revolution, the state and the dictatorship of the proletariat, party building, socialist construction, and philosophy. The second traces how the Party has treated Marxism-Leninism as an inseparable whole, from the early 1920s through Party constitutions to Xi Jinping. The third compares China's institutions with those of the Soviet Union and sets out the stages of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang argues that Chinese Marxists came to Marxism chiefly through the October Revolution and Leninist teaching, citing Mao Zedong and the finding that the journal New Youth carried 40 articles on Leninism and 16 on Marxism in 1919–1926. Wang insists that discarding Leninism means discarding Marxism, and criticises currents that try to separate the two. China's political system, ethnic policy, multiparty cooperation, mixed ownership economy, socialist market economy, the new development philosophy, rule of law and cultural policy are each presented as developments of the October path that also drew on Soviet shortcomings. Wang concludes that the Two Integrations and three leaps (Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era) have carried Marxism-Leninism to a new stage. Wang concludes that the best way to commemorate Lenin is to carry on his thought and unfinished work, and that Leninism will shine more brightly as socialism with Chinese characteristics and world socialism grow. The text is a Party-theoretical affirmation rather than a critical historical assessment. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists present continuity between Lenin, the Soviet experience and current Chinese policy.

Several concepts of Chinese culture embodied in the "Second Integration" “第二个结合”中蕴含的若干中华文化观念 Cao Yingwang Cao Yingwang asks which strands of traditional Chinese culture underlie the "Second Integration", the combination of the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article argues that six long-standing cultural concepts match certain Marxist ideas. In Cao's account, Chinese Communists have given them creative transformation and innovative development, and in this way they have become a cultural reason why Marxism can keep being adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article takes the six concepts in turn: a world-wide outlook (tianxia guan), valuing the foundation (guiben guan), self-reliance and self-strengthening (ziqiang guan), the relation of heaven and humanity (tianren guan), continuity and change (yingeguan), and the unity of knowing and doing (zhixing guan). For each it cites classical sources such as the Analects, Mencius and Xunzi. It then follows the concept through Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and, above all, Xi Jinping, from the revolutionary years to the post-2012 period. Cao's central move is to pair each concept with a Marxist counterpart and a Party doctrine. The ideal of "all under heaven as one family" is linked to communism and to a community with a shared future for mankind. Valuing the foundation is matched with the primacy of productive forces and the people, which Cao ties to the new development philosophy and to new quality productive forces. Self-reliance is paired with the dialectic of internal and external causes and with independence in Mao's thought. The heaven–humanity concept is linked to Marx on humans and nature and to Xi Jinping's ecological civilization thought. Continuity and change is read in the Second Integration itself and in the principle of upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground. Knowing and doing is read through Mao's "On Practice" and the line of seeking truth from facts, with Xi's stress on practical work. Cao concludes that the Second Integration has given these concepts new theoretical content and new vitality, and that over more than a century of Party history it has shown how to advance cultural construction. The article presents this as guidance for creatively transforming traditional culture and building a modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-historical account of how official scholarship ties particular classical Chinese ideas to Marxism and to Xi Jinping's thought, with many quotations from Mao, Zhou, Deng and Xi.

Mao Zedong's thought on governing Xinjiang and its major contemporary significance 毛泽东治疆思想及其重大现实意义 Li Qingxi Li Qingxi asks what Mao Zedong's approach to governing Xinjiang consists of and what it offers present-day policy. The article argues that Mao, applying Marxist principles to Xinjiang's conditions and drawing on traditional Chinese culture, developed a systematic body of thought on Xinjiang. In Li's view, this thought remains important for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation and for Xinjiang's stability and prosperity in the context of the "two overall situations". The article has four parts. It traces how the thought formed from the 1920s to the 1960s: early reflections on the nationalities question, formation between 1935 and 1949, and maturity after 1949 with the founding of the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in 1955. It then sets out five components: national equality and unity, regional national autonomy, cautious social reform, the Production and Construction Corps' land reclamation and border defence, and reliance on the people of all nationalities. It next identifies three distinguishing features and ends with contemporary implications. On Li's account, the thought has three features. First, it builds on a Marxist view of nationalities while departing from Soviet practice: Li says Mao criticised "Han chauvinism" and rejected a federal model, and presents the Soviet collapse as confirming his judgement. Second, it uses dialectical thinking, such as identifying the principal contradiction of each period, guarding against secondary ones, and proceeding gradually yet flexibly, for example on religion and reform. Third, it consciously draws on traditional Chinese governance, including regional autonomy that accommodates local custom and the ancient policy of garrison farming. From this, Li derives five present-day tasks: firmly uphold national equality and treat all groups by one standard, including opposing both Han chauvinism and local nationalism; make Xinjiang's security the first priority, with high pressure on the "three forces"; forge the sense of community of the Chinese nation through heart-to-heart work, ideological education for young people and minority cadres, and mixed residence and exchange; strengthen the Corps; and give sincere, long-term economic, cultural and social aid, especially to southern Xinjiang. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Mao-era ethnic and frontier policy is being used to justify current Xinjiang policy.

The spirit of the Zunyi Meeting shines forever 遵义会议精神永放光芒 Li Zhongjie Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, Li Zhongjie takes up the Zunyi Meeting of January 1935 and asks what its lasting spirit means for the Party today. Li argues that the meeting saved the Party, the Red Army and the Chinese revolution at a moment of extreme danger. Drawing on Xi Jinping's 2021 remarks in Guizhou, the article defines the Zunyi Meeting spirit as firm conviction, adherence to truth, independence and self-reliance, and unity and solidarity. The article is organised in four sections, one for each element of this spirit, each headed by the formula that it "shines forever". Each section first recounts the historical circumstances: the heavy losses of the Central Red Army at the Xiang River, the pressure for a change of leadership, the meeting of 15–17 January 1935, the subsequent manoeuvres of the Long March and the follow-up meetings. Each then draws lessons for the present, quoting Zhou Enlai, Liu Bocheng, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Li holds that the meeting corrected the "Left" dogmatist errors, added Mao Zedong to the Politburo Standing Committee and began forming a leadership core around him. In Li's account, it was also the first time the Party decided major political and military questions without intervention from the Communist International, with which contact had been lost. Li further presents the series of meetings held on the march, with open debate and decisions by majority, as an early form of inner-Party democracy that strengthened unity rather than damaging it. Li links adherence to truth to a leadership core and a mechanism for correcting mistakes. Li concludes that the Party must keep firm ideals, correct errors promptly, rely mainly on its own strength while opening up, and preserve unity. For the new journey, Li calls on Party members to grasp the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, strengthen the "four consciousnesses", the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and stay in step with the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, so as to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian presents the Zunyi Meeting as a source of current Party-building doctrine.

Re-examining the concepts of "globalization", "anti-globalization" and "deglobalization" “全球化”“反全球化”“逆全球化”概念再考察 Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin asks what it means to "uphold the correct direction of economic globalization", a formulation that appeared for the first time in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article argues that the answer starts with conceptual clarification. In Zhou's account, "economic globalization" is not the same as "globalization", and "anti-globalization" and "deglobalization" each carry specific historical meanings that are often confused. The article moves through the three concepts in turn. It traces the Western history of the word "globalization" and the periodisations of its stages, then proposes its own four-period history of economic globalization from 1500 to the present. It then examines the anti-globalization movement from the 1999 "Battle of Seattle" onwards, and finally distinguishes three usages of "deglobalization". A closing section draws out the implications for policy language. Zhou's central claim is that "globalization" in Western discourse has mostly meant the neoliberal "capitalist globalization" of recent decades, whereas the Chinese concept of economic globalization rests on historical materialism and Marx and Engels's account of the division of labour and world history. Anti-globalization protest is read, with reference to Kofi Annan and Joseph Stiglitz, as a reaction to flaws in global governance and to the shifting of capitalism's internal contradictions, not to economic globalization as such. "Deglobalization" is separated into Walden Bello's original, constructive proposal for the Global South, a broad equation with protectionism and state intervention, and the current usage. Zhou adopts the third: the policy turn in developed capitalist countries after the 2008 financial crisis, marked by Brexit, Trump's election, "small yard, high fence" and "decoupling". Zhou also points to the short-term effect of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, which makes re-industrialisation in developed countries possible. Zhou concludes that this deglobalization is a strategy by rentier interests in developed countries to protect monopoly positions, that it cannot resolve capitalism's contradictions, and that Western blame of China is misplaced. In Zhou's view the issue is not whether to have globalization but how to meet global governance challenges, through more inclusive, beneficial and resilient development, genuine multilateralism and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist conceptual genealogy of the globalization debate and the intellectual basis of the Party Congress formulation.

Striving to paint a new ecological picture of building liveable, workable and harmonious rural areas 奋力绘就宜居宜业和美乡村建设的生态新画卷 Ma Mingchong Writing in a Party-theory journal in 2024, Ma Mingchong asks how the ecological side of building "liveable, workable and harmonious" villages should be advanced under rural revitalization. The article argues that the shift from "beautiful countryside" to "harmonious and beautiful countryside", announced at the 20th Party Congress (2022), reflects Xi Jinping's grasp of the laws of rural development. Ma holds that the work has achieved notable results since the 18th Party Congress (2012) but is still in a "tackling key problems" phase of raising quality and efficiency. The piece has three parts. The first reviews achievements in four areas: ecological-civilization awareness among villagers, protection and restoration of the natural environment, improvement of the rural living environment, and the ecological transformation of agriculture. The second names four continuing challenges. The third sets out four measures for comprehensive advancement. Ma draws on Xi Jinping's statements throughout and cites official figures for 2023. On results, Ma cites figures such as over 90 per cent of administrative villages with household waste collected and treated, rural sanitary toilet coverage above 73 per cent, and rural domestic sewage treatment (or control) above 40 per cent. Ma also cites utilisation rates above 78 per cent for livestock manure, 88 per cent for straw and 80 per cent for agricultural film, and over 68,000 certified green and organic products. The challenges are long-term ecosystem restoration, upgrading rural infrastructure, non-point-source agricultural pollution, and uneven, over-exploitative agricultural development with weak digital foundations. Ma's remedies are to strengthen grassroots Party organizations as leaders (including through selecting graduates, resident cadres and returning entrepreneurs, and through online tools), to build harmonious natural ecology through compensation and protection systems, to improve rural human ecology through pollution control and village planning, and to develop green, circular agriculture. Ma concludes that these four lines of work, aimed at prosperous industry, ecological liveability, civilised customs, effective governance and affluent living, will support high-quality development of agriculture and rural areas. On the industrial side, Ma calls for turning "ecological resources" into "ecological products" and brands, integrating the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors, and cultivating new quality productive forces in the countryside. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-theory journals present rural ecological policy, with 2023 official statistics and the standard policy checklist.

How new quality productive forces empower the digital development of ideological and political education A logical path 新质生产力赋能思想政治教育数字化发展的逻辑进路 Lu Lan Lu Lan asks how new quality productive forces, with digital technology as their chief representative, can drive the digital transformation of ideological and political education. The article argues that borrowing concepts and methods from other disciplines is not enough and may even obscure the essence of the field. Lu contends that the field must instead grasp the characteristics of 'digital existence', where human life is increasingly rendered as data, and use this to optimise the structure and upgrade the functions of ideological and political education. The article has three main sections, published in the journal Party Building and Ideological Education. The first describes the shift from experience-driven to data-driven education and the risks and opportunities this creates. The second examines changes in ways of thinking and the 'technological arming' of the field. The third turns to practice: how digital resources become educational value, how that value is placed in concrete scenarios and organised as an ecosystem, and where the limits of digital methods lie. Lu's core argument rests on several moves. Internet thinking and ecological thinking, the author says, should reshape the discipline, with technology kept secondary to ideological and political education and anchored in fostering virtue and the all-round development of the person. Digital tools bring new subjects (human–machine relations), quantitative and algorithmic research, and virtual presence through VR and AR that widens the space of teaching. Lu then sets out a chain from digital resources to digital value, to scenario-based application, to an ecological scenario system. This system is described as moving data collection from static to dynamic, and as taking educational work down into people's everyday settings and grassroots grid organisations. Lu cautions that algorithms driven by capital can crowd out mainstream values, and that over-reliance on technology risks alienating people and treating living individuals as objects of algorithmic control. The author calls for data security and shared access, and for a balance between humanistic values and technology. The article closes by invoking Weber's remark that the light of great problems still shines. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education connect the concept of new quality productive forces to digitalisation, algorithms and educational practice.

Teachers are the key to the high-quality development of ideological and political courses in universities in the new era 教师是新时代高校思政课高质量发展的关键 Duan Yan Duan Yan takes up Xi Jinping's 2019 statement that the key to running ideological and political theory courses well lies in teachers, and in drawing out their initiative, enthusiasm and creativity. Writing five years after the symposium of March 2019, the author argues that building a trustworthy, respected and capable teaching force is an inherent requirement for the high-quality development of these university courses. It is also presented as a necessary step in advancing education modernization and training talent suited to new quality productive forces. The article has three sections. The first traces the Party's long attention to teachers, from revolutionary-era institutions such as the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University to Deng Xiaoping's 1978 remarks, and reports that the number of university ideological and political course teachers has risen to 145,000. The second explains why teachers' initiative matters, and the third sets out three proposals for strengthening the teaching force. In Duan's account, the courses are 'essentially about reasoning', and this is hard to do well. The content spans Marxist philosophy, political economy, scientific socialism, the 'four histories' and domestic and international affairs. The students are active, curious and ready to raise sensitive questions, and the courses must constantly be renewed with modern teaching methods. Hence the 'six requirements' for teachers: strong politics, deep feeling, innovative thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline and upright character. Duan proposes three measures. Teachers should master the 'craft', 'scholarship' and 'way' of teaching, and teaching should follow the 'eight unities' set out by Xi. Party committees at all levels should lead, consolidate the 'great ideological and political education' pattern, expand case and material banks, run rotating training and reform evaluation and incentive systems. The author concludes that these courses should train more talent for building a strong nation and for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship frames teacher development in ideological and political education under Xi Jinping.

Opening a new realm in the Marxist thought on the relationship between humanity and nature A four-dimensional reading of Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization 开创马克思主义人与自然关系思想新境界 Xu Hengbing Xu Di Responding to Xi Jinping's call to study and practise Marxism's thinking on the relationship between humanity and nature, Xu Hengbing and Xu Di ask how Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization innovates on and develops that classical thinking. Their answer is that, at each of four levels, it takes the classics' basic positions and extends them to new historical conditions in China. The article does not survey the full "ten upholds" of the Thought. It selects four dimensions: humanity and nature, protection and development, ecology and civilization, and environmental governance. These move in sequence from a view of nature to a view of development to a view of civilization, ending with practical innovation. Each section sets out the position of Marx and Engels, notes how Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao carried it forward, and then shows what Xi adds. In the authors' account, the idea that humanity and nature form a "community of life" adds a factual claim (the objective organic link, requiring limited exploitation of nature) and a normative one (rebuilding unity at a higher level). They also take the "two mountains" theory ("lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets") to bring the ecological environment into the productive forces and to widen the Marxist concept of wealth. Against Western degrowth and steady-state thinkers, they argue that Marx traced ecological destruction to the logic of capital, not to growth as such, so limiting growth misreads capitalist production. For China, they say Xi locates ecological problems in the mode of development and way of life, not in socialist relations of production. The authors present the claim that "when ecology thrives, civilization thrives" as deepening Marx's account of civilization, and as placing ecological civilization within the overall plan for socialism with Chinese characteristics. On governance, the authors summarise Xi's programme as shifting the development model and way of life toward green and low-carbon forms, cultivating an ecological outlook across society, and building strict institutions and rule of law. Examples include central environmental inspections, ecological compensation and carbon-emissions trading. They conclude that this programme broadens the Marxist path to a rational relationship between humanity and nature under socialist conditions. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account of how Xi's ecological thought is tied to Marx's and Engels's texts and to earlier Chinese leaders' formulations, including its engagement with Western degrowth and ecological Marxist arguments.

A brief analysis of several basic categories of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and their interrelations 中国化时代化马克思主义若干基本范畴及其相互关系简析 Tian Xinming Responding to Xi Jinping's call to promote the systematization and academic grounding of the Party's innovative theory, Tian Xinming asks how the core categories of that theory relate to one another. The article argues that a scientific theoretical system is a web of concepts, and that Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times can be systematized only by clarifying the logical links between its basic categories. Those links, Tian holds, mirror the historical logic of China's path since the early twentieth century. Tian identifies five pairs of overall categories as the first tier of the system: modernization and Chinese modernization; civilization, Chinese civilization and the modern civilization of the Chinese nation; scientific socialism and socialism with Chinese characteristics; Marxism and adapted Marxism; and the Chinese people and the Communist Party of China. Each section takes one pair in turn, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and the article ends by tying the pairs together. Tian's central move is to treat each pair as a relation of the universal to the particular. Reading the Communist Manifesto, the author takes revolutions in the instruments of production, in production relations and in all social relations as the general features of modernization, which Western modernization carries in bourgeois form and Chinese modernization carries in socialist form under Party leadership. Tian equates the new form of human civilization with the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, described as a unity of socialism and Chinese civilization. Socialism with Chinese characteristics is said to uphold the basic principles of scientific socialism, above all the lofty ideal of communism, while giving them distinctive Chinese features. Tian then traces these achievements back to the claim that Marxism works, but not unconditionally: it works because the Party applies it scientifically through the Two Integrations, which produce a Marxism fully Marxist and fully Chinese. The creating subject is the Chinese people led by the Party, whose nature and aims are set out in the Party constitution. Tian concludes that systematizing the theory means following the unity of the logical and the historical, so that the system reflects the Party's century of struggle and guides the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how a senior Party theorist arranges the key concepts of Xi Jinping Thought into a logical hierarchy.

Deng Xiaoping's exploration of and contribution to the theory of Chinese modernization 邓小平对中国式现代化理论的探索与贡献 Yu Chunxi Yu asks what Deng Xiaoping contributed to the basic framework of the theory of Chinese modernization. The article argues that Deng, as chief architect of reform and opening up and of socialist modernization, put forward a series of ideas that laid that framework and deepened understanding of modernization. Yu holds that summing up these contributions matters for building the theory system and for advancing Chinese modernization in practice. The article is organised around six contributions. They are the concept of a "Chinese-style modernization", the goal of common prosperity, the "three-step" development strategy, the thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force, opening up to the outside world, and the theory of the socialist market economy. Yu draws on Deng's talks and speeches from 1978 to 1988, on Marx's analysis of capitalism and the world market, and on modernization theory, dependency theory, Stalin and Mises. Yu first argues that Deng's 1979 concept challenged the equation of modernization with Westernization promoted by classical modernization theory, which Yu says the United States sponsored. The concept takes socialism and the primary stage of socialism as its coordinates and reflects Deng's reflection on the "Left" errors before reform. Yu reads it as treating socialist and capitalist modernization as two particular forms of a shared universal process. On common prosperity, Yu says modernization brings wealth but not necessarily shared wealth, so only socialism can secure the latter. On opening up and markets, Yu argues that globalization follows the logic of capital and risks Westernization and dependency, so opening must keep to the socialist road and the Four Cardinal Principles. Yu adds that the market is a means of allocating resources, not the preserve of capitalism, and that Deng's separation of the market economy from capitalism freed it to serve socialism. Yu concludes that these ideas covered the concept, essential requirements, strategic arrangements, direction and principles of Chinese modernization. Deng also stressed Party leadership, spiritual as well as material civilization, and socialist democracy. In Yu's view, this enriched Chinese modernization theory and deepened the Party's understanding of general and Chinese laws of modernization, laying a foundation for later theoretical and practical innovation. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Deng's statements are presented as the origin of Chinese modernization theory, with extensive quotations from his speeches.

Promoting systematic integration of reform, highlighting priorities and achieving real results 推动改革系统集成突出重点取得实效 Liu Zhichang This newspaper commentary, published in August 2024, interprets the methodological formula of "three greater emphases" in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. The decision calls for reform to give greater attention to systematic integration, to highlighting priorities and to real results. Liu Zhichang argues that these three emphases strengthen the systematic, holistic and coordinated character of reform and sum up the practice and methodology of comprehensively deepening reform. The article has one section for each emphasis. The first treats systematic integration as a requirement of the systems concept and as the basic guide for further reform. The second treats highlighting priorities as a requirement of materialist dialectics. The third links reform results to Chinese modernization. Liu draws on the history of reform from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee onwards, and on the record since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu grounds systematic integration in the dialectical-materialist view that things are interconnected. The author holds that China, a large developing country in the primary stage of socialism, finds that reform and the adjustment of interests tend to affect the whole. Highlighting priorities rests on the law of contradiction: reform should identify the principal contradiction while also balancing secondary ones, combining the "two-point" and "focal-point" approaches. Liu cites the record since rural "household contract" reform, which started in Xiaogang village, as showing that economic reform leads other fields. Real results are tied to institution-building and to liberating and developing the productive forces. Liu cites Xi Jinping's criterion that reform is judged by whether it promotes economic and social development and gives people tangible benefits. Liu concludes that the 2035 and 2029 targets set out in the decision should guide a roadmap and timetable. Reform should focus on a high-standard socialist market economy, whole-process people's democracy and the other priorities the decision lists, with economic reform in the lead. Liu calls for turning institutional strengths into governance effectiveness, so that reform supplies institutional guarantees and strong momentum for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise official-style exposition of the methodological reasoning behind the Third Plenum's reform decision.

Taking institution-building as the main thread 坚持以制度建设为主线 Chen Zhigang This newspaper commentary, published shortly after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), takes up one of the principles set out in the Plenum's decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization: "taking institution-building as the main thread". Chen Zhigang argues that this principle is a valuable lesson of reform and opening up, especially since 2012, and that it must guide the next stage of reform. Its aim, in Chen's account, is to convert institutional advantages into effective national governance and supply a firm institutional guarantee for Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first reviews how the Party's understanding of institutions has developed, from the establishment of the basic socialist system and the market-economy reform goal to the 18th Party Congress era (2012 onwards). The second explains why institution-building is inherent in the overall goal of further deepening reform. The third sets out how institutions can secure Chinese modernization. Chen's core argument rests on three moves. First, the overall goal is read as one whole: the first half fixes the direction of upholding the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, rejecting both a closed, rigid old path and an "evil path" of changing banners, while the second half points to improving institutions and modernizing governance. Second, Chen holds that reform has entered a stage of tough problems and entrenched interests, so good experience must be fixed in institutional form. Third, the article stresses confidence in the institutions together with innovation: confidence is not complacency, existing systems need improving and gaps need filling, while foreign governance experience may be used selectively. Chen concludes that reform must combine top-level design with coordinated measures, use the dialectic of breaking and establishing (establish before breaking, to avoid institutional gaps), and treat the three tiers of institutions differently: fundamental institutions are to be consolidated, basic ones improved, and important ones innovated. Only so, the author says, can institutions help to prevent risks and open new prospects amid crises. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the Third Plenum's institution-building principle and its three-tier institutional scheme.

Ecosocialism for realists 现实主义者的生态社会主义 Michael Albert This is an abridged Chinese translation of Michael Albert's article "Ecosocialism for Realists". Albert asks why ecosocialism, now a major global alternative to "green capitalism", has said so little about how a transition would actually happen. The article argues that ecosocialists are held back by an "abstract utopian" habit of describing ideal futures without analysing the path, and by neglect of the trade-offs and dangers a ecosocialist regime would face. It proposes a "realist utopian" approach in their place. Albert first sets out three shared principles of ecosocialism: use-value over exchange-value, collective ownership and planning that shape and constrain markets, and "contraction and convergence" in consumption between the Global North and Global South. The article then reviews the Green New Deal as a possible transition platform and examines the choice between degrowth and growth-oriented paths. It closes with the risks of emergency rule, negative-emission technologies, solar geoengineering and mineral extraction. Albert draws on Löwy, Foster, Richard Smith, Sam Gindin, Erik Olin Wright, Andreas Malm and others. The central move is an analysis of why a growth-based Green New Deal may not stabilise capitalism. Albert gives three reasons: falling net energy as renewables with lower energy returns spread, over-promised "green jobs", and rising private and public debt without the growth needed to service it. On this reading the Green New Deal is a "temporary way station" before a fork: deeper socialisation with rationing and job guarantees, or a return to right-wing growth at any cost. Albert then argues that any ecosocialist government may be pushed towards institutionalised "state of emergency" measures such as carbon rationing, and would face resistance from the far right allied with capital. Two equilibria are sketched. One is degrowth emerging from Green New Deal crises around 2030–2050. The other is a slower transition around 2050–2080, dependent on negative-emission technology, geoengineering and intensified extractive conflict. Albert concludes that ecosocialists and their allies should put more intellectual effort into strategy and into the limits of the best-case scenario, without abandoning utopian imagination. Facing these risks may strengthen rather than weaken belief in a new world, he suggests. He also calls for a stronger red-green alliance and a changed narrative of prosperity. Read the original if you study ecosocialism, degrowth or the Green New Deal and want a critical, strategy-focused account of the dilemmas of transition in core countries.

Mao Zedong and the development of philosophy and social sciences in China 毛泽东与中国哲学社会科学事业发展 Song Yuehong Zhou Jin Song and Zhou ask what Mao Zedong contributed to laying the foundations of Marxist philosophy and social sciences in China, and what that legacy offers for building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics today. They argue that Mao explored the laws and features of this field, set out guiding policies for it, and left a body of historical experience that bears directly on current tasks. The article has four parts. The first treats Mao's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times as the path that opened the field. The second examines his formulas "weeding through the old to bring forth the new" and "making the past serve the present". The third covers the "Hundred Flowers" and "Hundred Schools" policy. The fourth draws lessons for the present, citing Xi Jinping's statements throughout. The authors argue that Mao's theoretical works, from the theory of New Democratic revolution to the writings on contradictions among the people, themselves embody the stance and method of Marxist social science, whose living soul they identify as seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. On tradition, they trace the formula from Mao's 1938 call to inherit China's historical legacy critically, through the 1942 inscription for the Yan'an Peking opera institute, to postwar projects: the Academy of Sciences' philosophy and social sciences division (1955) and the new punctuated edition of the Twenty-Four Histories (completed 1978). On the "Hundred Flowers" policy, they stress three features: it operates under Marxist guidance, which Mao held would strengthen rather than weaken Marxism's leading position; it upholds academic democracy by separating political from academic questions; and it is inclusive, rejecting both xenophobia and uncritical borrowing from abroad. Examples include the founding of Historical Research (1954), Mao's 1957 logic seminars and his remark on the Lanting Preface debate. Drawing on Mao, the authors call for problem-oriented research on major practical questions, with Marxism as guidance and the people as the research standpoint. They also want an independent Chinese knowledge system, with discipline, academic and discourse systems built on Chinese conditions rather than copied from abroad. They add a call for talent programmes and incentives for scholars. They present Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the current guide. Read the original if you want an official-academic account of how Mao's cultural and scholarly policies are being drawn on in current discussions of China's philosophy and social sciences.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating to advance the content-based development of ideological and political courses 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Zhou Zhou Writing in Guangming Daily on 7 August 2024, Zhou Zhou takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction on school ideological and political courses (sizheng ke). The commentary argues that these courses should advance "connotative" development by upholding fundamental principles while innovating, so as to raise their relevance and appeal. The piece is organised around four commitments, each paired with a method of innovation: the socialist direction of education, the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, a Chinese cultural standpoint, and the goal of cultivating new-era talent. Zhou argues that the courses are above all about transmitting ideas and belief, so Marxist guidance and Party leadership are their political foundation. The Party's innovative theory, above all Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, should run through professional, compulsory and elective courses and become students' own convictions. Zhou also holds that students' confidence rests on Marxist truth, the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the depth of Chinese civilisation, which should help them grasp the Two Integrations. Finally, Zhou calls for a "big ideological and political course" pattern in which classroom, professional, social and online teaching work together and other courses move in the same direction. Zhou concludes that these measures serve the education of new-era talent who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and ready to take on national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state discourse on ideological education is framed for university teachers.

Reform and institutional innovation as the institutional guarantee for vigorously developing new quality productive forces 改革创新为大力发展新质生产力提供体制保障 Pang Jinju Since 2023, developing new quality productive forces has become a major theme of Chinese policy and scholarship. Pang Jinju notes that most discussion has focused on science and technology, industry and talent, and approaches the question from the angle of reform and institutional innovation. The article argues that deepening reform, with economic reform at its centre, and innovating institutions are an intrinsic requirement for developing new quality productive forces and promoting high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first sets out why reform is required, drawing on Xi Jinping's definition of new quality productive forces, Marx's and Engels's statements on productive forces and relations of production, and the record of reform and opening up. The second addresses the relationship between government and market. The third sets out reforms in other fields: science and technology, education and talent systems, the transfer of research results, green development, and opening up. Pang's central argument is that, on the Marxist principle that relations of production must suit the productive forces, a revolution in productive forces demands new relations of production. Without reform, the author says, researchers' initiative is constrained, factors of production cannot be innovatively allocated, and industrial upgrading stalls. On government and market, Pang holds that the market should play the decisive role in allocating resources while government plays its role better. In China, the author stresses, "government" differs from the Western category because Party leadership is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, so strengthening that leadership comes first. Pang lists concrete tasks: support state-owned and private firms alike under the Two Unwaverings, unify basic market rules on property rights, market access, fair competition and social credit, build a national unified market, and reform Party and state institutions. Pang concludes that continued comprehensive reform is needed for new quality productive forces, just as past reform liberated productive forces. The article cites figures such as an economy of 126 trillion yuan in 2023 and 921,000 invention patents granted. It observes that too few patents become real productive forces, which makes reform of the transfer of research results important. It also calls for green transformation, institutional opening up, and a modern industrial system that serves the real economy. Read the original if you want a Party-school-style political-economy account of how institutional reform is linked to new quality productive forces, with detailed policy recommendations.

Accurately grasping the relationship between Chinese culture and the cultures of the various ethnic groups 准确把握中华文化与各民族文化的关系 Ma Hui Wang Yanzhong Ma Hui and Wang Yanzhong take up a question that, they say, Xi Jinping has made central to cultural work since 2019 and especially at the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Affairs: how Chinese culture relates to the cultures of China's ethnic groups. Their thesis follows Xi's image of Chinese culture as the trunk and ethnic cultures as branches and leaves. Ethnic cultures are parts of Chinese culture, not independent of it, and handling the relationship correctly provides the ideological and cultural basis for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first defines the two concepts and their scope, drawing on Fei Xiaotong's idea of the Chinese nation as a pluralistic unity. It treats the formation of the two kinds of culture, their scope (national versus regional) and their layers (geographic, everyday-practice and industry-based). The second part explains how ethnic cultures merge into Chinese culture. The third proposes three practical paths for strengthening the 'trunk' role of Chinese culture. Examples run from Neolithic sites and the Zhongyuan (Central Plains) cultural sphere to the Hani terraces, the Epic of King Gesar and the 'Hu' costume and music borrowed into the Central Plains. The core argument is that ethnic cultures have never been pure or isolated. The authors identify three mechanisms of integration: connected geographic units that spread Central Plains culture outward while drawing in frontier cultures; political culture embedded in ethnic cultures, which in their account steers them toward a shared national culture in which the national outlook replaces ethnic sentiment; and mutual borrowing and sharing, including the listing of ethnic cultural heritage on national and world registers. In the authors' reading, listing turns local ethnic traditions into collective Chinese culture, as with the Hani terraces and the Gesar epic, whose spread they credit to state policy and translation into the national common language. The authors propose three paths. The state should guide the creative transformation of ethnic cultures through policy and top-level design around the mainline of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Local stories of ethnic interaction, such as Zhang Qian's mission to the Western Regions or Princess Wencheng's journey to Tibet, should be told widely. Ethnic cultures should also be modernised through innovation, cultural industries and works on ethnic unity. They conclude that this strengthens the 'Five Identifications', cultural confidence and the building of a culturally strong country. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars frame ethnic culture policy in terms of the 'trunk and branches' model and the heritage listing of ethnic traditions.

Xi Jinping's key assertions on developing new quality productive forces 习近平关于发展新质生产力的几个重要论断 Zhang Lin Zhang Lin, a lecturer at Chongqing University's School of Marxism, examines a series of statements by Xi Jinping on new quality productive forces made since July 2023. The article argues that these statements answer why, what kind of and how to develop such forces. In Zhang's reading, they innovate on the Marxist theory of productive forces and open a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, while also guiding practice on high-quality development. The article selects seven representative assertions and explains each in turn. They cover the claim that new quality productive forces have already taken shape in practice; their relation to high-quality development; their essence as advanced productive forces; their identity as green productive forces; the central role of scientific and technological innovation; the need for new production relations through deeper reform; and the principle of developing them according to local conditions. Zhang quotes Xi's speeches, Politburo study sessions and regional inspection remarks throughout. Zhang's core reasoning links theory to practice. Tracing Xi's wording from forces being "accelerated" to "already formed", Zhang concludes that China has moved from the formation stage to the development stage. Zhang describes new quality productive forces as an upgrade of labourers, means of labour, objects of labour and their combination, marked by high technology, high efficiency, high quality and a large rise in total factor productivity. The author presents them as inherently green, since protecting the ecology is protecting productive forces, and as driven by original and disruptive innovation, basic research, the fusion of technological and industrial innovation, and talent. On production relations, Zhang reports Xi's call for deeper reform of the economic, science and technology, education and talent systems, together with high-level opening up. Zhang also stresses the method of "establishing before breaking", selective choices suited to each locality, and differentiated guidance, with specific directions for the northeast, Tianjin, Jiangsu, central China and the west. The article concludes that Xi's statements form part of Xi Jinping Thought on the economy and are of major practical significance for high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned exposition of Xi's formulations on this concept, with dated quotations and regional examples.

Forging souls and nurturing people with Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to strengthen students' cultural confidence 用习近平文化思想铸魂育人，增强学生文化自信 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng asks how ideological and political education in universities should use Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, formally set out at the national conference on propaganda and ideological work in October 2023, to strengthen students' cultural confidence. Starting from Xi Jinping's "3.18" speech on ideological and political theory courses (2024), which names the Four-sphere Confidence as a direct goal of such teaching, Wu argues that this body of thought supplies the fundamental guidance for the task. The article is a short essay in three parts, each linking Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to one educational task: fostering students' theoretical awareness of the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation, giving cultural confidence the support of an independent knowledge system, and guiding students to take up the mission of building a modern Chinese civilization. It was published in a journal on teaching and research in Marxist theory in 2024. In the first move, Wu defines subjectivity as the capacity of an individual or community to make cognitive and practical judgements independently, and treats it as a condition of freedom. A nation shows cultural subjectivity when it holds to its own culture and is not penetrated by others. Wu reads China's unbroken civilisation of more than 5,000 years as proof of this, and holds that only Xi Jinping Thought on Culture has theorised it systematically. In the second move, Wu calls cultural confidence the subjective form of cultural subjectivity and says it must rest on theoretical understanding rather than blind pride. Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, with the Two Integrations (especially the "second integration" with traditional Chinese culture), supplies this understanding and counts as an independent knowledge system. Wu adds that who is educated depends on whose theory is used, and that students should be equipped to resist what the article calls Western cultural hegemonism and colonialism. Wu concludes that educators should guide students to adopt a "grand view of history", use Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method, creatively transform and innovatively develop traditional culture, and take part in building the modern Chinese civilization. The article describes that civilization as a new form created under Party leadership, which rejects "Western-centrism" and the "clash of civilizations" and offers a Chinese approach to the difficulties of capitalist civilization. Read the original if you want to see how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture is being set out as a teaching framework for ideological and political courses in Chinese universities.

Building a new type of worker–peasant and urban–rural relationship oriented towards coordinated development and common prosperity 构建以协调发展和共同繁荣为取向的新型工农城乡关系 Zheng Yougui Zheng Yougui asks how China should handle the relationship between industry and agriculture and between town and countryside in the new era. The article argues that a new type of worker–peasant and urban–rural relationship, built around coordinated development and common prosperity, is an integral part of Chinese modernization. In Zheng's account, the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has stopped treating the "three rural issues" in isolation and handles them as a question of overall strategy. The article is organised in two parts. The first traces how the strategic goal of coordinated development has been widened and upgraded since the 18th Party Congress (2012), from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping through Jiang Zemin's call to resolve the dual economic and social structure. The second examines how common prosperity was written into the definition of the new relationship, citing Xi's speeches, the 19th Central Committee's Fifth Plenum (2020) formulation and central documents. Latin American cases of the "middle-income trap" serve as a foil. Zheng makes two main moves. First, the principal contradiction in Chinese society has shifted to one between the people's desire for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. Coordination has therefore moved from balancing farm and factory output, as in Zhou Enlai's 1962 couplet, to a goal of "four-sphere synchronisation", of rural modernization, and of hundreds of millions of peasants advancing together. Second, adding common prosperity shifts the aim from breaking the urban–rural dual structure to shared prosperity. Zheng says this requires peasants to take part equally in modernization and share its fruits, and holds that only Party leadership and the socialist system can deliver it. Zheng names five institutional paths: prioritising agriculture and rural areas and rural revitalisation; planning town and country as a whole; strengthening collective ownership while separating land rights and activating resources; building industries that serve farmers; and giving farmers equity stakes to bind them to commercial capital. The article concludes that the new relationship is a historic upgrade and an innovative development of the Marxist theory of worker–peasant and urban–rural relations, suited to China's large rural population. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how rural policy since 2012 is framed in terms of common prosperity and the Marxist tradition.

Mao Zedong's insistence on independence and self-reliance in advancing Chinese modernization: historical motives and present-day guidance 毛泽东坚持独立自主推进中国式现代化的历史动因和现实指引 Liu Lyuhong Zun Shuaihui Liu Lyuhong and Zun Shuaihui ask why Mao Zedong made independence and self-reliance the guiding principle of socialist modernization, and what this offers for Chinese modernization today. They argue that Mao wove this principle through the whole of socialist modernization, giving it a distinctive national posture and a note of 'autonomy'. In their account it is one of the fundamental marks separating Chinese modernization from Western modernization. After a literature overview, the article is organised in four parts. It first sets out the problem and the reasons why independence was necessary in the early People's Republic. It then identifies three historical motives: lessons from modern China's failed modernization attempts, the formation of independence thinking during the revolution, and the new tasks of socialist construction. The third part analyses three dimensions of Mao's thought, and the fourth draws lessons for the present. The authors argue that reformism and imitation of the West led nowhere in semi-colonial, semi-feudal China, from the Westernizing faction to the 1911 Revolution and the New Culture Movement. Independence thinking matured through conflict with Comintern directives and dogmatism, culminating, they say, at the Zunyi Conference. After 1949 Mao rejected both capitalist modernization and copying the 'Soviet model', as in On the Ten Great Relationships and the call for a 'second integration' of Marxism with Chinese realities. The authors read his thought as covering sovereignty, the path of construction and spiritual independence, giving respectively the precondition, freedom from path dependence and ideological grounding. They add that self-reliance did not mean closing the door to foreign aid and learning. For the present, the authors call for building Chinese modernization theory independently, drawing on the Two Integrations, and for self-reliance in science and technology, secure supply chains and no dependence on others, without decoupling from the world. They also urge continuing to 'walk our own road' and rebutting distortions of Chinese modernization, which they say has broken the equation of modernization with Westernization. Read the original if you want a Party-school-style account of how Mao's independence principle is being linked to Xi Jinping-era Chinese modernization discourse.

Deng Xiaoping's major contributions to Chinese modernization 邓小平对中国式现代化的重大贡献 Tian Keqin Zhao Yecheng Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) formula that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, Tian and Zhao ask what Deng Xiaoping contributed to it. They argue that after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), Deng and the Communists around him made an epoch-making contribution to the path, concepts and major measures of Chinese modernization. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces Deng's coining of "Chinese-style modernization" in 1979 and how its content was later enriched by successive Party congresses. The second examines the "three-step" development strategy and the goal of a xiaokang society. The third treats the Party's basic line and the "two hands" approach as the guiding direction and method of modernization. Each part ends by linking Deng's ideas to later Party documents and to Xi Jinping. The authors contend that Deng first said in March 1979 that construction, like revolution, must "suit Chinese conditions", and that he defined it as socialist, coordinated between material and cultural-ethical progress, and peaceful in orientation. They describe the move from a "two-step" to a "three-step" plan (1987), with targets of per capita GNP of 500, then 1,000, then about 4,000 US dollars, and report that the first two steps were reached early or exceeded. They present Deng's insistence on holding to the basic line of "one centre, two basic points" and his "two hands, both firm" method as the political and methodological foundation. In their account, later formulations, such as the new two-step arrangement of the 19th and 20th Party Congresses, apply and deepen these ideas. Tian and Zhao conclude that modernization practice since reform and opening up has underpinned the Chinese path and the system of theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that Deng's blueprint is being realised step by step, citing Xi Jinping. The article is a continuity narrative from Deng to the present. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Party theorists trace the lineage of Chinese modernization back to Deng's statements of 1979–1992.

Building the foundation of strength for ideological and political theory courses on three cultures 以三种文化夯实思政课的力量根基 Zhao Yiliang Zhao Yiliang takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction that ideological and political theory courses (sizheng courses) should treat excellent traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture as their "foundation of strength". The article argues that these three cultures should underpin the courses' content, their value orientation and their teaching methods, and that doing so is a consistent requirement of the Party Central Committee for the courses' "connotative development". The article is built around three "logics", each applied in turn to the three cultures. The first, a knowledge logic, treats the cultures as sources of cultural depth. The second, a value logic, treats them as the basis of students' beliefs and "confidence". The third, a method logic, treats them as a spur to innovation in teaching. Zhao draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and writings, with occasional citations of Engels. On the knowledge logic, Zhao argues that traditional culture supplies philosophical, moral and value resources, such as "all under heaven for the common good", the idea that rule should rest on virtue, and the people-centred idea of government. Revolutionary culture, including relics, heroes' stories and red sites, supplies teaching material and the "red bloodline". Advanced socialist culture, formed through the Two Integrations, supplies the spirit of patriotism and reform and the core socialist values. On the value logic, Zhao links traditional culture to historical and cultural confidence, revolutionary culture to confidence in the path and the system, and socialist culture to theoretical consciousness. Zhao adds that courses should uphold Marxism's guiding position and reject "non-Marxist", "pseudo-Marxist" and historically nihilist views. On method, Zhao proposes tracing origins and linking past and present when teaching traditional culture, and storytelling that joins knowledge with values, including virtual-reality and AI tools, for revolutionary culture. For socialist culture, Zhao proposes combining ideological guidance with scholarly explanation. Zhao concludes that the three cultures should be treated as a foundational project for "fixing the root and forging the soul". They should run through the whole of ideological and political education and talent training, so as to raise the courses' relevance and appeal. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars connect official cultural doctrine to the design and teaching of compulsory ideological and political courses.

Practical explorations in special-topic education on the Marxist view of religion in universities The case of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences 高校马克思主义宗教观专题教育的实践探索 Yang Tianjiao Chen Tianjia Yang Tianjiao and Chen Tianjia ask how the Marxist view of religion, together with the Party's religious policy, can be taught more effectively in Chinese universities. They note that university ideological and political courses lack a dedicated chapter on the subject, so it is usually taught as scattered points of knowledge. Drawing on the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (UCAS), the authors argue that a stand-alone special topic is feasible and welcomed by students, but that it needs better content, discourse and institutional support. The article has three parts. It first describes the design and practice of a religion topic that UCAS has run since 2019 within a compulsory postgraduate course on Chinese Marxism and the contemporary world. It then evaluates the results through a questionnaire and interviews covering 1,365 master's and doctoral student responses. Finally it offers strategies and recommendations for strengthening such education. On design, the authors describe a topic organised around the Marxist view of religion, drawing also on philosophy, sociology, psychology and brain science. It starts from students' own questions, such as why Party members may not hold religious beliefs, and links religion to the holistic national security outlook through cases of alleged foreign religious infiltration, cults and spiritual pyramid schemes. According to the survey, 93.7% of respondents were satisfied with the teaching, and 65.71% had vague understandings of the Marxist view of religion. Nearly half had encountered alien-themed cult or spiritual-practice content online. Only 23.22% correctly answered a question on the principles of religious affairs management. The authors conclude that students want systematic knowledge but find classical formulations abstract and know the policy background poorly. The authors recommend understanding the regularities of teaching this subject, with an atheist foundation and interdisciplinary rigour. They call for an educational discourse that is authentic, sincere and appropriate, avoiding command and preaching. They also propose stronger Party leadership in universities, academic support, training for ideological and political teachers to compensate for a shortage of specialist scholars, and a dedicated national textbook. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese example of how religion is taught in university ideological courses, including the survey data and the authors' own assessment of weaknesses.

Raymond Aron's reflections on the Marxist philosophy of history and their limits 雷蒙•阿隆对马克思主义历史哲学的思考及其局限 Jia Xiangyun Raymond Aron, the French liberal thinker long overshadowed by Sartre and the left, described himself as a socialist but not a Marxist. Jia Xiangyun asks what Aron made of the Marxist philosophy of history and where his thinking fell short. The article argues that Aron's view of history overlaps with Marx's in important respects and that parts of his account of historical knowledge concretise and enrich historical materialism. It also holds that his "probabilistic determinism" slides into scepticism and that his stance remains that of an observer, not an actor. The article has four parts. It begins with Aron's reading of Marx and his notion of "metascience". It then places the philosophy of history as a discipline, from Vico and Herder through Hegel and Ranke to Marx and Engels, and sets Aron's 1938 doctoral thesis, Introduction to the Philosophy of History, within that line. Next it sets out Aron's general problems of historical knowledge: history versus natural science, individual and totality, and objectivity. A conclusion weighs his contributions against his limits. Jia reports that Aron distinguished Marx from Marxism and found two tendencies in Marx, an objectivising, law-governed one and a subjectivising one centred on class struggle. In Aron's view these could be reconciled only through some metascience, and the rival existentialist, structuralist and orthodox Marxist-Leninist schools each emphasise one side. Jia calls this attribution of the schools to Marx's own tendencies a misreading, because Marx's texts form a developing whole, and cites Lukács on the dialectic of subject and object. On historical knowledge, Aron held that history, unlike natural science, depends on understanding and narrative. He favoured William Dray's rational-explanation model over Carl Hempel's covering-law model. Jia argues that these views embody the disciplinary character and totalising method of historical materialism. Jia concludes that Aron's account of the subject–object relation parallels Marx's claim that people make their own history, though not as they please. The article nonetheless finds two limits. Aron's pessimism about the historical subject yields historical nihilism and no account of history's meaning. His stance as an "engaged spectator" stays at analysis and enlightenment, whereas Jia presents Marx as a revolutionary actor committed to human emancipation and the free development of each individual. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Aron's debt to and distance from Marx, and of his place in debates on historical knowledge.

The spirit and essence of the "Second Integration" as embodied in Mao Zedong Thought “第二个结合”的精神实质在毛泽东思想中的体现 Zhang Yunyi Liu Songlin Zhang Yunyi and Liu Songlin ask how far the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, was already present in Mao Zedong's thought. Starting from Xi Jinping's 2023 formulation of the Two Integrations, they argue that Mao Zedong Thought embodies the spirit and essence of the Second Integration and that Mao made a foundational contribution to it. In their reading, the First Integration concerns practical application to Chinese reality, while the Second concerns the "national form" of Marxism in thought and culture. The article has three parts. The first traces the historical logic of the First Integration, from Li Dazhao and Mao's 1930 critique of bookism to the 1938 report On the New Stage and the 1945 Party resolution on history. The second sets out three core views of the Second Integration that the authors find in Mao: a pluralist view of culture, a view of national culture as an inheritance, and a view of foreign culture. The third reads the "three magic weapons" of the revolution (the united front, armed struggle and Party building) as products of this integration. The authors' central move is to treat the Second Integration as the "spiritual core" and deeper driving force of the First, not a simple addition to it. They argue that Mao's "Hundred Flowers" policy fits Marxism's leading position, that he separated the "essence" from the "dross" of tradition through class analysis and the test of practice, and that his "ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign" method meant absorbing foreign culture selectively, with Marxism as its "soul" and Chinese culture as its "body". The third part gives examples. The united front draws on ideas of great unity and harmony, military thought draws on Sunzi's Art of War and the Laozi, and Party building draws on seeking truth from facts, serving the people and the Two Musts. The authors conclude that Mao's creative explorations laid the foundation for the Two Integrations. They say Xi Jinping carried this forward by making cultural confidence the core category of the Second Integration, which they describe as providing spiritual impetus for Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Revisiting Mao's contribution, they add, helps in understanding Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Read the original if you want a detailed account, with textual citations, of how Chinese scholars trace the Two Integrations back to Mao's writings.

Skilled at reasoning: the fundamental guideline for strengthening Marxist atheist education in university ideological and political theory courses 善讲道理：高校思政课加强马克思主义无神论教育的根本遵循 Ren Baolong Ren Baolong asks how university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) can carry out the Marxist atheist education that a 2021 Party and State Council opinion on ideological and political work required. The article takes Xi Jinping's April 2022 statement that the essence of these courses is 'reasoning' (jiang daoli) as its guideline. Ren argues that 'being skilled at reasoning' means teachers must explain, in depth and thoroughly, the atheist principles embedded in each course. In Ren's view this bears on cultivating reliable successors and on securing Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere. The article has three parts: why the approach is necessary, what is to be taught, and how to teach it. The first part contrasts what should be done with the actual situation. The second goes through six required courses in turn: Basic Principles of Marxism; the Introduction to Mao Zedong Thought and the Theoretical System of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics; the Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; the Outline of Modern and Contemporary Chinese History; Ethics and the Rule of Law; and Situation and Policy. The third part sets out teaching methods. Ren holds that atheist education in these courses suffers from three absences: it is silent in the discipline of ideological and political education, missing from the unified textbooks, and unvoiced in teaching, because teachers are afraid to, unwilling to or unable to teach it. Drawing on Marx's remark that theory grips the masses when it is radical, Ren argues that a thorough theory still needs 'thoroughness of persuasion' to win over students. Each course is assigned its own atheist content. Examples are the people as makers of history in the principles course, atheism in the thought of Mao and later Party leaders, the Party's current religious work theory, missionaries and imperialism in the history course, and online fads such as burning incense in the ethics course. Ren also proposes lecture, practical and online teaching methods, teaching that is deep, thorough and lively, and teacher–student interaction. Ren concludes that teachers must master and believe in Marxist atheism and set an example, while students must reflect on it actively. Teaching should use cases, everyday language and technology such as VR to answer students' sharp questions directly rather than avoid them. Ren argues that only this can resist the growing reach of theistic ideas among young people. Read the original if you want a detailed, course-by-course account of how Chinese university ideological and political courses are expected to integrate atheist education.

Drawing fully on the treasure of fine traditional Chinese culture to advance the intensive development of ideological and political theory courses 充分挖掘中华优秀传统文化宝藏，推进思政课建设内涵式发展 Liu Shulin Liu Shulin takes up Xi Jinping's instruction, conveyed at the 11 May 2024 conference on school ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke), that these courses should rest on Marxism and draw strength from fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. The author argues that, following the Second of the Two Integrations (Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture), mining traditional culture is a major driver of what the article calls the intensive development of these courses. By this the author means real gains in guiding ideas, content, theoretical grounding and teaching method, rather than formalism. The article is organised around five areas in which traditional culture can be put to use: experience of running schools and educating the people; ideals and beliefs; the people-based (minben) tradition; the historiographical heritage and the grand view of history; and China's tradition of proactive exchange with the outside world. Liu draws on the Book of Rites, the Book of Documents, Xunzi, the Records of the Grand Historian and other classics. These are set beside statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.
