Liu's central claim is that classical ideas can be adopted selectively, with their feudal political content rejected, in line with Mao's call for critical use of the cultural heritage. The Book of Rites principle of mutual growth of teaching and learning is offered as a pedagogical lesson. Its contrast between the Great Unity and the moderately prosperous society (xiaokang) is read as showing that China has kept its highest ideal while setting achievable stage goals, which Liu links to Deng Xiaoping's use of xiaokang. The boat-and-water image of ruler and people, found from Xunzi to Wei Zheng, is presented as an ancestor of the Party's mass line and the people-centred approach. Historiography and the Party's two answers to the historical cycle are tied to the grand view of history, which Liu says supports opposing historical nihilism and teaching Party history. The Silk Road and Xuanzang are cited to show that Chinese civilisation was never closed. Liu concludes that teachers should combine critical selection with absorption, using the past to serve the present and foreign learning to serve China. They should view the world through the grand view of history and support the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Doing so, the author holds, would improve the relevance and appeal of the courses and serve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Tsinghua Marxism scholar maps classical Chinese sources onto current Party doctrine for teaching ideology and politics.

Correctly understanding and scientifically grasping the theory of new quality productive forces 正确认识和科学掌握新质生产力理论 Li Zhengtu Li Zhengtu asks where the theory of new quality productive forces comes from and what it is. Writing in 2024, after Xi Jinping's calls to develop new quality productive forces and his statement that high-quality development needs a "new theory of productive forces", Li argues that the theory derives from Marxist political economy's theory of productive forces and extends it. The article presents itself as a systematic reading of that extension and of the policies that follow from it. The article has three main parts. The first sets out five elements of productive-forces theory: advanced productive forces, the determining role of productive forces, productive forces as the criterion, the reaction of relations of production, and the development of productive forces. It draws on Marx, Lenin and Deng Xiaoping. The second part builds a theory of how productive forces develop, tracing factors of production from William Petty through Marx to neoclassical growth models. The third part reviews policy choices since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and judges them against the resulting framework. Li's central move is to apply each of the five elements to new quality productive forces, giving a "five-theory" scheme: advancement, determination, criterion, reaction and development. He then adds a "three-theory" account of their development. Science and technology are the fundamental driver. New factors of production, above all data, change the structure of productive forces. A qualitative change in productive forces brings a qualitative change in relations of production. Li holds that every era has its own new quality productive forces, which today are digital and green. He gives the formula: new quality productive forces = digital productive forces × green productive forces. Li concludes that policies on strategic emerging industries, the digital economy, future industries, innovation-driven development, talent, incentives, deepening reform, opening up and green development are all scientifically sound. In his account they follow from the theory, and he adds that practice came before theory, which in turn confirms the policy choices. He also states that new quality productive forces call for new relations of production under socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned attempt to derive new quality productive forces systematically from Marxist productive-forces theory and to use it to justify current policy.

Deng Xiaoping's historic contribution to exploring Chinese modernization 邓小平对探索中国式现代化的历史性贡献 Sang Xuecheng Guo Kai How did Deng Xiaoping shape the idea of Chinese modernization before the term took its present form? Sang and Guo argue that Deng, as chief architect of reform and opening up, was a principal pioneer of the path. They hold that his concept of a "Chinese-style modernization" (中国式的现代化) inherited and developed the "four modernizations" thinking of Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai, and that it has had a lasting influence on the Party's current leadership of national rejuvenation. The article has four parts. It traces how the concept was proposed in 1978–79 and revised in 1983. It then examines the goal of a "moderately prosperous family" and the three-step development strategy. It sets out a series of principles for modernization, and closes by comparing Deng's formulation with Xi Jinping's "Chinese modernization". The authors rely mainly on Deng's speeches, meetings with foreign leaders and Party congress documents. The authors read the shift from "four modernizations" to "Chinese-style four modernizations" and then "Chinese-style modernization" as a deepening grasp of how modernization works. They link it to Deng's visits to Japan, Singapore and the United States, and to China's large population and weak economic base. In their account Deng's aim was to oppose rash advance and wholesale copying of Western models. They say this developed into the idea of a moderately prosperous society (xiaokang) and the theory of building socialism with Chinese characteristics. The three-step strategy was endorsed at the 13th Party Congress (1987). The principles they list are Party leadership, starting from the national conditions, common prosperity rather than polarisation, the basic line of "one centre, two basic points", and balanced material and ethical-cultural progress. Sang and Guo conclude that the two concepts are continuous. Both answer the questions of their historical moment and insist on seeking truth from facts. They argue that Xi's "Chinese modernization" is a creative development of Deng's concept, with richer content and a wider international outlook. Deng's version, they say, was more concerned with principle and direction, while the current one is more holistic and systematic. Read the original if you want a Party-school account of how the Dengist formulations are linked to today's official concept of Chinese modernization.

Using scholarship to teach politics is the key to teaching ideological and political theory courses well 用学术讲政治是讲好思政课的关键 Luo Yuting Liu Hongchang How should university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) persuade students rather than simply instruct them? Luo and Liu argue that the essence of these courses is to "explain the reasons" behind politics, and that the key is "using scholarship to teach politics": offering a Marxist, theory-based account of major historical and current political questions. In their view this strengthens the scientific and logical force of the courses and helps students build firm ideals and convictions. The article has three parts. The first takes Xi Jinping's formula that political firmness comes from theoretical clarity and breaks firmness into political direction, the ability to judge right and wrong, and steady political resolve. The second traces theoretical clarity to three sources: the universal truth of Marxism, Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and the unity of Marxism's truthfulness and its value orientation. The third sets out what the authors call the key requirement for teaching the courses. The authors hold that political character is the fundamental attribute of these courses and academic rigour their essential feature, so the two must be united. They propose three methods. Teachers should explain historical trends through the basic contradictions of capitalism and the claimed inevitability of socialism's victory. They should use international comparison, citing GDP and purchasing-power figures for China, the United States, India and Japan and contrasting China with Western political systems, to build political confidence. They should use the Party's century of struggle to deepen political identification. The authors also urge teachers to engage sensitive student questions and to criticise erroneous social trends, and they quote Mao Zedong that people must be persuaded, not coerced. The authors conclude that teachers who themselves hold Marxist convictions and have real theoretical command can win students over by the force of truth. Students would then support Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics and take part in Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese ideological-education scholars justify and operationalise the link between academic argument and political education, including the comparative data and China–West contrasts they recommend using in class.

Focusing on advancing Chinese modernization to further deepen reform comprehensively 紧紧围绕推进中国式现代化 进一步全面深化改革 Wei Chuanguang Published in Guangming Daily shortly after the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), this commentary interprets the Party's Decision on further deepening reform comprehensively to advance Chinese modernization. Wei Chuanguang argues that Chinese modernization has advanced through reform and opening up and will open broad prospects only through further reform. Reform, in the author's words, is always in progress and never complete. The piece is organised around three of the Decision's formulations: bringing the relations of production and the productive forces, the superstructure and the economic base, and state governance and social development into better alignment. Each section applies one of these pairs. They address, in turn, new quality productive forces, economic-system reform as the leading element, and the fit between governance and social development. In the first move, Wei draws on the classical Marxist view that productive forces and relations of production move in contradiction. Relations of production can act as a midwife and accelerator of new technology or as a fetter on it, so new quality productive forces require new relations of production, which in turn require deeper reform of economic, science-and-technology and industrial-policy systems. In the second, Wei treats economic-system reform as the lead reform. It centres on a high-standard socialist market economy, the Two Unwaverings, a unified national market and stronger property-rights protection, and it is meant to pull along reforms in democracy, rule of law, culture, welfare, ecology and Party building. In the third, Wei sets out four relationships that governance and development must balance: an effective market and a capable government; making the cake bigger and dividing it well; free vitality and good order; and material and cultural-ethical progress. Wei concludes that reform must be coordinated, systematic and integrated across fields, with the goal set by the Decision for 2035 of a high-standard socialist market economy and basic modernization of the system and capacity of national governance. Institutions should give the Party's and the state's decisions long-term stability and support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of the Third Plenum Decision, organised by the Marxist pairs of productive forces and production relations and base and superstructure.

The innovative development of Marxist political economy in contemporary China 马克思主义政治经济学在当代中国的创新发展 Zhang Yu Zhang Yu asks how Marxist political economy has been developed in contemporary China and what original contribution Xi Jinping's economic thinking makes to it. The article argues that Xi Jinping Thought on the economy is the economic part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Zhang's account it is the latest theoretical result of Marxist political economy in contemporary China and the twenty-first-century world, and it marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article first traces the Party's handling of political economy: Mao Zedong's call to study socialist political economy, Deng Xiaoping's proposal for a political economy joining Marxist principles with Chinese practice, and the formation of Xi's economic thought after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out, in thirteen thematic sections, the components of this body of thought, from Party leadership of economic work and the people-centred approach to development to methodology for economic work. Each section lists a series of Xi's statements and then says what it adds to a branch of Marxist theory. Zhang's central claim is that these components form a systematic, internally connected theoretical system. It answers questions that, in the article's words, the Marxist classics did not address, earlier Chinese Communists never faced, and Western economic theory cannot resolve. Examples include new quality productive forces, the new development philosophy, high-quality development, the new development pattern, and the basic economic system of public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse forms of ownership. Zhang presents each as extending a classical theme, such as the relation of economics to politics, the aim of socialist production, social reproduction, productive forces, urban–rural relations, globalisation and economic modernization. Zhang concludes that this thought is both specifically Chinese and universal. It addresses questions Zhang says concern all humanity, such as the choice between socialism and capitalism, and between putting people first and putting capital first. The article states that Chinese modernization has broken the equation of modernization with Westernisation. It calls on Chinese theorists to summarise the experience of socialist economic construction, of economic modernization and of globalisation, and to offer Chinese wisdom and solutions. Read the original if you want a systematic official-line overview of the components of Xi Jinping's economic thought and how Qiushi's author ties each to Marxist political economy.

The deepening of universal intercourse under the revolution of new quality productive forces 新质生产力革命背景下人类普遍交往的深度发展研究 Zhang Jianyun Zhang Jianyun asks how the revolution in new quality productive forces, led by digital technologies, changes the universal intercourse (交往, Verkehr) that Marx and Engels tied to the development of productive forces. The article argues that the 19th-century machine system produced only an atomised, accidental and superficial universal intercourse. In Zhang's view, the digital technology system now creates "digital intercourse", which deepens universal intercourse and drives it towards organic unity. The article has four main parts. It first defines intercourse in Marx and Engels and traces how technology and productive forces shaped it, from isolated peasant production to machine industry and the world market. It then describes the digital technology system (big data, AI, blockchain, cloud computing) and the forms of digital intercourse. Next it examines production and exchange, and it ends by discussing the significance of these changes for efficiency, human development and a community with a shared future for mankind. Zhang's core claim is that digital intercourse transcends time, space and trust, is free "anytime, anywhere, on the person", and lets individuals interact as individuals rather than as members of bureaucratic units. In production, blockchain-based networks allow real-time cooperation and data, technology and business integration. Workers can then act together like Marx's "one social labour-power" in the Robinson Crusoe passage of Capital. In exchange, disintermediation merges producers and consumers, reduces alienated, thing-mediated relations and moves towards planned, flexible production according to social and individual needs. Zhang concludes that deeper universal intercourse raises efficiency, supports all-round human development by letting individuals appropriate the totality of productive forces, and helps build a community with a shared future for mankind. Digital capitalism, in this account, produces difficulties because private ownership conflicts with the demands of new quality productive forces, not because of the technology itself. The technology "will not remain trapped in capitalism for ever". Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Marx's concept of intercourse to blockchain, AI and the Party's new quality productive forces discourse.

Striving to build China's independent knowledge system 努力建构中国自主的知识体系 Wei Lei This newspaper commentary examines "China's independent knowledge system", one of the signature concepts of Xi Jinping's cultural thought, first set out systematically at the national conference on propaganda, ideological and cultural work on 7–8 October 2023. Wei Lei argues that the concept is a defining marker of that thought's originality. It reflects, in the author's account, three things: the objective requirements of China's cultural development, the social development of the new era, and the exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. The article is organised under three headings that follow these points. It begins with a historical sketch, from the knowledge system of ancient China and its Ming-Qing framework of the Six Arts and the four categories of classics, history, philosophy and belles-lettres, to its crisis after the Opium War. It then turns to the link between contemporary practice and theory, and finally to China's relationship with Western knowledge. Xi Jinping's speeches supply most of the supporting quotations. Wei contends that, from the late Qing on, Western-derived disciplines were adopted in China but did not adequately explain or solve Chinese problems, so the task of rebuilding a Chinese knowledge system remained unfinished. Xi's concept answers that task on three conditions: guidance by Marxism, inheritance of fine traditional Chinese culture through creative transformation and innovative development, and a focus on what China is doing now. Wei says neither traditional nor Western-derived knowledge can explain China's success, so new theory must come from reform and development practice. On the West, the author describes a global discursive hegemony built on Eurocentrism, the "end of history" thesis and Orientalism, and holds that the concept rejects copying Western models while drawing on their reasonable elements. Wei concludes that the concept sums up the laws governing the development of China's knowledge system and grasps the trend of its construction amid civilizational exchange. It also reflects a world-minded outlook, in which China's knowledge contributes "Chinese wisdom" to what the author calls the questions of the world. Philosophy and social science scholars are urged to take answering the questions of China, the world, the people and the times as their academic duty. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how Chinese scholars present the "independent knowledge system" within Xi Jinping's cultural thought.

The threefold critique of contemporary capitalism and its new interpretation 当代资本主义的三重批判及其新阐释 Kong Ming'an Kong asks how to understand contemporary financial capitalism, led by the United States, when it appears to have weathered the 2008 subprime crisis and the 2023 Silicon Valley Bank run and returned to apparent prosperity. The article draws mainly on Slavoj Žižek's psychoanalytic critique, supplemented by Alfred Sohn-Rethel's account of commodity fetishism. Kong argues that, beneath its legitimating surface, capitalism conceals contradictions in three areas: finance, political democracy and ecology. The article has three main sections and a short conclusion. The first treats financial capital, digital capital and welfare capital. The second examines the form and paradoxes of capitalist democracy. The third covers the inevitability of ecological crisis and Žižek's rejection of what he calls the ecology of fear. Kong draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Habermas, Adorno and Dan Schiller, and sets Žižek's Lacanian readings beside them. On finance, Kong reports Žižek's claim that speculators are paradoxical subjects, empty and desiring, driven by both greed and fear, in the way Lacan's object a works. Expansionary money creation after a crash only postpones crisis to the future. Digital capital, in Kong's reading with Sohn-Rethel, extends the abstract "oneness" of money into digital fetishism, and welfare capital, including billionaire philanthropy, merely delays collapse and strains public finances. On democracy, Žižek's "forced choice" (choosing between bad and worse, as in Sophie's Choice) and the lift "close door" button are used to argue that elections are formal and misrecognised, though Kong stresses that Marx credited bourgeois democracy with historic progress. On ecology, Žižek's claim that "nature does not exist" casts humanity as nature's wound. Kong reports that he therefore rejects both return to nature and fear-based ecology, and advocates a Bartleby-like refusal of capitalism. Kong concludes that none of the three forms alters the capitalist system, and that only institutional opposition can end its alienation. Capitalism, in Kong's words, is neither about to perish nor immutable. Žižek's analysis is called incisive but also radical or extreme, and Kong calls for a fuller assessment grounded in Marx and in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's critical reception of Žižek's psychoanalytic account of finance, democracy and ecology.

A critique of capitalist political economy from the perspective of parallax dialectics 视差辩证法视域下的资本主义政治经济学批判 Shi Fengge Shi Fengge examines how Slavoj Žižek's "parallax dialectics" yields a critique of capitalist political economy. The article argues that, seen through this lens, the contemporary capitalist economy shows systemic antagonisms that differ from the path Marx took in Capital, namely the exploitation of surplus labour, but still expose the system's inner contradictions. Shi presents this as a new theoretical angle on global capital and a possible resource for the Left in rethinking emancipatory politics. The article has five parts. It first reconstructs parallax dialectics: Žižek takes Kojin Karatani's "parallax" from Transcritique, reads it through Kant's antinomies and Lacan's Real, and grounds it in ontological difference and "minimal difference". Three sections then take up three parallax splits: the "Real" economy versus actual economy, the depoliticisation of the economy versus the primacy of politics, and material versus immaterial labour. A short conclusion assesses Žižek's approach. In Shi's account, Žižek separates the "Real" economy, an absent quasi-cause that shapes society, from the actual economy, a symbolised sub-system. Class struggle mediates economy and politics, so the mainstream claim of a purely objective market economy is an ideological illusion. Shi reports Žižek's view that depoliticisation serves the unrestricted global movement of capital and produces semi-monopoly power in internet giants and gene-patenting firms. On labour, Shi follows Žižek's critique of Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt. They treat immaterial labour as dominant, capital as merely parasitic, and "exodus" as the route to liberation. Žižek replies that outsourcing separates knowledge workers from sweatshop workers, so capital still organises and unites global production. He holds that liberation requires collective ownership of the "commons" and of the management of things. Shi concludes that Žižek offers the Left a distinctive way back to political economy critique. Shi also judges the approach "seemingly Marxist but not" (si "ma" fei "ma"): its philosophical deduction departs from Marx's historical-materialist analysis, which starts from the commodity, and risks sliding into idealist speculation. The author calls for drawing on Žižek's method while holding to Marxism's historical-materialist account of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading and assessment of Žižek's economic thought, including his debate with Negri and Hardt.

On the conservative elements in Lukács's History and Class Consciousness 论卢卡奇《历史与阶级意识》中的保守主义成分 Yan Yan Lukács's History and Class Consciousness (1923) sought to rescue Marx's revolutionary dialectic by "returning to Hegel". Yan asks whether Lukács actually removed the conservative elements of Hegelianism, and whether he did the same with Max Weber's rationalisation theory, on which the book's concept of reification depends. The article argues that he did not fully succeed: Hegelian and Weberian conservatism survive in the book and leave it with unresolved paradoxes. The article relies chiefly on the critique of Lukács by his pupil István Mészáros, developed over five chapters of Beyond Capital. It has four parts. The first argues that Hegel's philosophy is a form of "uncritical positivism". The second traces the negative influence of Hegelianism on History and Class Consciousness. The third examines the "Weber burden" in the book's treatment of rationality, calculability and bureaucracy. A short conclusion follows, drawing on Mészáros, Ferenc Fehér and Zhang Yibing. On Hegel, Yan follows Mészáros in holding that his "political economy standpoint" takes the capital relation uncritically. His ethical state, his account of civil society and his teleological philosophy of history are read as indirect arguments for the eternity of capital and for its "virtue". Lukács's thesis that the proletariat is the identical subject–object of history is, in Yan's reading, a Hegelian remnant, as Lukács himself conceded. It also reflects an over-optimistic reading of the European revolutionary situation after 1917, an underestimation of capital and an overestimation of class consciousness. On Weber, Yan adds a criticism of Mészáros: Lukács condemns bureaucracy and reification at the level of values but accepts Weber's findings on efficiency and calculability. Yan holds that Lukács also confuses two senses of reification, the reification of production relations, which Marx criticised, and the objectification of the production process, which Marx affirmed. Weber's understanding thus prevails beneath Lukács's open opposition to him. Yan concludes, with Mészáros, that Lukács treated the crisis of capitalism as a crisis of consciousness. This weakened the primacy of the material and economic, left him dependent on intellectuals bringing consciousness from outside, and led to his late turn to ethics and aesthetics. Yan stresses that Mészáros and the Budapest School still regard the book as a landmark. A closing note adds that Mészáros overlooks the positive influence of Marx's historical method, which Yan thinks kept critical and revolutionary elements alive. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, Lukács's reception of Hegel and Weber, or Mészáros's critique of him.

Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England and the study of Britain's modernization: a visual analysis 《英国工人阶级状况》关于英国现代化进程研究的可视化分析 Liu Nana Liu Nana rereads Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England as a study of Britain's modernization, which Engels traces from the Industrial Revolution. The article argues that Engels's data and field observations expose a set of paradoxes in capital-driven modernization. From these Liu draws lessons for seeing how Chinese modernization goes beyond the Western path. The article has three parts. The first sets out the temporal and spatial features of British modernization, using figures and charts on population movement, transport, city growth and the world market. The second analyses three paradoxes that Liu finds in Engels's text. The third draws theoretical implications for Chinese modernization. In Liu's account, Engels treats industrialization and urbanization as mutually reinforcing, and sees British capitalism as opening world history through the division of labour, new technology and the world market. Liu identifies three paradoxes. Workers become appendages of machines and are harmed in body and mind. Urban space develops unevenly, with housing shortages, town–country opposition and the loss of public leisure space. Free trade benefits capital, not labour: it intensifies competition among workers, lowers their purchasing power and extends exploitation worldwide. Liu stresses that Engels traces these outcomes to the capitalist system itself and not to incidental causes. Liu concludes that Chinese modernization surpasses Western modernization in three ways. First, it is a modernization of people, in contrast to what Liu calls the Western modernization of things, and it aims at free and all-round human development under a people-centred approach. Second, it builds socialist town–country relations through "people's cities" and rural revitalization. Third, it widens its space through a new pattern of domestic and international dual circulation. Liu describes it as both open and endogenous, and as rejecting plunder and colonial expansion. Read the original if you want a data-driven rereading of Engels's early work that is tied to current Party discourse on Chinese modernization.

The "logic of Capital" as critique and transcendence of Hegel's speculative logic A methodological inquiry based on the relation between logic and history “《资本论》的逻辑”对黑格尔思辨逻辑的批判与超越 Liu Daoyi Liu Daoyi asks how Marx's principle of the unity of logic and history arose from, and went beyond, Hegel's opposite principle that history is unified within logic. The article argues that Hegel's inversion of the relation between thought and reality necessarily inverted the relation between logic and history. In Liu's account, Marx overcame this inversion in what Lenin called the "logic of Capital", where materialist logic, dialectics and epistemology are applied to a single science. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Hegel's principle through his treatment of the history of philosophy and of world history, and lists its defects. It then sets out Marx's counter-principle, drawing on the 1857–58 manuscripts and Engels. The last two parts follow the "logic of Capital" through two movements of concepts: from the concrete to the abstract, which Liu locates in Marx's critique of the history of political economy (chiefly Theories of Surplus-Value), and from the abstract to the concrete, which Liu locates in the three volumes of Capital. Liu identifies three defects in Hegel's approach. Its transitions are conceptual deduction that cannot be verified against facts. It leaves his material thin, as in his treatment of China, and so feeds Eurocentrism. It cannot grasp the role of economic factors. Marx, by contrast, starts from real contradictions in capitalism and gathers extensive factual material. He holds that the order of categories follows their relations within modern bourgeois society, not their historical order of appearance, although simple categories such as money or labour in general often did exist earlier. In Liu's reading, Marx's critique of political economy runs from the mercantilists through Smith and Ricardo to the vulgarisation of the Ricardian school. It shows how all economists studied surplus-value only in the special forms of profit and rent. On Liu's reading, the structure of Capital embodies the same unity. Volume I runs from commodity and money to the tendency of capitalist accumulation, which ends in the negation of the negation. Volume II treats the circuits and reproduction of capital. Volume III moves from profit to merchant capital, interest-bearing capital and ground-rent, each with a historical review. The article concludes that this method negated and surpassed Hegel's speculative logic, raised dialectics to a new level and offers a scientific methodological basis for social change and theoretical innovation today. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how the structure of Capital is read as applying the unity of logic and history against Hegel.

The origins, spread and social role of religion in Southeast Asia: an analysis 东南亚宗教的起源、传播及其社会作用探析 Wang Xiaofeng Wang Xiaofeng asks how religion in Southeast Asia arose, spread and functioned socially, and answers from the Marxist view of religion and historical materialism. The article argues that religious consciousness must be explained from material production and the level of the productive forces, not from ideas alone. It presents this as a theoretical and practical research task, since Southeast Asian politics, culture and diplomacy cannot be understood without religion. The article has five parts. It first traces the origins of primitive religion, then the spread of Buddhism and Islam through trade. It then examines how colonial powers used religion, and how religious figures took part in anti-colonial struggles. A closing section looks ahead. Cases include Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines, supported by many quotations from Marx and Engels and by studies from Southeast Asian and Chinese scholars. Wang makes three main moves. First, early peoples with weak productive forces were subjugated by nature, so they personified natural forces. Wang cites sun worship in Indonesia and Vietnam, bird totems in Vietnam, ancestor worship and Malay animism. Second, Buddhism and Islam travelled along trade routes: Indian merchants and monks brought Buddhism, and Arab merchants brought Islam, with Malacca as a centre. Third, citing Marx's 'opium of the people', Wang contends that French colonizers used Buddhism in Vietnam, and Spanish and later American rulers used Catholicism in the Philippines, to pacify the population. In Wang's account the Philippine church held wide political and economic powers. Yet Wang also reports that monks and Muslim leaders led or joined resistance in Vietnam, Malaya and the Philippines, with religious and national conflicts becoming intertwined. Wang concludes that religion will persist in Southeast Asia and keep shaping politics, because it is embedded in mainstream and popular culture and in a plural society. Malaysia is the main example. There, Wang says, Islamism and Malay nationalism are merging, religious bureaucracy is expanding, and religious identity is deepening social division. Wang warns of future 'religious risks' and calls for specialist study of Southeast Asian religion guided by the Marxist view. Read the original if you want a Marxist-framed account of Southeast Asian religious history, or a sample of how Chinese atheism-studies scholarship treats the region.

Building China's independent knowledge system on the basis of Chinese modernization 立足中国式现代化建构中国自主的知识体系 Han Qingxiang Han Qingxiang takes up Xi Jinping's 2022 statement that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means building China's independent knowledge system. In this People's Daily commentary, the author argues that the system should be built on the course of Chinese modernization. Its Chinese features, Han says, show the system's independence, and that independence in turn shows Chinese modernization's original contribution to world modernization. The article has two parts. The first sets out basic paths for building the system, defining a knowledge system in philosophy and social sciences as an independent body of experience and knowledge that pursues original results and addresses Chinese problems. The second goes through the features of Chinese modernization, each of which Han presents as a field for scholarly research: population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical progress, nature, peace, and a new form of human civilization. In the first part, Han lists four requirements: uniting fidelity to principle with innovation under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; turning the principled theoretical results of Xi's statements into distinctive concepts, then into academic discourse and research paradigms; drawing on traditional culture, foreign achievements and future trends; and breaking free of Western-centrism. Han describes Western-centrism as the theoretical form of Western modernization, and calls for critical reflection on its core categories. In the second part, Han argues that scholars should systematically summarise Chinese modernization's results in each field. These include high-quality population development, the relations between efficiency and fairness and between growth and distribution, the dialectical unity of material and cultural-ethical civilization, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. Han concludes that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and is a new form of human civilization. Scholars, Han says, should keep to China's own path, take what China is doing as the centre of their work, and explain its theoretical and practical breakthroughs. They should also help Chinese theory "go global", so that the world knows "China in scholarship" and "China in theory". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official discourse links Chinese modernization to the project of an autonomous Chinese social science.

The global significance of upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China 坚持我国宗教中国化方向的全球主义意涵 Li Weijian Yin Di Since 2015, Xi Jinping has called for upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China as part of guiding religion to adapt to socialist society. Li and Yin respond to foreign scholarship that, in their account, presents the policy as a uniquely Chinese measure to secularise, Hanify, control or eliminate religion, contrary to global trends and to religious freedom. They argue that the policy has a local, Chinese orientation but also carries rich "globalist" implications, and that the two are not in contradiction. The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2024, first notes that overseas research includes an edited volume distinguishing "top-down" from "bottom-up" sinicization. It then examines the policy from seven angles: its fit with the objective laws of religious development, its engagement with global religious realities, its consistency with religious freedom, its alignment with religious modernism, its respect for fine traditional culture, its value for global religious governance, and a closing synthesis. The authors' central move is to ground the policy in Marxist religious studies: religion is superstructure, shaped by economic base and society, so religions necessarily become localised and adapt to their times. Refusing this, they say, produces conflict, extremism and terrorism. They argue that sinicization is therefore a response to global religious conflict, which they say has reached China through extremism and "de-sinicization" currents. They hold that the policy is a form of guidance consistent with freedom of belief and with UN counter-terrorism resolutions. They also contend that it follows the global path of religious modernism and respects both Chinese and religious traditions. Finally, they cite France's burqa ban and US church-state separation as examples of other states steering religions to fit national values. Li and Yin conclude that the policy is "both Chinese and the world's" and offers a reference for global religious governance. They attribute foreign criticism to anti-China forces that, in their view, fear the policy's success will challenge their own governance models. They urge confidence in China's path, theory, system and culture, and continued application of the Party's theory of religious work in the new era. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars rebut foreign critiques of religious policy and frame it in terms of global trends and Marxist religious theory.

Derrida and Marx: the "hauntology politics" guiding future justice 德里达与马克思：引导未来正义的“幽灵政治学” Jia Liyan Jia Liyan examines Jacques Derrida's "politics of spectres" (the "politics of ghosts" of Specters of Marx) and asks why a deconstructionist, often accused of apolitical textual play, declared himself an heir to Marx. The article argues that Derrida's project is a deconstructive reading of Marxism that keeps its critical spirit and its messianic promise of emancipation, and that its real aim is future justice. The article is organised in three parts. The first places Derrida's book in the shock of the fall of the Berlin Wall and the "end of history" thesis of Francis Fukuyama. The second turns to the meaning of "spectres" and of Marx's "spirit" as an inheritance, drawing on Hamlet, the Communist Manifesto and the Western Marxist tradition of Lukács, Gramsci and Bloch. The third treats the "New International" and a "new politics", including Derrida's later work on law, hospitality and friendship. Jia reads Specters of Marx as, in Derrida's own words, a book of resistance against the post-1989 consensus that Marx and communism were dead. Derrida lists ten "plagues" of the "new world order", such as unemployment, exclusion of migrants, economic wars and arms trading, and concludes that justice is still absent and history unfinished. In Jia's account the spectres are victims of violence, colonialism and oppression, and inheriting Marx means a duty to them and to the future; Derrida speaks of many "spirits" of Marx, not one, and inheritance requires deconstructing what is received. Jia reports that Derrida rejects historical determinism and party-based Marxism, imagines a "New International" that is neither a state body nor a party, redefines revolution as an ethical rupture, and holds that law can be deconstructed while justice, as a messianic promise, cannot. Jia concludes that Derrida's "politics of spectres" is an ethicised extension of Marxist critique. It values the messianic call for justice but, as Jia points out, ignores Marxism as ontology, dialectical materialism and historical materialism. For Jia the case shows a longing for social solidarity and fairness in contemporary Western thought, and as long as real justice remains unrealised, many people are in some sense Marx's heirs. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of how Specters of Marx is read, from the Berlin Wall context through to Derrida's later politics of hospitality.

Chinese modernization: the effective combination of socialism and modernization 中国式现代化：社会主义与现代化的有效结合 Tang Aijun Tang Aijun asks how Chinese modernization can be understood as socialist modernization, and what distinguishes it from both capitalist modernization and earlier socialist models. The article argues that Chinese modernization is a new type of modernization built on an effective, two-way combination of socialism and modernization. Tang presents this as the core of a non-capitalist theory of modernization. The article first traces how socialism and modernization came together in economically and culturally backward countries, through Marx's late writings on Eastern societies and Lenin's reworking of the conditions for socialist revolution. It then examines the two directions of combination in turn: socialism must incorporate the demands of modernization, and modernization must adopt socialist principles and direction. Each section contrasts a flawed approach with the theoretical solutions Tang attributes to Chinese practice since reform and opening up. Tang argues that Marx, in his later years, allowed that backward countries might skip the 'Caudine Forks' of capitalism, and that Lenin changed the order of Marx's conditions from 'economics first, politics second' to revolution first, modernization afterwards. Tang holds that the traditional socialist model in China weakened the content of modernization, treating market mechanisms and urbanization as capitalist and judging reality by an idealised socialism. Chinese modernization is said to have corrected this through three theoretical moves: the primary stage of socialism as its starting point, the productive-forces criterion as its standard, and the socialist market economy as its core link. In the other direction, Tang rejects the 'ends–means' view that capitalism and socialism are merely alternative routes to the same modern society. Tang distinguishes them by ownership basis, by how contradictions are handled (including 'harnessing' capital) and by historical mission. Tang then identifies three links: Communist Party leadership as the decisive factor, a people-centred value orientation aimed at common prosperity, and the socialist institutional system. On the first, Tang contends that the superstructure can be embedded in the economic base. Tang concludes that socialist institutions better provide momentum, order and fairness than capitalist ones, and that this is the 'socialist logic' of Chinese modernization. The text is a theoretical argument for the legitimacy and distinctiveness of the Chinese path, framed within Marxist categories. Read the original if you want a detailed Party School account of how Chinese theorists reconcile Marx, Lenin and Deng Xiaoping on modernization and the base–superstructure relation.

A comparative study of Mao Zedong's and Deng Xiaoping's thought on modernization 毛泽东邓小平现代化思想比较研究论析 Zhang Yanguo Writing in 2004 (the article first appeared in the Journal of Wuhan University, Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), Zhang Yanguo compares the modernization thought of Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. Both men, Zhang argues, pursued the same goal: a strong modern country that benefits the people and consolidates the Communist Party's position as the ruling party. They differed in their historical starting points, their sense of what threatened the Party, and the development path they chose. Zhang concludes that Deng's innovations would not have been possible without the groundwork of Mao's exploration. Zhang defines modernization in the narrow sense used in academic circles: a backward country's planned economic and technological transformation, and its learning from advanced countries, in order to catch up with industrial powers. Sun Yat-sen is excluded because his model was 'Westernization'. The article has three sections: 'same goal, different starting points'; 'same anxiety, different readings'; and 'same exploration, different choices'. Each section sets Mao's statements against Deng's, with Mao's 1950s–60s speeches and the Eighth Party Congress (1956) as the main reference points. Zhang says Mao's thought took shape amid the rapid victory of the new-democratic revolution, which fostered optimism and expectations of fast construction. Deng's took shape after twenty years of 'Leftist' errors and the Cultural Revolution, which produced a sober and pragmatic outlook. On the Party's sense of danger, Zhang argues that Mao, after the Eighth Party Congress had defined the main contradiction as one between the people's needs and backward production, returned to class struggle as the principal contradiction. This led to the Cultural Revolution. Deng, by contrast, made 'what is socialism and how to build it' his central concern, held that poverty is not socialism, and set aside the 'socialist or capitalist' test in favour of the 'three favourables'. On models, Zhang holds that Mao's 'leaning to one side' kept him within the Soviet model of centralised planning. Deng treated reform as a revolution and sought a distinctively Chinese path of modernization. Zhang concludes that Mao's departure point confined him to the Soviet pattern, while Deng's focus on problems and on developing the productive forces opened a new road. Deng's theory, in Zhang's view, can also renew itself with the times. Mao's theory, despite its costly lessons, is still presented as a 'reliable starting point' and a valuable spiritual legacy. Read the original if you want a 2004 Chinese scholarly account of the Mao–Deng relationship, with extensive quotations from both leaders on class struggle, productive forces and the Soviet model.

Mao Zedong's exploration of building a large party and its lessons for today 毛泽东对大党建设问题的探索及其经验启示 Mao Sheng Mao Sheng asks how Mao Zedong approached the task of building the Chinese Communist Party into a large party that could lead the country's cause, and what this offers to present-day Party building. The author argues that Mao combined the Marxist theory of party building with Chinese conditions, set the aim of building a large party, and left experience that bears directly on what the 20th Party Congress (2022) called the "unique problems of a large party". The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's exploration through three phases: setting the aim of a large party from 1939, tied to national rejuvenation; the Yan'an-era "great project" of Party building, including the rectification campaign; and the period of governing, when he linked building a socialist large country to building a large party. The second part sets out four basic ideas he stressed. The third draws six lessons and links each to statements by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the core argument, Mao Sheng reads Mao Zedong's thinking as four requirements of a large party: great responsibility, as the "core force" leading the cause; great compassion, meaning wholehearted service to the people; great principles, meaning the "revolutionary and Bolshevik tradition" and ideological building; and great unity, with the Party made "as solid as iron". For the period after 1949, the author says Mao identified raising governing capacity and preventing degeneration as the two key issues, citing the "Three-anti" and "Five-anti" campaigns, the punishment of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan, and the creation of discipline inspection commissions. The author presents these as proof that the Party could build as well as destroy. The final part draws six lessons: serve the people and keep the original aspiration; unify thinking through ideological education; overcome the "fear of incompetence" through learning; keep up the spirit of struggle; carry out self-reform; and rectify Party conduct. Mao Sheng concludes that revisiting Mao's experience should help advance the Party's "new great project" and keep the Party from changing in nature. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how current large-party discourse is anchored in Mao's writings, with dense citations of his speeches from 1937 to 1958.

Religion does not play a prominent role in the shared spiritual home of the Chinese nation 中华民族共有精神家园中宗教角色并不突出 Wang Qichang Wang Qichang asks what makes up the shared spiritual home of the Chinese nation and what part religion plays in it. The short piece argues that, compared with the West, religion's role in building this home is not prominent. It opens by defining the shared spiritual home as the historically formed cultural and spiritual system of a unified multi-ethnic China, to which every self-identifying Chinese person is emotionally attached. Wang cites Xi Jinping's 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work, which listed building the shared spiritual home among its "twelve musts". The article then divides the concept into three levels: ideas, culture and everyday life. At each level it sets Chinese examples beside Western ones, including Plato, Thomas More, Hegel on Greece and Heidegger's "poetic dwelling". At the level of ideas, Wang points to the ideal of "great harmony under heaven" (datong) from the Book of Rites, later taken up by Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen. At the cultural level, the home is the continuous history and rich culture of China, including Confucian culture, the arts, the written script and classical poetry, whose popularity on television shows is offered as evidence. At the level of life, it is the unity of heaven and humanity and a love of nature, shown in Tao Yuanming's pastoral poetry and, in Wang's example, the popularity of the video creator Li Ziqi. Wang concludes that Daoist ideas of the unity of heaven and humanity and Buddhist compassion may have contributed to the shared spiritual home and may help in building it. Even so, the article holds that religion's role here is not prominent in comparison with the West. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar of atheism frames the nation's spiritual home in cultural rather than religious terms.

Plekhanov's critique of the "religious quest" and his exposition of Marxist atheism 普列汉诺夫对“宗教探寻”的批判和马克思主义无神论的阐释 Zhang Jiansong Zhang Jiansong asks what Georgi Plekhanov's long essay "On the So-called Religious Quest in Russia" offers for religious theory and for ideological struggle today. Zhang argues that, after the defeat of the 1905 revolution, Plekhanov used historical materialism to expose the "God-seeking" and "God-building" currents as theoretically weak and politically harmful. The article presents the essay as a model of Marxist criticism that still has practical meaning for religious work and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article follows the three parts of the essay that Plekhanov completed, using the texts in volume three of his selected philosophical works. Part one, "On Religion", sets out a basic theory. Part two, "Religion Again", criticises Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky. Part three deals with the "decadents" Merezhkovsky and Minsky. Zhang opens with the Stolypin reaction and closes with lessons for China. Zhang's central claim is that Plekhanov grounds religion in social being. His definition has three elements: ideas, feelings and ritual. Myth and animism arise from the low productive forces of hunting peoples, who reasoned by analogy. Totemism gave way as humanity gained control over nature, and later gods took on the shape of rulers and judges. Applying this framework, Plekhanov argues that every religion needs spirits, so the "atheist religion" of Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky is a verbal game. Zhang reports that Plekhanov attributes the quest to intellectuals who lost faith in revolution and turned to individual consolation. Against the decadents, Plekhanov defends the proletariat's economic struggle and argues that their individualism and fear of death drive their mysticism. He appeals to Feuerbach and Engels, and holds that only dialectical materialism resolves the problem of freedom and necessity. Zhang concludes that readers should learn two things. The first is to remain firm Marxists. Zhang cites the Soviet Union's collapse under Gorbachev's ideological pluralism and the Chinese Communist Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The second is to dare to struggle against erroneous trends. Zhang lists historical nihilism, constitutional democracy, "universal values" and neoliberalism, along with abnormal religious phenomena in some regions, as targets. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese reading of Plekhanov's religious theory and of how it is used in current Chinese ideological discussion.

New developments in the ideological sphere under new technological conditions 新技术条件下意识形态领域新变 Huang Xianghuai Writing in a newspaper commentary (China Social Sciences Today, May 2024), Huang Xianghuai asks how ideological work must change under new technological conditions. Huang credits the Party Central Committee since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with a fundamental turnaround in the ideological sphere. The author nevertheless stresses, citing the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), that "quite a few challenges" remain and that the work must keep renewing itself. The piece examines three new features: the changed communication landscape of the all-media era, a new form of struggle in the age of cognitive warfare, and the greater difficulty of safeguarding ideological security in the post-truth era. On the first, Huang argues that mainstream media are squeezed by self-media and capital, and that a dominant position is earned through influence, not held by default. Mainstream outlets should therefore be judged by what they achieve, not by whether they discharge their duties, and any outlet that sustains this function could be recognised as mainstream. On the second, the author says openly hostile statements have largely disappeared, but contention has shifted from disputes over doctrine to disputes over specific issues, using insinuation and incremental pressure that the author calls cognitive warfare. Responses must follow what works. On the third, Huang contends that narrative matters more than fact, that non-ideological problems turn into ideological ones, and that blocking and deleting content are losing effect. Huang proposes raising the ideological capacity and literacy of Party members and officials, alongside technical and legal measures, so that erroneous views lose influence. Huang also calls for a more open, inclusive attitude towards media outside the traditional mainstream. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar frames online ideological work in 2024.

The historical-materialist implications of building a modern Chinese civilization 建设中华民族现代文明的历史唯物主义意蕴 Dong Jianming Dong Jianming asks what historical materialism contributes to understanding the "new cultural mission" put forward by General Secretary Xi Jinping: building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. The article argues that this mission is firmly grounded in Marx's theory of history and is both required by the times and an inevitable step in historical progress. It presents the mission as part of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and as a source of theoretical guidance for creating a new culture for the present era. The piece is a short commentary, originally published in the China Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报) on 5 June 2024. It is organised in three parts: the historical necessity of the mission, the role of culture in social development, and the intellectual and cultural traditions accumulated by the Chinese nation. Dong draws on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong's \"On Contradiction\", the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and statements by Xi. First, Dong applies the principle that the economic base ultimately determines the superstructure. In this account, modern China's cultural subjectivity crisis stemmed from underdeveloped productive forces, while the Party-led advance from \"standing up\" to \"becoming rich\" to \"becoming strong\" and the progress of Chinese modernization now provide the material basis for cultural confidence. Second, citing Engels, Dong rejects economic determinism: culture interacts with the base and other superstructural elements. Cultural subjectivity does not grow automatically from economic growth but must be consciously built. Dong contends that in Western capitalist societies culture is dominated by capital and serves exploitation and accumulation, becoming a fetter on the productive forces. Third, Dong stresses the relative independence of forms of social consciousness, so that Chinese civilization's inherited traditions matter alongside economic factors. Dong concludes that shouldering the new cultural mission requires taking the Two Integrations, especially the \"second integration\" of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, as the basic guide. Marxism, in this view, activates the genes of Chinese civilization, while traditional culture enriches Marxism, producing a new cultural life-form. Dong presents this as both an application and a further development of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentators ground Xi Jinping's cultural thought in the classical Marxist base–superstructure framework.

Holding firmly to the soul and the root of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 坚守好马克思主义中国化时代化的魂和根 Wu Haijiang Jiang Hao Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Marxism must not be abandoned as the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture must not be abandoned as the "root" of the process, Wu Haijiang and Jiang Hao ask what it means to hold to both. Their thesis is that doing so is the foundation and precondition of theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece appeared in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in February 2024. The commentary has three parts. The first treats Marxism as the soul (hunmai, the "soul vein"). The second treats fine traditional Chinese culture as the root (genmai, the "root vein"). The third argues that the two must be integrated, and lists what this integration brings. Throughout, the authors rely heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). On Marxism, the authors argue that it is a scientific truth with lasting vitality, resting on historical materialism and the theory of surplus value. They also present it as the guiding ideology on which the Party and the state were founded, and as the "spiritual calcium" of the Party's new journey. They say Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has made original contributions to it. On the cultural root, they identify five features of Chinese civilization: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peace. They claim each of these shapes the Chinese path. In their account, for example, unity makes national unification the core of China's core interests, and peace explains why China imposes neither its values nor its political system on others. The authors conclude that the soul and the root must be "connected" so that the Party's theoretical innovation continues. They say this means injecting Chinese concepts, spirit and wisdom more deeply into Marxism. It also means building China's own autonomous knowledge system, with Marxism activating living elements of traditional culture. Finally, it means building a modern Chinese civilization as the cultural form of Chinese modernization. They present this as a contribution to human civilization with world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists in 2024 framed the relationship between Marxism and traditional culture, and which Xi Jinping formulations they drew on.

The historical-materialist grounding of the new form of human civilization 人类文明新形态的唯物史观根据 Ding Kuangyi Ding Kuangyi asks what historical materialism contributes to understanding the "new form of human civilization" that Xi Jinping associates with Chinese modernization. The article opens from Xi's statement that Chinese modernization is rooted in traditional Chinese culture, embodies the essence of scientific socialism and shows a path different from Western modernization. Ding argues that this new civilizational form has a deep basis in historical materialism, and that the basis can be traced along three lines. This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 11 April 2024, is organised in three sections. They cover innovation in the mode of production, the dialectical relation between material and spiritual civilization, and the idea of a "true community". Each section sets out the Marxist principle first and then applies it to Chinese modernization, with Western modernization as the contrast. In the first section, Ding restates that the mode of production, the unity of productive forces and relations of production, underlies culture and civilization. The contradiction between the two drives changes in the economic base and superstructure, and so the rise and fall of civilizational forms. On this basis Ding presents new quality productive forces, technological innovation and adjustments to relations of production (public ownership, a mix of distribution principles, common prosperity) as innovations that reshape civilization. In the second section, Ding cites Marx, Engels and Lenin on the mutual influence of material and spiritual life. Ding describes Western modernization as pursuing abstract material wealth, producing consumerism, instrumental rationality, utilitarianism and individualism. Chinese modernization is portrayed as grounded in a "logic of the human being" rather than capital, with material growth as a means, not an end. The third section describes capitalist community as mediated by money, capital and the market, which Ding calls an inverted and alienated form producing atomised, lonely individuals. Ding contrasts this with Marx's "true community", the association of free individuals. Ding concludes that Chinese modernization builds community at home through a governance community of shared construction, governance and benefit. Abroad it does so through a community with a shared future for mankind. The "true community" thus points, in Ding's account, to a civilization of equality, harmony and mutual help. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentators link Xi Jinping's formulations on civilization to classical Marxist categories in a short newspaper format.

Several questions requiring deeper reflection in studying the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 研究马克思主义中国化时代化需要深入思考的几个问题 Zhang Guozuo Zhou Xiaomei Zhang Guozuo and Zhou Xiaomei take up a question from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): why the Party stresses that it is specifically Marxism as adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times that "works". They argue that the answer lies in understanding two key words, "sinicization" (zhongguohua) and "adaptation to the times" (shidaihua), and the internal logic joining them. Their thesis is that the two are an inseparable whole and that continuing the process in the new era requires adherence to eight principles. The article is organised in five sections. It first traces the concept of adapting Marxism to China from Mao Zedong's 1938 report at the Sixth Plenum of the Sixth Central Committee through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. It then examines the meaning of adaptation to the times, sets out the relation between the two, and lists the eight principles. A final section presents Chinese modernization as a major theoretical innovation. The authors define the first as a spatial dimension (Marxism must suit Chinese conditions) and the second as a temporal one (it must answer the questions of each era). Because any Chinese reality belongs to a particular era, they say, debating which is primary or secondary violates the principle of wholeness. They hold that the basic principles of Marxism do not change, while specific conclusions tied to earlier conditions may be replaced, and they liken dogmatic repetition of old conclusions to "carving a mark on a boat to find a sword". The eight principles are: upholding Marxist fundamentals, the Two Integrations, keeping pace with the times, putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, problem orientation, a systems outlook, and a world-embracing outlook. In the final section the authors present Chinese modernization as the result of this process. They compare it with Western modernization across eight dimensions, including leadership, guiding theory, political system, ecological impact and moral foundations, and judge the Chinese model superior in each. The authors conclude that the three historic leaps in sinicized Marxism (Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era) are both sinicized and timely Marxism. They describe the theory of Chinese modernization as breaking the monopoly of "Western centrism" and offering developing countries a new option. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how the Two Integrations and the "eight principles" are presented in Chinese academic discourse.

Resolving the puzzle of social "institution": a critical reading of Castoriadis 破解社会“建制”之困：卡斯托里亚迪斯的批判解读 Qi Chuang Zhao Hu The article asks how the Greek-French thinker Cornelius Castoriadis, whom Axel Honneth called "the last Western Marxist", understood social "institution", and argues that this concept organises his whole theoretical development. Qi and Zhao propose rendering the French/English "institution" as "建制" (jianzhi, rendered here as "institution" in the sense of an instituting process) rather than the usual "制度", because it stresses a dynamic, ongoing act of construction over a fixed, passively executed result. Their thesis is that for Castoriadis institutions are condensations of social imaginary significations, and that this reading keeps his thought tied to the practical aim of changing the world. The article has four parts. It first traces the intellectual sources of the concept: Durkheim's sociology, Merleau-Ponty's late philosophy, and Marx's theory of alienation, together with Western Marxist figures such as Lukács, Gramsci, Adorno and Lefebvre. It then turns to signification, meaning and language, drawing on Heidegger's reading of logos and legein and on commentators including Olson, Adams, Arnason, Edgar and Sedgwick. A third part treats the essence of institution as social imaginary signification, and a fourth examines its "instituted" and "instituting" aspects. The authors argue that Castoriadis replaces Durkheim's "social" qualifier with "imaginary", stressing that institutions are changeable creations, and that alienation arises when the imaginary element becomes autonomous and dominates society. Signification, which they describe as a "magma" without fixed elements or limits, is expressed through language but cannot be reduced to linguistics or structuralist frameworks. Institution is then presented as a creation "out of nothing", with the original imagination as its source, yet the authors insist this is materialist, extending materiality from production and need to the whole of society. Institutions tend to harden into the instituted, disguising themselves as permanent, but the authors hold that the instituting dimension is more fundamental. Qi and Zhao conclude that the dialectic of the instituted and the instituting shows the necessity of change and affirms the revolutionary character of the social-historical. In their reading, where Marx indicates a direction of social development, Castoriadis stresses development itself, so that the legitimacy of the future is explained from revolution rather than the reverse. Read the original if you work on Western Marxism, post-Marxism or the Chinese reception of Castoriadis and want a detailed account of how the concept of institution links imagination, language and alienation.

Practical guidelines for ideological and political education in the digital age 数字化时代思想政治教育的实践遵循 Wang Tianmin How should ideological and political education respond to big data, algorithms and artificial intelligence? Wang Tianmin argues that it must accept the arrival of the digital age and adapt to it, but on a people-centred footing. Digital technology, in this view, is an objectification of human essence and so serves education, and the principle of 'putting people first' must remain the guide throughout. The article has three parts. The first justifies digitalisation theoretically, drawing on Marx's thinking on humans as 'objectifying' beings, on needs, and on the human essence as the ensemble of social relations. The second asks how digital tools can deepen the people-centred educational idea. The third turns to practice: how digital technology enters research and educational work, and how its quality can be raised. Wang's central move is that digital technology, like earlier technology, confirms human essence, since it turns people and their world into data that humans themselves invented. From this the author draws three advantages for educators. Aggregated data and big data give a holistic picture of the person, avoiding one-sided concepts. They track people as they develop, avoiding fixed and static definitions. And they present people together with their world, avoiding the separation of subject and object. In practice, Wang adapts a three-step model of AI-assisted research to education. The educator poses the problem, the system gathers data and generates plans, and the educator refines, tests and evaluates them against the goals set by the state and society. Wang calls for educators to convert principles, policy documents, cases and methods into digital information and to build a growing digital resource base that reflects the will of the Party and state. The article calls cyberspace a frontline of ideological work and says digital positions must be strengthened to train a new generation for national rejuvenation. It holds that digital education is still at an early stage and cannot fully replace offline, embodied teaching. Technology remains an auxiliary means whose outputs must be checked against educational goals, so that people are not dominated by machines. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar grounds the digitalisation of ideological and political education in Marxist philosophical anthropology and in practical workflows.

Keeping the development of ideological and political courses in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory 坚持思政课建设与党的创新理论武装同步推进 Qin Fayue This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2024, takes up an instruction Xi Jinping gave in May 2024: that the building of ideological and political courses (sizhengke) in schools should advance in step with arming people with the Party's innovative theory. Qin Fayue, a university vice-president, argues that the two tasks are inherently consistent. In Qin's account, the principle is a long-standing tradition of Party leadership, a requirement for opening a new phase of ideological education, and a safeguard for raising a new generation fit for the era. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the principle through four historical periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out what the principle demands today, and the third explains how it supports the cultivation of "new people of the era". It closes with a section on the role of teachers. For the historical part, Qin lists the courses offered at each stage, from Marxism and "political common sense" in revolutionary-era schools to the Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought courses of the 1950s. Qin concludes that each step in curriculum building coincided with a step in theoretical education. For the present, Qin calls for a curriculum and textbook system centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and led by the course introducing that thought. Qin also proposes AI-enabled smart classrooms and a "big ideological and political course" that joins the classroom, society and online spaces, with examples such as lessons held in fields, venues and workshops. Qin further argues that the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics since 2012 should serve as teaching content, so that students come to appreciate the system's advantages and strengthen their confidence in it. Qin calls for a teaching force that is politically strong and broad in vision, able to convey the substance of the Party's theory accurately. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on ideological and political education is presented, including its historical narrative and practical measures.

Grasping the relationship between religion and culture within the "Five-Sphere Integrated Plan" 在“五位一体”总体布局中把握宗教与文化的关系 Qiu Shi Qiu Shi, writing in the journal Science and Atheism, takes up how religion and culture should be related in Chinese theory and practice. The piece is an excerpted contribution to a seminar on traditional Chinese religion and traditional Chinese culture, held in Beijing on 21 April (2024) by the China Atheism Society and the CASS Centre for Science and Atheism. Qiu argues that, within the Five-Sphere Integrated Plan, religion is a political matter and not a cultural one, and that the "religion-as-culture" thesis has complicated the question. The article first clarifies the two terms, both of which Qiu calls elastic. It then examines Party congress reports and the Party's theory of religious work, and ends with a critique of Western religious studies. Qiu holds that "culture" in the Five-Sphere Integrated Plan means the spiritual-cultural sphere alongside the economy, politics, society and ecology, and that the discussion should be confined to this sense. Religion belongs to the political sphere as part of united front work. According to Qiu, the 19th and 20th Party Congress reports (2017, 2022) never mention religion in their cultural sections, and of the "nine musts" only the requirement of the sinicization of religion concerns culture. In that framework Chinese culture guides and permeates religion. Religion is culture, Qiu concedes, but a special kind that must be guided by fine traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. Qiu calls two Western claims fallacies: that primitive culture was religious culture, and that religion is the essence and soul of a culture. In Qiu's account, these inflate religion and set ancient superstition against modern scientific culture. Qiu calls for stronger critical analysis of Western religious studies to defend the scientific character of the Party's religious theory. Read the original if you want a short statement of the official Chinese argument for treating religion as a political rather than cultural question.

Integrating discourse into the classroom: methodological innovation in university ideological and political theory courses 话语融课：高校思政课的方法创新 Dai Yuqi Dai Yuqi, writing in Study Times in July 2024, asks how university ideological and political theory courses can become more attractive and effective. The commentary argues that innovating the discourse system should lead the renewal of teaching methods. It identifies persistent classroom problems: grandiose talk, stiff talk, stale talk and monologue by the teacher. The piece asks teachers to settle "for whom, what and how" they teach, while holding to fundamental principles and innovating. It is organised around four paired formulas for changing how things are said: big talk told small, hard talk told soft, old talk told anew, and talk shared by many. Dai's central move is to treat contrasting registers as complementary rather than opposed. Grand theory and Party achievements should be taught with political firmness, but introduced through small, everyday cases that reveal larger themes. Dai likewise pairs "indoctrination" with "inspiration", citing Xi Jinping: firm language states political positions and keeps teaching accurate, while gentler language builds an open atmosphere, and teachers should switch between them as the situation requires.
