Old content should be refreshed with new vocabulary, internet language, differentiated teaching for different student groups, and integration of ideological and political education across school stages. Finally, the author calls for a "big ideological and political course" in which schools, families and society cooperate, and in which policymakers, grassroots workers, beneficiaries and students themselves also speak in class. Dai concludes that discourse innovation makes these courses more targeted, approachable and effective. It is meant to unify students' knowledge, feeling, will and action, and to train new-era talents who take on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a short, practice-oriented example of how Party-affiliated academics frame teaching-method reform in ideological and political courses.

Is the socialist ideal being reborn in the West? Starting from the sharpening internal contradictions of the Western "elected system" 社会主义理想是否在西方重生？ Zheng Ruolin Zheng Ruolin asks whether the Western consensus that socialism died with the Soviet Union still holds. The author starts from Thomas Piketty's 2020 book Vivement le Socialisme!, in which the author of Capital in the Twenty-First Century says he now sees socialism as the best name for an alternative to capitalism. Zheng argues that Western capitalism's inequality is undermining the Western "elected system", and that this could lead either to a turn towards socialism or to a new era of conflict. The short commentary takes Piketty's two conditions for capitalism's survival, equality and the environment, and concentrates on inequality. It then analyses the split between national industrial capital and transnational financial capital, and uses the United States as its main case. It compares the present to the situation a century ago. Zheng cites Piketty's figures: the top 1% own 38.8% of global assets and the bottom 50% own 2%. In Zheng's account, the Western "democratic system" is really an "elected system" that depends on continuous growth and on economic superiority over other systems. Both conditions are eroding because of polarisation and China's rise. The author argues that globalisation once united the interests of the two forms of capital, but industrial capital now backs de-globalisation, with working-class support, while financial capital wants free movement. Zheng reads Trump's election and the Capitol riot as signs of this conflict and as a growth of the far right resembling the pre-war period. Zheng concludes that it is unclear whether the present will produce a Western move towards socialism, as Piketty hopes, or a conflict of "all against all", perhaps war or nuclear war. The author notes that the West has historically tried to resolve internal crises through external war, and that this needs serious study. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language view that links Piketty's turn to socialism with a class-fraction analysis of Western politics.

Telling the ideological and political course well, with the world-noted achievements as its content support 以举世瞩目成就为内容支撑讲好思政课 Yan Lianfu Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 13), Yan Lianfu takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction that schools' ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) should draw their content from the remarkable achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Yan's thesis is that teaching these achievements is a requirement of the new period and the way to make such courses reason in a deep, thorough and lively manner, and to help students strengthen belief, conviction and confidence. The article has three parts. The first sets out why achievements should anchor the courses. The second says which kinds of achievement teachers should draw on: theoretical, material and technological, spiritual and cultural, and institutional. The third proposes practical routes, each organised around one word: quan (all), xin (new), ji (technology) and gong (together). Yan argues that achievements supply facts, data and cases that verify the theory taught, so that courses can answer students' questions and respond to confusion in a complicated online ideological environment. Each type of achievement is tied to a form of confidence. Theoretical achievements, including the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, support confidence in theory. Material achievements support confidence in the path, spiritual and cultural ones support confidence in culture, and institutional ones support confidence in the system. On method, Yan calls for every course at every level to teach achievements, for new achievements to enter teaching promptly, for AI and digital tools to enrich resources and identify student needs, and for students as well as teachers to tell the story of achievements. Yan concludes that teachers should lead while students act as active subjects, so that students become communicators and practitioners of the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece shows how Party-line guidance on ideological and political education is turned into teaching practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese university ideological and political courses are told to use national achievements, digital technology and student participation in teaching.

Telling the story of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation well in university ideological and political courses: what should, must and can be done 高校思政课讲好中华民族现代文明的应然、必然与实然 Qi Weiping Bai Jinyan Qi Weiping and Bai Jinyan ask how university ideological and political courses (sizheng courses) should incorporate the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, a concept the authors link to Chinese modernization. Their thesis is that teaching it well is something the courses ought to do (yingran), must do (biran) and can do through concrete methods (shiran). The article is organised in three parts that follow this triad. The first argues that the concept enriches course content by connecting the Party's history, its present practice and its new mission. The second sets out why it is indispensable for moral education and the cultivation of talent (lide shuren). The third offers four practical approaches: political orientation, content, teaching formats and new media. A short conclusion draws on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). In the authors' account, the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is the sum of the material and spiritual civilization created under the Communist Party's leadership in the course of modernization. It continues Chinese civilization and expresses the Chinese path to modernization and a new form of human civilization. The authors argue that teaching it deepens study of the Party's innovative theory, including the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping's thought on culture. They also say it builds a shared ideological basis for national rejuvenation and supports the all-round development of the person, which they contrast with Western modernization under the logic of capital. They further claim it strengthens students' cultural confidence against trends such as money worship, hedonism and historical nihilism. On method, the authors call for adherence to the socialist orientation of education and for linking theory with practice through investigation and practical classes. They propose comparing Chinese modernization with world civilizational patterns, using Marxist social-formation theory to locate the present stage, and drawing on virtual and online teaching, social media and open online courses. They conclude that teachers should grasp all three dimensions in order to raise the effectiveness of the courses and build a youth base for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of Party education justify and operationalise new official concepts within the sizheng curriculum.

Leading high-quality development of ideological and political education in the new era through integrated construction 以一体化建设引领推动新时代思政教育高质量发展 Weng Tiehui Writing in the People's Daily on 22 July 2024, Weng Tiehui, a Vice Minister of Education, takes up the call from Xi Jinping to deepen the integration of ideological and political education across universities, secondary schools and primary schools. The piece appeared on the fifth anniversary of the 2019 symposium on school ideological and political theory teachers. Weng argues that integration bears on the basic educational questions of whom to train, how to train them and for whom, and that it should be pursued by following educational regularities and innovating in practice. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first gives reasons why integration is of the utmost importance for ensuring the Party has successors. The second sets out how to overcome difficulties by focusing on pertinence and effectiveness. The third lists key links and priority areas: curriculum, practical teaching, evaluation, teaching staff and overall support. It is framed as a study of the spirit of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and as a contribution to building a leading education country. Weng gives three grounds for integration: the political nature of education, which the Party has stressed through successive policy changes; the need to train talent for Chinese modernization; and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, which requires that courses, course-embedded ideological education and daily education not become isolated "islands". On method, Weng argues that stages should share one consistent direction while goals rise step by step. Patriotic education, for example, would start with emotional enlightenment in primary school and move to firm ideals and convictions at university. Weng also names unresolved problems, including weak links between knowledge and values, between theory and practice, and between teachers at different stages, and research on how students at each stage receive such education. Weng proposes unified curriculum and textbook planning, more interactive teaching, and practical teaching outside the classroom that builds the Four-sphere Confidence. Weng warns against turning specialist courses into political courses and against "low-level red" and "high-level black" distortions. Other proposals are multi-dimensional evaluation that prioritises teaching, stronger teacher training, family–school–society cooperation, and leadership mechanisms with ideological education written into school planning and Party-building assessments. Read the original if you want an authoritative Ministry of Education statement of how integrated ideological and political education is to be organised and assessed in 2024.

Deleuze's theory of affect and its critique of capitalism 德勒兹的情动理论及其资本主义批判 Hu Yaohui Since the mid-1990s the "affective turn" has spread across the humanities, and Hu Yaohui takes up its most important theoretical source, Gilles Deleuze's theory of affect. The article asks how Deleuze builds, through Spinoza, a philosophy set against Hegel, and what that philosophy can say about contemporary capitalism. Hu argues that affect theory offers a new view of capitalism's current forms of control, but remains distant from genuine Marxism. The article proceeds in three steps. It first places Deleuze's Spinoza in the French reaction of the 1960s against Hegelianism, a tradition shaped by Kojève's lectures and carried through Sartre and Merleau-Ponty, and contrasts him with Althusser's narrower critique of historicism. It then reads Deleuze's picture of the world through three concepts: power, affect and desire. Finally it turns to Anti-Oedipus and the "Postscript on the Societies of Control" to reconstruct his critique of capitalism. Hu's central reasoning is that Deleuze answers Descartes's problem of the ground of the world with Spinoza's doctrine of expression, then answers Hegel's charge of "acosmism" with a theory of becoming. Things differ only in degrees of power, that is, in their capacity to be affected. Affect is the change of state when bodies meet, joyful or sorrowful, and desire is presented as productive rather than a lack, as in Freud and Lacan. On this basis Hu reports Deleuze's account of capitalism as a tension between two affects: cynicism, which decodes and levels all flows of desire, and piety, produced by the Oedipal family, which recaptures them. In the later control society, Hu adds, fear becomes the governing affect, and individuals become "dividuals" modulated through data. Hu credits Deleuze with a creative reading of Marxism that points towards a materialist theory of desire and helps explain biopolitics and the consumer society. Yet Hu judges the critique too abstract: without touching ownership and wage-labour relations, no emancipation is possible, and radical change risks becoming aestheticism. Hu also questions how a society of differences, built on the "body without organs", could be organised or address intersubjectivity and social norms. Read the original if you want a compact, Marxist-oriented account of how Deleuze's Spinozism, affect and critique of capitalism fit together, together with a Chinese scholar's assessment of its limits.

Global change and China's governance The theoretical implications and international significance of Chinese modernization 世界之变与中国之治 Zhang Shuhua This is a speech by Zhang Shuhua, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum and printed in World Socialism Studies, 2024 no. 3. Zhang contrasts what the speech calls "China's governance" with disorder in the West, and argues that Chinese modernization is both distinctively Chinese and of wider value to the world. The speech places this against a background of crisis in the capitalist system and a revival of the world socialist movement. The speech has four parts. It asks what guarantees Chinese modernization's success, what it brings the world, what lessons it offers, and how to decode China's governance, build Chinese scholarship and spread the Chinese way. Zhang traces the goal of modernization from 1949 through the "four modernizations" of 1964 and the post-1978 shift of focus, to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang contrasts Western modernization, which the speech describes as built on colonial expansion and domestic oppression, with a Chinese path aimed at benefiting all people. Three political features are identified: Party leadership, a people-centred approach, and independence and agency. Success is attributed to handling reform, development and stability together. Zhang claims that China's experience has broken the "myth" of Western liberal democracy and free markets, and that it offers other developing countries a reference point through initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Zhang concludes that Chinese modernization is "China's and also the world's". The speech calls for an autonomous Chinese knowledge system that moves beyond Western-centric perspectives and distils core concepts from China's governance to share abroad. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior CASS political scientist presents Chinese modernization's international meaning at a 2024 socialism forum.

The historical starting point of combining Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture 马克思主义与中华优秀传统文化相结合的历史启程 Lu Kuan Lu Kuan takes up the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture, as a historical question. Lu notes that scholars have paid little attention to when and how this combination began. The article argues that it began with the early spread of Marxism in China from the late nineteenth century, and that this early history clarifies the meaning and mechanism of the Two Integrations. The article uses Edward Said's idea of "travelling theory" to ask what conditions of acceptance and resistance Marxism met in China. It is organised in four parts: the affinity between Marxism and Chinese tradition; their functional complementarity; the role of translators as a "bridge"; and lessons for research on the Second Integration. Its evidence comes from intellectuals such as Tan Sitong, Sun Yat-sen, Liang Qichao, Cai Yuanpei, Li Dazhao, Qu Qiubai and Mao Zedong, and from translated works including Looking Backward, Xingde Qiushui's The Essence of Socialism and Chen Wangdao's translation of the Communist Manifesto. Lu argues that Confucian ideals of great harmony (datong), Mohist thought, minben (people-as-root) ideas and the well-field system served as a "medium" through which Chinese readers understood socialism. This reduced resistance to Marxism and enriched its cultural life. Lu then argues that tradition could not answer the systemic crisis of modern China, so Marxism supplied a programme for social revolution and in turn revitalised Chinese culture. Translators are treated as the key agents. They used classical vocabulary, rewrote books as chapter-style novels, added "translator's comments" and localised examples, as Qu Qiubai did. Lu also notes a cost: reading Marxism through tradition sometimes obscured essential differences between them and produced simplification or misunderstanding. Lu draws three lessons for studying the Second Integration. Research should extend back to the early transmission history, including the translators. It should unite theory with history under a "grand historical view". It should keep pursuing innovation in discourse and ideas, using tools such as travelling theory and translingual practice. Lu concludes that Marxism became the "soul" and tradition the "root" of Chinese culture, supporting the building of a modern Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you study the early transmission of Marxism in China, translation history, or the intellectual genealogy of the Second Integration.

Key focal points for advancing ideological and political theory courses in the new era 推进新时代思想政治理论课建设的几个着力点 Pang Jinju Writing after Xi Jinping's fresh instructions on ideological and political theory courses (known as sizheng courses) on the fifth anniversary of the 2019 symposium for their teachers, and after a national promotion meeting on 11 May 2024, Pang Jinju asks how these courses should be built in the new era. The article's answer is that they must be tied to the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and cultivating successors to the socialist cause. Pang identifies five areas of emphasis. The article proceeds in five numbered sections. It covers the mission of the courses and the responsibility for training a new generation; the reform of the curriculum and textbook systems; the updating of teaching content; the combination of classroom teaching with social practice; and Party leadership and teacher training. Pang draws heavily on Xi's remarks from 2019 to 2024 and on official data about achievements since 2012. Pang argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should be the "soul" of moral education. The current curriculum rests on the 2005 "05 scheme", which Pang credits with a historic role but says must now be updated. Pang points to the new required course and textbook on the Thought as the direction of reform. Teaching content should bring in the Party's innovative theories and the achievements of the new era, citing poverty alleviation, GDP growth, reform and opening up, and improved livelihoods. Textbooks change slowly, so teachers must convert them into teaching. The "big ideological and political course" should join the classroom to social practice, covering past, present and future practice. Pang warns that practice must not replace classroom teaching, nor should teaching be confined to the classroom. Pang concludes that Party committees at all levels must take political responsibility for these courses, building a coordinated working pattern. Teachers are the foundation and the key. Pang calls for them to meet Xi's requirements of strong politics, deep feeling, fresh thinking, broad vision, strict self-discipline and upright character. Pang also calls for a sound teacher evaluation system and better status and conditions for teachers. Read the original if you want a Party-line account of how senior figures in the field frame current priorities for political education in Chinese universities.

On Mao Zedong and the historical consciousness of the Chinese Communist Party An analysis based on "The Bankruptcy of the Idealist Conception of History" 论毛泽东与中国共产党的历史自觉 Li Zhen Zhou Chunlin Li and Zhou ask what "historical consciousness" (lishi zijue) means in Mao Zedong Thought and why Mao's 1949 essay "The Bankruptcy of the Idealist Conception of History" is worth rereading today. They argue that historical consciousness is the essential attribute of Mao Zedong Thought and a key test of whether historical objectivity and the people's agency are truly united. In their account, the Party matured theoretically by leaving behind idealist views of history detached from Chinese reality, which produced the first leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's historical consciousness: his early reading of history as a source of general laws, his critique of Western capitalist claims to historical self-awareness, and his view of the relationship between China and the world. The second analyses the 1949 essay, the last in a series of five pieces on Sino-American relations written in August–September 1949 in response to the US State Department's white paper and Dean Acheson's letter to Truman. The third links this legacy to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and Chinese modernization. The authors argue that Mao read the failure of Western-style reform in modern China, and the aggression that accompanied Western 'teachers', as evidence that bourgeois claims to embody universal reason were false. They say Mao answered Acheson's explanations of the Chinese revolution, which cited overpopulation and imported Western ideas, by pointing to imperialist, feudal and bureaucrat-capitalist oppression. Marxism took hold, in their reading, because Chinese conditions required it and the people grasped it. They add that Mao used historical materialism to treat relations with the United States as a question of imperialism and struggle, and that he traced illusions about America to individualism and liberalism. Li and Zhou conclude that Mao and the Party showed a high degree of historical consciousness, and that Xi Jinping Thought has inherited and deepened it as historical, epochal and civilizational consciousness. They hold that the people are the real agents of history and its ultimate judges. They also contend that Chinese modernization, grounded in historical materialism and Chinese traditional culture, can help create a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated study connects Mao's 1949 anti-imperialist writing to present-day theory on history, China–US relations and civilization.

The historical-materialist basis of the new form of human civilization 人类文明新形态的唯物史观根据 Ding Kuangyi This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2024, asks what grounds in historical materialism support the claim that Chinese modernization amounts to a new form of human civilization. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization is a wholly new form of human civilization, different from the Western model, Ding argues that the concept rests on three historical-materialist foundations. The article is organised in three short sections: innovation in the mode of production, the dialectical relationship between material and spiritual civilization, and the "true community". Each section first sets out the relevant principle from Marx, Engels or Lenin, then contrasts Western modernization with Chinese modernization as the author presents them. In the first section Ding argues that civilizational forms ultimately derive from the mode of production, the unity of productive forces and relations of production, so that transforming productive forces is key to renewing civilization. Chinese modernization is said to advance this through technological innovation and new quality productive forces, and through adjusting relations of production: public ownership as the base, distribution combining work and factors of production, narrower income gaps and common prosperity. In the second section Ding holds that Western modernization pursues abstract material wealth, reduces rationality to instrumental reason and makes utilitarianism and individualism the basis of its spiritual life. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is said to coordinate material and spiritual civilization, treating wealth as a means rather than an end. In the third section Ding describes the capitalist "community" as mediated by money, capital and the market, producing atomised individuals and a lonely mass society, whereas Marx's "true community", the association of free individuals, overcomes this. Ding concludes that Chinese modernization advances community-building domestically, through a social governance community built, governed and shared by all, and internationally, through a community with a shared future for mankind. In this account, the new form of human civilization points towards equality, harmony and mutual aid. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese commentary derives the concept of a new form of human civilization from classical Marxist texts and contrasts it with Western modernization."

Holding fast to the soul and the root of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 坚守好马克思主义中国化时代化的魂和根 Wu Haijiang Jiang Hao Wu Haijiang and Jiang Hao, in a commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2024, take up Xi Jinping's statement that the project of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times rules out abandoning either Marxism, the "soul", or excellent traditional Chinese culture, the "root". The authors argue that holding fast to both is the foundation and precondition of theoretical innovation. Their thesis is that the two must be fused, not merely kept side by side. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why Marxism must remain the soul. The second lists the features of the root in traditional culture. The third explains what follows in practice from joining the two. It leans throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). In the authors' account, Marxism is a scientific truth with lasting vitality: historical materialism and the theory of surplus value reveal the laws of social development and of capitalism. It is also the Party's fundamental guiding thought, linked to the Two Integrations. The authors credit Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with a new leap in adapting Marxism. The root, they say, has five features: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peace. They claim these features explain why China keeps to its own path and peaceful development, and why it imposes neither values nor political systems on others. Wu and Jiang warn that forgetting one's ancestors severs both soul and root and leads to a "subversive" error. The authors conclude that Marxism's core ideas and the best of traditional culture must be linked, and name three outcomes. The first is continued Party theoretical innovation, with the nation's core ideas and wisdom injected more deeply into Marxism. The second is building China's own independent knowledge system, in which Marxism activates living elements of tradition. The third is building a modern Chinese civilization, a new cultural form for Chinese modernization, which they say carries world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-theory commentary frames the relationship between Marxism and traditional culture.

New changes in the ideological sphere under new technological conditions 新技术条件下意识形态领域新变 Huang Xianghuai This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2024, asks how new technology is changing ideological work in China. Huang Xianghuai argues that, despite what the author describes as a fundamental turn for the better since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the 20th Party Congress report (2022) acknowledges many remaining challenges. The author calls for study of their new forms so that ideological work becomes more targeted, proactive and effective. The article takes three features of the present in turn: the all-media communication landscape, the era of cognitive warfare, and the post-truth era. For each, Huang describes how the terrain of ideological contestation has shifted and what this requires of media organisations, institutions and Party members. In Huang's account, self-media and capital have squeezed traditional mainstream media, so that mainstream opinion no longer holds its lead automatically: it is earned by expanding influence, not by occupying a position. Media should therefore be judged by whether they achieve their function, not merely by whether they discharge their duties. Huang describes non-mainstream ideologies as shifting from doctrinal disputes to disputes over specific issues, using insinuation and individual cases to unsettle public perception. The author calls this cognitive warfare, an escalation of earlier information and propaganda battles. In the post-truth era, Huang argues, narrative outweighs fact, and non-ideological problems readily acquire ideological content, so blocking and deleting lose effect. Huang concludes that mainstream media should adopt a more open and inclusive attitude, matching tactics to how problems appear, and that Party members and cadres need stronger ideological ability and literacy, alongside technical and legal measures. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line view of how Chinese Party scholars frame ideological risk in the internet age.

The historical-materialist implications of building a modern Chinese civilization 建设中华民族现代文明的历史唯物主义意蕴 Dong Jianming This short commentary asks what historical materialism contributes to understanding the new cultural mission that General Secretary Xi Jinping has set out: building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. Dong Jianming argues that the mission rests firmly on Marx's historical materialism and is both required by the times and an inevitable result of historical progress. Grasping this, the author says, helps readers understand the core of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and take up the mission. The article is organised in three sections. The first treats the historical necessity of the mission through the base–superstructure relationship. The second discusses culture's role in social development. The third turns to the intellectual and cultural traditions that the Chinese nation has accumulated over its history. Dong draws on Marx, Engels and Mao Zedong's essay "On Contradiction", together with Xi Jinping's statements and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Dong's first move is that the economic base determines the superstructure only "in the last instance". In this reading, China's modern humiliation and its crisis of cultural subjectivity came from underdeveloped productive forces. The Party's leadership from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" and "becoming strong", and the advance of Chinese modernization, now supply the material foundation for cultural confidence and independence. Second, citing Engels's letters, Dong rejects economic determinism: culture reacts on the economy and other superstructural elements. The author adds that cultural subjectivity does not grow spontaneously out of economic growth and must be built consciously. Dong characterises Western capitalist culture as dominated by capital, serving exploitation and eventually fettering the productive forces. Third, Dong invokes the relative independence of forms of social consciousness. Chinese civilization's "five outstanding features" (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and the "Second Integration" of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture are presented as developing this point. Dong concludes that the Two Integrations, especially the Second, must guide the mission. Marxism is said to activate the genes of Chinese civilization, while traditional culture enriches Marxism's cultural life, producing a new cultural organism. The article presents this as both applying and further developing historical materialism, and as a way to create a new culture for the present era. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-line account of how Xi Jinping's cultural thought is linked to classical Marxist texts on base, superstructure and relative autonomy.

Plekhanov's critique of the "religious quest" and his exposition of Marxist atheism A reading of "On the So-Called Religious Quest in Russia" 普列汉诺夫对“宗教探寻”的批判和马克思主义无神论的阐释 Zhang Jiansong Zhang Jiansong studies Georgi Plekhanov's long essay "On the So-Called Religious Quest in Russia", written after the defeat of the 1905 revolution under Stolypin's reaction. The article asks how Plekhanov used Marxist theory to answer the mystical currents of the time: "God-seeking" among bourgeois thinkers and "God-building" inside the Social-Democratic movement. Zhang argues that Plekhanov's rebuttal was theoretically sound and timely, and that it still offers lessons for religious work and ideological struggle in China today. The article follows the three finished parts of the essay, as collected in the third volume of Plekhanov's selected philosophical works. It first treats "On Religion", the theoretical introduction. It then covers "Religion Again", which criticises Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky. Finally it covers the section on the Decadents, chiefly Merezhkovsky and Minsky. Zhang notes that a planned fourth article on the Vekhi group was never written. A short closing section draws contemporary lessons. In Zhang's account, Plekhanov first defines religion as a fairly coherent system of ideas, feelings and activities, and traces animism, myth, totemism and the gods to the level of the productive forces and the hunting way of life. Zhang reads this as an application of the principle that social being determines social consciousness, and stresses that Plekhanov also allowed for interaction between consciousness and being. Armed with this, Plekhanov argues that every religion, including the "atheist religion" of Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky, necessarily involves spirits and the supernatural. He treats these quests as a response to the despair of the intelligentsia after defeat. Zhang adds that Plekhanov attacks the Decadents for individualism, fear of death and contempt for the workers' economic struggle, and for substituting a consolation that Feuerbach had already dismissed as illusion. Zhang concludes that Plekhanov's critique steadied revolutionary morale and holds two lessons. One is to stay firmly Marxist, which Zhang contrasts with the Soviet collapse under Gorbachev and links to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The other is to dare to struggle against erroneous trends, such as historical nihilism and certain abnormal religious phenomena in parts of China. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese reading of Plekhanov's religious theory, or want to see how the history of Marxism is used to frame current ideological work.

Chinese modernization and an independent knowledge system of economics: fundamental guidance and theoretical reconstruction 中国式现代化与经济学自主知识体系：根本遵循与理论再造 Zhou Wen Bai Ji Zhou Wen and Bai Ji ask how Chinese modernization relates to the effort to build an independent knowledge system of economics. They argue that China's experience breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization, dismantles the Western discourse system in economics, and supplies both the guiding basis and the content for a Chinese economics that is not a variant of Western theory. The article has three parts. The first contrasts Chinese modernization with the Western model, drawing on figures such as Myrdal, Perkins and Fukuyama, on the record of the Washington Consensus and Russian shock therapy, and on the article's own statistics on China's growth and poverty reduction. The second explains why an independent economics is both enabled by and required by Chinese modernization. The third takes four "identifying concepts" and presents each as a shift away from a Western counterpart. The authors contend that mainstream economics abstracts from Western experience and cannot explain developing countries. They hold that Western hegemony and Western economic discourse grew together, and that China's success came from rejecting neoliberal prescriptions. In their account, the four shifts are: from capitalist to socialist market economy, with public ownership as the mainstay and distribution according to work; from demand management to supply-side structural reform, which the authors distinguish from Western supply-side economics; from market equilibrium and the "rational economic man" to common prosperity; and from methodological individualism to a systems perspective. Each is presented as a theoretical innovation grounded in practice. The authors criticise Chinese economics for over-relying on Western theory and mathematical modelling. They call for a new paradigm, neither a rewriting of Capital, nor a patching of Soviet-style political economy, nor a copy of Western economics. It should be guided by basic Marxist principles and combined with fine traditional Chinese culture, and should move from practice to experience to theory. They conclude that building this knowledge system is a call of the times and a historical choice, and that it can offer other developing countries Chinese wisdom and Chinese solutions. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars present the case for an autonomous Chinese economics, including the four paired concepts and the authors' critique of Western theory.

Mao Zedong's exploration of Chinese modernization: its civilizational terrain 毛泽东探索中国式现代化的文明境域 Huang Xianzhong Yuan Hongjuan Huang Xianzhong and Yuan Hongjuan ask how Mao Zedong's lifelong pursuit of modernization relates to the construction of a modern Chinese civilization. They argue that Mao took socialist civilization as both ideal and driving force, and then used Chinese modernization to build that civilization, so that Chinese modernization entered the terrain of modern civilization from the outset. The authors organise this terrain into three zones: a "highland", a "hinterland" and a "strategic ground". The article draws on Mao's life and writings from his youth to the 1960s. The first section covers his turn to Marxism, his socialist ideal and the revolution, and the founding of the People's Republic. The second examines how he built a socialist form of civilization in politics, economy and culture. The third turns to the roots of that civilization in the Marxism–China relationship, and in traditional culture. The authors link their account to Xi Jinping's 2023 remark on the mutual relation between Chinese civilization and Chinese modernization. The authors distinguish a "teleological" logic, in which the socialist ideal comes first, from a "generative" logic, in which modernization produces civilization. They hold that Mao's exploration began with the former. For the hinterland, they read Mao's "trinity" of politics, economy and culture as a Chinese-style development of historical materialism. It covers remaking social relations toward people's mastery of the country, industrialization and the Four Modernizations, and cultivating "new people" who are both "red and expert". For the strategic ground, they treat the "Second Integration" of 1956 as the key move. They also point to the link between Marxism and traditional culture, which prefigures the later Two Integrations. They identify three features of this civilization. Unity combined with particularity, democracy combined with centralism, and the joint development of individual and collective are said to draw on ancient and modern, Chinese and Western experience while avoiding the flaws of Soviet and capitalist models. The authors conclude that Mao was the founder of both Chinese modernization and Chinese socialist civilization. They propose that drawing on his practical wisdom from a civilizational perspective is necessary for building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on the new journey. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars tie Mao's thought to the current Chinese modernization discourse and its civilizational framing.

Class-based environmental analysis A new reading of The Condition of the Working Class in England 基于阶级的环境分析 Liu Li Liu Li asks how Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) should be read now that class analysis and environmental analysis of the book usually run on separate tracks. The article argues that the work's distinctive contribution was to join the two for the first time, treating capitalist exploitation through an environmental lens. On this reading, Engels remained committed to Marxist class analysis, in contrast to the stratification, race, community and identity frameworks that Liu says dominate environmentalism since the 1960s. The article draws on Engels's observations of Manchester, London, Liverpool and other industrial towns in 1842–1844. It is organised in four parts: how capital reshapes the environment in its natural, social and individual dimensions; class-based environmental differentiation and opposition; the environmental discipline and control of the working class; and a concluding section with four points. Liu sets Engels against Weber, Bourdieu, Giddens, Foucault and Braverman, and cites Ted Benton on Engels as an early ecological political thinker. Liu's central claim is that the environment is neither external nor neutral under capitalism but distributes class positions. Four mechanisms are identified: environmental stratification, such as the concentric layout in which factory zones, middle-class streets and bourgeois suburbs are ranked by exposure to pollution; environmental identification by housing, occupation, age and sex; closure and segregation, including the hiding of slums behind respectable streets; and a classification of disease, with occupational illness and shortened lifespans. The author then argues that capital controls workers through sanitary policing, workhouses and the factory system, which operates through space, time and the body. Liu concludes that labour exploitation and environmental exploitation are linked, and that housing and factories were the first and main sites of class segregation and control. In the author's reading, Engels traced the "social murder" of workers to the capitalist system itself and not to incidental abuses. The article also holds that environmental debates, including urban ecology and spatial justice, should not lose this class standpoint. Read the original if you study Engels's early work, Marxist ecology or class-based environmental justice and want a detailed reading of the book's environmental themes alongside Foucault and Weberian stratification theory.

The scientific modes of thinking in Xi Jinping's thought on culture 习近平文化思想的科学思维方法 Ma Jianqing You Zhichun Ma Jianqing and You Zhichun ask what scientific methods of thinking underlie Xi Jinping's thought on culture, and how they guide propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Their answer is that this body of thought rests on five connected modes of thinking: strategic, historical, bottom-line, dialectical and innovative. Together, the authors argue, these give the work its direction, historical initiative, security safeguards, handling of key relationships and creative vitality. The article is organised in five sections, one for each mode, and each section has three or four sub-points. It draws on Xi's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including his October 2023 call for "seven focuses" in this work. Topics range from the Party's leadership and traditional culture to ideological risk, the media, international communication and institutional rules. On strategic thinking, the authors say Xi defines the work as bearing on the Party's fate, national stability and national cohesion, and sets its mission as promoting cultural prosperity, building a strong cultural nation and building a modern Chinese civilisation. On historical and bottom-line thinking, they stress upholding Party leadership, drawing on fine traditional culture and resisting historical nihilism. They hold that there can be no compromise on ideology, citing the Soviet collapse as a warning. They also describe Xi's "red, grey and black zones" as a way to hold the ideological front and win over those in between. Dialectical thinking, in their account, treats Party leadership and the people's primacy as identical, and sees economic and cultural construction as mutually supporting. It balances positive publicity against struggle with negative phenomena and links domestic and international work. On innovative thinking, the authors point to the Second Integration as a new emancipation of thought, to the "three adaptations" method of working, and to a four-part institutional system of laws, Party regulations, administrative rules and normative documents. They conclude that these modes of thinking make Xi's thought on culture a coherent, scientific guide for work in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars present the methodology behind current propaganda and cultural policy.

The view of mutual learning among civilizations embedded in Chinese modernization 中国式现代化蕴含的“文明互鉴观” Liu Xianchun Zhang Yanxia Liu Xianchun and Zhang Yanxia ask what view of civilizations is built into Chinese modernization and why it matters amid global upheaval. They argue that Chinese modernization carries a distinctive 'view of mutual learning among civilizations'. In their account it replaces civilizational barriers with exchange, civilizational conflict with mutual learning, and civilizational superiority with coexistence, and so differs from the Western model of modernization. The article is organised around four theses, each paired with a Western idea it is said to refute. Sections one to four take in turn the diversity, equality, inclusiveness and openness of civilizations. Each section first sets out the principle, then shows how Chinese modernization is said to embody it. The authors draw on Xi Jinping's statements, Marx's remarks on Russia and on world history, Chinese historical episodes such as the Silk Road and Zheng He's voyages, and critiques of Toynbee, Huntington and Fukuyama. The authors argue that Western thought equates modernization with Westernization, ranks civilizations hierarchically, predicts a clash of civilizations and promotes closure, whether through trade protection or 'decoupling'. They hold that Western modernization rested on colonial plunder and still leads some Western powers to contain developing countries, citing wars, 'colour revolutions' and conditional aid. By contrast, they say, Chinese modernization moved from passive imitation to independent exploration under Marxist guidance, adopted the principle that civilizations are equal, rejected Cold War thinking and 'zero-sum' games, and drew on the Chinese ideal of 'harmony without uniformity'. They also point to the Global Civilization Initiative, the Belt and Road Initiative and the claim that China is open to learning from others while sharing its own experience. The authors conclude that the economic, cultural and ecological crises of the West show the limits of Western civilization as a 'yardstick' or 'model'. They present Chinese modernization as an alternative that is peaceful, pluralist and open, and as a reference point for other countries seeking paths suited to their own conditions. In their view it also points the way for the future of human civilization. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of how Chinese academic writing, in 2024, frames civilizational pluralism and criticises Western-centrism and the 'clash of civilizations'.

The cultural form of Chinese modernization An examination based on historical materialism 中国式现代化的文化形态 Zhou Dan Zhou Dan takes up the idea, tied to Xi Jinping's remarks on the Second Integration, that the new culture formed through the integration of Marxism with traditional Chinese culture is the "cultural form of Chinese modernization". Starting from the historical-materialist view that culture reflects the economy and politics, the article asks why this cultural form is proposed, what it contains, how it should be built and what significance it has. Zhou offers a preliminary answer to each question. The article has four parts. The first sets out the background: the need for economy and culture to develop in step, the building of a new form of human civilization and a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, and the push for cultural confidence and strength. The second defines the concept, distinguishing culture from cultural form and setting out its goal, its essential requirements and its philosophical ideas. The third discusses principles of construction. The fourth assesses significance. Zhou's core move is to treat cultural form as the conceptualised, self-aware stage of culture, in the relation of part to whole and form to content. The economic form of Chinese modernization ultimately determines the scope and pace of the cultural form, but culture in turn gives spiritual momentum to the whole. Its essential requirements are the "seven focuses" in Xi's guidance on propaganda, ideological and cultural work. These include Party leadership, a socialist ideology, core socialist values, the "four forces" of media, the creative transformation of traditional culture, and international communication. Its philosophical content is a distinctive set of "six outlooks" on the world, values, history, civilization, democracy and ecology. For construction, Zhou points to the Two Integrations, spiritual independence (said not to be cultural nationalism) and mutual learning among civilizations, drawing on Marx and Engels on world history. Zhou concludes that the cultural form shows the cultural subjectivity of Chinese modernization, leads the creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional culture, and helps build the civilizational system of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. In this account it serves as a spiritual force for taking Chinese modernization "wider, longer and more firmly" and offers Chinese wisdom to human progress. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher uses historical materialism to systematise the cultural dimension of Chinese modernization within current Party theory.

Grasping the civilisational vision of the Global Civilization Initiative 深刻把握全球文明倡议的文明境界 Qin Long Li Weiguang Qin Long and Li Weiguang examine the Global Civilization Initiative, which Xi Jinping set out on 15 March 2023 at the CPC in Dialogue with World Political Parties High-Level Meeting. The initiative has four parts: respecting the diversity of civilisations, advocating common values of humanity, valuing the inheritance and innovation of civilisations, and strengthening international people-to-people exchanges. The authors argue that it is China's answer to how different civilisations should coexist and where human civilisation is heading, and that it follows the earlier Global Development and Global Security Initiatives. The article is organised in three sections. The first treats the initiative as a product of the inheritance and renewal of Chinese civilisation. The second presents it as an expression of Chinese modernization's creation of a new form of human civilisation. The third presents it as support for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors draw on Xi's speeches, on Marx and Engels's idea of world history, and on classical Chinese ideals. In the first section the authors link the initiative to the outstanding features of Chinese civilisation (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness) and to the Two Integrations. They describe it as a modern Chinese contribution to humanity, continuing a historical role such as the Four Great Inventions. In the second section they contrast Western modernization, which they say is marked by capital domination, polarisation and ecological crisis, with Chinese modernization. They argue that the initiative breaks the equation of modern civilisation with capitalist or Western civilisation and rejects theories of civilisational clash and superiority. It also holds that each country should find its own path of civilisational development rather than copy a Western template. In the third section they say it enriches the civilisational content of the community with a shared future for mankind. Its common values of humanity are presented as going beyond so-called universal values, and China's hosting of dialogues and forums is cited as practical implementation. The authors conclude that the initiative reflects the Communist Party of China's dual mission of national rejuvenation and human progress. They say it shows China as a responsible major country and sets an example for other parties. They also say it shows a historical initiative by the Chinese nation to advance human civilisation through its own revival. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party scholarship presents the Global Civilization Initiative in terms of Chinese tradition, Chinese modernization and a critique of Western civilisational claims.

The deep logic and forms of cultural imperialism in Western left-wing discourse 西方左翼话语中文化帝国主义的深层逻辑与样态 Du Min Du Min asks what lies beneath cultural imperialism as Western left-wing and postcolonial writers describe it, and how it works in the contemporary world. The article argues that its core is a "spiritual interest–control" logic, which goes beyond the profit logic of trade in cultural goods. Du holds that this logic appears in two forms, "knowledge imperialism" and "spiritual imperialism". The article draws on thinkers including James Petras, Harold Innis, Syed Hussein Alatas, Syed Farid Alatas, Edward Said, Samir Amin, David Harvey and the Sri Lankan scholar Susantha Goonatilake. It first sets out the "commodity profit–capital" and "spiritual interest–control" dimensions. It then treats knowledge imperialism through intellectual property, research funding and academic dependence. Spiritual imperialism is traced from religious imperialism to non-governmental organizations, with cases from Africa, Central Asia and Sri Lanka. On knowledge imperialism, Du argues that developed countries hold superiority in knowledge production and use patent regimes, such as TRIPS, to monopolise technology and extract excess profit. Du sets this "knowledge–hegemony–rent" logic against Lenin's "finance–monopoly–excess profit" logic. Dependent countries are said to suffer intellectual subordination, a "captive mind" and brain drain. On spiritual imperialism, Du contends that since the 1990s religious bodies and other NGOs have served as covert channels of Western values. The 2004 tsunami relief in Sri Lanka is offered as a typical case. Du also cites American legislation on international religious freedom and funding for training journalists as ways of legitimising this influence at home. Du concludes that the two forms are complementary routes by which imperialism pursues its strategic interests under neo-colonial conditions. The article also holds that China's catching-up in knowledge and innovation has alarmed the United States. It notes that states such as Pakistan, Russia and Hungary have responded by expelling or banning foreign NGOs and strengthening ideological safeguards. Du presents these as forms of resistance to spiritual infiltration. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on Western left and postcolonial sources to build a typology of cultural imperialism.

Marx's thought on the "machine system" and its methodological implications 马克思的“机器体系”思想及其方法论意蕴 Chen Zhong Prompted by the rise of ChatGPT and debates over machines, technology and the fate of civilisation, Chen Zhong asks how artificial intelligence should be understood and what Marx would make of it. The article argues that Marx was not the first thinker to discuss the "machine system", but offered the most historically grounded and penetrating analysis of it. Its value, Chen contends, lies less in knowledge content than in method. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's account of the machine system from The Poverty of Philosophy, the Communist Manifesto, the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts and Capital, drawing on commentary by Mumford, An Qinian, Zhang Yibing and Gao Qiqi. The second extracts the methodological features of that account. The third applies them to artificial intelligence and digitalisation. Chen reads Marx's machine system in four dimensions: automated machinery, a society interconnected through machine industry, the replacement of workers' skills by machines (making workers appendages of capital-owned fixed capital), and the growing role of science. Methodologically, Marx starts from real historical processes and living relations rather than abstract concepts, as in his critique of Proudhon. He also judges machinery by its historical trend, as both progress in productive forces and a source of harm to labourers under capital. Applying this, Chen treats AI as an advanced "working machine" that externalises higher mental skills. In Chen's reading, its general progressive effect must be separated from the distribution of interests under particular institutions, and the idea of AI wholly replacing humans is science fiction rather than science. Chen draws three points for the intelligent age: the machine system is the systematisation of civilisation, and humanity increasingly forms a community with a shared future; conscious public adjustment of institutions is needed to civilise it; and people should become the conscious core of the system, with institutions that let all parties share its gains equally. Chen speculates that Marx would use ChatGPT for routine textual work but would still study the intelligent machine system from "real life relations". Read the original if you want a Marxist-methodological framework for AI that draws closely on Marx's texts on machinery.

A review of overseas scholarship on China's comprehensively deepening reform 海外学者关于中国全面深化改革的研究述评 Zhang Ke Liu Xinyue This is a literature review of representative English-language scholarship on the policy of comprehensively deepening reform, which has been pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang and Liu use outside views to understand the reform's achievements, historical significance and prospects. They also assess the theoretical contributions and limits of this literature, and they propose ways to improve the international narrative of China's reform. The review has three parts. The first covers overseas scholars' general assessments: the overall reform goal, the decision-making system and reform methods, and comparative perspectives. The second surveys studies by field: economic, political, cultural, social, ecological-civilisation and Party-building reform. The third describes the literature's main features, and a conclusion follows. Among the scholars named are Barry Naughton, Dwight Perkins, Shang-Jin Wei, Fabrizio Zilibotti, Rana Mitter, Elizabeth Perry, Kerry Brown, David Shambaugh and Andrew Wedeman. According to the review, many overseas authors judge the reform positively. They treat the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity as an innovation, credit the central leading body with coordinating reform, and see top-level design combined with local experimentation. Some also argue that Chinese reform borrows selectively from the West without copying it. On the economy, they stress the market's decisive role, the need to raise total factor productivity, and a shift to innovation-driven growth. In environmental and Party-building studies, they examine vertical management, cadre training and the anti-corruption campaign. The authors identify four features of the literature: macro and micro topics together; area studies dominant but disciplinary theory growing; a wide range of scholars with more Chinese–foreign co-authorship; and support, sincere advice and ideological bias existing side by side. Zhang and Liu conclude that this scholarship offers useful perspectives and some suggestions of reference value. They also say that some works misread the reform, show ideological bias, tie reform successes to the "China threat" thesis, or apply existing theories too mechanically. They propose four steps: understand the relation between institutional confidence and reform, use differentiated international communication, support Chinese scholars publishing abroad, and strengthen academic ties with overseas institutions and "China-friendly" experts. Read the original if you want a field-by-field guide to English-language studies of China's post-2012 reform, together with the Party School authors' view of how to respond to them.

Providing strong impetus and institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization Commentary by the Qiushi commentator on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee 《求是》杂志评论员：为中国式现代化提供强大动力和制度保障 This short commentary in Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party's theoretical journal, was published as the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (15–18 July 2024) was meeting. It argues that the plenum's decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization expresses the Central Committee's determination to improve socialist institutions and modernize national governance. Reform, the commentary holds, is the main source of momentum for Chinese modernization. The piece first places the plenum in the present period, which it calls critical for building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, amid a complex international situation, a new round of technological and industrial change, and public expectations. It then traces Xi Jinping's statements on reform from the 20th Party Congress (2022) to the Politburo meeting of June 2024. Finally it lists achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in eight areas: the economy, democracy and law, culture, livelihoods, ecology, Party building, the military and foreign affairs. The core claim is that reform since 2012 has been pursued with unprecedented resolve and has made the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics more mature and fixed. The commentary asserts that no other country or party has shown comparable political courage or carried out reform on such a scale and so quickly. It presents these results as proof of the importance of the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and of the leadership role of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. The commentary concludes that reform and opening up has no end point and calls on readers to study Xi's statements on reform, build consensus and keep pushing reform forward. Under the Party's leadership, it says, reform will supply strong impetus and institutional guarantees for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party press framed the Third Plenum at the time of its opening.

The theoretical contribution, connotation and development path of new quality productive forces 新质生产力的理论贡献、内涵特征和发展路径 Research Group on New Quality Productive Forces, Economic Committee of the CPPCC National Committee This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 17 July 2024 and written by a research group of the CPPCC National Committee's Economic Committee, explains what new quality productive forces are and how to develop them. It presents the concept as one that Xi Jinping put forward by combining the basic principles of Marxist political economy with economic practice in the new era. The group argues that the concept has three theoretical contributions, a definite set of defining features, and a clear path of development. The article follows Xi's remarks during inspection tours from July 2023 and his systematic exposition at the 11th collective study session of the 20th Politburo (January 2024). It has three sections. The first covers the concept's theoretical contribution, the second its connotation and features, and the third six lines of work for promoting it. On theory, the group places the concept in a lineage running from Mao Zedong's emphasis on liberating and protecting productive forces through Deng Xiaoping's "science and technology are the primary productive force", Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao's Scientific Outlook on Development. It describes the concept as an innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and as a development of Marx's three-element account of productive forces (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour) that adds digital technologies and data. It also treats the concept as a deepening of Xi Jinping's economic thought. On features, the group lists revolutionary technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors, deep transformation of development methods (intelligent, green and integrated), and a marked rise in total factor productivity as the core indicator. On the path forward, the group proposes high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, supported by basic research and a new whole-nation system; a modern industrial system; green and low-carbon transition; new relations of production suited to the new forces, including factor-market reform, data valuation and wider opening up; promotion of entrepreneurship; and new mechanisms for training and attracting talent. It argues that these measures would raise productivity, build material wealth and improve people's wellbeing. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how the concept is framed theoretically and what policy steps are linked to it as of mid-2024.

Adhering to reform and innovation to advance new quality productive forces 坚持改革创新推动新质生产力发展 Ding Jinqing Ding Jinqing, writing in the Economic Daily in July 2024, takes up the question of how new quality productive forces can be developed through reform. Citing Xi Jinping's statement that developing them requires further comprehensively deepening reform and forming new types of relations of production, Ding argues that the task is both a development question and a reform question. The article is a newspaper commentary rather than a research paper. It is organised in three parts. The first deals with deepening reform to release innovative vitality, mainly in science and technology institutions. The second concerns accelerating a modernised industrial system through intelligent, green and integrated industry. The third is about shaping new relations of production through reform of the economic system and of education, science and technology, and talent systems. Ding's central claim is that innovation, both technological and institutional, is the defining feature of new quality productive forces, so institutional barriers must be removed. On science and technology, Ding calls for perfecting the new whole-nation system, strengthening the Party Central Committee's centralised leadership of scientific work, using the socialist system's ability to concentrate resources on major tasks, and expanding international scientific cooperation, including through the Belt and Road Initiative. On industry, Ding urges supply-side structural reform to make industry more intelligent (artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure, new growth engines such as commercial space and the low-altitude economy), greener (carbon trading, green certificates, ecological compensation) and more integrated across sectors and regions. On relations of production, Ding invokes the Marxist principle that productive forces determine relations of production, and argues for a high-standard socialist market economy, a unified national market, support for private firms under the Two Unwaverings, and joined-up reform of education, science and talent so that innovative personnel can be trained and rewarded. Ding concludes that deepening reform and opening up at a higher starting point will clear the obstacles that hold back new quality productive forces and provide continuing momentum for high-quality development. The piece is a policy-oriented exposition that restates official lines on reform, industry and talent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary in 2024 linked new quality productive forces to institutional reform, industrial upgrading and talent policy.

Unwaveringly promoting the high-quality development of ideological and political theory courses in the new era 坚定不移推进新时代思想政治理论课高质量发展 Jin Nuo Jin Nuo takes up how ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) in Chinese schools and universities should develop in the new era. Writing after Xi Jinping's latest instructions on these courses, Jin argues that they are the key course for implementing the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education and the first front for teaching the Party's innovative theory. The article contends that high-quality development requires applying the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article is organised around four methodological principles drawn from that worldview: self-confidence and self-reliance, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and staying true to fundamental principles while breaking new ground. Each section links the principle to concrete measures, including policy documents, textbooks, teacher training, practice bases, digital platforms and Ministry of Education programmes. It draws on Xi's speeches, including his 2019 symposium with teachers of these courses, and on citations from Marx. In the first section, Jin argues that there are grounds for confidence in running the courses well. These are the Party Central Committee's attention to the work, the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, China's traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture, and accumulated experience. The second section holds that the courses must answer students' real questions by explaining reasoning in depth, thoroughly and vividly. Jin criticises teaching that reads from scripts, favours form over substance, or fails to refute erroneous trends of thought. The third section presents the 'big ideological and political course' as extending teaching beyond the classroom through links between these courses and course-embedded ideological education, between teachers and students, and between schools and society. In the fourth section, Jin calls for precise understanding of students' circumstances, content that joins theory, history and present reality, varied teaching methods, and digital tools such as cloud-based resource banks and smart classrooms. The conclusion calls on educators to be guided by Xi Jinping Thought and to do their utmost to run the courses well. Jin presents this as the way to raise the younger generation to meet the expectations of the Party, the state and the people. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of current policy, institutions and teaching practice in China's ideological and political education.

Making socialism with Chinese characteristics "the best system in the world" Deng Xiaoping's thought on institution-building and the further deepening of reform 让中国特色社会主义“成为世界上最好的制度” Zhao Lingyun Writing in 2024, the 120th anniversary of Deng Xiaoping's birth and the opening year of the "further comprehensively deepening reform" agenda, Zhao Lingyun asks what Deng's thinking on institution-building was and how it guided reform. Zhao argues that its core is Deng's 1980 aspiration that the socialist system would "become the best system in the world", and that reform and opening up is best read as a process of institution-building. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Deng's thought around four questions: what counts as the best system, why socialism with Chinese characteristics can become it, when, and how. The second traces institution-building in three phases: rectification and restoration (1975, 1977–78), reform and innovation from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the 18th Party Congress (2012), and institutional integration and operation since then. The third looks ahead to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Zhao argues that Deng offered evaluation criteria (political stability, popular unity and living standards, sustained growth of the productive forces) and tied the goal to the mid-twenty-first century, which Zhao links to the "Two Centenary Goals". Zhao claims the post-2012 reforms moved from building a basic framework (2014–16), through key reforms (2017–19), to system integration (2020–23), while also converting institutional strengths into governance effectiveness, citing the response to Covid-19. The "new development stage" is presented as the key step toward the "best system", a stage of quantitative accumulation approaching a qualitative leap. For further deepening of reform, Zhao proposes focusing on a complete, standardised and effective institutional system, supplying the institutions Chinese modernization needs (a common prosperity system, institutions supporting new quality productive forces), and expanding institutional openness. The last point rests on Deng's "two bold absorptions", with a clearer distinction between capitalism's fundamental and specific institutions. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory account of how Deng's institutional thinking is used to frame four decades of reform and the agenda of 2024.

Strengthening the building of the teaching force for ideological and political theory courses 加强思政课教师队伍建设 Zhang Jingmei This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's recent instruction on school ideological and political theory courses. Zhang Jingmei explains how to build a teaching force that is, in Xi's formulation, strong in politics, deep in feeling, new in thinking, broad in vision, strict in self-discipline and upright in character. Zhang treats these six requirements as general guidance for raising the quality of the teaching force in the new era. The article is organised as six sections, one for each requirement. Each section sets out three practical demands on teachers, and Zhang draws on Xi's earlier remarks on teachers and on the courses. On political strength, Zhang calls on teachers to hold to the Party's leadership, grasp the significance of the Two Establishes, practise the Two Upholds and take the Four-sphere Confidence to students. They should also truly believe in Marxism themselves, since belief must first take root in teachers before it can bear fruit in students. The sections on feeling, thinking and vision ask teachers to cultivate love of country, of the people and of education, to keep pace with the information age and avoid reciting textbooks, and to broaden their knowledge and compare China with other countries without being closed or servile to the West. The sections on self-discipline and character stress ethical conduct, consistency of word and deed online and offline, and loyalty to the Party, country and people. Zhang also asks teachers to treat students with care and be their mentors and friends. Zhang concludes that these six qualities together define what a high-quality teaching force requires. They are meant to produce a new generation committed to national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance on teacher conduct and the ideological and political courses is presented in the Party-state press.

Upholding the socialist market economy is the necessary path for comprehensively deepening reform 坚持社会主义市场经济是全面深化改革的必由之路 Dong Zhiyong Writing in mid-2024, after Xi Jinping's 23 May symposium with entrepreneurs and experts, Dong Zhiyong asks why the socialist market economy must remain the basis of further comprehensively deepening reform. The article argues that, as reform enters what it calls a "deep-water zone", only unwavering adherence to the socialist market economy can keep consolidating the institutional strengths of Chinese modernization and drive reform forward. The article has five parts. It first treats the socialist market economy as a product of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It then presents it as a great creation of the Communist Party, traced through successive Party congresses from the 12th to the 15th. Next it credits the system with China's economic achievements, then sets out what upholding it implies for deepening reform, and ends with a short conclusion. Dong contends that classical Marxism and Western neoclassical economics both assumed socialism and the market to be opposed, and that both drew mainly on Western experience. China, proceeding from the primary stage of socialism, held that planning and the market are both means of allocating resources and that the market economy is not the same as capitalism. Dong contrasts this with the Soviet model, whose partial reforms the author calls short-lived, and with the Soviet and East European turn to privatisation, which the author links to the collapse of those systems. The article credits the market's "decisive role" in resource allocation, citing shifts from planning targets to prices, from state protection to property-rights protection, and from officials to entrepreneurs, but insists that this role is not the "whole role". Party leadership, medium- and long-term planning and cross-cyclical macroeconomic regulation are presented as distinctive strengths. Dong concludes that building a high-level socialist market economy is the necessary path for deepening reform and advancing Chinese modernization, and that the qualifier "socialist" must never be forgotten. Upholding it is said to mean shifting growth towards innovation and new quality productive forces, pursuing common prosperity, reforming ownership structures, balancing development with security, and expanding institutional opening up, which the author says offers a reference for other developing countries. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party theorists link the market economy, reform and Chinese modernization after the 20th Party Congress (2022).
