Advancing Chinese modernization requires adherence to independence, self-reliance and self-strengthening 推进中国式现代化必须坚持独立自主自立自强 Party Leadership Group of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences This article, issued collectively by the Party leadership group of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and carried in Qiushi in 2024, sets out why Chinese modernization must rest on independence, self-reliance and self-strengthening. It argues that this principle is a historical conclusion of the Party's century of struggle, a necessity in the present international environment, and something to be upheld through strategic resolve, theoretical innovation, balanced opening up and determined struggle. It frames the principle with Xi Jinping's statements and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). The text has three parts. The first traces independence and self-reliance through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution under Mao Zedong, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up under Deng Xiaoping, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi. The second explains why the principle is needed now and what supports it. The third sets out four practical requirements. In the second part the authors make three main moves. They argue that universal laws of social development coexist with diverse national paths, citing Marx and Lenin, so that no country can be strong by following others, and China cannot copy Western modernization given its size and its more than 1.4 billion people. They describe a harsher external environment, with containment and suppression by the United States and other Western states, and weak original innovation and dependence on foreign core technologies, so that high-level scientific self-reliance becomes a priority. They also list the foundations they see for self-reliance: Party leadership, the socialist system's capacity to concentrate resources, economic and scientific indicators such as 2023 GDP above 126 trillion yuan, and cultural confidence. The conclusion lists the requirements: keep strategic resolve and avoid both a closed, rigid old path and an erroneous path of abandoning socialism; pursue the Two Integrations to advance theoretical innovation; treat self-reliance and opening up dialectically, building the new development pattern with domestic circulation as the mainstay while staying open; and meet risks with determined struggle. The authors hold that, on this basis, China can become a modern socialist great power. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of the official case for self-reliance as a principle of Chinese modernization, and the sources it draws on.

The world dimension of innovative development in ideological and political education in the new era 论新时代思想政治教育创新发展的世界向度 Zeng Linghui Bu Luping Zeng Linghui and Bu Luping ask how ideological and political education in China, forty years after it was established as an academic discipline, should develop beyond its domestic mission. They argue that, besides answering the questions of China and of the people, it must now answer "the questions of the world" against the backdrop of what official discourse calls changes unseen in a century. The authors propose four capacities that together form a new world-facing dimension: harmonious coexistence, narrative communication, discursive interpretation and self-confidence. The article is organised as four sections, one for each capacity. It draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements on civilisational diversity, telling China's story well and handling foreign theories critically. It gives examples from domestic practice, including implicit education, environmental education, ritual education and the "big ideological and political course", and lists channels such as Xinhua, CCTV international, social media, Confucius Institutes and academic exchange. It closes with a discussion of China's global governance proposals. First, the authors argue that harmonious coexistence means critically borrowing from other countries' ideological education without replacing one model with another, while holding to the basic Marxist standpoint when dealing with Western thought. Second, they say narrative communication requires creative transformation of paradigms, so that traditional Chinese culture, Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and online narratives become intelligible to international audiences. This also needs new carriers (text, image, digital) and platforms, so that China's reasoning no longer "cannot be voiced or spread". Third, discursive interpretation is said to be weak because the field still describes experience rather than explaining it; the authors call for new theory and shared international discourse on a community with a shared future for mankind. On self-confidence, Zeng and Bu hold that it rests on Marxist guidance, on active participation in international exchange and on communicating China's global governance proposals. They conclude that the field must "keep to principles and innovate", holding fast to the Marxist standpoint and to the stance of Chinese culture and modern civilisation, in order to build new discourse and narrative forms and to avoid falling silent in global exchanges. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese ideological education scholars frame the discipline's international communication tasks and the vocabulary they use for them.

The position and role of traditional Chinese religion in traditional Chinese culture Centred on the debates among Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism 中国传统宗教在中国传统文化中的地位和作用 Lü Jianfu Lü Jianfu asks what place and function traditional religion held within traditional Chinese culture. The piece is an edited set of remarks from an April 2024 symposium in Beijing on 'traditional Chinese religion and traditional Chinese culture'. The symposium was organised by the Chinese Atheism Society, the CASS Research Centre for Science and Atheism and the journal Science and Atheism, to carry out Xi Jinping's speech on cultural inheritance and development and to examine how traditional culture bears on the sinicization of religion. Lü's thesis is that religion was essentially subordinate to a Confucian-centred culture, with its role limited to faith and philosophical thought. The article first sketches religion's development from primitive nature worship through the Xia, Shang and Zhou periods to the shift towards a humanistic culture in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. It then traces how the Three Teachings came to be paired: Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism from the Han–Wei period onwards. A third section compares the three teachings' character, and a fourth assesses their influence on Chinese life, philosophy and art. Lü argues that describing Chinese culture as made up of the 'Three Teachings' is a modern idea. In Lü's account it stems from the historical comparison and debate among the three, from the use of Christianity as a template for classifying national cultures, and from later efforts to set tradition against the West. Lü contends that it overstates religion and blurs the line between religious and secular culture. On this view, the Han-era 'sole honouring of Confucianism' and the Six Arts created a complete cultural system, and Confucianism, as state ideology, stayed dominant. Its religious element lay in venerating Heaven and ancestors, while Buddhism and Daoism were religions proper. The author maintains that they never became coequal, and that when religion intruded into politics, as in the 'Three Wu persecutions of Buddhism', it was suppressed. Lü credits Buddhism with raising the level of Chinese dialectical thinking, with Sui–Tang Buddhist philosophy as a peak, though its idealism also influenced Neo-Confucianism. Lü also notes Buddhism's artistic legacy, such as the Dunhuang grottoes. Lü cites the saying 'Confucianism governs the world, Daoism the body, Buddhism the mind', and concludes that Confucian belief was universal while Buddhist and Daoist faith was a partial choice. Lü adds that this philosophical heritage helped China accept Marxist dialectical materialism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of religion, writing in an atheism-studies journal, positions religion as subordinate within traditional culture.

Mao Zedong and the outstanding characteristics of Chinese civilization 毛泽东与中华文明突出特性 Shao Yong Shao Yong takes up the five outstanding characteristics of Chinese civilization that Xi Jinping has summarised and asks what Mao Zedong said about each of them. The article argues that Chinese modernization continues Chinese civilization, and that Mao, drawing on wide historical knowledge and classical learning, offered incisive remarks on all five that are worth revisiting. Shao ends by urging adherence to the principle of upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, so as to carry the historical cultural lineage forward. The article is organised in five sections, one for each characteristic: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Each section assembles Mao's speeches, letters, poems, marginal notes on the dynastic histories and conversations with foreign visitors from the 1930s to the 1970s. Shao presents these sources largely in chronological order, with brief commentary. Examples include the 1938 report on the Party's place in the national war, the 1939 essay 'The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party', the 1937 sacrificial text for the Yellow Emperor's tomb and Mao's remarks on Qin Shihuang and Cao Cao. On continuity, Shao stresses Mao's formula that Marxist historicists must not cut off history, and shows him using Chinese history as a guide for the Party. Examples are the circulation of Guo Moruo's essay on Li Zicheng to guard against complacency after victory, and the call for research on the past century's history. On innovation, Shao reads Mao's idea of making the past serve the present and foreign things serve China as a creative method. Shao also treats Mao's 1959–60 view that socialism has an underdeveloped and a more developed stage as a basis for the later theory of the primary stage of socialism. On unity, Shao cites Mao's repeated praise of Qin Shihuang, Cao Cao and Xie An as unifiers, and his rejection of a 1949 proposal to divide China along the Yangtze. Shao shows Mao's inclusiveness in his support for letting a hundred flowers bloom and a hundred schools contend, and in his call to learn from every nation's strengths while adopting them selectively. His peacefulness appears in his calls for ending civil war in the 1930s, the Chongqing negotiations, and his statements on peaceful coexistence and resistance only to aggression. Shao concludes that Mao's thinking links closely to the five characteristics and that inclusiveness has principles, accepting what is good and rejecting what is not. Read the original if you want a dense, chronologically arranged collection of Mao's statements on Chinese history and tradition, organised around Xi Jinping's formulation of civilizational characteristics.

Mao Zedong's theoretical reflections and strategic planning on national political security 毛泽东关于国家政治安全的理论思考与战略谋划 Ye Zipeng Zheng Yifan Political security, the authors write, is the foundation of national security, covering sovereignty, state power, the system and ideology. The article asks what Mao Zedong understood by national political security and how he planned to achieve it. Ye and Zheng argue that Mao applied the basic principles of the Marxist view of national security to Chinese conditions, and so laid the groundwork for a national security path with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Mao's concept of political security: its four meanings (complete sovereignty, a stable state power, institutional security and ideological security) and its source and purpose in the people. The second sets out four strategic measures. The third draws lessons for the present, tied to the holistic national security outlook and to the new era. On the authors' account, Mao held that people are the decisive factor, more so than institutions, and that political security is both achieved through the people and meant to serve them. The strategic plan has four elements. The first is keeping the Party from degenerating, with the Soviet collapse offered as a warning. The second is a people's army backed by a modern defence industry. The third is struggle, which covers military action, diplomacy by means of the Five Principles, and internal struggle against corruption and in the ideological sphere. The fourth is training successors to the proletarian cause, as a defence against the "peaceful evolution" strategy associated with John Foster Dulles. The authors present Mao's emphasis on Marxist education and on remoulding workers as part of this effort. For the present, Ye and Zheng propose three tasks. The first is to strengthen the Party's leadership of political security, including its strategic thinking, its ability to mobilise the masses and its leadership in ideological struggle, with online ideological struggle singled out. The second is to use the people's role in safeguarding security, through identification with the system, wider outreach, and reporting and reward mechanisms. The third is to build a material base through Chinese modernization and common prosperity, with attention to distribution, to coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, and to tax and social security tools. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party scholars link Mao-era security thinking to current national security policy.

Preface to "Updating Cuba's socialist model: a path of development towards prosperity, democracy and sustainability" 《古巴社会主义模式更新：面向繁荣、民主与可持续的发展道路》序言 Carlos Miguel Pereira Hernández This is a Chinese translation of a preface by Carlos Miguel Pereira Hernández, Cuba's former ambassador to China, dated 18 May 2022. It was written for a 2024 book by He Qin of the Academy of Marxism, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, on the updating of Cuba's socialist model. Pereira presents the book as a panoramic account of Cuban socialism and argues that Cuban socialism is a home-grown model, forged in anti-imperialist struggle, whose viability has been proved over time. After recalling his 2010 meeting with He Qin and the interview that followed, Pereira summarises the book's nine chapters. They cover the course of the Cuban Revolution, the thought of its leaders, the formation of Cuban views of socialism and the milestones of Cuba's development. He also notes the book's treatment of macroeconomic adjustment, strategic economic sectors, education and science, environmental protection, social governance and foreign strategy. He ends by outlining Cuba–China exchanges, including the China–Cuba Party theoretical seminars of 2014 and 2022. Pereira's own argument runs from José Martí's four goals (independence, social justice, economic development, a Cuban democratic government) through the 1959 revolution and Fidel Castro's 1961 declaration of its socialist character. He argues that the US blockade, which he calls the longest and most unjust unilateral sanction in modern history, must be taken into account when judging Cuba's record, and that Cuba's problems should not be blamed on socialism. He names three features of Cuban socialism: people's democracy, social mission and national unity. He describes the update begun at the Sixth Party Congress (2011) as extending democracy, curbing bureaucracy and rigid hierarchy, retaining public ownership of the main means of production while recognising several forms of ownership, and renewing the economic structure. Pereira concludes that Cuban socialism is the institutional guarantee of national independence and self-determination, and that Cuba faces blockade, crisis, pandemic and climate change with confidence. He credits the book with affirming the central role of Fidel Castro's thought, and stresses shared goals and a close strategic relationship between Cuba and China, including joint opposition to blockades and unilateral coercive measures. He congratulates the author on behalf of the Cuban Communist Party, government and people. Read the original if you want a Cuban official's view of the Cuban socialist model, its update since 2011 and Cuba–China ties, or want to judge whether to consult He Qin's book.

The peaceful character of Chinese civilisation and its world significance 中华文明的和平性及其世界意义 Luo Wendong Luo Wendong takes up a thesis from Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development: that the peaceful character of Chinese civilisation fundamentally determines China's role as a builder of world peace, contributor to global development and defender of the international order. The article, published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2024, argues that peace is a defining trait and basic value of Chinese civilisation. In Luo's account, it has shaped China's own history and also bears on world peace and development. The piece moves in three steps. It first traces the cultural roots and historical record of Chinese peacefulness, from classics such as the Book of Documents, the Book of Songs, the Doctrine of the Mean and Sunzi's Art of War to the Silk Road, Zhang Qian and Zheng He. It then turns to the People's Republic, covering the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, Deng Xiaoping's reform-era foreign policy and Mao Zedong's statements against aggression. Finally it considers China's peace concepts and policies since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Luo's central claim is continuity: values such as "harmony in diversity" and "winning without fighting" are said to have guided exchange through trade and cultural influence rather than conquest. Luo cites Bodde, Bertrand Russell and Jomo Kenyatta as outside observers who recognised this, and says China did not expand even when its economy was a third of world output. The article presents the Communist Party as inheriting this tradition. In its telling, China's rise to the second-largest economy came through hard work and opening-up cooperation, not colonial plunder. For the present, when it describes a world of conflict, hegemonism and deficits in peace, development, security and governance, Luo lists China's initiatives as its answer. These are the community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives. Luo concludes that peace is the foundation of national stability and prosperity, and that China will keep to peaceful development and help build a community with a shared future for mankind. It is said to reject cultural hegemony, imposing its values or political system on others, and bloc politics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link classical Chinese culture to contemporary foreign-policy doctrine.

"French Theory" and the philosophy of the future: constructing a new philosophical paradigm “法国理论”与未来哲学：一种新哲学范式的构建 Ouyang Qian Why does contemporary French philosophy look so little like philosophy as traditionally understood? Ouyang Qian takes up the American-coined label "French Theory" and argues that it signals more than the "end of philosophy". In the author's reading, Foucault, Derrida, Deleuze, Lyotard, Baudrillard, Bourdieu and others are trying to end that "end" by building a new philosophical paradigm, which the article presents as a possible form of future philosophy. The article is organised in three movements followed by a short conclusion. It traces the shift from a "system of critique" to a "critique of systems", then from "grand narrative" to "micro-perspective", and finally from "philosophy of consciousness" to "cultural studies". It draws on Habermas, Rorty, Gary Gutting, Badiou and the French thinkers' own texts, and sketches five research paradigms within French cultural critique. Ouyang contends that traditional metaphysics, from Plato to Hegel, sought universal, eternal systems, and that French thinkers reject this as a totalising, identity-based mode of thought tied to power and reason's domination. Philosophy therefore turns to contingent events, to micro-analyses such as Foucault's archaeology and genealogy, and to Deleuze and Guattari's micropolitics of desire. The author describes this as replacing a telescope with a microscope. On the third move, Ouyang holds that, under the influence of structural linguistics and psychoanalysis, the subject is treated as produced by signs and culture. The five paradigms are Foucault's critique of reason, Derrida's deconstruction, Deleuze's analysis of desire, Baudrillard's critique of the political economy of the sign, and Bourdieu's "constructivist structuralism". The author notes that all of these maintain some link with Marxism, citing Derrida's praise of the Communist Manifesto. Ouyang concludes that whether the future of philosophy will look like French Theory cannot yet be decided. Even so, the author argues, French Theory's interdisciplinary, present-oriented and practice-oriented character, together with its creation of concepts, holds the seed of a new philosophy. Two lessons are drawn: the world needs philosophy more than philosophy supposes, and philosophy can no longer be done in the old way. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's synthesis of French poststructuralism and postmodernism as a paradigm shift in philosophy, with many citations from the thinkers themselves.

Overseas scholars' perceptions and assessments of Chinese-style agricultural and rural modernization 海外学者关于中国式农业农村现代化的认知与评价 Chen Yitao This literature review, published in 2024 in Contemporary China History Studies, surveys how scholars and institutions outside China have understood and evaluated Chinese-style agricultural and rural modernization since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Chen Yitao notes that Chinese scholarship has tracked overseas rural studies mainly by looking at researchers, theories and methods. The article instead samples English-language work from roughly the past decade, to offer an "other's perspective" and help "tell the story" of rural revitalization. The sources include journals such as The China Quarterly, think tanks such as the International Institute for Environment and Development, and bodies such as the Asian Development Bank and the OECD. Chen organises the material under four headings: achievements (agriculture, farmer incomes, rural public services, grassroots governance); driving forces; distinctive features; and global significance. A closing section describes the characteristics, contributions and limits of the overseas literature. In Chen's account, overseas writers see four mutually supporting drivers: Party leadership as the leading force, farmers as the main agents (including returning youth, the "new farmers"), institutional flexibility, and technological diffusion. They identify three distinctive features: combining top-level design with local pilot projects, urban–rural integration alongside green development, and a value orientation centred on farmers' welfare. They also credit China with contributing to global food security, to cooperation opportunities, and to rural governance and poverty-reduction models for developing countries. Chen largely presents these views as consistent with China's actual conditions. Chen concludes that overseas research is diverse in its authors, scope and methods, and is often driven by pragmatic policy concerns. It supplements domestic scholarship, though a minority of authors are said to remain bound by "Western-centrism" or to exaggerate rural problems. Chen calls for tracking foreign research, rebutting what the article regards as misrepresentation, and building a discourse system that is Chinese in character but intelligible abroad, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a catalogue of the overseas scholars, think tanks and reports that Chinese academics cite on rural modernization, and a sense of how they are being read.

The idea of inter-subjectivity in traditional Chinese culture and its contemporary significance 中国传统文化中的互主体思想及其现实意义 Cheng Long Cheng Long takes up a question raised by Xi Jinping's call to advance the Second Integration: what is the basic character of traditional Chinese culture? Some scholars locate it in 'subjectivity'. Cheng disputes this, since Western thought from Descartes through Kant and Hegel also champions human subjectivity. The article argues that the distinguishing trait is 'inter-subjectivity' (互主体性). Western culture proceeds from the 'self' and a subject–object split, and so is in essence single-subject. Chinese culture proceeds from the unity of self and other, and so favours pluralistic coexistence. The article has three parts. The first reads Confucian, Daoist, Mohist and some Legalist texts, plus modern figures such as Hong Xiuquan, Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen, for five kinds of relation between subjects: harmony and integration, mutual respect and love, equality, tolerance, and good faith. The second asks why the idea arose so early, drawing on a historical-materialist comparison with ancient Greece. The third sets out its present-day significance. Cheng gives three reasons for the contrast, each tied to China's formative period. First, humanism emerged early: belief in ghosts and spirits gave way, from the Yin–Zhou transition, to concern with people, whereas Greek thought looked outward to nature and was constrained by religion. Second, the rich river-valley geography made the 'person–person' relation the main problem, while Greece's poor, fragmented land pushed trade, expansion and a 'philosophy of struggle'. Third, clan kinship survived in China as a 'family–state unity', whereas in Greece it dissolved into contractual political relations, which in Cheng's account led to others being treated as objects. Cheng concludes that inter-subjectivity offers a window onto the distinctive value of traditional culture. It helps end the modern 'ancient–modern, East–West' dispute. It also supplements Marxism, which in Cheng's view says little concrete about how subjects cultivate themselves under socialism. Finally, it forms the cultural basis of a community with a shared future for mankind, set against what the author calls Western zero-sum hegemonic logic. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-by-text case for a China–West contrast built on inter-subjectivity, and its link to current Party discourse on the Second Integration.

On determining the principal contradiction of ideological and political education 论思想政治教育主要矛盾的判定 Kuang Ning Wang Xisheng Kuang Ning and Wang Xisheng take up a basic question in the theory of ideological and political education: what is its principal contradiction? They note that research on the topic is thin and that scholars disagree. Their thesis is that, in any given period, the principal contradiction is a single opposition-and-unity between ideological and political educators and the people educated, located at the level of their respective needs. The article has three parts. It first surveys four representative views in the 40 years since the discipline was founded. These identify the contradiction from the constituent elements of the field, from conflicts within the educational process, from tensions in practical work (for example a single guiding ideology versus diverse social trends), and from the function of nurturing people. It then sets out criteria for judging a principal contradiction, and finally applies them to identify its two sides, its object and its nature. The authors say a later study will trace historical practice under the Communist Party. The authors identify four disagreements: whether the contradiction is one or many, who its two sides are, at what level it operates, and whether it is mere difference or true opposition and unity. They answer by defining the concept, drawing on Mao Zedong's analysis of contradiction. A principal contradiction holds the dominant position, decides the nature and direction of the field and conditions the secondary contradictions. It changes between historical stages but is stable within one, and in any given period there can be only one. Two principal contradictions, they argue, would each be unable to dominate the other, which is incoherent. Applying these criteria, the authors argue that the two sides must be educators and educated, the most basic elements in every scheme of the field's components, rather than content, methods or environment. The educators are a collective representing the will of the Party and state, and the educated include all members of society. The object of the contradiction is need, not ideas, since explaining behaviour by thought rather than need would repeat the old materialism Engels criticised. Educators must guide people according to the demands of Party and state, while the educated have varied needs and may bargain over ideas. Read the original if you want a systematic conceptual account of how Chinese theorists define and justify a principal contradiction in ideological and political education.

A historical-political interpretation of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation Centred on how the Zhou–Qin transition shaped China's model of state governance 中华民族现代文明的历史政治学阐释 Huang Tao Huang Tao asks how the modern civilization of the Chinese nation should be understood in relation to China's ancient state. The article argues that this civilization is a politics-centred civilization that grew out of traditional Chinese civilization, so that its formation must be read with respect for historical continuity and close attention to major changes in the model of state governance. Using a historical-political approach, Huang takes the Zhou–Qin transition as the key moment for tracing that continuity. The article defines the Zhou–Qin transition as a comprehensive transformation of Chinese civilization, led by changes in governance and state form. It runs from the founding of the Zhou dynasty (1046 BCE) to the death of Emperor Wu of Han (87 BCE), more than 900 years. Huang then reviews what Zhou and Qin institutions bequeathed and where they fell short. The article goes on to the late-Qing crisis, the revolutions led by the Communist Party, and the two great transformations seen together. Huang's central claim is that the Zhou–Qin transition produced the core structure of Chinese civilization: six basic paradigms of state. These are the centralised state, the multi-ethnic state of diversity in unity, the all-under-heaven (tianxia) state, the unified state, the super-large-scale state and the secular state. From them derive features such as the county system, bureaucracy, a strong state, popular-basis (minben) thought and meritocracy. Huang argues that these formed the political and social setting for the modern revolutions, and that without these roots modern civilization would lose its foundation. The article also lists the limits of Zhou rule (weak centralisation, fragmentation, rigid hierarchy) and of Qin rule (excessive monarchical power, harsh law, a weak society). Huang holds that these limits were largely those of traditional civilization. It argues that the Party, guided by Marxism-Leninism and the Two Integrations, inherited the six paradigms. It also added socialism, republican democracy, the rule of law, the people's congress system and regional ethnic autonomy, reorganising them in a revolutionary way. Huang concludes that continuity and major change are dialectically united in Chinese civilization: the two great transformations form a relay across more than two thousand years, and neither is a break or a simple inheritance. Both began with changes in governance and state form, which for Huang confirms that Chinese civilization is politics-centred. The author holds that modern China is on a path combining Chinese subjectivity, historical continuity and human universality, a result of civilizational renewal rather than rupture, and that a universal political science cannot exclude China. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese scholars use ancient state history to ground claims about the continuity of Chinese modernity.

Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England and the study of British modernization: a visual analysis 《英国工人阶级状况》关于英国现代化进程研究的可视化分析 Liu Nana Liu Nana asks what Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England reveals about the process of British modernization, and what that account implies for Chinese modernization. The article argues that Engels read modernization through the interaction of industrialization and urbanization, and that he exposed the contradictions of capital-driven modernization. From this Liu concludes that Chinese modernization transcends the Western model. The article is built in three parts. The first analyses the temporal and spatial features of British modernization as Engels observed them: the Industrial Revolution as starting point, urbanization as spatial carrier, and world history as the wider setting. It draws on figures and historical records, presented in charts, on population movement, transport (roads, canals, railways, steamships) and the growth of cities such as Manchester and Glasgow. The second part sets out three paradoxes, and the third draws theoretical lessons for China. In Liu's reading, Engels shows that modernization brought no improvement for workers. The three paradoxes are these. First, workers become appendages of machines, damaged in body through child and female labour and long hours, and in spirit through the division of labour. Second, urban space develops unevenly: cramped and shoddy workers' housing, a city–countryside opposition, and the loss of common land and leisure space, which Liu connects to rising drinking that Engels traces to capitalist private ownership. Third, free trade, after protective tariffs had nurtured British industry, serves capital's freedom, intensifies competition among workers, lowers their purchasing power and enables the exploitation of poorer countries. Liu draws three lessons. Chinese modernization is a modernization of people, set against the Western modernization of things, and rests on a people-centred approach and Marx's stages of human development. Socialist urban and rural space should be built through "people's cities" and rural revitalization, not capitalist city–country opposition. Finally, a new development pattern in which domestic and international circulations reinforce each other is said to widen the space for Chinese modernization, which Liu describes as both endogenous and open. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses Engels's early empirical study, with charts and data, to support claims about Chinese modernization.

Building China's independent knowledge system requires strengthening theoretical thinking 建构中国自主的知识体系必须强化理论思维 Sun Laibin Sun Laibin takes up Xi Jinping's call, made in 2022, to build China's independent knowledge system, and asks what role theoretical thinking should play in it. The article argues that philosophers and social scientists must deliberately strengthen theoretical thinking, using theoretical insight, abstraction and creativity to summarise Chinese experience in terms of "Chinese principles" and raise it to the level of Chinese theory. The article has three parts. The first defines theoretical thinking, contrasts it with empirical thinking, and says why scholars in the new era should develop it. The second explains why building an independent knowledge system cannot do without it. The third sets out how the three capacities named above can each advance the project. Sun draws throughout on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Hegel and Einstein, and on Xi Jinping's speeches. Sun distinguishes empirical thinking, based on experience and common sense, from theoretical thinking, which uses scientific abstraction to reach essence and laws. Moving from the first to the second needs abundant, accurate empirical material and the power of abstraction. The author holds that theoretical thinking helps turn "external" problems (conflicts between existing theory and new practice) into "internal" ones, and so serves the three priorities of subjectivity, originality and systematicity in Chinese-style philosophy and social science. In practice, theoretical insight is meant to grasp China's real conditions and identify genuine problems. Abstraction distils identifying concepts, with "a community with a shared future for mankind" given as a model. Creativity then organises concepts into a systematic whole, in the manner of Marx's method in Capital, fusing Marxism, traditional Chinese culture and foreign scholarship. Sun concludes that scholars should use the Chinese worldview and methodology, in theoretical form, to explain Chinese modernization and turn its experience into theory. Sun lists high-quality development, new quality productive forces and similar concepts as new-era achievements that await further study. Read the original if you want to see how a Peking University Marxism scholar links the official project of an independent knowledge system to classical Marxist accounts of abstraction and theory-building.

An ideological and political education interpretation of "ideological reality" (sixiang shiji) “思想实际”的思想政治教育学阐释 Ye Fangxing Marking the 40th anniversary of ideological and political education as an academic discipline, Ye Fangxing takes up "ideological reality" (sixiang shiji), a phrase that appears constantly in Party documents and everyday speech but is usually treated as self-explanatory. The article argues that it should be recognised as a core concept of the discipline. In Ye's account it denotes the actual state of people's thinking and spirit, and it supplies the factual premise on which ideological and political education must be built. The article first defines the concept and distinguishes it from "work reality" (gongzuo shiji). It then sets out four features: its factual, structural, evaluative and typological character. Next it considers the concept's place in the discipline, and it ends with principles for investigating ideological reality. It draws on Marx and Engels (including The Condition of the Working Class in England), on Durkheim's Moral Education, and on Party documents and Chinese scholarship in the field. Ye's central move is to hold together fact and norm. Ideological reality is an observable, measurable "ideological fact", centred on values, especially political values. Yet it is "what is", not "what ought to be": it must be assessed against the aims of ideological and political education, and observing it is only the starting point of that work. Ye also divides it into three types (overall, group and individual) and into cognitive, emotional and value layers. Ye further argues that it reflects people's social being, since what people think corresponds to how they live. On this basis Ye treats ideological reality as a starting category of the discipline. Grounding work in it is described as a practical premise, a long-standing principle of the Party's ideological and political work, and a standard of effectiveness, because education that misses it becomes "ideological idling". Ye urges investigation that combines overall and differentiated views, fact and norm, and macro and micro approaches, with the individual and micro level needing the most strengthening through oral history, narrative and in-depth interviews. The article concludes that describing concepts of this kind gives theoretical research in the field an empirical footing. Read the original if you study the conceptual foundations of Chinese ideological and political education or the Party's tradition of investigation and research.

Seeking humanity's direction amid the deepening of great changes New developments and changes in foreign communist parties in 2023 在大变局深度演进中探寻人类前进方向 Yu Haiqing This annual survey asks how communist parties outside China fared in 2023, a year the author describes as marked by shifting great-power relations, geopolitical rivalry and a post-pandemic world full of uncertainty. Yu argues that these parties kept to their stance and struggle goals and adjusted to new conditions. Their overall development showed continuity and stability, with the defining feature of advancing amid a low tide. The article is organised in six sections. It covers anniversaries and commemorations, including Mao Zedong's 130th birthday and the deaths of several party leaders. It then reviews party congresses and Central Committee plenums, local and national election results, struggles against capitalism and for workers' rights, and the state of international solidarity. Cases range from ruling parties in Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and the DPRK to non-ruling parties in Germany, France, Britain, Pakistan, Venezuela, Ireland, Austria, Greece, Spain and Russia. Two moves carry the argument. On elections, Yu reports breakthroughs at regional and local level, such as the Austrian communists' rise in Salzburg from 0.31% to 11.66% and the Greek party's reported rise above 10%. Yu also notes setbacks, for instance in India's Tripura state, and concludes that overall strength changed little. On unity, the author sees the Ukraine crisis deepening divisions: the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe dissolved, and the Greek party founded a new European Communist Action. Meanwhile, a Global Anti-imperialist Platform, whose programme blames Western imperialism for the crisis, took shape as a rival channel. Yu adds that parties split internally, as in Cyprus, and that some parties moved towards cooperation, notably the merger of two Danish communist parties and the 23rd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties in İzmir, which issued a joint action plan despite differing views. Yu concludes that, as great changes deepen, unity and coordinated action are of practical importance and would speed the revival of world socialism. The author names the main task for foreign communist parties in the coming period as widening consensus, bridging differences and achieving cooperation. Read the original if you want a detailed, party-by-party chronicle of the 2023 congresses, elections and international networks of non-Chinese communist parties, as seen from a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences researcher.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground to promote the connotative development of ideological and political theory courses 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Cai Wencheng Responding to a recent directive from Xi Jinping on school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke), Cai Wencheng argues that these courses should develop 'connotatively', that is, by improving quality rather than expanding scale. The article, a commentary in the Party journal Qiushi's sister publication Hongqi Wengao (2024, no. 12), holds that this requires upholding fundamental principles while innovating, so as to make the courses more targeted and more appealing. Cai presents this as a scientific guide to running such courses well in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out the strategic significance of connotative development, the second its core meaning, and the third the practical requirements. It treats the courses as part of the wider course of the Party's cause, the building of a modern socialist country and national rejuvenation, and draws heavily on Xi's speeches and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). In Cai's account, the courses matter for three reasons: they carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, they serve the Party's aim of educating people for the Party and talent for the country, and they are integral to building a leading country in education. The core meaning is that the courses must be political, strategic and bound up with people's wellbeing. Cai identifies four pillars: a high-standard curriculum and textbook system centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; a high-quality teaching system integrated across primary, secondary and tertiary levels; a high-level theoretical research system; and an effective talent-cultivation system that draws on all subjects through 'ideological and political education across the curriculum'. Cai's practical requirements are to hold to the right political direction in an ideological field described as increasingly complex, and to apply Xi's 'eight unities' (for example, political and academic rigour, indoctrination and inspiration). Cai also calls for 'great ideological and political courses' that link classrooms to society, for new methods such as case-based and interactive teaching, and for teachers who are politically strong and ethically upright. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official line on how ideological and political courses are to be organised and taught in Chinese schools and universities after Xi's 2024 directive.

A panoramic examination of Mao Zedong's promotion of the innovative development of Chinese Marxist philosophy in the Yan'an period 延安时期毛泽东推进中国马克思主义哲学创新发展的全景式考察 Wang Yan Wang Yan asks how Mao Zedong, during the Yan'an period (1935–1947), built Chinese Marxist philosophy and gave Marxist philosophy a 'Chinese form'. The article argues that Yan'an was the most important stage of this work. In Wang's account, Mao created the first theoretical form of Chinese Marxist philosophy by combining Marxist principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article has four main sections plus a conclusion. It begins with the two foundational texts, 'On Practice' and 'On Contradiction'. It then turns to Mao's account of what Chinese Marxist philosophy means and how it is generated, and to his philosophical work in three fields: military, political and methodological. It ends with the Rectification Movement, the establishment of the line of seeking truth from facts, and the Party's adoption of Mao Zedong Thought at the Seventh Congress (1945). Wang first argues that the two essays gave a systematic philosophical basis to the ideological line of seeking truth from facts, in response to the dogmatism that had cost the revolution heavily. They drew critically on Soviet textbooks, for example by Mitin and Shirokov, while reorganising and extending their content. They also absorbed Chinese traditions, such as the unity of knowing and acting and the dialectics of the Book of Changes. Second, Wang reads Mao's call to 'sinify Marxism' (issued in 1938) as a two-way process: applying theory to Chinese conditions and raising Chinese revolutionary experience into theory. On the cultural side, Mao is said to have distinguished the feudal from the non-feudal in tradition, given old terms such as 'seeking truth from facts' new Marxist meanings, and translated Marxist language into national forms. Third, Wang shows Mao applying this philosophy to a Marxist military philosophy ('On Protracted War'), a political philosophy ('On New Democracy') and a methodology of thought, leadership and work. Wang concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy belongs to the Marxist philosophical tradition while taking a form distinct from Marxism elsewhere. It emerged from repeated struggle against dogmatism, from reflection on the Chinese–Western cultural debate, and from the summing up of experience in making Marxism concrete. Wang says it thereby 'realised the modern ideological enlightenment of the Chinese people'. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the Yan'an texts and the Rectification Movement are presented in Chinese scholarship as the origin of Chinese Marxist philosophy.

Deng Xiaoping and Chinese modernization 邓小平与中国式现代化 Shi Zhongquan Shi Zhongquan asks what role Deng Xiaoping played in Chinese modernization. The article's thesis is that, if Mao Zedong laid the foundations of the thinking behind Chinese modernization, Deng was the first to put forward the idea of a "Chinese-style modernization" and the great pioneer of the path that realises it. The article has three parts. It first places Deng within the first generation of Party leaders and their exploration of socialist modernization, then examines the historical background and initial meaning of the idea in 1979. It next traces how Deng opened the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, through theoretical preparation, major reform policies and the 13th Party Congress (1987). Finally it treats Deng's 1992 southern tour talks as lifting this thinking to a new level. Shi argues that Deng first used the phrase in March 1979 to describe a deliberately modest goal: a "xiaokang" (moderately well-off) standard, with per-capita GNP of around US$1,000 by the end of the century. Shi suggests Deng then preferred "the path of building socialism with Chinese characteristics" for four reasons: it was the more normative wording, the 1979 meaning did not reach beyond 2000, Deng was already planning for the 21st century, and the two concepts are related but not identical. Shi lists five theoretical "weapons" and three major policies behind the path, including letting some get rich first, the household contract responsibility system and the special economic zones. The 13th Party Congress added the primary stage of socialism, the basic line of "one centre, two basic points" and a three-step development strategy. The southern tour talks, Shi says, defended that basic line, set out the essence of socialism and the case for a socialist market economy, and served as Deng's "political testament". Shi concludes that Deng's talks were the direct source of the theory of building socialism with Chinese characteristics, later named Deng Xiaoping Theory and treated as the origin of the system of theories of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Shi reads Deng's 1989 and 1992 speeches as a unity, and presents Deng's three-step strategy as the roadmap to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's account of how Deng's 1979 formulation relates to later official terminology and to his policies and theory.

On the critical theory of "transitional capitalism" Its problem logic and contemporary value, from the perspective of "Political Marxism" 论“转型资本主义” 批判理论的问题逻辑及其当代价值 Feng Wangzhou Feng Wangzhou asks how the Anglo-American school of "Political Marxism" analyses the development of capitalism and the prospects for moving beyond it. The article argues that the school, whose leading figures are Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood, has built a systematic critical theory that Feng labels "transitional capitalism". Feng holds that this theory has real value for developing twenty-first-century Marxism, for foreign Marxist critiques of capitalism, and for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article first sets out the school's background: the collapse of the Soviet Union, the "end of history" thesis, and the retreat of many left intellectuals from criticising capitalism. It then traces three generations of scholars over some forty years, from Brenner, Wood and George Comninel to Benno Teschke and Hannes Lacher, and then to Xavier Lafrance and Eren Duzgun. The main section reconstructs the school's "problem domain" in six parts: the origins of capitalism, its stages of development, its ideology, the state and international relations, its general crisis, and ways of overcoming it. Feng's core claim is that the school keeps to Marx's historical materialism and places social property relations, understood as class relations, at the centre. On this view capitalism arose contingently in English agriculture, through market dependence, and not through trade, population change or commercialisation. It then moved from agrarian to industrial capitalism, to colonial imperialism, and finally to capitalist imperialism. In Feng's account, the school treats "progress", democracy, "endless war" and liberalism as a chain of ideology that supports capitalist rule. It also sees class struggle, economic, ecological and social crises combining into a general crisis. Feng reports that the school's way beyond capitalism has four elements: a renewed historical materialism, the working class as revolutionary subject, anti-capitalist struggle organised through the nation-state to achieve real democracy, and an international alliance of labour and new social movements. Feng concludes that the school continues earlier critiques of state capitalism, consumer society, late capitalism and global capitalism. Feng adds that it clarifies the revolutionary agency behind a revival of world socialism, and that it helps strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic overview of Brenner, Wood and their successors, and of how Chinese academics present this school's relevance to Chinese socialism.

Deepening basic theoretical research in ideological and political education in the new era An interview with Professor Zhang Yaocan of Central China Normal University 《思想教育研究》记者：深化新时代思想政治教育基础理论研究 续写学科高质量发展新篇章 This is an interview, conducted by a reporter for the journal Ideological and Political Education Research, with Professor Zhang Yaocan of Central China Normal University. Zhang is introduced as one of the founders of the discipline of ideological and political education in China, with more than 60 years of teaching. Marking forty years since the discipline was established, the interview asks how it developed, what lessons it has produced, and how it should "uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground" in the new era. Zhang begins with a personal account. After studying political education at Central China Normal University, they worked in student affairs, taught a moral-cultivation course, and published a university moral-education text in 1986. Zhang then divides the discipline's history into three stages: exploration (1978–1983), systematic construction (1984–1996) and innovative development (1996 to the present). The interview then turns to the role of basic theory and to tasks for the future. Zhang names three driving forces: the Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times through the Two Integrations, the practical experience of builders in many sectors, and the scholars and practitioners of the field. Five lessons follow: be guided by sinicised Marxist theory, combine theory with practice, combine history with theory, pursue cooperation alongside individual strengths, and treat the discipline, the undergraduate major and the ideological and political theory courses as mutually supporting. Zhang argues that basic theory is the first expression of the discipline's scientific character and also underpins its ideological character. Strengthening it requires "five adherences", including the unity of science and ideology, an interdisciplinary paradigm and cooperation among older, middle-aged and young scholars. Looking ahead, Zhang calls for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to guide the discipline. Zhang also wants ideals-and-convictions education tied to Chinese modernization, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind, and research kept oriented to practice. Zhang notes that metatheory has advanced, but that work on the discipline's basic categories is thin and lacks scholarly debate, which Zhang treats as a mark of a mature discipline. Read the original if you want a participant's periodisation of the field, with its policy milestones and course reforms, or an insider view of how the discipline defines its theoretical tasks.

Grasping the laws of Chinese modernization politically 从政治上把握中国式现代化建设规律 Bao Xinjian This commentary in the Party School newspaper Study Times takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Central Economic Work Conference that advancing Chinese modernization must be treated as "the greatest politics". Bao Xinjian argues that this formulation is a fundamental guide for understanding the laws governing modernization from a political vantage point. In Bao's account, it matters for strengthening the Party's overall leadership, keeping modernization on the right course and releasing its driving force. The article first sets out a Marxist view of politics: politics reflects fundamental interests and objective laws of economic and social development, is the operation and governance of the state, and concentrates the interests of the majority. It then identifies three sources of the political significance of Chinese modernization: the goal of national rejuvenation, the task of modernizing state governance, and the subjectivity and needs of the people. On rejuvenation, Bao traces the path from the Opium War through failed reform and revolutionary attempts to the founding of the Communist Party, and then from Mao Zedong's "four modernizations" through Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style modernization" to Xi Jinping's theoretical innovation. The author presents modernization as the only correct road to national rejuvenation, one that does not copy Western models. On governance, Bao holds that institutions play a fundamental, overall, stable and long-term role. The article links this to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). In this reading, institutional reform turns institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. On the people, Bao says modernization is fundamentally the modernization of people, and that it avoids the polarisation, extreme individualism and loss of human subjectivity the author attributes to Western modernization driven by the "logic of capital". Meeting people's growing needs for a better life through high-quality development is described as its core political value. Bao concludes that because Chinese modernization is the greatest politics, leaders must strengthen the Party's overall leadership from a political standpoint, hold to the people-centred orientation, and raise officials' political judgement, political understanding and political execution. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2024 justify the claim that modernization is "the greatest politics" through national rejuvenation, institutional reform and the people's role.

A political-economy interpretation of new quality productive forces 新质生产力的政治经济学阐释 Han Wenlong Han Wenlong takes up Xi Jinping's 2023–2024 formulation of new quality productive forces and asks how it can be understood as a category of Marxist political economy. The author argues that the concept is a new political-economy category which enriches Marxist productive-force theory, and that it can be explained by materialist dialectics, by identifying its drivers and by pairing it with a partial change in relations of production. The article has four parts. It first sets out the concept's meaning, covering the "new" and the "quality" in the term, the dialectic of quantitative and qualitative change, advancement of structure and content, and two unities that mark advanced productive forces. It then examines the motive force and sources of development, turns to the relations of production, and ends with practical paths. Han draws on Marx's remarks on means of labour, the productivity of labour, complex labour and distribution relations. Han holds that the "new" lies in new elements (workers with new skills, intelligent equipment, digital and deep-sea or deep-space objects of labour) and in new technologies, industries, business forms and fields. The "quality" has four aspects: a new essence, high-quality development, high-quality living and a "quality" advantage in international competition. Demand change is presented as the trigger, the organic combination of production-force elements led by complex labour as the internal driver, and contradictions among those elements as the source. Han then argues that relations of production must be partly restructured. The proposals include a mixed ownership system for data elements with a "three-rights separation" of property rights, a collaborative innovation system led by a new national system, distribution tilted towards data, technological and complex labour, a high-standard market system, and consumption relations that integrate natural and social dimensions. Han concludes that developing new quality productive forces is central to Chinese modernization and to building new competitive advantages. The practical agenda comprises high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, advanced manufacturing with strategic emerging and future industries, institutional reform of property rights, evaluation and incentives, and accumulation of high-quality human resources through complex labour. Read the original if you want a systematic Marxist-theoretical framing of the concept, including its treatment of data ownership, distribution and the labour theory, as well as its policy proposals.

Firmly grasping cultural discourse power in building school ideological and political courses in the new era 牢牢把握新时代学校思政课建设文化话语权 Gu Youren Zhao Li This short commentary asks how schools' ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) can be developed in the new era, and answers that the key is to build and consolidate "cultural discourse power". Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's recent instruction that these courses must uphold Marxism's guiding position and draw strength from fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, Gu and Zhao argue that all ideological, moral and political education takes place in a cultural context and relies on cultural discourse as its vehicle. The article moves through three sections. The first looks at what the authors call the ethical and character-forming nature of traditional Chinese culture. The second reviews the Chinese Communist Party's experience of cultivating virtue through culture, from Mao Zedong's policy of critically inheriting tradition to the present. The third turns to practical tasks for the new era. Gu and Zhao contend that, historically, rulers and ordinary educators alike shaped and defended cultural discourse power, which they credit for the effectiveness of traditional moral education and the vitality of Chinese culture. In the new era, they say, global upheaval, cultural pluralism and online information have changed the cultural environment and posed unprecedented challenges. They propose three measures: heightening awareness of risk, including what they describe as cultural infiltration by some Western countries; building mainstream culture, explaining socialism with Chinese characteristics in Marxist political language while stressing Party leadership, the people's standpoint and patriotism; and guiding popular culture. On the last point, the authors acknowledge that popular culture enriches daily life but argue that its commercialism undermines recognition of core values, so courses should be down-to-earth in idiom yet pitched high in the values they convey. The authors conclude that cultural discourse power determines whom the courses serve and how, and that it bears on carrying the Party's ideological and political work tradition into the future. They present securing it as a necessary choice for implementing Xi's instruction, fostering cultural confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics, safeguarding ideological security and offering Chinese wisdom to global cultural governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars link Party ideological education to culture, tradition and ideological security.

The multi-tense cultural form of Chinese modernization 多时态的中国式现代化文化形态 An Deming This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's formulation that the "Second Integration" produces a new culture that becomes "the cultural form of Chinese modernization". An Deming argues that this cultural form is not static. It develops alongside Chinese modernization and enriches its theory and practice, and it has a dynamic, multi-stage character that can be read in three tenses: completed, ongoing and future. The article is organised around these three tenses. The completed tense covers the cultural achievements of the Party-led revolution and socialist construction. The ongoing tense corresponds to cultural construction in the new era. The future tense concerns the goals and significance of that construction, both for China and for the wider world. In An's account, the completed form rests on the organic combination of two core elements: excellent traditional Chinese culture and the basic principles of Marxism. Marxism acts as a "catalyst" that activates the cultural genes of the tradition, and An links the inclusiveness of Chinese civilisation to Marxist internationalism. For the ongoing tense, An cites Xi's point that the Two Integrations is a "chemical reaction", not a "platter" of parts. An therefore warns against treating tradition in a homogenised, mechanical way and calls for historical materialism, dialectics and a sublating attitude. Three practical paths follow: raising the cultural literacy of workers and the public, attending to living popular cultural practice (including intangible cultural heritage), and contributing Chinese approaches to international cultural exchange. The future tense is said to face both inward, towards confidence in Chinese culture, and outward, towards offering solutions to global problems. An concludes that the multi-tense cultural form is both a result of Chinese modernization and a constituent part of its process. It shows, in An's view, that Chinese modernization is comprehensive, covering cultural and spiritual as well as scientific, technological and material dimensions. Emphasising this cultural form, An says, enriches the meaning of modernization and adds depth to the Chinese path. Read the original if you want a short, official-line account of how the Two Integrations is being framed as a cultural theory of Chinese modernization.

Collaborative innovation between specialist-course education and ideological and political theory course education from the perspective of curriculum-based ideological and political education 课程思政视域下专业课教育与思政课教育的协同创新 Ren Menglei Ren Menglei takes up a practical problem in Chinese university teaching: how specialist (professional) courses and the compulsory ideological and political theory courses can move 'in the same direction and together' under the policy of curriculum-based ideological and political education. Ren argues that some current practice wrongly treats the policy as 'specialist course plus political course', or tries to turn one type of course into the other. The thesis is that genuine coordination rests on the structural differences between the two kinds of course, aiming at 'harmony without uniformity' and at a combined force for fostering virtue and cultivating talent. The article has three parts. The first examines the 'heterogeneity' of the two course types, reviewing scholarly definitions of curriculum-based ideological and political education and the misconceptions that Ren says have appeared in practice. The second turns to teachers as the main agents of reform. The third turns to teachers and students together, using Nankai University's 'four togethers' model, virtual-reality classrooms, case-sharing platforms and feedback mechanisms as examples. Ren's core claim is that value is already embedded in knowledge, so bolting a few 'values' onto a specialist lesson is counterproductive. Reform therefore means drawing out the values inside each discipline's knowledge system, and building a Chinese independent knowledge system, while ideological and political theory courses build a complete scientific system of their own. Ren assigns the two types different strengths. Political theory courses are compulsory, reach all students and provide explicit, systematic Marxist education. Specialist courses reach fixed groups of students and offer implicit, tailored education. Teachers should share cases, borrow methods from each other (small-group seminars, a 'grand historical view', the chip-technology example) and keep value formation, knowledge transmission and ability building unified. Ren adds that students are active agents who internalise values, so their sense of gain should be a key measure of success. Ren concludes that the two reforms must interlock in a spiral, not run as parallel lines, or the 'two skins' problem will persist. Course design should replace simple stacking of resources with sensible sequencing, and teacher–student feedback should be routine. Reform is not an end in itself: its purpose is to foster virtue and cultivate people. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of how university teachers are urged to coordinate political theory courses and specialist courses, including Nankai's practices and the VR classroom debate.

The fourfold transcendence of Chinese modernization as the modernization of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature 人与自然和谐共生的中国式现代化的四重超越 Yan Xiaofeng Zhang Yanhong Taking up the 20th Party Congress (2022) statement that Chinese modernization is a modernization of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature, Yan Xiaofeng and Zhang Yanhong ask how it differs from the Western path. They argue that it surpasses Western modernization on four levels: the view of nature, value stance, global governance and practical model. In their reading, it amounts to socialist modernization transcending capitalist modernization and offers a theoretical form and practical template for resolving what they call the institutional ecological crisis of the West. The article is organised into four sections, one for each level, and each ends with a summary contrast with the West. It draws on Descartes, the Enlightenment, Marx's theory of metabolism between humans and nature, Lenin on raw materials and colonies, and classical Chinese thinkers such as Mencius, Zhuangzi and Xunzi. It also reviews Western "deep green" and "light green" currents, ecological modernization, and Chinese policy examples such as the Belt and Road Initiative and carbon targets. The authors' central move is to trace Western ecological failure to capital's logic of accumulation. On the view of nature, they say Western dualism and anthropocentrism treat nature as capital's "tap" and "raw-material store", and that both green currents stay within this dualism. Chinese modernization instead rests on the "life community" idea, which they present as joining Marxist ecological thought with the traditional view of the unity of heaven and humanity. On values, they hold that capital exploits both nature and workers, while Chinese modernization is people-centred. On global governance, they describe Western "eco-imperialism", which shifts pollution and resource extraction onto developing countries, and contrast it with a community with a shared future for mankind and common but differentiated responsibilities. On practice, they say Western ecological governance never challenges capitalist institutions, whereas socialist ecological civilization integrates green development into economic, political, cultural and social construction. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization overcomes dualism, capital-centredness, hegemony and one-sidedness. They call it an original Chinese contribution to world modernization and civilization, and a path for developing countries towards green, low-carbon and sustainable development. They say it shows the institutional superiority of socialism in ecological civilization. Read the original if you want a systematic statement of the official Chinese case that Chinese modernization is ecologically distinct from, and superior to, Western modernization.

Creating the cultural form of Chinese modernization 创造中国式现代化的文化形态 Yang Geng Yang Geng asks what cultural form Chinese modernization should take and how it is to be created. Writing in the Party-school newspaper Study Times (8 July 2024), Yang argues that the new culture produced by the Second Integration, joining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, is that cultural form. In this account the Second Integration makes Marxism Chinese and makes traditional culture modern, and the cultural form unites the spirit of the times with the spirit of the nation. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first sets out the theoretical basis and the guiding standard for combining Marxism with traditional culture. The second deals with absorbing new research results from Marxism outside China. The third addresses how this cultural form should embody the common values of all humanity. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on passages from Marx. Yang's central reasoning is that the combination is possible because the two traditions share points of convergence, which Xi Jinping calls a high degree of mutual compatibility. Yang adds that traditional ethics concern human relations, which are social relations, and that the further the feudal order recedes, the weaker the ideological character of traditional culture becomes. Because tradition has a dual character, the combination also requires separating its essence from its dross. What to inherit and what to transform, Yang says, depends on the practice of Chinese modernization, not on Marxism or tradition alone. On foreign Marxism, Yang holds that Western Marxist cultural critique, covering cultural hegemony, the culture industry and postcolonial theory, helps in understanding capitalist modernity and its culture. Yang says it should be studied critically, neither rejected wholesale nor copied, and then localised. Yang concludes that the new cultural form must reflect China's core values and the essential features of socialism, and also the common values of humanity: peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom. Yang presents this as consistent with building a community with a shared future for mankind and as a way to create a new form of human civilization. The author calls for a new cultural mission in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists connect the Second Integration, foreign Marxism and universal values in discussing Chinese modernization.

The value implications of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的价值意蕴 He Zhonghua This newspaper commentary asks what is at stake in building a "modern civilization of the Chinese nation", a task the author links to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, Chinese modernization and the creation of a "new form of human civilization". He Zhonghua argues that this is an ongoing, open-ended process with deep historical roots, and that its value lies in showing that a civilization grounded in national particularity can modernise without copying the West. The article is organised in three parts. The first presents the Chinese nation's modern civilization as opening new possibilities for a new form of human civilization. The second treats it as the objective marker of national rejuvenation. The third holds that Chinese modernization is the only path by which it can be built. He draws throughout on Marx, Engels and Hegel, and on classical Chinese sources. In the first part, He recounts, through Marx and Engels, the achievements and costs of capitalist civilization, namely ecological crisis and conflict among people. He contends that shifting from industrial to ecological civilization is needed for a new form of civilization, and that the Chinese case offers a route that is not the Western one. In the second part, he argues that the West modernised by returning to its classical heritage, so that China's modernization is likewise a renewal of its own tradition. Drawing on Marx's remarks on the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, he concludes that, in a world-historical setting, the decisive criterion of rejuvenation is the successful construction of this civilization. In the third part, He diagnoses the "dialectic of enlightenment" in the West, where reason produces both the discovery and the loss of the human being. He sets against it Chinese ideas such as "Dao follows nature" and an introspective way of understanding the person, which he says guard against reification. Chinese modernization is also socialist, owing to the adapting of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. He concludes that Chinese modernization can largely avoid the "terrible vicissitudes" of Western capitalist modernization. It must still draw critically on all human achievements, including science and technology, while keeping tension between history and morality, reason and value, and lawfulness and purposiveness. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese philosopher uses classical Marxist texts and Chinese tradition to justify the idea of a distinctive Chinese modern civilization.

Strengthening the reach and influence of Chinese civilization 增强中华文明传播力影响力 Liu Xiaoxin This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts, takes up the requirement in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to strengthen the reach and influence of Chinese civilization, together with Xi Jinping's October 2023 instruction on propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Liu Xiaoxin argues that this task is central to cultural confidence, to China's international discourse power and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Telling China's story well, in Liu's account, is the way to achieve it. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the task matters. The second says what stories should be told: those of traditional culture, of Chinese modernization and of the Communist Party. The third turns to practical capacity-building in international communication, covering the discourse system, communication platforms, think tanks and professional education. Liu argues that stronger international communication supports cultural confidence, gives China a voice commensurate with its overall national strength, and promotes dialogue among civilizations. Liu presents the community with a shared future for mankind as respecting civilizational diversity rather than imposing one civilization on others. On content, Liu says traditional culture should show China as a peace-loving, responsible power. Chinese modernization is described as a new form of human civilization that differs from the Western model and widens the options open to developing countries. Liu also wants the Party's history and character explained abroad in order to correct what the article calls overseas prejudice. On capacity, Liu calls for a strategic communication system with distinctive Chinese features. It would include leading new-type mainstream media, differentiated messaging for regional and specific audiences, and a role for overseas Chinese, Chinese enterprises and foreign friends.
