Liu also calls for 5G-enabled platforms and short-video and mobile formats, as well as regionally distributed think tanks and a dedicated academic discipline for international communication. Liu stresses speaking to audiences on equal and candid terms and finding common ground with them. Read the original if you want an example of how official Party-line writing links cultural confidence, discourse power and media strategy in China's international communication agenda.

Engels and the English working class 恩格斯与英国工人阶级 Paul Blackledge This is a Chinese translation of an excerpt from Paul Blackledge's book Friedrich Engels and Modern Social and Political Theory (2019). It takes up a paradox: critics who separate Engels's mature work from Marx's thought, the "Marx–Engels opposition" thesis, still praise The Condition of the Working Class in England. Blackledge argues that the book is continuous with the Marx–Engels worldview of The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto, so praising it while condemning Engels's later writings is incoherent. The chapter first surveys admirers and detractors of the 1845 book, from Henderson and Chaloner to Hobsbawm, McLellan, Carver and Gilbert. It then traces Engels's earlier writings: the Letters from the Wuppertal, his articles on English domestic crises, the London letters and the critique of Carlyle in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. Finally it works through the book's themes of industrialisation, humanism, gender, Malthusianism, Chartism and revolution, and closes with Marx's and Engels's later self-criticisms. Blackledge reads the book as an internal strategic guide for the German left, not an academic study. In his account, Engels grounds socialism in the workers' own movement against existing conditions, not in an ideology brought from outside. He credits Engels with seeing trade unions and strikes as training grounds for revolution. He also credits Engels with treating the state as a capitalist structure and law as a whip prepared by the bourgeoisie. Blackledge notes that Engels traces the 'surplus population' to the capitalist trade cycle, not to nature as Malthus did, and sees drunkenness and crime as products of social conditions. Blackledge concedes that the book is still marked by a youthful humanism and some fatalism. Its closing hope that communism might soften an otherwise bloody revolution, and its prediction of imminent revolution in England, reflect Engels's not yet fully Marxist outlook. Engels and Marx overcame these weaknesses in 1845 by breaking with socialist moralism, mechanical materialism and political fatalism. Blackledge concludes that the book is a foundation, not an aberration, of their shared view, which weakens attempts to draw a line between Marx and Engels. Read the original if you want a defence of Engels's early work against the Marx–Engels opposition thesis, or a guide to the scholarly debate over the book.

The "Fengqiao experience": Mao Zedong's governance philosophy and wisdom and its contemporary development “枫桥经验”：毛泽东治国理政的理念与智慧及其当代发展 Zhou Zhongzhi Zhou Zhongzhi asks what the "Fengqiao experience" reveals about Mao Zedong's approach to governing China, and why it still matters. Zhou argues that Mao's endorsement of this grassroots model (resolving conflicts locally and not passing them upward) expressed a coherent governance outlook. In Zhou's account, that outlook remains productive in the twenty-first century and has theoretical and practical value for Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first places the Fengqiao experience in Mao's writings of 1956–57, "On the Ten Major Relationships" and "On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People", and recounts how Mao praised the 1963 practice in Fengqiao, Zhuji, Zhejiang, and ordered it promoted nationally. The second reads the experience against traditional Chinese culture, in particular the joint rule of virtue and law and the people-as-foundation idea. The third follows it from Mao to Xi Jinping and sets out its current form. Zhou's central claim is that Mao's governance joined a "big picture" of top-level design with a "centre of gravity downward" in grassroots work. Three supports are named: dialectical analysis in which contradictions of different kinds can be transformed, so that negative factors become positive ones; the mass line, "from the masses, to the masses"; and continuity with the Chinese tradition. Zhou reads the village rules and mediation work in Fengqiao as modern forms of virtue-and-law governance, and the grassroots emphasis as an update of the people-as-foundation idea. For the present, Zhou cites the Party's 19th Central Committee Fourth Plenum and the 20th Party Congress (2022), and says the experience now rests on combining self-governance, rule of law and rule by virtue, and on uniting human effort with technology. Zhou concludes that, given external pressure and domestic risks, the Fengqiao experience is more urgent than before as a way to resolve risks at source and strengthen the base of state governance. Digital tools bring efficiency and fine-grained management, but Zhou warns that they cannot replace face-to-face work with the masses, because online-only contact breeds bureaucratism and formalism. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese account of how Party scholarship links Mao-era grassroots governance to Xi Jinping-era social governance and to claims about traditional culture.

Advancing Chinese modernization requires continually consolidating cultural subjectivity 推进中国式现代化要不断巩固文化主体性 Tong Ping Lei Bingjie Tong Ping and Lei Bingjie take up the claim that "the Integrations have consolidated cultural subjectivity", which they present as a major thesis about the deep roots needed to build a modern Chinese civilisation. Their answer is that Chinese modernization depends on continually strengthening cultural subjectivity, which they treat as the source of cultural confidence and a basis for building ideological and cultural strength. This is a Party-school commentary for a Party journal. The article has three parts. The first argues that consolidating cultural subjectivity is a requirement of the new journey. The second sets out the scientific meaning of the concept, using its foundation, core and underlying tone. The third lists the fundamental requirements for consolidating it. These are Party leadership and the guiding role of Marxism, the core socialist values, deeper reform of the cultural system, and a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. The authors argue that cultural subjectivity deepens the cultural base of Chinese modernization and builds a socialist ideology with strong cohesion. In their account it also protects cultural security, since they hold that losing cultural autonomy and confidence is the greatest cultural-security problem. They define its foundation as conscious awareness of and deep identification with one's own culture. Its core is the autonomous capacity to carry forward, develop and transform that culture, which they say is neither closed nor arrogant. Its underlying tone is ideological: they hold that every cultural system's character is set by its ideological attributes. They state that claims of value neutrality carry political purposes, and they warn that neglecting this leads to the loss of cultural leadership and discourse power under Western discursive hegemony. A culture that disarms itself, they say, would become a dependent "follower". The authors conclude that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Two Integrations and the Party's cultural leadership must guide the cultural work of the new era. They add that the core socialist values should draw on the creativity of the people, and that cultural reform should put social benefits first. Philosophy and social science should build Chinese discourse and contribute Chinese wisdom on shared human problems. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school writers present cultural subjectivity, ideology and cultural security as parts of Chinese modernization.

In Chinese modernization, people's livelihood comes first 中国式现代化民生为大 Zhang Yuanxin Taking as its starting point Xi Jinping's remark during an April 2024 inspection in Chongqing that "in Chinese modernization, people's livelihood comes first", this commentary asks why livelihood (minsheng) is central to Chinese modernization and what that requires in practice. Zhang Yuanxin argues that the principle fixes the value orientation and goal of Chinese modernization and marks it off from Western modernization. The article presents this as having both theoretical and practical significance for pursuing Chinese modernization through high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first explains why Chinese modernization must put livelihood first, drawing on the nature of the Party and of the socialist system. The second sets out the livelihood content of the goal, stated at the 20th Party Congress (2022), of building a modern socialist country by the middle of the century. The third turns to practical requirements for the new era. In the first part, Zhang reasons that the Party's founding purpose, original aspiration, ideals and mass line all commit a modernization it leads to serve the people. Socialism with Chinese characteristics, through its guiding ideology, political leadership, basic institutions, emphasis on developing the productive forces and commitment to fairness, is said to supply the guarantees for improving livelihood. Zhang contrasts this with Western modernization, which the author describes as capital-centred and as producing wide wealth gaps and polarisation. In the second part, five goals are tied to livelihood: common prosperity, the people being masters of the country, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, social harmony and stability, and harmony between humanity and nature. The third part recommends meeting people's aspirations for a better life, addressing urgent concerns in education, employment, income distribution, social security and health, and holding the bottom line while prioritising key groups and regions. Zhang concludes that livelihood work should do its best while acting within the country's means, advance step by step and persistently, combine Party leadership with popular participation and shared benefits, and tilt resources toward rural areas, the west and disadvantaged groups to narrow gaps. The text is a Party-theory commentary that restates and organises current official positions rather than adding new empirical material. Read the original if you want a compact view of how official Party scholarship links livelihood policy to the Party's nature, the socialist system and the contrast with Western modernization.

Keep advancing Chinese modernization on the new journey of the new era 新时代新征程上把中国式现代化不断推向前进 Management Committee of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (Chinese Academy of Governance) Published in Qiushi (2024, no. 13) under the name of the Party School's management committee, this is an authoritative study-and-implementation piece rather than a research article. It argues that Chinese modernization is the central task of the Party and state, and that completing it requires guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and Xi's statements on Chinese modernization. The text has three parts. The first reviews how, in the new era, the Party led the people to advance and extend Chinese modernization in understanding, strategy and practice. The second presents Xi's statements as a scientific guide: Party leadership, the Chinese characteristics, essential requirements and major principles, the handling of major relationships, great struggle, and a new form of human civilization. The third sets out four tasks: deepening reform, high-quality development, raising cadres' capabilities, and implementation. The article contends that Xi's discourse has begun to form a theoretical system of Chinese modernization, which it says enriches Marxist modernization theory and breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization. It sorts the content into five Chinese characteristics (what it is), nine essential requirements (what to do) and five major principles (how to do it). It presents Party leadership, backed by the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, as decisive for the direction and success of the project. It lists paired relationships to be balanced, such as top-level design and local exploration, efficiency and fairness, and vitality and order, and calls for a spirit of struggle against external pressure. In its account, Western-led modernization has left some imitating countries in political turmoil, economic stagnation and social division, whereas Chinese modernization offers a path for the Global South and a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization is the only correct road to national strength and rejuvenation. They call for deepening reform, pursuing high-quality development in line with the new development philosophy, developing new quality productive forces according to local conditions, training officials, and carrying out decisions with a nail-driving spirit. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party's own training institution frames Chinese modernization in mid-2024, including its official structure of characteristics, requirements and principles.

Self-education as practical wisdom in ideological and political education Three modes: knowledge, method and value 论作为思想政治教育实践智慧的自我教育样态 Yu Ying Yu Ying asks how self-education should be understood within ideological and political education, against a background of modernity in which people are drawn into other people's worlds and logics and lose sight of their own problems. Existing scholarship, the author says, treats self-education mainly as a methodological matter, either as a body of method knowledge or as an implementation technique. Yu argues instead that self-education is a form of practical wisdom that unites theoretical and practical reason, and that it has three practical modes: knowledge rooted in action, method that reproduces concrete situations, and value grounded in the subject's own reflection. The article is a theoretical essay in four sections. The first three take each mode in turn, each time criticising two prevailing approaches. The fourth section is a conclusion that places the argument in the setting of globalisation and industrial modernity. Yu draws on Confucius, Mencius and Wang Yangming's unity of knowing and doing, on Marx and Engels's "real human beings", and on Gadamer's account of the humanities. In the first move, Yu argues that empiricist and borrowing-oriented approaches both stress "a priori knowledge" of ideological and political education and overlook practical knowledge. Understanding the field is gained through lived experience in action, and self-education turns knowledge into wisdom through "unity of knowing and doing". In the second, Yu traces the "instrumental" and "technical" views of method to scientism. Drawing on Gadamer, the author holds that the meaning-world of human beings cannot be fully quantified, so self-education cannot be a standardised procedure. It is a method wisdom exercised according to time, person and circumstance, and it starts from the learner's own life world. In the third, Yu treats the value of ideological and political education as a relation to the needs of the educated subject. Needs vary, but Yu says they are social and share a common core, which is the improvement of political-ideological and moral quality. Classroom indicators such as attendance, the author suggests, do not capture this. Students must test and choose values themselves. Yu concludes that political-ideological and moral quality cannot be produced by an "industrial logic" of efficiency and standardisation, which leaves people "one-dimensional". Self-education should therefore be seen as an integrated capacity of knowledge, method and value, not as a tool for educating oneself. It would preserve "self-awakening" and the drive to self-realisation, and an orientation towards the true, the good and the beautiful. Read the original if you work on the theory or pedagogy of ideological and political education in China and want to see how current scholarship draws on practical wisdom, hermeneutics and Marxist concepts of the person.

Modernization alone is not enough; what matters more is the "Chinese-style" path A critical assessment of Jiang Tingfu's A History of Modern China 只讲现代化是不够的，更重要的是“中国式” Wang Xianming Liu Yanhong Prompted by a student's question about why Jiang Tingfu's A History of Modern China (1938), which narrates modern Chinese history around modernization, is praised by some and dismissed by others, Wang Xianming and Liu Yanhong offer a critical assessment. They argue that the book has real academic merits and lasting appeal, but that its theoretical framework is heavily Westernized and that it has two serious political flaws. In the authors' view, talking only about modernization is insufficient: the correct path and the right leadership matter more. The article opens with the book's publication history. Jiang wrote it in Wuhan in 1938 and described it as a preliminary report. The authors say it was out of favour after 1949, then reissued in dozens of editions since reform and opening up, and gradually elevated to a pioneering masterpiece. They note that contemporaries such as Cao Juren did not rank it among the three best works on the period. The authors then set out three parts: why the book has drawn long-term attention, why its framework is Westernized, and what its political defects are. On its appeal, the authors credit four features: the "Jiang Tingfu question" (can China modernize?), a simple structure built around four rescue plans (self-strengthening, the reform movement, the Boxers, Sun Yat-sen's programme), a comparative global setting including Japan, Russia and Turkey, and accessible prose. They contend, however, that its recent popularity mainly reflects the rise of Western modernization thinking, and that some use a "modernization paradigm" to displace the revolutionary narrative guided by historical materialism. Wang and Liu argue that Jiang equates modernization with Westernization, draws on Western-centrism and the "stagnant China" thesis of Hegel and H. B. Morse, and echoes imperialist justifications, for instance in treating Mongol and Manchu rule as invasions and describing China as an imperialist power. Politically, they link the book to the Kuomintang-backed Yiwen Research Society, whose leaders later defected to Japan, and say its "science first" logic amounts to defeatism. They also fault it for placing hopes of national rejuvenation in Chiang Kai-shek while disparaging the Communists. The authors conclude that Jiang the historian lacked sufficient moral and intellectual judgement. In their account, a semi-colonial, semi-feudal country could neither resist imperialism nor industrialize without a popular anti-imperialist, anti-feudal revolution. They close with Jiang's later quarrel with his former student John K. Fairbank, who adopted his paradigm but rejected his anti-Communist politics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of a widely reissued history, and of the modernization paradigm in modern Chinese historiography.

From development philosophy to form of civilization: the evolution of terminology and knowledge production in Chinese modernization 从发展理念到文明形态：中国式现代化的术语演进与知识生产 Zhang Mingzhi Zhang Mingzhi asks how the vocabulary of modernization in China has evolved, and how Chinese modernization, as a body of practice, produces a distinctive discourse, knowledge system and channels of communication for the wider world. The article argues that the shift from the "two civilizations" to the five-sphere overall plan, together with the new development philosophy, has given Chinese modernization its own character and opened what the author calls a new form of human civilization. The article has three main parts. The first traces the terminology from the "four modernizations" through the 1978 truth-criterion debate and the evolving reform goals to the Five-sphere Integrated Plan (economic, political, cultural, social and ecological construction). The second reads Chinese modernization through the new development philosophy, covering its essential attributes and its "new era" features. The third treats knowledge production, an autonomous knowledge system, international communication and civilizational significance, before closing with directions for future research. Zhang's central move is to treat development concepts as products of practice that then guide it. Chinese modernization is presented as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. Its core is common prosperity and a people-centred approach, and its outward character is peaceful, open and shared. The author sets this against a Western path driven by capital, which is said to produce class polarisation, a "centre–periphery" structure and ecological crisis. A second move links the new development stage, new development philosophy and new development pattern, with innovation and new quality productive forces as the main driver. Zhang then argues that the practice yields original concepts and narratives, offers developing countries an alternative to Western modernization and gives world socialism a new form. The author claims that this undermines the "end of history" thesis and the "clash of civilizations" thesis. In the conclusion, Zhang holds that traditional Western modernization theory cannot explain Chinese modernization and that the classics offer no ready answer. Four tasks follow for research: more rigorous concepts and terms, a wider range of methods (including AI-based modelling of discourse), a systematic autonomous knowledge system, and shared values. The author also calls for stronger international discourse power and for East–West dialogue mechanisms. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars frame modernization terminology, the new development philosophy and the building of an "autonomous knowledge system" as a theoretical project.

Soft narratives of historical nihilism: endogenous mechanisms and countermeasures 历史虚无主义软性叙事：内生机制与应对策略 Luo Hongjie Luo Hongjie takes up a shift in how historical nihilism, which the article treats as a harmful erroneous trend and a political problem, is spread. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping has repeatedly called for resisting it openly, and scholars and mainstream media have criticised it widely. Luo argues that, with digital technology, it has moved from "hard" to "soft" and from explicit to implicit narratives, which makes it harder to recognise and more likely to be believed. The article sets out to describe these forms, explain how they work and propose responses. The article moves in four steps. It first identifies two shifts: from grand narratives to micro-level "playful retellings" (personal memoirs, trivial details), and from abstract sophistry to embodied, audiovisual "performance" (short videos, newly compiled histories). It then describes four soft forms: everyday agenda-setting, emotive discourse, covert images and immersive audio-visual embedding. Next it analyses three internal mechanisms, and finally it sets out countermeasures. For the mechanisms, Luo proposes a sequence of "concealment–attraction", "consumption–stirring" and "interpellation–alienation". Nihilist content attaches to media that are easy to hide in and attractive, such as memes, short videos, games and murder-mystery role-play. Consumption then moves audiences from receiving to accepting the content. Drawing on Althusser's notion of interpellation, Luo holds that repeated exposure turns spontaneous reactions into conscious ones. Audiences are then "alienated" in their values and view of history, and become carriers of the trend themselves. Examples include the claim that burning the soldier Qiu Shaoyun alive contradicts physiology, jokes about Lu Xun's portrait and game versions of historical figures. Luo's response has three parts: effective identification, rational criticism and active construction. Identification means reviewing topics, discourse, images and audio-visual content, including platform screening and regulation of films, lyrics and games. Criticism means refuting the essence, the implicit mechanism and typical cases. Construction means establishing a Marxist view of history and a scientific view of "perceptual activity", and building the mainstream ideology's own soft narrative system at national, institutional and individual levels. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars frame digital media, popular culture and ideological work in the fight against historical nihilism.

Putting people's livelihood first: a key guideline for Chinese modernization 民生为大：中国式现代化的重要遵循 Pan Xun Cui Jianxi This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's remark during an inspection in Chongqing on 22 April 2024 that in Chinese modernization, "people's livelihood comes first" (民生为大). Pan Xun and Cui Jianxi argue that the statement clarifies the essential character of Chinese modernization as people-centred, identifies what decides its success or failure, and sets out a practical guideline for it. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces how livelihood expresses the 'people first' nature of Chinese modernization, through the Party's century-long history, the Marxist view of the people, and the need to meet the people's growing aspiration for a better life. The second examines livelihood as the key to the direction, mission and outcome of modernization. The third derives three practical principles. On the first two points, the authors read the Party's history from its 1921 programme to the new era as a continuous effort to realise modernization for the people's wellbeing. They contend that Chinese modernization has broken the 'modernization equals Westernization' myth and gone beyond Western modernization's logic of capital by following a human-centred logic. They link livelihood to the national mission of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to common prosperity, citing figures that rural per capita disposable income in poor areas rose from 6,079 to 12,588 yuan between 2013 and 2020. For practice, the authors call for strengthening primary-level Party organisations and grassroots governance so that livelihood projects reach people concretely, citing the 255,000 village-based work teams of the poverty-alleviation campaign. They also call for improving livelihood through development, treating better living standards as a measure of development, and relying on the people as the driving force of history. They present this as the Party's value stance and a code of action for modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary connects Xi's livelihood remarks to Marxist theory and Party history.

A theoretical analysis of new quality productive forces and paths for cultivating them 新质生产力的学理分析与培育路径 Cheng Enfu Liu Meiping Since Xi Jinping first raised the term in Heilongjiang in September 2023, "new quality productive forces" has become a central economic concept. Cheng Enfu and Liu Meiping take up three questions: what the concept means, what institutional conditions it requires, and how it can be cultivated. Their answer is that new quality productive forces are defined by new production factors, new science and technology, and strategic new industries. They say these can develop properly only within socialist relations of production under Party leadership. The article is organised in three main parts. The first analyses new quality productive forces along the three dimensions of factors, technology and industry. The second discusses the relations of production that support them: the dialectic between productive forces and socialist relations of production, the roles of government and market, and state-owned enterprises. The third sets out cultivation paths: new mechanisms, new fields of application, and a peaceful world environment. A short conclusion follows. On factors, the authors argue that information, data and networks have become core production factors. In their account these factors produce "intelligent labourers" and a digital economy that can steer traditional factors, including capital. On technology, they hold that new quality productive forces arise from cultural, institutional, basic-science and industrial revolutions together, and that frontier basic research is the source of original innovation. They say China needs a full group of high technologies, to be developed through a new national system, to resist external "chokehold" pressures. On relations of production, they hold that public ownership as the mainstay, a government that regulates markets, and strong state-owned enterprises keep capital under control and guide the new forces towards common prosperity. They cite platform monopolies and the real-estate sector as areas needing regulation, and Huawei's Mate60 Pro and its 5.5G chips as evidence of industrial upgrading. The authors also argue that war and the "new imperialism" obstruct new quality productive forces, while these forces in turn promote just exchange and peace. They conclude that new quality productive forces are the most important route to Chinese modernization and to catching up with the developed West. They call for Party leadership, full use of the socialist economic system, and coordination of new factors, technologies and industries. Read the original if you want a political-economy reading of new quality productive forces that links technology and industrial policy to public ownership, state enterprises and anti-hegemony arguments.

Lenin's critique of non-Marxist currents of thought in Russia and its implications for contemporary China 列宁对俄国非马克思主义思潮的批判及其对当代中国的启示 Jia Shupin Jia Shupin asks how Lenin identified and refuted the non-Marxist currents that flourished in Russia around the turn of the twentieth century, and what this offers China today. The article argues that such currents typically present themselves as 'developing' Marxism, which makes them more deceptive. Studying Lenin's critique, in Jia's view, helps in recognising the harm of present-day currents in a complex ideological struggle. The article has three parts. The first describes four currents the author treats as Russian variants of Bernstein's revisionism: Menshevism, economism, Narodism (populism) and Machism. The second sets out Lenin's criticism of each. The third draws lessons for contemporary China. Jia reads Lenin's critiques as defences of Marxism's organisational, political, economic and philosophical foundations. Against the Mensheviks, Lenin upheld a centralised party of committed members, with democratic centralism in place of a loose, self-governing association. Against the economists, he argued that socialist consciousness must be 'instilled' from outside the spontaneous labour movement by an organisation of revolutionaries. Against the Narodniks, he held that capitalism's development in Russia was objectively necessary and historically progressive, and against Mach's followers he defended the partisanship of philosophy and the primacy of matter. Jia adds that Lenin kept the party close to the masses, warning that separation from them was among its gravest dangers. For China, Jia calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position and the Party's leadership over ideology and culture, drawing on the lessons of the Soviet collapse. The author names historical nihilism, neo-liberalism, the 'end of ideology' thesis and online-driven currents as threats. Jia proposes better discernment among social trends, firm and open rebuttal of erroneous views, and stronger theoretical education, including study of the 'Four Histories' and of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal draws on Lenin's polemics to frame current ideological work.

The essence of law: examining the relations between law, state and society Rereading Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right 法的本质：从法与国家及社会关系 层面进行的审视 Xiong Guangqing Xiong Guangqing asks what Marx's early Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right reveals about the essence of law. The author argues that earlier readings often overlooked Marx's legal concerns, and that the work is Marx's first exploration of the nature of law. In Xiong's account, it marks the start of his critique of bourgeois legal thought and a turn towards historical and dialectical materialism. The article reads the text from a legal angle, drawing also on philosophy and political science. After a section on Hegel's Philosophy of Right and Marx's reasons for criticising it, four parts follow. They treat the relation of state and society, the class character of the state, the internal links among law, state and society, and the state as the embodiment of class and civil society. Xiong draws on the Introduction to the Critique, the Communist Manifesto, The German Ideology and Engels to show how Marx's views developed. Xiong's central claim is that Marx corrected Hegel's inversion of the relation between state and civil society. Hegel derived the state from the absolute Idea. Marx held instead that family and civil society are the presuppositions of the state, which in the author's reading establishes law's objectivity. Xiong then argues that Marx exposed the class nature of the Prussian state and of Hegel's defence of constitutional monarchy, since the state protects private property and law expresses the will of the ruling class. Marx's treatment of monarchy, bureaucracy and legislature as unreconciled elements of the state is read as showing law's material determination. Law, in this reading, is a product of class and society, conditioned by material life and not a tool the ruling class can use at will. Xiong concludes that the work set the intellectual foundation for Marxist theory and for Marx's later deepening of his account of law. It also helped move Marx from revolutionary democracy towards communism. The author highlights Marx's preference for democracy, in which the people create the constitution and popular sovereignty is realised, and reads it as pointing towards a "new state system", which Xiong identifies with the dictatorship of the proletariat. Read the original if you study the early Marx, Marxist jurisprudence or Chinese scholarly readings of the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right.

The Way of China: a philosophical interpretation of the outstanding characteristics of Chinese civilization 中华之道：中华文明突出特性的哲学阐释 Zhang Zhiqiang Zhang Zhiqiang takes up the five "outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilization named by Xi Jinping at the 2023 symposium on cultural inheritance and development: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. The article argues that these are not a loose list of traits but the law of development of Chinese civilization, which Zhang calls "the Way of China". Zhang presents the Way of China as both the result of Chinese history and the premise that keeps generating China. The text is the introduction to Zhang's 2024 book of the same title. The article first sets out why five characteristics, and why in this order, and proposes that they form three pairs: continuity and innovation, unity and inclusiveness, inclusiveness and peacefulness. It then takes each characteristic in turn, drawing on classical sources such as the Book of Changes, the Gongyang Commentary, the Doctrine of the Mean and the Book of Rites, as well as on Qian Mu and Fei Xiaotong. A closing section ties the argument to the Second Integration, building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, and the future of world civilization. Zhang's central move is to read continuity as the continuity of a unified historical subject. Through the notion of "tongji" (thread-gathering), legitimate succession and the state form are said to unify time, so that continuity and innovation presuppose each other as change and constancy, or the one and the many. Zhang links innovation to the Book of Changes idea of "casting off the old and taking up the new" and to the Party's self-reform. Unity is traced to the "great unity" tradition and to the ideal of "all under heaven as one family", and inclusiveness to the ethic of conscientiousness and reciprocity ("zhong-shu"). Zhang claims this ethic produces "common values", which differ from "universal values" in the way they are established: through mutual communication rather than by one side imposing them. Zhang contrasts a worldview of heaven and humanity as one with Western subject–object opposition and monotheism, and attributes peacefulness to the same cosmology, citing the absence of expansion and colonial plunder in Chinese history. Zhang concludes that adapting Marxism to Chinese tradition means using Marxist principles to activate these characteristics and bring out the laws of Chinese civilization. A modern civilization of the Chinese nation must therefore modernize all five and discard none of them. Zhang adds that such a civilization would not replace other civilizations with a single one, but would help form a larger community of human civilizations, a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated scholar derives Xi Jinping's five characteristics from classical Chinese philosophy and links them to the Second Integration.

The inner drivers, methods and laws of theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化理论创新的内在动因、方法和规律 Wang Gang Wang Gang asks what drives theoretical innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which methods achieve it, and which laws it follows. The article answers that innovation is driven internally by practice, problem-orientation and the Party's mission. It is carried out through methodological requirements and governed by three laws. Wang treats the three as unified: drivers supply the impetus, methods the path, laws the direction of development. The article has three parts, written in 2024 and published in a journal on ideological and political education. The first part treats the drivers across the Party's history, from the new-democratic revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The second sets out methodological requirements. The third formulates the laws of innovation. Wang repeatedly maps Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era onto this scheme. On drivers, Wang argues that each stage of Chinese practice posed questions the classic authors could not have met. Each also posed a defining question of its age, and the Party's mission as a Marxist "mission-oriented party" spurred it to answer them. On method, Wang stresses upholding fundamental principles while innovating, which means holding to Marxism as the "soul" and to fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". The article presents the Two Integrations and the "six musts" from the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the basic guide, and it adds systematization and scholarly grounding of theory as an internal requirement. On laws, Wang names three: the dialectical unity of upholding and developing Marxism, with dogmatism and pragmatism as the two errors to avoid; the positive interaction of theoretical and practical innovation; and learning from the creativity of the people. Wang concludes that the three sets of factors are mutually unified and jointly advance the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article treats the Party's mission and tasks as without limit, so theoretical innovation too has no end. It calls for following the mass line in theory-building, on the grounds that the people's practice is the inexhaustible source of theory. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present the logic, methods and regularities of theoretical innovation from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping.

The threefold logic and pathways of coordinated urban–rural development from the perspective of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化视角下城乡协调发展的三重逻辑与推进路径 Zhou Shaojie Zhong Xiaoping The article asks how urban–rural relations can be coordinated within Chinese modernization, and why coordination must precede integration. Zhou and Zhong argue that coordinated development is the precondition for urban–rural integration, and that the main weakness still lies in the countryside. Their answer is that comprehensive rural revitalization, rather than integration alone, is the strategic basis for narrowing the urban–rural gap. The study is organised around three "logics". The theoretical logic draws on Marx's account of urban–rural opposition and on the "synchronised development of the Four Modernizations" (industrialization, urbanization, informatization, agricultural modernization), alongside rural revitalization and the drive to build a strong agricultural country. The historical logic traces policy-driven phases from the planned-economy division of the two sectors to the present push for integration. The practical logic identifies six current difficulties, and the final section proposes seven pathways. Zhou and Zhong's central claim is that outside forces (industry supporting agriculture, cities leading the countryside) must combine with the countryside's own endogenous momentum. Using statistics, they report that the urban–rural income ratio fell from 2.88 in 2012 to 2.39 in 2023, but that the absolute gap widened from 15,738 to 30,130 yuan. They also report that inequality within the rural population exceeds that in towns, and that rural pension levels are far below urban ones. The six difficulties are weak county economies, thin village collective economies, rural ageing and a weakened farm workforce, and a fragile rural industrial system in which smallholders struggle to reach large markets. The authors also stress that revitalization cannot save every village and must follow population trends and local conditions. The authors propose invigorating county economies, strengthening village collective and cooperative economies, raising farmers' employability, innovating rural investment mechanisms, raising rural social security (including a large rise in the basic pension minimum by 2025), and improving rural governance under Party leadership. They present this as essential to common prosperity and to a modernized socialist country. Read the original if you want a data-rich, policy-oriented account of China's urban–rural gap and the measures an academic policy analyst proposes to close it.

Reflections on the development of part-time teachers of ideological and political theory courses in universities under the "Big Ideological and Political Course" initiative From role identity, knowledge production and professional identity “大思政课”背景下高校思政课兼职教师发展现状的若干思考 Zhang Nan Zhang Nan asks how part-time teachers of university ideological and political theory courses ("sizheng ke") are coping with their new position as the "Big Ideological and Political Course" policy expands their ranks. The article is an empirical study based on educational narrative. It argues that these teachers face difficulties in three linked areas: role, knowledge and professional identity. Zhang proposes that these can be eased by recognising the value of "practical knowledge" and by building stronger organisational support. The article opens with the policy background: Xi Jinping's 2021 remarks on the "Big Ideological and Political Course", the 2022 work plan issued by ten ministries, and Ministry of Education figures cited by the author, according to which part-time staff were 32.68 per cent of 106,411 such teachers in November 2021. The study draws on 20 valid interviewees from an initial 25. They are university counsellors, Party and administrative heads of departments, industry professionals and teaching staff from other subjects, drawn from four types of institution. Data came from semi-structured interviews, classroom observation and teaching documents. Three main sections follow: role, knowledge and professional identity. On role, Zhang uses role theory (Mead, Merton's "role set") to describe overload from combining a main job with part-time teaching, and confusion over whether to teach as administrator or as educator. One interviewee uses "role reminders" to manage this. Zhang argues that unclear institutional expectations of part-time staff deepen this confusion, and that teachers' own convictions and supportive organisations help build role identity. On knowledge, Zhang draws on distinctions between essentialist and non-essentialist views of knowledge, and between theoretical and practical knowledge. In this reading, part-time teachers' experience can count as practical knowledge only if it is reflected on and turned into public teaching resources, through dialogue with full-time colleagues and critical reflection. On professional identity, Zhang finds that counsellors adapt more easily, while industry professionals feel isolated and under greater pressure to master theory. Zhang concludes that universities should convert part-time teachers' practical experience into rational, teachable knowledge. They should also treat these teachers as an integral part of the "Big Ideological and Political Course" framework, not as a numerical supplement. The proposed measures are collaborative teaching models between full-time and part-time teachers, stronger group belonging and self-identity, and supporting platforms for training and exchange. Read the original if you want interview-based evidence on how part-time ideological and political teachers describe their work, or if you study teacher development in Chinese higher education.

Comparing the "two systems": three patterns of modernization theory and practice “两制”比较：现代化理论与现代化实践的三种样态 Zheng Yifan Zhou Miao Zheng Yifan and Zhou Miao ask how modernization theory and practice have developed under capitalism and socialism, and what this means for Chinese modernization. They argue that modernization since the Industrial Revolution has taken three forms: capitalist early-starting predatory, capitalist late-starting dependent, and socialist late-starting independent. In their account, capitalist modernization was flawed from the outset and is exposed in the third wave of modernization, while Chinese modernization is presented as the leading example of the socialist independent type. The article first reviews theory in three parts: post-1945 Western development economics (structuralist and neoclassical), the social-development thought of Marx, Engels and Lenin, and the radical left tradition of dependency theory and world-systems analysis. It then examines the practice of capitalist modernization, using Britain, France, the United States, Germany and Japan as predatory early starters and South Korea as a dependent case. Finally it turns to socialist independent modernization, taking the Soviet experience from the New Economic Policy to the five-year plans, and then China's path. The authors argue that structuralists and neoclassicals differ on the role of the market but share a class standpoint, since neither touches the question of ownership. Radical thinkers such as Paul Baran, Samir Amin and Immanuel Wallerstein, by contrast, belong to the Marxist paradigm and criticise the capitalist order. Drawing on Marx and Lenin, the authors define "predation" as unequal value transfer and colonial exploitation, and dependence as control of a country's economy, politics, culture and military by international finance capital. They cite South Korea's chaebol, foreign shareholding and US military command as evidence. They hold that public ownership and foreign-trade monopoly allowed the Soviet Union to modernise without plunder or foreign loans, and attribute its collapse to the degeneration of the Soviet Communist Party rather than to the Soviet model. For China, the authors identify four features of its independent path: strengthening Party leadership through self-reform, a people-centred orientation, theoretical innovation through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and independence and self-reliance. They conclude that only adherence to socialism can produce independent modernization. They also warn against copying Western models. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist typology of modernization that links dependency and world-systems theory to official accounts of Chinese modernization and the Soviet experience.

The elements, structure, distinctive features and systematic construction of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的要素结构、显著特征与系统建设 Luo Liang Responding to Xi Jinping's call, at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation as a new cultural mission, Luo Liang asks three questions: what this civilization is, what is distinctive about it, and how it should be built. The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2024, answers by treating the civilization as a complex system whose elements, relations, structure and functions can be analysed in turn. The text has three parts. The first sets out the system's element structure: five component civilizations, four pairs of relations, three structural levels and four functions. The second identifies four distinctive features. The third proposes construction paths organised around three system properties, which Luo calls self-activation, self-emergence and self-adaptation. In Luo's account, the five components are a material civilization of high-quality development, a political civilization of the people being masters of the country, a spiritual civilization of all-round human development, a social civilization that brings benefits to the people, and an ecological civilization of harmony between humanity and nature. The relations are tradition and modernity, upholding fundamental principles and innovation, the real and the virtual, and the local and the global. The structure comprises an ontological layer (civilizational thinking and existence), a categorial layer (ideas, artefacts, conduct, institutions) and an operational layer (cultivation, practice, creation). The functions are continuing the national spiritual lineage, the cultural lineage, the root lineage of traditional culture, and the soul lineage of Marxism. The four features are dynamism through casting off the old and establishing the new, unity of group and self, inward cohesion and wholeness, and an inclusive openness. Luo contrasts the last two with what the article describes as a capitalist hegemonic logic of Western-centrism. For construction, Luo calls for Party leadership at every level, the Two Integrations and socialist core values as the basis of practice, and evaluation by the people's interests. The article also urges strengthening the civilization's communication, influence and guiding power internationally, and its adaptation to global pluralism, digitalization, civilizational conflict and rival domestic currents of thought, which it says must be countered under Marxist guidance. Read the original if you want a systematic, system-theory framing of how official discourse conceptualises the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, with its component parts and proposed construction tasks.

Beyond "labelling" and bias A reflection on the abuse of the authoritarianism paradigm in Western political science 超越“标签化”与偏见 Lin Yi Wang Qiaochu Lin Yi and Wang Qiaochu ask why Western political science has so persistently classed non-Western political systems as "authoritarian", and what Chinese scholarship should do about it. Taking the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2022 Democracy Index as a starting point, they argue that the "authoritarianism" paradigm has become a standardised, prejudiced label that serves ideological competition more than analysis. The authors hold that Chinese scholars must move beyond it and build indigenous concepts if they are to explain Chinese modernization on its own terms. The article has three main parts. The first describes how overseas scholars apply the label (centralised authority, elections that fail liberal-democratic standards, state will placed above citizens' rights) and how the notion of "authoritarian resilience" explains survival within the same frame. The second traces the paradigm's abuse and its conceptual and theoretical roots in political development theory, the "transition paradigm" and the "democracy/non-democracy" dichotomy. The third sets out the political context and intellectual lineage behind the paradigm and then proposes alternatives. The core argument is that "authoritarianism" is a residual category between totalitarianism and democracy, defined against a Western liberal benchmark. Lin and Wang note that sub-concepts such as "fragmented", "competitive" or "participatory" authoritarianism pair a pejorative noun with neutral or favourable adjectives, which they read as patching a concept that cannot explain real achievements. They add that the "grey zone" of hybrid regimes shows the dichotomy's blind spots, that the third wave of democratization ended in reversals in many transition states, and that the label has been stretched even to Western cases such as the Trump administration. In their account, scholars such as Larry Diamond reveal how democracy itself is being ideologised and "exported" to protect Western international standing. The authors conclude that the paradigm fails both as theory and as description, and that democracy has many forms, so no single standard can define it. For Chinese political studies they propose four lines of work: the Second Integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, systematic study of the experience of the People's Republic, critical but creative borrowing from Western discourse, and a firm socialist orientation centred on the people. They also call for turning local concepts into discourse able to compete with Western ones. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic critique of the "authoritarianism" label in Western political science and the case for an indigenous political-science discourse.

Creative transformation and innovative development of China's fine traditional virtues in the new era 新时代中华优秀传统美德的创造性转化创新性发展 Xiao Guiqing Long Zhengwu Xiao Guiqing and Long Zhengwu ask how China's fine traditional virtues can be turned into something suited to the new era. Taking Xi Jinping's statements as their starting point, they argue that creative transformation and innovative development of these virtues must rest on the historical position of the new era and on the Two Integrations. The result, they say, should carry Chinese characteristics, style and manner. The article has three parts. The first sets out why inheriting traditional virtues matters: as the ethical basis of the Two Integrations, as spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and as a store of governing wisdom for the Party. The second divides the virtues into six levels: personal character, family virtues, professional ethics, public morality, virtue in government, and virtue in foreign relations. The third sets out a scientific attitude and method for inheritance. The authors' central claim is that traditional virtue and Marxism fit together closely, so that inheriting the first is part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Ideas such as 'the world belongs to all' and 'the people as the foundation of the state' are said to match communist ideals and the principle of putting the people first. At each level the authors pair a traditional virtue with a present-day practice: moral exemplars, family-conduct campaigns, honesty in a market economy, rural civility and poverty alleviation, the Party's self-reform and consultative democracy, and the Belt and Road Initiative. They also say that traditional virtue nourishes the core socialist values. On method, the authors call for critical inheritance guided by a Marxist view of ethics. They cite Engels that no universal morality fits all eras and peoples, and they urge keeping what is vital while discarding dross. They also insist on a people-centred stance, on using stories and moral models, and on avoiding doctrinaire indoctrination so that virtues are internalised as real values. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party theorists connect Confucian-era ethics, the core socialist values and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

Integrating the great founding spirit of the Party into university ideological and political courses: value, content design and practical strategies 伟大建党精神融入高校思政课教学的价值意蕴、内容设计与实践策略 Ruan Yifan Wu Dongyan How should the great founding spirit of the Party be brought into university ideological and political theory courses? Ruan and Wu argue that this spirit embodies the Party's original aspiration and mission, and so is a rich ideological and teaching resource. Their thesis is that it should be integrated through precise content selection, systematic design and a coordinated set of practical measures, in order to raise its educational effect and meet the goal of cultivating new-era young people. The article has three parts. The first sets out the value of integration: fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, safeguarding ideological security in universities, and deepening students' feelings for family and country. The second assigns content to each of the five core courses. The third proposes practical strategies, organised around systematic design, "three guarantees" and "six methods". In the authors' design, each course highlights one "logic" of the spirit. The basic principles of Marxism course explains its theoretical logic. The two courses on Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought explain its practical logic, with stress on the Two Integrations. The modern Chinese history course covers its historical logic, and the ethics and rule of law course covers its value logic, following a progression from knowledge to emotion, will, belief and action. Practice is built on three guarantees: management, teaching staff and evaluation. The six methods are standard textbooks, digital technology, case teaching, practical teaching activities, new media and immersive teaching with red culture and art. Ruan and Wu conclude that the spirit should be woven into the "big ideological and political course" pattern. This would link classroom, campus and society, relying on official policy documents, red educational resources, trained and part-time teachers, and clear evaluation standards. They present this as a way to strengthen students' political, ideological, theoretical and emotional identification with the Party. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party-history themes are mapped onto the five required university courses and the teaching methods proposed for them.

Practical paths for integrating excellent traditional Chinese culture into ideological and political education 中华优秀传统文化融入思想政治教育的实践路径 Wang Zengfu Wang Zengfu asks how excellent traditional Chinese culture can be built into ideological and political education in practice. The article holds that the two share an inherent fit, since both aim to cultivate patriotic feeling, sound character and cultural confidence. Wang argues that integration is both an urgent requirement for passing on traditional culture and a means of making ideological and political education more effective. The article sets out to answer three questions: what to integrate, who integrates it, and how. The article proposes five practical paths. These are systematically drawing out the educational resources in traditional culture; raising the traditional-culture literacy of those who carry out ideological and political education; building a graded chain of courses according to the principle of differentiated audiences; using digital technology to renew the technical and environmental carriers of integration; and establishing an evaluation mechanism. Wang places the whole programme under the Two Integrations and the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. On resources, Wang argues that selection must be guided by Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people as the foundation of the state" are said to fit the values of scientific socialism. They are to be transformed creatively and developed innovatively under the leadership of core socialist values, with the aim of cultivating mainstream values. On people and courses, Wang calls for teachers, responsible units, families, schools and society to work together. Wang also criticises "forced integration" that ignores audience differences and "loose links" between school stages, and proposes a sequence from primary school to university that links theory with practice and ideological-political courses with course-embedded ideological education. On digital technology, Wang points to storage, vivid presentation, shared resources and real-time feedback, plus immersive virtual and augmented reality, all within a secure campus culture. Wang concludes that evaluation should involve many parties and combine top-down guidance with bottom-up participation. It should use indicators that are complete, dynamic and differentiated, cover the whole cycle before, during and after teaching, and be updated continuously. Wang says this would strengthen learners' cultural identity and confidence and advance the high-quality development of ideological and political education in the new era. Read the original if you work on ideological and political education in China and want a detailed, policy-oriented framework for curriculum design, digital carriers and evaluation.

The dialectical logic of the development of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的辩证发展逻辑 Wang Jie Wang Jie asks how Chinese modernization should be understood in light of the dialectic of universality and particularity in contradiction. The article argues that, seen as universal, Chinese modernization shares historical, theoretical and practical continuity with the modernization of the Chinese nation, of socialist countries and of human society. Seen as particular, it has distinctive advantages and features that drive the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and offer a Chinese experience and Chinese approach to others. The article is organised in four parts. The first three each set Chinese modernization against one of the three larger processes: the Chinese nation's modernization efforts since the Opium War, the modernization of socialist states since the October Revolution, and world modernization. In each, Wang separates what Chinese modernization shares from what is new in it. A fourth part draws out its significance for Chinese, socialist and human civilization. In the first part, Wang traces over a century of exploration at the levels of material objects and industry, institutions and culture. Against this background, Chinese modernization is said to reach a new height through four features: a more advanced leading class, broad mass mobilisation under the Communist Party, comprehensive content, and a distinct path. In the second part, it is placed within the socialist modernizations that began from backwardness, relied on public ownership and a proletarian party, and faced competition from capitalism. Its innovations are the socialist market economy, support for the non-public sector alongside a stronger public sector, and distribution that breaks with egalitarianism. In the third part, it follows general laws, such as technology, industrialisation and markets. Wang adds five particular features: huge scale, "parallel" rather than sequential development, a people-centred orientation, peaceful development, and a socialist direction. Wang concludes that Chinese modernization continues and renews Chinese civilization and defends and confirms socialism against the "end of history" thesis associated with Fukuyama. It also enriches the forms of human modernization. In the author's account, it shows that developing countries can find a path that does not depend on developed countries and suits their own conditions. Read the original if you want a systematic official-style account of how Chinese modernization is positioned against national, socialist and global histories.

How human liberation generates enormous momentum for modernization 论人的解放何以催生巨大的现代化动力 Wu Zhongmin Wu Zhongmin asks how the historical tide of "human liberation" produces the driving force of modernization, and what limits that liberation needs. Wu defines liberation as the rise of people's practical and cognitive capacities with modern science and productive forces, which frees them from the constraints of traditional society. The article argues that without it modernization has no momentum, but that liberation can slip out of control and must be given reasonable boundaries. The article has four sections. Three examine the sources of momentum: the autonomy of society's members, the wide space for their activity, and their growing needs. The fourth sets out four limits. Wu contrasts traditional and modern society throughout, drawing on medieval Europe and traditional China. Marx supplies much of the framework, and Xi Jinping's statements are cited on Chinese modernization. In the first section, Wu argues that modern values of freedom and equality replace dependence with autonomous behaviour. Its features are independence, stronger self-interest, rationality and competitiveness, which the market economy rewards through distribution by contribution. The second section holds that large-scale social mobility, openness to the outside world, wider choice, more exchange and better cooperation raise creativity. Wu cites patent filings, including a rise in Chinese resident filings from 25,346 in 2000 to 1,344,817 in 2020. The third section claims rising needs push the economy up through successive sectors, from agriculture to industry to services. Wu then identifies four boundaries: liberation must not outrun the stage of productive forces, capital must not grow "wildly", materialistic demand must not dominate spiritual and cultural needs, and the ecological environment must not be damaged. Wu presents these as conditions for healthy, lasting momentum and for the goal of free and all-round human development. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Marxist ideas of human emancipation are linked to Chinese modernization and its stated limits.

New quality productive forces and national competitive advantage: inner logic and strategic priorities 新质生产力与国家竞争优势：内在逻辑与战略重点 Zhou Wen Yang Zhengyuan Zhou Wen and Yang Zhengyuan ask how new quality productive forces can be turned into lasting national competitive advantage as the new round of technological and industrial revolution deepens and great-power rivalry intensifies. They argue that, unlike the incremental innovation of traditional productive forces, new quality productive forces rest on disruptive innovation. Their logical starting point, in the authors' view, is rebuilding independent innovation capacity through an organic combination of government and market. The article has four parts. It first treats productive-force progress as the decisive factor in national advantage, contrasting incremental innovation (the expansion of existing stock) with disruptive innovation (the reconstruction of increments), with historical cases from Portugal and Spain, Britain's steam power and the United States' electrification. It then presents industrial competition as the modern form of rivalry between states. Next it criticises three theoretical misconceptions, and it ends with four strategic breakthroughs. The authors draw on Smith, Marx, Porter, Freeman, Acemoglu and Robinson, Stiglitz and others. The authors say that new quality productive forces mean original, disruptive breakthroughs, "from 0 to 1", rather than marginal technical improvement. Developed countries, they contend, protect patents and restrict technology cooperation, which forces developing countries to rely on independent innovation. Drawing on Freeman, Wen Yi and others, they hold that state action is needed to supply infrastructure and overcome market gaps. The three misconceptions are: full marketisation, as in institutionalist economics and the Latin American case; industrial hollowing-out and over-financialisation, which they analyse with Marx's account of credit and fictitious capital; and static comparative advantage, which they say locks developing countries into the middle and lower links of value chains. They cite US semiconductor controls as an example. The authors propose four priorities: building a new-type whole-nation system (xinxing juguo tizhi) that combines government and market and links science, industry and finance; integrating the digital and real economies, with platform regulation and anti-monopoly enforcement; building a modern industrial system that climbs to the middle and upper reaches of global value chains while safeguarding supply-chain security; and creating world-class enterprises, with state-owned firms as sources of original technology and private "little giants" in close cooperation. Read the original if you want to see how a Fudan political-economy team links new quality productive forces to industrial policy, technological rivalry and critiques of Western development theory.

The distinctive advantages of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的独特优势 Chen Congkai This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2024, asks what makes Chinese modernization distinctive and why this path could only have emerged in China. Chen Congkai argues that its advantages can be understood from cultural, historical, theoretical and practical angles, and sets out six: strong leadership, a distinctive cultural tradition, theoretical innovation, a people-centred value orientation, ecological civilization values, and a contribution to world peace. The piece is organised as six short sections, each pairing a feature of Chinese modernization with a contrast to Western modernization. It draws on speeches by Xi Jinping, on the five features of Chinese modernization named in official discourse, on Marx and Engels, and on Thomas Piketty's work on inequality. It also cites figures on forest cover and a list of twentieth-century pollution incidents in the West. Chen's central claim is that leadership by the Communist Party of China determines the nature, direction and momentum of modernization, whereas Western parties are described as offering slogans, short-term promises and a rotation of power controlled by large capital. The author traces each of the five features to Chinese traditional ideas such as 'harmony between humanity and nature' and 'enriching the people', and presents the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the theoretical guide. Chen contrasts a people-centred path, which is said to have eliminated absolute poverty, with a capital-centred Western path marked by rising inequality and a 'pollute first, clean up later' model. The article concludes that Chinese modernization pursues peaceful development, has no record of foreign aggression or colonies in the author's account, and offers an alternative to equating modernization with Westernization. Chen presents it as an opportunity for countries that want to develop without dependence, and as a step towards a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official-line commentary summarises the claimed advantages of Chinese modernization against a Western comparison.

Some theoretical questions on the formation and development of new quality productive forces 新质生产力形成与发展的若干理论问题 Hou Weimin Hou Weimin takes up the category of new quality productive forces, put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023 and endorsed by the Central Economic Work Conference (2023), and asks how it should be understood in theory and how it should be built in practice. Hou argues that the concept extends Marxist productive-force theory and answers the needs of a new stage of Chinese modernization. In Hou's view, it must be read through Marx's own texts, and its formation depends on state-led, publicly owned economic power. The article has four parts. It first separates the essential definition of new quality productive forces from their concrete forms, comparing Marx's "new productive forces", labour productive power and the subject–object relation. It then identifies three theoretical breakthroughs. The third part treats the new relations of production that fit these forces, and the fourth sets out the leading role of the state-owned economy. Hou draws throughout on Marx's Grundrisse, Capital, The German Ideology and letters, and on Xi's statements. Hou holds that Marx's "new productive forces" refer to qualitative change in total productive power tied to a change of social formation. The Chinese concept instead stresses the advanced quality of particular factors of production. A scientific discovery or invention is not a productive force until it is embodied in material means of production and absorbed into social production, so the concept cannot be reduced to technological determinism or to higher labour productivity. Hou counts data, computing power and artificial intelligence as new factors that extend the concept. On the relations of production, Hou argues that new quality productive forces call only for adjustments within direct production, not a change of social formation. These adjustments cover exchange and distribution, stable regulation of labour relations and the training of innovative talent. Hou concludes that public ownership should lead the process. Marx's remark that freedom depends on whether productive forces belong to the people is read as support for state-owned capital's decisive role. Hou says state-owned enterprises have greater cooperative productive power, and calls for state control of large digital platforms, state-led AI regulation, heavier state investment and policy support. Hou rejects the view that private firms are the main vehicle, and the proposal to capitalise labour-power through new share schemes. Read the original if you want a Marxist-political-economy argument, closely tied to Marx's texts, for a state-owned-economy-centred reading of new quality productive forces.

Can the West escape the crisis of neoliberalism? 西方能否摆脱新自由主义危机 Dai Weilai Dai Weilai asks whether the West can escape the crisis of neoliberalism, rebuild the international order and keep its dominant position. This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, argues that neoliberalism, which has shaped US economic policy since the 1970s, now faces crises in the economic, social and political spheres. Dai holds that escaping them will not be easy. The article first sets out the three crises in turn: the crisis of the free market, of social values and of political consensus. It then turns to the Biden administration's response at home and to its attempt to reshape the global order. On the economy, Dai argues that financial deregulation fed speculation, hollowed out industry and produced financialisation, and that the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic exposed the limits of self-regulating markets. Dai describes neoliberal "freedom" as freedom for capital owners to set rules in their own favour, and cites wealth inequality, protest movements and polarised politics as signs of lost consensus. The article reads the "New Washington Consensus" set out by Jake Sullivan in April 2023 as an end to neoliberal foreign policy. In Dai's account, it combines industrial policy, public investment, welfare expansion and labour protection at home with protectionism, high-technology barriers and a more fragmented global order abroad. Dai concludes that neoliberalism, presented as a "universal value", must change profoundly. The question, Dai writes, is also one of how Western values will be repositioned in a changing social order. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of how the US shift away from neoliberalism is being interpreted.

Hou Wailu's three identities in exploring the sinicization of Marxism 侯外庐探索马克思主义中国化的三重身份 Yuan Zhiwei How did the historian Hou Wailu approach the adaptation of Marxism to China? Yuan Zhiwei argues that Hou pursued it along three paths, revolution, historiography and thought, and so combined the identities of revolutionary, historian and thinker. In Yuan's reading, these three identities explain the purpose and the scholarly contribution of Hou's history writing. The piece appeared in the China Social Sciences Daily in November 2023. The article is organised around the three identities. It first looks at Hou as a revolutionary who "fought with the pen", then as a historian who sought truth for practical use, and finally as a thinker who explored the future of Chinese culture. Yuan draws on Hou's biography, from his student activism and contact with Li Dazhao to his translation work and wartime editing, and on his studies of Chinese thought and society from the Shang-Zhou transition to the early twentieth century. As a revolutionary, Yuan says, Hou joined the Communist-led national salvation movement and the New Democratic Revolution. He co-translated the first volume of Capital with Wang Sihua in 1936. Yuan holds that his scholarship was meant to supply historical grounds for the revolution and for Marxism's spread in China. As a historian, Hou built a "trinity" of economics, philosophy and history and combined social history with the history of thought. He also required a world-historical, comparative outlook, summed up as "a world perspective, Chinese problems". As a thinker, Yuan argues, Hou criticised the autocratic, religious and land-nationalising features of traditional thought while valuing its materialist, atheist and anti-despotic strands. He judged that Chinese tradition lacked an internal dynamic of self-transformation and needed scientific Marxism as a new cultural force. Yuan concludes that Hou's aim was to "ask after the future way out of Chinese culture", that is, to find answers for China's independence, prosperity and the liberation of the Chinese nation. In this account Hou also tried to build confidence in a Chinese scholarly paradigm grounded in historical materialism. Yuan says these experiences still offer theoretical reference for current discussion of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and of Chinese culture's direction.
