Read the original if you want a concise, sympathetic overview of Hou Wailu's career and method as a case of Marxist historiography in China.

Can the West escape the crisis of neoliberalism? 西方能否摆脱新自由主义危机 Dai Weilai Dai Weilai asks whether the West can escape the crisis of neoliberalism, rebuild the international order and keep its dominant position. This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, argues that neoliberalism, which has dominated US economic policy since the 1970s, now faces crises in three areas: the economy, society and politics. In Dai's view, escaping it will not be easy. The article first sets out the three crises: the failure of the free market, a crisis of social values and a collapse of political consensus. It then turns to the US response, both at home and in the international order, and ends by placing neoliberalism within the longer history of Western political thought. Dai argues that deregulated finance produced speculation, hollowed-out industry and rising inequality. The article cites a record "misery index", stagnant incomes for the bottom 90 per cent and protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street. It also describes political polarisation, with left and right both attacking neoliberalism. Dai reads the "new Washington consensus", which national security adviser Jake Sullivan outlined in April 2023, as a turn towards industrial policy, state-led development, labour protection and protectionism. The article presents this as a US attempt to restore its hegemony. According to Dai, it will diversify global economic policy, sharpen competition, put a "iron curtain" around high-technology trade and make cooperation on issues such as climate harder, while the rise of developing countries redistributes power. Dai concludes that neoliberalism, presented as a "universal value", cannot avoid crisis as social practice changes, and must undergo deep adjustment. Whether the West can escape is, in this view, a question about repositioning Western values in an evolving social order, not only about its political-economic system. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of the US shift away from neoliberalism.

"Rules-based" as a discursive trap of the United States and the West 基于规则”是美西方的话语陷阱 Wang Lei Wang Lei takes up the phrase "rules-based international order", which US and Western leaders use frequently. The commentary argues that these leaders are not defending international rules. In Wang's reading, the phrase carries a set of Western values and calculated self-interest. The piece first sketches the historical record. It runs from the Westphalian system through the Vienna, Berlin, Versailles–Washington and Yalta systems, which Wang describes as orders "based on power". It then covers the post-1945 UN-centred system and the post-Cold War promotion of the "Washington Consensus". It ends with the shift of power from West to East and from North to South. Wang argues that the vagueness of "rules" suits US instrumental needs, because international law would bind the United States. In this account, the United States subordinates international law to its "rules", reshapes them pragmatically (for example a "new Washington Consensus"), and applies them selectively. Wang cites three points: US non-participation in key multilateral treaties, policies at odds with general principles of international law, and the "trimming" of law in the name of rules. On this view the formula erodes the unity and authority of international law, and the United States becomes its "number one destroyer". It also divides friends from foes, labelling China and Russia "revisionist". Wang presents China as a firm defender of an order based on international law. Rules should be made jointly, serve public-goods values, and apply to all without exceptionalism or double standards. Only a return to such an order, together with reform of international law, would bring lasting peace and development, in Wang's view. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary criticises the "rules-based order" concept and sets it against international law.

The inner paradox of neoliberalism's anomalous survival 新自由主义反常存续的内在悖论 Chen Xuefei Neoliberalism is blamed for the Asian and Latin American crises of the 1990s and the US financial crisis of 2007–2008, yet it did not perish and has become the ideology of mainstream Western parties. Chen Xuefei asks why it persists and argues that this survival is anomalous. In Chen's view it has not resolved neoliberalism's underlying difficulties but deepened the internal crisis of modern Western society, so it cannot last. This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, traces neoliberalism genealogically. It moves from mercantilism and French physiocracy to classical liberalism, then to the two post-war neoliberalisms, German ordoliberalism and American neoliberalism, before turning to their domestic and international effects. Chen's central claim is that liberal governance has always carried a paradox between freedom and security: freedom must be produced and managed at once. Ordoliberalism made security subordinate to the freedom of market competition, and American neoliberalism pushed this furthest. It recast the population as human capital, treated every person as an enterprise, applied economic analysis to marriage, family and politics, and made the market a tribunal judging government. Domestically, Chen argues, the interest mechanism worsens the Matthew effect in income and wealth, and measures such as minimum-income schemes or pandemic relief protect freedom rather than the population. Internationally, Chen calls neoliberalism a new imperialism that globalises North Atlantic standards. Chen concludes that neoliberalism's persistence reflects not vitality or universality but the shelving of its own paradox by states that have become containers for global capital. Placing the freedom mechanism above everything else serves the hegemonic expansion of globalised capitalism and deepens Western society's crisis. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese critical genealogy of neoliberalism that draws on Foucault-style governmentality analysis.

The path and method by which Mao Zedong created the philosophical system of "practice theory" 毛泽东创立“实践论”哲学体系的路径与方法 Li Weiwu Li Weiwu asks how Mao Zedong created the philosophical system of "practice theory" (shijianlun), which the article treats as the core of Mao Zedong Thought. The author sets out to trace the stages of exploration, the logical links between them and the research method involved. The thesis is that the system arose from the needs of the Chinese revolution and was built step by step, moving from concrete reality to philosophical abstraction and back to concrete reality. The article is organised as six sections that follow Mao's path in order. It begins with the problem of the relation between the universal truth of Marxism and China's concrete conditions, which Mao met in rural investigation in the 1920s and 1930s and in the anti-dogmatist struggle within the Party. It then covers the materialist-dialectics movement in Shanghai and Beijing around 1930, his reading notes on Soviet textbooks, the 1937 lecture outline, and the texts "On Practice" and "On Contradiction". It ends with the 1943 decision on leadership methods and Mao's wartime writings on military, revolutionary and state theory. Li makes three main moves. First, Mao shifted the emphasis of dialectical materialism from ontology, the focus of Ai Siqi and Li Da, to epistemology, because his opponent was now dogmatism within the Party. Li argues that he justified this through Lenin's unity of dialectics, epistemology and logic. Second, the core is built from the concept of "social practice" and two formulas: "practice–cognition–practice" and "particular–general–particular". Mao's 1943 mass line, "from the masses, to the masses", adds a third formula, "masses–leadership–masses". Li reads this as folding historical materialism and political philosophy into the system, with collective subjects of cognition. Third, Mao derived a methodology from the system, the principles of "hitting the target with the arrow" and "seeking truth from facts". Li argues this produced a Chinese Marxist military theory (On Protracted War), a theory of revolution and a theory of the state (New Democracy). Li concludes that the system was not created at a stroke. In his account it answered the question of universal truth and Chinese reality in both theory and practice, and it armed the Party and the masses for victory in the revolution. He presents it as a model of adapting Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context that still guides that task in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based reconstruction of how Mao's philosophical writings of the 1930s and 1940s fit together and how a leading Chinese philosopher interprets them.

Building a modern Chinese civilisation requires firmly grasping both the "root" and the "soul" 建设中华民族现代文明要牢牢把握“根脉”和“魂脉” Li Jie Li Jie takes up Xi Jinping's goal, set out at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, of building a modern Chinese civilisation. Li asks what direction that work should take and argues that it rests on two lines of continuity: Marxism as the "soul vein" (hunmai) and excellent traditional Chinese culture as the "root vein" (genmai). The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, takes both from Xi's remark at the 20th Political Bureau's sixth collective study session that neither can be abandoned. The article has three parts. The first treats traditional culture as the root, placing it within China's 5,000-year history, the humiliations after 1840 and the Party's present aim of a culturally strong socialist country. The second treats Marxism as the soul, through the Two Integrations. The third sets out three questions on which, Li says, "political clarity" is needed: how to understand Chinese civilisation, Marxism, and the Two Integrations. In the first part, Li argues that cultural confidence, which the article calls more basic and more lasting than other forms of confidence, is needed to resist what Li calls a Western view of civilisation. In Li's account, that view treats Western modernity as the only modern civilisation and so confuses plurality with unity and equality with hierarchy. Li contrasts it with China's openness and inclusiveness, which Li sees as matching Marxism's own openness. In the second part, Li presents the First Integration (Marxism with China's concrete realities) and the Second Integration (Marxism with traditional culture) as two sides of one process. Li says traditional values such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the root of the state" fit scientific socialist values. Li concludes that without Marxism, modern civilisation lacks a soul and head, and without tradition it lacks a foundation and feet. Li holds that the Two Integrations are the necessary path to a modern civilisation. In this account they rest on mutual fit, produce "a new cultural life form", and consolidate cultural subjectivity, which Li sees embodied in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Li describes Chinese civilisation as continuous, innovative, unified, inclusive and peaceful. On that basis Li says it follows that China will go its own way, and that national unity is the core of China's core interests. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian ties the Two Integrations to the root-and-soul metaphor and to the project of a modern Chinese civilisation.

Advancing the building of a modern Chinese civilization through research on the history of Chinese civilization 以中华文明史研究推动中华民族现代文明建设 Chen Shilong This newspaper commentary, published in June 2024, asks how research on the history of Chinese civilization should serve the building of a modern civilization of the Chinese nation, which Xi Jinping named a new cultural mission. Chen argues that history as a discipline should take this goal as its central task in the new era. The article defines civilization as the sum of material, spiritual and institutional achievements. It then sets out four tasks: the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization, scholarly explanation of civilization's "five outstanding characteristics", mutual learning among civilizations, and new ways of writing civilizational history. On origins, Chen holds that the usual checklist of writing, bronzes, cities and ritual centres cannot fit every civilization. The author endorses the "Chinese approach" to civilizational criteria developed by the origins project: productive growth and cities, class differentiation, and kingship and the state. On the five characteristics (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness), Chen calls for combining archaeology with documents and breaking the topic into case studies, such as the shift from mixed commandery-and-kingdom rule to commanderies and counties, or the coexistence of Song, Liao and Jin regimes. Chen also wants a civilizational history guided by historical materialism, with a holistic view, multidisciplinary work, and room for agricultural, steppe and maritime civilizations. Chen concludes that building a modern civilization means creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional culture, not a return to the past. Research should identify positive and modern elements in Chinese institutions and thought, strengthen historical consciousness and cultural confidence, and supply intellectual resources for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short statement of how an archaeologist at CASS links civilization studies to current cultural policy.

The value of Mao Zedong Thought in China–Africa diplomatic practice 毛泽东思想在中非外交实践中的价值意蕴 He Jian Liu Shuaijun He Jian and Liu Shuaijun ask how Mao Zedong Thought, and the diplomatic thinking within it, shaped China–Africa relations in the Mao era and what value it retains today. They argue that Mao's foreign-policy ideas guided the move from almost no contact to a relationship of mutual support. In their view these ideas have historical, theoretical and contemporary value, and they still offer guidance for present-day China–Africa ties. The article has three parts. The first traces the history of China–Africa relations in four stages: early Chinese awareness of Africa before 1949, tentative contacts in 1949–54, the 1955 Bandung Conference, and aid and China's return to the United Nations in 1956–76. The second examines four strands of Mao's thinking: the three diplomatic guidelines of the early 1950s, the 'intermediate zone' idea, the international peace united front, and the theory of the three worlds. The third turns to the value of this legacy today. The authors read each strand as raising Africa's place in China's strategy. Mao's 'intermediate zone' formulations of the 1940s–50s and 1960s, they say, first gave Africa a conceptual place, then made it a force China could unite with. The peace united front, expressed in the Bandung principle of 'seeking common ground while setting aside differences', is presented as the basis for equal, non-interfering relations. Chinese aid, cited at about 7.7 billion yuan from the 1950s to the 1970s, is credited with winning political support. The authors note that 16 of the 23 sponsors of the 1971 UN resolution, and 26 of the 76 states voting in favour, were African. They also interpret the three-worlds theory as an application of dialectical materialism and as a rebuilding of China's international discourse power. The authors conclude that Mao-era thinking on national interest, independence and peaceful coexistence still helps China read the international situation and place itself within it. They describe the 'community with a shared future for mankind' as inheriting and going beyond Mao's diplomacy, and as moving China–Africa ties from 'all-weather friends' towards a China–Africa community with a shared future. They also hold that China's response to the 'two overall situations' draws on this legacy. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Mao-era diplomatic doctrine is linked to China–Africa policy and to current foreign-policy discourse.

The basic core, main features and value implications of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的基本内核、主要特征与价值意蕴 Li Mengyun Taking up Xi Jinping's call at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development to "build the modern civilization of the Chinese nation", Li Mengyun asks what this civilization consists of, how it is characterised and why it matters. The article argues that it is a Marxist-guided civilizational form with modern value orientations, rooted in fine traditional Chinese culture and carried forward through Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic core of the concept, the second its main features, and the third its value implications. Li draws on Hegel's distinction between what is actual and what merely exists, on Marx and Engels, and on Xi's speeches. The article also refers to earlier scholarship on the concept's theoretical emergence, philosophical narrative and practical exploration. On the core, Li argues that "modern" refers to a civilization's nature as well as its time. Western capitalist civilization, in Li's account, merely "exists" and lacks necessity, whereas the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is actual, inheriting and transforming the past while bearing the future. Its core has four elements: Marxism as guiding theory, fine traditional culture as intellectual root, Chinese modernization as practical basis, and the modernization of the human being as its value aim. Li identifies four features: inheritance, a people-centred character, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Western modern civilization is described as driven by the logic of capital and alienation, which the Chinese form is said to surpass. Li presents four implications: continuing the Chinese historical cultural line, gathering strength for building a modern socialist country, advancing the Second Integration, and taking on the mission of constructing a new form of human civilization. The author contends that the project strengthens cultural confidence, helps coordinate material and cultural-ethical progress, and offers developing countries an alternative to the Western single model. Li also criticises Western theories of a "clash of civilizations" and civilizational superiority. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account of how this concept is justified from Marxist and traditional sources, including its positioning against the West.

The historic contribution of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义政治经济学的历史性贡献 Zhang Yu Zhang Yu asks what the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics has contributed to the development of Marxist political economy. The article argues that it has taken Marxist political economy, and especially its socialist branch, to a new stage. In Zhang's account, four features mark this advance: a distinct subjectivity, prominent originality, a complete system, and a rich body of theoretical results that state general principles. The article first traces how Marxist political economy divides into a capitalist part rooted in Capital and a socialist part. It then follows the Chinese line: Mao Zedong's call to learn from the Soviet Union but find a separate path, the market-oriented reforms after reform and opening up, and Xi Jinping Thought on the economy since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Four sections follow, one for each feature. The first section covers the sources of subjectivity. The second lists some fifteen original theories. The third compares the traditional socialist economics textbook with the Chinese system. The fourth deals with the relation between the particular and the universal. Zhang contends that the theory has subjectivity because of theoretical self-awareness, a distinctive economic form, a Marxist worldview and method, and practical achievements. Western economics is described as an ideologically loaded summary of Western experience, to be borrowed from critically rather than copied. Zhang says the Chinese theory differs from traditional socialist economics in four ways. It starts from the primary stage of socialism, takes the socialist market economy as its premise, borrows critically from Western economics, and widens its scope to basic economic institutions, the economic system, operation, development and opening up. On principles, Zhang distinguishes three kinds of development of Marxist theory: deepening it (public ownership alongside other forms), innovating (economic modernization) and correcting it (capital under socialism). Zhang rejects the view that Chinese theory is only an application of classical principles, and argues that general principles also rise from particular practice, as Marx drew his from Britain. Zhang concludes that China, as the most developed real-world form of socialism, is the main object from which general principles of socialist political economy can now be drawn. The article presents Chinese socialism as a banner of twenty-first-century scientific socialism and as an option for developing countries. It calls on scholars to turn practical experience into a systematic economic doctrine. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists present Xi Jinping's economic thought as a theoretical advance within Marxism.

The origins, theoretical framework and critical assessment of "fossil capitalism" “化石资本主义”的概念源起、理论框架和理论评述 Huang Yinlin Huang Yinlin takes up "fossil capitalism", a concept developed by Western left-wing scholars to criticise a capitalist mode of production dependent on fossil fuels, and notes that Chinese scholarship on it is still thin. The article sets out where the concept comes from, what its framework contains and where it falls short. Huang's overall view is that the theory offers a useful lens on contemporary capitalism and ecological crisis, but has real limits that call for a dialectical reading that takes "the essence and discards the dross". The article draws mainly on Andreas Malm, Ian Angus, John Bellamy Foster, Naomi Klein and John Szabo. Part one traces the concept's historical origins in the industrial revolution's shift from water to steam power, its theoretical sources, and its practical logic. Part two reconstructs the framework: what fossil capitalism means, its main features, and how to overcome it. Part three assesses the theory's lessons and limitations. In Huang's account, fossil capitalism has economic, political and natural dimensions. Economically, fossil fuels are the lifeline of capital's drive for endless growth; politically, the fossil-fuel industry is a powerful interest group that shapes state policy through lobbying and donations; and its exponential growth pushes the Earth system into the Anthropocene. Huang identifies four features: capital's anti-ecological logic, escalation into "fossil imperialism", a rift in the global metabolism, and war driven by oil. The theory's remedy, drawn from Angus and Foster, is an eco-socialist movement. It would draw in "Green-Left" forces, adapt to new science, hold to internationalism and anti-imperialism, and involve many groups in ecological practice. Huang says the theory draws on historical materialism, Marx's metabolic rift and the proletariat as the revolutionary subject. Huang credits the theory with offering a dynamic view of contemporary capitalism and a critique of its destruction of nature. It also provides, in Huang's view, resources for China's socialist ecological civilisation and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Its limits, Huang argues, are a vague concept with utopian tendencies, a Western-centred viewpoint, a failure to uphold the basic principles of scientific socialism or to treat capitalism's basic contradiction as irreconcilable, and neglect of each citizen's responsibility. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Malm, Angus and Foster's eco-Marxist work on fossil fuels and climate.

World socialism amid the great upheaval in the international economic and political order 国际经济政治格局大变动中的世界社会主义 Zhou Miao Liu Tingting Zhou Miao and Liu Tingting ask how the development of world socialism has been tied to shifts in the international economic and political order, and what this implies for the present. Writing amid what the authors call changes unseen in a century, they argue that the rise and fall of socialist forces has followed the contradictions of the capitalist world economy and the changing balance among great powers. They conclude that the current acceleration of these shifts brings both opportunities and risks for socialism. The article has three parts. The first traces the historical logic from the Paris Commune and the October Revolution to the socialist camp, the post-war national liberation movements and the rise of the Third World. The second examines how the form and intensity of great-power struggle changed after the Second World War, covering relations among capitalist states, the two-system relationship, the Soviet collapse and the shift of competition towards economic and institutional rivalry. The third turns to the present: the post-2008 crisis, the Russia–Ukraine conflict, China's strategic environment and the condition of communist and left forces worldwide. The authors build on Lenin's thesis of uneven capitalist development and the imperialist chain's weakest link. In their account, wars and crises among capitalist powers opened historical windows for socialist revolution, as in Russia. After 1945, they argue, the United States exercised hegemony through neo-colonial economic, financial and military means rather than direct war among capitalist powers, and pursued 'peaceful evolution' of socialist states, citing oil-price pressure on the Soviet Union and the Plaza Accord against Japan. They hold that socialist states must therefore raise productive forces and institutional appeal while learning from the achievements of capitalist civilisation. For the present, the authors see relative decline of the United States and the West, the strengthening of BRICS and socialist countries, and a revival of left sentiment, including a new 'pink tide' in Latin America. They also identify weaknesses: communist parties are small, fragmented and doctrinally divided, and right-wing forces have often gained instead. They call for theoretical innovation, closer engagement with working people's demands, and stronger cooperation among parties, trade unions and left scholars, and they present China's strategic confidence as resting on its own development. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account linking great-power rivalry, the Soviet collapse and the prospects of the international communist and left movement.

Living up to a great era, shouldering a glorious mission 不负伟大时代 担负光荣使命 Peng Qinghong This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2024, asks what Chinese philosophers and social scientists must do to meet the expectations Xi Jinping set out at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work. Peng Qinghong takes Xi's call to "stand at the forefront of the times, connect the changes of past and present, and sound the first notes of new thought" as a framework. The author argues that this call gives researchers both a direction and a set of values to follow. The piece is organised under three headings drawn from Xi's formulation: standing at the crest of the times, being skilled at connecting past and present, and daring to voice new ideas first. Each heading is divided into three requirements. The text quotes Xi throughout, including on Chinese modernization, the Two Integrations, the people-centred orientation of scholarship, and academic misconduct. Under the first heading, Peng says scholars should solve problems, anticipate risks and lead, by focusing on the Party's and the country's major questions, moving from passive response to active foresight, and identifying the broad logic of social development. Under the second, the author calls for cultural confidence, adherence to the Two Integrations and "upholding fundamental principles while innovating". Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as a model of this approach. Under the third, Peng requires scholars to put the people first, practise seeking truth from facts, and show the boldness to speak. Peng cites the 1978 article "Practice is the sole criterion of truth" as an example of the second requirement. On the third, Peng calls on scholars to consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere and to counter what the author describes as demonization of China abroad. They should act as "fighters" rather than "gentlemen" who guard their reputations. Peng concludes that if scholars follow these three requirements, they will not fail in their mission and will make larger contributions to building a strong country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary translates Xi Jinping's expectations of social scientists into concrete duties, or if you are studying the language that frames academic work in China's new era.

The Party's practical path in building a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation 党推进中华民族现代文明建设的实践脉络 Chen Jianbo This short commentary, first printed in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2024, asks how the Communist Party of China has approached cultural construction and how it should now build a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation. Starting from Xi Jinping's June 2023 remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, Chen argues that this task is the Party's new cultural mission and follows from a long line of practice in developing socialist culture. The article moves in three steps. It first recalls the Party's cultural mission since its founding and in the early People's Republic. It then reviews what has been achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including Xi's theoretical contributions on culture. Finally it sets out the requirements for the new journey: cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and keeping to fundamental principles while innovating. Chen's central claim is that the Party has always led advanced culture and also inherited traditional culture. After 1949, in Chen's account, it established Marxism's guiding position, adopted the principles of making the past serve the present and foreign things serve China, and issued the "let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend" policy. Since 2012 the Party has combined Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, which the article treats as the basis for the Two Integrations, especially the "second integration". Chen lists many strands of Xi's thinking, among them the Party's overall leadership of ideological work, core socialist values, a Chinese philosophy and social science, the protection of cultural heritage, international communication and the Global Civilization Initiative. Chen holds that cultural confidence means turning Chinese experience into Chinese theory. Openness means drawing on all outstanding civilisational achievements. "Upholding fundamental principles" means keeping the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity, and never abandoning Marxism or traditional culture. Chen concludes that the new form of human civilisation created by Chinese modernization is both Chinese and global, and calls for guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article also calls for the Two Establishes, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, so that a model modern civilisation can be offered to the world. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated commentary presents the lineage and current requirements of the cultural mission.

Promoting the high-quality development of philosophy and social sciences 推动哲学社会科学高质量发展 Lü Peiming This commentary, published on 17 May 2024 in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work. Lü Peiming argues that the speech answers fundamental questions about the long-term development of the field and sets the direction for philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. The article asks how universities, taking Tongji University as the example, can turn this guidance into high-quality development. The piece has three parts. The first describes the new situation facing university philosophy and social sciences over the eight years since the 2016 symposium. The second reports what Tongji University has already done to promote interdisciplinary integration. The third sets out five new lines of action for the future. On the current situation, Lü names three factors: Xi Jinping's new requirements, including the call to build China's own knowledge system; new Party Central Committee plans such as the 2017 opinions on accelerating the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics and the 2022 action plan to 2035; and the challenge of a new technological revolution, which is pushing the restructuring of the humanities into a 'new liberal arts'. Lü presents Tongji's response as organisational innovation: discipline clusters, organised interdisciplinary research on topics such as AI governance and digital cities, cross-field platforms and think tanks focused on 'city' and 'Germany (Europe)'. The five future tasks are deepening research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era under the Two Integrations; moral education for a new generation; serving national strategy; developing the new liberal arts with AI; and building China's external discourse system. Lü concludes that universities should integrate Marxist theory with engineering, science and medicine, and train versatile talent. They should also produce original scholarship that supports the building of China's own knowledge system and the effort to build a community with a shared future for mankind. The text is a university leader's programmatic statement more than an analytical study. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese university translates central directives on philosophy and social sciences into institutional plans, platforms and priorities.

Understanding new quality productive forces as a key variable 理解作为关键变量的新质生产力 Linda Matar This text is a Chinese translation of a commentary by the Lebanese author Linda Matar. It takes up Xi Jinping's call of 31 January 2024 to accelerate new quality productive forces and asks what the concept means. Matar argues that it is a key variable of economic growth and should be read through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In this reading it is an upgrade of productive forces within a socialist, people-centred framework, not a paradigm shift or a turn to capitalism. The piece begins with China's development path since 1949, which Matar sums up as policy autonomy and a link between security and development. It then cites figures on research and development spending, export growth in the "new three" products (electric vehicles, lithium batteries, solar cells) and technological leadership. Further sections cover the Marxist theory of productive forces, the Party's reform-era policy, whole-process people's democracy, poverty reduction and inequality, and the place of innovation and national security in high-quality development. Matar contends that mainstream growth models, which treat technology as endogenous or exogenous, hide the question of which social forces direct development and who benefits. In her account, the difference between socialist and capitalist production lies in its purpose: satisfying people's needs rather than creating private surplus value. She argues that the state's control of capital, together with the Party's leadership, keeps workers united with the means of production. Matar rejects Western media claims that the concept repackages old slogans or that the Party commands from above, and points to consultative democracy. She presents democracy and development as mutually reinforcing: people's control of resources is, in her view, the substance of democracy. Matar concludes that new quality productive forces are a roadmap for China's socialist modernization and cultural-ethical progress. She holds that high-quality development keeps economy and politics united and protects China's global position and its voice in science and technology under Western restrictions. Development, innovation and national security form a "trinity", in her words, and technology serves the aim of making the economy serve the people. Read the original if you want to see how a foreign sympathetic commentator frames the concept, and how she answers Western media interpretations, for a Chinese-language audience.

Foreign literature on education governance 国外文献论教育治理 Tang Feng This is a review of foreign scholarly literature and policy documents on education governance from roughly the past five years, compiled by Tang Feng and published in Foreign Theoretical Trends in 2024. It opens from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's statement that education is a matter of fundamental importance for the nation and the Party. Tang says the aim is to inform China's strategy for building a strong education nation. The review selects three themes: measures to promote the digitalisation of education, ways of integrating research and teaching and reflections on them, and future strategies for education development. Because of space, only representative items are presented. Each entry gives a source and a short abstract. They include a Hechinger Report opinion piece, a Broadband Commission report, European Commission plans, academic studies of teacher educators and language courses, an OECD outlook and a US Department of Education plan. On digitalisation, the sources present the pandemic as a rehearsal for digital transformation. They cover personalised learning supported by artificial intelligence, dynamic learner records, school connectivity built on four pillars (Map, Connect, Finance, Empower), and the EU Digital Education Action Plan 2021–2027 with its two priorities and 14 actions. On research–teaching integration, a Finnish survey of 101 teacher educators identifies six forms of integration, with research-based content mentioned most often. A study of a graduate computer-assisted language learning course finds that teaching research skills through process-centred methods is harder than building research awareness through content. A UK study reports that law favours combining research and teaching, while other disciplines prefer separating them. The strategy documents set out the European Education Area, the OECD's finding that digitalisation is member states' top education priority, and the US Department of Education's five goals centred on equity, educators, student wellbeing, higher education value and departmental capacity. The article draws no overall conclusion of its own. It is an annotated guide to foreign sources, presented as a reference for Chinese education policy. It leaves the debates it reports open, for instance on how research and teaching should be combined. Read the original if you want a compact bibliography of recent English-language studies and EU, OECD, UNESCO-linked and US policy documents on digital education, research–teaching integration and long-term education strategy.

Ideological and political education resources in excellent traditional Chinese culture 中华优秀传统文化蕴含的思想政治教育资源 Shan Wenpeng Shan Wenpeng asks how excellent traditional Chinese culture can be systematically mined as a resource for ideological and political education, and how doing so can help build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system for the discipline. Writing in 2024, forty years after the discipline's founding, Shan argues that this culture is the 'root and lifeline' of the Party's theoretical innovation. The article holds that research should move from broad, general treatment to finer-grained discussion, guided by the Two Integrations. The article has four main sections plus a conclusion. The first argues that traditional culture is already an important part of the discipline's content, and notes shortcomings in how it has been integrated. Three further sections then set out the resources the author identifies: ideas and concepts, humanistic spirit, and moral norms. Each section closes with a statement of what teaching should stress. Shan's first move is to show that the culture serves the discipline's purposes: its goals of fostering virtue and cultivating people, the structure of its content, and its self-reliant knowledge system. The author criticises existing work for favouring grand narrative over systematic depth and quotation over logical interpretation. Second, Shan sorts the resources into three clusters. Ideas include the unity of heaven and humanity, governing by virtue, and the Great Harmony under heaven. Humanistic spirit covers self-strengthening, benevolence ('loving others') and harmony without uniformity. Moral norms cover righteousness over profit, filial piety extended into loyalty to the state, and self-cultivation. Shan presents each as the traditional answer to a basic relationship: humanity and nature, politics and governance, nation and world, person and person, family and state, self and others. In the conclusion, Shan calls for deeper scholarly study of how traditional culture enters ideological and political education, under the guidance of the Two Integrations. Three tasks follow. The first is to strengthen the work of fostering virtue and cultivating people. The second is to consolidate cultural subjectivity. The third is to build an autonomous disciplinary knowledge system able to answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Read the original if you study the theory of ideological and political education in China, or want to see which traditional concepts the discipline is now drawing on.

The contemporary significance of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的时代意蕴 Fang Zheng Following Xi Jinping's call at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation as a new cultural mission, Fang Zheng asks what this project means for its time. The article argues that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation embodies three qualities of the Communist Party's theoretical character: seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times, and upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground. The article is organised in three sections, one for each quality. The first treats the concept as a summation of the Chinese nation's history, from ancient civilization through the modern humiliations to the Party-led revival. The second places it within a Marxist view of civilization, the development of the productive forces and the contrast between Western and Chinese paths to modernity. The third deals with Party leadership, cultural subjectivity and national spirit. In the first section, Fang presents the concept as a systematic reading of socialist, Party, People's Republic, reform-era and national history. In the second, Fang argues that civilization and the productive forces are essentially linked, so that civilizational continuity requires rapid productive development. The author describes Western modernization as bound up with colonial plunder, neo-colonialism and cultural colonialism, and presents Chinese modernization as breaking the equation of modernization with Westernization. Marx and Engels, Fang notes, could not foresee a socialist modernization of a large, backward Eastern country, which had to be explored independently, with the Two Integrations as guidance. In the third section, Party leadership is called the key to building this civilization, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the expression of cultural subjectivity. The great founding spirit of the Party and the great national spirit are said to supply its spiritual content. Fang concludes that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is at bottom a socialist civilizational form and a marker of national rejuvenation. Only by adhering unwaveringly to Party leadership and Xi Jinping's cultural thought, the author contends, can its content be explained, its theoretical system built and its practical paths widened. Read the original if you want to see how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2024 justifies the concept of a modern Chinese civilization in Marxist and historical terms.

Intellectual characteristics of the peaceful nature of Chinese civilization and its contemporary presentation 中华文明和平性的思想特点及其当代呈现 Liu Feng Liu Feng takes up one of the "five outstanding characteristics" that Xi Jinping has attributed to Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and asks what philosophical roots lie behind its peaceful nature. The article argues that this peacefulness rests on Chinese philosophy's view of the cosmos as harmonious and on the doctrine of the unity of heaven and humanity. It holds that these roots shape the present-day Chinese commitment to peaceful development. The article has four sections. It first sets out the ontological basis of peacefulness, drawing on the Laozi, the Book of Changes and the Song philosopher Zhang Zai's idea of "supreme harmony". It then examines the unity of heaven and humanity in three forms: following the seasons, correspondence between heaven and humanity as in Dong Zhongshu, and the unity of human virtue with heaven and earth in Confucian and Neo-Confucian thought. A third section identifies three features of the Chinese idea of harmony, and the last turns to its contemporary expression. Liu's central claim concerns the three features of "harmony" (he). First, it is many-sided, linking self, family, society, nature and "all under heaven" in a single line from self-cultivation to bringing peace to the world. Second, it presupposes order and difference rather than erasing them. Liu draws on Yan Ying's contrast between harmony and sameness, on the Confucian pairing of ritual and music, and on the saying that "the gentleman seeks harmony but not conformity". Third, harmony is generative: citing Shi Bo's "harmony gives birth to things; sameness cannot continue", Liu says Chinese philosophy treats harmony of yin and yang as the source of all creation. Liu also reads Zhang Zai's "opposites are resolved through harmony" as another statement of the supreme-harmony philosophy. In the final section Liu presents a community with a shared future for mankind as the highest present-day expression of this civilizational trait, linking it to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and the aim of a harmonious world. Citing Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, Liu says Chinese modernization follows a path of peaceful development, unlike modernization achieved through war and colonial plunder. Liu argues that studying this trait has theoretical and practical importance in answering "clash of civilizations" and "strong countries inevitably seek hegemony" arguments. Read the original if you want a close account, with many classical citations, of how a Chinese philosopher grounds official claims about peaceful development in the Chinese philosophical tradition.

Understanding several important dimensions of Chinese modernization 深刻认识中国式现代化的几个重要维度 Yan Shuhan Yan Shuhan takes up the theory of Chinese modernization, which Xi Jinping has called a major theoretical innovation of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. The article argues that the Party as a whole needs to grasp it through four paired dimensions, each treated as a dialectical unity, so that practice can keep winning new victories in building a modern socialist country. The article moves through four pairings: commonality and particularity; importance and arduousness; historical continuity and stages; and strategic thinking and pragmatism. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report. It also draws on Marx's Capital, Mao Zedong, and Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remarks on a Chinese-style modernization, and it reviews the Party's record from the Yan'an period to the new era. On the first pairing, Yan says the five features of Chinese modernization set out at the 20th Party Congress show its particularity. It also shares the general features of all modernization, such as industrialization, urbanization and measurable indicators like GDP per capita. Yan treats the claim that modernization equals Westernization as a methodological error that substitutes one general pattern for particularity. The opposite error would be to discuss particularity without commonality, and the proposed community with a shared future for mankind is offered as an example of grounding a distinctive path in shared human values. On the fourth pairing, Yan describes strategic thinking, seen in medium- and long-term planning, as joined to a practical attitude of proceeding steadily from national conditions. On the third, Yan identifies two leaps in the Party's understanding. The first was Deng Xiaoping's 'Chinese-style modernization', which Yan equates with a moderately prosperous society and with per capita rather than total output as the key indicator. The second was Xi Jinping's 'Chinese modernization', aimed at a strong modern socialist country by the middle of the century. For Yan the dropped Chinese particle 'de' marks a real conceptual advance, not just a change of wording. Yan concludes that understanding of the laws of Chinese modernization has reached an unprecedented level, and that a preliminary theoretical system now exists. Many problems remain unsolved, however, and understanding is still deepening amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century. Yan therefore calls on the whole Party to stay confident, to guard against and defuse risks, and to keep up its fighting spirit. Read the original if you want a clear example of how Party theorists present Chinese modernization as a dialectical, historically staged project and as a contribution to world socialism.

Grasping the importance of consolidating cultural subjectivity 深刻把握巩固文化主体性的重要意义 Zang Hua This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in October 2023, asks why consolidating "cultural subjectivity" matters. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, Zang defines the concept as a clear understanding of, and strong identification with, one's own nation's cultural origins, development and standing. The author calls consolidating it a major task in building a modern Chinese civilization. The piece is organised around four reasons for its importance. It treats cultural subjectivity as the foundation of cultural confidence, as a source of cultural strength for the Party in leading the times, as a cultural basis for national identity, and as support for exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. On the first point, Zang argues that a firm cultural self gives cultural confidence its foundation. This subjectivity is rooted in more than five thousand years of civilization and in the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On the second, the author says the Party built it by integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as its strongest expression. Zang also holds that traditional ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the foundation of the state" feed national identity. In dealing with other civilizations, the author calls for adhering to Marxism as the "soul" and traditional culture as the "root", while learning from others on the principle of "putting ourselves first". Zang concludes that consolidating cultural subjectivity requires upholding Xi Jinping Thought, following the path of socialist cultural development, and transforming traditional culture creatively. It also requires open learning that brings together ancient and modern, Chinese and Western. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how cultural subjectivity was framed in Party discourse in late 2023.

The generative logic of the theoretical system of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化理论体系的生成逻辑 Dai Yuqi Dai Yuqi asks how the theoretical system of Chinese modernization came into being and what it consists of. The article argues that the system grew out of a historical process, a theoretical framework and a body of practice, and that it constitutes an independent body of knowledge with Chinese features and a new form of human civilisation. It was published in People's Forum in October 2023 and reposted in June 2024. The article is organised under three headings: historical logic, theoretical logic and practical logic. The first traces the waves of world modernization, the early Chinese attempts at modernization from the Self-Strengthening Movement to the May Fourth period, and the Communist Party's century of exploration. The second sets out the system's sources, structure and distinctive features. The third turns to practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the theoretical section Dai summarises the core of Chinese modernization as "115951": one basic premise (Party leadership), one fundamental guide (Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), five features, nine essential requirements, five major principles and one fundamental goal (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation). Dai describes the system as a dialectical unity of the general and the particular and of the local and the global, and as rooted in Marxism and traditional Chinese culture. The practical section presents methods for carrying it out: systemic thinking, handling major relationships such as efficiency and fairness or vitality and order, and bottom-line thinking and a fighting spirit against risks. Dai contrasts this path with a Western-centred model that some scholars treat as universal. Dai concludes that Chinese modernization is a self-shaped knowledge system integrating political, academic and everyday discourse. Dai calls on Chinese scholars to develop signature concepts and to lead international research. The author holds that the modernization of people, expressed in cultural values, should be the focus, and that Chinese modernization should keep offering ideas for global problems. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholarship frames the structure and origins of the Chinese modernization theory.

Features and value of theoretical research on jointly building the Belt and Road 共建“一带一路”理论研究的特点和价值 Zhai Kun Zhai Kun takes up the question of what theoretical research on jointly building the Belt and Road has become over the past decade, and what it contributes. Writing after the Third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation (October 2023), the author argues that this body of research supplies theoretical, intellectual and discursive support for the Belt and Road Initiative and carries both theoretical and practical value. It is presented as having grown up alongside the practice it studies. The article, a newspaper-style commentary first published in the People's Daily, has three parts. The first traces two phases of research since Xi Jinping proposed the initiative in autumn 2013 and sets out the research field's basic content. The second identifies three defining traits. The third assesses the field's value for theoretical innovation. In Zhai's periodisation, the first phase focused on definitions, essential attributes, causes, strategy, mechanisms, cooperation models and risks. After 2018, when Xi called for a shift to high-quality development, research became more multidimensional and began probing the initiative's underlying laws of development. The three traits are the unity of knowing and doing, a worldwide outlook (tianxia qinghuai), and openness and inclusiveness. Zhai cites examples such as think-tank work applied to infrastructure connectivity, and studies proposing inclusive economic globalization and a shift from national to common-interest modernization. On value, the author claims the research advances international economic theory by going beyond the traditional "centre–periphery" pattern. It also advances international relations theory through win-win cooperation without political conditions, and international development theory through infrastructure and small-scale livelihood projects. Zhai concludes that this research helps build China's independent knowledge system under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and offers the world public knowledge products. These include concepts of global governance, right approach to interests, security, development, cooperation and ecology. The author contends such ideas can help address the peace, development, security and governance deficits. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic account of how Chinese scholars frame the Belt and Road as a source of theory, and which concepts they treat as central.

Strengthening the fundamental role of consumption in economic development 增强消费对经济发展的基础性作用 Lin Zhaomu Lin Zhaomu's commentary takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to expand domestic demand and 'strengthen the fundamental role of consumption in economic development'. Lin presents this as both a key step in accelerating the new development pattern and in promoting high-quality development, and as a response to the current weakness of demand. The author argues that implementing it requires a deeper grasp of its meaning and significance. The piece has three parts. The first revisits Marx's account of the dialectical relation between production and consumption and the Party's experience of applying it. The second explains why expanding consumption is an inherent requirement of the new development pattern, with domestic circulation as the mainstay. The third sets out a package of coordinated measures across production, distribution, exchange and consumption. Lin draws on Marx's Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy: without production there is no consumption, and without consumption production has no purpose. Lin treats this as a general economic law that guides present policy, and reads the Party's successive judgements of the principal contradiction in Chinese society (1956, 1981 and the new era) as applications of it. On the international side, Lin cites weak global growth since 2008, protectionism, the pandemic and de-globalisation as reasons to rely more on China's domestic market, which the author calls the world's largest and most promising. Lin stresses that this does not downgrade investment, which remains an important part of domestic demand. In the 20th Party Congress formulation, however, its main role shifts towards optimising the supply structure. Lin's policy proposals follow the chain from production to consumption. They include deepening supply-side structural reform, raising the share of household income and labour remuneration in national income, and expanding education, health and social security spending. They also include building a unified national market, improving logistics, and building consumption infrastructure and protecting consumers. The author also calls for stabilising bulk consumption, expanding service and rural consumption, and developing new forms of consumption. Read the original if you want a concise, officially placed statement of how Marx's production–consumption theory is used to justify China's domestic-demand and consumption policy in 2023.

Deeply understanding and comprehensively grasping the theoretical system of Chinese modernization 深刻理解和全面把握中国式现代化理论体系 Chang Qingxin Chang Qingxin takes up the question of how to understand the theoretical system of Chinese modernization, which the article says has been initially constructed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Taking the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's central task of building a modern socialist country in all respects as its starting point, Chang argues that a deep and comprehensive grasp of this system is needed for the new journey to be 'clearer, more scientific and more tangible and workable'. The article is organised in three parts that follow the 20th Party Congress report. The first sets out the scientific value of Chinese modernization, the second discusses its five defining features (what kind of modernization it is), and the third examines the nine essential requirements (how it is to be achieved). Chang draws heavily on speeches by Xi Jinping and on Marx's writings on production and nature. In the first part, Chang argues that the key to its theoretical and world-historical significance is that it deconstructs and goes beyond Western unilinear evolutionism. Chang says it breaks the equation of 'modernization' with 'Westernization', offers developing countries an alternative to dependence on the Western model, achieves leapfrog development through institutional innovation, and forms a distinct discourse of 'comprehensive' modernization covering livelihoods, ecology and human development. The five features are then presented: huge population scale, common prosperity for all, coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Chang contrasts the last of these with colonial plunder and 'pollute first, clean up later' in capitalist countries. On the nine essential requirements, Chang treats Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee and commanding element, and socialism with Chinese characteristics as the main thread. Chang presents the remaining requirements (high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy, enriching people's spiritual world, common prosperity, harmony between humanity and nature, a community with a shared future for mankind, and creating a new form of human advancement) as an organic whole directed at shared goals. Chang concludes that, together, they amount to the practical achievement of a new form of human advancement and that they answer problems such as the 'middle-income trap' and ecological crises. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style overview of how Chinese modernization's features and essential requirements were systematised after the 20th Party Congress.

Jointly building the Belt and Road expands new practice in global governance 共建“一带一路”拓展全球治理新实践 Geng Xiefeng Writing after the third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation (October 2023), Geng argues that a decade of jointly building the Belt and Road Initiative has opened new practice and new models in global governance. The article presents the initiative as China's proposal for an open world economy and for balanced, sustainable development, and as evidence of China's responsibility for making the global governance system fairer. This short commentary, reprinted from the People's Daily, opens with Xi Jinping's keynote at the forum. It then takes four areas in turn: connectivity, institutional opening-up and global economic governance, regional governance, and development cooperation with the Global South. Geng's central claim is that the Initiative answers governance problems that arise from a rising tide of anti-globalization and sharpened geopolitical rivalry. Connectivity, pursued through the principle of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, is said to ease bottlenecks in globalization. The author says China's institutional opening-up, together with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the New Development Bank and the Silk Road Fund, strengthens developing countries' voice. The Initiative is described as an economic cooperation platform rather than a geopolitical tool, and its development cooperation as free of political conditions, unlike the aid of developed countries. Geng concludes that high-quality Belt and Road cooperation should align with high-standard international economic and trade rules, while balancing openness and security. The article also looks to linking the Initiative with the Global Development Initiative, which it says will help address development problems. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary framed the Belt and Road Initiative as global governance in 2023.

A preliminary study of the framework and content of the theoretical system of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化理论体系的框架轮廓和内容初探 Jin Chengwei Jin Chengwei takes up Xi Jinping's statement that the Party has "initially constructed" a theoretical system of Chinese modernization, making it clearer, more scientific and more tangible and workable. The article asks what the outline and content of that system are. Jin argues that it is an internally unified whole, which can be outlined through five pairs of categories and which contains at least ten components. Jin presents it as a major result of scientific socialism that enriches Marxist and world theories of modernization. The article has two parts. The first sketches the framework through five pairs: history and reality, theory and practice, inheritance and innovation, the general and the particular, and China and the world. The second lists the ten components: historical roots, essential requirements, core theme, major principles, overall goals, overall strategy, fundamental value, distinctive features, external relations and ideas and methods. Jin draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping. In Jin's account, the system links history and reality because Western-style attempts such as the Westernization Movement and the 1911 Revolution failed, and the Party then built the conditions for modernization stage by stage. It links theory and practice through the changing principal contradiction of each period. On inheritance and innovation, Jin says it draws on traditional ideas such as "a world of great harmony" and on Marx and Lenin on industrialization. On the general and the particular, Jin says following general laws of modernization does not mean taking the Western path, and describes China's industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization as advancing "in parallel". The ten components trace a line from industrialization and the "four modernizations" through the moderately prosperous society to Chinese modernization. They include nine essential requirements, such as Party leadership, common prosperity, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind, and five features, such as huge population size and peaceful development. Jin concludes that the theory answers what kind of modernized socialist country is to be built and how, and offers new support and new contributions to humanity's exploration of modernization. Jin adds that its distinctive worldview, values, and views of history, civilization, democracy and ecology merit further research and exposition. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned catalogue of how Chinese modernization is being systematised as a theory, with its main sources and categories.

Promoting high-quality development of the Belt and Road Initiative and achieving new results 推动共建“一带一路”高质量发展不断取得新成效 Contemporary World Research Center, International Department of the CPC Central Committee Marking ten years since Xi Jinping proposed the Belt and Road Initiative in autumn 2013, this commentary by the Contemporary World Research Center of the CPC International Department takes stock of the initiative. It argues that the initiative has become a welcome international public good and platform for cooperation. In the authors' account, it carries the values of peace, development, cooperation and mutual benefit, shows the resolve to build a community with a shared future for mankind, and extends practical exploration in reforming global governance. The piece has three parts. The first reviews achievements under five headings: building consensus on cooperation, improving infrastructure, promoting trade, facilitating finance, and deepening exchanges between civilisations. The second sets out the initiative's contemporary value and international influence. The third looks ahead, following the 20th Party Congress (2022) call for high-quality development of the initiative, and sets out three principles for the next stage. To support the first part, the authors cite figures. By June 2023 China had signed over 200 cooperation documents with more than 150 countries and 30 international organisations. They report that trade with partner countries totalled 19.1 trillion US dollars in 2013–2022, and that overseas economic and trade zones created 421,000 jobs. They also cite a World Bank estimate that the initiative will cut global freight times by 1.2–2.5 per cent. The authors present the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Silk Road Fund and debt sustainability guidelines as parts of a multi-tiered financial network. The initiative is described as 'open, green and clean', and as an alternative to closed 'small circles'. The authors say it consults all parties as equals and aims to give developing countries more representation and voice in global governance. Looking forward, the authors call for three commitments: equality among cooperating parties, openness of cooperation mechanisms, and broadly shared benefits. In practice this means improving platforms such as the China International Import Expo, upholding genuine multilateralism, and cooperating on climate change, poverty reduction, food security, the digital economy and clean energy. The authors also write that partners can share the opportunities created by Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese framing of the Belt and Road Initiative at its tenth anniversary, with the figures and slogans used to present it.

The "Two Integrations" as the necessary path “两个结合”是必由之路 Wang Nanshi This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in October 2023, asks what it means to call the Two Integrations the "necessary path" (bi you zhi lu) of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Wang argues that a necessary path is one chosen actively by people, yet determined by objective laws. On this reading, combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture has both an objective possibility and a necessity. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's formulation and a Lu Xun image of paths made by walking. It then moves through the philosophical affinity between Marxism and Chinese tradition, the historical process of integration led by the Communist Party, the effects on China's path, theory and institutions, and finally the global significance of the resulting "new cultural life form". On possibility, Wang points to an affinity in ontology. Western philosophy from Plato to Hegel mostly assumed a transcendent metaphysical ground, whereas Marx understood reality through the interaction of humans and their world. Wang calls this an ontology of "affairs" rather than "things", and finds a similar ontology in Confucian thought, while noting that the two differ in origin and nature. On necessity, Wang holds that cultures flourish only when rooted in their own history, drawing on others while keeping the self as the main body. The integration is presented as a "chemical reaction", not a mere mixture, which has made Marxism Chinese and tradition modern. Wang concludes that the Two Integrations opened up room for innovation and gave intellectual initiative. Examples include the people-centred tradition behind whole-process people's democracy and the harmony of humans and nature. They have also supported Chinese modernization and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Wang foresees broad prospects and a deep influence on human civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how the Two Integrations are justified philosophically and historically.

Refuting the claim that Mao Zedong's edition of "Since the Sixth Congress" falsified documents 批驳“毛泽东编辑的《六大以来》有篡改文献问题”的谬论 Wang Xuechao Did Mao Zedong tamper with documents when he edited "Since the Sixth Congress: Secret Inner-Party Documents" (Liu da yilai), the collection of Chinese Communist Party documents compiled in Yan'an in 1941? Wang Xuechao takes up this charge, made in Gao Hua's book on the origins of the Yan'an Rectification Movement. Gao argues that Mao put himself in the foreground, heavily cut some texts and altered dates to hide the truth. Wang contends that all three claims contradict the historical record and that Gao reads Party history only as a power struggle. The article is organised around the three charges. The first concerns how many of Mao's writings the collection contains and what share of the book they make up. The second concerns Mao's alleged "major surgery" on his 1938 report "On the New Stage". The third concerns the dating of documents, above all the political resolution of the First Party Congress of the Central Soviet Area. Wang draws on Hu Qiaomu's recollections, the original 1938 journal text, the Chronology of Mao Zedong, and later editions of the collection and of Mao's Selected Works. On the first charge, Wang says Gao relied on the 1980 revised edition, not the 1941 original. Wang distinguishes the collected and selected editions and estimates that the 1941 book held about 522 documents, of which 29 were by Mao, roughly 5 per cent. The impression of self-promotion, Wang argues, arose when later editions added titles from the Selected Works. On the second charge, Wang notes that the title "The Position of the Communist Party of China in the National War" was already a section heading of the original report, so no renaming occurred. Wang adds that the 1980 edition lists Mao's Selected Works pieces by title only, and that the text circulated too widely for secret rewriting. On the third charge, Wang finds 20 wrongly dated documents in the book and attributes them to lost archives and difficult collection work. Wang adds that Mao did not yet treat the Fourth Plenum as the start of the third "Left" line, so the supposed motive of warning Ren Bishi is far-fetched. Wang concludes that the three claims (self-promotion, major surgery, concealment) do not match the facts. The author presents the question of whether Mao falsified documents as both a scholarly and a political matter, because it bears on the historical evaluation of major leaders. Wang calls for analysis grounded in full documentary evidence and warns that a "power struggle" framework yields one-sided conclusions. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based Chinese rebuttal of Gao Hua's account of the editing of this Yan'an-era collection, including the editions' contents and the table of misdated documents.

A theoretical analysis of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的理论探析 Shang Zhixiao Shang Zhixiao takes up a concept introduced by Xi Jinping in 2023: "the modern civilization of the Chinese nation", presented as part of a new cultural mission alongside cultural prosperity and building a strong socialist culture. The article argues that this new formulation needs to be understood theoretically before it can be put into practice. Its answer is that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is, in essence, a socialist modern civilization: the latest form of Chinese civilization, built on socialism and the Party's leadership. The article has four parts. It first distinguishes civilization from culture and sets out what it sees as the distinctive features of Chinese civilization. It then traces how Xi came to the concept, from his remarks at the Yin Ruins in Anyang in October 2022 to the symposium on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023. The third part defines the concept and its internal structure. The fourth traces its historical course since 1949 and its link with Chinese modernization. Shang's core argument has three moves. First, Chinese civilization is described as unbroken, deep, distinctive and far-reaching, with five outstanding features (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness); the modern civilization is said to inherit these. Second, the concept is analysed on two levels. Conceptually it has a subject (the Chinese nation), a historical position (the modern era) and a form (culture). In practice it rests on the Party as leadership core, the people as the force relied upon, and socialism with Chinese characteristics and advanced socialist culture as guiding direction. Civilization is the inner essence and advanced socialist culture its outward form. Third, the author places its starting point in the founding of new China and the establishment of the socialist system, and argues that it grows together with Chinese modernization. In this reading the concept goes beyond both traditional Chinese civilization and capitalist civilization, and also escapes the constraints of "traditional" socialism. Shang concludes that building this civilization means promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture, combining Marxism's basic tenets with that culture, and developing socialist culture and Chinese modernization together. The author presents it as both a requirement of national rejuvenation and a new model within the diversity of world civilizations. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of how the concept is defined and justified, and how it is tied to Chinese modernization and the Marxism–tradition integration.

Marx's thought on modernization and Chinese modernization 马克思的现代化思想与中国式现代化 Xie Fusheng Jiang Nan Xie Fusheng and Jiang Nan ask how a backward country can modernize, given that post-1960s modernization theory took Western Europe as its ideal model and ignored the conflicts facing latecomers. Their answer is that Marx's texts supply a general theory of modernization, and that Chinese modernization combines the general features of that theory with specific features of China's own conditions. They present this combination as a theoretical innovation that breaks with Eurocentric accounts. The article has three main parts. It first reconstructs Marx's view of modernization: the essence, features and laws of motion of modern society.
