It then traces the Chinese Communist Party's course from the "four modernizations" through "Chinese-style modernization" under Deng Xiaoping to the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects and supply-side structural reform. Finally it sets out the general and particular features of Chinese modernization and draws a theory from them. The authors read Marx as treating industrialization of the mode of production as the basis of modernity, with political institutions, social relations, values and the world market changing in its wake. Society is an organic whole driven by internal contradictions between productive forces and relations of production. On this basis Xie and Jiang argue that the Party, by resolving the principal contradiction of each period, built an independent industrial system through collectivization and planning, then released the combined productive forces of social exchange through the socialist market economy, and now pursues high-quality development. The authors say the general features appear at all levels, including the developmental state's role in capital formation. The particular features are Party leadership, socialist basic institutions, huge population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony with nature and peaceful development, which the authors contrast with Western capital-centred modernization. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization confirms Marx's laws of modern society while showing China's distinctiveness, offers developing countries a feasible path, and is a great creation of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They credit the Party's organization, self-awareness and capacity for change. Read the original if you want a political-economy reading that ties Marx's organic-totality framework to the stages of China's post-1949 development, with the author's figures on accumulation, growth and poverty reduction.

The history and experience of integrating excellent traditional Chinese culture with ideological and political education 中华优秀传统文化与思想政治教育融合发展的历史与经验 Wang Yi Wang Yi asks how excellent traditional Chinese culture and ideological and political education have developed together over the forty years since ideological and political education became a formal academic discipline. The article argues that bringing traditional culture into the field's research agenda is a valuable experience of the discipline and a practical need for its continued development. Wang presents this as a way to build a Chinese-based body of disciplinary knowledge that serves Chinese modernization. The article opens with three reasons why the two should be fused: they deepen the discipline's historical and cultural roots, they serve the Party's work of teaching traditional culture, and they drive innovation in the discipline. It then divides the fusion into three phases. The first is the institutional start from the early 1980s, with the creation of the specialty in 1984. The second is the deepening after 2005, when Marxist theory became a first-level discipline. The third is the comprehensive advance since the 18th Party Congress (2012). A final section looks ahead. Wang describes the first phase as centred on socialist cultural-ethical progress, national spirit and histories of Chinese moral education, mainly Confucian. The author judges this work too focused on moral education to be clearly separated from the history of philosophy and ethics. In the second phase, research became more specialised and varied in perspective and moved towards practice, including work on the socialist core value system and on courses. Since 2012, guided by Xi Jinping's statements on traditional culture and the Two Integrations, studies have extended to cultural transmission, the core socialist values, family instructions, village rules and the reform of ideological and political theory courses, including guides for bringing traditional culture into textbooks. Looking forward, Wang calls for work guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture and the Two Integrations. The aim would be a Chinese-based knowledge system. Wang proposes using traditional humanistic values and methodological wisdom in teaching, and building the discipline, academic, discourse and textbook systems. Concrete proposals include deeper study of the history of ancient Chinese ideological and political education, telling stories drawn from the 'five histories', and writing textbook guides for all school levels. Read the original if you want a periodised, officially aligned account of how this discipline has treated traditional culture, or if you study how Chinese academics frame the construction of an autonomous knowledge system.

On Mao Zedong's far-sighted vision of escaping the cycle of order and disorder, rise and fall 论毛泽东跳出治乱兴衰周期率的远见卓识 Wang Chuanli Wang Chuanli takes issue with Richard Nixon's remark, in his book Leaders, that Mao Zedong, like the most revolutionary leaders, could destroy but not build. The article argues that Mao was equally skilled at building, consolidating and defending a new China, and made a historic contribution to the Communist Party's effort to escape the 'cycle of order and disorder, rise and fall' (zhiluan xingshuai zhouqilü). It presents his measures as an institutional base and a store of experience for the Party today. The article is organised in five sections, each treating one set of Mao's measures: the choice of state system and state structure; resistance to corruption and degeneration; the coordination of development and security; the 'new road' of people's democracy; and the building of a vigorous Marxist Party. Wang draws on Mao's speeches, letters and directives from the 1930s to the 1960s, and sets them against Lenin, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Historical cases include Guo Moruo's essay on Li Zicheng, the Three-Anti and Five-Anti campaigns, the Korean War, Third Front construction and the Nixon visit. Wang's central claim is that Mao rejected Western parliamentary and separation-of-powers models, describing them as bourgeois dictatorship, and chose people's democratic dictatorship, the people's congress system and a unitary rather than federal state. In the article's account, this guarded against disorder and separatism, which Wang links to the Soviet collapse. Mao is then portrayed as using anti-corruption campaigns, the 'Two Musts' and rectification to keep the Party vigilant against complacency. Wang also credits him with balancing economic construction against external threats, through the Soviet alliance, the Korean War, nuclear weapons and opposition to 'peaceful evolution'. Wang reads Mao's reply to Huang Yanpei, that only supervision by the people and everyone taking responsibility can prevent rule from collapsing with its leaders, as the core of the democratic answer. This includes mobilising all positive factors, multi-party supervision, and handling of petitions from the public. Wang concludes that a Party can escape the cycle only if it remains a vital Marxist party. Mao's means, in this account, were adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, a dialectical democratic centralism, hard work and thrift, rectification, and cadres taking part in manual labour. Wang says these supply lessons for today's Party, including full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the handling of security risks amid great changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how current Chinese scholarship reads Mao's governance record as a guide to Party-building and anti-corruption today.

Upholding a global outlook has deep cultural roots and a practical foundation 坚持胸怀天下具有深厚文化底蕴和实践基础 Liu Xingyun This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily on 27 October 2023, asks where the Party's principle of "embracing the world" (a global outlook) comes from. Liu Xingyun argues that it is a historical lesson of the Party's century of struggle and an important standpoint and method running through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Understanding its sources, in the author's view, helps in advancing Chinese modernization. The piece is organised around three sources: the values of Marxist theory, the intellectual heritage of traditional Chinese culture, and the practical exploration of Chinese modernization. It opens with a statement by Xi Jinping that the Party also works for human progress and world harmony. It closes with the present international situation. Liu first traces the outlook to Marxism's aim of emancipating all humanity, its ideal of a "community of free individuals" and the proletarian party's commitment to serve the majority. The author presents the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind as the contemporary expression of that ideal. Second, Liu cites classical Chinese ideals such as "all under heaven belongs to all" and "to cultivate oneself, regulate the family, govern the state and bring peace to all under heaven". These are said to have shaped a worldview of the world as one family and a tradition of peaceful, open relations. Third, Liu holds that Chinese modernization combines self-reliance with openness, drawing on other countries' experience while benefiting others. Since reform and opening up, the author says, this has been a key reason for its success. Liu concludes that, amid accelerating global change, China urges shared construction, shared benefit and win-win cooperation, to enlarge the "cake" of global modernization. China will do so by widening high-standard opening up and offering new opportunities to the world. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links Marxist theory, Chinese tradition and Chinese modernization to the Party's foreign-policy outlook.

Grasping the major trends in international trade and accelerating the building of a strong trading nation 把握国际贸易发展大势 加快贸易强国建设 Zhao Jin Zhao Jin takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to speed up the building of a strong trading nation. The article asks what trends are reshaping international trade and what policies China needs in response. Zhao argues that trade is becoming more inclusive, digital, green, integrated, service-based, re-globalised and security-conscious, and that China should act on each trend to raise the innovation, competitiveness, reach, influence and security of its trade. The article is a policy-oriented commentary organised in six sections, each pairing one trend with a set of measures. The trends are: inclusive trading actors; digital and green trade objects; the growth of services in trade structure; re-globalisation of the market structure through the rise of developing countries; the spread of high-standard international economic and trade rules; and the securitisation of the trade environment. Zhao supports these with figures, many attributed to the World Trade Organization, and with quotations from Xi Jinping. Zhao's core reasoning is that each trend corresponds to a mark of a strong trading nation. Private firms accounted for 50.9% of China's trade in 2022, so Zhao urges a better business environment and cooperation platforms for large, medium and small firms. Services made up only 12.3% of China's trade against a world average of 21.1%, so Zhao calls for opening up services, integrating them with manufacturing, and pursuing institutional opening up. On digital and green trade, Zhao proposes digital supply chains, a green trade system, and active participation in rule negotiations such as the CPTPP and the Digital Economy Partnership Agreement. Zhao presents the rise of developing economies as making re-globalisation unstoppable, and describes US, EU and Japanese security policies as driving a global turn to trade security. Zhao concludes that China should align with high-standard rules, use opening up to drive domestic reform, and build a global development community through the Belt and Road Initiative and South–South cooperation, including with Africa. Zhao also calls for a trade security system built around supply chain security, with export controls, investment screening and trade diversification, and stresses that a strong trading nation must first be strong in security. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how a Party-affiliated economist links global trade trends to China's trade policy priorities.

Advancing Chinese modernization must follow the path of high-quality development 推进中国式现代化必须走高质量发展之路 Tang Zhouyan Li Ye Tang Zhouyan and Li Ye ask how high-quality development relates to Chinese modernization. Their thesis is that the two are logically linked and internally consistent: high-quality development is both an essential requirement of Chinese modernization and the path by which it must be advanced. The authors open with Xi Jinping's statements at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the first session of the 14th National People's Congress (2023), which call high-quality development the primary task of building a modern socialist country. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscript, is organised in three sections. The first presents high-quality development as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization and ties it to the new development philosophy. The second matches the five features of Chinese modernization against the demands of high-quality development. The third sets out a methodology for advancing modernization through it: guiding principles, economic tasks and habits of thought. In the authors' account, each of the five features of Chinese modernization requires high-quality development. These are an enormous population, common prosperity for all, coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and a path of peaceful development. The authors argue that only such development can meet the needs of a huge population, 'make the cake bigger' while correcting imbalances, enrich spiritual life, avoid the Western path of polluting first and cleaning up later, and avoid the Western route of war, colonialism and plunder. They call this the only correct path and describe the linkage as an enrichment and innovation of the Marxist view of development. The methodology rests on five principles: upholding the Party's overall leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics, a people-centred approach, deeper reform and opening up, and a fighting spirit. It adds a new development pattern built around the domestic cycle, systematic and dialectical thinking, and a problem-oriented approach. The authors conclude that many theoretical and practical problems remain. They call for full study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for persistence with high-quality development in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists in 2023 tied high-quality development to the defining features of Chinese modernization.

The key to Chinese characteristics lies in the "Two Integrations" 中国特色的关键就在于“两个结合” Yang Ziqiang This commentary, originally printed in the People's Daily in October 2023, takes up a line from Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development: the key to socialism with Chinese characteristics is the Two Integrations. Yang argues that this path emerged under the guidance of Marxism and also from more than five thousand years of Chinese civilization. The Two Integrations, in Yang's account, are therefore the only way to open up and develop that path. The piece has three sections. The first presents the Two Integrations as the necessary road for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second sets out why they are called the Party's greatest "magic weapon" for success, through four effects. The third presents the theory of Chinese modernization as a major result of the Two Integrations. Yang traces the Party's history from the October Revolution, which brought Marxism-Leninism to China, to the "second integration" of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, which Xi put forward in the new era. Marxism, the author contends, stays vital only when rooted in a nation's own historical and cultural soil. The four effects are: giving the path its distinctiveness and deeper historical roots; stimulating the creativity of the theoretical system; strengthening the superiority of the institutions; and consolidating cultural subjectivity. Yang holds that Chinese modernization is a modernization that continues an ancient civilization and does not destroy it. It grows from Chinese soil, the author says, and is not a copy of other countries. The article calls it a new form of human civilization, different from the Western model, and links it to Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Yang concludes that universal truth becomes material force only when joined to concrete reality, and scientific theory becomes spiritual force only when joined to fine culture. The author calls for studying and expounding Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and for upholding the Two Integrations, so as to take on a new cultural mission, build a strong cultural nation and develop a modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents the Two Integrations as the basis of the Chinese path and of Chinese modernization.

Building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power 建设具有强大凝聚力和引领力的社会主义意识形态 Li Jie This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 25 October 2023, takes up ideological work as a task of the Party. Li Jie argues that building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power is a major issue for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. In Li's account it is also a strategic task for propaganda, ideological and cultural work, and a support for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece begins by describing the Party's ideological work since 2012 and then sets out two sets of tasks. The first concerns the continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The second concerns concrete measures to provide an ideological guarantee for national rejuvenation. Li draws throughout on Xi Jinping's statements and on Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Li holds that the situation in the ideological sphere has undergone a fundamental, overall change. Under the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the Party is said to have reversed a once passive position, strengthened Party leadership and raised cultural confidence and social cohesion. For Li, the strength of an ideology depends on whether Marxism keeps being adapted. This means arming the Party and the people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and holding to Marxism as the "soul" and traditional Chinese culture as the "root" of theoretical innovation. It also means answering new questions of the era in a timely way, since an ideology gains cohesion through its power to explain reality. On the practical side, Li calls for full Party leadership over ideological work, with firm control of leadership, management and discourse power, and for the ideological responsibility system to be enforced at every level of Party committee. Li also calls for institutions that secure Marxism's guiding position, such as study systems and a comprehensive education mechanism. The commentary further urges cultural confidence and the cultivation of core socialist values, patriotism, collectivism and traditional virtues. Li presents these steps as providing a firm ideological guarantee for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how the Party frames ideological work and its priorities after the 2023 propaganda conference.

A powerful ideological weapon and scientific guide to action for shouldering the new cultural mission 担负起新的文化使命的强大思想武器和科学行动指南 Qu Qingshan Writing in the People's Daily in October 2023, Qu Qingshan presents Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, which he says was formally put forward and systematically set out at the national work conference on publicity, ideology and culture, as the guiding framework for the Party's cultural work. His thesis is that this body of thought enriches and develops the Marxist theory of culture and supplies a "powerful ideological weapon and scientific guide to action" for shouldering the new cultural mission. The article is organised in four sections. It first treats the thought as a theoretical summary of the Party's practice in leading cultural construction, from the revolutionary period through reform and opening up and into the post-2012 era. It then presents it as a major result of the Two Integrations, sets out the timeline of Xi Jinping's speeches and meetings on culture, and finally lists the qualities that Qu says give the thought its strength. Qu argues that the thought grows out of the Party's accumulated experience and combines Marxism as the "soul" with fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". In his account, the Second Integration lets Marxism take on a Chinese style while Marxist truth revitalises traditional culture, which consolidates cultural subjectivity and yields the cultural form of Chinese modernization. He traces key milestones, among them the "new cultural mission" first put forward at the 19th Party Congress (2017), the Two Integrations formulated in 2021, and the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, and concludes that the thought forms the cultural chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He credits it with four features: scientific character, people-centred character, practical character and openness. Qu concludes that the thought is the fundamental guide for publicity, ideological and cultural work. He calls on the whole Party to grasp the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, strengthen the "four consciousnesses", hold to the Four-sphere Confidence and achieve the Two Upholds. In this way, he says, the Party can consolidate the shared ideological foundation, raise China's cultural soft power and provide ideological support for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an authoritative Party-press statement of how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture is officially framed and dated.

Accelerating the building of a modernized industrial system 加快建设现代化产业体系 Lin Muxi Wang Cong This commentary, first published in Economic Daily in November 2023, asks how a modernized industrial system should be understood and built as part of Chinese modernization. Lin and Wang start from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which treats high-quality development as the primary task of building a modern socialist country, and from Xi Jinping's repeated statements on the subject. They argue that accelerating this construction is strategically necessary and that it must follow specific requirements and priorities. The piece has three parts: the strategic significance of the modernized industrial system, the requirements for advancing it, and the key points to grasp in construction. Each part is anchored in Xi Jinping's remarks and in decisions of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, quoted from 2018, 2023 and the 19th Party Congress (2017). On significance, the authors present the system as the base of the new development pattern, the material and technological foundation of a modern country, and a means of gaining strategic initiative in international competition. They note that the industrial chain is still "large but not strong" and treat supply-chain security as a response to a changing international environment. On requirements, they read Xi's formulations as a sequence: innovation-led and coordinated development across the real economy, technology, finance and human resources; self-reliance and controllability; support from the real economy; and the "completeness, advancement and security" of the system, which they call mutually reinforcing and dialectically unified. On priorities, they stress balancing the real and virtual economies, avoiding blind duplication, integrating the three sectors, upgrading traditional industries instead of simply phasing them out, and keeping the system open. Lin and Wang conclude that building the system is a complex systemic undertaking. It calls for policy coordination, regionally differentiated planning, advanced manufacturing and strategic emerging industries, and openness combined with independent innovation. They argue that closed-door development means falling behind. Read the original if you want a compact guide to how Chinese official discourse in late 2023 linked industrial policy, supply-chain security and the real economy in the language of high-quality development.

Forging an organically unified new cultural life-form 造就有机统一的新的文化生命体 Han Qingxiang This short commentary in the People's Daily interprets Xi Jinping's remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development on the Two Integrations. Han Qingxiang argues that Xi's formulation, in which the integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture produces "an organically unified new cultural life-form", deepens understanding of how culture is built and points the way to a stronger cultural nation. The piece has three parts. It first explains why the integration is a "chemical reaction" rather than a mixture, then presents the new cultural life-form as a fresh starting point for resolving the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western. It closes with proposals for the new cultural mission. Han holds that the two sides enrich each other. Traditional culture nourishes Marxism and gives it a Chinese style, while Marxism activates the living elements of tradition and gives them contemporary meaning. The resulting culture is the cultural form of Chinese modernization. In Han's account it breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization, rejects Western-centrism, and differs from the colonial expansion and cultural unilateralism the author attributes to Western capitalism. It stresses civilizational exchange, mutual learning and coexistence. Han calls for cultural confidence, spiritual independence and openness to the best of human civilization, together with the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity. The aim is to renew Chinese civilization and move it towards a modern form. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line reading of Xi Jinping's "new cultural life-form" and the Two Integrations.

Chinese modernization lights up human civilization 中国式现代化点亮人类文明之光 Wang Xingsheng This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2023, asks what contribution China can make to humanity, recalling Mao Zedong's remark that China should make a larger contribution. Wang Xingsheng argues that Chinese modernization answers this by creating a new form of human civilization, which the author describes as a light the Chinese nation offers to the world. The piece has three parts. The first places modernization within the long history of human civilization and the Western origins of the modernizing process, then sets out how China came to its own path. The second, the longest, examines four sets of relations: between people, between people and things, between people and nature, and between China and other countries. The third turns to the global and historical significance of the path. Wang's central claim is that the novelty of this civilization lies in overcoming the congenital defects that Western modernization inherited from the capitalist mode of production. In the author's account, capitalism produces polarisation, inverts the relation between people and things through commodity fetishism, damages the environment and rests on colonial plunder. Chinese modernization is presented as the opposite on each count: it pursues common prosperity, unites material abundance with human development, places ecological civilization within the overall plan, and follows peaceful development and a community with a shared future for mankind. The author cites the elimination of absolute poverty since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the Occupy Wall Street movement as contrasting evidence. Wang concludes that the path's significance is world-historical. It is said to confirm the scientific truth of Marxism and to advance scientific socialism in the twenty-first century, to make the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation irreversible, and to break the myth that modernization equals Westernization, offering developing countries another option. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary presents Chinese modernization as a new form of civilization in contrast with Western capitalist modernization.

From "mutual fit" to "mutual fulfilment": the Second Integration of Marxism and traditional Chinese culture 由“彼此契合”到“互相成就” Shang Zhixiao Why should the basic tenets of Marxism be combined with China's fine traditional culture, and how can this "Second Integration" be achieved? Shang Zhixiao takes up these questions in a study framed by Xi Jinping's remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development (2 June). The article argues that Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture are highly compatible. In Shang's account, that compatibility leads through organic combination to "mutual fulfilment", and the result is a cultural form of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the compatibility of the two, historically and in terms of ideas. The second explains how each "fulfils" the other. The third clarifies what "integration" means and what it should produce. The historical section moves from Marx's writings on China during the Second Opium War, through the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement, to the founding of the Communist Party in 1921. Shang's core argument rests on three moves. First, the author finds parallels in content: communist ideals and the ancient ideal of "a world of great harmony"; the people-centred outlook of historical materialism and the tradition of "the people as the foundation of the state"; and revolutionary spirit and the ethos of constant self-renewal. Second, mutual fulfilment runs both ways. Marxism gives traditional culture a scientific worldview and method, enabling its "creative transformation and innovative development", while traditional culture gives Marxism Chinese style and cultural vitality. Third, integration is described as a "chemical reaction", not a physical mixture or a "platter". It does not merge the two into one: it aims to make Marxism Chinese and traditional culture modern. Shang concludes that the new cultural life-form created this way is the cultural form of Chinese modernization. It draws on traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, and on the achievements of other civilizations. In the author's view, it deepens the historical roots of socialism with Chinese characteristics and shows a higher level of the Party's historical and cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how the Second Integration is justified and what theoretical outcome it is meant to produce.

Grasping the meaning of high-quality economic development 深刻把握经济高质量发展的内涵要义 Lin Jiang Lin Jiang's commentary, first published in Economic Daily in September 2023, sets out what high-quality development means and why it is the first task of building a modern socialist country in all respects. The author argues that the judgement that China's economy has shifted from a stage of rapid growth to one of high-quality development rests on Xi Jinping's economic thinking and reflects the Party's deepening grasp of economic laws. The piece begins by tracing Xi Jinping's statements on the topic from the 19th Party Congress (2017) to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then reads high-quality development from five angles: the new development stage, the new development philosophy, the change in the principal contradiction in society, the laws of economic development, and the strategic timetable to the middle of the century. A second section links the judgement to basic Marxist principles, and a third names the new development pattern as the key to carrying it out. Lin distinguishes economic growth, a quantitative increase, from economic development, the unity of quantity and quality. Quality for the author means structure and efficiency, and quantity means scale and speed. In Lin's account, extensive, factor-input growth has reached its limits: resource constraints, a shrinking working-age population and weaker comparative advantages call for innovation-driven growth. Drawing on empirical research, the author describes a move from "structural acceleration" to "structural deceleration" and the "new normal". The author also maintains that the judgement embodies the dialectical relation of matter and consciousness, the law of quantitative into qualitative change, universal connection and the doctrine of contradiction. The new development pattern, with domestic circulation as the mainstay and domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other, is presented as the strategic base. Lin presents it as a response to weakened traditional international circulation and as an open, not closed, pattern. Lin calls for balancing expanded domestic demand with supply-side structural reform, speeding up technological self-reliance, closing gaps in industrial and supply chains, building a modern industrial system, promoting rural revitalisation and regional coordination, and deepening opening up. The aim is to provide a solid material and technological base for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party economists justify the shift to high-quality development in Marxist and policy terms.

Stimulating the spiritual strength to advance Chinese modernization 激发推进中国式现代化的精神力量 Hao Wenbin This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily on 26 September 2023, asks how the Party's moral and ideological resources can drive Chinese modernization. Hao Wenbin argues that the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists, whose source is the great founding spirit of the Party, supplies lasting strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Party members and officials should therefore carry it forward in order to innovate and make new breakthroughs. Taking up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), the piece is organised around four qualities drawn from that lineage: firm ideals and convictions, a sincere commitment to the people, a fighting spirit, and the character of self-reform. Each section opens with a statement by Xi Jinping and ends with practical demands on cadres. On ideals, Hao holds that conviction has carried the Party through hardship and must rest on the scientific truth of Marxism. This requires study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the people, Hao lists spirits such as the Yan'an spirit, the Lei Feng spirit and the spirit of the fight against poverty and the pandemic as expressions of devotion to the people. Hao links this to common prosperity, investigation and research, and the Party's mass line. On struggle and self-reform, Hao calls for vigilance against "black swan" and "grey rhino" events, and for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, with the Party's self-reform keeping it from losing its character. Hao concludes that drawing on this spiritual lineage will sustain officials' drive and diligence on the new journey. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists as a resource for modernization.

Advancing cultural self-reliance, confidence and strength under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture 在习近平文化思想指引下推进文化自立自信自强 Wang Menghui This commentary by Wang Menghui, Party secretary of Hubei Province, was published in the People's Daily in January 2024. It asks how Party members and officials should understand and apply Xi Jinping Thought on Culture. Wang's answer is that the thought rests on three linked commitments: cultural self-reliance, cultural confidence and cultural strength. Wang presents it as the theoretical summary of the Party's cultural work in the new era and as a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has an opening statement of the cultural mission, followed by three sections, one for each commitment, and a short regional close. It draws on the history from the Opium War onwards, on Mao Zedong's New Democracy writings, and on Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It ends by applying the framework to Hubei and the Jingchu cultural heritage. On self-reliance, Wang argues that national independence includes spiritual independence, and that this requires a firm cultural subjectivity. In Wang's account this means arming the Party and people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, following the path of socialist cultural development, and upholding the Party's leadership over ideology and the media. On confidence, Wang treats cultural confidence as the most fundamental of the Four-sphere Confidence and as an original contribution to Marxist cultural theory. It calls for telling China's story well, building Chinese-style philosophy and social science, and strengthening international communication. On strength, Wang links national rejuvenation to cultural flourishing and names the Two Integrations as the key to Chinese modernization. Wang concludes that cultural strength is needed for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He proposes promoting core socialist values and the spirit of Party members, encouraging virtues such as diligence and dedication, and building "complete communities" through Party-led grassroots governance. For Hubei, Wang calls for creative transformation of Jingchu culture and for building a province strong in culture. Read the original if you want a compact, official provincial-level statement of how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture is organised and put into practice.

Handling well the relationship between upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground 处理好守正与创新的关系 Yue Zongwei This commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts takes up how Chinese modernization, which it calls a pioneering undertaking without precedent, should balance "upholding fundamental principles" (shouzheng) with innovation (chuangxin). Yue argues that the two are dialectically unified and complementary. The author presents this as a key method of thought for the Party's governance in the new era. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping on the dialectic of continuity and change. It then traces the approach to Chinese cultural tradition and to the Party's commitment to emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts. Two main sections follow, one on upholding principles and one on innovation. On the first, Yue says that Chinese modernization must keep its "root and soul": leadership by the Communist Party of China, socialism, and the Party's basic theory, line and strategy. The author contends that its eventual success will show capitalism is not the only route to modernization. On the second, Yue says that Chinese modernization is exploratory and faces unknown territory, so innovation must be placed at the centre of national development. The author calls for implementing the new development philosophy, pursuing high-quality development, liberating thinking, innovating in theory, and reforming institutions and mechanisms. Leading cadres should change outdated ideas and become leaders of innovation. Yue concludes that principle without innovation leads to rigidity, and innovation without principle leads to loss of direction. Both are needed to steer Chinese modernization through a period of great global change. Read the original if you want a short, authoritative example of how Party-aligned writing frames continuity and innovation in Chinese modernization.

A theoretical reading of "the people's need for a better life" “人民美好生活需要”的学理性解读 Han Xiping Du Du Han Xiping and Du Du take up the concept of "the people's need for a better life", introduced at the 19th Party Congress (2017) when the principal contradiction in Chinese society was redefined. They argue that the concept must be read historically and dialectically: it is a stage-specific need, rooted in material conditions, that expands as society develops. Grasping it correctly, in the authors' view, is necessary for tackling unbalanced and inadequate development. The article has four parts. It first traces the concept's evolution, then sets out its specific content, then gives its theoretical and practical grounds, and finally identifies the basic guarantees for meeting it. It draws on Marx and Engels (the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology, Capital, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy), Engels's Dialectics of Nature, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The authors treat human needs and the productive forces as mutually driving each other. On this basis they trace a historical line in China from the need for independence, to subsistence, to prosperity, and now to a "better" life. They divide the concept's content into material needs, which are primary and must be richer, fairer and kept reasonable so as to avoid consumerism, and spiritual or social needs, which Marx treats as essentially human. They ground the concept in the Marxist value aim of free and all-round human development, in the essence of socialism as Deng and Xi state it (ending polarisation and achieving common prosperity), and in the Party's founding mission. Finally they argue that satisfying it requires mature, rational and green material production, and a sound ecological environment drawing on Xi's "two mountains" thesis. The authors conclude that the need for a better life is neither rigid nor quantitative but a changing, open and historical category. Meeting it requires the unity of the historical stage and the long term, of the material and the spiritual, and of production and ecology. They add that it cannot be achieved at one stroke but through continued development that resolves the principal contradiction. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the 19th Congress formulation is linked to Marx's theory of needs and to Xi Jinping's statements on ecology and common prosperity.

Upholding institutions as the guarantee for developing whole-process people's democracy 坚持以制度为保障发展全过程人民民主 Bao Xinjian Bao Xinjian takes up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls whole-process people's democracy the essential attribute of socialist democracy and an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. The article asks how this democracy is secured in practice. Bao's answer is that institutions are the guarantee: a complete 'chain' of democratic institutions is what makes it, in the official formula, the most broadly based, genuine and effective form of democracy. The commentary is built in three parts, drawing heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and Party Congress reports. The first part reviews the institutional system: the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation and political consultation under Party leadership, and grassroots self-governance. The second part concerns the 'true meaning' of democracy and its link to state governance. The third part treats popular support, equality and inclusiveness. Bao's core argument has two moves. First, whole-process people's democracy is a 'full-chain' institutionalised democracy. The fundamental, basic and important political institutions cover political and social life, and each has a specific function: the people's congresses for elections, legislation and oversight, consultative channels for building consensus, and grassroots autonomy for direct democracy. Second, Bao contends that this democracy joins democratic institutions to state governance, a problem the author says Western democratic models have never solved because procedure and efficiency seem to conflict. In Bao's account, Western democracies drift from the people's needs and become tools of politicians, whereas the Communist Party's 'people-centred' stance turns institutional strengths into governance capacity. Bao ties this to the principle that matters of common concern are discussed by everyone concerned, with consultation scaled to national, local, group and grassroots issues. Bao concludes that Chinese modernization requires the democratic institutions to be strengthened further and made more institutionalised, standardised and procedural. Broad, multilevel, institutionalised consultation is said to reach the largest common denominator of public opinion, to balance unity and diversity, and to consolidate the patriotic united front. Bao presents this as a creative development of the Marxist view of democracy, with continuing political value. Read the original if you want a representative, source-heavy statement of the official 2023 case for whole-process people's democracy as an institutional and governance system.

Progress and practical testing in adapting Marxist ownership theory to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义所有制理论中国化时代化的进展和实践检验 Hong Yinxing Hong Yinxing takes up how Marx's theory of ownership, which Hong calls the core of Marxist economics, has been adapted to China's reform practice. The article argues that reform and opening up used ownership as its breakthrough point and produced a framework of ownership theory for the twenty-first century. Hong holds that this framework is faithful to Marx's method rather than a departure from it, and that practice has confirmed it. The article is organised in five parts. It covers the ownership structure of the primary stage of socialism, the capital attributes of state-owned assets, mixed ownership, property-rights institutions, and household property rights and factor incomes. Hong draws on Capital, the Communist Manifesto and the preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, and on Party documents from 1993 to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Hong also briefly contrasts Western property-rights theory and cites Piketty on inequality. Hong's first move is that the form of ownership depends on the level of the productive forces, so private ownership cannot be abolished until the non-public sector has exhausted its capacity. This is said to justify public ownership as the mainstay alongside other forms, and the shift from the Two Unwaverings to the 'two inviolables' of public and non-public property rights. The second move is that state capital, though lacking the capital-labour relation, shares capital's other traits: profit-seeking, motion and accumulation. On this basis Hong defends the exit of state capital from uncompetitive sectors, mixed ownership through joint-stock firms, and the shift from managing assets to managing capital. The third move extends ownership from means of production to all factors, including data, so that distribution by factor contribution is explained as the economic realisation of factor ownership. Hong proposes narrowing income gaps by increasing the non-labour factors workers hold, not by denying factor incomes. Hong sums up the path as moving from abolishing private ownership to using it under public-sector dominance, from denying to affirming state assets' capital attributes, from ownership to property-rights systems, and from means of production to factor ownership with household property income. In Hong's view, this twenty-first-century ownership theory keeps pace with the times and has raised overall efficiency across forms of ownership. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese economist's account of how state-capital reform, mixed ownership and factor distribution are justified in Marxist terms.

The human-centred meaning of China's cultural modernization and paths to building it 我国文化现代化的人学意蕴及其建设路径 Zhang Zhonghua Feng Yanli Most scholars study cultural modernization by looking at how the economy and politics shape culture. Zhang Zhonghua and Feng Yanli accept this but argue that culture is a product of human practice, so its modernization is at core the modernization of people. The article contends that advancing China's cultural modernization in the new era therefore requires an anthropological (renxue) perspective, one centred on the human subject. The article has four parts. It first defines cultural modernization as part of modernization as a whole, using a three-layer model of culture (material, institutional, spiritual) and three features of modernization (transformative, developmental, comprehensive). It then argues that the modernization of people is the core of cultural modernization, and explains why China's version is marked by the primacy of the people. Finally it sets out three practical requirements: adequate understanding, effective measures and joint effort. The central move is that people's modernization, meaning knowledge, skills, social relations, psychology, values and ways of thinking, is both what produces culture and what culture shapes. The authors hold that imported educational models or cultural management methods will remain nominal if the public's mindset does not match them. They cite Alex Inkeles on psychological barriers to development. In the authors' account, Western cultural modernization is capital-centred and polarised, leaving workers with vulgar commodities and spiritual poverty. China's, they say, rests on four features: leadership by the Communist Party, a socialist character, service to the people and to socialism, and social benefits ranked above economic ones. In practice, the authors call for stronger awareness that cultural modernization advances people's modernization, self-liberation and civilisation. They urge adherence to the socialist path of cultural development with Chinese characteristics, coordinated material and spiritual progress, and skills support for disadvantaged groups. They also assign roles to government (policy and ideological security), society (cultural organisations and enterprises) and individuals (modern consciousness and practical ability). Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars link cultural modernization to a theory of the human subject and to the idea of the primacy of the people.

Drawing wisdom for theoretical innovation from the creations of the people 从人民群众的创造中汲取理论创新智慧 Ai Silin Ai Silin takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at a Politburo study session of the 20th Central Committee, to "pay attention to drawing wisdom for theoretical innovation from the creations of the people". The article reads this as an application of the Marxist theory of knowledge and the view of history centred on the masses, and as a summary of the Party's historical experience. Ai's thesis is that the people's creative practice is the inexhaustible source of Marxist theoretical innovation, so the Party must follow the mass line in developing theory. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical basis: the primacy of practice in Marxist epistemology and the people's role as the makers of history. The second reviews the Party's history, from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The third turns to practical requirements for theoretical innovation. In Ai's argument, practice is the basis and test of knowledge, and the masses are the main force transforming the world. The people's practice therefore decides which problems theory must address, supplies its content, and supplies a standard for judging results. Ai presents the results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times as the distilled experience and collective wisdom of the Party and the people. Examples include rural investigations behind Mao Zedong's strategy of encircling cities from the countryside, and household contract responsibility, township enterprises and ownership reform in the reform era. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is described as rooted in the people's practice. Ai proposes that the mass line be followed in theoretical work through three measures. The first is large-scale investigation and research, in which officials act as the people's pupils and go down to grassroots level. The second is to condense investigation findings into new theory, so that investigation does not become a "broken bridge" to research. The third is a lasting mechanism: education in the mass viewpoint, better evaluation of research, open channels for suggestions and criticism, and theorists who write their papers "on the land of the motherland". Read the original if you want to see how a Red Flag Manuscripts article links Party theory-making to the mass line and to investigation and research as methods.

Firmly holding the bottom line of economic security 牢牢守住经济安全底线 Ding Jinqing Writing in Economic Daily in December 2023, after the Central Economic Work Conference, Ding Jinqing asks how China can keep economic security secure while pursuing growth. The commentary argues that high-quality development and a high level of security must reinforce each other, and that economic security is the foundation of national security and part of the holistic approach to national security. Ding holds that this requires Party leadership across economic work and a firm grasp of four basic characteristics of economic security. The piece is organised around those four characteristics: stability, strategic nature, dynamism and interconnectedness. Each section gives three or four practical requirements, supported by statements from Xi Jinping and the Central Economic Work Conference. The dynamism section covers four priority fields: food, energy, key technologies and finance. On stability, Ding calls for seeking progress while keeping stability, handling reform, development and stability as an organic whole, and pursuing quality and quantity together without judging success by growth rates alone. On strategy, Ding stresses economic development as the central task, upholding and improving the basic socialist economic system, with the Two Unwaverings, and a people-centred approach. Ding says doubts about the basic economic system or about the role of private business should be clearly rebutted. On dynamism, Ding says food, energy, core technology and finance must each be secured, including through the 1.8 billion mu farmland red line, a new energy security strategy, self-reliance in science and technology, and comprehensive financial regulation to avoid systemic risk. On interconnectedness, Ding argues that economic security is a whole-system matter, so risks must be stopped from chaining together or escalating, for instance from economic risk into social and political risk, or from international risk into domestic risk. Ding concludes that development and security should be planned together, with a new security pattern matching the new development pattern, so that development builds security and security protects development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary frames economic security in the language of the Central Economic Work Conference and Xi Jinping's statements.

The threefold significance of building the new development pattern 构建新发展格局的三重意蕴 Chen Yanbin Why did the Party Central Committee decide to accelerate the building of a new development pattern? Chen Yanbin argues that the decision answers two pressures: insufficient domestic demand within the domestic cycle, and weakening momentum in the international cycle amid de-globalisation and uncertainty. The article sets out three aspects of the pattern's significance: it clears the domestic circulation and supports high-quality development; it promotes interaction between domestic and international circulations and builds new advantages in cooperation and competition; and it brings supply and demand into a higher-level dynamic balance while raising the efficiency of macroeconomic regulation. The piece is an explanatory essay in the Party journal Qianxian, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the 14th Five-Year Plan had both called for a pattern with the domestic cycle as the mainstay. It draws on World Bank and National Bureau of Statistics figures and on Xi Jinping's statements. Its three sections move from consumption and investment, to industrial chains and the super-large market, to macroeconomic policy. On the domestic cycle, Chen notes that household consumption was only 38.4 per cent of GDP in 2022, well below the global average and the middle- and high-income averages. Chen also reports that capital formation contributed 50.1 per cent of GDP but drove only 1.5 percentage points of growth, and that private investment's share fell to 52.9 per cent in the first half of 2023. The proposed remedies are fairer income distribution, a sounder social security system, a larger middle-income group and more productive investment. On the international side, Chen argues that the old low-end embedding in global value chains is no longer sustainable. China's complete industrial system and its super-large market could instead raise supply-chain resilience, help overcome 'chokepoint' technologies, and create a new 'gravitational field' for global resources. On regulation, Chen holds that traditional demand-side stabilisation cannot cope with interacting short- and long-term, supply and demand problems. Chen advocates the 'three-in-one' framework, which unifies stabilisation, growth and structural policies. Chen concludes that the new pattern is a systematic project and the strategic basis for high-quality development. For current conditions, the author calls for a growth target slightly above potential growth, moderately stronger monetary and fiscal policy, and combined use of structural and growth policies to remove bottlenecks. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official economic rationale for the new development pattern, together with the policy-framework proposals of a CASS macroeconomist.

Adhering to the general principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability 坚持稳中求进工作总基调 Han Baojiang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 27 September 2023, presents the "general principle of making progress while maintaining stability" as a guiding principle of Party governance and a methodology for economic work. Han Baojiang argues that, with the economy recovering but facing new difficulties, officials should study, grasp and apply this methodology so as to meet the year's economic and social targets with high-quality development. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the meaning of the principle, drawing on Chinese reform experience since reform and opening up and on a series of statements by Xi Jinping. It then discusses how to handle the dialectical unity of "stability" and "progress". Finally, it lists three areas for effort: high-quality development, deepening reform and opening up, and coordinating development with security. Han's central claim is that stability and progress must be understood as a whole. Stability is the premise, meaning steady growth, employment and prices, no systemic financial risk, and consistent policy direction. Progress means restructuring the economy and deepening reform, and stability does not mean inaction. Two relationships follow. Reform, development and stability must be balanced, so that the pace of reform and development stays within what society can bear, under the Party's leadership. Groping for stones to cross the river must also be combined with top-level design, as reform enters what Han calls its deep-water stage. Han's recommended measures include the new development philosophy, a unified national market, the Two Unwaverings, institutional opening up and the Belt and Road Initiative. They also include a holistic approach to national security, which Han describes as ensuring that security and development advance together. Han concludes that the Party should build on a secure foundation while working harder on "progress", aiming at an effective improvement in quality and a reasonable growth in quantity. The commentary also calls on leading cadres to master the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and use it to analyse economic questions. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how official commentary framed the "stability with progress" principle in economic policy in autumn 2023.

From the "first integration" to the "Two Integrations": an important development and innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context 从“一个结合”到“两个结合”：马克思主义中国化的重要发展和创新 Ren Guixiang Ren Guixiang asks how the "Two Integrations" put forward by Xi Jinping in 2021 relate to the earlier Party principle of combining Marxism with China's concrete realities. The article argues that the Two Integrations inherit, enrich and develop that "first integration". It presents the addition of a "second integration", with China's fine traditional culture, as a further innovation and leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has four parts. It first traces the first integration from Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. It then examines how Xi enriched the first integration after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third part reviews the Party's earlier attitudes to traditional culture and the stages by which Xi proposed the Two Integrations. The last part sets out the significance of the second integration. Ren argues that Xi's treatment of the first integration is macro-level and holistic, linking a century of Party history to five hundred years of world socialism. It is also dynamic and open to the times, and it extends to concrete cases such as the Zunyi Conference and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference. The Two Integrations took shape gradually in Xi's speeches from 2014 to early 2021. They were formally proposed on 1 July 2021, written into the Party's third historical resolution (2021) and elaborated in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Ren holds that Mao and later leaders handled the relation to traditional culture correctly but never framed it as an explicit proposition. In this reading, the first integration is the premise of the second and the second is its development. Ren draws four conclusions about the second integration. It is a new leap in adapting Marxism and creates a "new cultural life form". It is a further ideological emancipation, comparable to the New Culture Movement and the 1978 truth-criterion debate. It widens the cultural foundations of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It supplies the cultural soft power for Chinese modernization, national rejuvenation and building a strong cultural nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how the Two Integrations were developed and justified, with extensive citation of Xi's speeches.

Running school ideological and political courses to the "highest standard of the capital" to cultivate new-era talents who shoulder the task of national rejuvenation 以首善标准办好学校思政课 培养担当民族复兴重任的时代新人 Education Work Committee of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee This is an institutional report by the Education Work Committee of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024. It sets out how Beijing is implementing Xi Jinping's instructions on school ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke). The Committee argues that such courses are the key course for ensuring the socialist orientation of education, and that Beijing is meeting the "highest standard of the capital" in building them. The text follows five headings. These are: arming students with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; innovation in the content and quality of the courses; a capital-based "great ideological and political course" built around practical teaching; the "six requirements" for teachers; and Party leadership and social coordination. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi Jinping and then lists Beijing's measures, with figures and named programmes. In the Committee's account, Beijing was the first in the country to make the compulsory course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era" universal for new undergraduates (from autumn 2020). It also issued the first national guideline integrating ideological education across universities, secondary and primary schools, set up five pilot districts, and built digital teaching resources and a "Digital Marxism School" project. The Committee describes more than 200 immersive practice bases, student participation in events such as the 70th anniversary of the PRC, the Party's centenary and the Winter Olympics, and school-specific brands. It also describes teacher measures: a staff-student ratio of at least 1:350, Party membership for new recruits, separate promotion tracks, competitions, and dynamic removal of poorly rated teachers. The Committee concludes that sustained Party leadership is decisive. It cites annual reports to the municipal Party standing committee, "first-in-charge" responsibility for school Party secretaries and presidents, and cooperation among families, schools, museums and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. It presents these arrangements as the way to produce successors "whom the Party can rely on". Read the original if you want a detailed, official inventory of how a leading Chinese municipality organises ideological and political education, from curricula to teacher management.

Optimising the use of red historical and cultural resources in practical teaching of ideological and political theory courses in universities An examination based on red venues 红色历史文化资源在高校思政课实践教学中的优化运用 Xie Ruoyang Song Jian Xie Ruoyang and Song Jian ask how Chinese universities can make fuller and more effective use of red historical and cultural resources in the practical teaching of ideological and political theory courses. Starting from Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on using red resources and passing on the red gene, and from the current drive to build the "great ideological and political course", they argue that red venues such as memorials, museums and former revolutionary sites are an underused teaching platform. Their thesis is that a systematic, university–venue partnership is needed to resolve three identified problems. The article has three parts. The first analyses the ideological and political education functions of red venues, physical and digital. The second reviews problems in how these venues are used in practical teaching. The third proposes ways to optimise their use. The authors place the discussion within the principle of unifying theory and practice and of linking the "small classroom" of the course with the "big classroom" of society. The authors credit red venues with three functions: narrowing the temporal distance to history and building emotional identification; deepening historical understanding and theoretical thinking, strengthening confidence in Party history and helping students resist historical nihilism; and guiding young people's values so that they carry on the red gene. They then identify three problems. Universities, concentrated in cities, favour accessible urban venues, leaving rural and remote sites, where the authors say most revolutionary remains lie, neglected. Visits stay passive, and digital venues mainly display with little interaction. Evaluation also leans towards results and lacks feedback between venues and universities. In response, Xie and Song call for a shared online and offline information platform linking venues and universities, and for joint research and interactive, participatory activities. They cite as an example the national research centre for revolutionary cultural relics that Wuhan University set up with the Xinhai Revolution Museum. They also propose a collaborative evaluation mechanism running through the whole teaching process, with several evaluating parties and a combination of process and outcome assessment, in place of reliance on practice reports alone. The aim, in their account, is to fulfil the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent. Read the original if you work on ideological and political course pedagogy or museum–university cooperation in China and want a structured account of the officially stated problems and remedies.

The laws of truth embedded in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 推进马克思主义中国化时代化蕴含的真理规律 Yan Xiaofeng Yan Xiaofeng takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is a process of pursuing, revealing and putting into practice truth. The article argues that the process works because it follows the practical principle and the laws of truth. On that basis, theoretical innovation guides creative practice. The article has four parts. It first presents pursuing, revealing and practising truth as an essential requirement of Marxism, using Marx's and Engels's own careers as illustration. It then treats the adaptation of Marxism as such a process, and identifies the Two Integrations as its fundamental route. Finally it turns to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the tasks of the new journey after the 20th Party Congress. Yan holds that Marxism's truth rests on its advanced class character, on the historical law of human emancipation, and on a scientific spirit that rejects "ultimate truth" and dogma. Adaptation is described as the unity of the universal and the particular, so that adapting Marxism to China also means adapting it to the times. In this account the Party's ideological line, the Two Integrations and the successive theoretical results (Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, Xi Jinping Thought) each embody this truth-seeking. The "second integration", with fine traditional Chinese culture, is presented as a further liberation of thought that broadens the cultural base of socialism with Chinese characteristics and expresses cultural subjectivity. Yan concludes that Xi Jinping Thought carries a "truth character" shown in the "six musts" and a "truth force" of conviction, responsibility, creativity and practice. The article calls for further theoretical thinking on the questions of the new journey. These include the question "where is the world heading", Chinese modernization, and the problems peculiar to a large governing party, to which the article says the Party's self-reform is the second answer to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party theorist ties epistemology and the theory of truth to official doctrine on the adaptation of Marxism.

Revision notes on the 2024 edition of the textbook "Chinese Marxism and the Contemporary Era" Guidance for revising and teaching the doctoral political theory course 《中国马克思主义与当代（2024年版）》修订说明 Hou Huiqin This is an explanatory note by Hou Huiqin, chief expert of the project team, on the 2024 revision of the textbook Chinese Marxism and the Contemporary Era. It is the only ideological and political theory course taught to doctoral students nationwide. Hou says the revision, only two years after the 2021 edition but spanning the 20th Party Congress (2022), aims to build the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times into the book, and offers teaching advice for the new edition. The note has three parts. The first sets out the revision's guiding idea and principles: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is treated through the relationship between contemporary China and the world, the Two Establishes provide the political standpoint, and updating is balanced against stability. The second argues that teaching depends on rendering Marxism in rigorous scholarly terms ("xueli hua"). The third presents the course's purpose as cultivating socialist "new-era talents" with a world outlook, with comments on students, teachers and young people's responsibilities. Hou argues that new ideas should be integrated "organically" rather than pasted in as labels, and that about a third of the text was changed while keeping the 2021 structure. Each of chapters one to six moves from the world's problems, to how states respond, to China's answer. Chapters on contemporary capitalism and socialism are now set within the interplay of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes of the century. On scholarly rigour, Hou holds that doctoral teaching must pose problems that experience cannot answer, rebut "rational" hostile ideological challenges, and reconstruct theoretical results as historical laws grounded in a worldview, not in empiricism. Hou also says teachers should stress that Chinese modernization is fundamentally different from Western modernization and reject the view that modernization means Westernization. Hou concludes that the course should join ideological guidance with academic depth, so that doctoral students gain a Marxist worldview alongside specialist skills and take on responsibility for national rejuvenation. The closing section, on the dialectic of "when youth flourishes, the nation flourishes", urges young people to unite China's mission with the times' mission, cultivate virtue and real skills, and pair lofty ideals with hard work. Read the original if you want to see how the compilers of China's doctoral-level political theory course describe its design, its teaching method and its intended audience.

Several hot issues in current domestic research on new quality productive forces 当前国内新质生产力研究的几个热点问题 Dong Zhenrui Li Zhen This review, published in 2024, surveys how Chinese scholars have responded to the concept of new quality productive forces, which Xi Jinping first put forward during inspection tours from July 2023 and elaborated further in 2024. Dong and Li note that the concept drew wide attention, and they summarise the main debates in the field. They report that scholars from economics, science and technology and theory differ in sources and methods but largely converge in their basic conclusions. The review is organised around three questions: why the concept was proposed, what it contains, and what practical steps its development requires. On background, it lists five rationales: advancing Chinese modernization, high-quality development, higher-quality living for the people, seizing the new round of technological and industrial change, and offsetting profound shifts in the world political and economic order. A short concluding section assesses the research as a whole. On content, the review follows Xi's definition and reports scholars' discussion of the three elements (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour), technological innovation as the core factor, and a large rise in total factor productivity as the core marker. It also covers the role of traditional, emerging and future industries and the three keywords "innovation", "superior quality" and "advanced productive forces". On practice, it records scholarly proposals on high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, a modern industrial system, green transformation, deeper reform to build matching new relations of production, a virtuous cycle of education, science and talent, and development adapted to local conditions. Some scholars warn that the concept should not be over-extended or applied indiscriminately. Dong and Li characterise the literature as strongly oriented to real-world problems, solid in tracing theoretical sources, and rigorous in generalising practice. They acknowledge that research is sometimes insufficiently focused. Two open problems stand out: how to avoid both the over-broad labelling of everything as "new quality productive forces" and a narrow reading limited to technology and industry, and how to treat the relation among emerging, future and traditional industries. Read the original if you want a map of mainstream Chinese scholarly positions on the concept in its first year, with the Party-line framing intact.

The generative logic and meaning of the concept of "new quality productive forces" An understanding based on historical materialism “新质生产力”的概念生发逻辑与内涵探析 Zhang Xiaojing Since Xi Jinping first used the term in September 2023, "new quality productive forces" has become a national development priority. Zhang argues that much of the existing commentary blurs the concept: it equates new quality productive forces with "new economy", "new business forms" or "new industries", or treats their causes, conditions and functions as their meaning. The article's thesis is that the concept must be returned to Marx's definition of productive forces and traced through the practice of China's economic development. On that basis Zhang defines the essence of new quality productive forces as advanced labour productive force. The article has four parts. The first reviews Marx's concept of productive forces, including Chinese scholarship's departure from the Soviet-textbook "element theory" and its recovery of the concept's origins in The German Ideology and Marx's technology notebooks. The second explains why the concept arises necessarily from historical materialism and from the demands of high-quality development. The third gives a multidimensional account of the concept's meaning, with examples from agriculture, industry, the digital economy and daily life. A short conclusion follows. Zhang's central move is to read Marx's "productive force" as the capacity of useful, concrete labour to create use-value, which cannot be separated from the relations of production. Productive forces are formed within given relations, and the old quality dissolves as a new one forms. On this reading, "new quality" is not a break with earlier industrial productive forces: digital technology amplifies them through a "multiplier effect". The author cites figures from a 2023 China Academy of Information and Communications Technology report: a digital economy of 50.2 trillion yuan in 2022, 41.5 per cent of GDP. Zhang also argues that self-reliance in core technology, with chips as the example, is a necessary condition. New quality productive forces then appear in four forms: a leap in the means of production, high-quality development of natural forces, innovative use of collective force, and the broad distribution of "general intellect". Zhang's examples include public ownership of natural resources, the "East Data, West Computing" project and ride-hailing platforms.
