Zhang concludes that Marx's productive-forces theory is a living methodology, not a dogma. It is the theoretical root of the concept, and it keeps the people-centred character of socialism with Chinese characteristics in view. The author holds that "new quality" is not an isolated quality: it is the product of China's successive revolutionary, construction and reform stages. Developing it requires attention to labour, means of production, natural force, collective force and general intellect together. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars ground the concept in Marx's texts, and a view of how the concept is being defined and defended in academic debate.

How the Communist Party of Cuba strengthens unity and builds consensus 古巴共产党加强团结凝聚共识的实践 Liu Xiangyang He Qin Liu Xiangyang and He Qin ask how the Communist Party of Cuba has sought to keep the country united while it pursues the "updating of the model" (模式更新) of Cuban socialism in the 21st century. Their answer is that the Party and government have combined measures on political stability, Party unity, rule of law, an online ideological struggle and international solidarity. In the authors' account, these steps have eased internal and external pressures and improved the social base and external environment for the updating. The article opens with the background of the model update: Raúl Castro's 2007 concept, the 6th Party Congress's guidelines, the 7th Congress's aim of "prosperous and sustainable socialism", and the 8th Congress's self-criticism of slow progress. It then covers generational succession in the leadership, Party-building, legal reforms (the 2019 Constitution, the 2024 ethics law for revolutionary cadres, the 2022 Family Code), defence against hostile online activity, and Cuba's diplomacy and international forums. The authors argue that Cuba's reforms, which expand private and informal activity, have brought speculation, tax evasion, moral decline and wider social divisions, so consensus must be rebuilt. On leadership, they describe an "old with new" arrangement in which Miguel Díaz-Canel, a scientist-politician, succeeded Raúl Castro with the older generation's approval. On ideology, they report that the Party prioritises Marxism-Leninism and history education, party schools and a cadre ethics regime. They describe the July 2021 protests and those in Santiago de Cuba in March 2024 as results of foreign hostile interference. In their account, Cuba responds with cyber ideological struggle and international solidarity, citing the 2019 solidarity congress of 1,300 delegates from 95 countries. The authors conclude that Cuba's model update has reached a critical point of deepening, and that the Party, government and people must unify their thinking. They argue that only by consolidating the subjectivity of Cuban culture and holding the leading position in the ideological struggle can maximum consensus be reached and risks be managed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how the Cuban Party presents its efforts at political cohesion and ideological work, with dates and institutional details.

The "Second Integration" and the space for innovation “第二个结合”与创新空间 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang asks how the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, opens a space for innovation for the modern civilization of the Chinese nation. The article argues that it is a civilizational methodology and not merely a theoretical abstraction of specific cases. In Liu's view it breaks through the spatial pattern framed by Western modern civilization and shows the theoretical wisdom of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first explains how the Second Integration opens the innovation space. The second sets out its "overall perspective" and the value positioning of that space. The third examines its inclusive mechanism and the continuing construction of the space. Liu draws on Marx's account of world history and capitalist modernity, and on categories such as cultural space, spatial justice and the production of space. Liu's central move is to read the Second Integration as combining a diachronic totality (a historical process from past to future, from tradition to modernity) with a synchronic totality (a structure of social relations). Together these give the innovation space its coordinates and locate it as a cultural space, produced through cultural production and exchange across public and individual, urban and rural, real and virtual spaces. A second move contrasts Western modernity with the Chinese case. Liu says Western modernity rests on the logic of capital, which turns time into space, uses the world market to create spatial barriers, and reduces "inclusiveness" to homogenisation. By contrast, Liu argues, the Second Integration draws on the inclusiveness, continuity, innovativeness and unity of Chinese civilization. It therefore offers a mechanism for different civilizations to coexist, grounded in rational consensus and in the unity of conformity to laws and purposiveness, and of endogenous development and external extension. Liu concludes that the Second Integration is the necessary path to cultural identity and to a modern Chinese civilization with its own style. Liu presents it as a cultural strategy of the Party in the new era that takes up the problems of modernity within Marx's world-history framework, expresses the originality of Chinese modernization, and supplies civilizational strength useful to human society. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on spatial theory and the critique of capitalist modernity to interpret the Second Integration.

The concept of democracy: Mao Zedong's construction of democracy and its multidimensional reflections With a discussion of Mao Zedong's foundational contribution to the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 民主的概念：毛泽东的民主构境与多维镜像的阐释 Li Panqiang Li Panqiang asks what Mao Zedong's concept of democracy actually was, arguing that although Mao's democratic thought has been widely studied, it has rarely been treated as a conceptual whole. The article contends that people's democracy is the core concept of Mao Zedong Thought and that Mao built an independent Chinese body of knowledge about democracy. On this basis Li claims that Mao laid the foundations of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces how Mao's concept formed through the combined influence of Chinese tradition, modern Western thought and Marxism-Leninism, and presents it at two levels: the "idea" (people's democracy as the people being masters of the country) and its concrete "existence" in practice. The second examines four dimensions of Mao's democratic framework, drawing on his speeches and writings from the 1920s to the 1960s. The third sets out Mao's contribution to Chinese modern civilization. In Li's reading, Mao defined democracy plainly as ordinary people being able to speak and act, and as a means rather than an abstract end. The four dimensions are democracy as rights (freedoms of speech, assembly and association, and workers' right to manage the state and enterprises); as a method of realising Party leadership (the mass line, gathering popular opinion, opposing bureaucracy); as an institutional system (from the people's republic to the people's congress system, the people's political consultative conference and consultative democracy); and as a democratic spirit (mutual respect, the search for truth through discussion, and shared ideals). Li presents Mao's 1945 answer to Huang Yanpei, that democracy is the way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall, as a key moment. Li concludes that Mao contributed to the democratic ideal, path, institutions and form of Chinese modern civilization. In the article's account, Mao avoided copying Western liberal democracy, broke the presumed uniqueness of the Western path, and created a new form that combines consultative and electoral democracy and goes beyond Western voting democracy. Li presents this as the root of whole-process people's democracy in the new era. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-theoretical reconstruction of Mao's democratic thought, with dense citations of his texts, as one strand of current Chinese discourse on democracy.

The value essence, value composition and value orientation of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的价值本质、价值构成与价值指向 Yao Chong Writing in 2024, Yao Chong asks what Chinese modernization looks like when read through the theory of value rather than through economic or institutional description. The article argues that Chinese modernization is the Chinese Communist Party's value practice of understanding and changing the world. Its essence, content and orientation are all organised around meeting the needs of the human subject, in contrast with Western modernization, which Yao says serves capital. The article has three parts. The first sets out three aspects of the value essence of Chinese modernization. The second breaks its value composition into five elements: value fact, value goal, value principle, value driving force and value choice. The third identifies four value orientations, ranging from national rejuvenation to a new form of human civilization. Throughout, Yao draws on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Capital, The German Ideology and Engels's Anti-Dühring, together with speeches by Xi Jinping. In the first move, Yao holds that Chinese modernization is essentially the satisfaction of people's needs, the affirmation of the objectification of human essential powers, and a Chinese interpretation of free and all-round human development. Western modernization, by contrast, is said to satisfy the needs of capital and to turn labour into forced, repetitive activity. In the second move, each value element is tied to a Chinese policy theme. The huge population is the value fact, common prosperity the goal, coordinated material and spiritual civilization the principle, harmony between humanity and nature the driving force, and the path of peaceful development the choice. Yao presents these as expressions of Marx's view of humanity, nature and society. Yao concludes that Chinese modernization points towards four ends: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a modernized socialist country; the development of twenty-first-century Marxism and a new picture of modernization theory; a model for developing countries that respects their cultural agency; and a new form of human civilization built on a community with a shared future for mankind. The article claims that it breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and enriches common human values. Read the original if you want a value-theory reading of Chinese modernization that ties the official slogans to Marx's concepts of need, objectification and free development.

Making vigorous efforts to cultivate and practise the core socialist values 着力培育和践行社会主义核心价值观 Zhang Chuanhe Following the national work conference on propaganda, ideological and cultural work held shortly before publication, and Xi Jinping's instruction listing 'seven efforts', Zhang Chuanhe takes up the task of cultivating and practising the core socialist values. The article argues that this task is a spiritual force for advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In Zhang's account it bears on social harmony and long-term national stability, and is a major task of the new era. The piece, a commentary in a Party theoretical journal, has three parts. The first explains why the core values matter; the second sets out guiding principles for cultivating them; the third proposes concrete channels of implementation. It draws throughout on the 20th Party Congress (2022) report and on Xi Jinping's statements. In the first part, Zhang argues that a country of over 1.4 billion people and 56 ethnic groups without shared core values could easily become 'a sheet of loose sand'. The core values are presented as the soul of cultural soft power and an element of state governance capacity. The second part holds that the work must be guided by Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with ideals and convictions at its centre. Its focus is shaping 'new-era people' able to shoulder national rejuvenation, described as self-confident, ethical, dedicated, practical and enterprising, and fostered through patriotism and Party, national and reform-era history education. The third part proposes four channels: law and policy, as expressed in combining rule of law with rule by virtue; excellent literary and artistic works; families, schools, workplaces and online space; and practical activities such as Martyrs' Day commemorations, model selections and volunteer service. Zhang concludes that the core values must be built into legal construction, social governance, national education and cultural production so that society identifies with and consciously acts on them. Education alone is insufficient without institutional norms and policy backing. Online space needs close attention to value orientation, with content contrary to the core values to be firmly kept out. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the Party press frames the practical routes for implementing the core socialist values in law, culture, education and daily activity.

Scientific guidance for correctly handling major relationships in China's economic development 正确处理我国经济建设中重大关系的科学指引 Li Yuju Lian Xin This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 29 November 2023, argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought gives guidance for handling the major relationships in China's economic development. The authors describe that thought as an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and as a theoretical achievement of applying Marxist political economy to new-era practice. The piece takes up five relationships in turn: government and market; reform and the rule of law; development and security; self-reliance and opening up; and China and the world. For each, the authors summarise a series of statements by Xi Jinping and then state what must be done on the new journey. On government and market, the authors trace the Party's shifting formulation from the market playing a basic role to a decisive role, and report Xi's call for a unified national market and for government to maintain macroeconomic stability and correct market failures. On reform and law, they present the two as like a bird's two wings, with major reforms to rest on legal grounds. On development and security, they present the two as inseparable, citing the holistic approach to national security, food and energy security, and secure industrial and supply chains. On self-reliance, they stress high-level scientific and technological self-reliance alongside wider opening up, with the new development pattern described as a proactive choice rather than a stopgap. On China and the world, the authors cite the Belt and Road Initiative, the global development, security and civilization initiatives, and a community with a shared future for mankind, and call for using favourable trends while being ready to struggle against risks. Their overall message is to study and carry out Xi's economic thought in each of these areas. Read the original if you want a compact, official-style summary of how Party theorists frame these five relationships and the Xi statements they draw on.

The five dimensions of common prosperity 共同富裕的五重维度 Qiu Gengtian This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in October 2023, asks what the "common" in common prosperity means. Qiu Gengtian argues that common prosperity is the essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics and that its defining quality is "commonness": it applies to the whole population, covers all aspects of life and advances step by step. Qiu holds that this commonness has five dimensions, all of which are indispensable. The article takes the five dimensions in turn: coexistence (gongsheng), consensus (gongshi), joint action (gongxing), shared interests (gongli) and shared feeling (gongqing). Each is introduced briefly, with citations of Xi Jinping, and the piece closes by saying that the five support one another in practice. Qiu presents coexistence as the objective basis: the peoples of China live together in one territory as a community with a shared destiny. Consensus means a common understanding of what common prosperity is, why it matters and how to pursue it, which Qiu traces from the early reform-era view that poverty is not socialism to the current emphasis on the people's better life. Joint action means that prosperity comes from honest, lawful work by everyone, under the Party's overall leadership, not from unearned wealth. Shared interests mean prosperity is material and spiritual, short-term and long-term. Shared feeling refers to bonds among compatriots, and Qiu says it both tests the results of common prosperity and strengthens people's identification with the Party, the state and the socialist path. Qiu concludes that the five dimensions depend on and reinforce one another, so that people can see and feel common prosperity as a real fact. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned statement of how Chinese theorists break down the concept of common prosperity.

The meaning and sample features of the new form of human civilisation 人类文明新形态的内涵要义和样本特征 Xiang Yuqiao Xiang Yuqiao asks what the "new form of human civilisation" announced by Xi Jinping in 2021 actually means and why it can serve as a model for others. The article argues that the Communist Party of China, in leading the people through socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization, has created a new civilisational "sample" or paradigm. This sample, Xiang contends, is socialist, distinctively Chinese and relevant to the whole world. The article has three parts. The first places the concept in the history of civilisation, drawing on Engels, Morgan and Freud, and treats civilisation as tied to the rise of the state. The second sets out five components: material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilisation. The third lists eight features that make the new form a sample, and the author reads each against official texts, including Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Xiang argues that slave and feudal states belong to the past and that capitalist states cannot lead civilisational progress because of their unresolved contradictions. Socialist states are therefore said to carry civilisation forward. Each of the five civilisations is tied to a guiding aim: common prosperity, a people-centred approach, core socialist values, fairness and all-round human development, and harmony between humanity and nature. The eight features include Marxist guidance, Party leadership, innovation in the elements of civilisation, borrowing from other civilisations, organic unity, an ethical core drawn from Chinese tradition (citing Qian Mu and Liang Shuming), internal and external drivers, and the combination of what already exists with what is yet to be achieved. Xiang concludes that the new form is unfinished. Examples include social civility and the persistence of wealth gaps, which Xi himself says common prosperity cannot remove at once. The author calls for a scientific view of civilisation that inherits and goes beyond Chinese tradition and both criticises and learns from other civilisations. Xiang also sets this against what the article calls Western-centrism and civilisational conflict. Read the original if you want a systematic account, in official Chinese philosophical language, of how the "new form of human civilisation" is defined and structured.

Contributing the strength of historical scholarship to building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 为建设中华民族现代文明贡献历史学力量 Zhao Qingyun This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 13 October 2023, asks what Chinese historical scholarship should contribute to building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. Taking Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development as its starting point, Zhao Qingyun argues that historians must clarify the content of fine traditional Chinese culture and show its link to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. On that basis, the author calls for developing Chinese history in the new era. The article has two parts. The first discusses the place of fine traditional culture and the long Chinese historiographical tradition within it. The second turns to the tasks of historical studies today, covering the inheritance of past historical writing, the legacy of Marxist historiography, and the need for macro-level study of historical laws. In the first part, Zhao traces a distinctive historical consciousness from early patriarchal kinship structures through the office of court historian, Confucius's Spring and Autumn Annals and Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. In Zhao's account, writing history integrated culture, unified the people and helped establish legitimacy for each dynasty, while traditions of seeking truth and practical statecraft sustained cultural continuity. Modern Western aggression, the author says, damaged Chinese confidence in their own history and led some scholars into Eurocentrism. Zhao argues that Western theories now increasingly fail to explain Chinese history and reality, so historians must break free of them. In the second part, Zhao says historians should use historical materialism to give inherited scholarship a new meaning, combining national character with contemporary relevance. Chinese Marxist historiography, born in the early twentieth-century struggle for national salvation, is presented as a resource for building the discipline, academic and discourse systems of Chinese history. Zhao concludes that history must not be absent from the effort to renew the nation. Historians are urged to study historical change and its underlying principles, to give historical nourishment to Chinese modernization, and to lay deep historical roots for Chinese civilization. The author also calls for studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and applying it in research. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese historian frames the tasks of the discipline under the call to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation.

Systematic and academic research and interpretation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 体系化学理化研究阐释习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想 Zhang Yifan Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks at the sixth collective study session of the Political Bureau (30 June 2023), this article asks how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era can be interpreted in a more systematic (tixihua) and academically grounded (xueli hua) way. Zhang argues that this is an inherent requirement of theoretical innovation. In the author's view it is also the basis for embedding the theory across the disciplines of philosophy and the social sciences and for building an independent Chinese system of knowledge. The article proposes three research approaches, each treated in its own section: textual research, research on categories, and research on genesis (shengcheng). Zhang presents them as methods borrowed in part from the study of Marxist classics. The discussion ranges from Xi's early writings to the Party congress reports and resolutions that serve as comprehensive texts. On texts, Zhang calls for tracing the formation of Xi's writings through stages, from the early Zhi zhi shen, ai zhi qie to the mature Xi Jinping: The Governance of China volumes. The author also advises moving from specific fields to the whole, treating Xi's statements as "a block of solid steel". On categories, Zhang wants their meanings clarified, without "explaining China through the West" but drawing on the sum of human knowledge, and wants the relations among categories such as the Two Establishes, Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind read through dialectical and historical materialism. Categories are also to be followed dynamically, as when the first of the "Four Comprehensives" changed after the first centenary goal was met. On genesis, the author points to objective conditions of the new era, Xi's personal qualities and the guiding role of the Two Integrations, and asks scholars to show that results in practice demonstrate the theory's scientific truth. Zhang concludes that Marxist theorists should keep pace with developments, tracking new categories and shifts in their meaning as the building of a modern socialist country proceeds. They should also explain how the theory opens new realms of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the methodological agenda that Party-affiliated scholars are given for interpreting Xi Jinping Thought in an academic register.

Making distribution function and work as it should 发挥好分配的功能和作用 Lian Si Lian Si, writing in Economic Daily (8 November 2023), asks how the income distribution system should be designed so that the "cake" of economic growth is shared fairly. The article argues that distribution is the most direct way to turn development gains into shared benefits, and that a coordinated system of primary distribution, redistribution and third distribution is the institutional basis for common prosperity. The piece first traces the development of income distribution policy since the 18th Party Congress (2012), through the Third and Fifth Plenums of the 18th Central Committee, the 19th Party Congress (2017), the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then describes the three tiers of distribution and sets out the values the author sees in the system. It closes with proposals for further reform of each tier. Lian presents distribution as a decisive link in social reproduction and as the expression of interests among economic actors. In the author's account, primary distribution is market-led and stresses efficiency, redistribution is government-led and stresses fairness, and third distribution rests on voluntary charity, donations and volunteering. The author contends that the system embodies a people-centred approach, unifies efficiency and fairness, supports high-quality development by letting labour, capital, land, knowledge, technology, management and data take part in distribution, and carries on traditional Chinese cultural values through charity. Lian holds that distribution by labour as the mainstay, with several modes coexisting, suits the primary stage of socialism. For reform, Lian calls for mechanisms that reward factors by their contribution, a shift from indirect to direct taxes, larger transfer payments to less developed regions, better charity law and support for volunteering, and stronger public services and employment support. The author concludes that this coordinated system is a strong institutional guarantee for Chinese modernization and must be upheld and improved. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames the three-tier distribution system and its link to common prosperity.

The only correct path to building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation 强国建设、民族复兴的唯一正确道路 Song Yuehong Writing ahead of the 74th anniversary of the People's Republic (the piece first appeared in People's Daily on 28 September 2023), Song Yuehong reviews how the Communist Party led the people in exploring, advancing and expanding Chinese modernization. The article takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization is "the only correct path" to building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. Song argues that tracing this history deepens understanding of the path and should lead the Party and people to cherish, uphold and extend it. The article is a short historical-political commentary organised in three periods. The first covers the era of socialist revolution and construction after 1949. The second covers the period of reform and opening up and socialist modernization from 1978. The third covers the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). A closing section looks ahead to the tasks set by the 20th Party Congress (2022). Song's central move is to present the three periods as one continuous line. In the first period, the author says, the founding of the state, the socialist transformation completed by 1956, the basic political institutions and an independent, relatively complete industrial system supplied the political precondition, experience, theoretical groundwork and material base for modernization. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), reform and opening up gave modernization a vigorous institutional framework and rapid material growth, through the primary stage of socialism, the socialist market economy and opening to the world. Since 2012, Song says, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has guided the advance, the theory of Chinese modernization has taken shape, and absolute poverty has been eliminated. Looking forward, Song calls for upholding Party leadership, which the article says determines the fundamental nature of Chinese modernization, and for taking Xi Jinping Thought as the guide. The author describes Chinese modernization as a new form of human civilization and an innovation in world modernization theory and practice. Song also urges handling a series of major relationships correctly, such as efficiency and fairness, and vitality and order, while relying on self-reliance. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official periodisation of the Party's path to Chinese modernization as presented in the Party press.

Releasing innovation momentum to lead the development of new quality productive forces 释放创新动能引领新质生产力发展 Lu Yuanyuan Following the Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2023, this newspaper commentary argues that new quality productive forces, being new in field and high in technological content, require innovation momentum to be released faster and development to be led by scientific and technological innovation. Lu presents the concept as an innovation on, and development of, the Marxist theory of productive forces. The piece has three parts. It first explains what new quality productive forces are and why they matter, then stresses high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, and finally sets out four ways for innovation to lead. It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's remarks and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Lu argues that new quality productive forces differ from traditional ones: innovation is their primary driver, intelligence an important resource and data a core factor of production. In Lu's account they drive high-quality development, seize the opportunities of the new round of technological revolution and industrial change, and help upgrade traditional manufacturing. High-level self-reliance in science and technology is described as the reliable guarantee for forming them, and as the foundation of national strength and security. The four measures are: using technological innovation to drive industrial innovation; promoting high-quality development of key manufacturing industrial chains through a new-type whole-nation system; advancing new industrialization, both fostering emerging and future industries and upgrading traditional ones; and strengthening the position of enterprises as the main body of innovation, with deeper reform of the science and technology system. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in late 2023 framed new quality productive forces and the policy steps linked to them.

Grasping the scientific methods for doing economic work well in the new era 把握做好新时代经济工作的科学方法 Zhang Xiaojing Zhang Xiaojing asks what methodology underlies Xi Jinping's economic thought and how it should guide economic work in the new era. Writing in the Economic Daily in September 2023, the author argues that the thought rests on the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, summed up in the "six musts", and that reading it through its methods clarifies why it is the fundamental guide for economic work. The article selects six methodological principles from Xi's economic thought and treats each in turn: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, a systems perspective, the general tone of seeking progress while maintaining stability, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, and combining problem-orientation with goal-orientation. It closes by stressing the Party's centralised and unified leadership over economic work. Zhang ties each principle to concrete policy. Putting the people first is linked to livelihood measures and common prosperity, which the author describes as making the "cake" bigger through high-quality development and dividing it well through coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution aimed at an olive-shaped income structure. Self-reliance underpins the new development philosophy's companion, the dual-circulation pattern, which the author presents as a proactive move rather than an expedient. The systems perspective is said to require implementing innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing together, with examples of how innovation must not contradict openness or carbon goals. On stability and progress, the author reads the Politburo's description of recovery as "wave-like" as calling for stability in operations and progress in modern industry, reform and livelihoods. Socialist market economy is offered as the example of upholding fundamental principles while innovating, and the author stresses that problem-orientation alone yields only local optimisation. Zhang concludes that Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of correct economic methods. The author calls on readers to study Xi's economic thought methodologically, apply the new development philosophy in full, accelerate the new development pattern and pursue high-quality development in order to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how the methodology of Xi's economic thought is presented to a Chinese policy audience.

Providing fundamental guidance for comprehensively advancing rural revitalisation 为全面推进乡村振兴提供根本遵循 Tu Shengwei Tu Shengwei takes up Xi Jinping's important discourse on rural revitalisation and asks what kind of countryside China should build and how. The article, a commentary first published in Economic Daily in October 2023, argues that this discourse is an integral part of Xi Jinping Economic Thought. In Tu's account it supplies fundamental guidance and a guide to action for advancing rural revitalisation across the board, and it should be understood through its scientific implications, its rich content and its world significance. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the scientific implications of shifting the focus of work on agriculture, rural areas and farmers (the "three rural issues") to comprehensive revitalisation. The second unpacks the word "comprehensive" in four respects. The third discusses the international significance of China's approach for rural theory, global rural problems and late-developing countries. Tu draws on Marx's remarks on town and country and on the human being's all-round development, and on Xi's statements. On the first part, Tu names four features. The countryside's value is newly recognised: Tu contrasts Western modernisation, led by urban industry with the countryside in a subordinate role, with a Chinese approach that treats rural prosperity as a value goal of Chinese modernization. The work also continues a century of Party-led rural construction and follows a step-by-step path from poverty alleviation to rural revitalisation. It is further presented as a route to resolving the principal contradiction, since the greatest imbalance is between urban and rural areas and the greatest insufficiency is in the countryside. "Comprehensive" then means all fields (the "five revitalisations" of industry, talent, culture, ecology and organisation), all areas without identical models for every village, all rural residents sharing the results, and all factors of production mobilised, with the Party's leadership and the institutional strengths of socialism concentrating resources and urban–rural dual-structure barriers gradually removed. Tu concludes that China's practice breaks the general Western paradigm of rural modernisation and enriches international rural development theory. It also contributes to food security and poverty reduction, citing the 'Thousand Villages' project as a model, and offers late-developing countries options for modernising the countryside before industrialisation is complete. Tu cites figures such as feeding nearly a fifth of humanity on under 9 per cent of the world's farmland. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Xi's rural discourse is framed theoretically and internationally, as presented in the Party press.

Shouldering the new cultural mission: striving to promote the flourishing of the cultural industry 担负新的文化使命 着力推动文化产业繁荣发展 Wu Tian Hu Leming Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's recent instruction on propaganda, ideological and cultural work, this commentary asks how China's cultural industry can be made to flourish. Wu Tian and Hu Leming argue that a flourishing cultural industry meets the people's new expectations for spiritual and cultural life and underpins national cultural soft power. In their account it expresses cultural confidence and the new cultural mission, answers the need for high-quality cultural supply, and cultivates a new pillar industry serving Chinese modernization. The piece is organised around three tasks, each with sub-measures: integrating high-quality resources to raise the industry's attractiveness; coordinating multiple actors to raise management capacity; and focusing on innovation to widen the industry's influence. It draws on statistics for cultural relics, heritage sites, publishing, digital libraries and foreign cultural trade, and on examples of experiential tourism in Nanjing, Chengdu and Luoyang. It was first published in Guangming Daily on 23 October 2023. On attractiveness, the authors call for surveying and integrating cultural resources through an open, authoritative data platform, upgrading cultural experiences around public demand, and producing cultural products guided by core socialist values and enhanced by technology, such as immersive museums. On management, they propose top-level policy design under unified Party committee leadership, standardised cultural industry parks, dedicated investment funds and financial platforms, and a talent system covering leaders, composite managers and technical specialists. On influence, the authors point to digital industries accounting for over 40 per cent of cultural industry revenue and urge building a national cultural big-data system. They also call for new consumption scenes such as digital, night-time and culture-tourism formats, and for new trade channels, citing foreign cultural trade passing 200 billion US dollars in 2021, up 38.7 per cent. They propose export bases, public service platforms and wider use of big data, AI and blockchain. They conclude that such efforts will advance the creative transformation of traditional Chinese culture and the building of socialist culture. Read the original if you want a compact example of official-style policy recommendations for cultural industry development, with the statistics the authors cite.

Whole-process people's democracy is the most genuine democracy 全过程人民民主是最真实的民主 Wang Zhizhang Wang Zhiqiang argues that whole-process people's democracy is the most genuine form of democracy, and builds the case by returning to what Marxist classical writers said about democracy. The piece, a short commentary originally published in Guangming Daily in October 2023, opens with Xi Jinping's description of this democracy as the broadest, most genuine and most effective. In Wang's view, grasping the essence of democracy through the classics matters for practising it in the new era. The article moves historically. It begins with the classical democracies of ancient Greece and Rome, then turns to modern bourgeois representative democracy, then to the communist conception of democracy that Marx and Engels set against it. It closes by presenting whole-process people's democracy as a development of this Marxist theory. Wang draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin throughout. Wang reads Marx as praising classical democracy while criticising it as resting on slavery, so that the 'citizens' were a minority and slaves and foreigners were excluded. Representative democracy is credited with historical progress, but Wang follows Marx in arguing that it presupposes the separation of civil society from the political state. In this account that separation splits the person into a self-interested 'private' individual and an abstract 'citizen', leaves public affairs monopolised by the state and a bureaucracy, and reduces elections to a periodic ratification of class rule. Against this, Wang presents the Marxist goal of the liberation of labour and common ownership of the means of production, with a state whose officials serve the people and public offices open to workers, as the basis of genuine people's democracy. Wang concludes that whole-process people's democracy continues this tradition and is an innovation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article describes it as covering the full chain of democratic election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight. It also holds that this democracy unites process and outcome, procedural and substantive democracy, and direct and indirect democracy, under the unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country, and law-based governance. Wang calls for deepening the practice in order to build strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary grounds the Party's democracy concept in Marx's and Engels's critique of representative government.

Leading high-quality economic development with a systems perspective 以系统观念引领经济高质量发展 Zhang Jiangang This Guangming Daily commentary asks how high-quality development, which the 20th Party Congress (2022) called the primary task of building a modern socialist country, can be pursued. Zhang Jiangang argues that it must be understood, planned and handled as a system, following Xi Jinping's call for a systems perspective. Doing so means grasping the principal contradiction while also attending to every part of the system. The article identifies five relationships to be handled properly: quality and quantity, demand and supply, the domestic and international circulations, the real and the virtual economy, and strategic emerging industries and traditional industries. Each pairing is tied to a problem the author says must be solved systematically: aggregate balance, supply–demand fit, economic circulation, industrial structure and the drivers of growth. Zhang treats each pair as a dialectical unity, not a choice between opposites. Quality improvement is slow and cumulative, while growth in quantity must stay within a reasonable range. Supply and demand create each other, and the author sees a mismatch, with surplus products alongside outflowing demand, as a key obstacle. This is why supply-side structural reform is to remain the main line. Finance is described as the lifeblood of the real economy and must serve it. Strategic emerging industries should lead, while traditional manufacturing is upgraded through digital technology. Zhang calls for stronger macroeconomic policy, with proactive fiscal and prudent monetary measures, to expand domestic demand and manage risks. The author also urges reliance on the domestic circulation, combined with wider opening up and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy agenda for high-quality development, organised around Xi Jinping's systems perspective.

The symbiotic logic of the strategy of building a cyber power and a community with a shared future for mankind 网络强国战略与人类命运共同体的共生逻辑 Jiang Fei Jiang Fei asks how China's strategy of building a cyber power (wangluo qiangguo) relates to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that the two are mutually consistent and reinforce each other. In Jiang's account, the cyber power strategy is not only a Chinese development path but also carries a global mission of offering an "traffic logic" for equal exchange among diverse cultures. The piece opens with a historical frame of three civilisational forms: an agricultural civilisation driven by human and animal power, an industrial civilisation driven by capital and fossil energy, and an ecological civilisation that coordinates labour, capital, resources and information. Jiang then sets out three "logics" linking the strategy and the community idea: cooperation, empathy, and a balanced world media order. The discussion draws on speeches by Xi Jinping, the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and a white paper on building a community with a shared future in cyberspace. First, Jiang holds that seeking cooperation and mutual benefit is the underlying logic of the cyber power strategy and the high-level logic of the community idea, citing Xi's 2013 Moscow speech and his call at the World Internet Conference for a community with a shared future in cyberspace. Second, the Two Integrations (Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture) are said to supply an empathy logic for international communication. Jiang reads Chinese modernization as a term that international audiences can understand, linking the idea of socialism with Chinese characteristics to global notions of development. Third, Jiang argues that the network revolution widens the physical "highway" of the community idea while adding a new traffic logic. The article notes that online anonymity weakens cultural filters yet can amplify prejudice, and that cultural hegemony has contested global communication since the 1980s. Jiang concludes that China's cyber power building both retains and goes beyond primary economic cooperation. The strategy is said to align with the goal of a balanced international communication pattern in which Chinese voices, and those of weaker groups worldwide, are heard, and in which mutual learning among civilisations is promoted under Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese communication scholar links internet governance, international communication and the community with a shared future for mankind.

The Chinese civilisational foundations and world significance of the new development philosophy Studying the spirit of the 20th Party Congress 新发展理念的中华文明底蕴和世界意义 Tian Pengying Zhang Lin Tian Pengying and Zhang Lin ask where the new development philosophy comes from and what it means beyond China. They argue that it is the outcome of the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's fine traditional culture. In their account it is rooted in the people-centred aim of seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation, and it carries universal significance for human development. The article was published in Ideological Front in 2023 and draws on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article has three parts. The first examines the philosophy's "root and soul" as a theory of development for the people, by the people and tested by the people. The second traces its "source and stream": the traditional ideas it inherits and the way it transforms them. The third sets out its meaning for China, as one of the "five musts" in the Congress report, and for the world, in theory, path and goal. The core argument is that the philosophy is not a revival of tradition but a creative transformation of it under Marxism. The authors map each of its five components onto an older idea: innovation onto "discarding the old and establishing the new", coordination onto valuing harmony and the mean, green development onto the unity of heaven and humanity, openness onto "harmony among all nations", and sharing onto "the world as a shared commons", which in their reading is surpassed by common prosperity. They then claim that it surpasses Western development theory, which in their view follows the logic of capital and leads to polarisation, materialism and external expansion. They also claim that it extends Marxist development theory, with each component refining a Marxist doctrine. Finally, they present it as guiding a peaceful, fair and democratic path for humanity, reflected in the Belt-and-Road-style opening of China's own development, in global governance reform and in whole-process people's democracy. The authors conclude that the new development philosophy unites law-governed development with purposeful development and unites China's logic with the world's. They say it offers methodological guidance for modernising both people and human society, and that it will lead a new direction for human civilisation. They also present it as supporting the goals of a community with a shared future for mankind and a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese theorists link the new development philosophy to traditional culture, Marxist theory and claims of global significance.

Key focal points for advancing new industrialization 推进新型工业化的几个着力点 Chen Qingguo This newspaper commentary asks how China should advance new industrialization, the goal set by the 20th Party Congress (2022) of being basically achieved by 2035. Opening with Xi Jinping's recent instruction that new industrialization is a key task of Chinese modernization, Chen Qingguo argues that the effort should rest on five focal points, each tied to a category of industry. The article moves through the five in turn: upgrading traditional industries, moving strategic industries up the value chain, integrating advantageous industries, developing emerging industries in clusters, and laying out future industries. Each section assigns the category a role in the new industrial system and lists measures. Chen describes traditional industries as the foundation, to be upgraded through digital, intelligent and green transformation of raw-material supply, equipment, management and distribution. Strategic industries (basic, leading and pillar industries) are said to need independent innovation and stronger, repaired and extended supply chains led by core enterprises. Advantageous industries are to be integrated with digital technology and international markets. Emerging industries such as new energy and new materials call for cross-disciplinary platforms and a progression from firms to industrial chains, groups and belts. Future industries such as brain-inspired intelligence, quantum computing and aerospace information require basic research, control over standard-setting and the new whole-nation system. Chen concludes that these five emphases together would give Chinese modernization a strong material and technological base. The piece is a short policy-oriented outline rather than an analytical study. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style summary of how Chinese commentators break new industrialization into industry categories and policy tasks.

From regime transition to state governance: the shifting focus of overseas studies of contemporary Chinese politics 从体制转型到国家治理：海外当代中国政治研究的重心转换 Wang Keyuan Qi Weiping Wang Keyuan and Qi Weiping ask how overseas scholarship on Chinese politics has changed since 1949 and how Chinese scholars should respond. They argue that, as a general trend, the field has moved from a focus on regime transition, in which scholars judged China's system by liberal-democratic values and expected it to change, to a focus on state governance, meaning the practice and capacity of Party-led rule. They stress that this is a trend, not a shift shared by every scholar. The article first traces three earlier paradigms: totalitarianism in the 1950s and early 1960s, factional politics around the Cultural Revolution, and authoritarianism after reform and opening up. It then reviews work since the early 2000s, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), by scholars such as Thomas Heberer, Elizabeth Perry, Zheng Yongnian, Sebastian Heilmann, Daniel Bell, Francis Fukuyama and David Shambaugh. Finally it analyses the logic, strengths and weaknesses of the shift and proposes how to respond. The authors argue that the earlier paradigms were shaped by US global strategy, Cold War confrontation and scarce sources, and that all of them started from ideology and predicted transition or collapse. In their account, the governance-centred literature instead examines the Party's governance capacity, citing work on economic growth, social stability and poverty reduction. It also draws lessons from the Chinese experience, namely Party leadership, adaptive governance rooted in revolutionary and traditional practice, policy experimentation, and long-term planning. They name three causes of the shift: China's achievements, wider access for researchers, and the success of external communication work. The shift is described as more fair in its criteria, more scientific in method and more China-centred in perspective. They also see limits: change is slow, praise for governance does not mean endorsement of the system, and individual scholars' positions vary, as with Fukuyama and Shambaugh. The authors conclude that the shift is the general direction of travel, but not a straight line, and that US–China tensions may affect some American scholars. They propose three responses: assess the trend in the round and avoid treating overseas scholars as a monolith or exaggerating their approval; explain the link between the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics and governance effectiveness; and build a systematic Chinese theory and discourse of state governance. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly view of how Western China studies are evolving and how Chinese academics propose to engage with them.

The practical logic of building a modern Chinese civilization 建设中华民族现代文明的实践逻辑 Zhang Ming Guo Guangyin This short commentary asks how the "modern civilization of the Chinese nation" is to be built, which it presents as a new cultural mission of the new era. Zhang Ming and Guo Guangyin argue that, guided by what they call Xi Jinping's thought on culture, the task is a necessary requirement of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They set out four elements of its practical logic: leadership, spiritual foundation, fundamental method and route of advance. The article is organised in four numbered sections. The first deals with the leading force, the Party's cultural leadership. The second turns to the spiritual root, cultural confidence and historical initiative. The third treats the fundamental method, the Second Integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The fourth concerns the route of advance, which the authors define as unifying local rootedness with openness to the world. The piece draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and on Party documents. On leadership, the authors hold that culture is part of the superstructure and carries an ideological character. In their account, the Party's overall leadership, the guiding position of Marxism and the Party's innovative theory therefore guarantee the right direction. On method, they describe the Second Integration as a chemical reaction rather than a mechanical joining. Marxism activates traditional culture so that it becomes modern, while Chinese wisdom is injected into Marxism so that it becomes Chinese. They link this to the rebuilding of the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity after the modern era of national humiliation. On the route of advance, the authors say the new civilization must grow out of Chinese modernization, which they describe as continuing an ancient civilization rather than destroying it. It must also resolve the dispute between ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, by absorbing the achievements of other civilizations. They conclude that the nation's modern civilization is both national and worldwide, and that building it requires \"upholding the ancestors\" while \"speaking anew\". Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official 2024 rationale for this civilizational project and its use of Xi's cultural thought.

Laying a solid ecological foundation for the lasting development of the Chinese nation 夯实中华民族永续发展的生态基石 Dai Xin This newspaper commentary asks why ecological civilization matters for China's long-term future and what each part of society should do about it. Dai argues that building an ecological civilization is a thousand-year undertaking tied to the lasting development of the Chinese nation, the Party's mission and people's wellbeing. The author's answer is that the idea that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" should guide both development and daily conduct. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's call since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to place ecological civilization at the centre of the "Five-sphere Integrated Plan". It then proceeds in three steps: the meaning of the "lucid waters and lush mountains" idea, the claim that Chinese modernization is a modernization of harmony between humanity and nature, and practical duties for governments, enterprises and individuals. Dai reads the "lucid waters and lush mountains" idea as settling three relationships. It treats human beings and nature as interdependent, which the author calls a modern reading of the traditional notion of "unity of heaven and humanity". It treats the environment as the base on which economic growth rests, not a rival to it. It also treats ecosystems as a living source of positive value. The author then contends that Chinese modernization, by pursuing high-quality development together with high-level protection, seeks a balance between material prosperity and ecological health. By contrast, the author says, Western modernization brought pollution, resource depletion and ecological crisis, so the Chinese path is described as going beyond it and offering a new model for the world. Dai calls on Party committees and governments to treat ecological civilization as a priority, set ecological red lines, back green industry and the circular economy, and strengthen law and enforcement. Enterprises should adopt green technology and clean production, and citizens should consume green, sort waste and avoid waste. The author concludes that this requires Party leadership, a leading role for government and the mobilisation of the whole society, in the service of the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2023 presented the ecological-civilization agenda and the roles it assigns to different actors.

Keep advancing the great cause of Chinese modernization Studying the spirit of General Secretary Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth 把中国式现代化宏伟事业不断推向前进 Qi Yiping Tang Junfeng This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 8 January 2024, offers a study of Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium commemorating the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth. Qi and Tang argue that the best way to commemorate Mao is to carry forward the cause he began, and that Chinese modernization is the present form of that cause. Studying the speech, they say, strengthens political resolve and confidence and helps the Party keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised in four sections, each pairing a theme from Xi's speech with Mao-era experience: continuous struggle toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; Party leadership; goals, planning and strategy for modernization; and the spirit of struggle. It draws on Xi's quotations about Mao and on Mao's own statements about industrialisation, Party-building and the fighting spirit. Qi and Tang present revolution, construction and reform as one continuous undertaking to save, build and strengthen the country. In their account, Mao and his generation laid the political premise and institutional base, and built an independent industrial system and defence breakthroughs such as the "two bombs and one satellite", which later made reform and opening up and Chinese modernization possible. They hold that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization under Party leadership, which determines its basic nature and outcome, and they point to Mao's ideas on Party-building as a resource for the Party's ongoing tasks. They also describe Mao's two-step plan for the Four Modernizations, his insistence on a self-reliant path and his handling of the ten major relationships, arguing that Xi's elaboration of Chinese modernization continues this line of thinking. The authors conclude that today's tasks require inheriting Mao's legacy while innovating, holding to the Party's traditions, and sustaining a spirit of independence and struggle against hardship and external pressure under the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. They call for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and for exploring new problems in practice so as to open new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary links Mao Zedong's legacy to Chinese modernization.

Integrating the digital and real economies to support high-quality development 数实融合助力经济高质量发展 Yang Hutao Yang Hutao, in a newspaper commentary first published in Economic Daily in November 2023, asks how the deep integration of the digital economy and the real economy can serve high-quality development. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statements and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yang argues that this integration is a necessary requirement for a modern industrial system and a major driver of growth. The piece defines integration as the digitalisation of industry, mainly agriculture, manufacturing and producer services. It then sets out its dimensions at firm and industry level, the role of data, China's current position and its shortcomings, and the question of core technologies. Yang holds that deep integration means digitalisation spreading from a few large firms to most real-economy enterprises, including small and medium-sized ones. Data is the key factor, so institutional innovation is needed on data property rights, security oversight and infrastructure financing, with policy differentiated by level. Yang cites 2022 figures of 9.2 trillion yuan for digital industrialisation and 41 trillion yuan for industrial digitalisation, and credits China's scale, data volume and range of application scenarios. Yang also lists weaknesses: industry that is large but not strong, dependence on foreign core technology and unrealised data value. Solving these 'chokepoint' problems requires internationally competitive firms occupying irreplaceable nodes in the division of labour. Yang concludes that integration should be pursued by marketising data factors, building new infrastructure, supporting key technologies, finance and talent, and modernising industrial and supply chains. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official economic discourse in 2023 linked digital-real integration to high-quality development.

The "world-historical outlook" of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的“世界历史观” Wu Hongzheng Xiu Yuexuan Wu Hongzheng and Xiu Yuexuan ask what view of world history underlies Chinese modernization. Taking two passages of the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as their starting point, they argue that Chinese modernization is guided not only by the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation but also by a Marxist world-historical outlook that advances humanity's freedom and liberation. The article was published in Theoretical Investigation, 2023, no. 4. The article is organised around three questions: where the world is heading (peace and development versus war and destruction), whether humanity can grasp the objective trend of world history, and what orientation should guide it. It moves through Marx, Hegel and Kant, the Cold War and the Soviet and East European upheavals, Deng Xiaoping's judgement on peace and development, and the idea of a "world of great changes unseen in a century". Each section ties a theme to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The authors' core argument has three moves. First, they hold that capital's logic cannot be reformed: in qualitative terms it requires zero-sum exploitation, and in quantitative terms it requires excess profit, so new capitalist forms only produce new conflicts. Socialist relations of production, by contrast, are said to root peace and development in the system itself. Second, they contrast Marx's world-historical outlook, in which law-governed trends can be grasped in advance, with the fatalism they attribute to Kant and Hegel and, by extension, to capitalist ideas such as the "clash of civilizations" and the "end of history". The report's image of a "crossroads" is read as a dialectical metaphor: a road exists, and the question is which one to take. Third, they argue that Chinese modernization is oriented by a community with a shared future for mankind, common values of humanity, and a "dialectical view of civilizations" that unites diversity and unity. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization has opened a new realm for scientific socialism in the twenty-first century. They cite its solution to the "Eastern society" problem, its market economy within a socialist framework, and its move beyond the "East subordinate to West" order. They also hold that the world-historical outlook must become practical action in building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese theorists use Marx's theory of world history, and Hegelian dialectics, to justify Chinese modernization and to criticise capitalism's view of history.

Continuously realising the people's aspiration for a better life 不断实现人民对美好生活的向往 Cui Youping This newspaper commentary, originally published in Economic Daily in October 2023, explains the people-centred approach to development as a core element of Xi Jinping's economic thought. Cui argues that the approach expresses the people's principal position, embodies the value of putting the people first, and is a basic principle the new development philosophy must always uphold. The piece has three parts. It first traces the people-centred stance to Marxism and to the Communist Party's historical experience. It then presents Xi Jinping Economic Thought as a creative formulation of that stance, and finally sets out how the Party is working to meet the people's aspirations for a better life. Cui holds that the people's character is the essential attribute of Marxism, citing the Communist Manifesto on the movement of the immense majority. The author reads the Party's mass line and its purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly as outgrowths of this value. Cui lists achievements of the new era: GDP per capita above US$12,000, victory in the campaign against poverty, and the world's largest education, social security and healthcare systems. The author also links the approach to the change in the principal contradiction, now between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. Cui concludes that development must be for the people, rely on the people and have its fruits shared by them. The author ties this to the 20th Party Congress (2022) goals of a modern socialist country by mid-century and to common prosperity achieved through high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary presents the people-centred development idea and its Marxist lineage.

Shouldering the new cultural mission 担负起新的文化使命 Dong Zhenhua This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 13 October 2023, responds to Xi Jinping's recent instruction on propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Dong Zhenhua argues that this work bears on the Party's future, national stability and national cohesion. In Dong's reading, it can be carried out properly only by taking up the "new cultural mission" of promoting cultural prosperity, building a culturally strong country and building a modern Chinese civilization, guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The piece has three numbered sections. The first explains why propaganda, ideological and cultural work is of extreme importance, drawing on Party history and on lessons from the world socialist movement. The second sets out the principles of the new mission: firm cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and upholding fundamental principles while innovating. The third turns to the guiding role of Xi Jinping's cultural thought and to practical tasks for Party committees at all levels. Dong holds that a shared ideological foundation is the precondition for a party, a state and a nation to exist. The article cites the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party as the result of giving up Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, and calls for leadership, management and discourse power over ideological work to be kept firmly in Party hands. On the three principles, Dong argues that Marxism is the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture the "root" of the new civilization, and that the two must be linked together. Openness means mutual learning among civilizations. Because social thinking is increasingly diverse, the article contends, a single guiding ideology must lead varied social consciousness, with core socialist values as the leading force. Dong concludes that Party committees must treat this work as a major political responsibility. The proposed measures include studying and implementing Xi Jinping's cultural thought, strengthening positive publicity and public-opinion guidance, practising core socialist values, developing cultural undertakings and industries, improving international communication, and guarding against ideological risks. The stated aim is to bring the thinking and action of more than 1.4 billion people into line with central decisions in support of Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party commentators framed the "new cultural mission" in autumn 2023.

Grasping the inner connection between economy and culture 深刻把握经济与文化的内在联系 Qiu Haiping This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 27 November 2023, asks how economists should relate Xi Jinping's economic thought to his thought on culture. Qiu Haiping argues that the two are mutually connected and together reveal how economy and culture interact and merge. The commentary proposes that economists study them jointly. The piece begins with the National Conference on Publicity, Ideology and Culture, which presented Xi Jinping Thought on Culture as the cultural part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then sets out two directions of research: the cultural foundations of Xi's economic thought, and the economic foundations of his cultural thought. Qiu holds that the key task is to study the internal logic linking high-quality development, cultural construction and the building of a self-reliant Chinese system of economic knowledge. In Qiu's account, economists have mostly read Xi's economic thought through political economy. Qiu urges them to examine how it carries forward traditional Chinese economic thought and the Marxist theory of culture found in Marxist political economy. In the other direction, Qiu says understanding of Xi's cultural thought lacks social-science perspectives, including economics. Philosophy and social sciences, economics among them, are themselves part of social culture, which Qiu says accords with basic Marxist views. Literature and art have relative independence but cannot be discussed apart from economic development. Qiu concludes that economists, political economists especially, should unify the two bodies of thought and draw out the cultural substance and humanistic spirit in Xi's economic thought. This work should then inform the construction of a self-reliant Chinese system of economic knowledge. Qiu presents this as a remedy for treating culture and economy in isolation. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Chinese economists are being urged to link economic and cultural theory.

Unwaveringly following the path of financial development with Chinese characteristics 坚定不移走中国特色金融发展之路 Ding Xiaoqin Yan Xinqi Writing in Guangming Daily in November 2023, Ding Xiaoqin and Yan Xinqi comment on the Central Financial Work Conference held on 30–31 October 2023. They argue that Xi Jinping's speech there gives fundamental guidance for high-quality development of finance and for unwaveringly following a path of financial development with Chinese characteristics. The short commentary has five parts. It covers the Marxist theory of finance, the Party's centralised and unified leadership over financial work, financial supervision and risk prevention, high-standard opening up of the financial sector, and financial innovation. The authors present the Party's recent financial theory and practice as a continuation and renewal of Marxist financial theory, which deals with money, credit and financial crises. In their account, since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee has combined that theory with China's conditions and traditional culture, producing results that form part of Xi Jinping's economic thought. As evidence of leadership, they cite the 2023 creation of the Central Financial Commission and the Central Financial Work Commission. They describe supervision moving from "one bank, two commissions" to "one commission, one bank, one bureau, one commission", and report that the renminbi's SDR weight rose from 10.92% to 12.28% in 2022. The authors conclude that China must guide finance to serve the real economy, strengthen supervision, defuse risks and build skilled financial cadres in order to become a financial powerhouse. They call for wider institutional opening up and more work on technology, green, inclusive, pension and digital finance. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned summary of how Chinese scholars presented the October 2023 financial work conference.

Advancing green development under the Belt and Road Initiative to inject strong momentum into global sustainable development 推进共建“一带一路”绿色发展 为全球可持续发展注入强劲动能 Hu Sai Sun Juhong Marking ten years of the Belt and Road Initiative, this commentary (first published in Guangming Daily, 24 October 2023) takes up Xi Jinping's announcement at the third Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation that "promoting green development" is one of eight actions to support high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. Hu Sai and Sun Juhong argue that China, as a participant, contributor and leader in global ecological civilization, has made green development the defining colour of the Initiative and a strong driver of global sustainable development. The article has three parts. The first explains why green is the "base colour" of the Initiative and how the concept has been built into its top-level design. The second reviews progress in five areas of cooperation: policy coordination, infrastructure connectivity, trade, financial integration and people-to-people bonds. The third sets out how to continue, under four headings: practising green development concepts, strengthening green technological innovation, deepening green finance cooperation and improving green development institutions. The authors present green development as a way for partner countries to escape the path of "pollute first, clean up later". They cite the end of new overseas coal-power projects, the promotion of wind and solar, environmental technology transfer centres and the Green Silk Road Envoys Programme. As evidence of results, they report more than 50 ecological and environmental cooperation documents, a green development partnership initiative with 31 countries, and more than 40 major institutions signing the Green Investment Principles by the end of 2022. They also say cumulative green and low-carbon energy investment in partner countries now exceeds traditional energy projects, and that China became the world's largest green trade economy in 2021, supplying nearly 70 per cent of global photovoltaic capacity. For the future, the authors call for cross-border circular-economy cooperation mechanisms, a green institutional convention, green loans, bonds and funds, project classification systems, ecological risk early warning and protected areas for key ecological spaces. They also call for centralised, unified leadership of the Initiative's green work, along with assessment of its tasks. They conclude that these steps would make the Initiative a more competitive and influential platform and add to the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise official-style overview of how Chinese commentators describe the Belt and Road's green agenda, with the figures and programmes they cite.

Common prosperity from the perspective of fairness and justice 公平正义视阈下的共同富裕 Wang Li This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily, asks how common prosperity relates to fairness and justice. Wang Li argues that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a defining feature of Chinese modernization. In the author's view, it is also the core category through which Chinese thought explains its own conception of fairness and justice. Steadily advancing common prosperity for all the people is presented as both a concentrated institutional realisation of social justice and a practical basis for a socialist discourse on fairness and justice. The article has three parts. The first compares capitalism and socialism, arguing that whether common prosperity can be realised is an important measure of justice. The second considers what common prosperity means when seen through fairness and justice.
