The third sets out three ways in which Chinese practice offers a "Chinese approach" to justice: eliminating absolute poverty, uniting fairness with efficiency, and pursuing the free and all-round development of the human being. Drawing on Marx, Wang argues that under capitalism fairness and justice are separated from common prosperity. Liberty, equality and fraternity are described as the ideological expression of bourgeois material relations, and class opposition and private ownership of the means of production are said to rule out common prosperity. Under socialism, by contrast, public ownership unites owners with labourers and producers with beneficiaries, so that common prosperity and justice coincide in form and content. Wang adds that justice is not abstract: given the primary stage of socialism and the principal contradiction identified since the new era, it requires a system guaranteeing fair rights, opportunities and rules. Common prosperity is described as covering material and spiritual life, democratic participation, rights and a healthy environment, not only economic growth. Wang points to the victory over absolute poverty since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as the foundation for justice. The article also cites the socialist market economy, the coordination of three distribution tiers and the provision of basic livelihood guarantees as ways of combining efficiency with fairness. It concludes that the Party keeps productive forces and the people's interests, and the measure of things and of people, in unity, with the free and all-round development of the human being as the highest value. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary links common prosperity to a Marxist critique of bourgeois justice.

Understanding the significance of advancing high-standard opening up 深刻理解推进高水平对外开放重要意义 Yang Lu This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in September 2023, asks why China should keep expanding high-standard opening up to the outside world. Yang Lu argues that it is an objective requirement of the new development stage and a necessary base for high-quality development and Chinese modernization. The piece presents Xi Jinping's statements on opening up as part of Xi Jinping economic thought. The commentary is organised around four reasons. Opening up is tied to the change in China's principal contradiction, to high-quality development and the new development pattern, to balancing development and security, and to steering economic globalization. It closes with a call to follow Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Yang argues that the principal contradiction is now between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development. In Yang's account, imports, foreign investment, trade and regional opening help meet that need and create jobs. The new development pattern, Yang stresses, is not a closed domestic cycle but an open dual circulation of domestic and international flows, and China's past achievements came under open conditions. On security, Yang holds that openness brings the capital, technology, markets and talent that support a higher level of security. Yang also contends that cutting economic flows between countries is impossible and against historical trends. Yang proposes mutually beneficial opening, better top-level design of the open economy, institutional opening in rules and standards, wider market access, a better business environment, and high-quality Belt and Road Initiative cooperation. Yang concludes that China should unwaveringly expand opening up at every level. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official press justifies high-standard opening up in the framework of Xi Jinping's economic thinking.

Understanding the connotation of new quality productive forces 理解新质生产力的内涵 Yang Huixin Jiao Yong This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 22 December 2023, asks what new quality productive forces are and how to cultivate them. Yang Huixin and Jiao Yong argue that accelerating their formation is a key step for seizing the opportunities of a new round of technological revolution, building a modernized industrial system and shaping new development advantages. The authors first define the concept through its two components, "new" and "quality", and then set out four roles: supporting strategic emerging and future industries, building a modern industrial system, driving the shift from old to new growth drivers, and serving as a decisive factor in great-power competition. On definition, Yang and Jiao hold that "new" means innovation in technology, business models, management and institutions. "Quality" means that these forces are not a partial optimisation or simple iteration of traditional productive forces, but advanced forces born of revolutionary technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors and deep industrial transformation. Intelligent, numerically controlled, precise production tools, such as lithography machines and high-end machine tools, are named as important markers. The authors list priority sectors, including new-generation information technology, new energy and civil aviation, and future industries such as the metaverse, brain-computer interfaces, humanoid robots and quantum information. They also call for upgrading traditional industries and for digital transformation. They describe Western "small yard, high fence" technology restrictions as harmful to China, and call for self-reliance and a new-type whole-nation system. The authors conclude that China should use its complete industrial system and very large market to foster these forces. They propose tackling "chokepoint" technologies through open competitive selection of research teams, greater autonomy for researchers, support for young talent and a role for leading and specialised enterprises. Read the original if you want a concise early official-media statement of how new quality productive forces were defined and what industrial priorities were attached to them.

Questioning and seeking the ethical foundation of Chinese modernization 追问和追寻中国式现代化的伦理基础 Yan Hui Yan Hui asks what ethical foundation Chinese modernization rests on and how it can be secured. The article argues that this inquiry contains two tasks: an ethical-foundation argument, which identifies the ultimate good and the holistic 'good life' at stake, and a moral grounding, which supplies both a subjective basis (virtue) and objective conditions (norms and institutions). Yan's thesis is that Chinese modernization is the practical movement that turns what 'is' in reason into what 'ought to be' and then into reality. The article has three parts. The first sets out a philosophical method drawn from Hegel's account of reason and actuality and from a sequence of sensibility, understanding and reason. The second defines the 'ethical world' as the ultimate good and examines its economic, political and personal dimensions, discussing Adam Smith, Kant and Marx along the way. The third turns to how Chinese modernization is a new path and how it can be grounded morally through a revolution in ideas, institutional innovation and practice. Yan defines the ultimate good in three statements: an economic organisation that creates and fairly distributes wealth continuously; institutions through which everyone can voluntarily and rationally express a political will; and the capacity and conditions for everyone to live a holistic good life. Economy and politics are only means, and the good life is the end. Yan argues that the capitalist market economy, driven by the logic of capital, produces alienation and polarisation, and that Smith's 'invisible hand' ignores the difference between private and public ownership. The market therefore cannot distribute fairly by itself, and political power must be limited and used through institutions, which Yan presents as the fundamental advantage of the socialist system. Chinese modernization is said to differ from Western modernization in its origins (equal and mutually beneficial rather than colonial), its path and its goal of common prosperity. Yan calls for reconstructing the concepts of politics, wealth (material, social and spiritual) and happiness, and for institutions that combine incentive with coordination and include self-restraint for those who hold power. Yan concludes that inquiry into the ethical foundation of Chinese modernization must respect holism, complexity and conflict, since values and costs, opportunities and risks coexist, and difficulties can only be resolved through repeated practice. The article presents the Party's century of practice as having built a political system embodying common prosperity, democracy, equality and justice. Read the original if you want a philosophically dense, Hegelian and Kantian account of how Chinese modernization is given ethical justification in current Chinese theory.

Practical requirements for advancing common prosperity in the new era 新时代推进共同富裕的实践要求 Ai Silin Li Hanke This commentary, originally published in the Economic Daily in November 2023, asks what practical conditions are needed to move common prosperity forward in the new era. Ai Silin and Li Hanke present common prosperity as an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a defining feature of Chinese modernization. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), they argue that it must be pursued through four requirements: strategic resolve, internal motivation, developmental strength and institutional potential. The piece is organised under four short headings matching these requirements. It sets out the staged goals announced by the Party Central Committee: solid steps by the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period, more marked substantive progress by 2035, and basic realisation by the middle of the century. It then turns to the role of the people, to high-quality development, and to the income distribution system. On strategic resolve, the authors stress that common prosperity is a long-term goal and a political question bearing on the Party's governing base, not only an economic one. They cite the scale of China's population and regional disparities as reasons to expect a long, arduous process, and they argue that the Party's overall leadership and top-level design are decisive. On motivation and strength, they say prosperity must be created through the hard work of the people, who should share in reform and development outcomes, and that it must come through high-quality development guided by the new development philosophy, with innovation as the first driving force. On institutions, they call distribution the foundational system and propose coordinated primary distribution, redistribution and third distribution. Primary distribution should raise labour's share. Redistribution should "raise the low, expand the middle and regulate the high" to build an olive-shaped income structure. Charity should supplement both under stronger legal oversight. The authors conclude that, with the Party's leadership, consistent goals and a single blueprint carried through, China can make steady progress towards common prosperity and achieve more marked substantive progress. They urge making the economic pie bigger while dividing it more fairly, and they warn against polarisation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the policy agenda for common prosperity, especially the sequencing of distribution mechanisms.

Practical requirements for advancing common prosperity in the new era 新时代推进共同富裕的实践要求 Ai Silin Li Hanke This newspaper commentary asks what practical demands follow from the Party's current approach to common prosperity. Ai and Li treat common prosperity as an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a defining feature of Chinese modernization. They argue that, guided by Xi Jinping's ideas since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the task is to understand these demands fully and accurately so that "more notable substantive progress" can be made. The article is organised under four headings: maintaining strategic resolve, stimulating endogenous motivation, strengthening development capacity, and tapping institutional potential. It opens with the political significance of common prosperity and the staged targets set for the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period, for 2035 and for the middle of the century. It then moves from the role of the people and of economic growth to the income distribution system. The authors first present common prosperity as a political issue bearing on the Party's governing base, not only an economic one. They describe it as a long-term goal that needs the Party's overall leadership, top-level design and a single blueprint pursued consistently. They contrast this with developed countries, where, in their account, the social system has left wealth gaps widening. They then tie common prosperity to people's own effort and to a people-centred idea of development, with shared fruits of reform and open channels of upward mobility. They also argue that development, specifically high-quality development guided by the new development philosophy, remains the basis, given the primary stage of socialism. Finally, they set out a three-tier distribution system: primary distribution through the market and distribution according to work, redistribution through taxes, social security and transfers, and charity as a third distribution. Redistribution aims to "raise the low, expand the middle, regulate the high" so as to form an olive-shaped income structure. Ai and Li conclude that firm Party leadership, mobilised popular effort, sustained high-quality growth and a coordinated distribution system together make steady progress possible. They also call for regulating excessive and illegal income, and for better legal oversight of charity. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy framework for common prosperity as it stood in late 2023, including its staged targets and the three-tier distribution scheme.

Shouldering the new cultural mission at a new historical starting point 在新的历史起点担负起新的文化使命 Huang Maoxing Qiu Shuilin Published in Guangming Daily on 25 October 2023, this commentary responds to Xi Jinping's recent instruction on propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Huang and Qiu take up the "new cultural mission" of continuing to promote cultural prosperity, building a culturally strong country and building a modern Chinese civilization. They argue that the mission follows from history, the times and practice, and that it supplies a roadmap and a set of tasks for cultural work in the new era. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the mission is necessary, under three headings: continuing the Chinese cultural lineage, meeting the demands of developing socialist culture, and driving the building of a modern Chinese civilization. The second sets out what the mission requires. The third offers five practical directions for carrying it out. The authors' central move is to link three goals in sequence. Cultural prosperity is the foundation of a culturally strong country. Building a socialist cultural power is included in, and lays the groundwork for, the longer-term and larger aim of a modern Chinese civilization. That civilization is in turn said to grow out of Chinese modernization, which the authors describe as a new form of human civilization different from the Western model. The two are presented as mutually reinforcing: Chinese modernization gives Chinese civilization modern strength, and the civilization gives modernization its depth. Throughout, the authors rely on the Two Integrations, the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, and cultural confidence. For action, Huang and Qiu call for strengthening Party leadership over ideological work and its responsibility system, and for thorough study of Xi Jinping's cultural thought. They also call for protecting and passing on traditional culture through heritage protection, databases and education. Further proposals are to use modern technology to renew traditional culture, and to improve international communication so as to "tell China's story well". Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in late 2023 framed the new cultural mission and its practical tasks.

Creating a new culture that belongs to our era 创造属于我们这个时代的新文化 Gao Xiang Writing in Qiushi (2023, no. 24), Gao Xiang presents Xi Jinping Thought on Culture as the defining achievement of cultural work since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Gao argues that it enriches and develops Marxist cultural theory and serves as the banner and soul of cultural prosperity in the new era. The piece is an official-style exposition rather than an empirical study. The article has three parts. It first explains the "milestone significance" of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture for the history of Chinese civilisation and of Marxist cultural theory. It then sets out the thought's scientific content as a system of theoretical "substance" (ti) and, finally, its practical "application" (yong), meaning the tasks it sets for cultural work. On the theoretical side, Gao identifies several distinctive features. These include placing culture at the centre of the Party's and state's overall work, stressing the Party's cultural leadership, and giving cultural confidence a core place. The thought also advances the Two Integrations, above all the "second integration" of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, which Gao says gives cultural subjectivity to building a modern Chinese civilisation. Gao calls the new cultural mission, and the concept of a "modern civilisation of the Chinese nation", its major innovations. That civilisation is described as socialist, balanced across five dimensions, oriented to common prosperity and to a community with a shared future for mankind, and different from the Western model of modernization. On the practical side, Gao calls for arming the whole Party with its innovative theory, upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds in propaganda and ideological work, and strengthening the Party's leadership over that work. Gao also calls for fostering core socialist values, improving the reach and credibility of the media in the information age, protecting cultural heritage, and developing cultural undertakings and industries. Further tasks are building international communication capacity, analysing how the Western ideological apparatus operates, and constructing China's autonomous knowledge system. Read the original if you want a concise, authoritative statement of how the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences leadership frames Xi Jinping Thought on Culture and its practical agenda.

Strengthening digital technology innovation and application to accelerate the development of new quality productive forces 加强数字技术创新与应用 加快发展新质生产力 Qi Yudong Xu Kaige Qi Yudong and Xu Kaige ask how new quality productive forces can be formed and developed, and answer that digital technology innovation and application are the core driver. Starting from Xi Jinping's remarks on revitalising Northeast China, they present the concept as a Marxist innovation in productive-force theory. In their account it captures a leap in productive forces caused by the digital technology revolution, and it helps the country seize the current round of technological and industrial change, build a modern industrial system and gain new competitive advantages. The piece, which first appeared in Guangming Daily in October 2023, has two parts. The first explains why new quality productive forces are a leap brought about by digital technology. The second sets out how digital innovation and application supply the core impetus, and names four priority directions: technological self-reliance, industrial upgrading, changes in the mode of production, and digital talent. Along the way the authors compare strategies in the United States, Germany, the EU and Japan. The central argument starts from the two basic elements of productive forces, labourers and means of production. Citing Marx's view that the means of labour mark out economic epochs, the authors contend that digital technology gives the means of labour a digital character, with strong connectivity and penetration, acting on data as a new object of labour. They place the resulting leap after the steam and electrical eras. On this basis they argue that key core digital technologies must be mastered, through concentrated efforts under the new whole-nation system or through 'changing lanes' to leapfrog on disruptive innovation. They also argue that digital technology should be fused with the real economy, especially manufacturing, so that intelligent, customised production on industrial internet platforms, with data as a production factor, replaces mass standardised output. The authors conclude that self-reliance in digital technology is the most urgent task and industrial upgrading the key focus. They hold that changing production methods is the critical link, since intelligent customised production is still far from widespread in China. Talent is the foundation: they call for complementary types of personnel and a more tolerant research management system and innovation culture. Read the original if you want a concise Party-press statement of how digital technology is linked to new quality productive forces and of the policy priorities that follow.

Shouldering the new cultural mission with a high degree of cultural consciousness 以高度文化自觉担负起新的文化使命 Jin Minqing This commentary, first published in the Economic Daily in October 2023, sets out how Party members should understand and carry out the "new cultural mission" announced by Xi Jinping. The mission is defined as continuing to promote cultural prosperity, building a culturally strong country and building a modern Chinese civilization. Jin Minqing argues that taking up this mission requires a high degree of cultural consciousness and a sense of responsibility, guided by Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article has three parts. The first explains the historical grounds for the mission: the tasks of the new era, the changing principal contradiction in society, and the international and national situation. The second turns to the goal of building a modern Chinese civilization and the principles it must follow. The third discusses methods and paths, drawing on Xi's "seven focuses" for propaganda, ideological and cultural work and on his remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Jin contends that the mission follows from objective conditions. The principal contradiction is now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, which Jin says is still visible in public cultural provision and in the coordination of material and spiritual civilization. Jin adds that the "great changes unseen in a century" bring ideological and cultural-security risks, and that Chinese modernization requires spiritual as well as material prosperity. A modern Chinese civilization must rest on three things: Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its guiding "soul"; fine traditional Chinese culture as its "root"; and absorption of the achievements of other civilizations. Jin presents the Second of the Two Integrations, joining Marxism with fine traditional culture, as the key method. It is meant to make Marxism Chinese and traditional culture modern, and to strengthen China's cultural subjectivity. Jin concludes that the mission calls for firm cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and adherence to fundamental principles alongside innovation. The practical tasks Jin lists include strengthening Party leadership of ideological work, upholding Marxism's guiding position, promoting core socialist values, building Chinese philosophy and social science, improving international communication and encouraging exchange among civilizations. Jin holds that this provides ideological assurance and spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of how the new cultural mission and the Second of the Two Integrations are framed in Party discourse.

Making the resolution of problems unique to a large party the main line of attack 以解决大党独有难题为主攻方向 Zhang Chao Zhang Zhiming This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, interprets Xi Jinping's call at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to take "resolving problems unique to a large party" as the main line of attack in advancing the Party's self-reform. The authors argue that this is both consistent with the Party's historical practice of tackling its principal problems and a strategic priority for the Party's long-term rule. The article has three sections. The first traces how the Party identified key problems for self-reform in successive periods: the Land Revolution, the Yan'an rectification, the early People's Republic, the reform era under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second works through the "six questions of how to always..." that Xi set out as the content of these difficulties. The third explains the significance of the focus. In the authors' account, the six questions concern keeping to the original aspiration and mission; unifying thinking, will and action; sustaining strong governing capacity; maintaining a drive to get things done; finding and solving the Party's own problems in good time; and keeping a clean political ecosystem. For each, they describe the risks of a Party with over 98 million members ruling the world's most populous country, citing Xi's remarks, and propose remedies such as the Two Upholds, theoretical study, discipline education, institution-based Party governance, popular supervision and anti-corruption work. They draw on the fall of the Soviet Communist Party after 74 years in power to argue that a ruling position is neither innate nor permanent. The authors conclude that the focus shows deep awareness of risk, strategic vision and a methodology for self-reform. By "main line of attack" they mean concentrating forces and resources on deep-seated, complex problems rather than formal or superficial ones, while keeping systematic thinking and a problem-oriented approach. They present this as a way for the Party to avoid the historical cycle of rise and fall and open a new stage in its self-reform. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theorists frame the "unique difficulties of a large party" and the six questions attached to them.

Better shouldering the new cultural mission at a new historical starting point 在新的历史起点上更好担负起新的文化使命 Fan Xichun Fan Xichun's article, published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2024, expounds Xi Jinping's 2 June 2023 speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. In that speech Xi called on the Party to continue promoting cultural prosperity, build a culturally strong country and build a modern Chinese civilization, which he termed the new cultural mission of the new era. Fan argues that Xi's three stressed requirements (firm cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and upholding fundamental principles while innovating) provide scientific guidance and a guide to action for carrying out that mission. The piece is organised in three parts, one for each requirement. Each part defines the concept, traces its historical and theoretical basis, and links it to the mission. Fan draws heavily on Xi's speeches and Party Congress reports (the 19th Party Congress in 2017 and the 20th in 2022), with one citation from Marx on people making history under inherited conditions. In the first part, Fan argues that cultural confidence rests on cultural subjectivity. This subjectivity is formed by Marxism combined with China's concrete realities and its fine traditional culture, and by the creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Cultural confidence, Fan says, underlies confidence in the path, theory and system, and is the precondition for national rejuvenation. The second part holds that openness and inclusiveness are traits of Chinese civilization that sustain its vitality through exchange and mutual learning. Fan says this means localising foreign culture and rejecting both Westernisation and revivalism. The third part defines upholding fundamental principles as maintaining Marxism's guiding position, the Two Integrations and the Party's cultural leadership. Innovation is described as new ideas, discourse, mechanisms and forms. Fan presents the combination of Marxism and fine traditional culture as the route to a new cultural organism, with Marxism as the 'soul' and tradition as the 'root'. Fan concludes that the mission must be carried out under the guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. In practice this means continuing the Chinese cultural lineage, fostering cultural undertakings and industries, strengthening shared ideological ground and raising national cultural soft power. Fan also claims that the three requirements enrich historical and dialectical materialism and develop Marxist methodology. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-theory journals present Xi's cultural thought and its three guiding principles.

Resolutely winning the tough and protracted battle against corruption 坚决打赢反腐败斗争攻坚战持久战 Huang Rongsheng Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 8), Huang Rongsheng takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2024). The article asks why the Party must treat the anti-corruption struggle as both a hard-fought assault and a protracted war. Huang's answer is that corruption threatens the Party's survival, that the situation remains severe and complex, and that the struggle must therefore be pursued to the end. The article has three sections. The first presents anti-corruption as "the most thorough form of self-reform", citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. The second describes the struggle as a major political fight that "cannot be lost". The third sets out how to carry it through: Party leadership, an integrated approach, and popular supervision. Huang's central claim is that corruption is a political problem, not merely a disciplinary one. It damages the Party's vitality by cutting its ties to the people, and its combat capacity by hollowing out Party organisations and members. The article says the Party has gained the "overwhelming victory" since the 18th Party Congress (2012) but adds that this is not a thorough or fundamental victory. In Huang's account, the conditions that breed corruption persist, and new forms are emerging, such as shadow companies, shadow shareholders, revolving doors between officials and business, and "micro-corruption". Huang cites the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as a warning about privilege and corruption in a ruling party. Huang proposes three measures. First, strengthen centralised Party leadership over the whole anti-corruption process, integrating political, ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional work. Second, advance "dare not, unable to, and not wanting to" be corrupt as one whole, combining deterrence, institutional constraint and moral education. Third, widen popular supervision through petitions, online platforms and open government, while guarding against false accusations. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party-school line on anti-corruption and the Party's self-reform in 2024.

Strengthening discipline building is the fundamental measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 加强纪律建设是全面从严治党的治本之策 Kan Daoyuan Writing in 2024, as the Party launched a nationwide campaign of Party discipline study and education, Kan Daoyuan argues that strengthening discipline building is the fundamental measure (zhiben zhi ce) of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscript, presents the campaign as an important step in deepening that governance and as a way to make members and cadres learn, understand and observe Party rules. The article has three parts. The first treats strict discipline as a Marxist party's defining trait and as a Chinese Communist Party tradition, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Party history from the First Congress to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out how discipline can address both symptoms and root causes. The third turns to the practical task of the education campaign. Kan's core claim is that discipline-building rests on theoretical, historical and practical logic together. Citing Xi Jinping, the author holds that political discipline is the most fundamental discipline, and that if it is not upheld, other rules will collapse and the Party will become weak and slack. Discipline must therefore be a live "high-voltage line": rules are enforced without exception, leading cadres, especially Party-branch heads, set an example, and punishment, institutional constraint and raised awareness work together. The author also argues that Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline form an organic whole, with discipline as the safeguard of the other two, and that tackling bad work styles and corruption as sharing one root requires "whole-cycle management". For the campaign itself, Kan calls on members to study the revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions article by article, to learn both what is forbidden and what they may and should do, to internalise the rules, and to observe them unconditionally. The author further urges that the campaign become regular and long-term, that Party regulations keep being refined, that a zero-tolerance tone be maintained, and that study be tied to the Party Central Committee's key decisions and to local work. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party-building discourse in 2024 links the Marxist tradition of party discipline to the Party's self-governance.

Systematic dialectics and the New Reading of Marx: a comparative examination 体系辩证法与马克思新阅读：一个比较视角的考察 Lu Kejian Two schools of Capital interpretation, systematic dialectics in the English-speaking world and the New Reading of Marx (neue Marx-Lektüre) in the German-speaking world, have recently attracted Chinese researchers working on value-form theory. Lu argues that their histories and mutual relations remain poorly understood in China. Some Chinese scholars wrongly fold the German school into the English one, or treat systematic dialectics as an Anglophone variant of the New Reading. Lu contends that the two are independent yet bear a family resemblance, and that both share a flaw: they stress the value form and exchange at the expense of production. The article has five parts. It traces the origins of each school: systematic dialectics from Christopher Arthur's "new dialectic" (Arthur, Robert Albritton, Tony Smith, Geert Reuten and others), and the New Reading from the "logic of capital" school of Hans-Georg Backhaus and Helmut Reichelt, rooted in Adorno's critical theory. It then sets out five shared features and the problem-consciousness behind them, and surveys internal and external criticisms. It ends with a proposal for a new research paradigm. Lu identifies the family resemblance in five points: both reconstruct the category of "totality"; both replace dialectical materialism with a "dialectic of capital"; both stress value-form analysis, drawing on Isaak Rubin and Alfred Sohn-Rethel; both reject Engels's "unity of the logical and the historical" and "simple commodity production"; and both are anti-positivist. Lu links this to concerns about whether the labour theory of value applies in post-capitalist societies, which the article ties to the socialist calculation debate. Lu also points to concerns about how Marx's theory differs from classical political economy. Lu argues that, following Sohn-Rethel and partial readings of Rubin, both schools wrongly sideline production and quantitative analysis. In Lu's view this risks idealism, and critics such as Peter Ruben argued that use-value and the material dimension were neglected. Lu proposes moving from "value form" to "labour product and commodity form". The commodity, as Capital's starting point, contains a trans-historical premise, the labour product, and has both a natural form (use-value) and a value form. Lu argues that stressing the labour product leads to a philosophy of labour that merges with Marx's communist political philosophy. Stressing the commodity's natural form opens an ecological dimension in Capital. Chinese scholars should draw on both schools while avoiding their one-sidedness. Read the original if you want a detailed genealogy of systematic dialectics and the New Reading, and a Chinese critique of their treatment of value form and production.

Keeping the development of ideological and political courses in step with arming minds with the Party's innovative theory 坚持思政课建设与党的创新理论武装同步推进 Song Youwen Responding to a recent instruction from Xi Jinping on school ideological and political courses (sizhengke), Song Youwen asks how these courses should be built so that they advance in step with the Party's innovative theory. The author argues that this synchronisation is necessary because the courses now hold a prominent place in the Party Central Committee's overall strategy for governing the country, and that it requires deeper understanding of how Party theory develops and a content-led, high-quality development of the courses. The article, published in a 2024 issue of a journal on ideological and political education, has three parts. The first sets out the strategic position of the courses. The second traces the pattern of theoretical innovation, using the sequence of Party theories and the revisions of the course curriculum since the 1980s. The third turns to practical measures for what the author calls connotative development. In the first part, Song presents the courses as the key vehicle for four tasks: fostering virtue and cultivating people (the 'fundamental task' of education), building ideological consensus, forging a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation, and telling China's story to the world. In the second part, Song notes that curricula moved from the 1985, 1998 and 2005 schemes, and from courses on Mao Zedong Thought and Deng Xiaoping Theory to one on Xi Jinping Thought, and reads this as evidence that each theoretical advance is followed by theoretical arming and course reform. The author calls for systematisation and scholarly rigour (xitihua and xueli hua) in teaching, citing Engels's Anti-Dühring as a precedent, and insists that value education must rest on solid knowledge. The third part names three priorities: a curriculum and textbook system centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, grounded in the relation between Marxism and traditional Chinese culture; teachers' close reading of original works; and equipping students with the Party theory's worldview and methodology, including its account of the 'three laws' of Party governance, socialist construction and human social development. Song concludes that the courses should both absorb new theory into their content and use the achievements of the new era to enrich teaching and tell the story of the new era. Teaching should convey the truth, practical power and spiritual appeal of the theory, in plain language but with depth of research. Read the original if you want to see how a Renmin University scholar frames the official rationale and priorities for ideological and political courses in 2024.

Plekhanov's critique of the "religious quest" and his exposition of Marxist atheism 普列汉诺夫对“宗教探寻”的批判和马克思主义无神论的阐释 Zhang Jiansong Zhang Jiansong examines Georgi Plekhanov's long essay "On the So-Called Religious Quests in Russia", written after the defeat of the 1905 revolution and under Stolypin's reaction. In that climate, Zhang explains, bourgeois scholars read the defeat as divine punishment, and a "God-building" current even arose inside Social Democracy. The article argues that Plekhanov used historical materialism to clear away this fog, defend Marxist atheism and steady revolutionary morale, and that the work still has practical value for religious theory and religious work today. The article follows the three finished parts of the essay, found in volume three of Plekhanov's selected philosophical works. Part one, "On Religion", sets out the basic theory; part two, "More on Religion", criticises Tolstoy, Lunacharsky and Gorky; part three attacks the Decadents, chiefly Merezhkovsky and Minsky. A planned fourth part on the Vekhi group was never written. A short closing section draws lessons for present-day China. Zhang reports that Plekhanov defines religion as a system of ideas, emotions and activities (myth, religious feeling and ritual). Drawing on ethnology, Plekhanov traces animism, totemism and the idea of gods to hunting life and low productive forces, which Zhang takes as confirmation that social being determines social consciousness. Using this framework, Plekhanov argues that every religion contains supernatural spirits, so "atheist religions" such as Tolstoy's, Lunacharsky's "fifth religion" and Gorky's deification of humanity are illusory. He treats them as consolation sought by disillusioned intellectuals. He also argues that the Decadents scorned workers' economic struggles as vulgar while pursuing individualist, bourgeois comfort and mystical escape. In the closing section Zhang draws two lessons: remain firm Marxists, and fight wrong ideological currents boldly. Zhang contrasts Soviet collapse after Gorbachev abandoned Marxism's guiding role with the Chinese Communist Party's adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Zhang also lists historical nihilism, constitutional democracy, "universal values" and neoliberalism as currents to be confronted, together with abnormal religious phenomena in some regions. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Plekhanov's religious theory, or want to see how it is applied to current ideological and religious work in China.

Using the remarkable achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics as content to teach ideological and political courses well 以中国特色社会主义取得的举世瞩目成就为内容支撑讲好思政课 Chen Jinlong This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in June 2024, asks how the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics can be used to teach ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) in schools and universities. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's instruction that these courses should rest on such achievements, Chen Jinlong argues that they should present facts as well as doctrine, grounding principles in facts and using principles to interpret them. Using the achievements of reform and opening up, and especially of the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), is described as integral to the courses' task of fostering virtue and nurturing people. The article has three parts. The first sets out how the achievements strengthen the courses' explanatory power, their emotional appeal and their approachability. The second identifies three kinds of content support the achievements supply: practical effectiveness, theoretical soundness and spiritual elevation. The third offers three practical focal points for teachers. On the first part, Chen argues that theory alone cannot make arguments persuasive. Examples include high-speed rail, aerospace and the digital economy, which are said to illustrate new quality productive forces. Others are the 60.2 per cent gross enrolment rate in higher education in 2023 and the completion of poverty alleviation, which the article says met the UN 2030 poverty target ten years early. On the second, Chen contends that the achievements prove the success of the Party's path, confirm the scientific character of its innovative theory, and reflect the spirit of Chinese Communists. The three focal points are to apply a "big historical view" that places achievements in Party, national and world socialist history; to match specific achievements with specific teaching content, such as linking the principle of putting the people first to rising living standards and whole-process people's democracy; and to join the "small classroom" of the course with the "big classroom" of society through visits to fields, factories and development zones. Chen concludes that firsthand contact with the achievements helps students understand course content and strengthens their conviction in Marxism, in socialism with Chinese characteristics and in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is a short normative piece on pedagogy rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official guidance frames the use of national achievements in Chinese ideological and political teaching.

Lenin's philosophical critique of Russian Narodism 列宁对俄国民粹主义的哲学批判 Geng Renjie Scholarship on Lenin's philosophy has concentrated on Materialism and Empirio-Criticism and the Philosophical Notebooks, and Geng Renjie argues that his early thought has been neglected. The article holds that Lenin first set out his Marxist philosophy systematically in his critique of Russian Narodism (populism), much as Engels first presented Marxism's main components in his polemic against Dühring. This critique, Geng contends, was the starting point of Lenin's philosophical development and a philosophical foundation of Leninism. The article follows the Narodist tradition from Herzen, Chernyshevsky and Lavrov to the liberal Narodist Mikhailovsky. It sets out Lenin's response in three sections: epistemology, dialectics and the conception of history. It draws chiefly on What the 'Friends of the People' Are and The Development of Capitalism in Russia. A closing section traces how these early arguments recur in Lenin's later work. Geng argues that Mikhailovsky's 'subjective method in sociology' made the objective world conform to human wishes, and that Lenin countered it with a materialism that treats ideological relations as a superstructure of material ones. On dialectics, Mikhailovsky reduced Marx's method to Hegel's triad. Lenin replied that the task is to describe real historical processes accurately, and that the triad is only a relic of Hegelian expression. Geng adds that Lenin did not deny Marxism's Hegelian origins but stressed its present content. On history, Lenin rejected the Narodist idealist and 'hero' view, in which a few intellectuals lead a passive mass. In its place he set the view that social formations develop as a natural-historical process and that the masses are independent historical actors. Geng finds the seeds of later positions in this critique: the reflection theory and the principle of partisanship in philosophy (partiinost), the unity of dialectics, logic and epistemology, and the application of historical materialism to political economy. He also finds a lasting 'people's view of history' and a 'historical dialectics' that sifted Narodism's valuable democratic core from its utopian dross. He sees the critique as preparing the later one of empirio-criticism. He ends by linking Lenin's dialectical thinking, people's view of history and problem-consciousness to the 'six musts' of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Lenin's early philosophy and its continuity with his later work.

The new form of human civilisation in the perspective of world history, and its significance 世界历史视域下的人类文明新形态及其意义 Tian Yisong Chen Weici Tian Yisong and Chen Weici ask how the "new form of human civilisation", presented as an inherent part of Chinese modernization and an expression of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, can be explained theoretically. They argue that Marx's theory of world history is the appropriate tool. In their account, the new form of civilisation is a creative development of that theory and its realisation in practice. The article has three parts. The first compares Hegel's and Marx's theories of world history. The second argues that the new form of civilisation is the contemporary realisation of Marx's theory. The third presents its significance for answering Western doctrines, namely Fukuyama's "end of history" and Huntington's "clash of civilisations". In the first part the authors contrast the two thinkers on three points. Hegel makes absolute spirit the driving force, heroic individuals the subject, and the Germanic world the highest stage. Marx locates the driving force in productive forces, the subject in the popular masses, and the final direction in communism, which in his view can only exist as a world-historical movement. The authors then argue that the new form of civilisation applies this framework. It rests on the development of productive forces, particularly through reform and opening up. It is built on socialism with Chinese characteristics and the primary stage of socialism, and it is people-centred. It is also described as a "real movement" that keeps abolishing existing conditions through the Party's self-reform, not as a finished end-state. The authors say it adds to Marx's theory in economic institutions, whole-process people's democracy, the rule of law, harmonious society and ecological civilisation. Against Fukuyama, the authors argue that communism in Marx is an open movement, not a terminal state. They add that the new form of civilisation does not claim to be a necessary path for other nations. Against Huntington, they argue that his theory expresses Western-centrism and hides the economic and class roots of conflict. They present the new form of civilisation, together with a community with a shared future for mankind, as an alternative for developing countries to the civilisation led by capital. They conclude that it answers the "great changes unseen in a century" and surpasses Western modernization, and they call for developing it further through the creative transformation of traditional Chinese culture. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars ground official civilisation discourse in Marx's world-history theory and in a critique of Hegel, Fukuyama and Huntington.

Several Chinese cultural concepts contained in the "Second Integration" “第二个结合”中蕴含的若干中华文化观念 Cao Yingwang Cao Yingwang asks which strands of traditional Chinese culture underlie the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The article argues that six long-standing cultural concepts match certain Marxist ideas. In Cao's account, Communist Party members creatively transformed and innovatively developed these concepts, and they became a cultural reason why the Party has been able to keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The six concepts are the view of all under heaven (tianxia guan), valuing the foundation (guiben guan), self-strengthening, the relationship between heaven and humanity, continuity and change, and the unity of knowing and doing. For each, Cao sets out the classical sources, such as the Analects, Mencius and Wang Yangming. The article then pairs them with a Marxist counterpart and follows the concept through statements and policies of Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, from early Party history to the present. Cao's central move is to show parallels between each concept and a Marxist idea. The ideal of a world of great harmony (datong) is matched with communism and, today, with a community with a shared future for mankind. Valuing the foundation is matched with the primacy of the productive forces and the people as makers of history. Self-strengthening is matched with the primacy of internal over external causes, in Mao's On Contradiction and in the principle of independence and self-reliance. Heaven and humanity is matched with Marx's view of humans and nature and with Xi Jinping Thought on ecological civilization. Continuity and change is matched with dialectical development and with "upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground". Knowing and doing is matched with Marxist epistemology and Mao's On Practice. Cao presents the Second Integration itself as an example of continuity and change, and says Xi puts more weight on action than on knowledge. Cao concludes that the Party's practice since its founding has given these traditional concepts new theoretical content and renewed their life in a new era. Cao says this experience offers lessons for promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional culture and for building a modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source account of how official Party scholarship links classical Chinese ideas to Marxism and to the thought of Mao, Deng and Xi.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics and the revival of European socialism 中国特色社会主义与欧洲社会主义的复兴 Thürmer Gyula This is a Chinese translation of a speech by Thürmer Gyula, chairman of the Hungarian Workers' Party, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum. Thürmer argues that capitalism is in deep crisis and that European socialist parties must renew themselves, drawing on socialism with Chinese characteristics. The speech opens with a diagnosis of the present: the European Union's loss of competitiveness, the collapse of Europe's security structure and the danger of world war. It then lists several "needs" of the European socialist movement: theoretical revival, study of the Chinese Communist Party's experience, a break with the "end of history" thesis, new forms of cooperation, and a clear international orientation. Thürmer holds that Marxism is a living theory that each party must apply to its own national conditions, as the Chinese case is said to show. He endorses Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Two Integrations, and calls for Marxism to be combined with Europe's own cultural and civilisational heritage. He presents China's poverty eradication and Chinese modernization as evidence that hard problems can be solved, while stressing that this is a sharing of experience and not an imposed model. Thürmer concludes that European parties should replace profit-based capitalism with people-centred socialism, defend national sovereignty, work for a multipolar world and support a community with a shared future for mankind. He also states that some communist parties do not accept the CPC's theoretical innovations and that discussion with them should continue. Read the original if you want a European communist leader's own account of how Chinese theory is received and used in Europe's socialist debates.

Studying and grasping Xi Jinping's important statements on comprehensively deepening reform 深入学习领会习近平总书记关于全面深化改革的重要论述 Mu Hong Writing in Qiushi in 2024, Mu Hong sets out to explain what Xi Jinping has said about comprehensively deepening reform since the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The article argues that these statements answer why reform is needed in the new era and how to pursue it. In Mu's account, they form the richest and most creative part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and are the guiding thought and basic guideline for further reform and opening up. The piece is a study-and-interpretation text organised into ten numbered principles, followed by a short conclusion. Each section quotes Xi, says what question the statement answers, and then lists what the Party Central Committee has done on that front since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The ten principles are Party leadership, the socialist path, innovation, a people-centred approach, problem orientation, emancipating the mind, rule of law, scientific methodology, opening up, and the Party's self-reform. Mu's central claim is that reform is directed and bounded. It must follow the path of socialism with characteristics Chinese, avoiding both the 'old path of rigidity' and the 'evil path' of changing banners. The Party's centralised leadership, backed by the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, is presented as the fundamental political guarantee. The author also treats reform as the application of the Marxist principle that relations of production must fit the productive forces. Mu links this to theoretical innovations such as high-quality development and new quality productive forces. Reform is to be advanced systematically, with the rule of law and with opening up, so that institutional strengths become governance capacity. Mu cites people's grassroots experiences, such as the Sanming health reform and the 'Fengqiao experience', as sources of reform practice. Mu concludes that Xi's statements distil the historical experience of reform and opening up and the Party's understanding of the laws of socialist modernization, so they should be cherished and upheld over the long term. The author calls on Party members, especially leading cadres, to strengthen their political, intellectual and practical commitment to reform and to oppose formalism and bureaucratism. The text presents the Party's self-reform as leading a 'great social revolution', and sees reform as supplying momentum and institutional guarantees for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how Party theorists summarise and organise Xi's reform discourse in the lead-up to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024).

Striving to write a youth chapter of taking responsibility for Chinese modernization 奋力书写为中国式现代化挺膺担当的青春篇章 Lin Jiang This commentary responds to Xi Jinping's message to young people on Youth Day (4 May) 2024. Xi urged them to carry forward the May Fourth spirit, listen to the Party and follow the Party, and write a youth chapter of shouldering responsibility for Chinese modernization. Lin Jiang argues that the message sets the direction for the Party's youth work in the new era and should draw young people into building a strong country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised in three parts. The first asks how to inherit and develop the May Fourth spirit. The second sets out the trust and expectations the Party Central Committee places in youth since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to what young people should do in the race toward national rejuvenation. Lin draws throughout on Xi's speeches and on examples such as the winners of the 28th China Youth May Fourth Medal. Lin's core argument is that the fate of youth has always been tied to the times, and that the history of national rejuvenation is also a history of youth struggle. The author reads the May Fourth Movement as the starting point of Marxism's spread in China and of the new-democratic revolution. Young people's most active period, Lin says, now coincides with the new journey of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Lin calls on them to take the lead in technological innovation, rural revitalisation, green development, social services and national defence, linking new quality productive forces to a demand for technical and applied talent. The author also asks them to hold ideals, accept hardship, reject pampered habits, and fold their personal efforts into the national cause. Lin adds that young officials, as the "key minority", should practise Xi's "five consciousnesses". Lin concludes that young people should have confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics and unite with the people. Lin holds that the closer the nation comes to rejuvenation, the more youth must be mobilised and the less room there is for slackening. Read the original if you want to see how a Communist Youth League school official presents Xi's 2024 Youth Day message and the Party's current expectations of young people.

Upholding and developing the labour theory of value 坚持和发展劳动价值论 Yang Jing Liu Ying Yang Jing and Liu Ying ask how the labour theory of value, a basic theory of Marxist political economy, can be upheld and developed in the age of digital and intelligent technology. They point to three new phenomena: the widening scope of productive labour, new forms of labour, and the participation of non-labour factors such as data in distribution. Their thesis is that understanding of Marx's theory must keep deepening, but its core must not change: living labour is the only source of value. The article has three parts. It first restates the main tenets of Marx's theory: the two factors of the commodity, the dual character of labour, the magnitude of value, the value form and the law of value. It then sets out four areas where understanding needs to deepen: use value, productive labour, forms of labour, and the participation of production factors in distribution. Finally it proposes four distinctions as points of emphasis for further research. The authors hold that in Marx's day consumption centred on material goods, whereas now spiritual products and services account for a growing share. They conclude that the concepts of use value and social product must be widened, and that productive labour now extends into non-material production. They also treat digital labour, such as social-media work, livestreaming and platform development, as a new form of human–machine interactive intellectual labour whose value-creating or value-transferring character needs study. The four distinctions are these. Living labour creates value, while all factors together create use values, and knowledge, technology, management and data create no value so long as they appear as objectified labour. Complex labour is multiplied simple labour and so creates more value. Productive labour must be told apart from unproductive labour such as commercial and financial work, which only shares in newly created value. Finally, every form of income originates in value created by labour, so "contribution" in distribution by factor means a role in producing use values. The authors conclude that value creation and value distribution must be kept apart, and that distribution by factor according to contribution can be justified without abandoning Marx's thesis that only living labour creates value. They cite Xi Jinping on distribution according to work as the mainstay and on improving distribution by factor. They also cite the Digital China plan on data-based distribution. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Chinese Marxist economists reconcile the labour theory of value with data as a factor of production and with digital labour.

Opposing hegemonism and power politics and actively advancing a community with a shared future for mankind 反对霸权主义和强权政治，积极推进人类命运共同体建设 Kong Dan Wang Xiangsui Kong Dan and Wang Xiangsui argue that the hegemon-centred global political order is disintegrating and a multipolar world is emerging. In this short commentary, published in World Socialism Studies in 2024, they contend that building a community with a shared future for mankind requires opposing hegemonism and power politics. The article has three parts. It first describes the underlying logic of the current world order, then examines hegemonism and power politics as obstacles to common development and security, and finally sets out the principles of "extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits" for building the community. The authors hold that the modern world system, which grew out of Europe from the late fifteenth century, still runs on a "law of the jungle". Citing slavery, colonial plunder, the indemnities exacted from China and the wealth drained from India, they say the developed countries became rich largely by looting the South, and that global capital still depends on excess profit from the Global South, which they call a form of "national surplus value". Hegemonism, in their definition, is a product of the imperialist stage of capitalism. They list its political, economic, trade, technological, military, information and financial forms, and say hegemons will defend their "hegemonic dividend" whatever the moral criticism. China's initiative, they warn, will therefore meet hostility from global capital. Kong and Wang conclude that the community with a shared future for mankind means peace over war, development over poverty, cooperation over confrontation and win-win outcomes. They call for reform of existing international rules and a redesign of the global architecture, and describe opposition to hegemonism as inherent in China's view of global governance. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese statement linking the shared-future concept to a critique of capitalist hegemony.

Postmodern theory's misreading of Marx's conception of history 后现代理论对马克思历史观的误读 Fu Qiuye Ma Wanli This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2024, asks how far postmodern criticism of Marx's concept of history holds up. Fu and Ma argue that the critiques by Jacques Derrida and Jean-François Lyotard misread historical materialism and have clear limits. They contend that Marx's view can only be fairly assessed when it is placed in its specific historical context. The article first sets out the two critiques. Derrida, in Specters of Marx (1993), treats the conception of history as a modern ideology of a grand narrative with a single rational principle. Lyotard reads Marx's history as a singular, necessary, progressive process inherited from Enlightenment myth and still bound by metaphysics, and he favours small narratives. The authors then offer three objections. The first objection is methodological. Fu and Ma say Derrida and Lyotard combine Marx's dialectic of part and whole with their own philosophy of the event. This is contradictory, because history conceived as unpredictable events cannot be a whole. They also say the two reduce Marx's ascent from the abstract to the concrete to a move from parts to whole, and that 'deconstruction' and 'event' lack clear meaning as bridges to historical totality. The second objection is that, once grand narratives are discarded, no comparably strong framework remains for analysing enduring structures such as the economic base and class struggle. The third objection is that the critics overlook the historical relativity of Marx's theory, which rests on analysis of nineteenth-century Western social formations and which, in the authors' view, is open to change and rupture. The authors conclude that historical materialism seeks the dynamics and laws of social change rather than a final picture of history. Marx himself said his theory must be updated, so any critique should rest on understanding its historical conditions. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Derrida and Lyotard on historical materialism.

The scientific application of historical materialism in the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》对唯物史观的科学运用 Sun Min Zhao Feng Sun Min and Zhao Feng ask how the Communist Manifesto put historical materialism to work. They argue that although the materialist conception of history had largely taken shape in The German Ideology, it remained a hypothesis there, untested by a full analysis of a particular social formation. In the authors' reading, the Manifesto was the first time Marx and Engels publicly attempted, and partly completed, that task. The short piece, published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2024, is organised under four headings: a scientific understanding of capitalism, a scientific explanation of socialism, a scientific forecast of the future society, and a scientific revelation of historical laws. It draws throughout on passages from the Manifesto, Engels's 1883 preface, the 1872 German-edition preface and Marx's 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. On capitalism, the authors trace the rise of the bourgeoisie from medieval townspeople and guild masters to machine industry and a society split into two opposed classes. They stress that the Manifesto credits the bourgeoisie with a revolutionary historical role, yet holds that the contradiction between private ownership and socialised production makes capitalism's replacement by socialist relations of production inevitable. On socialism, they report the Manifesto's conclusions that the proletariat is both impoverished and united by large-scale production, that the bourgeoisie's fall and the proletariat's victory are equally inevitable, and that revolution requires the "two ruptures" with traditional property relations and traditional ideas. The authors list five principles in the Manifesto's forecast of the future: developing the productive forces, public ownership with planned production, real democracy and the abolition of major social divisions leading to common prosperity, a staged transformation, and the building of a new culture. They concede that the Manifesto's expectation of simultaneous revolution in several developed countries differs from today's globalisation, but hold that its core principles remain sound. They conclude that, despite the unfinished critique of political economy, the Manifesto tested historical materialism through class struggle and supplied the historical basis for Marx's classic 1859 formulation. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of the Manifesto as a demonstration of historical-materialist method.

Starting from Mao Zedong's reading life 从毛泽东同志的读书生活谈起 Chen Jin Writing for Qiushi in 2024, on the occasion of the third National Reading Conference, Chen Jin takes Mao Zedong's reading life as a model for building a "scholarly society" and for encouraging Party members and cadres to love reading, read good books and read well. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on reading as his greatest hobby and as a duty of leading cadres. Chen argues that Mao's breadth of knowledge and skill in applying it were rare in Party and world history, and that his example still offers lessons. The essay has three main sections: Mao's passion for reading, his wide-ranging reading, and his skill as a reader. It draws on anecdotes and records from his youth in Hunan, the Yan'an years and his later life. It ends by linking Mao's example to Xi Jinping's own reading habits and to Xi's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on study by leading cadres. Chen stresses that Mao read daily whatever his workload, using the methods of "squeezing" out time and "drilling" into problems, and kept reading until the day before his death in 1976. Mao's reading focused on Marxist-Leninist works, philosophy and history. He read Marxist classics in order to apply them to Chinese realities, philosophy as a "tool" of thought and method, and Chinese and foreign history to draw lessons and avoid cutting off the past. Chen identifies several habits of a skilled reader: rereading key texts, comparing works with opposing viewpoints, annotating and discussing in reading groups, and above all linking books to practice and to the "wordless book" of society. Chen concludes that Mao's reading helped establish a Party tradition of treating study as a necessary route to theoretical grounding and work competence. The article presents Xi Jinping as continuing this tradition. As the country advances the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization and faces serious tests, the article calls on cadres to treat reading as a way of life, a work responsibility and a spiritual pursuit. Read the original if you want an official Party-journal portrait of Mao as a reader, and of how reading is presented as a duty for cadres under Xi Jinping.

The meaning of Marx's concept of "world history" 马克思“世界历史”概念的意涵 Duan Guangpeng Duan Guangpeng asks what Marx's concept of "world history" means once it is separated from Hegel's. Hegel, the article says, understood world history "philosophically", as the externalisation and sublation of self-consciousness. Marx reworked the concept at the level of practice and sensuous activity and started from "real human beings". Duan argues that this gave the concept a new meaning and produced a new principle for explaining history. The article is a short essay in the history of Marxism, organised around three successive senses of world history in Marx's work. The first draws on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, where world history is the process by which humans are born through their labour. The second draws on The German Ideology, where it is the evolving history of material production. The third is a specific sense, in which world history is the expansion of the capitalist mode of production. In the 1844 Manuscripts, Duan finds two layers. Marx adopts Feuerbach's notion of the human species-essence and treats communism as the positive sublation of alienated labour. In this layer he still follows Hegel's speculative logic of alienation and return. Marx also separates alienated labour from objectifying labour. The latter is humanity's transformation of nature and cannot be abolished, so history becomes the history of objective activity. In The German Ideology, Duan argues, Marx explains ideas from material practice rather than the reverse. He starts from real individuals acting under given material conditions, treats the production of life as both a natural and a social relation, and concludes that all history is first of all a history of production, not of ideas. In the specific sense, Duan traces capital from landed property through medieval guild capital and merchant capital to industrial capital. Industrial capital, in Marx's account, dissolves naturally formed local and national limits and turns relations into money relations. As local and national production is drawn into the capitalist system, Duan writes, history becomes world history in the true sense. Marx mostly uses the term in this sense, Duan says. The article does not go beyond this exposition of Marx's texts. Read the original if you want a concise outline of how Marx moved from Hegelian alienation to a materialist and capital-centred account of world history.

Improving the teaching system of university ideological and political theory courses by explaining principles "in depth, thoroughly and vividly" 在“讲深讲透讲活”道理中完善高校思政课教学体系 Chen Xixi Following the May 2024 conference on building school ideological and political courses, which relayed Xi Jinping's instruction to "explain principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly", Chen Xixi asks how university teachers can turn the unified textbook system into an effective teaching system. Chen argues that the answer lies in uniting the courses' ideological and theoretical substance with their approachability and relevance. In this reading, neither side may be pursued at the other's expense. The article starts from Xi's 2019 speech to teachers of these courses and his 2022 remarks at Renmin University. It first explains why the courses must "go deep, thorough and vivid", citing their ideological nature and the training goals of socialist universities. It then devotes one section to each of the three requirements, offering concrete teaching proposals. These cover theoretical thinking, vertical links between school stages, reading original works, integrating the "seven histories" and the craft of classroom delivery. Chen holds that the courses are the explicit, not implicit, vehicle of Marxist ideology. The textbooks' official wording therefore has to be converted into teaching content, since a teacher who stresses only conceptual analysis or only entertainment fails. "Depth" means training students' theoretical thinking, pairing constructive with critical teaching, and building the curriculum around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It also means avoiding repetition between high school, undergraduate and graduate courses. "Thoroughness" means guiding students to read original texts and placing principles within the seven histories. "Vividness" means starting from shallow, student-relevant cases that lead to deep theory, choosing what to treat in detail and what briefly, and following the textbook without reciting it. Chen also calls for plainer, more practical writing and speech, warning against formalism and stilted language. Chen concludes that teaching should move from appealing to emotion to persuading by reason, from commenting on events to reasoning from them, from illustration to theoretical proof, and from covering everything to deepening step by step. Chen suggests this would raise both the courses' theoretical quality and their appeal to students. Read the original if you want a detailed, practice-oriented account of how Chinese university ideological and political courses are meant to be taught under current Party guidance.

Ideological and political theory courses grounded in fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture 思政课以中华优秀传统文化、革命文化和社会主义先进文化为力量根基 Gao Guoxi Gao Guoxi takes up Xi Jinping's instruction that school ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke) should rest on three cultural sources: fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. The article asks how these resources can give the courses their "power base" in cultivating students as builders and successors of socialism. Gao argues that, used well, they turn knowledge transmission into value guidance and move students from spontaneous to conscious understanding, building cultural confidence. The article, published in Research on Ideological Education (2024, no. 5), has three parts. The first explains what each of the three cultures contributes to understanding "why China is China". The second discusses how to make teaching more targeted and effective. The third sets out practical routes for putting the cultural resources to work in teaching. In the first part, Gao reads traditional culture as showing the continuity and cultural subjectivity of Chinese civilisation, the tradition of unity, and a view of the person within social relations that Gao finds consistent with collectivism and common prosperity. Revolutionary culture, in Gao's account, explains the historical, theoretical and practical logic of Party leadership and provides ideals and convictions against historical nihilism. Advanced socialist culture is tied to the Two Integrations, which Gao says consolidate cultural subjectivity and let Marxism "speak Chinese". In the second part, Gao says the courses must respect the laws of education, students' physical and mental development and ideological work. They should move from knowledge to values to belief, and combine the teacher's leading role with the student's own agency.
