For practice, Gao calls for integrated teaching across primary, secondary and university stages, coordination among the various ideological-political course types, and a family–school–community–government network. Gao also calls for making full use of the "great ideological and political course" (da sizhengke), which draws on social resources and practical teaching bases. Students should be drawn into volunteering and similar activity. Gao concludes that the three cultures give these courses a solid base for educating new people able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that this base needs further study. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxism-school scholar links cultural resources to the design and pedagogy of ideological and political courses.

Forty years of research on contradictions in ideological and political education: course, features and prospects 四十年来思想政治教育矛盾研究的历程、特征与展望 Hu Rui Bi Hongmei This review surveys four decades of scholarship (1984 to the present) on the contradictions that ideological and political education is meant to resolve. Hu and Bi start from the Marxist view that contradiction is the basic driver of development, so the discipline must say which contradictions it addresses and how. They argue that the research has moved from borrowing from pedagogy to building discipline-specific theory, and that it now needs more structural, concrete and forward-looking work. The article is built in three parts. The first divides the research into four stages: initial construction (1984–1988), theoretical standardisation (1989–2003), gradual deepening (2004–2011) and innovative development (2012 to the present). The second identifies six features of the literature. The third sets out prospects under three headings. On the history, Hu and Bi report that early work took over the moral-education theory of a basic contradiction between the educator's requirements and the educatee's actual moral level. Later scholars added layered and classified analyses, human-centred readings, and, after the shift in the principal social contradiction in the new era, contradictions linked to the need for a better life, online education and intelligent technology. The six features are Marxist guidance, grounding in the principal social contradiction, the laws of the discipline, the activity process, multidisciplinary borrowing and a focus on university students. For the future, they call for moving from multiplicity to structure by distinguishing basic from specific, principal from secondary, and inherent from new contradictions. They also call for linking abstract analysis to concrete goals, constraining factors and real problems, and for moving from adaptation to transcendence through traditional strengths, dialectical thinking and grassroots practical innovation. Hu and Bi conclude that the field has produced rich results and more consensus than disagreement, but must change its thinking, widen its approaches and update its methods for the new era. They identify gaps: few studies of specific activities or tasks, thin analysis of the conditions under which influences operate, and a split between theoretical work on contradictions and descriptive work on problems. Read the original if you want a periodised map of Chinese scholarship on the basic contradiction of ideological and political education, with the main scholars and positions.

Ideological and political education for university students in the perspective of social acceleration 社会加速视野下的大学生思想政治教育 Zhang Zhe Zhang Zhe asks how ideological and political education for university students should respond to what the article calls the era of social acceleration. The author argues that acceleration brings both opportunities and new challenges to this work, and that universities can meet them by guiding students in how they relate to the speed of others, to one another and to their own mental resilience. The article has three parts. It first examines social acceleration through historical materialism, noting that Western acceleration theory grew out of left-wing debates on accelerationism and capitalism. It then analyses effects on students' learning, perception of time and psychology, on the media of ideological and political education, and on its environment. Finally it proposes three countermeasures, drawing on Hartmut Rosa's idea of resonance and on concepts from Hegel, Heidegger and Debord. Zhang contends that, read through Marx, acceleration is not a single abstract process. It arises from the accelerating contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production, and it unites positive and negative aspects, such as technological progress alongside faster economic crises and environmental pollution. For students, the author reports greater learning autonomy, a compressed sense of time and more psychological confusion. Digital media enrich teaching, but image-based 'spectacle' and technological logic risk weakening critical awareness and alienating students. A 'time lag' opens between the fast-changing external environment and the more stable internal environment of the education, producing what Zhang calls 'galloping standstill'. Zhang proposes three responses. Students should be guided to coordinate with the 'social other's speed' by engaging dialectically with AI as a 'machine other' and by easing damaging competition over grades. They should be led to build wider 'relations of relations', with art as a bridge to resonance, since acceleration does not automatically mean a better life. Finally, a multi-layered support system should foster 'strong psychological traits', linking mental-health education and counselling with ideological and political education. Read the original if you want to see how contemporary social-acceleration theory is applied to Chinese university ideological and political education.

Cultivating new-era youth with the core socialist values 用社会主义核心价值观培育时代新人 Yang Xianjin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 9), Yang Xianjin, Party Secretary of Tianjin University, asks how universities should use the core socialist values to produce a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's message to young people for Youth Day 2024 and his October 2023 instruction on propaganda and ideological work, the article argues that universities must treat the cultivation and promotion of these values as a basic, strategic task. It describes the aim as young people who are idealistic, ready to take responsibility, able to endure hardship and willing to strive. The piece has four parts. The first explains why universities must take up the task. The second sets out four directions for guiding young people. The third turns to methods, and the fourth to institutional guarantees. Throughout, Yang draws on Xi Jinping's speeches and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and applies them to university governance and student life. Yang gives three reasons for the university's role: young people's values are forming and will shape society's future values; universities are cultural centres with a mission of cultural leadership; and a "world-class university with Chinese characteristics" must rest on distinctive values and Chinese traditional culture. Moral education (lide shuren) is described as the university's fundamental task. It is to proceed by strengthening ideals and convictions, deepening patriotism, which Yang defines as the unity of loving the country, the Party and socialism, fostering a sense of responsibility, and building moral character. The core method is a movement from recognition to internalisation to action. Education and guidance cover theoretical study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, ideals-and-convictions education and the use of "red resources". Cultural immersion works through campus culture, role models and traditional culture. Practice includes volunteering, academic integrity, online civility and encouraging graduates to take grassroots posts. On guarantees, Yang calls for strengthened Party leadership, with the university Party committee as the leading core. He also calls for teacher training under the "educator spirit", integration of the values into every stage of talent cultivation and university rules, and cooperation among family, school, government and society. The work is described as "building a mansion in the mind", a gradual process that must be regularised and institutionalised. Read the original if you want to see how a university Party secretary translates the Party's values-education agenda into concrete campus measures and organisational mechanisms.

Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on ideological work 认真学习贯彻习近平总书记关于意识形态工作的重要论述 Cai Jingfeng This article, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, takes up how Party cadres should understand and carry out ideological work under Xi Jinping's leadership. Cai argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee has strengthened centralised and unified leadership over ideology and has produced a fundamental shift in the situation in this field. The author calls on readers to study Xi's statements, take up the political responsibility of safeguarding ideological security, and build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. The piece is organised in three parts. The first explains why ideological work is of the utmost importance. The second sets out why it is urgent now, looking at the state of social thinking, economic and social development, the building of a strong socialist culture, information technology and the international situation. The third lists practical measures for the coming year, drawing on Xi Jinping's cultural thought and the national conferences on propaganda and ideological work. Cai's central claim, following Xi, is that ideological work bears on the Party's future, on the country's long-term stability and on national cohesion. The author argues that regimes often collapse first in the realm of ideas, cites the fall of the Soviet Union as a warning, and describes Western infiltration, "peaceful evolution" and "colour revolutions" as intensifying threats. Cai also says that Western "constitutional democracy", neoliberalism and historical nihilism keep reappearing in new forms, so Marxism must be established as the leading ideology amid plural currents. The article treats the internet as the main arena of struggle and says that growing competition between major powers has made the ideological contest more complex. For practice, Cai proposes five reinforcements: arming Party members with the Party's innovative theory, positive propaganda including economic messaging and international communication, risk monitoring and prevention, tighter control of ideological positions such as schools, media, publishing and emerging technologies like AI, and stronger Party leadership. On the last point, Cai calls for revising the ideological responsibility system, with risk assessment, summons, inspection and accountability so that it has "teeth". Read the original if you want a clear example of how official Party journals set out the tasks, rationale and mechanisms of ideological work in the Xi Jinping era.

The theoretical significance of accelerating the development of new quality productive forces 加快发展新质生产力的理论意义 Zhou Wen Zhou Wen asks what theoretical significance attaches to accelerating the development of new quality productive forces, a concept advanced by Xi Jinping. The article argues that the concept answers three questions: what these forces are, why they should be developed and how. In Zhou's account it innovates on Marxist productive-force theory, points to a new direction for productive-force development, and offers Chinese discourse and theory with world significance. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2024, has three sections. The first returns to Marx's treatment of productive forces: labourers, means of labour and objects of labour, together with cooperation, natural forces, management and science and technology. The second sets new quality productive forces within the history of industrial revolutions and in present-day international competition. The third links the concept to building China's own knowledge system and to the wider world. Zhou contends that the concept continues Marx's view that science is itself a productive force and that productive forces and relations of production interact. It is described as the adapting of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In Zhou's reading it stresses innovation-led technology, information and data as core factors, counts green development as part of the concept, and looks to an optimised recombination of labourers, tools and materials. Zhou reads each industrial revolution as the product of scientific breakthroughs, so that new quality productive forces arise from key, disruptive technological breakthroughs. 'New' marks a break from resource-intensive growth, and 'quality' means innovation-driven leaps. The author says some developed countries use technology monopolies and decoupling to slow China, and presents the present as a convergence of challenges that is also a strategic opportunity. Zhou concludes that the concept shows how to build Chinese discourse and theory from China's practice. Modernizing productive forces is described as the most fundamental task of Chinese modernization. Zhou holds that the concept will add momentum to world economic recovery, set an example for developing countries and become a Chinese theory leading world development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2024 tied new quality productive forces to Marx's productive-force theory and to the project of a Chinese autonomous knowledge system.

Accelerating the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学 Chen Yulu Chen Yulu asks how Chinese universities should carry out the Party Central Committee's call to speed up the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. Citing Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and a recent national meeting of publicity department heads, Chen argues that universities must link this task to Chinese modernization and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a Party-theory commentary that draws its institutional examples from Nankai University. The article has three parts. The first sets out the foundations: Marxism as the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". The second turns to the three systems named in Xi's formula, namely the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems, and ties them to Chinese modernization. The third sets out what universities should do, with Nankai's history, motto and current initiatives as illustration. Chen argues that the field must be guided by Marxism, specifically Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Researchers should be oriented to the people and to problems, and should "write their papers on the land of the motherland". The author also holds that traditional culture, patriotism and the Two Integrations give the field its roots. On the three systems, Chen calls for a balanced disciplinary layout that supports key, emerging, niche and weak subjects, and for new concepts and methods, including the use of big data and AI. Chen also wants a discourse that blends the best of Western scholarship with Chinese terms and gives China an international voice matching its standing. For universities, the central task is building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, which Chen presents as both a practical and a theoretical need, including breaking what the article calls the Western monopoly on knowledge. Chen concludes that universities, as one of the "five armies" of philosophy and social science, should lead in this work. Chen proposes four measures: building an autonomous knowledge system, cultivating talent under the principle of fostering virtue through education, expanding "organised research" around the major issues of modernization, and improving international communication. Nankai's forums and cultural events are offered as examples. Read the original if you want to see how a university leader presents the official agenda for Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and how Party guidance, traditional culture and institutional practice are linked in it.

Who judges democracy, and how? Studying and absorbing Xi Jinping's important statements on democracy 民主由谁评判、怎么评判 Si Li This study-and-commentary piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, asks who has the right to judge whether a country is democratic and by what criteria. Si Li answers by expounding Xi Jinping's statements on the subject. The core claim is that a country's own people, not a few outside states, judge its democracy, and that whole-process people's democracy meets the proper criteria. The article has three parts. The first treats the question of who judges. The second sets out how a political system should be assessed, drawing on the "eight abilities" standard Xi announced in 2014 and the later "four looks, four more-so looks" formulation. The third presents whole-process people's democracy as the "most broad, most genuine and most effective" democracy, a description Si traces to the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It closes by linking this to the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress. Si argues that democracy belongs to all peoples and cannot be a monopoly of a few states. Judging varied political systems by a single yardstick is, in Xi's words, itself undemocratic. In Si's account, bourgeois democracy began with popular sovereignty but in practice became rule by the wealthy, and only proletarian democracy frees the democratic subject from the constraints of capital. Si holds that the Chinese model grew from China's own history and conditions. Against a model in which people matter only at election time, the article stresses substantive participation, fulfilment of promises, enforcement of laws and supervision of power. It credits the system of people's congresses, multiparty cooperation under Communist Party leadership, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-government with giving institutional form to the people being masters of the country. Si concludes that whole-process people's democracy unifies process and outcome, procedure and substance, direct and indirect democracy, and the people's will and the state's will. The author presents this as a contribution of Chinese wisdom to human political civilization and calls for firmly following the path of political development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party commentary justifies China's democratic criteria and contests Western democratic standards.

Learning dialectics from Comrade Mao Zedong 向毛泽东同志学习辩证法 Qu Qingshan Marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, Qu Qingshan asks what Mao's dialectical thought contributed and why Party members should study it today. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech of 26 December 2023, the article argues that Mao's dialectics forms a core part of Mao Zedong Thought and gave the Chinese revolution and construction a "spiritual weapon". Qu holds that learning it remains necessary for advancing Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first surveys how Mao's dialectics guided the New Democratic Revolution, socialist construction, Party building, and the making of strategy and tactics, drawing on texts such as On Protracted War, On the Ten Major Relationships and the 1939 preface to The Communist. The second assesses its place in the Party's intellectual history. The third turns to what studying it means in the era of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Qu's central claim is that Mao's dialectics has three sources: the basic tenets of Marxism, fine traditional Chinese culture, and the concrete realities of China. Qu says Mao developed the law of the unity of opposites and the principle of the universality and particularity of contradiction, which laid a methodological basis for adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article presents Mao's use of terms such as "contradiction" and "unity of knowing and doing", and of proverbs and stories, as creative transformation of Chinese tradition. It also describes Mao's dialectics as a "dialectics of practice" drawn from the experience of victories and defeats. Qu calls for the Party to treat Marxist philosophy as its "essential skill", study materialist dialectics, and make the "six musts" from the 20th Party Congress (2022) the Party's new "common language". Qu also argues that the Two Integrations, especially the second, open a new horizon for dialectics and continue the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want an official Party-journal account of how Mao's philosophy is presented as a source for current ideological campaigns and for Xi Jinping Thought.

Logical dimensions, technical foundations and forms of realisation of big data analysis in ideological and political education 思想政治教育大数据分析的逻辑向度、技术基础与实现形式 Liu Hongda Liao Yinwei Liu Hongda and Liao Yinwei ask how big data analysis, which targets people's thoughts and behaviour, can be applied in ideological and political education. Citing Marx's remark that a science is truly developed only when it can use mathematics successfully, they argue that big data strengthens the discipline's capacity to capture, trace, describe, compute and predict people's behavioural, physiological, psychological and emotional states. Applying it, they say, requires clarifying its logical dimensions, mastering its technical basis and exploring its forms of realisation. The article has three parts. The first sets out four logical shifts in how data are thought about. The second reviews technical foundations in four areas: network behaviour, physiological signals from wearables, facial-expression capture and emotion computing from audio and video. It draws on foreign studies of learning-platform logs, stress management, facial-expression recognition and speech analysis of depressed patients. The third proposes a four-dimensional analysis platform covering environmental variables, knowledge cognition, emotional identification and behavioural tendency. On logic, the authors argue that analysis should move from social data to individual data, from known to unknown data, from logical data to computed data, and from quantitative to qualitative data. They stress that human thought is too complex to quantify fully, so qualitative analysis stays primary and quantitative analysis supplementary. Behavioural quantitative data can supply more objective support for qualitative judgements about thought. On realisation, each dimension yields analysis indices that support a practical scenario. Environmental data support a "dynamic environment" across home, school, community and internet. Cognitive data support a "dynamic teaching scenario" with personalised content, precise methods and intelligent procedures. Emotional data support a "smart psychological counselling scenario". Behavioural data support fuller, deeper and more accurate "student portraits" covering behaviour, thought and future tendencies. The authors conclude that combining these logics, technologies and platforms can make ideological and political education more targeted, proactive, predictive and effective. They present big data as a means of moving from experience-based judgement to data-supported analysis of students' thoughts and behaviour. The text does not discuss privacy, ethics or the limits of such measurement. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how big data, wearables and affective computing are being proposed for use in ideological and political education.

Zhou Enlai and the Nanchang Uprising of 1 August 周恩来与八一南昌起义 Shi Zhongquan Written for the 126th anniversary of Zhou Enlai's birth, this article asks how to understand Zhou's part in the 1 August 1927 Nanchang Uprising and how to assess the uprising's historical standing. Zhou had neither Mao Zedong's years in the new army nor Zhu De's formal military training. Shi argues that his earlier experience made him the natural leader of the uprising. Shi also argues that the uprising should be seen as part of the Party's exploration of a Chinese revolutionary road, not as a mere failure of 'urban-centred' thinking. The article has four parts. The first traces Zhou's career from 1924 to 1927: Guangzhou, the Whampoa Academy's political department, the two Eastern Expeditions, four months administering the East River region, the Ye Ting Independent Regiment, the Shanghai workers' uprising and the response to Chiang Kai-shek's coup. The second narrates the uprising, the southward march, the defeats around Shantou, Zhu De's 'three reorganizations' in southern Jiangxi, and Zhou's escape to Hong Kong. The third reassesses the uprising's status. The fourth follows Zhou's later work in the central leadership. Shi's central move is to separate historical evaluation from historical lessons. In 1927 no choice existed between urban insurrection and encirclement of the cities from the countryside, so Shi says the uprising cannot be faulted for lacking a later insight. Shi treats it as exploration, comparing failures to a red traffic light that warns 'no road this way'. Shi lists its significance as the first armed resistance to the Kuomintang, the beginning of an independent Party-led army, and the start of the agrarian revolutionary war. Quoting Zhou's own later self-criticism, Shi accepts that the main error was marching far south instead of carrying out land revolution locally. Shi concludes that the uprising belongs to the opening of the sinicization of Marxism, citing Hu Jintao's 2007 remark, and that Zhou was one of the great explorers of that road. After 1927, Shi says, Zhou guided the remnants of the uprising troops towards Jinggangshan and the Hailufeng base, and opposed 'putschist' leftism. Shi also credits Zhou with promoting Mao and Zhu's armed base-building and arguing the case for rural revolution to the Comintern. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-history account of Zhou's military role and of how current Chinese scholarship reframes the Nanchang Uprising within the Party's search for its revolutionary road.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground to promote the content-based development of ideological and political courses 守正创新推动思政课建设内涵式发展 Wang Yi Responding to Xi Jinping's recent instruction on school-level ideological and political courses (sizheng ke), Wang Yi asks how these courses can develop in depth under new conditions. The article argues that the answer lies in the method of "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" (shouzheng chuangxin), which Wang presents as both a worldview and a methodology. Wang writes that the two elements are dialectically unified: upholding principles gives innovation its direction, and innovation supplies the source and momentum for upholding principles. The piece is a commentary that opens with a general statement of the principle and then builds on four parts. The first concerns the core content of the courses, the second the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics as supporting material, the third the cultural foundations of the courses, and the fourth innovation as the driver of continuing improvement. It ties each part to quotations from Xi and to concrete measures, including course and textbook arrangements and teaching projects at Renmin University of China. Wang's central move is to treat the "fundamental principles" as Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author calls for courses and textbooks built around it, such as the introductory course on that Thought, offered to undergraduates since autumn 2022. Other proposed modules cover Xi's thinking on the economy, the rule of law, ecological civilization, the military, diplomacy and culture. Wang also wants the courses to explain the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics and their root cause, so that students grasp the significance of the Two Establishes and strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. The same section draws on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture, including core socialist values. On the innovation side, Wang proposes linking required and elective courses and combining the classroom with practice-based "big classrooms" in society. The article also proposes digital platforms with shared databases of problems, cases and teaching materials. Wang concludes that this approach will fulfil the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. It aims to train more young people of a new era who are reliable for the Party, patriotic and ready to take on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is a programmatic statement of how ideological and political courses are meant to be organised and taught. Read the original if you want to see how a Renmin University Party official translates Xi's 2024 instruction into specific curriculum, practice-teaching and digital measures.

How to write the "big" article of the "Big Ideological and Political Course" “大思政课”如何做好“大”文章 Zhang Ling This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 31 May 2024, asks how universities can realise the "big" in the "Big Ideological and Political Course" (大思政课). Zhang Ling argues that the shift from the ordinary ideological and political course to the "big" version is more than one word: it renews the concept, widens the vision and enlarges the pattern of teaching. In Zhang's reading, it joins the campus classroom to wider society and asks students to understand China and the world through history and reality. The article follows Xi Jinping's recent instruction on school ideological and political courses and his earlier remarks on the subject. It then sets out six requirements, each beginning with "big": a large pattern, a large personality, great teachers, large resources, large combined strength and a large system. Zhang's core argument is that each requirement ties teaching to Party leadership and to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Large personality means cultivating top talent in knowledge, ability and thought. Great teachers means strengthening the teaching corps, bringing in model workers, craftsmen and red-site guides, and exploring AI-era methods. Large resources means placing teaching within the long history of reform and opening up, New China, modern China, socialism and Chinese civilisation. Large combined strength and a large system mean opening the course to society, setting out responsibilities, and strengthening Party leadership through leading groups and accountability systems. Zhang concludes that ideological and political education has entered a stage of quality improvement and substantive development. Universities should use "big" course construction to foster a new generation for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a university Party official presents the official agenda for ideological and political education in 2024.

The Party's self-reform in the perspective of the history of the international communist movement 国际共运史视域中的自我革命观 Chai Shangjin An Yaqin Writing in 2024, Chai Shangjin and An Yaqin ask what the 170-plus years of the international communist movement show about why Marxist parties succeed or fail in power. Their thesis is that Marxist parties have led social revolution through self-reform, and that a ruling party can secure a complete victory for socialism and long-term rule only by keeping to its founding mission and carrying full and rigorous self-governance of the Party through to the end. The article moves chronologically through four stages. It begins with Marx and Engels and the founding of the proletarian party, from the Communist League to the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to Lenin's thinking on party-building after the Bolsheviks took power. Next it sets the Soviet Union under Stalin and Gorbachev, and the communist parties of Eastern Europe, against those of Vietnam, North Korea, Cuba and Laos. It ends with the Communist Party of China, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, and with the influence of its experience on other parties. The authors contend that Marx and Engels never used the term "self-reform" (自我革命) but supplied its principles: the Manifesto's "two ruptures" with traditional property relations and ideas imply that communists must remould themselves while changing the world. They present Lenin as systematising these principles into four requirements: theoretical guidance, the vanguard's advanced character and purity, democratic centralism with criticism and self-criticism, and strict organisation and discipline. In their account, Stalin's over-centralisation, suppression of dissent and personality cult cut the Soviet party off from the people, and Gorbachev's "democratisation" and ideological pluralism replaced self-reform and led to the party's dissolution in 1991. The authors conclude that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Chinese party has given a "second answer", self-reform, to the question of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall, alongside Mao's answer of supervision by the people. They claim this experience offers a model that parties in Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, Russia, Brazil and South Africa have drawn on. They call for treating full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as a permanent strategic task, since the "unique difficulties of a large party" require a long process. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theoretical account of how the history of the international communist movement is used to justify the doctrine of self-reform.

New developments in Xi Jinping's discourse on ideological and political theory courses in the five years since the "March 18" speech “3·18”重要讲话五年来习近平总书记关于思政课重要论述的新发展 She Shuanghao Marking five years since Xi Jinping's speech to a symposium of teachers of ideological and political theory courses on 18 March 2019, She asks how Xi's later remarks have extended his earlier statements. The article argues that these later remarks deepen the understanding of such courses in five respects and set higher requirements for their development. The piece has two parts. The first sets out the five deepenings: the status of the courses, the conception of the curriculum, the essence of teaching, the teaching process and the evaluation of courses. The second draws six practical implications for teaching, and the article ends with a short summary. In She's account, Xi has moved the courses from a "key course" for fostering virtue through education to a "top priority" of Party-led education work. The article says the "March 18" speech contained the outline of a "big ideological and political course" outlook, but that the concept was only named afterwards and extended to social practice and lived experience. It also says Xi later defined the essence of the courses as "explaining principles", described teaching as the teacher's "teaching" joined with the student's "comprehension", and proposed evaluation by whether the courses are taken seriously, suited to needs and done well. She calls for teaching centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, a wider conception of the curriculum, a renewed teacher–student relationship, continuous design across school stages and plural evaluation. The goal is the intensive, quality-focused development of the courses. Read the original if you want a concise account, from a Chinese education scholar, of how official guidance on political theory teaching has developed since 2019.

Class and race: the shift of discourse in mainstream Western social analysis and its implications 阶级与种族：西方主流社会分析中的话语转换及其寓意 Lin Deshan Lin Deshan asks how class discourse gave way to race discourse in mainstream Western social analysis after the Second World War, and what this says about identity politics. Existing discussion of racism, the author notes, has mostly stayed within culture and multiculturalism and has neglected how mainstream political forces moved between the two vocabularies. Lin's thesis is that the shift was driven mainly by the needs of political competition, above all electoral politics, and not by any real retreat of class. The article first sets out Marx's concept of class and the post-1950s challenges to it: a new middle class, the institutionalisation of class conflict, Cold War limits, and the cultural turn influenced by Gramsci and the rise of critical race theory. It then examines two mainstream forces in turn: liberalism, traced through Max Weber, Ralf Dahrendorf, T. H. Marshall and Anthony Giddens, and European social democracy, with the German and Swedish parties as main examples. A short conclusion draws out the significance of the two discourses. Lin argues that liberals led the move towards a politics without class. They absorbed Weber's ideas of social status and the "open society", and replaced equality and inequality with inclusion and exclusion. Race thus became a question of citizenship and identity, not of class. Liberal positions are said to be contradictory: they endorse pluralism yet doubt that a multicultural society can work, and they split into radical and conservative camps. Social democrats, in Lin's account, diluted their class identity to become "catch-all" parties courting the new middle class and adopted the radical liberal, multicultural view of race. This alienated traditional workers, many of whom moved to right-wing populism, and since the 2008 financial crisis some parties have partly returned to class politics. Lin concludes that identity consciousness is itself shaped by politics and culture and reflects the outlook of the dominant class, which the author says confirms Marx's view. Class discourse has not disappeared but survives in Weberian form, and mainstream theory abandoned Marx's version because it criticises capitalism and posits antagonistic class relations. Race, the author holds, cannot replace class as an analytical tool, though critical race theory can deepen understanding of capitalism, and its progressive wing's use of class analysis is not opposed to it. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of how liberalism and social democracy reframed class and race, with attention to the Swedish and German social democratic documents.

The fundamental guidelines for building school ideological and political courses in the new era Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important instructions on school ideological and political courses 新时代学校思政课建设的根本遵循 Xia Wenbin Xia Wenbin, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) and posted on this site in May 2024, sets out how schools should carry out General Secretary Xi Jinping's recent instruction that ideological and political courses must show "new prospects and new achievements" in the new era. The article treats Xi's instruction as the fundamental guideline for the work. Its stated aim is to train "new-era people" who can be trusted by the Party, love the country and shoulder the task of national rejuvenation. The commentary is organised in five parts. These cover guidance by the Party's innovative theory, the content system of the courses, innovation within a framework of upholding fundamental principles, the building of the teaching force, and Party leadership over the courses. Each part restates directives from Xi and the 20th Party Congress (2022) and turns them into practical requirements for schools at all levels. Xia's first move is that the courses must advance in step with the study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. This means a core course and unified textbooks, and integrated ideological and political education across universities, middle schools and primary schools. The second move concerns content and method. Content should rest on Marxism, on the achievements of socialism with chinese characteristics, and on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture. Teaching should "uphold fundamental principles and break new ground". In Xia's account this means defending the guiding status of Marxism and the Two Integrations, and criticising historical nihilism and neoliberalism. It also means student participation and explaining principles in a way that is deep, thorough and lively. Third, Xia stresses teachers, who should be politically strong, deeply committed, innovative in thinking, broad in outlook, strict in self-discipline and upright in character. Xia calls for evaluation that does not reward diplomas, papers and titles above classroom work. Xia concludes that Party committees at every level should put these courses on their agenda and keep a coordinated leadership structure. School Party secretaries and presidents should themselves teach the courses each term. The author presents strengthened Party leadership as the guarantee that the courses will fulfil the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party-theory guidance, curriculum design and teacher evaluation for school ideological and political courses are being framed in 2024.

Deepening the integrated development of ideological and political education across universities, secondary and primary schools 深入推进大中小学思想政治教育一体化建设 Wang Yi Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's instructions on school ideological and political theory courses, this article asks how ideological and political education can be integrated across universities, secondary schools and primary schools. Wang argues that such integration is necessary for the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, for improving the system of ideological and political work, and for the high-quality development of that education. The article presents integration as the way to raise a new generation to take on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a Party-theoretical commentary in three parts. It first sets out the significance of integration, then its defining requirements, and finally four areas for practical effort. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches and on central Party and State Council documents issued since the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the second part, Wang describes integration as vertical and horizontal at once. Vertically, goals, content and methods are linked across school stages: moral feeling in primary school, ideological foundations in junior secondary, political literacy in senior secondary, and a sense of mission at university. Horizontally, it joins dedicated ideological and political courses with ideological and political content in other subjects, classroom teaching with social practice, and offline with online education. The third part names four levers: strengthening the main channel through a curriculum and textbook system built around Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; pooling the efforts of Party committees, teachers, families and society; connecting resource supply; and setting an evaluation orientation based on results in fostering virtue. Wang concludes that Party leadership "can only be strengthened, not weakened" and that Party committees must treat these courses as a priority. The author also calls for a teaching force that is integrated in training, exchange and support, and for evaluation that moves away from a sole focus on exam scores. Other proposals include regular inspection and feedback to ensure the policy is implemented at every level. Read the original if you want a clear example of how Party leadership frames school ideological education and how it translates central directives into institutional measures for each school stage.

Building the ranks of young ideological and political theory course teachers in universities in the new era: logical basis, practical challenges and paths forward 新时代高校思政课青年教师队伍建设的逻辑依据、现实挑战与实践进路 Yu Anlong Yu Anlong asks how Chinese universities should build and strengthen their corps of young teachers of ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke), the compulsory courses that carry Party-led value education. Taking up Xi Jinping's 2019 remark that running these courses well depends on teachers, Yu argues that young teachers are the key group in this effort. The article contends that their development needs a systematic, multi-stage approach. The article has three parts. The first sets out why such teachers matter, the second identifies four present challenges, and the third proposes five practical measures. It draws on central policy documents from 2019 to 2022, including the Ministry of Education's 2019–2023 training plan and its 2020 regulations on teacher-corps building. It also cites figures reported for 2021: more than 127,000 full-time and part-time teachers, and 17,866 full-time teachers with doctorates, up 89% from 2016. Yu describes young teachers as a fresh force, as vanguard educators of a new generation of students, as pioneers of teaching innovation (for example, smart classrooms and virtual simulation) and as people with a strong inner drive to grow. Against this, Yu finds that growth in numbers has outrun quality. Some universities hired quickly, put weight on teaching and research credentials rather than political conviction and professional ethics, and drew staff from other disciplines or from student counsellor posts. Yu also identifies narrow knowledge, thin social experience, weak team support, cohort competition for promotion, and heavy pressure across teaching, research and social service. The proposed remedies are strict entry screening of political stance, professional ethics and psychological fitness; training that links pre-service and in-service, online and offline, theory and practice; and multi-dimensional, multi-party evaluation suited to the slow effects of value education. Further proposals are clearer promotion routes, dedicated funding and role models for incentives, and team mentoring and humane care for what Yu calls the young 'qingjiao' (underpaid junior lecturers). Yu concludes that the work involves many links and calls for coordinated measures at each of the five gates: entry, quality, evaluation, incentive and team. The aim is a corps that is politically firm, theoretically solid and capable of passing on the cause of university ideological and political education. Yu notes that the problems described are general and vary by region and institution, so they need case-specific analysis. Read the original if you study how Chinese universities manage and train ideological education staff and want a detailed, policy-oriented account of the problems and proposals.

Mazyar and Marxist historiography in Republican China 马札亚尔与民国马克思主义史学界 Li Ziqiang Li Ziqiang asks how the Hungarian-born Comintern scholar Ludwig Madyar (Mazyar, 1891–1937), the best-known exponent of the Asiatic mode of production, was received by Chinese Marxist historians in the Republican period, and why he has become a marginal and silenced figure in Chinese scholarship. The article argues that a political-history framework has reduced Madyar to a Trotskyist label. Li holds that a scholarly reassessment shows his work prompted Chinese historians to deepen their grasp of historical materialism and to rethink the particularity of China's path. The article has three parts. The first surveys the translations of Madyar's Chinese rural economy study and his later Outline of the Chinese Economy, along with the publishers' promotion, reviews and varied reactions of Chinese scholars. The second traces how his image shifted from international authority to Trotskyist and finally "counter-revolutionary", through the 1931 Leningrad discussion, the 1930s and the 1940s. The third weighs the weaknesses of his theory and the ways Chinese Marxist historians sublated it. Li argues that Chinese reactions mixed political, scholarly and national-sentiment factors. Trotskyist sympathisers tended to back Madyar, while Lü Zhenyu, Jian Bozan and others criticised him, often with real engagement. After the Soviet verdict of 1931 and the consolidation of a unified historical-materialist paradigm around 1938–39, criticism became ideological, and from 1949 Madyar was fused with the Trotskyists. Li identifies his fatal flaw as a contradiction between his Asiatic theory and his own evidence, which pointed to landlord–peasant exploitation and thus to feudalism. He also sees an over-reliance on natural-environment explanations and a European yardstick. Yet Li credits Madyar with prompting agrarian-economy research by Chen Hansheng and others and with forcing a rebalancing of the general and the particular, which led Lü Zhenyu and Hou Wailu beyond the "variant" theory. Li concludes that the Asiatic mode of production may be a "false problem", but a century of debate has left a rich scholarly legacy. He calls for abandoning binary thinking, recognising the historical relativity of orthodoxy and heresy, and avoiding a mechanical match between the Asiatic mode and the Chinese road. Li presents this clearing-up of the legacy as a necessary step in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you study the Asiatic mode of production debate, the Chinese social history controversy or the intellectual history of Chinese Marxist historiography and want detailed sources on Madyar's reception.

Zhang Zai's reworking of the "naturalist" view of ghosts and spirits inherited from the Qin–Han period 论张载对秦汉以来“自然主义”鬼神观的改造 Wang Jinchi Zhang Zai's (Song-dynasty Confucian) account of ghosts and spirits has often been treated as a representative of ancient Chinese materialism and atheism. Wang argues that a purely naturalist reading cannot capture it, because in Song–Ming Neo-Confucianism ghosts and spirits concern the substance of the Way. In Wang's view, Zhang Zai deliberately turned away from the naturalist view that had prevailed since the Qin and Han, and moved atheism from a narrow to a broader sense. The article has five parts. It first sets out the naturalist view and its limits, taking in the Guanzi, the Book of Rites, the Appended Remarks of the Book of Changes, Wang Chong and Fan Zhen. It then examines Zhang Zai's concept of "spirit" (shen) as substance and its link to the Great Void, and his reading of "ghosts and spirits" as function. The last sections turn to ritual sacrifice, the idea of "establishing teaching through the Way of spirits", and his rejection of belief in monstrous and malignant beings, before a brief conclusion. Wang says the naturalist view treated ghosts and spirits as refined qi and as the expanding and contracting of yin and yang. It denied that the dead survive as ghosts, culminating in Fan Zhen's thesis that the spirit perishes with the body. Wang judges this a narrow atheism: it attacks only concrete consciousness, strips Confucianism of its transcendent dimension, and fails to answer Buddhist objections, such as those of Zongmi. Zhang Zai, by contrast, separates finite perception from "spirit" as unlimited, constant and the substance of heaven. Ghosts and spirits are the "innate capacity" of the two qi: they are not qi itself, yet not apart from it. This avoids both naturalism and the Buddhist split between substance and function. In sacrifice, Zhang Zai rejects personified mountain-and-river deities and fixed ritual hierarchies, holding that sacrifice communes with the shared Void nature of ancestors and Heaven. He refutes tales of malignant beings by appeal to what all can see, as against private visions. Wang concludes that Zhang Zai kept the naturalist element, starting from the phenomenal world, but restored the transcendent dimension without becoming a thoroughgoing atheist. His view is not a deviation in the history of atheism but a "candid friend" (zhengyou) to it, and Wang Fuzhi later built on it. Read the original if you study Song–Ming Neo-Confucianism, Chinese debates on atheism, or Confucian responses to Buddhism and want a close reading of Zhang Zai's texts.

Generative AI and a new field of inquiry on the value movement of digital capitalism 生成式人工智能和数字资本主义价值运动新论域 Huang Zaisheng Huang Zaisheng asks how generative AI, represented by ChatGPT, reshapes the value movement of digital capitalism, and whether an "AI capitalism" is taking shape. Drawing on Marxist political economy, the article argues that capital uses technology to discipline labour and extract surplus value, while the "subjectification" of dead labour also erodes value. Huang concludes that generative AI produces digital wealth but deepens the contradictions of digital capitalism. The article is organised around four sets of questions. It examines commodity production and consumption under the "cognitive revolution", then human–machine collaboration and the new features of value creation in digital labour. It goes on to large-model competition and capital accumulation, and finally to new variables in the capitalist order of production. A brief conclusion follows. The evidence is drawn from industry reports and examples such as GPT-3, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Midjourney. On production, Huang argues that synthetic data, pre-trained foundation models and AI-generated content automate the supply of data and the making of digital content, so capital can monopolise "means of cognition" and free itself further from digital labour. On labour, collaboration splits the picture. Unpaid user labour, freelancers with distinctive skills and technical staff in new AI posts gain, while micro-task crowdworkers and ordinary workers lose out and risk becoming a "surplus proletariat". On accumulation, competition shifts to computing power and a few digital oligarchs, producing an "intelligent-computing monopoly". Huang also identifies new destabilising factors. Replacing living labour undermines capital's ability to absorb it through a "spatio-temporal fix", and AI-generated content strains the copyright regime that secures the value of knowledge commodities. Platform firms also gain "new power" over values and knowledge production, sharpening conflict with bourgeois states. Under "Silicon Valley private ownership", the author concludes, these contradictions cannot be reconciled. Only by going beyond the logic of capital, transforming the platform system and exploring digital socialism can universal AI benefit and the liberation of digital labour be achieved. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy framework for generative AI, with extensive Chinese-language industry sources.

Ideological and political work should pay attention to the role of negative teaching material 思想政治工作要注重发挥反面教材的作用 Luo Yuting Wang Fengyun Luo Yuting and Wang Fengyun take up a gap in ideological and political work. In their view it has long stressed positive education, telling people what they should do, and has paid too little attention to negative teaching material (fanmian jiaocai), which weakens its effect. They argue that such material has distinctive and irreplaceable strengths. In the new era, they say, it should be studied and used more fully while positive education remains primary. The article has three parts. The first sets out the value of using negative teaching material: negative figures, incidents and setbacks drawn from social life. The second identifies four distinctive advantages. The third discusses effective use under three headings: selection, vivid presentation and in-depth treatment. The authors draw on Mao Zedong, Chen Yun, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping. Their examples include Wang Ming, the Chiang Kai-shek coup of 12 April 1927, the Huang Kegong case, the collapse of the Soviet Union, and recent corruption cases. For the first part, the authors argue that using negative material is a fine tradition of the Party's ideological work. They add that it complements positive education dialectically, comprehensively and realistically, since society contains negative phenomena alongside mainstream positive ones. They also present it as an effective way to teach bottom lines, the limits beyond which a thing changes in quality, such as corruption by officials. The four advantages are: opposites that complete each other (xiangfan xiangcheng), comparison and discrimination, warning and alerting, and self-reflection. On the Soviet collapse, the authors say it prompted some former liberalising intellectuals to reconsider their views. On practice, the authors call for material matched to its audience, for example court hearings and cases of former students for officials and undergraduates. They also call for sensible timing and a sense of proportion, because over-exposure in mass and self-media may backfire and must not reverse the primary and secondary aspects. They propose live testimony from convicted officials, documentaries and short-video platforms, and interactive sessions after hearings. They further urge systematic classification, root-cause analysis and critical use. This last should build lasting mechanisms against recurrence, guided by Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese ideological-education scholars justify and operationalise 'negative teaching material' in Party discipline and anti-corruption education.

The emergence, application and risk prevention of datafication in ideological and political education 思想政治教育数据化的产生、应用与风险防范 Xie Yu Xie Yi Xie Yu and Xie Yi ask how big data and artificial intelligence are reshaping ideological and political education, and what limits should govern that change. They argue that the "datafication" of ideological and political education is an inevitable new research paradigm and practical orientation. In their view it can sharpen the precision and appeal of the field, but only if its risks are managed. The article has three parts. The first traces how datafication arose: the big-data social environment, the spread of data applications and "big data plus ideological and political education" research inside the discipline, and the borrowing of methods from computational social science. The second sets out four applications, and the third identifies three groups of risk. A short conclusion gives the authors' overall stance. On applications, the authors say datafication reaches the subjects, content, methods and platforms of education. They describe collecting and analysing big data, for example from social media or campus-card and library records. They also propose online experiments, such as comparing how a Party meeting's spirit spreads as text, image or video, or splitting students into experimental and control groups for micro-lessons. A further application is computer simulation, for example comparing "cramming" with "heuristic" teaching, and they add the development of research and guidance tools. On risks, they warn against over-reliance on data technology and "instrumental alienation", citing universities that build overlapping online learning platforms linked to assessment, which they say can produce formalistic compliance. They also warn of privacy violations and the weakening of human subjectivity. Their third concern is a loss of reliability and validity, from biased online data and from researchers lacking interdisciplinary skills. Xie and Xie conclude that datafication offers new research methods for online content, communication and management, and can increase interaction, personalisation and precision. They call for active exploration combined with "cautious optimism" and steady progress. They also call for verifying that data methods fit the discipline's value orientation and for ethical norms to bind the field. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language overview of how data-driven methods are being proposed for ideological and political education, and of the risks the authors flag.

Atheist propaganda and education in rural areas of China's southwestern border: current situation and countermeasures 西南边境农村地区无神论宣传教育现状与对策 Yue Zongfeng Yue Zongfeng asks how well Marxist atheist propaganda and education is working in rural areas along China's southwestern border, and what should be done to improve it. Writing in the context of central documents that call for strengthening atheist education in the countryside (the 2018 No. 1 Document on rural revitalization and a 2021 opinion on ideological and political work), the author treats the border as a weak point of ideological work. The article's thesis is that the overall situation is good, but that several problems, above all foreign religious infiltration and illegal religious activity, require a systematic set of countermeasures. The study is based on fieldwork on the China–Myanmar border in six prefectures and cities of Yunnan (Nujiang, Dehong, Baoshan, Lincang, Pu'er and Xishuangbanna), carried out in three rounds between December 2019 and November 2023. It draws on 812 valid questionnaires out of 1,000 distributed, plus 68 semi-structured and in-depth interviews. The article has three parts: the current situation, four problems that merit attention, and five groups of countermeasures. On the situation, Yue reports that 62.8 per cent of respondents held communist (atheist) belief and 22.4 per cent were religious believers. In the author's reading this shows that atheism remains dominant, although religious belief is still well above the level in inland China. Yue also cites low rates of superstitious practice, with 94 per cent reporting none, and high satisfaction with grassroots government work on atheist education. The problems identified are the inertia of ethnic religious tradition, foreign religious infiltration alongside illegal religious activity, inaction and even belief in spirits among some grassroots cadres and Party members, and spiritual emptiness linked to the hollowing out of villages next to the border. Yue argues that these conditions leave room for religious groups to compete with the Party for rural leadership. The proposed countermeasures are to promote border prosperity and agricultural modernization, since the author follows Marx in treating poverty as the soil of religion. They also include investment in education and culture, a joint early-warning and management system against infiltration, stronger Party leadership with accountability for cadres and atheism as a criterion for Party admission, and a drive to spread Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era together with local ethnic cultural activities. Read the original if you want survey figures on religion and atheist education in Yunnan's border villages, or an example of how Party scholars frame religious infiltration and policy responses in border regions.

Goals, experience and "upholding fundamental principles while innovating" in training talent for the ideological and political education major 思想政治教育专业人才培养的目标定位、宝贵经验与守正创新 Wang Shuyin Qu Pengfang Marking forty years since the Ministry of Education set up the ideological and political education major in 1984, Wang Shuyin and Qu Pengfang ask what the major has aimed to produce, what its training has taught, and how it should develop. They argue that talent training has consistently centred on specialised personnel for ideological and political work, and that past experience supports a new-era approach of upholding fundamental principles while innovating (守正创新). The article cites survey data from the "Sunshine Gaokao" platform, which put graduate numbers at 20,000–22,000 a year and student satisfaction at 4.1 out of 5. The article has three parts. The first traces training goals, specifications and levels through official documents from 1984 to 2024. The second distils experience under three headings: political direction, linking theory with practice, and strengthening disciplinary support. The third proposes four areas of innovation: broader training horizons, distinctive professional features, higher quality, and new training approaches. It draws throughout on Ministry of Education and State Education Commission documents and national teaching-quality standards. On goals, the authors describe a widening of aims from cadres in Party, government and enterprise posts, to senior teaching and research personnel, to "composite" talent able to work in both settings. They set out a three-part specification of political-theoretical grounding, professional knowledge and practical ability, and a ladder of levels running from diploma and bachelor's degrees through second bachelor's degrees to master's and doctoral study. On experience, they stress the Party's overall leadership, a firm socialist political stance and the guidance of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They also stress faculty, textbooks and Marxism schools as supports; the article notes more than 1,440 such schools by 2021. Looking ahead, the authors call for integrated bachelor's-master's-doctoral training with less repetition of courses across stages, and for clearer separation of the major from the university's required ideological and political theory courses and from the other second-level Marxist theory disciplines. They also want research topics kept between over-broad ("a basket for everything") and too narrow, better courses and practice teaching, wider international horizons, information literacy and a multidisciplinary background. They argue that these steps would raise quality and fit graduates to the needs of socialist modernization. Read the original if you study the institutional history and policy documents behind the training of ideological and political education specialists in China, or want a detailed account of how the major's goals and levels have been defined.

The basic contradiction of ideological and political education from the perspective of world history 世界历史视域下思想政治教育基本矛盾解读 Liu Juan Liu Juan asks what basic contradiction drives the continual evolution of ideological and political education, and why existing answers remain unsatisfactory. The article argues that scholars differ because they understand the nature of the field differently, and that the problem can be addressed by adopting a world-history perspective. On this basis Liu defines the basic contradiction as the dialectical relation between the mainstream ideology's demand for unity and the diversity of social consciousness. The article first diagnoses current research, in which the basic contradiction of ideological and political education is repeatedly confused with that of the educational process, and is shaped by the moral-education paradigm. It then explains what a world-history perspective offers, drawing on Gadamer's notion of horizon and on Marx and Engels's theory of world history. Next it reconsiders the nature of ideological and political education itself, and finally sets out the contradiction's two components. Liu cites Chinese scholars such as Lu Qingren, Zhang Yaocan, Yu Yangtao, Jin Linnan, Wang Ying and Shen Zhuanghai. Liu argues that after history became world history, spiritual interaction became global and modern states became its main actors and defenders of ideological security. Ideological and political education is therefore defined as a practice of spiritual interaction, with education as its basic form. In it a political group or ruling party uses the mainstream ideology to guide individuals' spiritual development nationwide. Within this frame the basic contradiction has two aspects. The first is between a state's mainstream ideology, with its strong sense of boundary, and other ideologies in the world, which Liu describes as diffuse, mobile and expansive. The second is between the unity of the mainstream ideology and the plurality of ideologies and individual spiritual worlds inside the country. Liu holds that the form of ideological and political education stays stable, is adjusted or is reshaped according to the changing balance between the 'one' and the 'many'. Ideological contradictions are ultimately constrained by changes in the social, political and economic base. Liu presents this reading as complementing earlier work, not rejecting it, by bridging macro and micro discourses in the field. The author concedes that the interpretation must still be tested by how well it explains actual ideological and political education, and that its argument needs further logical and historical support. Read the original if you study how Chinese scholars theorise ideological and political education as a discipline, or want to see Marxist world-history theory applied to the question.

Three major questions in building Marxist parties, seen through the historical course of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动历史进程视域下马克思主义政党建设的三个重大问题 Lin Jianhua Why has the international communist movement alternated between triumphant advances and serious setbacks? Lin Jianhua answers that the key lies in the Party, and that the quality of Marxist party-building can be judged by whether a party has a scientific theory, outstanding leaders and iron discipline. The article takes these as the three major questions of party-building, especially for a long-governing Marxist party. Lin proceeds historically, from the Communist League (1847) and the Communist Manifesto through the First, Second and Third Internationals to the Chinese Communist Party. The article has three main sections, one for each question, and draws heavily on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The Soviet Party's dissolution and the Chinese Party's growth serve as contrasting cases. On theory, Lin argues that Marxism guides the movement because it answers the questions of each era. Where its guiding role is upheld, parties develop; where it is neglected, parties suffer setbacks or dissolve. On leadership, Lin grounds the authority of leaders in historical materialism: leaders emerge from the people, see further and act decisively, and a party without a recognised leader or core cannot act in unison. The article presents the Two Establishes as the most important political achievement of the new era. On discipline, Lin stresses ideological unity, centralism and the ban on autonomy for Party organisations at each level. The author attributes the Soviet collapse partly to the abandonment of centralised leadership and cites Xi Jinping's discipline campaigns, including the 2024 Party discipline study and education drive. Lin concludes that the combination of scientific theory, an outstanding leader and iron discipline produced the movement's victories and gives the Chinese Communist Party its steel-like unity. For Lin, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds follow logically from history and from objective law. The Party's self-reform is presented as its second answer to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party scholarship uses the history of the international communist movement to justify the centrality of the leader and the Party's discipline.

Establishing and improving the "first agenda item" system with a high degree of political consciousness 以高度政治自觉建立健全“第一议题”制度 Yang Jianjun This commentary in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts takes up the "first agenda item" system, which the General Office of the Central Committee announced in an opinion of 23 February 2024 on consolidating the results of the study campaign on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Under the system, Party committees and Party groups at every level begin their standing-committee meetings and theory study sessions by studying Xi Jinping Thought and Xi's major speeches. Yang Jianjun argues that the system is an important lever for strengthening the Party's political building, raising political capacity and reinforcing the leadership role of Party organisations. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the system matters, the second the political requirements for establishing and improving it, and the third how to put it into effect. In the first part Yang draws on the Party's history, from Mao Zedong's call to turn the whole Party into a university, through the theoretical-education decisions of the socialist period, to reform and opening up and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yang gives three reasons for the system's importance. It is said to continue the Party's tradition of building the Party through ideas and theory. It is said to be necessary for the central task set by the 20th Party Congress (2022), advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. And it is presented as a practical need, because Xi Jinping Thought is described as the master key to development problems at a time of mixed opportunities and risks. On requirements, Yang calls for a deep grasp of the Two Establishes, a command of the stance, viewpoint and method of Xi Jinping Thought, and a demonstrative role for leading cadres as the \"key minority\". On implementation, Yang calls for linking study with practice, a problem-oriented approach, and institutional mechanisms such as immediate, regular and varied study, a closed loop from study to follow-up, tracking ledgers and supervision. Yang concludes that the system should become standardised, routine and effective, so that theory is turned into a guide for practice and a driving force for work. Study of Xi Jinping Thought is to be a required course and, in practice, a \"golden key\" and \"anchor\" for high-quality development. Read the original if you want to see how official Party commentary frames the purposes and working mechanisms of the \"first agenda item\" system in Party theoretical study.

Strictly strengthening the Party's discipline building 从严抓好党的纪律建设 Zhang Hao Writing in spring 2024, Zhang Hao argues that strengthening discipline building is the root-level remedy within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article treats the campaign of Party discipline study and education, announced at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (January 2024), as the occasion to make discipline building more rigorous. Its stated aim is to provide a firm disciplinary guarantee for Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts, opens by tracing how discipline building has risen in importance since the 18th Party Congress (2012), through the 19th and 20th Congresses. It is then organised in three parts: how to conduct the discipline study and education to a high standard; why political discipline and political rules must be given prominence; and how to observe and enforce Party discipline strictly. Throughout it draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements. On the first point, Zhang says the campaign extends the thematic education on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It should centre on the newly revised Regulations on Disciplinary Action, which the author says add 16 articles and revise 76 compared with 2018, and it should target leading cadres as the "key minority". On the second, Zhang calls political discipline the most fundamental discipline, requiring the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, adherence to the Party Constitution and absolute loyalty. The author says the revised Regulations now classify merely voicing support for central decisions without implementing them as a breach of political discipline. On the third, Zhang calls for discipline to become a "live high-voltage wire", with Party committees bearing primary responsibility and discipline commissions bearing supervisory responsibility. The author presents the "four forms" of supervision and discipline enforcement as graded safeguards, and warns against a "broken windows effect" from lenient enforcement. Zhang concludes that Party organisations should use the education campaign to make officials stand in awe of discipline, keep to bottom lines and grow used to working under supervision. The goal is a unified, iron discipline binding the whole Party at all times, which in the author's view will push full and rigorous self-governance of the Party into greater depth. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media framed the 2024 discipline education campaign, its priorities and its standard vocabulary.

Vigorously developing the cultural industry 大力发展文化产业 Ouyang Xuemei Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 8), Ouyang Xuemei asks how the cultural industry can be developed vigorously so that it supports high-quality development. The article's thesis is that, following Xi Jinping's call to promote high-quality development of the cultural industry, China should answer two "integration propositions": culture with technology, and culture with tourism. Ouyang presents this as key to raising the country's cultural soft power and the influence of Chinese culture. The piece has three parts. The first describes the industry's strengths and recent achievements: new cultural forms, the fusion of culture and tourism, and growth in cultural trade. The second sets out remaining problems. The third turns to remedies, based on Xi Jinping's remarks of 21 March 2024 in Hunan, and ends with rural cultural-tourism policy. Ouyang cites figures for 2023: 4.891 billion domestic tourist trips, up 93.3%, and 82.03 million inbound visitors. Foreign cultural trade is said to have risen from US$21.73 billion in 2012 to US$221.7 billion in 2022. Against this, Ouyang lists weaknesses: weak original output in traditional sectors, a shortage of talent in new formats, and cultural firms described as "scattered, small and weak". The author adds regional and urban–rural gaps, and weak cultural consumption, which was 10.8% of spending in 2023 against 11.7% in 2019. On remedies, Ouyang calls for a change of attitude so that spiritual needs count as much as material ones, and for further reform of the cultural system with more financial support. Technology such as generative AI, virtual reality and 5G is said to be cultivating new quality productive forces, with online games described as a testing ground. Ouyang says culture and technology empower each other. Ouyang calls for deeper integration of culture and tourism, using heritage, "national trend" culture, big data and smart platforms. For the countryside, the author proposes combined "agriculture, culture and tourism" products, with each village offering its own distinctive product, backed by policies on talent, land and finance. The article presents the rural cultural-tourism industry as facing an unprecedented opportunity. Read the original if you want a concise Red Flag Manuscripts statement of official thinking on cultural industry policy, with the statistics and policy documents it cites.
