Sustained effort and deeper advances in the anti-corruption struggle 持续发力、纵深推进反腐败斗争 Wang Chuanli This commentary, published in 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection to keep up the anti-corruption struggle and push it further in depth. Wang Chuanli argues that, although the struggle has won an "overwhelming victory" that has been consolidated, the situation remains severe and complex, so the Party must act with sustained, precise force. The article is organised around four reasons for continuing the struggle. It presents the effort as an expression of the Party's political consciousness in escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall through self-reform; as a response to the people's expectations of a clean political environment; as a sign of a sober reading of new trends in corruption; and as a demonstration of confidence in winning new victories. It draws on Mao Zedong's Yan'an cave dialogue, speeches by Xi Jinping, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the newly revised disciplinary regulations. Wang's central claim is that corruption is a question of the Party's survival, citing historical dynasties and the fall of the Soviet communist party as warnings. Self-reform is described as the "second answer" to the historical cycle, and the article lists Xi's "nine adherences" as its practical requirements. Wang stresses that the masses suffer most from corruption and privilege and are a force the struggle relies on, pointing to reporting and petition mechanisms. Because bad work styles easily rebound, the article says, the eight-point rules must be enforced continuously, with attention to hidden, mutated forms such as gift delivery by courier, and with linked investigation of misconduct and corruption. Wang describes the revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions (16 new articles, 76 revised) and the plenum's deployments: political supervision, work against corruption in finance, state enterprises, energy and other sectors, inspection tours, and reform of discipline-inspection bodies. The article concludes that victory depends on the Party's leadership and on the Party's continued self-reform, and it expresses confidence that the Party will deliver a "qualified answer sheet". Read the original if you want a representative statement of how official Party commentary in 2024 framed the case for continuing the anti-corruption campaign.

Taking the leadership of the great social revolution as the fundamental purpose On advancing the Party's great self-reform 以引领伟大社会革命为根本目的 Cao Wenze Cao Wenze takes up a formulation Xi Jinping put forward at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2024): the Party's self-reform must have leading the great social revolution as its fundamental purpose. Cao argues that this requirement reflects a new level of understanding of how self-reform works and defines the goal towards which it is directed. The article is a Party-journal commentary that urges study and implementation of Xi's ideas on the subject. The piece is organised in three parts. The first sets out the theoretical and practical logic linking the \"two great revolutions\", the social revolution and the Party's self-reform, drawing on Marx and Engels. The second reviews four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to present tasks tied to the Chinese modernization drive. Cao's core argument starts from the historical-materialist claim that landlord and bourgeois classes, once revolutionary, became targets of revolution because they represented only their own interests. By contrast, the Communist Party has no special interests of its own and can face problems and correct errors, so it preserves its vanguard character and purity through self-reform. Cao stresses that this character is not innate or permanent but forged through revolutionary struggle, and that it matters especially after taking power. Reading Party history, Cao presents examples such as the Yan'an rectification, the execution of Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan, and Deng Xiaoping's description of reform as a second revolution as evidence that the two revolutions have always accompanied and reinforced each other. For the present era, Cao says full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has produced a second answer to the \"historical cycle\" question. Cao concludes that the Party still faces long-term, complex and severe \"four tests\" and \"four dangers\" and that some aspects of Party building do not yet match the task of building a modern socialist country. Cao calls for three things: maintaining full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, centred on the \"key minority\" of leading cadres; serving the central task of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization; and keeping a fighting spirit through Party history and discipline education. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal frames the link between Party discipline and the social revolution in the Xi era.

Upholding the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership as the fundamental guarantee 以坚持党中央集中统一领导为根本保证 Wang Tingyou Zhao Puchen This article by Wang Tingyou and Zhao Puchen elaborates the first of nine issues that Xi Jinping said must be handled well in advancing the Party's self-reform, as set out at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The authors argue that the Party's self-reform proceeds under Party leadership, that centralised and unified leadership by the Party Central Committee is the highest principle of that leadership, and that it is therefore the fundamental guarantee of self-reform. In their view it must never be wavered on, under any circumstances. The piece has three sections. The first gives three reasons why such leadership is needed: to keep self-reform on the right course, to achieve its set goals, and because it is a basic lesson of the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second asks what the Central Committee's authority consists of, drawing on Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. The third sets out the practical routes by which that authority is to be safeguarded. The central claim is that the Central Committee is the Party's "brain and nerve centre", and that a very large Party facing what Xi calls the Party's distinctive problems can unify its thinking, will and action only if the Central Committee holds supreme and final authority. The authors read this as an organisational system running vertically from the Central Committee to local bodies, Party groups and grassroots branches, which they say ensures that decisions are carried out in full. They cite the 2016 intra-Party guidelines, the 2019 opinions on Party political building and the 2021 historical resolution. They present the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as the political consequence of this principle, and they describe the tradition of centralising on the basis of full democracy as a Party innovation. The authors propose five measures. They call for strengthening political building, so that members show absolute loyalty to the Central Committee. They want ideological building, using Xi Jinping Thought to unify thinking, and tighter discipline, especially for senior officials as the "critical minority". They also propose reforming the Central Committee's own decision-making and coordinating bodies, and building an institutional system of Party leadership based on the Party constitution and democratic centralism, with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as its aim. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how the Party's theoretical press currently links Central Committee authority, discipline and institutional reform to the Party's self-reform.

Analysing the contemporary virtual economy through Lenin's critique of finance capital 列宁金融资本批判视域下当代虚拟经济分析 Wang Danzhu Chen Jisheng Wang and Chen ask whether Lenin's critique of finance capital, set out in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, still explains the swollen "virtual economy" of today. They recall that Western economists such as Harry Magdoff and Paul Sweezy proposed answering stagnation with financialisation, yet the expansion of the virtual economy deepened crises such as 1997 and 2008. The authors argue that contemporary capitalist virtual economy has not moved beyond Lenin's framework, which remains a "scalpel" for dissecting it, and that the framework also offers lessons for China. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs how Lenin's theory arose from Marx's account of fictitious capital and from the concentration of production and banking around 1900, and sets out its core claims. It then applies the theory to the virtual economy in general, and tests it against three twenty-first-century developments: digital technology, the divergence between virtual and real sectors, and economic globalisation. A final part turns to risks facing China's virtual economy and to policy implications. The central move is to treat parasitism as the essential trait of finance capital under monopoly. The authors trace how financial monopoly and the "participation system" create the conditions for parasitism, how capital export extends it worldwide, and how it produces recurring crises. They then argue that each new feature confirms Lenin. Digital platforms and mergers deepen monopoly, and they cite Amazon's retail share and Google's search share. Citing US figures for 1960–2020, they say finance rose while manufacturing fell, which they read as parasitism on the real economy. Rising global liquid financial assets and the dollar's role are presented as a strengthened financial hegemony that is bound up with military and political power. Turning to China, the authors list three risks: weak coordination between virtual and real economies, rising external pressure, and difficult regulation. They call for four responses: the Party's centralised and unified leadership over financial work, a people-centred approach to finance, balanced development of the real and virtual economies, and stronger regulation through legislation, big-data supervision and internal governance. In their view, public ownership as the main body of the economy makes regulation effective in a way Lenin thought impossible under private ownership. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal links Lenin's theory of imperialism to debates on financialisation, digital monopoly and financial policy in China.

"Free from doubts at forty": a historical reflection on the development of the discipline of ideological and political education “四十不惑”：思想政治教育学科发展的历史沉思 Xiang Jiuyu Xiang Jiuyu takes the Confucian saying that at forty one is free from doubts as a metaphor for the discipline of ideological and political education after forty years of development. The article argues that the discipline has reached a stage of clear positioning, stable form and wide application. Xiang stresses that this does not mean problems have vanished, only that the discipline no longer doubts its direction and has the capacity to build its own knowledge system. The article has three parts. The first describes what "freedom from doubt" means in three respects: clarity of disciplinary belonging, maturity of principles and depth of application. The second asks where it comes from, pointing to scholars, scholarship and institutional bases. The third sets out reflections on future tasks: integrated development, high-quality development and development in service of Chinese modernization. In Xiang's account, the discipline's essence is "forging souls and cultivating people", with Marxism as the "soul". Its principles form a structure of "point" (the theory of inculcation), "line" (political work as a lifeline), "plane" (comprehensiveness) and "body" (integration). Scholars are said to hold three identities, as educators, as committed Marxists and as researchers, and Xiang holds that research, belief and action must be combined. The discipline is said to have moved from "seeking scriptures" from philosophy and sociology to building an autonomous knowledge system of six kinds of research. As institutional evidence the article cites 1,440-plus Schools of Marxism by 2021 and a 2021 survey in which ideological and political education had the most full-time teachers (5,650, 28%) and doctoral dissertations (341 of 953) among the Marxist theory sub-disciplines. Xiang proposes extending integration beyond schools to research and to lifelong, society-wide education. Xiang also calls for easing mismatches between supply and demand, knowledge and practice, and internal and external resources. Under Chinese modernization, the discipline should "multiply" its gains by working on frontier research, joining the building of a Chinese school of scholarship and opening an international outlook, while "subtracting" wasteful formal innovation. Read the original if you want a self-assessment of this discipline's identity, principles and agenda by a leading scholar in the field.

Data, labour and platform capital A study of digital capitalism from the perspective of historical materialism 数据、劳动与平台资本 Chen Meng Lan Jiang Chen Meng and Lan Jiang ask what data, labour and platforms are within digital capitalism, and whether digital technology amounts to a new mode of production. Opening with Michael Betancourt's image of the sixteenth-century 'cat organ', they argue that behind the apparently frictionless digital economy lie the material basis of production and living labour, as historical materialism holds. Their answer is that digital capitalism is a new dimension of capitalism, not a new mode of production. The article draws on Marx's Capital and on contemporary theorists such as Nick Srnicek, Christian Fuchs, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Maurizio Lazzarato and Paolo Virno. It is organised around three questions: how data becomes a commodity, whether digital labour is productive labour, and whether digital capitalism constitutes a new mode of production. A short conclusion considers the prospects for a transition to what the authors call digital socialism. On data, the authors reject Srnicek's comparison of data to oil, which they say makes it look like a freely available natural resource. In their account data is a product of human activity whose use-value depends on an institutionalised apparatus of algorithms, platforms and terminals. It is a commodity that serves both as a means of production and as a means of circulation, notably in targeted advertising. On labour, they apply Marx's three criteria for productive labour: it produces use-values, it is internal to capitalist production, and it produces surplus value. Digital labour meets these criteria, but only within the digital capitalist mode of production, and they say its definition should not become tautological. They fault theorists of immaterial labour for overestimating a utopia of 'free labour' and missing capitalism's material basis. On the third question they follow Fuchs: technology is not neutral, surplus-value production drives technical change and not the reverse, and platforms tend towards monopoly and rentier power. The authors conclude that the 'digital' is a refined form of capitalism and not an escape from it. In their reading, digital production could end drudgery, but within existing class structures it intensifies exploitation and domination. They call for the Party-neutral task of changing relations of production and social relations to fit modern productive forces, so that a move from digital capitalism to digital socialism becomes possible. Read the original if you want a Marxist, Nanjing-based critique of the theory of immaterial labour and of 'new mode of production' claims about the digital economy.

Lenin's reflections on how to carry out socialist economic construction in a backward country 列宁对如何在落后国家进行社会主义经济建设的思考 Vladimiro Giacché This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Italian scholar Vladimiro Giacché. It asks how Lenin, in 1922–1923, thought about building a socialist economy in a backward country. Giacché argues that Lenin's late writings on the New Economic Policy (NEP) redefined state capitalism, cooperatives and the state apparatus, and that they remain relevant a century later. The article reads Lenin's reports to the 11th Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1922 and to the Fourth Comintern Congress in November 1922. It then turns to two works dictated while he was seriously ill, 'On Co-operation' (January 1923) and 'Better Fewer, But Better' (March 1923). It also sets out the course of his strokes, and closes with a short assessment of the Soviet path that followed. Giacché draws out three moves. First, Lenin drew three lessons from the first year of the NEP: the link with the peasantry, the test of Communist management against private capital, and a new idea of state capitalism. In Giacché's account, Lenin held that state capitalism under a proletarian state, which controls land and the key industries, is a different thing from state capitalism under bourgeois rule. It is capitalism that is permitted and kept within limits, provided the Party learns how to do the limiting. Second, in 'On Co-operation', Lenin argues that once the workers hold power and the means of production, cooperatives can be a main route to socialism. The emphasis shifts to peasant cooperation and a 'cultural revolution', and Giacché notes that Stalin and Bukharin used the text in 1925 to argue that Russia could build socialism unaided. Third, 'Better Fewer, But Better' calls for caution, thrift and the cutting back of the tsarist bureaucratic inheritance. It sees the final victory of socialism as secured by the revolt of Russia, India and China, and the Soviet task as tactical survival. Giacché concludes that Lenin's last advice pointed to gradual internal accumulation with a minimal bureaucracy. The Soviet industrialisation that followed was not gradual, brought social trauma and expanded the bureaucratic machine, which he says ran against Lenin's final instructions. He identifies four lasting themes: the complexity of socialist construction, anti-dogmatism, state transformation together with workers' cultural emancipation, and the Asian peoples' role as subjects of history. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of Lenin's last writings on the NEP, state capitalism and cooperatives, written from outside China for a Chinese journal on world socialism.

Fully implementing the holistic approach to national security 全面贯彻总体国家安全观 Chen Yixin Marking the tenth anniversary of Xi Jinping's holistic approach to national security (announced in April 2014), Chen Yixin, Party secretary and minister of the Ministry of State Security, argues that the concept has driven a historic leap in Chinese theory and practice of national security. The article, published in Qiushi in 2024, presents the approach as the fundamental guide for security work in the new era and calls for it to be studied thoroughly and implemented in full. The piece has five parts. It sets out the concept's intellectual content and its development from 2014 through the 19th and 20th Party Congresses; reviews ten years of practical results; draws out five methodological requirements; lists five main tasks for security organs; and closes with six kinds of safeguards. Chen describes the approach as a theoretical system built around the word "holistic" and the "ten adherences". It places political security at the top, treats development and security as paired priorities, and requires Party leadership over all security work. On results, Chen cites the Central National Security Commission and the Party's leadership regulations, the National Security Strategy (2021–2025), more than twenty specialised security laws, the Hong Kong national security law, a national security education day, and global initiatives under a community with a shared future for mankind. The requirements are system-wide construction, all-domain risk control, coordination at home and abroad and online and offline, use of all means, and mobilisation of the whole society. The main tasks are countering subversion, hegemony, separatism, terrorism and espionage; Chen frames Taiwan, external pressure and ideological infiltration in these terms. Chen concludes that the Two Establishes provide the greatest certainty for meeting any challenge, and that the Party must keep absolute leadership over security work in support of Chinese modernization. The proposed safeguards cover politics, institutions, rule of law, science and technology, publicity and personnel, including loyalty and discipline within the security ranks. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement from China's state security chief of how the holistic approach to national security is to be put into practice, including the operational priorities of the security organs.

Cultivating new-era talents by passing on the red gene 在传承红色基因中培育时代新人 Wang Quanliang Wang Quanliang, Party secretary of Anyang Normal University, asks how universities should cultivate young people able to shoulder the task of national rejuvenation. Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, Wang argues that the "red gene" is the spiritual bond of the Chinese nation and the source of energy for such "new-era talents". Universities, in this account, must pass it on under the guidance of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. The article has three parts. The first presents passing on the red gene as a key way of studying and implementing Xi Jinping's thought on culture, citing Xi's repeated statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second explains why cultivating new-era talents requires it. The third sets out practical measures for higher education, organised under four headings: continuing the red bloodline, telling red stories, promoting red culture and using red resources. In the second part, Wang says the red gene gives young people three things: a cultural direction, value guidance and spiritual motivation. It is described as a living textbook that creates emotional identification, supports firm ideals and convictions, and helps answer the question of what kind of people to train, how and for whom. In the third part, Wang calls for red culture to be built into training plans, syllabuses and school-based textbooks, and for ideological and political courses to work together with "course ideology and politics". Wang also proposes using film, short video and livestreaming, putting red culture into campus life and landscape, and organising field study at revolutionary sites alongside online courses. Wang concludes that universities should make the red gene the source of moral education and integrate it into the whole process of running schools and training students. The aim is to strengthen students' confidence and resolve and to contribute to building China as a strong country in education, science and technology, and talent. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Party-led universities are told to turn red culture into teaching, media and practical activities.

An interpretation of Marx and Engels's methodology of investigation and research 马克思恩格斯的调查研究方法论阐释 Liu Ying Liu Ying asks what methodological principles guided Marx and Engels's investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu), and what they offer to present-day practice. The article starts from the Party's description of investigation and research as its "family heirloom" and from Mao Zedong's remark that scientific communism was reached only after a lifetime of such work. Liu argues that, although Marx and Engels never used the term, each step towards scientific socialism was in substance investigation and research, and that their methods still give guidance in the new era. Published in Theoretical Exploration in 2024, the article sets out five principles in turn and then a short conclusion. They are: standing on the proletarian position; combining problem awareness with a problem orientation; combining typical with general surveys; combining investigation with research; and organising and institutionalising the work. Liu draws on Marx's articles on the Moselle, his 1880 Workers' Inquiry, Engels's Letters from the Wuppertal and The Condition of the Working Class in England, the Brussels Communist Correspondence Committee and the International Working Men's Association. In Liu's account, investigation as such has no class position, but its use does. Marx and Engels worked for proletarian liberation in their aims, objects and findings, whereas bourgeois scholars, in Liu's view, distorted facts to hide class contradictions. Liu argues that Marx and Engels focused on fundamental questions of their era rather than isolated social problems. They treated England as the typical site of mature capitalism, while the International's statistical committees pursued general surveys of workers' conditions. Liu stresses that gathering evidence, from fieldwork and from libraries and blue books, was only a first step: the decisive stage was analysis, summed up in the saying "three parts investigation, seven parts research". Liu also emphasises the correspondence committees and the International's rules as ways of making investigation collective and regular. In the conclusion Liu draws lessons for today. Investigation must be people-centred, and Liu cites Xi Jinping's 1988 inquiry in Ningde and the "Four Down to the Grassroots" system as examples. Liu adds that it must be problem-oriented, combine breadth with typical cases, and turn scattered impressions into systematic understanding, as with the more than fifty inquiries Xi made before the "targeted poverty alleviation" approach. Liu also endorses the Party Central Committee's call to make investigation a long-term mechanism and routine work. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-line overview of how Chinese scholars link Marx and Engels's research practice to current calls for investigation and research.

The logic behind the formation of Marx's philosophical discourse: a discourse perspective 从话语视角看马克思哲学的生成逻辑 Liu Ying Yang Yi Liu Ying and Yang Yi ask how Marx's philosophical discourse was formed and what logic it followed. They treat Marx's philosophical revolution as also a revolution in discourse, which they define as a system of linguistic signs organised by a certain logical structure. Starting from Xi Jinping's calls to build a philosophy and social science discourse system with Chinese characteristics, the authors argue that returning to the original context of Marx's discourse can support that task. Their thesis is that its formation rests on four paired logics, each a unity of two sides. The article is organised in four sections: speculative and realist logic; implicit and explicit logic; critical and constructive logic; and revolutionary and practical logic. It follows Marx's path from his doctoral dissertation and the Rheinische Zeitung period, through the Hegelian Philosophy of Right critique, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The Holy Family, to the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. It draws on Hegel, Feuerbach, Deleuze and Althusser's symptomatic reading as points of reference. The authors argue that Marx moved from Hegelian speculation, through Feuerbach's humanism, to a realist logic grounded in practice. They hold that this shift appears on the surface as changes in terms and categories, for example from 'alienated labour' to 'relations of production'. Beneath it runs an implicit line, which the authors identify as the era's question of capital's appropriation of labour and the emancipation of the proletariat. In their account, terms sometimes lagged behind thought: 'human essence' and 'species' were kept while their meaning changed. They contrast Hegel's self-determining concept, as in his idealised notion of labour, with Marx's concepts drawn from real productive life. They conclude that Marx's discourse is both critical of the world and put into practice, unlike the Young Hegelians' 'phrase-revolution'. The authors conclude that Marx's discourse differs from speculative philosophy in one respect: practice. They say it works as a material force aimed at changing the world and guiding the proletariat. They present this as theoretical support for building a Marxist-guided academic discourse system in contemporary China. Read the original if you want a close, text-by-text account of how Marx's categories changed between 1841 and 1846, as seen by Chinese scholars of the history of Marxism.

Forty years of the ideological and political education discipline: a historical and contemporary survey 思想政治教育学科设立40年的历史与现实考察 Liu Shulin Marking 40 years since ideological and political education was established as a university discipline in 1984, Liu Shulin asks where the field's theoretical and practical foundations lie and how it has developed. The author argues that the discipline did not appear from nothing in the 1980s. It inherited the Party's accumulated experience from the revolutionary years and the first 30 years of the People's Republic, and it has matured through practice and through the lessons of setbacks. The article is organised in four parts. It begins with the ideological and political work developed under Mao Zedong, then turns to how Deng Xiaoping, Ye Jianying and others in the early reform period spoke about it. It next traces the institutional steps taken between 1949 and 1984, and it ends with the discipline's growth from the late 1980s to the era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Liu's central claim is that the discipline's roots lie in what the article calls the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. In this account, Mao's formulation of ideological work as the "lifeline" of all other work, together with persuasion, criticism and self-criticism, and patriotic, collectivist and socialist education, supplied the basis. The article then lists documents and figures from the early People's Republic: the 1949 Common Programme, the 1952 directive on training Marxist-Leninist teachers at Renmin University, and Liu Zizai's 1955 "four musts". Liu reads these as forerunners of the "main channel" of university ideological education and of "integrating ideological and political education into all courses". The author also cites Qian Xuesen's 1980 proposal for a "Marxist science of moral education" and the 1983–84 decisions that created the major. Liu says the discipline was tested in the late 1980s, when "abolition", "dilution" and "reform" theories challenged it. In the author's telling, practitioners held their ground and the lessons of that period led to new textbooks, doctoral programmes and Schools of Marxism. Since the 18th Party Congress, under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the author finds conditions for the discipline unusually favourable. Liu still lists shortcomings: academic and discourse systems, practical effectiveness, integration across school levels, and teacher quality. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how Chinese scholars trace the lineage and institutional history of ideological and political education.

Grasping the regularities of forty years of development of the discipline of ideological and political education, and prospects for the new era 思想政治教育学科40年发展的规律性把握与时代展望 Feng Gang Marking the fortieth anniversary of the formal establishment of the discipline of ideological and political education in 1984, Feng Gang asks what regularities can be drawn from its development and where it should go next. The article argues that the discipline's growth rests on Party leadership, service to the task of educating people, fit with social and individual needs, and a combination of local roots and global outlook. It holds that future development should proceed through Chinese modernization, high-quality development and a stronger scientific image. The article has three main parts. The first draws four regularities from the period since the reform and opening up. The second sets out four features of the discipline since the 18th Party Congress (2012): synchrony with Party theoretical innovation, fuller policy support, stronger endogenous drive and a clearer innovation orientation. The third looks ahead, and a short conclusion follows. In the first part, Feng presents the discipline as an original product of the Communist Party, created in response to the decline of the work-unit system and to value confusion amid economic reform. Feng also stresses that it drew on both traditional Chinese culture and the moral and civic education of other countries. For the new era, Feng cites Xi Jinping's speeches and a series of policy documents from 2015 to 2022, including the "big ideological and political course" initiative, as providing theory and institutional backing. The forward-looking section proposes building the discipline's internal, public and international images, and linking it in "four connections" with ancient Chinese thought, other Marxist theory sub-disciplines, the humanities and overseas practice. Feng adds that it should draw on cultural strength by treating culture as an extending, flowing and diverse force. Feng concludes that the discipline's basic experience is the combination of theoretical research and practical exploration, and that its inner logic lies in the dialectic between the universal and the particular in moral education. In Feng's view, Marxist guidance and the Party's innovative theory give it vitality. Only by following this path, Feng argues, can it fulfil its mission within Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an insider's account of how the discipline understands its own history, policy framework and agenda, written by a leading figure at Beijing Normal University.

Making good use of digital technology to build the "Great Ideological and Political Course" 善用数字技术 建好“大思政课” Peng Qinghong Peng Qinghong asks how digital technology can be used to build the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke), the policy push to open ideological and political theory teaching beyond the classroom to the whole of society. Writing in 2024 and drawing on Xi Jinping's calls to integrate the traditional strengths of ideological work with information technology, Peng argues that the two are mutually reinforcing. The author holds that technology serves the course, and that the relationship needs careful management. The piece, published in China Higher Education (2024, no. 9), has three parts. It first sets out why digital technology and the Great Ideological and Political Course fit together. It then names five points where the two can be joined, and finally discusses five relationships that must be handled correctly. In the first part, Peng contends that 5G, big data, the Internet of Things and AI suit the course's aims, and suit students born after 2000 who expect immersive learning. In the other direction, the scale of the course is said to spur technological innovation and to bring schools, enterprises and government into building a joint digital support system. The five points of integration are: linking the different actors through virtual teaching-research offices and platforms; shared resource platforms such as the National Smart Education Platform; digital tools for teacher–student interaction; virtual reconstruction of scenes through VR and "cloud visits" to revolutionary sites; and a systemic change in resources, interaction and evaluation. Peng then lists the five relationships. The classroom stays primary and technology is auxiliary. "Red" (political orientation) must lead "expert" (technical competence), so mainstream ideology guides design and use. Technology should reshape teaching and not become mere display. Privacy and digital ethics must be balanced against shared public space. Rollout should be gradual and suited to teachers' abilities, without uniform mandates. Peng concludes that technology is a "double-edged sword". Used properly it gives the course a stronger sense of the times and more appeal, and used carelessly it departs from the aims of reform. The author calls for a phased, differentiated approach that keeps the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent at the centre. Read the original if you want a practical view from a university leader of how digitalisation is being fitted into Party-guided ideological and political education in China.

Stage characteristics and trends of capitalist digitalization 资本主义数字化的阶段特征与趋向研判 Chen Wenxu Chen Wenxu asks how digitalization should be located in the development of capitalism and what it reveals about the system's future. The article argues that digitalization is both a precondition for and the core feature of a new stage of capitalism, usually discussed as digital capitalism. In Chen's view it has not changed the institutional essence of capitalism or produced a higher social formation; it has produced new forms of labour, capital and exploitation. The article has three parts. The first traces the historical positioning of digitalization from the third scientific and technological revolution of the 1940s–50s. It follows successive Western concepts: Daniel Bell's post-industrial society, Manuel Castells's informational society, and Nicholas Negroponte's digital society. It contrasts these with continuity-minded critics such as Dan Schiller, Frank Webster and Habermas. The second part describes four new features: digital technology, digital labour, digital capital and digital exploitation. The third part assesses four trends. Chen's central move is to read digital phenomena through Marx's labour theory of value. Users' online activity is treated as labour that creates use value and abstract value. The data it generates becomes digital capital once platforms analyse it by algorithm, and platforms appropriate it without pay. Chen rejects arguments that platform services are equivalent to wages, or that digital labour lies outside production and so outside exploitation, calling these misreadings of Marx. The four trends are monopoly among a few top internet firms, with unequal positions in the global data value chain; the uncertain prospects of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and central bank digital currencies; the expansion of digital hegemony, which Chen illustrates with US actions against 5G suppliers and the Clean Network programme; and a potential "cyber proletariat". Chen concludes that digitalization must be analysed from the standpoint of historical materialism and the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete. Criticism should not reject digital technology, since, citing Marx on machinery, the contradictions arise from its capitalist application. The article argues that the basic contradiction of capitalism has only been modernised and that the cyber proletariat could unite globally. It ends by pointing to China's digital development as a path towards a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account that links Western theories of the information society to a political-economy critique of platforms, data and digital hegemony.

An analysis of Yan Yuan's atheist thought 颜元的无神论思想探析 Xu Jiulin Yan Yuan, a thinker of the late Ming and early Qing, is often described as an Enlightenment figure, but Xu Jiulin argues that scholarship has misread his atheism. Earlier studies, Xu says, focus on his attacks on Buddhism and Daoism and treat his atheism as theoretically unoriginal. Xu's thesis is that Yan's atheism is aimed chiefly at the religionised Confucianism of Cheng–Zhu Neo-Confucianism, which Yan believed had absorbed Buddhist and Daoist ideas, and that it can only be understood through his materialist theory of qi and his practical learning. The article has four parts. It first examines Yan's qi-based ontology and his epistemology, then his practice-oriented thought summed up as getting one's hands on the matter and doing it. A third section assesses the significance and limits of his atheism, and a short conclusion follows. Xu draws on Yan's own writings and, at points, on Marx and Engels as comparison. Xu argues that Yan reversed the Cheng–Zhu priority of principle (li) over qi, holding that li exists only within qi. On this basis Yan rejected a pure, transcendent world of li, the claim that qi is the source of evil, and the Buddhist and Daoist views of the world as empty and still. His epistemology of seeing principle in affairs likewise denies that ghosts, reincarnation, hell or immortals can be known. Yan's practical doctrine affirms the body and its desires. It rejects quiet-sitting, the Cheng–Zhu maxim of preserving heavenly principle and eliminating human desires, and fatalism, and it widens practice to include military, agricultural and economic matters. Xu reads all this as a critique of religious alienation. Xu concludes that Yan helped Confucianism shed Buddhist and Daoist influence and move from speculative learning towards practical learning, and that this makes his thought significant for the Enlightenment. Xu also notes limits: Yan prayed to a supreme deity at night, his qi theory kept some idealist and agnostic traces, and he sought liberation from religion through moral cultivation rather than through the growth of productive forces. Read the original if you study Chinese materialism, Neo-Confucianism's religious dimension, or how Chinese scholars read Confucian thinkers alongside Marxist critiques of religion.

The deep logic and forms of cultural imperialism in Western left discourse 西方左翼话语中文化帝国主义的深层逻辑与样态 Du Min Du Min asks what lies beneath cultural imperialism as it is analysed by Western left and critical scholars. The article argues that, besides a "commodity profit–capital" logic, cultural imperialism rests on a deeper logic of "spiritual interest–control", in which cultural exchange serves the strategic interests of imperialist states and ideological domination matters more than trade volumes. Drawing on James Petras, Harold Innis, Edward Said, Syed Hussein Alatas, Syed Farid Alatas, Samir Amin, David Harvey and others, Du divides this logic into two forms. The first is "knowledge imperialism", based on technological hegemony and control. The second is "spiritual imperialism", based on ideological penetration. The article treats each form in turn, with examples from Asia, Africa, Latin America and the former Soviet space. On knowledge imperialism, Du describes a sense of civilisational superiority inherited from colonial rule and a monopoly over knowledge production backed by intellectual property regimes such as the TRIPS agreement. Du also cites figures on patents and research spending. On this account, a "knowledge–hegemony–rent" logic differs from Lenin's finance-capital monopoly. It leaves dependent states with intellectual dependence, a brain drain and what Alatas calls the "captive mind" and the intellectual "comprador". Spiritual imperialism is traced from religious imperialism to non-governmental organisations, which Du says have become agents of Western values since the 1990s. Du cites Soros-funded foundations, the post-tsunami conversions and Sinhala Buddhist backlash in Sri Lanka, and US measures such as the International Religious Freedom Act. Du argues that this penetration is more concealed than old colonial methods. Du concludes that the two forms are complementary routes to imperialist strategic interests in the post-colonial world. Du adds that China's catch-up in knowledge production has, in this reading, alarmed the United States. Spiritual penetration, the article claims, tends to provoke resistance, and Du points to Pakistan's expulsion of international aid organisations in 2018 and Russia's 2015 bans on US foundations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar draws on Western and postcolonial critics to frame knowledge, religion and NGOs as instruments of imperialism, with case material from Sri Lanka and Central Asia.

Key issues in further advancing the sinicization of religion in China 深入推进我国宗教中国化的几个关键问题 He Xinyuan How can the Party more effectively advance the "sinicization of religion" (zongjiao zhongguohua), which Xi Jinping stressed in 2021 and which the 20th Party Congress report (2022) again set as a task? He Xinyuan, a researcher at the Academy of Marxism, argues that, beyond supporting religious circles in interpreting doctrines in line with contemporary China and fine traditional Chinese culture, three things must be grasped. These are the core socialist values as the "greatest common divisor", Marxist atheism, and the Party's leadership. The article is organised in three sections matching these points. It begins from the premise that religion must adapt to its society and will long exist in socialist China. It cites the 2018 white paper figure of nearly 200 million believers and over 380,000 clergy. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and later Party leaders, and on Xi Jinping's speeches, including the 2021 National Conference on Religious Work. In the first section, He argues that unity among believers and non-believers should be sought at the level of shared values. Their fundamental political and economic interests are said to coincide, and the core socialist values are presented as the value consensus all can accept. Using them to guide religion does not mean asking believers to abandon faith, but a "political bottom line" must hold: upholding Party leadership, patriotism and socialism with Chinese characteristics. In the second, He holds that Marxist atheism is a "major principle". Unchecked spread of theism is said to threaten the Party's guiding ideology and governing position. Atheist education is described as aiming neither to eliminate religion nor to set believers against non-believers, but to help people view religion scientifically. Patriotism, collectivism and socialism education in religious circles, including the "four histories", is proposed as the practical route. In the third, He argues that religion is never a private matter for a Marxist party, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin and successive Chinese leaders. Party leadership is said to work through political leadership, ideological guidance and guidance of interests, and through the Party's cultural leadership, with ideological work at its core. He concludes that guidance by the core socialist values, adherence to Marxist atheism and atheist education, and strengthened Party leadership are essential to advancing sinicization. In his view, this brings out religion's positive role, respects the laws of religion's survival, and addresses prominent problems in the religious field. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Party-affiliated scholar of atheism frames religious policy in the Xi Jinping era.

Ideological and political education oriented to individual needs in the new era: a multidimensional reflection 新时代思想政治教育面向个体需要的多维审思 Zhao Benyan Wang Jianxin Zhao Benyan and Wang Jianxin take up a question in ideological and political education: what does it mean for this work to be oriented to individual needs (面向个体需要) in the new era, and why and how should it be? They argue that such an orientation applies Marxist theories of the human being to the field. In their account it raises educational effectiveness and gives concrete form to the people-centred principle of ideological and political work. The article has three parts. The first sets out the meaning of the orientation along three dimensions: goal, content and method. The second analyses three reasons for it, concerning how moral character forms, the problems of individualisation, and high-quality development. The third proposes three practical directions: matching supply and demand, optimising the structure of needs, and putting the people first. The authors note that individual needs are increasingly complex and varied, while the desire for free personal development and spiritual enjoyment has moved up the order of needs. The core argument starts from Marx's aim of the free and all-round development of every individual. The authors hold that ideological and political education therefore has to proceed from the "real individual" and from that person's needs, above all spiritual ones such as belief, morality and cognition. It must both satisfy these needs and guide them towards social needs, so that the "natural person" becomes a "socialised person". They add that individuals accept educational content selectively, according to their needs and motives. They also hold that individualisation sharpens the conflict between diverse personal values and a unified dominant value orientation, and that high-quality development calls for "precise drip irrigation" in place of "flood irrigation". In practice, the authors call for equal, interactive relations between educators and students. They propose using big data, algorithms and artificial intelligence to identify needs, and building a varied supply of content that fits each stage of an individual's development. Education should focus on the people's need for a better life, enrich needs and screen out false, radical or improper ones. It should also advance common prosperity in spiritual life under the principle of "leaving no one behind" and encourage individual striving within Chinese modernization. Read the original if you study the theory of ideological and political education in China, especially how individual needs, precision and data-driven methods are being brought into it.

Cybernetic proletarianisation Spiralling devaluation and conflict in digitalised production 控制论无产阶级化 Simon Schaupp This text is a Chinese translation, abridged, of an article by Simon Schaupp first published in Capital & Class (2022). Schaupp asks how digitalisation affects manual labour and argues that, rather than mainly polarising jobs, it produces a spiral of devaluation that he calls "cybernetic proletarianisation". Algorithmic control, he claims, both expels living labour from production and reintegrates it in devalued form. Workers are caught in digital feedback loops, and part of their work is to make themselves superfluous. The article combines Marxist class analysis with empirical labour-process research in Germany, a leading economy in production digitalisation. It draws on participant observation from 2017 to 2019 in four anonymised firms: a mechanical engineering company, a food-delivery platform, a chemicals manufacturer and an online retailer. The author took assembly work and bike-courier work and attended works-council meetings. The study rests on 55 interviews with workers, engineers and managers. After a theoretical reconstruction of proletarianisation, drawing on Marx's Theories of Surplus Value and on Nick Dyer-Witheford's "cybernetic vortex", the empirical sections cover expulsion, reintegration and conflict. Schaupp identifies three mechanisms of expulsion. First is "deskilling flexibilisation": workers encode their know-how into digital systems, which then equip low-skilled replacements and allow flexible scheduling. Second is cybernetic intensification: real-time measurement and feedback induce workers to "self-adjust" and eliminate idle time. Third is data-based automation: data gathered from workers is used to automate their tasks, such as robotic picking or driverless vehicles. Expulsion does not produce technological unemployment. It is followed by reintegration into labour-intensive, low-paid, precarious work, often by migrants, which starts the next cycle. Against views that algorithmic management atomises workers, Schaupp describes "technopolitics from below": technological disobedience, oppositional worker cultures and organised action. He reports informal resistance, strikes and platform-courier protests, and finds that union strength was weaker where cybernetic proletarianisation was more advanced. Schaupp concludes that cybernetic proletarianisation is a dynamic process rather than a fixed social group. It is defined by computer-issued instructions, digital performance evaluation, use of collected data to replace labour, and precarious pay, and it is shaped by shared subjective experiences of lost autonomy and dignity. The four stages form a spiral, and the four firms are placed at different turns of it. Whether the process becomes a general trend, he says, depends on workers' own technopolitical action, which has in some cases halted or reversed devaluation. He notes that the qualitative design cannot measure its full extent. Read the original if you study digital labour, algorithmic management or the Marxist theory of proletarianisation and want an empirically grounded German case study.

A survey of research on "Political Marxism" abroad 国外“政治马克思主义”研究述要 Feng Wangzhou This literature review surveys scholarship, in China and abroad, on "Political Marxism", a current of Marxism outside China that emerged in the 1970s and is influential among Anglo-American left scholars. Feng identifies Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood as its founders and presents their "political-historical materialism" as an attempt to reject non-historical readings of Marxism while keeping historical materialism as the best tool for criticising capitalism. The article reports that research on the school has entered a period of steady growth. The review is organised in nine thematic sections: the meaning and formation of the school; the origins of capitalism and theories of social development; the theory of new imperialism; historical materialism; the nation-state; capitalist crisis and class struggle; globalisation and modernity; the critique of post-Marxism and postmodernism; and the critique of capitalist ideology. Feng draws on commentators such as David McNally and Vivek Chibber, and on Chinese scholars' work on Brenner, Wood and Benno Teschke. Several arguments recur in the work Feng summarises. On origins, Brenner and Wood are said to trace capitalism to a shift in social property relations in English agriculture, rejecting commercialisation and demographic models, though critics are reported to find the approach overly focused on class struggle. On imperialism, Wood is described as locating the novelty of the new imperialism in domination by economic means and as differing from David Harvey over the relation between the logic of capital and the logic of territory. On method, Wood is credited with reading historical materialism as a critique of capitalism's historical specificity rather than as a set of universal laws, and with defending class and totality against postmodernism. Feng also notes critical assessments: Brenner's crisis theory is said to neglect the preconditions of competition, and Wood's anti-postmodern critique is called narrow in places. Feng concludes through the surveyed literature that Political Marxism has not departed from Marxism but has clarified questions about the origin, nature and forms of capitalism and strengthened the historical-materialist method, thereby showing Marxism's contemporary value. The survey also shows a shared view that capitalist ideologies such as progress, democracy and liberalism will be dissolved by proletarian revolutionary movements. Read the original if you want a structured map of Chinese and international scholarship on Brenner, Wood and Teschke, with references to the key debates.

Innovative mechanisms for universities to prevent and defuse the risk of online religious infiltration 高校防范和化解网络宗教渗透风险的创新机制研究 Zhang Aihui Gao Jianjun Zhang Aihui and Gao Jianjun take up the question of how Chinese universities can more effectively guard against what they call online religious infiltration by hostile Western forces. They argue that the internet has made online religion a new form of religious life and that infiltration through it threatens ideological security on campus. Their answer is a five-part "innovative mechanism" combining Marxist religion education, reformed ideological and political education, campus culture, legal regulation and a dedicated anti-infiltration team. The article first sets out why the task matters: in the authors' account it answers Western ideological "containment", supports students' healthy development, and raises the effectiveness of ideological and political education. It then reports a questionnaire survey of 1,080 valid responses at three universities in northern Jiangsu, plus 20 case interviews, to describe how online religion reaches students. A section on causes precedes the proposed mechanisms. The survey finds that 44.71% of students learn about religion mainly through online platforms, that most are curious but ambivalent about religion, and that 85.32% see online religious propagation as having both benefits and drawbacks. Students are fairly cautious about online information but, the authors say, underestimate the danger of deliberate infiltration. The authors attribute infiltration to the reach of converged media, students' weak critical judgement, shortcomings in ideological and political education (no student named a politics teacher as a first source of help, and few universities teach Marxist views of religion as a dedicated subject), and some universities' limited awareness of the risk. The proposed remedies include strengthening Marxist religion education and scientific atheism, teaching the "four histories", integrating ideological content into all courses, using local and red culture, student societies against cults, campus network rules based on the 2018 Regulations on Religious Affairs and the 2021 measures on internet religious information services, and a team ranging from teachers and counsellors to parents, IT staff and student Party members. The authors conclude that universities should combine education, humane care for students, cultural influence, legal supervision and coordinated staffing to build a long-term defence, and they call for regular training for the anti-infiltration team. The text relies on Xi Jinping's statements at the 2015 and 2016 work conferences to frame the policy. Read the original if you want survey data on Chinese students' attitudes to online religion, or an example of how Party-aligned scholarship frames religion, ideological security and university governance.

The formation and collapse of the Japanese Communist Party's united front in the twenty-first century 21世纪日本共产党统一战线的建立与破裂 Li Ming Li Ming asks why the Japanese Communist Party (JCP) managed to build a united front with other opposition parties in the early twenty-first century and why that front collapsed after two national election defeats. The article starts from the JCP's stated strategy of seeking a democratic coalition government through elections rather than one-party rule. Li argues that the collapse had both external and internal causes, with the external ones, above all the allies' withdrawal, decisive. The article first traces the process in three stages. It covers the JCP's policy adjustments from 2002 to 2015, the formal 'opposition-party joint struggle' of 2016–2021, and the breakdown after the 2021 lower-house and 2022 upper-house elections. It then analyses external factors (the form, purpose and environment of cooperation) and internal factors, before a short conclusion on future prospects. Li draws on JCP statements, election results and party-strength statistics. On external causes, Li describes the opposition-party joint struggle as a 'lower' form of united front. In this account it rests on agreements signed between party leaders, with no organisational structure and little backing from either side's voters, so a change of leader can void it. Partners such as the Constitutional Democratic Party sought votes and seats rather than shared long-term goals, and they differed from the JCP on core issues like the US alliance. Li adds that anti-communist propaganda by the authorities left the public wary of the JCP in government, and that the trade union federation Rengo discouraged cooperation. On internal causes, Li points to the JCP's declining membership and Akahata readership, and to weakening traditional mass organisations, which have shrunk. Li also cites the 2023 expulsions of members who called for an elected party leader, which opponents used to attack democratic centralism. Li concludes that the united front remains the JCP's strategic goal, as Shii Kazuo affirmed at the party's centenary. The party's eighth plenum of the 28th Central Committee (June 2023) adopted a 'go it alone' approach for the next general election. Li notes that centre-left parties may waver before elections, and urges the JCP to take the initiative whether or not cooperation is rebuilt. It should recover some revolutionary character and principle, set out clearer policies, extend inner-party democracy and consolidate the mass line. Read the original if you study the Japanese left, communist parties in parliamentary systems, or how Chinese scholars assess united-front strategy abroad.

Word–image intertextuality: the two-element advance of narrative in ideological and political education 语图互文：思想政治教育叙事的二元进阶 Li Weijun Li Weijun asks how storytelling in ideological and political education can be made more effective by combining its two basic media, written or spoken language and images. The article starts from Xi Jinping's call to tell good stories, especially stories of the new era. It argues that the two media are different in kind but complementary, and that joining them produces "intertextuality" (huwen) with a "1+1>2" effect. Li calls this the "two-element advance" of narrative in ideological and political education. The article has three parts. The first sets out a theory of word–image intertextuality built on three components: shared rules, metaphor and context. The second examines the logic of each medium, treating language as temporal and images as spatial. The third turns to practical strategies drawn from cognitive psychology. Li draws on Engels, Marx, Roland Barthes, Lessing, Rudolf Arnheim and Ernst Cassirer, and on the Chinese tradition of "images on the left, text on the right". The 2022 controversy over illustrations in a people's education textbook serves as the main case. Li's central claim is that language and images each have to cross into the other's territory. Language unfolds in time, so listeners must turn it into spatial mental pictures. A still image is a frozen moment, so it has to be put back into a temporal sequence to recover its context. Li links the media to two cognitive mechanisms. Images attract attention quickly and engage a "heuristic" mechanism that works through feeling and intuition. Language engages a "systematic" mechanism that works through rational analysis. The article proposes a sequence: an image first evokes perceptual memory, then concise language interprets and distils its meaning. Information then moves from short-term to long-term memory and forms a persuasive "rhetorical image". Li also stresses metaphor, citing Xi Jinping's figures such as "calcium for the spirit" and "the first button", and the cultural and technological context of Chinese modernization, the whole-media environment, digitalization and the metaverse. Li concludes that combining word and image gives ideological and political education a stronger persuasive and memory-forming power than either medium alone. Educators are urged to use images, including VR, AR and metaverse tools, to convey truth, immersive setting and emotion, and then to use language to explain and consolidate their meaning. Read the original if you work on ideological and political education, narrative or visual rhetoric and want a detailed theoretical framework for teaching practice.

Contemporary Western left-wing scholars' critique of green capitalism 当代西方左翼学者对绿色资本主义的批判研究 Yao Xiaohong This review surveys how Western left-wing scholars have responded to green capitalism, the discourse of "green economy", "green growth" and "green new deal" that Western states and monopoly capital promoted after the 2008 financial crisis. Yao asks whether green capitalism can reshape the human–nature relationship, whether continued capital accumulation is compatible with the environment, and what social alternative should replace it. The author reports that these scholars broadly reject green capitalism, and then assesses the field as useful but flawed. The article has three main parts. The first sets out the left's exposure of green capitalism as false. The second traces the degrowth debate, from Malthus, the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth, Georgescu-Roegen, Daly and Andre Gorz to Giorgos Kallis and Jason Hickel, and the objections of David Schwartzman, Eleanor Finley, Ulrich Brand, John Bellamy Foster and Stefania Barca. The third examines proposals for a social-ecological transformation. A brief conclusion evaluates the whole body of work. Yao reports three lines of critique of green capitalism. It serves capital's drive for endless accumulation (Kallis, Wanner, Naomi Klein, Hickel). Eco-Marxists such as Foster, Pepper and Burkett argue that it rests on a mode of production that separates producers from the means of production, producing a "metabolic rift". It also deepens ecological injustice between rich and poor and between core and periphery. On degrowth, Yao shows critics accusing it of dualism and idealism, of neglecting relations of production and class, and of denying that socialism needs growth. Schwartzman and Brand reply that socialist growth serves human need rather than profit. On transformation, the author notes a more measured view of green capitalism, a stronger role for the state, and attention to political alliances with ecological movements in the Global South. In the conclusion, Yao credits this scholarship with helping to understand changes in contemporary capitalism and with extending Marxism's relevance. The author nonetheless finds it scientifically weak, because some scholars abandon historical materialism or apply it inconsistently. The author also finds it theoretically fragmented, and sometimes utopian or pessimistic, so that it risks serving Western states. Yao concludes that only adherence to Marxist standpoint and method, together with the Four-sphere Confidence in socialist ecological civilization with Chinese characteristics, can achieve harmony between humanity and nature. Read the original if you want a map of Western eco-Marxist and degrowth debates on green capitalism, with names and positions, as seen from a Chinese Marxist perspective.

The dance of spatial dialectics: the reception, dispute and dialectics of Lefebvre's theory of the production of space in the English-speaking world 空间辩证法的舞蹈：列斐伏尔空间的生产理论在英语世界的传播、争辩与辩证 Liu Huaiyu Half a century after Henri Lefebvre published The Production of Space (1974), Liu Huaiyu asks how its central idea, the 'triple' or three-dimensional spatial dialectic, has been received and contested in the English-speaking world. Liu argues that Anglophone scholarship has often misread the late Lefebvre as a postmodernist or post-Marxist. In Liu's view, the book's real contribution is not a postmodern 'spatial turn' but a critical epistemology of social space and a dialectic of spatial contradiction, which can only be understood by returning to its German dialectical context. The article first traces the book's difficult style (a fugue-like, dictated text) and three waves of Anglophone reading: David Harvey's urban political economy from the 1970s, Edward Soja's postmodern geography from the 1980s, and a broad empirical wave since 2000. It then sets out Lefebvre's several versions of the triad (spatial practice, representations of space, representational spaces; physical, mental and social space; perceived, conceived and lived). Liu next examines the readings of Harvey, Soja, Fredric Jameson, Shields and Stuart Elden, before turning to Christian Schmid's German-language interpretation. Liu's central move is to follow Schmid in separating a three-dimensional epistemology from a three-part ontology. Harvey is read as giving a structural-functionalist reading and as privileging spatial practice. Soja is read as turning the triad into an ontology of 'Thirdspace' alongside historicality and sociality, thereby, Liu says, covertly repeating Hegelian thesis-antithesis-synthesis. Shields's 'other' and Elden's Nietzschean 'overcoming' are likewise said to retain a way of ending contradiction. Jameson's cognitive mapping is credited with escaping postmodern ontology, though Liu finds it over-weights representational space. Liu adds that Schmid may still hide a pluralist eclecticism. Liu concludes that Lefebvre's spatial dialectic is Marx's dialectic of social contradiction expressed in space, a synchronic concentration of historical contradictions, and that the book's weight lies in chapters five and six rather than the introduction. Liu lists five contradictions: use value and exchange value; production and consumption of space; global homogeneity and local fragmentation; centre and periphery; domination and appropriation. Lefebvre, Liu notes, hesitates over the way out, naming only 'differential space', and so returns to the triad. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, spatial theory or Western Marxism and want a Chinese Marxist critique of Harvey, Soja and Jameson.

The evolution of contemporary Western Marxist currents and their core problematic 当代西方马克思主义思潮的嬗变及其核心问题意识 Xia Ying Western Marxism has no precise boundaries, and since the 1970s many thinkers working under its name have weakened their Marxist foundations through political, economic and cultural critique. Xia Ying asks in what sense such work still belongs to the tradition. The article proposes a problematic that runs through the whole century: whether revolution against capitalist society exists and how it is possible, and who or what its subject (subjectivity) is. Xia argues that this criterion shows Western Marxism has not ended. The article proceeds chronologically. It begins with Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci in the 1920s–40s, who were Party leaders and revolutionary participants, and with the Frankfurt School. It then turns to the post-1945 shift to philosophical critique, Marcuse and the 1968 May events, and the later radical left (Badiou, Negri and Hardt, Žižek, Agamben, Rancière). It engages Perry Anderson's verdict that Western Marxism ended in the mid-1970s, and Axel Honneth's account of the Frankfurt School's unity. It closes with a two-stage periodisation around the Bretton Woods collapse of the 1970s. Xia contends that early thinkers took revolution's legitimacy for granted and treated the proletariat as a given, a priori subject, as in Lukács. After the 1970s financialisation and dispersed ownership, later thinkers treat the subject as generated within each situation, as in Badiou's 'event subject' and the 'multitude'. The author argues that the critique of political economy gradually left critical theory: Pollock's state capitalism led to pessimism, Horkheimer shifted towards philosophy and culture, and Habermas and Honneth moved to communication and recognition. Xia therefore describes Western Marxism as turning from changing the world to interpreting it, from an ontological analysis of capital's logic to an epistemological one. In the second stage, labour and capital are said to be in 'complicity', and 'revolution' becomes 'innovation'. Xia concludes that the shared problematic is the critique of the capital logic permeating social life. Its heirs, however, have split into two paths: normative ethics and political philosophy (Honneth), and radical-left thought-experiments (Agamben, Negri and Hardt). Xia judges both to be accommodations with capital, so that Western Marxism has moved from critical theory to uncritical theory. Even so, the author holds that studying it reveals capitalism's trajectory and possible lines of critique, and that it helps in building China's autonomous Marxist discourse system. Read the original if you want a periodised, critical account of Western Marxism's post-1970s thinkers and an argument for why they still count as Marxists.

Beyond the green illusion of capitalism 超越资本主义的绿色幻象 Tian Anqi Jiao Pei Can the "green economy" promoted by late capitalism resolve the twin crises of economy and ecology? Tian Anqi and Jiao Pei answer in the negative. They argue that "green capitalism", which seeks a green turn without changing the capitalist system, builds only a "green illusion". Overcoming it, they contend, requires moving beyond capital's logic through institutional and value change, drawing on China's experience of building ecological civilization. The article has three parts. The first traces the background of the Western "green turn", from Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, the Club of Rome's Limits to Growth and the 1972 Stockholm conference to later climate policies in Britain, the United States and the EU. It then sets out two pillars of green capitalism: faith in market pricing of nature and faith in technology. The second part examines the harms of this illusion, and the third presents the proposed alternative. The authors argue that market solutions such as carbon trading and payment for ecosystem services turn nature into a commodity and an appendage of capital, deepening the subject–object split and encouraging greenwashing. They hold that technological optimism ignores the Jevons paradox and domestic political divisions, citing Foster, Richard Smith, David Pepper and Kohei Saito. They further charge that Western states externalise environmental costs through polluting industries moved to the Global South, evade "common but differentiated responsibilities", and wage wars for resources, citing Middle East oil, Agent Orange in Vietnam and depleted-uranium munitions. They describe these practices as ecological imperialism and ecological colonialism. The authors conclude that ecological crisis cannot be solved under private ownership of the means of production, and that socialist public ownership is the institutional guarantee of ecological justice. They add the ideal of harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature, which they say transcends both anthropocentrism and ecocentrism. As practical evidence they cite China's ecological civilization under Xi Jinping's thought, the carbon peak and carbon neutrality goals, the green Belt and Road Initiative, South–South cooperation, and China's role in COP15. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of green capitalism that draws on eco-Marxist literature and ends with an endorsement of China's ecological path.

Always maintain a high degree of political sensitivity 始终保持高度的政治敏锐性 Zhang Tingguang This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in April 2024, takes up Xi Jinping's call for Party officials to "always maintain a high degree of political sensitivity" and to be prepared for danger in times of peace. Zhang presents political sensitivity as the combined expression of political standing and political insight, and as a precondition for leading cadres' political judgement, political understanding and political execution. Zhang notes that Xi made the point at a special democratic life meeting of the Political Bureau held during the thematic education campaign on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Against a complex international and domestic situation, the article sets out three requirements: mastering Marxism, putting Party political building first, and guarding against risks. First, Zhang argues that the depth of one's grasp of Marxist theory determines the degree of political sensitivity. Citing Mao Zedong's image of Marxism as a telescope and microscope, the author calls for thorough study of Xi Jinping Thought. Second, Zhang holds that political advancement distinguishes a Marxist party, so cadres must analyse problems politically, understand the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, and carry out the Two Upholds. Third, the article urges bottom-line thinking and a sense of hardship, with particular vigilance towards political risks, sensitive factors and erroneous ideological trends. Zhang concludes that these practices will keep all undertakings on the correct political course and improve cadres' ability to grasp direction, the overall situation and the general trend. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Party-press commentary frames political sensitivity as a cadre competence.

Cultivating a new generation for the new cultural mission 培养更好担负起新的文化使命的时代新人 He Xiuchao This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 10 April 2024, asks how universities can train students to take up the new cultural mission set out in Xi Jinping's thought on culture. That mission is to keep promoting cultural prosperity, build a strong cultural nation and build a modern Chinese civilization. He Xiuchao argues that universities should do so through three tasks: upholding cultural self-reliance, strengthening cultural confidence and achieving cultural self-strengthening. The article takes each of the three tasks in turn, quoting Xi Jinping on each, and then sets out what the author thinks universities, ideological and political theory courses and teachers should do. It is addressed to higher-education leaders and teachers, and the author writes as a university Party secretary. On cultural self-reliance, He holds that China's cultural subjectivity was built by the Party's combination of Marxism with the Chinese context and with fine traditional Chinese culture. In He's account, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is its strongest expression. On cultural confidence, He presents the Second Integration as evidence of the Party's confidence, and calls on universities to improve cultural curricula and teaching quality. He also wants ideological and political courses to teach Party theory and the histories of the Party, the People's Republic and socialism, so as to counter the pull of a more plural cultural environment. On cultural self-strengthening, He links culture to Chinese modernization and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He concludes that universities should carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education, keep Marxism as the guiding ideology and run Xi's cultural thought through the whole process of educating students. Teachers are urged to embody the spirit of educators and to bring Marxist views of the world, of life and of values into their teaching. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-state leaders frame university education around the new cultural mission.

The expansionist and exclusionary nature of the American road to modernization 美国现代化道路的扩张性、排他性 Liang Haoguang Liang Haoguang asks how the United States modernized and how that path underpins its present strategy of competing with China. The article argues that American modernization rests on expansion and exclusion: each sphere of development has been turned into an instrument of hegemony.
