Liang contends that Washington's policy towards China since the 18th Party Congress (2012) follows from this logic, and that China needs a differentiated response in each sphere. The article first sets out the multiple senses of modernization: a world phenomenon, a civilizational shift and a development goal. It then reviews eight American "roads": agriculture and grain monopoly, industrialization and "re-industrialization", science and technology, culture, finance, military power, and global governance. For each, Liang pairs a historical account with the corresponding US policy towards China, supported by figures on trade, innovation, dollar share, voting rights and military bases. A second part proposes countermeasures in economics, technology, finance, security and governance, and a short conclusion returns to Chinese modernization. Liang's central claim is that the US maintains its position through linked instruments. These include food-trade control, export controls and "democratic technology alliances", cultural and ideological infiltration, dollar dominance (supported by petrodollars, IMF veto power and currency swaps), a global base network, and alliance groupings such as the Quad. Liang says this makes the US the largest obstacle to reform of global governance. Liang adds that copying the American model has led most countries into development traps, and cites Daniel Bell and Cyril Black as rejecting the equation of modernization with Westernization. Liang advises China to work "within the system" through incremental reform rather than challenge it from outside, and to avoid "extreme competition" and "hybrid confrontation". The proposals include building a modern industrial system and new quality productive forces, self-reliance in technology combined with greater openness, non-dollar payment systems and a multipolar currency order, a stronger Asia-Pacific position, and cooperation with Belt and Road and Global South countries. The article concludes that Chinese modernization offers developing countries a new paradigm. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Chinese Academy of Sciences scholar frames US–China rivalry as a contest between modernization paths, with data and policy recommendations.

Guiding research on a new theory of productive forces with Xi Jinping's economic thought 用习近平经济思想指导新的生产力理论研究 Hong Yinxing Writing in the People's Daily in April 2024, Hong Yinxing takes up the call by Xi Jinping that high-quality development needs a new theory of productive forces. Hong argues that the concept of new quality productive forces continues and renews Marxist productive-forces theory, and that research on it should be guided by Xi Jinping's economic thought. The short commentary is a programme for research rather than an empirical study. Hong selects three theoretical questions among those needing study. The first is the leap in the elements of the productive forces and in their optimal combination. The second is the deep integration of scientific and technological innovation with industrial innovation. The third is the new type of relations of production suited to the new productive forces. Each section starts from Marx or Xi's formulations and ends with a list of research tasks. On the first question, Hong follows Marx's three elements (labourers, means of labour, objects of labour) and argues that the aim is a qualitative leap, not just more input. For labour, this means innovative and strategic talent as the first resource and a workforce suited to the new technological revolution. For means of labour, it means digital platforms and intelligent tools. For objects of labour, it means a new energy revolution and green development. On the second, Hong cites Marx on science becoming a direct productive force once applied to production. Hong holds that scientific and industrial revolutions now occur almost simultaneously, so research should cover the new-type whole-nation system, the transformation of traditional industries, and the digital economy. On the third, Hong holds that relations of production must fit the productive forces and should take the form of institutions that reward innovation. Hong proposes four research areas for the new relations of production. They are collaborative innovation platforms linking industry, universities and research institutes; the cultivation of technology entrepreneurs and the entrepreneurial spirit; innovation highlands built on science and industrial parks; and institutions for future industries. The last covers the roles of market and government and an error-tolerance mechanism for innovation. Hong's overall aim is theoretical support for cultivating new quality productive forces and for high-quality development. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned outline of the research agenda that Chinese economists were setting for new quality productive forces in spring 2024.

The important theoretical status of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture: an understanding based on the unity of the historical and the logical 习近平文化思想的重要理论地位：基于历史与逻辑相统一的认识 Fang Shinan Fang Shinan asks what place Xi Jinping Thought on Culture occupies in theory, and answers by applying the method of the unity of the historical and the logical, which Marx and Engels developed by sublating Hegel's idealist version. The article contends that this thought is the cultural chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Fang's account it is an open, rigorous and developing body of theory that guides socialist cultural construction as a worldview and methodology. The article is organised around three angles. It first looks at the thought's value and status through the interaction of economic base and superstructure, and through its historical context. It then reads the thought as a major result of the Two Integrations, and finally as the cultural chapter and theoretical guide of Chinese modernization. Throughout, Fang ties the analysis to Party documents, to speeches by Xi Jinping and to classical passages from Marx and Engels. Fang's first main move is to argue that scientific theories arise from the needs of their era and from existing intellectual material. On this reading, Xi Jinping Thought on Culture is a theoretical summary of the Party's experience of cultural work since its founding, and of work since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Second, Fang presents the thought as an exemplar of the Two Integrations. It combines Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, and each integration serves as the other's foundation or precondition. Third, Fang describes it as providing the cultural form of Chinese modernization. The article links cultural prosperity to national rejuvenation and to coordinated material and spiritual civilisation, and it treats cultural justice and cultural rights as conditions for the all-round development of the individual. Fang concludes that the thought makes an original contribution to Marxist cultural theory and opens a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article lists the "seven focuses" Xi has set for propaganda, ideological and cultural work, including Party leadership, socialist ideology, core socialist values, media influence, continuing the Chinese cultural lineage, cultural undertakings and industries, and international communication. In Fang's view these set out a cultural form for Chinese modernization and a modern Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a close example of how Chinese scholars use the historical-logical method to establish the theoretical standing of Xi Jinping Thought on Culture.

An assessment of the new wave of socialist thought in the United States 美国新一轮社会主义思潮评析 Gao Jianming Gao Jianming asks what Bernie Sanders's 2016 and 2020 campaigns have produced in American socialist thought, and what that means for socialism's prospects in the United States. The article argues that since 2016 four programmes have emerged: liberal socialism, twenty-first-century socialism, class-struggle social democracy and new anarchism. In Gao's account they differ in vision and method but share enough ground to form a single new wave, whose future depends on whether the currents stress their differences or their commonalities. The article presents each current through its leading figures. Liberal socialism is traced to James Livingston, Ira Katznelson and Michael Walzer. Twenty-first-century socialism is associated with Fred Block, Nancy Fraser and Erik Olin Wright, building on Heinz Dieterich's Latin American usage. Class-struggle social democracy is drawn from the Jacobin circle (Bhaskar Sunkara, Vivek Chibber), and new anarchism from David Graeber. A fifth section compares the currents, and a final section assesses prospects. Gao identifies two shared features: rejection of revolutionary socialism and absorption of left populism. On the first, the currents disavow violent revolution and comprehensive planning and keep markets, partly because support comes mainly from young people. On the second, the currents endorse direct or participatory democracy and integrate class struggle with new social movements, drawing on Chantal Mouffe's populist strategy; even Sunkara and Chibber use an expanded notion of the working class that blurs into "the people". The differences lie in the vision of socialism, from social-democratic liberal socialism to Sunkara's call for nationalising banks and private firms and Graeber's opposition to the state. They also lie in method: electoral politics, class struggle or Graeber's "prefigurative politics". Gao concludes that the prospects for American socialism are unclear. Sectarian disputes would weaken the left, and Gao cites the split and membership decline of the Democratic Socialists of America after its 2021 peak. If the currents instead build on their shared rejection of revolution and their populism, they could reach a minimal consensus around liberal socialism, treated as an intermediate stage. Gao holds that this would widen its social base and let Wright's strategy of eroding capitalism be carried out. Read the original if you want a detailed survey of post-2016 American socialist currents and their internal disagreements, as seen by a Chinese Marxist scholar.

China and Vietnam join hands to contribute to the development of contemporary world socialism 中越携手为当代世界社会主义的发展作出贡献​ Vu Van Phuc This is a Chinese translation of a speech by a senior Vietnamese Communist Party theorist, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum. The speaker argues that China and Vietnam, guided by Marxism-Leninism that each adapts to national conditions, share similar socialist features. In the speaker's account, both countries therefore contribute to the development of contemporary world socialism. The speech compares the two parties' guiding ideologies and economic systems. It then surveys China's modernization record and sets out, in eight points, the theoretical views the Vietnamese party has formed after nearly 40 years of renovation (Doi Moi). Wu notes that China's system rests on public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to work, and a socialist market economy. Vietnam is said to be practising a socialist-oriented market economy during its transition to socialism. Wu holds that despite the different names, both are new types of market economy under Communist Party leadership. The eight Vietnamese points include Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought as the party's foundation, the socialist direction and the Party's ruling position, a socialist rule-of-law state, a distinctive national culture, international integration, the ruling-party theory, and great national unity as the driving force. Wu concludes that the achievements of China's reform and opening up and Vietnam's renovation embody the persistence of Marxism-Leninism in line with national realities. The speech presents them as a joint contribution to world socialism and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an official Vietnamese Party view of China–Vietnam ideological affinity and a concise list of the Vietnamese party's theoretical summary of renovation.

Examining the global digital divide in the 21st century and China's solution 21世纪全球数字鸿沟审视与中国方案 Chen Wenxu Nie Jiaqi Chen and Nie ask why a gap in digital capacity has opened between developed and developing countries, and how it might be closed. Drawing on Marxist political economy, they argue that the digital divide, understood mainly as the "third divide" (unequal outcomes from using digital technology), is a product of digital capitalism, neoliberal policy and the digital hegemony of the United States and other Western states. They present the "Digital Silk Road" as China's solution, one that would help build a community with a shared future for mankind in the digital age. The article has three parts. The first sets out the conditions that produced the divide. The second classifies it into four kinds (access, capability, output and talent), explains its logic of generation, and diagnoses obstacles to governing it. The third explains the content and scope of the Digital Silk Road and the governance subjects and mechanisms needed to build it. The authors cite figures on 2021 internet penetration, 4G coverage and broadband, and examples such as the Japan–US semiconductor disputes, Huawei sanctions and control of root servers. The authors argue that digital capitalism leaves capitalism's exploitative essence unchanged. In their account, developed countries export digital capital, monopolise technology and data, and appropriate "digital surplus value" from paid and unpaid digital labour. They say these countries restrict latecomers on grounds of "national security" once those latecomers approach core standards. Governance fails, the authors say, for lack of a cooperative environment, effective actors and workable security and cooperation mechanisms. The Digital Silk Road, which they describe as combining China's digital economy with the Belt and Road Initiative, is presented as non-zero-sum cooperation. It rests on joint consultation, respect for digital sovereignty and the non-competitive character of digital networks. The authors call on China to strengthen its digital technology and cyber security, and to build digital government, society and individuals. They also call for aligning top-level design with partner countries, cooperating across institutional, technical, material and commercial dimensions, and admitting willing developed countries. They add that the divide does not show a flaw in digital technology itself: under capitalism it serves a few, under socialism it could serve the majority. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account that links digital-divide theory to digital hegemony and the Belt and Road Initiative.

Data-driven innovation in ideological and political education: trends, predicaments and supporting mechanisms 数据驱动思想政治教育创新发展的态势、困境及助推机制 Yan Jie Zhang Xiao Yan Jie and Zhang Xiao ask how big-data technology can be used to renew ideological and political education, and what risks must be managed along the way. They argue that data-driven innovation expresses an internal unity of value rationality and instrumental rationality. In their view, the field should seize the opportunity, use big data reasonably, head off technological crises, and build an education mechanism guided by "technology for good", so as to improve educational results. The article has three parts. The first describes three current trends: faster open sharing of data, continuing technological empowerment, and deepening cross-boundary integration. The second identifies three practical predicaments: data barriers, data risks and data anxiety. The third proposes three matching mechanisms, for data sharing, data security and data motivation. It opens with Xi Jinping's call to combine the traditional strengths of ideological and political work with information technology. On the trends, the authors say that data technology enables precise identification, analysis, supply, evaluation and feedback about students. They add that VR, AR and MR create immersive scenes that turn abstract argument into something perceptible. They also say it shifts methods towards full-sample data and correlation analysis. The predicaments are set out in three groups. Data silos and monopolies obstruct the supply and circulation of educational data and leave room for social trends to exploit platforms. Leakage, misuse and theft threaten students' privacy. Over-reliance on figures, which neglects quality and causes anxiety, and over-rejection of data both undermine the work. The proposed remedies run as follows. For sharing, the authors call for trust and identity recognition among educational actors, a defined list of shareable data with graded management, and agreed rules of conduct. For security, they propose data-processing, data-perception and encryption technologies, including node, link and end-to-end encryption. For motivation, they call for precise student profiling, an integrated intelligent data platform built with schools, government, enterprises and technical staff, and varied learning scenarios that move teaching from instrumental to human-centred. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how ideological and political education researchers frame digital technology, its risks and institutional safeguards.

An analysis of Qu Qiubai's scientific atheism 瞿秋白科学无神论思想探析 Xiao Kaiqiang Xiao Kaiqiang examines how Qu Qiubai (1899–1935), an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party, developed a fairly systematic scientific atheism. The article argues that Qu applied dialectical and historical materialism to criticise religious theology and popular superstition, and in doing so advanced the spread of early Marxist atheism in China. Xiao presents this as relevant to research and propaganda on Marxist atheism in the new era. The article has four parts. It first traces the theoretical and practical roots of Qu's thought, from his early exposure to Daoism, Buddhism and Tolstoy's ethics of love, to his turn to Marxism after 1920, including his years as a journalist in Soviet Russia. It then sets out the content of his atheism under four headings. A third part assesses his historical contribution, and a short conclusion follows. Xiao argues that Qu's thought arose from two sources: a deliberate choice of Marxist atheism, and the need to fight imperialism and feudalism in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, where missionaries and the doctrine of the divine right of kings were used to dull resistance. On content, Qu held that religion is a product of social labour and changes with social development. He judged its role dialectically, as once useful in primitive society but later a tool of class rule that confined thought and obstructed science. He treated religious theism and idealism as kin, differing in form but not in essence. To free the masses from religion, Qu proposed advancing science, popular education and a cultural revolution against superstition. Xiao concludes that Qu was a pioneer of Marxist atheism in China. He cites Qu's translations of works such as Gorev's on materialist philosophy, which Mao Zedong praised in 1943, and his drafting of a 1923 programme calling for the separation of education from religion. Xiao also credits Qu's practical proposals for propaganda and for handling religious questions. In Xiao's view, theistic ideas now spread in more hidden ways, which gives Qu's work contemporary significance. Read the original if you want a detailed account of early Chinese Communist views on religion and superstition, drawn largely from Qu's own writings.

Restless hegemony: the US far-right political movement and its impact 躁动的霸权：美国极右翼政治运动及其影响 Zhao Mínghào Zhao Minghao examines the rise of the far-right political movement in the United States and asks what it means for American politics, for the wider world and for China. The article argues that, amid social division, ethnic antagonism and political polarisation, far-right ideas have moved towards the mainstream. In Zhao's account the movement has become a national security threat, is linked to far-right forces in Europe and elsewhere, and has a strongly anti-China hawkish tendency that drives US China policy. The article has three parts. It first describes the movement's ideology, membership, characteristic features and likely future threats, citing the Biden administration's own assessments and episodes such as Charlottesville (2017) and the 6 January 2021 Capitol attack. It then explains why the movement is growing, tracing it from the Ku Klux Klan through the Tea Party to the Trump era. Finally it turns to the movement's international networks and its effect on US–China relations. Zhao offers four causes of growth: widening inequality and economic distress among lower-middle-class whites; ethnic tension and white 'survival anxiety' over projected demographic change; social media and 'tribalism', which spread conspiracy theories; and defects in the electoral system and polarised parties, aggravated by Trump's tolerance of groups such as the Proud Boys. Zhao says the movement links with European populists, notably through Steve Bannon's foundation 'The Movement', on shared anti-elite, nationalist and anti-immigrant positions. On China, the author contends that far-right propaganda shapes Republican voters' hostile views, that politicians then gain by taking a tough line, and that this vicious circle was worsened by 'China virus' rhetoric during the pandemic. Zhao concludes that the movement's influence deserves close attention and could reach a new high if Trump wins the 2024 election. Zhao warns that US political turmoil will spill over into relations with China, and calls on China to guard against it and to respond properly to the growing 'restlessness' of American hegemony. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly view of how American domestic extremism is linked to US foreign policy and to Sino-American relations.

Domestic research on Lenin's view of religion since reform and opening up: a review and outlook 改革开放以来国内列宁宗教观研究：综述与展望 Zhang Wanjie Gao Yuzheng This article, published in Science and Atheism in 2024, reviews how Chinese scholars have studied Lenin's view of religion since reform and opening up. The authors say the topic matters because religious work occupies an important place in Chinese modernization, and Lenin's outlook is presented as a living application of the Marxist view of religion in Russia. They conclude that the field has produced solid results but is now thin, repetitive and in need of renewal. The review is organised around four clusters of work: the theoretical sources of Lenin's view; its periodisation and the grounds for it; its content and distinctive features; and assessments of its theoretical significance and present-day value. A fifth section evaluates the field as a whole and sets out five directions for future study. On sources, Zhang and Gao report broad agreement that Marx and Engels were the most direct influence, with additional influences from Plekhanov and Dietzgen, Russian revolutionary democrats such as Herzen and Chernyshevsky, and the French materialists. On periodisation, most scholars treat the October Revolution of 1917 as the dividing line between a stage of theory and a stage of practice. Others propose three-stage schemes with different dates, such as those of Liu Yaqiong, Li Jie and Ma Yingjie, Guo Ruike and Li Danyang. On assessment, the review distinguishes studies of single components, such as religious freedom or atheist propaganda, from wholly affirmative evaluations and from dialectical ones. Chen Rongfu, Li Jie and Ma Yingjie note historical and regional limits, and Lü Daji later concluded that parts of Lenin's approach leaned 'Left'. The authors identify five gaps. These are the weak study of contemporary relevance, which they say has cooled in recent years; the reliance on three main texts; the lack of an agreed periodisation standard; the scarcity of systematic monographs; and the absence of detailed comparison with later Soviet leaders and with practice in China and other socialist states. They call for Lenin's view to be studied further so that it can inform Party religious work, the sinicisation of religion and the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese-language scholarship on Lenin and religion, with names and works to follow up.

From the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom: the practical direction of AI development 从必然王国到自由王国：人工智能发展的实践指向 Chen Shuxing Zhang Mingming Chen and Zhang ask how artificial intelligence (AI) should be understood from a Marxist standpoint, given that its capitalist application deepens exploitation and traps workers in what Marx called the realm of necessity. They argue that AI's own contradictions point its development towards the communist realm of freedom, and that the article demonstrates the historical necessity of a leap from the one to the other. The article has three sections. The first describes how AI operates within the realm of necessity under capitalism. The second presents AI as a historical opportunity for escaping that realm. The third sets out the real possibility that AI carries human society into the realm of freedom. The authors draw mainly on Capital and the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse), together with contemporary commentators such as Yuval Noah Harari. In the first section, the authors argue that capitalist ownership turns AI into a tool for extracting surplus value. In their account it displaces both manual and mental labour, creates a 'useless class' of surplus population, concentrates wealth in the hands of owners of intelligent machines, and enables intensive surveillance of workers. In the second section they draw on Marx's Grundrisse passage on the 'explosive' conditions that capital itself creates. As automation reduces living labour towards zero, they contend, value cannot be measured by labour time, exchange value and the money form come under strain, and the basis of capitalist value relations erodes. The same process shortens necessary labour time and expands free time, which they treat as the precondition of free labour. In the third section the authors contend that AI dissolves the opposition between labour and leisure, makes labour a first need of life rather than a means of survival, and allows all-round individual development. Disposable time, not surplus labour time, becomes the measure of wealth, which they link to common prosperity and distribution according to need. They conclude that the social practice of AI increasingly breaks through capital's constraints, which raises the likelihood that society enters the realm of freedom. They add that individuals must keep learning to meet the new demands. Read the original if you want a systematic reading of AI through Marx's Grundrisse theory of labour time, value and free time.

The theoretical connotations, value implications and practical requirements of "not believing in evil, not fearing ghosts, not fearing pressure" “不信邪、不怕鬼、不怕压”的理论内涵、价值意蕴及实践要求 Duan Ganghui Duan Ganghui takes up the formula "not believing in evil, not fearing ghosts, not fearing pressure", which Xi Jinping set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as part of the call to strengthen the Party's fighting spirit. The article argues that the formula is a coherent theoretical system rather than a slogan. In Duan's account it runs through the Party's spiritual lineage, and it equips the Party to face the "two great global and domestic situations" of the current era. The article has three parts. The first traces each of the three phrases through statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Xi. The second sets out the formula's value for great-power rivalry, for Chinese modernization and for the Party's "unique problems". The third lists practical requirements for Party members. In Duan's reading, each phrase corresponds to one quality. "Not believing in evil" means upholding truth and independence and is tied to aspiration (zhiqi). "Not fearing ghosts" means revolutionary momentum plus tactical skill and is tied to backbone (guqi). "Not fearing pressure" means a sense of hardship and bottom-line thinking and is tied to confidence (diqi). Duan treats them as a logical sequence concerning direction, overcoming difficulty and long-term rule, answering questions about the path, national rejuvenation and strengthening the Party. The article says the formula gives the Party initiative in the contest with the United States and the West in ideological, material and strategic terms. It describes the formula as a spiritual force behind Chinese modernization and as the key to the Party's "unique problems", which it says include loss of fighting spirit among some cadres, a "skills panic" and weakening of moral and disciplinary bottom lines. For practice, Duan calls for firm belief built on scientific theory, Party history, current achievements and Chinese civilization. Duan also calls for preserving revolutionary momentum while using the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to fight flexibly, holding firm on principle and adapting on tactics. In addition, Duan urges cadres to build "inner skills" through study and "outer skills" through investigation and research, so as to anticipate internal and external risks. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the Party's current discourse on struggle is organised and justified, with references to Mao, Deng, Jiang and Xi.

Strengthening Party building requires adherence to Marxist atheism 加强党的建设必须坚持马克思主义无神论 Wang Lili Dai Lixing Wang Lili and Dai Lixing argue that Marxist atheism is a requirement of Party building, not a private matter for Party members. Taking as their starting point the National Conference on Religious Work (April 2016), which called Marxist atheism a great principle, they contend that the Communist Party of China, as a Marxist governing party, must apply it to its own construction. The article is organised in three parts. The first links atheism to the Party's vanguard character and purity; the second to the mass base of the Party's rule; the third to the Party's self-reform. The authors draw on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Chen Yun and Xi Jinping, as well as on the December 2023 revised Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China. In the first part, the authors reason that the Party's nature, goals and discipline all require members to be thoroughgoing atheists. They argue that allowing members to hold religious beliefs would let idealism and materialism coexist inside the Party and split it ideologically. They read the cases of corrupt officials who consulted fortune-tellers or worshipped Buddha as evidence of a flawed worldview. In the second part, they set "people-centred" thinking against "god-centred" thinking and say the Party must work wholly for and rely on the people, not on deities. They hold that this is compatible with respecting religious freedom and uniting believers, but that atheist education must continue. They also present religion as a channel for foreign infiltration, which they describe as a political problem. In the third part, they link atheism to a fighting spirit, citing Mao's remarks on "ghosts" and Lenin's "militant materialism", and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform. The authors conclude that atheist propaganda and education must be sustained to protect the Party's ideological security and its leading position. They also hold that it should secure the initiative in the ideological field and win over the masses and the younger generation, while uniting believers around the Party. They present this as part of the effort to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated atheism journal justifies the ban on Party members holding religious belief and ties it to Xi Jinping's discourse on ideals, the people and self-reform.

The "Second Integration" and the emergence of Marxist atheism in modern China A study centred on the critique of "spiritualism" in New Youth, 1918–1919 “第二个结合”与马克思主义无神论在近代中国的出场 Liu Yan Hu Zhaoyang How did Marxist atheism come to appear in modern China? Liu and Hu argue that the answer lies partly in the campaign waged in the journal New Youth in 1918–1919 against "spiritualism" (lingxue), a current that used the name of science to promote belief in ghosts and spirits. In their account, the victory of Chen Duxiu and other New Culture advocates was a self-directed choice of advanced intellectual weapons. It also displayed traits of excellent traditional Chinese culture that, the authors say, fit the people-centred, scientific and open character of Marxist atheism and so prepared the ground for its spread. The article has three main parts. The first describes the spread of Western psychical research into China, where it merged with native soul-beliefs and planchette divination (fuji), and the activities of the Shanghai Spiritualist Society (Shanghai Lingxue Hui). It then narrates three concentrated rounds of criticism in New Youth between May 1918 and April 1919, involving Chen Duxiu, Liu Bannong, Chen Daqi, Liu Shuya, Wang Xinggong and others. The second part treats the campaign as cultural soil for Marxist atheism. The third matches its features to Marxist atheism, and a short conclusion follows. Liu and Hu's central move is to identify three inherited traits in the campaign: patriotism, continuity with the ancient struggle between atheism and theism, and an inclusive attitude to foreign ideas. They read the campaign as anti-imperialist and anti-feudal, since spiritualism was said to serve foreign cultural control and the restorationist forces of the Beiyang government. They also point to the critics' use of Wang Chong's thought alongside Darwinian evolution and material monism. The authors then pair four features with Marxist atheism. The critics' emphasis on human beings over gods matches its people-centred stance, and their monist materialism matches its theoretical basis. Their exposure of pseudo-science matches its scientific character, and their inclusiveness matches its openness. The authors concede that the critics' atheism was still pragmatic, mechanical and short of dialectical materialism. The authors conclude that the campaign was a landmark in Chinese atheist history and, in their phrase, announced Marxist atheism before it arrived. They say the Marxist introductions in New Youth then displaced Enlightenment-style atheism, followed by the 1922 anti-Christian movement and the 1923–1924 debate on science and metaphysics. They add that, today, only adherence to scientific atheism can realise freedom of religious belief and bring out the strengths of Chinese traditional culture, and they call this a task of the new era. Read the original if you study the early history of Chinese atheism, the New Culture Movement, or how Chinese scholars link the Two Integrations to Marxist atheism.

Building a community with a shared future for mankind and opposing the future of hegemonism and power politics 构建人类命运共同体反对霸权主义和强权政治未来 Rossana Duron Cambron This text is a Chinese translation of a speech by Rossana Duron Cambron, co-chair of the Communist Party USA, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum. Cambron argues that science and production already allow humanity to end hunger, homelessness and poor education and healthcare, and that only the capitalist system prevents this. In her view, building a community with a shared future for mankind therefore means confronting the minority that controls resources and power. The speech moves from a diagnosis of US hegemony to the domestic situation in the United States. It then surveys the left in Latin America, and finally describes her party's ideological and peace work. She cites labour struggles, polling of young Americans, and the electoral record of left governments in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Cuba. Cambron describes the United States as an imperialist power abroad that presents itself as a democracy at home. She claims the greatest domestic threat is fascism, advanced by an extreme right that grew under Reagan and gained strength with Donald Trump's election in 2016. Against this she points to rising worker militancy, including auto workers, UPS drivers, and Amazon and Starbucks workers, and to polls showing most Americans under 35 prefer socialism. She also points to a new Latin American "pink tide", with 12 countries governed by the left in 2023. She says the struggle against hegemonism is above all ideological: it must counter "American values" of individualism and competition, which she links to high depression, suicide and drug-use rates. She also links it to military spending of over 900 billion dollars and more than 800 overseas bases. Cambron reports that her party held a peace conference in November 2023. It put forward proposals for a ceasefire in Gaza, cuts to military spending, a ban on nuclear war, and measures against poverty. She holds that peace means achieving justice rather than the absence of conflict, and that all struggles are linked, so funds must shift from the military to the people. She welcomes the Chinese comrades' call for a new society built on more advanced values and cooperative international relations, and says she is convinced that the new form of human civilization will be socialist civilization. Read the original if you want a US communist's view of hegemonism, US politics and Latin American left governments, and of the community with a shared future for mankind.

Lessons from atheist propaganda and education since reform and opening up 改革开放以来无神论宣传教育的经验启示 Su Bin Su Bin takes up the record of atheist propaganda and education in China since reform and opening up (1978 onwards) and asks what experience can be drawn from it. The article describes a path from a brief revival in the early period, through decline and a situation in which 'theism has its speakers, atheism has none', to a turnaround around the turn of the century and a new phase since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Su argues that success rests on four mutually supporting conditions: the Central Committee's commitment, scholars' responsibility, implementation by localities and departments, and the mobilisation of the masses. The article is organised in five parts: one section for each of the four conditions, followed by a conclusion. It draws on statements and documents of successive Party leaders from Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping, on the careers of scholars such as Ren Jiyu and Du Jiwen, and on regional cases. These include Gansu and Henan on schools, Zhejiang and Wenzhou on Party members who hold religious belief, Shanxi on rural superstition, and Xinjiang and Ningxia on de-extremification. In Su's account, the Central Committee has consistently kept Marxist atheism within the mainstream ideology, held that Party members may not believe in religion and must propagate atheism, and ruled that atheist education does not conflict with freedom of religious belief. The article presents the 2003 instruction from Hu Jintao as having settled the scholarly dispute on this point. Scholars supply the political conviction, scholarly integrity, policy advice and early action, as in the 1995 'Two Sciences Alliance' campaign against superstition. Localities and departments turn directives into practice in schools, in Party organisation and discipline work, in publicity and online governance, and in ethnic regions. Su holds that atheist education is in essence mass work. In Xinjiang, Su describes the campaign against religious extremism as combining it with outreach to specific groups. The author also notes mobilising ordinary people to monitor violations through new media and through community watch networks. Su cautions against treating religious difference as political opposition or linking extremism to particular ethnic groups. The conclusion calls for atheist ideas to be woven into scientific and cultural knowledge, 'like salt dissolved in food', and for unity among all actors so that Marxist atheism remains dominant in people's thinking. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how atheism work is organised across Party, academia, local government and mass campaigns, with concrete regional cases.

From reason to culture A study of Jack David Eller's atheist thought 从理性走向文化 Ping Huijiang Chen Fayang This article studies the atheist thought of Jack David Eller, an American anthropologist and prominent atheist writer. Ping and Chen ask how Eller moves from rational refutation of theism towards a broader cultural struggle. They argue that his thought is marked by rationalism, an anthropological perspective, a combative spirit and a commitment to developing atheism further, and that it is valuable for studying atheism across cultures despite certain limits. The article draws mainly on Eller's Natural Atheism and Atheism Advanced, together with his articles defending atheism. It is organised in four parts: atheism grounded in rationalism; atheism seen through anthropology (tolerance, morality, language and everyday life); atheism as struggle; and atheism as a developing, evolving position. A closing section sets out the authors' assessment of its shortcomings. In Ping and Chen's account, Eller first treats atheism as identical with reason. He places the burden of proof on theists, rebuts the cosmological, ontological and teleological arguments plus experiential and social ones in twelve steps, and defends a "presumption of atheism". In Atheism Advanced he then judges this insufficient, because religion succeeds by controlling people, not persuading them. Drawing on anthropology, he treats religion as one cultural creation among many. He denies that tolerance and morality derive from religion, locating them in culture, nature and reason. He urges atheists to stop speaking Christian language, to see how Christianity colonises time, space, art and habits, and to build their own vocabulary, organisations and education. Ping and Chen conclude that Eller's thought is theoretically innovative and practically suggestive, and that his anthropological approach widens the paths of atheist critique. They also identify limits. In their view he loads atheism with tasks it cannot bear, since it is not a complete worldview. He also remains tied to rationalism and Western-centrism. His doubts about atheist collective action, and his choice of Henry VIII's England over the Soviet and Chinese cases, are cited as examples. Read the original if you study Western atheism, the American atheist movement, or how Chinese scholars of atheism assess foreign thinkers.

Restless hegemony: the US far-right political movement and its impact 躁动的霸权：美国极右翼政治运动及其影响 Zhao Minghao Writing in 2024, Zhao Minghao asks why the far right has become a serious force in American politics and what that means beyond US borders. The article argues that the movement has moved from the margins into the mainstream, that it is now treated as a national security threat inside the United States, and that it has an international reach and a hawkish anti-China orientation that will spill over into China–US relations. The article opens with the movement's ideas, membership and tactics, citing groups such as the Proud Boys, Patriot Front and American Vanguard. It then traces its roots from the Ku Klux Klan and the Civil War through the civil rights era, the Tea Party and the Trump presidency. The final sections cover its links with European and other far-right forces and its effects on China–US relations. Zhao attributes the movement's growth to four factors. These are economic hardship among lower-middle-class whites, which the author ties to globalisation, automation and financialisation. They are also white anxiety about demographic change and affirmative action, the echo-chamber and conspiracy dynamics of social media, and a polarised, "vetocratic" political system whose electoral flaws the Trump years exploited. Abroad, the author describes Steve Bannon's attempt to build a "new nationalist international" through European populist parties, and contacts with groups in Ukraine, Japan and Latin America. On China, Zhao argues that far-right actors shape Republican voters' hostile views, promote conspiracy theories such as the "China virus", and encourage politicians to win votes through tough China policies, producing a vicious circle. Zhao concludes that the far right's influence deserves close attention. He suggests that prosecutions of Trump could further inflame it, and that a Trump victory in 2024 might raise its influence to a new peak. The article calls on China to guard against the spillover of American political disorder and to respond to what it calls the growing internal restlessness of US hegemony. Read the original if you want a Chinese international-relations scholar's account of the US far right, its transatlantic networks and its implications for China–US relations.

A scientific-atheist interpretation of Engels's contradiction between the "expected" and the "unexpected" 恩格斯“预期与非预期”矛盾的科学无神论诠释 Li Wen Engels observed late in life that the purposes of human action are anticipated, while the results the action actually produces are not. Li Wen asks why history, made by purposeful people, so often yields outcomes nobody intended, and why theistic readings cannot answer this. The article argues that Engels's treatment of the "expected and unexpected" contradiction starts from real people and their practice, and therefore refutes every theistic interpretation. In this way it shows the force of Marxist scientific atheism. The article has four parts. It first sets out theistic readings, tracing them from traditional theology through Vico to Kant's "Nature" and Hegel's "cunning of reason". It then argues that the "unexpected" is not the work of divine will, and that the "expected" has nothing to do with deities. A short conclusion draws out theoretical and practical implications. Li's central move is that Vico's providence, Kant's plan of nature and Hegel's absolute reason are, in the article's reading, new gods replacing old ones, and so are refined forms of theism. Behind them lies a mystified expression of objective historical law, together with hidden human purposes. Engels, in Li's account, strips this veil away. For Engels, historical necessity is determined by the conditions of real life, and people are the authors of their own history. The unexpected arises from two sources: the tension between historical law and human purposes, and the clash of individual wills, whose resultant is something nobody willed. For the "expected", Li cites Engels's view that gods are humanity's own projections and reflections of alienation. Realising expectations therefore depends on practice moving from conflict to agreement between conformity to law and conformity to purpose. Li concludes that Marxist scientific atheism is a mature atheism that rejects both traditional and rationalist theism. The contradiction, a "Gordian knot", can only be cut by humanity itself. Li adds that theism is sometimes used by states and interest groups for political and economic gain, and that removing it frees people's initiative to change the world. The article claims relevance for deeper study of the contradiction, for people's pursuit of real happiness, and for the Party's religious work and atheist education in the new era. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars of scientific atheism apply Engels's late historical writings to Western philosophy of history and to religion.

An assessment of the new wave of socialist thought in the United States 美国新一轮社会主义思潮评析 Gao Jianming Gao Jianming asks what the revival of socialism in the United States since Bernie Sanders's 2016 and 2020 campaigns amounts to intellectually, and where it may lead. The article argues that four current programmes (liberal socialism, twenty-first-century socialism, class-struggle social democracy and new anarchism) share enough ground to make a lasting revival possible, but only if their advocates play down ultimate disagreements. After framing socialism as one of three competing ideologies alongside liberalism and conservatism, the article takes each programme in turn. Liberal socialism is associated with James Livingston, Ira Katznelson and Michael Walzer. Twenty-first-century socialism is associated with Fred Block, Erik Olin Wright and Nancy Fraser. Class-struggle social democracy is drawn from the Jacobin circle (Bhaskar Sunkara, Vivek Chibber). New anarchism is represented by David Graeber's "prefigurative politics". Gao then compares similarities and differences and ends with the prospects for American socialism. Gao identifies two shared features. First, all the currents reject revolutionary socialism: they renounce violent revolution and comprehensive planning and keep markets, even where, as with Sunkara and Chibber, they treat Soviet experience more sympathetically. Second, they absorb left populism in the sense of Chantal Mouffe. They stress direct or participatory democracy and fold class struggle together with new social movements, and Sunkara and Chibber use a widened notion of the working class that blurs into "the people". The differences lie in vision and method. Liberal socialists want to tame capitalism, twenty-first-century socialists to end it while keeping some private ownership, class-struggle social democrats to abolish private ownership, and anarchists to oppose the state. They also differ over whether electoral, class or prefigurative politics should lead. Gao concludes that the prospects are unclear. Factional dispute could weaken the left, and Gao cites the split and falling membership of Democratic Socialists of America after its 2021 peak of 95,000. Alternatively, the other currents could treat liberal socialism as an intermediate stage, which would broaden its social base and let Wright's strategy of eroding capitalism from above and below be put into practice. Gao holds that toning down ultimate conflicts and attending to present common ground is an indispensable subjective condition for the revival to continue. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's map of post-2016 American socialist currents, their key texts and their disagreements.

Why Western economic models no longer work 西方经济学模型为什么不灵了 Ye Shuhong This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 24 February 2024, asks why Western economic models forecast so poorly. Ye argues that mainstream Western economics suffers from a severe "explanatory deficit" in reading both the world economy and China's, and that it needs to bring in humanistic factors. The piece opens with recent criticism from within the West: the European Central Bank's president Christine Lagarde, AFP, and Nobel laureate Esther Duflo. It then cites central banks that have revised their forecasting systems after missing inflation, turns to Western reporting on China, and ends with a proposed remedy. Ye contends that traditional Western economics starts from an abstract, homogeneous "economic man" and builds a logic driven purely by calculation. History, values and cultural and institutional influences are treated as "interference" and excluded. In Ye's account, this makes the models ill-suited to a more complex, non-linear world shaped by globalisation and technological revolution. Ye presents China as the typical case the models cannot explain, noting past predictions of collapse. Citing the Chinese economist Zhu Tian, Ye says China's growth owed much to institutions, policy and Confucian culture, especially its emphasis on saving and education. Ye concludes that understanding China's economy requires adding more humanistic "parameters" and treating people as concrete social and cultural beings. Ye says this would explain why government can be a "necessary good" and why projects such as loss-making high-speed rail, rural revitalisation, the "dual carbon" policy and the Belt and Road Initiative go ahead. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese official newspaper frames the limits of Western economics.

Scientific guidance for advancing theoretical innovation 推进理论创新的科学指引 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang asks what Xi Jinping's statements on theoretical innovation tell the Party about how to renew its theory. Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024), Liu argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi has answered a series of major questions on the subject. In Liu's account, this has raised the Party's understanding of the laws of theoretical innovation to a new level and offers guidance for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is a short commentary in four sections. Each takes one pair of concepts from Xi's remarks: the "soul" and "root" of innovation; the age as the mother of ideas and practice as the source of theory; the people as the subject of innovation and their aspirations as its value; and systematization and doctrinal rigour (xueli). Liu first holds that Marxism is the "soul-vein" and excellent traditional Chinese culture the "root-vein" of innovation, and that the two must interpenetrate. Marxism activates the living elements of traditional culture, while Chinese Marxists must draw on Chinese ways of thinking and living. Combining them is both a method and a result of innovation, and Liu ties it to the Two Integrations. Second, Liu says theory must respond to the age and to practice. It cites the "great changes unseen in a century", a community with a shared future for mankind and Chinese modernization as the practical ground for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Third, the people are the subject of innovation because their creative practice supplies fresh experience, and their aspiration for a better life is its value core, aimed at common prosperity. Liu also distinguishes system, which concerns links among parts, from doctrinal rigour, which concerns the passage from phenomena to essence. Without doctrinal rigour, innovation remains an accumulation of sensory experience and particular events. Liu concludes that these four sets of ideas make up Xi's account of the laws of theoretical innovation. Following them, the author says, will open new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and will show the truth-power of Xi's thought. The piece is a Party-theory exposition rather than a critical study. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how current official theory frames the sources, subjects and methods of theoretical innovation.

The basic functions and practical foundations of cultural inheritance and innovation in ideological and political education 思想政治教育文化传承创新的基本功能和现实根基 Wang Xuejian Gong Changrui Wang and Gong ask what role ideological and political education plays in the inheritance and innovation of culture, and how that role can be put on a firm footing. They argue that the two are fused in practice. In their account, ideological and political education carries out a mission of cultural inheritance and innovation, and that mission in turn gives it a deeper cultural root and distinctive strengths. The article opens by defining cultural inheritance and innovation, drawing heavily on Xi Jinping's statements on 'keeping to fundamental principles while innovating', creative transformation of traditional culture and cultural confidence. It then sets out four basic functions of ideological and political education, and finally proposes four practical foundations for exercising them. It is a normative, policy-oriented discussion rather than an empirical study. The authors present inheritance and innovation as mutually conditioning: inheritance supplies the basis for innovation, and innovation drives inheritance forward. The four functions are guiding (setting direction for mainstream culture and steering subcultures towards it), integrating (reconciling clashing cultures under mainstream values), innovating (supplying new content and methods) and disseminating (acting as a carrier for mainstream and traditional culture). The four foundations follow the same logic. These are Marxism as the guide, with Xi Jinping Thought on culture as core content; an integrative stance that upholds mainstream culture, draws on traditional culture and screens foreign culture; effective methods such as practice, healthy lifestyles, libraries and cultural exchange; and advanced channels of communication, including better-trained educators, new media and a healthy online environment. Wang and Gong conclude that ideological and political education is an important support for cultural inheritance and innovation and a route to cultural confidence. They call for it to be guided by Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, so that cultural development keeps its direction against rival currents of thought. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of ideological and political education link the discipline to cultural policy and to the official line on traditional culture.

What is democratic socialism in the United States? 什么是美国的民主社会主义 Carlo Invernizzi Accetti This is a Chinese translation of an article by the political scientist Carlo Invernizzi Accetti on the ideology of contemporary American democratic socialism. Writing after the movement's rise since Bernie Sanders's 2016 campaign and its slowdown after 2020, the author asks what holds the movement together. The thesis is that its ideology rests on four constitutive concepts, socialism, democracy, class and revolution. Participants agree on each only in broad terms, and the movement is united by continuing debate rather than settled doctrine. The article opens with the movement's recent trajectory: Sanders's primaries, growth of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) from under 5,000 to over 95,000 members by 2021, and its persistence in Congress after the 2022 midterms. It then takes each of the four concepts in turn. The evidence is drawn from Sanders's speeches, DSA documents, and writers such as Bhaskar Sunkara, Paul Adler, Chris Maisano, Gary Dorrien and Naomi Klein. A conclusion draws on Adam Przeworski's work on European social democracy. Accetti shows that each concept splits when made concrete. Socialism ranges from Sanders's Rooseveltian 'economic rights' and a Nordic-style welfare state to worker ownership of the means of production and, for Adler, democratic management of the whole economy. Democracy raises the dilemma of working inside the Democratic Party or breaking from it, with positions from grassroots pressure to a 'dirty break'. Class is disputed between income-based and production-based definitions, between class priority and intersectionality, and over environmentalism and the Green New Deal. Revolution means lawful, majoritarian and gradualist change toward a non-capitalist utopia, but it is understood variously as winning policies, as empowering workers, and as quick or generational. Drawing on Przeworski, Accetti argues that social-democratic parties face a tension between their industrial working-class base and the need to attract wider voters, which dilutes ideology. The author contends that American democratic socialism displaces this tension into its ideology through populist elements. These help it appeal beyond the small working-class electorate but leave it a loose coalition of actors with differing goals. Accetti suggests only hard organising work can build a cohesive constituency, and concludes that 'left populism' must shed its populist elements to become truly popular. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based map of the internal debates of the US democratic socialist movement and an outside political-science diagnosis of its strengths and weaknesses.

Raising high the banner of building a community with a shared future for mankind and working together for a better world 高举构建人类命运共同体的鲜明旗帜 携手建设更加美好的世界 Guo Yezhou This is a speech by Guo Yezhou, then Deputy Head of the International Department of the CPC Central Committee, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum and published in World Socialism Studies, 2024 no. 1. Guo argues that Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, together with the Global Development, Global Security and Global Civilization Initiatives, answers the question of what to do in a world undergoing great changes unseen in a century. The speech first sets out three Marxist qualities that Guo attributes to these ideas: scientific character, popular character and practical character. It closes with a call to communists worldwide and a statement of what the Chinese Communist Party will do in its party-to-party diplomacy. On scientific character, Guo contends that the ideas rest on dialectical and historical materialism and develop Marx and Engels's theory of world history, replacing confrontation with peaceful development and zero-sum games with mutual benefit. On popular character, Guo traces them to traditional Chinese ideas such as "all under heaven is shared by all" and cites the Belt and Road Initiative, which the speech says has drawn nearly 1 trillion US dollars in investment, produced over 3,000 projects and helped lift nearly 40 million people out of poverty. On practical character, Guo reports that the idea has appeared for six consecutive years in UN General Assembly resolutions, that over 100 countries support the development and security initiatives, and that China has built various communities of shared future with dozens of countries and regions. Guo calls on communist parties and progressive forces to follow a new type of inter-party relations based on seeking common ground, mutual respect and mutual learning. The Party, Guo says, will hold more bilateral and multilateral exchanges, such as the forum of the Communist Party of China with Marxist parties. Read the original if you want an official statement of how Chinese party diplomacy presents this concept to foreign communists.

Why Western economic models no longer work 西方经济学模型为什么不灵了 Ye Shuhong This short commentary, first published in Economic Daily in February 2024, asks why Western economic models increasingly fail to forecast or explain the world economy and China's economy. Ye argues that these models suffer from a serious "explanatory deficit" because they strip out historical, cultural and humanistic factors. The piece opens with recent doubts voiced in the West: ECB president Christine Lagarde's remark that some economists form a closed "tribe", Esther Duflo's joke about economists' standing, and central banks in Britain and Canada reviewing their forecasting systems after failing to predict inflation. It then turns to Western media coverage of China and closes with a prescription. Ye contends that traditional Western economics starts from an abstract, homogeneous "economic man" and treats history, values and institutions as "interference". In Ye's account, globalisation and technological revolution have produced diverse national development models and non-linear relations that linear formula-based thinking cannot capture. China is presented as the typical case the models cannot explain: Western economists have repeatedly predicted its collapse, yet reforms that mainstream theory judged mistaken succeeded. Ye cites Zhu Tian's finding that Confucian culture, especially its emphasis on saving and education, helped drive growth alongside distinctive institutions and policies. Ye concludes that understanding China's economy requires more humanistic "parameters", returning the abstract economic man to a concrete social and cultural person. Only then, Ye says, can one grasp why the state can be a "necessary good", why some loss-making high-speed railways are built, and why rural revitalisation, dual-carbon policy and the Belt and Road Initiative are pursued. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese official-media commentary criticises Western mainstream economics and frames China as its test case.

Upholding financial services for the real economy as the fundamental purpose 坚持把金融服务实体经济作为根本宗旨 Huang Maoxing Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2024, Huang Maoxing takes up Xi Jinping's instruction, given at a study session for provincial and ministerial leaders on high-quality financial development, that finance must make serving the real economy its fundamental purpose. Huang argues that the real economy is the foundation of finance. Cut off from it, finance becomes "water without a source", and the sector should therefore treat service to the real economy as its starting point and goal. The commentary has three sections. The first sets out why serving the real economy is finance's central mission. The second names priority areas for high-quality financial services. The third proposes five ways to strengthen financial service functions: the monetary and financial environment, financial infrastructure, multi-level capital markets, high-standard financial opening up, and regulatory effectiveness. Huang's core reasoning rests on three claims, each presented as following from Marxist political economy. First, finance arises from an industrial-capital-centred real economy, so the two form a dialectical unity, summed up in Xi's image of the economy as the body and finance as its blood. Second, finance concentrates dispersed money capital and so supports a modern industrial system. Third, Huang says some capitalist countries, driven by financialised capital, let finance circulate apart from the real economy. In Huang's account this produced excessive virtual-economy expansion and crises, and only a real-economy orientation can prevent systemic risk under the socialist market economy. The priority areas Huang lists are product and service innovation, a better structure of funding supply, support for manufacturing upgrading, and credit access for private firms. Huang adds that funding should favour science and technology, green development, inclusive finance, pension finance and digital finance. Huang calls for steady monetary policy with structural tools, better financial infrastructure and credit-reporting systems, deeper equity financing and institutional investors, and opening up that keeps a floor of financial security. Huang also calls for stronger Party leadership over financial work and regulation that covers all financial activity, including local government debt and real-estate firms. Since 2012, Huang says, the financial system has made progress in these areas. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2024 linked Marxist political economy to concrete financial policy priorities.

Deepening supply-side structural reform and expanding effective demand in tandem 坚持深化供给侧结构性改革和着力扩大有效需求协同发力 Xu Kangning This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscript in early 2024, interprets one of the "Five Musts" set out by the Central Economic Work Conference: that China must deepen supply-side structural reform and work to expand effective demand at the same time. Xu Kangning argues that the two should be pursued together, not separately. In Xu's account, doing so would balance demand and supply dynamically, draw on China's ultra-large market and strong productive capacity, and advance the new development pattern and high-quality development. The article has four sections. The first explains why expanding domestic demand and optimising supply must move together and why a unified national market is needed. The second sets out the theoretical relation between supply and demand. The third calls for innovation-led measures on both sides, covering consumption, investment, rural markets, strategic emerging industries and the digital economy. The fourth extends the argument to the international circulation, using examples from foreign trade. Xu's central claim is that demand and supply are mutually dependent: demand pulls supply, and supply creates demand. Managing only the demand side, Xu holds, cannot reach deep structural problems. Smartphones and online music serve as examples of new supply generating new demand. Xu describes overcapacity in some industries as structural, not absolute, because high-quality supply still sells, citing domestic phones and new-energy vehicles. On this reading, technological innovation drives industrial and market innovation, and new quality productive forces, strategic emerging industries and future industries are the key directions for improving supply. Xu also proposes extending demand-side measures to the countryside through rural logistics, e-commerce and infrastructure investment, alongside institutional reform and support for private investment. On trade, the article cites the shift from the "old three" exports (clothing, appliances, furniture) to the "new three" (new-energy vehicles, lithium batteries, photovoltaics), and calls for more digital trade and higher-standard opening up. Xu concludes that this combined approach fits Chinese modernization and raises the quality of both domestic and international circulation. Read the original if you want an official-line reading of the Central Economic Work Conference's supply-and-demand guidance, with the examples and policy priorities used to support it.

Upholding positive interaction between high-quality development and high-level security 坚持高质量发展和高水平安全良性互动 Han Xiping Han Xiping takes up the relationship between development and security, and argues that high-quality development and high-level security must interact positively and keep a dynamic balance. The author starts from Xi Jinping's statement at the Central Economic Work Conference (December 2023) that this is a regular pattern to follow in economic work in the new era. In Han's account, security is the precondition of development and development is the guarantee of security. The article, published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscript (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, has three parts. The first explains why the principle matters. The second sets out its basic requirements. The third proposes practical paths: one for achieving high-quality development and one for achieving high-level security. On significance, Han presents the principle as an inherent requirement of building a modern socialist country in all respects. The author also treats it as a strategic response to a changing international and domestic environment, citing great-power rivalry, a setback for economic globalisation, uneven development and "chokepoint" technologies. Han further calls it a theoretical innovation within Xi Jinping's economic thought. On requirements, the author stresses seeing how the two interact, making them support each other, and continually reassessing the balance through early identification and handling of risks. On paths, Han calls for speeding up the new development pattern by expanding domestic demand, achieving technological self-reliance and opening up at a higher level. Han also calls for a stronger national security system covering food, energy, finance and the ecological environment. Han concludes that the holistic approach to national security must be implemented so that the "two miracles" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability become more sustainable, and so that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation proceeds smoothly. The author says development results should be turned into security capacity, while security should create a stable environment for development. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-line reasoning on development and security, together with its policy checklist for key sectors.

Xi Jinping's original contributions to Marxist atheism: a study 习近平总书记关于马克思主义无神论的原创性成果研究 Zhu Xiaoming Zhu Xiaoming takes up Xi Jinping's statements on upholding and propagating Marxist atheism, drawn mainly from the national religious work conferences of 2016 and 2021 and from Xi's speeches on organisational and propaganda work. Following Xi's call (June 2023) to study the original theoretical results of the Party's new concepts, Zhu argues that four of these statements are original: neither the classics nor earlier Party leaders made them. In Zhu's account they continue earlier thought while adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article takes the four statements in turn: upholding Marxist atheism is a "major principle"; Marxist atheism must always remain the mainstream ideology and hold the leading place in people's thinking; the relationship between freedom of religious belief and ideological struggle must be handled correctly; and atheist propaganda must be strengthened in a targeted way so that atheism "takes root in people's hearts". A closing section sets out how the four fit together. For the first statement Zhu gives four reasons. The Party's dialectical and historical materialism is itself thoroughly atheist. Atheism, unlike religious freedom, which Zhu says applies to religious work, covers all areas of Party and state work. The author reads the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as showing that atheism disappeared and religion and ethno-religious separatism returned. And rising spiritual needs in China pose new ideological challenges. On the second and third, Zhu argues that inclusiveness towards believers must not weaken atheism's leading role, and that religion is both an ideology and a social entity, so policy must address both. On the fourth, Zhu stresses party schools, universities and schools as venues, and engaging with scientific unknowns. Zhu concludes that the four statements form a framework running from principle to leading position, key relationship and practical requirement, and that they guide new research and propaganda work on atheism. Zhu also holds that this work is a long-term foundation for preventing religious risks, not a campaign. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how Xi's atheism statements are being systematised in Chinese religious and ideological policy discourse.

A study of the religious beliefs of American youth 美国青年的宗教信仰状况研究 Han Qi This is a literature review of nearly a century of American research on the religious beliefs of young people, from the early twentieth century to the late 2010s. Han Qi argues that the field mirrors both social and religious change in the United States. In Han's account, the research traces secularisation and privatisation of religion, and offers lessons for studying religious belief among Chinese youth. The review divides the field into three stages, using 1960 and the start of the twenty-first century as dividing lines. Before the 1960s, studies were mainly descriptive quantitative surveys of college students' attitudes. From the 1960s to the end of the century, work moved to the science–religion relationship, the measurement of religiosity and long-term tracking, notably Hoge's studies. Since 2000, studies of 'emerging adults' and spirituality have dominated, with qualitative and mixed methods. Han stresses two main moves. First, Hoge's longitudinal work showed declining commitment and church participation to the mid-1970s, then a conservative turn described as a 'return of the 1950s'. Han treats this as an episode within a continuing secularising trend. Second, drawing on Christian Smith's National Study of Youth and Religion and Souls in Transition, Han reports that only about 15 per cent of emerging adults are spiritually open. Most see religion as a private matter, and parents' religious practice remains a strong influence. Han presents therapeutic individualism as the cultural background to spiritual seeking, and follows Smith in holding that claims of a youth turn to 'spiritual but not religious' are exaggerated and do not yet threaten the traditional religious structure. Han concludes that the research has advanced through better methods and richer perspectives, and that its findings are rooted in American culture and cannot simply be transferred elsewhere. For China, Han calls for Marxist theory of religion as the basis of study, and for uniting believing and non-believing youth around the core socialist values. Han also proposes more rigorous questionnaire design and sampling, longitudinal analysis of existing surveys, and research perspectives of Chinese origin. Read the original if you want a guide to the main American studies of youth religion and to how a Chinese Marxist researcher draws lessons from them.

Antonio Negri and the encounter with his times 安东尼奥·奈格里与时代的际会 Lan Jiang Marking the death of the Italian Marxist theorist Antonio Negri on 15 December 2023, this commemorative commentary asks what his thought can still offer in the digital age. Lan argues that Negri, though mainly a twentieth-century thinker, kept meeting each new era with his concepts of general intellect and immaterial production. In the age of intelligent technology, Lan contends, those concepts must be reinvented rather than simply repeated. The piece follows Negri's career in three stages: Italian workerism (operaismo) of the 1960s and its factory-centred politics; the network era of Empire and Multitude, shaped by post-Fordist production; and the present age of algorithms and data. It ends with a short biographical note covering his role in Potere Operaio and Autonomia Operaia, his arrest in 1979, exile in France, return to prison in Italy in 1997, and main works. Lan traces Negri's key ideas to the circle around Raniero Panzieri and the journal Quaderni Rossi, and to the reading of Marx's "Fragment on Machines" in the Grundrisse. Panzieri's idea that workers are really subsumed under machines became, in Negri's hands, a non-material "general intellect": workers' shared language, affect and cooperation, which capital cannot see and which supports a strategy of exodus. With the move from factory to metropolis, Lan says, Empire and Commonwealth extend this to networked white-collar workers, producing biopolitical power but also the multitude, a technologically united counter-force. Lan then offers a critique: in the present planetary computation system, people take part not as subjects but as data, objectified and subordinated to algorithms and hidden protocols. For this reason Lan holds that Negri's subject-based general intellect has become indifferent "general data", and that exodus no longer works as a strategy. Lan nonetheless judges Negri's direction correct: only by taking possession of general data can intelligent machines and big-data algorithms become a public instrument for everyone rather than a profit tool for a few platforms. Reinventing Negri in the intelligent age therefore means letting the multitude regain control of general data. Lan closes with a Matrix image of Negri as Neo offering the "red pill" of general intellect. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese appraisal of Negri that links workerism and Empire to debates on data, platforms and digital capitalism.
