Capital valorisation, alienated labour and algorithmic power Three dimensions of contemporary Western left critiques of capitalist digital labour 资本增殖、劳动异化与算法权力 Liu Zhuohong Guo Xiaoqing Liu and Guo ask how contemporary Western left thinkers understand digital labour under capitalism. They argue that digital technology couples naturally with the logic of capital: digital labour is at once a "paradise" for valorisation and a "hell" that erodes labour's stability and the worker's essential powers. The article organises the Western left critique along a three-part framework: capital valorisation, labour alienation and algorithmic power. The article opens with a survey of Western schools: Dallas Smythe's communication political economy, Hardt and Negri's autonomist Marxism, Christian Fuchs's systematic critique of digital labour, and the left accelerationism of Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams. It also lists Chinese scholars working on platform capitalism, biopolitics and the prospects of digital labour. Three sections then treat valorisation, alienation and algorithmic power, drawing on Marx, Andrejevic, Standing, Byung-Chul Han, Rosa, Harvey, Žižek and Dyer-Witheford. A final section assesses the critique. The authors contend that data has become a core means of production and that platforms extract unpaid audience and user-generated labour. In their reading this moves capital from the "formal" to the "real" subsumption of society. Alienation, they argue, is not ended but extended: work and life merge, workers become precarious (Standing's "precariat"), and "prosumer" labour deepens colonisation of everyday life. Algorithmic power then works through internalised control, echo chambers and ideological effects. Proposed forms of resistance include the precariat, Hardt and Negri's multitude, Žižek's "excluded" and Dyer-Witheford's networked communism. The authors judge most of these abstract or utopian. Liu and Guo conclude that the Western left's analysis of digital capitalism is sharp and confirms Marx's critique. They fault it for being absorbed by capital's logic, departing from historical materialism, compromising with liberalism and offering diagnosis without a programme of transformation, so that it remains "micro-politics". They call for a dialectical view of digital labour and for comparing the Western critique with Marxist critiques of capital and socialism with Chinese characteristics. They claim this would show the institutional advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics in curbing the harms of digital labour and developing new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey and assessment of Western left theories of digital labour, from Smythe to Fuchs, Han and Žižek.

The reproduction of labour subjectivity under the logic of capital A contemporary dimension of Western Marxist critical theory of capital 资本逻辑下劳动主体性的再生产 Niu Ziniu Niu asks why the strengthening of workers' subjectivity under contemporary capitalism has not liberated them but has coincided with worse conditions. The article argues that the inherited framework of "subject–object inversion", in which capital usurps and objectifies the worker's subjectivity and liberation means restoring it, is tied to one historical form of capitalism. Niu holds that Western Marxists since the 1960s built a theory of the reproduction of the labouring subject because they saw a hidden complicity between worker subjectivity and capital's rule. The article is in three parts. It first criticises what Merleau-Ponty called "Weberian Marxism": Lukács, the first-generation Frankfurt School and their influence on Chinese Marxist philosophy. It then traces the line of thought on subject production through Kojève, Lacan, Althusser and Foucault. It ends with Deleuze's theory of desire-production and later work by Byung-Chul Han, Antonio Negri's autonomism and the cognitive capitalism school. Niu contends that Lukács's reification theory fitted Fordist industrial capitalism and linked the commodity form to rationalised labour through Weber, bypassing Marx's theories of valorisation and relative surplus-value. Capital's principle is non-identity, ceaseless self-exceeding, so a critique of uniformity and a liberation of difference turned out to serve neoliberalism and also struck at trade unions, welfare states and socialist countries. The later tradition, Niu argues, treats power as affirmative. Althusser's ideological state apparatuses and Foucault's account of how workers are constituted as willing labourers and, under neoliberalism, as entrepreneurs of the self, lead to Deleuze's claim that workers themselves desire surplus labour. Niu says Deleuze still retains a negative notion of power through "reterritorialisation", and that Negri and the cognitive capitalism school repeat the Weberian error by expecting flexible, cognitive labour to be emancipatory. Niu concludes that expanded worker subjectivity can be a contemporary form of labour's subordination to capital, with capital accumulating itself in workers through "human capital". The author calls for a distinction, drawn from Althusser, between the wage-labouring subject and the political subject, and for a political process that turns the former into the latter. Without it, revolutionary action would fail or prove false. Read the original if you are interested in how Western Marxist theories of subjectivity, ideology and power are assessed from within Chinese Marxist philosophy, and in a critical reading of Lukács, Foucault, Deleuze and Negri.

The essence, crisis and alternative of neoliberal globalization A commentary on David Lane's recent lectures 新自由主义全球化的实质、危机和替代 Song Chaolong Shao Xianyue This commentary reports and assesses a series of lectures given at Peking University on 24–26 May 2023 by David Lane, emeritus professor of sociology at Cambridge, whose recent book is Global Neoliberal Capitalism and the Alternatives: From Social Democracy to State Capitalisms. Song and Shao present Lane's view that neoliberal globalization is the ideology and framework of a transnational capitalist class, that it is in crisis, and that China's rise as a "semi-core" power points to a possible socialist alternative. After introducing Lane's research and publications, the article follows his lectures in three parts: the essence of neoliberal globalization, its defects and crises, and its alternatives. It traces capitalism after the Second World War from "internationalism", with varied national models, to globalization from the late 1970s. It then sets out Lane's critique of Wallerstein's world-system model and closes with a short conclusion. Song and Shao report Lane's claim that neoliberal globalization is in essence a modern form of imperialism, driven by multinational corporations and a transnational capitalist class made up of corporate owners, officials, international-institution executives, think-tank members and media. In Lane's account it fails in three ways: it cannot avoid crises such as that of 2007–2008, it erodes state sovereignty and public welfare, and it deepens social conflict and produces a new populism, such as Brexit, that stays within the neoliberal framework. Lane holds that the crisis cannot be resolved inside the capitalist world system. He credits China's mixed ownership, socialist market economy, strong public power and advocacy of a community with a shared future for mankind with offering a different model. He replaces Wallerstein's "semi-periphery" with "semi-core" and cites the growing BRICS share of world GDP. Song and Shao conclude that Lane regards China's constructive proposals as a positive alternative to neoliberal globalization. They also add a critical note: Lane's "semi-core" label does not accurately describe China's place, since it risks fitting China into a capitalist-dominated world system, and it stresses competition while neglecting cooperation between socialism and transnational capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic reading of a Western sociologist's account of globalization, the transnational capitalist class and China's role in it.

The environmental politics of the Communist Party USA since the 21st century: theory, policy and action 21世纪以来美国共产党的环境政治：理论、政策与行动 Gao Ze Gao Ze asks how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), founded in Chicago in 1919, has approached environmental questions since 2000, a subject the author says Chinese scholarship has neglected. The article argues that the CPUSA has built a distinctive Marxist environmental politics that joins theory to practical struggle. In the author's assessment, the party has little power over US policy but has an influence larger than its size and is an unavoidable part of the American left's environmental spectrum. The article has three main parts: the CPUSA's theoretical critique of contemporary capitalist ecology, its policy positions, and its forms of action. It draws on CPUSA theorists and organisers such as John Bachtell, Mark Brodine and Anita Waters, on party congress reports and on the 2008 global warming report. It also covers the party's stance on the Green New Deal, its work with marginalised groups and its international cooperation. A short conclusion lists three features of the party's environmental politics. On theory, Gao reports that CPUSA thinkers return to dialectical materialism and to Capital, using the metabolic rift framework and coining notions such as the "dialectics of climate change" and "ecological necessity". They hold capitalism responsible for the ecological crisis, say that only systemic change can resolve it, and treat the crisis as a "planetary emergency". They see the working class as the key agent and propose "working-class environmentalism". On policy, the slogan "people and planet before profit" guides the party's positions. The party gives the Green New Deal "reserved" support while demanding a larger role for workers and unions, and it presses for environmental rights for poor communities, immigrants and minorities. Its actions include joining the People's Climate Marches (2014 and 2017) and global climate strikes, publishing reports, running Marxist education, and backing technology transfer and ecological agriculture for developing countries. Gao concludes that the party's theory serves its movement, that its populist propaganda shapes public opinion beyond its organisational weight, and that it combines American environmentalism with a global critique of capitalism. The author adds that the CPUSA praises China's ecological civilization, and calls for Marxist parties to cooperate on global ecological governance and on building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you study Western communist parties, the American left's environmental politics or how Chinese scholars present foreign Marxist parties.

Strengthening patriotic education in the new era to gather mighty strength for Chinese modernization 加强新时代爱国主义教育 凝聚中国式现代化建设磅礴伟力 Hu Guodong Hu Guodong, who is Youth League secretary at Peking University, asks how patriotic education should be carried out among young people in the new era. The article argues that the Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China, in force from 1 January 2024, secures such education through law. In Hu's view this helps gather strength for building a modern socialist country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The short commentary has three parts. It first traces patriotism as an inherited spirit, from five thousand years of history through the Opium War, the May Fourth movement and the Party's leadership. It then explains why patriotic education matters now, citing Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally it sets out tasks for university Youth League organisations, with Peking University's practice as illustration. Hu contends that the "two overall situations" (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and profound global change) bring confusion of thought and value conflicts, which makes building young people's spiritual world urgent. The author draws on Xi's formula that patriotism must be united with love of the Party and of socialism. Hu proposes three approaches: teaching Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era through combined teacher lectures and youth presentations; holding activities such as song concerts, poetry events and runs tied to national anniversaries; and linking ideals to practice, for example through volunteering during epidemic control and the Winter Olympics. Hu concludes that patriotic education is a systematic project of consolidating foundations and forging the soul. Youth League bodies should follow Xi Jinping Thought, root patriotism in young people and cultivate a new generation able to carry the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party youth organisations describe the practical implementation of patriotic education in universities.

Grasping the foundations of cultural confidence 深入把握文化自信的根基所在 Zeng Rongfeng Yin Yungong This short commentary asks what cultural confidence rests on and how it should be strengthened. Zeng and Yin argue that it has three foundations: cultural subjectivity, Chinese civilisation, and Chinese modernization. They present cultural confidence as an important part of Xi Jinping's thought on culture and as an original contribution to Marxist cultural theory. The piece is organised in three parts, one for each foundation. Each opens with a statement by Xi Jinping and ends with a task for the new era. The authors tie the discussion to building a culturally strong country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. First, the authors hold that cultural subjectivity is the fundamental support of cultural confidence. They say it was built under Party leadership through the Two Integrations, and that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is its strongest expression. Second, they describe Chinese civilisation as continuous, innovative, unified, inclusive and peaceful. In their account, cultural confidence is therefore open and inclusive, not a matter of stagnation, simple restoration or blind exclusion of the foreign. Third, they argue that Chinese modernization supplies the practical ground for cultural confidence. They say it has rejected capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist Western modernization and has broken the equation of modernization with Westernization. The authors call for upholding the Party's cultural leadership, following the path of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, and learning from other civilisations. They also call for turning Chinese experience into Chinese theory, so that cultural confidence and Chinese modernization reinforce each other. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party theorists currently ground cultural confidence.

Comparison and mutual learning: similarities and differences in Chinese and Vietnamese socialist modernization 比较与互鉴：中越社会主义现代化的异同 Pan Jin'e Since the 20th Party Congress (2022) set out Chinese modernization, socialist modernization has become a focus of debate among Marxist scholars in China and abroad. Pan Jin'e compares China and Vietnam, the two main socialist states today, and argues that both pursue a modernization that differs in nature from Western capitalist modernization. Their aims are shared even though their concepts, priorities and stages of development differ. The author hopes the comparison will inform Chinese modernization and offer a reference for other socialist and developing countries. The article has four parts. It first reviews theories of modernization (Chinese scholars such as He Chuanqi, Luo Rongqu and Han Qingxiang, and Western ones such as Dirk Bendix, W. W. Rostow and Samuel Huntington) and Vietnamese understandings of the term. It then traces Vietnam's industrialization and modernization in three phases: early exploration from the Third Party Congress (1960), the Doi Moi (renovation) period from the Sixth Congress (1986) to the Twelfth (2016), and a new phase of improved quality and efficiency from the Thirteenth Congress (2021). The third part draws out five features of the Vietnamese path, and the fourth compares China and Vietnam. Pan identifies five features of Vietnam's path. It is modernization premised on industrialization, oriented towards socialism, mutually reinforcing with renovation and international integration, a catch-up path that seeks to shorten the process, and one whose content keeps being enriched, for example by sustainability and the digital economy. On this basis Pan lists seven commonalities with China: socialist attributes and values, comprehensive Party leadership, a people-centred approach, interaction with reform and opening up (Doi Moi), coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, alignment with national rejuvenation goals set for mid-century, and a path of peaceful development. Four differences are traced to scale and stage. China speaks of a new journey of Chinese modernization, while Vietnam, which the author places at an early stage of industrialization, stresses industrialization. China emphasises its huge population and common prosperity, while Vietnam stresses its demographic dividend and enterprises. The two countries also differ in their stance towards the new technological revolution. Pan concludes that the success of both countries breaks the myth that modernization equals Westernization and demonstrates the diversity of paths to socialism. The author further claims that socialist modernization is more efficient than the capitalist kind, upholds social fairness better, and shows the vitality of Marxism. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of Vietnam's Party congress policies on industrialization from 1960 to 2021, together with an official-line comparison with China.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics and the revival of European socialism 中国特色社会主义与欧洲社会主义的复兴 Thürmer Gyula This is a Chinese translation of an address-style article by Thürmer Gyula, chairman of the Hungarian Workers' Party. Writing in 2024, Thürmer argues that capitalism is in deep crisis, that Europe's security structure has collapsed and that world war is a threat. In his view European socialist parties must revive, and socialism with Chinese characteristics can help them do so. The text lists a series of 'needs' for European socialism: theoretical renewal, study of the Chinese Communist Party's experience, a break from the 'end of history' thesis, new forms of cooperation, and a clear international orientation. It draws on Chinese examples such as the Two Integrations, Chinese modernization, poverty eradication and party dialogues. Thürmer holds that the collapse of European socialism caused ideological confusion, with some parties turning to revisionism and others to dogmatism. Marxism, he says, is a living theory that each party must apply to its own national conditions, and Chinese practice proves this. He suggests Europe follow the Two Integrations by combining Marxism with its own cultural and civilisational heritage, while insisting this is a sharing of experience and not an imposed model. He also praises the 2023 high-level dialogue between the Party and world political parties and the conferences organised by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Thürmer calls for a multipolar world in which states with different systems coexist, and for efforts to avoid world war and build a community with a shared future for mankind. He says European socialist parties will try to regain lost ground and he expresses support for China's drive to build a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want to see how a European communist party leader presents Chinese socialism as a resource for his own movement.

The complex reality and new prospects of the socialist movement 社会主义运动的复杂现实与新前景 Pradeep Kumar Gyawali This is a Chinese translation of an article by Pradeep Kumar Gyawali, Deputy General Secretary of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist–Leninist). Gyawali asks how the world socialist movement should respond to the contradictions of globalization and to a shifting global balance of power. The answer is that socialism is "the only correct choice", pursued along nationally specific paths, and that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind offers a framework for cooperation. The article has five parts. It begins with the challenges of the present: unequal globalization, climate crisis, disruptive technology, extremism and the Covid-19 pandemic. It then discusses the significance of a community with a shared future for mankind and argues the case for socialism. It goes on to describe the Nepali communists' record, and ends with proposals for global cooperation. Translator's notes explain Nepali history, including the Panchayat system and the 2006 April movement. Gyawali argues that Western dominance of two centuries is declining. In the author's account, the West's military record is discredited, and emerging economies, including BRICS members, are challenging Western economic primacy. Western powers, the author says, are obstructing this rise rather than adjusting to it. The author presents China's peaceful rise as a new phenomenon that has lifted 800 million people out of poverty. Gyawali holds that persistent inequality, with nearly 1 billion people in absolute poverty, requires an alternative. Marxism, in this reading, is not a ready-made formula but a way of analysing and transforming society, so each country must take its own socialist road and answer new questions creatively. The author sees socialism as defensive after the Soviet collapse but now reviving, through communist parties, trade unions and social movements. On Nepal, Gyawali credits the party with a role in the 1951 democratic struggle, the campaign against the Panchayat system and the 2006 April movement. In government, it says, the party established social security, carried out post-earthquake reconstruction and signed a transit agreement with China, and it is laying foundations for socialism with Nepali characteristics. The author concludes with calls to respect each country's choice of political system, reject bloc politics and zero-sum thinking, uphold the UN Charter and promote mutual learning, while acknowledging the task is not easy. Read the original if you want a South Asian communist party leader's view of globalization, China's role and the Nepali socialist project, as published in a Chinese theoretical journal.

Critique and reflection: the emergence, causes and lessons of the equality crisis in contemporary capitalist welfare states 批判与反思：当代资本主义福利国家平等危机的生成、原因及启示 Wang Qing Why have Western welfare states, long seen as models of social solidarity, produced the Occupy Wall Street and Black Lives Matter movements, France's Yellow Vests and pension protests, and Britain's Brexit impasse? Wang Qing takes up this question through the French scholar Pierre Rosanvallon's account of equality. Wang argues that these states face a "second equality crisis" of capitalism, which Rosanvallon cannot explain because he stays within reformism. The article's own answer is that the roots lie in capital's logic and private ownership, and that common prosperity within Chinese modernization offers a way beyond the crisis. The article has three parts. The first traces the welfare state's classic redistributive tools: progressive income tax, social insurance and collective bargaining. It then sets out the forces that undermined them from the 1970s. The second part gives Wang's Marxist explanation of the crisis. The third draws lessons for China, in the form of three principles for promoting common prosperity: a people-centred approach, differentiation and dialectical thinking. Wang follows Rosanvallon in describing a shift from "similarity" equality and mechanical solidarity to a society of individuals who demand equality of difference. Individualization, the tearing of Rawls's "veil of ignorance" as risks become differentiated, finance-led accumulation, flexible work and capital flight all weakened redistribution. Wang then criticises Rosanvallon and Rawls for avoiding the ownership of the means of production. In Wang's reading, injustice in distribution is only the surface, and "relational equality" is a veil over capitalist domination. Drawing on David Harvey's "capital fix", Wang also contends that platform work hides exploitation of digital labourers, and that welfare is an instrument capital uses to ease class conflict, not something that overcomes capital's drive to expand. Wang concludes that common prosperity, as a union of productive forces and relations of production, substantively surpasses the capitalist equality crisis. The practical proposals include prioritising employment, social protection for the 84 million workers in new forms of employment, equalising basic public services, and reforming income distribution. Wang also stresses that common prosperity does not mean egalitarianism, and that it must balance joint building with joint sharing, material with cultural life, and an effective market with an enabling government. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School author uses Rosanvallon's theory of the welfare state to build a Marxist critique of Western welfare capitalism and to justify common prosperity policy.

An action guide for advancing comprehensive rural revitalization effectively 有力有效推进乡村全面振兴的行动指南 Huang Chengwei Huang Chengwei offers a study-and-implementation commentary on Xi Jinping's important instruction on "agriculture, rural areas and farmers" (the "three rural issues"), issued around the 2023 Central Rural Work Conference. Huang argues that the instruction sets out the strategic requirements and main thrust of comprehensive rural revitalization. In this reading it is the fundamental guide and action guide for pushing revitalization forward "effectively" in the new era, and it ties accelerated agricultural and rural modernization to Chinese modernization. The article, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, is organised in five parts. These cover the positioning of rural revitalization as the overall lever of rural work, lessons from the "Thousand Villages Demonstration, Ten Thousand Villages Renovation" project, the two bottom lines plus the twin drivers of technology and reform, three "levels" of improvement with farmers' income, and Party leadership. Huang's first move is to present rural revitalization as the "overall lever" of rural work, assessing achievements and new difficulties such as rising production costs and market volatility. Huang lists favourable conditions: Party leadership, national strength, rural potential and accumulated experience. The second move is to treat the Zhejiang "Thousand Villages" experience as a teaching model with three features: a people-first value orientation, a systematic and coordinated approach, and tailoring policy to local conditions. The third move is a package of measures. These aim to guarantee grain security and prevent large-scale return to poverty, to drive rural development through science and technology and reform, and to raise rural industry, construction and governance while strengthening measures to raise farmers' incomes. Huang concludes that the Party's overall leadership is the fundamental guarantee. This includes the principle that the Party manages rural work, a responsibility system running from the central level to counties and townships, grass-roots Party organisations, rural talent and risk prevention. The article is an authoritative-style reading of the policy line, not an independent empirical study. Read the original if you want a systematic outline of how official commentary framed the priorities of rural policy in early 2024, including the specific measures listed for grain security, poverty-return monitoring and rural reform.

The logical starting point of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics is the primary stage of socialism 中国特色社会主义政治经济学的逻辑起点是社会主义初级阶段 Yu Bin Chinese scholars have proposed many different logical starting points for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Yu Bin asks why they disagree and which answer is correct. The article's thesis is that the starting point is the primary stage of socialism. Yu treats Chinese modernization as the logical main line that unfolds from this point. The article first diagnoses four causes of the disagreement. It then reviews candidate starting points for general socialist political economy, among them socialist commodities, public ownership, quotas, funds, associated labour and "socially organised commodities". It then turns to a long list of proposals specific to China: commodities, productive forces, economic resources, consumption needs, Party leadership, the basic economic system, the "people as principal body" theory, surplus product, capital, ownership, "labour for the people", the "real person" and the principal contradiction. Yu criticises each in turn. Yu traces the disagreement to four causes: neglect of results already achieved by Marxist political economy, interference from bourgeois economics, one-sided attention to economic reality, and treating the starting point in isolation from the logical main line that must develop from it. Using Capital as the model, Yu argues that a starting point must be able to generate the whole system, must not be a result or a means, and must not presuppose what it has yet to explain. Yu holds that for general socialist political economy the starting point is associated labour on the basis of common ownership of the means of production, as in Marx's "negation of the negation" passage. Because socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism at its primary stage, its political economy must first show why it differs from general socialist political economy. On Yu's reading, Deng Xiaoping's remarks on the primary stage and on Chinese modernization make that stage the starting point of the main line, which is the movement of Chinese socialism towards higher stages. Yu concludes that, since a mature socialist political economy does not yet exist, a textbook could proceed from general political economy to socialist political economy and then to the Chinese case, and would then begin with political economy in general. If socialist principles are already presupposed, the logical starting point is the primary stage of socialism. Yu also argues that early PRC practice after the 1950s should be analysed critically, because it ran ahead of the primary stage. Read the original if you want a detailed critical survey of Chinese debates on the starting point of socialist political economy, argued from Capital's method.

Leninism and "war and peace" in the twenty-first century 列宁主义与二十一世纪的“战争与和平” Lü Xinyu Lü Xinyu asks why war has returned to Europe and the Middle East after the Cold War, and argues that the answer lies in the "de-communization" that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article contends that the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the Israel–Palestine war and the US "new Cold War" against China are extensions of twentieth-century Cold War logic. In Lü's view, lasting peace requires a return to Leninism. The article has four parts. It first examines Cold War historiography and what Lü calls "reversal-of-verdict historiography" (翻案史学), including the "Lenin as German agent" rumour, and its echo in China. It then turns to civilizational discourse (Fukuyama, Huntington, Dugin) and the expansion of NATO. The third part reviews Cold War episodes from Churchill's Fulton speech to Mearsheimer's "offensive realism", and the fourth returns to Lenin's writings on the national question, the state and peace. Lü argues that Western-dominated Cold War history, much of it reproduced in China, presents the Chinese and Russian revolutions as Soviet manipulation and so undermines their legitimacy. Balance-of-power theory, "civilizational conflict" and ethnic nationalism are described as the new guises of imperialism and as breeding grounds of war. Lü reads Russia's treatment after 1991, including what the article calls broken promises on NATO and the Minsk agreements, as a repeat of the Versailles settlement. The post-1917 contest between Leninism and Wilsonism is presented as the root dispute: Wilson's self-determination rests on ethnic nationalism, Lenin's on the liberation and eventual merging of oppressed nations. Lü concludes that the Soviet failure does not show the failure of socialism and peace, and that suppressing socialism is what undermines peace. Lü calls for a fresh reckoning with the whole Cold War narrative and describes socialism with Chinese characteristics as the major historical result of Leninism. China's patriotism is distinguished from Western ethnic nationalism, and China is urged to help build a united front of the Global South and to treat the three global initiatives on development, security and civilization as a unity. Read the original if you want a long, polemical Chinese Marxist reading of the Cold War and the Ukraine war that ties them to Lenin's theory of nation and state.

Collective force: on the logical foundation of common prosperity 集体力：论共同富裕的逻辑基础 Li Fenghua Yi Xilin How can common prosperity be achieved under a socialist market economy, where the law of value tends to produce polarisation? Li Fenghua and Yi Xilin argue that Western welfare-state and market-failure remedies cannot answer this, since they rest on individualism and private ownership. They find the answer in the concept of "collective force" (jitili) from Marx's Capital, which they present as the logical and economic-philosophical foundation of common prosperity. The article has three parts. The first defines collective force and shows how it operates across modern industrial society: in material production, knowledge production (science, patents, platform economies) and social interaction (markets and political institutions). The second examines how capitalism privatises collective force, through global plunder, appropriation of audience labour, technological hegemony and international financial dominance. It also notes partial public ownership, in public utilities and welfare states. The third sets out how making collective force public leads to common prosperity. The authors read Marx's passage on cooperation as showing that cooperation and division of labour create a productive force that cannot be reduced to individuals. Since this force is social in origin, they hold that it should belong to society, and that capital's unpaid appropriation of it is the main source of surplus value and of wealth gaps. They argue that collective force exists at several levels, from workshop and city to nation and world. This yields "multi-level ownership", combining public ownership at each level with respect for individual ownership of individual contributions. They claim this fits Marx's twin formulas of abolishing private ownership and re-establishing individual ownership, and that it covers mixed-ownership economies in the primary stage of socialism. The authors conclude that distribution theory has focused on labour versus production factors and neglected the contribution of collective force, which they say has let a few individuals capture it as factor income. They propose identifying the collective component of outputs and returning it through taxes and public accumulation, citing inheritance, property and windfall taxes as useful precedents. This, they argue, is a Pareto-improving, gradual path of socialist "self-reform" rather than violent expropriation. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-economy attempt to ground common prosperity in a reading of Marx's Capital and in ownership theory.

Showing the dual character of Chinese modernization through the "big history" perspective The distinctive features of Chinese modernization and the common features of modernization across countries 从大历史观展示中国式现代化的双重属性 Li Jie Every country's path to modernization, Li Jie argues, must follow the general laws of modernization while also fitting national conditions. Chinese modernization therefore has both features shared with other countries and features of its own, and the universal lives within the particular. Li proposes that a "big history" perspective (dà lìshǐ guān) can show this dual character. The piece appeared in Beijing Daily on 22 April 2024. The commentary goes through five features of Chinese modernization: a huge population, common prosperity for all, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and a path of peaceful development. For each, Li sets the Chinese case against how Western capitalist modernization handled the same problem. The text also draws on Marx on machinery, Mao Zedong on the value of people, Deng Xiaoping on the essence of socialism, Xi Jinping on ecology and culture, and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). In Li's account, each Chinese feature answers a problem that every modernizing country faces. Western countries met labour shortages through land enclosure, the slave trade and factory machinery, which Li says sacrificed workers and peasants to capital accumulation. China instead treats its population as a resource rather than a burden. Li argues that capitalist modernization can create wealth but cannot distribute it fairly, and that it fosters hypocritical morality, ecological damage and colonial expansion. Socialist modernization is presented as a remedy, through distribution and social security systems, balancing efficiency with fairness and vitality with order, combining material and spiritual wealth, and rejecting the logic that a strong country must seek hegemony. Li concludes that the Chinese features and the common features of modernization are inseparable and highly unified. He attributes this unity both to the dual nature of modernization itself and to the historic achievements and changes of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Li also presents China's experience as a model for developing countries seeking non-capitalist paths and cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a short, official-style statement of how Party-aligned scholars frame Chinese modernization against Western modernization.

Promoting the building of a case bank for integrated ideological and political theory teaching across university, secondary and primary schools through quality evaluation 以质量评价推动大中小学思政课一体化教学课例库建设 Liu Jie How should quality evaluation be used to build a bank of model teaching cases for the integrated teaching of ideological and political theory courses across universities, secondary schools and primary schools? Liu Jie argues that evaluation is a deep intervention in the case bank's construction and bears on the high-quality development of integrated ideological and political education. In the author's view, evaluation can produce "typical cases" only if it reflects the particular ecology and developmental regularities of this education. The short commentary, written in 2024, is organised in three parts. The first sets out basic principles of quality evaluation, the second proposes a system of evaluation standards, and the third discusses relationships that must be handled correctly in integrated teaching. It draws on Xi Jinping's statements on ideological and political courses, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and the project on big-data support for integrated teaching that funded the work. On principles, Liu holds that ideological and political courses should be judged by whether they "explain principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly". This means building on the Party's established practice of mass ideological education, using Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and strengthening ideals and convictions step by step from primary school to university. The proposed standards are a value standard that coordinates ideological and political courses with ideological and political education running through other courses; an effect standard that joins a grand historical perspective to political identification; and a standard that combines each school stage's comparative advantages with targeted measures and feedback. The relationships to be handled are those between textbook content and teaching content, between quantitative and qualitative indicators (including big-data monitoring of public opinion on cases), and between existing conditions and the teachers and students involved. Liu concludes that principles, standards and the handling of these relationships should all be anchored in fostering virtue and nurturing talent and in improving students' core competencies. The author links this to the strategy of building a strong education system and to supplying talent for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academics frame evaluation criteria for integrated ideological and political teaching, and how they tie them to Party-defined educational goals.

On Slavoj Žižek's idea of communism 论齐泽克的共产主义理念 Li Xixiang Li Xixiang examines Slavoj Žižek's idea of communism, asking what it consists of and whether it holds up. The article argues that Žižek's critique of capitalism is forceful and his call for communism is more radical than Alain Badiou's. In Li's assessment, however, it remains ambiguous and wavering, and its account of the revolutionary subject falls into a kind of utopianism that deserves critical reflection. The article has three parts. It first sets out Žižek's critique of capitalism and his case for communism, drawing on his rejection of Fukuyama's end of history and his claim that the 9/11 attacks and the 2008 financial crisis show capitalism in a terminal impasse. It then identifies four dimensions of his idea: the necessity of communism, the critique of capitalist ideological utopia, a new proletarian subject, and an eschatological conception of time. Finally it compares Žižek with Badiou and with Ernesto Laclau's critique. Li reports that Žižek sees four antagonisms capitalism cannot resolve: ecological catastrophe, the inadequacy of private property for 'intellectual property', the social and ethical implications of biogenetics, and new forms of apartheid. Communism is therefore an 'eternal' idea only in the Hegelian sense of having to be reinvented in each historical situation. His proletariat is every individual stripped of substance, so that 'we are the ones we have been waiting for', and he acts in 'time of the end' by intervening in the present from the standpoint of a possible future disaster. Badiou, by contrast, treats communism as a hypothesis through which individuals become subjects after an event occurs. Li finds Žižek's immediacy more radical but sees hesitation behind it, citing his remark that he is not wholly opposed to capitalism and his treatment of it as an ontological fact, which Li says brings him close to Fukuyama. Li concludes that Žižek's critique of capitalism is incomplete, his revolutionary subject is to some extent empty, and his call for radical action cannot be carried out. In this account it becomes an empty gesture that quietly supports existing reality, so that Žižek himself falls into a form of the cynical realism he criticises. Li cites Laclau's charge of 'political nihilism' in support. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist academic's critical assessment of Žižek's communism, set against Badiou and Laclau, especially on the revolutionary subject.

Western left-wing digital socialist theory: drivers, features and resistance 西方左翼数字社会主义理论：动力、特征与抗争 Li Quan Du Min Li Quan and Du Min examine the family of Western left-wing theories that tie socialism to digital technology. Since Kevin Kelly coined 'digital socialism' in 2009, the authors say, the concept has been debated and extended. They argue that, in a broad sense, cybercommunism, communicative socialism, platform socialism and Kelly's narrow 'digital socialism' share a common aim. All of them rest on reflection on socialist elements generated by digitalisation and on a critique of capitalism. The article has four parts. It first sets out the historical types of digital socialism and the forces driving them. It then identifies the theory's features, covering its themes, its lines of development and its practical prospects. Next it discusses how these theories resist capitalism, through ideology, plunder and the logic of capital. It closes by assessing their value and limits. Thinkers discussed include Paul Cockshott, Christian Fuchs, Dimitris Boucas, James Muldoon, Evgeny Morozov and Dan Schiller. Li and Du name three drivers: the revision of traditional socialism, the critique of contemporary capitalism, and the critique of digital exploitation. On the first, they trace cybercommunism to the old debate over whether central planning is computable, citing Soviet planning and Allende's Chile. They say theories of digital socialism rest on three kinds of judgement. The factual judgement is that networked communities already contain non-capitalist, shared relations; the authors consider Kelly's version a mere description that ignores private ownership. The value judgement is that digital work is 'free' and 'autonomous'; Fuchs's analysis of alienation is cited against this. The logical judgement concerns spontaneous versus conscious transformation, and the authors side with the conscious view of Morozov and others. They argue that these theories grow from capitalist cultural and platform soil and say little about political change. The authors credit digital socialism with forward-looking thought and with critical value against ideological concealment, appropriation of digital labour and the privatisation of infrastructure. They nevertheless judge it historically limited. Citing Lenin on the dictatorship of the proletariat, they argue that the theories neglect class consciousness among digital workers and the movement needed to overthrow capitalism. In their view the revolutionary spirit stays confined to theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey and assessment of Western digital-socialist currents, from cybercommunism to platform socialism.

The Communist Party of Vietnam's indigenous exploration of modernization 越南共产党推进现代化建设的本土探索 Wang Chengjiu Lai Huiting Wang Chengjiu and Lai Huiting ask how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has pursued socialist modernization, and what this shows against the idea that modernization means Westernization. Starting from the debate prompted by Chinese modernization, they present Vietnam as a second case. They argue that the CPV has broken with the Soviet model and kept industrialization and modernization 'socialist-oriented', and that this has produced notable results alongside serious problems. The article has four parts. It first traces three stages: early exploration through industrialization (1954–1986), a turning point from 'industrialization' to 'industrialization and modernization' (1986–1996), and fast-track advance since 1996. It then lists five main measures, sets out achievements with statistics, and ends with current problems. The authors draw on CPV congress and plenum documents, including the 2022 Resolution 29 that extends the programme to 2030 and 2045. In the authors' account, early policy followed the Soviet example by prioritising heavy industry at 'fast, vigorous, steady' speed, and this unbalanced the economy and led to crisis. After 1986 the CPV is said to have corrected course. It made agriculture the 'front of first importance', adopted a 'fast and sustainable' growth concept, and revised its phased targets. It also developed a socialist-oriented market economy, opened to the world while treating domestic resources as primary, and used the science and technology revolution, the knowledge economy and digital transformation as levers for leapfrogging. The authors cite GDP growth, structural change, urbanization, rural development, poverty reduction and rising life expectancy as results. The authors also list problems: slowing growth, heavy reliance on foreign direct investment, low local content and a place at the bottom of value chains, weak state-owned and private enterprises, and shortages of skilled personnel. They conclude that Vietnam's path, like China's, goes beyond the Soviet model and refutes 'modernization equals Westernization', and that it adds to socialist countries' experience. They also see the recent China–Vietnam joint statement on a community with a shared future as a favourable opportunity. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Vietnam's modernization policy since 1954, with its statistics and Party documents, as seen from the Chinese debate on socialist modernization.

Youth ideological and political education in light of the evolution of educational digitalization 基于教育数字化演进之路的青年思想政治教育探究 Feng Pei Marking 40 years since the establishment of the ideological and political education discipline and 30 years since China's full internet connection, Feng Pei asks what the history of educational digitalization teaches about how to guide young people ideologically. The article argues that, although digital technologies keep changing, certain constants run through them, and that youth ideological and political education should use these constants to lead students' new needs as digital education moves from informatization to full digitalization. The article first traces three stages of Chinese educational digitalization, seen from the perspective of ideological and cultural communication: a text-based 1.0 era around 2000 (desktop computers, BBS forums, blogs), an image-based 2.0 era after 2010 (mobile phones, MOOCs, Weibo, WeChat, short video), and an intelligent 3.0 era since 2013 (big data, virtual simulation, generative AI). It then draws three lessons from this history and three directions for guidance. Feng frames the discussion with Xi Jinping's remarks on the internet and AI and with the "seven focal points" of Xi Jinping's thought on culture. Feng's central move is to distinguish the "constant within change" from the "new within the constant". The three constants are that content is king, that meeting individual needs is fundamental, and that connection and resonance are essential. Feng draws on Marx's account of needs as driving history to support the second. For each constant, Feng identifies a new feature of today's students and a matching task. Students born after 1995 and 2000 are said to be fragmented in their information intake, more emotionally expressive online, drawn to "shallow socializing", and inclined to conceal their real thinking in closed peer circles. Feng warns that algorithmic "information cocoons" and generative AI carry risks, including simulated empathy displacing real contact. The article also notes that ideological and political work suffers from weak sensitivity to student needs, staff turnover and costly, hard-to-scale virtual simulation. Feng concludes that educators should keep the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent as the guiding orientation, and renew it in three ways. They should respond sensitively to students' changing needs, supply precise and vivid content that is neither sensationalised nor pandering, and link the seven subsystems of university ideological and political work online and offline. Concrete proposals include "one-stop student communities", AI corpora for career, mental health and academic guidance, open feedback systems to evaluate staff performance, and regional university alliances to share simulation resources. The aim is to serve Chinese modernization by raising a new generation. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how ideological and political educators propose to respond to generative AI, algorithms and youth online culture.

Forging strong organizations and building a sound contingent of cadres as an important focus 以锻造坚强组织、建设过硬队伍为重要着力点 Wang Tingda This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, interprets one of the "nine requirements" that Xi Jinping set out at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection: advancing the Party's self-reform by forging strong organizations and building a sound contingent of cadres. Wang argues that a tightly knit organizational system is the source of a Marxist party's strength. Pursuing this focus, in the author's view, shows the Party's resolve to build such a system and to coordinate Party building at every level and in every field. The article has three parts. The first explains why organization matters, drawing on Xi's statement that the Party's strength comes from its organization, and on the Party's record since its founding more than a century ago. The second sets out how to strengthen the political and organizational functions of Party organizations, as laid out at the 20th Party Congress (2022). The third turns to cadres, Party members and talent. Wang's core claim is that the Party's central, local and primary-level organizations form a chain from the "first kilometre" to the "last kilometre" of carrying out the Central Committee's decisions. The author says the political and organizational functions reinforce each other, and proposes five areas of work. These are political building, theoretical education, tighter implementation, the mass line, and "immunity" through the Party's self-reform. On cadres, Wang calls for the principle that the Party manages cadres, with political reliability ranked first among the criteria for a "good cadre". The author also calls for strict entry and exit rules for membership, more recruitment from workers, farmers and young intellectuals, and the gathering of patriotic talent. Wang concludes that comprehensive Party organization and a leadership that can command the whole Party to act together is an advantage no other party in the world has. Deepening the Party's self-reform through strong organizations and sound cadres, the author holds, will supply continuing momentum for high-quality development. Read the original if you want to see how Party-building discourse in 2024 linked organization, cadre selection and membership management to the Party's self-reform.

Contributing the strength of higher education in the new era to accelerating the development of new quality productive forces 为推动新质生产力加快发展贡献新时代高等教育力量 Zhang Jun Written after Xi Jinping's speech at the 11th collective study session of the Political Bureau (31 January 2024), this article asks what role universities should play in speeding up new quality productive forces. Zhang argues that higher education is the key point where education, science and technology, and talent converge, and so a foundational link in developing productive forces. Universities should therefore study Xi's statements on the subject and carry out education reform, scientific innovation and talent training accordingly. The article has three parts. The first treats accelerating new quality productive forces as an important mission of higher education. The second sets out the tasks this places on universities. The third proposes routes for the new era. Zhang draws heavily on Xi's remarks, especially on innovation, high-quality development and the 'Party's leadership of universities'. In the first part, Zhang reasons that each major leap in productive forces has produced demand for new kinds of workers and changed education, from papermaking and printing to the three industrial revolutions. Three justifications follow: the modernization of education, the building of a major world centre for talent and an innovation highland, and the creation of world-class universities with Chinese characteristics, whose disciplines, teaching and governance new quality productive forces are said to restructure. The second part names three tasks: raising the quality of home-grown talent, advancing original and disruptive technological innovation toward high-level scientific and technological self-reliance, and speeding the conversion of research results into industry. The third part's routes are: strengthen Party leadership of universities, including the president responsibility system under the Party committee; pursue research at the world frontier and on national strategic needs; reshape talent-training goals, methods and evaluation; and let discipline building lead the modern industrial system through basic, emerging and interdisciplinary fields. Zhang concludes that universities should build education, science and technology, and talent into a unified strategic base, innovation highland and stronghold. The article gives concrete measures: basic-discipline training bases, technology-transfer bodies, organised industry–education integration, and interdisciplinary teams and platforms for fields such as quantum and life sciences. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal translates Xi's new quality productive forces discourse into a programme for university governance, talent training and discipline planning.

Upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership 坚持和加强党的全面领导 Li Haiqing Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 6), Li Haiqing takes up the first of the "thirteen upholds" that the June 2023 national organisation work conference used to summarise Xi Jinping's thinking on Party building: upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership. Li argues that this is an inherent requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics, that it must be put into practice in a comprehensive, systematic and holistic way, and that it depends on full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and on the Party's self-reform. The piece is a short theoretical commentary in three numbered sections. The first explains why Party leadership is essential to socialism with Chinese characteristics and to Chinese modernization. The second unpacks the 20th Party Congress (2022) formula that Party leadership is "comprehensive, systematic and holistic". The third links leadership to the Party's self-reform, with a historical survey from the 1927 August 7 Meeting to the present. Li builds on Xi Jinping's statements that Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Li's reading, a complex international and domestic environment raises the demands on the Party's capacity to set direction, manage risk and push reform. Li concludes that without Party leadership, national strength and rejuvenation would be illusory. Li then defines the three terms. "Comprehensive" covers the objects, content, process and methods of leadership, though the Party "oversees but does not take over" and must act within the constitution and law. "Systematic" means a complete system of leadership institutions. "Holistic" means every level of Party organisation, and the Party and state apparatus, functions in coordination. The first priority is upholding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee, through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. In the third section Li holds that willingness to undertake self-reform distinguishes the Party from other parties and explains how it has escaped the historical cycle of rise and fall. Li presents the Party's history as both a social revolution and a self-reform, and credits the anti-corruption campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with removing serious hidden dangers and reversing lax Party discipline. Li concludes that self-reform supplies the political guarantee for national strength and rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party scholars justify the doctrine of overall Party leadership and link it to Party discipline.

Building the spiritual foundation and cultivating new people of the era Ideological and political theory courses in the new era 铸牢精神之基 培育时代新人 Han Hua Han Hua's article, published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, asks how ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) in schools and universities can cultivate "new people of the era" (shidai xinren). Drawing throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Han argues that these courses are the key vehicle for implementing the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent. They are, in this account, central to ensuring that the Party's cause and the building of a modern socialist country have successors. The article is organised in three parts. The first deals with education in ideals and convictions, which Han calls the red thread running through the courses. The second turns to teaching scientific ways of thinking. The third treats the cultivation of new people of the era as a systematic project in which the courses occupy a pivotal place across the stages of a young person's development. Each part is built around dated statements by Xi, from the 2016 national conference on ideological and political work in universities to the 2023 study campaign on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Han's central claims are that firm convictions come from scientific theory, and that teachers must therefore present Marxism and Xi's thought in a way that is deep, thorough and lively, rather than as empty preaching. The courses should explain why the Party, Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics are, in the author's words, effective and good, and help students merge personal ideals with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Han adds that students need Marxist standpoints, viewpoints and methods, including historical, dialectical, systemic and innovative thinking, not just abstract concepts. The courses should also move progressively from primary school to university, address practical problems in study, careers and daily life, and put moral education first. Han concludes that the courses must be reformed in teaching concepts, content, methods and means, so that students are willing to learn and can apply what they learn. The aim is talent who support Party leadership and the socialist system and commit their lives to socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact, Xi-quotation-based statement of how Party publications frame the purpose and method of ideological and political courses in the new era.

Consolidating and extending the results of the theme education campaign and advancing the modernization of grassroots governance 巩固拓展主题教育成果 奋力推进基层治理现代化 Beijing Institute of Party Building This commentary by the Beijing Institute of Party Building takes up Xi Jinping's speech of 31 January 2024 on consolidating and extending the results of the Party's theme education campaign. It asks how those results can be turned into progress in modernizing grassroots governance. The authors argue that Party building must lead grassroots governance, and that doing so supports Chinese modernization. The article is organised around four slogans from the campaign: learning to forge the soul, to increase wisdom, to correct work style and to promote action. Under each it sets out one task: building the ideological foundation, innovating ideas and measures, forging the governance workforce, and ensuring tasks are carried out. Each section draws heavily on Xi's remarks on grassroots work and pairs them with recommendations. The first move is to justify the priority given to the grassroots. Citing Xi, the authors present grassroots governance as the base of the Party's rule, a way to meet people's aspirations for a better life, and a precondition for modernizing national governance. The second move is institutional. They call for fuller Party leadership, noting that Party-led governance risks becoming diluted or hollow. They also call for a streamlined grassroots management system, with resources, management and services moved down to the street and township level. Further proposals are wider participation by residents, social organisations and market actors, and combining self-governance, rule of law and moral governance. The third move concerns cadres and delivery. The authors call for the "Fengqiao experience" and the "four go-to-the-grassroots" practice. They also want sustained correction of formalism and bureaucratism to lighten the burden on grassroots officials, and training for village and community Party secretaries. They add a closed-loop, full-cycle management system with a performance evaluation in which residents' satisfaction carries weight, plus more funding and better community service facilities. The authors conclude that grassroots governance works as a foundation for national governance, summed up in the phrase "good governance at the grassroots" underpinning "the governance of a great country". They propose that Party committees and governments at every level keep these tasks in view and take responsibility for results. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party research body translates Xi Jinping's speeches into a practical agenda for grassroots governance, including its stated problems and its remedies.

Re-examining the labour theory of value in the age of artificial intelligence 人工智能时代劳动价值论再审视 Li Nan Li Nan takes up the doubts that "machines replacing humans" and "unmanned factories" have raised about Marx's labour theory of value. The article asks how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes labour, whether the theory still applies, and how it should be put into practice. Li answers that AI changes the forms of labour and the realisation of value without displacing living labour as the sole source of value, so the theory remains a scientific guide. The article has three parts. The first describes how AI reshapes labour and shifts value. The second clarifies three points of dispute: the uniqueness of the source of value, the standing of the worker as subject, and the nature of capital. The third sets out how to uphold the theory in practice, and cites Xi Jinping on AI as support for the Party's people-centred orientation. In the first part, Li argues that the relation between living and objectified labour grows more complex, with objectified labour taking a larger share. New forms such as digital labour appear, and working time and space extend. Higher organic composition of capital and falling value per commodity make use-value and value move in opposite directions. In the second part, Li rejects autonomist and knowledge-theory claims that intellect or knowledge creates value. Following Marx's view of labour as a totality, Li says unmanned factories must be assessed together with the upstream and downstream work of R&D, assembly, maintenance and distribution, where living labour adds value. AI is still a "technical being" created by human labour, and humans still supply the purposes of labour. Li also rejects the accelerationist hope that AI can transcend capitalism. In Li's account, AI intensifies the opposition between capital and labour, monopoly, and exploitation, and makes exploitation less visible, for instance through users' unpaid "non-employment labour" that trains models. Li calls for three things. The first is to uphold the monistic view of living labour as the source of value while broadening the concept to cover digital labour. The second is to keep the worker's subject status, through innovation-oriented training, AI education and all-round human development. The third is to treat capital and AI dialectically, using the basic economic system, fair distribution and anti-monopoly and data regulation to curb the disorderly expansion of capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of the labour theory of value against claims that AI makes living labour obsolete, together with the policy proposals Li draws from it.

Cultivating the course (yangke): the essential skill for ideological and political theory teachers who want more effective teaching 养课：思政课教师提高教学实效性必须练就的功夫 Lu Binghui Five years after Xi Jinping's 18 March 2019 speech at the symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses, Lu Binghui argues that teachers have become technically proficient at preparing and delivering lessons. Even so, the author holds that this is not enough to raise student attendance and attentiveness. The article proposes "yangke" (cultivating the course) as a further requirement: the teacher's own work on personal character, on abilities and qualities, and on the teaching environment. The article is built around three headings that match the three dimensions of yangke. Part one reads the speech's "six requirements" for teachers as a path to moral cultivation. Part two takes the "eight unifications" as the key to building ability. Part three treats creating a good classroom atmosphere as the practical measure. Lu draws on classical Chinese sayings, Marx, Lenin and the speech itself, and cites an Anhui provincial policy from 2022 on appointing student ideological-political officers. Lu groups the six requirements into three qualities: genuine feeling (strong politics and deep commitment), skill (new thinking and broad vision, combining specialist depth with breadth) and good character (strict self-discipline and upright personality). The eight unifications are applied to the teacher's professional stance, content and methods. Lu distinguishes facts, cases and materials as three ways of telling stories, and says methods should emphasise the constructive over the critical, diversity over uniformity, inspiration over indoctrination, and implicit over explicit education. The author's most distinctive move is an analogy with a pop star's concert. A teacher meets strangers with no build-up, so the first lesson is decisive, and the teacher must create a good "soft environment". For university teaching, Lu urges teachers to relax their habitual absolute dominance of the classroom and move closer to students. Suggested steps include appointing class representatives and ideological-political officers and forming interest groups. Teachers should also join campus cultural activities and summer social practice, and show family-like concern for students' thinking and daily lives. Lu contends this will strengthen rather than weaken the teacher's guiding role. Read the original if you study ideological and political education in Chinese universities and want a detailed, practice-oriented reading of Xi Jinping's 2019 speech.

Climate-political positions of Europe's radical left parties and the social-ecological transformation 欧洲激进左翼政党的气候政治立场与社会生态转型探析 Wang Congcong How have Europe's radical left parties responded to the climate and ecological crisis, and how do their positions differ from those of other party families? Wang argues that these parties blame capitalism for the crisis. They reject the EU's neoliberal "European Green Deal" and offer a "Left Green New Deal" built on social-ecological transformation, which stresses social justice more than the positions of the Greens and social democrats. The article has four parts. It first surveys radical left responses at the organisational level (the "Now, The People" platform, the European Left Party, the GUE/NGL parliamentary group) and at the level of manifestos and policy reports. It then reconstructs the theory of social-ecological transformation, which draws on the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation and Ulrich Brand. Next, it compares climate and energy positions of Germany's and Sweden's parties across the left–right spectrum. A conclusion assesses the theory and the practice. Wang identifies three strands in the radical left's transformation project. The first is a critique of the roots of the crisis: capitalist growth and profit-seeking, "green growth" as a corporate slogan, and climate injustice between rich and poor and between North and South. The second is a "red-green" vision with a new economic model under democratic planning, public ownership and control of energy, and a "just transition" with retraining and secure jobs. The third is a broad alliance of parties, unions and social movements, for example the European Forum of Left, Green and Progressive Forces. In the German and Swedish comparison, Wang finds the radical left and the Greens setting earlier carbon-neutrality targets than social democrats. Centre-right parties favour market and technological means, and the far right is divided: Germany's AfD is sceptical of climate policy, while the Sweden Democrats support national targets and nuclear power. Wang concludes that the radical left's discourse offers an alternative to neoliberal "green capitalism" and helps explain its limits. Its response is shaped by ideology, history and internal factions as well as external conditions. In practice, Wang says, the parties' proposals are poorly integrated, their influence on mainstream policy is limited, and the programme still needs testing. Wang calls on them to sharpen their distinct "red-green" profile against social-democratic and Green eco-modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed survey of party documents and national cases on the European left's climate and energy policy.

Advancing the integrated development of ideological and political courses across primary, secondary and tertiary schools: following the fundamental principles, strengthening practice, seeking innovation 推进大中小学思政课一体化建设：循根本、强实践、求创新 Xu Rong Five years after Xi Jinping called in March 2019 for the integrated development of ideological and political courses (sizheng ke) from primary school to university to be treated as an important project, Xu Rong asks how that work can reach a new stage of high-quality development. The article argues that integration should rest on clearly understood fundamental principles, be driven by practice that confronts concrete bottlenecks, and be renewed through innovation suited to a changed educational and technological environment. The article has three parts. The first sets out the guiding principles: serving national strategic needs, promoting students' growth, and improving teaching effectiveness. The second examines the practical logic of integration through a practice-oriented outlook, a strong problem awareness and effective coordination mechanisms. The third looks ahead to innovation under three headings: new qualities in the teaching ecosystem, new domains opened by digital and intelligent technology, and new strategies for cooperation between school stages. Xu reviews official documents issued since 2019, including guidance on teacher development and on building integration communities. Xu identifies obstacles that persist despite the progress. Teachers tend to stay within their own stage, there is too little drive for communication between stages, and knowledge is sometimes repeated without deepening students' values. Costs and benefits of developing resources are also hard to share across institutions. The author warns against superficial or patchwork integration. They propose mutual supervision and feedback between stages, and argue that students' thinking does not develop linearly, so links between stages must be dynamic. On technology, Xu raises questions about data connectivity, digital twins and human–machine relations. Xu also argues that cooperation lacks a leading body and a cross-boundary governance mechanism, and calls for both so that stage boundaries become overlapping zones of shared knowledge. Xu concludes that integration is fundamentally a collective undertaking that needs coordination, a lead organisation and cross-domain governance. It must also adapt to the digital and intelligent age. The article mostly poses questions and sets directions rather than reporting empirical results. Read the original if you study how Chinese educational policy conceives the coordination of ideological and political education across school stages, or want to see how the field is taking up digital technology.

Building a spiral-ascending curriculum for teaching a sense of community of the Chinese nation across primary, secondary and university ideological and political courses 大中小学思政课中华民族共同体意识教学内容的螺旋上升式构建研究 Li Chunhui Li Chunhui asks how teaching on the sense of community of the Chinese nation (Zhonghua minzu gongtongti yishi) should be organised across primary school, secondary school and university ideological and political courses. The article argues that content should be built in a "spiral-ascending" way, deepening stage by stage to match students' cognitive development. Li presents this as important for strengthening students' "five identifications" and for advancing the building of the Chinese national community. The article has four parts. It first defines the concept and its scope, dividing it into political, economic, cultural and shared-destiny dimensions, drawing on Fei Xiaotong's "pluralism within unity" formula and on Xi Jinping's statements. It then sets out why a spiral structure matters, proposes three guiding principles, and finally gives concrete teaching paths for each of the four dimensions at primary, secondary and university level. Li's core argument rests on three claims about significance: the spiral design moves from shallow to deep as students' cognition and values develop; it fills out the integrated construction of ideological and political courses from simple to complex; and students, as carriers of the idea, spread it from "points" to a wider "surface" of society. The three principles are to combine a top-level goal with stage goals, completeness with continuity, and gradual progression with continuity across stages. Concretely, primary teaching is activity-based (films, museum visits, ethnic food and costume exchanges, group projects); secondary teaching is theory- and case-based (national security cases, poverty alleviation, large-scale West-to-East resource projects, the Covid-19 response); university teaching is systematic and classics-based, using Marx and the Party's history. Li also proposes discussions that rebut Western criticism of China's ethnic affairs. Li concludes that coordinated, step-by-step content design, with teachers drawing on Xi Jinping's thinking on ethnic work and enriching resources at each stage, is the route to embedding the sense of community in students. This is framed as serving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want detailed examples of how Chinese educators propose to translate the official concept of forging a sense of community of the Chinese nation into stage-specific classroom content.

Lenin's thought on the correct tactics of the proletarian party and its implications A textual analysis based on "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder 列宁关于无产阶级政党的正确策略思想及其启示 Kang Rui Hong Yan Kang Rui and Hong Yan ask what Lenin meant by "correct tactics" for a proletarian party and how such tactics should be formulated. Working from "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder, they argue that Lenin there set out a systematic theory of tactics against the "Left" currents in the early twentieth-century international communist movement.
