In their account it offers a guide for the Communist Party of China as it builds a modern socialist great power. The article has three parts. The first defines correct tactics through three features: they guide the Party's political activity, they combine firmness of principle with flexibility, and they help to "develop, aid and arouse" revolutions elsewhere. The second part draws four methodological requirements from the text. The third turns to what the authors call contemporary lessons for the Chinese Party, citing Xi Jinping and the 20th Party Congress (2022). On definition, the authors stress Lenin's distinction between reasonable compromise, which serves proletarian interests and raises the movement's consciousness and fighting capacity, and the compromise of traitors, which they describe as capitulation to the bourgeoisie. On method, they say tactics must rest on a correct grasp of Marxist theory, on the basic features of the epoch (the Bolsheviks' reading of the shift from bourgeois parliamentarism to the dictatorship of the proletariat is the example), on the experience of earlier revolutions adapted to "national and state differences", and on a sober estimate of all class forces rather than revolutionary mood. The "Left" communists, they argue, failed on each count, for instance by dogmatically rejecting parliaments and any compromise. The authors conclude that the Party must uphold and develop Marxism, grasp the pulse of the times, use dialectical thinking and unite all who can be united. They present the new development philosophy, the answers to the "questions of China and of the world" in the 20th Party Congress report, and the expansion of the united front as applications of Lenin's tactical thinking. Read the original if you want a close reading of Lenin's tactical writings as they are presented in Chinese Party-theory scholarship, and an example of how that reading is tied to current Party policy.

Three paths for building an autonomous knowledge system in the discipline of ideological and political education 思想政治教育学科自主知识体系建构的三重进路 Zhang Yixiang Zhang Yixiang takes up a question for the discipline of ideological and political education, which the article says has developed for forty years into one of the most dynamic fields within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. The question is how it should build its own autonomous knowledge system and pursue high-quality development in the new era. Zhang argues that this requires attention at three levels: scholarly self-awareness, the deepening of the discipline's internal content, and innovation through coordination. The article was published in 2024 in Ideological and Theoretical Education Research and opens with Xi Jinping's call to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. The article has three main sections, each divided into three sub-points. The first concerns scholars' initiative and confidence, and distinguishes three levels of autonomy in the discipline's knowledge. The second works through the discipline's content along the dimensions of breadth, depth and boundary. The third turns to innovation: guidance by Marxism, grounding in Chinese modernization, and coordination of resources. Zhang draws on the three-part framing of discipline system, academic system and discourse system throughout. Zhang holds that the discipline has not fully left its early 'apprentice' state of borrowing from pedagogy, ethics, management, psychology and political science. Some scholars, the author says, lack confidence and drift to other fields. Knowledge is classed as fully autonomous (core theory such as the nature, structure and laws of the field), predominantly autonomous (cross-disciplinary areas such as the psychology or management of ideological and political education) and jointly studied (such as Xi Jinping's thought on culture or social trends). Zhang sees meta-theory as lagging, the branch subjects as underdeveloped, and the discourse system as the weakest link, with little international influence. Contested points such as whether the process has a single or dual subject also need settling. The author proposes new fields, including work with new economic organisations, new social organisations and new employment groups, and judges that research on these is almost absent. On innovation, Zhang calls for Marxism as the guide, with nourishment from the classics, the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, fine traditional Chinese culture, and critically absorbed foreign scholarship. The discipline should also study Chinese modernization, including its content, value and implementation paths. Zhang further urges coordination among academic resources (including artificial intelligence and engineering fields), researchers and practitioners, publishing platforms and policy support. Read the original if you want a view from within the discipline of its perceived weaknesses and agenda for building an autonomous knowledge system in ideological and political education.

The resurgence of anti-intellectualism in contemporary America Rooted in the internal contradictions of meritocracy 当代美国反智主义的再兴起 Sun Chenghao Zhang Chenghao Why has anti-intellectualism returned to American life, and why did earlier predictions of its decline fail? The authors argue that Richard Hofstadter's 1960s explanation, built around religion, McCarthyism and educational shortcomings, no longer accounts for the current wave. They propose that meritocracy, understood as both a distribution system and an ideology of 'equal opportunity' and 'rewards for the able', is the main driver of the new anti-intellectualism. The article begins by reviewing the concept of anti-intellectualism (drawing on Hofstadter and Daniel Rigney) and the existing literature on its causes. It then analyses meritocracy's origins, its turn into a conservative ideology after the 1980s, and its defects. It goes on to trace how meritocracy feeds anti-intellectualism through education, elite–mass antagonism and the loss of work dignity and civic spirit. It ends with the features and consequences of the new wave. The authors make three main moves. First, they hold that meritocracy masks substantive inequality: elites monopolise elite schooling through inherited cultural capital, so education becomes class-stratified and instrumental and no longer cultivates independent, reflective thought. Second, they argue that meritocratic morality casts the successful as deserving and the unsuccessful as lazy or stupid, while elite domination of public office breaks representation. As evidence they cite Congress, where no member of the 118th Congress was formerly an industrial worker, and the educational split in the 2016 vote. Third, they claim that the resulting resentment is directed less at knowledge itself than at elites, and that it expresses itself in more radical, populist forms, including refusal of masks and vaccines and the storming of the Capitol. The authors conclude that the new wave makes social issues more conservative (climate change, abortion), erodes the legitimacy of American democracy, and weakens national cohesion and the country's international standing and hegemony. They add that the United States cannot simply abandon meritocracy for hereditary hierarchy, and that whether it can calm angry, anti-elite citizens remains an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of American populism that links education, representation and distribution to anti-intellectualism, with the supporting data they cite.

Main achievements, key lessons and innovation directions in building university ideological and political theory courses in the new era 新时代高校思政课建设的主要成就、重要经验和创新向度 Yang Xiaohui Yang Xiaohui takes stock of how university ideological and political theory courses (sizheng ke) have developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and especially in the five years after the 2019 symposium for teachers of these courses. The article argues that guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has produced a fundamental shift in the field. In Yang's account, this shift has delivered historic achievements, transferable lessons and clear directions for further innovation. The article has three parts. The first lists five achievements: the courses' higher strategic standing, more developed guiding concepts, the progress of Party theory 'entering textbooks, classrooms and minds', a larger and better teaching force, and stronger safeguard mechanisms. The second distils six lessons from this record. The third sets out five directions for innovation, drawing on official figures such as growth in teacher numbers and degree-granting programmes, and on a 2017 national survey of student satisfaction. Yang's argument rests on a few moves. The achievements are tied to concepts such as integrated course-building across primary school to university, the 'big ideological and political course', and the new Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought course and textbook. The lessons stress strengthening Party leadership, putting students at the centre, combining top-level planning with grassroots experiment, and balancing preserving fundamentals with innovation. Yang also pairs problem-orientation with goal-orientation and joins the 'big course' concept to mechanisms for cooperation. For the future, Yang calls for systematic study of Xi's statements on these courses, stronger conviction and creativity among teachers, and support from Marxism schools and the Marxist theory discipline. Yang also calls for clearer duties for Party and Communist Youth League organisations and for better coordination among university departments, which Yang says still sometimes work at cross purposes. Yang concludes that building these courses should be treated as a systematic project under Party leadership, one that adapts to changing circumstances while keeping the courses' political nature. The article is written from within the official education system and relies on policy documents and official statistics rather than independent evaluation. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese higher-education authorities describe their achievements and priorities in ideological and political course reform.

The content of building an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of ideological and political education 思想政治教育学科自主知识体系的建构内容 Zhong Qidong After four decades of disciplinary development, ideological and political education has built a knowledge system centred on its principles and methods. Zhong Qidong asks what knowledge supports an autonomous version of that system, in what sense it is autonomous, and how knowledge about ideological and political education relates to the knowledge used to carry it out. The author argues that the two are closely interlinked and that the autonomous system must integrate both. The article has three parts. The first sets out a historical-materialist basis, asking whether ideology is itself knowledge. The second examines the Chinese context for building autonomous knowledge through four relationships. The third lays out the content of the system, divided into constitutive knowledge (what ideological and political education is) and functional knowledge (how it operates). Zhong draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Xi Jinping and existing work by Chinese scholars in the field. Zhong reads Marx and Engels as rejecting ideology as false consciousness while not denying that ideology is knowledge. Ideology generalises, so it counts as knowledge, but only a Marxism grounded in real individuals' material life is, in the author's reading, "genuine knowledge" and a "scientific ideology". On this basis the author describes a concentric knowledge spectrum around the discipline's own knowledge. Autonomous knowledge, in Zhong's definition, is new knowledge generated by applying existing knowledge, not self-certified knowledge. It requires handling four relationships: with Western knowledge, with traditional moral cultivation, with Chinese practice and experience, and with other disciplines. Constitutive knowledge is built from concepts (with ideology as the base concept), categories ("thought and reality"), propositions and ideas. Functional knowledge comprises laws (ideological laws), methods (with materialist dialectics as the master method) and a supporting body of substantive knowledge borrowed from other disciplines. Zhong concludes that the main tasks are to reflect on and go beyond Western knowledge, inherit and sublate traditional moral education, interpret Chinese practice for the world, and clarify disciplinary boundaries. Autonomy is only relative, and knowledge borrowed from other fields should be recast as the discipline's own concepts and principles through creative transformation. The author also asks scholars to build a conceptual system around Xi Jinping's description of the Second Integration as a further liberation of thought. Read the original if you study the theoretical foundations of ideological and political education as a discipline, or how Chinese scholars link Marxist ideology theory to disciplinary autonomy.

The development of Vietnam's theory of socialist democracy since Đổi Mới (reform and opening up) 革新开放以来越南社会主义民主理论发展研究 Ruan Yinping Ruan asks how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has developed its theory of socialist democracy since the Đổi Mới policy of renovation and opening up began in 1986. The article argues that, guided by Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, the CPV has steadily revised its understanding of democracy and built a distinctive body of theory. In Ruan's account this theory treats democracy as both the goal and the driving force of socialist construction. It holds that the state should belong to the people, come from the people and serve the people. The article has three parts. The first sets out the background: economic transition, political reform, and social change such as the rise of a middle class, which Ruan says made the older theory inadequate. The second traces how the CPV's understanding of democracy's essence, subject, status and content changed across its successive national congresses. The third presents the theory of democratic construction, which Ruan summarises as one overall model, two key relationships, three basic forms and five principles. Ruan argues that the CPV moved from the earlier language of "collective mastery" and the working people to "the people" as a whole, including entrepreneurs and the private sector. Democracy was placed ahead of fairness in the 2011 platform and became the theme of the 12th Congress. The overall model is "the Party leads, the state manages, the people are masters", to which the 13th Congress (2021) added the Fatherland Front and other organisations. The two relationships are democracy with national unity, and democracy with law and social order; Ruan quotes CPV leaders rejecting multiparty politics and pluralism. The three forms are direct, representative and grassroots democracy. The five principles are popular sovereignty, Party leadership, democratic centralism, the rule of law, and checks and supervision over power. The author presents Vietnam's socialist democracy as a surpassing of Western "liberal democracy", as the CPV sees it. Ruan concludes that, through renovation, the CPV has produced distinctive concepts and institutional arrangements that secure Vietnam's democratic construction. The author says these also offer theoretical understanding and practical experience for building socialist democratic theory in a period of great global change, and for developing democracy under a socialist market economy. Read the original if you study Vietnam's official political theory, the CPV's congress documents on democracy, or comparative work on socialist-oriented democratic discourse as presented from China.

The logic of constructing an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of ideological and political education 思想政治教育学科自主知识体系的建构逻辑 Li Hui Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's call to build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences, this article asks how the discipline of ideological and political education should construct its own autonomous knowledge system. Li Hui argues that the task answers four questions: for whom and by whom the system is built, what it contains, and how it is built. In Li's account these correspond to five constructive logics, and Li holds that the effort has a dual effect: the discipline is to serve as a model for others, and the work marks a new stage in its own development. The article is organised in five sections, each devoted to one logic: the logic of subjectivity, grounded in Communist Party leadership; the logic of guidance, grounded in Marxism; goal orientation centred on fostering virtue and cultivating talent; the holistic logic of systems thinking; and the logic of knowledge production through critical inheritance. Li draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches on philosophy and the social sciences and on Party documents, and refers to debates within the discipline. On subjectivity, Li separates the "value subject" from the "building subject" and resolves a long-running dispute over whether the discipline serves scholars or the Party. Li concludes that it serves the Party and the people, and that its builders form a layered system of leadership, administrative and academic actors, with the Party holding leadership, management and discursive power. On guidance, Li holds that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is itself the process by which an autonomous knowledge system emerges. On goals, Li rejects value-neutrality and value-clarification positions, arguing that the discipline is both knowledge education and value education. Under systems thinking, Li treats the whole person, integrated education, socialist ideology and social development as the bases for constructing the system. Under critical inheritance, Li calls for drawing on Marxism, Party experience, traditional culture and foreign scholarship while criticising Western ideology. Li concludes that the five logics support one another. Subjectivity and guidance secure autonomy, goal orientation makes them concrete in the educational process, holistic construction secures systematicity, and knowledge production secures scholarly rigour. Neglecting any one, Li warns, would damage the whole project. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of ideological and political education justifies Party leadership and Marxist guidance as the basis of disciplinary knowledge construction.

The content, social background and essence of the Biden administration's "middle-class" foreign policy 拜登政府“中产阶级”外交政策的基本内容、社会背景与实质 Ma Feng Ma Feng examines the "foreign policy for the middle class" that the Biden administration adopted in place of Donald Trump's "America First". The article argues that the policy responds to domestic crisis and declining international standing, and that in essence it does not differ from "America First". In Ma's view both are devices by which US monopoly capital and the upper elite try to rescue themselves, and Biden, like Trump, is a political agent of that capital who cannot change the country's basic direction. The article has three parts. The first traces how the policy took shape: a Carnegie Endowment report, Biden's 2020 Foreign Affairs essay, his February 2021 State Department speech, the accompanying memorandum, statements by Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan, and the 2022 National Security Strategy. The second sets out the social background, namely the shrinking middle class, rising inequality and inflation. The third offers five claims about the policy's essence. Ma first argues that "middle class" is a non-class "class" mixing proletarians, petty bourgeoisie and part of the bourgeoisie. The author cites figures on the shrinking middle class, the Gini coefficient, billionaire wealth and food insecurity to show that its position has not improved under Biden. Ma attributes inflation and polarisation to the contradiction between private ownership of the means of production and socialised large-scale production. The five claims are that the policy expresses economic nationalism and national egoism, for example through \"Build Back Better World\" and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework; that it exports domestic contradictions abroad; that it continues the tradition of putting US interests first; that it adjusts long-term foreign policy to preserve hegemony; and that it fosters bloc confrontation, as in the Ukraine crisis and policy towards China. Ma concludes that whatever form or slogan it takes, the policy serves to maintain US unipolar hegemony and the domestic rule of the upper class. In the author's account, spending on war while cutting taxes for the rich deepens inequality, and the United States has lost its moral appeal. Ma contends that Washington should instead reform at home and compete with China on a basis of mutual respect. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Biden-era US foreign policy, with its class analysis and the sources it cites on inequality and inflation.

Lenin's critique of non-Marxist currents in Russia and its lessons for contemporary China 列宁对俄国非马克思主义思潮的批判及其对当代中国的启示 Jia Shupin Jia Shupin asks what Lenin's polemics against non-Marxist currents in Russia around the turn of the twentieth century can teach China today. The article argues that such currents typically wear Marxist dress and claim to renew Marxism, which makes them deceptive. Jia holds that mastering Marxist fundamentals through Lenin's critiques helps identify and resist comparable currents in present-day ideological struggle. The article has three parts. The first describes four currents the author treats as Russian variants of Bernsteinism: Menshevism, Economism, Narodism (populism) and Machism. The second sets out Lenin's criticism of each. The third draws lessons for contemporary China, with particular attention to ideological leadership and theoretical education. In Jia's account, Lenin answered the Mensheviks' loose, self-governing party model by defending centralism and the vanguard party, while also insisting on close ties between the party and the masses. Against the Economists he argued that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers from outside, since workers alone develop only trade-union consciousness. Against the Narodniks he argued that capitalism in Russia was historically progressive and arose from existing conditions. Against Machism he defended philosophical materialism and the Party principle in philosophy, claiming that its claim of neutrality masked idealism. Jia draws three lessons. China should uphold Marxism's guiding position and the Party's leadership over ideology, and Jia names historical nihilism, neoliberalism and the 'end of ideology' thesis as current erroneous currents. It should recognise that ideological work is complex and long-term, strengthen the ability to discern harmful currents, and take a firm stand against Western capitalist ideological infiltration. It should also deepen theoretical education, including the study of Party history and the promotion of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a Party-theory reading of Lenin's polemics and how Chinese scholars apply them to current ideological work.

Reflections on how artificial intelligence can empower the precision development of ideological and political education in universities 人工智能赋能高校思想政治教育精准化发展的思考 Tang Pingqiu Liu Tingting Tang Pingqiu and Liu Tingting take up a practical problem in Chinese higher education: how artificial intelligence (AI) can help make university ideological and political education more "precise". They start from the 2019 national education work conference, which called for "precision ideological and political education" to address weak targeting, poor fit between content and student needs, and low accuracy. The authors argue that AI has inherent strengths in precision, coordination and adaptation, so it can empower this approach and shape students' thinking gradually and unobtrusively. The condition they set is that it be steered by values and run by people. The article has two parts. The first sets out three advantages of AI for precision education: timeliness, "intelligence" or wisdom, and targeted delivery. The second proposes three strategies: value guidance to set direction, human–machine collaboration, and platform construction. The authors give a short account of AI's technical layers (foundation, technology and application) and draw on technologies such as GPUs, face recognition, natural language processing, adaptive learning systems and virtual reality. On the advantages, Tang and Liu argue that AI processes large volumes of student data quickly, frees teachers from routine tasks and builds cross-media "precise portraits" of students. Because its algorithms can optimise themselves, they say, AI can detect students' emotions and attention, mine patterns in unstructured data, and filter out "noise" from the infiltration of Western values. Unlike the earlier big-data stage, which stayed at the level of mass lectures and meetings, AI can adapt content to individuals and build immersive teaching scenes. On strategy, the authors insist that value rationality must direct instrumental rationality, and that shared values must anchor individualised education so that it does not simply cater to students' preferences. They hold that AI remains "weak AI", so teachers must lead, guard privacy and ideological security, and add emotional care. On platforms, the authors call for a big-data collection platform with graded confidentiality and school–enterprise cooperation, a smart teaching platform with VR learning scenes and a knowledge graph of ideological and political education resources, and a management and service platform kept up to date by technical staff. They conclude that AI should serve the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating talent, guided by Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese university Party and ideological-education researchers frame the use of AI and student data in political education.

The rich connotations, methodological implications and practical requirements of "the essence of ideological and political theory courses is reasoning" “思政课的本质是讲道理”的丰富内涵、方法论意蕴和实践要求 Ai Silin Ai Silin examines Xi Jinping's 2022 statement at Renmin University of China that "the essence of ideological and political theory courses is reasoning" (讲道理). Ai asks why this was raised to the level of the courses' essence and what it requires of teachers. The article argues that the statement deepens understanding of how such courses should be taught, and that it points to higher effectiveness for university courses in the new era. The article has four parts. It first traces Xi's remarks on these courses since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the 2019 teachers' symposium. It then sets out the meaning of "reasoning", the methodological guidance of "making arguments profound, thorough and lively", and three practical requirements. Ai draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and closes with a note on the discipline of Marxist theory. Ai gives three reasons for the emphasis: the courses' theoretical and scientific character, the logic by which their goal of fostering conviction is reached, and the need to address teaching that "cannot reason well". Examples are reading from the textbook, stating conclusions without argument, superficial treatment and one-sided treatment. The reasoning taught is not ordinary reasoning. It unites truth with ethics and feeling, political principle with academic grounding, and general principles with concrete cases. Ai reads the methodological formula as follows. "Profound" means asking why, teaching standpoint and method, and moving from phenomena to essence. "Thorough" means teaching holistically, through students' questions, by comparison, and by criticising wrong ideas while affirming correct ones. "Lively" means accessible language and varied methods, including integrating artificial intelligence. Ai treats the three as mutually supporting. Ai draws three practical requirements. Teachers should put heart and effort into every class and manage the tensions between teaching and learning. They should raise their scholarly level, because the courses are themselves scholarship and a lack of academic substance produces "filler courses". Finally, the discipline of Marxist theory should provide stronger support, including through the new first-level discipline of CPC history and Party building, more research funding and platforms, and teaching that explains Chinese modernization and builds the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want an authoritative-line account of how Party theorists in higher education justify and operationalise "reasoning" in ideological and political courses.

Uncovering the critical dimension of the labour theory of value 发掘劳动价值论的批判性维度 Niu Ziniu Niu Ziniu takes up a gap in how the labour theory of value is read. Chinese Marxist scholars, the author says, have long stressed its constructive dimension: labour creates value, capitalism's main defect is the unpaid appropriation of surplus value, and a post-capitalist order should distribute value fairly. This is a kind of 'distributive justice' reading. Niu argues that Western left scholars, citing Moishe Postone, now stress a critical dimension. On this view, 'labour appearing as value' already contains a degree of alienated labour, so the problem goes beyond unjust distribution. Niu presents recovering this dimension in Capital as a task for today's Marxist scholars. The piece appeared in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2024. It has four sections: the social constructedness of categories, the historicity of the labour theory of value, the organic object and dialectical method of Capital, and the relation between the labour theory of value and the theory of surplus value. It draws mainly on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital. It closes by linking the argument to present-day labour conditions. First, Niu argues that 'labour' and 'value' are historical categories. Marx asked why labour appears as value, which the classical economists never did. Niu distinguishes the early, ontological concept of labour as sensuous object-activity from the Capital concept tied to abstract labour, which belongs to capitalist wage labour. Second, Niu rejects a 'linear logic' reading in which the labour theory of value is an axiom from which capitalism is deduced. Capitalism is an 'organic totality' in which each element is both condition and result. The ascent from the abstract to the concrete reproduces that totality in thought; it is not a historical genesis. Third, value rests on money and capital, and capital on surplus value. So 'labour creates value' in reality means 'wage labour creates profit'. Niu adds that, on Marx's Grundrisse argument, abolishing capitalism means abolishing the value form, so that labour time is no longer the measure of wealth. Niu concludes that the labour theory of value is neither a pure premise of Capital nor a standard of critique that exists independently of capitalism. It is an abstract aspect of the capitalist totality and holds the seeds of labour alienation. Niu notes that deepening contradictions have brought intensified labour, unstable labour relations, sharper competition and meaningless work. Grasping the critical dimension, Niu argues, would revive the value of Capital and give a philosophical account of these problems. Read the original if you want a short statement of the 'critical' reading of value theory, which draws on Postone, and of how it differs from the distributive-justice reading common in Chinese scholarship.

Is labour the foundation of Marx's critique of capitalism? On Moishe Postone's interpretation of Marx's critical theory 劳动是马克思资本主义批判的基础吗？ Wu Meng Wu Meng takes up a common assumption in contemporary scholarship: that labour is the cornerstone of Marx's social theory, both as an ontological basis for human society and as the fulcrum of his critique of capitalism. The article examines the challenge to this view posed by the late American left thinker Moishe Postone, and argues that Postone is right to raise the question of historicity but fails to answer it convincingly. In Wu's reading, Marx does not treat labour as the foundation of capitalist society at all. The piece is a short newspaper commentary built in three steps. It first sets out Postone's claim, in Time, Labor, and Social Domination, that the idea of labour as creator of the social world and source of wealth applies only to capitalist society, not to society in general. It then criticises Postone's account of abstract labour, and finally returns to Marx's own texts, notably the 1857–58 manuscripts, to reposition labour within Marx's thought. Wu credits Postone with restoring a historical dimension: separating trans-historical labour from specifically capitalist labour guards historical materialism against metaphysics. But Wu argues that Postone misreads abstract labour as labour's function as a social mediating activity. For Marx, Wu says, abstract human labour expresses the equalisation of different concrete labours, a 'social effect' of the whole capitalist production mechanism and of a total 'world of commodities', not a form of labour. Wu traces this error to Postone's 'foundationalism', which looks for a homogeneous basis for capitalist totality and, in Wu's view, also obscures the class domination workers suffer from the bourgeoisie. Citing Marx, Wu contends that capitalist social structure precedes labour's apparent foundational role, which is an 'appearance'. The real question for Marx is why labour appears as value, not whether labour constructs it; the view that labour constructs value is the classical political economy Marx criticised. Wu concludes that Postone mistook classical political economy's emphasis on labour's foundational status for Marx's own position, and so did not adequately reflect on labour's place in Marx's thought. Wu calls for facing changes in contemporary life as Marx did, in a historical-materialist way, without presupposed concepts. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese critique of Postone's reading of abstract labour and of the labour-ontology view of Marx.

Upholding the Party Central Committee's centralised and unified leadership as the fundamental guarantee for advancing the Party's self-reform 以坚持党中央集中统一领导为根本保证深入推进党的自我革命 Wang Libing Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 5), Wang Libing takes up one element of Xi Jinping's thinking on the Party's self-reform: that the work must be carried forward with \"upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee as the fundamental guarantee\". Wang argues that this leadership is the highest principle of the Party's self-reform, and that the Party must firmly uphold the Central Committee's authority and keep fully in line with the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. The article has three sections. The first sets out why centralised and unified leadership is the highest principle, in theoretical, historical and practical terms. The second reviews what Wang describes as historic and pioneering achievements of the Party's self-reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to what it means in practice to take this leadership as the fundamental guarantee. Wang's theoretical case cites Marx, Engels and Lenin on centralism and authority, and then Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The historical case runs from the Zunyi Meeting to the present and concludes that when the Party stresses self-reform and upholds central leadership, its cause advances, and that the reverse brings setbacks. The achievements are grouped under several heads: leading by example from the top, with the Central Committee and senior cadres setting the standard; strengthening the Party's overall leadership; the claimed decisive victory in the anti-corruption struggle; a more mature supervision system and body of Party regulations; and the Two Establishes, which Wang calls the most important political result. For practice, Wang calls for three things. The Party should advance self-reform unwaveringly under central leadership, turning the Two Establishes into the Two Upholds. It should implement the Central Committee's decisions on self-reform to the letter. It should also use self-reform itself to defend central authority, by struggling against words and deeds that weaken Party leadership, tackling the \"seven haves\" problems, tightening political discipline and improving the institutional system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how the official line ties Party discipline, anti-corruption and institutional reform to central authority.

Carrying forward the Marxist style of study that links theory with practice 发扬理论联系实际的马克思主义学风 Jiang Zexun Jiang Zexun takes up Xi Jinping's call, in his preface to the sixth batch of national cadre training textbooks, for officials to carry forward the Marxist style of study that links theory with practice and to act as resolute doers in building Chinese modernization. The article, published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscript (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, argues that this style of study is a major political question bearing on the fortunes of the Party's cause. In Jiang's view, whether theory is tied to practice decides the quality of Party conduct and the success of national rejuvenation. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the style matters: it is a defining trait of Marxist theory, a requirement for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, a practical necessity for Chinese modernization, and a continuation of the traditional Chinese unity of knowing and doing. The second says what cadres should link theory to: their own thinking, their work, and historical and cultural conditions. The third lists methods for doing so. Jiang draws on Marx, Engels and Mao Zedong, and above all on Xi Jinping's statements, to argue that Marxism is a method and a guide to action rather than dogma. On the work side, cadres are told to tie study to Chinese modernization, high-quality development, the pressing concerns of the people, problems in Party building, and the domestic and international situation. The methods are mastering the theory, problem orientation, field investigation that avoids showy or superficial visits, the mass line (including online), a practical, results-oriented work style, and theoretical innovation drawn from practice. Jiang also invokes the traditional idea of the unity of knowing and doing as a cultural root of the approach. Jiang concludes that the effectiveness of theory depends on how far it meets real needs and how deeply it enters practice. Cadres are urged to study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era thoroughly, to curb formalism and bureaucratism, and to produce results that withstand scrutiny by history and the people. Jiang adds that practice must keep generating new concepts, so that the theoretical framework of Chinese modernization continues to develop. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-school line on study style and cadre work methods, with the key Xi Jinping formulations gathered in one place.

Scientific guidance for advancing theoretical innovation 推进理论创新的科学指引 Liu Tongfang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2024, no. 4), Liu Tongfang asks how the Communist Party of China should understand and carry out theoretical innovation. Liu argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping's remarks on the subject have raised the Party's grasp of the laws governing theoretical innovation to a new level. In Liu's reading, these remarks set out its basic principles and significance and its scientific method, and so give guidance for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is a commentary in four parts. Each part takes one pair of concepts from Xi's statements: the "soul" and "root" of theory; the times as "mother of thought" and practice as "source of theory"; the people as the subject of innovation and the value it serves; and the systematization and scholarly grounding of theory. It draws mainly on Xi's formulations and on the Party's experience of more than a century. Liu's first claim is that Marxism is the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture the "root" of innovation, and that the two interpenetrate. Marxism gives scientific, people-centred, practical and open principles; traditional culture gives continuity and the Chinese character of theory. Liu treats the Two Integrations as both a method and a result of innovation. Second, Liu holds that the times and practice generate theory. Liu cites the world's "changes unseen in a century", Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind as practices that theorists must answer and guide. Third, Liu names the people as the subject of innovation and their aspiration for a better life as its value, aimed at common prosperity and human emancipation. Systematization links the different parts of theory, while scholarly grounding lifts it from perceptual experience to rational knowledge. Liu concludes that continued innovation guided by these four sets of insights will open up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It will also show the truth-power of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The text is a Party-theory exposition rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise account of how current official discourse frames the logic, subject and method of theoretical innovation.

Lenin's critique of the liberal Narodniks on Russia's path of development, and its lessons 列宁在俄国发展道路问题上对自由主义民粹派的批判及其启示 Wang Jinfen Du Qianwen Wang and Du examine how Lenin criticised the liberal Narodniks (populists) such as Mikhailovsky, Vorontsov, Yushakov and Danielson in the debate over "where Russia is going" at the turn of the twentieth century. The authors argue that the liberal Narodniks offered a reformist, petty-bourgeois programme that denied capitalism's necessity in Russia, and that Lenin's rebuttal remains instructive for socialist construction today. The article reconstructs Lenin's critique in three parts: the "non-capitalist path", the question of which social force should lead, and the Narodniks' claim to speak for "the people". A fourth part draws three lessons for contemporary China, citing Xi Jinping's statements on each. The authors rely on Lenin's writings, including The Development of Capitalism in Russia. In the authors' account, Lenin first refuted the claims that capitalism was unworkable and destructive in Russia. He argued that the social division of labour, commodity production and the ruin of small producers were already enlarging the home market, and that Danielson and others misunderstood the realisation of products. Capitalism, Lenin held, was therefore both inevitable and progressive, because it socialised labour and created the material basis and class forces for socialism. Second, he analysed the peasantry as dual and vacillating, the intelligentsia as dependent on the bourgeoisie, and the proletariat as the "only fighter" for emancipation, so that a proletarian party must lead through research, propaganda and organisation. Third, he exposed the Narodniks' "revival of the people's economy" as patching up capitalism and treating the masses as a mob, and insisted that the path must start from the interests of working people and rely on them as makers of history. The authors draw three lessons. Socialism must learn from the beneficial achievements of capitalist civilisation, while staying alert to its contradictions and rejecting the equation of modernization with Westernization, since Chinese modernization is socialist modernization. Adherence to the leadership of the Communist Party of China must be unwavering. The authors cite the Soviet collapse as a warning, attributing it to ideological and political pluralism under Gorbachev and to a Party that became a privileged bureaucratic group cut off from the people. The Party must also represent the people's interests and rely on them, developing whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholars use Lenin's polemic with the Narodniks to support current Party-leadership and development arguments.

A critique of US digital hegemony from the perspective of digital imperialism 数字帝国主义视阈下美国的数字霸权批判 Hu Ying Hu Ying asks what US digital hegemony consists of and what it is in essence. The article argues that digital imperialism is the latest form of imperialism and that US digital hegemony is its main expression. In Hu's account, the classical Marxist theory of imperialism has not become outdated: it remains the tool for seeing that the new technical forms conceal the same plunder of global surplus value. The article is built in five parts. It first treats digital capital and digital oligarchs as the basis of US hegemony, drawing on figures on platform concentration and the Wintel alliance. It then describes how the US controls other countries' data and digital space, and how it uses digital advantages to consolidate cultural and political hegemony. A fourth part addresses the essence of this hegemony through Marx, Lenin, Luxemburg and world-systems writers such as Wallerstein and Frank, and a short conclusion turns to policy. Hu identifies three means of control: the digitalisation of unequal exchange, in which raw data from peripheral countries is processed and sold back as software or advice; control of the access routes to digital space, such as operating systems, cloud infrastructure and network equipment; and digital colonisation through "digital technology assistance", illustrated with Africa. Using Lenin's view that monopoly is the essence of imperialism, the article treats digital monopoly capital as the logical starting point. It names four accumulation mechanisms: data extraction, digital enclosure, the fusion of digital capital with industrial and financial capital, and digital export. Hu also claims that platforms exploit unpaid "prosumer" labour and spread US values through search engines and social media. Hu concludes that digital hegemony changes the form of imperial power but not its predatory purpose, and that digital imperialism is only a "new solution" that cannot resolve capitalism's basic contradiction. The article calls for a community with a shared future for mankind in digital space. It cites Xi Jinping's remarks on cybersecurity and China's 2020 Global Initiative on Data Security, and rejects data monopoly, digital colonisation and double standards. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical Chinese account of US digital power that combines classical imperialism theory with detailed company and market data.

The "Three Initiatives": a three-dimensional presentation of the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind “三大倡议”：人类命运共同体理念的立体化呈现 Liu Zhigang Liu Zhigang asks how China's Global Development Initiative (2021), Global Security Initiative (2022) and Global Civilization Initiative (2023) relate to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that the three initiatives follow one logic and make the idea concrete and theoretical. In Liu's account they answer three global problems, namely development, security and civilisation, and extend the Belt and Road Initiative. After a framing section on the three initiatives as a set, the article gives one section to each. The development initiative is presented as laying the material foundation, the security initiative as ensuring lasting peace, and the civilisation initiative as building value consensus. Each section sets the initiative against Western counterparts, which the author labels "development first for the West", "absolute security" and the "clash of civilizations". Each section also lists practical steps, such as the Group of Friends of the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative Concept Paper, the Saudi–Iran reconciliation and dialogue forums among civilisations. Liu's central claim is that the initiatives are complementary. Development supplies the material conditions for security and cultural exchange, security supplies a stable environment, and shared values supply a spiritual and ethical base. In Liu's reading, each initiative also surpasses a Western model: capital-first and self-first development, bloc-based "absolute security", and civilisational superiority and "universal values". The author cites figures to support this, including China's average contribution of 38.6 per cent to global growth over ten years and more than 70 per cent of global poverty reduction. Liu also draws on the Chinese tradition of harmony in diversity and holds that the common values of humanity differ in kind from Western "universal values". Liu concludes that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind is a set of concrete public goods rather than empty rhetoric. The author holds that the three initiatives reshape the global economic, governance and civilisational orders. They also express a dialectical unity of the universal and the particular, and give the idea a basis in the laws of historical development. The article is written in the official voice and assesses foreign powers throughout in sharply critical terms. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars frame the three global initiatives as one system and contrast them with Western models.

Making good use of the "Great Ideological and Political Course": three narratives of connotation, value and practice Characteristics, value orientation and practical path 善用“大思政课”三重叙事：内涵特征、价值旨归与实践理路 Fu Hong Cai Chen Since Xi Jinping told education-sector delegates in 2021 that the "Great Ideological and Political Course" (da sizheng ke) should be used well, scholars have debated what it means. Fu Hong and Cai Chen, writing in 2024, argue that the project has reached a "deep-water zone" in which unclear actors, weak results and even wrong direction have appeared. They hold that its basic questions must be clarified, and that the concept is best understood through three linked narratives: cognitive, value and practical. The article first reviews existing scholarship on the concept's meaning, value and structure. It then sets out its own account in three parts: what "great" and "using well" mean and the course's basic features; the value of the approach for moral education and for fostering "new-era talents"; and the practical path for building it. Throughout, it draws on Xi Jinping's speeches on ideological and political courses and on the 2022 Ministry of Education work plan for promoting the course. On connotation, the authors argue that the "great" course inherits the breadth already inherent in ideological and political courses, innovates on it, and builds a wider pattern of cooperation between school and society. They insist its emphasis remains on the "course", not on a loose "big ideology and politics", and that its test is effectiveness rather than size. "Using well" is read as using it truly, widely and flexibly, and as treating it as a system with holistic, structural, three-dimensional and dynamic features. Its characteristics are said to be problem orientation, practice orientation and cross-field coordination. On value, the authors present it as a way to carry out the fundamental task of fostering virtue and cultivating people, to resolve persistent difficulties in moral education, and to answer the questions of whom to train, how and for whom. For practice, the authors call for three things. First, Party committees at all levels should give overall leadership by setting direction, planning and coordinating. Second, construction should rely on the ideological and political course itself, strengthening its theoretical depth, linking it to reality and using social resources, while course-embedded ideological education works alongside it. Third, three kinds of elements should be coordinated: people (educators, learners, outside participants), things (such as red resources and practice bases) and operational methods. Read the original if you study ideological and political education in Chinese universities and want a detailed, officially aligned account of how the "Great Ideological and Political Course" is conceptualised and what practical measures are proposed.

Moral development of youth in the new era: current situation, problems and paths 新时代青年道德建设的现状、问题及路径分析 Wang Jianmin Wang Jianmin asks how the moral development of young people aged 14 to 35 is faring in the new era and how it should be strengthened. Taking up the call of the 20th Party Congress (2022) to implement a citizen moral development project, Wang argues that the overall trend among youth is positive but that significant problems remain in how young people understand, feel, will and practise socialist morality. The author concludes that these problems can be addressed through seven coordinated paths. The article first defines youth and socialist morality, which it describes as centred on serving the people, with collectivism as its principle and the core socialist values as its guide. It then assesses the current situation along four dimensions: moral cognition, moral emotion, moral will and moral conduct. A second section sets out problems in each dimension, and a third identifies causes and proposes paths. These paths are guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Party leadership, family education, schools, the social environment, institutional mechanisms and young people's own moral cultivation. On the situation, Wang cites patriotic sentiment, online expressions of national pride, acts of rescue and volunteering (over 90 million registered volunteers aged 14 to 35 by the end of 2021) as evidence of a healthy trend. On problems, Wang identifies shallow understanding of socialist morality, including belief that morality is useless or that it should wait for economic development. The author also points to uneven moral emotions, the downplaying of national history, uncritical admiration of Western moral culture, utilitarian motives, hesitation over helping others, online abuse, and indifference to wrongdoing. Wang attributes these to weak ideals and convictions, gaps in school and family education, negative social influences and limited self-cultivation. For remedies, Wang calls for Party leadership over ideological work, stronger family education and family traditions, and school curricula on ideals, public and private morality and national security. Wang also proposes cleaner online spaces, community and red-culture education sites, combined rule-of-law and rule-of-virtue mechanisms, systems of reward and punishment, and several forms of oversight. The author ends by urging young people to be exemplary in public and private morality and to promote civic morality themselves. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated youth researcher frames youth moral problems and prescribes institutional and educational remedies in the language of ideological and political education.

Cheng Jing's Marxist historiography 程憬的马克思主义史学研究 Li Changyin Li Jiahuang Cheng Jing (1902–1950) is little discussed in current scholarship, though Republican-era scholars noted his work. This article asks where he belongs in the history of Chinese Marxist historiography. Li and Li argue that he was an important early pioneer: he accepted historical materialism in the early 1920s, and between 1928 and 1933 he published studies of Chinese social history whose approach matched that of Guo Moruo and Lü Zhenyu and which appeared no later than theirs. The article first traces Cheng's route to Marxist historiography: the New Culture and May Fourth setting, study under Hu Shi, Marxist reading at Peking University, and training at the Tsinghua Institute of Chinese Classics under Liang Qichao and Wang Guowei. It then examines his social history of ancient China, followed by his history of Chinese philosophy, covering pre-Qin thought and early modern Neo-Confucianism. A final section assesses the distinctive value of his work. On social history, the authors argue that Cheng set out a fairly complete scheme of social formations. It ran from primitive society that developed from the "horde" into the clan, through a patrilineal clan society under the Shang, to a feudal Western Zhou and a "disguised feudalism" from the Eastern Zhou and after the Qin. The authors hold that his Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn views preceded Lü's formulations and that he was closer to Lü than to Guo. On philosophy, they show him moving beyond Hu Shi's positivist model. He explained Laozi's thought through the collapse of the feudal order and answered why Confucianism suited post-Qin society. He also divided early modern Neo-Confucianism into three schools, based on principle, mind and qi, which they compare with Zhang Dainian's later scheme and place near Hou Wailu's method. The authors conclude that Cheng's work has two distinctive values. He broke through positivist historiography from inside that camp, since he was a former secretary to Hu Shi and a friend of Gu Jiegang. His work also shows an internal, scholarly path to Marxist historiography, independent of political events such as the failure of the Great Revolution and the social history debate. They concede that his depth generally fell short of Guo and Lü. Read the original if you study the early history of Marxist historiography in China, the debates over periodising ancient Chinese society, or the Republican-era relation between positivism and historical materialism.

The essence, crisis and alternative of neoliberal globalization A commentary on David Lane's latest lectures 新自由主义全球化的实质、危机和替代 Song Chaolong Shao Xianyue This commentary reports and assesses three lectures given at Peking University on 24–26 May 2023 by David Lane, emeritus professor of sociology at Cambridge and author of Global Neoliberal Capitalism and the Alternatives: From Social Democracy to State Capitalisms (2023). The authors present Lane's thesis that neoliberal globalization is the ideology and framework of a transnational capitalist class, and that it is in crisis. They add that the rise of China as a "semi-core" power points to an alternative, which Lane calls socialist globalization. The article has four parts: the essence of neoliberal globalization, its defects and crisis, the alternative, and a short conclusion. It begins with Lane's account of postwar capitalism, which moved from internationalism to globalization. Competitive market, coordinated market and social-democratic welfare models existed side by side before the 1970s. The authors then set out his critique of Wallerstein's world-system model and add their own reservations at the end of the third part. On Lane's account, from the late 1970s Thatcher and Reagan pushed a neoliberal ideology that dissolved national borders and let multinational firms and a transnational capitalist class rule. Lane describes this class as including corporate owners, officials, the managers of the IMF, World Bank and WTO, think-tank members, and businesspeople and media. He sees three failures: it cannot avoid crises, as the 2007–2008 financial crisis showed. It weakens state sovereignty and welfare provision. It also fuels new populism such as Brexit, which Lane regards as a continuation of neoliberalism rather than a challenge to it. Lane holds that the crisis cannot be solved inside the capitalist world system, so a different globalization is needed. He credits China with a mixed-ownership market economy under socialist regulation and with a strong public-power state. He also credits it with building regional organizations and promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Lane traces three stages since reform and opening up: peripheral dependence, competitive symbiosis and a new equilibrium. He proposes replacing Wallerstein's "semi-periphery" with "semi-core". The authors conclude that China's constructive proposals on globalization offer a positive alternative to neoliberal globalization. They also criticise Lane's structural analysis as inaccurate. In their view, labelling China "semi-core" assumes that it belongs to a single capitalist world system. The label also stresses competition and confrontation while overlooking cooperation and exchange between socialism and transnational capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of a Western sociologist's view of neoliberalism, world-system theory and China's role in globalization.

The distinctiveness of the development of the discipline of ideological and political education since reform and opening up 改革开放以来思想政治教育学科发展的特殊性 She Shuanghao Lu Yuqiang Why did the discipline of ideological and political education grow so quickly in the roughly forty years after reform and opening up? She Shuanghao and Lu Yuqiang answer that, among many lessons, the most fundamental cause is the discipline's distinctiveness. The article traces how the Chinese Communist Party moved ideological and political education from a social phenomenon to a practice, then to a science, and finally to an independent academic discipline with its own undergraduate programme. The article is organised around five aspects of this distinctiveness: the discipline's Marxist, ideological nature; the practical base in the Party's own ideological and political work; the particular circumstances of its establishment; its position within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory; and its development model. It draws on Party and State Council documents from 2004–05, on the 1979–80 debate on making political work scientific, on textbook series from the 1980s and 1990s, and on statements by Deng Xiaoping, Hu Yaobang and Jiang Zemin. The authors argue that, unlike the education that other ruling classes gave in their own interests, Marxist ideological and political education serves the fundamental interests of the proletariat and working people. In their account it works by reasoning, persuasion and consultation rather than coercion, and it rests on a century of Party practice that sometimes met difficulties when it borrowed from Soviet experience. They identify six factors behind the discipline's founding: objective need, the attention of the Party Central Committee, strong promotion by the education authorities, the efforts of theorists, academic societies and journals, and the results of talent training. Finally, they present the "programme first, discipline later" model as a source of strength. In their reading, it produced a textbook system, a conceptual vocabulary (notably the 1986 definition in Principles of Ideological and Political Education) and a body of specialist knowledge. They also describe the discipline as the point where all Marxist theory disciplines land in application, and say it helped bring about the first-level Marxist theory discipline. The authors conclude that this distinctiveness explains past growth and should guide future development. They call on the discipline to clarify its nature, firm up its foundations, keep its distinctive features and original purpose, and follow its own laws of development. Read the original if you want a Chinese disciplinary insider's account of how ideological and political education became an academic field, including the documents, textbooks and institutions involved.

The rise and fall of late-developing modernization and the state: an analysis based on state autonomy and state embeddedness 国家与后发现代化的荣枯——基于国家自主性和国家嵌入性的分析 Sun Daiyao Diao Weiqi Sun Daiyao and Diao Weiqi ask what kind of state, and what kind of state–society relationship, helps late-developing countries modernize. Their answer is that two variables, state autonomy and state embeddedness, each high or low, decide whether the state plays a positive role. The authors argue that only a state combining fairly high levels of both can steer modernization well. The article first reviews theories of state autonomy: Marx and Engels on Bonapartism, Weber on bureaucracy, the relative-autonomy debate between Poulantzas and Miliband, Huntington's political order thesis, the East Asian 'developmental state' (Chalmers Johnson), the 'bringing the state back in' school, and the later 'state in society' and 'embedded autonomy' approaches of Migdal, Evans and Weiss. It then defines the two concepts and builds a four-quadrant model. Four cases illustrate it: Argentina and India (low autonomy, high embeddedness), Nigeria (low autonomy, low embeddedness), Saudi Arabia (high autonomy, low embeddedness) and South Korea (high on both). The authors criticise Evans for using autonomy and bureaucratic completeness interchangeably and for leaving the path from 'embedded autonomy' to performance unexplained. They define autonomy as the state's capacity to decide and enforce policy against social forces, and embeddedness as the channels through which it gathers information from, and consults, society broadly rather than only some groups. Taking resource allocation and industrial upgrading as the mediating mechanism, they argue that the state must remove barriers to resource mobility and also concentrate resources on strategic industries, withdrawing in time. In their account, early democratization in Argentina and India left the state unable to concentrate resources or overcome entrenched interests. Strong groups or ethnic forces captured resources in Nigeria, and a rentier bureaucracy absorbed them in Saudi Arabia. South Korea's planning, infrastructure and industrial policy under Park Chung-hee is presented as the successful case. The authors conclude that late developers need relatively high autonomy and embeddedness throughout modernization, but that pushing either to an extreme, such as total state takeover of society, backfires. They acknowledge limits: the industry-and-resources lens misses political, social and cultural dimensions, and the determinants and variability of the two traits need further study. They add that a state can raise either through reform, or slide down the scale as interest groups grow. Read the original if you want a comparative framework for the state's role in late development, with case material on Argentina, India, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and South Korea.

Clarifying the basic questions of ideological and political education in the curriculum 厘清课程思政的基本问题 Li Heliang Ideological and political education in the curriculum (kecheng sizheng) has become a buzzword in Chinese higher education, yet scholars disagree about what it is and how to strengthen it. Li Heliang argues that it is not a new discipline or a theoretical breakthrough but a logical return to the original purpose of education, which is to cultivate people morally as well as intellectually. The article was published in the journal Party Building and Ideological Education in Schools and posted on the Academy of Marxism site in 2024. The article proceeds in six sections. It first places curriculum-based political education within the nature of education itself, then distinguishes it from dedicated ideological and political theory courses. It goes on to discuss how to draw out the ideological elements already inside each course, what the practice is for, what drives it forward, and how universities should plan it as a whole. Li draws on Vygotsky, Xi Jinping's remarks on education, and the Ministry of Education's May 2020 Guidelines for Ideological and Political Education in the Curriculum in Higher Education. Li's central claim is that education is inseparable from society and from the free and all-round development of the person, so every course already carries a moral function. Long-standing instrumentalism has stressed knowledge and skills and let this moral element fade. Li distinguishes the dedicated theory courses, which are explicit and ideological, from curriculum-based education, which is mainly implicit and works through content and the teacher's conduct. The two are said to be in collaboration, not in a primary–supplementary relation. Li criticises teachers who bolt political content onto professional courses, or who create separate moral courses for students, arguing that such steps provoke resentment and weaken the effect. Poetry teaching is offered as an example of drawing out historical context and patriotic feeling. Li concludes that the approach should not be applied uniformly: pure natural-science or highly technical courses need not carry it, and sometimes a few words from the teacher are enough. Universities should experiment, adapt to their own specialisms and students, and draw up common standards and even negative lists. Li calls for systematic coordination among Party committees, administrative departments, faculties, teachers and students, and for teachers to use methods from related disciplines. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's critique of mechanical practice in university ideological and political education and a view of how it should be managed.

Class, assets and work in rentier capitalism 食利资本主义中的阶级、资产和工作 Brett Christophers This is a Chinese translation of an article by the economic geographer Brett Christophers (Uppsala University), first published in Historical Materialism in 2021. It asks how class and inequality should be understood in what the author calls an age of rentier capitalism. Christophers argues that recent work on assets and inequality overlooks the fact that most rent-generating assets belong to corporations, not households. In his account, class position increasingly depends on how an employee's work relates to the assets the employer owns. The article has three parts. The first reviews Thomas Piketty, Guy Standing and Lisa Adkins, Melinda Cooper and Martijn Konings, who bring asset ownership into class analysis, and sets them against Erik Olin Wright's employment-based schema. The second examines corporate ownership of seven asset types: property, financial assets, intellectual property, natural resources, digital platforms, long-term service contracts and infrastructure. The third asks what this means for Marx's categories. Christophers defines rent broadly as income from owning or controlling scarce assets under limited competition, which extends Marx's concept of ground rent beyond land. Christophers argues that employees in rentier firms stand in four privileged relations to corporate assets: creating them, demonstrating their value (accountants), protecting them (lawyers, for example through patent 'evergreening') and maximising rent (lobbyists, tax lawyers and accountants). Most staff, by contrast, simply 'sweat' the assets, and the pay and class gap between the two groups is wide. He presents these roles as speculative hypotheses needing empirical testing. Applying Marx's distinction, he notes that labour exchanged against rent is unproductive, since it creates no surplus value. This poses two problems: whether Marx's concepts fit an economy centred on rent, and what class position these workers hold. Citing Ian Gough, he says Marx's argument that commercial workers are exploited does not extend to workers paid out of rent, so they challenge Marx's class theory more sharply than commercial workers do. Christophers concludes that more empirical and theoretical work is needed. He proposes that class be understood through two questions: whether people own housing or other valuable assets, and what labour relation they have to employer-owned rent-yielding assets, whether sweating, creating or protecting them. As capital changes form, he says, the concepts used to understand it must change as well. Read the original if you work on Marxist class theory, rentier capitalism or the productive/unproductive labour debate and want an argument that tests Marx's categories against corporate asset ownership.

The internal structure, construction logic and advancement paths of an autonomous knowledge system for the discipline of ideological and political education 思想政治教育学科自主知识体系的内在结构、建构逻辑及推进路向 Zheng Jingbin Zheng Jingbin asks how the discipline of ideological and political education should build its own autonomous knowledge system, a task that Xi Jinping has placed at the centre of building a Chinese philosophy and social science. Citing Xi's 2016 and 2022 statements, Zheng argues that the knowledge system is the foundation of the "three systems" (discipline, academic and discourse systems), and that the discipline, as a basic part of the social sciences, must now construct one. The article was published in 2024 in a journal on ideological and theoretical education. The article first gives four reasons the problem is pressing: the discipline's composite, multi-source character; its relatively recent founding (about forty years ago) and weak intensive growth; scholars' limited capacity for knowledge creation; and new practical questions that exceed existing explanations. It then reviews scholarly views on the system's components (two-, three- and four-element models), proposes its own structure, and surveys proposed features of an "autonomous" system, from which it selects four. It closes with five proposed routes for advancing construction. Zheng divides the system into four blocks: theoretical knowledge (what is it), practical knowledge (what to do), methodological knowledge (how to do it) and institutional knowledge (what outcome to aim for), each an interdependent subsystem. From 28 keywords drawn from the literature, Zheng picks the four most frequent features as the logical thread of construction: localness in knowledge production, interconnectedness with other bodies of knowledge, systematicity of structure, and originality in application. Localness means drawing concepts from Chinese practice and traditional culture. Interconnection means integrating Marxist theory, technology, natural science and neighbouring social sciences. Originality means posing new propositions for Chinese problems and issues of wider human concern. For advancement, Zheng calls for guidance by Marxist theory (the people's standpoint, Marxist worldview and method, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era). Further proposals are textbook-system reform with vertical coordination across school stages, a shift in research paradigms towards data-driven and interdisciplinary work, international dialogue that avoids mechanical borrowing from the West, and a problem-oriented approach. The aim is for knowledge to move from national to global significance and offer "Chinese wisdom" for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed map of how scholars in this field conceptualise disciplinary knowledge-building under the current policy agenda.

Digital ideological and political education and the reshaping of teachers' competence structure in ideological and political theory courses 数字思政与思政课教师能力结构再塑 Jiang Hong Zhou Hongjiang Jiang Hong and Zhou Hongjiang ask how ideological and political theory courses ("sizheng ke") in Chinese universities can undergo digital transformation, and answer that the decisive factor is teachers. The article argues that "digital ideological and political education" is an important direction for such courses in the new era, and that its construction depends on reshaping teachers' competence structure around digital literacy. The article opens from the call of the 20th Party Congress (2022) to advance the digitalisation of education, then proceeds in three steps. It first explains why digital ideological and political education matters, then argues that teachers are its key element, drawing on Xi Jinping's 2019 symposium on these courses (the "3·18" symposium). Finally it sets out four areas in which teachers' capacities should be rebuilt, before a short conclusion. On the first point, the authors say that students' "networked existence" and the technological shifts of the age require the courses to adapt. They also warn against the "pan-entertainment" that excessive use of technology could bring to the classroom. For teachers, they stress personal charisma and professional ethics, based on Xi's "Six Requirements" and "four-have" good teacher standards. They also stress analysing students' interests and arming oneself with the Party's innovative theory. The four areas of capacity are improving network use (platform skills, training, shared digital resource banks); adopting a human–machine collaborative teaching philosophy; exploring digital teaching methods; and conducting immersive teaching with VR, AR and MR. In the authors' account, collaboration shifts communication from "person–person" to "person–machine–person", and teachers become guides and designers of resources, while technology lacks human value rationality and warmth. They link digital methods to Xi's "Eight Unities", for example combining explicit and implicit education through virtual scenes of revolutionary history. The authors conclude that digital transformation must first settle whether teachers' competence structure is adequate, with digital literacy at its core. They add that digital ideological and political education is not merely a technical means but must carry educational ideals and values. Teachers should therefore keep to the Eight Unities, strengthen political conviction and cultural confidence, and act as guides to students' growth. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Chinese scholars in ideological and political education link digital technology, teacher training and Party guidance for classroom practice.

Integrating Party history study and education into university ideological and political theory courses 把党史学习教育融入高校思政课教学 Gai Yixin Writing in Guangming Daily, Gai Yixin, dean and professor at a school of Marxism, takes up the question of how Party history study and education can be built into university ideological and political theory courses. The commentary is prompted by the Regulations on Party History Study and Education issued by the CPC Central Committee in February 2024. Gai argues that Party history is the most vivid and persuasive textbook for these courses and that using it is necessary if they are to reach students' hearts, stimulate thinking and inspire commitment. The piece is organised under three headings, each opening with a call from Xi Jinping: to form a broad view of history and of the times, to unite theory with practice, and to explain principles in depth, thoroughly and vividly. Gai sketches how the Party has used history-related courses since the new-democratic revolution, at Shaanbei Public School and North China United University, and after 1949.
