The commentary then gives teaching suggestions under each heading. Gai's first move is that a broad historical outlook links the present-day classroom to Party history. It does so by showing students the Party's achievements and the significance of its century of struggle. The author adds that digital tools such as VR and AR can make red historical resources more engaging. Second, Gai calls for combining the "small classroom" of the course with the "big classroom" of society. This means building a "big ideological and political course" through reading, discussion, visits to red sites and fieldwork, so that students see the Party's material, institutional and spiritual strength and link personal goals to national rejuvenation. Third, Gai proposes three ways to "explain principles": telling small stories about ordinary people and local changes, breaking big principles into smaller ones close to student life, and learning through practice. One concrete proposal is to award course credit for students' vacation activities at home, such as volunteering at red exhibition halls, so that they move from passive listening to active explaining. Gai concludes that Party history teaching should help students understand why the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics have succeeded. It should also lead them to tie individual aims to national needs and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The commentary is a practical, officially aligned account of teaching method, not a scholarly study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party history education is being presented to university teachers of ideological and political courses after the 2024 Regulations.

Advancing digital ideological and political education and strengthening online education capacity 推进数字思政建设 提高网络育人能力 Sun Chuhang Luo Liang Sun Chuhang and Luo Liang, in a commentary first published in Guangming Daily on 12 October 2023, take up Xi Jinping's call to improve online education capacity and to carry out ideological work in schools well in the internet age. They argue that cyberspace has become the "first environment" of young students. In their view, "digital ideological and political education" (digital sizheng) is a paradigm shift for the field, not a simple addition to traditional teaching or a mere refinement of method. The piece is built around four elements: the value of digital ideological and political education, its goals, its content, and the practical work needed to build it. It closes with a short note on top-level design and teacher capacity. On value, the authors say the field should replace "inculcation" with interactive methods that draw out individual potential. It should also strengthen mainstream ideology in digital space and build a "firewall" against online infiltration. On goals, they name three: using value guidance to overcome technological alienation and addiction, easing the isolation and "information cocoons" of digital life, and using moral norms to reduce risks such as data leaks and algorithmic discrimination. On content, they stress digital thinking, digital ethics and digital skills. Practical measures include new methods such as virtual reality and immersive teaching, ideological and political data centres, algorithm governance across the student life cycle, and integrated monitoring and service platforms. The authors conclude that progress requires stronger top-level design, innovation in concepts, content and methods, higher digital literacy among teachers, and a sustainable disciplinary theory and long-term working mechanism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese educators propose to use big data, algorithms and platforms in ideological and political education.

Understanding propaganda, ideological and cultural work as an extremely important task 深刻认识宣传思想文化工作是一项极端重要的工作 Li Yi This commentary, written by a vice president of the Central Party School, expounds Xi Jinping's directive on propaganda, ideological and cultural work. Xi called it "extremely important" work that bears on the Party's future and destiny, on the country's long-term stability and on the cohesion and centripetal force of the nation. Li Yi argues that these "three bearings" deepen the Party's understanding of the work's strategic and overall significance and show the way to shoulder the "new cultural mission". The article is organised in three sections, one for each "bearing". The first traces the Party's treatment of propaganda work from the Communist League's 1847 rules and Lenin's writings through the Party's founding in 1921, the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform-era periods, to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second turns to cultural security and ideological struggle, and the third to culture as the basis of national cohesion and to Xi Jinping Thought on culture. Li's central argument is that in every historical period this work has supplied ideological guarantees for the Party's tasks, and has therefore been the Party's "lifeline". On national security, Li contends that Western hostile forces export "cultural hegemony" and promote liberalism, historical nihilism and "universal values" in order to push the Party to change its banner. The Soviet collapse and "colour revolutions" are cited as showing that socialism can be undone in the ideological sphere when it cannot be defeated by arms or economic pressure. Li holds that the Party can make no compromise there and must act from the standpoint of survival. On cohesion, Li presents the continuity and unity of Chinese civilisation as the source of national strength, and says the "second integration" of Marxism with fine traditional culture consolidates Chinese cultural subjectivity. Li concludes that Xi Jinping's new ideas on culture are a theoretical summing-up of practice, form the cultural part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and constitute "Xi Jinping Thought on culture". Li calls for studying and applying them, strengthening the Party's overall leadership of this work, building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion, fostering core socialist values, improving news communication and international communication, and promoting Chinese traditional culture. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how a senior Party School official frames ideological work, cultural security and the "new cultural mission" at the end of 2023.

Promoting patriotic education in the new era so that it is broad, in-depth, lasting and effective 推动新时代爱国主义教育广泛深入持久有效开展 Jin Xin This short news report, originally carried in the People's Daily, covers a press conference on the Patriotic Education Law, which took effect on 1 January 2024. Jin Xin reports how officials presented the law as a legal guarantee for making patriotic education in the new era broad, in-depth, lasting and effective. The press conference was jointly organised by the Legislative Affairs Commission and the General Office of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress. Officials from the Publicity Department of the Central Committee, the Cyberspace Administration, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism and the Ministry of Education answered reporters' questions. Yang Heqing of the Legislative Affairs Commission lists four roles for the law: legal support for patriotic education, spiritual momentum for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, support for traditional culture, and a basis for safeguarding national security, honour and interests. Tang Lei describes existing laws, regulations and rules on online content, including the Cybersecurity Law and the Regulations on the Online Protection of Minors. Zeng Jianli says that putting patriotic education into law reflects deeper understanding of its importance, the integration of core socialist values into the legal system, and the advance of law-based governance. Zhou Jiucai and Wang Daquan outline measures on cultural heritage, red tourism and intangible heritage, and on schools, where students are the key group. The report concludes that the law is meant to consolidate shared values, strengthen national unity and gather strength for national rejuvenation. Education authorities say they will fulfil their statutory duties by integrating patriotic education into curricula, strengthening practical education, running signature activities and deepening cooperation between schools and families. Read the original if you want a brief official account of how Chinese state bodies describe the aims and implementation of the Patriotic Education Law.

Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of biocapitalism in the twenty-first century 21世纪国外左翼学者对生物资本主义的批判 Liu Pengfei Gu Yongchun This review surveys how Western left-wing scholars since 2006 have analysed biocapitalism, the form of capitalism that extracts profit and accumulates capital through the life sciences and biotechnology. It starts from Kaushik Sunder Rajan's Biocapital: The Constitution of Postgenomic Life, which combines Marxist political economy with Foucauldian biopolitics. Liu and Gu argue that these scholars, though illuminating, remain at the level of phenomena and need a fuller Marxist political-economy critique. The article draws on Rajan, Nikolas Rose, Clayton Pierce, Melinda Cooper, Joseph Dumit and others. It has three main sections: biocapitalism as the latest form of capitalist domination; its instrumental and "redemptive" character under the joint operation of capital logic and power logic; and its expression as neoliberalism and new imperialism in biological form. A short concluding section assesses the literature and raises questions for China. In the authors' account, the foreign scholars hold that biocapitalism continues capitalism rather than breaking with it: private ownership, class exploitation of "bio-labourers" and profit-driven monopoly persist. What changes is the route of exploitation, which shifts from people as bearers of labour-power to people as biological organisms. Value is drawn from speculative "future products" and expectations, and extraction extends from working time to the whole of life, blurring work and leisure. The review adds that state funding, patent monopolies and a "pseudo-religious" ideology of national salvation legitimate this process. It also cites the deCODE genetics database in Iceland, the Human Genome Project's treatment of the Guaymi, and transnational organ trafficking as cases of what the scholars call bio-imperialism and biocolonialism. Liu and Gu conclude that biocapitalism results from capital's rent-seeking in biotechnology and that its problems come from capital logic and the power logic it manipulates. They judge that most foreign left scholars stop at description and offer "reformist" or "utopian" remedies, and they call for a Marxist critique of political economy as the proper tool. They add that biotechnology has become a field of great-power rivalry, making biosecurity urgent for China, and they leave open whether biocapitalism might move towards "biosocialism". Read the original if you want a Chinese-language overview of Western left debates on biocapital and the way a Chinese Marxist assessment frames them.

The causes of "anti-globalization" and how to respond “逆全球化”的成因与应对 Dan Qing Dan Qing's short commentary asks why the United States and other Western countries, once champions of globalization, have turned to "anti-globalization" measures such as "de-risking", trade "decoupling" and the chips act. The author argues that these moves serve Western hegemony and domestic interests, and that China and other countries should answer by promoting an open, inclusive and mutually beneficial globalization. The piece has three parts: the main forms of anti-globalization, its root causes, and the proposed responses. It draws on examples such as the 2023 Munich Security Conference, the growth of the US "Entity List", and US withdrawals from agreements and organisations. Dan describes the US as using political bloc-building, economic sanctions and diplomatic withdrawal to slow the rise of emerging countries. The causes are said to be the outward projection of domestic contradictions (financial crises, industrial hollowing-out, widening inequality), a negative-sum strategy of containing rivals even at a cost to itself, and global governance that lags behind the declining Western share of the world economy. In the author's reading, Western countries choose globalization or its reverse purely according to their interests. Dan concludes that China should keep expanding opening up, help build a "new type of globalization" with more voice for developing countries, and work for a community with a shared future for mankind. The author cites the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative and Global Civilization Initiative as the means. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Party-journal commentary presents the Chinese official view of Western decoupling policies.

The reproduction of labour subjectivity under the logic of capital A contemporary dimension of Western Marxist critical theories of capital 资本逻辑下劳动主体性的再生产——西方马克思主义资本批判理论的一个当代面向 Niu Ziniu Niu asks why the strengthening of workers' subjectivity under contemporary capitalism has not liberated labour but has coincided with worse conditions. The article challenges the "subject-object inversion" paradigm, inherited from Lukács and influential in Chinese Marxist philosophy, which treats capital as usurping workers' subjectivity and liberation as its restoration. Niu argues that Western Marxists since the 1960s recognised a hidden complicity between labour subjectivity and capital's power, and developed theories of how capital reproduces labour subjects. The article has three parts. It first criticises what Merleau-Ponty called "Weberian Marxism" (Lukács, Adorno, Marcuse). It then traces a line of thought on the production of subjects through Kojève, Lacan, Althusser and Foucault. Finally it examines Deleuze's theory of desire-production and its later development by Byung-Chul Han, followed by a critique of Negri's autonomism and the cognitive capitalism school of Yann Moulier-Boutang. Niu contends that Lukács reached the rationalised labour process through Weber's rationalisation theory rather than through Marx's theories of valorisation and relative surplus value. The critique therefore fitted Fordist industrial capitalism, not the essential law of capital. Because capital's valorisation principle is non-identity, a ceaseless drive for "more", liberating differentiated subjectivity served capital. Niu says this fed neoliberalism and the post-1968 movements, and also hit bureaucratic unions, welfare states and socialist states. Althusser's ideological state apparatuses and Foucault's biopolitics treat power as productive. Deleuze defines surplus labour as a qualitative form internal to the worker's desire, so that workers "desire capital's desire". Niu adds that Deleuze's call to extend deterritorialisation still suits capital. Negri and the cognitive capitalism school repeat the Weberian error by treating more flexible, cognitive labour as emancipatory. Niu concludes that under neoliberalism domination takes the form of liberation, and that the wage-labour subject is not automatically a political subject. Following Althusser's distinction, Niu calls for specific political procedures to turn capitalism's "labour subjects" into "political subjects", without which revolutionary action would fail. Niu says this also invites reflection on the existing paradigm in Chinese Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you want a critical account of how Western Marxist theories of the subject, from Lukács to Deleuze and Han, relate to capital accumulation and neoliberalism.

Drawing vitality for ideological and political theory courses from reform and innovation 思政课建设要向改革创新要活力 Wang Yi Marking five years since Xi Jinping's March 2019 symposium for teachers of ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke), this Guangming Daily commentary takes up how these courses can keep gaining vitality. Xi said then that their development must "draw vitality from reform and innovation". Wang argues that the five years have produced clear results, and that the next stage should rest on strengthened Party leadership, innovation, coordinated action and digital empowerment. The piece has three parts. The first surveys results in four areas: guiding ideas, the overall pattern of work, the content system and teaching methods. The second extracts three basic lessons: upholding Party leadership, innovation as a driving force, and coordinated linkage. The third proposes how to deepen reform from "a new historical starting point". In Wang's account, the guiding ideas are set by Xi's statements and by central policy documents, which supply top-level design. The pattern of work has changed through stronger Marxism schools, research funding for the courses, and a school–family–society effort. The content system is built around the course "Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era", the "Great Ideological and Political Course" and integration across primary, secondary and university stages. Methods include case-based, inquiry-based and experiential teaching, as well as virtual classrooms. The lessons Wang draws stress that Party leadership "can only be strengthened, not weakened". They also cite university Party secretaries and presidents as first persons responsible, and a teacher–student ratio of no less than 1:350 for full-time teachers. For the next stage Wang proposes three measures. The first links compulsory and elective courses, with the Xi Jinping Thought introduction as the core of a "gold course" system. The second joins the small classroom to the wider social classroom through practice bases, volunteering and fieldwork. The third uses digital platforms, resource banks and XR/VR simulation to move from using technology to being empowered by it, and from individual teachers to team effort. Read the original if you want an official-academic account of how Chinese universities describe their ideological and political course reforms, with concrete policy instruments and examples.

The evolution of Kishida's "new capitalism" policy: theory and practice 岸田“新资本主义”政策的演进：理论与实践 Liu Rui Liu Rui examines the "new capitalism" programme that Fumio Kishida first put forward in September 2021 as Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party chose its leader. The article asks how the policy has developed, what lies behind it, what theory it draws on and how far it has worked. Liu's answer is that the policy corrects neoliberalism only in part: in practice it continues the main methods of "Abenomics", stays within Japan's traditional neoliberal framework and addresses short-term problems rather than long-term ones. The article has four parts. It first traces the policy from the October 2021 framework and the new headquarters chaired by the prime minister through the 2022 and 2023 basic policy documents. It then sets out the background: long economic stagnation, a "disparity society", weak corporate innovation, feeble consumption and investment, and a changed international environment. The third part reviews the theoretical foundations, and the fourth assesses results and obstacles. In Liu's account, the policy has three features: it stresses distribution, but this fades as it is folded into the growth strategy ("investment in people", structural wage rises); it takes on extra functions, notably economic security, which Liu says follows the United States in restraining China and works against the growth goal; and it widens government–private cooperation. Liu locates its theory in criticism of neoliberalism, stakeholder capitalism and the "public-interest capitalism" of Hara Joji, which draws on Japanese business traditions. Liu concludes that "new" means a correction of neoliberalism, not a rejection of capitalism. On results, Liu argues that the 2023 wage rises mainly reflect rising prices, so real wages kept falling. Growth was driven by external demand and a weak yen, while domestic demand declined and corporate retained earnings reached record highs. Liu identifies three obstacles: a severe fiscal position and a fiscal-reconstruction target that is hard to meet; large funding gaps for defence, measures against the falling birth rate and green transformation; and an excessive emphasis on economic security that could hinder growth. Liu closes by asking how the government can strengthen growth, raise real wages and potential growth, and reform social security, and says these questions test the Kishida government. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's detailed, data-heavy assessment of Kishida's economic programme and its intellectual sources.

Mao Zedong's reflections on major questions of the Chinese revolution during the Great Revolution: an analysis of "The Significance of Commemorating the Paris Commune" 大革命时期毛泽东对中国革命重大问题的思考——基于《纪念巴黎公社的重要意义》的分析 Tang Zhihua Chen Honghui Tang and Chen examine a short lecture Mao Zedong gave in 1926 at the Kuomintang's political training class to mark the 55th anniversary of the Paris Commune. The text is only about 2,000 characters long, yet the authors argue that it deals systematically with the conditions, significance and lessons of the Commune. Their thesis is that, by reading the Commune closely against Chinese conditions during the First United Front, Mao thought through a series of major questions of the Chinese revolution. In their account this laid a theoretical foundation for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and for the later theory of the New Democratic revolution. The article is organised around four themes drawn from the lecture. It first treats changes in the revolutionary situation, namely the revolution's character, its strategy and its goal. It then turns to the forces of revolution, to armed struggle as the basic form of revolution, and finally to principles and strategies for moving the revolution forward. The authors set Mao's lecture beside his other writings of the 1920s and 1930s, and beside the positions of the Comintern, the early Party congresses and Chen Duxiu. The authors make three main moves. First, they argue that Mao saw the revolution shifting from a movement of the few to one involving the majority of workers and peasants, to be mobilised politically and aimed at a workers' and peasants' state on the Soviet model. Second, they say Mao insisted that the proletariat and its Party must lead, against the then-dominant underestimation of the working class, and that armed struggle was the basic form of revolution, to be pursued by drawing flexibly on the Commune and the October Revolution rather than copying them. Third, they report that Mao read the Commune's failure as stemming from the lack of a unified, disciplined party and of severe treatment of enemies. The authors link these points to the Party's centralised and unified leadership, to Party building, and to the principle of delivering a decisive blow to the enemy, which they contrast with Chen Duxiu's conciliatory line. Tang and Chen conclude that the lecture marks an early, pioneering step in Mao's theoretical and practical awareness of adapting Marxism to China. They see in it the seeds of the later path of encircling the cities from the countryside and seizing power by armed force. They also urge readers today, in a period of great changes unseen in a century, to study it so as to strengthen the fighting spirit and overcome risks to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you study Mao's early thought, the Party's official historiography of the Great Revolution, or how Commune lessons are used in Chinese Marxist theory.

Sources and practice of Mao Zedong's idea of "proletarian revolutionary utilitarianism" 毛泽东“无产阶级的革命的功利主义”思想的源头与实践 Miao Guishan Miao Guishan examines the origins and practice of the idea of "proletarian revolutionary utilitarianism" that Mao Zedong put forward at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art in May 1942. In that talk Mao said Communists take as their starting point the unity of the present and future interests of the great majority, and so aim at the "broadest and most distant" goals rather than narrow, local ones. Miao argues that the idea has several distinct theoretical roots and was carried out in the Party's revolutionary practice, as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article first summarises the idea's content: it is a question of standpoint (serving workers, peasants and soldiers) and of method (the mass line), it applies equally to military and cultural work, and it differs in kind from feudal, bourgeois and petty-bourgeois utilitarianism. It then has four sections on sources. These are the young Mao's reading of Friedrich Paulsen's ethics and of utilitarianism; the Communist Manifesto and the theory of the Chinese revolution; Lenin and Lu Xun on literature; and the practice of the new-democratic revolution. Miao's central move traces the idea to Mao's 1917 annotations of Cai Yuanpei's Chinese version of Paulsen's System of Ethics, studied under his teacher Yang Changji. Mao took from Paulsen a teleological theory of self-realisation, which Miao links to his own ideal of the heroic individual and to the Chinese tradition of sacrificing life for righteousness. Miao says this ideal turned into a proletarian value outlook once Mao embraced Marxism around 1920. Miao adds that the Manifesto's claim that proletarian movements serve the immense majority, together with Mao's wartime analyses of class forces and revolutionary stages, supplied the theoretical premise. Lenin's "literature for the millions of working people" and Lu Xun's couplet about serving the people like an ox supplied the standpoint. Mao's own formula that Communists' words and actions must meet "the greatest interests of the greatest number" echoes Bentham and Mill, as mediated by Yang Changji's history of Western ethics. In the new-democratic period Mao made this a productive-forces standard, and the Party's "serve the people" purpose followed from it. Miao concludes that the idea is true because it accords with the people's interests and has been tested in China's revolution and construction. The article also presents it as an ethical consciousness in individual Communists and an ethical spirit in the Party as a political community, citing Mao's three principles in On Coalition Government. Read the original if you study Mao's intellectual formation, the links between Chinese ethics and Marxism, or how official scholarship traces the origins of Mao Zedong Thought.

New developments in the Middle East amid great changes: features, challenges and prospects 大变局下中东地区新发展：特征、挑战及前景 Wang Lincong Wang Lincong asks how the Middle East is changing as the international order shifts, and what obstacles and prospects follow. The article argues that the region has reached a historic turning point: states prioritise development, reconcile with one another and act with greater strategic autonomy, becoming an important force in the Global South. It holds that China's global initiatives can help the region leave its security and development predicaments and shape a "new Middle East". The article has three parts: new features of regional development, the challenges it faces, and its prospects. The features are examined at three levels: national, regional and global. Wang draws on opinion surveys (Arab Opinion Index 2022, Arab Barometer), national vision plans such as Saudi Vision 2030, and events from 2019 to 2023, including the Saudi–Iranian rapprochement, the Ukraine crisis and BRICS enlargement. Wang argues that the Arab upheavals deepened rather than resolved the region's development, security and governance deficits. Citizens now care more about economic livelihood than abstract democracy, and elites want to catch the fourth industrial revolution. The "wave of reconciliation" is presented as a rational choice based on security and economic costs, helped by US strategic contraction and Chinese mediation. Wang also stresses persistent obstacles: structural economic problems, debt crises and slow diversification in oil-rich states; continuing US pressure, which Wang describes as sanctions, proxy conflicts and exclusive "mini-multilateral" schemes such as I2U2 and IMEC; and layered security risks, including Gaza, Sudan, the Turkey–Syria earthquake and Libya's floods. Wang concludes that the region's progress will be difficult and uneven, since strategic trust and security institutions are lacking. China is credited with a constructive role, shown in trade figures, the 2022 China–Arab summits, naval escorts in the Gulf of Aden and the brokering of the Saudi–Iranian deal. Wang proposes cooperation under the global development, global security and global civilization initiatives, together with the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Middle East realignment and China's role are framed, with figures and examples from 2019–2023.

The paradigm shift in research on foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义研究的范式转向 Sun Ying Sun Ying asks how Chinese research on foreign Marxism (Marxism outside China) has changed since the start of the new era, and where it should go next. The article argues that the field is already in a period of paradigm transition. It moves from object-oriented translation and exposition towards what Sun calls subject-centred, dialogical research that serves the development of contemporary Chinese Marxism. Sun first summarises five scholarly positions on the shift: the contemporary-significance, problem-orientation, change-of-centre, change-of-role and breaking-disciplinary-walls views. The article then organises the change along three axes: content (from translation and introduction to genealogical research), method (from text commentary to theoretical system-building), and value orientation (from drawing direct lessons to returning to the Marxist classics and stressing China's significance). Examples include biopolitics, urban space, financial capitalism and ecological Marxism. Sun argues that translation remains the foundation, but it mainly transports knowledge and cannot sort out tendencies in foreign thought that depart from Marxist fundamentals, such as instrumentalization, fragmentation and deconstruction. Genealogical research therefore compares thinkers such as Foucault, Agamben, Hardt and Negri and works across disciplines. Under a principle of wholeness, scholars compare Chinese and Western approaches, for instance Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization against Western ecological Marxism, which Sun describes as theoretically stagnant and ineffective in practice. They also place Western Marxism in the history of thought and build their own analytical paradigms. The third move is a new "return to the classics", after the "return to Marx" of the turn of the century. It draws on the Capital revival after the 2008 crisis and on MEGA2, and on studying texts of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, in dialogue with foreign studies of China. Sun concludes that the core issue is the critique of capitalist modernity, with Marxism as guide, sinicized Marxism as centre and foreign Marxism as resource. Guided by the Two Integrations, the author expects future work to focus on capitalist modernity, paths of human emancipation and forms of civilization. It should also stress grand historical narrative and strengthen the construction and international spread of Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want to understand how a Chinese scholar maps the field's methodological self-reassessment and its stated aims.

The historical logic of East European neo-Marxism On the contemporary significance of research on East European neo-Marxism 东欧新马克思主义的历史逻辑——兼论东欧新马克思主义研究的当代意义 Song Tieyi Song Tieyi takes up a question about classification: East European neo-Marxism has long been treated as a branch or appendage of Western Marxism, so its own theoretical significance has gone under-recognised. The author argues that the two traditions share a source in Lukács's turn in Marxist theory but differ in historical logic, and that East European neo-Marxism should not be equated with Western Marxism. This short newspaper commentary also draws out what studying it means today. Song begins with the two usual reasons for the conflation: the shared Lukácsian origin, and the fact that, apart from the Budapest School, East European currents did not survive as continuing schools. The article then uses the Czech philosopher Karel Kosík and his Dialectics of the Concrete as its main case. It proceeds in three steps: Kosík's totalising cultural critique, its extension into a critique of political economy, and its openness to history. It closes by relating the discussion to Marx's late thought and to present-day research. The central claim is that Lukács left a double path of cultural critique and critique of political economy, and a split between methodology and ontology. Western Marxism, in Song's reading, carried on mainly as theoretical critique, whereas East European neo-Marxists, working from the practice of socialist states, tried to unite the two paths in a 'humanist socialism'. Song reads Kosík's concrete dialectics as the key example. Kosík criticises the 'pseudo-concrete' world of reified, fetishised everyday utilitarian practice, then argues that the 'economic man' of classical economics is a product of economics itself, not its premise. For Song, his dialectic is at once the self-unfolding of the 'thing in itself' and the method for pursuing it, which heals the split Lukács left. Song also links this to Marx's late writings on the Asiatic mode of production, the 'Kaufine Gorge' idea and the reply to Zasulich. Song concludes that East European neo-Marxism was itself an expression of historical practice and stayed open to diverse historical paths on a humanist, national-cultural basis. The author connects this to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and to the Two Integrations, which are said to have answered the questions Marx left in his late work. Further study of East European experience is said to deepen understanding of how Marxism becomes localised worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language case for separating East European neo-Marxism from Western Marxism, centred on Kosík.

Re-examining Marx's concept of abstract labour 重新审视马克思的抽象劳动概念 Wang Shaoliang Wang Shaoliang takes up a long-running dispute over what Marx meant by abstract labour. Citing the Soviet economist Isaak Rubin's contemporary Rozenberg's early objection (1930s) to treating it as merely a physiological expenditure of labour-power, Wang argues that the physiological reading takes an epistemological sense of "abstraction" for Marx's own. In Wang's account, abstract labour is a social and ontological category specific to capitalism, not a natural property of human labour in every era. The piece is a short theoretical commentary in three parts. It first traces the philosophical history of "abstraction" from Aristotle and Plato through Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, and shows how this lineage produces a naturalistic reading. It then turns to Marx's ontological critique, drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts and Capital, and finally to the social determination of abstract labour and the "abstraction of labour" as a historical process. Wang also notes that Marx uses varying formulations and qualifiers such as "common", "universal" and "undifferentiated". Wang argues that the physiological definition in Capital is a result reached "after the event", a post festum analysis that expresses capitalist commodity economy in the language of natural science and so makes wage labour look eternal. Marx, in this reading, moves abstraction into ontology: value has a "phantom-like objectivity" that is real yet detached from sensuous objectivity, and socially necessary labour time acts as a hidden structural power over workers and capitalists alike. The Latin root abstrahere, meaning separation, points to the historical separation of labourers from the means of production and from ethical ties, so that abstraction is a real, daily process in production. Wang accordingly distinguishes abstract labour from "labour in general", and criticises Paul Sweezy for equating them. Wang concludes that abstract labour becomes the subject of modern social development only under definite historical conditions, and that attributing the substance and source of value to it can be explained only within the movement of capitalism. The analysis in Capital is said to unite scientific analysis with critique of value, since abstraction both negates individuality and gives private labour a social character. Read the original if you work on Marx's value theory or the philosophical background to Chinese debates about abstract labour and want a compact ontological alternative to the physiological interpretation.

Strengthening political guidance for youth and cultivating new-era talents for the Party 加强青年政治引领 为党培育时代新人 Zhu Hanmo This commentary, by the secretary of Nanjing University's Communist Youth League committee, responds to Xi Jinping's remarks in a collective conversation with the new leadership of the League's Central Committee. Xi stressed strengthening political guidance for young people. Zhu argues that this is the League's fundamental task: it follows from the League's founding mission and from the Party's need for qualified builders and reliable successors. The piece first explains why political guidance matters. It then sets out Xi's working path for the League: take a political perspective, start from ideology, and proceed from the characteristics of young people. The second half turns to four "logics" through which guidance is to be carried out: theoretical, historical, practical and one based on present-day reality. Zhu holds that "listening to the Party and following the Party" is the League's political lifeblood and what distinguishes it from other youth organisations. On the theoretical side, young people should study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era through regular thematic education. On the historical side, Party history and its "red genes" should be taught. Achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) are to serve as "achievement education" supporting the Four-sphere Confidence. The practical logic links practice to young people's specialist skills, to national priorities and to political commitment. Zhu also notes that today's "Z generation" requires new methods. Zhu concludes that the League should unite, organise and mobilise young people to act as a vanguard and shock force for building a strong country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated youth work is framed and operationalised after the 20th Party Congress (2022).

The theoretical value and practical significance of Lenin's intellectual legacy for the world revolution and the Vietnamese revolution 列宁思想遗产对世界革命和越南革命的理论价值与实践意义 Nguyễn Xuân Thắng Wei Lichun Pan Jin'e Written to mark the 150th anniversary of Lenin's birth (2020) and published in 2024, this article asks what Lenin's legacy means for world revolution and for Vietnam. The authors, a senior Vietnamese Party leader with two Chinese scholars, argue that Lenin defended and creatively developed Marxism, and that his thought gave Ho Chi Minh and the Communist Party of Vietnam the basis for combining national independence with socialism. The article moves through seven sections. The first four deal with Lenin: his theory that revolution could succeed in the imperialist era and the October Revolution, his ideas on socialist construction and the New Economic Policy, his struggle against opportunism, and his theory of the national and colonial question. The fifth and sixth sections turn to Vietnam, covering Ho Chi Minh's conversion to Leninism and the Party's current line of renewal (đổi mới). A short conclusion restates the commitment to Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought. The authors argue that Lenin built on Marx's expectation of simultaneous revolution in advanced countries. From the law of uneven development, they say, he concluded that socialism could win first in a single country, and that Russia was the weakest link in the imperialist chain. They present the October Revolution as an objectively necessary outcome, not an accident. They read the shift from war communism to the New Economic Policy as a model for reforming existing socialism, which includes a multi-sector economy and learning from capitalism. In their account, the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe was the failure of a flawed model, not of socialism or Marxism-Leninism. The authors also stress Lenin's extension of the slogan to 'workers of all countries and oppressed nations, unite'. They hold that Ho Chi Minh's thesis that colonial revolutions may precede metropolitan ones, and that independence must be tied to socialism, enriched Marxism-Leninism. The authors conclude that the Communist Party of Vietnam, guided by Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, has produced historic achievements through renewal. They cite a socialist-oriented market economy, stronger Party building and an anti-corruption campaign since the 12th Party Congress. They call for firmness in the goals of national independence and socialism and for Vietnam to become a developed, socialist-oriented country. Read the original if you want an official Vietnamese Party-theoretical account of how Lenin's legacy is used to legitimise renewal and the Party's leadership.

Deconstruction and restoration: the road to rebuilding the history of Chinese Marxist historiography 解构与还原：中国马克思主义史学史的重建之路 Chen Feng Chen Feng notes that research on the history of Chinese Marxist historiography has become a fast-growing field, drawing many young scholars, and asks how it can move beyond routine work. The article argues for two tasks: deconstructing long-standing presuppositions, and restoring the real picture of the field by returning to primary sources and engaging critically with them. The article has two parts. The first examines four presuppositions that Chen traces to a "revolutionary history paradigm", in which Marxist historiography becomes a branch of revolutionary history. The second sets out how to restore the field's actual shape, covering which sources to read, how to read them, and the part played by the researcher's own standpoint. In the first part, Chen challenges four assumptions. These are that Marxist historiography is the final form of historical scholarship; that it must fuse politics and scholarship; that it is the same as "Chinese Communist Party historiography"; and that its unity hides its internal differences. Chen argues the first is teleological and unhistorical, since Marxism treats everything as developing. Chen also holds that Marxism is both a revolutionary theory and a social science, so scholars could use it without sharing the political faith. Chen further distinguishes official from academic Marxist historiography and stresses breaks and disputes among its figures and periods. In the second part, Chen urges reading far beyond the few canonical authors. Suggested sources include non-Marxist periodicals, reviews, diaries and letters, popular works, ultra-left-period writings, and hostile Kuomintang criticism. Chen also proposes shifting from "confirmatory" to "discovery" reading, and treats restoration as also a reconstruction in which the researcher's present outlook meets the objective record. Chen concludes that the field is dominated by orthodox, uneventful studies and must deliberately "defamiliarise" itself. It should dare to question inherited theories and conclusions, and aim at a "new Marxist historiography history", modelled on the shift to the "new revolutionary history" in modern Chinese history. The result, Chen says, would be a new scholarly map that is closer to the past and guides future Marxist historiography. Read the original if you study Chinese historiography or the self-critical turn in Chinese scholarship on Marxism, or want concrete source suggestions for the period before and after 1949.

New trends in British Marxist historiography since the 1990s 20世纪90年代以来英国马克思主义史学新趋向 Liang Minsu How has British Marxist historiography developed since the 1990s, after the generation of Hobsbawm and E. P. Thompson? Liang argues that the school has lost momentum and no longer produces figures of equal stature. Even so, its themes, core concerns and historical outlook remain a reference point for international historiography, and a second generation and later followers have extended its legacy in two areas: the new labour history and Marxist feminist history. The article has three parts. The first describes the new setting after the end of the Cold War: British works defending or applying Marxist method, non-Marxist studies of Hobsbawm and Thompson, new histories of the Communist Party of Great Britain, and institutions and journals such as the Socialist History Society (1992), the Marx Memorial Library and Workers' School (1993), and periodicals like Past and Present, History Workshop Journal and New Left Review. The second part treats the new labour history under the "cultural turn". The third treats Marxist feminist history. Liang's central claim is that Thompson's "culturalist" paradigm, which approached class consciousness through experience and a history "from below", is the theoretical base of the new labour history. Later historians turned it towards global labour history, partly in response to criticism that stress on experience and language fragmented the field. In feminist history, Sheila Rowbotham, Catherine Hall, Sally Alexander and Barbara Taylor are presented as building on Thompson while criticising his marginalising of women. Their move from women's history to gender history, joined with class analysis, widened the field in three ways: geographically (Scotland, Ireland, Australia), in historical context (second- and third-wave feminism, imperial and global history), and in theory (a call to return to class analysis and a critique of patriarchy). Liang concludes that, over the past three decades, later British Marxist historians have mostly worked on the writings and thought of the first two generations, especially Thompson's culturalist model. In the article's account, British Marxist historiography still shapes British historical scholarship and receives international attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of post-1990 British Marxist history, with many names and titles on the Communist Party's historiography, labour history and feminist history.

Xi Jinping's inheritance and enrichment of Mao Zedong's view of traditional culture 论习近平对毛泽东传统文化观的继承与丰富发展 Zhang Guozuo Sun Yafang Zhang Guozuo and Sun Yafang ask how Xi Jinping's attitude to traditional Chinese culture relates to that of Mao Zedong. They argue that Xi has creatively inherited Mao's view of traditional culture and enriched it with new ideas, judgements and strategic plans. The article, published in Social Sciences Journal (2024, no. 2), defines traditional culture as mainly Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist thought, and presents Xi's contribution as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first identifies four strands in Mao's view: valuing national history, keeping the national culture primary, applying Marxism in light of Chinese characteristics, and absorbing the essence while discarding the dross. For each, the authors pair a Xi counterpart, using quotations from speeches between 2012 and 2022. The second part lists Xi's additions, and the third assesses their significance. In the authors' reading, each Maoist idea is carried a step further. Valuing history becomes strengthening cultural confidence. Giving priority to national culture becomes holding to a Chinese cultural standpoint. Applying Marxism with Chinese characteristics becomes the Two Integrations, notably combining Marxism's basic principles with excellent traditional culture. Mao's selective method becomes 'discriminating treatment and sublating inheritance', which adds creative transformation and innovative development. The authors say Xi deepens the standing of this culture as the nation's 'root and soul' and as the root of Party theoretical innovation. They also say he gives it practical roles in governance, core socialist values, philosophy and social sciences, and literature and art. Finally, they say he sets out a systematic programme covering research, education, display, and legal protection of cultural heritage. The authors conclude that Mao's era mostly concerned breaking down old culture and left the value, transformation and development of tradition unexamined theoretically. Xi's contribution, they argue, lies mainly in 'establishing'. They say it strengthens cultural confidence, opens a new horizon through the Two Integrations, supplies resources for a new form of human civilization and Chinese modern civilization, and underpins cultural soft power amid what they describe as hostile international pressure. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present continuity and development between Mao's and Xi's cultural policy, with many dated Xi quotations.

Ownership in the digital age: from digital capitalism to digital socialism 数字时代的所有制议题：从数字资本主义到数字社会主义 Hao Zhichang Hao Zhichang asks how ownership should be understood in the digital age and whether it points towards digital capitalism or digital socialism. The article argues that ownership, as the foundation of the relations of production, is the underlying logic of any digital civilisation, and that debates on data rights or privacy law stay superficial if they ignore it. Hao holds that the digital form of ownership is at a crossroads: under capitalism it yields new hidden forms of exploitation, while a socialist form of ownership can open a new digital civilisation. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's concept of ownership: its elements (objects of labour, means of labour, labourers, non-labourers and purposive activity), the attribution of the means of production, and the specific way labourers and means of production are combined. It then maps these elements onto digital forms. The second part analyses digital capitalist ownership, drawing on Nick Srnicek, Christian Fuchs, Kevin Kelly, Byung-Chul Han and others. The third sets out digital socialist ownership and relates it to China's basic economic system. Hao's central move is to treat user data as the digital counterpart of Marx's 'filtered' raw material, and algorithms, cloud computing and AI as digital means of labour. Under digital capitalism, these digital means of production belong to platform owners, not to users. Users are combined with them through a 'non-standard' digital wage-labour system, in which 'free services' function as wages. The 'public use' model replaces exclusive private use and turns exploitation into self-exploitation. Hao disputes Han's claim that users own their means of production: in Hao's view they only use them, and are newly recruited wage-labourers. Against this, digital socialist ownership requires common or social ownership of data and platforms. It also requires a higher-level direct combination of labourers with the means of production, which Hao reads as the digital form of Marx's 're-establishing individual ownership'. Hao concludes that 'public use' without public ownership is a new deception, and that open, shared digital means of production resist privatisation. The article presents the 'Digital China' project and China's basic economic system, with public ownership as the mainstay, as providing institutional guarantees for this path. It describes a Chinese model of digital socialism with global significance. Read the original if you want a Marxist, ownership-centred critique of platform capitalism that ends in an argument for digital socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Strengthening theoretical and empirical research on China's culture and civilization 加强我国文化、文明的理论和经验研究 Li Peilin This short editorial introduction argues that research on culture and civilization in China needs to be strengthened, both theoretically and empirically. Li Peilin notes that 'culture' is among the most widely studied yet most variously understood concepts in the humanities and social sciences. He holds that its importance in China is tied to the country's long civilizational history and to Chinese modernization, in which cultural development is one of five areas of construction. The piece first sketches how Chinese intellectuals have treated traditional culture since the Opium War of 1840. It then distinguishes culture from civilization, notes the lack of a discipline of 'culturology', and introduces three articles by young scholars on a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences project. Li argues that the dominant modern intellectual current, from the Westernizing Movement to the May Fourth Movement, leaned towards a break with tradition, unlike the European Renaissance. He cites Hegel and Weber as Western thinkers sceptical that Chinese culture could modernize. Two parallel strands, he says, are often overlooked: the persistence of culture in everyday life, and the deep influence of tradition on reform thought, which grew into cultural self-awareness after reform and opening up. Li also separates culture, understood as 'humanization', from civilization, which he links to writing, cities and social ritual. He says culture research is treated as interdisciplinary and mostly humanistic, which limits scholarly consensus and calls for more empirical disciplines. Li presents building a culturally strong country and shaping a modern Chinese civilization as current tasks for Chinese social science. He introduces a 2023 national survey of residents' satisfaction with cultural development and three articles drawing on it, on cultural needs and confidence, cultural subjectivity, and cultural governance. He hopes more scholars will join, making the field more standardized and mature. Read the original if you want a brief view from a leading Chinese sociologist on how culture and civilization research is being organised in China.

Revisiting the Lenin–Kautsky debate on the October Revolution from the perspective of revolutionary will 革命意志视角下列宁和考茨基关于十月革命理论论争的再探讨 Ding Guanghao Sun Daiyao Ding Guanghao and Sun Daiyao ask why Lenin and Kautsky, after the 1917 October Revolution, reached such opposed judgements of it. They argue that the root of the dispute lies in how each understood 'revolutionary will'. Lenin held a logic of 'manufacturing' will under special revolutionary conditions, while Kautsky held a logic of 'generation', in which will arises naturally on a mature economic base. The article opens with a review of earlier scholarship. It notes early Western Marxists' critique of Second International economic determinism, Cold War 'Leninology' that treated Kautskyism as Leninism's source, and Chinese studies of democracy and dictatorship, imperialism and revolutionary strategy. It then compares the two thinkers on three questions: the objective conditions for progressive will in backward Russia, how will is shaped through Soviet democracy, and whether wartime will can be carried into socialist construction. A final section traces the differences back to their understandings of historical materialism. On conditions, the authors report that Lenin saw Russia's backwardness and crisis as an advantage for starting the revolution, though not for completing it. Kautsky, in The Dictatorship of the Proletariat, judged that will born of backwardness was blind mass psychology and not socialist. On shaping, Lenin favoured centralised leadership and training through struggle and practical work; Kautsky held that 'pure democracy' and free will were prerequisites, and that Soviet rule produced only 'unified opinion'. On the limits of will, Kautsky warned of 'barracks socialism', which Ding and Sun call a salutary warning that overlooked the survival logic of War Communism. Behind these differences, the authors argue, Kautsky's naturalist, scientistic reading led to 'economic fatalism' and a rigid use of general laws. Lenin's historical dialectic stressed the interplay of base and superstructure, the particular within the general, and the unity of Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character. The authors conclude that the debate epitomised the clash between Russian Marxism and Second International 'orthodoxy'. After October, they say, revolution in relatively backward countries became the 'general' case. They cite Mao Zedong's view that seizing power precedes developing productive forces, and Xi Jinping's call for fighting spirit and will in building socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. They argue that a Marxist governing party must keep its revolutionary spirit. Read the original if you study the Lenin–Kautsky controversy, debates on 'skipping stages', or how Chinese scholars link Lenin's theory to contemporary Party discourse.

Financial hegemony and its effects in the light of Lenin's theory of imperialism 列宁帝国主义论视野下的金融霸权及其影响 Xing Wenzeng Prompted by the US Federal Reserve's rate rises and Western sanctions on Russia since 2022, which Xing Wenzeng says have caused currency collapses and debt crises in many developing countries, the article asks how financial hegemony became a tool for plundering global wealth and what deeper effects it has. Xing argues that its roots lie in Lenin's theory of imperialism, above all in the rule of finance capital and the financial oligarchy. The article has four sections. It first sets out the institutional, military and technological foundations of present-day US financial hegemony. It then examines how the United States and its Western allies use it as a weapon of control and plunder, through financial sanctions, dollar hegemony and the engineering of crises abroad. The third section discusses how it sharpens capitalism's deeper contradictions, among developed countries and between the hegemon and developing ones. The last section turns to de-dollarisation and the case for a fairer international order. Evidence includes Russia, Sri Lanka, Egypt, Vietnam, South Korea and Latin America. Xing's central move is to read Lenin's finance capital as the basis of hegemony. Banking and industrial capital merge, finance capital dominates, and a few states hold a special position over the rest. Since 1945, Xing says, this has been reinforced by financial monopoly, about 750 US military bases and technological control. The author cites the rising share of finance in US corporate profits and US stakes in major semiconductor firms. The second move applies Lenin's law of uneven development and his picture of a world split into a few usurer states and many debtor states. In Xing's account, the Fed alternates between easing and tightening to shift costs onto others, as with the Plaza Accord and Japan, pressure on the euro, and Asian and Latin American debt crises. Xing concludes that dollar-based finance is losing trust. Russia, India and others are de-dollarising and building alternatives to SWIFT, and the author calls this trend irreversible. Xing says the remedy is genuine multilateralism, a multipolar order and greater developing-country solidarity, and presents China's call for diversified settlement currencies, debt relief and a community with a shared future for mankind as a contrast to US hegemony. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist application of Lenin's Imperialism to the Fed, dollar and sanctions debates since 2022, with data and cases.

An investigation of the Chinese Bureau of the Communist Party of the USA 美国共产党中国局考论 Wang Mingliang Wang Mingliang takes up the history of the Chinese Bureau of the Communist Party of the USA, an underground organisation of Chinese students, workers and overseas Chinese founded in 1927. Little is known about it, and even its founding date and its Chinese and English names have been unclear. Wang argues that the Bureau grew up independently of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), belonged organisationally to the American party, and nonetheless deserves a place in the CCP's organisational history. The article draws mainly on the US Communist Party files held in the Russian State Archive of Socio-Political History. It supplements them with American, mainland Chinese and Taiwanese archives, memoirs and oral accounts. It first reconstructs the origins, names, membership and phases of the Bureau, from the "Chaotao" student group of Tsinghua graduates to its dissolution in the early 1950s. It then examines the Bureau's relations with the American party, the CCP and the Comintern. Finally it surveys five areas of united-front and propaganda work. On relations, Wang compares two conflicting recollections, those of Zhang Bao and Cai Fujiu, and reconciles them. In Wang's account the early members were recruited by the American party under Comintern guidance, and the CCP, distant and preoccupied after 1927, gave little direct guidance. Close CCP contact came only after the Pacific courier route opened in 1941, and above all after 1945, when the Bureau, reorganised under Dong Biwu, became the CCP's leading group in the US. The American party gave little money or attention, which Wang attributes to its factional strife, its dependence on Comintern funds and the Bureau's small size. Wang also cites CCP constitutional provisions of 1923 and a 1978 foreign ministry notice to support counting these members as CCP members. The Bureau's work, in Wang's list, covered organising overseas Chinese labourers, publishing newspapers and pamphlets to counter Kuomintang information blockades, and campaigning against US trade with Japan. It also covered lobbying against US intervention in the civil war and mobilising scientists and students to return after 1949. Wang notes that the standard Party organisational history omits the Bureau and calls this a gap in Party history research. Wang hopes more scholars will study it. Read the original if you are interested in CCP overseas organisation, the Comintern's national-party structure, or archival work on Chinese communists in the United States.

Anxiety over market value in early capitalist England Money, commodities and national security in Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida 英国早期资本主义时期的市场价值焦虑——莎士比亚《特洛伊罗斯与克瑞西达》中的货币、商品与国家安全 Tao Jiusheng Tao Jiusheng asks how Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida (1609) registers the anxieties of England's early capitalist market economy. The article argues that the women Helen and Cressida are commodified in a Trojan–Greek market and function like money on the foreign-exchange market. Like coin, their value swings between intrinsic value, which comes from the bearer's own qualities, and extrinsic value, which comes from external relations such as supply, scarcity and the judgement of others. In Tao's reading, the Trojans' decision to rely on Helen's inflated market value leads to the fall of Troy, which expresses the playwright's worry that market-based valuation endangers the state. Tao first reviews earlier criticism, including David Hawkes and Jonathan Harris, and says it has not tied the value debates to national security in the historical setting of rising capitalism. Part one covers the Renaissance background: enclosure, wage labour, the commodification of women and chastity, the analogy of people to stamped coin, and early modern theories of money from Malynes, Mun, Buridan, Oresme and North. Part two reads the play's value disputes over Helen, Cressida, Achilles and Ajax. Part three turns to anxieties about merchants, social order, fraud, the "just price", debased coinage and exchange-rate manipulation. Tao's central move is to match the characters' conflicting valuations with the period's money theories. Hector's appeal to Helen's own worth corresponds to bullionist intrinsic value, while Troilus's insistence that value is set by those who judge corresponds to market value. Her scarcity, uniqueness and the lovers' subjective feelings also make her value unstable. Second, Tao links this instability to contemporary fears. Ulysses's advice to act "like a merchant" erodes aristocratic hierarchy in the Greek camp. Thersites likens a man to a counterfeit coin. Malynes and Thomas Smith, meanwhile, describe foreign bankers and counterfeiters exploiting the gap between a coin's face and metal value. Tao concludes that the play implicitly points to the need for government regulation of the market, since the Trojan court appears but does not supervise valuation. The article notes that mercantilist writers themselves worried that monarchs were subject to larger commercial forces, and that Mun recognised that rulers could not overcome them. Tao also links the play's subjective, market-driven valuation to Hobbes's Leviathan and to later cultural theory. Read the original if you work on Shakespeare, early modern literature and economic thought, or Marxist literary criticism of commodification and want a detailed, text-based account of how money theory is mapped onto the play.

The state, challenges and prospects of the Nepali communist movement in light of the 2022 general election 从2022年大选看尼泊尔共产主义运动的现状、挑战与前景 Yuan Qun Why did Nepal's two main communist parties lose the November 2022 elections, form an alliance, then split within weeks, and what does this mean for the communist movement? Yuan Qun takes up these questions, focusing on the CPN-UML and the CPN (Maoist Centre), which finished second and third behind the Nepali Congress. The article argues that the movement remains Nepal's largest political force but faces fragmentation, factional self-interest and foreign interference, and that its future depends on unity and on balancing party identity with parliamentary transformation. The article opens with the election results at local, provincial and federal levels, comparing them with 2017, when the left alliance won 174 House seats. It then narrates the post-election manoeuvres: Prachanda's power-sharing deal with Oli, his third term as prime minister in December 2022, the split over the presidential candidate in February 2023, and the Maoist Centre's turn to the Nepali Congress. The central section analyses three challenges; a final section sets out three aspects of the movement's outlook. Yuan identifies three challenges. First, party fragmentation: the article reports that eleven governments have come and gone since 2008, that turnout fell to 61.85%, the lowest since 1990, and that newer parties, such as the Rastriya Swatantra Party and the Hindu-monarchist Rastriya Prajatantra Party, took votes from the two mainstream communist parties, whose share of House seats dropped to 40%. Second, disputes over office and interest: Yuan attributes the repeated collapse of coalitions and the 2018 merger to Oli and Prachanda's quarrels over the premiership and presidency. Third, outside pressure: the author describes India as working behind the scenes to split the communists and favour the Nepali Congress, and the United States as using the Millennium Challenge Compact and democracy promotion to counter China's influence. Yuan concludes that, since five communist parties still hold 122 House seats, setbacks do not signal decline and the movement will advance by a winding, spiral path, citing Lenin. Unity among communist factions is presented as the key to escaping the current difficulties, with the June 2023 Socialist Front as an example. The author also holds that, as parties in a parliamentary system, they must preserve their distinct character while transforming, and points to the decline of Western social democracy and West European communist parties as warnings. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic view of Nepali communist politics after 2022, including the author's account of Indian and US roles.

Raising the international reach of research on contemporary Chinese history 提升当代中国史研究的国际传播力 Zhang Xingxing This is a reflective essay by Zhang Xingxing, editor-in-chief of Contemporary China History Studies from 2008 to 2019, written for the journal's 30th anniversary in 2024. Zhang asks how the only specialist academic journal on the history of the People's Republic could strengthen the international reach of research in this field. The answer, drawn from the author's own twelve years in post, is a combination of four practices: attending international academic events, recruiting overseas authors, co-organising conferences abroad, and publishing an English-language edition. The essay is organised in four numbered sections, each built on dated examples. It covers the author's participation in the 2007 Beijing congress of the International Committee of Historical Sciences, the 2010 Amsterdam International Congress of Historical Sciences, and a 2015 Melbourne conference on the global nuclear order. It then lists foreign contributors, including the Russian scholar Mikhail Titarenko, Ezra Vogel of Harvard, and scholars from Japan, Sweden, Germany, Korea and Vietnam. Further sections cover joint seminars in Moscow and Hanoi, and the troubled path to an English edition with the Dutch publisher Brill. Zhang's central claim is that the field's influence grows when Chinese scholars actively seek a voice on international platforms and build lasting institutional ties, such as the quinquennial International Senior Forum on Contemporary Chinese History run by the Institute of Contemporary China Studies. The author argues that foreign scholars' articles supply multi-perspective views and that comparative exchanges, for example between China's reform and opening up and Vietnam's renovation, help Chinese researchers understand their own development more clearly. The English edition is presented as a cautionary case: the first volume took five years, drew criticism of its translation quality, and the second carried an unapproved 21-page introduction. Zhang reports that the journal responded with stricter translator standards, content control, and a sign-off procedure before printing. Zhang concludes that the journal is an important platform for external exchange but that much remains to be done to make it a first-rate international journal. The author calls for firm political and academic orientation, continued experimentation, and broad cooperation with scholars at home and abroad, so as to explain the Chinese path, summarise Chinese experience and tell China's story well. The essay is dedicated to the late Vogel and Titarenko. Read the original if you want a practitioner's first-hand account of how a Chinese state-sponsored history journal handled foreign collaboration, translation and publisher relations.

Theoretical precursors and practical paths in the formation of Western social law 西方社会法形成的理论先导与实践进路 Yu Shaoxiang How did "social law" (shehuifa), a legal branch concerned with the livelihood of the weak, come into being in the West? Yu Shaoxiang argues that from the mid-nineteenth century the private law and market economy of capitalism produced growing social problems. Public and private law proved inadequate to them, and the two began to merge. The result was a "third domain" of law containing social law, economic law and environmental law. The article has three parts. The first sets out five theoretical precursors: utopian socialism, the theory of state responsibility, human rights theory (including the right to subsistence), "new property" theory, and welfare economics. The second traces practice through four periods: before the Industrial Revolution, its early and late phases, and the post-industrial period. Its cases include English Poor Laws, Bismarck's social insurance in Germany, French relief and accident legislation, and the US Social Security Act of 1935. It also covers Britain's Beveridge-era reforms. The third part analyses the nature, values, aims and functions of social law. Yu holds that social law arose from the guarantee of the right to subsistence and corrects the limits of formal equality under private law. Its values are ethical care, social security and social fairness. Its stated aims shifted over time. Bismarck's insurance is presented as an "investment" to weaken revolution, and August Bebel is cited as saying it blunted trade-union action. In modern societies, Yu says, the ideological colouring has faded and the aim is a basic safety net for all citizens. Social law also stabilises society and supports the market economy by redistribution and by stimulating consumption. Yu concludes that social law answers objective economic and social needs and is determined by the material mode of production. The author takes this to confirm Marx's view that legal relations are rooted in material life, and that social law mainly serves to ease class conflict and resolve complex social problems. The article presents its development as a mark of a modern state's maturity. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language overview of the Western intellectual and historical sources of social law, as background to how Chinese legal scholars frame the field.

Korsch and the problem of worker education Marxism of, by, and for the people 柯尔施与工人教育问题 Edward Baring This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the intellectual historian Edward Baring. It asks why Karl Korsch's 1922 pamphlet The Essence of Marxism, which stresses the economic base, appears to resemble the "vulgar Marxism" he attacked in Marxism and Philosophy (1923). Baring argues that intellectual historians neglect worker education, and that Korsch was a teacher who used his theoretical writing to solve the problem of how to convey Marxism to the working masses. The article follows Korsch from his early Fabian-influenced socialism and the failed socialisation commissions of 1919 to his turn to the German Communist Party. It then covers his educational pamphlets, his reading of Karl Kautsky, and the argument of Marxism and Philosophy. It ends with his break with the Comintern and the Party, his later editions of Marx, and a comparison with Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Mariátegui and Senghor. Baring contends that Korsch's key concept of "expression" is often misread, for example by Althusser and Martin Jay, as meaning that theory flows directly from workers' practice. For Korsch, Marxism arises from the proletariat's unsystematic class outlook combined with an inheritance of bourgeois philosophy, so education is both necessary and difficult. Philosophy matters for three reasons: it explains the importance of ideological struggle, it allows bourgeois contamination of workers' views to be "purified", and it requires Marxism to be renewed with each historical moment. Baring distinguishes three levels: Party intellectuals, theoretically minded workers (the pamphlet Fundamentals of the Materialist Conception of History) and the rank and file (The Essence of Marxism). On this reading, the last pamphlet presents the economy as objective truth but is meant to shape how workers understand it, and so is not vulgar Marxism. Baring traces how Korsch's view of the Party's guiding role shifted after his clash with Zinoviev and the Comintern. Korsch came to suspect that Party leaders used education to control workers, and by 1932 he was editing a cheap edition of Capital, volume 1, for workers to read themselves. By 1950 he was urging revolutionaries to move beyond Marxist theory. Baring adds that worker education pushed Western Marxists to "provincialize" Marxism for local audiences, and he treats this as a route to understanding its European specificity. Read the original if you work on Western Marxism, Korsch or Marxist pedagogy and want a reinterpretation of Marxism and Philosophy through the practice of worker education.

Traditional elements in the medieval German political system 德意志中世纪政制中的传统要素 Wang Yaping The article takes up the German "special path" (Sonderweg) thesis, which holds that nineteenth-century Germany industrialised without establishing a liberal society and constitutional state, and so drifted towards Nazism. Wang argues that an explanation needs a long-term view reaching back to the Middle Ages. In Wang's account, three traditional elements shaped the German political system and set it apart from England and France: the elective kingship, the dual structure of church and state, and the Germanic Mark system. After a review of the historiography, from Hans-Ulrich Wehler's Bielefeld school to the 1980s work on the Reformation, the article proceeds in six sections. It begins with the Frankish heritage and the divergence of East and West Francia. It then examines the elective monarchy, the church–state mechanism, the Mark principles and the cities, the loosely organised empire, and the territorial states. Wang draws on German, French, British and American historians, and on Marx and Engels's remarks on the Mark. Wang argues that the elective kingship, from Henry I (919) through the Golden Bull of 1356, let secular and ecclesiastical princes check royal power. Concessions such as the statutes of 1220 and 1231/32 and the system of seven electors entrenched territorial sovereignty and blocked centralisation. The Ottonian imperial church tied emperors to the papacy, and the Investiture Controversy, the Canossa episode and later the principle cuius regio, eius religio kept political and religious fragmentation going. The Mark principles of protection and freedom, in Wang's reading, preserved free peasants in the east, fed urban growth and city leagues, and produced several regional economic centres but no unified market or currency. England and France, by contrast, moved to absolutist monarchy and nation-states. Wang concludes that these traditional elements delayed the modernisation of the German political system into the nineteenth century, even though capitalist elements had already appeared in the economy, including merchant houses, joint-stock mining and metallurgy, Prussian large estates and princely universities. The collision of political tradition with modernity, Wang says, led Germany onto its "special path". Read the original if you want a long-term medieval account of the Sonderweg debate, with extensive German-language historiography on elective kingship, church–state relations, the Mark and territorial states.

Mao Zedong's thought on comprehensive balance of the national economy: a re-examination 毛泽东国民经济综合平衡思想再探讨 Zhou Shaodong Zhou Shaodong re-examines Mao Zedong's thinking on the comprehensive balance of the national economy, which the article treats as an important part of Mao's economic thought. The author argues that Mao, applying the dialectical idea of the unity of opposites, developed a systematic account of what such balance means, what it rests on and how it is achieved.
