Zhou contends that, although the institutional basis and micro-level carriers of the Chinese economy have changed greatly, the core of this thought still offers guidance today. The article has four parts. It first sets out the background: the economic recovery of 1949–52 and the sharp fluctuations in growth during the Great Leap Forward, the people's communes and the post-1959 disasters. It then discusses the meaning and nature of comprehensive balance, compares how balance is reached under capitalism and socialism, and analyses the means Mao proposed. It closes with the thought's present-day value, drawing on Mao's critical notes on the Soviet Political Economy textbook, On the Ten Major Relationships and On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People. Zhou reads Mao's idea of balance from the theory of contradiction: imbalance is absolute and balance only temporary and relative. Balance is therefore comprehensive rather than symmetrical, meaning coordinated proportions among sectors, regions, accumulation and consumption, and centre and localities. It is also dynamic, and imbalances in the economy are in essence contradictions among the people, to be handled by unity–criticism–unity and by the principle of 'from the masses, to the masses'. Under socialism, public ownership and planned, proportionate development, led by the Party, make active balance possible. Mao's means were the 'simultaneous development' of industry and agriculture, centre and localities, large and small enterprises, modern and indigenous methods, and coastal and inland regions. Zhou links this to a 'wave-like' pattern of non-equilibrium growth and notes its resemblance to Albert Hirschman's unbalanced growth theory. For the present, Zhou draws three lessons. Supply-side structural reform should be combined with expanding domestic demand, so as to reach a dynamic balance in which demand leads supply and supply creates demand. Macroeconomic regulation should give way to broader macroeconomic governance. Balance also needs the Party's centralised leadership, the basic socialist economic system, and the Two Unwaverings, supporting both state-owned and private firms as micro-level carriers, together with five-year plans. Zhou presents this as an example of building an autonomous knowledge system for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao's dialectics of balance is being used to frame current Chinese macroeconomic policy.

Knowledge and sociality: the sociology-of-knowledge logic of English School international relations research 知识性与社会性：英国学派国际关系研究的知识社会学逻辑 Ren Dongbo Feng Shuai Ren and Feng ask how the English School of international relations (IR) can be understood through the sociology of knowledge, a lens they say Chinese scholarship has barely applied to it. Drawing on social-network theory, they treat the School as a 'social–knowledge' network with two features. 'Knowledge-ness' is its role as producer, transmitter and critic of IR knowledge; 'sociality' is its ties to world events and the academic community. The authors argue that the two are distinct but interdependent, and that both are built into the School's practice. The article has five substantive sections. It first links the School's agenda to British decline, decolonisation and the Cold War, and then to the post-Cold War and information-age revival. It then looks at the School as an academic community: the British Committee on the Theory of International Politics, the Rockefeller and Ford foundations, and universities such as the London School of Economics (LSE), Cambridge, Oxford and the Australian National University. Next it examines the School's 'social practice' in the second great debate with American IR. The last section covers its core theme, international society, in two phases: the expansion narrative and the later regional turn, with East Asia and China as the main cases. The authors argue that the School's agenda followed shifts in world politics. Its early themes of international society, order and justice fit a declining imperial power, and it gained wider audiences when the post-Cold War field turned to norms and institutions. They stress that the School's institutional life came from the British Committee, whose funders did not push it towards policy relevance, and that the School has since become a looser, global network. In the Bull–Kaplan debate, they present the School's historical, interpretive and normative approach as opposed to American scientism, a contrast they trace to different academic and political settings. Its expansion narrative is criticised as Eurocentric and as neglecting colonialism. The authors report that the regional turn partly corrects this, through work on China's and Japan's entry into international society, China's peaceful rise and the Chinese School. Ren and Feng conclude that the School is both an intellectual and a social phenomenon: its ideas reflect social facts and are also socially constructed by scholars through their practice. They say its internal debates, interaction with other scholarly groups and the fusion of knowledge-ness and sociality shape its development, and that this will continue through an open academic network. Read the original if you want a sociology-of-knowledge account of the English School, including its institutional history and its treatment of China, from a Chinese perspective.

Mao Zedong's strategic guidance in the great War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea 毛泽东在伟大抗美援朝战争中的战略指导 Mao Xinyu Marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, Mao Xinyu asks how Mao and the Party Central Committee won the Korean War against a militarily superior United States. The article argues that victory came from a distinctive art of strategic guidance, which allowed a weaker side to defeat a stronger one and which, in the author's view, still offers lessons for handling today's risks and challenges. The study is arranged in four parts, each ending with a short set of "lessons" for the present. It covers the decision to send troops abroad, the management of the war's course from preparation to ending, the creation of new strategy and tactics against a modernised enemy, and the use of people's war and total-war methods. Evidence comes mainly from Mao's telegrams, speeches and instructions, and from campaign history. In the author's account, the decision to fight rested on putting political and long-term interests above immediate ones. Mao balanced economic reconstruction against survival of the new state, and chose a limited war fought outside China's borders, using the name "volunteers" and confining the conflict to the peninsula to prevent a larger one. Mao then steered the war by preparing for the worst case, shifting from counter-offensive to protracted active defence, and pursuing a negotiated settlement backed by military strength. Mao's adaptation to a modern opponent is summed up as learning from the war itself, assessing the enemy's strengths and weaknesses (US "much steel, little spirit" against Chinese "little steel, much spirit"), and devising tunnel defence, night fighting and "iron" supply lines. Finally, Mao mobilised the whole population, the Sino-Soviet alliance, diplomacy and propaganda, and fought while negotiating. Mao Xinyu concludes that war decisions must serve the strategic whole, that war leaders must master uncertainty and develop asymmetric methods from battlefield practice, and that modern wars are won by relying on the people and on the state's total capacity. Looking to current great-power rivalry, the author calls for integrated national strategic systems, an international united front against the main adversary, and preparation for cognitive warfare, citing the Russia–Ukraine conflict. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese military-academy researcher draws on Mao's Korean War leadership to frame contemporary strategic and defence thinking.

Searching for light: recollections and reflections at Marx's birthplace 寻找光明：马克思故居前的追忆与思考 Huo Qinghua This is a first-person travel essay, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2024. Huo Qinghua recounts a visit in summer 2022 to Marx's birthplace in Trier, Germany, made at the end of a Sino-European study tour of vocational colleges. Huo's point is that the visit, and the exhibits in the house, show Marx's enduring significance and the continuing vitality of Marxism, above all in China. The essay follows the visit in order. It describes the train journey from Saarbrücken, the history of Trier, and the house on Brückenstraße. It recounts how the house was identified in 1904 from a removal notice in a local newspaper, then bought by the Social Democratic Party in 1928, seized by the Nazi authorities and reopened as a memorial in 1947. Huo then goes through the three floors: the reception and family rooms, the floor on Marx's and Engels's lives, and the attic with manuscripts and editions. Huo draws several lessons from the exhibits. Marx came from a comfortable middle-class family but chose a life of exile and struggle, in line with the school-leaving essay in which he wrote of choosing work for the welfare of humanity. Huo presents the Marx–Engels partnership as a model of comradely cooperation, with Capital as its fruit. Beside the first edition of the Communist Manifesto and the first volume of Capital, Huo notes the earliest Chinese translation by Chen Wangdao, and links them to Marx's two great discoveries, historical materialism and surplus value. Huo goes on to say that socialism suffered a setback after the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, while socialism with Chinese characteristics has since achieved remarkable results and revitalised scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China. Huo concludes that, nearly 150 years after Marx's death, his theory still shines and will remain a beacon of human progress, thanks to its scientific, revolutionary, practical, people-centred and developmental character. Huo suggests Marxism can help in understanding the contradictions and crises of the world economic system amid what the essay calls changes unseen in a century, and in thinking about fairer and more sustainable governance. Huo ends by writing a tribute in the visitors' book. Read the original if you want a short personal account of a visit to the Trier house, with the commemorative tone in which Chinese writers present Marx's legacy to a general readership.

Creative transformation and innovative development of China's fine traditional legal culture 中华优秀传统法律文化的创造性转化和创新性发展 Li Lin How should China's fine traditional legal culture be inherited and made usable for a modern socialist rule-of-law country? Li Lin argues that such culture is defined by three features: universality and commonality, advancement and civilisation, and practicality and popular orientation. Its creative transformation and innovative development should combine comparative study of foreign experience with the Two Integrations, so as to build an autonomous Chinese system of legal knowledge. The article has three parts. The first defines key concepts, from culture and legal culture to rule-of-law civilisation and "traditional Chinese legal culture", and sets criteria for what counts as "fine". The second surveys the Chinese legal family, its influence on Japan, Korea, Vietnam and other Asian states, and China's own borrowing from abroad in civil, administrative and criminal legislation. The third introduces the author's analogy between "traditional Chinese medicine jurisprudence" and "Western medicine jurisprudence". Li sorts inherited legal culture into three groups: elements reflecting universal human values, such as fairness, the rule of virtue assisted by punishment and cautious penal policy; elements that once served governance but are now dross, such as collective punishment and presumption of guilt; and elements, including some Legalist ideas, that were marginal then but useful now. Li then defines "Chinese-medicine jurisprudence" as China's own legal culture, legal family and Party-led rule-of-law experience, and "Western-medicine jurisprudence" as legal theory imported from the Soviet socialist, civil-law, common-law and international systems. Li holds that the two share goals as law and medicine do, and that their differences make integration both possible and necessary. Integration is to be guided by Marxism, the "soul" of the system, and by traditional culture, its "root". Li calls for a "self-reform" of legal scholars, who should reject both the superiority of Western-style jurisprudence and the view that Chinese tradition is outdated. Li also proposes holistic study of traditional legal culture, a search for the "greatest common divisor" between the two traditions, and integration through the core branches of law, avoiding a "two-skins" outcome. The aim is a new realm of legal civilisation for Chinese modernization that supports a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a leading CASS jurist links traditional legal heritage, comparative law and the Party's theory of an autonomous legal knowledge system.

Rawls's threefold critique of utilitarianism 罗尔斯对功利主义的三重批判 Wang Li Rawls's criticism of utilitarianism, more than fifty years old, remains the standard backdrop for work on utilitarianism. Wang Li asks how Rawls's "justice as fairness" sought to replace it, and whether his critique holds. The article's thesis is that Rawls attacked three forms of utilitarianism with steadily weaker force, which Wang reads as showing that utilitarianism exerts a pressure on his theory that is hard to dispel. The article follows the structure of A Theory of Justice. Three sections reconstruct Rawls's critique of classical utilitarianism (Hume, Smith, Bentham, Mill, Sidgwick), average utilitarianism and "limited" utilitarianism, each set against his two principles of justice. A fourth section then criticises the critique, drawing on rule utilitarianism and debates about decision-making under uncertainty. A short conclusion follows. Wang reports that Rawls opposes classical utilitarianism on three contrasts: aggregate welfare against the priority of liberty and rights; extending individual choice to society against the separateness of persons; and teleology against a non-teleological view that puts the right before the good. Against average utilitarianism he cites the difficulty of calculating probabilities, the lack of a unified measure of expectation and the risk of sacrificing individuals. Limited utilitarianism, which blends the average principle with constraints such as a social minimum, is the hardest case because the argument from liberty no longer works against it. In Wang's reading, Rawls's counter-arguments are a vague utility standard and the claim that its constraints depend on intuition or on the difference principle. Wang then argues that rule utilitarianism escapes much of this critique, that Rawls's maximin reasoning is implausible, and that limited utilitarianism is best read as a special form of rule utilitarianism. Rawls's claim about the indeterminacy of utility fails once the comparison is confined to wealth and income. His claim that the difference principle secures a higher social minimum is also left without clear reasons. Wang concludes that Rawls was not defending utilitarianism. Wang argues, however, that utilitarianism has its own strengths and resources for replying, and that "justice as fairness" would need fuller reasons to displace it entirely. The author calls for treating the two theories on equal terms through mutual critique. Read the original if you work on Rawls, contemporary utilitarianism or Chinese scholarship on political philosophy and want a detailed, sympathetic re-examination of how Rawls argued against utilitarianism.

A critique of erroneous views that negate the lofty ideal of communism 否定共产主义远大理想的错误观点辨析 Shi Zhenping Shi Zhenping takes up a trend that, in the author's account, belittles or rejects the lofty ideal of communism, understood as Marx and Engels's scientific prediction of the basic features of a future society. The article argues that this trend aims at undermining the Party's spiritual pillar, and that its arguments rest on three methodological errors, each of which Shi sets out to refute. The piece builds on Xi Jinping's repeated stress since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on communist ideals and convictions. The article opens by describing the views it opposes: that public ownership by society, planned economy and distribution according to labour are empty abstractions or misjudgements, and that Marx's vision is a "classical socialism" now consigned to the grave. Shi then lists five harms of such views, including undermining Marxism as a whole, the twentieth-century socialist path, the Party's leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The remaining sections answer the three methods in turn, the last through close readings of passages from Marx and Engels. First, Shi argues that actually existing socialism and Marx's future society are two linked but distinct stages. The latter presupposes fully developed productive forces, social ownership, no commodity relations, classes or state, and a worldwide scope. Present-day socialism, with mixed ownership and markets, is therefore still in a transition period, and the Soviet model or the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics cannot be set against communism. Second, Shi reviews Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping to claim that each developed new understandings of socialism without abandoning the founders' prediction. Third, Shi holds that the founders refused detailed blueprints of the future but never gave up its basic features. Shi rereads Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge, Engels's 1893 Figaro interview, and the letters to Nieuwenhuis and Pease, as being quoted out of context. Shi concludes that developing Marx's view of socialism must proceed from upholding the founders' prediction, and rejects both dogmatism and development that abandons the ideal. Reading Marx and Engels's statements against detailed blueprints as a denial of their predictions is said to conceal their consistency and to sow risks for the communist ideal. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory scholar in China defends the communist ideal against revisionist readings, especially the close textual analysis of Engels's letters and interview.

The atheistic implications of Song-dynasty Neo-Confucianism 论宋代理学的无神论意蕴 Zhou Yun Wang Minmin Zhou Yun and Wang Minmin ask how Song-dynasty Neo-Confucianism (lixue), a movement whose thinkers firmly believed in ritual sacrifice and spirits, nevertheless advanced atheism. Their thesis is that the Neo-Confucians introduced philosophy in order to explain spirits and human–spirit communication more clearly, but in doing so disenchanted nature and dissolved the spirits' independence. The authors stress that this effect was unintended and that no complete atheism existed in Chinese history; it is atheistic only in terms of a developmental process. The article has three parts. The first documents the Neo-Confucians' devotion to sacrifice and spirits, citing Zhou Dunyi, Cheng Yi, Zhang Zai and Zhu Xi on ritual, Zhu Xi's ancestral halls, divination, and Yang Jian's mystical experiences. The second examines their rational critique of popular belief and their theoretical reworking of the spirits. The third draws out the atheistic implications in two respects. The authors argue that Zhang Zai, the Cheng brothers, Zhu Xi, Zhang Shi and Chen Chun attacked 'strange beings and wicked spirits' and opposed idol-making, partly in a Song scientific climate. They then recast Heaven and spirits through principle (li) and qi, so that Heaven becomes principle and spirits become traces of natural transformation. Zhou and Wang read the diagram of the Supreme Ultimate as a philosophical account of the generation of things that removes a willing Heaven or Lord on High. The emphasis on sincerity (cheng) also made spirits dependent on the worshipper's subjective effort, which Chen Chun carried toward treating sincerity as the spirits' ontological basis. The authors also find internal contradictions that, in their account, exposed the vanity of belief in spirits: Zhang Zai and Zhang Shi treated ritual or divination as tools of governing yet defended them as classical doctrine, and Chen Chun criticised spirit-writing while conceding that spirits act through people. They conclude that Neo-Confucianism reached the peak of contemporary rational thought and dealt superstition a heavy blow, while only unintentionally advancing atheism; such contradictions drive further theoretical development. Read the original if you want a close textual study, with Song sources, of how religious and rationalist elements coexisted in Neo-Confucian thought and how Chinese scholars frame this as a stage in the history of atheism.

The atheist thought in Mao Zedong's Xunwu Investigation and its lessons for today 《寻乌调查》中的无神论思想及其启示 Liu Fujun Zhang Ruxu Liu and Zhang examine the atheist thought contained in Mao Zedong's Xunwu Investigation, the social survey of Xunwu county that Mao carried out in May 1930 during the Agrarian Revolutionary War. They argue that chapters three to five of the report deal in depth with theistic questions and embody Marxist standpoint and method. In their view this thought is an important milestone in the Sinicization of Marxist atheism and still offers guidance for research on religion and atheist education today. The article has four parts. It first sets out why religious organisations, believers and ideas had to be handled correctly in the revolutionary base areas. It then reconstructs four sets of views in the report: on religion, folk belief, feudal superstition and secret societies, the last chiefly the Tongshan Society. A third part assesses the historical standing of this thought, and a fourth draws present-day lessons. Liu and Zhang argue that Mao analysed each form of belief by class position and economic exploitation, not by belief alone. They cite his category of 'deity landlords' (temples, monasteries, shrines and altars), his breakdown of the social composition of believers and his reading of motives for joining churches. On superstition, Mao found geographical, psychological and economic roots: peasants' reluctance to move house when land was divided reflected real material loss, not merely outdated thinking. The authors trace how these findings fed Soviet-period policy on clerics' land and voting rights, the treatment of clan and communal land, and freedom of religious belief. They also see in the report the three bases of Mao Zedong Thought: seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. For the present, the authors propose that research on theism be guided by the 'six musts' of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and that Marxist atheism be adapted to the Chinese context through the Two Integrations, including linkage to traditional Chinese atheistic ideas. Atheist education should go deep into reality, daily life and the masses, in the primary stage of socialism. They also call for implementing the policy of religious freedom fully while resisting infiltration by foreign religious currents and cults. Read the original if you study the history of Chinese Communist policy on religion, Mao's survey method, or how current Party writing on atheism draws on early revolutionary sources.

Defining the concept of extremism under the rule of law: rules and definition 极端主义概念法治化界定研究:规则与定义 Wang Xiaofei Zhuang Ying Chinese statutes such as the Criminal Law, the Counter-Terrorism Law and the Regulations on Religious Affairs use the term "extremism" without giving it a clear legal definition. Wang and Zhuang ask how China should define the concept within a rule-of-law framework, as a basis for a future dedicated counter-extremism or de-extremification law. They argue that the concept should be defined as a "composite" whose content is exclusion or "sole existence", and that the definition must follow five rules. The article is a combined philosophical, legal and criminological study. It first surveys scholarly views on the genus concept (the broader category) of extremism, with five positions: statement and conduct, conduct, theory or statement and conduct, ideology and belief, and leaving it blank. It also surveys views on the differentia (the feature separating extremism from related concepts), which range from one element to four. It then classifies legal texts from Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, China and a draft Russian federal law into five types: evasive, blank, transferred, differentia-specified and fully determined. The authors argue that the disagreements stem mainly from different rankings of two values: individual cultural-spiritual freedom and the public interest of state and society. They hold that composite genus concepts breach the logical rule that a genus must be one level above the defined term. They also hold that existing definitions cover only part of extremism's extension and rely on vague evaluative vocabulary. Their five rules are: the genus must be the next-higher concept; the definition's extension must equal that of extremism, with exemptions for legitimate self-protection, necessity and consent; the law's purpose and title must be consistent; linguistic vagueness must be reduced; and both values must be balanced. Drawing on the traditional Chinese idea of "zhongyong" (the mean) and "coexistence", they propose that extremism's essential features are exclusionary means, aims contrary to coexistence, and expression through theories, conduct, social systems or statements. They favour "counter-extremism" over "counter-extremist activity" or "de-extremification" as the legislative aim. Wang and Zhuang conclude that defining extremism is unavoidable for counter-extremism legislation touching national security. They say the definition must rest on China's traditional culture and national conditions, align with international practice and follow rule-of-law rules. They call for supporting instruments, such as concrete criteria for identifying extremism and a dynamic catalogue of extremist materials, and propose after-the-fact punishment and indirect intervention as safeguards. Read the original if you work on Chinese counter-extremism legislation, comparative Central Asian anti-extremism laws, or the legal theory of defining contested concepts.

The socialisation question in the British Labour Party: origins, evolution and future 英国工党的社会化问题：缘起、演变与未来 Wang Yao Wang Yao asks what "socialisation" (shehuihua) has meant for the British Labour Party over more than 120 years and why it has mattered so much. The article argues that the issue defines Labour's socialist identity, is the focus of factional struggle between left and right and between unions and party elites, and sets the limits of the party's policy choices. Wang's overall reading is that socialisation shaped social democracy, while Labour's gradual retreat from it has left the party without a clear political direction. The article divides Labour's history into five periods: 1900–1918, 1918–1945, 1945–1979, 1980–2010 and 2010 to the present. It first traces how the concept shifted from "social" or "collective ownership" to nationalisation, and later to "indirect socialisation" through economic democracy, the welfare state and state intervention. Each period is tied to specific party documents, leaders and electoral outcomes, from the 1918 Clause Four and Attlee's government to Blair's rewriting of Clause Four, Corbyn and Starmer. Wang's central claim is that socialisation moved from an end to a means and was then largely abandoned. Early Labour was an electoral alliance of unions and socialist societies, pursuing labourism rather than a socialist goal. After 1918 it equated "socialism = socialisation = nationalisation", and after 1945 the welfare state and planning displaced nationalisation as the policy focus. Wang describes the Blair-era "third way" as "de-socialisation": it accepted markets, limited public ownership and shifted from "democratic socialism" to "social democracy", though Wang says this was not simple neoliberalism. Corbyn's "re-socialisation", centred on democratising ownership and decision-making, is presented as crude, unconvincing on funding, and unable to escape the electoral system and political culture. Wang suggests Starmer's Labour offers nothing new on the subject. Wang concludes that Labour now clings to nostalgia for Keynesianism, the welfare state and public ownership, which in Giddens's phrase meets a radicalised conservatism with a conservative socialism. Wang adds that, in Bernstein's formula, "the movement is everything" leaves social democracy unable to say where it leads, because its goals of freedom, justice and solidarity are close to social consensus. Even so, Wang holds that socialisation remains politically relevant while capitalism's basic contradictions and the tension among market, society and democracy persist. Read the original if you want a periodised, Chinese-academic account of how the Labour Party's ownership policy and relation to socialism changed from 1900 to the Starmer era.

New progress in Laos's socialist modernization drive 老挝社会主义现代化建设新进展 Guo Mingrui Fang Wen Since the 11th Congress of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP) in 2021 set the goal of achieving modernization, how has Laos advanced its socialist modernization? Guo and Fang argue that, under Party leadership and a development path suited to national conditions, Laos has made new progress through a combined set of measures. The article is a descriptive overview of that record, written from a standpoint sympathetic to the LPRP. The article is organised around six areas: Party building, economic development, poverty reduction, the socialist rule-of-law state, foreign affairs, and a closing outlook. Its economic section covers agriculture, tourism, the China–Laos Railway and the digital economy. Its foreign-affairs section reports on Lao General Secretary and President Thongloun Sisoulith's visits to China in November–December 2022 and October 2023, including his meetings with Xi Jinping. Guo and Fang present Party building as the foundation of the whole project. They describe stronger ideological work (Marxism-Leninism and Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, internet management, youth education), comprehensive Party leadership, closer ties to the masses and a purer membership. On the economy, they credit agriculture, tourism and the China–Laos Railway, which they call a flagship Belt and Road Initiative project, with driving growth. They also cite national digital-economy plans and joint poverty-reduction work with China, including the "4×100" projects. They report that over 50 districts, 4,700 villages and 900,000 households have escaped poverty. They add that the Lao state has passed more than 180 laws and moved to institutionalise Party-led governance by law. The authors conclude that Laos and China, both Communist-led socialist states, share ideals, systems and similar development paths, and that Thongloun's visits show mutual support for each country's modernization and will give new impetus to world socialism. Looking ahead, they expect Laos to continue comprehensive renewal, to adapt Marxism to Lao conditions and the needs of our times, to improve its socialist-oriented market economy and to pursue green, sustainable, high-quality development. Read the original if you want a Chinese-academic account of how Lao Party-state development and China–Laos cooperation are framed, including the policy documents and figures it cites.

Guidelines and policies of the Chinese Communist Party on religious work during the War of Liberation 解放战争时期中国共产党宗教工作的方针政策探析 Zhou Wei Zhou Wei examines how the Chinese Communist Party handled religion in the liberated areas during the War of Liberation (1945–1949), when several religions and competing religious forces coexisted. The article argues that, guided by Marxism, the Party framed practical policies that implemented freedom of religious belief, advanced democratic reform of religion and won over religious figures and believers, building consensus and strength for founding the new China. Zhou holds that studying this record enriches the Party's theory of religious work in the new era. The article is a historical-policy study built on Party documents, newspaper reports and local cases from North, Northeast, Inner Mongolia, Suiyuan and other areas. It has four main parts: forming a people's democratic united front with religious circles; gradually deepening democratic reform of the old religious system; implementing freedom of religious belief; and resolutely striking at illegal and reactionary religious forces. A short conclusion draws out lessons for today. On the united front, Zhou describes the Party condemning Nationalist persecution of religious communities, admitting believers to trade unions and peasant associations, guaranteeing their voting rights, and mobilising them against civil war. On reform, the Party is said to have abolished clerical exploitation, adjusted religious landholding while leaving religious bodies enough land to support themselves, separated religion from education, and protected religious property and relief. Freedom of belief covered lawful missionaries, ethnic minority customs and atheist propaganda. The Party is also described as treating religion differentially, prosecuting missionaries accused of espionage and banning reactionary secret societies (huidaomen) while protecting law-abiding believers. Zhou concludes that, following Marx, the Party understood religion would eventually die out only after a very long process, so administrative force should neither ban nor promote any religion. In the author's account, the period raised the Party's prestige among religious circles, advanced the legalisation and democratisation of religious work, and furthered the adaptation of Marxist views of religion to China. Zhou calls for fully implementing religious freedom, governing online religion, deepening Marxist atheist education and improving religious laws so religion can adapt to socialist society. Read the original if you want a source-rich account of early Communist religious policy and its framing in current Party discourse.

Self-revolution in the depths of thought: Mao Zedong's high regard for ideological and political work 思想深处的自我革命：毛泽东对思想政治工作的高度重视 Cao Yongxin Cao Yongxin asks why Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communists treated ideological and political work as a core, strategic task, and what lessons this holds today. The article argues that such work is a distinguishing feature of the Chinese Communist Party and the 'lifeline' of all other work. It holds that, under the primary stage of socialism and a socialist market economy, any slackening would put the Party's cause at risk of 'subversive mistakes'. The article has three parts. The first traces how building the Party ideologically and building the army politically gave rise to ideological and political work. It covers the 1929 Gutian Conference resolution, Mao's 1955 remark that political work is the lifeline of economic work, and later Party documents repeating the formula. The second part sets out five lessons from Mao's leadership. The third turns to the new era and links this work to self-liberation, self-reform and historical initiative. Cao's five lessons are theoretical preparation through Mao's writings, coordinated organisational leadership by Party committees and first secretaries, unity of knowing and doing through practice, the mass line and investigation, and a policy of 'punishing the past to warn the future and curing the sickness to save the patient'. On the last, Cao stresses persuasion over coercion. Cao also contrasts this unity of thought and practice with the self-cultivation of ancient thinkers. In the final section, Cao presents the work as the means by which the proletariat awakens its own subjectivity and liberates itself without saviours. The Party's self-reform is, in Cao's words, essentially an ideological struggle 'in the depths of the soul'. Cao concludes that this work mobilises the most active factor in production, people, and cannot be replaced by material incentives, legal penalties or empty preaching. Citing Deng Xiaoping's 1989 remarks on weak ideological education, Cao treats neglect as costly. The article cites the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as warnings, and calls for firm leadership and initiative in this field. It also holds that historical initiative shows itself through intellectual emancipation, theoretical consciousness, active practice and a conscious choice of path. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Mao's ideological work is being used to frame the Party's self-reform today.

The formation of Marx's historical-materialist view of religion and its critique of capitalist fetishism 马克思历史唯物主义宗教观的形成及其对资本主义拜物教的批判 Gu Jianhong Gu Jianhong asks how Marx's view of religion took shape and how it was applied to capitalist society. Starting from the claim that capitalism's advance has produced a spiritual crisis and that religious questions are increasingly prominent, Gu argues that Marx's historical-materialist view of religion supplies the intellectual basis and guiding principles for handling such questions today. The article holds that this view emerged through a move from theism to atheism and through struggle with idealism and old materialism, grounded in Marx's practical engagement with social life. The article has four parts. It first traces Marx's shift from the rationalist Jewish faith of his youth to atheism, then follows the formation of his historical-materialist position through the Rheinische Zeitung, Feuerbach, the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question, the 1844 Manuscripts and the Theses on Feuerbach. It then turns to Marx's critique of fetishism, from early uses of the word to Capital, and ends with brief conclusions on contemporary relevance. Gu's central move is to distinguish stages. Under Enlightenment rationalism and Bruno Bauer's influence, Marx's atheism still moved within speculative criticism of religion's 'content', which Gu calls illusory. Journalism on Moselle peasants and wood theft, followed by Feuerbach's materialism, redirected him to earth rather than heaven. Gu argues that the Theses on Feuerbach then went beyond Feuerbach's abstract humanism, so that religious alienation is traced to social alienation. The second move is that Marx carried this stance into political economy. Fetishism, Gu says, moves from a matter of social consciousness to one of social being: commodity, money and capital hide relations between people behind relations between things, and the 'economic trinity' in Capital completes this inversion. Gu concludes that religion is rooted in real social life and that any religious view detached from social reality is unreliable. Marx's analysis of fetishism, in this account, shows the stance at work and points toward the free and all-round development of the human being. Gu calls for upholding this view in building socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, so that religion's relations with the economy, politics and culture are handled correctly and Chinese modernization has a spiritual foundation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of the textual sources of Marx's religion critique, linked to fetishism and to contemporary religious policy.

The crisis of human existence under the "new alienation" of temporal rhythm, and its resolution A critical analysis of Jonathan Crary's critique of capitalism's "sleepless" regime 时间节奏“新异化”背景下人的存在危机与化解 Li Shibo How has the temporal structure of contemporary life been distorted, and how can people escape it? Li Shibo takes up this question through Jonathan Crary's account of the "24/7" regime, which the article presents as a round-the-clock social time covering consumption, work, leisure and sleep. In Li's reading, Crary describes a "new alienation" of time without time and rhythm without rhythm. Li argues that Crary's diagnosis is illuminating but stops short of Marx's analysis of capitalism, so his remedies remain at the level of a moral appeal. The article reconstructs Crary's book 24/7: Late Capitalism and the Ends of Sleep in three sections. The first covers the loss of natural and cyclical rhythm, read against Henri Lefebvre's rhythmanalysis and the history of everyday life. The second covers technological acceleration, attention, digital surveillance and the illusion of autonomy. The third covers Crary's two proposed exits, a community of "waiting" and the defence of sleep. Li brings in Byung-Chul Han, Hartmut Rosa, Arendt, Žižek and Nancy Fraser as points of comparison. Li reports Crary's claim that 24/7 capitalism strips out pauses and rhythm, shrinks sleep, and turns users' attention and data into a form of surplus value. Apparent self-direction online is described as an illusion in which people become "sleepless workers" and self-exploiting "achievement subjects". Crary's responses are "waiting" (queuing, taking turns), which creates shared, unproductive time, and sleep, which capital cannot fully colonise. Li's critique is that Crary never reaches the capital-valorisation logic or the contradiction between the productive forces and the relations of production. His "waiting community" is therefore a soft ethical expectation that leaves competition intact, and sleep as refuge is judged utopian because capital and data keep operating while people dream. Li concludes that Han, Rosa and even Fraser's more radical call to abandon the capitalist system share the same difficulty. None identifies a subject able to build a real community or negate capitalism. The author calls for a return to historical materialism and the critique of political economy, with communism as the true community. In this account the proletariat of the digital age remains the force that ends capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Crary, Han and Rosa on time, sleep and digital capitalism, and how it sets those thinkers against Marx.

Why left-wing governments returned in Latin America and their possible impact 拉美国家左翼政府回归的原因及可能影响 Han Qi Han Qi asks why a second wave of left-wing governments took office in Latin America so soon after the first receded, and what it may mean at home and abroad. The article argues that the return was not accidental but the product of several internal and external factors. It holds that the pendulum will swing again unless the underlying causes, above all poverty and inequality, change substantially. The article first recalls the first wave, which began with Hugo Chávez's victory in 1998 and had broken up by the 2010s. It then traces the second wave from López Obrador's win in Mexico in 2018, through Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Honduras, Colombia and Brazil. By January 2023, the author says, left-wing states accounted for about 90 per cent of the region's area and population. The text then moves through causes, challenges facing the new governments, and effects on domestic policy, regional integration and relations with China and the United States. On causes, Han distinguishes the institutional basis (normalised electoral politics and alternation in power), the fundamental cause (long-standing inequality and poverty), external shocks (the pandemic, inflation, the Ukraine crisis, and weaker US pressure after Trump), and short-term factors. The short-term factors are right-wing governance failures and flexible left campaigns that built broad coalitions and added agendas such as indigenous, gender and environmental rights. Han stresses that 'left' here is defined only within the bourgeois camp and relative to 1990s neoliberalism. The challenges include narrow electoral margins and minority legislative positions, as in Peru's Castillo case. Others are limited fiscal room without the earlier commodity boom, the need for growth, and a shift in development model. Han concludes that the second wave will last only if it handles crisis well in the short run and makes a breakthrough on poverty and inequality in the long run. The author expects policies that favour lower and middle strata, renewed regional integration, and closer cooperation with China, citing the shared goal of common prosperity and Belt and Road participation. Han also expects a more critical stance towards US hegemony, while noting that Chinese firms should be ready for resource nationalism. Read the original if you want a China-based scholar's account of the 2018–2023 leftward turn in Latin America and its implications for China–Latin America ties.

Drivers and impact of the rise of the "Global South" “全球南方”崛起的动因与影响 Cui Shoujun Why has the "Global South" become a prominent concept in international debate, and what follows from its rise? Writing in late 2023, Cui argues that the rise is not accidental but the inevitable result of developing countries rising as a group, in a period of what the article calls great changes unseen in a century. Cui holds that clarifying its causes and effects can strengthen the geopolitical cohesion of these states. The article opens with the concept's history: its first use by the US activist Carl Oglesby in 1969, its descent from the "Third World" idea of Alfred Sauvy and Peter Worsley, and its spread through the Brandt Report, the South Commission and the UN Development Programme. It then gives the concept three meanings: geographical, economic and geopolitical. The main body discusses three drivers of the rise (economic, political, and global governance), followed by three global effects. Cui identifies economic growth as the direct driver. Drawing on Raul Prebisch's centre–periphery theory, Cui argues that the fragmentation of global value chains after the Cold War let developing countries industrialise, and cites a PwC projection that the E7 economies would overtake the G7. Political influence is the deeper driver, built through South–South cooperation since the 1955 Bandung Conference and through regional integration. The fundamental driver is the author's critique of Western-dominated global governance, citing unequal IMF and World Bank voice, sanctions, the pandemic and unmet climate-finance pledges. The effects are the faster reshaping of international order (the author points to BRICS expansion, the New Development Bank and the COP27 loss-and-damage fund), new opportunities for South–South cooperation through the Belt and Road Initiative, and intensifying Western competition to win over and divide the Global South. Cui concludes that the rise of the Global South is an irreversible historical trend. The concept, in this account, avoids the older binary logic of centre and periphery or East and West. Cui stresses that it is not an organisation but a diverse community of development, and that the US and its allies will keep trying to court and divide it. Cui calls on Global South countries to build consensus in the "Bandung spirit" and become a mainstay of development cooperation and fairness. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the Global South concept arose and how Chinese scholars link it to BRICS, the Belt and Road Initiative and criticism of Western-led governance.

Atheist thought in Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State 恩格斯《家庭、私有制和国家的起源》无神论思想的探讨 Ding Qiang Mou Degang Ding Qiang and Mou Degang ask what Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State contributes to the Marxist atheist view of religion. The book gives little space to religion as such, and the authors note that existing studies approach it through women's emancipation, marriage and the state. They argue that it applies scientific atheism to primitive society and shows religion to be a historical category, shaped by the economic base and changing as society moves from gentile to class order. The article first situates the book in the development of Marx's and Engels's views of religion. It names two leaps: the move to a historical-materialist view around The German Ideology, and a later clarification of primitive society through their anthropological studies. It then works through three themes: that religion must be verified within historical processes, that its function must be sought in social life, and that its character differs between the barbarian and civilised eras. The evidence is mainly Engels's discussion of the Iroquois, Greeks, Romans and Germans, drawing on Morgan and Marx's notes. On the first theme, the authors argue that for Engels the gens created its gods, not the reverse. Ancestor worship, they say, shifted from a female to a male ancestor with the move from matriarchal to patriarchal clans, and some practices, such as cannibalism, persisted as ritual as productive forces advanced. They contrast this with Bachofen's view of religion as a decisive lever of history, which Engels said leads to mysticism. On the second theme, they argue that early religion regulated conflicts within the clan and between the clan and nature, as in Iroquois initiation rites and agricultural festivals. On the third, they say that with private property and the state, Engels's "spontaneous" religion became "artificial" religion: religious powers were stripped away, sacred customs such as temple prostitution were degraded, and religion's purpose served the ruling class. The authors conclude that where Engels's earlier works treated religion in broad historical or epistemological terms, the Origin approaches it from material production and social organisation. This, they say, completes the case that religion is a historical category and shows its shift from a force binding the clan against nature to a tool of minority rule. They acknowledge that the book does not discuss the features of artificial religion in civilised society or religion's final fate, but argue that it underlies Engels's account of religion's emergence, development and eventual disappearance in Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy. Read the original if you study Marxist theories of religion, Engels's late anthropological work, or how Chinese scholarship on scientific atheism reads the classics.

A review of Chinese research on several key figures in the history of the international communist movement 国际共产主义运动史几位重要人物研究介评 Fan Xin This literature review surveys how Chinese scholars have studied five major figures in the history of the international communist movement: Lenin, Stalin, Plekhanov, Bukharin and Trotsky. Fan opens by citing Xi Jinping on the value of historical research and links the work to the question of how to build a long-governing Marxist party. The review covers the period from the founding of the People's Republic to the early 2020s. Each figure gets a section that divides the scholarship into phases and then sets out the main debates. For Lenin the phases run from a revolution-and-struggle perspective, through peace and construction, to multi-dimensional study after 1990. Stalin's are polemical, reflective and re-evaluative. Plekhanov's are initial study, interruption during the Cultural Revolution, and renewed study after reform and opening up. Bukharin and Trotsky each pass from total negation, through re-evaluation, to what Fan calls objective assessment. Fan shows how the shifting political climate shaped the scholarship: Soviet-era verdicts, the Sino-Soviet polemics, the Soviet collapse and reform at home. Within each section the review lists the live disputes. On Lenin these include the nature of the New Economic Policy, his late thought and his ideas on party-building. On Stalin they cover the definition and causes of the Soviet model, its link to the Soviet collapse, and his merits and faults. On Plekhanov they cover his philosophy and his split with Lenin. On Bukharin they concern his equilibrium theory and his idea of growing into socialism. On Trotsky they concern permanent revolution. Fan reports that mainstream Chinese media see the Soviet model as a highly centralised system that served a purpose in its historical conditions. Fan concludes that Lenin research is rich and multi-dimensional, while Stalin research still lacks weighty works that substantiate the mainstream verdict. Plekhanov studies are mostly thematic and need a more systematic overview. Bukharin research is relatively weak and unsystematic. Trotsky research, Fan says, is clearly insufficient in breadth and depth and has the most room to grow. Fan argues that strengthening this work would help build the discipline of international communist movement history. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese-language scholarship, with titles and dates, on these five figures and on how official and academic assessments changed over time.

Ai Siqi's atheist thought and its lessons A textual study based on Popular Philosophy (Dazhong zhexue) 艾思奇的无神论思想及其启示 Guo Zuquan Huang Xiaodan Guo Zuquan and Huang Xiaodan examine the atheist thought in Ai Siqi's Popular Philosophy, the popular exposition of Marxist philosophy that began as lectures in 1934 and was serialised in the journal Dushu shenghuo. They argue that the book does more than popularise Marxism: it analyses theism and atheism in philosophy and proposes ways of combating theism. From this the authors draw lessons for atheist work today. The article has three parts. The first traces the sources of Ai's atheism: the spread of modern scientific knowledge, his study of Marxist classics in Japanese and German during two stays in Japan, and his family background, including a childhood experiment that tested a nun's superstition. The second sets out the book's content: Ai's critique of theism, his atheist positions, and his use of materialist dialectics as a "weapon of struggle". The third derives three contemporary lessons. On the core argument, the authors report that Ai finds theism concealed in several philosophical positions, among them idealism, fatalism, pseudo-materialism, pragmatism and mechanism. For Ai, idealism is "a bridge" to religion, and theistic ideas are often used to control the masses. Against these he sets practice, the objectivity and self-motion of matter, and the laws of dialectics: contradiction, the transformation of quantity into quality, and the negation of the negation. Ai explains change by internal contradiction rather than a "magician", and uses the collapse of the Leifeng Pagoda as an example. The authors' lessons are that Marxist atheism should be integrated with the Party's purpose and essential character, that it should hold the ideological high ground, and that it should be popularised. The authors conclude that Party members must be firm Marxist atheists, citing Xi Jinping's 2016 remarks, and that atheism education should be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They call for religious studies with Chinese characteristics to rest on atheism, and for ideological and political education to be oriented by it. They also propose popularising atheism among cadres and the public, using new media, and building atheism as a university discipline with accessible textbooks and student lecture teams. Read the original if you want to see how Ai Siqi's 1930s philosophical popularisation is used to support current Party-line arguments for atheist education.

A study of the socialist thought of the New Zealand New Left 新西兰新左翼的社会主义思想研究 Zhao Ting Liu Shiyuan This research article examines the New Zealand New Left, which the authors say emerged in the 1950s and declined in the 1970s. It asks what this current thought about capitalism and socialism and what it achieved. Zhao and Liu argue that the New Left sought a socialist path beyond traditional communism and social democracy, paid particular attention to colonial history and Māori rights, and shifted its main struggle from social movements to academic theory. They also argue that it was limited by fragmentation and weak theory. The article is organised in five parts. It first traces three stages: origins after the failed 1951 waterfront strike (1951–1968), the new-social-movements period (1968–1976), and a turn to academic critique from 1976 onwards. It then covers the New Left's critique of the welfare state and neoliberalism, its reassertion of a Marxist class standpoint, and its proposals for moving towards socialism. A concluding section assesses strengths and limits. On the welfare state, the authors report that New Left scholars such as David Bedggood saw it as a product of capital accumulation. In their account it legitimised capitalist power and alienated people. On neoliberalism, Bruce Curtis is said to have called it in New Zealand a 'lie' that strengthened transnational monopoly capital, and David Neilson is said to have read the pandemic through capitalist globalisation and ecological exploitation. In class analysis, Patrick Eagleton-style debates on the 'new middle class' and Rob Steven's four-class model are presented. The New Left also criticised Althusser and Erik Olin Wright and defended Marx's concepts of class and the formal and real subordination of labour to capital. Its political programme combined opposition to colonialism and 'neo-colonialism', replacement of financial-capital rule, a 'Māori socialist economy' and an alliance of workers and ethnic minorities. Neilson's democratic-socialist regulation model is judged by the authors to be utopian. The authors conclude that the New Left advanced New Zealand's left movement in both theory and practice. They fault it for distance from the working class, an unsystematic grasp of Marxism influenced by Weber and Bourdieu, factional division, and no workable strategy for socialism. They add that the Labour–Green alliance has pushed it further to the margins, though they hold that its critique of capitalism still merits attention. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of an under-studied Western left current, including its debates on class, colonialism and neoliberalism in a settler-colonial setting.

Liu Shibai: a Marxist economist in step with his times 刘诗白：与时代同频共振的马克思主义经济学家 Ding Renzhong Ding Renzhong offers an appreciative portrait of Liu Shibai (b. 1925), a leading theoretical economist at Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, as a Marxist economist whose work moved in step with China's reform practice. The piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in November 2023, argues that Liu's research path traces a logical thread in the innovation of economic theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article opens with Liu's biography: his education-oriented family, his early reading of Capital, his studies at Wuhan University from 1942, and his teaching at Sichuan University from 1946. It notes his shift after 1958 from contemporary capitalism to socialist economic theory. Ding names three features of his scholarship: comprehensive study of economic reform, grounding in Chinese conditions, and unity of theory and practice. The body then takes up four themes: the socialist market economy, plural forms of ownership, the primary stage of socialism, and the theory of people's wealth and macroeconomic operation. Ding stresses several of Liu's positions. In 1979 he defined the socialist economy as a socialist commodity economy and argued that a market economy is a general category, not peculiar to capitalism; Ding says this idea later entered the 1984 Party decision on economic reform. Liu argued that compatibility between the market and public ownership is settled in practice, and that state enterprises needed clear property rights and a legal-person property system. He held that socialist ownership is plural and "incomplete". Using both relations of production and productive forces as criteria, he classed China among countries emerging from a backward semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, which must pass through a long primary stage of socialism. Ding also covers Liu's idea of political economy as a study of "people's wealth", his analysis of demand shortfalls and overcapacity in the transition period, and his account of cycles under a socialist market economy. Ding concludes that Liu consistently relied on Marxism, applied it to Chinese practice, and so advanced the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Liu is presented as a firm believer in communist ideals and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Ding adds that his analyses of overcapacity and cycles remain useful today. Read the original if you want a concise, officially sympathetic overview of Liu Shibai's main contributions to Chinese economic thought from 1979 to the 2000s.

Wu Yifeng: a people's economist grounded in Marxism 吴易风:立足马克思主义的人民经济学家 Zhang Lin This is a biographical tribute, originally published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2023, to Wu Yifeng (b. 1932), a first-class professor at Renmin University of China. Zhang, who was Wu's doctoral student, presents him as a Marxist economist who was also learned in Western economics and the history of economic thought. The article's thesis is that Wu combined firm Marxist conviction, critical engagement with Western economics and a commitment to serve working people, and so exemplified the "people's economist". The piece is organised under four headings. It first traces Wu's path as a member of the first generation of economists trained after 1949, from teaching cadres in 1953 to Renmin University and the writing of his major works. It then covers his defence of Marxian economics in several debates, his work on adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, and his role as a textbook author and educator in Western economics. A final section gives a personal portrait of Wu as a teacher and friend. Zhang reports that Wu answered critics of Marxist economics point by point. Against the claim that it ignores resource allocation, Wu argued in 1997 that allocation is subordinate to the mode of production. Against the claim that Coase had a property-rights theory and Marx did not, he argued that Marx built a scientific and systematic one a century earlier. Against the view that Marxism cannot be expressed mathematically, he co-authored work on Marx's models, while warning against using mathematics as packaging. On Western economics, Wu held that it has a dual character, class bias and usefulness under specific conditions. In Zhang's account he rejected both wholesale acceptance and wholesale rejection, calling for criticism of the ideological elements and for selective borrowing of the useful ones. Zhang also describes Wu's textbooks with Gao Hongye and his role in the 1990s seminars that countered what participants saw as the over-promotion of Coase's theorem and of privatisation-oriented theories. Zhang concludes that Wu's emphasis on the class character of economics and on the leading place of Marxist economics in China amounts to a call for economics to serve the broad masses. Wu is said to have urged others to be "people's economists" and to have lived by this over more than sixty years of scholarship. Read the original if you want a sympathetic portrait of a leading Chinese Marxist economist, with details on his main debates, textbooks and view of Western economics.

Moses Hess and the young Marx in historical perspective 历史性视野中的赫斯与青年马克思 Kang Zhai Since the 1960s, revived interest in Spinoza and the publication of Moses Hess's original writings have prompted renewed study of Hess's role in the formation of Marx's thought. Some scholars, including David McLellan, Isaiah Berlin, Hiromatsu Wataru and Leszek Kołakowski, stress Hess's decisive influence and even count him among the founders of the materialist conception of history. Kang Zhai accepts that Hess influenced the young Marx's communism but argues that the two men's theories differ decisively. In this account Marx's communism holds to historicity, whereas Hess's remained, in Marx's words, a "non-historical abstraction" full of moral zeal. The article, which appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in November 2023, compares the two thinkers on three points. It first looks at their theoretical routes to communism: Marx through critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, Hess through the philosophy of history. It then asks what each meant by communism and by economic alienation. Finally it considers the political and practical consequences of these differences and closes with a critique of Hiromatsu's reading. Kang argues that Marx reached communism by identifying the separation of civil society from the political state as the modern world's basic problem and by concluding that civil society has priority over the state. Overcoming the separation therefore meant sublating civil society. This led from the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher texts to the critique of private property through alienated labour in the 1844 Manuscripts. Hess, by contrast, moved from the religious "sacred history" of his early work, through a Fichtean philosophy of action, to a critique of money as alienated social intercourse and a vision of communism as an ethical community of love. Both used the idea of overcoming the split between individual and species. Hess's alienation, however, operates in the sphere of circulation and remains a Hegelian-Feuerbachian reworking of French socialism. Marx locates alienation in capitalist production and in the relation between labour and capital, and Kang says this reflects a deeper engagement with classical political economy. Kang concludes that Hess's philosophical limits led him to a gradualist, morally grounded reform programme that rejected force and class struggle, with communism justified as right rather than as necessary. Such reform could not touch capitalism's basic structure, so communism stayed an "abstract ought". Kang credits Kołakowski and Hiromatsu with breaking dogmatic ideology's long concealment of Marx's early development. Kang nonetheless says Hiromatsu overstates Hess's influence and confuses Hess's view of the human essence as "intercourse and joint activity" with Marx's view of it as the ensemble of social relations. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's historical standpoint is distinguished from Hess's ethical communism in current Chinese scholarship on the history of Marxism.

Hegel's philosophy of right and the critique of Western modernity 黑格尔法哲学与西方现代性批判 Sun Leqiang Marking the 180th anniversary of Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Sun Leqiang asks how the work's scholarly value and contemporary relevance should be understood afresh, in the context of intellectual history and of East–West differences. The short essay, which first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2023, argues that the work lays bare the internal structure of Western modernity: individual, civil society, state. It also argues that Marx's claim that civil society determines the state still holds today. Sun begins with the setting of Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right, the "dual revolution" of English industry and French politics, against which Germany appears as an anachronism. The essay then traces how the relation between civil society and the state changed: from identity in ancient Greece and the Middle Ages to separation after the French Revolution. It next follows how the concept of civil society narrowed from a bourgeois political community to a system of needs, and closes with Marx's critical route and its present value. Sun contends that Hegel rebuilt the concept of civil society on Adam Smith's account of labour, division of labour and exchange, but did so in order to surpass Smith. Where Smith relied on the "invisible hand" and laissez-faire, Hegel held that individual reason is mastered by civil society, so that the state's collective reason must overcome its antinomies. In Sun's reading, Hegel's philosophy of the state is therefore itself a critique of political economy. Marx, by contrast, first criticised the "copy" (Hegel's speculative philosophy of the state) and then the "original" (the modern representative state). Marx saw this state as a regime of private property, so Hegel's state could only reinforce civil society's dominant logic. Sun adds that Marx at this stage had not yet studied classical political economy or the civil-society section of Hegel's text. Sun concludes that, despite their disagreements, Hegel and Marx agree on the evolution of modern Western society, with civil society as the basis of Western modernity. Marx's further step was to carry the narrow concept of civil society to a critique of the capitalist mode of production. Sun notes the irony that state intervention, as Hegel envisaged it, later appeared in the New Deal, Keynesianism and the welfare state, yet as a bourgeois political state. Neither Smith's nor Hegel's logic resolved civil society's paradoxes. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how Hegel's civil society and state, and Marx's early critique of them, are linked to the critique of Western modernity.

Cultural enlightenment and the shaping of belief: the formation of atheist knowledge in New Youth 文化启蒙与信念塑造：《新青年》无神论知识的生成 Yang Lan Yang Lan examines how atheist knowledge took shape in the journal New Youth (Xin qingnian) and how its orientation shifted from cultural enlightenment to revolutionary mobilisation. Earlier scholarship, the article says, has mostly traced the journal's themes, circulation and impact, or the atheist thought of Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao. Yang instead takes the interaction of knowledge and practice as a lens. The thesis is that atheism in the journal moved from a critique of old religion in support of the republic to a scientific atheism tied to proletarian liberation and, ultimately, to the activities of the Chinese Communist Party. The article follows New Youth from 1915 to the mid-1920s in three stages. The first covers the attack on Confucianism as a state religion and on spiritualist ghost-belief, in the political setting of Yuan Shikai's sacrificial ceremonies and attempted restoration. The second covers the 'replace religion with science' project, and the third the turn to the 'sacredness of labour' and to Marxism. Yang draws on pieces by Chen Duxiu, Yi Baisha, Wang Xinggong, Gao Xian, Qu Qiubai, Li Dazhao and others, as well as translations. Yang argues that in the first stage contributors such as Chen Duxiu, Liu Bannong, Qian Xuantong and Chen Daqi used Western precedents and modern science to criticise the 'Confucian religion', the Spiritualist Society and religion's social role. They then tried to build positive content: they mined Chinese philosophers for atheist ideas, wrote the history of religion and life, and introduced scientific method and a 'scientific' outlook on life. After 1919, Yang contends, atheism was linked to socialism and the labour movement. Qu Qiubai's 1923 'new manifesto' extended science to social science, and Comintern texts connected atheist education to proletarian culture. The use of historical materialism to explain human origins and social development turned a plain atheism into scientific atheism. Yang concludes that atheism ran through the journal's whole life and registered changes in its enlightenment aims. Cultural enlightenment drew on modern science to defend the republic and attack feudal autocracy and superstition. Labour enlightenment stressed proletarian culture and class liberation, and after 1920 the increase in Soviet-Russian sources changed the journal's Euro-American models. Yang presents the shift to scientific atheism as a distinctive course in the transformation of Chinese revolutionary thought, and says the Party's popularisation of these ideas among students and workers made them an ideological weapon. Read the original if you study the early history of Marxism, atheism and science propaganda in China, or want a detailed list of New Youth articles on the subject.

Lenin's socialist value orientation during the New Economic Policy period 新经济政策时期列宁的社会主义价值取向 Wang Min Yu Liangzao Since reform and opening up, Chinese scholars have studied Lenin's theory of the New Economic Policy (NEP) extensively. Wang and Yu argue that this work has paid too little attention to how Lenin justified and advanced the NEP from a socialist standpoint. Their thesis is that Lenin held a firm socialist value orientation throughout the policy's shift, formulation, implementation and development, and that identifying it clarifies the NEP's socialist character. The article has three parts. The first examines Lenin's texts of 1921–22 on why the NEP was necessary and correct. The second sets out five areas in which he applied socialist principles in practice. The third draws lessons for the Chinese Communist Party today. In the first part, the authors read Lenin as presenting the shift from War Communism as a response to Russia's peasant-dominated conditions. In their account, he held that a compromise with the peasantry was the only way to save the revolution until revolutions abroad arrived, and that the NEP was a "detour" and a "strategic retreat" towards socialism. They also cite his 1922 confidence that NEP Russia would become socialist Russia. In the second part they argue that Lenin put improving peasants' living and production conditions first, through the tax in kind and free trade. They add that he promoted electrification and concessions to raise productive forces, and urged the Soviet state to develop commerce while keeping socialism as its direction. They also credit him with a cultural revolution centred on literacy and teachers, and with strengthening the Party's leadership, unity and fight against bureaucracy. The authors conclude with three lessons for China, which they link to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Party should uphold its leadership and give ideological work a foundational place in Party building. It should put the people first and pursue common prosperity. It should also adhere to the Two Integrations, combining Marxism with China's realities and its fine traditional culture. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-scholar reading of Lenin's late writings on the NEP, and of how they are tied to current Chinese policy language.

Understanding the standpoint, viewpoint and method of Xi Jinping's important statements on religious work through the "Six Musts" 从“六个必须坚持”认识和把握习近平总书记关于宗教工作的重要论述的立场观点方法 Zuo Peng This short essay, one of three written contributions to a journal feature on studying Xi Jinping's statements on religious work, asks how the Party's religious work in the new era should be understood through the "Six Musts" (liu ge bixu jianchi) set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Zuo Peng argues that Xi's statements on religious work are the religious-work chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and that each of the six principles supplies a standpoint, viewpoint or method for that work. An editors' note places the piece after a June 2023 symposium on the statements, addressed by Wang Huning. The article is organised in six numbered sections, one for each principle: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systematic thinking, and a global vision. Each section opens with the principle's general meaning and then applies it to religion, quoting Xi and the Party congress report. The author cites 2018 figures of nearly 200 million religious citizens and over 380,000 clergy. Zuo's central moves are as follows. First, religious work is treated as mass work and united-front work: the author says that respecting believers' faith while protecting their practical interests will draw them around the Party and strengthen its social base. Second, the Sinicization of religion is presented as Xi's theoretical and practical innovation, grounded in the historical Sinicization of imported religions. Zuo pairs it with "fundamental principles" (upholding the Marxist view of religion) and "breaking new ground" (adapting that view to new conditions). Third, the problem-oriented section lists the issues Zuo sees: growing numbers of believers, foreign infiltration, commercialisation, illegal proselytising and Party members taking part in religious activity. The remedy is Marxist atheism as the mainstream ideology, stronger rule of law and firm atheism among Communists. The systematic-thinking section stresses "guidance" (dao) through education, culture, policy, administration and law. Zuo concludes that the global-vision principle requires telling China's religious story abroad. The author says that Chinese religious policy handles religious questions effectively and offers "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" to problems such as safeguarding freedom of belief and curbing religious extremism. The author describes foreign criticism of Chinese religious policy as hostile distortion, and this characterisation is the author's own. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party theorists map religious policy onto the Six Musts.

The Soviet collapse began with the Soviet Communist Party's wholesale denigration of its own history 苏联崩溃起自苏共对苏共历史的全面诋毁 Zhang Shuhua How a party treats its own history and its leaders is, in Zhang Shuhua's view, a test of its maturity. The article argues that the Soviet collapse began when the Soviet Communist Party (CPSU) leadership under Gorbachev and Yakovlev, in the late 1980s, set about discrediting the Party's entire past. Zhang calls this a wholesale negation that served current political needs and repeated earlier errors. The article gives a short background: the fixed official interpretation of Soviet history after the 1938 Short Course, Khrushchev's 1956 attack on Stalin's cult of personality, and Brezhnev's later criticism of Khrushchev. It then identifies four features of the late-Soviet 'reflection on history' campaign: it was organised from the top, it was tied to mass rehabilitations, it was led by non-specialist writers and journalists, and it ended in nihilism about Soviet history and socialism. Zhang's central claim is that the campaign was deliberately steered by the top leadership. He cites Gorbachev's 1986 demand for new textbooks, the 1987 speech marking the October Revolution's 70th anniversary, and the Politburo's 1988 decision to build a monument to Stalin's victims. He also describes the 1988 Nina Andreyeva letter and the sharp reply in Pravda. Zhang notes dissent from Ligachev, Chebrikov, academicians and ordinary Party members. In his account, the attack moved from Stalin to the Soviet system, then to Lenin, the October Revolution and Marxism-Leninism. Zhang says it also fed admiration for the West and for tsarist Russia, and he quotes remarks that even welcomed colonial status. He presents this as the ideological basis of post-Soviet Russian neoliberalism.
