Zhang concludes that, in the name of re-evaluating history, Gorbachev and Yakovlev opened the way to dismantling the CPSU ideologically and put the Party on trial before history. The article implicitly offers this as a warning about historical nihilism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how the late-Soviet history debates are used as a cautionary case, with detailed episodes from 1986 to 1989.

Guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, strengthening cultural confidence in the practice of the Sinicization of religion 以习近平文化思想为指导，在宗教中国化实践中增强文化自信 Zhang Xinying This short commentary, one of three written reflections solicited by the journal Science and Atheism, asks how Xi Jinping Thought on Culture, first formally proposed at the national conference on propaganda, ideological and cultural work in October 2023, should guide the work of making religion Chinese. Zhang argues that the 'Second Integration' of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture is the key criterion and path for the Sinicization of religion, and that this process shows the reach of Xi's cultural thought beyond propaganda work into religious affairs. An editors' note places the piece after a June 2023 symposium on Xi's important expositions on religious work. Zhang first locates the 'Second Integration' within Xi's 2023 speech on cultural inheritance and development. The author then turns to the 'five identifications' (with the motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Communist Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics) and reviews the religions one by one: Buddhism, Daoism, Tibetan and Theravada Buddhism, then Catholicism, Protestantism and Islam. The closing section sets out cautions. Zhang reads the five identifications as political and, above all, cultural identification, which Xi calls the deepest level of identification. The main path is to immerse each religion in fine traditional culture, gradually and by category. In the author's account, Han Buddhism and Daoism, already well Sinicized, face a task of 're-Sinicization'. Catholicism, Protestantism and Islam, by contrast, are said not yet to be fully 'religions of China', and the author cites Western 'ideological infiltration' and 'Arabization' tendencies as challenges. Zhang also contrasts China's utilitarian polytheistic tradition with Western monotheism's 'alienated' theocentrism, and suggests that reassessing polytheism would strengthen cultural confidence. Zhang warns against idealising a religion's historical Sinicization, against treating minority religious forms as models without change, and against using the slogan to expand proselytising. Sinicization is not meant to attract more believers. It is described as gradual and practical, 'more a matter of doing than of saying', and not to be reduced to slogans or showpiece projects. Zhang calls on academics, as the 'third team' in religious work, to do field research and study the history, experience, rationale and paths of Sinicization. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholars link Xi Jinping Thought on Culture to religious policy and to the Sinicization of specific religions.

Drawing theoretical innovation wisdom from the creations of the people 从人民群众的创造中汲取理论创新智慧 Ai Silin Ai Silin takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the sixth collective study session of the 20th Politburo (2023), to "draw theoretical innovation wisdom from the creations of the people". The article reads the call as an application of the Marxist theory of knowledge and the mass view of history, and as a summary of the Party's historical experience. It argues that the call fixes the standpoint, direction and route for advancing the Party's theoretical innovation. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first sets out why the people's creative practice is the inexhaustible source of Marxist theoretical innovation. The second reviews the Party's history, from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The third turns to practical measures for following the mass line in theoretical work. Ai's core reasoning starts from the primacy of practice in Marxist epistemology and the people-centred nature of Marxism. Practice is a social activity carried out by the masses, so the masses are the decisive force in changing the world and a source of theory. The article presents the rural investigations behind Mao Zedong's strategy of surrounding the cities from the countryside, and the household contract responsibility system and township enterprises under reform and opening up, as examples. It treats Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as rooted in the people's practice. On method, Ai calls for large-scale investigation and research in which cadres learn humbly from the people. Investigation gathers raw material, and research must then distil from it theory that applies generally. Ai describes investigation without research as a "broken bridge". Ai concludes that the Party should build long-term mechanisms for following the mass line. These include education in the Marxist mass viewpoint, stronger research skills with incentives for evaluating research results, and open channels for suggestions, criticism and supervision. They also include a body of theorists who learn from the people and "write their papers on the land of the motherland". Ai ties this to the current study campaign on Xi Jinping Thought and to a period of rapid change, which is said to call for respecting the people's initiative. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists justify theoretical innovation as coming from the masses and how they link it to investigation and research methods.

Hegel's reconciliation and the young Marx's revolution 黑格尔的和解与青年马克思的革命 Zhang Donghui Why did Hegel counsel reconciliation with social reality while the young Marx demanded revolution? Zhang Donghui argues that the difference rests on how each understood 'essence'. Hegel, in Zhang's reading, takes an anti-essentialist stance that dissolves and weakens essence, and so views social contradiction and historical change through becoming and reconciliation. The young Marx tends towards essentialism, which is the premise of his theory of alienation, and he chooses revolution in order to sublate alienation. The article, a short piece first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in November 2023, has three parts. The first compares the two thinkers' conceptions of essence, drawing on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Science of Logic and on the young Marx's critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and his determinations of religion, money, labour and the human being. The second sets Marx's alienation against Hegel's 'becoming' (Werden). The third turns to reconciliation versus revolution as practical attitudes. Zhang defines essentialism as grasping the laws and essence of things from empirical phenomena. The young Marx, on this account, presupposes an essence, reads the actual state of things as alienation from it, and then uses revolution to return things to their ideal state. Hegel, by contrast, treats essence as the reflection of thought in itself and as a transitional moment on the way to the absolute Idea, so alienation in Marx's sense cannot arise for him. Becoming is a broader concept that contains alienation. Reconciliation is not an excuse for existing evils: Zhang notes that Hegel allows for reform and even revolution when social contradictions, such as extreme inequality, make society unworthy of reconciliation. Zhang describes Hegel's stance as present-oriented realism and Marx's as future-oriented idealism. Zhang adds that Marx moved from political towards social revolution, stressing the material conditions and development of productive forces, as in The German Ideology. That emphasis, Zhang says, links his theory of revolution to Hegel's dialectic of becoming and gives it some compatibility with reconciliation. Zhang concludes that Hegel's anti-essentialism remains entangled with essentialism, that Marx's revolution partly destroys essentialism, and that the essentialism lens is only one angle of reading. Read the original if you want a brief, concept-focused comparison of Hegel and the young Marx through the essence/alienation framework.

Carl Schorlemmer and the Marxist philosophy of chemistry 肖莱马与马克思主义化学哲学 Yu Ping Li Xuechen This short piece asks what the work of the German chemist Carl Schorlemmer (1834–1892), a close associate of Marx and Engels, contributes to a Marxist philosophy of chemistry. Yu Ping and Li Xuechen present him as a scientist who consciously applied materialist dialectics to research and as a committed communist. They argue that his achievements show the value of theoretical thinking for natural science and of natural science for Marxism. The article has four parts: Schorlemmer's work in chemistry and the philosophy of chemistry; his work on the history of chemistry; the character of his scientific conduct; and the lessons the authors draw for today. It draws on Engels's judgements of Schorlemmer, on his textbook and history of organic chemistry, and on a letter from Marx to Engels of 3 January 1868. The authors argue that Schorlemmer borrowed the method of Marx's Capital and treated aliphatic hydrocarbons as the "cell" from which all organic compounds derive. On this basis he did experimental and theoretical work on hydrocarbons and their derivatives. In the authors' account he also traced a dialectical path from inorganic chemistry through organic chemistry and biochemistry to biology, and showed how chemistry rests on physics and mechanics, which they say matches Engels's view of the transformation of forms of motion. In the history of chemistry, his 1871 textbook, the first organised by chemical structure, and his 1879 history of organic chemistry are presented as pioneering works shaped by historical materialism. The authors add that he came from a poor family, lived frugally, was generous to friends and students, and thus models the spirit of the scientist. The authors draw two lessons. Natural scientists should actively learn and use Marxist theoretical thinking in their research. Adapting Marxism to the needs of our times also requires drawing on new natural-science results and on study of Marx's theory of science and technology, in order to keep Marxism vital. Marx's request, passed through Engels, for Schorlemmer's advice on agricultural chemistry while writing on ground rent is cited as evidence that Marx valued natural science. Read the original if you want a brief, officially oriented introduction to Schorlemmer and to how Chinese Marxist scholars link the history of science with the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

How Marx transcended Rousseau's Romantic view of science and technology 马克思对卢梭浪漫主义科学技术观的超越 Zhu Huabin Rousseau, the Romantic thinker, acknowledged the importance of science but dwelt mainly on its harmful effects, holding that it corrupted social customs and degraded human nature. Zhu argues that Marx inherited Rousseau's critical spirit but placed science and technology within historical materialism. In this account Marx revealed their social and humanistic character and treated them as a revolutionary force for progress, thereby overcoming Rousseau's Romantic imagination. The short commentary, which first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, is organised around three themes: the essence of science and technology, their alienation, and their revolutionary power. It ends with three lessons for promoting scientific and technological innovation in the new era. On essence, Zhu contrasts Rousseau's claim that science springs from moral vice (astronomy from superstition, mathematics from greed) with Marx's view that curiosity and desire are only drivers. For Marx, the real basis of natural science is labour practice, and the value of the human being and that of science and technology are unified. On alienation, Zhu says Rousseau saw science's damage to morals but not its root. Marx traced the harm to workers' bodies, minds and individuality to the capitalist production process, and located the cause in the capitalist application of machinery rather than machinery itself, which in itself lightens labour and shortens working time. On revolutionary power, Zhu says Marx rejected Rousseau's anti-science stance. He saw technology as raising productivity, saving labour time and enlarging free time, and he regarded alienation as a necessary stage on the road to communism. Zhu draws three lessons for innovation in the new era: keep a human-centred orientation aimed at the people's aspiration for a better life; apply dialectics to the 'double-edged sword' of technology, maximising its positive effects and limiting its negative ones; and hold to the historical-materialist position that alienation is avoided by promoting innovation under the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's relation to Rousseau on technology, and of how it is linked to current innovation policy.

Lenin's account of the proletarian party's tactics of struggle and its lessons Based on "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder 列宁对无产阶级政党斗争策略的阐释及启示 Sun Shoutao Zhu Fanghan Sun Shoutao and Zhu Fanghan take up Lenin's treatment of the tactics of struggle of the proletarian party, which Lenin ranked alongside Marx's philosophy, economics and socialist doctrine. They note that existing scholarship on "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder mostly introduces and interprets the single text, and that its tactical thought has been discussed only sparsely. The article argues that Lenin's tactics form a systematic body of thought that carries a dialectical methodology and still offers practical lessons for Communist parties, above all the Communist Party of China. The article has three parts. The first sets out five tactical lessons Lenin drew from the Bolshevik experience and from other revolutionary parties. The second identifies three methodological features of that thought. The third turns to the present and draws three lessons for the Communist Party of China (CPC). On the tactics themselves, the authors report Lenin's insistence on iron discipline and unconditional centralisation. They also cover his distinction between the compromise of the traitor and the compromise forced by circumstances, and his call to work in trade unions and bourgeois parliaments to win the masses. They further cover his account of the relations among leaders, party, class and masses, and his demand for skill in changing forms of struggle. In the authors' reading, the methodology rests on three elements. These are revolutionary dialectics applied in practice, which guards against both dogmatism and empiricism; the combination of principle with flexibility; and class analysis aimed at winning allies and isolating enemies. The authors present the Bolshevik tactics as the model for all proletarian parties, related to them as the particular to the general. For the present, the authors call for upholding the Party's centralised and unified leadership and strict discipline, citing the response to the Covid-19 epidemic and the campaign against poverty as examples. They also call for close Party–masses relations and for cadres who solve the masses' practical problems and encourage popular participation in governance. Finally, they urge following a Chinese path by applying materialist dialectics, pointing to Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up and Xi Jinping's continuation of it. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Lenin's tactical thought is connected to current Party-building and to the CPC's own historical experience.

The scientific positioning, rich content and worldview and methodology of General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work 习近平总书记关于宗教工作的重要论述的科学定位､丰富内涵和世界观､方法论 Zhu Xiaoming Zhu Xiaoming asks how Xi Jinping's important expositions on religious work should be placed within the Party's theory, what they contain, and how they should be studied and applied. The article argues that they form part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the third major theoretical achievement of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It also holds that they supply a basis for building Marxist religious studies as an academic discipline. The article has four sections. The first locates the expositions historically, tracing religious-work theory from Mao Zedong Thought through the reform-era theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics to the present. The second sets out their content in "three levels". The third turns to the worldview and methodology behind them, and the fourth to the implications for the discipline of Marxist religious studies. Zhu's central move is to organise the "Nine Musts" from Xi's 2021 national conference on religious work into three levels. The first three concern how religion is understood: the importance of religious work, strong leadership mechanisms, and developing socialist religious theory with Chinese characteristics. The next three concern how religious issues are handled: the Party's basic principles, the Sinicization of religion, and uniting believers around the Party and government. The last three concern methods: positive and healthy religious relations, support for religious bodies' self-building, and rule of law. Zhu then links the "Six Musts" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, staying true to fundamental principles while innovating, problem orientation, systems thinking, and a global outlook) to the worldview and methodology of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Applying them together with the Two Integrations, Zhu says, yields scientific understanding and keeps the theory current. Zhu calls on scholars to treat Marxist religious studies and Marxist atheism as priority disciplines. They should interpret Xi's expositions accurately, study the new concepts and judgements as principled theoretical results, and pursue integrated innovation. The aim is to make the discipline more systematic and academically grounded, drawing on Xi's 2023 remarks on systematising theory. Zhu also urges continuing the tradition of Marxist religious studies begun by Ren Jiyu. Read the original if you want a compact Party-orthodox account of how religious-work theory is periodised and structured, and how it is linked to disciplinary development.

Understanding the great achievements and key lessons of reform and opening up 深刻认识改革开放的伟大成就和重要启示 Fourth Research Department, Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee This commentary, written by a research department of the Party's central history and documents institute and published in the People's Daily in December 2023, takes stock of 45 years of reform and opening up. It was issued after the Central Economic Work Conference stressed relying on reform and opening up to strengthen endogenous momentum for development. The authors argue that the record of achievements and the lessons drawn from it matter for deepening reform on the "new journey" and for reaching the second centenary goal. The article has two parts. The first surveys five areas of achievement: economic strength, socialist democracy and the rule of law, cultural soft power, the sharing of reform outcomes, and ecological progress. The second sets out six lessons for the future. Throughout, the authors link the period since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the new stage opened by the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). On achievements, the authors cite figures: GDP rising from 368.7 billion yuan at the start of reform to 121.02 trillion yuan in 2022, the world's second largest; the elimination of absolute poverty; the world's most complete industrial system; per capita disposable income up from 171 yuan in 1978 to 36,883 yuan in 2022; and life expectancy of 78.2 years. They also point to whole-process people's democracy, a largely formed framework of law-based governance, a reversal in the ideological sphere, and better air and water quality. From this record they derive their lessons: uphold the Party's centralised and unified leadership, put the people at the centre of development, and keep to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They add that Marxism must continue to be adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, that institutional strengths should become governance effectiveness, and that cultural confidence supplies spiritual strength. The authors conclude that the practice of reform and opening up proves the correctness of Chinese modernization, which they call the only correct path to national rejuvenation. They call for unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and for guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a compact, officially framed summary of how Party theorists present the achievements and lessons of reform and opening up at the end of 2023.

Forever remember Comrade Mao Zedong's great achievements and noble example 永远铭记毛泽东同志的丰功伟绩和崇高风范 Party History and Literature Research Institute of the CPC Central Committee Written for the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, this commemorative piece by the Party History and Literature Research Institute of the CPC Central Committee asks what the Party should draw from Mao's legacy today. Its answer is that remembering Mao means deepening understanding of the Two Establishes, adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, holding to the socialist road, pursuing Chinese modernization, and continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The article opens with an assessment of Mao as a founder of the Party, the army and the People's Republic. It then proceeds in four sections, each introduced by the phrase "today, to cherish the memory of Comrade Mao Zedong, we must…". These cover his role as the core of the first generation of central leadership, his pioneering role in adapting Marxism to China, the socialist path, and modernization and Party building. Each section links Mao's record to Xi Jinping's leadership and thought. The piece draws on quotations from Mao, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. The authors argue for continuity across eras. They hold that the Zunyi Meeting established Mao's leadership and that Deng judged the revolution would have groped in darkness longer without him. They present the Two Establishes as the major political outcome of the new era. In their account Mao Thought was the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to China, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is a further leap. They say it keeps the "living soul" of Mao Thought (seeking truth from facts, the mass line, independence) and carries it forward through the Two Integrations. The article acknowledges that Mao took detours in exploring socialist construction. It insists that the periods before and after reform and opening up are linked, and that the achievements of each must not be negated. It credits Mao's era with the industrial base and the "two bombs, one satellite" breakthroughs, and treats Chinese modernization as confirming his forecasts. On Party building, the authors present Mao's "two musts" and his answer to the historical cycle of rise and decline (letting the people supervise the government) as forerunners of the Party's self-reform. They conclude that the best commemoration is to carry forward his cause, to follow a path that is neither rigid nor a change of banner, and to unite around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's central research institute frames Mao's legacy in relation to Xi Jinping Thought and current slogans in an official anniversary text.

Mao Zedong's thought of independence and self-reliance and its value for our times 毛泽东同志的独立自主思想及其时代价值 Yang Fengcheng Writing in Guangming Daily in December 2023, Yang Fengcheng takes up Mao Zedong's idea of independence and self-reliance (duli zizhu), which Yang calls the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought and a key to the success of China's revolution and construction. The article's central claim is that its core is placing national development on the basis of one's own strength and having Chinese affairs decided and handled by the Chinese people themselves. Yang argues that this principle keeps its value in the new era. The piece has five numbered sections. The first traces the idea's sources in Marxism and in Chinese traditional culture, and the Party's gradual, hard-won grasp of it from the Zunyi Conference onward. The next sections treat independence in choosing a development path, self-reliance in economic and technological work, the relation between self-reliance and openness, and the spirit of struggle. Each section links Mao-era examples to present-day concerns. Yang holds that independence was not automatic for Chinese communists. Dogmatism and Comintern directives, in Yang's account, bore heavy responsibility for the defeats of the Great Revolution and of the 'Left' line in the land-revolution period. Mao's answers were the path of encircling the cities from the countryside and the 'second integration' of Marxism with Chinese reality after 1949, seen in 'On the Ten Major Relationships'. Yang credits these with building an independent, relatively complete industrial system and avoiding the dependent development of some newly independent states. Self-reliance is illustrated by the Nanniwan production campaign and the 'two bombs, one satellite' programme after the Soviet withdrawal of experts. Yang stresses that it does not mean closing the country: Mao favoured learning critically from all nations, and the article presents reform-era opening up as continuing this. Yang concludes that no nation has become strong by depending on outsiders or copying foreign models, and that China must keep strengthening confidence in its path, theory, system and culture. Because key technologies still face 'chokehold' problems, the article says they cannot be begged or bought and must be developed independently. Yang also calls for a fighting spirit that is both brave and skilful, citing Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping on never being anyone's appendage. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party scholars present Mao's independence principle as a basis for current policy on technology, openness and sovereignty.

The impact of the new round of left-wing governments on Latin America's socialist movement 新一轮左翼执政对拉美社会主义运动的影响 Yuan Dongzhen Yuan Dongzhen asks how the latest wave of left-wing governments in Latin America, which began around 2018–2020, has affected the region's socialist movement. The article argues that the new wave has changed the region's political landscape and substantially improved the overall environment for socialism. It also holds that the fortunes of the left and of socialism remain closely linked but are constrained by weak party-building, alternating left and right rule, and outside pressure. The article has three parts. The first describes the wave's features: a clustered, 'contagion'-style pattern, a cyclical left–right alternation, and spillover effects across borders. Yuan traces the first 'pink tide' from Venezuela in 1999, the rightward turn after 2015, and the left's return from Mexico in 2018 to Brazil in 2022–2023. The second part examines four effects on the socialist movement. The conclusion then draws general lessons about the left–socialism relationship. Yuan argues that left-wing rule is favourable to socialism because the left's social base (middle and lower strata), its support for state intervention and social equity, and its anti-US stance overlap with socialist positions. The article contrasts the right-wing period, when Venezuela, the main bearer of 'twenty-first-century socialism', was isolated by the Lima Group and Prosur, with the period after 2020. In the later period, Bolivia, Peru, Colombia and Brazil restored ties with Caracas and the right-wing blocs dissolved. Yuan also shows communist parties in Brazil, Chile and Colombia joining governments, and cites party congresses, regional forums and left intellectuals calling for struggle against capitalism and neoliberalism. Yuan concludes that the strength of socialist parties largely determines how the movement develops. Many left parties, the author says, are immature and depend on charismatic leaders, which risks patronage and bureaucratism. Frequent alternation of left and right, in Yuan's view, means socialism can only advance gradually and in waves. Yuan adds that US and European conservative opposition, including the US strategy of 'supporting the right and striking the left', is a lasting external obstacle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Latin American left politics, with a country-by-country chronology and details of communist party participation in government.

Escaping the misconceptions of Western ecologism 走出西方生态主义思潮误区 Zhang Xiuqin Zhang Xiang Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the national conference on ecological and environmental protection, this commentary asks how to view Western ecologism critically. The authors argue that it puts the environment above economic and social development, stresses protection one-sidedly and so has practical limits. They contend that the Marxist view of ecology, as developed in Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, offers the way out. The article first sketches the main strands of Western ecologism, from the late nineteenth-century conservation movement to the environmentalism of the 1960s and 1970s. It then lists animal liberation and rights theory (Peter Singer), biocentrism, ecocentrism and ecological postmodernism (Charlene Spretnak). It then sets out three theoretical flaws and ends with the Marxist corrective. The authors credit ecologism with revising traditional anthropocentrism but call it one-sided. In their account it exaggerates the opposition between humans and nature, treats economic growth and protection as contradictory, and blames technology and modern civilization instead of capitalism. Against this, they hold that capitalist private ownership and the profit motive are the root of ecological crisis, so values and development methods alone cannot fix it. They say Marxism treats the relation dialectically, keeps human agency and purposes in view, and is tested in practice, whereas ecologism remains dualist and sees development and protection as zero-sum. The authors conclude that eliminating ecological crisis requires changing the social system and ending capitalist private ownership, so that humans and nature coexist harmoniously. They present the "ten adherences" of ecological civilization in socialism with Chinese characteristics and China's reported achievements as confirming the Marxist view. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese Party-journal writing criticises Western green thought from a Marxist standpoint.

Debates among foreign left-wing scholars on the theory of digital socialism 国外左翼学者关于数字社会主义理论的论争 Li Quan Du Min This review surveys how left-wing scholars outside China have argued over "digital socialism", a concept Kevin Kelly introduced in 2009 as an alternative to capitalism for the age of big data and the internet. Li and Du note that the literature is varied and sharply divided, and that it includes related notions such as communication socialism and platform socialism. They organise the disputes around four questions: whether digital socialism is socialist in character, whether it can drive social change, whether it can move into practice, and whether it can promote people's free and all-round development. The article is built as a sequence of four debates, followed by a short conclusion. It draws on Kelly, Christian Fuchs, Donatella Della Ratta, Richard Sprague, Michael Peters, Evgeny Morozov, Dimitris Boucas, Aaron Bastani, Paul Cockshott, James Muldoon, Don Tapscott and others. It also cites protest movements such as the Arab Spring and Occupy Wall Street as evidence for the mobilising power of digital networks. On the first question, the authors report that Kelly treats sharing as the core of a decentralised "new socialism". Fuchs, Della Ratta and Sprague reply that sharing under private platform ownership rests on commodity forms and capitalist class relations, so it is not communism; Peters proposes "knowledge socialism" as a more accurate term. On social change, optimists point to growing socialist elements, while realists such as Morozov and Boucas hold that private ownership of infrastructure must first be broken. On practice, the review separates three routes: Bastani's "fully automated luxury communism", which Li and Du fault for lacking a theory of class struggle; digital feedback systems for planning, as in Cockshott; and autonomous, publicly owned platforms, as in Fuchs and Muldoon. On human development, Kelly and Barbrook stress autonomy and "free gifts", whereas Fuchs and Sevignani argue that digital labour is hidden alienated labour, which they call "playbour". Li and Du conclude that digital socialism emerged after the 2008 financial crisis and that its variants, including cyber-communism, platform socialism and communication socialism, share a revolutionary aim of replacing capitalism despite their differences. In their view these theories contribute to twenty-first-century socialist movements and increasingly press for practical effect beyond cyberspace. Read the original if you want a structured map of Western left debates on digital labour, platforms and post-capitalist planning, with names and works to follow up.

Foreign communist parties' assessments of the current stage of socialist development and new trends 国外共产党关于当前社会主义发展阶段及新态势的判断 Yu Weihai Li Yuwei Yu Weihai and Li Yuwei take up a question Xi Jinping has posed as a major research task: what is the present state of world socialism? They approach it through the judgements of communist parties outside China, since these parties are the main force of the international communist movement. The article argues that these parties share one view of the historical era but differ on the stage world socialism has reached, and that they are pursuing new strategies for revival. The article has three parts. The first shows that foreign communist parties broadly hold that the present is still the epoch of transition from capitalism to socialism, citing the Greek, Swedish, Canadian, Turkish and other parties and joint statements of 2021–22. The second sorts their assessments of the current stage into four positions. The third surveys new trends in theory, practice and international cooperation, and ends with the authors' own assessment. On the stage of development, the authors report four views. Some parties, such as the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, the Communist Party of Sweden and the Danish Workers' Communist Party, see a major opportunity for revival after the 2008 financial crisis. Others, including the British, American and Turkish parties, see a tense struggle to leave the ebb, with membership gains alongside weak organisation, sectarianism, theoretical drift and low class consciousness. The Greek party and the New Communist Party of Yugoslavia see a continuing period of crisis. The fourth group regards China as leading a "new era of hope". The authors then describe trends: adapting Marxism to national conditions (for example the French party's "eco-communism" and the British party's three-step programme), reform in ruling parties of Vietnam, Laos, Cuba and the DPRK, parliamentary and mass activity, and new international networks such as the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. The authors conclude that world socialism is in a critical period of slow revival, shaped by the capitalist crisis and what they call the shift from "the East rising, the West declining" toward socialism rising and capitalism declining. They criticise parties that stress proletarian internationalism at the expense of national and era-specific adaptation, naming the Greek and Spanish workers' parties, and say most parties reject this. They hold that China is increasingly seen as the new hope of the movement and can contribute more after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Read the original if you want a detailed, China-framed catalogue of what foreign communist parties say about their own condition and the state of world socialism.

Foreign left-wing scholars' critique of biocapitalism in the twenty-first century 21世纪国外左翼学者对生物资本主义的批判 Liu Pengfei Gu Yongchun This review surveys how Western left-wing scholars have analysed biocapitalism since the early 2000s, as biotechnology spread through production and daily life. It starts from Kaushik Sunder Rajan's Biocapital: The Constitution of Postgenomic Life (2006), which combines Marxist political economy with Foucauldian biopolitics. Liu and Gu argue that these scholars show biocapitalism to be a continuation of capitalism in the age of the life sciences, with some new features. They also argue that the scholars stop short of a structural critique. The article draws on Rajan, Nikolas Rose, Clayton Pierce, Melinda Cooper, Joseph Dumit and others. It has four parts. The first treats biocapitalism as both continuity and change. The second examines how capital logic and power logic work together, giving biocapitalism an instrumental and a redemptive character. The third covers neoliberalism and new imperialism in biological form. A closing section assesses the literature and its relevance for China. On continuity, the authors report that biocapitalism still depends on capital seeking rents from biotechnology, on patents as legal monopolies and on the exploitation of "bio-labourers", many of them from the Global South. On novelty, they report that value extraction becomes more virtual, as firms trade on "future products" and patent knowledge, and that it reaches into the whole of life time. States are said to supply funding and a quasi-religious discourse of national salvation, drawing on cases such as the deCODE genetics database in Iceland and Rajan's study of Indian laboratories. The cited examples of "biocolonialism" and "bio-imperialism" include cell patenting involving the Guaymi and transnational organ trafficking. In the closing section the authors credit the foreign scholars with a multi-dimensional picture of biocapitalism's hidden exploitation. They judge, however, that most remain at the level of phenomena because of their standpoint and theoretical limits. In their view the proposed remedies therefore fall into reformism and utopianism. The authors call for Marxist political economy critique as the means to reach the deeper structure and to frame solutions. They also stress the importance of China's biosecurity and biotechnology and ask whether biocapitalism might eventually give way to "biosocialism". Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western critical scholarship on biotechnology and capital, with its sources and case examples.

Foreign communist parties' understanding of, and response to, a new stage of capitalist development 国外共产党对资本主义发展新阶段的认识与应对 Wang Xiaoqing Has contemporary capitalism entered a new stage, and how should socialists respond? Wang Xiaoqing surveys how communist parties outside China have answered this question in recent years. The article argues that these parties have explored the issue independently, producing a range of judgements on the current stage of capitalism. In the author's reading, they nonetheless agree that capitalism's changes have not resolved its inherent contradictions and that the inevitable victory of socialism stands. The article has four parts. It first sets out the basis on which parties judge capitalism's stage: the historical-materialist view of an epoch of transition from capitalism to socialism, Lenin's theory of imperialism, and changes in the productive forces and relations of production. It then reviews five perspectives found in party programmes and documents. It next compares the parties' strategies and tactics, and closes with an assessment. The cases include the New Communist Party of the Netherlands, the Communist Party of Canada, the Communist Party USA, the Communist Party of Poland, the Communist Party of Spain, the Communist Party of Norway and the Colombian Communist Party. The core of the survey is the typology of stage judgements. Some parties hold that capitalism remains in Lenin's monopoly capitalism; others speak of state monopoly capitalism or transnational monopoly capitalism. Others describe globalised imperialism, digital capitalism, "green imperialism" or "new capitalism". Wang then links these judgements to two strategic lines: immediate socialist revolution, held by parties that see capitalism as still moribund imperialism, and gradual, staged replacement, held by those that see a partial qualitative change. Both camps stress broad domestic alliances of popular forces and an international anti-imperialist, anti-monopoly front. Wang's assessment credits the parties with innovation and says their analyses guide practice, for example environmental campaigns and left-front electoral alliances. The author also criticises two positions. The idea of globalised imperialism, in this view, confuses capital with capitalism, since five socialist countries remain. The claim that capitalism is still Lenin's monopoly stage, with immediate revolution as the strategy, is called conservative, because the productive forces continue to develop and the era's theme has shifted to peace and development. Read the original if you want a detailed survey of how foreign communist parties classify present-day capitalism, together with a Chinese academic's critical evaluation of those views.

Problem awareness and practical orientation in research on the critique of contemporary imperialism 当代帝国主义批判研究的问题意识和现实旨趣 Qin Shiya Qin Shiya examines the wave of critical research on contemporary imperialism produced by Western left-wing scholars since the turn of the twenty-first century. The article asks what problems this literature took up, what it contributed and where it fell short. Qin argues that it combines 'intervening in reality through theory' with 'developing theory from reality', and that its contributions and limits offer useful lessons for developing twenty-first-century Marxism. The article surveys works from around 2000 to 2006 by Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Leo Panitch, Samir Amin, David Harvey, Ellen Meiksins Wood, John Bellamy Foster, Alex Callinicos, William Robinson and others. It sets out three disputes: whether classical imperialism theory still applies, whether imperialism should be analysed through a capital–state dual logic, and the status of historical materialism as method. It then turns to the structure and contradictions of the new imperialism: global production and class structure, the nation-state, and the subjects and forms of anti-capitalist struggle. It closes with an assessment. In Qin's account, scholars split three ways on classical theory. Callinicos would extend it, Harvey would draw on it selectively, and Panitch and Gindin would reject it as economic reductionism. Qin presents the dual-logic debate (Callinicos, Harvey and Wood on one side, Robinson on the other) as a dispute over historical materialism. Qin sides with Callinicos, saying that the primacy of the economic base does not deny the state's role, and calls Panitch and Gindin's reading of historical materialism undialectical and one-sided. On the nation-state, the 'strong state' view of Harvey, Wood and Callinicos is set against the 'transnational state' view of Robinson, Hardt and Negri. Amin and others criticise the latter as a myth of globalization. Qin also reports the divisions over Hardt and Negri's 'multitude' and over whether resistance should be transnational (Robinson, Harvey) or nationally based (Wood). Qin credits the literature with exposing new forms of capitalist exploitation, bringing the state's transformation into view and recording new anti-capitalist trends. The article also notes weaknesses. Hardt and Negri lack political-economic evidence, Harvey and Wood say little about the revolutionary subject, and Robinson is charged with building a globalization myth. Qin holds that capitalism's essence, including its basic contradiction and exploitative character, has not changed, so Marxist critique remains valid. Marxism is described as an open system that develops through answering real problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of the Harvey, Wood, Callinicos, Panitch and Robinson debates on imperialism and the state.

Marxist atheism and two questions in building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 马克思主义无神论与中华民族现代文明建设的两个问题 Tian Xinming In June 2023 Xi Jinping called, at a symposium on cultural inheritance and development, for building a \"modern civilization of the Chinese nation\". Tian Xinming takes up two questions: what this concept means, and how upholding Marxist atheism relates to building such a civilization. Tian argues that the concept is equivalent to a new form of human civilization and to Chinese modernization, and that Marxist atheism supports both the unity and the inclusiveness of that civilization. The article has two parts. The first clarifies the concept by linking it to Xi's other formulations, in line with Xi's call to make theory more systematic and academically grounded. The second takes two of the five \"outstanding characteristics\" of Chinese civilization that Xi has described, unity and inclusiveness, and asks how atheism bears on each and on their relationship. Tian draws on Xi's speeches, the Constitution and Lenin and Mao Zedong. In the first part, Tian reads the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, a new form of human civilization and Chinese modernization as one object seen from three angles. In Tian's account, it is civilization of the Chinese nation, socialist in character, and modern, formed through the Two Integrations under Party leadership. In the second part, Tian argues that unity now rests on Marxism as the guiding ideology. Marxism is a thoroughly materialist and atheist worldview, and the Party's mission and ultimate goal rest on it. Tian warns that if theism spread and religious believers multiplied, it would erode the ideological base, weaken unity and affect the Party's governing foundation. Inclusiveness, by contrast, appears in constitutional provisions on freedom of religious belief. Tian holds that unity and inclusiveness are inseparable and that atheist propaganda is consistent with religious freedom. Tian concludes that atheist work must be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and must balance ideological struggle against religious freedom. Propaganda should target the masses, especially young people, and keep Marxist atheism dominant in mainstream ideology. It should also stay within ideological limits: no administrative measures, no propaganda in places of worship or aimed specifically at believers, no priority over the Party's central tasks, and no equating of criticism of theism with rejecting all religious culture. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist atheism scholar links official civilizational concepts to policy on religion and ideological work.")

"What is Chinese communism?": American observers' reflections on the Chinese revolution during the War of Resistance “何为中国共产主义”:全面抗战时期美国观察家对中国革命的思考 Lu Xiaona Lu Xiaona asks why American observers who travelled to North China after the full-scale outbreak of war in 1937 kept asking "what is Chinese communism?", how their deep prejudice against the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) dissolved, and how their revised views bore on US Far Eastern strategy. The article argues that field investigation convinced them the CCP was organisationally independent of the Soviet Union and pursued a communist programme rooted in Chinese conditions. Lu presents this as a Marxism adapted to China, which the observers publicised in an effort to shift American policy. The study follows several groups: the Amerasia group of 1937, Marine officer Evans Carlson (1937–38), missionary Stanton Lautenschlager (1940), and, in 1944, the foreign press party (Harrison Forman, Gunther Stein, Israel Epstein and others) and the US Army Observation Group at Yan'an (John S. Service, John P. Davies, David Barrett, Raymond Ludden and others). Four sections cover the CCP's independence from Moscow, its "own" communism, its wartime economic experiments as a "testing ground for a new China", and Yan'an as a "miniature of China's future". A short conclusion traces the policy consequences. Lu's central claim is that the observers' changing qualifiers for the party, from Carlson's "so-called" communists to "Yan'an's", "their own" and finally "fitting" communists, reflect the CCP's continuing effort to adapt Marxism to Chinese conditions. The evidence includes interviews with Mao Zedong, Zhu De and Zhou Enlai, Service's report finding no sign of Soviet remote control, and Stein's view that nationalism outweighed doctrine in the party's programme. Lu also examines the policies of rent and interest reduction, encouragement of private capital, and cooperatives and labour-exchange teams built on private holdings. The article contrasts these with Marx's and Lenin's cooperative theories, arguing they did not fit China's unfinished revolution and peasant base. Lu concludes that the observers' reports improved the CCP's image and for a time encouraged US-CCP military cooperation, with Carlson and Barrett urging closer ties and arms aid. After the failure of Hurley's mediation and Stilwell's recall in late 1944, US policy turned sharply rightward. In Lu's account, decision-makers dismissed the reports as biased because of ideological fixation, which reflected a two-sided American China policy. Read the original if you study US-CCP relations in the War of Resistance, or want a Chinese scholarly account of how American eyewitnesses framed the "Sinification of Marxism".

Capital's critique of capitalist civilisation and its world-historical significance 《资本论》对资本文明的批判及世界历史意义 Lu Shaochen Lu Shaochen asks what kind of critique Marx's Capital offers of what the author calls "capital civilisation" (capitalist civilisation), and where it points historically. Lu argues that the work is a political-philosophical critique, not only a critique of capitalist exploitation. It exposes the political preconditions of capitalist civilisation and shows the path from political emancipation to human emancipation, meaning the all-round development of the person. The piece appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023. The article is a short essay that sets Marx's argument beside modern Western political thought and contemporary philosophy. It draws on Fergusson, Machiavelli, Hobbes, Hegel, Kant, Tönnies, Weber, Tocqueville and Adam Smith, and on later writers such as Byung-Chul Han, Dorothea Dörmer (Dallmayr-style commentary on subjectivity), Robert Bellah and Habermas. It moves from the totality of the system, through individualism and the loss of community, to poverty and the world system, and ends with Marx's alternative. Lu's first move is that capitalist civilisation is a total system, not the sum of individual choices, so criticism and transcendence must also be total. Following Marx and Han, Lu describes a rule without a ruler in which competition imposes capital's laws on everyone. Individuals are reduced to egoistic, mutually opposed bearers of exchange relations, and the ideal of self-realisation becomes compulsive "self-exploitation". Lu says this produces narcissism, nihilism and, in the long run, populism, fundamentalism and renewed conflict between nation-states. Lu argues that only Marx showed absolute individualism to be a result of generalised exchange rather than its starting point. A second move is that the logic of reification becomes power, appearing as polarisation of wealth and poverty within states and as a centre–periphery order globally. Against Hegel's reliance on colonial expansion, Lu says Marx proposed active state governance. Through education it would steer people living by direct labour towards work in invention and artistic creation, and shift production from labour time to free time. Lu adds that this requires treating political economy first as political critique and seeing individuals as community members. Lu concludes that humanity now calls for a new freedom based on community and all-round development, achieved through long-term state governance that gives human relations back to people. Lu also links this to the significance of the Chinese traditional culture of family-and-country feeling and responsibility. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar reads Capital as political philosophy and ties it to Chinese cultural themes.

Marx's historical thinking and its contemporary perspective 马克思的历史性思想及其当代透视 Yuan Bei This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (9 November 2023), asks what is distinctive about Marx's way of thinking historically. Yuan Bei argues that Marx's break with speculative philosophy lay not simply in starting from social reality, but in analysing that reality historically. The piece also asks how Marx's emphasis on objective laws can be reconciled with contingency and the possibility of emancipatory politics. The article begins with the materialist conception of history of 1845 and the claim in The German Ideology that there is only one science, the science of history. It then contrasts Marx with classical political economy and Hegel, and turns to later disputes: the Second International's economic determinism, the stress on subjectivity from Lukács to the Frankfurt School, and Louis Althusser's "materialism of the encounter", read with Badiou and Žižek on the "event". Yuan argues that for Marx the social world is a product of industry and social conditions, not something given from the beginning. Historical analysis therefore does two things. It affirms objective laws, grounded in the production and reproduction of material life, and it attends to concrete historical conjunctures, in which elements meet in relations of forces. Classical political economy, in Yuan's account, was "supra-historical" because it treated capitalist production and economic categories as natural and eternal, whereas Marx saw capital as a process and its categories as historical and transitory. Hegel, by contrast, focused on the self-knowledge of absolute spirit, while Marx focused on real individuals engaged in material production, with the aim of breaking the rule of capital and achieving the liberation of the proletariat and humanity. Yuan holds that Althusser's emphasis on contingency is not groundless, since Marx himself, in his 1871 letter to Kugelmann, said that chance affects the acceleration and delay of development. Yuan concludes that emancipatory politics requires recognising both historical necessity and the contingent event. Drawing on Badiou's two kinds of temporality, Yuan suggests that revolutionary possibility depends on whether individuals can seize fleeting situations opened by an event. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how Marx's historical method is positioned against Hegel, classical political economy and Althusser's aleatory materialism.

The technological (Technologie) import of machinery and large-scale industry in Capital 《资本论》机器大工业的工艺学意旨 Li Jiayi Li Jiayi asks how Marxist political philosophy can grasp the political essence of modern capitalism in an age of highly developed machine industry. The short piece, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, answers that the route is Marx's 'technology' (工艺学, the study of how production is carried out) in Capital. Li contends that this approach exposes how bourgeois power relations are built into both material and mental production, 'from below'. The article has three parts. The first distinguishes the general and the specific meanings of technology in Capital: the general study of humanity's active relation to nature, and the study of the direct production process under a particular social form. The second examines how machine industry builds the modern logic of technology, through the replacement of the human organism by an objective productive organism and through the principle of decomposition and synthesis. The third turns to political philosophy and to how technology works as a form of power. Li argues that under capitalism the machine becomes capital and makes the labour process subordinate to it. Machinery creates no value but yields surplus value by shortening the part of the working day the worker spends for themselves. Workers, owning nothing but their labour-power, must be merged into the machine system, so that, in Marx's words, the means of production use the worker. Li lists four features of this domination by things: capitalist ownership of means of production and products; the machine as a screen that makes capital's power less visible; the machine as objectified general intellect and the separation of manual from mental labour; and a shift of workers' struggle from direct to indirect confrontation. Technology then reproduces itself as management science, culture and ideology. Li, drawing on Foucault, reads management technology as a 'political anatomy' and 'mechanics of power' that disciplines bodies and measures even leisure time. Li concludes that analysing the labour process behind the value-expansion process reveals the historical character of capitalist power. Because modern industry's technical basis is revolutionary, Li holds, it must come into irreconcilable conflict with the logic of capital's valorisation and eventually undermine it. Compared with deriving power relations from political economy, Li claims, the technological route better reveals the micro-mechanisms of capitalist power. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language reading of Marx's technology concept as a bridge between political economy and political philosophy, including its use of Foucault.

The three dimensions of Marx's critique of political economy 马克思政治经济学批判的三重维度 Liu Yiwen Liu Yiwen asks in what sense Marx's critique of political economy is a critical theory, and answers that it is at bottom a critique of justice. Drawing on Gould's remark that in this critique Marx revealed the ethical substance of his theory of justice, Liu argues that the critique carries Marx's thinking on justice. It exposes a substantive injustice behind capitalism's apparent justice in exchange and distribution. The article takes up the debate on "Marx and justice" that began in the 1970s, including the "Tucker–Wood thesis". It works through three dimensions of Marx's critique in turn: alienation, exploitation and crisis. For each, it asks why the phenomenon should count as a cause of capitalism's injustice, since Liu says no self-evident link joins them. The text appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 21 December 2023. On alienation, Liu reads it as capital's structural, self-perpetuating domination over labour, a relation that labour itself produces. Free and equal exchange hides this relation, and it generates fetishism that naturalises historical social relations. It also exposes a contradiction between the spheres of exchange and production, since capitalism violates the justice standard it set for itself. Exploitation is treated as the other side of the same process: capital appropriates the product of labour without payment, in a coercive and permanent way. For crisis, Liu argues that treating it as a purely economic matter hides its link to the system. The injustice lies in the logic of capital that causes, conceals and tries to sustain comprehensive social breakdown, not in the breakdown itself. Following Marx, crises end only with capitalism's collapse from within and proletarian revolution from outside. Liu concludes that alienation, exploitation and crisis are each grounds for Marx's justice critique, but the final target is the operating logic of the capitalist system. In Liu's account, the shift from the laws of commodity production to the laws of capitalist appropriation serves unlimited capital accumulation and the system's perpetuation. The critique is therefore a distinctive holistic, comprehensive and developmental theory. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how Marx's critique of political economy can be read as a theory of justice.

Capital's critique of Locke's labour theory of property 《资本论》对洛克劳动所有权理论的批判 Cheng Tong Cheng Tong asks what exactly Marx criticised in John Locke's theory that labour gives rise to ownership. The article takes issue with a widely held scholarly view that Marx simply pointed to a 'separation of ownership and labour' in capitalism, which supposedly made Locke's 'identity of ownership and labour' obsolete. Cheng argues instead that Marx's real objection is that this identity still holds formally under capitalism but has changed its content, so that it now serves the capitalist rather than the labourer. The piece opens with Locke's Two Treatises of Government and the 'identity of ownership and labour' at the core of his argument. It then reviews the 'separation' reading, citing the Japanese scholar Mochizuki Seiji and Marx's well-known formulations in the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts and in the German editions of Capital, Volume I. The article then turns to textual evidence from the French edition and to Marx's own concepts in Capital and its manuscripts. Cheng's first move is philological. The famous passage on the separation of ownership and labour was deleted from the French edition of Capital, Volume I, the last version Marx revised, and replaced by a sentence about the disappearance of the appearance of equivalent exchange. Marx's lists of revisions and his annotated copy of the second German edition confirm that later editions were to follow the French text. 'Separation of labour and product' became 'separation of product and producer'. Cheng reads this as Marx recognising that the earlier wording was imprecise or erroneous. The second move is conceptual. Marx distinguishes the 'bearer' of labour from its 'owner'. Once the capitalist buys labour-power, its use-value, which is labour itself, belongs to the capitalist, and so does the product. Ownership and labour are therefore identical in the capitalist, which entails the separation of ownership from the labourer. Cheng concludes that Locke's error lies not in ignoring a separation but in applying a pre-capitalist, small-producer identity to capitalist property, thereby defending it with an ideology of labour-based property. Read the original if you want a close textual argument, drawn from the Marx manuscripts and the French edition, on how Marx answered Locke.

Showing theoretical value through the tempering of social critique Developments in foreign Marxism in 2022 在社会批判的淬炼中展现理论价值 Jia Keqing This annual survey by Jia Keqing reviews the main research of 2022 by Marxist and Marxist-influenced scholars outside China. Jia defines foreign Marxism as a diverse body of thought with no unified system. In Jia's account it is realistic, critical, open and scholarly, and it persists because the problems of capitalism remain unresolved. The review is organised by school and theme: the Frankfurt School from the first to the fourth generation; eco-Marxism; post-Marxism; critiques of digital capitalism; and a final section on other fields. These include progressive taxation, market socialism, class analysis, feminist political economy and racial capitalism. Each section reports the work of named scholars at Western universities. Among the positions Jia reports, Tom Rockmore argues that the first two generations of critical theorists neglected the economic dimension Marx stressed. Werner Bonefeld and Chris O. Kane read Adorno's negative dialectics as a basis for the critique of political economy, and Nancy Fraser calls contemporary capitalism "cannibal" capitalism. John Bellamy Foster ties eco-Marxism to ecological revolution and to ecological civilization, and he regards China's ecological civilization as a gift to the world. On post-Marxism, Jia presents Laclau and Mouffe's discourse theory as still relevant to politics. Scholars of the digital economy, including Christian Fuchs, Michael Kwet and James Muldoon, are reported as treating digital capitalism as a threat to democracy and a form of digital colonialism. Jia concludes that these scholars combine academic rigour with concern for real problems, which keeps the field alive. Jia also finds that the Frankfurt School's critical and revolutionary edge is fading, and that many digital critiques stop at the technology without addressing capitalist relations of production. In Jia's view, foreign Marxism is often absorbed by mainstream Western ideology and so helps stabilise the existing order, which gives it a dual role. Jia adds that post-Marxism, though a challenge, can act as a whetstone for Marxism. Read the original if you want a broad, name-by-name map of 2022 Western Marxist scholarship as seen from the Chinese academy.

New trends in the development of world socialism amid great changes 大变局下世界社会主义发展新趋势 Chen Mingfan Chen Mingfan asks where world socialism is heading in what the article calls the great changes unseen in a century. The author's answer is that capitalism has passed its "golden age" and is declining, while socialism is moving towards revival. Chen holds that this prospect should give confidence in socialism's future, while the path will remain arduous and winding. The article first traces the history of the socialist movement through successive world upheavals. It runs from the utopian socialists and the Communist Manifesto, through the Paris Commune, the First World War and the October Revolution, to the Chinese revolution of 1949 and the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. It then surveys the movement's divisions: communist parties in power (China, Vietnam, Cuba, the DPRK, Laos), communist and left forces in capitalist and developing countries including Latin America, democratic socialism, and the "national socialism" of some post-colonial states. Chen's central claim is that two irreversible factors are pushing the movement towards revival: capitalism's decline and China's development. On the first, the author cites the financial crisis, the pandemic, political paralysis in the United States and mass protest, and judges that these open a rare opportunity. Drawing on Lenin's conditions for a revolutionary situation, Chen adds that ruling classes still hold strong state machinery and proletarian parties are immature, so the movement faces a long period of tempering. On the second, the author presents the Communist Party of China as the mainstay of world socialism. Chen points to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Party's self-reform, whole-process people's democracy, Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Chen contrasts the democracy with Western electoral politics and cites foreign communists' praise for China's experience. Democratic socialism is described as having departed from socialism and become reformed capitalism. Chen concludes that the Party bears a "two rejuvenations" task: achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and leading world socialism out of its trough. Building China into a leading modern socialist power by mid-century is said to have an immeasurable influence on the movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how Party-aligned scholarship periodises world socialism and ranks its currents, with China as the movement's centre.

The ideological character of Western party-system theory 西方政党制度理论的意识形态特性研究 Zhang Fei'an Zhang Fei'an takes up a question that, in the author's view, existing scholarship on China's new-type party system has neglected: not what is new about it, but what is 'old' about the Western party system and why it must be transcended. The article argues that Western party-system theory is not value-neutral science. It is an ideology dressed as science, built on a typology of liberal democracy, which defends the legitimacy of Western capitalist political institutions and cannot accept the legitimacy or longevity of Communist Party rule in China. The article has four parts. It first traces the rise of the theory to Cold War social science in the United States. It then examines how party-system theory became tied to liberal-democratic discursive hegemony. A third part analyses the 'competitiveness' standard through two branches of the theory, typology (Duverger, Blondel, Dahl, Rokkan, Sartori, Mair) and the study of causes (Duverger's law, Lipset and Rokkan's social-cleavage theory). A short conclusion draws out the implications for China. Zhang's central claim is that party-system theory took off in the mid-twentieth century as a deliberate piece of 'conceptual politics'. Drawing on Schumpeter's procedural definition of democracy, and on Schattschneider and Sartori, US scholars equated democracy with competitive elections. This turned the contest between capitalism and socialism into one between liberal democracy and totalitarianism, so that one-party systems were excluded from the concept of a party system altogether. Using the Marx–Engels account of ideology in The German Ideology, Zhang reads this as the ruling class presenting its particular interests as universal. The same competitive premise, the author argues, runs through every branch of the theory: definitions reject non-competitive systems, typologies do not count non-competing parties, and accounts of origins never study non-Western systems. Zhang adds that these systems are treated only as objects of 'transition' studies. Zhang concludes that, on this theory, the function, rationality and advantages of China's system of multiparty cooperation and political consultation cannot be understood. The article says that cooperation among China's parties is ignored because Western theory counts only competing parties. Following historical materialism, the author ties the competitive and divisive character of Western party systems to private ownership of the means of production. Zhang calls for greater theoretical self-awareness in building a Chinese party theory and in defending China's discursive power in party studies. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western party-system theory, with a detailed survey of its typologies and causal theories, and an example of how the new-type party system is theorised in Chinese scholarship.

Taking the right path of modernization for a large country with an enormous population 走好人口规模巨大的大国现代化道路 Ouyang Yao Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization is modernization of a huge population, Ouyang argues that population scale is a defining feature of the Chinese path and the basic starting point for decision-making. The article contends that three tasks follow from this feature: promoting common prosperity, building a leading country in education, and driving growth mainly through domestic demand. The commentary is organised under three headings, one for each task. It draws on World Bank figures for 2021, national statistics on educational attainment, and Xi's remarks on China's market size and population. On common prosperity, Ouyang notes that China's roughly 1.41 billion people moving into modernity would, in the author's figures, raise the number of people in high-income countries by 1.28 times. The author proposes coordinated regional development and rural revitalization to address regional and urban–rural imbalances. On education, Ouyang argues that population size is an asset rather than a constraint. Having turned labour quantity into an advantage in early reform and opening up, China now needs a human-capital dividend, built through equalised basic education, vocational training, diversified higher education and lifelong learning. On demand, the author says the export-oriented model suited the period of low incomes, whereas rising incomes make a domestic-led model, a unified national market, secure industrial and supply chains and technological self-reliance the best choice. Ouyang concludes that these three priorities are the urgent requirements for realising Chinese modernization under conditions of huge population scale. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary links population size to policy priorities in distribution, education and domestic-demand-led growth.

The transformation of the Marxist view of history in the new era and its intellectual effects 新时代马克思主义历史观变革及其思想效应 Jin Xingyu Jin Xingyu takes up the many references to "history" in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and asks what view of history lies behind the achievements of the decade since 2012. The article argues that this view, built on dialectical and historical materialism, enriches and deepens the Marxist conception of history. It also claims that the view lays a cultural foundation for building China into a modern socialist country. The article is organised in three parts that follow the classic division of a theory into ontology, epistemology and methodology. The first part treats the ontology of history through four features: essence, process, driving force and form. The second treats the epistemology of history through five forms: historical time, position, mission, experience and spirit. The third treats historical methodology through five practices, from the "big view of history" to taking historical initiative in the world. Jin's core claim is that Xi Jinping's statements turn the Marxist view of history into a framework for understanding the Party's own record. On ontology, history is presented as a practical history centred on the mode of production. It is a comprehensive history spanning the histories of the Party, New China, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation. It is driven by the principal contradiction, which the 19th Party Congress (2017) redefined, and it is written by the people. On epistemology, the author places the Party at a "critical moment" between the first and second centenary goals. The third historical resolution (2021) draws ten lessons from the past century. On methodology, Jin links the big view of history to assessing the two periods before and after reform and opening up as continuous in essence. The author also links it to judging historical figures within their conditions and to opposing historical nihilism, which the article says aims to deny Marxism's guiding role and the Party's leadership. Jin concludes that the three theoretical dimensions form an organic whole within socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author says this view strengthens historical confidence and the authority of the Party Central Committee and its core leader. Jin calls on the Party to keep "historical clarity" and to take historical initiative in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Party theorists organise Xi-era statements on history into ontology, epistemology and methodology.

Consciously guiding all discipline inspection and supervision work with Xi Jinping's important thinking on the Party's self-reform 自觉用习近平总书记关于党的自我革命的重要思想统领纪检监察一切工作 Gong Tanghua This commentary, published in Study Times on 12 January 2024, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the Third Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI). Gong Tanghua, who heads the CCDI's supervision team at the State Council's SASAC, argues that discipline inspection and supervision bodies must bring their thinking and action into line with the speech. In the article's account, they must treat Xi's important thinking on the Party's self-reform as the guide for all their work. The article has three parts. The first interprets the content and significance of the thinking, which Gong calls the plenum's most important political outcome. The second turns to the strategy for a decisive and protracted anti-corruption struggle, and applies it to central state-owned enterprises. The third sets out requirements for building up discipline inspection and supervision cadres themselves. Gong presents the thinking as powerful in three ways: in the truth of its theory, in its practical guidance and in its spiritual appeal. It answers why, how and by what means the Party can reform itself, and forms the self-reform chapter of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For SASAC and the central enterprises, Gong would advance the “three no's” together: not daring to be corrupt, not being able to and not wanting to. Under the first, the article names key sectors (finance, energy, pharmaceuticals, infrastructure) and key links (mergers, personnel decisions, procurement, bidding, overseas investment). Under the second, it calls for institutional reform, case analysis and supervision of top leaders. Under the third, it proposes disciplinary education, warning-education bases and a rejection of the idea that central enterprises are special. Gong concludes that discipline inspection personnel must turn the blade inward and be models of self-reform. He asks them to lead in theoretical study, political loyalty, struggle and personal integrity, and to resist what the article calls corrupt Western values. He also proposes measures on selecting and rotating cadres and on talent pools. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party discipline official applies the Party's self-reform doctrine to the state-owned asset sector and to the supervisors themselves.

Pan-Africanism or Classical African Marxism? 泛非主义还是经典非洲马克思主义？ Ntongela Masilela This is a Chinese translation of an article by the South African historian and Marxist Ntongela Masilela. It asks how classical Pan-Africanism gave way to what Masilela calls Classical African Marxism. He argues that the latter emerged from the encounter between Pan-Africanism and classical Marxism, and that it became the living philosophy of the African revolution once Pan-Africanism had won its political goal and then failed. The article moves from late-nineteenth-century Pan-Africanism, a response to the 1885 Berlin Conference, to the 1960 independence wave and the 1960–61 Congo crisis. It treats C. L. R. James, George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah and W. E. B. Du Bois as the first generation to join Pan-Africanism with Marxism, and it discusses the historians Cheikh Anta Diop and Joseph Ki-Zerbo.
