Most of the text is given to Frantz Fanon and Amilcar Cabral, whom Masilela presents as the founders of the tradition, shaped by the Algerian and Guinea-Bissau revolutions. Masilela makes three main moves. First, he contrasts Classical African Marxism with Western Marxism. In his account the former is a product of victory, political and joined to practice, while the latter is a product of defeat, philosophical and aesthetic. He also criticises Perry Anderson's response to Martin Bernal's Black Athena. Second, he sets Fanon against Cabral. He says Fanon's view of the peasantry as the sole revolutionary class misread colonial society. In his reading, Cabral corrected this by treating the peasantry as a material force and the working class as the historical force. Third, he summarises Cabral's contributions: a theory of history in which the mode of production drives change, a class analysis of Guinea-Bissau, culture as a ground of resistance, and principles for the revolutionary party and revolutionary democracy. Masilela concludes that Classical African Marxism will lose its historical legitimacy once neo-colonialism is expelled from Africa, just as Pan-Africanism did after colonialism ended. He says its historical task is unfinished. Its open questions include the socialist direction of the 1970s revolutions, the form of African socialist democracy, the continent's political and economic unity, and the coming South African revolution. Read the original if you study African Marxism, Fanon and Cabral, or comparisons between Western Marxism and Third World revolutionary theory.

New developments in foreign eco-socialist research since the 2008 financial crisis 2008年金融危机以来国外生态社会主义研究新进展 Gao Ze Huan Qingzhi This is a literature review of foreign eco-socialist research over the decade and more since the 2008 financial crisis, published in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2023, no. 1). Gao and Huan argue that the crisis and the limited results of 'green capitalism' opened new room for eco-socialist theory. In their account, the field has since renewed its textual base, widened its theoretical schools and turned to concrete environmental problems. They present the survey as a first step to draw the attention of Chinese Marxist ecologists. The review has three main sections. The first covers new readings of Marx and Engels, centred on Kohei Saito, Camilla Royle, Paul Blackledge and John Bellamy Foster. The second covers five schools that critique capitalism ecologically and propose alternatives: world-systems Marxism, radical socio-ecological transformation, post-development theory, democratic eco-socialism and Gramscian political ecology. The third covers 'red-green' analysis of labour-environmental movements, climate change, food security, biodiversity and the Anthropocene. Gao and Huan describe Saito as using the MEGA2 edition and Marx's natural-science notebooks to reject the view of Marx as a 'Promethean' and to place the 'metabolic rift' at the centre of a late Marx's ecological critique. Among the schools, they single out Jason Moore's world-ecology, Ulrich Brand's critical political ecology, Latin American post-development thought, and the democratic eco-socialism of Michael Löwy and Hans Baer. The last of these rests on common ownership of the means of production and participatory democracy, and is partly a response to the shortcomings of Soviet-style socialism. They also report work on 'climate capitalism', on Vandana Shiva's defence of local agriculture against commodification, and on the Anthropocene and related terms such as the Capitalocene. The authors conclude that the field has entered a new stage, marked by continuity with the textual work of Foster and Burkett and by a markedly wider scope. They hold that a global, cross-disciplinary eco-socialist movement is needed and that China should stay open to experience from elsewhere while continuing to build a modern socialist country in which humanity and nature coexist in harmony, and to build ecological civilization with Chinese characteristics. They also warn that many foreign 'green left' scholars lack a Marxist theoretical and methodological basis and are limited by their own social systems, so their views should be treated with caution. Read the original if you want a map of recent Western and Latin American eco-Marxist and eco-socialist authors and schools, seen through a Chinese Marxist lens.

New changes and characteristics of contemporary capitalism 当代资本主义的新变化及特点 Tan Youzhi Tan Youzhi asks how contemporary capitalism has changed since the Second World War, and especially in the twenty-first century, and what those changes mean for its long-term fate. Citing Xi Jinping's call to study contemporary capitalism, the article argues that capitalism has gained new vitality from technological revolution while facing a rising tide of anti-globalisation. In Tan's reading, neither development alters its historical destiny of being replaced by socialism, though that replacement will be long and arduous. The article has two parts. The first, on 'new changes', takes technological revolution and the course of globalisation as the two main forces shaping contemporary capitalism. It reviews the first three technological revolutions, from steam to electricity to atomic energy and computing, and links each to a stage of capitalist development. It then turns to the fourth, digital and intelligent, revolution. The second part, on 'characteristics', discusses the limits of capitalism's adaptive capacity and the slow pace of its replacement. Tan argues that new technology has revived capitalism after the 2008 financial crisis by raising productivity and temporarily easing class conflict, citing Dan Schiller's notion of 'digital capitalism'. Globalisation, by contrast, has produced uneven gains, global problems and a backlash of unilateralism, populism and protectionism, which Tan says exposes the flaws of Western democracy. Drawing on Marx's 1859 Preface, Tan presents the 'two inevitables' (capitalism's demise and socialism's victory) as consistent with the 'two never wills' (no social formation perishes before its productive forces are exhausted). Capitalism still retains 'room for expansion'. But welfare and state intervention leave wage labour untouched, widen inequality, and sow new crises, and Tan describes capitalism as a 'dual' society, citing Michel Albert. Tan concludes that capitalism is in transition towards socialism and is accumulating its material basis, yet will not collapse suddenly. Analysts should combine the 'inevitability' of its demise with the 'long-term' nature of the process, and avoid blind optimism. Tan also says the West still holds the upper hand overall but that 'the West declines, the East rises', and that capitalist powers, above all the United States, shift crises onto others and warrant vigilance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese international-relations scholar uses Marx's 'two inevitables' and 'two never wills' to frame contemporary capitalism and its prospects.

The state, challenges and prospects of Nepal's communist movement in light of the 2022 general election 从2022年大选看尼泊尔共产主义运动的现状、挑战与前景 Yuan Qun Why did Nepal's two largest communist parties lose the 2022 general election, form a coalition and then break apart within months? Yuan Qun asks this question and what it means for the future of Nepal's communist movement. The article argues that the movement still has a strong base but faces fragmentation of the party system, infighting over office and foreign interference. In Yuan's view, its prospects depend on left unity and on balancing party identity against parliamentary transformation. The article opens with a chronological account. It covers the 2017 victory of the left alliance, the 2018 merger and 2021 court-ordered split of the Nepal Communist Party, and the 2022 local, provincial and federal results. In the House of Representatives the Nepali Congress took first place, the CPN-UML second and the CPN-Maoist Centre third. Yuan then describes the post-election bargaining. Prachanda broke with Deuba and allied with Oli, then left Oli's camp over the presidential election, and the UML withdrew from the government in February 2023. The second half analyses three challenges and then three aspects of the future outlook. Yuan identifies three challenges. The first is fragmentation: after 11 governments in 14 years, voters grew disillusioned, turnout fell to 61.85%, and new and regional parties gained seats, so the two communist parties' share of House seats fell to about 40%. The second is the pursuit of immediate interests, such as the prime ministership and presidency, which Yuan traces through repeated broken power-sharing deals since 2008. The third is outside intervention. The author describes India as treating communist-led governments as pro-China and as helping to undermine them, and the United States as using the Millennium Challenge Corporation compact and pressure for Western-style democracy to constrain China's influence. Yuan concludes that the movement remains Nepal's largest political force. Five communist parties together won 122 seats, and communists led eight of the 11 governments, so progress will be "tortuous", in a spiral rather than a straight line. Unity is the key, and Yuan cites the 2023 Socialist Front as a step in that direction. The author also warns, citing European social democracy and Western European communist parties, that diluting party character leads to marginalisation. Read the original if you want a China-based reading of Nepal's communist politics, with detailed electoral data and a timeline of coalition manoeuvres.

The Communist Party of Cuba's practice of strengthening ideological work 古巴共产党加强意识形态建设的实践 Liu Yumeng Liu Yumeng examines how the Communist Party of Cuba has strengthened its ideological work since its Eighth Congress in April 2021. The article argues that the Party treats ideological construction as a strategic task. In Liu's account, this response to a hostile international environment and to the difficulties of Cuba's "updating" of its socialist model has helped safeguard national security and social stability, and offers lessons for other socialist countries. The article has three parts. It first identifies three sources of ideological risk: US economic blockade combined with ideological pressure, worsened by the pandemic; domestic wavering of public sentiment; and the swing between left and right in Latin American politics. It then describes four sets of measures drawn from the Eighth Congress and the plenums of the Eighth Central Committee. Finally, it draws three lessons, supported by a review of ideological work from the 1959 revolution to the present. On the risks, Liu contends that the US pairs sanctions on medicines, food and energy with funded organisations and online campaigns aimed at young people, artists and journalists. Liu also points to a lag between ideas and economic reform, citing Raúl Castro's remark that outdated thinking is Cuba's biggest obstacle. On the response, the author reports four measures: improving Party leadership through a Programme for the transformation of political-ideological work; promoting Cuban culture and a legal culture; theoretical innovation that preserves the Marxist-Leninist, Martí and Fidel Castro foundations while renewing discourse; and work among youth through the Union of Young Communists. Liu draws three lessons for socialist states. Ideological work should be a strategic measure for consolidating socialism; its direction must remain Party leadership and the socialist system, as in the 1991 and 1997 congresses and the pledge against restoring capitalism; and its priorities must shift with circumstances, from moral education after 1959 to Marxist education in the "special period" and consensus-building during the "updating". The author presents Cuba's "battle of ideas" as a useful reference for China, which Liu says also faces ideological risks. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Cuban Party documents and speeches on ideology, and of what Chinese analysts draw from them.

The origins and evolution of Egyptian Marxist historiography in the twentieth century 20世纪埃及马克思主义史学的缘起与流变 Zhao Yueqing Zhao Yueqing takes up a field that, in the author's account, has received almost no attention in Chinese scholarship: Egyptian Marxist historiography. Chinese work has focused on Western and socialist-bloc cases or on the history of Egyptian communism, while foreign studies are said to lack systematic treatment and to show ideological bias. Drawing on Arabic sources and a historical-materialist method, Zhao argues that Egyptian Marxist historiography grew from Western socialist thought, classical Marxism and the Sinicization of Marxism. It developed distinctive theories, notably "dependency theory" and the "pseudo-Islam" thesis, that influenced global Marxist historiography. The article traces the subject from the nineteenth century to the end of the twentieth. It first covers theoretical sources: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi and Saint-Simonian ideas, Salama Musa and Fabian socialism, the translation of classics by Henri Curiel's movement, Rifaat al-Said, and the reception of Mao Zedong's writings and of Samir Amin. It then follows three periods: the early stage from the October Revolution to the 1952 revolution; the Nasser era; and the post-Nasser period of infitah (economic opening) under Sadat and Mubarak. A final section assesses the value of this historiography and its limits. Zhao's central claim is that each period shaped a different emphasis. Early historians used the left-wing press as their base and applied political economy to colonialism, with Fu'ad Mursi's 1949 study of capitalism and class struggle as the main example. Under Nasser, Zhao argues, historians merged Marxism with nationalism, adopted structural analysis, and professionalised through archives and institutions. After the 1970s, Amin's dependency theory enriched Marxist political economy, and Rifaat al-Said's "pseudo-Islam" thesis turned criticism towards religious extremism. Women historians such as Amina Shafiq also extended class analysis to gender. Zhao credits the tradition with building a Marxist vocabulary, a "history from below" focused on peasants and workers, and a broader range of fields. Zhao also identifies limits. Party competition after the return of multi-party politics, the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood and the tension between religion and atheism constrained the tradition. Some historians, Zhao says, overstated economic determinism and neglected non-class factors. Zhao concludes that Egyptian Marxist historiography reflected its cultural and social setting, and that examining its gains and lessons can help the study of Middle Eastern historiography. Read the original if you work on Marxist historiography, Middle East intellectual history or Chinese scholarly views of Marxism in the Arab world, and want a detailed survey of Egyptian thinkers and their Arabic-language works.

Reform and opening up and the founding and development of socialism with Chinese characteristics 改革开放与中国特色社会主义的开创和发展 Qin Gang Marking 45 years since the Party's decision to launch reform and opening up, Qin Gang asks how that policy and socialism with Chinese characteristics relate to each other. The article argues that the two form a single, integrated process: reform and opening up gave rise to socialism with Chinese characteristics and keeps driving its development, while the latter displays the achievements of reform. Qin holds that the policy's greatest historical contribution is precisely the founding and growth of this form of socialism. The article has three parts. The first sets out four ways reform and opening up contributed: it laid a foundation, opened space for innovation, gathered strength and supplied lasting momentum. The second describes innovative development in the new era under Xi Jinping, in five respects: faster pace, demonstrated superiority, governance effectiveness, contributions to the world and a demonstration effect. The third distils six lessons from experience. Qin's central reasoning is that freeing thought led to reform, and reform in turn moved socialism beyond rigid thinking and rigid institutions. The article credits two historic shifts, from a highly centralised planned economy to a socialist market economy and from a closed to an open country, with reshaping ownership and distribution structures. For the new era, it cites poverty alleviation, ecological protection, ethnic unity, the Belt and Road Initiative, whole-process people's democracy and Chinese modernization as evidence of governance capacity and wider influence. Qin also reports 2022 per capita GDP of 12,741 US dollars and a middle-income group of over 400 million. The six lessons are: theoretical innovation grounded in practice; independent exploration; putting people's rights and interests first; giving society stable expectations through phased goals and five-year plans; actively integrating national development into world development; and the Party's leading role. Qin presents the last as a distinctive strength, arguing that the Party represents the whole of society rather than any interest group. Qin also acknowledges remaining problems, such as entrenched interests and institutional defects, and calls for deeper reform and opening up. Read the original if you want an official-line overview of how Party theorists link reform and opening up to socialism with Chinese characteristics and to the new era.

A critique of erroneous views that negate the lofty ideal of communism ​否定共产主义远大理想的错误观点辨析 Shi Zhenping Shi Zhenping takes up a current of opinion that, in the author's account, belittles or rejects communism as the Party's lofty ideal. Opening with Xi Jinping's statements on the importance of communist conviction, Shi argues that such views amount to negating Marx's scientific prediction of the basic features of a future society. These views, Shi contends, are logically untenable and harmful to Marxism, the Party and socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article first describes the claims it opposes: that public ownership by society is an "empty abstraction", that planning was a "misjudgement", and that "classical" and "traditional" socialism are finished. It lists five harms of such claims, including undermining Marxism as a whole, the twentieth-century socialist path and the Party's leadership. It then rebuts three methods of argument in turn: equating the Soviet model with Marx's prediction, setting Marx's successors against the founders, and separating upholding Marx's view of socialism from developing it. The third rebuttal includes a close rereading of passages by Marx and Engels. Shi's central move is to distinguish actually existing socialism from the socialism Marx and Engels described, which Shi treats as two linked stages of one process. In Shi's reading, Marx's socialism, which he treats as synonymous with communism, presupposes fully developed productive forces, social ownership, no commodity relations, classes or state, and a worldwide scope. Existing socialism, with multiple ownership forms, markets and a state, is still a transitional stage, so it neither contradicts nor refutes the prediction. Shi then argues that Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping each deepened understanding of socialism without abandoning the founders' prediction. Finally, Shi maintains that Marx and Engels rejected detailed blueprints of the future, not the prediction of its basic features. Shi supports this with the 1843 letter to Ruge, Engels's 1893 "no final goal" interview, and the 1881 letter to Nieuwenhuis. The letter to Edward Pease is read as a refusal of a 600-word summary, not a retraction. Shi concludes that developing Marx's view of socialism must proceed from upholding the founders' prediction, and that dogmatism and "development" that discards the prediction are both mistaken. Quoting Engels, Shi urges readers to read authors "as they wrote" and not to find in them what is not there. Selective quotation, Shi warns, hides the founders' steadfastness and prepares the ground for rejecting the communist ideal. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how contemporary Chinese Marxist scholarship defends the classical prediction of communism through close reading of Marx and Engels's texts.

Beyond "labelling": re-examining Europe's new radical parties 超越“标签化”——重新审视欧洲新激进主义政党 Xiang Zuotao Gu Feng Xiang Zuotao and Gu Feng ask why European parties that traditional parties, mainstream media and many scholars brand "extreme", "xenophobic" or "populist" have won growing support since the 2008 financial crisis. Their thesis is that these labels reflect the bias of established forces. In the authors' account, the rise of the "new radical parties" results from the under-representation of lower- and middle-income groups in Western representative democracy. The article covers a broad set of parties, including Fidesz in Hungary, the National Rally and La France Insoumise in France, Brothers of Italy, the Sweden Democrats, Podemos, Syriza, ANO 2011 and Alternative for Germany. It has four parts: the labels applied by traditional parties, media and Western academics; the parties' platforms on domestic politics, economy, society and foreign relations, along with their records in office; the social and geographical profile of their voters; and a short conclusion. It draws on 2022 election results and polling from France, Italy, Sweden, the Czech Republic and Hungary. The authors argue first that the parties are an ideologically heterogeneous group. Their platforms are pragmatic: direct democracy and anti-corruption pledges, stronger state intervention in industry, agriculture and prices, welfare reform, restrictive positions on migration (with exceptions), and Euroscepticism of varying degrees. Their results in office are mixed. Hungary's Fidesz is presented as relatively successful, while Syriza and Italy's Five Star–League coalition are described as having been constrained. Second, they argue that the parties' supporters share a socio-economic position rather than a class ideology. These are blue-collar workers, farmers, the self-employed and the less educated, concentrated in economically declining regions and hurt by globalisation, austerity and the weakening of the nation-state. Their grievances are insecurity, with migrants seen as competitors, and the neglect of their material concerns by traditional parties. The authors conclude that the parties largely follow existing electoral rules and do not aim at fundamental institutional replacement, so the "extreme" label is misplaced. They also say Western critics fail to link these parties to the inherent contradictions of capitalism. While noting that some proposals are utopian or treat only symptoms, they present the parties as an alternative response for the "disappointed" middle and lower strata. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic reading of European radical-right and radical-left parties, with country-level voter data, that challenges Western framings of populism.

A model of combining general principles with historical conditions A theoretical interpretation of the prefaces to the Communist Manifesto 一般原理和历史条件相结合的典范 Jiang Tianlun This short commentary asks what the seven prefaces that Marx and Engels wrote for later editions of the Communist Manifesto show about how Marxism should be applied. Jiang Tianlun argues that, although the prefaces were written at different times, for different audiences and about different problems, together they exemplify combining the general and basic principles of Marxism with historical conditions and concrete realities. The author treats this combination as the methodological core running through them. The piece first sketches the Manifesto's drafting for the Communist League in 1848, its predecessor drafts by Engels and its four-part structure. It then argues that the prefaces re-elaborate scientific socialism in light of conditions in particular countries. Jiang organises the discussion around three themes: the terminology of communism versus socialism, the path of development for non-Western societies, and the relation between the unity of the world's proletarians and national independence. On terminology, Jiang follows Engels's explanation in the 1888 and 1890 prefaces. In 1847 socialism was a bourgeois movement and communism a working-class movement, so the Manifesto could not be called a socialist manifesto. Jiang adds that the choice also criticised the petty-bourgeois socialist currents of later decades, such as Lassalleanism, Proudhonism and Fabianism. On Russia, Jiang reads the 1882 Russian preface and Marx's reply to Vera Zasulich as refusing to apply the Western sequence of social formations mechanically. The rural commune could become a starting point for communist development if a Russian revolution signalled, and complemented, proletarian revolution in the West. On the Polish and Italian prefaces, Jiang reads Engels as holding that international proletarian cooperation requires each nation's independence, so that "Workers of the world, unite!" is tied to national industrial development and the socialist movement. Jiang concludes that Marx and Engels never set an abstract, rigid "law" or single path for historical development. In the author's account, their attention to each nation's circumstances and traditions, also seen in Engels's remarks on the English and German workers' movements, is a model of applying and innovating theory. Jiang also suggests that the communism–socialism distinction offers a methodological basis for understanding the unity of the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the lofty ideal of communism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how the Manifesto's prefaces are used to support the principle of integrating general theory with specific conditions.

The context and mechanism of social self-criticism 社会自我批判的语境与机制 Lü Jingmei Lü Jingmei takes up "social self-criticism" as a theoretical and practical problem, arguing that it must be approached through a historical-materialist reading of the classic texts. The article holds that notions such as social self-adjustment, self-development, self-improvement and self-transcendence all belong to this category and are in essence processes of society's self-movement. To grasp it systematically, Lü proposes to clarify its context, its concept and its mechanism. The piece is a short commentary in three parts: the context in which the topic arises, a conceptual clarification, and an analysis of mechanism. It draws chiefly on the Communist Manifesto, Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy and the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. It also looks at the transformations of capitalism since the nineteenth century and at socialism with Chinese characteristics. On context, Lü sets the Manifesto's optimistic judgement of the two inevitabilities beside the Preface's more cautious point that new relations of production never appear before their material conditions mature. Capitalism, in Lü's account, has moved from free competition to organised, welfare-state and neoliberal forms without resolving its basic contradiction. On concept, Lü argues that "social self-criticism" fits better than "social criticism" because society is both the object and the subject of critique, and finds the idea implicit in Marx's phrase "self-criticism of bourgeois society". It has a real form (the "criticism by weapons") and an ideal form (the "weapon of criticism"). On mechanism, Lü argues that it starts from concrete individuals whose critique spreads into a collective effect, and that it needs an objective condition (deep-rooted contradictions) and a subjective one (a class-conscious proletariat). It also needs a reference frame of social reality and social ideal, and a unity of retrospect, tracking of the present and prospect. Lü concludes by distinguishing three routes of social self-criticism according to the relation of individual, society and state: an individualist route starting from the atomised individual, a statist route starting from the nation-state, and a socialist route starting from concrete individuals in social relations. The author presents the third as going beyond the other two, since it holds that the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. Read the original if you want a concise conceptual framing of Marx's "self-criticism of bourgeois society" and its link to contemporary questions about capitalism and socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Locke's theory of property rights and its influence on Marx 洛克财产权理论对马克思的影响 Zhang Shoukui Marx read Locke's Two Treatises of Government and his economics closely, yet Zhang observes that Chinese Marxist theory has paid little attention to how Locke shaped Marx's social and political philosophy. The article argues that Locke is both an important source of that philosophy and the starting point from which Marx criticised and went beyond liberalism and classical political economy. Zhang takes property rights as a preliminary case, offered as an opening for further discussion. The piece, a short newspaper article, first sets out the essence of Locke's property theory, then turns to Marx's reflections on property, and finally to the ways Marx surpassed Locke. Hegel and Rousseau appear as intermediaries, and Adam Smith as the thinker who raised labour to a principle of political economy. Zhang draws on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and Theories of Surplus-Value. Zhang reads Locke's politics as a defence of property because property is the concrete form of freedom. Government is secondary and instrumental, and Locke grounds property both in natural law and in labour being "mixed" with nature. Marx inherited two things: labour as the justification of property, and the link between property and human freedom. He also saw Locke as a spokesman of the rising English bourgeoisie, progressive against feudal claims but conservative in presenting private property as natural and eternal. Marx's break comes through his distinction between objectified labour and alienated labour, and between "private property as labour" and "private property as capital". Zhang argues that Locke missed this distinction and so treated capitalist property as the product of objectified labour. For Marx, property in Locke's sense is property as capital. It springs from alienated labour, is therefore historical rather than natural, and has its own emergence and demise. Zhang concludes that Marx did not justify private property as the basis of individual freedom, as Locke did, but exposed the capital relation as an obstacle to self-realisation. Marx treated property as an economic and social question of human emancipation, not a matter of natural right or political emancipation. On this reading, property and ownership can be settled only through social and political revolution that abolishes private property as capital. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Locke, Hegel and Rousseau figure in Marx's early critique of property.

The scientific disclosure of the inherent laws of the innovative development of Marxism in the new era 新时代对马克思主义创新发展内在规律的科学揭示 Liu Jianjun Qiu Anqi Liu Jianjun and Qiu Anqi ask whether the innovative development of Marxism follows identifiable laws, and argue that it does. In their account, since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi Jinping and the Chinese communists around him have not only created Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era but also scientifically disclosed the basic laws governing how Marxism develops through innovation. The authors present this as a major new theoretical contribution and a research topic that scholars should take up. The article first justifies speaking of laws of 'innovative development' rather than of Marxism's development in general. It cites Marx, Engels and Lenin, then Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, before tracing Xi's statements from 2013 to 2023. From these the authors distil four basic laws, each treated in its own section: the dialectical unity of upholding fundamental principles and innovation; the cross-fusion of localization and adaptation to the times; the organic combination of differentiated and fusion development; and the benign interaction of theoretical and practical innovation. On the first law, the authors argue that 'upholding what is correct' (shouzheng) is the precondition of innovation, because of Marxism's truth content and its guiding role for Party and state; it means keeping its core, not its letter. They cite Bernstein's revisionism and Wang Ming's dogmatism as failures to hold the two together, and Lenin and Mao as models. On the second, localization (spatial) and adaptation to the times (temporal) are inseparable, and the Two Integrations are presented as the Chinese form with wider applicability. On the third, innovation either unfolds from within an existing proposition (for example from one integration to two) or fuses with other thought, as Xi puts it, in a 'chemical reaction' rather than a 'platter'. On the fourth, practice supplies the basis for theory and theory guides practice, provided practice does not violate theoretical logic and theory does not outrun practice. The authors conclude that these laws are embodied in the formation of Xi Jinping Thought, described as contemporary Chinese Marxism and Marxism of the twenty-first century. They call for upholding fundamentals without wavering and innovating without pause, for continuing the Two Integrations, and for advancing Chinese modernization so that theory and practice enrich each other. Read the original if you want a systematic statement, in the official Chinese framework, of how Party theorists conceptualise the rules of Marxist theoretical innovation under Xi.

Rebuilding the state's political system from society The 1871 Paris Commune in the eyes of the communards 从社会出发重构国家政制 Shan Chengxiu Was the Paris Commune a new kind of state, or only a municipal revolt, a local self-government experiment or an anarchist negation of the state? Shan Chengxiu notes that Marx and his followers read the Commune as the embryo of a proletarian state, while Versailles, moderate republicans and Bakuninists portrayed it as "non-state". To settle the dispute, the article reconstructs how the communards themselves understood their project. It argues that they were concerned with the state throughout and tried to rebuild its political system starting from society. The source base is the Commune's official gazette and the minutes of its sessions, supplemented by communards' later memoirs. The article first shows how the "commune" and the "republic" were equated in the Commune's own language. It then follows the changing powers of the Executive Commission up to the creation of the Committee of Public Safety, and the split of the Commune into majority and minority. It examines the Neo-Jacobin and Blanquist majority, and the Proudhonist minority, before a closing assessment. Shan contends that the communards sought a "social republic" rather than municipal autonomy. Its social dimension appears in secularising decrees, anti-despotic democracy (universal suffrage, recall, capped officials' pay, mass associations) and measures restraining capital. The vote of late April 1871 on a Committee of Public Safety exposed two conceptions: for the majority, dictatorship was a transitional means to promote democracy, whether in the Jacobin tradition or Blanqui's "Parisian dictatorship". For the Proudhonist minority, communal sovereignty could not be surrendered, and the state could only be a bottom-up federation resting on mutual associations. Because the Commune lasted only 72 days, Shan says neither programme went beyond Paris and the Commune showed only a potential for a new state form. In the conclusion, Shan holds that the communards' view contradicts both the municipalist reading and the anarchist reading. After defeat, survivors divided among radical republicans, Bakuninists, Blanquists and a small group turning to Marxism, while in the 1880s the labour movement stressed the Commune's socialist character. Shan sees in Commune democracy an early exploration of people's democracy: a composite democracy combining elections with consultation, whose dilemma over centralisation holds lessons for democratic centralism, and whose debate on dictatorship bears on the dictatorship of the proletariat. Read the original if you want a source-based study of the Commune's internal debates, with Chinese Marxist theory in view, on democracy, dictatorship and federalism.

The neo-fascist turn of neoliberal capitalism: roots and ways out 新自由资本主义的新法西斯主义转向：根源与出路 Lu Shaochen Lu asks why neoliberal capitalism has turned towards neo-fascism and what could stop it. Drawing on Western left scholarship, the article argues that the root lies in neoliberalism's absolutisation of market and money power. Lu holds that Western left remedies resting on morality or ethics cannot answer this, and that an answer requires a return to, and going beyond, Hegel through historical materialism. The article has three parts. The first describes the crisis of neoliberal capitalism through Foucault, Giroux, Jodi Dean, Byung-Chul Han, Wolin, Galbraith and others, and surveys scholars who link it to neo-fascism, including Cox, Foster, Robinson, Patnaik and Chomsky. The second reviews left proposals for alternatives: confrontation (Chomsky, Chibber), a renewed internationalism (Traverso, Alkin), a minimum programme (Foster), Hardt and Negri's commons, and moral or cultural renewal (Sweezy, Mason, Brown, Snyder). The third turns to Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Marx's critique of it, and the Chinese context. Lu reports that, in these accounts, neoliberalism hollows out social bonds and democracy, subordinates the state to finance, and leaves unemployed people to channel resentment into identity politics. Lu argues that most left alternatives share neoliberalism's premise that state intervention is inherently authoritarian, and that moral appeals therefore remain utopian. In Lu's reading, Hegel already saw that civil society generates poverty and a resentful rabble, which Allen Wood treats as the mechanism behind fascism. Hegel's reliance on desire and private property also seeded the problem. Lu holds that Marx's notions of the positive essence and positive existence of the human being, together with free time, point beyond this. Lu concludes that neo-fascism can be avoided only under the leadership of a Party and state that grasp historical necessity and draw on cultural resources that move people from their positive essence to their positive existence. Lu says this gives great significance to studying the spirit of Chinese civilisation, with its benevolence, people-centredness, good faith, justice, harmony and aspiration to great unity. Lu adds that Western left ethical proposals could be worth drawing on once a socialist revolution and communist party have prevailed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western left responses to neoliberalism and the far right, built around Hegel's theory of civil society.

The background, atheist content and contemporary relevance of "Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts" 《不怕鬼的故事》的编写背景、无神论蕴含及其现实镜鉴 Ren Baolong Chong Juan Ren Baolong and Chong Juan examine Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts (《不怕鬼的故事》), a collection of folk tales from classical Chinese notebook fiction that Mao Zedong personally decided to compile and helped edit in the early 1960s. They argue that understanding how the book came about and what atheist ideas it carries is useful for atheist propaganda and education in the new era, and for consolidating Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere. The article has three parts. It first sets out the domestic and international situation of the late 1950s and early 1960s and the book's editing and publication. It then reads the stories as atheist texts. It finally draws four practical lessons for present-day atheist education. On background, the authors describe Sino-Soviet disagreement, Western pressure and the persistence of feudal superstition at home. Mao took 'ghosts' as a metaphor for enemies and difficulties, and from 1959 told ghost stories on several occasions. The Institute of Literature of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, under He Qifang, compiled the book, and Mao followed the selection and the preface closely. It was published in 1961 with 70 items, and a revised edition with 66 followed that October. On content, the authors identify three themes: 'there are no ghosts in the world'; 'the more one fears ghosts, the more ghosts there are'; and contempt for ghosts strategically but respect for them tactically. They illustrate each with specific tales, such as Wang Jia, Song Dingbo and Chen Zaiheng. For the present, the authors call for four things. Atheist propaganda should be openly and boldly Marxist, and general Marxist education should not replace it. It should focus on Party cadres and young people. It should draw on atheist resources in traditional Chinese culture. Its language should be renewed through stories, short videos, memes and plain or online speech. They also call for flexible tactics that combine courage in strategy with care in each concrete case. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how this Mao-era text is now read as a model for atheist education, with plot summaries of the tales and a list of recommended methods.

The psychoanalytic critique of capitalism and its elements 资本主义的精神分析批判及其要素 Julien-François Gerber This is a Chinese translation (abridged) of an article by Julien-François Gerber, a scholar at the International Institute of Social Studies in The Hague. Gerber notes that psychoanalysis has rarely been applied systematically to economic questions. The article seeks to organise scattered psychoanalytic work on capitalism into a single field of critique and to encourage dialogue across schools. It asks what the psychic foundations of capitalism are, why it holds so many people, and how people unconsciously shape and sustain the economy. The article first sketches the history of the field. It starts with Freud's analogies between libido and money and the early analysts' studies of money and the 'anal character'. It then covers Edward Bernays and Ernest Dichter on the right, Otto Gross and Wilhelm Reich on the radical left, and the post-war work of the Frankfurt School, the Tavistock Institute and French post-structuralism. Finally it covers Lacanian and Jungian critiques since the 1980s. The main part offers a typology of four currents, each symbolised by a mythic figure. Gerber's core move is this typology. Eros stands for repressed libido and resulting alienation (Reich, Marcuse, Deleuze and Guattari, Dejours, Rosa). Thanatos stands for compulsive repetition and the endless movement of desire. In the Lacanian account, capitalism exploits primordial loss and its superego now commands people to 'enjoy'. Ahriman stands for hedonistic will to power, centred on money and technology (Dufour, Harsch, Lietaer). Lucifer stands for narcissistic, rationalising arrogance, seen in Weisskopf's study of neoclassical economics and Fromm's 'monocerebral man'. Gerber adds that individuals both introject and project economic norms, which reinforces unjust systems. Gerber suggests that each current fits a different social group: workers, consumers, the wealthy, and managers and economists. He identifies tensions among them over whether the superego represses or commands enjoyment, over whether alienation is universal or historical, and over whether desire should be released or restrained. He holds that the schools are not irreconcilable and calls for more dialogue, for attention to class, gender, race and non-Western contexts (Fanon, Nandy), and for use of under-exploited thinkers such as Klein and Winnicott. He argues that psychoanalysis can inform post-capitalist politics only alongside wider political, economic and ecological change. Read the original if you work on psychoanalysis and Marxism, Freudo-Marxism or Lacanian critiques of capitalism and want a mapped overview of the literature.

Basic experiences, main lessons and contemporary implications of a century of the communist movement in the United States 百年来美国共产主义运动的基本经验、主要教训及其当代启示 Li Dongming Li Dongming asks what a century of the communist movement in the United States, centred on the Communist Party USA (CPUSA, founded in 1919), can teach the present-day world socialist movement. The article argues that the movement's survival inside the heartland of capitalism rests on a few durable experiences, while its stagnation stems from identifiable errors, and that both yield lessons for communist parties in capitalist and socialist countries alike. The article has three parts. It first sets out four basic experiences, then five main lessons, and finally two contemporary implications. Li's evidence is drawn mainly from the party's internal history: the two liquidation crises (under Earl Browder in the 1940s and after 1956 under the Gates group), factional struggles involving William Z. Foster, Jay Lovestone, Gus Hall and others, and the party's constitutions through to the 2014 revision. On experience, Li credits the party with upholding Party leadership, holding firm to socialist and communist conviction, defending Marxism-Leninism against revisionism, and standing up to fight at critical moments. On lessons, Li identifies "Left" sectarianism, dogmatism and dependence on Moscow; overestimating the radicalism of the American working class; recurrent factional splits that weakened the organisation; a failure to understand American capitalism's capacity for self-adjustment and its cultural achievements; and a mishandled balance between democracy and centralism, including Hall's long tenure, an ageing membership and loose discipline in the 2014 constitution. Li draws two implications. First, communists must distinguish the historical trend (the "two inevitables" of capitalism's replacement) from the actual situation, bearing in mind Marx's "two never" qualifications, and so avoid rash strategies. Second, Marxism must be applied creatively to national conditions without dogmatism and without diluting it in the name of localisation or American "exceptionalism". Li also cites Xi Jinping to argue that parties must not copy others' experience and must follow their own independent path. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of CPUSA history and the lessons it draws for the world socialist movement.

Lenin's theory of the new-type proletarian party and its contemporary value 列宁的新型无产阶级政党理论及其当代价值 Yuan Xiuli Ma Zhangxu Yuan and Ma ask what Lenin's theory of the new-type proletarian party consists of and why it still matters. They argue that the theory, developed against Bernstein's revisionism and Russian 'Economism', remains a basic principle and scientific guide for proletarian parties today. In their account, whether a socialist country correctly assesses and keeps to this theory, and to the party's leadership, determines its future. The article has three parts. The first sets out why Lenin judged a new-type party necessary and urgent in Russia around 1900. The second reconstructs the theory itself, in six elements: Marxism as guiding ideology, an organisation of revolutionaries, the core role of leaders and a leading group, the 'inculcation' of socialist consciousness, the party programme, and the party rules with democratic centralism. The third turns to Xi Jinping's statements on party-building and to the Soviet collapse. In the authors' reading, Lenin answered a workers' movement that was growing but led by a disorganised, 'amateurish' party whose Economist wing separated economic from political struggle and celebrated spontaneity. Lenin held that workers alone produce only trade-union consciousness, so socialist consciousness must be brought from outside. He also held that the party must be a disciplined vanguard distinct from the whole class, and that centralism, binding rules and discipline were needed against federalism and autonomy. For the present, the authors argue that upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership is a major principle of a mature Marxist governing party. They reject the view that these principles suit only a revolutionary party seeking power, citing Xi's statement that the Communist Party of China is both a Marxist governing party and a Marxist revolutionary party. The authors take Gorbachev's reforms as a negative case. In their account, 'unrestricted openness' and radical democratisation, together with the amendment of Article 6 of the Soviet constitution in 1990, ended the party's leading position and led to the party's collapse and the Soviet Union's disintegration. They conclude that the Communist Party of China must keep to Marxist-Leninist party-building principles, defend its leadership and long-term governing position, and resist calls for multiparty or Western-style systems. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholarly article uses Lenin's party theory and the Soviet case to justify centralised Party leadership today.

The practical logic of building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation 建设中华民族现代文明的实践逻辑 Zhang Ming Guo Guangyin This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in January 2024, asks how the new cultural mission of building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation is to be carried out in practice. Zhang and Guo argue that the task follows from the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and must be guided by Xi Jinping's thinking on culture, which they present as the cultural component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article is organised around four elements: the leading force, the spiritual foundation, the fundamental method and the path of advance. Each is introduced with extensive quotation from Xi Jinping's speeches and addressed in turn: Party leadership over culture, cultural confidence, the Second Integration, and the unity of local rootedness with openness to the world. The authors first argue that culture is part of the superstructure and carries a class position, so the Party's leadership over cultural work and Marxism's guiding role in ideology secure the right direction. In their reading, the "modern" in the new civilization comes from Marxism's scientific truth, which "activates" traditional civilization. They then treat the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, as the core method. It is described as a chemical reaction rather than a mechanical joining: Marxism gives tradition a modern form, and Chinese wisdom makes Marxism "Chinese". The authors say this process rebuilds the cultural subjectivity damaged in the modern era. Finally, they hold that Chinese modernization supplies the practical ground, and that the civilization must be both national and global, overcoming the polarised debate between wholesale Westernization and conservative revivalism. The authors conclude that building the new civilization requires unwavering Party leadership, cultural confidence and independence in theory, deepening the Second Integration, and combining "upholding the ancestors" with "speaking new words". They add that this means drawing on the achievements of all human civilizations while creating a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-aligned commentary in early 2024 framed Xi's cultural thought and the Second Integration.

Two decades of Japanese reflection on the Aum Shinrikyo affair 二十余年来日本社会对奥姆真理教事件的反思 Huang Lüping Huang surveys how Japanese society has reflected on the Aum Shinrikyo affair over more than twenty years. The cult carried out the March 1995 sarin attack on the Tokyo subway, which, according to the article, killed 14 people and injured about 6,300. Its founder Asahara Shoko and twelve others were executed in July 2018. Huang's thesis is that the affair resulted from several interacting factors, that Japan's lack of religious regulation was the fundamental one, and that Japan's experience offers lessons for China's work against cults. The article is a review of scholarship, journalism, memoirs by former members and court reporting. Authors cited include Shimazono Susumu, Shimada Hiromi, Ota Toshihiro, Egawa Shoko, Murakami Haruki and the former member Hayashi Ikuo. It is organised in three parts: the cult's defining features, the causes of its rise, and proposed countermeasures. A concluding section draws implications for China. Huang reports that the literature identifies three features: a doctrine pieced together from existing religions and bent to justify crime, a hierarchy with personal worship and mind control, and a pursuit of money and political power. Scholars dispute the "mind control" thesis. The article groups the proposed causes into five: Japan's social system, lax religious oversight, a social current seeking spirituality, sensationalist media coverage, and scholars' mistaken endorsements. In Huang's own ranking, the first and fourth are environmental, media and scholarly errors are incidental, and absent regulation is the fundamental cause. The 1951 Religious Corporations Act limited oversight. Revisions after 1995 and the 2022 assassination of Abe Shinzo, in Huang's account, show that governance remains weak. On countermeasures, Huang describes individual vigilance, critical thinking, neutral media, university education, and exit counselling by the Japanese association for leaving cults. Huang judges these efforts useful but limited, since individuals bear the risks of religious freedom and civic groups lack unified leadership. For China, the author calls for deeper study of online cults, vigilance against commercialised "mind-body-spirit" courses, mobilising social forces, and above all strong regulation. Huang says Japan's experience confirms the correctness of China's anti-cult work. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source guide to Japanese Aum scholarship and to how Chinese anti-cult research draws on it.

Guiding the practice of reform and opening up in the new era with the grand view of history 以大历史观指导新时代改革开放实践 Xiong Daohong Cai Ziwei Xiong Daohong and Cai Ziwei ask how the grand view of history that Xi Jinping has urged the whole Party to adopt can be used to understand 45 years of reform and opening up and to guide its continuation. Their answer is that reform and opening up should be read within a wider frame of time and space, and that doing so strengthens historical consciousness and historical confidence. In their account it also supports a spirit of historical initiative in deepening reform and opening up in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out the foundations: historical materialism, the correct view of Party history, and the Central Committee's repeated summings-up of reform and opening up, from the 1981 historical resolution to Xi's 2018 speech marking 40 years. The second says that grasping the history means grasping its theme, its main thread, its position and its relation to the world. The third turns to practice in the new era. In the authors' account, the theme is upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, and the main thread is theoretical innovation, running from the truth-criterion debate through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They place reform and opening up within the "five histories" (Party, New China, socialism, the Chinese nation, and reform and opening up itself). The periods before and after 1978 are treated as a unified whole, not as opposites. For the new era the authors identify three features: continuity, as Chinese modernization is advanced and the people remain the subject of history while the country stays in the primary stage of socialism; particularity, because the principal contradiction has changed and reform now means harder institutional construction; and a worldwide dimension. The authors conclude that the experience of 45 years must be carried into current practice. They call for a firm grasp of historical trends and the world situation, a people-centred approach, and a more active attitude toward change and openness. They also call for explaining China to the world and promoting mutual learning among civilizations. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars apply the grand view of history to reform and opening up, and how that history is periodised and framed in official discourse.

The fascist culture of violence of neoliberalism and the way out 新自由主义的法西斯主义暴力文化和未来出路 Henry Giroux This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Canadian-American critical theorist Henry Giroux. It asks why cruelty and violence have become so visible and normalised in the contemporary United States. Giroux answers that the country has entered what he calls "neoliberal fascism": a new historical conjuncture in which neoliberalism, having lost its legitimacy, fuses with white supremacy, ultranationalism and a politics of disposability. The article moves through five parts: cruelty as a core feature of fascist politics and its long history in the US; the return of fascism's spectre and the absence of any systemic analysis; neoliberalism as a stage of "gangster capitalism"; the near-complete militarization of American society; and a conclusion on resistance. Giroux draws on Etienne Balibar, Stuart Hall, Karl Polanyi, Hayek, Friedman, Paul Mason, David Harvey and others. His examples include mass shootings, attacks on transgender children, cuts to social safety nets, the military budget and right-wing extremist killings. Giroux's central move is to read neoliberalism not as a break from fascism's heritage but as its enabling ground. In his account, a market ideology that treats society as nonexistent and freedom as market freedom strips away social responsibility and solidarity. Once it can no longer justify poverty and inequality, it turns to open racism and the dehumanization of people deemed surplus. He argues that the aestheticization of violence in media and entertainment normalises it and diverts attention from its systemic causes. Fragmented, issue-by-issue analysis by intellectuals and media, in his view, prevents people from seeing these connections. Giroux concludes that voting alone is insufficient. He calls for mass collective resistance and sustained uprisings, and for a broad anti-capitalist movement guided by socialist democratic principles. In his view, capitalism is the "laboratory of fascism", so resistance must begin from abolition rather than reform, and he rejects ideas of compassionate capitalism. He also urges rebuilding critical mass consciousness, a multiracial progressive movement and radical political education. Read the original if you want a Western critical-left account of American politics as neoliberal fascism, as selected for a Chinese foreign-Marxism audience.

The internal logic of atheistic thought in the Laozi 论《老子》无神思想的内在逻辑 Qi Xiangyang Zhang Rui Is the Laozi (Daodejing) a theistic or an atheistic text? Qi Xiangyang and Zhang Rui note that modern scholarship has split into three camps: those who read the Dao as idealist and therefore theistic, those who read it as materialist and therefore atheistic, and those who accept the Dao's materiality while conceding that the text still affirms ghosts and spirits. The authors argue that the first two camps apply a Western idealism-versus-materialism test that does not fit the text. They propose that the lower (empirical) and upper (metaphysical) realms must be read together, and that the text's dialectical outlook produces a systematic, if not absolute, atheism. The article is built in four parts. It first examines the lawlike character of the Laozi's dialectical outlook, then its removal of divine agency from the empirical world, then the atheisation of the realm of origins, and finally the text's place in the history of Chinese atheistic thought. Evidence comes from close readings of chapters of the received text, the Guodian bamboo slips and the Mawangdui silk manuscripts. It also draws on commentators from Wang Bi to Feng Youlan, Xu Fuguan and Guo Qiyong. The authors' central move is to argue that the Laozi's doctrine that the myriad things 'carry yin and embrace yang' is a cognition of objective regularity, even if it lacks the conditions and laws of modern dialectics. Because society is itself a unity of contradictions, rulers should practise non-action (wuwei) rather than rely on Heaven's mandate or spirits. The Laozi also explains natural phenomena, such as rain, through the union of heaven and earth. Ghosts and spirits survive only as marginal symbols without power over human affairs. The second move is that the Dao was abstracted from critical observation of the empirical world, from the bottom up. Unlike the traditional Heaven, with its will and personality, the Dao has no purpose, will or values, acts only through non-action, and is closer to a law. The authors judge it materialist in Marxist terms, while citing Liu Xiaogang's warning against retrospective reading. The authors conclude that earlier figures such as Zichan and Yan Ying produced only scattered atheistic remarks and kept Heaven as the supreme ground. The Laozi, they argue, replaced Heaven with the Dao and offered the most systematic atheistic worldview of the Spring and Autumn period. They add that later cosmogonies, including Taiyi Sheng Shui, the Huangdi Sijing and the Huainanzi, place spirits in a subordinate position within the generative sequence. Read the original if you study early Chinese philosophy, the history of Chinese atheism, or how Chinese scholars apply Marxist categories to classical texts.

A reader's guide to Heine's On the History of Religion and Philosophy in Germany 《论德国宗教和哲学的历史》导读 Qin Ming This is a reader's guide, published in the series on classic Marxist works, to Heinrich Heine's On the History of Religion and Philosophy in Germany (1834). Qin Ming starts from Engels's remark in Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy that Heine was the first to see the revolutionary content of Hegel's philosophy. Qin argues that the book helps readers understand Engels, and Marx's 1843 claim that the critique of religion is the premise of all critique. Qin notes that Heine wrote the book to explain German religion and philosophy to a French audience, so that they could read German literature. Qin calls it a short and simply organised work, a recognised entry point to Marxist theory, and a prime example of Heine's polemical writing, in which poetic language carries deep philosophical thought. The guide follows Heine's three parts in turn. The first covers Christianity, Catholicism, Luther's Reformation and the emergence of German philosophy. The second is a transitional survey of the philosophers from Descartes to Lessing. The third covers Kant through Hegel. Qin's central line is that, in Heine's account, philosophy emerged from the Reformation, freed itself from religion and became a revolutionary force. Qin reads Heine's Luther as the figure who gave reason the right to interpret scripture and so opened intellectual freedom. The second part is organised around the dispute between sensualism (materialism) and spiritualism (idealism), seen in Locke against Leibniz, Plato against Aristotle, and Spinoza's synthesis. In the third part Kant's Critique of Pure Reason is the blade that cut off the head of deism, and Fichte, Schelling and Hegel complete the line. Qin also sets Heine's thesis beside Engels: thought precedes action, and Germany's philosophical revolution will precede a political one, which when it comes will shock the world. Qin concludes that reading Heine clarifies how philosophy separated from religion and gained revolutionary force. In Qin's view it also illuminates the prehistory of Marxism and its historical continuity with earlier thought. Qin adds comments of their own, for example that Kant's obscure style in the first Critique may have been a defence against religious persecution. Read the original if you want a concise guide to Heine's text and to how Chinese Marxist scholarship links it to Engels and early Marx.

The theoretical content and contemporary value of Mao Zedong's thought on Party discipline building 毛泽东关于党的纪律建设思想的理论内涵及时代价值 Party Committee of the China Academy of Discipline Inspection and Supervision This article, a collective piece by the Party Committee of the China Academy of Discipline Inspection and Supervision, asks what Mao Zedong's thinking on Party discipline contains and what it offers the Party today. It argues that Mao applied Marxist principles to Chinese conditions and built a body of thought whose constant themes were strengthening Party leadership, enforcing political discipline and stressing ideological education. In the authors' view, this thought remains relevant to strengthening discipline in the new era. The article has three parts. The first traces the origins of Mao's thought: the proletarian party's nature and original mission, the adaptation of Marxist party-building theory to China, and practical needs in revolution and construction. The second sets out five elements of its content: the status of discipline, its core requirements, ideological education, institutions and rules, and enforcement. The third draws lessons for the present. On the authors' account, Mao defined discipline as the "guarantee for carrying out the line" and made the "four subordinations" (individual to organisation, minority to majority, lower level to higher level, the whole Party to the Central Committee) the most important discipline. The article treats ideological education as the "first-class task" for cultivating "conscious discipline", and cites Mao's insistence that discipline be codified in rules such as reporting systems and the Party committee system. It also presents the principle of "punishing past errors to prevent future ones and curing the sickness to save the patient" as pairing strictness with care, citing Mao's stress that Communists must meet a stricter standard than ordinary citizens. For the present, the authors call for guiding discipline building with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, centring on political discipline, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. They also call for treating Party spirit, Party style and Party discipline together, integrating discipline building into the wider system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and advancing the "three no-corruptions" (not daring, not being able, not wanting to be corrupt) as one whole. Read the original if you want an official Party-institutional account of how Mao's discipline thinking is linked to current anti-corruption and Party-building doctrine.

Lenin's critique of erroneous currents of thought on Russia's path of development 列宁在俄国发展道路问题上对错误思潮的批判 Wang Jinfen Between the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the question "where is Russia heading?" divided Russian intellectuals. Wang Jinfen argues that its core was whether economically and culturally backward Russia should take the capitalist or the socialist road, and how socialism and capitalism should be related. The article contends that Lenin met a series of mistaken currents with systematic criticism, and that his arguments still matter under new historical conditions. The article is organised chronologically around four targets. Before 1917 these were Narodnik (populist) "non-capitalist road" theory and the "legal Marxism" of Struve, which treated capitalism as eternal. After the October Revolution came the "historical catastrophe", "premature birth" and "economic determinism" charges of Plekhanov, Kautsky and Sukhanov. Last came the "petty-bourgeois reformism" and "petty-bourgeois revolutionism" aroused by the New Economic Policy (NEP). Wang's first move is that Lenin rejected both utopian bypassing of capitalism and its glorification. Narodnism, in Lenin's view, expressed small producers' interests and ignored that socialism presupposes developed productive forces and a proletariat. Legal Marxism concealed capitalism's contradictions, which Lenin said prove its historical transience. Hence Russia must both use capitalism and move beyond it. Second, against Plekhanov and others, Lenin accepted that Russia lacked the economic preconditions but denied this barred revolution. Wang reads this as "revolutionary dialectics": a country can seize power first and then create the cultural and material conditions for socialism, an approach different from Western modernization. Third, on the NEP, Lenin opposed those who abstractly set capitalism against socialism, arguing that in a small-peasant country state capitalism is an intermediate link. He also warned against the Change-of-Landmarks group, who expected the NEP to restore capitalism. Wang concludes that Lenin's central lesson is how a backward country that has chosen socialism treats capitalism. It must make use of capitalism while the Party keeps socialist direction. In Wang's reading, this depends on Communists learning to harness capital and delivering results that persuade the people the new order is better than the old. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Lenin's polemics on Russia's development path, along with the Chinese scholarly framing of their contemporary relevance.

Out of monotheistic religion, not yet out of monotheistic thinking Zhao Tingyang and Alain Le Pichon on the monotheistic mode of thought 走得出一神教，未走出一神论 Xiao Jianfei Liu Haichun This is a review essay on The Shadow of Monotheism: Correspondence between a Philosopher and an Anthropologist, a book of letters exchanged over about three years between the Chinese philosopher Zhao Tingyang and the French anthropologist Alain Le Pichon. Xiao and Liu present it as an experimental transcultural dialogue rather than a conventional exchange of ideas. They argue that the book's central insight is that the world has largely left monotheistic religion behind but has not left monotheism as a way of thinking, which persists in modern secular forms. The review first sets out the two correspondents' concerns: Le Pichon asks about China's place and role in the world, while Zhao asks how the world can escape the clash of civilizations and ideological conflict. It then covers three themes. The first is the contrast between China's direct relation of heaven and humanity and the European need for mediators between God and humans. The second is the shift from religious monotheism to modern monotheism built on absolute subjectivity. The third is the ontological problems this creates, ending with resources from Chinese thought for reordering the world. In the reviewers' account of Zhao's argument, modern Western thought replaced God with the sovereign, rational individual, whose self-justification mirrors Trinitarian theology and amounts to a "pseudo-religion" (the human rights doctrine is cited as an example). Combined with universalism, this mode of thinking is said to produce clashes of civilizations and ideological struggles. Its logical extension is the self-made human, gene editing and superintelligent AI, which could judge humans as worthless and create a "qualitative inequality" in the right to life. Against this Zhao proposes a relational ontology of co-existence, drawing on Confucian ren and a "New Tianxia System", and replaces innate human rights with "prepaid human rights", which are conditional on fulfilling one's duties to others. The reviewers conclude that monotheistic thinking is spreading through global language, law, markets, technical standards and popular culture. They note that Le Pichon's optimism about China's cultural influence is judged premature, and that Zhao's more sober view is closer to the facts. They add that transcultural exchange can break the "spell" of monotheism, but that belief runs deeper than reason, and that the ten letters amount to groundwork for mutual learning among civilizations. Read the original if you want a detailed guide to Zhao Tingyang's critique of Western subjectivity and monotheistic thinking, and to how Chinese scholars present the exchange with Le Pichon.

Why the Australian Labor Party won the 2022 election: causes and assessment 2022年澳大利亚工党胜选的原因及评析 Dong Muxi Dong Muxi asks why the Australian Labor Party (ALP), a centre-left force within the capitalist framework, returned to government in the May 2022 federal election after nine years in opposition, defeating the Liberal–National Coalition and installing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. The article argues that the win rested on changed external conditions and on internal adjustments by the party, but was a limited return that leaves Labor facing serious difficulties. The article has three parts. The first treats external factors since the 2008 financial crisis: widening inequality, a revival of class consciousness among wage earners, and the relative decline of the Coalition. The second covers internal factors: a leftward shift in policy, a drive to recruit members and widen intra-party democracy, and the reshaping of the leader's image. The third assesses the victory, setting out its limits and the party's future challenges, and a short conclusion places the result in the wider Western context. Dong contends that the crisis dissolved middle-class illusions among white-collar workers, moving the class structure from an 'olive' towards a 'dumbbell' shape and pushing voters leftward. Under Bill Shorten and Albanese, Labor moved away from the neoliberal 'Third Way' towards opposing economic inequality, a more inclusive Indigenous and multicultural policy, and stronger climate commitments. Dong then argues that the return is limited in three ways: Labor's primary vote (32.58%) was a record low and the win depended on preferential voting; its leftward turn is a pragmatic, limited adjustment that mainly criticises neoliberalism without a new social-democratic discourse; and its 77 of 151 seats leave it constrained by crossbenchers. Dong concludes that Labor's future depends on defining its position between class loyalty and a broader coalition, overcoming a theoretical bottleneck, and escaping policy constraints under a continuing capitalist structural crisis, with high public debt already forcing compromises such as retaining tax cuts for high earners. As a reformist party, Labor's capacity to break through remains, in Dong's view, highly uncertain, and the wider decline of Western social democracy has not been reversed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-oriented assessment of contemporary Australian social democracy, with figures on votes, seats and policy pledges.

A critical analysis of Messianic Marxism 对弥赛亚式马克思主义的批判性分析 Jia Jinyue Jia Jinyue examines "Messianic Marxism", the strand of thought that joins Marxism to messianic motifs and reads socialist revolution and communism as a quasi-religious story of redemption. The author argues that this reading misrepresents Marx. In Jia's account it is a variant of religious teleology that strips Marxism of its class character, its critical edge and its scientific standing. Only historical materialism, Jia holds, can show what the school is and why it fails. The article has three parts. The first sets out how Messianic Marxism arose in response to the crisis of postmodernity and what it claims. It draws on Karl Löwith, Walter Benjamin, Jacques Derrida and Wilhelm Dilthey, and the author also names Fredric Jameson and Arnold Toynbee as representatives. The second part tests the school's claims against Marx's early texts and its method of reading. The third part reinterprets the school from the standpoint of historical materialism and considers what this means for understanding Chinese modernization. Jia presents the school's claims as follows: Marx's "prehistory" and future history echo a Judaeo-Christian scheme, exploitation is treated as a moral "original sin", and the proletariat becomes a chosen people. The rebuttal rests on two moves. First, Marx's study of the Book of Isaiah under Bruno Bauer in 1839 took place in the heyday of biblical criticism, so Jia reads it as critical reflection rather than reception. Jia adds that Marx later attacked Christian-tinged socialism in The Eighteenth Brumaire and Moses Hess's messianic tendencies in The German Ideology. Second, the school is said to cut Marx's texts apart, treat materialism as speculation and ignore its scientific character. Jia concludes that it is religious teleology, lacks revolutionary practice, is detached from the people and material interests, and remains Eurocentric. Jia concludes that the school's ambiguous critique of capitalism amounts at most to a despairing struggle on the way back to Christian theology. Real solutions to the dilemmas of modernity lie in changing relations of production, not in waiting for redemption. The author adds that China's path differs because it has kept to the materialist conception of history instead of turning Marxism into religion, and that this offers another angle on Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Benjamin, Löwith and Derrida's theological readings of Marx, or if you are interested in how Chinese scholarship frames Marxism and religion.

Intelligent international communication of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind: significance, communication system and pathways 人类命运共同体理念的智能化国际传播：意义向度、传播体系与路径 Xu Yanling Taking up the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to build a community with a shared future for mankind and to strengthen international communication capacity, Xu asks how artificial intelligence can help spread this concept abroad. The article argues that intelligent communication, driven by big data, computing power and algorithms, can turn the concept from a "Chinese discourse" into a "world discourse". It holds that this requires both exploiting the technology's advantages and overcoming political and cultural obstacles. The article has five parts. It first describes how data, computing power and algorithms form a new platform for international communication. It then sets out the value dimensions of intelligent communication, namely discursive effectiveness, discursive confidence and discursive appeal, and the bottlenecks that limit it. The last two parts propose a communication system built on "warmth", "breadth" and "precision", and six practical choices. Xu draws repeatedly on Xi Jinping's statements on international communication. Xu's core argument is that AI-based translation, virtual reality, agenda-setting and metaverse narrative networks can lower cultural barriers and let the concept reach audiences through immersive, personalised, point-to-point delivery.
