Against this, the author identifies three constraints. Western capital and Western-dominated opinion are said to intensify profit-driven competition over communication rules. Nationalist approaches to AI governance are said to breed ideological bias against the concept. Differences in values are said to open a "discourse gap" and to keep developing countries "voiceless". Xu portrays the concept's call for a fairer international order as in direct conflict with Western monopoly capital's interests. Xu proposes six measures: adopting scene-based thinking, strengthening value guidance, building a dual-track mechanism of intelligent technology plus value concepts, using algorithms to identify friendly, neutral and hostile audiences for point-by-point communication, using blockchain to build trust, and raising intelligent communication to a strategic communication system with trained specialists and theoretical research. The author also warns against over-reliance on technology and calls for filtering ideas such as neoliberalism, populism and historical nihilism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links AI, algorithms and the metaverse to official goals for international discourse power.

Raising the level of rule of law in the administration of internet religious affairs 提高互联网宗教事务管理法治化水平研究 Zhang Xiaochen Zhang Xiaochen asks how the administration of religious affairs on the internet can be placed more firmly on a legal footing. The article argues that such administration bears directly on national security and social stability. In the author's account, China has built a policy framework and a growing body of law, but faces real gaps that call for a more complete legal system. The article has four parts. It first defines internet religious affairs administration as government administration of individuals and organisations engaged in online religious activity, and links it to political, ideological and social security. It then traces developments from the late 1990s, when the first temple-run website appeared, to the present. Next it sets out three challenges. Finally it offers proposals. Zhang's core move is to present policy and law as a "two-wheel drive". The policy side is a four-way framework of Party leadership, government administration, social coordination and religious self-discipline. The legal side runs from the National Security Law and Cybersecurity Law to the 2017 Regulations on Religious Affairs and the 2021 Measures for the Administration of Internet Religious Information Services. Zhang identifies three problems. Few laws address the topic: three laws, one administrative regulation and one departmental rule. Enforcement is harder because of low entry barriers for proselytising, algorithmic push and closed online groups. Public legal education is weak, so some platforms stay out of the matter and some believers misread the rules. Zhang proposes a dedicated regulation on internet religious affairs and rules on religious apps and algorithmic recommendation. Zhang also proposes provisions for foreigners' online religious activity, local regulations, and stronger enforcement, judicial and legal-education mechanisms. Zhang concludes that stronger rule of law is part of carrying out the Party's and state's major decisions on religious work, with Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee. The article adds that this guarantee needs trained legal personnel and technology such as big data and artificial intelligence. It acknowledges that further work could examine legal supervision and Party regulations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames internet religion as a security and legal-governance issue, with concrete examples of regulations and local measures.

The philosophical code of the creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture A historical-materialist perspective 中华优秀传统文化创造性转化和创新性发展的哲学密码 Zhang Ruitao Guo Binbin Zhang Ruitao and Guo Binbin take up the policy of the "creative transformation and innovative development" of excellent traditional Chinese culture, abbreviated as the "Two Creations". They note that existing scholarship mostly discusses its background, mechanisms, value and practical paths, and that its inner logic is under-examined. The authors ask what the Two Creations are, why they are "inevitable" and how to deepen them. Their answer is that, read through historical materialism, they follow necessarily from the relation between social being and social consciousness. The article has four parts. It first defines the philosophical meaning of the two terms and the logical relation between them. It then sets out the historical logic, covering practice, human agency and the Chinese Communists' changing attitudes to tradition from Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu to Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The third part gives the theoretical logic, and the fourth the practical logic: who carries it out, in what direction, and by what means. The authors treat "creative transformation" as the dialectical unity of cultural continuity and change, an enlarged reproduction of culture, and an interplay of content and form. "Innovative development" is the replacement of old cultural forms by new ones, the absorption of modern and foreign culture, and the extension of culture's essential content. They argue that cultural change follows changes in material production. Culture's historical inheritance, its uneven development relative to the material base, and the mutual influence of the elements of social consciousness all require traditional culture to be remade. Examples include turning the idea of family-and-nation sentiment into a basis for patriotism and a sense of community while discarding its patriarchal and autocratic elements. They also cite the concept of "harmony and unity" (hehe) as a guide for relations between people, nature and civilizations. In practice, the authors name the people as the decisive force and Party leadership as the political guarantee. They set four directions: scientific truth under Marxism, "Chinese characteristics", conformity to the times, and openness to the world. They propose four paths: coordinating cultural time and space through media; building a discourse system; improving legal protection of heritage and intellectual property; and improving national education. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholars ground the Two Creations in historical materialism and in the Party's evolving view of tradition.

Returning to the economic context: how East European neo-Marxism supplements humanist readings of Marx 回归经济学语境：东欧新马克思主义对马克思人道主义解读视角的补充 Du Hongyan Du Hongyan asks how East European neo-Marxism read Marx's humanism from within his economic writings rather than from philosophy alone. The article argues that these thinkers supplemented the humanist interpretations of Western Marxism by returning to the context of political economy. Doing so, in Du's account, countered both the economic determinism of Soviet Marxism and the abstract humanism of Western humanist currents. The article has four parts. It first sets out why a return to economics is needed. It then examines the "super-economic" character the East European thinkers found in Marx's economic work. Next it shows how they developed Marx's critique of "economic man" against economism in East European socialism. A final section assesses their contribution. Du draws mainly on Petrović, Kosík, Adam Schaff, Márkus and Marković, and on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Grundrisse and Capital. Du's central claim is that Marx completed his study of the "real human being" in economics, by analysing the alienated relation between people and production. In Marx's formula, in antiquity "man appears as the purpose of production", whereas under capitalism production and wealth become the end. Schaff criticises existentialism for an asocial, ahistorical individual, and criticises ethical-humanist readings of the early Marx for discarding scientific socialism. Petrović reads Marx's economics as a critique, whose point is that humans are free, creative practical beings and not "economic animals". Marković and Kosík extend the critique of "economic man" to economism in East European socialism and to the world of pseudo-concreteness. Du adds that Schaff took the Grundrisse as evidence against Althusser's thesis of a break in Marx's thought. Du concludes that the East European approach offers a case for the continuity of Marx's thought. It also moves beyond economic determinism, since Marx's historical determinism leaves room for human choice among real possibilities. The thinkers applied this to argue that East European socialism had not overcome the condition in which production is the human end, and they called for its humanisation. Du presents rereading Marx to analyse existing society as an important paradigm of Marxism outside China. Read the original if you study Marxism outside China, the debates over the young and mature Marx, or the Yugoslav Praxis school and its Polish and Czech counterparts.

The environmental politics of the Communist Party USA since the 21st century: theory, policy and action 21世纪以来美国共产党的环境政治：理论、政策与行动 Gao Ze Gao Ze asks how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) has approached environmental questions since the turn of the century, a topic the author says Chinese scholarship has neglected. The article argues that the party has built a distinctive radical-left environmental politics that joins Marxist theory to practical campaigning. In Gao's reading, this has given the CPUSA a visibility in the American left that exceeds its small size. The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The first reconstructs the party's theoretical work, the second sets out its policy positions, and the third describes its forms of action. Gao draws on figures such as John Bachtel, Mark Brodine, Anita Waters and Donald Donato, on the party's 31st National Convention report, and on its 2008 global warming report. On theory, Gao says CPUSA writers return to Marx and Engels, especially dialectical materialism and the idea of a metabolic rift. They treat capitalism as the root of ecological crisis, so that only systemic change, not reform, can resolve it. They frame the crisis as a 'planetary emergency' and propose the notion of 'working-class environmentalism', which keeps the working class as the key agent of change. On policy, the slogan 'people and planet before profit' leads the party to give qualified support to the Green New Deal, while pressing for workers' voice in it. It also defends marginalised communities against environmental racism and calls for green technology transfer to developing countries. In action, the party joins climate marches and strikes, publishes reports, runs Marxist education, and backs international cooperation. Gao concludes that the party's theory serves its movement work, that it influences public opinion more than policy, and that it combines American environmentalist currents with a global critique of capitalism. The article also notes the party's praise for China's ecological civilization, and Bachtel's view of the Communist Party of China as a model. Gao calls for closer cooperation among Marxist parties worldwide on global ecological governance and on building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how a Western communist party frames climate politics, and how that account links to Chinese ecological discourse.

The Party of Labour of Austria's exploration of the road of socialist revolution 奥地利劳动党对社会主义革命道路的探索 Wang Ximan Xue Lijun Wang Ximan and Xue Lijun examine the theory and practice of socialist revolution developed by the Party of Labour of Austria (PdA), the country's only party guided by Marxism-Leninism, in its first decade. The party was founded in 2013 out of a split from the Communist Party of Austria, whose turn to democratic socialism and entry into the European Left Party some members rejected. The authors argue that the PdA has built a distinctive revolutionary theory and made modest gains, but that its youth, weakness and limited grasp of national conditions leave theory and practice poorly connected. The article has four parts. It first traces the theory through the party's five congresses (2013–2022) and the conditions behind it: the contemporary era and changes in capitalism, Austria's economic and political situation, and a revolutionary tradition running from the Austromarxists to the 1980s slogan of 'socialism in Austrian colours'. It then sets out seven strands of the theory, describes party-building, parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle and international work, and closes with an assessment. In the authors' account, the PdA holds that the present era remains one of transition from capitalism to socialism and that contemporary capitalism is imperialism, bringing destruction and war. Austria is described as a subordinate member of the imperialist pyramid with a weakened bourgeois ruling system. The party rejects democratic socialism and reformism, and takes the core of revolution to be the political power of the organised working class and socialisation of the means of production. Its programme has three planks: nationalised production, democratised decision-making and class solidarity. It also calls for an anti-monopoly alliance, combines parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, and envisages a planned economy in a future society. In practice, the authors report, the PdA has set up regional organisations, a youth front and its own press, won a seat on a municipal council in Lower Austria in 2020, and built ties with communist parties abroad. They judge its progress to be real: it continues the revolutionary tradition, adapts Marxism to Austria and opposes imperialism and monopoly. They also list its problems: fewer than a thousand members, scarce funds, harsh criticism of other left parties, and positions against the EU and the market economy that have little appeal. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-scholarly account of a small European communist party's programme and organisation, with the authors' evaluation of it.

Basic practices of the Communist Party of Vietnam in Party political building since Đổi Mới 革新以来越南共产党党的政治建设的基本做法 Yan Jiehua Zhang Shengjie Yan Jiehua and Zhang Shengjie ask how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) has carried out Party political building since the start of reform (Đổi Mới, 'renovation') 37 years ago. They argue that the CPV has gradually placed political building first among its Party-building tasks, using it to lead ideological, moral, organisational and cadre building, and that this has raised its leadership and governing capacity. They present the experience as a reference for Marxist ruling parties. The article is organised around five areas of practice, followed by a conclusion on remaining problems. These are: setting the political direction and keeping the Party's working-class character; holding a 'people-based' political stance; anticipating political risks and strengthening political resolve; raising cadres' political capacity; and reshaping the political ecology. The authors draw on CPV congress documents (from the Sixth in 1986 to the Thirteenth in 2021), plenum resolutions and regulations, and statistics on training and discipline. On direction, the authors report that the CPV drew from the Soviet and East European collapse the lesson that the failure was of a dogmatic model, not of socialism. It set out 'five basic principles' in 1989 and 'five adherences' in 2021. On the people, the authors describe the formula 'people as centre and subject' and the aim of unifying the 'Party's will' with 'the people's hearts', including public consultation on congress drafts and stronger grassroots organisations. On risks and cadres, they describe policy research bodies, lists of manifestations of 'self-evolution' and 'self-transformation', a four-tier Party school system, quantified cadre evaluation, rotation of posts, and protection for 'six-dare' cadres. On discipline, they cite 2012–2022 figures, including some 168,000 disciplined members, and anti-corruption law revisions. The authors conclude that political building has unified Party thinking, curbed unhealthy tendencies, strengthened ties with the people and consolidated the CPV's ruling position. They identify four continuing problems: weak translation of Party decisions into policy ('hot above, cold below'); persistent 'self-evolution' and formalism; the long task of developing 'six-dare' cadres; and an incomplete system of hard rules lacking 'soft' cultural constraints. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based Chinese account of Vietnamese Party-building policies, with figures and regulation numbers, for comparison with Chinese Party-building discourse.

The relationship between the Anti-Christian Movement and the founding of the Chinese Socialist Youth League 非基督教运动与中国社会主义青年团成立的关系探析 Peng Ruikang Chen Jing The article asks how the Anti-Christian Movement of 1922 related to the founding of the Chinese Socialist Youth League. Scholars disagree: some hold that the League initiated and led the movement, others that members took part only as individuals, and others that the Comintern reports on Party leadership are unreliable. Peng and Chen argue that local League branches deliberately launched the movement, and that it in turn consolidated those branches and prepared the League's national founding in May 1922. They also argue that the League never achieved unified leadership of the movement. Drawing mainly on contemporary newspaper reports and participants' memoirs, the authors first trace the movement's background: the 1920 religion debate of the Young China Association, and the spread of Lenin's theory of imperialism, especially through the Congress of the Toilers of the Far East in early 1922. They then examine the League branches in Shanghai, Beijing and Guangdong, and the First National Congress in Guangzhou. A short conclusion assesses the movement's end and legacy, including its return in 1924 as the campaign to recover educational rights. Peng and Chen argue that the three branches played different roles. Shanghai launched the movement in March 1922 and framed Christianity as a vanguard of capitalist and imperialist aggression. In Beijing the League's call produced a larger but Enlightenment-style anti-religion alliance, whose mixed membership put it beyond Communist and League control, so it never turned decisively anti-imperialist. In Guangdong the League led through the press and by organising student and anti-religion alliances. The authors note that a Comintern representative's claim that the movement had wrecked the Christian conference is inaccurate. They cite the First Congress's resolution on relations with other organisations, which called for both struggle against and use of the YMCA, and for efforts to win leadership of non-Christian groups. The authors conclude that the movement gave the League its practical setting, spread Marxism-Leninism, enlarged its influence among students and trained early members. The League's plan to expand its leadership after the congress was frustrated by the Zhili–Fengtian war, political change in Beijing, the shift of attention to the labour movement and the students' summer departure. Read the original if you study the early history of the Communist Party and the Youth League, or the debate over Comintern sources and who actually led the Anti-Christian Movement.

A typology of the communist parties of Central and Eastern Europe A comparative analysis based on differences in the indigenization of Marxism 中东欧共产党的类型学划分 Xiang Zuotao Gu Feng Xiang and Gu ask how the communist parties of Central and Eastern Europe, which were largely cast in the Soviet mould before 1989, have differed since the upheavals of 1989–91 in adapting Marxism to their own countries. They argue that differences in the parties' willingness and capacity to indigenize Marxism have split them into three types: traditional, intermediate and pragmatic. In their account, this split shows the growing diversity of the contemporary international communist movement. The article first reviews existing typologies of post-1989 communist parties (those of John Ishiyama, Baukje/Bakke-style 'traditional versus reformed' schemes, and Luke March's conservative versus renewed distinction). It finds them unsuited to the region, because they study large parties such as those in France, Russia or the Czech Republic, or they treat nearly all Central and East European parties as 'traditional'. The authors then take each type in turn, with examples including the New Communist Party of Yugoslavia, the Hungarian Workers' Party, the Communist Party of Poland, the Communist Party of Bohemia and Moravia (KSČM), and the Bulgarian and Serbian communist parties. The authors classify parties by theory, mode of activity and political influence, and hold that external conditions such as party systems and transition outcomes were roughly the same for all, so subjective will and capacity explain the differences. Traditional parties treat the Soviet model as the only road, denounce 'revisionism', reject parliamentary politics and mainly stage protests and commemorations. Intermediate parties draw on national experience (for example Kádárism and Titoism), adopt some new-left causes, put forward ideas such as 'communal socialism' and 'open socialism', and contest elections while guarding their revolutionary identity. Pragmatic parties accept regional integration, globalization and a market economy under state control, and ally with social democrats. The authors say this brings electoral seats but risks social-democratization, and that cooperation with populists has proved self-damaging, citing the KSČM's loss of parliamentary representation in 2021. The authors conclude that indigenizing Marxism is a challenge for every communist party, and that balancing revolutionary ideals against practical activity is a dynamic task. They say it depends on capitalism's capacity to generate an industrial reserve army, on how far capitalist institutions meet workers' demands, and on how parties handle their relationship with the proletariat. They attribute the general 'downturn' of the region's communist parties to failures on these fronts. Read the original if you want a structured comparison of small and often overlooked communist parties in Central and Eastern Europe, with party-level examples and electoral figures.

Learning from Mao Zedong's strategic foresight 学习毛泽东的战略远见 Bi Jingjing Bi Jingjing, a retired senior officer of the PLA National Defence University, takes up Mao Zedong's strategic foresight (zhanlüe yuanjian) as a core element of strategic leadership. Bi argues that Mao made a pioneering contribution to shaping the Chinese Communist Party's capacity for foresight. Studying it, in the author's view, is of major strategic significance for building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation amid a complex international situation. The article has three parts. The first explains how Mao's foresight formed: as a product of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, as a cognitive outlook drawing on Marxism and traditional Chinese culture, and as guidance for revolution and construction. The second sets out its practical structure in six aspects. The third discusses its philosophical basis. Examples run from the Jinggangshan base area and the Anti-Japanese War to the Civil War, the Korean War and early socialist construction. Bi's central claim is that foresight is a combined quality of aspiration, belief, prediction, decision, patience and vigilance. The six aspects are national rejuvenation as aspiration, anticipation of the future, willingness to make trade-offs, confidence in victory, patience and wariness in times of safety. Illustrations include On Protracted War, the decision to give up Yan'an in 1947 to win all of China, the decision to enter the Korean War, and the 'going to the capital to take the examination' remark. Bi then roots these in dialectical materialism and historical materialism, in five unities: seeking truth from facts with far-sighted vision, a bright future with a tortuous road, strategic resolve with tactical flexibility, summing up history with opening the future, and individual with collective wisdom. Bi concludes that Mao's foresight is a model for the Party's strategic thinking. The author states that, with instability and uncertainty rising in the external environment, understanding it should help the Party broaden its strategic horizon, strengthen strategic thinking and create new achievements. The text draws on Xi Jinping's assessments of Mao's decisions as reference points. Read the original if you want a Party-military view of how Mao's strategic thinking is presented as a resource for current leadership training and Party history education.

Mao Zedong and the historical evolution of the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation 毛泽东与中华民族现代文明形态的历史演进 Tian Keqin Written for the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth (26 December 2023), the article asks how Mao contributed to the formation of a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation. That is the task the Party set itself in the new era. Tian argues that Mao, by combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities, made an indelible contribution to the creative transformation of Chinese culture from tradition to modernity. In Tian's account, this laid the theoretical foundation for the present call to build a modern Chinese civilisation. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical context: the clash between Western capitalist civilisation and traditional Chinese civilisation, and the failed attempts to find a path forward before the Communist Party. The second examines Mao's contributions in politics, the economy and culture. The third draws four lessons for today and links them to statements by Xi Jinping. Tian's core argument is that Mao's contribution rested on three tasks: breaking down the old order and building a new one. In politics, this meant the people's democratic dictatorship, the system of people's congresses, multi-party cooperation under Party leadership, and regional ethnic autonomy. In the economy, it meant socialist transformation of ownership and industrialisation, which Tian credits with building a fairly complete independent industrial system. In culture, it meant the New Democratic cultural programme (national, scientific, mass), a selective attitude towards tradition, and the 'Hundred Flowers, Hundred Schools' policy. Tian presents these as the political premise, material basis and cultural roots of the modern civilisation of the Chinese nation. Earlier attempts, from 'Chinese learning as the base, Western learning for use' to 'wholesale Westernisation', are said to have failed because they did not handle the relation between Chinese and Western civilisation correctly. Tian draws four lessons from Mao: keep to the standpoint of the Chinese nation, rely on the strength of the Chinese people, unswervingly follow China's own path, and treat the achievements of human civilisation with openness. Tian concludes that the Party must make building this civilisation its cultural mission, uphold the Two Integrations, and promote the coordinated development of material, cultural-ethical, political, social and ecological civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school scholar links Mao's cultural thought to current official discourse on civilisation.

Mao Zedong and seeking truth from facts 毛泽东与实事求是 Zhang Xiaofei This short commentary, published in Study Times in December 2023, examines the place of "seeking truth from facts" in Mao Zedong's thought. Zhang argues that it is one of the three basic aspects of the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought and its starting point, and that Mao created that body of thought by applying the basic tenets of Marxism-Leninism to Chinese realities. The article is built in three parts. The first traces Mao's path from his youth to the post-Mao period: the Hunan tradition of practical statecraft, his early social investigations, the Jinggangshan base and the Central Soviet Area, the Yan'an-era writings and Rectification campaign, the early People's Republic, and the return to the principle after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The second part sets out Mao's original ideas on the subject, and the third draws lessons for the present. Zhang's central argument is that Mao made seeking truth from facts the basis of the Party's ideological line. In the author's account, Mao insisted that theory must come from practice and be proved in practice, that Marxism must be "concretised" in China and developed rather than treated as dogma, and that dogmatism and subjectivism must be opposed. Zhang gives particular weight to investigation and research: Mao's slogan that without investigation there is no right to speak, his 1930 essay on opposing book worship, and his 1961 call for a year of investigation after the losses of the Great Leap Forward. The article also presents Mao as a lifelong reader of Marxist classics, especially the Communist Manifesto, and quotes Mao's remark that Chinese problems can only be solved by the Chinese. Zhang concludes that Communists must remain models of seeking truth from facts, and ties this to Xi Jinping's description of the principle as the Party's basic method of thinking, work and leadership. The author calls for raising theoretical level, upholding the Two Integrations, linking theory with practice, and using investigation and research as a family heirloom. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of how Mao's approach to investigation and theory is presented to Party cadres today.

Hegelian elements in Marxism outside China 国外马克思主义中的黑格尔思想元素 Lu Shaochen Lu Shaochen asks how Marxism outside China has dealt with Hegel, and why its relation to him has produced a mismatch. The article argues that these thinkers criticise modern society in a "near-Hegelian" way, drawing on Hegel's work on the state and national spirit. When they turn to practice and reconstruction, however, they fall back on a "near-Kantian" position that predates Hegel. Lu proposes a new Marxist scheme that stays Hegelian in method of critique and practice but replaces Hegel's ontology with the "positive existence" and "positive essence" of human beings. The piece, a short newspaper article, moves through foreign Marxist thinkers in roughly chronological order. It starts with Georg Lukács and Antonio Gramsci, then covers Herbert Marcuse, Theodor Adorno, Jürgen Habermas and Axel Honneth. It cites Martin Jay, Allen Wood, Michael Feola, Kurt Leidecker and Perry Anderson as commentators. It ends with Hegel's own limits and Marx's critique of him. Lu's central claim is that Hegel's lasting achievement was to explain the substantive spirit of Western modern society through the state idea and national spirit. Any serious critique of that society must therefore engage him. In Lu's reading, Lukács inherited the category of totality but detached the revolutionary subject from building the state idea and national spirit. Gramsci enriched Hegel on civil society and hegemony but did not grasp that national spirit is the state idea reproduced downward. Marcuse defended Hegel against the charge of proto-Nazism but could not show how a totalising revolution was possible. Adorno rejected totality altogether, and Habermas and Honneth retreated towards communicative and social-liberal solutions that Lu finds weak on objectivity. Lu treats Hegel as neither a plain statist nor a liberal. Lu concludes that Hegel's real flaw was to treat Western capitalist state ideas as the only form of world history, a distortion that Lu says especially affects his reading of the East. Lu finds Marx's critique of political economy the way past Hegel, because it reveals that humans generate themselves through labour and addresses the problem of poverty that Hegel could not solve. Lu endorses Anderson's complaint that foreign Marxism neglects labour and the reproduction of human beings, and says that refuting Hegel in a Kantian way was doomed to fail. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language assessment of how Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and Habermas relate to Hegel, framed by the state and national spirit.

Practical lessons of Lenin's historical analysis for the Party in formulating correct policies and tactics 列宁的历史分析法对党制定正确的政策策略的现实启示 Liang Haifeng Liang asks how Lenin's method of historical analysis helped the Bolsheviks set policy and tactics, and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. The article argues that Lenin treated dialectics as inseparable from historicity, and that this method let him adjust policy to each specific stage and set of conditions. In Liang's view, it remains a methodological reference for Party policy-making in the new era. The article, published in 2023, has two parts. The first defines Lenin's historical analysis and traces its use in three areas: flexible tactics through the 1905 and 1917 revolutions, firm struggle to consolidate Soviet power, and the critique of mistaken currents. The cases include Narodism, the Economists, Machism and revisionism. The second part draws three lessons for the Chinese Party. On Lenin, Liang's central claim is that he derived tasks from the actual course of events rather than from fixed principles. Examples include rejecting the Mensheviks' copying of Western bourgeois revolution in 1905, the April Theses and the decision for armed uprising in 1917, the Brest-Litovsk peace, and the wartime policy toward peasants. Liang also says Lenin's critiques rested on extensive historical research, as in The Development of Capitalism in Russia and Materialism and Empirio-criticism. The Chinese lessons follow from this. The Party should study history seriously, citing Marx and Engels, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. It should respect historical stages and conditions and draw on past failures. Liang names Chen Duxiu's compromise with the Kuomintang, Wang Ming's and Bo Gu's errors, and the Great Leap Forward. It should also adopt the "grand view of history" (da lishi guan), which Liang describes as long-term, broad and steady in direction. Liang concludes that Lenin's method is a tested scientific worldview and methodology. Studying history, learning from experience and holding a long-term global perspective will help the Party formulate correct lines. In this reading it will also support Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and strengthen confidence in socialism's eventual victory. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of how Lenin's historical method is used to justify Party history study and the Xi-era "grand view of history".

Interpreting the young Marx's Paris text cluster 青年马克思的巴黎文本群解读 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing takes up the long dispute over the young Marx's Paris writings, namely the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the contemporaneous Paris Notebooks, which together form a "Paris text cluster". The article argues that the key to reading this cluster is what Zhang calls the "labour-alienation construct", which bears on the sources of Marx's thought and on his later economic thinking. Zhang first explains why the cluster is contested: Marx's thinking was unsettled, with Hegel, Feuerbach, political economy and Enlightenment history competing in his mind. The texts were also found only after his death, and their interpretation is tied to ideological struggles over the legitimacy of historical materialism. The article then reconstructs the order of writing and traces the construct from On the Jewish Question through the Paris Notebooks to the 1844 Manuscripts and later economic manuscripts. Zhang holds that the Paris Notebooks contain a complete research plan: Say, Smith and List, then the Mill excerpts, then the Hegel excerpts. Since Marx did not normally excerpt and write at once, Zhang concludes that the Notebooks preceded the 1844 Manuscripts. Zhang distinguishes three stages: a first construct in the Mill notes, based on "need" and alienated exchange; a second in Notebook I of the Manuscripts, drawing on Hegel and Smith; and a scientific third construct in the later economic manuscripts. Zhang reads the construct as Marx's first systematic "critical epistemology", Hegelian phenomenology applied to social materialism. It sees relations behind visible commodities and property, yet still ends in Feuerbach's human species-being, which Zhang calls implicitly idealist. Zhang concludes that Marx abandoned this humanist epistemology from the Theses on Feuerbach onwards, and that a new critical epistemology emerged in the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts, completing two shifts in his epistemology. Read the original if you want a concise statement of Zhang Yibing's periodisation and reading of the young Marx's alienation theory.

The concept of class in the "Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right" 《〈黑格尔法哲学批判〉导言》中的阶级概念 Huang Du Liu Ling Huang Du and Liu Ling start from the observation that the concept of class is receding from politics, sociology and even philosophy, where "stratum" has largely replaced it. They argue that treating class as an empirical ranking of wealth or social status is the greatest misreading of Marx. Their thesis is that Marx's concept of class can be grasped fully only by returning to his early texts, above all the 1843–44 Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, where the proletariat first appears in a philosophical determination that underlies his later theory. The article, originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2023, reconstructs why and how the concept enters this text. It does so through three "logics": textual, practical and theoretical. The authors also address the common scholarly view that the Introduction is immature because Marx had not yet mastered political economy or formed historical materialism. On the textual side, a word-frequency count in the Marx–Engels Collected Works (Chinese second edition, vol. 1) shows "class" appearing 41 times in the Introduction, 13 of them as "proletariat", against one occurrence in the Critique itself. The authors read this as a turning point. In the practical account, Marx's work on the Rheinische Zeitung, especially the debates on wood theft, confronted him with the "perplexing questions" of material interests and left Hegel's rational state unconfirmed. In the theoretical account, Marx moves from seeking a political solution to the split between state and civil society towards the interior of civil society. There he turns that split into the antagonism between proletariat and bourgeoisie, using a transformed Hegelian dialectic. The authors conclude that class concerns human "species being" and real freedom, not merely poverty or ownership of the means of production. They offer three initial propositions. The proletariat is a product of history and of industrial, modern capitalist society. It marks the loss of human universality and is not simply observable workers or paupers. It is a special class with self-negating and transcending character, since it must abolish the bourgeoisie and thereby itself. Without this framework, they warn, the later notion of the working class risks empiricism and Lukácsian reified consciousness. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based argument for a philosophical rather than sociological reading of Marx's class concept.

The three-dimensional historical foundations of historical materialism 历史唯物主义的三维历史底蕴 Jin Xingyu This short theoretical piece asks what gives historical materialism its character as a totalizing philosophy of history. Jin argues that it inherits, criticises and goes beyond the "general philosophy of history" represented by Hegel. Its break, in Jin's account, is to "return the content of history to history": it grounds history in the productive practice of "real individuals" and so offers a scientific answer about history in general. The article claims that this is built on three dimensions. Jin takes the dimensions in turn: natural history and human history, past and future, and national history and world history. Each is tied to texts by Marx and Engels, mainly The German Ideology, Engels's account of natural evolution, and their late reflections on Russia. The piece is a compact exposition rather than a survey of secondary literature, with a brief nod to E. H. Carr on the link between past and future. On the first dimension, Jin argues that natural history and human history are structurally parallel on the basis of practice. Externally, both show diverse forms. Internally, both are governed by laws rooted in the metabolism between humans and nature. In capitalism, Jin says, the logic of capital makes human history move blindly, like natural history, which bourgeois ideology then defends. Overcoming this alienation requires a return to active practice. On the second, historical materialism is described as a philosophy oriented to the future. It links "interpretation–critique–prediction" and uses a "practical reflection" that works backwards from developed forms. It ties historical logic to the real movement of communism. On the third, Jin says Marx and Engels went beyond a Eurocentric view of history. They treated world history as a system of mutually dependent nations. Their late attention to Russia's possible path past the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, Jin argues, shows that varied national paths do not negate general laws. Jin concludes that these three dimensions give historical materialism's totality a unified, diverse and open character. Jin presents this "big view of history" as an important intellectual resource for the Communist Party of China's governance. In Jin's reading it fits the theme of a century of Party history, supports Chinese modernization and the building of a new form of human civilisation, and opens a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how Chinese theorists currently frame the historical-materialist "totality" of nature, time and world history, and how they link it to Party doctrine.

Advancing Chinese modernization requires strengthening strategic thinking 推进中国式现代化必须强化战略思维 Cheng Zhangchun This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscript in 2023, argues that Chinese modernization can only be advanced by cadres who are good at strategic thinking and at viewing problems from a strategic standpoint. Cheng Zhangchun takes as the framework a speech by Xi Jinping at the study seminar on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022). In Cheng's account, the speech identifies four qualities of strategy that cadres must strengthen. The article is organised in four sections that follow these qualities: foresight, a global (whole-picture) perspective, stability, and the combination of strategic principle with tactical flexibility. Each section explains what the quality means and what Party members and cadres are expected to do in practice. The text relies heavily on quotations from Xi Jinping and on the documents of the 20th Party Congress rather than on external cases. On foresight, Cheng contends that strategy concerns the long term and the general trend, so that cadres must move from passively "encountering" risks to actively "foreseeing" them, guided by scientific theory and by knowledge of historical laws. On the global perspective, the author holds that planning must start from the "two overall situations" (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and profound changes unseen in a century), grasp the principal contradiction, and use systems thinking, including the nine essential requirements of Chinese modernization and the five-sphere integrated plan. On stability, Cheng calls for historical patience, strategic resolve and a broad mind among leading cadres, who should be willing to build on predecessors' work and avoid frequent policy reversals. The final section argues that strategy and tactics form a dialectical unity: firm principles must be kept in line with Party theory and the Party line, yet need not become rigid, and strategy should be adjusted as conditions change. Cheng notes that the content of the current period of strategic opportunity has changed profoundly and calls for new strategic responses, together with flexible, locally adapted policies, bottom-line thinking and the capacity for struggle. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school-style writing translates Xi Jinping's formulation of strategic thinking into concrete expectations for cadres.

Reflections on Xi Jinping's important speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development 对习近平在文化传承发展座谈会上重要讲话的若干思考 Marco Rizzo Alberto Lombardo This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by Marco Rizzo and Alberto Lombardo of the Communist Party (Italy), responding to Xi Jinping's remarks of 2 June 2023 at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. Xi called for building a modern Chinese civilization and a cultural powerhouse. The authors read this as a prompt for Western communists to reflect on the state of capitalist civilization and on Italy's position. They argue that Chinese modernization, which balances material and spiritual civilization, stands in sharp contrast to a degenerating West. The commentary has five sections. It contrasts the coordinated development of modern Chinese civilization with Western decline, and China's intellectual independence with the subordination of Italy and Europe. It then compares China's openness with Western narrowness, presents multipolarity as the direction shown by Chinese civilization, and ends with China's stress on harmony and peace in the face of US policy. Italian history, NATO, the Belt and Road Initiative and Africa serve as the main cases. The authors take Xi's five features of Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and read them as the basic principles of a multipolar order. They set this against a US-led unipolarity that they describe as imperialist, marked by double standards, war, financialization and cultural homogenization. In their account, bourgeois nationalism and cosmopolitanism are two complementary faces of class rule, opposed by internationalism and patriotism of the oppressed. They argue that Italy has lacked independent choice since the Cold War, citing US bases and Washington's pressure over its Belt and Road memorandum and trade with Russia. They hold that China's self-reliant path, lifting about 800 million people out of absolute poverty, shows what independence makes possible. The authors conclude that modern Chinese civilization, under Communist Party leadership and Marxist guidance, can contribute more to a world in which countries are guided rather than dominated. They call China the strongest bulwark against Western imperialist aggression and hope that Italians and Europeans will take up Xi's call for spiritual independence. The text is openly polemical and partisan in its characterisation of the United States and Europe. Read the original if you want to see how a European communist party leadership interprets Xi Jinping's cultural policy and China's international role.

A century of British communist parties: historical evolution and the causes of decline 百年英国共产主义政党历史演变与衰败的原因分析 Song Xiongwei Why have British communist parties remained split and marginal for a century? Song Xiongwei takes up this question, arguing that existing Chinese-language studies stress external shocks (the dissolution of the Comintern, Soviet actions, the Khrushchev "secret speech", the Sino-Soviet split) and neglect internal causes. The article contends that decline stemmed chiefly from ideological wavering, lack of independence from Moscow and organisational slackness. The article first reconstructs the lineage of British communist organisations, which existing studies often conflate. It follows the Communist Party of Great Britain (CPGB) from its founding in 1920, through its wartime peak of over 56,000 members, to the 1956 exodus, the Maoist, Trotskyist and Eurocommunist splits, the 1988 founding of the Communist Party of Britain, and the CPGB's 1991 reorganisation as Democratic Left. It then offers six internal explanations and ends with lessons for the Chinese Communist Party. Song's core claim is that the CPGB was formed in 1920 largely under Soviet pressure, without resolving deep ideological disagreement, notably over parliamentary participation. Song then argues that the party repeatedly negated its own line: documents of 1944 and 1951 pursued socialism by parliamentary means, Eurocommunism undermined the dictatorship of the proletariat and democratic centralism, and in 1990–91 the party abandoned Marxism-Leninism. Song adds that pro-Soviet factions dependent on Soviet funding hardened, that sectarian expulsions bred rival groups (over 70 Trotskyist bodies), that its programme resembled the Labour Party's, and that lax discipline and loose membership left weak branches. Song concludes that wavering in the ideological sphere, absence of independence and a disorganised structure cost these parties public support. Drawing on this history, Song calls for upholding Marxism's guiding position in ideology, strengthening the Chinese Communist Party's overall leadership and the authority of the Central Committee, unifying thinking through the Party's innovative theory, tightening organisation and building a high-calibre cadre corps. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school account of the fragmentation of British communist organisations and how Chinese scholars draw governing-party lessons from it.

New displays of the appeal of Chinese civilisation in the new era and a new realm for research on the "Two Integrations" 新时代中华文明魅力的新展示与“两个结合”研究的新境界 Liu Shulin Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Shulin asks what Chinese civilisation shows in the new era and what that implies for research on the Two Integrations: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. Liu argues that Chinese civilisation has regained a leading position, and that Marxist scholars now have a new mission to realise the Two Integrations through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first describes three new aspects of Chinese civilisation's appeal: an expanded historical timeline supported by archaeology, its continuity, and an endogenous dynamic arising from interaction between centre and periphery. The second examines how the civilisation passed through a low point in modern times and revived. The third sets out three requirements of the Two Integrations in the new era. Liu draws on Xi Jinping's speeches, Chinese historians such as Bai Shouyi and Lei Haizong, and Arnold Toynbee. Liu's central argument concerns historical regularity. Early advance in the feudal stage, Liu holds, gave China a durable institutional shell, which later made the transition to new social formations harder. Citing Lei Haizong, Liu says countries that enter a new social formation first are usually relatively backward in the previous one, and that China's modern humiliation is explained by two lacks: guiding ideas and a unifying organisation. Marxism-Leninism and the Communist Party, in Liu's account, supplied both and 'activated' the civilisation's vitality, so that China is again at the starting point of leading development. Liu rejects cultural revivalism and historical nihilism, and endorses 'creative transformation and innovative development' of tradition under Marxist guidance. Liu concludes that Marxist scholars must carry forward the tradition of adapting Marxism, keep Marxism firmly in the guiding ideological position, and use tradition to educate people, especially the young. Liu frames this as a contest of soft power with hegemonic forces and calls for building academic, disciplinary and discourse systems on Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how the Two Integrations are tied to claims about civilisational continuity and the social-formation sequence.

The inner connection and practical orientation of firm historical confidence and steadfast ideals and convictions 坚定历史自信与坚守理想信念的 内在关联与实践指向 Mei Ping Chen Jiao Mei Ping and Chen Jiao take up a pairing first put forward by Xi Jinping at the Second Plenary Session of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): that Party members should "stand firm in historical confidence" and "consciously hold to ideals and convictions". The authors argue that the two are highly coupled. Both aim to unify thought and action around the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, though they differ in content: historical confidence rests on a scientific grasp of historical laws and achievements, while ideals and convictions mean belief in Marxism, communism and the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first treats the inner connection between the two; the second, their active role in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; the third, four practical orientations for the "new journey of examination". It draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches, the 2021 Party resolution on history and the Marxist classics, and relates the argument to the Party's centenary history. On the connection, the authors contend that historical confidence affirms and supports ideals and convictions. It affirms them because it is confidence in the "two inevitables" and in a century of achievements, and it supports them because Party history supplies facts, heroes and collective memory. In return, steadfast conviction gives historical confidence its rational self-awareness, since it is grounded in Marxist truth, and its deepest source of strength, the aim of seeking happiness for the Chinese people and "great harmony" for the world. On their active role, historical confidence strengthens historical consciousness and initiative, while conviction supplies socialist direction and gathers the people's strength through the common ideal. The practical orientations are strengthening the Party's self-confidence and upholding its overall leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; consolidating the spiritual foundation through the Party's spiritual genealogy to advance Chinese modernization; clearing ideological fog by opposing historical nihilism, with the collapse of the Soviet Union cited as a warning; and honing the capacity for struggle against risks and challenges. The authors conclude that, amid the interplay of the "two overall situations", the whole Party and people must keep both qualities to advance national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party theorists link historical confidence, ideological conviction and the Party's political tasks.

Hegelian elements in foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义中的黑格尔思想元素 Lu Shaochen Lu Shaochen asks how Marxism outside China has dealt with Hegel, and why its theoretical results have been uneven. The article, a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in September 2023, reads the relationship through Hegel's notions of the state idea and the national spirit. Lu argues that these thinkers criticised society in a largely 'near-Hegelian' manner but drew back to a 'near-Kantian' position when it came to practice and constructive proposals. Lu holds that this mismatch deserves study, and proposes a new Marxist approach that stays Hegelian in method and critique but replaces Hegel's ontology with 'the positive existence and positive essence of the human being'. The article moves through foreign Marxism roughly in sequence. It begins with the inheritance of the totality method in Georg Lukács and Antonio Gramsci. It then turns to Herbert Marcuse's defence of Hegel and to Theodor Adorno's rejection of totality, followed by Jürgen Habermas and Axel Honneth, who Lu says retreat towards social liberal democracy. A final section sets out how one might return to Hegel and then go beyond him, drawing on Marx and on critics of Hegel such as Kurt Leidecker and Perry Anderson. Lu's central claim is that Hegel's strength lay in explaining the substantial spirit of Western modernity through the state idea and national spirit, and that any critique of that modernity must therefore pass through him. In Lu's reading, Lukács's proletarian subject floats free of state idea and national spirit, Gramsci enriches Hegel on culture and hegemony but underrates the contest for state power, and Marcuse speaks only abstractly of historical reason. Adorno's negative dialectics and Habermas's communicative paradigm, Lu argues, give up totality and fall back on contractarian contingency. Lu also contends that Hegel is neither a simple statist nor a liberal, since he insisted that totality and individuality must be united. His real flaw, on this account, is treating Western capitalist forms as the only pattern of world history. Lu concludes that Marx's critique of political economy supplies the way forward. Marx located the secret of human history in people producing themselves through labour, and so could address the poverty and 'rabble' problem Hegel could not solve. Lu endorses Anderson's complaint that foreign Marxism neglects labour and the reproduction of human beings, and judges that refuting Hegel in a Kantian manner was bound to fail. Lu also links this to the values of Eastern civilisation, such as attention to humaneness and labour. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-authored assessment of how Lukács, Gramsci, Marcuse, Adorno, Habermas and Honneth relate to Hegel, and of the case for a Marx-based return to him.

The Mill Notes in the context of political economy and the evolving logic of alienation 政治经济学语境中的《穆勒笔记》及其异化逻辑演进 Zhang Fugong Zhang Fugong examines the Mill Notes, the young Marx's first extended encounter with political economy, and asks how the logic of alienation develops within them. Drawing on MEGA2, the article argues that the Mill Notes should be read against the economic literature Marx was excerpting, and that this reading helps settle current scholarly disputes. Originally a newspaper article from 2023, it is a short piece. The article first reviews the long debate over the Mill Notes' date and status relative to the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. It identifies three positions: written before the Manuscripts, between Notebook I and Notebooks II–III, or after Notebook III. It then follows the Paris Notes on Say, Skarbek, Smith and Ricardo to trace how Marx moves from alienated exchange to alienated labour. Zhang rejects the claim that the Mill Notes' alienation of communication (交往异化) is more advanced than the alienation of labour in Notebook I. In Zhang's reading, the social relations in the Mill Notes are mainly exchange relations, whose freedom and equality are an ideological appearance concealing the exploitation behind private property. From Say, Skarbek and Smith, Marx obtains the picture of a commercial society and treats money as the alienated mediation of human activity. He then turns to wage labour for subsistence through the line division of labour, labour machine and exploitation-based private property, which he takes from Ricardo. Zhang concludes that Marx's early theory of alienated labour grows out of this political-economy context. Its four forms are already sketched, and attention to capital–labour exploitation begins to break the exchange framework. The theory still lacks sublation of alienation, which Zhang says Marx later supplies by drawing on Hegel's negative dialectic. Read the original if you study the young Marx's development or the dating debate over the Paris writings and want a source-based argument against treating alienation of communication as the higher stage.

The internal structure of the young Marx's theory of alienation 青年马克思异化理论的内在结构 Kong Weiyu Kong Weiyu asks how the many theoretical sources of the young Marx's theory of alienation (political economy, Hegelian philosophy, Feuerbach's humanism) were arranged in his thinking. The author treats this as a foundational question to settle before any original interpretation. The thesis is that two logics coexisted in Marx's mind in a structured field of forces, which polyphony theory and field theory together can describe. The piece appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2023. The article first reviews the "two logics" reading of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, associated with Sun Bogao, Zhang Yibing and Tang Zhengdong. It then borrows the concept of polyphony from musicology and from Mikhail Bakhtin's account of Dostoevsky's novels, and adds Pierre Bourdieu's theory of the field. Kong reads the two logics as polyphonic: an objective logic starting from economic reality and an alienation logic starting from humanism, each independent yet jointly forming a whole. Because polyphony leaves the whole unfinished, Kong suggests, it helps explain why later scholars interpret the young Marx so openly. Field theory is then used to show how the logics relate. The objective logic is explicit, since the Manuscripts use terms close to those of the political economists, and even production, practice and communism appear. The humanist alienation logic stays implicit but dominates, so that the return point for overcoming alienation remains human species-essence. Kong argues that this changed only after Marx's Brussels and Manchester notebooks and his encounter with large-scale machine industry. Kong adds that each logic has mixed sources. The objective one draws on Smith and Ricardo and also on the humanist economist Schulz-type thinkers such as Skarbek, while the alienation logic draws on Feuerbach and on Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit. Kong concludes that opening up this structural field is difficult but rewarding, and requires sustained work on the texts. Read the original if you want a short methodological sketch of how the young Marx's thought can be modelled with polyphony and field theory.

Rethinking the totality of Marx's concept of "history" 重新理解马克思“历史”概念的总体性特征 Wu Meng Wu Meng asks how the totality of Marx's concept of "history" should be understood, and argues that the influential reading by Georg Lukács needs to be revised. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2023, holds that this concept shapes both the horizon of historical materialism and our theoretical attitude towards contemporary life. Wu's thesis is that the totality of Marx's "history" is a historical feature tied to the capitalist mode of production. It is not a whole that contains and determines its parts. The piece has three parts. The first sets out Lukács's account in History and Class Consciousness. The second identifies three internal inconsistencies in it. The third presents Wu's own reading of Marx's dialectic and of totality in the critique of political economy. In Wu's account, Lukács treats method as the core of Marxist orthodoxy. He reads Marx through a Hegelian dialectic of part and whole and of subject and object. Reification, on this reading, is a partial appearance, and the proletariat can grasp the social totality behind it. Wu credits the insight that history is more than a set of empirical facts but argues that the logic fails on three counts. Part–whole dialectics work in Hegel's logic because the Absolute Idea unites individuality and totality, whereas capitalist social structure is not an individual phenomenon alongside others. Lukács's mediating concepts, the "structural principle of construction" and the "real tendency of development", are vague and hard to operationalise. Reading Marx's move from the abstract to the concrete as a move from part to whole also turns Marx's historically specific concept into an abstract one applicable to any era. Wu locates the root of these problems in equating Marx's dialectic with Hegel's, although Marx called his method the direct opposite of Hegel's. Wu's positive proposal is that totality is the capitalist mode of production itself. It is not a ready-made entity but a structural operation that gives phenomena their "mode of givenness". It is a functional whole that accompanies objects yet cannot be objectified, a "collusion" of human and material factors. Totality is therefore a historical feature belonging only to capitalism, where universal relations between persons and between things arise. Marx, Wu argues, begins from this universality, which classical political economists took to be eternal, and asks about its historical preconditions. Read the original if you are interested in Western Marxism's debates over totality and in a Chinese critique of Lukács's use of Hegel in reading Marx.

The "war without end" of contemporary imperialism and its inner logic 当代帝国主义的无限战争及其内在逻辑 Kong Ming'an Chen Yu Kong Ming'an and Chen Yu ask why the dominant war form of contemporary imperialism has shifted from territorial colonial war to what Ellen Meiksins Wood called "war without end", and what drives it. Drawing on Wood and Slavoj Žižek, they argue that this war mode is a ghost-like, open-ended form of objective violence that remains bound to the logic of capital. Published in the Journal of Hubei University in 2023, the article is a work of foreign Marxism studies. The article has five parts. It first sets out four dimensions in which war without end is "unlimited": duration, military purpose, means and spatial reach. It then reads the concept through Žižek's idea of the ghost, and classifies its violence using Žižek's typology of subjective, objective and symbolic violence. The fourth part ties it to capital logic by way of Lacan's object a, and a short conclusion follows. The authors use the post-1945 United States as their main case, with the Iraq and Afghanistan wars as examples. The authors contend that, once the costs of holding colonies became prohibitive, imperialism detached war from specific military goals while keeping a clear political aim, namely global hegemony. In their account the resulting war is ghostly: it persists, shifts shape, threatens unlimited destruction and is presented as justice while serving capital's interests. Its violence is objective, systemic and anonymous, in the sense of Žižek, and of Hardt and Negri's "Empire", rather than the act of individual rulers. The authors then argue, with Žižek, that capital now works like Lacan's object a, becoming invisible through finance and digital money. They cite figures on US military spending to show that war and capital reinforce each other, and they say this fits Marx's political economy and Lenin's view of imperialism as moribund capitalism. The authors conclude that war without end is driven and served by imperial capital, so it can be eliminated only by overthrowing the capitalist system, as Lenin held. They add that opposing imperialist hegemonic logic, in order to safeguard world peace and build a community with a shared future for mankind, is a new task of the age. Read the original if you study Marxist theories of imperialism, Žižek or Wood, or want to see how Chinese scholars combine psychoanalytic concepts with Leninist analysis of contemporary war.

The "anti-ecological" nature of eco-capitalism: a critique from Marxist political economy 生态资本主义的“反生态性”——基于马克思主义政治经济学批判视角 Li Weiran Li Weiran asks whether eco-capitalism, the mainstream Western approach to environmental problems in developed capitalist countries, can solve those problems. Li argues from a Marxist standpoint that it cannot. In Li's account it overlooks the real source of ecological problems, which is the mode of production and the social system tied to it, and the capitalist system's logic is by nature "anti-ecological". The article has three parts. The first sets out the two schools of eco-capitalism: eco-market-ism, which relies on free markets and price mechanisms, and eco-Keynesianism, which relies on state planning and macro-regulation. The second offers a political-economy critique of the "anti-ecological" character of capitalism. The third turns to public ownership as the basis for solving ecological problems and to the Chinese case. In Li's reading, eco-market-ism turns ecological resources into commodities through eco-tax reform and tradable pollution permits. Eco-Keynesianism criticises this as a "fallacy of composition" and calls for state-led ecological investment and eco-friendly technology. Li treats both as reformist strategies within capitalism. Drawing on Marx, Michael Löwy and John Bellamy Foster, Li locates the anti-ecological character in three features of capitalist logic: expansion ("grow or die"), profit-seeking (production for exchange-value and money) and short-sightedness. Private ownership of the means of production, Li adds, splits humanity from nature and pushes environmental costs onto developing countries. Eco-capitalism therefore only gives capitalism a "green coat" and can at most ease problems, not cure them. Li concludes that socialism has advantages in value orientation ("people-centred" rather than value-expansion), institutional basis (public ownership) and economic system (a socialist market economy in which government plans and regulates). On China's own environmental problems, Li attributes them to extensive growth, to exploring a market economy without precedent, and to pollution transfer from developed countries, not to public ownership. Li notes that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and so calls for guiding capital, helping it shift from industrial to ecological capital, on a path of socialist ecological civilisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar classifies and criticises Western eco-capitalist theories and links the critique to China's ecological civilisation policy.

The Communist Party of Argentina's exploration of the road to socialism and an assessment of it 阿根廷共产党对社会主义道路的探索及对其评析 Li Donghua Ding Bowen Li and Ding examine a century of the Communist Party of Argentina (the first communist organisation in Latin America) and its search for a road to socialism. They argue that the party's exploration has not succeeded. In their view this is a common fate of non-governing communist parties in developing countries, whose root cause is that the subjective and objective conditions for socialism are not yet in place. The article divides the party's history into three stages: the revolutionary struggle period (1918–1945), the stage of peaceful struggle (1945–1990), and the period of transition and adjustment from 1990 to the present. It then identifies five features of the party's approach: peaceful transition through parliament, the pursuit of democracy and anti-dependence politics, united fronts, economic struggles for workers' basic rights, and ties with left forces in the region. A final section offers an assessment and outlook. In the authors' account, the early party relied on class struggle, strikes and trade unions, but was repeatedly repressed and spent long periods as an illegal organisation. After 1945 it turned to parliamentary and legal means, and since the 1990s it has run in electoral coalitions led by the Justicialist (Peronist) Party. It won only a handful of seats and, the authors say, remains a marginal participant rather than a leader of fronts. Li and Ding give four reasons for its limited results: harsh conditions of survival; dependence on the Justicialist Party, which in their view merely uses the communists against the right; strong influence from outside socialist movements, which produced shifts and reversals; and internal weaknesses, including four major splits in the second half of the twentieth century and a membership that fell from nearly 200,000 in the early 1980s to 170,000 in 2021. The authors expect the party to remain a political force in Argentina and a member of the Latin American left, but to stay a small party for a long time. They conclude that its search for a socialist road is still unfinished, with a long road ahead. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of Latin American communist parties and of the limits facing non-governing communist parties in developing countries.

The development of the Communist Party USA since its 30th National Convention and its prospects 美国共产党三十大以来的发展图景与前景探析 Li Haiyu Feng Xiaoxu Li Haiyu and Feng Xiaoxu ask how the Communist Party USA (CPUSA) has developed since its 30th National Convention in June 2014 and what lies ahead for it. They treat that convention as a turning point. It replaced the leadership of Sam Webb, who had urged abandoning Leninism, democratic centralism and the vanguard party and changing the party's name. The authors argue that the new leadership corrected this rightward line and that the party has since grown, though favourable conditions are offset by serious weaknesses. The article has three parts. The first surveys CPUSA's development in five areas: party building, revised ideas about capitalism and socialism, opposition to the far right, assessment of the Biden administration, and involvement in strikes and anti-racist movements. The second sets out opportunities, namely continuing systemic crisis in the United States, a revival of socialist sentiment, and the revitalisation of world socialism. The third sets out challenges, both internal and external. On party building, the authors report that the party kept its name, reaffirmed Leninism and democratic centralism, expanded Marxist education and local clubs, and grew from about 5,000 members in 2018 to roughly 11,000. They describe the opportunities through inequality figures, political polarisation, racial injustice and the pandemic, and through polling and election results showing wider interest in socialism, including the growth of the Democratic Socialists of America. The challenges include a small membership, financial strain, loosened admission rules, and disputes before the 31st Convention (2019) over Black self-determination and a revived Communist International. The authors also cite persistent anti-communist prejudice, a far right that remains strong, and weak class consciousness among American workers. The authors conclude that CPUSA's influence among young people, who lack Cold War memories, will probably grow, and that its marginal position may ease somewhat. Its challenges, however, mean no fundamental change or breakthrough in the short term, and its effect on mainstream politics should be rationally assessed. They call for further localisation of Marxism, steady accumulation of strength, spreading of ideas, worker mobilisation and patience. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of CPUSA's post-2014 organisation, strategy and membership data, including its internal disputes.

"The scar of democracy": critical theory's critical response to the New Right “民主的伤疤”：批判理论对新右翼的批判性回应 Li Li Zhou Aimin Li Li and Zhou Aimin start from Ralf Dahrendorf's 1997 forecast that the twenty-first century might be an authoritarian one. They ask where the contemporary New Right comes from, what drives it and why it attracts support. Their thesis is that the Frankfurt School's critical theory, early and contemporary, offers important intellectual resources for answering these questions. The article has three main parts. The first traces the New Right in the United States, from Barry Goldwater in 1964 through Nixon, Reagan, the post-Cold War break-up of "fusionism" and Trump. It then traces the European New Right, from Alain de Benoist's 1968 research group to the electoral successes of parties such as Fidesz, the AfD, Vox and the Sweden Democrats. The second part examines early critical theory (Horkheimer, Adorno, Löwenthal, Fromm and others), and the third examines Habermas and his successors. Drawing on early critical theory, the authors identify three levels of explanation. At the level of society, fascism and the far right are products of conditions that advanced capitalism generates, such as capital concentration, the "declassing" of the bourgeoisie and the threat of technological unemployment. At the level of the individual, studies such as Studies on Authority and the Family and The Authoritarian Personality treat authoritarian character as a product of social structure, not of nature. At the level of propaganda, agitation works on unconscious mechanisms through stereotyping, personalisation and ritual. The authors then turn to Habermas's legitimation-crisis theory. In this reading the New Right is a defensive reaction to the political system's loss of capacity under financialised globalisation, and Habermas treats its prejudices as symptoms and not as the underlying disease. He therefore urges "de-thematisation" of the right's agenda and supranational, EU-level cooperation to politically shape economic globalisation. The authors conclude that, in the critical-theory tradition, the danger of the New Right lies in the fact that it grows out of Western democracy itself. In Adorno's phrase it is a "scar of democracy". Opposing it therefore requires examining the inner contradictions of Western democratic politics, including inequality, exploitation and mechanisms that exclude minorities and migrants. They call for critical absorption and transformation of these ideas in order to respond to the changes in international politics that the New Right's rise has caused. Read the original if you want a compact survey of how Frankfurt School thinkers from Adorno to Habermas are being mobilised to explain the contemporary Western far right, as seen from Chinese academic debate.

The workers' movement in Kazakhstan since the disintegration of the Soviet Union 苏联解体以来的哈萨克斯坦工人运动 Kang Yanru Kazakhstan has recovered economically faster than most former Soviet republics, yet ranks near the bottom of the International Labour Organization's global rights index for workers and has seen almost continuous strikes since independence. Kang Yanru asks how the workers' movement developed, what marks it out, why it has stayed combative, and what lessons it offers. The article argues that the movement's deeper roots lie in neoliberal reform and privatisation, reinforced by a state-monopolised trade-union system and double oppression by local oligarchs and transnational capital. The article first divides the period since 1991 into four phases: fragmented and declining activity to 2007; a first peak from 2008 to 2011, culminating in the eight-month Zhanaozen oil strike; a lull from 2012 to 2019; and a revival after the pandemic that led to the unrest of January 2022. It then lists five features of the movement, analyses three causes, draws lessons from its successes and setbacks, and ends with four current difficulties. Kang's central claims are these.
