Because manufacturing collapsed and the economy centred on oil and mining, labour became concentrated in the energy sector, which supplies the movement's main force. The article cites the Mangystau region, where unemployment is high and oilfields may be exhausted by 2030. Privatisation in two waves, pension, health and education reforms on Chilean and American models, and rising inequality are named as the fundamental cause. The 2014 revision of the Trade Union Law, which in the author's account left only a state-controlled federation and led to the dissolution of over 600 independent unions, pushed workers towards strikes rather than bargaining. The author notes that the movement combined economic demands with calls for nationalisation and workers' control, and that some demands were met. The article also warns that unorganised workers, about two-thirds of the total according to the ILO, are exposed to manipulation, and describes the January 2022 events as a 'colour revolution' in which, it says, external forces probably played a part. Kang draws three lessons: coordinate action across sectors and regions, link the workers' movement to the socialist movement, and prevent strikes from being turned into 'colour revolutions'. The article lists four obstacles: the lack of a legal communist party, unions that cannot meet workers' demands, the difficulty of organising against transnational firms, and legal and coercive repression. On unions, it cites John Foster's suggestion that socialists work inside official unions. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of labour struggles in post-Soviet Central Asia, including the article's treatment of the January 2022 unrest and of the Kazakh left.

Resolving the dilemmas of global governance through the Silk Road spirit Dilemmas and pathways 论以丝路精神破解全球治理的困境与路径 Yin Xuepeng Xu Xiujun Yin Xuepeng and Xu Xiujun ask how global governance can be improved at a time of what they call accelerating changes unseen in a century. Their answer is that the Silk Road spirit, defined as peace and cooperation, openness and inclusiveness, mutual learning among civilisations, and mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, can offer ideological guidance for building a more just and reasonable global governance system. The article first traces how Xi Jinping formulated the Silk Road spirit between 2013 and 2017 and sets out its four meanings: a driving force of the ancient Silk Road, a system of ideas with a practical basis, the guiding principle for high-quality development of the Belt and Road Initiative, and the spiritual core of a community with a shared future for mankind. It then analyses four conflicts of governance ideas, assesses the spirit's value for resolving each, and ends with four practical paths. The authors describe global governance as split between confrontation and cooperation, protectionism and openness, decoupling and connectivity, and zero-sum thinking and win-win outcomes. They attribute the first term of each pair mainly to the United States and its allies, citing tariffs, sanctions, withdrawal from the TPP and 'conscious decoupling', and the second to China and other emerging economies. Each principle of the Silk Road spirit is then matched to one problem. Peace and cooperation counter Cold War thinking, openness counters protectionism, mutual learning counters the 'clash of civilizations', and mutual benefit counters zero-sum games. The four paths are to promote the common values of all humankind, to practise the global governance outlook of extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, to practise 'true multilateralism', and to innovate governance ideas through initiatives such as the Global Development Initiative and the Global Security Initiative. Yin and Xu conclude that the Silk Road spirit, which they say is the only foreign-affairs spirit included in the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists, summarises China's diplomatic thinking in the new era and helps move the international order towards greater justice and reason. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars link the Belt and Road Initiative to global governance and to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Lefebvre as founder of the urban philosophy of Western Marxism 列斐伏尔为西方马克思主义城市哲学奠基 Guan Wei This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2023, asks how Henri Lefebvre turned the scattered reflections on cities in Marx and Engels into a theoretical resource for a Marxist urban philosophy. Guan Wei argues that Lefebvre's systematic study of these texts, and his thinking about a path to human liberation through the city, make him the founder of Western Marxist urban philosophy. The article follows Lefebvre's reading in sequence. It begins with his claim that Marx and Engels lived through the rise of the industrial capitalist city but never treated it systematically. It then turns to his separate treatments of Engels and of Marx, and to his account of the city as a subject and a historical category. It ends with his handling of the reproduction of the relations of production. Guan reports that Lefebvre gathered Marx's and Engels's "fragments" into an approach grounded in historical materialism and the critique of political economy. In this reading Engels described the concrete life of the working class in the capitalist city, where civilisation and barbarism sit side by side as two faces of one coin. Marx, by contrast, worked from abstract principles that are intelligible only in an urban setting. For Lefebvre, the transition from feudalism to capitalism is a contradictory movement between town and country, and the city is itself a subject and a work, whose participants hold a "right to the city". That right may be marginalised, but it signals the possibility of change and points toward the "complete urbanisation of society". Guan adds that Lefebvre treats reproduction as the key to everyday alienation, space and the survival of capitalism. In his account capitalism creates new sectors of exploitation, including leisure, everyday life, knowledge, art and urbanisation, and it produces space as capital and capital as space. Guan concludes that Lefebvre's work is more than a gathering of fragments. It brings the urban question into the field of historical materialism and lays epistemological and methodological foundations for urban studies. It also exposes the contradictions and alienation of the capitalist city. Lefebvre hopes for a new urban philosophy that holds out human liberation and a new urban form, order and set of relations. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of how Lefebvre read Marx and Engels on the city and of the roots of his notions of the right to the city and complete urbanisation.

Lenin's critique of "freedom of criticism" and its lessons 列宁对“批评自由”的批判与启示 Fang Guangshun Du Chunqiu Fang and Du examine how Lenin answered the slogan of "freedom of criticism", which Eduard Bernstein put forward to "revise" Marxism from a bourgeois standpoint and which spread into the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party. The article argues that Lenin, in What Is to Be Done? and other works, exposed the slogan as a vehicle for bourgeois ideology and gave a scientific restatement of Marxism. It holds that this critique still offers guidance for ideological work today. The article first traces the origins of the slogan: the late nineteenth-century changes in capitalism, the Second International's revisionist turn, and Bernstein's demand at the 1901 Lübeck congress. It then follows its Russian variants through four periods: "legal Marxism" and economism, Menshevism after 1903, liquationism after 1908, and social chauvinism in the First World War. Four sections then set out Lenin's critique from the standpoint of Marxism's view of the people, its holistic view, its view of practice and its view of development. A final section draws lessons for China. The authors argue that Lenin treated the slogan as a cover for political aims: turning the workers' movement into a liberal "tail" and the revolutionary party into a reformist one. Against it, Lenin upheld the people's standpoint, mass initiative and the Party's ties to workers and peasants. He also defended Marxism as an integral worldview, "cast from a single piece of steel", whose parts cannot be separated. On practice and development, the authors report that Lenin demanded that theory rest on the full body of facts and be tested in revolutionary action. He also held that theory must advance with history, with proletarian struggle and with the best of human thought. The authors draw five lessons. They call for vigilance toward currents that present themselves as Marxist, for a firm people's standpoint, and for a complete and clear worldview. They also stress starting from reality and carrying theory into practice, and continuing theoretical innovation. They quote Xi Jinping on ideology as the point where hostile forces first breach a society, and link these tasks to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school style reading of Lenin's polemic against revisionism is turned into current ideological guidance.

The ideological character of Western party-system theory 西方政党制度理论的意识形态特性研究 Zhang Fei'an Zhang Fei'an asks why Western party-system theory, which presents itself as neutral science, cannot accommodate the party system led by the Communist Party of China. Taking up Xi Jinping's 2018 description of the multiparty cooperation and political consultation system as a "new type of party system", the article asks what makes the Western system "old" and why it must be transcended. Zhang's thesis is that this theory is an ideology defending the legitimacy of Western capitalist political institutions, and that Chinese scholars need to see through its "scientific illusion" before building their own party theory. The article has four parts. It first traces the rise of the theory to Cold War social science in the United States after the 1950s. It then links the theory to the hegemony of liberal-democratic discourse. The third part examines the "competitiveness" norm in the theory's branches: definition, typology and causes (and, more briefly, transition). A short conclusion draws out the implications for China. Zhang draws on Duverger, Sartori, Schattschneider, Schumpeter, Dahl, Rokkan, Lipset, Mair and others. Zhang's core argument is that party-system research was marginal until the Cold War, when the contest between the United States and the Soviet Union turned on who could claim "democracy". In Zhang's account, Schumpeter's procedural definition of democracy as competition for votes, together with Schattschneider's claim that democracy is a by-product of party competition, let liberalism annex democracy, tie it to multiparty elections and brand one-party socialism anti-democratic. Zhang says competition then became the "meta-standard" of the field. Definitions deny that non-competitive systems are party systems, typologies by party number (Duverger, Sartori) count only parties that compete for seats, and explanations of origin, whether Duverger's electoral-law approach or Lipset and Rokkan's social cleavages, never study non-Western systems. Zhang reads this through the Marx–Engels account of ideology as the ruling class presenting its interests as universal. Zhang concludes that Western theory cannot grasp the functions, rationality or advantages of China's system, because that theory rests on social division and competition and aims to prevent a party representing the people's overall interest from taking power. Understanding the Western system's "oldness" through historical materialism, Zhang argues, will strengthen Chinese scholars' theoretical self-awareness and discourse power in building a Chinese party theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Cold War political science and its party typologies, or want to see how the "new type of party system" is theoretically contrasted with Western models.

From critique to reaction: the New Right, critical theory and international relations 从批判到反动：新右翼、批判理论与国际关系 Jean-François Drolet Michael C. Williams This is a Chinese translation of an article by Jean-François Drolet and Michael C. Williams, first published in the Journal of International Political Theory (2022). It asks why radical conservatism has been so effective on the world stage and argues that the answer lies partly in the New Right's appropriation of themes from critical theory. The authors contend that Gramsci's hegemony, the Frankfurt School's analysis of capitalist mass society, and postmodernism have been turned to reactionary ends, which challenges the assumption that critical theory is inherently tied to progressive politics. The article defines the New Right as the intellectual vanguard of the radical right's revival since the end of the Cold War. It traces its origins to the French Nouvelle Droite of 1968 (Alain de Benoist and others) and its counterparts in Italy, Germany and the United States, including the paleoconservatism of Paul Gottfried and Sam Francis and today's white-nationalist "alternative right". It is organised in three main sections, on Gramsci, on the "New Class" and the Frankfurt School, and on postmodernism, followed by a conclusion. First, the authors argue that the New Right adopted a "right-wing Gramscianism": a long-term "metapolitics" of cultural struggle, on the premise that political power rests on cultural hegemony that the left now holds. Second, it draws on Frankfurt School critiques of consumerism and the culture industry, together with James Burnham's idea of a managerial "New Class", to portray liberal managerialism, identity politics and Habermasian deliberative democracy as instruments of elite control. It also accuses critical intellectuals of being co-opted. Third, it reworks postmodern distrust of Enlightenment universalism into "identitarianism" and "differentialism", in which culture and ethnicity are defended against mixing, and into Faye's "archeofuturism". The authors add that the New Right seeks to create self-conscious social agents among those "left behind" by globalisation, the very agent that critical theory has failed to find. The authors conclude that the New Right is not simply anti-intellectual or a continuation of historical fascism, though its rhetoric can foster violent, conspiratorial politics. They say it aims to take control of globalisation and build an alternative order in which capitalism thrives within a myth of shared civilisational heritage and the West is defined against "Global Islam" and the Global South. They contrast this confidence with a critical international theory paralysed by self-doubt and losing momentum. They offer no solution, but say critical scholars can no longer avoid these questions. Read the original if you study the intellectual genealogy of the contemporary radical right or the political uses and limits of Gramscian and Frankfurt School ideas in international relations theory.

The new industrial revolution and the development of socialism in the twenty-first century 新产业革命与21世纪社会主义发展 Li Caiyan Li Caiyan asks how the fourth industrial revolution, driven by artificial intelligence, big data and cloud computing, changes the conditions for socialism in the twenty-first century. The article argues that, as with the three earlier industrial revolutions, the new one brings both challenges and fresh opportunities. In Li's view, socialism's institutional advantages allow it to turn the technology towards human development. The article treats four areas in turn: the exponential growth of productive forces and the global polarisation between rich and poor; the changing make-up and agency of the working class; the effect of digital technology on proletarian unity; and artificial intelligence and the free and all-round development of the human being. Li draws on figures for China's digital economy, on Western left-wing scholars such as Judith Butler and Guy Standing, and on classic passages from Marx, Engels and Mao Zedong. Li holds that digital technology raises output while producing a "digital divide" between countries and inside Western societies, which the author links to digital capitalism and a "winner-takes-all" economy. Against Western and Russian scholars who propose plural or new middle-class agents of change, Li argues that gig workers and the "precariat" remain working-class, because Marx and Engels defined the proletariat by its relation to the means of production, not by the form of labour. Rising class conflict, protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and online organising are read as signs of reviving class consciousness. Li also lists obstacles to unity: dispersed workplaces, individualisation, gaps between countries and competition for cheap labour. Artificial intelligence is said to free time but also to produce a "new alienation". Li concludes that big data can make planning more scientific and complement the market, that socialist relations of production can narrow the digital divide in pursuit of common prosperity, and that the sharing character of the internet fits socialist values. Li adds a caution drawn from Mao Zedong against easy optimism and calls for serious institutional and cognitive responses. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how digital technology bears on class, internationalism and alienation, with references to Western left debates.

The growing overseas influence of Mao Zedong Thought and its lessons 毛泽东思想海外影响力的提升与启示 Ding Yi Ding Yi asks how Mao Zedong Thought, which the article presents as the theoretical result of the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, built up its influence abroad, and what that history teaches about promoting Chinese theory and culture internationally today. The author argues that the process passed through three stages and that its experience offers practical guidance for taking Chinese theory "global" in the new era. The first half is a historical periodisation. The early stage (to 1949) covers translations and publications through the Comintern, the Paris-based Salvation Times and a Yan'an English edition of On Coalition Government. It also covers foreign journalists, above all Edgar Snow and his Red Star Over China. The second stage (1949–1978) covers state-organised multilingual publishing of the Selected Works, with the article citing 18 languages and 48 editions in the 1960s and 70s. It also covers dissemination in Asia, Africa and Latin America. The third stage (1978 to the present) is described as a calmer, scholarly phase with research centres in South Korea, Australia, the United States and Japan. The second half draws four lessons from this record, organised by the elements of communication. On communicators, Ding argues that state leadership must be complemented by media, enterprises, think tanks, universities and non-governmental bodies, because politicised or state-led channels in some Soviet-bloc countries limited the effect. On channels, the author calls for combining traditional publishing with internet-based and other new media. On content, Ding stresses adapting to local cultures and the role of translation, citing the audience-aware Japanese translations of the Selected Works. On methods, the author points to cultural diplomacy and soft power. Ding concludes that cultural diplomacy, supported by the country's "hard power", helps shape a positive national image and a favourable international opinion climate. The author calls for Chinese theory to be communicated through a global system based on a community with a shared future for mankind, using new concepts that connect Chinese and foreign audiences, and for translation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to be standardised. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academic account of how Mao Zedong Thought's overseas reception is used to frame current international communication strategy.

The time of our lives: reflections on work and capitalist temporality 我们生命中的时间：对工作和资本主义时间性的反思 Bryan D. Palmer This text is a Chinese translation (abridged) of an essay by the Canadian historian Bryan D. Palmer, first published in Socialist Register. Written in 2020 as Covid-19 dissolved the boundaries between work and home, it asks how capital controls time and why time must again become a central socialist question. Palmer argues that the struggle over time is a class struggle that cannot be resolved by shorter hours or the slogan of 'a fair day's wage for a fair day's work', and that only abolishing the wage system would free time. The essay moves through a historical sequence. It starts with Marx's analysis of the working day and the nineteenth-century struggles for shorter hours. It then turns to the early twentieth century: the 1913 Paterson strike, the October Revolution, Taylorism and the stopwatch. It next examines the 1960s debates on leisure and alienation, centred on E. P. Thompson's 'Time, Work-Discipline and Industrial Capitalism'. It ends with the post-1973 period, the gig economy, and a critique of André Gorz. Palmer's central move draws on Marx's picture of capital as a vampire that turns the many's free time into surplus labour. The working day is therefore a variable, and capital answers legal limits by intensifying work. He credits Thompson with showing how time discipline was internalised under early industrial capitalism. He faults Thompson, however, for romanticising task-oriented pre-capitalist work and for underrating women's oppression and the incomplete reach of capitalist time among colonised and marginalised groups. Palmer reads the gig economy as both new and old, a return to the 'putting out' system with round-the-clock surveillance, and cites figures on rising working hours and automation-driven job losses. Palmer rejects Gorz's call for 'abolishing work' and a leisure society within reformed capitalism, and calls his argument a false utopianism. In Palmer's reading, Gorz misread Marx's dialectic of necessity and freedom, ignored imperialism, and treated time as a problem only of the wealthy countries. Palmer concludes that the eight-hour day no longer suffices and that a new commitment to abolishing the wage system is needed, closing with the 1968 graffiti 'beneath the paving stones, the beach'. Read the original if you want a Marxist history of working time that links Marx, Thompson and the present-day platform economy, together with a polemic against Gorz.

Plekhanov and Lenin on the October Revolution: the political disagreement and its theoretical roots 普列汉诺夫与列宁关于十月革命的政治分歧及其理论根源 Wang Zhongru Why did Georgi Plekhanov, the "father of Russian Marxism", reject the October Revolution that Lenin led? Wang argues that the break between the two men, which ran from 1903 to Plekhanov's death in 1918, was not a matter of loyalty to Marx. It came from different abilities to apply theory to practice: Plekhanov is cast as a theorist and propagandist, Lenin as a theorist who also seized the pulse of society to advance revolution. The article has four parts. It first sets out Plekhanov's rejection of the democratic dictatorship of workers and peasants and of the October Revolution, drawing on his response to Lenin's April Theses and his open letter to the Petrograd workers. It then examines his case for class cooperation during the First World War, and Lenin's philosophical defence of October in "Our Revolution" and related late writings. The last part traces the methodological roots of Plekhanov's error. Wang contends that Plekhanov treated the level of the productive forces as an absolute precondition for socialism. He quoted Marx and Engels selectively, for example on the "premature seizure of power" in Engels's Peasant War in Germany, in ways that Wang says cut across Engels's own purpose. Against this, Wang presents Lenin's "revolutionary dialectic": the general laws of history presuppose particular forms and sequences of development. Wang notes that Lenin, citing Marx's remark on a peasant war supporting a proletarian revolution, argued that a revolutionary seizure of power could create the preconditions for cultural and economic advance. Wang finds Plekhanov's dialectics confined to the conceptual level. They stressed the objective, economic side of revolution and ignored the subjective side. Plekhanov denounced dogmatism while turning some Marxist propositions into absolute dogma, and he fell into self-contradiction. Wang draws a parallel with Hegel and quotes Bukharin's verdict of a "bookish dialectician". The lesson Wang draws for Communists is to combine theory with practice and to use dialectical and historical materialism creatively. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Lenin's critics on the Marxist side are assessed, with extended quotations from Plekhanov's 1917 writings.

Lenin's thought on Party leadership in "The Tax in Kind" 列宁《论粮食税》中党的领导思想解析 Zhu Lixia Jin Doudou Zhu Lixia and Jin Doudou ask what Lenin's 1921 pamphlet "The Tax in Kind" (Lenin's Chinese title: Lun liangshi shui) contributes to the theory of Party leadership. They argue that, beneath its surface role of explaining the New Economic Policy, the text is about how a Marxist party can strengthen its leadership in a country dominated by small peasant farming. They hold that its ideas remain relevant a century later for the Communist Party of China's effort to strengthen Party leadership. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's statement at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article first sets out the background: war communism, the surplus-requisition system, the fuel and grain crises of early 1921, strikes and peasant uprisings, and the "Left" communists' attacks on the new policy. It then draws out three elements of Lenin's thinking on leadership. These are replacing requisition with a tax in kind, using capitalism to develop socialism, and opposing bureaucracy. A final section derives three lessons for the Party in the new era. On the first element, the authors argue that the tax in kind eased tension between the ruling party and workers and peasants. They say it left peasants free to dispose of their surplus, strengthened the worker-peasant alliance, and thereby reinforced centralised and unified Party leadership. On the second, they present Lenin's use of state capitalism as an intermediate link between small production and socialism, under proletarian state limits. In their account this was progress, not retreat, and it improved the Party's own building. On the third, they follow Lenin in tracing bureaucracy to feudal remnants and to the scattered small-producer base. They say it was worsened by old-regime officials entering state organs, and that Lenin proposed promoting workers from below and sending officials to investigate at grassroots level. The authors conclude that the Party today should safeguard the people's fundamental interests, uphold Party leadership over all work, and combat bureaucracy and formalism. On the last point they mention removing falsified performance indicators and using 5G, cloud computing and big data for real-time supervision in rural areas. They link China's reform and opening up to Lenin's use of capitalism to develop socialism. They also claim the Party's leadership explains China's rapid economic growth. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-building scholarship draws on Lenin's New Economic Policy writings for present-day arguments on leadership.

A century of exploration by Latin American communist parties and their present state 拉美共产党的百年探索与发展现状 Xu Shicheng Xu Shicheng, a Latin Americanist, surveys more than a century of communist organisation in Latin America and the Caribbean and asks where the parties stand today. The article argues that these parties have survived repeated setbacks and remain an important left-wing force, but that they have never become the mainstream. Apart from the Communist Party of Cuba, none has governed alone. The text opens with a historical sketch. It covers the founding of parties after the Russian Revolution, the splits of the 1950s–70s under the influence of the Sino-Soviet dispute, guerrilla warfare, the Chilean parliamentary road under Allende, the military dictatorships, and the shock of the Soviet collapse. It then profiles individual parties in three groups: those that take part in government (Brazil, Chile, Uruguay), legal opposition parties (Venezuela, Argentina, Colombia), and parties without legal registration (the two Peruvian parties and Bolivia). Each profile gives founding dates, membership, seats, leaders and guiding ideology. The central section identifies shared theoretical shifts since the 21st century. Xu reports that the parties have moved from dogmatic Marxism-Leninism to its "localisation", for instance by pairing it with Mariátegui's thought in Peru or with Bolívar's in Venezuela. Several have redefined themselves from a vanguard of the proletariat to a party of working people or a "mass" party. Most have abandoned armed struggle for legal and electoral struggle, and they reject neoliberalism while seeking a path to socialism. In practice, Xu lists electoral participation, influence on government decisions, leadership of trade unions, use of party media and social networks, and regional coordination through the São Paulo Forum and party conferences. He also lists pandemic relief measures and solidarity with Cuba and Venezuela against US sanctions. Xu also traces relations with the Communist Party of China. In his account, ties were broken in the 1960s and 70s and then restored, and many Latin American parties now praise the Chinese path. His conclusion is that the leftward turns in regional politics offer openings. To avoid marginalisation, the parties must integrate Marxism-Leninism with national conditions, innovate in theory and propose policies suited to their countries. Read the original if you want a party-by-party reference on Latin American communist parties, including membership and parliamentary strength, together with a Chinese academic view of their orientation.

Left and right: on the Labour Party's economic policy and party positioning Original title: "Labour, Left and Right: On Party Positioning and Policy Reasoning" 左与右：论英国工党的经济政策和政党定位 Michael Jacob Andrew Hindmoor This is an abridged Chinese translation of a 2022 article by Michael Jacob and Andrew Hindmoor, both of the University of Sheffield. It asks why the British Labour Party has swung between left and right since 1945. Many commentators expected Keir Starmer to move Labour towards the centre after the 2019 defeat. The authors call this the "electoral–ideological" explanation: Labour must choose between ideology and winning votes. They propose a "political economy–policy" alternative. Labour moves right and favours redistribution when the economy performs well, and moves left towards structural reform when it is seen to perform badly. The article first sets out two economic programmes. The "redistributive" programme, associated with the right, relies on growth to fund public services and welfare. The "structural reform" programme, associated with the left, stresses planning, public ownership and regulation of finance and labour. The authors use the Manifesto Project's left–right scores for Labour's election manifestos from 1945 to 2019. They test both explanations against Attlee, Gaitskell, Wilson, Kinnock, Blair and Brown, Ed Miliband and Corbyn. They give most attention to the Wilson years (1960–75), and they end with Starmer's Labour. The authors tie each leftward turn to a perceived economic problem: postwar reconstruction, the stagflation and IMF loan of the 1970s with the 1983 "Alternative Economic Strategy", and the post-2008 crisis and austerity. They tie rightward turns to sustained growth in the 1950s, the 1980s recovery and the 1992–2008 boom. Wilson's radical 1964 and 1966 economic plans, they argue, do not fit the claim that moving right wins elections. Jacob and Hindmoor add that parties and voters shape preferences as well as follow them, so the "centre" is constructed. Drawing on the Rawlsian-style critique of Anthony Downs's rational-choice model, they stress policy reasoning ("policy deliberation"): internal debates in which actors change their minds as conditions change. Examples are Stuart Holland's influence in 1973, the New Labour revisionists in the 1990s, and Peter Mandelson's revival of industrial strategy in 2008–10. The authors conclude that the economic conditions behind Labour's turn left after 2010 persist. They cite low investment, insecure work, regional inequality, an unreformed banking system and a cost-of-living crisis. They expect Labour's next manifesto to move towards the centre of the 2019 one but not necessarily back to Blair, since public opinion on economic policy remains fairly left-leaning. They also note that Rachel Reeves has proposed structural reforms. Read the original if you study the Labour Party, party-positioning theory or the debate between rational-choice and policy-reasoning accounts of party change.

The historical evolution and present state of the socialist movement in West Asia and North Africa 西亚北非地区社会主义运动的历史演变与现状 Chai Shangjin Chai Shangjin surveys socialism in the Arab world of West Asia and North Africa, from its mid-twentieth-century origins to the present. The article, a chapter in a 2023 yearbook on the international communist movement, argues that Arab nationalism and political Islam have weakened in recent years while communist and left-wing parties in Turkey, Iraq, Egypt and elsewhere have become more active. In Chai's account, these parties remain weak in the regional party landscape, and their overall rise will take time. The chapter has four parts. It first sets out the rise and main features of "Arab socialism". It then traces the history of left-wing parties in three groups: Marxist-type, socialist-type and nationalist-type. Next it reviews party developments since the "Arab Spring" of 2011 in Egypt, Tunisia, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Turkey. It ends with the movement's current characteristics and likely trends. Chai argues that Arab socialism, associated with Michel Aflaq, Gamal Abdel Nasser and the Ba'th parties, rests on three shared features: the aim of Arab liberation and unity, a strong nationalist orientation, and an Islamic basis opposed to exploitation. Socialism served as a means to national revival and was often a label covering other aims. The Egypt–Israel peace treaty of 1979 is said to have undermined Arab nationalism and with it Arab socialism. Communist parties, many founded in the 1920s under Comintern influence, are described as frequently banned and small, then struggling after the Soviet collapse. Chai finds the current movement marked by engagement with domestic struggles (for example the anti-"Islamic State" fight in Iraq), efforts at left unity, and friendly ties with the Communist Party of China. The article reports that these parties back Beijing's positions on Taiwan, Xinjiang and Hong Kong. It expects them to adjust theory and policy to new conditions, to sharpen their socialist profile, and to stay constrained by political Islam, populism and internal fragmentation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-affiliated country-by-country overview of Arab and Turkish left parties and their links with the Chinese Communist Party.

Lenin's New Economic Policy thought from the perspective of reform and its contemporary value 改革视角下的列宁新经济政策思想及其当代价值 Zhang Wei Zhang Wei asks what Lenin's New Economic Policy (NEP) can teach about reform in a socialist state. The article argues that the shift from War Communism to the NEP was a major reform in the history of socialism. In Zhang's reading, Lenin was both an advocate and a practitioner of that reform, and his thinking on it holds lessons for China's drive to comprehensively deepen reform. The article has three parts. The first traces how NEP thought took shape, from early ideas on state capitalism in 1918, through the crisis of War Communism and the peasant revolts, to the Tenth Party Congress (1921), Lenin's essay "On the Tax in Kind" and the later acceptance of markets and money. The second part organises Lenin's thinking under five headings: the motives, methods, risk prevention, implementation and safeguards of reform. The third part draws five lessons for present-day China. In Zhang's account, Lenin held that War Communism had become detached from Russia's conditions, with a small-peasant economy and little large-scale industry. It damaged the peasants' incentive to produce and worsened the lives of workers and peasants. Lenin therefore turned to using private capitalism and state capitalism, including the tax in kind and concessions to foreign capital, to promote socialism. He also treated the NEP as a retreat that needed a limit: capital had to stay under Soviet power's "supervision and calculation", with the commanding heights in state hands. Zhang adds that Lenin required Communists to learn management, even from bourgeois specialists, and to keep the Party united. Drawing on Xi Jinping's statements, Zhang proposes five lessons for comprehensively deepening reform: stay problem-oriented, lead with theoretical innovation, hold to bottom-line thinking, build cadres' capabilities, and strengthen Party leadership. The author argues that the contrast between reform in China and in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe turned largely on whether Party leadership was kept. Zhang concludes that the NEP and today's reform face similar questions, such as how to treat capital and how to build socialism in a backward country, and urges continued study of Lenin's NEP thought. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory journal links Lenin's NEP to the current reform agenda.

The world and the left 世界与左翼 Göran Therborn This is a Chinese translation, abridged, of an essay by the Swedish sociologist Göran Therborn that first appeared in New Left Review in 2022. Therborn asks where the global left stands at the end of the first quarter of the twenty-first century. He argues that the twentieth-century left was shaped by two systemic dialectics, industrial capitalism and colonialism, which had stalled by century's end. The new left of the twenty-first century, in his account, is a creative response to neoliberal globalization rather than a continuation of the old left. The essay moves through six parts. It first reviews the twentieth century's achievements and exhaustion, then the rise and current decline of neoliberal hegemony. It then profiles the new left through the alter-globalization protests, climate mobilisation and the socialist turn in Latin America and the United States. A comparison of old and new left practice follows, across social base, organisational tools, democracy, strategy and protest. The essay ends by assessing gains and losses and naming the challenges ahead. Therborn contends that digital financial capitalism no longer produces its own opponents as industrial capitalism did. Protesters are therefore mostly outsiders damaged by neoliberalism, not its key economic agents. The new left appeals to \"the people\" and radical democracy, favours movements over parties, and works through protests and uprisings. It lacks a programme or a strategy for winning power, which Therborn sees as its main difference from the twentieth-century left. He lists four tasks: the climate crisis, the risk of war under a new imperial geopolitics (which he ties to US-led sanctions and the rise of Asia), and class struggle against extreme inequality. He credits the new left with putting inequality and climate action onto mainstream agendas and with reducing inequality in Latin America. He faults it for scant institutional results beyond China, Vietnam and Cuba, which he credits to the twentieth century. Therborn concludes with cautious optimism, based on the left's creativity and mass mobilisation. He says the twentieth century left no recipe, only a heritage of experience. He calls for a left with a global outlook that opposes US hegemony and works to prevent a new world war. He also argues that the loss of a socialist vision is serious and that a long march needs a direction. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist sociologist's periodisation of the twentieth- and twenty-first-century left, including his views on geopolitics and Asia's rise.

Mechanisms by which high-quality Party building in universities can lead high-quality development of ideological and political work among university students 高质量党建引领大学生思想政治工作高质量发展的机制研究 Zhang Yao Zhang Yao, a university Party official, asks how Party building in Chinese universities can guide and raise the quality of ideological and political work among students. The article argues that the two are unified in the practice of running socialist universities rooted in Chinese soil, and that both serve the mission of educating people for the Party and talent for the country. Zhang's answer is a set of four mechanisms: organisational management, coordination and linkage, evaluation and assessment, and support and guarantees. The article has three parts. The first sets out why high-quality Party building leading high-quality ideological and political work matters. The second explains the internal logic linking the two. The third proposes the four mechanisms and illustrates them with examples from Huazhong University of Science and Technology and other unnamed universities. Zhang quotes Xi Jinping repeatedly, on ideological and political work as the lifeline of all work, on the Party's overall leadership of education, and on moral education as the fundamental task. On significance, Zhang points to three pressures: the traits of present-day students, who are described as capable and public-spirited but still forming their values and so open to competing currents of thought and online influence; new demands on student Party work; and external challenges. In this last point the author says Western countries, led by the United States, are containing China and attempting ideological infiltration, so universities must hold their ideological ground. On internal logic, Zhang says Party building guides ideological work politically, organisationally and culturally. Ideological work in turn gives Party building its goals, working models and teaching staff, and both share the aim of cultivating a new generation for the era. The four mechanisms are concrete. Party committees would join decision-making and oversight, and the student affairs department would take the lead. Platforms and teams would be integrated through one-stop student communities, unified Party-Youth League-class organisation and "walking ideological and political classes". Student Party members would be assessed over their whole membership cycle, with results used for rewards and discipline. Support would come from political-leadership requirements, standardised student Party branches and a strengthened staff of counsellors and class advisers. Read the original if you want a practitioner's account of how a university leader frames Party building and student ideological work, with institutional examples from Huazhong University of Science and Technology.

Building the new development pattern and seizing the initiative in future development 构建新发展格局把握未来发展主动权 Wang Tinghui Writing in the Party-state newspaper Economic Daily in October 2023, Wang Tinghui asks why the Party Central Committee under Xi Jinping decided to build a new development pattern and how it should be built. The pattern is defined as one with the domestic circulation as the mainstay and the domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. Wang argues that it is a strategic response to changes in China's stage of development, environment and conditions. In this reading it will secure China's economic foundations and its "initiative" in future development. The commentary has two parts. The first sets out three aspects of the pattern's strategic significance. The second identifies four priority areas for systematic deployment. Throughout, Wang draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on the official framing of the principal contradiction in society and of the "two overall situations". On significance, Wang argues that the pattern fits the new stage of development and the changed principal contradiction. It also helps coordinate the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with what the article calls the world's "great changes unseen in a century", at a time of rising unilateralism, protectionism and weakened traditional international circulation. Finally, it draws on China's changing comparative advantages: rising labour costs and resource constraints on one side, a very large market, a middle-income group of over 400 million and a complete industrial system on the other. On priorities, Wang calls for stronger endogenous momentum in the domestic circulation through expanded domestic demand and deeper reform. Wang also urges a modern industrial system built on high-level scientific and technological self-reliance and a real-economy focus. Further proposals are coordinated urban–rural and regional development with a unified national market, and a higher-quality international circulation through high-standard opening up. Wang concludes that making the domestic circulation the mainstay does not mean closing the door. Instead, domestic demand potential should be used to link domestic and international markets more closely and to attract global resources. This, Wang says, will strengthen China's capacity to allocate resources globally and keep the strategic initiative. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese policy writers justify and operationalise the dual circulation strategy.

The problem of gender identity in contemporary Western feminist research 当代西方女性主义研究中的性别身份问题 He Cuixiang He Cuixiang asks what a woman is and how gender identity should be understood, a question the author treats as central to contemporary feminist research. The article argues that neither biological essentialism nor pure social constructivism gives an adequate answer. Gender identity, in the author's view, should rest on the mutual fit of biological, sociocultural and psychoanalytic factors. The article moves through three ways of defining woman. It begins with biological definitions, from traditional patriarchal norms (the Chinese 'three obediences and four virtues') to radical feminism and Shulamith Firestone's The Dialectic of Sex. It then turns to social constructionism, from Simone de Beauvoir to Judith Butler's theory of performativity, and to Lacanian psychoanalysis and its account of feminine jouissance. A fourth section reviews current disputes in identity politics. He sets out three debates. The first concerns the relation between sex and gender: Butler treats even the body as constructed, while critics such as Somer Brodribb hold that ignoring biological difference denies the female body. The author adds that gender must also be read through class, race, colonialism and capitalism. The second concerns whether a unified category of 'woman' is needed. Butler rejects it as exclusionary, but Iris Marion Young, Seyla Benhabib, Nancy Fraser and Martha Nussbaum reply that the concept is necessary for criticising patriarchy. The third concerns the goal of liberation. He argues that identity politics in the third wave produces a 'difference dilemma' that fragments feminism and undermines universal rights, and cites US debates over gender policy and political correctness. Nussbaum's capabilities approach is offered as a way beyond it. He rejects radical feminism's proposal to abolish women's reproductive role through technology. The author accepts cultural tolerance of gender plurality but urges caution in social construction and in law and policy. Feminism, the article says, should move beyond identity politics towards social emancipation and the cultivation of basic human capabilities, with attention to poor working women. The author adds that standards for a good life for women vary across societies, and that China's family-centred culture differs from Western individualism. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese overview of Western debates on sex, gender and identity from Beauvoir to Butler, Lacan and Nussbaum.

Towards a culturally conservative critique of modernity Kołakowski's twofold critique of utopianism and liberalism as a vantage point 走向一种文化保守主义的现代性批判 Yan Yan Utopianism and liberalism are usually treated as sworn enemies in Western political thought, and Marxism is often wrongly labelled a utopianism. Yan Yan examines how the Polish neo-Marxist Leszek Kołakowski, writing from a position of cultural conservatism, criticised both. In Yan's account, Kołakowski held that both can lead to totalitarianism and that the right course is to resist the temptation of uniformity and seek balance among competing values. Yan defends Marxism's scientific character while treating Kołakowski's ideas as partly instructive. The article has three parts. The first covers Kołakowski's critique of utopian 'future society', including his types of utopia (epistemological, political, revolutionary) and his 'three motifs' reading of Marx. The second covers his critique of the liberal 'open society' in dialogue with Karl Popper, Karl Polanyi and Friedrich Hayek. A closing section places his thought in its Central and East European context and compares his idea of inconsistency with Aristotle's mean. Yan argues that Kołakowski attacks a specific, levelling kind of utopia that promises final reconciliation and the end of evil, then wrongly attributes it to Marx. Drawing on Ernst Bloch and Agnes Heller, Yan distinguishes a 'good' utopia, a value-rational orientation towards a goal, from a 'bad', ahistorical one, and cites Marx and Engels in The German Ideology to show that communism is a real movement and not an ideal. Against liberalism, Kołakowski holds that the open society's values (market, democracy, individual freedom) conflict with one another. Pursuing them uniformly would threaten that society, and a measure of tradition and 'irrational' taboo is indispensable. Yan finds his critique of liberal equality of opportunity pertinent, since it would require abolishing the family and imposing collective education, though Yan sets aside his turn to Christian theology as religious mysticism. Yan concludes that Kołakowski rejects uniformity without defending difference unconditionally: he seeks a dynamic balance between universality and particularity, and says one can be a 'conservative-liberal-socialist'. For him history has no happy endpoint, and every improvement carries a cost. Yan reads this against the Central and East European experience of the twentieth century. Yan warns against his misreading of Marxism but finds philosophical wisdom in his stress on human finitude and the universal–particular relation. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese Marxist assessment of Kołakowski, or of the debate over whether Marxism is utopian.

Laos: the 11th Party Congress and new progress in socialist renovation 老挝：召开党的十一大，社会主义革新事业取得新进展 Fang Wen Hai Xian This year-in-review chapter, from a 2021–2022 report on the international communist movement, examines how the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP) advanced what it calls socialist renovation in 2021. Fang and Hai argue that the Party's 11th Congress, followed by the second and third plenums of the 11th Central Committee, set a five-year course. In their account, the Party's centralised leadership, applied during the pandemic, produced progress at home and in foreign relations, above all with China. The chapter has four parts. It first reviews the 11th Congress (January 2021): the achievements of the previous five years, four lessons of renovation, and the targets of the Ninth Five-Year Plan for 2021–2025. It then covers domestic developments in 2021: the two plenums, laws on budget losses, drug control and the environment, the 30th anniversary of the 1991 constitution, and the pandemic response. A third part treats diplomacy with China, Vietnam and other states. A short conclusion looks ahead to 2022. The authors report Secretary-General Thongloun Sisoulith's findings: average GDP growth of 5.8% over five years despite Covid-19, 3.5% growth in 2021, and social security coverage of 94%. The four lessons are strengthening Party-building, developing distinctive industries, developing human resources, and strictly carrying out Party decisions. The plan aims at average growth of over 4% and per capita income of 2,887 US dollars by 2025, within a socialist-oriented market economy. The chapter gives particular weight to the China–Laos Railway, opened in December 2021. In the authors' reading it is a flagship of the Belt and Road Initiative, linking it to Laos's shift from a 'land-locked' to a 'land-linked' country, and a model of cooperation between socialist states. They also describe Chinese vaccine and medical aid, and the building of a China–Laos community with a shared future. For 2022 the authors list five tasks. They are to localise Marxism-Leninism in Laos and apply Kaysone Phomvihane Thought, to strengthen Party-building, to keep the line of principled comprehensive renovation, to build a socialist rule-of-law state and modernise governance, and to integrate into regional and international processes. They present resistance to 'peaceful evolution' by hostile forces, and to 'self-evolution' within, as part of the ideological task. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-aligned Chinese account of Lao policy documents, statistics and China–Laos–Vietnam relations in 2021.

Primitive accumulation and the contemporary critique of capitalist patriarchy An autonomist feminist perspective based on Federici 原始积累与资本主义父权制的当代批判 Dai Xuehong Wu Jiacheng Dai and Wu take up the work of Silvia Federici, the Italian autonomist Marxist and feminist theorist, whom they say Chinese scholarship has neglected. Chinese research on autonomism, they note, has concentrated on Antonio Negri and Michael Hardt and overlooked autonomist feminism, the school's most important branch. The article argues that Federici extended Marx's analysis of primitive accumulation to women's social position and the reproduction of labour-power. On this reading, the 16th–17th century witch hunt was a foundation of capitalism and wage labour, and a source of capitalist patriarchy. The article has four parts. It first outlines Italian autonomist Marxism and its feminist wing (Dalla Costa, James, Fortunati and Federici) and the Wages for Housework campaign. It then presents Federici's mature theory, developed from the 1980s and above all in Caliban and the Witch (2004). A third part follows her argument into the era of neoliberal globalisation, drawing on her experience teaching in Nigeria in the 1980s. A conclusion assesses her influence on feminist Marxism, Negri and Hardt, Christian Fuchs's theory of digital labour, and social reproduction theory in the United States. The authors argue that, for Federici, primitive accumulation separated producers from the means of production and also separated production from reproduction. The witch hunt, in this account, pushed women out of waged work and made their bodies a machine for producing workers. This created what she calls the patriarchy of the wage: men gain power through wages, while women are controlled through unpaid reproductive labour. In the second move, Dai and Wu say Federici treats primitive accumulation as a permanent mechanism within capitalism, not a one-off prehistory. She combines Luxemburg's and Harvey's ideas of an "outside" that capital must keep appropriating, and counts women's domestic labour as such an outside. Contemporary violence against women, including enclosure of their bodies and repression of their resistance to land privatisation, is read as class conflict and not merely gender conflict. The authors conclude that Federici developed Marxist-feminist gender theory and, in their words, achieved a real union of Marxism and feminism. They credit her with showing patriarchy to be intrinsic to capitalism and with opening a new field of critique around non-productive or dispossessive accumulation. They hold that she deserves more attention and deeper discussion. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of autonomist feminism and Federici's theory of primitive accumulation, or want to see how Chinese Foreign Marxism studies receives Western feminist Marxism.

North Korea: Holding the Eighth Party Congress and advancing socialist construction 朝鲜：召开党的八大，推进社会主义建设 Li Chengri This chapter from a report on the international communist movement examines the Eighth Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea, held in Pyongyang in January 2021, and the steps taken in 2021 to carry out its decisions. Li argues that the Congress reinforced Kim Jong Un's sole leadership, kept the line of concentrating all efforts on economic construction, and strengthened Party discipline. In Li's account, North Korea will keep to this course despite sanctions, the pandemic and a stalled international situation. The article has three parts. The first describes the Congress itself: the revised Party rules, the restored post of General Secretary, the personnel changes and the new five-year economic plan for 2021–2025. The second surveys 2021 implementation under four headings: the sole leadership system and 'unity of one mind'; economic construction; livelihood, science and technology; and external relations, covering China, other socialist states and the Korean peninsula. The third offers a short outlook, drawing on the Fourth Plenum of the Eighth Central Committee in December 2021. Li makes three main moves. First, the Congress is read as consolidating Kim's absolute authority through Kimilsungism-Kimjongilism, the General Secretary post and a merged, strengthened Central Inspection Commission, together with the 'people-first principle' as the Party's basic political method. Second, Li points to the shift in delegate composition from military to administrative and economic personnel, new economic bodies, Kim's open admission that the previous plan largely failed, and 2021 figures. These include the report to the UN on the 2030 Agenda, which Li cites to show that the economy was still growing rather than shrinking continuously, as some overseas media reported. Third, Li presents foreign policy as giving priority to traditional friendship with China, as shown by exchanges of congratulatory messages and a new export processing zone at Musan. North Korea's line towards the United States is described as 'strength for strength, goodwill for goodwill'. Li concludes that, although North Korea faces great difficulties and sanctions are unlikely to ease soon, it will keep to the line of concentrating on economic construction and the 2021–2025 plan. Its external policy is expected to move in a positive and peaceful direction, and China–DPRK friendly cooperation is expected to expand. The article is largely descriptive and takes North Korean and Chinese official statements at face value. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of the Eighth Congress and the 2021 follow-up measures, with dates, personnel and policy details.

Innovating the research paradigm of foreign Marxism 创新国外马克思主义研究范式 Lan Jiang Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2023, Lan Jiang argues that Chinese research on foreign Marxism, which has been productive since the 1980s, has reached a turning point. In the author's view, the field must move beyond translating and analysing foreign Marxist thinkers. It should reinterpret them through a Chinese discourse system, be guided by problems, and contribute to building China's own independent knowledge system. The piece first describes the historical mission of the field after reform and opening up. It then reviews three decades of expansion, from individual thinkers to schools and national traditions, and to new areas such as ecological, postcolonial and feminist Marxism. It next sets out two current problems and closes with a proposal for a new research structure. Lan names early Chinese translators and the main figures introduced, from Lukács, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School to French and analytical Marxists. Lan identifies two weaknesses. Early work concentrated on texts and ideas and neglected their historical setting. Lan argues that figures such as Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, Baudrillard and John Bellamy Foster responded to specific stages of capitalism, so reading text against text is like buying the casket and returning the pearl. Lan also holds that these thinkers often read Marx through Western ideological discourse. Fromm's humanist reading, which sets the young Marx against the Marx of Capital, is the example given. Lan then describes Chinese scholarship as a coordinate system. The existing vertical axis sorts thinkers by period, country and school, which Lan says clarifies lineages but separates national traditions. The proposed horizontal axis would re-frame foreign Marxism with Chinese questions, concepts and discourse. Lan calls for foreign Marxism to be reread in the context of the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and drawing on China's concrete conditions and traditional culture. Lan's example is the digital economy: scholars should use critics such as Marcuse, Stiegler and David Harvey without simply repeating their critiques. They should consider how to avoid new inequality from capital monopoly and let the digital economy benefit all people. The author presents this as expressing scholarly self-confidence and as a foundation for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a short statement of how a Chinese philosopher proposes to reorient the study of Western and foreign Marxism.

"Being" or "existence"? A discussion of Hegel's Science of Logic “是”还是“存在”——关于黑格尔《逻辑学》的讨论 Wang Lu Wang Lu reflects on a lecture he gave at a reading group on Hegel's Lesser Logic organised by the Marxist philosophy history section of the Institute of Philosophy, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The question is how Hegel's core concept Sein should be rendered in Chinese: as 'shi' (roughly the copula 'is') or as 'cunzai' (existence). Wang maintains that translating Sein as 'existence' is a mistranslation and that it must be read as 'is', in the sense of the copula, if Hegel is to be understood. The piece opens with the history of Chinese translations. He Lin first rendered Sein as 'you' (have/there is), then as 'cunzai', and sometimes used both; Yang Yizhi used 'you' for the Science of Logic, while Liang Cunxiu and Xue Hua followed 'cunzai'. Wang then reports the discussion after his talk, which centred on whether Sein is 'is' or 'existence', and sets out two main objections and several lesser ones. Wang answers the first objection, that Hegel speaks of the beginning of logic and so means 'existence', by arguing that Hegel says the beginning is logical and must therefore start from the logic inherited from Aristotle. In that logic the basic form is 'S is P', from which one can find 'is' and 'not' but never 'existence' or 'nothing'. Against the second objection, that 'existence' is the most abstract, undetermined concept, he argues that the Chinese word is a verb with its own content, close to 'there is', so it lacks the immediacy and indeterminacy Hegel requires. Only the copula taken out of a sentence loses its determination and becomes Hegel's 'pure is'. He adds that Dasein is the noun form of 'ist da', and that Hegel distinguishes Existenz separately. Wang also criticises how his critics argue: they bring in material from elsewhere rather than discuss the passages in question, and they speak of 'is all the way through' in general terms without engaging his many quoted texts. He attributes the objections to knowledge structures built on translations full of 'existence', and suggests that adding logical theory might change the outcome. He welcomes the reading group as academic progress. Read the original if you are interested in the Chinese debate over translating being and Sein, and in a logic-based reading of Hegel's starting concepts.

A critical reflection on three modes of ecological critique in contemporary foreign Marxism 批判性反思当代国外马克思主义生态批判的三种模式 Feng Wangzhou Feng Wangzhou asks how contemporary Marxism outside China has criticised the ecological crisis of capitalism, and where that critique falls short. Writing in a Chinese Social Sciences Today piece of July 2023, Feng argues that since the 1960s foreign Marxism has taken an "ecological turn". Three modes stand out: ecological Marxism, eco-socialism, and historical-geographical materialism. Feng judges each valuable but marked by shared theoretical weaknesses. The article first outlines each mode in turn. Ecological Marxism, associated with James O'Connor, John Bellamy Foster, Joel Kovel, William Leiss, Ben Agger and André Gorz, among others, is presented as the theoretical base. Eco-socialism is traced through three generations, from Adam Schaff to Leiss, Agger and Gorz, then to Georges Labica, Reiner Grundmann and David Pepper. Historical-geographical materialism, linked to Henri Lefebvre, David Harvey and Edward Soja, ties ecological questions to space. A final section sets out the three shortcomings and draws a conclusion for China. In Feng's account, ecological Marxism traces the crisis to capitalism as a whole and offers theories such as the dialectic of disappointed expectations, the double crisis and the metabolism concept. Eco-socialism blames the capitalist system for the crisis and favours grassroots democracy, non-violent gradual reform and a steady-state economy. Historical-geographical materialism holds that capital turns space into a site of accumulation, making nature a "tap" and a "sink". This produces what Feng calls ecological imperialism at the global level. The three shortcomings are these. The modes stress theory over revolutionary practice and so risk utopianism. They remain inside the capitalist system, offer no path beyond it, and ignore the global significance of ecological civilization under socialism with Chinese characteristics, which Feng says leaves them Eurocentric. They also "rebuild" Marx's and Engels's ecological thought in ways that exaggerate or distort it. Feng concludes that the roots of the ecological crisis must be understood through the capitalist system and its mode of production, with a dialectical view of capital's logic and vigilance against ecological traps. China should be guided by Xi Jinping's thought on ecological civilization and shift towards green, coordinated development under the five development concepts. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of how three strands of Western Marxist ecological thought are classified and criticised from the standpoint of Chinese official ecological theory.

The "dangers" and "opportunities" of generative artificial intelligence 生成式人工智能的“危”与“机” Tang Xinghua Writing in August 2023 in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), Tang Xinghua asks how humans should assess generative AI, which the author says is beginning to show human-like creativity. Tang's thesis is that its arrival is both a danger and an opportunity (the Chinese word "wei ji" combines the two). The author calls for a combined judgement of both sides and a search for the "best possible way" of living with the technology. This short commentary is divided into two parts, "Challenges" and "Opportunities", and closes with a general conclusion. It draws on several Western thinkers: Bernard Stiegler on technology and "proletarianization", Thomas Kuhn's paradigm theory, Maurice Merleau-Ponty on embodied perception, and Norbert Wiener and Yuval Noah Harari on automation and the future of work. On the challenges, Tang argues that technological unemployment is unavoidable as more mental labour is replaced, although earlier industrial revolutions show that many workers found new jobs after retraining. Following Stiegler, the author describes technology as stripping people of craft knowledge, life knowledge and finally rational knowledge, and says generative AI is approaching the second and third stages. Using Kuhn, Tang adds that most mental work is routine, like "normal science", and so is replaceable. On the opportunities, Tang holds that AI still cannot do work that needs high creativity, flexibility, organisation or personal presence. Drawing on Merleau-Ponty, the author says embodied, emotional and memory-laden cognition is beyond AI. Tang therefore urges learning through direct experience in real settings, and a love of knowledge pursued freely rather than for its usefulness. Tang concludes that generative AI calls for changes in learning, education and social structure. The author also says philosophy and ethics must become a "study of the future" that anticipates problems, so that technology serves a good life for humanity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese philosophy scholar draws on Stiegler, Kuhn and Merleau-Ponty to frame generative AI in 2023.

The radical feminist theory of social reproduction Informal labour, the majority world and the need for inclusive theory and politics 激进女性主义的社会再生产理论 Alessandra Mezzadri This text is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by Alessandra Mezzadri of SOAS, University of London, first published in Radical Philosophy. It asks whether social reproduction, meaning the daily and generational reproduction of workers and labour-power, creates value in the Marxist sense. Mezzadri answers yes. She argues that this is especially clear once attention moves from the West to the "majority world", where most people work informally. The article first reviews recent Social Reproduction Theory (SRT), notably the collection edited by Tithi Bhattacharya, with Nancy Fraser, Susan Ferguson and David McNally among its contributors. It then returns to earlier radical feminist work by Selma James, Maria Rosa Dalla Costa, Leopoldina Fortunati, Silvia Federici, Maria Mies, Rhoda Reddock, Angela Davis and Antonella Picchio. A further section contrasts the Western focus of SRT with the geography of informal labour, citing International Labour Organization figures. The article ends by discussing the politics that follows from this. Mezzadri contends that SRT tends to attend to care institutions in Europe and North America, and that it sometimes treats use-value activities as non-value-producing. She calls this reasoning circular, because it assumes what it needs to prove. Drawing on the cases of India and China, she argues that in contexts of informal and informalised labour, a strict line between productive and reproductive spheres is misleading. She says reproductive spheres add to value generation in three ways. They tighten control over labour beyond working hours, as in factory dormitories. They externalise the costs of reproduction onto households and communities, which amounts to a de facto subsidy to capital. And they sustain the formal subsumption of labour under capital, as in home-based work within fragmented global production. Mezzadri concludes that theoretical divisions are political. Excluding unpaid work from value creation, she argues, implicitly ranks forms of exploitation and gives paid labour a priority that undermines solidarity. She calls for inclusive theory and politics that link struggles over production and reproduction. She also warns against a capitalist "monism" that rests on Western experience and creates new dualisms of its own. Read the original if you study Marxist-feminist value theory, informal labour in the Global South, or the debate between early domestic-labour analysis and Social Reproduction Theory.

Rosa Luxemburg's theory of socialism and its limits With a note on the fundamental divergence between Luxemburg and Lenin 卢森堡的社会主义理论及其限度——兼论卢森堡与列宁理论的根本分歧 Shu Xin Hu Hui Shu Xin and Hu Hui ask how Rosa Luxemburg's theory of how to achieve and how to build socialism should be understood, and why it clashed so sharply with Lenin's. They argue that her theory has distinctive strengths, notably its commitment to revolution and to the people as the subject of socialism. In their view it is nonetheless limited by the historical conditions of her time and by a detachment from the actual workers' movement in both West and East. The article, published in 2022, begins with a short history of how Soviet and Chinese scholarship has treated Luxemburg, from Stalin's 1930s charge of 'Menshevism' to later Chinese reassessments. It then has three parts. The first reconstructs the logical premises of her theory in The Accumulation of Capital and her view of the early twentieth century. The second sets out her answers on how to achieve socialism (against Bernstein's revisionism) and how to build it (in her critique of the Bolsheviks). The third examines the theory's limits. On the core of her theory, the authors report that Luxemburg saw capitalism as bound for collapse once non-capitalist environments disappeared, so that the proletariat had to make revolution before then. She held that reform cannot grow peacefully into socialism, that the masses are the primary subject of revolution, and that the party should follow them. She also held that socialism needs democracy, including bourgeois democratic forms emptied of class content, with the dictatorship of the proletariat as its guarantee. The authors locate the root of the Lenin dispute in the question of the revolutionary subject: Lenin held that class consciousness must be 'imported' into the movement by the party, whereas Luxemburg stressed the workers' 'self-centralism'. They identify three limits: she discarded Marx's reproduction schema yet reduced every new feature of imperialism to the general logic of accumulation; she viewed Russia through 'Western European spectacles' and missed the revolutionary role of backward nations; and she criticised revisionism without examining its roots in workers' everyday legal struggles. The authors conclude that, despite flashes of insight, Luxemburg's theory was too abstract and detached from the real conditions of socialist movements in East and West, which restricted its influence. They judge that Lenin's innovations had far greater historical impact and that his criticism of her was necessary. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Luxemburg that sets her against Lenin on party organisation, democracy and imperialism, and that shows how her work is evaluated in Chinese scholarship.

Lenin's view of the essence of socialism: economic and political perspectives 列宁的社会主义本质观：经济与政治的视角 Wang Zhongru How did Lenin understand what socialism fundamentally is? Wang Zhongru argues that Lenin kept to the basic position of Marx and Engels, but, by contrasting socialism with capitalism and by working through the difficulties of building it in Russia, reached conclusions of both theoretical and practical value. In Wang's reading, Lenin's view can be reconstructed along two dimensions, the economic and the political. The article has four main parts. It first looks at Lenin's limited direct treatment of human liberation and development, drawing mainly on the Party programmes of 1902 to 1919 and on his definition of class. It then turns to his understanding of the essence of capitalism, before setting out the economic essence and the political essence of socialism. A short conclusion links the findings to contemporary Chinese practice. Wang holds that the Party programmes treat public ownership of the means of production as a means, while the welfare and all-round development of all members of society is the end and the essence of socialism. Lenin defined capitalism by commodity production and the commodity status of labour-power. Wang finds a logical gap here, since this excludes commodity production under any later social formation. Wang argues that the programme's stress on capitalist relations of production, above all ownership, gives a more accurate account than the market mechanism, citing later practice, especially socialism with Chinese characteristics. For Lenin's socialism, Wang distinguishes a theoretical socialism (the "ought") from a practical one (the "is"). Its economic essence is large-scale industry, public ownership, and organising labour and distribution through the state or society rather than the market, ending anarchy in production. Its political essence is the dictatorship of the proletariat, understood as one class holding power and exercising political leadership, with the Soviets as one form and not a universal model. Wang concludes that Lenin located the essence of socialism in the welfare and all-round development of all members of society. This is realised economically through a mode of organising production and distribution different from capitalism, and politically through proletarian leadership of society via its vanguard. Wang says that drawing on Lenin's findings is part of the Chinese Communist Party's drive to build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The Party's own understanding of the question is left for separate study. Read the original if you are interested in a Chinese Party-school reading of Lenin's concepts of capitalism, socialism and the dictatorship of the proletariat, including its critical remarks on his stress on non-market planning.

What is the "matter" in the materialist conception of history? 何为唯物史观的“物”？ Zhou Jiaxin Zhou Jiaxin takes up a recurring question in discussions of the basic principles of Marxist philosophy: how should the "matter" or "thing" (wu) in the materialist conception of history be understood? The common answer is that it refers not to ordinary empirical objects but to concrete, historical social relations. Zhou accepts that this points to the methodological essence of the theory but argues it does not exhaust the issue. A full grasp of the method, the author contends, must go beyond asking what the "thing" is and return to real social and historical life, seeking a scientific answer to the relation of thought and being in practice that changes the world. The piece, a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2023, begins with the historical development of the concept of materialism. It traces its use from the seventeenth century and mechanical materialism, through the vulgar materialism of the nineteenth century that Engels criticised, to twentieth-century Marxist-Leninist, Western Marxist and physicalist currents. It then turns to Marx's own vocabulary and closes with the Capital section on commodity fetishism as a worked example. Zhou argues that Marx and Engels never posed the question of what the \"thing\" in historical materialism is. For them, materialism meant rejecting Hegelian speculation, Feuerbach's anthropology and the metaphysics of political economy in favour of the actual process of material production.
