Zhou instead distinguishes four German categories in Marx: material or stuff (Material, Stoffe); the thing (Ding); the object-like thing (Sache), linked to property rights as the counterpart of personhood; and the object (Gegenstand). In the fetishism section Marx moves among these terms deliberately, to remind readers that behind a heap of commodities lie social relations. Value is an \"ideal thing\", yet the social relations it expresses are objectively real, grasped through the power of abstraction rather than a microscope. Zhou concludes that the answer lies not in finding the substance that materialism is \"of\", but in grasping the methodological essence of the theory as it is applied. The author points to Engels's basic question of thought and being, Lenin's definition of matter as objective reality, and Mao Zedong's formulation of seeking truth from facts. Zhou calls on those who uphold historical materialism today to engage the real historical process, identify the idealist nature of erroneous currents of thought, and grasp the objective material reality that underlies thought. Read the original if you want a compact philological and conceptual account of how Marx's different German words for \"thing\" bear on debates about materialism.

Certainty in the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义发展的确定性 Ronnie Lins Ronnie Lins, a Brazilian scholar of China, offers a short commentary on why China's path can offer certainty in an uncertain world. Lins argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) socialism with Chinese characteristics has entered a new era, and that the Communist Party of China, through its distinctive model of governance, will lead the people past structural and practical challenges. Lins expresses confidence that China will build a modern socialist country by the middle of this century. The article is organised under four headings: certainty amid uncertainty; building a modern Chinese civilization; sharing a better future with humanity; and a closing assessment. It draws heavily on the reports of the 19th and 20th Party Congresses and on speeches by Xi Jinping, including the declaration of victory over absolute poverty in February 2021. Lins surveys policy areas in turn: livelihoods, health and employment, education and culture, economic development, ecology, and peace and security. Lins's central claim is that China's planning system links theory to practice and keeps the people's wellbeing first. In this account, targets are adjusted over time through the Party Congress, the National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, with deputies feeding public concerns into plans. The author presents high-quality development as resting on five areas: a high-level socialist market economy, a modern industrial system, rural revitalization, coordinated regional development and high-level opening up. Lins adds that technological self-reliance, green and low-carbon transition, and defensive national defence policy together support what the article calls Chinese modernization. On education, Lins offers a personal view that "integration" is the entry point for future challenges and that the government should systematically evaluate teaching methods. Lins concludes that China has shown the world the path of a prosperous, democratic, civilised, harmonious and beautiful modern socialist country. The author voices admiration for China's successes and firm belief that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is near, crediting Party leadership, clear planning and broad popular participation. Lins also says these achievements benefit the world and that the Chinese people wish to share a better, more equal future with humanity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Brazilian China specialist presents the official narrative of China's new era for a Chinese readership.

A rebuttal of foreign claims that Chinese history and culture were interrupted 对国外有关中国历史文化中断的驳议 Zhang Haipeng Responding to Xi Jinping's remarks at the June 2023 symposium on cultural inheritance and development, which stressed the continuity and innovativeness of Chinese civilization, Zhang Haipeng takes up a question debated abroad: whether Chinese history was broken in 1949. Zhang rejects the view of some foreign and Chinese scholars that the founding of the People's Republic ended historical continuity, calling it a superficial opinion. The article argues that institutional change and cultural continuity belong together in Chinese history. This short commentary, published in a newspaper, first surveys Chinese dynastic history from the Zhou to the Qing. It picks out the Qin centralised state, the Tang imperial examination system, and the Yuan and Ming provincial system as moments of reform. It then turns to the late Qing reforms, the 1911 Revolution and the Republic, and the adoption of Marxism after the October Revolution. It cites foreign discussion by Harvard's William Kirby and by Japanese scholars including Yamada Tatsuo and Kubo Toru, but does not engage their arguments in detail. Zhang's central move is that changes of social character and system, from slave society to feudal society, then semi-colonial and semi-feudal society, then socialism, have always occurred in Chinese history and are not ruptures. The article describes the transition to socialism with Chinese characteristics as a great innovation within continuity. Continuity is to be judged by whether national unification, central authority, ethnic interaction and ideological consistency were kept, and by whether people's wellbeing improved. It also looks at cultural values such as 'the world belongs to all' and the people-as-foundation idea. The author contends that Republican parliamentary and party politics failed because they were imported and cut off from the people. In this account, the Party's adaptation of Marxism and its people-centred institutions have realised the old minben idea at a higher level. Zhang concludes that the Chinese nation's progressive spirit, which keeps what is sound without clinging to the old, should be built into the Party's spiritual lineage and the Two Integrations. On this basis the author says China can create a new cultural form of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Chinese historian answers the 'rupture of 1949' thesis in official terms and links it to current Party cultural policy.

German scholarship on Marx's London Notebooks: a review 德国学界关于马克思《伦敦笔记》的研究综述 Wu Ting This literature review surveys German research on Marx's London Notebooks of 1850–1853, concentrated in the 1970s to 1990s. Wu Ting notes that this work appeared when 'bourgeois Marxology' was fashionable in the West. German scholars therefore stressed that the Notebooks are an internal link in Marx's intellectual development and an important foundation of Capital and its manuscripts. The review has three parts. The first covers the Halle research group on Marx and Engels, led by Wolfgang Jahn, which edited Notebooks I–XIV for the second Marx-Engels Complete Works (MEGA2) before its dissolution in 1991. The second covers overall readings of the Notebooks, centred on Jahn and Dieter Noske's 1979 study, together with specialist work on money, credit, banking and the major texts. The third covers studies of pre-capitalist modes of production and Asiatic landownership in the later, still unpublished notebooks. Wu reports that Jahn read the Notebooks as the prehistory of Marx's 1858 'six-book plan' for his critique of political economy. Jahn and Noske, in this account, reject the Marxological split between Marx's research method and his mode of presentation and between a 'young' and a 'late' Marx. They hold that the 1848–49 revolutions led Marx to crisis theory and that the Notebooks prepared the discovery of surplus-value theory. Other scholars (Vasina, Müller, Schellhardt, Arnhold) trace the monetary and credit analyses, and Jahn treats the 'Reflections' of 1851 as a high point. The review then turns to Schellhardt's reading of Marx's extracts from Karl Hüllmann on medieval towns and finance, and to Winkelmann's work on Prescott's histories of Mexico and Peru. It ends with Wolfgang Rein's study of the Asiatic landownership extracts, which Rein links to Marx's later account of primitive accumulation and the subordination of pre-capitalist structures to capital. Wu concludes that the Halle group made major contributions through its collection and editing of sources and its reconstruction of the historical thread of Marx's economic research. The review adds that the pre-capitalist and Asiatic material is little known among Chinese scholars because it lies in notebooks not yet fully published. Wu presents the German work as offering a way to examine the inner logic of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a guide to German-language scholarship, names and sources on the London Notebooks, especially the Halle group and the unpublished later notebooks.

The development, main content and historical assessment of Yun Daiying's atheist thought 恽代英无神论思想的发展脉络、主要内涵及历史评价 Zhou Wei This article examines the atheist thought of Yun Daiying (1895–1931), an early leader of the Chinese Communist Party and a pioneer in spreading atheism in modern China. Zhou argues that Yun applied Marxist atheism to criticise religious theology and feudal superstition, and in doing so built a relatively complete atheist outlook of his own. The article sets out its origins, content and value, and also names its limits. The piece has three parts. The first traces the development of Yun's atheism: its theoretical foundations in materialism and the doctrine of knowability, the late Qing and Republican climate of rampant superstition, and his move from youthful atheism to a Marxist position after he joined the Party in 1921. The second sets out five areas of content: the basic questions about religion, religious freedom, faith versus scientific belief, theism and science, and methods of dealing with theism. The third assesses his contribution and shortcomings. Zhou's central claim is that Yun's thought matured when he left behind his early ambivalence, including admiration for Jesus's personality, and began to explain religion through political and economic systems, imperialism and feudal exploitation. In Zhou's account, Yun held that religion is a human creation with six psychological and historical sources, that its positive functions will fade until it dies out, and that it should not be forcibly suppressed, though illegal activity must be punished. He saw scientific belief as open to doubt while religious belief is exclusive, and he saw theism as obstructing science and reason. His remedies were guiding religion to adapt to society, including church self-government, atheist education, popularising science, and breaking superstition through cultural and political revolution. Zhou credits Yun with exposing religious mysticism, spreading scientific knowledge and advancing the adaptation of Marxist atheism to the Chinese context. Zhou also finds two weaknesses: theoretical inconsistency, with traces of Daoist and Confucian ideas and statements that leave room for belief in gods, and an emotional, one-sided view of Christianity as a tool of imperialism, as in his remark that every Christian is a 'foreign slave'. Zhou says he should not be judged by present-day standards and that studying him can inform research on Marxist atheism and the handling of religious questions and superstition today. Read the original if you study the early Chinese Marxist treatment of religion, or the history of atheist propaganda in the Republican era.

The artistic critique in the construction of Marx's scientific atheism 马克思科学无神论思想的艺术批判建构 Jiang Xuebin Marx's atheism is usually read through his philosophical critique of religion and theology. Jiang Xuebin asks whether it also has an artistic dimension, and argues that it does. In Jiang's account, Marx built a distinct 'artistic critique' of divinity, which adds a further strand to the development of his scientific atheism. The article follows Marx's thinking in three steps, running from his early creative writing to his mature theory. It begins with the poems, the novel Scorpion and Felix and other youthful literary work. It then turns to Marx's statements on the nature of art, and finally to his writings on 'artistic production'. Jiang contrasts Marx throughout with the idealist aesthetics of Schelling, in which art is bound up with God. Jiang's central claim is that each stage removes divinity from art in a different way. In the early poems, gods, stars and spirits are said to be projections of nature and of human limits, while inspiration comes from real love and real life. Marx's mature view of art rests on materialism, practice and social need, so that art is a conscious human activity and not a divine emanation. Under the heading of artistic production, Marx treats art and religion as particular modes of production. Art then becomes a lens for criticising capitalism, in which the writer is a wage-labourer and artistic work turns into a commodity. Jiang holds that these problems come from capitalist contradictions, which gods cannot solve and only human practice and emancipation can. Jiang concludes that Marx's artistic critique traces a line from poetic intuition, through the theoretical grounding of art in philosophy, practice and society, to a practical critique of artistic production under capitalism. On this reading, art is a human practice and a mode of production, and is neither a vehicle of the divine nor a tool for manipulating people in God's name. The article presents this as showing how Marx's atheism matured and as opening a literary and artistic path for contemporary research on scientific atheism. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's aesthetics, his early poetry, or how Chinese scholars of atheism link literature and the theory of artistic production to the critique of religion.

Chinese modernization's mastery of capital 中国式现代化对资本的驾驭 Dong Biao Dong Biao asks how Chinese modernization relates to capital, given that modernization has historically been driven by capitalism. The article argues that Chinese modernization moves beyond the binary of 'abolishing capital' and 'putting capital at the centre'. In Dong's account, it has opened a new path of using and mastering the logic of capital, so that economic and social development advances together with human development. The piece, a newspaper commentary, has three parts. The first defines the logic of capital and links it to the general features of modernization. The second sets out what is distinctive about Chinese modernization. The third turns to practice and proposes how to guide the healthy development of capital under Chinese conditions. Dong draws on Marx to argue that industrialization, marketization, bourgeois democracy and secularization all depend on the logic of capital. Under capitalist dominance, the author says, these tendencies produce economic, political, ecological and value crises, so capital-led modernization completes only 'the first half' of the task, and socialism must supply a shift of paradigm. Chinese modernization, led by the Party and centred on the people, treats capital as a means. Dong lists four features: common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development that rejects colonial expansion. For the present, Dong calls for Marxist guidance in understanding capital, capitalism and modernization, and for a dialectical view of capital's dual role under the socialist market economy. Public and non-public capital share a profit-seeking, mobile and expansionary nature, but public ownership as the main body sets the basic rules. Citing recent 'disorderly expansion' of financial and platform capital, Dong proposes 'traffic lights' for capital: Party leadership over capital, a people-centred orientation, the Two Unwaverings, better distribution systems, and a law-based business environment. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese framing of capital governance and its Marxist justification.

"Harnessing capital" and advancing Chinese modernization “驾驭资本”与推进中国式现代化 Xu Ge Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2023, Xu Ge takes up what the article calls the major question of how a socialist society should "harness capital". Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that regulating and guiding capital is at once an economic, political, practical and theoretical problem, Xu argues that harnessing capital is the key to Chinese modernization. In this reading, Chinese modernization combines the general laws of modernization with Chinese characteristics because the Party and the socialist system use capital's positive role while restraining its negative effects. The commentary has three parts. The first treats the precondition: a change in the mode of modernization, linked to the new development philosophy and high-quality development. The second treats the key task: preventing capital from swelling into a "totalizing" power. The third sets out the basic path by which harnessing capital advances Chinese modernization. Xu's core claim is that modernization either remains subject to the "logic of capital" or treats capital as a factor serving development. Drawing on Marx, Xu says capital tends to expand into an all-dominating power, which in Western modernization happened above all through exchange between capital and political power. Xu rejects abolishing capital or the market. The article calls instead for regulating and guiding capital by law, setting "traffic lights" for it and fighting corruption and rent-seeking. Xu also distinguishes lawful state guidance of capital from "exchange" between capital and public power, which is held to be illegitimate and to violate fair exchange. A further distinction is that neither capital nor the market equals social life, so commodity exchange should not colonise moral and cultural life. Xu also separates the "social form" of modernization from its "material content", saying socialism absorbs the achievements of modern civilization while shedding their capitalist form. Xu concludes that Chinese modernization places capital in a "non-central", "limited" position, as an important factor, link and force under the dominant influence of the socialist mode of production. Xu lists what this means in practice: a people-centred modernization, common prosperity rather than polarization, coordination of material and cultural-ethical advance, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Read the original if you want a concise statement, in the official theoretical idiom, of how Chinese Marxist scholars frame the relationship between capital, the market and public power in the socialist market economy.

Continuing to advance the emancipation of thought on the question of capital 持续推进对待资本问题上的思想解放 Rong Xin Writing in China Social Sciences Today (August 2023), Rong Xin asks why Chinese modernization can claim to surpass earlier theories of modernization. The author argues that classical modernization theory, dependency theory, world-system theory, globalization theory and post-modernization theory all take capital and its logic as their premise. In Rong's reading, this confines them to fixed centre–periphery and dependent–dominant structures. Rong holds that the decisive difference is the sustained emancipation of thought on how to treat capital over more than four decades of reform and opening up. The commentary has three sections. The first draws on Marx's critique of modernity to set out capital's nature and the internal contradictions of its logic. The second traces the Party's practice of treating capital, from abolishing it to using it, then regulating and guiding it, and finally going beyond it. The third places Chinese modernization within the problem of how socialist modernization can exist alongside a world dominated by capital. Rong's central move is to distinguish capital as a social relation from capital as a factor of production, while holding that the two are dialectically united. The author says a rigid, essentialist view, which treated the social relation as the precondition for capital's civilising function, blocked earlier attempts to use capital under socialism, including Lenin's New Economic Policy and Mao Zedong's remarks of 1956. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the Party in Rong's account separated the two, treating capital as a tool for market allocation of resources that a socialist state may use. Rong adds that capital's drive for self-expansion produces blind production, social division and distorted human nature, so it must be regulated and guided to prevent its disorderly expansion. Using capital as a factor to abolish capital as a social relation is presented as the aim of socialist modernization. Rong concludes that the classical Marxist framework treated socialism and modernization as incompatible categories, and that socialist modernization became a task only after Lenin's theory of socialism's victory in one country. Chinese modernization is described as having found a path by staying open to the world, handling capital's dual logic dialectically and using capital without losing its direction. The author says this both releases market vitality and upholds social fairness and justice. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists justify using capital under socialism through Marx's distinction between capital as social relation and as production factor.

The new industrial revolution and the development of socialism in the twenty-first century 新产业革命与21世纪社会主义发展 Li Caiyan Li Caiyan asks how the new industrial revolution, also called the fourth industrial revolution and driven by artificial intelligence, big data, cloud computing and digital networks, changes the conditions for socialism in the twenty-first century. The article argues that, as with the three earlier industrial revolutions, this one brings socialism both new challenges and new opportunities. Li holds that Marx's analysis of class relations remains valid and that socialism can use its institutional advantages to overcome the negative effects of the new technologies. The article places twenty-first-century socialism on the footing of the new industrial revolution and examines four areas: the growth of productive forces and global polarisation, the subjectivity of the working class, the unity of the proletariat, and the free and all-round development of the human being. It draws on Chinese digital-economy statistics, PwC forecasts, Western left-wing scholars such as Judith Butler, Guy Standing and Kees van der Pijl, and protest movements in the United States, France and India. Li closes with a section on how socialism can respond. Li's central move concerns class. Against Western and Russian scholars who propose plural agents of change or a 'new middle class', Li argues that gig workers and the 'precariat' remain workers, because Marx and Engels defined the proletariat by non-ownership of the means of production, not by the form of labour. Digital labour, in Li's account, still yields surplus value, only in a more concealed way. Automation, the 'double diamond' class structure and the 'digital divide' are said to sharpen class contradictions and revive class consciousness, as shown by Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests. Li then weighs digital media, which aid organisation, against fragmented workplaces, individualisation and competition between workers in developed and developing countries, which hinder unity. AI is described as both freeing people from drudgery and producing a 'new alienation'. Li concludes that big data and the Internet of Things can make planning more scientific and supplement market allocation under the socialist market economy. Socialist relations of production, the author argues, can narrow the digital divide in pursuit of common prosperity, and the shared character of information technology fits socialist values. Citing Mao Zedong, Li warns against blind optimism and calls for careful institutional responses. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar uses Marxist class theory to interpret digital capitalism, platform labour and AI.

Historical experience and lessons from the Communist Party's handling of religious issues in southern Xinjiang in the 1950s 20世纪50年代中国共产党处理南疆地区宗教问题的历史经验与启示 Yan Shaohua Yan Shaohua asks how the Chinese Communist Party dealt with religion in southern Xinjiang in the 1950s, and what that record offers for religious work today. The article argues that the Party's approach was cautious, steady, flexible and gradual. In Yan's account it achieved its aims without major social upheaval, and it gave local people real freedom both to believe and not to believe. Yan says this had no precedent in the region's history and that it still instructs the handling of religion in Xinjiang. The article first reviews four strands of 1950s practice, drawing on speeches by Wang Enmao, Party directives and local gazetteers. They are publicising the policy of freedom of religious belief; carrying out the democratic reform of religious institutions; building an anti-feudal united front with religious figures; and, last, lessons for the present. It uses Kashgar, Aksu, Hotan and Zepu as examples. Yan's core claim is that policy was tied to the Party's central task of each period. Early on, the Party stressed freedom to believe in order to counter the Nationalist rumour that communists would abolish religion. Atheist education and the freedom not to believe were promoted fully only from 1958. Yan argues that separating religion from administration, justice, marriage and education, and then abolishing religious feudal privileges, waqf land and religious levies, rested on gradualism. The Party distinguished clerics from landlords and brought religious figures into land-reform committees and study classes. Yan says this narrowed the target of struggle and widened unity. Yan draws three lessons for the new era. Religious work must serve the Party's central task, now stability and long-term security in Xinjiang. The separation of religion and state must be upheld, so that religion is a private matter and is not tied to ethnicity; Yan states that there is no such thing as a "Muslim nation". The Sinicization of Islam in Xinjiang, Yan argues, requires Party leadership and the principle of the "state's presence". Yan calls for Party and government bodies to guide scriptural interpretation and the governance of religion. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Xinjiang religious policy of the 1950s is framed as a model for current policy, with extensive local sources.

An outline of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明论要 Shang Zhixiao Taking up Xi Jinping's call, at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023, to build "the modern civilization of the Chinese nation" as a new cultural mission, Shang Zhixiao asks what this civilization is, what defines it and how it should be built. The article argues that it is the latest form of Chinese civilization, created since 1949 under the leadership of the Communist Party, and that it has four defining features and four paths of construction. The article moves in five steps. It first defines civilization and its relation to culture, drawing on classical Chinese texts and Engels. It then turns to Chinese civilization and the five "outstanding characteristics" that Xi names: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Next it sets out the basic meaning and the essential determinations of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, and it closes with routes for building it. On unity, Shang cites a statistic that, over about 4,000 years since the Xia dynasty, roughly 2,700 years were periods of unification and 1,200 of division. Shang reads the concept in three ways. It corresponds to ancient and modern phases of Chinese civilization; it is a comprehensive civilization (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological) that combines Marxism with Chinese reality and traditional culture and aims to surpass both ancient Chinese and capitalist civilization; and it is the cultural form of Chinese modernization. Its essential determinations are Party leadership, Marxism as ideological foundation, a socialist character, and the primacy of the people as the civilization's subject. For construction, Shang proposes four paths: following the practice of Chinese modernization, merging with the building of advanced socialist culture, linking up with the historical lineage of Chinese culture, and opening to a global outlook. Shang concludes that the Party must keep leading, that Marxism must be adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that traditional culture must be handled by sublating its dross and keeping its essence, opposing both cultural nihilism and cultural revivalism. Internationally, the author calls for exchange and mutual learning, in contrast to "Western-centrism", and for contributing to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a systematic exposition, in the official idiom of 2023, of how Chinese scholarship defines the "modern civilization of the Chinese nation" and its Party-led construction.

New features of capital movement in Western developed countries since the 21st century 21世纪以来西方发达国家资本运动的新特点 Hu Leming Li Lianbo Responding to Xi Jinping's call to understand correctly the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital, Hu Leming and Li Lianbo ask how capital has moved in the developed capitalist countries since 2000. The authors argue that capital accumulation always follows three logics of scale, space and power. In their account, these logics have unfolded fully since the 2008 financial crisis: capital achieves unprecedented accumulation, opens new spaces for valorisation and becomes a power that dominates everything. They say studying Western theories of capital helps to deepen understanding of capital's laws and to regulate capital's behaviour in China. The article surveys mainly Western Marxist and critical scholarship, including Dan Schiller, Christian Fuchs, John Bellamy Foster, David Harvey, Brett Christophers, Jodi Dean and Cecilia Rikap-style work on rents and platforms. It is organised in five parts. After an introduction, it covers three new capital forms (digital, natural and financial capital), changes in how surplus is extracted (rentierism, economic rent, a new enclosure movement), and the spread of capital's logic from daily life to ideology. It closes with four lessons for China. The authors argue that the three forms are all, in Marx's terms, circulating capital detached from material production. Digital capital is chiefly commercial capital, green capital is fictitious capital, and financial capital is a pure means of appropriating income. The three increasingly interlock, for example in the financialisation of platforms and in green finance. In the authors' reading, surplus is now extracted less through value creation than through rents, patents, digital 'enclosure' of the internet and what some scholars call neo-feudalism, so that contemporary capitalism shifts from producing value to distributing it. Capital also builds ideologies of its own: the claims that digital technology brings equality and that markets are the best route to environmental protection. It further reshapes everyday life through household debt and the digitalisation of leisure into labour. The authors draw four lessons. Capital should be seen neither as a monster nor as a cure-all: as a production factor it can advance productive forces, but as a social relation it is exploitative. Markets and government regulation must both be improved to curb disorderly expansion. Social value norms, including the core socialist values, are needed as a third barrier where markets and government both fail. Finally, they contend that only the socialist market economy, based on public ownership with public capital as the leading form, can successfully harness capital. Read the original if you want a dense survey of Western critical theories of digital, green and financial capital, read from the standpoint of Chinese debates on regulating capital.

Foreign left-wing rethinking of the global climate crisis in the twenty-first century 21世纪国外左翼对全球气候危机的再思考 Chen Feng This survey, published in World Socialism Studies in 2023, reviews how communist and workers' parties and left-wing scholars outside China have analysed the global climate crisis. Chen Feng reports that these actors link the crisis to capitalism, building on Marx's idea of a rift in the metabolism between humanity and nature. The article's main finding is that the foreign left treats socialism as the fundamental way out, while also proposing supplementary measures. The review covers a wide range of sources: European and North American communist parties, the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties, the European Left Party and the Party for Socialism and Liberation. It also draws on scholars such as John Bellamy Foster, Andreas Malm, Michael Löwy, Martin Empson and Alex Callinicos. It is organised in four parts: the flaws of capitalist green policies, capitalism as the root of the crisis, socialism as the fundamental solution, and other practical routes. According to Chen's account, the left argues that carbon taxes, carbon trading and "green growth" serve monopoly capital. In this reading they widen inequality, burden low-income groups, fuel what the article calls environmental racism, and reinforce an unjust international order. The surveyed authors hold that capitalism is in essence a fossil-fuel system driven by profit, short-termism and accumulation, so that green capitalism and technological innovation cannot resolve the contradiction. Against this, they present socialism as offering planning, public ownership of energy and finance, and democratic ecological planning. Several argue that the survival crisis will push people towards it. Chen also reports the left's complementary proposals: curbing consumerism, fair carbon taxation, new jobs and retraining for workers leaving fossil-fuel sectors, left unity, and alliances between labour, environmental and other progressive movements. The conclusion is that the foreign left has deepened its critique of capitalism but still needs further theoretical and practical exploration. Read the original if you want a catalogue of the positions of Western communist parties and left scholars on climate, as presented from a Chinese academic standpoint.

The absolute limits of capital and their rational transcendence With a commentary on Mészáros's "theory of going beyond capital" 资本的绝对界限及其合理超越 Yan Yan Writing in 2023, Yan Yan asks how Marxists should assess István Mészáros's claim, in Beyond Capital, that capital runs into "absolute limits" and must therefore be superseded. The author sets this against a practical problem: Marx and Engels did not foresee a market economy under socialism, so they did not analyse how a socialist society should treat capital. Yan argues that Mészáros's analysis of the limits follows Marx's line of thought and develops Marxist critique of capital, but that his demand to supersede capital rests on a metaphysical, one-sided view that does not fit China's conditions. The article first sets out Mészáros's position, presenting him as a Hegelian Marxist, a student of Lukács, who nonetheless rejects Hegel's "uncritical positivism". It then goes through four limits in turn: the conflict between transnational capital and nation-states; the destruction of the natural conditions of social metabolic reproduction; women's emancipation and substantive equality; and chronic unemployment and the population crisis. Each is discussed against opposing thinkers, including Kant, Hegel, Smith, the Club of Rome, Sombart, Weber, Hayek and Malthus. A final section evaluates Mészáros's overall theory. In Yan's account, Mészáros holds that the "no alternative" ideology of bourgeois thinkers is mistaken. He argues that capital's drive to expand cannot be contained by the state, by scale economies, by technology or by redefining needs, and that each attempt to manage contradictions reproduces them on a larger scale. In the critical section Yan accepts the distinction Mészáros draws between capital and capitalism. Yan objects, however, that for Marx the target is mainly capital in its social attribute, capital under capitalist relations of production, not capital in general. On Yan's reading Mészáros therefore wrongly presents the choice as binary: either capital controls you or you destroy it. Because of this, Yan says, he declares market socialism absurd and overlooks the diversity of socialist models and the way a socialist market economy can bring out "the civilising side of capital" while curbing its negative side. Yan also argues that the Soviet problem lay in failing to use capital effectively, not in retaining it. Yan concludes that "going beyond" Marx is legitimate only if it supplements and develops Marxism in light of capitalism's new changes, given the unfinished and open character of Capital. It is not legitimate if it aims to overturn Marxism's basic views and method. For China in the new era, Yan says, the task is not to supersede capital but to regulate and guide its healthy development, while recognising that capital promotes productive forces. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Mészáros's Beyond Capital and of how capital should be treated under socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Totality, totalization and negative dialectics The idea of totality in foreign Marxism in the mid-twentieth century 总体性、总体化与否定的辩证法 Yang Haifeng How did the Marxist concept of totality change after Lukács revived it, and what stayed constant? Yang Haifeng argues that between the 1930s and the post-1970s period, totality shifted from a critical method and a utopian ideal to an object of suspicion, then to a reconstructed open totality. Through these shifts, Yang holds, the constant theme was critical reflection on capitalist society and the search for a better one. The article proceeds in five stages. It examines the Frankfurt School's critical theory and Marcuse's negation; the humanist rereading of the 1844 Manuscripts by Marcuse, Henri Lefebvre and Erich Fromm; Jean-Paul Sartre's move from totality to totalization; Adorno's critique in Negative Dialectics; and post-Marxism (Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida). Althusser appears briefly as someone who replaced the humanist basis of totality with an objective structural one. Yang's central distinction is between totality as a fixed structure and totality as an open, unfinished process or a differently conceived whole. Horkheimer and Marcuse treat the organized, monopoly-capitalist whole as a reified pseudo-totality, which leads to total critique and Marcuse's Great Refusal. For Lefebvre and Fromm the 'total human being' is the aim of liberation. Sartre treats structure as congealed and dialectic as movement, using the progressive–regressive method. Adorno reads Hegel's world spirit as the mirror of commodity exchange and identity-thinking. He answers with non-identity and the 'constellation'. Laclau and Mouffe, and Derrida, dissolve essentialist totality in favour of open articulation and difference. Yang credits post-Marxist deconstruction with questioning the post-Cold War 'end of history' and the power structures behind it. The article contends, however, that a loose totality with no dominant element cannot reveal the structure of society. Overstressing difference in a globalized world, Yang argues, risks erasing the ruling logic of capital. Yang concludes that drawing on modern philosophy while preserving Marxism's critical force still needs exploration. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language genealogy of the totality concept from Lukács to post-Marxism, with close readings of Marcuse, Sartre and Adorno.

Critique and transcendence of justice On Agnes Heller's interpretation of Marx's theory of justice 正义的批判与超越 Yan Yan Does capitalism contain distributive justice, and does communist society transcend justice? Yan Yan takes up these questions through the Hungarian Marxist Agnes Heller, in particular her Beyond Justice and her writings on Marx's idea of justice. Yan argues that Heller mixes misreadings of Marx with useful ideas. Sorting the two, Yan holds, helps in building a Marxist theory of justice suited to China, where capital remains a production factor in the socialist market economy and the primary stage of socialism sets the context. The article is organised in five parts. Four sections follow Heller on capitalist distributive justice, whether distribution according to labour can transcend justice, the alleged contradictions in Marx's principle of distribution according to need, and whether freedom or justice is more fundamental. A short closing assessment weighs the strengths and weaknesses of her position. Yan compares her with Marx, Adam Smith, Kant, István Mészáros, John Rawls, Jürgen Habermas and critics such as Jean Cohen and Michael Walzer. Yan's central move is to separate Heller's "formal justice" from Marx's view that the mode of production determines distribution. Heller holds that market rules applied to everyone make capitalist distribution just. Yan replies that Marx does not deny this formal side but regards it as an empty appearance resting on an unjust mode of production. On distribution according to need, Yan rejects Heller's claim of a clash between unlimited needs and finite lives. Following Mészáros, Yan says unlimited needs are shaped by capital's logic, so Heller's ethical-value solution is a subjectivist utopia. Yan also traces her reading of communism as a merely regulative ideal to Kant. On freedom and justice, Yan sees her priority of freedom as shaped by hostility to Soviet-bloc socialism and by Eastern European dissident experience. Yan adds that whether communism transcends justice resembles the question of whether it abolishes the state: it can be called both a transcendence of justice and a new type of justice. Yan concludes that Heller's theory is liberal and utopian in tendency and fails to grasp the unity of the empirical and transcendent dimensions of Marxism, or the coercive force of capital. Yan still credits her analysis of dynamic justice, plural needs and the opposition to fixed norms, and her question of how plural cultures can be bound together. Yan says her alternative to Rawls offers a useful reference for realising fairness and justice under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese-Marxist assessment of Heller on justice, with links to current debates on capital and the socialist market economy.

Innovating the research paradigm of foreign Marxism 创新国外马克思主义研究范式 Lan Jiang Writing in September 2023, Lan Jiang argues that research on foreign Marxism in China, productive since the 1980s, has reached a turning point. With socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era, the author holds that the field must move beyond translating and analysing foreign Marxist thinkers. It should reinterpret them in Chinese discourse, take a problem-oriented approach, and contribute to building China's own independent system of knowledge. The commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, has three parts. It first sets out the historical mission of introducing foreign Marxism after reform and opening up, then names problems in the field after three decades of growth, and finally proposes a new research framework. Lan describes the framework as a coordinate system with a vertical and a horizontal axis. Examples range from Lukács, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School to Baudrillard, John Bellamy Foster and debates on the digital economy. Lan says early introduction of foreign Marxism supplied a critique of capitalism from inside its own mode of production, a perspective that socialist countries outside the West lacked. In Lan's view it also helped Chinese readers face Western capitalist elements while avoiding wholesale Westernisation. Two problems follow. Early work stressed texts over their historical setting, although thinkers such as Marcuse, Baudrillard and Foster answered concrete stages of capitalism. Foreign Marxists also read Marx through Western ideological discourse, as Erich Fromm did when he set a humanist young Marx against the later author of Capital. The vertical axis, Lan says, is the existing work by period, country and school, which risks cutting links across regions. The proposed horizontal axis would reframe the field with Chinese questions, concepts and discourse. Lan calls for foreign Marxism to be read against the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and with resources from fine traditional Chinese culture. On the digital economy, Chinese scholars should not simply echo Marcuse, Stiegler or David Harvey. They should ask how to prevent new inequality from capital monopoly and let the digital economy benefit all. Lan sees this as a way to enrich philosophy, sociology, politics and communication studies, to show academic confidence, and to lay a creative basis for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism sees the field's methodological shift towards an autonomous Chinese knowledge system.

Paying tribute to history and creating a new cultural brilliance 礼敬历史，创造新的文化辉煌 Dou Zhaorui Writing in 2023, Dou Zhaorui offers a study-and-interpretation piece on Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. The article asks how the call to build a modern Chinese civilization should be understood and pursued. Dou argues that the speech is a political and theoretical declaration of the Communists of the new era, a guide to action and a milestone in the history of Chinese culture. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the "five outstanding characteristics" of Chinese civilization (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness) and draws from each a requirement for building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. The second treats the Two Integrations as the necessary path. The third sets the goal of creating a new form of human civilization, with three tasks tied to Party leadership, institutions, reform and global initiatives. Dou's central reasoning is that each characteristic yields a practical direction. Continuity means going one's own way and adapting traditional culture creatively. Innovation means avoiding both a closed, rigid old path and an "evil path" of changing banners. Unity means defending national unification and territorial integrity and strengthening the sense of community of the Chinese nation. Inclusiveness means deepening opening up, and peacefulness means rejecting cultural hegemony. Dou then argues that Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture are highly compatible, citing materialist and dialectical thought, the ideal of "all under heaven for the public good" and the people-as-foundation idea. This compatibility is said to be the basis of the Two Integrations, which make Marxism Chinese and make traditional culture modern. The "second integration" is presented as a fresh liberation of thought that consolidates the cultural subjectivity of the Chinese nation. Dou concludes that Party leadership over propaganda, ideological and cultural work is the political precondition for a modern Chinese civilization, and that without it Chinese modernization is impossible. Traditional ideals, the spirit of innovation and the philosophy of peaceful coexistence should be combined with the Party's mission, the Chinese socialist system, reform and opening up, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The aim is a civilization marked by common prosperity and balanced material, cultural, political, social and ecological progress. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated historians present Xi Jinping's 2023 cultural speech and link it to the Two Integrations and Chinese modernization.

Some reflections on atheism and the sinicization of religion from the perspective of the "Second Integration" “第二个结合”视角下对于无神论与宗教中国化问题的几点认知 Zhang Xinying This text is a summary of a speech by Zhang Xinying, delivered on 9 July 2023 at a symposium on "the Second Integration and atheism" organised by the editors of the journal Science and Atheism. It responds to Xi Jinping's remarks of 2 June 2023 describing the "Second Integration" (combining Marxism with China's fine traditional culture) as a fresh emancipation of thought. Zhang asks whether traditional culture contains religious elements, what role its atheistic factors play, and whether its beliefs can serve the sinicization of religion. The answer is that traditional culture does contain such elements, and that they can support religious sinicization. Zhang says each question could fill a long study and offers three fragmentary observations. The first concerns the historical sources of the "fine traditional culture" that Xi repeatedly cites. The second takes up the claim that Chinese culture is humanist rather than god-centred. The third applies both points to the direction of sinicizing religion, including foreign religions such as monotheistic faiths. Zhang argues that the core values of fine traditional culture were largely fixed by Confucian-led pre-Qin thinkers in the "Axial Age", before Buddhism and Daoism existed as complete religions. The "three pillars" description of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism is therefore conditional, and Zhang warns against equating tradition with the backward features of late feudal society. In Zhang's reading, the early Chinese view of the gods dissolved the boundary between gods and humans and made religion serve worldly life. Zhang calls this an original humanist undertone, quite unlike the "god-centred" monotheism of other cultures. Zhang adds that it made Marxism easier to embrace in China. Zhang cites Paul Tillich's 1957 remark that Confucianism was a positive condition for the success of communist faith. Zhang concludes that traditional beliefs can supply useful resources for the sinicization of religion. Traditional religions should open a new chapter, while foreign monotheistic religions should learn from Chinese culture how to coexist with mainstream politics and ideology. They should also link up with the core socialist values and play their social role within Chinese modernization. Zhang presents this as a goal of the Second Integration and as a way of joining Marxist religious studies with Marxist atheist education. Read the original if you want to see how a senior scholar of religion links the Second Integration to official policy on religion and atheism.

Building a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation through the Two Integrations 在“两个结合”中建设中华民族现代文明 Bie Ronghai Bie Ronghai argues that the "new cultural mission" set out by Xi Jinping, namely building a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation, rests fundamentally on the Two Integrations. The Two Integrations join the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Writing in September 2023 in a newspaper commentary, Bie draws on Xi's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development. The article has three parts. The first shows that the Two Integrations and the building of this civilisation are internally unified in their subject, goal and direction, in their historical continuity, and in the paths they provide. The second describes the new form that the Two Integrations give the civilisation, along three dimensions: subjectivity, historical vision and world consciousness. The third discusses its contemporary significance, the forces that drive it, the Chinese chapter it writes and its global meaning. Bie holds that the subject of both is the Party and the people, that both aim at a strong modern country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that both follow the path of Chinese modernization. The Two Integrations supply the route: unwavering Marxist guidance, the ideological line of seeking truth from facts, and a firm Chinese cultural stance of remembering origins, facing the future and absorbing foreign ideas. They also give the civilisation a distinct character. It combines Chinese civilisation's wholeness with its subjectivity, its continuity with its capacity for innovation, and its rootedness in China with openness to other civilisations. Bie says the Party leads, the people form the main force, and socialism with Chinese characteristics fuses with the traits of Chinese civilisation. Bie concludes that this path differs from Western, capital-centred modernization. In Bie's account it offers developing countries experience, refutes the "end of history" and "failure of socialism" theses, and draws on ideas such as "harmony in diversity" and ecological wisdom to contribute to world peace and civilisational exchange. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how official Party discourse links the Two Integrations to civilisation-building and to Chinese modernization.

Traditional Chinese culture and atheism 中国传统文化与无神论 Li Shen This is the record of a speech by Li Shen at a symposium on "the Second Integration and atheism", organised on 9 July 2023 by the editorial office of the journal Science and Atheism. The symposium followed Xi Jinping's 2 June 2023 talk on cultural inheritance and development, in which he called the "second integration" (of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture) a further liberation of thought. Li's theme is how traditional Chinese culture relates to atheism. Li holds that Chinese tradition combined near-universal belief in gods with a long, continuous line of thinkers who rejected crude sorcery and superstition. Li first sketches the development of Chinese culture from the legendary Yellow Emperor and Flame Emperor era through the Shang and Zhou, the Qin unification and the Han decision to honour Confucianism alone. He then follows Confucian thought through Wang Bi, Kong Yingda, the Song Neo-Confucians and the Four Books, noting parallel changes in Buddhism and Daoism. The second half is a chronological survey of atheist thinkers from Confucius and Xunzi to Wang Chong, Fan Zhen, Han Yu, Liu Zongyuan, Liu Yuxi, Ouyang Xiu, Cao Duan and Xiong Bolong. Li argues that Confucianism gave the ancient state stability and cultural continuity, making Chinese culture the only one uninterrupted for five thousand years, and that unity was treated as normal and division as abnormal. In his account, Chinese rulers and people alike believed in gods, and the deities of the state faith were regarded as protectors of the state, which fostered tolerance. He contrasts this with world religions centred on individual salvation, which, he says, treated other peoples' gods as idols to be removed and, with capitalist expansion, nearly destroyed the cultures of tolerance and peace. Within this setting, thinkers from Confucius onwards corrected sorcery and excessive worship. Examples include Xunzi on unusual celestial events, Wang Chong's rejection of the correspondence between heaven and humanity, Fan Zhen's analogy of the blade and its sharpness, and Ouyang Xiu's refusal to record supposed omens. Li concludes that these ideas form a sequence within fine traditional culture and supply valuable material for present-day atheism. He adds that ancient atheism spread with difficulty and its proponents suffered hardship. Scientific, thoroughgoing atheism, he says, can flourish only in a socialist society guided by Marxism. Confucianism, by his account, was good at preserving order but could not cope with modern imperialist aggression, so the Qing abolished its ruling status before the 1911 Revolution and the founding of the People's Republic gave tradition new life. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese atheism scholars link the "Second Integration" to the history of Chinese irreligious thought.

Through a century of vicissitudes, confident of a brighter tomorrow Analysis and forecast of the international communist movement, 2021–2022 历尽百年沧桑 坚信明日辉煌 Pan Jin'e This is the general report of the annual "yellow book" on the international communist movement, edited by Xin Xiangyang and Pan Jin'e. Pan takes up the movement's development in 2021–2022, a year that marked the centenary of the Communist Party of China and of several other communist parties. The report argues that, despite setbacks, the Party's century of experience and the vitality of socialism with Chinese characteristics keep alight the hope of the international communist movement and of world socialism. The report has three parts. The first reviews historical memory: the 150th anniversary of the Paris Commune, thirty years since the Soviet collapse, and the anniversaries of Rosa Luxemburg (150 years since birth) and Antonio Gramsci (130 years). The second covers the Party's centenary, its summing-up of experience, its 2021 achievements, and congratulations from foreign parties and scholars. The third surveys the 2021 Party congresses of Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea and Laos. Three moves carry the argument. On the Commune, Pan reports that parties and scholars saw it as enriching Marxism and as a forerunner of the Soviet state, and lists its principles, including smashing the old state machine and paying officials skilled workers' wages. On the Soviet collapse, Pan collects explanations from Chinese, Vietnamese and Russian voices, among them Gennady Zyuganov, and stresses abandonment of Party leadership, ideological decay and historical nihilism. Pan cites Xi Jinping's warning that China must not follow the Soviet path, and presents Luxemburg and Gramsci as thinkers still relevant today. Pan then gathers tributes from foreign communists and scholars to the Party's achievements, which the report presents as showing the superiority of the socialist system. The country sections describe, among other things, Vietnam's leadership rotation, anti-corruption drive and 2.58% growth in 2021, Cuba's economic updating and its handling of the July 2021 protests, which the Cuban leadership attributed to US-backed subversion, and the opening of the China–Laos railway. Pan concludes that the Party's centenary achievements display the superiority of the socialist system and will guide the direction of world socialism. The ruling parties of China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea and Laos are described as combining pandemic control with economic stability. Other parties are said to criticise their bourgeois governments and seek alternatives to capitalism. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese state-academic survey of how the movement was assessed in 2021–2022, including summaries of Vietnamese, Cuban, Korean and Laotian congresses and of foreign communists' statements about the CPC.

Monopoly capitalism over the past 40 years 过去40年的垄断资本主义 Malcolm Sawyer This is a Chinese translation, abridged, of an article by the British economist Malcolm Sawyer (Leeds University Business School), first published in the Cambridge Journal of Economics in 2022. Sawyer asks how neoliberalism, globalisation and financialisation since about 1980 relate to the theory of monopoly capitalism. His thesis is that "actually existing neoliberalism" has in practice been monopoly capitalism, now transnational and financialised, and that it has produced slower growth and rising inequality. The article opens with the analytical basis of monopoly-capitalism theory: industrial economics (structure–conduct–performance), Kalecki's "degree of monopoly" and the work of Keith Cowling. It then takes in turn neoliberalism, globalisation and financialisation. It follows with empirical evidence on industrial concentration, markups and "Big Tech", and a section on secular stagnation that draws on Steindl, Kalecki and Hansen. Most of the evidence is drawn from the United States and Britain. Sawyer argues that neoliberal doctrine promises competitive markets, yet the era saw rising concentration, merger-driven consolidation and weak antitrust enforcement. Cowling and Sugden are cited for the view that multinationals strengthen monopoly power, not weaken it, as intra-firm trade and foreign direct investment grow. On financialisation, Sawyer holds that the pursuit of shareholder value and financial payments shifts income from wages to profits and weakens investment and innovation. Studies he cites report rising markups and concentration, with a large role for intangible assets and knowledge monopolies held by technology firms. On stagnation, he follows the Steindl–Kalecki line: monopoly conditions lower the propensity to invest and innovate, and redistribution towards profits depresses demand. Sawyer concludes that market-promoting, deregulatory policy has fostered monopoly capitalism and delivered growth below that of the postwar "golden age". Analyses of monopoly capital and of financialisation together explain the near-stagnation of the past two decades. Future growth, he adds, will probably stay low for climate and environmental reasons and will have to differ structurally from past growth, an adjustment he says financialised monopoly capitalism cannot make. Read the original if you want a Post-Keynesian and Kaleckian empirical case that links neoliberalism, financialisation and Big Tech to monopoly capitalism and stagnation.

The workers' movement in Kazakhstan since the disintegration of the Soviet Union 苏联解体以来的哈萨克斯坦工人运动 Kang Yanru Kang Yanru asks why Kazakhstan, one of the stronger post-Soviet economies yet near the bottom of the International Labour Organization's global labour-rights ranking, has seen a persistent and combative workers' movement since independence. The article argues that the immediate causes are economic crisis and falling living standards, while the fundamental cause is neoliberal privatisation. Kang adds two further factors: a state-monopolised vertical trade-union system, and the double pressure of domestic oligarchs and transnational capital. The article periodises the movement into four stages: 1991–2007, a first peak in 2008–2011 culminating in the Zhanaozen oil strike, a low tide in 2012–2019, and a revival after 2020 that led to the January 2022 unrest. It then sets out five features of the movement, discusses causes, draws lessons from its results, and ends with the difficulties it faces. Kang's core argument is that an unbalanced, energy-dependent economy concentrated the workforce in oil and mining, which became the movement's class base. Two rounds of privatisation, pension, health and education reforms, and rising inequality, in the author's account, fed grievances. The 2014 revision of the Trade Union Law removed the right to strike from the union's functions, and more than 600 worker-founded unions were dissolved. Kang argues that workers therefore turned to strikes and demonstrations rather than bargaining. Independent unions and left organisations, notably the banned Communist Party and the Socialist Movement of Kazakhstan, are credited with raising demands such as nationalisation and workers' control, not only wages. The author also warns that, with about two-thirds of workers outside official unions, strikes risk disorder and exploitation by outside forces, and cites the "colour revolution" label applied to January 2022. Kang draws three lessons: coordinate action across sectors and regions, link the workers' movement with the socialist movement, and prevent strikes from being turned into "colour revolutions". Four obstacles are listed: the lack of a legal communist party, unions that cannot meet workers' demands (where the author notes John Foster's suggestion of working inside official unions), the difficulty of organising against transnational firms, and legal and coercive repression. Kang sees little sign that the 2022 constitutional reform will change labour relations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of post-Soviet labour struggles in Central Asia, with data on privatisation, union law and the January 2022 events.

The path to concretising historical materialism 历史唯物主义的具体化路径 Yuan Liguo Yuan Liguo asks how historical materialism can be made concrete rather than treated as a formula applied to any society. Starting from Engels's 1890 letter to Conrad Schmidt, which complained that "materialism" had become a label for young German writers, Yuan argues that Marx's own route to concreteness lay in a "social epistemology". On this reading, historical materialism becomes a theory of bourgeois society, reached through the critique of political economy, and is oriented to transforming that society. The piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2023, has four parts. It begins by criticising the reading of historical materialism as a "general theory". It then turns to the reconstruction of the object of knowledge, the "concrete totality", and finally to the path of social epistemology, which Yuan treats from an objective and a subjective side. Yuan draws on Marx's 1857–58 methodological writings, the German Ideology and Capital, and refers to Althusser and Lukács. Yuan holds that categories such as productive forces and relations of production, base and superstructure, or class lose their meaning when detached from empirical processes and used as supra-historical rules. In the critique of political economy Marx moved to the most developed form, bourgeois society, and Yuan reads his "backward-thinking method" as a way to grasp the structure of earlier forms and the tendency of society to sublate itself. Marx's object of knowledge is the "totality of bourgeois society", set against the empiricism of classical political economy, which Yuan says produces fetishised knowledge. It is also set against Hegel's rationalism, in which thought's self-movement replaces the real world. On the objective side, Yuan says capitalism's universality is its unprecedented development of productive forces, which creates the basis for the "individual ownership" Marx anticipates and for cooperative factories. On the subjective side, Yuan follows Lukács in treating class consciousness as the means by which workers cease to be reified as a commodity and become agents of change. Yuan concludes that concrete historical materialism is not a value-neutral positive science but a "science of real human beings and their historical development", aimed at revolutionising the existing world and reaching scientific socialism. Knowledge of bourgeois society's totality is produced from within it and also helps to reshape it, in a unity of theory and practice. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Marx's critique of political economy can be read as an epistemology of historical materialism, with an emphasis on totality and class consciousness.

Understanding correctly the dialectical negation of capital in Capital 准确认识《资本论》对资本的辩证否定 Zhang Junshan Zhang Junshan takes up the common view that profit-seeking is capital's nature and that capital can multiply itself. Zhang argues that this view carries a fetishistic assumption and misreads Marx. In the author's account, Marx's statements that capital 'breeds' do not show that he thought capital multiplies as a thing. The piece follows the order of Volume I of Capital, from the second part on money becoming capital through the chapters on the labour process, constant and variable capital, and the later chapters on capital's 'life instinct'. It reads this sequence as a series of abstractions in which each stage negates the one-sidedness of the stage before. The central claim is that Marx's method of scientific abstraction proceeds by dialectical negation: deeper attributes negate surface ones while preserving the link to them. Money is first negated as capital, though capital still takes the money form. Then 'capital multiplies' is negated by the finding that workers' surplus labour creates surplus value. Zhang adds that Marx's definitions must not be taken from wherever he first states something, which is the mistake Engels criticised. Finally, self-valorization is traced to capitalist relations of production. Capitalists monopolise the means of production and subsistence and so control the labour process and its product. Capitalist relations of production are therefore the essence of capital, and capital is their reified form. Zhang concludes that valorization is not capital's innate nature but a phenomenon produced by capitalist relations of production. Marx's later stress on capital's drive to expand is, on this reading, an exposure of class exploitation, not a claim that capital is naturally self-expanding. Zhang says that views separating capital from these relations, and so defending its permanence, ignore the dialectical negation in Marx's analysis. Read the original if you want a compact, method-focused reading of how Capital's categories develop and how this bears on critiques of capital fetishism.

The factive turn in contemporary epistemology 当代知识论中的事实转向 Zhou Hongyu This short piece, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2023, asks what the "factive turn" in Anglo-American analytic epistemology is, what produced it, why it came only in the last twenty-odd years, and whether it is a real turn. Zhou's answer is that epistemology has increasingly come to hold that reasons for belief can only be factive things, not subjective mental states. Zhou notes that this follows closely on the earlier "value turn" in the field. The article is organised under three headings: what the factive turn is, its causes, and the resistance it met. Zhou first sets out the traditional view that perceptual experiences and other beliefs serve as reasons for belief. The piece then identifies three contributing forces and finally discusses sceptical scenarios and internal disagreement among supporters of the turn. Zhou defines a factive item as one that entails how things actually are. Facts, veridical perceptual experiences and knowledge qualify, whereas beliefs and ordinary perceptual experiences do not. The three driving forces are epistemological disjunctivism, which gives veridical experience a justificatory standing that illusions and hallucinations lack; Timothy Williamson's knowledge-first epistemology, with its principle E=K (evidence is knowledge); and an earlier factualist shift in the philosophy of action, in which Jonathan Dancy and others treat reasons as facts. As for the delay, Zhou points to the Cartesian demon scenario: a victim and a normal subject share the same experiences and seem equally rational, which suggested that reasons must be mental states. Recent philosophers answer that being justified differs from being blameless, so the deceived twin is excused but not justified. Zhou presents this distinction as removing a key obstacle. Zhou concedes that doubts remain about whether a unified turn exists. Supporters disagree on whether reasons are facts, veridical experiences or knowledge, and some pluralists hold that no single kind of thing can play every role reasons play. Zhou concludes that the turn is not a uniform movement and its details need refining, although its advocates share the core view that only factive things can constitute reasons for belief. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language orientation to this debate in analytic epistemology and its main sources.

Distinguishing abstract labour from the concept of labour 抽象劳动与劳动概念辨析 Qian Jin Labour is the basic concept of Capital and the starting point of the labour theory of value. Qian Jin argues that abstract labour is identical with the concept of labour, and that it should not be given an interpretation different from that of labour in general. The piece first appeared in China Social Sciences Today in May 2023, and it reads as a polemic against readings that treat abstract labour as something narrower or historically specific. The article is a short theoretical commentary in four steps. It begins with the logical status of "labour" as a genus concept, then rejects the equation of abstract labour with simple labour. It next sets out a view of economic history to deny that abstract labour belongs only to capitalism, and it ends by warning against inventing new readings of the concept. Qian draws on Marx's remarks on the dual character of labour in Capital. Qian's first move is logical. Labour is an abstraction from all the varied productive and service activities that people undertake, and in ordinary usage it means human labour, not animal labour. Every use of "labour" is therefore already a use of "abstract labour", in the way that "horse" abstracts from a particular white horse. The author notes that Marx's value theory has always been called the labour theory of value, never the "abstract labour theory of value". The second move concerns complexity. Abstract labour covers both complex and simple labour, Qian says, and treating it as simple labour is unfounded. Human labour has grown ever more complex, and the author points to the technological revolution of the mid-twentieth century as an example. The third move is historical. Qian holds that humanity has known three economic forms: natural economy, commodity economy and market economy. Commodity economy arose at the end of primitive society and ran through slave and feudal societies, while market economy arose with capitalism. Commodity value and abstract labour therefore existed before capitalism, and the author says Marx never claimed otherwise. Qian concludes that abstract labour is labour, and labour is human labour, which has driven social development since human origins. It is neither a concept specific to capitalism nor to developed capitalism. Qian accepts that studying Capital calls for innovation and keeping pace with the times. Even so, the author insists that such work must respect basic historical facts and basic logic, and must not build new understandings on speculation. Read the original if you want a concise statement of one Chinese scholar's position in debates over the meaning of abstract labour and its historical scope.

New viewpoints and significance of the 22nd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties 第22次共产党和工人党国际会议的新观点和价值意蕴 Luo Lizhang This article examines the 22nd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, hosted by the Communist Party of Cuba in Havana on 27–29 October 2022. According to the author, 145 delegates from 78 parties in 60 countries attended. Luo argues that the meeting gave communist parties a platform for exchange and strengthened the international standing of world socialism. The author also stresses that it exposed unresolved disagreements over the Russia–Ukraine conflict. The article first sets the context: an intensifying imperialist offensive led by the United States, and the Covid-19 pandemic. In this context Luo credits socialist-led states and non-ruling communist parties with advancing the socialist movement. It then reports the meeting's 'new viewpoints' under five heads: the condition of the working class during the pandemic, the nature and causes of the Russia–Ukraine conflict, calls for international solidarity, support for Cuba and other peoples' struggles, and a joint Action Plan. A closing section assesses the meeting's value and shortcomings. Much of the argument consists of positions taken by individual parties. On the pandemic, parties from Greece, Spain, Brazil and Mexico, among others, are reported as holding that capitalism's profit-first logic and its drive to extract surplus value worsened workers' conditions. On the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the author sets out two camps: parties that call it an inter-imperialist war, and parties that deny Russia is imperialist and describe the war as a response to NATO expansion. Two opposing resolutions were adopted, each signed by about 20 parties with no overlap. Luo also describes the shift of communist cooperation from 'one road, one centre' to a model of equality, independence, voluntary participation and plural levels. Luo concludes that the meeting's value lies in mutual learning, in raising the international voice of socialist forces and in drawing parties together. The author lists three weaknesses: differences of theory and stance still divide the parties, the means of reaching the stated goals remain vague, and the meeting's function needs strengthening, since some delegates doubt its role. Luo calls for further efforts to narrow differences and build broader consensus against imperialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how parties in the international communist movement positioned themselves on the pandemic, the Ukraine war and solidarity with Cuba.

The historical variations, theoretical logic and contemporary symphony of "the people above all" 人民至上的历史变奏、理论逻辑与时代交响 Tang Shaolian Tang Yanmei Tang Shaolian and Tang Yanmei ask how to read the core "code" behind the Communist Party of China's hundred years of achievement, and answer that it is the principle of "the people above all" (人民至上). Placed first among the "six musts" at the 20th Party Congress (2022), the principle is presented as opening a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, in its view of the people. The authors argue that in the new era it comprises three layers: the people as masters, as the main body (subject) of history, and as the chief examiner. The article has three main parts. The first traces a historical shift from the traditional Chinese "people-as-foundation" (minben) outlook to modern democratic ideas, through Confucian texts, late-Qing reformers and early Marxists such as Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu. The second sets out the theoretical logic of why the people are supreme, moving from Marxist epistemology and historical materialism through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. The third develops the new-era "symphony" of the three layers, drawing mainly on Xi Jinping. On the traditional view, the authors argue that minben thinking could not solve two problems: how popular will could constrain supreme monarchical power, and how the people could cease to be objects of rule. Late-Qing reinterpretations did not escape this, and in their account only early Marxists achieved the move to democracy, though even they only laid a preliminary basis. Theoretically, the people are supreme because they are the subject of practice and the creators of material and spiritual wealth. Each leader supplies an answer: for Mao the Party is a tool of the people; for Deng the people's interests are fundamental; for Jiang respecting the people's status as subject follows from respecting social laws; for Hu the people are the most reliable source of strength. The "masters" strand holds that power is conferred by, used for and controlled by the people.
