The "subject" strand holds that people are real, self-liberating agents and bearers of interests, with common prosperity as the goal. The "examiner" strand develops Mao's "sitting the exam" metaphor into the claim that the times set the paper, the Party answers it and the people mark it. The authors conclude that the Party's hundred years have been a century of affirming the people's mastery, drawing on their strength as subject and implementing their right to judge. Citing Zheng Yongnian, they contrast Western parties, described as vote-seeking tools, with the Communist Party as a "mission-driven" party whose legitimacy comes from fulfilling its mission. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how "the people above all" is traced from traditional minben thought through successive leaders to Xi Jinping's formulations.

Socialist thought and practice of the Venezuelan left The United Socialist Party of Venezuela under Maduro 委内瑞拉左翼的社会主义思想与实践 Yang Jianmin Zhang Xiaoxu This research article examines how the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), founded by Hugo Chávez in 2008, has governed under Nicolás Maduro since 2013. Yang and Zhang argue that the party has survived the severe "Venezuelan crisis" and is now using a more favourable environment to adjust its leadership and organisation and to innovate in governing ideas and methods. They nonetheless judge that the party's governing philosophy is far from scientific socialism and is better seen as another exploration of a development path distinct from the Western model. The article begins with the party's origins, its founding documents and Maduro's rise to the chairmanship in 2014. It then moves through five parts: the improved governing environment since about 2021; changes to leadership and organisation after the Fifth Congress (2022); the new governing concept and its practical projects; the challenges still facing the party; and a short conclusion. On the environment, the authors cite the end of hyperinflation, GDP growth of over 15% in 2022, the party-led coalition's landslide wins in the 2020 and 2021 elections, an easing of US sanctions and the leftward turn in Latin America. On innovation, they present Maduro's "3R.Nets" concept as the core guide: resistance, rebirth and revolution, within a "new period of transition to socialism" fixed at 2022–2030. They read two initiatives through it: the "Good Government 1×10" online complaint system and the planned special economic zones meant to attract foreign investment. Organisational changes include a new 13-member Politburo, regional "contact persons" and grassroots elections in which non-party members could vote. The authors list four challenges: the Homeland Plan 2019–2025 targets (oil output of 685,000 barrels a day in 2022 against a goal of 5 million), obstacles to the special zones such as vague incentives and weak investor trust, criticism from dissidents and the Venezuelan Communist Party that the party has drifted towards capitalism, and a legitimacy problem shown by falling turnout and votes between 2012 and 2018. They conclude that whether the party can implement these measures and meet these challenges will test its governing capacity and decide whether the economy recovers. Read the original if you want a Chinese Latin Americanist assessment of the PSUV's recent organisational and policy changes, with election and economic figures.

The theoretical experiments of the French Communist Party 法国共产党的理论尝试 Yu Hui This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2023, asks how the French Communist Party (PCF) has tried to survive and renew itself as a communist party in a developed capitalist country. Yu Hui argues that the PCF's recent theoretical and organisational experiments, built around the programme "Common France", are worth attention, but that they have not stopped its marginalisation. In Yu's reading, the party remains caught in a double bottleneck between theory and reality. The article opens by presenting "upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground" (守正创新) as both a worldview and a method for studying the world socialist movement. It then sets out the PCF's external and internal difficulties, links them to social contradictions in France, and describes the measures the party took in the twenty-first century. The measures discussed are the 38th Congress resolution, the Common France programme, the "Europe of the people" position and efforts to strengthen the central committee's role in grassroots organisation. Yu identifies two kinds of challenge. Externally, the 2022 elections ended the old left–right duopoly and pointed to a three-way contest between the centre, the radical left and the far right, with Marine Le Pen's National Rally rising. Internally, Yu holds that the party's "new communism" is all-encompassing but lacks a core idea, so its policies and alliance strategies keep shifting. Yu also contends that the party has lost its ideological identity by turning from a "vanguard party" into a "mass party" and taking a "centrist road". The 32nd and 35th Congresses' radical turn and Left Front brought no lasting gains, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon's "La France Insoumise" displaced the party. As Yu describes it, Common France sets out six goals: popular control of investment and distribution, a Sixth Republic, support for employment and development, real gender equality, an open and united France, and sustainable production. It treats the parliamentary road as preparation for overthrowing capitalism and calls for ecological, labour, information and monetary revolutions. Yu concludes that this evolution has not reversed the party's decline and that its understanding of capitalism and of socialist practice constrains its transformative aims. Read the original if you want a short Chinese academic view of the PCF's post-2020 strategy and its difficulties.

The main practices of the Communist Party of Cuba in strengthening Party building 古巴共产党加强党的建设的主要做法 Liang Xiaoyu Liang Xiaoyu asks how the Communist Party of Cuba has kept its ruling position and public credibility despite the US blockade, the shock of the Soviet and East European collapse, and a narrow economic base. The article argues that the Party has done so through a set of mutually reinforcing Party-building practices, and that these offer lessons for any Marxist ruling party. After a short introduction to Cuba and the history of the Party, from its founding organisation in 1961 to the Eighth Congress in April 2021, the article organises the Cuban experience under four headings: ideological and theoretical work, the anti-corruption struggle, serving people's livelihood, and the mass line with close Party–people ties. A concluding section draws out four general lessons. The evidence consists of Party documents, congress decisions, membership figures and examples of cadre discipline and consultation campaigns. Liang's core argument is that the Party's strength rests on theory that is both firmly Marxist-Leninist and localised, and on ties with ordinary people. On theory, the article describes a tiered network of Party schools and training centres and the writing of José Martí's thought into the Party statutes, which it presents as an adaptation of Marxism to Cuban conditions. On conduct and the masses, it reports strict punishment of corrupt senior officials, publicly known and modest cadre salaries, no special privileges, and mass organisations covering almost the whole population. It also describes large consultations on congress documents, citing 3.5 million participants in the debate before the Fourth Congress and over seven million in the discussion of the Sixth Congress guidelines. Free education and health care, and attention to food security, are presented as the material basis of popular support. Liang concludes that a Marxist ruling party must accept supervision by the masses, maintain a good work style, pursue theoretical innovation rooted in national conditions, and build strong grass-roots organisations. The author holds that Cuba's experience has also advanced Marxism in the twenty-first century and carries significance for world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school scholar's account of how the Cuban Party's discipline, mass-line and welfare practices are presented as models for Party building.

On Rosa Luxemburg's socialist conception of culture 论罗莎·卢森堡的社会主义文化观 He Ping Research on historical materialism, He Ping observes, has shifted from macro-level theories of the transformation of social formations to micro-level cultural critique. The article asks how that shift occurred, how the two levels relate, and whether their theoretical gains can be joined. It takes Rosa Luxemburg's socialist conception of culture as a case study. He argues that her conception was a key turning point, produced in her fight against Millerandism, and that it links the macro theory of revolution to micro cultural critique. The article has four parts. It first reconstructs the Millerand affair of 1899, in which a French socialist joined a bourgeois cabinet, and Luxemburg's critique of it. It then examines what the author calls the rational construction of socialist culture, drawing on her readings of Marx's early writings and of Capital. Next it covers the ideological construction of socialist culture: the concept of the working class, the critique of religion, and the party's relation to the trade unions. It ends with three lessons for current research. He's central move is that Luxemburg recast legal reform through the dialectic of whole and part. Reform has a socialist character only if it forms a stage within the proletariat's overall struggle. Otherwise it is bourgeois, however it presents itself. On this basis she argued that Marx's doctrine is the proletariat's spiritual culture. In He's account, that culture cannot arise spontaneously within bourgeois culture. It emerges at the point of rupture with it, and the Social Democratic Party must hold cultural leadership over parliamentary and trade-union work. He reads her accounts of Marx's early development, of the rate of profit in Capital volume 3, and of religion as 'political fetishism' as parts of this project. In the same spirit she rejected Bernstein's praise of British trade unionism. He concludes that Luxemburg's conception diagnosed the crisis of the Second International and reflected on socialist modernity. He draws three lessons. First, socialist modernity should become a topic of historical-materialist research. He argues that Western Marxism and the Eastern European Budapest School failed to distinguish capitalist from socialist modernity, and he links this to the collapse of Eastern European socialism. Second, research should look for the point where macro and micro perspectives meet. Third, a theory of socialist modernity must be built from China's own practice, not transplanted from Luxemburg. This bears on the study of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese reading of Luxemburg's writings on Millerandism, religion and trade unions, and the author's case for linking cultural critique to revolutionary theory.

An analysis of the Communist Party of Vietnam's practical model of advancing state governance 越南共产党推进国家治理的实践模式探析 Xu Qinfa Zhang Rui Xu Qinfa and Zhang Rui ask how the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) organises state power and why it rejects Western-style separation of powers. They argue that the CPV's "division of labour among the three powers" (sanquan fengong) is a governance model that joins Marxist-Leninist theory of state power to Vietnamese practice. In their account it differs from Western separation of powers because the powers are not separated or set against each other. State power stays unified and belongs to the people, under CPV leadership, while state organs divide tasks, cooperate and supervise one another when exercising legislative, executive and judicial power. The article has three parts. The first traces the model's logic: its theoretical basis in Marx, Engels and Lenin, its historical development from the 1946 constitution through the 1959 and 1980 constitutions to the 2001 amendment and the 2013 constitution, and its origin in the CPV's response to "peaceful evolution". The second sets out the model's basic principles. The third discusses its practical value. The authors identify three principles. First, the CPV exercises "overall leadership" as the sole ruling party. They say it does not directly wield state power but leads politically, organisationally and ideologically. Second, state power is unified and belongs to the people, who exercise it through direct and representative democracy as provided in the 2013 constitution. Third, the legislature (National Assembly), government and courts divide functions, cooperate and supervise one another, which the authors present as a guard against the alienation of state power. They describe calls for separation of powers, a multiparty system or "civil society" as part of peaceful evolution. They note that a 2017 Party regulation makes advocating them grounds for expulsion. The authors conclude that the model keeps Vietnam on a socialist path, realises people's mastery of their own affairs, and helps build a clean and strong political system. They cite Vietnam's results against Covid-19 as evidence of the model's advantages. The article is largely affirmative and relies on CPV documents and speeches by Nguyen Phu Trong and Ho Chi Minh. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly presentation of how Vietnam's official doctrine justifies one-party rule and rejects separation of powers.

Lessons and implications of the failure of the Soviet model of socialist modernization 社会主义现代化苏联模式失败的教训及启示 Zhao Hong Zhao Hong asks why the Soviet model, the first attempt to build a socialist alternative to capitalist modernization, failed, and what that failure offers to countries still exploring socialist modernization. The article argues that the Soviet experience should not be dismissed one-sidedly but weighed dialectically, since it provides, in Zhao's words, a complete 'model' running from experience to lessons for Chinese modernization. Drawing on Barrington Moore's typology of modernization paths and on Russian and Soviet sources, including Lenin, Stalin, Gorbachev's memoirs and Deng Xiaoping, the article first diagnoses three failures. It then draws three implications for the present. The analysis runs from Peter the Great to the Soviet collapse, with extended attention to the New Economic Policy and to Stalin's economic writings. The three failures are as follows. First, the Soviet model never escaped Russian historical and cultural tradition. Zhao describes a catch-up modernization driven by state coercion and military expansion, citing figures on military spending and territorial growth, which left living standards and political life stagnant. Second, it never resolved the relation between socialist practice and the essence of socialism. Zhao contrasts Lenin's shift from War Communism to the New Economic Policy with Stalin's pursuit of ever 'larger and purer' production relations, which Zhao says detached them from the level of the productive forces. Third, it mishandled the absorption of capitalist modern civilisation. Lenin favoured learning from foreign technology and management, whereas Stalin's late 'two parallel world markets' thesis, in Zhao's account, produced closure and a lopsided military-industrial economy. Zhao's implications for China are that the ruling party must always put the people's interests first, citing a late-Soviet survey in which 85 per cent said the CPSU represented officials, and linking this to the Party's self-reform; that modernization must not depart from national conditions or treat Marxism as dogma; and that it must advance through mutual learning among civilisations. Zhao adds that Chinese modernization and the Soviet model are both catch-up modernizations, so resolving the imbalances this produces remains a major task. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Soviet failure is used to frame lessons for Chinese modernization.

The path to concretising historical materialism 历史唯物主义的具体化路径 Yuan Liguo Yuan Liguo takes up a long-standing misreading of historical materialism as a "general theory" of history or society, and argues that the theory has to be made concrete. Starting from Engels's 1890 letter to Conrad Schmidt, which warns against using "materialism" as a mere label, Yuan holds that Marx and Engels offered a guide to research rather than a system. The article, a short piece from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2023), proposes that the route to concreteness is a "social epistemology" worked out through the critique of political economy. The piece has three parts. The first criticises readings that treat the forces and relations of production, base and superstructure, and class and exploitation as abstract categories detached from empirical processes. The second turns to how Marx rebuilt the object of knowledge, setting his notion of totality against classical political economy and Hegel. The third sets out the route of social epistemology, which Yuan describes from an object-side and a subject-side perspective. Yuan's central move is to trace a shift from the "general" production of The German Ideology to Marx's work from 1858 on bourgeois society, the most developed form of production, which Marx's "backward-looking method" uses to understand earlier social forms. Political economy fixes alienated relations as given, so Yuan poses what they call Marx's social-epistemological question: how objective knowledge of reified bourgeois relations is possible. Marx's answer, in Yuan's reading, makes the "totality of bourgeois society" the object of knowledge. This avoids both the empiricism of political economy and Hegel's idea of thought's self-movement. Yuan also cites Althusser on the irreducibility of this totality to any single cause. On the object side, Yuan reads capitalism's universality as its unprecedented development of productive forces, which outgrows capitalist relations. Yuan points to Marx's re-established individual property and to worker cooperatives in Capital, volume 3, as signs of a way beyond capitalism. On the subject side, drawing on Lukács, Yuan treats class consciousness as the working class's knowledge of its own position, which turns workers from "commodity labour-power" into agents of change. Yuan concludes that concrete historical materialism is a theory of revolutionary practice and not a value-neutral positive science. Read the original if you want a compact account of how a Chinese scholar links Marx's critique of political economy, Lukács and Althusser to the question of what "concrete" historical materialism means.

Subject and revolution: the transformation and development of themes in Western Marxist theory 主体与革命：西方马克思主义理论主题的嬗变及发展 Miao Cuicui This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2023, asks how Western Marxism has handled the problem of revolution in countries where proletarian revolution did not occur. Miao argues that, in response to different social realities, Marxism in the East stressed objective laws and scientific character, while Marxism in Western capitalist countries stressed subjective agency, social critique and humanism. Its central claim is that Western Marxism's themes of subject and revolution follow a line from awakening a missing class consciousness, to critiquing ideological state apparatuses, to reconstructing a new revolutionary subject. The article opens with the historical emergence of proletarian revolution in early capitalism and its later predicament. In the stage of state monopoly capitalism, Miao notes, capitalism flourished, the Soviet Union dissolved, and Western liberal democracy proclaimed the "end of ideology" and "end of history". The piece then surveys Lukács, Gramsci, Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse and Habermas, before turning to contemporary radical left thinkers: Negri, Hardt, Virno, Karatani Kojin, Agamben and Badiou, with a reference to Žižek. Miao reads Lukács's theory of reification and his distinction between psychological and imputed class consciousness as the entry point for awakening proletarian consciousness. Gramsci's "war of position" over cultural hegemony and the Frankfurt School's critique of the culture industry and technology extended this line. According to Miao, however, such cultural and ideological critique lacked the practical force to shake capitalist society, so the theme shifted to remaking the revolutionary subject. Contemporary radicals do this along four paths: the "multitude" in production (Negri, Hardt, Virno); consumer boycott (Karatani); resistance to the state of exception in everyday life (Agamben); and fidelity to the event in politics (Badiou). Miao concludes that these theorists use the subject's difference to oppose capitalism's uniformity, but focus on independent individuals without domination or centre. In Miao's judgement, this cannot achieve real enlightenment, freedom or individuality. The author holds that a new subject and a reversal of power are possible only if the individual is fused into the social human whole, and individual freedom into the proletariat's self-emancipation and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how Western Marxist themes moved from class consciousness to ideology critique to subject-formation, and of how a CASS scholar assesses the contemporary radical left.

The theoretical focus of contemporary social epistemology 当代社会认识论研究的理论聚焦 You Yang You Yang takes up the question of what the "social dimension of knowledge" means and argues that it is the theoretical focus of contemporary social epistemology. Published in the China Social Sciences Today in July 2023, the article presents social epistemology as a philosophical study of knowledge-production practice. It claims that this study shares a value orientation with the Marxist view of productive forces and can therefore help to uphold and develop Marxist epistemology. The article first traces how twentieth-century epistemology moved beyond the "solitary knower" of rationalism (Descartes, Leibniz) and empiricism (Locke, Hume). It then sets out three ways of clarifying "knowledge" and "society": science-policy studies, the social organisation of knowledge, and the social attributes of knowledge. It goes on to name the field's core problems and main schools, and ends by placing the discussion within a historical-materialist framework of knowledge. You argues that knowledge is social in its production, acquisition and transmission, citing Alvin Goldman on language and Martin Kusch on the normative task of organising collectives to produce knowledge well. In You's account, the field's core problems are testimony, disagreement among experts and the choice between them, and collective knowledge and collective justification. The article distinguishes philosophical approaches, such as Goldman's truth-oriented social epistemology, from the sociological social-constructionist approaches that stress social interest and class oppression. It adds that contextualism, citing Guo Guichun, can balance the normativity and the sociality of scientific knowledge. You concludes that epistemology must integrate the normative features of traditional theory with the social features of knowledge, and that it should be located within a historical-materialist framework. The article lists three values of the social-dimension view: it shows the direction of epistemology's development, deepens its value orientation and driving forces, and reveals free exchange of ideas. It also states that turning epistemology towards social life and practice will be an important direction for a long time to come. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language overview of how social epistemology is being presented within a Marxist framework.

State governance: the philosophical thought of Marx and Engels and its lessons 国家治理：马克思恩格斯的哲思与启示 Xu Yaotong Xu Yaotong, in a commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in March 2023, asks what Marx and Engels said about state governance (guojia zhili) and what it offers for China today. Xu argues that the two thinkers built a system of thought on governance out of their political-philosophical theory of the state. Their analyses of Germany, Britain and France, Xu holds, carry major lessons for modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. The piece is organised in three sections, each built around a quotation from the classics and a national case. The first takes Marx's 1842–43 defence of the Moselle correspondent in the Rheinische Zeitung, on peasant poverty in Germany. The second turns to nineteenth-century Britain and Engels's remarks on universal suffrage. The third covers France under the Second Empire and the Paris Commune of 1871. On Germany, Xu reads Marx as showing that governance exists for the state and not the state for governance. Poverty on the Moselle therefore stemmed from the state apparatus and its officials, who blamed the governed instead. Solving governance problems requires tackling bureaucratism and the substantive problems of the state system and political structure. On Britain, Xu says Engels's mockery of governing by universal suffrage targeted an incomplete democracy, with property qualifications and bought parliamentary seats, and not suffrage itself. Governance must rest on power granted by the people, which in Xu's account means thoroughgoing socialist democracy. On France, Xu stresses the costly, parasitic bureaucracy and military of the Second Empire. Marx and Engels held that effective rule requires capacity, that the bourgeoisie had lost it, and that the Commune showed the proletariat taking power. Xu concludes that the proletariat, once in power, must be able to govern well and keep strengthening that capacity, increasing productive forces and meeting the people's interests as the Communist Manifesto indicates. Xu adds that Marx's Germany needed proletarian revolution first, whereas present-day socialist states must deepen reform of political structures and governance methods while upholding and improving the basic socialist system. Read the original if you want a short, text-based account of how a Chinese scholar draws contemporary governance lessons from Marx and Engels on Germany, Britain and France.

Basic features of Western Marxism's critique of technological rationality 西方马克思主义技术理性批判的基本特征 Zhang Xingping Zhang Xingping, in a commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today (27 June 2023), asks what is distinctive about Western Marxism's critique of technological rationality. The author argues that, despite disagreements over ethics, politics, ecology and gender, Western Marxist thinkers share one defining feature: they join the critique of technology to a critique of the capitalist system. In Zhang's account this produced a humanist technology ethics and widened the horizon of Marxist philosophy of technology. The piece is organised around three features: the rationality of technology as the central theme, the double logic of value critique and institutional critique as the line of approach, and human freedom and emancipation as the underlying aim. Zhang moves from Rousseau, Nietzsche, Simmel, Spengler and Heidegger to Lukács, the Frankfurt School, ecological Marxism and feminist Marxism. Later figures named include Marcuse, Gorz, James O'Connor and John Bellamy Foster. Zhang contends that earlier critics of modernity mistook technology itself for the source of alienation and slid into anti-technology positions. Western Marxists, by contrast, locate the root of society-wide reification in the capitalist use of technology. On the value side, reason has shrunk into instrumental rationality cut off from value rationality, which sustains positivism, consumerism and the idea of "controlling nature". On the institutional side, technology and capital together turn science and technology into an ideology that steers attention towards consumption and shores up the legitimacy of capitalist rule. Zhang also distinguishes two emancipation strategies: early Western Marxism and ecological Marxism stress the collective liberation of the proletariat or of humanity and nature, while the Frankfurt School and feminist Marxism stress the individual. Zhang judges that combining institutional change with a change of values avoids the emptiness of speculative humanist philosophy of technology and the narrowness of engineering-minded approaches. The author also holds that, by relying too heavily on cultural-ideological critique, Western Marxism strayed from the basic line of Marxist political economy and ended in a moral utopianism. Zhang therefore calls for historical materialism to be upheld and for China, as it moves from a major to a strong science and technology power, to draw on this critique selectively, "with analysis and discernment", without rejecting or copying it wholesale. Read the original if you want a compact, officially minded assessment of how Chinese scholars evaluate Western Marxist theories of technology.

Why a great ecological civilization can emerge in socialist China An interview with the ecological Marxist theorist John Bellamy Foster 为什么伟大的生态文明能够在社会主义中国产生 John Bellamy Foster Guo Jianren This is an interview in which Guo Jianren of Zhongnan University of Economics and Law questions John Bellamy Foster, editor of Monthly Review and sociologist at the University of Oregon. It follows Foster's lecture "Ecological Civilization and Ecological Revolution: An Ecological Marxist Perspective", given at the invitation of the Sansheng Valley Cobb Eco-Academy. Foster's central claim is that the ecological civilization the world needs must move towards socialism, and that this is why the idea has become a real force in China but hardly exists in capitalist countries. Guo's questions cover five topics. They ask how ecological Marxism can draw on natural science, Whitehead's organic philosophy and traditional Chinese culture, and why Foster rejects Jeremy Lent's reading of Chinese ecological civilization. They ask about the political-economic mechanisms behind ecological civilization, including monopoly capitalism and the Green New Deal. They ask about Marx's "metabolism" concepts and China's urbanisation and rural revitalisation, about the "environmental proletariat", and about China's role in global ecological governance. Foster answers the first question through Joseph Needham, whom he presents as combining Marxism, ecological materialism, Whitehead's process philosophy and Chinese Daoist thought, all opposed to capitalism. On the second, he argues that the Western Green New Deal is only a slogan or "green Keynesianism" that the capitalist system rejects. He says monopoly capitalism produces stagnation, waste and financialisation and leaves no room for ecological civilization, whereas China treats it as a core task of socialist construction and has a roadmap for ecological transition. On the third, he says Marx's "universal metabolism of nature", "social metabolism" and "metabolic rift" form a unity. He wonders whether rapid urbanisation may widen China's rift, yet he welcomes collective rural land ownership, rural revitalisation and poverty reduction. He then proposes the "environmental proletariat", a broader class concept drawn from Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England, which would include ecological peasants and the workers and peasants of the Global South. Foster concludes that ecological civilization and the socialist movement reinforce each other. He describes China's ecological civilization as perhaps the greatest gift socialist development has given the world. He also notes that the idea first appeared in the Soviet Union in the 1980s. Read the original if you want Foster's own account, addressed to a Chinese audience, of ecological Marxism, his metabolic rift theory and his view of Chinese ecological civilization.

"Marxism in the Anthropocene": origins of the issue, content analysis and theoretical assessment “人类世的马克思主义”：议题源起、内容探析与理论评述 Zhao Ruifu This 2023 article, published in the Journal of China University of Geosciences (Social Sciences Edition), reviews the debate on "Marxism in the Anthropocene" that emerged in Euro-American thought around 2010. Zhao Ruifu asks what the issue actually says and how it should be assessed. The author's answer is that eco-Marxist and green-left scholars have used the Anthropocene concept to deepen the ecological critique of capitalism and to revise eco-Marxism's anthropocentric value basis and its vision of eco-socialism. Zhao first traces the Anthropocene concept from Buffon, Stoppani, Pavlov and Vernadsky to Stoermer and Crutzen (2000) and the Anthropocene Working Group's wider impact after 2008. A chronology of texts follows: Andreas Malm's "Capitalocene" (2009), Gerda Roelvink on species-being (2013), John Bellamy Foster's formal intervention from 2015, and works by Ian Angus, Kohei Saito, Camilla Royle, Alf Hornborg and others. Zhao marks 2009, 2015 and 2019 as stages of the debate. The article ends with an assessment from the standpoint of Marxist studies, eco-Marxism and China's socialist ecological civilization. Zhao sorts the debate into three clusters. The first concerns the start date of the Anthropocene: Foster and Saito favour the "Great Acceleration", while Malm and Hornborg reject blaming humanity as a whole and place responsibility on fossil capital. The second concerns an "update" of anthropocentrism: Foster, against what he sees as monistic anthropocentrism, defends a "dialectic of the Anthropocene" that keeps human agency within a dialectic of humanity and nature. The third concerns eco-socialist proposals, including Angus's and Foster's lists of concrete measures (16 in Foster's 2022 book) and Malm's "eco-Leninism", which Zhao says still lacks systematic form. In assessing the issue, Zhao credits it with giving Marxism abroad new momentum and activating its ecological content. Zhao also notes a risk of Marxism being "taken up at will", citing Simon Boxley's reading as an example. The author argues that engaging with the debate would help domestic scholars overcome what Zhao sees as China's relative silence on the Anthropocene. Zhao also holds that it could supply resources for the theory and practice of socialist ecological civilization and for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a mapped chronology and bibliography of Western eco-Marxist work on the Anthropocene, together with a Chinese scholar's view of its relevance to ecological civilization.

The historical practice of Chinese modernization: agrarian transformation and peasant life in contemporary Liangshan Yi areas through oral history 中国式现代化的历史实践：口述史视野下当代凉山彝族地区农政变革与农民生活 Ruan Chiyin Research on Chinese modernization has mostly worked at the macro level, and Ruan Chiyin argues that concrete empirical studies are still thin. This article takes up the socialist agrarian practice of the 1950s–1970s in a frontier mountain minority region, which the author says has been less studied than Han plains villages. Using oral history, Ruan contends that collectivization and the democratic reform dismantled a slave-holding hierarchy and gave poor peasants and women new standing. The author presents this as a distinctive path of agricultural and rural modernization, different from the Western one. The evidence comes from fieldwork in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan and in Yunnan between 2013 and 2016, combined with archives and published scholarship. The article opens with the rigid caste order of pre-1956 Yi society and the effects of opium cultivation. It then presents eight elders' accounts of the democratic reform of 1956–1958 and a case study of one multi-ethnic village, "X Village", under the people's commune. It ends with the village's changes after household contracting in the early 1980s. Ruan's central claim is that collective land ownership removed the material basis of lineage-based hierarchy. In the author's reading, the democratic reform of 1956–1958 freed slaves and redistributed land and tools. Collective production in X Village, with multiple cropping, livestock raising, processing and a "specialist team" that helped weaker teams, raised output and curbed inequality. The author also says it drew different ethnic groups into joint work. After decollectivization, Ruan reports, the two-harvests-in-a-year system and the combination of crops and livestock were abandoned. Irrigation and storage facilities decayed, and the lineage organisations regained influence. Women cadres became rare, land distribution became more uneven, and young adults left for wage work. Ruan sums up the achievements in three areas: the economic (sustainable integrated farming and less inequality), the political (equal status for the poor and for women) and the ideological (dignity and a collective spirit). The author sees these as laying the groundwork for common prosperity. The article ends by calling for lessons from this history to guide efforts to narrow wealth gaps in a market environment. It frames this within the Party's current stress on promoting common prosperity through high-quality development and on going beyond the crisis of modernity under Western capital logic. Read the original if you want first-hand oral-history testimony from Liangshan and a village-level account of collective agriculture and its dissolution in a minority region.

Chen Liang's atheism and his critique of Confucianism as a religion 陈亮无神论思想及其对儒教的批判 Liu Yu Chen Liang, a Southern Song utilitarian thinker long regarded in Chinese scholarship as a representative of ancient materialism, is the subject of this article. Liu asks what his atheism amounted to within Confucian thought. Liu argues that it was an attack on the religious-theological elements of Confucianism (rujiao, 'Confucian religion') and a defence of human value, and that it helped keep Confucian learning (ruxue) from turning into a full religion. Prior scholarship, Liu notes, has mostly studied Chen's atheism through the 'relation of Heaven and man' and views on ghosts and spirits, without stating clearly that it criticised Confucianism as a religion. Liu builds on Ren Jiyu's thesis that Confucianism is a religion, and on Hou Wailu's reading of Chen's debate with Zhu Xi as 'militant atheism'. The article has three parts: Chen's rejection of Confucianism's mystical elements; his affirmation of human value and agency; and an assessment of his place in Confucianism's self-correction, with a short conclusion. In the first part, Liu argues that Chen's materialist epistemology held that the boundary between Heaven and man is 'plainly knowable'. On that basis Chen denied the sacredness of sages and classics, and reinterpreted the 'Way' (dao) as something inseparable from concrete things and everyday affairs. He also attacked the Neo-Confucian 'Heavenly principle' (tianli) as a disguised theism that suppresses human desires. In the second part, Liu presents Chen's slogan that the Way's survival depends on people as an answer to Zhu Xi. Chen stressed human agency, defended legitimate desire, criticised the introspective doctrines of mind and nature, and valued heroes and human planning over fate. Liu cites Marx and Engels to frame this as negating the divine in order to affirm the human. Liu concludes that Confucian learning is a 'study of the human' rather than a religion. The author holds that Confucianism was repeatedly corrected from within, and that Chen played this role against the Song-Ming Neo-Confucians, whose system Ren Jiyu called the completion of the Confucian 'god-making movement'. Liu concedes that Chen's atheism was incomplete: he still showed some reverence for Heaven's mandate and wrote prayers for rain. Liu still judges the flaws minor. In the context of promoting excellent traditional Chinese culture today, the author calls for removing the religious-theological elements of Confucianism and drawing on its positive components. Read the original if you want a Marxist-atheist reading of the Chen Liang–Zhu Xi debate, with extensive quotations from Chen's writings and letters.

Relying on tenacious struggle to open up new horizons for our cause 依靠顽强斗争打开事业发展新天地 Bu Xianqun Bu Xianqun, writing in 2023 after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up the Congress report's call to "rely on tenacious struggle to open up new horizons for our cause". The commentary argues that the report embodies the Party's spirit of great struggle and that this spirit should guide the Party's work in the new era. In Bu's view, the spirit is a necessary mental quality and capacity for the struggles that lie ahead. The article is organised in three parts: the theoretical, practical and cultural foundations of the spirit of struggle; its new meanings in the new era; and the guidance it offers for the future. It draws on Marxist theory, the history of the Party, the long history of Chinese civilisation, and Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also refers to the 19th Party Congress report (2017) on the links among great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream. Bu contends that the spirit of struggle is inherent to Marxism, because Marxism treats the unity of opposites as the basic law of development and sees struggle as part of the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production. It is also described as the Party's spiritual base across revolution, construction and reform, and as a trait of the Chinese nation seen in reform, self-strengthening and vigilance in times of peace. The article lists what Xi has said the "great struggle with many new historical features" demands: firm ideals, Party leadership, vigilance against major risks, and the Party's self-reform. It notes that the 20th Party Congress report made upholding the spirit of struggle one of five major principles and called on cadres to "dare to fight and be good at fighting". Bu concludes that great struggle is a judgement based on real conditions, an integral part of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a requirement for safeguarding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee. After the 20th Party Congress, the Party's central task is to build a modern socialist country in all respects and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, and struggle is to proceed along that path. Bu calls on readers to understand the spirit of struggle through Marxism, Party and national history, and the history of Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated historians present the 20th Congress's language of struggle and its claimed theoretical, historical and cultural roots.

The Lao People's Revolutionary Party's exploration and practice of the people's standpoint, and its main lessons 老挝人民革命党人民立场的探索实践与主要经验 Xu Qinfa Zuo Yuntian Xu Qinfa and Zuo Yuntian ask how the Lao People's Revolutionary Party (LPRP) has upheld a "people's standpoint" since leading Laos through the anti-French, anti-Japanese and anti-American wars of national liberation and founding the Lao People's Democratic Republic in 1975. They argue that the Party's persistence in this standpoint explains its achievements in revolution and in the reform era, and that summarising it offers international experience for socialist countries, world socialism and the international communist movement. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical basis: the views of Marx, Engels and Lenin on the masses as makers of history and on the danger of a ruling party losing contact with them, and the thought of Kaysone Phomvihane, which the authors present as the Lao localisation of Marxism-Leninism and the Party's basic guide. The second reviews practice in three fields: perfecting the political system of people's democracy, raising living standards, and keeping open channels for gathering the people's strength. The third draws out the main lessons. In the practice section, the authors describe the LPRP's shift from "proletarian dictatorship" to "people's democratic dictatorship" and its theory of people's democracy as a stage towards socialism, followed by the 1991 constitution and more than 140 laws by 2017. They cite figures on per capita GDP rising from US$325 in 2000 to US$2,664 in 2020, public-health coverage of 98 per cent in rural areas, and growth in schools. They also cite mass organisations, Buddhism treated as a positive force, leaders' grassroots visits, and anti-corruption rules such as asset declarations. The authors draw three lessons. The Party builds a systematic "people's theory" from experience, arms cadres with it and spreads it among the people to win hearts. It improves Party building, in ideology, politics, organisation and conduct, so as to gather popular strength. It treats protecting the people's fundamental interests as both the starting point and the aim in meeting risks such as the Asian financial crisis, Covid-19 and Western "peaceful evolution". Read the original if you want a Chinese-academic account of the Lao Party's governance record, with dates, policy documents and statistics, as seen from the Chinese scholarship on world socialism.

From the pursuit of perfect order to the practice of cultural theory Zygmunt Bauman's exploration of paths beyond the crisis of modernity 从完美秩序的追寻到文化理论的实践 Zhou Laishun Gao Yan Among Western thinkers who have criticised modernity since the mid-twentieth century, Zygmunt Bauman is read by Zhou and Gao as offering a distinctive response to its crisis. The article argues that Bauman diagnoses the crisis through metaphors of order, then looks for a way out in culture understood as creative practice, which in their account restores human creativity and subjectivity. The article has three parts. The first sets out the manifestations and essence of the crisis of modernity, drawing on Bauman's images of the panopticon and the gardening ambition and on his work on the Holocaust. The second treats culture as modern society's self-consciousness and as a bearer of internal ambivalence. The third turns to cultural practice as a way of dissolving the crisis, through structuration and utopian practice. The authors situate Bauman between Marx, Gramsci, Foucault, Lévi-Strauss and existentialism. For Bauman, as the authors present him, modernity is essentially the production of order, and the drive for perfect order must expel whatever cannot be assimilated, so it produces disorder and ambivalence. The panopticon (after Foucault) and the gardener-state of Legislators and Interpreters show how this order standardises individuals; Modernity and the Holocaust treats Auschwitz as a product of the same bureaucratic and technical rationality. Culture is both creative and a tool of regulation, because humans build their social world and are bound by it. The way out lies in culture as practice rather than as structure. Structuration is endless and revolutionary activity that resists fixed order. Utopian practice, set out in Socialism: The Active Utopia, criticises alienation and historical necessity and opens possibilities without describing a concrete future society. Zhou and Gao conclude that Bauman offers a humanist, Marxist-anthropological path beyond modernity's crisis, aimed at recovering the individual's self-determined freedom. They also note a limit. Utopia always lies ahead as a vision, supplies no specific remedy, and would be dangerous if turned into a concrete social blueprint. Read the original if you study Bauman, foreign Marxism or critical theories of modernity and want a Chinese scholarly reading that links his cultural theory to Marx and Gramsci.

The two-way interaction between Chinese philosophy and Marxist atheism and its significance Han-dynasty philosophy in Ren Jiyu's history of philosophy 中国哲学与马克思主义无神论的双向互动及其意义 Wang Shiliang Wang Shiliang asks how the work of Ren Jiyu (1916–2009), a leading Marxist historian of Chinese philosophy and religion, linked the study of Chinese philosophy with Marxist atheism. The article argues that Ren fused two approaches: a Marxist history of philosophy and his thesis that Confucianism is a religion. In Wang's reading, this fusion produced a two-way interaction between Chinese philosophy and Marxist atheism, and it still carries methodological meaning for atheism research and education today. The article opens with Ren's 'three histories' of Chinese philosophy (the four-volume History of Chinese Philosophy, the Concise History, and the History of the Development of Chinese Philosophy) and his work on the 'three teachings' of Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism. It then traces Ren's conception of the history of philosophy, including a shift in emphasis between the early textbook and the later multi-volume history. The central case study is Ren's interpretation of Han-dynasty philosophy: Dong Zhongshu, the Baihu tong, Wang Chong, and the relation between philosophy and natural science. Wang shows that Ren first defined philosophy's history as a history of struggle between materialism and idealism, shaped by Zhdanov's definition and class analysis. Later Ren gave greater weight to the history of human cognition and described Chinese philosophy as advancing through struggle with religion. In the Han case, Ren reads Dong Zhongshu's doctrine of heaven–human correspondence as a theology serving centralised autocracy, and the Baihu tong as completing a 'state religion of feudal society'. Wang Chong appears as a 'militant atheist' whose empiricism hit at the core of Confucian doctrine, although Ren also notes contradictions, such as fatalism, that stopped him from being a thoroughgoing atheist. Han medicine and agriculture, Ren argues, show the practical knowledge that undercuts theology. Wang concludes that Ren applied Marxist principles to the concrete course of Chinese philosophy and deepened understanding of its cognitive history. Wang adds that Ren carried out Mao Zedong's call to criticise theology and so widened the 'ideological front' of Marxist atheism. For the present, Wang suggests that atheism research and education should link up with the new liberal arts, ideological and political courses, and textbook systems. Read the original if you want a detailed account of Ren Jiyu's reading of Dong Zhongshu, the Baihu tong and Wang Chong, or of how Chinese Marxist scholarship treats religion and Confucianism.

Paradigms and practical paths for the global communication of a community with a shared future for mankind 人类命运共同体全球传播范式与实践取径 Sun Lijun Writing in 2023, Sun Lijun asks how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, first written into the Party Congress report at the 18th Party Congress (2012) and reaffirmed at the 20th (2022), can be spread effectively worldwide. The article argues that the idea's global communication is moving through three successive paradigms: mass-media diffusion, multi-actor participation and idea reproduction. It holds that China must lead the shift from the first to the second and prepare for the third. The article first traces how the concept was enriched over a decade, from the 2011 white paper on China's peaceful development through the Belt and Road Initiative to the "five communities" (health, security, development, humanistic and human–nature life communities). It places the concept in a longer intellectual history of "community", from Marx and Engels's The German Ideology to Ferdinand Tönnies and Western communitarianism. Using Thomas Kuhn's notion of paradigm, it then periodises the idea's communication. It closes with four practical shifts: in values, channels, narrative and discourse strategy. Sun reports a discourse analysis of mainstream media in 18 countries and regions. In the author's account, US coverage was negative, European coverage mixed, and Belt and Road and African media most attentive, with coverage rising since 2018 and the Covid-19 pandemic. From this the author argues that government-led, single-voice diffusion has limited effect, and that NGOs, transnational firms and individuals should take part, mainly through social media. The four shifts are from "issue-based" to "people-centred" values, from one-way to multidimensional channels, from fact-based to story-based narrative, and from monologue to dialogue. Sun cites the spread of an Italian girl's thank-you cartoon and China's COVAX vaccine supply as examples. Sun concludes that global communication is overcoming Euro-centrism and that China should raise its communication capacity, widen participation and upgrade its view of global governance. The author expects the third, reproduction paradigm to arrive only slowly, once states accept that no country can stand apart from global crises. In that stage the idea would be re-created from each country's own conditions and would also reproduce Marxist social theory under new globalisation. Read the original if you study Chinese international communication strategy, or want to see how a Chinese media scholar applies Kuhn, Rogers and social-media theory to a Party concept.

The innovative value of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and its future development 中国特色社会主义道路的创新价值及其未来发展 Zhao Yong Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which lists adherence to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics as a major principle for building a modern socialist country, Zhao Yong asks what is innovative about this path and where it is heading. The article, published in Theory and Reform in 2023, argues that the path should be examined through a "grand view of history", placed within the histories of the Party, the People's Republic, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation. Zhao concludes that the path is the necessary route to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and that it offers an original option for human modernization. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundation (Marxism), the historical depth (the evolution from the new-democratic revolution to socialist revolution, socialist construction and socialism with Chinese characteristics) and the practical basis of the path since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The second identifies four forms of innovation: in path, theory, institutions and culture. The third looks ahead, proposing three perspectives for the future: subjectivity, historical initiative and international vision. Zhao argues that the path embodies the diversity of modernization routes, both as a whole and through its many specific sub-paths, from economic and political development to the rule of law and peaceful development. In theory, Chinese modernization is said to enrich world modernization theory, to end the "end of history" thesis, to undermine the basis of "Western-centrism" and to reject capital-centred, polarising, expansionist modernization. Institutionally, Zhao sees a "three-in-one" logic of fundamental, basic and important systems that unites upholding and developing socialism with using and transcending capitalism. Culturally, the path draws on traditional Chinese civilization and offers a new form of human civilization, answering the "clash of civilizations" with exchange and mutual learning. For the future, Zhao calls for stronger subjectivity amid great changes unseen in a century, noting that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and must keep its development in its own hands. Zhao also urges greater historical initiative, grounded in a people-centred approach, and a Chinese discourse and narrative system that raises China's international discourse power. The article is a statement of the official framing of the path and its global significance. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Party-affiliated scholarship presents the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics after the 20th Party Congress.

Mao Zedong's incisive analysis of why the "road of capitalist society" could not work in China 毛泽东对“资本主义社会之路”在中国行不通的深刻剖析 Cao Mingchen Cao Mingchen takes up a question from modern Chinese history: why China did not and could not follow the European and American capitalist path. Drawing on Mao Zedong's writings and speeches, the article argues that the national bourgeoisie's proposals for a bourgeois republic, in whatever form, were repeatedly shown to be unworkable. In Cao's account, China's only viable course was the New Democratic and then socialist road under Communist Party leadership. The article begins with the post-1840 semi-colonial, semi-feudal setting and then works through five reasons drawn from Mao, before a short conclusion. These are: imperialism did not permit it; socialism, as a new force in world history, did not permit it; the big landlords and big bourgeoisie firmly opposed democracy; the national bourgeoisie was weak, compromising and vacillating; and the struggle was led by the proletariat. Cao cites Mao texts from the 1920s to the late 1940s, including "On New Democracy" and his 1949 report to the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee. Cao groups the reasons into external and internal ones. Externally, Mao held that imperialism aimed to keep China a semi-colony and so blocked its national capitalism, while the October Revolution and the Soviet Union opened a new era in which colonial revolutions belonged to the world proletarian socialist revolution. Internally, the Guomindang regime represented big landlords and the bureaucratic bourgeoisie, and Chiang Kai-shek never became a Chinese "Kemal". The national bourgeoisie, economically small and afraid of the masses, was dual in character and could not lead the revolution. Cao calls proletarian leadership, exercised through the Communist Party, the decisive factor and presents Mao's "two-step" idea of a New Democratic revolution followed by a socialist one. Cao concludes that the failure of the capitalist road had both objective and subjective causes: China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions allowed neither the old Western path nor a direct leap to socialism, and the bourgeoisie lacked the strength to lead. In this reading, the founding of New China and the socialist system confirm the historical necessity of socialism. Cao says Mao's analysis helps strengthen confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a systematic, source-based account of how Mao explained China's rejection of the capitalist road, as presented in Party-history scholarship.

The spirit of historical initiative: its genesis, identity-building function and paths of deepening 历史主动精神：生成逻辑、认同功能与深化路径 Sun Chongya Gao Fujin Against a background of turbulence in world history, the article asks how the Chinese nation can keep its historical resolve and confidence. It takes up the leadership's call to "strengthen historical confidence and historical initiative" and argues that the spirit of historical initiative (lishi zhudong jingshen) is a cultural form that leads people to understand and make history correctly. The authors contend that it unleashes subjects' conscious agency and strengthens popular identification with the path of Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first traces the spirit's genesis along three lines: a theoretical logic grounded in historical materialism, a historical logic rooted in the Chinese tradition of innovation, and a practical logic based on the spirit of struggle. The second sets out three identity functions: identification with a mission, with an order, and with a memory. The third proposes three ways to deepen the spirit, each aimed at a specific risk. On genesis, the authors argue that historical materialism, with its focus on labour practice, gave birth to the spirit. They read classical Chinese ideas such as "self-strengthening without rest" and the reform programmes of Wang Anshi and Kang Youwei as sources of its innovative content, and they treat the Communist Party's struggle as its practical form. On function, the authors hold that the spirit supports the legitimacy of Chinese modernization through its "people-centred" values. They also hold that it carries national governance towards "good governance" (shanzhi) through a principle of justice, and that it consolidates historical confidence through the collective memory of national rejuvenation. On deepening, the authors prescribe a "grand historical outlook" against historical nihilism, which they link to Western "colour revolutions". They also call for "subject rationality" to disenchant capital logic and consumerism, and for strengthened "spiritual production" against technological rationality, with attention to digital technology, "technology for good" and humanism. The authors conclude that the deeper a people's grasp of historical laws, the more it controls its own destiny. They hold that the "great changes unseen in a century" are both an opportunity and a challenge, and that seizing historical trends through initiative lets humanity advance. The text uses the vocabulary of Party theory of its period, and it reads as an attempt to ground that vocabulary in classical Marxist concepts. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link historical materialism, traditional culture and national identification to the idea of historical initiative.

Whole-process people's democracy as a necessary requirement and path of realization for Chinese modernization 全过程人民民主是中国式现代化的必然要求和实现路径 Li Feng Li Feng argues that Chinese modernization and whole-process people's democracy have so far been studied separately: the first mostly in macro-economic and social terms, the second mainly as democratic ideas and institutions. The article sets out to link them, contending that whole-process people's democracy is both a necessary requirement of Chinese modernization and its political path of realization. Without that link, the author holds, democracy lacks a long-term goal and modernization lacks a democratic dimension. The article opens by presenting Chinese modernization as a new form of human modernization and whole-process people's democracy as a new form of human political civilization. It then proceeds in two directions. The first runs from the five features of Chinese modernization (an enormous population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement in step, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development) to the need for this form of democracy. The second runs from democracy's five links (election, consultation, decision-making, management, supervision) to their role in carrying modernization forward. In the first part, Li draws on the scale of China's population and territory, which the author describes as imposing a heavy governance load and requiring a democracy that integrates interests under Communist Party leadership. Common prosperity is said to need both market mechanisms and economic democracy, balanced by state regulation and a guard against populism and egalitarianism. The author also rejects Western modernization theory, citing Lipset and Coppedge, as tying modernization to Western-style democracy through biased democracy indices. In the second part, Li assigns each link a task: election supplies legitimacy and efficient information processing; consultation handles complex, conflicting interests; democratic decision-making manages risk and combines democracy with centralism; management and supervision turn participation into governance effectiveness. Li contrasts this with what the article calls the gridlock and 'veto politics' of Western democracy. Li concludes that the five features of Chinese modernization can be realized only with the values and institutional guarantees of whole-process people's democracy, and that its core meaning can be understood only within the horizon of Chinese modernization. The article promises further development of democratic forms and greater effectiveness so as to achieve modernization 'faster and better'. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how whole-process people's democracy is tied to the official framework of Chinese modernization, and of how its five links are assigned governance functions.

"People-masses-first-ism" in North Korea under Kim Jong Un ​金正恩时代朝鲜的“人民群众第一主义” Li Yongchun Li Yongchun asks how the Workers' Party of Korea under Kim Jong Un came to define its guiding ideology, "Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ism", as in essence "people-masses-first-ism" (renmin qunzhong diyi zhuyi), and what this means in practice. Li notes that scholarly work on the topic is scarce. The article argues that the formula has become the core governing idea of the Kim Jong Un era, replacing the earlier emphasis on military-first politics. The article has three main parts followed by a conclusion. It first traces the concept through three stages: its germ in 2012, its formal proposal in 2013, and its deepening from the Seventh Party Congress (2016) to the Eighth (2021). It then sets out the concept's content, drawing on published speeches and writings by the leaders. Finally it surveys implementation in the political, economic and social fields. Li points out that the party's internal study materials on the ideology are not public, so the account rests on openly available sources. Li presents the concept as having four components: it descends from the Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il maxim of treating the people as heaven; it treats the people as masters of revolution and construction; it relies on the people's strength to advance the revolution; and it requires selfless service to the people. On implementation, Li describes a sustained and public campaign against abuse of power, bureaucracy and corrupt practices, including the dismissal of officials in 2020 and a strengthened party inspection body after the Eighth Congress. Li also cites economic measures (agriculture, light industry, a livestock base, large housing projects, five-year plans) and social ones (12-year compulsory education, health facilities, cultural and tourist sites). Li reads the Eighth Congress's decision to write the concept into the party rules as the basic political method of socialism, in place of military-first politics, as a shift from "military-first" to "people-first" politics. Li concludes that the concept has strengthened unity around Kim Jong Un and domestic stability, and says that predictions of North Korean collapse have proved wrong. Li names natural disasters, sanctions and the pandemic as the "three mountains" in the way, and expects the party to keep applying the principle to economic development and living standards. Li also expects it to be treated as a guiding ideology on a par with the Juche idea and military-first thought. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how North Korean official sources frame Kim Jong Un's ideology and its policy applications, with dated citations of speeches and party meetings.

Towards everyday life: tracing the distinctive qualities of socialist consultative democracy 走向日常生活：社会主义协商民主的特质探源 Zhang Liwei Why should consultative democracy move into people's daily lives, and what does it look like when it does? Zhang Liwei starts from the claim that consultative democracy is an important form of whole-process people's democracy. Zhang argues that moving it into everyday life takes democracy beyond its confinement to politics and makes it a way of life. This, the article holds, shows what is distinctive about the Chinese path of democracy. The article has four parts. It first sets out why democracy should be built in everyday life, drawing on participatory democratic theory and its critique of liberal democracy. It then examines the qualities of everyday consultative democracy through historical inheritance and modern reconstruction. A third part discusses its value, engaging Henri Lefebvre's critique of everyday life and Marx on human emancipation. A short conclusion draws out the implications. Zhang's first move is to argue that everyday life gives "participation" a social foundation. Because it is tied to personal interests, everyday participation mobilises people from below, builds trust in democratic institutions, and supplies methods for political democracy. The second move traces the inheritance of consultative democracy from the Chinese cultural ideal of harmony in diversity and the saying "when there is a problem, discuss it", which Zhang reads as seeking consensus through overlapping preferences rather than compromise. Zhang says it must also be rebuilt for the individual, social and ethical sides of the person, through equal participation, social capital and communicative ethics. The third move is that consultation restores meaning to daily life by countering alienation and strengthening intersubjectivity. Zhang links it to Marx's idea of social emancipation, citing its popular character, problem orientation and educative function. Zhang concludes that democratic research should look beyond the political sphere and treat daily life as a new vantage point. In Zhang's account, everyday democracy complements political democracy, forms its social basis and supports a harmonious relationship between state and society. The author presents this as a creative transformation of Marxist democratic theory and a contribution to a new form of political civilisation and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you study Chinese theories of consultative democracy or want to see how Marxist, participatory and Confucian-style concepts are combined in one argument.

"New materialism" and the philosophical foundations of a community with a shared future for mankind “新唯物主义”与人类命运共同体的哲学根基 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang asks what philosophical ground underlies the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) describes as where the future of the world's peoples lies. Liu argues that it is rooted in Marx's "new materialism", whose standpoint, set out in the Theses on Feuerbach, is "human society or social humanity" rather than civil society. The article presents this shift of standpoint as an ontological revolution and as the basic precondition for the community's appearance in the new era. The article has three parts. The first contrasts civil society and human society along three lines: the logical starting point, the mode of thinking, and the ultimate destination. The second links civil society to capitalist economic globalization and the "centre–periphery" order. The third moves from human society to the community with a shared future for mankind, drawing on Marx, Hegel, Lenin, Rousseau, Althusser and Western communitarian thought. Liu contends that old philosophy begins from the abstract human being, thinks through empirical intuition and the subject–object divide, and ends in a "false community". Marx's new materialism begins from real individuals engaged in production, thinks dialectically, and aims at a "true community". Liu argues that the private interests of civil society, driven by the logic of capital, spread worldwide as unequal hierarchies of core and periphery, which the bourgeois state and its "universal values" justify. The community with a shared future, in Liu's reading, sublates this alienation as a realist and not an altruist or idealist scheme. It recognises differences between states, seeks shared interests, answers "global problems" through joint consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, and offers a measure of ethical security against modern anxiety. Liu concludes that the community with a shared future continues Marx's project of "changing the world" in the new era and carries real world-historical significance. China's promotion of it is said to show a major-country sense of responsibility. Liu calls for deeper philosophical study of its theoretical resources and of its inheritance from new materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed philosophical genealogy that ties Chinese foreign-policy language to Marx's early writings and to the civil society debate.

Three misreadings of Lenin's New Economic Policy and their correction 关于列宁新经济政策的三大误读与正解 Liu Jun Sun Cuiping Liu Jun and Sun Cuiping take up the question of what Lenin's New Economic Policy (NEP, introduced in 1921 in place of War Communism) actually was, and argue that it has been persistently misread. They identify three representative misreadings: the "temporary expedient" view, the "retreat" view and the "preparation for an offensive" view. Their thesis is that the NEP was a long-term, systematic exploration of how a backward country can move towards socialism by an indirect route, not a stopgap, a capitulation or a pause before attack. The article takes each misreading in turn, citing its holders: Preobrazhensky, a 2009 Russian teachers' handbook and Ryazanovsky and Steinberg's history of Russia for the first; the Smenovekhovtsy ("change of landmarks" émigrés), Leszek Kołakowski and Evgenia Gnatenko for the second; and Zinoviev and Stalin, in the latter's late-1920s dispute with Bukharin, for the third. It then sets out three methodological principles for reading the NEP correctly. These are drawn from Lenin's own texts and linked to remarks by Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Against the first view, the authors stress Lenin's phrase that the policy would be pursued "seriously and for a long time" and was meant to carry Russia through the whole transition period. Against the second, they argue that state capitalism under the dictatorship of the proletariat is capitalism that the workers' state can restrict and delimit, so the NEP changed the method of economic construction, not the nature of the state. Against the third, they read Lenin's call to "halt the retreat" as meaning no further concessions, not an end to the NEP, and as calling for regrouping and selecting capable personnel rather than attacking. They treat his talk of an "offensive" as a way of placating radicals in the Party. The three principles are the dialectical unity of the universal and the particular in historical development, of retreat and advance, and of using capitalism and going beyond it. The authors note that state control of land and of the commanding heights of production formed the bottom line that guaranteed the NEP's socialist character. They conclude that the NEP was the first exploration of developing productive forces beyond a single form of public ownership, and that it offers lessons for reform in China. These include keeping public ownership dominant while using markets and multiple forms of ownership in the primary stage of socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of the NEP that draws on Lenin's texts and ties them to current Chinese debates on reform and the relation to capitalism.

Upholding a world-embracing outlook: theoretical sources, a century of practice and present-day lessons 坚持胸怀天下的理论溯源、百年历程及现实启示 Sun Xiuling The article examines "upholding a world-embracing outlook" (jianchi xionghuai tianxia), which the 20th Party Congress report (2022) lists as part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The 2021 Party history resolution also names it as one of the historical lessons of the Party's first century. Sun argues that the principle reflects the Party's Marxist stance on China's relations with the outside world. In Sun's account, it has deep theoretical roots and has guided a century of practice. It also yields lessons for advancing Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first traces three sources: the Marxist idea of world history, the "all under heaven" sentiment of traditional Chinese culture, and the foreign-policy thought developed in the Sinicisation of Marxism. The second surveys the Party's practice in four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third draws four lessons. Sun's core argument is that the principle joins Marx's analysis of world history with Chinese cultural concepts. From Marx and Engels, Sun takes the claim that capitalism created the world market and world history but will not end it. On this view, individual liberation and communism depend on history becoming fully world history. From the Chinese tradition Sun draws ideas such as the world as shared by all, harmony without uniformity, and benevolence towards others. Sun then follows foreign-policy thought from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. The article presents the practice in each period as foreign relations serving domestic tasks while pursuing independence, peace and shared development. It cites the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, foreign aid, the Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind, and poverty reduction. Sun draws four lessons. The first is to master the worldview and methodology of the Party's Sinicised Marxism. The second is to preserve centralised, unified Party leadership as the basis for handling external relations. The third is to pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, taking on greater international responsibility. The fourth is to keep to independence and self-reliance while learning from other civilisations. Sun concludes that the principle will help Chinese modernization create "a new form of human civilisation". Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how official scholarship traces the lineage of the world-embracing outlook from Marx and classical Chinese texts to Xi Jinping's diplomacy.

An important milestone on the Chinese nation's road to great rejuvenation The victory in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea and its spirit 中华民族走向伟大复兴的重要里程碑 Tang Junfeng This commentary was published in the People's Daily on the 70th anniversary of the victory in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea. Tang takes up Xi Jinping's description of that victory as a declaration that the Chinese people had stood up, and as an important milestone on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author argues that remembering the war and carrying forward its spirit should inspire the Chinese people to advance on the new journey of building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the victory matters historically. The second identifies four components of the Great Spirit of Resisting US Aggression and Aiding Korea. The third turns to the present and lists four resolves that remembering the war is meant to strengthen. In the first part, Tang describes China's intervention as a just act by a just army, taken at the request of the Korean Party and government after US forces crossed the 38th Parallel and, in the author's account, threatened China's security. Tang presents the outcome as a victory of the weak over the strong.
