In this account it secured the new state's footing, displayed the strength of the people's army, deterred later armed attempts against China and encouraged oppressed peoples elsewhere. The four elements of the spirit are fearlessness towards bullying and hegemony, national unity under Party leadership, a willingness to fight to the death, and innovative wisdom. Tang links each to a present task: meeting risks with courage, building the broadest unity, refusing to flinch from struggle, and pioneering Chinese modernization. Tang concludes that China must hold firm in four resolves: unity under the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, building a strong country and achieving rejuvenation, building a world-class military under Xi Jinping Thought on Strengthening the Military, and defending world peace and justice. The last is tied to opposing hegemonism and power politics and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official commentary in 2023 used the Korean War to support themes of Party leadership, military strengthening and national rejuvenation.

The cultural construction of a community with a shared future for mankind and its world significance 人类命运共同体的文化构建及其世界意义 Liu Tongfang Liu Tongfang asks what the cultural dimension of building a community with a shared future for mankind consists of, and what it offers the world. Writing in 2023, Liu argues that this cultural construction is the spiritual side of the community and has an internal structure that unites subjectivity, diversity and leadership (主导性). It has three levels, material, political and spiritual, and performs three functions: integrating, transcending and reproducing. The article has four sections. It first defines the three features of cultural construction, then sets out the three levels, then the three functions, and finally the way cultural construction shapes a new "world civilisation body". Liu draws on Marx and Engels, Gramsci's cultural hegemony, Fei Xiaotong's idea of cultural subjectivity, Heidegger, Daniel Bell, Althusser and Bourdieu, and criticises Hegel, Fukuyama and Huntington. Liu's central move is to ground culture in material production. The material level is the foundation, the political level (the state, institutions, political identity) is the safeguard, and the spiritual level (a spiritual home, shared values) is the aim and reacts back on the other two. The author holds that capitalist globalisation sets "universal values" against exploitation and capital accumulation, and that this produces cultural hegemony and Western "cultural centrism". The three functions are described as follows: integrating means individuals identify with community norms, transcending means critique of reality oriented to people's free and all-round development, and reproducing means cultural output is constantly renewed to meet spiritual needs. Liu concludes that this cultural construction answers Western cultural centrism and offers a way to resolve civilisational conflict through dialogue and mutual learning, with the principle of harmony in diversity. It also points toward a new pattern of inclusive world civilisation. The author presents it as a form of Chinese wisdom that shows China's cultural consciousness and confidence and has milestone significance for human civilisation. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-academic account of how the cultural dimension of the community with a shared future for mankind is theorised, using both Marxist and Western sources.

The shifting centre of gravity of the world socialist movement and China as its mainstay 世界社会主义运动重心转移现象与中国成为社会主义事业中流砥柱 Wang Chuanli Zhu Siyuan Wang Chuanli and Zhu Siyuan ask why leadership of the world socialist movement has moved from country to country, and where it now lies. Their thesis is that uneven development explains the shifts, and that China, under the leadership of the Communist Party, has become the mainstay (zhongliu dizhu) of the movement's revival. They present this as the realisation of Lenin's thesis of a "backward Europe and advanced Asia". The article has three parts. The first traces the movement's centre of gravity through Britain (Chartism), France (June 1848 and the Paris Commune), Germany (the Second International) and Russia (the October Revolution and the Third International), relying mainly on quotations from Marx, Engels and Lenin. The second sets out four reasons why China now holds this role. The third discusses the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The authors argue that shifts depend on objective circumstances and subjective preparation. Objective conditions are decisive, but once they mature a strong proletarian party becomes the key factor, as in the case of the Bolsheviks. They contend that the Communist Party of China meets this condition. Their reasons are its handling of the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, its adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, its "Chinese solution" to global disorder, and its size, discipline and capacity for self-reform. They compare it with the Soviet, Eastern European, Western European, Greek and Japanese communist parties, all of which they say failed in some respect. In the third part they claim that China's success refutes Fukuyama's "end of history", Western-centrism and Huntington's "clash of civilizations". They say it offers developing countries a path to Chinese modernization that avoids colonial plunder and dependence. The authors conclude that the new era marks the start of the epoch Mao Zedong predicted in 1962. In their account, China's "new form of human civilisation" shows the superiority of socialism over capitalism and points the way to the revival of world socialism, to modernization in developing countries and to peaceful development. The article is a Party-aligned, openly affirmative account of China's global role. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholars periodise the history of the world socialist movement and justify China's claim to lead it.

The impact of Christian missions on the sense of community of the Chinese nation, and how to respond The case of Christian missions in the China–Burma border region in the 1930s 基督教传播对中华民族共同体意识的影响及应对 Gao Tietai Gao Tietai takes up the question of how Christian missions weakened the national identity of ethnic groups on the China–Burma border in the 1930s, and what lessons that history holds today. The article, published in the journal Science and Atheism (2023, no. 3), uses 'Christianity' in the broad sense of Catholicism and Protestantism. Its thesis is that missionary activity diluted local attachment to the motherland and to Chinese culture, and that contemporary efforts to forge a stronger sense of community of the Chinese nation, together with the 'Sinicisation' of Christianity, can draw on the responses of that period. The article has four parts. It first describes confused national identity among border peoples during the boundary disputes of the early twentieth century, citing the 1933 Banhong incident and the Sino-British boundary survey commissions of 1935–37. It then sets out three channels of missionary influence. A third part reviews how officials, scholars and the public understood the problem and responded. A final part draws implications for Yunnan today. Gao argues that missionaries gained great appeal among converts, whom the author says 'knew only the pastor, not the government'. They ran church schools with texts in missionary-created scripts or in English and Burmese, and the author says some lessons were hostile to Han Chinese. They also recast historical memory, for instance by presenting Jesus as the brother of Zhuge Liang, whom many local peoples revered. Contemporary Chinese commentators, in Gao's account, did not interfere directly with belief. They promoted border education, the national language, textbooks on shared history and the thesis that the Chinese nation is one. They also favoured localised churches and political propaganda carried by itinerant teaching teams. Gao concludes that the 1930s measures partly resisted missionary division and prompted early thinking about Christianity's 'Chinese-isation'. For the present, the author calls for the Sinicisation of Christianity in border areas, wider use of the standard national language and script, and stronger historical memory of the Chinese nation. The stated aim is to resist overseas religious infiltration and to consolidate the sense of community of the Chinese nation as the main line of ethnic work. Read the original if you study Party ethnic and religious policy, Christianity in Yunnan, or how Republican-era frontier history is used in current Chinese policy discourse.

A scientific demonstration of the decisive significance of the communist ideal 共产主义理想决定性意义的科学论证 Hou Huiqin Hou Huiqin takes up the claim that the communist ideal is only a "result" of historical events, a distant "other shore" and not a real force, so that it plays no decisive role in history. Hou argues that this claim rests on a crude reading of historical materialism, and that the ideal's decisive role can be established scientifically, in theory and in practice. Citing Xi Jinping, Hou treats wavering ideals and convictions as the most dangerous kind of wavering for a Marxist party. The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic theory: the dialectic of matter and consciousness, the two senses of "determining" and the two senses of "reaction". The second argues that Marxism created a scientific form of belief, after surveying earlier religious and traditional Chinese forms. The third examines the features of communist belief, its link to Chinese modernization, and the standards and mechanisms for testing Party members' convictions. Drawing on Engels, Hou separates economics as determining "in the last instance" from the actual course of history, where politics, culture and ideas can be decisive. Hou argues that Western "economic determinism" is aimed at the communist ideal. Hou distinguishes a spontaneous agency, such as capitalist production, from agency guided by a scientific worldview, which can accelerate history. In Hou's account, Marx's critique of German ideology, of the modern state and of commodity fetishism resolved the two keys to scientific belief: the knowability of the thing-in-itself and the unity of relative and absolute truth. This, Hou says, grounds a belief based on the unity of working-class and human interests. Hou describes communist belief as real, because it runs through the transition process, as staged, like a relay, and as lofty, because it ends humanity's "prehistory". Hou criticises Popper and Hayek for rejecting conscious historical creation, and presents Chinese modernization as conscious modernization under Party leadership, as against Western spontaneous modernization. In peacetime, Hou proposes loyalty to the Party as the test of conviction, applied through the "key minority" of leading cadres, learning and supervision systems, and the Party's self-reform, with a stated target of "two-faced" officials. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher links the epistemology of belief to Party discipline and ideological work.

The impact of the new round of left-wing governments on Latin America's socialist movement 新一轮左翼执政对拉美社会主义运动的影响 Yuan Dongzhen Writing in 2023, Yuan Dongzhen asks how the recent return of left-wing governments in Latin America has affected the region's socialist movement, and what this shows about the link between the left and socialism. The article argues that the new round of left rule has improved the overall environment for socialism, while the movement's development remains constrained by party weaknesses, left–right alternation and outside hostility. The article first sets out three features of the new left cycle: its clustered, region-wide character, its cyclical nature, and its spillover effects. Yuan traces the first 'pink tide' from Venezuela in 1998–99, the right-wing turn after 2015, and the left's return from Mexico (2018) to Brazil (2022–23). The second part examines four effects on socialism, drawing on cases from Venezuela, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Uruguay and Bolivia. A short conclusion draws the lessons together. Yuan argues that left governments are more favourable to socialism than right-wing ones. In the author's account, the left's social base, support for state intervention and social equity, and anti-US foreign policy overlap with socialist positions. The author holds that rising phases of Latin American socialism have coincided with left cycles and low points with right cycles. The author cites the right-wing Lima Group and Prosur, which targeted Venezuela and have since dissolved, and the restored diplomatic ties with Caracas after 2020, as evidence that pressure on '21st-century socialism' has eased. Yuan also reports that communist parties in Brazil, Chile and Colombia have become governing partners, and that left parties, regional bodies and intellectuals keep up a critique of capitalism and neoliberalism. In conclusion, Yuan identifies limits. Many left parties, such as Ecuador's Citizen Revolution and Bolivia's Movement for Socialism, are said to be organisationally immature, dependent on charismatic leaders and prone to clientelism and bureaucratism. Frequent left–right alternation means socialism can advance only gradually and in waves. Yuan adds that US and European conservative forces continue to oppose it, and that this resistance will be hard to remove in the short term. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's survey of the 2018–2023 left cycle in Latin America, including detailed data on communist party participation in government.}

Questions to be answered in upholding the direction of the sinicization of religion in China 坚持我国宗教中国化方向需要回答的几个问题 Dong Xiaoqin Dong Xiaoqin takes up misunderstandings that, according to the author's fieldwork, have arisen at the grassroots as the Party promotes the sinicization of religion. Believers ask what sinicization means, why it is needed and what will happen to their religion afterwards. Dong argues that these questions come from missing or one-sided understandings, and that the policy's meaning is clarified by answering three questions: whether it aims to "transform away" religion, whether it politicises religion, and whether it develops religion. The answer to each is no. The article has three main sections and a short conclusion. It draws on speeches by Xi Jinping, Mao Zedong's 1945 report On Coalition Government, early constitutional documents and the 1954 Constitution. It also uses the historical cases of Buddhism and Islam in China, and statistics on believers and religious venues cited by the author. On the first question, Dong holds that sinicization leaves "basic beliefs, core doctrines and ritual systems" intact. What changes is how doctrine is interpreted so that it fits socialist society and traditional Chinese culture, as Buddhism and Islam did historically. Dong proposes an official platform for interpreting scriptures, run under Party and government leadership, whose representatives must be politically reliable, learned, law-abiding and trusted by believers. The author presents this as protecting religious discourse power and security against what is described as hostile Western infiltration and religious extremism. On the second, Dong traces the Party's record on religious freedom and says sinicization is not "Party-run religion" or control. The author adds that freedom of belief is bounded by law. On the third, Dong says the aim is to guide religion to adapt to socialism, not to promote it. The Party's stance is that administrative force should neither develop nor abolish religion, and religion is cast as a "harmony" voice in China's plural culture. Dong ties this to the "one guidance, five identifications, three loves and four histories" education. Dong concludes that sinicization is a gradual strategic task to be pursued under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It should be led by the Party, with religious circles as the main actors and scholars as support. The goal is a religious system of thought, institutions and governance with Chinese characteristics, and the author also calls for a stronger academic discourse system. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism answers, in official terms, the grassroots and foreign objections to the sinicization of religion.

From left-wing guerrilla to left-wing ruling party: the experience of Nicaragua's Sandinista National Liberation Front 从左翼游击队到左翼执政党：尼加拉瓜桑地诺民族解放阵线的经验 Li Han Li Han asks how Nicaragua's Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) turned itself from a guerrilla organisation into a lasting left-wing party of government. The article presents the FSLN as a rare success among Latin American guerrilla movements: of the 127 armed groups active between 1980 and 2010, only 15 tried to form parties, and the author cites a success rate of about 4% for new parties in the region. Li's thesis is that the FSLN's transition and its continuous rule since 2006 rest on organisational strength, discipline, broad social alliances and growing pragmatism, though new governing problems now threaten that position. The article has three parts. The first traces the transition from guerrilla force to party, from the 1961 founding under Carlos Fonseca through the 1979 revolution, the electoral defeat of 1990 and the return to office in 2006–2007. The second explains the party's long hold on power. The third lists the difficulties the FSLN faces after Daniel Ortega's re-election in 2021, and a short assessment places the party within the Latin American left. On the transition, Li points to the party's inherited vertical command structure, a national leadership, provincial and municipal committees and base committees, and to the discipline reinforced after the split of 1995 and the 2002 statute. Li also stresses its alliances with trade union, peasant, women's and youth organisations, and its shift from open Marxism-Leninism in the 1980s towards a pragmatic 'Christian, socialist, solidarity' Nicaragua. On continuity in power, Li cites reconciliation with the Church and private business, economic growth and poverty reduction (national poverty down from 42.5% to 24.9% between 2009 and 2016), low homicide rates, and a stand against US hegemony. Li adds that the party controls the army and police, which it created, a feature said to distinguish it from many other left-wing governing parties. Li also cites the fragmentation of the opposition and ties with left-wing governments in the region and with China. Li identifies four challenges: rigid organisation, an incomplete theoretical system and weak cadre development; economic contraction in 2018–2020 and falling foreign aid; the unresolved political and social crisis that began in 2018; and Western sanctions and non-recognition of the 2021 election. Li concludes that the FSLN is a pragmatic Latin American left party with some social-democratic traits, with deep social roots but defects it struggles to overcome. Read the original if you study Latin American left-wing parties, the transformation of guerrilla movements into parties, or Chinese scholarly assessments of the Sandinista government.

The First International and the historical origins of socialist parties' external exchanges 第一国际与社会主义政党对外交往的历史起源 Yang Xiuwen Wang Shaoxing Scholars disagree about when party diplomacy began: some trace it to the First and Second Internationals, others to the October Revolution or the Third International, and others reject any origin before 1919. Yang and Wang take up this dispute as a weakness in the basic theory of party diplomacy. They argue that the International Working Men's Association (1864) marks the historical origin of socialist parties' external exchanges, which they distinguish from party diplomacy proper. The article first builds a conceptual framework. It separates 'external exchanges' by parties not yet in power from 'party diplomacy' by ruling parties, and it sets out the content, values and origins of socialist external exchanges. It then examines the First International's practice: support for strikes, national liberation and the Paris Commune; its statutes; its programmatic tactics; and its opposition to imperialist war. Finally it draws out the International's theoretical views and legacy. The authors rest the argument on a few moves. They hold that external exchanges belong to parties not in power, and so form the logical precursor of party diplomacy. They read the International's statutes as guaranteeing each member's ideological, organisational and action independence, and they derive from this a rule: independence and joint action condition each other. They also argue that the International's rise and eventual collapse show that struggle requires strong party leadership. They describe its tactics as 'firm in substance, moderate in form' and as 'unity and sincere criticism', combined with open struggle against sectarian currents such as Proudhonism and Bakuninism. Yang and Wang conclude that the International's practice was early and tentative but laid the foundations for later socialist external exchanges and for the party diplomacy of socialist states. They call for stronger theoretical awareness of the principles and tactics involved, for leadership of external exchanges by the party, and for the Marxist theory of inter-party relations to be combined with national conditions. They also say this work can supply resources for the Communist Party of China's own theory of party diplomacy. Read the original if you study the history of inter-party relations, the First International, or how Chinese scholars ground party diplomacy theory in Marxist classics.

The social regulation of digital capitalism How platforms govern 数字资本主义的社会调节 Petter Törnberg This is a Chinese translation of an article by Petter Törnberg, published in Big Data & Society. It asks whether digital platforms mark a break with neoliberal capitalism or an intensification of it. Using regulation theory, Törnberg argues that digital capitalism is both a continuation of financialised post-Fordism and a rupture with it. Its common core, in his account, is the digitalisation, privatisation and financialisation of market regulation. The article first places digital capitalism within the history of capitalist transformation, tracing the shift from Fordism (state-regulated national markets) to post-Fordism (state-regulated transnational markets) to platform-owned proprietary digital markets. It then examines how platforms compete with states, drawing on cases such as Uber, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta. Finally, it analyses three shifts in social regulation: from neoliberalism to techno-feudalism, from Taylorist hierarchy to algorithmic groups, and from postmodern to automated consumer culture. Törnberg contends that platform profit rests on rents extracted by controlling access to key resources, through infrastructural lock-in, data monopolies and network effects. Platforms exploit regulatory grey areas, expand quickly with venture capital, and present themselves as neutral to shift legal responsibility, as when Uber labels drivers "independent contractors". Platforms thus take over functions once performed by public institutions, such as setting market rules, enforcing contracts and organising labour relations. In his view this produces a "predatory" form of governance, closer to feudal lordship than to classic neoliberal markets. It also brings algorithmic control of workers and consumption shaped by manipulation, resting on what he calls a "techno-liberal" faith in the algorithmic invisible hand. Törnberg concludes that digitalisation, since digital goods can be reproduced at near-zero cost, leads platforms to create artificial scarcity. He cites scholars who therefore see a pre-capitalist rather than post-capitalist outcome. Drawing on Gramsci, he describes the present as an interregnum and outlines three paths: continued laissez-faire platform capitalism; state use of platform capacities for control; or treating platform infrastructure as a public utility, possibly through platform cooperativism. He insists the outcome remains open and political, and that code must be subordinated to political life. Read the original if you want a regulation-theory account of platform power and its links to financialisation, rent and the state.

Mao Zedong's economic thought: a review of research on its foundations, theoretical content and practical achievements 毛泽东经济思想的生成基础、理论内涵与实践成就研究述论 Yang Yan This review surveys Chinese scholarship, published since the 1980s, on Mao Zedong's economic thought, which Yang Yan treats as an important part of Mao Zedong Thought and as comparable in value to his political, military and philosophical thought. Written to mark the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth, it both explains the content of the thought and assesses the state of research. Yang's overall position is that the thought guided the historic economic changes of twentieth-century China and deserves fuller, more systematic study. The review is organised around three dimensions: the foundations from which the thought arose, its theoretical content, and the practical achievements achieved under its guidance. It draws on monographs and articles by a long list of Chinese scholars and quotes the American scholars Maurice Meisner and Paul Samuelson on the Mao-era record. A final section sets out directions for further research. On foundations, Yang reports that scholars trace the thought to Marxist theory, to revolutionary practice and social investigation (such as the Xunwu and Xingguo surveys), and to Chinese history and traditional thought, which Mao is said to have inherited critically. On content, the review sorts the literature into three bodies of thought: new democratic economics, the theory of socialist transformation, and socialist economic construction. The last includes stages of development, contradictions in socialist society, economic relations such as agriculture, light and heavy industry, and socialist commodity production. The review notes that scholars largely defend the General Line for the transition period, while acknowledging errors such as a single ownership form and over-hasty transformation after 1955. On achievements, it cites figures on industrial output, grain, schooling, health and life expectancy. It concludes that the Mao era was neither a utopia sustained by a personality cult nor a period of mere stagnation. Yang concludes that research remains fragmented, because it tends to treat theory, policy and results separately, and that few studies examine how ideas were put into practice. The author calls for a full chain of logic and data running from practice to understanding and back to practice. Yang also proposes combining Marxist theory with Party history methods, and drawing on local archives and case studies, to deepen work on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Chinese scholarship on Mao-era economic thought and policy, and of how that scholarship defends the Mao period's economic record.

The spatial production of platform capital and its limits 平台资本的空间生产及其限度 Wang Huan Yang Yuling Since the 2008 crisis, the "gig", "sharing" and "digital" economies have grown around platforms such as Google, Facebook and Amazon. Wang and Yang ask why and how digital platform space is produced, what role it plays in capital's valorisation, and whether platform capital has permanently overcome spatial limits. They argue that platform companies continue capitalism's tradition of spatial reorganisation by building a virtual spatial paradigm, and that this paradigm remains bound by limits inherent in capital. In their conclusion, only a socialist spatial configuration can remove these limits. The article, published in Socialism Studies in 2023, has three main sections. The first treats the "spatialisation of capital", tracing platform capital from industrial and finance capital to the "space of flows", and describing how it builds virtual physical space, virtual social space and a psychological space of trust. The second treats the "capitalisation of space", examining the platform's capital attributes, its production process and its absorption of labour. The third examines the contradictions this process produces. The authors draw on Marx, Lenin, Harvey, Lefebvre, Giddens, Castells and Deleuze and Guattari. In the authors' account, platform space is both a means of production and a form of capital. Virtual physical space works as a "digital factory" and is rented out for ground rent. Virtual social space turns concrete labour into homogeneous abstract labour and standardises exchange globally. Platforms extend the formal subsumption of labour into everyday life, as workers bring their own workspaces and means of production, and extend it into real subsumption by appropriating socialised collective force. The authors then identify three limits. Virtual space is infinite while real space is finite, immediate while real space is slow, and comprehensive while real purchasing power is fixed. As platform space becomes universal, the authors expect it to become structurally homogeneous, to divide users into centre and periphery, and to run out of external space for "spatial fixes". Self-driven labour and algorithmic "enslavement" are said to deepen total plunder of society and approach a new "spatial implosion". Wang and Yang conclude that platform space production eases capital's survival crisis and carries humanity into a virtual world, but that it also exposes the exploitation of workers and of society as a whole. They hold that its spatial limits are embedded in the nature of capital and become more concrete as capital changes form. Read the original if you want a Marxist spatial-theory analysis of digital platforms that combines Marx's critique of capital with Harvey and Lefebvre.

An analysis of Lenin's strategy for socialist moral education 列宁社会主义道德教育方略论析 He Jinglei He Jinglei asks how Lenin approached moral education under socialism and what it offers China today. The article opens from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which makes civic moral construction a strategic task of the Party, and from the need to cultivate a new generation fit for national rejuvenation. He argues that Lenin, though he never used the term 'socialist morality' directly, developed a systematic strategy of socialist moral education for an economically and culturally backward country. The article is organised in five parts, each presented as one principle of Lenin's approach: making the masses the main actors; setting clear goals; building the educational environment by breaking with the old and establishing the new; applying systems thinking to the overall layout of practice; and strengthening the political leadership and exemplary role of the Communist Party. He draws mainly on Lenin's writings from the pre-revolutionary years, the period after October 1917, and the New Economic Policy. In He's account, Lenin set five goals: a sense of ownership among working people, collectivism, a sense of role models, correct internationalism and patriotism, and loyalty to the communist cause. To create a favourable environment, Lenin called for criticising bourgeois morality and petty-bourgeois habits, intensifying Marxist propaganda and a Party press, and using trade unions, the Communist Youth League and schools as moral educators. The author identifies four practical pillars: youth as the strategic starting point, communist ideals and convictions (with realism about how long and winding the road is), discipline of several kinds, and communist labour such as the 'communist subbotniks'. He concludes that, although Lenin's thinking bears a Russian and period imprint, it sets out general requirements, ways of thinking and points of action for moral education in less developed countries. The article presents it as relevant to cultivating a new generation for the new era, to civic moral construction, and to the goal of making China a strong socialist modernised education power. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language synthesis of Lenin's scattered remarks on morality, discipline and the Party's role, framed for current Chinese moral-education policy.

Experience and prospects of Marxist atheism propaganda and education in the new era Report on the 10th Scientific Atheism Forum and the 2022 annual conference of the China Atheism Society 新时代马克思主义无神论宣传教育的经验与展望 Zhang Ge This is a report on the 10th Scientific Atheism Forum of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, held together with the 2022 annual conference of the China Atheism Society. The meeting took place online on 27 November 2022 under the theme "Marxist atheism propaganda and education in the new era: experience and prospects". It was convened to put into practice Xi Jinping's speeches at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and at the national religious work conferences of 2016 and 2021. It was organised by the CASS Academy of Marxism, Heilongjiang University and the Society, with more than 130 scholars and officials attending. After the opening and closing addresses, the report sorts the papers into six themes. These are the history and experience of atheism education; basic theory, including early Party leaders' atheist thought; practical experiments with different audiences (students, peasants, cadres, border regions); the relationship between Marxist atheism and Marxist religious studies; building Marxist religious studies as a discipline; and the Party's religious work, including the "sinicization of religion". Each section summarises individual speakers in a sentence or a short paragraph. Several threads recur. Historical overviews divide the new era into stages and argue that atheism work lapsed after 1987, so that research must be rebuilt before propaganda can succeed. Zhang Ge's own paper identifies five teaching models, from fragmentary inclusion in ideological courses to independent systematic courses. On the discipline, speakers such as Li Shen, Zhang Xinying, Xi Wuyi and Jia Runguo describe atheism as the "hard core" of Marxist religious studies. Lü Jianfu and Zuo Peng warn of Western religious studies, "de-ideologisation" and overstating religion's positive cultural functions. Tian Xinming treats ideological struggle and freedom of religious belief as a unity that contains opposition, and says atheist education should target society at large, not believers specifically. The closing summary by Jia Runguo judges the conference a success and says the atheism cause is developing well since the 2021 conference called for strengthening Marxist religious studies. It adds that the work is long and demanding, and that the "Three Musts" from the 20th Party Congress apply to it. Practical proposals include wider teaching of atheism courses, more teachers, and a clearer leadership system, with Party organisation, propaganda and education departments leading the work among cadres and young people. Read the original if you want a detailed map of the speakers, institutions and positions in current Chinese official debates on Marxist atheism, religious studies and religious policy.

The crisis of the neoliberal global order in the perspective of the critique of political economy 政治经济学批判视域中的新自由主义全球秩序危机 Hu Xiaokun Hu Xiaokun asks how the neoliberal global order can be understood as monopolistic and crisis-ridden when read through Marx's critique of political economy and Lenin's theory of imperialism. The article, a newspaper-length commentary first published in 2023, presents the analysis of contemporary Russian left-wing scholars, above all Alexander Buzgalin and Andrei Kolganov. Hu reports their claim that twenty-first-century capitalism is returning to monopoly, which they see as the outcome of competition's own logic. The text begins with Lenin's view that imperialism is economically monopoly growing out of free competition. It then turns to Marx's account of competition, the average rate of profit and the relation between 'capital in general' and 'many capitals'. The second half sets out Buzgalin's periodisation of monopoly capitalism since the early twentieth century and his analysis of its current forms. It ends with the Russian scholars' reading of the present world situation. Hu argues, following Marx, that capital's inner tendencies assert themselves through competitive compulsion. Competition among many capitals produces concentration and centralisation and so turns into its opposite, monopoly. Buzgalin, in Hu's account, distinguishes three stages: early-twentieth-century imperialism, a post-war stage of social reformism, and neoliberal globalisation since the 1970s. In his view the last is reverting towards the first, under the domination of financial monopoly capital. Hu lists the features Buzgalin identifies: corporate manipulation of public life, the sale of simulated goods, speculative financial ecosystems, 'desocialisation' and escalating geopolitical conflict. Buzgalin also stresses a counter-tendency. Socialisation of production, trade unions and public-sector services built up socialist elements inside capitalism, and these now obstruct monopoly profit. The great powers respond with protectionism, militarisation and sanctions, producing what he calls a new imperialism of centre over (semi-)periphery. Hu concludes that the Russian scholars restore Lenin's theory and Marx's critique in order to strip away neoliberal ideology's concealment of capital's logic. They also trace how the basic contradiction of capitalism spreads globally. Starting from Russia's position as a (semi-)peripheral capitalist formation, they combine geopolitical logic with the logic of capital. Hu presents this as a distinctive theoretical perspective on the 'great changes unseen in a century'. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese introduction to how Russian Marxists such as Buzgalin interpret neoliberal globalisation, de-globalisation and new imperialism.

Rethinking the theoretical sources and logical course of Marx's first intellectual transformation 重思马克思第一次思想转变的理论渊源与逻辑进程 Zhang Fugong Zhang Fugong takes up a long-debated question in studies of the development of Marx's thought: which theoretical sources and what logical course produced his first intellectual transformation, from idealism to materialism and toward communism. Zhang argues that earlier scholarship, which centred on Hegel and Feuerbach, neglected the latent influence of Proudhon, Moses Hess and Engels. Taking these figures into account, the article contends, gives a more exact picture of the plural background and the complicated path of the shift. The piece was published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2023. The article first reviews two interpretive routes. One, begun by Lenin, judges the shift by philosophical logic and political stance; it was hardened into a Soviet "one transformation" thesis, rejected by Western Marxism, and revived by Chinese scholars such as Sun Bo'ao through the "two transformations" thesis. The other route analyses changes of object and theme, for instance from critique of the state to critique of civil society. Zhang then proceeds in two parts: the plural theoretical background, and the stage-by-stage course through the Rheinische Zeitung period, the Kreuznach notebooks, the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question and the Introduction to the Critique. Zhang's central claim is that Marx took over Feuerbach's anthropological materialism, not his naturalistic one, as Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge shows. Extending it to politics and economics, Zhang argues, drew on others. Proudhon offered a critique of bourgeois right and property from a theory of human nature; Hess moved from critique of political alienation to critique of monetary alienation; Engels added empirical economic study and a firmer revolutionary communist stance. Zhang holds that the "civil society determines the state" idea in the 1843 critique of Hegel was only latent social materialism, since Marx still viewed civil society negatively. The dominant logic there, Zhang suggests, was a Hess-like critique of political alienation. In On the Jewish Question Marx moved to economic alienation, and in the 1844 Introduction he tied philosophy to the proletariat, probably under Engels's influence. Zhang concludes that in the period of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher Marx achieved a first, general transformation in philosophical logic and political stance together: Feuerbachian anthropological materialism and revolutionary communism based on it. Zhang stresses that no complete system yet existed, since alienation was still treated at the level of exchange and money, not labour, and the link between sublating alienation and communism was left to the Paris Manuscripts. Read the original if you study the early Marx and want a compact argument that Proudhon, Hess and Engels shaped his turn to materialism and communism.

Main problems and solution paths in the process of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化进程中面临的主要问题与解决路径 Zhao Ruyu Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhao Ruyu asks what the main problem facing Chinese modernization is. Starting from the principal contradiction between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, the article argues that the central problem is the contradiction between a new industrial revolution and the urban–rural gap. The new industrial revolution is presented as the key to inadequate development, and narrowing the gap as the key to unbalanced development. The article has five parts: the framing of the problem, the case that this contradiction is the main one, an analysis of how it arises, the paths to resolve it, and a conclusion. The historical section compares the earlier industrial revolutions and the information revolution of the 1990s in Britain, France, Germany, the United States, Japan and South Korea with the present. Zhao then examines the effects of the new industrial revolution on the countryside and the effects of the urban–rural gap on that revolution. Zhao argues that developed countries avoided a lasting clash between industrial revolution and urban–rural relations for four reasons. Natural resources gained importance, labour-intensive industries absorbed large workforces, populations were relatively small, and the international division of labour allowed those countries to exploit developing ones. The new industrial revolution, in Zhao's account, has a dual effect. It promotes sustainability and efficiency, but it also devalues natural endowments, thins out the industrial system, expels labour and concentrates resources in very large cities, which tends to widen the rural gap. The gap in turn affects the revolution in two ways. Putting rural catch-up first could slow the revolution, whereas letting the gap widen would burden local finances, endanger food security and social stability, and weaken rural consumer demand. Zhao concludes that neither side can be abandoned and that the gap cannot be put on hold until the revolution is finished and the 'cake' divided. The proposed path is for cities and countryside to build a modern industrial system together. It has three parts: extending new technologies such as smart agriculture, biotechnology and e-commerce to rural areas; redistributing industry spatially through metropolitan circles, virtual research clusters and small towns; and upgrading rural infrastructure and public services through in-situ urbanization. Read the original if you want a policy-oriented economic analysis of how technological change and the urban–rural divide interact in discussions of common prosperity.

Lenin's critique of Russian Narodism and its contemporary implications 列宁对俄国民粹主义的批判及其现实启示 Xu Wenwen Xu Wenwen asks why and how Lenin set out to criticise Russian Narodism (populism) at the turn of the twentieth century, and what that critique offers today. The article argues that Lenin's critique was not a routine intellectual quarrel. It aimed to build a "scientific ideology" and establish Marxism as the only scientific revolutionary theory, combining construction with refutation. Xu presents this as consistent with the present-day call to unite the constructive and the critical in ideological work. The article has four parts. The first sets out why the intellectual dispute needed Lenin's judgement: Russia's cultural choices during its social transition, the long evolution of Narodism from Herzen through revolutionary and liberal phases to the Socialist Revolutionaries, and the shortcomings of earlier critics. These critics were the "legal Marxists" and Plekhanov. The second part reconstructs Lenin's critique. The third draws out its essence. The fourth turns to implications for China. In Xu's account, Lenin made three main criticisms. He rejected the Narodniks' "non-capitalist" path by using statistics on peasant differentiation and the growth of the domestic market to show that capitalism was developing in Russia. He traced the petty-bourgeois roots of Narodism, which in his view was the ideology of the peasant democracy and a utopia that was also an expression of a historically limited democratic struggle. He also attacked Mikhailovsky's "subjective sociology" for starting from human nature rather than objective economic facts. Xu adds that Lenin defended historical necessity as compatible with individual action and the role of leaders. Lenin also held that no non-class ideology exists, so the proletariat must lead ideologically. Xu concludes that Lenin's critique is a matter of political principle. Quoting Xi Jinping's remark that positive publicity does not mean giving up the struggle in public opinion, the author draws four lessons for China in the new era. These are to confront erroneous trends and draw a line between Marxism and anti-Marxism; to strengthen theoretical confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics; to proceed from national conditions and develop Marxism through contemporary practice; and to uphold Party leadership and discourse power in ideological work. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory reading of Lenin's early polemics and of how they are applied to current ideological work.

The atheist thought of Marx's doctoral dissertation and its significance in the new era 马克思博士论文的无神论思想及其在新时代的意义 Wang Xiang Wang Xiang asks what Marx's doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature (written 1839–41), contributes to the history of Marxist scientific atheism. The article argues that, despite its debt to Hegelian idealism and Bruno Bauer's philosophy of self-consciousness, the dissertation is the true opening work of Marx's critique of religion. In Wang's reading it is the logical starting point of scientific atheism and a first decisive step towards it. The article has three parts. The first traces the atheist motives behind the choice of topic, from Marx's Rhineland upbringing and two school essays to his time in Berlin among the Young Hegelians. The second sets out three strands of atheist thought in the dissertation. The third draws four lessons for atheist theory and education in the new era, with reference to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Wang's core argument is that the dissertation does three things. First, by defending Epicurus' doctrine of the atomic swerve through "self-consciousness", Marx sets out an ontological atheist principle and places philosophy above religion. Second, Marx applies an early theory of alienation to nature worship, treating religion as alienated self-consciousness. Wang presents this as the first stage of a path from religious to political, labour and money alienation, and as giving atheism a practical, combative character. Third, Marx's rebuttal of Plutarch on the immortality of the soul grounds an atheist humanism that is a precursor of communist thought. Wang concedes the idealist limits of this stage but argues they were products of their time. Wang draws four requirements for the new era. Scientific atheism must keep its thoroughgoing critical spirit and confront theism, including hostile religious influence from inside and outside China, in order to protect ideological security. Its development must be viewed historically and dialectically, and dismissing the dissertation for its idealism is called mistaken. The doctrine must be pursued in a spirit of truth, avoiding decontextualised misreadings of the classics. Atheism must also keep its philosophical concern with ultimate values, aimed at communism and the free, all-round development of the person. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-academy account of how Marx's early writings are used to ground scientific atheism and current policy on religion.

The content, characteristics and methods of Sinicized Marxist psychology of religion 中国化马克思主义宗教心理学的内容、特点及方法 Zhou Puyuan Li Ping Zhou Puyuan and Li Ping take up the question of how the psychology of religion should be built in China. They argue that, since Wundt founded experimental psychology, work on the mind has split into a philosophical tradition and a quantitative natural-science tradition that do not meet. In their account, a psychology of religion adapted to Chinese conditions and guided by Marxism ("Sinicized Marxist psychology of religion") can bridge the two. It does so by joining quantitative and qualitative work, and rational and non-rational factors, in practice. The article has three parts: the field's content, its characteristics and its methods. On content, the authors sketch the field's origins in the introduction of Western psychology of religion into China, which they divide into beginning, stagnation and start-up periods. They then discuss the field as both psychology and religious studies, and offer a definition. The second part lists seven characteristics. The third sets out research methods, ending with the "new liberal arts" agenda. The core argument places the field within social psychology and treats religion through Lü Daji's four elements: ideas, feelings, behaviour and institutions. Religious consciousness is described as a distorted reflection of reality, religious feeling as a bond of identity, and religion as a special ideology. The authors give the seven characteristics as clear guiding ideology, critical spirit, interdisciplinarity, atheism, usefulness to policy-making, practice and guidance. They describe the field as scientific atheism in worldview and method. In their view it criticises Western theistic currents, such as Freud's reduction of religion to neurosis, and offers theoretical support to the Party and government in religious affairs. On method, the authors call for dialectical logic, which they break down into the contradiction-as-motive-force approach, statistics (fieldwork data) and classification. They also call for historical materialism as the overarching guide, and for a wide range of discipline-specific methods, from history to anthropology and theology. They conclude that this diversity, though it complicates theory, gives the field greater inclusiveness than other disciplines. They also hold that it should help build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system and guide believers towards compatibility with socialist society. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars of scientific atheism define and justify a Marxist psychology of religion and its policy role.

Chinese modernization: how a local narrative can become a world discourse 中国式现代化：何以从本土叙事转向世界话语 Li Jiali Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Li Jiali asks how Chinese modernization can be turned from a locally rooted political phrase of the new era into a discourse with universal standing. The concern is practical: the author wants to guard against misreadings, especially in Western scholarship, that would turn the concept into fresh evidence for distorted accounts of China's development. Li's answer is that its universal significance must be explained in scholarly terms. The article has three parts. The first traces the historical narrative of Western modernization discourse as Enlightenment discourse, capital discourse and development discourse, including dependency theory (Samir Amin) and Said's Orientalism. The second follows modern China's own narratives since 1840: the "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application" approach, wholesale Westernization, and socialist modernization under the Communist Party. The third sets out three ways in which a world discourse is possible. Li argues that modernization as a concept and its theory were built by Western thinkers, who tied it to capitalism and Western-centred world order. In Li's view, dependency theory and Orientalism remain inside Western frameworks, as anti-Western-centrism built on Western-centrism. China's earlier schemes failed, the author says, because the first kept feudal foundations and the second took capitalism as the template. Socialist modernization, from the 1945 Seventh Party Congress through the "four modernizations" to reform and opening up, is presented as surpassing both traditional socialism and Westernization. To make the concept universal, Li calls for three moves. China's modernization should be seen as part of human modernization, sharing common features with other countries, as the 20th Party Congress report says. Its five features should be read as answers to the general problems of modernity, such as tensions between people and nature. And it should be understood as advanced because it breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and escapes the "spell of capital". Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how the concept is positioned against Western modernization theory and of China's modernization debates since 1840.

Lenin's communist faith and flexible measures of socialist construction in spring 1918 1918年春列宁的共产主义信仰和灵活的社会主义建设措施 Yu Min Yu Min opens with Xi Jinping's January 2022 remark that strategy and tactics stand in a dialectical relationship, so that firmness of strategy must be combined with flexibility of tactics. The article asks how Lenin combined the two in spring 1918, between the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March and the outbreak of civil war in July. Yu's thesis is that in this period Lenin held unwavering faith in communism while advocating flexible measures to develop Soviet Russia's industry and economy. The article has three parts. The first sets out four strands of Lenin's communist conviction. The second reads Lenin's call to "go our own way" and sets out six flexible measures. The third assesses Lenin's thought, tracing the same pairing to Marx and Engels and then to Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The main sources are Lenin's The Immediate Tasks of the Soviet Government, his "Left-Wing" Childishness and the Petty-Bourgeois Mentality, and his speeches of 1918. For conviction, Yu argues that Lenin saw Soviet achievements as part of a world socialist movement. Lenin treated the economic task as one link in a chain leading to international revolution. He expected a "new giant" of revolution to grow in the West, and he called the struggle for grain "living socialism". For flexibility, Yu lists strict labour discipline, well-paid bourgeois specialists, compromise with the old co-operatives, a reworked Taylor system, German-style state capitalism, and learning management from trust organisers. Yu stresses that these departed from principle, for example the Paris Commune rule on pay, and from Marx and Engels's original vision. In Yu's reading Lenin took these steps because he started from actual conditions rather than from dogma. Lenin also rejected 'Left' Bolshevik objections that quoted Marx. Yu concludes that Lenin continued and enriched the Marxist tradition of joining firm principle to flexible tactics, which Marx and Engels had shown in the Communist Manifesto. The author then argues that the Chinese Communists have kept this tradition through reform and opening up and in the new era. As evidence Yu cites Deng Xiaoping's remarks on communist ideals and Xi Jinping's statements, together with the poverty-alleviation campaign. Yu says that the new era's Party has enriched Lenin's thought on a higher footing. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Lenin's 1918 economic policy that links it to current Party theory on strategy and tactics.

Mao Zedong's thought on ideological and political education in universities and its contemporary implications (1949–1966) 毛泽东关于高校思想政治教育的思想及其现实启示(1949—1966) Luo Xiong Luo Xiong asks how Mao Zedong approached ideological and political education in Chinese universities after 1949, and what that experience offers today. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that this work answers the fundamental questions of what kind of people universities train, how, and for whom, the article argues that Mao made a series of creative adjustments and reinforcements. In Luo's reading, these still hold lessons for cultivating a new generation capable of shouldering national rejuvenation. The article is organised chronologically and then thematically. The first part covers 1949–1956, when Mao adjusted university work in the transition from new-democratic to socialist construction. The second covers 1956–1966, the period of comprehensive socialist construction, when Mao strengthened it. The third draws three present-day implications for the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The evidence is mainly Party directives, instructions Mao reviewed or approved, and the Sixty Articles on Higher Education (1961). For 1949–1956, Luo describes three measures. Party leadership was extended through Party organisations, with Party cadres installed in university leadership. The content of teaching was revised to counter 'feudal, comprador and fascist' ideas among staff and students. Teachers of political theory were trained through Party schools and Marxism-Leninism classes. For 1956–1966, Luo identifies three developments. Party secretaries were made first-responsible persons for ideological work. Courses were reshaped around the 'three educations, two haves' guideline (moral, intellectual and physical education, producing cultured workers with socialist consciousness), with growing emphasis on opposing revisionism. Education was also to serve proletarian politics and be combined with productive labour, through the Socialist Education Movement and farm and factory work. By the end of 1965, the article says, about 395 universities and over 220,000 staff and students had taken part. Luo concludes that Party leadership produced many 'both red and expert' intellectuals, while acknowledging deviations. These included leftist tendencies after the expanded anti-Rightist campaign, with politics prioritised over academic study, and labour time that sometimes exceeded study time. For the present, Luo calls for upholding Party leadership with Party secretaries as first responsible persons, and for keeping the right political direction under Xi's 'four services' formulation to cultivate a new generation. Luo also calls for strengthening both dedicated political theory courses and 'ideological and political education across the curriculum'. Read the original if you want a documented account of Party directives on university political education in the Mao era, and of how a Chinese scholar draws on it to support current policy.

The logic, features and paths of intelligent algorithms empowering Marxist atheist propaganda 智能算法赋能马克思主义无神论宣传的逻辑、特征与路径 Luo Guoqing Luo Guoqing asks how intelligent algorithms, which now steer online information input, processing and distribution, can be used to strengthen Marxist atheist propaganda and education. Writing in 2023 and citing Party documents since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that call for strengthening atheist education, Luo argues that combining the two is theoretically necessary, practically required and technically feasible. The article presents algorithms as a new form of power with an ideological function that Marxist atheism must learn to steer. The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic of the combination. The second identifies three features of algorithm-enabled atheist propaganda. The third proposes four practical paths. Examples come from Chinese social media, including Sina Weibo accounts that promote science and oppose superstition and cults, and the WeChat account of the journal Science and Atheism. Luo's core argument is that algorithms are double-edged. In the article's account, online religious propagation, cults and hostile overseas forces exploit recommendation systems, "information cocoons" and the Matthew effect to push fortune-telling and theistic content and to draw users toward religious belief. Atheist propaganda should therefore be built into the algorithmic system, following Xi Jinping's call to "master algorithms with mainstream values". Luo describes the technical route as tagging atheist content, profiling users and matching the two, and as creating immersive "simulated environments" and "smart fields" for data analysis and prediction. The resulting propaganda is said to shift from one-way output to multi-party interaction, from mass broadcasting to personalised delivery, and from grand narrative to concrete, everyday and emotional storytelling. Luo proposes four paths. The first is upgrading algorithms: raising the weight of atheist content, filtering sensitive terms and adding reverse-push programmes that show atheist material to users who browse theistic content. The second is innovating content and discourse, including short-video accounts, while keeping the scientific rigour of the theory. The third is raising the atheist theoretical competence of algorithm designers, content moderators and audiences. The fourth is strengthening regulation under the rules on internet religious information services and algorithmic recommendation, with responsibilities assigned to government departments and platforms. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar links algorithmic governance, online religion and ideological security, with concrete platform examples.

Mao Zedong's creative use and development of the traditional concept of "tianxia" (all under heaven) 毛泽东对传统天下观的创造性运用和发展 Ding Junping Jia Shuheng Ding Junping and Jia Shuheng ask how Mao Zedong drew on the traditional Chinese concept of tianxia ('all under heaven') and what he made of it. They argue that Mao creatively used and developed the tianxia outlook of China's fine traditional culture, and that this shows the way Mao Zedong Thought combines the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities. The article first sets out four value components of the traditional tianxia view: tianxia as a personal responsibility, as an ideal of great harmony (datong), as an account of rise and fall tied to popular support, and as one family. It then examines Mao's handling of each in turn, from his youth to the post-1949 period, drawing on his writings and speeches. A final section assesses the significance of this development, and a short conclusion links it to the thought of Xi Jinping. The authors' central claim is that Mao kept the emotional and ethical core of each idea but replaced its philosophical content with Marxism. In their account, the duty to bear responsibility for tianxia acquired concrete goals once Mao used class analysis and the theory of contradiction. His datong ideal was purged of absolute egalitarianism, identified with communism, and given a practical route: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution, then gradual transition to communism. On winning popular support, Mao grounded it in historical materialism, in which the people are the driving force of history, rather than in imperial favour, and he answered Huang Yanpei's question about the 'historical cycle' of dynasties with democracy and popular supervision. For the 'one family' view, the authors cite Mao's treatment of the Chinese revolution as part of world revolution, his call for peaceful coexistence of different systems, and his stress on learning from all nations. The authors conclude that this adaptation helped Marxism take root in China, renewed the content of the old tianxia view, produced correct policies for revolution and construction, and shaped the Communist spirit of serving country, nation and people. They add that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping has carried the line forward, including through a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Mao is presented as drawing on classical Chinese ideas of responsibility, utopia, popular support and world order.

New trends in Sri Lanka's socialist movement 斯里兰卡社会主义运动的新动向 Du Min Du Min asks what role Sri Lanka's left-wing parties played in the economic and political crisis that, in the author's account, brought down the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government and led to the declaration of national bankruptcy in July 2022. The article also asks how the crisis changed the socialist movement. Du argues that the crisis pushed the left towards three shifts: new strategy, a broader ideological appeal and a wider political base. The article first sorts Sri Lankan left parties into traditional (the Lanka Sama Samaja Party and the Communist Party), new (the People's Liberation Front, JVP) and radical (the National Freedom Front and the Frontline Socialist Party), and sets out how they read the crisis. It then covers strategy, ideological struggle and political foundations, and ends with the reasons for these changes. Du draws on party statements, rallies and campaigns from 2020 to 2022. On strategy, Du describes a weakening of the 'politics of dependence', in which traditional left parties tied themselves to the Sri Freedom Party and the Rajapaksa family. A conversion of 'politics of confrontation' from armed struggle to non-violent street and parliamentary opposition has also occurred, and a 'politics of policy' is strengthening. The last includes crisis-exit programmes and the traditional left's 'solidarity economy', which would transfer loss-making firms to employee ownership. On ideology, the parties tie the crisis to capitalism and neoliberalism, claim patriotism for socialism against racialized nationalism, and stress ethnic equality and class analysis. On organisation, Du points to the National People's Power alliance, the 2022 'Supreme Alliance' of radical and traditional parties, and a push to mobilise peasants. Du attributes these trends to three needs: rescuing the nation, winning the ideological contest against non-Marxist explanations of the crisis, and acting independently of bourgeois parties. The article presents the movement as being in a stage of a 'new revolution' after crisis, in Engels's phrase, and argues that workable policy proposals are a precondition for popular recognition. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language account of how Sri Lanka's left parties differ and how a Chinese Marxist scholar interprets their strategy after 2020.

Subject and revolution: the transformation and development of themes in Western Marxist theory 主体与革命：西方马克思主义理论主题的嬗变及发展 Miao Cuicui Miao Cuicui asks how Western Marxism has handled the problem of revolution after the proletarian revolution Marx anticipated failed to occur in the developed capitalist West. The article, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2023, contends that Marxist theory takes different themes in East and West: in socialist countries it stresses objective laws and scientific character, while in the West it stresses subjective agency, critique and humanism. On the theme of subject and revolution, Miao traces a line from awakening a missing class consciousness, through critique of the ideological state apparatus, to the remaking of new revolutionary subjects. The article begins with the historical emergence of proletarian revolution in early capitalism and the predicament it later met: capitalism flourished, the Soviet Union dissolved, and Western liberal democracy proclaimed the 'end of ideology' and 'end of history'. Miao then reviews, in order, Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse) and Habermas. The final section turns to contemporary radical left thinkers: Negri, Hardt, Virno, Kojin Karatani, Giorgio Agamben and Alain Badiou, with Žižek cited as a framing voice. Miao argues that the early Western Marxists located the failure of revolution in missing consciousness rather than immature material conditions. Lukács's theory of reification distinguished psychological from imputed class consciousness, while Gramsci pursued cultural hegemony through a 'war of position'. Frankfurt School critiques of the culture industry and technology, and Habermas's discourse ethics, could not, in Miao's view, shake the ideological state apparatus because cultural critique lacks a real force behind it. The theme therefore shifted to new subjects along four routes: the 'multitude' in production (Negri, Hardt, Virno), consumer boycott in consumption (Karatani), resistance to the state of exception in everyday life (Agamben), and fidelity to the 'event' in politics (Badiou). Miao concludes that these contemporary constructions of political subjects set difference against capitalist uniformity but centre on independent, decentred individuals, and so cannot achieve real enlightenment, freedom or individuality. In the author's view, only by fusing the individual into the social human whole, and individual freedom into the proletariat's self-emancipation and human emancipation, can power be reversed and a true force for changing the world be found. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how a Chinese Marxist scholar sketches the Western Marxist development from class consciousness to the multitude and the event, together with the author's critique of it.

The Communist Party of China's major contributions to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress 论十八大以来中国共产党对国际共产主义运动的重大贡献 Zhuo Mingliang Zhuo Mingliang asks how the international communist movement should be assessed three decades after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and what the Communist Party of China (CPC) has contributed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that the movement's condition should be judged not by the number of ruling communist parties but by the real influence and guiding power of existing socialist states. On that basis it describes a situation of an "overall ebb" alongside a "local high tide", the latter being the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out five ways in which the CPC has raised its standing in the movement. The second surveys the roughly 950 communist organisations in over 130 countries, classified by relation to state power, membership size, guiding ideology, attitude towards China and choice of revolutionary road. The third turns to what the CPC should do to promote the movement in the twenty-first century, drawing on lessons from the Soviet period and on statements by foreign communist figures. In the first part, Zhuo credits the CPC with advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It also credits the Party with building a community with a shared future for mankind, opposing hegemonism, hosting party-to-party exchanges, and winning favourable assessments from foreign communist parties, which the author illustrates with statements from several of them. The survey stresses diversity and division: parties follow Marxism-Leninism, Maoism, Trotskyism and other lines, and differ sharply on whether China is socialist. Zhuo reads the overall trend as combining independent national paths with growing calls for international unity. Zhuo concludes that the CPC, as the world's largest ruling party, should supply a "CPC answer" for the movement's revival. The author calls for avoiding the great-party chauvinism attributed to the Soviet Communist Party, and for leading by example rather than by command. Concrete proposals include a "twenty-first-century internationalism", deeper ties with international communist and left organisations, wider forms of party cooperation, an international coordinating body of Marxist parties and a "community with a shared future for communist parties worldwide". Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated account of how Chinese scholars map the world's communist parties and envisage the CPC's role among them.

A review of Mao Zedong Thought research in Chinese academia in 2022 2022年度国内学界毛泽东思想研究述论 Che Zongkai This is a literature review of how Chinese scholars studied Mao Zedong Thought in 2022. Che Zongkai treats it as an important result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and as a continuing focus of attention. By the author's count, 2022 produced four substantial academic monographs, 1,094 journal articles with "Mao Zedong" as a keyword (297 in CSSCI or core journals), and 105 master's and doctoral theses. The review is arranged by theme: the overall formation and development of the Thought; Mao's writings and their textual versions; political thought; philosophy; economic thought; cultural and educational thought; Mao's life and experiences; and studies of Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun and other first-generation leaders. It notes that research on Zhu De produced few high-quality results that year. A final section sets out priorities for further work. Among the highlights, scholars read the three Party historical resolutions as texts that interpret Mao Zedong Thought, and link Mao's thought to Xi Jinping's writings on Mao. Work on the Yan'an Talks, in their 80th anniversary year, examines textual versions and Mao's literary and aesthetic ideas. Textual study of the revisions to Mao's essays and poems, and of his reading notes, is described as opening new materials. In economics, Meng Jie is reported as presenting Mao as a forerunner of institutional economics of socialism in contemporary China. Other scholars trace Mao's ideas on modernization and industrialization. Wu Xuan's survey of competing views on when the young Mao became a Marxist is summarised as arguing that this was a gradual process, not a single point. Che proposes four directions: Mao Zedong Thought and the Party's theoretical innovation; its relation to Chinese modernization; study of Mao's writings and versions, including text-criticism methods and links to current problems; and the contributions of other leaders and Party theorists such as Hu Qiaomu, Ai Siqi and Zhang Ruxin. With the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth in 2023 approaching, Che calls for a comprehensive, historical and dialectical approach. Read the original if you want a bibliographic map of 2022 Chinese scholarship on Mao, with named authors and topics, or a sense of the research agenda officially encouraged for it.

Accelerating the building of a leading education country with Chinese characteristics 加快建设中国特色社会主义教育强国 Zhang Donggang Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, Zhang Donggang, identified as Party secretary of Renmin University of China, takes up Xi Jinping's formulation of what a 'leading education country' (jiaoyu qiangguo) with Chinese characteristics must be. Zhang argues that universities, as the 'leading edge' of this project, should grasp and apply each element of Xi's definition, and should treat building world-class universities and strong disciplines with Chinese characteristics as the top priority. The article is organised around the components of Xi's statement, delivered at a Political Bureau study session: the fundamental guarantee, fundamental task, fundamental goal, important mission, basic path and core function, ending with the aim of education that satisfies the people. Each of the seven sections first explains why the element matters, citing Xi and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and then lists measures for universities. Zhang's core claim is that the Party's overall leadership over education is the 'fixed anchor' of the whole undertaking, and that the other elements follow from it. Moral education (lide shuren) is presented as the basic task because every society trains people to meet its own political requirements. Talent cultivation serves the Party and the country and the second centenary goal. Education is also said to support Chinese modernization, which the article defines as the modernization of the whole population. The measures proposed include the presidential responsibility system under Party committee leadership, ideological and political courses, a self-reliant Chinese system of knowledge in philosophy and social sciences, and cultivation of top innovative talent. They also include modernization of educational concepts, institutions and governance through digital transformation, international exchange, and fairer, higher-quality provision. Zhang concludes that the ultimate purpose is education 'satisfying to the people', which is meant to lay the foundation of national strength and popular well-being. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a senior university Party official translates Xi Jinping's education directives into concrete institutional tasks.

Lenin's communist conviction and flexible measures of socialist construction in spring 1918 1918年春列宁的共产主义信仰和灵活的社会主义建设措施 Yu Min Yu Min opens with Xi Jinping's January 2022 remark that strategy and tactics stand in a dialectical relationship, so that firmness of strategy must be combined with flexibility of tactics. The article takes this as a method for reading Lenin's thought in spring 1918, the period between the Brest-Litovsk peace (March) and the outbreak of civil war (July). Yu argues that Lenin at once held an unshakeable communist conviction and advocated flexible measures to develop Soviet industry, and that the two embody this unity. The article has three parts. The first sets out four strands of Lenin's conviction. The second takes his phrase "walking one's own road" from The Immediate Tasks of the Soviet Government and examines six flexible measures. The third assesses Lenin's thought against Marx and Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On conviction, Yu reads Lenin's statements as showing that he treated Soviet achievements as part of the world socialist movement and as a torch for revolution elsewhere. He saw the economic effort as a "link" leading to the next one, international proletarian revolution. He expected a "new giant" of Western revolution to grow, and he cast the struggle for grain as a fight for "living socialism". On flexibility, Yu lists six measures.
