These were strict labour discipline, a high-salary system for bourgeois specialists, compromise with old cooperatives, a reformed Taylor system, German-style state capitalism, and learning management from trust organisers. Yu stresses that Lenin chose each from concrete conditions, not from theory or principle, and that he accepted tension with Paris Commune principles. Yu concludes that Lenin continued the Marx–Engels tradition, visible in the Communist Manifesto, of joining the final goal to present struggle, and developed it through practice instead of theory alone. Yu says the Chinese Communists' practice shows the same continuity, citing Deng Xiaoping's remarks on communist ideals and Xi Jinping's on ideals as the "calcium" of the spirit and on people-centred development. In Yu's view, the Party in the new era follows Lenin's spirit and enriches it from a higher standpoint. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Lenin's 1918 economic policy, framed through Xi Jinping's strategy-and-tactics formula.

Four preconditions for contemporary Marxist studies in China 当代中国马克思主义研究的四个前提性问题 Chen Xueming Chen Xueming asks what must be settled before contemporary Marxist research in China can proceed on firm ground. The article argues that such research continues the history of Marxism and of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, so it must first reach a reasonably shared view of four major questions. Chen holds that vagueness on these questions would seriously impair further study. The four preconditions are: how to understand the stages of Marx's own intellectual development; how to understand the development of Marxism after Marx and Engels died; how to understand the fierce struggles that accompanied Marxism's spread in China; and how to assess the competing interpretations of Marxism produced by Chinese scholars since reform and opening up. Each section sets out a typology of positions, then states what contemporary research should take from it. Chen identifies three turning points in Marx's thought: from social democrat to communist in the mid-1840s; from historical idealism to historical materialism around 1850; and, in the late 1850s and early 1860s, the move to the critique of political economy, which gave the "two inevitables" a scientific basis beyond what the Communist Manifesto could offer. Only the Marx of this third stage, Chen argues, is the real founder of Marxism, so Capital should be read mainly as political economy and not as an ontological philosophy. Chen also distinguishes three post-Marx currents (Second International, Third International and so-called Western Marxism), three directions in China since the May Fourth Movement (cultural conservatism, wholesale Westernisation, socialism), and three readings since reform and opening up (Enlightenment-style, postmodern, and one centred on Marx's "two great discoveries"). Chen presents the first two readings as one-sided or mistaken, because their standpoints were superseded within Marx's own development. Chen concludes that Chinese research should build theoretical innovation on the post-turning-point Marx, treat the Third International tradition as the main line to inherit while learning from the other two currents, prepare to debate the conservative and Westernising tendencies that persist, and adopt the third interpretive path as the mainstream. Chen also calls for continued study of how the three paths relate and where their limits lie. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Fudan Marxist philosopher defines orthodoxy, and what he rejects, in Chinese Marxist scholarship around 2023.

Theoretical programme and policy adjustments of the Socialist International since its split An assessment 社会党国际分裂以来理论纲领与政策主张调整评析 Wang Zhao Wang Zhao asks how the Socialist International has reshaped its theory and policy in the decade since the founding of the Progressive Alliance in 2013 split the social-democratic movement into two parallel international organisations. The article argues that the adjustments are an attempt to revive social democracy by turning left under the banner of "progressive politics". In Wang's assessment this turn has some progressive value, but it lacks theoretical innovation and, judged from scientific socialism, remains structurally limited. The article has four parts. It first describes three predicaments since the split: organisational (member parties falling to 132 against 140 in the Progressive Alliance, weaker cohesion and fewer meetings), ideological, and financial (large Western European parties cutting or stopping their dues). It then examines changes to the theoretical programme and to policy in organisation, democracy, the economy, migrants and refugees, and climate. A closing assessment treats the features, effects and essence of these changes. Wang reports that the Socialist International now presents "progressive politics" as its goal. It rejects neoliberalism's idea of freedom in favour of responsibility, treats equality as an organising principle, and gives new weight to solidarity, democracy and peace. Policy follows from this: dues are tied to voting rights, competitive leadership elections and a one-third minimum of women in the presidium, opposition to austerity, and a climate policy built on common but differentiated responsibilities. Wang characterises the changes as value-centred, pragmatic, eclectic and reformist, increasingly global in outlook, and positioned to the left of the Progressive Alliance, which the author places centre-right. Wang concludes that the changes aim to adapt social-democratic values to a changed era and to redefine the movement's relationship with liberalism and neoliberalism. The article credits them with limiting further fragmentation and speaking for developing countries and the vulnerable. It faults them for a gap between theory and practice, tension between internationalism and national interests, and no systematic vision of progressive politics. From the standpoint of scientific socialism, Wang argues, the programme ignores class conflict and the class nature of the state and stays within capitalism, so its structural predicament will persist. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of the post-2013 Socialist International and how Chinese scholars assess social democracy.

Grasping the formation and development of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics through the "big history" perspective Analysis of key and difficult points in Chapter 5 of the 2023 edition of the textbook "Introduction to Mao Zedong Thought and the Theoretical System of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics" 以大历史观把握中国特色社会主义理论体系的形成发展 Wang Heng This is a teaching-oriented guide to a newly added chapter of the 2023 revised university textbook on Mao Zedong Thought and the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Chapter 5 gives an overall account of the social and historical conditions in which that theoretical system formed and of its developmental stages. Wang argues that instructors should use a \"big history\" perspective, showing the unity of theoretical, historical and practical logic, so that students understand the system as a coherent whole. The chapter links the earlier chapters on Mao Zedong Thought with the later chapters on Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Wang organises the teaching points under four headings: the international background, the historical conditions, the practical basis, and the stages of development together with the system's historical standing. Each heading lists specific questions teachers should make clear. On the international background, Wang stresses that peace and development became the theme of the age partly through Mao Zedong's opening of Sino-American normalisation and his \"three worlds\" strategy. Wang warns against the simplistic idea that changes in the world automatically produce theoretical innovation, and ties each leader's contribution to a particular international challenge. On historical conditions, Wang says the theory drew on lessons from the periods before and after 1978, which the author holds are not to be set against each other. It also rested on judgements about the primary stage of socialism and on a succession of \"questions of the times\". On the practical basis, Wang points to household contract responsibility, special economic zones and the socialist market economy. Wang also stresses continuity across generations and the claim that the masses' creativity is the source of theoretical innovation. Wang concludes that the four component theories are \"of one lineage\" (yimai xiangcheng) and \"advance with the times\". In the author's account they share the same guiding sources, themes, qualities, basis in the primary stage of socialism, and goal of serving the people's fundamental interests. Teachers should also mark the key dates when propositions emerged and the theory matured. Wang presents the system as continuing and developing Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, and as the guiding ideology the Party and state must uphold over the long term. Read the original if you teach or study the official framing of this textbook chapter and want to see how its key themes are meant to be taught.

The Guide weekly and the early spread of Marxism in China 《向导》周报与马克思主义在中国的早期传播 Liang Dawei Ru Yahui The article examines the Guide (Xiangdao) weekly, the first political organ of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, and asks what it contributed to the early spread of Marxism in China. Liang and Ru argue that, from its launch in September 1922 to its forced closure in July 1927, the paper spread Marxism-Leninism, explained Party policy and guided the workers' movement. They describe it as a faithful and courageous 'guide' to the Chinese revolution. Drawing on press sources and related documents, the authors place the paper in the historical setting of early Marxist dissemination. They note that it ran for 201 issues, moved between Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou and Wuhan, and grew from several thousand copies to more than 100,000. The article has three main parts: the exposition of Marxism-Leninism and the Party's revolutionary programme; the rebuttal of 'Dai Jitao-ism' and the 'statist faction'; and the class analysis of the revolution's forces. In the first part, the authors count the paper's 1,474 articles. They report that 171 dealt with the relation between economic base and superstructure, and they cite special issues on Lenin, the October Revolution and the national-colonial question. In the second part, they argue that Chen Duxiu, Qu Qiubai and the short-commentary column 'Cunthie' defended the Marxist theory of the state, class struggle and historical materialism against Dai Jitao's appeal to benevolence and the statists' supra-class 'all-people revolution'. In the third part, the Guide stressed that the proletariat must hold leadership, treated the peasantry as its most reliable ally, and described the national bourgeoisie as politically dual: revolutionary at times, vacillating and compromising at others. The paper also helped shape opinion in favour of the first KMT–CPC cooperation. The authors conclude that the Guide recorded the Party's early search for a revolutionary path and prepared rich ideological material for it. They say the paper's Fourth Congress (1925) assessment gave it a 'leading position in public opinion'. They also treat its practices as part of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, and as useful today: holding to the Marxist standpoint, strengthening positive propaganda and confronting erroneous ideas firmly. Read the original if you want a detailed, sourced account of how a Party newspaper of the 1920s presented Marxism, class analysis and polemics, as the Party's official historiography now tells it.

A historical examination of the mutual fit between Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture 马克思主义同中华优秀传统文化相互契合的历史考察 Bu Xianqun Bu Xianqun takes up a formulation from Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development: that Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture have different origins but are highly compatible, and that only mutual fit allows organic integration. Writing in the Guangming Daily in June 2023, Bu argues that the Marxist encounter with Chinese tradition, and the opening of socialism with Chinese characteristics, were no accident. In the article's account they rest on historical, philosophical, cultural and social foundations. The short commentary has three parts. The first presents "mutual fit" as a historical insight, in three respects: it explains why the two could be combined, it affirms traditional culture, and it deepens the historical roots of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second part treats the fit as a grasp of historical regularity. The third considers its value as a resource for theoretical and institutional innovation. Bu's central argument is that the acceptance of Marxism in China was historically necessary and culturally prepared. Changes since the Ming and Qing dynasties are cited as background: sprouts of capitalism, a rising urban stratum, critiques of autocracy and the transformations after the Opium War. Bu holds that among the paths tried in modern China only socialism suited the people's aspirations and conditions. Bu also points to the openness of Chinese culture, which absorbed Confucianism, Buddhism and Neo-Confucianism, and lists elements said to echo historical materialism: the Five Phases and yin-yang as early dialectics, the unity of knowing and doing, the ideal of "all under heaven is public", and the people-based (minben) tradition. Bu concludes with three requirements. Scholars should recognise the continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness of Chinese civilization. They should draw critically on historical governance experience, including unitary centralised rule, the bureaucracy, supervisory and remonstrance systems, merit-based selection and law combining virtue with punishment. They should also ground theory in the practice of the Chinese nation and turn Chinese experience into Chinese theory, in order to build a modern Chinese civilization and strengthen cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated historians present the Two Integrations and the continuity of Chinese civilization with Marxism.

Deeply understanding the value implications of the new form of human civilization 深刻认识人类文明新形态的价值意蕴 Wang Bo This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2023, asks what theoretical value lies in the "new form of human civilization" that Xi Jinping links to Chinese modernization. Wang argues that it sums up the Party's century of struggle, carries forward the Marxist view of civilization, goes beyond Western civilizational theory and practice, and opens a new realm of scientific socialism. The piece follows Xi's remarks at a study session on the 20th Party Congress (2022) and has three sections. The first traces how Party thinking on civilization developed from the reform era to the present. The second places the new form within Marx and Engels's critique of capitalist civilization. The third treats it as an advance for scientific socialism. Wang says Chinese modernization promotes the coordinated development of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. This is said to build on earlier formulas, from the "three civilizations" to the "five-sphere integrated plan". Wang reads Marx and Engels as showing that capitalist civilization is brilliant yet contradictory, driven by surplus-value and by a Western-centred, hegemonic logic of the "law of the jungle" and zero-sum games. Against this, Xi's call for mutual respect and learning among civilizations is presented as a basis for world peace. Under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, rural revitalization, poverty alleviation and ecological governance are cited as evidence of socialism's advantages. Wang concludes that, facing great changes in the world, the era and history, China must firmly uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics and keep creating the new form of human civilization through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a short, official-style statement of how Chinese modernization is tied to the Marxist theory of civilization.

Understanding the Chinese revolution from the standpoint of "Chinese modernization" 立足“中国式现代化”理解中国革命 Qu Jun Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which put forward Chinese modernization, Qu Jun asks how the Chinese revolution should be understood from that standpoint. The author takes Xi Jinping's 2018 remark that the Party does not treat revolution and governing as two entirely different things as the starting point. Qu argues that modernization and revolution are interfused rather than opposed, and that the revolution is still continuing in a new-era form. The article has three parts. The first criticises the older opposition between a "modernization view of history" and a "revolution view of history". The second describes the hopes and practice of the revolution led by the Communist Party. The third turns to how the "Chinese revolution" of the new era should be advanced, drawing on the 20th Party Congress report and Xi's speeches. Qu first contends that separating modernization from revolution narrows the meaning of revolution. In the author's reading, a social revolution has a violent, overturning side and also a constructive and creative side. Reforms and popular enlightenment over the past century belong to it, so the revolution is part of Chinese modernization and a pivot of its key stages. Second, Qu says the Party's revolution combined three historical tasks: changing the state of the country, of the people and of Chinese civilization. It did so by taking the people as the centre, judging Chinese conditions independently, and combining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Qu sets this against rival socialisms that remained bookish, imitative or confined to small circles. Third, the author says the new-era revolution is carried forward through the Party's self-reform, which "leads the social revolution". Qu names four requirements: continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, stronger basic institutions, a "great struggle" with many new historical features, and a firm belief that the Party remains a revolutionary party. Qu concludes that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is "always on the road". Understanding the revolution through Chinese modernization is meant to sustain socialism with Chinese characteristics under Party leadership. The author warns against complacency over achievements. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party historians now link revolutionary history to the Chinese modernization framework and to current Party-building.

The logic of a new type of international relations in the path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化道路的新型国际关系逻辑 Ouyang Xiangying Writing in 2023, as what official discourse calls changes unseen in a century accelerate, Ouyang Xiangying asks what logic underlies the new type of international relations that China advocates and how it serves Chinese modernization. The author argues that this new type of relations, whose core Xi Jinping first described in 2013 as win-win cooperation, ultimately points towards a community with a shared future for mankind. Since building such a community is, in Ouyang's account, an essential requirement of Chinese modernization, the new international relations must serve both. The commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper, is organised around the three components named in the 19th Party Congress (2017) formula: mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation. Each section sets the Chinese approach against what the author presents as the outdated logic of some Western powers, especially the United States: bullying the weak, zero-sum games and plunder. The text draws on reports of the 19th and 20th Party Congresses, speeches by Xi Jinping, political philosophers such as Rawls and Habermas, and aid figures from a government white paper. On mutual respect, Ouyang contends that equality among states, rooted in the Chinese idea of harmony in diversity, suits an era of networked, multipolar power better than hierarchy derived from Machiavellianism and social Darwinism. The author lists four channels for building the new relations: great-power ties, neighbourhood ties, ties with developing countries, and exchanges between political parties. On fairness and justice, Ouyang charges that US trade disputes, export controls, unilateral sanctions and rule-manipulation violate basic justice, while China, in the author's description, pursues peaceful development, pledges never to seek hegemony and promotes the Global Security Initiative. On cooperation, the author blames dollar hegemony and US interest-rate policy for instability in developing countries, and contrasts this with the Belt and Road Initiative and Chinese aid. The author cites 270.2 billion yuan of foreign aid in 2013–2018, 47.3 per cent of it grants, given without political conditions. Ouyang concludes that China, as a builder of peace, contributor to global development, defender of the international order and provider of public goods, will advance under Party leadership and win new victories on the path of Chinese modernization. The Global Development Initiative is presented as a call to build a community of shared development. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS researcher frames China's diplomatic principles and sets them against US conduct.

Agricultural and rural modernization as the foundation of building a strong agricultural country 农业农村现代化是建设农业强国的根基 Liu Changquan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, Liu Changquan takes up Xi Jinping's statements that a strong agricultural country is the foundation of a strong modern socialist country. The article argues that socialist modernization is incomplete without agricultural and rural modernization, and that the latter is the base on which China's agricultural strength must be built. It presents the piece as an interpretation of Xi's remarks to the Jiangsu delegation at the first session of the 14th National People's Congress and of his article in Qiushi (2023, no. 6). The article has three parts. The first sets out why accelerating agricultural and rural modernization matters. The second describes its basic requirements. The third argues that reform and science and technology must work together as a "twin-wheel drive". Topics range from food security and rural revitalization to green and low-carbon farming, urban–rural integration, new types of farm operators and diversified food supply. Liu holds that agricultural and rural modernization is part of Chinese modernization and the weakest link in it, lagging behind industrialization, informatization and urbanization. In the article's account it is a precondition for a strong agricultural country, a guarantee of stable food supply for a large population, the overall goal of rural revitalization, and the basis of green development. It requires no copying of foreign models, and it rests on self-reliance in agricultural science and technology, above all seeds and key equipment. On reform, Liu says the main task is the relationship between farmers and farmland. This means deepening the separation of ownership, contract and management rights while keeping household contracting central, and fostering family farms, cooperatives and socialised services to link smallholders to modern agriculture. Liu concludes that agricultural and rural modernization is a long and arduous task running through the whole process of building a modern socialist country. It calls for a shift from scale and speed to quality, efficiency and competitiveness. The article proposes a "big food concept" that widens food sources beyond arable land to grassland, forests, oceans and biotechnology, and covers non-staple foods such as meat, eggs, dairy and vegetables. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official policy reasoning on agricultural modernization, food security and rural reform as presented in a Party theoretical journal in 2023.

Making real efforts to ensure that study and implementation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era go deep and take root 在推动学习贯彻习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想走深走实上下功夫 Liu Xiaoxin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts and posted in June 2023, Liu Xiaoxin discusses the thematic education campaign on studying and implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article takes up Xi Jinping's instruction that the campaign should "make real efforts" to make study go "deep and solid". Liu argues that without real understanding and practice, the study would become a formality and would fail to unify thinking, resolve the Party's prominent problems or advance the Party's and the country's work. The piece is a three-part exposition of Xi's remarks, framed as guidance for Party organisations at all levels. The first part sets out principles for study. The second sets out four aims of the campaign: forging loyalty and conviction, increasing wisdom, correcting work style, and promoting practical work. The third part treats investigation and research as the means of solving real problems. In the first part, Liu calls for reading original works, including the Selected Readings of Xi Jinping's works and the 2023 edition of the Study Outline. Liu also stresses grasping the "six musts" listed in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): put the people first, stay confident in our own path, uphold fundamental principles and break new ground, stay problem-oriented, apply systems thinking, and keep the world in view. Study should combine knowing, believing and doing, and Liu cites the Marxist view that practice determines cognition. The second part ties the four aims to ideals and loyalty to the Party, to mastering Marxist methods, to rectifying formalism and bureaucracy, and to delivering high-quality development and common prosperity. The third part calls for cadres to go to the grassroots with problems in mind, listen to criticism as well as praise, and treat investigation and analysis as equally important. Liu says results should be judged by whether problems are actually solved. Liu concludes that the campaign should turn study into practical results, with the Party's full and rigorous self-governance and the Party's self-reform continuing without end. Investigation and research are presented as a way to keep close ties with the people and to put the decisions of the 20th Party Congress into effect. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-affiliated scholars present the aims and methods of the 2023 thematic education campaign.

Understanding the genesis and logic of the "grand historical view" 深刻认识和把握大历史观的生成逻辑 Wang Guang This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2023, asks where the "grand historical view" (da lishi guan) put forward by Xi Jinping comes from. Wang Guang argues that the concept, which Xi has advanced since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a scientific way of understanding, drawing on and grasping history, rests on three sources: Marxist historical materialism, China's fine traditional culture, and the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article is organised in three parts, one for each source. It moves from theoretical origins to historical grounding to practical basis, quoting Xi's remarks throughout, together with a line from Liang Qichao on Chinese historiography. In the first part, Wang presents the grand historical view as a development of historical materialism, the \"only scientific view of history\". Faced with what Xi calls changes unseen in a century, it calls for analysing events within the long flow of history, the tide of the times and global currents. In the second, Wang treats it as a creative transformation of Chinese historiographical tradition, citing the continuity of Chinese civilization and the practical, statecraft orientation of Chinese historical writing. In the third, Wang says the concept is a theoretical summing-up of the new era's practice. Xi has asked that work on philosophy and social sciences, the \"three rural issues\" and literature and art all be viewed within it. Wang concludes that the ten years of change in the new era supplied the practical foundation for the concept and, in turn, enriched its content. Firmly establishing the view, Wang says, helps draw experience and wisdom from a broad historical perspective for building the future. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line account of how Chinese scholars trace the intellectual sources of the grand historical view.

Studying and implementing Xi Jinping's strategic thought on the Party's self-reform and building up discipline inspection cadres themselves 学习贯彻习近平总书记关于党的自我革命战略思想 扎实推进纪检干部队伍自身建设 Liao Wenhui Writing in 2023, Liao Wenhui presents a study-and-implementation commentary on what the author calls Xi Jinping's strategic thought on the Party's self-reform. Liao argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi has set out this thought as an original contribution to the Marxist theory of party building. In Liao's account it also deepens understanding of how to build a Marxist party that stays in power for the long term. The article then applies the thought to the ongoing education and rectification of discipline inspection and supervision cadres. The text has two parts. The first sets out the content of the thought: Xi's statements from 2016 to the 20th Party Congress (2022), why self-reform is needed, and how it has been carried out. The second turns to the discipline inspection cadre corps itself and lists four requirements: political tempering, theoretical armament, a fighting spirit, and strict self-discipline. On why self-reform is needed, Liao points to problems the 20th Party Congress report attributed to the period before 2012, including weakened Party leadership, formalism, bureaucratism and corruption. Liao adds that the Party's "four tests" and "four dangers" will persist, so full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is "always on the road". Liao presents self-reform as the Party's defining trait. It rests on the Party's nature and purpose, which Liao says include having no special interests of its own. On method, Liao lists eight measures, among them political building, centralised education, the eight-point regulations, discipline, inspection tours, Party regulations and an anti-corruption campaign that targets "tigers", "flies" and "foxes". Liao concludes that discipline inspection bodies are political organs and must hold themselves to higher standards than the cadres they supervise. Liao calls on them to carry out self-examination, guard against the "darkness under the lamp", and become a more disciplined "iron army". They are also to uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a clear example of how the Party's official discourse links self-reform theory to the internal discipline of its own inspection apparatus.

Between nationalism and internationalism: the evolution and political participation of the Communist Party of Israel 在民族主义与国际主义之间：以色列共产党的发展演变与政治参与 Ge Shuzhen Ge Shuzhen asks how the Communist Party of Israel has fared since its origins in Mandate Palestine, caught between Jewish and Arab national feeling and the proletarian internationalism it professed. The article argues that the party was never able to reconcile the two. Ge treats this tension as the root of its internal splits, its marginal place in Israeli politics and its limited influence. The article is a historical survey in five parts. It begins with the Palestine Communist Party under the Mandate, from the Socialist Workers Party of 1919 and its admission to the Comintern in 1924. It then covers the reorganised party's activity after 1948, the 1965 split into Maki and Rakah, and the party's theoretical positions after the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union around 1989–91. A short conclusion assesses the party's difficulties. Ge's central claim is that the party's early Jewish nationalist stance clashed with Comintern internationalism. Under Comintern and Soviet pressure the party moved from a Jewish to an Arab line in the 1930s, a shift Ge says wounded Jewish members and led to a wartime division. After 1948 the party defended Arab citizens' equality, workers' interests and opposed US and German aid, which Ge says kept it on the margins of a mostly Jewish society. Disputes over the Arab–Israeli conflict, Zionism, Arab nationalism and Soviet policy then split it in 1965. Ge reports that the Jewish-led Maki lost its seats and dissolved in 1975, while Rakah continued as the Communist Party of Israel, increasingly dependent on Arab votes. Ge notes that since the 2000s the party has criticised contemporary capitalism, described socialism as a continually renewed path, and put forward a peace programme for Israel and Palestine. It has also kept democratic centralism and a Jewish–Arab democratic front. Even so, Ge argues, Arab nationalist parties have drawn away its Arab support, its parliamentary seats have not exceeded four since the 1990s, and its weak capacity for self-renewal and the low tide of world socialism limit its prospects. Ge says it must strengthen itself, widen its public influence and deepen cooperation with left forces abroad. Read the original if you study communist parties in the Middle East, the national question within Marxist parties, or the history of Arab–Jewish politics in Israel.

Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's strategic thinking on the Party's self-reform and building up discipline inspection cadres 学习贯彻习近平总书记关于党的自我革命战略思想 扎实推进纪检干部队伍自身建设 Liao Wenhui Liao Wenhui, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in mid-2023, sets out to explain Xi Jinping's strategic thinking on the Party's self-reform and to draw out what it requires of the Party's own discipline inspection cadres. The article presents the thinking as an original contribution to the Marxist doctrine of party building and as an important part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It argues that it deepens understanding of how to build a Marxist party that governs for the long term. The piece has two parts. The first reviews the thinking itself, tracing Xi's statements from 2016 through the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It then asks why the Party needs self-reform and how it has been carried out. The second part turns to the campaign of education and rectification among discipline inspection and supervision cadres, launched in 2023, and sets four requirements for them. Liao gives two reasons for self-reform. Before the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article says, the Party faced serious problems: weak Party leadership, wavering convictions, formalism, bureaucracy, privilege and corruption. The Party also still faces what it calls the four tests and four dangers, together with the problems peculiar to a large party, so self-reform must be permanent. Liao presents the Party's nature and mission as the source of its willingness to correct itself, since it claims no special interests of its own. Eight measures are listed: political building, centralised education, organisational rectification, the eight-point decision on conduct, discipline, supervision, rule-based governance and anti-corruption work. Liao concludes that discipline inspection cadres must meet a higher standard, because their organs are political organs. They should show absolute loyalty to the Party Central Committee, with Xi at its core, and build their convictions through theoretical study. They should also develop a fighting spirit and the skills to go with it, and hold themselves to strict personal standards. These include self-examination and guarding against the problem of those who police others failing to look at themselves. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal official frames self-reform and the tasks assigned to discipline inspection cadres in the 2023 rectification campaign.

Foreign scholars and media on Chinese modernization in recent years: research and interpretation 近年来国外学者和媒体关于中国式现代化的研究和解读 Li Hanke This literature review, published in 2023, surveys how foreign scholars and media outlets have studied and interpreted Chinese modernization since Xi Jinping formally put forward the concept (2020–2021) and the 20th Party Congress (2022) wrote it into the Party report. Li presents these views as a "stone from other hills" that can help Chinese researchers answer the question of modernization and deepen their own work. The review draws on a wide range of sources, including Agence France-Presse, Vietnamese and African media, Latin American television, Japanese and US outlets, Monthly Review, and scholars from Italy, South Africa, Russia, Cambodia, the US and Cambridge. It is organised in three parts: the background to the concept (practical achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and theoretical lineage); its content and features, following the six aspects named in the Party report; and its worldwide significance. Li reports that foreign observers see Party leadership as the decisive force, with the Party's self-reform and anti-corruption work often cited. Foreign voices described in the review contrast Chinese modernization with Western modernization, which they portray as based on capital accumulation, colonial expansion and ecological damage. In their accounts, common prosperity, harmony between humanity and nature and peaceful development set China apart. Li also notes cautionary views about economic growth and geopolitical pressure. On significance, the review reports three claims: that modernization is not the same as Westernization, that China offers developing countries a reference path, and that it opens a new form of human civilization. Li concludes that the foreign literature offers three lessons for Chinese research: raise the theoretical level beyond tracking current events, study Chinese modernization as an integrated whole across economy, politics, society, ecology and foreign affairs, and strengthen international comparison of modernization paths. The review treats the foreign material mostly as supporting evidence and relays it largely without critical assessment. Read the original if you want a catalogue of foreign commentary on Chinese modernization, as selected and framed by a Chinese academic.

Bringing the strengths and role of the People's Political Consultative Conference into play in advancing Chinese modernization 在推进中国式现代化中发挥人民政协的优势和作用 Jiang Zelin Writing in 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Jiang Zelin asks how the People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) can contribute to Chinese modernization. Jiang argues that, as the broadest patriotic united front organisation, the CPPCC is a symbol of great unity and solidarity. Its strengths should therefore be considered as part of the systematic project of Chinese modernization, so as to rally all forces that can be rallied. The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2023, is organised around five strengths of the CPPCC. Each is tied to one dimension of modernization: the Party's leadership, high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy, scientific and technological progress, and common prosperity. Jiang draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report to frame each section. Jiang first argues that Party leadership is the greatest advantage of Chinese modernization and the political foundation on which the CPPCC unites different parties, groups and ethnicities in one political community. The CPPCC's role is said to lie in coordinating relations and focusing its consultation on the central tasks of the Party and state, in the service of high-quality development. On democracy, the article presents the CPPCC as an important institutional result of whole-process people's democracy. In Jiang's account it takes part in elections through prior consultation, in decision-making, management and oversight, with participants consulting on an equal footing. The last two sections emphasise the CPPCC's concentration of talent for innovation, and its broad sectoral links for reflecting interests and consolidating the Party's governing base, which Jiang treats as a political matter as well as an economic one. Jiang concludes that the CPPCC should make use of its strengths as a united front organisation and let its members play their part. The aim is to build unity through diligent performance of duty, cooperation and common struggle, and to form a strong joint force among Chinese people at home and abroad. Read the original if you want to see how a former provincial CPPCC head presents the body's functions in official 2023 terms, within the framework of Chinese modernization.

The historical and theoretical logic of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation 中华民族现代文明的历史与理论逻辑 Luo Wendong Luo Wendong offers a commentary on Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development (2023), which called for taking on a new cultural mission and building a modern civilization of the Chinese nation. Luo argues that the speech shows the Party's understanding of cultural construction and the laws of civilizational development has reached a new height. In Luo's reading, it also makes an original contribution to Marxist cultural theory and is a milestone in the history of both the Chinese nation and human civilization. The article is organised in three parts. The first sets out the historical roots and cultural foundation of Chinese civilization. The second traces the distinctive path and essential character of the modern civilization the Party is building, from the late Qing to the new era. The third turns to the guiding ideas and fundamental principles for building it, drawing on Xi's cultural thought since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Luo first presents the five outstanding features of Chinese civilization that Xi identifies: continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness and peacefulness. Luo holds that these features explain why China must follow its own path and why understanding them is a precondition for grasping the historical inevitability of the Chinese path. Next, Luo recounts how failed attempts to revive national heritage or imitate the West gave way to Marxism-Leninism and the Party's efforts at civilizational modernization. The Two Integrations, of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture, are presented as producing a new organic cultural entity, strengthening cultural subjectivity and opening room for innovation. Luo describes the resulting civilization as socialist, as combining material and spiritual advance and harmony between humans and nature, and as oriented to common prosperity and a community with a shared future for mankind. Luo claims it goes beyond both ancient Chinese and modern Western civilization. Luo concludes that building this civilization is a long, exploratory undertaking that cannot be done quickly. Luo urges philosophers and social scientists to link their work to the current thematic education campaign, to apply the Two Integrations, and to deepen research on the laws and major questions of cultural and civilizational development. Read the original if you want a concise official-line academic account of how Party scholars frame Chinese civilization, the Two Integrations and the modern civilization of the Chinese nation after Xi's 2023 speech.

The mission of passing on the red gene in the context of media convergence 媒体融合背景下红色基因传承的使命任务 Guo Jianhui Xiong Wen This newspaper commentary asks how the "red gene" (the revolutionary ideals, style and spirit of Chinese Communists) can be passed on in an age of media convergence. Guo and Xiong argue that 5G, artificial intelligence, big data and cloud computing have changed the media landscape and the way information spreads. In their view this brings both opportunities and challenges, and they say the task can be met only by using the technological, channel and platform advantages of converged media to develop red resources and spread red culture. The authors open by citing Xi Jinping's repeated calls since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to make good use of red resources and hand the red gene down through the generations. They then set out five tasks, each introduced by Xi quotations and followed by practical measures: ideological foundation, mainstream public opinion, the cultivation of young people, cultural confidence, and international communication. The core argument is that the red gene is rooted in belief in Marxism, so passing it on means promoting Marxist theory in a form suited to new media. The authors describe the internet as a front line where ideas contest each other. They claim hostile forces use it to sell Western political views to young people, and they cite a survey putting minors' internet penetration above 90 per cent. Their remedy is to tell the stories of the Party, the revolution and its heroes through smarter production and distribution, short videos, games, animation, cultural-creative products and tourism. They also propose digitised databases of red cultural resources and a digital red-culture industry. For overseas audiences they call for tailored, region- and audience-specific expression, use of international social media, and specialist foreign-communication staff. The authors conclude that media convergence is a major opening for carrying the red gene forward. They present the five tasks as ways to consolidate Marxism's guiding position in ideology, build consensus, train new-era young people, strengthen cultural confidence and project a credible, lovable and respectable image of China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars link digital media strategy to red culture, youth education and external communication.

New symptoms of cultural nihilism from the perspective of algorithms, and strategies for responding 算法视阈下文化虚无主义新症候及应对策略 Wei Yong'an Wei Yong'an asks how cultural nihilism, which the author describes as a long-standing tendency to disparage, doubt and negate mainstream cultural values, has changed in the age of algorithmic media. The article argues that the negative effects of algorithms (black boxes, information cocoons, the 'eyeball effect', deepfakes, discrimination) give cultural nihilism new room to spread. This produces new forms of dissemination that challenge socialist mainstream culture and call for a response built on value guidance, content, innovation and regulation. The article has three parts. The first sets out four cultural tensions in the algorithmic society: value versus instrumentality, popularisation versus vulgarisation, precision versus circle-formation, and dominance versus pluralism. The second analyses five ways algorithms strengthen cultural nihilism, namely its content, targets, form, channels and effects. The third proposes countermeasures under four principles: orientation as the soul, content as king, innovation as the key, and regulation as the base. Wei's core claim is that algorithms add no new content to nihilism but make its delivery more effective at each stage. Deepfakes and AI face-swapping are said to fabricate or alter images of ancient figures and revolutionary heroes. Tag-based matching and collaborative filtering are said to deliver such material precisely to receptive users. Entertainment-saturated formats are said to create addiction, the algorithmic black box to hide the material from oversight, and filter bubbles to produce blind identification while crowding out mainstream content. Wei also names historical nihilism, neoliberalism, 'universal values' and populism as currents that ride on this entertainment-style packaging. In response, Wei calls for mainstream values to govern algorithms, citing Xi Jinping's call to steer algorithms with mainstream value orientation. Wei also proposes raising the algorithmic literacy of engineers and users, and winning over online opinion leaders. High-quality content should be given more weight in recommendation pools, and the same deep-synthesis technology should be used for cultural innovation, with the examples of AI-colourised photos of Chinese People's Volunteers and a digital human on Xinhua. Wei further urges a multi-actor governance system covering filing, ethics review, industry self-discipline and embedding mainstream culture in algorithm design. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-official-academic account of how algorithmic recommendation is framed as an ideological risk and how regulatory and content strategies are proposed in response.

Chinese modernization amid the predicament of world modernity: a systemic-structural response 世界现代性困境下的中国式现代化：系统结构性应对方案论析 Zhu Wenting Zhu Wenting asks how Chinese modernization can be understood as a Chinese response to the current predicament of world modernity. The article argues that its effectiveness lies in its "systemic-structural" character, a term Zhu takes from materialist dialectics to describe the interaction of a thing's internal elements. In Zhu's account this character runs through three levels: values, institutional principles and practical forms. The article opens with the nature of world modernity and its three predicaments, as Zhu describes them: deepening value alienation, institutional divergence, and the entanglement of modernization with de-globalization. It then reviews Western-centric modernity theory and several "multiple modernities" approaches: neo-Marxist theory, developmentalism and dependency theory, and world-systems theory. It next sets out the three-level structure of Chinese modernization, and ends with the mechanisms Zhu draws from it. Zhu judges the alternative theories inadequate. Western-centric models only adjust capitalism, and the multiple-modernities schools remain within capitalist market logic or neglect the agency of late-developing countries. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is presented as moving from "value ideals" (the all-round development of the person, common prosperity, a community with a shared future for mankind) through the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics to practical forms. Those forms are the deepening of the socialist market economy and the parallel advance of new-type industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization. Zhu then names three mechanisms: a Party–people–humanity pattern of multiple actors that gathers modernizing forces; a handling of the socialist–capitalist relationship that, Zhu argues, releases the advantages of the socialist system; and the creation of a new form of human civilization through improved relations between humans and nature, society and the world. Zhu concludes that Chinese modernization offers a reliable model for escaping the predicament of world modernity. In this reading it also enriches modernity theory and supports the idea of a new form of human civilization. Zhu treats capitalism as the root of the predicament and presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as correcting capital-centred, polarising and expansionist modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-theory account of how Chinese modernization is positioned against Western modernity theories, dependency theory and world-systems theory.

"Geyi" and "reverse geyi": Western Marxism studies in China in the 1980s Chinese research on Western Marxism around the 1980s “格义”与“反向格义” Chen Xiangqin How did Chinese theorists understand Western Marxism when it entered China around the 1980s, in the era of reform and opening up and "thought liberation"? Chen Xiangqin argues that every study of a Western Marxist school, general or specific, was subordinate to a prior judgement about the nature of Western Marxism and its relation to Marxism. This produced a "geyi" and "reverse geyi" between Marxism modelled on the Soviet textbook system and Western Marxism, which in Chen's view enriched Chinese Marxist research and opened new theories and scholarship. The article first traces the origins of Western Marxism's introduction, from translations of Lukács, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty in the 1960s–70s and the pioneering work of Xu Chongwen, to the research boom after the 1978 truth-criterion debate. It then divides the period into four stages: 1978–82, 1982–87, 1987–89 and 1989–91. Next it surveys debates on philosophical questions (practice, dialectics, materialism) and political ones (the critique of capitalism, of Soviet socialism, and theories of revolution and utopia). It ends with the 1988 Xu Chongwen–Du Zhangzhi controversy. Chen's central distinction concerns direction. Initially the Soviet textbook was used to judge, or "geyi", Western Marxism as a bourgeois, revisionist current. In 1987–89 some scholars reversed the process, treating Western Marxism as part of Marxism's history and using ideas such as practical ontology, totality and subjectivity to question the textbook's "objective" dialectics and material monism. Most Chinese critics, Chen reports, rejected practice-ontology as idealism and held that Western Marxism shifted from political economy to philosophical and cultural critique, leaving only utopian longing. The 1988 debate turned on whether the concept exists, how to classify Western Marxism, and whether Marxism is "one" or "many". Chen notes that the disputants' criteria for what counts as Marxism differed. Chen concludes that Western Marxism was the only Western current to become deeply entangled with Marxism in 1980s China, taking part in debates on humanism and alienation, subjectivity and enlightenment, and the form of Marxist philosophy. Chen holds that it advanced thought liberation by supplying resources for understanding contemporary capitalism and for reflecting on the Soviet model, freeing Chinese theory from dogmas of both Soviet and Western systems. The article presents the post-1989 outcome as a move towards "two-way geyi", studying Western Marxism under the guidance of Marxism. Read the original if you want a detailed periodisation of Chinese reception of Western Marxism and the Xu–Du debate, as told by a Chinese scholar.

The Yucatán socialist movement in Mexico and its causes, 1917–1924 墨西哥尤卡坦社会主义运动始末及其成因（1917—1924） Han Qi Jiang Yuyan Between 1917 and 1924 a socialist movement in Mexico's Yucatán state produced a government proclaimed to be the 'first socialist regime in the Americas', led by Felipe Carrillo Puerto. The authors note that Chinese studies of Latin American history have said little about it and that no specialist article had appeared. They narrate the movement and then ask why it arose in Yucatán. Their answer is a combination of six factors, from the spread of socialist ideas to Carrillo's own leadership. The movement ultimately failed but left a lasting legacy. The article has three parts. The first narrates the movement in two stages: a preparatory phase (1917–1922), from Carrillo's election as head of the Socialist Party to his governorship, and his period as governor (February 1922 until his murder on 3 January 1924). It lists his reforms in land, rationalist education, women's rights, Maya cultural revival and law. The second part analyses causes, and the conclusion assesses the failure and the movement's afterlife. On causes, the authors argue that socialist ideas had circulated in Mexico since the nineteenth century, including through Ricardo Flores Magón and Zapata's movement, where Carrillo worked. Maya communal traditions, in their reading, offered a cultural basis for socialism. A sisal monoculture tied to US capital, with debt peonage, created a polarised society. They also argue that Salvador Alvarado's earlier top-down reforms mobilised the population, though he was no Marxist and favoured class conciliation. They credit the party and its 'resistance leagues', a fusion of party and government with democratic-centralist features, and Carrillo's organising ability and alliance with President Obregón. The authors also note that his reliance on local caciques later fed corruption. The authors attribute the defeat to several factors. Carrillo lacked military backing, and sisal prices fell, which cut revenue. His use of caciques bred corruption, and his radical land decrees alarmed planters and foreign capital. His goals also ran against the federal government's direction, and Obregón could not protect him during de la Huerta's 1923 rebellion. They nonetheless trace his influence on Cárdenas's collectivisation and socialist education, on Mexican cultural nationalism and on later Latin American memory, citing Armando Bartra's link to Bolivia's communitarian socialism. Read the original if you study Latin American socialism, the Mexican Revolution or Chinese scholarship on foreign socialist experiments and want a detailed account of the Yucatán case.

Chinese modernization and the creation of a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化与人类文明新形态创造 Yuan Zushe Yuan Zushe asks what distinguishes Chinese modernization from the Western modernization that began in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and why the former can be said to create a new form of human civilization. The article argues that Enlightenment modernity, built on rationalism and individualism, has produced wealth but also a comprehensive civilizational crisis. In Yuan's account, Chinese modernization corrects this path by grounding itself in a value commitment to the good life of the people as the principal agent (people's subjectivity). The article begins from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and its summary of the essential requirements and features of Chinese modernization. It then proceeds in three sections: a critique of Western rationalism and its cultural-value consequences; the need for independent nation-states to develop their own approach to modernity; and the value commitment of Chinese modernization. Yuan draws on Marx and Engels, and on Western and Japanese writers including Jeffrey Alexander, Max Weber, Amartya Sen, Baudrillard, Samuel Huntington and Tomio Futaki. Yuan holds that Western modernization, driven by technical rationality, markets and the logic of capital, equated development with growth and gave rise to ecological damage, inequality, nihilism, neo-colonialism and a loss of rooted tradition. Revisionist 'new modernization' studies and development ethics are cited as partial corrections, but the author maintains that Western modernity cannot distinguish what is modern from what is Western. Yuan therefore calls for a Chinese theory of modernity, with a 'Chinese logic' and 'Chinese solution', and notes that scholars have so far neglected questions such as what marks its success and how it should be communicated abroad. The article concludes that Chinese modernization succeeds because of Party leadership, the socialist system, inheritance of traditional culture and, above all, its commitment to the people's good life and the free and all-round development of the person. Yuan cites the new development philosophy, common prosperity, harmony with nature and peaceful development as marks of a modernization that holds the moral high ground. The author expects it to correct the older Western model and lead humanity towards a better future. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese philosopher draws on Western modernization theory to frame Chinese modernization as a critique of Enlightenment modernity.

The new form of human civilization sublates the paradox of capitalist civilization 人类文明新形态扬弃资本文明悖论 Zhao Ruize Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls for regulating and guiding the healthy development of capital by law, Zhao Ruize asks how the new form of human civilization deals with capital's contradictory effects. The author argues that this civilization, a new type oriented towards socialism, distinguishes capital's dual nature as a relation of production and as a factor of production. It thereby uses capital's positive role while avoiding its negative limits, and in doing so sublates the paradox of capitalist civilization. The piece appeared in China Social Sciences Today in May 2023. The article moves in four steps. It first sets out how capitalist civilization arose through capital's civilizing role, then the paradox built into that form. It next places the new form of human civilization in Marx's account of the succession of civilizational forms, and finally draws out the significance of continuing to enrich and develop it. Zhao relies mainly on Marx and Engels, including the Grundrisse's three social forms and the Communist Manifesto. In Zhao's reading, capital's civilizing role consists in the rapid growth of productive forces and the universalization of social exchange, which opened world history. Yet capital's aim is self-valorization, and its drive to expand keeps pressing against natural and social limits. The result, the author argues, is ecological crisis and social crisis, rooted in private appropriation set against socialized production and in domination of the periphery by the centre. Zhao presents the new form of civilization as a transitional socialist form between capitalist and communist civilization. It absorbs capitalism's material achievements while carrying communism's requirements, and it is the product of integrating Marxism with China's concrete reality and its fine traditional culture. Under it, socialist relations of production dominate, so capital's factor-of-production attributes can be used while its valorizing attributes are held in check. Zhao draws three implications. First, "traffic lights" for capital (green for its civilizing function, red for its valorizing drive) are a way to "harness" capital, with the final aim of "eliminating" it in a higher mode of production. Second, material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization are coordinated, in contrast to what the author calls capitalism's one-dimensional civilization. Third, respect for civilizational diversity and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind show that capitalist modernization is not the only road and that capitalist civilization is not the final form. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese commentary links Marx's theory of capital's civilizing role to Chinese modernization and the policy of regulating capital.

Marx's philosophy establishes a scientific concept of practice 马克思哲学确立科学的实践概念 Gao Juan This short piece, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2023, asks how Marx's concept of practice became a scientific one and why it matters. Gao Juan argues that practice is the pivot by which Marx broke with the idealist philosophical tradition. In Gao's reading, it is also essential for grasping the scientific system of Marxist philosophy and the coherence of Marx's thought as a whole. The article follows the concept from The German Ideology back to its origin in the Theses on Feuerbach. It first traces a movement from the abstract to the concrete in Marx's treatment of practice. It then examines the "five kinds of production" that The German Ideology treats as the main forms of practice. It closes by placing practice as the starting point of Marx's philosophy. Gao contends that the Theses on Feuerbach fixed practice as the mark separating new materialism from old materialism. There Marx criticised Feuerbach's humanism, redefined the human essence as the ensemble of social relations, and made sensuous human activity the logical starting point. In Gao's account, The German Ideology deepened this into material production, so that "object-related activity" became concrete. The five kinds of production are the production of material means of life, their reproduction, the production of human beings themselves, of social relations and of social consciousness. Gao says the first three are basic and that new needs arising from satisfied ones drive history. Social consciousness is derived from the other four. Gao notes that the word "practice" appears in The German Ideology mostly indirectly, through terms such as "sensuous activity" and "industry and commerce". Gao concludes that the German Ideology filled the gap of abstraction left at the time of the Theses, grounded the new view of history in real individuals and production, and marked an essential break with Feuerbach. Practice is described as the core of the universal principles of Marxism. Gao calls for understanding, inheriting and developing Marx's scientific conception of practice so that it can be combined with China's realities to address practical difficulties. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology are linked through the concept of practice.

Western Marxism's changing evaluations of Engels's philosophy and its "theoretical bombast" 西方马克思主义对恩格斯哲学评价的历史演变及“理论浮夸” Yi Xianfei How have Western Marxists judged Engels's philosophy since 1923, and why? Yi Xianfei argues that their assessments passed through two turns, tracking changes in Western capitalism and divisions within Western Marxism. The article concludes that the critics' attacks on Engels amount to what Marx called theoretical bombast, produced by a lack of revolutionary practice. The article reviews three currents in turn. These are early Western Marxism (Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci), the humanist Marxism of the mid-twentieth century (Merleau-Ponty, Sartre), and the scientistic current of the 1960s (Althusser, Colletti). For each, Yi sets out the criticisms of Engels under dialectics, ontology and epistemology, then lists the current's main features and explains its stance by political context, philosophical background and attitude to Marxism. Yi argues that early Western Marxists rejected Engels's extension of dialectics to nature and found his concept of practice too narrow. Even so, they did not reject him wholesale, and they judged him from Marx's standpoint. Humanist Marxists, shaped by the Second World War and the rediscovery of Marx's 1844 Manuscripts, moved to a general rejection. They treated Engels as having no philosophy, took him as a separate individual, and judged him from existentialist or other standpoints. The scientistic current, led by Althusser, partly returned to Engels, praised his genius, and criticised him for inheriting Hegel's flawed dialectic and so making Marxism metaphysical. Yi also notes the principle of 'abandoning Engels to protect Marx', in which the periphery of a theory is revised to save its core. Yi contends that these critiques mostly serve to set off each school's own theory by casting Engels as its opposite. In Yi's account Marx and Engels agreed on the dialectics of nature, and Western Marxist critiques of contemporary capitalism fit Engels's view of nature and society. Yi holds that the critics, cut off from proletarian revolutionary practice and tied to bourgeois or petty-bourgeois outlooks, produce inflated theory and will end as dust of history. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how Western Marxism has judged Engels, and of how that debate is framed within Chinese scholarship.

Party-building thought in "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder and its contemporary implications 《共产主义运动中的“左派”幼稚病》中的党建思想及其当代启示 Wang Youchen Zhao Feng Wang Youchen and Zhao Feng ask what Lenin's 1920 pamphlet "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder contributes to the theory of proletarian party building, and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. They argue that, beyond guiding the new communist parties of its time, the work sets out general principles on discipline, theory, leadership and tactics that can inform the new great project of Party building in the new era. The article has three parts. It first sets the historical background: after the October Revolution, ultra-left sectarianism and adventurism appeared in the European and American workers' movements, including refusal to join parliaments and slogans such as "down with the leaders" and "abolish the party". It then reconstructs four strands of Lenin's Party-building thought. It closes with four lessons for the contemporary Chinese Communist Party. In the authors' reading, Lenin's four strands are: iron discipline and theoretical construction; a struggle on two fronts against "Left" and Right opportunism; the authority of leaders; and correct strategy and tactics, including reasoned compromise. The authors stress that Lenin's discipline rests on democracy and combines voluntary and compulsory elements. They also stress that leadership authority is exercised by a stable collective, not an individual, and that Lenin distinguishes revolutionary compromise from the compromise of traitors. From this the authors draw four implications. Discipline-building should be systematic, linked to ideological education, the mass line and the Party's political line. The Party should guard against "Left" deviation first while watching for Right deviation in opposing it. The Two Upholds should be realised in both knowledge and action, avoiding personality cults and blind adulation. Finally, the Party should promote inner-Party harmony by allowing principled yet flexible compromise on inner-Party contradictions, which the authors treat as non-antagonistic. The authors conclude that the Chinese Party's approach to Party building stands in a continuous line with Lenin's pamphlet. Learning from it, they say, can widen and deepen Party building and support theoretical innovation and practical breakthroughs. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party-theory scholarship in 2023 draws on a Leninist text to support current positions on discipline, the Two Upholds and inner-Party harmony.

The major contributions of the Communist Party of China to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress 论十八大以来中国共产党对国际共产主义运动的重大贡献 Zhuo Mingliang Tan Guoqing Zhuo Mingliang and Tan Guoqing ask what the Communist Party of China (CPC) has contributed to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what it should do next. They argue that the movement is currently marked by a 'general ebb' alongside a 'local high tide'. In their account, the 'local high tide' is the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics, which they call the movement's main 'growth point' since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article has three parts. The first lists five contributions of the CPC in the new era. The second surveys the roughly 950 communist organisations in over 130 countries, sorted by relation to state power, membership, guiding ideology, attitude towards China and choice of revolutionary path. The third sets out how the CPC should advance the movement in the twenty-first century, from historical review to concrete mechanisms. The authors draw on statements by foreign communist figures, including Mick Kelly, Michael Hooper, Mincho Minchev and Mauro Alboresi. The authors' five contributions are: advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its result; promoting a community with a shared future for mankind and opposing hegemony; offering 'Chinese solutions' to global problems; building a 'Chinese platform' for exchanges among communist parties; and winning more positive appraisals from foreign communist parties. The survey stresses diversity: some parties praise China's path, others, such as the German Marxist-Leninist Party and the Revolutionary Communist Party USA, doubt its socialist character. The authors say that parties seek both independent development and international unity, and that the failure of parliamentary roads to socialism means the feasibility of violent revolution should not be ignored. Zhuo and Tan call on the CPC, which they describe as the world's largest ruling party, to supply a 'CPC answer, plan and contribution'. They urge it to learn from Soviet great-party chauvinism and to lead by 'exemplary demonstration' rather than coercion. Their proposals are a 'twenty-first-century internationalism', deeper ties with international communist and left organisations, wider forms of party cooperation, an international coordinating body of Marxist parties, and a 'community with a shared future for communist parties of the world'. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the CPC sees its role in the global communist movement, with a classification of the world's communist parties.

Understanding the great significance of the "Two Integrations" 深刻理解“两个结合”的重大意义 Li Zhen Li Zhen takes up the formulation of the Two Integrations, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and asks why it matters for the Party's long effort to adapt Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article argues that the formulation enriches the content and practical paths of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, points to a scientific direction for that work in the new era, and deepens the Party's understanding of how to uphold and develop Marxism. It further claims that the formulation has universal methodological value beyond China. The article is organised in three parts. The first examines the "first integration", combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities, and traces it from Mao Zedong's 1938 call for the "sinification of Marxism" through the Yan'an rectification movement and the 7th Party Congress (1945). The second turns to the pairing of the two integrations, adding integration with China's fine traditional culture, and links it to Xi Jinping's statements. The third treats the Two Integrations as a general law of the nationalisation of Marxism. Li's central claim is that the second integration answers a question the first left open: the cultural foundation of adapting Marxism. In the article's reading, a scientific theory takes root only in a nation's own historical and cultural soil, so fine traditional culture is the first object of integration. Li cites Xi Jinping on the "high degree of compatibility" between that culture and the values of scientific socialism, and presents the second integration as both implicit in and a logical development of the first. Li also ties the Two Integrations to the formation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which the article describes as a new leap in adapting Marxism. In the third part Li draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao and Deng Xiaoping to argue that applying Marxism always depends on national conditions, so that the Two Integrations, though framed around China, express a general principle. Li concludes that the Two Integrations offer a methodological reference for nationalising Marxism more widely in the world and constitute an original theoretical contribution by Chinese communists to developing Marxism. The text is a concise, officially oriented exposition of the concept and its lineage in Party discourse. Read the original if you want a short account of how Party scholarship traces the Two Integrations from Mao's 1938 formulation to Xi Jinping Thought and claims for them universal significance.

Strengthening discourse-system building depends on bringing out "Chinese characteristics" 加强话语体系建设重在彰显“中国特色” Huang Ju This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2023, asks how China should build its discourse system so as to gain the initiative in international public opinion. Huang argues that the key is to bring out "Chinese characteristics", which the author presents as following objective laws of both discourse construction and discourse communication. The piece first gives two reasons for this claim, one theoretical and one practical. It then sets out three routes for strengthening the subjectivity and originality of a Chinese-characteristic discourse system: Marxist guidance, contemporary Chinese practice and traditional Chinese culture. On theory, Huang holds that every discourse system combines the general and the particular. Citing Marx, the author treats discourse as an expression of real life that is determined by an economic base, while different bases, institutions and traditions give each system its own character. On communication, Huang contends that distinctive discourse spreads more widely, and that building such a system is necessary to end the position of being "voiceless and abused" and to reverse Western strength and Chinese weakness in international discourse. The three routes are then spelled out: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the guiding worldview and method; Chinese modernization as the practical source of new concepts, categories and theories; and the creative transformation of traditional culture's concepts and terms. Huang concludes that Chinese philosophy and social science can develop their own strengths only by starting from China's realities and producing original theory. The result, the author says, would be a discourse with Chinese features, style and manner that better tells China's story. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and recommended method for building a Chinese-characteristic discourse system.

Chinese modernization creates a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化创造人类文明新形态 Dong Tianmei Written in 2023 as part of the study campaign on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, this commentary asks what it means to say that Chinese modernization has created a "new form of human civilization". Dong argues that the formula, taken from the 2021 Party resolution on history, expresses the Chinese Communist Party's view of civilization in the twenty-first century. It is presented as a scientific conclusion reached through Marxist standpoint and method. The article first sets out the formula's meaning: a civilization marked by the advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics, guided by the new development philosophy, and balancing material, political, cultural, social and ecological progress. It then proposes four dimensions for understanding it: a socialist form of modern civilization, a Chinese form of socialist civilization, a contemporary form of Chinese civilization, and a new form of world civilization. Each section draws on the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and on statements by Xi Jinping, with occasional references to Marx and Deng Xiaoping. Dong's central move is to separate modernization from Westernization.
