Drawing on historical materialism, the author says modernization is a natural historical process, and that its Western capitalist version rests on exploitation and an unresolved contradiction between private ownership and socialized production. Chinese modernization is said to go beyond capital-centred, polarized, materialist and expansionist models. The author describes a "human-centred logic" overcoming the "logic of capital", and treats Party leadership as what determines the socialist nature of the project. The article also roots Chinese modernization in traditional Chinese culture, claiming that ideas such as "all under heaven is for the common good" fit the values of scientific socialism. Dong concludes that the new civilization form offers developing countries a fresh option. It is said to refute the "clash of civilizations" thesis and the claim that strong states inevitably seek hegemony, replacing them with exchange, mutual learning and coexistence among civilizations. The author links this to a community with a shared future for mankind and to the Global Civilization Initiative proposed by Xi in 2023, reading the former as a contemporary version of Marx's idea of history becoming world history. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholarship during the 2023 study campaign framed Chinese modernization as a civilizational claim.

The people's happiness and well-being as the ultimate purpose of promoting high-quality development 人民幸福安康是推动高质量发展的最终目的 Chen Hongqi Writing in 2023 in New Xiangtan Review, Chen Hongqi takes up Xi Jinping's statement, made to the Jiangsu delegation at the first session of the 14th National People's Congress, that "the people's happiness and well-being is the ultimate purpose of promoting high-quality development". Chen argues that the statement explains the inner logic linking popular well-being and high-quality development, shows Xi's consistent concern for the people, and gives high-quality development its direction and basic guidance. The commentary has two main parts. The first places the principle in Marxist and Party tradition, as an expression of the Party's people-centred stance and of its aim of fulfilling the people's yearning for a better life. The second sets out five practical tasks for realising people's happiness and well-being within high-quality development. Chen draws on Xi's speeches, the 19th and 20th Party Congress reports (2017, 2022) and statistics for 2022. In Chen's account, Marxism holds that the people are the creators of history and that the future society aims at the free development of all. The Communist Party has pursued this aim since its founding, and under Xi it has been formulated as a people-centred philosophy of development. Chen argues that economic growth is the material basis of better livelihoods, while improving livelihoods in turn lifts consumption expectations and supplies endogenous momentum for growth. The two are therefore dialectically unified. The article cites 2022 figures: per capita disposable income of 36,883 yuan, basic pension coverage of 1.05 billion people, and basic medical insurance enrolment above 95 per cent. Chen's five tasks are: protecting and improving livelihoods through development; solidly advancing common prosperity, including by improving primary, secondary and tertiary distribution and building an olive-shaped society; focusing on people's most pressing concerns, including equalised basic public services; strengthening and innovating social governance, including the "Fengqiao experience"; and deepening the building of a Safe China under the holistic national security outlook. Chen concludes that the Party must treat the people's happiness as its fundamental purpose and keep consulting the people, since the people are the "ultimate judge" of the Party's work. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2023 tied high-quality development to livelihood, distribution and security policy.

The complex context of the young Marx's turn to materialism 青年马克思唯物主义思想转变的复杂语境 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing, in a piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (6 June 2023), returns to the young Marx's first intellectual shift, from idealism to materialism. The article asks three questions: how this shift should be studied, why Marx made it, and where its theoretical sources lay. Zhang argues that the shift was driven by the "problem of material interests" and that it drew on more sources than Feuerbach alone. The article starts from Lenin's 1914 account of Marx's turn during the Rheinische Zeitung period and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, and from Sun Bokai's "two shifts" thesis, which separates general materialism from historical materialism. Zhang divides the first shift into five stages. They run from the 1842 Rheinische Zeitung articles, through the 1843 Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and the Kreuznach notebooks, and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher texts, to the 1844 Paris Notebooks and Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The fifth stage is the second shift after 1845, toward historical materialism, together with Marx's later explicit and implicit returns to the first shift. On method, Zhang sets three principles. These are working from the German, French and English originals and the MEGA2 manuscripts; tracing the genesis of Marx's ideas; and reconstructing his thought in its own context without teleological projection. Zhang's example is that reading the 1843 "civil society" as the "economic base", or reading alienated labour through Capital, mistakes later concepts for earlier ones. On motive, Zhang holds that Marx's encounter with material interests, as in the debates on wood theft, shook his Hegelian faith in state reason. The problem was only partly resolved in 1843–44, when Marx turned to economics. It persisted through the theory of alienated labour and later through the "sachlich" forces and "Versachlichung" of historical materialism, and it shaped his critical sequence from civil society to bourgeois society to the capitalist mode of production. On sources, Zhang accepts Feuerbach's importance but, following Sun Bokai, stresses that Marx never accepted him without reservation and sublated his humanism through Hegelian dialectics. Zhang adds Eduard Gans, whose Hegel edition and remarks on class opposition left a lasting mark. Zhang also names Engels and Moses Hess, who supplied economic critique and the notion of "economic alienation". The last source is the classical economists excerpted in the Paris Notebooks, who in Zhang's view brought Marx to what Zhang calls "social materialism". Read the original if you study the young Marx's intellectual development, MEGA2-based textual method, or the Chinese scholarly debate following Sun Bokai's "two shifts" thesis.

Reflections on building an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese historiography 对构建中国历史学自主知识体系的思考 Chen Qitai Chen Qitai asks how Chinese historical scholarship can build its own autonomous knowledge system under the guidance of the materialist conception of history. The article argues that historiographical theory guides the whole discipline, and that the task requires two things: drawing together the theoretical achievements of the reform era and drawing out the theoretical value of traditional Chinese historiography. The article opens by presenting China's long, continuous history, its developed feudal society, the modern revolution and the decades since 1949 as a source of theoretical problems. Chen then credits two forces for the vitality of historical theory since reform and opening up: clearing out dogmatism and returning to Marxism's founding principles, and developing the materialist conception of history to match new conditions. Section two lists 13 theoretical achievements of the period and discusses several in detail. Section three takes the history of historiography as a test case. Among the 13 achievements, Chen examines Fei Xiaotong's theory of the pattern of diversity in unity of the Chinese nation, the cultural-identity thesis in Qu Lindong's five-volume work, and Liu Danian's 'two basic problems' (national independence and modernization) as the main thread of modern Chinese history. He presents the last as an integration of earlier approaches centred on revolutionary high tides and on modernization. In section three, Chen argues that historical compilation is not a mere technical matter. He identifies 'compilation thought' as its core, and takes Sima Qian's Shiji as an example. Its five-part form embodies what Chen calls a 'multi-dimensional historical vision', later adapted in Bai Shouyi's multi-volume General History of China. Chen concludes that creative use of the materialist conception of history is the unshakeable direction. He calls for more systematic summaries of theoretical results, both across the discipline and within its branches such as political, economic, intellectual and cultural history. In his view this would strengthen cultural confidence. Chen describes his list of 13 achievements as a personal and incomplete selection. Read the original if you want a Chinese historian's survey of reform-era historical theory, including the debates on ethnic relations and modern history, and of how traditional historiography is being reframed for a contemporary Chinese knowledge system.

The new form of human civilization sublates the paradox of capital's civilization 人类文明新形态扬弃资本文明悖论 Zhao Ruize Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (23 May 2023), Zhao Ruize asks why the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) calls for regulating and guiding the healthy development of capital by law. The answer offered is that capital has a great civilizing role, but if left to grow wildly and expand without order it brings disastrous consequences. Zhao argues that the new form of human civilization distinguishes capital's dual character, as a relation of production and as a factor of production. It uses the positive side and avoids the negative, and in doing so sublates the paradox of capital's civilization. The commentary has four sections. The first sets out how capitalist civilization arose through capital's civilizing role, and the second the paradox that role contains. The third places the new form of human civilization in Marx's account of historical stages, and the fourth lists three ways in which it can be enriched and developed. Drawing on Marx, Zhao holds that capital's civilizing role lies in the rapid growth of productive forces and the universalization of social exchange, which opened the way to world history. Yet capital's aim is self-valorization, so its drive to expand keeps hitting the external limits of nature and society. In Zhao's account this triggers ecological and social crises and, at the level of the world system, domination of peripheral regions. Zhao reads Marx's three social forms in the Grundrisse as pointing to communism, which inherits capitalism's civilizational achievements while overcoming its alienation. On this view the new form is a transitional socialist civilization, "in progress" rather than complete, in which two kinds of production relations coexist. Zhao draws three implications. First, capital can be "harnessed" by giving it "traffic lights": green for its productive-factor role, red for its valorizing role as a production relation. The ultimate aim is to "eliminate capital" within a higher set of production relations. Second, the new form coordinates five dimensions (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological), in contrast to what Zhao calls capitalism's one-dimensional civilization. Third, it respects civilizational diversity and promotes a community with a shared future for mankind, showing that capitalist modernization is not the only road. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese Marxist commentary links Marx's theory of capital to official claims about Chinese modernization and the regulation of capital.

Upholding rule-based governance of the Party: the code behind "China's governance" 坚持依规治党:“中国之治”的密码 Wang Jianqin Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Jianqin asks why governing the Party according to its rules has become what the author calls the distinctive governance code of "China's governance". The thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), rule-based Party governance, backed by intra-Party regulations and a system for the Party's self-reform, has become the political guarantee for the Party's governing capacity and for national governance. The article has three parts. The first traces the Party's tradition of "building the Party through discipline" from the First Congress programme, the 1922 constitution and the Jinggangshan period to Mao Zedong's "four subordinations" and the Party constitutions of later congresses. The second examines the conceptual shift to "institutional governance of the Party" and rule-based Party governance in Xi Jinping's statements. The third links these to the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and to Chinese modernization. Wang argues that Marxist parties are distinguished by strict discipline, which Lenin treated as a condition for overthrowing private ownership. Through democratic centralism, discipline takes on both a "Party" and a "legal" character, and over time discipline rules have turned into formal intra-Party regulations. The author presents rule-based governance as a change in the Party's ideas, thinking and methods, which combines the tradition of strict governance with the rule of law. It was written into the Party constitution in 2017, and Xi's "ten adherences" at the Second National Conference on Intra-Party Regulations are described as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang says the Party's governance moved from "lax, loose and soft" to "strict, tight and hard", and holds that the Party's leading role under the constitution makes its position in governance different from that of Western and other ruling parties. Wang concludes that only by keeping strictness as the keynote, and by strengthening the authority and enforcement of intra-Party regulations, can the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party reach a stage of high-quality development. The author holds that the Party's self-reform is the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall, and that Chinese modernization depends on this political guarantee. Wang claims this offers Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to party governance and legal civilisation worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party discipline, intra-Party regulations and the rule of law are linked in current Chinese Party-building discourse.

The value implications of the "Three Musts" “三个务必”的价值意蕴 Yi Kaifa This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2023, asks what value the "Three Musts" carry. The report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) told all Party members they must keep to the original aspiration and founding mission, stay modest, prudent and hard-working, and dare and know how to fight. Yi Kaifa argues that these requirements do four things: guide Party building, support long-term rule, shape the Party's image and supply spiritual strength for national rejuvenation. The article has four sections, one for each function. It takes the three requirements in turn within each section. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks, on the Party's history and on a definition of party image as public perception. On Party building, Yi links each "must" to a field of work. The first concerns ideological building, the second work style and discipline, and the third political building and governing capacity. On long-term rule, Yi attributes the Party's historical selection by the people to the three qualities. The Party still faces the "four tests" and "four dangers", so Yi calls for keeping the clarity and resolve of the "exam" in aims, work style and capability. On image, Yi describes party image as a public impression formed from everything people can see and feel of a party. In Yi's reading, the Three Musts embody a caring and responsible image, an advanced and striving one, and a capable and effective one. Yi concludes that the Three Musts also supply the spiritual strength needed for national rejuvenation. They would do this by reinforcing belief, restraining complacency and strengthening the will to struggle, among Party members and the public alike. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party commentary presents the Three Musts as requirements for Party building and the Party's image.

The ideological content and practical paths of building a community with a shared future for mankind 构建人类命运共同体的思想内涵与实践路径 Sun Xihui Sun Xihui asks what ideas underpin the building of a community with a shared future for mankind and how it is to be pursued in practice. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2023, Sun argues that the concept, together with the related global initiatives, rests on Marxist principles and a set of universal values, and that it can be advanced through specific diplomatic and cooperative channels. The article presents the concept as an essential requirement of Chinese modernization and a key part of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought. The piece is organised in three parts: the moral and value foundations, the core content, and the basic paths. It draws on Xi Jinping's speeches at the United Nations and the Boao Forum, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative and the Global Civilization Initiative. It also cites figures on the Belt and Road Initiative. Sun first claims that the concept inherits and develops Marx's idea of the community, charting a route from an "abstract" or "illusory" community to a "true community". The author treats the common values of all humanity (peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom) as its moral basis, with peace and development the first prerequisites and fairness and justice the core pursuit. Second, Sun sets out its core content through the Global Development Initiative, which is people-centred, innovation-driven and attentive to developing countries, and the Global Security Initiative, which stresses respect for sovereignty, opposes bloc confrontation and unilateral sanctions, and links traditional and non-traditional security. Third, Sun identifies the paths: a new type of international relations, including relations among major powers, a correct approach to righteousness and interests, partnership without alliance and genuine multilateralism; communities of shared future with particular countries and regions as intermediate steps; and the Belt and Road Initiative. For the last, the author cites more than 200 cooperation documents signed by 151 countries and 32 international organisations. Sun concludes that great practice produces great thought and that great thought guides practice. The author calls for deeper study and implementation of Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought, so as to open new prospects for major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics and create a favourable external environment for the second centenary goal and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars link the community with a shared future to Marxist theory, the global initiatives and the Belt and Road.

Key focal points for steadily advancing common prosperity for all the people 扎实推进全体人民共同富裕的着力点 Ye Bing This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2023, asks where policy should concentrate in order to advance common prosperity. Ye Bing argues that, with a moderately prosperous society now built, the historical stage of steadily promoting common prosperity has arrived. The author treats it as an essential requirement of socialism and a defining feature of Chinese modernization, to be pursued under Party leadership by making the "cake" bigger through high-quality development and dividing it fairly through institutional arrangements. The piece draws on two Xi Jinping articles in Qiushi (2021 and 2022) and on his phased targets for the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan, 2035 and the middle of the century. It then moves through Party leadership, high-quality development, employment, the regulation of capital, the distribution system, social security, and rural and urban-rural gaps. Ye holds that Party leadership is the political guarantee and must run through every field, including drawing up an action outline for common prosperity. High-quality development, supported by technological self-reliance, a modern industrial system and a strong real economy, is called the fundamental route. On capital, Ye accepts its role in a socialist market economy but calls for "traffic lights" against disorderly expansion: strengthening state capital in strategic sectors, regulating the platform economy and enforcing anti-monopoly rules. Distribution is to combine primary distribution, redistribution through taxes and transfers, and philanthropy as a third distribution, with labour-based distribution as the mainstay. Ye further urges wider social security coverage for migrant and flexible workers, and equalised basic public services in rural education and health care, since the heaviest tasks remain in the countryside. The author concludes that common prosperity shows the superiority of socialism with Chinese characteristics and will be achieved along the path of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise, policy-oriented summary of the official agenda for common prosperity as framed in 2023.

Rhythmanalysis: a new perspective in foreign Marxist critical theories of time 节奏分析：国外马克思主义时间批判理论的新视域 Lu Bao Why do people feel short of time and anxious about falling behind, and what can Marxism say about it? Lu Bao takes up Henri Lefebvre's late concept of "rhythmanalysis", which the author says has received too little attention in Chinese scholarship. Lu argues that it extends Marxist social critique to the abstraction and politicisation of time, and can explain the present acceleration of social life. The article has four sections. The first traces the genealogy of rhythmanalysis through Gurvitch, Bachelard, Nietzsche, Lukács, the Frankfurt School and Debord, and shows how Lefebvre set it against Freudian psychoanalysis. The second covers the shift from pre-modern cyclical time to capitalist accumulation time, drawing on Le Goff, Marx, Postone, E. P. Thompson and Foucault. The third turns to "hypermodernity" and social acceleration, citing Virilio, Rosa, Lipovetsky, Nowotny and Jonathan Crary. The fourth sets out a way out. Lu's central claim is that capital splits time into labour time and life time, and then extends linear, homogeneous, abstract time from the factory into all of everyday life. In Lu's account, this is a "colonisation" of the everyday that reproduces capitalist relations through control of bodily rhythm. Lu then argues that in hypermodern society acceleration forms a closed, self-driving loop of technological, social and everyday acceleration. Its costs, as Lu lists them, are exhaustion, anxiety, depression, the commodification of life itself, the erosion of sleep, lost local identity and "systematic stupidity". Lu criticises accelerationism as a new technological determinism that ignores the need to change the relations of production. Lu concludes that the answer is deceleration, not a return to pre-modern life: a relative, harmonised slowing in which technology, institutions and daily rhythm are brought into step, and natural cycles and linear time coexist. Lu finds an echo of this in the Book of Changes. Lu then turns to Marx's view that the measure of wealth will become disposable free time once capitalist private ownership is overthrown, which opens the way to a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Western Marxist theories of time, or critiques of social acceleration and want a Chinese reading that links them to Marx's labour-time analysis.

Totality, totalization and negative dialectics The idea of totality in mid-twentieth-century foreign Marxism 总体性、总体化与否定的辩证法 Yang Haifeng Yang Haifeng asks how the concept of totality, revived by Lukács, changed in foreign Marxism from the 1930s to the post-1970s period. The article argues that totality shifted in both definition and orientation. It began as a critical method and a utopian ideal of the "total human being", became a target of critique once capitalist society was seen as a reified totality, and was then deconstructed and reconstructed by post-Marxism. Yang holds that one theme stays constant: reflection on and critique of capitalism, and the search for a better society. The study moves through five stages. It starts with the Frankfurt School's critical theory (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse). It then covers readings of the 1844 Manuscripts by Marcuse, Lefebvre and Fromm. Next come Sartre's distinction between totality and totalization, and Adorno's critique of totality in Negative Dialectics. The last section treats postmodernism and post-Marxism (Lyotard, Laclau and Mouffe, Derrida). Yang mentions Althusser's structural totality along the way. Yang's first move is that the Frankfurt School saw the organised, monopoly capitalism that followed the First World War as a "pseudo-totality" built on reification and private ownership. Critical theory therefore opposes it with interdisciplinary, totalising critique, which in Marcuse becomes the "Great Refusal". The second move is Sartre's: he treats totality as a congealed, reified structure and totalization as an open, ongoing process, which in Yang's reading restores the movement of Marxist dialectics. The third is Adorno's. He reads Hegel's world spirit as the philosophical image of commodity exchange and its identity principle, a source of domination, and answers with non-identity and the "constellation". Yang reads Laclau, Mouffe and Derrida as deconstructing closed, essentialist totality in order to build an open, non-dominating one. Yang sees positive value in this as a response to post-Soviet claims about the "end of history". Yang also argues that stressing difference and looseness makes it hard to reveal the structure of society and risks obscuring the dominance of the logic of capital under globalisation. In Yang's view, how to draw on modern philosophy while keeping Marxism's critical force still needs exploration. Read the original if you study Western Marxism, the Frankfurt School or Sartre and post-Marxism and want a long, text-based account of how totality evolved as a concept.

A study of Xi Jinping's important statements on religious work in Xinjiang in the new era 习近平总书记关于做好新时代新疆宗教工作重要论述研究 Jia Youjun Pu Lixia Jia and Pu set out to systematise what Xi Jinping has said about religious work in Xinjiang since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They argue that these statements form part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and of the Party's strategy for governing Xinjiang. In their account, the statements offer a complete framework for religious work in the region and guidance for the whole country. The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2023, has three parts. The first sets out five strands of Xi's statements: Party leadership of religious work; the Sinicization of Islam in Xinjiang; governing Xinjiang according to law; building 'three contingents' of personnel; and combating religious extremism. The second identifies five modes of thinking in the statements: political, innovative, strategic, dialectical and systems thinking. The third assesses their theoretical and practical value. On Sinicization, the authors argue that Islam in Xinjiang has been well localised but is less Sinicized than in inner China, because its Chinese outlook and standpoint are not firmly grounded. They present Xi's remedy as strengthening identification with Chinese culture, guiding religious figures towards interpretations suited to the times, and resolving whether Xinjiang looks 'east or west'. On law, they stress the principle of protecting what is legal, stopping what is illegal, curbing extremism, resisting infiltration and cracking down on crime. They also stress meeting believers' normal religious needs. They define religious extremism as a political struggle, not an ethnic or religious question, and cite a 2016 Kashgar survey of clergy to show how weak the clergy's education is. The authors conclude that Xi's statements opened a new level of understanding of Xinjiang religious work and set out its direction and methods. They also credit the statements with strengthening Party leadership and with guiding the handling of incidents involving religion. They cite the regional government's 2022 report of five consecutive years without violent terrorist cases as evidence of results. They also argue that formulations first devised for Xinjiang, such as the 'five identifications' and forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, now guide ethnic and religious work nationwide. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the policy rationale for religious governance in Xinjiang.

Annual development planning meeting of the CASS Research Centre for Science and Atheism and the journal Science and Atheism: a summary 中国社会科学院科学与无神论研究中心和《科学与无神论》年度发展规划会综述 Zhang Ge This is a report on the annual development planning meeting of the Research Centre for Science and Atheism at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) and its journal Science and Atheism, held on 4 February 2023 at the Academy of Marxism. Gong Yun, deputy director of the Academy and director of the Centre, chaired. He set two agenda items: the Centre's main work for the year and the building of the journal. Both were treated as platforms for strengthening the discipline of scientific atheism. About thirty scholars attended, from CASS bodies (the Party committee, the Institute of Contemporary China Studies, the Institute of World Religions, the Academy of Marxism), the China Research Institute for Science Popularization, Shanghai Normal University, the Central Institute of Socialism, the United Front Work Department, Tsinghua University, Renmin University and the People's Public Security University. Huang Yanhong first reviewed 2022: publication of Principles of Scientific Atheism, a draft reader on atheist education for rural areas, courses for united front cadres and for a Marxism school in the north-west, and the tenth scientific atheism forum. She also gave journal figures: 62 papers, a composite impact factor of 0.521 and a comprehensive one of 0.244, with page counts to rise further in 2023. Participants then made proposals on the Centre. Zhu Xiaoming argued that atheism underpins the Party's guiding ideology and should not be treated as optional. He distinguished the struggle between theism and atheism, which he assigned to the propaganda, education and organisation departments, from the struggle with extreme or separatist ideas inside religious circles, which he assigned to the united front department. He attributed a 'rebound' of religious fervour to the pandemic and economic fluctuations. Li Shen held that Marxist religious studies is in essence Marxist atheism, and proposed a research society under the China Atheism Society. Others proposed an introduction to Marxist atheism, an atheism dictionary and library, 'atheism lecture halls' at universities, more work in Xinjiang and Tibet, and closer ties with science popularization bodies and the anti-cult association. On the journal, speakers asked for new columns on scientific spirit and method, more translations of foreign atheists, and topics such as religion among students, rural religion, religious infiltration and the science-fiction work The Three-Body Problem. Several urged entry into core-journal indexes (CSSCI, AMI, Peking University core list) and wider circulation, and Zhang Xinying cautioned that scientific atheism remains a marginal discipline with manuscript-supply problems. Speakers also asked for more publicity, a website and joint conferences. Read the original if you want a detailed record of how Chinese atheism researchers set their institutional priorities in 2023.

Mutual fit: the deep foundations for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture 彼此契合:马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合的深厚底蕴 Zhang Taiyuan Taking up Xi Jinping's remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, this newspaper commentary asks why combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture was possible at all. Zhang Taiyuan's answer is that a combination presupposes mutual fit: although the two have different origins, the author argues that they are highly compatible in values and habits of thought, and this made an organic union possible. The article is built around a brief introduction and four paired themes, each setting a traditional Chinese idea beside a Marxist one: 'the world belongs to all' and human emancipation; 'unity of heaven and humanity' and materialism; 'the people as the foundation of the state' and the people as makers of history; and the Great Harmony (datong) society and communism. Zhang draws on Mao Zedong, Li Dazhao, Liang Qichao, Qu Qiubai, Ai Siqi and the French sinologist Jacques Gernet, as well as on Xi Jinping and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Zhang's central claim rests on Xi's phrase that Marxism took root in China because it connected with values the people lived by 'without being aware of it'. The author reads this as an unconscious convergence of thinking that formed the cultural basis for the combination. In the examples, Zhang finds in Chinese tradition a practical, worldly orientation, naturalistic and atheistic strands, a long-standing concern with the people, and an ideal of a society free of exploitation. Early Chinese Marxists such as Li Dazhao and Qu Qiubai are presented as understanding communism through the Great Harmony, and Ai Siqi as seeing 'seeds' of Marxism in Chinese thought. Zhang concludes that this affinity helps explain why Chinese intellectuals chose Marxism among competing currents after the May Fourth Movement. Citing Xi, the author adds that the combination is mutually enriching: it makes Marxism Chinese and traditional culture modern, and yields a new cultural form for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholarship in 2023 presents the cultural compatibility of Marxism and Chinese tradition, with quotations from early Chinese Marxists.

The political narrative of the rise and decline of "labour socialism" in Brazil's Workers' Party 巴西劳工党“劳工社会主义”兴衰逻辑的政治叙事 Wang Shaoyuan Why did Brazil's Workers' Party (PT), which governed from 2003 to 2016 under the banner of "labour socialism", rise and then fall? Wang Shaoyuan argues that this doctrine could achieve only limited results. In the short run its effects depended on whether the international market environment favoured Brazil. In the long run, Wang contends, it was not a scientific governing philosophy, because it left untouched the domestic factors that constrain Brazilian growth. The article first sets out the party's "labour socialism", adopted as its guiding ideology in 1990, and its policy approach of change through peaceful, gradual means and of winning the interests of the "C class", the so-called new middle class. It then divides the PT's time in office into a prosperous phase (2003–2010, under Lula) and a declining phase (2011–2016, under Rousseff). It uses figures on GDP growth, exports, minimum wages, credit, poverty and the Gini coefficient. A final section reflects on why the party lost power. Wang's core claim is that the PT's success came from resisting neoliberalism, while its decline came from never abandoning capitalism. Lula kept parts of Cardoso's neoliberal framework, including fiscal and monetary austerity, a floating exchange rate and inflation targeting, and appointed orthodox figures to economic posts. Growth rested on commodity exports, rising minimum wages and consumer credit. When external conditions turned, the article reports structural supply problems, inflation, a deteriorating current account and persistent income polarisation. It also describes a party split over identity, with critics seeing a "left government without a left agenda". Wang names three failings. Labour socialism is not scientific socialism. The party lost ideological leadership by lurching between developmentalism and neoliberalism. It also lacked the people as a real subject, covering the gap with "radical democracy" and broad alliances. Wang concludes that the PT must keep its original socialist aims while adjusting to history's laws and to national and world conditions, and must stand firmly with the people. The article notes Lula's 2022 candidacy and Bolsonaro's weak record as signs that the left may return. It also says the Brazilian case matters for China in guarding against neoliberal erosion and building socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Latin American left governments, with the economic data and a critique based on scientific socialism.

The threefold logical meaning of abstract labour in Marx's "Paris Manuscripts" 马克思“巴黎手稿”中抽象劳动的三重逻辑意涵 Kou Dongliang Most scholarship on Marx's concept of abstract labour concentrates on Capital and its manuscripts. Kou Dongliang asks what the term meant in its first appearance, in the 1844 "Paris Manuscripts". The article argues that Marx did not yet offer a scientific concept there. Instead, within the theory of alienated labour, he implicitly gave abstract labour three connected meanings: separation, inversion and non-objectivity. These opened the "revolution in terminology" that later led to the critique of political economy. The article is organised around three pairs of logic, one for each meaning: "alienation–freedom", "making a living–human-centred" (谋生—人本) and "idea–sensuousness". It draws on Marx's critique of classical political economy (called "national economy" in the manuscripts) and of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit and Philosophy of Right. It also uses Feuerbach's anthropology and the Comments on James Mill. Kou notes that Marx had not seen Hegel's Jena texts, where the term abstract labour first arises. First, abstract labour means separation. Labour is cut off from the means and objects of labour, which become capital. Kou reads this through the "fourfold separation" of alienated labour: from the product, from the activity, from the human species-essence, and from other people. Marx's phrase about reducing "the greatest part of mankind" to abstract labour is read from the standpoint of workers, set against an ideal of free, species-defining labour. Second, abstract labour is inverted labour: a means of subsistence for the worker and of profit for the capitalist. It reduces the worker to a machine and distorts human needs into the need for money. Third, drawing on Feuerbach's sensuousness, Marx judges Hegel's labour to be "abstract spiritual labour", non-objective and merely logical. He counters with labour as sensuous, objective activity. Kou concludes that the "Paris Manuscripts" follow Feuerbach's anthropological principles and reject the classical labour theory of value. Abstract labour there is therefore an ethical, metaphorical term, at most an idea, and not yet a defined theoretical concept. Yet it sketches an economic-philosophical outline and an \"embryo\" for later work. Only in Capital does Marx define abstract labour scientifically, as a material social function of capitalist production and as a conceptual movement. Kou calls for further study of how the concept was built. Read the original if you study the genesis of Marx's value theory or the relation of the young Marx to Hegel, Feuerbach and classical political economy.

Analysing rural land transfer through Marx's theory of ground rent 马克思地租理论视域下农地流转问题分析 Chai Shu Chai Shu asks how Marx's theory of ground rent can explain the problems of rural land transfer in China, and whether it still applies under the socialist market economy. The article argues that it does. Land ownership and the separation of ownership from use exist in China as well as under capitalism, so ground rent exists too, and the theory can guide reform of land transfer. The article has three parts. It first summarises Marx's ground rent thinking against the background of English enclosures and the rise of the three classes of landlord, capitalist and wage labourer. It then applies the theory to China's current land transfer, under the system in which collective ownership is kept while contracting and management rights are separated ("three rights separation"). Last, it draws policy conclusions. On Marx, Chai stresses that ground rent is the economic form through which land ownership is realised and that it is a converted form of surplus value created by agricultural wage labour. The author distinguishes differential rent I and II from absolute rent. Applying this to China, Chai holds that absolute rent and differential rent I belong to the collective as owner, and differential rent II to the contracting households. In practice, the author argues, the "household contracting" system has stressed dispersed farming over unified collective management. This has weakened village collectives, and industrial and commercial capital entering the countryside has deepened the weakness. Chai says capital then dominates pricing, leaves farmers scattered and with little bargaining power, and captures rent that should go to collectives and farmers, which widens the rural wealth gap. Chai concludes that collective land ownership must be upheld and the collective strengthened. The author proposes that the Party organise farmers through cooperatives led by village Party branches. These would pursue moderate-scale operation, give the collective a voice in setting transfer prices and in distributing rent, and advance common prosperity. Chai also suggests that government set up bodies to assess land transfer prices. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar applies Marx's Capital, Volume III, to current debates on rural land circulation and collective ownership.

The predicaments facing the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) and how to overcome them 尼共（毛主义中心）面临的困境与克服 Tang Xin Tang Xin examines the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre), described as one of Nepal's two largest communist parties and its third-largest party overall. The article argues that, since the republic was founded in 2008, the party has lost its earlier edge and faces long-standing difficulties. Whether it overcomes them, Tang contends, will shape the direction of the whole Nepali communist movement. The article first sets out four predicaments: identity, organisation, mass base and external pressure. It then reviews the party's own diagnosis and response in the political report of its Eighth Congress (26 December 2021 to 2 January 2022). A final section assesses early results and prospects in the run-up to the 2022 general elections, drawing on the party's performance in the 2017 elections and the May 2022 local elections. On identity, Tang argues that the party has become an electoral, within-the-system party. It dropped armed struggle and the language of "protracted people's war" and new democratic revolution, and its patriotism is questioned over its stance on the US Millennium Challenge Corporation compact. On organisation, Tang points to the 2012 split, Baburam Bhattarai's 2015 exit, the failed 2018 merger into the Nepal Communist Party and weak democratic centralism. The mass base has shrunk, Tang says, as vote totals fell and corruption and opportunism spread. The party is also squeezed between the Nepali Congress and the CPN (UML). The Eighth Congress report, in Tang's account, declares Nepal to be in a socialist-revolution stage and calls for a united front, party discipline and self-criticism. Tang concludes that the party's first task is to keep its political influence, which it did for now through its coalition with the Nepali Congress. Its way out of the identity crisis, Tang says, is theoretical innovation, because the Congress report does not clearly distinguish its line from the UML's "people's multiparty democracy". Tang also calls for broad communist unity, with theoretical dialogue and management of factionalism. The article further urges firmer defence of national sovereignty, proletarian internationalism and closer ties with the Communist Party of China and the People's Republic of China. Read the original if you follow Nepali communist politics, or want a Chinese academic assessment of a Maoist party's move into parliamentary politics.

The significance of Engels's late-life research on religion 论恩格斯晚年宗教研究意蕴 Wang Liangbin Jing Tao Why did Engels, after Marx's death in 1883 and while completing Capital, devote so much effort to religion? Wang and Jing treat this research as a significant side-strand of his late work and ask what it was for. They argue that it served three purposes: the needs of the revolutionary struggle, the defence and development of historical materialism, and the resolution of Engels's own lifelong engagement with the Bible. The article is organised in four parts: the practical needs of the international workers' movement; the defence of historical materialism; Engels's personal "Bible complex"; and a conclusion. It draws on Engels's letters, Anti-Dühring, his writings on early Christianity and his remarks on Bruno Bauer. It also traces Engels's early religious development through his letters to the Graeber brothers and his engagement with German biblical criticism. On the first purpose, the authors say Engels rejected two errors: radical atheism and forced abolition of religion (Bismarck's Kulturkampf, the Blanquists, the Bakuninists, Dühring), and Christian socialism, which blurred the line between religious faith and communist ideals. For the second, they argue that Engels used the idea of "intermediate links" between economic base and ideology to answer economic determinism. They also read his warning against treating the materialist method as a ready-made formula, aimed at the Party's "Young Ones", as a call to study history in depth. On the third, they hold that his 1894 essay on early Christianity resolved an interest begun in 1841. In it Engels reassessed Tübingen School and Bauer's criticism, crediting Bauer but correcting what he saw as Bauer's idealist errors. The authors conclude that Engels's critical stance towards religion was consistent, and that critique means sublation rather than simple negation. They claim that he moved from criticising heaven to criticising its worldly basis, so no "mild turn" occurred in his late years. They also reject the view that late Engels diverged from Marx, since he worked throughout from historical materialism. In their view, his late writings enriched Marxist religious theory and hold an unshakeable place in it. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Engels's late writings on religion and early Christianity, and of the debates about continuity between Engels and Marx.

Chinese modernization's answer to the question of common prosperity and its world-historical significance 中国式现代化对共同富裕问题的解答及其世界历史意义 Liu Xingang Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Xingang asks how modernization can coexist with a narrowing wealth gap. The article argues that in Western modernization the degree of modernization and the degree of common prosperity stand in an antinomy-like paradox, with widening inequality treated as something close to an iron law. In Liu's account, Xi Jinping and the Party have answered this world-historical problem through Chinese modernization, whose essence includes common prosperity for all the people. The article has three parts. The first traces the problem in capital-centred modernization, from the English path after the 16th century through Adam Smith, the utopian socialists, Marx, Lenin, the Washington Consensus in Latin America (with Brazil as the example) and Thomas Piketty's data. The second sets out China's answer since the 18th Party Congress (2012): a new worldview and methodology, a practical programme and a modernized governance system. The third draws out the world-historical significance of the answer. Liu draws on Marx's distinction between "capital in general" and "many capitals" to argue that capital's power to divide social wealth, especially that of financial capital, is the root of polarisation. Against this, the article presents Chinese modernization as people-centred, led by the Party and secured by the basic economic system with public ownership as the mainstay. It also describes it as phased, with differences between people and regions acknowledged, and as coordinating primary distribution, redistribution and the third distribution. Liu says it avoids two failures: Western welfare-state capitalism, which in the article's reading shifts the costs onto the middle-income groups, and Latin American over-reliance on high welfare, which led to the "middle-income trap". Liu concludes that the elimination of absolute poverty and the building of a moderately prosperous society show that modernization with common prosperity is feasible. In this reading, it breaks the equation of "modernization = Westernization", widens the routes open to developing countries and enriches a new form of human civilization. Liu presents this as a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Chinese scholars frame inequality, capital and the Chinese path as a response to Western modernization.

Should Marx and Engels's critique of religion be divided into a narrow and a broad sense? 马克思恩格斯宗教批判是否应有狭义、广义之分？ Zhu Fengkai Ma Fengqiang The article asks whether the concept of Marx and Engels's "critique of religion" should be understood in two senses. Zhu and Ma observe that Chinese scholarship mostly uses a narrow sense, treating the critique as the early views from the Rheinische Zeitung to the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period. A second, looser usage simply equates it with Marx and Engels's religious theory as a whole. The authors argue that both senses are legitimate and that distinguishing them is worthwhile. The piece first sets out the two usages through examples. For the narrow sense it cites Zhao Dunhua, who sees Marx's critique as a sublation of Bauer and Strauss, and Tang Xiaoyan, who extends it to Capital, Volume 1. For the broad sense it cites Tang Xiaofeng and Hu Jian. It then assesses the rationale and purpose of each sense, and ends by considering what the distinction means, including for building Marxist religious studies as a discipline after the 2021 national conference on religious work. For the narrow sense, Zhu and Ma note that before historical materialism the early Marx and Engels criticised religion itself, exposing its falsity and artificiality, rather than the capitalist economic base behind it. Studying this phase helps separate their views from those of the Young Hegelians. For the broad sense, the authors ask why Marx and Engels criticised religion and why they did so in successive stages (political, economic, cultural, social). Their answer is that the aim was always to sublate human self-alienation and achieve human emancipation, and that criticism of religion alone could not do this. On this reading, later theories of the essence, origin and withering away of religion, and of the workers' party's attitude to religion, still belong to one critique of religion. The authors conclude that the broad sense is a valid concept that shows continuity and wholeness in Marx and Engels's thinking on religion and illustrates the openness and developmental character of Marxism. Citing Xi Jinping's December 2021 call to strengthen Marxist religious studies, they claim that a continuous, comprehensive theory suits better as a theoretical basis for the discipline than a stage-bound one. Read the original if you work on Marxist theories of religion in China, or on how Chinese scholars frame the foundations of Marxist religious studies.

Engels's inheritance and development of Marx's thought on culture, and its contemporary value 恩格斯对马克思文化思想的继承、发展及当代价值 Wang Xiuhan Hou Yanshe Marx and Engels never gave a formal definition of culture, yet Wang Xiuhan and Hou Yanshe argue that human freedom and all-round development runs through their thought on it. The article asks what Engels inherited from Marx's thought on culture, what he added, and what this means for cultural construction in China today. Its thesis is that Engels fully inherited Marx's narrow sense of culture, extended the broad sense, completed the account through historical materialism, and supplied a theoretical basis for present-day socialist cultural work. The article has four parts. The first examines the concept of culture, the second Engels's use of historical materialism to supplement Marx, and the third his treatment of culture and freedom and of the class character of culture. The fourth turns to contemporary value, drawing on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and statements by Xi Jinping. The authors work mainly from Engels's late letters, Anti-Dühring, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, and The Housing Question. On the concept, the authors say Marx used culture narrowly for spiritual products such as ideas, art, morality and science, and broadly for stages of social development. Engels followed the narrow sense but separated culture from civilisation. In their reading, culture precedes civilisation, which is a higher stage of cultural development with a positive value orientation, while culture itself is value-neutral. Against charges of 'economic materialism', Engels held that the economic base is decisive only 'in the last instance'. Culture has relative independence and reacts back on the base, and people make their own history. The authors add that Engels treats freedom as both the driving force and the goal of culture, and that different classes have different cultures that also serve as tools in class struggle. For the present, the authors draw four implications. Cultural construction should put the people first, since people are its subject and its beneficiaries. Party leadership is its fundamental guarantee, because of culture's class character. Material and spiritual civilisation must develop in coordination, which they present as a feature of Chinese modernization. Culture is both a driving force and a goal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They call for continued Marxist guidance in building a socialist cultural power. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Engels's texts are used to ground current Party cultural policy.

On the value system of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化的价值体系 Tang Renwu Taking up the strategic arrangements of the 20th Party Congress report (2022), Tang Renwu asks what separates Chinese modernization from Western capitalist modernization. The article's answer is that "modernization" is in itself an abstract, neutral concept, and that only its value system makes it capitalist or socialist. Tang argues that studying the value orientation, pursuits and realization of Chinese modernization is therefore essential to achieving it. The article has four main parts. It first presents the value system as the "soul" of modernization, made up of value standards, orientation, pursuit, goals and realization. It then treats Chinese modernization's value orientation, "people-centred" development, as a sublation of capitalist modernization. The longest sections set out four value pursuits and four routes to value realization, and a short conclusion deals with the handling of capital. Tang contends that capitalist modernization runs on the logic of capital, in which people are ruled by things. Drawing on Marx, Tang describes this as exploitation at home and colonial plunder abroad, with formal equality masking real inequality. Chinese modernization is said to reverse this logic so that material development serves human development. The four pursuits are a socialist modernized great power, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, harmony among state, society and citizen (via core socialist values), and a community with a shared future for mankind. Realization depends on Party leadership, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Tang cites tree-planting and carbon-neutrality pledges, and the voyages of Zheng He, and claims that Chinese culture lacks any gene for aggression. The article's characterisations of Western history and of US policy are the author's own. In the conclusion, Tang says Chinese modernization is distinguished by "harnessing capital". Capital is to be used and guided but also guarded against and regulated, within a socialist market economy. Its "effect boundary" is whether it benefits socialist productive forces, national strength and living standards. Its "scope boundary" is the economic sphere, so that it cannot spread into politics, society or the spiritual realm. Read the original if you want a systematic, official-line account of how Chinese scholars use the language of value to contrast Chinese and Western modernization.

Several major theoretical questions on opening up a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 关于开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界的几个重大理论问题 Qu Qingshan Writing in Dang Jian (Party Building) in mid-2023, as the Party launched a campaign of study and education on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Qu Qingshan asks how that body of thought should be understood. Qu argues that it has achieved a new leap and opened a new realm in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is a theoretical commentary by the president of the Institute of Party History and Literature. The piece has three parts. The first treats the Two Integrations as the fundamental path of theoretical innovation, tracing the move from the earlier single "integration" to the present two. The second presents the "six musts" (put the people first, stay confident in our own path, uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground, take problem-oriented approach, adopt systems thinking, and have a world perspective) as the core and "living soul" of the thought. The third sets the six musts against three other bodies of theory: the Marxist worldview and methodology, the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought, and the Party's ideological line. Qu argues that the shift from one integration to two is neither a numerical change nor a simple addition. In Qu's account, Mao Zedong first posed the integration of Marxism with China's specific conditions. Later leaders developed it, and since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi Jinping has added integration with fine traditional Chinese culture. The first integration, Qu says, resolves the relation of theory to reality; the second resolves that of past to present and China to abroad. Qu holds that the first is the premise of the second and the second its deepening, and that the second also supplies a cultural foundation for Chinese modernization. On the six musts, Qu contends that they are the worldview and methodology of the thought, and that they relate to the three bodies of theory as "source" to "stream". They are said to be a creative application of Marxist dialectical and historical materialism, a new-era expression of Mao's seeking truth from facts, mass line and independence, and a concrete unfolding of emancipating the mind, seeking truth from facts, keeping pace with the times and being pragmatic. Qu concludes that grasping the six musts is the basis for deeper understanding of the thought and for further theoretical innovation. Read the original if you want an official Party-history view of how the Two Integrations and the six musts are positioned within the lineage of Chinese Marxism.

Chinese modernization and the qualities of a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化彰显人类文明新形态的品质向度 Hou Yanshe Ge Shujin Hou Yanshe and Ge Shujin ask how Chinese modernization shapes what the Party calls a new form of human civilization. Taking up Xi Jinping's statement at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that Chinese modernization is "a brand-new form of human civilization", they argue that each of its five features expresses a distinct quality of that civilization, and that together they mark a path different from Western modernization. The article is organised in six sections. Five sections take the five features in turn: a huge population, common prosperity, coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Each is paired with a quality of the new civilization: its popular character, justice, coordination, lawfulness and inclusiveness. A sixth section generalises these into four further qualities (transcendence, principledness, generativity and exemplarity) and presents Chinese modernization as a "comprehensive innovation". In each section the authors set capitalist modernization against the Chinese path, drawing on Marx and Engels. Capitalist modernization, driven by the logic of capital, is said to produce fetishism, alienation, polarisation of wealth, a split between material and spiritual life, ecological destruction and colonial expansion. Chinese modernization is described as placing the people first, working towards common prosperity, advancing the "five-sphere" overall plan, pursuing ecological civilization and rejecting plunder and hegemony. The authors cite China's elimination of absolute poverty, its contribution to world growth and the Belt and Road Initiative as evidence. The final section argues that the new civilization surpasses capitalist civilization, unites the objective laws of history with human purposes, takes shape through practice, and offers an example for other developing countries. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization, led by the Party and guided by historical materialism, has broken the equation of modernization with Westernization and shown a different picture of modernization. They claim it points the correct direction for world modernization and human civilization in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-theory account of how the five features of Chinese modernization are linked to the concept of a new form of human civilization, and of how that account contrasts Chinese and capitalist modernization.

Re-examining Marx's concept of "sociality" 重新审视马克思的“社会性”概念 Wang Juan Wang Juan asks what Marx actually meant by "sociality" (shehuixing), a term the author says is widely used but rarely defined. Marx never gave it a dedicated treatment, and the article notes that the Chinese edition of the Marx-Engels Collected Works mentions it explicitly only 49 times. Wang argues that, since the surge of Chinese research on Marx's theory of the human being from the 1990s, the concept has habitually been read through "social relations", and that this reading is too shallow. The article has three parts. The first sets out three common approaches: groupism (including Western communitarianism), a social-relations ontology, and sociological social structuralism (Durkheim, Weber, Simmel, Blau, Parsons). The second returns to Marx's original context, tracing his critique of social contract theory (Hobbes, Locke) and of Hegel's ethical state through the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question, the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. The third turns to the critique of political economy, taking the three equations of the value-form in Capital, Volume 1. Wang argues that each common approach falls short. Groupism, in Wang's account, dissolves the individual into the collective and cannot separate humans from social animals. Reading sociality as social relations is "primary" sociality only, and structural sociology reduces it to a model of linkages. For Marx, the argument runs, sociality has two layers: relations between people, and the relation between particular and universal interests. It names real social relations grounded in the unity of the two. Wang reads the value-form analysis as showing how, through the money form and commodity, money and capital fetishism, social relations between people are masked as relations between things and sociality is split apart. Wang also contends that some Western Marxists shifted critique to culture, consumption and everyday life, offering only a "phenomenological" analysis without a critique of political economy. Wang concludes that Marx's concept only becomes clear through the critique of political economy, which shows that conflicts between private and common interest cannot be resolved while private property exists. Re-examining it is presented as a response to the fragmentation and reification of contemporary society, and as a source of methodological guidance for analysing present social problems. Read the original if you want a systematic reading of Marx's "sociality" against communitarian, sociological and Western Marxist alternatives, with close attention to the value-form analysis in Capital.

Principles and methods for building an autonomous knowledge system in the study of foreign Marxism 国外马克思主义研究自主知识体系建构的原则与方法 Han Qiuhong Han Qiuhong asks how the study of foreign Marxism, a second-level discipline within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory, can build its own autonomous knowledge system in line with the call to accelerate a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that the system must rest on Marxism and the results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that the field has already moved from following its object to a more independent, dialogical research model. The article has three parts. The first presents the basic framework of the discipline as "one theory, two histories": an introduction to foreign Marxism, the history of Marxism's worldwide spread and theoretical development, and the history of foreign Marxism research in China. The second sets out a methodological stance called "one body, two faces". The third proposes a practical route, "one core, three dimensions", covering the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. Han divides Chinese research since Xu Youyu's 1982 book into three paradigms: a "nature" debate over whether Western and foreign Marxism is Marxism at all, an intellectual-history paradigm of translation and textual study, and a problem-oriented paradigm engaging Western scholars on digital capitalism, biopolitics, ecological crisis and artificial intelligence. The "one body" is Marxism as guide. The "two faces" are facing China and the world, and facing reality (critiques of capitalism and modernity) and the future (scientific socialism and the international communist movement). Han treats foreign Marxism as a source of critical concepts and academic targets but warns against copying it. The article lists, as deviations to be criticised, replacing proletarian revolution with the "multitude", ecological crisis replacing economic crisis, and "green parties" replacing proletarian parties. Han concludes that the discipline should define its place within Marxist theory and train scholars versed in both Chinese and Western thought. It should renew its academic paradigms by returning to Marx and the classics, and build original discourse that draws on the conceptual vocabulary of foreign Marxism without adopting its methods wholesale. The guiding principles are a Chinese standpoint, Chinese problems and the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese specialist in foreign Marxism frames the field's history, its guiding principles and its purpose for Chinese Marxist theory.

Several major theoretical questions on opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 关于开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界的几个重大理论问题 Qu Qingshan Writing in mid-2023, as the Party launched a thematic education campaign on studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Qu Qingshan takes up how that body of thought should be understood. Qu argues that it has opened new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that two things are central to grasping it: the Two Integrations and the "six musts". The commentary, published in the journal Dangjian, has three parts. The first traces how the single integration of Marxism with China's concrete realities developed into the Two Integrations. The second presents the "six musts" as the essence and living soul of Xi Jinping Thought. The third explains how the "six musts" relate to three other bodies of theory: the Marxist worldview and methodology, the living soul of Mao Zedong Thought, and the Party's ideological line. Qu holds that the Two Integrations, the integration of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture, are the fundamental route for adapting Marxism. Dogmatism and empiricism, he says, caused early setbacks, and Mao Zedong's call to combine Marxism with China's specific features raised the first integration. The shift to two integrations is, for Qu, a summation of long experience and not a mere numerical addition. The first integration is said to address theory and practice, the second the relation of past and present and of China and the outside world. The first is the premise and foundation of the second, and the second extends and deepens the first. Qu adds that the "six musts" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systematic thinking, and a global vision) distil the worldview and method running through Xi Jinping Thought. He describes them as a creative application of Marxism, a new-era expression of Mao Zedong Thought's living soul, and a concrete unfolding of the ideological line of emancipating the mind and seeking truth from facts. Qu concludes that Chinese modernization draws its cultural roots from the Two Integrations and offers a different picture from Western modernization, and that studying the "six musts" lets Party members grasp the thought's underlying logic and apply it flexibly. Read the original if you want an official Party-history perspective on how the Two Integrations and the "six musts" are presented in 2023 as part of one theoretical lineage.

A new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化的新境界 Wang Binglin Taking the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as its starting point, this article asks what is new about the latest stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang Binglin argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has opened a "new realm" through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Wang's account this realm rests on practical achievements, on the Two Integrations and on a distinctive worldview and methodology. The article has three parts. The first sets out the practical basis: the Party's answers to four questions, which Wang calls the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. The second treats the Two Integrations, especially the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The third examines the "six commitments" that the Congress report presented as the stance, viewpoint and method running through the Thought. In the first part, Wang links each question to a response: Chinese modernization for China, a community with a shared future for mankind for the world, a people-centred approach and common prosperity for the people, and the long-term development of socialism for the times. The article also cites the Party's centenary activities, the entry into a new era and the victory over absolute poverty. Wang's second move is cultural. Marxism and traditional culture are said to be highly compatible, and the article cites ideas such as harmony between humanity and nature, a world of "all under heaven for the common good", the people as the root of the state, appointing people on merit, and constant renewal. Wang holds that this compatibility explains why Marxism took root in China. Third, Wang reads the six commitments (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systematic thinking, and a global vision) as a unity of worldview and method. Wang presents them as the basic guide for further theoretical innovation. Wang concludes that the new realm is both a theoretical leap and a practical achievement, and that it shows why Marxism, and Marxism adapted to China and the times, "works". The Thought is described as contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism, with significance for China and for the development of scientific socialism. Wang calls for creative transformation of traditional culture under Marxist guidance and for continued theory-building based on practice. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how the 20th Party Congress framed theoretical innovation, culture and method.

A new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化的新境界 Wang Binglin Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Binglin asks what is new in the latest stage of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and how that progress can be continued. The author argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has produced a new leap and opened a "new realm". In Wang's reading, this vindicates the claim that Marxism, in its Sinicised and contemporary form, "works". The article has three parts. The first treats the practical basis of the new realm: the Party's answers to four questions, namely those of China, the world, the people and the times, together with the three major events of the past decade named in the Congress report. The second presents the Two Integrations as the fundamental requirement, with extended discussion of Marxism's fit with traditional Chinese culture. The third turns to the "six commitments" as the worldview and methodology to be followed. Wang's central move is to treat the new realm as a product of practice. Chinese modernization answers the question of China. A community with a shared future for mankind answers the question of the world. Common prosperity and the poverty-alleviation campaign answer the question of the people. Wang then argues that combining Marxism with excellent traditional culture is a major theoretical innovation. The author cites ideas such as "all under heaven is for the common good", people-as-the-foundation, harmony between humanity and nature, and ceaseless self-renewal as highly compatible with scientific socialism. The final move reads the six commitments as the core of the Thought's standpoint, viewpoint and method. These are putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, problem orientation, systems thinking, and a global vision. Wang presents them as a unity of worldview and method, and as the basis for further theoretical innovation. Wang concludes that the Thought is contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism, with significance for China, for scientific socialism and for human civilisation. Continued innovation depends on mastering the six commitments and keeping the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official account of the 20th Party Congress's theoretical framing, including its use of classical Chinese sources to support the Two Integrations.

A Marxist text offering a preliminary systematic exposition of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 对新时代坚持和发展中国特色社会主义初步系统阐述的马克思主义文献 Zhu Jiamu Writing ten years after Xi Jinping's speech of 5 January 2013 (the "1.5 speech"), delivered to newly elected Central Committee members after the 18th Party Congress (2012), Zhu Jiamu asks what place the speech holds in the new era. Zhu argues that it is an important Marxist document, the opening work of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era and the foundation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Zhu's reading, it is the first written answer the Party leadership gave "to history and to the people". The article sets the speech against the background of problems the 20th Party Congress (2022) report said existed a decade earlier, including wavering faith, formalism and historical nihilism. It then works through seven themes: that socialism with Chinese characteristics is socialism and not another "ism"; that modernization must start from China's conditions; the unity of the periods before and after reform and opening up; the aim of historical nihilism; the deepening of understanding of socialism; communist ideals; and long-term cooperation and struggle between socialism and capitalism. For each, Zhu traces how Xi's later statements and policies developed the speech's points. Zhu's central moves are, first, to read the speech as a response to a "bourgeois liberalization" current since the 1980s. The speech's insistence that the basic principles of scientific socialism cannot be abandoned is taken to mean that reform has a fixed direction and that some things must not be changed. Second, Zhu holds that the two historical periods are essentially one exploration of socialist construction. Third, Zhu argues that historical nihilism is a political project to incite the overthrow of Party leadership, citing the Soviet collapse as a warning. Zhu also draws the speech's later lineage: Chinese modernization, the Four-sphere Confidence, and the division of the primary stage of socialism into sub-stages such as the new development stage. Zhu concludes that the speech is the upstream source of Xi Jinping Thought. Zhu presents ideological and political security, firm communist ideals, and long-term cooperation and struggle with capitalist states as continuing tasks. Zhu also calls on historians of the PRC to take up a "defend the country" function and to resist historical nihilism. Read the original if you want a Party-aligned account of how the 2013 speech is retrospectively framed as the origin of core themes in Xi-era ideology.
