The common values of all humanity embedded in the new form of human civilization, and their contemporary significance 人类文明新形态内蕴的全人类共同价值及其当代意义 Wang Yuchen Peng Yiwei Wang Yuchen and Peng Yiwei ask how the new form of human civilization created by Chinese modernization relates to the common values of all humanity. They argue that this civilization unites the core socialist values, which are specific to China, with the common values of all humanity, which they treat as a universal ideal. The article, published in 2023, frames the relationship through two dialectical pairs: universality and particularity, and the reality of civilizational development versus its ideal aims. The article has three sections. The first presents the new form of human civilization as a unity of the core socialist values and the common values of all humanity, drawing on a typology of 'early-developing endogenous' and 'late-developing exogenous' modernization and on Marx and Engels's account of capitalist civilization. The second treats the common values themselves, and sets them against the core socialist values and against the actual civilization. The third sets out their historical significance. It traces the core socialist values through successive Party leaders, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. The authors contend that so-called 'universal values' rest on theories of civilizational superiority, clash and end, and absolutise the Western model as the only one. Their account is that the common values (peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom) rest instead on civilizational equality and mutual learning, and take different forms in each country according to its history and interests. The core socialist values apply only to China and are described as the 'greatest common divisor' of its people. The common values are the minimum requirement of the socialist ones and are the greatest common divisor among nations. The new civilization is already real, while the common values are still mainly an aspiration. Wang and Peng say that building a community with a shared future for mankind is what can bridge the two. Wang and Peng conclude that the common values express the Party's people-centred orientation and its sense of responsibility for humanity. They say the 'Chinese approach' answers the questions of the world, the people and the times raised by the great changes unseen in a century. They also say it resolves the relationship between diversity and unity in civilization, and guides the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. They add that China does not export its model, and that its appeal depends on further enriching the new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese account of how the common values of all humanity are distinguished from 'universal values' and tied to the core socialist values.

Making the study and implementation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era go deep and take root 在推动学习贯彻习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想走深走实上下功夫 Liu Xiaoxin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2023, no. 9), Liu Xiaoxin comments on the thematic education campaign on studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, launched across the Party in 2023. Liu presents the campaign as a major measure for implementing the 20th Party Congress (2022) and as a route for the Party's self-reform. The article argues that, following Xi Jinping's call to make study 'go deep and take root', Party organisations must ensure that learning is genuinely understood and applied rather than performed as a formality. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first sets out the methods of study: reading original works, grasping the worldview and methodology, and linking knowledge to practice. The second lists four aims of the campaign: forging conviction, increasing wisdom, correcting work styles and promoting practical work. The third turns to investigation and research as a way to solve concrete problems. Liu's central claim is that study must unite learning, thinking and applying, and knowing, believing and acting. Party members and cadres are told to read prescribed texts, including the Selected Readings of Xi Jinping and the Outline for Studying the Thought, and to master the 'six musts' named in the 20th Congress report: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, a systems approach, and a global vision. Liu invokes the Marxist view that practice is the source and aim of knowledge, and requires that the campaign be judged by whether it solves problems and satisfies the people. On investigation, Liu calls for going to the grassroots with questions, listening also to unwelcome views, and giving equal weight to investigation and analysis. Liu concludes that the campaign should strengthen ideals and loyalty to the Party, correct formalism and bureaucratism, and turn study into results in high-quality development, common prosperity and the management of risks. The Party's tasks, the article says, include full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which is described as 'always on the road'. Read the original if you want a sample of how Party-school-style guidance on the 2023 education campaign was framed for cadres, including its reading list and its stated criteria of success.

Consciously using Xi Jinping Thought to transform the subjective and objective worlds 自觉用习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想改造主观世界和客观世界 Cao Wenze Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, Cao Wenze addresses Party members and cadres taking part in the thematic education campaign on studying and implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article's thesis is that cadres must use this body of thought to remould both their own inner world and the external world of practice. Cao describes the thought as contemporary Chinese Marxism, twenty-first-century Marxism, and the essence of Chinese culture and spirit for the present age. The piece is a hortatory commentary in three parts. The first sets out how the thought should be studied; the second deals with transforming the subjective world; the third with transforming the objective world. Cao draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and a list of recommended texts, including the 2023 edition of the Study Outline. In the first part, Cao argues that study must be comprehensive, systematic and in-depth, treating the thought as a single complete system. It should be based on reading original works and applying its worldview and methodology, including the Party's stress on people-centred development, systems thinking and a global outlook, and should link theory to practice. In the second part, the subjective world is reshaped by firming up ideals and convictions, strengthening Party spirit and upholding the principle of putting the people first. Cao treats the distinction between public and private interest as the basic measure of Party spirit. In the third part, the objective world is changed through four tasks: conducting investigation and research, improving the seven abilities required of cadres, implementing the 20th Party Congress decisions with a focus on high-quality development, and delivering practical benefits to the public. Cao adds a call for a willingness to struggle and take responsibility. Cao concludes that cadres should turn learning into stronger conviction, better skills and tangible results in their own posts, so that thought and action are unified. The text is a statement of the official line on the campaign, and it frames the thought as a guide to both self-cultivation and to the tasks of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party publications presented the aims and method of the 2023 thematic education campaign to cadres.

The Chinese form of Marx's thought on labour justice: logic, historical evolution and contemporary orientation 马克思劳动正义思想的中国样态：逻辑理路、历史演进与现实指向 Shao Xianping Liu Lu Shao Xianping and Liu Lu ask how Marx's thought on labour justice (the evaluation of labour activity, labour relations and labour methods) has been taken up in China, and what form it takes today. They argue that Marx resolved the modern question of justice by tracing it back to labour, the human mode of production, and that the realisation of labour justice is the defining feature of socialism. In their account, the Communist Party of China has carried this thought forward through state reconstruction and institutional change, producing a distinctive Chinese form in the new era. The article, published in Study and Practice in 2023, has three parts. The first reconstructs the logic of Marx's thought as a unity of critique and construction. The second traces its historical evolution in modern China, from the revolution to reform and opening up and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third examines its present orientation under institutional construction, value guidance and cultural incentive. On Marx, the authors identify three shifts: from formal to substantive justice, from common labour to shared labour, and from labour in thrall to things to the liberation of labour. Drawing on the theory of surplus value, they say Marx exposed the justice of equal exchange in circulation as an illusion, because injustice lies in production and in the separation of labour from ownership. In China, they present three stages: the revolution and workers' movement, which addressed substantive justice; land reform, socialist transformation and the basic distribution system, which institutionalised sharing; and livelihood measures such as labour legislation and employment policy, which laid the basis for liberation. For the new era, they call for institutions that regulate public and private capital, including digital capital, and for putting the people first through employment, distribution and public services. They also call for a culture that respects labour dignity, decent work and the spirit of labour, model workers and craftsmanship. The authors conclude that Marx's thought has become an endogenous intellectual force in the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and that its Sinicisation offers a Chinese form, wisdom and strength in answering contemporary ideas of justice. They urge that the value stance, policy arrangements and practical strategies of labour justice be upheld in building a modern socialist country, so as to promote people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how labour justice is linked to common prosperity, capital regulation and the Party's historical record.

The formation of the path of Chinese modernization: historical review and practical expansion 中国式现代化道路的成型：历史审视和现实拓展 Qi Weiping Qi Weiping takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's account of Chinese modernization as the product of long exploration since 1949, and argues that the Congress's full exposition of the theory marks the path's maturation and formation. Qi holds that this path emerged through setbacks, costs and trials, and is presented as the only correct road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Looking at its history, the article says, shows how hard-won the result is and strengthens the resolve to broaden and deepen it. The article follows the three time markers in the Congress report: the founding of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). After a brief look at modernization as a goal since the Opium War, it moves through four sections: laying the foundation with the "four modernizations"; opening the path with the "moderately prosperous society" concept; the theoretical and practical breakthroughs of the new era; and six requirements for the next stage. Qi's central argument is that each stage built on the last. The pre-1978 period is credited with setting a socialist direction distinct from Western modernization, building an industrial base and producing theoretical groundwork, despite detours caused by copying the Soviet model and the Cultural Revolution. Deng Xiaoping's idea of a moderately prosperous society, which he distinguished from Western models and pitched at a realistic level, became the programme that carried modernization forward until it was declared achieved in 2021. Since 2012, Qi says, the Party has summed up the features, essential requirements and major principles of Chinese modernization, so that a preliminary theoretical system now exists. Qi claims this offers a new option for other countries and breaks Western discursive dominance over modernization theory. For the future, Qi calls for adherence to Party leadership, full application of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, political clarity, use of the Party's historical experience to build unity, a fighting spirit against external risks, and the Party's self-reform. Qi concludes that cherishing and extending the achievement is the Party's sacred mission. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account that periodises the path of Chinese modernization from the four modernizations to the 20th Party Congress.

Understanding the threefold logic of common prosperity 深刻理解和领悟共同富裕的三重逻辑 Zhou Wen Tang Jiaocheng Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called for steadily advancing common prosperity and described Chinese modernization as a modernization of common prosperity for all the people, Zhou Wen and Tang Jiaocheng ask what laws and logic govern common prosperity. They argue that it should be examined along three dimensions: theory, history and practice. Their thesis is that common prosperity is the organic unity of a theoretical, a historical and a practical logic. The article is divided into four parts: three analytical sections, one for each logic, and a short conclusion. The theoretical section draws on Marx's Capital and Critique of the Gotha Programme. The historical section runs from the founding of the People's Republic through reform and opening up to the new era after 2012. The practical section covers Party leadership, the market system, the public and non-public sectors, and the distribution system. The theoretical logic, in the authors' account, is a "labour logic". Labour is the source of wealth, and distribution according to labour, which they argue fits the primary stage of socialism with public ownership as the main body, motivates workers and promotes fairness and shared wealth. They treat common prosperity as the counterpart of the liberation of labour, with capital logic replaced by labour logic. Historically, they trace a sequence: socialist political and economic institutions as the institutional base, the path of "some getting rich first" as the productive-forces base, and poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society as an improvement in relations of production. In practice they call for centralised, unified Party leadership of economic work, a high-standard socialist market economy combining an "effective market" with an "effective government", and the Two Unwaverings to "make the cake bigger". They also call for coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution to "divide the cake well", and note remaining gaps between urban and rural areas, regions and industries. The authors conclude that common prosperity must run through the whole process of Chinese modernization. This means coordinating productive forces and relations of production, advancing high-quality development, and refining the theory through the cycle of practice and understanding. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese political-economy account of common prosperity, with its framing in labour theory, Party history and policy measures, and its use of the 20th Congress language.

Mastering Marxism's "essential skill": study, practice and the theme education campaign 把马克思主义看家本领学到手 Ling Haiqing This newspaper commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today on 27 April 2023, takes up the Party's theme education campaign on studying and implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It was written after a work conference on the campaign held in Beijing on 3 April 2023. Ling argues that the campaign is a means of improving the Marxist level of the whole Party and that it demands effort in three areas: ideological study, linking theory to practice, and concrete action. The piece is organised under three headings that follow this scheme. It begins with Xi Jinping's remarks at the conference about the goals of national rejuvenation and the need to strengthen theoretical armament. It then discusses the campaign's general requirements and its fundamental task, citing Xi's formulations at length. It closes with the call to read original texts and to turn theory into practical results. Ling's core claim is that the campaign's requirements, "learn the thought, strengthen Party spirit, emphasise practice, build new achievements", embody the Marxist theory of knowledge, which joins understanding with practice and the remaking of the subjective world with the remaking of the objective one. On this reading, the unity of study, reflection and application and of knowing, believing and acting expresses the Two Integrations and keeps Marxism vital. Ling also presents ideals and convictions as the Party's spiritual "calcium", and holds that Party members must use the thought to face contradictions, analyse them and resolve them. The author further links this to the Party's self-reform, with members urged to take political check-ups, accept public supervision and correct deviations at once. Ling concludes that the Party's success rests on Marxism and that rising challenges in reform, development and governance require cadres to apply the thought to major risks and problems, in pursuit of Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Each step in theoretical innovation, the author says, must be followed by theoretical armament and then practice, and cadres should read original works to grasp the thought as a whole. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2023 theme education campaign was justified in Marxist epistemological terms in the Party-aligned press.

Truly mastering Marxism as the essential skill 真正把马克思主义看家本领学到手 Gong Yun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2023, no. 9), Gong Yun takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the work conference for the thematic education campaign on studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, that Party members and cadres should "truly master" Marxism as their essential skill (看家本领). Gong argues that doing so means, above all, studying and applying Xi Jinping Thought in depth, and that theoretical armament has been a constant priority of the Party for over a century. The commentary has two parts. The first sets out why Marxism is the soul and banner of the Communist Party of China. It draws on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. The second explains how to deepen the study and implementation of Xi Jinping Thought, under three headings: comprehensive study, comprehensive grasp and comprehensive implementation. In the first part Gong presents Marxism as a unity of truth and values, with the people as its essential attribute. Gong describes it as a scientific, practical and open theory whose fate is bound up with that of the Party, the Chinese people and the Chinese nation. In Gong's account it supplied the ideological weapon for revolution, construction and reform, and cadres who master it gain stronger political judgement, understanding and execution. The second part calls Xi Jinping Thought "contemporary Chinese Marxism" and "Marxism of the twenty-first century". Gong says it should be studied as a complete system rather than in fragments, with attention to its worldview, methodology and the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and applied in practice. Gong concludes that study must lead to action, linking theory with practice, so that learning is turned into results that advance the work of the Party and state. Gong calls on cadres to use the Thought to remould their own outlook, to resolve problems and defuse major risks, and to advance Chinese modernization, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated theorists frame Marxist study for cadres during the 2023 thematic education campaign.

The theory of Chinese modernization as a major innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 中国式现代化理论是马克思主义中国化时代化的重大创新 Yan Xiaofeng Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yan Xiaofeng argues that the theory of Chinese modernization is a major theoretical innovation and a significant achievement in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article, which opens by citing Xi Jinping's remarks at a study seminar on the Congress, presents the theory as an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Yan contends that building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation require developing this theory further. The article has three parts. The first explains why opening new horizons for the adaptation of Marxism calls for developing the theory, tracing the Party's history through the New Democratic Revolution, the socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out what the theory contributes. The third discusses its role in guiding the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Yan's central claim is that Marxism advances by answering major questions of the era, and that modernization is one of them. In the author's account, Western capitalist modernization proved unworkable in China after the Opium War, and no ready-made answers exist for how to avoid its defects while using socialist institutions. The article lists the theory's contributions: modernization is not Westernization and has no single model; Party leadership is its most essential feature; it has distinctive Chinese characteristics (a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony between humanity and nature, peaceful development); and it has stated essential requirements and a strategic layout. Yan describes it as a product of the Two Integrations that rejects capital-centred, polarising, materialistic and expansionist paths. Yan concludes that the theory must keep answering new questions: external risks, deep-seated domestic contradictions, problems of Party building, and the "questions of modernization" Xi has raised for humanity. The author calls for guidance from Xi Jinping Thought and for enriching the theory on the basis of practical innovation. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party theorists in 2023 linked Chinese modernization to the longer project of adapting Marxism to China.

Accelerating the new development pattern as the strategic fulcrum for promoting high-quality development 加快构建新发展格局是推动高质量发展的战略基点 He Zili Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, He Zili takes up Xi Jinping's remark to the Jiangsu delegation at the first session of the 14th National People's Congress. Xi said that high-quality development is the first task of building a modern socialist country in all respects, and that accelerating the new development pattern is its strategic fulcrum. He argues that the new development pattern, with the domestic cycle as the mainstay, is both required by and a means of achieving high-quality development. The article has three parts. The first explains why the new stage of development requires high-quality development. The second sets out how the new development philosophy should guide it, through innovation, coordination, green development, opening up and sharing. The third describes the features of the new development pattern and how each supports high-quality development. In the first part, He gives three reasons. Extensive growth, driven by larger inputs of labour and other factors, is becoming unsustainable: the demographic dividend is fading, returns to capital are falling and resource constraints are hardening. Popular aspirations have moved from having goods to having good ones. The principal contradiction is now unbalanced and inadequate development, which He traces to extensive methods, low quality and efficiency, and weak momentum. In the third part, He holds that the new pattern supports high-quality development in five ways. It is oriented to self-reliant innovation, including a new whole-nation system for core technologies. It aims to expand domestic demand through investment and consumption. It rests on self-reliance and security of industrial and supply chains. It strengthens the real economy and manufacturing, and guards against finance circulating within itself. It also calls for a higher level of opening up, which He presents as consistent with economic globalisation. He concludes that high-quality development, led by the new development philosophy and anchored in the new pattern, is the way to meet the people's aspirations and advance common prosperity. He also links higher-level opening to a community with a shared future for mankind. The piece is a policy exposition in the official register. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Chinese economists in 2023 tied the new development pattern to high-quality development.

The development of Marxist social investigation methodology in the new era 马克思主义社会调查方法论的新时代发展 Liu Jie Gao Yang Liu Jie and Gao Yang take up a gap they see in work on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times: the methodology of social investigation (diaoyan, survey and investigative research) is scattered through studies of Party history and has not been systematically distilled. Their thesis is that this methodology originates in Marx's turn to real individuals and their way of life. In their account the Chinese Communist Party then extended it to the lives of the masses, and in the new era it is developing along three lines. The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of the methodology in Marx and Engels's critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and of Feuerbach. It then reviews the Chinese exploration of the method from Li Dazhao and Qu Qiubai through Mao Zedong's investigations to the socialist construction period. The third part, on the new era, draws on the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and Xi Jinping's call for a renewed culture of investigation. A short conclusion follows. The authors argue that for Marx, knowing society requires starting from living individuals and their mode of life, which led him to take civil society as the empirical object of study. They cite Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England and Marx's workers' questionnaire as examples. Marx and Engels, they say, divided the masses by class but did not fully explain the masses as practical subjects of investigation. The authors credit the Party with filling this gap: it refined classifications of the masses, treated them as subjects of investigation, and replaced civil society with the everyday life of the people as the object. They also credit it with producing principles such as seeking truth from facts. For the new era, the authors identify three paths. The first is respecting the people's right to speak, with whole-process people's democracy as the institutional platform. The second is embedding investigation in grassroots democracy, which the authors contrast favourably with capitalist representative systems. The third is improving people's livelihood projects to stimulate the people's own initiative. They conclude that the methodology puts the people at the centre, supplies tools for building a socialist democratic system, and underpins Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese sociology and ethnology scholarly team links Marx's early philosophy to the Party's current investigation and research campaign.

Letting Marxism show a stronger and more persuasive power of truth on Chinese soil 让马克思主义在中国大地上展现出更强大更有说服力的真理力量 Li Yang This commentary, published in 2023, is a study-and-reflection piece on volumes one and two of the Selected Readings from the Works of Xi Jinping. Li Yang argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is a process of seeking, revealing and practising truth. In Li's account, the Selected Readings show the truth-power and practical strength of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and Marxism can show a stronger and more persuasive truth-power in China only if new horizons keep being opened. The piece has three parts. The first treats the response of Xi and the Party Central Committee to great changes in the times and the situation: development, common prosperity, foreign relations and the banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second covers the continuing adaptation of Marxism, the creation of Xi's Thought, and the Party's historical experience, including the Two Establishes. The third presents the principle of putting the people first as the distinguishing mark of a Marxist party. Li argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has met overlapping global upheaval, the pandemic and serious risks with strategic thinking, a fighting spirit and historical initiative. The new development stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern are described as mutually dependent and as the basis of high-quality development, through which common prosperity is to be advanced. Li presents Xi Thought as answering the major questions of the new era, as innovating in Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and as opening a new realm of Marxist party-building theory. The Two Establishes are described as the "golden key" to the new era and the core of the Party's historical experience. Putting the people first is presented as both the essence of Marxism and a creative transformation of the traditional Chinese idea that the people are the foundation of the state. Li concludes that the Selected Readings unite upholding and developing Marxism, and that the Party should keep a spirit of historical initiative and creativity on the new journey. Only repeated, fresh study of the texts, the author says, will let readers absorb the truth-power of contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese academic and Party-affiliated writers present the Selected Readings and the official narrative of Xi Jinping Thought.

Lenin's conception of cultural anti-poverty work in a socialist state and its implications 列宁关于社会主义国家文化反贫困的构想及其启示 Lin Ke Lin Ke asks how Lenin, during the New Economic Policy (NEP) period in Soviet Russia, conceived of lifting the masses out of "cultural poverty" and what this offers present-day China. The article argues that Lenin's approach joined the leadership of the Marxist party with the principal role of the people, and that its methodological lessons can inform a Chinese anti-poverty discourse. Lin notes that existing scholarship has dwelt on Lenin's basic principles or their sinicisation, leaving this practical side less studied. The article has five sections. The first treats the socialist system as the basic guarantee for eliminating cultural poverty; the second, the vanguard party's guiding role in changing social attitudes; the third, embedding propaganda and education in everyday life. The fourth examines the parallel pursuit of enlightenment and political mobilisation, and the fifth draws lessons for China. Lin draws on Lenin's speeches and drafts, Soviet literacy and education measures, and the system of worker and peasant correspondents. Lin's central claim is that cultural anti-poverty work needs a socialist institutional base, such as the People's Commissariat for Education and the literacy campaign. It also needs a vanguard that moves the masses from intuitive, emotional grievance to rational understanding of a complicated revolution, including the use of state-regulated capitalism under the NEP. Propaganda must be tied to practical livelihood questions, with newspapers presenting concrete local experience instead of abstract slogans. Lin singles out the worker and peasant correspondents, who wrote for the press and fed material to the Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate on bureaucracy and corruption. In Lin's reading, this turned readers from an audience into agents of revolutionary consciousness and of supervision. Lin draws three lessons for China. The Party's vanguard role should guide changes in social attitudes, tying Chinese modernization to material conditions and advanced socialist culture. Varied forms of participation should turn popular aspirations into conscious action against poverty, supporting whole-process people's democracy. Cultural work should follow the principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability, avoiding impatience and rashness. Read the original if you want a close account of how Lenin's cultural and propaganda thinking is linked to China's current anti-poverty and governance discourse.

How Chinese modernization has successfully avoided the "modernization traps" 论中国式现代化对“现代化陷阱”的成功规避 Wu Zhongmin Wu Zhongmin asks why Chinese modernization has succeeded since reform and opening up, and answers that a major reason is its success in avoiding "modernization traps". Wu defines these as relatively hard problems or predicaments that any country meets in modernizing, and argues that a country's success depends largely on whether it can avoid sinking into them. The article lists several traps, including dependency, capital supremacy, economic transition, growth, de-industrialization, the "Tacitus trap" and excessive wealth gaps. It then examines five that Wu regards as most important, each tied to one dimension of modernization: dependency (national autonomy), de-industrialization (material economic base), capital supremacy (economic institutions), excessive welfare (social protection) and social turmoil (safe social functioning). For each, Wu cites cases such as Latin America, Africa, Japan after the Plaza Accord, Brazil and the Philippines, then sets out China's practice. Wu's central contrast is between countries that lost autonomy, hollowed out their industry, let capital or welfare logic run unchecked, or tolerated corrupt public power, and China. Wu credits China with combining self-reliance with openness through the "dual circulation" pattern, keeping a complete industrial system and curbing financial and property bubbles. Wu also credits China with improving livelihoods and regulating the market against capital supremacy, and with tying social spending to economic capacity. For stability, Wu points to prioritising economic growth, livelihood improvement and an anti-corruption campaign backed by Party rules and laws. Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and Mao Zedong are cited throughout as guidance. Wu concludes that the five traps can interlock and compound if left unchecked, and that Chinese modernization has so far avoided them only in a staged, not permanent, way. Risks of old traps returning and of new kinds of traps remain, and the second centenary goal depends on continued avoidance. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's systematic account of how mainstream Chinese theory frames development pitfalls, with comparative cases and policy data.

Striving to write a new chapter of high-quality development in the old revolutionary areas 奋力谱写革命老区高质量发展新篇章 Cai Songtao Writing in 2023 in Red Flag Manuscripts, Cai Songtao, the Party secretary of Xinyang in Henan, takes up how the Dabie Mountains, an old revolutionary area, can achieve high-quality development. Citing the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and Xi Jinping's remarks during his inspection of Jiangxi, Cai argues that the area should set an example in accelerating such development and compete for the lead in the rise of the central region. The article holds that this is a requirement for improving the lives of people in old revolutionary areas. The piece is a policy-oriented commentary in three parts. The first concerns upholding a people-centred approach to development. The second concerns raising the quality and efficiency of growth. The third concerns seizing opportunities and making full use of national policy. It is linked throughout to the Party's thematic education campaign and to the Dabie Mountains' revolutionary history. On the people-centred approach, Cai presents the aim of making old revolutionary areas "better" and the lives of their people "better" as the starting and end point of revitalisation. Cai calls for stronger public services and social security, and for consolidating poverty-alleviation gains through "precise" identification, assistance and management to prevent a return to poverty. On growth quality, Cai argues for ecology-first green development, the faster replacement of old growth drivers with new ones through technological innovation, talent and green finance, and a better business environment through streamlined administrative services and "clean and amicable" government–business relations. In the third part, Cai calls on the area to use the 2021 State Council opinions on supporting the revitalisation of old revolutionary areas, together with special bonds and major projects. Cai also urges it to play to local strengths, including red culture and ecological assets, and to turn its status as a latecomer region into an advantage, since it has fewer burdens from legacy industries and more room for emerging ones. The author concludes that the area must carry forward its revolutionary heritage and strive to be first in regional competition. Read the original if you want an example of how a local Party leader translates national high-quality development and common prosperity language into a programme for a former revolutionary base.

Foreign Marxist scholarship on digital capitalism 国外马克思主义学者关于数字资本主义的研究 Zhou Shaodong Zou Sai This review surveys how Marxist scholars outside China have studied digital capitalism, which the authors define as the digital economy under capitalist relations of production. The authors find that this scholarship is strong on critique but weak on forward-looking proposals. They add that it suffers from four tendencies, which they set out in an assessment at the end. The review follows the historical course of digital capitalism in three stages. The first, from the post-war US information industry to the dot-com crash of 2001, is the stage of germination. The second, from 2001 to the financial crisis of 2008, is expansion and crisis. The third, from 2008 onwards, is decline followed by a recovery from about 2014 with mobile internet. It draws on Dan Schiller, Herbert Schiller, Christian Fuchs, Nick Dyer-Witheford, Hardt and Negri, Bernard Stiegler, Nick Srnicek, Fredric Jameson and others, on themes such as digital labour, immaterial labour, the culture industry, the digital divide and surveillance. In the authors' account, foreign Marxists generally keep to historical materialism and stress that state power and commercial interests shaped digital technology. In their assessment, however, recent work leans towards cultural and ideological topics such as digital fetishism and cultural hegemony. It therefore drifts from material production and offers little on building a new economic base. The authors also say the literature stretches the category of labour to cover everyday activity and dissolves the proletariat into the "multitude", which they call a retreat from class analysis. Many works treat digital capitalism as a new historical formation, whereas the authors hold that it remains within large-scale machine industry and Marx's second social formation. In their view data has value only because of labour and capital invested in it. They also charge that the literature neglects the theory and practice of twentieth-century socialist countries. The authors conclude that digital capitalism has not escaped capitalism's crisis tendencies. They point to platform cooperativism and online occupation movements as signs that digital tools can serve proletarian struggle. They suggest that "digital socialism" may emerge in developing countries, citing China's policy limits on capital in the digital economy and the early results of the sharing economy and digital commons. They propose public ownership of data and the use of digital technology for centralised, dynamically adjusted planning. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Western digital-capitalism theory, with a broad bibliography of the field.

On the theoretical preconditions of research on foreign Marxism 论国外马克思主义研究的理论前提 Juan Hongfei Juan Hongfei asks what foundations Chinese research on foreign Marxism must rest on, given the field's growth and, in the author's view, its fragmentation. The article argues that the field has paid too little attention to its own theoretical preconditions, which has seriously hampered its development. It names three: the study of Marx's thought, the history of ideas, and the real history of the twentieth century. The article is organised in three sections, one for each precondition, and ends with a short summary. It takes in the Western Marxism of Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci, humanist and scientistic Marxism, and the pluralised currents after 1968, including feminist, ecological and digital-capitalism critiques. It also covers the neo-Marxism of Eastern Europe and the changing attitude of Chinese scholarship since reform and opening up. First, Juan holds that foreign Marxism should be judged by its stance and method, not by whether it uses Marx's concepts. Grasping Marx's thought as a whole is therefore the base for judging these currents. Humanist and scientistic Marxism, in this reading, each take only one of two logics that are unified in Marx: human emancipation and the critical analysis of capitalism in Capital. Second, the history of ideas supplies the wider view. It lets researchers place new thinkers and concepts, avoid chasing novelty, link thinkers across schools, and see how Chinese attitudes moved from negative criticism to positive borrowing and from indirect appropriation to direct dialogue. Third, each major turn in foreign Marxism is tied to a real historical problem. These include the contrast between the October Revolution and the failed European revolutions, the May 1968 upheaval, the 2008 financial crisis, and the Eastern European experience of socialist reform. Juan concludes that foreign Marxism can be correctly located, and used as a resource for building Marxist theory in China, only when these three foundations are combined. The article criticises the long-dominant 'introduce and review materials' paradigm for detaching theorists from their social and intellectual contexts. It also calls for dialogue between Chinese and foreign Marxism in light of the 'great changes unseen in a century', while maintaining the leading position of Marxism. Read the original if you want to understand how a Chinese scholar sets out the methodological premises and aims of the foreign Marxism field in China.

The poverty of Popper's critique of communism With a discussion of historical laws and the necessity of communism 波普尔共产主义批判的贫困 Wei Xu Karl Popper's doubts about communism, set out in The Poverty of Historicism and The Open Society and Its Enemies, have been influential. Wei Xu argues that his critique is itself "impoverished": it treats communism as a form of historicism, rests on his theory of knowledge growth, and contains an "Achilles' heel" in the relation between knowledge growth and the course of history. The author contends that Marx's argument for communism strikes exactly this weak point. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Popper's chain of five theses against historicism, his falsifiability criterion and his alternative of "piecemeal engineering". The second exposes the ambiguities and conservative standpoint behind this reconstruction and shows how Popper misreads Marx. The third sets out Marx's grounds for historical laws and for communism, drawing on Engels, Lenin and Lukács, and closes with a note on China's experience. Wei argues that Popper concedes too much: he allows testable social-scientific predictions, partial regularities, holistic "Gestalt" study and trends, yet still denies any prediction of history. His demarcation criterion, in Wei's view, only fixes what counts as "science" and does not settle whether historical claims are true. The fact that knowledge shapes history does not rule out laws or trends that knowledge growth cannot divert. Against this, Wei presents the laws of historical materialism as abstracted from the structure of society as a whole. They do not require omniscience about history, and they are conditional, resting on the movement of the productive forces. Communism is then derived in two steps: productive forces advance cumulatively because production is continuous, creative and irreversible, and capitalist private property negates itself through the contradiction between socialised division of labour and private ownership, the "negation of the negation" described in Capital. Wei concludes that communism is a natural-historical process, grounded in laws and reliable trends, and compatible with an open future. Wei adds that historical materialism meets Popper's own criterion of falsifiability, while progress toward public ownership is better called a "trend" that needs dialectical thinking. The article closes by presenting the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization as further empirical evidence for the necessity of communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist reply to Popper's anti-historicism that engages his epistemology in detail and sets out the logic of Marx's case for communism.

Marx's "circle of friends" 马克思的“朋友圈” Shu Xin This short piece, from 2023 (the 205th anniversary of Marx's birth and 140th of his death), introduces a book published by People's Publishing House, Marx's Circle of Friends (《马克思的朋友圈》). Shu presents it as a popular, illustrated account of Marx's relationships, meant to help Party members, cadres and the public grasp the spirit of Marxism. The book's editor-in-chief is Gong Yun, deputy director of the Academy of Marxism at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The piece describes the book as grounded in authoritative historical record and written in lively language. It sorts Marx's contacts into intellectual partners (Engels, Heine, Wolff, Westphalen, Feuerbach), comrades and students (Liebknecht, Bebel, Kugelmann, Weydemeyer, Dietzgen, Lafargue and others), and theoretical opponents (Proudhon, Bauer, Lassalle, Bakunin). The book contains over 100 images styled as social-media posts. Most of the piece sketches two friendships. Engels, Marx's "top friend", is called his "second self"; Shu recounts their meeting in Paris in 1844 and their worried letters, and notes Engels's material help to Marx's family. Heine, a poet 21 years older, is said to have learned communism from Marx, whose influence Shu links to Heine's poem Germany. A Winter's Tale. Shu argues that Marx chose friends by shared theory, revolutionary stance and goals rather than personal gain, so that his friendships trace his intellectual development. Shu concludes that Marx's approach to choosing friends is a lesson for today's Party members and cadres, who should combine warmth ("情") with integrity ("清"). The piece urges readers to hold to truth and ideals and not to judge friendship by utility. Read the original if you want a brief, officially oriented introduction to this popular book and to how Marx's friendships are used in Party education.

The evolving logic of Marx and Engels's critique of the city and its contemporary implications 马克思恩格斯城市批判思想的演进逻辑及其现实启示 Li Xiaoguang Niu Siqi Li Xiaoguang and Niu Siqi ask how Marx and Engels's critique of the industrial capitalist city developed into a historical-materialist theory, and what it offers for urban work today. They argue that the critique has original significance for contemporary urban theory and that its method is best grasped by returning to the classic texts and tracing the logic of their evolution. The article follows the texts in chronological order. It begins with Marx's journalism for the Rheinische Zeitung and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher and with Engels's early empirical observations in the Wupper valley and England. It then turns to the works of the 1840s, from the 1844 Manuscripts to The German Ideology, The Poverty of Philosophy and the Communist Manifesto. Finally it covers the later period: Capital, 'On the Nationalisation of Land', The Housing Question, Anti-Dühring and The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. The authors identify three stages. The starting point is political critique of civil society and empirical observation. Marx's 1842 defence of equal rights for town and country is an early example, and Engels's accounts of industrial pollution and worker poverty are another. The second stage builds a social-historical and urban–rural framework. The German Ideology is called a watershed, introducing 'urban–rural opposition' and tracing it to the division of labour and private property. The Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy describes modern history as the 'urbanisation of the countryside', in contrast with the ancient 'ruralisation of the city'. In the third stage, Capital treats urban–rural separation as both a driver of accumulation and a source of the paradoxes of capitalist modernity. Marx's writing on land nationalisation and Engels's polemics on housing and the division of labour then present urban–rural integration as achievable only through abolishing private ownership, eliminating the old division of labour, balancing industry across the country and highly developed productive forces. The authors draw three lessons for Chinese modernization in the new era. Urbanisation should be people-centred, meaning public participation, attention to livelihood problems and public satisfaction as the test of urban work. It should also rest on harmony between humans and nature, with ecological red lines and green, intensive development. Finally, it should aim at urban–rural integration and common prosperity, through supporting the countryside with industry and cities, rural revitalisation and new-type urbanisation. Read the original if you want a text-by-text account of how Marx and Engels's views on city and countryside developed, and of how a Chinese scholarly article links them to current urban policy.

Chinese modernization in the light of modern Chinese history 从近代历史进程看中国式现代化 Guo Ruoping Guo Ruoping asks how Chinese modernization, set by the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the Party's mission for the new era, should be understood against more than a century of modern Chinese history. The article argues that every modernization plan since the mid-nineteenth century was conditioned by the principal contradiction of Chinese society at the time. Only by tracing those contradictions, Guo holds, can one grasp what is distinctive and epoch-making about Chinese modernization. The article moves through three periods. The first covers the late Qing quest for "self-strengthening", in its Westernisation-movement, reform-movement and constitutional phases. The second covers modernization thinking in the revolutionary years under the Communist Party, from 1921 to the eve of 1949. The third covers the People's Republic: the Four Modernizations, reform and opening up, and the formulation of Chinese modernization after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Guo's central move is to read each period through Mao Zedong's analysis of principal contradictions. The late Qing efforts are described as limited reforms led by the court and some elites, meant to preserve dynastic rule, and so unable to resolve the conflict between imperialism and the Chinese nation. The Communist Party is presented as changing the political subject that could resolve that conflict. Its early programmes on industrialization, its debates with agrarian conservatives, and Mao's vision of a New China in 1945 are treated as the first conceptions of socialist modernization. After 1949, Guo traces how redefinitions of the principal contradiction (1956, 1981, 2017) tied the goals of modernization to the Eighth Party Congress, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the 19th Party Congress (2017). Deng Xiaoping's 1979 phrase "Chinese-style modernization" is cited as the origin of the concept, which Guo says the 20th Party Congress expanded into five features and an integrated, system-wide strategy. Guo concludes that Chinese modernization rejects "Westernization" and one-way "integration with international norms", and pursues an autonomous socialist path. It is described as comprehensive, covering the economy, national governance, ecology, people's livelihoods and national security. Guo also presents it as a new option for countries that want development while keeping their independence, and as creating a "new form of human civilization". Read the original if you want a historian's account that places Chinese modernization in a long line of modern Chinese modernization projects, organised by the changing principal contradiction.

Several questions on comprehensively advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化全面推进中华民族伟大复兴的几个问题 Sun Tanghou Sun Tanghou takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) formula that the Party's central task is to "comprehensively advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization". Sun argues that the formula gives Chinese modernization a distinct strategic position and a direct causal link to national rejuvenation. Understanding its "reasoning, theory and philosophy" is said to be essential for grasping the Congress's strategic plans. The article, published in 2023, is a study-oriented exposition of that formula. The article has four parts. The first sets out four "logics" behind the formula: political, historical, theoretical and practical. The second traces the origins of Chinese modernization from Mao Zedong's 1945 remarks and the "four modernizations" through Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style modernization" to Xi Jinping's 2020 formulation, then lists its five features and nine essential requirements. The third covers the overall goals for 2035 and the mid-century, and the "two-step" strategic arrangement. The fourth examines the new strategic situation, the major principles and nine practical routes. Sun argues that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Party, and that this defines its nature and direction. Drawing on the Two Establishes, Sun treats the Party's leadership as the decisive guarantee. Sun distinguishes Chinese modernization from what the article calls Western modernization, which it describes as driven by capital, materialist, human-centred in its ecology and tied to colonial plunder. At the same time Sun holds that it shares common features and general laws of modernization, such as industrialization, urbanization and market allocation. Methodologically, Sun draws four lessons: autonomy, innovation, diversity and inclusiveness. Sun also describes a hostile external environment, attributing it to the United States and the West, and calls for a spirit of struggle. Sun concludes that Chinese modernization is the only correct path to national rejuvenation. Success is said to depend on five principles: the Party's overall leadership, the socialist path, a people-centred approach, deepening reform and opening up, and the spirit of struggle. Sun lists nine practical tasks, including high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity, green development, national security, a community with a shared future for mankind and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned survey of how Chinese academics systematise the 20th Congress's modernization theory.

Development and innovation of the fundamental institution of upholding Marxism's guiding role in the ideological field 坚持马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位根本制度的发展与创新 Wu Xueqin Wu Xueqin examines the institution of 'upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological field', which the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) formally named a fundamental institution (根本制度). The article argues that this institution, which Wu says bears on the Party's banner, direction and fate, took shape over a century of Party history and has been developed and given new content in the new era. The article has three parts. The first traces four stages: germination in revolutionary struggle (night schools, peasant training institutes, Communist Youth League, periodicals, the Yan'an rectification), formation and a twisting course after 1949, improvement during reform and opening up, and maturity in the new era. The second sets out the new-era achievements, and the third discusses how the institution is to be put into effect. In the core argument, Wu draws five lessons from the historical record: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times as the first task; propaganda and education as the core requirement; absorbing outstanding cultural achievements as a resource; a Party-led cultural and educational system as the key instrument; and seizing ideological leadership and discourse power as the guarantee. Wu says the new era has built on these in five respects: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the 'soul', constitutional and Party-charter provisions as the 'four beams and eight pillars', governance of cyberspace, a supporting enforcement system including responsibility for ideological work, and coordination with other fundamental institutions. For implementation Wu proposes five pairings: cultural confidence with institutional confidence, adherence to fundamentals with innovation, systematisation with workability, accountability built into institutions with institutionalised accountability, and outward conformity with inward conviction. Wu concludes that the institution is a necessary result of China's historical, theoretical and practical logic, and that it works fully only if people internalise it as a way of life. Practical measures include better organisational leadership, management and early-warning mechanisms for ideological work, stronger Party leadership of media and online space, and distinguishing questions of political principle, of understanding and of academic opinion, with scholarly debate bound by propaganda discipline. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-official account of how ideological leadership is being institutionalised in China and which mechanisms are proposed for it.

Upholding fundamentals and breaking new ground: the internal logic and basic guideline of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 守正创新：马克思主义中国化时代化的内在逻辑和根本遵循 Zhang Zhengguang Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Zhengguang asks why Marxism keeps its vitality and how the Communist Party of China has advanced the process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The answer, in the article, is the paired principle of "upholding fundamentals and breaking new ground" (shouzheng chuangxin): holding to Marxism's basic principles, stance and method while innovating in step with practice. Zhang presents this as both Marxism's "secret code" of renewal and the internal logic of its Sinicization. The article has three sections. The first traces the principle through the history of Marxism, from Marx's early development and the revisions to the Communist Manifesto to Engels and Lenin. The second reads the Party's century as a history of the same principle, moving through the new-democratic revolution, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to the Two Integrations as the present path, and to how the two integrations relate to each other. Zhang argues that social-science theory is a dialectical unity of absolute and relative truth and must stay open to practice. On this reading, Marx and Engels never treated their theory as final, and they developed it through involvement in working-class struggle and through polemics against rival currents. Zhang rejects Bernstein's view, echoed by some Western Marxist scholars, that such development amounts to "revisionism", and says it confuses theoretical innovation with abandoning fundamentals. In the Chinese case, Zhang names successive theoretical results: Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Each, the article says, held to basic principles while responding to new conditions. Zhang concludes that integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture is the fundamental route by which Marxism stays vital. The two integrations are said to be equally important: without the first, theory becomes rigid and rootless, and without the second it loses its "roots and soul". The article also holds that the present era is still the historical epoch Marxism identified, so Marxism is not outdated. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese academic account of how the Party's theory frames Sinicization as continuity plus innovation, with its historical narrative and its response to the "revisionism" charge.

The theoretical system of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的理论体系 Xiang Jiuyu Xiang Jiuyu takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that Chinese modernization has become a preliminary, relatively stable theoretical form, and asks what that theoretical system consists of. The article argues that Chinese modernization is a new body of theory: it rests on a distinct philosophical foundation, breaks with existing modernization narratives and has a definite core and distinctive features. Xiang presents grasping it as a key to understanding the changes of the new era and to building China's independent knowledge system. The article is organised in four parts. The first sets out the conceptual foundations, the second the historical change the theory represents, the third its theoretical "hard core", and the fourth its distinctive traits. Along the way Xiang engages Francis Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis and Western-centrism, and cites Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi. On foundations, Xiang argues that the theory goes beyond Fukuyama's thesis through historical materialism, combining the general necessity of modernization with China's particularity. It rejects the equation of modernization with Westernization and takes a people-centred stance as its value core. The change it brings is described as a "revolution in terminology" (concepts such as high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind), a shift of research paradigm, and an original theoretical narrative. The hard core has five parts: leadership by the Communist Party, socialist institutional character, Chinese characteristics, the nine essential requirements and distinctive advantages in material production, state governance and social development. Xiang ranks the advantage in material production as fundamental. Xiang concludes that the system is shaped by three unities. These are the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, the fine traditional Chinese culture, and socialist modernization. In this reading it enriches socialist modernization theory, applies scientific socialism to China's conditions, and is still developing. Xiang also claims that it breaks the West's monopoly on modernization theory and offers guidance to other developing countries. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars map the structure and sources of the theory of Chinese modernization.

Winning the cyber ideological struggle of the new era with a spirit of historical initiative 以历史主动精神打赢新时代网络意识形态斗争 Wang Yonggui Writing in 2023, Wang Yonggui asks how the Party can win the ideological struggle in cyberspace, which the article treats as a main arena for clashing ideas and a key area of political and ideological security. The answer is to apply the "spirit of historical initiative" that Xi Jinping has stressed since the new era began. Wang argues that this spirit combines respect for objective laws, readiness to seize opportunities and a talent for summing up experience. It operates at three levels: cognitive, practical and methodological. The article follows these three levels in three parts. The first part analyses the risks of the online environment, to build "cognitive consciousness". The second part sets out opportunities and supports for action, to build "practical consciousness". The third part draws on the experience of the new era to supply methods, for "methodological consciousness". Wang supports the argument throughout with quotations from Xi Jinping's speeches, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and a small number of scholarly sources. Wang identifies four features that make the online struggle harder. Open, free cyberspace weakens the old propaganda-based model and makes anonymous attacks hard to trace. A multiplicity of online actors blurs the line between ordinary users and hostile forces. Entertainment content can carry historical nihilism and other "erroneous trends", and can feed capital's collusion with technology. Algorithmic "information cocoons" and closed communities undermine a common value base. Wang then proposes five supports: a new view of cybersecurity that is scientific, holistic, dynamic and coordinated; cultural supports, including the guiding position of Marxism; talent; infrastructure; and rule by law. The article's methods are fought as four campaigns: positional, public opinion, hearts-and-minds, and technology. Wang concludes that experience of the new era should be turned into method so that the Party keeps the initiative in cyberspace. Concrete proposals include promoting "positive energy" and expanding the "red zone" against "grey" and "black" zones. Officials are to take the mass line online and answer public opinion crises quickly while resolving the real-world problems behind them. Wang also calls for breakthroughs in core technologies and for China to gain a voice in international rule-making. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Chinese Party-theory scholarship frames online ideological security and the policy measures it ties to it.

Rallying minds and strength for the new journey 为奋进新征程凝心聚力 Liu Guangming Wang Qiang Liu Ke This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 9 May 2023, explains why the Party is running a campaign of thematic education on studying and applying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu, Wang and Liu take their cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the work conference launching the campaign. They argue that the campaign, aimed chiefly at leading cadres at county and department level and above, is a major step in implementing the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article is organised around three "necessary requirements" that, in the authors' account, make the campaign significant. The first is unifying the Party's thinking, will and action. The second is spurring Party members to take responsibility and open up new prospects for the cause. The third is advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform. On the first point, the authors argue that each advance in Party theory must be followed by theoretical arming of the membership. They present Xi's thought as a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, reached through the Two Integrations. Leaders are called the "critical minority" who must set an example, grasp the Two Establishes and carry out the Two Upholds. On the second, they argue that the tasks set by the 20th Party Congress, pursued through Chinese modernization, face uncertain risks, so cadres must turn study into firmer ideals, stronger Party spirit and practical work, guided by the "six musts". On the third, they argue that the campaign addresses problems unique to a large party and the lasting "four tests", "four dangers" and "four impurities". It does so through political health checks, correcting deviations and strengthening the Party's capacity for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-advancement. The authors conclude that the campaign should be carried out thoroughly so that the Party stays united, remains the leading core of socialism with Chinese characteristics and never loses its character. The text is an official-style mobilisation piece rather than an analytical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's press justified the 2023 thematic education campaign and linked it to ideology, governance and Party building.

Deeply understanding and grasping the "Two Establishes" 深刻理解和把握“两个确立” Zhang Yanguo Xiao Chun This newspaper commentary, published in 2023, sets out how the authors think the Party should understand the Two Establishes. Zhang and Xiao point to the amended Party Constitution adopted at the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls the Two Establishes a major political outcome of the new era. They argue that the formula is a sound historical conclusion and that its decisive significance should be grasped. The piece has two parts. The first shows that the Two Establishes rest on the Party's century of history and on the practice of the new era. The second sets out three requirements for understanding them: the Two Upholds, theoretical armament, and the link between upholding the core and the guiding ideology. On history, the authors contend that the Party has endured because it has stressed the Party's self-reform and, at each stage, formed a strong leadership core and openly set its guiding ideology. They trace a line from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which they describe as a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On practice, they say that the achievements of the past decade show that the Party can lead the people to new victories only with a leader recognised by the people as its core and with this thought as its guide. The authors call for loyalty to the core and for treating the Two Upholds as the highest political principle. They also call for deeper study and propagation of Xi Jinping Thought, including the Party's thematic education campaign, and for firm political discipline alongside theoretical confidence. They present these steps as ensuring that Chinese modernization advances steadily. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary justifies the Two Establishes through Party history and the achievements of the new era.

From alienated labour to alienated time: the contemporary transformation of Marx's social critical theory 从劳动异化到时间异化：马克思社会批判理论的当代转化 Xie Yazhou Chen Nannan The article asks how the concept of alienation, central to Marx's social critical theory, can be carried into a present that differs sharply from Marx's own. Xie and Chen argue that alienation has moved from the sphere of labour to that of time. They hold that Hartmut Rosa's theory of time alienation gives a useful diagnosis of late modern society, but that it needs to be corrected by Marx's critique of capital. The text has three parts. The first traces Marx's own development from humanist to scientific alienation, through the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology, the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse) and the 1861–63 manuscripts. The second turns to the Frankfurt School and to Rosa, a fourth-generation Frankfurt thinker, covering his definition of time alienation, his three dimensions of social acceleration and its driving mechanisms. The third compares the critical paths of Marx and Rosa and ends with remarks on Chinese modernization. On Marx, the authors argue that the 1844 theory, with its four determinations of alienated labour, still rests on a humanist notion of species-essence and a Hegelian pattern of return. After The German Ideology, they say, alienation is grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Its resolution then lies in communism, not in a restored essence. On Rosa, they report his view that acceleration of technology, of social change and of the pace of life drives alienation from space, things, action, time, self and society. Competition, the cultural promise of a full life and a self-reinforcing acceleration cycle sustain this process. His critique has a normative side, since time norms undermine modernity's promise of reflexivity and autonomy. It also has a functional side, since desynchronization points to the system's eventual breakdown. His remedy is 'resonance' rather than slower living. The authors judge that Rosa offers a phenomenological analysis that does not reach the deeper cause. In their account, he denies that acceleration follows from capital's drive to valorise itself and reduces it to psychological and cultural factors, and his resonance proposal remains abstract. They call for placing acceleration within the logic of capital, following Marx's critique. For Chinese modernization they draw two implications: expanding public ownership while regulating private capital, and building a sound legal and administrative system. Read the original if you want a Marxist assessment of Rosa's social acceleration theory set against the development of Marx's own concept of alienation.

Chinese modernization and common prosperity 中国式现代化与共同富裕 Han Xiping Wang Siran Han Xiping and Wang Siran ask how common prosperity relates to Chinese modernization and how it can be achieved. They argue that, unlike capitalist modernization, which they say produces polarisation between rich and poor, Chinese modernization takes common prosperity as its essential requirement and basic feature. The article draws on the 20th Party Congress report (2022) and on Xi Jinping's statements on the subject. The article has three parts. The first sets out why common prosperity is a defining feature of Chinese modernization, in four respects: socialism's essence, China's cultural heritage, the Communist Party's historical goals, and a claimed new form of human civilisation. The second lays out strategic steps by stage: the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan period, 2020 to 2035, and 2035 to the middle of the century. The third proposes three sets of measures: high-quality development, a better distribution system, and a fuller social security system. On theory, the authors cite Marx, Engels and Deng Xiaoping to place common prosperity at the heart of socialism. They also trace it through Chinese ideals such as "great harmony" and a moderately prosperous society, and through the Party's record from land reform to poverty alleviation. They hold that Chinese modernization breaks with "Western centrism" and the "end of history" thesis, because it rests on public ownership as the mainstay with several forms of ownership developing together. On policy, they stress that common prosperity does not mean equal or simultaneous wealth. They call for innovation-driven growth, rural revitalisation and coordinated regional development, and for coordinating primary distribution, redistribution and the "third distribution" (charity). They also warn against "welfarism", which they say only adjusts capitalist relations and cannot alter the basic divide between bourgeoisie and proletariat. The authors conclude that common prosperity is a long-term, gradual process that cannot be rushed. They propose milestones such as an olive-shaped income distribution, equalised basic public services and a Gini coefficient below 0.3. They present Chinese modernization as offering developing countries a new option for balancing efficiency and fairness. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how official discourse links common prosperity to Chinese modernization, with the staged targets and policy tools it cites.

Applying historical wisdom to create great undertakings in the new era 运用历史智慧开创新时代伟业 Zhang Yanguo Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Yanguo takes up the report's call to "firm up historical confidence, strengthen historical initiative". The commentary asks how studying history can help the Party and people achieve great undertakings in the new era. Zhang's answer is a sequence: a correct view of history leads to historical cognition, then to historical confidence, historical consciousness and historical initiative, and finally to great historical undertakings. The piece is organised under five headings. These cover the origin of historical confidence in a correct view of history, historical cognition as its basis, and confidence as the deepest and most fundamental form of confidence. They continue with historical consciousness as the route to initiative, and the creation of new-era undertakings. Zhang draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks, on Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, and on the Party's official summaries of its historical experience. Zhang distinguishes fragmentary, emotional perception of history from rational cognition that works from facts, from surface to essence. Historical confidence, in this account, rests on the second kind, guided by dialectical and historical materialism and on the history of the Chinese nation, the Party, New China, reform and opening up and the past decade. Zhang calls it the foundation of the Four-sphere Confidence and says it should also become confidence that others share. The author also sets confidence against two threats: domestically, historical nihilism that denies the Party's achievements, and abroad, "hostile forces" promoting Western-centred views of history, "universal values" and "Westernization". Zhang urges the Party to answer these ideological struggles directly. Zhang concludes that historical confidence is the Party's greatest source of assurance, historical consciousness its distinguishing feature, and historical initiative its particular strength. The Party's "five historical significances", "ten historical experiences" and "six musts" are presented as the grand narrative that roots the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation in history.
