As challenges grow more complex, Zhang calls for firmer historical resolve and a fresh "answer sheet" for history and the people. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-aligned scholars present historical confidence and the struggle against historical nihilism after the 20th Party Congress.

Marx's critique of Proudhon's economic philosophy 马克思对蒲鲁东经济哲学思想的批判 Luo Chengyi Liu Cuifeng This article revisits The Poverty of Philosophy (1847), which Marx wrote in French as a reply to Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty (1846). Luo and Liu argue that in this polemic Marx used his new worldview, historical materialism, to criticise Proudhon's economic philosophy comprehensively. They hold that the work was not an immediate success against Proudhon's influence among workers, but that it retains lasting value as the first public, scientific statement of historical materialism's core ideas. The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The parts take Marx's critique of the foundation of Proudhon's thought (an idealist view of history), of his method (the "serial" dialectic), and of his core theories of value and property, including ground rent. The conclusion places the book in the personal and political history of the two men and links it to the present-day guiding role of Marxism. On the foundation, the authors report Marx's view that Proudhon treats economic categories as eternal and derives them from abstract thought, with the division of labour as the motor of history. Marx, by contrast, locates the motor in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, so categories are only historical and transitory. On method, they argue that Proudhon borrowed only the terminology of Hegel's thesis–antithesis–synthesis, dividing each category into a "good" and a "bad" side and hoping to keep one and remove the other. In their account this ends the dialectical movement and produces a "system of economic contradictions" that exists only in thought. On theory, they set Ricardo, who started from real economic relations, against Proudhon's chain of assumptions about constituted value and the equal division of surplus labour. They also cover Marx's argument that property and rent are expressions of changing social relations, so that "rent comes from society, not from the soil". The authors conclude that the critique of Proudhon's economics and philosophy shifted into a political critique of his petty-bourgeois class position. In their reading, Marx saw Proudhon as an opponent of feudalism but also an obstacle to the communist movement and a defender of small property owners. They add that the book put proletarian revolution at the centre and offered a path to human emancipation. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language account of how Marx's 1847 polemic is read today as a statement of historical materialism, including its treatment of value theory and ground rent.

Mao Zedong's historical contribution to China's modernization drive 毛泽东对中国现代化事业的历史贡献 Zhu Siyuan Marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth in 2023, Zhu Siyuan asks what Mao contributed to China's modernization and why it matters for Chinese modernization today. The article argues that Mao made pioneering and decisive contributions: he created the social conditions, the political and institutional premise, the material base and the theoretical foundation on which later modernization rests. The article is organised in four parts that follow Mao's career. They cover the victory of the new-democratic revolution, the socialist transformation and the founding of the basic socialist system, socialist construction from 1953 to 1978, and Mao's strategic thinking on modernization. Throughout, Zhu argues against what the author calls historical nihilism, including the view that Mao understood only revolution and class struggle and neglected construction. In the first two parts, Zhu argues that independence, unification and liberation were preconditions for a modernization that is neither Western nor dependent on the West. The author uses historical materialism, and Engels's critique of economic determinism, to reject the idea that revolution delayed modernization. Zhu also rejects the view, which the author labels a 'productive forces first' position, that China should have consolidated new democracy for a long period. In Zhu's account Mao, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai held that new democracy was a transitional form that had to move toward socialism, so the socialist transformation completed in 1956 secured the political premise for modernization. The third part cites GDP and industrial output growth figures for 1949–1978, a quotation from the historian Maurice Meisner, and the creation of an independent and relatively complete industrial system. Zhu concedes setbacks and errors but says they cannot erase these achievements. The fourth part credits Mao with drawing lessons from the Soviet model and calling for the 'Second Integration' of Marxism with Chinese realities. Zhu also credits him with the 'Four Modernizations', the 'two-step' strategy, the principle of overall balance, and the theory of contradictions among the people. Zhu concludes that reform-era achievements were built on the basic system and the material foundation of the Mao period. The author presents Deng Xiaoping's 'three-step' strategy and Xi Jinping's new 'two-step' strategy as continuations of Mao's staged approach. Mao's ideas are said to remain a guide for building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Chinese case for continuity between the Mao era and later modernization, set against historical nihilism.

Beware of overseas regional history's attempts to deconstruct historical China 警惕海外区域史研究解构历史中国的企图 Kong Yingchuan Kong Yingchuan takes up a trend in recent American China studies: regional histories of China's frontiers that claim to be "region-centred" but, in the author's view, end up deconstructing historical China. The article, a critical commentary first published in Historical Review in 2022, argues that this work uses Western concepts to cut the frontiers out of Chinese history. Kong says the real intent behind it deserves vigilance. The piece first sketches the development of American regional-history writing on China, from Fairbank, Lattimore and Wittfogel in the 1930s and 1940s, through the "China-centred approach" of the 1960s and Skinner's regional systems theory, to a post-1990 shift under postmodern and postcolonial influence. It then examines specific works on Taiwan, Guizhou, Yunnan and Xinjiang, by authors including Teng Emma Jinhua, Laura Hostetler, Bin Yang, Peter Perdue, James Millward and Michael Clarke. Kong closes by setting these works against what the article presents as the historical record of a unified multi-ethnic China. Kong contends that these works label ancient China an "empire" and treat the Yuan and Qing as non-Chinese "conquest dynasties". On this reading, Qing map-making, ethnography and frontier governance are equated with Western colonialism, and Yang's account of Yunnan is said to make its Chinese identity depend on a provincial identity. Kong answers that such claims ignore the long Chinese traditions of cartography and local gazetteers. The author adds that they also ignore the institutional continuity of the province system, which Kong traces back to the Wei–Jin, Sui and Tang dynasties. Kong further cites the gradual fusion of nomadic and agrarian peoples. Kong concludes that the "colonial empire" framing plays down modern Western colonial aggression against China and serves a political aim. In the article's reading, "decolonisation" of the regions amounts to "de-Sinicisation", a return to a Han-only China acceptable to the West, or a "China history without China". Kong insists that China's unity came from the natural coalescence of its peoples and was settled in the modern struggle against colonial invasion. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese historians of the frontiers respond to the "New Qing History", Inner Asia approaches and postcolonial scholarship in the United States, and which books they single out.

Understanding in depth why Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times works 深入理解中国化时代化的马克思主义为什么行 Yang Weijun Wang Yannan Yang and Wang comment on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which extended the "three whys" formula with a second "works" (xing) claim: that Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times works. The authors read this as marking both the spatial and the temporal dimension of Party theoretical innovation. They present it as an expression of theoretical confidence and historical consciousness. The short piece, first printed in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2023, is organised in three parts. It sets out the theoretical character that makes Marxism "work", then the routes by which it does so, then the methodological principles involved. A brief closing section lists where the "works" lies. On character, the authors attribute four qualities to Marxism: scientific rigour, a people-centred stance, practicality and openness. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is described as twenty-first-century Marxism. On routes, they stress the Two Integrations, of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. On method, they list putting the people first, self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, problem orientation, systematic dialectics and a global outlook tied to a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors conclude that adapting Marxism has a starting point but no end point. In their account it works because it continues the Marxist tradition, realises the Two Integrations, rests on the worldview and methodology of Xi's thought, and is carried by a Party that believes in, practises and spreads Marxism. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how the official reading of the "works" formula was presented to Chinese readers in 2023.

Accelerationism and its critique from the perspective of historical materialism 历史唯物主义视域中的加速主义及其批判 Lei Yu Lei Yu takes up accelerationism, a radical Western theoretical current that proposes alternatives to capitalism. The article argues that in opposing the myths of neoliberalism, accelerationism has produced myths of its own and so become a new ideology. It also contends that accelerationism distorts Marx in order to present him as its forerunner. Lei calls for vigilance towards novel discourses and a methodological self-awareness grounded in historical materialism. The text first appeared as a newspaper article in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2023. The piece has three parts. The first traces accelerationism's history in three stages. The first is the 1970s French thinkers Deleuze, Guattari, Lyotard and Baudrillard, writing after the failure of May 1968. The second is the right-wing accelerationism of Nick Land in the 1990s. The third is the left-wing accelerationism of Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams, whose 2013 manifesto brought the current to wide attention. The second part dissects five myths. The third turns accelerationism into a "model" that can be analysed and assessed. Lei identifies five myths. In ideology, accelerationism is a product of the Enlightenment and capitalism, leading on the right towards fascism and on the left towards what Lei calls totalitarian socialism, such as Aaron Bastani's "fully automated luxury communism". In historical narrative, it is a "hyperstition" that reverses the order of history. In technology, it is a Promethean cult in which technology becomes destiny. In politics, it is a struggle for hegemonic discourse. In textual reading, it is a one-dimensional reading of Marx that cites the free-trade speech and the "fragment on machines". Lei argues that Marx always viewed capitalism through the contradiction between the forces and relations of production, whereas accelerationism affirms only the productive forces. As a model, its political hopes for an alternative remain unrealised. It grafts Marxism onto Nietzsche, post-structuralism and science fiction. Drawing on Althusser, Lei says its problematic stays inside capitalism and follows reality rather than critically transcending it. Lei concedes that accelerationism offers some critical insight. It reflects the inherent contradiction of capital valorisation and the powerlessness of the Western left, and it draws attention to global capitalism's challenges to socialist theory and practice in China. Lei concludes that Marxists should stay alert to radical Western currents, strengthen their ability to answer them and deepen their own theoretical self-understanding. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist assessment of accelerationism, from Land to Srnicek and Williams, and of how Chinese scholars frame its relation to Marx.

Always holding on to the hearts of the people 始终守住守好人民的心 Wang Gaohe Fang Hongtao This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2023, reads the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) through Xi Jinping's statement that in winning and defending the country the Party is defending "the hearts of the people". Wang and Fang argue that winning popular support is both the secret of the Party's first century of achievement and the key to future success. The piece is organised in five steps. It begins with the improvement of living standards over the decade since 2012, then turns to the people-centred stance underlying the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. It goes on to common prosperity as a mark of Chinese modernization, the Party's measures on livelihoods, and finally the creative power of the people. The authors cite poverty alleviation and the building of a moderately prosperous society as evidence of improved lives, including nearly 100 million rural people lifted out of poverty and life expectancy rising to 78.2 years. They argue that Marxism took root in China because its defining attribute is its people-oriented character, whereas other currents failed to represent Chinese people's interests. They contrast Chinese modernization, which they describe as aiming at common prosperity of material and cultural life, with Western modernization, which in their account cannot solve widening wealth gaps. Wang and Fang conclude that the Party should keep improving livelihoods through income distribution, employment, social security and health policies. It should also apply the mass line and combine whole-process people's democracy with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which they present as the two answers to the "historical cycle" question. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary presents the 20th Congress report's people-centred themes.

Upholding the supremacy of the people as a defining trait of vivid practice in the new era 坚持人民至上是新时代生动实践的鲜明品格 Ma Dekun This newspaper commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today on 3 January 2023, takes up the principle of putting the people first (人民至上) as it appears in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Ma Dekun notes that the word "people" occurs more than 170 times in the report and calls it a manifesto of the supremacy of the people for the new era. The author argues that this principle is a defining feature of the Party's practice since 2012 and an expression of the Marxist idea of the free and all-round development of the human being. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the Party's new journey and mission require upholding the supremacy of the people. The second sets out four components of the principle as the author understands it. The third turns to practice and names three tasks: close ties with the masses, firm fairness and justice, and common prosperity. It draws throughout on speeches by Xi Jinping and on the Party Congress report. On the first part, Ma argues that the Party's historical mission, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, points in value terms towards the people's happiness. Its realisation also depends on the joint effort of all the people under Party leadership, so the mission itself demands that the people come first. The four components are taking the people's stance, attending to the will of the people, respecting the people's principal position, and promoting the people's wellbeing. The author links the second to whole-process people's democracy and the people's congress system, and the fourth to the high-quality development the Party pursues in order to meet the people's needs. In the practical section, Ma holds that the mass line, "from the masses, to the masses", must be maintained and that the Party grew through its ties with the people. The author lists measures for fairness and justice: improving the distribution system, prioritising employment, strengthening social security and building a healthy China. Ma treats common prosperity as the final aim of the principle, while acknowledging that, because China is in the primary stage of socialism, the road to it remains long. The author expresses confidence that the Party can meet the people's aspirations for a better life. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how the people-first principle was presented after the 20th Party Congress.

The historical logic of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times "New judgements, new interpretations" written discussion, part 1 马克思主义中国化时代化的历史逻辑 Sun Daiyao Taking its cue from the 20th Party Congress report (2022), which says that what works is Marxism "adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times", Sun Daiyao asks what historical and theoretical logic underlies this process. The article argues that localisation and contemporisation are inherent requirements of Marxism as an open, developing theory. In Sun's account, the Chinese Communist Party's repeated theoretical innovation around China's practical problems forms the historical basis of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is organised in three parts. The first examines the theoretical character and development of Marxism, drawing on Marx, Engels and Lenin. The second traces the laying of foundations and deepening of Sinicisation from Li Dazhao and Yun Daiying through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. The third treats the "new leap" since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the formation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Sun's central claim is that Marxism is a method, not a ready-made dogma, so it must change with time and place; Lenin's "concrete analysis of concrete conditions" and Mao's "seeking truth from facts" express this. The article presents each stage as a response to new problems: Mao Thought as the first historic leap, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the second, and Xi Jinping Thought as a new leap. For the latest leap, Sun identifies its practical basis as the three "major questions of the times" and its theoretical mark as original ideas such as the "Ten Affirmations". Its philosophical basis is the view that truth is pursued through practice, together with the Two Integrations, which Sun reads as including a "penetrating" fusion of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Sun concludes that, because theory that stands still falls behind real life, continued innovation depends on grasping the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought and applying its stance, viewpoint and method. The article calls for historical initiative and theoretical confidence in writing new chapters of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-historical genealogy of Sinicisation, from Mao to Xi, as presented in an official-academic account.

The logical relationship and value convergence between fine traditional Chinese culture and the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind 中华优秀传统文化与人类命运共同体理念的逻辑关系与价值融通 Shi Si Shi Si asks how the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind relates to fine traditional Chinese culture, and how the two connect in value terms. The article argues that traditional culture is the concept's cultural foundation and source of values, and that the concept is in turn a creative transformation and innovative development of that culture, carried out under Marxist guidance. Without this cultural root, Shi contends, the concept would lose its "root and soul". The article opens with the "great changes unseen in a century" and the questions of where the world and humanity are heading. It then reads the concept's proposals on politics, security, the economy, culture and ecology as expressions of traditional philosophy. Next it traces four lines of development, from "harmony and integration", benevolence, people-as-the-root thinking and the righteousness–profit debate. The final part sets out five "convergences" of values, citing classical sources such as Mencius, the Book of Rites, Zhuangzi and Zhang Zai. In Shi's account, the concept develops each tradition rather than simply repeating it. Benevolence is carried from the "small self" to the "greater self" and from family-state to humanity, removing the hierarchical limits of Confucian feudal ethics. The people-as-root idea expands from the Chinese people to the peoples of the world. Under the Marxist theory of contradiction, the opposition between righteousness and profit becomes a dialectical unity in which states build economies together. The five convergences pair traditional ideas with goals: harmony with a lasting peaceful world; "all under heaven as one family" with a universally secure world; mutual aid with common prosperity; harmony in diversity with an open and inclusive world; and the unity of heaven and humanity with a clean and beautiful world. Shi concludes that the concept is a theoretical crystallisation of the convergence between contemporary Chinese Marxism and fine traditional culture. In this reading it marks a new height of theoretical confidence and practical consciousness in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article presents it as a Chinese solution to global problems, drawing on remarks by Xi Jinping throughout. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links classical sources to current foreign-policy language, and which traditional concepts are used to ground the community with a shared future for mankind.

The distinctive "six outlooks" contained in Chinese modernization 中国式现代化蕴含的独特“六观” Xin Xiangyang This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today takes up a statement by Xi Jinping of 7 February 2023. Xi said that the distinctive world outlook, values, view of history, view of civilization, view of democracy and view of ecology contained in Chinese modernization are a major innovation in the theory and practice of world modernization. Xin Xiangyang argues that unpacking these "six outlooks" helps explain the global influence of Chinese modernization. The article takes the six outlooks in turn, giving each a short section: world outlook, values, view of history, view of civilization, view of democracy and view of ecology. Each section lists a few defining propositions rather than developing a sustained case. On the world outlook, Xin contends that Chinese modernization is part of world modernization and follows its general laws. In the author's account it also breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and the idea that only capitalism makes a country strong. The values are said to have four sources: traditional Chinese culture, scientific socialism, the core socialist values and common values of all mankind. The view of history exposes the violence behind Western modernization, citing Marx on primitive accumulation, and stresses China's independent exploration. The view of democracy holds that without whole-process people's democracy there is no Chinese modernization, and that Western modernization achieved only a democracy of capital. The ecological view criticises capital's plunder of nature and calls for harmony between humanity and nature. Xin concludes that these outlooks make Chinese modernization an alternative picture of modernization and offer developing countries another path and a "Chinese solution". Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned summary of how Party theorists present the worldview behind Chinese modernization.

Safeguarding the foundation and source, the root and soul of Chinese modernization 守好中国式现代化的本和源、根和魂 Wang Mingyi Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2023, Wang Mingyi comments on Xi Jinping's address at the study session on the 20th Party Congress (2022) spirit. Xi called on the Party to "safeguard the foundation and source, the root and soul" of Chinese modernization by holding firmly to its Chinese characteristics, essential requirements and major principles. Wang argues that doing so ensures the correct direction of Chinese modernization and keeps this unprecedented undertaking moving forward. The piece is organised in three parts, each taking one of the three elements Xi named. It moves from Chinese characteristics, to the essential requirements, to the major principles, and quotes Xi throughout. Wang presents these as the answer to a set of major theoretical and practical questions and as a guide to action for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. On Chinese characteristics, Wang argues that no single or universal model of modernization exists. Wang presents the five features of Chinese modernization, namely a huge population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development, as growing out of China's national conditions and traditional culture. On the essential requirements, Wang stresses that Party leadership is the greatest strength and fundamental guarantee of Chinese modernization. Wang treats advancing modernization as the Party's central task from now on, and reviews the 20th Party Congress goals for 2035 and for the next five years. On the major principles, Wang lists five commitments: Party leadership, the socialist path, a people-centred approach, deepening reform and opening up, and a fighting spirit. Wang says these answer the risks and challenges the undertaking will meet. Wang concludes that the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has summarised these three elements and begun to build a theoretical system of Chinese modernization, making it clearer, more scientific and more workable. Holding to them, the author argues, will widen the path to a modern socialist country and increase the significance of Chinese modernization in the history of human civilization. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party-school-style commentary presents Xi's three-part formula on Chinese modernization.

How Chinese modernization was successfully advanced and expanded in the new era 新时代何以成功推进和拓展中国式现代化 Chen Li Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in May 2023, Chen Li asks how the Communist Party has succeeded since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in advancing and expanding Chinese modernization. The piece is a study session commentary built on Xi Jinping's speech at the opening of a seminar on studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Chen argues that Chinese modernization is the major result of long exploration under Party leadership, and that the new era produced theoretical and practical breakthroughs in understanding, strategy and practice. The article opens with a historical survey. It runs from the failed attempts after the Opium War (the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1898 reforms, the 1911 Revolution) through the New Democratic Revolution, the socialist revolution and construction after 1949, and the reform and opening up period. It then devotes three sections to the new era, covering deepening understanding, improved strategy and enriched practice. Chen's central claim is that earlier reformers failed for lack of advanced scientific theory, and that the Party succeeded by integrating Marxism with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. On understanding, Chen holds that the creation of Xi Jinping Thought is the greatest achievement of the decade. The 20th Party Congress report, in Chen's account, set out the features, essential requirements and principles of Chinese modernization and began to build its theoretical system. On strategy, Chen cites the five-sphere integrated plan, the Four Comprehensives and the two-step plan towards a modern socialist country by mid-century, and says the 20th Congress set higher targets for 2035. On practice, Chen cites institutional maturation, GDP growth from 54 to 114 trillion yuan, and the elimination of absolute poverty. Chen also lists gains in Party discipline, ecology, the military, Hong Kong, cross-Strait relations and diplomacy. Chen concludes that the decade's achievements gave Chinese modernization a more complete institutional guarantee, a firmer material base and greater spiritual initiative. Chen asserts that practice has shown it to be the only correct path to national rejuvenation, and calls for stronger confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, avoiding both a closed, rigid old path and an "evil path" of abandoning socialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official narrative links its history to the new-era claims about Chinese modernization.

Enriching the people's spiritual world is an essential requirement of Chinese modernization 丰富人民精神世界是中国式现代化的本质要求 Wang Xinsheng Wang Xinsheng, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2023, comments on a formulation in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The report listed enriching the people's spiritual world among the essential requirements of Chinese modernization, alongside the claim that it is a modernization of material and cultural-ethical advancement in coordination. Wang argues that this places spiritual civilization and spiritual strength at the centre of the national project, and that material and spiritual civilization are like a bird's two wings or a cart's two wheels. The article has three parts. The first explains why enriching the people's spiritual world matters, in theoretical and practical terms. The second reviews cultural work in the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012), presented as the foundation for this goal. The third turns to the 20th Party Congress agenda of building a socialist cultural power and sets out what it requires. Wang's core argument is that Chinese modernization is socialist and must therefore create a new form of human civilization that meets both material and spiritual-cultural needs. In this account, spiritual enrichment is a measure of social development, of all-round human development and of socialism's superiority. Wang credits the past decade's achievements to several measures: establishing Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, promoting core socialist values, creatively transforming traditional Chinese culture, and a people-centred orientation in cultural production and public cultural services. The article also treats cyberspace as a shared spiritual home. It cites Xi Jinping's remarks that regulation must cover all media and cites the Cybersecurity Law, and it calls for the Party to hold the initiative in online ideological work. Wang concludes that cultural construction is a long-term systemic project, covering content, talent, institutions, the cultural industry and the dissemination of Chinese civilization, to be carried out as the Congress specified. Success would, in this view, supply a powerful spiritual impetus to national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior academic restates the 20th Party Congress's cultural and ideological priorities and links them to the concept of Chinese modernization.

The elements, models and evolution of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的要素、模式与变迁 Tong Dezhi Wang Xu Tong Dezhi and Wang Xu ask what elements make up Chinese modernization, how those elements relate, what models they form and how these have changed across periods. Taking up the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, they argue that it is best defined as the strategic goal of the Communist Party leading the people, through reform and opening up, to promote development and build socialism. They contend that it has passed through three successive models and moves from the inheritance of core principles to innovation, and from emphasis on a centre to comprehensiveness. The study builds a corpus from five sets of leaders' writings: Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping's Governance of China. It extracts the words adjacent to "modernization", about 320,000 characters, and checks the results against a supplementary corpus of Party document compilations since 1978. Using Nvivo 11 coding, co-occurrence and coverage statistics, the authors combine quantitative and qualitative analysis. The article sets out the elements, then three models, then patterns of change. From the most frequent co-occurring words, the authors derive four features: modernization led by the Party and carried out by the people, socialist modernization, modernization driven by reform and opening up, and modernization aimed at development. They trace the shift in the notion of development from rapid growth to high-quality development. They then periodise three models. The first is the "four modernizations" (industry, agriculture, national defence, science and technology), whose frequency peaks in Deng's writings and then drops. The second is a moderately prosperous society (xiaokang), and the third is the modern socialist country. In the authors' reading, this sequence shows social and state-level modernization converging. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization combines continuity, meaning Party leadership, socialism and common prosperity, with innovations such as whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind. They say its scope has widened from key sectors to an overall layout, the three-in-one to five-in-one arrangement, culminating in the 20th Congress's account. They concede that word-frequency analysis assumes frequency equals importance and that conclusions rest on texts alone and need further empirical testing. Read the original if you want a corpus-based, quantitative reading of how Party leaders' modernization discourse has evolved from Mao to Xi.

Philosophical distillation of the great practice of the new era Studying and applying the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 新时代伟大实践经验的哲学升华 Zhao Jianying Zhao Jianying takes up the call in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to grasp the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article, first published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2023, argues that the "Six Musts" are the concentrated expression of that worldview and methodology. In Zhao's account they are a philosophical summation of the experience of the new era, the core of the Thought, and the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has three parts. It first places the Six Musts in the lineage of Marxist philosophy and of earlier Chinese Marxism. It then takes each of the six in turn: put the people first, be self-confident and self-reliant, uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground, stay problem-oriented, apply systems thinking, and keep the whole world in view. A final section sets out how Party members should use this worldview in the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Zhao's central move is to tie each "Must" to a named Marxist principle. Putting the people first is linked to the materialist conception of history and to a value orientation of people-centred development. Self-reliance is linked to the unity of the universal and the particular and to the dialectic of internal and external causes, so that no single modernization model is universal. Problem orientation and systems thinking are tied to epistemology and to the principle of universal connection, and the "world in view" is tied to world-history theory and to traditional Chinese ideas such as "great harmony under heaven". Zhao also traces continuity from Mao Zedong's independence and self-reliance and Deng Xiaoping's "our own road" to Xi, presenting the Six Musts as consistent with earlier thought while moving with the times. Zhao concludes that this worldview should serve as an ideological weapon for transforming both the subjective and the objective world. The proposed applications are to read the era and the strategic picture of national rejuvenation, to advance Chinese modernization and common prosperity, to guard against major risks, to handle international relations and work toward a community with a shared future for mankind, and to pursue full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how the Six Musts are presented as Marxist philosophy and as a continuation of Mao and Deng.

Guiding China's high-quality economic development with Xi Jinping Thought on Economy 以习近平经济思想指引中国经济高质量发展 Ren Baoping Ren Baoping, in a commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2023, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Economy is a major theoretical innovation that answers the question of how China can achieve high-quality development. In Ren's account, the thought arose from the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era and the shift of the economy from rapid growth to high-quality development. It is presented as both a scientific guide and a programme of action for the new stage of development. The piece has two main parts, preceded by a short framing of the thought's place in the Party's theory. The first part sets out five theoretical contributions, tracing the concept from the 19th Party Congress report through the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee to the 20th Party Congress report (2022). The second part lists six practical requirements for high-quality development and ends with a call to study and implement the thought. Ren contends that the thought adapts Marxist political economy to Chinese conditions and extends it. The five contributions are: starting from the change in the principal contradiction of society; a people-centred approach; the new development philosophy, whose innovation, coordination, green, open and shared dimensions are each described as a theoretical advance; reforms in quality, efficiency and drivers of growth, aimed at raising total factor productivity; and using high-quality development to advance Chinese modernization. The practical requirements are high-level self-reliance in science and technology, building a new development pattern, orienting growth towards people's well-being, supply-side structural reform focused on the real economy, the digital economy as a new engine, and high-level opening up. Ren concludes that high-quality development is the first task of building a modern socialist country in all respects, and that Xi's expositions on it form an important part of the thought. The author calls on readers to study, interpret and follow the thought so that the economy moves steadily forward on the path of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned summary of how Chinese scholars frame the theory and policy priorities of high-quality development in 2023.

Marx's thought on combating spiritual poverty and its implications for our times 马克思反精神贫困思想及其时代启示 Yu Chunling Zhou Hequn Yu Chunling and Zhou Hequn ask what Marx's critique of capitalist "spiritual poverty" (jingshen pinkun) contributes to understanding that phenomenon and to pursuing spiritual prosperity today. They define spiritual poverty as a cultural phenomenon of social-wide loss of spirit and impoverished mental life, and focus on its social form. They argue that capitalist spiritual poverty is a relative poverty, a serious imbalance between spiritual and material development driven by the logic of capital. Marx's anti-poverty thought, in their view, offers theoretical guidance for "common prosperity" in spiritual life. The article has four parts. The first reconstructs Marx's diagnosis of five symptoms: withered creative capacity, lowered aesthetic level, declining morality, alienated spiritual intercourse and lack of self-conscious awareness. The second traces roots at three levels: material and technological, institutional, and ideological. The third sets out Marx's route to spiritual prosperity. The fourth draws lessons for contemporary China. The authors draw on the 1844 Manuscripts, Capital, the Communist Manifesto and The German Ideology. The central argument is that spiritual poverty arises from capitalist use of technology, private ownership and bourgeois ideology rather than from technology as such. Machine industry reduces workers to fragments of persons and takes away their free time. Private property and the logic of capital make usefulness and money the sole measure of value. The ruling class, which controls material production, also controls the means of mental production, including education. The authors conclude that Marx's way out has three conditions: material abundance through developed productive forces and technological innovation, escape from the logic of capital by abolishing capitalist private ownership, and proletarian revolution. In the final part the authors draw lessons for China in the new era. They call for using the advantages of the socialist system and holding to the Two Unwaverings, while recognising the dual role of capital. They want regulation to prevent its disorderly expansion and its corrosion of cultural life. They call for coordinating material and spiritual wealth in pursuit of common prosperity, with Marxism guiding ideology and core socialist values guiding cultural work. They also want better public cultural services to meet people's growing cultural needs. They say that reform-era commodity economy has brought moral anomie, hedonism and vulgar tastes. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language reading of Marx on alienation and culture, linked to current Party policy on spiritual common prosperity.

The young Marx's critique of private property and his turn to civil society Centred on the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right 青年马克思的私有财产批判和市民社会转向 Wen Quan Tang Liwei Wen and Tang take up the question of how the young Marx moved from criticising Hegel's theory of the state to focusing on civil society. The usual account credits Feuerbach's materialism with this turn. The authors argue that this idealist–materialist and state–civil society framework is too simple. They contend that around 1843 Marx used the contradiction between private property and the state, and his scrutiny of property's legal relations, to grasp the practical limits of Hegel's philosophy of right. In their reading, this gave him the premise of historical materialism. The article has three parts. The first traces the modern link between private property and the state, from the ancient city-state through Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau to Hegel, in order to reposition Marx's concerns at the Rheinische Zeitung. The second follows Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right on estates, primogeniture and landed property. The third considers the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Introduction to the Critique, and The German Ideology, to assess what the turn means theoretically. The authors argue that Hegel tried to reform the natural-law tradition by building property and personality into objective spirit and by making the ethical state mediate civil society's conflicts. Marx judged the estates a 'political illusion' of civil society. In his analysis, hereditary landed property makes private property the highest constituent of the political state and so pushes law back to a Germanic private-law level. Hegel's scheme therefore could not overcome the split in modern civil society. Wen and Tang add that Marx saw the Philosophy of Right as an extension of Hegel's Logic. He accordingly replaced its abstract personality with real social human beings and made civil society the real subject, historically situated. The authors conclude that the turn to civil society deepened the same problem and did not swap one object of study for another. They say it was an essential event in the formation of historical materialism. They also argue that the critique of private property should not be used to divide Marx's work into a political-critique phase and a political-economy phase. In their view the critique of political economy is internal to historical materialism, and Marx's dialectic was not completed in 1844. They suggest that Feuerbach's relation to Marx be reassessed. Read the original if you study the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Marx's relation to Hegel and natural-law theory, or the early roots of historical materialism.

Further strengthening research on basic theoretical questions of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 进一步加强马克思主义中国化时代化基础理论问题的研究 Tian Keqin Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called for opening up new realms for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, Tian Keqin asks which basic theoretical questions in this field need deeper study. The article argues that research should be strengthened in five areas: core concepts, the historical standing of theoretical achievements, themes, the system of theoretical achievements, and the fundamental path and method. Tian presents this as necessary for grasping the Party's internal laws of adaptation and for serving the scholarly mission of building arguments for the Party and the people. The article is organised in five sections, each tied to a guiding reference point: the relationship between the two processes ("sinicization" and "contemporization" of Marxism); the "three leaps"; the overall theme of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; the three Party "historical resolutions" (1945, 1981, 2021) as documentary basis; and the Two Integrations. It draws on Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation, the 13th, 14th, 15th and 17th Party Congresses, and the 2021 resolution. It closes by linking the research agenda to Xi Jinping's call to let the world know "China in academia" and to build an autonomous knowledge system with Chinese characteristics. Tian makes three main moves. First, the two processes are distinct but inseparable: Mao did not stress contemporization in 1938 because China's situation still fell within Lenin's imperialist era and the pressing task was to correct dogmatism, whereas from the 1980s changed world conditions led the 14th Party Congress (1992) to add the "features of the times". Second, on the "three leaps", the 2021 resolution speaks of one "first historic leap" (Mao Zedong Thought) and two "new leaps" (the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era). Tian says the latter two need more study, including Deng Xiaoping Theory's foundational role and the logical relation between those two achievements. Third, Tian identifies four theme shifts culminating in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and holds that "the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" is the overarching theme. Tian also reads the 20th Congress's selective restatement of earlier summaries as showing that the content system of Xi Jinping Thought is still being developed. On the Two Integrations, Tian argues that the second (with fine traditional Chinese culture) was already implicit in Mao's call to inherit China's historical heritage, rests on the first, and answers present needs of cultural confidence. Tian concludes that advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization requires both integrations and thorough study of Xi Jinping Thought. Theorists are urged to speak both accurately and freshly. Read the original if you want a Party-theory scholar's map of the research agenda on adapting Marxism in China, including how the official periodisation and terminology have shifted since 1938.

The cultural dimension of the "Two Integrations" and the development of Sinicized Marxism “两个结合”的文化维度与中国化马克思主义的发展 Hong Jun Hong Jun asks why integrating Marxism with China's fine traditional culture, alongside its integration with China's concrete realities, has come to be stated as a principle only now. The article takes up Xi Jinping's formulation of the Two Integrations, made in the 2021 speech marking the Party's centenary and repeated at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Hong argues that the cultural dimension emerged gradually through a century of debate and struggle, and that its explicit affirmation moves Sinicized Marxism to a new and higher stage. The article is a historical-theoretical survey in four parts. It begins with Engels's and Lenin's thoughts on adapting Marxism to local conditions and with Stalin's formula of proletarian content in national form. It then turns to Mao Zedong's writings of the late 1930s and 1940s, followed by wrong views of the Marxism–tradition relationship, both inside and outside the Marxist camp. The final part sets out the grounds on which the two can be integrated. Hong makes three main moves. First, Mao's idea of Marxism's adaptation to Chinese conditions already had a realistic dimension and a historical-cultural one. Mao studied Mohist and Confucian philosophy with Chen Boda and Zhang Wentian, yet in formal statements he stressed integration with China's realities, so recognition stayed at a single integration for decades. Second, Hong traces obstacles: Comintern and Soviet hostility, cultural conservatives from Zhang Zhidong to the Kuomintang, and nihilist attitudes among early Communist intellectuals and later scholars who treated tradition as feudal or unscientific. Third, Hong argues that Marxism and traditional culture share an "affinity". The evidence offered includes the Confucian ideals of Great Harmony and the moderately prosperous society, the people-as-basis tradition, and early Chinese Marxists' use of Datong language, as well as Li Zehou's and Jacques Gernet's observations. Hong concludes that influence ran both ways: Chinese tradition was transformed by Marxism, while foreign Marxism took national form and was nourished by fine traditional culture. In Hong's view, the 20th Congress formulation clears away a century of confusion, shows cultural self-awareness and self-confidence, and supports the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a Chinese path to modern civilization. Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual history of how the Marxism–traditional culture question was fought over in China, with citations from Mao, Chen Duxiu, the Kuomintang and conservative thinkers.

Marking a new height in understanding Chinese modernization 标注中国式现代化认识的新高度 Tian Pengying Tian Pengying takes up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and its account of Chinese modernization. Tian argues that the report gave a comprehensive, systematic theoretical summary of its Chinese characteristics, essential requirements and major principles, and so formed a complete theoretical system. In Tian's reading, this marks a new height in the Party's understanding, building on a line of work running from the First Five-Year Plan to the Fourteenth. The article is a commentary in three parts. The first sets out the Chinese characteristics of Chinese modernization against a reflection on world modernization theory. The second turns to the major principles to be upheld in what Tian calls a great and arduous undertaking. The third discusses the basic dimensions of modernization through several major relationships that Xi Jinping has said must be handled correctly. In the first part, Tian contrasts Chinese modernization with Western paths. Tian says neoliberal theories hold that modernization means following the West, and that countries copying Western models have developed slowly and with difficulty. By contrast, Chinese modernization is said to proceed from national conditions, pursue common prosperity and avoid polarisation, balance material and cultural-ethical progress, and pursue harmony between humanity and nature. It also follows a path of peaceful development, which Tian presents as dissolving the historical logic that a rising power must seek hegemony. The second part lists principles: upholding the Party's overall leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics, the people-centred approach, deepening reform and opening up, and a fighting spirit. The third part pairs top-level design with practical exploration, strategy with tactics, fundamental principles with innovation, efficiency with fairness, vitality with order, and self-reliance with opening up. Tian presents these as applications of materialist dialectics. Tian concludes that Chinese modernization is the fundamental route to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Tian calls on the whole Party to strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, hold firm the Four-sphere Confidence and carry out the Two Upholds, while staying alert to new contradictions in a complex international environment. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how the 20th Party Congress report's framework on Chinese modernization is presented to Party cadres and academic readers.

The logical starting point of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义政治经济学的逻辑起点 Xie Fusheng Kang Meng Xie Fusheng and Kang Meng take up a question they say has been unresolved since the founding of China's socialist economic system: what category should serve as the logical starting point of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Citing Xi Jinping's call to turn practical experience into a systematic economic doctrine, they argue that a correct starting point is the first task of building the theoretical system. Their answer is the commodity. The article first sorts existing positions into three groups by the type of category chosen: complex categories (the state, the economic system), indirect categories (labour in its various forms, 'the people') and simple categories (product, surplus product, commodity, and variants such as 'planned commodity'). It then returns to Hegel's account of the 'beginning of science' in the Logic and to Marx's method in Capital. Finally it applies that method to the socialist market economy, ending with the specific features of the Chinese system. The authors argue that, following Hegel and Marx, a starting category must be simple, abstract and mediating, and that complex categories can only be results of the ascent from the abstract to the concrete. In their reading, labour and 'the people' are mediated categories, and product or surplus product do not express social relations. Marx himself began Capital with the commodity as the 'cell form' containing the germs of all later contradictions. Because socialism with Chinese characteristics, in the primary stage of socialism, still rests on commodity production and market exchange, the commodity keeps the same character. The law of value, realised through the coercive law of competition, mediates the move to enterprises, labour relations, industrial chains, urban–rural and international relations. The authors conclude that the socialist commodity, like the capitalist one, can anchor the system, which differs from the capitalist one through five general features of the economic base: centralised Party leadership of economic work, the people-centred new development philosophy, the three-part basic economic system, building a community with a shared future for mankind, and seeking progress while maintaining stability. They claim these combine an 'effective market' with a 'capable government' and capture the positive results of capitalist commodity production while curbing blind market development. Read the original if you want a detailed survey of Chinese debates on the starting category, and a Hegel–Marx methodological defence of the commodity as the starting point for socialist political economy.

Towards a reasonable Enlightenment: Engels and Nietzsche 走向合理启蒙：恩格斯与尼采 Liu Senlin Comparisons of Marx and Nietzsche are well established, but Liu Senlin observes that no comprehensive comparison of Engels and Nietzsche exists. The article treats both as Enlightenment thinkers who began from a radical critique of religion and later moved to a more 'reasonable' Enlightenment position. Liu argues that they overlap, often in the very years they wrote, on Christianity, eternal recurrence, a return to nature, traditional morality and the limited legitimacy of metaphysics, while differing in important ways. The article has three main sections. The first compares the young Engels (his 1840s review of Carlyle's Past and Present) with Nietzsche on the critique of Christianity and the 'death of God'. The second takes up eternal recurrence and metaphysics, drawing on Engels's Dialectics of Nature and Anti-Dühring and on Nietzsche's Human, All Too Human and Beyond Good and Evil. The third addresses morality and 'natural right', setting Engels's 1886 critique of Feuerbach beside Nietzsche's On the Genealogy of Morals. Liu argues that both men read religion as a symptom of real suffering and as a falsification of reality, but they diverge at the point of resolution. Engels moves to atheism and locates religion's secret in society and history; Nietzsche exposes its psychological secret and offers a new god, Dionysus. On recurrence, Engels's concept is cosmological and independent of human activity, so it does not exclude progress, whereas Nietzsche's is a critique of modern progress. Both grant metaphysics a historical and psychological justification, though Nietzsche extends it to far more people and rejects dialectics as itself metaphysical. On morality, both hold that moral judgement can obscure reality and that a 'natural right' persists that society cannot abolish. Liu says Engels treats it as historically bound and sorts social 'natural right' into three cases: ideological deception to be exposed, what suits the productive forces, and aspirations for the future. Liu concludes that, as they matured, both adjusted their early radical Enlightenment stance into a more reasonable one, marked by a return to nature, qualified acceptance of natural right and a dialectical attitude to tradition. Engels's future philosophy lies in the critique of political economy, whereas Nietzsche turns to a new humanism and rejects modern economics and sociology. Liu says Engels would criticise Dionysus. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based comparison of Engels and Nietzsche on religion, metaphysics and morality, written from within Chinese Marxist philosophy.

The historical evolution and development trends of the socialist movement in West Asia and North Africa 西亚北非地区社会主义运动的历史演进与发展趋势 Chai Shangjin Lian Ying Chai and Lian ask how socialism has developed in the Arab region of West Asia and North Africa, and where it is heading. They argue that, as nationalist and political-Islamist forces weaken, Arab left-wing parties and communist parties in Turkey, Iraq, Egypt and elsewhere are becoming more active. In their view the movement is still growing, but it remains weak and of limited political influence. The article moves from ideas to organisations to the present day. It first examines Arab socialism, from Michel Aflaq's 1940s formulation to the state-led socialisms of Nasser's Egypt, Algeria, Syria, Iraq and Libya. It then sorts the region's left-wing parties into Marxist, socialist and nationalist types. Next it surveys the period since the "Arab Spring" country by country, covering Egypt, Tunisia, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Turkey, and ends with the movement's features and trends. The authors identify three shared traits of Arab socialism. It aims at national liberation and unity, with the Palestine question as its test. It is strongly nationalist, treating socialism as a means to national revival. It is rooted in Islam, which the authors say left parties see as containing egalitarian elements, while opposing Islamist fundamentalism. They argue that communist parties were hampered by dogmatism, dependence on the Soviet Union, poor understanding of national conditions and wavering positions on the national question. The authors also say many regimes used a socialist label to cover ethnic, nationalist or religious aims. Chai and Lian describe the present movement as engaged in national politics, focused on left unity (for example the Arab Left Forum), and keen on ties with the Communist Party of China. They expect parties to adjust theory and policy flexibly, to sharpen their socialist profile after the pandemic, and to need considerable time before rising as a whole. They give the main obstacle as the dominance of political Islam and populism, and the left's lack of agreement on how to respond. Read the original if you want a party-by-party survey of Arab and Turkish left organisations, written from a Chinese perspective that stresses their friendly relations with the Chinese Communist Party.

Chinese modernization and the construction of China's independent knowledge system 中国式现代化与中国自主知识体系构建 Sun Leqiang Writing in 2023, Sun Leqiang asks how Chinese philosophy and social science can build what Xi Jinping in 2022 called an independent knowledge system, and how this relates to the theory of Chinese modernization. The article takes up Xi's 2016 call for discipline, academic and discourse systems with Chinese characteristics. Sun judges that, seven years on, scholarly work still falls well short of what the Party and state expect. The thesis is that such a system must start from the autonomy of Chinese practice, be measured against world history, and rest on theorising that practice. The piece is organised in three parts: starting from "China", taking "all under heaven" as the yardstick, and grounding the work in practice. The first part sets out three ways of understanding China. The second compares Chinese and Western paths, and the third turns to the tasks of scholars. Sun draws on Marx on civil society and the Germanic form of property, on Engels's warning to Germany's "young ones", and on extensive quotation from Xi. Sun argues that the narrative "modernization equals Westernization" is a product of capital-led world history. Seen through Western yardsticks, China appears as a distorted "mirror image". Sun treats China as a generative process, as a totality of history and structure, and as an autonomous practical totality that never passed through an independent Western-style civil society. Against both "universalism" and "particularism", Sun contrasts the two paths. Capitalism is described as centred on private property, individuals and nation-states. Chinese modernization is described as public-ownership-based, people-centred, ecologically harmonious and oriented to a pluralistic civilisation and to a community with a shared future for mankind. Sun adds that it transcends capitalist modernity and represents a new form of human civilisation. Sun calls for concrete research that turns Marxist principles into the specific universality of Chinese society, for example by contrasting the Asiatic mode of production and public ownership with Germanic and capitalist forms. Such work should theorise China's particular experience as Smith, Ricardo, Hegel and Marx did for the British, German and Western paths, with the aim of producing a Chinese counterpart to The Wealth of Nations and Capital. Sun also urges enriching the "three laws" and rejecting a linear reading of the five social formations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist philosopher links Xi's calls for a self-reliant knowledge system to world-historical claims about Chinese modernization.

Three dimensions of Marx's conception of civilization 马克思文明观的三重维度 Huang Weiming Xue Xiujun This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2023, asks how Marx understood civilization. Huang and Xue argue that his view rests on three basic dimensions: human practice as the basis for analysing civilization, human development as the yardstick for assessing it, and human emancipation as the ideal pursued by communist civilization. The article is organised in three sections, one for each dimension. It begins by contrasting Marx with modern Western research on civilization, citing Guizot's historical work and Morgan's anthropology. It then turns to Marx's assessment of capitalist civilization, and ends with his picture of a communist stage of civilization. On practice, the authors say Enlightenment-influenced scholarship asserted human agency against theology but grasped the human being as an abstract generality. In their account, this led it into idealism, treating civilization as a product of ideas and desires. Marx instead started from material production, so that civilization is, in Engels's words quoted by the authors, a matter of practice. Productive forces are its ultimate determining force, and practice makes civilization a practical, historical and social category. On development, Huang and Xue say Marx credited capitalism's "civilizing side": vast productive forces, world-wide interaction, mastery over nature and free time for workers. He also condemned its "anti-civilizing side": exploitation for the sake of valorising capital, workers reduced to appendages of machines, and a dependence on things that leaves people as capital's "sacrificial victims". The authors conclude that Marx's aim in studying civilization was human liberation and the free and all-round development of the individual. They describe communist civilization as unifying three pairs: individual and others' development, labour and human development, and all-round human development and social progress. Labour there becomes self-realisation rather than a compulsory means of livelihood. Read the original if you want a compact, quotation-based outline of how Marx's account of civilization links practice, capitalism's contradictions and communist emancipation.

Marx and Engels's critique of the paradoxes of capitalist society 马克思恩格斯对资本主义社会悖论的批判 Liu Shuhui Liu Shuhui, writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (23 February 2023), asks how to understand the claim in the Communist Manifesto that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are "equally inevitable". The article argues that the claim can be understood through three paradoxes of capitalist society that Marx and Engels identify: wealth, freedom and civilization. Each, in Liu's reading, is an opposition produced by capitalism itself, and together they make bourgeois rule unsustainable. The piece is a short commentary on the history of Marxism, organised under three headings, one for each paradox. Liu draws mainly on the Manifesto and links it to other works by Marx and Engels, including The Poverty of Philosophy, Wage Labour and Capital, Capital, Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy and Marx's speech on free trade. A closing section ties the three paradoxes back to the Manifesto's thesis. On wealth, Liu describes the opposition between the accumulation of wealth and the accumulation of poverty. The bourgeoisie must guarantee workers at least a bare subsistence in order to rule, yet cannot do so, and in that sense society can no longer live under its rule. On freedom, Liu reads Marx's analysis in Capital as showing that freedom of buying and selling presupposes workers who have no means of production and are compelled to sell their labour-power. Free competition is likewise described as the highest form of private property, so that the worker's only freedom is the freedom to choose by whom to be exploited. On civilization, Liu follows Marx and Engels in holding that the bourgeoisie draws all nations into "civilization" while forcing them to adopt its mode of production and subordinating the East to the West through colonialism. The result, the article says, is a lopsided world. Liu concludes that the first two paradoxes lead workers to unite against their own national bourgeoisie, while the third leads the proletarians of the world to unite against the bourgeoisie as a class. In this sense the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are, as the article presents it, equally inevitable. Liu notes that the opposition between wealth and ecological destruction is not treated in the Manifesto and is therefore left aside. Read the original if you want a concise, text-based outline of how Chinese commentary reads the Manifesto's thesis of bourgeois collapse through the themes of wealth, freedom and civilization.

Continuously fulfilling the people's aspiration for a better life 不断实现人民对美好生活的向往 Peng Pingping This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today on 30 March 2023, interprets a passage of the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The passage calls for safeguarding and improving people's livelihoods through development and for continuously fulfilling the people's aspiration for a better life. Peng argues that this formula shows the Party's firm stance of standing with the people. In the author's account it also gives the Party a fundamental guide for keeping to its founding mission on the new journey. The piece has four sections. The first presents the aspiration for a better life as an expression of the Party's original aspiration and founding mission. The second traces the idea through the Party's century of struggle, from the revolution to the era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third and longest section sets out how the Party should move forward actively, under four headings: grasping the general trend of the times, starting from actual national conditions, focusing on real problems, and applying bottom-line thinking. Peng's central claim is that the Party has no interests of its own and represents the fundamental interests of the overwhelming majority. In this reading, every stage of its history, including the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and reform and opening up, was driven by the goal of people's happiness and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. For the present, the author stresses that China remains in the primary stage of socialism. The principal contradiction is described as the one between the people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, so economic development must stay the central task. The author adds that this lays the material basis for common prosperity and for Chinese modernization. Peng also calls for attention to people's most immediate concerns, for historical patience, and for stronger risk awareness and fighting spirit. Peng concludes that if the Party treats fulfilling the people's aspiration for a better life as the starting point and goal of modernization, and works for common prosperity, it will gather great strength and build a brighter future. The text is an official-style interpretive commentary on the congress report, not an independent analysis. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists present the link between the Party's mission, its history and the new journey after the 20th Party Congress.

Western left-wing scholars' critique of digital capitalism from the perspective of global governance 全球治理视域下西方左翼学者的数字资本主义批判 Song Jianli Song Jianli asks what Western left-wing communication scholars reveal about the risks that digital capitalism poses to global governance. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2023, Song argues that the critiques of Dan Schiller, Christian Fuchs and Dallas Smythe show how capital's logic widens the digital divide and installs invisible control. In Song's reading, this undermines both the equality and the democratisation of global governance. The article has three parts. The first treats the digital divide and its effect on equality, drawing on Schiller and Fuchs. The second turns to Smythe's "consciousness industry" and to later theories of surveillance and transparency (Foucault, Deleuze, Byung-Chul Han, Shoshana Zuboff, Christoph Kucklick), and considers algorithmic power and Herbert Schiller's "information geopolitics". The third part sets out the governance deficit in the digital economy and the prospect of a new form of human digital civilisation. Song reports that Fuchs shows how "productive consumers" supply unpaid labour to internet firms, which hides the unequal relation between capital and labour and supports global exploitation of digital labour. Schiller, in this account, denies that digitalisation relieves capitalist crisis or inequality, and argues that it strengthens transnational firms and marketisation. Song adds that US-led "digital imperialism" relies on data hegemony and knowledge monopoly. Smythe's work, together with Han's "transparency society", is used to argue that the democratic promise of networks is an illusion. Audiences labour unseen, voluntary self-exposure perfects surveillance, and transparency erodes trust. Kucklick's paradox of opaque machines producing transparency is presented as a governance dilemma. Song adds that "big-data positivism" depoliticises governance and threatens national political and cultural security. Song concludes that digital technology can either deepen global inequality or help reverse it, depending on whether it escapes the domination of capital interests. Governments should build open, fair and non-discriminatory rules for cyberspace and close the digital divide, with cooperation as the only viable path. The author expects China to play a more constructive role by acting on a global governance outlook of dialogue, inclusiveness and expanding common interests. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese overview of how Western critical communication scholarship on digital capitalism is being used in debates on global digital governance.

The cultural dimension of the "Two Integrations" and the development of sinicized Marxism “两个结合”的文化维度与中国化马克思主义的发展 Hong Jun Hong Jun asks why the requirement that Marxism be integrated with China's fine traditional culture, set out in Xi Jinping's 2021 speech on the Party's centenary and restated at the 20th Party Congress (2022), matters for the development of Marxism in China. The article argues that the cultural dimension of the Two Integrations is a conclusion drawn from more than a century of debate and practice. In Hong's account, giving it prominence clears away long-standing confusion and moves sinicized Marxism to a higher stage. The article is a historical-conceptual survey in four parts. It begins with Engels and Lenin on the "localisation" of Marxism, and with Stalin on national form and proletarian content, and notes the early Chinese Communists' attempts at adaptation. It then examines Mao Zedong's discussions of sinicization, followed by the mistaken views on the relation between Marxism and Chinese tradition, from both outside and inside the Marxist camp. The last part sets out the grounds on which the two are said to be compatible. Hong argues that Mao's 1938 report already contained two dimensions, a practical one (applying Marxism to Chinese conditions) and a historical-cultural one (critically inheriting the heritage "from Confucius to Sun Yat-sen"). Mao's letters to Chen Boda on Mozi and Confucius are cited as evidence of his classical learning. Even so, Mao and later formulations stressed the practical dimension, so understanding stayed at "one integration" for a long time. Hong attributes this to historical conditions and to widespread mistaken views. Cultural conservatives, Guomindang right-wingers and some dogmatists inside the Party all treated Marxism and Chinese culture as incompatible. Many early Communist leaders, shaped by the New Culture Movement, were nihilistic about tradition. Hong holds that the historical record refutes the claim that Marxism does not suit Chinese conditions, and points to an "affinity" between the two. Examples are the Confucian ideals of datong (great harmony) and xiaokang, the minben (people-as-basis) tradition, and ancient materialist and dialectical ideas, with support from Li Zehou. The influence ran both ways: tradition underwent modern transformation, and Marxism was enriched by it. Hong concludes that the 20th Congress formulation reflects cultural consciousness and confidence and provides theoretical support for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual-historical account of how Party theorists and their critics treated Marxism and Chinese tradition from the 1920s to the present.

How is the integration of Marxist basic principles with fine traditional Chinese culture possible? An examination centred on the social justice of the classical Marxist thinkers' attention to Chinese questions 马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合何以可能 Wang Shengyu Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and Xi Jinping's speech of 1 July 2021, the article asks how the basic principles of Marxism can be combined with fine traditional Chinese culture, which it abbreviates as the "Two Combinations" in the narrow sense. Wang argues that the answer lies in a shared "social justice" dimension: Marxist theory and Chinese culture are compatible because both express justice, and Marx and Engels's writings on China show this. The combination is therefore described as both legitimate and necessary. The article has three sections. The first sets out a "justice context" for the combination, addressing three doubts in the scholarly literature and reviewing five existing lines of interpretation. The second reads Marx and Engels's 1850s writings on China, including those on the Opium Wars and the opium trade, to show where the two traditions meet. The third draws practical implications for contemporary China under three headings, each beginning "着力于" (focusing on). Wang first treats the doubts as constructive. The "change of nature" worry is that Marxism's revolutionary character is lost. The "change of flavour" worry is that Chinese culture's distinctiveness is diluted. The "change of score" worry is that the integration stays theoretical and detached from practice. Wang then reads Marx and Engels as holding that a just nation raises a just cry, a just people pursues a just cause, and just practice needs just theory.
