On this reading, they backed Chinese resistance to aggression while criticising fatalism and the idea that violence drives development. Wang finds affinities between their views and values such as "the world belongs to all", people-centredness and harmony between humanity and nature. Wang concludes that the combination should aim to meet the people's need for a better life, advance the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics. For the last of these, the article points to institutional improvement, distributive justice and Chinese modernization. It presents social justice as a lens that unites the scientific character of theory with its practical necessity. Read the original if you want a justice-centred reading of Marx and Engels's China texts within current Party discourse on the Two Integrations.

The spread of "isms" in the May Fourth period and the opening of the path of Chinese modernization 五四时期“主义”传播与中国式现代化道路的开启 Sun Shan Sun Shan asks how the historical process now called Chinese modernization began, and answers that it was opened by the spread of Marxism as an "ism" during the May Fourth period. Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) formulation that Chinese modernization advances the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the author argues that the early dissemination of Marxism formed the essential link between China's modernization and scientific socialism. Combining intellectual history with social history under a "grand historical view", the article examines how Marxism spread after the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. It is organised in four parts, each tied to a core element of Chinese modernization: socialist direction, the path, the leading force, and the driving force. Evidence comes mainly from writings, letters and periodicals of Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Li Da and others, plus societies such as the Awakening Society and the New People's Study Society. Sun's central claim is that Marxism's propagation shaped each element in turn. Through debates with reformism, anarchism and Guild Socialism, Marxism gained discursive authority and fixed a socialist orientation, after the First World War had, in the author's account, shown capitalist modernization to be necessary but impossible for China. The turn to "learning from Russia" produced a "revolution–modernization" path, replacing reform with social revolution and moving Chinese modernization, in Sun's phrase, from passive to active. Early Marxist societies trained a core of cadres, and the Marxist theory of the proletarian party prepared the founding of the Communist Party as modernization's leading core. Finally, mobilisation of workers and peasants ("going to the people"), stress on popular agency and adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions formed its driving force. Sun concludes that the May Fourth spread of Marxism gave modernization in China its direction, path, leadership and driving force. It also sidestepped the capital-centred logic of Western modernization and gave China theoretical self-awareness and historical initiative. The author presents this as the value and historical starting point of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich account of how Chinese scholarship links early Marxist propagation to the origins of the current official modernization narrative.

Guiding and regulating the healthy development of capital under the socialist market economy 社会主义市场经济条件下引导和规范资本健康发展 Cai Wanhuan Cai Wanhuan takes up a question that Xi Jinping has described as a major theoretical and practical problem for Marxist political economy in the new era: how capital, which must exist in a socialist market economy, can be used for productive purposes while its negative effects are held to a minimum. The article argues that this requires a Marxist understanding of capital's nature and laws of behaviour, a clear definition of capital's place under socialism, and concrete rules for guiding and regulating it. The article has three parts. The first sets out the general attributes of capital under market conditions and its specific character under capitalist private ownership. The second examines capital under the socialist market economy, covering its historical positioning and the institutional advantages of socialism. The third proposes principles for regulation, including the Two Unwaverings, rules governing capital's conduct, and "red and green lights" for capital's entry into different sectors. Drawing on Marx's Capital, Cai holds that capital is not a thing or a real factor of production but a social relation of production embodied in a thing. Its profit-seeking drives cooperation, technical innovation and resource allocation, yet it also produces exploitation, monopoly, financialisation, a gap between expanding production and narrow worker consumption, and ideological influence. Under the socialist market economy, Cai says, capital is a tool and not an end, and the state should "master" it, rejecting both liberal opposition and Keynesian supplementation. Three institutional safeguards are named: a public sector as the mainstay, Communist Party leadership, and the balancing of long-term and short-term, whole and part. Cai argues that public enterprises are more efficient when measured by new value (v + s) created for society, not by profit alone. Cai concludes that public and non-public capital must be distinguished in nature and positioned clearly, with the Two Unwaverings applied only on the basis of public ownership as the mainstay. Regulation should cover labour's share of distribution, anti-monopoly enforcement (especially against platform and digital capital), enforcement of labour contract law, and restricted private capital in housing, healthcare and other livelihood areas. Capital must not be allowed to turn from servant into master. Read the original if you want a Marxist-economics account, from a Tsinghua scholar, of how Party theory justifies regulating private capital after the 20th Party Congress (2022).

From "categorical sophistry" to "critique of capital": how Engels surpassed the classical political economy of poverty 从“范畴诡辩”到“资本批判”：恩格斯对古典政治经济学贫困理论的超越 Wu Dajuan Xue Junqiang Wu Dajuan and Xue Junqiang ask how Friedrich Engels's theory of poverty broke with that of classical political economy. They argue that existing scholarship treats Engels mainly as a "bridge" to Marx's critique of political economy and as a subordinate of Marx's own poverty theory, and neglects his original contribution. In their account, Engels lifted the question of poverty from "categorical speculation" to a "critique of capital", opening a scientific path distinct from classical economics. The article has three parts. The first characterises classical political economy (Adam Smith, Ricardo, Malthus) as ahistorical and uncritical. The second sets out Engels's critique in three steps: of the "economic man" premise, of the way classical economists explain the roots of poverty, and of their remedies. The third draws out the spirit and value of Engels's break, drawing on Althusser, Marcuse, Harvey, Foucault and Polanyi as supporting voices. The authors claim that classical economists treated capitalist relations as eternal natural law and reduced poverty to individual failings or to distribution. Engels, they argue, showed that capital is not accumulated labour but a social means by which people rule people, and that poverty springs from capitalist private property and competition rather than from "small abuses". They read his phrase "social murder" as exposing a hidden form of capitalist exploitation, and compare it to Foucault's panopticon. Engels also treated political economy as a "historical science", embedding poverty in the history of industry, politics and the workers' movement. The authors conclude that Engels offered a new "problematic" rather than a correction of the old one. On their reading, he held that small repairs are futile unless the ownership system built on the propertylessness of the majority is abolished, and that poverty is overcome only through the workers' liberation and communism. They present his fieldwork, journalism and later work on Capital and the Second International as combining scientific rigour with humanistic concern. Read the original if you study Engels's independent role in Marxist poverty theory or the Chinese reception of his early economic writings.

Advancing Chinese modernization through informatization and contributing to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 以信息化推进中国式现代化为中华民族伟大复兴贡献力量 Zhuang Rongwen Writing in 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhuang Rongwen, a senior official in China's cyberspace administration, argues that informatization should be pursued deliberately as a route to Chinese modernization. The article says the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the "great changes unseen in a century" and the information revolution are converging historically. In Zhuang's account, informatization enriches the setting, path, driving forces and goals of Chinese modernization and offers a rare opportunity. The piece is organised in six sections. It begins with Xi Jinping's statements on informatization, such as "without informatization there can be no modernization". It then covers the Party's achievements in cyberspace work since 2012, the major principles of Chinese modernization, and the five features of Chinese modernization set out in the 20th Party Congress report. It also covers the key relationships to be handled and the strategic arrangements for building a cyber power. Each section ends with tasks for the cyberspace and informatization field. Zhuang's central move is to read the principles and features of Chinese modernization as direct guidance for internet work. Informatization is said to be an accelerator of the "four modernizations" (new-type industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization), which the article says must develop in parallel rather than in sequence as in the West. The author cites digital economy growth from 11 trillion yuan in 2012 to 45.5 trillion yuan in 2021 and 1.051 billion internet users by June 2022. Party leadership is treated as decisive. The principle that the Party manages the internet is said to have ended the earlier fragmented "nine dragons controlling the water" arrangement. Zhuang also pairs each feature of Chinese modernization with a task. These include using the world's largest user base, spreading the gains of the internet to all, developing the digital economy alongside online culture, promoting green digital transformation, and building a community with a shared future in cyberspace. Zhuang concludes with a list of priorities. They are digital infrastructure, breakthroughs in core technologies through the new whole-nation system, a stronger digital economy, digital government and society, digital culture, digital ecological civilization, cybersecurity, and international cooperation including a "Digital Silk Road". The author calls for building a cyber power in step with the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Chinese official presents the cyberspace and digital agenda within the official framework of Chinese modernization.

Chinese modernization broadens the paths to modernization open to developing countries 中国式现代化拓展发展中国家走向现代化的路径选择 Chai Shangjin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2023, no. 6), Chai Shangjin asks what Chinese modernization offers developing countries. The article opens from Xi Jinping's remark that each country's people are best placed to judge which modernization suits them. Chai argues that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of "modernization = Westernization" and gives developing countries a new model for independent modernization. The piece has three parts. The first treats Chinese modernization as an innovation in world modernization theory and practice, tracing the Communist Party's role through the new-democratic revolution, the founding of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second contrasts Chinese modernization with the Western pattern. The third sets out its significance for humanity's common problems and for developing countries. Chai's central claim is that Chinese modernization differs from Western modernization in kind. In the article's account, Western modernization began with enclosures and colonial plunder and has always been bound by the "logic of capital", which produces polarisation between rich and poor. Chinese modernization is described as people-centred and aimed at common prosperity, balancing material and cultural-ethical progress and harmony between humanity and nature. Chai also holds that Party leadership determines its fundamental direction and success. Chai adds that it follows the path of peaceful development rather than hegemony or resource plunder, and that the West-led model has brought widening North–South gaps, crises and conflict. Chai concludes that no country has succeeded by copying developed countries' models, that no fixed model of modernization exists, and that each country should explore a path suited to its own conditions. Chinese modernization, in this reading, shows the Western road is not the only one and will keep widening developing countries' options, while China seeks shared development with them. Read the original if you want a concise statement, in the official register of 2023, of how Chinese modernization is presented as a model and a contrast to Western modernization for the Global South.

Serving Chinese modernization through high-quality educational modernization 以高质量教育现代化服务支撑中国式现代化 Zhang Jun Writing in Guangming Daily in 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Jun asks how universities should carry out the Congress's guidance on Chinese modernization. The author argues that educational modernization and Chinese modernization are dialectically united, and that universities must place themselves within the larger picture of national development and serve what the article calls the "matters of greatest national importance". The commentary is organised around four perspectives: the political, the systemic, the long-term, and digitalisation. It draws on the experience of Beijing Institute of Technology, where the author is Party Secretary, as an illustration. Zhang contends that Chinese modernization requires educational modernization to come first, and that Party leadership is its political guarantee. Universities are to cultivate talent through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and red cultural resources. Zhang then reads the Congress report's joint planning of education, science and technology, and talent as a "trinity" and calls for a "big education view". Disciplines are treated as the core unit of this trinity, with talent training, technological self-reliance and talent-team building all tied to national strategic needs, including "bottleneck" technologies. Zhang calls for a high-quality education system, with the Double First-Class initiative shifting from "catching up in quantity" to "surpassing in quality". Zhang also urges an education digitalisation strategy and a modernised system of school governance, and says this could offer a Chinese approach to global education governance. Read the original if you want a short example of how a senior university Party leader links Party leadership, discipline building and digital education to Chinese modernization.

Independent innovation in the path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化道路的自主创新 Luo Yuting Luo Yuting asks what makes the path of Chinese modernization distinctive and answers that its defining feature is independent innovation (zizhu chuangxin). Independence and self-reliance, in Luo's account, are the soul of the national spirit, and innovative development is the essence of the spirit of the times. The article presents the path as one the Communist Party opened by proceeding from China's concrete realities and the fundamental interests of the people. The article is organised around four 'combinations' that Luo treats as innovations of the path: national independence with independent exploration; universal truth with concrete conditions; socialism with the market economy; and primary reliance on indigenous innovation with learning from others as a supplement. Each section sets out the historical, theoretical and policy grounds for the claim. Evidence ranges from modern Chinese history and the 'two bombs, one satellite' programme to industrial statistics and the experience of Japan and South Korea. Luo first contrasts independent modernization with modernization permitted within the bounds of imperialism, which the author describes as dependent on international monopoly capital. In this reading, the failures of the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1898 reforms and the 1911 Revolution show that dependent modernization cannot succeed. Luo argues that Japan and South Korea became 'vassal-type' modernizers, constrained by the United States. By contrast, the author stresses China's complete industrial system, which the article says includes every category in the UN industrial classification. Luo then argues that the path rests on Marxist principles, including socialized large-scale production and science and technology as a productive force, applied to China's national conditions, culture and the goal of common prosperity. The central 'combination' of socialism and the market, in Luo's view, produces a 'two-way coupling' of state macro-regulation with market vitality, of regulating capital with preventing its disorderly expansion, and of efficiency with fairness. Luo concludes that China must rely mainly on its own innovation, especially in science and technology, because core technologies cannot be bought, particularly amid what the author calls a technology war waged by the United States and its allies. Learning from other countries remains a necessary supplement, so that self-reliance does not become self-isolation. Luo contends that adhering to this path is essential to building a modern socialist country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a representative Party-theory account of how Chinese modernization is justified as independent, Marxist and innovation-led.

Upholding and developing Marxism requires integrating it with China's fine traditional culture 坚持和发展马克思主义，必须同中华优秀传统文化相结合 Zhang Lu This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 18 April 2023, explains the statement in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) that upholding and developing Marxism requires combining it with China's fine traditional culture. Zhang argues that this integration deepens the Party's understanding of how to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and expresses the Party's cultural confidence and cultural self-awareness. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks that traditional culture is the "root" of the Party's theoretical innovation. It then moves through the historical reasons for the integration, the influence of traditional culture on China's path, theory and institutions, and the tasks ahead on the "new journey". Zhang's central claim is that Marxism took root in China because it resonated with values the Chinese people had inherited over millennia and held without always noticing. In this account, the values of fine traditional culture are highly compatible with those of scientific socialism, which is the precondition for the integration. Citing Xi, Zhang holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics carries a "genetic code" from traditional culture, and that the national governance system draws on it. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article says, ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the foundation of the state" have been reinterpreted as sources for the core socialist values. The relationship is presented as mutual: Chinese Marxism gains Chinese style, while tradition gains new content from Marxism's truth. Zhang calls for stronger historical and cultural confidence and a deeper grasp of the Two Integrations. The article urges drawing out the philosophy, humanism, values and moral norms of traditional culture, so as to give the Party's innovative theory distinct Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of why the Chinese Communist Party links Marxism to traditional culture.

Raising political capacity through stronger theoretical cultivation 在加强理论修养中提高政治能力 Li Linbao This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in April 2023, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks at the 90th anniversary of the Central Party School. Xi said that the firmer a leading cadre's grasp of Marxism, the higher their political standing and the stronger their political judgement, political comprehension and political execution. Li argues that theoretical cultivation is the core of a leading cadre's overall quality and largely determines their political capacity. The piece first explains why openly emphasising politics is a mark of Marxist parties and a long-standing strength of the Party. It then takes the three capacities in turn: political judgement, political comprehension and political execution. For each it sets out what theoretical study should contribute. On judgement, Li holds that systematic mastery of Marxist theory, especially the Party's innovative theory of the new era, sharpens the ability to read situations, tell right from wrong and resist risks. Cadres should use Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to "forge their souls" and spot political problems early. On comprehension, the author calls for deep study of that thought, an understanding of the Two Establishes, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and close alignment with the Central Committee. On execution, Li says cadres must check their work against Party theory, line and Central Committee decisions, carry out what the Centre decides, and face problems directly. Li concludes that theoretical maturity underpins political maturity, and that study should end in faithful implementation of Central Committee decisions. The aim is to keep advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary links theoretical study to cadres' political capacities.

Demonstrating the power of scientific modes of thinking and working Lessons from China's three-year COVID-19 response 展现科学思想方法和工作方法的强大力量 Ding Jinqing Writing in the People's Daily in April 2023, after China moved to a new phase of COVID-19 management, Ding argues that the pandemic response shows the strength of the scientific ways of thinking and working that the Communist Party has long stressed. The commentary holds that the response, led by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, reflects both the advantages of Party leadership and of the socialist system, and the practical power of these methods. The piece is a short official commentary organised under five headings: strategic resolve and decisive decision-making; seeking truth from facts; a systems approach; bottom-line thinking; and respect for scientific spirit and technology. Each heading opens with a statement by Xi Jinping and then links it to episodes of the pandemic response, from the closing of outbound routes from Wuhan and Hubei in January 2020 to the downgrading of management of the infection on 8 January 2023. Ding's central move is to read each stage of the response as an application of a named method. The shift from the "dynamic zero-COVID" policy to category B management is presented as flexible adjustment to the weakened pathogenicity of Omicron, wider vaccination and accumulated experience, and as evidence of seeking truth from facts. The principle of "containing the epidemic, stabilising the economy, ensuring development security" is described as a systems approach, supported by the "six stabilities" and "six guarantees" and by the author's figure of a 2022 GDP of 121 trillion yuan. Bottom-line thinking appears in preparing for worst cases, in support for small firms and the most vulnerable, and in strengthening the public health emergency system. The final section stresses science-led decisions, research on vaccines, tests and treatments, and public science education. Ding concludes that these methods let the Party keep the strategic initiative, and that the outcome shows the power of scientific thinking and working methods. The article offers no critical appraisal of the response; it is an affirmative account that also serves as a guide to how Party theory frames the pandemic experience. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2023 presented the pandemic response as a demonstration of Marxist methodology.

Treating science with a scientific attitude and pursuing truth in the spirit of truth 以科学的态度对待科学 以真理的精神追求真理 Zhong Xiaowu This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in April 2023, takes up Xi Jinping's call to treat science with a scientific attitude and pursue truth in the spirit of truth. Zhong argues that Marxism is the Party's fundamental guiding ideology but is not a fixed dogma. In Zhong's account, it is an open theoretical system that develops with the times, practice and science, and its vitality lies in uniting adherence to Marxism with its development. The piece moves from Marxism in general to the Chinese Communist Party's own record and then to present tasks. It first recalls what Marxism reveals about social development and capitalism, then reviews more than a century of Party practice, then sets out what is required now. Zhong notes that Marx and Engels described their theory as a guide to action, applied according to historical conditions. Marxists have therefore kept their theory alive by adjusting it to national circumstances, history and the demands of the age. The Party, in this reading, has done the same through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, combining its basic principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Zhong says, this produced Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, described as a new leap and an original theoretical contribution. Zhong concludes that practice and theoretical innovation have no end, and that Chinese communists today have a historic duty to keep writing new chapters. Citing Xi, Zhong rejects both dogmatism and pragmatism. Zhong calls for attention to major practical and strategic problems in building a modern socialist country, close links with the creative practice of the masses, and absorption of the achievements of other civilisations. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the official press justifies continuing theoretical innovation in Marxism.

Showcasing the distinctive character of "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" in the new era 彰显新时代守正创新的鲜明气象 Qin Gang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 12 April 2023, takes up one of the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): the requirement to uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground (shouzheng chuangxin). Qin Gang argues that this principle is a regular pattern the Party has drawn from a century of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In the author's account it is also a distinctive mark of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and of the new era itself. The piece is built in three parts, each opened and anchored by quotations from Xi Jinping. The first treats the principle as an experience of Party theory and practice. The second presents it as an objective requirement for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third presents it as methodological guidance for advancing Chinese modernization. The article was written to support the study campaign on Xi Jinping Thought launched in 2023. Qin's first move is to root the principle in both Marxism and Chinese tradition. The author reads Marx and Engels's statements that the application of the Manifesto's principles depends on historical conditions, and that theory is not a dogma to be repeated mechanically, as early expressions of the idea. The author then pairs these with classical Chinese sayings about renewal and adapting to the times, and presents the principle as the outcome of combining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. Second, Qin defines the relationship between the two halves. Upholding principles means not wavering on Marxism, the Party's overall leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, but it is not rigid adherence to old formulas. Innovation, in turn, must have roots and a source. Third, Qin credits this approach, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), with the new ideas and strategies of the new era, the elimination of absolute poverty and the building of a moderately prosperous society. The author also credits it with a theory of Chinese modernization that presents it as a new form of human civilisation, distinct from the Western model. Qin concludes that the Party must keep to this method as the world undergoes what the article calls changes unseen in a century, and as it faces new risks and challenges. By keeping national development based on its own strength, the author says, the Party can win new victories in building a modern socialist country. Qin calls on readers to turn the worldview, methodology and standpoint of Xi Jinping Thought into their own intellectual tools. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2023 presented "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" as a methodology that links Marxism, Chinese tradition and Chinese modernization.

Embracing the world: demonstrating the responsibility of a major Party and a major country 胸怀天下彰显大党大国责任担当 Su Changhe This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 17 April 2023, explains one of the "six musts" (liù ge bìxū jiānchí) in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era: the requirement to "embrace the world" (xiōnghuái tiānxià). Su Changhe presents this as a standpoint and method that the Communist Party of China uses to understand and handle its relations with the outside world. The author argues that it shows the global outlook and sense of responsibility of a major Party and a major country. The piece is organised under three headings. The first concerns grasping global trends and the tide of the times. The second concerns placing China's own development within the framework of human development. The third concerns building a community with a shared future for mankind. It draws throughout on statements by Xi Jinping, and it opens by situating the topic at the point where the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation intersects with what it calls changes unseen in a century. In Su's account, Xi applies dialectical and historical materialism to the international situation. Xi reaches several judgements: peace, development, cooperation and win-win outcomes remain the main line; economic globalization is a historical trend despite setbacks; and China is still in a period of strategic opportunity. Su then argues that the Party pursues its own development in step with the world's. The Belt and Road Initiative, trade expos and regional trade agreements are cited as ways of sharing opportunities, and Chinese modernization is described as rejecting colonial plunder and the path of a strong country seeking hegemony. The third section lists the principles, initiatives and values Xi has put forward to build a community with a shared future for mankind. These include the Global Development, Global Security and Global Civilization Initiatives and the "common values of all humanity". The article contends that hegemonic power, zero-sum games and ideological confrontation push the world towards division. Su concludes that, whatever happens internationally, the Party will remain consistent in embracing the world. It will use Chinese modernization to advance national rejuvenation, add stability to the cause of peace and development, and uphold the common values of all humanity. The text reads as an authoritative exposition of official foreign-policy thinking in the early period after the 20th Party Congress. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Chinese official discourse in 2023 framed the link between domestic development, Chinese modernization and the idea of a shared-future community.

How to kill the greedy capitalist glutton: reading Nancy Fraser's Cannibal Capitalism 如何干掉贪婪的资本饕餮——解读南希·弗雷泽的《食人资本主义》 Lan Jiang This is a review essay on Nancy Fraser's Cannibal Capitalism (Verso, 2022). Lan asks why Fraser calls contemporary capitalism, especially after the Covid-19 pandemic, 'cannibal', and how it 'eats' people. Lan's answer is that the book marks Fraser's break with the feminist identity politics and redistributive reformism of her early career, and her return to a thoroughgoing critique of the capitalist system itself. The review first traces Fraser's intellectual path: her feminist and Frankfurt School background, her debate with Axel Honneth over recognition and redistribution, and the later influence of Rahel Jaeggi. It then turns to the two resources Fraser draws on, Marx's critique of political economy and Karl Polanyi's The Great Transformation. It closes with the book's periodisation of capitalism, its account of the financial stage, and its reading of the pandemic. Lan argues that Fraser first treated redistribution as a supplement to Honneth's recognition theory, but that this already implied capitalism cannot solve inequality from within. A 2016 conversation with Jaeggi, later published as Capitalism: A Conversation in Critical Theory (2018), pushed her to see capital as a self-propelling subject that feeds on humans. Fraser then extends Marx: exploitation of workers rests on the 'expropriation' of colonies, racialised groups, women's care work and nature. Following Polanyi, she separates the economic system from the social and natural conditions that make it possible. In Fraser's periodisation, merchant, liberal-colonial, state-managed and now financialised capitalism each consume these foundations in new ways. The ouroboros on the cover expresses a system that devours its own base. Lan's example is the care work that financialised firms commodify, such as paying for surrogacy and egg freezing for female employees. Lan concludes that Fraser regards the pandemic as the point where the contradictions of cannibal capitalism converge, and as proof that the system must be abolished. Lan reads the book as showing that equality can only be reached by discarding the capitalist order, and ends with Fraser's call to 'starve the beast'. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Fraser's shift from recognition politics to anti-capitalist critique, or a concise map of her debts to Honneth, Jaeggi, Marx and Polanyi.

The genesis, theoretical construction and contemporary value of Lenin's organisational building A re-examination from the perspective of democratic centralism 列宁加强组织建设的生成逻辑、理论建构与时代价值 Liu Jinxu Li Genshou Liu Jinxu and Li Genshou ask how Lenin's thinking on Party organisation, and above all his doctrine of democratic centralism, arose, what it consisted of, and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. They argue that Lenin inherited Marx and Engels's Party-building theory and shaped it through the practical problems of the Russian revolution. In their view it remains a classic body of theory with direct lessons for the Party's governance. The article, published in Tangdu Journal in 2023, has three parts. The first traces the origins of Lenin's thinking in Marx and Engels's Party theory and in Russian revolutionary practice, from the 1890s to the formal adoption of democratic centralism at the Fourth Congress of the Russian Social-Democratic Labour Party in 1906. The second reconstructs the theory itself. The third draws out four lessons for the present. In reconstructing the theory, the authors identify four concerns. The first is organisation: a tightly disciplined vanguard, with Party members' quality prized over their numbers, against Menshevik proposals for a looser membership. The second is democracy: the Party congress as supreme authority, convened regularly, with elected rather than appointed committees whose members can be recalled. The third is members' agency: rights to be informed and to decide, and wider discretion for local organisations. The fourth is unity: free discussion and comradely criticism, minority rights, majority rule and a single programme and statute, together with opposition to the Economists, the Mensheviks and factionalism. The authors present these as developing the Marx–Engels model of congresses, elections and reporting systems. For the present, the authors draw four lessons. They call for a better-developed institutional system, so that institutional strengths become governance capacity. They call for stricter discipline and Party spirit, with the Party's self-reform leading social revolution; they cite figures from anti-corruption investigations since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They also urge holding to a people-centred stance and upholding collective leadership together with the Two Upholds. Democratic centralism is described as the Party's greatest institutional advantage. Read the original if you want to see how Lenin's Party-building is turned into a Chinese Party-building agenda, and how Chinese scholarship links Lenin to current Party discipline and leadership.

Opening up a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Lin Zhenyi This commentary, published in the People's Daily on 29 March 2023, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's statement that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is a process of seeking, revealing and acting on truth. Lin Zhenyi, a secretary-general at the Central Party School's research centre on Xi Jinping Thought, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era achieves a new leap in this process and opens a new realm for it. It is presented as the latest in a line running from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The article is organised in four sections. The first deals with how the thought answers the major questions of the era. The second considers its original theoretical contributions. The third turns to its guiding role in practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The fourth discusses its contribution to the world through Chinese wisdom and Chinese solutions. Lin's core claim is that the thought answers the questions of the new era: what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold, how to build a modern socialist country, and how to build a Marxist party that stays long in power. In Lin's account it offers an answer on Party building through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, which is said to be a way of escaping the historical cycle of rise and decline. Theoretically, Lin says it combines Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, and has become a coherent system summarised in the 'ten affirmations', the 'fourteen commitments', the 'thirteen areas of achievement' and the 'six stances' of the 20th Party Congress report. Lin credits the thought and the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core with the achievements of the past decade, and calls the Two Establishes the most important political outcome of the new era. Lin concludes that a great theory is necessarily global in reach. The article lists the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind, the Belt and Road Initiative, the Global Development, Security and Civilization Initiatives and common values of humanity as contributions to peace and development. It presents these as evidence of the world significance of twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily framing of Xi Jinping Thought as a new stage in the adaptation of Marxism.

How to keep up an enterprising spirit at all times Maintaining the drive to get things done and start new undertakings 如何始终保持干事创业精神状态 Huang Jian This short commentary, first published in People's Daily and posted in May 2023, asks how the Communist Party can always keep the mental state needed to get things done and start new undertakings (ganshi chuangye). Huang Jian calls this a problem peculiar to the Party that it must solve. The author argues that only by keeping this spirit can the Party lead the people in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The piece first explains why the question matters, pointing to historical cases in which rulers grew complacent after long peace and their governments collapsed. It then recalls the Party's long awareness of the danger, citing Mao Zedong's call before national victory to keep up a modest, prudent and hard-working style, and Xi Jinping's warnings. It lists measures taken since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with practical requirements for Party members and cadres. Huang contends that the Party's rise and the nation's revival came from struggle, and that complacency or love of comfort would endanger the Party's vanguard character and vitality. The author describes cadres' mental state as the combined expression of ambition, responsibility, drive and work style, which decides whether the Party's blueprint becomes reality. Three problems must be solved: willingness, through study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and firm ideals; ability, through learning from books, practice and the masses; and courage, through combining strict management with care, and through a mechanism that tolerates and corrects errors. Huang concludes that cadres should take on heavy responsibilities in economic development, grassroots work and service to the people. Those who dare to struggle and take responsibility should be backed and boldly promoted. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary frames cadre morale and incentives in 2023.

Advancing theoretical and practical innovation in Chinese modernization through a systems perspective 以系统观念推进中国式现代化理论和实践创新 Zang Fengyu Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2023, Zang Fengyu takes up the theory of Chinese modernization set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and asks how a systems perspective can guide its theoretical and practical development. The article argues that Chinese modernization is a "systematic project" that must be understood through universal connection, comprehensiveness and development, and managed through forward-looking thinking, overall planning and integrated advancement. The piece has two main parts. The first applies the systems perspective to the content and essence of Chinese modernization, covering its institutional guarantees, material foundation and spiritual strength, its five distinctive features and the nine essential requirements listed in the Congress report. The second turns to six pairs of relationships that Xi Jinping named as needing correct handling, and ends with a note on the habits of thought required. Zang's central claim is that the features, essential requirements and major principles of Chinese modernization are themselves systematic, so the theory is "clear, scientific" and workable in practice. In the account given, Party leadership determines its basic character, and it is said to have discarded the antagonistic contradictions produced by the logic of capital and to offer a new form of human civilisation. The second part treats top-level design and practical exploration, strategy and tactics, upholding fundamental principles and innovation, efficiency and fairness, vitality and order, and self-reliance and opening up. Each is presented as a dialectical pair whose two sides define and condition each other. Zang gives, for example, innovation as the key and "upholding principles" as the foundation, and describes China's rapid growth and long-term social stability as two "miracles". Zang concludes that these relationships will keep generating new contradictions, and calls for stronger strategic, historical, dialectical, systems, innovative, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. The aim is development that is higher in quality, efficiency, fairness, sustainability and security, and further practical creation of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Xi Jinping's "major relationships" framework is applied to Chinese modernization.

The evolution of Party Congress themes since the 15th Party Congress and adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 党的十五大以来党代会主题演进与马克思主义中国化时代化 Duan Yan Duan Yan asks what the themes of the six Party Congress reports since the 15th Party Congress (1997) reveal about the process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article argues that this process runs through the whole sequence. In Duan's account, the Party has repeatedly judged the era, the national conditions and the Party's own situation, and has used these judgements to advance theoretical innovation. Duan notes that the 15th Congress was the first to condense its content into a stated theme, and that later reports have opened with one. The article is built in four parts, followed by lessons for the present. It first traces how the themes reflect the Party's reading of the era (peace and development), of the basic national condition (the primary stage of socialism) and of the historical position (the new era). It then follows the phased goals named in the themes, from building a moderately prosperous society to a modern socialist country. Third, it reviews the guiding ideology each theme proclaims, from Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Duan's central claim is that each theme joins a judgement of the times to a concrete task and a theoretical banner. The goals are said to apply Marx's and Lenin's idea of socialism and communism as developing in stages, linking long-term and near-term aims. The ideological sequence is presented as continuous innovation: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and finally Xi Jinping Thought, which the 20th Party Congress (2022) described as a new leap. Duan credits the Two Integrations with giving Marxism Chinese features and with drawing on traditional culture. Duan draws six lessons for further adaptation: put the people first, maintain self-confidence and self-reliance, uphold fundamental principles while innovating, remain problem-oriented, use systematic thinking, and keep the whole world in view. The author insists that holding to fundamental principles means rejecting dogmatism and ossification as well as distortions of Marxism, and that self-reliance does not mean closing the door to other civilisations. Read the original if you want a close reading of how Party Congress themes since 1997 are officially tied to the theory of adapting Marxism.

Where it lies and what to do: new thinking on the creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture 何在与何为：中华优秀传统文化创造性转化的新思考 Zuo Yuhe Starting from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls for combining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, Zuo Yuhe asks which traditional resources are truly "fine" and how they can be creatively transformed. The article argues that such resources exist in China's ideas of governance, morality and the conduct of life. It holds that they must be sifted with a Marxist standpoint, method and viewpoint, and renewed so as to serve contemporary socialist culture. The article is organised in five parts and draws heavily on Xi Jinping's remarks on traditional culture. It first treats the ideological core and "cultural genes" of Chinese civilisation. It then surveys political resources, namely the people-as-foundation idea (minben) and the Confucian ideal of the Great Harmony (datong), and moral and life-philosophy teachings from Confucius, Mencius, Mozi, Xunzi, Fan Zhongyan, Zhang Zai and others. The last two parts discuss the method of transformation and warn against two wrong tendencies. Zuo's central argument is that the tradition falls into three kinds: elements that are progressive and democratic in character and should be inherited, elements serving the ruling class that should be criticised and removed, and a large mixed category that is hardest to judge. Confucian ren (benevolence) is the example: it is bound to hierarchical ritual, yet also expresses universal love with humanist and popular content. Even apparent dross such as ritual, loyalty and filial piety may be reinterpreted in an egalitarian sense once their patriarchal content is stripped away. Zuo reads the Great Harmony ideal and minben thought as sources that helped Chinese thinkers move towards modern democracy and socialism. Zuo identifies two errors to guard against. Cultural and historical nihilism, rooted in cultural inferiority, is said to lead to Westernisation and to denial of the revolution, reform and opening up, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Cultural restorationism, rooted in complacency, is said to include attempts to "Confucianise" Marxism. Zuo insists that the Party's guiding ideology is Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought and the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, not Confucian culture. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated historian's account of how Chinese scholars are expected to sort the "essence" of tradition from its "dross" in the Marxist-Chinese culture agenda.

Is there "civil society" in the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right? 《黑格尔法哲学批判》中存在“市民社会”吗？ Kong Weiyu Kong Weiyu starts from Engels's 1885 claim that it is civil society that conditions and determines the state, and from the habit of reading that claim as the state of the young Marx's thought in 1843–44. The article asks what Marx meant by "civil society" in his manuscript Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, which Engels had not seen. Kong's answer is that the concept there is ambiguous and unfinished, and is neither Hegel's concept nor the later historical-materialist one. The piece is a short theoretical commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2023. It is organised around four questions: whether the concept exists at all in the manuscript, whether it exists in Hegel's sense, whether it exists as an "economic base", and whether it exists in a humanist sense. Kong draws on Marx's German terminology, the structure of Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right, and Marx's later retrospective remarks. On terminology, Kong notes that the manuscript is loose in its wording. Marx sometimes replaces "civil society" with "the individual", which Kong reads as showing that he then conceived civil society as made up of individual rights. Kong also distinguishes the French-derived term for aristocratic "society" from "bürgerliche Gesellschaft", and argues that the former is pejorative and must not be confused with civil society. On Hegel, the surviving manuscript begins at the "State" section (§261), and Kong argues that no lost part could have treated the long civil-society chapter, so no sustained analysis of it exists. Marx's civil society is a flat, non-structured body of private citizens held together by marriage, contract and legally conceived property. In Kong's view, this is why Marx could not carry out a materialist inversion of Hegel's structured "state–civil society–family" system and "only turns in circles within abstract right". Political economy had not yet been studied systematically, so the concept only emerges properly in the 1844 Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. Kong concludes that the manuscript's civil society has a humanist side: it must first sublate the feudal political state, and in the future it would itself be sublated, so that the "true human being" appears. Kong sees this as an expression of Marx's humanist materialism of the time. Read the original if you study the young Marx's development, the translation of bürgerliche Gesellschaft, or the gap between his 1843 manuscript and Engels's later reading of it.

The meaning and connotations of common prosperity in spiritual life 精神生活共同富裕的意义内涵 Wan Ping Writing in a newspaper commentary in March 2023, Wan Ping asks what common prosperity in spiritual life means, taking as a starting point Xi Jinping's call at the tenth meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission to promote it under the guidance of core socialist values. Wan notes that scholars still debate the concept and mostly stress the functional, mutually supportive relation between the spiritual and the material. The author argues that this neglects the concept's "generative" dimension, and that common prosperity in spiritual life is an organic unity of three ideals. The article is built around these three ideals: an ideal of inner richness in personal life, a social ideal of harmony between individual and society, and a national dream of promoting all-round human development. A closing section ties them to the core socialist values. On the first ideal, Wan holds that material abundance does not automatically produce spiritual prosperity and that some groups may fall into a "spiritual poverty trap". The author calls for drawing on Zhuangzi and Kant, promoting a view of life based on contribution and goodness, curbing consumerism, and giving spiritual support to disadvantaged groups. On the second, Wan points to Confucian ethics and to digital technology's potential for "warm" social ties. On the third, Wan argues that earlier states, limited by class, could do little for all-round development, whereas the socialist state makes it a national aim, which Xi Jinping raised to the level of the Chinese Dream after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Wan concludes that the first two ideals are the starting point of the third, while the third guarantees their realisation. Core socialist values at the national, social and individual levels are said to guide all three, and spiritual and material civilization are to advance together. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars link common prosperity to spiritual life, core socialist values and human development.

Grasping the meaning of the fighting spirit through materialist dialectics 基于唯物辩证法领悟斗争精神意涵 Zhang Tinghui This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2023, asks how the Party's call to be "bold and skilful in struggle" can be understood philosophically. Zhang argues that the fighting spirit is rooted in materialist dialectics, specifically the Marxist theory of contradiction. The piece follows the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which told the whole Party to be "bold and skilful in struggle". The article has four sections, each tying one aspect of contradiction theory to the practice of struggle. They cover the basic properties of contradiction, its universality and objectivity, the method of contradiction analysis, and the struggle aspect of contradiction. Zhang draws on Mao Zedong, Marx and Xi Jinping, and traces the wording of the 18th, 19th and 20th Party Congress reports on "great struggle". Zhang holds that contradictions exist everywhere and independently of human will, so the willingness to acknowledge, expose and analyse them is the philosophical basis of daring to struggle. Skill in struggle comes from the method of contradiction analysis: distinguishing principal from secondary contradictions, concentrating on the former while coordinating the latter, and analysing each concrete problem on its own terms. This includes judging the timing, effect and degree of struggle. On the struggle aspect, Zhang says unity of opposites is conditional and relative while struggle is absolute, so the Party should unite all forces it can and work to shift the balance between the two sides. Zhang concludes that this orientation shows the Party's resolve in dealing with the problems unique to a large Party in the world. The author states that, with unity around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the Party can draw on Marxism to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary grounds the official language of struggle in the vocabulary of dialectical materialism.

Building a discourse system of institutions from the perspective of conceptual history 概念史视角下的制度话语体系建构 Yang Binbin This commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) on 30 March 2023, asks how a discourse system for the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics can be built. Yang Binbin argues that conceptual history, a method that traces how concepts evolve in order to present historical logic as a whole, is a workable path. In Yang's view, it can support efforts to strengthen confidence in China's institutions and to tell the story of those institutions in a way suited to the times. The article treats the institutional discourse of socialism with Chinese characteristics as a developing and open system of concepts, assertions and propositions with different historical, cultural and practical sources. It sorts these sources along three dimensions, each with three types: cultural origin, historical position and the form in which concepts are generated in practice. Yang acknowledges that conceptual history has several strands (social history, history of ideas, history of words) but holds that its methodology has distinctive value for this task. On cultural origin, Yang distinguishes endogenous concepts, imported concepts and fusion concepts. The last are traditional Chinese terms that the Party has given new content, which Yang presents as an expression of combining Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. On historical position, Yang separates summarising or reflective concepts (oriented to the past), guiding or anticipatory concepts (oriented to the future) and responsive or judgemental concepts (oriented to present reality). Many political concepts, the author notes, combine factual and value judgements. On form, Yang lists inherited, borrowed and reworked concepts, with a further case of concepts re-imported. Concepts must be read in their specific historical context, Yang argues, or they will be misattributed or earlier thinkers wrongly criticised. Yang concludes that introducing conceptual history into the study of the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and into Party history, the history of reform and opening up, the history of the People's Republic and the history of socialism, has important value. In Yang's account, it would help build China's own knowledge system, make better use of discursive resources, make institutional explanation more self-aware and theoretical explanation more thorough, and show the values and wisdom in China's political path. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars propose to use conceptual-history methods to systematise the vocabulary of institutional confidence and discourse building.

Marx and Engels's critique of the paradoxes of capitalist society 马克思恩格斯对资本主义社会悖论的批判 Liu Shuhui This short commentary asks how to understand the claim in the Communist Manifesto that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable. Liu Shuhui argues that the claim can be grasped through three paradoxes of capitalist society that Marx and Engels identified: those of wealth, freedom and civilisation. The author presents the Manifesto as the first comprehensive statement of the principles of scientific socialism, built on dialectical and historical materialism and on the law that society's basic contradictions drive its development. The article takes each paradox in turn and traces it through the classical texts. For wealth, Liu draws on The Poverty of Philosophy, Wage Labour and Capital, the Manifesto and Capital. For freedom, the sources are Marx's speech on free trade, Capital and Engels's writing against Karl Heinzen. For civilisation, Liu turns to Engels's early outline of a critique of political economy and the Manifesto. A brief closing section ties the three paradoxes to the forms of working-class struggle. On wealth, Liu argues that capitalist production relations generate wealth and poverty together. Accumulation at one pole, in Marx's words in Capital, goes with an accumulation of misery at the other. In Liu's reading, the bourgeoisie cannot guarantee even a bare subsistence to its wage-slaves, so it can no longer rule. On freedom, the freedom of buying, selling, trade and competition presupposes workers who own nothing but their labour-power. Liu says such workers are free only to sell themselves, and to choose by whom they are exploited. On civilisation, the bourgeoisie draws every nation into its mode of production and subordinates the East to the West through colonialism. The article calls the resulting world lopsided and deformed. Liu adds that the wealth paradox also covers ecological destruction, which the Manifesto does not address. Liu concludes that the first two paradoxes lead workers to unite against their own national bourgeoisie, while the third leads proletarians worldwide to unite against the bourgeoisie as such. In this sense, the author says, the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based outline of how the Manifesto and related classics ground the thesis of the bourgeoisie's inevitable downfall, as presented in the Chinese official press.

Whole-process people's democracy: the unity of discourse construction and practical path 全过程人民民主：话语建构与实践路径的统一 Chen Chengxin Writing in a newspaper commentary in February 2023, Chen Chengxin asks what distinguishes whole-process people's democracy among the world's democratic forms. The author's answer is that it unifies the construction of democratic discourse with the practical path of democracy, making it a form of democracy in which words and deeds agree. Chen traces this to three features: a people-centred starting point, democracy running through the entire process, and Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee. The piece has three sections. The first deals with the people-centred logical starting point, discussed under two headings: the 'whole subject' (all the people) and the 'whole domain' (all fields of life). The second sets out the comparative advantages of whole-process people's democracy, especially relative to electoral democracy. The third explains why Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee that discourse and practice stay aligned. Chen argues that 'the people' in this model includes respect for individual rights but unites them within a systemic 'whole subject'. The article presents the basic socialist economic system, with the means of production owned by all the people, as ensuring that democracy is not controlled by interest groups. It then claims that two kinds of 'completeness' give the model its advantage: a complete institutional procedure (the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation, regional ethnic autonomy, grassroots self-governance) and complete participatory practice, described as full-chain, all-round and full-coverage. Unlike 'one election decides everything' formal democracy, Chen contends, it is oriented to whether problems are effectively solved, with consultation and supervision running through the whole term of office and the whole decision cycle. Because the Party both constructs the discourse and leads the practice, the author argues, its leadership secures direction, orderly implementation and efficient governance, with the people's evaluation as the standard. Chen concludes that Party leadership lets discourse and practice develop together, citing people's congress supervision and the People's Daily Online 'message board for leaders' as examples of democratic innovation in the new era. The author adds a caution that 'whole process' operates within a certain context and scope, so its discursive boundaries and operating limits should be kept in view. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Chinese scholars present whole-process people's democracy as superior to electoral democracy and as inseparable from Party leadership.

The social-scientific methods of the dialectics of nature 自然辩证法的社会科学方法探赜 Wang Yuexin Wang Yuexin asks how the dialectics of nature, usually read as Marx and Engels's thinking about nature and science, relates to the social sciences. The article, a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, argues that the dialectics of nature rests on a thorough use of social-scientific methods. This, Wang says, is why it avoids becoming a mere "dialectics of the natural world" and joins with the dialectics of history. The piece opens with Bonifaty Kedrov's view that Engels's Dialectics of Nature is an important introduction to Capital and that it makes Marxist doctrine more complete. It then takes three methods in turn: the study of the social subject (the social body), the historical method, and class analysis. Wang draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on commentators including Lukács, Alfred Schmidt, Sidney Hook and John Bellamy Foster. Wang first argues that, seen from the social subject, "nature" in the dialectics of nature is not the bare natural world. It is mediated by labour and forms the basis of productive forces, and science and technology are likewise a social activity, driven by social need. Second, the historical method here is that of historical materialism, not natural-history explanation of the kind Marx criticised in Büchner's social Darwinism. Wang reads the unity of natural history and human history as implying a duty to future generations to treat the earth like "good heads of households". Third, class analysis exposes the ecological damage that capitalism does through its exploitation of workers and its seizure of resources worldwide. It also points to the liberation of the proletariat, which Wang links to the ecological liberation sketched in the 1844 Manuscripts as the unity of thoroughgoing naturalism and humanism. Wang concludes that social-historical methodology runs through the dialectics of nature and completes Marx and Engels's thought on nature, science and technology. Ecology and technology then no longer appear as inert matter but are internally united with historical dialectics. The text relates the dialectics of nature to ecological concerns, including the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. Read the original if you want a compact account of how one Chinese author links Marxist ecology, historical materialism and class analysis within the dialectics of nature.

How the proposition of "adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" inherits and develops "the Sinification of Marxism" “马克思主义中国化时代化”命题对“马克思主义的中国化”的继承和发展 Chen Xixi Wang Jicheng Chen Xixi and Wang Jicheng ask how Xi Jinping's call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to open up new realms for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times relates to Mao Zedong's 1938 proposition of the "Sinification of Marxism". They argue that the relation cannot be read literally, as if "times" were simply added to "China". In their view the new proposition both continues the old one and deepens it. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Mao's proposition through its theoretical basis, its practical logic and its scope. The second identifies three points of continuity with the later formulation. The third identifies three ways in which the later formulation deepens the earlier one. On the theoretical basis, the authors argue that Marxism is "concrete" because it applies the universal materialist conception of history to the particular contradictions of European capitalism. Applying it in China therefore needs a dialectical movement between universal and particular, not a formal-logic addition of Chinese "specific differences" to a general whole. Mao's 1925 class analysis and his 1956 call for a "second integration" are presented as examples. Continuity lies in making Chinese experience Marxist, combining Marxism with traditional culture, and placing it in a world frame. The deepening lies in three moves. First, combining Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture is made the historical foundation of the new formulation. Second, creating Chinese modernization gives Marxism worldwide significance, since the authors say its five Chinese features address problems capitalist modernization could not solve. Third, developing twenty-first-century Marxism takes Sinification further towards "worldization". This requires studying contemporary capitalism, exchanges with Marxism outside China, and a community with a shared future for mankind grounded in common values of humanity. The authors conclude that because Marxism is concrete it needs and can undergo Sinification, and that continuing this process must enrich its adaptation to the times. They hold that the two formulations are therefore continuous and also deepened. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese theorists derive the logic of Sinification from universal–particular dialectics and use it to frame current Party theory.

Chinese modernization and promoting the all-round development of the human being 中国式现代化与促进人的全面发展 Hao Lixin Hao Lixin asks how Chinese modernization relates to the all-round development of the human being, a question raised by the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which describes Chinese modernization as unifying material abundance with people's all-round development. Hao argues that promoting all-round human development is the fundamental value goal of Chinese modernization, and that the practice and theory of the new era have in turn enriched Marxist thinking on the subject. The article has two main parts. The first grounds the value goal in three sources: the founders of Marxism on the nature of socialist society, the Chinese Communists' exploration of modernization from Mao Zedong to the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second part examines how new-era practice has extended the idea, through the people-centred approach, the thesis that the essence of modernization is the modernization of the human being, and the stages by which all-round development is realised. Hao draws on Marx's account of human essence, alienation and the division of labour, and on his sequence from relations of personal dependence to dependence on things to free individuality. Capital-driven modernization, in Hao's view, cannot deliver all-round development, and the author cites Ellen Meiksins Wood's account of rising inequality in the United States as evidence. Chinese modernization is instead said to rest on common prosperity. Hao reads Xi's 2013 thesis that modernization is the modernization of the human being as meaning that people are its subject and its purpose. Hao also distinguishes this from Alex Inkeles's Western notion, which is said to neglect social systems and historical difference. Hao concludes that all-round development is realised gradually, through common prosperity, high-quality development, a richer spiritual life, harmony between humans and nature, world peace and a community with a shared future for mankind. Hao adds practical demands: more free time for workers and an education system that combines moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour training. Chinese modernization and human development are described as dialectically unified, offering what the author calls Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to other countries. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how the Marxist idea of the free and all-round development of the individual is placed within Chinese modernization.

Festival commemorations and youth mobilisation in the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region 节日纪念活动与晋察冀边区的青年动员 Fan Yanli Liu Rongzhen This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in May 2023, asks how the Chinese Communist Party used commemorations of revolutionary festivals to mobilise young people during the War of Resistance against Japan. Fan and Liu argue that after the full-scale outbreak of war the Party turned such commemorations into a key arena for awakening youth, building a sense of national identity and drawing them into the resistance. They treat the Shanxi-Chahar-Hebei Border Region, described as a model anti-Japanese base area, as the place where this practice was most extensive. The article is organised in three parts, drawing mainly on reports in the Jin-Cha-Ji Daily (Jin-Cha-Ji is the Chinese name of the region) and on archival documents. The first part covers the Party's recognition of youth and its protection of their rights; the second describes the content of festival activities and their results up to 1942; the third turns to the rectification campaign and its integration into youth commemorations. In the authors' account, festival speeches affirmed the May Fourth and December Ninth movements as symbols of justice and progress and presented youth as a driving force of history. The Border Region government backed this with guarantees in politics (voting rights from age 18), culture (the 'four great educations' in the Ten-Ten Programme), marriage and labour. Youth Day, May Fourth and related campaign weeks combined military, political, sporting and entertainment events, and slogans and contests pushed enlistment and wartime production. The authors cite 1942 figures of 470,000 organised young people and children in the Northern Yue district, 430,000 of them in the Youth Vanguard, and four-year totals for operations, land reclamation and school enrolment. Fan and Liu note that subjectivism, rigid leadership and detachment from reality also affected youth work, so rectification study was built into festival activities through inspections, self-criticism and renewed education. In their reading, this made mobilisation more effective, deepened young people's national consciousness and political identification with the Party and revolutionary government, and made them a backbone of the resistance. Read the original if you want a concise, source-based account of how commemorative events served political mobilisation in a wartime base area, as presented from the Party's perspective.

Strengthening the exposition of the Marxist stand, viewpoint and method 加强对马克思主义立场观点方法的阐释 Yang Wenming Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yang Wenming asks how research on Party documents should respond to the Congress report's claim that the Party succeeds because Marxism, in its form adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, "works". Yang's thesis is that the historic achievements of the past decade are, at root, a victory for applying Marxist materialism and dialectics. The task for document researchers is therefore to strengthen exposition of the stand, viewpoint and method (lichang guandian fangfa) running through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. This short commentary has three parts. The first links the decade's results to the Party's use of dialectical and historical materialism, citing Politburo study sessions on these subjects and the handling of major relationships such as the whole and the part, or the long term and the present. The second sets out the worldview and methodology of the Party's innovative theory, summarised in the Congress report as the "six musts". The third turns to practical guidance for the China Society for CPC Documents Research. In Yang's reading, the six musts are: put the people first; stay confident in our own path and self-reliant; uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground; be problem-oriented; adopt a systems approach; and keep the world in view. Each is tied to a Marxist root: people-centredness to historical materialism, self-confidence to concrete analysis of concrete conditions, and a systems approach to the core of materialist dialectics. Yang holds that the people's stand is the most fundamental, since without it even sound-looking views and methods slide into idealism and subjectivism. This stand is presented as what distinguishes a Marxist party from other parties. Yang proposes that researchers explain which stands, viewpoints and methods the Party has used across its work, why, how, with what results, and with what consequences if they were abandoned. Exposition should treat the three as one whole, with stand determining viewpoint and both shaping method. It should rest on primary documents, be mainly positive but include comparison and rebuttal of erroneous positions, and speak to current public concerns in plain language. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated documents researcher sets out the political and methodological tasks of Party literature research after the 20th Party Congress.

On Marcuse's defence of Hegel's thought 论马尔库塞为黑格尔思想的辩护 Gao Haiyan Zhu Huanghe Herbert Marcuse's Reason and Revolution: Hegel and the Rise of Social Theory was written when Hegel's rationalism was under suspicion, since Nazism claimed his philosophy as a foundation. Gao and Zhu ask how Marcuse defended Hegel, and what that defence shows about the relation between Hegel and Marx. They argue that Marcuse recovers the critical and revolutionary side of Hegel's reason and thereby defends Marxist philosophy. They also argue that his reading stays at the level of Hegelian speculation and misses the philosophical revolution Marx carried out. The authors say Chinese scholarship has paid the book too little attention, because Marcuse soon turned to comparing Marx and Freud. They examine the book through the dialectic between reason and history and between reason and reality. The article is organised into four themes in Marcuse's defence: the universality of reason, its historicity, its actuality, and its dialectic. A short conclusion follows. Gao and Zhu report that Marcuse reads Hegel's reason as a universal principle that rebuilds unity after Kant's split between subject and object. It becomes a historical force, so that Hegel brings history into idealist philosophy.
