Marcuse also reads Hegel's actuality as the unity of essence and existence, so that "the real is rational" carries a hidden critical edge. Through the negativity of dialectic, Marcuse links Hegel to Marx, since both treat negation as the essence of reason. The authors then criticise this reading. In their account, Marcuse and Hegel treat actuality as abstract reason, whereas Marx treats it as concrete human activity. Marcuse's dialectic begins and ends in reason, while Marx's begins and ends in real people and their practice. Marcuse stresses Hegel's continuity with Marx rather than the break between them. The authors conclude that Marx's ontological transformation of Hegel's dialectic turned the dialectic of reason into a dialectic of practice and made the "revolution of reason" real. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Reason and Revolution and of how Marcuse relates Hegel to Marx.

The new form of human civilization in the perspective of the Marxist view of civilization 马克思主义文明观视域中的人类文明新形态 Tang Aijun Tang Aijun takes up the concept of the "new form of human civilization", which Xi Jinping linked to Chinese modernization in his 2021 speech marking the Party's centenary and which the 20th Party Congress (2022) called an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. Tang argues that the concept can be explained through a Marxist view of civilization built from Marx's and Engels's historical materialism. Read this way, the new form is a civilization that moves towards an information-age civilization, is integrated across five domains, and takes human all-round development as its value goal. The article first defines the Marxist view of civilization as a system covering the nature, origin, structure, driving forces and forms of civilization. It then uses three lenses as its framework: a theory of civilizational forms, a theory of civilizational structure, and a theory of the civilizational subject. Each lens gets a section, and each is tied to a practical orientation for Chinese modernization. On forms, Tang draws on Marx's "technological social formations", classified by tools and industrial structure, to distinguish agricultural, industrial and information civilizations. Tang holds that the new form's direction of evolution is information-age civilization, which is not the same as the new form itself. Because China's industrialization is unfinished, Tang describes a "parallel" path in which industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization advance together, unlike the "serial" Western sequence. On structure, Tang reads Marx and Engels as implying material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization, and presents the new form as a coordinated whole whose political core is a new institutional civilization. On the subject, Tang uses Marx's three stages of human development to argue that the new form criticizes the reification produced by modern capital-centred civilization and takes people, not capital or things, as the measure. Tang concludes that Chinese modernization should move beyond traditional industrial civilization, beyond a single material-civilization model, and beyond capital-led modernization. The article says this means pursuing a new type of industrialization with the four modernizations in step, and promoting all five civilizations together. It also means harnessing capital to serve socialism and human all-round development, since capital remains usable in the primary stage of socialism. Read the original if you want a systematic Marxist-theoretical grounding of the Party's concept of a new form of human civilization, as presented by a Central Party School scholar.

The succession of early Chinese Marxists' theories on the evolution of social formations 我国早期马克思主义者关于社会形态演变理论的递嬗研究 Wang Xiangqing Liang Yanli Wang Xiangqing and Liang Yanli ask how the first generation of Chinese Marxists understood the evolution of social formations, a core category of historical materialism, and what their work contributed. Before Marxism arrived, they note, Chinese scholars largely held an idealist view of history. The authors argue that thinkers from Cai Hesen to Mao Zedong moved step by step towards a scientific account that spread Marxist social-formation theory in China and served the cause of national salvation. The article first sets out the background and intellectual sources. The background is the debates over "ancient and modern, China and the West" and over "problems versus isms"; the sources are the Marxist classics, Soviet and Japanese Marxism, and traditional Chinese philosophy. It then follows five stages: Cai Hesen's foundation-laying, Zhang Bojian's advance, Fan Shoukang's innovation, Li Da's deepening and Mao Zedong's refinement. A final section draws out three general features of the early Marxists' work. In the authors' reading, each thinker added something and left gaps. Cai's Social Evolution History (1924) used Morgan's three-stage scheme but said little about feudal, bourgeois and socialist formations. Zhang's eight-stage scheme was more concrete but unorthodox. Fan and Li used five-stage schemes, and Li stressed the special features of each formation and of the transitional period. Mao analysed China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal formation and emphasised class struggle as the driving force. The authors identify three features. The early Marxists used historical materialism to sublate evolutionism, shifting from the vocabulary of evolution to class struggle and the unity of evolution and revolution. They moved from general theory to the realities of China. They also moved from a plurality of views towards acceptance of the five-formation theory, which the authors say became orthodox after the 1938 Short Course of the Soviet Communist Party. They conclude that this work shifted Chinese historical outlooks, strengthened the Communist Party's leadership and was confirmed in revolutionary practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-language account of how Cai, Zhang, Fan, Li and Mao each periodised history and how the five-stage scheme became dominant in China.

Chinese modernization and the question of capital: theoretical framework and practical wisdom 中国式现代化与资本问题：理论架构及其实践智慧 Xia Ying Cui Juran Xia Ying and Cui Juran ask how Chinese modernization differs from Western modernization, and how capital can be regulated in practice. They argue that Marx's critique of political economy, centred on the logic of capital, offers the key. On this basis, they hold that Chinese modernization sublates that logic: it keeps capital as a factor of production while removing it as a relation of production, producing development with "capital" but without "capitalism". The article moves from theory to practice in four sections. It first traces how modern society, civil society and classical political economy emerged in the West, through Habermas, Hegel, Marx's reversal of Hegel and Adam Smith. It then examines the dual character of the logic of capital in modernization, and the limits Marx identified for it, with a side-look at Sismondi. The last section sets out the practical wisdom of Chinese modernization. The authors' central move is Marx's distinction between capital as a factor of production and capital as a relation of production. As a factor, capital in the Grundrisse drives market expansion, productivity, innovation, scientific discovery and new needs, and may create free time for human development. As a relation, it forces workers into wage labour and alienation, and meets internal limits: a falling rate of profit and overproduction crises. Sismondi saw the demand-side contradiction but sought only government correction, which Marx judged superficial. The authors then argue that three features of Party leadership contain capital. The Party's proletarian character gives modernization a socialist orientation. Marxism guides its grasp of capital's nature. Its people-centred approach prevents polarization of wealth. In practice they point to a socialist market economy with public ownership as the mainstay, checks on the disorderly expansion of capital, and an "effective market" joined with an "enabling government". The authors conclude that, as the Party deepens its understanding of capital, its capacity to harness it will grow. Capital's drive to expand and the technical progress that follows can then serve prosperity and give people free time, and capital's operation can become a ladder to common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Marx-based, philosophically framed account of how Chinese scholars justify using capital under socialism, set against Hegel and classical political economy.

The new path of Chinese modernization and new developments in the modernization of the human being An analysis based on Marx's theory of world history 中国式现代化新道路与人的现代化新发展 Qiao Yuqiang Qiao Yuqiang asks what Chinese modernization contributes to global modernization when read through Marx's theory of world history, which traces how national and regional histories become world history and how individuals move from one-sided to all-round development. The article argues that Chinese modernization is a new type of modernization. By critically reconstructing and going beyond modernization led by the logic of capital, it widens the paths open to other states and advances the modern attributes of the human being. The article has three main parts. The first describes how capital and Enlightenment reason together opened the modern era in the West, and where their combined role reaches its limits. The second sets out four contributions of Chinese modernization to global modernization: its subject, its driving force, its values and its goal. The third examines how three attributes of the human being (sociality, historicity and practicality) develop further on this path. A short conclusion closes the piece. Qiao holds that capital, with Enlightenment reason as its legitimating partner, drove productive forces, markets and political revolutions, but then reduced people to instruments of profit and left the world in global risk. Against this, the article says Chinese modernization makes the people, not capital, its subject and "sublates" capital critically, so that capital serves human development. Its "endogenous" driving force, built on the state, the market and the people, is contrasted with the "outward-oriented" force of commercial, industrial and finance capital. Its "common values" replace Western "universal values", which the author describes as a metaphysical expression of Western centrism. Its goal is cooperative interaction, sustainable development and the liberation of humanity as a "species" being, in place of a centre–periphery hierarchy. On the attributes of the human being, the author points to common prosperity (sociality), the shift of the people from onlookers to masters of the country (historicity), and the people's practice at home and a community with a shared future for mankind abroad (practicality). Qiao concludes that the essential task of modernization is the modernization of the human being as a species being. In this account Chinese modernization, led by the Communist Party and using Marxist methodology, makes up for the theoretical and practical shortcomings of Western capitalist modernization and ends its monopoly. It offers an original contribution and useful experience to states that want to modernize while staying independent. Read the original if you want a worked example of how Marx's world-history theory is used to place Chinese modernization within a philosophy of history and of human development.

Capital, world history and communism as a trinity An examination of Capital and its manuscripts 资本、世界历史与共产主义的三位一体 Liu Jingdong Liu Jingdong asks what historical structure underlies Marx's critique of capital and of political economy. The article argues that Capital and its manuscripts contain a three-part scheme, "capital, world history and communism", in which capital's mode of production and the world market, through their own crises and self-sublation, form the historical bridge to a communist association of free individuals. Liu presents this as the basic structure of Marx's capital theory and, more broadly, of his whole theory of society and history. The article has four main sections plus a conclusion. It begins with Marx's plans for his economic work, in the 1857–58 Manuscripts, the 1858 letter to Engels and the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. It then turns to the world market and crisis, to the self-sublation of capitalist ownership and the re-establishment of individual property, and to credit, joint-stock companies and banking in Volume III. The last substantive section covers the transition from the realm of necessity to the realm of freedom. Liu supports each step with extended quotations from Marx. Liu's central claim is that Marx's concept of capital has a double character, historical and class-based. Historically, capital's drive for surplus value creates the world market, develops needs and capacities, and lays the material basis for communism. In class terms, capital exploits labour, and the "freedom" of the wage-worker is only formal. Liu reads Marx's three social forms (personal dependence, dependence on things, free individuality) as the same scheme. Liu also argues that Marx saw joint-stock companies, credit, banking and workers' cooperative factories as transitional forms in which capitalism sublates itself within its own limits. In Liu's account Marx also warned against overstating this, and criticised Proudhon's hopes for reform through credit. Revolution by the proletariat is still required. Liu concludes that, across the manuscripts, letters and volumes of Capital, Marx traced a consistent logic by which capital's self-sublation on the world market leads to communism. Liu also holds that Marx exposed the claim that capital or free competition is eternal as a bourgeois myth, an early critique of the "end of history" idea. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reconstruction of how Marx's writing plans and quotations from Capital are used to support a unified reading of capital, world history and communism.

The rebuilding of community: a historical-materialist examination of Chinese modernization 共同体的重建：中国式现代化的历史唯物主义审视 Yan Song Yan Song asks how Chinese modernization relates to the dissolution of community under capitalism, and answers that it rebuilds community in a way Western modernization cannot. In Yan's account, Western modernization dissolved traditional communities and put in their place a "false community" in the form of the capitalist state. Chinese modernization, drawing on Marx's ideas about modernity, is said to produce a different path, expressed in what the article calls Xi Jinping's thought on community. The article is in three parts. The first traces the dissolution of community in Western modernization: civil society and the political state, atomised individuals, commodity and capital fetishism, and the harms caused within capitalist states and across the world system. The second sets out four kinds of community in Xi's discourse: a community with a shared future for mankind, together with its cyberspace variant; the Chinese nation community; the social governance community; and the human–nature community of life. The third assesses the theoretical, institutional and practical significance of this rebuilding. Yan notes that existing scholarship tends to treat each type separately. Yan's central move is to read Marx's critique of civil society and the state as showing that capitalist modernity turns people into atomised wage-labourers. In this reading, the bourgeois state offers only formal belonging and welfare that secure the capitalist mode of production. Against this, Yan treats the four communities as one system embedded in the features of Chinese modernization: a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advance in step, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Yan also argues that China's development is "parallel" rather than the Western "serial" sequence, and so did not pass through bloody primitive accumulation. Because it rests on a socialist system aimed at communism, the article claims, it moves toward Marx's "real community". Yan concludes that Chinese modernization theoretically criticises Western dissolution of community, institutionally supplies the security and belonging people have lost, and practically promotes harmony between people and nature, society, nations and states. It is also presented as a model for late-developing countries, and as no return to premodern community, since it combines the "common good" of traditional communities with modern features. Yan adds that the theory is still being developed in practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal links Marx's concepts of false community and fetishism to the Party's current vocabulary of community.

Further strengthening research on basic theoretical questions of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 进一步加强马克思主义中国化时代化基础理论问题的研究 Tian Keqin Zhang Zeqiang Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called for opening up "new horizons" in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, Tian Keqin and Zhang Zeqiang ask which basic theoretical questions research in this field must now deepen. They argue that studying the Congress report's new formulations, and the core concepts, historical course, theoretical results, themes and methods they touch on, is necessary to grasp the inner laws of the Party's project and to fulfil scholars' task of serving the Party and the people. The article is organised around five areas of research. These are the core concepts and the relation between "Sinicization" (zhongguohua) and "contemporization" (shidaihua); the historical status of the "three leaps"; the theme of the process; the system of theoretical results as set out in the Party's three historical resolutions; and the method of the Two Integrations. Each section combines a historical account with a list of questions the authors regard as still open. The authors argue that the two "hua" are distinct yet inseparable. In their account, Mao Zedong stressed Sinicization in 1938 because Leninist-era conditions and the fight against dogmatism demanded it, while the Party's turn to "the features of the times" came with the changes of the 1980s and was written into the 14th Party Congress (1992). On themes, they identify four major shifts and conclude that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is the overarching theme, above "socialism with Chinese characteristics". They also maintain that the Two Integrations rest on one another: the first, combining Marxism with China's concrete realities, was the groundwork for the second, combining it with fine traditional Chinese culture, and Mao's own idea of Sinicization already contained the second. They hold that the 2021 resolution's wording of one "historic leap" and two "new leaps" requires clearer study of Deng Xiaoping Theory's foundational role and of how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era relates to the earlier theoretical system. The system of Xi's thought is, they say, still being summarised and not finished. The authors conclude that such work fits Xi Jinping's call to let the world know "academia in China" and "theory in China", and that it strengthens the discipline and a self-reliant Chinese knowledge system. Scholars should "speak accurately and speak anew" on the basis of the third historical resolution and the 20th Congress. Read the original if you want a detailed map of the research agenda that Party-theory scholars set for the "two hua" after the 20th Congress, and of how they periodise the Party's theoretical results.

A brief discussion of state capital in the socialist market economy 略论社会主义市场经济中的国有资本 Meng Jie Meng Jie asks in what sense state capital is the form that socialist ownership by the whole people takes under market conditions, and what this implies for reform of state-owned enterprises since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that state capital is a transformed form of that ownership relation. Its decisive dimension is the relation between state and enterprise, which sets it apart from private capital analysed in Marx's Capital. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theory of state capital and its goals. The second turns to the reforms after the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013): classified reform of state-owned enterprises, the shift to "managing capital", and the overall governance structure of the state economy. The third addresses how to judge the dominant position and efficiency of the state sector and the role of Party leadership. Meng draws on asset and ranking data, including Fortune Global 500 figures, to support the argument. Meng holds that ownership by the whole people has two internal moments, the state and the enterprise. Reform therefore changes how the state acts, replacing administrative orders with economic and legal means, but cannot fully separate ownership from management. State capital has three dimensions: state–enterprise, capital–labour and capital–capital. Its goals are plural, combining profit with use-value goals set by national strategy. In Meng's reading, the capital–labour relation shifts from zero-sum antagonism toward distribution according to labour. Meng classifies enterprises by function rather than by market structure or profit motive, and presents state enterprises as tools of national economic governance. Meng also warns that "managing capital" through state financial capital risks subordinating industrial capital to short-term returns, which would call for guiding and regulating state financial capital. Meng concludes that the state sector remains dominant, citing 2018 data on state-controlled enterprises' share of assets, especially in finance, and its weight among the largest firms. Claims that state firms are inefficient are described as one-sided, because they ignore reform lag, long-run recovery and the wider economic functions of state capital. Meng calls for Party leadership to be built into corporate governance in order to make the state economy stronger, better and larger. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy account of state capital in China, linked to current state-owned enterprise reform.

The historical setting of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化的历史场景 Cao Yongxin Cao Yongxin starts from Marx's point that people make history under inherited conditions. On that basis the article argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has to be understood through its concrete historical settings. Cao holds that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era unites the localisation of Marxism in China with its adaptation to the age, and that the new context must be linked to earlier ones. The article has five parts. It first clarifies concepts: the relation between 'Chinese' and 'of the times' content, and the universal significance of localised Marxism. It then sets out the setting in which Xi Jinping Thought emerged, at home and abroad since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Next it compares the settings of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization, and then the setting for combining Marxism with traditional Chinese culture. It closes with the Party's historical experience and the risks it faces. Cao argues that 'of the times' is the key content of the formula, since each theoretical advance bears the mark of its period. In Cao's account the 'Chinese characteristics' formula originally contrasted with the Soviet and East European model, whereas Chinese modernization is defined against Western capitalist modernization. The author describes a favourable strategic window after the 1970s that was followed by Western containment after the 2008 financial crisis. From this the author concludes that opening up cannot be relied on and that self-reliance and independent innovation are needed. Cao also claims that a developing country on the capitalist road would be suppressed anyway, so only socialism can bring national rejuvenation. The cultural combination is presented as a defence against capitalist corrosion and against a revival of feudal ideas, the 'two preventions'. Cao names three sources of risk for the Party: external containment by the West, divergent interests within society after market development, and corruption inside the Party. Cao calls for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Party's self-reform, common prosperity and the Four-sphere Confidence. The present setting is described as composite: reform-era modernization, the new era and 'great changes unseen in a century' in the world. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads current theory through domestic and international history, and how the article frames risks to Party rule.

Rebuilding the community: a historical-materialist examination of Chinese modernization 共同体的重建：中国式现代化的历史唯物主义审视 Yan Song Yan Song asks how Chinese modernization relates to the problem of community under modernity. The article argues that Western modernization dissolved traditional communities and replaced them with a "false community" serving one class against another. Chinese modernization, in Yan's reading, rebuilds community, and this rebuilding is expressed in what the author calls Xi Jinping's thought on community. Yan says existing scholarship treats individual community concepts separately and neglects their overall unity and internal links. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs, mainly from Marx and Engels, how Western modernization dissolved community. It covers the split between civil society and the political state, the atomised individual, the "false community" of the capitalist state, and the consequences within nations and across the world market. The second part sets out four forms of community in Xi's discourse: the community with a shared future for mankind (including its cyberspace version), the Chinese nation as a community, the social governance community, and the community of life between humans and nature. The third part assesses the theoretical, institutional and practical significance of this rebuilding. Yan argues that Western modernization produced atomised wage-labourers, whose lives are governed by commodity and capital fetishism and by reified relations. Welfare and citizenship are described as devices that stabilise capitalist rule. Against this, the four forms of community are presented as one system, each tied to a feature of Chinese modernization: a huge population, common prosperity, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful development. Yan adds that Chinese modernization is socialist, so its value orientation is communism and Marx's "real community". The author also contends that it skipped the bloody primitive accumulation of the West by following a "parallel" rather than "serial" path. Yan concludes that rebuilding community is one comparative advantage of Chinese modernization and shows the strengths of the socialist system. The author also presents it as an option for developing countries that want modernization without losing independence. The framework is described as unfinished and still developing, and not a return to premodern community. Instead it is said to combine the "common good" of traditional communities with the features of modern society. Read the original if you want to see how Xi Jinping's community concepts are fitted into a Marxist critique of Western modernity and linked to Chinese modernization.

The succession of early Chinese Marxists' theories on the evolution of social formations 我国早期马克思主义者关于社会形态演变理论的递嬗研究 Wang Xiangqing Liang Yanli Wang Xiangqing and Liang Yanli ask how early Chinese Marxists understood the evolution of social formations, a core category of historical materialism, and how their successive studies built up Marxist theory on the subject in China. They argue that, guided by historical materialism, these thinkers moved from borrowed general schemes towards a theory fitted to Chinese conditions. In the authors' account, the work spread Marxism and helped answer the question of where China was heading. The article has three parts. The first sets out the background: the debates over "ancient and modern, China and the West" and over "problems versus isms", plus the intellectual sources, namely the Marxist classics, Japanese and Soviet Marxism, and traditional Chinese philosophy. The second traces five stages through five figures: Cai Hesen, Zhang Bojian, Fan Shoukang, Li Da and Mao Zedong. The third draws out the general features of this body of work. The authors assess each figure by his periodisation and its limits. Cai's Social Evolution (1924) used Morgan's three-stage scheme and is judged pioneering but vague. Zhang's eight-stage scheme is described as more concrete and accessible, though some of its divisions are called contentious. Fan and Li are credited with a five-stage division and with attention to China's specificity. Mao is credited with stressing class struggle and analysing China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal formation. Three features are identified. Historical materialism was used to criticise evolutionism. Attention shifted from general theory, through the study of ancient society, to the present reality of China. Diverse views gave way to acceptance of the five-formation theory, which the authors say was consolidated by the Stalin-edited History of the CPSU(B) in 1938 and Mao's praise of it. The authors conclude that this research moved from spontaneous to conscious, from individual to collective and from theory to practice. They say it promoted a shift from an idealist view of heroes to a materialist view of the masses. In their view it also strengthened the Communist Party's leadership by gathering mass support for socialism, and revolutionary practice confirmed the theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-historiographical account of how Chinese Marxists periodised history before 1949 and how the five-formation scheme became orthodox.

The expression and characteristics of whole-process people's democracy from the perspective of "China's governance" 中国之治视域下全过程人民民主的表达与特征 Zhang Shuhua Writing amid what the article calls a "great change unseen in a century", Zhang Shuhua asks how China answers the question of democracy, and argues that the answer is whole-process people's democracy. The author places this democracy within "China's governance" (zhongguo zhi zhi), a concept treated as the political dimension of Chinese modernization and as the counterpart of what Zhang describes as growing disorder in the West. The article has six sections. It sets out the theoretical and international significance of China's governance; compares Chinese modernization with Western and Soviet-bloc paths; and lists the civilizational traits and advantages of China's governance. It then draws out the "principles" (zhongguo zhi li) behind it, traces the Chinese people's search for democracy from the late Qing to the new era, and ends with the characteristics of whole-process people's democracy. Zhang draws on foreign scholars such as Barry Buzan, George Lawson, Martin Jacques and Russian sinologists, and also notes critics such as Nadège Rolland. Zhang contends that China's governance rests on an independent path rather than imitation of foreign models, on Party leadership as a stable political core, and on the people's principal position. Politically it is marked by stability, development, practicality, coordination and efficacy, and it unifies democracy, order and efficiency. On this basis Zhang says it has produced a "new view of democracy", a comprehensive view of development and a view of global governance linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as rooted in Chinese soil, socialist in essence, consensus-based, effective through election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and continually innovating. Zhang cites grassroots legislative liaison offices as an example. By contrast, the author portrays Western democracy as suffering institutional failure and as a source of global disorder. Zhang concludes that whole-process people's democracy is China's choice and reply to the world's question about democracy. It must uphold the organic unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance. The author holds that it offers Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to political civilization, and that no country has a monopoly on democracy. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese political science presents whole-process people's democracy as a comparative and civilizational claim against Western democracy.

The young Marx's inversion and transformation of Hegel's conception of philosophy 青年马克思对黑格尔哲学观问题的颠倒和转换 Lü Shirong How did Marx move beyond Hegel's abstract and inverted view of what philosophy is, and bring German philosophy "down from heaven to earth"? Lü Shirong takes up this question through the young Marx's treatment of Hegel's "problem of the conception of philosophy". The article argues that Marx first inverted that conception and then transformed it. Marx thereby left Hegel's framework of absolute spirit and turned philosophy towards real social problems, though the author stresses that the task was not yet complete in the early works. The article has four sections. The first reconstructs Hegel's conception of philosophy as the culmination of traditional Platonic metaphysics and as a distinctively "German metaphysics" tied to Germany's backward transition from feudalism to capitalism. The second covers Marx's student-period legal-metaphysics experiment, his doctoral dissertation and his notes on Epicurus. The third turns to the Rheinische Zeitung articles of 1842–43. The fourth examines the Kreuznach notes, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and the introduction to that critique. Lü holds that Hegel kept the Platonist opposition between a supersensible and a sensible world, and that Marx's dissertation began to invert it by affirming the reality of the sensible world and the activity of thought towards it. In the newspaper articles Marx then moved philosophy into political practice on behalf of "the people". He turned Hegel's "dialectic of concepts" into a "dialectic of practice", giving it a materialist content. In the Kreuznach notes Marx performs an "ontological reduction" of Hegel's philosophy of right: Hegel made the idea of the state the subject and real existence its predicate. Marx reverses this, so that family and civil society determine the state. Lü reads Marx's critique of political emancipation as exposing Hegel's metaphysics as a theoretical support for bourgeois rule, and as pointing to the proletariat's human emancipation. Lü concludes that the young Marx turned Hegel's abstract speculation about the age into a new conception of philosophy that engages reality directly. He also began to show how rational metaphysics is bound up with German bourgeois domination, and so started building his own philosophy on the ground of real society. The author adds that Marx had not yet given a fully historical-materialist account of reason, the state and right. Read the original if you study the early Marx–Hegel relationship, the Kreuznach notes or the genesis of Marx's materialist turn, and want a systematic Chinese reading organised around "conception of philosophy".

The genesis and contemporary value of Lenin's "theory of inculcation" 列宁“灌输论”的生成逻辑与时代价值 Hong Yan Wang Shengzhen Hong Yan and Wang Shengzhen take up the long-running dispute over Lenin's "theory of inculcation" (灌输论). They note that, after Dewey and others, "inculcation" shifted in Western educational debate from a near-synonym of education to its opposite, and became a target of criticism. The authors argue that, against such charges, Lenin's theory should be understood completely and accurately from a Marxist standpoint, restoring its original meaning and bringing out its value for the present. The article has three sections. The first traces the theory's genesis, from Marx and Engels's ideas on communist education through Kautsky's first formulation to Lenin's mature version. The second sets out what the authors regard as the theory's genuine content. The third turns to its value in the "new era", drawing on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It was published in a 2022 issue of a journal on Party building and ideological education. On genesis, Hong and Wang identify three needs in Russia: the Social Democratic Party had to separate itself from the "Economists", who revered the spontaneity of the workers' movement; the Russian movement needed a theory suited to Russian conditions rather than copied from abroad; and a backward country swamped by petty-bourgeois influence made the task of bringing Marxist theory to the proletariat urgent. On meaning, they argue that social-democratic consciousness cannot arise spontaneously, because it is a class consciousness (they cite Lukács) rather than the sum of individual workers' thoughts. It is also a consciously created theory that intellectuals must develop. They hold that the Marxist claim that social being determines consciousness does not mean consciousness emerges automatically. Inculcation is therefore, in their view, a unity of theoretical innovation (the writer) and theoretical education (the agitator). The authors conclude that the theory remains relevant in three ways: as a basis for continued theoretical innovation, including the creation of Xi Jinping Thought; as support for ideological and political education in a period of sharp ideological struggle against hostile forces; and as a guide for the ideological side of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They claim that Chinese practice shows the theory has not become outdated but is a "key" to the Party's successes. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party-journal scholarship defends Lenin's inculcation theory and links it to current ideological work.

Marx's decoding of the process of modernization and the distinctiveness of Chinese modernization 马克思对现代化进程的解码与中国式现代化的独特性 Liu Weibing Responding to the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which says Chinese modernization shares features with other countries' modernization but has Chinese characteristics, Liu Weibing asks how to grasp its distinctiveness on the basis of modernization's general laws. The article argues that Marx, though he never proposed a concept of modernization, in fact developed a theory of it, and that this theory lets us see what sets Chinese modernization apart. For Liu, the distinctiveness rests on adapting to national conditions while using the Party's historical initiative. The article has three parts. The first traces three shifts in Marx's logic: from alienation to production to capital. The second sets out the dual character of modernization as a historical process. The third turns to Chinese modernization, which Liu discusses under three headings: Party leadership, the free and all-round development of the human being, and the move from spontaneous to conscious history. In Liu's reading, Marx moved from criticising political, labour and historical alienation (1844 texts), through the division of labour and the forces and relations of production, to capital as a social relation whose self-valorisation shapes production, distribution, exchange and consumption. From this Liu derives three paired features of modernization: time acceleration with spatial expansion, totalisation with difference, and alienation with liberation. Marx, Liu stresses, criticised capitalist modernity rather than modernization as such, and allowed the East a path that might avoid the 'Caudine Forks' of capitalism. Chinese modernization, Liu argues, is led by a mission-driven party that differs from parliamentary parties, and the Party's self-reform guides the broader social revolution. Capital is treated as a means rather than the subject of modernization. Through the socialist market economy, public ownership as the mainstay and distribution according to work, surplus labour time is said to be converted into free time for people. Liu describes the process as conscious in theory, values and path. Liu concludes that studying Chinese modernization requires Marxist perspectives, knowledge of modernization's general laws, and attention to Chinese conditions and Party practice. Chinese modernization, in this account, will increasingly show world-historical significance and may open a new form of human civilization. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical case, framed through Capital and the Grundrisse, for why Chinese modernization is held to differ from capitalist modernization.

Understanding and grasping the scientific content of the theory of Chinese modernization 认识和把握中国式现代化理论的科学内涵 Pei Changhong Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Pei Changhong asks what the theory of Chinese modernization rests on and what makes it scientific. The article argues that the theory, systematised in the Congress report as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, rests on three bases: the Party's understanding of its own governing laws, of the laws of socialist construction, and of the laws of human social development. The article is organised in three main sections, followed by a short conclusion. The first treats the practice and theory of scientific socialism, the second the logic of Marxist political economy, and the third the logic of historical materialism. Pei compares China with Britain, the United States, Japan, South Korea, India, Latin America and Africa, and traces the evolution of Party formulations from the Four Modernizations to the Five-sphere Integrated Plan and the Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy. In the first section Pei contends that Chinese modernization differs from the Western path in its political foundation (a people's republic led by the Party rather than a bourgeois republic), its basic economic system (public ownership as the mainstay, a socialist market economy centred on the people rather than on capital), its values, its peaceful development and its independent, self-reliant opening up. The second section holds that China's path differs in the government–market relationship, in compressing industrialisation, informatisation, urbanisation and agricultural modernization into parallel development, and in aiming at the people's wellbeing rather than GDP alone, with the digital economy and modernised governance as markers. The third section draws on Marx to argue that civilisation is the overall expression of a given level of productive forces, that it is diverse, and that exchange and mutual learning among civilisations are its norm. Pei criticises Huntington's clash-of-civilizations thesis and the 'end of history' idea. Pei concludes that the theory is an original theoretical achievement that deepens scientific socialism, Marxist political economy and historical materialism. In the article's account, it shows that modernization is not a Western monopoly, that it requires Party leadership in China, and that it offers other developing countries seeking independence a new option. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading economist in the Party-state system grounds Chinese modernization in Marxist theory and contrasts it with Western and other developing-country paths.

Five methods of Mao Zedong's investigation and study 毛泽东开展调查研究的五种方法 Xu Zhongyuan Xu Zhongyuan, writing in Study Times in April 2023, presents Mao Zedong as the Party's model of personally practising investigation and study (diaocha yanjiu). The article opens with Mao's remark that when he was at a loss for a solution, he went to investigate, and that once he had done so, the answer appeared. Xu's thesis is that Mao's investigations were distinctive because they followed identifiable methods, which the piece sets out as five. The text is a short commentary built from anecdotes rather than theoretical exposition. It draws on episodes from the Jinggangshan and Jiangxi period, the Yan'an years, the early People's Republic and Mao's last decades. Each method is introduced with a heading-like phrase and illustrated by one or more stories involving ordinary villagers, bodyguards, newly appointed ambassadors and commanders. The first method is to read people's faces and manner (chayan guanse): Xu recounts Mao telling the cadre Jiang Hua to observe how villagers eat, dress and feel. Second, Mao used his security guards, sending them home to investigate rural conditions and asking for their letters. Third, he found major issues by reading newspapers and historical works, for example choosing northern Shaanxi as the Long March destination after a newspaper report, and urging a regional commander to read Gu Zuyu's geographical work. Fourth, he took villagers' grievances and complaints as prompts for inquiry, as when he looked to his own policy failures after a farmer's angry remarks and then helped cut a grain levy. Fifth, he helped people solve practical problems while investigating, citing the Shazhouba well, his concern over the Yellow River, and a conversation with an unrecognised fisherman at Beidaihe. Xu concludes implicitly through these cases that Mao's investigation combined genuine feeling for the people, self-examination and attention to detail. The article does not draw explicit policy lessons, but it presents these practices as an example for cadres. Read the original if you want a compact set of anecdotes from official Party commemorative writing on Mao's working style, or if you study how investigation and study is being promoted as a model of leadership practice.

Advancing Chinese modernization in the historical process of the new era 在新时代历史进程中推进中国式现代化 Song Caifa Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Song Caifa asks how Chinese modernization was established, how it advances in the new era, and what it contributes to humankind. The article argues that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization under Communist Party leadership, rests on the basic socialist economic system, and has created a "new form of human civilization" that offers developing countries an alternative to Western modernization. The article has three main sections. The first traces how the Party established and leads Chinese modernization, from Sun Yat-sen's early blueprints through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second links modernization to the transformation of the principal social contradiction in the new era. The third assesses the world significance of Chinese modernization and its relation to a community with a shared future for mankind. Throughout, Song draws heavily on Xi Jinping's speeches and Party documents. Song's central moves are as follows. First, Party leadership and public ownership as the mainstay of the economy are presented as the foundations of modernization: the nature of ownership shapes production relations, so modernization must be "of all the people" and move from public ownership to common ownership to common prosperity. Second, the shift in the principal contradiction, now between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, defines modernization's priorities. Song cites the elimination of absolute poverty, the passage from a moderately prosperous society to a modern socialist country, and high-quality development as the route to common prosperity. Third, the author contends that Chinese modernization breaks with Eurocentric and single-model theories and surpasses capital-centred, polarising and expansionist Western paths as well as the rigid Soviet model. Song also criticises a minority view that stressing a Chinese model means self-isolation, and rejects "universal values" promoted by Western hegemonism. Song concludes that Chinese modernization is an original contribution that rewrites the world map of modernization, given China's population of over 1.4 billion, and that it enriches scientific socialism in the twenty-first century. The author adds that modernization is a stage in socialist development, not its final aim, which remains communism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing presents the Party's official narrative of modernization, with extensive references to Party documents.

A three-dimensional logical examination of the emergence of contemporary "soft" historical nihilism 当代软性历史虚无主义思潮登场的三维逻辑审视 Cheng Litao Gao Jiazhe Cheng and Gao take up what they call "soft" historical nihilism, which they present as a recent variant of historical nihilism. They argue that, after sustained criticism by the Party, the state and academia, historical nihilism has taken a more concealed form, with subtler methods that make it easier to mislead people's understanding of history. Their thesis is that this variant can be understood, and countered, by examining three connected logics: its intellectual roots, its real-world conditions and its inner mechanism, all from the standpoint of historical materialism. The article is organised in three sections. The first, the "ideological logic", traces soft historical nihilism to postmodernism and to nihilism in the line of Nietzsche, Heidegger and Weber. The second, the "practical logic", looks at the domestic and external environment and at cyberspace. The third, the "mechanism logic", examines the ideological impact of the trend and the way it distorts historical narrative. The authors illustrate their claims with examples drawn from the War of Resistance against Japan, representations of Mao Zedong, and comparisons of Republican-era and early People's Republic economic data. The authors argue that postmodern historiography, with its stress on the reader's subjective reading of history as "text", supplies the root of the trend, while nihilism supplies its philosophical base by negating historical value, especially the Communist Party's leadership and the socialist path. In their account, it flourishes because mainstream criticism has forced a softer disguise, because visual and entertainment culture and Western consumerist and ideological influence give it channels, and because the internet speeds its spread through memes, parody videos and self-media. They contend that its content assaults historical materialism in ontology, by promoting subjectivism and a "heroes make history" view, and in epistemology, by promoting subjective truth. Its core method, they say, is narrative distortion: it misuses microhistory to decentre narrative, positivist historiography to blur objectivity, and comparative history to steer values, as in the \"two 30 years\" argument. Cheng and Gao conclude that, whatever form it takes, historical nihilism remains nihilistic about history, so criticism of it is an important task for safeguarding ideological security. They call both for exposing its substance through the "weapon of criticism" and for removing its real-world foundations through the "criticism of weapons". Concretely, they propose stronger study of Party history and national history, a cleaner climate of public opinion and deeper understanding of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing defines and categorises the latest forms of historical nihilism and the cases it cites.

Engels's conception of nature and his outstanding contribution to Marxism 恩格斯自然观对马克思主义的卓越贡献 Zhou Ye Zhu Yao Zhou Ye and Zhu Yao ask what Engels's view of nature added to Marxism. They argue that Engels moved from "empirical natural science" to "theoretical natural science". By using materialist dialectics to explain, know and transform nature, they say, he revealed general laws common to nature, human society and thought, and brought about a major change in the history of natural science. The article is organised in four parts. The first treats Engels's definitions of matter, motion, time and space. The second turns to the three basic laws of materialist dialectics as Engels set them out. The third examines his historical-materialist account of primitive society, and the fourth his dialectics of nature on the relation between humans, nature and society. Evidence comes mainly from Anti-Dühring, Dialectics of Nature, The German Ideology and The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. In the authors' reading, Engels refused to treat matter as a contemplated "pure object". He grounded it in human practice, and defined motion as matter's mode of existence and time and space as its forms of existence. The authors present the three laws as the transformation of quantity into quality, the interpenetration of opposites, and the negation of the negation. They stress that Engels drew examples from mechanics, physics, chemistry and biology, and understood negation as sublation, a unity of overcoming and preserving. On society, they discuss Engels's "two kinds of production", meaning the production of the means of life and the production of human beings themselves. These explain how kinship-based clan society gave way to private property, classes and the state. The authors also highlight Engels's claim that "labour created man" and his warning that nature takes revenge for human victories over it. From this they draw a principle of "two elevations" of humanity. People must come to understand natural laws and the consequences of intervening in nature, and must also come to grasp and regulate the indirect social effects of production. Only then, the authors say, does human society pass from a spontaneous to a conscious stage, and humans become true subjects of natural history. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language overview of Engels's dialectics of nature, with extensive quotation from his texts.

Marx's critique of religion and the formation of the materialist conception of history An analysis centred on Marx's early writings 马克思的宗教批判与唯物史观的形成 Huang Jinhui Min Li Huang Jinhui and Min Li take up the relationship between Marx's critique of religion and the emergence of the materialist conception of history. They argue that the materialist conception of history was formed in the course of criticising religion and the Prussian state that religion defended, so the two stand in an "endogenous" relation. In their view this link is a key to understanding how Marx's thought developed, yet it has not received due attention among Chinese scholars. The article first reads Marx's early writings in three stages. The first is the doctoral dissertation period (1836–1841). The second covers the Rheinische Zeitung and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (1842–1844), including "On the Jewish Question" and the "Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right: Introduction". The third runs from 1844 to 1846, with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Holy Family, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. It then assesses the role of the religion critique in forming the theory, and ends with what the study means today. The authors contend that Marx's explanation of religion moved from ideas (lack of reason or self-consciousness), to politics (the state and its interests), to the economy (alienated labour, money, material production and exchange). His method moved correspondingly from speculative philosophy, through Feuerbach's humanist materialism, to historical materialism. In the authors' reading, criticising Feuerbach and the Young Hegelians for explaining religion without material production and social relations pushed Marx to the "practice" category and to the view that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. They add that the aim shifted from theoretical critique to changing the world. The German Ideology is presented as the first systematic statement of the theory and of a Marxist view of religion: religion disappears only when the real social relations that produce it are overthrown. Huang and Min conclude that the religion critique was both the entry point and a driving force for the theory. They say it also led Marx on to the study of capitalist production and surplus value, and so to political economy and scientific socialism. They argue that neglecting this link produces misunderstandings. They also draw a policy lesson. On their account, Marx's view implies that religious work in China should avoid both "left" and right errors and should build laws guiding religion to adapt to socialism with Chinese characteristics. They add that raising education and science, improving income distribution and advancing common prosperity would gradually remove the conditions on which religion rests. Read the original if you study the development of Marx's early thought, or the theoretical basis of Chinese religious policy.

How a community with a shared future for mankind changes the world 人类命运共同体何以改变世界 Chen Shuguang Chen Shuguang asks what the Chinese proposal to build a community with a shared future for mankind contributes to global governance and to world history. The article argues that the proposal changes how global governance is conceived, offers a vision of international order, and marks out a new form of human civilization. It also holds that the proposal opens room for socialism and capitalism to coexist and sets the programme for the present stage of world history. Chen presents it as a contemporary Chinese form of the Marxist theory of world history and universal intercourse. The text is organised in five parts: a shift in the paradigm of global governance thinking; the Chinese proposal for reconstructing world order; a new form of civilization; a contemporary design for coexistence of the two systems; and a programme of action for world history. Chen draws on Marx's idea of world history, Durkheim's "organic solidarity", Hegel on relations between states, and Western authors such as Huntington and Michael Barr. The article also cites speeches by Xi Jinping and Deng Xiaoping. Chen's central claim is that the existing order is a "centre–periphery" structure serving transnational capital. On this account, Western-led governance no longer fits the material content of globalization, so a crisis arises between its "social form" and that content. Against this, the community with a shared future replaces homogeneous, linear and subject–object thinking with pluralist, complex and intersubjective thinking. It is said to rest on five concepts of equal status, common security, cooperative development, civilizational diversity and ecological harmony. Chen insists it reforms the UN-centred system rather than overthrowing it, and denies that it is nationalist or an "Eastern-centrism". Drawing on Marx's "two never" principle, Chen holds that capitalism still dominates the world while the balance is shifting "east rises, west declines". The community is therefore the only realistic option, ahead of a "true community" that remains the long-term goal. Chen concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind is China's contribution to international relations theory, a banner of new civilization, and the stage-specific goal of world history, to be pursued through six action plans. These include the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development, Global Security and Global Civilization Initiatives. Chen acknowledges that the task is long, faces unilateralism and Cold War thinking, and is not the end of human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist theoretical defence of the concept, set within world-history and two-systems debates.

The Western tradition, core orientation and intellectual effects of Marx's thought on community 马克思共同体思想的西方传统、核心指向与思想效应 Shen Jiangping Ding Yaopeng Shen Jiangping and Ding Yaopeng ask how Marx's thought on community (gongtongti) relates to the long Western lineage of such thinking, and what it can still contribute today. Marx never defined the term, and his remarks are scattered across his career. The authors argue that he sublated earlier Western ideas of community, that his core contribution lies in a revolutionary path to a "true community", and that this thought should not be read as a fixed dogma. The article, published in Nanjing Social Sciences in 2023, has three main parts. It first surveys pre-Marxian thought: the "moral community" of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the contract community (Augustine, Hobbes, Rousseau), the rational communities of Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, and utopian socialists such as Saint-Simon, Owen and Fourier. It then reconstructs Marx's own position from early writings to Capital and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. Finally it turns to later developments: Lenin, Western critics, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, and the Chinese idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors identify three structural themes in the earlier tradition: the relation of individual to community, the gradual separation of "community" from "state" (clearest in Kant), and the projection of an ideal society. In their reading, Marx developed the first into two relations and three principles, drawn from his early journalism and philosophy. He treated the capitalist state as an "illusory community" and the "association of free individuals" as the true community. The authors say this involves abolishing private ownership, the withering of the state and free, all-round individual development. Marx's route there is the "re-establishment of individual property" on the basis of cooperation and common possession. The authors also hold that the community/state distinction still needs defending against Fukuyama, Berlin and Hayek, and they criticise Hardt and Negri for stressing political "exodus" while neglecting economic revolution. The authors argue that the community with a shared future for mankind should not be read as a linear continuation of Marx's true community. In their view it addresses a different level, namely coexistence of different systems in the long period before communism, when Marx allowed the state to persist. They hold that the ultimate aim of abolishing private ownership and building the true community remains the Communists' highest programme. They also call for adapting Marx's thought to changed conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Marx's community concept is positioned against both the Western tradition and the current Chinese diplomatic concept.

Upholding the Marxist standpoint in research on ideology 坚持意识形态问题研究的马克思主义立场 Shi Xiaoning Song Wenyuan This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in December 2022, asks why research on ideology must be conducted from a Marxist standpoint. Shi and Song argue that ideology is vital to the survival of a party, a state and a nation. They hold that a Marxist standpoint supplies both a scientific analytical perspective and a practical necessity for China. The authors begin with the place of ideology in the history of Marxism. They list classic works, Second International theorists and Western Marxists such as Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and Althusser as evidence of its importance. They then trace the Chinese Communist Party's handling of ideological work from the New Democratic Revolution to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Their central theoretical move concerns Marx's own legacy. Many scholars treat ideological critique as the core of Marx's theory. Shi and Song accept this partly, but say that treating ideology as "false consciousness" is only the logical starting point. In their reading, the deeper purpose is to build a "proletarian system of ideas", so the critical and the functional dimensions together make up the whole doctrine. Their second move is practical: because Marxism is the guiding thought of the Party and the state, ideology research must keep to it. The authors credit the Party with clarifying ideological confusion through the debate on the criterion of truth and the Four Cardinal Principles. They also credit it with a mature ideological theory in the twenty-first century. Since 2012, they say, the leadership has secured Marxism's guiding position, strengthened responsibility systems for ideological work, and criticised historical nihilism. They conclude that a Marxist standpoint is both extremely important and urgent. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-affiliated scholars frame ideology work and its Marxist lineage.

The place of the theory of human development in Marxism 人的发展理论在马克思主义中的地位 Chen Xinxia Chen Xinxia asks what position the theory of human development holds within Marxism as a whole. The article argues that the complete emancipation and free and all-round development of the human being is the core value of Marxism. The theory that expresses this value orientation is, in Chen's account, an important part of Marxism: it rests on Marxism and is generated and developed within it. The article has three parts. The first shows that the theory of human development is grounded in Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. The second argues that human development is the core value running through all three components. The third sets out the theoretical and practical significance of making this position explicit, including for contemporary China. Chen's central moves are as follows. Philosophically, the practical standpoint and historical materialism define the human subject, the meaning of development and its social conditions. Political economy, through the theory of surplus value, explains why capitalism blocks development and why free time and shorter working hours matter. Scientific socialism supplies the path of emancipation, and Chen treats emancipation as the premise of development: emancipation is the task of revolutionary periods, development that of periods of construction. Chen then argues that Marxism's components are usually seen as unified in their scientific understanding, while their unity of value orientation gets too little attention. Recognising human development as the shared value would confirm Marxism as, in Lenin's phrase, a single 'piece of steel'. On the practical side, Chen holds that the point strengthens Marxism's capacity to answer deep questions of social life and to guide social progress. In China, where the principal social contradiction has shifted, the article proposes human development as a higher value standard for relating the two problems of unbalanced and inadequate development. Chen argues that inadequate development is addressed through further growth and unbalanced development through adjusting social relations, and that both should be judged by whether they benefit human development. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how human development links Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and how one Chinese scholar applies it to current policy.

Marx forever: commemorating the 205th anniversary of Marx's birth 永远的马克思——纪念马克思诞辰205周年​ Hao Guisheng Hao Guisheng, a professor at Tianjin Normal University, writes a commemorative essay on the anniversary of Marx's birth. It presents Marx as the greatest leader and teacher of the world's proletariat and working people. The author's thesis is that Marx's life had three defining features, learning, struggle and innovation, and that all three carry direct lessons for Chinese Communists today. The essay is organised as three biographical sections followed by practical conclusions. The first follows Marx's learning from childhood and the Trier school, through Bonn and Berlin and his doctoral thesis on Democritus and Epicurus, to his work on the Rheinische Zeitung. It then covers political economy and the writing of Capital, and his late studies in mathematics, world history and early society. The second section surveys his struggles against feudal absolutism, the Young Hegelians, Proudhon, reactionary governments, poverty and various opportunists. The third presents his theoretical innovations. In Hao's account, Marx's learning was driven by a sense of mission to serve humanity and by the principle that theory must engage with life. His struggle, in Engels's words, was his "element". Hao names as his two great discoveries the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value, which Hao says turned socialism from utopia into science. Hao attributes Marx's capacity for innovation to three causes: critical inheritance of earlier culture, revolutionary practice, and the vantage point that historical materialism provided. Hao draws three lessons for Chinese Communists. First, the Party should launch another campaign to "reform our study", on the model of Mao Zedong's 1942 call, since the author sees the Party and society as impatient, utilitarian and poor at studying Marxism. Second, they should join the struggle between socialism and capitalism, which the author says persists. Hao argues that this means guarding against capitalist restoration, returning to the people power that has degenerated, and fighting opportunism and revisionism inside the Party. Third, innovation must rest on inheritance and on practice in class struggle. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich biographical survey of Marx that is also an example of a hard-left Chinese reading of Party tasks today.

Four dimensions for understanding the distinctive features of Chinese modernization and its world-historical significance 理解中国式现代化特质及其世界历史意义的四重维度 Sun Leqiang Sun Leqiang takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022). The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks how Chinese modernization and its world-historical significance should be understood. Sun argues that this requires a 'grand view of history', a world-historical perspective, China's own autonomy and a comparison with the Western path. The piece is organised around four paired dialectical relations: understanding China from China, China from the world, the world from China, and the world from the world. Each pair is treated in a short section, and together they move from China's historical continuity to global debates about modernization. In Sun's account, Chinese modernization cannot be understood within a single period. It is rooted in traditional Chinese culture and tied to Party leadership and the adaptation of Marxism to China, so it must be placed in the long sweep of Chinese history. Sun contends that the Western path is only one national path, characterised as capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist. The 'modernization equals Westernization' narrative is therefore a myth, and Chinese modernization, with its five features set out in the 20th Party Congress report, shows that modernization takes plural forms. Sun adds that it sublates the defects of the Western model and offers a new form of human civilisation, citing a community with a shared future for mankind and whole-process people's democracy. Sun concludes that historical materialism gives the unity of history, while concrete paths are diverse. Western modernization began world history but will not complete it, and Chinese modernization is said to represent the direction of human progress. Sun predicts that a new pattern breaking out of the capitalist world system will inevitably arrive. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists frame Chinese modernization against Western modernization in 2023.

The historical logic of the exploration of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化探索的历史逻辑 Chen Zhigang This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks how Chinese modernization came about historically. Chen argues that it is a great creation of the Communist Party of China, produced by successive generations of Party members who explored, opened up and extended it. Chen presents it as the only road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece draws on Xi Jinping's speech at the study session on the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article follows four periods in turn. These are the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For each, Chen names the condition it supplied for modernization: social conditions, political prerequisites and material foundations, institutional vitality, and finally a more complete institutional, material and spiritual base. Chen argues that each stage built on the one before. The revolution ended semi-colonial, semi-feudal society and won national independence. After 1949 the basic socialist system, the Two Integrations' precursor of a 'second integration' of Marxism with Chinese conditions, and an independent industrial system laid the foundations. Deng Xiaoping's idea of a moderately prosperous society and the 'three-step' strategy then combined socialism with the market economy. For the new era, Chen credits Xi with a theoretical system that surpasses neoliberalism and dependency theory and breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. Chen also points to strategic plans and to practical results such as the elimination of absolute poverty. Chen concludes that practice has proved Chinese modernization to be the Party's creation and the necessary road to national rejuvenation. Only by keeping to it, the author says, can that rejuvenation be achieved. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-aligned scholarship narrates Chinese modernization as a continuous, staged historical process.

New features of mass work and the growth of young cadres 群众工作新特点与年轻干部成长研究 Sun Yingshuai Sun Yingshuai takes up the question of how the Party's mass line and mass work must adapt to new conditions, and what this means for young cadres. Starting from the premise that the mass line is the Party's lifeline, Sun argues that the transformation of the principal contradiction and the spread of the internet have changed the environment of mass work. Young cadres, who are more attuned to the internet, are said to be well placed to build an online–offline "concentric circle" of mass work. The article was published in People's Forum in 2022. It identifies four features of mass work in the new era: online mass work as a new model of public governance; truthfulness, speed, openness and transparency as new requirements; the coordination of group interests as the new normal; and the need to eradicate bureaucratism and formalism by putting the people first. Sun draws on internet-usage and education statistics, and on cases such as the Fengxian incident, the Zhengzhou "7·20" rainstorm, the Baiyin ultramarathon deaths and the MU5735 crash. Sun's first move is to argue that, with 1.032 billion internet users by December 2021 according to the article's figures, gaps in information access between young, old and rural users are narrowing. Mass work therefore now spans physical and virtual society, and the pressure of analysing and guiding public opinion has grown. Officials, Sun says, must be willing to speak out, speak promptly and speak truthfully, or face a "crisis of trust". The second move turns to the principal contradiction: disputes over lift installation, neighbourhood clean-ups, epidemic controls and family matters show that mediating among diverse interests is now routine, and that small matters can become public incidents online. Sun concludes that bureaucratism and formalism, although curbed, persist and must be tackled by keeping the people at the centre, feeling for the masses and judging achievements by popular experience. Cadres should also avoid arbitrary decisions and wait patiently until the majority are ready for reform. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of internet-era mass work, with domestic cases of public-opinion handling and community mediation.

Chinese-style democracy as inheritance and development of the Marxist view of democracy 中国式民主对马克思主义民主观的继承和发展 Sun Yingshuai Sun Yingshuai asks how democracy as practised under the Communist Party of China relates to the Marxist conception of democracy. The article argues that over more than a century the Party has held to the essential content of that conception while adapting it to China's revolution, construction and reform. In Sun's account, this produced Chinese-style democracy, which unites democracy with dictatorship, democracy with centralism, procedural with substantive democracy, and the people's democracy with the will of the state. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remark of October 2021 that democracy is a common value of all humanity. The article is organised around three themes: the substance of democracy (from class democracy to people's democracy), its guiding principle (from "complete democracy" to democratic centralism) and its forms (from representative democracy to whole-process people's democracy). Sun draws on Marx and Engels, on Lenin's Soviet experience, and on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. Historical illustrations include Athenian democracy, the bourgeois Enlightenment thinkers Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau, the Paris Commune and the 1954 Chinese constitution. On substance, Sun argues that Marx used historical materialism and class analysis to show earlier democracies, from slave-owning Athens to bourgeois states, to be democracies of a minority. Marx treated democracy as a question of the state and held that the proletariat must win rule to realise majority democracy. Sun presents Mao's analysis of China's classes and the doctrine of "people's democratic dictatorship" as widening the proletarian base to an alliance of workers, peasants and other classes. On principle, Sun traces Marx's elected and recallable organisation, Lenin's centralism, and the Chinese formula of "centralism on the basis of democracy, democracy under centralised guidance", noting that the Russian term stresses centralism. On form, Sun treats the people's congress system, the political consultative conference and consultative democracy as realising the Commune's principle of combining legislative and executive work. Sun concludes that whole-process people's democracy, put forward since the 18th Party Congress (2012), completes this line of development. As evidence, the article cites direct election of over 90 per cent of county- and township-level deputies by more than one billion voters, and more than 3 million suggestions on over 200 draft laws. Sun holds that Chinese-style democracy goes beyond "minority democracy" and "one-off democracy" and ensures that the people are masters of the country. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how Chinese scholars link Marx, Lenin and Mao to the official concept of whole-process people's democracy.
