Engels's view of nature and its outstanding contribution to Marxism 恩格斯自然观对马克思主义的卓越贡献 Zhou Ye Zhu Yao This article asks what Engels's conception of nature added to Marxism. Zhou and Zhu argue that Engels moved from "empirical natural science" to "theoretical natural science", using materialist dialectics to explain, understand and transform nature. In their account, this revealed the general laws governing nature, human society and thought, and brought a major change in the history of natural science. The article is organised in four parts, each based on Engels's texts, chiefly Anti-Dühring, Dialectics of Nature, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, and The German Ideology. It covers his definition of matter and its forms of existence; the three basic laws of materialist dialectics in nature; his account of primitive society through the theory of the "two kinds of production"; and his dialectic of nature as a way to understand the harmony of humans, nature and society. On matter, the authors argue that Engels rejected old materialism's intuitive treatment of nature as a pure object. Matter is for him an abstraction grounded in human practice, existing as motion in space and time. The authors then present the laws of the transformation of quantity into quality, the interpenetration of opposites, and the negation of the negation, illustrated with Engels's examples from mechanics, physics and chemistry. Negation is read as sublation, an inner self-movement of things. In the history section, Zhou and Zhu stress that social systems are conditioned by both the production of the means of life and the production of human beings themselves. They set out the shift from blood-kin groups to class society and the state. The final part reads Engels's "labour created man" thesis and his warning that nature takes revenge for each human victory over it as the basis of the unity of natural history and human history. The authors extract from this the principle of the "two elevations" of humanity: learning nature's laws and their consequences, and learning to control the wider social effects of production. They conclude that only then does society move from a spontaneous to a conscious stage, with humans becoming subjects of natural history. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based survey of Engels's natural dialectics and its links to historical materialism as presented in Chinese scholarship.

The Communist Party of Denmark's exploration of socialism and the reasons for its decline 丹麦共产党对社会主义的探索及衰落原因 Bai Hu Chen Jinxiang Bai Hu and Chen Jinxiang ask why the Communist Party of Denmark, once an organisation of some influence in the Nordic countries, ended its 70-odd years of existence in decline and collapse. They argue that its theory and practice of socialism centred on parliamentary struggle and peaceful transition, and that its demise resulted from a combination of objective and subjective factors, with the external environment the main one. The article first traces the party's history in three phases: founding and growth through revolutionary struggle (1919–1945), the search for a new path in the Cold War (1946–1989), and survival and extinction after 1990. It then surveys four areas of the party's exploration: the peaceful road to socialism, the labour movement and anti-capitalist struggle, bilateral and multilateral inter-party activity, and the struggle for peace. A final section sets out three reasons for failure. In the authors' account, the party dropped the phrase "dictatorship of the proletariat" from its 1952 programme and later held that an anti-monopoly democratic struggle could reach socialism without civil war. It joined strikes, such as the 1973 national strike, May Day rallies, Nordic communist conferences, and campaigns for peace and a nuclear-free Nordic zone. The authors attribute its decline to three factors: nearly ten splits over ideological disputes, including those after the 1956 Soviet Party Congress and the expulsion of Axel Larsen, who then founded the Socialist People's Party; its long confinement in the shadow of the Social Democrats and that party; and an uncritical pro-Soviet, anti-Chinese stance that, they say, eroded its independent judgement. They report that its membership fell to about 2,000 by 1992. They also state that the party calling itself the Communist Party of Denmark today is a different body, re-formed in 1993. The authors conclude that the party's fate resembles that of many Western communist parties and reflects a general problem. For all foreign communist parties, they say, adapting Marxism to local conditions and to the times remains a long and arduous task. Understanding the Danish case, they suggest, helps explain why socialism in Western countries has fallen into a trough. Read the original if you study Western European communist parties, Nordic left politics or how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars assess the decline of foreign communist parties.

Building a discourse system for institutions from the perspective of conceptual history 概念史视角下的制度话语体系建构 Yang Binbin Yang Binbin asks how a discourse system for the institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics can be built so that institutional confidence is strengthened and China's institutional story is told well. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2023, argues that conceptual history, which traces how concepts evolve in order to present the underlying historical logic, is a feasible path. Yang holds that this discourse is a developing and open system whose concepts, assertions and propositions have different historical sources, cultural roots and practical uses. The article does not survey schools of conceptual history in detail. It notes that social history, the history of ideas and the history of words are distinct approaches, and says the method as a whole is valuable for examining a concept's historical starting point, logical starting point, semantic turning points and internal features. Yang then sorts institutional concepts under three headings: cultural origin, historical position and form of present-day generation. Each heading yields a threefold typology. By cultural origin, Yang distinguishes endogenous or indigenous concepts, characterised by originality; exogenous or imported concepts, whose meaning shifts in transfer into Chinese; and fusion or interactive concepts, in which old Chinese terms receive new content from Party practice, which Yang links to the Two Integrations. By historical position, there are summarising or reflective concepts (historical), guiding or anticipatory concepts (future-oriented, normative) and responsive or judgemental concepts (tied to present reality, often combining fact and value). By form of generation, there are inherited, borrowed and transformed concepts, plus a case of concepts re-imported. Yang insists that concepts must be read in their specific historical context, using historical materialism, or the result is misattribution and unfair criticism of predecessors. Yang concludes that bringing conceptual history into the study of the history of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Communist Party, reform and opening up, the People's Republic and socialist development has real value. In Yang's account it offers a window onto building China's own knowledge system and onto the transformation of traditional culture. It would also help excavate discourse resources, make institutional explanation more self-aware and thorough, and show the values and wisdom in China's political path. Read the original if you want a compact typology of how Chinese scholars classify the sources of institutional concepts and a sense of how conceptual history is being enlisted for discourse construction.

The influence of traditional Chinese culture on the early spread of Marxism in China 中国传统文化对马克思主义在中国早期传播的影响 Wu Zengli Hu Peng Wu Zengli and Hu Peng ask how traditional Chinese culture shaped the early transmission of Marxism in China. Writing in the framework of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, they argue that the process of making Marxism Chinese was also one of continual influence by traditional culture. The influence was complex: it created tension, steered the selection and interpretation of Marxist content, and made transmission both winding and gradual. The authors define the early-transmission period as running from 1899, when the missionary Timothy Richard's Datong xue first mentioned Marx and socialism in Chinese, to the late 1920s. The article has three main sections: how traditional culture affected the entry of Marxism, the content that was chosen and how it was interpreted, and the course of dissemination. It draws on figures such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Liang Qichao, Sun Yat-sen, Qu Qiubai, Hu Shi and Mao Zedong, and on press and education statistics. In the first section, Wu and Hu stress the heterogeneity of Confucian-centred, agrarian culture and Marxism, which they describe as a modern Western doctrine that arrived amid anti-Confucian radicalism. They argue, however, that the decline of traditional culture opened conditions for Marxism: the end of the examination system and the monarchy, the new culture movement, a changed view of the West, a booming periodical press, and a new-style educated intelligentsia. In the second section they argue that Chinese intellectuals combined old and new and kept Chinese needs central. They often rendered socialism in traditional terms such as the Great Harmony, the well-field system or equalising wealth, and emphasised different parts of Marxism according to practical needs. The authors say this made early understanding partial and unsystematic. In the third section they claim that cultural inertia, habitual thinking, custom and warlord repression slowed transmission. They also hold that the openness of Chinese culture and its affinity with Marxist values, as in the Sinicisation of Buddhism, aided it. The authors conclude that traditional culture, as a rich resource, helped Marxism take root in Chinese soil. They add that influence ran both ways: Marxism now guides the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. They present a precise grasp of the fit between fine traditional culture and Marxism as necessary for developing contemporary Chinese Marxism. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-rich account of the cultural-historical conditions and mechanisms of Marxism's early reception in China, as presented in current Chinese scholarship.

New understandings of the essence of socialism 关于社会主义本质的新认识 Bao Xinjian Bao Xinjian takes up what he calls a fundamental question of socialist theory and practice: what the essence of socialism is. Writing thirty years after Deng Xiaoping's 1992 southern tour talks, he argues that Deng's definition of socialism's essence was an original contribution, and that Xi Jinping's thinking has developed it into a fuller, four-dimensional formulation suited to the new era. The article has three parts. The first assesses Deng's definition: liberating and developing the productive forces, eliminating exploitation, eliminating polarisation and ultimately achieving common prosperity. The second reconstructs Xi's statements on the essence of socialism and condenses them into a new formulation. The third draws out what this means for grasping socialism's essence comprehensively in the new development stage. Bao relies heavily on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng and Xi, and on the 2021 Party resolution on its century of struggle. Bao argues that Marx, Engels and Lenin never systematically defined the essence of socialism, and that Mao's exploration was marred by errors such as "taking class struggle as the key link". In his account Deng clarified the relationship between essence, characteristics and principles, and freed thinking from disputes over whether a measure is "socialist or capitalist". For Bao, Deng's definition also kept reform and opening up on course. Bao then summarises Xi's contribution as a new formulation: upholding Marxist party leadership and the people's position as masters of the country; fully liberating and developing the productive forces; upholding fairness and justice and achieving common prosperity; and promoting all-round social progress and human development. Each element corresponds to a level: fundamental nature, mode of production, core values and ultimate goal. Bao contrasts the "people-centred logic" of socialism with the "logic of capital". Bao concludes that, in the new development stage within the primary stage of socialism, the essence of socialism must be grasped as a whole. He calls for upholding the principle of putting the people first, keeping to the socialist market economy with an effective market and a capable government, and giving greater weight to common prosperity and all-round human development. These measures also include regulating capital and curbing its disorderly expansion. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how Deng's definition of socialism is presented as continuing into Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

The "five-dimensional scale" for judging Marxism's guiding role in the ideological sphere 判定马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位的“五维尺度” Liang Jianxin The Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) established upholding Marxism's guiding role in the ideological sphere as a fundamental system. Liang Jianxin asks how one can tell whether that role is actually being upheld. The article answers that socialist ideology rests on five fundamentals: theoretical foundation, ideals and convictions, values, moral concepts and discourse. These five are proposed as the dimensions of assessment, and other ideological phenomena are treated as their reflection. Drawing on the 19th Party Congress report (2017), Liang compares the five to a building: theory is the foundation stone, ideals, values and morality are the pillars, and discourse is the outer decoration. The article has five main sections, one for each dimension. Each combines quotations from Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping with practical recommendations. It ends by arguing that the five together form a "five-pointed star". On theory, Liang says Marxism must be explained in four ways: the Marxist rationale behind Party lines and policies; the claim that the Communist Party has no special interests of its own; Marxism's superiority over rival theories; and its contemporary relevance, illustrated by the response to Covid-19. On ideals, communism is presented as a direction of social development that is pursued through accumulated stages, and the author calls for resolving three tensions: individual existence and transcendence, the personal dream and the Chinese Dream, and the long-term and the staged. On values, the core socialist values must be tied together as abstract and concrete, theory and practice, individual and society. On morality, Liang draws on Engels's critique of eternal moral dogma and asks for a detailed system of moral norms, rooted in everyday life, that combines breadth with vanguard standards. On discourse, Liang argues that it must be practical, critical and of its time. The author cites the "universal values" discourse as a "discourse trap". Liang concludes that judging whether Marxism's guiding role is upheld depends on action as well as words, and that the five dimensions must work as an organic whole. The article is a Party-theoretical text on ideological work. It writes in the official register and treats the contrast between Marxism and liberalism or individualism as settled. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholars operationalise the ideological-leadership system, or if you study Party discourse on values, morality and communication.

An economic interpretation of Chinese modernization: a "six-in-one" logical framework 中国式现代化的经济学阐释：“六位一体”的逻辑框架 Zhou Mi Liu Lifan Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhou Mi and Liu Lifan ask how Chinese modernization can be explained in economic terms. They argue that existing studies mostly restate official documents and leave its logic unclear. To fill the gap they propose a "six-in-one" framework and derive from it a set of implementation paths. The article opens by tracing the idea of modernization from the 1950s "four modernizations" to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 use of the term. It then reviews foreign theories (Rostow's stages, Chenery's three-stage account) and Chinese scholarship on industrial, technological and social modernization. It then sets out the framework and its six strands. It ends with six paths for putting the framework into practice, and a short conclusion. The framework has six parts: government action as an endogenous variable; a return to the labour theory of value; active matching of heterogeneous labour to the national economic circulation; effective combination of supply and demand; guidance by a multi-level vision linking people, nation and world; and high-quality development. The authors contrast Western modernization, which they say rests on a technology theory of value, with a Chinese path that combines it with the labour theory of value. They argue that Smith, Ricardo and Marx all assumed homogeneous labour, whereas Chinese practice recognises productive, research, cognitive and distributive labour. They describe four stages of matching: distributive labour with natural resources, productive labour with foreign capital, research labour with knowledge, and entrepreneurs' cognitive labour with the market. They present the government's roles as guide, shock absorber and amplifier, citing dual-track pricing and local experimentation as examples. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization has a complete logical framework and is a blueprint for future modernized states. They propose six paths: upholding Party leadership to modernize governance; cultivating craftspeople, scientists, entrepreneurs and officials; unblocking production, distribution, circulation and consumption; meeting varied demand through measures on housing, trade and rural consumption; pursuing a national vision tied to a community with a shared future for mankind; and advancing high-quality development. Read the original if you want an economist's attempt to build a systematic theoretical scheme around Chinese modernization, including a heterogeneous-labour argument that revises the classical labour theory of value.

The "five-dimensional scale" for judging whether Marxism guides the ideological sphere 判定马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位的“五维尺度” Liang Jianxin Since the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) made upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere a fundamental system, Liang Jianxin asks how one can tell whether that position is actually being upheld. The article proposes a "five-dimensional scale": theoretical foundation, ideals and convictions, values, moral concepts and discourse. Liang argues that every other ideological phenomenon is a reflection or echo of these five fundamentals. Liang derives the five from the 19th Party Congress (2017) call for a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power, which unites people in ideals, values and morality. Ideals, values and morality rest on a theoretical base and are expressed through a distinctive discourse. The article uses an architectural image: theory is the cornerstone, ideals, values and morality are the pillars, and discourse is the outer decoration. Five sections take each dimension in turn, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On theory, Liang says Marxism must be explained under "four clarifications": the Marxist rationale behind Party policy, the claim that the Communist Party has no special interests of its own, Marxism's superiority over rival theories, and its contemporary relevance, illustrated by the response to Covid-19. On ideals, Liang defines communism as a direction of development, a revolutionary movement and a gradual accumulation of qualitative change, and says three relationships must be clarified. On values, morality and discourse, Liang says core socialist values must link the abstract to the concrete, theory to practice, and the individual to society. Morality needs a detailed system of moral norms (a "guiding principle" plus specific items) that is both broad and advanced. Discourse must be practical, critical and of its time. Liang cites the "universal values" discourse as a "discourse trap". Liang concludes that the five dimensions together form a "five-pointed star" supporting Marxism's guiding position, and that the test lies in action as well as in what is said. Ideals must show in reform, development and improving livelihoods. Liang also calls for stronger international communication so that China's story can be told in terms Western audiences can accept. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic turns the abstract principle of Marxism's ideological leadership into a checklist of criteria.

Lenin's epistemological thought and its contemporary value 列宁的认识论思想及其当代价值 Gao Bin Gao Bin takes up Lenin's theory of knowledge as it appears mainly in the Philosophical Notebooks, and asks what it inherited from Marx and Engels, what it criticised, and what it still offers today. The article's thesis is that Lenin developed a "practice-based epistemology" in which knowledge arises from practice, is tested by practice and aims at objective truth. Gao presents this as an important part of Marxist philosophy with continuing relevance. The short article has three main parts: Lenin's inheritance and development of Marxist epistemology; his critique and transcendence of modern epistemological schools; and the contemporary value of his thought. It refers to Machism, Second International opportunism and Bogdanov's revisionism as the setting for Lenin's turn from historical questions to epistemology. It closes with a brief note on artificial intelligence and cognitive science. Gao argues that Lenin defended the materialist position that the real world exists independently of consciousness, and described cognition as a dialectical movement from sensory to rational knowledge and back to practice. Lenin is said to have developed Marxist views of practice as the criterion of truth, of the objectivity of truth, and of subjective initiative. Gao then reports Lenin's criticism of idealism, metaphysics, empiricism, neo-Kantianism and logical empiricism, each charged with one-sidedness. Lenin is said to have gone beyond both rationalism and empiricism by joining sensory and rational knowledge, and by stressing contradiction between thought and being as the driver of cognitive progress. Gao adds that Lenin treated knowledge as historical and class-conditioned. Gao concludes that Lenin's epistemology keeps its value in four ways. It puts practice first, stresses the historicity of knowledge, encourages theoretical innovation and promotes critical thinking amid globalisation and informatisation. Gao also claims that AI and neuroscience have moved epistemology from the relation between matter and consciousness to that between neural activity and consciousness. On this view, cognition is an active, dialectical process rather than simple stimulus and response, and Lenin's principles should guide the study of objective laws. Read the original if you want a brief, introductory Chinese overview of how Lenin's epistemology is presented for present-day teaching and research.

Grasping the dialectical thinking in the strategic thought of self-reform 科学把握自我革命战略思想中的辩证思维 Wu Fulai Wu Fulai takes up the strategic thought on the Party's self-reform that took shape after the 18th Party Congress (2012) and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) presented as the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Wu notes that scholarship has concentrated on theoretical sources, history, discourse and experience, while the dialectical thinking behind self-reform has been little studied. The author argues that this gap feeds a mistaken view that the Party has changed from a "revolutionary party" into a "governing party". The article's thesis is that self-reform follows the dialectical negation of the negation, and that this logic explains its meaning, its practice and its future course. The article has three main parts plus a short conclusion. The first traces the changing meaning of "revolution" in Chinese and Western contexts and reads self-reform through five lenses: the subject–object relation, historical experience, contradiction, the Party's character, and escape from the historical cycle. The second identifies four pairs of dialectical unity in practice. The third sets out routes for opening a "new realm" of self-reform in the new journey. In Wu's account, self-reform is the Party taking itself as the object of revolution. This is possible, the author says, because the Party has no special interests apart from those of the country, the nation and the people. Western parties, by contrast, are described as defending particular class interests and therefore incapable of such self-reform. In practice, Wu finds dialectical unity between self-discipline and discipline imposed from outside (including popular supervision), between consolidating foundations and innovating, between overall momentum and key priorities (with anti-corruption as the "most thorough" self-reform), and between turning the blade inward (self-reform) and outward (social revolution). Wu presents "people's supervision" and self-reform as the two complementary answers to the historical cycle, and rejects multi-party rotation and separation of powers as arguments against self-reform. For the new journey, Wu calls for four things: combining Party leadership with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, including the Two Establishes; regulating the use of power and improving the system of Party regulations; continuing the Party's spiritual lineage and ideals-and-convictions education; and standing with the people while innovating supervision. The conclusion holds that dialectical thinking is key to understanding the Party as a mission-driven party, and that it must keep its revolutionary character and long-term vigilance. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists ground the doctrine of self-reform in Marxist dialectics and in the Party's own historical narrative.

On the original contributions of Chinese Marxist philosophy 论中国马克思主义哲学的原创性贡献 Zhao Shifa Does Chinese Marxist philosophy have any originality? Zhao Shifa takes up a question he says is much disputed at home and abroad. Some critics call Chinese Marxist philosophy a copy of the Soviet textbook system. Others reject the idea of adapting Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context, preferring "Marxist philosophy in China". Zhao argues that these critics work with too narrow a notion of originality. On a broader, practice-based notion, he holds, Chinese Marxist philosophy is an original theoretical creation. The article has four parts. It first redefines originality. It then sets out the original content of Chinese Marxist philosophy across what Zhao calls three historic leaps: Mao Zedong's philosophy, the philosophy of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics (Deng Xiaoping, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development), and the philosophical thinking of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third part draws out three lessons. The fourth assesses the significance of this body of thought. Zhao distinguishes a narrow sense of originality (first or earliest creation) from a broad one, which he equates with independent innovation arising from practice. In this broad sense originality means creative solutions to practical contradictions. It rests on the unity of critique and inheritance, of content and form, and of theory and practice. Because Marxist philosophy was combined with Chinese realities for the first time by Chinese intellectuals and communists, Zhao says, the result counts as original. He names three lessons: keeping practice at the centre, exercising the Chinese nation's subjectivity, and opposing dogmatism. He treats dogmatism as the chief enemy, citing the Wang Ming line, the "Two Whatevers" and neoliberalism as "foreign dogma". He also lists Xi's contributions to the theory of practice and dialectics, to historical materialism, to ideology and discourse power, and to the unity of Chinese and global perspectives. Zhao concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy enriches Marxist theory. He also says it guides the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and offers what he calls Chinese wisdom for a new form of human civilization and a community with a shared future for mankind. He admits that its discipline, academic and discourse systems are still taking shape and that textbooks have not yet fully achieved a Chinese form. He describes Western modernity as facing internal contradictions and crisis. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language argument for the originality of Chinese Marxist philosophy, from Mao to Xi, and for the criteria it uses to judge originality.

Review of frontier issues in contemporary foreign Marxism research 当代国外马克思主义研究的前沿问题述评 Kong Ming'an Writing in Foreign Theoretical Trends (2023, no. 1), Kong Ming'an surveys the latest developments in foreign Marxism, the field that has existed as a discipline in China since the 1980s. The review opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the Politburo's 43rd collective study session (2017), which valued contemporary Marxist currents for their critical analysis of capitalism's structural contradictions, crises and new forms. Kong organises the field into ten thematic clusters. The clusters are: ideology theory; digital capitalism and new imperialism; consumer society and the labour theory of value; political philosophy of fairness and justice; eco-Marxism; contemporary populism; the Frankfurt School's critical theory across four generations; biopolitics and life philosophy after COVID-19; postmodernism and post-Marxism; and spatial critique and urban Marxism. The thinkers discussed include Althusser, Žižek, Christian Fuchs, David Harvey, Hardt and Negri, Baudrillard, G. A. Cohen, Habermas, John Bellamy Foster, Laclau, Mouffe, Agamben and Lefebvre. A short conclusion notes further schools, including analytical, structuralist and feminist Marxism and recent Japanese Marxism. Within each cluster Kong traces a line from Marx and the classical tradition to current theorists. Ideology moves from Marx's "false consciousness" through Gramsci to Althusser's interpellation and Žižek's ideological fantasy. Digital capitalism is presented as a new form of exploitation, through digital labour and "playbour", and as an extension of imperialism, discussed through Harvey's "spatio-temporal fix" and Hardt and Negri's immaterial labour. Kong also reports debates over justice (Habermas against Rawls, Cohen's critique of Nozick and Rawls), Foster's "metabolic rift", and Laclau and Mouffe's left populism against Žižek's criticism. Kong's own evaluations appear mainly in the populism section, which describes populism as destructive in practice and as present in China's online sphere. Kong concludes that foreign Marxism is open and inclusive, and that its theorists try to combine Marxism with the features of the present age. In Kong's view this shows Marxism's vitality and explanatory power. Kong adds that Chinese scholars need not accept these thinkers' specific views, but should attend to their methods and the questions they raise. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-academy map of the main currents of foreign Marxism, with names and works, as a guide to how this field is presented to Chinese readers.

Religion and politics in the perspective of Marx and Engels 马克思恩格斯视域中的宗教与政治 Tang Zixiang Tang Zixiang asks how Marx and Engels understood the relationship between religion and politics, a question the author sets against the persistence of religion in contemporary politics (the Iranian revolution, 11 September 2001, Hindu nationalism). Tang notes that primordialists such as Huntington treat religion as a cause of conflict, while instrumentalists treat it as a tool of material forces. The article argues that Marx and Engels resolve this by tracing religious questions back to their social and economic roots, so that religion has both a positive and a negative political face, and its final resolution lies in human emancipation. The article is built in three parts. The first treats religion as the sacred cloak of mass resistance, drawing mainly on Engels's The Peasant War in Germany and his essay on Ludwig Feuerbach. The second treats religion as an instrument of class oppression and aggressive expansion, using Marx on the Eastern Question and Engels on Russia, Spain and England. The third reconstructs the path from criticism of religion to political emancipation to human emancipation, drawing on Marx's On the Jewish Question and the introduction to his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. Tang argues that, in medieval Europe, theology absorbed all ideology, so peasant and plebeian movements, such as Thomas Müntzer's, had to take religious form. The author reads Engels as comparing early Christianity with the modern workers' movement. The cloak is dropped, Tang says, in the French bourgeois revolution, and socialism seeks salvation in this world. On the negative side, Tang holds that rulers use religion to deceive their own people and to justify wars, but that religious wars are at root class struggles over material interest, not caused by ideas. Tang also reads Marx as saying that political emancipation does not require abolishing religion. The modern state can separate from religion while religion flourishes in civil society, as in the North American states, but this emancipation remains partial and abstract. Tang concludes that criticism of religion is the premise of all criticism, and that the problem is solved only by overcoming alienation and restoring to people their own world and relations. In this account the proletariat, armed with philosophy, is the agent of universal human emancipation. With high productive forces and the disappearance of classes, the state and religion would leave the historical stage. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how Marx and Engels linked religion, class struggle and the state, written for a Chinese journal on science and atheism.

An outline of the atheist thought in the Guanzi chapter "Neiye" 《管子˙内业》无神论思想举要 Lu Mingl un Lu Minglun asks what atheist thinking can be found in "Neiye" (Inward Training), a chapter of the ancient Chinese compendium Guanzi. Lu argues that the chapter, a representative work of the Daoist current of the Jixia Academy in the Warring States period, built a fairly systematic outlook whose account of matter and of life carries a distinct atheist consciousness and is an early and original contribution. The article has four parts. The first examines how the chapter denies that ghosts and spirits have a ruling will. The second looks at how it affirms human subjectivity, in knowledge and in personal growth. The third turns to its exploration of the mechanisms of life, including health and longevity. A short conclusion assesses the chapter's place in the history of Chinese thought. Lu sets the discussion against Shang-dynasty belief in a personified Lord on High and the Zhou sense of a heavenly mandate. Lu's central claim is that "Neiye" takes refined qi (jingqi) as the origin of all things, including human beings, so that "ghosts and spirits" are only a mode of circulation of this qi. On this reading, insight comes from concentrated qi and not from spirits, and divination is dispensable. Statecraft depends on rulers' sound decisions and agriculture on the natural seasons, so the "heaven of will" becomes a "natural heaven". Lu then argues that the chapter makes sagehood the result of cultivating body and mind, with a calm heart and upright posture, and not a divine endowment. The same logic governs health: longevity follows from preserving qi, from controlling emotions and from relaxed, undistracted practice, so life span lies with the person and not with the gods. Lu cites Marx's remark that atheism affirms human existence through the negation of God. Lu concludes that "Neiye" elevates the human and lowers the divine, and had an enlightening effect. Lu concedes that it was a product of its age, that its theory is not fully consistent (it does not clearly separate matter from mental activity) and that its ideas on life-nurturing remain partly idealised. Lu calls on contemporary philosophers to mine such ancient texts for atheist ideas and develop them creatively for the needs of the new era, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you are interested in early Chinese materialist and atheist thought, or in how Chinese scholars present classical Daoist texts in an atheist framework.

Peasant cooperatives and common prosperity in rural areas: classical theory and Chinese practice 农民合作社促进乡村共同富裕的经典理论与中国实践 Han Yujie Xu Xuchu Han and Xu ask how peasant cooperatives relate to common prosperity in the countryside. They argue that the Marxist classics treated cooperatives as the necessary road for peasants towards common prosperity. On this view, cooperatives and common prosperity are bound in a relationship of mutual formation, and Chinese practice has put the idea to work. The article has three parts. The first reviews theory: the utopian socialists (More, Saint-Simon, Fourier, Owen), Marx and Engels, and Lenin. The second sets out the "symbiosis" of cooperatives and common prosperity in their conditions of emergence, social functions and ideals. The third traces Chinese practice from the revolutionary period to the post-18th Party Congress (2012) era, drawing on examples such as Yan'an consumer cooperatives and the Zhejiang, Sichuan and Shandong models. On theory, the authors read Marx and Engels as implying common prosperity without using the term. Cooperatives would abolish the town–country opposition and exploitation, and they should rest on public ownership of land, scaled-up operation, voluntary mutual benefit and gentle transformation of small peasants. Lenin is said to have turned cooperatives into a gradual, locally adapted route to socialism. For China, the authors claim cooperatives gave peasants land and means of production and brought them into socialist relations of production. They also credit the "two leaps" proposed by Deng Xiaoping with building a material base. In the primary, secondary and tertiary distributions, cooperatives are said to raise incomes, share value along the chain and embody a moral duty to help the weak. The authors conclude that, under Chinese modernization, cooperatives, collective economic organisations and composite cooperative bodies can drive rural revitalisation and narrow the town–country gap. Three paths are named: high-quality development of cooperatives, comprehensive reform of supply and marketing cooperatives, and the cooperative transformation of collective economies. They cast these forms as a "third road" for the policy of letting some get rich first to lead the rest. They note that absolute poverty has been eliminated but no lasting mechanism against relative poverty exists yet. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account that links the Marxist cooperative tradition to current rural policy and to named local cooperative models.

The formation and development of Marx and Engels's critique of religion and its scientific transcendence of the bourgeois view of religion 马克思恩格斯宗教批判思想的形成发展及其对资产阶级宗教观的科学超越 Meng Fei Yuan Xiaomin Meng Fei and Yuan Xiaomin ask how Marx and Engels's critique of religion took shape and why it should count as a scientific advance over bourgeois views of religion. They argue that the critique grew out of the founding of dialectical and historical materialism, takes the material conditions of life as the basis for understanding religion, and supplies a method for practical religious work in different countries. The article has three main parts. The first traces Marx and Engels's path from theism to atheism, from humanist to social psychology, and from economic reality to historical materialism. The second turns to Engels's later years, covering Anti-Dühring and Dialectics of Nature. The third sets out three ways in which the critique goes beyond bourgeois thinking about religion, and a short conclusion follows. In the authors' account, Marx moved from Hegel through Bruno Bauer and Feuerbach, breaking with Bauer in On the Jewish Question and with Feuerbach in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Feuerbach, they say, traced religion to alienated human nature but treated the human being as abstract and isolated, whereas Marx and Engels start from economic relations and class society. The authors argue that this yields three claims. Religion is an alienated fantasy and a special form of ideology. Its social roots lie in conditions human beings cannot master, and religious struggles are in essence struggles for political power between classes. It will wither away as science advances and as private ownership of the means of production is abolished and production is planned. They credit Engels with linking religion to the natural sciences, criticising pseudo-science and rejecting Dühring's call to ban religion in a future society. The authors conclude that the critique was an indispensable step in making the Marxist view of religion scientific. They draw a practical lesson from Engels: religion should be guided appropriately rather than prohibited, and freedom of religious belief is defended. They call for Marxist religious studies in the new era to draw on this body of thought and, in light of China's national conditions and the specific realities of religion in China, to build a sinicised Marxist study of religion. Read the original if you want a compact survey, from a Chinese Marxist perspective, of how Marx and Engels's views on religion developed and how they are applied to religious work in China today.

Building a social governance community in rural revitalisation 乡村振兴中的社会治理共同体建设 Zhao Xiaofeng Zhao Xiaofeng asks how a social governance community can be built in the countryside during rural revitalisation. The concept was first put forward by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and restated in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as a community in which everyone has responsibility, does their duty and shares in the benefits. Zhao's thesis is that local government must convert its monopoly power over public services into service rights granted to social and market actors. This must be done while four "hidden traps" are avoided and a relationship model of joint participation, consultation, shared responsibility and shared benefit is built. The article has four parts. It first sets out the starting point: the growth since reform and opening up of village committees, farmers' cooperatives, leading enterprises and rural social organisations. It then reviews governance theory, specifically delegation (principal–agent) theory and empowerment theory. Next it analyses the traps facing county and township governments, social organisations, enterprises and ordinary villagers. Finally it proposes four practical paths. Zhao criticises delegation theory for treating governance as power and control and leaving out the people, and mutual-empowerment theory for assuming that cooperatives help government. Zhao proposes shifting from a perspective of power and control to one of rights and services. Local government is a "power-monopolising" participant, while social organisations and enterprises are "right-expanding" participants who must win service rights. The four traps follow from this. Government may take over everything, driven by administrative subcontracting and promotion tournaments. Social organisations may fall into contests over rights. Enterprise capital may expand without order and squeeze out small farmers and "backbone farmers". Villagers, increasingly individualised, may participate without rules, as in profit-driven petitioning. Zhao proposes four mechanisms. The first is shared governance ideas under Party leadership, with the Party–people relationship as decisive. The second is joint construction: fostering more actors, avoiding both government-centred and society-centred models, and allocating or withdrawing service rights according to performance. The third is consultation and coordination, with local government as the likely coordinator and primary-level Party organisations stepping in when it fails. The fourth is benefit sharing, through common prosperity and coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, without coerced donations. Read the original if you want a sociological account of rural governance in China that draws on field observation and on the principal–agent and empowerment literatures.

The development, rich connotations and far-reaching significance of the contemporary Chinese view of human rights 当代中国人权观的发展脉络、丰富内涵及深远意义 Xu Xianchun Xu Xianchun sets out to explain the "contemporary Chinese view of human rights", which the author presents as the theoretical counterpart of a "Chinese path of human rights development" formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Xu argues that this view is a major result of integrating the Marxist view of human rights with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. It guides officials in respecting and safeguarding rights and points the way forward for the cause in the new era. The article has three parts. The first traces the sources and history of the view: Marx and Engels, traditional ideas of people-centredness, and the Party's explorations from the New Democratic Revolution through the Mao, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao periods. The second sets out the content of Xi Jinping's statements on human rights under the heading of the Party's leadership, the people's standpoint, subsistence and development rights, health, a systematic approach, vulnerable groups, rule of law and global governance. The third assesses the view's significance. Xu's core claim is continuity. Marxist classics held that rights are social, class-based and historical, and that bourgeois human rights are both historically progressive and hypocritical. Each generation of Party leaders, in Xu's account, added to this: Mao tied rights to national independence and the people's mastery of the country; Deng stressed development and rejected "human rights over sovereignty"; Jiang named subsistence and development as the primary rights; Hu stressed a people-centred approach and the Scientific Outlook on Development. Xi's "six adherences" distil the Chinese path: Party leadership, the people's principal position, China's actual conditions, subsistence and development rights first, rule of law, and participation in global governance. Xu argues that no single model fits all countries, and that criticism of China by some Western states is a strategic effort at Westernization and containment. Xu concludes that the view widens the Chinese path, lays a human rights foundation for Chinese modernization, and enriches the diversity of human rights civilization. It does so by promoting the "common values of all mankind" in place of Western "universal values" and by offering developing countries an alternative. The author calls for firmness and strategic resolve in following this path. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists trace the genealogy of the Chinese human rights discourse from Marx to Xi Jinping.

The intellectual sources and original theoretical contributions of the "Two Integrations" “两个结合”的思想渊源和原创性理论贡献 Jin Minqing Jin Minqing asks where the thesis of the Two Integrations came from and what is original about it. The thesis, put forward by Xi Jinping, calls for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Jin argues that it distils a century of Party theoretical innovation, reveals the laws of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and makes an original contribution to that process. The article has three parts. It first traces the history of attempts to link Marxism with Chinese conditions and culture, from Liang Qichao, Zhu Zhixin and Wang Zichen to Li Dazhao, Cai Hesen, Chen Duxiu and the early Party. It then follows the Party's accumulated experience from Mao Zedong's sinification of Marxism through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, up to Xi's formulation at the Party's centenary (2021) and the 20th Party Congress (2022). The third part lists the original contributions of the new era. Jin's central claim is that the two integrations were pursued unevenly. Earlier generations, facing national independence and construction, concentrated on the first integration, while the second was relatively underdeveloped; Mao spoke of a "deep integration" with culture but never turned it into a clear proposition. Jin holds that the new era's historic mission made the second integration especially important. Jin then argues that Xi's theory joins Marxist principles to Chinese tradition at specific points. Marxism's view of the people as makers of history is joined with the minben (people-as-foundation) tradition, and the communist ideal of a "true community" with the ideal of "all under heaven as one family", yielding a community with a shared future for mankind. Marxist views on nature are joined with the unity of heaven and humanity, yielding ecological civilization, and Party purity with traditions of self-examination, yielding the Party's self-reform. Jin also credits Xi with analysis of the contemporary epoch, the "new contradiction" of the new era, Chinese modernization and a Marxist stance toward traditional culture. Jin concludes that the Two Integrations work in both directions. Marxism takes root in Chinese culture and in popular values, and traditional culture is raised to the level of Marxism through creative transformation and innovative development. Jin presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the exemplar of this process and as a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars trace the lineage of the Two Integrations from the early twentieth century to Xi's thought.

Mao Zedong's exploration of the path of Chinese modernization: process, main contributions and contemporary value 毛泽东对中国式现代化道路的探索历程、主要贡献及当代价值 Yang Xiaojun Shao Yan Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which presents Chinese modernization as the product of long exploration since 1949, Yang Xiaojun and Shao Yan ask what Mao Zedong contributed to that path. They argue that Mao was a pioneer of Chinese modernization, and that his explorations, including his errors, prepared its opening and development. They hold that studying them has theoretical and practical value for pursuing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first traces Mao's exploration in three phases: the revolutionary period, when he sought national independence and industrialization; the early People's Republic, when he imitated the Soviet heavy-industry model; and the period after 1956, when he sought a path suited to China's conditions. The second lists his contributions in theory, institutions, strategy and development model. The third draws a line from Mao to Xi Jinping on theory, Party leadership and methodology. On the authors' account, Mao's New Democracy theory supplied the first theoretical outline of modernization. The socialist transformation then built the basic economic and political institutions: public ownership, the people's congress system, multi-party cooperation and regional ethnic autonomy. Mao's strategy moved from industrialization to the "four modernizations", and from a catch-up campaign against Britain and the United States to a "two-step" plan. His model moved from "learning from the Soviet Union across the board" to independent exploration, marked by On the Ten Major Relationships and the "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese realities. The authors concede that the Great Leap Forward was a failure but say Mao reflected on it and corrected course. For the present, the authors argue that Xi Jinping inherited and developed Mao's legacy in three ways. He built the theoretical framework of Chinese modernization, he placed the Party's overall leadership first, and he extended Mao's seeking truth from facts through investigation, problem orientation and practical action. They present the Party's self-reform as the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall, following Mao's "supervision by the people". They conclude that Mao's exploration is the historical and logical starting point of Chinese modernization, and that it broke the claim that capitalist modernization is the only model. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese academics now link Mao-era modernization thinking to Xi Jinping's Chinese modernization narrative.

Displaying the mighty power of the manned spaceflight spirit on the new journey of the new era 在新时代新征程上彰显载人航天精神的磅礴伟力 Xu Chuan This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in April 2023, asks how the spirit forged in China's manned spaceflight programme can serve the Party's central task after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Xu Chuan argues that the manned spaceflight spirit, part of the Party's spiritual lineage that begins with the great founding spirit, will supply strong spiritual power for advancing Chinese modernization. The article is organised around the four components of the spirit as Xu presents them: being especially able to endure hardship, to fight, to tackle key problems, and to dedicate oneself. Each section follows the same pattern. It first explains how the quality arose in the spaceflight workforce, then traces its roots in Chinese civilisational tradition and the Party's history, and finally says how it should be carried forward in the new era. Xu draws heavily on speeches by Xi Jinping and on classical Chinese verse. In Xu's account, endurance of hardship came from harsh conditions and a weak technical base, and fighting spirit from the scale and risk of the project. Tackling key problems relied on the nationwide system of concentrated effort, which Xu says filled technological gaps, and dedication meant generations giving up personal interests, even their lives. Xu presents each trait as both a legacy of the Chinese nation and a reflection of the Communist Party leading the people. The author links them to present tasks: young cadres should be tempered at the grassroots and in hard regions, struggle is needed amid mounting risks, key core technologies cannot be bought or begged, and selflessness is needed in a turbulent world. Xu concludes that these four qualities should be promoted on the new journey, and calls for turning spiritual wealth into inexhaustible material creativity. The piece calls for a new, improved nationwide system for science and technology, for more breakthroughs "from 0 to 1", and for dedication that ties personal development to the country's fate. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary links a specific national project to the Party's spiritual lineage and to the goals of Chinese modernization.

The dual logic of Marx's study of capital Between economic philosophy and economic anthropology 马克思研究资本问题的双重逻辑 Yan Hui Yan Hui asks what the theoretical and practical value of Marx's critique of capital is for the present, and argues that Marx approached capital through a dual logic. The author distinguishes economics, economic philosophy and economic anthropology as three dimensions of his inquiry, though Marx never named them so. Economic anthropology comes first logically, because Marx had already fixed the anthropological meaning of labour and capital before analysing them. Economic philosophy comes first in time, because it concerns the historical emergence of capitalism. The article has three parts. The first reads Marx's early manuscripts, notably the excerpts from James Mill and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, on money, alienation, species-being and communism. The second turns to Capital and the Grundrisse, covering the movement from commodity and money to surplus value, and the historical standing of capitalism. The third takes up the passage from economic anthropology to philosophical anthropology and the real road back to a "human world". Yan draws on Hegel, Weber and Marxist classics throughout. Yan holds that economics alone, treated as value-neutral natural science, would make exploitation look like a natural law. Marx therefore added a value logic of what people "ought to do" to the fact logic of what they "can do". Capital is abstract and also concrete: it is the starting point from which commodity, money, class and state relations unfold. Yan reads the mystery of surplus value through the gap between labour-power and labour, and through the fact that workers advance their labour to the capitalist on credit. Capitalism is analysed as a value outlook, a mode of production and a social formation. It is progressive because it dissolves relations of personal dependence and builds a system of universal exchange, but it is historically limited. The shift from dependence on things to social dependence is placed in public ownership, where sociality is the premise of production and not its alienated result. Yan also develops a threefold account of time (natural, social and meaningful) and argues that rising productivity should expand free time. Yan concludes that Marx's study of capital was never an end in itself. It was a means of uncovering the secret of exploitation and finding a basis for moving beyond capitalism towards communism. The sequence economic philosophy, economic anthropology, philosophical anthropology gives Marx's mode of thought, while the movement from lower to complete private ownership to communist public ownership gives the objective historical logic. The author describes Marx as both an idealist and a realist, and sees continuing significance in his philosophical anthropology in an age of globalization. Read the original if you want a philosophical, early-Marx-centred reading of Capital that links alienation theory to the critique of political economy and to questions of public ownership and free time.

Marx's idea of "species-being" and its contemporary value Based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 马克思的“类存在”思想及其当代价值 Wu Ning Li Xinglin Marx rarely uses the vocabulary of the "species" in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, yet Wu Ning and Li Xinglin argue that a developed idea of "species-being" runs through the text and survives the formation of Marx's new materialist worldview. The article claims that Marx took the terminology from Feuerbach but gave it a different foundation and content. It also holds that this idea has practical value today for building a community with a shared future for mankind. The article has three parts. The first traces the idea from Feuerbach's concept of the species to Marx's transformation of it, and answers critics, above all Louis Althusser and his thesis of an "epistemological break". The second reconstructs the content of species-being through three categories: species-relations, species-characteristics and species-essence. The third draws out the idea's contemporary significance. The authors' central contrast is that Feuerbach understands the species through consciousness, feeling and religion, and stays abstract, while Marx locates it in free, conscious labour and objectifying practice. On this reading, species-being is not given by nature but forms through human practice, in two relations: with nature and with society. The authors say Althusser mistook Marx's Feuerbachian vocabulary for Feuerbachian humanism and overlooked the role of labour, so his "two Marxes" is, in their view, a misreading. They argue that the early and later Marx are continuous, and that Marx's early exploration made his later thought more mature. They also hold that alienated labour reduces people to creatures of physical need and one-dimensional existence, which restricts their all-round development. The authors conclude that species-being offers a way of thinking for the community with a shared future for mankind. In their account it stresses openness, inclusiveness and unity, and treats the individual and the species as a dialectical pair in which each enriches the other. They argue that it asks states to tolerate differences of system and culture while seeking deeper unity through mutual learning, and that it points to reconciliation between humanity and nature. They present the community with a shared future as a concrete application of Marx's idea in Chinese reality. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of the 1844 Manuscripts that rejects Althusser's break thesis and links species-being to current Chinese foreign-policy language.

The theory of Chinese modernization as a major innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 中国式现代化理论是马克思主义中国化时代化的重大创新 Yan Xiaofeng Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yan Xiaofeng takes up a question of Party theory: how the theory of Chinese modernization relates to the long project of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Following Xi Jinping's remarks at a study seminar on the Congress, Yan argues that the theory is a major theoretical innovation and a major achievement in advancing that project. In this account it is also an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article, a commentary in a Party theoretical journal, has three parts. The first argues that opening up a new horizon for the adaptation of Marxism requires developing the theory, and traces how the Party formed it through the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out the theory's contributions. The third considers its role as guidance for the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects. Yan's central claim is that the Party advances the adaptation of Marxism by answering major questions of each era, and that Chinese modernization is such a question. Since the Opium War, the author holds, the Western capitalist road to modernization has proved unworkable in China. The contributions Yan lists include the claim that modernization is not Westernization and that countries may choose their own paths. Others are that Party leadership is the most essential feature, and that the Chinese features are a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Yan also credits the theory with defining the essential requirements, a new form of human civilization, and a strategic layout. The article presents the Two Integrations as the fundamental route, and as the source of the theory. Yan concludes that the new journey brings fresh strategic conditions and risks, including external challenges, deep-seated domestic contradictions and problems within the Party. These call for further theoretical answers, including to the \"questions of modernization\" Xi raised at the dialogue with world political parties. Yan calls for adherence to Xi Jinping Thought, study of the 20th Congress, and enrichment of the theory on the basis of practice. Read the original if you want to see how a Party theorist frames Chinese modernization within the official narrative of the adaptation of Marxism in the Chinese context.

Understanding the theory of Chinese modernization through historical materialism 以唯物史观理解中国式现代化理论 Liu Tongfang Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Tongfang asks how the theory of Chinese modernization should be understood from the standpoint of historical materialism. Liu argues that the theory grasps the combined situation of "changes in the world, changes of the times and changes in history", anticipates the basic direction of modernization, and links China's development to the common development of the world. In this reading it is both a major theoretical innovation and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. The article has four sections. It first examines how the theory understands "historical change" dialectically; it then treats the theory as opening a turn in the epoch of world history; third, it considers how the theory helps build a pattern of common development in the contemporary world; and finally it places the theory within scientific socialism. Throughout, Liu draws on Marx and Engels's theory of world history, the unity of the historical and the logical, and the totality of social relations. Liu's central claim is that the theory rests on three sets of historical relations: humanity and nature, China and the world, and material and spiritual civilization. Against the Western-dominated idea of modernity, which Liu describes as equating modernization with Westernization or capitalization, Chinese modernization is presented as a "part" of world history that advances the whole. Liu says it does so through a community with a shared future for mankind, common values of humanity and reform of global governance. On this account it sublates the capitalist form of civilization and creates a new form of human civilization. The theory is also said to apply historical materialism's totalising method to the Party's leadership and its people-centred approach. Liu concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era guides the practice of Chinese modernization. This practice, in Liu's account, answers "the people's question", "the world's question" and "the question of the times", and gives scientific socialism a contemporary Chinese form with a global character. Liu urges Marxist researchers to grasp contemporary Chinese Marxism through the "Chinese logic" of historical materialism and to strengthen the reach of Chinese governance experience abroad. Read the original if you want a philosophical, world-history-centred account of how official Chinese modernization theory is justified through historical materialism.

Peripheral liberation in Samir Amin's perspective: substance, logic and possibilities 萨米尔·阿明视域中的边缘解放：实质、逻辑及其可能性 Li Xiaole Can the periphery of the capitalist world system carry the hope of human liberation? Li Xiaole takes up this question through the Egyptian Marxist Samir Amin (1931–2018), especially his book The People's Spring (2017) on the Arab uprisings. Li argues that Amin's account of the Arab movement as a peripheral, national-liberation struggle has real insight but that peripheral liberation does not express a necessary law of human liberation. The article has three parts. The first traces, on Amin's account, how the Arab world moved from centre to periphery. The second sets out the form and substance of the Arab movement as Amin reads it. The third is Li's own assessment, which weighs practical and theoretical weaknesses and ends by naming what Amin's work still offers Chinese scholarship. In the first two parts, Li reports that Amin extends the world system back to the tributary systems of antiquity and treats Europe's rise and the decline of the Middle East as shifts in the centre–periphery structure. In Amin's view the Arab movement is anti-imperialist and potentially anti-capitalist, aimed at 'collective imperialism' (the United States, Europe and Japan). Its driving force is the popular masses, and its goals are social justice, national independence and thorough democracy. Li then criticises Amin on two grounds. In practice, the movement lacked a long-term socialist strategy, a strong organised leadership and a clear historical subject, and Amin's prescription of 'delinking' from the world market does not fit reality. In theory, Li says, Amin neglects uneven development inside peripheral countries and departs from Marxist production and class analysis, since he stresses accumulation and exchange over production. Li also holds that centre–periphery contradiction is only a particular contradiction, not the basic contradiction of the contemporary world. Li concludes that peripheral liberation cannot be equated with human liberation. Li presents a community with a shared future for mankind as the correct solution to the basic contradiction of the present international order. Li still credits Amin with prompting questions about how to explain the distinctiveness and world-historical significance of China's socialist path, and how to discuss global and domestic justice from a modernity different from that of the capitalist world system. Read the original if you want a Chinese critical appraisal of Amin's dependency and world-system theory, and of his reading of the Arab uprisings, set against Marxist production and class analysis.

The History Workshop at the University of the Witwatersrand and the rise of social history in South Africa 金山大学历史工作坊与南非社会史研究的兴起 Li Pengtao Li Pengtao asks how the History Workshop at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits) helped reshape South African historiography from the 1970s. The article argues that the Workshop, formed amid the anti-apartheid struggle and influenced by British Marxist historiography and African history, was the core institution that made "history from below" the dominant mode of South African social history. Li notes that Chinese scholarship has surveyed South African historiography but has not yet studied the Workshop in a dedicated piece. The article has four parts. It first sets out the Workshop's origins: the labour movement and the Soweto uprising of 1976, the influence of British Marxist historians such as E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm, African independence and oral-history scholarship, and changes in English-medium universities. It then describes its activities, including the triennial conferences from 1978, the interdisciplinary network and its conference themes after apartheid. Next it assesses four scholarly contributions and ends with a general evaluation and the criticisms the Workshop has faced. Li's central move is to place the Workshop within the lineage of revisionist (radical) history. In Li's account it grew out of a critique of the structuralist revisionists, influenced by Althusser and Poulantzas, who stressed that capital shaped apartheid and paid little attention to African agency. The Workshop instead stressed divisions within the apartheid state, the fluidity of race and class, and black urban culture. Li identifies four contributions: local and urban history, public history (popular textbooks, open days, the apartheid museum in Johannesburg, teacher workshops), oral history as a way around the lack of written records of black lives, and gender history. Li concludes that the Workshop widened the scope of modern South African history and later contributed to rebuilding the new South Africa. Li also reports three lines of criticism: too little theory, compared with India's Subaltern Studies; a mainly white membership and a neglect of racial oppression; and weaknesses in method, including "history in the town" rather than "history of the town" and inattention to power in oral interviews. Li adds that its steady commitment to oral and local history, and its real-world concern, still shape South African historical writing. Read the original if you study South African or African historiography, the reception of British Marxist history from below, or the links between scholarship and anti-apartheid politics.

On the theoretical construction of Marxist religious studies 关于马克思主义宗教学理论建设的有关问题 Lü Jianfu Responding to Xi Jinping's call at the 2021 National Conference on Religious Work to "strengthen the disciplinary construction of Marxist religious studies", Lü asks what that discipline is and how it relates to the "Marxist view of religion". The author argues that the two concepts share the same content and differ only in register. Marxist religious studies is, in Lü's view, a scientific and fully formed discipline, and efforts to deny it or fold it into Western religious studies are misguided. The article has three parts. The first defends the scientific status of Marxist religious studies, drawing on Ren Jiyu's 1979 definition and on the debates in two textbooks, the General Theory of Religious Studies and its New Edition. The second traces how the "Marxist view of religion" became an ideological concept in the 1990s, in the context of Xinjiang. The third examines the discipline system and proposes a structure for it. Lü rejects the textbooks' claim that Marx and Engels offered only a "view" of religion, not a "study". In Lü's account, their criteria of independence and systematicness are flawed: a discipline is defined by the quality of its principles, methods and objective laws, not by quantity. Marxist religious studies, following Ren, is a science of the laws of religion's emergence, development and eventual disappearance, grounded in dialectical and historical materialism and in scientific atheism. Lü holds that the "Marxist view of religion" arose from 1990s propaganda and education work after the 1990 Baren unrest and was later stretched to absorb Western religious studies and the "religious culture" theory. Lü further argues that Western religious studies has no general discipline and no real sub-disciplines. Comparative religion, the philosophy of religion and the sociology of religion are described as theology repackaged or as branches of other fields. The author reads the proliferation of such sub-disciplines, including "Marxist" versions of them, as religious infiltration of philosophy and the social sciences. Lü proposes building on the discipline that has actually taken shape over 60 years and dropping "general religious research" as a separate field. Three areas would be strengthened: Marxist religious theory, scientific atheism, and the theory and policy of proletarian parties' religious work, each with a detailed list of sub-topics. Read the original if you want a detailed, polemical statement of one position in Chinese debates over Marxist religious studies, including its account of the 1990s background and its proposed disciplinary framework.

The Lei Feng spirit as a spiritual coordinate for the new social ethos of our times 时代新风新貌的精神坐标 Chen Peng Writing in Guangming Daily in 2023, on the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other veteran revolutionaries' inscriptions for Lei Feng, Chen Peng takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to foster a new social ethos. Chen argues that the Lei Feng spirit matches five spirits named in that report and is a 'spiritual coordinate' for the new ethos. This short commentary links each of the five spirits to episodes from Lei Feng's life: labour, striving, dedication, creativity, and thrift and frugality. Each section pairs an anecdote or quotation with a statement from Xi Jinping or a claim about the Party and nation. Chen presents Lei Feng as a model labourer, honoured at work in Wangcheng, on the Weishui project and at Anshan Iron and Steel. His seven-day flood-control effort at a reservoir in 1960 is offered as an example of striving. His maxim of 'benefiting others without thought of self' and his help to strangers on a train illustrate dedication. His fuel-saving truck modification and a mud-hauling device illustrate creativity, and his refusal of a second uniform and his donations from a small allowance illustrate thrift. Chen contends that the Chinese people and the Party have advanced through these qualities, and that Lei Feng has become a common name for selfless contributors. Chen concludes that Lei Feng, a 'people's hero', embodies the spirit of the age, and that his example has lit people's hearts for 60 years. Chen calls for deeper study of Xi Jinping's statements on promoting the Lei Feng spirit, so that it is passed on and builds strength for the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party publicity officials link the Lei Feng model to the 20th Party Congress's language on spiritual civilization.

Whole-process people's democracy as a transcendence of Western democratic politics An analysis based on the system of people's congresses 全过程人民民主对西方民主政治的超越 Cheng Enfu Sun Shaoyong Cheng Enfu and Sun Shaoyong ask what institutional vehicle makes whole-process people's democracy real, and argue that it is the system of people's congresses. Published in 2022, shortly before and in the light of the 20th Party Congress, the article presents this system as a wholly new political institution that goes beyond Western democratic politics. The article has three parts. The first describes the nature and features of the people's congress system and compares it with earlier Chinese options (constitutional monarchy, the Kuomintang presidential system) and with Western models, namely the separation of powers in the United States and cabinet government in Britain. The second argues that the system embodies a democracy that is the most extensive, the most genuine and the most effective. The third sets out Xi Jinping's eight \"whether" tests and four \"look at, but look more at\" criteria for judging whether a political system is democratic and effective, and applies each to China and the United States. The authors hold that the form of state follows its content: the people's congress system is the form of government that corresponds to the people's democratic dictatorship. They argue that it is extensive because Party leadership and democratic centralism cover a huge population. In their account it is genuine because it joins electoral and consultative democracy at the \"input end\" with decision-making, management and supervision at the \"output end\", all under the rule of law. They argue that it is effective because it keeps the people as masters of the country. By contrast, the authors describe American democracy as elite or oligarchic. In their reading it is dominated by money, lobbying and a politics of vetoes, and it reduces popular participation to periodic voting, with unfulfilled promises. Chinese practice, they say, offers orderly leadership succession, collective decision-making, merit-based recruitment and layered supervision. The authors conclude that the people's congress system unifies Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance.
