They call for upholding and improving it, strengthening its lead role in legislation and the effectiveness of its supervision, and rejecting what they call superstitious faith in Western-style democracy. They expect this to raise governance capacity and contribute to human political civilisation. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese scholars use the people's congress system to contrast whole-process people's democracy with the American model, and to see how the official criteria for judging democracy are applied point by point.

Continuously raising the level of urban safety governance 不断提升城市安全治理水平 Wu Aiqun This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in 2023, asks how cities can improve their safety governance as part of public safety governance. Wu Aiqun argues that, guided by Xi Jinping's statements on urban work and the strategic plans of the 20th Party Congress (2022), cities should pursue reform and innovation in three areas: evaluation standards, safety safeguards and governance effectiveness. The piece is organised under three headings that follow these areas. It draws heavily on quotations from Xi Jinping and on central Party and State Council documents on work safety and urban safety development. It closes the opening framing with the aim of weaving an all-round, multi-layered public safety net. On evaluation, Wu holds that the city is a complex system, so assessment must use a systems perspective. Accident counts are an outcome measure, while hazard checks, supervision and enforcement, and rescue capacity are process measures that should also be included, moving governance towards prevention. On safeguards, Wu calls for strengthening grassroots foundations and responsibility systems, improving laws and local regulations under Xi Jinping's thought on rule of law, and expanding technology such as data sharing and urban lifeline projects. On effectiveness, Wu stresses a people-centred approach, the principle that development must not come at the expense of safety, governance innovation, and systemic governance that breaks down departmental and regional fragmentation. Wu concludes that urban safety should be treated as comprehensive and holistic, with "whole-chain" supervision and "all-hazard" rescue capacity, and with Party committees, governments, departments and enterprises each bearing their responsibilities. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames urban safety governance in the terms of the 20th Party Congress.

On historical confidence, cultural confidence and civilizational confidence 论历史自信、文化自信和文明自信 Chen Jinlong Chen Jinlong takes up three concepts that appear in recent Party discourse: historical confidence, cultural confidence and civilizational confidence. The 20th Party Congress report (2022) called for firm historical and cultural confidence, and Xi Jinping had earlier put forward civilizational confidence. Chen argues that the three are distinct in content yet closely linked, and that clarifying their meanings, features and relations is the basis for strengthening them. The article has four sections. The first three deal with each concept in turn, tracing when Xi Jinping first used it, defining it and listing its characteristics. The fourth examines how the three relate. Chen draws mainly on Xi's speeches and on the Party's third historical resolution (2021). Chen holds that historical confidence, as Xi uses the term, refers specifically to confidence in the history of the Communist Party. It covers the Party's major achievements over a century and the spirit of its struggle. Cultural confidence means confidence in socialist culture with Chinese characteristics, meaning fine traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. Civilizational confidence covers confidence in Chinese civilization and in the "new form of human civilization" that Chinese modernization is said to have created. The author describes this new form as people-centred, aimed at all-round human development, and as having moved beyond the defects of Western capitalist civilization and corrected the deviations of traditional socialist models. On their relations, Chen argues that history comes first, so historical confidence underlies the other two. Culture precedes civilization, which Chen treats as the refined, progressive part of culture. Cultural confidence therefore rests on historical confidence and prepares the ground for civilizational confidence. Chen concludes that civilizational confidence grows out of, and sublimates, the other two. It is the higher and more lasting form, and it shows more fully the world significance of Chinese civilization and the new form of human civilization. Listing the three together follows both a temporal logic, the order in which history, culture and civilization form, and a spatial logic of decreasing scope. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Party theorists define and rank these three "confidences" and of the Xi Jinping speeches they cite.

"Human emancipation" in the perspective of community theory 共同体理论视域中的“人的解放” Zhao Zixu Wang Shirun Zhao Zixu and Wang Shirun argue that "community" (gongtongti) was long dismissed as an immature element of the early Marx under the influence of the Soviet system of Marxist theory. Reflection on that system, translations of Marxist scholars from abroad, and Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, they say, offer a chance to reread the concept. Their thesis is that community runs through Marx's whole thought as a changing category: if "human emancipation" is the theme and aim of Marx's philosophy, community theory is its foundation and guarantee. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2023, follows Marx's treatment of community through four stages. These are his rejection of Hegel's view in the early writings, the community thinking of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology, the historical account of pre-capitalist forms in the Grundrisse manuscripts of Capital, and the "time economy" through which capital prepares the restoration of community. Hegel, Feuerbach, Aristotle, Kant and Gramsci appear as reference points. The authors read Marx's development as a triad of thesis, antithesis and synthesis. In the 1844 Manuscripts, they say, the unalienated "species life" is lost through private property and alienated labour, and communism as community restores it. The German Ideology supplies the "false community" (antithesis) and the "true community" (synthesis) but leaves the thesis missing. The authors hold that the Grundrisse fills this gap with the "original community", in which labour and ownership are undivided. They describe Marx's three forms of ownership (Asiatic, ancient, Germanic) and argue that only the Germanic form, resting on individual ownership, contained the conditions for free labour and wage labour. Once civil society emerged and the world market formed, the authors say, capital seemed to make emancipation impossible. They contend, however, that Capital shows capital's civilising role: by creating surplus labour and shortening necessary labour, it makes possible a "time economy" under workers' own control, which supports the return of community. They conclude that Marx's vision of community will be realised in the move from theory to reality, and they link this to Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of how community underpins Marx's idea of emancipation, from Hegel's critique to the Grundrisse.

The historical-materialist foundations of Marx's thought on the "real community" 马克思“真正的共同体”思想的唯物史观基础 Sang Mingxu Sang Mingxu asks how Marx's idea of the "real community" ("true community", 真正的共同体) should be understood and used. The article, a short piece first published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2023, argues that the idea did not arrive as a finished scientific theory. In Sang's account it passed from a humanist (anthropological) position to historical materialism, and only the later, historical-materialist formulations should serve as the main basis for research. The article follows the concept through three texts. It begins with the 1844 critique of "The King of Prussia and Social Reform", then turns to The German Ideology, and finally to the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse). It then sets out eight features of the real community as Marx developed it on a historical-materialist basis. The last section draws out three implications for present-day theory and practice. Sang reads the 1844 formulation, "the essence of man is the true community of man", as a humanist proposition shaped by Feuerbach's influence. It defines human essence abstractly, apart from concrete social relations. In The German Ideology the real community is contrasted with the illusory communities of the past, which rest on the division of labour and private property. It presupposes highly developed productive forces, universal intercourse and the disappearance of private property and the division of labour. In the Grundrisse Marx ironically calls money and capital the inverted "community" of capitalism. Sang's eight features cover the community's definition, its historical position beyond the capitalist mode of production, its characteristics, its subjects (real individuals), its inner principle (free association), its ownership basis (individual ownership rebuilt on common possession of the means of production), its dialectical structure and its means of realisation. Sang distinguishes the real community from a community with a shared future for mankind. In Sang's account the latter is a global community of development that stands on this side of capitalism, with nation-states as its subjects and a mixed global ownership structure, while the former is its long-term goal. For building contemporary communities, such as communities of social governance, Sang proposes four principles: realism, dialectics, historicity and agency. Sang warns that citing Marx's humanist-stage statements as the main evidence weakens Marxism's explanatory power. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based outline of how Marx's concept changed and how a Chinese scholar links it to the community with a shared future for mankind.

Advancing the Party's self-reform with a great spirit of historical initiative 以伟大的历史主动精神推进党的自我革命 Luo Lizhang Lin Wenkang This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to advance the Party's self-reform. Luo and Lin argue that, under new historical conditions, the Communist Party can complete its mission only if it pursues self-reform with a great spirit of historical initiative. They present willingness to reform itself as what marks the Party out from other parties. The article builds its case around three requirements: historical consciousness, historical self-confidence and historical responsibility. Each is divided into two aspects and supported by quotations from Xi Jinping, the 2021 Party resolution on its century of struggle, and Marx. On consciousness, the authors say the Party must grasp historical laws and put the people first, accepting supervision from the people and judging the results of self-reform by whether they approve. It must also hold to its founding mission and inherit its tradition of self-reform. On self-confidence, they hold that the Party's achievements and the historical experience set out in the resolution are the source of confidence, and that these must be fully summed up. On responsibility, they call for a clear reading of historical trends and of the Party's historical position, meaning the new era. They link this to the "great changes unseen in a century" and to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The authors conclude that the key to building a modern socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation lies in the Party. They call on it to stay vigilant, rally around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and so guide a "great social revolution". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how official Party discourse in 2023 framed self-reform in terms of historical initiative.

Interpreting the classics and innovating discourse 经典诠释与话语创新 Shan Chuanyou How should Chinese Marxists read the Marxist classics so that their language can renew itself? Writing in a newspaper commentary in March 2023, Shan argues that classical interpretation and discourse innovation form one process. Drawing on hermeneutics, Shan holds that interpretation must be historical, mediating and applied, and that it should aim at adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times rather than at repeating quotations. The piece is built in three parts, each pairing a feature of interpretation with a feature of discourse innovation: historicity and the precondition of innovation; mediation and dialogue; application and practice. It engages Western hermeneutics (Schleiermacher's methodological hermeneutics, the idea of the text's autonomy, the limiting of interpretation to understanding and explanation). It also cites Xi Jinping, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, and takes Chinese modernization as the main problem to which the classics are addressed. Shan first rejects dogmatism and the ideal of returning wholly to an author's original meaning. Texts, authors and interpreters are all products of history, and interpreters carry the cultural tradition, including a Marxism that has by now become part of China's own pre-understanding. Second, interpretation is a dialogue organised around problems. Shan names the questions of modernization as today's problem field: whether it means Westernization, and whether it must bring polarisation, material supremacy and zero-sum competition. Marx's warning against turning his account of Western European capitalism into a universal philosophy of history is read as showing that modernization is not Westernization. Third, following Marx's emphasis on changing the world, Shan calls hermeneutics a practical philosophy in which understanding, explanation and application cannot be separated, and in which application is the core. Shan warns against pragmatism, which is said to use relative truth to deny absolute truth and so treat the classics as valid only for their own time. Shan concludes that, in the new era, interpreters should return to the classics repeatedly, starting from the practice of Chinese modernization. In this way they can draw on the classics to generate innovation and use localised Marxist discourse to rally the people for building a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese theorists use Western hermeneutics to justify reinterpreting Marxist texts in support of discourse innovation and Chinese modernization.

Revisiting the claim that the logical starting-point category of Capital is the commodity "labour-power" 再论《资本论》逻辑起点范畴是“劳动力”商品 Cheng Hao Cheng Yanjun Which category serves as the logical starting point of Marx's Capital? Cheng Hao and Cheng Yanjun argue that it is the commodity "labour-power", not the ordinary commodity as a "thing" analysed in the opening chapters. They call the first view the "thing-commodity theory" and their own the "labour-power commodity theory". In their account the choice decides whether Capital is read as a rigorous, scientific logical system of human emancipation, and it matters for building a political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics modelled on Capital. The article surveys Hegel's Logic and Marx's remarks on method, and then recent Chinese scholarship on starting points. It sets out a broad meaning of "commodity" in Capital as a pair of categories, then criticises the thing-commodity theory for internal contradiction and vulgarity. It ends by outlining the content and significance of the labour-power theory. The authors also draw on the late statement of Wei Xinghua, a prominent Capital scholar, that the commodity cannot be the logical starting point of capitalist political economy. The authors distinguish an "analytical starting point" from a "logical starting point". In their reading the opening analysis of the thing-commodity is only an "overture", while the labour-power commodity of the second part is the "main melody", to which the first part is subordinate. They hold that the two commodities form an opposed yet organically unified pair, and that the logical starting point must be unique. They argue that the thing-commodity existed long before capitalism and has no inherent emancipatory determination, so treating it as the starting point contradicts Capital's emancipatory and scientific character. They also say the thing-commodity theory ends up quietly substituting the capitalist mode of production, and so labour-power, for its own starting point. The authors tie this to Marx's path from "alienated labour" in the Paris Manuscripts to labour-power in Capital. The authors summarise the labour-power theory as "one core, five key points" and link labour-power's emancipatory determination to the process of overcoming alienation, which they place in socialism and then communism. They connect this to the primary economic system of the Xi era, a public sector as the mainstay, and to common prosperity. They also sketch their own system built on "human-capital property rights" as a starting point. They call for more study of how Marx moved between 1844 and 1867 from "labour" and "alienated labour" to labour-power. Read the original if you work on the logic of Capital, on debates over its starting category, or on how Chinese economists draw on Marx's method to build a socialist political economy.

Marx's critique of the "Holy Alliance" and the value concepts of a new world order 马克思对“神圣同盟”的批判与新型世界秩序的价值理念 Lan Yang Du Yue Lan Yang and Du Yue ask what Marx's analysis of the Holy Alliance, the conservative alliance of European monarchs formed after the French Revolution, can tell us about today's international order. They argue that the Alliance was a system of power, institutions and ideology, and that the US-led alliances and groupings of the present (NATO, the "Summit for Democracy", the Five Eyes, AUKUS) share its essence, whatever their outward differences. Against these they set a new type of international relations built on mutual respect, fairness and win-win cooperation. The article has three parts. The first reads Marx's and Engels's remarks on the Holy Alliance through a historical-materialist "trinity" of power structure, institutional system and ideology. The second applies the same lens to contemporary hegemonic alliances. The third discusses the value concepts of a new world order, drawing on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors rely on Marx's 1859 Preface, Engels's writings, Marx's articles on Poland and the Crimean War, and Gramsci's theory of hegemony. On the Holy Alliance, the authors argue that its legitimist ideology was only the surface. Beneath it lay a balance-of-power arrangement meant to contain France, prop up Habsburg Austria and provide quasi-collective security. Its deepest basis was the combined dominance of British sea power and Russian land power, and the Crimean War marked its collapse. The authors treat this as a case of base and superstructure appearing "inverted", which historical materialism sets right. Applying this to the present, they say US-led alliances rest on capital's logic of accumulation and the core's domination of the periphery. They add that these alliances serve as institutional tools of a declining hegemon and rely on an exclusionary universalism. The authors list four features: conquest-based power politics, a disguised universalism, a confrontational centre–periphery structure and a hierarchical political order. The authors contend that China's rejuvenation has world-historical significance because it replaces the principle of capital with that of labour, civilizational conflict with mutual learning, and zero-sum games with cooperation. They call for strengthening China's economic and technological base, deepening institutional innovation and global-governance participation, and building Chinese discourse. They also call for a community with a shared future for mankind, pursued through partnership without alliance. Power politics and zero-sum thinking, they conclude, have no future. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist scholars use Marx's nineteenth-century analysis of the Holy Alliance to interpret US alliance policy and justify China's vision of a new international order.

Accelerating the building of a strong agricultural country 加快建设农业强国 Han Yang Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in spring 2023, Han Yang takes up the Party Central Committee's call, restated in the 2023 No. 1 Central Document, to speed up the building of a strong agricultural country. Han's thesis is that agricultural strength is the foundation of a modern socialist country, so that agriculture must move from being a large sector to being a strong one. The piece presents itself as a study of Xi Jinping's remarks at the Central Rural Work Conference of December 2022 and of the Document. The article has two parts. The first sets out why the task matters, in five points. The second sets out routes to achieving it, in five more: stable output and supply, international competitiveness, technological self-reliance, a green and low-carbon rural environment, and rising farmers' incomes. Han frames the whole as guidance for work on agriculture, rural areas and farmers (the "three rural issues") in the coming period. On significance, Han argues that without agricultural modernization national modernization would be "incomplete, unbalanced and unsound". The author notes that goals for building a strong country rose from four at the 18th Party Congress (2012) to twelve at the 19th (2017) and thirteen at the 20th (2022), the last including agriculture. Han adds that China's agriculture is still "large but not strong", lagging behind industrialization, informatization and urbanization. Food demand has also shifted from eating enough to eating well and safely, widening food security into a broader notion of food supply. On the routes, Han calls for grain security based on domestic supply, a greater say in global agri-food rules, pricing power and diversified imports, and breakthroughs in seeds and machinery. Han also calls for resource-saving green development and raising farmers' incomes through integrated rural industries, urban–rural integration, land-market reform and fairer distribution. Han concludes that this is a long-term historic task that will run through the whole process of building a modern socialist country. Agriculture is cast as the "ballast stone" for coping with a changing world. The author ties it to common prosperity, saying the hardest part of achieving it lies with farmers and rural areas. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the policy logic and priorities behind the agricultural-power goal as it stood in 2023.

How to deepen research on Chinese modernization 如何深化对中国式现代化的研究 Wu Zhongmin Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which made Chinese modernization the Party's central task, Wu Zhongmin asks how scholarship can supply the theoretical support the project needs. The article argues that research should be deepened in two main directions: study of Chinese modernization itself, and study of modernization 'meta-theory', meaning the general theory and laws of modernization. A closing section adds three methodological recommendations. The first part takes up five topics: why China places such weight on modernization, its gradualist way of advancing, the advantages and disadvantages of being a very large country, how to inherit valuable elements of traditional civilisation, and the leadership role of the Communist Party. The second part covers reflection on existing modernization theories, new trends in modernization worldwide, the 'welfare excess trap', and win-win cooperation among states. The final section concerns Marx and Engels, interdisciplinary work and comparative country studies. Wu contends that Chinese modernization combines features common to all modernization with features rooted in China's conditions, so general theory underpins the study of the specific case. The author describes China's approach as gradual: easy tasks first, balanced development, and a 'security first' principle. Wu judges that size brings strategic depth, a large market and global influence, but also uncertainty, path dependence on quantitative expansion and complacency, since per capita indicators lag. The author criticises Western-centric theory, postmodern theory, dependency theory and world-system theory, each credited with contributions but faulted for specific flaws. Wu also holds that post-war modernization has entered an 'intermediate stage' in which market competition and social protection must be balanced, and that many states are caught in a welfare-excess trap. The author attributes the stability of China's modernization to the Party's leadership, and attributes recent international turbulence mainly to US hegemonism. Wu concludes that research should take Marx and Engels's ideas on modernization as its theoretical starting point and develop them in light of the necessity of the market economy and China's conditions. It should be interdisciplinary without becoming an all-inclusive 'pan-modernization' field, and should draw on comparative studies of other countries to avoid insularity. Read the original if you want a systematic agenda of research topics on Chinese modernization, and an example of how a Central Party School scholar frames modernization theory, welfare and international order.

The place of the theory of human development within Marxism 人的发展理论在马克思主义中的地位 Chen Xinxia Chen Xinxia asks what position the theory of human development holds within Marxism. The article argues that the complete liberation of humanity and the free and all-round development of the individual form the core value of Marxist theory. The theory of human development, in Chen's account, is the theoretical expression of that value orientation: it rests on Marxism, and the value it carries runs through all of Marxism's component parts. The article has three sections. The first shows that the theory is grounded in Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. The second argues that human development is the core value running through those same three parts. The third explains why it matters to clarify this position, both theoretically and for contemporary China. On the first point, Chen draws on the Marxist view of practice and historical materialism to define the 'real human being engaged in practical activity', the meaning of human development and its social conditions, including the role of productive forces and social systems. Chen reads Marx's theory of surplus value as showing that, under capitalism, workers lose free time and cannot develop, so that abolishing private ownership becomes the precondition of liberation. On the second point, Chen argues that human development is the highest-level, most inclusive value orientation in Marxism and the shared value dimension of its three parts. Liberation is its logical and historical precondition, associated with revolution, while development is its goal, associated with construction. Chen holds that this value orientation took scientific socialism beyond modern humanism and utopian socialism. Chen concludes that clarifying this position confirms the unity of Marxism as 'a single block of steel'. In Chen's view, scholars have affirmed the consistency of its scientific cognition but neglected the consistency of its value orientation. Chen also argues that it strengthens Marxism's capacity to guide social progress. In contemporary China, where the principal contradiction has shifted, Chen proposes human development as the higher value yardstick for handling the relation between unbalanced and inadequate development. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language argument that human development is the core value linking Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and its application to current policy.

The philosophical contribution of the new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times Review of the 2022 annual meeting of the Chinese Society for Historical Materialism and academic symposium 马克思主义中国化时代化新飞跃的哲学贡献 Fang Jue This is a report on the 2022 annual meeting of the Chinese Society for Historical Materialism, held online on 10 December 2022 with a symposium on the philosophical contribution of the new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The Society and Sun Yat-sen University co-hosted it in Guangzhou, with the journal Studies on Marxism and the university's Institute of Marxism among the co-organisers. According to Fang, more than 300 scholars from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Peking University, Tsinghua, Renmin University, Wuhan University and other institutions took part. Fang organises the proceedings under four themes. These are the original contribution of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to Marxism; dialectical and historical materialism as the worldview and methodology of Chinese communists; building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power; and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Speakers were mostly vice-presidents or standing council members of the Society, including Hou Huiqin (president), Zhao Jianying, Jin Minqing, Yang Haifeng, Xin Xiangyang, Yan Xiaofeng, Feng Yanli and Ai Silin. Participants agreed that Xi Jinping Thought represents a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that adherence to historical materialism guarantees it. Hou argued that only by studying historical materialism can one grasp the significance of the Two Establishes and the Two Integrations, and he located the thought's philosophical contribution in a new leap in dialectical thinking, including community thinking behind a community with a shared future for mankind. Others treated "six musts" as its philosophical summation, innovation within fundamentals as its logic, and Marxist philosophy as open and historical. Xin Xiangyang used the two methods to interpret changes in the principal contradiction of Chinese society, and Lin Jinping examined how to uphold them within the Two Integrations. On ideology and modernization, speakers drew on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Feng Yanli described it as a programme for fairness and justice; Yang Shengping gave philosophical definitions of a new form of human civilization; Wang Yan set out the value claims of whole-process people's democracy. Ai Silin, Yuan Yinchuan, Hou Yanshe and Dong Hui each analysed Chinese modernization's methodology, common features and Chinese characteristics, essential requirements and historical-materialist meaning. Read the original if you want a quick map of who in China's Marxist philosophy circles presented which positions on Xi Jinping Thought and Chinese modernization at the end of 2022.

Digital scorched earth and surplus data The survival of modern people in digital capitalist society 数字焦土和剩余数据 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang asks whether digital capitalism brings a new prosperity or leaves a "digital scorched earth", and how modern people can live on such ground. Starting from pessimistic diagnoses by Byung-Chul Han, Jonathan Crary (Scorched Earth) and Nancy Fraser, the article argues that users are reduced to interchangeable "data–traffic" units. Lan's answer is that hope lies in a "surplus data" archaeology that recovers what platform algorithms leave behind. The article moves in three steps. First it traces the rootless modern person through Heidegger's "profound boredom" and his notion of Gestell (enframing), Henri Lefebvre's abstract space, Karl Polanyi and Simone Weil's uprootedness. Second it reads Crary's 24/7 regime and his idea of scorched earth, supported by Han and Slavoj Žižek. Third it turns to Walter Benjamin, Schelling's "indivisible remainder", Foucault's archaeology and Bernard Stiegler's tertiary retention. Lan argues that industrial capitalism abstracted workers into points in a network of space and time, and that digital capitalism goes further. In the author's reading of Crary, users become abstract registered accounts moving between platforms, with data extracted from them. The "scorched earth" is therefore the digital interface that screens off the living earth, not the physical ground. Because platform protocols already filter out whatever does not fit, the interface is smoother than Benjamin's arcades, and the rag-picking or parallax view of Benjamin, Foucault and Žižek is no longer open to individuals. Following Stiegler, Lan holds that platforms use only a tiny part of the data users leave, while the rest sits unexamined on servers like sealed archives. Lan concludes that resistance cannot come from inside the platform system or from changes of subjectivity. It must rest on "inter-objectivity", direct communication between data and data, and between objects, through new algorithms that bring surplus data into view. When this happens, the author suggests, the capital-controlled Charon of the digital gate will fade and a path to the real will reappear. Read the original if you want a Foucault-, Benjamin- and Stiegler-inflected philosophical critique of digital capitalism and a speculative proposal for "surplus data archaeology".

Reasons for the return of left-wing governments in Latin America and their possible impact 拉美国家左翼政府回归的原因及可能影响 Han Qi Why did a second wave of left-wing governments take power in Latin America so soon after the first wave receded in the 2010s? Han Qi argues that the return was not accidental but the product of several internal and external factors acting together. The article also asks what the new governments face and what their rule will mean at home and abroad. The article opens with the first wave (from Hugo Chávez's 1998 victory in Venezuela) and its decline after the 2009 Honduran coup. It then dates the second wave from López Obrador's 2018 win in Mexico and lists later victories in Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Honduras, Colombia and Brazil. According to Han, by January 2023 left-wing states covered about 90% of the region's area and population. The text has three parts: causes, challenges, and domestic and international effects. On causes, Han names regular electoral politics as the institutional basis and long-standing poverty and inequality as the fundamental cause. Covid-19, inflation, the Ukraine crisis and the easing of Trump-era "maximum pressure" from the United States are the external triggers. In the short term, Han points to right-wing governments' failures on corruption, violence and pandemic management, and to the left's flexible tactics. Those tactics included broader agendas on gender, indigenous and environmental issues, and centrist coalitions such as Lula's and Petro's. Han stresses that "left" and "right" here are relative to the neoliberal governments of the 1990s, not to a traditional left standard. The challenges are narrow electoral margins and weak legislative bases, as in Peru and Chile, the limited fiscal room for social reform without a commodity boom, the need for growth, and a shift in development model. Han concludes that the left will probably govern for a shorter or longer period depending on how well it handles crisis and on whether it makes a real breakthrough against poverty and inequality. The author expects improved welfare for lower and middle strata, with examples from Colombia and Bolivia, and a revival of regional integration. Han also expects closer cooperation with China, citing trade and Belt and Road Initiative figures, and more outspoken left-wing criticism of US policy, though left governments may follow resource nationalism. Read the original if you want a China-based scholar's account of Latin America's "pink tide" and how it bears on China–Latin America relations.

The major contributions of the 20th Party Congress to world socialism 党的二十大对世界社会主义的重大贡献 Wu Degang Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wu Degang asks what the Congress contributes to world socialism. Taking his cue from Xi Jinping's report, he argues that scientific socialism has taken on new vitality in twenty-first-century China and that the Congress has made major contributions on four fronts: theory, practice, the revival of world socialism, and global problem-solving. The article is organised in four numbered sections. It first traces the successive theoretical achievements of the Party, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then reviews the record of the past decade and Chinese modernization, places socialism with Chinese characteristics within five centuries of world socialist history, and ends with the Party's international outlook and its proposals for a community with a shared future for mankind. Wu's central claim is that Xi Jinping Thought, by answering questions that the classic Marxist writers, earlier socialist states and developed Western countries did not resolve, marks a new milestone in scientific socialism and adapts Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author cites a rise in GDP from 54 trillion to 114 trillion yuan, a world economic share of 18.5 per cent, and the removal of all 832 poor counties from the poverty list. In Wu's account, these results refute the claims of the 'obsolescence of Marxism', the 'end of socialism' and the 'collapse of China'. He also argues that China halted the ebb of world socialism after the Soviet collapse and that Chinese modernization widens the options of developing countries that want both growth and independence. Wu concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics is becoming the banner of twenty-first-century scientific socialism and a mainstay in reviving world socialism. He presents the Belt and Road Initiative, a new type of international relations and a community with a shared future for mankind as Chinese contributions to global challenges. The text is an affirmative interpretation of the Congress and offers little critical engagement. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian frames the 20th Party Congress as a contribution to world socialism and to Chinese claims of international leadership.

On socialism with Chinese characteristics and the revitalisation of world socialism 论中国特色社会主义与世界社会主义的振兴态势 Zhang Zhiyuan Li Juanjuan Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Juanjuan ask how socialism with Chinese characteristics relates to the current revival of world socialism after its low ebb. Writing in the first issue of 2023 of a Chinese journal on ideological and theoretical education, they argue that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the most consequential component of twenty-first-century world socialism. In their account it supplies the central force, the new prospects and the historical direction of that revival. The article opens with the path from Thomas More's Utopia (1516) to the Communist Manifesto (1848) and then proceeds in three parts. The first treats Chinese achievements of the past decade as a pillar of world socialism: the people as principal force, the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, and the drive towards a modern socialist country. The second turns to Chinese modernization, a new form of human civilisation and a community with a shared future for mankind. The third reviews the historical course from the lessons of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe to the present. Their central claim is that China's experience offers other countries a model. They hold that poverty eradication, achieved by the socialist economic system, shows the superiority of the system. Chinese modernization, they say, gives developing countries a new option that is neither a closed, rigid old path nor a path of abandoning socialism. They also present the new form of civilisation and the community with a shared future as Chinese answers to Western-centred models and to global governance deficits. Historically, they contrast the Soviet and East European reforms of the late 1980s, which they associate with abandoning Party leadership and Marxist guidance and ending in collapse, with China's reforms. They credit the latter with holding the banner of scientific socialism, and with reaching the stage where capitalism, hit by the financial crisis, populism and de-globalisation, faces a rising socialism. The authors conclude that the centre of world socialism has shifted to China in the twenty-first century. They state that socialism with Chinese characteristics in some sense represents the future of world socialism and is becoming its mainstay and banner. They add that the Party has the responsibility, confidence and capacity to contribute more to scientific socialism. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Chinese Party-school scholars frame China's role in the international socialist movement.

The international environment of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era, seen through new changes in contemporary capitalism 从当代资本主义的新变化看新时代中国特色社会主义面临的国际环境 Lin Deshan Sun Han Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which speaks of changes in the world, the era and history unfolding in unprecedented ways, this article asks how new changes in contemporary capitalism shape the external environment of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Lin and Sun argue that capitalism is undergoing a new 'change of the century'. In their reading, this change both alters the conditions of the world socialist movement and makes China's international environment more complex and more competitive. The article has three parts. The first describes capitalism's economic transformation through globalisation, financialisation and digitalisation, and its systemic crisis after 2008. The second assesses what these changes mean for the world socialist movement, setting out new opportunities and new problems. The third turns to their effects on the international setting in which China operates. On the crisis, the authors point to social tearing between 'winners' and 'losers', political polarisation and the spread of populism, which they say cast doubt on representative democracy itself. Rising inequality, they argue, opens space for radical and progressive politics: 'red-green' politics, direct democracy, digital socialism, and a younger base around figures such as Sanders and Mélenchon. At the same time, the shrinking industrial working class, the erosion of collectivism and state-centred politics, the challenge that digital capitalism poses to classical critiques, and disputes over left populism all trouble traditional socialism. For China, the authors identify three effects. Uneven development intensifies competition over the international economic order, and restraining China's rise has become a consensus among developed capitalist states. Domestic political changes in the West, including populist right parties and a generational split between conservatism and radical liberalism, spill over into China policy. Competition between the two systems over development paths becomes a lasting factor. Lin and Sun conclude that China's international environment will be more complex and that competition will run through its relations with developed capitalist countries. They hold that its form and limits depend on both sides' strategic choices. They end by affirming China's commitment to peaceful development, in line with the 20th Party Congress report. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account, from the CPC's theoretical perspective, of how Western political and economic change is read as shaping China's external conditions and the prospects of world socialism.

The history of Chinese philosophy as a coordinate system for studying the sinicization of Marxist philosophy 马克思主义哲学中国化研究的中国哲学史坐标系 Li Weiwu Li Weiwu takes up a question raised by Xi Jinping's call to combine the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture (the Two Integrations). How can research on the sinicization of Marxist philosophy show that Chinese Marxist philosophy has moved from being a 'philosophy in China' to being a 'philosophy of China'? Li argues that this requires a neglected framework: the history of Chinese philosophy, rather than only the history of Marxist philosophy. The piece, printed in Guangming Daily in April 2023, first sets out two complementary coordinate systems for this research. It then explains what the Chinese philosophy coordinate system contains, with attention to the 'ancient-to-modern change' (gu-jin zhi bian) after the Opium War. Finally it reads the sinicization of Marxist philosophy within that change, drawing on Mao Zedong's philosophical writings and on concepts such as 'seeking truth from facts'. Li holds that the Marxist-philosophy-history framework places sinicization within the worldwide spread of Marxism and shows its universality. The Chinese-philosophy-history framework instead links it to the sources and traditions of Chinese philosophy and shows its particularity. Earlier studies, Li says, mostly used the first. In Li's account, Chinese philosophy changed form after the Opium War, from an ancient to a modern form and from an ancient to a modern tradition, through two movements: the sinicization of Western philosophy and the modernization of Chinese philosophy. Li insists this was not a rupture or mere 'Westernization'. Marxist philosophy, in this reading, took part in the change by answering questions that other currents could not: a materialist conception of history replacing cyclical and evolutionary views, New Democracy as an answer to 'where is China going', and a Chinese form of dialectical materialism built on practice. Li concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy did not grow directly out of ancient Chinese philosophy. Yet by shaping and settling into the modern tradition, and by reactivating ideas such as 'seeking truth from facts', 'the ideal of great harmony' and 'a moderately prosperous society', it has entered the Chinese philosophical tradition. Li calls for future research on combining Marxist philosophy with that tradition to start from the Chinese philosophy coordinate system. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese philosophers frame Marxism's place in the history of Chinese thought.

Four suggestions for raising the level of research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 努力提高习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想研究水平的四点建议 Wang Chuanli Wang Chuanli takes up a practical question: how scholars can raise the quality of research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Wang acknowledges that the field has grown rapidly, with dedicated institutes, large projects and many publications, but argues that research must still go deeper. The article offers four suggestions: cultivate a good scholarly and writing style, strengthen intellectual content and linguistic appeal, bring out historical depth through comparison, and adopt a lofty outlook grounded in a 'people first' and national sentiment. The article is a normative essay in four numbered sections. It draws on the history of the Communist Party of China, especially Mao Zedong's Yan'an rectification campaign and his attack on 'Party stereotyped writing', and on the collapse of the Soviet Union as Wang reads it. It cites Russian authors Lisichkin and Shelepin on Soviet textbooks, praises particular articles in Chinese journals, and refers to Xi Jinping's own comparative history and personal experience at Liangjiahe. It also quotes Marx's school essay on choosing a profession. Wang's central claim is that style is not a minor matter: in Wang's account, a party's creative theoretical capacity and vitality show in its scholarly and writing style. Dogmatic, empty writing is linked to the Party's early setbacks and to the Soviet decline. Wang therefore criticises research that lacks 'problem awareness', is written from the study rather than from practice, and rearranges leaders' phrases. Wang also criticises papers that list points in numbered sequences and that overuse 'logic' in titles (historical logic, practical logic and so on) while merely listing facts. Wang asks instead for comparison with the history of Marxism, world socialism, past regimes and anti-corruption experience, and for scholars whose motives are service to the people rather than careers, bonuses or publication prominence. Wang concludes that researchers should combine love of country and people with their work, so that study of the new thought becomes work with warmth and high purpose. Wang argues that without a people-first outlook scholars cannot understand Xi Jinping's thinking and will produce only empty results. Read the original if you want to see how a Tsinghua Marxism scholar frames scholarly style, language and motivation as questions of political and intellectual standards for research on Xi Jinping Thought.

Understanding and advancing Chinese modernization from the height of Marxist philosophy 从马克思主义哲学高度理解和推进中国式现代化 Zhao Jianying Zhu Huabin Writing in Guangming Daily in April 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhao Jianying and Zhu Huabin argue that Chinese modernization should be understood through Marxist philosophy. They contend that doing so gives the theory sound scholarly grounding and guides practice. Their starting point is Xi Jinping's elaboration of Chinese modernization at the Congress and in later speeches, which they say has produced an initial theoretical system. The commentary has three parts. The first treats the goal of Chinese modernization through the Marxist view of history and values. The second applies the dialectic of universality and particularity to the features Chinese modernization shares with other countries and those specific to China. The third turns to the dialectics of advancing it: coordination, and the systems approach to major relationships. On goals, the authors hold that the people are both the makers and the value-bearers of history. From this they derive Xi's claim that the essence of modernization is the modernization of the human being, with the free and all-round development of the person as its final aim. They contrast this with Western modernization, which they say freed people from religious and royal authority but left them under the rule of capital and money fetishism. On commonality and particularity, they list shared features such as industrialization, urbanization and modernized governance. They set against these the five features named at the Congress: a huge population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical advance, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. On method, they cite Xi's list of relationships to be balanced, including top-level design and practical exploration, efficiency and fairness, and vitality and order. They stress finding the right measure and a dynamic balance. The authors conclude that the theory of Chinese modernization is an integrated whole, the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. They say it opens a new stage in adapting Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They also say it breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers developing countries a model. They call for deeper study of the theory. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2023 framed Chinese modernization in Marxist-philosophical terms.

Theoretical features and historical evolution of the contemporary adaptation of Marxism to the times 马克思主义时代化的理论特征和历史演进 He Haigen Sun Daiyao He Haigen and Sun Daiyao take up the idea of Marxism's "adaptation to the times" (shidaihua), which the 20th Party Congress (2022) report names, together with adaptation to the Chinese context, as a historic responsibility of Chinese communists. They argue that adapting Marxism to the times is an internal requirement of Marxist development. In their account it runs through the history from the birth of scientific socialism to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and it must always stay within the direction of the "big era" of transition from capitalism to socialism. The article first sets out a framework. It distinguishes "big eras" (social formations such as feudalism or capitalism) from "small eras" (stages defined by technology and shifting themes). It then lists two preconditions for adaptation: real needs, and objective conditions in which the character of the age changes substantially. The second part traces three historical stages: scientific socialism after the first technological revolution, a "Russian stage" after the second, and a "Chinese stage" after the third. The third part identifies four features of Xi Jinping Thought. The authors link each stage to a technological and economic shift. In their reading, the first revolution gave socialism a real basis, so it could move from utopia to science. Monopoly capitalism and imperialism, with Russia as a weak link under heavy foreign capital, led Lenin to a new stage of theory. After 1945 the third revolution and the turn to "peace and development" exposed the Soviet model. The authors cite East–West German comparisons of productivity and incomes, and say that socialism with Chinese characteristics arose from Deng Xiaoping's reassessment of the age. For Xi's thought they list four features: grasping what changes and what does not in the age; the "two-in-one" unity of Sinicisation and adaptation to the times; continuing to answer basic questions of socialism from within the big era; and answering the "question of the world" through a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors conclude that Marxism remains the guide for an era still marked by capitalism's basic contradictions, and that Xi's thought is both Chinese and of world significance. They present Chinese modernization as an answer to questions that are at once China's and the world's. Read the original if you want a detailed periodisation of Marxism's development by technological revolution, or an account of how Party theorists justify the link between Sinicisation and adaptation to the times.

Adhering more consciously to the Two Integrations as the fundamental path for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 更加自觉地坚持“两个结合”推进马克思主义中国化时代化的根本途径 Liu Dehai This short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 22 March 2023, takes up a question raised by Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): by what path is adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times to be advanced? Liu Dehai answers that the fundamental path is the Two Integrations, meaning the combination of Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with excellent traditional Chinese culture. Liu presents this as the reason the tree of sinicised Marxist theory is deeply rooted and leafy. The piece is organised in three sections. The first treats the Two Integrations as a summing-up of experience and a revealed regularity in the Party's history of more than a century. The second turns to the new era, and the third to what the Party must do on its new journey. Liu argues that Marxism is a guide to action rather than a dogma, and that the Party's rejuvenation path grew from drawing on both China's realities and its traditional culture. In Liu's account, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era was formed through the Two Integrations. Liu describes it as contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism, and as a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Liu calls for more conscious adherence to the Two Integrations, so as to produce theoretical innovation on the basis of practice. This means answering new practical problems, deep-seated issues and pressing public concerns. It also means promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture, and linking Marxism with the values of ordinary people. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how the Two Integrations were presented in the press after the 20th Party Congress.

A deeper understanding of "ultimately, it is Marxism that works — Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" 深刻理解“归根到底是马克思主义行，是中国化时代化的马克思主义行” Bai Xianliang This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in March 2023, interprets a formulation from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): why the Communist Party of China "can", why socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good", and why, ultimately, "Marxism works", specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Bai argues that the three claims form a dialectical chain and that the formulation expresses the internal logic and historical necessity of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is organised in four numbered sections. The first draws out the basic Marxist principles contained in the formulation. The second presents it as the historical wisdom of the Party's century of struggle. The third sets out the fundamental route by which Marxism takes effect, and the fourth outlines directions for Party-building and the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Bai's central reasoning rests on three claims about theory and practice. Theory guides practice, so Marxism is fundamental to the Party's revolution, construction and reform. Its value is realised only in concrete, historical conditions, so what actually guided the Chinese revolution, in Bai's account, was not dogmatic, book-bound Marxism but a Marxism that had been adapted to China. Marxism also does not "work" spontaneously: it needs the Communist Party as its practical agent, the integration of its basic principles with China's realities and fine traditional culture, and mastery by the people. Bai accordingly states three conditions: Marxism must be applied in practice, localised and updated, and taken up by the masses. The author also reads the Party's century of struggle as a unity of theoretical innovation, Party leadership and the Chinese path. Bai concludes that the new era requires firm theoretical confidence, strengthening the Party through theory, and a stronger conscious commitment to applying Marxism to major practical problems. The author calls for arming the whole Party with the latest results of Marxism, and for using the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to pursue Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary explains the link between Marxism, Party leadership and the Chinese path after the 20th Party Congress.

Upholding the Two Integrations and continually opening up new horizons for Marxism 坚持“两个结合”，不断开辟马克思主义发展新境界 Jin Nuo Writing in the People's Daily in March 2023, Jin Nuo takes up a question that follows from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): how the Communist Party of China can keep Marxism vital while developing it. Jin's answer is the Two Integrations, which the article presents as the fundamental route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and as a key to the Party's success. The commentary is built in three parts. The first explains why the Two Integrations are the basic path of adaptation, treating the link with China's concrete realities and the link with fine traditional Chinese culture in turn. The second reviews their significance across more than a century of Party history and for the present task of advancing Chinese modernization. The third sets out three requirements for further theoretical innovation. Jin argues that Marxism is not a closed body of truth and cannot be treated as dogma, so it must be tied to national conditions in each period of revolution, construction and reform. It must also be tied to traditional culture, which Jin says shares a high degree of fit with the values of scientific socialism, so that Marxism takes root among the people and acquires distinct Chinese features. The article credits this method with Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It describes the last as a model of the Two Integrations, rooted in traditional culture and answering the major questions of the new era. For the future, Jin calls for innovation that takes people's aspiration for a better life as its starting point and end point, keeps answering new questions, and gives theory distinctive Chinese features. The article names four sets of questions: those of China, the world, the people and the times. It links this work to common prosperity and to supporting Chinese modernization, which it calls a pioneering undertaking with unknown terrain and risks. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how the Party presents the Two Integrations and the tasks of theoretical innovation after the 20th Party Congress.

Bearing in mind the "five musts": steering the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics steadily into the future 牢记“五个必由之路”，引领新时代中国特色社会主义事业行稳致远 Jiang Zeting This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in March 2023, takes up the "five musts" (wuge biyou zhi lu) that Xi Jinping put to the whole Party in his report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Jiang argues that they are the key to the historic achievements of the Party's first century and especially of the new era. In Jiang's reading, they express three qualities of Communists today: firm historical confidence, a high degree of theoretical consciousness and a strong sense of responsibility. The article is organised in three parts that match these three qualities. The first reads the five principles as a summary of a hundred years of Party experience. The second treats them as a deepening of understanding of three laws: those governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. The third presents them as practical guidance for the future. The first part takes each principle in turn. Jiang holds that the Party's overall leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics, unity and struggle, the new development philosophy, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party are each tied to the achievements of the Party's first century and the past decade. The second part assigns the principles to the three laws. Party leadership and self-governance are said to advance understanding of how Communist parties rule, including self-reform as the \"second answer\" to the historical cycle. Socialism with Chinese characteristics is said to enrich the laws of socialist construction. Unity and struggle and the new development philosophy are said to deepen understanding of the laws of social development, including the role of the people's state of mind. In the third part Jiang calls on Communists to follow the five principles as a guide to action on the new journey towards the second centenary goal. Five tasks are set out. They are upholding Party leadership, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; innovating theory on the basis of practice; strengthening the patriotic united front and a sense of community among the Chinese nation; applying the new development philosophy to build a new development pattern and promote high-quality development; and continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 20th Congress formula was presented to a general Party readership in 2023.

Accurately grasping the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era 准确把握习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想的世界观和方法论 Shen Jiangping This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, takes up a line from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that theoretical innovation must begin by grasping the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Shen Jiangping argues that this formulation lifts the Thought to the philosophical level and distils its theoretical essence. In Shen's reading, it is a concentrated expression of contemporary Chinese Marxism and opens a new realm for Marxist worldview and methodology. The article has two parts. The first traces the sources of this worldview and methodology: inheritance from Marxist philosophy, development of earlier Sinicized Marxism, and nourishment from fine traditional Chinese culture. The second sets out its theoretical significance under three headings: innovating Marxist worldview and methodology, guiding the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and advancing world governance and human civilization. Shen holds that the worldview is not self-generated but rests on dialectical and historical materialism, and that it continues the Party's long practice of summarising each period's theoretical innovation at the level of worldview and method, with seeking truth from facts as the constant stance. The "six must-haves" are presented as the essence and soul of the Thought and as its stance, viewpoint and method. Shen also says that concepts from traditional culture, such as harmony between humanity and nature, the people as the foundation of the state, and good-neighbourliness, are fused into this worldview through the Two Integrations, giving Marxism Chinese features. Shen concludes that grasping this worldview is the precondition and applying it the key. The author calls on the whole Party to study the 20th Congress in this way, to arm minds and guide practice, and to keep advancing theoretical innovation so that the Party's cause stays on course. The article also presents the worldview as relevant beyond China, through the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary justifies the claim that the Thought is a philosophical advance in Marxism.

Communism as a "real movement" is by no means illusory Viewed through Lenin's "A Great Beginning" 作为“现实运动”的共产主义绝非虚无缥缈 Fan Xin Fan Xin takes up Lenin's 1919 pamphlet "A Great Beginning", written after Pravda reported that Moscow–Kazan railway workers had launched voluntary "communist subbotniks". The article asks what the text shows about communism and answers that communism is a "real movement" visible in actual labour, not a distant fantasy. Fan uses this to rebut the claim that communism is "illusory" (the "vague and remote" thesis). The article has three parts. The first reads Lenin's three quoted Pravda reports as evidence of a concrete form of communist labour organisation and spirit. The second examines why Lenin saw labour productivity as the decisive ground of competition between social systems, and how the pamphlet treats the two stages of communist society. The third turns to the Chinese Communist Party's own statements on communism, from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping, and to the setbacks and recovery of socialism since 1989–91. Fan argues that earlier scholarship either treated the pamphlet as a description of subbotniks or simply stressed raising productivity. In Fan's reading, Lenin's real point is that the proletarian dictatorship must embody a higher type of social labour organisation than capitalism, and that this guarantees communism's victory. Fan reads Lenin's definition of communism as higher labour productivity created by voluntary, associated workers using advanced technology. Lenin also shows how voluntary initiative can break the "vicious circle" between hunger and productivity. Lenin's caution that subbotniks could not yet be universal, and that the work is long-term, is presented as proof that communists are not utopians. Fan concludes that Lenin's lesson of nurturing the "shoots" of the new remains relevant. Citing Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, Fan holds that building socialism with Chinese characteristics is already a practical step towards the highest ideal. Fan also contends that socialism's setbacks, including the Soviet collapse, are temporary twists in a historical trend. The article calls for firmer ideals, a proletarian character in state power and higher labour productivity. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Lenin's text to official Party discourse on communist ideals and the "illusory communism" argument.

New trends in the development of world socialism amid great global change 大变局下世界社会主义发展新趋势 Chen Mingfan Writing in early 2023, Chen Mingfan asks where world socialism is heading in a period of what Chinese official discourse calls great changes unseen in a century. The article argues that capitalism has passed its "golden age" and is inevitably declining, while socialism is advancing irresistibly. Chen holds that a scientific, long-run view of history should give confidence in socialism's future while preparing for a difficult and winding road. The article has three parts. The first traces the socialist movement through successive global upheavals: the utopian socialists, the Communist Manifesto, the Paris Commune, the First World War and the October Revolution, the post-1945 socialist camp, and the setback after the Soviet and East European collapse. The second examines how the movement split into revolutionary and reformist currents and surveys its present branches: ruling communist parties, communist and left forces in capitalist and developing countries, democratic socialism, and so-called national socialism. The third turns to China's role. Chen argues that the movement's history, though marked by defeats, rises overall, and that Marx's and Mao Zedong's accounts of revolutionary setbacks support this. In Chen's reading, democratic socialism has abandoned socialism and become reformed capitalism, a "doctor at the sickbed" of capitalism, whereas communist parties that adapt scientific socialism to national conditions form the mainstream. Two irreversible forces are said to be reviving the movement. One is capitalism's decline, which Chen sees in the post-2018 financial crisis, the pandemic, US political division and popular protest. The other is China's example, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, whole-process people's democracy, Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind, which Chen supports with remarks by foreign communist figures. Citing Lenin, Chen adds that objective crisis does not by itself produce revolution, since Western proletarian parties remain immature. Chen concludes that world socialism is gradually moving from low ebb to revival, with good prospects but a long period of testing ahead. The Chinese Communist Party is described as bearing a "two rejuvenations" task: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the revival of world socialism. Chen expects that building China into a leading modern socialist power by mid-century will strongly influence the movement. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar presents the history of socialism, the role of the Chinese Communist Party and the future of the left abroad in early 2023.

A century of the Communist Party of Australia: development, positions and challenges 澳大利亚共产党百年发展历程、主张及挑战 Xu Ke Zheng Yifan Xu Ke and Zheng Yifan examine the hundred-year history of the Communist Party of Australia (CPA), its theoretical and policy positions, and the difficulties it now faces. They take the Party's 14th National Congress (February 2022), the first of its second century, as the occasion for the study. They present the CPA as a small Marxist-Leninist party that remains marginal, but that has kept to Marxism-Leninism and to friendship with China amid strong anti-China sentiment in Australia. The authors argue that studying it helps Chinese scholars understand the current state of the world socialist movement and unite progressive forces in Western countries. The article has three parts. The first divides the Party's history into four phases: growth from 1920 to 1945; decline and dissolution from 1946 to 1990, shaped by Cold War repression, the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, the Sino-Soviet split and repeated splits; refounding in 1996 on the basis of the Socialist Party of Australia; and the period since 2020. The second part sets out the CPA's views on party building, revolution, economic policy, social policy and foreign policy. The third part names four challenges. In the authors' account, the CPA holds that the working class remains the main force for revolution, citing survey data on class identification in Australia. The Party combines electoral work, now concentrated on local councils because the 2021 rise in the membership threshold for registration makes national contests hard, with class struggle through trade unions. It calls for public ownership of key sectors, for the rights of Indigenous people, women, temporary-visa workers and LGBT people, and for ending Australia's alignment with the United States, including AUKUS. The authors describe the Party's defence of China and its criticism of the Australian authorities as proletarian internationalism. The four challenges the authors identify are worsening conditions and a fragmented left; a continuing risk of splits, given weak ideological education, discipline and institutions after the 2019 split; propaganda work that lags behind in the digital age, with website traffic figures cited for comparison; and an ageing membership with too few successors. They nonetheless see the 2019 split as not wholly a loss, citing a remark by Engels, and report that membership has grown. They conclude that China should follow left parties abroad, spread Chinese modernization and build its international discourse power, and that the Communist Party of China should lead the revival of world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of the CPA's history, internal debates and organisation, and of how Chinese researchers frame foreign communist parties.

The problematic and theoretical tensions of classical Western Marxism 经典西方马克思主义的问题意识与理论张力 Gao Xiaoxi This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2023, asks what problem animated classical Western Marxism, the tradition running from Lukács to Althusser between the 1920s and 1960s. Gao Xiaoxi argues that its problematic grew out of a strategic dispute over how to make socialist revolution in advanced capitalist countries, and that this dispute took theoretical form as a debate over the essence of Marx's philosophy. The article first sets out the historical conditions of twentieth-century capitalism: oligopoly, a divided working class including a "labour aristocracy", and a shift from open repression to ideological manipulation through consumerism and mass culture. It then contrasts classical Western Marxism with the Second International, and finally divides the tradition into humanist and scientistic currents and traces its legacy. Gao contends that the Second International read Marxism as a deterministic doctrine, confusing historical laws with natural laws and neglecting the subjective dimension of historical materialism. Classical Western Marxists, in Gao's account, instead treated Marxism as a philosophy of subjective practice and stressed class consciousness and cultural-psychological revolution. The tension lies in uniting ideology critique with revolutionary practice, which Gao says exposed a subjectivist and romantic tendency. Hegelian Marxists, the Frankfurt School and existentialist Marxists took the humanist route, while Althusser's structuralism took the scientistic one, which Gao says ended in a theoretical monologue. Gao concludes that after May 1968 the tradition declined as a movement, yet its tensions (history–structure, time–space, class–individual and others) still shape ecological Marxism, post-Marxism and late Marxism. Grasping this problematic, Gao argues, is needed to understand foreign Marxism and to avoid misjudging the history of Western Marxism's interpretation and reception. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-academic map of how classical Western Marxism is positioned within the wider field of foreign Marxism.

On socialism with Chinese characteristics creating a new form of human civilization 论中国特色社会主义创造了人类文明新形态 Liu Jianjun Liu Jianjun examines the claim, made by Xi Jinping in 2021 and repeated in the Party's 2021 historical resolution and at the 20th Party Congress (2022), that socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a new form of human civilization. The article asks why the Party advanced this claim, what it means and what theoretical and practical significance it has. Liu answers that the claim is a coherent and scientifically grounded proposition, and argues that it will be borne out by future development. The article has five parts. It first sets out the background: the maturing and success of socialism with Chinese characteristics, rising assessments of it, the growth of a Party discourse on civilization, and the Party's historical, practical and future confidence. It then analyses the phrase semantically, treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as a civilization form, and explains why it is a new one. It closes with the world-historical significance of this form. Liu draws on the historical-materialist notion of social formations rather than the comparative approach of Spengler, Toynbee and Kishimoto Takuro, which treats civilizations as separate cycles. Liu argues that the new form is a composite, "atypical" one, produced by the interaction of three civilizations. It is a contemporary form of Chinese civilization, a Chinese form of socialist civilization, and a form of modernization civilization that transcends industrial, Western-centred and capitalist modernity. Liu reads the perfect tense of "has created" as meaning "has taken shape" rather than "has been completed", with the decisive period running to 2035 and 2050.
