On the world stage, Liu says this civilization enriches civilizational diversity, promotes exchange and mutual learning, advances civilization through innovations such as whole-process people's democracy, and offers guidance for the future, partly through its communist elements. Liu concludes that the new civilization form is a major creation of the Chinese nation and a landmark in the history of human civilization, with its scientific validity to be confirmed by later development. Throughout, the author presents the Chinese path as a peaceful alternative to colonial and Western-centred modernization, and as one that coexists with other civilizations without replacing them. Read the original if you want a detailed, theoretically structured account of how Chinese scholarship justifies the Party's "new form of human civilization" thesis, including its use of Marxist social-formation theory and civilizational discourse.

Strategic blueprint and theoretical-system elevation of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的战略擘画和理论体系升华 Gu Hailiang On 7 February 2023, at a study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022), Xi Jinping stated that a theoretical system of Chinese modernization had been "initially constructed". Gu Hailiang reads this judgement as a summary of the Party's century of struggle and of the practical and historical logic of Chinese modernization. The article argues that the judgement rests on historical initiative and theoretical confidence, and that it deepens Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has four sections. The first traces the exploration of modernization through the New Democratic Revolution, the Mao-era building of socialism and the period of reform and opening up, then sets out the theoretical innovations since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second lists the components of the theoretical system, from Xi's 2020 account of five features to the 20th Party Congress report. The third relates the theory to the three major questions of the new era. The fourth examines the worldview and methodology behind it. Gu's central move is to treat Chinese modernization as a system with defined parts. These include its Chinese characteristics, five main features, nine essential requirements, eight goals for 2035, five major principles and its roots in traditional Chinese culture. Gu further reads it as the answer to three questions: what socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold, what kind of modern socialist country to build, and what kind of long-governing Marxist party to build. Gu holds that Party leadership determines the fundamental nature of Chinese modernization. The article also draws out six "views" in Xi's account (on the world, values, history, civilization, democracy and ecology). It links them to dialectical and historical materialism and to six relationships to be handled in a "systematic process", such as top-level design and practice, or efficiency and fairness. Gu concludes that Xi's judgement shows the historical basis of Chinese modernization as an innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In Gu's account it also shows the integrated innovation in the content of the theory and its answers to the three major questions. It further brings out the scholarly and philosophical reasoning of the system, which Gu says raises contemporary Chinese Marxism to a new level. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists organise Chinese modernization into a theoretical system, including the historical debates of the 1920s–30s.

Upholding and developing Marxism requires integrating it with China's fine traditional culture 坚持和发展马克思主义，必须同中华优秀传统文化相结合 Zhang Lu This short commentary, published in People's Daily in April 2023, explains why the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) stated that upholding and developing Marxism must be combined with fine traditional Chinese culture. Zhang argues that this principle deepens the Party's understanding of how to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that it shows cultural confidence and cultural awareness. The piece opens with quotations from Xi Jinping and the Congress report, then moves through the historical conditions for Marxism's reception in China, the influence of traditional culture on China's path, institutions and governance, and the task ahead. It is built largely around Xi's statements. Zhang's central claim is that Marxism took root in China not by chance but because it resonated with values handed down over thousands of years. In this reading, the values of fine traditional culture closely match those of scientific socialism, which makes the combination possible. Zhang cites Xi's view that socialism with Chinese characteristics carries a cultural "gene", and argues that traditional ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the foundation of the state" feed the country's institutions, governance system and the core socialist values. Marxism, Zhang says, gains Chinese style from this culture, while the culture gains new content from Marxism. Zhang calls for stronger historical and cultural confidence and a deeper understanding of the Two Integrations. The commentary urges drawing out the philosophy, humanistic spirit, values and moral norms of traditional culture, so that the Party's innovative theory acquires distinctive Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the cultural integration is justified in Party theory around the 20th Party Congress.

A scientific-atheist interpretation of Engels's contradiction between the "expected" and the "unexpected" 恩格斯“预期与非预期”矛盾的科学无神论诠释 Li Wen Engels observed late in life that the purposes of human actions are anticipated while the results they actually produce are not. Li Wen asks why a history that people make purposively so often yields outcomes contrary to their aims. Li argues that theistic answers, which place the cause in gods or providence, do not resolve the problem. Engels's practical-materialist account, which starts from real human beings and their practice, does resolve it, and in doing so it shows the spirit of Marxist scientific atheism. The article has four parts. It first reviews theistic readings of the contradiction, moving from traditional theology to the "rational theology" of Vico, Kant and Hegel. It then explains why unexpected outcomes are not the work of divine will. A third section argues that anticipated outcomes have nothing to do with gods. A short conclusion draws out the practical implications, including for the Party's religious work in the new era. Li contends that Vico's divine providence, Kant's "nature" and Hegel's "cunning of reason" all install a new deity above history and so amount to subtler forms of theism. In Li's reading, the "divine will" in these systems is a mystified expression of objective historical law, while human purposes lie hidden beneath it. Engels removes the mystification: historical necessity is set by real conditions of life, and people are the authors of their own history. Unexpected results arise because historical law and human purposes constrain and disturb each other. They also arise because individual wills conflict and merge into a resultant that no one intended. Li adds that Engels treats gods as human projections and reflections of human self-alienation, so that "God is man" and anticipation becomes a human affair. Li concludes that the contradiction can be resolved only through human practice. Practice must move from conflict towards fit between conformity to law and conformity to purpose, with human aims approaching historical law and law incorporating human aims. Li adds that theism is sometimes used by states and interest groups for political and economic gain and can leave people passive in the face of the unexpected. Removing it, Li says, frees human agency and has value for the Party's religious work and for scientific-atheist education. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of scientific atheism reads Engels's late theory of history against Vico, Kant and Hegel.

Crisis and transformation: the French left on the crisis of contemporary capitalism 危机与变革：法国左翼对当代资本主义危机的思考 Ni Jingjing Since the 2008 financial crisis, capitalism has entered a new round of global expansion under the banner of neoliberalism. This article asks how the French left has analysed the crisis of contemporary capitalism: its causes, features, harms, likely course and alternatives. Ni argues that French left thinkers read the crisis not as a mere financial event but as a total, multidimensional crisis of the capitalist system, and that they point towards several routes of transformation. The article ends by drawing lessons for China. The article has two main parts. The first, "Crisis", takes up the French left's claim that capitalism has always been an unstable system, citing Marx on primitive accumulation and Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. It then examines four dimensions: the mode of production, democracy, spiritual life and ecology, with a brief note on social unrest such as the "yellow vests" and pension protests. The second part, "Transformation", sets out four alternatives associated with figures including Piketty, Jacques Bidet, Alain Badiou, Jacques Rancière, Henri Lefebvre, Michel Foucault and André Gorz. On the crisis, Ni reports that Baudrillard's idea of "implosion" is applied by Gallo to overproduction, shrinking markets and widening inequality. Rancière's distinction between "police" and politics explains how democratic representation silences dissent, and consumer society is said to produce a loss of meaning. On the alternatives, the author presents French thinkers as: reviving political economy as a study of "society as a whole" (Piketty, Bidet, Duménil and Lévy); rebuilding political ontology around the "event" (Badiou, Rancière); countering the "self-division" caused by reification with an aesthetics of existence (Lefebvre, Foucault); and replacing economic rationality with ecological rationality, as in Gorz's ecosocialism and its slogan "less production, better life". In the conclusion Ni treats each current as offering a lesson for China. These include deepening understanding of Marx's critique of capital, attending to the interests of diverse groups, integrating green development into Chinese modernization, and caring for people's physical and mental health. Ni also urges upholding the Party's core leadership and the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in a world where capitalism's overall crisis is visible and the two systems coexist and compete. Read the original if you want a Chinese overview of how French left thinkers, from Piketty to Badiou and Gorz, are framed in Chinese scholarship on contemporary capitalism.

Understanding several theoretical questions 谈谈对几个理论问题的理解 Ren Dakui Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Ren Dakui takes up four questions in Party theory on which, in the author's view, some scholars' formulations are imprecise or mistaken. The article argues that the Party's century-long struggle has one theme, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, with modernization as the path; that the market economy can be a basic economic institution only in a limited sense; that the community with a shared future for mankind must not be confused with communism; and that Party leadership is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has four numbered sections. The first treats the Party's historical theme and socialist modernization, including how Chinese modernization differs from capitalist modernization, and it criticises historical nihilism and some assessments of the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1898 reforms and the 1911 Revolution. The second examines the "three basic economic systems" set out by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). The third discusses the community with a shared future for mankind. The fourth explains why Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Ren holds that treating modernization and rejuvenation as twin themes blurs the line between goal and path. Modernization is neutral in the abstract, and since the October Revolution it has split into capitalist and socialist forms. On the economy, Ren reads the three systems as basic in three separate domains: public ownership as main body in ownership, distribution according to work in distribution, and the socialist market economy in resource allocation. Only the ownership system determines the nature and direction of society. On the community with a shared future, Ren rejects readings that call it a "green channel" to the "association of free individuals", a driver of change in the mode of production, or something grounded in human nature, arguing these ignore class and risk convergence theory. Ren concludes that Party leadership underpins every other feature of socialism. The Party can reform itself because of its nature and purpose and its acceptance of supervision by the people, which Ren links to Mao Zedong's answer to Huang Yanpei on the historical cycle. Ren defends the Two Upholds against charges of a personality cult and warns of lessons from the Soviet and East European collapse. The article ends by urging students to study Marxism and follow the Party. Read the original if you want a worked example of how a senior Party-school theorist polices orthodox formulations on modernization, the economic system and the community with a shared future.

The new-era "theory of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" 新时代“中华民族伟大复兴论” Wang Huxue Wang Huxue takes up Xi Jinping's statements on the Chinese Dream and treats them as a coherent body of thought, which the author calls the new-era "theory of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation". The article argues that these statements answer, at the level of "where is the Chinese nation heading", what kind of rejuvenation is to be achieved and how. In Wang's account, the theory defines the concept's scientific content, identifies the path, names the leading force and draws up the blueprint. The article is organised in four parts that follow those four claims. It draws on speeches by Xi, the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and passages from Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. It also gives a historical outline of the Party's century of struggle in four periods and the two-step timetable to 2035 and mid-century. Wang first reads the Chinese Dream through "one core, two levels, three dimensions": rejuvenation as the core, national and individual dreams as the two levels, and national prosperity, national rejuvenation and people's happiness as the three dimensions. Rejuvenation is said not to mean reviving past imperial glories or seeking hegemony, but peaceful development and a community with a shared future for mankind. The path requires Chinese modernization, described as socialist rather than capitalist, together with the "Chinese spirit" of patriotism and reform and innovation, and the unity of the people as "Chinese strength". The leading force is the Communist Party, which Wang calls the only party able to lead the nation to rejuvenation, and rejuvenation is presented as the single theme of its hundred years of struggle. Wang concludes that the Chinese nation has moved from "standing up" and "growing rich" to "becoming strong", and that rejuvenation is now an irreversible historical process. The author cites the strategic arrangement of a basically modernized country by 2035 and a great modern socialist country by the middle of the century, and calls for continued fighting spirit under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical exposition of how the Chinese Dream and national rejuvenation are defined and tied to Chinese modernization and Party leadership.

Organising and mobilising the masses: the logic of Mao Zedong's "rise up" revolutionary discourse (1921–1949) 组织动员群众：毛泽东“起来”革命话语的逻辑建构（1921-1949） Xia Quan Kang Qingyue This research article asks how Mao Zedong built the word "qilai" (rise up, stand up, get organised) into a revolutionary discourse that mobilised the masses between 1921 and 1949. Xia and Kang argue that Mao's use of the term formed a systematic discourse within the Chinese Communist Party's organisational language, and that it helped the Party win popular trust and the victory of the New Democratic revolution. The authors begin with the word's meanings and historical setting. They trace the stages from which Mao's discourse emerged: the failures of reformism, the Party's alliance with the Kuomintang, the period of Soviet-influenced revolutionary language, and the wartime construction of a New Democracy discourse. They then analyse the first to fourth volumes of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong and the first to fifth volumes of the Collected Writings of Mao Zedong, sorting uses of "qilai" into three semantic types and drawing conclusions about the discourse's features. The core of the argument is the three meanings. The first, "to rise up, stand forward, take up arms", is the discourse's core: Mao applied it to peasants, workers, students, women, Party members and oppressed peoples abroad, and, in the authors' account, adapted it to each moment, from the anti-imperialist struggle to the war against Japan and the civil war. The second, auxiliary sense appears in compounds such as "unite", "organise" and "mobilise" with "qilai"; the authors say Mao deliberately preferred "unite the masses" in this form, giving colloquial speech revolutionary force. The third, "stand up", expresses the goal and result, culminating in the 1949 declaration that the Chinese people had stood up. According to the authors' count, the two collections contain 1,138 instances of the word, and about 66 per cent of the roughly 958 uses of the second type have revolutionary significance. Xia and Kang conclude that the discourse was mass-oriented, easy to spread, firm in conviction, and marked by class identity and exclusivity that separated "revolution" from "counter-revolution". They see the three meanings as mutually reinforcing: the first supplies the content, the second its vivid forms, and the third confirms its success, building a bond of trust between Party and people. Read the original if you study Mao-era political language, Party mobilisation methods or quantitative discourse analysis of Mao's texts.

Marx's transformation of Hegel's conception of the state and its theoretical effects 马克思对黑格尔国家观的变革及其理论效应 Wang Daiyue Why did Marx criticise Hegel's theory of the state when Hegel clearly recognised modern subjective freedom? Wang Daiyue answers a long-running objection, raised by liberal-leaning Western readers, that Marx misread or treated Hegel unfairly. The article argues that the real dispute concerns where the state's universality comes from: Hegel treats it as prior to the people, while Marx traces it to the people's material activity. Overcoming Hegel's political metaphysics in this way, Wang contends, prepared the ground for historical materialism. The article goes beyond the usual restriction of Marx's critique to the period before 1844 and draws on a wider body of early texts, combining philosophical and economic perspectives. It moves through five parts: a re-examination of the critique and its critics (Avineri, Fine, Ilting); the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, with Feuerbach's influence; Marx's 1844 economic studies, the 1844 Manuscripts and the dialectic of particularity; The German Ideology on the state and the proletariat; and a conclusion. Wang's central reasoning has three steps. First, in the Critique, Marx makes the people the source of the constitution and proposes true democracy and universal suffrage to overcome the split between civil society and the political state. Marx's own analysis of landed property and of the labouring class, however, shows civil society to be divided, so that suffrage without structural change cannot work. Second, Marx's reading of Smith and Mill, then the 1844 Manuscripts and The German Illusion-free account in The German Ideology, shows universality arising in civil society itself through exchange, division of labour and objectified labour, not through a transcendental human essence. Third, The German Ideology distinguishes particular, common and "general" interests. It presents the state as having a double face: an abstraction of social interaction that the bourgeoisie has appropriated as an illusory community. Only the proletariat can reclaim that universality. Wang concludes that the basic divide is the people-centred character of the state. By making universality emerge in material production, Marx removed the divine basis of Hegel's state and what Wang calls "superstition" in the philosophy of right. He also gave the proletariat's revolutionary role a scientific justification. The article presents the Paris Commune as confirming the German Ideology's vision, with universal suffrage as a transitional measure. Read the original if you work on the Marx–Hegel relationship, the early Marx's texts, or the genesis of historical materialism, and want a detailed rebuttal of the claim that Marx's critique of Hegel was unfair.

Western left critiques of the "new alienation" of humans under digital capitalism and their implications 西方左翼对数字资本主义人的“新异化”的批判及其启示 Gong Yongdan Gong Yongdan asks how Western left thinkers have analysed the alienation of human beings in digital capitalism, and what this offers for China's own digital development. The article argues that the alliance of capital and digital-intelligent technology produces a "new alienation" in which people are ruled by an abstract force, digital capital logic. In Gong's assessment, Western left critics describe it well but do not go beyond Marx's critical logic and find no way to sublate it. The article draws on Slavoj Žižek, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri, Giorgio Agamben, Andreas Reckwitz, Hartmut Rosa, Jodi Dean, Christian Fuchs, Byung-Chul Han and others. Part one gives an ontological critique of digital existence, rights and communication. Part two gives a political-economy critique of how digital capital screens labour, how algorithms control people, and how digital activity is requisitioned. Part three turns to what China can draw from these critiques. Gong reports that, for these critics, people are changing from real entities into abstract "virtual bodies", from "persons with status" into "status without personhood", and from independent individuals into "singularised" groups competing for visibility. In the political-economy part, Gong presents digital capitalism as the general realisation of the real subsumption of labour under capital. It leaves some people "surplus" or "useless" and impoverished as "digital poor". Algorithms turn people into "data persons" and "particle persons", while digital capital appropriates their intellectual, emotional and communicative activity. Gong holds that the culprit remains capital logic, which Western critics leave unresolved. For China, Gong calls for three measures. First, uphold the principle of putting the people first and govern digital capital logic with the logic of human labour, including limits on digital capital and distribution rules built on data property rights. Second, build a community with a shared future in cyberspace, so that a genuine community constrains the virtual community of digital capital. Third, maintain public ownership of digital means of production, with shared data to close the "digital divide". Gong presents Chinese modernization, guided by common prosperity, as having avoided the alienation seen in the West. Read the original if you want a systematic survey of Western left theories of digital alienation, together with an official-line Chinese response to them.

China's ecological civilization construction and its contribution to the development of human civilization 我国生态文明建设对人类文明发展的贡献 Cao Mengqin Writing in Guangming Daily in 2023, Cao Mengqin asks what China's ecological civilization construction offers to human civilization as a whole. Cao argues that its achievements belong to the world as well as to China, and that it supplies experience for a new form of civilization beyond the predicament of industrialisation. Cao presents the topic as important for breaking what the article calls the West's discursive monopoly and ideological hegemony over green development. The short commentary opens from the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which describes historic changes in environmental protection, and then sets out three kinds of contribution: theoretical, practical and institutional. On theory, Cao presents Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization as a complete scientific system summed up in the "ten adherences". Its original contributions, in this account, include the principle that when ecology thrives civilization thrives, the idea that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets, and a green vision linked to a community with a shared future for mankind. On practice, Cao points to ecological red lines, a development path said to differ from the Western model of "pollute first, clean up later", international recognition of projects such as the Three-North Shelterbelt and Saihanba, and carbon peaking and neutrality efforts. On institutions, Cao lists systems such as ecological compensation, river and forest chief systems, the "same responsibility for Party and government" principle, and carbon-market mechanisms. Cao concludes that this theory, practice and institutional system offer Chinese wisdom, a Chinese approach and Chinese strength for global green development and the progress of civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official scholarship frames China's ecological policy as a model for the world.

Telling the story of Chinese modernization in the capital of a major country in the new era Beijing as material for ideological and political theory courses 讲好新时代中国式现代化的大国首都故事 Ding Yun Ding Yun asks how university ideological and political theory courses (sizhengke) can tell the story of Chinese modernization through the example of Beijing. Taking up Xi Jinping's call to tell good stories about the new era, the article argues that the capital's development over the past decade offers vivid teaching material. Telling it well, Ding contends, is an important route to reforming these courses and raising them to a new level. The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical basis, namely the distinctive features of Chinese modernization as presented in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The second reviews what Ding calls the Beijing chapter of Chinese modernization, drawing on five areas of Beijing's development. The third turns to teaching practice and the idea of the "big ideological and political course" (da sizhengke). It was published in Ideological and Educational Research, 2023, no. 3. In Ding's account, Chinese modernization combines features common to all modernizations with Chinese ones: an enormous population, common prosperity, coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Ding presents these as going beyond Western modernization. Beijing's story is then told through five themes: reduced-scale development and the relocation of non-capital functions within Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei coordination; innovation backed by education, science and talent; green development and air-pollution control; people-centred urban governance, including the "respond to complaints" mechanism, which the article links to whole-process people's democracy; and opening up, including hosting the Belt and Road Forum and the Winter Olympics. Ding proposes three steps for teaching. Courses should link the classroom to society by using Beijing's museums and mass activities. They should assemble a "big teaching corps" that includes model workers, heroes, scientists and officials, together with guides from memorial sites. They should also carry a "big mission": teaching students the national standpoint, innovation, green practice and a sense of responsibility for a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxism-school scholar links official accounts of Beijing's development to the design of ideological and political courses.

Mao Zedong's historical contribution to exploring the correct path of resolving ethnic issues with Chinese characteristics 毛泽东对探索中国特色解决民族问题正确道路的历史贡献 Li Taojun Starting from Xi Jinping's statement at the Fifth Central Conference on Ethnic Work that the Party's greatest achievement in ethnic work is the "correct path of resolving ethnic issues with Chinese characteristics", Li Taojun asks what role Mao Zedong played in opening that path. The article argues that Mao and the Communists around him began the exploration, supplying the basic policies, the institutional foundation and the value principles of socialist ethnic relations in China. The article is organised in three parts, which Li describes as moving along a historical axis and a thematic one. The first follows Mao's thinking and the Party's minority policy from the early 1920s through the Long March and the War of Resistance. The second covers the shift from federalism to regional ethnic autonomy and how that system was refined. The third sets out the values behind the system, which Li presents through the traditional contrast between "instrument" and "way". Li's central claim is that the Party began with Soviet-influenced ideas of national self-determination and federation, which were never put into practice and were gradually abandoned. Mao's route to the Common Programme of 1949 ran through a class analysis of ethnic oppression, cautious and non-coercive work on the Long March, and the Inner Mongolian autonomous government of 1947 as a model. Li cites Mao's remarks of 1958 that China's demographic make-up, with Han people at 94 per cent, ruled out a Soviet-style union of republics. The article presents regional autonomy as socialist in character, dependent on training minority cadres, written into the 1954 constitution with flexibility for Tibet, and bound to central directives. It then identifies the guiding values as a multi-ethnic view grounded in the Chinese nation, ethnic equality and unity, opposition to both Han chauvinism and local nationalism, and religious harmony with freedom of belief. In the conclusion Li traces the successful experience summed up in the 1992 formulation of the correct path back to Mao's theory and practice. The article states that Mao's approach accords with the laws governing the rise and decline of nations and with dialectical and historical materialism. It holds that the basic framework and good traditions of China's ethnic work follow from Mao's aim of great unity of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao's ethnic policy is presented in current Chinese Party scholarship, including his statements on autonomy, cadres and religion.

Mao Zedong's strategic thinking on major questions of the Chinese revolution from a global perspective during the New Democratic Revolution 新民主主义革命时期毛泽东以世界眼光对中国革命重大问题的战略思考 Liu Huiqiang Lian Tong Liu Huiqiang and Lian Tong ask how Mao Zedong, during the New Democratic Revolution, placed the Chinese revolution within world history. They argue that from his earliest explorations, with the 1920 aim of 'remaking China and the world', Mao treated Chinese questions as world questions. In their account, this global perspective ran through his judgements on the revolution's stages, position, nature, path and significance, and helped the Party find a path suited to China. The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The first covers the new epoch opened by the October Revolution and Mao's division of the revolution into two steps. The second examines the world-historical factors behind the revolutionary path: the rural-encirclement strategy, the interaction of world and Chinese history in shaping modern China, and the international united front. The third treats China's place in the world revolution and the global significance of the War of Resistance against Japan. Mao's texts, such as On New Democracy (1940), are read against Marx, Engels and Lenin. The authors contend that Mao read the age as one of revolution and war, in which imperialism's contradictions were sharpening and capitalism was declining. On this basis, the revolution after the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement was 'new democratic' and part of the proletarian socialist world revolution, so a bourgeois republic was no longer a viable prospect. They argue that 'encircling the cities from the countryside' and armed seizure of power was the Chinese form of the world revolution's general experience. In this reading, it followed from China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions, and the 'Left' dogmatists erred by copying the Russian model mechanically. Mao's united-front principles combined broad alliance with differentiation, and self-reliance with foreign aid. The authors conclude that the victory of the New Democratic Revolution was among the most significant political events of the twentieth century, alongside the October Revolution and the Second World War. In their view, it altered the global political balance and offered other colonised nations a path and experience. They propose that revisiting Mao's strategic thinking can help coordinate the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation with the world's 'great changes unseen in a century', and guide China's dealings with the outside world. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how Mao's wartime texts connected Chinese revolutionary strategy to Marxist-Leninist theories of world history and imperialism.

A manifesto for the age: "the point is to change the world" A philosophical reflection on the path of Chinese modernization “问题在于改变世界”的时代宣言 Yuan Zushe Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yuan Zushe asks what philosophical significance lies in the path of Chinese modernization as set out in Xi Jinping's report. The article, a commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, argues that this path offers a new model of modernization suited to a new form of human civilisation. In Yuan's account it also opens a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Yuan frames the discussion by combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and its fine traditional culture. The reflection is then organised under four headings: ontology (worldview), practice (the view of the subject), the conception of history, and values. Each section contrasts Chinese modernization with what the author calls Enlightenment modernity and the capital-centred modernization of the early-developing Western countries. On ontology, Yuan contends that the Western worldview rests on free-market logic, the logic of capital, narrow instrumental rationality and relations of domination, and that it produces environmental, peace, development, trust and governance deficits. Chinese modernization, in this reading, stresses a community with a shared future for mankind and harmony between humans and nature. On practice and history, Yuan holds that Western modernization is marked by one-dimensional conquest of nature, hegemony and historical nihilism, while the Chinese path tests and develops Marxist truth through practice. Yuan also argues that it replaces a nation-state-centred view of history with one prioritising shared human values. On values, Yuan argues that Western modernization maximises the interests and desires of the bourgeoisie. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is said to correct this by exposing the supposed universality of Western freedom, democracy, equality and human rights as illusory. It aims at common prosperity for over 1.4 billion people, adheres to the principle of putting the people first, and is presented as advancing the Marxist view of history centred on the masses, with the free and all-round development of the human being as its ultimate goal. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Marxist philosophers frame Chinese modernization against Western modernity in ontological, practical, historical and axiological terms.

Understanding institutions from the perspective of the philosophy of social science 从社会科学哲学视角理解制度 Li Jianmin This short piece from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (10 January 2023) asks how institutions are established and sustained, and what philosophy of social science can add to sociological accounts. Li argues that the debate on collective intentionality, which spread in analytic philosophy from the 1980s, opened a new route. In this view the 'collective acceptance' account of John Searle and Raimo Tuomela explains the logical structure of institutions and underpins their social ontology. The article has three parts. It first describes an 'ontological turn' in institutional research, setting sociological definitions (Jonathan H. Turner's) beside Searle's critique of social science. It then examines how institutions are created and maintained. Finally it considers two developmental trends of human institutions, which Li calls homogenisation and 'circle-isation'. Li reports Searle's claim that social science has copied the natural sciences and treated money or government as objects like those of physics, while neglecting the ontological presuppositions of its own objects. Institutions are social constructions that exist only if collectively accepted. Humans assign 'status functions', such as a piece of paper serving as money, and these are observer-relative, so ontologically subjective but epistemically objective. This objectivity is what makes disciplines such as economics possible. Maintaining an institution requires continued acceptance and collective action. Tuomela adds 'collective commitment' as a guarantee of joint attitudes, giving acceptance the character of an action equilibrium in game theory. On this basis Li sees two trends. Under homogenisation, similar institutions (universities, governments, money, hospitals, science) converge in function across cultures as background culture loses influence. Under 'circle-isation', institutions divide people into groups, such as the 'DINK circle' or the 'e-sports circle', that communicate poorly with each other. Some circles, such as the 'science circle', hold authority across the whole social network. Li concludes that human institutional action is caused by collective intentionality and that institutions are an important collective phenomenon. Explaining their creation and maintenance through collective acceptance may not strengthen the explanatory power of social-scientific theories of institutions, Li concedes. Even so, the author holds that this transcendental ontological account offers a new approach to institutional research. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language introduction to Searle's and Tuomela's social ontology as applied to institutions, including the author's own account of institutional trends.

The logical orientation of promoting a community with a shared future for mankind 推动构建人类命运共同体的逻辑指向 Zheng Xiaowei This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, reads the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) on building a community with a shared future for mankind. Zheng argues that the report treats the idea systematically, grounding it in Chinese modernization and aiming it at creating a new form of human civilization. The author organises the analysis around three parts of the report: the great changes of the new era, the essential requirements of Chinese modernization, and the promotion of world peace and development. Each part is used to bring out a different layer of the concept's logic. Zheng first presents the community as the practical realisation of Marx's theory of community, which runs from the critique of capitalist society's "illusory community" to a "true community" or "association of free individuals". Xi Jinping's ideas from 2012 to 2017 are described as a creative development of that theory. Second, the author lists what the report's essential requirements imply for the community: Party leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics and whole-process people's democracy as its political guarantee; high-quality development as its economic base; an enriched spiritual world as its cultural element; common prosperity as its social condition; and harmony between humanity and nature as its ecological condition. Zheng contends that Chinese modernization differs fundamentally from colonial, plundering capitalist modernization. Zheng concludes that the community is one of the latest achievements of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that it answers the question of where the world is heading. The author sums up the report's stance as peaceful diplomacy, mutually beneficial opening up, reform of global governance and shared human values. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 20th Party Congress report links Marx's community theory, Chinese modernization and foreign policy.

On the philosophical significance of the young Engels's "other path" Centring on The Condition of the Working Class in England 论青年恩格斯“另一条道路”的哲学意义 Liu Huaiyu Was Friedrich Engels merely the "second violin" to Marx, or did he reach historical materialism by a path of his own? Liu Huaiyu takes up this long-running dispute between the "second violinist" and "other path" readings. The article argues for the "other path" view and gives it a new interpretation. In Liu's account, Engels's importance lies not only in his late systematisation of Marx's doctrine but also in the originality of his youthful, independent route to historical materialism, which also speaks to twenty-first-century urbanisation and globalisation. The article first reconstructs Engels's intellectual development from the Bremen period to the 1842–1845 years in Manchester, Paris, Barmen and Brussels. It then surveys more than 170 years of readings of The Condition of the Working Class in England: Soviet and East European scholars, sociological and ecological readings, and Western accounts that treat the book as the founding text of \"urban Marxism\". Liu then sets out the classical significance of the \"other path\", before closing with its relevance today. Liu makes three main moves. First, Engels reached communism through field investigation of advanced English capitalism, which served as an antidote to Young Hegelian abstraction and to the \"true socialists\". The book is also read as Hegelian historical dialectics: it traces how industrial revolution produced the proletariat as a new historical subject. Liu notes that the book is still immature, since its proletariat and communism concepts owe much to philosophical logic, and that Engels later gave the path up while Marx carried the critique of political economy forward. Second, Liu argues that Engels's treatment of Manchester anticipates later urban theory. This includes his critique of alienated urban interaction, of class segregation and of uneven development. It also includes his view that big cities foster working-class consciousness. Liu stresses that Engels held capitalist production, not the city, responsible for workers' conditions, so he was not a founder of \"urban Marxism\" as a substitute for the critique of capitalism. Liu concludes that Engels's path was obscured because he abandoned it and because it was read dogmatically. Defending his originality, the author says, fights dogmatism and academic impoverishment. For the twenty-first century, Liu calls for a \"re-spatialised\" Marxism. It would study how capitalism turns cities into instruments of control, and how disadvantaged groups can gain the right to the city. It would also treat urban space as a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you are interested in the Engels–Marx relationship, the reception history of the 1845 book, or Chinese philosophical engagement with Marxist urban theory.

High-quality development of the Marxist theory discipline in the new era 新时代马克思主义理论学科高质量发展研究 Zhang Leisheng Li Mengyun Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Leisheng and Li Mengyun ask how the first-level discipline of Marxist theory, which studies the Party's guiding ideology and its theoretical innovation, can achieve high-quality development on the new journey. They argue that this requires three things: a firm awareness of high-quality development, a clear sense of the discipline's positioning, and stronger institutional and personnel construction. The article first takes stock of the discipline's achievements and problems over the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then discusses positioning, with the academic system as its core, using the history of Marxism and the basic principles of Marxism as examples. It closes with three paths of construction: strengthening Schools of Marxism, raising the quality of teachers, and improving the training of specialist graduates. On achievements, the authors cite incomplete statistics: by the end of 2022 there were 106 doctoral and 279 master's programmes, 125,000 ideological and political theory teachers, and over 1,440 Schools of Marxism. They name four problems: research fields that stray from the discipline's content, uneven teaching staff with few leading scholars, weak organised research with low-quality output, and homogenised or loosely regulated curricula. Their central claim is that the academic system underpins both the disciplinary system and the discourse system. It should be built on the unity of the "doctrine, theory and philosophy" of the Party's innovative theory and on the premise that Marxism, and Marxism adapted to China's conditions and the needs of our times, works. The authors also warn against "de-Marxification" of teachers and graduate training. They recommend that teachers read the classics, study history and grasp basic principles. The authors propose concentrating resources on distinctive and leading sub-disciplines in key Schools of Marxism. They want the discipline kept distinct from Marxist studies in general, from ideological and political course teaching, and from the work of the Schools themselves. They also call for stricter control of graduate curricula, dissertation topics and research skills. They present these steps as the way to turn high-quality development from an aim into practice. Read the original if you want a Party-school-internal view of how Marxist theory is organised as an academic discipline in China, including its staffing, curricula and quality problems.

Deconstructing the American democratic discourse system and discourse power 美式民主话语体系及话语权解构 Lu Yizhi Lu Yizhi asks how the United States constructs and uses its discourse system and discourse power on democracy, and why non-Western countries so easily fall into it. The article argues that, after the Cold War and especially in the twenty-first century, the US has used 'democracy, freedom and equality' as an ideological weapon to hold back the development of non-Western states. In Lu's view, those states often rely on American concepts, standards and theories of democracy and have not built their own democratic discourse. Lu proposes dismantling the American system in terms Americans can understand, exposing its false universality. The article is organised in five parts: the theoretical basis of American democratic discourse, its main technique, its main purpose, its essence, and its methodology. It draws on Western thinkers such as Ranke, Hegel, Huntington, Fukuyama and Joseph Nye, on political-science works such as Huntington's The Third Wave, and on episodes such as the 'colour revolutions' and the 'Arab Spring'. It also describes how the US treats rival economies and cultures. Lu argues that the foundation is Western centrism: racial superiority, democratic superiority and cultural superiority, with the US inheriting and radicalising earlier European views. The main technique is discourse hegemony, which Lu says works by smearing non-Western democracy, setting agendas and indices, promoting 'democratisation' as equivalent to modernisation, and using sanctions or force. Its purpose, in Lu's account, is extreme egoism: seizing strategic, economic, political and cultural gains. Its essence is concealing the hypocrisy of American democracy, which Lu describes as redefining democracy as elections, as money politics, as elite rule, as 'veto politics' and as privilege for powerful interest groups. Among the methods Lu lists are vague democratic ideals, a binary of democracy versus despotism, double standards at home and abroad, and academic innovation that hides ideology. Lu concludes that non-Western countries need to deconstruct the theory, aims, techniques, paths and essence of American democratic discourse and expose its flaws. They should also build a national democratic content and institutional system suited to their own conditions and to the times. Lu warns scholars against uncritically adopting Western theories. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship in 2023 criticises American democracy and 'discourse power', and what remedies it proposes.

The historical starting point, main connotations and mission of the Chinese path to modernization 中国式现代化道路的历史起点、主要内涵与使命追求 Jiang Yingzhou Wang Chuangyu Scholars disagree about when the Chinese path to modernization began, and Jiang and Wang argue that the answer shapes how its meaning and mission are understood. Taking China as a late-developing country whose modernization passed through several shifts in development model, the article contends that the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 is the historical starting point. Reform and opening up, in this reading, was a qualitative leap within a continuous process rather than a restart. The article first reviews five candidate starting points in the literature: the Self-Strengthening Movement, the 1911 Revolution, the founding of the Communist Party, the founding of the PRC, and reform and opening up. It then surveys how scholars define the path's connotations, in formulas such as the "six unities" or "four unities", and its mission. The authors then set out five features of the path and five missions, and close with a conclusion. The authors build the case on the nature, leadership, goals and continuity of modernization. They cite Deng Xiaoping's statements that the Four Modernizations were set under Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai and were socialist in character. The five features are: universality combined with particularity; a path forged under pressure from both Western capitalist and Soviet-style models; a socialist character; leadership by the Communist Party; and common prosperity. On this account the path is not an extension of the capitalist modernization begun in 1911, though it must still answer questions raised by the Self-Strengthening Movement and the 1911 Revolution. The five missions the authors name are advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, meeting the people's aspiration for a better life, writing the "big article" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, creating a new form of human civilization, and making new and greater contributions to humanity. The authors present the path as transcending capitalist and traditional Soviet models and as a Chinese approach for developing countries. They add that its success demonstrates the truth of Marxism adapted to China. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-language account of the debate over the starting point of Chinese modernization and the official framing of its features and missions.

Vigorously promoting revolutionary culture in the historical process of advancing Chinese modernization 在推进中国式现代化历史进程中大力弘扬革命文化 Fan Xichun Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Fan Xichun argues that revolutionary culture is an important component of socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and a powerful source of momentum for Chinese modernization. Fan contends that building a modern socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation depend on its ideological guidance, value orientation, spiritual nourishment and cultural support. The article therefore calls for promoting revolutionary culture vigorously and for continually enriching it in practice. The article opens by defining revolutionary culture as an advanced culture formed under Communist Party leadership across the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It then sets out the present context: the 20th Party Congress goals of basic modernization by 2035 and a modern socialist country by mid-century, pursued amid what Fan calls profound global change, deep-seated domestic contradictions and external pressure. The main body applies a three-layer model of culture (ideas, material products, institutions and customs) and ends with a short section on adapting revolutionary culture to the times. Fan's central move is to assign revolutionary culture a role at each of the three layers. At the level of ideas, Marxism and its Chinese theoretical achievements, communist ideals, a people-centred standpoint and core socialist values secure the nature and direction of modernization. At the level of material products, revolutionary literature, art and relics, which the article says include over 36,000 immovable sites, inspire the public. At the level of institutions, Fan points to Party leadership, whole-process people's democracy and a long lineage of revolutionary spirits, from the Jinggangshan spirit to the spirit of poverty alleviation, as the political guarantee and driving force. Fan concludes that revolutionary culture stays vital only when it fits the demands of practice and of the age, and invokes Xi Jinping's call for creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. The author calls for enriching its contemporary content and forms so that it becomes a mark of the new era. Fan presents this as an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization and a historical responsibility of Communists. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party-affiliated writers frame revolutionary culture's role in Chinese modernization, including its full catalogue of named revolutionary spirits.

A preliminary analysis of historical trends of thought 历史思潮初析 Yu Pei Yu Pei takes up a concept that, he notes, has no entry in major encyclopaedias and no agreed definition: the "historical trend of thought" (lishi sichao). He argues that such trends are a specific form of social consciousness, rooted in a society's economy, politics, culture and mass psychology, and that studying them gives theoretical and practical value for forecasting and strategic judgement in a period of world upheaval. The article has three parts. The first defines historical trends of thought, distinguishes them from social and academic trends, and traces their evolution in the West, in modern China and in Meiji Japan. The second examines their changing "themes of the era", moving from Marx's theory of world history to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The third takes the postwar "global history" movement as a case of a historiographical trend, discussing Geoffrey Barraclough and L. S. Stavrianos. Yu's central move is to apply historical materialism. Historical trends of thought are said to reflect the historical current (lishi chaoliu), which is primary and material, while the trend of thought is secondary and ideational. Yu rejects the claim that academic trends can be kept "pure" of politics, arguing that they are never outside ideology and that scholarly and social trends belong together. He also contends that no historical trend can be judged by a single standard, since it depends on one's worldview, and he cites Western claims that modernization and globalization mean Westernization. Global history is presented as a product of anti-colonial movements and the rise of developing countries after 1945, with Barraclough's rejection of Eurocentrism and Stavrianos's A Global History (later editions stressing new technology) as examples of a new era requiring new historiography. Yu concludes that the current theme has shifted from "world history" to a community with a shared future for mankind, which he describes as enriching Marx's world-history thought. He holds that the world will remain one of "one globe, two systems" for a long time. He urges researchers to study theory, history and present conditions rigorously, so as to grasp the laws of historical development, strengthen historical confidence and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how "trends of thought" relate to ideology, historiography and world-historical change, with global history as a worked example.

How can artificial intelligence be made to do good? Reflections on technological threats and state responsibility 人工智能如何向善：基于技术威胁与国家责任的思考 Mei Lirun Mei Lirun asks how artificial intelligence can be steered towards good when public attitudes have moved from enthusiasm, after AlphaGo's victory, to widespread anxiety about an AI threat. The article argues that, for a state whose core mission is to promote the well-being of its people, calming this anxiety is a new and unavoidable responsibility. Mei holds that the state should answer each main type of AI threat with a matching pair of measures. The article first traces the rise of the AI threat discourse, citing warnings from Elon Musk and Stephen Hawking, a 2015 Oxford risk assessment and the spread of media alarm. It then examines three threats that Mei says attract most concern: unemployment, privacy and loss of meaning. The final section, the longest, sets out state responsibilities for each, drawing on examples from China, the United States and the European Union. On unemployment, Mei accepts that earlier industrial revolutions created more jobs than they destroyed. Mei argues, however, that this precedent may fail now, because AI replaces white-collar as well as blue-collar work and demands higher skills. On privacy, Mei describes companies "hunting" data, which makes anonymisation weak and leaks irreversible. On meaning, Mei argues that algorithmic "information cocoons", AI's superiority in fields humans take pride in, and the handing over of decisions to algorithms narrow the space in which people find meaning through growth and autonomy. Mei proposes that the state conduct a survey of automation ("mapping") and provide a safety net of subsidies, retraining and job information for the unemployed. For privacy, Mei calls for legislation, including AI-specific laws, and periodic special campaigns of inspection and punishment. For meaning, Mei urges the state to encourage "reverse recommendation" in algorithms and to publish "technology forecasts" of what AI can and cannot do. Mei also asks the state to promote a notion of human–machine symbiosis. Read the original if you want a Chinese political-science account of AI governance that ties public anxiety to state responsibility and cites Chinese regulatory campaigns from 2017 to 2019.

Marx and Engels on collective ownership of land 马克思恩格斯关于土地集体所有制的论述 Chen Wenxue Chen Wenxue asks what Marx and Engels actually said about collective ownership of land, and what their statements imply for rural land reform in China today. The article argues that Marx and Engels treated collective ownership as a form of public ownership alongside nationalisation, and that cooperatives were the route to it. On this basis Chen concludes that China should neither privatise nor nationalise rural land. The article has three parts. It first sets out why Marx and Engels wrote on land ownership: the aim of communist revolution, the need to win the peasantry as an ally, and concrete questions of land title in revolution. It then reads their texts from 1843 to the 1880s, including Engels's "The Peasant Question in France and Germany" and Marx's replies to Vera Zasulich on the Russian village commune. The final part turns to China's land history since 1949 and to current reform. Chen's central move is to trace how "collective ownership" shifted from a general term for public ownership, opposed to private property, to the ownership of the working masses. In Chen's account, the cooperative ideas of Marx and Engels supplied that content. Large estates were to be expropriated and passed, first by lease, to agricultural workers' cooperatives under state ownership. Small peasants were not to be dispossessed by force: they were to be brought into cooperatives through example, social help and time, and Engels backed the Danish model of direct pooling. Chen adds that for Russia, Marx held that the commune could move straight to collective ownership, without passing through the stage of bourgeois smallholding, provided proletarian revolution succeeded. Chen draws five conclusions about collective land ownership, covering its place in communism, its negation of capitalist property, its use in winning peasants, its basis in large-scale socialised production, and cooperatives as the route. For China, Chen defends the household contract responsibility system and the separation of ownership, contract and management rights, with homestead reform in progress. Privatisation is rejected as contrary to Marxism and the constitution. Nationalisation is rejected because of the urban–rural divide, fiscal burden and political risk, so reform must protect peasant interests and proceed by category and by stages. Read the original if you want a close, text-based survey of the classical sources on land and cooperatives, together with their use in current Chinese policy debate.

Marx and Engels on social character 马克思和恩格斯关于社会性格的思想探析 Ouyang Kang Zhao Beisite Ouyang Kang and Zhao Beisite ask what Marx and Engels thought about "social character", a group-level psychological trait pattern and the behaviour it produces. They argue that, although the two never used the term in a strict sense, their writings on national character, class character and universal personality contain a coherent body of thought. The authors present it as a theoretical source of Erich Fromm's concept and as a resource for current concerns: building a sense of community among the Chinese nation, meeting the spiritual needs of the people in the new era, and responding to modern anxiety, depression and loneliness. The article first defines social character and places it within Marx's and Engels's account of social consciousness. It then examines three dimensions: national character, class character, and a universal human personality form tied to Marx's three forms of human development. A final section draws out four underlying orientations of this thought: social, historical, practical and humanistic. The evidence comes mainly from Engels's The Condition of the Working Class in England, Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire and Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and Marx's account of the three forms of human development in the Grundrisse. The authors argue that social character is a stable system of low-level social consciousness, an intermediate link through which social psychology develops into systematic ideology. National character is shaped by modes of production and life, by the mode of social change, and by war and migration. Class character, they say, increasingly replaces national character as the real "nationality", with feudal lords, capitalists and workers each expressing their relation to a form of private property. The article reads the three forms of human development as a history of personality, from dependence on persons, through independence resting on dependence on things (with isolation and anxiety), to the free individuality of the third form. The authors also hold that, since all consciousness is social, no purely individual character exists. The authors conclude that Marx and Engels linked healthy social character to the reform of social institutions and to proletarian revolution. In their reading, the subjects of social character are practising people who can change their own character, and its goal is the spiritual liberation and all-round development of each person. They also read Marx and Engels as rejecting both forced erasure of national character and the placing of narrow national particularity above human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx and Engels treated national and class psychology, and how a Chinese scholar links Fromm's concept to the Marxist theory of human development.

Some reflections on combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture Studying and implementing the spirit of the 20th Party Congress 关于马克思主义基本原理与中华优秀传统文化相结合的若干认识 Yang Yanqiu Yang Yanqiu takes up a proposition that Xi Jinping first put forward in his 2021 speech marking the Party's centenary and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) elaborated: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. Written as a study note on the Congress, the article asks why the two must be combined, why they can be, and how. Yang's answer is that the combination is the necessary route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that it rests on a real inner compatibility between the two. The article has four sections: the necessity of the combination, the inner affinity between Marxism and traditional culture, the grounds on which they can be joined, and methods and paths. Yang draws on Engels, on Mao Zedong's view of history, and above all on the historian Liu Danian and the Marxist historiography of Li Dazhao, Guo Moruo, Hou Wailu and Du Guoyong. Yang also cites Marx's writings on China and the Congress report's "six adherences". On necessity, Yang argues that Marxism could take root in modern China only by explaining Chinese history and responding to the problems of the country's modern transformation, and that Chinese Marxist historiography was founded in the very act of interpreting traditional culture. Traditional culture in turn needs Marxism for its "creative transformation and innovative development". On feasibility, Yang points to Marx's and Engels's sustained attention to China and to the openness of Chinese culture, which Yang says absorbed Buddhism, Islam and Western learning in three major exchanges. Yang warns that compatibility must not be examined only as ideas set against ideas, but in relation to economic base and superstructure, citing the early Marxist historians' shift from a single economic-formation method to a more dialectical view. On method, Yang lists several principles drawn from the six adherences: putting the people first and looking for inner spiritual affinity rather than surface resemblance; self-confidence and self-reliance; upholding fundamental principles while innovating, with a problem-oriented approach; a systematic outlook; and an open, world-embracing stance. Combination, Yang stresses, is not a blend or compromise but a process of both breaking and establishing under Marxist guidance, and research must serve practice rather than revive the past for its own sake. Read the original if you want an official-academic account of how Chinese historians frame the "Two Integrations", with extensive references to Marxist historiography.

The Kreuznach Notebooks and the young Marx's turn to materialism 《克罗伊茨纳赫笔记》与青年马克思的唯物主义转向 Liu Bingjing How did the young Marx come to adopt materialism in 1843? Liu Bingjing notes that the usual account points to the material-interest problems of the Rheinische Zeitung period and to Feuerbach's philosophy. Drawing on the MEGA2 text of the Kreuznach Notebooks, Liu argues that Marx's own independent historical research was also indispensable to the turn. The article draws on Marx's stay in Kreuznach from May to September 1843, when he studied the political history of England, France and other countries and wrote both the Notebooks and the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right. It follows the Notebooks in sequence: Notebook I's broad chronicle of French history, the narrowing focus from Notebook II onward, readings of Daru, Rousseau and Bailleul, and a long comment in Notebook IV on Ranke's journal. It then compares these with the Critique. Liu contends that through excerpts on Venetian privilege, Rousseau's remarks on property and law, and feudal and bourgeois France, Marx came to see that property relations in civil society shape the state and politics. Land ownership underpinned feudal personal dependence, and property ownership underpinned bourgeois political status. On this basis Marx reversed Hegel's claim that the state determines civil society, as his Ranke comment on Hegel's state idea as 'subject' shows. The Critique then restates this argument, including its treatment of primogeniture and the claim that political estates become social estates. Liu adds a qualification: Marx had not yet grasped the objective historical content of civil society. He still criticised the dominance of private property in ethical terms, citing Vergniaud and Robespierre, and called for restoring the human essence of social forms. In Liu's reading, Marx had inverted Hegelian speculation and turned to materialism, but his view of social history kept an implicit idealist tinge. Starting from concrete history nevertheless pointed him toward the political-economy study of civil society. Read the original if you want a short account of how the Kreuznach Notebooks bear on the origins of Marx's materialism and the limits of his 1843 position.

Clarifying Marx's "philosophy of history" and its orientation for our times 马克思“历史哲学”的澄明及时代定向 Wu Hongzheng Against the backdrop of what Chinese discourse calls changes unseen in a century, Wu Hongzheng asks whether Marx's thought contains a philosophy of history capable of answering the question of where the world is heading. Wu argues that it does: Marx's theory of world history, set out in works such as the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto, is the core of an implicit philosophy of history. This has been neglected in scholarship, and Wu holds it should be recovered and given a contemporary orientation. The article has three parts. The first explains why Marx's philosophy of history has receded from view. The second reconstructs its basic content by contrasting Marx with Kant and Hegel on the conception of history, its subject, its value and its laws. The third turns to the present and identifies three orientations: changes in contemporary capitalism, the new form of human civilization, and a community with a shared future for mankind. Wu names three causes of the recession: Marx never built a separate system or used the term in his own materialist framework; his critique of Hegel gave the false impression that he rejected the field; and the emphasis on "historical science" overshadowed it. Wu replies that Marx attacked only the speculative "general philosophy of history", which offers abstract universality and treats history as a set of ideas. Marx's own version, in Wu's account, rests on concrete universality and on labour as the creator of history. It places the value of history in human freedom and emancipation, and finds historical necessity in the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production, a necessity that can be grasped in advance rather than only in retrospect. Wu also argues that Marx's view is not a linear one: the Renaissance and the October Revolution show necessity that includes contingency, so the author calls it a dialectical conception of progress. Wu concludes that Capital is both Marx's economic philosophy and, at a higher level, part of his philosophy of history, so the surplus-value law belongs to the logic of social formations. In Wu's view, recent shifts such as unilateralism and de-globalisation do not change that orientation. Civilizations advance through sublation rather than clash or simple replacement, and the community with a shared future for mankind becomes the era's theme. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese philosophical argument that Marx has a philosophy of history, set against Kant and Hegel and linked to current Party-state concepts.

A deeper understanding of why Marxism adapted to China and our times "works" 深刻理解中国化时代化的马克思主义行 Zhang Hui Taking up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which states that the Communist Party's success and the merits of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rest on Marxism "working", and specifically on Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, this theoretical commentary asks how the two claims relate. Zhang argues that this "works" can be understood from three angles: method of thought, mechanism of formation and practical results. The thesis is that adapted Marxism is a theoretical product of upholding fundamental principles while innovating, a fruit of the Two Integrations, and the key to China's "two miracles". The article has three sections, one for each angle. It first traces the spread of Marxism-Leninism in China after the October Revolution and the founding of the Party. It then covers the move from a single "integration" to the Two Integrations. Finally it surveys the Party's record from Mao Zedong to the new era, citing Engels, Mao and the philosopher Ai Siqi along the way. Zhang's first move treats Marxism as a method rather than a dogma. Because it offered no ready answers for a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China, the Party had to avoid mechanical application and foreign models and instead fit the theory to national conditions. Zhang calls this "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground", the internal logic by which adapted Marxism arises. Second, Zhang argues that the combination of Marxism with Chinese reality was long studied mainly in terms of theory and mission, while cultural affinity was neglected. Drawing on Ai Siqi, Zhang says traditional Chinese culture has a deep compatibility with Marxism, which provided a cultural-psychological basis for its acceptance and fostered the creative transformation of that culture. Third, the author names adapted Marxism as the "secret code" of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. Zhang says it guided the new-democratic revolution, the socialist market economy, the theoretical system, the institutions and the culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhang concludes that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It is presented as the guide for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author urges Party members to hold firm to Marxist belief and study the latest achievements of this adaptation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school-style scholarship explains the 20th Congress formula that Marxism "works" through method, the Two Integrations and developmental results.

Persist in using Marxism to observe, grasp and lead the times 坚持用马克思主义观察时代把握时代引领时代 Dong Zhenhua Dong Zhenhua takes up the formula repeated in Xi Jinping's speech at the Party's centenary (2021) and in the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle: use Marxism to "observe the times, grasp the times and lead the times". Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress, Dong argues that only by doing so can the Party keep answering the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and produce theory that keeps pace with the age and guides practice. The article is a short theoretical commentary in three parts. The first concerns holding to Marxism's worldview, methodology and basic standpoint. The second concerns problem awareness and a problem-oriented approach. The third concerns upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, which the author links to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Dong draws on Xi Jinping, the 20th Party Congress report, Marx and Lenin, and on episodes from Party history. In the first part, Dong argues that the Party has kept its initiative because it applies Marxist method to analyse situations. Examples are Mao Zedong's "a single spark can start a prairie fire" after the failed uprisings, and the 1978 debate on practice as the sole criterion of truth, which Dong says opened reform and opening up. In the second part, citing Marx on problems as "the voice of the epoch", Dong holds that Marxism offers principles and methods rather than ready-made answers. Dong says the present era far exceeds what the classic authors foresaw, and that China's socialism is still in its early decades in the primary stage of socialism. In the third part, Dong treats "upholding fundamental principles" and "innovation" as two sides of one question: innovation means "continuing the discourse" in Marxism's authentic spirit, neither merely repeating texts nor starting afresh elsewhere. Dong concludes that upholding fundamental principles means three unwaverings: Marxist basic tenets, the Party's overall leadership, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. This must go together with "saying new things" that the founders did not say. Dong calls it a solemn duty of today's Communists to keep writing new chapters of Marxism adapted to China and the times, starting from the worldview and methods of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Central Party School scholars present the logic linking Party history, problem orientation and theoretical innovation in 2023.

Wang Zhen's early encounters with Chairman Mao 王震早年与毛主席的交往 Li Shenming Written to mark the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth and the 115th of Wang Zhen's, this is a historical memoir-style account rather than a research article. Li Shenming, who worked at Wang Zhen's side for over a decade, reconstructs Wang's early dealings with Mao from Wang's own oral recollections and from interviews with his old comrades and subordinates. Li presents Wang as a true Communist and Mao as a leader of exceptional breadth, openness and strategic clarity. The article is organised chronologically in three sections. The first covers Wang's youth as a railway worker, his 1925 escort of Mao by rail handcar, and their 1930 meeting near Changsha, where Mao advised on forming the Xiangdong Independent Division. The second covers Wang's talks with Mao at the First National Soviet Congress in Ruijin (1931–32).
