The third covers their meeting during the Second Congress in January 1934, and the later Xiang-Gan battle at Shashi. Li's central thread is Mao's guidance on guerrilla and mobile warfare against the 'left' line of Wang Ming and the advisers Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De). Mao urged Wang to use the 'sixteen-character' formula, avoid costly attritional fighting, and reject 'fortress against fortress' tactics. He also told Wang to correct the over-extension of purges, to treat captured troops generously, to study revolutionary theory, and to follow the path of encircling cities from the countryside. Li notes that Mao said all this while himself sidelined from leadership, yet voiced no complaint. Li then reports that Wang carried this guidance back to the Xiang-Gan base, and cites a veteran's testimony that it explained the victory at Shashi in April 1934. Li concludes that the Shashi victory, achieved by Ren Bishi, Wang Zhen and Xiao Ke by applying Mao's instructions, eased pressure on the Central Soviet Area. The account also stresses Mao's personal warmth and his criticism of localism. It is offered as a tribute to both men. Read the original if you want a participant-sourced, commemorative narrative of Mao's military and political advice in the early 1930s, or want to see how Party-affiliated writers present Mao's role in the inner-Party struggle with the Wang Ming line.

The strategic blueprint of Chinese modernization and the elevation of its theoretical system 中国式现代化的战略擘画和理论体系升华 Gu Hailiang On 7 February 2023, at a study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022), Xi Jinping stated that a theoretical system of Chinese modernization had been "preliminarily constructed". Gu Hailiang's article is an interpretive exposition of that judgement. It argues that the formulation sums up the practical and historical logic of Chinese modernization, answers the three major questions of the era posed by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and rests on a distinctive Marxist worldview and methodology. The article has four sections. The first traces the historical initiative behind the exploration of modernization, from the new-democratic revolution through the Mao era to reform and opening up. The second sets out the components of the theoretical system as Xi presented them, from the five features of 2020 to the 20th Party Congress report. The third links the system to the three major questions of the era, and the fourth examines the six "views" (worldview, values, view of history, view of civilization, democracy and ecology) and the relationships within the "systematic process" of modernization. Gu's central move is to read the theory as the product of accumulated historical conditions: the revolution's "fundamental social conditions", the political premises of the socialist period, and the institutional and material base of reform and opening up. Gu cites debates of the 1920s–30s and the Four Modernizations, with Deng Xiaoping's 1979 "Chinese-style" modernization as the origin of the term. The article then lists six innovations in the Congress report: the central task, the five features, the essential requirements, the 2035 goals, the major principles and cultural roots. It argues that the Party's leadership determines the fundamental nature of Chinese modernization, and that the six "views" apply the dialectical and historical materialist worldview. They are tied to the "six musts" of Xi's thought and to six relationships, such as top-level design and practical exploration, and efficiency and fairness. Gu concludes that the theory is a major theoretical innovation of the 20th Party Congress and a new stage in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In this account it presents a new form of human civilization that breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists systematise the official account of Chinese modernization and trace its historical lineage.

The first step in the origins of Chinese civilisation, eight thousand years ago 八千年前中华文明起源迈开第一步 Han Jianye Han Jianye asks when the origins of Chinese civilisation began, distinguishing them from its formation, which the author dates to the first early states on Chinese soil. The short piece argues that the first step in the origins process was already taken around 8,000 years ago. It is an excerpt from a longer article on the origin, formation and longevity of Chinese civilisation, first published in Study Times in 2022. The article draws on archaeological finds from the Yellow River basin, the Yangtze region and the West Liao River basin. It moves from agriculture, to calendrical knowledge and belief, to social order, and then summarises what these show. Han begins with the rough formation, by about 8,000 years ago, of two farming systems: rice in the south and millet in the north. In Han's account, China's large farmland area and this dual system secured a stable food supply. Han then cites the Jiahu site in Henan, where bone instruments may have been used for "observing celestial phenomena to determine the seasons", along with divination symbols on tortoise shells and dragon images in distant regions, which the author reads as signs of early worship of heaven and a unified cosmology. Clan cemeteries and orderly ring-ditch villages point, in Han's reading, to ancestor veneration and a settled social order. Han concludes that by 8,000 years ago most of China had an ordered society, some social differentiation and a developed system of ideas and knowledge, including cosmology, ethics, historical consciousness, astronomy, mathematics, symbols and music. In Han's view this system forms the core of Chinese civilisation, and a cultural sphere of an "early China" was emerging. Read the original if you want a brief statement of one archaeologist's case for dating the beginnings of Chinese civilisation to the Neolithic.

Mao Zedong's successful way of turning crisis into opportunity 毛泽东化危为机的成功之道 Chen Mingfan Zhang Xuesen Chen and Zhang ask how Mao Zedong repeatedly turned crises facing the Chinese Communist Party into opportunities, and what this offers the Party today. They argue that his method rested on three linked capacities: advance planning, calm strategic resolve under threat, and seizing the strategic initiative. The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to "turn danger into opportunity" and presents Mao as the model for it, against a background of what it calls changes unseen in a century and rising anti-globalization. The article is built in four sections. The first three each take one element of Mao's approach and illustrate it with episodes from the revolution and the early People's Republic: the anti-"encirclement" campaigns, the Seventh Party Congress, Third Front construction, the Khrushchev demands of 1958, Fu Zuoyi's threatened raid on Xibaipo, the response to the US blockade, the Korean War, and the campaign against schistosomiasis. The fourth section draws lessons for the present from Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report (2022). On advance preparation, the authors stress Mao's "bottom-line thinking", citing his refusal of Soviet naval proposals and the "one principle, four points" formula on Taiwan, and his claim that thorough preparation can deter an enemy. On strategic resolve, they cite his decision to delay recovering Hong Kong to keep a trade window open, the "rubber for rice" deal with Ceylon, and his insistence on despising the enemy strategically while respecting it tactically. On initiative, they say Mao held that people, not weapons, decide outcomes, and that subjective initiative must still respect objective laws. They note that the "Left" errors and the Great Leap-era setbacks came from ignoring those laws. Chen and Zhang conclude that danger and opportunity are a unity of opposites, and that strategic initiative is the condition for turning one into the other. They call on the Party to prepare for major risks, hold firm strategic resolve and seize the initiative, citing Xi's "black swan" and "grey rhino" warnings. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars use Mao's wartime and early-PRC decisions as a template for crisis management under Xi Jinping.

The worldview and methodological significance of adhering to systems thinking 坚持系统观念的世界观和方法论意义 Yang Hongyuan This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, starts from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which says the Party must adhere to systems thinking (系统观念). Yang Hongyuan asks how this idea should be understood and used to guide the work of the Party and state. The answer is that systems thinking is both a worldview and a method, and that the Marxist classics help to explain it. The piece has three parts. The first traces the idea in Marx, Engels and Lenin. The second shows how the Chinese Communist Party has applied it, from Mao Zedong to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third takes up current conditions and the demands they place on systems thinking. Yang argues that dialectical materialism treats the material world as universally connected, so that every thing is an organic whole, or system. In Yang's account, Marx's idea of the organic system and his analysis of bourgeois society in Capital, and Engels's use of the concept of system in his writings on nature, are foundational, and Lenin summarised the method. Yang holds that making systems thinking part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is an original contribution to Marxism. It is linked to strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. Yang concludes that, given the strategic opportunities and risks at home and abroad, systems thinking is needed to advance high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Yang calls for balancing domestic and international affairs, development and security, central and local initiative, and the short and long term. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register account of how Party theorists ground systems thinking in Marx and Engels.

Chinese modernization raises human civilization to a higher dimension and level 中国式现代化促进人类文明升维提级 Liu Liangjian Taking Xi Jinping's speech at the study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022) as its starting point, this short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2023, asks what Chinese modernization means beyond China. Liu argues that its proposal, its successful advance and the first construction of its theoretical system mark a step up in dimension and level (shengwei tiji) on three fronts: in Chinese civilization's understanding of itself, in the world concept of modernization, and in human thinking. Liu expects these to lead in practice to a similar step up in the form of human civilization. The piece first reviews the paradigm that has governed Chinese self-understanding since the mid-nineteenth century, then turns to each of the three upgrades in turn. It draws on classical Chinese sources (the Book of Songs, the Analects, Zhou Dunyi) and sets Western critiques of modernity, from postmodernity to multiple modernities, against Chinese experience. It closes with a reflection on Hegel's and Fukuyama's views of history. Liu describes the old paradigm as 'modernization equals Westernization': China learned first techniques, then institutions, then ideas, in a process assumed to follow a single line with the West ahead. In this account the more closely China imitated the West, the more it lost itself. Chinese modernization, Liu argues, breaks this myth by showing world history as simultaneous advance at many points, and recasts China's modern renewal as an interaction of Western and Chinese civilizations that produces a new civilization that is both Chinese and universal. Western thinkers have criticised Eurocentric modernity but, Liu says, they seldom recognise a Chinese form as independent and in some respects pointing to the future. As an example Liu cites harmony between humanity and nature, which Liu sets against a Western faith in conquering nature, drawing on the Chinese debate on heaven and humanity. On thinking, Liu invokes the idea of the unity of substance and function (ti-yong buer) to argue that no single universal standard of modernization exists apart from its varied concrete forms. Liu concludes that Chinese civilization should take on, with confidence, the mission of bringing forth a new form of human civilization. This requires creative transformation of tradition rooted in living practice. Liu holds that history has neither been completed in Prussia nor ended in the West, and that people everywhere will take part in making it. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese scholars present Chinese modernization as a philosophical and civilizational claim with world significance.

Staying firmly confident in economic work 坚定做好经济工作的信心 Gao Peiyong Wang Hongju Writing in the People's Daily in March 2023, Gao Peiyong and Wang Hongju take up Xi Jinping's remarks to the Jiangsu delegation at the first session of the 14th National People's Congress, where Xi called high-quality development the first task of building a modern socialist country. The authors argue that 2023, the first year of implementing the 20th Party Congress (2022), calls for a correct reading of the economic situation, better social expectations and stronger confidence. Their thesis is that the economy is already improving and its long-term fundamentals are sound. The commentary has three parts. The first reviews 2022 and early 2023 data and identifies positive changes in domestic demand, supply and market expectations. The second lists the strengths behind the claim that the long-term fundamentals have not changed. The third turns to the December 2022 Central Economic Work Conference and sets out four sets of tasks for guiding business entities and stabilising expectations. On the first part, the authors cite GDP above 120 trillion yuan in 2022, growth of 3% and consumer price inflation of 2%. They also cite average growth of 4.5% over three years and an IMF upgrade of China's 2023 forecast from 4.4% to 5.2%. They say demand is recovering as pandemic controls are eased, supply is improving as commodity prices fall, and PMI readings have moved into expansion territory. On the second part, they name the leadership of the Party and the socialist system, a hardworking population, Chinese modernization, a solid industrial base, 170 million business entities, a huge domestic market and the dividends of reform and opening up. In their account these make up the "fundamentals". The policy section calls for expanding consumption and investment, and for implementing the Two Unwaverings through state-enterprise reform and a better environment for private firms. It also calls for opening up at a high level to attract foreign investment, and for coordinated fiscal, monetary, industrial, technology and social policy. The authors present these steps as the way to turn the economy's potential into results and consolidate the overall recovery. Read the original if you want an example of how official economic commentary in early 2023 framed the post-pandemic recovery and the policy agenda behind it.

Coordinating the expansion of domestic demand with the deepening of supply-side structural reform 搞好统筹扩大内需和深化供给侧结构性改革 Liu Yuanchun Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2023, Liu Yuanchun takes up Xi Jinping's statements on coordinating the expansion of domestic demand with the deepening of supply-side structural reform. Liu argues that the two are unified rather than opposed. The author presents their integration as necessary for high-quality development, for building the new development pattern, and for coping with external shocks and current macroeconomic problems. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why both policies are needed and how they relate. The second sets out the principles that should guide their coordination, under Xi Jinping's economic thought. The third turns to concrete tasks, drawing on the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, the 2022 Central Economic Work Conference and the Outline of the Strategic Plan for Expanding Domestic Demand (2022–2035). Liu holds that insufficient demand is one of the main obstacles to economic recovery. As evidence, Liu notes that final consumption has stayed above 50 per cent of GDP for twelve years but remains below the roughly 80 per cent of major developed economies and the roughly 70 per cent of India and Vietnam. Supply-side reform, by contrast, is described as the fundamental remedy for deeper structural problems, since the principal contradiction has shifted from weak aggregate demand to a mismatch between supply and demand structures. Liu sees the two as complementary: demand expansion is macro, short-term and demand-side, and works through regulation, while supply-side reform is micro, medium-term and supply-side, and works through reform. Liu therefore calls for action on both supply and demand, and on both policy and institutions, guided by high-quality development, a domestic circulation of high-level dynamic balance, and the principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability. For practice, Liu calls for forming a complete domestic demand system and raising consumption backed by income, investment with reasonable returns, and financing subject to capital and debt constraints. Liu also calls for technological and institutional innovation to strengthen industrial and supply chains, for promoting mutual reinforcement of domestic and international circulation, and for deeper reform and opening up, including a unified national market and institutional opening-up. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official macroeconomic line of early 2023 links demand-side and supply-side policy.

Accelerating the improvement of the socialist market economy system 加快完善社会主义市场经济体制 Yang Jing This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, argues that the socialist market economy system must be improved more quickly and understood accurately. Yang Jing holds that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has made the system an integral part of the basic socialist economic system. In Yang's account, this has deepened understanding of market laws, advanced Chinese modernization and enriched Marxist political economy's theory of the market economy. The piece follows the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which makes building a high-standard socialist market economy system a strategic task. The article has three parts. The first places the market economy within the basic socialist economic system. The second deals with the relationship between market and government. The third takes up how to understand and handle capital's characteristics and patterns of behaviour. Throughout, it relies heavily on statements by Xi Jinping and on Party documents, and it presents Xi Jinping's economic thought as the guiding framework. Yang first notes that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) placed the market economy system alongside public ownership as the main body and the distribution principle of 'to each according to work' in a 'trinity' framework. Combining the socialist system with the market economy is described as a great innovation that unites ownership, distribution and economic operation. On government and market, Yang says the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) set out that the market plays the decisive role in allocating resources while government plays its role better. In practice this means reducing direct government interference in micro-level activity and also reforming government functions, macroeconomic governance and public services to make up for market failure. On capital, Yang lists state, collective, private, foreign and mixed forms. Yang says capital's negative effects under capitalism, such as crises, ecological damage and polarisation, are largely overcome under socialism, but its profit-seeking nature can still lead to disorderly expansion. Capital therefore needs regulation by law, with 'traffic lights', so that its positive role is used and its negative role controlled. Yang concludes that accelerating improvement of the system, with the market and government uniting organically, accords with the law that relations of production must suit the state of the productive forces. It would, in this view, liberate and develop the productive forces and meet people's growing needs for a better life, while serving common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party-line exposition of the socialist market economy, the government–market relationship and the treatment of capital as framed after the 20th Party Congress.

We must adhere to self-confidence and self-reliance 必须坚持自信自立 Liu Jun This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, argues that adhering to self-confidence and self-reliance (zixin zili) is an integral part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu Jun contends that it is a dialectical unity of theoretical, historical and practical logic. The piece is organised along those three logics. The theoretical logic concerns firm belief in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The historical logic presents self-confidence and self-reliance as a key instrument behind the Communist Party's century of struggle. The practical logic treats it as a requirement for what the article calls the new "road of examination" towards the second centenary goal. Liu draws throughout on statements by Marx, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. On theory, Liu argues that confidence rests on the conviction that Marxism works, and specifically Marxism adapted to China through the Two Integrations, with Marxist principles combined with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Liu reads dialectical materialism and historical materialism as implying that there is no universal development model, so each country must find its own path. On history, the author claims that self-reliance opened the road to national rejuvenation, from the New Democratic Revolution through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and revitalised scientific socialism through successive theoretical innovations. Liu states that Chinese modernization rejects what the article describes as the old Western path of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization, creating a new form of human civilization. For the new journey, Liu calls for three things: firm belief in Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics, together with continued adaptation of Marxism; independence and a path of China's own, neither copying classic Marxist templates nor foreign models; and open opposition to historical nihilism as well as to complacency and arrogance. Liu urges vigilance towards "black swan" and "grey rhino" events and an awareness of risk. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2023 linked self-confidence and self-reliance to Xi Jinping Thought, Chinese modernization and the Party's historical narrative.

Overall strength rising, marked regional differences: new developments in foreign left-wing movements in 2022 总体力量上升 区域差异显著——2022年外国左翼运动新动态 Zhou Miao Writing in early 2023, Zhou Miao surveys how left-wing forces outside China fared in 2022, a year the author describes as marked by the pandemic, the Ukraine crisis and growing global deficits in peace, development and governance. The article's thesis is that the left's overall strength is rising, but unevenly: gains in Latin America and parts of Africa and Oceania sit beside a pronounced right-wing and far-right turn in Europe and weak showings in much of Asia and the Middle East. The article is organised by region: North America and Europe, Asia, Oceania and the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa. Each section lists election results, strikes and protests, and party membership figures country by country. Examples include the UK strike wave, the French left alliance's rise to 142 National Assembly seats, Lula's victory in Brazil, Gustavo Petro's win in Colombia, and parliamentary results in Senegal, Angola, Kenya and Lesotho. For Europe, Zhou sorts left parties into three groups: those that are strong or governing, those that govern but face a surging right, and those that have lost power or are fading, as in Italy, Sweden, the Czech Republic and Latvia. In North America the author points to growth in membership of the Democratic Socialists of America and the Communist Party USA. For Latin America, Zhou describes a new "pink tide" under which over 80 per cent of the region's population live in states governed by the left. The author cautions that economic problems, corruption, right-wing pressure, outside intervention and the Peruvian president's removal make the "pendulum effect" hard to end soon. In the concluding section Zhou sees opportunity in the political and economic crises of the West: labour unrest, higher union support and the exposure of capitalism's contradictions. The main obstacle named is internal division, notably over the nature of the Ukraine crisis, with left forces in India, Vietnam, South Africa and Bolivia judging Russia more positively than northern left forces. Zhou calls on left forces to tell mainstream from tributary, set aside disputes, exchange ideas and replace competition with "solidarity and symbiosis". Read the original if you want a country-by-country record of 2022 elections and left-wing mobilisation, as compiled by a CASS specialist on foreign left-wing thought.

The world-historical significance of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的世界历史意义 Zhu Andong Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhu Andong asks what significance Chinese modernization holds beyond the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that it has major world-historical significance: it gives scientific socialism new vitality in twenty-first-century China, offers humanity a new option for achieving modernization, and offers Third World countries a theoretical and practical alternative to the Western path. The article has three parts. It first sets out Marx's theory of world history and its two stages. It then reviews Western modernization theory and the criticisms made of it. Finally it turns to Chinese modernization, defined as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China. Zhu draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on the 20th Party Congress report and on Rostow's stages-of-growth model, dependency theory and world-systems theory. Zhu reads Marx as dividing world history into a stage opened by capitalism and a transition towards a "communist" world-historical stage. Capitalism, in this account, developed the productive forces and prepared its own gravediggers. Zhu holds that no social formation exits history on its own, so the bourgeoisie presents capitalism as natural and permanent. After the Second World War the United States and other Western countries, according to Zhu, built modernization theory to keep Third World states from turning to socialism. Zhu argues that the theory erased colonial plunder and presented Western capitalism as the only route, and that neoliberal modernization later served Western, especially financial, hegemony. Zhu says dependency theory and Western left scholars such as Stiglitz and Ha-Joon Chang criticised this but did not dislodge its mainstream standing. Zhu concludes that China's achievements and the systemic crisis of contemporary capitalism show there is no single modernization model and no universal standard. Zhu sets the five Chinese features named in the 20th Party Congress report against what the article calls Western modernization, marked by polarisation, violence and plunder. The article says China's record of rapid growth and long-term stability attracts other countries and has loosened US-led hegemonic control, making non-capitalist paths more feasible for them. Zhu holds that this moves humanity further through Marx's second stage of world history, creates a new form of human civilization and contributes to eventual communism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Marx's world-history theory to a critique of Western modernization theory.

Marxism and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义和中国化时代化的马克思主义 Hou Huiqin Hou Huiqin takes up a question the author treats as the first-order issue for the Communist Party of China: how to understand the relationship between Marxism and Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Hou notes that doubts persist about whether Marxism is outdated, and that some tendencies pull the two apart. The article's thesis is that they form an organic unity of "one body, two sides", and that the Party must keep to two unwaverings: Marxism as guide and continued adaptation of it. The article has three parts. The first defines the relationship through the unity of the scientific system and of the Party's guiding thought. It then sets out how the two sides interact and how their routes to knowing historical laws differ. The second part considers whether Marxism is a "foreign" culture and revisits the old debate over "substance and function" (ti–yong). The third takes up the Two Integrations, concentrating on integration with fine traditional Chinese culture. Hou argues that Marxism supplies the general, shared theory, while its Chinese form supplies the particular, so the two cannot be separated. The founders moved from general laws to specific ones. Chinese Marxism starts from the most pressing concrete problems and moves upward to general laws. On the foreign-origin question, Hou holds that culture has a dual character, class and human, in which class character is decisive. Marxism, as the class consciousness of the working class, is a "world-historical" presence and not a foreign import. It is foreign only in two limited senses: it must be brought to a spontaneous working class from outside, and its European idiom needs localising. Hou therefore distinguishes Marxism as guiding ideology from Marxism as a cultural element. Integration with tradition must operate first at the ideological level, because tradition does not clarify or renew itself without Marxist guidance. Hou concludes that continuing to adapt Marxism is itself the process of unifying it, and that the Two Integrations, especially with traditional culture, strengthen confidence in Chinese modernization. Hou warns against cultural revivalism, historical nihilism and any pluralism in guiding thought. The article closes by stressing that abandoning Marxism would cost the Party its soul. Read the original if you want a detailed statement of how a leading Party ideologist reads the Two Integrations and defends the unity of guiding ideology.

Chinese modernization: common features and Chinese characteristics 中国式现代化：共同特征与中国特色 Luo Yuting Luo Yuting takes up a question raised by the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): how Chinese modernization can hold both the features shared by all modernizations and its own Chinese characteristics. The article argues that the two form an organic unity. A modernization with only common features, or with only Chinese characteristics, would in Luo's view not be Chinese modernization. The article has three parts. The first defines modernization and sets out its common features. The second describes six Chinese characteristics, which Luo labels institutional, national-conditions, value, development, ecological and peace characteristics. The third discusses what the author calls China's choice, meaning how to combine the two sides in practice. In the first part Luo defines modernization as the shift from an underdeveloped to a developed state, driven by science and technology and by socialized production. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Luo identifies four core indicators: modernized science and technology, modernized productive forces, modernized ways of life, and modernized social institutions. Chinese modernization shares these, Luo says, as the process by which China's productive forces and living standards catch up with and surpass advanced world levels. Its Chinese characteristics, following the 20th Party Congress report, are a huge population, common prosperity for all, coordinated material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Luo adds the leadership of the Communist Party and the socialist system as institutional features. Luo treats the common features as the universal and the Chinese characteristics as the particular, and likens their combination to the dialectical link between universality and particularity in contradiction. Luo draws three requirements from this. Production development must go together with institutional innovation, so that the socialist basic economic system is improved and polarisation under capitalist modernization is avoided. Science and technology leadership must go together with independent innovation, which Luo presents as necessary given what the article calls trade wars, tech wars and decoupling by hegemonic powers. The exploration of a path must go together with confidence in that path, and Luo contrasts it with the Western capitalist model, which the author describes as built on war, colonialism and plunder. Read the original if you want a systematic account, from a Marxist-theory scholar writing in an official-theory journal, of how Chinese modernization is placed within a general theory of modernization.

The value and significance of Mao Zedong's speech at the opening ceremony of Yan'an University With a discussion of the Chinese logic of running higher education institutions in the Yan'an period 毛泽东《在延安大学开学典礼上的讲话》的价值与意义 Zeng Luping Prompted by Xi Jinping's April 2022 remarks at Renmin University of China that Chinese universities should take root in Chinese soil rather than copy foreign models, Zeng Luping returns to Mao Zedong's speech at the opening of the reorganised Yan'an University in May 1944. The author argues that the speech sets out a Chinese 'logic' of running universities: institutions must first serve the Party's central tasks, national strategy and economic and social needs. In wartime conditions, this meant serving the anti-Japanese base areas. The article has four parts. It first reviews the history of Yan'an University, from its founding in 1941 through the mergers of 1943 and 1944, and places it within the Yan'an Rectification Movement. It then analyses the speech's content, traces its roots in Mao's educational thought, and finally examines the university's practice and legacy under seven headings: educational policy, disciplines, management, curriculum, links with practical work units, research, and productive labour. Zeng contrasts two logics. Western-influenced universities, including most pre-1949 Chinese ones, followed a 'disciplinary logic' in which scholarly output is the measure of success. The Rectification Movement, in the author's account, criticised this and established a 'social-demand logic', with 'new-type regularisation' acceptable only if consistent with adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Zeng reads Mao's speech, with its concrete targets for self-sufficiency, literacy and public health, as a rejection of dogmatism that applies the principle of seeking truth from facts. The author stresses that this does not abolish disciplines or scholarship, but subordinates them to the Party's central tasks. Zeng concludes that Yan'an University embodied the 'Yan'an model' of higher education and that, after 1949, its principles shaped the new China's system: Marxist guidance, education serving proletarian politics and combined with productive labour, Party committee leadership with presidential responsibility, and priority for engineering. The author holds that the 1952 reorganisation of departments fully applied the social-demand logic. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese account of Yan'an-era university history and of how Party scholarship links it to current calls for a distinctively Chinese higher education.

The historical contribution of the "Two Integrations" and its practical requirements “两个结合”的历史贡献及实践要求 Xu Fengzhen Xu Fengzhen asks what the formula of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, the Two Integrations, contributes to the theory of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article treats it as an original theoretical creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Xu argues that it unites content and method, and epistemology and practice, and that it opens a new stage in the adaptation of Marxism. The article is organised around five angles: concept, theory, history, cognition and practice. It first traces the discourse on adapting Marxism from Li Dazhao, Chen Weishi, Zhang Wentian and Ai Siqi to Mao Zedong and the post-1949 formulations. It then examines how Marxism came to be chosen in China, the stages of integration from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, and two mistaken ways of thinking. It ends with methodological requirements. Xu's core claims are that the Two Integrations reorganises earlier wording into a unified framework. "Marxism" replaces "Marxism-Leninism", "China's specific realities" absorbs earlier stage-specific formulas, and fine traditional culture is placed alongside those realities. Xu describes the structure as "one body, three wings" (theory, practice, culture) and "one root, two foundations". Xu explains the affinity between Marxism and the Communist Party through five points: people-centred stance, human emancipation, revolutionary character, the highest programme of communism, and practicality. Xu also points to correspondences between Marxism and Chinese traditional thought. Xi's rejection of the "template" and "master copy" views serves as the corrective to dogmatism and cultural nihilism. Xu contrasts the periods before and after the Zunyi Conference as positive and negative lessons. In practice, Xu calls for close study of Marx's original texts, for strengthening both the Marxist "root" and the two Chinese "foundations", and for pursuing creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. Xu proposes extending adaptation to parts of Marxism beyond philosophy, such as Marx's thinking on modernization, party building and the united front. The author also proposes moving from one-to-one mutual adaptation to a one-to-two form, with the three elements reinforcing one another. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of how the Two Integrations is theoretically framed and what research agenda it sets for studies of the adaptation of Marxism.

Socialism's transcendence of capitalism, seen from the all-round development of the human being 从人的全面发展看社会主义对资本主义的超越 Dong Jianming Dong Jianming asks why capitalism can realise only a one-sided, abstract development of human beings, while socialism contains the possibility of their all-round development. Taking its cue from the 20th Party Congress report (2022), which lists all-round human development among the goals for 2035, the article argues that capitalism's internal logic of capital limits human development. Socialism, in Dong's reading, transcends that limit, and Chinese modernization shows the possibility becoming real in practice. The article reconstructs Marx's and Engels's notion of all-round development on three levels: the material basis of productive forces, the all-round development of labour and of human abilities, needs and individuality, and the forms of social intercourse. Each of the first three sections takes one level, first setting out the contradictory role of capitalism and then the corresponding Chinese practice. Dong draws on Marx's analysis of exploitation, alienation, the cooperative factory and the "illusory community", and on Weber, Horkheimer and Adorno, and Marcuse. On the material basis, Dong argues that capitalism created the productive forces needed for all-round development but deprived workers of the means to realise it, and then became a fetter on those forces. Socialised ownership of the means of production is presented as the way to remove that fetter. On labour, capital shapes workers, the industrial reserve army and capitalists alike into one-sided, "one-dimensional" individuals, whereas socialism can reverse the relation between people and capital, as Marx's workers' cooperative factory foreshadows. On intercourse, capitalist world history produced a state that is an "illusory community" and an unequal order of "East subordinate to West"; the "true community" is the alternative. Dong cites as Chinese counterparts the public-capital logic, land reform from household contracting to the "three rights separation", state guidance of capital with "traffic lights", the dignity of labour, a community with a shared future for mankind, and a distinct path to modernization. Dong concludes that capitalism cannot truly achieve all-round human development, while socialism provides its real basis and, in the author's account, this possibility is being realised under socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article presents common prosperity, a people-centred approach and adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times as the vehicles of this realisation. Read the original if you want a detailed Marxist-philosophical argument, anchored in Marx's texts, for why Chinese theorists treat all-round human development as the measure of socialism's superiority over capitalism.

The historical logic of "daring to struggle and being good at struggle" and its contemporary value “敢于斗争、善于斗争”的历史逻辑及其当代价值 Xiao Guiqing Liu Jiarong Writing in 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Xiao Guiqing and Liu Jiarong take up the injunction in Xi Jinping's report that the whole Party must "dare to struggle and be good at struggle". The article argues that this principle is a consistent historical logic running through the Communist Party's first century, and that it remains a guiding requirement for building a modern socialist country and reaching the second centenary goal. The article moves chronologically. It first reviews the Party's experience in the new-democratic revolution, in socialist revolution and construction, and in the reform period. It then turns to the "great struggle" of the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering its meaning, its "new historical characteristics" and its achievements. A final section looks ahead to the new journey towards the second centenary goal. The authors' central move is to split the principle into two parts: daring to struggle is a matter of courage and spiritual drive, while being good at struggle is an art of strategy. Drawing on Mao Zedong, they cite the policy of "both unity and struggle" and the criteria of being justified, advantageous and restrained, and on Deng Xiaoping the strategy of "hiding our capabilities and biding our time", which they say did not mean abandoning struggle on core interests. For the new era, they present Xi's view that struggle must keep to the leadership of the Party and the socialist system, and that it spans political, economic, cultural, social and ecological security. They credit it with the Party's centenary, the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era, and poverty alleviation. They describe the external environment as marked by Western containment, trade and technology wars, and a US that they say will not tolerate Chinese modernization. The authors conclude that the second centenary goal will be accompanied by long and complex struggles, and that the key lies in the Party and in its cadres. They call for cultivating a fighting spirit, strengthening fighting skills through ideological, political and practical training, and holding the initiative in struggle, while stressing that the Party has no wish to make enemies. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-affiliated scholars after the 20th Party Congress trace the concept of struggle through Party history and apply it to current domestic and international tasks.

The two dimensions of the human–nature relationship in Capital and their contemporary implications 《资本论》中人与自然关系二维向度思想及当代启示 Dou Ling Geng Rumeng Dou Ling and Geng Rumeng ask how Marx's Capital treats the relationship between humans and nature, a question they describe as both a major practical problem and a major theoretical concern in current scholarship. They argue that, unlike Marx's early philosophical reflections, Capital treats the question scientifically from the standpoint of historical materialism. In their reading, the human–nature relationship is in essence the relationship between human productive activity and nature, and it is shaped by two dimensions: the productive forces and the relations of production. The article has four parts. The first examines the productive-force dimension, from natural conditions as the basis of production, through small-scale production, to machine industry and the double-edged effect of science and technology. The second examines the production-relations dimension under capitalism: separation of producers from the means of production, unlimited expansion, technology in the hands of capital, and private ownership of land. The third considers how the contradiction between humans and nature can finally be resolved. The fourth draws implications for global environmental governance and for building a "Beautiful China". The authors' central move is that the productive forces determine how far humans can exploit or improve nature, while the relations of production determine which tendency prevails. They contend that capital's pursuit of profit, the capitalist use of machinery and the split between landowner and tenant farmer, who has no motive for long-term improvement, give capitalism an inherent mechanism of ecological destruction. Citing Marx's passage on associated producers regulating the metabolism with nature, they argue that most scholars read it only through production relations. In their view it requires both highly and rationally developed productive forces and public ownership of the means of production, and the contradiction can arise under any system while society remains in the "realm of necessity". On global governance, the authors criticise Western eco-socialism and argue that capitalist states shift pollution abroad and resist environmental agreements. They call on China to cooperate internationally while uniting with others against "ecological imperialism", and they hold that a final resolution requires fundamental change to capitalist private ownership. For China, they describe the shift from passive to conscious environmental protection since reform and opening up. They treat ecological civilization and the aim of a "Beautiful China" as expressions of socialism's essence, to be advanced by institutional reform and public conscientiousness. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Capital's ecological thought that links it to current Chinese ecological civilization policy and to criticism of Western eco-socialism.

Marx's view of the modern and the theoretical foundations of the new path of Chinese modernization 马克思的现代观与中国式现代化新道路的学理基础 Zhuang Yougang Gu Yi Marx never defined "the modern" in one place, and the authors argue that existing scholarship has treated only fragments of his scattered remarks. Zhuang and Gu set out to reconstruct Marx's view of the modern as a systematic whole. They contend that this view supplies the fundamental theoretical basis for the new path of Chinese modernization. The article has four parts. It first sets out Marx's methodological principles, then the main dimensions through which he presents the content of the modern. It next examines his understanding of the modern as a historical process, and finally draws out implications for Chinese modernization. Marx's own texts, including the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, the Manifesto and Capital, are the main evidence. In the authors' reading, Marx understands the modern first as a transformation in how people exist, from dependence on persons to independence resting on dependence on things. He compares classical and modern society along four dimensions: handwork giving way to machine production, widening exchange that makes history world history, natural economy giving way to commodity economy (with labour-power sold as a commodity), and the reversal of town–country relations. The authors then argue that Marx treats the arrival of modernity as lawlike and unavoidable, as both progressive and historically narrow, and as uneven across countries. Late-developing countries may enjoy advantages, and Marx's remark that a society can shorten and lessen the birth-pangs implies several possible routes into modernity. From this the authors conclude that modernization is essentially a transformation of human existence, with one goal but many possible paths. Because historical conditions have changed, they argue, China cannot repeat the Western European route, which relied on internal dispossession and external plunder. They hold that the uneven course of modernity makes a new path both possible and necessary. They describe Chinese modernization as socialist modernization, which must complete tasks that capitalism completed in the West while serving the people as a whole. In their account it is the direct theoretical result of socialism with Chinese characteristics and points towards a new form of civilization. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Chinese Marxist scholars derive a theory of modernization from Marx's writings.

Theoretical features and historical evolution of the contemporary adaptation of Marxism to the needs of our times On Marxism's "timeliness" (shidaihua) from scientific socialism to Xi Jinping Thought 马克思主义时代化的理论特征和历史演进 He Haigen Sun Daiyao He Haigen and Sun Daiyao examine what it means to "adapt Marxism to the needs of our times" (Marxism's shidaihua) and trace how this has unfolded historically. Taking up the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to keep writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, they argue that shidaihua is an internal requirement of Marxist development. In their account it means combining Marxism with the features of an era so that it answers the questions that era poses. The article first sets out a conceptual framework. It distinguishes the "big era", defined by a social formation such as capitalism and lasting centuries, from "small eras" defined by shifting themes, principal contradictions and technological change. It then divides the history of Marxism into three stages tied to the three scientific and technological revolutions: the birth of scientific socialism, the "Russian stage" of Leninism, and the "Chinese stage". It closes with four features of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The authors argue that shidaihua requires a real need and objective conditions, and that it must not depart from the direction of the big era, the transition from capitalism to socialism, or it would degenerate. In their reading, the first technological revolution gave socialism a material basis, moving it from utopia to science. The second, with the shift to monopoly capitalism, produced Lenin's analysis of imperialism and Russia as a weak link; the authors cite figures on foreign capital in Russia. The third, they say, changed the class structure in the West and exhausted the Soviet model, which they illustrate with East–West German comparisons. They contend that Deng Xiaoping's reassessment of the era as one of "peace and development" opened the Chinese stage. For the present, the authors identify four features of Xi Jinping Thought. It grasps what has changed and what has not in the era: peace and development remain the theme, while the world faces changes unseen in a century and a new technological revolution. It treats nationalisation and timeliness as an inseparable "two-in-one". It keeps answering the basic questions of socialism within the big era. It responds to the "question of the world" through a community with a shared future for mankind and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-school account of how Chinese theorists periodise Marxism's development and link it to technological revolutions.

Heller's construction of a Marxist anthropology centred on "feelings" 赫勒以feelings为中心的马克思主义人类学建构 Sun Jianyin Sun Jianyin examines "feelings", the core concept of Ágnes Heller's early philosophical anthropology, and asks how Heller used it to build a Marxist anthropology. Sun argues that, guided by Wittgenstein and Kant, Heller took elements of Marx's thought to go beyond both, and so joined Marxism with psychoanalytic and psychological analysis. Sun also holds that the result has real limits from the standpoint of Marx's historical materialism. The article has five parts. It first sets out the context: the split between Anglo-American empirical anthropology and the continental tradition of philosophical anthropology, the question of whether Marxism and psychoanalysis are compatible, and Heller's planned series on instinct, feelings, needs, morality, personality and history, which she did not complete. It then traces the concept's philosophical sources in Wittgenstein's analysis of sensation and private language and in Kant's Anthropology from a Pragmatic Point of View. A third part reconstructs Heller's conceptual system, a fourth assesses its value, and a closing section compares it with Marx's own texts. Sun's central claim is that Heller solved two problems. First, she joined sensation (Wittgenstein's focus) and feeling (Kant's) in one plural concept, "sensation/feeling", which rises from simple sensation through perception, memory and emotion to stable feeling and is inseparable from thought and action as forms of "involvement". Second, she rejected an a priori view of feeling by treating feelings as socially learned motivations, "built in from within" through social practice. Sun draws on her use of Marx's account of human essence and of objectification, alienation and sublation. In Sun's reading, this renews the field of philosophical anthropology, deepens the philosophical understanding of psychology, and offers a route between psychoanalysis and orthodox Marxist anthropology. In the conclusion Sun is critical. Heller's anthropology abstracts from socialisation and never takes economic life as its basis. It draws its "experience" largely from literary depictions of individual psychology, and so yields an abstract universality that fits any social formation. Sun says this misreads the objective stance of Marx's late anthropological work, which tied ideas to historical conditions, and that it foreshadows her later turn to the "postmodern". Even so, Sun credits Heller with a dialectical account of how feelings arise and develop, and with one possible path towards a Marxist anthropology. Read the original if you work on the Budapest School, Marxism and psychoanalysis, or the history of philosophical anthropology and want a detailed Chinese critical reading of Heller's early work.

On the holistic wholeness of Marxism 论整体的马克思主义整体性 Yu Bin Yu Bin asks what it means to grasp the wholeness (zhengtixing) of Marxism as a whole. The article argues that most existing studies of Marxist wholeness fail to do so, because each takes one feature, theme or angle and treats it as the key. Yu proposes instead a "holistic" wholeness that covers the whole of Marxist theory and the whole of its practice. The article opens with a survey of Chinese scholarship on the question. It sorts the positions into groups: those that identify a core (scientific worldview, scientific socialism, critique, practice); those built on a unifying theme (abolishing private property, human liberation, critique of the logic of capital); those that use one or several perspectives or dimensions; those that stress unity of several aspects; and those that stress completeness. Yu then develops two parts of the author's own account: the wholeness of Marxist theory, and the wholeness of theory and practice. Yu argues that the three component parts of Marxism (philosophy, political economy, scientific socialism) cannot be linked by a neat formula, such as philosophy guiding economics. Citing Engels on the "negation of the negation" in Capital and on the separate routes by which the English, French and Germans reached communism, Yu holds that the parts are independent and complementary, and valuable for their differing content. On this view, wholeness means mastering all the classic works, including Engels's military writings and Marx's mathematical manuscripts, so that useful parts can be found when new problems arise. On practice, Yu holds that unity of theory and practice means using practice to realise truth, not using theory to explain reality. The article offers Lenin's New Economic Policy and Deng Xiaoping's "second leap" in rural reform as examples. It also defends the agreement of logic and history against Meng Jie. Yu concludes that the holistic wholeness of Marxism covers Marx, Engels and Lenin's theory, plus later theories that practice has tested and the people have endorsed. The article lists Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Yu says it excludes work by parties or scholars that departs from basic Marxist principles, naming some Soviet leaders and some Western Marxists. Yu also contends that partial mastery of Marxism has weakened its ability to answer real problems and contributed to its marginalisation. Read the original if you want a critical map of Chinese debates on Marxist wholeness, or an argument for reading the Marx-Engels Collected Works in full.

The inherent logic of Marxism leading the system of philosophy and social sciences 马克思主义引领哲学社会科学体系的内在逻辑 Han Xiping Wang Siran Han Xiping and Wang Siran take up the call to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, which they describe as ultimately the construction of China's own autonomous knowledge system. Their thesis is that this system should be led by Marxism, and that this follows from three sources: a historical logic, a practical logic and a theoretical logic. The article first reviews how Marxism shaped China's revolution, construction and reform, from the Mao Zedong Thought tradition through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Chinese modernization. It then argues from present needs and from the state of Western social science, and from Marxism's own theoretical character. It ends with five concrete measures. In the historical argument, the authors hold that the Communist Party's century of success rests on Marxism's continual adaptation to Chinese conditions, so that a new knowledge system should be built on the same foundation. In the practical argument, they say a China that has become strong needs social sciences that are strong and autonomous, and that liberal-led Western social science, built on market-centred assumptions and fragmented disciplines, cannot explain or solve today's interlinked problems. In the theoretical argument, they claim that Marxism's scientific, people-centred, practical and open character, with historical materialism and dialectics as method, suits the holistic study of complex problems. The proposed measures are: strengthening Marxist theory as a first-level discipline (its doctoral programmes rose from 39 in 2016 to 104 by 2021, according to the authors) and ending its perceived marginalisation; applying Marxist standpoint and method across disciplines while drawing on traditional Chinese culture; promoting interdisciplinary "new liberal arts"; absorbing outstanding human social-science achievements critically; and shifting paradigms so that Chinese experience is turned into original theory and the habit of imitating the West is dropped. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official case for a Marxist-led autonomous knowledge system in Chinese academia, together with its policy references and proposed disciplinary measures.

Lenin on the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks)'s courage in self-reform: practice and thought 列宁关于俄共(布)勇于自我革命的实践和思想 Wang Yijuan Yu Liangzao Wang Yijuan and Yu Liangzao ask how Lenin led the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) to confront its own errors, and what this offers the Chinese Communist Party today. They argue that readiness for self-reform is the mark distinguishing a Marxist party from other parties and a requirement for fulfilling the proletariat's historical mission. In their account, Lenin consistently admitted the party's mistakes openly, fought them and drew lessons from them. The article, published in 2023, has three parts. The first reviews four episodes of Lenin's practice after the October Revolution: the struggle against "revolutionary phrase-mongering" over the Brest-Litovsk peace, the reflection on the trade-union controversy, the admission of errors in War Communism, and the criticism of Communists' inability to manage the economy under the New Economic Policy. The second part sets out Lenin's ideas on the significance of self-reform, and the third draws lessons for the Chinese Communist Party. The authors identify three strands in Lenin's thinking. Admitting errors keeps the party clear about its mission, as in his remark that a party that is unafraid to acknowledge mistakes will reach the summit. It also drives theoretical innovation, they say, citing the commissar system in the Red Army, state capitalism as a transitional stage and the specificity of Russia's path. Finally, self-criticism strengthens organisation and the party's vanguard character and purity, including through measures against bureaucracy and the 1921 purge informed by the views of non-party workers. The authors present the shift from grain requisition to a tax in kind and free trade as the model case of correction in practice. The authors conclude that Lenin's experience speaks to the Chinese Communist Party in three ways. Party political building should take the lead, as should the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, to uphold the authority of the Central Committee and avoid factions. Rural questions, poverty-reduction gains and rural revitalisation deserve priority. The "danger of insufficient capability" among the "four dangers" must be met through study, practice and firm ideals, in line with Xi Jinping's statement that the Party's self-reform is always on the road. Read the original if you want a Party-journal reading of Lenin's early Soviet policy debates as a precedent for the Chinese Communist Party's current self-reform discourse.

New explorations of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) on the socialist road 印度共产党(马克思主义）对社会主义道路的新探索 Zhang Qingzheng Zhang Qingzheng asks how the Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), has explored the socialist road since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and what that record implies for its prospects. The article argues that the party's theoretical and practical innovations let it grow into what the author calls the largest communist party in the capitalist world. It also credits the party with decades of continuous local rule won through elections. The author adds that in recent years the party has run into serious difficulties. The article has four parts. It first sets out the CPI(M)'s view of world socialism: its reading of the Soviet collapse, its critique of democratic socialism and neoliberalism, and its outlook on the socialist movement. It then traces the development of the party's theory of the "people's democratic revolution" since its founding in 1964. Next it reviews practice: membership and mass organisations, state governments in West Bengal, Tripura and Kerala, and relations with other parties. It ends with an assessment of lessons, problems and prospects. Zhang argues that the party treated the Soviet collapse as the failure of a distorted model, not a refutation of Marxism-Leninism. On that basis it revised its theory: capitalism and socialism would coexist for a long period, and it adopted new "four contradictions". It held to peaceful and parliamentary struggle but kept other options open, and it widened its class base to four classes, with the working class leading. Its united-front line shifted over time, and a split has opened over whether to ally with the Congress party against the BJP. Zhang names four successes: ideological firmness, adapting Marxism to Indian conditions, mass struggles and land reform, and attention to party-building. Five problems are uneven regional strength with sharp electoral losses, laxity in party-building, falling membership, factionalism, and weakened propaganda. Zhang concludes that the CPI(M) has gained useful experience but that its road "will still not be smooth". The author lists favourable conditions: the constitutional preamble's commitment to socialism, India's multiparty system, a large rural population, and the development of China and Vietnam. Unfavourable factors include religious and communal divisions and, in the author's account, repression and violence from the BJP and the state. Read the original if you study communist parties outside China, India's left, or how Chinese scholars assess the CPI(M)'s record and party-building.

From industrial machines to interpretive machines Shifting themes in foreign studies of Marx's theory of machinery 从工业机器到解释机器 Zhu Chunyan Gao Qin This review surveys how Marxist schools outside China have understood and developed Marx's theory of machinery over roughly a century, following the actual development of technology. Zhu and Gao argue that the themes have shifted from mechanisation to automation to digitalisation, while the underlying logic of capital has stayed constant. They present this as a reason to see the theory as still valid for analysing digital capitalism. The article is organised in three historical stages plus a conclusion. The first covers Soviet Marxism (Lenin, Bukharin, Stalin-era industrialisation) and early Western Marxism (Lukács, Horkheimer and Adorno, Marcuse). The second covers labour process theory (Harry Braverman, David Noble) and Italian autonomist Marxism (Hardt and Negri) on automation. The third covers contemporary accelerationism (Williams and Srnicek) and the British scholar Larry Lohmann's... in the article's account, Larry Roman's "interpretive machine" theory of artificial intelligence. Zhu and Gao draw contrasts at each stage. Soviet Marxism treated machines as neutral productive forces and affirmed mechanisation, whereas early Western Marxism treated them as historical phenomena bearing reification and domination. Labour process theory stressed how automated and numerically controlled machines deskill workers and extend capital's control, while autonomism stressed the general intellect, immaterial labour and the chance for workers to "escape" with the machine. For the digital age, accelerationism proposes to accelerate productive forces and democratise technology, whereas Roman's account treats AI as the mechanisation of human interpretive skills, continuous with industrial machines, relying on unpaid living labour and sustaining an ideology of "full automation". The authors conclude that what changes is the form of machine technology and the reach of capital's domination, and what stays the same is capital's leading role in machine use. They hold that today's technological reality has not gone beyond the scope of Marx's theory, and that the real problem lies in the capitalist economic structure rather than in the machines' dual effects. They call for further research with Marx's scientific method on new technological conditions. Read the original if you want a compact map of Western Marxist positions on machines, automation and AI from Lenin to accelerationism and Roman.

The historical experience of the Communist Party of China in maintaining its vanguard character over a century: a perspective from the international communist movement 百年中国共产党永葆先进性的历史经验——基于国际共产主义运动的视角 Lü Weizhou Writing for the Party's centenary in 2021, Lü Weizhou asks why the Communist Party of China has grown from a small force into a ruling party and what lessons the international communist movement offers on keeping a party "advanced". The article holds that maintaining "advanced character" (xianjinxing) is the essential attribute of a Marxist party and the fundamental reason for the Party's success. It also treats this as a permanent task bearing on a party's survival. The article has two main parts. The first draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on the Soviet and East European experience, to identify four foundations of a vanguard party: guidance by scientific Marxist theory, communist ideals and convictions, the support of the people, and democratic centralism as the organisational principle. The second part traces how the Chinese party has realised each of these over its hundred years. A short conclusion looks ahead to the "two centenary goals" and the building of a modern socialist country. Lü reads the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and of the East European parties as a negative test of each foundation. In this account, the Soviet party abandoned Marxism by adopting "humane, democratic socialism", lost its ideals, developed bureaucratic privilege that cut it off from the people, and weakened democratic centralism through past repression and later through Gorbachev's "unconditional democracy". The Chinese party, by contrast, is presented as having kept each foundation. The author names the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context (from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), a spiritual lineage of ideals and sacrifice, the mass line, and democratic centralism, citing the Zunyi Conference and the Zhang Guotao split as successes and the Cultural Revolution as a failure. Lü concludes that vanguard status is neither achieved once and for all nor permanent. Under long-term rule, factors that weaken the Party are always present, so the Party must treat maintaining its vanguard character as a major strategic task, keep drawing on historical experience and improve its governing capacity. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account that sets the Chinese party's history against the Soviet collapse and the wider communist movement.

New readings of Gramsci's thought in Chinese and foreign scholarship from a historical perspective, and their implications 历史性研究视角下国内外理论界对葛兰西思想的新解读与启示 Pan Xihua Marking the 85th anniversary of Antonio Gramsci's death, this review surveys roughly the last ten years of Chinese and foreign research on Gramsci's thought. Pan Xihua argues that understanding Gramsci requires returning to his own historical setting, and that research adopting such a historical perspective has produced new readings of long-contested questions. The article is a literature review that also draws lessons for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has three parts. The first lists new historically oriented publications: new Chinese editions of the Prison Notebooks (2014, 2016), the forthcoming direct translation from Italian by Tian Shigang, Chinese monographs on Gramsci's historicism and cultural hegemony, and works from Italy, Mexico, France and the Anglophone world on the reception of Gramsci. The second part examines three clusters of new interpretation: Gramsci's historical standing, the relation of his philosophy of praxis to Marxism, and fresh uses of his cultural hegemony in analysing historical events. The third part draws implications for China. On historical standing, Pan reports that Chinese scholars now largely agree Gramsci is a founder of Western Marxism, while foreign scholars such as Eric Hobsbawm stress his priority in developing Marxist political theory. Pan notes that evaluations bear the mark of their era, citing a Russian scholar who says Gramsci's emphasis on consent was alien to Soviet ideology. On the philosophy of praxis, Pan describes one Chinese view equating it with Marxism, used partly to evade prison censorship, and another stressing its originality. Pan reports that most scholars, including Yohann Douet and Michael Löwy, see it as an innovative development of Marxism rather than an identity with it. Pan also highlights a newer trend abroad of applying cultural hegemony to the history of the communist movement, such as Aleksandr Maisuryan's account of how dissidents eroded the Soviet Communist Party's hegemony before the Soviet collapse. Pan says this trend has not yet drawn attention in China. Pan draws three implications. Studying the "five histories" (of the Party, new China, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation) should strengthen confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Marxism should continue to be localised and innovated, as Gramsci did against dogmatic "orthodox Marxism". Because ideological hegemony must be built and maintained continuously, the Party must hold leadership and discourse power in ideological work in the new-media era, where Pan sees historical nihilism and Western ideological infiltration as threats. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language bibliographic map of recent Gramsci scholarship and an example of how Chinese Party scholars draw political lessons from him.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 守正创新推进马克思主义中国化时代化 Deng Chundong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2023, Deng Chundong takes up one of the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): the requirement to uphold fundamental principles and break new ground. Deng argues that this pairing is the key to enriching Marxism and to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The two sides are held to be dialectically united and inseparable. The article has three parts. The first draws on the history of world socialism and of the Communist Party of China to show why the pairing matters. The second sets out what upholding fundamental principles requires, namely the \"three unwaverings\". The third explains how innovation should proceed, in four directions: following objective laws, starting from China's realities, answering the questions of the era, and guiding new practice with the Party's innovative theory. Deng contends that abandoning fundamental principles betrays Marxism and leads socialism to setbacks, while dogmatism leaves socialism stagnant. The three unwaverings are: the basic tenets of Marxism, the Party's overall leadership, and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Deng insists that rigid adherence to old formulas or past mistakes is not real upholding of principles. Equally, policies that depart from the Marxist standpoint or from the basic socialist system, or that copy the governance models of Western capitalist countries, are not real innovation. Innovation, in this reading, means respecting objective laws, combining Marxism with China's circumstances and with fine traditional Chinese culture, studying contemporary capitalism and Marxism outside China selectively, and developing the theory of Chinese modernization. Deng concludes that the strength of the Party and of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rests on Marxism, in its Chinese and contemporary form. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. Deng calls for arming the whole Party with it and for opening new horizons through the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists in 2023 explained the relationship between orthodoxy and innovation in the Party's theoretical work.

Opening up a new realm of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 He Xinyuan He Xinyuan asks how Marxism can keep guiding practice in individual countries, and answers that it must be localised and adapted to its era. The article argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era achieved a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In He's account, it thereby opened up a new realm of that process. The article has three parts. The first presents localisation and timeliness as a general law of the world socialist movement, citing Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ism and Ho Chi Minh Thought in Korea and Vietnam. The second examines the Two Integrations. The third sets out the basic guidelines for continuing the work on the new journey, drawing on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). He contends that the Two Integrations are a law-like understanding of the process. These are combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The first, in He's reading, is the Party's most valuable experience, and dogmatism and bookishness caused earlier setbacks. The second is described as a distinctive feature, resting on a claimed high degree of fit between scientific socialism's values and traditional Chinese culture. He holds that the Two Integrations are specific to China yet also universal, offering a basic guide for working-class parties elsewhere. For the new journey, He lists six principles: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, staying true to fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global vision. These rest on dialectical and historical materialism. He concludes that theoretical innovation has no end and that the Party must keep adapting Marxism through the Two Integrations and these principles. He claims that the Two Integrations will also open broad prospects for Marxism's localisation in other countries. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the Two Integrations and the guidelines for adapting Marxism after the 20th Party Congress.

Three "coats" of historical nihilism 历史虚无主义的三件“外套” Zhao Guanghui Zhao Guanghui, in a short commentary, asks how historical nihilism has changed form now that it is under pressure.
