The author argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), its spread has been checked, so it has become more concealed and has put on new "coats". These are "secret history", "art" and "scholarship". Each coat makes its claims more persuasive. The piece takes the three coats in turn. It opens with Xi Jinping's call, at the Party history study and education mobilisation meeting, to oppose historical nihilism openly and to clarify vague understandings of major issues in Party history. It then gives a short section to each coat and closes with a general assessment of the shift in method. Zhao argues that "secret history" exploits the public appetite for hidden political and personal details. In the author's account, it turns policy disputes among Party leaders into power struggles and invites readers to take fiction as reliable history. Under the "art" coat, the author says, artistic form is used to carry ideological content, through "playful retellings", the mocking of the sublime and a calligraphy example that builds a "upright" image of Chiang Kai-shek. The "scholarship" coat, Zhao claims, uses academic reflection and selective sources to dismantle historical materialism, the theory of five social formations and class analysis, and to undermine the historical basis of Party leadership. Zhao concludes that historical nihilism has moved from crude defamation of heroes to forging history by treating a detail as the whole, detached from its context. The author calls on readers to use their judgement so as to see the mainstream, the essence and the general trend. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese official scholarship classifies and rebuts the forms of historical nihilism.

The purpose and significance of Marx's "commentary on Greek art" 马克思“希腊艺术评论”的目的和意义 Zhou Zimao Zhou Shixing Marx's well-known remarks on Greek art in the Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy have usually been read within aesthetics and art studies. Zhou and Zhou argue that their purpose and significance go well beyond this. In the authors' view, the commentary is a large-scale social theory about the future direction of human society and the ideal mode of human existence and development. The short piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2023, reads the commentary through its textual structure and logic of argument. It takes up the several "difficult problems" Marx names and draws out their methodological meaning. It treats Greek art, Greek myth, the critique of capitalist production and Marx's late turn to anthropology and history in turn. The authors make three moves. First, Marx insists on rising "from the abstract to the concrete": the general principle that material production determines spiritual production is not enough, and Greek art must be tied to Greek myth and to the conditions of low productive forces. Once nature is actually mastered, myth disappears, so Greek art's decline in modern society is unavoidable and imitation of it is bound to fail. Second, the commentary is part of Marx's critique of capitalism. The authors say it refutes the bourgeois belief that material and artistic production advance in balance, and shows that capitalist production, which seeks exchange value, is hostile to art as free spiritual production. Third, studying ancient society offers a "prototype" for predicting modern trends. The authors conclude that Marx answers the puzzle of Greek art's "eternal charm" by turning an artistic question into one of social development. For them, Greek society, as humanity's childhood, serves as a "norm" and "model". Its simple original relation between humans, nature and society, its "natural individuality" and its imaginative power still instruct modern people. Read the original if you want a concise argument for treating Marx's remarks on Greek art as social theory and not only as aesthetics.

Whole-process people's democracy: the unity of discursive construction and practical path 全过程人民民主：话语建构与实践路径的统一 Chen Chengxin Chen Chengxin asks what distinguishes whole-process people's democracy from other democratic forms and answers that its main comparative advantage is the unity of democratic discourse and democratic practice. In Chen's account it is a democracy in which words and deeds agree. The piece first appeared in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in February 2023, and the author attributes this unity to three constants: a people-centred logical starting point, the running of people's democracy through every stage of political life, and Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee. The commentary has three parts. The first treats the people-centred starting point, the second the comparative advantages of whole-process people's democracy, and the third the Party leadership that Chen presents as its basic guarantee. Chen draws on the Constitution, the revised Organic Law of the National People's Congress, the basic political institutions, and examples of recent democratic innovation such as NPC oversight and the People's Daily Online "message board for leaders". Chen argues that "the people" in this democracy is a systemic "all-subject" concept that includes respect for individual rights but unifies them within the whole people. The author also stresses coverage of "all domains", from the struggle for independence to poverty alleviation and Chinese modernization. Compared with electoral democracy, which Chen portrays as a formal system of "one election decides all", the author presents whole-process people's democracy as resting on two kinds of completeness: complete institutional procedures and complete participatory practice, the latter described as covering the whole chain, all fields and the whole process. It is oriented towards whether problems are effectively solved rather than towards votes alone, and Chen says it applies consultation, supervision and public input throughout decision-making and an official's whole term. Chen concludes that Party leadership secures the direction, order and efficiency of this democracy, through institutional mechanisms, the mass line, rule of law and consultative governance. In this reading, the Party both constructs the democratic discourse and leads its practice, and people's evaluation is the standard by which discourse is tested against practice. Chen adds a caution that "whole process" applies within a given context and scope, so the discourse has boundaries and operating limits. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars present the comparative case for whole-process people's democracy against electoral democracy.

The civilisational implications of the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》的文明意蕴 Wang Jing Wang Jing reads the Communist Manifesto, the programmatic document marking the public emergence of Marxism, through the lens of civilisation. The short piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, argues that the Manifesto applies historical materialism to reveal both the historical significance and the inherent defects of modern capitalist civilisation, and to explain why humanity must move on to a new communist civilisation. In Wang's formulation, the text is at once a critique of modern capitalist civilisation and a manifesto for a new communist one. The article has two main sections. The first, on the Manifesto as a critique of capitalist civilisation, sets out what Marx and Engels credit to the bourgeoisie and then the contradictions they trace to capital. The second, on the Manifesto as a declaration of a new civilisation, draws chiefly on the third part of the Manifesto, on socialist and communist literature, and on its account of the communist future. Wang argues that Marx and Engels recognised the bourgeoisie's revolutionary role: the expansion of productive forces, the replacement of feudal and patriarchal ties by wage-labour relations, and the creation of a world market and world history. The defects, Wang says, stem from the logic of capital's self-valorisation, which produces three imbalances: unequal social standing between bourgeoisie and proletariat, uneven development between nations, and strained relations between humans and nature. Wang then explains that the Manifesto rejects reactionary, conservative and critical-utopian socialisms as not genuinely communist, because they leave the relation of capital and wage labour intact or refuse revolutionary action. Wang concludes that, for Marx and Engels, communist civilisation is a sublation of capitalist civilisation: it must absorb capitalism's positive achievements while overcoming its defects. It abolishes bourgeois property rather than property in general, reverses the rule of the past over the present, and ends the subordination of living labour to accumulated labour. Wang adds that, in the Manifesto's account, this requires a communist revolution that breaks radically with traditional property relations and leads to an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese statement of how the Manifesto can be read as a theory of civilisation, in the context of official discussion of civilisation.

The problem consciousness and theoretical tensions of classical Western Marxism 经典西方马克思主义的问题意识与理论张力 Gao Xiaoxi Gao Xiaoxi, in a short piece first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2023, asks what questions drove classical Western Marxism, the current running from Lukács to Althusser between the 1920s and 1960s, and what tensions it left behind. Gao argues that its problem consciousness grew out of the dispute over how to make socialist revolution in advanced capitalist countries, and that this dispute took the form of a rethinking of the nature of Marx's philosophy. The piece first sets out the conditions of twentieth-century capitalism: oligopoly, a divided working class including a "labour aristocracy", and a shift from direct repression to ideological control through consumerism and mass culture. It then contrasts classical Western Marxism with the Second International, divides the tradition into humanist and scientistic camps, and traces its afterlife in later foreign Marxism. Gao contends that the Second International read Marxism as determinism, treating historical laws like statistical natural laws and falling into dogmatism. Classical Western Marxists, in Gao's account, instead took Marx's philosophy as a subject-centred theory of practice and urged a revolution grounded in cultural and psychological change and class consciousness. The tension lay in uniting ideological critique with revolutionary practice, which Gao says exposed subjectivist and romantic tendencies. Humanists such as Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci and the Frankfurt School followed Hegelian elements in Marx; Althusser's structuralism, with its "theoretical anti-humanism", is judged to have lapsed into theoretical monologue. Gao concludes that ecological Marxism, post-Marxism and later Marxist themes such as space and the body descend from this problem consciousness, and that foreign Marxism can be read through paired tensions such as history–structure and time–space. Without grasping this, Gao warns, one may misjudge the history of Western Marxism and weaken the contemporary and global outlook of sinicized Marxism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese overview of how classical Western Marxism is positioned within the wider field of foreign Marxism.

The relationship between government and market in high-quality development 高质量发展中的政府与市场关系 Fang Fuqian Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2023, Fang Fuqian asks how the relationship between government and market bears on high-quality development, which the author defines at base as stable, sustained and harmonious growth. Fang's thesis is that high-quality development requires raising the "fit" (shipeixing) between government and market, so that the two combine better. The short piece has two parts. The first sets out how to understand the government–market relationship, contrasting Western economics with the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second discusses how to advance market-oriented reform and government reform together, drawing on the 19th Party Congress (2017) and 20th Party Congress (2022) reports. Fang argues that neoliberal schools oppose government intervention and hold that markets stabilise themselves, whereas in Chinese political economy the two are complementary, not opposed. The author cites Xi Jinping's call to use both the "invisible hand" and the "visible hand", and treats the formula of the market playing the decisive role and the government playing its role better as a breakthrough beyond Western economics. Fang grounds the fit in China's basic economic system, with public ownership as the mainstay and distribution according to work as the main form. Markets allocate resources most efficiently, but monopoly, incomplete information, externalities and unfair income distribution cause market failure, while government can also fail through poor decisions and policy lags. Fang concludes that China faces a double task because of its transition from a highly centralised planned economy. It must deepen market reform, including property rights, factor markets and a unified national market, and it must reform government by reducing direct intervention, placing government conduct under the rule of law and building a service-oriented government. The author stresses that government should act in a moderate, effective and scientific way, not simply more actively. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese line on government and market in the language of high-quality development.

Continuously advancing and expanding Chinese modernization 不断推进和拓展中国式现代化 Chen Jin Writing in the People's Daily in February 2023, Chen Jin takes up Xi Jinping's description of the theory of Chinese modernization, set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022), as a major theoretical innovation and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. The commentary asks how Party members should understand this path in order to keep advancing and expanding it. Chen's answer is that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, and that it is inseparable from socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece is organised under six headings: the historical logic of Chinese modernization, its link with building a moderately prosperous society, the innovations achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012), its Chinese characteristics, its essential requirements, and its far-reaching influence on world modernization. It traces the idea from Mao Zedong's calls for industrialisation and the 'four modernizations' to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remarks on 'Chinese-style modernization'. It then follows the stages from the 16th to the 19th Party Congress. Chen argues that Deng used the 'xiaokang' (moderately prosperous) idea to give Chinese modernization its meaning. In Chen's reading, this idea rejects rashness and copying of the West, treats modernization as staged, and aims at social progress and all-round human development, not only economic growth. For Chen, the distinctive features are an enormous population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical advance, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Its essential requirements are Party leadership and socialism, together with the five-sphere overall plan and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Chen also contends that capital-driven Western modernization carries built-in limits such as wealth gaps, polarisation and spiritual emptiness, and that Chinese modernization overcomes them and breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. Chen concludes that Chinese modernization and socialism with Chinese characteristics have advanced as one process, and that Party leadership is its most prominent advantage and a principle that must be upheld. The author presents the path as a new option for developing countries that want faster growth while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account, by a Party-history scholar, of how Chinese modernization is linked to earlier Party goals and to socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Gaining a deep understanding of the "six musts" 深刻领悟“六个必须坚持” Qiao Maolin Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, Qiao Maolin offers a study-guide commentary on the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). These are the requirements to adhere to the principle of putting the people first, to self-confidence and self-reliance, to being committed to the fundamentals while breaking new ground, to a problem-oriented approach, to a systems approach, and to thinking with the world in mind. Qiao argues that together they give a basic route to understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a basic guide for continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The commentary opens by presenting Marxism as an open system that develops with the times, and the Thought as the latest step in that development. It then takes each of the six musts in turn, using a similar pattern. Qiao first gives the theoretical basis, then shows how the principle runs through the Thought and the work of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally lists what it requires for the new journey ahead. Qiao's central claim is that each principle joins a Marxist premise to a feature of the Thought. The people-first principle rests on the materialist view that the people create history and on the idea that Marxism is by nature a theory of the people. Self-confidence and self-reliance is tied to Chinese modernization and the Four-sphere Confidence, since China's problems must be answered by Chinese people on the basis of national conditions. The "commitment to fundamentals" is defined as holding firm to Marxism's basic tenets, the Party's overall leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, while "breaking new ground" means saying and doing what predecessors have not. The problem-oriented approach reflects the universality of contradiction. The systems approach is linked to the coordinated overall plans Xi has put forward. Thinking with the world in mind is tied to the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind. Qiao concludes that the six musts form an organic whole that unites upholding Marxism with developing it. The commentary calls them a "golden key" to the essence of the Thought and a guide for theoretical innovation grounded in practice. It urges readers to understand their theoretical content, method and practical meaning so as to keep writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 20th Party Congress's methodological principles are being explained to Chinese readers.

The rich connotations and contemporary significance of the "Three Musts" “三个务必”的丰富内涵和时代意义 Shen Chuanliang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 3 March 2023, interprets the "Three Musts" set out in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): stay true to the founding mission, remain modest, prudent and hard-working, and dare and know how to fight. Shen argues that the formula is a major judgement grounded in historical regularities and the demands of the times. In Shen's account, it deepens understanding of how a communist party governs and how it builds itself, and it helps the whole Party unify its thinking and will on the new journey. The article has three parts. The first traces the "Three Musts" to the Party's experience over a century, starting with Mao Zedong's "Two Musts" of 1949 and moving to the Party's recent efforts to govern itself rigorously. The second takes each of the three requirements in turn, with historical examples and statements by Mao and Xi. The third sets out what the formula means for Party building and for the national goals ahead. Shen presents the "Three Musts" as both a whole and a set of distinct emphases. On the founding mission, Shen says the Party's understanding has widened: it now covers spiritual as well as material well-being, the influence of Chinese civilization, and contributions to human progress. On modesty and hard struggle, Shen sees continuity with the "Two Musts" and with a tradition the Party carried forward from revolution to the present. On struggle, the article holds that all of China's achievements came through struggle, and that the new journey requires "great struggle". Shen links this to the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decline, namely self-reform, and to the long-term persistence of the "four tests" and "four dangers". Shen concludes that the "Three Musts" deepen understanding of the laws of Communist Party governance. The article also calls them a firm grip for strengthening Party building across ideological and work-style fields, and a political guarantee for realising the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Shen proposes continued Party-wide education campaigns, a more complete body of Party regulations, and the promotion of the spirit of the Party's founding. Read the original if you want an authoritative-style account of how Party theorists connect the 20th Party Congress formula to Mao's 1949 "Two Musts" and to the self-reform agenda.

The socialism of humanist Marxism A review of Kevin B. Anderson's view of socialism 人本主义马克思主义的社会主义观 Guo Lishuang Liu Yang Guo Lishuang and Liu Yang present and assess the conception of socialism developed by the American Marxist scholar Kevin B. Anderson. The article reports that Anderson treats socialism as the thorough negation and transcendence of capitalism, and regards both Stalinism and democratic socialism as inadequate to present challenges. In its own assessment, the article finds Anderson's critique of capitalism comprehensive and his socialist vision insightful, but argues that his socialist vision is thin and that his reading of China under Mao Zedong is mistaken. After a short introduction to Anderson's career as a MEGA2 researcher and author, the article is built in three parts. The first sets out his analysis of capitalism through six core features. The second covers his account of Stalinism and democratic socialism, followed by a critical response. The third reconstructs his humanist Marxist socialism and offers an evaluation, closing with remarks on foreign Marxist scholars more generally. According to the authors, Anderson names exploitation, alienation, racism and imperialism, gender subordination, the strengthening and centralisation of the state, and environmental destruction as capitalism's defining traits. Socialism must therefore overcome alienated labour, end capital accumulation and the critique-free embrace of technology, address hierarchies of race, gender and sexuality, and tackle ecological damage. Anderson draws on Marx's three stages of communism, with the Paris Commune as a transitional form. The authors then dispute his claim that Mao-era China was wholly Stalinist: they cite decentralisation in the Ten Great Relationships and the 1957 reforms, the role of markets, and intra-Party and multi-party democracy. They also reject his claim that workers and peasants were ruthlessly exploited, arguing that workers laboured voluntarily, as in the Daqing oilfield. The authors conclude that Anderson's negation-based method deepens understanding of capitalism, but that his socialism mainly targets capitalism's ills. They also say he does not clarify how humanist socialism differs from communism, and that his view of China rests on Western yardsticks and scarce primary sources. They see him as typical of foreign Marxist scholars whose systems are theoretically complete but weak in practical strategy, and they call for more dialogue and tolerance of socialist models that arise from different national conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's critical account of a Western humanist Marxist's theory of socialism and of his view of Mao-era China.

From digital inequality back to Marx Contemporary foreign Marxist scholars' critique of digital capitalism 从数字不平等到重新回到马克思 Lan Jiang Lan Jiang's short commentary asks how Marxist thinkers outside China read digital capitalism, a new type of capitalism that has emerged as digital technology, communications and algorithms spread through industry, consumption and logistics. The author argues that these scholars find in digital capitalism widening inequality and a destruction of the conditions of life. Lan reports that they therefore turn back to Marx as the only resource able to address the abuse and plunder of technology by capital. The article is organised in three parts. It first treats digital capitalism and expanded inequality, then what it calls the scorched earth of life under digital capitalism, and finally the call to return to Marx in the digital age. Its main interlocutors are Étienne Balibar, Nancy Fraser (Cannibal Capitalism, 2022), Jonathan Crary (Scorched Earth, 2022, and 24/7), Alain Badiou, Christian Fuchs, Guy Standing and Yuval Noah Harari. Habermas and Giddens appear as foils from the neoliberal era. Lan's first move is that the dialogue ethics and deliberative democracy of the neoliberal period promised greater equality, whereas digital platforms, the digital divide and the commercialisation of biological and medical data are widening the gap. In this account inequality shifts from spatial to biological, producing a precariat that Lan describes with Standing's term. The second move follows Crary: 24/7 biopolitical control, drugs and the Chinese '996' work schedule make bodies more productive. Life is abstracted into screens and data and cut off from the earth. The third move follows Badiou, who holds that the problem is not the technology but capital, especially finance capital, monopolising data and algorithms, so that the struggle must target ownership. Fraser, in Lan's reading, abandons a purely identity-based feminism for Marx's critique of political economy. Lan concludes that the way out of inequality and 'scorched earth' lies in returning to the Communist Manifesto and to the critique of political economy in Capital and its manuscripts. Citing Fuchs's Rereading Marx in the Age of Digital Capitalism, the article endorses breaking private ownership so that everyone can share equally in the benefits of digital and AI technology. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how Balibar, Fraser, Crary, Badiou and Fuchs are being presented to Chinese readers as critics of digital capitalism.

Institutional predicaments and new changes in contemporary Western capitalism 当今西方资本主义制度困境与新变化 Zhao Junjie Writing against the backdrop of Xi Jinping's thesis of "great changes unseen in a century", Zhao asks what new changes Western capitalism is undergoing, what institutional predicaments it faces, and where capitalism is heading in the twenty-first century. The article's answer is that the West faces overlapping political and economic crises that reflect a systemic crisis of the capitalist system itself, not merely a cyclical downturn. Zhao concludes that the contest between the two systems has shifted in socialism's favour. The article has three parts. The first describes four institutional predicaments: the economy (deindustrialisation and failed state intervention), politics (decline of establishment parties and malfunctioning democracy), society (the welfare state and inequality), and theory (the fading of Western values and the failure of neoliberalism). The second part traces the causes of the "systemic crisis" in economic, political and social-ecological terms, including the effects of the Ukraine crisis. The third part assesses what these changes mean. Evidence comes largely from statistics on manufacturing shares, voting results, deficits and debt, and from remarks by Western figures. Zhao attributes the crisis chiefly to the "disorderly expansion of capital" and financial liberalisation, which hollowed out manufacturing and produced the 2008 financial crisis and the European sovereign debt crisis. In the author's account, Western democracy has degraded: leaders are short-sighted, elections are captured by interest groups, and populism and polarisation are rising. Zhao also argues that the generous European welfare system, the Green parties' policies and the West's handling of the Ukraine crisis have worsened deficits, energy shortages and inflation. Zhao presents the Ukraine crisis as a product of capitalist expansion, which the US uses to deflect domestic contradictions and to bind Europe to its interests. Zhao expects capitalism to undergo major restructuring and prolonged "pangs" over the next two or three decades, possibly under labels such as green, ecological, national-debt or populist capitalism. The author holds that state intervention under state monopoly capitalism cannot cure the system's inherent defects, and that the Western hegemonic order centred on the US dollar is declining. Meanwhile, socialism with Chinese characteristics has, in Zhao's view, shown vitality, so the historical contest between the two systems has turned in Marxism's favour. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar in 2022 framed Western crises, populism and the Ukraine war as evidence of capitalism's systemic decline.

Theoretical and practical explorations of Party discipline building in the New Democratic Revolution period 新民主主义革命时期党的纪律建设的理论与实践探索 Huang Bingqiong Huang asks how the Communist Party of China developed its discipline in theory and practice between its founding and 1949, and what that record offers today. The article argues that the Party kept adjusting its disciplinary rules to the revolutionary situation, its organisational growth and its internal needs. In Huang's account, this adjustment gave the Party the cohesion and fighting capacity to win the New Democratic Revolution. The article follows five stages in chronological order. It begins with the founding period, covering early Marxists' debate on "iron discipline" and the programme and constitution of the First and Second Congresses. It then treats the Great Revolution (1923–27), the Agrarian Revolutionary War, the full-scale War of Resistance against Japan, and the War of Liberation. A short conclusion draws lessons for the present. Huang's central claim is that discipline expanded in content and became more specific at each stage. The Second Congress constitution (1922) set out democratic centralism and expulsion as a penalty. The Fifth Congress (1927) first named "political discipline", issued the first anti-corruption notice (1926) and created a Central Supervisory Commission. After 1927 the Party refined rules on secrecy, organisation and relations with the masses, and rebuilt inspection bodies. Mao Zedong's wartime formulations are central: discipline is compulsory but must rest on members' consciousness, and the "four subordinations" were set out in 1938. In the late 1940s, Huang says, the Party used request-and-report systems, discipline education and strict enforcement to end indiscipline and "anarchism" and prepare to govern nationally. The article also notes that mechanical or excessively harsh enforcement under mistaken lines in the 1930s drew correction, which it describes as a combination of persuasion and strict enforcement. Huang concludes that the Party always treated iron discipline as a basis of survival and adapted it to changing conditions. The author attributes this to the Party's willingness to face problems and to turn the blade inward. For the "new era", Huang calls for drawing on this history to perfect full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, strengthen conduct and discipline, and advance the Party's self-reform. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based chronology of how Party discipline rules, bodies and enforcement practices developed from 1920 to 1949, as Party historiography presents it.

"Cosmopolitanism" in Marx's perspective 马克思视野中的“世界主义” Feng Ziyi Feng Ziyi takes up a gap in scholarship on Marx. Researchers have studied his theory of world history extensively but paid little attention to his views on cosmopolitanism. Feng argues that these views cannot be reduced to the world-history theory and have a distinct value. Marx opposed false cosmopolitanism, which in Feng's reading serves narrow nationalism or capital, and upheld a true cosmopolitanism grounded in the people and in human emancipation. The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of Marx's engagement, from Stoic and Christian universalism through Kant and Hegel to the German 'ideological fervour' of the 1840s. It then distinguishes four aspects of the concept in Marx's writings: critique of political economy, value critique, description of modern society, and the theory of the international workers' movement and human liberation. A third part sets out his method, and a fourth draws implications for today. Feng's central claim is that Marx's cosmopolitanism differs from earlier versions in four methodological respects. It rests on historical materialism rather than reason, human nature or absolute spirit, deriving world history from productive forces and from capital's expansion. It holds a people-centred standpoint, in contrast to the Young Hegelians, 'true socialism' and bourgeois economics. It treats the universal as 'concrete' and historical, so that world culture presupposes national cultures. And it uses contradiction analysis, exposing colonial plunder and hypocritical appeals to a world-historical view, as in Engels on Poznań and Marx's writing on China. Writing in 2023, Feng draws three lessons. The civilizational value of cosmopolitanism should be upheld against what the author describes as the false and opportunistic cosmopolitanism of some Western states, especially the United States, and against 'reverse globalization'. A new cosmopolitanism should be built on a community with a shared future for mankind, which Feng distinguishes from earlier versions by its subject (humanity, not the individual), its horizon and its goal of cooperation. The international economic and political order should also be rebuilt on mutual respect and shared global governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of Marx's scattered remarks on cosmopolitanism and of how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher links them to current foreign-policy concepts.

Marx's theoretical reflections on the modernization of Eastern countries and their implications 马克思关于东方国家现代化进程的理论思考及启示 Ma Jun Ma Jun asks how Marx explained the late and stalled modernization of Eastern countries, and what that analysis offers for Chinese modernization today. The article argues that, from the 1850s, Marx's scattered writings on China, India and Russia form a second side of his theory of modernity, alongside his analysis of Western industrial capitalism. In Ma's reading, Marx located the causes of Eastern lag in internal structures, saw modernization there as started by Western pressure, and did not fall into Eurocentrism. The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical background: the Crimean War, the Opium Wars and British rule in India as the mid-nineteenth-century divide between East and West. The second examines how modernization was set in motion in the East and how East and West interacted. The third draws three lessons for Chinese modernization. Ma draws on Marx's articles on China and India, Capital, The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte and the letter on Russia, and also cites scholars such as Luo Rongqu, Edward Said and Hannah Arendt. On causes, Ma identifies three. One is the durability of a self-sufficient natural economy built on small peasant farming joined to household handicrafts. Another is the fusion of the feudal state and society, with no separation between political state and civil society. The third is a feudal and small-peasant mentality that favoured submission and conservatism. On interaction, Ma uses Luo Rongqu's term "transmitted great change" for modernization imposed from outside, and cites Marx's image of the mummy exposed to fresh air. Against charges of Eurocentrism, including from Said and postcolonial critics, Ma argues four points. Marx used Western Europe as a reference point on the basis of productive forces. He rejected treating the Western path as a universal model. He saw Eastern events, such as the Taiping Rebellion, as acting back on Europe. He also condemned colonial aggression morally. Ma draws three implications. Modernization requires comprehensive reform of economy, politics, culture and society, and the remnants of peasant consciousness, official-centred culture and weak rule of law still hinder it. Marx's idea of "social revolution" as a total transformation should be kept, joining personal, national and world emancipation. China should also raise its level of opening up, while aiming to break the capitalist "centre–periphery" pattern and promote common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of how Marx's Eastern writings are used to defend him against Eurocentrism charges and to ground Chinese modernization.

Clarifying the concept of the "class for itself" “自为阶级”概念辨析 Jia Tianyu Zhang Youkui Jia Tianyu and Zhang Youkui take up the concept of the "class for itself" (自为阶级), which Marxism uses to state the proletariat's historical mission and its relation to the Communist Party. They argue that earlier studies have identified what the concept points to (historical mission, class consciousness, Party leadership) but have not explained the dialectical logic of the concept itself. Without that, the authors say, the internal links among these three elements remain unclear. Their thesis is that these three elements together make up the concept's content. The article first traces the concept's formation. It starts from Hegel's category of "being-for-itself" in the Logic and Marx's use of it to separate a stage of wage struggle from a stage of political class-against-class struggle. It then follows Lenin's account of spontaneity and consciousness, including his theory of "inculcation", and Mao Zedong's definition of the class for itself through the "three understandings". The three main sections then take the three elements in turn: human emancipation as the historical task, correct knowledge of class relations, and leadership by the Communist Party. The authors argue that the class for itself is the proletariat whose class interest is universal, namely the abolition of classes and human emancipation, and that this follows from the full development of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Class consciousness, they say, is not a subjective awakening but a correct, reflective grasp of the essence of class relations, which is both scientific and revolutionary. It can arise only from the proletarian position under developed capitalism. The Party is presented as an internal component of the class for itself rather than an external instrument: communists may differ from workers in class origin, but not in class standpoint or relation to the movement. The authors conclude that inculcation is not the transfer of knowledge from outside. In their account, the proletariat becomes a class for itself through the practice of class struggle, and the process also reshapes the educators into Communist Party members. They criticise readings that treat the Party as external to the class, or that explain its vanguard role by members' qualities or workers' wage interests. Read the original if you want a close, Hegel-informed reading of how Marxist-Leninist-Maoist theory ties class consciousness to Party leadership.

On the methodological innovation of the Two Integrations in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 论“两个结合”对推动马克思主义中国化时代化的方法论创新 Li Hongwei Li Hongwei takes up the Two Integrations, first announced by Xi Jinping at the Party's centenary in 2021 and set out systematically in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article argues that existing scholarship has mostly traced their history, content, results and experience, and that their epistemological and methodological contribution has been little examined. Li's thesis is that the Two Integrations are both a worldview and a methodology, and that they carry out methodological innovation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is organised around four classic disputes that the Two Integrations are said to resolve: space and time (differences between cultures), substance and function (ti and yong), knowing and doing, and things and people. Each section pairs a conceptual problem with a method. Li draws on Chinese philosophical categories, Mao Zedong's, Deng Xiaoping's and Xi Jinping's statements, and passages from Marx, and traces the move from the earlier single "integration" with Chinese reality to the present two-part formula. First, Li holds that integration works by seeking common ground while preserving differences. Marxism and fine traditional Chinese culture, though of different origin, are said to share features such as an orientation to practice, an ideal of great harmony, and a belief that the people make history. Integration is described as a chemical-like reaction, not simple addition, and as guarded against both dogmatism and cultural nihilism. Second, on substance and function, Li reads the Two Integrations as giving Marxism's basic principles the leading role, with Chinese reality as the site of theoretical and practical innovation and fine traditional culture as a source of spirit and wisdom. This is presented as an answer to the late-Qing formula "Chinese learning for substance, Western learning for application" and as an expression of cultural confidence. Third, Li argues that integration must be carried out in practice. Theorists and Party cadres are named as its key agents, and formalism and detached theorising are criticised. Li adds that the Two Integrations must serve the people. In content they should be close to the people, and in form they should be welcome to them, meaning plain language and a Chinese style. Li links this to Chinese modernization, to a community with a shared future for mankind, and to a "new form of human civilization". The article concludes that the Two Integrations have underpinned the Party's achievements over a century and remain necessary for high-quality development, common prosperity and building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese theorists frame the Two Integrations as a methodology, with its sources in Chinese philosophy and Party texts.

Innovations in major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era, seen from a historical perspective 从历史发展的视角看新时代中国特色大国外交的创新 Zuo Fengrong Zuo Fengrong asks what is new about the major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and answers by placing it against four histories: Marxism, international relations, world socialism and the diplomacy of the People's Republic. The article argues that this diplomacy, which serves the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind, both inherits and innovates on each of them. In theory, Zuo says, it develops Marxist international relations theory and rejects the traditional view that defines a state's standing by its power. The article has four main sections. The first compares the new-era diplomacy with Marx, Engels and Lenin on international relations. The second takes up the traditional 'strong states inevitably seek hegemony' logic and China's path of peaceful development. The third draws lessons from Soviet-model diplomacy, and the fourth turns to practice: China's role as a responsible major country, the coordination of the 'two overall situations', and a global network of partnerships. Zuo's core argument is that the new diplomacy inherits Marxism's concern for humanity, its holistic view of the world and its opposition to hegemony. It departs from Marx's emphasis on class struggle by building on the coexistence of different social systems and on common values. Against realist theory, which the article presents as locked in power competition, Zuo contends that China offers new-type international relations and new-type major-country relations, built on partnership rather than alliance. Zuo reads Soviet diplomacy as a negative lesson: a dogmatic belief in war and revolution, exporting its model, standing outside the world economic system, and bloc hegemonism. In the author's account, China by contrast integrates into the existing international order, does not export its model, and conducts inter-party exchanges on the basis of equality. Zuo concludes that this diplomacy goes beyond the traditional diplomacy of struggle for hegemony and interests, enriches socialist foreign policy and gives China a favourable external environment for national rejuvenation. The article credits China with promoting globalization, taking part in global governance, advancing the Belt and Road Initiative and widening its partnerships, and argues that this also makes the changing world more predictable. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars place current diplomacy within Marxist theory and the history of Soviet and Chinese foreign policy.

Marx's thought on the subject of state governance and its practice in contemporary China 马克思国家治理主体思想及其在当代中国的实践 Wang Daiyue Wang Daiyue asks how China's drive to modernize state governance relates to Marx's theory of the state, which stresses the state's dependence on society and its eventual withering away. The article argues that Marx's view of who governs the state, namely the people, gives theoretical grounding to this project. It holds that the project is guided by Marxism rather than Western liberal theory, citing Xi Jinping's statement that modernizing governance is not Westernization or capitalization. The article is organised in five parts. It begins with the people as the governing subject, drawing on Marx's critique of Hegel's monarchical sovereignty, The German Ideology and later political economy, and on Claus Offe and James O'Connor. It then turns to the role of a Marxist party, the material foundation in ownership, and Marx's 'true democracy'. Each section pairs Marx's texts with present-day Chinese institutions and Xi Jinping's statements. Wang's core argument has three strands. First, the people cannot govern in a society where capital is the real subject, so only socialism can make them governors. Second, the people are not a homogeneous entity and need a Marxist party to organise, educate and ally them with peasants and the urban poor; the Communist Party of China, in Wang's account, has no interests of its own and works through the mass line. Third, Marx's idea of rebuilding individual ownership through common possession of socialised means of production is read as the material basis of popular governance. Wang says this is secured today by the dominant place of public ownership, with state-owned enterprises addressing regional imbalance and welfare, while non-public sectors are steered by the socialist relations of production. Wang presents Marx's 'true democracy' as an ethical ideal that Marx later tied to the dictatorship of the proletariat and the Paris Commune. It was left unresolved as to how the people could govern in a socialist state. The article claims that whole-process people's democracy answers this question by covering election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and by extending democracy to the economy and culture. Wang concludes that the Marxist party and public ownership make the Marxist view of the people distinct from populism. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical justification of Chinese state governance, grounded in Marx's early critique of Hegel and in the Paris Commune.

Capital accumulation and the inner logic of capitalist ownership A theoretical examination based on Capital 资本积累与资本主义所有制的内在逻辑 Cai Ling Cai Ling argues that the theory of surplus value has become a shorthand for Marx's critique of capitalism, and that this hides how Marx reached the system's deepest structure. In Cai's reading, Marx got there by tracing the recapitalisation of surplus value, that is, capital accumulation, and this leads to the inner logic of capitalist ownership. Earlier research, the article says, has stayed with the basic nature of accumulation or its technical analysis and has not reached the question of ownership. The article has three sections, all drawn from the three volumes of Capital. The first covers the realisation and limits of accumulation: its general law in Volume 1, the conditions of realisation in Volume 2 (circuits of capital and the two departments of reproduction), and its tendencies towards crisis in Volume 3. The second sets Marx's account of how the law of capitalist appropriation forms and consolidates against classical economics and modern political philosophy. The third examines how accumulation sustains and expands capitalist ownership. Cai also rejects David Harvey's view that the three volumes' theories of accumulation are fractured and contradictory. Cai's central claim is that capitalist ownership is not a legal relation of persons to things, as classical economics assumes. It is an appropriation relation, reproduced through accumulation, in which capital takes the labour activity of wage workers and its value. Cai gives three steps: the conversion of the commodity-production law of ownership into the law of capitalist appropriation, through the social character of labour and labour-power becoming a commodity; primitive accumulation, with its expropriation and colonial violence, as the historical origin of appropriation; and the continuous reproduction of the capital relation itself, capitalists on one side and wage workers on the other. On this basis Cai argues that Marx's model of simple reproduction is essential, because it shows how labour-power is appropriated and the class relation reproduced. Cai concludes that capitalist ownership is sustained mainly by expanding the scale of accumulation, which pushes capital to compete, concentrate and seek new markets. Capitalists are described as puppets of accumulation's own logic. Accumulation is limited by the opposition between capital and wage labour and by consumption, and these limits appear as crises of relative overproduction. Read the original if you want a close reading of Capital that links accumulation, appropriation and ownership, and that contests classical economics and Harvey on these points.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground: a defining trait of contemporary Chinese Communists' attitude to Marxism 守正创新：当代中国共产党人对待马克思主义的鲜明品格 Yang Zengdong Dang Jiamei Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which lists "upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground" among the "six musts", this article asks what the formula says about how Chinese Communists treat Marxism. Yang and Dang argue that it expresses a scientific attitude towards theoretical innovation. In their account, "upholding fundamental principles" is the precondition and "breaking new ground" the source of vitality, and the two are dialectically unified. The article has three parts. The first shows how the Party has upheld Marxism's basic principles in four respects: historical materialism, materialist dialectics, the people-centred character of Marxism, and the unity of knowing and doing. The second explains how this foundation supports the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context through the Two Integrations. The third presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the latest result of the approach. Yang and Dang read the Party's "big history" outlook as a Chinese form of historical materialism, and problem orientation as an application of dialectics. They treat "putting the people first" as the practical expression of Marxism's people-centred stance. They argue that the Two Integrations, combining Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional culture, are not a simple extension of the earlier single integration. They describe a reciprocal relationship: the first integration supplies the practical basis for the second, and the second widens the theoretical space for the first. The authors claim that the Marxist-compatible ideas in traditional culture include people-as-root thinking, dialectical thought and the ideal of "all under heaven for the common good". They also contend that this combination is a historical necessity rather than Max Weber's "elective affinity". The authors conclude that the "six musts" condense the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought and carry forward the nineteenth-century Marxist worldview. They hold that Xi Jinping Thought both defends the truth of Marxism and develops it in political economy, scientific socialism and philosophy. Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground today means adhering firmly to this body of thought, applying its stance, viewpoint and method, and maintaining the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party-affiliated theorists link the Two Integrations, the "six musts" and the idea of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context.

Understanding and interpretation: a study of Marx's thought on the ideological stratum 理解与阐释：马克思意识形态阶层思想研究 Zhang Zhidan Research on Marx's theory of ideology has concentrated on its essence and functions, on ideological critique and on proletarian ideological construction, and Zhang Zhidan argues that it has neglected the subject dimension. The article takes up Marx's scattered remarks on the "ideological stratum" (yishi xingtai jieceng). It reads them as a historical-materialist account of who produces, spreads and practises ideology. Zhang's thesis is that Marx treated this stratum as professional thought-rulers who are historically specific, dependent on the ruling class and internally complex. The article has three parts. The first defines the stratum and sets out its material basis. The second examines its functions. The third rebuts four misconceptions: the "end" thesis, the "non-dependence" thesis, the "ossification" thesis and the "mechanistic" thesis. Zhang draws on Capital, Theories of Surplus-Value, The German Ideology and The Eighteenth Brumaire. They also bring in Gramsci, Althusser, Mannheim, Lukács and Daniel Bell. Zhang treats "class" and "stratum" as interchangeable here, as Marx and Engels sometimes did. Zhang reconciles the "false consciousness", "ruling ideas" and "revolutionary consciousness" readings of ideology by treating ruling ideas, in the end a systematised class consciousness, as the common thread. The stratum is grounded in two structures. In the production structure, material production determines mental production, and the stratum's non-productive labour serves surplus-value production. In the class structure, the class that controls material production also controls mental production, and keeps its thinkers on a salary. Its functions are ideological production in a broad and a narrow sense, and legitimation of rule through deconstruction of rival ideas and construction of justifications. This legitimation can be deliberate deception or an unwitting reflection of real relations. Zhang adds that revolutionary classes have their own ideological thinkers. Against the four misconceptions, Zhang holds that the stratum is historical and will vanish with class society. It cannot float free of class, so the "public intellectuals" trend is described as an echo of Mannheim. It is not monolithic, and Zhang calls for case studies of influential Western thinkers such as Fukuyama and Hayek. It is not merely passive, since a proletarian stratum exists to serve the working class, socialist construction and human emancipation. Zhang concludes that Party ideological ranks, leadership over ideas and ideological security need strengthening. Read the original if you want a close textual reconstruction of Marx's ideological stratum, together with a Chinese academic argument about its bearing on contemporary ideological work.

Whole-process people's democracy: an essential requirement of Chinese modernization 全过程人民民主：中国式现代化的本质要求 Liu Xiuhua Gu Zhaoming Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Xiuhua and Gu Zhaoming ask how whole-process people's democracy relates to Chinese modernization. Their thesis is that developing it is an essential requirement of Chinese modernization. In the authors' words, without democracy there is no socialism, no socialist modernization and no rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The short commentary is organised in three parts. The first presents the development of whole-process people's democracy as a consequence of the Party's people-centred stance and its reading of the historical trend towards national rejuvenation. The second treats it as an institutional guarantee of modernization, tracing the people's congress system and the basic economic system from the founding of the People's Republic through reform and opening up. The third describes how it renews the value concepts of socialist democracy across the economic, political, cultural, social and ecological spheres. In the first part the authors argue that Chinese modernization aims at common prosperity and at meeting the people's growing needs. They hold that this requires relying on the people and drawing on their creativity, for which whole-process people's democracy is the means. Drawing on historical materialism, the second part holds that a public-ownership economic base requires a superstructure of democratic politics, institutionalised and placed under the rule of law. The authors present the unity of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance as the core of that system. In the third part they claim that this democracy joins elections, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight, and is therefore the 'most extensive, most genuine and most effective' democracy. They contrast it with what they call capitalist party-competition democracy, Western capital-centred modernization, one-dimensional materialist capitalist modernization and the polarisation of wealth and poverty. The authors conclude that whole-process people's democracy is a democracy of the whole chain, in all respects and with full coverage. They say that practising a broader, fuller and more sound form of it will unite hundreds of millions of people on the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Their account is a statement of official positions and does not engage in empirical comparison. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the concept was tied to Chinese modernization in the official press immediately after the 20th Party Congress.

Adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and Chinese modernization 马克思主义中国化时代化与中国式现代化 Zhang Shengen Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Shengen asks how the Communist Party's century-long theoretical exploration of modernization relates to the process of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article argues that Marxism "works" in China because the Party has combined its basic principles with China's concrete conditions and the features of the age. In Zhang's account, this process has guided Chinese modernization at every stage and has produced its latest result in the 20th Congress's account of Chinese modernization. The article is a chronological survey of Party documents and leaders' statements in four stages. It begins with national independence and liberation as the precondition for modernization, covering the failures of late-Qing and Republican-era efforts and Mao Zedong's 1945 remarks. It then treats the 1950s–1970s search for a Chinese industrialization path, from Soviet-style heavy industry to "On the Ten Major Relationships" and the Great Leap Forward. The last two stages cover Deng Xiaoping's formulation of a Chinese-style modernization in 1979 and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang's central move is to present each stage as a lesson in adaptation. Early dogmatic copying of Soviet experience brought setbacks in the revolution, and the later Soviet-style industrial model, though judged broadly successful in the First Five-Year Plan, was corrected by Mao's call to learn selectively and to "take the Soviet Union as a warning". The Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution are described as departures from seeking truth from facts, though the author says the exploration still laid foundations. After the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), the concept widened under Deng, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao. Zhang then sets out Xi Jinping's five features of Chinese modernization, the nine essential requirements and the five major principles of the 20th Congress, arguing that the first two requirements derive from Party history and the other seven from recent practice. Zhang concludes that the 20th Congress's treatment of Chinese modernization raised the Party's understanding of the laws of socialist modernization to a new level and answers the question of what kind of modernizing socialist power to build and how. The article acknowledges severe external pressures and internal contradictions, and calls for unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core in order to achieve the second centenary goal by the mid-21st century. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how Chinese modernization is placed within the narrative of adapting Marxism, with many quotations from Mao, Deng and Xi.

Using dialectical thinking to handle several major relationships in Chinese modernization 运用辩证思维处理好中国式现代化若干重大关系 Zhou Renjie Writing in March 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhou Renjie takes up Xi Jinping's statement that advancing Chinese modernization is a systematic project requiring overall planning and coordination. The commentary argues that this demands dialectical thinking: handling a set of major relationships correctly is, in Zhou's account, the way to meet risks and keep the project on course. Zhou presents the approach as an expression of Marxist materialist dialectics and a deepening of the Party's understanding. The piece has three parts. It first explains why dialectical thinking is needed for a pioneering undertaking that will meet foreseeable and unforeseeable challenges, and links the approach to Mao Zedong's 1956 speech On the Ten Major Relationships. It then discusses six pairs of relationships. The last part turns to practical work for 2023, the first year of the new journey, drawing on the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2022. In Zhou's account, each pair must be held in balance rather than treated as a choice. Top-level design must be combined with practical exploration, and strategy, which should be forward-looking and stable, with flexible tactics. Upholding fundamental principles (守正) must go together with innovation. Efficiency, which means growing the economy, must be paired with fairness, meaning sharing the results and pursuing common prosperity. Vitality, the movement of production factors, must go with order, meaning lawful regulation and governance. Self-reliance in science and technology must go with opening up. Zhou argues that fairness rests on efficiency and efficiency needs fairness to last, and that China can achieve a lively yet orderly balance. For 2023 Zhou proposes speeding up the new development pattern, with expanded domestic demand and a modern industrial system. Zhou also calls for better macroeconomic regulation that combines an efficient market with a capable government, and for deeper reform and opening up, including rule-of-law protection of property and wider institutional opening. Zhou concludes that mastering dialectics and applying the new development philosophy will bring high-quality development that is more efficient, fair, sustainable and secure. Read the original if you want an example of how official commentary frames Chinese modernization through Xi Jinping's six relationships and applies them to economic policy in 2023.

Overall strength rising, regional differences marked New developments in foreign left-wing movements in 2022 总体力量上升 区域差异显著 Zhou Miao Zhou Miao's survey asks how left-wing forces outside China fared in 2022, a year the author describes as shaped by recurring COVID-19 waves, the Ukraine crisis and growing global deficits in peace, development and governance. The thesis, given in the title, is that the left's overall strength rose, but with sharp regional differences. Zhou argues that left forces must exchange experience and build consensus in response. The article moves region by region. It covers North America and Europe, Asia, Oceania and the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa. Each section lists strikes, protests, membership figures and election results country by country. A short conclusion then assesses the opportunities and challenges facing the left. Zhou reports a clear contrast. In North America and Europe, strikes in Britain and France and membership growth in groups such as the Democratic Socialists of America and the Communist Party USA sit alongside a structural rightward shift in European politics. Zhou sorts European left parties into three types: those that gained or kept influence, those in office but threatened by the far right, and those that lost power or declined. Latin America, in Zhou's account, has a new "pink tide" under which Petro in Colombia and Lula in Brazil won office and more than 80 per cent of the region's population lives under left-led governments. Zhou adds that corruption, economic problems, right-wing opposition and external interference still constrain the left there. Results in Asia, Oceania, the Middle East and Africa are described as mixed, with gains in Australia, Papua New Guinea, Senegal and Lesotho and setbacks in Japan, Israel and The Gambia. In the conclusion, Zhou names political and economic crisis in the West as the main opening for the left. The evidence cited is rising labour unrest and a record 71 per cent approval of US unions in a Gallup poll. The main obstacle, in Zhou's view, is internal division. The Ukraine crisis is the example: left forces in India, Vietnam, South Africa and Bolivia judged Russia relatively positively, while northern left forces mostly criticised it. Zhou calls on left forces to separate the mainstream from side currents, set aside disputes, and replace "competition and confrontation" with "solidarity and symbiosis". Read the original if you want a dense country-by-country record of 2022 elections, strikes and party results, seen from a Chinese state-affiliated academic perspective.

Vigorously promoting the Lei Feng spirit to help the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 大力弘扬雷锋精神 助力中华民族伟大复兴 Gao Wenxue Marking the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other older-generation revolutionaries inscribing tributes to Lei Feng, this newspaper commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call to let the Lei Feng spirit shine in the new era. Gao Wenxue argues that the spirit can supply strong moral force for building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised around four qualities attributed to Lei Feng. Each is presented as a source of strength for national rejuvenation: conviction, broad love for the people, selfless devotion to work, and an enterprising will. Each section recalls Lei Feng's words or conduct and then says what people today should continue to do. Gao presents conviction as the political soul of Communists and the base of the Party's century of struggle, and describes Lei Feng's loyalty to the Party and socialism as an example. Service to the people is tied to the Chinese Dream, which Gao calls fundamentally the people's dream, and to the mass line. Lei Feng's image of the "screw" is used to argue that rejuvenation depends on countless people doing concrete jobs well, and his remark that difficulties are "paper tigers" is used to call for fighting spirit against hardship. Gao concludes that people should continue Lei Feng's idealism, spirit of dedication, professionalism, hard work and thrift, and willingness to take on responsibility and struggle. In this reading, these qualities would help consolidate belief, unity and effort for national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Party press links a model figure from the 1960s to current rejuvenation rhetoric.

Mao Zedong's theoretical guidance and practical example in the popularisation of Marxism 毛泽东对马克思主义大众化的理论指引和实践示范 Chen Ying Chen Ying takes up the question of how Mao Zedong led the popularisation (dazhonghua) of Marxism, meaning its spread among Party cadres and ordinary people. The article opens with the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) on putting the people first. It argues that Mao pioneered this path in both theory and practice. In the author's view, his ideas still offer direction for equipping the Party with theory in the new era. The article has four parts. It first sets out Mao's early advocacy and groundwork, from the Gutian Conference resolution through the Yan'an rectification to the Seventh Party Congress. It then examines his methods, the third part draws out the values behind his approach, and the last part turns to present-day relevance. The evidence is drawn from Mao's writings, letters, speeches and directives between the 1920s and the 1960s. Chen makes three main moves. First, Mao is said to have treated propaganda and education as central. He wanted theory to "grip the masses", and he insisted on tailoring content to the audience ("look at the target"). He also held that popularisation is the goal and plain, vivid language the means, as in his praise for Ai Siqi's popular philosophy and his own analogies. Second, the author summarises his methods as "one writing, two establishing" (yixie liangban): writing, running newspapers and running schools. Examples include Xiangjiang Review, Xinhua Daily, the Yan'an schools and the call to turn the whole Party into a university. Third, Chen finds four values in this work: Marxism as an ideological weapon, as truth, as an expression of care for the people, and as a source of strategic vision. Chen concludes that Mao's leading role and foundational position in popularising Marxism are pronounced, and that this popularisation continues in an unbroken line to the present. The author proposes using the Party's innovative theory to arm Party members, educate the people and guide practice, so that it "flies into the homes of ordinary people". It should also be combined with China's concrete conditions and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao's propaganda, newspaper and school work is presented in current Party scholarship on theoretical education.

An analysis of Mao Zedong's theoretical exposition of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 毛泽东关于马克思主义中国化的理论阐释论析 Wu Wenhao Wu Wenhao examines how Mao Zedong, who first put forward the proposition of the "adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context" in 1938, explained the process in theory. The article argues that Mao answered four core questions: why Marxism must be adapted, what is adapted, how, and by whom. Wu presents this exposition as a pioneering contribution and offers a systematic reconstruction of it, aiming to deepen research on Mao Zedong Thought. The article has three parts. The first traces the formative logic of Mao's exposition: the earlier ideas of Marx, Engels and Lenin on applying Marxism to national conditions, the practice of the Chinese revolution and construction, and Mao's own qualities, which Wu lists as firm ideals, theoretical mastery, a practical bent, a pioneering spirit and cultural learning. The second part sets out the core content under the four questions. The third draws lessons for the present, citing Xi Jinping's formulations. On the core content, Wu argues that the "why" rests on philosophy and conditions: Mao's On Practice and On Contradiction ground adaptation in the unity of theory and practice and of the universal and the particular, while theory takes effect only if it answers a real need, links to actual conditions and is grasped by the masses. The "what" has two sides: making Marxism concrete in China, including through traditional Chinese culture, and "Marxizing" the rich realities of the Chinese revolution. The "how" covers theoretical study, investigation of Chinese conditions and aiming Marxism at specific targets. On "by whom", Wu names the Communist Party as leading core, the people as the fundamental support, and cadres, leaders and theorists as important individual agents, linked by the mass line. Wu concludes that Mao's exposition remains a guide for continuing adaptation in the new era and draws four lessons. These are: strengthening theoretical study, assessing China's actual conditions under global change, realising the Two Integrations, and deepening the "China path", meaning the socialism with Chinese characteristics path, through distinctive features, comparative advantages and a discourse system. Wu says this path shows advantages over the Western path. Read the original if you want a structured account of how Chinese scholars present Mao's theory of Sinicisation and link it to current Party theory-building.

China's approach and experience in comprehensively implementing supply-side structural reform 全面实施供给侧结构性改革的中国方案与经验 Zhong Ying Zhong Ying examines supply-side structural reform, which the Party Central Committee has stressed since 2015, and asks what it means, why it was adopted and what experience it offers. The article argues that the reform was a major adjustment of economic thinking, adopted after analysis of the world economic cycle and of the new normal of China's economic development. In Zhong's account it has produced marked results and a distinctive 'Chinese approach' that differs from Western macroeconomic theory. The article has three parts. The first sets out the international and domestic background, including the post-2008 slowdown, protectionism, the 'three-phase overlap' and the nine trend changes identified in 2014, and then defines the reform's content. The second traces the policy path: the key factor-market directions (population, land, finance, micro-level vitality, innovation, institutions), the 2015–2017 tasks of 'cutting overcapacity, destocking, deleveraging, lowering costs and strengthening weak links', and the later 'consolidate, enhance, improve, unblock' guideline. The third presents achievements, with statistics on steel and coal capacity, housing inventory, leverage, tax and fee cuts and infrastructure, and then distils five lessons. Zhong's central claim is that the main contradiction lies on the supply side and is structural rather than one of aggregate volume. Demand-side stimulus after 2008 showed diminishing returns and side effects such as overcapacity, local debt and property bubbles. The author distinguishes Chinese reform from demand-side management and from Western supply-side economics. Zhong holds that it takes demand into account and pairs supply reform with the strategy of expanding domestic demand. It also aims at innovation, which Zhong says Keynesian, neoclassical and new Keynesian theory do not. And it treats market and government as a dialectical unity, in contrast to the Western school's emphasis on tax cuts and the market alone. The five experiences Zhong lists are: reform on the premise of demand, support from the succession of old and new growth drivers, combining priority tasks with orderly expansion, using both the market and government, and anticipating risks. Zhong concludes that practice has proven the decision correct, that the reform enriches Xi Jinping's economic thought, and that it reflects the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of supply-side reform policy stages, with the statistics the author cites, and of how Chinese scholars contrast it with Western economics.

An analysis of the conception of practice in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》实践观探析 Tian Changsheng Tian Changsheng asks what view of practice is contained in Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and why it matters for understanding Marxist philosophy. The article argues that the Manuscripts, which it calls the birthplace of Marxist philosophy, contain an early form of a scientific conception of practice. In Tian's reading, this conception differs from both Hegel's objective idealism and Feuerbach's old materialism and opens the path to a "new materialism". The article is organised around four aspects of practice, each treated in its own section. These are the precondition of practice (sensuous nature), its essential content (objectifying activity), its distorted form (alienated labour) and its moment of return (the humanisation of nature). Tian draws mainly on passages from the Manuscripts, with supporting references to The German Ideology and to Engels on nature's "revenge". Tian first argues that practice presupposes nature. Nature supplies the means of production, the means of subsistence and the "spiritual nourishment" of practice, and the human subject is both an active and a passive natural being. Practice is then defined as objectifying activity: unlike other living things, humans realise their essence in objects, change those objects and so enrich their own nature, including their senses. Alienated labour is presented as a distorted form of this relation, arising from practice itself through surplus products, the division of labour and private property. Tian reads Marx as holding that alienation can be overcome only through practice, leading to communism as the return of the human being to itself. Tian concludes with a dialectic of the "humanisation of nature" and the "naturalisation of humanity". The first reflects human civilisation and the capacity to transform nature, and the article notes that it risks provoking nature's counter-effects. The second is presented as a reflection on that civilisation, which the author ties to ecological damage and consumerism, and as a return to harmony with nature. Practice mediates between the two. Tian holds that the Manuscripts founded a new worldview and settled accounts with Hegel, although traces of Feuerbach's humanism remain.
