Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how the early Marx's concept of practice links alienation, objectification and the human relation to nature.

Three preliminary questions on "the Marxism that has been adapted to China and the times works" “中国化时代化的马克思主义行”的三个前提性思考 Zhang Yan Chen Weifeng Zhang Yan and Chen Weifeng take up a formula from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that the Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good because Marxism works, and specifically because "the Marxism that has been adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" works. The authors argue that understanding this "second works" requires settling three preliminary questions: what adapting Marxism to China and the times means, what that adapted Marxism is, and why it works. The article is organised in three sections, one per question, each ending with a stated conclusion. The first traces the terminology from Mao Zedong's 1938 formulation of "Sinification", through the "three-ization" (Chinese, contemporary, popular) of 2009, to Xi Jinping's 2018 fusion of the two terms. The second distinguishes the process of adaptation from its theoretical results and places Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era among those results. The third examines the theory's strengths. The authors argue that the new wording is not a mere change of vocabulary. In their account, "Chinese" adaptation is a spatial dimension of theoretical innovation and "of the times" a temporal one; they note that scholars such as Li Junru and Gong Yuzhi had held that "Sinification" already contained both. Adding a second "works" is, they say, not tautological but an emphasis that marks the Party's own theoretical achievements and builds confidence. They locate the reasons for success in four things: the scientific character of Marxism itself, its combination with China's concrete realities, its combination with fine traditional Chinese culture (the Two Integrations), and the "six musts" of the Congress report (the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, problem orientation, systems thinking, and a world outlook). They add that the ten years since 2012 have tested the theory in practice. The authors conclude that the Marxism adapted to China and the times is the theoretical product of a century of Party effort, with Xi Jinping Thought as its current form, and that it works because Marxism works and because the Party holds to the Two Integrations and the six musts. They call for further theory-building on a practical basis as China pursues the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from within the official discourse, of how the 20th Party Congress formula was built up and justified.

The power of truth: the Communist Manifesto and the founding of the Communist Party of China 真理的力量：《共产党宣言》与中国共产党的创建 Li Jian Li Jian examines how Chen Wangdao's complete Chinese translation of the Communist Manifesto, published in August 1920, shaped the founding of the Communist Party of China. The article argues that the text served as the core of early ideological enlightenment and theoretical acculturation, and that its publication and spread illuminate the internal logic and practical path of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The study first considers the agents of transmission: the Marxist-trained intellectuals around Chen Duxiu, Li Hanjun, Chen Wangdao, Li Da and Yu Xiusong in Shanghai, with Voitinsky's funding for the printing house. It then traces three channels of dissemination: the founding of Party organisations, the training of cadres, and the awakening of ordinary people. Finally it looks at why the text spread so widely, citing Shanghai's publishing network, reprint figures, cover design and the way the translation was synchronised with Party-building. Li contends that, with Marxist literature scarce, the Manifesto became the basic study text for early members, the course book at the Foreign Languages School and Shanghai University, and a source for the Party's early declarations. Memoirs by Dong Biwu, Bao Huiseng, Mao Zedong and others are used to show how reading it formed political belief. Li also describes workers' schools, leaflets and the 1922 Marx commemorative booklet as ways of turning theory into popular mobilisation, and argues that early Communists stressed class struggle and proletarian dictatorship as tools for analysing China's conditions, while treating the Manifesto's principles as needing adaptation to specific circumstances. Li concludes that early Communists turned the Manifesto's spirit into an organisational driving force and into the political and cultural formation of Party members, which established the Party's character as a 'learning party' and laid a foundation for later theoretical innovation. Read the original if you want a source-rich account of the Manifesto's translation, circulation and use in the early Party, drawn from memoirs and Comintern-era reports.

Marx's idea of the "productive force of capital" A study based on Capital and its economic manuscripts 马克思关于“资本的生产力”思想探析 Xu Shuihua Yang Zeguang Scholars disagree about whether Marx actually held a notion of the "productive force of capital". Xu Shuihua and Yang Zeguang argue that he did, that he used the concept explicitly, and that it carries two meanings: capital's power to command other productive forces, and capital's role as a real historical force that is itself a productive force. The article proceeds in three steps. It first traces the textual basis through the 1857–58 manuscripts and Volumes I, II and III of Capital. It then sets out what Marx meant by the concept. Finally it examines how Marx weighed the concept's effects on capitalist society, both affirming and critical. On the textual side, the authors find the phrase first mentioned in Marx's notes on Ricardo and developed in the 1857–58 manuscripts. In Volume I it appears in the treatment of relative surplus value, covering cooperation, the combination of labour, machinery, science and natural forces. In Volume II the idea is said to be implicit in the continuity and turnover of capital, and in Volume III it appears in passages on rent and on free natural forces. On meaning, the authors hold that capital's ownership of the means of production makes it the subject of production. Collective, scientific and natural productive forces therefore appear as capital's own. They also hold that capital, as a historical force, moved society from feudal "barbarism" to capitalist "civilisation" and supplies the material conditions for communism. Marx's assessment is dialectical in the authors' account. He credits capital with material abundance, the world market, scientific advance and the free time and conditions from which a revolutionary subject emerges. He also condemns it for one-sided human development and for damaging nature. The authors conclude that Marx treated capital both as a relation of production and as a productive force with a historical limit. When capital stops advancing productive forces and begins to fetter them, history discards it. They present the productive force of capital as a mode of exercising the productive force of social labour under capitalism, one that turns against both people and ecology. Read the original if you want a text-by-text survey of where Capital and the manuscripts use the phrase, or a Chinese-language argument that capital is both a relation of production and a productive force.

The value orientation, practical implications and contemporary enlightenment of Marx's thought on social relations 马克思社会关系思想的价值旨趣、实践意蕴与当代启示 Bi Guoshuai Bi Guoshuai asks what Marx's thought on social relations offers for improving social relations and promoting all-round human development today. The article argues that Marx's account is organised around human emancipation as the core of historical progress. It holds that this thought supplies guidance for building what Bi calls "people's relations" (renmin guanxi) in contemporary China. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the value orientation of Marx's thought: its starting point in "human beings engaged in sensuous activity", its goal of the "free individuality" of persons, and its overall horizon of social-historical development. The second sets out the practical implications, as a dual logic of transforming reified relations and constructing human relations. The third draws lessons for present-day China under three headings. Bi contends that Marx overcame both Hegel's idealist reduction of social relations to relations of consciousness and Feuerbach's intuitive, ahistorical "natural" ties, thereby uniting their materiality and historicity. Marx's three stages of social relations (natural, reified, human) are said to correspond to the three stages of emancipation. In the reified stage, capital-dominated production and exchange invert the relation between persons and things. Changing this requires overthrowing bourgeois political rule and gradually abolishing capitalist private property, which Bi says cannot be done by ignoring the level of the productive forces. Human relations must then be built up under socialism by developing the productive forces and perfecting socialist institutions, with public ownership at their core. Bi concludes that China, at the primary stage of socialism, has largely passed beyond the stage of transforming reified relations but lacks the conditions for human relations. Its task is therefore to build "people's relations" as a transitional form, by giving them direction, strengthening their foundation and shaping their form. In practice, Bi calls for upholding the socialist road, Party leadership and the people's principal position; pursuing high-quality development; and building institutions that combine public ownership, common prosperity and harmony between humanity and nature. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's relational theory of the human being and its policy application to contemporary China.

On the historical experience of the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 论中国共产党百年奋斗的历史经验 Yuwen Li Xi Jiameng Yuwen and Xi take up the historical experience that the Communist Party of China draws from its century of struggle, as set out in the 2021 Party resolution on major achievements and historical experience (the Resolution). They argue that summing up experience is a defining trait of the Party and one reason it can remain in power, correct its mistakes and manage risks. In their view, the Resolution's "ten upholds" explain why the Party succeeded in the past and how it can keep succeeding. The article has three parts. The first shows how the Party has valued experience-summing from the 1945 and 1981 historical resolutions to the successive theoretical innovations of Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second analyses the ideas and logic of the "ten upholds". The third sets out requirements for applying this experience in the new era. The central argument is that the ten upholds form a coherent whole in three senses. They revolve around three laws: those governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and the development of human society. They continue earlier summaries, from the first two resolutions through the "nine musts" of Xi Jinping's 2021 speech, and they form a closed loop in which upholding Party leadership and the Party's self-reform stand at the head and tail. They also verify the "three logics" of history, theory and practice, which the authors say are consistent from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping. For applying the experience, the authors propose three requirements: uphold Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the core position of Xi Jinping in the Central Committee and the whole Party; uphold the people's position as the subject of history; and exercise historical consciousness and initiative in facing great struggles. They distinguish spontaneity from consciousness in history. They hold that grasping historical laws lets the Party seize the initiative on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese Party theorists interpret the Resolution's ten upholds and their theoretical logic.

Letting the Lei Feng spirit shine more brightly in the new era 让雷锋精神在新时代绽放更加璀璨的光芒 Pang Lisheng Marking the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other revolutionary leaders' inscriptions for Lei Feng, Xi Jinping issued an instruction on deepening the campaign to learn from Lei Feng. This commentary, written by Pang Lisheng, takes that instruction as its guide. Pang argues that the Lei Feng spirit has enduring value and that its contemporary meaning must be grasped so that it can supply spiritual strength for building a modern socialist country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first explains why promoting the Lei Feng spirit matters. The second sets out its contemporary content. The third proposes practical ways to carry it forward. Pang treats the spirit as originating in the period of socialist revolution and construction, with its meaning enriched as the times change. In the first part, Pang contends that the Lei Feng spirit embodies the core socialist values, continues the traditional virtues of the Chinese nation and expresses the moral character of Communists. Promoting it is therefore described as an inherent requirement for cultivating those values, for advancing cultural confidence and strength, and for gathering spiritual force as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation meets greater risks. The second part identifies three elements: firm ideals and convictions, including Marxist belief and study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; dedication to one's work, whose core Pang names as serving the people wholeheartedly; and a spirit of innovation and struggle. For practice, Pang calls for making learning from Lei Feng routine and institutionalised, and for linking it closely with volunteer service in families, schools, communities and social services. Pang also urges new platforms and media, deeper research on the spirit, the selection of model figures, and supporting systems such as incentive and recognition schemes, social credit and volunteers' rights protection. These measures are meant to build a lasting mechanism and a civilised social atmosphere. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-theory journals present the Lei Feng spirit in connection with core socialist values and cultural confidence, and what institutional measures they propose.”

Mao Zedong's systematic construction of the theory of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context: an intellectual-history study 毛泽东对马克思主义中国化理论的系统建构：一项思想史的考察 Xiong Chengshuai Research on the theory of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, Xiong Chengshuai argues, has produced many results that repeat one another or talk past each other. The author attributes this to the lack of a clear knowledge structure and to a concept stretched to cover everything. Distinguishing the theory from the practice of adaptation, Xiong proposes that the theory built up by Mao Zedong during the War of Resistance against Japan has three layers: basic theory, mid-level theory and applied theory. The article is an intellectual-history study of Mao's wartime writings, read in their historical setting. It first treats the basic theory in the 1937 lecture outline on dialectical materialism and in "On Contradiction" and "On Practice". It then turns to the mid-level theory of revolutionary stages and periodisation, drawing on Robert Merton's notion of middle-range theory, used here only in the sense of lying between grand theory and detail. Last come two examples of applied theory: united front theory and guerrilla warfare theory. Xiong's core argument is that Mao built this structure to counter dogmatism after the failures of the early 1930s. In the basic theory, the world is always changing, so no theory is absolute. The particularity of contradiction is the main object of knowledge, and knowing moves repeatedly from the particular to the general and back. The mid-level theory sorts Chinese history into old-democratic, New Democratic and socialist revolution, with the May Fourth Movement as the dividing line, and sets the direction of work at each stage. The applied theories are said to rest on both layers. The united front is justified by the Party's weak position and by the stage of revolution. Guerrilla warfare is raised from a tactic to a strategy built on base areas, and it is expected to develop into mobile warfare. Xiong concludes that the three layers differ in stability. The basic theory changes least, applied theories must be revised in each new period, and the periodisation long guided the Party. The author suggests that this structure could connect separate studies and support more detailed work on each layer. Read the original if you want a text-based account of how Mao's wartime writings are said to form a layered theoretical system, or a case study of how Chinese scholars try to make the study of adapting Marxism more academic.

The new form of human civilization as a continuation and innovation of Marx and Engels's theory of civilization An analysis from the perspective of world history 人类文明新形态对马克思恩格斯文明理论的守正创新 Liu Hao Liu Hao asks how the "new form of human civilization" created through Chinese modernization relates to the theory of civilization that Marx and Engels developed in the nineteenth century from a world-historical perspective. The article argues that the Communist Party of China has both preserved the core of that theory and innovated on it, and that this is visible in three areas: historical trend, path of development and mode of interaction between peoples. The author presents this as opening a new chapter of Marxist civilization theory. The article is organised in three parts that follow these three areas. The first treats the historical trend from capitalist to socialist civilization and the Chinese case. The second takes up Marx's late idea of bypassing the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism and Chinese modernization as a distinct path. The third examines Marx's idea of the "meeting of extremes" in his writing on the Taiping rebellion and the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind. Liu closes with a summary of the significance of these contributions. In the first part, Liu reads Marx and Engels as showing the dual character of capitalist civilization: historically progressive, yet trapped in contradictions rooted in capital, so that socialist civilization must replace it. The author contends that the new form of civilization puts "the people first" against capitalism's primacy of capital, and that, by combining public ownership as the main body with a socialist market economy, it governs capital without abolishing it, something Marx and Engels did not address. In the second part, Liu argues that Marx's late writings reject a linear view of history and allow backward countries distinct paths, which Chinese modernization is said to confirm and extend by showing how to consolidate socialism after such a leap. In the third part, Liu holds that Marx foresaw China as one pole of world history, and that a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative turn this antagonistic interaction into mutual benefit and replace the claimed superiority of Western civilization with coexistence. Liu concludes that the new form of civilization answers the questions of where socialism and socialist civilization are heading, and points a direction for how human civilization should be built. The author presents it as altering the pattern of world development and as carrying universal world-historical significance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames current Party theory as a continuation of Marx and Engels's writings on civilization, world history and the East–West relationship.

The history of rhythm and the rhythm of history The Communist Manifesto's historical analysis of the bourgeoisie and its methodology 节奏的历史与历史的节奏 Liu Tongfang Why does the Communist Manifesto, a political programme, open its main text with a historical account of the bourgeoisie? Liu Tongfang argues that the answer lies in the historical consciousness Marx and Engels developed in the age of the 'dual revolution'. To bring this out, the article uses 'rhythm' as an analytical lens, distinguishing a 'history of rhythm' from a 'rhythm of history'. The article first treats history as grounded in 'social structure', meaning the mode of production and exchange, and shows how the bourgeoisie's expansion of productive forces sped up historical tempo. It then turns to the rhythm of history, understood as the recurrence of historical laws, and illustrates it through capitalist crises and changes in property relations. Finally it draws out three methods in the Manifesto: class analysis, historicity and totality. Liu engages Vico, Kant, Hegel, Croce, Collingwood, Lefebvre, Braudel and Karatani Kojin along the way. Liu contends that Marx and Engels go beyond both speculative and analytical philosophy of history by treating all history as a history of rhythm. Class struggle repeats its essential content (exploitation and resistance) in changing forms. What recurs, in Liu's reading, is neither events (Marx's 'tragedy and farce' remark) nor structures (Karatani's view) but the necessity of laws. Capital's rhythm of production and destruction, with periodic crises, and the shifting of property relations from feudal to bourgeois and onward show that the bourgeoisie produces its own 'gravediggers'. This points to the inevitable fall of capitalism and victory of communism. On method, Liu holds that class analysis explains how the bourgeoisie arose through class struggle. Historicity treats it as a transient product of development. Totality allows capitalism to be assessed both for its historic achievements and for its alienating effects, without denying either. The article concludes that the Manifesto's analysis retains lasting theoretical value, and it calls for close reading of the classic texts to draw out their historical-materialist methodology. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholars read the Manifesto's historical method, or in the 'rhythm' framing that links Lefebvre and Braudel to historical materialism.

Carrying forward the Lei Feng spirit to achieve new breakthroughs in Liaoning's revitalisation 弘扬雷锋精神 推动辽宁振兴发展取得新突破 Study Group of the Theoretical Learning Centre of the CPC Liaoning Provincial Committee Marking the 60th anniversary of the inscriptions by Mao Zedong and other revolutionary leaders in honour of Lei Feng, this commentary by the Party committee study group of Liaoning province argues that the Lei Feng spirit should be actively carried forward to support Liaoning's revitalisation. Published in the People's Daily on 15 March 2023, it presents Liaoning as the birthplace of the Lei Feng spirit and says that the spirit supplies the moral support needed for a new breakthrough in the province's comprehensive development. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's recent instructions on Lei Feng study activities and his 2018 visit to the Lei Feng memorial hall in Fushun. It then recalls Lei Feng's 3 years and 9 months of work in Liaoning and names local models inspired by him, such as Guo Mingyi and Luo Yang. Four sections follow, each opening with 'carrying forward the Lei Feng spirit means…': gathering the energy of conviction, cultivating great love, showing selflessness, and sharpening an enterprising edge. The authors argue that firm communist belief is the essence of the Lei Feng spirit, and that serving the people wholeheartedly is its substance. In their account, loyalty to the Party means taking up the political task Xi and the Central Committee have assigned to Liaoning. They report that the province's economic base, political ecology and business environment have improved and that it has passed its most difficult period. In the 'Liaoshen Campaign' metaphor they use, a three-year action plan is to deliver comprehensive revitalisation. The authors link the 'screw that never rusts' and the spirit of 'squeezing' and 'drilling' to high-quality development, the real economy, innovation, and reform. They also tie the fighting spirit to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, anti-formalism and thrift, and to the province's red heritage. The authors conclude that Liaoning will continue its red heritage and promote the Lei Feng spirit to strengthen its resolve, backbone and confidence. They say this will serve Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They call on cadres and the public to embed personal aspirations in the Party's cause, and to work towards common prosperity and shared benefits for Liaoning's 42 million people. Read the original if you want an example of how a provincial Party leadership links a national moral exemplar to regional economic and political tasks in official discourse.

Understanding the two dimensions of "Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times works" 理解“中国化时代化的马克思主义行”的双重维度 Jiang Hong Zhao Qiuyuan The 20th Party Congress (2022) declared that the Party succeeds, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good, ultimately because "Marxism works", specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Jiang and Zhao ask why this Marxism works. They answer that it must be read through two dimensions drawn from Xi Jinping's speeches: a worldview-and-methodology dimension, and a stance-viewpoint-method dimension. The article is built in three parts. The first treats the Marxist worldview and methodology, covering the truth-claim of Marxism and then Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The second examines the "Six Upholds" (六个坚持) set out in the 20th Party Congress report. The third argues that the two dimensions are dialectically united and places them in the historical context of the "two great trends" (两个大局). Jiang and Zhao argue that Marxism's truth lies in a scientific worldview, dialectical and historical materialism, and in a method tested through practice that has changed the world, from the October Revolution to China's own revolution. They claim Xi Jinping Thought deepens understanding of three sets of laws. These are the laws of Party rule, where the Party's self-reform is presented as a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall; the laws of socialist construction; and the laws of human social development, shown in Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. The Six Upholds are grouped as value stance (putting the people first, global vision), spiritual character (self-confidence and self-reliance, preserving fundamental principles while innovating) and dialectical method (problem orientation, systematic thinking). The authors trace these to Marxism and to traditional Chinese culture. The authors conclude that Marxism remains the true understanding of our era, since capitalism's contradictions have sharpened since the 2008 financial crisis. They hold that continued theoretical innovation must bind "Chinese context" and "our times" together within the two great trends, and that adapted Marxism has acquired world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Party theorists in 2023 justified the "Marxism works" thesis and the Six Upholds.

The contemporary value and significance of whole-process people's democracy from an international perspective 国际视角下全过程人民民主的时代价值与意义 Yu Yunquan Yu Yunquan asks what whole-process people's democracy means for the world and how China should communicate it abroad. Writing in 2023, Yu argues that the concept carries global significance and practical effectiveness, and that this is confirmed by a 2022 opinion survey. The author concludes that China should now strengthen the international communication of its democratic ideas. The article draws on a poll run in 2022 by the Institute of Contemporary China and the World, whose president is the author. The poll covered 23 countries across five continents and was compared with 2021 results. The text has three parts: the world significance of whole-process people's democracy, its practical effectiveness, and ways of telling the story of Chinese democracy. Yu makes three claims about world significance. The concept is said to embody common values of all humanity and to draw on China's continuous civilisation, and it is presented as offering a Chinese approach to governance problems and to democratising the world order. On effectiveness, Yu reports that respondents rated highly the Communist Party's leading role, the economy and technology, social fairness and stability, Chinese culture, and China's part in global governance. The article cites figures such as 95.7% agreement on common values and a leadership-role approval above 90%. Yu contrasts China with Western states, which the author accuses of exporting 'colour revolutions' and of following Fukuyama's prediction, while China is said not to export values. The article holds that a country's democracy should be judged by its own people. Yu proposes four paths for international communication. These are deeper theoretical research, a distinctive external discourse built on core concepts and new media, and visits by foreign experts, journalists and young people to see Chinese democratic practice. The fourth is civilisational exchange and mutual learning through party, think-tank and people-to-people channels. The aim is to build a credible, lovable and respectable image of China. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese think-tank uses survey data to support whole-process people's democracy and to set out a plan for communicating it abroad.

The Communist Party of China's understanding and re-understanding of the essence of socialism 中国共产党对社会主义本质的认识和再认识 Wang Huaichao Wang Huaichao asks how the Communist Party of China has come to define the "essence of socialism", understood as the fundamental attribute that distinguishes a socialist society from all others. The article argues that the Party's understanding has deepened in stages through practice, moving from the abstract to the concrete and from the general to the particular. It ends by proposing its own new formulation of that essence. The article moves chronologically. It begins with Marx, Engels and Lenin, noting that Marx and Engels never used the term itself, and then turns to Stalin's "traditional" view of socialism. It then covers Deng Xiaoping's 1992 formulation and later additions under Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. A closing section sets this development against the Marxist theory of knowledge, citing Lenin and Mao Zedong on practice. Wang reads Deng's 1992 definition (liberating and developing the productive forces, eliminating exploitation and polarization, and finally achieving common prosperity) as an original contribution to scientific socialism. In Wang's account it unites productive forces with relations of production, purpose with means, and efficiency with fairness. Later leaders added to it: the all-round development of the human being (Jiang), social fairness and justice and social harmony (Hu), and, under Xi Jinping, Party leadership as the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, with sharing as an essential requirement. Wang treats the Party's progress as a cycle running from practice to understanding and back to practice, and from the particular to the general and back. Mao's account of knowledge frames this cycle. Wang proposes that socialism is essentially a new type of social system, led by a proletarian party, with the people as the principal body. Through liberating and developing the productive forces, it gradually achieves common prosperity, realizes social justice and promotes the free and all-round development of the human being. The article lists six elements: Party leadership, the people's principal position, productive forces, common prosperity, social justice and all-round human development. Wang says this formulation rests on the historical experience of socialism with Chinese characteristics and that understanding will keep rising to new levels. Read the original if you want a compact, Party-school account of how official definitions of socialism's essence have developed from Deng to Xi.

The Lei Feng spirit never goes out of date 雷锋精神永不过时 Tao Ke Zhai Yuanbin Marking the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other revolutionary leaders' inscriptions for Lei Feng, and following a recent instruction from Xi Jinping, the authors argue that the Lei Feng spirit remains valid however the times change. Their commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, presents sixty years of the nationwide 'learn from Lei Feng' campaign as proof. The article first recounts the campaign's history. It begins with local activities in Shenyang and Fushun in 1960, passes through the People's Daily coverage of February 1963 and the publication of Mao's inscription on 5 March 1963, and ends with Xi Jinping's recent directive. It then traces how the concept of the Lei Feng spirit was formed. The authors' central move is to describe a shift from learning from Lei Feng's deeds to learning from a spirit. They report that Mao defined its essence as good thinking, work style and character, and wholehearted service to the people. Zhou Enlai's inscription, they say, set out its content, and Hu Qiaomu in 1983 called it a 'crystallization' and 'symbol' of a collective spiritual core, not an individual's qualities. They also contend that it combines traditional Chinese culture, red revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture, and keeps developing with the times. The authors conclude that its enduring vitality drives the campaign. In their account it supplies values for individuals and a spiritual force for social progress. Following Xi Jinping, they call for Party members and cadres to set an example, for stronger support for volunteer service, and for learning from Lei Feng to become everyday practice, especially among young people, so as to build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise official account of how the Lei Feng spirit has been defined and promoted since 1963.

On the logic of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化的逻辑 Han Qingxiang Han Qingxiang reads the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as an important sample text of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context, and argues that one master logic runs through it: the logic of Chinese modernization. Its core, Han says, is using Chinese modernization to build a modern socialist country in all respects and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article holds that this logic has four parts: a generative, a theoretical, a practical and a world logic. The article follows these four dimensions in turn. The generative logic traces how the Party advanced and extended Chinese modernization from the "four modernizations" to socialist modernization and then to modernizing national governance. The theoretical logic sets out the Congress report's account of the orientation, shared features, Chinese characteristics and essential requirements of Chinese modernization. The practical and world logics then cover the strategic arrangements of the report and China's place in global modernization. Han argues that the Congress report, for the first time, built an overall theoretical and discourse system for Chinese modernization and so gained the power to define it. In Han's reading, the "new path of Chinese modernization" put forward in 2021 extends the "Chinese-style modernization" of Deng Xiaoping, whose goal was a moderately prosperous society, in five respects. These are common prosperity, coordinated development of five civilizations, harmony between humanity and nature, peaceful development, and the goal of becoming strong ("qiang qilai") rather than merely rich. Han describes Western modernization as marked by polarization, material excess, ecological damage and colonial expansion, and presents Chinese modernization as surpassing it. The five features and the nine essential requirements are presented as a system, running from Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics to a new form of human civilization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Han concludes that China has moved from "the world losing sight of us" to "the world having a place for us" and now towards "the world turning to us". On this view Chinese modernization offers developing countries a new option for modernizing while keeping their independence. It also gives scientific socialism new vitality in twenty-first-century China. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists organise the 20th Congress report around Chinese modernization.

A comparative study of the theories of capital circulation in Capital and the Tableau économique 《资本论》与《经济表》资本循环理论的比较研究 Liu Xingang Lu Xin Marx praised Quesnay's treatment of circulation many times, and Quesnay's Tableau économique (1758) and Marx's Capital (Volumes II and III) deal with closely related themes. Liu and Lu ask how the two theories of capital circulation relate. They argue that the two share many specific views but differ fundamentally in methodology, and that this coexistence is explained by a shared intermediate step: the analysis of economic relations. The authors link the topic to China's strategy of a new development pattern with the domestic cycle as the mainstay and domestic and international cycles reinforcing each other. The article first reviews two existing positions. The 'similarity thesis' (Schumpeter, Richard Stone, Leontief) points to shared systemic methods, a common internal logic running to growth and national accounting, and shared practical uses such as input–output analysis. The 'transcendence thesis' stresses Quesnay's feudal standpoint and Marx's critique and reworking of him. The authors judge both inadequate: the first rests on logical continuity, the second on class standpoint and orthodox tradition, and neither examines the substance of the doctrines. The article then compares main views, compares methodology, explains the coexistence, and draws implications. On main views, Liu and Lu identify four similarities. Both distinguish annual advances from original advances, producing discontinuity in circulation, a point on which Marx says Adam Smith fell behind Quesnay. Both see capital taking different forms under different laws. Both see a tendency for capital to drift away from productive sectors, notably towards finance. Both hold that laissez-faire markets need forces outside the market to keep circulation orderly. On methodology, the authors argue that Marx abstracts to 'labour in general' and treats economic relations as a conscious core category. Quesnay stays with agricultural labour and a 'natural order' that Marx rejects, which they say gives Quesnay's approach an apologetic character towards capitalism. Citing Engels on the 'intermediate links' that classical economists neglected, they argue that both thinkers pass through the analysis of economic relations, so similar conclusions can coexist with different methods. The authors conclude that method and conclusions stand in a dialectical unity, not a linear relation in which method determines viewpoint. Marx absorbed Quesnay's concepts, judgements and inferences, reworked them within his own framework and supplied what Quesnay lacked on economic relations. They draw three implications: study Marx's circulation theory through this unity; follow it in theoretical innovation; and use it to critique and absorb contemporary schools such as behavioural and information economics, in support of political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's relation to the Physiocrats, the history of Capital Volumes II and III, or how Chinese economists frame the absorption of non-Marxist economics.

Dialectical relations and innovative paths for steadily advancing common prosperity through Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化扎实推进共同富裕的辩证关系与创新路径研究 Wen Fengan Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wen Fengan asks how common prosperity can be achieved in a socialist country of well over a billion people, and what relationship holds between common prosperity and Chinese modernization. The article argues that the two are dialectically unified: common prosperity is an important feature of Chinese modernization, Chinese modernization embodies the inner requirements of common prosperity, and advancing the one through the other is the necessary road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article opens with a literature review of Chinese scholarship on the meaning and significance of common prosperity, on Chinese modernization, and on the main obstacles, which Wen groups under regional and urban–rural gaps, income gaps and gaps in public services. Wen concludes that scholars still disagree on how the two concepts and their relationship should be understood. The second part sets out their dialectical relationship, and the third proposes five paths of implementation. In the article's account, Western modernization rested on industrial revolution, colonial plunder and unequal international rules, and produced prosperity for a minority of people and countries. Wen contends that common prosperity for 1.4 billion people fixes the character of Chinese modernization: it is led by the Communist Party, follows socialism with Chinese characteristics, and combines material and spiritual wealth, efficiency and fairness, and development and sharing. Common prosperity is described as staged rather than simultaneous, and as compatible with moderate differences, not egalitarianism. Wen's five paths are: upholding the Party's overall leadership; unifying material and spiritual advancement while preventing alienation, through education, cultural supply and talent policy; coordinating regional and urban–rural development; combining efficiency and fairness within high-quality development, with the market and government both playing a role; and joining co-construction with sharing, including intellectual property protection and incentives for work and innovation. Wen calls for these measures as the basis for the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the official framing of common prosperity under Chinese modernization is built up in Chinese academic writing, including a survey of domestic scholarship on the topic.

Re-examining Marx's thesis of the "natural history" of economic social formations From the perspective of Hegel's "natural history of spirit" 马克思“经济社会形态的自然史”论断再探 Liu Zhenjiang Marx's preface to the first edition of Capital describes the development of the economic formation of society as 'a process of natural history'. Liu Zhenjiang takes up the long-running debate in Chinese scholarship over what this means. One camp (Chen Zhiliang, Yang Geng) reads it as saying that social formations are merely 'similar to' natural history in having their own laws. The other (Luo Bozhong) reads it as saying that social development is 'naturally' so, driven by the dialectic of human productive agency rather than material necessity. Liu argues that both are partial, and that the direct theoretical basis of Marx's thesis is Hegel's 'natural history of spirit'. The article has four parts. It begins with Marx's reading of Hegel's 'pure-thought dialectic' in the 1844 Manuscripts and in Capital. It then reconstructs Hegel's natural history of spirit from the Philosophy of Right, the Lectures on the History of Philosophy, the Phenomenology of Spirit and the Philosophy of History. The third part examines Marx's concept of natural history and the negation of the negation in free labour. The last part turns to the concrete forms of the economic formations: the 'five formations', the 'three forms' of personal development and the 'three historical states' of the Capital manuscripts. Liu's central claim is that Marx sublated Hegel's account, replacing the self-realisation of spirit with real human beings and their material productive labour. For Hegel, 'nature' includes human natural drives and needs, and history is the process in which freedom reconciles itself with natural necessity. Marx, in Liu's reading, defines natural history as the process by which nature becomes human, driven by the satisfaction of needs through labour. The first camp therefore wrongly equates human history with natural history in the sense of the natural world, while the second wrongly denies material necessity. On this account, capitalism's own 'natural laws' lead to the negation of private property based on individual labour and to the re-establishment of individual ownership on the basis of cooperation and common possession of the means of production. Liu concludes that the development of economic formations is a natural history of human modes of production, in which the unity of lawfulness and purposiveness is realised as human freedom grows. Society cannot skip or abolish natural stages of development by decree, but knowledge of its laws can shorten and ease the 'birth pangs'. The 'realm of freedom' rests on the 'realm of necessity'. Read the original if you work on the Hegel–Marx relationship, the historical-materialist theory of social formations, or the Chinese debate over 'natural history' and want a detailed textual argument drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and Capital.

Marx's "Chapter on Capital" as a pioneering exploration of capital theory With a discussion of capital theory under the socialist market economy 马克思“资本章”对资本理论的开创性探索 Gu Hailiang Gu Hailiang asks what Marx's "Chapter on Capital" in the Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58 contributed to capital theory, and what it offers for studying capital under China's socialist market economy. The article argues that the chapter made three "firsts": it first explored the structure of a theory of capital, it first used "capital in general" and "many capitals" to frame the study of capital's characteristics and laws of behaviour, and it first treated capital as a "totality", disclosing its historical, social and class character. The article has three main sections, one for each "first". The first traces Marx's successive plans: the five-part plan of the 1857 Introduction, the "six-part" and "three-part" structures for capital, the six-book plan of 1858, and the four-part structure for the book on capital. The second follows the pair "capital in general" and "many capitals" into the three volumes of Capital. The third examines the totality and then turns to Party documents from the 1990s to the 2010s on capital under the socialist market economy. Gu reads the pair "capital in general" and "many capitals", derived from Hegel's "one and many", as the key to Capital. Volumes I and II analyse capital's nature at the level of capital in general, while Volume III moves to competition, the average rate of profit and prices of production, which Gu calls Marx's original contribution. Drawing on Marx's image of capital as the "universal light" that gives other relations their colour and weight, Gu reads Xi Jinping's concept of a "capital structure" of state, collective, private, foreign and mixed capital in the same way. In this account public capital is the "universal light" that changes the character of the other forms. Xi's call to grasp capital's "characteristics and laws of behaviour" is presented as a creative application of Marx's two themes. Gu concludes that private capital under socialism keeps its profit-seeking nature, so that it has both positive and negative effects. The aim is orderly development, not abolition, and curbing "disorderly expansion" is not meant to suppress competition or accumulation. Marx's analysis of the limits capital meets is also said to bear on the specific limits that may arise among public and non-public, and domestic and foreign, capital, and on building an effective structure of capital governance. Read the original if you want a close reading of how the 1857–58 manuscripts' plans for capital theory are linked to current Chinese policy language on capital.

Space and capital: homogeneity and heterogeneity in the spatial thought of Lefebvre and Marx 空间与资本：列斐伏尔与马克思的空间思想的同质性与异质性 Li Shule Li Shule takes up a question raised by the "spatial turn" in Western Marxism: how does Henri Lefebvre's thinking on space relate to Marx's? The article argues that existing scholarship, in stressing continuity between the two, over-interprets their homogeneity and obscures real differences. Li's thesis is that the two share a logical starting point, but that Lefebvre's theory of the production of space has a specific content that goes beyond Marx's framework. The article, published in Teaching and Research in 2022, has three parts. The first traces how each thinker's spatial thought arose, treating the relation between space and capital as the common thread: the starting question of how capital comes to dominate space, the unfolding of urbanization, and the spatial metaphors Marx built on the logic of capital. The second sets out the criteria for judging homogeneity and heterogeneity. The third analyses three differences: spatial discourse, the form in which space is constructed, and the structure of spatial power. A brief conclusion turns to socialism and China. Li distinguishes the logical premise of Lefebvre's theory from its specific content. In the premise, Lefebvre follows Marx: historical materialism and the critique of political economy, with each mode of production having its own space. Marx's "spatialization of capital" and "capitalization of space" are said to be an important source for Lefebvre. Yet Lefebvre holds that modern capitalism differs from the capitalism Marx criticised, because the production of space itself has replaced the production of things in space, and the totalizing logic of space production has replaced the logic of capital. On this basis Li reads Marx's space as scattered metaphor, with land ownership and the "trinity formula" as the core of spatial construction. Lefebvre, by contrast, builds a systematic discourse in which real estate, land speculation, state intervention and urban planning produce an abstract, homogenized and fragmented space. His politics shifts from violent revolution to a struggle for "differential space" against abstract space. Li concludes that the move from Marx's scattered metaphors to Lefebvre's systematic logic marks capitalist space construction becoming self-aware. It also deepens the critique of modern capitalism. Li notes, however, that Lefebvre said socialism had not yet produced its own space and did not analyse concrete socialist cases. Li then argues that in China's urbanization, capital over-accumulation, over-urbanization and land speculation reflect a contest between the socialist system and market logic. The superiority of that system is said to lie in keeping space production oriented to the people. Read the original if you work on Lefebvre, Marxist spatial theory or Chinese debates on urbanization and want a case for treating Lefebvre and Marx as distinct rather than continuous.

The historical logic of the Communist Party of China's exploration of Chinese modernization 中国共产党探索中国式现代化的历史逻辑 Guo Guangyin Writing in 2023, soon after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Guo Guangyin asks how Chinese modernization came to be, and answers that it is the product of the Communist Party of China's long exploration, one the author describes as logically connected across four historical periods. Guo argues that this path, won at great cost, is the only correct road to building a strong socialist country and achieving the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is a short commentary organised chronologically. It covers the failed early attempts at modernization in modern China, the New Democratic Revolution, the period of socialist revolution and construction, the period of reform and opening up, and the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Each section identifies what that stage contributed to the present path. Guo's central claim is that each stage supplied a necessary condition. Earlier efforts to copy Western models failed, in the author's account, because they neither avoided dependence nor secured national independence, liberation and freedom for the people. The New Democratic Revolution removed these political obstacles. Socialist revolution and construction then established the basic system, an independent industrial system and the concept of the 'four modernizations'. Reform and opening up, beginning with Deng Xiaoping's 1979 formulation of 'Chinese-style modernization', added a mixed ownership structure, a socialist market economy and openness, and developed the goals from 'three-in-one' to 'four-in-one'. Since 2012, Guo says, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has widened the goals to 'five-in-one' and begun to build a theoretical system. Guo concludes that Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics are what distinguish Chinese modernization from Western modernization. The author claims it has regional and national value and also world-historical significance, offering a reference for late-developing countries and helping to overcome the problems of Western-style modernization. Guo adds that the achievements of the new era have strengthened institutions, material foundations and spiritual drive. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2023 presented a continuous historical narrative of Chinese modernization from the Opium War to the new era.

The centennial development and historical logic of Chinese Communists' view of communism 中国共产党人共产主义观的百年发展与历史逻辑 Geng Renjie Geng Renjie asks how Chinese Communists' understanding of communism (what it is, what it will be like, how it is to be realised) has developed since the Party's founding in 1921, and what logic runs through that development. Writing in 2023, Geng argues that the Party built a scientific view of communism through the combination of Marxist principles with Chinese realities, and that this development has four mutually supporting dimensions. The article follows these dimensions in turn: practice, understanding of the concept's content, the path to realisation, and the construction of the ideal. It draws on figures from Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Qu Qiubai and Li Da in the early years, through Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi and Chen Yun in the revolutionary period, to Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Xi Jinping. Sources include early lectures and essays, Mao's writings, Deng's talks of the 1980s and Party congress documents. Geng's central claim is that each dimension moves along a distinct trajectory. In practice, the Party shifted from "following the Russians' road" to "taking our own road", a stance Geng credits with helping it withstand the crises of 1956 and 1989–91. In content, understanding deepened from a preliminary acceptance of historical materialism to full command of Marxist philosophy; Mao's 1940 definition of communism as a proletarian ideology and a new social system marks, in Geng's account, the maturing of this view. On the path, early emphasis on proletarian dictatorship gave way, after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), to liberating and developing the productive forces with economic construction at the centre, a shift Geng traces to Deng and sets against the radical transition attempts of the Great Leap Forward. On the ideal, early vague longing for a "Great Harmony" society became the Party's "political soul", and the Party consistently opposes both empty talk of the ideal and abandoning it as remote. Geng concludes that communism is, in turn, a unity of class character and revolutionary character, of necessity and long-term process, of science and justice, and of idealism and realism. The author holds that Chinese Communists must keep developing this scientific view as they pursue the second centenary goal and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, especially amid intense ideological competition between China and the West. Read the original if you want a periodised, source-rich account of how the CPC's official line on communism is traced from the early 1920s to the 20th Party Congress (2022).

The establishment and initial operation of the administrative supervision system in New China (1949–1954) 新中国行政监察体制的建立与初步运行（1949—1954年） Xu Xing Xu Xing asks how New China's administrative supervision system was built and how it worked in its first five years, a stretch that earlier scholarship has covered thinly. Existing work, the author notes, concentrates on intra-Party supervision or on today's national supervision reform. Xu argues that the 1949–1954 system, created under Party leadership and shaped above all by Zhou Enlai, played a real historical role in fighting corruption and bureaucratism and still offers lessons for current reform. The article opens with the roots of the system in the revolutionary base areas: the Soviet-period Workers' and Peasants' Inspection departments, the border-region assemblies of the anti-Japanese war, and the North China People's Supervisory Court of 1948. It then describes the founding of the People's Supervisory Commission under the Government Administration Council, its 1950 trial organizational regulations and its internal departments. Next it covers how the commission operated, including the national supervision conferences of 1951 and 1953, and assesses its results. A closing section draws four implications for the present. Xu identifies three main achievements. The commission focused on financial and economic management, investigating accidents such as the Yiluo coal mine gas explosion; it joined the Three-Antis campaign, disciplining thousands of cadres and helping to handle the Liu Qingshan and Zhang Zishan case; and it built a five-level network that, by September 1954, reached nearly 4,000 organs with close to 20,000 supervisory cadres. The author highlights working principles such as combining top-down inspection with bottom-up supervision by the masses, and combining punishment with education. Xu also reports the dual leadership structure, the abolition of the large administrative regions in 1954, and the replacement of the commission by a Ministry of Supervision. Xu concludes that Zhou Enlai's supervisory thinking supports clean government, mass participation, rigorous management of supervisory cadres and Party leadership. The article links the 1950s move from separate Party and state supervision bodies to later reform, ending with the 2018 National Supervisory Commission and the Supervision Law. Xu presents this as evidence that merging Party and state supervision strengthens constraints on power. Read the original if you want a detailed institutional history of early People's Republic supervision, with figures, regulations and case examples, written from an official Party-history perspective.

Continuously opening up new horizons in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 不断开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Zhang Shihai Zhou Yongwei Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which says Marxism, and specifically Marxism adapted to China and the times, is what ultimately "works", Zhang and Zhou ask why Marxism "works" and how the Party should keep extending its adaptation. They argue that Marxism succeeds because of its own scientific and truth-bearing character. They add that the Chinese Communist Party has consistently pursued theoretical innovation with a high degree of theoretical self-awareness. Writing in 2023, the authors organise the article in three parts. The first examines the sources of Marxism's truth-force. The second reviews how adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has been advanced scientifically. The third looks at the achievements of the past decade and the tasks ahead. A short conclusion discusses the laws governing this process. The authors derive Marxism's truthfulness from four features: its scientific character, grounded in historical materialism and the theory of surplus value; its orientation to the people; its practical character; and its openness as a method rather than a dogma. They then argue that adaptation has run through the Party's history, from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They link each stage to the leaps from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". For the authors, continued adaptation requires basing theory on China's national conditions and experience, drawing on excellent traditional Chinese culture, and upholding the Two Integrations. They present the decade's "three major events" and "three historic victories" as proof that Marxism works in China. The authors conclude that adaptation is never finished. They present Xi Jinping Thought as a model of innovation and as "Marxism of the twenty-first century", and they call for the whole Party to study it and apply it through Chinese modernization. In their closing section they say that opening new horizons demands both a full understanding of the underlying laws and a conscious use of them, and that theory must answer the problems of each era. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-school scholarship in 2023 explained the 20th Congress's "Marxism works" formula and the logic of continuous adaptation.

From the "one integration" to the "Two Integrations": continually opening new horizons in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 从“一个结合”到“两个结合” 不断开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Li Yi Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which stressed combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture, Li Yi asks what the move from the "one integration" to the Two Integrations means. Li argues that the "second integration" extends and logically completes the first. In Li's account it enriches the content of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and marks a new level of understanding of how that adaptation works. The article, published in Marxism Studies in late 2022, has four parts. It first traces the Party's path from Marx and Engels' warnings against dogmatism, through the Zunyi Conference, Mao Zedong's "second integration" of the 1950s and the reform era, to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then treats the Party's historical responsibility as heir to traditional culture, the link between national rejuvenation and cultural revival, and finally how traditional culture should be creatively transformed and innovatively developed. Li's core claim is that the two integrations share the premise of upholding Marxism's basic tenets but differ in emphasis. The first stresses socio-economic reality, with history and culture included in it in a broad sense. The second stresses historical and cultural reality, culture in a narrower sense, which Li treats as a deeper and more lasting force that reacts upon economy and politics. Li holds that Marxism has criticised the dross of tradition most thoroughly and inherited its essence most authentically, because the two agree in moral ideals and values rather than in wording. The Two Integrations are also presented as an answer to the early-modern dispute over ancient and modern, Chinese and Western, in which Li says cultural conservatism and liberal Westernisation both opposed such a union. Li concludes that Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization arise from the Two Integrations, and differ from both Western and Confucian modernization. Li calls for work on three questions: what counts as "fine" in tradition, why integrate (rejecting wholesale Westernisation, "Chinese learning as substance" and cultural conservatism), and how, through practice rather than mere interpretation. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-school account of how the "second integration" is justified historically and theoretically within official discourse.

On the practical character of Marx In commemoration of the 140th anniversary of Marx's death 论马克思的实践品格 Jiang Yingchun Marking the 140th anniversary of Marx's death in 2023, Jiang Yingchun asks what it means to keep Marx "alive among us". The article answers that the best way is to grasp the practical character (shijian pinge) of Marx and his thought, and to keep developing Marxism through practice. Jiang presents this character as the core and soul of Marxism's practical character in general, citing Xi Jinping's remark that Marxism seeks both to "interpret the world" and to "change the world". The article has three sections. The first treats Marx as a revolutionary in the history of thought who settled accounts with idealism and with philosophy detached from life. The second discusses Marx as a unity of the "man of thought" and the "man of action", drawing on obituaries from 1883, Franz Mehring's biography, and Mao Zedong's 1945 remarks on the October Revolution's effect in China. The third examines Marx as leader and promoter of the practice of scientific socialism, through three activities. Jiang argues that Marx grounded his work in practice and that idealist "conjectures" keep reappearing to defend backward social orders. Phenomenology is given as one example, described via a Chinese scholar's judgement as subjective idealism. Following Mehring, Jiang holds that the fighter in Marx always outweighed the thinker, because thought has value only when it guides human emancipation. Jiang criticises scholars who study Marx's texts in detail but will not act as he did. Marx's leadership is traced in three areas. He helped build international workers' organisations: the Communist League and the Communist Manifesto, and the First International. He defended the vanguard character and purity of workers' parties, as in the Critique of the Gotha Programme and the 1879 circular letter, with the German Social Democratic Party's later degeneration offered as a warning. He also fought erroneous currents inside the socialist movement that left private ownership of capital intact. Jiang concludes that reactionary forces will always try to stifle socialism, so studying Marx's practical character is needed for real struggle, for acquiring the skills of struggle and for advancing the cause. Socialist China's continuing efforts to change the world in its own way are called the best way to honour Marx. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how the unity of theory and practice is used to criticise academic detachment and to frame the lessons of the history of the communist movement.

The logic of alienation, the logic of production, the logic of capital Three important shifts in the development of Marx's philosophy 异化逻辑·生产逻辑·资本逻辑 Yang Haifeng How should one grasp the development of Marx's philosophy from the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 to Capital? Yang Haifeng argues that a philosopher is best understood through the cognitive framework that governs each phase of their thought. On this basis Yang holds that Marx passed through three frameworks: a logic of alienation built on alienated labour, a logic of production built on material production, and a logic of capital aimed at the self-valorization of capital. The article is organised in three sections, one for each shift. The first reconstructs the theory of alienated labour against Hegel's philosophy of right, classical political economy, the communist currents of the day (Weitling, Proudhon) and Feuerbach's anthropology. The second follows the turn to historical materialism in The German Ideology and related works. The third reads Capital, including Marx's letters on the dual character of labour, the contradictions of capital and the realm of freedom. Yang's central claim is that Capital is not simply an application of the historical materialism of 1845–46. The logic of production defines production through material means of life, that is, use-value. In Capital, however, use-value only carries exchange-value, and production serves the valorization of capital, so the logic of production is subordinated to the logic of capital. Yang treats this as the deepest of the three shifts and as the key to the specificity of capitalist production. Moral critique of capitalists, on this reading, falls back into capital's own logic, and the contradictions of capital arise from its operation rather than from an a priori human essence. Yang also criticises scholars who say they start from the logic of capital but in fact derive it from the logic of production, a route Yang traces back to Lukács's ontology of social being. Yang concludes that each shift deepened Marx's scientific understanding of history while rebuilding his critique of capitalism on a deeper footing. Only at the stage of the logic of capital could Marx show the historicity and distinctiveness of capitalist production, its internal contradictions and its possible futures. Marx also separates himself from Hegel, since capital's contradictions cannot be resolved by reconciling state and civil society and require overturning capital's logic, with the realm of freedom as the horizon. Read the original if you study the internal development of Marx's thought or the debate over capital-logic versus production-logic readings of Capital.

On the generative mechanism of the Chinese Communist Party's historical confidence 论中国共产党历史自信的生成机制 Chen Jinlong Chen Jinlong asks where the Chinese Communist Party's "historical confidence" comes from. The concept was first put forward by Xi Jinping at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), and the 20th Party Congress (2022) repeated the call to "stand firm in historical confidence and strengthen historical initiative". Chen argues that the Party's historical confidence is produced by four linked elements: historical accumulation, historical consciousness, the grand historical view and historical initiative. The article is a conceptual and interpretive study, built on Xi Jinping's speeches, the third historical resolution (2021) and the report to the 20th Party Congress. Its four main sections take the four elements in turn, and a short conclusion sets out how they relate to one another and to cultural confidence, civilizational confidence and the Four-sphere Confidence. Chen holds that historical accumulation is the objective basis. It consists of the history of the Chinese nation and its civilization, the Party's revolutionary, construction and reform achievements and its spiritual lineage, and the record of Chinese modernization since 1949. Historical consciousness, meaning a clear grasp of historical position, experience and laws, supplies the cognitive basis. Examples are the "ten adherences" of the resolution, laws governing Communist Party rule and socialist construction, and the idea of a new form of human civilization. The grand historical view supplies the methodological basis. It judges Chinese history over a long span and within world history, citing Marx on gunpowder, the compass and printing, and the influence of Chinese culture on the European Enlightenment. Historical initiative turns confidence into practice, and Chen says it is also accompanied by a sense of historical concern. Chen concludes that accumulation, consciousness, confidence and initiative form an organic whole, in which confidence turns into initiative and initiative in turn strengthens confidence. In the author's account, historical confidence is the starting point, cultural and civilizational confidence are embedded in it, and the Four-sphere Confidence and historical confidence contain each other. Respect and reverence for history, Chen says, mark a mature party. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Party theorists explain the sources of historical confidence and its link to the Four-sphere Confidence.

The Nanniwan spirit: a bright banner of "doing it ourselves for ample food and clothing" 南泥湾精神：自己动手、丰衣足食的光辉旗帜 Bi Yuanning Writing in 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Bi Yuanning asks what the "Nanniwan spirit" is, how it arose and why it still matters. The article argues that this spirit, born in the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region's production campaign, embodies revolutionary heroism, the nature and purpose of the people's army, and a tradition that remains relevant today. Bi opens by noting that Xi Jinping led the Politburo Standing Committee to Yan'an soon after the Congress and urged the promotion of the Yan'an spirit. The piece is a Party-journal commentary in three parts: the formation of the Nanniwan spirit, its content, and its value for the present. The historical section covers the Anti-Japanese War's stalemate phase after 1938, the blockade of the border region, and the Eighth Route Army's 359th Brigade, which began reclaiming wasteland at Nanniwan in March 1941. It credits Mao Zedong's call to \"do it ourselves\" (1939) and Zhu De's survey work as the leadership guidance behind it. Bi defines the spirit's core as self-reliance and hard struggle, and breaks it into themes: obeying the Party, overcoming difficulties by one's own hands, serving the people, frugality, officers sharing hardship, and innovation. The evidence includes the brigade's claimed self-sufficiency in grain and funds by 1943 and, citing a 1945 Liberation Daily report, about 354,000 mu cultivated and 37,000 shi of grain harvested, with 10,000 shi paid to the government. Bi also lists organisational innovations such as soldiers' cooperatives, a mixed farming–industry–transport–commerce economy, and labour competitions. Bi cites Mao's praise of this as a \"miracle\" and a \"material basis\" that could not be conquered. Bi concludes that promoting the Nanniwan spirit serves three present needs. It sustains the Party on its \"new road to the examination\", through the \"Three Musts\", the Party's self-reform and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It is also required for advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, in the face of risks and challenges. Finally, it unites the people through a people-centred approach and whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want an example of how Party media present wartime Yan'an traditions as resources for current Party-building and ideological work.

How to keep a clean and healthy political ecosystem at all times 如何始终保持风清气正的政治生态 Jiang Laiyong Writing in 2023, Jiang Laiyong takes up one of the "unique problems" that the Party says a century-old governing party must solve: how to keep a clean and upright political ecosystem at all times. Jiang defines the political ecosystem as the conditions and environment in which political actors operate, made up of political relations, customs, tendencies and character. The article argues that this goal is both essential and very hard to achieve, and that it requires Marxist dialectical thinking and effective measures. The article has three parts. The first sets out why a healthy political ecosystem matters; the second explains why it is arduous and complex to sustain; the third proposes measures under three headings: putting the people first, daring and knowing how to struggle, and a systems approach. On importance, Jiang contends that the political ecosystem shapes the cadres who live in it, so it is key to producing good cadres. It also underpins the solution of the Party's other unique problems and supports Chinese modernization. On difficulty, Jiang says good and bad ecosystems always coexist as contradictory aspects, and the bad one corrupts faster than the good one forms. Causes are complex, including a historical culture of official-centred thinking and reliance on personal connections, uneven development, and gaps in full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Jiang adds that corruption tends to rebound once pressure eases, so the work is long-term. Jiang's proposals include greater transparency and supervision of power, and lifelong accountability for livelihood projects. They also include tackling formalism, bureaucratism and officials' inaction, partly through exit rules for underperforming public employees. Jiang further calls for criticism and self-criticism, and for advancing the three-pronged approach of making officials not dare, not be able and not want to be corrupt. Other proposals are strict cadre-selection standards, supervision of top leaders ("first in command"), rule-of-law methods, assessment indicators for the political ecosystem, and heavier penalties for bribe-givers. Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated scholar's account of how political ecology is framed in anti-corruption and cadre-management policy around 2023.

The formation, sources and logic of the narrative discourse of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 中国化时代化马克思主义叙事话语的形成、来源与逻辑 Jia Huize Responding to the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to build a Chinese discourse and narrative system and tell China's story well, Jia asks how the theoretical narrative discourse of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times took shape. The article treats this discourse as a core part of Chinese discourse and of the wider narrative system. It argues that it can be understood through three basic questions: its formation, its sources and its internal logic. The article is built in three parts. The first periodises the discourse into four stages: from the founding of the Party to 1949; from 1949 to reform and opening up; from reform and opening up to the 18th Party Congress (2012); and the period since 2012. The second identifies six sources of discourse. The third sets out six principles that Jia presents as the discourse's internal logic. In the historical part, Jia traces how each generation of Party leaders produced its own vocabulary: Mao Zedong's revolutionary and socialist-construction terms, the reform-era terms of Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and, since 2012, Xi Jinping's terms such as Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. The six sources are Marxist discourse (the basic source), the discourse of Chinese practice, traditional Chinese culture, the language of ordinary people, Western and other foreign discourse, and domestic and international scholarship.
