Jia ranks them: Marxist discourse supplies the foundation and method, while practice and tradition carry the Chinese context, and the rest are supplements. The logic is summarised as being based on practice, grounded in national conditions, problem-oriented, people-centred, referenced to the times and oriented to popularisation. Jia concludes that this discourse grows out of Marxism and is continually refined from the experience of Chinese practice, drawing on traditional culture, popular speech and other resources. The author sees the three questions as the basis for developing the discourse further and explaining why Marxism works in China. Jia adds that further research should cover textual carriers, political standpoint, modes of thinking and discursive techniques. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-theoretical account of how Chinese leaders' signature phrases are classified by period, source and logic.

Core socialist values: the unity of "what" and "how to build" socialism with Chinese characteristics 社会主义核心价值观：中国特色社会主义“是什么”与“怎么建”的统一 Sun Weiping Yin Bangwen Sun Weiping and Yin Bangwen ask how the core socialist values relate to socialism with Chinese characteristics. They argue that the values express what that socialism is and also show how it should be built. In their account, the values are a concrete form of the communist values of Marx and Engels in contemporary China, and an organic part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article has four sections. It first traces how the core socialist values emerged as a product of the Party's "value consciousness", from Marx and Lenin through Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then maps the three levels and twelve concepts onto the essence of socialism, and examines the relation between these values and "common human values". The last section sets out how the values bear on building socialism with Chinese characteristics. The authors argue that each value matches a feature of socialism's essence as Deng Xiaoping defined it. Prosperity and common prosperity answer the liberation of the productive forces; democracy and the rule of law answer people's mastery of the country; civilisation and harmony follow from public ownership. They hold that the values absorb common human values such as peace, democracy and freedom, while the socialist values should in turn guide those common values. They contrast this with Western "universal values", which they say rest on private ownership and the "logic of capital". On practice, Sun and Yin call for three things. The values should serve as the shared ideological basis for uniting a plural and fragmented society. They should guide institutional reform and top-level design, in a two-way interaction between values and institutions. They should direct national education so as to train "new people of the era". They conclude that the values give socialism with Chinese characteristics its direction and its spiritual core. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theory account that links the core socialist values to the essence of socialism, to common human values and to institution-building.

A glimpse of the transcendence of Marx's labour theory A counter-critique of Arendt's critique of Marx's theory of labour 马克思劳动理论的超越性管窥 Han Meiqun Yi Huanhuan Hannah Arendt, in The Human Condition and her writings on Marx and the Western tradition of political thought, questioned and criticised Marx's theory of labour. Han and Yi argue that, because Marx and Arendt start from different points and aim at different ends, her criticisms rest on many misunderstandings. They contend that Marx's labour theory does not return to traditional Western philosophy but transcends its order and its traditional view of development. The article first sorts existing scholarship on Arendt's critique into three views: complementarity, misreading and enrichment. It then takes up two charges in turn: the "dichotomy" charge, and the charge that Marx's theory contains an "unnatural growth of the natural". Each section sets out Arendt's position and then Marx's reply. A final section sets out four aspects of Marx's theory: labour and human essence, social practice, capitalist production, and free and all-round human development. On the first charge, Arendt places Marx within the tradition running from Plato, so that he merely inverts the hierarchy of contemplative and active life. She also reads him as wanting to "abolish labour" and as treating violence as action. The authors reply that this misreads Marx's critique of alienated labour. In their account, Marx raises labour, the lowest activity of active life, to the highest place, and defines the human being as a labouring animal rather than a political one. They add that his aim is changing the world, so that philosophy ends in practice rather than in contemplation. On the second charge, Arendt holds that the theory carries totalitarian elements, dissolves the public and private realms into a labouring society, and leads through automation to a consumer society. The authors answer that it frees labouring subjects and gives them freedom of association and self-realisation. They argue that automation shortens necessary labour time and widens free time for all-round development, and that the theory overcomes the opposition between humans and nature. The authors conclude that Arendt's objections amount to a utopian construction of classical political philosophy that seeks a spiritual refuge for capitalist elites. They call for returning to the authentic Marx and grasping the transcendent character of his labour theory. The aim is a socialist view of labour suited to China, one that respects labour, knowledge, talent and creation, in the context of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Arendt's reading of Marx on labour, or an example of how labour theory is tied to the socialist view of labour in China.

Commemorating International Women's Day means fighting for women's freedom and equality Mao Zedong's 1939 Yan'an speech and a Party chronology of the women's movement 纪念三八妇女节，就是要争取妇女的自由与平等 Mao Zedong This compilation, posted on International Women's Day 2023, is not a research article. It combines excerpts from Mao Zedong's speech of 8 March 1939 in Yan'an with a Party-centred chronology of the Chinese women's movement. Its message is that women's liberation depends on organisation and on joining the wider struggle for national and social liberation. The first part reproduces Mao's speech and his 1939 inscription poem for the magazine Chinese Women. The second part is a chronology from 1921 to 2023, drawn from sources such as Xinhua and CCTV. It covers the Soviet areas, the War of Resistance against Japan, the first national women's congress of 1949, the 1954 Constitution, the reform era and the Party congresses since 2012. In the speech, Mao says the Chinese nation and people lack freedom and equality under imperialism and feudal forces. He argues that no great task, whether resisting Japan or increasing production, can succeed without women. He adds that women's strength is scattered unless they form organisations. He also holds that social liberation requires mobilising women, and that women's own liberation requires joining that struggle, with rights to manage affairs, to hold meetings and to speak. The chronology presents equality policy as continuous under Party leadership. It cites the Party's gender-equality commitments in the 18th Party Congress (2012) report, repeated in the 19th and 20th, and a greeting from Xi Jinping on 6 March 2023. The compilation presents women's emancipation as a project realised under Party leadership, from Mao's call for organisation to current policy. Read the original if you want Mao's 1939 wording on women and the national struggle, or a short official chronology of the women's movement and its legal milestones.

Arming young people with the Party's scientific theory 用党的科学理论武装青年 Han Xiping Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which told the whole Party to treat youth work as strategic work, Han Xiping asks why young people must be armed with the Party's scientific theory and how this should be done. Han argues that this theoretical arming is a distinctive strength of the Communist Party of China and that it matters more in the new era. The piece is a commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts. The article has three parts. The first presents theoretical arming as the Party's advantage. The second explains why the new era makes it more urgent. The third sets out three ways to carry it out. Han draws throughout on Xi Jinping's remarks on youth work, and also cites Marx and Lenin. Han's first claim is that Marxism is scientific and open to development, so the Party can answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. In this account the Party has won over young people because Marxist parties, unlike bourgeois parties, treat youth as friends and successors rather than as tools. The second claim is that today's young people will be the main force of modernization up to mid-century, and that hostile forces are trying to Westernize and divide them. Han describes this as a struggle the Party cannot afford to lose, and calls for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to follow each theoretical innovation. Third, Han proposes three ways to deliver this arming. It should be systematic, with staged and differentiated programmes coordinated by Party organizations, the Communist Youth League, Party schools and universities. It should be practical, showing young people the results of the past decade and building lasting mechanisms for social practice. It should be modern, using the internet and platforms such as Study Xi Strong Nation (Xuexi Qiangguo) in language that young people find accessible. Han concludes that the quality of youth education will shape China's future. Arming young people with the Party's theory is described as a proven path that sets the Party apart from other parties. The goal is to raise qualified successors who can take on building a modern socialist country and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists justify ideological work among youth and what institutional measures they propose.

Chinese modernization: a great creation in "skipping the Caudine Forks" 中国式现代化：“跨越卡夫丁峡谷”的伟大创造 Wang Gonglong How can an economically and culturally backward country modernize? Wang Gonglong takes up this question through Marx's late hypothesis that Russia might "skip the Caudine Forks" of capitalism. Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang argues that Chinese modernization is a socialist path taken by a non-Western country without passing through the capitalist system. In this reading it both verifies Marx's hypothesis in practice and develops it creatively. The article has four sections. The first traces the origins of the hypothesis against Marx's critique of Western capitalist modernization. The second presents Chinese modernization as the successful "answer" to a problem that Marx only "posed" and that the Soviet Union, in Wang's account, failed to solve. The third sets out three ways in which China's experience confirms the hypothesis. The fourth lists five creative developments of it. Wang reconstructs the hypothesis in three logical steps: skipping is necessary, possible and conditional. The conditions are economic (absorbing capitalism's positive achievements, including advanced productive forces and the market), historical (socialist victory in the West) and revolutionary (a mutually reinforcing revolution in East and West). Wang observes that the last two conditions never materialised, which left the question open. The author's answer is that China built socialist institutions that in turn drove productive forces forward, combined rapid growth with long-term stability, and set out to avoid capitalism's "chain of problems". The article lists these problems as polarisation, alienation, crisis, plunder abroad and ecological strain. Wang names five creative developments: the socialist market economy; a "parallel" strategy that integrates industrialisation, urbanisation, agricultural modernization and informatisation, in contrast to the Western "serial" sequence; a path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; a framework for coexistence between two systems through a community with a shared future for mankind; and inspiration for other developing countries. The author concludes that the path answers a major question in the history of socialism and will shape world socialism and human modernization in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholarship links Marx's late writings on Russia to the official narrative of Chinese modernization.

Major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era: strategy and practical requirements 新时代中国特色大国外交战略及其实践要求 Gao Zugui Gao Zugui, director of the Institute of International Strategy at the Central Party School, asks what strategy and practical requirements the 20th Party Congress (2022) set for major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics. The article argues that as the world faces profound change, Chinese diplomacy should be built on a single overall goal, a community with a shared future for mankind, pursued through a peaceful development path, an independent foreign policy of peace, opening up and reform of global governance. It also holds that China must be ready to struggle when its core interests are threatened. The article begins with Gao's reading of the international situation, then moves through eight areas of practice. These cover the aim and overall goal of foreign work; the peaceful development path; the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and a new type of international relations; opening up as a basic national policy; global governance; the Global Development Initiative and Global Security Initiative; and common values of humanity. A final section calls for daring and skilful struggle. Gao draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report. Gao describes the "great changes unseen in a century" as a change in the world, in the era and in history. In his account, developed countries' share of world GDP fell from 78.85 per cent in 2001 to 59.08 per cent in 2021, while emerging and developing economies rose to 40.92 per cent. He also points to rising unilateralism and protectionism, and to a renewed coexistence of capitalism and socialism. Against this background, the article presents the community with a shared future for mankind as a Chinese contribution that does not replace one system or civilisation with another. It treats China's development as peaceful by character and rejects the claim that a strong country must seek hegemony. It sets "extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits" against hegemonic and bloc politics. It presents the "common values of humanity" as going beyond Western "universal values" and the clash-of-civilisations thesis. Gao concludes that China must keep the initiative over its own development and security by relying chiefly on its own strength. He expects external containment to intensify, with the United States named as the main source of pressure. He says China must keep its strategic resolve, hold to bottom-line thinking and be prepared for severe tests, while working for peace and common development. Read the original if you want a systematic Party School account of how the 20th Party Congress's foreign policy line is framed and justified.

On the theoretical premises of research on foreign Marxism 论国外马克思主义研究的理论前提 Juan Hongfei Juan Hongfei takes up a methodological problem in Chinese research on foreign Marxism. The author argues that the field, though large and productive, pays too little attention to its own intellectual premises. Citing another scholar's criticism, Juan describes a dominant 'data-introduction' style that reads thinkers' texts in the abstract, cut off from their historical setting. In Juan's account, this makes research increasingly empirical and fragmented. The article proposes three premises: study of Marx's own thought, the history of ideas, and the real history of the twentieth century. The article has three main sections, one for each premise. The first treats research on Marx as the root of the field. The second treats the history of ideas as its overall perspective. The third treats twentieth-century world history as its real-world foundation. Juan draws on cases including Georg Lukács, Karl Korsch and Antonio Gramsci, Sartre and Althusser, ecological and feminist Marxism, East European new Marxism, and digital capitalism. In the first section, Juan holds that any current can be called Marxist only in relation to Marx's thought. Judging it requires grasping Marx's stance, viewpoint and method, not merely whether it uses his concepts. On this reading, humanist and scientistic Marxism each took up one of two logics in Marx: human emancipation and the critical analysis of capital. Juan holds that Marx's system unites them, and that post-1970s currents often draw only resources from Marx and in places depart from him. In the second section, Juan says the history of ideas lets researchers place new thinkers and concepts, link currents and avoid fragmentation. It also lets them read the field alongside China's own shift from negative criticism to affirmative borrowing. In the third, Juan ties each major turn in foreign Marxism to a historical problem. These include the contrast between the Russian and European revolutions, the May 1968 events, financial capital and the 2008 crisis, and the Eastern European reform experience. Juan adds that China's rise and what the article calls 'the great changes unseen in a century' now reshape capitalism. Juan concludes that foreign Marxism can only be properly understood and positioned if these three premises are combined. Research should also involve real dialogue with foreign thinkers and scholars. Done this way, the field can supply theoretical resources for addressing China's practical problems and for building Chinese Marxist theory, while Marxism keeps its leading position. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's methodological critique of how foreign Marxism is studied in China, or a compact account of how that field is periodised and justified.

Marx's critique of the bourgeois view of interest 马克思对资产阶级利息观的批判 Liu Huajun Why does capital bear interest, and should interest exist at all? Liu Huajun takes up this old question, which Böhm-Bawerk framed as one of what 'is' and what 'ought' to be, and examines how Marx answered bourgeois political economy on it. The article argues that Marx treats interest as a share of surplus value, that is, of unpaid labour. On this reading, bourgeois economists tried to make interest look rational by hiding that origin. The article is organised in six parts. It begins with the denial of a 'natural rate of interest' (Locke against Massie). It then turns to the relation between interest and profit in Hume, Smith, Ricardo, Say and the Currency School. Next come Marx's dissolution of the 'qualitative division' of profit, his rejection of the claim that interest is the 'price of capital', and his view that interest belongs to labour, followed by a short conclusion. Liu draws on Capital Volume III and the 1861–63 manuscripts, comparing the two texts' wording. Liu argues that bourgeois writers wanted both to keep interest and to lower it, and so invented a natural rate. Marx, citing Massie, counters that supply and demand for money cannot fix interest, whose determination is empirical and contingent. Liu holds that the economists blur the link between interest and industrial profit so that profit appears unconnected with labour. For Marx, by contrast, interest only divides surplus value between money-capitalist and functioning capitalist. Interest-bearing capital is mere form, and money lent circulates as M + ΔM, with ΔM drawn from surplus value. Liu then reads Marx's remark that interest as the 'price of capital' is irrational. In Liu's account, the absurdity lies in treating capital as a commodity, whose use-value is then presented as interest. This move hides the fact that capital extracts surplus labour. Liu concludes that interest expresses capital's 'unlimited and endless' drive beyond its limits, and that interest-bearing capital hides this drive most completely. Equating interest with ground rent makes capital look like a thing that creates value in itself. Liu says that for interest to produce value it must return to the production process, where labour is the core of capital. The author also notes that the relation between labour and capital, on which realising interest depends, needs a separate treatment. Read the original if you want a close textual reading of Marx's critique of interest, including the comparison of Capital Volume III with the 1861–63 manuscripts.

Foreign Marxist views on the nature of the socialist road with Chinese characteristics: an analysis 国外马克思主义的中国特色社会主义道路性质观辨析 Ma Jinrun Yu Kaiyue Ding Xiaoqin How do Marxist scholars outside China characterise the road of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and where do they go wrong? The authors argue that a sizeable body of foreign Marxist work reaches mistaken or one-sided verdicts on the nature of this road. In their view, a correct judgement is the precondition for assessing its achievements and its global significance fairly. The article sorts foreign views into four types: "market socialism" (David Schweickart, G.A. Cohen, John Roemer, Nat Weinstein, M.J. Gordon); "capitalism", including neoliberalism and state capitalism (Robert Weil, Martin Hart-Landsberg, Paul Burkett, David Harvey, Samir Amin); "combination of several economic systems" (Pivovarova, Schaff and others); and a "third road" (Arif Dirlik, David Laibman). It then examines three causes of these errors and sets out the authors' own account of the road's nature. The authors reject each label in turn. Market socialism, they say, is vaguely defined, and Schweickart's and Roemer's versions differ from China's primary stage of socialism, which retains private ownership and wage labour. The capitalist verdict, they argue, rests on opposing socialism to the market and on inequality. China, they respond, keeps public ownership as the mainstay, treats widening gaps as temporary on the way to common prosperity, and differs from capitalism, where polarisation springs from the system itself. They fault the mixed-economy view for adding systems mechanically, and the third-road view for ignoring continuity of principle. The authors trace the errors to deviant criteria for what socialism is, an economics-only research perspective, and neglect of Communist Party leadership, which they link to a Western-style view of democracy. Their own account rests on Xi Jinping's formula of the dialectical unity of the theoretical logic of scientific socialism and the historical logic of China's development. They test the road across seven dimensions: goals, leadership, market economy, democratic politics, culture, a harmonious society and ecological civilization. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese critique of named Western Marxist positions on China's system, set out in the Party's own terms.

The internal logic, scientific connotation and fundamental guidelines for establishing a correct view of Party history 树立正确党史观的内在逻辑、科学内涵与根本遵循 He Xinchun Li Wenrui Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls for sustained education in the histories of the Party, New China, reform and opening up, and socialism, this article asks how a correct view of Party history should be established. The authors define such a view as people's overall understanding of the history of the Communist Party of China. They argue that it rests on historical materialism, materialist dialectics and seeking truth from facts, and that it is a political question bearing on the fate of the Party and the state, not merely an academic topic. The article has three parts. The first sets out the internal logic behind a correct view: historical materialism as its theoretical base, the "big history" outlook as its method, the Party's hundred-year achievements as its practical foundation, and the educational and advisory functions of Party history as its inner driving force. The second sets out the scientific connotation of the view through five components: political, popular, spatio-temporal, mission-related and learning-related. The third turns to the fundamental guidelines, drawn mainly from Xi Jinping's statements on Party history since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors hold that a correct view starts from social being determining social consciousness, and that it must place the Party's century within 5,000 years of Chinese civilisation, 500 years of world socialism and 180 years of modern Chinese history. Each component carries a principle: Party history "belongs to the Party", Party spirit and the people's character are united, the Party's historical position is fixed in time and space, the Party is a mission-driven party, and study follows seeking truth from facts. The guidelines they list include grasping the theme running through Party history, namely the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They also include studying the "three historical resolutions" and evaluating major problems without letting achievements hide mistakes or mistakes cancel achievements. The authors name historical nihilism as the main present threat. They describe it as rooted in idealist history, exaggerating Party errors, slandering leaders and heroes, and using fragments to deny the whole. To counter it they propose theoretical education, grasping the significance of the Two Establishes, strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, tightening ideological work and legal measures against defaming history, and promoting core socialist values. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how Chinese Party-history scholars frame the "correct view of Party history" and the campaign against historical nihilism.

The course and experience of Party political building in the new era 新时代党的政治建设历程及经验 Li Zhenghua Gu Xunbao Li Zhenghua and Gu Xunbao ask how the Communist Party of China has developed its "political building" (political construction) since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what lessons follow for the new journey ahead. They argue that the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has raised political building to the leading position within Party building, advancing it in both theory and practice, and that this is significant for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is organised chronologically and then thematically. The first section covers the five years after 2012, when new concepts and measures appeared. The second covers the period from the 19th Party Congress (2017), when political building was placed first among the Party's tasks. The third draws four basic lessons. The authors define political building as work on political conviction, political leadership, political capability and a clean political ecosystem, aimed at unity and consistent action across the Party. In the authors' account, the first phase introduced the Two Upholds, the "four consciousnesses", "political ecology" and "intra-Party political culture", and "political capability". It also brought measures such as political inspection tours, stricter intra-Party political life, the anti-corruption campaign and a people-centred stance. After 2017, they say, a conceptual system took shape, with over 70 concepts grouped under four headings. Political building was defined as the "fundamental" building that guides all others, and the Two Establishes were put forward. In practice it was made to guide ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional work, while the Party's basic line was updated and its overall leadership reinforced. Li and Gu draw four lessons: strengthen Party regulations (they cite 3,615 currently valid by 2021); focus on the "critical few" leading cadres to bring along the "vast majority"; raise political awareness and capability through Party-spirit education and training; and keep the fundamental aim of serving the people and meeting their aspirations for a better life. They present each as guidance for the new journey. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned chronology of Party political building, with the key documents and dates, for study of Party-building discourse.

Zhou Enlai and the second large-scale import of complete sets of technology and equipment in New China 周恩来与新中国第二次大规模引进成套技术设备 Chi Aiping Chi Aiping takes up a gap in the existing scholarship: the background and outline of the 1972–1975 import of complete sets of technology and equipment from Western countries have been studied, but Zhou Enlai's role in deciding and carrying it out has not. The article argues that, with Mao Zedong's support, Zhou led the State Council's working group in launching and steering what it calls the "second large-scale import", which followed the Soviet-aided 156 projects of 1954. It presents the programme as a major spur to later economic and technological progress and as a showcase of Zhou's strategic judgement. The article has three parts. The first traces how the decision was made and started, from the international and domestic situation of the late 1960s and early 1970s to the State Planning Commission's January 1972 report on chemical-fibre and fertiliser plants, and then to the "4.3 Plan" of 1973. The second examines Zhou's organisational and strategic guidance during implementation. The third assesses the programme's significance and the thinking behind it. Chi draws on leaders' marginal notes, commission reports and Zhou's talks with foreign guests. Chi's central claim is that Zhou made the key choices at each stage. He set the working line of "learn, use, adapt, create", picked negotiators, accepted a price concession to secure the French fibre contract, and told the commission to merge scattered departmental requests into one larger plan. The 4.3 Plan finally covered 26 projects worth about 4.3 billion US dollars, later raised by 880 million. In implementation, Chi says, Zhou strengthened the working group by bringing in Chen Yun and then Deng Xiaoping, backed the use of bank deposits and deferred payment for foreign exchange, and promoted export earnings through the Guangzhou trade fair and processing of imported materials. Chi adds that Zhou's remarks on bank ties, foreign capital and cheap labour anticipated later opening-up practice, and that he worked against the "Gang of Four" and ultra-leftist interference. Chi concludes that the programme brought advanced technology, management ideas and market information, and trained cadres and specialists who later supported reform and opening up. In the article's account, the 18 fertiliser, fibre and alkylbenzene projects, 63.84 per cent of investment, laid the material base for solving China's food and clothing problems. Chi holds that the six principles of the plan, including self-reliance and combining learning with original creation, remain a useful reference. Read the original if you want a documented, Party-history account of how Zhou Enlai's role in the early 1970s opening to Western technology is presented in official Chinese scholarship.

The Lei Feng spirit as a spiritual summit of faithfully carrying forward the Party's original aspiration and mission 雷锋精神是忠实传承党的初心使命的精神高地 Yan Xiaofeng Marking the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other senior leaders' inscriptions for Lei Feng, this commentary (first published in People's Daily, 5 March 2023) asks how Lei Feng should be understood on the new journey after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Yan Xiaofeng argues that the Lei Feng spirit should be grasped from the standpoint of the great founding spirit of the Party, and that its core is the Party's original aspiration and mission, which runs through the whole spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists. The article has three parts. The first places the Lei Feng spirit within the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists, whose source is the founding spirit. The second presents Lei Feng as a model of putting the original aspiration and mission into practice. The third links the spirit to what Yan calls the problems unique to a large party, and to the Party's tasks in advancing Chinese modernization. Yan contends that the Lei Feng spirit grew out of the founding spirit and became part of the genealogy in its own right. In Yan's account it belongs to the period of socialist revolution and construction, arose among ordinary grassroots Party members, and was formed by the People's Army in peacetime. Yan defines it as lofty ideals and faith, a spirit of service, dedication to one's work, innovation and hard struggle. Yan reads it as the continuation of the Zhang Side spirit under socialism, and cites Lei Feng's diary and conduct as examples of unity of word and deed. The central move is to treat remembering the original aspiration and mission as the first of the Party's unique problems. Learning from Lei Feng is said to help Party members withstand the "four tests" and overcome the "four dangers": the tests of long-term governance, of reform and opening up, of the market economy and of the external environment. Yan says it also helps against spiritual slackening and corruption. Yan concludes that Party members and officials must lead by example so that learning from Lei Feng becomes everyday practice, especially among young people. Doing so would strengthen the Party's bond with the people and its commitment to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Every step towards the second centenary goal is described as putting the original aspiration and mission into practice. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-affiliated scholarship ties the Lei Feng model to the spiritual genealogy and to Party-building themes after the 20th Party Congress.

The political-civilisation implications of the Chinese modernization path Centred on the new type of state system 中国式现代化道路的政治文明意蕴探析 Li Yingrui Li Yingrui asks what the political-civilisation content of Chinese modernization is, and answers by looking at China's "new type of state system" (xinxing guojia zhidu). The article argues that the path's political-civilisation meaning is concentrated in this system, which it presents as both distinctively Chinese and as enriching the forms of human political civilisation. Li treats the topic as relevant to developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, modernising national governance and telling China's story abroad. The article has three parts. The first traces the system's century-long evolution in five "historic developments": early Soviet-republic experiments, the New Democratic republic, the establishment of the socialist state system in the 1950s, the formation of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics after reform and opening up, and the more mature and defined system of the new era. The second part sets out the system's threefold meaning and six defining features. The third assesses its contributions to human political civilisation. Li defines the system as socialist, as a system with Chinese characteristics, and as a new kind of modern state system. On the last point, Li says it has not fully escaped the logic of capital, yet it criticises and goes beyond the capitalist modern state through what the article calls "new modernity". Its six features are a economic base with public ownership as the mainstay, Communist Party leadership, the political value of putting the people first, democratic centralism, whole-process people's democracy, and a united-front "base colour". Li then claims three contributions: a "people's logic" that breaks capital's domination of state-building, a Chinese democratic discourse that criticises and goes beyond Western democratic discourse, and a demonstration of institutional diversity that guides developing countries. In Li's account, Western liberal democracy faces crises and the "end of history" thesis has been refuted. Li concludes that the system, as a product of the Party's creative development of the Marxist theory of the state, can promote China's development and has world-historical significance. Li calls for building a theoretical, discourse and academic system for China's institutional construction, rebutting distortions of the Chinese path, and turning institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Chinese Party theorists narrate the state system's history and present its comparison with Western political models.

Four dimensions for understanding the distinctive features of Chinese modernization and its world-historical significance 理解中国式现代化特质及其世界历史意义的四重维度 Sun Leqiang Responding to Xi Jinping's speech at the study session on the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022), this newspaper commentary asks how Chinese modernization should be understood. Sun Leqiang argues that its distinctive features and world-historical significance can be grasped only through a "big view of history" and a comparison with the Western path. The piece is organised into four dialectical pairs, each a way of reading Chinese modernization: understanding China from China (the stage and the whole), China from the world (the global and the national), the world from China (the particular and the universal), and the world from the world (diversity and unity). In the first two dimensions, Sun holds that Chinese modernization is inseparable from Party leadership, the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and China's fine traditional culture, and must be placed within the continuity of Chinese history rather than a single period. Against the Western claim that modernization equals Westernization, the author describes the Western path as capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist, and presents the five features named at the 20th Party Congress as a different model. In the last two dimensions, Sun argues that this particular path has universal meaning, because it sublates the defects of Western modernization and offers a new form of human civilisation. Historical materialism supplies unity, while concrete historical paths are diverse. Sun concludes that Western modernization opened world history but cannot complete it, and that Chinese modernization represents the direction of human progress. As the "great changes unseen in a century" deepen, the author predicts that a new pattern breaking through the capitalist world system will inevitably arrive. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists frame Chinese modernization against Western modernization in 2023.

Chinese modernization and the exploration of a new form of intelligent civilization 中国式现代化探索智能文明新形态 Gao Qiqi Gao Qiqi, in a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks how Chinese modernization can shape the coming age of artificial intelligence. Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Chinese modernization offers a picture different from the Western model, Gao argues that it has distinct advantages for exploring a new form of intelligent civilization under the framework of common prosperity and high-quality development. The article first reviews China's modernization during the third industrial revolution, which Gao divides into the computer, internet and mobile internet stages. It then turns to the fourth industrial revolution, the intelligence revolution, and to the rivalry between modernization models. A final section sets out China's institutional strengths for what Gao calls intelligent civilization. Gao holds that China has moved from distant to close pursuit of the leading countries and that this reflects a learning from, and surpassing of, both the Soviet and American models. In artificial intelligence, Gao concedes that the United States leads in general large-model technology such as ChatGPT, while China has strengths in market scale, talent and institutional planning. Gao describes US entity lists, restricted cooperation and technology alliances as an attempt to wall off advanced productive forces. Because the intelligence revolution may bring creative destruction, unemployment and social polarisation, Gao argues that a new-type whole-nation system, shared computing and data platforms, intellectual property protection and common prosperity are needed. Gao concludes that intelligent civilization requires innovation combined with responsibility: original innovation to bring China to the front in productive forces, and institutional design so that most people share the gains. Gao expects Chinese modernization to be refined further and to become a model for this new civilization. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese scholar links the AI competition with the United States to the claims of Chinese modernization.

Party members' reading activities in the early years of the Party and the Great Revolution period 建党之初和大革命时期党员读书活动的开展 Yi Fenglin Organising Party members to read in a planned way is described by Yi Fenglin as a fine tradition of the Communist Party of China and a basis for its later study system. The article asks how the Party, in the years after its founding in 1921 and during the Great Revolution (1924–27), set about organising reading among its members. Yi argues that these early efforts laid the groundwork for later systems of Party study. Using the approaches of reading history and organisational history, and combining macro and micro perspectives, the article draws on Party and Communist Youth League reports, letters, memoirs and resolutions from Hankou, Shanghai, Nanjing, Beijing, Guangdong, Jiangxi and elsewhere. Because Party and League work overlapped heavily at the time, Yi also includes League members. The article is organised in five parts: the background, the planned content of reading, the methods, the material conditions provided, and the results. Yi argues that reading became a key route for training members because weak theoretical grounding and discipline were widely reported, while teachers, funds and time made large training schools hard to run. The Party therefore planned reading lists (for example Yun Daiying's 1927 list and the Guangdong League's 1926 list) that stressed Marxist theory, Party documents and periodicals such as Xiangdao. Reading combined individual study with branch-level group discussion, supported by guidance, tests of understanding, supervision and links to practical work. The Party guaranteed supply through translation and editorial committees, its own publishing bodies, Party and League periodicals, and libraries. According to the article, the results were firmer communist conviction, better revolutionary skills such as judging political disputes, and organisational growth, as members recommended readings to others and local Party founders in Jiangxi used reading to recruit. Yi concludes that organised reading strengthened members' ideological level and working ability and increased the cohesion and fighting capacity of the Party organisation. The article presents this early practice as part of the Party's tradition of self-building. Read the original if you are interested in the early history of Party education, reading practices and local Party organisation, and want archival examples of specific reading lists and methods.

An analysis of Marx's early communist thought A reading based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 马克思早期共产主义思想探析 Xie Xiaojuan Li Shuting Xie Xiaojuan and Li Shuting ask what Marx's first systematic account of communism, in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, contains and why it matters. They argue that the Manuscripts set out a communism grounded in the sublation of private property and the human being's return to itself. In their view this work prepared Marx's later "new worldview". They also claim that revisiting it helps strengthen belief in communism and the shared ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in support of the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The article has three parts. The first treats the critical premises of Marx's thinking: his critiques of crude communism, of political communism, and of Hegel's idealist view of nature. The second sets out the basic content of communism in the Manuscripts. The third examines the route to its realisation. The authors close by linking the Manuscripts to The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. In the authors' reading, Marx judged earlier communisms to be incomplete. Crude communism, they say, merely redistributes property mechanically, never reaches the level of private property, and negates human individuality. The two political forms recognised alienation but remained "unfinished". Against these and against Hegel's abstract treatment of labour, Marx defined communism as the positive sublation of private property and alienated labour. The authors present this as three unities: the real appropriation of human essence, the return of the human being to a social existence, and the fusion of humanism and naturalism. On the path to communism, the authors argue, Marx held that it must draw on all the wealth created under private property. It also rests on large-scale industry and the natural sciences, and it requires the full liberation of human needs, senses and individuality. They conclude that the Manuscripts, despite Feuerbach's influence, already go beyond his outlook and contain the seeds of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of the 1844 Manuscripts' account of communism and how it is linked to Marx's later works.

Upholding fundamental principles and breaking new ground in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 守正创新推进马克思主义中国化时代化 Deng Chundong Deng Chundong takes up a principle from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), 'We must stay committed to the principle of upholding fundamental truths and breaking new ground' (守正创新). The article, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2023, argues that this principle is the key to continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. In Deng's account, abandoning fundamentals leads to betrayal of Marxism, while abandoning innovation leads to dogmatism and stagnation. The piece is a three-part commentary in the style of Party theory writing. It first sets out why the principle matters, drawing on the history of Marxism, world socialism and the Party's century of struggle. It then explains the 'three unwaverings' that make up fidelity to fundamentals, and finally the requirements of innovation. Deng relies heavily on Xi Jinping's statements and the 20th Party Congress report. On fidelity, Deng calls for unwavering commitment to the basic principles of Marxism, to the Party's overall leadership, and to socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author calls Party leadership the 'core code' of past achievements. On innovation, Deng presents the two as dialectically unified: both rest on respect for objective laws, namely the laws governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. Deng warns against treating rigid dogmatism or repeated past errors as fidelity. Deng also warns against treating policies that depart from Marxist fundamentals, or the copying of Western capitalist governance, as innovation. Deng proposes that theoretical innovation start from China's actual conditions and combine Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. It should also answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. This means studying contemporary capitalism and the 'great changes unseen in a century', and engaging with Marxism outside China selectively, neither rejecting it wholesale nor copying it. The article ends by calling for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to guide practice and for new openings under the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists frame the balance between orthodoxy and innovation after the 20th Party Congress.

The Western tradition, core orientation and intellectual effects of Marx's thought on community 马克思共同体思想的西方传统、核心指向与思想效应 Shen Jiangping Ding Yaopeng Marx never defined "community" (Gemeinschaft, Gemeinwesen) explicitly, and his remarks on it are scattered across his works. Shen and Ding ask how his thought on community grew out of the Western tradition, what its core is, and how it should be read today. They argue that Marx sublated earlier Western ideas of community, and that his idea of a "true community" is a scientific theory but not a fixed dogma. It has to be developed in step with changing historical conditions. The article has three main parts. The first surveys pre-Marxian Western thought: the moral community of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the contract communities from Augustine and Hobbes to Rousseau, the rational communities of Kant (right), Hegel (ethical life) and Feuerbach (love), and the utopian socialists Saint-Simon, Owen and Fourier. The second reconstructs Marx's own account from his early journalism to Capital and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. The third follows later developments: Lenin on the state, Western critics such as Hayek, Hardt and Negri's "multitude", and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Shen and Ding identify three persistent themes in the tradition: the relation of individual to community, the gradual separation of "community" from "state", and the anticipation of an ideal society. Marx, in their account, turns the first into two relations (individual and whole, self-consciousness and universal consciousness) and three principles (freedom, unity of collective and private interest, human emancipation beyond political emancipation). He treats the capitalist state as an "illusory community" and the "association of free individuals" as the true one. He proposes to reach it by abolishing bourgeois private property and "re-establishing individual property". The authors judge Hardt and Negri's call for the multitude to "exit" capital and state to be right about capitalism's property form but without an economic basis. They also argue that the community with a shared future for mankind, part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is not a linear development of Marx's true community. In their view it answers a different question: coexistence among states and systems in a long period before communism, when Marx allowed the state to persist. The authors conclude that the true community will be realised only in a future communist society. Until then, Marx's thought offers resources for handling individual-community relations, coexistence between differing systems and ideologies, and the question of ownership reform grounded in the productive forces. They warn that merging the two ideas would undermine the scientific character of Marxism. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language account of how Marx's community concept is placed within Western intellectual history and how it is distinguished from the community with a shared future for mankind.

Upholding the Marxist standpoint in the study of ideology 坚持意识形态问题研究的马克思主义立场 Shi Xiaoning Song Wenyuan This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in December 2022, argues that research on ideology must keep to a Marxist standpoint. Shi and Song hold that ideology is vital to the survival and development of a party, a state and a nation, and that it occupies a central place in the whole history of Marxism. The authors first survey the classical texts and later thinkers in which ideology is discussed, from The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto and Capital to the Second International theorists, Western Marxism (Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School) and Althusser. They then turn to the Chinese Communist Party's own record on ideological work, from the new-democratic revolution through the reform era to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Their central claim is that ideology has two sides in Marx. Critique of ideology as "false consciousness" is, in their account, only the logical starting point, shaped by Marx's materialist reworking of Kant's critical philosophy and by the needs of proletarian struggle. The more important purpose is a "functional" one: to build an ideological system for the proletariat. Together, critique and function make up what the authors call Marx's "ideological legacy". On the practical side, Shi and Song say Marxism is the guiding ideology on which the Party and state were founded. They credit the Party with reaching a mature ideological theory and, since 2012, with strengthening Marxism's guiding position, criticising "historical nihilism" and promoting core socialist values. They conclude that studying ideology from a Marxist standpoint is both extremely important and urgent. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese view of how Marx's theory of ideology links to current ideological work.

The historical logic of the exploration of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化探索的历史逻辑 Chen Zhigang This commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks how Chinese modernization came about and what historical logic runs through its exploration. Chen argues that it is a great creation of the Communist Party of China, the result of successive generations building on one another, and the only path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece takes its framing from Xi Jinping's speech at the study session on the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article moves through three periods. These are the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and reform and opening up, followed by the new era that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012). For each stage Chen identifies what it supplied to modernization: social conditions, a political premise and a material base, an institutional and material framework, and then fuller institutional, material and spiritual support. Chen holds that the revolution ended semi-colonial, semi-feudal China and created the basic social conditions. In Chen's account, the socialist system and an independent industrial system then laid the political and material foundations. After reform and opening up, Deng Xiaoping's xiaokang goal and the 'three-step' strategy, combined with a socialist market economy, produced rapid growth and what the article calls a new form of human civilisation. For the new era, Chen credits Xi Jinping with advances in theory, strategy and practice. Theory is said to have gone beyond neoliberalism and dependency theory and broken the equation of modernization with Westernisation. Strategy covers the 'two-step' plan, and practice covers poverty alleviation, the new development philosophy and cultural confidence. Chen concludes that practice has proved Chinese modernization to be the Party's creation and the necessary road to national rejuvenation, which can be achieved only by adhering to it. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned periodisation of how Party writers present the continuity between the revolutionary, Maoist, reform-era and Xi-era stages of modernization.

New features of mass work and the growth of young cadres 群众工作新特点与年轻干部成长研究 Sun Yingshuai Sun Yingshuai asks how the Party's mass work must change under the conditions of the new era, and what this means for younger cadres. Starting from Xi Jinping's call to study the characteristics and patterns of mass work in the new situation, Sun argues that the mass line remains the Party's basic working method but now has to be carried out both online and offline. Young cadres, in Sun's view, are better placed than older ones to notice difficulties and blind spots among the public on the internet and should build "concentric circles" linking the two spheres. Published in People's Forum in 2022, the article is organised around four themes: online mass work as a new mode of public governance; the requirements of truthfulness, speed, openness and transparency in handling online opinion; the coordination of group interests as the normal state of mass work; and the need to keep a people-centred approach while eliminating bureaucratism and formalism. Sun draws on internet-usage and education statistics, and on cases such as the Fengxian incident, the Zhengzhou "7·20" floods, the Baiyin ultramarathon deaths and the MU5735 crash. Sun's first argument is that mass work now spans physical and virtual society, because in the "self-media" era citizens have unprecedented rights to information and expression. If cadres respond more slowly than information spreads, the pressure of opinion guidance rises. Cadres should therefore speak up, speak promptly and speak truthfully, and must not delete posts or conceal facts. Sun also holds that, since the principal contradiction in society has shifted, conflicts of interest among groups are routine, and cites disputes over lift installation, clearing illegal structures and pandemic-related labour disputes. Handling such petty matters badly, Sun says, can turn them into public incidents. Sun concludes that cadres must hold to a people-centred approach and feel real affection for the people. They should judge their achievements by how the people feel and avoid arbitrary decision-making, while Sun treats persistent bureaucratism and formalism, including during pandemic control, as the key point for improving work style. The title's reference to young cadres is developed mainly in the introduction rather than in a separate section. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-journal account of how internet governance, opinion management and interest coordination are framed as tasks of mass work.

How Chinese-style democracy inherits and develops the Marxist view of democracy 中国式民主对马克思主义民主观的继承和发展 Sun Yingshuai Sun Yingshuai asks how democracy as practised under the Communist Party of China relates to the Marxist conception of democracy. The article argues that the Party has kept the essential content of that conception while developing it to fit China's revolution, construction and reform. In Sun's account, this produced a set of unities: democracy and dictatorship, democracy and centralism, procedural and substantive democracy, direct and indirect democracy, and the people's democracy and the will of the state. The article is organised around three themes: the substance, the principles and the forms of democracy. Each is traced from Marx and Engels through Lenin to the Party's own practice. It begins with Athenian and bourgeois democracy as Marxism criticised them, then covers the Party's organisational doctrine, and ends with institutions from the Paris Commune and the Soviets to the people's congress system and whole-process people's democracy. On substance, Sun argues that Marx used historical materialism and class analysis to show earlier democracies, from Athens to bourgeois republics, to be democracies of a minority. Mao Zedong's class analysis of semi-colonial, semi-feudal China led the Party to widen proletarian class democracy into "people's democracy" and the people's democratic dictatorship. On principle, Sun traces the move from Marx's "complete democracy" to Lenin's centralism and then to democratic centralism. Sun notes that the Russian term stresses centralism, and that the Party's 1945 constitution used "democratic centralism" in that sense. On form, Sun presents the people's congress system as a Chinese realisation of the Marxist idea of unified legislative and executive power. It is supplemented by consultative democracy, regional ethnic autonomy and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), whole-process people's democracy. Sun concludes that Chinese-style democracy has gone beyond "minority democracy", "one-off democracy" and "pseudo-universal democracy". It aims to be broad, genuine and effective, and Sun describes it as a democracy of governance, efficiency, driving force and systematic verifiability. Sun cites figures, including that directly elected county and township deputies make up over 90 percent of deputies, and that over 200 draft laws were put out for public comment. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholarship links Marx, Lenin and Mao to the current doctrine of whole-process people's democracy.

A review of research on whole-process people's democracy since 2019 2019年以来全过程人民民主研究述评 Liang Haifeng This literature review, published in the Journal of the Jinggangshan Cadre Academy of China in 2022, surveys scholarship on whole-process people's democracy since Xi Jinping first used the phrase in November 2019. Liang counts more than 1,400 related items on CNKI by June 2022, including over 850 journal articles. The review argues that the topic has quickly become a research hotspot with solid results, but that the work is limited in scope, comparison, empirical depth and method. Liang organises the field into three clusters. The first covers meaning, features, status and significance: democracy centred on the people, completeness, institutional procedures, participatory practice, social effectiveness and innovation. The second covers the concept's historical, theoretical and realisation logics. The third covers practical paths: the people's congress system, consultative democracy and grassroots democratic practice, with examples from Guangzhou. On the core debates, Liang reports that scholars define the concept by its comprehensiveness, in contrast to what they describe as the narrowed, election-centred "intermittent" democracy of the West. Scholars trace its roots to traditional Chinese ideas of people-based governance and to Marxist theories of democracy. Many hold that Party leadership is a necessary condition of its realisation and that the Party and the people's mastery of the country are not opposed. Several argue that consultative democracy followed by voting produces efficiency gains. Liang identifies four weaknesses: homogeneous work that mostly interprets leaders' speeches, thin comparison with Western democracy, shallow practical research, and a narrow method that lacks surveys, statistics and case studies. The review proposes a wider temporal and international outlook, more attention to implementation problems, richer methods including cross-disciplinary and systematic research, and greater unity of understanding. Liang also notes some officials' bureaucratism and some citizens' passivity, and links research to building China's international discourse power on democracy. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese scholarly positions on whole-process people's democracy in 2019–2022, with names of the main authors and the field's self-criticism.

The basic guidelines for building a modern socialist country in all respects 全面建设社会主义现代化国家的基本遵循 Xia Yipu This newspaper commentary, published in February 2023, explains the five major principles set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the basic guidelines for building a modern socialist country in all respects. Xia argues that the task is great and arduous, carried out at a time when strategic opportunities coexist with growing risks and uncertainties. The principles are therefore presented as essential for meeting severe tests. The piece takes the five principles in turn: upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership, keeping to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the people-centred approach to development, deepening reform and opening up, and carrying forward the fighting spirit. Xia assigns each a role: fundamental guarantee, banner and direction, value stance, source of motivation, and spiritual outlook. Together they are described as a logically tight organic whole. Xia argues that Party leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of the system. In this account it lets Chinese modernization avoid the harms of capitalist modernization and ensures common prosperity and peaceful development. Western modernization is characterised as following the logic of capital and as bound up with plunder and exploitation, so Chinese modernization neither should nor can repeat it. Reform and opening up is called the key move that brought China abreast of the times, and the fighting spirit is framed as a feature of Marxism needed to face risks. Xia concludes that the Party must uphold the authority of the Central Committee, follow the Four Cardinal Principles, rely on the people, deepen reform to turn institutional strengths into governance capacity, and stay vigilant while coordinating development and security. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how the 20th Party Congress's five principles are explained to a Chinese readership.

Sixty years of the "Learn from Lei Feng" campaign: development and lessons 学雷锋活动六十年来的发展历程及启示 Ouyang Xuemei Marking the 60th anniversary of Mao Zedong and other senior revolutionaries' inscriptions for Lei Feng, this commentary (published in Guangming Daily, 1 March 2023) asks how the campaign to learn from Lei Feng has developed and what it teaches. Ouyang argues that Lei Feng has grown from an individual model into a social culture, a moral marker and spiritual benchmark of socialist China, and that the Lei Feng spirit "never goes out of date". The piece draws on Xi Jinping's recent instruction on the campaign. The article is organised chronologically in four stages. It begins with the campaign's rise in 1960–63, moves to its place in socialist spiritual civilization building after 1977 and in the early reform years, then to its role as a vehicle of the socialist core value system from 1989 onward, and ends with the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Each stage is illustrated with documents, commemorative events, publications and model figures. Ouyang describes how the campaign spread from the army to the whole country after Mao's 1963 inscription, which set 5 March as Learn from Lei Feng Day. In the reform era it was tied to civility campaigns and, from the 1990s, to volunteer service and the slogan of learning from Lei Feng at one's post. In the new era, the author reports, it was given top-level design: institutionalised volunteering (2014), annual national model selections from 2015, a 2019 outline on civic morality, and the inclusion of the Lei Feng spirit in the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists in 2021. Ouyang concludes that the campaign has endured because the Lei Feng spirit emerged from socialist construction, accords with the Party's purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and inherits traditional national virtues. Its vitality lies, in this view, in keeping pace with the needs of each era and in serving as a vehicle for moral standards and civic ethics. Read the original if you want a concise official-line chronology of the Lei Feng campaign, with its key documents and dates, up to 2023.

Telling the story of the Communist Party of China well 讲好中国共产党的故事 Qu Qingshan Marking the publication of the English edition of The Centenary of the Communist Party of China (Zhongguo Gongchandang de yibai nian), Qu Qingshan, head of the Party's central institute for Party history and literature, argues that the book gives a basis for presenting the Party to foreign readers. This is a commentary rather than a research article. Qu presents the English edition as a major event for Party history work, theoretical education and external publicity. He ties it to the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to build Chinese discourse and narrative systems and to present a credible, lovable and respectable image of China. The piece has three parts. The first describes the book as an authoritative official history and says the English edition is faithful to the Chinese original. The second sets out what readers can find in the four-volume work. The third explains how to use it to tell the Party's story, organised around the Party's image as seen through its members, its internal character and its international role. Qu characterises the book as a standard history marked by authority, scientific rigour, accuracy, completeness, systematic treatment and responsiveness to current questions, including rebuttal of historical nihilism. He says it does three things: it recounts the Party's struggles and achievements through documented facts; it shows the Party's spirit and the lineage of Communist spirit that begins with the founding spirit; and it explains why the Party has succeeded and how it can continue to do so. Qu holds that this can correct what he calls foreign, especially Western, bias and distortion, and shift the Party's image from one shaped mainly by others to one shaped mainly by itself. On storytelling, he calls for explaining the Party's purpose of serving the people, its ties with the people, its scientific theory and policy continuity, its discipline and self-correction, its rigorous self-governance and its contributions to world peace and a community with a shared future for mankind. Qu concludes that the English edition gives China a new platform for telling the Party's story. He describes it as an outward declaration of the Party's historical self-confidence, and a means of spreading the Party's history, theory and voice. He expects it to help more foreign readers understand China and to support exchange with other countries. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian presents the aims and intended international use of the official centenary history.

The fundamental cause of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state: lessons and implications (Part 1) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(上) Li Shenming Writing in 2022, a century after the founding of the USSR and 31 years after its collapse, Li Shenming asks what was the decisive cause of the loss of the Soviet Party and state. The article argues that, although many factors contributed, the fundamental cause was the ideological and political degeneration of the leadership group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev. This is the first instalment of a two-part study. Li opens by invoking Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping on the Soviet case, and by citing Russian reflections after 1991. The first half then has two parts. One sets out eight areas in which the leadership is said to have degenerated: belief, theory, politics, the economy, organisation, work style, foreign policy and outlook on life. The other briefly assesses twelve rival explanations from among the more than fifty Li says exist. The central move is a Maoist distinction between principal and secondary contradictions, together with the claim that a correct ideological and political line decides everything. Li traces a continuous descent. Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin and his theories of a 'party of the whole people' and 'state of the whole people' are said to have prepared Gorbachev's 'humane, democratic socialism', privatisation, abolition of the Party's leading role, nepotistic personnel policy and concessions to the West. The article draws on memoirs, Russian commentators and US figures such as David Kotz and Jack Matlock. It rejects as one-sided explanations including the 'original sin' of the October Revolution, the rigidity of the Stalin model, nationalities policy, the arms race, external pressure, one-party rule, 'blame Gorbachev alone' and the 'convergence of factors' view. Li holds that popular abandonment of the Party was a result of the leadership's degeneration, not its cause. Li concludes that research on the cause is never purely academic, because historical nihilism uses attacks on Soviet history to attack the Chinese Communist Party and Mao. He insists on a clear political standpoint and warns that a wrong conclusion could shake the foundations of the Party and the People's Republic. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese account of the Soviet collapse, with its critique of competing explanations, and are ready to read it as an argument for Party leadership and ideological discipline today.

Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 2) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(中) Li Shenming This is the middle instalment of a three-part essay marking the centenary of the USSR's founding (published in World Socialism Studies, 2022 no. 10). Li Shenming asks what lessons the fall of the Soviet Communist Party and state holds. The author's answer is that the decisive lesson concerns the Party's own building, especially problems inside its leadership group, and that these lessons bear directly on China. Part 2 sets out nine lessons. They cover the link between a big party's self-construction and the fate of nation and people; leaders' convictions and theoretical grounding; ideological and political clarity; embedding fundamental institutions in the constitution; communist ideals; two kinds of reform; ideological work; Party leadership of the army; and Western "peaceful evolution". Li draws on the records of Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev, post-Soviet Russian commentators, and the writings and statements of Allen Dulles and other Western figures. Li argues that after Lenin and Stalin the CPSU lost a strong leadership core. A privileged bureaucratic stratum grew, and the leadership abandoned Marxism for "abstract humanism", class conciliation and Western values. Gorbachev's "reform" is described as a reform of a fundamentally non-socialist kind that aimed at capitalisation, in contrast to the Marxist view of reform as socialism's self-improvement. Li presents abolition of Article 6 of the Soviet constitution, "depoliticisation" of the army and a flood of historical nihilism, including slanders against war heroes such as Matrosov, as steps that dismantled the Party's legal and military base. In Li's account, the Western strategy of "peaceful evolution" worked through exchanges, foundations, prizes, NGOs and the cultivation of a "fifth column" inside the leadership. Li names Gorbachev, Yakovlev, Shevardnadze and Yeltsin, citing Russian memoirists and statements by Western leaders. Li calls the infiltration of the leading group an "undisputed fact". Li then links each lesson to China, criticising "constitutional democracy", stressing ideological leadership, absolute Party command of the army and a reform that never changes direction. The essay ends with "to be continued". Read the original if you want to see how a leading CASS scholar reads the Soviet collapse and ties it to current Chinese Party-building and ideological policy.

Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and state (Part 2) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(下) Li Shenming This is the second and final part of Li Shenming's study of why the Communist Party of the Soviet Union lost power and the USSR dissolved, published in World Socialism Studies in late 2022 to mark the Soviet Union's centenary. Having treated causes and lessons in the first part, Li turns here to what he calls the important implications for the Communist Party of China. His thesis is that China can avoid the Soviet fate only if it keeps Marxist leaders at the head of the Party, preserves public ownership, wins the ideological struggle and stays close to the people. The article sets out ten imperatives, each drawn against the Soviet record: leadership and succession; the Party's self-reform; the economy and common prosperity; ideological work; the Party's purpose and style; Party control of the army; foreign policy; cadre selection and education; Marxist theoretical study; and a correct view of the era. Li draws on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on episodes from the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. Li argues that a Party leader's firm Marxism is often decisive, and he presents the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as essential safeguards, calling for guarding against 'two-faced' people and 'ambitious schemers'. On the economy, he holds that without public ownership there is no socialism, and that Soviet collapse followed the plundering of the public-ownership base by a degenerate leadership. He also criticises one-sided reform practices in China, including neglect of class analysis, downplaying of collective farming and income polarisation. On ideology, Li contends that class struggle persists within limits, denounces historical nihilism and calls for stronger leadership in universities and research bodies. He defends Party command of the army against 'nationalisation of the army', and reads the present as still an age of imperialism, requiring courage to struggle. Li concludes that the Soviet experience warns the Party to treasure its hard-won leadership core, to reform itself so as to escape the 'historical cycle' of rise and fall, and to keep faith with the people. He makes concrete proposals: five political standards and public notice periods for promoting senior cadres, institutionalised Marxist study tied to appraisal, and further volumes of Mao's Selected Works and full collections of Xi Jinping's writings. He expects world socialism to enter an active period in the coming decades. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Party theorist draws practical political and ideological conclusions from the Soviet collapse for China today.

Advancing the Two Integrations to write a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 推进“两个结合”谱写马克思主义中国化时代化新篇章 Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance) Council Published in Qiushi after the 20th Party Congress (2022) and signed by the Party School's governing council, this commentary asks how theoretical innovation should continue on the new journey. Its answer is that the Two Integrations must be upheld consistently. These are combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The article presents this as the fundamental route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The text has three parts. The first reviews the integration of Marxism with China's concrete conditions since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second covers integration with fine traditional Chinese culture. The third sets out tasks for the future. It draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches and the 20th Party Congress report, and gives examples of what it calls original contributions.
