The article argues that the Party has tied theory to the changing national situation. Examples are the judgement at the 19th Party Congress (2017) that socialism with Chinese characteristics had entered a new era and that the principal contradiction in society had changed. It says this is not a break with orthodoxy: Marx's and Engels's analysis of capitalism's basic contradictions has not become outdated, and "keeping to the fundamental" does not mean conservatism. It lists new ideas it considers original, including the Party's leadership as the defining feature of the system, a people-centred approach, the new development philosophy, and the Party's self-reform. On culture, it says Xi has joined the essence of Marxism with traditional ideas. Examples are harmony between humanity and nature behind ecological civilization thought, and the 'all under heaven' worldview behind a community with a shared future for mankind. It also links people-as-the-foundation thought to whole-process people's democracy. For the future, the article proposes holding to the worldview and methods summed up in the "six musts" of the 20th Party Congress report. It also calls for organising theory around the Party's central task of building a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. A third call is for firm historical and cultural confidence, so that theoretical innovation becomes what it calls comprehensive innovation in a civilizational sense. The article closes by urging the Party to arm itself with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how Party institutions present the Two Integrations and the link between Marxism and traditional culture.

The scientific connotations and major significance of the "five paths that must be followed" “五个必由之路”的科学内涵与重大意义 Xin Xiangyang This commentary in Guangming Daily interprets a formulation from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): the "five paths that must be followed" (wu ge biyou zhi lu). These hold that the Party's overall leadership, socialism with Chinese characteristics, unity and struggle, the new development philosophy, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party are each the indispensable route to, respectively, developing socialism, national rejuvenation, historic achievements, national growth and the Party's lasting vitality. Xin Xiangyang argues that the formulation is at once a summary of history, a conclusion about the present and a roadmap for the future, and that its principles, theory and philosophy should be grasped in depth. The article has two parts. The first sets out four aspects of the formulation's meaning. The second sets out three aspects of its significance, and a closing paragraph ties the formulation to the Party's century of struggle, more than seventy years of the People's Republic, over forty years of reform and opening up, and the ten years of the new era. On meaning, Xin reads "biyou" as implying that there is no other way, and treats the formulation as the core code of the Party's achievements. It is presented as a law-like conclusion drawn from the Party's century of experience, as an answer to the questions of which banner to raise, which road to take and which goal to pursue, and as an organic whole rather than five separate items. Party leadership is described as the skeleton running through all five, and Xin urges that they be studied together with the "ten adherences" and the "nine musts". On significance, Xin presents the formulation as a methodological principle to be cherished and upheld, as the basis for meeting the people's expectations on the "new road to the examination" (the Party's new test of governing), and as the path for going beyond Western modernization and creating a new form of human civilization. Xin concludes that the formulation bears on the Party's future, the nation's destiny, the people's wellbeing and human progress, and so must be cherished and upheld consistently. He also states that it offers a reference for other developing countries and "Chinese wisdom" for human problems. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 20th Party Congress formulation was interpreted in official Party-theory commentary soon after the Congress.

How is the creation of a "Chinese original Marxist philosophy" possible? 创建“中国原创性马克思主义哲学”何以可能 Liu Tongfang Liu Tian Liu Tongfang and Liu Tian ask whether and how a "Chinese original Marxist philosophy" can be created, taking their cue from the 20th Party Congress (2022) call to keep writing new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They argue that such a philosophy is necessary, faces two real difficulties, and is now feasible. In their view it should function as a scientific community that drives theoretical innovation and as a platform on which Chinese and Western thought can coexist and reinforce each other. The article is organised in three parts: why creation is necessary, why it is difficult, and why it is feasible. It draws on hermeneutics, Thomas Kuhn's notion of paradigm and scientific community, and Ferdinand Tönnies' distinction between community and society. It also uses the Frankfurt School, as analysed by Rolf Wiggershaus, as a reference case for how a school coheres. Domestic examples include the textbook-system debates of the reform era and Chinese Marxist archaeology. On necessity, the authors say Western-centred social science holds a discursive hegemony that treats its own perspective as universal, while Chinese Marxist philosophy suffers a paradigm crisis, scattered individual research and theory that lags behind practice. On difficulty, they identify a relative lack of autonomous, original concepts, though they list examples such as \"Chinese modernization\", and a lack of shared recognition among scholarly communities divided by lineage, region and method. On feasibility, they hold that the Frankfurt School's real \"inner principle\" was a problem-consciousness oriented to its own era. For Chinese scholars they derive three requirements: shared research questions centred on Chinese modernization; resource sharing and integration that produces internationally influential work, in a \"harmony without uniformity\" polyphony and without isolation from Western scholarship; and a critical and self-critical character aimed at construction, not nihilism. The authors conclude that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the necessary conditions, including a large research workforce and funding, are in place. They present clarifying necessity, difficulties and community principles as only a starting point, with further theoretical and practical work left to the scholarly community. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Marxist philosophers frame the project of a self-reliant knowledge system and use the Frankfurt School as a model for school-building.

Several features of how Gongjin spread Marxism 《共进》传播马克思主义的若干特点 Zhou Jianhua Shen Weifang Gongjin (Advancing Together) was one of the earliest progressive periodicals to spread Marxism in Shaanxi province. The authors ask how it did so and identify five characteristics of its dissemination work. Originally a magazine that reported popular suffering and attacked warlord rule, it turned towards Marxism in June 1922, when its 17th issue carried the Chinese Communist Party's statement on the political situation. The short article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, belongs to the history of Marxism in China. It works through the five features in turn, citing individual articles and issue numbers from the journal as evidence. The first two features concern interaction. Gongjin answered letters from young intellectuals on questions such as gradualism versus radicalism and the Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, and it worked alongside other red periodicals, notably Gongxian, run by Shaanxi students away from the province. It also reprinted pieces on the October Revolution and Lenin from New Youth, The Guide and China Youth. The next two features concern occasions and topics. The journal used anniversaries of the October Revolution, Marx's birth and Lenin's death to explain class struggle, surplus value and the Communist Manifesto, and it commented on local issues, such as a warlord's massacre of peasants in Xingping, to argue for national revolution with peasants as its main force. The fifth feature, according to the authors, was adjusting content to readers. Articles for progressive youth and educators gave theoretical argument on surplus value and Leninist imperialism theory. Pieces for ordinary readers used plain language, for example a simplified five-stage account of social development. The authors present these methods as the reason Gongjin advanced Marxism in Shaanxi. Read the original if you want a concise, source-based account of early Marxist propaganda in a regional Chinese periodical.

Basic experiences and lessons of the early adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 早期马克思主义中国化的基本经验及启示 Liu Zhenjin This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks what the Communist Party of China learned during the early exploration of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times (1919–1938). Liu argues that the Party then lacked experience and struggled to combine Marxism-Leninism with Chinese revolutionary practice. Its setbacks, in Liu's view, yield lessons relevant to the Two Integrations today. The article is built around four "persistent" principles drawn from the early period: applying Marxism's basic tenets to China's concrete realities; combining them with fine traditional Chinese culture; upholding the principal position of the people; and actively guiding currents of social thought. Liu illustrates each with episodes such as the Long March, Mao Zedong's early writings and the debates of the 1920s. On the first point, Liu holds that treating Comintern directives as sacred and copying Soviet experience produced Chen Duxiu's "Right" error, the failure of the Great Revolution and the near-collapse of the Long March. The Party then reflected, and the Tongdao and Liping meetings under Mao's leadership changed the route. Liu presents Mao's "no investigation, no right to speak" as the outcome of that reflection. On thought, Liu describes three major debates, including Li Dazhao's reply to Hu Shi that "problems" and "isms" cannot be separated. They are said to have drawn a line between Marxism and liberalism, guild socialism and anarchism. Liu concludes that early progress came from independence in solving China's problems, a dialectical stance towards tradition, firm Party leadership with reliance on the people, and struggle against erroneous trends. Liu offers these as the main inspiration for adapting Marxism in the new era. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style summary of how Party scholars draw lessons from the 1919–1938 period for current theory.

The qualities behind the early successful spread of Marxism in China 马克思主义在中国早期成功传播的品质 Ling Yingsheng Zhu Xuedan Why did Marxism spread successfully in China in the early twentieth century? This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in February 2023, argues that the answer lies in qualities of Marxism itself and in how Chinese communists handled it. Ling and Zhu distinguish a necessary condition, Marxism's advanced character, from sufficient conditions: its fit with the needs of the Chinese revolution and the Party's scientific attitude towards it. The article opens with the rise of Leninism and the October Revolution, which it says strengthened the confidence of Chinese intellectuals seeking a way to save the nation. It then sets out four qualities in turn: Marxism as the proletarian ideology that fits the trend of social development; its capacity to keep pace with the times; its integration with Chinese conditions and with fine traditional Chinese culture; and the role of the Communists who carried it. The authors contend that Confucian ideology collapsed with its feudal base, while the Three Principles of the People lost popular support once, in their account, they served a minority and were reshaped under Chiang Kai-shek. Marxism, by contrast, took the people's standpoint. Ling and Zhu also hold that its aim of free and all-round human development matches the traditional ideals of great harmony and shared wealth. In the New Democratic Revolution, they say, dogmatism weakened Marxism's social base until Mao Zedong and others established the line of seeking truth from facts. The authors conclude that Marxism's advanced and revolutionary character became effective because Communists applied it to China's realities. They present this as the foundation of the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-history explanation of why Marxism, rather than rival ideologies, won acceptance in early twentieth-century China.

The influence of Japanese Marxism on the early adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context 日本马克思主义对早期马克思主义中国化的影响 Li Aijun Zhang Yan This short piece, first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks how Japanese Marxism shaped the early adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. Li and Zhang argue that Chinese students in Japan and exiled reformers or revolutionaries translated Japanese-language Marxist texts. In their account, this had an important effect on early Marxism in China. The authors move through three themes. They describe how Japanese socialists coined Marxist terminology, why Japan became China's main channel for absorbing it, and how much Japanese-channel literature reached China. They then turn to the formation of a Chinese Marxist discourse. Li and Zhang say Japanese translators either gave new meanings to classical Chinese words or coined new terms from Chinese characters. They contend that shared characters and a common cultural sphere made Japan a shortcut for Chinese translators. The authors cite 231 translated works between 1902 and 1949 and a peak around 1919. They also cite a German scholar's count of 35 Marxist terms borrowed directly from Japanese, such as 'capitalism' and 'socialism'. Terms were not borrowed uncritically: 'means of production' was first rendered through the Japanese 'means of production' wording in the 1938 Capital, then revised in 1957 after the German original. The authors conclude that China's understanding was at first passive but not slavishly imitative. Japanese terminology spared Chinese translators the difficulty and inconsistency of working directly from the originals or English translations, so it sped up the spread of Marxism in China. Read the original if you want a concise overview of the Japanese route by which Marxist vocabulary and texts entered China.

The founding of Marx's materialist conception of history seen from the perspective of discourse transformation 话语变革的视角看马克思唯物史观的创立 Liu Ying Most studies of Marx's materialist conception of history stress that it uncovered general laws of human history and revolutionised the understanding of history, but Liu Ying observes that few approach its founding through discourse. Opening with Xi Jinping's repeated calls to study historical materialism, the article argues that Marx's philosophical discourse passed through three forms: an early Hegelian speculative discourse, a humanist discourse with Feuerbachian colouring, and a new materialist discourse. In Liu's account, the change of discourse was the formation of the materialist conception of history itself. The article follows Marx's texts in chronological order across three sections. The first covers the Doctoral Dissertation and the Rheinische Zeitung period. The second covers the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, the Paris manuscripts and The Holy Family. The third covers the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Liu tracks logic, narrative mode, terminology and field of problems in each, drawing on Plekhanov, Althusser, McLellan and Engels. Liu argues that each stage already held elements pointing beyond it. In the speculative period, "real factors" appear: Marx criticises Epicurus's freedom detached from the world and begins to speak of "objective relations" independent of individual will. In the humanist stage, Marx reverses Hegel on civil society and the state, introduces the proletariat, and in The Holy Family first uses "mode of production". He still derives economic categories and communism from alienated labour, which Liu reads as a logic of alienation rather than historical necessity. The decisive shift comes with the Theses on Feuerbach, which drop "species" and "alienation" and put practice at the centre. The German Ideology then makes real production practice the starting point, replacing "self-consciousness" and "human essence" with productive forces, forms of intercourse and material production, and so completes the new materialist discourse. Liu concludes that the Theses were a rehearsal of the new discourse and The German Ideology marks its formation and the founding of the materialist conception of history. Liu concedes that some terms in the latter remain imprecise, for example "forms of intercourse" where later texts say relations of production. The Poverty of Philosophy and the 1859 Preface are presented as refinements within this framework. Liu also suggests that this view can inform building a discourse system for contemporary Chinese philosophy and social science under Marxist guidance. Read the original if you want a close, text-by-text account of how Marx's vocabulary shifted on the way to historical materialism, as seen by a Chinese scholar.

On the theoretical foundations of modern monetary policy 论现代货币政策的理论基础 Li Bin Sun Siyi Modern monetary policy rests on Western monetary theory, which the authors trace back to the quantity theory of money. Li and Sun ask why a policy built on this theory has gained weight over decades of macroeconomic regulation, yet produces uncertain effects and cannot prevent periodic financial crises. Their answer, drawn from Marxist political economy, is that the quantity theory inverts cause and effect, so that policy based on it stays detached from the analysis of reproduction. The article first describes the framework of narrow monetary policy, the shift from precious-metal to credit money, and two policy tendencies: single-target inflation targeting (the euro area, South Korea) and multi-target, New Keynesian-leaning frameworks (the US Federal Reserve, Japan), compared in a table of central banks. It then traces the quantity theory from Locke, Hume and Ricardo through Fisher, Marshall, Pigou, Wicksell, Keynes, Phillips, the new classical economists and Modern Monetary Theory. It ends with the limits of monetary policy and lessons for China. The core claim is that prices are determined by value and that money supply is only an influencing factor. The authors list five defects of the quantity theory: it ignores money's function as a measure of value, ignores the social relations money represents, reverses causation, lacks a view of money as money capital, and misreads credit money, which is essentially a debt relation and is endogenous to production. Prices, interest rates and money stock are therefore functions of the reproduction process. In crises, the authors argue, monetary policy faces a dilemma: tightening cuts output and employment, while loosening worsens sectoral disproportions. They also say that indicators such as price levels do not register serious imbalances such as overcapacity, high leverage and property bubbles. For China, the authors call for treating price changes as ultimately driven by value, respecting the conditions for the realisation of total social capital, and using monetary policy dialectically and in moderation. They also call for keeping a proper ratio between industrial and fictitious capital, with money directed mainly to material production. They regard supply-side structural reform as a return to a policy mix grounded in the labour theory of value, and reject treating real and value variables as separate policy targets. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of the quantity theory and central-bank frameworks, together with policy implications drawn from the reproduction schemes.

On common prosperity in spiritual life and the all-round development of the human being 论精神生活共同富裕与人的全面发展 Liu Ying Liu Ying asks how common prosperity in spiritual life relates to the all-round development of the human being. Starting from Xi Jinping's 2021 statement that common prosperity covers both material and spiritual life and is highly unified with all-round human development, the article argues that the answer lies in the original context of Marx's theory. Marx formed the idea by criticising how private ownership under capitalism alienates spiritual life and so produces one-sided development. Liu concludes that in the new era, raising material living standards should go together with promoting common prosperity in spiritual life. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's account of alienated spiritual life under capitalism and its consequences. The second discusses socialism and communism as the conditions that make spiritual common prosperity and all-round development possible, and the unity of the two. The third turns to practical measures for contemporary China. Drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts, the Grundrisse, The German Ideology and Capital, Liu argues that labour alienation leads to alienation of spiritual needs, spiritual production and spiritual communication. These in turn make people's needs, social relations and individuality one-sided, turning them into "reified" beings. Liu holds that public ownership of the means of production and the abolition of forced division of labour remove the economic basis of this alienation. In the author's account, as material wealth grows, spiritual life carries more weight in human development, and eventually spiritual and material production converge. Liu treats present problems in China, such as money worship, hedonism and consumerism, as "growing pains" that socialist development will resolve. Liu proposes four measures: strengthening the guiding role of core socialist values; raising the level of ideological and moral education; strengthening publicity on spiritual civilization, including through new media and internet governance; and improving the public cultural service system, including digital culture and greater investment in remote regions. The author presents these as ways to build people's spiritual home and advance all-round development. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links the theory of alienation to current policy on cultural and ideological work under common prosperity.

The contemporary value of the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系的时代价值 Zhao Xue This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks what the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists offers the Party today. Zhao argues that this body of spiritual wealth, running from the founding spirit to the spirit of poverty alleviation, is the "spiritual code" that has kept the century-old Party moving forward. The piece is organised under three headings: the lineage supplies strength for the Party's self-reform, it shows why the Party's century of struggle succeeded, and it gathers the sources of strength for national rejuvenation. Zhao draws on the Zunyi Meeting, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as examples. Zhao treats the Party's courage in self-reform as the main thread running through the lineage. Marxism is called its soul, formed by combining Marxism's essence with fine traditional Chinese culture and the shared values of the people. The article also holds that the lineage developed around the theme of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, through the revolutionary, socialist construction, reform and new-era periods. Zhao concludes that on the new journey the lineage should be turned into strength for taking on responsibility and into lasting motivation for strengthening the "four consciousnesses", the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. Self-reform is meant to ensure the Party never changes in character. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary presents the Party's spiritual lineage after the 20th Party Congress (2022).

The Marxist classics' methodological critique of positivism 马克思主义经典作家对实证主义思潮的方法论批判 Guo Taihui Fu Zhengfa How did Marx, Engels and Lenin criticise positivism, and where exactly did the two currents part ways? Guo and Fu argue that the nineteenth-century clash between positivism and Marxism began as a dispute over what philosophy is, carried over into methodology, and ended in opposed views of society and history. The critique varied in emphasis from Marx to Engels to Lenin, but the authors say it never altered the underlying epistemological position. The article re-reads the classic texts of both camps and draws on existing scholarship. It treats positivism through Comte, Spencer and Mach, and argues that Chinese scholarship has compared the two currents without tracing the move from worldview to method or the internal changes within each. Its sections cover the philosophical basis of the critique, its main methodological dimensions, and its expression in conceptions of society and history, followed by a conclusion. On philosophy, the authors argue that positivism rejects metaphysics but also discards philosophy's worldview function, confining knowledge to phenomena in a way they call neo-Humean. Marxism, by contrast, is said to sublate traditional philosophy, keeping Hegel's dialectic and the rational core of Feuerbach's materialism, and joining them in historical materialism. On method, Marx is presented as rejecting Comte's search for eternal social laws, since laws are historically specific. Engels is said to hold that positive science needs dialectical thinking and to find Comte's method mechanical and his classification of sciences unoriginal. Lenin is shown attacking Mach's reduction of matter to sensations as idealism. On history, positivism is said to ground progress in intellectual and moral change, to stress order, and to defend capitalism and class conciliation. Marxism is said to locate the basis of change in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and to look to revolutionary practice. The authors conclude that the conflict concerns social goals and the means of achieving them as well as worldview and method. They hold that Marxism enriches itself by engaging rival theories, and that Marxist methodology should be applied consciously in both natural and social science. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Marx, Engels and Lenin each criticised Comte, Spencer and Mach, as presented in Chinese Marxist scholarship.

Marx's critique of the productive presupposition of capitalist distribution relations An inquiry into Notebook I of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 马克思对资本主义分配关系的生产前提批判 Li Shumei Li Shumei asks how the young Marx, in Notebook I of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, criticised bourgeois political economy's account of wages, profit and rent. The article argues that the economists described the income forms of different classes but never examined their presupposition, the separation of capital, landed property and labour. Marx, in Li's reading, traced distribution back to this separation and showed that it is necessary, essential and harmful only for the worker. The article has four parts. The first treats wages and the separation itself, set against Adam Smith and Proudhon. The second examines capital's command over labour and the profit and accumulation that follow. The third follows landed property and rent from feudal holdings to capitalised property, including the debate over dividing estates. The fourth sets out the significance of Marx's critique, links it to Capital, and closes with remarks on China's current practice. Li contends that Marx read wages as the result of the separation, not a free contract, since workers must sell their labour to live. In every state of society, whether declining, growing or at its peak, the worker stays in poverty. Capital is accumulated labour and the power to command others' labour, and competition concentrates it in few hands. Landed property follows the same path, and Marx concluded that both Proudhon's wage equalisation and the division of estates leave private ownership untouched. Li adds that Marx also exposed classical economics for valuing labour while despising the labourer, and that this critique prepared his later rejection of the 'trinity formula' in Capital. Marx's picture of free labour and free enjoyment, with land as 'true individual property', is read as anticipating the Communist Manifesto and Capital. Li concludes that Notebook I is Marx's earliest text on production and distribution and has lasting theoretical value. Marx did not yet distinguish labour from labour-power, nor state the problem as the separation of producers from the means of production. The article then ties Marx's ideas to China, citing the primary stage of socialism, a basic economic system with public ownership as the mainstay, regulation of capital, distribution according to work, common prosperity and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you study the early Marx's economic thought, or how Chinese scholars link the 1844 Manuscripts to contemporary Chinese policy.

Firmly grasping the key guide for historical research in China in the new era 牢牢把握新时代中国史学研究的重要指针 Yu Xinhua This commentary, originally published in the People's Daily on 8 November 2021, asks how Chinese historians should study and apply Xi Jinping's statements on the science of history. Yu Xinhua argues that these statements are an integral part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and serve as the key guide and basic principle for historical research in the new era. Historians are urged to study them closely and put them into practice. The piece is organised under three headings: innovating and developing the Marxist theory of history; strengthening research on major historical questions centred on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation; and promoting the integration of disciplines. It begins by noting that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi has addressed studying, writing and using history across Party history, national history, the history of the Chinese nation and world history. On theory, Yu calls for work on the history of Marxist historiography in China, from the early spread of historical materialism, through the debates on Chinese social history and the "five golden flowers" discussions, to the rise of social, environmental, cultural, medical and women's history after the 1980s. Yu also wants Marxist historical theory tied to contemporary conditions such as artificial intelligence and shifting international patterns. On major questions, Yu lists the origins and development of Chinese civilization, the contemporary value of fine traditional culture, academic support for forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, and historical wisdom for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Historians should draw on China's historical record of peace-seeking values and on the Silk Roads to show the logic of a peaceful development path. Yu holds that these questions cannot be answered with traditional methods alone, and urges closer ties between Chinese and world history, archaeology and textual studies, and with other humanities, the natural sciences, big data and AI. The article concludes that historians should grasp the core meaning of Xi's statements and the Marxist standpoint, viewpoint and method running through them. They should build a discipline, academic and discourse system for history with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise official statement of the research priorities set for Chinese historians in 2021.

The milestone significance of the great transformation of the past decade in the new era 新时代十年伟大变革的里程碑意义 Gong Yun This commentary, first published in the People's Daily and posted on the Academy of Marxism site in February 2023, asks what the changes of the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012) mean in historical terms. Gong Yun argues that the "great transformation" of the new era is a milestone in the history of the Party, of New China, of reform and opening up, of socialism worldwide and of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised as a series of five claims about what the decade achieved. These concern the Party's strengthened leadership, the renewed historical initiative of the Chinese people, the irreversible progress of national rejuvenation, the revitalisation of scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China, and the decisive role of the Two Establishes. It closes with a call to unity, citing Mao Zedong's 1957 remarks on the path to an ideal society. On the Party, Gong says that under the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Eight-point Regulations and an unprecedented anti-corruption campaign produced an "overwhelming victory". The author presents this as finding a "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decline through the Party's self-reform. On development, Gong cites GDP growth from 54 trillion to 114 trillion yuan, a world share of 18.5 per cent, urbanisation of 64.7 per cent, the eradication of extreme poverty and a moderately prosperous society as evidence that national rejuvenation is now irreversible. Gong also contends that Chinese modernization surpasses capitalist modernization, has revived the standing of socialism after the Cold War, and offers humanity a new option, citing the Italian Communist Party leader Mauro Alboresi. Gong concludes that these achievements were won by struggle and that the Two Establishes are their decisive factor and the Party's greatest source of certainty. The author calls on the whole Party and people to rally around the Central Committee, uphold the banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and continue the drive toward a modern socialist country and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative of the new era's first decade is framed for a mass readership in the People's Daily.

Advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through Chinese modernization 《求是》杂志评论员：以中国式现代化全面推进中华民族伟大复兴 Qiushi commentator This commentary by a Qiushi journal commentator, republished from Hongqi Wengao in February 2023, is a study guide to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Its starting point is Xi Jinping's statement that the Party's central task is to lead the people in building a modern socialist country and to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The commentator argues that this path is the bright road to national rejuvenation, and that it must be grasped in its distinctive features, essential requirements and guiding principles. The text has four sections. The first traces the history of modernization goals from Sun Yat-sen's Plans for National Reconstruction through the periods of revolution, reform and opening up, and the 19th Party Congress's two-stage plan to 2035 and mid-century. The second sets out the five features and nine essential requirements of Chinese modernization set by the congress report. The third presents five major principles for the road ahead. The fourth turns to the opening phase of the new journey and to economic work in 2023. The commentator contends that, before the Communist Party was founded, every attempt at a modernizing path to national revival failed. Under Party leadership, in this account, China completed in decades an industrialization that took Western countries centuries, and achieved rapid growth together with long-term stability. Chinese modernization is described as socialist modernization led by the Party and serving the majority, set against Western modernization characterised as capital-centred, polarising, materialist and based on expansion and plunder. The five principles are upholding the Party's leadership, the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a people-centred approach, deepening reform and opening up, and fighting spirit. The text also calls for vigilance and bottom-line thinking in the face of severe tests. For the near term, the commentator names high-quality development as the primary task and says 2023 is the first year of implementing the congress's decisions. The article acknowledges weak demand, supply shocks and weakening expectations, but maintains that China's economy is resilient and that the long-term fundamentals are sound. It calls for steady progress, a new development pattern and greater market confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official Party press summarised and promoted the 20th Congress's modernization agenda in early 2023.

Chinese modernization seen through the coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement 从物质文明和精神文明相协调看中国式现代化 Xi Jinping Economic Thought Research Center Taking up the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article from the Xi Jinping Economic Thought Research Center examines one of the five features of Chinese modernization: the coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement (wuzhi wenming and jingshen wenming). The authors argue that material abundance and spiritual richness together are the fundamental requirement of socialist modernization, and that this coordination must run through the whole modernization drive. The piece, published in Qiushi's Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2023, has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical and historical logic of the principle, drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin and the Party's own record. The second describes the vision for 2035 and the mid-century goal in both material and cultural-ethical terms. The third lists practical requirements. In the authors' reading, Marxism treats the two civilizations as a dialectical unity: material production conditions cultural life, while ideas react back on material conditions. They hold that the Party has long pursued both, from Mao Zedong's early statements through Deng Xiaoping's strategy of 'grasping with both hands' to the efforts since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on ideology and values. They contend that development of material wealth alone, without cultural-ethical progress, would not be genuine socialist modernization. The vision joins a prosperous China (economic strength, innovation, national security, better livelihoods) with a culturally flourishing one (core socialist values, common prosperity, strength in education and culture). The practical section calls for promoting 'all-round abundance of material things' through high-quality development and the new development philosophy, widely practising core socialist values, promoting fine traditional Chinese culture through creative transformation, and advancing 'all-round human development' under a people-centred approach. The authors conclude that economic development must remain central while cultural-ethical work is pursued with equal persistence, so that the nation gains both material strength and spiritual force. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists in 2023 explained this feature of Chinese modernization and the policy tasks they attached to it.

Firmly grasping the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the history of New China 牢牢把握新中国史的主题主线、主流本质 Song Yuehong This newspaper commentary responds to Xi Jinping's congratulatory letter on the 30th anniversary of the Chinese Society for the History of the People's Republic of China. Song Yuehong takes up the letter's call to firmly grasp the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the history of New China. The author argues that studying the letter requires an objective, comprehensive and accurate understanding of New China's development, achievements and experience, so that research, publicity and education on that history can advance with high-quality development. The piece has three parts. The first sets out the theme and main threads of New China's history, tracing how the Party's goals and its reading of the principal social contradiction changed from the socialist revolution and construction period through reform and opening up to the new era. The second defines the mainstream and essence of that history. The third draws out what this means for research, with proposals on topics and on building the discipline. On the theme, Song states that New China's history is a history of entrepreneurship, exploration and struggle, and that its theme is to keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to found and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics, and to build a modern socialist country and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Citing Engels' image of history as a resultant of many forces, Song lists four main threads: safeguarding sovereignty and world peace and building a community with a shared future for mankind; upholding Marxism and the Party's self-reform; advancing Chinese modernization and common prosperity; and achieving complete national reunification. The mainstream is described as building and strengthening the country, taking its own path and benefiting the people. Song acknowledges mistakes and a serious setback in the socialist construction period, but presents them as part of exploration whose theoretical results and material base prepared the ground for later reform. Song concludes that research should clarify the historical necessity of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, study Chinese modernization as running through New China's history, and build the discipline, academic and discourse systems of New China history. The author also calls for combining source collection with theory and for openly opposing historical nihilism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party historians are told to frame the history of the People's Republic and set research priorities.

Chinese modernization: inheriting and innovating Marx's thought on modernization 中国式现代化：马克思现代化思想的传承与创新 Dou Yongchao Dou Yongchao takes up Chinese modernization, set out systematically in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), and asks how it relates to Marx's own thinking. The article's thesis is that Chinese modernization is essentially an inheritance and creative development of Marx's thought on modernization, and that it should therefore be examined at the level of Marxist theory rather than only through its historical, comparative or world-significance dimensions, which Dou says dominate current scholarship. The article has two main parts. The first reconstructs the theoretical logic of Marx's thought on modernization, although Marx never used the term itself. The second sets out how Chinese modernization carries forward and innovates on this thought in four respects: value standpoint, development path, civilizational structure and ideal goal. A short conclusion follows. In Dou's reconstruction, Marx understood modernization through the "economic formation of society", as the transition to the modern bourgeois mode of production, and criticised its capitalist form dialectically. Capital produced vast productive forces, cities, modern states and a world market, but also economic crisis, ecological crisis and alienation between people, nature and things. Marx therefore pointed to a new type of modernization, aimed at the free and all-round development of the individual and, in his late reflections on Russia, possibly reachable without passing through capitalism. Dou argues that Chinese modernization carries this forward. Its people-centred standpoint develops Marx's "interests of the immense majority" and draws on Chinese minben (people-as-foundation) ideas. Under Party leadership it seeks to steer capital rather than be ruled by it, pursues harmony between humanity and nature, and treats material modernization as serving the modernization of people. The five-sphere layout and the goals of high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy and common prosperity extend Marx's account of future civilization, while the community with a shared future for mankind is presented as the present-day expression of communist ideals fused with the traditional Datong (Great Harmony) ideal. Dou concludes that Marx's thought supplies the theoretical guidance for Chinese modernization, while Chinese practice provides the ground for developing that thought further. Chinese modernization is described as an important result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. It is said to move socialism with Chinese characteristics towards communism, and Dou calls for continued theoretical and practical innovation, guided by Marx's thought, Chinese conditions and traditional culture, in a world where capitalism and socialism coexist. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar derives the official concept of Chinese modernization from Marx's critique of capital and from his late writings on non-Western paths.

Artificial intelligence and the transformation of the capitalist mode of production 人工智能与资本主义生产方式的变迁 Wang Wenze This article reviews recent work by scholars outside China on how artificial intelligence is changing the capitalist mode of production, and analyses it through Marxist political economy. Wang's thesis is that AI has not altered the essential features of capitalism. In the author's reading, it has reshaped machine systems, forms of work and the capital–labour relation in ways that deepen capital's control and exploitation of labour and sharpen class contradictions. The review begins with Marx's definition of the capitalist mode of production in Capital and a sketch of successive technological revolutions, from steam to electricity to computers and then AI. It is organised in three parts: AI's remaking of the machine system, its effects on workers, and new features of the capital–labour relationship. The sources are mainly Western and other foreign scholars, including Nick Srnicek, Jamie Woodcock, Mary L. Gray and Siddharth Suri, Christian Fuchs, Shoshana Zuboff, Bernard Stiegler and Janine Berg. Wang first argues that AI is essentially the intelligent upgrading of the 'control machine' added by automation to Marx's three-part machine. This produces platforms as a form of production organisation and the 'gig economy', including 'ghost work'. On labour, the review reports digital labour, the polarisation of the workforce as middle-skill jobs are replaced, and weakened worker solidarity. On the capital–labour relation, it identifies three tendencies: stronger control through what Zuboff calls surveillance capitalism, including remote control, monopoly over data and absolute power in the labour market; heavier exploitation through longer hours, lower pay, reduced autonomy and new forms such as 'playbor' and affective labour; and the concealment of the contradiction behind algorithms, platform 'neutrality' and the 'algorithmic black box'. Wang concludes that, under the logic of capital, AI raises productivity but also reshapes organisation, employment and labour forms so that exploitation of surplus labour intensifies. The review holds that this confirms Marx's claim that capitalist development strengthens exploitation of the individual worker. It adds that the capitalist use of AI re-intensifies the conflict between bourgeoisie and working class and is brewing a general crisis within capitalist society. Read the original if you want a Marxist-framed map of Western and other foreign scholarship on platforms, digital labour and AI-era exploitation.

The internal logic of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系的内在逻辑 Zhao Yaping This short commentary asks how the "spiritual genealogy" of Chinese Communists came to be formed and developed. Zhao argues that it rests on three interlocking logics: theoretical, historical and practical. Understanding them, the author says, matters for carrying forward the Party's spiritual lineage and for achieving new successes in the new era. The piece opens with the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which traces the genealogy to the great founding spirit of the Party. It then takes the three logics in turn, moving through the periods of the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. On the theoretical side, Zhao holds that the genealogy derives from Marxism and its revolutionary spirit, and that each stage of Marxism's adaptation to Chinese conditions, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, nurtured it. On the historical side, the author lists the spirits formed in each period: the Red Boat, Jinggangshan and Long March spirits before 1949; the Korean War resistance, Daqing and \"Two Bombs, One Satellite\" spirits afterwards; the reform and opening up, flood-fighting and women's volleyball spirits; and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the poverty-alleviation, craftsmanship and anti-epidemic spirits. On the practical side, Zhao argues that these spirits were distilled from experience in leading revolution, construction and reform. Zhao concludes that spirits formed in different periods together make up a complete genealogy expressing the Party's character. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style outline of how Party commentary periodises and classifies the named \"spirits\" of the Communist Party.

The great founding spirit of the Party as the wellspring of the Communist Party of China's spirit 伟大建党精神是中国共产党的精神之源 Xu Jinghui Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, Xu Jinghui takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the Party's centenary celebration (2021) that the great founding spirit is "the wellspring of the Communist Party of China's spirit". Xu argues that this founding spirit is the source, the nourishing spring and the common thread of the Party's whole genealogy of spirit. The short commentary has three parts, one for each of these roles. It runs through the Party's historical periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. It names the spirits associated with each, including the Red Boat spirit, the Jinggangshan spirit, the Resisting US Aggression and Aiding Korea spirit and the "two bombs, one satellite" spirit. Xu contends that the later spirits grew out of the founding spirit's convictions, fundamental purpose and good work style. In the author's account, each emerged from a concrete achievement: the Korean War victory, the nuclear and space breakthroughs, reform and opening up, the fight against Covid-19 and the Beijing Winter Olympics. The author then reads the four parts of the founding spirit as a "red bloodline": upholding truth and ideals, practising the original mission, fearless struggle, and loyalty to the Party and the people. Xu concludes that the founding spirit is the root and soul of the Party's spirit, giving direction and spiritual support against domestic and international risks in every period. The piece is a brief, affirmative statement of the official reading of this theme. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party commentary links the founding spirit to later named spirits.

Distinctive features of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系的鲜明特质 Ma Zhen This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks what characterises the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists. Ma describes it as a valuable legacy of the Party's century of struggle that expresses its fundamental purpose and fine traditions. The author argues that the spirit forged in different historical periods has distinct features yet forms an organic whole. The piece identifies four features: fearlessness in sacrifice together with love of country and people; self-reliance and hard struggle; bold exploration and daring to be first; and upholding fundamental principles while innovating, joined with moral responsibility. It draws on the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and on examples such as the Nanniwan spirit and the Red Flag Canal spirit. Ma presents patriotism as the core of the national spirit and links it to the Party's aim of serving the people wholeheartedly. Self-reliance is tied to the claim that China's problems must be answered by Chinese people on the basis of national conditions. In the new era, the author cites comprehensive deepening of reform and the anti-corruption campaign as expressions of daring to be first. Moral responsibility is said to be rooted in both traditional Chinese culture and Marxism, which Ma says transcends narrow nationalism, unilateralism and protectionism. Ma concludes that this genealogy should be passed on to give Communists a continuing spiritual source for firm ideals and convictions. The author also presents China's conduct abroad as an example of the moral responsibility involved in building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary summarises the character of the Party's spiritual tradition.

Leadership of the Communist Party of China gives modernization its "Chinese" meaning 中国共产党领导赋予现代化“中国式”意涵 Xie Lixia Li Bin This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, asks what makes modernization "Chinese" in the phrase Chinese modernization. Xie Lixia and Li Bin answer that the leadership of the Communist Party of China is the decisive factor. In their account, the Party's leadership gives Chinese modernization four defining features and is what allows China to move closer to the centre of the world stage. The authors trace the pursuit of modernization from the Party's founding through the early socialist exploration, the period of reform and opening up, and the new era under Xi Jinping. Each period is linked to a Party leader's formulation: the Four Modernizations, Deng Xiaoping's call to take a "Chinese-style" path, and Xi's statement that the modernization being pursued is socialist modernization led by the Party. The text is organised in four sections: socialism as the political meaning, Chinese characteristics as the paradigm, coordinated development as the philosophical trait, and common prosperity as the goal. Xie and Li argue that Western powers presented Western, capitalist modernization as the universal model, and that the rise of socialism put a socialist banner on modernization. In their reading, the Party's insistence on independence and self-reliance produced a new paradigm, since no single model or universal standard of modernization exists. They present coordinated development as the Party's way of handling the principal contradiction of Chinese society, citing Mao Zedong's \"On the Ten Major Relationships\" (1956), the mid-1990s guidance on major relationships, and the \"Five-Sphere Integrated Plan\" since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Common prosperity is traced from early revolutionary aims through Deng's moderately prosperous society to the 2021 declaration that poverty alleviation had been won and a moderately prosperous society built, and the 2035 and mid-century targets. The authors conclude that Party leadership is the key to Chinese modernization. They contrast its socialist character with capitalist modernization, its Chinese characteristics with the Western paradigm, its coordination with one-sided and distorted development, and its common prosperity with wealth for a minority. They claim this path offers developing countries a reference and contributes a Chinese approach to human civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how Party writers tie the four features of Chinese modernization to Party leadership across historical periods.

The solemn historical responsibility of contemporary Chinese Communists 当代中国共产党人的庄严历史责任 Guo Jianning Published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2023, this short commentary takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's statement that continually writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is the solemn historical responsibility of contemporary Chinese Communists. Guo Jianning argues that this is also the mission of philosophy and social science scholars, and that the report gives direction for theoretical innovation grounded in practice. The piece is organised under three headings: the "two capabilities" (that Marxism works, and that Marxism adapted to China and the times works), the Two Integrations as the fundamental path, and the "six commitments" as the core of the ideas. Guo contends that the Party's success rests ultimately on Marxism's scientific, practical, people-centred and open character and on the Party's own sustained adaptation of it, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Integrating Marxism with China's realities is said to have produced Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilisation, which the author describes as rejecting capital-centred, polarising Western modernization. Integrating it with fine traditional culture is presented as a matter of mutual connection, with examples such as "the people as the foundation of the state" and people-centred development. The "six commitments" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global vision) are described as the worldview and methodology running through the Thought. Guo concludes that the six commitments should be studied as the key to the spirit of Xi Jinping Thought, so that Chinese Communists can keep advancing the adaptation of Marxism and write new chapters. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 20th Party Congress formulations were presented to scholars in early 2023.

On the core themes of Western ecological Marxism Joel Kovel's ecological critique of capital and its contemporary value 论西方生态学马克思主义的核心论题 Hu Xiaojie Li Xiaochun Hu Xiaojie and Li Xiaochun ask what distinguishes the American eco-socialist Joel Kovel within Western ecological Marxism, which emerged in the 1970s. They argue that, while the school shares the view that the capitalist system is inherently anti-ecological, Kovel is distinctive in starting from capital itself as the root of ecological crisis. The authors say existing scholarship mostly systematises Kovel's theory, whereas they set it against contemporaries in order to bring out its original features and its lessons for China. The article has four parts. It first surveys James O'Connor, Leiss and Ben Agger, and John Bellamy Foster as representatives of the critique of capitalism, covering the second contradiction of capitalism, technological rationality and alienated consumption, and the metabolic rift. It then reconstructs Kovel's critique of capital, industrialisation, globalisation, technology, the ecosystem and use-value. It next compares Kovel's commonalities with and departures from the school, and finally draws implications for an ecological civilisation in the Chinese form. In the authors' reading, Kovel follows Marx in treating capital's drive to expand as destructive of its own conditions of production, so that ecological crisis is a historical necessity under capitalism. He rejects the idea that technological progress can reform the crisis, calling it crude mechanical materialism, since technology cannot be separated from social relations. Kovel also draws on the second law of thermodynamics to treat the ecosystem as a dissipative structure whose order capital disrupts, and he insists on the priority of use-value over exchange-value. The authors identify three marks of originality: Kovel begins from capital rather than from a revision of historical materialism or from alienation; he holds an ecocentric value orientation unlike most ecological Marxists; and he holds that capitalist society can be transformed into eco-socialism. They conclude that China's ecological civilisation should combine institution-building with ecological values, treat humans and nature as a 'community of life', and pursue ecology-centred production, linking these to Xi Jinping's statements and the 'two mountains' formula. Read the original if you want a comparative overview of ecological Marxists and a Chinese reading of Kovel's relevance to ecological civilisation policy.

Strengthening the Party's overall leadership of Chinese modernization from a political height 从政治的高度切实加强党对中国式现代化的全面领导 Bao Xinjian Writing in Guangming Daily shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Bao Xinjian argues that the Party's political leadership is the most fundamental element of its overall leadership, and that it decides the direction and fate of Chinese modernization. In the article's account, whether Party organisations and leading cadres can raise their political judgement, political understanding and political execution bears directly on whether modernization succeeds. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out the distinctive features and inner logic of Chinese modernization. The second discusses the major principles and correct direction needed on the new journey. The third treats the promotion of whole-process people's democracy as a key link in strengthening Party leadership. It relies heavily on the 20th Party Congress report and on speeches by Xi Jinping. Bao's central move is to contrast two modernization logics. Chinese modernization follows a "people-centred logic" aimed at all-round human development, while Western modernization, in this reading, follows a "capital logic" that produces one-sided social development and a loss of human subjectivity. The author adds that the people-centred approach does not reject capital: in the primary stage of socialism, capital must be used while its negative effects are curbed, through an "effective market" and a "capable government". Bao then ties leadership to the "five adherences" of the Congress report, to seizing historical initiative amid global upheaval, and to relying on the people. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as a measure of the Party's leadership capacity, to be developed in three ways: people-centred, problem-oriented and institution-based. Bao names the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-governance as its institutional chain. Bao concludes that Party organisations and cadres at every level must stand firmly with the people, hold to the political principles and direction set by the Central Committee, and raise the institutionalisation, standardisation and proceduralisation of democracy. Doing so is presented as a precondition for Chinese modernization to avoid deviating from its course. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party theory in early 2023 linked Party leadership, the critique of capital logic and whole-process people's democracy.

Implementing Party leadership comprehensively, systematically and holistically Further advancing the great new project of Party building in the new era 《人民日报》评论部：全面、系统、整体落实党的领导 People's Daily Commentary Department This commentary from the People's Daily commentary department (2 February 2023) takes up the question of how the Party should uphold its leadership. It argues that, to govern a large Party and a large country, Party unity, centralised and unified leadership, and the authority of the Central Committee are of paramount importance. Party leadership, in the words it quotes from the 20th Party Congress report (2022), must be implemented comprehensively, systematically and holistically. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's 2021 visit to the Yangjiagou revolutionary site in Shaanxi, where the Central Committee was based during the civil war. It then moves through the achievements of the past decade, the practical meaning of upholding Central Committee authority, and the 20th Party Congress's plans for improving Party leadership. The commentary presents centralised and unified leadership as the main political guarantee of the period's successes, citing poverty alleviation and the response to COVID-19. For the latter it gives figures such as more than 4.6 million grassroots Party organisations. It calls the Two Establishes the decisive factor behind these changes. Upholding leadership is described as concrete: it means the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, plus following the Central Committee in all circumstances and absolute loyalty to the Party. It adds that leadership must also be improved, through stronger political discipline, democratic centralism and better decision-making bodies. The commentary concludes that speaking out clearly on politics and ensuring Party unity are the Party's lifeblood. Deeper understanding of the Two Establishes and higher political judgement, understanding and execution, it says, will make the Party more united. Read the original if you want an example of official 2023 Party-press language on leadership, loyalty and centralisation after the 20th Party Congress.

Deepening research on the history of New China to encourage firm historical confidence 深化新中国史研究 激励人们坚定历史自信 Yang Shengqun Writing in early 2023, Yang Shengqun takes up Xi Jinping's congratulatory letter to the History Society of the People's Republic of China on its 30th anniversary. The letter asked researchers of national history to help people "firmly establish historical confidence" and strengthen historical initiative. Yang argues that this task combines political and scientific requirements and that research on the history of New China should be deepened so that it can educate people through history. The article is a commentary organised under four headings. They are: the historical logic and inevitability of socialism with Chinese characteristics; the major achievements and historical experience of socialist construction since 1949; the intellectual, theoretical, institutional and cultural legacies of earlier generations; and the scholarly transmission of the history of the Chinese nation's progress since modern times. Yang draws on Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era writings, Deng Xiaoping, and the Party's two historical resolutions of 1981 and 2021. Yang's central claim is that historical confidence must rest on a grasp of historical logic and inevitability. In this account, socialism with Chinese characteristics is the conclusion of more than 180 years of modern Chinese history, over 500 years of world socialism and more than 5,000 years of Chinese civilisation. Yang holds that summing up achievements and experience is both a political and Party-spirit requirement and a scientific one, since good history highlights the "essence and mainstream" of events. Yang also calls for more study of the thought and institutional legacies of Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi, Zhu De, Deng Xiaoping and Chen Yun, within a people-centred view of history that still credits leading figures. Yang concludes that New China history, the "soul" of which is Party history, is the composite vehicle for what the article calls the "four histories". Yang admits it began late and has not yet fully formed the features of an independent discipline. Yang urges researchers to organise the field around the theme of national rejuvenation and the three leaps of standing up, becoming prosperous and becoming strong, so as to strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian links the discipline's tasks to official guidance on historical confidence in 2023.

The distinctive strengths of the Communist Party of China as a century-old large party 中国共产党百年大党的独特优势 Liu Honglin Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Honglin takes up the Congress report's call to stay clear-headed and resolute about solving the "unique problems of a large party". Liu argues that to meet this demand the Party must draw on lessons from its hundred years of struggle and understand the distinctive strengths it has as a century-old large party. The article identifies five: political, theoretical, institutional, organisational and spiritual, together with Party building as a "magic weapon". Liu begins by reading the Congress wording closely: the emphasis falls on "clear-headedness and resolve", and the unique problems are specific to the world's largest Marxist governing party remaining in power for the long term. Liu links them to supervising power, opposing corruption, self-reform and escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. Each of the five sections then traces one strength from the Party's early congresses and revolutionary bases through the reform era to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), quoting Mao Zedong, Xi Jinping and the 2021 Party history resolution. The core argument is a ranking of the five strengths. Putting the people first is the political strength and the "red thread" running through all the others. Theoretical innovation that keeps pace with the times, through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, gives guidance. Centralised and unified Party leadership is the key institutional strength. A tight organisational system, which Liu says has at least ten levels, 96.712 million members and 4.936 million primary organisations at the end of 2021, and strict discipline supply support. The spirit of self-reform, shown in anti-corruption campaigns from the 1920s to the present, supplies drive. Liu contends that no other party in the world pursues Party building and self-reform so consistently. Liu concludes that these advantages become decisive only if they are turned into a winning position through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and continued work on the new great project of Party building. Party building is therefore presented as the means of preserving existing strengths and creating new ones. The article answers the Party's historical-cycle question with Xi Jinping's "second answer", the Party's self-reform, alongside Mao's earlier answer of popular supervision. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Party scholarship frames the Party's strengths, and how it uses the 20th Party Congress concept of the "unique problems of a large party".

A programmatic document for advancing the rule of law in China in the new era and on the new journey 新时代新征程推进法治中国建设的纲领性文件 Zhou Youyong Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhou Youyong presents the Congress report's chapter on "upholding law-based governance in all respects and advancing the building of a rule-of-law China" as a programmatic document for the new era. The article argues that the chapter, the first in a Congress report to treat the topic in a dedicated section, sets out the direction and tasks of legal construction under Xi Jinping Thought on the rule of law. Zhou takes it as showing the Party's determination to pursue the rule of law, and as the guide for the new journey. The piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts, has three parts. The first reviews the achievements of the decade since 2012 and credits them to Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law. The second links Chinese modernization to law-based governance. The third summarises the report's general requirements and four priority tasks: the legal system centred on the Constitution, law-based administration, fair justice, and a law-based society. Zhou's central claim is that modernization and the rule of law are internally bound together. Law is both a basic guarantee of national modernization and part of its content, so a country that modernizes must also move to the rule of law. The article cites Xi Jinping's view that this must proceed through top-down and bottom-up interaction. It reads the report's call to "advance law-based governance in all areas of work" as meaning that law should run through economic, political, cultural, social and ecological development, as well as national security, the military, "one country, two systems" and international relations. Zhou also lists the guiding requirements: keep to the socialist rule-of-law path with Chinese characteristics, keep Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee, and keep a people-centred stance. Zhou concludes that the Party must stay guided by Xi Jinping Thought on the rule of law, hold to the goals set for a rule-of-law China, and provide long-term legal safeguards for building a modern socialist country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The text is an authoritative-style exposition of the report rather than an independent analysis. Read the original if you want a concise, Party School-style account of how the 20th Party Congress framed the rule of law and its link to Chinese modernization.

Integrating the essence of Marxist thought with the shared values people live by without noticing 把马克思主义思想精髓同人民群众日用而不觉的共同价值观念融通起来 Jiang Chang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily and posted on 27 February 2023, asks how Marxism can take firm root in China. Jiang Chang argues that the Two Integrations require the essence of Marxist thought to be fused with the common values that people hold and act on daily without being aware of them. Doing so, the author says, strengthens the historical and popular foundations for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has three parts. The first describes how Marxism has already entered Chinese people's values. The second concerns consolidating a shared value system led by Marxist values. The third sets out how the fusion can be achieved gradually and almost imperceptibly. Jiang holds that fine traditional Chinese culture contains distinctive values, such as the unity of heaven and humanity, the unity of knowing and doing, and governing by virtue, and that many of them are compatible with Marxism. This, in the author's account, helped Chinese people accept Marxism, and basic principles such as the primacy of matter and the people as makers of history are now widely held. The author presents the socialist core values as continuous with Marxist values, citing improved livelihoods, fairness and justice, and free and all-round human development. Both Marxist theory and core values, Jiang says, come from the people's practice and must work through it. Jiang calls for two measures. The first is to make the Party's innovative theory, above all Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, take hold among the people, moving them from recognising Marxism to truly understanding and using it. The second is to promote the unity of knowing and doing, through Party-wide study and a learning society and through individual moral cultivation and practice. Read the original if you want a short example of how official commentary links Marxism, traditional culture and the socialist core values.

Linking up the essence of Marxism with the best of traditional Chinese culture 同中华优秀传统文化精华贯通起来 Shang Zhixiao This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in early 2023, takes up a formula from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): linking up the essence of Marxist thought with the best of traditional Chinese culture. Shang argues that doing so requires understanding the essence of Marxism, drawing out the best of that culture, and studying the inner logic that connects the two. The piece has three parts. The first presents Marxism as open to the achievements of human civilization and as a method rather than a dogma. The second traces how the Party has drawn on traditional culture since Marxism reached China. The third sets out what must be done next. Shang notes that Marxism's three components built on German classical philosophy, British classical political economy and French utopian socialism. On this basis Shang holds that Marxism must be combined with each country's actual conditions, and that in China this is the work of the Two Integrations. Shang's examples include Mao Zedong's "seeking truth from facts", Deng Xiaoping's "moderately prosperous society" and Hu Jintao's "harmonious society". Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Shang says, Xi has linked the Marxist view of the masses to the idea of the people as the foundation of the state. He has also drawn on classical sayings on reform and patriotism, and on the ideal of "all under heaven as one family" to explain a community with a shared future for mankind. In Shang's account, Marxist dialectics in turn revitalise traditional culture. Shang calls on Party members to grasp the essence of Marxism, in its worldview and methodology. They should also use that standpoint and method to mine the classic values of traditional culture, which Xi's report describes as highly compatible with scientific socialism. The aim is connection in content, fit in method and convergence in values. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Chinese commentators justify combining Marxism with traditional culture.

Advancing economic theoretical innovation grounded in practice: making original contributions to developing Marxist political economy 不断推进实践基础上的经济理论创新 为发展马克思主义政治经济学作出原创性贡献 Zhou Wen This short commentary, first published in People's Daily, argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought, formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), makes important original contributions to Marxist political economy. Zhou Wen presents it as upholding the basic principles and methods of Marxist political economy while summarising the Party's understanding of economic laws, especially those of socialist economic construction, and opening a "new realm" for the discipline. The article is organised around three areas of contribution: deepening understanding of the laws of socialist economic construction, answering major questions of economic development in the new era, and resolving the relationship between government and market. On the first area, Zhou argues that the stress on the Party's overall leadership of economic work enriches Marxist theory on the relation between economics and politics. The people-centred approach and the pursuit of common prosperity are said to clarify the nature and purpose of socialist production.
