Treating public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse forms of ownership, distribution according to work alongside other methods, and the socialist market economy as the basic economic system is said to enrich theory on the market economy. On the second, Zhou describes the new development philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing as a systematic framework that answers questions about development's purpose, driving force, method and path. On the third, Zhou holds that combining the market's "invisible hand" with the government's "visible hand" overcomes the drawbacks of capitalist market economies and goes beyond Western mainstream economics in theory and practice. Zhou concludes that this approach offers a fundamental guide for building a Chinese-style disciplinary, academic and discourse system in economics. In the new stage of development, Zhou calls for further research and practice on combining socialism with the market economy, so as to bring together an efficient market and a capable government. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style statement of how Chinese scholars frame Xi Jinping's economic thought as a contribution to Marxist political economy.

Supporting high-quality development: strengthening the building of the industrial workforce in the new period 为推动高质量发展提供支撑 加强新时期产业工人队伍建设 Zhou Jianjun This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in February 2023, asks how China should build up its industrial workforce to support high-quality development. Zhou argues that industrial workers are the main supporting force within the working class, and that stable industrial and supply chains, smarter, more digital and greener manufacturing, and more world-class firms all depend on a high-calibre workforce. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's call for a large army of knowledge-based, skilled and innovative industrial workers, and links it to the Reform Plan for Building the Industrial Workforce in the New Period. It then sets out three areas of work: skills improvement, diverse incentives and the protection of workers' rights. On skills, Zhou calls for enterprises to draw up training plans, for large leading firms to host demonstration training bases for highly skilled personnel, and for skills competitions tied to major national projects and key industries. On incentives, the author proposes distribution that favours front-line workers, portable social insurance across ownership types, sectors and regions, and ending the dual-track system separating personnel management from worker management. The author also proposes allowances for highly skilled staff and distribution according to skills and innovation as factors of production. On rights, Zhou urges strengthening democratic management through workers' congresses, open factory affairs, and worker directors and supervisors, with trade unions fulfilling their rights-protection duties and collective consultation institutionalised. The aim, in the author's words, is to build harmonious labour relations with Chinese characteristics and a social climate that respects labour and prizes skill. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style statement of the policy measures for industrial workers promoted in China in early 2023.

A political-economy critique of "algorithmic capitalism" “算法资本主义”的政治经济学批判阐释 Sun Liang Sun Liang asks why algorithms have become central to contemporary capitalism, how they exercise control, and whether they leave any route to emancipation. The article argues that algorithms should not be equated with control: algorithms in general are an anthropological, accumulated human skill, and their coercive, profit-seeking features come from the capitalist form that has captured them. Critique should therefore target the capital form of algorithms, not algorithms as such. The article has three parts. The first describes how algorithms embedded in capitalism produce a paradox with modern civilisation, at the levels of cognition, governance and production. The second identifies three mechanisms by which designers' interests and the capital principle shape algorithmic operation. The third turns to Marx's critique of political economy to propose a direction for correcting algorithmic capitalism. Sun draws on Lessig, Deleuze, Han Byung-chul, Zuboff, Hardt and Negri, Virno and others. On cognition, Sun argues that algorithms promise an accurate picture of the world but breed a cartographic, computational belief that erodes subjects' capacity to imagine the future. On governance, they open a space of freedom that becomes biopolitical regulation. On production, they are meant to enable shared resources but become a means of capital valorisation, since they make social and affective activity measurable and so subject to value form. The three mechanisms are: algorithms embody designers' interests and are not neutral; data-guidance capacity reproduces the inequalities of private ownership; and ownership of platforms and servers is capitalist in character, producing data monopoly and what Sun calls "data colonialism". Against Virno and Negri's "crisis of measure" reading of the "Fragment on Machines", Sun argues that they read Marx's labour theory of value in a Ricardian way. In Sun's account, value-form analysis shows that algorithms cannot change the social character of exchange value, and the Grundrisse's collapse thesis was superseded by the dual character of labour in Capital. Sun concludes that general intellect can serve human development only if it is withdrawn from capital's possession, which requires changing the ownership structure of the means of production. Algorithms should be steered towards regulation and "de-capitalisation" under a tension between suffering from algorithmic development and suffering from its absence. Sun suggests that, under socialism's drive to develop the productive forces, algorithms can support Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Marxist value-form rebuttal of post-operaist and Western left optimism about digital technology, set against critical theories of surveillance and biopolitics.

Three dimensions of ecological thought in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》生态思想的三个维度 Luo Junli Luo Junli asks what ecological thought can be found in the young Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and what it offers in a period of worsening global ecological crisis. The article argues that the text contains an ecological outlook that can be read along three dimensions: nature, society and institutions. Together they run from the human–nature relation, through the capitalist roots of ecological crisis, to its resolution in communism. The article is organised in three main sections followed by a short conclusion. The first deals with the dialectical relation between humans and nature. The second treats labour, alienated labour and private property as the social origins of ecological crisis. The third takes up communism as the way out. Luo draws mainly on Marx's own formulations in the Manuscripts, such as nature as the human being's "inorganic body" and the species-specific character of human production. In the nature dimension, Luo argues that humans depend on nature for both material and spiritual needs, yet differ from animals in being self-conscious and active, producing "in accordance with the laws of beauty". In the social dimension, labour is the mediating link through which humans and nature produce and confirm each other, a relation Luo describes as objective activity. Under capitalism this link is alienated. Luo holds that alienated labour is the fundamental cause of ecological crisis and private property its direct cause, because nature becomes a mere profit-making instrument and science and human needs are alienated as well. In the institutional dimension, Luo reads Marx's communism as the positive sublation of private property and human self-alienation, distinct from earlier crude communism. It brings two reconciliations: between humans and nature, and between people. Luo concludes that communism means both the full liberation of humanity and the full revival of nature, and that the Manuscripts remain a useful reference for easing present environmental problems. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language reading of the 1844 Manuscripts as a source for Marxist ecological thought, organised around alienated labour and communism.

Rethinking Stalin's theory of building socialism in one country 斯大林“一国建成社会主义”理论的再思考 Tang Desen Jiang Li Tang Desen and Jiang Li take up a question raised by the Soviet collapse and the upheavals in Eastern Europe: did these events refute Stalin's theory of building socialism in one country? The authors note that some Western scholars treated the theory as bankrupt, or as Stalin's personal invention rather than Lenin's idea, and that some Chinese commentators since the 1990s have blamed it for Soviet failures. They argue that the theory deserves an objective assessment, that its historical role cannot be erased, and that it still offers lessons for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article, which first appeared in the journal Studies on Marxism in 2014, has four parts. It first sets out the background: Lenin's thesis of victory in one country, the encirclement of the Soviet state, the risks that grew under the New Economic Policy, and the 1924–1927 disputes with Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev. It then presents the theory's content, assesses its contributions, and closes with five lessons for China. On content, the authors stress Stalin's distinction between building socialism in one country and the "final victory" of socialism. The first, as they report him, means defeating the national bourgeoisie through a worker–peasant alliance and a unified industrial and agricultural economy. The second requires protection against armed intervention and restoration, which in Stalin's view depends on revolutions elsewhere. The authors credit the theory with four contributions: it justified the existence of Soviet power, it inspired confidence in building socialism, it unified the Party's guiding ideology and organisation, and it enriched Marxism-Leninism. They also hold that Stalin later made it absolute, set the standard for socialism too low, and neglected the productive forces. Tang and Jiang conclude that building socialism with Chinese characteristics can be seen as a completion and development of the theory. They draw five lessons: hold high the banner of socialism; integrate Marxism-Leninism with national conditions in the primary stage of socialism; recognise that socialist construction is a long process and avoid skipping stages; prioritise the productive forces and aim for a high standard of socialism; and rely on self-reliance while seeking a favourable international environment. Read the original if you want a mid-2010s Chinese defence of Stalin's theory and the lessons it draws for China's own path.

Ren Bishi and the Northwest Bureau senior cadres conference 任弼时与西北局高干会 Wang Guangxin This article, from the journal Party Literature (2022, no. 3), examines the senior cadres conference of the CPC Central Committee's Northwest Bureau, held from 19 October 1942 to 14 January 1943. Mao Zedong called it an "examination" in the Rectification campaign. Wang Guangxin argues that Ren Bishi, entrusted by the Central Committee, guided the conference from start to finish and contributed decisively to its success and to the implementation of its decisions. The author also presents the conference as significant for the Party-wide Rectification campaign. The article follows three stages. The first covers the preparation: Ren's promotion of rectification study in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, and his investigations into Party–government–army–people relations, the border region economy and Party history. The second covers the conference itself, under three headings: Party centralised and unified leadership, shifting the focus of work to production, and resolving historical problems of the Northern Shaanxi Party. The third covers the aftermath in the border region and other base areas. Wang's central claim is that Ren's guidance combined theory with fieldwork. Ren traced disunity, such as disputes over salt transport and over the garrison corps' relation to the Northwest Bureau, to weak Party spirit among some cadres. At the conference he argued that the Party is the highest form of proletarian organisation and that democratic centralism is not to be shaken. He told cadres that production was now the "central link" and that wartime mobilisation habits had to change. He also proposed using familiar labour-exchange teams rather than a new name for labour mutual-aid. On historical problems, Wang describes Ren's long investigation of the mistaken 1930s purges in Northern Shaanxi. It led to the Central Committee's December 1942 re-examination decision, which the article says Mao endorsed. Wang concludes that the conference strengthened centralised leadership, drove the production campaign (the article cites 1943 figures for land reclaimed and self-sufficiency), clarified Party history and strengthened unity. Wang presents this as a good result in the "examination" and as a model for other base areas. Read the original if you study the Yan'an Rectification campaign, Ren Bishi's role, or the Party's wartime handling of leadership, economy and history.

The spiritual quality of "perseverance" in the historical experience of the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 中国共产党百年奋斗历史经验中“坚持”的精神品质 Shen Chengfei Jin Tao The 2021 Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, uses the word "persevere" (jianchi) 160 times. Shen and Jin ask what this recurring verb reveals about the Communist Party of China (CPC). They argue that the spirit of perseverance, steadfastness and tenacity running through the "ten adherences" is the volitional guarantee and source of strength that made the Party's whole historical experience possible. The article is organised around three questions: why the Party perseveres, what it perseveres in, and how it does so. The first part traces the origins of the "persevering" struggle in the four historical periods of the century and in the Party's ideals and sense of foreboding. The second sorts the ten adherences into three levels: the subject, the object and the path of development. The third sets out the mechanisms that sustain the quality. Shen and Jin contend that perseverance was forced by the hard road of national rejuvenation and grew from lofty ideals and a collective consciousness of hardship, expressed as concern for the nation, the people and the Party itself. On the subject level, they place leadership by the Party, self-reform, the united front and daring to struggle. On the object level, they place putting the people first and having the world in mind. On the path level, they place an independent Chinese road, now Chinese modernization, together with theoretical and practical innovation. They then identify three sustaining mechanisms. The first is an inner drive: founding the Party for the public good and governing for the people. The second is an external corrective: summing up experience, learning from setbacks and holding a correct view of Party history. The third is the logical unfolding of perseverance through a consistent guiding ideology (Marxism), a continuous genealogy of Party spirit traced to the great founding spirit, and stable policies since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The authors conclude that the Party's perseverance appears concretely as perseverance in guiding thought, in spiritual genealogy and in institutions and policy. In their account, guiding thought fixes its nature, the spiritual genealogy gives it character and policy expresses it in action. Only when the abstract and the concrete are united, they argue, can the quality be passed on and developed. Read the original if you want a close reading of how a Party-affiliated academic account derives a psychological and moral "quality" from the 2021 Resolution's historical summary and ties it to the Party's account of its own legitimacy.

Scientifically understanding and grasping the Party's innovative theory of the new era 科学理解和把握新时代党的创新理论 Liu Dehai Writing in Economic Daily on 21 December 2022, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Dehai takes up how the Party's innovative theory of the new era should be understood. Liu argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the major theoretical achievement of the Party's exploration, and that it marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The commentary is organised in three parts. It first describes the content and structure of the Thought, then explains the Two Integrations, and finally turns to the Thought's worldview and methodology as summarised in the Congress report's "six musts". Liu presents the "ten affirmations", the "fourteen commitments" and the "thirteen areas of achievement" as mutually reinforcing parts of one scientific theoretical system. On the Two Integrations, Liu says integration with China's specific realities means looking at the primary stage of socialism, the changed principal contradiction, and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation alongside global change. It means applying Marxism's worldview and method, not reciting its conclusions or treating it as dogma. Integration with fine traditional Chinese culture rests, in Liu's view, on the compatibility of ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people as the foundation of the state" with the values of scientific socialism, and calls for creative transformation of that culture. Liu reads the "six musts" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global vision) as an organic whole. In Liu's account, they answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Liu calls on readers to use Marxism as the arrow aimed at the target of China in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style overview of how the Thought is framed after the 20th Party Congress.

Green development reflects the responsibility of a major country 绿色发展体现大国担当 Men Jing This commentary, published in Economic Daily on 30 October 2022, argues that green development, one element of the new development philosophy, both benefits China and shows China acting as a responsible major country. Men presents it as a guiding principle and a method of modernization. The piece has two parts. The first, on how green development benefits China, links it to the report of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and to Chinese modernization, one of whose features is harmony between humanity and nature. The second, on how it benefits the world, reviews China's part in global climate, biodiversity and development governance. In the first part Men quotes Xi Jinping's formula that protecting the ecological environment protects productive forces. Men then cites figures for the past decade: 960 million mu of afforestation, forest coverage of 24.02%, a 34.4% fall in carbon intensity, and coal's share of primary energy consumption falling from 68.5% to 56%. In the second part Men lists China's pledges and initiatives: peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality before 2060, the Global Development Initiative, South–South cooperation, the Kunming Declaration, and a green Belt and Road Initiative with partner agreements and an international coalition. Men concludes that China has both positions and commitments, offers successful experience and public goods, and has won broad international recognition. The article holds that China's continued development and opening up will energise the global green economic recovery. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary in 2022 presented environmental achievements and global climate diplomacy as proof of major-country responsibility.

Xi Jinping Thought on Economy has enriched and developed Marxist political economy 习近平经济思想丰富发展了马克思主义政治经济学 Yan Maoxu This short commentary, published in People's Daily in January 2023, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Economy has enriched and developed Marxist political economy. Yan presents it as an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Yan's account, it grew out of practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and opens a new horizon for contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. The article is organised around three sets of "original contributions", each pairing a policy idea with the questions it answers and the Marxist theory it is said to extend. These cover the Party's leadership of economic work, the shift to high-quality development, and the reform of the market economy and opening up. First, Yan holds that centralised, unified Party leadership of economic work and the people-centred approach to development answer the questions of the fundamental guarantee and standpoint of economic development. Yan links this to the Marxist relationship between economic base and superstructure. Second, the judgement that China has moved from high-speed growth to high-quality development, together with the new development stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern, is said to answer questions of historical position, guiding principles and path. Yan presents this as continuing and innovating Marx and Engels's ideas on development principles, stages and social reproduction. Third, improving the socialist market economy, supply-side structural reform and the healthy development of economic globalization are said to address institutional foundations, the main line of work and opening up. Yan concludes that these ideas deepen the Party's understanding of the laws of socialist construction, the socialist market economy and economic globalization, and extend Marxist theory on the economy and politics, on market economy and on the world economy. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary frames Xi Jinping's economic thought as an innovation within Marxist political economy.

On the global significance of Xi Jinping's economic thought 论习近平经济思想的世界意义 Zhou Wen Writing in the Party-run Economic Daily in October 2022, Zhou Wen asks what Xi Jinping's economic thought offers beyond China. The author argues that, formed in practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), it answers questions such as "what is wrong with the world and what should we do" and gives "the key of wisdom" for resolving global development problems under today's complex conditions. The commentary is organised in four parts: an introduction and three thematic sections. These present the thought's significance through high-quality development and the sharing of Chinese experience, the path of Chinese modernization as a Chinese approach to world development, the combination of an efficient market with an enterprising government, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind in global governance. Zhou supports the argument with economic figures, quotations from Xi, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Zhou's central claims are that modernization is not Westernization and that Chinese modernization is not a copy of Western models. According to the author, many developing countries that copied the West lost their autonomy and fell into stagnation and instability, whereas China industrialised in decades and rose peacefully, without colonial expansion. The author adds that China's socialist market economy, which combines public ownership with the market, has dispelled the "myth" of neoliberal economics and offers a model for handling the state–market relationship. Zhou cites GDP growth from 53.9 trillion yuan in 2012 to 114.4 trillion in 2021, and a World Bank assessment that the Belt and Road Initiative would lift millions out of poverty. Zhou concludes that Xi Jinping's economic thought extends Marxist political economy, including its theory of the world economy, and that it points to a path for countries seeking both faster development and independence. The author presents China's initiatives, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the New Development Bank and South–South cooperation funds, as steps towards narrowing the global development gap and reforming the global economic order. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Chinese commentary presents the international relevance of Xi Jinping's economic thought.

The decisive significance and inner logic of the "Two Establishes" “两个确立”的决定性意义及内在逻辑 Han Qingxiang This commentary, first published in Economic Daily on 9 October 2022, explains why the Two Establishes are of decisive significance. Han Qingxiang argues that the Party's establishing of Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party, and of the guiding position of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is both necessary and decisive for the Party and the country. Han opens with the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, which describes Xi as the main creator of this body of thought. The article then reads the Two Establishes through three "logics": theoretical, historical and practical (or realistic). It ends with a call to strengthen political, intellectual, theoretical and emotional identification with the Two Establishes. On the theoretical side, Han grounds the Two Establishes in the historical-materialist unity of objective laws and subjective initiative. The objective tasks of the new era are building a modern socialist country, common prosperity and national rejuvenation. Han holds that achieving them depends on the masses and on the guiding role of leaders. On the historical side, Han points to the Zunyi Conference of 1935 and the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as showing that the Party succeeds when it has a strong leadership core and correct guiding thought. On the practical side, Han argues that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is now irreversible and that no fundamental mistakes can be allowed. Han says that standing on the right side of history and keeping the initiative requires centralised Party leadership, continued adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and the two core establishments themselves. Han concludes that, under Xi's leadership and guided by his thought, China has achieved the first centenary goal and is moving towards the second. The Two Establishes are presented as the fundamental guarantee of national rejuvenation. Han calls on Party members to turn identification with them into conscious action in carrying out the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official case for the Two Establishes was framed in the weeks before the 20th Party Congress.

Making willingness, courage and skill in taking responsibility a prevailing norm 让愿担当、敢担当、善担当蔚然成风 Yin Yuping Writing in early 2023, Yin Yuping takes up how the Communist Party can make its cadres willing, bold and skilled in taking responsibility (dandang zuowei). The commentary starts from Xi Jinping's speeches of December 2022 and January 2023, which list keeping up a drive to get things done among the unique problems the Party must solve. Yin argues that building incentive, protection and care mechanisms will make such conduct the prevailing norm. This, the author says, provides organisational support for building a modern socialist country and for national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. The piece has four parts. The first sets out why taking responsibility is required by the new journey of the new era. The second covers incentive and accountability mechanisms that build willingness to take responsibility. The third turns to mechanisms for tolerating and correcting errors, which aim to make cadres bold enough to act. The fourth deals with care for cadres, which Yin presents as the basis for building their skill. Each part draws heavily on Xi Jinping's remarks. Yin first presents responsibility-taking as a political quality of the Party, a hallmark of the "good cadre" standard of loyalty, integrity and responsibility, and a practical route to the goals of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Yin sets these goals against warnings of "black swan" and "grey rhino" risks. The core institutional proposals follow. Evaluation should put political standards first, define specific cases of inaction, and reward those who take on difficult tasks. Accountability should be precise, since Yin says that over-broad or crude accountability produces the perverse result that those who act make more mistakes and those who do nothing make none. The error-tolerance mechanism should rest on Xi's "three distinctions", which separate inexperienced or exploratory mistakes from knowing violations of discipline and law, and it should follow clear procedures that guarantee cadres' right to appeal. Yin adds that tolerance is not an end in itself and must be paired with correction. Yin concludes that rewards, tolerance and care must work together: strict management combined with warm concern, with particular support for grassroots cadres. Care is to take the form of trust and guidance at work, attention to daily and family difficulties, and moral support through honours and protection of reputation. The commentary offers no new theory but sets out how current Party policy on cadre management is meant to operate. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the Party's official reasoning on cadre incentives, accountability and error tolerance after the 20th Party Congress.

Advancing and expanding Chinese modernization under the leadership of the Party 在党领导下推进和拓展中国式现代化 Yue Kui This short commentary, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), argues that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China. Yue Kui notes that the Congress report lists "upholding the leadership of the Communist Party of China" first among the essential requirements of Chinese modernization. In Yue's view, building a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation require that Party leadership be applied in every field and link of the process. The article has three parts. The first reviews how the Party has advanced and expanded Chinese modernization over more than a century. The second covers the blueprint set out by the 20th Party Congress. The third addresses how to gather the strength needed to carry it out. Yue traces the Party's modernization goals from the revolutionary and construction period, through the reform and opening up era's concept of "Chinese-style modernization" and the three-step strategy, to the innovations since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On this account, history and reality show that Chinese modernization is led by the Party and suited to China's conditions. The author presents the Congress's two-stage plan, which calls for basic modernization by 2035 and a modern socialist country by the middle of the century, as consistent with China's reality and the people's wishes. Yue also contends that the Party, as the core of leadership, has united the whole nation, and that this unity produced the achievements of socialist modernization. Yue concludes that the Party's overall leadership must be upheld and strengthened. The author calls for mobilising all positive factors, consolidating unity among the peoples of China and strengthening unity with Chinese people overseas. The article is a brief, official-style exposition of the Party-leadership theme in the Congress report. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars presented the link between Party leadership and Chinese modernization soon after the 20th Party Congress.

China's responsibility in promoting fairer development of the global governance system 促进全球治理体系公平发展的中国担当 Zhao Zhongxiu Writing in early 2023 in the wake of the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhao Zhongxiu asks how China has taken part in global governance and what further role it should play. The commentary, first published on Guangming Online, argues that under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era China has pursued high-level opening up and offered Chinese solutions to the world's "great changes unseen in a century". Zhao presents this as the conduct of a responsible major power. The piece has two halves. The first surveys five fields in which China is said to have contributed: economic governance, health governance, poverty governance, security governance and climate governance. The second turns to the future, setting out five matching tasks. A short passage between them warns of obstacles in the international environment. In the first half Zhao cites concrete evidence. It includes a fall in China's average import tariff from 15.3% to 7.4%, the negative-list system for foreign investment, and the declared completion of poverty eradication in 2020, ten years ahead of the UN 2030 Agenda target. It also includes a 48.4% cut in carbon intensity against 2005 and agreements on climate cooperation with 38 developing countries. Zhao contrasts this with protectionism, unilateralism, localism and pragmatism in the economic policies of developed countries, which in Zhao's view harm global development cooperation. China is cast as a "constant" amid a changing world economy. For the future Zhao calls for several steps. These are multilateralism through the WTO, APEC and the G20 and high-quality Belt and Road cooperation; a global public health system and a Chinese global health strategy; and poverty reduction tied to the Belt and Road Initiative and to Chinese firms going abroad. Zhao also proposes opposing hegemonism, double standards and unilateral sanctions while giving developing countries a larger voice on security, and leading South-South climate cooperation while meeting the dual carbon goals. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese university leader presents China's global governance role, in official language, across economy, health, poverty, security and climate.

Continuously shaping new drivers and new advantages for development 不断塑造发展新动能新优势 Pan Yuteng This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in February 2023, reads the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) on education, science and technology, and talent. Pan notes that the report for the first time gave "implementing the strategy of invigorating China through science and education and strengthening talent support for modernization" its own section. In Pan's view, this shows a strategic outlook that treats the three fields as one whole in building China into a leading country in each. The piece first sets out the three fields' place in building a modern socialist country, then cites achievements of the past decade. It then turns to three headings: giving education priority, self-reliance in science and technology, and talent as a leading and driving force. Pan holds that education is the foundation, science and technology the key, and talent the fundamental factor of Chinese modernization. Pan cites the claim that science and technology are the primary productive force, talent the primary resource and innovation the primary driving force. As evidence, Pan gives figures: national R&D spending rose from 1 trillion to 2.8 trillion yuan over the decade, ranking second in the world, and China has the largest number of researchers. For each field Pan lists tasks, including a high-quality education system, a new system for mobilizing national resources, a national laboratory system, work on "bottleneck" technologies, and the principle of the Party managing talent. Pan concludes that the strategies for invigorating China through science and education, for strengthening the country through talent, and for innovation-driven development should be implemented in depth, so as to open new fields and keep shaping new drivers and advantages for development. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how the 20th Party Congress linked education, science and technology, and talent.

Better playing the role of trade unions around the Party's central task 围绕党的中心任务更好发挥工会作用 Leading Party Group of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions Published in the People's Daily and reposted in February 2023, this commentary by the Party group of the All-China Federation of Trade Unions takes up how trade unions should act after the 20th Party Congress (2022). It starts from the Congress report's statement that the Party's central task is building a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. The authors argue that trade unions, in keeping with their tradition, must centre their work on this task and serve the overall agenda under Party leadership, so as to gather the strength of the working class. The text is organised in five sections, each opening with a part of the Congress report and ending with what unions should do. The sections cover Party leadership and the Two Establishes; study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; the skills of the workforce and high-quality development; a people-centred approach and workers' status as masters; and trade union reform and building. The core argument is that each element of the Party's central task gives unions a concrete duty. In the authors' account, Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of Chinese modernization, so unions must make it their political principle and uphold the Two Upholds. Unions are to spread Party theory "into enterprises, workshops and teams" and consolidate the Party's class and mass base. For high-quality development they are to build a knowledgeable, skilled and innovative industrial workforce through skills competitions, mass innovation activities and the promotion of the model worker, labour and craftsman spirit. On the people-centred approach, the authors call for protecting workers' legitimate rights, applying whole-process people's democracy through workers' congresses, raising labour's share in primary distribution, strengthening protection for flexible and new-form employment workers, and enriching cultural life in support of common prosperity. The authors conclude that unions should keep and strengthen their political, advanced and mass character as a bridge between the Party and workers. They propose strengthening grassroots organisations, building a high-calibre professional cadre of union officials, improving online union work and using high-quality Party building to guide innovation. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the national union leadership framed the unions' tasks after the 20th Party Congress.

The generative logic, mechanism and contemporary cultivation of the cultural gene of common prosperity 共同富裕文化基因的生成逻辑、作用机理及时代涵育 Cui Haiying Cui Haiying asks what cultural resources sustain the pursuit of common prosperity, beyond its economic conditions and institutional guarantees. The article argues that there is a "cultural gene" of common prosperity: a stable, inheritable and evolving spiritual structure that Cui describes as the "genetic code" of how the Chinese people think and act in pursuing a better life. It is presented as the cultural root of the Party's effort to seek happiness for the people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts: how the gene was formed, how it operates, and how it should be cultivated in the present. The first part traces its formation through historical, theoretical and practical logics. The second examines its effect through the Party's nature and purpose, its original aspiration and mission, and its spiritual lineage. The third sets out measures drawn from the gene's stability, inheritance and evolution. In Cui's account, the historical logic runs from early notions of equitable distribution and the pre-Qin thinkers (Confucius's "not worrying about poverty but about inequality") to Sun Yat-sen. The theoretical logic draws on three features of Marxism: its people-centredness, openness and progressiveness. The practical logic follows the Party from land reform through the first use of the term common prosperity, Deng Xiaoping's formulations, and Xi Jinping's statements in the new era. Cui argues that the gene shapes the Party's direction, for example in distribution policy, anchors its values across generations of leaders, and sustains its drive through spirits such as the Daqing spirit and the poverty-alleviation spirit. For cultivation, Cui proposes upholding Party leadership, the socialist system and the people's principal position. Cui also proposes drawing on traditional, revolutionary and advanced socialist culture, and balancing preserving fundamentals with innovation, openness with confidence, and understanding with practice. Cui concludes that cultivating this gene gives common prosperity a value foundation and a source of strength. The article also warns against what it calls egalitarianism, "lying flat", Western-style welfarism and ideas of "robbing the rich to help the poor", and calls for building a Chinese discourse on common prosperity. Read the original if you want a culturalist, Party-centred account of how Chinese scholars link the Party's history, Marxism and traditional thought to the common prosperity agenda.

The value implications, strategic design and development path of building a modern socialist country in all respects 全面建设社会主义现代化国家的价值意蕴、战略设计及发展路径 Li Nan Zeng Lihua Taking the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as its starting point, this article asks what kind of modern socialist country China is to build and how. Li Nan and Zeng Lihua argue that building a modern socialist country in all respects carries a distinct set of values. They also argue that it rests on a systematic strategic design and requires a coordinated set of development paths, which they regard as necessary for Chinese modernization in the new stage of development. The article has three parts. The first sets out four value implications: moving people from "one-dimensional" to all-round development, putting into practice the Party's original aspiration and founding mission, securing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and opening a new realm of modern civilization. The second reviews the strategic design: eight goals for 2035, five guiding principles, the staged steps from the Two Centenary Goals onward, and six methodological choices. The third proposes six paths, covering Party leadership, high-quality development, whole-process people's democracy, cultural confidence, common prosperity and harmony between humanity and nature. The authors' central claim is that this modernization differs in kind from the Western model. They describe the Western model as capital-centred, built on plunder and exploitation, and equating "modernization" with "Westernization". Chinese modernization, in their account, rests on people-centred development and an all-round development of the person, with material, cultural and ecological foundations. They say it turns the model of world modernization "from singular to plural". Leadership by the Party is presented as the fundamental guarantee, and the authors offer evidence for readiness to advance, including per capita GDP of 12,551 US dollars in 2021 and China's climb in the Global Innovation Index from 34th in 2012 to 11th in 2022. The authors conclude that the two-step plan, basic modernization by 2035 and a strong modern socialist country by the middle of the century, should be pursued through stronger Party leadership. They also call for deeper reform and opening up, for the Two Unwaverings, for a rounded income distribution structure and for green, low-carbon development. They add that the struggle in the ideological and cultural sphere must be sustained. The article is a systematic exposition of the congress report's themes in official terms, not a critical or comparative study. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based overview of how Chinese academics organise the 20th Party Congress's modernization agenda around values, strategy and policy paths.

The dialectics of technological innovation in Capital 《资本论》中技术创新思想的辩证法 Wang Cheng Wang Cheng asks how technological innovation should be understood in Capital and its manuscripts, where it forms an implicit line of thought. The article argues that Western economics, lacking dialectics, explains only the surface effects of innovation. Marx, in Wang's reading, treats innovation dialectically, as an expression of capital's essential character in the interaction of productive forces and relations of production. The article has four parts. It first criticises Western readings of Marx as a technological determinist or evolutionist, covering Schumpeter's methodological individualism, paradigm-based models such as the Rae–Marx–Schumpeter growth idea, and David Harvey's structuralist reading. It then follows Hegel's logic of essence through Marx's work: the inner driving force (essence), the phenomenon, and actuality. A final part considers how capitalist innovation is transcended. Wang's core claim is that the inner driving force of capitalist innovation is the reproduction of capitalist social relations, mediated by social labour as traced through Marx's three major manuscripts. Innovation is therefore not the same as productive-force progress. At the level of phenomenon, it appears as a contradiction between producing and realising surplus value. Wang reads this as a three-stage cycle of individual innovation, generalisation through competition, and a new round of innovation driven by the average rate of profit. Volume II is read as showing how innovation intensifies discontinuities in circulation, hides value transfer and deepens crises, while Volume III's falling profit rate completes the account. Wang concludes that Marx's dialectic differs from Hegel's closed circle by adding human agency. Wang concludes that innovation has a dual character. It strengthens capital's control over workers, yet it creates the material basis of a future society and the conditions for overturning capitalist relations. Human beings, as the actors in innovation, move from enslavement by things toward real liberation and all-round free development, in what Wang calls an objective reversal of the logic of subjugation. Read the original if you want a Hegelian-dialectical reading of Marx's theory of technology, set against Schumpeterian and Harvey-style interpretations, with close reference to the Capital manuscripts.

The basic demands and fundamental flaws of Proudhon's conception of justice An analysis based on the materialist conception of history 蒲鲁东正义观的基本诉求和根本缺陷 Wang Fengming Wang Luyuan Research on Proudhon has concentrated on his theory of value and his reform schemes, and has paid less attention to his theory of justice. Wang and Wang argue that without understanding that theory one cannot understand the other two, and that it carries a petty-bourgeois appeal which still shapes ideas of justice today. Using the materialist conception of history as method, they contend that Proudhon's conception of justice is abstract, idealist and in the end a petty-bourgeois fantasy of turning back history. The article follows three questions in Proudhon's work. First, why justice is 'necessary': for Proudhon it underlies law, institutions, order, cooperation and exchange. Second, what justice is: an eternal principle, human sociality, equality, and finally absolute equality of property. Third, how justice is to be realised: through a 'constituted value' theory and through a social form that keeps individual private ownership. Each section sets out Proudhon's position and then criticises it, mainly with Marx's texts, including Capital, the Grundrisse and The German Ideology. On the first question, the authors argue that Proudhon inverts the relation between social life and ideas. In their account, ideas of justice reflect existing economic relations, and law and institutions are tools by which the ruling class consolidates a given economic order. On the second, they hold that Proudhon's demand to abolish property targets only bourgeois ownership based on exploiting others' labour. It leaves intact the property of small producers in simple commodity production, so his ideal of 'eternal justice' is drawn from the legal relations of commodity production. On the third question, the authors raise three objections. Proudhon's theory ignores socially necessary labour time and treats the value of labour as a measure of value, which they say undermines the labour theory of value. Individual private ownership, they argue, inevitably develops into capitalist private ownership and polarisation. Equivalent exchange also holds only as a tendency and on average, so 'full' exchange of equal labour is utopian. The authors conclude that real equality would require abolishing commodity exchange and private ownership and building a society on public ownership of the means of production. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of Proudhon's ethics and a view of how Chinese scholars use the materialist conception of history to assess petty-bourgeois theories of justice.

The documentary value of Zhou Enlai's "The Current Situation and Tasks of the War of Resistance" in elaborating "protracted resistance" 周恩来《目前抗战形势及任务》阐发“长期抗战”的文献价值 Li Liangming Wu Qinghua This article examines a little-noticed report outline by Zhou Enlai, "The Current Situation and Tasks of the War of Resistance" (Mudian kangzhan xingshi ji renwu), which the authors present as an important early statement of the idea of "protracted resistance" against Japan. The text survives in Bai Shui's book Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao, first published in Hankou in April 1938 and reissued in 2014. The authors argue that the outline shows Zhou applying Marxist standpoint and method to China's concrete conditions, and that it is a valuable source for studies of Zhou's thought and of the War of Resistance. The article has three parts. The first traces the document's publication history: Li and Wu compare it with entries in Zhou's chronology and with four pre-1949 versions under slightly different titles, and conclude that it is the outline of Zhou's report of 17 December 1937 to representatives of Xi'an organisations. The second summarises the content in three sections: lessons from four months of full-scale war, the crisis of resistance and the way out, and the tasks of sustaining a long war. The third assesses the document's value. On the first section, the authors report Zhou's view that the war had raised national self-confidence and begun to create a unified political authority through Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. Early military setbacks, in his analysis, came from Japan's greater strength and long preparation, from collaborators and pro-Japanese elements, and from weak mobilisation. The article reads Zhou as locating the real crisis not in lost territory but in wavering inside the anti-Japanese camp and the rise of capitulationism. His remedy was to consolidate and expand the anti-Japanese national united front on the basis of Kuomintang–Communist cooperation, build a unified national defence government and army, and mobilise and organise millions of people. The authors also cite Zhou's refusal in February 1938 of Chiang Kai-shek's proposal that the Communist Party dissolve into the Kuomintang, as evidence of both independence and flexibility in the united front. The authors conclude that the document enriches research on Zhou's military thought. They place it in a sequence of his statements from July to December 1937 in which his understanding of a protracted war deepened as the situation changed. They also hold that it offers further angles for the history of the War of Resistance, notably its treatment of protracted resistance through the united front. Read the original if you are a historian of the Chinese Communist Party, of Zhou Enlai or of the anti-Japanese war and want the source-tracing of this outline and its place among Zhou's wartime texts.

Accelerating the construction of the "three major systems" of historical theory research in the new era Preface to a five-volume series and an account of the founding of the Institute of Historical Theory 加快构建新时代历史理论研究“三大体系” Xia Chuntao Xia Chuntao, writing in early 2023, introduces a five-volume series, Frontier Series of Historical Theory Research in the New Era, and uses it to explain why the Institute of Historical Theory was founded and what it should do. The series collects articles from the institute's journal, and it is the institute's first collective publication. Xia's thesis is that historical theory research must be built up quickly into the "three major systems" (discipline, academic and discourse systems), with historical materialism as its guide. The piece has three parts. The first reads the institute's name and gives three reasons for its creation. The second goes through its nine research offices and their projects. The third reviews the journal's transformation since 2019, the contents of the five volumes, and what Xia calls the "founding spirit" of unity, pragmatism and perseverance. Xia argues that the name "historical theory", rather than "historiographical theory", signals the primacy of historical materialism, and that the concept of historical theory takes priority over that of historiographical theory. The three reasons are these. First, a correct view of history is needed against historical nihilism. Second, history should serve contemporary China, and Xia criticises scholarship that is detached from reality, "fragmented" and heavy on textual criticism but light on theory. Third, Chinese historiography has a weaker international voice than the country's standing warrants. Xia urges selective, critical engagement with Western currents such as postmodern historiography, global history, the "New Qing History" and the history of emotions. The nine offices, Xia says, link ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign. Xia stresses that upholding historical materialism and developing it go together, citing the Party's treatment of the five-social-formations theory as a guide rather than a dogma. Success, Xia says, is measured by producing results and talent, because people are the core element of the three systems. Xia concludes that the new era offers historical theory unprecedented opportunity, and calls on the institute to combine basic theory with applied policy research, and historical with contemporary research. Xia also acknowledges that the four newer offices started late and lack accumulated scholarship, and that traditional strengths in historiographical studies have weakened. The text is an institutional self-presentation as well as a programme. Read the original if you want to understand how a leading Chinese institute defines its mission, structure and priorities in historical theory under the current political guidance.

Accelerating the improvement of the socialist market economy system 加快完善社会主义市场经济体制 Yang Jing Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yang Jing asks how the socialist market economy system should be understood and further improved. The commentary argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has accelerated this improvement, treating the system as an important part of the basic socialist economic system. Yang holds that this has deepened understanding of market-economy laws, extended Chinese modernization and enriched Marxist political economy on the market economy. The piece has three sections. The first places the socialist market economy system within the basic socialist economic system. The second discusses letting the market play the decisive role in allocating resources while the government plays its role better. The third concerns correctly understanding and handling the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital. It draws throughout on statements by Xi Jinping and on the 20th Party Congress report's call to build a high-standard socialist market economy system. Yang first notes that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) placed the system alongside public ownership as the main body and the primary role of distribution according to work. Together these form a \"three-in-one\" framework. In Yang's reading, combining the basic socialist system with the market lets ownership, distribution and economic operation form an organic unity. Yang argues that this serves people-centred development, the principal contradiction and common prosperity, by enlarging the \"cake\" and then dividing it well. Second, Yang traces the Party's evolving view of the state–market relation to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The author calls for less direct government interference in micro-level activity and for better macroeconomic governance, regulation and public services to remedy market failure. Third, Yang acknowledges the many forms of capital in China today. The author argues that capital's profit-seeking can cause disorder if unchecked, and calls for equal access, orderly competition and legal oversight with \"traffic lights\". Yang concludes that perfecting the system in this way conforms to the law that relations of production must suit the state of the productive forces. The author contends that it frees and develops the productive forces and meets people's needs for a better life. Capital should be guided to promote productive forces, wealth creation and livelihood protection, and kept from drifting away from the real economy. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Chinese commentary in early 2023 framed the state, market and capital relationship after the 20th Party Congress.

Putting health first and building a Healthy China 坚持健康优先 建设健康中国 Yao Jianhong Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yao Jianhong asks what it means to give priority to people's health and how this principle should drive the building of a Healthy China. The author argues that health-first development is both an important principle and a key mechanism of Healthy China, and that it requires changes in government priorities, in the health system and in individual attitudes. The article has three parts. The first sets out the meaning of health-first development from three angles: health's place in economic and social development, a fundamental change in how the health sector operates, and citizens' own sense of responsibility. The second gives four reasons for its significance, and the third lists the priority tasks, from high-quality development and public health to medical science, talent and local experimentation. Yao's central reasoning is that health is a basis of development as well as its goal. The author sums up the first angle as 'three priorities and one continuing effort': prioritising health spending, medical science and technology breakthroughs and the training of health workers, while keeping health integrated into all policies. The health system is to shift from a treatment-centred to a people's-health-centred model, with prevention first. Yao also stresses that individuals are the 'first persons responsible' for their own health. As reasons for health priority, the article cites the people-centred development philosophy, the fragmentation of services and weak coordination of medical care, medical insurance and medicines, the risks of epidemics and chronic disease in an ageing society, and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The proposals include a government-led non-profit health service system, a stronger four-tier public health network, early warning and biosecurity law, and public health spending that grows faster than overall health spending. Yao also suggests health-risk taxes and labels on tobacco and high-salt, high-sugar foods, and insurance incentives for healthy behaviour. They further call for more funding for medical research and for local authorities to treat health as a major livelihood project and to share good practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Healthy China policy priorities were framed after the 20th Party Congress.

Improving the comprehensive governance system and building a healthy online ecosystem 健全综合治理体系 营造良好网络生态 Yang Liqun Writing in early 2023, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yang Liqun, a Jiangsu provincial propaganda and cyberspace official, takes up how China should carry out the Congress's call to "improve the comprehensive governance system for cyberspace and foster a good online ecosystem". The commentary argues that this system is a political necessity and a core part of Xi Jinping's thinking on building China into a cyber power. Yang holds that it needs a systematic, whole-of-society approach under Party leadership. The piece has three parts. It first explains why the system matters, then reviews recent achievements and the challenges that remain, and finally sets out six areas of work for applying the 20th Party Congress's guidance. It traces the policy line from the 19th Party Congress (2017) through the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) to the 20th Congress, and refers to the national meeting of cyberspace administration heads held on 4–5 January 2023. Yang's core argument is that the internet has become the main arena of ideological struggle, so governing it is tied directly to political and national security and to the Party's long-term rule. Comprehensive governance is also presented as part of modernizing the system and capacity of national governance, and as a condition for high-quality development of the cyber sector. On results, Yang cites ideological-responsibility inspections, the "Qinglang" (clear and bright) campaigns, online legal education and cadre training. The stated problems are fast-changing technologies such as the metaverse and AI, weak influence of mainstream new-media platforms and internet firms, and a few platforms that neglect their responsibilities. The remedies are organised under image-laden headings: clarified lines of responsibility, a stronger multimedia opinion landscape, cleaner online content, online civility work aimed at young people, law enforcement, and cybersecurity and data-security checks. Yang concludes that governance should move from after-the-fact management to process-based governance, and from fragmented to coordinated control, with integrated online and offline governance. The guiding formula is that positive energy is the overall requirement, control is the hard principle and good use is the real skill. Read the original if you want to see how a provincial Party cyberspace official translates central internet-governance doctrine into operational tasks and slogans.

New changes in the world landscape and new features of great-power competition 世界格局新变化与大国博弈新特点 Wang Wen Writing in early 2023, the tenth anniversary of the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind and of the Belt and Road Initiative, Wang Wen asks how China should read the world situation and great-power rivalry in the third decade of the century. The author argues that the 'great changes unseen in a century' are continuing to unfold and that great-power competition is intensifying. China therefore needs strategic resolve and policy patience, and should view its problems as a 'protracted war' in the long term. The piece was published in the Party journal Qianxian. The article has three parts. The first sets out three dimensions of the continuing transformation: world politics, the international economy and global ideas, drawing mainly on events of 2022. The second warns that the change will be uneven and that China must prepare for severe tests in political security, economic and financial affairs, and ideology. The third lists three guidelines for 2023, namely focusing on development, daring to struggle, and expanding opening up and cooperation. Wang's central claim is that non-Western countries are rising collectively and independently, citing Russia, Latin America's leftward turn, ASEAN, India, Central Asia, the Arab world, Africa and RCEP. The author describes a 'de-Westernisation' of economic development, pointing to falling shares of the US dollar in reserves and Europe in world output, and a 'demythologising' of Western democracy, with development replacing it as the dominant global discourse. At the same time Wang cautions that Western strengths persist and that the trend will not be linear. The author portrays the United States as pursuing an Indo-Pacific strategy, provoking possible conflict in the western Pacific and over Taiwan, imposing chip embargoes and other economic measures, and using cultural influence to shape ideas, all in the author's account aimed at delaying the decline of Western hegemony. Wang concludes that China should keep its independent, peaceful foreign policy and win-win opening, restore the economy through high-quality development, resist hostile forces while distinguishing politicians from ordinary people, and push for a community with a shared future for mankind. The author also calls for stronger ideological security. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese international-relations scholar close to Party discourse framed the post-2022 world order and the rivalry with the United States for a Party-journal audience.

Only unity brings victory, only struggle brings success 团结才能胜利 奋斗才会成功 Sun Xiuling This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily, takes up Xi Jinping's formulations at the 20th Party Congress (2022) that "unity is strength" and that "only unity brings victory, only struggle brings success". Sun Xiuling argues that unity and struggle are the key to the Party's past achievements and a requirement for building a modern socialist country in all respects. The author presents the slogan as a rule drawn from long practice. The piece is organised in three numbered sections. The first treats unity and struggle as a lesson of the Party's hundred-year history. The second presents them as the most distinctive spiritual hallmark of the Communist Party and the Chinese people. The third explains why they are indispensable for the new journey towards a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Sun first gives the slogan a philosophical grounding in the Marxist law of the unity of opposites: possibility and reality depend on each other and convert into one another under certain conditions. In this reading unity and struggle are the basis and path of victory, and victory is their result, linked through human subjective initiative. Historically, the author holds that unity within the Party, and the centralised and unified leadership of the Central Committee, have been decisive, from the Zunyi Meeting under Mao Zedong to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping as core. Sun then traces the spirit of unity and struggle to five thousand years of Chinese civilisation, which the Party is said to have inherited. Finally, the author calls for resolutely upholding the Two Establishes, strengthening the Two Upholds, forging a sense of community of the Chinese nation as the main thread, and consolidating the broadest patriotic united front. Sun concludes that the project of national rejuvenation is a relay race that requires even greater unity, together with a fighting spirit embedded in the effort to unite, given what the author calls the long-term, complex and arduous nature of the great struggle. The author calls on readers to align thinking and action with the 20th Party Congress and to unite all forces that can be united. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school commentary links the 20th Congress slogan on unity and struggle to Party history, national spirit and loyalty to the Central Committee.

Clarifying the direction of Chinese modernization: a deep grasp of its Chinese characteristics 明确中国式现代化建设的方向 深刻把握中国式现代化的中国特色 Shao Changjun This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily, interprets a passage from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The report describes Chinese modernization as socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, with features common to all countries and Chinese characteristics rooted in national conditions. Shao argues that these characteristics set the direction of modernization and reflect the Party's mission and the essential features of socialism. The article takes the five characteristics in turn: a huge population, common prosperity for all, coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and a path of peaceful development. Each section opens with a quotation from Xi and then sets out practical requirements. For Shao, the huge population of over 1.4 billion brings unprecedented difficulty and potential, and calls for steady, step-by-step progress, a people-centred approach and a shift from a large to a strong country in human resources. Common prosperity is described as a long historical process that combines market and government and enlarges and then fairly divides the "cake". On material and cultural-ethical progress, the author puts high-quality development first and calls for advancing socialist culture. Shao says the ecological path rejects pollution first and clean-up later, and that the peaceful path rejects war, colonialism and plunder. Shao concludes that these characteristics should be applied in every field and link of socialist modernization. The article ends by calling for a community with a shared future for mankind, the Global Development Initiative and the Global Security Initiative. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style summary of how the five Chinese characteristics of modernization were presented to a wide readership in early 2023.

On the dissemination and Sinicization of the concept of revolution in the Communist Manifesto 论《共产党宣言》革命概念传播与中国化 Dai Juntan Pan Qin Taking up Wolfgang Fritz Haug's remark that the question of revolution is the "source code" of Marxism, the article asks how the Manifesto's concept of revolution was established, translated and adapted to the Chinese context. Dai and Pan argue that the classic passage on the tasks of proletarian revolution, which Lenin expounded in The State and Revolution, became the "revolution code" of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that Chinese Communists gradually decoded it through practice. The study has three parts. It first traces the European word revolution from Greek and Latin terms through the English, American and French Revolutions to Marx, Engels and Lenin. It then follows the Chinese word geming, its Japanese re-coining as a translation of revolution, and its return to China, tracked through early English–Chinese dictionaries from Morrison (1822) to 1916. The third part examines Chinese renderings of the Manifesto's key passage, from Zhu Zhixin and Cheng Shewo through Chen Wangdao and Li Da to the two Chinese translations of The State and Revolution. The authors make three main moves. First, they hold that Marx treated revolution as the highest expression of class struggle, centred on state power and aimed at remaking the socio-economic structure, a sense that sets it apart from rebellion or dynastic change. Second, they argue that the Chinese term moved from its classical meaning of dynastic mandate-change to a positive modern concept through Japanese mediation, with reformers, democrats and liberals stressing different aspects. Third, they read successive translations as steadily deepening understanding: Chen's literal rendering left room for the new state form, Li Da cited Lenin to defend the dictatorship of labour against anarchist readings, and Ke Bonian's vernacular translation of The State and Revolution, which Mao Zedong carried with him, stressed the violent first step. The 1929 Manifesto of the Fourth Red Army is presented as the passage's practical application to Chinese land revolution. The authors conclude that Chinese Communists clarified the defining features of proletarian revolution: smashing the old state machine, establishing a new state form, and reshaping ownership relations. They say the contemporary Chinese dictionary definition preserves this content, whereas Western scholars still dispute the term and a Webster's definition, in their account, describes only pre-proletarian political revolution. Read the original if you are interested in conceptual history, translation studies of the Manifesto, or how Chinese scholars narrate the Sinicization of Marxist revolutionary theory.

Lenin's late view of socialist civilization and its major value 列宁晚年社会主义文明观及其重大价值 Tian Hui Sun Laibin This article, published in Research on Ideological and Political Education in 2023, asks how Lenin in his last years (roughly from spring 1921) thought about building a socialist civilization in a country with a backward economic and cultural base. Tian and Sun argue that Lenin worked out a distinctive path by which relatively backward countries can reach modern civilization through socialism. They present it as a new view of civilization that surpassed earlier Western, populist and Marxist models. The authors first clarify Lenin's use of 'civilization' and 'culture', which he did not divide into the later categories of material, political and spiritual civilization. They then work through five parts: seizing power first and building afterwards; the indirect route to socialism; using capitalism; Lenin's final plan for Russia's civilizational development; and the value of this thinking. Sources include 'On Our Revolution', 'On the Tax in Kind', the 'testament' writings of 1922–23 and Li Dazhao's idea of a 'third new civilization'. The core argument is that Lenin answered critics such as Sukhanov by holding that taking political power first does not violate the general laws of historical development. He treated Russia's particularities as a legitimate variation in the order of stages. After the setback of War Communism, the authors say, Lenin shifted from direct to indirect transition, from revolution to reform and from advance to strategic retreat, through the New Economic Policy. This meant using state capitalism, concessions, cooperatives, bourgeois specialists and Taylorism while controlling capitalism through law, taxation, statistics and supervision. Lenin's final design combined commodity-money relations and electrification, a reform of state organs and Party democracy, and a cultural revolution built on mass literacy and learning from past human achievements. Tian and Sun conclude that Lenin's late thought went beyond the West European path, the populists' village-commune socialism and Marx's late 'non-capitalist path'. They also claim it opened a new route to world modernization that Western theory has obscured. For present-day China, they draw four lessons for Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization: balance universality and particularity, accept that the task is long and hard, combine inheritance with innovation, and balance overall coordination with key priorities. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Lenin's NEP-era writings are being used to ground contemporary Chinese claims about socialist modernization.

The Communist Party of China's war behind enemy lines through Norman Bethune's eyes, 1938–1939 Based on the Bethune archives held overseas 白求恩眼中的中国共产党敌后抗战（1938-1939） Guo Yonghu Zhu Bo The article asks how Norman Bethune, the Canadian Communist surgeon who came to China in 1938 and died in Hebei in November 1939, saw the Communist Party of China and the resistance war it led behind Japanese lines. Guo and Zhu argue that Bethune was not merely an observer but a participant. In their account he recorded conditions faithfully, judged the Party's line highly and publicised its war effort abroad. The source base is the newly digitised Norman Bethune Papers at the Osler Library of the History of Medicine, McGill University, which hold more than 300 items in five collections. The authors first survey the archive in three groups: material from before China, Bethune's letters, reports, diaries, writings and photographs from his time in China, and later Sino-Canadian commemorative records. They then analyse his China-period documents under two headings: his record of the battlefield, and his evaluation and promotion of the Party's resistance. On the first heading, the authors cite Bethune's reports and letters on Japanese bombing and atrocities, and on severe shortages of trained medical staff, drugs, instruments and food for the wounded in the base areas. They also cite his diary impressions of Yan'an and the Anti-Japanese Military and Political University, where he noted egalitarian practice and high morale. On the second, they say Bethune called the Party the best national Communist party he had seen. He endorsed its protracted-war strategy, united front policy and guerrilla warfare, and held that mass mobilisation was the key to survival and growth. The authors describe Bethune's propaganda work as four-fold: a 1938 dispatch for the Manchester Guardian, the story 'The Dud Shell' and the essay 'Wounds' for North American publications, a Jin-Cha-Ji branch of a foreign-publicity association, and the use of treated Japanese prisoners as material. They conclude that his writings show the Party leading the war in the right direction and sustaining national hope, and that he brought this to international audiences. Read the original if you want a source-based account of foreign perceptions of the Communist-led resistance, or a guide to the Bethune materials at McGill.

Meeting challenges with a fighting spirit, opening up the future through striving 以斗争精神迎接挑战 以奋进拼搏开辟未来 Zhou Junjie Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2023, Zhou Junjie takes up the question of why the Communist Party of China must keep and develop a "fighting spirit" (douzheng jingshen) on the new journey after the 20th Party Congress (2022). The article contends that the Party has reached its present position through struggle and must rely on struggle to win the future. It places this within Xi Jinping's call for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform. The piece has three parts. The first presents daring and skilful struggle as the "spiritual code" behind the Party's achievements, drawing on Marxist dialectics and the Party's history. The second sets out why struggle is especially needed now, looking in turn at the international situation, domestic conditions and the state of the Party.
