The third sets out how to carry out struggle on the new journey. Zhou argues that contradiction is universal and that new things grow only through hardship, citing Mao Zedong and Engels. The article describes the world as undergoing changes unseen in a century, with technological competition, geopolitical tension, supply-chain disruption and what it calls hegemonic bullying. At home it lists unbalanced development, dependence on imported key components and Western pressure over trade, technology, finance, Taiwan and the South China Sea. Within the Party it identifies slackness, official inaction and the persistence of corruption risks. Its prescription has three strands: keep historical initiative and the correct political direction, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; build confidence and take the initiative in struggle, with leading cadres setting an example; and raise capabilities and a sense of responsibility. It adds that struggle is an art: seize the principal contradiction, hold firm on principle, stay flexible on tactics, and unite all forces that can be united. Zhou concludes that, with the first centenary goal achieved, the Party must meet the second with a strong sense of responsibility and a willingness to fight, and must solve the "unique problems of a large party". The article is a Party-theoretical commentary that conveys how the official line links struggle, Party discipline and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want to see how a military-academy Party theorist presents the fighting spirit in official discourse after the 20th Party Congress.

Dare to struggle and be good at struggle 敢于斗争 善于斗争 Guangdong Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era This commentary, first published in the People's Daily and written by a Guangdong provincial research centre on Xi Jinping Thought (drafted by Zhang Hao), takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) that all Party members must be willing and able to struggle. It argues that the Party was born amid domestic and foreign troubles and has grown through hardship. In the authors' account, a spirit of struggle runs through every period of its history and must now be carried into the new journey. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the 'great struggle' with 'many new historical features' is long-term, complex and arduous. The second explains where confidence for that struggle comes from. The third lists what the Party must do to win new victories: sharpen awareness of danger, strengthen will and skills, and keep strategic confidence and resolve. On long-term, complex and arduous, the authors point to the changing world, China's continued position in the primary stage of socialism, and the Party's lasting tests and dangers, such as self-complacency, corruption and detachment from the masses. They add that 'black swan' and 'grey rhino' events may occur at any time, and that the nearer the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation comes, the greater the risks. Confidence is said to rest on four sources: the Party's firm leadership, with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; the advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics; and the united effort of the people. The authors conclude that the Party, having reached today through struggle, will win the future the same way. They call for awareness of potential danger and bottom-line thinking, for cadres to build fighting will and capability and take the lead in crises, and for strategic confidence combined with tactical flexibility. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated research centres present the 20th Congress's language on struggle and risk to cadres.

Qiushi commentator: advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party without pause 《求是》杂志评论员：一刻不停推进全面从严治党 Qiushi commentator This commentary, issued under the label of a Qiushi magazine commentator in early 2023, responds to Xi Jinping's 9 January speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. It presents the speech as a strategic deployment for continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and argues that the Party must advance it "without pause" and carry the Party's great self-reform through to the end. The piece first frames the issue historically, then turns to the speech's main themes. It recalls Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era answer to escaping the historical cycle of rise and decline (popular supervision of government) and presents self-reform as the second answer. It then covers the "unique problems of a large party", the building of a governance system, and seven practical tasks for the new journey. The commentary's core claim is that a decade of rigorous Party governance has produced results, which it supports with a 2022 opinion survey by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Bureau of Statistics. According to the survey, 97.4 per cent of respondents considered the effort effective, 22.4 points higher than in 2012. It then lists the "six how-to-always" challenges Xi set out, such as keeping the original aspiration, unifying thought and will, and spotting and solving the Party's own problems. The tasks it derives are political supervision, the eight-point regulations and the "four forms of decadence", discipline building, anti-corruption work, a stronger supervision system and a loyal inspection corps. Anti-corruption is to advance through making officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt, with zero tolerance. The commentary concludes that Party organisations and members should study the speech, grasp the Two Establishes, and strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds. It says political supervision should guarantee that the 20th Party Congress (2022) decisions are carried out and give a firm start to building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how Party media presented the 2023 anti-corruption and discipline agenda, with its official vocabulary and survey figures.

Promoting the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists, with the great founding spirit of the Party as its source 弘扬以伟大建党精神为源头的中国共产党人精神谱系 Theoretical Study Centre Group of the Party Affairs Meeting, Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee This Qiushi article, written collectively by the theoretical study group of the Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee, responds to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Congress put promoting the great founding spirit of the Party into its theme and wrote that spirit into the Party Constitution. The authors argue that the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists, which has the founding spirit as its source, is a core strength of the Party and should be turned into spiritual support for building a modern socialist country and achieving national rejuvenation. The piece has three sections. The first reads the Party's century of history as a unity of a history of struggle and a history of spirit. The second explains why the lineage is the Party's "genetic code". The third sets out how to apply it on the new journey. The first section goes through four periods: the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. For each it names the main task and a list of "spirits", from the Jinggangshan and Yan'an spirits to the poverty-alleviation, anti-epidemic and scientists' spirits. The authors' central claim is that great undertakings give rise to great spirit, and great spirit leads great undertakings. They attribute the Party's vitality to four traits that the lineage embodies: advanced thought and firm belief in Marxism and communism; an unchanged original aspiration to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the nation; tenacity and fine conduct, illustrated by casualty and sacrifice figures; and loyalty to the Party and to the people. For the present, they call for drawing four kinds of strength from the lineage: the power of truth, of practice and struggle, of personal character, and of wisdom (historical initiative). Each is tied to a task, such as studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, sustaining a fighting spirit, standing with the people, and taking a long historical view. The article concludes by calling on the whole Party to rally around the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to promote the lineage as it sets out toward new goals. It cites Xi's visit to Yan'an after the Congress as a sign of the leadership's intent to carry on the Party's red heritage. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how Party theorists framed the "spiritual lineage" and the founding spirit after the 20th Party Congress, including its periodisation and its list of named spirits.

Carrying the Party's great self-reform in the new era through to the end 把新时代党的伟大自我革命进行到底 Yang Fei Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2023, Yang Fei, a Guangzhou Party discipline official, takes up Xi Jinping's call of December 2022 to see the Party's "great self-reform" through to the end. The article argues that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has produced an "overwhelming victory" against corruption, but that the struggle is far from finished and must be sustained with firm political resolve. The piece is a study-and-implementation essay on Xi's Politburo speech and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It has three parts: why self-reform is the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall; what full and rigorous self-governance has achieved over the past decade; and what discipline inspection and supervision organs must now do. It closes with a note on Guangzhou's own tasks. Yang's central claim is that willingness to undertake the Party's self-reform follows from the Party's nature and purpose: it has no interests of its own and represents none of the interest groups or privileged strata. Self-reform and social revolution, in this account, reinforce each other, and a Party of over 96 million members must watch for problems peculiar to large parties, as the Soviet collapse is said to show. For the decade since 2012, Yang credits the Eight-point Regulations, the anti-corruption campaign and the Two Establishes with strengthening Party unity. Yang cites a poll in which 97.4 per cent of respondents rated the campaign effective, 22.4 points above 2012. The practical agenda covers political supervision, a stronger system of Party regulations, continued correction of the "four undesirable work styles", and zero tolerance of corruption, including "new-type" and hidden forms. Yang concludes that discipline organs must keep a tough tone and uphold the centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee as the basis of self-reform. Yang also calls for tighter oversight of top leaders and of corruption involving officials' relatives, and for joint punishment of bribe-givers. Guangzhou, described as at the "two frontlines", is urged to pioneer measures against cross-border and new corruption. Read the original if you want an example of how a local discipline-inspection chief translates the 20th Party Congress line on Party self-reform into concrete anti-corruption tasks.

The "ideational", "material" and "real" content of the ideology of socialism with Chinese characteristics 论中国特色社会主义意识形态的“观念”“物质”和“现实”内容 Kou Qingjie Li Pingping Kou Qingjie and Li Pingping ask what the ideology of socialism with Chinese characteristics actually consists of. They argue that existing scholarship has studied how to strengthen its discourse power and summarised the Party's experience of ideological work, but has not examined its content in a broad sense. Their thesis is that this ideology should be understood as having three components: an "ideational" one, a "material" one and a "real" one. The article is organised in three sections, one for each component. It draws on Marx and Engels's The German Ideology, on Louis Althusser's notion of ideological state apparatuses, on Lenin's What Is to Be Done? and on speeches by Xi Jinping. The authors treat Marxism, Sinicised Marxism and traditional Chinese culture as ideas; institutions, Party organisation and state apparatuses as material form; and people and their practice as the lived dimension. The authors hold that ideas depend on a material base and that both ideas and material structures stay "dead" without human subjects. For the ideational content they list Marxism as truth and method, Sinicised Marxism (from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, in three stages: revolutionary, constructive, and both since the 18th Party Congress of 2012) and fine traditional culture such as people-centred thought. The material content is the socialist system, the Party's organisational system, and education, communication and propaganda bodies, which the authors treat as ideological state apparatuses following Althusser. The real content is Party members, Marxist researchers and communicators, and ordinary people, together with practices such as propaganda work, poverty alleviation and ideological and political theory courses. In the authors' account, exemplary figures are "walking" ideology. The authors conclude that a full account of the ideology must cover all three dimensions, because each is necessary for it to operate. In practice they call for stronger education of young people, better ideological and political discipline among Party members, and more training of Marxist researchers. Read the original if you want a systematic account, from within Chinese academia, of how ideology is conceptualised as ideas, institutions and practice, including its use of Althusser.

Visual imagery in Marx's narrative of historical materialism and its implications The case of The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte 马克思唯物史观叙事的视觉形象呈现及其启示 Zhang Guoqi Zhang Guoqi asks how Marx's historical-materialist narrative in The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte produces vivid visual images, and what that offers present-day China. The article argues that the images of bayonets, the Phrygian cap, the calendar, Napoleon's statue on the Vendôme column and the 'cackling of geese' are not literary decoration. In Zhang's reading they are the concrete form of a scientific analysis of French class struggle, and they show Louis Bonaparte as a 'mediocre and ridiculous' figure who staged a coup on his uncle's model. The article has four parts. The first sets out three rules governing visual imagery in historical-materialist narrative: its scientific character, its value-orienting character and its practical character. The second reads the Brumaire through four devices: the buffoon figure, the decoding of the 'Napoleonic ideas', scenes suited to the characters, and symbolic props. The third examines the self-consistent logic behind these images, partly in contrast to Italo Calvino's account of how visual images arise. The fourth draws lessons for contemporary China. Zhang's central claim is that visual images arise from real life, not from spontaneous fantasy. On this view the coup and its imagery reflect a specific economic base and the class struggle in France, which let a mediocre figure play the hero. Marx's images are tied to four principles: acting 'in the real world and with real means'; discovering the new world through criticism of the old; the aim of revolutionising the existing world; and the unity of interpreting and changing the world. Zhang adds that French workers lacked revolutionary theory and a strong leading class, and that Marx urged the peasantry to ally with the urban proletariat. Zhang also holds that such narrative must remain non-fictional, though artistic treatment is allowed. Zhang concludes that this method offers guidance for telling China's story well, in line with Xi Jinping's call to highlight Chinese cultural features and the 'visual image of the Chinese nation'. The article also draws on the 20th Party Congress (2022) goal of presenting a credible, lovable and respectable China. Zhang calls on theorists to use concrete imagery to portray the Party's vanguard role and China as a responsible major country, and to cultivate young people as 'new people of the era' fit to carry out the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you study Marx's historical writings as narrative, or want to see how Chinese scholars link them to current ideological and cultural-communication work.

Chen Yun's explorations in advancing the Party's political building in the Yan'an period 延安时期陈云推进党的政治建设的探索 Liu Dong Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), which stressed strengthening the Party's political building, Liu Dong asks what Chen Yun contributed to this task during the Yan'an period. Liu argues that Chen, then head of the Central Organization Department, worked out a substantial body of ideas on political building through practice and summing up experience. These ideas, the article holds, still offer guidance for the new great project of Party building in the new era. The article is organised around four themes that mirror the 2019 Central Committee opinions on strengthening the Party's political building: firm political belief, upholding the authority of the Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership, building political capacity, and carrying measures through in organisation and implementation. Liu draws on Chen's speeches and writings from 1935 to 1947, including 'How to Be a Communist Party Member' (1939), his writings on branch work, and his drafting of Organization Department decisions on cadres. The material is set against the Party's rapid expansion and the mixed class background of its new members. Liu's central claim is that Chen tied belief, discipline and practice together. On belief, Chen required members to study Marxist theory, led a study group in the Organization Department, and insisted that the interests of the people and the Party are identical. On authority, he backed Mao Zedong as the leading core, demanded the 'four subordinations' (individual to organisation, minority to majority, lower level to higher, whole Party to the Central Committee) and held that a core leadership forms only through strict democratic centralism. On capacity and implementation, Liu reports Chen's four tasks for Party branches, his insistence on mass work led by the Party, his view that theory must be combined with practical experience, his emphasis on criticism and self-criticism, and his rule that cadres be selected with politics first and ability second, 'with virtue primary'. Liu concludes that Chen's Yan'an ideas are a valuable asset of the Party and should be studied and drawn on today, so that the Party's political building can play its leading role and the Party remains the firm leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article is largely expository, presenting Chen's views through extended quotation. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Chen Yun's Yan'an-era thinking on Party discipline, cadre selection and branch work, as it is presented in current Party-history scholarship.

Basic experience of the Communist Party of China's century-long construction of political identification 中国共产党百年政治认同建设的基本经验 Wang Shuqin Li Jing Wang and Li ask how the Communist Party of China has built and kept the political identification of the people over its first hundred years. Political identification, they define, is members of society's psychological belonging, emotional attachment and behavioural support towards their political system. The authors argue that the Party worked along four dimensions: interests as the foundation, institutions as the safeguard, emotion as the key link, and values as the point of belonging. Together, they say, these formed a unified force behind what they call the two miracles of rapid economic growth and long-term social stability. The article takes each dimension in turn and traces it through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and also cites Aristotle, Rawls and Freud. It closes with a short conclusion on how the four dimensions fit together. In the authors' account, interest identification comes first: land reform, the consolidation of people's status as masters of the country, the end of hunger and poverty, and a better life for all. Because interests are changeable, institutional identification is needed, and it rests on fair and just institutions such as the 1954 Constitution, the basic economic system and whole-process people's democracy. Emotional identification is built through the Party's moral conduct in office: rectification campaigns, discipline, anti-corruption work and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Value identification, the most stable and highest level, comes from ideological work, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and from core socialist values. Wang and Li conclude that the four dimensions follow a logical progression and priority order, and that stable identification requires all four to be fused. They hold that, in a period of great global change and national rejuvenation, the Party must keep its close ties to the people if it is to preserve its legitimacy as a long-term ruling party. Read the original if you want a structured, officially aligned account of how Party theorists explain popular support for the CPC across its history.

Continuously improving the effectiveness of cyberspace governance 不断提升网络空间治理效能 Lin Xiaowen This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily, takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to improve the system of comprehensive internet governance and foster a healthy online ecosystem. Lin argues that cyberspace governance must be strengthened so that China can move from being a large internet country to a strong one. The piece opens by noting that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee has pursued the strategy of building China into a cyber power, which Lin says has brought historic achievements. It then sets out three directions for further work: a people-centred approach, governance by law, and multi-party participation. On the first, Lin cites Xi Jinping's call for internet development to serve the people and urges stronger online content building, with a positive, healthy online culture nourished by core socialist values. On the second, Lin lists laws such as the Cybersecurity Law, the Data Security Law and the Personal Information Protection Law, plus more than 300 national standards. Lin calls for faster supporting legislation, tougher enforcement, cross-departmental coordination, platform accountability and a mix of campaign-style and routine governance. On the third, Lin describes a pattern led by Party committees, with government management, corporate responsibility, social oversight and netizen self-discipline. A 2019 opinion on this system, Lin says, shifted governance from after-the-fact management to process governance. Lin concludes that the Party's overall leadership, better coordination among agencies, platform responsibility, industry self-regulation and netizens' ability to recognise false information together create a good online ecosystem. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on internet governance was presented to a general readership in early 2023.

Contributing the strength of veterans' work to building a modern socialist great power 为社会主义现代化强国建设贡献退役军人工作力量 Pei Jinjia This commentary, first published in the People's Daily and written by the Party secretary and minister of the Ministry of Veterans Affairs, sets out how veterans' work should serve the goals laid down at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Pei Jinji argues that, because the Party's central task is now to build a modern socialist great power and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, the veterans' affairs system must make studying and implementing the Congress's spirit its first political task. The article takes Xi Jinping's report to the Congress as its framework and organises the discussion into five areas of work. These are modernizing the governance system and capacity of veterans' affairs; contributing to economic and social development; serving the modernization of national defence and the armed forces; supporting the modernization of the national security system; and rallying unity and morale for the national goal. Each section opens with a passage from the report and then lists practical tasks. Pei's central claim is that veterans' work is an integral part of the work of the Party and state and must be organised around its central tasks. On governance, Pei calls for stronger Party leadership, standardised service centres and stations, tighter accountability mechanisms, information platforms and a fuller legal and policy framework, including the Veterans Protection Law and revised regulations on resettlement and pensions. On development, Pei presents veterans as a talent pool and proposes training, job fairs, placement in grassroots Party and village committees, and individualised, file-based services. On defence and security, Pei describes the system as an extension of military modernization: aligning policy with military reform, supporting combat readiness and wartime response, easing soldiers' family concerns, resolving grievances through the 'Fengqiao experience', and organising veterans for emergency rescue. In its final section Pei calls for keeping veterans closely united around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, through campaigns such as 'Veterans Always Follow the Party' and 'Most Beautiful Veterans'. Pei also urges consolidating unity between the military, government and people through the 'double support' work, and using red resources and martyr commemoration to promote the national spirit. Read the original if you want to see how the Ministry of Veterans Affairs translated the 20th Party Congress report into concrete policy priorities for veterans' services in early 2023.

Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China 中国式现代化是中国共产党领导的社会主义现代化 Qi Yingyan This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily and posted in February 2023, takes up a formulation from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China. Qi Yingyan argues that this statement sets out the fundamental character of Chinese modernization and is the core marker distinguishing it from, and in the author's view making it superior to, Western modernization. The piece is organised under three headings. The first treats the Party as the leading force of Chinese modernization and traces its role from the 7th Party Congress (1945) through the industrialisation goals of the 1950s and reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as the source of the basic nature and direction of modernization. The third derives the principle of the people's principal position from the Party's leadership and from the scale of China's population. Qi's core argument is that the Party's leadership and the socialist system together fix what kind of modernization China pursues. Drawing on Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, the author says this is socialist modernization and nothing else, marked by common prosperity, the coordination of material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful development. Western modernization is contrasted as driven by the logic of capital, aimed at extracting surplus value, treating people as reified factors of production, and, in the author's account, bringing ecological damage, colonialism and plunder. Because a population of over 1.4 billion is larger than that of all existing developed countries combined, Qi holds that China has no ready model to follow and must rely on itself, proceed patiently and share the fruits of development among all the people. Qi concludes that upholding Party leadership is the highest principle and the greatest political advantage of Chinese modernization. Development must be for the people and rely on the people, and the Party's leadership must be carried into every sphere of work in order to mobilise popular initiative. The author also presents the Chinese path as widening the options for developing countries that want to modernise while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line exposition of how the 20th Party Congress report links Party leadership, socialism and the people-centred approach to Chinese modernization.

Promoting a community with a shared future for mankind is an essential requirement and unremitting pursuit of Chinese modernization 推动构建人类命运共同体是中国式现代化的本质要求和不懈追求 Fu Xiaoqiang Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary asks how Chinese modernization relates to the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Fu Xiaoqiang argues that promoting such a community is an essential requirement of Chinese modernization and one of its unremitting pursuits. In Fu's account, Chinese modernization points the way and opens a path for both the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the building of that community. The article, first published on Guangming Online in February 2023, has three parts. The first sets out the international responsibility and global contribution of Chinese modernization. The second draws lessons that Chinese modernization offers for building the community, under the headings of common prosperity, openness and inclusiveness, harmony between humanity and nature, and universal security. The third describes four paths Chinese modernization opens: shared development through cooperation, peaceful development through mutual learning among civilizations, comprehensive and coordinated development, and independent development that draws on others. Fu presents the idea as a theoretical innovation that draws on the Marxist theory of world history and of the community, and on traditional Chinese views of "all under heaven". Chinese modernization is portrayed as surpassing Western modernization, which Fu describes as driven by capital and marked by war, colonialism, plunder, wealth polarization and ecological damage. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is said to centre on the people, seek peaceful development, and ease the "security dilemma" through dialogue and partnership without alliances. Fu argues that it breaks the monopoly of "Western-centrism" and encourages developing countries to find their own paths, since no single model of modernization exists. Fu concludes that Chinese modernization offers humanity a new choice and an inexhaustible impetus for the community with a shared future for mankind. The article states that the Communist Party and the Chinese people will offer more Chinese wisdom, solutions and strength, and will advance the Global Development Initiative and the Global Security Initiative. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese official discourse after the 20th Party Congress links domestic modernization to its vision of global order.

The deep meaning and contemporary value of the new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化新的飞跃的深刻意涵与当代价值 Zhang Zhongmin Zhang Zhongmin takes up the claim, made in the Party's third historical resolution (2021) and the 20th Party Congress report (2022), that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has achieved a "new leap" in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article asks what this judgement means and what value it has. Zhang argues that the leap is a real historical process that is still under way. In Zhang's account it grows out of the interplay between theory and practice, and between "using Marxism to transform China" and "using China to transform Marxism". The article has four parts. The first reads the leap through historical materialism, looking at its strategic meaning, its concrete referents and its causes. The second sets out the theoretical form and essential content of the leap. The third discusses its historical significance. The fourth turns to its contemporary value, set against the history of the Party, of the People's Republic, of reform and opening up, and of world socialism, and ends with practical proposals. Zhang ties the three leaps to the Chinese nation's progress from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" to "becoming strong". The third leap is said to answer three major questions and to move the Party's formulation from "eight clarifications" to "ten clarifications". Zhang also credits it with finding the Party's self-reform as a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. The causes are analysed under four logics: historical, practical, political and internal. The political logic rests on the Two Establishes, and the internal logic on the tension between the goals of the "two centenaries" and real conditions. Zhang holds that the leap fuses Marxism with the cultural genes of Chinese civilization through the Two Integrations. It is presented as proof that Marxism remains vital and as a challenge to the "end of history" thesis. Zhang concludes that the leap closes the first century of adapting Marxism to China and opens a new starting point. It is also presented as a scientific programme for world socialism and a source of reference for developing countries. The article proposes studying the whole history of this adaptation with a "big history" outlook and balancing "upholding fundamental principles" with "innovation". It also proposes turning the leap into practical results for Chinese modernization, covering Party building, military modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the official narrative of the "new leap" is justified through historical materialism and the Party's three historical resolutions.

Problems unique to a large party: what is "unique" and where lies the "difficulty" 大党独有难题：“何为独有”又“难在何处” Xu Yanling Xu Yanling takes up a formulation from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that the Communist Party of China, as the world's largest Marxist governing party, must stay clear-headed and firm in solving "problems unique to a large party". Writing in the People's Forum, Xu reads the phrase as a deepening of Xi Jinping's earlier remark that a large party has "large difficulties". The article argues that these problems are best understood at three levels: governing the Party, governing a large country, and global governance. The article is organised into three sections, one for each level. The first concerns Party governance and the "historical cycle" of rise and decline. The second concerns the governance of a vast and complex country in the course of Chinese modernization. The third concerns the Party's role in reforming global governance and building a community with a shared future for mankind. Each section ends with a short summary of why the difficulty is distinctive. On Party governance, Xu cites official figures of 96.712 million members and 4.936 million primary organisations at the end of 2021. The author argues that growth in size brings new problems: diverse membership, "detached" members, weakened organisation in some places, and a wider age range. Xu sets "four tests" (governing, reform and opening up, the market economy, the external environment) as external causes against "four dangers" (slackening of spirit, insufficient capacity, detachment from the masses, corruption) as internal causes. Their combination is said to catalyse the historical cycle, and self-reform is presented as the second answer to it. On governing the country, Xu identifies a basic difficulty in a huge and uneven society, a process difficulty in pursuing Chinese modernization as a late developer under Western pressure, and a goal difficulty in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, where haste and complacency must both be avoided. On the global level, Xu describes an objective difficulty (deficits in peace, development, security and governance), a difficulty of agency (reduced willingness among states, with the United States and its allies accused of abandoning treaties and organisations), and a practical difficulty (value consensus and public goods). The author attributes resistance to Western ideology and to "Thucydides trap" and "Kindleberger trap" thinking. Xu concludes that the Party faces both difficulties specific to the era and difficulties of its own in promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. In the author's account, it is meeting them as a responsible century-old party, joining its own development to that of the world. Read the original if you want a structured Chinese-language account of how Party theorists frame the "unique problems" formula, and of how they link Party building, domestic governance and foreign policy.

We must always remain clear-headed and resolute in tackling the problems unique to a large party 必须时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定 Zhan Chengfu Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2023, Zhan Chengfu takes up a formula from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): to keep the people's support and consolidate its long-term governing position, the Communist Party must stay clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large party. Zhan presents this as a deepening of Xi's argument that the Party escapes the historical cycle of rise and fall through the Party's self-reform. The article is an interpretive commentary that treats confronting such problems as a mark of the Party's vanguard character. The piece has three parts. The first explains why the Party is distinctive and lists the difficulties that follow, citing figures of 96.712 million members and 4.936 million primary organizations at the end of 2021. The second reviews a decade of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out eight tasks for continuing it. Zhan names three distinctive features: the Party's heavy historical mission, its long-term single-party rule, and its unmatched size. From these Zhan derives three problems. The first is keeping unity of thought, will and action under a firm leadership core, illustrated by the Zunyi Conference, Zhang Guotao, Wang Ming and the Yan'an rectification campaign. The second is keeping the original aspiration and spotting its own faults, with the Soviet Communist Party cited as a party that became a privileged bureaucratic group. The third is keeping up drive and a clean political climate against the "four dangers". Zhan argues that the past decade's measures covered ideology, responsibility, discipline, cadres, work style and anti-corruption. In Zhan's account these produced a system of self-purification and showed that self-supervision, a worldwide puzzle, can be solved under one-party rule. Zhan concludes that the Party must keep pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform to the end. Zhan lists eight measures. They include strengthening the Central Committee's centralized and unified leadership, arming the Party with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and improving the rules governing self-reform. They also cover building a high-calibre cadre corps, strengthening Party organizations, correcting work style, and fighting corruption as a protracted campaign. Read the original if you want an official-line account, from a senior government official, of how the Party frames its own organizational problems and the anti-corruption agenda after the 20th Party Congress.

Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party depends on improving the system 全面从严治党重在健全体系 Zhao Xusheng Writing in Guangming Daily in early 2023, Zhao Xusheng takes up a new task set by the 20th Party Congress (2022): improving the system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The commentary argues that this system-building is the key to carrying the governance effort forward. In Zhao's reading, it is a comprehensive and pioneering part of Party building in the new era. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why such a system is necessary, the second defines its content and place, and the third proposes ways to improve it. Zhao draws throughout on Xi Jinping's speeches, the Party Congress report and plenary session documents, including the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee and the Second Plenum of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Zhao gives three grounds for the system. First, building a Marxist party follows a basic law that combines ideological work with governance through institutions and Party regulations. Second, the achievements of the past decade have laid a foundation: Zhao says lax and soft Party management has been fundamentally reversed, and cites Xi's six experiences. Third, the "unique problems of a large party", summarised as "six how's", can be solved fundamentally only through institution-based governance. Zhao defines the system as a dynamic whole of five subsystems: core (the Party's overall leadership), elements (organisations, members and cadres, with leading cadres as the "critical few"), structure (the overall layout of Party building), standards (strictness) and responsibility. To improve it, Zhao calls for top-level design with systems thinking, closer linkage between governance by Party regulations and the rule of law, and coordinated integration with full coverage of content, targets, responsibility chains and institutions. Zhao concludes that building out this system is how the Party can address the problems peculiar to a large party through self-reform. The author calls for fragmented, piecemeal efforts to be avoided. Responsibility should be placed on Party committees, with secretaries treating Party building as their first responsibility and discipline commissions carrying out supervision. Read the original if you want a concise, Party School-style account of how the 20th Party Congress framed Party discipline and institution-building as a system.

The governance advantages of a century-old Party 百年大党的治理优势 Chen Zhongkui Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Chen Zhongkui asks why the Communist Party of China governs so well and why China has developed so quickly. The article's answer is that the Party holds three governance advantages: its leadership as the core governing agent, a clear people-centred value orientation, and a strong capacity for organisation and mobilisation. Chen presents these as strengths that should be upheld, consolidated and improved. The piece is a Party-theory commentary built on three headed sections: the advantage of the governing subject, the advantage of values, and the advantage of effectiveness. It draws on Xi Jinping's statements, episodes from Party history from the 1927 repression to the Huaihai Campaign and poverty alleviation, and repeated contrasts with Western parties and political systems. Chen also cites Edgar Snow on Mao Zedong and Francis Fukuyama's revised view of the 'end of history'. On the first advantage, Chen argues that any party that is to be a strong governing agent needs three conditions: lofty belief, severe trials and organisational self-renewal. In Chen's account the Party meets all three, citing the sacrifices of revolutionaries, the failure of repeated Western predictions of China's collapse, and the Party's record of self-reform from the Gutian and Zunyi meetings to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On values, Chen contends that the Party represents the fundamental interests of all the people, whereas Western parties represent segments of voters and so fall into endless partisan conflict. The article points to the elimination of absolute poverty as evidence. On effectiveness, Chen says the Party's tight organisation, the unity of Party spirit and the people's will, and its roots among the people let it mobilise society when needed. Chen concludes that Party leadership is the root of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics and that without it the 'China model' would not have succeeded. The article ends with a call for all Party members to remember the Party's founding mission, stay close to the people and work toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Party-school style commentary frames the case for Party leadership as a governance advantage and contrasts it with Western party politics.

From the "Two Musts" to the "Three Musts": new vistas, new requirements and new expectations on the road of the Party's "examination" “两个务必”到“三个务必”：赶考路上的新图景、新要求、新期待 Zhao Maosheng Fan Mingyang Zhao Maosheng and Fan Mingyang start from the image of the Communist Party as a "mission-driven party" that is always sitting an "examination" (gan…kao). They ask what situation the "Three Musts" face, what they demand and what they expect, compared with Mao Zedong's "Two Musts" of 1949. The "Three Musts" are Xi Jinping's call, made after the first centenary goal had been met, that Party members must never forget the original aspiration and keep the mission in mind, must stay modest, prudent and hard-working, and must dare and know how to struggle. The authors argue that the two formulations are continuous but that the later one is more comprehensive and systematic. The article has three parts. The first compares the historical settings: the Second Plenary Session of the Seventh Central Committee at Xibaipo (1949), when the Party was about to become the governing party, and the present stage of national rejuvenation, with what the authors call great changes unseen in a century. The second compares the requirements each slogan places on Party members. The third compares the expectations attached to each. The authors draw on Mao's speeches and letters, Xi's statements and a few passages from Marx. In the authors' reading, Mao's "Two Musts" (modesty and prudence, plus hard struggle) drew on the Party's earlier style of work. They were meant to guard against complacency and corruption after victory, and to help the Party escape the "historical cycle" of dynastic rise and fall. The "Three Musts" are set out as answers to three questions. "For what" is the value goal of serving the people and national rejuvenation. "Why able" is the work-style guarantee of modesty and hard work. "How" is the practical call to struggle with both courage and skill. The authors present the three as an organic whole: the first supplies the premise and goal, the second the safeguard, and the third the capacity and method. The authors conclude that the "Three Musts" are expected to sustain firm conviction in building a modern socialist country. They are also expected to secure the path to national rejuvenation and to supply the character needed for the Party's self-reform, so that it can solve the problems unique to a large party and avoid the historical cycle. They call on Party members to keep close ties with the people and to cultivate struggle skills. They also call on them to resist hostile external forces and to correct internal weaknesses in responsibility and practical ability. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists link Mao's 1949 warning to Xi Jinping's Party-building discourse after the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Striving to the fore on the track of national rejuvenation 在实现民族复兴的赛道上奋勇争先 Guan Jian This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily and posted on the Academy of Marxism site in February 2023, takes up Xi Jinping's 2023 New Year address. Guan Jian, a professor at Nankai University, argues that realising the Chinese Dream is a historical relay race and that each generation of young people must strive to the fore on the track of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised under three headings: merging personal ideals with the cause of the Party and the state; contributing wisdom and strength in the broad arena of the new era; and keeping youthful vitality and an uplifting spirit. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks on youth, a historical sketch from the May Fourth period to the present, and a line attributed to Marx on the spirit of youth. Guan reads modern Chinese history as one in which young people were a vanguard force. The author cites the May Fourth generation's choice of Marxism-Leninism and the 13 delegates, averaging 28 years old, at the Party's first congress in 1921. Today's youth, in this account, live in the best and most critical era for national rejuvenation, and the Party Central Committee supports them through the principle that the Party manages youth affairs and a policy of youth-priority development. Guan notes that young people face competing social currents and doubts, for example between ideals and reality or the individual and the collective. Guan concludes that firm ideals and convictions are the remedy: faith in Marxism, belief in socialism and communism, and confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author calls for arming youth with Party theory so that they join Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary frames youth, ideals and Party leadership around the Chinese Dream.

Comprehensively raising the capacity to train legal professionals, to provide solid personnel support for law-based governance 全面提升法治人才培养能力 为全面依法治国提供坚实人才保障 Hu Ming Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), which gave law-based governance its own chapter in the work report for the first time, Hu argues that training legal professionals is a basic, supporting part of comprehensively governing the country by law. The article is a short commentary by the Party secretary of China University of Political Science and Law. It contends that law schools, as the main place of such training, must follow Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law and turn out large numbers of legal professionals loyal to the Party, the country, the people and the law. The piece sets out four lines of work for law schools: value guidance, curriculum, textbooks, and collaborative and practical teaching. Each is presented as a requirement drawn from Xi Jinping's remarks, including his 2017 visit to the university. Hu first calls for combining moral and legal education. Xi Jinping Thought on the rule of law should enter textbooks, classrooms and students' minds, ideological-political content should be built into law courses, and professional ethics should be taught alongside skills. On curriculum, Hu proposes cross-disciplinary study, a full course system for foreign-related legal work, and possible new fields such as Party regulations, national security law and data law, together with digital teaching platforms. On textbooks, they should start from China's conditions and absorb foreign experience selectively, not copy Western theory. They should also draw creatively on traditional Chinese legal culture. Hu closes by urging joint training between institutions, citing the university's law-and-English joint degree with Beijing Foreign Studies University. Law schools should also build internship bases with courts, procuratorates, law firms and government bodies, and appoint practitioners as part-time professors and practice mentors. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a leading law-school leader translates Party legal-education policy into concrete measures.

Chinese modernization displays a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化展现人类文明新形态 Hu Changshuan Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Hu Changshuan asks what distinguishes Chinese modernization from the modernization of the Western developed countries, and what responsibility follows from that difference. The author argues that Chinese modernization is socialist in essence, goes beyond capitalist modernization, and carries a solemn duty to create a new form of human civilization. The commentary has three parts. The first contrasts capitalist and socialist modernization. The second traces how the pursuit of modernization has been tied to national rejuvenation, from the late Qing reform efforts through Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the two-stage plan for the second centenary goal. The third sets out the contributions Hu attributes to Chinese modernization. In Hu's account, Western modernization is driven by the logic of capital, the limitless drive to accumulate, and rests on plunder, aggression and the exploitation of the majority, as Marx's Capital is cited to show. Chinese modernization is described as comprehensive, covering the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology, and as aiming at common prosperity, coordination of material and spiritual civilization, harmony between humans and nature, and peaceful development. Hu argues that Western-style paths failed in modern China, and that the Communist Party chose its own route. On this basis the author names three contributions: a reference point for developing countries, a way of overcoming the ills of capitalist modernization (ecological damage, world wars), and a new form of civilization. Hu describes that form as the coordinated development of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization, people-centred and committed to all-round human development. It is said to combine a Marxist view of civilization with traditional Chinese views. Hu concludes that, with capitalist modernity in what the author calls an unprecedented crisis, Chinese modernization offers developing countries a new option and carries the task of promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official narrative presents the link between Chinese modernization, national rejuvenation and a new form of human civilization shortly after the 20th Party Congress.

Comprehensively advancing rural revitalisation is an important task of building a strong agricultural country in the new era 全面推进乡村振兴是新时代建设农业强国的重要任务 Huang Chengwei Huang Chengwei, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2023, takes up the question of how rural revitalisation should be advanced as part of building a strong agricultural country. The article is an exposition of Xi Jinping's speech at the Central Rural Work Conference and of the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Huang's answer is that two bottom lines must be held, three aspects of the countryside must be handled together, new sources of momentum must be generated, and Party leadership must be strengthened. The piece is organised in four parts. It begins with the two bottom lines: national food security and preventing large-scale return to poverty. It then turns to the coordinated promotion of rural development, rural construction and rural governance. The third part covers four sources of new momentum: deepening rural reform, pooling assistance forces, digital villages, and county-township-village coordination of infrastructure and public services. The last part concerns Party leadership over agriculture, rural areas and farmers (the "three rural issues"). On the bottom lines, Huang argues that feeding more than 1.4 billion people is always the top priority. The article calls for holding the 18-billion-mu farmland red line, building high-standard farmland, achieving self-reliance in seed technology, and strengthening incentives for grain farmers and major grain-producing regions. It also calls for better monitoring and assistance mechanisms and stronger minimum-guarantee social assistance. On the three aspects, Huang proposes industrial integration and local employment for development, planning-led and quality-first construction, and a governance system combining self-governance, rule of law and moral governance under Party leadership. Reform is to centre on the farmer–land relationship, including land requisition, homestead and contracted-land reforms. Huang concludes that the Party's leadership is the key to rural work. The article calls for the five-level Party secretary mechanism, with county Party secretaries as "frontline commanders", and for a responsibility system running from the centre through provinces to cities, counties and townships, with differentiated targets and tolerance for error. It also urges more resident first secretaries and work teams, and wider mobilisation of private enterprises and social organisations. Read the original if you want a detailed, policy-oriented summary of the official agenda for rural revitalisation and agricultural modernisation after the 20th Party Congress.

Effectively preventing and defusing major economic and financial risks 有效防范化解重大经济金融风险 Li Jianjun Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2023, Li Jianjun interprets the fifth of the policy priorities set by the Central Economic Work Conference of 15–16 December 2022: effectively preventing and defusing major economic and financial risks. Li argues that this task is the key to coordinating development and security, and that it must be pursued under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the spirit of the 20th Party Congress (2022). The commentary has three parts. The first deals with the property sector, the second with financial risk and local government debt, and the third with the policy measures needed to keep the economy stable. Li sets the discussion against what the article calls triple pressure: shrinking demand, supply shocks and weakening expectations. On property, Li reads the Conference's line of guaranteeing completed housing, people's livelihoods and stability as a way to avoid unfinished projects, stop debt risk from spreading to finance and hold the bottom line of no systemic risk. Li treats the principle that housing is for living in, not for speculation, as the fundamental remedy. It would de-financialise real estate and move the sector away from high debt, high leverage and high turnover, towards a new model combining market and affordable housing, rental and purchase together, and urban renewal. On finance, Li points to external shocks, such as central-bank tightening abroad, and to weak small banks, rural banks and trust companies at home. Li calls for stronger centralised Party leadership over financial work, rigorous Party self-governance and anti-corruption campaigns in the sector. For local debt, Li proposes halting new hidden debt, resolving existing stock through market-based and law-based default mechanisms, and holding to the principle that the central government does not bail out localities. Li concludes that economic and financial risks ultimately stem from obstructed circulation in the real economy. Li therefore urges stable growth, employment and prices, support for innovation, fuller use of domestic demand and steadier foreign trade and investment. Citing the 20th Party Congress report on "black swan" and "grey rhino" events, Li calls for greater awareness of danger and bottom-line thinking. Read the original if you want a Party-school-style reading of the 2022 Central Economic Work Conference on property, financial supervision and local debt.

Engels's method of criticising Bakunin's "anti-authority theory" and its lessons A textual study based on "On Authority" 恩格斯对巴枯宁“反权威论”的批判方法与启示 Li Zijuan How did Engels dismantle Bakunin's rejection of all authority, and what does his method offer today? Li Zijuan argues that in "On Authority", written in the 1870s after the defeat of the Paris Commune, Engels used dialectical and historical materialism to expose the idealist basis of Bakunin's anarchism. In Li's account, this also set out a Marxist theory of authority and a model for criticising erroneous currents of thought. The article has three parts. It first reconstructs Bakunin's four core positions: an abstract, absolute notion of freedom; the equation of authority with the state and with evil; the absolute opposition of authority and autonomy; and the abolition of the state in place of proletarian revolution. It then examines how Engels answered each position through philosophy, history, dialectics and class standpoint. Finally it draws four methodological lessons, with a short survey of Western and Chinese thinkers on authority, including Weber and Follett. Li's central claim is that Engels grounded authority in material production. Using examples such as the cotton mill and the railway, Engels showed that large-scale production requires a unified will, so that authority is an objective necessity. Subordination tends to shift from compulsion to voluntary acceptance. Li reads Engels as treating authority and autonomy as a dialectical unity of opposites whose scope changes with the stage of social development. Engels is also said to have argued that revolution is "the most authoritarian thing there is", that the Paris Commune fell for lack of centralisation and authority, and that Bakunin mistook the state rather than capital for the main evil. Li adds that Bakunin contradicted himself by running a secret organisation with strict discipline. Li concludes that authority must be studied on a materialist basis, from a historical and class standpoint that rests on the people, and with a dialectical view of authority and autonomy. Theories of authority should be inherited critically and developed creatively. Li links this to the Party's maintenance of the authority of the Party Central Committee, arguing that it is compatible with grassroots self-government and regional ethnic autonomy, and sees authority and autonomy as a form of the relation between democracy and centralism. Read the original if you want a close, Party-theoretical reading of Engels's "On Authority" and of how it is used to defend the authority of the Central Committee.

Improving the institutional and normative system for the Party's self-reform 完善党的自我革命制度规范体系 Liu Chang This commentary in Guangming Daily (February 2023) takes up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to improve the institutional and normative system for the Party's self-reform. Liu Chang, a professor at Jilin University, argues that three components are central: the system of intra-Party regulations, the Party and state supervision system, and the integrated pursuit of the "three no-corruptions". The piece opens by presenting self-reform as the second answer the Party has found to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. It then has three sections, each treating one component as a precondition, an institutional environment or a driving force for the system. On regulations, Liu holds that the intra-Party regulatory system is the Party's code of conduct, rooted in full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and defined by its political character. It needs better enforcement, links with law enforcement and the judiciary, and a case-guidance system. On supervision, Liu says intra-Party supervision must lead and other forms of supervision must work in coordination. Discipline, supervisory, dispatched-office and inspection supervision are to form a "trunk" force backed by clear lists of responsibilities. On the "three no-corruptions", Liu argues for pursuing them together under the lead of Party political building. This would use mechanisms that combine early warning with punishment and accountability with tolerance of error, and would be supported by a culture of integrity. Liu concludes that these measures turn self-reform into a lasting, stable and effective institutional system, which in turn lets it guide social revolution and modernize state governance. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party-affiliated scholars framed the institutional agenda for self-reform after the 20th Party Congress.

Holding firmly to the "ruler" of discipline in governing the Party in the new era 抓牢新时代管党治党的“戒尺” Liu Xiaochuan This newspaper commentary, originally published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at the second plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that discipline is the "ruler" (jièchǐ) for governing the Party. Liu Xiaochuan argues that discipline-building must be given greater prominence in the new era so that rules have "teeth" and officials come to respect them, take warning and know their limits. The piece has three parts. It first presents strict discipline as a glorious tradition and distinctive strength of the Party. It then explains why discipline-building is the fundamental measure of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It closes with practical requirements for holding on to the "ruler". In the first part, Liu cites Marx, Engels and Lenin on the need for Party discipline, along with early Chinese communists and later Party documents, to portray a continuous tradition up to the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the second, Liu contends that some ruling parties around the world lost power because they weakened discipline, and that the Party's "four tests" and "four dangers" will persist. Liu adds that discipline secures the unity the Party needs to govern a large developing country. In the third, Liu sets out three tasks: put political discipline first as the most fundamental kind; focus on leading cadres as the "critical minority", who should set an example in observing the Party constitution and the law; and enforce discipline so that it does not become a "scarecrow". Enforcement means equality of all members before Party discipline, no exceptions, and linking discipline enforcement with law enforcement under governing the country by law and the Party by rules. Liu concludes that gripping the "ruler" of discipline is necessary for raising the standard of Party governance, keeping the Party vital and passing the new "examination" of the new era. The text is a short, official-style exposition of current Party-building doctrine rather than an empirical study. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school commentary presents discipline-building under Xi Jinping, including its citations of the Marxist classics.

Developing a positive and healthy intra-Party political culture 发展积极健康的党内政治文化 Sang Xuecheng Writing in Guangming Daily shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Sang Xuecheng asks how intra-Party political culture can be developed so that it helps purify the Party's political ecology. The author argues that a positive and healthy culture is an important basis for keeping the Party advanced and pure. Its ideals, beliefs, values and conduct are meant to shift Party building from "treating pollution" to "clearing the source", and from treating symptoms to treating root causes. The short commentary follows the Congress's call to persevere with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. It sets out four components of intra-Party political culture: a culture of belief, an organisational culture, a culture of conduct and an institutional culture. Each is paired with a means of building it: Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, democratic centralism, thoroughgoing self-reform, and a complete system of intra-Party regulations. In Sang's account, belief is the spiritual core of the culture. It is built through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and through firm confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and it must resist ideas that distort or negate Marxism. Organisational culture rests on democratic centralism and on the Two Upholds. It should combine unity of thought, will and action with initiative from all quarters, and it rejects individualism, cliques and similar negative habits. Conduct culture depends on the Party's self-reform, which Sang calls the second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall. Rigorous Party life, criticism and self-criticism, and the "Four Work Styles" campaign are the means. Institutional culture is carried by intra-Party regulations, and the author cites 221 central, 170 departmental and 3,327 local regulations as of June 2022. Sang concludes that the regulatory system must keep developing, tighten its "institutional cage", and fix the Party's cultural values in rules. The author points to personnel selection and intra-Party supervision as priority areas. The text presents these steps as ways to keep the Party from degenerating and to make a healthy political ecology permanent. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars frame political culture, the Party's self-reform and the role of regulations in Party building after 2022.

Continuing to promote the flourishing development of research on the history of the People's Republic 不断推动国史研究繁荣发展 Song Yuehong Song Yuehong, writing in the People's Daily in February 2023, asks how research on the history of the People's Republic (guoshi, 'national history') should develop. Prompted by Xi Jinping's congratulatory letter to the Chinese Society for the History of the People's Republic on its 30th anniversary, the article argues that this field must hold to the main theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the country's history. It presents the field's growth as a story of steady progress under correct political guidance. The commentary has three parts. The first traces how national-history research began inside Party history research, then grew through the Mao-era compilation of local gazetteers and five-, seven- and ten-year histories, and became a discipline after the 1981 resolution on Party history. The second summarises results of the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012) in content, forms and publications. The third sets out four tasks for the new journey. Song contends that the 1981 resolution, which divided the period to 1981 into four stages, spurred the writing of national history. Two works are called pioneering: the multi-volume Contemporary China series and the Draft History of the People's Republic of China. For the new era, Song cites research on the dialectical unity of the periods before and after reform and opening up, the 'Recording a Moderately Prosperous Society' database project, and short histories used in Party history study and education. For the future, Song calls for stress on research into the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for study of Chinese modernization's theoretical system and practice. Song also urges comprehensive general histories of the People's Republic and a wider international perspective, including new concepts that foreign audiences can understand. The author insists that historical nihilism must be firmly opposed. Song concludes that national-history research should contribute to building a modern socialist country in all respects and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is an official-style programmatic overview, not a detailed historiographical study. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the Party-state frames the development, achievements and priorities of People's Republic history research as of early 2023.

Historiographical criticism as the foundation of the historiography of CPC history 史评是中共党史学史之基础 Zhou Liangshu Zhou Liangshu argues that criticism of historical writing (shiping) is the foundation of the historiography of Chinese Communist Party history, the field that studies how Party history has itself been written. The short commentary draws mainly on the thinking of the Party historian Zhang Jingru. Zhou begins with the long tradition of historiographical criticism in China and the West, citing Confucius, Liu Zhiji, Zhang Xuecheng and Herodotus. The commentary then notes Li Dazhao's early theoretical work and the revival of research on the subject from the 1980s. The remainder follows Zhang's reflections on the status, function, object, principle and method of criticism in Party history studies. Zhou reports that Zhang planned a history of Party historiography from 1980 and needed ten years to finish it. Zhang blamed weak criticism in the field, where book reviews mostly summarised content or offered praise. On Zhang's view, criticism drives the field's development, because it links historical scholarship with society. Its main objects are historians and their works. Its fundamental principle is seeking truth from facts, with all authors treated equally whatever their status. Its basic method is "knowing the person and the age", which Zhou sets against abusive polemic. Zhou concludes that criticism helps and guides later scholars and should rest on reasoned argument and sound sources, not on labelling opponents. Zhang's own verdict on his book was that it lacked a base in criticism. Read the original if you want a brief account of how one leading Party historian saw the role and ethics of scholarly criticism in the discipline.

Law-based governance in all fields is an inherent requirement and an important safeguard of Chinese modernization 全面依法治国是中国式现代化的内在要求和重要保障 Zhai Guoqiang This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's call to run the country in all respects according to law. Zhai Guoqiang argues that law-based governance is both an inherent requirement of Chinese modernization and an important safeguard for it, since a modern country must be one governed by law. The article is organised around five features of Chinese modernization named in the report: a huge population, common prosperity for all, coordinated material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and a path of peaceful development. For each, Zhai explains why comprehensive law-based governance is needed. Zhai holds that the rule of law is the most reliable and stable form of governance, and that modernizing a country of over 1.4 billion people in the primary stage of socialism, amid mounting risks, requires law to consolidate foundations, stabilise expectations and secure long-term stability. On common prosperity, social fairness and justice must be turned into legal institutions covering distribution, public services, taxation and property rights. On civilisational balance, the author reads the principal contradiction as now also appearing in law, and calls for combining rule by law with rule by virtue. On ecology, Zhai attributes environmental problems to weak and poorly enforced rules, and urges strict, enforceable ecological legislation. On peaceful development, the author links China's constitutional principles to upholding international law and building a foreign-related legal system. Zhai concludes that law-based governance will carry growing responsibilities as Chinese modernization advances. Domestic and foreign-related rule of law should be advanced together, so that China helps shape international rules and supports a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the 20th Party Congress linked rule of law to each feature of Chinese modernization.

Promoting the unity of material abundance and spiritual richness 促进物质富足和精神富有相统一 Chen Juan Writing in early 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Chen Juan asks how common prosperity should be understood and pursued. The commentary, originally published on Guangming Online, argues that common prosperity means abundance in both material and spiritual life, and that the two must be advanced together as a unity. The piece has three parts. It first sets out why prosperity in both spheres belongs to the socialist view of common prosperity. It then presents material abundance and spiritual richness as the basic requirement of socialist modernization. Finally it offers practical directions for making the two integrate and reinforce each other. Chen describes the material and spiritual as dialectically unified: material needs come first, citing Engels, but spiritual life, once formed, gains relative independence and in turn sustains material prosperity. In Chen's account, Western modernization is capital-centred, sees things rather than people and produces exploitation, polarisation and materialism. Chinese modernization, by contrast, is people-centred and pursues human all-round development. Chen also links this to the change in the principal contradiction of Chinese society in the new era, where people's needs for a better life now extend to spiritual and cultural demands. Chen calls for improving the socialist market economy, narrowing urban–rural, regional and income gaps, applying the new development philosophy, advancing rural revitalisation, and developing advanced socialist culture guided by core socialist values. Chen also urges stronger public cultural services and guidance of public opinion. Material and cultural construction are to reinforce each other, with cultural undertakings and industries opening new sources of material growth. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary on the 20th Party Congress frames common prosperity as both material and spiritual.

Science and technology innovation for building a great modern socialist country 面向社会主义现代化强国的科技创新 Chen Jin Chen Yuanzhi Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this short commentary asks how science and technology innovation can serve the goal of building a great modern socialist country. The authors argue that science and technology, as the primary productive force, should underpin all five dimensions of modernization: economic, political, cultural, social and ecological. The article is organised as six sections, each linking innovation to one strategic task: a modernized economic system, common prosperity, peaceful development, advanced culture, ecological civilization and the modernization of national governance. On the economy, the authors call for breakthroughs in key core technologies, secure and controllable industrial and supply chains, and a stronger national innovation system integrated with rural revitalization and regional strategies. On common prosperity, they say innovation should combine wealth creation with wealth sharing, widen participation beyond firms, and supply solutions for health, ageing, disaster prevention and green development. On security, they hold that control of core technologies is the basis of economic and defence security, and propose a new whole-nation system to overcome "stranglehold" problems and achieve "de-dependence". On culture, they stress the scientist spirit, model-worker spirit and craftsman spirit; on ecology, technical work on carbon peaking and neutrality.
