For governance, the authors propose organised research on frontier technologies, reformed management, evaluation and talent systems, and use of big data, cloud computing, blockchain and AI to make public decisions more scientific. They conclude that innovation must be systematically aligned with every part of the modernization agenda. Read the original if you want a compact view of how Chinese scholars link technology policy to the 20th Congress agenda.

Understanding the new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times from three dimensions 从三重维度深入理解马克思主义中国化时代化新的飞跃 Li Youxin Li Youxin takes up an official judgement found in the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). That judgement holds that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era has achieved a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Li argues that the claim can be understood along three dimensions: the development of practice, the combination with culture, and theoretical innovation. The article, published in Mao Zedong Studies in late 2022, is built as three sections, one for each dimension. The first places the Thought within the sequence of historical periods and their leading theories, from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The second looks at Xi Jinping's treatment of traditional Chinese culture since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third lists the main original contributions that Li attributes to the Thought. On practice, Li argues that a theoretical leap is measured first by whether real practice has entered a new era. Each earlier leap answered the practical themes of its own period, and the new era is a distinct historical period with new tasks, which the Thought is said to answer. On culture, Li says Marxism can take deep root in China only if combined with its excellent traditional culture. Li reports that Xi set out principles for treating tradition, defended cultural confidence, and put forward the Second Integration. Li also lists creative transformations, such as a community with a shared future for mankind drawing on the idea of "great harmony under heaven", and the Belt and Road Initiative drawing on the ancient Silk Road. On theory, Li names eight areas, including Party leadership as the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Chinese modernization, and common prosperity. Li concludes that the Thought is the theoretical crystallisation of the historic achievements and changes since 2012. It is also the contemporary essence of Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit, and it is Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. These three aspects together are presented as the grounds for the new leap. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars justify the claim of a "new leap" in the Sinicisation of Marxism, and of how the Second Integration is presented.

An action guide for advancing Chinese modernization 推进中国式现代化的行动指南 Qu Qingshan This commentary, published in the Party discipline newspaper China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News in February 2023, studies Xi Jinping's speech at the opening of a seminar for newly elected Central Committee members and provincial and ministerial leaders. Qu Qingshan calls the speech a brilliant Marxist document, the culminating work of the Party's innovative theory of Chinese modernization and an authoritative elaboration of the 20th Party Congress (2022). In Qu's account, it gives direction and fundamental guidance for building a modern socialist country and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Qu first sets the background: the "three-step" strategy, the Two Centenary Goals, the completion of the first goal, and the 20th Party Congress report's summary of Chinese modernization. That summary comprises five Chinese features, nine essential requirements and five major principles. The article then goes through the six questions Xi addresses in the speech, one section for each. Qu argues that the six questions form one coherent theoretical system. They cover how Chinese modernization came about, through long exploration by the Party and the people. They cover its fundamental character, which Qu describes as socialist modernization under Party leadership, "the first and most important question". They cover its Chinese features, understood as a unity of general laws and national particularity, and its creation of a "new form of human civilization". In Qu's reading, this form breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and offers developing countries a new option. The last two questions are methodological. One is the six relationships to be handled correctly, including top-level design and practical exploration, efficiency and fairness, and vitality and order. The other is the need for "great struggle", which requires strategic clarity, confidence and initiative. Qu concludes that Xi's speech raises the Party's understanding of Chinese modernization to a new level and should guide efforts to implement the 20th Party Congress. He calls for steadfastness on this path and says struggle must be undertaken without hesitation against forces seeking to contain or obstruct national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of Xi's 2023 seminar speech and how the Party's leading historian presents its six themes.

Letting Marxism take firm root in China 让马克思主义在中国牢牢扎根 Zhao Yuanjie This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 6 February 2023, interprets a passage in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The passage calls for giving scientific theory distinct Chinese characteristics and consolidating the historical and popular foundations of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Zhao argues that this passage explains why Marxism has taken root in China and how it can keep doing so. The piece begins with Marx's remark that a theory is realised in a country to the degree that it meets that country's needs. It then treats the two foundations in turn, historical and popular, and ends by relating them to each other. It uses the Party's record since its founding and examples from the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). On the historical foundation, Zhao holds that Marxism must be applied to China's concrete conditions in each period, so that practical and theoretical innovation reinforce each other. The article lists Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought as products of this process. On the popular foundation, Zhao stresses the Two Integrations, in particular combining Marxist principles with fine traditional Chinese culture. As examples, the author cites the people-centred development philosophy, said to draw on ideas such as "the people as the foundation of the state", and the idea of a community of life for humanity and nature. Zhao concludes that the two foundations support each other dialectically. A firmer historical foundation strengthens the people's historical self-awareness and confidence in Marxism. A firmer popular foundation lets the people understand and apply the theory, and so turn it into a material force. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official Party commentary presented the 20th Congress's line on Marxism and Chinese tradition.

Linking the essence of Marxist thought with the best of traditional Chinese culture 把马克思主义思想精髓同中华优秀传统文化精华贯通起来 Shang Zhixiao Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary asks how the essence of Marxist thought can be connected with the finest elements of traditional Chinese culture. Shang argues that this requires understanding Marxism's core, continually drawing out the ideas in traditional culture, and studying the inner logic that joins the two. The text first appeared in the People's Daily in February 2023. The piece has three parts. The first treats Marxism as open to all the achievements of human civilisation and as a method rather than a dogma. The second traces how Marxism's adaptation in China has drawn on Chinese historical culture. The third sets out tasks for the present. Shang holds that Marxism's three components built on German classical philosophy, British classical political economy and French utopian socialism, and that Engels described it as a method, not a doctrine. Applied in China, it met an ancient culture, and the Party has advanced the Two Integrations through successive theoretical achievements. Shang cites Mao's "seeking truth from facts", Deng's "xiaokang", Hu Jintao's "harmonious society" and, under Xi, the people-centred idea and a community with a shared future for mankind as examples of Marxism and traditional culture combined. In this account Marxism gains a Chinese flavour while dialectical materialism gives traditional culture new vitality. Shang calls for firmly grasping the essence of Marxism, digging out the best of traditional culture with Marxist standpoint and method, and pursuing continued integration in content, method and values. Shang presents this as a historical responsibility of today's Communists and as a sign of the Party's cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a short, official-line statement of how Party theorists justify combining Marxism with traditional culture.

Improving the distribution system to consolidate the foundational institution for promoting common prosperity 完善分配制度 夯实促进共同富裕的基础性制度 Wei Zhimin Yang Xiubo Published in the People's Daily on 8 February 2023, this short commentary by Wei Zhimin and Yang Xiubo takes up how the distribution system can serve common prosperity. Starting from the 20th Party Congress report (2022), which calls the distribution system the foundational institution for promoting common prosperity, the authors argue that improving it is of great importance for the new journey ahead. The article first gives three reasons why distribution matters, then sets out measures for each of the three levels of distribution. It closes its framing by stressing that common prosperity is a long historical process that cannot be achieved at one stroke. Wei and Yang argue that the distribution system is the key to combining effective incentives with reasonable distribution: it must make the 'cake' bigger and also divide it well. They treat a distribution system with distribution according to labour as the mainstay and several modes coexisting as part of the basic socialist economic system, suited to the primary stage of socialism. They describe primary distribution as the foundation, redistribution as the safeguard and the third distribution as a supplement, and claim that together these form a 'three-wheel drive' of an efficient market, a capable government and a caring society. For primary distribution, the authors call for raising the share of household income and of labour remuneration and for building an olive-shaped income structure. For redistribution, they propose improving taxation, equalising basic public services, strengthening transfer payments and regulating the order of income distribution. For the third distribution, based on voluntary charity, they call for supportive rules, charity law and oversight, and better public mobilisation. Read the original if you want a concise official-style outline of the policy measures linked to the three levels of distribution.

Persisting in deepening reform and opening up to build a high-standard socialist market economy system 坚持深化改革开放 构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制 Zhou Shaopeng Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary asks what a "high-standard socialist market economy system" means and how it is to be built. Zhou Shaopeng defines it as a socialist market economy in which a modern enterprise system with Chinese characteristics is combined organically with an effective market and a capable government. The piece first appeared in Guangming Daily on 7 February 2023. The article opens by defining the economic system, the market economy system and the socialist market economy system, with resource allocation as the core criterion. It then takes up three requirements in turn: improving the modern enterprise system with Chinese characteristics, building a high-standard market system, and letting the government play its role better. It refers throughout to Xi Jinping's statements, the 20th Party Congress report and the 2022 Central Committee and State Council opinions on a unified national market. Zhou treats the enterprise system as the micro-foundation of the economic system. In Zhou's account, a modern enterprise system rests on corporate legal personhood, limited liability and a governance structure of shareholders, board, supervisors and managers. The Chinese version adds Party leadership of state-owned enterprises, to be combined with the modern enterprise system, and Zhou lists five reform areas: shareholding reform, governance, cadre management, pay and personnel systems. A high-standard market system is described as unified, open, orderly and efficient. Zhou argues that it can help the economy withstand shocks and, in special circumstances, circulate internally. On government, Zhou assigns macroeconomic stability to the central government and public services and market supervision to local governments. The article stresses coordinating fiscal and monetary policy under the principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability, along with antitrust enforcement, removal of local protectionism and planning that guides investment and consumption. Zhou concludes that a high-standard socialist market economy system will only be truly established if government is made capable ("有为政府") alongside effective markets and modern enterprises. The text is mostly a policy exposition, restating the Congress's directions with definitions and a list of measures. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese economists framed the post-2022 market-economy reform agenda, including state enterprise reform and the unified national market.

Advancing economic theoretical innovation grounded in practice and making original contributions to developing Marxist political economy 不断推进实践基础上的经济理论创新为发展马克思主义政治经济学作出原创性贡献 Zhou Wen This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 31 January 2023, asks how Xi Jinping's economic thought contributes to Marxist political economy. Zhou Wen argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi has drawn on China's experience to put forward new ideas and strategies, which together form Xi Jinping Thought on economics. In Zhou's account, this body of thought upholds the basic principles and methods of Marxist political economy and makes important original contributions that open a new realm for it. The article is organised under three headings: deepening understanding of the laws of socialist economic construction; answering major questions of China's economic development in the new era; and resolving the relationship between government and market. Zhou argues that the stress on the Party's overall leadership of economic work enriches Marxist theory on the relation between economics and politics. The people-centred approach and the commitment to common prosperity are said to clarify the purpose of socialist production and the nature of the socialist economy. Treating public ownership as the mainstay, with multiple forms of ownership, distribution according to work as the mainstay, and the socialist market economy as the basic economic system is presented as an enrichment of Marxist market theory. The new development philosophy of innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing is described as a systematic answer to questions of the purpose, driving forces and paths of development. Zhou claims that combining the market's "invisible hand" with the government's "visible hand" resolves a worldwide problem in economics and goes beyond both Western development models and mainstream Western economics. Zhou concludes that this provides a basis for a Chinese economics with its own disciplinary, academic and discourse systems. The author calls for further research and practice on combining socialism with the market economy, so that an efficient market and a capable government work together better. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of how Chinese commentators present Xi's economic thought as an original contribution to Marxist political economy.

Deeply grasping the decisive significance of the "Two Establishes" 深刻领悟“两个确立”的决定性意义 Li Junru Li Junru takes up the Party's call, issued at the 20th Party Congress (2022), to understand the "Two Establishes" in depth. The commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 7 February 2023, argues that establishing Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and the whole Party, and establishing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the guiding ideology, is of decisive significance for the Party and country in the new era and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is built in three parts under separate headings. The first presents the Two Establishes as the decisive factor behind the changes of the past decade. The second argues that they reflect the shared wish of the whole Party, the military and the people of all ethnic groups. The third names grasping them as the most pressing task of the new journey and sets out what Party members should do. Li's central claim is that the achievements of the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012) came under the leadership of the Central Committee with Xi as its core and under the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought. The author lists economic gains, poverty reduction, the anti-corruption struggle, ideological work, disaster relief and epidemic control, and attributes each to Xi's personal leadership. Li then grounds the Two Establishes in history and popular will. Citing the Zunyi Conference and Deng Xiaoping's remark that a leadership collective needs a core, Li holds that a Party without a core drifts into weak leadership. Li also reports that at the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), localities, departments and the military all wanted Xi's core status made explicit. The Thought is said to answer the major questions of the era and to give practice its direction. Li concludes that, amid what the text calls great changes unseen in a century and possible \"black swan\" and \"grey rhino\" events, the Party needs a helmsman and a compass. Li calls on Party members to defend Xi's core status \"emotionally, ideologically, politically, organisationally and in action\" and to strengthen centralised, unified leadership. Li also urges them to apply the Thought's worldview and methodology and to turn it into practical work. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how the Two Establishes were explained to Party cadres after the 20th Party Congress.

Arming young people with the Party's scientific theory 用党的科学理论武装青年 Han Xiping Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called on the whole Party to treat youth work as strategic work and to arm young people with the Party's scientific theory, Han Xiping asks why this task matters and how it should be carried out. Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2023, Han argues that arming youth with Party theory is an advantage of the Party, that it is especially necessary in the new era, and that it needs systematic, practice-oriented and internet-aware methods. The article has three parts. The first presents theoretical arming of youth as a Party strength and a reason the Party has won young people. The second explains why the new era makes it more urgent. The third sets out three approaches to the work: systematism, practicality and responsiveness to the times. Han contends that Marxism, as a science and not a fixed dogma, lets the Party keep answering the questions of China, the world, the people and the age. In the author's account, bourgeois parties treat young people as instruments and so cannot win their lasting allegiance, whereas Marxist parties rely on the mass line and guide youth to understand their own interests. The author describes the next dozen or so years to basic modernization, and about thirty to a strong modernized country, as a period in which today's youth are the main force. Han claims that hostile forces try to Westernize and divide Chinese youth, so winning them is a struggle the Party cannot afford to lose. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is named as the content to be taught. On method, Han calls for a system run under the principle of Party leadership over youth work. It would coordinate Party organizations, the Communist Youth League, Party schools and universities, vary teaching by age and occupation, and institutionalize proven schemes such as the Young Marxists training project. It would also tie theory to practice, citing Lenin's warning against book knowledge cut off from work, by presenting the achievements of the past decade and creating lasting mechanisms for social practice. Finally, it would use online platforms such as Xuexi Qiangguo with plainer language. Han concludes that this is the Party's distinctive path for producing qualified successors. Read the original if you want to see how a university Party official presents the rationale and methods of youth ideological work after the 20th Party Congress.

Deeply grasping the decisive significance of the "Two Establishes" and continuously strengthening the Party's political development on the diplomatic front 深刻领悟“两个确立”的决定性意义 不断加强外交战线党的政治建设 Tang Chengyao Sun Pengyuan This article, published in early 2023 and written by a research group of the Foreign Ministry's Party organisation, asks how the diplomatic front should strengthen the Party's political development in light of the Two Establishes. Tang and Sun argue that grasping the decisive significance of the Two Establishes and carrying out the Two Upholds is the political guarantee for what they call major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article has three parts. It first sets out why political development matters for diplomacy, then describes the main practices adopted in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the missions abroad, and finally draws lessons from them. The authors draw on ministry measures, survey results and research visits, and the work won a 2022 national award for Party-building research in central Party and government organs. The authors give three reasons for the task: diplomacy is by nature political work and must be led by the Party; a world of rapid change requires the diplomatic corps to be politically sound; and loyalty to the Party is a long tradition, which they trace to Mao Zedong's appointment of generals as ambassadors and Zhou Enlai's sixteen-character guideline for diplomats. Their account of practice has four strands. These are treating the ministry as a political organ and putting head-of-state diplomacy at the centre; arming officials with Xi Jinping Thought, including study of Xi's diplomatic thought; reinforcing a people-centred stance through education on the original aspiration and mission, consular protection and countering what the authors describe as US and Western attacks over Xinjiang, Hong Kong and human rights; and cultivating a clean political environment through discipline, cadre selection and anti-corruption work. From these practices the authors draw five lessons: keep the correct political direction, hold to a people-centred position, raise political capability, guard against political risks, and preserve the Party's political essence while pressing responsibility down the chain. They cite a questionnaire in which over 80 per cent of respondents said leaders increasingly treat Party building as their main achievement and 98.1 per cent rated the work as good or fairly good. The authors conclude that political development must remain the first task of the diplomatic front. Read the original if you want a detailed, insider account of how Party-building measures are organised in China's foreign ministry and of the official rationale behind them.

The interaction between modernization and modernity in the Party's century of exploration 党的百年探索视阈下现代化与现代性的互动关系 Ma Yunzhi Zhao Rongfeng Ma Yunzhi and Zhao Rongfeng ask how the Communist Party of China's century-long pursuit of modernization has related to the construction of a distinctively Chinese modernity. They argue that socialist modernization has been closely tied to the model of modernity it produces. In their account, modernization conforms to the basic features of modernity while, as it advances, building a Chinese modernity that differs from the Western one. The article follows the Party's history in three stages, which it labels the emergence, presence and future logic of Chinese modernity. It begins with the early exploration from the founding of the Party through the first decades of the People's Republic, then turns to modernization under socialism with Chinese characteristics, from Deng Xiaoping Theory through the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It ends with the goal of building a modern socialist country in all respects. The authors first define the two concepts, treating modernization as the outward form of modernity's inner values. They hold that Marx located modernity's pillars in the logic of capital and metaphysical rationality, and that China's modernity began logically with the Party's founding, which linked modernization to Marxism. They then argue that each theoretical stage added a dimension: Deng Xiaoping Theory set the tone of Chinese characteristics, the Three Represents added the twin aims of liberating productive forces and liberating people, and the Scientific Outlook on Development moved from putting things first to putting people first. For the future, they say China is crossing three "traps" (middle-income, Thucydides and Kindleberger), advancing economic, political, cultural, social, ecological and Party modernization together, and keeping a people-centred orientation that they say surpasses the capital-centred modernity of the West. The authors conclude that building modernity in China is still unfinished, but that the Party's path has produced a modernity fundamentally different from Western models. They contend that this offers other countries a Chinese approach to modernization and a new form of human civilization. They add that the process advances the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Party-history account that reads the post-1921 modernization story through the concept of modernity and its official theoretical milestones.

Correctly understanding the importance of Xi Jinping's statements on bottom-line thinking and preventing and defusing major risks 正确认识关于坚持底线思维着力防范化解重大风险论述的重要性 Cai Qinyu Liu Zhen Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Cai and Liu take up Xi Jinping's repeated call to uphold "bottom-line thinking" and to focus on preventing and defusing major risks. They argue that this body of statements is a new judgement and requirement for Party building in the new era, grounded in theory, history and practice. The short commentary is organised in three parts: the theoretical source in basic Marxist principles, the historical evidence drawn from positive and negative experience, and the practical need to build a modern socialist country in an all-round way. On theory, the authors contend that bottom-line thinking embodies the unity of subjective initiative and objective laws, a systemic outlook that treats risks in politics, ideology, the economy, technology and other fields as one whole, and the dialectic of contradiction. On history, they cite Mao Zedong's "two musts" in 1949, the decision to enter the Korean War, and the "three musts" in the 20th Party Congress report. On practice, they present four needs: consolidating the socialist system amid external pressure, building the new development pattern and high-quality development, modernising national security, and maintaining the Party's advanced and pure character through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The authors conclude that the path of Chinese modernization is long and difficult, so the Party must hold to bottom-line thinking to prepare for the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school commentary links Xi's risk discourse to Marxist theory, Party history and current policy priorities.

Firmly grasping the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the history of New China 牢牢把握新中国史的主题主线、主流本质 Song Yuehong Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2023, Song Yuehong takes up the congratulatory letter that Xi Jinping sent for the 30th anniversary of the Chinese Society for the History of the People's Republic. The letter calls on historians to hold firmly to the "theme, main thread and mainstream essence" of the history of New China. Song argues that studying and teaching that history requires an objective, comprehensive and accurate grasp of its course, achievements and experience, and that these three concepts supply the basic framework for doing so. The piece is a short commentary in three parts. The first sets out the theme and main thread of New China's history, tracing the Party's changing goals and its reading of the principal social contradiction across the socialist revolution and construction period, the reform era and the new era. The second defines the mainstream and essence of that history. The third turns to practical directions for research. Song defines the theme as the continuous adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, together with the founding and development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Its purpose is to build a modern socialist country and achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Four main threads follow: safeguarding sovereignty and promoting a community with a shared future for mankind; upholding Marxism and the Party's self-reform; advancing Chinese modernization and common prosperity; and promoting national reunification. The mainstream is described as founding, enriching and strengthening the country, taking its own path and benefiting the people. Song acknowledges serious setbacks, above all in the socialist revolution and construction period. In the article's account, however, these were part of exploration, and the period's achievements and lessons prepared the ground for the reform era. Song concludes that research should clarify the history, necessity and regularities of the socialist path with Chinese characteristics, and should study Chinese modernization as a process running through New China's history. The article also calls for building the discipline, academic and discourse systems of New China history, combining theory with the collection of sources, and openly opposing historical nihilism. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party historians are told to frame the history of the People's Republic and what research agenda follows from it.

New changes and characteristics of contemporary capitalism 当代资本主义的新变化及特点 Tan Youzhi Writing in a journal issue of early 2023, against a background of the pandemic, the Ukraine crisis and what the article calls the 'four deficits' in global governance, Tan Youzhi asks how contemporary capitalism has changed since 1945 and especially since the turn of the century. The article takes up Xi Jinping's call to strengthen research on contemporary capitalism. Tan's thesis is that capitalism has gained new vitality and is still adjusting, but that its historical fate of being replaced by socialism is unchanged, and that the replacement will be long. The article has two parts. The first, on 'new changes', reads these changes through historical materialism and names two main drivers: successive scientific and technological revolutions, and the course of globalization. Tan reviews three past technological revolutions (steam, electricity and internal combustion, atomic energy and computing) and a fourth now under way around the digital economy and intelligent manufacturing. The second part sets out two characteristics of contemporary capitalism. On the changes, Tan argues that each technological revolution has renewed capitalism, and that the fourth has helped Western economies recover from the 2008 financial crisis and eased class conflict for the time being. Globalization, by contrast, has met a counter-current of unilateralism, populism, protectionism and 'decoupling', which pandemic disruption to supply chains has intensified. On the characteristics, Tan reads Marx's 'two inevitables' together with his 'two never wills' of 1859 (the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy). The first concerns the specific law of capitalist development and the objective certainty of socialism's succession. The second concerns the general law and the long and arduous character of that succession. Welfare policy and state intervention, Tan holds, cannot remove the contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation, so inequality, crises and instability persist. Tan concludes that capitalism still has a capacity to expand, so it will not collapse soon, and calls for combining the necessity of its demise with the long duration of the process. The author also calls for combining capitalism's decay with its continuing possibilities, and the stages of history with its direction, so as to avoid blind optimism. The article describes a 'strong capitalism, weak socialism' pattern alongside a trend of 'the West declining, the East rising'. It also says the United States shifts crises onto others through rule-setting, sanctions and intervention. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholarship in 2023 applied the 'two inevitables' and 'two never wills' to contemporary capitalism, technology and globalization.

On the requirements of the new era for upholding historical confidence and strengthening historical initiative 论坚持历史自信、增强历史主动的新时代要求 Wang Tingyou Pei Yanan Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Tingyou and Pei Yanan take up the Congress report's call on the whole Party to "uphold historical confidence and strengthen historical initiative", alongside the newly formulated "three musts". The authors argue that this twofold requirement rests on three things: grasping historical laws and trends, seizing opportunities through innovation, and treating history, including its errors, correctly. The article has three numbered sections, each opening with a statement of one condition for historical confidence and initiative and closing with practical requirements for studying the Congress's spirit. It moves from the Party's century of struggle and the Marxist view of historical laws, through innovation in theory, practice, institutions and culture, to the Party's three historical resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021) and the fight against historical nihilism. It was published in a journal on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping theory. In the first section the authors hold that history is objective and governed by laws, so a Marxist party must align itself with its direction. They read the Party's path from the founding goal of socialism and communism through reform and opening up to the two centenary goals and Chinese modernization as a record of following those laws. In the second, they argue that necessity makes its way through the practice of the people. The Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, together with the Two Integrations, is presented as the source of its vitality, and the authors list historic shifts in economy, opening up, development philosophy and Party building. In the third, they say that mistakes, including the Cultural Revolution, were unavoidable in exploring a new path, and that what counts is the attitude toward them. Historical nihilism is described as an attempt to deny Party leadership by distorting history. The authors call for viewing history in its concrete conditions and with a long-term perspective. Wang and Pei conclude that Party members must systematically study Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, keep a spirit of struggle, continue innovation, and learn Party history and the history of the People's Republic, reform and socialism. They present this as the way to ensure that socialism with Chinese characteristics keeps widening its path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a close, officially aligned account of how Party theorists linked historical confidence, historical nihilism and the 20th Congress agenda in late 2022.

The Communist Party of China's historic contributions to enriching and developing scientific socialism 中国共产党丰富和发展科学社会主义的历史贡献 Huang Guangyou Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Huang asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has enriched and developed scientific socialism over its century-plus history. The article argues that the Party, by combining Marxist fundamentals with Chinese conditions, has become the mainstay of the international communist movement in the twenty-first century. Huang presents its contributions as original ones in theory, in practice and in institutions. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats theory: the path to power, stages of socialist development, the essence of socialism, and Chinese modernization. The second treats the practice of the socialist movement, from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist transformation and reform to the new era. The third treats institutional innovation, from the Chinese Soviet Republic to the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Huang repeatedly contrasts Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin with the Party's own responses. Huang's central move is to show that each Chinese innovation filled a gap left by the classics. Marx and Engels gave no concrete guidance for semi-colonial countries, and saw peasants as incapable of representing themselves. Mao Zedong's New Democratic Revolution, relying on the peasantry and encircling cities from the countryside, is described as a second model after the October Revolution, later borne out in Vietnam, Korea and Cuba. Huang likewise credits the theory of the primary stage of socialism, Deng Xiaoping's definition of socialism's essence (liberating and developing the productive forces, eliminating exploitation and polarisation, reaching common prosperity), and the break from the Soviet model as moving socialism from one model to many. Huang concludes that Chinese modernization, led by the Party, breaks the Western equation of modernization with capitalism and offers developing countries a path of independent exploration. The author also holds that China's governance experience and the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind show the advantages of socialist governance. The article ends by listing the Party's theoretical achievements, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, as results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Party scholars frame China's relation to the classics of scientific socialism and to the Soviet experience.

The scope and boundaries of intelligent labour 智能劳动的范围与边界 Shang Xiwei Chen Xiaohui Writing in a newspaper commentary in January 2023, Shang and Chen ask how far AI-driven "intelligent labour" can replace human labour. They note the pessimistic view that machines will displace workers and usurp their status as labourers. They argue instead that Marxist labour theory remains valid and that intelligent labour has clear limits. The piece first describes what intelligent machines already replace, such as cash machines, unmanned warehouses, automatic ticketing and securities-analysis software. It then explains how an intelligent machine system (algorithms, data and robotic arms) takes over functions of the brain and muscles. Finally it sets out three boundaries drawn from Marx's historical materialism and his view of labour. According to the authors, replaceable work is repetitive, patterned and programmable. Human knowledge is objectified in machines, turning living labour into objectified labour. The first boundary is that AI cannot produce something from nothing, because it depends on data supplied by humans. The second is that AI creates no value: living human labour remains the only source of value, and the machine is only a "measurer" and "indicator" of social relations. The third is that AI lacks emotion, will and aesthetic sense, so it cannot respond to unexpected situations and its output lacks uniqueness. The authors conclude that AI remains a tool and cannot shed its character as a thing. They still regard it as a historical advance over handicraft and mechanical tools, one that produces new forms of labour alienation but also holds positive significance for the liberation of human labour. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-labour-theory answer to fears of AI replacing human work.

The problem consciousness and theoretical tensions of classical Western Marxism 经典西方马克思主义的问题意识与理论张力 Gao Xiaoxi Gao Xiaoxi, in a short piece for the Chinese Social Sciences Today (January 2023), asks what question drove classical Western Marxism, the current running from Lukács to Althusser between the 1920s and 1960s. Gao argues that its core concern was how to make socialist revolution in advanced capitalist countries, and that this strategic dispute was expressed as a debate over the nature of Marx's philosophy. The article first sketches twentieth-century capitalism: oligarchic monopoly, a divided working class including a "labour aristocracy", and a shift from open repression to softer ideological control through consumerism and mass culture. It then contrasts classical Western Marxism with the Second International, divides the former into humanist and scientistic wings, and traces its afterlife after the events of May 1968. Gao contends that the Second International read Marx in a deterministic, dogmatic way and so could not meet these changes. Classical Western Marxists, by contrast, treated class consciousness as decisive and understood Marxism as a philosophy of subjective practice joining philosophy, history and politics. Its central tension, in Gao's account, is how to unite critique of capitalist ideology with revolutionary practice, which exposes a subjectivist and romantic tendency. The humanist wing (Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, existentialist Marxism) is set against Althusser's structuralist "theoretical anti-humanism", which Gao says slides into theoretical monologue. Gao concludes that Marxism outside China can be read as shaped by tensions such as history–structure and liberation–disengagement, which trace back to classical Western Marxism. Without grasping this problem consciousness, Gao warns, one risks misjudging the interpretation and reception of Western Marxism and weakening the contemporary and global outlook of Marxism adapted to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how classical Western Marxism is positioned within the wider field of foreign Marxism.

Firmly grasping the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the history of New China 牢牢把握新中国史的主题主线、主流本质 Song Yuehong Marking the 30th anniversary of the Chinese Society for the History of the People's Republic, Xi Jinping sent a congratulatory letter urging historians to firmly grasp the theme, main thread and mainstream essence of the history of New China. This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 15 February 2023, sets out how Song Yuehong reads that instruction. Song argues that studying the letter requires an objective, comprehensive and accurate account of the course, achievements and experience of New China, and a deeper understanding of these three categories. The piece moves in three steps. It first defines the theme and the four main threads of New China's history, tracing the Party's changing statements of its goals across the socialist revolution and construction period, the reform and opening up period and the new era. It then sets out the mainstream and essence of that history, including how the author treats its setbacks. Finally it draws out tasks for research on the history of New China. In Song's account, the theme is the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, together with building and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics and rejuvenating the Chinese nation. The four threads are safeguarding sovereignty and promoting a community with a shared future for mankind; upholding Marxism and the Party's self-reform; advancing Chinese modernization and common prosperity; and achieving national reunification. Song admits that the path was not smooth and that mistakes and serious setbacks occurred. The author nonetheless holds that the exploratory achievements of the early period prepared the ground for later reform, so the mainstream is founding, enriching and strengthening the country, taking its own path and benefiting the people. The essence is a history of socialist development, of the people's united struggle and of national rejuvenation. Song calls for research to explain the historical logic of the socialist path with Chinese characteristics and the course of Chinese modernization. It should also build a disciplinary, academic and discourse system for the history of New China, combine source collection with theory, and openly oppose historical nihilism. Studies should foster historical confidence and the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated historians frame the periodisation and interpretive guidelines for studying the People's Republic after Xi's 2023 letter.

Firmly grasping the requirements of our times for unity and struggle 牢牢把握团结奋斗的时代要求 Li Haitao This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 11 January 2023, interprets "unity and struggle" as a key phrase of the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Li notes that Xi Jinping, in discussion with the Guangxi delegation, listed "five firm grasps", one of which is firmly grasping the requirements of the times for unity and struggle. Li argues that the Party and people must understand its strategic significance, political meaning and practical demands in order to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is organised in three parts. The first presents unity and struggle as the most distinctive spiritual hallmark of the Party and the Chinese people. The second sets out what unity and struggle mean in the new era, namely acting under the Party's banner. The third explains how the "Three Musts" from the Congress report apply to the task. In the first part, Li traces the roots of unity and struggle to some 5,000 years of civilisation and to the resistance to aggression in modern times. Li also grounds it in the Party's character: its lofty ideal, its guiding theory, its purpose of serving the people, and its strict organisation and discipline. The second part calls for uniting will and action through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It also calls for closer unity around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core, supported by the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Li adds four further kinds of unity: within the Party, between Party and people, between the military and government and between the military and civilians, and among Chinese at home and abroad. The third part reads the Three Musts as, respectively, the source of strength, the proper spirit and the essential feature of unity and struggle. These are staying true to the founding mission, remaining modest and plain-living, and daring and being skilled at struggle. Li concludes that the Party's central task is to lead the people in building a modern socialist country and advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization. In Li's account, a complex international and domestic environment, including the Russia–Ukraine conflict, rising anti-globalisation and unresolved domestic problems, makes unity and struggle indispensable. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory commentary in early 2023 presented the 20th Congress's unity-and-struggle theme and its links to the Two Establishes and the Three Musts.

Continuing to write new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 不断谱写马克思主义中国化时代化新篇章 Yang Genqiao Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2023, Yang Genqiao takes up the task of continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, which the author calls the solemn historical responsibility of today's Communist Party members. Yang argues that the 20th Party Congress (2022) supplied the fundamental guidance for this task through the Two Integrations and its account of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The short commentary first explains why Marxism matters to the Party and the country, citing the Congress report's claim that it is Marxism adapted to China and to the times that "works". It then reviews the Party's century-long record of theoretical innovation, from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory to Xi Jinping Thought. A final section sets out what must be done on the new journey. Yang's central claim is that the Party's achievements rest on continually updating Marxism. Quoting Xi Jinping, Yang reads Marxism's "localization" and "timeliness" as its spatial and temporal dimensions of development. Xi Jinping Thought is presented as the latest result of this process, credited with helping the Party meet risks and produce historic changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yang rejects both dogmatism and pragmatism: the classics' words should not be mechanically applied to today's China, since present conditions exceed what Marx, Engels and Lenin could imagine. Yang calls for adherence to Marxism's guiding position together with theoretical innovation grounded in practice. This means applying the six "musts" of the Thought's worldview and methodology: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while innovating, problem orientation, systems thinking, and a global outlook. It also means pursuing the Two Integrations, linking Marxism to China's concrete realities and to its fine traditional culture. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how the Party presents its theoretical lineage and the 20th Congress's guidance on Marxist innovation.

Fully, accurately and comprehensively applying the new development philosophy to drive high-quality development 完整、准确、全面贯彻新发展理念 着力推动高质量发展 Lu Mingchuan Zhang Yixiu Published in Guangming Daily on 20 January 2023, this short commentary by Lu Mingchuan and Zhang Yixiu takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report and the 2022 Central Economic Work Conference. Both stressed applying the new development philosophy and promoting high-quality development. The authors argue that this is a necessary task for the Party's central mission in the new era and on the new journey. The article is organised around the five elements of the new development philosophy: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. Each receives a section that links the principle to a set of policy priorities. On innovation, the authors call for new mechanisms, focused national science and technology projects, and a stronger role for enterprises, together with self-reliance in science and technology and home-grown talent. On coordination, they tie the task to the principal contradiction in Chinese society and urge a modern industrial system, rural revitalisation and regionally coordinated development. They also propose green and low-carbon transition, with carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, and high-standard opening up that relies on the domestic market while drawing in global resources. On sharing, which the authors call an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics, they list priorities. These are employment, basic public services, social security and a distribution system that supports common prosperity. They also propose raising low incomes, expanding the middle-income group and regulating excessive and illegal income. The text works as a policy outline built on official documents. Read the original if you want a compact summary of how the five concepts were translated into policy priorities in early 2023.

Taking the Chinese modernization path of common prosperity 走共同富裕的中国式现代化道路 Li Heliang Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which describes Chinese modernization as modernization for the common prosperity of all the people, Li Heliang argues that China must unwaveringly follow a path of Chinese modernization built on common prosperity. The piece, a short commentary first published in Guangming Daily on 3 January 2023, holds that this path comprehensively transcends the modernization model dominated by the logic of capital. The article has three parts: why common prosperity goes beyond Western capital logic, why it is a defining feature of Chinese modernization, and how it is to be advanced in practice. In Li's account, Western modernization, resting on capitalist production, is built on exploitation and deprives proletarians of the right to modernize. China, by contrast, keeps public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to labour as the main form, and the central place of labour, and since the 18th Party Congress (2012) has eliminated absolute poverty and built a moderately prosperous society. Li then analyses common prosperity by its subject, content, process and goal. It is not egalitarian sameness. It covers material and spiritual life and all five forms of civilization. It requires both creating and fairly distributing wealth, and it provides the basis for the free and comprehensive development of the human being. Li proposes three tasks: upholding the Party's overall leadership without wavering, improving the top-level design across the five-sphere integrated plan (including the Two Unwaverings, ecological civilization and social governance), and advancing with historical initiative and creativity, guided by dialectical and historical materialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated theorists link Chinese modernization, common prosperity and a critique of capital logic.

Developments in Western European left-wing social movements amid political upheaval 政治变局下西欧左翼社会运动的发展动向 Wu Huiping Wu Huiping asks how left-wing social movements in major Western European countries have grown since the early 2000s, and why many have turned into new radical left parties. Writing in early 2023, Wu argues that these movements, through innovative political mobilisation and organisation, offer a strong case for observing how left-wing thought spreads and develops in Europe. The article holds that their rise reflects globalisation, technological change and political disorder, but that weak governing capacity and right-wing populist competition limit their future. The article first surveys the movements country by country. These are La France Insoumise under Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Italy's Five Star Movement, Spain's Podemos and Germany's Aufstehen. Wu then identifies common features: policy agendas centred on social justice and an explicit left-populist stance. A section on organisational traits follows, and then one on four underlying drivers. The text closes by assessing bottlenecks and likely directions. In Wu's account, the movements differ from traditional parties in three ways. They mobilise through social media and online platforms, which Wu calls internet democracy. They adopt loose, parallel, bottom-up structures with easy online membership, which Wu describes as direct democracy. Their supporters are younger, better educated and cross-class, unlike the working-class base of traditional left parties. Wu traces their rise to four drivers. Neoliberal inequality has deepened, and youth unemployment in Spain and Italy has been severe. Traditional party systems are fragmenting. Digital technology lowers the cost of organising. A series of European crises, including the financial, euro and refugee crises, has fuelled populism and Euroscepticism. Wu concludes that the movements' mobilisation methods and organisational innovations offer lessons for the modernisation of traditional parties. Their growth is constrained, however, by a lack of governing experience, as shown by the Five Star Movement's decline after taking office. It is also constrained by competition from right-wing populists such as the National Rally and Alternative for Germany. Wu notes that the pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict deepen Europe's crises and give the left openings. Whether it can use them depends, in Wu's view, on improving its governing capacity and offering more credible alternatives. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic overview of the new European left's organisation, social base and prospects.

Marching steadily on the road of human progress New developments and trends among foreign communist parties in 2022 坚定行进在推动人类发展进步的道路上 Yu Haiqing This annual survey, published in early 2023, asks how communist parties outside China fared in 2022 and what trends marked their activity. Yu Haiqing argues that the parties held to their ideals and kept working for peace and social justice. The author also finds that they remained in a long-running phase of struggle against adversity, with electoral setbacks and deepening internal divisions. The article is organised around five themes. It begins with commemorations: the 105th anniversary of the October Revolution, the centenary of the Soviet Union, and party anniversaries in Brazil, Japan and the Netherlands. It then reviews election results, mainly in Europe, Brazil, Japan, the Czech Republic, Russia and Nepal. Next it covers party congresses and plenums in ruling and non-ruling parties, and the parties' international meetings and disputes. It closes with their campaigns on peace, workers' interests, anti-communism and women's rights. Yu's core assessment is that electoral and parliamentary politics were largely unfavourable. The author cites Portugal's worst-ever result, about 2% for the French candidate, and a divided Italian communist movement that won no seats. Nepal's communist reunification and return to government is the exception, which Yu describes as an expedient and fragile alliance. The more important point is the split inside the movement. Yu describes two clashes: one between the Communist Party of Greece and the Workers' Party of Hungary over ideology and unity, and one over the Russia–Ukraine conflict. In the latter, a joint statement backed by 23 parties blamed the United States and NATO, while a Greek-led resolution called the war imperialist and said only ending capitalism would end war. Yu reads these as a widening of internal contradictions. Yu concludes that the parties are entering a new cycle, with more in-person contact and clearer goals, but that fundamental disagreements on major theoretical and practical questions obstruct unity and cooperation. The author calls on the parties to respect one another, seek common ground while setting aside differences, and look for a "greatest common divisor". Read the original if you want a detailed, country-by-country chronicle of communist party congresses, elections and international meetings in 2022, as seen by a scholar at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

The threefold basis for the principle that religious activities must not interfere in social life, and how to put it into practice 宗教活动不得干涉社会生活的三重依据及践行理路 Yang Yansheng Qian Hanfei Yang and Qian take up a line from Xi Jinping's speech at the National Conference on Religious Work (December 2021): "religious activities must not interfere in education, the judiciary, administrative functions and social life." They note that religion's willingness to engage in society has grown in recent years, with more frequent conflicts and group incidents involving religious demands. Their thesis is that the principle rests on a theoretical basis, an institutional basis and a practical basis, and that it needs further institutional and social measures to be carried out. The article has four parts. It first derives the principle from Marxist theory, then from Party policy documents and state law since reform and opening up. The third part draws on the authors' own collection of public-opinion cases, gathered with monitoring software using Buddhism, Islam and Christianity as keywords. The last part sets out three practical routes. On theory, the authors argue that Marxist views of religion clash with the nature of modern social life in three ways: the illusory nature of religion against the practical character of social life, the private nature of faith against the public nature of social life, and religious mysticism against modern rationality. They hold that religion must therefore stay in the private sphere. On practice, they describe three problems: religious infiltration of politics, education, culture and daily life; the disorderly expansion of house churches, which they say disrupts rural kinship ties and campus life; and the entanglement of ethnic and religious issues. In their account this entanglement produces biased law enforcement in civil disputes and lets extremist, terrorist and separatist forces use religion, citing the 2009 and 2014 violent incidents in Urumqi. For implementation, Yang and Qian call for the principle to be written consistently into Party documents and laws, with new departmental rules such as norms for managing house churches, an early-warning and response system for religion-related public opinion, and revision of religious doctrines and regulations. They also propose greater practical care for the people, tailored to why people turn to religion, so that Party and government care comes before religious care. They further want the governance pattern of Party leadership, government management, social coordination and religious self-discipline strengthened, with interdisciplinary research and better-trained officials. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholarly journal on science and atheism justifies limits on religious activity in public life, with examples of the cases it cites.

Atheist thought in Mao Zedong's Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan and its implications 《湖南农民运动考察报告》中的无神论思想及其启示 Liu Fujun Liu Fujun examines the atheist thought contained in Mao Zedong's 1927 Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, a text usually read for its theory of peasant revolution. Liu argues that the Report also answered a major question of the National Revolution: how to understand and treat "theocratic authority" (shenquan, the rule of gods and spirits over peasant life). In Liu's view, this thought marked the start of the Sinicization of Marxist atheism and still offers guidance today. The article is organised around four sets of "threes". It first sets out the background: the weight of spirit-belief on the peasantry, Marxist atheism as the Party's theoretical basis, and Mao's own path from childhood Buddhist belief to firm atheism. It then reconstructs the Report's content, assesses its historical standing, and draws lessons for the present. Liu draws on Mao's other investigations (Xunwu, Changgang, Xingguo), early Party documents and writings by Zhou Enlai, Yun Daiying and Qu Qiubai. Liu's core claim is that the Report treats theocratic authority as one part of the feudal-patriarchal order, alongside political, clan and patriarchal authority, and as a tool of spiritual oppression and economic exploitation. Its answer to how to overthrow it has four elements: overthrow landlord rule, lead peasants in economic struggle, raise their education and culture, and propagate atheism. Liu stresses the Report's principle that belief declines as a result of political and economic victory, not coercion; in Mao's words, peasants would discard the idols themselves, without others doing it for them too early. Liu adds that Mao's Xunwu concept of "deity landlords" (temples, shrines and monasteries holding land) linked belief to material exploitation, and that Mao distinguished folk belief from institutional religion. Liu concludes that the Report's lessons are three. The roots of theism will persist for a long time under socialism, so atheist education must continue. Marxist atheism must keep being adapted to Chinese conditions and the needs of the times. Atheist propaganda must serve the Party's central tasks and respect the Party's policy of freedom of religious belief, uniting religious believers rather than setting them apart. Liu supports these points with Lenin and with Xi Jinping's remarks in Liangshan (2018). Read the original if you want a Party-theorist account of how Mao's early rural investigations are used to ground current atheist education and religious policy.

What is "new" about contemporary Western New Atheism 当代西方新无神论“新”在何处 Chen Weihua Chen Weihua asks what the adjective "new" actually signifies in "New Atheism", the cultural phenomenon that emerged in Britain and the United States in the early twenty-first century. Critics, the article notes, have called it blind, radical, "old wine in new bottles" and a trend driven by publishing profits. Chen argues that "new" carries a historical dimension, marking both a break with traditional atheism and a response to new circumstances, and that New Atheism is a new stage in the development of Western atheism. The article is organised around four senses of "new": a new stance, new forms of communication, new goals, and a new choice of way of life. It draws on the term's origin in 2006, the books of Sam Harris, Richard Dawkins, Daniel Dennett, Christopher Hitchens and Ayaan Hirsi Ali, critics such as the theologian Hoult and Thomas Zenk, and studies of American atheist organisations and online resources. Chen closes by assessing New Atheism from the standpoint of Marxist atheism. Chen's central argument is that New Atheism differs from earlier atheism in posture, medium and aim. Its authors do not pose as neutral observers, claim that religion's core assertions are false and that Western culture gives religion too much respect, and reject accommodation even with moderate belief. The internet, the article says, created a community of otherwise "hidden" atheists and let groups such as the Secular Coalition of America organise campaigns. Drawing on Stephen Drew and Mary Bernstein, Chen presents identity-building and political demands as the movement's main goals, including church–state separation and progressive positions on social issues. The article adds that atheists remain marginalised in the United States. Chen concludes that New Atheism inherits the Enlightenment's combative spirit but is also a social and cultural phenomenon, a post-9/11 ideological response to religious fundamentalism and terrorism. In Chen's account it is the most radical current in contemporary Western atheism. Its appeal also draws on a Western desire for a middle path between it and the religious right, so that atheism becomes "a possible way of life" and cultural choice. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-atheism scholar's overview of how New Atheism is characterised, and of the Western sources behind that characterisation.

Major innovations of Chinese modernization seen from history 从历史看中国式现代化的重大创新 Yu Heping Writing in early 2023, Yu Heping asks in what sense Chinese modernization is a major innovation in world modernization theory and practice. Taking up Xi Jinping's claim that it breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization, Yu argues that it contains four innovations: a new summing-up of the course of human civilization, a new direction and form of civilization, a new picture of world modernization, and a new creation in modernization theory. Yu holds that these are concentrated in its stated connotations and fit the historical facts. This short commentary approaches the question through the changing meaning of "modernization". It moves from the early modernizers, who imitated Britain or the West, to the spread of the concept and Western theory, and then to Chinese ideas of socialist modernization after 1921. It ends with the five connotations set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Yu distinguishes an early stage of intuitive, "perceptual" modernization, largely imitation without a theory of modernization, from later rational understanding. Western modernization theory, in Yu's account, grew from Western experience and mainly meant capitalist industrialization and democratization, so it amounted to a theory of Westernization. Chinese modernization, Yu says, contains these general elements, especially industrialization and democratization, and adds five distinctive features, including a huge population, common prosperity and the harmonious coexistence of humanity and nature. Its decisive difference is a people-centred ultimate purpose. Capitalist modernization, Yu argues, centres on capital accumulation and shares benefits only passively and unevenly. Yu concludes that Chinese modernization theory is the newest, most comprehensive and highest understanding of modernization so far, and an epoch-making innovation. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a CASS historian uses the history of the modernization concept to support the official claim of Chinese modernization's originality.

On the relationship between the discipline of CPC history and Party building and the construction of ideological and political theory courses 中共党史党建学科与思想政治理论课建设关系刍议 Song Xueqin Yang Zongru In September 2022 the Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council and the Ministry of Education added "CPC history and Party building" as a first-level discipline under law. Song Xueqin and Yang Zongru ask how this new discipline relates to the compulsory ideological and political theory courses taught in Chinese universities. They argue that the two are mutually dependent and inseparable, and that building the discipline well requires treating them together. The article has three parts. The first argues that the discipline needs the courses; the second that the courses supply momentum for the discipline's "three systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse systems); the third that building an autonomous body of knowledge in the discipline can raise the quality of the courses. The authors draw on Xi Jinping's statements, central Party documents from 2019 and 2022, and a historical review of how Party history was taught from the 1950s onward. In the first part, the authors say courses largely decide a discipline's standing. They trace Party history's strong periods (the 1950s–60s and the 1980s) to its close tie with required political theory courses, and its weakening to later course reforms in 1998, 2005 and 2008 that separated them. They set out two current proposals: replace or merge existing courses into one on CPC history and theory, or keep the present course structure and have several disciplines jointly support three named courses. Both are called feasible, but the authors favour a dedicated course platform. In the second part, they argue that the courses' principle of unity of political and academic quality guides the disciplinary system. Student questions raised in teaching become research problems for the academic system, and the courses bring different discourse resources together for the discourse system. In the third part, the authors say the autonomous knowledge system should enrich course content through the Sinicization of Marxism and the spiritual lineage of Chinese Communists. It should also supply research methods, including the 2021 historical resolution's guidance on a correct view of Party history and opposition to historical nihilism, and strengthen problem orientation in teaching. They cite weak problem awareness, for example in teaching modern Chinese history, as a current shortcoming. They conclude that the discipline and the courses should interact in a virtuous circle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the new first-level discipline is meant to connect to compulsory political theory teaching, including the course-reform options under discussion.

The Party's investigation and research work during the full-scale War of Resistance Methods, results and lessons of the Yan'an-era campaign 全面抗战时期党的调查研究工作 He Lei Liu Shuru He Lei and Liu Shuru examine how the Chinese Communist Party carried out investigation and research (diaocha yanjiu) between 1937 and 1945, a period they call the full-scale War of Resistance against Japan. They argue that the campaign, promoted above all by Mao Zedong, was a high point in the Party's history of fact-finding. In their view it offers lessons for improving the investigative skills of Party members and cadres today. The article has three parts. The first explains why such work was necessary. The second describes four methods used in the anti-Japanese base areas: comprehensive survey, typical-case survey, survey by conference, and pilot-point survey. The third reviews the results and draws four lessons. The authors illustrate each method with a case: Li Zhuoran's Gulin survey, surveys of village Party branches in the Taihang area, Zhang Wentian's Yan'an rural investigation, and Xi Zhongxun's Haojiaqiao survey. On necessity, the authors argue that the Party's rapid growth and the lingering subjectivism and dogmatism after the Zunyi Conference called for investigation. They present it as a bridge between the universal truths of Marxism and China's concrete conditions, and therefore as a means of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions (Marxism's Sinicization) and unifying Party thinking. They also treat it as a way of practising the mass line, since measures cut off from local needs had strained Party–people relations. The four lessons are: give the work high priority in thinking; build and improve investigation institutions, as the 1941 Central Committee decision did by creating a Central Investigation and Research Bureau and local research offices; adhere to seeking truth from facts; and keep to the principle of going 'from the masses, to the masses'. The authors conclude that when the Party emphasised investigation its policies fitted reality, and that neglect led to losses. They hold that the wartime experience can help today's cadres improve their investigative ability, apply theory to practice and keep close ties with the people. Read the original if you want a historical account of Yan'an-era survey methods, with named cases and Mao's remarks on them, framed as guidance for present-day Party work.

Badiou's philosophy of the event and the "Chinese question" 巴迪欧的事件哲学与中国问题 Liu Xin Alain Badiou's philosophy of the event is usually seen as a Western theory travelling east. Liu Xin argues that the influence ran both ways: Badiou's theory of the event was itself shaped by his encounter with Chinese thought. The article treats this interaction, and the "Chinese question of Western theory" it produces, as a way of seeing how event philosophy operates "in the world". The article has four sections. It begins with Chinese and French readings of Hegel in the 1960s and 1970s, then turns to Badiou's "rediscovery" of the Hegel scholar Zhang Shiying. It next considers the place of literature and art in Badiou's event philosophy, citing Quentin Meillassoux and Slavoj Žižek as commentators. A short conclusion assesses the limits of Badiou's engagement with China. Liu's central claim is that Badiou, dissatisfied with Althusserian and Kojèvian Hegel, found a revolutionary Hegel in Chinese Marxism. He set Zhang Shiying's reading of the "rational kernel" of Hegelian dialectics, which runs through Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong, against He Lin's conservative, state-centred and mystical reading. Badiou drew on Mao's principle of "one divides into two" and on Zhang's account of the leap from quantitative to qualitative change. In his reading, these ideas open space for a rupture that breaks an existing structure and gives rise to the event. Liu also notes that Badiou counts the Chinese Revolution and the poet Ai Qing among the events and subjects of the twentieth century. For Badiou, art can restore the sensuous force of an event in a way that retrospective political history cannot. Liu concludes that Badiou's theory is the product of a two-way dialogue with Mao, He Lin, Zhang Shiying and Ai Qing. The author also criticises it as abstract. Badiou's event is portrayed as miraculous and unexplainable, and people can only wait passively for it. In Liu's view, Badiou had no direct experience of China, and his "revolutionary China" was a projection of the French cultural and political crisis after May 1968. Liu warns that bringing Badiou back into China as a hermeneutic tool should acknowledge the "misreading" involved and the theory's limits. Read the original if you are interested in Badiou's debts to Maoism and Chinese Hegel scholarship, or in how Chinese scholars critically assess Western radical theory's use of "China".

Rethinking the relationship between the Sinicization, modernization (keeping pace with the times) and popularization of Marxism 关于马克思主义中国化、时代化与大众化关系的再思考 Chen Peiyong Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Chen Peiyong asks how three long-discussed categories relate to one another: the Sinicization of Marxism (zhongguohua), its adaptation to the times (shidaihua) and its popularization among the masses (dazhonghua). The article's thesis is that the first two are inseparable yet distinct, and that the third has a different focus. It holds that the Congress's emphasis on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with popularization no longer named alongside it, does not make popularization less important. The article first traces the history of the formulations. It covers Mao Zedong's 1938 proposal of Sinicization, the pause in its use after 1952, Deng Xiaoping's formulations about combining universal truth with Chinese realities, and the post-2001 revival. It also covers the 2009 Fourth Plenum document that first listed all three terms together.
