Chen then analyses each term's meaning, and ends by comparing the Congress reports' wording with the earlier triple formula. Chen defines Sinicization as the unity of transforming Marxism and transforming China, and adaptation to the times as the unity of transforming Marxism and transforming the age. Both oppose dogmatism, and since China's concrete reality is changing and set within the world, Sinicization already contains adaptation to the times. The difference is that Sinicization stresses space and the times stress time. For a country that lags behind the world's front rank, Chen argues, localization may run against 'keeping up with the times', as in the revolutionary period, when pursuing urban proletarian revolution would have failed. As China's standing has risen, the two requirements are said to be converging, so that Sinicized Marxism now also aims to lead the era. Popularization is defined as the unity of transforming Marxism and reaching the masses. It concerns the form of expression, whereas the other two concern theoretical content. Chen sees possible tension: popularization can slide into vulgarization or trivialization and misread new theoretical results. Chen nonetheless insists that the task is far from finished and that its success should be a standard for judging whether Sinicization and adaptation to the times succeed. Read the original if you want a conceptual and textual history of how the Party's official triple formula developed, and a Party-theorist's reading of why popularization dropped out of the 20th Congress wording.

A comparative study of Critique of Hegelian Philosophy and Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right With remarks on the origin, birth and development of historical materialism 《黑格尔哲学批判》与《黑格尔法哲学批判》比较研究 Chai Peng Ding Sanqing Chai Peng and Ding Sanqing compare Ludwig Feuerbach's Critique of Hegelian Philosophy with Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, the first systematic critiques of Hegel written by each thinker. They ask what the two texts reveal about the link between Feuerbach's materialism and historical materialism. Their thesis is that Feuerbach laid a philosophical foundation but stopped at materialism in general, whereas Marx's unfinished text is a transitional work that already contains the germ of historical materialism. The article has four parts. It first examines Feuerbach's breakthrough, omissions and misplaced emphasis, then Marx's text: its transitional character, its layout and its limits. The third part compares the two works on six points: aim, standpoint, method, subject matter, significance and limitations. A short conclusion draws out the consequences for the origins of historical materialism. The authors draw on Engels, Althusser, and Chinese scholars such as Han Lixin and Zhu Xueping. On Feuerbach, the authors argue that he traced Hegel's roots in Fichte, Schelling and Kant. By inverting subject and predicate and taking a genetic approach, he made sensuous, real being the starting point of philosophy. But he discarded Hegelian dialectics along with idealism. His 'natural man' therefore stayed an isolated, unhistorical figure, and he relapsed into dependence on religious morality when he addressed social change. On Marx, they stress the context of writing: material-interest disputes at the Rheinische Zeitung, a growing sense of the Prussian state's class character, and Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy. Marx criticised Hegel's monarchy, bureaucracy and estates assembly and argued for democracy. Yet he still hoped to overcome political alienation through the state, and his claim that civil society is the state's presupposition was, in the authors' view, only a logical inference from the inversion. The authors conclude that Feuerbach's limits come from his inability to escape modern idealism and metaphysics. Marx's limits come from a mind in transition, where Hegelian, Feuerbachian and historical-materialist tendencies collided. Marx later developed 'civil society determines the state' in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher and The Holy Family. He then turned to material production and economic relations as the real starting point. For the authors, the 1843 manuscript shows the beginnings of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the young Marx's break with Hegel and Feuerbach, or want a structured six-point comparison from a Chinese perspective.

The historical and theoretical foundations of "Marxism works" “马克思主义行”的历史和理论基础 Hu Changshuan The report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) states that the ultimate reason the Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good is that Marxism works, specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Hu Changshuan takes up how this claim should be understood. The author argues that "Marxism works" and "sinicized, contemporary Marxism works" are essentially unified, and that grasping this is a theoretical precondition for further advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article has three parts. The first treats the historical and theoretical grounds for confidence in Marxism as such. The second treats the grounds for confidence in sinicized, contemporary Marxism. The third explains how the two relate, drawing on Marx's remarks on theory and practice. In the first part, Hu locates the strength of Marxism in its scientific and elevated character, and in its practical value. Scientific character means that Marxism emerged from the best natural and social science of its day and revealed general laws of social development. Its elevated character lies in its proletarian standpoint and its commitment to human emancipation. In practice, Hu says, it moved socialism from utopia to science and from theory to reality. The second part holds that the 20th Party Congress conclusion expresses the achievements of practice and the theoretical results of Marxism's adaptation, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Hu reads the Soviet collapse as confirming the conclusion, because it resulted from departing from Marxism. The third part presents a two-way relation. Sinicized Marxism shares with Marxism the logic of historical materialism, the aim of communism, the people's standpoint and the dialectical-materialist method. Hu also argues that most other Marxisms remain at the level of theory and have not realised its practical essence. Hu concludes that studying the classics and the conditions in which Marxism arose will deepen conviction in sinicized Marxism. Conversely, sinicized Marxism must be understood on a larger world-historical scale, where it embodies the unity of theory and practice. The author describes Xi Jinping Thought as the most influential, creative and practically significant Marxism in the world today. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists justify the claim that Marxism works and the standing of sinicized Marxism within global Marxism.

Marx's view of world history and its contemporary value 马克思的世界历史观及其当代价值 Wu Hongzheng Wu Hongzheng asks what Marx's view of world history is and what it offers today. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Communist Party (2021), the article argues that the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics must be understood within the process of world history. It frames the problem through three basic questions: whether world history is created by human practice or by a supernatural power, whether its laws can be known, and whether it should lead to peace or destruction. The article has three parts. The first sets Marx's critique of German classical philosophy, mainly Kant and Hegel, against these three questions. The second defines the core of Marx's view of world history, drawing on the Theses on Feuerbach, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto. The third draws out its present-day value for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Wu argues that Kant locates world history in a hidden plan of nature and Hegel in the Absolute Spirit, so that both stand outside history and regard its laws as unknowable or fatalistic, and neither commits to lasting peace. Marx, in Wu's account, reverses this: humans create world history through practice, its laws are knowable as historical materialism, and the world is to be changed, not merely interpreted. World history begins with the "universal intercourse" produced by capital's expansion, and the proletariat, as a "universal class" without particular interests, is its creating subject. Private ownership is identified as the root of conflict, so peace requires its abolition. Wu concludes that three lessons follow today. Peace and development remain the theme of the age, while the Hegelian priority of national interest survives in Western "cold war thinking" and zero-sum logic. Historical nihilism, which Wu calls an expression of the capital-led view of history, must still be fought. A community with a shared future for mankind needs the "common values of all humanity" as its spiritual basis, and Wu presents it as inheriting Marx's call to change the world. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Marx's critique of Kant and Hegel that is tied directly to current Chinese foreign-policy language.

The theoretical implications of the idea of "serving the people" in the new era 新时代“为人民服务”思想的理论意蕴 Feng Gang Feng Gang examines the idea of "serving the people" (wei renmin fuwu) in the new era. The article presents it as the fundamental purpose of the Communist Party of China, a moral demand placed on the people, a proposition within the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, and a body of thought and culture. Feng argues that deepening its theoretical implications is needed to consolidate the Party's governing foundation and to meet the "four tests" and "four risks". The article has three parts. The first identifies the Marxist theoretical core of the idea. The second traces its cultural roots in traditional Chinese culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture. The third shows how the idea is carried forward in governance practice since the 18th Party Congress (2012), in the rule of law, in the building of ethics and cultural-ethical progress, and in Party building. The text draws on classic texts and on Xi Jinping's speeches and Party documents. Feng grounds the idea in three Marxist pillars. The conception of history centred on the masses explains why one serves the people, because they create material and spiritual wealth and drive social change. Marxist views of interest explain how: they respect objective interests and aim at the interests of the great majority. The labour theory of value, read through Marx's account of species-being and alienated labour, explains how it is possible, since everyone is both a subject and an object of such service. On the cultural side, Feng points to the people-as-foundation thought of Confucius, Xunzi and Mencius and to benevolent government, which the idea is said to have dialectically sublated. Revolutionary ideals, the Party's spirit and revolutionary values then shaped it, and advanced socialist culture is said to sustain it through cultural consciousness, confidence and strength. In governance, Feng reads the principle of the people's principal position in comprehensive rule of law and in judicial reform as the idea's contemporary expression. In ethical-cultural progress, it calls for attention to people's real social relations, to their needs given the shift in the principal contradiction, and to their active participation. In Party building, it is embedded in the mass line, in full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and in the "original aspiration and founding mission". Feng concludes that the Party should distil its century of experience, strengthen its sense of purpose, and raise the level of modernising national governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style account links Marxist theory, Confucian people-centred thought and current Party-building language around a single core slogan.

The Communist Party of China's self-reform in the perspective of the Marxist view of revolution 马克思主义革命观视域下中国共产党自我革命研究 Zeng Wei Zeng Wei asks where the Communist Party of China's "self-revolution" (rendered here as the Party's self-reform) comes from in Marxist theory, and why it arises. The article argues that self-reform should be read through the Marxist view of revolution, as a continuing, internally necessary part of the proletarian party's revolutionary practice. On this reading it is not a one-off campaign. Writing in early 2023, Zeng links the idea to the Party's historical experience and to the "two great revolutions" of the new era. The article has three parts. The first defines self-reform within Marx's and Engels's accounts of revolution: dialectical negation of oneself, political revolution and social revolution. The second sets out why self-reform arises, under three headings: the proletariat's historical emergence, the historical mission of its party, and revolutionary strategy. The third turns to practice and gives five requirements for self-reform under the Party. It draws on Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping. Zeng's central move is to separate two tasks of the proletarian party. In political revolution the task is confrontation and destruction, and the proletariat must also shed the "old filth" of the society it grew up in. In social revolution the task shifts to construction, and the party must become both a revolutionary party and a governing party, as Lenin's call for self-education under the New Economic Policy is said to show. Zeng then argues that self-reform is necessary because of the proletariat's class character, because of the party's historical mission, and because it is part of revolutionary strategy, which must raise the party's own consciousness and capacity. On this basis Zeng calls for self-reform that holds to the fundamental direction of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It should grasp the new features of the new era, rely on the people's主体 position, recognise that social revolution is long and arduous, and carry forward a spirit of self-reform. The article presents the Soviet collapse as a case of drift from the socialist direction, and credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party with strengthening the Party's ties to the people. It also calls for combining "breaking" (tackling corruption) with "establishing" (institution-building). Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic grounds the Party's self-reform in classical Marxist theories of revolution.

Opening up a new realm for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Tao Wenzhao This newspaper commentary, published in Economic Daily in February 2023, argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Tao contends that the Party's success and the strengths of socialism with Chinese characteristics ultimately rest on Marxism in this adapted form. In Tao's account, the thought answers major questions of the new era and opens a new realm of that adaptation. The piece is organised around six headings: answering the major questions of the new era; revealing the innovative mechanism of the Two Integrations; its original content; its scientific worldview and methodology; and its guidance of the great changes of the new era. It draws on Marx's remark that true philosophy is the essence of its own age's spirit, and it sets the thought against the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and what Tao calls changes unseen in a century. Tao argues that the thought arose from the practice of the new era and addresses what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics, socialist modernised power and long-governing Marxist party should be built, and how. Combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture is presented as the fundamental path of Marxism's innovative development in China. Tao says the thought, summarised in the “Ten Clarifications”, “Fourteen Commitments” and “Thirteen Areas of Achievement”, has made original contributions to Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. It also embodies a worldview and method: people-centredness, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, problem orientation, systematic thinking and a global outlook. Tao concludes that the great changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012) were achieved under the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and under the guidance of this thought, and that the Two Establishes are the decisive political achievement behind them. In this reading, the changes strengthened the Party, advanced the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and gave Chinese modernization as a new option for other countries. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line in early 2023 presented Xi Jinping Thought as a theoretical innovation within the Sinification of Marxism.

Why high-quality and full employment should be emphasised 为什么要强调高质量充分就业 Zhang Binbin This short newspaper commentary takes up a line from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which calls for strengthening the employment-first policy and promoting high-quality and full employment. Zhang asks what the term means, why it deserves emphasis and how it can be achieved. The answer is that employment of this kind meets the needs of employers and workers alike and supports wider economic upgrading. The article first defines high-quality and full employment through four features, then sets out four policy directions. It is a compact policy explainer rather than a theoretical study, and it closes by calling the task a systematic project. On definition, Zhang describes such employment as meeting enterprises' demand for human resources, as decent work for employees, as supporting a unified, competitive and flexible national labour market, and as promoting technological change and industrial restructuring. Decent work is understood as adequate pay, good working conditions, harmonious labour relations and secured rights. Zhang notes that labour supply has fallen short of demand in recent years and that structural mismatches persist. The four policy directions are keeping the economy within a reasonable range, strengthening firms' capacity to absorb workers, matching workers' skills to market needs, and improving supporting labour-market institutions. Zhang's proposals include relief for firms, a better environment for private enterprise, lifelong vocational training, reform of the household registration and social security systems, and better protection for flexible and platform workers. The author concludes that labour-market institution building and related reforms must go further, with social policy providing a safety net. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line account of how Chinese policy commentary framed employment goals after the 20th Party Congress.

How Chinese modernization resolves the problems of China's modernization, and why it matters 中国式现代化对中国现代化难题的解决及其意义 Wang Yuchen Wang Yuchen asks how Chinese modernization differs from earlier attempts to modernize China, and what it offers the world. The article argues that Chinese modernization is modernization led by the Communist Party, and that it solved four problems that China's modernization faced: forming a political leadership force, combining efficiency with common prosperity, overcoming ecological constraints, and pursuing peaceful development through exchange and mutual learning among civilizations. After defining modernization in broad and narrow senses, Wang classes China's case as "late-developing, externally stimulated" modernization, a challenge-and-response type, in contrast to the "early-developing, endogenous" Western type. Four sections treat the four problems in turn, drawing on the Party's historical record from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. A final section sets out the significance for late-developing countries and for human civilization. On leadership, Wang holds that the late-Qing reform efforts and the 1911 Revolution failed for lack of a mature political leader, whereas the Party's founding mission and its Marxist, people-centred character made it that force. On common prosperity, the article contrasts capitalist modernization, which it says produces polarization and alienation, with the Party's explorations from Mao's socialism through Deng's "some get rich first" approach to Xi's staged targets for 2035 and the middle of the century. On ecology, Wang traces a shift from industrial-era environmental protection to ecological civilization, and presents Xi's "lucid waters and lush mountains" approach, legal institutions and "community of life" ideas as a path distinct from the West. On peace, Wang says Chinese modernization rejects colonial plunder, the "clash of civilizations" thesis (Huntington) and the "end of history" thesis (Fukuyama). Wang concludes that Chinese modernization offers late-developing countries a model of building mature political leadership while developing independently rather than copying others. It also overcomes what Wang calls the one-sided, distorted character of Western modernization, and so creates a new form of human civilization. In this reading it deepens understanding of the laws of human and socialist development and is a new development of contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-line account of how Chinese modernization is positioned against Western modernization and dependency-type development paths.

The spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army: an enduring monument between the White Mountains and Black Waters 东北抗联精神：白山黑水间永立的不朽丰碑 He Weizhi This commentary, published in the Party journal Dangjian in 2023, takes up the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, the Communist-led guerrilla force that fought Japanese occupation in north-east China. He argues that this spirit, forged in blood in the mountains and forests of the north-east, is a lasting part of the Party's spiritual heritage. It remains, in his account, a resource for the Party and the country in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out how the spirit formed and where it stands historically. The second analyses its content under three headings. The third lists its present-day value. He draws on statements by Mao Zedong (1949) and Xi Jinping (2015 and 2016) to support the spirit's standing. In the first part, He identifies four features of the Northeast struggle: it lasted 14 years, it was cut off behind enemy lines without Nationalist aid, its hardship reached the limits of human endurance, and it was marked by setbacks, including the influence of "Left" errors in the Party. He names five conditions behind the spirit: Party leadership, firm ideals and convictions, strong political and ideological work, the example of Communist commanders such as Zhao Shangzhi, Li Zhaolin and Zhao Yiman, and the harsh environment. Its core content, he argues, is loyalty to the Party, the national righteousness of answering the call of national crisis, and a heroic determination to fight to the end. The last includes mountain guerrilla warfare and cooperation with Korean and Soviet anti-Japanese forces, which he calls internationalism. For the present, He calls for five tasks. These are to strengthen Party members' ideals and convictions through regular, institutionalised education, and to promote patriotism in pursuit of the Chinese Dream. He also calls for a fighting spirit to meet the "great struggle" with many new historical features, and for the Party's absolute leadership over the armed forces. Finally he calls for a global outlook that advances a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an example of how Party publications present a regional anti-Japanese war history as part of the Party's spiritual lineage and link it to current political tasks.

The spiritual force for realizing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation: connotation, relationships and paths 实现中华民族伟大复兴的精神力量：内涵、关系与路径 Zhang Zhiyong Zhang Zhiyong takes up a theme highlighted in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): strengthening the "spiritual force" (jingshen liliang) for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that national rejuvenation needs spiritual as well as material strength. It defines this force as the confident, self-reliant, innovative and proactive energy the Chinese people show under Party leadership, and proposes ways to strengthen it. The article opens with a literature review. It covers the Marxist theoretical basis of spiritual force, how scholars explain its content and origins, and the paths they propose for promoting it, such as the great founding spirit of the Party, the spiritual lineage built on it, and core socialist values. Zhang finds the field short on historical-process studies, interdisciplinary work and innovative findings. The body then has three parts: the connotation and distinctive features of this force, four relationships to be handled, and a set of practical paths. On connotation, Zhang draws on Marx to say that spirit is a reflection of social being, and that rejuvenation is a practical and historical undertaking, not a purely spiritual one. Theory guided by Marxism turns into material force when it grips the masses. Zhang identifies three features: autonomous initiative, selection and creativity, and mature self-confidence. The four relationships are material and spiritual needs in a good life, material and spiritual civilization in Chinese modernization, material and spiritual prosperity in common prosperity, and positive and negative mentalities in the pursuit of happiness. Zhang says material gains do not automatically bring spiritual ones, and cites problems such as money worship, "lying flat" (tangping) and "involution" (neijuan). For the paths, Zhang calls for five efforts. The first is to study Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era so as to take spiritual initiative. The second is to teach the Party's centenary achievements and the changes of the past decade, to build confidence. The third is to produce literary and artistic works built around patriotism and core values. The fourth is to promote a fighting spirit. The fifth is to celebrate striving, with officials, model workers and youth as examples. Zhang concludes that a theoretical system of Chinese spiritual force remains an important research task. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-scholar account of how the spiritual dimension of national rejuvenation is conceptualised and how it is to be cultivated in policy.

Scientifically understanding and guarding against ideological risks in the new era 科学认识和防范新时代意识形态风险 Zhang Zhidan Taking up the call in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) to safeguard ideological security and strengthen the capacity to prevent ideological risks, Zhang asks what such risks actually are and how they should be handled. The article argues that ideological risk is above all an endogenous problem: a gap between a ruling ideology and social practice, not mainly the effect of outside influence. Zhang holds that mishandled ideological risk could delay or even interrupt the building of a modern socialist country. The article has three parts. The first defines the essence of ideological risk, drawing on Marx, Sartre and the notion of ideology as the ruling class's systematised thought. The second sets out basic principles for guarding against such risk in the new era. The third proposes four practical paths, quoting Xi Jinping's remarks on risk prevention throughout. Zhang's central move is to define ideological risk as the ruling ideology's inability to answer major problems in practice, which leaves it "floating" and powerless. In this reading, an "internal tension" between theory and practice is a source of renewal if turned into productive "internal tension" (tension as creative force), but it makes a crisis logically inevitable if ignored. The principles that follow are: uphold Marxism's guiding position through four kinds of research (textual, practical, absorptive and anticipatory); use institutional confidence and the mutual shaping of ideology and institutions; and strengthen communication power to win discourse power at home and abroad, with zero tolerance for erroneous trends. The practical paths are responsibility and a sense of duty among those in charge, monitoring and early warning (using a "social combustion theory" and the stages of public-opinion development), scientific and refined governance moving towards intelligent governance, and attention to timing, degree and effect so that small risks do not grow into systemic ones. Zhang concludes that guarding against ideological risk is systematic work. It requires continuous innovation in mainstream ideology, institutional safeguards, effective propaganda and education, and accountable officials. The author presents the Party's ideological innovation since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a successful precedent. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account, written for cadres, of how ideological risk is conceptualised and managed under Xi Jinping.

Model, paradigm, exemplar: the methodological lessons of the third historical resolution for research on the history of New China 范本、范式、范例：第三个历史决议对新中国史研究的方法示范 Zhu Hanguo Zhu Hanguo asks what the third historical resolution, adopted by the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee in November 2021, offers as method for scholars studying the history of the People's Republic. The article contends that the resolution sets a standard for such research in three ways: it supplies a model (the 'grand view of history'), a new paradigm (the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation) and a set of methodological exemplars drawn from the correct view of Party history. The article has three main sections. The first sets out four perspectives on New China's history that follow from the grand view of history. The second reviews the two existing paradigms in the field, a 'national history' paradigm and a 'socialist history' paradigm, citing scholars such as Zhu Jiamu, Cheng Zhongyuan, Li Li'an and Zhang Qihua and works such as the five-volume Draft History of the People's Republic of China. The third draws three methodological lessons from the resolution's correct view of Party history. Zhu argues that the grand view of history places New China within five thousand years of Chinese history, within the century of Party struggle, within the history of the world socialist movement and within contemporary world history. Against the two existing paradigms, Zhu presents the resolution as proposing a 'rejuvenation paradigm' that divides the period into three phases (to the start of reform and opening up, to the 18th Party Congress of 2012, and the new era since then), each laying foundations for national rejuvenation. On method, Zhu calls for viewing history in concrete, objective and connected terms, so that the periods before and after reform and opening up are not set against each other. Zhu also calls for grasping the main theme and main thread, allowing several themes such as rejuvenation and modernization to coexist, and for treating errors in context. The Cultural Revolution is a nationwide error to be fully rejected, but Zhu holds that its period cannot be dismissed wholesale. The first thirty years' achievements are the 'mainstream' and the errors 'tributaries'; Zhu cites Taiwan's high-school textbooks as an example of one-sided negation. Zhu concludes that research on New China's history has moved from its founding through development to maturity, and that the resolution is a classic text on how to understand, analyse and write history. Its historiographical attitudes and methods, in Zhu's view, are an example for deepening the field. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese historian of the Party and the People's Republic translates the 2021 resolution into research method and into positions on the periodisation and evaluation of the pre-reform decades.

Tracing the concept of "the spirit of historical initiative" and the logic of its evolution “历史主动精神”概念溯源及其演进逻辑 Hou Yanshe Lü Mingyang The 2021 Party resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's first century uses the phrase "the spirit of historical initiative" twice, once for the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and once for the Chinese people. Hou and Lü ask where the concept comes from and how it took shape. They argue that its roots lie in Marx's notion of the proletariat's "historical initiative", and that it developed through Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao into a defining trait of the Party under Xi. The article has three main parts. The first traces the idea in Marx and Lenin, including Marx's 1871 letter on the Paris Commune and Lenin's comments on the Russian revolution of 1905. The second sets out the Chinese context, moving from the Chinese people's passage from \"spiritual passivity\" to initiative, through Mao's \"conscious dynamic role\", to the reform era. The third covers the concept's formal establishment and its content since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and ends with proposals for the future. In the authors' reading, Marx and Lenin treat the proletariat's historical initiative as heroism, self-awareness of its mission, revolutionary capacity and creative remaking of society according to objective laws. They contrast this with utopian socialists, who they say treated workers as passive. Lenin's Saturday volunteer labour is presented as an example that moves the concept's focus towards Communists. Mao's \"conscious dynamic role\" is treated as the key link in China: it joins respect for objective laws with the mobilisation of the people and cadres. The authors say Jiang Zemin first formally used the term in 1989, when speaking of the working class. They list six features of the spirit under Xi, including dialectical-materialist method, a people-centred stance, theoretical innovation, Party study campaigns, global strategic vision and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. They condense its meaning into five elements: a scientific spirit that respects laws, a spirit of the people as subject, conscious initiative, foresight and a spirit of responsibility. The authors conclude that the achievements of the decade since 2012 result from this spirit, and that it must be turned from an idea into practice as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation enters a critical stage. They propose five dialectical pairings to guide this: Party leadership and the united front; respect for laws and respect for the people; theoretical and pioneering innovation; assessing the situation and seizing momentum; and the Party's self-reform and social revolution. Read the original if you want a detailed genealogy of this official concept, from Marx's letters to the 2021 resolution, and the Party-theory framing around it.

A historical-materialist interpretation of the Communist Party of China's self-reform 中国共产党自我革命的历史唯物主义阐释 Dai Yuqi Dai Yuqi takes up the Party's self-reform (自我革命, often rendered "self-revolution"), which official discourse presents as a defining trait and advantage of the Communist Party of China. Dai notes that existing scholarship concentrates on its practical significance, value, measures and comparative advantages, and argues that its historical-materialist interpretation is underdeveloped. The article's thesis is that self-reform can be explained through three strands of historical materialism: social epistemology, the mass view of history, and practical dialectics. Dai also contends that ancient ruling classes and Western electoral parties could only adjust themselves, not carry out self-reform, because of their class standpoints and interests. The article has four parts. The first treats the origins of self-reform, the second its value, the third its methodology, and the fourth its prospects. The first part traces self-reform through four periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part draws on Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping on the people's standpoint and the mass line. The third part works through problem- and goal-orientation, and criticism and struggle. The last looks ahead to the Party's second centenary goal. In the first part, Dai argues that social being, in the form of world conditions, national conditions and Party conditions, determines the theme of self-reform in each period, while consciousness actively responds to it. Examples include ideological Party-building in the Yan'an rectification, discipline and style in the 1950s, and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era. The second part holds that self-reform rests on the people's standpoint and the mass line. Dai presents popular supervision as an external constraint and self-reform as an internal one, and says the two are organically united as answers to the question of escaping the historical cycle. The third part sets out the dialectic of problem-orientation and goal-orientation. Dai names self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-enhancement as the Party's capacities, and warns against both a view that self-reform is unnecessary and an excessive one. Looking ahead, Dai calls for perfecting the institutional norms of self-reform, with the Party constitution and democratic centralism at the core, plus high-quality personnel and strict supervision. Dai also urges tackling the \"unique problems of a large party\" raised at the 20th Party Congress (2022), and says the Party should further deepen whole-process people's democracy. Dai suggests this would offer a \"Chinese approach\" and a new model for party politics elsewhere. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style account of self-reform is built from Marxist philosophical categories, with detailed periodisation of the Party's campaigns.

The evolution of the Socialist International's conception of democracy 社会党国际民主观的演进研究 Wang Zhao Wang Zhao asks how the Socialist International (SI) has understood democracy since its refounding in 1951 and what its shifts reveal about world social democracy. The article argues that democracy has been the core of SI theory throughout, and that its conception of democracy has passed through three successive "third ways". The first lay between capitalism and communism, the second between traditional social democracy and neoliberalism, and the third, now emerging, between traditional social democracy and social liberalism. The article is organised chronologically in three parts. The first traces the historical starting point, from the 1848 revolutions and Bernstein's revisionism to the 1951 Frankfurt Declaration, and the later broadening of its "four democracies" (political, economic, social and international). The second covers the post-Cold War period: the shift from "democratic socialism" to "social democracy", the promotion of democracy abroad, the rightward turn of the Blair-style "third way", and a democratic conception of global governance. The third examines the period since the financial crisis, the split of 2013 and the SI's recent adjustments. Wang's central claim is that the SI's democracy has moved along the ideological spectrum from left to centre-left to "centrist", then back left. Before the Cold War ended, the SI treated democracy as a reform tool within capitalist parliamentary systems, while still retaining a European-centred standard. After 1991 it dropped the "socialism" label and converged with bourgeois liberal democracy, which Wang says cost social-democratic parties their distinct identity. After the 2008 crisis, a dispute between a Western European "reformist" camp and a "traditionalist" camp of southern European and developing-world parties over political, social and organisational democracy led to the 2013 founding of the Progressive Alliance. Wang presents this as the ideological cause of the split. Since the split, Wang reports, the SI has shifted left and added "progressivism" to its democratic vision. This takes in political democracy, economic democracy opposed to neoliberalism, a revived welfare state, and democratisation of the UN and of globalisation, with attention to weaker groups and developing countries. Wang judges that this brings no theoretical breakthrough, and that a fourth theoretical transformation of social democracy remains at an exploratory stage. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of Socialist International congress resolutions and declarations as seen from a Chinese contemporary-socialism research perspective.

The civilizational implications of Marx's theory of Eastern society and its contemporary significance 马克思东方社会理论的文明论内涵及其当代启示 Duan Feifei Che Yuling Duan Feifei and Che Yuling ask what Marx's late writings on Russia and the East contribute to thinking about civilization today. They argue that Marx's idea of 'skipping the Caudine Forks' was a civilizational proposal grounded in the particular form of Eastern society, not a universal law of development. In their account, this idea is being continued in practice by Chinese modernization, which they present as a new type of civilization. The article has three sections. The first asks how an Eastern civilization is possible, examining Russia's geography, culture and communal landownership. The second revisits Marx's 1850s–1880s engagement with India and Russia, including his correspondence with Vera Zasulich and the 1877 letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski. The third turns to the present, discussing Western capitalist civilization, Fukuyama and Derrida, and the community with a shared future for mankind. The authors argue that Marx moved from an early Eurocentric view, in which the bourgeoisie subordinates East to West, to treating the East as a coexisting civilization. They locate the key difference in ownership: in their reading, the absence of private landownership is the 'key' to the East, as Engels put it. Marx's view of the Russian village commune shifted from scepticism to conditional affirmation. He saw its dual character, combining communal and private elements, as a source of both vitality and dissolution, and held that it could become a point of social renewal only with a Russian revolution and by absorbing Western material achievements. The authors say Marx explicitly limited the 'historical inevitability' of capitalism's rise to Western Europe. The authors conclude that the Russian attempt was difficult but did not disprove the proposal, and that China is realizing it by developing socialism without repeating capitalism's evils. They describe the community with a shared future for mankind as sublating capitalist civilization through plural civilizations, open cooperation, ecological balance and 'mutual learning' in place of civilizational conflict. They claim the Chinese approach has world-historical significance comparable to English industry, French politics and German philosophy. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical reading of Marx's late Russian texts and of how they are used to ground claims about a new form of human civilization.

Strengthening the spiritual force for realizing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 增强实现中华民族伟大复兴的精神力量 Shen Zhuanghai Shen Zhuanghai takes up a strategic requirement set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022): strengthening the spiritual force needed to realize the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Shen argues that a nation without spirit cannot stand, and that the achievements of Chinese civilisation, of the Party and people over the past century, and of the decade since 2012 all depended on such spirit. On this basis the article holds that the new journey toward a modern socialist country requires an even more buoyant spiritual state. This is a short commentary published in Qiushi in early 2023. It is organised around six conditions, each introduced with the same formula: spiritual force cannot be strengthened without scientific theory, a conscious and firm development strategy, the inheritance and renewal of spiritual traditions, a flourishing culture, advanced institutions, and, finally, concrete practice. Each section ends with what Shen says must be done on the new journey. Shen's central claim is that spiritual force becomes deeper and more lasting only when scientific theory is fused with it. Theory, in this account, gives spirit direction, cohesion, purity and firmness. Marxism, and now Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is to be the guiding ideology that turns conviction into practice. Shen also stresses that spirit and institutions shape each other. The 20th Party Congress report's emphasis on Chinese modernization, on coordinating material and spiritual civilisation, and on a more complete institutional guarantee is read as showing that institutional strength must be converted into governance capacity and into united spiritual force among the people. Shen further calls for passing on traditional Chinese virtues and the Party's spiritual lineage, which begins with the spirit of the founding of the Party. This is to be done through education in Party history and the history of the People's Republic. Shen also calls for building a socialist cultural power under Marxist ideological leadership and the core socialist values. The article ends by arguing that spiritual force becomes real only through practice, and that the new era is both a time of struggle and a time to build a new spiritual highland for the nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party theorists in 2023 linked ideology, culture, tradition and institutions to the national rejuvenation agenda.

Three errors in the theory of "wholesale Westernization" “全盘西化”论的三个错误 Zuo Yuhe Zuo Yuhe takes up the theory of "wholesale Westernization" (quanpan xihua), a cultural current that was influential in modern China, and argues that it is flawed in theory. Zuo holds that although Hu Shi was the first to use the slogan, its genuine advocates were Chen Xujing of Lingnan University and a group of like-minded scholars. The article identifies three core errors. The piece is a short commentary. It first sets out Chen Xujing's position, developed in his 1930 essay and his 1932 book on the future of Chinese culture, then examines the premises on which it rests: the claim that Western culture is superior, the denial that Chinese civilisation can modernise itself, and a doctrine of cultural wholeness and indivisibility. Zuo concedes that the West was more advanced in Chen's time and that the advocates' aims of democracy, science, individual liberation and attacks on feudal hierarchy were progressive. Against them, Zuo argues first that civilisation has both a temporal and a national character, so backwardness in era does not prove national inferiority, and that the fine traditions of Chinese culture can be creatively transformed. Second, civilisation has material, institutional and spiritual levels that are connected but relatively independent, so wholesale acceptance does not follow. Third, the equation of modernization with Westernization is false: Zuo points to new factors in Ming–Qing China and treats Westernization as only one model among several. Zuo concludes that the advocates neglected national character, absolutised the unity of culture and equated Western civilisation with world civilisation, which Zuo calls Eurocentric. Zuo adds that China has opened a distinctive path of Chinese modernization that points to a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese historian's critique of the 1930s Westernization debate, framed in terms of present-day official discourse on modernization.

The historic contributions of the Party Constitution adopted at the Seventh Party Congress 中共七大党章的历史性贡献 Huang Wei This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, asks what the Constitution of the Communist Party of China adopted at the Seventh Party Congress (Yan'an, 23 April to 11 June 1945) contributed to Party history. Huang Wei argues that it was the most complete and detailed Party constitution of the democratic revolution period, a summary of the 17 years of struggle since the Sixth Congress (1928), a mark of the Party's maturity and a milestone in the development of Party constitutions. The article is organised around three contributions. The first is the constitution's statement that Mao Zedong Thought is the Party's guiding ideology. The second is its full presentation of the programme of the New Democratic revolution. The third is its strengthening of the Party's own building, through organisational principles, institutions, work style and discipline. Huang draws heavily on Liu Shaoqi's report on revising the Party constitution (published as "On the Party") and on the constitution's text. On the first point, Huang notes that the general programme defines Mao Zedong Thought as the unity of Marxism-Leninism with the practice of the Chinese revolution and the guide to all of the Party's work, and makes studying it a duty of every member. In Huang's reading, this reflected the Party's ideological and political maturity and led to the first historic leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On the second, Huang stresses that the constitution for the first time placed a general programme before the articles, a practice later followed. It defined the Party's nature, its goal of New Democracy and its final aim of communism, and set out the revolution's character, leading force, tasks and targets. On Party building, Huang cites a 1943 decision on strengthening Party spirit, which criticised members who acted without consulting the centre, as the background. Huang lists a series of "firsts" in the constitution: codified duties and rights of members, the mass line and the aim of serving the people wholeheartedly, criticism and self-criticism, democratic centralism, admission by conduct rather than class origin, the powers of national conferences, and graded disciplinary measures. Huang concludes that these show the constitution's pioneering character and its place linking past and future in Party history. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars present the 1945 Party constitution and its place in Party-building history.

The origins of Marx's concept of exploitation and its contemporary value 马克思剥削概念探源及其当代价值 Emmanuel Renault This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the French philosopher Emmanuel Renault, first published in Actuel Marx. Renault notes that Marx borrowed the concept of exploitation from the Saint-Simonians, and that it is now often dismissed as outdated. Some economists reject the labour theory of value it presupposes. Some philosophers and sociologists see economic reductionism in it, and some empirical researchers hold that today's profit-making no longer matches Marx's analysis. Renault takes the view that capitalist exploitation persists, and he defends the concept while updating its use. The article has four parts. It traces the concept from the Saint-Simonians to the Communist Manifesto, then examines how exploitation is developed in Capital. It then answers three objections, and finally asks how far the concept explains neoliberalism. Renault says that a full test of the neoliberal case lies beyond a single article. Renault argues that Capital turns exploitation into a theory with three strands: an economic theory of the source of profit, a sociology of structural inequality, and a socio-economic account of economic dependence and domination at work. He holds that the labour theory of value remains useful. It separates necessary from surplus labour, and it shows why labour must be commanded and disciplined in a way machines and raw materials need not be. Renault also argues that replacing it with a notion of injustice captures only one of three features of exploitation: the appropriation of surplus labour. It leaves out dependence and domination. Against the Foucauldian charge that Marx neglects micro-power, Renault notes that Foucault himself took Marx's analysis as a methodological model. On neoliberalism, Renault contends that its defining trait is a return to absolute surplus-value production. Evidence offered includes longer hours and working lives, greater work intensity, electronic monitoring, wage cuts, outsourcing, unpaid work and informal employment. Renault cites 'death from overwork' (karoshi) in Japan and South Korea. This return, Renault adds, is combined with the 'real subordination' of labour associated with relative surplus value. Renault concludes that Marx's theory remains valid. It helps to distinguish forms of exploitation under neoliberalism. It also reveals a general logic of capitalist exploitation, which joins capital accumulation to mechanisms that constantly renew the extraction of surplus labour. Even without the value theory, Renault says, the distinction between absolute and relative surplus value still helps identify changes in the logic of accumulation. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist philosopher's defence of the exploitation concept against economic, Foucauldian and justice-based critiques, together with an analysis of neoliberal labour relations.

Comprehensively advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization 以中国式现代化全面推进中华民族伟大复兴 Zhang Airu This article is a study of the 20th Party Congress (2022) thesis that Chinese modernization should be the means of comprehensively advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Zhang argues that this path is rooted in China's own conditions, is shaped by distinctive Chinese features and advantages, and offers a new option for other countries. The text follows Xi Jinping's report to the Congress closely and quotes it often. The article is organised in three parts. The first presents Chinese modernization as the necessary road to national rejuvenation and traces how Party leaders set modernization goals in different periods. The second sets out the features, essential requirements and principles that the report attributes to Chinese modernization, and stresses two defining elements. The third considers its significance for the world and for the Global South. In the first part, Zhang reads Xi's remark that China's modernization is both "the most difficult" and "the greatest" as reflecting a late-developing, populous Eastern country that lost the chance of the Industrial Revolution and had to find its own way. The article lists Mao Zedong's goal of the four modernizations, Deng Xiaoping's use of a moderately prosperous society (xiaokang) to define Chinese-style modernization with a three-step strategy, and Xi's formulation since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part argues that Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics are the two features that matter most in the long run. Zhang presents them as the basis of two achievements, rapid economic growth and long-term social stability, and of the coordinated development of five forms of civilization. In the third part, Zhang says the path rejects modernization through war, colonialism and plunder, and cites Xi's statements that no single modernization model exists and that diverse paths should be respected. Zhang concludes that Chinese modernization has driven national rejuvenation into an irreversible historical process and has brought the goal into the lives of ordinary people. The article presents the path as a "new form of human civilization" that gives developing countries seeking both growth and independence a new choice. It also promises Chinese wisdom, proposals and strength for humanity's shared problems. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned exposition of how Party scholars summarised the 20th Party Congress line on Chinese modernization and national rejuvenation shortly after the Congress.

A critique of the fragmentation syndrome of historical nihilism 历史虚无主义的碎片化症候批判 Li Jinrong Li Jinrong takes up a feature that scholars have noticed in historical nihilism: its fragmentation. The article argues that historical nihilists break up holistic historical thinking into disconnected pieces, in their minute focus, cut-and-paste narration, fragmented communication and splintered value judgements. Li holds that merely describing this negatively is not enough, and that it must be analysed through historical materialism in order to clear away its ideological space and secure ideological security in the new era. The article is organised around four dimensions in which fragmentation operates: historical facts, historical laws, historical narrative and historical action. Each of the first four sections names what is dissolved (certainty of facts, necessity of laws, wholeness of narrative, consciousness of action) and the resulting effect on the public (cognitive confusion, wavering conviction, flippant speech, practical retreat). It draws on Ranke, Collingwood, Becker, Hayden White, Karl Popper, Lyotard and Derrida as Western sources, and on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Lukács as counterweights. A final section sets out four countermeasures. Li's central move is to argue that nihilists exploit relativism and positivism: they treat texts as free interpretation, mistake selected fragments of evidence for facts, and use contingency and individual experience to deny regularity in history. Against this, Li defends the unity of objective and subjective in historical knowledge and the interplay of necessity and chance in historical events. Li also holds that micro-narrative and individual narrative, set against grand and collective narrative, leave history as 'free-flowing grains of sand' with no theme or mainstream. The article treats abstract human-nature theory as a vehicle for this, citing literary works that dwell on desire and portray revolution as mere violence, and online short-video platforms where history is commercialised. Li says these erode shared memory and the Party's sense of historical initiative, while distinguishing them from legitimate micro-history. Li proposes four measures. These are to end fragmented Party-history study in favour of systematic study, to keep historical research holistic under a grand historical outlook, to improve governance of online dissemination, and to build a multi-actor system for resisting historical nihilism. The article closes by calling for the historical initiative of the Party to be exercised in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how current Chinese Marxist scholarship frames historical nihilism as a problem of method, narrative and media, and how it ties that critique to ideological security.

Developments in Western European left-wing social movements amid political upheaval 政治变局下西欧左翼社会运动的发展动向 Wu Huiping Since the turn of the century, left-wing social movements in major Western European countries have gained momentum and, after an initial social impact, quickly turned into new radical left parties. Wu Huiping argues that their political mobilisation and organisation are innovative, and that they are a good case for observing how left-wing currents spread and develop in Europe. The article traces their rise, their shared features, their drivers and their limits. The article first surveys four national cases: La France Insoumise under Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Italy's Five Star Movement, Spain's Podemos, and the much weaker "Aufstehen" (Stand Up) movement in Germany. It then identifies three common traits: digital mobilisation, flat and loose organisation, and a young, cross-class support base. A third section gives four drivers, and a final section sets out the obstacles and likely direction. Wu describes these movements as combining a pluralist programme centred on social justice with an openly left-populist stance that pits "the people" against elites. On the four drivers, Wu cites neoliberal inequality and youth unemployment, the weakening of traditional party systems, the digital revolution, and Europe's overlapping crises. In Wu's account, Italy and Spain succeeded most where those crises hit hardest. Wu argues that the internet allows leaders and even political outsiders to speak directly to the public and to replace hierarchical party machines with parallel, online structures. On this reading, the movements' ability to dismantle the existing order exceeds their ability to build a new one. Wu concludes that the movements' innovations in mobilisation and organisation offer lessons for the modernisation of traditional parties. Wu names two main bottlenecks: a serious lack of governing capacity, illustrated by the Five Star Movement's decline after taking office, and fierce competition from right-wing populists such as the National Rally and the Alternative for Germany. Wu adds that the pandemic, the Russia–Ukraine conflict and the energy and price crisis may open space for further growth. Their future depends on raising governing capacity and offering a more convincing alternative programme. Read the original if you want a concise, China-based account of the new European left, with country data and a view of how Chinese scholars assess it.

Telling good stories to shape an image A century of the Communist Party of China's external publicity work 讲好故事塑形象 Zhai Jiaqi Published in the journal Party Building (Dangjian) in early 2023, this article takes up the Party's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which called for building Chinese discourse and narrative systems, telling China's story well and presenting a credible, lovable and respectable China. Zhai surveys the Communist Party of China's external publicity work (duiwai xuanchuan) over a hundred years. The author argues that the Party has consistently adapted this work to changing international conditions, national circumstances and Party circumstances, and that it has created a favourable international climate of opinion for revolution, construction and reform. The account is chronological and divided into four stages. The first covers the revolutionary years from the early 1920s to 1949, from the Comintern congresses to the Long March, the War of Resistance and the Liberation War. The second covers the early People's Republic under Cold War isolation. The third covers reform and opening up from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the 16th and 17th Party Congresses. The fourth covers the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhai's central claim is that each stage had a distinct task. Before 1949, the Party worked through limited channels and foreign journalists such as Edgar Snow, whose Red Star Over China is cited, to counter Nationalist propaganda and win international support. After 1949, the aim was to break the Western bloc's blockade and replace the image of a semi-colonial country, through foreign-language publications, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and public diplomacy. Under reform and opening up, the Party introduced a spokesperson system and press conferences and answered Western criticism with white papers on human rights and Tibet. Since 2012, the article describes a broader, multi-actor publicity pattern involving the Belt and Road Initiative, cultural exchanges, documentaries and the circulation of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China in 37 language editions. It also describes publicity struggles over trade, Hong Kong, Taiwan and human rights. Zhai concludes that the achievements of this work rest fundamentally on the strong leadership of the Party Central Committee and the guidance of its theory. The author calls for implementing the 20th Party Congress's requirements under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, so as to strengthen international communication, the appeal of Chinese culture and the persuasiveness of Chinese discourse. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed periodisation of the Party's foreign-facing propaganda and the cases it highlights at each stage.

New trends in the development of world socialism amid great changes 大变局下世界社会主义发展新趋势 Chen Mingfan Chen Mingfan asks where the world socialist movement is heading in what the article calls a once-in-a-century transformation of the world. The thesis is that the movement, now emerging from a trough that followed the Soviet and East European upheavals, is gradually moving towards revival. Chen attributes this to two irreversible forces: the decline of capitalism and the development of China under the Communist Party. The article has three parts. The first reviews how socialism rose through successive world upheavals, from the British industrial revolution and the French Revolution to the Paris Commune, the First World War and the October Revolution, the postwar expansion of socialism, and the setback of 1989–91. The second traces the movement's division into currents: communist parties, parties in capitalist and developing countries, democratic socialism, and 'national socialism' in the developing world. The third turns to China's role and the prospects for revival. Chen argues that after Engels's death the movement split into a revolutionary line, scientific socialism, and a reformist line, democratic socialism. The latter, in Chen's account, has in essence abandoned socialism and become reformed capitalism, acting as the 'doctor at the sickbed' of capitalism. Chen presents the Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the movement, with Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the DPRK also holding to the socialist course. Chen then credits Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Chinese modernization, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind with offering models and theoretical tools to socialists abroad, citing favourable comments from foreign communists and commentators. Chen cites Lenin's conditions for a revolutionary situation to caution that the Western crisis alone is not enough. Rulers still control strong state machinery, proletarian parties remain immature and mass discontent has not yet become rational political demand, so the movement faces a long period of tempering. Chen says the Party bears a 'two rejuvenations' task: national rejuvenation and leading socialism's revival. Chen expects China's goal of becoming a leading modern socialist power by mid-century to have an immeasurable effect on the movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the world socialist movement's history and prospects that casts China as its leading force.

Five dimensions of the critique of historical nihilism 历史虚无主义思潮批判的五重论域 Jing Hui Jing Hui takes up historical nihilism, which the article treats as a foreign import and an ongoing threat to China's ideological security. The article argues that it should be criticised systematically from five angles: its existence, essence, harms, duration and methodology. Its stated aim is to clear away the value confusions the trend creates and so strengthen the ideological defences of the Party and the country. The article opens by citing Xi Jinping's calls since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to oppose historical nihilism openly, in the context of the goal of the Two Consolidations. It then proceeds through five sections. The first maps where historical nihilism now appears: academic research, literary and artistic work, and cyberspace. The second identifies its essence. The third sets out its harms. The fourth explains why the struggle against it will be long. The fifth proposes a method of critique. Jing's central claim is that historical nihilism is, at root, a denial of Marxism's guiding role, of the Communist Party's leadership and of the historical necessity of China's path to socialism. The author describes its tactics as selective deconstruction, fragmentation and subjective arrangement of history, and in online settings the use of big data, algorithms and recycled old content. The author holds that it fragments historical understanding, dissolves national spirit and erodes cultural confidence, and points to Xi's remarks on the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Soviet Communist Party. Its persistence is attributed to the coexistence of several forms of ownership, lingering cultural inferiority, anxiety about reform, and what the article calls ideological infiltration by hostile forces at home and abroad. Jing calls for a methodological response grounded in historical materialism, which is meant to expose the idealist basis of historical nihilism. It also calls for class analysis, which is meant to reveal its bourgeois standpoint, and for a rigorous, fact-based approach to historical scholarship. That approach would treat the mainstream and tributaries of history dialectically and refuse to let isolated errors cancel out achievements. The author also urges preparing for a long struggle rather than expecting quick results. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist education journal frames historical nihilism as an ideological-security problem and what counter-method it proposes.

The translation and dissemination of the Communist Manifesto in China 《共产党宣言》在中国的翻译与传播 Li Xinhao Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (22 December 2022 issue dated 29 December), Li Xinhao traces how the Communist Manifesto reached and was rendered in China over roughly 120 years. The article argues that this translation history is also the history of Marxism taking root in China and of the Communist Party's pursuit of truth and its self-reform. It treats the Manifesto's reception as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece is a short historical overview in three parts. The first divides the Chinese versions into three stages: excerpts and quotations (1899–1919), full-text translations (1920–1949) and revised editions (1949 to the present). The second takes the opening sentence about the "spectre" as a case study of translators' deliberations. The third turns to how Chinese scholars have interpreted the text and what the 20th Party Congress (2022) implies for its continued dissemination. Li's central example is the rendering of the German words Gespenst and umgehen. Chinese translators tried many renderings, and Cheng Fangwu revised his several times over decades, from "huge shadow" to "demon shadow" to "demon". The Central Compilation and Translation Bureau fixed "youling" (spectre) and "youdang" (to wander) in 1964 and 1995, checking the German original against other-language versions. Li also reads Marx's choice of the pejorative term as ironic self-description that opens the Manifesto like a theatrical monologue. On interpretation, Li distinguishes three levels: terminological translation studies, annotated readings, and evidential scientific exegesis that links the text to present Chinese practice. Li holds that readings screened by revolutionary and construction experience become part of adapting Marxism to China. Li concludes that Manifesto scholarship now includes histories of its dissemination, discourse and ideas, and treats this as a creative use of the classic. Citing the 20th Party Congress's stress on the Two Integrations and on the Manifesto's own preface, which says application of its principles depends on historical conditions, Li calls for drawing out ideas that were previously neglected but matter for current practice. Read the original if you want a compact account of the Chinese editions of the Manifesto and of how Party-aligned scholarship frames their significance.

The people-centred character of the Communist Manifesto 《共产党宣言》的人民性品格 Shao Xiaoqiu This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) on 29 December 2022, asks in what sense the Communist Manifesto embodies the 'people-centred' (renminxing) character that Shao Xiaoqiu treats as the essential attribute of Marxism. Shao argues that the Manifesto grew out of the practice of the masses and aims at the liberation of humanity, so that it shows this character in an exemplary way. The piece has two main parts. The first traces how the Manifesto arose from the proletariat's struggles and from Marx and Engels's own practice. It also covers the seven prefaces added over later decades. The second part examines the Manifesto's account of the Communist Party's relation to the people and of the stages leading to human emancipation. Shao contends that nineteenth-century workers' uprisings, such as those in Lyon, Silesia and the Chartist movement, all failed and so called for a scientific theory. In Shao's reading, Marx and Engels distilled these experiences, with Engels spending over twenty months among factory workers. The prefaces then adjusted the text to new conditions after the 1848 revolutions, the First International and the Paris Commune. On emancipation, Shao sets out three steps drawn from the Manifesto: establishing proletarian rule, socialist transformation of ownership, and developing production towards communism. Shao stresses that the Party has no interests apart from those of the proletariat as a whole. Shao concludes that the Manifesto's people-centred essence has contemporary value across time. Its insistence on keeping theory abreast of the times reflects the 'people-centred' idea that the Chinese Communist Party has consistently upheld. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary links the Manifesto's prefaces and its idea of emancipation to current Party language about the people.

From digital inequality back to Marx Contemporary foreign Marxist critiques of digital capitalism 从数字不平等到重新回到马克思 Lan Jiang This newspaper commentary by Lan Jiang asks how contemporary Marxist thinkers outside China understand digital capitalism and what remedy they propose. Lan argues that these scholars find digital technology and biopolitics deepening inequality and hollowing out human existence, and that they converge on a return to Marx, above all to the critique of private ownership. The piece opens with Etienne Balibar's 2021 remark that capitalist productive forces have reached a 'totalising stage' touching every individual life, and with Nancy Fraser's 2022 image, in Cannibal Capitalism, of capitalism as a snake devouring its own tail. It then moves through three steps: the widening inequalities of digital capitalism, the 'scorched earth' of life under it, and the call to return to Marx. Thinkers discussed include Habermas, Giddens, Yuval Noah Harari, Guy Standing, Jonathan Crary, Alain Badiou, Fraser and Christian Fuchs. On inequality, Lan contrasts the neoliberal-era faith in dialogue and deliberative democracy (Habermas, Giddens) with the 'digital divide' and with monopoly platforms that control data and algorithms. After the Covid-19 pandemic, Lan says, biological and medical data become objects of capital, so that the wealthy can buy enhanced bodies while a 'useless class' of precarious workers (Standing's precariat) falls behind. Lan reads this as a shift from spatial to biological inequality. Drawing on Crary's Scorched Earth and 24/7: Late Capitalism and the Ends of Sleep, Lan then describes capital's round-the-clock control of bodies and the abstraction of life into screens, user identities and data, which leaves people rootless. As the remedy, Lan presents Badiou's September 2022 argument that the problem lies not in digital technology but in the capitalist, especially financial, monopolisation of data and algorithms, so that the struggle must target ownership. Fraser, in Lan's account, abandons a purely identity-based feminism for Marx's critique of political economy, and Fuchs's book on rereading Marx in the age of digital capitalism calls for ending private property so that all share the benefits of digital and AI technology. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how Balibar, Badiou, Fraser, Crary and Fuchs are being presented to Chinese readers as critics of digital capitalism.

The Marxist outlook of Communists in the new era 新时代共产党人的马克思主义观 Han Meng Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in November 2022, Han Meng takes up a formulation in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that the Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good ultimately because Marxism works, specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Han argues that this sentence condenses the Marxist outlook of Communists in the new era. The short commentary has two parts. The first asks which Marxism is said to "work", drawing on Marx, Engels, Lenin and the history of the Chinese revolution. The second asks how this Marxism should be grasped philosophically, and compares two wordings found in Party documents. Han contends that Marxism is easily mistaken for fixed dogma, a danger that Marx, Engels and Lenin themselves noted. In Han's account, Chinese revolutionary history shows the cost of applying Russian experience as an abstract formula, as in the strategy of armed uprisings in central cities. Success came with the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside, which joined principles to Chinese conditions. Han then distinguishes "adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" (a verb, a process of theoretical integration) from "Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" (an adjective, an intrinsic attribute and the result of that process). Han locates this attribute in Marxism's worldview and methodology, and lists six aspects, including the creative practice of the people, independent exploration, unity of theoretical and historical logic, problem-solving, systematic thinking and a world-historical character. Han concludes that the adaptation of Marxism is a development from theory to practice, from the spontaneous to the conscious, and from the national to the world. Han presents the practical task for Marxists, especially theorists, as laying foundations for the independent development of Chinese modernization and for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the 20th Congress wording on Marxism is interpreted philosophically in Chinese official theory.
