Seizing the historical initiative and answering the questions of history Continuously opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 把握历史主动 回答历史之问 Zhang Lichang Sun Tiantian This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today on 29 December 2022, asks how the Party can seize the historical initiative and answer the questions of history. Zhang and Sun answer that it can do so only under the guidance of Marxism that has been adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They present upholding Marxism's guiding position and opening new horizons for that adaptation as the historic mission of Chinese communists. The piece surveys more than a century of revolution, construction and national rejuvenation. It then turns to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the latest theoretical result of this process, and to the Two Integrations as the method for developing it further. The authors argue that adapting Marxism means combining its basic principles with China's actual conditions, the world's conditions and historical conditions, rather than reciting conclusions or applying them dogmatically. In their account, Xi Jinping Thought gives original answers to the questions of the new era. They name the new historical position of socialism with Chinese characteristics and the redefined principal contradiction in society. That contradiction is between people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, and the authors say it enriches Marxist contradiction theory. They describe the second of the Two Integrations, with fine traditional Chinese culture, as a major theoretical innovation. It requires historical and cultural confidence, and it gives Marxism distinctive Chinese features, style and character. The authors conclude that practice and theoretical innovation have no end. They call on every thinker to take up the theoretical and historical task of opening new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line frames the Two Integrations and Xi Jinping Thought at the end of 2022.

The theoretical foundations of why the sinicised and contemporary Marxism "works" 中国化时代化的马克思主义行的理论根基 Zhang Tao Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2022, Zhang Tao takes up a line from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): that the Party's success and the merits of socialism with Chinese characteristics come down to the fact that Marxism "works", specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The commentary argues that this efficacy rests on two foundations: the Two Integrations and the answers the theory gives to four sets of questions. The piece is short and has two main sections. The first examines the Two Integrations, the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second shows how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era answers what the author calls the questions of China, of the world, of the people and of the times. It opens with a lineage running from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. On the first foundation, Zhang argues that Marxism is to be used as a worldview and method for solving China's problems, not as dogma or a set of phrases to recite. The author cites Marx and Engels as models, since they refused to apply their theory mechanically and kept revising it. On culture, Zhang holds that ideas such as "the world belongs to all" and "the people are the foundation of the state" are highly compatible with scientific socialism's values. On the second foundation, the author says the Thought answers the question of China through Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It answers the question of the world through a community with a shared future for mankind. It answers the question of the people through a people-centred standpoint, and the question of the times by addressing the tasks of the new era. Zhang concludes that upholding Xi Jinping Thought amounts to truly upholding and developing Marxism, and that practice in guiding China and the world will further show that sinicised, contemporary Marxism works. The text is an official-line explanatory commentary rather than a scholarly study. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 20th Party Congress formula that Marxism "works" is explained and justified in Chinese theoretical writing.

Making an original contribution to developing Marxist political economy 为发展马克思主义政治经济学作出原创性贡献 Zhou Wen In this short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 31 January 2023, Zhou Wen asks what Xi Jinping's economic thinking adds to Marxist political economy. Zhou argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) Xi has drawn on China's economic experience to form Xi Jinping's economic thought, which upholds the basic principles and methods of Marxist political economy. In Zhou's account, it makes important original contributions and opens a new horizon for the discipline. The piece is organised under three headings: deepening understanding of the laws of socialist economic construction, answering major questions of China's economic development in the new era, and resolving the relationship between government and market. Under the first heading, Zhou lists three contributions. The first is strengthening the Party's overall leadership of economic work, which Zhou says enriches Marxist theory on the relationship between economics and politics. The second is the people-centred approach and the pursuit of common prosperity, which Zhou says clarifies the purpose of socialist production. The third is a basic economic system combining public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to work and the socialist market economy. Zhou then presents the new development philosophy as a systematic theory that answers questions about the aims, drivers, methods and paths of development. On government and market, Zhou describes Xi's formula of letting the market play the decisive role while the government plays its role better. In Zhou's reading, this goes beyond both Western development models and mainstream Western economics. Zhou concludes that this approach supplies a fundamental guide for building a Chinese system of economic disciplines, scholarship and discourse. Zhou calls for continued research and practice on combining socialism with the market economy, and for better integration of an efficient market with a capable government. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style summary of how Chinese commentary frames Xi's economic thought as a contribution to Marxist political economy.

Theoretical foundations for advancing the new great project of Party building in the new era 新时代深入推进党的建设新的伟大工程的理论依据 Wang Chuanli Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Chuanli asks what theoretical grounds support the Congress report's decision to keep up full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and to push forward the new great project of Party building in the new era. The article argues that these arrangements are not only policy but apply and enrich Marxist doctrine on party building, as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang takes four parts of the report in turn and matches each to a classical Marxist principle. Upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee is tied to Engels's view of authority. Forging minds and souls through Party theory is tied to the theory of inculcation. Stricter discipline and conduct is tied to the vanguard character of the Party. Unceasing self-governance is tied to the theory of permanent revolution. The article draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Xi Jinping, and on episodes from Party history. In the first part, Wang reads Engels's On Authority as showing that more social cooperation requires more authority. Wang argues that China's higher degree of socialisation, with big data and artificial intelligence, makes the case for the Central Committee's authority stronger, and that this is compatible with democratic centralism. In the second, Wang follows Lenin's What Is to Be Done? to hold that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers from outside. By the same logic, Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era could not arise spontaneously from the masses and must be summed up by outstanding leaders, with Xi as its main founder. In the last part, Wang cites the "four tests" and "four risks" and the "four-fold 'until'" and "four-fold 'to'" formulas of Marx and Engels. Wang reasons that, as a disease can recur, corruption and bad work styles can rebound even after the anti-corruption campaign's reported "overwhelming victory". Wang concludes that the Marxist theory of permanent revolution supplies the basis for continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and for using the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. In Wang's account, Party members must therefore keep their revolutionary spirit, purge corrupt elements, overcome privilege and preserve the purity of the proletarian vanguard. Read the original if you want to see how a Tsinghua Marxism scholar ties the 20th Congress's Party-building agenda to Engels, Lenin and the theory of permanent revolution.

Stimulating powerful momentum for high-quality development 激发高质量发展的强大动力 Han Baojiang Published in Guangming Daily on 15 November 2022, shortly after the 20th Party Congress, this commentary asks how the Congress's priority of high-quality development can be achieved. Han argues that it requires applying the new development philosophy fully, accurately and comprehensively, accelerating the new development pattern, and mobilising society as a whole. High-quality development is presented as the essential requirement of Chinese modernization and as the primary task of building a modern socialist country. The piece is organised in three parts, each anchored in the Congress report and in quotations from Xi Jinping. The first sets out what high-quality development means and how the new development philosophy should be built into social reproduction, the new development pattern and the modern economic system. The second, the longest, deals with the new development pattern. The third turns to the social forces needed to carry the effort through. Han's core argument draws on Marxist political economy. Citing the theory of the realisation of the total social product, Han holds that quality ultimately depends on whether goods find buyers, so aggregate demand must validate aggregate supply. After more than 40 years of reform and opening up, the author says, China faces relative oversupply, and this makes expanding domestic demand the strategic basis. Han ties this to supply-side structural reform, with innovation, a strong manufacturing base, "long boards" strengthened and "short boards" repaired in industrial chains, agricultural modernization, and balanced development of finance, property and the real economy. The third lever is reform and opening up, which Han says should remove blockages in the economic cycle through a high-level socialist market economy and high-level opening. Han concludes that the new development pattern can be built only by drawing on the creativity of the people, as historical materialism holds. The author proposes arming officials and the public with Xi Jinping's economic thought, deepening state-owned enterprise reform, protecting private and foreign-invested firms, and building a capable cadre corps with accountability and error-tolerance mechanisms. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how a prominent Party School economist links the 20th Congress economic goals to Marxist circulation and realisation theory.

The value orientation and generative logic of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的价值旨归和生成逻辑 Zhao Chaofeng Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhao Chaofeng asks what Chinese modernization is for and how it came about. The article argues that Chinese modernization is the necessary path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, that it was created through the Party-led socialist practice of the People's Republic, and that it fits Chinese realities while also embodying scientific laws. The 20th Congress slogan of comprehensively advancing national rejuvenation through Chinese modernization, Zhao says, gives modernization a clearer value orientation. The article has three parts. The first treats modernization as the fundamental route to rejuvenation and as the shaper of a new form of human civilization. The second traces the historical formation of the path: the New Democratic Revolution, industrialization under the Five-Year Plans, the Four Modernizations, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third explains why the path suits China's conditions and reflects three sets of laws. Zhao draws on Marx, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Party congress documents from the 13th (1987) to the 20th. Zhao's central move is to identify modernization with rejuvenation in both logic and timing. Both goals, the article says, were placed in the same period by the theory of the primary stage of socialism and the later two-centenary targets, so rejuvenation is the arrival of a modern socialist country that leads its age and is not a return to the past. Zhao then equates socialism with Chinese characteristics with the Chinese modernization path, as two expressions of one thing. Modernization fits Chinese conditions through staged strategies and a 'parallel' catch-up model that combines industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization. It embodies socialist laws through Party leadership, the liberation and development of the productive forces, and common prosperity. It also embodies general laws of social development: the movement of contradictions, human liberation and all-round development, and a rejection of the Western capital-centred route and of Western-centrism. Zhao concludes that Chinese modernization has taken China from 'catching up with the times' to 'leading the times', and that it will continue after the building of a modern socialist country, lifting the primary stage of socialism to a higher level. The path is said to have created a new form of human civilization, to give the Party a concrete route towards the Second Centenary Goal, and to offer developing countries a Chinese option. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Chinese modernization is tied to rejuvenation, socialism with Chinese characteristics and the primary stage of socialism, with references to Party congress documents.

Marx's theory of "world history" and the international workers' movement 马克思的“世界历史”理论与国际工人运动 Liu Enzhi Liu Enzhi asks how Marx's concept of "world history" differs from the idealist versions in German classical philosophy, and what it implies for proletarian politics. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2022, argues that Marx grounded world history in the real economic relations of capitalism. On this basis he drew a practical programme, world revolution, and a conception of peace opposed to Kant's. The piece opens by contrasting Marx with Kant and Hegel. Kant's "perpetual peace" and Hegel's absolute spirit as ruler of world history are treated as speculative constructions with no historical reality. Two sections follow. The first, on how world history is presented, deals with the world market and world revolution. The second, on world history and proletarian emancipation, compares Kant's and Marx's routes to peace and ends with the First International. In Liu's reading, Marx treats the world market opened by the bourgeoisie as the material carrier of world history. Capital globalises its own contradictions, so world revolution is both possible and necessary. It is possible because crises spread everywhere and because Eastern countries are drawn into the market. It is necessary because an isolated crisis can be exported through war or colonial expansion, and because local communism would be swallowed by expanding capitalism. Liu then argues that Kant's perpetual peace is a transcendental, abstract imperative, and that his league of states would remain bourgeois. Marx instead sought elements of peace within objective conditions. For Marx, lasting peace rests on the revolutionary union of the proletariat, which abolishes bourgeois states, classes and war together. Liu concludes that world revolution is the concrete practical form of Marx's concept of world history, aiming at abolishing bourgeois rule globally. The First International is presented as Marx's key attempt to unite workers across countries, with Marx as its guiding figure. According to Liu, it fostered the international workers' and world socialist movements that pressed on bourgeois rule and shaped world history. Read the original if you want a short, source-based account of how Chinese Marxist scholarship distinguishes Marx's world history from German idealism and links it to internationalism.

The historical significance of Engels's "Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy" 《国民经济学批判大纲》的历史意义 Sun Lin This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2022, asks what Engels achieved in his 1844 Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy. Sun argues that Engels did more than expose the alienation of economic categories. In Sun's reading, he found a logical starting point that undoes the mystical system of Hegel's speculative philosophy, moving from an undetermined immediacy to the reality of concrete human beings, and so laid a foundation for the materialist conception of history. The article has two main parts after a discussion of the logical beginning of the text: Engels's critique of capitalist production, and his critique of the essence of capitalist private ownership. Sun draws on Engels's passages on factors of production, capital as accumulated labour, price and value, overproduction and crisis, and the concentration of property. Feuerbach's influence is traced through Engels's remarks in the Outlines and in The Holy Family. Sun's central claim is that Engels, like Feuerbach, inverted Hegel's logic and replaced it with a starting point of the sensuous and objective ("感性—对象性"). On this basis, Sun says, Engels could enter bourgeois society and analyse the alienated realities of private ownership. Sun credits Engels with identifying nature and humans as the two factors of production, treating capital as accumulated labour, finding hidden theft in the price-value gap, and tracing crises to overproduction. For Sun, private ownership is the source of exploitation and class polarisation, since living labour is ruled by dead capital. Sun concludes that Engels held that the evils of private ownership can be removed only by abolishing it, and that he pointed to public ownership as the future direction of social development. Read the original if you want a brief, Chinese-language account of how the Outlines is read as a bridge between Feuerbach's critique of Hegel and the materialist conception of history.

The decline of Western European parties and the rise of populism 西欧政党衰败与民粹主义的崛起 Zeng Sen Why have populist parties surged in Western Europe in recent years? In this short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, Zeng Sen argues that the decay of mainstream parties is the basic precondition for that rise. Since the 1970s, the author notes, Western European countries have entered post-industrial society, with major shifts in class structure and values, and parties have declined over the long term as a result. The article is organised around three aspects of this decline, which Zeng presents as the political setting for populism: the weakening of party organisation, the ideological convergence of mainstream parties, and growing electoral volatility. It draws mainly on Britain, France and Denmark, and on the scholarship of Richard Katz and Peter Mair, Robert Putnam, Arend Lijphart, Francis Fukuyama and others cited in passing. On organisation, Zeng reports that membership of the main Western European parties fell by almost half between 1980 and 2008, that activism and party identification weakened, and that parties became 'cartels' reliant on state resources, which cut their ties with voters and produced a crisis of representation. On convergence, the author argues that the centrist 'Third Way' consensus politics left left and right parties alike embracing European integration, globalisation and immigration. This is said to have neglected the grievances of blue-collar workers and allowed populists to claim to be the only true voice of the people, especially in consensus-style systems. On volatility, Zeng argues that the postwar 'frozen' party system has thawed. The article cites a fall in the average mainstream vote to 72% in 2015 and the exit of both main French parties in the first round of the 2017 presidential election. Zeng singles out centre-left parties, which in the author's account turned from economic equality to the identity politics of marginal groups and lost working-class voters to right-wing populists. The article concludes that populist parties have partly reshaped Western Europe's political map, and says it is still an open question whether they act as a corrective or a threat. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of party-system explanations for European populism and of how it is framed for Chinese readers.

New developments in contemporary ecological Marxism 当代生态马克思主义研究新进展 Lin Zhaoxia This short review in a Chinese social-science newspaper surveys how ecological Marxism has developed since the start of the twenty-first century. Lin Zhaoxia presents it as one of the most influential current schools of thought, arising from the worsening ecological crisis and from Marxism's practical mission. The review's central claim is that these scholars treat the ecological crisis as in essence a crisis of the social system, to be resolved only through a thoroughgoing critique and transcendence of capitalism. Lin reviews work by André Gorz, John Bellamy Foster, Grundmann, James O'Connor, Paul Burkett, Joel Kovel, Saito Kohei and others on the causes, forms, critical dimensions and ways beyond ecological crisis. The text is organised in four sections: capital accumulation as the direct cause of crisis; the rift in metabolism as its form of appearance; the critical dimensions of ecological Marxism; and a renewed construction of historical materialism. A short conclusion places the school in the history of Marxist research since the 1960s. On causes, Lin reports that capital's endless accumulation demands raw materials and energy. O'Connor's 'second contradiction' sets capitalism's unlimited production against the limited conditions of production, while Foster describes accumulation as producing a rift in the metabolism between society and nature. On forms, the review describes three features: the contradiction between use-value and exchange-value, alienated consumption and commodity fetishism, and the estrangement of people from nature. On critique, Gorz is said to seek a 'paradigm shift' that frees use-value from exchange-value, and Kovel to locate the crisis in social relations and to stress restoring producers' control over production. Foster, Peter Dickens-type thinkers such as Pepper, and Grundmann are said to argue that historical materialism has an ecological dimension, which Saito systematically reconstructs as continuous with Marx's critique of political economy. Lin concludes that ecological Marxism is both a value orientation for social development and a critical theory of capitalism's internal contradictions. The review adds that these scholars treat ecological problems as common to all human society, and cites the Russian scholar Shevchenko's remark that capitalism's development model is 'a dead end'. In this account the ecological crisis can be overcome only by a complete critique and transcendence of capital and capitalist society. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of how ecological Marxist thinkers are presented to a Chinese readership.

Viewing the new thought of the new era from a historical perspective 从历史角度看新时代的新思想 Zhou Liangshu Following the 20th Party Congress (2022), which declared that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era marks a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, Zhou Liangshu asks how the new thought should be understood. The author argues that it must be placed inside the Party's own history, as a relationship of adherence and development, inheritance and innovation. Zhou takes this reading from Xi's own remarks that socialism with Chinese characteristics is a "big essay" which each generation of leaders continues to write. The article proceeds chronologically through four stages. It begins with Mao Zedong's founding of China's socialist cause, then turns to Deng Xiaoping and the 1981 Resolution on Party history as the basis for continuity and development. It then covers the exploration of a new path under reform and opening up, and finally the contributions of Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. At each stage Zhou draws on speeches and Party documents. Zhou's first move is to trace methods of thought across generations. Mao's 1956 "Ten Relationships" and his 1957 analysis of contradictions among the people are said to survive in Jiang's twelve relationships, Hu's Scientific Outlook on Development, Xi's call for a systems approach, and the identification of the principal social contradiction. The second move concerns Deng. The article describes his handling of Mao's legacy as evaluating a figure through the whole of history rather than a fragment of it, and presents "socialism with Chinese characteristics" as a unity of inheritance and development. Zhou also rejects both a return to a "closed and rigid" old road and a "wrong road" of abandoning socialism, and links Deng's combative style and leadership method to Xi's "great struggle" and emphasis on the "key minority". Zhou concludes that the Three Represents, a harmonious society and the Scientific Outlook on Development each answered problems that history had made ripe for solution, and warns against judging predecessors with hindsight. The article credits the new era with three achievements: Xi's thought, the Party's self-reform as a second answer to the historical cycle of rise and fall, and the launch of a new journey toward a modern socialist country. Zhou presents these as continuous with earlier generations' work. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how Chinese scholars link Xi's thought to Mao, Deng, Jiang and Hu.

Understanding and grasping the historical responsibility of opening up new realms of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 深刻认识和把握开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界的历史责任 Huang Yibing Writing in Guangming Daily on 16 November 2022, shortly after the 20th Party Congress, Huang Yibing argues that writing new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is the solemn historical responsibility of today's Chinese communists. The commentary reads the Congress as a summing-up of the Party's experience with Marxism, an elaboration of the Two Integrations, and a call for theoretical innovation grounded in practice. Huang's thesis is that this work depends on a scientific attitude toward Marxism, on the Two Integrations, and on the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece has four numbered sections. The first treats the Party's attitude to Marxism. The second presents the Two Integrations as a major original contribution of Xi Jinping Thought. The third explains the "six commitments" that the Congress report used to summarise that Thought's worldview and methodology. The fourth turns these into requirements for future theoretical work. On attitude, Huang holds that the Party's century of achievement rests on upholding Marxist fundamentals and seeking truth from facts. In this account Marxism is an open system, so the Party opposes both dogmatism and pragmatism. Huang notes that Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping each stressed development, and that today's China has outrun what the classical authors could imagine. On the Two Integrations, Huang says Marxism must be combined with China's concrete realities, to solve Chinese problems rather than recite conclusions, and with fine traditional Chinese culture, which is said to be highly compatible with scientific socialism. This second integration is credited with turning "Marxism in China" into "Chinese Marxism". The six commitments are: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systemic thinking, and a global vision. Huang concludes that the six commitments are a "golden key" and a "bridge and boat" for further theoretical innovation, and sets out what each requires. These include firm adherence to Marxist fundamentals, the Party's overall leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, attention to new problems, and learning from other civilisations. Practice has no end, Huang says, so adapting Marxism has none either, and continuing the Two Integrations will open new realms. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned reading of how the 20th Party Congress framed theoretical innovation and the Two Integrations.

Three dimensions for a scientific grasp of the "Two Integrations" 科学把握“两个结合”的三个维度 Sun Laibin Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this Guangming Daily commentary asks how the "Two Integrations" should be understood. Sun Laibin argues that the report presents them as the inner mechanism by which Marxism keeps developing. In Sun's reading, they can be grasped along three dimensions: why they are necessary, why they are possible, and how they are to be advanced. The article first reviews the historical record of combining Marxism with Chinese realities, from early Party mistakes to the Sinicization of Marxism under Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping. It then turns to the relationship between Marxism and traditional culture, drawing on Engels and on Lenin's critique of Bogdanov. It ends with practical routes for carrying the Integrations forward. On necessity, Sun contends that Marxism can guide practice only if it is joined to China's specific conditions. Sun cites the early Party's mechanical borrowing of Soviet experience as a costly lesson. Marxism can flourish only if rooted in the nation's own historical culture. On possibility, Sun argues that Marxist principles are universal, having grown from the sum of world revolutionary experience. Sun also claims that excellent traditional culture closely matches scientific socialism's values, and lists four areas of fit: cosmology (the unity of heaven and humanity), the vision of "all under heaven" and a world of great harmony, social harmony amid difference, and ethics. The Party's "historical initiative" is the third ground. Sun holds that the Party has repeatedly taken the initiative in advancing the Integrations. On the path forward, Sun calls for two things. The first is to integrate Marxism with present-day realities by identifying the basic national conditions and by being problem-oriented. The second is to let Marxism and traditional culture interact. Marxism should guide and revitalise the culture, for instance by reading "unity of heaven and humanity" as harmony between people and nature. In turn, the culture should enrich Marxism with ideas and terms such as "seeking truth from facts" and "a moderately prosperous society". Sun stresses that the Integrations do not happen automatically. They require centralised Party leadership and a sense of responsibility among scholars and the public. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the Two Integrations were explained after the 20th Party Congress, including its examples of cultural parallels with Marxism.

Upholding the fundamental requirement of putting the people first 坚持人民至上的根本要求 Han Zhenfeng This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 14 November 2022, takes up the principle of "putting the people first" (renmin zhishang), which the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) lists as part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Han argues that it is a fundamental requirement of the Marxist materialist conception of history and a key lesson of the Party's century of struggle. The piece is short and organised as a sequence of six requirements, each introduced by a classical Chinese maxim and supported by quotations from Xi Jinping, and in one case Mao Zedong. It opens by defining "the people" as a historical and political category whose core is the working masses who produce material goods. Han's six requirements are: take a firm people's standpoint; give priority to the people's interests; improve the people's wellbeing; respect the people's creativity; draw on the people's wisdom; and ensure that the people share in development. The author links these to the mass line, to the principal contradiction in Chinese society, defined as that between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, and to the claim that the people are the creators of history. Reform and development are said to be judged finally by whether the people share in their results. Han concludes that, on the new journey towards the second centenary goal, Party members and cadres should treat the fundamental interests of the great majority as the starting and end point of all work. Whether the people support, approve, are happy with and agree to a policy is presented as the basic test of success. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-line commentary links people-centred development to Marxist historical materialism.

Building a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power 建设具有强大凝聚力和引领力的社会主义意识形态 Lin Yangzhi Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary in Guangming Daily asks how to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. Lin argues that ideological work is the work of giving the country and the nation their "heart" and "soul", and that it decides their survival, prospects and fate. The author's answer is that Marxism's guiding position must be upheld and the Party's leadership over ideological work firmly held. The piece is organised in four numbered sections. It first explains why ideological work matters, then turns to the Party's leadership over it. It next sets out how to consolidate mainstream thought and public opinion, and ends with governance of the internet. Almost all of its authority comes from extended quotations of Xi Jinping. Lin's core argument runs as follows. Ideological work is paired with economic work as mutually supporting, and the author presents a world of sharper ideological struggle, in which hostile forces are said to seek "colour revolutions" and to subvert Party leadership. Control of positions (zhendi) is therefore the key: Lin says the Party must hold the leadership, management and discourse power over ideology and defend its positions actively. Mainstream opinion is to be strengthened in four ways: arming the Party and people with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, practising core socialist values, developing a Marxist-guided philosophy and social science "with Chinese characteristics", and building an integrated all-media communication system under the principle that the Party manages the media. The internet is described as the main battlefield of ideological struggle. Lin calls for a comprehensive online governance system and rule-of-law management of cyberspace. Lin concludes that a strong socialist ideology will unite the whole people in ideals, values and morality. In the author's account, that unity will generate the force needed to advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Cadres at all levels are urged to strengthen their ability to manage and use the internet. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official Party line on ideological work after the 20th Party Congress, including how it frames ideological security, media and the internet.

The Second Party Congress and the Party's mass work 中共二大与党的群众工作 Li Chuanbing Marking the 100th anniversary of the Second National Congress of the Communist Party of China (1922), this newspaper commentary asks what the congress contributed to the Party's mass work (qunzhong gongzuo). Li Chuanbing argues that the congress made a pioneering exploration of how to work among the masses, and that revisiting it helps summarise historical experience and grasp the characteristics and rules of mass work. Li ties this to the people-centred approach to development in the new era. The article opens with the Resolution on the Party's century of struggle adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). It then has two main sections. The first covers how the Second Congress deepened theoretical understanding of the importance of mass work. The second covers the policies it set. A closing section assesses the historical contribution of these ideas. In Li's account, the congress's resolution on Party organisation defined the Party as a large "mass party" and a vanguard that must not become a "minority of communists" cut off from the masses. Li holds that the congress also analysed Chinese social classes in a scientific and realistic way. It affirmed the leading role of the workers, treated the peasantry as the largest element of the revolution, saw the bourgeoisie as having a revolutionary side while noting its tendency to compromise, and counted handicraftsmen and small shopkeepers as participants. On this basis it proposed a democratic united front and measures on Party discipline, trade unions and youth work. Li stresses that the proletariat's temporary alliance with democrats was not surrender to the bourgeoisie. Li concludes that these ideas guided the mobilisation of workers, students and youth after the congress and helped bring about the first high tide of the revolution. They are also presented as a theoretical precedent for the Party's mass line and for the united front, later named one of the Party's "three magic weapons". Read the original if you want a short, official-style account of how Party historiography now links the 1922 congress to the mass line and united front doctrine.

Persistently and thoroughly advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 持之以恒深入推进全面从严治党 Li Lifeng Published in Guangming Daily on 15 September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes its starting point from Xi Jinping's remarks to a seminar of provincial and ministerial leaders. Li Lifeng argues that the Party, as the world's largest Marxist governing party, can consolidate its long-term rule only by pursuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party without letup. The article presents this as the means by which the Party's self-reform can lead social revolution. The piece has three parts. The first presents full and rigorous self-governance as a great practice of self-reform in the new era. The second explains why the effort is "always on the road". The third sets out concrete directions for opening up a new realm of self-reform. Li's central reasoning is that self-governance serves the Party's founding mission and its great struggle, cause, project and dream. The article names the "four tests" and "four dangers" as long-lasting, and treats the Party's willingness to correct its own errors as the reason it has endured. It points to global turbulence and to the pressures of national rejuvenation, and it says that impurities in political stance, thinking, organisation and conduct remain unresolved. Quoting Xi, it holds that the struggle against corruption is still fierce and that the Party can ensure it never degenerates only by sustained effort. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article says, this effort has ended lax governance and found a way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Li proposes six lines of action. They are: political development as the guiding principle, including the Two Upholds and the Two Establishes; ideological development through study of Marxism and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; stricter discipline and conduct, including the eight-point regulations; a sustained, zero-tolerance anti-corruption campaign targeting both "tigers" and "flies"; stronger Party organisations and a cadre corps willing to struggle; and a system of Party regulations and supervision. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official press framed self-governance and anti-corruption on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

Guidance by Marxist scientific theory as the Communist Party of China's distinctive political character and strong political advantage 马克思主义科学理论指导是中国共产党的鲜明政治品格和强大政治优势 Ruan Huarong Chen Shuguang This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 19 September 2022, ahead of the 20th Party Congress, takes up Xi Jinping's statement that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Party's distinctive political character and strong political advantage. Ruan and Chen argue that, in the end, the reasons the Communist Party of China "can do it" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good" come down to the fact that Marxism "works". The piece has three sections. The first presents Marxism as the choice of history and of the Chinese people since the Opium War of 1840. The second runs through four historical periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third looks ahead to the continuing task of developing Marxism in China. In the first section the authors say that capitalism, reformism, liberalism, social Darwinism, anarchism, pragmatism and other currents were each tried and failed to resolve China's fate. The Chinese people therefore chose Marxism and the Party formed from its union with the workers' movement. The relationship is described as reciprocal: the Party did not fail Marxism, because it has defended, upheld and developed it through successive theoretical achievements, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Marxism did not fail the Party, because the Party grew from weak to strong under its guidance. The authors write that the Party was founded, flourished and grew strong through Marxism. For each period they pair a theoretical innovation with a historic leap: "standing up", "becoming prosperous" and "becoming strong". The authors conclude that Marxism is not dogma but a guide to action, which must be adapted to China and to the times (adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times) in order to take root. They hold that this adaptation is far from finished, since contemporary change exceeds what the classical authors could imagine and China is still in the primary stage of socialism. The Party's theoretical mission is to keep combining Marxist principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, opening up new horizons for twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars framed Marxism's role in the Party's legitimacy on the eve of the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Achievements and experience of the Communist Party of China in pioneering innovation during a century of struggle 中国共产党在百年奋斗中坚持开拓创新的成就和经验 Cheng Enfu Sun Shaoyong Taking its cue from the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over a century, this article asks how the Communist Party of China has sustained innovation in its hundred years of struggle. Cheng Enfu and Sun Shaoyong argue that the Party's history is a continuous process of innovation, and that this has been a fundamental reason for its successes. They summarise achievements and lessons in four fields: theory, practice, institutions and culture. The article opens with the revolutionary heroism and optimism of the New Democratic Revolution, which the authors present as a spiritual precondition of victory. It then takes each of the four fields in turn. For each, it sketches the historical record from Mao Zedong through reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), and then lists several lessons. The institutional section also reviews the framework set out by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). On theory, the authors credit the Party with adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. They name three lessons: proceed from national conditions and combine Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture; be problem-oriented; and keep thought liberated while opposing opportunism and dogmatism. On practice, they stress strengthening Party leadership, putting the people at the centre, and holding to a scientific worldview. On institutions, they call for fidelity to objective laws, integration with national governance, and firm enforcement, including keeping power and capital 'in the cage of institutions' and opposing private capital monopoly and disorderly expansion. On culture, they stress the dialectic of economic base and superstructure, the policy of letting a hundred flowers bloom, and reliance on the people. The authors conclude that innovation in all four fields has given the Party a body of experience that underpins the building of a modern socialist country and national rejuvenation. They present these lessons as a guide for deepening understanding of the laws of Communist Party rule, socialist construction and social development. They also call for cultural works to avoid pursuing ratings, box office or circulation alone, and to follow socialist core values. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how Chinese scholars summarise the Party's innovation record across theory, practice, institutions and culture.

Raising traditional Chinese medicine to a level that contributes to the whole world Mao Zedong's role in reviving traditional Chinese medicine in the early People's Republic 把中医提到对全世界有贡献的高度 Han Honghong Han Honghong asks how Mao Zedong shaped the revival of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) after 1949. Writing in 2014, Han draws on the six-volume Chronology of Mao Zedong (1949–1976), published in December 2013, which for the first time disclosed several of his remarks on the subject. The article argues that Mao treated TCM as a cultural heritage to be critically inherited, unified with Western medicine and raised to the point of contributing to the world. The article is organised in five parts. It begins with Mao's assessment of TCM's historical and practical value between 1949 and 1958, including his edits to a 1954 Central Committee directive. It then examines his campaign against contempt for TCM, his principle of combining Chinese and Western medicine, and the movement for mutual learning between the two. A final section draws three lessons for present-day TCM policy. Han's central claim is that Mao combined respect for TCM with a demand that it be scientifically examined. Han reports that Mao described TCM as a product of agrarian and handicraft society, to be accepted critically, keeping what is rational and discarding the dross. Mao denounced disdain for TCM as a servile, pro-foreign attitude and blamed sectarianism among Western-trained doctors. Han shows how Mao's position developed into the principle of integrating traditional Chinese and Western medicine, with Western-trained doctors learning TCM and TCM practitioners learning modern science, aiming at a unified new Chinese medicine. Han cites concrete measures: the 1955 Central Committee approval of a report on improving TCM work, and the training courses that released Western-trained doctors to study TCM. According to the article, about 36,000 such doctors were studying TCM by 1960. Han draws three lessons. TCM development should rest on national conditions and balance inheritance with innovation, in line with Xi Jinping's call for creative transformation and innovative development of traditional culture. Integration of Chinese and Western medicine should be maintained as mutually complementary, which the article says has influenced the rise of integrative medicine worldwide. TCM should also follow a healthy and sustainable path, supported by talent, industry and overseas outreach. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's account of Mao's recorded remarks on TCM and of how they are used to frame current policy.

The internal mechanism and implementation path of state-owned enterprises in promoting common prosperity 国有企业促进共同富裕的内在机理及其实现路径 Di Minxue Di Minxue asks how common prosperity can be advanced in practice and why state-owned enterprises should take the lead. The article argues that the main obstacle is distribution, that distribution is at root a question of ownership, and that state-owned enterprises, because of their ownership character and strength, should act as pilots by raising workers' pay. The text has three parts. The first sets out the problems facing common prosperity and the theoretical analysis behind them, drawing on Marx, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and the economist Liu Guoguang. The second explains the mechanism by which state-owned enterprises contribute. The third proposes a micro-level pilot scheme with four steps: creating a favourable environment, enterprise applications, approval and supervision, and guiding policies. Di frames the issue as "making the cake" and "dividing the cake", and holds that after four decades of rapid growth, division is the main problem. The article cites a Gini coefficient of 0.465 in 2019 and an urban–rural income ratio of nearly 2.6 in 2020. Following Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, Di maintains that production conditions determine consumption distribution, so widening gaps reflect the shift from public to private ownership and the growth of private employment, and that public ownership must stay dominant. State-owned enterprises are said to be specially suited because they are owned by the whole people and under Party leadership, and because they are strong in technology and capital. Di credits them with supplying cultural products, paying higher wages than private firms (using wage tables for 2011–2020), remitting profits for transfer payments, investing in the western regions and Xinjiang, and serving as a "universal light" that steadies markets and strengthens private-sector wage bargaining. Di proposes that the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission set up a working group on raising labour remuneration. It would select pilot firms that are large, technology-based, and have good labour relations. These firms would put into practice the shared development philosophy through joint consultation, joint construction of mechanisms, joint creation of benefits and shared results. Incentives would include honours, priority in national projects and legislation treating wage increases as profit remitted to the state, preferably at a lower credited rate. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-economics case for assigning state firms the lead in common prosperity, including a concrete institutional design.

Belt and Road research seen through the global value chain of ideas 从全球思想价值链角度看“一带一路”研究情况 Wang Wen Wang Wen gives this keynote speech at a Zhejiang seminar on area studies and the Belt and Road Initiative, held with the opening ceremony of Zhejiang Normal University's African area-studies institute. He argues that the Initiative is reshaping the global value chain of ideas, and that research on it has cooled at home while being distorted abroad. The speech first sets out the decline in publication, then explains why research has cooled, and ends with proposals for rebuilding the chain of ideas and organising future work. Wang also lists gaps the Initiative fills in global public goods, trust, governance and multilateralism. Wang cites falling numbers: Chinese-language journal articles peaked at over 30,000 in 2017 and fell by 2021 to a third of that, and books fell to 447 in 2021. Foreign-language books fell from 37 in 2019 to 3 in 2021. Meanwhile, according to Wang, over 1,400 international think tanks issued 674 reports in the first nine months of 2021, twice the previous year's figure, mostly negative, citing debt traps, opacity and vaccine diplomacy. Wang attributes the domestic cooling partly to a clearing-out of superficial, trend-chasing work, and partly to a lack of new topics and an underestimate of how long and contested the Initiative will be. In Wang's view, it faces a short-term contest over public opinion and a long-term contest over quality. Wang calls for firm rebuttal of what are described as US distortions, and for more in-depth, innovative work by Chinese think tanks and scholars. Proposals include a dedicated research fund, a transnational research association, and combining strategic firmness with tactical flexibility. Read the original if you want a Chinese think-tank leader's account of how the Initiative's research and international image are framed as a contest of ideas.

Opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 开辟马克思主义中国化时代化新境界 Guo Jianning Wei Yueyan Guo Jianning and Wei Yueyan take up a central theme of the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): opening up new horizons for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Writing in early 2023, they argue that this task is the theme, general outline and guiding thread of the Party's theoretical innovation in the new era, and that it expresses a high degree of theoretical consciousness. In their account, theoretical innovation, like practice, has no end point. The article is organised in four parts. It sets out the theoretical form of the new horizon, centred on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then examines the practical achievements, above all Chinese modernization and a "new form of human civilization". Next it discusses the cultural foundations, and finally the features of the era that shape the theory. The authors' core claim is that the Party's strength rests on Marxism that has been adapted to China and the times. They present the Two Integrations (of Marxist principles with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture) and the "six persistences" as the essence of the Thought. They see Chinese modernization as the main practical result: they describe its five distinctive features, nine essential requirements and five major principles, and argue that it is not a copy of foreign models. They contrast it with a Western modernization that, in their characterisation, is capital-centred, polarising and expansionist. On culture, they argue that traditional ideas such as people-based governance and harmony are activated by Marxist truth, so that Marxism takes root in China. They add that the "two overall situations" (national rejuvenation and global change unseen in a century), a community with a shared future for mankind, a fighting spirit and "taking the historical initiative" define the era. The authors conclude that the Party must keep a vigorous spirit and take the historical initiative in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. They also link this task to the Party's central mission of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned reading of the 20th Party Congress theoretical framework, with the major slogans of the Two Integrations, Chinese modernization and cultural confidence laid out in one place.

Continuously writing new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 不断谱写马克思主义中国化时代化新篇章 Shen Chuanliang Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Shen Chuanliang asks how the Party should keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author's answer is that this requires treating Marxism scientifically, treating Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its latest achievement, and holding to the Two Integrations as the fundamental route. Shen also calls for mastering the stance, viewpoint and method that run through that body of thought. The article is a study-and-interpretation piece in five sections. It begins with why Marxism must be localised and how the Party has done so over a century. It then sets out the content of Xi Jinping Thought: the "ten affirmations", the "fourteen commitments" and the "thirteen areas of achievement". The third section treats the Two Integrations, the fourth the "six musts" of the Congress report, and the fifth the role of the Thought in the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Shen argues that any scientific theory has to be localised to work, citing Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao on applying theory according to concrete conditions. Integrating Marxism with China's concrete realities means grasping both what stays constant and what changes: the primary stage of socialism, the principal social contradiction and popular expectations. The author says integration with fine traditional Chinese culture is possible because the two share values, such as "all under heaven for the public good" and the people as the foundation of the state, and the ideal of a great harmony. Shen presents the "six musts" (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, problem orientation, systematic thinking, a global vision) as a logically connected system. The article also stresses that the Thought is open and still developing, and that the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds are decisive for the Party. Shen concludes that the Thought gives the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation its basic direction (socialism with Chinese characteristics), spiritual support and scientific method. The author calls on the whole Party to study the Thought's worldview and methodology and apply them to risks and challenges. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's systematic, officially aligned reading of the 20th Congress report's theoretical formulations, including the "ten affirmations" and the "six musts".

New developments in North Korea's socialist theory and practice in the ten years of Kim Jong Un's rule 金正恩执政十年朝鲜社会主义理论与实践的新发展 Qian Zhengyu Qian Zhengyu asks what has changed in North Korea's socialist theory and practice since Kim Jong Un took over the Workers' Party of Korea and the army in December 2011. The article argues that the Party moved from songun (military-first) politics and the "parallel line" to a "frontal breakthrough" strategy centred on economic construction. In Qian's account, it made theoretical and practical gains even under heavy sanctions, natural disasters and the Covid-19 pandemic. The article opens with the Seventh Party Congress (2016) and the Eighth Party Congress (January 2021), summarising how each assessed past work and set tasks. It then covers theory: the Party's guiding ideology, a sole leadership system, Party purposes, the basic political mode, the judgement of the international situation and of the present era, the nature of the socialist economy, and the place of science and technology. A third section reviews practice in five areas: Party and cadre building, economic work and living standards, ideological struggle, foreign relations, and the anti-epidemic campaign. Qian presents the sequence as a consolidation of Party leadership. Kim-Il-sungism–Kim-Jong-Ilism became the sole guiding ideology (2012), and the 2021 congress replaced military-first politics with "the people-first principle" as the basic political mode. On the economy, Qian traces early experiments with enterprise autonomy and the "field responsibility system", which raised market activity. Citing Kim, Qian says these also disrupted planning and state control. The Eighth Congress therefore defined the economy as self-reliant, planned and people-serving, and re-emphasised the cabinet and unified state direction. Qian also describes a declared "our-state-first era", a hardening ideological front against Western and South Korean influence, summit diplomacy with South Korea, the United States and China, and strict border closure that kept the country free of Covid-19 infections. Qian concludes that North Korea's exploration of a socialist path suited to its conditions, since the Soviet and East European upheavals, has enriched the theory and practice of the world socialist movement. The author adds that studying it helps China consolidate traditional Sino-Korean friendship, and that the peninsula's stability matters for Northeast Asia. Qian treats the article as a snapshot of the current stage. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-school scholar's sympathetic, source-rich account of how North Korean official discourse and policy changed under Kim Jong Un.

Four "defeats" in Mao Zedong's own account: Gaoxingxu, Nanxiong Shuikou, Tucheng and Luban Chang 《党史博采》：毛泽东眼中的四次“败仗” This is a popular Party-history feature from the journal Dangshi Bocai (2023, first issue). It takes up a remark Mao Zedong made on 10 September 1956 at a preparatory meeting for the Eighth Party Congress. There he said openly that he had personally commanded battles that were lost: Gaoxingxu, Nanxiong, Tucheng and Maotai (Luban Chang). The text presents the four engagements as evidence that Mao, though celebrated as a brilliant strategist, never claimed to be undefeated. The article is built as four short military narratives in chronological order. The first is the Gaoxingxu fighting of September 1931 during the Third Encirclement Campaign in the Central Soviet Area. The second is the Nanxiong–Shuikou campaign of July 1932 against Guangdong forces. The third is the battle of Tucheng in January 1935, the first fight after the Zunyi Conference. The fourth is the attack on Zhou Hunyuan's column at Luban Chang in March 1935. Each section gives troop movements, orders, casualties and what went wrong. The article's central point is that each "defeat" had a specific cause. At Gaoxingxu, the Red Army's forces were not concentrated, it ran short of ammunition and lost heavily, though it wiped out an enemy brigade. At Nanxiong Shuikou, false reports that the enemy had withdrawn, and the mistaking of ten enemy regiments for four, produced a costly victory. The article quotes Mao's later remark that such battles, "usually counted as victories", were ones "we have never welcomed". At Tucheng, a one-character intelligence error (a brigade rendered as a regiment) meant the enemy was far stronger than expected. At Luban Chang, the enemy's fortifications, fierce fire and air support forced a withdrawal. The article concludes that these setbacks did not end in failure overall. The Tucheng reverse pushed the Red Army to cross the Chishui River westward, which opened the Four Crossings of the Chishui, described as one of Mao's finest strokes. Luban Chang, in the article's view, rested on a correct decision and did not prevent that success. Read the original if you want a detailed, narrative-style account of these four engagements and the Chinese Party-history framing of Mao's admission of failure.

Striving to promote common prosperity for all the people on the new road of the "examination" 在新的赶考路上着力促进全体人民共同富裕 Jiang Shuping Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Jiang Shuping takes up a new formulation in Xi Jinping's report: for the first time, "achieving common prosperity for all the people" is named an essential requirement of Chinese modernization, beyond being one of its important features. Jiang argues that this reflects the Party Central Committee's conscious commitment to its original aspiration and founding mission, and that it places common prosperity at the centre of the new journey of building a modern socialist country. The piece is a short interpretive commentary built in three parts. The first reviews how the Party has pursued common prosperity, from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping through to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second traces how the issue has been raised in priority, from the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020) to the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission meeting of August 2021 and the 20th Congress report. The third sets out how substantive progress is to be made. Jiang presents the pursuit of common prosperity as a basic Marxist position and as a continuous line of Party exploration, citing Mao's "common wealth, common strength" and Deng's definition of the essence of socialism. For the recent period, the author points to the elimination of absolute poverty, the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, and the large education, social security and health systems. Jiang notes the three-stage goals set in 2021 (narrowing gaps by the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan, equal access to basic public services by 2035, basic realization by mid-century). The author concedes that unbalanced and inadequate development and urban–rural, regional and income gaps remain large, and argues that progress requires doing one's best within one's means, improving the distribution system and social security, and pursuing high-quality development under the new development philosophy. Jiang concludes that, on the new "examination" road, the Party must uphold its overall leadership, keep economic development as the central task, rely on the people and persevere to produce a better answer for history and the people. Common prosperity is described as a long-term yet practical task for more than 1.4 billion people, one that can be neither rushed nor delayed. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the 20th Congress report positions common prosperity within Chinese modernization.

Marxism of China in the new era and twenty-first-century Marxism 新时代的中国马克思主义与21世纪马克思主义 Vladimiro Giacché The Italian Marxist Vladimiro Giacché, vice-president of the Association Marx XXI (Italy), asks how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era should be understood by readers used to discussing Marx in a Western political culture. The text is a Chinese translation of his article, published in World Socialism Studies in 2022. Giacché argues that this body of thought is non-static, non-dogmatic Marxism and a developing twenty-first-century Marxism. He begins by naming three obstacles for Western readers: the habit of splitting Marx's and Engels's thought into isolated aspects, the weakening of the link between Marxism and political practice in the West, and the differing background of Chinese Marxism, which serves to build socialism rather than mainly to critique capitalist relations. The article then proceeds through Xi's speeches and writings. It covers the development of theory through practice, the role of traditional Chinese culture, dialectical materialist method, trends in the contemporary world, and the competitive advantages of China's socialist system. Giacché's central claim is that the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics develops Marxism rather than merely recording policy. He notes that Marx and Engels had no experience of governing a socialist state and that Lenin made a similar point about state capitalism, so Chinese communists had to find their own solutions. He identifies contradiction, relations, institutions and systematic thinking as the core categories of Xi's method. He reads the community with a shared future for mankind as a universalism that rejects imperialism and a single model of civilisation. He also reads the Chinese system's advantage as lying in public ownership as the mainstay, a socialist market economy and Party leadership, which he says allow long-term strategy not dominated by bourgeois interests. In six concluding points, Giacché stresses that practice runs through the evolution of the thought, that traditional culture provides fertile soil, and that China's stance is rooted in independence rather than any inferiority complex towards the West. He observes that the features Xi stresses, the role of the state and Party leadership, are the same ones Western critics target, and says this is no coincidence. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist's systematic, sympathetic reading of Xi Jinping Thought, and of how it frames institutional competition with capitalism.

The development and prospects of Chinese political science in the new era 新时代中国政治学的发展与前瞻 Wang Bingquan Writing just after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wang Bingquan takes stock of a decade of Chinese political science since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that the discipline, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, has entered a stage of self-reliance and self-direction. Wang holds that its central task is to build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system and to advance the "three systems" (disciplinary, academic and discourse) of Chinese political science. The article proceeds in six parts. It sets out the new demands on the discipline: the "great changes unseen in a century", the modernization of national governance, social transformation and a growing native awareness. It then surveys research themes, from the Party's leadership system, institutional reform and grassroots governance to whole-process people's democracy and common prosperity. Next it reviews ten sub-fields (historical, rural, ethnic, comparative, technology, spatial, environmental, political communication, political psychology and the history of political thought) and new methods such as big data, experiments and cross-disciplinary work. Wang's core argument is that the discipline's growth is explained by a set of internal and external drivers: the guidance of Party theory, practical demands of reform, a turn from imitating Western concepts to local ones, international competition, new technology and openness. In Wang's account, earlier reliance on Western frameworks could not capture China's experience, and the contrast between "China's order" and "Western disorder" strengthened the case for indigenous theory. The article also presents the Party's leadership, the new type of party system and Chinese governance theory as innovations that go beyond Western theories. It says Marxism and a creatively transformed traditional political culture should remain the foundations. Wang concludes that the discipline should strengthen four forms of awareness: self-awareness, strategic awareness, community awareness among scholars and integration across disciplines. Political scientists are urged to build new concepts and analytical frameworks from Chinese practice and to raise them to general theory. They are also urged to centre research on Chinese modernization and to place political reform research within the modernization of national governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned overview of how Chinese political science describes its own sub-fields, themes and methods since 2012.

China and Africa jointly building the Belt and Road with high quality: concept, foundations, difficulties and responses 中国与非洲高质量共建“一带一路”：理念、基础、困境及应对 Tong Fei Writing in late 2022, Tong Fei asks how China and Africa can move their Belt and Road cooperation from rapid expansion to high-quality development. The article argues that the concept behind the cooperation, the material, institutional and popular foundations built over nearly a decade, and a set of targeted adjustments together make this shift feasible, even though serious obstacles remain. The article has three parts. The first sets out five features of the China–Africa Belt and Road concept: a new view of international order, common development and win-win cooperation, keeping promises, step-by-step practical progress, and the goal of a China–Africa community with a shared future. The second describes the foundations of cooperation, and the third analyses four difficulties and proposes four responses. Tong draws on trade and investment figures, summit documents and opinion surveys such as Afrobarometer. On foundations, Tong cites 2021 bilateral trade of 254.2 billion US dollars, 46 African countries with signed Belt and Road agreements by January 2021, the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation as a multilevel institutional platform, and survey data showing mainly positive African views of China. On difficulties, Tong identifies the unsustainability of China-financed contracting, a trade deficit of 43 billion dollars for Africa, coups and insecurity, uneven African perceptions (including 'debt trap' concerns), and growing competition from the United States, the EU's Global Gateway, India and Japan. Tong attributes part of the negative perception to Western narratives. Tong proposes matching projects precisely to Africa's weak sectors such as agriculture, manufacturing and infrastructure, and improving institutions by linking the Belt and Road with African integration and the African Union. Tong also calls for fostering Africa's autonomous development through evaluation of Chinese-financed projects, diversified financing, greater transparency and the involvement of local firms. A fourth proposal is to tell the China–Africa story through localised communication. The article concludes that the cooperation should aim at 'high standards, sustainability and improved livelihoods'. Read the original if you want a Chinese policy-studies view of Belt and Road cooperation with Africa, with survey and trade data and a list of difficulties and recommendations.

The exploration of world socialism and the forward direction of human civilization 世界社会主义的探索历程与人类文明的前进方向 Liu Chenguang Writing just after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Chenguang asks what the history of world socialism reveals about its underlying logic and about where human civilization is heading. The article argues that world socialism is part of the transition from world capitalism to world socialism that Marx called "world history". In Liu's account, Chinese modernization and the new form of human civilization it has created will deeply shape that direction. The article has three parts. The first reviews the exploration of world socialism, drawing on Xi Jinping's 2013 periodisation of five hundred years of socialism, and sets out four lessons. The second identifies three logics running through that history. The third projects three trends in human civilization. Liu draws on Marx's three social forms, Toynbee's plurality of civilizations, Kissinger, and the scholar Jiang Hui. On the historical record, Liu stresses that socialism is a real movement rather than a finished doctrine. It has had to cross the "Caudine Forks" in backward countries, it aims at modernization, and it has no fixed model. The Soviet model is criticised as rigid and as having taken a "great-party chauvinist" stance. The core argument is that three logics overlap. The logic of doctrine is the historical necessity Marx identified, which unfolds unevenly. The logic of power covers class struggle, imperial rivalry and national liberation movements. The logic of civilization covers capitalism's claim to be the only civilization, set against the plural civilizational forms of socialism. Liu warns against a linear, idea-led view of history and describes world history as "polyphonic", with multiple modernities emerging against capitalist modernity. Liu forecasts three trends: a reordering of the world as US unipolarity and Western dominance decline, a revival of socialism with China as its banner and mainstay, and the coexistence of diverse civilizations moving towards a community with a shared future for mankind. The rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is presented as a rejuvenation of Chinese civilization, fusing Marxism with that civilization. The article claims that the future of human civilization depends largely on how this new form develops. Read the original if you want to see how a Central Party School scholar links world-historical theory, civilizational discourse and official claims about China's role in world socialism.

An analysis of the content of intra-Party political culture in the Yan'an period 延安时期党内政治文化内涵探析 Feng Liujian Jiang Wei Feng Liujian and Jiang Wei ask what constituted the political culture inside the Chinese Communist Party during the Yan'an period, which they date from October 1935, when the Central Committee reached Wuqi in northern Shaanxi, to March 1948, when its leaders crossed the Yellow River. They define this culture as the Party values and behaviour found among members and organisations, including political belief, cognition, style, norms and values. Their thesis is that it formed an organic unity of three layers: political ideas, political institutions and political conduct. The article is organised around these three layers. Ideas are called the 'soul' of intra-Party political culture, institutions its 'guarantee' and conduct its outward 'manifestation'. Under ideas, the authors treat Marxism as guiding ideology, communism as fundamental political belief, and wholehearted service to the people. Under institutions, they cover the Party's leadership system, democratic centralism and cadre management. Under conduct, they cover the three work styles, the Party's political image and its clean, honest character. The evidence is drawn from Party resolutions, speeches by Mao Zedong and Liu Shaoqi, and accounts by visitors such as Edgar Snow, Anna Louise Strong and Huang Yanpei. In the authors' account, the Sinification of Marxism, the idea of adapting Marxism to China's conditions, gave the Party a theoretical, ideological and practical self-awareness. They cite the 1942 decisions on unified leadership, the system of reporting to superiors, and the 1941 decision on strengthening Party spirit as institutional means of upholding the authority of the Central Committee. Democratic centralism is presented as balancing inner-Party democracy with centralised unity. The authors credit the cadre system, which they say rested on merit and virtue, study systems, screening, supervision and anti-corruption rules, with building a capable leadership.
