Feng and Jiang present the three work styles of linking theory with practice, keeping close ties with the masses, and criticism and self-criticism as the visible form of this culture. They describe the Party's image as rooted in correct political direction, seeking truth from facts, serving the people, self-reliance and hard struggle, and integrity. Examples include the production campaign, 'crack troops and simple administration' and rewards and punishments for officials. They conclude that the three layers are inseparable and that Yan'an political culture shows the Party's political and spiritual strength, with lasting historical and contemporary value. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars frame Yan'an-era Party culture and its sources.)

Marxism adapted to China and our times works 中国化时代化的马克思主义行 Wang Shuyin This short commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement, repeated in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), that the Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good because Marxism works, and specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang Shuyin argues that the formulation expresses Marxism's theoretical character and gives a basic guide for opening up new horizons in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece has three parts: the Party's innovative theory guiding new practice; the continual opening of new horizons for Marxism; and the Party's role in writing what Wang calls the grandest epic in the history of the Chinese nation. Wang argues that Marxism is a method and guide to action, not a dogma, and that it is a developing theory. It works because the Party keeps combining its basic principles with China's realities and the features of the era, and solves practical problems in revolution, construction and reform. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as the latest leap in this process, and Wang lists six stances and methods for further theoretical innovation, including putting the people first and keeping a problem-oriented approach. Wang concludes that the Party's guidance by Marxism underlies its historical initiative and the achievements of the past decade, which he describes as setting the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on an irreversible course. He calls for grasping the decisive significance of the Two Establishes and fully applying Xi's thought in building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars explain the 20th Party Congress formula on Marxism.

On common prosperity and value guidance 论共同富裕与价值引领 Luo Yuting Liu Shuhao Luo Yuting and Liu Shuhao, writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), treat common prosperity not only as an economic and political question but as a question of values. Their thesis is that Chinese modernization, which the Congress report defines as the modernization of common prosperity for all the people, requires deliberate value guidance to build a social consensus on what common prosperity means and how to reach it. The article has three parts. The first sets out why such guidance is needed now: China has entered a historical stage of making solid progress towards common prosperity, common prosperity is described as an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and creating a better life for the people requires shared values. The second identifies four value tendencies to correct. The third proposes five ways of advancing value guidance: policy orientation, public opinion, cultural cultivation, behavioural norms and model demonstration. In the authors' account, each of the four value questions is a pairing of a principle to uphold and a deviation to resist. "Prosperity for all" must guard against polarisation, but also against absolute egalitarianism, which the authors say contradicts the law of value and distribution according to labour. "Comprehensive prosperity" means material and cultural-ethical wealth together, against a one-dimensional "materialism". "Gradual prosperity" rejects "simultaneous prosperity", which the authors link to the influence of Nordic welfarism and call unrealistic for the largest developing country. "Prosperity through joint building" rejects getting something for nothing, which they call parasitic and tied to exploiting classes' values. On implementation, the authors call for policies that embody the idea that labour is honourable and prosperity comes through struggle. They also call for positive publicity that answers mistaken views at home and abroad, and for drawing on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture. Legal and institutional norms should help hard-working, honest and innovative workers become prosperous, and exemplary cases, such as the Zhejiang common prosperity demonstration zone, should be promoted for emulation. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party-oriented theory frames common prosperity as an ideological and moral task as well as an economic one.

The primary stage of socialism and socialism in the primary stage (part 2) Keynote report to the 8th Forum on Marxist Theory and Contemporary Chinese History, 12 August 2022 社会主义初级阶段与初级阶段社会主义（下） Zhu Jiamu This is the second half of a keynote report that Zhu Jiamu, president of the Chinese Society for the History of the People's Republic of China and former vice-president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, gave at the 8th Forum on Marxist Theory and Contemporary Chinese History on 12 August 2022. Zhu asks how to tell whether practice in the primary stage of socialism is guided by the theory of socialism as practised in that stage, rather than departing from scientific socialism. Zhu's answer is that policies suited to the primary stage must be combined with fidelity to the basic principles of socialism. This part sets out three further tests, continuing from the first half: holding to the communist ideal alongside the Party's basic programme; upholding the Four Cardinal Principles alongside the policies of socialism with Chinese characteristics; and resisting Western "peaceful evolution". The argument draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Chen Yun and Xi Jinping, on the Soviet collapse, and on the 2021 Party resolution on history. On the first test, Zhu argues that the Party's "minimum" programmes in each period have differed but that its "maximum" programme of communism has kept it from losing direction and slackening its will to struggle. On the second, Zhu holds that combining reform and opening up with the Four Cardinal Principles is the main reason for China's success, that hostile forces attack precisely this combination, and that Gorbachev's abandonment of those principles caused Soviet failure. Zhu goes through each principle. Public ownership must remain dominant, judged by control of the economy's lifelines rather than by the private sector's share of output or employment. The "dictatorship of the proletariat", in Zhu's account, still has a target in subversion and bourgeois liberalization. Party leadership and the guiding role of Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought must continue, while theory keeps developing. On the third test, Zhu presents peaceful evolution as concentrated in the political and ideological spheres. Zhu treats corruption, especially collusion between officials and private capital, as a product of it and as a route for "colour revolutions". Zhu concludes that China must neither attempt what is beyond the primary stage nor violate socialist principles, so that it can advance to a higher stage and eventually to communism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a senior Party historian justifies the limits of marketization and the case for strict ideological vigilance.)

The primary stage of socialism and socialism in its primary stage (Part 1) 社会主义的初级阶段与初级阶段的社会主义（上） Zhu Jiamu This is the first part of a keynote report that Zhu Jiamu gave on 12 August 2022 at the Eighth Forum on Marxist Theory of Contemporary Chinese History. Zhu argues that, just as understanding the nature of Chinese society was decisive for the revolution, understanding the nature of the present stage explains the achievements of reform and opening up. In Zhu's account, that stage is the primary stage of socialism, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is the theory and policy suited to it. Zhu asks readers to grasp how the two ideas in the title relate. The speech has two main sections. The first traces how Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping understood the length and internal divisions of socialist society. The second asks whether China's rise since the late 1990s means it has left the primary stage. Zhu draws on Party Congress reports and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). Zhu holds that Marx and Engels treated socialism as the first phase of communism but did not say how long it would last. Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and the Great Leap Forward in China, Zhu says, all tended to underestimate the time required. Mao later stressed a long period, and Deng tied socialism's task to developing the productive forces. Zhu presents distinguishing a primary stage within socialism as a major theoretical innovation, and treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as the system of theory and policy for that stage. The Party's judgement that the new era is a higher phase within the primary stage rests, Zhu says, on a changed principal contradiction and on advances in GDP, poverty reduction, social security and international standing. Zhu nonetheless lists reasons why China has not reached an advanced stage. Per capita indicators are still low, growth is resource-intensive and uneven, and core technologies remain foreign-held. Demographic and external pressures persist, and the standards for industrialization and modernization keep rising. Zhu concludes that after more than 70 years of effort China has entered a new stage of development in the new era. That stage is still insufficiently developed and remains far from the advanced world level. It can therefore only be a higher level within the primary stage of socialism, not the advanced stage of socialist society. The text ends with "to be continued". Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian justifies, historically and statistically, the claim that China remains in the primary stage of socialism.

Getting off to a good start in building a modern socialist country in all respects 为全面建设社会主义现代化国家开好局起好步 Wang Changlin Writing in the People's Daily in January 2023, Wang Changlin interprets the Central Economic Work Conference held at the end of 2022 and the speech Xi Jinping gave there. The article's thesis is that China's economy has withstood severe tests, that its long-term fundamentals remain sound, and that the conference's priorities can bring about an overall recovery in 2023. In Wang's account, this recovery would mean an effective improvement in quality and a reasonable growth in quantity, and so a good start to building a modern socialist country in all respects. The piece has three parts. It first reviews the 2022 economic record, then assesses short-term and long-term prospects, and finally sets out how to carry out the conference's tasks. The review cites figures on growth, high-tech manufacturing, investment, exports, prices, employment and food output. It compares China's inflation and trade performance with that of the United States, the eurozone and Japan. Wang argues that, despite a growth dip to 0.4% in the second quarter, a package of stabilising measures produced annual growth of 3.0% and GDP above 120 trillion yuan. For 2023 the author sees favourable conditions in the recovery of contact consumption, continued infrastructure and manufacturing investment, policy effects and a low 2022 base. Over the longer term Wang points to a working-age population of nearly 900 million, a large middle-income group, a complete industrial chain and room for fiscal and monetary policy, and puts potential growth at 5%–6%. The author also admits that three pressures remain: shrinking demand, supply shocks and weakening expectations. Wang calls for coordinated management of several pairs of tasks and for improving social expectations and confidence. The priorities are expanding domestic demand, especially consumption; building a modern industrial system with key technology breakthroughs and food and energy security; implementing the Two Unwaverings; attracting more foreign investment; and defusing financial and property-sector risks. Read the original if you want a concise official-economist reading of the 2022 Central Economic Work Conference and the policy priorities it set for 2023.

Advancing the adaptation of Marxism to China and the times through great practice 以伟大实践推进马克思主义时代化中国化 Zhou Jiaxin This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in November 2022, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's claim that Marxism, adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, explains the Party's success. Zhou Jiaxin argues that further theoretical innovation rests on grasping the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The piece first treats the standpoint of practice as the basic viewpoint of Marxist philosophy. It then sets out six principles that Zhou presents as the method for advancing adaptation, each tied to the Party's "historical initiative". Zhou argues that practice unites historical, truth and value perspectives: it is concrete and historical, carries social relations, and is the test of truth. Citing Fang Jun of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, Zhou holds that a scientific view of history is in essence a scientific view of values. Chinese modernization is described as a world-historical practice that is highly distinctive, profound and complex. Zhou then lists six commitments: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systems thinking, and a global vision. Each is said to strengthen historical initiative. Zhou concludes that these six commitments form an interrelated whole. In this account they make up the method for understanding Xi Jinping Thought and for the Two Integrations, and they express the unity of historical, truth and value perspectives in the new journey of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party-affiliated philosophers link practice, the 20th Party Congress's six commitments and the adaptation of Marxism.

A Marxist philosophical reflection on Chinese modernization 对中国式现代化的马克思主义哲学思考 Gao Chao Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in November 2022, Gao Chao takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's statement that Chinese modernization shares common features with other countries' modernization while having distinctive Chinese characteristics. Gao argues that this is both a political and a theoretical judgement, and that Marxist philosophy in the new era must explain what is common, what is specific, and how the two relate. This short commentary first challenges the popular view that modernization has a single model, the Western one. It then draws on Marx and Engels, turns to the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and ends with research agendas that Gao, citing the researcher Fang Jun, assigns to Marxist philosophy. Gao reasons from historical materialism that modernization is, at root, the modernization of productive forces, and that the scientific and industrial revolutions first occurred in the West. Quoting Engels on the interaction between economic base and superstructure, Gao holds that Marx's remark that advanced countries show backward ones their future does not imply one road only. In Gao's account, problems such as polarisation, imbalance between material and cultural-ethical progress, ecological damage and conflict between states are common to all modernizing countries, but China addresses them differently: through common prosperity, ecological harmony and peaceful development, not through aggression, expansion or the sacrifice of the majority. Gao concludes that Marxist philosophy should "illuminate reality with theory", and endorses Fang Jun's two priority questions: why socialism was first established in less developed capitalist countries, and why it was not consolidated in some of them. Answering these would, Gao says, explain why socialism can be built well in China, and show that Chinese modernization is a new path, not one valid for China alone. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how the official line on Chinese modernization is framed in philosophical terms.

Chinese modernization and the modernization of the human being 中国式现代化与人的现代化 Zhou Ke This short review, first published in Chinese Social Sciences Today on 24 November 2022, uses Fang Jun's book Scattered Leaves of Thought (思想的散叶) to discuss how Chinese modernization should be understood. Zhou Ke argues that approaching it through the modernization of the human being requires attention to the unity of the historical outlook and value theory in Marxist philosophy. In Zhou's reading, Fang's book upholds and develops that unity. The piece has three parts. The first reads Chinese modernization, as set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), in terms of human modernization. The second reviews value-theory research in Chinese Marxist philosophy since the 1980s. The third discusses the book's pairing of practical concern with theoretical reflection. Zhou holds that modernization includes changes in people's psychology, values and conduct, not only in technology, economy and politics. Chinese modernization, the author says, affirms human needs and development through common prosperity, balanced material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony with nature and peaceful development. Zhou therefore rejects simply copying Western personality-and-psychology approaches. The review credits Chinese scholars with moving value theory beyond a purely epistemological frame and defining value through the contradictions of practice. It also credits them with treating ethical questions, such as institutional ethics, as questions of historical outlook. Zhou concludes that the book exemplifies turning real problems into scholarly ones, following Liu Ben's principle that research on real problems should drive foundational theory and foundational theory should deepen research on real problems. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese account of how value theory and human development are linked to Chinese modernization, and of how one strand of Chinese Marxist philosophy has developed since the 1980s.

Chinese modernization and the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the times 中国式现代化与马克思主义哲学的时代化 Lin Qing Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which set out the features and requirements of Chinese modernization, Lin Qing asks how Chinese modernization relates to the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the needs of our times. The short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in November 2022, argues that the relationship can be grasped through two dimensions: the original historical setting of Chinese modernization, and the move from a formal to a substantive crossing of the "Caudine Forks". The first part addresses why modernization in China is socialist. Lin notes that for Marx, socialism was not itself a project of modernization, since it was built on surpassing capitalist industrial modernity. The second part turns to Marx's late reflections on the Caudine Forks, prompted by Vera Zasulich's question, and to the concept of appropriation in The German Ideology. Lin reads Mao Zedong's On New Democracy as concluding, from a historical-materialist analysis of China's situation, that national independence required a path from new-democratic to socialist revolution. Lin then argues that China crossed the Caudine Forks only formally through revolution, and must now cross them substantively: appropriating the means and achievements of Western-style modernization without its suffering. Drawing on Marx and Engels, Lin says appropriation is conditioned by its object, by the individuals who appropriate (hence the stress on modernization of the human being) and by the manner of appropriation, which means joint appropriation by united people. Lin reads the features listed in the Congress report as building social commonality. Lin concludes that Marxist philosophy should offer a general interpretation of Chinese modernization as a world-historical effect, first imposed and later actively pursued, while refusing a "philosophy of history" reading. Lin adds that understanding socialism remains the essential question as the process unfolds. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese philosopher links the Caudine Forks debate to current Party theory on modernization.

Advancing the adaptation of Marxism to China and our times through great practice 以伟大实践推进马克思主义时代化中国化 Zhou Jiaxin This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in November 2022, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's claim that it is Marxism, adapted to China and the times, that explains the Party's success. Zhou argues that theoretical innovation grounded in practice depends first on grasping the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and on applying its stance, viewpoint and method. The piece begins with the standpoint of practice in Marxist philosophy, then turns to the Chinese practice of the new era, which Zhou characterises as extremely distinctive, profound and complex. It closes with six principles that the author presents as the methodological requirements of the Thought. Zhou argues that practice opens Marxist philosophy to social and historical depth, supplies a test of truth, and sketches a better future. Drawing on Fang Jun, the piece holds that a scientific view of history is in essence a scientific view of values, so that taking historical initiative means unifying views of history, truth and value. Adaptation of Marxism is then tied to six commitments: putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, a problem-oriented approach, systemic thinking, and a global vision. Each is said to be the ground on which historical initiative grows. Zhou concludes that these six commitments form an interrelated whole. In the author's account, they embody the scientific unity of views of history, truth and value achieved on the basis of practice, and they keep advancing adaptation of Marxism on the new journey of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated philosophers link the standpoint of practice to the six methodological principles drawn from the 20th Party Congress report.

Chinese modernization: our road to rejuvenation 中国式现代化：我们的复兴路 Qi Si This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in November 2022, reads the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) as setting out Chinese modernization as the means of advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Qi argues that the Party must grasp the strategic plan and world-historical significance of Chinese modernization and draw on a spirit of historical initiative as the country begins a new journey. The piece has three parts. It first summarises the great changes since the 18th Party Congress (2012), then sets out the features, requirements and guiding principles of Chinese modernization, and finally places it in three historical frames: the history of the Chinese nation, of socialism, and of human society. Qi's core claim is that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, with Party leadership as its fundamental political guarantee and socialism as its fundamental political direction. The author lists its Chinese characteristics as a huge population, common prosperity, coordination of material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Historically, Qi presents it as marking the nation's leap from standing up to becoming prosperous and then strong. It is also said to reject the old path of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization, creating a new form of human civilization and offering other countries a new option. Qi concludes that following its own path is the Party's historical conclusion from a century of struggle, and that this path serves the Chinese people and nation as well as human progress. The author calls for stronger awareness of risks, deeper reform and opening up, and a fighting spirit among Party members and cadres. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line summary of how the 20th Congress report framed Chinese modernization and its global significance.

The foundational act for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation Mao Zedong's leadership of socialist transformation and its great significance 实现中华民族伟大复兴的奠基之举 Li Youxin Wang Xia Li and Wang ask what the socialist transformation of the 1950s, led by Mao Zedong, contributed to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. They argue that it was the foundational act of that project. In their account it laid three bases: the socialist road, the basic economic system and the material foundation. The article has three main sections, one for each base. The first covers Mao's choice of direction and the Party's General Line for the transition period (1953). The second covers the change in ownership of the means of production and the resulting public-ownership-based economic system. The third draws on statistical tables for 1949–1957 on output, infrastructure, living standards, health, education and defence. A closing section answers critics of the transformation. The authors argue that by 1952 changes in the principal contradiction, the economic structure, popular enthusiasm and the international situation had made the transition timely. They credit Mao with a distinctively Chinese path: industrialization and transformation pursued together, agricultural cooperation before mechanization, and peaceful transformation of capitalist industry and commerce. They argue that public ownership and distribution according to work removed the basis of exploitation and enabled the concentration of resources on major undertakings. To rebut claims that the transformation held back productivity, they cite figures. These include industrial output up 128 percent from 1952 to 1957, life expectancy rising from 35 to 57 years, and the nuclear and satellite programme (the "two bombs and one satellite"). Li and Wang conclude that reform-era institutions inherit the basic economic system of the transformation period and develop it rather than negate it. They present Xi Jinping's "two non-negations" as the proper stance toward the periods before and after reform and opening up. They say some critics of the transformation are driving historical nihilism, aimed at discrediting the socialist road and Party leadership. Read the original if you want a representative Party-historiography defence of the 1950s transformation, with its statistical evidence and its framing against historical nihilism.

Sinicized and modernized Marxism works 中国化时代化的马克思主义行 Dong Zhenhua Taking its title from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary asks why the Communist Party of China has succeeded and why socialism with Chinese characteristics is judged good. Dong Zhenhua answers that, in the end, it is Marxism that works, specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The piece appeared in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2022 and presents continued theoretical innovation as a solemn historical responsibility of today's Communists. The article has three parts. The first reviews more than a century of the Party's history as a process of seeking, revealing and putting truth into practice. The second explains why writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is a duty. The third sets out the stances, viewpoints and methods that Dong says theoretical innovation must rely on, drawing on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In the historical section, Dong presents three leaps for the Chinese nation: from being weak to standing up under Mao Zedong, from standing up to growing rich under Deng Xiaoping and reform and opening up, and from growing rich to becoming strong in the new era. Each is attributed to combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and, more recently, with fine traditional Chinese culture, which the article calls the Two Integrations. Dong argues that success has come whenever the Party kept Marxism open and used a developing Marxism to guide practice, and setbacks followed when it did not. Looking forward, the author lists six commitments: put the people first, be self-confident and self-reliant, uphold fundamental principles while breaking new ground, be problem-oriented, apply systems thinking, and keep the whole world in view. Dong concludes that the 20th Party Congress report is the Party's political declaration and action programme for the new journey. The author calls on readers to improve their ability to analyse and solve practical problems with Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and to arm themselves with Xi Jinping Thought. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party School scholars present the official narrative of Marxism's adaptation in the months after the 20th Party Congress.

Inquiry into several questions on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 关于马克思主义中国化时代化的若干问题探赜 Li Sicong Writing in early 2023, after the 20th Party Congress (2022) made advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times a Party duty, Li Sicong asks how this formula arose, what it means, how it relates to a century of Party theory, and how it should be pursued. Li argues that existing scholarship leans towards grand theoretical narrative and has not examined these points closely. The article's answer is that the formula is a systematic summation of the Party's century of theoretical innovation and a dynamic process of applying Marxism to China's realities and the features of the era. The article has four parts. It first traces how the formula was proposed, then defines its "scientific connotation". It then reads the Party's century as three leaps (Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era). Finally it sets out how Xi Jinping Thought opens up a "new realm" of this adaptation. On origins, Li adds two conditions to earlier scholarly explanations: the "spatial extension" (local modes of production, culture, religion) and the "temporal continuity" (era, stage, tasks) that bound any theory's development. Li divides the formula's emergence into three phases: a period from the 18th Party Congress (2012) when its meaning was carried by older phrases; a preparatory period after the 19th Congress (2017), when Xi first used it as an independent concept in 2018; and a period of establishment from the Party's centenary in 2021, via the third historical resolution and the 20th Congress. Li holds that the new formula does not merely add to the earlier "sinification, adaptation to the times, popularisation" formulations but sublimates them, uniting their theoretical, era-related and popular dimensions. Li then treats the "Six Musts" as the worldview and methodology for the Party's pursuit, revelation and practice of truth: putting the people first, global vision, self-confidence and self-reliance, innovation while upholding fundamental principles, problem orientation and systems thinking. Li stresses that the political stance in "upholding fundamental principles" matters because judging what counts as "science" and "truth" requires a position. The article concludes that Party members should grasp Xi Jinping Thought's worldview and methods to shoulder the duty of continued theoretical innovation. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the formula was periodised and defined, and of how it is tied to the Six Musts.

Chinese advanced intellectuals and the integration of Marxism-Leninism with the Chinese workers' movement An important perspective on research into the founding of the Communist Party of China 中国先进知识分子与马克思列宁主义同中国工人运动的结合 Huang Guangqiu Official Party documents repeatedly present the founding of the Communist Party of China as the product of the integration of Marxism-Leninism with the Chinese workers' movement. Huang Guangqiu asks how this integration should be understood and how it came about. The article argues that placing China's advanced intellectuals inside this process is an important angle for studying the Party's creation, and that they played a major role in bringing the two together. The article is organised in four parts. It first sets out why intellectuals were needed, given the character and weaknesses of the Chinese working class. It then traces how intellectuals such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Mao Zedong, Cai Hesen, Dong Biwu and Qu Qiubai came to Marxism through comparison and reflection. The third part examines how the May Fourth Movement showed them the strength of the workers, and how they then went among workers in Shanghai and Beijing. A short conclusion links these steps to the First National Congress in July 1921. Huang's central argument is that the working class, despite its revolutionary qualities, could not by itself reach class consciousness. The author describes workers as marked by feudal habits, low education and peasant small-producer outlooks, so Marxism had to be brought to them by intellectuals. Intellectuals, in this account, turned to Marxism because other Western doctrines and the capitalist road had failed in China, because the First World War and the Paris Peace Conference disillusioned them, and because the October Revolution showed a workable alternative. The author cites Li Dazhao's and Chen Duxiu's shift away from bourgeois democracy as evidence that this was a reasoned choice. After the May Fourth strikes they surveyed workers, organised May Day events and founded journals, and in the process their own outlook shifted towards the proletariat. Huang concludes that because intellectuals chose Marxism after repeated comparison, recognised the workers' strength and propagated Marxism among them, the integration of Marxism-Leninism with the workers' movement occurred and the Party could be founded. The article presents this as the basis for the Party's later achievements. Read the original if you want a Party-history account of how early Marxist intellectuals are said to have linked theory and the labour movement, with many quotations from Li, Chen, Mao and their contemporaries.

A profound transformation in the form of human civilisation 人类文明形态的深刻变革 Feng Ziyi Feng Ziyi, in a short commentary first published in the China Social Sciences Today (2022), argues that China's development has produced not only a path of Chinese modernization but also a new form of human civilisation. Feng presents the step from a "new path" to a "new form" as a major rise from development to civilisation, and as China's highest achievement and greatest contribution to world civilisation. The article first clarifies what "new form" means, then sets out six ways in which the new form of human civilisation advances and leads human civilisation: expanding it, changing its configuration, widening its paths, guiding its direction, adding momentum, and reshaping its mode of development. On the meaning of the term, Feng holds that it is a comprehensive view of civilisation rather than a set of indicators, that it forms a new paradigm of ideals, values and norms, and that it is still unfolding. Feng argues that it enriches existing civilisation with values such as mutual respect, fairness and win-win cooperation, and that it reinterprets categories such as the core socialist values. In Feng's account, China's rise rests on moral and value-based influence rather than capital or hegemony, and shows that there is more than one Western-style route to modernity. A community with a shared future for mankind points a way forward amid the "great changes unseen in a century". Poverty alleviation and the Belt and Road Initiative are cited as sources of momentum. Mutual respect and exchange, Feng says, replace hostility and isolation. Feng concludes that the new form is an "upgraded version" of civilisation that is still a work in progress. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese scholars frame Chinese modernization as a civilisational contribution.

Chinese modernization and a new form of civilization 中国式现代化与文明的新形态 Yang Geng This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks in what sense Chinese modernization generates a new form of civilization. Yang argues that the novelty lies in three features: how China handles tradition and Western civilization, its socialist character, and the fusion of several social transformations in one period. The piece is organised around the repeated phrase that each point is where the "newness" of the civilization lies. Yang approaches modernization through a typology (endogenous versus exogenous), through social formation (capitalist versus socialist modernization), and through the historical sequence of marketization, industrialization and reform. Yang classes China's modernization as exogenous, set off by the challenge of Western capitalism and bound up from the start with national rejuvenation. Its central tension is therefore between native tradition and Western modernity. Yang holds that the measure for what to borrow and what to inherit is neither Western civilization nor tradition itself but contemporary Chinese practice. Yang adds that capitalist modernization produced capitalist civilization, whereas Chinese modernization is socialist, aims at common prosperity and removes class and capital–labour antagonism, while still absorbing rational elements of capitalist civilization. In the West marketization preceded industrialization, but in China modernization, marketization and socialist reform proceeded together. Yang concludes that this "triple transformation" and "trinity" will constitute a new form of human civilization. The text is a compact statement of one scholar's framing of the topic. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher links modernization theory to the idea of a new civilizational form.

A major enrichment and development of the theory of world modernization 对世界现代化理论的重大丰富和发展 Yu Chunhui This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 19 December 2022, takes up the 20th Party Congress (2022) report's account of Chinese modernization. Yu argues that the theory of Chinese modernization, formed through long practice, raises the Party's understanding to a new level and is a major enrichment and development of the theory of world modernization. The piece first recounts the Party's exploration of its own path: the goal of a modern socialist country in the period of revolution and construction, the phrase "Chinese-style modernization" and the "three-step" strategy after reform and opening up, and the advances since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then summarises Xi Jinping's exposition of the theory and ends with a contrast with Western modernization. Yu stresses that modernizing a developing country whose population exceeds that of all existing developed countries combined has no precedent and no ready-made road. In Yu's account, Xi's statements form a rigorous theoretical system covering the distinctive features, essential requirements and major principles of Chinese modernization. The author claims there is neither a single modernization model nor a universal standard. Chinese modernization is said to go beyond the older Western paths, described as capital-centred, polarised, materialist and expansionist, and to widen the routes open to developing countries. Yu concludes that the theory fits China's reality and reflects both the laws of socialist construction and those of human social development. The author calls on readers to focus on problems arising in the process, to propose new ideas and methods, and to produce further innovations in modernization theory and practice. Read the original if you want a brief, official-register statement of how Chinese modernization was presented as a contribution to world modernization theory after the 20th Party Congress.

Grasping the essential features of Chinese modernization accurately 精准把握中国式现代化本质特征 Liu Renying Yang Li'na Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today asks what the distinctive, essential features of Chinese modernization are and how it differs from Western modernization. Liu and Yang argue that only by answering this can Chinese modernization be grasped in thought and advanced in practice. The article goes through six features in turn: modernization led by the Communist Party and socialist in character; modernization of a huge population; modernization toward common prosperity; coordinated development of material and cultural-ethical advancement; harmony between humanity and nature; and the path of peaceful development. Each is set against a contrasting account of Western capitalist modernization. For the authors, Party leadership and the socialist system are the most essential feature and the basic dividing line. Western modernization, they write, is driven by the bourgeoisie's pursuit of surplus value and so produces polarisation, crises, consumerism, ecological damage and external plunder. Chinese modernization is described as people-centred rather than capital-centred, citing the eradication of absolute poverty (98.99 million rural people lifted out of poverty under current standards) and the principle that clear waters and green mountains are invaluable assets. Marx's Capital is invoked on polarisation and on workers' need for time for spiritual needs. The authors conclude that the idea that 'modernization equals Westernisation' is a myth, and that Western 'modernization traps' should be recognised as deceptive and unsustainable. They call for practice grounded in China's realities and experience, offering other countries a reliable alternative. Read the original if you want a compact, official-line outline of how Chinese commentators contrast Chinese modernization with Western modernization.

Deepening philosophical reflection at a major historical juncture 在重大历史关键节点深化哲学思考 Zhang Wu Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in November 2022, Zhang Wu argues that the 20th Party Congress (2022) marks a historical turning point. The commentary contends that this moment obliges Marxist philosophy to leave its "comfort zone" and ask a new overarching question: how is Chinese modernization possible? Zhang first reads the Congress's central task, advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, against several histories: the Chinese nation, socialism, the Communist Party, the People's Republic, and reform and opening up. The text then turns to the history of Marxism itself and to the idea of "living history" producing "living Marxism". In Zhang's account, nineteenth-century Marxism had developed Western Europe as its stage, and twentieth-century Marxism backward Eastern countries. The twenty-first century's stage will be a developed Eastern country, a situation Marx never faced. Zhang holds that Chinese modernization is possible theoretically because of the Two Integrations, since Marxism's critique of modernity and China's fine traditional culture both rule out the capitalist road. Its difficulty, notably its huge population, should be turned into momentum by developing people into talent, which calls for a theory of human development grounded in historical materialism rather than copied from the West. Philosophically, Zhang says, Chinese modernization is building a "post-capital-logic" form of philosophy, one that sublates capital logic instead of rejecting it, so that capital serves human development. Zhang concludes that this juncture is an opportunity for Marxist philosophy to innovate, likened to Rhodes, the place to dance. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher frames the 20th Party Congress as a task for philosophical theory.

Staying clear-headed and resolute in solving the problems unique to a large party 时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定 Liu Zhiming This newspaper commentary, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up Xi Jinping's call to remain clear-headed and resolute in solving the problems unique to a large party. Liu Zhiming argues that, for the world's largest Marxist governing party to keep the people's support and consolidate its long-term rule, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must be treated as a permanent strategic task. Any relaxation, the author warns, risks a rebound. The article moves in three steps. It first presents the willingness to carry out the Party's self-reform as a tradition and a lesson of a century of struggle. It then explains why a problem-oriented, cautious attitude is still needed, citing the speech by Xi at the second plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (2023 session of the new Commission). It closes with five practical directions for the new journey. Liu's central claim is that the Party's strength lies not in avoiding mistakes but in correcting them through criticism and self-criticism, democratic centralism and service to the people. On this reading, the Party has no interests apart from those of the nation and people, which is why it can face its own problems. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the author says, the anti-corruption campaign and rigorous self-governance have solved many prominent problems. Even so, impure thinking, politics, organization and work style persist, and the "four tests" and "four dangers" remain. Liu presents the Party's self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and fall, and says only the Party itself can defeat it. Liu calls for the Party to keep to its original aspiration and mission and to unify thinking, will and action under the Party Central Committee, with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. The author also proposes strengthening governing capacity and rule-based Party governance, sustaining cadres' drive through both strict management and encouragement, and building self-correcting mechanisms around the Party constitution and organizational life. The last proposal is a healthy political ecology, starting with how officials are selected and promoted. Liu is confident that the Party will keep renewing itself through self-reform. Read the original if you want an example of how a CASS Party-building scholar presents the official line on the Party's self-reform after the 20th Party Congress.

Staying clear-headed and resolute in tackling the problems unique to a large party 时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定 Liu Zhiming This newspaper commentary, published in Hunan Daily and posted in January 2023, takes up a formula from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): to keep the people's support and consolidate its long-term governing position, the Party must stay clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large party. Liu Zhiming argues that this is a strategic response to the question of what kind of long-ruling Marxist party to build and how to build it. In Liu's reading, the Party must see the task through and carry its great self-reform to the end. The piece has three parts. The first presents the courage for self-reform as a tradition and a lesson of the Party's century of struggle. The second explains why the problems remain pressing under long-term rule. The third sets out five areas of work for the new journey, drawing mainly on Xi Jinping's remarks at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. Liu's central claim is that the Party's strength lies in its capacity to correct itself rather than in avoiding mistakes. Liu credits this capacity to the Party's people-centred commitment, democratic centralism and criticism and self-criticism, and says the Party has no interests of its own apart from those of the nation and the people. Liu accepts that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since 2012 has solved many problems. Even so, the author argues, impurity in thinking, politics, organisation and work style persists, and the "four tests" and "four dangers" will endure. Liu treats the Party's self-reform as the "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decay, and says only the Party itself can defeat it. Liu proposes five measures: remember the founding mission; unify thinking, will and action through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; improve governing capacity through institutional and rule-based Party building; sustain officials' drive through incentives; and uncover and fix problems through democratic centralism and criticism and self-criticism. A healthy political ecology depends on proper selection of officials and a sound political culture. Liu concludes that a governing Party led by Xi Jinping's core will keep renewing itself. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars presented the post-20th Congress agenda of Party self-governance to a general readership.

The Chinese Communist Party's changing understanding of modern China as "semi-colonial" 中国共产党对近代中国“半殖民地”社会性质的认识历程 Zhai Yu Zhai Yu takes up a question of Party history: how and when the Chinese Communists came to describe modern China as "semi-colonial", the first half of the "semi-colonial and semi-feudal" formula that became the standard characterisation of China's modern society. The article argues that the Party's semi-colonial designation was largely an independent judgement made from its own observation of China. It was not a conclusion handed down by the Comintern, although Lenin's usage inspired it. The article begins with the standard account of the formula and its consequences for the targets and tasks of the revolution. It then traces the term from Lenin's writings of 1915–1920 through the early Party. It examines Tian Cheng's 1921 pamphlet, Zhang Tailei, Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen, Zhang Guotao and Qu Qiubai, and the documents of the Second and Third Party Congresses. It ends with Mao Zedong's usage from 1923 and his 1939 text On the Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party. Zhai makes three main moves. First, Lenin's "semi-colony" meant a state's semi-independent international position, whereas the Chinese formula extended it to the nature of society. Second, Zhai corrects claims in the literature about priority. Tian Cheng's 1921 pamphlet, not Cai Hesen or Chen Duxiu, is likely the first use by a Chinese person in China. The Second Congress (1922) documents already called China semi-colonial about five months before the Comintern's Fourth Congress did the same. They did not use the term "semi-feudal" or the full formula, which the Second Congress documents lack. Third, usage was uneven. Leaders such as Qu Qiubai and Li Lisan still wrote "colony" after 1922, while Party documents were more consistent and in 1928 even influenced a Comintern resolution. Zhai presents Mao as the most consistent user of the term, who never used "colony" for China beforehand. In the 1930s Mao treated China as semi-colonial overall but with colonial parts, notably the north-east after Japan's invasion. Zhai concludes that the formula was already in frequent use by Mao in the year or two before 1939, so the 1939 text did not originate it, though it gave the systematic theoretical statement. The origin of "semi-feudal" and of the fixed wording is left for a separate study. Read the original if you study early CPC history, the Party's relationship with the Comintern, or the textual genealogy of the "two halves" theory.

Pressing ahead with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party without pause: taking responsibility for solving the problems unique to a large party Studying Xi Jinping's important speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection 一刻不停推进全面从严治党 在解决大党独有难题上担当使命责任 Zhong Jiyan This commentary, published in the China Discipline Inspection and Supervision News on 19 January 2023, is a study piece on Xi Jinping's speech at the Second Plenary Session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The author argues that the speech gives the fundamental guidance for advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. In the author's account, the speech sets out why the problems unique to a large party arise, how they show themselves and how to resolve them. Discipline inspection and supervision bodies, the author says, must therefore keep a clear head and firm resolve in tackling them. The piece has three parts. The first explains the demand to keep up the fight against these problems and to see the Party's self-reform through to the end. The second covers the goals and tasks of building a system of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The third turns to the priority tasks of Party conduct, clean governance and the anti-corruption struggle, and to the high-quality development of discipline inspection and supervision work. The author lists six problems unique to a large party: keeping the original aspiration and mission; unifying thought, will and action; maintaining governing capacity; keeping up a spirit of enterprise; spotting and correcting its own errors; and sustaining a clean political ecosystem. The author says these call for treating full and rigorous self-governance as a long-term strategy and rejecting any hope that the tone will soften. The author describes the self-governance system as covering every aspect of Party building and rests it on institutions and Party rules. For discipline bodies, the author sets out six tasks: concrete, precise and routine political supervision; persistent enforcement of the central Party's eight-point regulations against the 'four undesirable work styles'; stronger discipline; a protracted anti-corruption fight that stresses 'one who is in charge' and 'flies' (petty corruption); a sounder Party and state supervision system; and a disciplined, loyal inspection corps. The author concludes that these bodies, as political organs, must support the Party's overall leadership and the Two Upholds. They must also make sure the decisions of the 20th Party Congress (2022) are carried out, and must reform themselves so that the Party never degenerates. The text is an authoritative official reading, not an independent analysis. Read the original if you want to see how the Party's discipline apparatus presented its tasks at the start of 2023, including its list of the six problems and its priorities for supervision and anti-corruption work.

Xi Jinping's creative development of Mao Zedong's view of labour 习近平对毛泽东劳动观的创造性发展 Liu Jia How does Xi Jinping's thinking on labour relate to the labour view of Mao Zedong? Liu Jia argues that Mao's view of labour, formed in the New Democratic Revolution and socialist construction, combined Marxism-Leninism with traditional Chinese labour culture. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Liu says, Xi has treated labour as a strategic question for national development and has developed Mao's view creatively, providing a basic guide for labour practice in the new era. The article has three parts. The first sets out four components of Mao's view: the foundational role of productive labour, the Marxist theory of labour factors, labour education and reform, and the cultivation of a socialist labour spirit and culture. The second turns to Xi's discussions of labour, grouped under happiness, values and education. The third draws lessons for present-day labour practice. On Mao, Liu stresses the slogan of increasing wealth through labour, the Yan'an-era production campaign, the use of labour as a criterion for class analysis, mutual-aid labour organisation, mechanisation of agriculture, the principle of combining education with productive labour, and the promotion of model workers such as Lei Feng. For Xi, Liu identifies three developments. Labour is the source of all happiness, linking individuals, society and the Chinese Dream. The model-worker, labour and craftsman spirits are presented as embodiments of the national spirit and the spirit of the times. Labour education is returned to its essential function of fostering moral character, in the framework of all-round moral, intellectual, physical, aesthetic and labour education. Liu also credits Xi with adding the concept of creative labour in 2013. Liu concludes that Xi's ideas orient labour toward the shift from becoming prosperous to becoming strong. The author calls for an innovation-oriented view of labour, to address the economy's weakness in innovation and "bottleneck" technologies, and for stronger labour education for young people. Liu also urges promotion of the model-worker spirit to build consensus on the value of labour. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese academic writing presents continuity between Mao Zedong's and Xi Jinping's thought on labour.

How Mao Zedong read the Marxist-Leninist classics 毛泽东如何读马列主义经典著作 Lu Weiming Ren Xin Lu Weiming and Ren Xin ask how Mao Zedong read the classic works of Marxism-Leninism and what that method offers readers today. They argue that Mao's approach was clear and well thought out, and that it still instructs Party members who want to read original texts, study original wording and grasp principles. In their account, this reading underpinned Mao's contribution to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article is organised around five features of Mao's reading: systematic and wide-ranging; selective and close; tied to history; tied to practice; and carried out against blind obedience. It follows Mao from the Jinggangshan base and the Long March through Yan'an, the civil war and the founding of the People's Republic. Examples include the Communist Manifesto, Lenin's Two Tactics and "Left-Wing" Communism, State and Revolution, and the Soviet Political Economy textbook. It also traces Party study institutions such as the Yan'an study groups, the 12 required books of 1949 and the Compilation and Translation Bureau of 1953. The authors contend that Mao read the whole body of the classics steadily and over decades, and urged the Party to do likewise, rather than quoting fragments. He read a few key works many times, including the Manifesto, at least 100 times by the authors' account, and changed his focus as circumstances changed. He read them against Party history, annotating Lenin and a Soviet philosophy text to trace Li Lisan-ism and adventurism to subjectivism. He also read them against practice, as in the 1958 turn to the Soviet textbook after the Great Leap Forward's problems. There, the authors say, he followed the book while doubting parts of it and offering his own views. Lu and Ren stress that Mao held the basic principles of Marxism to be unchanged but treated particular conclusions as tied to their historical setting. In this account, his opposition to dogmatism and "bookism" in the 1930s and the Yan'an rectification campaign led to his 1938 call for the sinification of Marxism. The authors conclude that studying his methods helps Party members raise their theoretical level and make reading the classics a lifelong habit, so that theory guides practice in the new era. Read the original if you want a Party-journal account of Mao's reading habits, with dated examples of the books he read and how Party study was organised.

From "heading for Yan'an" to "people-centred": Yan'an art under the influence of the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art Yan'an fine art after the 1942 Forum 从“奔赴延安”到“以人民为中心” Jin Xin Jin Xin asks how the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art, held by the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party in May 1942, changed the fine art produced in the Yan'an base area. The article argues that Mao Zedong's Talks at the Forum were a watershed for Yan'an art. In Jin's account, they turned artists who arrived with revolutionary enthusiasm but petty-bourgeois habits into revolutionary "literary soldiers" whose work was people-centred. Jin draws on artists who attended the Forum and on their works and recollections, including Cai Ruohong, Hua Junwu, Gu Yuan, Li Qun, Wang Shikuo, Zhang Ding and Jiang Feng. Contemporary comments by Lu Dingyi, Hu Man and Mao Dun also feature. The text has three main sections followed by a conclusion: the ideological remoulding of artists; the shift in their tasks, audience and creative focus; and changes in content and form. The central claim is that the Talks settled three questions for artists: who they are, whom they serve and how they serve. Jin describes many artists as trained in urban art schools and the Left-wing Artists' League, admiring Western modernists such as Matisse and Picasso, and producing satire and exposure of dark sides. After the Forum, going down to villages, factories and army units is said to have changed their standpoint and led them to adopt folk forms. Jin's key evidence is Gu Yuan's two woodcuts titled Divorce Suit. The 1940 version, with strong chiaroscuro influenced by Käthe Kollwitz, drew criticism from villagers. The 1943 version used clean outlines and folk-print methods and was accepted. Jin also cites Wang Shikuo's Reforming the Idler and Li Qun's Repairing a Spinning Wheel for the Villagers as works rooted in everyday life. Jin concludes that artists abandoned imitation of Western painting and drew on folk and local art. They produced new woodcuts, New Year pictures, comic strips and paper-cuts that, in the article's view, combined strong content with strong form. The Forum is presented as a turning point that began a new era of people-centred Chinese art, pointed it towards national and popular forms, and shaped art in the People's Republic and socialist literature and art more broadly. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholarship describes the Yan'an Forum's effect on visual art, with named artists, works and contemporary reviews.

Development and innovation of the fundamental system of upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere 坚持马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位根本制度的发展与创新 Wu Xueqin Writing after the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Wu Xueqin asks how the Chinese Communist Party came to make "upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere" a fundamental system, and how that system can be effectively implemented. The article argues that the system is one of the Party's basic institutions and an important component of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics. In Wu's account, it has been built up over a century and matured in the new era. The article has three parts. The first traces four historical stages: its emergence in revolutionary struggle, its formation and uneven development after 1949, its improvement during reform and opening up, and its maturation in the new era. The second sets out what the new era has achieved since the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) formally designated the system as fundamental. The third discusses five pairings through which the system should be implemented. Wu draws five lessons from the century of experience: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, propaganda and education, absorbing other cultural achievements, a Party-led cultural and educational structure, and winning discourse power. For the new era, Wu describes five achievements: a first task of implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; "four beams and eight pillars" that write the principle into the Party Constitution, the state Constitution and other laws; cyberspace governance; a responsibility system for ideological work; and coordination with other fundamental systems. On implementation, Wu pairs cultural confidence with institutional confidence, and preserving fundamentals with innovation. The author also pairs a coherent system with practical operability, accountability with the institutionalisation of accountability, and external rules with internalised conviction. Wu insists that academic debate be distinguished from questions of political principle. Wu concludes that the system must be made part of people's way of life if it is to work and to secure the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Wu calls for better organisational leadership, management and environmental mechanisms for ideological work, including online ideological security and stronger accountability. Read the original if you want a Party-theoretical account of how ideological leadership is institutionalised in China, with its periodisation, policy documents and prescriptions for ideological work.

A study of the editions of Capital 《资本论》版本考究 Cui Youping Hu Yi Marking the 155th anniversary of the first volume of Capital, this article surveys the principal editions that have appeared as the work spread worldwide. Cui and Hu argue that collecting and studying the editions of Marxist classics is foundational work for theoretical research. They present the editions as a way to retell the history of Capital's circulation, from its German origins to the twenty-first century. The article has four parts. It begins with the German editions, including Marx's three stages of preparation and writing, Engels's editing of Volumes 2 and 3, Kautsky's edition of Theories of Surplus Value, and later German collected works and the MEGA2 edition. It then covers the Russian, French, English and Japanese editions, followed by a shorter list of other languages. The third part treats publication in China, before 1949 and after, in minority languages and in Taiwan. The authors stress the special status of the German text as the main reference for all translations. They describe the second German edition of 1872 as the last Volume 1 that Marx revised himself, and the fourth edition of 1890, edited by Engels, as the most widely used. They note that the French edition of 1872–75 was personally revised by Marx, who added new material and restructured it, so that it has independent scientific value. For China, they trace a path from fragmentary excerpts to the Guo Dali and Wang Yaonan complete translation of 1938, then to the translations of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau, including those in the second Chinese edition of the Collected Works (2001–03). They also list popularisations, from Kautsky's and Borchardt's abridgements to illustrated and comic versions, and cite figures: 22 editions in nine languages in Engels's lifetime and over 220 editions in 43 languages by 1967. In the conclusion, the authors say the circulation of Capital expanded after the October Revolution and after the Second World War. It fell silent for a time after the Soviet collapse and has again become popular reading since the start of the twenty-first century. They end by calling for study of the basic principles of Marxist political economy under Xi Jinping's economic thought, to advance economic theory in serving socialist economic construction. Read the original if you need a detailed bibliographic guide to Capital's editions and translators in German, Russian, French, English, Japanese and Chinese, including the Chinese publishing history.

The three historical resolutions and Mao Zedong Thought 三个历史决议与毛泽东思想 Fan Xianlei Fan Xianlei asks how the Chinese Communist Party's three historical resolutions (1945, 1981 and 2021) treat Mao Zedong Thought, and argues that the treatment shows both continuity and development. In Fan's reading, the drafting of the three documents mirrors the formation, evaluation and ongoing innovation of Mao Zedong Thought. Studying them together is said to help in understanding Mao Zedong Thought correctly and in advancing the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article takes the resolutions in turn. It begins with the 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party and the establishment of Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology at the Seventh Party Congress. It then turns to the 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party since the Founding of the People's Republic, drafted under Deng Xiaoping's direction. It closes with the 2021 resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee. Each section ends with lessons Fan draws for the Party today. On the first resolution, Fan argues that it never uses the term "Mao Zedong Thought" but describes the same content under other names, so the signifier differs while the signified is the same. By criticising the "Left" line and presenting Mao's positions on new democracy, armed struggle, the mass line and seeking truth from facts, it prepared the theoretical ground for the Seventh Congress. For the second resolution, Fan reports Deng's insistence that defending Mao's historical standing and Mao Zedong Thought was the most important task. Deng treated the question as political, separated Mao's late-period errors from Mao Zedong Thought, and called the thought the collective wisdom of the Party. The resolution also summarised its living soul as seeking truth from facts, the mass line, and independence and self-reliance. For the third resolution, Fan stresses that it follows earlier conclusions while adding new understandings since the 18th Party Congress (2012). One example is recognising Mao's idea of a "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese realities as an enrichment of Mao Zedong Thought. Fan concludes that the Party's guiding ideas form an organic whole that is continuous and still developing, so that its stages must not be set against one another. Theory must be tested in practice and must keep summing up fresh experience. Leaders should be judged with dialectical and historical materialism, using Xi Jinping's "six cannots" standard. Fan presents the three resolutions as models of how the Party evaluates its leaders and promotes theoretical innovation. Read the original if you want a detailed account, from an official Party-history researcher, of how Mao Zedong Thought is positioned across the Party's three authoritative history documents.

Root causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 1) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（上） Li Shenming Writing on the centenary of the USSR's founding and thirty-one years after its end, Li Shenming asks why the Soviet Party and state collapsed. Li's answer is that, among many causes, the decisive one was the ideological and political degeneration of the leading group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev. Li presents this as the first part of a two-part study and ties it to Mao Zedong's call to study the Soviet case and to Xi Jinping's warnings about it. The article first argues that the top leadership, and the ideological and political line it follows, determine whether a ruling party keeps its character. It then sets out eight dimensions of degeneration: belief, theory, politics, economics, organisation, work style, foreign policy and outlook on life. Each is traced across the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods with Soviet and Russian testimony, memoirs and some American commentators. A closing section assesses twelve other explanations of the collapse. Li contends that Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin, his theories of the 'party of the whole people' and 'state of the whole people', and his 'peaceful' foreign policy line began the break with Marxism-Leninism. Brezhnev's period brought theoretical neglect, patronage networks, privilege and corruption. Gorbachev then completed the turn through 'humane, democratic socialism', abolition of the Party's leading role, privatisation and concessions to the West. Li presents Gorbachev's circle as a product of the Khrushchev line, not an accident, and as conspirators who concealed their aims. Li rejects rival explanations as one-sided or as reversing cause and effect. These include the 'original sin' of the October Revolution, the rigid Stalin model, nationality conflicts, the arms race, economic failure, Western pressure, one-party rule, and blaming Gorbachev alone. Li holds that the 'combined forces' view must identify the principal contradiction. Li warns that historical nihilism, which uses the denial of Soviet history to attack the Chinese Communist Party, must be resisted, and that a wrong conclusion could shake the foundations of the Party and the People's Republic. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Chinese Party theorist explains the Soviet collapse and its lessons for the Chinese Party today.

The root causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 2) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（中） Li Shenming This is the second part of a serialised article by Li Shenming, written for the centenary of the USSR's founding, on why the Soviet Communist Party and state collapsed. Li argues that the most serious lesson is that the Party's own construction failed, above all within its leading group. He presents the collapse as a catastrophe for the Soviet peoples and a gain for the United States, and draws warnings for China. This instalment sets out nine lessons. They cover Party-building and the fate of nations; the leader's convictions and the need for a strong leadership core; ideological and political clarity; constitutional entrenchment of Party leadership; communist ideals; two conceptions of reform; ideological work; absolute Party leadership of the army; and Western 'peaceful evolution' and the 'fifth column'. Li moves from Khrushchev through Brezhnev to Gorbachev, with citations from Russian officials, economists and former Soviet leaders. Li holds that from Khrushchev onwards the Soviet leadership drifted from Marxism-Leninism: it promoted 'peaceful coexistence', an 'all-people's party' and abstract humanism, and a privileged bureaucratic stratum grew up that was cut off from the masses. Gorbachev's 'reform' is described as a rejection of socialism itself, marked by abolishing Article 6 of the constitution, introducing a multiparty system, depoliticising the army and spreading historical nihilism, such as slanders of war heroes like Matrosov. Li then contends that the West ran a long strategy of peaceful evolution. In his account this worked through scholarships, foundations, Nobel prizes, NGOs and the cultivation of a 'fifth column' that put figures such as Gorbachev, Yakovlev and Yeltsin in power. He supports this with claims about CIA files, Masonic membership and statements by Soviet and Western figures. Li concludes that socialist states must never change their banner. They need a firm leadership core, Marxist guidance, control of ideological work, absolute Party command of the army and vigilance against infiltration. He ties these lessons to China, criticising 'constitutional democracy' as echoing Gorbachev's proposals and endorsing the post-2012 leadership's stress on ideology, struggle and the 2018 constitutional amendment on Party leadership. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist scholar draws political lessons for China from the Soviet collapse, including claims about Western subversion that readers will want to weigh against other sources.

Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and state (Part 2) Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示（下） Li Shenming This is the second part of Li Shenming's study of why the Soviet Communist Party lost power and the USSR dissolved, written for the 100th anniversary of the Soviet Union's founding. Part 2 turns from causes to implications for the Communist Party of China. Li's thesis is that the Soviet collapse is a warning to heed. He argues that China can avoid a similar fate only by upholding the Party's leadership core, its Marxist-Leninist orientation, public ownership and ideological struggle. The text sets out ten "implications", each beginning with "must". They cover leadership and succession, the Party's self-reform, economic construction and public ownership, ideological work, the Party's purpose and style, Party control of the army, foreign policy against hegemonism, cadre selection and youth education, Marxist theoretical study, and the correct judgement of the historical era. Li draws on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Chen Yun and Xi Jinping, and contrasts the Soviet record from Khrushchev to Gorbachev with China's practice. Li argues that the Party leader's being a firm Marxist can be decisive, so he calls for "unwaveringly" upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds and for guarding against "two-faced" people and conspirators in the leadership. He holds that the Soviet collapse resulted from a degenerated leadership dismantling public ownership. He also holds that class struggle persists in socialist countries and that historical nihilism, Western ideological infiltration and calls to depoliticise the army must be countered. Li reports shortcomings in China's own reform record, among them widening income gaps and one-sided promotion of household contracting. Finally, he contends that the world is still in the era of imperialism described by Lenin, so that courage to struggle comes first. He predicts a revival of world socialism within two or three decades. Li proposes concrete measures. These include education on the relations between leaders, Party, class and masses, five political criteria and public notice periods for senior cadre promotions, institutionalised Marxist study tied to appraisal and promotion, and the continued publication of Mao's Selected Works and of Xi Jinping's collected writings. He closes by expressing confidence in a bright future for world socialism and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Chinese Party theorist, writing before the 20th Party Congress (2022), draws policy lessons from the Soviet collapse in ideology, personnel and foreign policy.

Deeply grasping the important experience of Party building in the new era 深刻把握新时代党的建设的重要经验 Chen Zhigang Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Chen Zhigang asks what lessons can be drawn from the decade of Party building since 2012.
