Chen argues that under the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, the Party has been strengthened through a series of new ideas and strategies, has reversed what the article calls a lax and soft approach to Party discipline, and has found a path for escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. The article presents six lessons as valuable for understanding the laws of Communist Party governance and for advancing the "new great project" of Party building. The article is a commentary organised in six numbered sections, each stating one lesson: upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership; adhering to fundamental principles while breaking new ground; leading full and rigorous self-governance of the Party with political building; upholding the Party's nature and purpose; problem orientation; and a systemic approach to self-reform. Each section combines extended quotations from Xi Jinping with the author's summary of measures taken since 2012. In Chen's account, the first lesson is that the Party's leadership has been extended from political, ideological and organisational leadership to leadership over all work. It rests on the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, which Chen presents as the decisive factor behind the decade's achievements. Chen lists theoretical innovations, including the move from strict Party governance to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and from the "two musts" to the "three musts". These are said to have solved the problem of self-supervision and given a "second answer" to the historical cycle question. Chen links the Party's closeness to the people (the mass line, whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity) with an uncompromising anti-corruption stance. The article also describes a "combination of punches" of self-reform: political, ideological and institutional building, work-style rectification, and anti-corruption work. Chen concludes that these hard-won experiences must be continued and developed so that the Party remains the strong leadership core of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Chen calls for continued work on formalism and bureaucratism, corruption in key projects and posts, and new mechanisms for supervising top leaders. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-building lessons of the Xi era, as presented in a Chinese Party-building journal in late 2022.

Assessment of political developments in Vietnam in 2021 2021年越南政治发展动态评析 Pan Jin'e Pan Jin'e reviews Vietnamese politics in 2021, a year that combined the 13th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam, the five-yearly National Assembly and local elections, and a severe Covid-19 wave. The article argues that the political cycle ran smoothly overall and showed the Party's ability to set the country's course. It also contends that the year exposed unresolved problems: leadership succession, factional balance, weak governance in the pandemic and poor coordination between Party and state organs. The article is organised in four parts. It first covers the Party congress of January–February 2021 and its personnel outcomes. It then sets out the congress's medium- and long-term development strategy. A third part describes the elections and the work of the National Assembly and the Fatherland Front. A closing assessment draws conclusions. Throughout, Pan frames Vietnamese politics through the formula of Party leadership, state management and the people as masters of the country. Pan reads the congress's personnel arrangements as breaking established norms: Nguyen Phu Trong's third term as General Secretary, age exemptions granted through a 'special circumstances' rule, and a Politburo of 18 members with fewer southern members. Pan interprets this as a bid for stability and a sign that no agreed successor exists, and possibly a transitional arrangement. On strategy, the article lists Vietnam's 'two centenary' goals, with high-income developed status by 2045, plus twelve directions, six key tasks and three strategic breakthroughs. Pan notes that the congress report put little emphasis on theoretical work. In the assessment, Pan reports that Vietnam went from a model of pandemic control in 2020 to a major outbreak, that growth in 2021 was 2.58 per cent against a target of 6–6.5 per cent, that local authorities did not carry out central orders, and that strikes followed in 2022. Pan links these failures partly to a weakening of Party authority as 'rule of law' reforms advanced. Pan concludes that Vietnam's politics ran steadily but met real difficulties, and that meeting the two centenary goals will require more effort from political actors at all levels. The author argues that democratisation should avoid the flaws of Western political models, which the article describes as being in decline. It should instead preserve the strengths of Communist Party-led democracy and the capacity to concentrate resources on major tasks. Read the original if you want a China-based specialist's detailed, mixed assessment of the 13th Congress, Vietnamese elite politics and the pandemic's political consequences.

"Permanent struggle is extremely important" Understanding Mao Zedong's view of struggle in four dimensions “永久奋斗是非常要紧的” Cao Yingwang This newspaper commentary, published in Beijing Daily in January 2023, asks what Mao Zedong meant by "struggle" (fendou) and why he stressed it throughout his life. Cao Yingwang argues that Mao's outlook on struggle has four dimensions: struggle must be hard, united, permanent and selfless. In Cao's account, struggle ran through Mao's practice and is also visible in his poems and writings. The article takes the four dimensions in turn, moving through Mao's student years, the revolutionary period, the War of Resistance against Japan and the years of socialist construction. Cao draws on Mao's notes from his school days, his speeches, his essay On Protracted War, the 1939 talk "Permanent Struggle", the Seventh Party Congress (1945) and the inscription for the Monument to the People's Heroes. Lines from Mao's poems are used throughout as illustrations. On hardship, Cao reports Mao's view that plain living and hard struggle are the Party's "political qualities". Mao held that the weaker side could prevail only through hardship and that a poor country could become strong only by long effort, an outlook Cao also links to Chinese folk tradition. On unity, Cao says Mao treated it as the source of strength, but as a unity with principles, reached through the formula "unity–criticism–unity" and broad enough to include people who disagreed with or had opposed him. On permanence, Cao stresses Mao's demand that struggle last to the end of life and pass from generation to generation, since each victory brings new struggles and complacency is dangerous. On selflessness, Cao cites Mao's tributes to martyrs as proof that sacrifice for the people underlay the revolution's success. Cao concludes that China now stands in a time of "mountain flowers in full bloom" in which Mao could "smile among them", but argues that the country must still think of danger in times of safety. In Cao's view, the spiritual legacy Mao left remains a motivating force for the Chinese people's continued, successive struggle. Read the original if you want a short, source-rich presentation of how official Party historians present Mao's ideas on struggle, hard work and unity for a general readership.

A brief discussion of Mao Zedong's view of history and its practice 简论毛泽东的史学观及其实践 Zhou Suyuan Zhou Suyuan asks how Mao Zedong understood history and how that understanding shaped his political practice. The article argues that Mao's wide reading in historical works gave him a coherent view of history. In Zhou's account, this view treated the past as a valuable heritage to be respected, critically sifted and used for present purposes, and it informed his leadership at several decisive moments. The article has four parts. The first sets out Mao's historical outlook, together with the aims and methods of studying history that Zhou draws from his writings and talks. The second shows Mao drawing on history at key junctures: choosing Marxism-Leninism and the socialist road, the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside, the theory of protracted war, and the call to carry the revolution through to the end. The third examines three episodes the article calls the "Jiashen dialogue", the "Yaodong (cave dwelling) dialogue" and the "Ganka (sitting the exam) dialogue". The fourth considers how historical wisdom runs through Mao Zedong Thought and his education of cadres. Zhou's central claim is that Mao treated history as the place where laws of development are found and lessons drawn, and that he combined respect for the past with critical analysis. The article lists several features of his method: giving history a scientific place, studying failures as well as successes, reinterpreting old texts for current needs, and separating the fine from the dross. Zhou presents the three dialogues as warnings against the complacency of victory, using the fate of Li Zicheng's rebel army, and as Mao's answer to the "historical cycle" of dynastic rise and fall, which he said democracy and popular supervision would break. Zhou also argues that the three living aspects of Mao Zedong Thought, seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance, each have roots in classical sources, and that Mao redefined "seeking truth from facts" from a philological method into a Marxist epistemology. Zhou concludes that Mao's historical knowledge underlay his foresight and his optimism, which the article traces to his grasp of social development and to his view that errors are instructive. Mao also used historical anecdotes to urge cadres to study, guard against corruption and stay modest. Zhou presents these as lasting guidance on the laws of governing. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Mao's use of history is presented in official-academic writing, with many quotations from his speeches and letters.

An assessment of Bidet and Duménil's view of "another Marxism" 比岱与杜梅尼尔“另一种马克思主义”观评析 Wang Yicheng Wang Yicheng examines the claim by the European left theorists Jacques Bidet and Gérard Duménil, in Altermarxisme: Un autre marxisme pour un autre monde, that a new "other Marxism" is needed for a different world. The article asks what changes in contemporary capitalism led the two authors to say that the era of classical Marxism must be surpassed. It also asks what theoretical qualities "other Marxism" inherits and whether it really goes beyond Marxism in standpoint and method. Wang concludes that it contributes a sharp reading of capitalism's structural changes but departs from historical materialism. The article has three parts. The first traces how Bidet and Duménil place "other Marxism" in the history of Marxism, in relation to classical Marxism and what they call neo-Marxism. The second sets out their analysis of present-day struggle: a three-step strategy, the "world-state" and the age of "ultimate modernity". The third assesses contributions and limits. Wang links these ideas to Bidet's earlier "meta-structure" theory, developed in his work on Capital, Theory of Modernity and General Theory. Wang reports that Bidet and Duménil see modern society as ruled by two poles, market/capital and organisation. Class struggle is therefore a "three-way game" among capitalists, holders of organisational power and a "fundamental class" of wage-earners and other dominated groups. Their strategy runs from unification of this class, to an alliance with the organisational power-holders against capital, to continuing self-reform of new organisations so that new class structures do not form. They also argue that a "world-state" is emerging, which brings a "world people" into being and requires the struggle to be joined with Third World national liberation. Wang's critique has four points. The "meta-structure" dialectic is formal-logical deduction on a single plane, not materialist dialectic, so it cannot reach capitalism's essential contradictions. Class conflict is read as a purely political matter, resting on a critique of unrealised freedom, equality and reason. The authors dismiss the Leninist role of the Communist Party as vanguard and rely on spontaneity and plural social movements. Treating market and organisation as trans-historical leaves the organisation of the fundamental class absent. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Bidet's meta-structure theory and of Western left strategies of alliance and the world-state.

The Communist Party of China's creation of a new form of rule-of-law civilization: a historical narrative 中国共产党创造法治文明新形态的历史叙事 Fu Zitang Fu Zitang asks what is new about the rule-of-law civilization created under the Communist Party of China (CPC) over its first century. Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Fu argues that Chinese modernization includes a Chinese path of rule-of-law modernization, and that the Party's century of struggle has produced a new form of rule-of-law civilization. In the author's account this form breaks what Fu calls the West's monopoly over narratives of legal modernization. The article follows the Party's history from its Second Congress (1922) through the Jinggangshan land law, the Soviet-era constitutional outline, the 1954 constitution, the post-1978 reform period and the Xi Jinping era. It is organised around three dimensions of innovation: mechanisms, texts and discourse. Fu calls mechanisms the fundamental driving force, texts the visible result and discourse the inner construction. A closing section compares this with Western legal development. On mechanisms, Fu holds that the Party's leadership of law is a matter of constitutional fact. Fu traces the shift to governing in accordance with law and describes a mechanism in which the Party leads legislation, ensures law enforcement, supports the judiciary and takes the lead in obeying the law. Fu treats "is the Party or the law greater" as a false question and says the real one is whether power or law is greater. On texts, Fu sets out four moments: dawn, new beginning, system and codification. The last is marked by the 2020 Civil Code and by planned codes in administrative, environmental and educational law. On discourse, Fu points to two successive "sixteen-character" formulas, to rule-of-law faith, to good law and good governance, and to the "rule-of-law system" as an original category. In conclusion, Fu contrasts China's path with Western ones. Mechanisms are described as "autonomous" rather than home-grown or transplanted. Texts are said to follow neither common law nor civil law. Western legal discourse is described as stagnant and facing a "discourse deficit". Fu says the Chinese form favours exchange and mutual learning among civilizations over a clash of civilizations or imposed models. Fu calls for continued work guided by Xi Jinping's thought on the rule of law. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned periodisation of Party legal history and its main concepts, or an example of how Chinese legal scholarship frames comparison with the West.

Theoretical origins and contemporary lessons of Mao Zedong's thought on Party spirit 毛泽东党性思想的理论渊源与当代启示 Liu Zhifeng Liu Zhifeng asks where Mao Zedong's thought on Party spirit (dangxing) came from and what it offers Party building today. The article argues that the idea grew out of the practical needs of building the Party rather than from abstract theory, and that its development ran parallel to the Party's move towards unity. In Liu's account, ideological education and rectification campaigns were its main means of strengthening Party spirit. The article first traces how Mao's use of the concept changed, from a descriptive philosophical notion in 1936 to a practical tool after the Southern Anhui Incident, with the concept essentially formed by the Seventh Party Congress (1945). It then examines Mao's methods, drawing on his reports and resolutions of 1928–29 and on the Yan'an rectification movement of 1941–43. A final section draws lessons for the new era, citing the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Liu holds that Party spirit concerns the relation between part and whole, and between individual and organisation. Individuals and units have legitimate interests of their own, but if left unchecked these threaten the Party's unity. Lacking Party spirit therefore means failing to carry out the central leadership's directives, and Mao also counted dogmatism and subjectivism as such failures. Rather than replacing peasant-origin members with workers, Mao chose to change their thinking, building the Party ideologically. Liu describes the Yan'an rectification as the first large-scale, top-down programme of Party-spirit education. It relied on studying documents, writing reflection notes that Party bodies inspected, and criticism and self-criticism in a "curing the sickness to save the patient" spirit. Liu says this differed from Confucian self-cultivation because it was organised, political and compulsory. Liu concludes that Party spirit is a mark of a party's capacity, citing the contrast between the Communist Party and the Guomindang, and that it remains vital for a governing party, where its loss leads to corruption. The author calls for opposing the view that Party spirit is useless, for linking Party-spirit education to concrete problems, and for treating it as a tool of the Party's self-reform. Liu also argues that Party spirit does not conflict with human nature and individuality, and that its content must change with the times. Read the original if you want a Party-school scholar's account of how Mao's Yan'an-era methods are drawn on in current Party-building discourse.

Unity and struggle: the only way for the Chinese people to create historic achievements 团结奋斗是中国人民创造历史伟业的必由之路 Li Qinggang This commentary, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up one of the "five musts" (五个必由之路) that Xi Jinping's report presents as lessons drawn from the Party's long practice: unity and struggle as the only way for the Chinese people to create historic achievements. Li Qinggang argues that unity and struggle are the most distinctive spiritual hallmark of the Communist Party and the Chinese people. On this view, they carried the nation from "standing up" to "becoming prosperous" and now "becoming strong", and they must continue to guide the new journey. The article has three parts. The first traces unity and struggle through Marxist-Leninist tradition, classical Chinese sources and the Party's history. The second argues that unity must form around clear goals, and surveys the programmes the Party set in the revolutionary, socialist-construction and reform periods. The third sets out four requirements for the new journey toward the second centenary goal. In the second part, Li argues that unity without a goal is illusory and struggle without action is false. Li reads the Party's slogans and programmes as mobilising devices: the minimum and maximum programmes of the Second Congress (1922), the anti-Japanese united front and the "three-thirds" system, rent and interest reduction, land reform, the four modernizations, and Deng Xiaoping's "moderately prosperous family" goal. These, Li says, led to the building of a moderately prosperous society in 2021. The third part states four conditions: upholding Party leadership, guidance by scientific theory and shared ideals, maintaining the united front (with the People's Political Consultative Conference as its organisation), and being willing and skilled in struggle. Citing Mao Zedong, Li holds that unity comes through struggle and that seeking unity by concession destroys it. Li concludes that unity formed around clear goals is the firmest, and that the Party must keep to this method under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The text is a Party-school exposition for cadres rather than a historical study, and it draws on classical quotations, Party documents and a few foreign scholars such as Fairbank and Huntington. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party-school scholars present unity, struggle and Party leadership as continuous lessons of history after the 20th Party Congress.

Lenin's critique of the "Economists" in What Is to Be Done? and its lessons for today 列宁《怎么办？》对“经济派”的批判及其当代鉴示 Li Dongming Writing 120 years after Lenin's What Is to Be Done? (1901–02), Li Dongming asks what Lenin's polemic against the "Economists" was meant to achieve and what it offers the Chinese Communist Party now. The article argues that the critique served several purposes: defending the Party's leadership core and centralised, unified leadership, consolidating Marxism's guiding position as the Party's ideological basis, and strengthening its political leadership of the workers' movement. From these, Li draws practical lessons for Party building today. The first part examines the Economists' positions and the Russian Social-Democratic Party's condition around 1900. Li describes a Party with little central leadership, strong circle mentality, police repression and exiled leaders, in which the group around Martynov flourished. The second part treats economism as a Russian variant of Bernstein's revisionism, citing the 1899 \"Credo\" and the Economists' slogan of \"freedom of criticism\". The final parts turn to the present, and the text closes with a section on unity and struggle after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Li's central argument is that the Economists, by worshipping spontaneity, equating workers' economic associations with revolutionaries' organisations and denouncing a centralised organisation of professional revolutionaries as undemocratic, undermined the leadership core. Li adds that economism spread mainly because many members had little theoretical training. Lenin's response, in Li's reading, rested on the claim that there is no non-class \"third\" ideology, so that any disparagement of socialist ideology strengthens bourgeois ideology. Li reports that the struggle ended in 1902, when the Economists' main periodicals closed. Li draws four lessons for the Party today. It must struggle against words and deeds that weaken the leadership core and the authority of the Central Committee. It must strengthen Marxist theoretical study across the Party. It must criticise erroneous currents, which Li names as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, constitutional democracy and \"universal values\", and win the masses with the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. And it must \"speak politically\" and raise its political leadership, in support of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-school-style reading of Lenin's early polemic is used to justify present-day demands for discipline, ideological unity and leadership authority.

The Communist Party of China and the four historic leaps of Chinese modernization 中国共产党与中国式现代化的四次历史性跨越 Huang Yibing Following the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article asks how the Communist Party of China has advanced and extended Chinese modernization, which it defines as socialist modernization led by the Party. Huang Yibing argues that the Party's century of effort can be read as four historic leaps, each setting the course for the next. The article appeared in the journal Dang de wenxian (Party Literature) in late 2022 and was posted online in January 2023. The article moves chronologically. It begins with the failed modernization attempts after the Opium War of 1840 and the democratic revolution led by the Party. It then covers the Mao-era drive for the "four modernizations", Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style four modernizations" and the three-step strategy, and finally the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The last part sets out Xi Jinping's remarks on Chinese modernization, the 20th Congress's plans, and the significance of the Chinese path for socialism and for the world. Huang's core argument is that modernization could not succeed in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, so the Self-Strengthening Movement, the reformers and Sun Yat-sen's camp all failed. Citing Mao Zedong, Huang holds that new productive forces require prior revolution of the relations of production and superstructure, so national independence and liberation were the precondition. After 1949 the Party built an independent industrial system, avoided what it calls the Soviet one-sided emphasis on heavy industry, and set the four-modernizations goal. Deng's formulation, tied to the idea of a moderately prosperous society, adapted the goal to China's conditions. Huang credits the post-2012 period with five Chinese features of modernization, five major principles, and a comprehensive blueprint covering the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology. Huang concludes that Chinese modernization, as the article describes it, enriches modernization theory, offers a new path for governing a socialist state, widens routes to modernization for developing countries, and contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. The text closes by calling for firm adherence to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and to the Party's leadership in building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want an official Party-history account of how the leadership periodises Chinese modernization and links it to the 20th Congress line.

Comprehensively advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires continuing to uphold and strengthen the leadership of the Communist Party of China 全面推进中华民族伟大复兴必须继续坚持和加强中国共产党的领导 Zhu Jiamu Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhu Jiamu asks why the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation must continue to rest on the leadership of the Communist Party of China. Taking up the Congress report's statement that the key to building a modern socialist country lies in the Party, Zhu argues that Party leadership was the decisive factor in past progress and remains indispensable for the next stage. The article appeared in a journal on ideological and theoretical education. The article has three parts. The first reviews modern Chinese history to claim that only the Party was qualified to lead national rejuvenation. The second sets out seven contributions the Party made to that goal since its founding. The third turns to the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the tasks and risks ahead, and the practical, legal and theoretical grounds for Party leadership. Zhu's core reasoning is historical and class-based. Earlier efforts, from the Taiping movement to the 1911 Revolution, failed for lack of an advanced class and a correct path. In Zhu's account the bourgeoisie could not lead, so the working class, joined with Marxist intellectuals, formed the Party, which carried both socialism and anti-imperialism and feudalism. Zhu lists seven contributions: a socialist path, the political precondition of independence, three historic opportunities (the Korean War, the opening to the United States, and opening up), a stable environment, fitting development strategies, progress on national unification, and a revitalised national spirit. Zhu then argues from Marxist base-and-superstructure theory that public ownership as the main body of the economy explains China's one-party leadership under multi-party cooperation, and the Party's absolute command of the army. Zhu rejects multi-party electoral competition as the measure of democracy, calling Party leadership the primary form of whole-process people's democracy. Zhu concludes that without Party leadership there would have been no revolutionary victory, no new China and no rejuvenation. Zhu stresses that the remaining tasks are harder: modernization, unification, world peace and common prosperity, amid domestic problems and external pressure the author attributes to US-led hegemonism. Zhu calls for upholding Party authority and the Party's self-reform, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Read the original if you want a representative statement of how a senior Party historian grounds Party leadership in history, class analysis and Marxist theory after the 20th Party Congress.

Mao Zedong's considerations in handling Sino-Soviet relations and their contemporary value 毛泽东处理中苏关系的考量及其当代价值 Xu Hao Xu Hao takes up three claims about Mao Zedong's dealings with the Soviet Union that the author says circulate under the banner of "restoring history". The claims are that Mao's 1939 statement on the Soviet–German pact was meant to win Stalin's support, that he readily accepted leaving the old 1945 treaty unchanged, and that after Stalin's death he sought the leading seat in the communist camp. Xu argues that all three distort the record and slander the Party's leader. In Xu's account, Mao acted throughout from China's own interests, state sovereignty and the principle of equality. The article has four parts. The first treats Mao's 1939 remarks on the Soviet–German Non-Aggression Pact. The second covers the negotiation of the 1950 Sino-Soviet treaty, the return of the Changchun Railway, Lüshun (Port Arthur) and Dalian, and the 1969 Zhenbao Island clashes. The third examines relations between the two parties, Mao's assessment of Stalin, and the dispute over who should lead the socialist camp. The fourth draws lessons for present-day diplomacy and party-to-party relations. Xu argues that Mao assessed the 1939 pact dialectically and in light of the War of Resistance against Japan. In Xu's reading, the pact isolated Japan and strengthened China's position, and it was not a bid for Stalin's favour. On the 1949–50 talks, Xu says Mao did not endorse the old treaty. He pressed for a new one because the old treaty had been signed with the Nationalist government and would leave the People's Republic without political legitimacy. Mao's 1957 statements that the Soviet Union should "head" the camp, Xu says, meant only a convener of meetings, and he said China lacked the qualifications to lead. Xu says Mao opposed great-power chauvinism and the "father-son party" relationship. The polemics of the 1960s are presented as a struggle for equality, not for leadership, and Xu cites Deng Xiaoping's remark that the real issue was inequality. Xu concludes that Sino-Soviet relations under Mao yield three lessons. Sovereignty and territorial integrity cannot be bargaining chips, and Xi Jinping is cited in support. Equality should be the first principle of party-to-party relations, and Xu links this to the Party's present-day stance of neither "importing" nor "exporting" models. Foreign relations should also rest on the people's standpoint, which Xu connects to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends Mao's Soviet policy against Western and Russian accounts, and how that history is tied to current Party diplomacy.

How Mao Zedong read the Marxist-Leninist classics 毛泽东如何读马列主义经典著作 Lu Weiming Ren Xin Lu Weiming and Ren Xin ask how Mao Zedong read the classic works of Marxism-Leninism, and what that practice offers to Party members studying theory today. They argue that his method had five connected features: reading systematically and widely, reading closely with priorities, reading in light of history, reading in light of practice, and reading without blind obedience. In their account, this method helped Mao advance the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. The article moves through the five features in turn. It draws on episodes from Mao's life across the Jinggangshan years, the Long March, Yan'an, the civil war and the period after 1949. It also covers the Party's institutional study arrangements, such as study groups, a reading list of twelve books and the 1953 founding of the Compilation and Translation Bureau for Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin's works. On the first two points, the authors say Mao insisted on studying Marxism "systematically, not piecemeal". They cite his gathering of books under wartime conditions and his repeated reading of the Communist Manifesto, which they say he read at least a hundred times in several editions. On the next two, they describe Mao tying texts to Party history, for example Lenin's Two Tactics and "Left-Wing" Communism, annotated against right and "left" errors. They also describe him tying them to current tasks, such as the Yan'an rectification campaign and his 1959 reading of the Soviet Political Economy textbook after the Great Leap Forward. On the fifth, they present Mao as opposing "book worship" and dogmatism. In their reading, he held that the basic principles of Marxism are unchanged while particular conclusions may change, a stance they link to his 1938 call for the "sinification" of Marxism. The authors conclude that studying Mao's reading method can help today's readers master correct ways of studying theory. They quote a call to make reading the Marxist classics a habit and a spiritual pursuit. Their aim is to raise theoretical competence so that Marxism can guide practice and advance socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Mao's reading habits and of the Party's institutionalised theory study, as presented in an official Party-history journal.

From sense of adversity to bottom-line thinking: continuity and development across generations of Party leaders 从忧患意识到底线思维：党的几代领导人的坚持和发展 Yang Yucheng Yang Yucheng asks how the traditional Chinese sense of adversity (youhuan yishi) became the working method now called "bottom-line thinking" in Xi Jinping's leadership. The article argues that Chinese Communists combined the basic principles of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture and so creatively transformed the older outlook. In Yang's account, bottom-line thinking guards against risks that could delay or interrupt the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It also gives practical guidance on the question of escaping the "historical cycle of rise and fall". The article has three main parts. The first traces the sense of adversity from pre-Qin Confucian, Daoist and Mohist texts through later historians and officials. It then follows the Party's leaders: Mao Zedong's "prepare for the worst" at the Seventh Party Congress, Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and Xi Jinping's explicit formulation after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part defines the concept of a bottom line. The third part sets out what the method adds to the traditional outlook. Yang defines bottom-line thinking as setting the lowest objective, standing on that minimum, and striving for the best result. It has three linked elements: looking at the worst case, preparing fully, and working towards the best outcome. The author reads it through Marxist dialectics, as a form of "two-sided" analysis and an application of the law of the transformation of quantity into quality. A bottom line is the limit of the "measure" beyond which a thing degrades into a lower state, for example a socialist society that abandons the basic principles of scientific socialism. Yang adds that merely holding the line is not the aim, since the core value is achieving more while holding it. In Yang's view, traditional youhuan thinking was a warning rather than a scientific method, lacking tools for identifying crises or plans for resolving them. Yang concludes that bottom-line thinking makes traditional prudence concrete and operational. Combined with strategic, historical and innovative thinking, it points to two linked answers to the historical cycle. These are modernizing state governance through comprehensive deepening of reform, and the Party's self-reform through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Yang presents the two as a "two-wheel drive" and says the Party can thereby take solid steps beyond the cycle. Read the original if you want a Party School philosopher's account of how risk-prevention language in the Xi era is tied to Mao-era texts, classical Chinese sources and Marxist dialectics.

Comrade Mao Zedong's teaching on "studying Marxist-Leninist theory with a purpose" and the study of Capital 毛泽东同志关于“要有目的地去研究马克思列宁主义的理论”的教导与《资本论》研究 Wang Yanan Writing in 1965 (the text is dated Xiamen, April 1965 and was first published in China Economic Problems), Wang Yanan asks what Mao Zedong meant by studying Marxist-Leninist theory "with a purpose", and why that means "finding stand, viewpoint and method" in the theory. Wang argues that this is a question of principle, and that Capital is the best test case. Studying Capital for a concrete political task, rather than for its own sake, is in Wang's account the only way to avoid both dogmatism and revisionism. The essay opens from Mao's "Reform Our Study" and its contrast between subjectivist study and the Marxist-Leninist attitude of shooting the arrow at the target. It then discusses the universal truth of Marxism and the unity of stand, viewpoint and method. Next it asks why these must be sought in Capital and works through a case: the 1958 "Capitalist Manifesto" and the revisionist theory of socialised means of production. It ends by showing how Lenin, Stalin and above all Mao developed these principles. Wang's central move is that universal truth in Marxism is not a set of ready-made conclusions but the proletarian stand and the materialist-dialectical viewpoint and method. Because Marx and Lenin built their theories for their own conditions, later readers must ask what problems the theories solved and on what basis, then test how far they fit new conditions. Wang says readers tend to treat Capital as dogma, so a political task is needed. Applying this, Wang rebuts the "new exploitation" and "class harmony" theories, which Wang says rest on a doctrine of the productivity of capital. Wang argues, from Marx's analysis of constant capital and the reserve army of the unemployed, that rising organic composition intensifies exploitation, and reads Marx's "rebellion is justified" as the opposite of the bourgeois and reformist "exploitation is justified" and "struggle is useless". Wang concludes that each advance in Marxist theory also enriches the principles of stand, viewpoint and method. Mao's class analysis, On Practice and On Contradiction are presented as results of studying Marxism-Leninism and Capital with a purpose, applied to China's semi-feudal, semi-colonial class relations. Marxism, Wang says, has developed this way and must continue to. Read the original if you want a primary example of 1960s Chinese Marxist economics, with its method of reading Capital, its polemic against Western and revisionist theories, and its account of Mao's contribution.

The Communist Party of China's work to strengthen scientific and technical personnel during the full-scale War of Resistance 全面抗战时期中国共产党加强科技人才工作的实践 Wang Mengxin Wang Mengxin examines how the Communist Party of China handled scientific and technical personnel in the period of full-scale resistance to Japan (1937–1945). The author notes that existing scholarship mostly deals with Party science policy and intellectual policy at the macro level, and sets out to study the work on technical personnel itself: why it was strengthened, what was done and with what results. Wang's thesis is that the Party's systematic measures eased a severe shortage of talent and underpinned economic construction in the base areas. The article has three parts. The first explains the reasons: backward, blockaded base areas with little education, an urgent need for technicians, and mistaken attitudes among some Party cadres. The second, the longest, describes four sets of measures: training, recruitment, deployment and material treatment. The third assesses the outcomes and their bearing on the period after 1949. Evidence comes mainly from Party directives, regulations, editorials and recollections, with cases from the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region and the Jin-Cha-Ji Border Region. On the reasons, Wang cites the claim that 90 per cent of adults in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region were illiterate. Production drives and blockade-breaking needed engineers and agricultural experts, while some cadres belittled technical work or suspected experts of being used by Nationalist agents. On the measures, Wang describes the founding of schools such as the Yan'an Academy of Natural Sciences (1940), research societies and technical exhibitions. Wang also covers the 1939 decision on absorbing intellectuals and the 1942 regulations on treating cultural and technical cadres. The 1942 directive's formula of 'tolerate, transform, employ' (rong, hua, yong) is presented as the guiding approach to deployment, alongside responsible posts, working conditions, stipends, housing, food and rewards. Wang concludes that these measures produced a cohort of technical talent in chemistry, machinery and oil, and stimulated their revolutionary enthusiasm. As evidence the article cites grain output in the Shaan-Gan-Ning region rising from 1.116 million to 1.817 million shi between 1937 and 1944, and more than eighty public factories by July 1944. Wang argues that this laid an economic foundation for the new China and that the personnel stayed on as backbone forces after 1949. Read the original if you want a documented account, drawn from Party sources, of wartime Communist policy on technical experts and the Party's own view of it.

Advancing the new great undertaking of Party building Studying General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on Party building in the new era 推进党的建设新的伟大工程 Wu Chuanyi This article is a study-and-exposition piece on Xi Jinping's statements about Party building since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It asks what guides, structures and secures the Party's work in the new era. Wu argues that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has strengthened Party cohesion, and that the task is to build a Marxist governing party that can stay in power over the long term. The text is organised in three parts. The first sets out the fundamental guidance: guiding thought, the main thread and the overall goal. The second describes a strategic layout of seven areas: political, ideological, organisational, conduct, discipline and institutional building, plus the anti-corruption struggle. The third discusses three safeguards: serious intra-Party political life, methodological innovation through inspection and supervision, and the responsibility of Party committees. Wu treats long-term governance as the decisive question among the three major propositions of the Xi-led leadership. The author points to the Soviet Communist Party and India's Congress Party as former ruling parties that lost power, and presents Xi's thinking as a way to avoid that fate. The main thread is strengthening long-term governing capacity, advanced nature and purity. The overall goal is a strong leadership core, which Wu says is needed to unite a large, diverse country and build value consensus under a socialist market economy. Political building comes first, and the author calls it the Party's fundamental building. Wu draws on Chinese history, such as the late-dynasty corruption of land annexation and the ancient censorate. The author contrasts the censorate, which served imperial rule, with the Party's inspection and supervision system, which is said to answer to the Party and the people. Wu also reads the Party's internal regulations as drawing on traditional Confucian moral requirements. Democratic centralism is described as requiring both democracy and centralisation. Wu says its weaknesses appear as unchecked "top leaders" and as inadequate implementation of higher-level intentions. Wu concludes that advancing Party building must take account of a complex international and domestic situation and of diversified interests under the market economy. The author calls on the Party to hold to self-reform, to preserve its advanced nature and purity, and to let self-reform lead social revolution toward a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned overview of how Party-building priorities in the Xi era are categorised and justified.

Mao Zedong's opposition to "peaceful evolution" and its significance for Party building 论毛泽东反对“和平演变”及其对党建的意义 Cang Nan Wang Songping Cang Nan and Wang Songping ask how a socialist state can consolidate the dictatorship of the proletariat and avoid capitalist restoration through "peaceful evolution", the Western strategy of corrupting a movement from within. They open with Lenin's remark that the bourgeoisie, unable to suppress the workers' movement, seeks to "buy up its upper layer" and corrupt it from inside. The authors argue that Mao Zedong and the Chinese communists, building on Marxism-Leninism and earlier experience, answered this question in both theory and practice. In their account, this was a major contribution to the international communist movement. The article has two parts. The first traces Mao's warnings from 1949 onwards: the "sugar-coated bullets" speech to the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee, the "examination" metaphor of Li Zicheng, the 1951 "Three-Antis" campaign, and statements from the mid-1950s and 1962–64. The second part assesses what these ideas mean for Party building. In the authors' reading, Mao held that class struggle persists in socialist society and that the socialist road, people's democratic dictatorship, Party leadership and Marxism-Leninism must be upheld. From this they derive three measures against "peaceful evolution". Cadres must take part in collective productive labour, which they say changes cadres' outlook, brings them closer to the masses and gives equality a material basis. Ideological and political work must be strengthened as the "lifeblood" of economic work, because politics reacts back on the economic base. Successors must be trained according to five principles: practise Marxism-Leninism rather than revisionism; serve the majority; unite the majority; work democratically; and be open, modest and self-critical. The authors conclude that these ideas form part of Mao's theory of Party building, covering ideological, organisational and work-style construction. They say it shows that Marxism must remain the guiding ideology of the Party, that cadres and successors must be cultivated strategically, and that members' ability to discern right from wrong must be raised. They argue that some members fall to bourgeois values because they joined the Party organisationally but not ideologically, and that the remedy is serious study of Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic restatement of Mao-era anti-corruption and cadre-training doctrine as an argument for Party building today.

Rectifying research on Mao Zedong's ethical thought 毛泽东伦理思想研究辨正 Hu Dan Hu Dan asks how scholarship on Mao Zedong's ethical thought should be corrected so that it can contribute to a Sinicized Marxist ethics and to rebuilding China's contemporary ethical order. The article argues that existing research is weak in its paradigm, logical structure, theoretical standpoint and assessment of present-day significance. It proposes remedies on each of these four points. The article is organised in four sections. The first builds a distinct paradigm of Mao's 'practical ethics'. The second reconstructs a coherent line of development around self-realisation. The third fixes the theoretical coordinates of the research in historical materialism. The fourth sets out the contemporary significance of Mao's ethics. Each section first describes a tendency in the literature, then explains why it hinders further research. Hu first criticises the use of Western normative-ethics frameworks, which in Hu's account reduce morality to rules and neglect practical wisdom. Mao's practical ethics, the author says, differs in theme, object and task from descriptive, meta-, virtue, normative and applied ethics. It draws on Friedrich Paulsen's self-realisation idea and on Marx's practical materialism. Hu then rebuilds Mao's ethics as a four-stage system of rights, morality, ethical life and history. In this system, the early 'spiritual individualism' becomes, after Mao's turn to Marxism, the self-realisation of the proletariat and of humankind. Hu argues that Mao's ethics must be read through historical materialism, in which 'real people' and history explain morality rather than the reverse. Hu rejects both the view that Mao's ethics is obsolete and the proposal to replace collectivism with individualism in a market economy. Hu concludes that, in the new era, Mao's ethical thought should be read within a world-historical horizon and the aim of human emancipation. Combining it with the achievements of reform and opening up could, in the author's view, rebuild the ethical order and balance individual and society, and freedom and order. This would also help to construct an ethics with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese doctoral researcher frames the case for a distinct Maoist 'practical ethics' and rejects Western ethical categories and the 'obsolescence' thesis.

Re-examining Plekhanov's thought in the course of the Russian Revolution 俄国革命进程中的普列汉诺夫思想再审视 Ma Jiahong Ma Jiahong argues that Georgi Plekhanov's life and ideas can be understood only within the internal logic of the Russian Revolution. Earlier studies, the author says, concentrate on his theory or on verdicts about his merits and faults, and neglect the particular features of Russian revolutionary history. The article re-examines his political activity to explain both his early achievements and his later failures, and to sharpen understanding of what made the Russian Revolution distinctive. The article moves chronologically through four sections. It begins with Plekhanov's turn from Narodism to Marxism and the founding of the Emancipation of Labour group in 1883. It then covers his theoretical work of the 1880s and 1890s against the Narodniks. Next it looks at his clashes with Lenin over party organisation, the bourgeois-democratic revolution and the First World War. It ends with the deeper historical reasons for those clashes, drawing on Plekhanov's own writings on monism and the role of the individual in history. Ma first rejects the common view that Plekhanov's conversion simply reflected Russian capitalist growth and a rising working class. In Ma's account the economy of the 1880s was stagnant and the workers politically immature. The turn instead came from Russian intellectual history meeting Western Marxism, so Russian Marxism carried a "leap-over" tendency from the start. Ma then defends Plekhanov's historical materialism against charges of fatalism or mechanism. Plekhanov's tragedy, Ma contends, was that he refused to recognise the peculiarity of Russia, where a mature party and theory had formed before the working class had. This led him to oppose Lenin's tactics, treated as Blanquism, to reject seizing power in 1917, and to take a defencist line in the war. Ma adds personal factors: long exile, a bookish life and ties to the Second International. The deeper cause lay in a changing world-historical situation that theory could not yet resolve. Ma concludes that Plekhanov deserves credit for bringing Russian and Eastern socialism into the world movement, but that his theoretical outlook limited his political agency. He was remote from Russian conditions, strong in abstraction but weak in judging concrete situations and building a revolutionary organisation. He tended to ask whether revolution was feasible rather than what it made possible. For Ma, universal theory takes effect only through particular experience, and political possibility comes from uniting the two. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reassessment of Plekhanov that sets him against Lenin and the specific path of the Russian Revolution.

Relying on the Party's self-reform to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall 依靠党的自我革命跳出历史周期率 Yan Xiaofeng How can a Marxist party that has ruled for a long time keep its nature and purpose and escape the cycle of dynastic rise and fall? Yan Xiaofeng, writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), argues that the Party's self-reform is the "second answer" to this question, following Mao Zedong's first answer of supervision by the people. The article presents self-reform as the deepest logic of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and as the key conclusion on building a long-ruling Marxist party. The article has four sections. It first sets out why the cycle is a fundamental problem, drawing on imperial dynasties, peasant uprisings and the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party. It then traces the Party's search for an answer from the Yan'an "cave conversation" of 1945 to the present. A third section reviews six areas of Party building under Xi Jinping: political, ideological, conduct and discipline, anti-corruption, organizational and institutional work. The last draws four conclusions about building a long-ruling party. Yan reads the cycle through historical materialism: earlier ruling groups represented a minority and so could not resolve their conflict with the people, and could not reform themselves. The two answers form an organic whole, with supervision by the people acting from outside and self-reform from within. Yan argues that supervision by the people supplies the political guarantee and motivation for self-reform, while self-reform internalises that supervision. Each is incomplete without the other. In Yan's account the Soviet party failed because it became a privileged bureaucratic group unable to reform itself. Yan concludes that a long-ruling Marxist party must hold to a Marxist view of power ("the country is the people"), have no special interests of its own, and keep its founding mission. It must also keep the resolve to turn the blade inward so that the Party does not change in nature, colour or flavour. Anti-corruption is described as the most thorough form of self-reform, and Yan stresses that self-governance "is always on the road". Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the 20th Party Congress framed self-reform as a way out of the historical cycle.

Mao Zedong's arduous exploration of China's path of socialist construction and its contemporary value, in the perspective of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 中华民族伟大复兴视阈下毛泽东对中国社会主义建设道路的艰辛探索及其当代价值 Li Liangming Lin Li This article, published in Theoretical Journal (Lilun xuekan) in 2022, asks how Mao Zedong's search for a path of socialist construction should be understood in light of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and what it offers for the second centenary goal. Li and Lin argue that Mao's exploration, though marked by errors, laid the political, institutional and theoretical foundations for later reform and for socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article opens with the socialist transformation of the early 1950s and then has three parts. The first treats the mid-1950s: the speeches "On the Ten Major Relationships" (1956) and "On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People" (1957). The second examines theoretical results from the corrective work of 1958–59 after the Great Leap Forward and the people's commune movement. The third draws three lessons for today. A passage in the middle also rebuts Western scholars whom the authors accuse of historical nihilism. In the authors' reading, Mao used the Soviet experience as a warning. He called for the Second Integration of Marxism with Chinese conditions, and he shifted the emphasis towards agriculture and light industry, local initiative and balanced interests. The authors credit the corrective period with four original results: the idea of an "underdeveloped socialism" stage, an endorsement of commodity production and the law of value, "to each according to his work" as the socialist distribution principle, and insistence on seeking truth from facts against exaggeration. They hold that mistakes arose from limited experience and a leftist climate, and that the Party after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) completed what Mao began. They cite Xi Jinping to insist that the periods before and after reform and opening up must not be set against each other. The authors draw three lessons. First, keep both the global and the domestic situation in view and keep developing Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions. Second, combine fidelity to fundamentals with innovation, so that Chinese modernization stays within the bounds of Party leadership and the socialist direction, and differs from capital-centred Western modernization. Third, use socialist political economy with Chinese characteristics, tracing the line from Mao's commodity-economy ideas to the socialist market economy, the dominant public sector alongside multiple forms of ownership, and a market-plus-government mix. Read the original if you want a Party-historiography account that links Mao's 1956–59 writings to current official theory on modernization, ownership and the market, and to the official line on the two periods.

Zhou Enlai's eight contributions to the cause of the Party and the people 周恩来对党和人民事业的八大贡献 Liu Chunxiu Liu Chunxiu sets out to summarise Zhou Enlai's career under eight headings, presenting him as an outstanding Party leader who emerged from the historical conditions in which the Communist Party of China was founded a century earlier. The article, a commemorative biographical overview, argues that Zhou made distinguished contributions to nearly every major victory of the Party and the people, and that his conduct remains a model for Communists. The article follows Zhou's life chronologically within thematic sections. It covers his early search for truth and joining the Party in Paris in 1921; his military work from the Whampoa Academy to the Nanchang Uprising, the Long March, the war against Japan, the civil war and the building of national defence; and his direction of the Party's secret work. It then treats his support for Mao Zedong's leadership, his united front work, his role as premier in economic construction after 1949, his diplomacy, and his personal character. Liu's central claims are that Zhou was loyal to the Party at moments of crisis and that he put the Party's unity first. After the 1927 defeat he organised the evacuation of Party members, and he later accepted the dominance of the dogmatist 'Left' line for the sake of unity. At the Zunyi Conference (1935) he took responsibility for the military failure and backed Mao, which Liu says was decisive for Mao's leadership position. Liu also credits him with founding the Central Special Branch, the Party's radio communications and code-breaking work, and the united front with the Kuomintang. After 1949, the article says, he helped design and carry out the First Five-Year Plan and shaped the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, his diplomacy at the Geneva and Bandung conferences, and the normalisation of relations with the United States and Japan. Liu concludes that Zhou's faith, selflessness, probity and diligence made him an 'immortal banner' for Communists, citing Xi Jinping's assessment, and that his spirit helped build the Party's image among the people. The article's tone is celebratory and it relies on official evaluations of Zhou. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese account of Zhou Enlai's career and of how Party historians present his role beside Mao Zedong.

Some reflections on building an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese historiography 关于建构中国历史学自主知识体系的几点思考 Zhu Hu Writing in Guangming Daily in January 2023, Zhu Hu asks how Chinese historical scholarship can build its own autonomous knowledge system, in response to Xi Jinping's call to construct an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in philosophy and the social sciences. Zhu argues that this task is necessary both for the internal development of the discipline and as part of criticising the cultural hegemony of Western knowledge systems. The piece is a short commentary rather than a full research article. The article opens with Xi's statements that history underpins all social sciences and with his hope, expressed in a letter to the Chinese Academy of History, for a discipline, academic and discourse system with Chinese characteristics. It then sketches Chinese historiography from its long premodern tradition through the shock of Western academic influence, to Marxist historiography in the revolutionary, construction and reform periods. Zhu next diagnoses current problems and closes with four proposed directions for construction. Zhu identifies several problems. Marxist guidance has weakened since the late twentieth century, which Zhu attributes partly to unresolved dogmatism and partly to imported Western schools, some of which are said to have encouraged historical nihilism. Zhu also points to fragmentation, with ancient and modern history, world history, archaeology and the auxiliary fields each retreating into their own walls. The discipline's scope is said to be narrowed and its practical function weakened, because specialised histories within economics, law or politics lack proper historical training. The four proposals are: adhere to Marxist guidance and practical application; honour traditional foundations such as the 'four keys' of official posts, geography, bibliography and chronology, together with the Marxist theory of social formations; broaden vision and answer the questions of the era, including those of Chinese modernization; and integrate fields and interdisciplinary work in a professional way. Zhu concludes that philosophy and the social sciences, history included, reflect a nation's intellectual capacity and comprehensive national strength. Zhu calls for accelerating the discipline, academic and discourse systems of Chinese historiography under historical materialism, while engaging in international exchange. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese historian, writing in an official newspaper, links Xi Jinping's guidance on autonomous knowledge systems to concrete diagnoses of the history discipline.

The new-era logic of the period of strategic opportunity A strategic-philosophy analysis based on Marx's thought on world history 战略机遇期的新时代逻辑 Xin Ming Xin Ming asks how China's "period of strategic opportunity" should be understood in the new era. The article reads it through Marx's thought on world history and the methods of what the author calls strategic philosophy. Xin argues that the period is not a gift of circumstance. It is a objective strategic situation that the strategic actors, China included, jointly bring about through correct strategy. Its content has changed substantially since the 1980s, and the Party's continued use of the term signals what Xin calls a high degree of strategic self-awareness. The article has four parts. The first traces how the concept was formed. It was formally put forward at the 16th Party Congress (2002), but it builds on Deng Xiaoping's judgments from the 1980s about peace and development. The second analyses changes in the strategic environment: the world pattern, the era and history. The third examines how China's strategic goals have moved from the "three-step" plan to the present two-step plan for a modern socialist country. The fourth sets out strategic responses suited to the new era. Xin's core argument is that environment and goals together reshape the period's meaning. On the environment, the author describes the rise of emerging economies, the weakening of Western dominance and the drive of new technology towards a more interconnected world. Xin draws on Lenin's account of a revolutionary situation and on Marx's statements about world history to read these shifts as part of a historical logic. On goals, Xin cites the shift from solving subsistence needs to building a modern socialist power that is "leading" in comprehensive national strength. Because the West now treats China as its main strategic competitor, the author contends that earlier restraint (taoguang yanghui) no longer fits. Xin proposes three responses. The first is active struggle backed by strength. The second is turning two-sided rivalry into multi-actor games, as in Mao Zedong's "three worlds" idea. The third is reshaping strategic perceptions through shared human values and cooperation. Xin concludes that, although risks have multiplied, time and momentum remain on the side of China and the emerging countries. China can therefore still treat its present stage as an important period of strategic opportunity if it acts in line with historical trends. The author presents the Party's persistence with the concept as proof of a historical initiative that goes beyond opportunism. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar combines Marxist world-history theory with strategic analysis to justify the continued use of the "strategic opportunity" judgment.

How the Communist Party of China came to understand modern China as "semi-colonial" 中国共产党对近代中国“半殖民地”社会性质的认识历程 Zhai Yu The article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) arrived at the "semi-colonial" half of the standard characterisation of modern China as "semi-colonial and semi-feudal". Zhai Yu argues that the judgment was largely the Party's own independent conclusion, reached from its reading of China's circumstances, and not a verdict handed down by the Communist International (Comintern). Lenin supplied the term, but early CPC figures applied it to China before Comintern documents did. Zhai first sets out the standard theory and Lenin's use of "semi-colony" between 1915 and 1920. The article then corrects several claims in the CPC-history literature about who first used the term, taking in Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen, Zhang Tailei, Qu Qiubai, Zhang Guotao, Li Lisan and Mao Zedong. It follows the Second, Third and Fourth Comintern-related meetings and the CPC's Second and Third Congresses, and ends with Mao's writings of the 1920s and 1930s. On priority, Zhai holds that Cai Hesen was not the first to apply the term to China, since Chen Duxiu did so a month earlier in 1922. A pamphlet signed "Tian Cheng", dated June 1921, probably contains the first use by a Chinese author inside China. Zhai also argues that the Second Congress (1922) used the idea of China as a semi-colony months before the Comintern's Fourth Congress did, so the common claim that Comintern meetings gave the CPC this view is, in Zhai's account, historically wrong. Zhai adds that the Second Congress documents do not call China "semi-feudal" or use the fixed phrase. Zhai then shows that leaders' usage wavered between "colony" and "semi-colony" until the mid-1920s, while Party documents were more consistent and later influenced the Comintern's 1928 resolution. Mao used "semi-colony" consistently from 1923 and tied it to the survival of Red base areas amid imperialist rivalry. In the 1930s he warned that Japan sought to turn China into a full colony, and Zhai notes that Mao's 1939 essay The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party gave the systematic statement of the theory, though he had used the phrase earlier. Zhai leaves the origins of the "semi-feudal" half for separate study. Read the original if you are interested in CPC history, the Comintern's role in early Party thought, or detailed source-based disputes over who first used key terms.

From deism to militant atheism The evolution of modern Western atheism 从自然神论到战斗的无神论 Zhang Heng Zhang Heng asks how atheism developed in modern Europe and what it handed on to Marxist atheism. The article argues that, from the English revolution of 1640 onwards, the rising bourgeoisie needed to criticise religious theology to free thought, develop science and attack the divine right of kings. In Zhang's account, this produced a sequence running from deism and pantheism to the thoroughgoing materialist 'militant atheism' of eighteenth-century France, which in turn became a source of Marxist atheism. The article has four sections. The first treats deism in England, with Francis Bacon, Hobbes, Tindal and Locke. The second treats pantheism and Spinoza's philosophy of substance. The third covers the French atheists La Mettrie, Helvétius, Diderot and d'Holbach. The fourth sets out what Marxist atheism inherited from them and ends with lessons for present-day atheist propaganda and religious work. Zhang's central claim is that each stage dislodged God a little further. Deism kept God as a rational lawgiver outside nature. Pantheism, above all Spinoza's 'God or nature', dissolved God into nature and denied creation and the divine right of kings. The French thinkers, in Zhang's reading, joined atheism to a monist materialism: matter in self-generated motion, with some dialectical features, an emphasis on both sensory and rational knowledge, and the idea that humans are products of their environment. They also treated religion as a tool of feudal absolutism, and Zhang presents this as the revolutionary significance of the French Revolution's 'theoretical banner'. Zhang follows Marx in judging that the French atheists explained religion's origins superficially, since they treated reason and education as the motor of history. Their critique of religion was only the 'embryo' of a critique of the real world, and Marx and Engels carried it on towards communism. Zhang then calls for atheist education that reflects its era, draws on Chinese and foreign atheist heritage, and views religion through historical materialism so as to guide it to adapt to socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language survey of how the Marxist tradition narrates the lineage from deism to French materialism, and how that history is tied to current atheism work.

An analysis of Mao Zedong's discourse on "not fearing ghosts" 毛泽东关于“不怕鬼”的论述探析 Tang Zhengmang Wang Juan Tang Zhengmang and Wang Juan examine Mao Zedong's call in the late 1950s and early 1960s not to fear "ghosts", a metaphor for external enemies, natural disasters and difficulties at home. The article opens from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which urges the whole Party and people to carry forward a fighting spirit that is "not afraid of ghosts". The authors argue that Mao's remarks showed courage and a conscious art of struggle, and that they remain a resource for the present. The article has three parts: the historical background, the main content of Mao's remarks, and their influence. For the background, the authors describe an international and domestic setting in which, in their account, the United States, Britain, India and the Soviet Union all put pressure on China. At home, they point to the setbacks of the Great Leap Forward, the people's communes and severe natural disasters. They also trace Mao's proposal for the 1961 booklet Stories of Not Fearing Ghosts, edited by He Qifang, and his revisions to its preface. The core argument has three strands. First, Mao's "ghosts" are not supernatural. The authors say they stand for imperialism and reactionaries, severe natural disasters, and faults, errors and setbacks in work. Second, Mao held that "the more you fear ghosts, the more ghosts there are", and the authors read the shelling of Jinmen and the suppression of the 1959 Tibetan rebellion as applications of this view. Third, they stress his formula of despising ghosts strategically while taking them seriously tactically, which they present as a development of his earlier principle that reactionaries are "paper tigers". They link the strategic part to dialectical reversal through struggle and to breaking superstitions about imperialism, and the tactical part to careful, shrewd handling of each concrete case. On influence, the authors claim that the "not fearing ghosts" spirit strengthened resistance to external pressure, including the Soviet withdrawal of experts in 1960. They also credit it with supporting the post-Great Leap economic readjustment, the 1961 investigation drive and the "sixty articles" on agriculture. They add that translations of the booklet spread the message abroad. They conclude that the discourse expresses a spirit and working method of daring and skilful struggle, and urge readers to revisit it on the new journey towards the second centenary goal and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of how Mao's "ghost" metaphor is being presented in official scholarship after the 20th Party Congress.

The view of the times embedded in Mao Zedong's On Protracted War 毛泽东《论持久战》蕴含的时代观 Cao Yingwang Cao Yingwang asks what conception of the historical epoch underlies Mao Zedong's On Protracted War (1938), the programmatic text for the Communist Party's leadership of the War of Resistance against Japan. Cao argues that Mao's attention to era, situation and trend is central to his method, and that the work's view of the times explains why the war would be protracted and why China would win. In Cao's reading, China was in an "age of progress" and Japan in an "age of regression", and the Communist Party's existence and leadership were the decisive marker of China's progress. The article has three parts. The first sets out the foundation of Mao's analysis, the contrast between the two belligerents' four features, and the epochal characteristics Mao identifies. The second examines five marks of China's "age of progress" named in the text: the Communist Party, an awakened people, the bourgeoisie and proletariat with a broad united front, a politically progressive army, and decades of revolutionary experience. The third assesses the historical influence of this analysis, including its treatment of the Nationalist Party. Cao contends that the defeatist view of "national subjugation" could not be refuted by China's size alone, since history offers cases of small, strong states conquering large, weak ones. Mao's further ground, as Cao presents it, is the character of the era: Japan's decline and isolation against China's progress and international support, shaped by the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. Cao ties each marker to the Party: mobilising the people through the mass line, the army's three political principles, the united front, and Marxist ideological, political and military lines that supported guerrilla warfare. The Nationalist Party, in Cao's account, had a dual character and made only limited progress, while mistaken views that downplayed Communist-led guerrilla war reflected a flawed view of the times. Cao concludes that, under the conditions of that era, Communist leadership organised the people, sustained protracted war through guerrilla warfare and enabled China to shift from weakness to strength. Abandoning that leadership and independence, Cao says, would have rewritten China's fate. Cao links this to the present: upholding the Party's centralised and unified leadership, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform are presented as what the rereading of On Protracted War should reinforce. Read the original if you want a Party-historian's interpretation of Mao's wartime thought, with extensive quotation from Mao's texts, and of how the Party's leading role is justified through the idea of historical epoch.

Atheist thought in the Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan and its implications 《湖南农民运动考察报告》中的无神论思想及其启示 Liu Fujun Liu Fujun asks what atheist thought is contained in Mao Zedong's 1927 Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, and what it offers today. The article argues that, besides setting out basic theory and policy on the peasant movement, the Report answered the question of how to understand and treat "divine authority" (shenquan). In Liu's reading, it thereby opened a path for adapting Marxist atheism to Chinese conditions. The article was published in Science and Atheism, 2022 no. 6. The article is organised in four parts, each built around a triad. It first sets out the background to the Report during the 1924–1927 National Revolution: Mao's 32-day, 700-kilometre survey of five Hunan counties, and the Report's wide circulation. It then analyses the Report's content, assesses its historical standing, and ends with lessons for the present. Liu draws on Mao's earlier writings and later investigations, including the Xunwu, Changgang Township and Xingguo surveys, as well as texts by Zhou Enlai, Qu Qiubai, Yun Daiying and Lenin. Liu argues that the Report's atheist thought took shape from three conditions: divine authority had become a rope binding the people and obstructing the democratic revolution; Marxist atheism had become the Party's scientific theory; and Mao had become a firm Marxist atheist. Its core content answers three questions. What is divine authority? It is part of the feudal clan system, subordinate to political power. Why overthrow it? It exerted spiritual oppression and economic exploitation. How? By overthrowing landlord power, leading economic struggle, expanding education and culture, and propagating atheism. Liu stresses the Report's principle that peasants should discard the idols themselves, without coercion or premature substitution by others. He adds that propaganda should be tied to solving practical problems such as land and rent. Liu draws three present-day lessons. The long-term roots of theism, which Liu lists as natural, epistemological and psychological, persist in the primary stage of socialism. Marxist atheism must keep being adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Atheist education must serve the Party's central tasks while respecting freedom of religious belief and uniting believers, citing Xi Jinping's 2018 remark that ignorance, backwardness and poverty are the real "ghosts". Read the original if you want a Party-line account of how Mao's early rural investigations are used to ground current official policy on atheist propaganda and religion.

The Communist Party of China and the four historic leaps of Chinese modernization 中国共产党与中国式现代化的四次历史性跨越 Huang Yibing Written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has advanced and extended Chinese modernization over a century. Huang Yibing argues that the process can be read as four historic leaps, each led by the Party: finding the correct direction, striving for the "four modernizations", defining a distinctively Chinese version of them, and now building a modern socialist country in all respects. The article stresses that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization under Party leadership and rejects both a closed, rigid old path and a path of changing the Party's banner. The article follows a chronological structure. It begins with failed modernizing projects after the Opium War (the Self-Strengthening Movement, the reformers around Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, and Sun Yat-sen's industrial plans) and then the New Democratic Revolution.
