It moves to the Mao-era industrial system and the "four modernizations", then to Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style" modernization, the "three-step" strategy and the goal of a moderately prosperous society. The last section covers the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the 20th Congress blueprint. Huang's central claim is that modernization in a semi-colonial, semi-feudal China was impossible without first revolutionizing the social order. Citing Mao Zedong, the author holds that new productive forces cannot grow under imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, so national independence and popular liberation were preconditions. Later leaps are presented as continuous adaptation to national conditions, from avoiding the Soviet pattern of neglecting light industry and agriculture to Deng's modest "xiaokang" target. For the present, Huang summarises Xi Jinping's statements on the five features of Chinese modernization, its essential requirements and five major principles, and the Congress's plans in the economy, politics, culture, society and ecology. Huang concludes that Chinese modernization offers a new path for socialist governance and gives developing countries an alternative to the Western model. The author describes it as a "parallel" process, with industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization advancing together, in contrast to the "serial" Western sequence. The article also presents it as a peaceful path that contributes to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an official-line, Party-history narrative that links the Opium War, Mao, Deng and Xi into a single account of modernization just after the 20th Party Congress.

Rethinking Marx's "threefold transcendence" of Bauer's critique of religion A textual interpretation based on On the Jewish Question 重思马克思对鲍威尔宗教批判思想的“三重超越” Zhang Man Zhang Man asks how Marx's On the Jewish Question relates to Bruno Bauer's The Jewish Question, and argues that Marx surpassed Bauer's critique of religion in three respects: the object of criticism, the theoretical line, and the proposed solution. The article starts from a complaint about existing scholarship. In the author's account, Bauer is usually read only through Marx's quotations and paraphrases, so his insights are neglected and his contribution to Marx's thought is underrated. The article uses the two titles as its core texts and is organised in three sections matching the three points of divergence, followed by a short conclusion. It draws on commentators such as David McLellan, David Leopold, David Ingram and Michael Maidan, and on Marx's later remarks in Capital. Zhang first reconstructs Bauer's own position, then sets Marx's replies beside it. On the object of criticism, Zhang says Bauer treated the "so-called Christian state" as the target, and so held that Jews lack human rights and civil rights because of their religion and egoism. Marx, drawing on the French and North American declarations of rights, shows that freedom of belief and egoism are themselves recognised in the rights of man. He turns attention to the "truly Christian state", a democratic state that treats religion as one element of civil society. On the theoretical line, Zhang argues that Bauer stayed within theology, whereas Marx moved the question into civil society, money and egoism, converting theological questions into worldly ones. This, Zhang suggests, prepared Marx's later turn to political economy. On the solution, Bauer demanded the abolition of religion. Marx replied that political emancipation does not require this, since religion persists in states that have achieved it. Zhang adds that Bauer confused political emancipation with human emancipation, which Marx distinguished. Zhang concludes that Bauer's thinking was shallow and offered no workable solution, yet it opened a window for Marx and left a lasting mark on his method, as McLellan says. The author adds that Marx's approach to religion in this text still has value today. In Zhang's view it can guide the application of Marxist religious theory to contemporary religious questions. Read the original if you study the Marx–Bauer relationship, the young Marx's critique of religion, or how Chinese scholarship presents Marxist religious theory.

Why Mao Zedong called the Rectification Documents a "classic" 毛泽东为何称《整风文献》为经书 Hu Weixiong In November 1942, speaking to a conference of senior cadres in north-west China, Mao Zedong called the documents of the rectification campaign "a classic" (jingshu). Hu Weixiong notes that scholars have rarely asked why, and that some, influenced by foreign scholarship, hold that the collection contains no Marxist classics. The article analyses the choice of items and the structure of the Rectification Documents (Zhengfeng wenxian) to explain in what sense Mao could call them a classic. Hu concludes that the collection is a classic of Party-building whose core is the union of Marxist-Leninist truth with Chinese revolutionary practice. Hu first reconstructs the editions: 18 documents in April 1942, 22 after additions, then a revised edition rising to 27 items by 1943. Taking the 27-item version, the article sorts the contents into four groups: rectifying the Party's style of study, Party work and writing; Party members' self-cultivation and organisational building; leadership, cadre policy, inner-Party struggle, discipline and democracy; and the Party's mission, propaganda and leadership, including Bolshevization. It describes the main items in each group, then assesses the collection's place in the history of Chinese Marxism. Hu's central claim is that the first group is the core. He singles out Mao's "Reform Our Study", "Rectify the Party's Style of Work" and "Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing" as foundational texts attacking subjectivism, dogmatism, sectarianism and formulaic writing, and urging investigation of Chinese conditions and history. The remaining items, by Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun, Stalin, Dimitrov and Lenin, supply standards for Party members, discipline and self-criticism. Hu also stresses that Mao selected and reviewed every item, and that ten of the texts are his own. He places the collection beside two other study series for cadres, the "Party books" on Party history and the compilation of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin on methods of thinking, and presents the whole as a Marxist study campaign in the form of rectification. Hu argues that the campaign removed the dogmatism and sectarianism associated with Wang Ming's line, made the Party a tightly organised Bolshevik-style party, and prepared the successful Seventh Party Congress. He treats Mao's principles of uniting theory and practice and seeking truth from facts as holding universal significance for Marxist parties. Hu also reads Mao's 1943 letter, which called only some rectification documents "fragments" of his thought, as consistent with their central role. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-by-document account of what the rectification canon contained and how a Party School scholar justifies its status.

A brief discussion of Mao Zedong's view of history and its practice 简论毛泽东的史学观及其实践 Zhou Suyuan How did Mao Zedong's deep reading of history shape his views and decisions? Zhou Suyuan argues that Mao respected, studied and used history throughout his life, and that this gave him foresight, a grasp of historical regularities and a distinctive method of learning from the past. The article presents this as a coherent view of history that Mao applied at critical junctures of the revolution and in governing. The article has four parts. It first sets out Mao's view of history and his stated aims and methods in studying it. It then looks at how Mao drew on history at key turning points: choosing Marxism-Leninism and the socialist road, the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside, the protracted-war thesis, and carrying the revolution through to the end. A third part treats three famous exchanges, the "Jiashen dialogue", the "cave dialogue" and the "examination dialogue". The last part considers the historical wisdom in Mao Zedong Thought and in his education of cadres. Zhou contends that Mao treated history as a heritage to be respected but critically sifted, rejecting both historical nihilism and uncritical revival of the past. He is said to have studied failure as well as success, reinterpreted old texts ("new readings of ancient books, using the past to serve the present") and separated essence from dross. In Zhou's account, the three living aspects of Mao Zedong Thought, seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance, each have roots in classical sources; "seeking truth from facts" was lifted from textual scholarship into a Marxist epistemology. Zhou reads the three dialogues as warnings, drawn from the fall of Li Zicheng's rebels and the historical cycle of rise and decline, against complacency after victory and as the basis for the answer that democracy lets the people supervise government. Zhou concludes that Mao's use of history gave him far-sighted judgement, an optimism rooted in his understanding of social development, and a lasting method of drawing lessons from others' experience. After 1949, the article says, Mao's concern shifted to guarding against corruption and degeneration among cadres. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how Mao's historical outlook is presented within official Party history, with many cited episodes and classical allusions.

The "Yan'an Road" as a Third World path and a new world history 作为第三世界的“延安道路”与新的世界史 Lü Xinyu Lü Xinyu asks how China's place in the world should be understood amid what the author calls a Western-imposed "new Cold War". The article argues that a Third World perspective, together with a return to the "Yan'an Road", is indispensable for answering where China comes from and where it is going. In Lü's reading, China's rise is the extension of a twentieth-century socialist and anti-colonial line, and its path belongs to more than China alone. The article opens by contrasting two ideas of the "Third World": Mao Zedong's and Deng Xiaoping's 1974 Three Worlds theory, and Leften Stavrianos's Global Divide (1981), which describes Third World failure under neo-colonialism. It then compares China with the neoliberal West through David Harvey, before turning to Samir Amin's "delinking" and Immanuel Wallerstein's account of ecology. It ends with China's anti-poverty, green development, Belt and Road and pandemic-aid measures, and with questions about the Party's "self-reform". Lü's core moves are as follows. First, drawing on Stavrianos, the author holds that China was the exception among Third World revolutions because the Yan'an "mass line" built a political subject on egalitarian participation, whereas other movements were bourgeois-nationalist. Second, drawing on Harvey, Lü argues that neoliberalism and right-wing populism are two sides of one coin, and that the Western left's failure ceded the state to the right. China's patriotism should therefore not be equated with Western nationalism. Third, Lü reads Amin's call for sovereignty-based "delinking" and internal change as describing the Chinese road, and treats Chinese measures on poverty, state-owned enterprises, ecology and aid as evidence that it is not "state capitalism". Lü concludes that the Party's historic task is now to prove that "only China can save socialism", as it earlier showed that only socialism could save China. The Yan'an Road is described as the starting point of the "China road", and the Party's self-reform as a new test. Lü also raises open questions, including whether China can resist great-power chauvinism and keep supplying infrastructure to the Third World. Read the original if you want a Chinese left-wing scholar's argument linking Yan'an, Third World theory (Amin, Wallerstein, Harvey) and current geopolitics.

Rebutting the "plagiarism thesis" of McLellan and Rosen How Marx surpassed Bruno Bauer's view of religion in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period 驳麦克莱伦和罗森的“抄袭说” Hao Wenli Hao Wenli takes up a charge made by Western scholars: that Marx's early writings on religion borrowed heavily from Bruno Bauer. The author names David McLellan, who points to Marx's reuse of Bauer's wording in the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, and the Polish scholar Zvi Rosen, who holds that most of Marx's remarks on religion are copied from Bauer. Hao argues that Marx's views in this period corrected Bauer and expressed the issues more precisely, and so surpassed him. The article is published in the journal Science and Atheism. The article first sets out four elements of Bauer's critique of religion: his dispute with David Friedrich Strauss over "self-consciousness" versus "substance"; his idealist account of historical motive force; his low estimate of the masses and trust in elite intellectuals; and his opposition to communism. It then compares Marx's Introduction with Bauer on three points, and does the same for On the Jewish Question. A final section gives biographical and textual grounds against the plagiarism claim. Hao contends that in the Introduction Marx grounds religion in an inverted real world, not in self-consciousness, and treats religious critique as a means to social critique. He also locates historical progress in practical criticism of German institutions and philosophy, and he looks to the proletariat as the agent of human emancipation. In On the Jewish Question, Hao says, Marx separates political from human emancipation, so that Jews need not abandon Judaism to be politically emancipated. The question is then a secular matter of the split between political state and civil society, not a theological one. Against the plagiarism claim, Hao cites Marx's independent writing schedule around the unfinished second part of Bauer's The Trumpet of the Last Judgment, and his break with the Berlin "Free" group at the Rheinische Zeitung, which Hao reads as a growing distance from Bauer. Hao also notes that the "opium" image appears earlier in Holbach, Maréchal and Hegel, so that on the critics' logic Bauer would be a plagiarist too. Hao concludes that Marx's Introduction is an original contribution to the Marxist view of religion, and that the plagiarism thesis inflates Bauer and belittles Marx's independent thought. The article also faults Chinese scholars for noting Marx's criticism of Bauer without analysing the relationship closely enough to answer Western critics. Hao proposes neither exaggerating nor minimising Bauer's role in forming Marx's outlook, and presents this as important for firm conviction in the Marxist view of religion. Read the original if you want a Chinese defence of the originality of Marx's early religious thought, or want to see how Chinese scholars answer McLellan on Bauer.

The theory of evolution and the development and spread of Marxist atheism 进化论与马克思主义无神论的发展与传播 Han Jingyi Xu Baojun Fan Yangcheng The article asks how evolutionary theory became a natural-scientific foundation of Marxist atheism and how it then travelled through different political settings. The authors argue that, from Darwin and Haeckel onward, evolution showed that humans arose through natural processes, and so became a scientific premise of dialectical and historical materialism. They describe its role as shifting with context: a rebuttal of creationism in Marx and Engels's day, an 'accelerator' in Russia, and a 'catalyst' in China. The study is organised in four parts plus a conclusion. It first treats Marx and Engels, including Marx's 1861 letter to Lassalle on Darwin, Engels's Dialectics of Nature and Anti-Dühring, and their reading of Haeckel. It then turns to Lenin and Russia before and after the October Revolution. The third part covers modern China, from Yan Fu's Tianyan lun (1897) and Chen Duxiu to the young Mao Zedong, and the final part draws general conclusions. On Marx and Engels, the authors argue that evolution dealt a blow to teleology and gave a materialist account of human origins, and that heredity and adaptation supplied evidence for dialectics. In the Russian section they stress Lenin's distinction between vulgar evolutionism, which derives from Spencer and which they call anti-dialectical, and scientific evolutionism. They report that Lenin praised Haeckel's Riddle of the Universe in Materialism and Empirio-Criticism and sought alliances with natural scientists, while holding that religion's real roots lie in unequal social systems under capital. For China, the authors say evolution broke the cyclical view of history and prepared acceptance of historical materialism. They add that it was often misread through competition and 'survival of the fittest', which opened the way to social Darwinism. The authors conclude that evolution's ideological and atheist character faded after the mid-twentieth century as Marxism became dominant, and its influence returned to natural science. They warn of two opposite errors, idealism that ignores natural laws and social Darwinism that transfers them wholesale into society. They call for dialectics and historical materialism to guard against both, and for continued attention to the natural sciences as support for Marxist atheism. Read the original if you want a survey of how evolutionary theory is placed within the history of Marxist atheism in Germany, Russia and China.

The Party's century of struggle has profoundly shaped the course of world history 党的百年奋斗深刻影响了世界历史进程 Feng Yanli Taking its cue from the 2021 Party resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's first century, this commentary asks how the Communist Party of China's hundred years of struggle have affected world history, and why it has become the world's largest governing party with major global influence. Feng argues that the Party's work is an integral part of humanity's progress and that its influence rests on three foundations: the advantages of the socialist system, great development achievements and the spirit of self-reform. The piece appeared in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), no. 23, 2021. The article has two parts. The first sets out the forms the influence takes: the Party's record on peace, justice and win-win cooperation; its role in inter-party exchanges, in world socialism and in international organisations; and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. The second part explains the underlying logic under three headings: the political foundation, the material guarantee and the source of momentum. In Feng's account, Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilisation and shown that no single model of modernization exists, giving countries that want both development and independence a fresh option. Feng credits the Party with leading world socialism after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and with maintaining regular contact with more than 500 parties and political organisations. The political foundation is the system's combination of Party leadership, the people as masters of the country and law-based governance; Feng contrasts what is called Chinese order with Western disorder, citing economic crises and unrest in the West. The material guarantee is rapid growth, the elimination of absolute poverty and the building of a moderately prosperous society in 2020. The driving force is the Party's self-reform, including anti-corruption work and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Feng concludes that the Party must keep to Marxism, particularly Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and keep combining it with China's fine traditional culture, so as to contribute more to human civilisation. Self-reform is presented as what keeps the Party from degenerating while it serves both the Chinese people and global progress. Read the original if you want a representative example of official Party-theory commentary on the Party's international significance around the centenary in 2021.

Upholding and developing Marxism through the Two Integrations 在“两个结合”中坚持和发展马克思主义 Wang Huxue This short commentary, published in Economic Daily in December 2022 shortly after the 20th Party Congress, asks why and how Marxism should be upheld and developed through the Two Integrations. Wang argues that combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture is both an inner requirement of theoretical development and an objective need of China's present development. The piece opens by tracing the formulation of the Two Integrations from Xi Jinping's speech marking the Party's centenary (2021) through the Sixth Plenum's historical resolution to the 20th Party Congress report (2022). It is then organised in two sections, one for each integration, and draws mainly on Xi's remarks and the Congress report. On the first integration, Wang holds that Marxism is a guide to action rather than dogma, and that it takes root only when Sinicized. Upholding it therefore means using its worldview and methodology to solve China's problems, not reciting phrases or conclusions. On the second, Wang describes a two-way relationship. Marxism activates Chinese civilization, citing parallels between Marx's view of humans as natural beings and the ideal of harmony between heaven and humanity, between the law of unity of opposites and "harmony without uniformity", and between dialectics and the reformist spirit of the Zhou. In turn, traditional culture nourishes Marxism, giving it Chinese features and a stronger historical and popular foundation. Wang concludes that only a Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times can take root in the hearts of hundreds of millions of Chinese people. The Two Integrations are presented as a summation of the Party's experience of theoretical innovation and as an expression of cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Two Integrations were explained to a general readership just after the 20th Party Congress.

Giving full play to the political function of primary-level Party organizations 充分发挥基层党组织的政治功能 Wang Binglin Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2022, Wang Binglin asks how the Communist Party of China's grassroots organizations can better perform their political function. Wang argues that the Party is a Marxist party whose basic attribute is political and whose basic function is political, so primary-level organizations must remain "fortresses" and not turn into mere service bodies. The article opens with the Party's size, citing 96.712 million members and 4.936 million primary-level organizations at the end of 2021. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the political function matters; the second reviews what has been achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the weaknesses that remain; the third offers four lines of work for Party building in the new era. Wang gives five reasons why the political function is necessary. It is required by the Party's overall leadership, by the people-centred approach, by the consolidation of the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and by full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Wang credits primary-level organizations with firmer political direction, with the Two Upholds, with "Party member shock teams" in the Covid-19 response and disaster relief, and with poverty alleviation work. Wang also lists problems: some organizations apply Party policy half-heartedly, chase economic targets while neglecting people's demands, leave gaps in coverage (especially in emerging sectors), have an ageing Party-affairs workforce, stress service over politics, and fall into formalism such as paperwork and record-keeping. Wang proposes four remedies. Primary-level organizations should be secured as the leading core of grassroots governance. They should meet the people's needs for a better life, with management and service combined. Their organizational strength should be raised through full coverage, better-chosen leaders, and more resources and authority. Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party should extend downward through study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, criticism and self-criticism, and checks on petty power. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party theorists in 2022 framed the political role of grassroots Party branches and the weaknesses they acknowledged.

On the basic foundations of Chinese modernization 论中国式现代化的基本立足点 Wang Junwei Written shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), this article asks what Chinese modernization rests on. Wang Junwei answers that it has three basic footholds: China's basic national conditions, its fine traditional culture, and the Chinese Communist Party's founding mission. The author presents this as the reason China had to take its own path, since neither Western models nor the Soviet one, in Wang's account, solved China's problems. The article opens with a historical sketch. It covers the failed attempts to learn from the West after 1840, the Party's pre-1949 struggle, the pursuit of the "four modernizations", Deng Xiaoping's concept of a Chinese-style modernization, and developments since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then devotes one section to each of the three footholds. It ends by placing Chinese modernization in a changing world, and it draws on statistics, classical Chinese sources and foreign commentators such as Arnold Toynbee and Jean-Paul Sartre. On national conditions, Wang argues that the basic condition remains the primary stage of socialism, summed up as a large population, a weak foundation and uneven development. Wang says the specifics have shifted: the birth rate and working-age population are falling, GDP and wealth have grown, yet per capita indicators, technological self-reliance and inequality still lag. The article therefore links common prosperity and high-quality development to these conditions, and quotes Xi Jinping that the Party's leadership is China's greatest national condition. On culture, Wang contends that the Party inherits and renews traditional culture. In this reading, communism echoes the ancient ideal of a harmonious society, and "serving the people" echoes "the people as the foundation of the state". The Two Integrations are presented as the route for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. On mission, Wang holds that the Party's outlook extends to human progress, so that Chinese modernization offers developing countries an alternative to capital-centred, polarising and expansionist Western modernization. The article describes China as never imposing its model on others and as playing a stabilising role in past crises. It criticises some developed countries for shifting burdens onto others and suppressing latecomers. It concludes that a modernization built on these three foundations will create new achievements for China and the world. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party theorists ground Chinese modernization in national conditions, tradition and Party mission.

The structure, main themes and influence of Mao Zedong's annotations on A System of Ethics 毛泽东《〈伦理学原理〉批注》的结构、主旨和影响 Han Qi Tian Linian Han Qi and Tian Linian examine the more than 12,000 characters of marginal notes that the young Mao Zedong wrote in 1917–1918 on Cai Yuanpei's Chinese translation of Friedrich Paulsen's System of Ethics. They ask what moral philosophy Mao developed there and how it shaped his later practical character. They argue that the notes contain a distinctive moral ontology and two ethical positions, individualism and realism, which together unify value and truth. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Mao's chain of eight paired concepts, from good and evil down to "mind and principle" (xinli), and the two positions drawn from it. The second analyses how these positions relate to value, truth and the "force of mind" as moral foundation. The third traces two chains of thought and their later Marxist transformation into On Practice and On Contradiction. The authors engage Kondo Kuniyasu, Zhang Hao, Wakeman, Li Zehou, Xiao Yanzhong, Tian Chenshan and Schwartz, and draw on Yang Changji's teaching. The authors read Mao's "spiritual individualism" as a subjective moral law, and his realism as the historical and concrete condition for realising it. Mao's notes thereby overcome the flaws they find in the British Hegelian self-realisation ethics that Yang Changji had introduced, and in moral theology. The central principle is sincerity (cheng), through which value governs truth. From it come two chains: mind, individualism, value and subjective initiative; and principle, realism, truth and objective regularity. The authors situate these in the thought of change (tongbian) in the Book of Changes, in Rousseau and Kant, and in May Fourth individualism and social reform. The authors conclude that after Mao's turn to Marxism, "seeking truth from facts" replaced sincerity, and practice replaced force of mind. The individual was then understood as a member of a class within social relations. They argue that Mao's late thought on socialist construction should be read within this lifelong trajectory, and not reduced to "philosophy of struggle", moralism or populism. Read the original if you study the early Mao, the roots of his practical philosophy, or the Sinicisation of Marxist philosophy.

Why Mao Zedong called the Rectification Documents a "classic text" 毛泽东为何称《整风文献》为经书 Hu Weixiong In November 1942 Mao Zedong told a meeting of senior cadres in the Northwest that the documents for rectifying the Party's "three work styles" were "a classic text" (jingshu). Hu Weixiong notes that scholars have paid little attention to why Mao said this. Some foreign scholars hold that the collection contains no Marxist classics. Hu argues, from the selection and structure of the Rectification Documents, that the collection deserves the label because it is a coherent programme for building the Party, grounded in the union of Marxist-Leninist theory with Chinese revolutionary practice. The article first traces the editions: 18 documents in the April 1942 version, 22 after the Propaganda Department's additions, and 27 in the revised 1943 edition, which Hu takes as the object of study. It sorts the 27 texts into four groups: rectifying the Party, study and writing styles; Party members' self-cultivation and organisational building; leadership, cadre policy, inner-Party criticism and struggle, discipline and democracy; and the Party's mission, propaganda, leadership methods and Bolshevisation. Hu summarises the main texts in each group, from Mao's own reports to pieces by Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun, Stalin, Dimitrov and Lenin. Hu's central claim is that Mao's writings supply the core and the guiding spirit. Reform Our Study, Rectify the Party's Style of Work and Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing attack subjectivism, dogmatism and sectarianism, and ask that Marxism-Leninism be used as an \"arrow\" aimed at the \"target\" of the Chinese revolution. The Bolshevisation texts, the Stalin and Dimitrov selections and the Liu and Chen pieces then supply norms for members, discipline, self-criticism and cadre selection. Hu also places the collection beside two other study series, the \"Party books\" and Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin on Methods of Thought, and treats it as the only one containing original works. Hu reads the campaign as a Marxist study movement against the dogmatism of Wang Ming, and cites Mao's remark that he did not wish his thought presented as a system. Hu concludes that the Rectification Documents hold a landmark place in the history of Chinese Marxism. They answered the question that had troubled the Party for nearly twenty years, namely how to combine universal truth with Chinese practice. They helped turn the Party into a cohesive, Bolshevik-style body able to lead the War of Resistance and the New Democratic revolution, and its seventh congress marked its transformation into a modern party. Hu adds that the principles of linking theory with practice and seeking truth from facts apply to Marxist parties worldwide. Read the original if you want a document-by-document account of what the 1942–43 rectification texts contained and how a Party School scholar reads their role in Mao's thought.

Striving to write a new chapter in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 奋力谱写马克思主义中国化时代化新篇章 Duan Hong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in December 2022, responds to the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The report calls writing ever new chapters in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times a solemn historical responsibility of today's Communists. Duan Hong argues that Marxism is a scientific system that keeps developing with the times, and that this task is both a theoretical necessity and a practical one. The piece has two parts. The first reviews the Party's history of more than a century as a history of theoretical innovation, running from the New Democratic Revolution through socialist revolution and construction and reform and opening up to the new era. The second sets out what the author says is required to write the new chapter: the Two Integrations, the "six musts", and theoretical innovation grounded in practice. Duan reads each historical stage as a theoretical achievement, from Mao Zedong's "second integration" to Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. On the Two Integrations, the author holds that Marxism must keep answering the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and must take root in fine traditional Chinese culture. For each of the six commitments (putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, staying true while innovating, a problem-oriented approach, systematic thinking, and a global vision), Duan argues that neglecting it would cost Marxism its essential character, direction or capacity to grow. Duan concludes that theory and practice must interact productively, so that innovation does not become "closed-door" work. Innovation should be rooted in contemporary Chinese practice and guided by Xi Jinping Thought, so that new theory guides new practice. Read the original if you want a short example of how Party-affiliated scholars presented the 20th Party Congress's line on the adaptation of Marxism.

Re-examining the course of the young Mao Zedong's worldview transformation With comments on the 1920 "summer", "winter" and "process" theses 青年毛泽东世界观转变历程再考察 Wu Xuan When did Mao Zedong become a Marxist? Wu Xuan takes up a long-running debate in Chinese scholarship over the date and the criteria of the young Mao's worldview transformation, including the "summer" thesis (1920), the "winter" thesis and the "process" thesis. Wu argues that the change was a complex, gradual process in which Marxist elements came to dominate Mao's thinking, and that it cannot be pinned to a single season or to the reading of particular books. The article has four parts. It first treats Mao's second stay in Beijing (1919–20) and his own account to Edgar Snow that by summer 1920 he was a Marxist "in theory, and to some extent in action". It then follows his practice after returning to Hunan in 1920: the Cultural Book Society, the Russian Studies Society, contacts with Chen Duxiu, and the founding of the Changsha communist group and Socialist Youth League. The third part assesses the Hunan self-government movement and the method for judging worldview change, and a short conclusion follows. Wu concedes that the three books Mao named (the Communist Manifesto, Class Struggle, History of Socialism) were published after August 1920. The author denies that this undermines Mao's claim, since what matters is whether he had broken with reformism and anarchism and accepted class struggle and the dictatorship of the proletariat. Wu reads Mao's Hunan activities as evidence of this shift, and reads the self-government movement's reformist and anarchist traces as a secondary current, not the main one. A transformation, Wu holds, means that Marxist elements became dominant, not that non-Marxist ones vanished; the same was true of Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu. Wu cites Mao's letters and the 1921 New People's Study Society meeting as marking completion by early 1921, when he was a Marxist in both theory and action. Wu concludes that Mao's transformation followed a path of knowing, practice, re-knowing and re-practice, moving from idealism to materialism and from radical democrat to communist. The author presents this path as typical of early Chinese communist intellectuals and as the basis of the Party's later achievements. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the Chinese historiographical debate over the dating of Mao's turn to Marxism and the evidence marshalled on each side.

Why Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times works 中国化时代化的马克思主义为什么行 Chen Jinlong This commentary, published in Economic Daily in December 2022, takes up the line from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) that the Party succeeds and socialism with Chinese characteristics is good because Marxism works, specifically Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Chen Jinlong argues that this adapted Marxism works because it suits China's conditions, answers the questions of the age and speaks to the people's concerns. The piece is organised in three parts after a short introduction, one for each reason. It draws on Marx and Engels, on the stages of China's revolution and construction, and on concepts from Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It closes by restating the author's call for a continuing effort to renew Marxism in China. First, Chen holds that Marxism rests mainly on European history, so applying it mechanically elsewhere would be dogmatism. In the author's account, it has been fitted to China through the Two Integrations: with China's concrete realities, including the nature of society and its principal contradiction, and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Examples given are the unity of heaven and humanity feeding ecological ideas, and the idea of the people as the foundation of the state feeding the people-centred approach. Second, Chen says each era sets its own questions. The author presents Xi Jinping Thought as the response to the questions raised by great changes unseen in a century (globalisation and deglobalisation, great-power rivalry, AI and big data). Third, because the people are the main body of practice, theory must come from and serve them, and their practice tests its truth. Chen lists the principal contradiction, whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity and harmony between humanity and nature as questions the theory addresses. Chen concludes that this Marxism is close to national conditions, the times and the people, and that this is why it works. Practice and theoretical innovation have no end, and the author calls it the historic responsibility of today's Communists to keep writing new chapters. They call for using Marxism to observe, grasp and lead the times, for drawing on China's practice, and for absorbing the achievements of other civilisations. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of the standard rationale for the adaptation of Marxism in China after the 20th Party Congress.

Deeply grasping the core meaning of the "six musts" 深刻领悟“六个必须坚持”的核心要义 Han Qingxiang This commentary, published in Economic Daily in December 2022, explains the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). Han Qingxiang argues that they form a tightly linked organic whole. In the author's reading, they are the worldview, methodology, standpoint, viewpoint and method that must be followed in opening up new realms of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article first places the "six musts" within the Congress report's call to advance theoretical innovation grounded in practice. It then takes each in turn: putting the people first, being self-confident and self-reliant, upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground, adopting a problem-oriented approach, applying systems thinking, and taking the whole world into account. Han assigns each "must" a distinct function. The people-first principle is the fundamental standpoint, and self-confidence and self-reliance the foothold. Upholding fundamental principles while innovating is the scientific attitude, and the problem orientation is theory's central task. Systems thinking is the method of thought, and a global outlook is the worldview. Han presents these as an expression of materialist dialectics, in which continuity and change, principle and creativity are unified. The author also calls for advancing the Two Integrations and addressing problems at home and abroad together. Han concludes that the "six musts" are the basic points for understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for continuing theoretical innovation. The author calls for applying them so that the Thought is carried through every area of Party and state work. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how the 20th Congress "six musts" are explained and organised.

A century of change in the Party Constitution 党章的百年演变 Yao Jintao Chen Jian Published in the Party discipline newspaper on 15 December 2022, shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary traces how the Constitution of the Communist Party of China has developed since the first formal text of 1922. Yao and Chen argue that, over a hundred years, the Party Constitution has become more complete in structure and content, and that it records the evolution of the Party's theory, political positions, line and institutions. The article follows the Constitution through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, the exploration of the socialist road, reform and opening up and modernization, and the new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It runs from the 1921 first Programme and the 1922 Second Congress text (six chapters, 29 articles) through the 1927 revision, the 7th Congress text, the 8th Congress text, the texts of the Cultural Revolution years, and the revisions of the 12th to 19th Congresses. Yao and Chen present each revision as a response to the Party's circumstances. The 1927 text fixed the basic framework later used. The 7th Congress text added a general programme and established Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology. The 12th Congress text, in their account, removed the 'Left' errors and became the model for the new period. The authors then list what each later congress wrote in: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For the 20th Congress they report 50 amendments (37 in the general programme, 13 in articles). These concern the Thought's positioning and the Two Integrations, the Party's century of experience, common prosperity and security, whole-process people's democracy, the Party's overall leadership, and the Party's self-reform. The authors conclude that the 20th Congress amendments reflect theoretical, practical and institutional innovation since the 19th Congress (2017), and that revising the Constitution to keep pace with the times is a Party convention. They call on all Party organisations and members to study, observe, implement and uphold it. Read the original if you want a compact, officially framed chronology of each Party Constitution from 1922 to 2022 and a summary of the 20th Congress amendments.

The theoretical implications of the maturation and consolidation of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义制度成熟定型的理论意涵 Ren Peng Ren Peng takes up a formulation from the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the socialist system with Chinese characteristics has become "more mature and more定型" (more fully formed). The article asks why this became possible in the new era, what marks a system as mature and consolidated, and how it should be developed once it is. Ren argues that the maturation rests on advanced productive forces and on the system's own self-improvement, that it can be recognised by identifiable criteria, and that it carries significant theoretical and practical weight. The article has four parts. It first sets out the theoretical necessity of maturation, then the signs of it, then its contributions, and finally its theoretical value, meaning the tasks that follow. Ren draws mainly on historical materialism, on speeches by Xi Jinping, and on the Party's documents from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). Ren's central move is to define a mature system by three marks. The outward mark is a system that is scientific, complete and stable. The inward mark is institutional confidence, value identification and compliance among the people. The third is orderly creation and revision of rules, smooth operation and good performance. On this account the system's performance shows in efficiency, in effectiveness against risks such as poverty alleviation and the Covid-19 epidemic, and in wider benefits. Ren then argues that maturation shows the Party has deepened its grasp of three laws: those governing Communist Party rule, socialist construction and human social development. It also means a new stage for the modernization of national governance and, in Ren's reading, supports entry into the "new development stage" of the primary stage of socialism. The article describes the system's advantages in comparison with Western systems and as a model for developing countries. Ren stresses that maturity is both absolute and relative, because it holds only under given productive forces and conditions. The article proposes three tasks. These are to persist in institutional reform and innovation, including measures for common prosperity; to strengthen institutional awareness and enforcement, especially among leading cadres as the "key minority"; and to balance stability with development so that institutional advantages become governance effectiveness. Ren holds that the Party's leadership system must remain unshaken. Read the original if you want a systematic statement, in the Party-theoretical idiom, of how Chinese scholars define institutional maturity and tie it to national governance modernization.

The idea of ideological leadership in Lenin's What Is to Be Done? and its contemporary implications 列宁《怎么办？》中的意识形态领导权思想及其当代启示 Lan Botao Lan Botao asks what Lenin's What Is to Be Done? contributes to the question of how a proletarian party secures ideological leadership, and what that offers the Communist Party of China today. The article argues that the book is a theoretical guide for Russian Social Democracy and that its ideas remain relevant. Lan frames ideological leadership as a strategic question that decides the Party's future, not a slogan, and cites Xi Jinping's demand that leadership, management and discourse power in ideological work never be allowed to slip away. The article has three parts. The first sets out the content of Lenin's idea of ideological leadership, drawing on his critique of 'freedom of criticism' and of the 'Economists'. It covers the role of scientific theory, the emphasis on conscious workers' movements, the organisation of revolutionaries, and the founding of an all-Russia political newspaper. The second part discusses the guiding significance of these ideas. The third draws lessons for the Party in the new era. Lan's central reasoning follows Lenin against the Economists, who exalted spontaneous workers' movements. Lan reports Lenin's view that a purely workers' movement cannot create an independent ideology and so stays under bourgeois ideological domination, remaining at the level of trade-unionism. Socialist consciousness therefore has to be instilled 'from outside' by the party, which Lan presents as a necessity because the working class under capitalism cannot produce its own ideology. Lan adds that Lenin saw a centralised all-Russia newspaper as the means to propaganda, agitation and the unification of local organisations. The struggle is described as irreconcilable, with a strengthened bourgeois ideology meaning a weakened socialist one. Lan draws three lessons for today. The Party should arm minds with its latest theory, upholding Marxism's guiding position and the principle that the Party manages ideology. It should also keep using the 'theory of inculcation', which Lan says should rely mainly on positive propaganda rather than rote teaching. Lan adds that this includes online and offline work, using media convergence to win hearts in a 'competition for identification' and to establish socialist core values against erroneous trends of thought. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads Lenin's early party-building text to support the Party's current ideological work.

An assessment of the predicaments of British neo-Marxist cultural studies 英国新马克思主义文化研究的困境评析 Li Xintong Li Xintong examines the path of British neo-Marxist cultural studies from culturalism to structuralism and then to cultural hegemony and articulation theory. The article argues that all three paradigms set out to overcome the "reflection theory" of culture, which treats culture as a mere reflection of the economic base. In Li's account, they ended in an original predicament and a contemporary one, both rooted in an unresolved view of the base–superstructure relation. The article first reconstructs the three paradigms. Culturalism (Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams, E. P. Thompson) stresses experience, human agency and culture as a whole way of life. Structuralism (Perry Anderson, Terry Eagleton, and Stuart Hall's turn to signification) treats culture and ideology as the precondition of experience. The third paradigm draws on Antonio Gramsci's hegemony and Ernesto Laclau's articulation, and is represented by the later Williams and by Hall. Li then discusses the "original" predicament and the "contemporary" predicament of cultural identity and openness. Li contends that culturalism and structuralism stand in an either/or antinomy: humanism against anti-humanism, the logic of history against the logic of structure. Hall's articulation, in this reading, merely overlays two incompatible paradigms and discusses "unity in difference" only inside ideology. Li argues that it drifts into post-Marxism and away from Marxist political economy. Williams's revision of "base" as a process and Eagleton's historical account of culture are discussed as other responses. By the 1990s, Li says, the stress on autonomy had become an autonomy of the economy alone, and reflection on historical materialism was suspended. On the contemporary side, structuralism makes identity a closed belonging, while culturalism's openness empties identity. Li proposes reading identity as a dialectical tension, drawing on Hall, Zygmunt Bauman and Jacques Derrida, with structure understood as an open "field". Li concludes that culture is meaningful only when studied within historical materialism, through social relations and practice. The author poses questions about Marx's broader conception of culture and practice, and about whether a new concept of culture could be derived from it. The article ends by claiming that socialism with Chinese characteristics, building on shared values and Chinese tradition, offers an open space for cultural dialogue. Read the original if you want a critical Chinese account of the Birmingham-school lineage and its theoretical dead ends, written from a historical-materialist standpoint.

From awareness of hardship to bottom-line thinking: continuity and development across generations of Party leaders 从忧患意识到底线思维：党的几代领导人的坚持和发展 Yang Yucheng Yang Yucheng asks how the traditional Chinese consciousness of hardship and danger (youhuan yishi) has been carried forward by successive generations of Chinese Communists and turned into the method of "bottom-line thinking" associated with Xi Jinping. The article argues that Communists combined the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, creatively transforming the old ideal of being prepared for danger in times of peace. Mao Zedong's generation first turned it into the method of "thinking from the worst possibility", and Xi Jinping's generation refined it into bottom-line thinking for preventing major risks. The article first traces the tradition from pre-Qin Confucian, Daoist and Mohist texts through later historians and officials such as Sima Qian, Wei Zheng, Ouyang Xiu and Wei Yuan. It then follows Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and Xi Jinping's speeches from the 18th Party Congress (2012) to the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). A central section defines what a "bottom line" is and what bottom-line thinking involves, and a final section assesses its innovation over the tradition. Yang defines a bottom line as the lower limit of the "measure" within which a thing keeps its present qualitative state, a critical point beyond which it degrades. Bottom-line thinking has three linked elements: looking from the worst case, preparing most fully, and striving for the best result. Yang reads this as an application of materialist dialectics, including the law of the mutual transformation of quantity and quality. Holding the bottom line is presented as a precondition for achieving more, not an end in itself. Yang says traditional awareness of hardship was a kind of cautionary warning with little operability, and that bottom-line thinking supplies identifiable lines, contingency plans and concrete steps. Yang contends that bottom-line thinking also bears on the question of "escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall", which Mao raised in his cave-dwelling talk with Huang Yanpei. In Yang's account the answer has two parts: modernizing the system and capacity of national governance through comprehensive deepening of reform, and the Party's self-reform through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which Yang says leads the first. Yang concludes that bottom-line thinking gives the old wisdom new vitality in the new era. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Xi Jinping's risk-prevention doctrine is placed in a lineage from Mao to the present and in Chinese tradition.

On the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital in the socialist market economy 论社会主义市场经济中资本的特性和行为规律 Liu Fengyi Following the Central Economic Work Conference of December 2021 and Xi Jinping's speech at the Politburo study session of April 2022, Liu Fengyi takes up the task of correctly understanding the characteristics and behavioural laws of capital under a socialist market economy. Liu argues that Marx's analysis of capital remains the basis, but that Marx did not foresee the combination of socialism and the market, so Marxist political economy must work out how capital's laws are modified in that setting. The article holds that the aim is to use capital well and to rein it in, with regulation as the main aspect. The article has four parts. It first sets out the starting points for studying capital theory, then derives capital's behavioural laws from its essence, then from its forms, and finally proposes ways to use institutional strengths to make good use of capital and to govern it. Liu separates public from private capital, and organises capital's forms by production, circulation and distribution, drawing on Marx's Capital throughout. Liu first defines capital in Marx's terms as a social relation that seeks self-expansion of value, not a thing, a sum of money or a production factor. Liu rejects the idea that capital has a natural attribute alongside a social one. Under capitalism, competition and money's limitlessness drive endless accumulation, which promotes productive forces but also produces exploitation, polarisation and crises. In the socialist market economy, Liu contends, public capital has a dual character: it follows market rules in form, while internally it embodies socialist production relations. Private capital keeps its wage-labour relation, but its laws are 'deformed' because production aims at meeting people's needs and public capital serves as the 'universal light'. Liu also stresses that capital prefers to 'divide the cake' in the virtual economy rather than 'make the cake' in the real economy. Liu concludes that capital's profit-seeking nature must be harnessed through the strengths of the socialist system, using six measures. These are the Two Unwaverings, using capital to serve the people, improving economic governance under Party leadership, supervising capital in direct production, setting 'traffic lights' for green development, and ideological and political work with private entrepreneurs. Liu says red lights for a few kinds of capital are meant to create green lights for most, and that the new development pattern follows the laws of capital circulation and turnover. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how a Chinese Marxist economist links Capital's categories to current policy on regulating capital.

The development path, internal difficulties and way forward of the Latin Americanisation of Marxism 马克思主义拉美化的发展理路、内在困境及其出路 Zheng Xiangfu Ling Zhehong Following Lenin's Russianisation of Marxism, the Peruvian Communist Party founder José Carlos Mariátegui began what Zheng Xiangfu and Ling Zhehong call the Latin Americanisation of Marxism. The article, published in 2022, asks why this localisation has produced real achievements yet also persistent difficulties. The authors argue that the answer lies in how Latin American Marxists understood the essence of Marxism and in the region's realities, and they trace the process historically to explain its necessity and mechanism. The account is divided into three periods. From the late nineteenth century to 1917, Marxism was mechanically mixed with local currents, as in the work of Juan B. Justo, Manuel Ugarte and Luis Emilio Recabarren. From 1918 to 1959, it fought the thesis of 'Latin American exceptionalism' and dogmatism, through Mariátegui, Julio Antonio Mella, Victorio Codovilla and Vicente Lombardo Toledano. After 1960 it took diverse forms: Castroism and Guevarism, dependency theory and the philosophy of liberation, Cuba's 'updating' of socialism, and Hugo Chávez's 'socialism of the twenty-first century'. A final section sets out the difficulties and proposed remedies. The authors present Mariátegui's call for a 'heroic creation', not a dogmatic copy of European models, as the turning point. They credit his Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality with finding Indigenous peoples to be the revolutionary subject and with applying historical materialism to local conditions. They then identify theoretical problems: the influence of Trotskyism, Stalinism and Browderism; a selective reading of Marxist conclusions that neglected its methodology; and the worship of Comintern directives or revolutionary leaders' slogans in place of concrete analysis. In practice, they say, the collapse of the Soviet Union weakened the communist parties, many of which became opposition or participating parties or turned to social democracy, leaving the socialist movement in a trough. The authors propose four requirements. Marxism must be grasped as an organic whole of philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, and socialisms detached from historical materialism are rejected as unscientific. Indigenous peoples and their traditions must be the foundation. Party-building is the key to success. Communist parties must also study their own historical experience and explore a socialism with Latin American characteristics. The article is a historical survey rather than a case study. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of Latin American Marxism from Justo to Chávez, and of how Chinese researchers assess its limits.

The historical necessity of building an independent knowledge system in Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and paths towards it 中国哲学社会科学自主知识体系建构的历史必然与路径探索 Han Xiping Han Xiping takes up Xi Jinping's statement that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics comes down to constructing China's own independent knowledge system. Writing in 2022, after the April release of the national 14th Five-Year Plan for philosophy and social sciences, Han argues that such a system is a call of the times and a historical necessity. In Han's view it also accords with the general laws of how the discipline develops. The article first defines knowledge, knowledge systems and "independent" knowledge, drawing on Aristotle, Russell, Polanyi and the OECD. It then traces how Western liberalism, with its "rational economic man" assumption, came to dominate the world's philosophy and social sciences and produced "Western centrism". Four sections follow on why the system is needed: by the era, by China, by the world, and then a section on practical routes. Han contends that Chinese scholarship remains in an "apprenticeship" to Western paradigms. The author says Chinese practice, such as poverty alleviation, the socialist market economy and ecological civilization, has not been distilled into its own theory, and that concepts like the "China model" are often defined by Western scholars. Liberal theory, in Han's account, can explain neither the current global turbulence nor the question of where humanity is heading. Chinese modernization is presented as transcending capitalist modernization and sublating its oppositions between humans and nature, capital and labour, and states. The author presents a community with a shared future for mankind and a new form of human civilization as Chinese answers to these questions. For the path forward, Han calls for Marxism as the guiding theory, a real break from imitation rather than the addition of some Chinese terms, and creative transformation of fine traditional Chinese culture combined with Marxism. The author also calls for theory that addresses both Chinese and global problems, supported by think tanks, and a new explanatory paradigm for Chinese experience built on Marxist standpoint and method. The aim is to end the "absence" of Chinese discourse in disciplines, textbooks and forums. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the 2022 official case for an independent Chinese knowledge system and its justification.

An investigation of the precious editions of Socialism: Utopian and Scientific 《社会主义从空想到科学的发展》珍贵版本探考 Xu Meng Guo Xiaoli Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, which Marx called an introduction to scientific socialism, was excerpted and revised from Anti-Dühring. This article by Xu Meng and Guo Xiaoli asks how the work's many language editions published before 1949 differ in publication history, format and content. The authors argue that each edition is in effect an independent work shaped by its translator, editor and historical setting. The article is a bibliographic survey based on editions the authors located, many of them held in China. It proceeds language by language: French, German, English, Japanese, Dutch and Chinese. For each it lists editions, publishers, prefaces, appendices, chapter divisions and annotations, and it also traces how the text circulated between languages. The authors make three main moves. First, they follow Engels's own adaptations: the French text (1880) was shaped for French readers, the German edition (1883) roughly doubled the content and introduced the now standard three-chapter structure, and the 1892 English edition carried a long new introduction. Second, they show how editors and translators added their own material: Japanese editions by Sakai Toshihiko and others carried headings, notes and political commentary, and some bore the marks of state censorship. Third, they trace the Chinese editions, many translated via Japanese, German, French or Russian sources. These include a 1912 serialisation, Ke Bonian's 1925 full translation, Wu Liping's 1938 version and Bogu's 1943 Yan'an edition, which the authors say became the standard text of a cadres' required-reading series. They also raise unresolved dating and attribution questions, such as the Dutch translation and an undated publisher's note in a US edition. The authors conclude that differences between editions reflect Engels's adaptation to different audiences and the translators' own understanding and circumstances. In their view each edition therefore has its own research value and historical limits. They argue that only by placing the editions in their historical and social contexts can the work's theoretical value and present significance be understood fully. They present the survey as a reference for tracing how Marxist classics spread worldwide and for understanding the sources of Marxism adapted to China. Read the original if you work on the textual history, translation or circulation of Engels's writings and need a detailed catalogue of early editions in several languages, especially the Chinese and Japanese ones.

Chinese modernization makes new and greater contributions to mankind 中国式现代化为人类作出新的更大贡献 Chai Shangjin Published in Guangming Daily shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), this commentary asks what Chinese modernization offers the wider world. Chai Shangjin argues that it breaks the claim that Western modernization is the only model, promotes global sustainable development, and both develops China and benefits other countries. The piece leans heavily on Xi Jinping's statements to frame these claims. The article opens by summarising the Party's account of Chinese modernization: a modernization of a huge population, of common prosperity for all, of material and cultural-ethical progress, of harmony between humanity and nature, and of peaceful development. Three sections follow. The first contrasts Chinese and Western paths, the second deals with ecological civilization and green development, and the third covers peaceful development and China's international initiatives. Chai supports the last section with a quotation from the British scholar Martin Jacques. Chai's central move is a contrast. In the author's account, Western modernization is essentially capitalist, centred on capital, expansionist and predatory, and it widens wealth gaps and political division at home and abroad. Chinese modernization, led by the Communist Party, is described as people-centred and aimed at common prosperity, and as having overcome the materialism and alienation from nature that accompany the Western path. Chai then argues that harmony between humanity and nature is intrinsic to this path. As evidence, the article cites figures for the past decade: average annual energy consumption growth of 3% supporting average economic growth of 6.6%, and a cumulative 26.2% fall in energy intensity. It adds that China pursues the new development philosophy and the carbon peak and carbon neutrality pledges. On peace, Chai states that China has never sought hegemony and will not, and links modernization to a community with a shared future for mankind and the Global Development and Global Security Initiatives. Chai concludes that the Chinese path has solved China's practical problems and, in a certain sense, answers the common question of how less developed countries can modernize. It is presented as both the proper road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a correct choice for leading global modernization trends. The text is an official-line commentary rather than a detailed analysis. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated writers presented the international significance of Chinese modernization right after the 20th Party Congress.

Clean-government building in the Chinese Soviet Republic and its valuable experience 中华苏维埃共和国廉政建设及其宝贵经验 Chen Shifa Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), which restated that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform are "always on the road", Chen Shifa looks back to the Chinese Soviet Republic (founded at Ruijin, Jiangxi, in the early 1930s). The commentary argues that this republic was a pioneering attempt at a new type of state power, a prototype of the later People's Republic and a testing ground for Party governance. In Chen's view, it was also an important early stage of the Party leading social revolution through its own self-reform, with clean government as its core content. The piece is a short newspaper article organised around four contributions of the Soviet period: building a broadly democratic new regime, creating an unprecedentedly clean government, constructing a comprehensive supervision mechanism, and spreading a culture of integrity in the service of the people. It draws on the Constitutional Outline of the Chinese Soviet Republic, election regulations, anti-corruption decrees and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhang Wentian and Xiang Ying, together with descriptive detail about the government's offices and staffing. Chen's central claim is that clean government rested on institutional design and not only on personal virtue. Democracy is said to have been made real through mass election campaigns, small electoral districts, universal suffrage for the exploited, and rights of supervision, dismissal, re-election and recall over deputies. The government is portrayed as lean and close to the masses: thirteen bodies housed in an ancestral hall, unpaid officials living on small food allowances, and systems such as the duty-deputy and cadre-labour arrangements. Supervision is described as multi-layered, with Party supervisory committees, a workers' and peasants' inspection department, "light cavalry" teams, press columns exposing misconduct, revolutionary courts, and zero tolerance of both embezzlement and waste. Chen concludes that the Soviet Republic opened a new chapter in building clean government in Chinese history, and that its experience and "red genes" retain strong practical value as a revolutionary lineage the Party must carry forward. The article offers no new archival research but gives a concise official-historical account of how the early Soviet period is now presented in the anti-corruption discourse. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars link the Jiangxi Soviet era to the current campaign for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The centenary evolution and basic experience of the Communist Party of China's propaganda work 中国共产党宣传工作的百年演进与基本经验 Zhong Xiaowu Zhong Xiaowu takes up the history of the Communist Party of China's propaganda work over its first hundred years. The article starts from the formula that propaganda is an "extremely important" task of the Party and a fine tradition and political advantage in winning victories in revolution, construction and reform. Zhong argues that tracing this history and distilling its experience offers a historical reference for keeping to fundamental principles while innovating (守正创新) in propaganda and ideological work in the new era. The article has three parts. The first divides the century into four periods, each with a defining trait: the New Democratic Revolution (revolutionary), socialist revolution and construction (rebuilding), reform and opening up (innovative), and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics (transformative). The second lists six achievements. The third draws nine "basic experiences", each tied to a feature of propaganda work. In Zhong's account, early propaganda joined the "gun" to the "pen", mobilised workers and peasants, and used Marxist education to build the Party and army. After 1949 it reshaped socialist ideology and culture, and from 1978 it was institutionalised through guidelines and regulations. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping's statements on propaganda and ideological work and the Regulations on Propaganda Work of the CPC are presented as bringing the work to "high maturity". The nine experiences are Party leadership (political character), propaganda as an extremely important task, Marxism's guiding position (ideological character), a people-centred approach (mass character), serving the central tasks (service), coordinated material and spiritual civilization (constructive), promoting correct and resisting erroneous ideas (struggle), a "big propaganda" pattern involving the whole Party (systemic), and innovation (artistic). Zhong concludes that propaganda history is also a history of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and that it has shaped a distinctive Party theory of propaganda. The author calls for continued Party leadership, a combative stance against "left" and right deviations, and innovation such as county-level media convergence centres and the Xuexi Qiangguo platform. Read the original if you want a systematic, officially aligned periodisation of Party propaganda work and its guiding principles, as presented by a provincial academy scholar.

Lenin's important thought on being good at "looking at problems politically" and its contemporary value 列宁关于要善于“从政治上看问题”的重要思想及其当代价值 Li Dongming Li Dongming asks what Lenin meant by the injunction that a proletarian party must be good at "looking at problems politically", and what the idea offers Party-building today. Li argues that Lenin treated this as a defining trait of the Bolshevik party. In Li's reading it helped the party seize the political initiative and defuse political risks, and it gives a model for strengthening a party's political construction and political leadership. The article, published in Marxism Studies in 2022, opens with Xi Jinping's December 2020 call to be good at looking at problems politically. It then draws almost entirely on Lenin's writings and speeches from the period of the transition from War Communism to the New Economic Policy (NEP), including the trade-union debate and the 10th Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks). Three sections reconstruct Lenin's thought: grasping political factors when assessing a situation, avoiding political dangers and errors, and putting political requirements into practice. A fourth section draws out its present-day value. Li stresses that Lenin's remark that politics must take precedence over economics does not mean politics determines or replaces economics. It means that economic questions such as the food tax must first be judged by the relation between the working class and the peasantry, on which the survival of Soviet power depended. Li presents the Trotsky–Bukharin trade-union dispute as a failure of this approach. In Li's account Lenin saw danger in factional activity, in a debate that hostile forces could exploit, and in a split that could open the way to capitalist restoration. Li adds that Lenin demanded real ideological unity, not just an end to argument. On implementation, Li reports Lenin's calls to learn to trade, to master economic management, to avoid empty talk, and to "grasp the main link in the chain". Li concludes that Lenin's approach still bears on Party-building in China. Li links it to three capacities set out by Xi: political judgement, political comprehension and political execution. Li calls on cadres to read situations through their political factors, to avoid political errors that endanger the Party's governing position, and to turn the Central Committee's decisions into concrete, creative work. Li holds that political initiative is the most advantageous initiative and political passivity the most dangerous. Read the original if you want a close account of how Lenin's NEP-era writings are used to support current Chinese Party discourse on political awareness and political risk.

The China best suited to "China": the historical evolution and inner meaning of the CPC's visions of state-building 最适合“中国”的中国：中国共产党建国构想的历史演进与内在意蕴 Li Chaoqun Li Chaoqun asks how the Communist Party of China has understood and led the building of a modern Chinese state, and what its successive state-building blueprints reveal. The article argues that these blueprints, adjusted to each period's revolutionary situation, national conditions and the logic of modernization, together show the Party exploring a path of national construction that Li calls the "China best suited to 'China'". The first part traces six stages. These run from the early communists' idea of a "state of the labourers" (Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Mao Zedong) through the Second Congress (1922) plan for a democratic republic and federation, then the workers' and peasants' democratic dictatorship of the Soviet period and the wartime adjustments. They continue to the New Democratic republic and the people's democratic dictatorship, consolidated in the 1949 Common Programme and the 1954 Constitution. The last two stages are socialist industrialization and the "four modernizations", and the post-1978 goals of a modern socialist country, from "three-in-one" through "four-in-one" to "five-in-one" and the strategy of the 19th Party Congress (2017). The second part draws out three implications. Li's core claim is that the sequence shows the Party's lofty founding mission, its theoretical creativity and the people's agency in its path. Li contrasts the Guomindang's one-party rule with a Party that Li says consistently served the people's fundamental interests. On theory, Li argues that the Party adapted the Marxist theory of proletarian dictatorship and developed New Democratic theory, in line with the Two Integrations. It also dropped the early federalism and national self-determination borrowed from Soviet Russia and the Comintern, for a unitary multi-ethnic state with regional ethnic autonomy, which Li attributes to China's tradition of political unity. Third, Li holds that the blueprints tied people's democracy to state-building, and treats whole-process people's democracy as the latest form of this. Li contrasts this with what the article describes as capital-driven "Western-style democracy". Li concludes that the Party, as the core of state-building, has led the country through saving, founding, reviving, enriching and strengthening the nation. In Li's account this unified the Party's growth with that of the modern state and produced a distinctive Chinese logic of state-building. The experience is presented as lasting support for building a modern socialist great power. Read the original if you want a periodised, document-based survey of the Party's changing state-building formulas from the 1920s to the 2010s, as presented in mainstream Party-history scholarship.

The historical position and academic principles of Marxist religious studies 马克思主义宗教学的历史地位和学术原则 Li Shen Li Shen asks what Marxist religious studies is, where it comes from and what principles should govern it.
