The article, published in the journal Science and Atheism in 2022, argues that Marxist religious studies is the science of religion guided by Marxism. In Li's account it grew from the same root as Marxist philosophy, takes the abolition of religion as 'illusory happiness' as its final aim, and must continue to criticise theology and spread atheism. The article is organised in ten numbered sections. It begins with the origins of Chinese Marxist religious studies in the 1950s and 1960s, marked by Ren Jiyu's Buddhist research and Mao Zedong's 1963 instruction to strengthen the study of religion. It then traces the intellectual lineage through eighteenth-century French materialism and German classical philosophy (Kant, Hegel, Strauss, Bauer, Feuerbach). Later sections cover the historical-materialist method, freedom of religious belief, the turn of the bourgeoisie towards religion, and the global trend of religious decline. Li makes three main moves. First, Marx and Engels inherited the critique of religion from the French and German tradition but cut off the 'religious tail' that Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach retained. Their basic principle is to explain religion through history, not history through religion, so religion disappears only when the real conditions it reflects disappear. Second, on this basis Li holds that religion cannot be abolished by coercion, so freedom of belief is upheld, yet the proletarian party aims to free belief 'from the witchcraft of religion' by criticising theology and propagating atheism. Third, Li argues that after the mid-nineteenth century a 'modern bourgeois religious studies' emerged (Max Müller, religious psychology, sociology and phenomenology). In Li's reading it flatters religion by treating it as a permanent feature of human nature. Li concludes that religion is declining overall, citing Whitehead on Europe, and that revivals are minor setbacks. He claims that Western religious forces and bodies such as the US Commission on International Religious Freedom are pursuing 'religious infiltration' of the Global South and China, which he calls a threat to China's ideological security. For Li, criticising theology, spreading atheism and resisting infiltration are the tasks and 'glorious responsibility' of Marxist scholars of religion. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of atheism presents the orthodox Marxist theory of religion and its implications for religious policy and scholarship today.

The idea of self-reform in the Communist Manifesto and its contemporary value 《共产党宣言》的自我革命思想及其当代价值 Miao Ruidan Miao Ruidan asks what the Communist Manifesto contributes to the Chinese Communist Party's current effort at self-reform. The article argues that the Manifesto holds a rich body of thought on how a proletarian party purifies, perfects, renews and improves itself, and that this thought forms the theoretical source of the Party's present self-reform. Miao sets this against the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which named perseverance in self-reform as a historical lesson of the Party's first century. The article has three parts. The first draws out four strands of thought from the Manifesto: purity (the basis of self-purification), vanguard character (the inner driving force of self-perfection), thoroughgoing revolutionary spirit (self-renewal) and party tactics (self-improvement). The second sets out the internal logic that links them. The third turns each strand into a requirement for the Party in the new era, presented under the Party's four capacities: self-purification, self-perfection, self-renewal and self-improvement. In Miao's account, the logic runs from motive to aim to purpose. The motive comes from the proletarian party's essential nature: it has no special interests of its own, so it must keep its purity and advanced character in order to represent the future of the movement. The aim is to temper revolutionary spirit and capacity through renewal and improvement, a process that includes turning the blade inward. The ultimate purpose is to honour the original aspiration and mission of liberating the proletariat and all humankind. Miao then maps the Manifesto's themes onto current Party practice. Ideological, political and organisational purity correspond to ideals-and-convictions education, political building and disciplinary rules. The Manifesto's account of vanguard character is tied to a problem-oriented approach to institution-building and the mass line. Its continuous revolution is tied to upholding fundamental principles while innovating, to criticism and self-criticism, and to using self-reform to lead social revolution. Its tactics are tied to coordinating the 'two overall situations' at home and abroad. Miao concludes that grasping the Manifesto's self-reform ideas as a theoretical source and 'political gene' has both theoretical value and practical relevance. It matters for advancing the Party's self-reform and for the great project of Party building in the new era. Throughout, the Manifesto is read as a source for contemporary Party-building doctrine. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists derive the Party's four-part self-reform formula from a classic Marxist text.

Advancing social development with a people-centred approach 以人民为中心推进社会建设 Yu Jianxing Wu Jiebing Published in Guangming Daily on 7 October 2022, this short commentary reviews a decade of "social development" (shehui jianshe) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Yu Jianxing and Wu Jiebing argue that Xi Jinping's new ideas have answered why and how social development should be pursued in the new era. In their account, these ideas raised the Party's understanding of the subject and drove theoretical and practical innovation. The article has two parts. The first summarises practice and experience since 2012 under four headings: a people-centred concept of social development, the joint advance of social and economic development, the balance between order and vitality, and the interaction of government and society. The second part identifies remaining problems and sets out five areas for reform of the institutions and mechanisms of social development. The authors say that before 2012 social development was understood mainly as improving people's livelihoods. They hold that the 18th Party Congress report added the innovation of social governance, so that social development became a large system spanning resource allocation, social interests, livelihoods, social organisations and social undertakings. They cite GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000, an olive-shaped income distribution, and legal and organisational reforms such as the Civil Code and the Charity Law. They also note the Fengqiao experience and the decoupling of trade associations from administrative organs. They then name three imbalances in some regions: economy over society, livelihood services over social governance, and stability over vitality. They add that local governments treat social development as a weak incentive because results are slow to appear. The authors propose strengthening Party leadership, for instance through Party committee social work or social development commissions. They also call for treating social development like economic development, narrowing the urban–rural, regional and income gaps, and building community resilience and emergency capacity. Further proposals are classified, dynamically empowered management of social organisations, funded by project subsidies rather than service outsourcing, and digital and intelligent reform that reshapes power structures and cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned summary of how Chinese scholars framed social development and its reform agenda in 2022.

The essential attributes and contemporary concerns of the path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化道路的本质属性和当代关切 Xu Ping Yu Miao Published in Guangming Daily in September 2022, this commentary asks what defines the path of Chinese modernization and what concerns it addresses today. Xu Ping and Yu Miao argue that its essential attributes are Party leadership and socialism, and that it differs from Western modernization in three practical features: independence, rootedness in Chinese soil and a people-centred orientation. The authors present it as a path that creates a new form of human civilisation and offers developing countries a new option. The piece opens by citing the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's centenary achievements and historical experience. It then has three sections: the essential attributes of the path, its distinctive practical features compared with Western modernization, and its contemporary content. The contemporary content is organised around Xi Jinping's account of the five features of Chinese modernization and the new development philosophy. The argument rests largely on quotations from Xi Jinping, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. In the authors' account, Party leadership is the decisive element and the fundamental political advantage of the path. Socialism is its institutional basis and fundamental direction, and the path aims to unite a high level of modernization with socialism and so go beyond capitalist modernization. The authors say this rejects the old Western routes of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization. Independence, they argue, follows from a history of subordination to the West and from the lesson that no nation can prosper by depending on others. Rootedness means gradual, endogenous evolution from Chinese civilisation. The people-centred character draws on Marxism, with development for the people, by the people and shared by the people. The authors conclude that the path must be advanced by acting on the new development stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern. They call for coordinating the "five-sphere" overall plan and the "four-pronged" strategy. They say innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing steer modernization toward higher quality, efficiency, fairness and harmony. A framework centred on whole-process people's democracy and common prosperity is said to be taking shape. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2022 presented Chinese modernization's defining attributes and its contrast with Western models.

The key to building a modern socialist country in all respects lies in the Party 全面建设社会主义现代化国家关键在党 Wang Binglin Liu Kui Published in the People's Daily on 18 October 2022, during the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's statement in the Congress report that the key to building a modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation lies in the Party. Wang and Liu argue that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, and that the Party's overall leadership must therefore be upheld and strengthened. The piece has three parts. It first traces how the Party led the people onto the path of Chinese modernization across four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era from the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then explains why Party leadership is the fundamental guarantee of the project, and finally turns to the role of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On the second point, the authors give three reasons. Party leadership keeps Chinese modernization on the right direction and in line with the essential requirements of socialism. It keeps modernization people-centred. It also gathers great strength, because the Party is said to share the people's interests and fate. The authors credit this leadership with letting China complete in decades an industrialization that took developed countries centuries, and with two miracles of rapid growth and long-term social stability. The authors conclude that upholding leadership requires improving it, and call for the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. Their agenda covers political, ideological, organizational, conduct and discipline building, institutional improvement, and an integrated approach to fighting corruption. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed statement of how Party commentary linked Party leadership to Chinese modernization on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

Stand firm in historical confidence and strengthen historical initiative 坚定历史自信 增强历史主动 Li Hua Written on the eve of the 20th Party Congress (2022) and first published in Guangming Daily, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call, made during a visit to the exhibition "Forging Ahead in the New Era", for the whole Party and people to stand firm in historical confidence and strengthen historical initiative. Li Hua argues that historical confidence rests on understanding history: the more fully the historical process is grasped, the more initiative the Party has over the future. The article is organised around three sources of the Party's historical confidence, each tied to one Chinese character: Marxism "works" (xing), the Communist Party "can" (neng), and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good" (hao). It moves from the modern failure of Western doctrines in China, through a periodised account of the Party's record, to the achievements of the new era. Li's first claim is that Marxism is the source of this confidence. After the Opium War, reformism, liberalism, social Darwinism, anarchism, pragmatism and other imported doctrines were tried and failed; the October Revolution brought Marxism-Leninism, and the Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has led China from "standing up" through "becoming rich" to "becoming strong". Second, Li reviews four periods: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The article credits each with historic breakthroughs, including national independence, the basic socialist system, the rise to the world's second-largest economy, and the first centenary goal. Third, Li presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as the practical expression of that confidence, citing industrialisation completed in decades, the elimination of absolute poverty, and Chinese modernization as a path that, in the author's account, rejects capital-centred, polarising and expansionist Western models. Li concludes that the Party's confidence rests on its achievements, its capacities and its fighting and self-reforming spirit, and ultimately on a commitment to the people's wellbeing, national rejuvenation and human progress. The piece cites Xi's statement that the Party, state and nation have the most reason to be confident. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2022 official discourse on historical confidence was framed for a general newspaper readership on the eve of the Congress.

The normative dimension of Marxism 马克思主义的规范性维度 Xu Mengqiu Marxism's standard self-descriptions include practicality, class character, criticality, revolutionary character and scientific character, but not "normativity". Xu Mengqiu argues that the concept should now be introduced, both to answer Western Marxism and Western scholars who criticise or misread Marxism and to widen the field of Marxist research. Xu's thesis is that Marxism has a normative dimension and normative content, and that its normative basis is fairly clear. The piece appeared in Guangming Daily on 26 September 2022. The article has two parts. The first defines the "normative dimension" and contrasts it with a "cognitive dimension", using examples from Mencius, Confucius, daily life and engineering acceptance checks. The second turns to Marxism. It reports Habermas's claim that Marxist social theory lacks a clear normative basis, and the view of Allen Wood and Richard Miller (named in the text as Wood and Miller) that Marx was not concerned with justice and morality. It then answers these claims with passages from Marx and Engels. Xu defines the normative dimension as starting from an "ought" grounded in some value outlook. From that position one affirms or negates what actually exists, then defends, corrects or reconstructs it. Xu groups description, explanation and empirical verification under a "cognitive dimension", and holds that the normative dimension also includes practical action. On Hume's problem of deriving "ought" from "is", Xu argues that the two activities arise together in practice, so neither is logically prior. Against Habermas, Xu holds that Marx's critical standpoint shifted with his worldview and his target, but two features run throughout. The first is a value foundation in the fundamental interests of the proletariat and working people, combined with a scientific grasp of historical laws, which together yield a revolutionary ideal. The second is a critique of capitalist reality and bourgeois ideology by both theoretical and material weapons, in the service of socialism and communism. Xu cites the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach and Capital as evidence of this dimension. Xu concludes that Marxist normativity is the unity of its value outlook and its sense of the "ought", with proletarian interests and historical laws as its ground. It joins the value yardstick to the scientific yardstick. Normativity and scientific character are essentially different but mutually dependent. Without science, Marxism would fall into utopian or ethical socialism. Marxists, Xu adds, do not claim value-neutrality, and openly present their doctrine as the proletariat's intellectual weapon. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language reply to Habermas and to the debate on Marx and justice, and a view of how Chinese Marxist theory is starting to adopt the vocabulary of normativity.

Guidance by Marxist scientific theory as the Chinese Communist Party's distinctive political character and powerful political strength 马克思主义科学理论指导是中国共产党的鲜明政治品格和强大政治优势 Ruan Huarong Chen Shuguang Writing in Guangming Daily on 16 September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Ruan Huarong and Chen Shuguang take up Xi Jinping's statement that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Party's distinctive political character and powerful political strength. They argue that the Party's achievements and the merits of socialism with Chinese characteristics come down, in the end, to the fact that Marxism works. The commentary is organised in three parts. The first presents the adoption of Marxism as the choice of history and the people in modern China. The second reviews four historical periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third turns to the continuing task of developing Marxism in China. The authors first claim that after 1840 many programmes and isms were tried and failed, including reformism, liberalism, anarchism and pragmatism, and that only Marxism could resolve the nation's historic problems. They then describe a mutual relationship: Marxism did not fail the Party, and the Party did not fail Marxism. In their account Marxism gave rise to the Party and armed it, while the Party upheld and developed Marxism, defended it during a low ebb of world socialism and put it into practice in the largest developing country. Period by period, they link Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era to the successive leaps from 'standing up' to 'becoming prosperous' to 'becoming strong'. The authors conclude that the adapting of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is far from finished. They hold that Marxism is a guide to action, not dogma, and that China's present practical innovation requires further integration of its basic principles with China's realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Theoretical innovation, they say, will let Marxism show greater persuasive force in China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official narrative of Marxism's role in its history was presented to a general readership on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

Keep advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 把新时代中国特色社会主义不断推向前进 Liu Guangming Hu Dezhi Liu Yongliang Published in the People's Daily on 19 October 2022, this commentary responds to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and its theme of holding high the banner of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The authors argue that the Party will keep advancing this cause and winning new victories on the new journey of building a modern socialist country. The piece is organised under three headings. It first treats socialism with Chinese characteristics as the renewal of scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China. It then presents it as the only correct path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Finally it calls for consistent adherence to and development of the cause. The authors contend that socialism with Chinese characteristics upholds the basic principles of scientific socialism while giving them Chinese features. They list Party leadership, the people's democratic dictatorship, public ownership as the mainstay, the guiding role of Marxism and a people-centred stance. They also claim that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has enriched theories of development stages, social contradictions and modernization. In their account, this shows the path is correct and will be walked steadily and well. The authors call for full implementation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and for pursuing high-quality development, common prosperity and whole-process people's democracy amid what they call great changes unseen in a century. They stress the "five musts" set out in the Congress report, including Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Persistently and deeply advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 持之以恒深入推进全面从严治党 Li Lifeng Writing in Guangming Daily on 15 September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Li Lifeng argues that the Party must keep advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the way to consolidate its long-term governing position. Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's speech to a seminar of provincial and ministerial leading cadres, the commentary treats this governance as the Party's self-reform, which Li presents as leading social revolution. The piece has three sections. The first presents full and rigorous self-governance as a great practice of self-reform in the new era. The second calls for a political awareness that this work is "always on the road". The third sets out measures for opening "new realms" of self-reform. In the first section Li ties the policy to five tasks: the great struggle, the great cause, the great project of Party building, the great dream, and the Party's founding mission. Li holds that courage in self-reform is the Party's most distinctive trait and has let it solve its own problems repeatedly. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Li says, the Party has reversed laxity in Party governance and found a path to escape the "historical cycle" through self-reform. The second section argues the work must continue because of the "four tests" and "four dangers", a turbulent international environment, and unresolved impurities in the Party's politics, thinking, organisation and conduct. Li quotes Xi on the continuing struggle against corruption. The third section gives six measures: political building as the guiding principle, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; ideological building through theoretical study; strict discipline and a campaign against formalism, bureaucratism and extravagance under the eight-point rules; a sustained anti-corruption drive with "zero tolerance", hitting "tigers" and "flies"; stronger Party organisations and a cadre corps willing to struggle; and a system of Party regulations and supervision. Li concludes that only persistence will keep the Party from degenerating and keep the "red country" from changing colour. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of how Party theory framed self-reform and anti-corruption on the eve of the 20th Party Congress."

The world significance of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的世界意义 Guo Qingsong This newspaper commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in October 2022, asks what Chinese modernization means beyond China. Guo argues that it breaks the myth that "modernization means Westernization", develops modernization theory, and offers the world a new form of human civilisation, a different path for developing countries and a fresh vitality for scientific socialism. The piece opens with Xi Jinping's five defining features of Chinese modernization. It then proceeds in three numbered sections: the creation of a new form of human civilisation, the reshaping of the international order, and the strengths of the socialist system. In the first section, Guo contends that Chinese modernization abandons four features of the traditional model: capital-centred development and polarisation, material growth as the sole aim, disregard for ecology, and expansionist plunder. In their place it puts common prosperity, balance between material and cultural-ethical advance, harmony between humanity and nature, and a community with a shared future for mankind. The second section describes an irreversible trend of "the East rising and the West declining" and cites 2021 trade and foreign-exchange-reserve figures, as well as a population of over 1.4 billion entering modernity. The third section argues that people-centredness shields modernization from the logic of capital and so expands scientific socialism. Guo concludes that the socialist character under Communist Party leadership and the people-centred orientation are the essential features of Chinese modernization and the root of its success. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the international meaning of Chinese modernization.

Reading the great changes unseen in a century through principle, theory and philosophy A review of Great-Power Games and the Future World: International Relations in the Perspective of the Philosophy of History 从道理学理哲理解读世界百年未有之大变局 Lin Jianhua This book review, first published in Guangming Daily in September 2022, introduces Han Zhen's Great-Power Games and the Future World: International Relations in the Perspective of the Philosophy of History (Central Party School Press, June 2022). Han is a professor at Beijing Normal University. Reviewer Lin Jianhua presents the book as an original work that uses the philosophy of history to interpret what Xi Jinping has called the great changes unseen in a century, and sums up its three main features. According to Lin, the book examines how international relations and the international order ought to be built and how they actually are, the basic pattern of interaction between China and the future world, and the general laws of social development. The review is organised around the three features, each ending with one dimension of explanation: the philosophical (zhéli), the theoretical (xuéli) and the practical (daoli). The first feature is that the book takes historical materialism and materialist dialectics as its basic guide. In Lin's account, Han holds that world history is driven by contradictions between productive forces and relations of production, not by good intentions, and that dialectics joins idealist "ought" with realist "is". The second is looking beneath appearances through unity of opposites. Three chapters treat North–South, East–West and capitalism–socialism, and Han reads the changing balance in each as favouring the South, the East and socialism. The third is strategic clarity and confidence and historical consciousness. Lin reports Han's view that the United States regards China as its chief strategic rival, so hopes of an American change of heart contradict historical materialism. Lin concludes, following Han, that China should combine resolute and skilful struggle with promotion of shared human values and a community with a shared future for mankind. The review treats this as both the fundamental theme of the philosophy of history and a rational demand for the future. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language introduction to how a Party-affiliated scholarly book frames great-power rivalry through Marxist philosophy of history.

Achievements of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 马克思主义中国化时代化的成就 Elias Jabbour This short commentary is a Chinese translation of a piece by the Brazilian economist Elias Jabbour, written just after the 20th Party Congress (2022). Jabbour argues that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is the key to understanding China's achievements in the new era and its future changes. The text takes Xi Jinping's report to the Congress as its starting point. It touches on the economy, state-owned enterprises, national security, technological innovation, socialist democracy and the lessons of the Soviet collapse. Jabbour contrasts the Chinese approach with capitalist states, whose ruling classes in his account turn state power into control over the people and serve only a rich minority. In China, he says, the large state-owned enterprise system, public finance and state asset management allowed innovative growth of the public sector, including in 5G, big data and artificial intelligence. He reads Marx as holding that technology can advance society but is monopolised by a few under capitalism, whereas under socialism it serves the people. He also points to risks from operating inside Western-dominated international rules and from an unstable world. Jabbour concludes that a government system guided by Marxism is vital for socialist countries. He attributes the Soviet collapse largely to a failure to localise Marxism and to leaders abandoning it. He also presents the anti-corruption struggle and close ties between Party and people as strengthening China's capacity to meet challenges. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a foreign Marxist economist framed the 20th Party Congress for a Chinese readership.

China's cause of common prosperity continues to develop with remarkable achievements 中国的共同富裕事业持续发展成就斐然 Tang Mai This is a Chinese translation of a short commentary by Tang Mai (a British scholar, emeritus professor at the University of Sussex), published in Guangming Daily in October 2022. Tang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Communist Party of China has given common prosperity growing priority, and that its policies have achieved notable results in material, ecological, cultural and governance terms. The article surveys the policy areas it associates with common prosperity: innovation-driven high-quality development, regulation of illegal and excessive incomes, primary and secondary distribution, housing, education and health costs, targeted poverty alleviation, rural revitalisation, ecological civilisation and pandemic protection. It closes with China's international role. In Tang's account, the Party encourages hard work and innovation while curbing corruption, financial and property risks, platform monopolies and entertainment-sector tax evasion. It expands the middle-income group, builds social insurance and basic public services, and uses the "double reduction" policy and affordable housing to stop key sectors being "hijacked by capital". The article cites targeted poverty alleviation as lifting nearly 100 million people out of extreme poverty. Tang also contends that the capitalist international division of labour widens global inequality, and that China's rise shows emerging economies can overcome this with good governance and help others, through the Belt and Road Initiative and the new development banks. Tang concludes that common prosperity and high-quality development are the necessary path to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that better distribution strengthens a domestic-demand-led model. The call for a community with a shared future for mankind is presented as the international expression of common prosperity. Read the original if you want to see how a foreign scholar presented China's common prosperity agenda to a Chinese Party-affiliated readership in 2022.

Always at the forefront of the cause of the Party and the people Commemorating the 120th anniversary of the birth of Peng Zhen 永远站在党和人民事业的最前线 Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee Published in the People's Daily on 12 October 2022, the 120th anniversary of Peng Zhen's birth, this commemorative article from the Party's central history and documentation institute presents Peng (1902–1997) as a proletarian revolutionary, a staunch Marxist and the chief founder of socialist legality in New China. Its thesis is that he spent his whole life at the forefront of the Party's and the people's cause, and that his career offers lasting lessons for Party members today. The article is organised chronologically in four sections. The first follows Peng from a poor peasant family in Shanxi through Party organising in Taiyuan and Tianjin, imprisonment, work in the north during the War of Resistance, the Jin-Cha-Ji base area, the Yan'an rectification movement and the Northeast. The second covers the early People's Republic, when Peng sat on the Secretariat and led Beijing for 17 years. The third covers the period after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), when he headed the legal and legislative work of the National People's Congress Standing Committee. The fourth draws lessons. In the article's account, Peng's most important contributions were in Party building, in Beijing's development and above all in law. It credits him with ideas on keeping the Party free from corruption, on collective leadership and democratic centralism, and on the people's congress system. It reports that between 1979 and 1988 he oversaw 88 laws and 35 legal decisions, drafted the preface to the 1982 constitution revision, and promoted standing committees of local people's congresses, competitive elections and direct elections to county level. It also credits him with directing the trial of the Lin Biao and Jiang Qing cliques, and notes that he suffered persecution during the Cultural Revolution. The closing section draws four lessons, each tied to a statement by Xi Jinping: firm conviction and fidelity to the original aspiration, a people-first public-servant outlook, seeking truth from facts, and an enterprising spirit. The article calls on readers to rally around the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core and to greet the 20th Party Congress (2022) with practical action. Read the original if you want an official Party-history portrait of Peng Zhen and an example of how the Party's central history institute presents a revolutionary leader's legacy for current political purposes.

Liu Shaoqi's reflections on socialist construction in China Centred on his speeches at the study and discussion meetings on the Soviet Political Economy textbook 刘少奇对我国社会主义建设的思考 Ma Huiyi Ma Huiyi examines what Liu Shaoqi said about socialism in the study and discussion meetings on the Soviet Political Economy textbook (third edition), which he organised in November 1959. Mao Zedong had urged officials to read the textbook from late 1958 in order to correct the 'Leftist' errors of the Great Leap Forward and the people's commune movement. Ma argues that Liu, reading the textbook critically against Chinese realities, deepened the Party's understanding of 'what socialism is and how to build it'. The article is organised in three parts, followed by a short conclusion. It first sets out Liu's account of the basic features of socialist society, then his view of the essence and purpose of socialist construction, and finally the methodological principles he advanced for exploring a distinctively Chinese path. Ma draws mainly on Liu's speeches, later published in a volume on China's economic construction, and places them against the experience after the Eighth Party Congress (1956). On socialist society, Ma reports that Liu defined it as a lower stage of communism that still bears marks of the old society. Its four features are planned, proportionate development, in which speed and proportion are a unity of opposites; public ownership as the main body, retaining forms such as money and commodities to be used and eventually discarded; distribution according to labour, combined with political and ideological work rather than reliance on 'material incentives'; and attention to relations among working people, especially between leaders and led. On the essence of construction, Liu is said to have treated it as the continual handling of contradictions between productive forces and relations of production, with relations adjusted consciously, and as aiming at the free all-round development of people in step with social development. On method, Ma highlights three points: Soviet and Chinese experience each have both universal and particular aspects; errors are possible and must be corrected promptly; and principle must be combined with flexibility. Ma concludes that these ideas deepened the Party's understanding of the laws of socialist construction and laid an intellectual basis for later exploration of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article stresses Liu's method of linking theory with practice. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-history account of Liu Shaoqi's critical reading of the Soviet textbook, with extensive quotations from his speeches.

Chinese modernization offers important lessons for the world 中国式现代化具有重要启示意义 Wen Hongyu Wang Yuchen This short commentary, first published in People's Daily on 10 October 2022, argues that Chinese modernization carries significant lessons for other countries. Opening with Xi Jinping's list of its five features, Wen and Wang present it as supplying a Chinese theory and a Chinese approach that other countries can draw on. The piece is organised as a series of claims, each beginning with a feature of Chinese modernization and ending with the lesson the authors draw from it. They address modernization theory, the pace of development, the relation between growth and distribution, international relations, and the relation between traditional and modern civilization. On theory, the authors contend that the West has long held discursive dominance and that many scholars equate modernization with Westernization. In their account, Chinese modernization shows that modernization is not a single-choice question, and that its theory fully surpasses capital-centred Western theory. They also say that, unlike the Western 'serial' sequence, China pursued industrialization, informatization, urbanization and agricultural modernization in parallel. On distribution, they say it first makes the 'cake' bigger and then divides it through institutional arrangements, in pursuit of common prosperity. The authors conclude that Chinese modernization breaks the myth that modernization means Westernization. They hold that it gives developing countries a new perspective, path and model, and that it creates a new form of human civilization under Marxist guidance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press presented Chinese modernization's international significance just before the 20th Party Congress.

Persisting in advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization 坚持以中国式现代化推进中华民族伟大复兴 Chen Shuo Guo Guangyin Published in the People's Daily on 11 October 2022, this commentary by Chen Shuo and Guo Guangyin takes up Xi Jinping's instruction, given at a study session for provincial and ministerial leaders, that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation must be advanced through Chinese modernization. The authors argue that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. In their account, the Party's leadership, the socialist direction and the goal of national rejuvenation are what make the path both distinctive and sustainable. The piece is built in three parts, each opening with a statement by Xi Jinping. The first treats Party leadership as the fundamental guarantee of Chinese modernization. The second treats socialism as its fundamental direction. The third presents national rejuvenation as its goal. The authors frame the discussion by the achievements of the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012), which they describe as historic and as making rejuvenation an irreversible process. On leadership, Chen and Guo argue that the Party gives modernization a firm leading core, keeps it on the correct course and sustains its vitality. For the last point they cite full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform. On socialism, they set Chinese modernization against Western modernization, which they describe as capital-centred, polarising, materialistic and expansionist. They credit Chinese modernization with a people-centred approach, common prosperity, all-round human development and a path of peaceful development, and they cite poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society as evidence. On national rejuvenation, the authors say China was drawn passively into a Western-led modernization after the modern era began. They conclude that the search for a modern path has always carried a double meaning, modernization and rejuvenation. They describe the Party as holding to this mission through successive theoretical and practical innovations, and they cite the two-step plan to build a modern socialist country by mid-century. They also point to the spiritual drive that the mission provides. They conclude that continuing on the chosen path will build China into a great modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary linked Chinese modernization, socialism and national rejuvenation just before the 20th Party Congress.

A typology and stage theory of modernization, and Chinese modernization Also on how Chinese modernization responds to the predicaments of Western modern civilization 现代化类型学、阶段论与中国式现代化 Yang Dian Yang Dian takes up two questions in this short piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2022: whether modernization is the same as Westernization, and whether it is a one-off state or an evolving process. Taking a global-sociology perspective, Yang proposes a typology and a stage theory of modernization. The article argues that modernization is not Westernization and that Western leadership is not permanent. The piece first sets out two roads and five types of modernization, then three historical stages. It next applies this framework to the origins, distinctive features and eight characteristics of Chinese modernization. It closes by listing predicaments of Western modern civilization and seven ways in which China's path is said to respond to them. Yang divides capitalist modernization into market-led, state-led and coordinated types, and socialist modernization into the Chinese and Soviet types. Yang contends that socialist modernization suits latecomer countries better, because it eases the tension in capital's dual nature and supplies a strong government able to pursue catch-up. In the stage theory, industrialization and urbanization (led by Britain) gave way to informatization, globalization and financialization (led by the United States). A third stage, built on artificial intelligence, is in Yang's account now contested by China and the United States, so non-Western countries may lead later stages. Yang concludes that Chinese modernization is theoretically and practically viable and offers "Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach" for going beyond Western-centred, one-model views of modernity. The proposed responses include whole-process people's democracy, curbing the disorderly expansion of capital, common prosperity, green development and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how a Chinese sociologist frames modernization theory to support the case for Chinese modernization.

What is new about the Chinese path to modernization 中国式现代化道路新在哪里 Huang Qunhui Writing in the People's Daily on 10 October 2022, just before the 20th Party Congress, Huang Qunhui asks what is new about the path of Chinese modernization. Huang argues that it fits China's realities, reflects the laws of socialist construction and of human social development, and comprehensively surpasses Western modernization theory. The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's formulation of a new path and a new form of human civilization. It then proceeds through four themes: the people-centred development philosophy, the use of national conditions to shape modernization's driving mechanism and strategy, exchange and mutual learning among civilizations, and the path of peaceful development. Huang contends that Chinese modernization follows the general laws of industrialization, marketization and globalization but rejects the Western logic of subordinating productive forces to capital, which the author associates with polarization, materialism and external plunder. Instead, it pursues common prosperity and the coordinated development of five civilizations. Huang credits the socialist market economy, which combines an effective market with an effective government and curbs the "reckless expansion" of capital, along with phased strategic planning. The author also contrasts Western views of a "clash of civilizations" and a "strong countries seek hegemony" logic with China's promotion of civilizational mutual learning and its pledge never to seek hegemony. Huang concludes that China's experience shows a late-developing country can achieve leapfrog development by independently exploring a path suited to its own conditions. Against a backdrop of what the article calls great changes unseen in a century, it presents China's initiatives as offering the world "Chinese wisdom" and solutions. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Chinese modernization was contrasted with the Western model on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

A community with a shared future for mankind: inheritance and innovation of Marx and Engels's theory of world history 人类命运共同体：马克思恩格斯世界历史理论的继承与创新 Gong Liuji Li Jing Marking the 90th anniversary of the publication of The German Ideology in 2022, Gong Liuji and Li Jing ask how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind relates to the theory of world history that Marx and Engels developed in that work. They argue that the idea, put forward by Xi Jinping, upholds the core of the theory while innovating on it. In their view, understanding the link requires first grasping the theory's main content and then identifying what the idea adds. The article has three main parts. The first reconstructs the theory of world history in The German Ideology: world history as an objective process, productive forces and universal intercourse as its basic drivers, and communism as its direction of development. The second shows how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind inherits the theory in three dimensions: theoretical, practical and value. The third sets out three innovations, in development path, development method and development subject. On inheritance, the authors say the idea follows the historical trend in a period of what they call great change unseen in a century, and keeps the theory's concern for harmony between humanity and nature, including green and sustainable development. They also argue that it carries on the value goal of the free and all-round development of the human being, contrasting the "false community" with the "true community" of The German Ideology. On innovation, they claim that Marx and Engels offered a scientific prediction without a concrete programme, whereas the idea supplies a practical plan. They further argue that its method is win-win cooperation rather than the violent revolution Marx and Engels envisaged, and that its subject extends from the proletariat to the peoples of the world. In their account, Marx and Engels were limited by their era in not foreseeing how capitalist societies would adjust themselves and improve welfare systems. The authors conclude that the theory of world history provides the foundation for the idea, while the idea inherits, develops and renews the theory. They hold that it gives the theory a contemporary spirit and helps in viewing global trends and major problems through a world-historical lens, so as to promote common development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars present Xi Jinping's concept as a continuation and update of Marx and Engels's world-history theory.

Grasping Marx and Engels's thought on ecology and science and technology 把握马克思恩格斯的生态科技思想 Yang Xiaobin Zhang Tian Yang Xiaobin and Zhang Tian ask how Marx and Engels related science and technology to the natural environment. Writing in a newspaper commentary of 2022, they argue that the two thinkers developed a mature "ecological science-and-technology thought". In it, technology stands in a dialectical unity with humanity and nature, and its ecological effects depend on the social system that controls it. The piece opens by noting that environmental protection has become a global concern in which technology is central. It then proceeds in three steps: the unity of technology, humans and nature; the damage done when technology is subordinated to capital; and the role of technology under communism. In the authors' reading, nature is the basis of human activity, and technology emerges from humans' knowledge and transformation of nature. Technology can also open new sources of value by raising resource efficiency and recycling waste, which Marx called production excretions. Under capital, they argue, technology serves profit and accumulation. It leads to over-exploitation, pollution, the transfer of ecological damage worldwide, and a "rift" in the metabolism between humans and nature. Capitalist remedies are described as only temporary and superficial. Under communism, production would aim at use-value and meeting reasonable needs, with the means of production held in common. Technology would then transform nature in accordance with its laws and support the free and all-round development of the individual. The authors conclude that technology itself does not damage nature and that the root of the problem lies in capitalist control. Only the replacement of capitalism by communism, in their account, can bring a lasting, rational metabolism and a "dual liberation" of humans and nature. Read the original if you want a concise overview of how Marx and Engels's classic passages are used to link ecology and technology.

Why confidence in our institutions has grown firmer 制度自信何以更加坚定 Ren Lixuan This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 28 September 2022, asks why confidence in China's institutions (zhidu zixin) has become firmer in the new era. Ren Lixuan answers that the institutional system has become more mature and settled, and that it has shown strong governance effectiveness in practice. In the article's account, these two grounds are the basis for stronger confidence in the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece has three parts. The first reviews institution-building since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which dealt with modernizing the system and capacity of national governance. The second sets out the governance results of the "Chinese system" in tackling long-standing problems and in meeting risks. The third turns to what must be done on the new journey. Ren describes the institutional system as complete, scientific and standardised, and effective in operation. The article lists 13 areas of institutional innovation, with the Party's leadership system holding the commanding position. Ren treats governance effectiveness as the test of any system and cites poverty alleviation, major technological projects and ecological protection as results. The article adds the response to Covid-19, external pressure from the United States and the West, and the Party's self-reform as further evidence. It contrasts "Chinese governance" with "Western disorder". It attributes this effectiveness to the Party's leadership as the greatest advantage and to the coordination of institutions across levels, which it says yields a whole greater than the sum of its parts. For the new journey, Ren calls for three things. These are to keep drawing on the Party's leadership as the greatest advantage, including through the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, to hold to fundamental principles while innovating, and to turn institutional advantages into governance effectiveness. The last requires strict implementation, with leading cadres as the "key minority" setting an example, and comprehensive supervision of enforcement. Ren concludes that the aim is to modernize national governance by the time a modern socialist country is built.

Read the original if you want a representative example of the official People's Daily case for institutional confidence in the Xi Jinping era, including its list of the 13 institutional areas.

How cultural confidence has become more firm 文化自信何以更加坚定 Ren Lixuan Writing in the People's Daily in September 2022, Ren Lixuan asks why cultural confidence among the Party and the Chinese people has grown firmer over the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Ren's answer is that cultural work under Xi Jinping has produced "historic achievements" and that this confidence is a basic, deep and lasting force on which national rejuvenation depends. The piece is an authoritative commentary on Party cultural policy rather than a scholarly study. The article has three parts. The first sets out six areas in which cultural confidence is said to have strengthened: Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, the treatment of fine traditional Chinese culture, the meeting of people's spiritual and cultural needs, responses to risks and challenges, and exchange and mutual learning among civilisations. The second part explains how the Party's "cultural consciousness" and Xi Jinping's leadership and thought guide this process. The third turns to the future and sets out three tasks. Ren argues that cultural confidence is built on Marxism as the guiding ideology, since abandoning it would mean losing one's soul and direction. It also rests on a "scientific" attitude to tradition, meaning creative transformation and innovative development. The author cites the Party's elevation of cultural confidence into the Four-sphere Confidence, the Party's control over propaganda, ideology and media, and Xi's speeches and cultural diplomacy. Examples include popular television dramas, free public cultural venues, the "great anti-epidemic spirit" and the poverty-alleviation spirit, and the 2019 Dialogue of Asian Civilizations. Ren presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the theoretical guide that gave the Party's understanding of culture a new level. Looking ahead, Ren calls for adherence to the cultural development path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, which the article calls the only correct path. This means learning from other cultures without treating foreign things as superior. Ren also urges cultural creation grounded in practice, with reform of cultural management systems and use of advanced technology, and the full release of the spiritual force in cultural confidence for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of the official People's Daily framing of cultural confidence and Party leadership over culture after 2012.

How theoretical confidence becomes firmer 理论自信何以更加坚定 Ren Lixuan Writing in the People's Daily in September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Ren Lixuan asks why the Party and the whole country should hold firmer confidence in theory. The answer is that Marxism, repeatedly adapted to Chinese conditions, has proved itself in practice. The commentary presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the latest result of that process, and as the basis for stronger theoretical confidence. The piece has four parts. It first reviews modern Chinese history to explain why "Marxism works". It then sets out how the Thought opens up "new realms" of Marxism. A third part treats the Thought as a theory that arises from practice and guides it, citing the achievements of the decade since 2012. A final part gives practical requirements for the new journey. Ren's central claim is that the Party's successes come from adapting Marxism to China's realities and to traditional Chinese culture. The author traces this through Mao Zedong Thought and Deng Xiaoping Theory to the new Thought, which is called twenty-first-century Marxism. The Thought is said to answer major questions in four areas: national rejuvenation, Chinese modernization, building a Marxist party in long-term power, and the world's future. Under the last heading the author lists the community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. In Ren's account the Thought has guided the response to external pressure and to the pandemic, the Party's anti-corruption and self-reform drive, and economic and social progress. The author cites GDP of 114 trillion yuan and per capita GDP above 12,000 US dollars. Ren calls for three things: studying and absorbing the Thought thoroughly, applying it to solve concrete problems, and continuing to innovate while upholding fundamental principles, so that Marxism is further adapted to China. The author argues that theoretical innovation never ends and that confidence rests on understanding. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party commentary justified theoretical confidence on the eve of the 20th Party Congress (2022).

How confidence in the path has become firmer 道路自信何以更加坚定 Ren Lixuan Writing in the People's Daily on 26 September 2022, during the press-conference series "China's Decade" and shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Ren Lixuan asks why confidence in the path (daolu zixin) of socialism with Chinese characteristics has grown firmer. The commentary answers that the achievements of the past decade and a deepened understanding of that path justify firmer confidence. Ren concludes that China will neither return to a "closed and rigid old path" nor take the "evil path" of changing the Party's banner. The piece has three parts. The first reviews what the path has achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out four "unities" that the author says capture the new understanding of the path. The third lists four requirements for going forward. Throughout, Ren draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements. In the first part, Ren credits the path with three results. It has produced Chinese modernization, which Ren says rejects the Western model of modernization centred on capital, polarisation, materialism and external plunder, and breaks the notion that modernization means Westernization. It has created a "new form of human civilization". And it has brought the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation into an irreversible process, with the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, GDP of 114 trillion yuan in 2021, and the leap from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong". The second part presents the four unities: Party leadership with the people's主体 role, scientific socialism's theoretical logic with China's historical logic, conformity to laws of development with conformity to purpose, and promoting Chinese civilization with promoting common human values. For the future, Ren calls for upholding and improving Party leadership, including the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. Ren also urges independence and self-reliance, coordinated advancement of the "five-sphere integrated plan" and the "four-pronged comprehensive strategy", and development as the first priority with solid steps toward common prosperity. The author holds that doing so will secure the second centenary goal and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official Party commentary in 2022 framed the "path" as a justification for continuity ahead of the 20th Party Congress.

New features of contemporary capitalism Neo-feudalism or communism 当代资本主义发展的新特征 Jodi Dean This is a Chinese translation of an article by the American political theorist Jodi Dean. It responds to McKenzie Wark's provocation in Capital Is Dead: what if we are no longer in capitalism but in something worse? Dean answers by tracing trends rather than saying yes or no. Echoing Rosa Luxemburg's 'socialism or barbarism', Dean argues that the choice is between communism and neo-feudalism, and that digital capitalism is drifting towards the latter. The article first defines capitalism, communism and the premise that capitalism has always lived off other modes of production. It then sets out four linked features of neo-feudalism: divided sovereignty, new hierarchies of lords and peasants, a split between privileged cities and desolate hinterlands, and amplified insecurity and apocalyptic feeling. It goes on to contest liberal talk of a 'democracy versus fascism' struggle, argue that neo-feudalism continues imperialism, and criticise parts of the contemporary left. It closes with a communist response to each feature. Dean's central claim is that accumulation now works through rent, debt and coercive power more than through profit from production, so that the value-form is weakened as capital escapes the factory. Platforms such as Uber and Airbnb, land privatisation, private investor tribunals, fine-based municipal policing and data extraction are cited as examples. Drawing on Barabási's work on networks, Dean holds that power-law distributions make hierarchy inherent to digital networks, so that only political action can abolish it. The author also argues that the rightward turn comes from economic desperation and weak labour, not from fascism as such, and that localism, basic income and 'post-work' visions mirror neo-feudal tendencies. Dean proposes reading divided sovereignty as the weakening of nation-states that a transnational communist order would need. The author also calls for siding with peasants and proletarians against the new lords, abolishing private ownership of the means of production, dissolving the town–country divide, and cultivating comradeship, courage and discipline. The author mentions Mao Zedong's strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside as one possible reference. The trend is not fixed, but without organised struggle the path leads to neo-feudalism. Read the original if you want a Western Marxist account of digital capitalism, rent and the hinterland, or a case study in how foreign Marxist work is presented to Chinese readers.

The essence of America's external "political infiltration" 美国对外“政治渗透”的本质 Guo Yonghu Writing in 2022, Guo Yonghu asks what lies behind the United States' external "political infiltration", which the article defines as using political means, together with economic, military, cultural and diplomatic resources, to shape the ideology, perceptions and behaviour of other countries' leaders, elites and publics. Guo argues that, whatever President Biden says about not seeking a new Cold War, the historical record shows a consistent pattern. In the author's account its aims are to dominate world order, consolidate the capitalist world system and promote "peaceful evolution" in socialist states. The article has three parts. The first traces the history of US infiltration from the 1820s Monroe Doctrine and Caribbean interventions, through hostility to the Russian Revolution and Cold War CIA covert action, to the post-Cold War period. The second sets out what Guo calls its essence. The third surveys how other states have resisted, then proposes responses for China. Examples include the 1964 Chilean election, Carter's human rights diplomacy, the National Endowment for Democracy under Reagan, the "Greater Middle East" plan and the Arab Spring. Guo's central claim is that infiltration is first of all a tool for consolidating US hegemony, since national interest governs the behaviour of a hegemonic power. Its core content is "exporting democracy": installing pro-US regimes and then transplanting the American system. Its goal, the author argues, is the "absolute security" of American ideology. Guo reads current pressure on China in this light, saying that the Party's "new form of human civilization" is seen in Washington as a challenge to Western capitalist civilization. Guo reviews counter-measures abroad. Russia has tightened laws on "foreign agent" organisations and passed a sovereign internet law. Kazakhstan and Belarus have controlled organisations and the opposition. Cuba has waged an "ideological battle" against neoliberalism, and left-wing Latin American states have formed regional alliances. For China, Guo calls for perfecting whole-process people's democracy, building a full ideological security system and forming an international united front against Western infiltration, promoting a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese academic frames US democracy promotion as hegemonic strategy and what counter-measures the article recommends.

The German Greens' return to federal government and the likely direction of their China policy 德国绿党重返联邦政府及其对华政策走向 Xuan Chuanshu Zhao Xiaohui After the 2021 Bundestag election, the German Greens won 14.8 per cent of the vote, became the third-largest party and entered a "traffic light" coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Free Democrats (FDP), taking five cabinet posts including the foreign ministry. Xuan and Zhao ask what kind of party the Greens are, why they succeeded, how the coalition formed, and what stance they will take towards China. Their thesis is that the Greens have moved from the radical left to a pragmatic centre but remain strongly ideological, so their left-wing label gives no grounds for assuming better Sino-German relations. Working within a framework of parliamentary politics, the article is organised in five parts. It divides the party's development since 1980 into three stages: grassroots opposition, "junior partner" in the 1998–2005 red–green government, and opposition from 2005 to 2021. It then examines the objective and subjective causes of the 2021 result, the reasons the SPD, Greens and FDP formed a government, and the Greens' positions on China. On the causes of success, the authors point to Western fatigue with political polarisation, including Trump-era politics and signs of a return to moderation in France and the 2019 European Parliament "green wave". They also cite the hollowing-out of Germany's political centre: voters leaving the CDU/CSU, SPD and Die Linke for the Greens, and a campaign built on optimistic messaging and a reconciliation of "moral purity" with "electoral viability". On China, the authors argue that the Greens label it a "competitor, partner and systemic rival", pursue values-based diplomacy, tie trade to human rights, and may press on Xinjiang and Tibet. They also say that the party needs Chinese cooperation on climate and that Foreign Minister Baerbock's "dialogue and toughness" line reflects this tension. The authors conclude that Greens' hard line is not pro-American, since the party also urges Europe to reduce dependence on the US and is harsher towards Russia, and that campaign rhetoric need not determine policy in office. In government, they argue, the Greens face a dilemma between value principles and the need to cooperate with China, Germany's largest trading partner for five years. The authors see room for improved relations in shared commitments to sustainability and peace, while warning China to stay sober about the Greens' influence. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of how the Greens' China policy was read in Shanghai in 2022, and of the party's electoral history.

"Defending the country means defending the people's hearts" The Communist Party of China's feeling for the people “守江山，守的是人民的心” Zhang Quansheng This short commentary, written after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up Xi Jinping's statement in the congress report that the country is the people and the people are the country, and that the Party, having won the country with the people, defends it by defending their hearts. Zhang argues that the phrase expresses the Party's working-class vanguard character, its fundamental purpose of serving the people wholeheartedly, and its original aspiration and mission. The article is organised around three claims about the phrase, followed by two practical requirements. It runs through the Party's history from its founding to the post-2012 period, using the sequence of stages "stood up, grew rich, became strong". Zhang first presents the phrase as the clearest expression of the Marxist view of the people as creators of history, and as the Party's decisive explanation for its successes in revolution, construction and reform. Zhang then calls it a necessity for the "new road to the test" and the second centenary goal, since the Party's tests and dangers will persist and, in Xi's words, the greatest danger after taking power is losing touch with the masses. Zhang cites the Party's record, from land reform and industrialisation to poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society, as evidence of its commitment. Zhang concludes that the Party must take the people's standpoint, put the people first in its heart, and work for their wellbeing. The article contends that if Communists keep their founding mission, the people will keep following the Party and the socialist state will endure. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-building commentary after the 20th Party Congress presents the Party's relationship with the people.

Maintaining a distinctive political character and bringing strong political advantages into play 保持鲜明政治品格 发挥强大政治优势 Liu Jianhui Writing shortly before the 20th Party Congress (2022), Liu Jianhui elaborates Xi Jinping's statement that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Communist Party of China's distinctive political character and strong political advantage. Liu reads Xi's conclusion that Marxism is ultimately the reason why the Party "can" and socialism with Chinese characteristics is "good" as the fundamental explanation of past success and the condition of future success. The piece is a Party-theory commentary rather than an empirical study. The article has three parts. The first argues that Marxism has profoundly changed the course of Chinese history. The second reviews how the Party has used Marxism to observe, interpret and lead its era across four historical periods. The third turns to the tasks of the new journey, namely study of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and continued theoretical innovation. Liu's central claim is that Marxism works in China because it has been adapted to Chinese conditions and to the needs of the times. Liu cites the Party's growth from about 50 members at its First Congress to over 96 million today as evidence of this political advantage. Liu then traces successive theoretical leaps: Mao Zedong Thought in the revolutionary and socialist-construction periods, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics after reform and opening up, and Xi Jinping Thought since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Each is presented as an answer to the problems of its period and as proof that the Party adheres to Marxism while developing it. Liu concludes that adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times has no end point, especially amid what the article calls great changes unseen in a century. Liu calls on the whole Party, and leading cadres in particular, to study Xi Jinping Thought as the primary political task. The thought is to be linked with the Marxist classics and Party history, and is to be combined with Chinese realities and traditional culture. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Party theorists in late 2022 presented Marxism as the Party's political advantage and described the sequence of theoretical "leaps".

Staying clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large party 时刻保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定 Han Bing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 28 October 2022, takes up a line from Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): to win popular support and consolidate its long-term governing position, the Party must stay clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large party. Han Bing argues that grasping why the Party has succeeded in the past, and how it can keep succeeding, matters for the new journey of building a modern socialist country. The piece is organised around four such problems, each introduced as one the century-old Party must solve. They concern holding to the original aspiration, maintaining unity, staying alert to danger, and carrying out self-reform. Each section quotes Xi Jinping, adds a short historical reference, and ends with what the Party must do on the new journey. On the original aspiration, Han holds that the Party represents the fundamental interests of the people and has no special interests of its own. Forgetting this, the author warns, would change the Party's nature. On unity, Han presents the Party's ideological, political and organisational building as the basis of its cohesion, and describes the Two Establishes as a judgement reflecting the shared will of the whole Party. On vigilance, Han recalls Mao Zedong's "cave dialogue" with Huang Yanpei and the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee, and stresses avoiding the historical cycle of rise and fall. Han concludes that the Party must keep to a people-centred stance, strengthen the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, and apply bottom-line thinking to risks. It must also continue full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which Han says is never finished, so that it can purify, improve and renew itself. Read the original if you want a concise, official-register statement of how Party commentary frames the Party's governing challenges after the 20th Party Congress.

Self-reform as the Party's second answer to escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall 自我革命是党跳出历史周期率的第二个答案 Dong Ying This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in October 2022, takes up a question raised in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): how a long-ruling Marxist party can escape the historical cycle of order, disorder, rise and decline. Dong argues that the Party's self-reform is the "second answer" to this problem, and that it keeps the Party from degenerating in nature, colour or flavour. The piece first recalls the 1945 "cave dwelling conversation" between Huang Yanpei and Mao Zedong, in which Mao named democracy as the first answer. It then traces Xi Jinping's statements on the cycle from 2013 to 2021, and reviews the work done since the 18th Party Congress (2012), before turning to the tasks set by the 20th Congress. Dong's central claim is that self-reform is what distinguishes the Communist Party from other parties. In the author's account, the Party has applied full and rigorous self-governance of the Party through a "combination of punches": a system of rules for self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation, tighter supervision and accountability, and a focus on the "critical few". The author also describes the campaigns against "tigers", "flies" and "foxes" as having removed serious hidden dangers in the Party, state and army. Dong concludes that the Party must keep its Marxist character by carrying out the "three musts" and staying alert to corruption. The author calls for self-reform to lead social revolution and social revolution to promote self-reform, so that the Party can lead the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's self-reform is presented in official commentary after the 20th Party Congress.

The "firewood and fire" analogy: Zhuangzi's view of life and death and his atheistic thought “薪火之喻”：庄子生死观及其无神论思想 Yan Wei The closing lines of the "Yangsheng zhu" chapter of the Zhuangzi compare a finger feeding firewood to a fire that passes on without end. Commentators have long read this "firewood and fire" analogy as a statement about the relation of body and spirit. Yan Wei disputes that reading. The article argues that the analogy expresses Zhuangzi's view of life and death, and that this view contains atheistic thought. The article has three parts. It first surveys four traditional readings of the analogy and rejects each of them. It then reconstructs Zhuangzi's outlook on life and death, drawing on the "Yangsheng zhu" story of Qin Shi mourning Lao Dan, the doctrine of "transformation of things" and the concept of qi. The third part turns to the atheistic implications. Yan draws on commentators from Cheng Xuanying and Lin Xiyi to Liu Xiaogan and Fukunaga Mitsuji. Yan sorts the rejected readings into four: body and spirit (often with spirit understood as a soul), life and knowledge, body and nature, and the transmission of culture. Yan holds that the body–spirit reading owes more to the Han–Wei–Six Dynasties debate on form and spirit than to the text, since believers in the immortal soul, such as Huiyuan, borrowed the image. In Yan's reading, the firewood is the individual life and the fire is the continuing great transformation of the cosmos. Because all things are qi gathering and dispersing, individual death is absorbed into cosmic change, and the fear of death is overcome in the mind alone. Yan finds atheism in two places. Life and death are natural, so individual death is both necessary and final, with no rebirth. And because transformation is a circulation of qi, there is no spirit that leaves the body, and so no soul. Yan concludes that the analogy joins individual life and death to cosmic transformation and is about transcending death. Its atheistic content lies in the naturalness of life and death and in the denial of an immortal soul. Later uses of the analogy in the form-and-spirit debate, Yan adds, distorted this content, and the author leaves that question for separate study. Read the original if you are interested in Zhuangzi scholarship, Chinese philosophical atheism, or the history of the debate over whether the spirit perishes with the body.
