The Seventh Party Congress and the great victory of the New Democratic Revolution 党的七大与新民主主义革命的伟大胜利 Yang Fengcheng Writing in 2022, Yang Fengcheng asks how the Seventh National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, held in Yan'an in 1945, contributed to the final victory of the New Democratic Revolution. The article argues that the Congress secured that victory in three ways: it drew on the Party's historical experience, it established Mao Zedong's leadership and Mao Zedong Thought as the guiding ideology, and it set out a sound strategy for post-war China. The article has three main parts. The first places the Congress in the whole history of the New Democratic Revolution. It traces the repeated postponements from 1937 onwards and the way the Party reviewed its past errors, through the rectification movement and the 1945 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party. The second part examines the Congress's endorsement of Mao as leader and of Mao Zedong Thought. The third turns to the political line, the peasantry, Party leadership, cadres, and the 'two transformations'. Yang draws on speeches by Liu Shaoqi, Zhang Wentian, Zhou Enlai, Ren Bishi, Zhu De, Chen Yun, Peng Zhen and others. Yang argues that the long delay had an unintended benefit: the Party had by then gathered experience from the War of Resistance and could set the lessons of its earlier detours against the way to victory. By moving the review of Party history to the Sixth Central Committee's Seventh Plenum, the leadership kept the Congress focused on present tasks and avoided prolonged settling of old scores. Yang reads the delegates' endorsement of Mao as resting on comparisons of correct and mistaken lines. Liu Shaoqi's report defined Mao Zedong Thought as the unity of Marxism-Leninism with Chinese revolutionary practice. On strategy, Yang stresses the peasantry as the main force, the independence of the Party within the united front, cadre unity and self-criticism, and the shift of work from countryside to city and from guerrilla to mobile warfare. Yang treats the last as the key military and political plan for victory, and describes Party maturity as both 'soft power' and 'hard power'. Yang concludes that the Seventh Congress ensured the victory of the New Democratic Revolution by summing up historical lessons, establishing Mao's position and Mao Zedong Thought, and making correct decisions on Party building and strategic transitions. The article closes with the hope that Party congresses in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics will, like the Seventh, become new milestones. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of the Seventh Congress as presented in Chinese Party-history scholarship, with many quotations from delegates' speeches.

The Yan'an Rectification Movement and strengthening the Party's centralized and unified leadership 延安整风与加强党的集中统一领导 Tan Huwa This article, originally published in Guangming Daily on 12 October 2022, asks how the Yan'an Rectification Movement (1941–1945) was linked to the strengthening of the Chinese Communist Party's centralized and unified leadership during the War of Resistance against Japan. Tan argues that this strengthening was a historical necessity and a core outcome of the movement. In Tan's account, it laid an ideological and political foundation for victory in the War of Resistance and in the democratic revolution. The piece has three parts. The first sets out why strengthening unified leadership reached the historical agenda. The second traces the central decisions of 1941–1943. The third examines how the policy was applied in the Northwest Bureau and the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. Tan draws on Party directives, speeches by Mao Zedong, Ren Bishi, Wang Jiaxiang and Chen Yun, and regional documents. Tan names four reasons for the policy. These were the surviving subjectivism and sectarianism, including the mountain-top mentality (shantouzhuyi) Mao criticised in 1944. They were also the harsher conditions behind enemy lines, the mistaken view that the "three-thirds" system made Party presence unimportant, and the weak coordination among Party, government, army and mass organizations. The key documents are the 1941 decision on strengthening Party spirit and the 1 September 1942 decision on unifying Party leadership in the base areas. The latter holds that the Party should lead all other organizations, that lower levels must obey higher ones, and that Party leadership should be a matter of principle and policy, not interference in every detail. Tan adds that leadership cores were set up at military-region level, and that the 1943 reorganization made Mao chairman of the Politburo and the Secretariat. In the Northwest Bureau, Tan reports, the policy was applied to mass organizations, Party broadcasting, relations with the army and the salt industry. By the end of 1943 the border region had achieved positive results. Tan notes that Party control of the army and financial departments was still weak, and that some government bodies still stressed government-system unity. The bureau responded with continued education, tighter organizational control and a stronger Party grip on overall affairs. Read the original if you want a documented account of how the Party's centralized leadership system was built in Yan'an and applied in the Border Region.

The essential attributes of the path of Chinese modernization and its contemporary concerns 中国式现代化道路的本质属性和当代关切 Xu Ping Yu Miao Published in Guangming Daily on 27 September 2022, this commentary asks what defines the path of Chinese modernization and what concerns it addresses today. Xu Ping and Yu Miao argue that the path shares general features of modernization but is distinguished by Chinese attributes. Its essential attributes, they hold, are Party leadership and socialism. The article has three parts. The first defines modernization as the historical shift from traditional to modern society and sets out the two essential attributes. The second identifies three practical features that set the Chinese path apart from Western modernization: independence, rootedness in local history and culture, and a people-centred character. The third turns to the contemporary meaning of the path, drawing on Xi Jinping's account of its distinctive features and on the new development philosophy. The authors present Communist Party leadership as the decisive factor in the path and as its fundamental political advantage. Socialism, in their account, is its institutional basis and basic direction, so that Chinese modernization seeks to unite a high level of modernization with socialism. They say this surpasses capitalist modernization and discards the older Western routes of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization. On the three features, they argue that independence follows from the historical choice between dependence on the West and self-reliance, citing Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. They say local roots come from Chinese civilization and the path's own evolution, and that the people-centred character follows from Marxist theory and the Party's founding mission. The authors conclude that the path, defined by Xi Jinping as modernization of a huge population, of common prosperity, of material and cultural-ethical advancement, of harmony between humans and nature, and of peaceful development, is a logical framework for coordinated progress. They claim it has widened the routes open to developing countries and offers a new choice to states that want faster development while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official Chinese discourse in 2022 framed the Party's leadership, socialism and the new development philosophy as the core of Chinese modernization.

The rich connotations and significance of the path of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化道路的丰富内涵与意义 He Degui This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in September 2022, asks what the path of Chinese modernization contains and why it matters. He Degui argues that the path, explored by the Party from "industrialization" and the "four modernizations" to Chinese modernization, shares features with other countries' modernization but carries distinct Chinese characteristics. In He's account it has produced a "new form of human civilization" that goes beyond Western modernization. The piece has three parts. The first describes the path's nature and its link to the Party's century of struggle. The second sets out the characteristics of the new form of human civilization. The third assesses the practical, historical and theoretical significance of the path. He contends that the path rests on the Party's leadership, mobilises the state, the market, society and the people, and aims at developing the productive forces, common prosperity and all-round human development. The new form of civilization is said to stress shared development, openness and inclusiveness, and a shared human destiny. He presents it as having overcome ills attributed to Western capitalist modernization, such as wealth polarisation and class conflict, and as having broken the idea that modernization means Westernization. He concludes that the path widens the routes to modernization open to developing countries and shows socialism with Chinese characteristics to be a successful road. In He's view it also ends the "end of history" thesis and the "failure of socialism" thesis, and advances the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official 2022 narrative links Chinese modernization to the idea of a new form of human civilization.

The normative dimension of Marxism 马克思主义的规范性维度 Xu Mengqiu Jürgen Habermas holds that the normative foundations of Marxism are unclear, and some Anglophone scholars deny that Marx cared about justice and morality. Writing in Guangming Daily, Xu Mengqiu argues that Chinese Marxists must answer this charge. Xu's thesis is that Marxism has a normative dimension and normative content, and that its normative basis is fairly clear. The article has two parts. The first defines the "normative dimension" and contrasts it with a "cognitive dimension", using examples from the Confucian tradition, daily life and engineering acceptance checks. The second sets out Habermas's critique, replies to it, and reads Marx's own texts, including the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach and Capital. Xu defines the normative dimension as starting from an "ought" grounded in some value outlook. From that standpoint one evaluates what exists, then defends, corrects or reconstructs it. The cognitive dimension, which Xu says covers description, explanation and empirical verification, treats things as they are. Xu holds that the two are interdependent and arise together in practice, so Hume's problem of deriving "ought" from "is" does not arise. Against Habermas, Xu argues that Marx's normative standpoint changed over time and differed by target. Two features run through all of it. The first is a value cornerstone, the fundamental interests of the proletariat and working people, joined to a scientific cornerstone, the grasp of historical laws. Together these yield a revolutionary ideal of the future society. The second is the use of both theoretical and material weapons, meaning the workers' movement, to criticise and deconstruct capitalism and its ideology. Xu cites Marx's critique of alienated labour, his remark that humans build "according to the laws of beauty", and the architect-and-bee passage in Capital as evidence of a normative standard. Xu concludes that Marxism's normativity expresses its value pursuits and lofty ideals, and that the unity of value and scientific standards is its basis. Normativity and scientific character are distinct yet interdependent. Without science, Marxism would fall into utopian or ethical socialism. Marxists, Xu adds, never claim value neutrality and openly present their doctrine as the proletariat's intellectual weapon. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reply to Habermas's charge about Marx's normative foundations, or a view of how Chinese scholars define "normative" and "cognitive" dimensions.

Reasoned, powerful, effective, useful Reflections on why Marxism works 有理有力有效有用 Ji Zhengju Writing in Guangming Daily in September 2022, Ji Zhengju takes up the question of why Marxism "works" (xing). The commentary argues that Marxism's strength rests on four defining traits: it is scientific, rooted in the people, practical and open. On this basis, Ji holds, Marxism has changed the world and China, and it remains a guide for the future. The piece has four sections. The first sets out the four traits. The second surveys Marxism's effects on world history: human civilisation, the history of socialism, national liberation movements, intellectual history, daily life, party development and the critique of capitalism. The third deals with China, and the fourth looks ahead and rebuts critics. Ji quotes Marx, Engels and Lenin, and also David McLellan and Robert Heilbroner. Ji argues that Marxism's scientific character, its discovery of laws of history, socialism and proletarian party rule, is joined to a class standpoint that serves working people, so that it carries both truth and moral force. Its practical orientation, summed up in the call to change the world, and its openness to development explain its vitality. Ji traces this development from Lenin's theory of imperialism through to the sinified Marxism of Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. For Ji, the October Revolution, the socialist camp and the rise of socialism with Chinese characteristics show Marxism's effect, and Western disorder shows that contemporary capitalism faces systemic crisis. Ji concludes that critiques of Marxism, such as the theories that it has failed, is utopian or is outdated, have been refuted by facts. In Ji's view the basic contradictions of capitalism and the "two inevitables" still hold, and we still live in the historical era Marxism identified. Ji calls for continuing to uphold and develop Marxism and to arm minds with its latest sinified achievements. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated theorists present the case for Marxism's continuing validity in the Xi Jinping era.

Building China's spiritual strength in the new era 构筑新时代的中国精神力量 Tian Feng This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 28 September 2022, reviews what the author presents as the achievements of socialist cultural-ethical progress (spiritual civilization building) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Tian argues that the key to new breakthroughs has been adherence to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a people-centred approach to development. The article first surveys three strands of work: creating civilized cities, villages and families; expanding civilized practice through volunteer service; and cultivating civilized conduct through moral role models, festival activities and youth education. It then draws out the principles said to underlie these results. In Tian's account, the work has produced wider and more credible national civilized-city programmes, rural customs reform linked to poverty alleviation and rural revitalization, and new practice centres in county-level districts across the country. The author sets out four requirements: keep the people's interests first, uphold fundamental principles while innovating in forms and carriers, seek truth and practical results, and persevere over the long term with broad participation. Each is tied to raising people's sense of gain, happiness and security and to strengthening cultural confidence. Tian concludes that, under Xi Jinping's personal guidance, this work should keep deepening civilized creation, practice and cultivation so as to raise society's level of civility. The stated aim is to build Chinese spirit, values and strength for achieving the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style summary of how Party-aligned writers framed spiritual civilization building in autumn 2022.

Relying on tenacious struggle to open up new horizons for the cause 依靠顽强斗争打开事业发展新天地 Liu Zhiming Writing in Guangming Daily on 22 September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Liu Zhiming argues that struggle is the decisive means by which the Communist Party of China has achieved its results and the means it must keep using. The short commentary contends that the future, like the past, has to be won through struggle rather than received as a gift. The piece has three parts. The first reviews the Party's history since 1921 and claims that all the achievements of the Party and people came through continuous struggle. The second explains why struggle is needed now, citing the current international situation and complacency inside the Party. The third sets out how a spirit of responsibility and struggle should be cultivated. Liu's reasoning starts from a Marxist premise: society advances through contradictions, and struggle is the form in which development and practical innovation are realised. The author describes a world of accelerating great changes unseen in a century, with unilateralism, protectionism and hegemonism, and says China faces more complex risks than before. Liu also points to cadres who seek a comfortable post, avoid difficulties or pass problems upward, and warns that a party or country that loses its will to struggle is close to collapse. Struggle in this sense is not for its own sake or for private gain. It serves the people's aspiration for a better life and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu calls for selflessness and courage, a spirit of historical initiative, and a focus on what the commentary calls "matters of national importance", with local interests subordinate to the whole. Struggle capacity is not innate, the author says, and must be tempered through theoretical study, including understanding the Two Establishes, strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence and achieving the Two Upholds, and through practice in hard places. Liu concludes that cadres should take the initiative in struggles, never yielding on matters of principle, as the country advances towards the goal of a modern socialist country and national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2022 framed struggle as a duty for cadres in the new era.

Continuously advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context through the "Two Integrations" 在“两个结合”中不断推进马克思主义中国化 He Bingbing Writing in Guangming Daily on 29 September 2022, He Bingbing asks what is required to keep advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context through the Two Integrations: combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The short commentary argues that this work rests on four supports: theoretical, practical, cultural and political. The piece is organised into four numbered sections. Each takes one support in turn: upholding the basic principles of Marxism, grasping China's concrete realities, transforming and developing fine traditional Chinese culture, and deepening the Party's self-reform. On theory, He insists that Marxism's guiding position must never waver. The author calls both for rejecting a rigid, stagnant attitude towards Marxism and for opposing attempts to distort its principles in the name of "reality" or to deny their universal validity in the name of "particularity". On practice, He treats the interplay of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes unseen in a century as the starting point. Questions such as common prosperity, high-level scientific self-reliance and social fairness are named as problems that theory must answer. On culture, He rejects both cultural nihilism and cultural conservatism, and urges drawing the essence from traditional culture and giving it contemporary form. In the fourth section, He argues that the Party's leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, driven by a people-centred orientation and the mass line, guarantee that adapting Marxism stays on the right course. The author presents the Party's self-reform as leading broader social transformation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a 2022 official-press commentary frames the Two Integrations in terms of theory, practice, culture and Party leadership.

Drawing nourishment for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics from fine traditional Chinese culture 从中华优秀传统文化汲取中国特色社会主义政治经济学的养分 Chen Xudong Chen Xudong, in a short newspaper commentary first published in Guangming Daily in September 2022, asks how the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics can draw on traditional Chinese economic thought. The author argues that it should systematically extract, summarise and elevate the ideas of fine traditional Chinese culture, because economics is essentially a historical science. The piece has three parts. It first notes that Marx's Theories of Surplus Value and Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations both built on earlier doctrines, and it describes the history of Chinese economic thought as a weak discipline in Chinese universities, lacking an authoritative textbook spanning ancient and modern times. It then discusses the historical influence of Chinese thought abroad. Finally it maps traditional ideas onto the new development philosophy. Chen observes that ancient China had no professional economists, so economic ideas lie scattered through political and philosophical writings and must be "refined" by researchers. The author cites claims of Chinese influence on the French Physiocrats and on American agricultural legislation during the Great Depression, via the "ever-normal granary". Chen then pairs each element of the new development philosophy with a tradition: innovation with the Book of Changes, coordination with the Doctrine of the Mean, green development with "unity of heaven and humanity" and ancient environmental offices, openness with Silk Road and Song-Yuan maritime trade, and sharing with Laozi, Confucius and Guanzi on common prosperity. Chen concludes that these resources offer useful intellectual and practical reference for the Belt and Road Initiative, institutional opening up and the pursuit of common prosperity, even though many ancient ideas were never put into practice. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars link classical Chinese texts to current policy concepts.

"People first" and the logic of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics “人民至上”与中国特色社会主义政治经济学的逻辑理路 Hu Leming Hu Leming asks how the principle of putting the people first (人民至上) can serve as the organising thread of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article, published in Guangming Daily in October 2022, argues that this principle gives the discipline a coherent logic. In Hu's account, the logic runs from people's everyday needs, through micro-level and macro-level analysis, to common prosperity and the all-round development of the person. The piece is built in four sections: the logical starting point, the micro logic, the macro logic and the logical destination. Hu draws on Marx's treatment of needs and of labour, capital and relative surplus population. Hu also draws on a Party resolution on the Party's century of struggle, a Report to the 19th Party Congress (2017) and remarks by Xi Jinping. Hu first proposes "living needs" as the starting category. Marx never defined it clearly, Hu says, yet it played a hidden role in his theories of value, surplus value and crisis, and it links life activity to production. Starting from the sequence of life process, needs and production process, Hu argues, the discipline can unfold the tensions between production and consumption, government and market, and public and private goods. At the micro level, Hu holds that the central issue is a harmonious and stable cooperation between labour and capital. Hu calls for worker participation in management through staff and workers' congresses, shared enterprise surplus with pay rising in step with productivity, and government and social organisations that curb monopoly and "disorderly expansion of capital". Hu also calls for extending labour protection to platform and flexible workers. At the macro level, Hu argues that employment should come first, and that the discipline should abandon the Western mainstream's one-sided stress on GDP growth. Hu cites Marx to warn that if capital and market logic alone steer technological change, a large relative surplus population results. Hu therefore urges labour-biased innovation, employment-oriented policy and social security for flexible workers and migrant workers. Hu concludes that common prosperity and the all-round development of the person are the destination of this political economy. Meeting needs is its precondition, labour–capital cooperation its micro foundation and employment-first its macro safeguard. Hu stresses that common prosperity in the primary stage of socialism falls short of Marx's vision of distribution according to need. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese economist links "people first" to the structure of a Marxist political economy, covering labour–capital relations, digital-era employment and common prosperity.

What underpins our Party's firm convictions and its grasp of historical initiative 我们党坚定信仰信念、把握历史主动的根本所在 Chen Shuguang This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 21 October 2022 during the 20th Party Congress, asks why the Communist Party of China holds firm to its convictions and keeps the historical initiative. Chen Shuguang answers that the decisive factor is guidance by Marxism, and specifically by Marxism adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Chen builds on the Congress report's statement that the Party's success ultimately rests on Marxism "working". The piece has two sections. The first explains why Marxism is said to work and traces the Party's record of adapting it. The second looks ahead to the Party's responsibility to keep writing new chapters of this adaptation on the new journey. In the first section, Chen presents Marxism as revealing universal laws of nature, society and thought, as standing for people's liberation and free, all-round human development, and as both interpreting and changing the world. Chen argues that Marxism's effectiveness comes from the Party's continual adaptation of it, citing Mao Zedong's 1938 statement and Deng Xiaoping's 1982 opening speech. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Chen says, this effort has produced Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, which Chen calls twenty-first-century Marxism and a new leap in adaptation. In the second section, Chen says Marxism is a guide to action, not dogma, and that theory must develop with practice. Chen lists principles to uphold, including putting the people first, self-confidence and self-reliance, and a global outlook. Chen calls on Party members to keep Marxism's guiding status, deepen theoretical innovation and answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times. Chen also urges them to study Xi Jinping Thought thoroughly and turn that study into practical results. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official line at the 20th Congress presented Marxism's adaptation as the source of its historical initiative.

The dialectical relationship between the two answers of the Communist Party of China to escaping the historical cycle 中国共产党跳出历史周期率两个答案的辩证关系 Ding Zhongyi Ding Zhongyi takes up the question of how the Communist Party of China can escape the 'historical cycle' of rise and fall, and how its two official answers relate to each other. The first answer is Mao Zedong's 1945 reply of 'people's supervision'. The second is the Party's self-reform, which Xi Jinping named in 2021. Ding argues that the two are distinct in emphasis but internally unified, and that they restrain and reinforce each other. The article has three parts. The first sets out how the two answers differ. The second, the longest, identifies three shared features: a commitment to 'putting the people first', public-power supervision as a method, and the security of the Party's governing position as a goal. It then examines how the answers condition each other. The third part draws out practical implications for the Party's present 'examination road'. Ding draws on Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi, and on recent Chinese scholarship on the topic. In Ding's reading, the first answer stresses external constraint, heteronomy and external momentum, while the second stresses introspection, self-discipline and internal momentum. Ding applies the Marxist theory of internal and external causes: external factors work through internal ones. People's supervision supplies social momentum and helps the Party see its own problems. Self-reform in turn improves the quality of people's democracy and moves the Party from passively accepting supervision to seeking it. Ding grounds the shared method in an account of public power as prone to expansion and misuse, so that supervision, both inside and outside the Party, is needed to prevent abuses of power. Ding proposes that each answer be used for its particular strengths and that their mutual reinforcement be encouraged. Whole-process people's democracy is presented as raising Mao's answer to a new level. Ding also calls for turning institutional advantages into governance effectiveness. This means making democracy effective as well as participatory, and resolving the tension between regulating power and keeping officials active, for example through mechanisms that tolerate errors. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how people's supervision and self-reform are meant to work together, with its Marxist and Chinese-source references.)

A vivid narrative of the Communist Party's firm ideals and convictions: what revolutionary cultural relics "say" 中国共产党坚定理想信念的生动叙事：革命文物的“言说” Han Ling Tang Song Han Ling and Tang Song ask how revolutionary cultural relics can convey the firm ideals and convictions of the Communist Party of China and pass them on to today's young people. They argue that relics "speak" (yanshuo, rendered as narrative): they tell the story of the revolution and turn abstract belief into something that can be seen, heard and touched. In the authors' view this makes them an indispensable tool for the ideological education of youth. The article has three parts. The first sets out the logic of this "narrative" function and the formula "relic + scene + story + spirit". The second reads particular relics as expressions of the spiritual qualities of the Party's convictions. The third draws out the present-day value of this narrative for educating young people. The authors claim that relics reconstruct historical scenes and, through "embodied cognition", place visitors inside them. This moves them from the material object to revolutionary spirit, such as the Jinggangshan and Long March spirits. Examples include Li Dazhao's gallows, Fang Zhimin's manuscript, a peasant Party member's handwritten oath, and a mortar at Jinggangshan that visitors may touch. Relics are then linked to three qualities. Mao Zedong's 1929 letter, "A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire", stands for innovative optimism. The Xunwu investigation, Red Army slogans and the "Three Main Rules and Six Points of Attention" stand for a people-centred outlook. The "branch built on the company" and the Ruijin complaint box stand for the Party's self-reform. The authors cite the fall of the Soviet Communist Party to argue that firm conviction and self-reform depend on each other. The authors propose that educators pair classroom teaching with visits to relics and sites, and to red family letters. Young people's ideals should rest on rational acceptance of scientific theory (Marxism), on a correct grasp of historical laws, and on an accurate assessment of revolutionary figures. Such experience is also meant to help them resist historical nihilism, which the authors say spreads through online media and distorts the image of revolutionary fighters. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-history and ideological-education study uses specific relics and anecdotes from Jinggangshan and Ruijin to argue for experiential teaching of ideals and convictions.

A good tradition of our Party: studying and applying philosophy in practice 我们党的一个好传统在实践中学哲学用哲学 Tan Qunyu This short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 24 October 2022, takes up the Party's tradition of studying and applying philosophy. Tan Qunyu argues that this tradition rests on the Marxist principle that practice is the basis of knowledge, and that it must continue to guide the Party in its new journey. The piece first sets out four propositions about practice drawn from Marx, Engels, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping: practice is the source of knowledge, the driving force of its development, and the sole criterion of truth, and it has the character of direct actuality. It then turns to the Party's history over more than a century and to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Tan contends that knowledge, including indirect knowledge, ultimately derives from direct experience, and that cognition advances through repeated cycles of practice and understanding. A theory counts as true only after testing across many fields and regions, and it then becomes a material force. In Tan's account, the Party has built theory on the practice of the people. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the judgement that the principal contradiction in Chinese society has changed, high-quality development, targeted poverty alleviation and ecological civilization are all presented as results of the practice–cognition–practice process. Tan concludes that the aim of studying philosophy is to improve understanding and guide practice, in pursuit of the second centenary goal. Party members should master the principle that matter determines consciousness, the analysis of contradictions, materialist dialectics, the analysis of society's basic contradictions, and the view that the people create history. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party commentary links Marxist epistemology to the legitimation of current policy.

The generative logic of the experience of putting the people first in the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 中国共产党百年奋斗中坚持人民至上经验的生成逻辑 Wan Guangxia Following the Party's 2021 historical resolution, which lists 'putting the people first' among the lessons of its century of struggle, Wan Guangxia asks how that experience came into being. The article argues that it rests on three interlocking logics: a theoretical logic, a historical logic and a practical (contemporary) logic. Together, in Wan's account, they explain why the principle is both a product of the Party's history and a requirement for the present. The article is organised in three parts that follow this scheme. The first traces theoretical sources: the classical Marxist view of the people as the subject of history, its adaptation in China from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, and the people-based (minben) thought of traditional Chinese culture. The second part covers the historical path from the nation 'standing up' to 'becoming prosperous' and 'becoming strong', together with lessons drawn from the ruling experience of proletarian parties, especially the Soviet Union. The third part addresses present-day requirements. In the theoretical part, Wan identifies three elements in Marx and Engels: the 'real individual' as premise, the people as makers of history, and all-round human development as the goal. Wan then links successive Party leaderships to formulations such as serving the people wholeheartedly, raising living standards as a test of socialism, representing the fundamental interests of the overwhelming majority, putting people first, and the people-centred development philosophy. Traditional ideas of respecting, loving, pacifying and benefiting the people are presented as the cultural root. In the historical part, Wan reads the Soviet case as a warning: a rigid planned economy that neglected livelihoods, weak intra-Party democracy, and a Party that lost its vanguard character and its mass ties through privilege and corruption. On the practical side, Wan argues that putting the people first is an inherent requirement of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics: its path, theory, system and culture. It is also required for the new journey of building a modern socialist country that is prosperous, democratic, civilised, harmonious and beautiful. Wan sets out what this means for the material, political, cultural, social and ecological spheres, including whole-process people's democracy, improved livelihoods and green development. Read the original if you want a systematic account, in the Party-theory idiom, of how Chinese scholars derive the principle of putting the people first from Marxist, traditional and Soviet-historical sources.

Staying clear-headed and resolute about the problems unique to a large Party through self-reform 以自我革命保持解决大党独有难题的清醒和坚定 Zhang Zhiming Writing shortly after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhang Zhiming asks how the Communist Party of China can keep its character under what the author calls the problems unique to a large Party. The central one, in Zhang's account, is how to govern the Party well and keep it from changing in nature, colour or flavour under opening up, a market economy and long-term rule. Zhang argues that the Party has always faced this problem soberly and that its answer is the Party's self-reform, as Xi Jinping presents it. The commentary moves through Party history. It begins with the overseas Chinese leader Tan Kah Kee's 1940 visit to Yan'an and his worry, recorded in his memoirs, about whether the Communists could stay clean if they controlled wealthy regions. It then covers the new-democratic revolution, with Mao Zedong's reply to Huang Yanpei, the "two musts" of 1949, the early anti-corruption struggle, and the later turn to mass campaigns and then to rule by institutions after reform and opening up. Finally it sets out four features of the path opened since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Zhang's core argument is that Xi identifies two answers to the "Yan'an cave question": Mao's answer that the people must supervise the government, and the second answer, self-reform. The article treats Mao's "new road of democracy" as consistent in substance with self-reform, since it depended on a Party made strong through its own building, on Party leadership, and on the rule of law. On the post-2012 path, Zhang lists four features. The first is full and rigorous self-governance of the Party driven from within. The second is governing the Party through institutions and Party regulations, combined with ideological education. The third is treating intra-Party supervision as the most fundamental form of supervision, with a system of inspections, supervisory commissions and a National Supervision Law. The fourth is leading the people in developing whole-process people's democracy. Zhang concludes that self-reform is the Party's innovative, distinctively Chinese way to break out of the historical cycle of rise and fall, and that its institutional rules must keep being refined, with gaps filled and enforcement strengthened. Zhang presents the Party's leadership and the people's mastery of the country as mutually reinforcing. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how self-reform is linked to earlier Party history and to Xi Jinping's formulations on Party governance.

The Party's century of struggle has fundamentally changed the future and destiny of the Chinese people 党的百年奋斗从根本上改变了中国人民的前途命运 Yang Fengcheng This commentary, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2021, explains a claim made in the Resolution on the Major Achievements and Historical Experience of the Party's Centenary Struggle, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): that the Party's hundred years of struggle fundamentally changed the future and destiny of the Chinese people. Yang Fengcheng argues that the change is visible in three areas: China's international standing, the people's political status, and the country's economic condition and living standards. The article is organised as three historical arcs, each running from the pre-1921 situation to the present. The first goes from the insult of being called the "sick man of East Asia" to "standing up" and approaching "the centre of the world stage". The second goes from feudal autocracy to the people becoming masters of the country and then to whole-process people's democracy. The third goes from poverty and a weak industrial base to economic independence and finally to a moderately prosperous society in all respects. Yang's core argument is that each shift was brought about by the Party's leadership at successive stages. On national dignity, Yang points to the anti-imperialist struggles of the 1920s, the war of resistance against Japan, the abolition of unequal treaties in 1949 and the Korean War, then to reform-era diplomacy and the Belt and Road Initiative. On democracy, the article credits the Party with politically educating and organising the peasantry, and with building the people's congress system, multiparty cooperation, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots democracy. It also warns that Western "constitutionalism", multiparty rotation and the separation of powers must be guarded against. On the economy, Yang describes China as having avoided the dependent development of some former colonies, and cites figures such as GDP above 100 trillion yuan in 2020, per capita GDP above US$10,000, and a middle-income group of more than 400 million. Yang concludes that a century earlier China appeared to the world as a picture of decline, whereas it now shows vigour, and that the founding of the Party was an epoch-making event that changed the direction of the Chinese nation. The author presents the achievement of the first centenary goal as a milestone and sees the country moving towards the second, a modern socialist power. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how Party historiography frames the Party's century in terms of national independence, democracy and prosperity.

Why Mao Zedong called the Rectification Documents a "classic" 毛泽东为何称《整风文献》为经书 Hu Weixiong In November 1942, speaking to a conference of senior cadres in north-west China, Mao Zedong described the documents used to rectify the Party's "three work styles" as "a classic" (jingshu). Hu Weixiong notes that scholars have paid little attention to why he said so. Existing studies discuss editions and contents, and some, influenced by foreign scholars, hold that the collection contains no Marxist classics. Hu argues that the choice and arrangement of the texts show the collection to be a classic of Party-building, and that it marks a milestone in the development of Marxism in China. The article first traces the editions: an 18-document version issued in April 1942, a revised edition of 22 documents in 1943, and a final set of 27 documents, which Hu takes as its object of study. It then sorts the 27 texts into four groups. These are rectification of the Party's style of work, of study and of writing; the training of Communists and Party organisation; Party leadership, cadre policy, inner-Party criticism and struggle, discipline and democracy; and the Party's mission, propaganda, leadership methods and Bolshevisation. Hu summarises the main texts in each group, including works by Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Chen Yun, Stalin, Dimitrov and Lenin. Hu's central claim is that the collection's core is Mao's own work, above all \"Reform Our Study\", \"Rectify the Party's Style of Work\" and \"Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing\", with the preface to Rural Surveys. In Hu's reading, these texts demand that Marxism-Leninism be combined with the concrete practice of the Chinese revolution, and they attack subjectivism, dogmatism and sectarianism. Hu also argues that the whole is a coherent programme. Mao supplied the original theory, while the Soviet and Comintern texts and the Party's own decisions supplied standards for discipline, self-criticism and cadre selection. Hu places the collection beside two other reading sets used in rectification, and presents it as a Marxist study campaign aimed at the dogmatism associated with Wang Ming. Hu concludes that rectification matured the Party and prepared its transformation into a modern party at the Seventh Congress (1945). He also holds that the principle of uniting theory with practice and seeking truth from facts applies to Marxist parties generally. Hu cites a 1943 letter in which Mao said that only some of the rectification documents, not his thought as a system, should be promoted. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-by-text account of what the Rectification Documents contained and how Party historians present their role in the Yan'an rectification campaign.

Did Lenin not know of the "Caudine Forks" hypothesis? A perspective based on textual verification 列宁不知道跨越“卡夫丁峡谷”设想吗 Zhu Huanghe Yang Wei Most Chinese scholars hold that Lenin did not know Marx's hypothesis that Russia might skip the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism, because the term never appears in his works and key Marx and Engels texts were unpublished in his lifetime. Zhu and Yang ask whether this is true and answer that, on textual evidence, Lenin did know the hypothesis. They argue that it served him as a weapon against the Russian Narodniks (populists) and as a theoretical basis for the October Revolution. The article first reconstructs the publication history of the relevant texts by Marx, by Engels and by the two jointly. It separates items published in Lenin's lifetime from those that were not: Marx's draft replies to Vera Zasulich (1924), his ethnological notebooks (after 1958) and Engels's 1893 letters to Nikolai Danielson. It then checks Lenin's writings and marginal notes for traces of the published texts. A final section considers how the hypothesis, the "theory of victory in one country" and the October Revolution relate. The authors' evidence is that Lenin quoted Marx's letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski at length against Mikhailovsky and marked the key passage "Note". He also asked for and praised Engels's 1894 Afterword to "On Social Relations in Russia", annotated it in 1906, and showed close familiarity with the 1882 Russian preface to the Communist Manifesto. The authors argue that Lenin used this knowledge against the Narodniks on three points: capitalism and the dissolution of the commune were already facts, peasants were backward small producers rather than "born communists", and Russia could leap forward only through proletarian-led social revolution. On this basis Zhu and Yang reject the view that Lenin's "theory of victory in one country" merely coincides with Marx's hypothesis. In their account the hypothesis is its theoretical cornerstone, Lenin's theory of imperialism supports it, and it in turn guides the October Revolution. They conclude that establishing Lenin's knowledge of the hypothesis explains this logical chain and gives Russia, China and other backward countries a theoretical basis of legitimacy for taking the socialist road first. Read the original if you want a source-by-source account of the publication history and of Lenin's references to Marx and Engels on the Russian commune.

Did Marx really think the circulation process creates value? Upholding the monism of "productive labour creates value" and its lessons for the new era 马克思真的认为流通过程能创造价值吗？ Wang Xianpeng Wang Xianpeng takes up a long-running dispute in Chinese economics: whether labour in circulation (trade, transport, services) creates value. The question has returned with the rise of the tertiary sector, after earlier debates in the 1960s and the early reform years. Through a close reading of Marx's texts, Wang argues that Marx did not hold that circulation creates value, and that only productive labour does. The article has four parts. It first establishes productive labour creating value as the cornerstone of Marx's critique of political economy. It then examines the main passages in Volume II of Capital that are cited to show circulation creates value, namely those on transport costs, storage costs and the transport industry's "useful effect". Next it draws four conclusions about how to read Marx's monism. It ends with the significance of this stance for contemporary socialist practice. Wang's central move is textual. Citing the 1861–63 manuscripts, Wang says Marx's "labour" means labour directly exchanged with capital in material production, and that services and "total labour" fall outside it. Wang then reads the Volume II passages closely. Marx speaks of value "added" (zhuijia), not "created". His remarks that costs act as value-creating are limited to the "single capitalist" and concern price mark-ups, not value. And what transport sells is a "useful effect", not a commodity. Wang adds a logical test: if circulation created value, the value of the same good would differ by transport distance, which contradicts the determination of value by socially necessary labour time. Wang says the proponents cannot explain where the extra value would come from. Wang concludes that abandoning the monism would dissolve the coherence of Marx's system and, in socialist practice, split theory from practice and open the way to claims that Marxism is outdated. Circulation and non-productive labour are still said to be necessary for realising value and use-value. Wang adds that separating them from value creation helps clarify the nature of trade, finance and intermediary services, strengthen the real economy, guard against the disorderly expansion of capital and advance common prosperity. Read the original if you want a text-by-text defence of the view that Marx confined value creation to production, or want to see how this debate is tied to current economic policy.

Engels's threefold contribution to defending Marxist ideological discourse power in his later years 恩格斯晚年维护马克思主义意识形态话语权的三重贡献 Tang Xiaoyan Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article notes, strengthening the Party's capacity for ideological discourse and holding firmly to ideological discourse power has been a central task. Tang argues that Chinese scholarship on the Marxist lineage of this theme remains fragmentary because Marx and Engels never used the term itself. Tang's thesis is that Engels, after Marx's death in 1883, was the first to defend Marxist ideological discourse power systematically, through three linked contributions: polemic combined with defence, refinement combined with development, and transformation combined with popularisation. The article first argues that Engels's role has been obscured by Western interpretations, notably the 'Marx–Engels opposition' thesis of Western Marx scholarship, and by Chinese research that follows Western Marxism or Marx studies. It then takes the three contributions in turn, drawing on The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Anti-Dühring and Engels's late letters on historical materialism. It closes with lessons for contemporary China. On polemic, Tang argues that Engels countered the bourgeois claim that the state is eternal, the revival of neo-Kantian and neo-Hegelian thought, Paul Barth's charge of 'economic materialism', and the dogmatic reading of the 'Young Ones' such as Paul Ernst. Against the last two, Engels held that the economic factor is decisive only 'in the last instance', and Tang reads this phrase as meaning necessity, mediation and non-exclusivity. On development, Tang credits Engels with defining ideology as 'false consciousness', mapping its layers by distance from the economic base, introducing the relative independence of ideology and stressing its reaction on the base. On popularisation, Tang presents Anti-Dühring as the first complete systematic presentation of Marxism, and Socialism: Utopian and Scientific as the model for turning a theoretical system into a discourse workers could grasp. Tang concludes that grasping Engels is necessary for understanding Marxism, and that his account of the interaction of economic base and superstructure still guides practice. Tang links this to Xi Jinping's 2013 statement that ideological work is an extremely important task of the Party. Tang calls on Chinese scholars to adopt a 'fighter, not gentleman' attitude toward anti-Marxist currents, combine critique with construction, and join theoretical development with popularisation in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading of Engels's late letters and polemics as a source for current ideological discourse power.

A decade of pursuing the Chinese Dream and building a shared future for humanity 追求中国梦与构建人类共同未来的十年 José Ricardo dos Santos This Chinese translation of a newspaper commentary by the Brazilian business figure and lawyer José Ricardo dos Santos looks back on China's last ten years ahead of the 20th Party Congress (October 2022). Dos Santos argues that since 2012 the Chinese Dream has moved from an idea some doubted to a concrete achievement under Communist Party leadership. He also holds that China's international role has become more important amid global crises. The piece begins with the Chinese Dream and the two centenary goals. It then turns to domestic development: innovation-driven development, the five-sphere plan, environmental commitments and high-quality development. Its final sections cover global governance, BRICS and the Belt and Road Initiative. Dos Santos treats the first centenary goal, the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, as already met. He credits people-centred policies and the slogan "leave no one behind", and expects the next goal to arrive on schedule or early. Abroad, he presents China as a pillar of BRICS and says the Belt and Road Initiative has added cultural exchange to trade and infrastructure. He describes both as expressions of a community with a shared future for mankind. He says the United States is trying to contain China, and that the Party has responded calmly while continuing to stress cooperation, respect for different social systems and common human values. Dos Santos concludes that China works both for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and for a common future for humanity. He says the community with a shared future for mankind has moved from concept to practice and drawn wide international praise. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Latin American business commentator, published in a Chinese Party-affiliated newspaper, presents China's decade under Xi Jinping.

Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is China's fundamental guide 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想是中国的根本引领 Charles Onunaiju This short commentary is a Chinese translation of an article by Charles Onunaiju, director of a Nigerian centre for China studies. It argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the basic guide for China's deepening governance reform. Onunaiju presents it as the Communist Party's latest guide to governing, adopted as the Party's guiding ideology at the 19th Party Congress. After a brief account of the Party's twentieth-century liberation and post-reform growth, the author takes the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a new starting point. Three areas of achievement are examined in turn: Party discipline, sustainable and inclusive development, and China's approach to global governance. On the first, Onunaiju holds that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, carried out through the Party's self-reform, is the precondition for other reforms. The author contrasts this with African parties that lost power after their ideas and organisation decayed. On the second, high-quality development is said to link growth with livelihoods, ecology, fairness and regional balance, whereas some developing countries, including some African ones, grow without real development. On the third, the author describes the Belt and Road Initiative and the Global Development Initiative as cooperative, win-win alternatives to what is called Western zero-sum thinking. Onunaiju concludes that these achievements strengthen the case for the Party's governance and bring benefits for world peace and development. The author also says that developing countries, Africa included, welcome China's contribution to South–South cooperation and North–South dialogue. Read the original if you want an example of how a Nigerian China specialist's view of the Party's new-era governance was presented to Chinese readers in the state press.

China's elimination of absolute poverty is a bright sight for the world 中国消除绝对贫困是世界亮丽风景线 Alessandra Ciattini This is a Chinese translation of a short commentary by Alessandra Ciattini, a professor at the University of Rome (the byline gives only her Chinese-rendered name). She argues that China's elimination of absolute poverty by the end of 2020 is one of the most notable achievements in the world today, and that it contrasts sharply with growing impoverishment in the West. Ciattini opens with figures on poverty reduction since 1981 and with UN Secretary-General António Guterres's praise in 2021. She then compares Western labour's loss of rights since the 1960s and 1970s with China's reform and opening up, rural reforms, targeted poverty alleviation, Party organisation and the shift in the principal social contradiction. She closes with poverty in Italy and the United States. She holds that rural and agricultural development, combined with a socialist market economy, was the key to victory. She rejects the Western description of China's path as "neo-liberalism with Chinese characteristics" and cites Joseph Stiglitz that the government never confused the end, people's well-being, with the means. In her account, China avoided "shock therapy" and tailored reforms to national conditions. She also stresses that poverty is multidimensional and that policy gave poor areas the capacity to generate their own income rather than mere transfers. Targeted poverty alleviation, she says, relied on household identification, digital monitoring and Party-led mobilisation of work teams and cadres. Ciattini concludes that China's anti-poverty campaign also advanced the modernization of national governance, and that the moderately prosperous society differs from Western consumerism. She calls on Western scholars to study the details of poverty alleviation to dispel misunderstandings. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a foreign scholar's praise of China's poverty alleviation is presented to a Chinese readership.

Why China has been able to win a comprehensive victory in poverty reduction and alleviation 中国为何能取得减贫脱贫的全面胜利 Mohammad Syed Islam Zhu Rui This is a Chinese translation of a newspaper commentary by a Bangladeshi researcher, published in Guangming Daily in October 2022. It asks how China won what Xi Jinping declared in February 2021 to be a comprehensive victory in the fight against poverty. The author's answer is that targeted poverty alleviation, backed by Party leadership and a people-centred approach, produced a historic achievement that other countries could learn from. The piece first sketches the long-term strategy since reform and opening up, including the 1994–2000 plan and two rural poverty-reduction outlines, and then cites the headline results. It goes on to list the measures used and ends with a short response to Western scepticism. The author cites official figures: 770 million rural people lifted out of poverty over four decades, and 98.99 million people, 832 counties and 128,000 villages removed from poverty under current standards. The author says this met the UN 2030 target ten years early and gave China a contribution of over 70% to global poverty reduction. The mechanisms named are targeted poverty alleviation, first proposed in Hunan in 2013, and more than three million cadres posted to villages. The author also lists industrial support, relocation, ecological compensation, education and social security, with infrastructure ("to get rich, first build roads"), tourism, e-commerce and livestreaming as key means. The author acknowledges that some Western critics find ending poverty in a country of 1.4 billion implausible. The author replies that the task was necessary because the fundamental purpose of socialism is common prosperity, and credits Party members and officials acting under a people-centred outlook. The author suggests that countries serious about ending poverty could adapt China's experience. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a foreign scholar's endorsement of China's poverty-alleviation record was presented in the Party press.

A contemporary decoding of Marx's philosophical revolution Analysis of major theoretical questions in the Theses on Feuerbach 马克思哲学变革的当代解码 Hou Huiqin Hou Huiqin takes up a long-running dispute over Marx's Theses on Feuerbach (1845). One influential reading, which Hou says is often presented as consensus in Chinese scholarship, holds that the Theses mark a 'practical turn' founding 'practical materialism' and a 'practice ontology'. Hou rejects this reading. The article argues that the Theses perfect a worldview Marx had already reached in 1843–44, and that practice belongs to the epistemology of dialectical materialism, not to ontology. The article has four parts. It first places the Theses in intellectual history through a critique of Louis Althusser's 'epistemological break'. It then examines the 'two transformations' that Marx completed in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period, and asks why the Theses target Feuerbach. It ends by locating the scientific view of practice within Marxist philosophy and by reading the eleventh thesis. Hou draws on Marx's Rheinische Zeitung articles, the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, and statements by Engels and Lenin. Hou makes three main moves. First, against Althusser, Hou separates two kinds of Feuerbachian influence: the materialist standpoint, which Marx never abandoned, and abstract humanism, which Marx held at a distance from the start. Marx's materialist turn, Hou argues, came with the discovery of the proletariat and the communist standpoint, and so preceded the Theses. The Theses supplied a scientific way of stating that worldview. Second, Hou distinguishes materialist from idealist activity: Marx's innovation lies in the objective conditioning of the subject, not in subjective initiative. Feuerbach grasped the 'sensuous object' but not 'sensuous activity'. Third, Hou holds that 'the priority of external nature' is the premise of historical materialism. Practice, citing Lenin and Mao Zedong, mediates the transformation of the 'thing-in-itself' into a 'thing-for-us' and cannot be an ontological foundation. Hou concludes that materialism, not practice, is the primary core of Marxist philosophy. Hou reads the eleventh thesis as saying not that earlier philosophers only interpreted the world, but that they lacked a scientific knowledge of it and a real social force to change it. Hou warns that stressing practice apart from this premise leads to a 'value socialism' and to the rejection of scientific socialism. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-philosophy defence of dialectical materialism against 'practical materialism' readings, built on close citation of Marx, Engels and Lenin.

Innovative development of Marxist philosophy 对马克思主义哲学的创新性发展 Liu Jun Writing in the People's Daily on 24 October 2022, during the 20th Party Congress, Liu Jun argues that Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, while inheriting the basic standpoint, viewpoints and methods of Marxist philosophy, has produced a series of innovative developments of it. The piece is a short commentary that treats Marxist philosophy as the "core skill" the whole Party is urged to study and apply. The article is organised in three parts: the continuation and development of Marxism's basic standpoint; the enrichment of its viewpoints; and the upholding and innovation of its methods. The second part takes four areas in turn: the view of practice, the view of nature, the view of contradiction and the view of development. Liu supports each point with passages from Marx, Engels and Xi. On standpoint, Liu holds that putting the people first expresses historical materialism and runs through Xi's thought like a "red thread". The article says it answers the questions of for whom, on whom to rely and who we are, by describing the people as the "examiner" of the era. It also says the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind develops Marx's "real community" and the aim of human emancipation. On viewpoints, Liu credits the thought with an advance from a "dialectical unity" of humanity and nature to a "community of life", and with the judgement that the principal contradiction in Chinese society has changed. It also credits the new development philosophy and Chinese modernization, said to break the equation of modernization with Westernization. On method, Liu stresses seeking truth from facts, keeping to fundamentals while innovating, a problem-oriented approach and systems thinking, together with strategic, historical, dialectical, innovative, rule-of-law and bottom-line thinking. Liu concludes that these elements enrich the Marxist philosophical "treasury" of methodology and constitute original contributions to the theory of social contradictions, the laws of civilisational development and the world-historical theory. The text is a concise, officially framed overview rather than a detailed philosophical analysis. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese Party theorists in October 2022 presented Xi Jinping Thought as a development of dialectical and historical materialism.

Embedding the requirement of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the Party's leadership of economic work 把全面从严治党要求体现在党领导经济工作之中 Ye Xiaowen Writing in Economic Daily on 24 October 2022, just after the 20th Party Congress, Ye Xiaowen takes up how the Party's comprehensive leadership of economic work can be secured. Ye argues that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must be built into that leadership, linking discipline and anti-corruption work with deepening reform, improving institutions and promoting development. The commentary opens from the first of the thirteen components of Xi Jinping's economic thought, the Party's overall leadership of economic work. It then proceeds under three headings: restraining power through institutions, strengthening ideological foundations, and ensuring the Party does not 'change in quality, colour or flavour'. Ye draws throughout on the 20th Party Congress report and on Xi Jinping's remarks. Ye contends that the Party faces lasting tests, including that of the market economy, which makes self-reform especially urgent. In Ye's account, a socialist market economy brings the risk of corruption from collusion between power and capital. Ye credits the post-2012 anti-corruption system with an 'overwhelming victory' but says residual corruption remains and has taken new forms. The remedy has two sides: institutional checks that make officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt, and ideological education through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, ideals and convictions, and traditional Chinese virtues. Ye concludes that the high-pressure stance against corruption must be kept up, while mechanisms are also built to motivate officials to act. These aim to make cadres willing and able to get things done as well as loyal, clean and responsible. This, Ye says, would let the Party lead economic work better and advance towards common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building discourse after the 20th Party Congress ties anti-corruption to economic governance.

The three national conferences held in the history of the Communist Party of China 党史上召开过的三次全国代表会议 Wu Rongsheng Published in Study Times shortly before the 20th Party Congress (2022), this short historical commentary explains a lesser-known Party institution: the national conference, which differs by one character from the national congress. Wu notes that the Party Constitution allows committees to convene delegate conferences when necessary to decide major issues that need prompt resolution. Wu presents the national conference as an important organisational system and a useful supplement to the congress. The article reviews the three national conferences in Party history: the 1937 Soviet Areas Delegates' Conference in Yan'an, the 1955 national conference in Beijing, and the 1985 national conference. For each, Wu gives the dates, the participants, the agenda and the speeches and resolutions. Wu describes the 1937 conference, with over 200 delegates representing more than 40,000 members, as the only such conference of the new-democratic revolution period. It endorsed the Central Committee's line since the Zunyi Meeting and prepared the Party for the War of Resistance. The 1955 conference approved the First Five-Year Plan outline and set up supervisory commissions; Wu quotes Mao Zedong calling it another rectification meeting. The 1985 conference adopted the proposals for the Seventh Five-Year Plan and adjusted the central leadership to speed generational turnover. Wu concludes that all three conferences were convened urgently, at key historical junctures, and resolved major problems. The latest revised Party Constitution specifies the conference's powers: discussing and deciding major issues, and adjusting or adding members of the Central Committee and the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. In Wu's account, the conference is therefore retained as a regular organisational system. Read the original if you want a concise factual overview of an obscure Party institution and its three precedents.

Adhering to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and advancing Party building Officials of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the Organization Department and the Central Policy Research Office brief the press 坚持全面从严治党 深入推进党的建设 Gong Liang This is a report, compiled by Guangming Daily journalist Gong Liang, on the second press conference of the 20th Party Congress press centre, held on the afternoon of 17 October 2022. Three officials spoke: Xiao Pei of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Supervisory Commission, Xu Qifang of the Central Organization Department, and Tian Peiyan of the Central Policy Research Office. The theme was unwavering full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the new great project of Party building in the new era. The report arranges the officials' answers under short thematic headings. These cover full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the defining theme of Party building, the implementation of the Party's organizational line, theoretical innovation, the Two Establishes, rule-based governance of the Party, strict management of cadres, and the comprehensive nature of Party leadership. Four sidebar items give figures from opinion surveys, inspections, Party regulations and poverty-alleviation work. Xiao Pei describes the past decade's anti-corruption struggle as unprecedented and says it reversed lax and soft Party governance and kept the Party from degenerating or being infiltrated by interest groups. Xu Qifang lists six strands of organizational work, from strengthening Party leadership to talent strategy, and stresses strict supervision of officials, including reporting of personal matters and rules on the business activities of officials' relatives. Tian Peiyan presents Xi Jinping's ideas on Party building as an original contribution to Marxist theory. He calls the Two Establishes the major political achievement of the new era and says rules-based governance is the fundamental remedy. He adds that Party leadership must be implemented comprehensively, systematically and as an integral whole. The sidebars cite a survey in which 97.4 per cent of respondents considered the effort effective, and say that nearly 4,000 Party regulations are in force, over 70 per cent of them newly made or revised in the past decade. The speakers say the 20th Party Congress (2022) set out a strategic plan to deepen Party building, and they promise further work on strengthening centralized leadership, improving the Party's self-reform, and winning the long-term anti-corruption campaign. They present this as a guarantee for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a compact official statement of how Party leaders framed Party discipline, cadre management and regulation at the start of the 20th Party Congress, together with the figures they cited.

Strengthening Party-building leadership to empower rural construction 强化党建引领 赋能乡村建设 Wu Shuxian Peng Li This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, asks how rural construction can be carried through to the modernization of the countryside. Wu and Peng argue that Party building must run through the whole effort. In their view, ensuring that the Party "takes overall charge and coordinates all sides" in rural work is the key to success, and they set out three forms of leadership: ideological, organisational (through personnel) and capacity-based. The piece is organised under these three headings. The first covers how Party members, cadres and villagers should understand rural construction. The second covers four groups: township cadres, the village two committees, resident work teams and local talented people. The third covers three capacities that the authors say grassroots Party organisations need. On ideological leadership, the authors say cadres should study Xi Jinping's statements on agriculture, rural areas and farmers. They should see rural construction as important, arduous and long-term, and should mobilise villagers into a mechanism of Party leadership, self-governance and peasant participation. On personnel, they call for wider recruitment of township cadres, training for the village Party branch and village committee, and stronger Party membership among returning entrepreneurs, young people and graduates. They also want resident teams to coordinate with village leaders and local talents to be drawn in and cultivated. On capacity, they propose better mobilisation, including digital tools, farmers' participation in decisions, consultative village governance, and emergency response that prevents risks early. Wu and Peng conclude that these measures would give rural construction a firm political guarantee and activate its endogenous drive. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building language is applied to rural governance and cadre training in 2022.

"Harnessing capital" and the path of Chinese modernization “驾驭资本”与中国式现代化道路 Xi Ge Xi Ge, in a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, asks how the path of Chinese modernization should treat capital. The author argues that its distinctive character lies in sublating and going beyond the Western, capital-centred road to modernization. The key issue, in Xi's account, is understanding capital's characteristics and laws of behaviour and learning to "harness" it. The piece presents itself as a call to Marxist theory and the philosophy and social sciences to study these questions in connection with General Secretary Xi Jinping's speech of 17 May. It has two main parts. The first sets out what Marxist theory must clarify about capital; the second takes up the rational harnessing of capital as a frontier issue and a practical task. Xi argues that going beyond capital-centred modernization does not mean abandoning capital. It means using and controlling capital to serve socialist modernization, developing its positive role while restraining its negative effects. Capital has a dual character as a relation of production and as means of production. Its "logic" brings contradictions: valorization dominating the labour process, social polarization, commodity fetishism and expansionist hegemony. Harnessing it therefore means following capital's laws of motion and using the superiority of the socialist system, so that socialist relations of production direct capital towards socialized productive forces and all-round human development. Xi concludes that Chinese modernization can create a new form of human civilization because it consciously applies and develops Marxist principles, especially the theory of capital. Through this the path is said to be rooted in China's particularities while offering universal demonstration value and world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Chinese theorists frame the "harnessing capital" formula within Marxist theory.

The "concept" mode of thinking in Marx's critique of political economy 马克思政治经济学批判的“概念”思维 Zi Yang Zi Yang asks what allowed Marx to see through the errors of bourgeois political economy, and answers that it was a mode of thinking built on the "concept" (Begriff). The short essay, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, argues that this mode was inherited from Hegel and remade on the basis of historical materialism. The article begins with Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, where Zi locates the start of the critique of political economy and treats the Rheinische Zeitung period only as its "prehistory". It then moves through three stages: the task of the critique, the forms of empiricism Marx found in political economy, and the formation of the concept-based method. Zi's examples come from Smith, Ricardo and vulgar economics, and from Hegel's Logic and Marx's Capital. Zi argues that the basic task of the critique is to "comprehend" (begreifen) the laws and categories of political economy. Bourgeois economics fails to do so because it takes private property as given and cannot derive its categories from it or connect them with each other. Zi traces this failure to the ahistorical treatment of the bourgeois mode of production. Zi sorts the resulting empiricism into three types. Smith places inner connections beside surface ones, as in his confusion of labour embodied with labour commanded. Ricardo tries to show directly that categories agree, and so skips the mediations between value, market price and production price.
