Vulgar economics takes forms of appearance for inner relations, as in its capital–interest formula. Zi then explains Hegel's concept as a subjective form of thought that also expresses the essence of the thing and grounds its truth. Marx, in Zi's reading, grounds it materialistically through Feuerbach's sensuousness and a social account of consciousness. In this sense a concept is a category that grasps the essential determination of a social relation, with "purity" and "inwardness". Zi concludes that the critique of political economy can be completed only when the essential determinations of social relations are grasped through concepts and then traced through the necessary mediations to surface phenomena. Categories such as "wages" and "circulating capital" are criticised because they either miss the most adequate form of a social relation or confuse it with empirical appearance. Read the original if you want a compact account of the Hegelian roots of Marx's method and of how Smith, Ricardo and vulgar economics are classified as types of empiricism.

The basic character of the materialist conception of history at its inception 唯物史观形成伊始的基本特征 Ohmura Izumi Was the materialist conception of history, when it first took shape, a "law of development of human history" (Engels's description) or a "guiding thread" for Marx's own research (Marx's description)? Ohmura Izumi, a Japanese Marx-Engels scholar, argues in this short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2022) for the second reading. The author holds that Engels and Marx differed here, even though Marx did not object to Engels's name for the theory. The piece starts from the history of the term. Engels coined "materialist conception of history" in his 1859 review of A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, and at Marx's funeral in 1883 he set the theory beside Darwin's theory of evolution. The commentary then turns to The German Ideology, in particular chapter 1 ("Feuerbach") and the dating of the theory's formation. Ohmura rejects the view, associated with the new historical-critical edition of the Marx-Engels Complete Works (MEGA), that the critique of Stirner in the draft of chapter 3 is the decisive moment. The author identifies three core elements: the base–superstructure relationship, class struggle, and social revolution. Ohmura argues that these appear on manuscript pages 22–24, before the Stirner critique. The later discussion of ideology, on pages 30–35, is read as an extension of that framework, and the author says it also refined the framework itself, notably the thesis that conflicts arise from the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse. Ohmura concludes that in 1845 the theory was a hypothesis guiding Marx's study of socio-economic history. Surplus-value theory did not yet exist, and the structure of Capital was not yet in view. The author finds it strained to call the theory an evolutionary law at its birth, and calls for further discussion of how its character developed, including whether Engels's formulation is sound. Read the original if you follow the MEGA debate over The German Ideology and want a compact case for dating the theory's formation to chapter 1.

The basic spirit of Western modernity from a critical perspective 批判视角下的西方现代性基本精神 Luo Qian What is the basic spiritual condition of Western modernity, and what do its achievements and limits look like when examined critically? Luo Qian argues that in modern society people have become masters of their own lives and no longer submit one-sidedly to external others or transcendent principles. The article holds that the modernity that began in the West rests on five basic aspects of spirit: secularity, individuality, creativity, practicality and positivity. Each marks a great achievement of modern emancipation and also its fundamental historical limit. This short piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in 2022, takes the five aspects in turn. Luo contrasts each with the pre-modern world, mainly medieval Christian theology. Luo also draws on Nietzsche, Heidegger and Marx, and refers to critiques of instrumental rationality. The closing section turns from the level of ideas to the social and historical foundations of these ideas. For Luo, secularity removes the transcendent realm as the source of value, so that human reason, interests, rights and desires gain legitimacy, but belief, the sublime and great things fade and value nihilism arrives. Individuality then frees the person from family, caste and rank, and Luo cites Marx on the historical roots of this individual in the dissolution of feudal society and the new productive forces. Creativity makes reality a product of human practice, so that nature, society and life become human artefacts, and Luo warns this may yield a reified world in the human image. Practicality turns relations into calculation, in which human dignity becomes exchange value and reason is reduced to instrumental reason. Positivity makes verifiable science the governing norm and an ideology, which squeezes out the sacred, the mysterious and the poetic. Luo concludes that interpreting or criticising modernity cannot stop at the level of ideas and must reach its social and historical basis. In this reading, Marx's critique of capitalist modernity supplies the ontological foundation of historical materialism for such criticism. It shows the historical conditions, achievements and limits of Western modernity's spirit. Luo adds that this critique provides the intellectual basis for Chinese modernization and for a new form of human civilisation, and points toward the sublation of Western modernity. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese philosophical account of modernity's five spiritual principles and of how Marxism is used to criticise them.

The historical logic of the early spread of Marxism in the East 马克思主义在东方早期传播的历史逻辑 Sun Laibin Sun Laibin asks why Marxism, which first spread in advanced capitalist Western Europe, found its next centre of gravity in the East, and what historical logic governed that shift. Taking Russia (loosely counted as Eastern) and China as examples, Sun argues that early diffusion combined features common to all scientific theories with differences arising from social setting, cultural tradition and revolutionary conditions. This combination, the author contends, produced a distinctive dialectic that helps explain how Marxism rose in the East. The article is organised around four "laws" of theoretical diffusion: the law of theoretical need, the law of diffusion through struggle, the law of practical orientation, and the law of advanced sacrifice. Each is illustrated with parallel cases from Russia, from the 1860s to the October Revolution, and from China, from the 1900s to the founding of the Communist Party. Sun draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on figures such as Plekhanov, Zasulich, Chen Duxiu, Cai Hesen and Qu Qiubai. Sun's central claims are as follows. First, Marxism spread in economically backward Russia and China because it answered a pressing need. The author presents the "strange" pairing of backwardness and revolutionary leadership as an instance of the dialectic of the general and the particular, avoiding both Narodnik theories of backwardness as advantage and Second International economic determinism. Second, Marxism advanced by contending with other Western currents, among them Narodism, "legal Marxism", anarchism, and in China the debates over "problems" and "isms" and over socialism. Sun describes these currents as at once fellow-travellers, competitors and opponents, owing to disputes over national paths, varied responses to capitalism, and the "Easternisation" of imported ideas. Third, translators were also revolutionaries, and many early propagators came from propertied families, so their move to the proletarian standpoint demanded sacrifice. Sun cites Qu Qiubai's self-criticism of his "dualistic personality". Sun concludes that Russian and Chinese intellectuals treated Marxism as a weapon for changing the world, not as pure doctrine. The author holds that without these class-standpoint shifts, the adaptation of Marxism to Russia and China would have been very different. Revisiting this history, Sun suggests, helps in understanding how Marxism rose in the East and in advancing its contemporary spread. Read the original if you want a conceptual account of early Marxist diffusion in Russia and China, framed through four named laws and illustrated with biographical and documentary detail.

A new form of human civilization and developing twenty-first-century Marxism 人类文明新形态与发展21世纪马克思主义 Han Qingxiang Writing in a newspaper piece of September 2022, Han Qingxiang argues that "path" and "civilization" are the fundamental questions for developing Marxism, and that twenty-first-century Marxism should be built on the path of Chinese modernization and the new form of human civilization it creates. Han treats these two "creations" as the foundation of a Marxism suited to the present century. The article begins from the claim that the essence of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times is the question of the path: of revolution, construction, reform and national rejuvenation. It then lists six things the "two creations" are said to contain: the growth point and centre of Marxism, the features of the age, the theme, the fundamental questions, the capacity for development, and the core elements. It closes by turning these elements into a theoretical structure and linking it to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Han first proposes that the Chinese path has "originary" significance: Chinese theory, institutions, culture and discourse all rest on it, so that disputes between Chinese and Western theory are, in the end, disputes over the path. On this basis Han argues that the centre of the world socialist movement has moved to contemporary China, and that the growth point of Marxism has moved with it. Han also identifies the age's defining feature as "transformation and reconstruction", produced by the interaction of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the world's "great changes unseen in a century". Han sets the theme of twenty-first-century Marxism beside those of Marx and Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, each tied to a path. It is to show the superiority of the socialist system and to choose the right path and civilization for China and the world. Han names five fundamental questions: people's wellbeing, national strength, world peace, the Party's strength and the vitality of Marxism. From the "two creations" Han extracts seven elements of strength: Party leadership, the people's principal role, market allocation, social mobilization, cultural cohesion, ecological nourishment and global harmony. Han calls their combination, under Party leadership, the "Party-led theory of a systemic structure of forces" and presents it as an expression of Xi Jinping's emphasis on systematic strategic planning and strategic thinking. Han calls for this structure to be further theorised. Read the original if you want to see how a prominent Chinese theorist ties the Chinese path, the new form of human civilization and the future of Marxism together in one framework.

Understanding the valuable experience of "persisting in pioneering and innovation" 深刻理解“坚持开拓创新”的宝贵经验 Shi Jingwen This commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, takes up one of the ten lessons of historical experience set out in the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience over the past century, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). That lesson is "persisting in pioneering and innovation". Shi argues that this has been a defining source of the Party's successes and remains a requirement for the current period. The piece first traces the historical roots of the principle, then reviews the Party's achievements by period, and finally draws out what the principle demands today. The historical roots are found in Marxism itself and in Chinese civilisation. The periods covered are the new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. Shi's central move is to present innovation as built into both Marxism and Chinese civilisation. Marxism is described as an open theory that is "not a dogma but a guide to action", and the Chinese nation's five-thousand-year history is said to show a continual search for change. Each period of Party history is then read as a case of innovation: the strategy of surrounding the cities from the countryside, the establishment of the basic socialist system, the socialist market economy, and the formation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The author links these to the first and later leaps in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. For the present, Shi names three requirements: a problem orientation, since problems are the starting point of innovation; a spirit of initiative, meaning grasping historical laws, strengthening historical awareness and acting on it; and reliance on the people's strength, through a people-centred approach and the cultivation of talent, especially young people. Shi concludes that the Party's century of struggle shows that only persistent innovation can win great struggles and realise great dreams. Because practice never stops developing, theoretical and practical innovation must continue, and the lesson must be inherited and carried forward in advancing Chinese modernization and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party commentary presents innovation as a historical lesson in the official narrative of the Party's first century.

The value and significance of the great founding spirit of the Party for national rejuvenation 伟大建党精神对民族复兴的价值意蕴 Wei Qiang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, Wei Qiang takes up the "great founding spirit of the Party", the concept Xi Jinping put forward in his 1 July 2021 speech. Wei argues that this spirit, formed when the Party was founded, has guided the whole historical course of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. In the article's account it is the spiritual source of the Party's struggles, sacrifices and creations. The short commentary is organised in four parts, each tied to one element of the founding spirit. They deal with faith and ideals, a sense of responsibility, strength of will, and political guarantees. Wei draws on episodes from the Party's history, from the Second Congress to reform and opening up and the new era. Wei's central claim is that the spirit supplies the rejuvenation project with beliefs, a mission, character and discipline. Marxist truth, in its Sinified forms from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and the communist ideal give faith its content. The original aspiration to seek happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation is said to have stayed constant through revolution, industrialisation, reform and opening up, and poverty alleviation. Fearlessness in struggle and loyalty to the Party, together with a commitment never to fail the people, are presented as the inner and political guarantees of rejuvenation. Wei concludes that the spirit is not abstract but carries practical concern. The author calls for its value to be turned from inner spirit into outward practice, giving strong spiritual force to national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2022 tied the founding spirit to the narrative of national rejuvenation.

Seen from the standpoint of civilization or culture: plural philosophies and the mutual transformation of the lifeworld 从文明或文化的观点看：多元哲学与生活世界的互变 Sun Litian This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what philosophy means if it is viewed through culture and civilization rather than only through science and cognition. Sun Litian argues that, from the scientific standpoint, a single philosophy is nearest to truth and others are error, whereas from the cultural standpoint many differing philosophies may have value. Marxist philosophy, in Sun's account, is both the scientific truth of our era and the high ground of its civilizational and moral values. Sun traces a cultural conception of philosophy from Hegel's turn to the spirit of the age and Marx's description of philosophy as the living soul of civilization, to Cassirer, Rorty and Chen Lai. The text then turns to Gao Qinghai's idea of a practical standpoint as the mode of thinking of Marxist philosophy, and to the concept of the lifeworld. Sun treats the natural, existence, consciousness, logic and language standpoints as different worldviews, or horizons for understanding the world. Borrowing Deleuze, Sun calls them distinct planes of thought that shape the lifeworld directly. The lifeworld, the pre-reflective world given before philosophy and science, carries stable beliefs that set limits on philosophical imagination: naive realist intuition, the Chinese intuition that people are good at the outset, and Rawls's intuitions about distributive justice. Philosophy must listen to the lifeworld yet also enter it with estranging, negating ideas that bring new norms and ways of living. Sun concludes that in an age of world history and globalization, plural philosophies will meet in a long dialogue of mutual interpretation, which is a dialogue of civilizational souls. A world with only one philosophy would mean the end of philosophy and of civilization. Sun adds that such dialogue must be tested against lifeworld intuition, as in Rawls's "reflective equilibrium", and that its calm voice is welcome as nationalism and populism rise against globalization. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese philosopher links Marxist philosophy, cultural pluralism and the lifeworld.

Theory and history: the twofold requirement of contemporary Marxist philosophy research 理论与历史：当代马克思主义哲学研究的双重要求 Zhang Milan Lai Shiqi This short report, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, surveys the lecture series "Theory and History: Lectures by Young Scholars of Marxist Philosophy", hosted by the School of Philosophy at Fudan University. Zhang and Lai argue that the lectures show young Chinese scholars working on real problems of the era, which they present as the aim of contemporary Marxist philosophy. In their reading, such work grasps the contemporary relevance of Marxist philosophy through both theory and practice, and contributes to building a distinctive discourse system of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. The report groups the lectures under three headings: the social-critical dimension of Marx's critique of political economy, new work on classic texts, and the history of ideas linking Marx to the Western tradition. It names speakers from Renmin University of China, Capital Normal University, Nanjing University, Shandong University, Jilin University, Sun Yat-sen University, Fudan University and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, and summarises each contribution in a sentence or two. On political economy, Xi Ge is reported as holding that capitalism has developed only at the level of natural necessity and alien necessity, while generating the material basis for sublating both. Huang Zhijun is cited on Marx's two senses of "averaging", which he reads as pointing to Marx's communist orientation. Adorno's concept of "exchange abstraction" is presented as showing that the critique of political economy remains tied to social reality. On texts, Yang Hongyuan treats the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right as the start of Marx's discussion of human emancipation, and Zhou Jiaxin traces the private-property question back into the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. On intellectual history, Feng Bo, Zhang Yin, Tian Guanhao and Huang Xuesheng are cited on Marx's relations with Spinoza, Rousseau and the Enlightenment. Huang describes Marx as a "new" Enlightenment thinker. The authors conclude that contemporary Marxist philosophy combines close textual work with new methods and a wider disciplinary horizon. They also call for scholars to engage the essential dimensions of social being, meet national needs and answer the questions of the age. Read the original if you want a quick map of current topics and names among younger Marxist philosophers in China, from Marx's critique of political economy to Marx and Spinoza.

The Belt and Road as a new engine driving world development “一带一路”是助推世界发展的新引擎 Luoke Lakeerte [罗科·拉科尔特] This short newspaper commentary, a Chinese translation of a piece by Nankai University associate professor Luoke Lakeerte (罗科·拉科尔特), argues that the Belt and Road Initiative is a new engine of world development. The author presents it as a successor to the ancient Silk Road, built on consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits and on genuine multilateralism. The article moves through several areas: inclusive globalisation, infrastructure in developing countries, financing, poverty reduction, pandemic cooperation and South-South cooperation. Its main example is the China–Laos railway, completed in December 2021. The author contends that, while the West promotes anti-globalisation and a "China threat" narrative, the Belt and Road Initiative offers an open globalisation aimed at a community with a shared future for mankind. In this account, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Silk Road Fund and the New Development Bank help developing countries escape a cycle of no capital and no infrastructure. The author cites a World Bank study that investment linked to the initiative could lift more than 34 million people out of moderate poverty, 29.4 million of them in participating countries. Lacorte concludes that the initiative is a model of South-South cooperation and will draw in more developing countries, whatever Western criticism says. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a foreign scholar's favourable account of the Belt and Road Initiative was presented to Chinese readers in 2022.

Chinese initiatives make a major contribution to improving the international landscape 中国倡议对改善国际格局作出重大贡献 José Luis Centella This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by José Luis Centella, president of the Communist Party of Spain, written shortly before the 20th Party Congress (2022). Centella asks what China's initiatives have contributed to the international order over the past decade. He argues that, in a world fragmenting amid the pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict, three proposals by Xi Jinping are especially valuable. The piece reviews the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), the Global Security Initiative (announced at the Boao Forum, April 2022) and the Global Development Initiative (put forward at the UN General Assembly, September 2021). It treats them as a linked set of Chinese proposals. Centella contrasts the Belt and Road Initiative's stated principles of voluntary participation, equality and transparency with what he calls the colonial, discriminatory and opaque practices of the United States and the European Union. He presents the Global Security Initiative as a multilateral, UN Charter-based alternative to what he describes as a new Cold War mentality, unilateral sanctions and double standards. The Global Development Initiative, in his reading, is inseparable from it, since it seeks technology transfer and knowledge sharing and aims to end colonial-style inequality between rich and poor countries. Centella concludes that the initiatives are people-centred Chinese solutions within the UN Charter framework. He describes China as a participant and partner rather than an aggressive competitor or new hegemon, and says that ignoring or slandering them deserves condemnation. Read the original if you want to see how a foreign communist party leader framed China's global initiatives for a Chinese Party-newspaper audience.

An assessment of class determination in post-Western Marxism and its characteristics 后西方马克思主义的阶级判定及其特点评析 Tang Jianlong Tang Jianlong asks how left theorists of the "post-Western Marxist" era determine class, and what this means for Marxist class theory. The article argues that these thinkers partly inherit and develop Marx's theory but also drift from it, dissolve it or turn against it. Because the criteria used to identify classes shape judgments about society, confidence in Marxism and the strategy of the communist movement, Tang holds that evaluating them helps in upholding Marxist class theory and handling real problems. The article first reconstructs how Marx and Lenin determined class, drawing on Capital and Lenin's \"A Great Beginning\". It then surveys Western Marxists such as Lukács, Gramsci, Marcuse and the early Gorz, before setting out seven post-Western Marxist types. These are Poulantzas's overdetermination approach, Gorz's work and class-consciousness approach, Roemer's property-and-market approach, Wright's exploitation-centred approach, Elster's endowment approach, Laclau and Mouffe's multi-field approach, and the de-classing tendency in Hardt and Negri's \"multitude\". Tang closes by assessing the characteristics and defects of these approaches and how to view both classical and post-Western Marxist theory. Tang reads Marx and Lenin as locating class in production: relation to the means of production, position in social labour, and the manner and share of wealth received. Political, cultural and educational factors matter, but economic position is ultimately decisive. By contrast, the later thinkers are said to stress politics, ideology, discourse or individual choice, and to move from essence to appearance and from abstraction to experience. Tang identifies four defects: exaggerating single non-economic factors, lacking a clear value goal, sliding into discourse politics and \"language games\" that Tang calls utopian, and negating the proletariat, class struggle and Marxism itself. Tang calls for reading the classics historically: Marx studied class to reveal capitalism's trajectory, not to sort people into classes, so his stance and framework should be kept while particular judgments are handled flexibly. Hostile attacks should be resisted, while criticisms within the left should be examined dialectically. Tang also credits the post-Western thinkers with reflecting real changes in capitalist class structure, countering dogmatism, and treating the working class as dynamic and historically formed. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Poulantzas, Wright, Roemer, Laclau and Mouffe, and Hardt and Negri on class.

A century of American Marxist historiography and its influence 美国马克思主义史学的百年流变及其影响 Xu Liang Marking a century since the founding of the Communist Party USA in 1919, Xu Liang asks how Marxist historiography developed in the United States and what difference it made. The article argues that, despite a winding course shaped by domestic and international conditions, American Marxist historiography has had a deep and wide influence on both American historical writing and American society. The article divides the century into three phases and then assesses impact. It first traces origins from utopian socialism, the 1848 exiles and the labour movement to the 1920s–40s. It then covers the flourishing of the 1960s–70s, and the challenges after the Cold War. Xu closes with two sections on influence, one on historiography and one on society. Xu presents the early "Old Left" (William Z. Foster, Philip Foner, Herbert Aptheker) as a first community of Marxist historians, who studied workers, Black Americans and women and rejected "American exceptionalism". They remained outside the mainstream. In the 1960s–70s, Xu says, a "New Left" (William A. Williams, Eugene Genovese, Howard Zinn) joined them, criticising US foreign policy and slavery and writing history "from below". After 1989–91 the field declined, but Xu describes a turn to interdisciplinary work and to rebuilding Marxism (Erik Olin Wright, Ellen Meiksins Wood, market socialism). On influence, Xu casts radical Marxist historiography as the counterweight to a conservative paradigm that denied class conflict. In this account, it opened labour, Black, women's and children's history and exposed class oppression, racial discrimination and inequality. Xu also credits it with feeding movements from Progressive reform and the New Deal to the 1960s–70s equality movements. Xu concludes that the clash between radical and conservative paradigms has been a main thread of American historiography, and that without Marxist history the field would have lost much of its momentum. The author adds that critique by successive Marxist historians has kept the ideal that "all men are created equal" moving forward and deepened public understanding of capitalism. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of American Marxist historians, their major works and how this tradition is evaluated from within China.

The British paradigm of twentieth-century Marxist historiography and its scholarly directions 20世纪马克思主义史学的英国范式及学术路向 Liang Minsu Liang Minsu asks how the British school of Marxist historians took shape in the twentieth century, how its two generations differed, and where research on it should go next. The article argues that the school, though never mainstream in British historiography, built a distinctive paradigm of 'new social history' that combined Marxist theory with holistic social-historical writing. It also holds that the shift from the first generation to the second marks a move from empirical social-historical narrative to social-theoretical critique. The article begins by defining the British Marxist historiographical paradigm and naming its two generations: Dobb, Hilton, Hill, E. P. Thompson, Hobsbawm and others, followed by the 'New Left' historians Perry Anderson, Robin Blackburn, Raphael Samuel, Tom Nairn and Stuart Hall. Liang then reviews Anglophone scholarship since the 1980s, such as the work of Harvey Kaye, Michael Kenny and Georg Iggers, and notes what it leaves out. The second half surveys Chinese research from Hong Kong and Taiwan and the mainland, and sets out future research routes. Liang periodises the school into formation (1930–1950), development (1960–1970) and transition (1980–1990), and ties each stage to the cultural turn led by Thompson. The core argument is that both generations rejected mechanical economic determinism and the crude base–superstructure model, treating Marxism as a guide to research rather than a ready-made formula. They stressed class experience, culture and popular agency, the first generation writing 'history from below'. The second generation, from Anderson's editorship of New Left Review in 1962, turned to continental Marxism, especially Althusser's structuralism, widening a political rift into an intellectual gulf. Liang nonetheless holds that this generation drew theoretical resources that raised the theoretical level of British history, notably in women's history, slavery studies and the new cultural history. Liang finds existing studies, at home and abroad, still lack a systematic comparison of the two generations and of their ideas of past, present and future. The article calls for firmer archival groundwork, including Communist Party records and biographical material, and for approaches from global historiography and global intellectual history, such as tracing the role of journals like Past & Present and New Left Review. It also names a weakness of the paradigm: the lack of a consistent historical thought and academic system, which Liang says weakened its creative influence. Read the original if you study Marxist historiography, the British New Left or Chinese scholarship's reception of Thompson and Hobsbawm, and want a bibliographic overview with a proposed research agenda.

Shaping the proletariat in the age of digital capitalism Forms, predicaments and corrections of contemporary Western left theories of the subject 数字资本主义时代无产阶级的形塑 Gong Yongdan Does Marx's revolutionary subject, the proletariat, still exist under digital capitalism? Gong takes up this question, which the article presents as a central concern of contemporary Western left scholars. The article argues that the new subjects these scholars propose are not true proletarians, and that the proletariat remains present because the logic of capital still governs labour. The article has three parts. The first surveys new subject-figures: the 'cognitive proletariat' and 'multitude' (Paolo Virno, Franco Berardi, Yann Moulier-Boutang, Maurizio Lazzarato, Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri), the 'user proletariat' (Slavoj Žižek), the 'divided' or 'left-over' people (Jodi Dean), and the 'cybernetic proletariat' and 'digital workers' (Nick Dyer-Witheford, Christian Fuchs). The second part criticises these constructions, and the third sets out a corrective. Gong contends that these theorists depart from Marx's class analysis in four ways. They replace labour-power with 'general intellect' as the condition of the subject. They widen the proletariat into an inclusive mass of the poor, migrants, users and fans. They redefine it as those 'without part' rather than those without means of production. And they dissolve its historical mission as 'gravedigger' into that of the 'new poor'. Against this, Gong holds that classes arise from relations of production, not from intellect, which belongs to all humans. The proletariat is defined by lacking means of production and being employed by capital. Gong therefore calls for a return from the 'logic of intellect' to the 'logic of capital', from virtual to embodied subjects, and from 'digital activity' to 'digital labour'. Only those who produce surplus value for digital platforms are digital workers, whereas ordinary users, even if alienated or poor, are not strictly proletarians. Gong concludes that digital capitalism remains capitalism, with the contradiction between capital and labour intact, so Marx's proletariat needs neither rewriting nor replacement. Gong credits the Western left with theoretical courage but warns against both mythologising the proletariat and discarding it. As long as capital's logic is present, its opposite does not leave the stage. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of autonomist and post-Marxist theories of the digital subject, set out through Marx's concepts of class, labour-power and productive labour.

The leftward turn of party politics in the Nordic countries and its prospects 北欧政党政治左翼化态势及其前景 Li Hong Why did centre-left parties return to power across the Nordic region while populism was rising elsewhere in Europe? Li Hong takes up this question after Norway's September 2021 election, when the Labour Party became the largest party and a centre-left bloc ended eight years of centre-right rule. Li argues that Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark have collectively "turned left", but that this leftward shift carries a populist imprint and faces serious tests. The article was published in Contemporary World, 2022 no. 2. The article first recalls the Nordic region's past as a "fortress of European social democracy" and the decline of its social democratic parties in the early twenty-first century, when right-wing populist parties such as the Sweden Democrats and the Danish People's Party surged. It then traces the recovery in Sweden (2014), Finland and Denmark (2019) and Norway (2021), with vote shares and seat counts. Three further sections cover the reasons for the victories, the character of the new left-leaning politics, and the governments' prospects. Li gives three causes of the victories. The first is the negative effects of neoliberal globalization, which Li says produced a political pendulum swing. The second is that centre-left parties adjusted their policies: they returned strongly to the welfare state, took over the centre-right's tight control of refugees, and treated climate change as a priority, favouring gradual measures over the Greens' radical ones. The third is a fragmented party system and the relative weakness of the centre-right. Li holds that the new leftism is real, as seen in the end of austerity and support for the EU. Even so, it is populist-marked because the parties kept restrictive refugee policies, replaced multiculturalist integration with a "dominant culture" approach, and stressed that welfare recipients carry responsibilities. Li identifies four challenges: the lead parties' low vote shares (under 30 per cent, and under 20 per cent in Finland); the instability of multiparty coalitions, illustrated by the fall of Finland's first government after six months; the strength of right-wing populists, especially in Finland; and the need to deliver results, since voters largely rejected the centre-right rather than endorsing the left. Li concludes that long-term rule depends on balancing party principles against voters' needs, a strong welfare state against growth, and climate action against sustainable development. Read the original if you want a concise, data-rich Chinese account of recent Nordic social democratic revival and its compromises on migration and welfare.

The elephant in the room: the crisis of Europe's left-wing parties 房中象：欧洲左翼政党的危机 Asbjørn Wahl This is a Chinese translation of an essay by the Norwegian trade-union activist and writer Asbjørn Wahl. It asks why Europe's left-wing parties avoid the question of their relationship to the European Union, which the author calls the "elephant in the room". Wahl argues that this evasion lies at the heart of the parties' wider political and ideological crisis, and that the EU cannot be reformed from within as many of them assume. The essay surveys the weak electoral position of left parties after the 2019 European Parliament elections. It compares rival left alliances: the European Left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon's "France Unbowed" with the Lisbon Declaration, and Yanis Varoufakis's DiEM25. It traces the historical roots of left attachment to European integration, including Mitterrand's failed programme of the early 1980s. It then examines the eurozone crisis, the Syriza government's capitulation in Greece, the "Plan B" initiative and the Brexit debate. Wahl contends that the left's pro-EU orientation rested on the promises of peace and social progress, which he says the EU's neoliberal and increasingly authoritarian structures have undermined. He lists seven institutional obstacles to reform from within, among them the democratic deficit, constitutionalised neoliberalism, treaties that require unanimity to change, the euro and the European Court of Justice. He criticises Varoufakis's reform-from-within strategy as naive. He also finds Plan B, which envisages breaching treaties if a left government is blocked, strategically underdeveloped. In his reading, some parties, such as the Swedish Left Party, have dropped exit demands for fear of allying with racists and nationalists, which has left criticism of the EU to the far right. Wahl concludes that the left must build its own internationalist, anti-racist opposition to what he calls the authoritarian neoliberal EU, and that leaving the eurozone or the EU may become a necessary option if a left government meets the Greek scenario. He argues that the rise of the far right stems from EU policies, not from left criticism of them. He calls for an honest recognition of the crisis, study of the EU's role, and a genuinely anti-capitalist strategy, to which Plan B could contribute. Read the original if you want a critical left-wing account of the EU debate among European parties, including detailed discussion of Syriza, Mélenchon, Varoufakis and the Brexit referendum.

Clearly and firmly strengthening the Party's political development 旗帜鲜明加强党的政治建设 Xiao Guiqing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 13 October 2022, takes up Mao Zedong's 1944 dictum that "the key to all problems lies in politics", which Xi Jinping cited in January 2021. Xiao Guiqing argues that politics is as decisive in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics as it was in the New Democratic revolution, and that strengthening the Party's political development is therefore the "golden key" to the Party's tasks. The piece is short and built around a repeated formula: the more complex the situation and the heavier the tasks, the more the Party must act in four areas. These are political direction and political leadership, the people as the political foundation, political capability, and political discipline. Xiao argues that political direction is the first question for the Party's survival and development, and that upholding it means upholding the Party's leadership and the central leadership's centralised, unified authority. Citing Mao's follow-on remark that the key of all politics is the masses, the author ties the people-centred approach to the Party's original aspiration. The author also stresses political capability as the first of the abilities cadres need, especially senior cadres, who must understand "matters of national importance" and see problems politically. On discipline, Xiao presents the Party's self-reform and the anti-corruption campaign since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a second answer to the "historical cycle" question. Xiao concludes that Mao's dictum has been confirmed by more than 70 years of practice. Communists now face a "new test" and a "fresh departure" at the junction of the two centenary goals, and the author calls on the Party to use political development to address the major questions of the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists framed political development in the run-up to the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Major historic achievements in the Party's political building in the new era 新时代党的政治建设取得重大历史性成就 Fan Dezhi Yang Shifu Published in Guangming Daily on 12 October 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes up the Party's "political building" (dang de zhengzhi jianshe) since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Fan and Yang argue that the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core placed political building first among the Party's fundamental tasks, and that original ideas and transformative practice have produced major historic achievements. These, they say, give a firm political guarantee for the "great new project" of Party building. The piece has three parts. The first presents Xi Jinping's statements on political building as an original contribution to Marxist theory of Party building. The second sets out the achievements and basic experience of the new era under five headings. The third treats political building as a permanent task and lists four directions for further work. In the first part the authors identify four claims: that taking a clear political stand is the Party's political advantage; that the first task is ensuring the whole Party obeys the Central Committee and upholds its authority and centralised, unified leadership; that political building is the fundamental form of Party building, deciding its direction and effect; and that the Party must consolidate its governing base, nurture a healthy political ecology, guard against political risks and raise political capability. The second part reviews the record: arming the Party with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, institutional rules on Party leadership, the people-centred approach (including poverty eradication and the eight-point regulations), training leading cadres, and anti-corruption work, which the authors say has achieved an overwhelming victory. Fan and Yang conclude that, because the Party's political advanced character cannot be secured once and for all, political building is a permanent task and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must continue. They propose strengthening ideological guidance, implementing the Two Upholds, improving political capability and purifying political life inside the Party. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Party-history researchers frame political building on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The Yan'an Rectification Movement and strengthening the Party's centralised and unified leadership 延安整风与加强党的集中统一领导 Tan Huwa Published in Guangming Daily in October 2022, this short historical commentary asks how the Yan'an Rectification Movement (1941–45) helped the Chinese Communist Party build centralised and unified leadership. Opening with Xi Jinping's 2021 remark that rectification brought the Party 'unprecedented unity', Tan Huwa argues that the movement was an ideological education campaign. In Tan's account it taught the whole Party to apply Marxism-Leninism to China's practical problems and to understand Marxist Party-building principles, and so it strengthened centralised leadership. The article has three parts. The first sets out why strengthening centralised and unified leadership reached the historical agenda during the War of Resistance. The second follows the central documents and institutional steps of 1941–43. The third takes the Northwest Bureau and the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region as a model case of implementation, using speeches by Chen Yun, Ren Bishi and Mao Zedong and local directives of 1943. Tan gives four reasons for the need: the survival of sectarianism and 'mountain-top' tendencies from the Land Revolution period and the influence of Wang Ming's dogmatism; harsher conditions behind enemy lines, which demanded unified command; mistaken ideas arising from the 'three-thirds' system, such as the view that Party organisation hardly mattered in government; and the new burden of local governance. The key document, the 'September 1' decision of 1942, is presented as affirming that the Party leads all other organisations. It required lower levels to obey higher ones and the whole Party to obey the Centre. It also limited Party leadership of government to principles and policy, not substitution for it. Tan then links this to the formation of a leadership core, including the 1943 decision making Mao Zedong chairman of the Politburo and Secretariat. In the Northwest Bureau, the Party committee was made the centre of unified leadership over mass organisations, propaganda broadcasts, army relations and economic bodies such as the salt industry. Tan also notes shortcomings that remained by late 1943, especially weak Party control over the army and finance. Tan concludes that rectification further cleared away subjectivism and sectarianism, raised the standards of Party building and comprehensively strengthened centralised leadership. In Tan's view, this laid an important ideological and political basis for victory in the War of Resistance and in the democratic revolution. Read the original if you want a compact, officially framed account of the documents and Northwest Bureau practice through which Yan'an-era Party unity is presented today.

Mao Zedong's firm resolve in upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee during the revolutionary war years, and his major contribution 毛泽东在革命战争年代维护党中央权威的坚定意志及其重要贡献 Zheng Zhiqiang Zheng Zhiqiang takes up a question the author says earlier scholarship handled mostly in broad narrative: how Mao Zedong upheld the authority of the Party Central Committee during the democratic revolution. The article argues that the turn from danger to victory in the Chinese revolution cannot be separated from Mao's defence of that authority. In Zheng's account, Mao showed firm resolve from the early years and became an outstanding example of loyalty to centralised, unified Party leadership. The article follows Mao through three periods. The first runs from Jinggangshan to Ruijin, the second from the founding of the Soviet-area Central Bureau to the early Long March, and the third from the Zunyi Conference to the eve of the People's Republic. A final section distils lessons. Zheng frames the study as relevant to the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. In the first period, Zheng contends, Mao carried out the Central Committee's general line of armed struggle and land revolution. Where he disagreed, he did so through democratic centralism, discussion and voting, and through formal reports to the Centre. In the second period, when the Provisional Central Committee criticised his line and stripped him of military posts, Zheng argues that Mao kept to his views but accepted each reassignment for the sake of unity. The author sets this against Luo Zhanglong, Zhang Guotao and others who opposed the centre or split the Party. After Zunyi, Zheng says, Mao's core position was consolidated through the Sixth Plenum, the Seventh Congress and ideological work, including the Yan'an rectification, the stress on Party spirit and new Party regulations. Zheng draws three lessons: a revolutionary party needs strict discipline and a Central Committee with authority; it must follow the mass line and carry out investigation so that its line is correct and can be transmitted downwards; and it must practise criticism and self-criticism. The article closes by linking these lessons to the Party's centenary, the new stage of development and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and calls for stronger Party history education. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of Mao's conduct toward the Central Committee from the Jinggangshan base through the Seventh Congress, including the specific conferences and personnel decisions Zheng cites.

The image of the hero in Mao Zedong's poetry 毛泽东诗词中的英雄形象 Wang Jianxin Wang Jianxin, in a commentary first published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) on 23 September 2022, asks how heroes and heroism are portrayed in Mao Zedong's poems and lyrics. The author argues that the heroic spirit is the enduring thread running through Mao's verse. It rests on a deep ideological content, and Mao combined an intense admiration for heroes with a firm rejection of the 'heroes make history' view. The article opens with Mao's boyhood reading in 1910 of a collection of biographies of world heroes, which, Wang says, made him see China's need for strong figures. It then proceeds in thematic sections: Mao's own youthful heroic self-image and sense of mission; his judgements on figures of the past, from the Yellow Emperor and Qu Yuan to Jia Yi, Cao Cao, Zu Ti, Liu Fen and Lu Xun; his tributes to revolutionary and patriotic fighters; and his verse on the people as makers of history. Wang's central argument is that Mao's heroism develops from individual self-confidence into a materialist view of history. Early lines such as 'Rebuking the warlords of the day as dung' show a young man's resolve to save the nation, which led him to Marxism after the May Fourth Movement. Wang reads the lines on emperors such as Qin Shihuang and Genghis Khan, and on slave and peasant rebel leaders, as a critique of the old history centred on kings and generals. The poems honouring Huang Gonglue, Peng Dehuai, Yang Kaihui, Luo Ronghuan, Ding Ling, Dai An'lan and the Nanjing Road 'Good Eighth Company' show a revolutionary pantheon. Wang then claims that Mao's 'people-centred view of history' holds the masses to be the true heroes, citing the line that 'the people of the proletariat' are the 'heroes of today'. Wang concludes that after 1949 Mao's poetry turned to celebrating the builders of the new China and a new generation, while keeping its confidence in a people who 'fear neither ... nor'. The people's standpoint is presented as both the theoretical foundation of Mao Zedong Thought and the emotional tone of his verse. Read the original if you want a short, Party-press survey of how Mao's poems are interpreted as expressions of heroism and the people's role in history, with many of the lines and figures identified.

Socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a new form of human civilization 中国特色社会主义创造了人类文明新形态 Liu Jianjun This short commentary from 2022 takes up the claim, first made explicitly by Xi Jinping at the celebration of the Communist Party's centenary, that socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a new form of human civilization. Liu Jianjun argues that the claim is both a political declaration and an academic proposition that needs scholarly explanation. In Liu's account, it expresses the Party's confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article first traces how civilization discourse, latent in the Marxist classics, became explicit and systematic among Chinese communists after reform and opening up. It then clarifies concepts: civilization versus culture, civilization form versus social formation, and the place of socialist civilization within a communist civilization that is to surpass private-property civilizations. Finally it sets out three dimensions in which the new form can be understood. Liu holds that every social formation is also a civilization form, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics is a more specific form within socialist civilization. It is a complete civilization form because it unites path, theory, system and culture, and also material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. Liu calls it complex and "atypical", to be grasped through three combined dimensions: a new form of Chinese civilization (its modern form, arising in a period of renewal), of modern civilization (a path to modernization different from the West's, described as a contemporary or surpassing form), and of socialist civilization (its Chinese form, achieved by a large, historically old but relatively backward Eastern country). Liu concludes that this civilization form enriches the diversity of world civilizations, promotes exchange and mutual learning, and advances and leads human civilization. It is still developing and will show a clearer outline and a more mature form in future. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists conceptually define the "new form of human civilization" formula.

The threefold critique of modernity in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》对现代性的三重批判 Liu Rongjun Zhang Leiyu Liu Rongjun and Zhang Leiyu ask how Marx criticises modernity in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. They define modernity as the union of the logic of capital with modern metaphysics, a union that shapes the economy, politics, culture, ecology and the structure of thought. Their thesis is that the Manuscripts mount a threefold critique: an economic-philosophical one, a socio-political one and a critique of the philosophy of subjectivity. The piece first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022. The article moves through the three critiques in turn. The first concerns classical political economy; the second concerns false forms of communism and Marx's own account of communism; the third concerns Hegel's philosophy of the subject and his dialectic. The authors present the three as stages from surface to depth, each sublating the one before. Their starting point is Marx's reading of Hegel's philosophy of right, which led him to treat the relation of industry and wealth to the political sphere as a main problem of the modern age. On the first level, the authors argue that classical economics defends a "capital justice" that treats the separation of labour from its object as legitimate. In their account it affirms labour in theory while negating the human being in practice, because workers live under fourfold alienation. It never examines private property, the premise of that justice, and so cannot identify capital as the abstract subject governing modern society. On the second level, Marx criticises "crude communism" for levelling private property and so leaving the logic of capital intact. He also criticises a politically minded communism that grasps only capital's negative side. Against these he sets communism as the positive sublation of private property and self-alienation, realised in an "association of free individuals". On the third level, Marx rescues the real, sensuous, objectifying human being from Hegel's abstract subject. The authors argue that he builds a materialist dialectic from Hegel's historical sense and judges that Hegel grasped labour only as abstract mental labour, so that his result is a "revolution inside the skull". The authors conclude that the three dimensions form a totalising dialectical picture that helped drive Marx's critique of ideology and the founding of historical materialism. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that we still live in the historical epoch Marxism identified, they hold that Marx's way of thinking and method remain useful for reading the present era. They tie this to the generation and development of a new form of human civilisation that sublates capitalist modernity. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-language reading of the 1844 Manuscripts as a layered critique of modernity and of its links to Hegel and classical economics.

Capital and the absurd "Sybel debate" 《资本论》与荒谬的“西贝尔之辩” Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing, in a newspaper commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2022, revisits a little-known episode after the publication of Marx's Capital. In March 1872 the Munich historian Heinrich von Sybel gave two public lectures to entrepreneurs, "The Teachings of Contemporary Socialism and Communism", attacking Marx's theory of surplus value and defending capitalists. Zhang calls this the "Sybel debate" and argues that it is absurd and cannot hide the objective laws of the capitalist mode of production that Capital reveals. Zhang first sets the background. Sybel's attack came mainly in the first lecture, and Marx knew of it. The Russian populist Mikhailovsky later amplified Sybel's views in an 1877 article. In his letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski, Marx answered only the misreading of his views on paths of social development, not Sybel's claims. The commentary then reports Sybel's two main arguments and answers them in turn. Sybel first denies primitive accumulation in Germany. Zhang reads this as a cover for his real aim, which is to deny that capitalists appropriate workers' surplus value without payment. Sybel cites Marx's passage on the architect and the bee to argue that purposeful labour belongs to whoever sets the goal. In factories that is the manufacturer, while workers are merely "living tools". Engineers and managers, he says, only serve the owner's goals, so the owner's "mental labour" creates value and surplus value. Zhang replies that Sybel confuses two kinds of purpose: the concrete aim of labour in making use-values, and the capitalist's drive to accumulate profit. The worker's subjective representation of the task cannot be separated from the worker, even on an automated line. Zhang lists five further flaws. Sybel misreads how the position of workers changes under mechanised production. He ignores the creative role of scientists and technicians. He misses that the factory owner is only a personification of capital relations and a puppet of the law of value. He overlooks that the owner's managerial and coordinating work is in essence capital's appropriation of the social combining power and technological productivity that workers and scientific staff create. Zhang concludes that, over 150 years after Capital, Marx's theory of surplus value remains a powerful tool for analysing contemporary capitalism. Read the original if you want a short Chinese Marxist rebuttal of a nineteenth-century apologist for capital, or an example of how Chinese scholars currently defend the labour theory of value.

The dialectic of modernity in Capital 《资本论》的现代性辩证法 Bai Gang Bai Gang asks how Marx's Capital, as a critique of political economy, offers a comprehensive account of modernity. This short commentary, first published in Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2022, argues that Capital is a 'higher-level' exposition of modernity. In Bai's reading, it identifies capital as the secularised successor to God, and then proposes to limit and transform capital in order to move beyond it. The article is organised in three parts. The first treats modernity as the process of 'secularising God', drawing on Nietzsche, Weber, Leo Strauss and Scheler. The second examines capital as the 'fetish' that expresses modernity. The third sets out what Bai calls Capital's 'scheme' for modernity: putting 'traffic lights' on capital. Bai draws throughout on Marx, and on Engels's review of Capital. Bai holds that modernity replaces the medieval order of faith with the rule of capital. Capital moves from commodity capital to money capital to interest-bearing capital, an 'automatic fetish' that Bai says carries the 'spiritual honour' God lost in the modern age. It rules through 'equality' and exchange, not force, which Bai links to the three fetishisms of commodity, money and capital. People gain independence from gods, but remain dependent on things. Bai argues that Marx neither rejects capital nor accepts it as eternal. He recognises its 'civilising side' and seeks to reshape it. Cooperative factories and joint-stock companies, and the replacement of wage labour by cooperative labour, are the means. The aim is the all-round developed individual and the 'realm of freedom'. Bai concludes that the dialectic of modernity in Capital transcends capitalism and also capital itself, 'surpassing capital through capital'. Marx's remedy for a modernity dominated by capital is a fuller modernity of free, all-round individual development, reached by re-establishing individual ownership and abolishing wage labour. Bai calls Capital the 'highest-level revolution of modernity' and of freedom. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist interpretation of Capital through the themes of secularisation, fetishism and the limits of capital.

Marx's concept of cooperation and its contemporary significance 马克思的协作概念及其当代意义 Pan Shenyang This short newspaper article, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what role the concept of cooperation plays in Marx's thought. Pan argues that cooperation is the standpoint from which Marx criticises capitalism, and also the basis of his idea of a socialist and communist economy. The piece first sets out Marx's definition of cooperation in Capital and its manuscripts and lists four features: internal interconnection, planning, the joining of labourers with their products, and the generation of new productive power. It then covers two themes: cooperation in the critique of capitalism, and cooperative production in Marx's view of socialism, including his engagement with the cooperatives of his day. Pan reads Marx as holding that under capitalism the social productive power created by cooperation is appropriated without payment and appears as the productive power of capital. Capitalist management, the author says, hides exploitation behind the neutral need for coordination, and workers become mere parts in the labour process. In the second half, Pan traces Marx's interest in cooperative production in the 1860s to the struggle against Lassalleanism, the First International and the influence of Owen and Ernest Jones. Marx and Jones criticised cooperatives that were isolated and competed with one another, but valued those that shared profits with members and society. Marx called such cooperatives "possible" communism. Pan concludes that Marx gave the cooperative only two principles, not a detailed blueprint: the dictatorship of the proletariat as a political precondition, and the use of new social elements that capitalism itself produces. According to Pan, this stresses both individual self-emancipation and objective conditions, so that Marx's idea avoids both utopianism and blind action. Read the original if you want a brief account of how Marx's theory of cooperation links his critique of capitalism to his view of the path towards communism.

The internal paradox of the aesthetic dimension in Marxism outside China 国外马克思主义审美之维的内在悖论 Wang Qi This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks why foreign Marxism has invested so much hope in the aesthetic dimension as a way of critiquing modernity. Wang Qi argues that this dimension hides paradoxes it cannot resolve, so it cannot deliver the revolutionary, world-changing significance it promises. The article first lists the thinkers who drew on aesthetics: Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Benjamin, Eagleton, Plekhanov and Jameson. It then examines two paradoxes, one at the starting point of the aesthetic critique and one in its practical aim. It ends with remarks on what this means for Chinese Marxist aesthetics and for cultural work in China. On the first paradox, Wang says foreign Marxism begins from social critique, such as Marcuse's "one-dimensional society", and concludes that domination now works through ideology and mass culture. Struggle therefore shifts from seizing power to contesting consciousness. In Wang's reading, this turn makes critique focus on thought and ideas rather than reality, and it ends in a utopia of reforming consciousness. On the second, Wang identifies three practical paths: aesthetic politics (Marcuse, Eagleton), aesthetic production (Benjamin, Lifshitz) and aesthetic existence (Adorno, Foucault). Wang argues that all three shrink revolution into individual self-formation, so they either stay in the study or sink into self-technique, an existentialist self-salvation. Wang concludes that these paradoxes confirm the scientific character of Marx's answer on the relation of thought and being. Chinese Marxist aesthetics should return to Marx and Engels, on the wholeness of sensibility, all-round human development and a harmonious ideal society. It should not copy this critical framework onto China's cultural problems. Wang calls for joint efforts in ideological and cultural development and aesthetic education, to raise a new generation developing morally, intellectually, physically, aesthetically and in labour. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist critique of the Frankfurt School and related aesthetic theory, and its link to current cultural policy.

How the Chinese miracle happened Based on a political-economy interpretive framework 中国奇迹何以发生 Zhou Wen Zhou Wen asks how China's economic miracle came about and argues that it needs a new political-economy explanation. In this short commentary, Zhou holds that the answer lies in persistently modernizing the state's governance system and capacity, and in a dialectical, organic combination of market and government. Zhou presents this as a critical reconstruction of neoliberal theory and the seed of a distinctive Chinese economics. The piece begins with the Western-centric view that modern China fell behind because of despotism and an underdeveloped market economy. It then turns to the historical role of government in the rise of capitalism and the early industrial revolution. Finally it sets out the analytical framework Zhou attributes to contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. Zhou contends that China's modern backwardness stemmed from the government's absence from the economy and weak governance, not from a lack of markets. Claims that a free market and limited government suffice for development are, in Zhou's words, theoretically baseless and poorly supported in practice. In place of the Western binary of government versus market, Zhou describes a three-dimensional framework of the Party, government and market. Under it, the Party exercises centralized, unified leadership over economic work, and the market plays the decisive role in allocating resources while government makes up for market failure. Zhou concludes that economic development has always been driven by the state, and that the rise and fall of governance capacity is its main thread. Zhou calls for a new political-economy discourse centred on development and the state. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese economist frames the Party–government–market relationship as an alternative to neoliberal theory.

The national character and global significance of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics 中国特色社会主义政治经济学的民族性与世界性 Liu Wei This short newspaper commentary asks how the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics can be both specifically Chinese and universal. Liu Wei argues that political economy, as a social science, is a dialectical unity of national particularity and worldwide significance, and that the Chinese version shows this unity in a particular way. The piece begins with a general point about learning across national traditions. It then develops two themes: the historical staging that gives the Chinese theory its national specificity, and the movement of socialism from a single country to the international sphere. Liu holds that comparative critique of different schools requires a fixed standard, namely the class standpoint and historical value orientation of political economy. It also requires scientific method and a thorough understanding of the object being criticised. The national specificity of the theory depends on the historical stage of the Chinese socialist mode of production. Liu locates this in the primary stage of socialism, whose basic programme is socialist modernization, to be achieved by 2050 under the "two-step" plan set out at the 19th Party Congress (2017). Liu then argues that socialism has been international since its origins and is now at a stage where it exists in individual countries. As Chinese socialism develops, the author says, it moves from the national to the global, and its political economy expands from a narrow to a broad sense. Liu concludes that the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics should explain the laws of motion of the Chinese socialist mode of production, and that it develops from national to international scope. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese economist links the stages of socialism to the claim that Chinese political economy is universal.

Upholding fundamental principles and innovating: the path of economic development in the new stage of development 新发展阶段经济发展道路的守正创新 Hong Yinxing Writing in a newspaper commentary of August 2022, Hong Yinxing argues that China's economic development path combines fidelity to the right direction of reform and opening up ("upholding fundamental principles") with continuous innovation. As China enters the new era and the stage of an upper-middle-income country, Hong says, this path is moving towards development that is higher in quality, more efficient, fairer, more sustainable and safer. The piece is organised around four paths: changing the mode of economic development, synchronised development of the "four modernizations", common prosperity for all the people, and open development under the new development pattern. Each is tied to statements by Xi Jinping and to what Hong calls Xi Jinping's economic thinking. On the first path, Hong holds that crossing the "middle-income trap" requires a shift from factor- and investment-driven growth to innovation-driven growth, with supply-side structural reform and green development as means. On the second, Hong describes China's "parallel" development of industrialisation, informatisation, urbanisation and agricultural modernisation as shortening the process and lowering its costs compared with the West's "serial" path. On common prosperity, Hong stresses that it does not mean egalitarianism or levelling incomes. Instead, it implies a "reasonable range" of income gaps, a larger middle-income group and a distribution system balancing efficiency and fairness across primary distribution, redistribution and the third distribution. Finally, Hong presents the new development pattern, with the domestic circulation as the mainstay and domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other, as the route to economic modernization, while coordinating security and development. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line overview of how an economist close to Party theory links Xi's economic ideas to China's development path.

Karl Marx and English socialism 卡尔·马克思与英国社会主义 David Leopold This is a Chinese translation (abridged, with subheadings added by the translator) of an article by the Oxford political theorist David Leopold. It takes up the neglected question of how far British life shaped Marx, who lived in London for over thirty years. Leopold argues against the views that Britain left little mark on him, that its influence was confined to economics, and that France was the only country whose socialism mattered to him. By "English socialism" he means the socialism of Robert Owen and the Owenite movement, which he says is often dismissed as merely "utopian". The article opens with a survey of eight areas of British influence: Scottish and English political economy, Scottish historical sociology, Chartism, Marx's journalism for the New-York Daily Tribune, his struggle against Palmerston, the International Working Men's Association, his London friendships (notably Edward Spencer Beesly) and English literature. It then concentrates on Owenism in four steps: Marx's assessment, his criticisms, the positive influences, and the channels through which he learned of it during his Brussels exile (1845–48). Leopold reads Marx's critique as aimed at four points: the claim that socialism must be blueprinted, Owenite paternalism toward the proletariat, its "unhistorical" character and its "anti-political" stance. He suggests these criticisms do not fit the full variety of Owenite theory and practice and served partly to highlight Marx's own emphases. He then identifies five positive influences: Owen's critique of alienated labour, the Owenite political economy of exploitation and class antagonism, elements of a socialist vision (the abolition of the town–country divide, early forms of combined education and labour), the link between materialism and socialism, and the cooperative movement, whose seed Marx said Owen sowed. For the Brussels years, Leopold identifies three probable channels: Engels, who had been involved with Owenites in Manchester; the 1845 research trip to Manchester, whose notebooks include extracts from Owen, Thompson, Bray, Edmonds and Watts; and the friendship with the poet and merchant Georg Weerth, who knew Bradford Owenism and Chartism. He concludes that Marx's knowledge of and engagement with English socialism was wider and more active than usually thought, and that Owen deserves respect rather than blanket classification as a utopian. Read the original if you study Marx's intellectual formation, the Manchester Notebooks, or the relation between Marxism and Owenism.

Providing a firm guarantee for advancing the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics Reading Xi Jinping's "Implement the Party's organizational line for the new era and keep making the Party stronger and more powerful" 为推进中国特色社会主义事业提供坚强保证 Feng Zhifeng This commentary, first published in Study Times and posted in October 2022, reads Xi Jinping's speech of 29 June 2020 at a Politburo study session of the 19th Central Committee. Feng presents the speech as a guide to action for carrying out the Party's organizational line for the new era. The article argues that this line gives the Party a firm organizational guarantee for upholding and strengthening its overall leadership and for advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece has three parts. It first sets out the scientific content of the organizational line, which Xi first formulated in full at the 2018 national organization work conference. It then reviews achievements in Party organization since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Finally, it lists measures for implementing the line. Feng reports four points on content: arming the whole Party with scientific theory, focusing on the organizational system, choosing and using the right people, and subordinating the organizational line to the political line. On achievements, the author cites 96.712 million Party members and 4.936 million primary-level organizations at the end of 2021. Feng also cites the "five systems" for cadre training and selection, and a series of regulations on primary-level organizations. The implementation measures include Party leadership over organizational work, the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, a tight organizational system, putting the people at the centre, and improving organizational rules. Feng concludes that a tightly organized Party can unite its members, gather talent and mobilize the public to meet major risks and challenges. Together, these measures are meant to raise the Party's creativity, cohesion and combat effectiveness. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media present the organizational line for the new era and its claimed results.

How to overcome the "fear of lacking skills" when facing online public opinion 面对网络舆情如何克服“本领恐慌” Guo Pengyuan Yuan Xia This short commentary, first published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao), asks how Party leading cadres can overcome the "fear of lacking skills" (benling konghuang) when dealing with online public opinion. The authors observe that, in recent hot-button online incidents, some cadres at first ignored the issue or treated it lightly, then panicked or avoided it, so that incidents escalated and rebounded on them. They argue that the remedy lies in correct views of news and public opinion, institutional and organisational capacity, and practical analytical tools. The piece sets out three steps in turn. It begins with ideological orientation, then moves to systems and organisation, and ends with concrete methods for judging public opinion. It draws on Xi Jinping's call to become expert in using new media and on Mao Zedong's remarks on running newspapers. First, the authors call for a Marxist view of news that combines Party spirit with the people's character, and a view of public opinion that relies on the masses. Cadres should not trust a few influential online "big Vs", since the "silent majority" matters more. Second, they propose a routine system of monitoring, early warning, response and review, a streamlined organisation for rapid "discover–decide–execute" action, legal and disciplinary oversight, and a young, media-literate team backed by outside experts. Third, they recommend four tools: monitoring notes, emotion-volume charts, communication-path maps and process-analysis charts. Each helps cadres track a case's platforms, emotions, key accounts and life-cycle stages. The authors conclude that these measures can raise cadres' sensitivity to online opinion and their ability to anticipate its course. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party media commentary frames cadre training in online public-opinion work, including its practical tools.
