Grasping the characteristics of young people to teach ideological and political courses well 把握青少年特点上好思政课 Han Liying This short commentary, published in the People's Daily and reposted in October 2022, asks how ideological and political theory courses in schools can be taught more effectively. Han Liying argues that they must be designed around the characteristics of young people, in line with Xi Jinping's remark that ideological and political education is a continuous process that should target each stage of growth. The aim, in the author's account, is to cultivate a new generation able to take on the task of national rejuvenation. The article is organised under three headings: building a firm ideological foundation, following the laws of young people's development, and enriching the forms of teaching. Each is presented as a requirement for fulfilling the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. On content, Han calls for sustained education in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, in the histories of the Party, New China, reform and opening up and socialism, and in patriotism, collectivism and socialist core values. On developmental stages, the author distinguishes early adolescence, with vivid, image-based thinking suited to experiential learning, middle adolescence, with emerging abstract thinking suited to commonsense learning, and late adolescence, with more complex thinking suited to inquiry-based learning. On method, Han urges teachers to answer students' real questions through case-based, experiential and interactive teaching, turning 'big principles' into 'small stories', respecting students' central position and using modern information technology. Han concludes that tiered course content, matched to the stages of growth and delivered in lively forms, will gradually raise young people's ideological and political awareness and strengthen the appeal of the courses. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese education scholar sets out the official rationale and teaching approach for school ideological and political courses.

Providing the people with more reliable and fuller social security 为人民提供更可靠更充分的保障 Jiang Wenling This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in October 2022, asks how China can give its people "more reliable and fuller" social security. Jiang Wenling, a regional civil affairs official, argues that meeting people's needs for a better life and steadily advancing common prosperity require a social security system with full coverage that is sustainable. Opening with a statement by Xi Jinping on social security as a basic institutional safeguard, the piece is organised around four principles: Party leadership, putting the people first, reform and innovation, and service first. Jiang first claims that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee has given social security top-level design, producing a functionally complete system built around social insurance, with social assistance, welfare and special care for veterans and their families. Jiang then presents the people-first principle as the starting point of the system, tied to common prosperity and to improving livelihoods from childcare to elderly care. The author says reform must respond to population ageing, urbanisation and more varied forms of employment, and must target the people's most pressing concerns. Jiang calls for multi-tier, multi-pillar pension insurance, provincial-level pooling of basic medical, unemployment and work-injury insurance, better urban–rural social assistance, and more accurate identification of beneficiaries. The author also urges a unified online–offline service platform, digital transformation of social insurance administration, and an emergency response mechanism for major risks, drawing on experience from routine epidemic control. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style statement of the policy priorities for social security after the 18th Party Congress.

Gathering great strength through unity: setting the banner and direction for united front work 以团结汇聚伟力为统战举旗定向 Liu Jiaqiang Writing in 2022, a hundred years after the Communist Party first formally put forward a united front policy, Liu Jiaqiang offers a study-and-implementation reading of Xi Jinping's speech at the Central United Front Work Conference. Liu presents the speech as a programmatic document that gives fundamental guidance for strengthening the patriotic united front in the new era. The article is a commentary by a senior figure from one of China's non-communist parties. The piece is organised in five sections. They cover the importance of developing the patriotic united front, the guiding thought for united front work, the Party's leadership as its basic principle, the historical responsibility of unity, and the task of making multi-party cooperation more standardised and vigorous. Liu draws heavily on Xi's own formulations and on the Party's 2021 resolution on its history. Liu's central claim is that the united front is a key instrument for the Party in winning struggles and governing, and for uniting Chinese people at home and abroad behind the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Liu reports Xi's "three more important" roles: defending sovereignty, security and development interests; serving the central tasks of national development; and broadening the Party's class and mass base amid social change. The article lists the "twelve musts" that summarise Xi's important thinking on united front work and says this thinking draws on Marxist united front theory, the Party's century of practice, socialism with Chinese characteristics and traditional Chinese culture. Liu argues that Party leadership is the first political principle, pointing to the Central United Front Work Leading Group and the revised united front work regulations. Liu also stresses unity as a historical responsibility, to be pursued through the "unity–criticism–unity" tradition and by seeking common ground while respecting diversity. Liu concludes that the democratic parties should treat studying Xi's speech as a political task. Liu calls on them to uphold Party leadership, strengthen their own theoretical education and organisation, and serve the central tasks of the country, in preparation for the 20th Party Congress (2022). Liu describes the multi-party cooperation system as a new type of party system grown from Chinese soil. Read the original if you want to see how a leader of a non-communist party presents the official reading of the 2022 united front conference and the role assigned to the democratic parties.

Dare to struggle, dare to win 敢于斗争 敢于胜利 Qiu Xin This short commentary, first published in People's Daily and dated October 2022, argues that a willingness to struggle and to win is the Chinese Communist Party's invincible spiritual strength. Qiu Xin takes as a starting point Xi Jinping's call to the whole Party to heighten awareness of danger, hold to bottom-line thinking and strengthen the will and ability to struggle. The piece moves from the Party's history to the present and then to what is required of its members. It describes the Party's first century as one long history of great struggle, reviews the risks of the past ten years, and sets out why struggle will continue. Qiu argues that society advances through contradictions, so struggle is unavoidable. In the author's account, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation will not be easy, and the world is undergoing changes unseen in a century, which means more risks. The author lists achievements of the new era as results of struggle, among them the victory in poverty alleviation, the results of balancing economic development with epidemic control, and changes in ecological protection. Qiu holds that struggle will accompany the whole process of reaching the second centenary goal, and that complacency or avoiding contradictions is wrong. The author names tasks that demand struggle, including full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, high-quality development, rural revitalisation and national security. Qiu concludes that the ability to struggle is not innate. It must be built through ideological tempering, political experience, practice and professional training, so that Party members and cadres can stand firm on principle and take responsibility in a crisis. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the official press framed the theme of struggle shortly before the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Carrying forward the spirit of historical initiative to create new great undertakings 发扬历史主动精神开创新伟业 Sun Cunliang Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in October 2022, Sun Cunliang takes up Xi Jinping's repeated call, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to grasp the general trend of history and seize the historical initiative. Sun defines this as exercising human subjective initiative on the basis of historical laws, so as to analyse the trend of history scientifically and overcome obstacles. The article argues that the Party's mastery of historical initiative rests on historical materialism, has deep roots in Party tradition, and answers present needs. The piece has three parts. The first explains historical materialism as the ideological basis of the spirit of historical initiative. The second treats the Party's consistent hold on the initiative as a historical tradition and political strength. The third sets out how to walk the "new road to the examination" (the new journey towards the second centenary goal) while keeping the initiative. In Sun's account, historical laws are objective, but people are not passive before them. The Party must unite conformity with law and conformity with purpose, combining respect for objective laws with creative practice. Sun reads the Party's whole history, from its founding through new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution, reform and opening up, and the new era, as a history of seizing the initiative. Three reasons are given for continuing to do so: it is a lesson of a century of Party history, an element of strategic thinking, and a requirement for meeting major risks as national rejuvenation draws nearer. Sun contends that risks must be anticipated rather than met passively. For the new journey, Sun proposes six tasks: studying historical laws and summing up experience; strengthening historical confidence through a correct view of Party history under historical materialism; heightening awareness of opportunity, risk and bottom-line thinking while keeping strategic resolve; carrying forward the fighting spirit; and daring to undertake self-reform. Self-reform is tied to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, anti-corruption work and reliance on the people. Sun's aim is a Marxist governing party that remains in the forefront of the times and enjoys the people's support. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholarship in 2022 linked historical materialism to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Party's self-reform.

Promoting the great unity of all Chinese sons and daughters 促进中华儿女大团结 Theoretical Study Group of the Party Leadership Group of the Central Institute of Socialism Published in the People's Daily in 2022, this commentary by the Party leadership group's theoretical study group at the Central Institute of Socialism takes up Xi Jinping's statement that promoting the great unity of all Chinese sons and daughters is the historical responsibility of the patriotic united front in the new era. The authors argue that unity guarantees the Chinese people's ability to overcome risks and challenges, and that the united front must keep consolidating unity among all ethnic groups, all the people and all Chinese at home and abroad in order to support the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has four parts. It first traces the united front from the Second Party Congress of 1922 through the revolutionary periods, the founding of the People's Republic, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the new era. It then reviews achievements in united front work since the 18th Party Congress (2012), grouped as theoretical, institutional and practical results. The final and longest part sets out five tasks for the Central Institute of Socialism, which the authors describe as a higher political college of a united front character. The authors argue that unity is the essence and permanent theme of the united front, which "arose from unity and prospers through unity". In their account the new-era front is the Party's broadest alliance and has been embedded in the system of national governance. They credit Xi Jinping's important thinking on united front work as theory, new regulations and leading groups as institutions, and results in multiparty cooperation, ethnic work, religious work, non-public-sector figures and outreach to Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan and overseas Chinese as practice. The five tasks they list are upholding Party leadership as the "centre of the circle", teaching the Party's innovative theory, anchoring unity in the goal of national rejuvenation, promoting patriotism, and strengthening cultural identity. The authors conclude that the Institute should train united front personnel and build a shared ideological and political foundation. This means bringing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era "into textbooks, classrooms and minds", and fostering the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds among students. It also means promoting Chinese modernization, patriotic education and the overseas spread of Chinese culture. Read the original if you want a concise official statement of how the united front's history, achievements and training tasks are presented in 2022 for a Party-school audience.

The Communist Party of Cuba and the Communist Party of China amid changes unseen in a century An interview with Balaguer Cabrera, a founder of the Communist Party of Cuba 百年未有之大变局下的古巴共产党与中国共产党 José Ramón Balaguer Cabrera Lou Yu This is an interview by Lou Yu, a reporter for World Socialism Studies, with José Ramón Balaguer Cabrera, born in 1932, a founder of the Communist Party of Cuba and a Central Committee member since 1975. He has also served as head of the Party's International Relations Department, Cuban health minister and ambassador to the Soviet Union. Asked about relations between the two parties and about the Communist Party of China (CPC), Balaguer presents them as a model of friendship between Marxist parties and praises the CPC's leadership, achievements and contribution to world socialism. The interview has three parts. The first covers the history and present of Cuba–China party ties; the second the CPC's achievements and experience; the third the CPC's contribution to Marxism and world socialism, including the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Balaguer speaks of the world being in a period of 'changes unseen in a century'. On bilateral ties, Balaguer traces mutual trust to the first Chinese labourers arriving in Havana in 1847 and to Chinese participation in Cuba's independence war. He recalls Fidel Castro's 1960 decision to recognise the People's Republic and later gestures, including Jiang Zemin's 1993 visit during Cuba's 'Special Period'. On the CPC, he holds that its main strength is its leadership: long-term planning, analysis of the principal contradiction at each stage, collective wisdom, and willingness to correct errors. He cites the end of absolute poverty in 2020 and nearly 800 million people lifted from poverty in forty years. He says the CPC's adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions and traditional culture, and its steadfastness after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, showed that socialism had not died. Balaguer concludes that China has become a world centre of Marxist research. He argues that capitalism's problems are structural and that the only solution is a transition to socialism, which he expects to prevail in the medium to long term. He describes the CPC as building a more equal, multilateral international order, opposing sanctions and Cold War thinking, and calls for reform of international organisations. Read the original if you want a Cuban Party veteran's first-hand view of Cuba–China party relations and of how he sees the CPC's role in world socialism.

Re-examining the causes of the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia 南斯拉夫联邦解体原因再探析 Ma Xipu Thirty years after the collapse of the Yugoslav federation, Ma Xipu asks why a state that built a distinctive self-managing, non-aligned socialism disappeared. The article argues that the break-up cannot be explained by one factor. In Ma's account it resulted from a flawed founding of the Yugoslav state, a series of internal failures in the economy, nationalities policy and the ruling League of Communists, and the direct and indirect intervention of outside powers. The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the state from the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (1918) through the royal dictatorship, the 1939 Croatian autonomy agreement, the 1941 invasion, the postwar six-republic federation, the declarations of independence of 1991 and the short-lived Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of Serbia and Montenegro. The second part examines internal causes under three headings. The third turns to external causes, including the fall of the Soviet bloc and Western policy. Ma holds that the first Yugoslavia was an ill-constructed, partly artificial creation of the Versailles order, with unresolved Serb–Croat tensions over centralism and federalism. Among internal causes, he cites the economic crisis of the 1980s (inflation of more than 2,000 per cent, mass bankruptcies, heavy foreign debt) and nationalities policy errors. These included recognising Bosnian Muslims as a nation, applying 'equal opportunity' and rotation mechanically, weakening Serbia by enlarging the powers of Kosovo and Vojvodina, and treating the national question as solved. He also argues that the League's 'guiding role' formula, the 'federalisation' of the Party, consensus replacing democratic centralism, the purges of Djilas and Ranković, and a rotating collective presidency removed the unifying centre. On external causes, Ma accepts that internal factors are primary but says outside powers bear heavy responsibility. He cites declassified material said to show that West Germany sought Yugoslavia's dissolution from 1976–77, and he describes the 1999 NATO action and Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence as the continuation of this aim. Ma concludes that Yugoslavia should receive fair historical judgement and respect. He also stresses that the national question is long-term and complex and that a central government must work to narrow regional gaps. He ends with hope for the revival of the region's peoples, Serbia above all. Read the original if you want a Chinese historian's integrated account of Yugoslavia's dissolution that gives particular weight to nationalism, Party organisation and Western intervention.

The political-ethical dimension of common prosperity 共同富裕的政治伦理之维 Wen Changchun Distributive justice, Wen Changchun notes, is a perennial theme of political philosophy, and the questions of what is distributed, by whom and how shape the contested ground of contemporary political ethics. This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, argues that common prosperity, described as an essential requirement of socialism and a defining feature of Chinese modernization, overcomes four ethical dilemmas that Western modernity could not resolve. The article is organised around four pairs of values: the individual and the collective, freedom and equality, fairness and efficiency, and government and market. For each pair, Wen first sets out what the author presents as the Western approach, drawing on liberalism, utilitarianism and economists such as Arthur Okun, and then contrasts it with the Chinese conception of common prosperity. Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping are cited in support. On the first two pairs, Wen contends that Western individualism and negative liberty make wealth an exclusive private good, defended through formal equality of opportunity and leading to polarisation between rich and poor. Chinese culture, in the author's account, is group-centred, so that prosperity is shared. Common prosperity permits some people and regions to get rich first, but is not egalitarianism: it seeks substantive equality, with no one left behind. On the third and fourth pairs, Wen argues that fairness must not be sacrificed to efficiency, nor efficiency to fairness, and that material wealth must go together with spiritual and cultural richness. Western societies are said to leave distribution as an afterthought to capital's logic and to favour the market over the state, whereas China combines an effective market with a capable government. Wen sets out three tiers of distribution: primary distribution by the market, redistribution by the state through taxes, social security and transfers, and a third distribution through charity and voluntary giving. Wen concludes that China has entered an era of gradually realising common prosperity for all the people, and that this conception of prosperity has produced a Chinese modernization distinct from the Western one. In the author's view, it effectively overcomes and dissolves the political-ethical predicaments of Western modernity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary in 2022 framed common prosperity as a normative alternative to Western political philosophy.

The contemporary value of whole-process people's democracy 全过程人民民主的时代价值 Zhou Meilei This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 15 June 2022, asks what whole-process people's democracy contributes in the present era. Zhou argues that it takes the people's position as masters of the country as the essence of democracy, grows out of China's own history and conditions, and at the same time expresses a democratic aspiration shared by all humanity. In Zhou's account it also enriches the forms of human political civilization. The article has three parts. The first traces the roots of this democracy in modern Chinese history, in the Party's institutional building and in traditional culture. The second describes its practical features and the sense of gain it gives ordinary people, set against Western electoral democracy. The third presents its contribution to socialist democratic theory and to other countries, particularly late-developing ones. Zhou's central claim is that this democracy is more complete than Western models. Western systems, in the author's reading, give citizens the vote but leave policy to interest groups and lobbyists, so that the people are 'awake' only at elections. Whole-process people's democracy is instead described as covering the whole chain (election, consultation, decision-making, management and supervision), all areas of life, and all levels from centre to grassroots. Zhou says this joins procedural and substantive democracy, and direct and indirect democracy, and rests on public ownership as the basis of the economy. As evidence the article cites survey figures on satisfaction with the Chinese government and on views of US democracy, and lists channels such as hearings, deputies' liaison offices and online participation. Zhou concludes that democratic development should follow a country's own characteristics and reality, which the author calls a basic lesson of China's experience. The article claims that this approach has raised governance capacity, produced economic and social stability, and given other developing countries confidence in finding their own paths, offering 'Chinese wisdom' to world political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official case for whole-process people's democracy was framed for a general readership in 2022.

Promoting win-win development through exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations 在文明交流互鉴中推动共赢发展 Thierry Meynard Thierry Meynard, a French sinologist and professor of philosophy at Sun Yat-sen University, offers a personal commentary (originally published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2022) on how cultures can learn from one another. Drawing on his years of living and teaching in China, he argues that exchange among civilizations should be open, plural and mutually beneficial, leading to what he calls win-win development. The piece begins with Meynard's impressions of progress since reform and opening up, especially in education, and notes that he joined Sun Yat-sen University in 2006 after doctoral study at Peking University in the 1990s. He then sets out three principles for his academic work, drawing on history, his teaching and his reading of the philosopher Liang Shuming. It closes with remarks on the pandemic and China's growing international educational influence. Meynard's three principles are: understand Chinese cultural traditions deeply and avoid applying Western values directly to China; encourage interaction between teacher and student; and avoid a simple opposition between Western and Chinese thought. Following Liang Shuming, he favours a triangular structure that includes Indian Buddhism, and says that dialogue should extend to the Arab world, Africa and Latin America. He cites early Jesuit-era exchange, such as Chinese examinations influencing Europe and the Xu Guangqi–Matteo Ricci translation of Euclid, as cases where both sides benefited. He observes that foreign philosophy in China remains mostly European and American, and links the ideal of great harmony (datong) to respect for difference. Meynard concludes that China should be both open to other cultures and distinctive in its own, and that Chinese culture is both national and global. He cites the numbers of Confucius Institutes and international students as signs of rising influence, and expresses his belief that China can open a model path for exchange and mutual learning among diverse civilizations. Read the original if you want a foreign scholar's personal, broadly favourable view of China's educational and cultural exchange, framed through Liang Shuming and Sino-Western intellectual history.

The international order from the perspective of the philosophy of history On Great-Power Games and the Future World 历史哲学视域中的国际格局 Yang Haifeng This is a book review, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2022. Yang Haifeng reviews Han Zhen's Great-Power Games and the Future World: International Relations from the Perspective of the Philosophy of History (Central Party School Press, 2022). Yang argues that the book treats history, the present and the future as one whole, and so offers a distinctive way of understanding today's global order and the place of socialism with Chinese characteristics within it. Yang credits it with academic and practical value for grasping current upheavals. Yang first sets out why a country's development now depends on the global order, since the world has moved from a trend of world history in Marx's day, through the imperialist era and late-twentieth-century globalization, to close interdependence. The review lists the book's eight chapters and concluding remarks. They run from the new development pattern and the North–South and East–West divides, through capitalism versus socialism and geopolitics, to China–US rivalry, future trends and the humanistic basis of a community with a shared future for mankind. Yang identifies three strengths. First, the book uses a large-scale historical outlook rooted in Hegel's and Marx's philosophy of history. It stresses that geopolitics shifts with changes in economic, political and military strength, and it treats culture as the basis of international relations. Second, it applies contradiction analysis. It traces the internal contradictions of states, for example the economic, political, identity and cultural crises Han attributes to the United States, and it identifies the principal contradictions among powers. In Yang's account, Han reads China–US rivalry as a result of US efforts to keep its post-1991 superpower status against a rising China. Third, Yang presents a community with a shared future for mankind as a solution that moves beyond the contradictions of power balances. In Yang's reading, it develops Marx's idea of an association of free individuals and also draws on Chinese ideas such as harmony and the mean. Yang concludes that the book takes a pragmatic line. It asks readers to recognise the continuing capacities of advanced capitalist countries as well as their problems, and to weigh these against China's own features and strengths when deciding strategy and pace. This, Yang says, strengthens historical confidence and initiative, and becoming a conscious historical subject is both the core theme of the philosophy of history and the self-understanding China should seek in the global order. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist assessment of a recent Party School work on geopolitics, China–US relations and the philosophical grounding of the community with a shared future for mankind.

Engels's dialectics in the perspective of the critique of political economy 政治经济学批判视域中的恩格斯辩证法 Zhou Dan Zhou Dan takes up a long-running claim in Western and Second International scholarship (Bernstein, Schmidt, Lukács's History and Class Consciousness, and 'Marxologists' such as Lichtheim and Levine) that Engels's dialectics is confined to nature and diverges from Marx's social-historical dialectics. Zhou argues that this misreads Engels. Seen through the critique of political economy, Engels's dialectics has a clear social-historical line and is fundamentally consistent with Marx's, to which it made distinct contributions. The article proceeds in three stages. It first examines Engels's early philosophical, social and economic writings, from the Schelling essays to the Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, The Holy Family and The German Ideology. It then turns to his reviews of Marx's A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and Capital, Volume 1, and his letters on Capital. Finally it considers the political-economy sections of Anti-Dühring. Zhou makes three main moves. First, Engels moved from the Young Hegelian primacy of reason to grounding dialectics in 'real experience', through his studies of English society. Zhou holds that this approach preceded Marx's and helped fix the methodological basis of historical materialism. Second, in his reviews Engels presented Marx's dialectic as the 'only correct form of intellectual development', resting on a new materialism and on the unity of logic and history. Zhou says Engels saw it as a tool for penetrating the reification of social relations under capitalism. Third, in Anti-Dühring Engels unified method and object: he derived general laws from historically specific ones and traced the interaction of production, exchange and distribution. He also defended the 'negation of the negation' behind Marx's re-establishment of individual property against Dühring's charge of incoherence. Zhou concludes that Engels's dialectics extends well beyond nature. His stress on real experience, his reading of Marx's dialectic and his grasp of its modern, critical character show a basic agreement with Marx on foundation, form and practical aim. They also show a clear understanding of how Marx's dialectic differs from Hegel's. In Zhou's view this answers attempts to diminish Engels or to set him against Marx. Read the original if you want a close, text-based Chinese defence of Engels's place in Marxist dialectics, built on his political-economy writings rather than the Dialectics of Nature.

The value content of China's governance and its contribution to the world 中国之治的价值蕴涵与世界贡献 Zhang Shuhua Zhang Shuhua asks what the political development of the People's Republic over more than seven decades, which the author labels "China's governance" (Zhongguo zhi zhi), offers to China and to the wider world. The commentary, published in 2022, argues that this experience has broken the "myth" that Western-style liberal democracy and free markets are the only successful model. In Zhang's view it has opened a new realm for scientific socialism and given other developing countries a new option. The piece is a short newspaper commentary. It places China's governance within Chinese modernization, identifies its distinctive features and the principles behind its success, draws out two theoretical products, and ends with the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind. Zhang names three keys to success: not copying other countries' political models but following a path rooted in China's own history and culture; adhering to the leadership of the Communist Party, which gives governance a stable political core; and keeping the people's principal position. Chinese politics, the author says, integrates democracy, order and efficiency, and unites Party leadership, law-based governance and the people as masters of the country. Its path is marked by stability, developmental orientation, continuity, coordination and practical effectiveness. Zhang rejects abstract and simplified debate on "democracy, freedom and human rights". The theoretical result is a "new view of democracy" and a "view of comprehensive development". Zhang presents the community with a shared future for mankind as the step from one country's comprehensive development to "common governance" worldwide, going beyond the unilateralism and "own country first" attitude of some major powers. The author calls for global governance based on consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, together with multilateralism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS scholar frames the general principles and international significance of China's political model.

The fetishistic character of time and the spiritual crisis of contemporary capitalism 时间的拜物教属性与当代资本主义精神危机 Liu Yunshan Liu asks how social time has become an object of belief under capital, and what this does to the inner life of people in contemporary capitalism. The article argues that, as capital's reach extends from material production into culture, institutions and ideology, social time acquires a fetishistic character comparable to that of the commodity and money. This fetishism, in Liu's account, is a root of capitalism's present spiritual crisis. The article has four parts. It first traces how capital and social time have combined historically, from pre-capitalist natural and religious time, through the clock-measured working day of early industrial capitalism, to the subtler regimes of today. It then sets out the fetishistic properties of time, and next turns to the production of spirit and its crisis. A short conclusion considers remedies. Liu draws on Marx's Capital, Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger and Hartmut Rosa's theory of the "accelerated society". Liu contends that capital's mode of rule has shifted from coercing the body to capturing the mind. Surplus labour time is converted into mind-controlling labour time, and leisure time is filled with consumption and entertainment. Scientific-technical rationality, together with a collective morality that condemns lateness and idleness, makes people accept the time regime willingly. Time becomes ideological, interchangeable with money ("time is money") and, finally, an end in itself rather than a tool. Liu identifies two spiritual effects: Heidegger's "vulgar time" closes off the possibilities of the spirit, while acceleration brings emptiness, shallow sensory stimulation, anxiety and social atomisation. Liu concludes that Nietzsche, Heidegger, Simmel and Rosa diagnose the symptoms but look to spiritual awakening or fall into pessimism, because they overlook the mode of production. In the author's view, Marx's diagnosis points to practice: critical reflection that exposes the logic of capital and raises economic rationality to political rationality. Only the sublation of capital's logic can open the genuinely free time of socialism and communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist reading of time, acceleration and alienation that engages Heidegger, Rosa and Western critical theory.

The roots and impact of inequality in contemporary capitalism 当代资本主义不平等问题的根源及其影响 Lin Deshan Inequality has accompanied capitalism throughout its history, but Lin Deshan argues that since the 1980s growing inequality and polarisation have become a defining feature of the contemporary system. The article asks what produced this trend in developed capitalist countries and what it has done to them. Lin's answer is that technological and global change played a part, but that the decisive factor was state policy under the neoliberal agenda, which spread under the banner of adapting to globalisation. The article has three parts. It first documents the widening of income and wealth inequality, drawing on Thomas Piketty, the OECD and the IMF. It covers the United States, Europe and Japan, with special attention to the US, and to the effects of the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. It then sorts explanations into globalisation and technology, government policy, and the decline of organised labour, adding education, discrimination and the structure of household wealth. A final part discusses social and political consequences. Lin treats globalisation and technology as real but limited causes. Piketty's finding that the return on capital exceeds economic growth explains the pull of the top, while the "skill premium" operates mainly among wage earners and cannot explain the gap between the very top and the majority. The main weight falls on policy, following Joseph Stiglitz, who calls inequality largely a product of policy and politics. Lin points to "market-friendly" policy and a race to the bottom, falling top marginal tax rates, a tax burden shifted onto wages, the retrenchment of welfare states and the shrinking of public wealth. Lin also points to the squeezing of the middle class and the weakening of unions and collective bargaining. Lin argues that the promised trickle-down effect has failed and that the Kuznets curve is only partly supported by the evidence. On consequences, Lin reports three widely shared findings. Inequality undermines equality of opportunity, a core Western value, and erodes the American Dream. It also depresses growth and raises the risk of crises, and it feeds political polarisation and damages democracy. Lin concludes that inequality has led people to a new understanding of capitalism's essential characteristics, and that neoliberal politics shaped the process more than any other force. Read the original if you want a data-rich survey of Western research on inequality, with an assessment of its causes from a Chinese Marxist-studies perspective.

Contemporary capitalist concepts of democracy and their critique 当代资本主义民主理念及其批判 Lei Xiaohuan Lei Xiaohuan asks how two recent concepts in capitalist democratic theory, digital democracy and supranational democracy, arose, what they amount to, and how Marxists should assess them. The article argues that both remain within bourgeois thought and, in essence, serve the interests of the bourgeoisie. Lei concludes that contemporary capitalist democracy is limited and false, and is in what the author calls vertical decline. The article begins with the historical background: the spread of the internet from the late twentieth century and the deepening of economic globalization, which led Western scholars to look for alternatives to representative democracy. It then reviews digital democracy (Kenneth L. Hacker, Jeanette Hofmann, digital parties such as Podemos and the British Labour Party's 2016 manifesto) and supranational democracy, covering James Bohman on transnational democracy and John Dryzek and Christopher Chase-Dunn on global democracy. Later sections give a general assessment of capitalist democracy and examine its recent trends. Lei makes three main moves. First, digital democracy cannot deliver broad deliberation under capitalism. It reduces democracy to voting, is hampered by the digital divide, and is exposed to monopoly control by technology firms, disinformation and algorithmic manipulation. Second, supranational democracy undermines the authority of sovereign states, masks the class nature of democracy and has little real practice. Lei cites Robert Keohane and the European Union's 'democratic deficit', and argues that bodies such as the IMF and World Bank serve transnational capital. Third, drawing on Lenin, Marx and Engels, Nancy Fraser, Wolfgang Streeck and Ralph Miliband, Lei argues that capitalist democracy has been limited from its origins, that its expansion resulted from popular struggle, and that its basis in private ownership means it ultimately consolidates bourgeois rule. As evidence of decline, Lei cites the loss of trust after the 2008 financial crisis, the fall in US trust in government from 77% in 1958 to 19% in 2015, the Occupy Wall Street and Yellow Vest protests, and the US handling of COVID-19. The article concludes that capitalist democracy is not identical with democracy, and that elites use limited liberalization to hold democratization at bay. Lei says this analysis is meant to strengthen confidence in whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Western democratic theory, with a survey of the Western literature on digital and global democracy.")

Imperialism's democracy and human rights, and the democracy and human rights of imperialism 民主和人权的帝国主义与帝国主义的民主和人权 Radhika Desai This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Canadian political economist Radhika Desai. She asks why Western states, above all the United States under Joe Biden, make democracy and human rights the centrepiece of their confrontation with China. Her thesis is that these slogans are an ideological weapon of imperialism: the Western powers, she argues, are themselves major violators of democracy and human rights, and the gap between their rhetoric and their practice is widening. The article first sets out how imperial justifications have shifted from the racism of the nineteenth century, to promises of development, to the present stress on rights and democracy. It then turns to the decline of liberal democracy in the United States, using Abraham Lincoln's formula of government of, by and for the people. A section follows on the Canadian Marxist C. B. Macpherson, then an assessment of Biden's December 2021 virtual Summit for Democracy. The last section takes up the graves found at Canadian Indigenous residential schools in 2021. Desai's central move is to trace Western democratic decay to neoliberalism and financialisation, which she says ended the postwar compromise between workers and capital. On her account, US politics is now plutocratic: Congress is rich, campaign finance decides elections, and both parties share a neoliberal consensus. She draws on Macpherson to argue that liberal democracy was designed to protect property, and that socialist and developing countries have a real historical claim to the name of democracy. She presents China's whole-process people's democracy as a serious alternative and sees Chinese development as bearing out Macpherson's prediction. She calls the Xinjiang genocide charge baseless and the summit's guest list inconsistent, and she contrasts the charge with Canada's treatment of Indigenous peoples, which she describes as genocide. Desai concludes that Western powers cannot hide the fact that they are leading violators of the rights they invoke, and that Canada would have to stop being an extractive settler-capitalist state for Indigenous rights to be restored. She suggests this may require a transformation akin to socialism. Democracy and human rights, in her closing formulation, serve capitalism's class oppression and imperial strategy. Read the original if you want a Marxist critique of Western democracy discourse, as it is translated for a Chinese academic readership, with its use of Macpherson and the Canadian Indigenous case.

Democracy at home and tyranny abroad 对内的民主与对外的暴政 Patrick Tourret This is a Chinese translation of an essay by Patrick Tourret, identified as a former editor-in-chief of the French journal International Communication. Writing against the background of a Western campaign against China in the name of democracy and human rights, Tourret argues that Western democracy has always had two faces: consensual rules among insiders and exclusion, coercion and violence towards outsiders. In his account, the United States and its allies act as both plaintiff and judge in an economic, commercial and ideological conflict. The essay moves through seven short sections. It defines democracy as the power of the people and the majority, then considers where real power lies in Western states and how foreign intervention works. It traces the inside/outside logic from Greece, Rome, Venice, the Netherlands and Britain to colonial empires and capitalism, uses the American Civil War as a test case, and discusses the limits and ideals of democratic forms. It ends with the struggle for democracy, socialism and popular well-being. Tourret holds that real power lies not in universal suffrage or parliaments but in the economic and social power of a class or class alliance, which will negotiate everything except its own supremacy. When that power feels threatened, coups and armed intervention follow. Abroad, he argues, interventions in the name of democracy (he cites Spain in 1936, Chile in 1973, Venezuela, Bolivia, Iraq, Libya and Syria) destroy popular sovereignty, and the targets are punished for disobedience rather than for being dictatorships. He reads the Civil War as a conflict over union and secession in which abolition came only through the course of the war, and he stresses that Western democratic forms were won by popular struggle, then discredited by being imposed by force. Tourret concludes that the main contradiction today is between a dominant minority imposing its system and the dominated majority asserting popular and national sovereignty. He cites Xi Jinping's 2013 remarks on the long, winding road to socialism's victory, and a joint article by the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to the US. He calls for a harmonious world free of domination, in which different forms of democracy can flourish. Read the original if you want a French left-wing critique of Western democracy and intervention, as selected for a Chinese Marxist journal in 2022.

An assessment of 30 years of capitalism in Ukraine 乌克兰资本主义化30年评析 Chen Airu Writing after the outbreak of the Russia–Ukraine conflict in 2022, Chen asks why Ukraine, which abandoned socialism on independence in 1991 expecting to become a prosperous, free and democratic developed country, ended up as, in the author's words, the poorest country in Europe. The article's thesis is that three decades of capitalization produced dependent economic decline, politics steered by the West through repeated "colour revolutions", and the neglect of popular opinion, to the benefit of oligarchs. Chen presents the case as a warning to other countries to follow an independent development path suited to national conditions. The article is organised in three sections. The first assesses Ukraine's economy, using GDP series, poverty rates, population loss and emigration figures. The second traces the colour revolutions from the 1948 Italian election through the events of 1989–91 in the Soviet bloc to Ukraine's 2004 "Orange Revolution" and the 2014 "Revolution of Dignity". The third draws on Ukrainian opinion surveys about capitalism, privatization, the role of the state and fairness. Chen's central claim is that Ukraine took the road of "dependent capitalism", which the author links to Immanuel Wallerstein's "peripheral capitalism" in The Modern World-System. The article reports that GDP never regained its 1991 level, that 60 per cent of Ukrainians lived below the poverty line in 2020, that the population fell from 52 million to under 34 million, and that the 50 richest families controlled about 85 per cent of GDP in 2013. Chen contends that the United States, drawing on declassified material and the CIA's methods, designed the colour revolutions, which put compradors and far-right forces in power. In Chen's reading, their ethnically divisive policies led to secession in Crimea and the Donbas, civil war and the present conflict. Survey data are cited to show majorities opposing capitalism, large-scale privatization and land privatization, favouring a mixed economy, and judging the economic system to serve only the rich (71.3 per cent). Chen concludes that the thirty years were ones of real gain for oligarchs and big capital, and of lost prosperity, security and hope for most Ukrainians. A state captured by oligarchs, the author argues, cannot make national or popular interests its core concern, and extreme policies of either right or left harm development. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar frames Ukraine's post-Soviet trajectory, with the survey data and economic figures it cites, in the context of the 2022 conflict.

The "value-critique group" in the context of contemporary German research on Capital 当代德国《资本论》研究语境中的“价值批判小组” Sun Liang Sun Liang introduces the German "value-critique group" (Wertkritik, or Krisis group), a current of Capital interpretation far less known than the New Marx Reading and almost unknown in China. The article asks what the group's central theme is and what principles organise it. Sun's answer is that its core is a critique of "value-immanence", the treatment of value and labour as fixed, natural categories, and that this leads it to demand the abolition of labour itself. Sun judges the approach partly valid but ultimately flawed. The article first explains why the group is neglected: it resists classification, its key figures (Robert Kurz, Ernst Lohoff, Roswitha Scholz, Norbert Trenkle) are mostly non-academic, and its work was long untranslated. It then traces the group's origins to the journal Krisis (Nuremberg, 1986) and the later Exit and Streifzüge, and to influences including Lukács, Adorno, Sohn-Rethel, Luxemburg, Grossman, Mattick and Rubin. The body has three parts: the critique of earlier breakdown theories, the critique of labour ontology, and the group's rejection of class struggle and its vision of emancipation in the age of fictitious capital. Sun reports that Kurz faults Luxemburg for staying within circulation and Grossman for a mathematical, quantitative model of falling profit rates. For Kurz both leave the value relation itself intact. Trenkle then argues that labour is not an anthropological constant but a historically specific form of coercive activity, so abolishing abstract labour requires abolishing labour as such. Kurz ties this to automation in the "third industrial revolution", where expelling living labour undermines the production of value. Sun adds that the group sees labour and capital as two sides of one value-form, so class discourse is ineffective, especially as fictitious capital becomes the real driver of accumulation. The group's answer is "against labour", a society whose material production no longer depends on capital accumulation. Sun credits the group with reminding readers that value is historical and with tracing value back to labour, which Sun sees as more perceptive than other left critiques. Sun argues, however, that it never explains why labour appears as value and ignores the capitalist relations of production built on the division of labour and private property. By dropping the internal contradiction between labour and capital, the group is said to reach an "aesthetic illusion" in calling for the abolition of labour. Sun holds that this contradiction must be understood within the movement of social history, via Marx's dual character of labour. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Wertkritik, its sources and its dispute with traditional crisis theory and class analysis.

Critical theory today Reflections on its legacy and recent developments 今日批判理论 Gerard Delanty Neal Harris This is a Chinese translation of a handbook chapter by Gerard Delanty and Neal Harris on the state of critical theory. The authors restrict the term to the Frankfurt School and its heirs, which they call, in effect, a euphemism for Marxist-influenced social research. They argue that the tradition keeps its coherence across generations through its roots in German idealism, especially Left Hegelianism. They also hold that it now faces challenges that require serious attention. The chapter has three parts. The first traces four or five generations: Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, Benjamin and Fromm; then Habermas; Axel Honneth's theory of recognition; and a possible fourth generation around Rainer Forst, alongside Nancy Fraser, Amy Allen, Rahel Jaeggi and Andrew Feenberg. The second part sets out shared themes: a Hegelian understanding of reason, immanent transcendence, the link between philosophy and social research, the diagnosis of social pathologies, and the exposure of false consciousness. The third part turns to present-day challenges. The authors read the tradition as a movement from Adorno and Horkheimer's negative critique of modernity, which they say ended in an impasse, to Habermas's communicative reason and then to Honneth's recognition theory. Habermas is credited with breaking the deadlock, but the authors suggest his work looks dated in the age of digital platforms and has lost the earlier Marx–Weber analysis. Honneth's later work, especially Freedom's Right, is said to move towards liberal ideal theory. Citing Michael J. Thompson and Stathis Kouvelakis, they argue that this move abandons the Frankfurt School's Marxist–Weberian heritage. They name three challenges: Eurocentrism and the neglect of colonialism, which Allen and Coulthard press; a loss of coherence as Foucault, Bourdieu, Boltanski and decolonial thought are absorbed; and a dilution of social research into philosophy. The authors conclude that the Frankfurt School's concepts remain useful for contemporary social research but must engage critics, including decolonial ones. They propose a mild self-correction of Left Hegelianism to keep theoretical coherence, and a return to the original sociological and philosophical programme. They warn that critical theorists may split into smaller, competing camps. Even so, they see room for strong interdisciplinary work on the basis of its core concepts and methodology. Read the original if you want a compact overview of Frankfurt School generations and the debates over recognition, decolonial critique and coherence, as presented in a Western handbook and translated for a Chinese readership.

The anti-sorcerer campaign in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region and the transformation of rural society 陕甘宁边区反巫神运动与乡村社会改造 Wu Chengwang Wu Chengwang asks how the Chinese Communist Party, after the outbreak of the War of Resistance against Japan, used the campaign against 'sorcerers' (wushen) in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region to reshape rural society. The article argues that the sorcerers were a 'parasite' on village life and an obstacle to social mobilisation. In Wu's account, the campaign carried revolutionary ideology down to the 'nerve endings' of village governance and into ordinary people's mentality, and so extended Party power at the grassroots. Drawing mainly on reports in the Party newspaper Liberation Daily (Jiefang ribao), Wu traces the campaign's origins, methods and results in three sections. The article focuses on the narrow sense of wushen: healers who claimed to drive out ghosts and cure illness in order to make money. It notes that the Border Region counted more than 2,000 of them, and that most of the press coverage appeared between February and October 1944. Wu explains popular belief in sorcerers by poverty and famine, long disorder under warlords and bandits, illiteracy (cited as 95–99 per cent) and the lack of doctors and medicine. Wu adds that sorcerers drained villagers' wealth, sometimes colluded with bandits and enemy agents, and spread rumours against modern medicine. On this basis the article calls them incompatible with the New Democratic culture described by Mao Zedong. The campaign had three strands: science education and Marxist study campaigns; an information space built from newspapers, reading groups, blackboard newspapers and village acquaintance networks, since most villagers could not read; and a 'medical revolution' of free treatment, effective care and cooperation between Chinese and Western medicine. Wu concludes that the campaign removed the spiritual element from healing and daily life, and brought villages into the government's mobilisation system. It also fostered new customs, such as yangge plays on the theme, and built popular identification with the Party and enthusiasm for production and war. Wu holds that the experience, including Party leadership, propaganda and education, and respect for the masses' wishes, informed later work on marginal social groups and still has present-day value. Read the original if you study Yan'an-era rural mobilisation, Party–peasant relations, or the Party's campaigns against superstition and for public health.

Shifts in human civilization and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind 人类文明变局与“人类命运共同体”理念 Liu Liangjian Liu Liangjian takes up the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which the author presents as an important contribution China has made in recent years. Liu argues that it is also a generative concept that could become a breakthrough point for innovation in Chinese philosophical discourse. The question "where is the world heading?" is described as both a practical issue of global governance and one of the most basic philosophical questions of the age. The short commentary, originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, begins with a sketch of world civilizations. It runs from the rough balance among Europe, the Middle East, India and China before the mid-nineteenth century to Western dominance afterwards, and then to the May Fourth Movement of 1919. It then turns to the philosophical foundations of the concept and to its implications for world political order. Liu holds that the world is entering a new "cultural germination period" in which different civilizations interact on Chinese soil. Drawing on Feng Qi's formulation of China's basic modern question, Liu reframes the contemporary question as where Chinese and human civilization are heading amid the "compression of time and space". This requires a "contemporary" view of time and history distinct from ancient and modern ones. Liu suggests "global-locality" as a political concept for a world moving beyond nation-states, with a world government as centre that still accommodates plurality. The idea is also tied to the ancient ideal of great harmony (datong), to a Marxist view of world history and to traditional Chinese emphasis on harmony. Liu concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind should be built up in theory on a philosophy of history grounded in a rich concept of "contemporaneity". Because it includes nature and "heaven", it aims to let people realise their nature within a community of heaven and humanity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese philosopher links this official concept to Feng Qi, Confucian ideas and world-historical theory.

Distinctive features of China's five thousand years of civilisation 中华五千年文明的特质 Liu Qingzhu This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what marks out Chinese civilisation over five thousand years. Liu Qingzhu argues that it is distinguished by continuity without rupture and by an inclusiveness summed up in the phrase "yourong nai da" (tolerance makes greatness). Liu starts from Engels's remark that the state is a summary of civilised society, and from Yi Jianping's etymological claim that "civilisation is the state". The author treats the state's material carriers as its people, its territory and the people's shared idea of the state. The text first applies an archaeological reading of non-rupture to each of the three, then turns to inclusiveness, internal and external. On continuity, Liu cites genetic studies showing that most people in China today are genetically close to populations of the middle Yellow River valley five thousand years ago. Liu adds that 99 per cent of surnames derive from the Yan-Huang lineage system. The author traces a stable territory from the Miaodigou culture to the Qin-Han dominions. Shared identity is shown in the idea of "zhong" (centrality) and "zhonghe" (harmony): capitals, Liu says, were sited at the "centre" from the Xishuipo tomb onward, expressing fairness towards all quarters. On inclusiveness, Liu points to non-Han dynasties such as the Northern Wei, Liao, Jin, Yuan and Qing, which are regarded as part of Chinese civilisation, and contrasts the Silk Road with the colonialism of the Age of Discovery. Liu concludes that these features, continuous people, land and identity together with an inclusive outlook, explain the vitality of Chinese civilisation. The Silk Road, in the author's account, shows friendship and cooperation rather than colonial expansion. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a leading Chinese archaeologist presents the continuity of Chinese civilisation in official-style terms.

Cultural identity and Chinese civilization amid great changes in the world 文化认同与世界大变局中的中国文明 Li Yuji Li Yuji takes up the claim, made by some Western scholars such as Lucian W. Pye, that China is "a civilization pretending to be a state". Li reads this as showing both a vague Western grasp of how civilization, state and nation relate in ancient China and the real uniqueness of that relationship. The article, a short newspaper commentary, argues that Chinese civilization is distinctive in combining national, state and cultural identity in a "trinity", and that this helps China in today's globalization. The piece begins with the origins of Chinese civilization, then looks at the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties and the Spring and Autumn period. It turns to Confucian thought as an expression of this trinity. It ends with the contemporary era of modernization and globalization. Li traces the trinity to China's particular agricultural environment and to a prehistoric faith centred on ancestor deities. In Li's account, this faith was this-worldly and tied to kinship and territory, and it blocked the rise of a transcendent universal god. Cultural identity therefore became the basis of national and state identity, as shown by the slogan "revere the king, expel the barbarians" and by the pairing of saving the nation and saving the state in modern times. Li credits Confucianism with fusing these elements, and lists openness, compatibility and the state's duty to protect its people as traits that let Chinese civilization survive repeated conflicts and divisions. Li concludes that these traits help China avoid the cultural contradictions and civilizational conflicts that Li says trap some non-Western countries torn between modernization and localization. Li lists five advantages, including openness, ethnic and religious compatibility, a practical work ethic, strong state backing, and vitality in building a "new form of human civilization". Li holds that China is following a path suited to its own traditions and circumstances. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars use the civilization-state idea to argue for the continuity of Chinese culture.

Grasping the materialist conception of history through the dual character of labour 从劳动的双重属性把握唯物史观 Li Jili How should labour be understood, and what place does it hold in the materialist conception of history? Li Jili, in a newspaper article from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2022), argues that the question decides the future of historical materialism. The article contends that Marx's concept of labour has a natural and a social aspect, and that this dual character is the key to the materialist conception of history as a whole, not only to political economy. The article begins with two rival misreadings. Li says Jürgen Habermas, a figure of Western Marxism, reduces Marx's labour to Weberian purposive-instrumental action and so proposes to reconstruct historical materialism. Moishe Postone, in Li's account, treats labour as a form peculiar to capitalism and so cuts Marx's thought in two. Li then moves from labour as a philosophical concept, through the concepts of productive forces and relations of production, to the objective laws of social development, and finally to Capital. Li first argues that Marx's labour is a philosophical concept, taken from Hegel's insight into labour and then freed of its idealism. Labour in this sense is the real social labour of a whole society, not that of an isolated individual. It therefore contains both the object-relation between people and nature and the social relations among people. Second, Li holds that the productive forces come from labour's natural side and the relations of production from its social side. Productive forces and relations of production are not two independent things that interact. They are two aspects of material production. Li maintains that productive forces determine relations of production by way of objectified labour, in which "dead labour" becomes the material carrier of objectified social relations. Third, Li says the same route explains why the products of human activity can harden into an objective material force that escapes human control. This force has its own logic, which is why historical laws can count as objective laws unlike natural ones. Li concludes that Marx's remark in Capital that the dual character of labour is "the pivot" for understanding political economy has long been read too narrowly. In Li's view the dual character is equally the pivot for understanding the materialist conception of history. If it is treated only as a feature of capitalism, Li warns, historical materialism is denied universal validity, and it cannot then guide socialist practice. Read the original if you want a short, philosophically oriented Chinese reply to Habermas and Postone on labour and historical materialism.

Marx's concept of cooperation and its contemporary significance 马克思的协作概念及其当代意义 Pan Shenyang Pan Shenyang asks what Marx's concept of cooperation (Kooperation) contributes to his critique of capitalism and to his vision of socialism. The short commentary argues that cooperation is the footing of Marx's critique and, in later work, the basis of his account of a practical path towards communism. The article draws on Capital and its manuscripts, Engels's letter to Bebel, and Marx's engagement in the 1860s with Lassalleanism, the International Workingmen's Association, Owen and the Chartist Ernest Jones. It first sets out four features of cooperation, then turns to its role in the critique of capitalism, and finally to cooperative production under socialism. Pan holds that under capitalism the social productive power created by cooperation is appropriated without payment and appears as the productive power of capital. Two further critiques follow: capitalist management presents itself as neutral while concealing exploitation, and workers within cooperative labour are reified into mere parts. Marx and Jones, Pan says, criticised isolated, competing cooperatives such as Rochdale while valuing features of others, and Marx called cooperatives "possible" communism. Marx gave no detailed blueprint but two principles: proletarian dictatorship as the political precondition, and drawing on new social elements generated within capitalism, such as the factory and credit systems. Pan concludes that Marx's cooperative conception stresses both subjective self-emancipation and objective conditions, so it avoids being either utopian or blindly activist. The piece offers little explicit discussion of present-day application beyond this. Read the original if you want a compact guide to how Marx's notion of cooperation links his critique of capitalism to the cooperative form.

Continuously advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times 不断推进马克思主义中国化时代化 Wang Haiwen Wang Wei Published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the study session for provincial and ministerial-level leading cadres on implementing the sixth plenary session of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Wang and Wang aim to explain why Marxism "works", why it works specifically through being adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and how that adaptation should continue. Their answer is that Marxism's scientific and practical character requires constant adaptation, which they say the Party's history confirms. The article follows the three questions in three sections. The first treats the nature and mission of Marxism, drawing on Xi's 2018 speech marking Marx's 200th birthday. The second argues that Marxism has to be adapted to China, citing Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong and then surveying the Party's theoretical stages from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The third sets out requirements for the new era. In the authors' account, Marxism works because it reveals the laws of social development, is the first system of thought for the people's own liberation, and is an open theory that develops with the times. They hold that since Marxism supplies only general principles, applying them in a country means examining national particularities, and that adapting Marxism to China combines upholding it with developing it. On this reading, the Party's history is one of successive adaptations: Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought. The authors say this success has shifted the contest between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour. For the new era, the authors call for continuing the Two Integrations, combining Marxist principles with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture, so that China makes original contributions to adapting Marxism to the times. They also call for a global outlook, citing the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, and say that answering questions such as how to rebuild the post-pandemic world requires effort from Marxists worldwide. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the logic and history of adapting Marxism to China.

The value content of China's governance and its contribution to the world 中国之治的价值蕴涵与世界贡献 Zhang Shuhua Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, Zhang Shuhua asks what is distinctive and universally meaningful in what he calls "China's governance" (zhongguo zhi zhi), the political development that accompanies Chinese modernization. The author argues that it contains elements specific to China but also general principles that other countries can compare and learn from. The short commentary begins with the leap from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong" over more than seven decades. It then sets out the sources of China's governance, the features of its political development path, and its two theoretical products, before turning to its international significance. Zhang names three keys to success: no copying of foreign political models, leadership by the Communist Party of China, and the principal position of the people. He lists five features of the political path under socialism with Chinese characteristics: stability, developmental character, continuity, coordination and effectiveness. The author says this path integrates democracy, order and efficiency and rejects abstract, simplified debates on "democracy, freedom and human rights". Its theoretical crystallisation, in Zhang's account, is a "new view of democracy" and a "comprehensive view of development", which treat political stability, order, performance, capacity, mobilisation and integrity as parts of political development. Zhang contends that this experience broke the "myth" that Western-style liberal democracy and free markets are the only successful model, and offers other developing countries a new option. He presents a community with a shared future for mankind as the extension of "comprehensive development" into "common governance", surpassing the unilateralism of some major powers. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS scholar frames China's political model and its claimed global relevance.

Common prosperity and the intelligent revolution Reflections starting from Marx 共同富裕与智能革命 Gao Qiqi Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2022, Gao Qiqi asks how the intelligent revolution (AI and digital technology) bears on common prosperity. Starting from Marx's critique of alienated labour and theory of surplus value, Gao argues that common prosperity cannot be realised under capitalism because of surplus-value exploitation. The article's thesis is double-edged: the intelligent revolution may deepen inequality and exploitation, yet it is also a necessary condition for common prosperity. The piece begins with the Chinese Communist Party's adoption of common prosperity as its value choice for social justice, and with its practical exploration of the concept. It then sets out the risks of the intelligent revolution, turns to its enabling potential, and ends with a proposal for "common labour". On the risks, Gao says intelligent technology may replace workers across industries, lower the weight of labour and land in production, and widen income inequality and "social exclusion". Under the dominance of financial and monopoly capital, the author argues, digital exploitation produces digital labour alienation. Algorithms turn a "digital proletariat" into an appendage of machines, shift exploitation from other-directed to self-directed, and extend it to emotions, which prompts "lying flat". On the other side, Gao holds that the sharing and digital economies support high-quality development and can erode private-ownership concepts, creating new conditions for public ownership of the means of production. Gao adds that they can also improve state precision in governance and resource allocation, and strengthen political participation and information processing. Gao concludes that common labour, built on public ownership, is the key to overcoming digital alienation. It would reunite workers with the material conditions of labour, expand use-value, and let individuals find self-fulfilment and "poetic dwelling". Its final aim is the free and all-round development of the human being, for which the intelligent revolution saves labour time. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar links Marx's alienation theory, digital labour and common prosperity.

Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization and the building of an ecological civilization 习近平生态文明思想与生态文明建设 Huan Qingzhi Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (August 2022), Huan Qingzhi argues that since the early 21st century, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), China's ecological civilization construction has become a relatively independent and complete system of discourse and theory, institutions and policy, and social practice. In Huan's account it forms part of Chinese modernization and of a "new form of human civilization". The short commentary is organised around three levels: theory, institutional policy and social practice. It then turns to the global significance of this construction, outlines three "green story" narratives, and ends by asking what stays the same and what changes for ecological civilization in the post-pandemic period. At the level of theory, Huan reads Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization as a political-philosophical justification whose core is modernization marked by harmony between humanity and nature. He describes this as a conscious union of "green" ecological sustainability and "red" socialist politics, tying ecological priority to socialist fairness and justice. At the institutional level, he cites the "eight systems" of the Overall Plan for Reforming the Ecological Civilization System and four requirements from the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). He holds that institutionalisation will be long and gradual. In practice, he points to pilot zones and indicators such as GEP accounting. He sees the Party and government leading from above, while the broad masses increasingly become the "self-conscious" main actors. Huan holds that this construction has global universality, because it answers worldwide demands to rebalance humanity and nature and would raise global environmental work as China moves from participant to contributor and leader. He concludes that its foundations and goals are unchanged, but that since the 2020 pandemic its international environment has changed. He expects the "low politics" advantage of ecological issues to fade and competition to become more visible. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic summary of how ecological civilization is framed theoretically, institutionally and globally.

Strengthen Party building as the lead and consolidate the cornerstone of epidemic prevention and control 强化党建引领 夯实疫情防控基石 Qin Jingran Guan Suye Writing in a newspaper commentary published in June 2022, Qin Jingran and Guan Suye ask how grassroots governance can be strengthened in light of China's experience with COVID-19. They argue that the most important lesson of the response has been Party-building-led reinforcement of the grassroots defence line of joint and collective prevention and control. They treat this as a marker of modernising the system and capacity of social governance. The piece focuses on the 'smallest unit' of grassroots organisation, described as the 'last kilometre' of governance and the 'last metre' of serving the public. It is organised around four measures, each tied to a function of grassroots Party organisations: leadership and linkage, a combat-ready organisational structure, personnel support, and coordination. Qin and Guan call for clear working areas, staff groupings and duties, and for villages and communities to act as self-governing bodies in early warning and emergency response. They propose a tiered structure of village or community Party organisations, neighbourhood (grid) organisations and building-level Party groups. In peacetime this structure handles publicity, information and services, and in an outbreak it is reorganised into flatter task-based groups. They also urge mobilising Party members, grid workers, volunteers, retired soldiers and enterprise staff, and setting up Party member shock teams and vanguard posts.
