The authors add that information should be shared among grid workers, medical staff and police, and that channels for residents' concerns should be kept open, drawing on the 'Fengqiao experience' and 'Tongxiang experience'. The authors conclude that grassroots Party organisations are the 'lead geese' of epidemic control, and that strengthening the smallest unit is key. They hold that the Party's political, organisational and mass-work advantages should be turned into practical results under a 'grassroots Party building+' approach. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building language was applied to community-level epidemic management in 2022.

The third industrial revolution and management change 第三次工业革命与管理变革 Wang Qin Writing in 2013, Wang Qin asks what the so-called third industrial revolution means for management and for enterprises. The commentary argues that the revolution should not be understood only as a change in technology, production organisation and lifestyle. In Wang's view its deeper content is institutional and managerial change, a transformation in how social resources are allocated. The piece first distinguishes two readings of the third industrial revolution: an energy-based view (renewables, distributed energy, hydrogen storage, new-energy vehicles) and a view centred on structural technologies (big data, artificial intelligence, robots, digital manufacturing). It then describes how big data, intelligent manufacturing, 3D printing and wireless networks are altering relations inside and between firms, and closes with two contrasts: enterprise manufacturing versus social manufacturing, and large enterprises versus platform enterprises. Wang's central claim is that the logic of management change is now the "rebalancing" of social resources. For about a century, the author says, management change followed Fayol's five functions, adding, removing or recombining them, and this logic can no longer guide firms whose boundaries are shifting. Firms must instead treat user resources as strategic, seek complementary resources from other firms, focus on newly created rather than existing resources, and push resources down through organisational layers. Wang argues that consumers become co-creators of value through "micro-manufacturing" and open, parallel innovation, and that competition will be between platforms, citing Apple's App Store as an example. Wang concludes that firms worldwide stand at a new starting line and must look for management and institutional innovation suited to the era. The author suggests that classical bureaucratic theory, scientific management and divisional organisation, drawn from the first two revolutions, face challenges to their applicability. Read the original if you want a brief 2013 Chinese management-studies view of how digital manufacturing and platforms were expected to reshape firm organisation.

The implications of building China into a country of strong civilization 中国文明强国建设的意蕴 Xin Xiangyang This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what kind of civilizational power China should become. Starting from the 19th Party Congress (2017) goal of a modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful by mid-century, Xin Xiangyang argues that a strong civilization has several defining features, and that it requires the balanced advance of five civilizations. The article moves through a series of marks of a civilizational power: a flourishing cultural sector and cultural industries, a rich and uplifting spiritual life for the people, stronger cultural communication abroad, and the modernization of the human being. It closes by discussing the coordinated development of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. Xin ties each feature to Chinese modernization and common prosperity. Western modernization, the author says, is marked by expanding materialism, so Chinese modernization must coordinate material and spiritual civilization. Common prosperity, in this reading, covers spiritual as well as material life. Xin follows Xi Jinping in treating the modernization of people as the essence of modernization. The author argues that advanced socialist spiritual civilization can resolve the "Adam Smith problem" and "Rousseau's question". Both, in Xin's view, reflect the basic contradiction of capitalist society and cannot be solved within it. Xin concludes that a civilizational power means the integrated development of all five civilizations by mid-century, not excellence in one field. The author also calls for China's own philosophy and social science, scholar-thinkers versed in Chinese, Western and Marxist thought, and wider global dissemination of Xi Jinping's ideas on governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese theorists in 2022 linked civilizational strength to Chinese modernization and spiritual common prosperity.

The materialist conception of history and the construction of civilisation 唯物史观与文明建构 Li Jingyuan Writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper (August 2022), Li Jingyuan asks what lies at the base of Deng Xiaoping Theory. Li argues that its foundation is Deng's restoration of the correct understanding of historical materialism. The piece is a short commentary, and despite its title it concentrates on Deng rather than on civilisation as such. Li begins from two questions Deng posed: what has changed since Marx's death more than a century ago, and how Marxism should be understood and developed under changed conditions. Li then sets out three parts of Deng's view of Marxism, which Li calls the theories of the system, of the essence, and of development. The piece closes by linking these to the Party's basic line of the reform period. Li contends that setting right the traditional view of Marxism is the soul of Deng Xiaoping Theory, and setting right the traditional view of socialism is its core. Both rest on clearing up the conception of history. In the first part, Deng held that Mao Zedong Thought must be grasped as a whole system, and Li presents the "Two Whatevers" as a product of an idealist view of history. In the second, seeking truth from facts is the essence of Marxism and of Mao Zedong Thought, and the ideological line underpins the political line. In the third, Marxism develops by solving China's pressing problems, so that it becomes sinicised. Li concludes that Deng, guided by historical materialism, set the basic line of "one central task, two basic points" and turned historical materialism towards everyday life. In Li's view, restoring historical materialism gave philosophical grounding to replacing "class struggle as the key link" with economic construction as the centre, and to the line of reform and opening up. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese philosopher links Deng Xiaoping Theory to historical materialism.

The task of our times: building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 构建中国特色哲学社会科学的时代任务 Wu Xiaoming Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (August 2022), Wu Xiaoming argues that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics is a major task entrusted to Chinese scholarship by the age. The author holds that the era is changing so deeply that it can only be understood once those changes become objects of scholarly theory. The short piece has three numbered parts. It first defines what kind of scholarship "Chinese characteristics" refers to, then considers the task from the side of theory, and finally places it within a new historical position and the world-historical significance of China's practice. Wu draws on Hegel, Marx and Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2016 symposium on philosophy and the social sciences. Wu contends that Chinese characteristics concern the nature and standpoint of scholarship, not its form: adding Chinese elements or topics misreads the task. What is required is scholarship that has left its "apprenticeship" and developed its own claims, with subjectivity and originality. Apprenticeship, the author says, was necessary but is dependent and imitative, and tends towards Hegel's "external reflection", which Wu equates with dogmatism: applying abstract principles to any content without engaging its substance. Wu concludes that scholarship must be freed from external reflection and enter social-historical reality, above all that of present-day China, while continuing to learn from others. Because China's practice has reached a new historical position, the author says, it generates a theoretical need that falls to this generation of scholars. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher frames the "subjectivity" of Chinese scholarship.

Finance capital and the financialization of contemporary capitalism 金融资本与当代资本主义金融化 Liu Xinyu Since the 1970s, financialization has become a defining feature of contemporary capitalism. Yet Rudolf Hilferding's systematic account of finance capital has received little attention, and some scholars deny that it has any contemporary relevance. Liu asks whether finance capital still has explanatory power for Marxist economics. The article, a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2022, argues that Hilferding's concept remains the theoretical foundation for understanding financialization, and that it in turn needs the test of present-day developments. The article first sets out three dimensions of Hilferding's finance capital: the monopolisation of bank and industrial capital, their fusion, and the dominant position of bank capital. It then reviews objections from Paul Sweezy, John Bellamy Foster and Costas Lapavitsas. Finally it turns to the Monopoly Capital school and its account of financialization since the 1970s, which Liu criticises. Liu reads Hilferding as treating monopoly as the precondition for finance capital, since without it ownership and use of money capital cannot be structurally separated. Bank capital then merges with industrial capital and dominates it through loan capital and fictitious capital. Industrial capital does not vanish but becomes one moment in the accumulation of finance capital. Finance capital's internal structure must therefore be grasped through both productive and non-productive accumulation. The Monopoly Capital school keeps Hilferding's split between production and finance but treats the two as absolutely opposed, equating financialization with fictitious capital. Liu calls this one-sided. In Liu's view, the school concentrates on circulation and on how surplus is absorbed, neglects how it is produced, never defines finance capital ontologically, and so cannot show why finance capital arises as the highest form of capital. Liu concludes that only a dual understanding of accumulation, in the real and the fictitious economy, reveals finance capital's structure and so grounds a theory of financialization. This would allow Marxist finance-capital theory to be developed into a world system combining economics, politics and international relations. Liu also holds that contemporary financialization should be used to renew the theory's modern relevance. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist statement of why Hilferding's Finance Capital still matters in debates with Sweezy, Foster and the Monopoly Capital school.

A critique of biopolitics in the context of digital capitalism 数字资本主义背景下的生命政治批判 Qu Liming This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks how biopolitics, a hot topic in Marxism outside China, should be understood once data has become the organising principle of society. Qu argues that data-based identity and "general data" mark a turning point that changes how political power reaches individual lives, and that this turning point is best analysed through Marx's critique of political economy. The article draws on Western thinkers: Agamben, Deleuze, Foucault, Dan Schiller, Cass Sunstein, Byung-Chul Han and Roberto Esposito. It first treats data identity as the condition of the new biopolitics, then distinguishes types of the "control society", and finally compares critical and affirmative accounts of biopolitics. Qu describes data identity as combining biometric data, records of social activity and algorithmic profiles of preferences. Without it, the author says, citizens cannot access travel, medical care or shopping, and individuals become "transparent", a society-wide Foucauldian panopticon. Control also works through performance metrics that split workers into competing units, and through "information cocoons" that isolate groups from each other. Qu reads Han's "psychopolitics" as a further extension of biopolitics. Agamben's "bare life" and "form-of-life" are set against Esposito's affirmative biopolitics of community and openness to others. Qu concludes that data becomes a new ruling force only when it acts as a general equivalent and operates as capital, just as the mere appearance of money did not create capitalism. Critical and affirmative biopolitics share one aim: a more complete society, with new technology bringing both challenges and possibilities. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how Western biopolitical theory is being reframed around digital capitalism.

The transmission of Marx's Capital in Tsarist Russia, Soviet Russia, the USSR and the Russian Federation 马克思《资本论》在沙俄/苏俄/苏联/俄罗斯的传播历程研究 Liu Xun Liu Xun asks how Marx's Capital has travelled through Russian-language culture over more than 150 years, and what that history reveals about the spread of Marxism in Russian and worldwide. The article argues that the transmission passed through four distinct phases. Each had its own achievements and distortions, and each shaped both Russian social thought and the global textual legacy of Marx. The article is organised chronologically. It covers the period before 1917, the years from the October Revolution to the mid-1950s, the period from the mid-1950s to 1991, and the post-Soviet years. It draws on publication histories, editorial projects such as MEGA1 and MEGA2, the Russian-language collected works, and the work of individual Russian and Soviet scholars. It ends with contemporary Russian research, including the critical Marxist school around Alexander Buzgalin and Andrei Kolganov. Liu's first main argument is that Capital's early Russian reception was tied to the question of Russia's development path. The first Russian translation appeared in 1872. Populists read it as a critique of autocracy but held that its laws did not apply to Russia's village commune. Plekhanov, and then Lenin in The Development of Capitalism in Russia and Imperialism, answered them. In Liu's account Lenin's work gave the 'final answer' that Russia, as a weak link in the imperialist chain, could move to socialism. Second, Liu credits the Soviet period with major achievements: the Marx-Engels Institute's collection of manuscripts, the 1857–58 manuscripts, mass editions, the second Russian edition of the Collected Works, MEGA2 cooperation and about 10 million copies in 25 languages. Liu also identifies a rigid 'textbook system' between the 1930s and the mid-1950s. In this system, creative research was criticised, readings were politicised, and Capital was reduced to its political-economy component. Third, after the mid-1950s Soviet scholars did work on Capital's formation history and its method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete (Vygodsky, Rosenthal, Ilyenkov). After 1991, Liu says, Capital was briefly marginalised, then regained interest, especially after the 2008 financial crisis. Russian editors continued to contribute to MEGA2. Liu reports that the Buzgalin–Kolganov school offers a critique of global capital, a call to update Capital's method, and an analysis of present-day Russia as 'oligarchic bureaucratic capitalism'. They treat Russia as still in transition towards a new socialism. Liu concludes that the Russian transmission has given Capital both textual and theoretical resources. Read the original if you want a detailed chronological survey, with names, editions and institutions, of Capital's Russian and Soviet reception and editorial history.

Resisting overseas religious infiltration in Chinese universities from the perspective of holistic governance: current state, reflection and mechanism building 整体性治理视域下我国高校抵御境外宗教渗透的现状、反思与机制构建 Lu Jianhua Lin Huaiyi Lu Jianhua and Lin Huaiyi, writing in the journal Science and Atheism (2022, no. 4), ask how Chinese universities can better resist what the article calls overseas religious infiltration. They argue that the dominant approach, built on top-down control and emergency response, should give way to "holistic governance", a framework oriented to problem-solving that seeks to integrate fragmented actors and policies. In the authors' view this offers a more scientific, coordinated and effective approach than traditional control. The article has three main parts. It first reviews existing practice: a Party-led organisational system with working groups and a line-style chain of command, a body of laws and regulations (the Constitution, the Education Law and ministry rules that separate education from religion), and ideological education through ideological and political theory courses, campus culture and pastoral care for students. It then diagnoses problems in governance concepts, actors, methods and system coordination. Finally it proposes a four-link governance mechanism and closes with remarks on the international context. The authors argue that current work is mainly reactive: universities act as "firefighters", treat students only as objects of protection, fail to integrate outside bodies such as local United Front, religious affairs, public security and cyberspace departments, and lack coordination and performance indicators. To remedy this they propose four linked mechanisms. A cognition-and-prevention mechanism would place a special leadership group under the university Party committee. A monitoring and early-warning mechanism would track students, online opinion, campus conditions and teaching and research. A judgement-and-response mechanism would cover information sharing (including a blacklist), expert assessment and intervention. A supervision-and-evaluation mechanism would check implementation, duties and outcomes, for example through student surveys. In the conclusion the authors cite Peter Berger's revised view and Pew Research Center projections to claim that religion is resurging globally. They describe religious infiltration as a tool of Western ideological pressure on China, and a long, complex struggle. They call for continuous innovation in university institutions and mechanisms to resist it. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese academic writing frames religion in universities as an ideological security issue and what institutional machinery it recommends.

A study of the dissemination of Marx's Capital in Italy 马克思《资本论》在意大利的传播历程研究 Li Jingwen Li Jingwen asks how Marx's Capital and its manuscripts were translated, read and used in Italy from the late 1860s to the present, and what interpretive traditions resulted. The article, a stage result of a national social science fund project on foreign scholarship on Capital, argues that Italian work on Capital forms a continuous line. That line is shaped by Hegelian influences, by a persistent concern with the falling rate of profit and by close ties to class struggle. Since the mid-twentieth century it has also been marked by a shift from opposed readings to a fusion of two paradigms. The article proceeds chronologically in four stages. It covers the early period from the 1860s to the early twentieth century, including anarchist translators and Antonio Labriola and Benedetto Croce. It then treats the two world wars and the Fascist period. A third section deals with the post-war decades to the 1970s, and a fourth with the period from the 1980s to the present. Li follows translations and editions (Italian editions of Marx and Engels's collected works, and MEGA2-based versions) alongside the thinkers and movements that used them. Li stresses three moves. First, early reception was driven by anarchists such as Cafiero and then shaped by the controversy over Achille Loria's critique of the falling rate of profit. Labriola defended historical materialism against it, while Croce moved towards an idealist reading and set the problems Gramsci later took up. Second, after 1945 the translation of manuscripts such as the Grundrisse opened a new phase. The Della Volpe school and Lucio Colletti offered a scientistic reading against Hegelian and humanist ones, while the workerist tradition of Panzieri, Tronti and Negri read Capital as a guide to factory struggle. Third, Li holds that after the 1970s the decline of the workers' movement brought a lull, followed by a revival through international scholarly cooperation, the Italian Marx–Engels edition and post-2008 rereadings. Li concludes that Italian study of Capital has deepened with the relaunch of the collected works and the spread of MEGA2. In Li's account, international collaboration has grown, and scientistic and humanist readings have moved from opposition to mutual influence and fusion. Li illustrates this with Colletti's attention to the Paris Manuscripts and Bellofiore's interest in the German new reading of Marx. Read the original if you want a detailed bibliographic and historical survey of Italian editions, translators and schools of interpretation of Capital.

Giving full play to the political function of primary-level Party organisations 充分发挥基层党组织的政治功能 Wang Binglin Writing in Guangming Daily on 30 September 2022, Wang Binglin asks how the Communist Party's primary-level organisations can be strengthened so that they carry out the Party's line effectively. Wang's answer is that these organisations must give full play to their political function. The author starts from the claim that a Marxist party's basic attribute is political and its basic function is political. The article cites official figures of 96.712 million Party members and 4.936 million primary-level organisations at the end of 2021. The article has three parts. The first sets out why the political function is necessary. The second reviews what primary-level organisations have achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the weaknesses that remain. The third proposes four areas of work for Party building in the new era. Wang gives four reasons why the political function is necessary: it is required by the Party's overall leadership, by the people-centred approach to development, by upholding and developing the socialist system with Chinese characteristics, and by full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The author insists that primary-level organisations are a "fighting fortress" and must not become mere service bodies, even though service is one of their functions. Achievements cited include the Two Upholds, the extension of branches into villages, communities and research teams, the work of Party members in the Covid-19 response and disasters, and poverty alleviation. Wang also lists shortcomings. These include weak implementation of policy, an emphasis on economic targets at the expense of responding to people's demands, gaps in coverage (especially in emerging sectors), an ageing cadre pool, and formalism such as time spent on forms and records. Wang calls for work in four areas. The first is to secure the leading position of primary-level organisations in grassroots governance. The second is to meet people's growing needs for a better life by combining management with service. The third is to raise organisational capacity: set up organisations in step with social change, choose and strengthen leaders, promote capable Party workers, and give primary-level organisations more resources and powers. The fourth is to extend full and rigorous self-governance of the Party downwards through theoretical education, criticism and self-criticism, and checks on petty powers. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic statement of how Party-building scholars justify and prescribe the political role of grassroots Party branches after 2012.

The Chinese Communist Party's atheist propaganda and education in the New Democratic Revolution period: explorations, experience and implications 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党无神论宣传教育的探索、经验及启示 Yang Mingyan Zhang Qianyuan Yang and Zhang take up a topic they say has received little attention in Chinese scholarship, partly because sources are scattered: how the Chinese Communist Party carried out atheist propaganda and education before 1949. They argue that, guided by Marxism and the principle of struggling against religion set out by Lenin, the Party treated atheist education and the raising of the masses' scientific and cultural level as an important part of its ideological work. They present this as a pioneering effort that offers lessons for atheist education today. The article has three parts. The first traces the practice through the May Fourth period, the Land Revolution period, and the War of Resistance and Liberation War periods. The second distils five lessons from this history. The third draws four implications for the new era, and is framed by Xi Jinping's call to draw on the Party's centenary experience. On the history, the authors describe the New Youth journal's scientific attacks on spiritualism, the 1922 Anti-Religion Alliance, and leaflets, lectures and the volume Anti-Religion Theory. In the Soviet areas they cite constitutional separation of religion and state, schools whose textbooks carried anti-superstition content, and newspapers such as Red China. During the anti-Japanese and civil wars they point to Marxist philosophy courses, plays, radio and a plague-prevention film. Their five lessons are guidance by historical materialism, Party leadership, linking theory to practice through the mass line, drawing on natural science and classic texts, and audience-specific methods. Examples include well-digging at Shazhouba, a 1944 locust campaign and plague control in the Northeast. The authors note that early crude methods provoked resistance. They also stress that Party members must hold to atheism while religious believers keep freedom of belief. For the new era, the authors call for firm Party leadership and Marxist guidance over atheist education. They also want a people-centred approach that connects with ordinary life and combines argument with emotional appeal. They propose a broader coordination mechanism that mobilises social organisations, enterprises and individuals beyond cultural and media bodies. They further propose an "Internet plus atheist education" pattern using platforms such as Weibo, WeChat and Douyin, together with tighter online supervision against theistic content. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based Party-history account of atheist propaganda methods before 1949, and of how Chinese scholars draw present-day policy lessons from it.

An interpretation of Marx and Engels's constitutional thought An examination based on the drafting of the Communist Manifesto, 1843–1848 马克思恩格斯宪法思想诠释 Liu Jianxiang Wu Jinle Liu and Wu ask whether the Communist Manifesto, usually read as a programme of class struggle and a landmark of Marxist jurisprudence, also contains a developed theory of the constitution. Tracing the document's roughly ten-year drafting history and Marx and Engels's sustained attention to constitutions from 1843 to 1848, they argue that it does. They support this with the German and English editions of the Manifesto. The article sets out four propositions. These are that a constitution should recognise human rights and civil rights and reflect the people's demands; that the working class needs a democratic constitution to achieve political emancipation and establish political rule; that a constitution is determined by, and must suit, the material conditions of life of a given society; and that each country must follow a constitutional path suited to its own national conditions. The evidence ranges from Marx's early critiques of Hegel and his notes on the French and American constitutions to the programmes of the League of the Just and the Communist League, Engels's draft credo and Principles of Communism, and the polemics against 'true socialism'. In the authors' reading, Marx held that democracy is the 'solved riddle of all constitutions' and that new constitutions arise through revolution. In On the Jewish Question, Marx distinguished the rights of man from the rights of the citizen and judged political emancipation both a real advance and not yet human emancipation. Liu and Wu stress that this critique did not reject individual freedom or equality as such. Next, they argue that Marx and Engels tied constitutions to the rise of the bourgeoisie, large-scale industry and free competition. Where the bourgeoisie had not yet won power, as in Germany, communists should support its revolution against absolutism while preparing the struggle against it. Where it ruled, as in Britain, France and the United States, workers should use constitutional rights for lawful class struggle. After a proletarian revolution, a democratic constitution is the first step in establishing proletarian rule. The authors conclude that the Manifesto's general principles must be applied according to historical conditions, which they take as a constitutional lesson: no country should copy another's constitutional path. They present Marx and Engels's criticism of 'true socialists', who transplanted French texts into Germany, as the model case. They also cite Lenin's continuation of the same democratic-constitution theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the drafting history of the Manifesto bears on Marxist constitutional and legal theory, including the rights debates of the 1840s.

Making historical materialism concrete: Marx's exploration and its significance 唯物史观具体化：马克思的探索及其意义 Tang Zhengdong Western scholarship has recently returned to Marx's two early-1850s political histories, The Class Struggles in France, 1848 to 1850 and The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, often reading them as a politics of action or a history of events set against economic determinism. Tang Zhengdong argues instead that they are Marx's first attempt to make historical materialism concrete (具体化), meaning to apply it to the real problems of a particular country. The article claims this reading clarifies the preconditions, theoretical marks and methodological features of such concretization. The article takes the two texts in three steps. It first shows that the inherited ideas and illusions Marx describes are products of social relations not yet sharpened into acute class antagonism. It then identifies two theoretical results of Marx's concretization, and finally draws out implications for the history of Marxism and for the adaptation of Marxism in China. Tang compares Marx with Victor Hugo and Proudhon, and with Engels's The Peasant War in Germany. Tang's first result is that Marx treats France's apparently farcical political struggles as the outward, mediating form of the internal contradictions of the French mode of production. Because France's development was atypical and lagged behind Britain's, its classes were underdeveloped, so class struggle could not take the pure form of capital against labour. Marx therefore traces the June defeat, the incoherent conduct of the parties and the peasants' support for Bonaparte to class position, not to tactics, party principles or the autonomy of state power. The second result is that Marx lifts this history to the level of laws of political struggle. He argues that small-holding peasants and the petty bourgeoisie would be driven towards the proletariat, and he formulates the idea of permanent revolution and the class dictatorship of the proletariat, which Tang says sets the texts apart from ordinary event history. Tang concludes that Marx's post-1848 thought should be read as an exploration of concretization, not merely an application of historical materialism, and that concretization is as central to the theory as its basic content. In Tang's view this marks what counts as success in combining basic principles with the analysis of a specific country. The article ties this to Mao Zedong's 1938 call to make Marxism concrete in China and to the Party's later study of principal contradictions and development laws under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a close reading of these two Marx texts that challenges event-history interpretations and links them to debates on adapting Marxism.

Review of Chinese and foreign scholarship on Western Marxism and economics 国内外学者关于西方马克思主义与经济学研究述评 Wang Qingchao This literature review, published in the Journal of Chongqing Jiaotong University (Social Sciences Edition) in 2021, asks how Western Marxism has treated Marx's economic theory, and how scholars in China and abroad have described that treatment. Wang's answer is that Western Marxism's orientation has shifted over time. It first moved away from economics towards philosophy and culture, then, after the 1970s, towards a broad and diffuse engagement with economics. Wang judges both phases to be flawed. The review has three parts. The first covers foreign scholars (Perry Anderson, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, David McLellan, Russell Jacoby, Robert Gorman, Michael Howard and John King, Joan Robinson, Herbert Gintis). It sets a 'philosophy thesis' for the period before the 1970s against a 'turn thesis' for the period after. The second covers Chinese scholars (Chen Xueming, Zhang Yibing, Tai Lihua, Han Yuli, Sun Chengshu, Cheng Enfu and Zhu Kui, Hu Leming). They trace a move from 'de-economization' to 'pan-economization'. The third part is Wang's own assessment. Wang's central move is to reconcile the two sets of scholarship. Both periodize Western Marxism around the May 1968 events in France. Before then, in this account, Western Marxism reacted against the economic determinism of the Second and Third Internationals. It downgraded political economy and favoured totality, which Chinese scholars call a dismemberment of Marxism. Afterwards, the pan-economizing trend widened the objects of study to include feminism and minority questions, and treated the economy as a political and cultural relation. Wang notes that this brought interdisciplinary breadth but blurred the subject matter of Marxist political economy. Wang concludes that cultural and economic critique have always been out of balance in Western Marxism. Contemporary Western Marxist economics has three defects: fragmented theory, methodological pluralism that blocks dialogue, and a ruptured theoretical system. Wang cites Sweezy's 'underconsumption', Baran's 'economic surplus' and Roemer's 'general exploitation' as examples of the fragmentation. Wang calls on Western Marxism to make political economy its main focus, and says that understanding its shifts can help develop contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy. Read the original if you want a map of the Chinese and Western debate over whether Western Marxism abandoned or diluted Marxist economics.

The loss of direction and the path to revival of Western Marxism A review of Domenico Losurdo's Western Marxism: How It Was Born, How It Died, How It Can Be Reborn 西方马克思主义的迷失与复苏之路 Li Wei This is a book review by Li Wei of Il marxismo occidentale: Come nacque, come morì, come può rinascere (2017) by the Italian historian of philosophy Domenico Losurdo (1941–2018). The Chinese edition, titled in Chinese Reconstructing Western Marxism, was published by Contemporary China Publishing House in April 2022 in a series planned by the Academy of Marxism, CASS. Li presents the book as a thought-provoking account of how Western Marxism fell into Eurocentrism, drifted towards liberalism and might be reborn through contact with Eastern Marxism. The review first introduces Losurdo as a scholar of Hegel, Marxism and liberalism, then sets out how the book defines Western Marxism. The term goes back to Merleau-Ponty (1955) and was popularised by Perry Anderson's 1976 study, which traced it to Lukács and Korsch and placed the Frankfurt School, Sartre, Lefebvre, Althusser, Della Volpe, Colletti and even Gramsci within it. Li then follows Losurdo's history from the First World War and the October Revolution, and his survey of individual thinkers. In Li's account, Losurdo identifies four differences between Eastern and Western Marxism. The West stressed anti-war revolution, the abolition of private economy and money, and fear of technology, while the East gave priority to national independence, treated trade and money as sustaining the revolution, and pursued development of the productive forces. Cultural factors also mattered: Western Marxism was shaped by Judeo-Christian messianism, while Eastern traditions made reception more pragmatic. Losurdo argues that Western Marxism declined because it ignored anti-colonial struggle, the real turning point of the twentieth century. He cites Colletti, Tronti, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Arendt, Foucault, Agamben, Negri and Hardt, and Žižek, and exempts only Gramsci and Lukács. For its rebirth he proposes three principles: Hegel's understanding of one's time, Marx's changing of the world and Lenin's revolutionary transformation. Li endorses Losurdo's criticism of Horkheimer, Bloch, Adorno and Colletti but finds that of Žižek and Badiou excessive. Li adds that Western Marxism remains an important philosophical tendency, and that Chinese scholars tend to draw out its critical potential. Li sees its present problem as confinement to academia, cut off from social movements and global inequality, and cites the Italian commentator Oscar Oddi, who suggests that lessons from the development and reform of socialist countries in the East may help revive it. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly assessment of Losurdo's anti-colonial critique of Western Marxism and its place in current CASS discussion of foreign Marxism.

Building firm faith on a theoretical foundation 以理论之基筑牢信仰根基 Lü Hongbo Writing as a young cadre working in theory and publicity, Lü Hongbo takes up Xi Jinping's 2021 call for young cadres to be firm in conviction and loyal to the Party. Lü argues that firm ideals and convictions come from firm theory, and that only a solid theoretical foundation can anchor faith. This short commentary in Study Times is organised around three linked claims: theoretical clarity gives firm conviction, theoretical confidence gives steadfast faith, and theoretical consciousness gives political consciousness. It ends with a note on the author's own work in Fujian. Lü contends that ideals rest on a rational acceptance of scientific theory, of historical laws and of national conditions. In Lü's account, Marxism has guided the Party through a century of ordeals, and studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is a required course for young cadres. Lü contrasts the delegates to the First Party Congress who abandoned the cause with those, such as Mao Zedong, who kept their faith. Lü also holds that the depth of one's grasp of Marxism determines political sensitivity and breadth of vision, and that Marxism should serve as a compass for new problems. Lü calls for continuous, in-depth study of the Thought and for deeper work on tracing its origins, drawing on Xi Jinping's 17 and a half years in Fujian. The aim is stronger political, intellectual, theoretical and emotional identification with the Two Establishes. Read the original if you want an example of how Party theory cadres present ideological study as the basis of conviction.

Making Party history study and education in universities regular and long-term 推进高校党史学习教育常态化长效化 Han Yun This short commentary, published on Guangming Net in 2022, asks how universities can turn Party history study and education into a regular, long-term practice. Han Yun argues that, following Xi Jinping's repeated requirements since the 18th Party Congress (2012), universities must consolidate the results of the Party history campaign, especially among young people. The piece has two parts. The first sets out why such education matters; the second proposes practical paths for universities. On value, Han claims that Party history education strengthens students' ideals and beliefs, helps them build a correct view of history and resist what the author calls erroneous social trends, and trains 'new-era people' who can serve as builders and successors of socialism. On practice, Han makes three proposals. First, build a systematic body of content, with top-level planning that presents the Party's theoretical exploration, revolutionary struggle and self-development, combining macro narrative with vivid detail, answering student concerns and adding recent achievements. Second, innovate teaching methods beyond lectures: themed talks on exemplary Party members such as Jiao Yulu, quizzes, role-play, visits to red heritage sites and new media. Third, guide and persuade rather than preach, letting students understand how knowledge developed, and linking past, present and future. Han concludes that this approach should lead students to value present-day well-being, recognise what the article describes as the distinct advantages of socialism with Chinese characteristics through comparison with the West, and take up their responsibilities. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party history education in higher education is framed and what teaching methods are recommended.

Three dimensions for understanding "leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform" 三个维度理解“以党的自我革命引领社会革命” Li Xiaodong Published in Guangming Daily in September 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call to "lead social revolution through the Party's self-reform". Li Xiaodong argues that the Communist Party of China's ability to carry out great self-reform is what has allowed it to lead great social revolution. The author presents the two as an organic unity, with self-reform as the driving force. The piece is organised around three "dimensions". The first treats the principle as an inherent requirement for a Marxist party to fulfil its historic mission. The second treats it as valuable experience from the Party's revolution, construction and reform. The third presents it as the key to meeting changes in the world, in the times and in history. Throughout, Li draws on Xi's speeches, with citations from Engels and Lenin on internal struggle and on a party's attitude to its own mistakes. In the first dimension, Li defines a Marxist party's self-reform as continuous self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. Li argues that the Party's historical height in self-reform determines the depth of social revolution, and that new revolutionary tasks in turn set new demands for self-reform. Old parties and dynasties, in this reading, failed because they lacked the courage to resolve their own serious problems. For the second dimension, Li traces the Gutian, Zunyi and Yan'an rectification episodes, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), and the campaign of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Li credits these with helping the Party escape the "historical cycle" of rise and fall. In the third dimension, Li stresses the unprecedented breadth, sharpness and difficulty of today's social revolution and the "four dangers" and "four tests" the Party still faces. Li concludes that self-reform is never finished and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is "always on the road". Li calls on the Party to strengthen its mechanisms for self-reform, to guard against any loss of its advanced and pure character, and to raise cadres' capacity to carry out modernization. Li expresses confidence that the Party will keep winning victories on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building theory was presented to a general readership on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The Party's distinctive political character and formidable political strength 党的鲜明政治品格和强大政治优势 Wang Xinsheng This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in September 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's statement at a seminar for provincial and ministerial-level leading cadres that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Party's distinctive political character and formidable political strength. Wang Xinsheng reads the statement as explaining why the Party has kept its vanguard character and purity, and why it has won victory after victory. The piece moves from the Party's history to the present. It first recalls the Party's century-long adherence to Marxism, then discusses how theory underpins political maturity, then turns to the way Marxism is applied in China, and ends with a call to keep to Marxism's guiding position. Wang argues that Marxism gave the Party a scientific worldview and methodology, which in the author's account freed it from the self-interested limits of earlier political forces. This is said to have let it correct errors, keep the historical initiative and complete tasks no other Chinese political force could. Marxism, however, is treated as a guide to action rather than dogma: its effect depends on combining its basic principles with Chinese realities and fine traditional Chinese culture, which the author calls adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Wang presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a new leap in this process and cites the past decade's achievements as proof. Wang concludes that the guiding position of Marxism must never be shaken, since it is the foundation of the Party and the state and the source of confidence in meeting turbulence. The author calls on the whole Party to study the worldview, methodology, standpoint and method of Xi Jinping Thought. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed Marxism as the Party's core political asset.

Consciously putting Communists' values into practice 自觉践行共产党人价值观 Wang Peizhou Wang Peizhou, in a commentary originally published in Study Times, asks what values Chinese Communists should concretely follow today. The author argues that Communist values are both an old and a new subject: old because the Party's political nature fixes their basic orientation, new because the present era demands specific value norms. The piece first distinguishes three layers: the lofty goal of communism, understood as the free and all-round development of every person; the core orientation of serving the people wholeheartedly; and concrete norms shaped by the times. It then cites Xi Jinping's statements from the 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection plenary session, the 19th Party Congress report and a Politburo study session. Wang reads Xi's wording as shifting from "uphold" to "promote" to "promote and put into practice", which signals unity of knowing and doing. The trailing "etc." suggests the list will expand as full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform advance. Four norms are examined in turn: loyalty and honesty, fairness and decency, seeking truth from facts, and integrity and incorruptibility. Wang links each to a present problem: officials who are politically two-faced, distorted views of power, formalism and bureaucracy, and the intrusion of commodity-exchange logic into inner-Party life. Wang concludes that these four norms are basic requirements of the Party's self-governance and self-reform, and that officials with greater power should hold greater reverence for it. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-press commentary presents the values expected of cadres and links them to Xi Jinping's formulations.

Jiangxi: the birth and continuation of the Red statistics enterprise 江西：红色统计事业的发祥与发扬 Theoretical Study Centre Group of the CPC Jiangxi Provincial Committee Marking the 70th anniversary of the founding of the PRC government's statistical agency, this commentary by the Jiangxi Provincial Party Committee's theoretical study group asks where Party-led statistics began and what lessons it holds today. The authors argue that the "Red statistics enterprise" originated and took root in Jiangxi during the Land Revolution period, and that its spirit should be carried forward in present-day statistical work. The piece has three parts. The first traces the institutional history from the Jinggangshan base area to the Central Soviet Area. The second distils the "spiritual connotation" of Red statistics into five principles. The third describes how Jiangxi applies these principles in what the authors call high-quality development of statistics in the new era. It is written in the authoritative, programmatic style of a provincial Party document. In the authors' account, a specialised statistical system took shape step by step. An investigation section was set up under the Party's Organisation Bureau from 1927. In 1931 the provisional central Soviet government in Ruijin placed statistical units in several ministries. In April 1933 a National Economy Department with its own Investigation and Statistics Bureau was created, with matching offices at provincial and county level. The authors present this as the prototype of the PRC's statistical organs. They treat Mao Zedong's Xunwu investigation as the source of its guiding ideas, "going deep, being practical, seeking truth". The five principles are Party leadership as the fundamental principle, the mass line as the core requirement, seeking truth from facts as the essential feature, rule by law and regulation as the safeguard, and efficiency with integrity as the hallmark. The authors illustrate the last with Mao's surveys done during military pauses and with the "knapsack government". For the present, the authors report that Jiangxi acts on Xi Jinping's directives on statistics by upholding the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds. They describe a shift towards giving social statistics equal weight with economic statistics, a drive against statistical falsification, and a modernised survey system with data-sharing platforms. They also cite the Jiangxi Statistics Management Regulations, a "data responsibility system", and training of cadres at sites such as the Central Soviet Area investigation and statistics history museum. Read the original if you want an example of how a provincial Party body uses revolutionary-era history to frame current statistical governance and anti-falsification policy.

Creative theoretical contributions to the socialist market economy 对社会主义市场经济的创造性理论贡献 Gu Hailiang Writing in the Party-run Economic Daily in September 2022, Gu Hailiang argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought makes creative theoretical contributions to the socialist market economy. Gu identifies three areas: the government–market relationship as the core issue of economic reform, the basic economic system as the defining character of the socialist market economy, and the nature and behavioural laws of capital. In Gu's account, these contributions enrich the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics and give Marxist political economy a new content for the twenty-first century. The article follows the Party's changing positions from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). It then turns to the methodology Gu finds in Xi's thinking and ends with a section on capital under socialism. It is built as four sections, each pairing documents and Xi's statements with Gu's commentary. Gu first traces a progression from adjusting economic mechanisms, to reforming the economic structure, to settling the system. Along the way, the market's role moved from supplementary to "basic" and then, in 2013, to "decisive" in allocating resources. Gu reads this as a shift from the market being merely compatible with socialism to being combined with it. Second, Gu holds that treating the socialist market economy as part of the basic economic system is an original contribution: public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to work and Party leadership give the market economy its socialist character, and "dialectics" and "two-sidedness" govern the state–market and public–private relationships. Third, Gu notes that Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin did not address capital under socialism. Gu presents Xi's approach as recognising several forms of capital, state, collective, private, foreign and mixed, whose positive role should be used and whose negative effects controlled. This means curbing the disorderly expansion of capital and setting "traffic lights" for it. Gu concludes that upholding the direction of socialist market-economy reform is a key principle of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Gu also concludes that Xi's economic thought gives that theory a new content in the sense of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party theorists trace the doctrinal stages of the socialist market economy and frame the Party's approach to capital.

The Two Establishes as the source of the strong cohesion and guiding power of ideological discourse in the new era “两个确立”是新时代意识形态话语强大凝聚力和引领力的力量之源 Wu Xueqin Writing in 2022, Wu Xueqin takes up the call in the Party's third historical resolution, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), to build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. The article argues that the Two Establishes (establishing Xi Jinping's core position and the guiding status of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era) are the source of that power. Wu presents them as grounded in theory, history, practice and institutions. The article first defines cohesion and guiding power and proposes four tests of whether an ideology has them. It then devotes four sections to the theoretical, historical, practical and institutional strength of the Two Establishes. The historical section runs from the Zunyi Meeting through the Deng Xiaoping era to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On theory, Wu answers critics at home and abroad who equate establishing a leader's authority with personal despotism or a personality cult. The author draws on Marxist accounts of the relation between outstanding individuals and the masses, and of social being and social consciousness, to argue that a leader's authority arises from historical conditions and cannot be reduced to worship. Wu adds that the relationship between the leading core and the guiding ideology is dialectical, as with Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. On history, Wu holds that the Party gained cohesion each time it established a core and a guiding thought, and that each period produced its own ideological discourse: revolution, construction, reform and now rejuvenation. On institutions, Wu contrasts China's merit-based cadre selection and intra-Party democracy with Western electoral democracy, which the author describes as money-driven. Wu also cites Party regulations that embed the Two Establishes in the system of Party leadership. Wu concludes that the Two Establishes strengthen the Party's leadership over ideological work, give the whole Party and people a firmer backbone, improve safeguards against ideological risk in new media, and consolidate Party unity. Wu says they also help China answer Western discursive dominance and strengthen national identity. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Party theorists justify the Two Establishes and rebut the charge of personality cult, or if you want to see how ideology, history and Party-building are linked in this literature.

How the Party served the interests of the masses in the Central Soviet Area period 中央苏区时期党如何为群众谋利益 Zhu Yihua Huang Yingxi This short commentary, first published in Study Times, asks how the Party worked for the interests of ordinary people in the Central Soviet Area. Zhu and Huang argue that the Party came to see protection of mass interests as the foundation of revolutionary victory. They point to the call of the provisional central government of the Chinese Soviet Republic to represent the poorest workers and peasants "wholeheartedly". The article covers three areas of practice: political structure, economic work and social welfare. It draws on examples from the Soviet organs, land reform, cooperatives, public health, relief and education, with figures from Jiangxi and Fujian, especially Guangchang county. On politics, the authors hold that protecting political rights was the basis for all other rights. They cite the Soviet Organic Law, which gave voting rights to non-exploiting men and women aged 16 and over, and report that women made up over 25 per cent of delegates in Jiangxi's elections. On the economy, they say land distribution made peasants masters of the land. Cooperatives then eased shortages of labour, oxen, seed and capital; by March 1933 the authors count 1,423 cooperatives in 17 counties. On social work, they describe mass hygiene campaigns, mutual aid societies and donation drives for relief, and Lenin primary schools, night schools and literacy classes. In Guangchang, they report 124 such primary schools by the end of 1933. The authors conclude that these measures improved livelihoods, raised political enthusiasm and won peasant support. They describe relief work under wartime scarcity as a direct sign of the advanced character of a Marxist party. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of Central Soviet Area governance, with local statistics, as presented in a Party newspaper.

Mao Zedong's far-reaching considerations in editing Party history document collections in the Yan'an period 延安时期毛泽东主持编辑党史文献集的深远考虑 Wan Ruijia Zou Weishao Why did Mao Zedong personally lead the compilation of a series of Party history and theory collections during the Yan'an period (1938–1945)? Wan Ruijia and Zou Weishao argue that the work was a deliberate political and ideological undertaking, not merely archival. In their account it was meant to unify the Party's thinking, summarise its historical experience and change its work style, and it is presented as a tradition of the Chinese Communist Party that began at Yan'an. The article is organised in three parts. The first describes the collections Mao edited and sorts them into three types: political documents (Since the Sixth Congress, Before the Sixth Congress, Two Lines), writings of the Marxist classics (Methodology of Thought of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin; Lenin, Stalin and the Comintern on China), and investigation material (Rural Surveys). The second part sets out Mao's reasons, and the third assesses the effects of the collections. For the authors, the context was the stalemate phase of the War of Resistance, the Wannan Incident (1941) and the lack of agreement inside the Party about past 'Left' and Right errors. They identify three purposes. The first was to unify thinking before the long-delayed Seventh Party Congress, linking the collections to the Rectification Movement. The second was to give cadres original documents with which to tell right from wrong, above all about Wang Ming's 'Left' dogmatist line. The third was to change the Party's style, tackling dogmatism and the separation of theory from practice, and promoting investigation and research. The authors conclude that the collections helped bring the Party 'unprecedentedly' together under Mao's banner and established the guiding position of Mao Zedong Thought. They also supplied the documentary and methodological basis for the Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party, and encouraged a style of linking theory with practice, ties with the masses and self-criticism. They claim that without these collections the Resolution would have been hard to produce. Read the original if you study the Rectification Movement, Party document compilation or the Party's own account of Mao's role in Yan'an.

Let the lamp of the Chinese spirit shine on the literary and artistic peaks of the new era 让中国精神的灯火在新时代的文艺高峰上闪亮 Tie Ning Writing in Qiushi in 2022, Tie Ning asks what it takes for Chinese literature and art to reach new peaks in the new era. The essay marks the eighth anniversary of Xi Jinping's Talk at the Forum on Literature and Art (2014). It also recalls Xi's call in December 2021 for literary masters and peaks. Tie's answer is that writers and artists should be guided by three fundamental ideas: the times, the people and innovation. The essay is a reflective address in an essayistic, personal register rather than a systematic study. It moves from Beijing's long cultural history, through Cao Xueqin and Lu Xun, to modern and contemporary writers such as Zhou Libo, Liu Qing and Ma Feng. It then turns to recent works: the television drama Shanhai qing (Ocean of Mountains and Seas), the dance-drama Zhi ci qinglü and the Beijing Winter Olympics ceremonies. Each of the three keywords is anchored in a few such examples and in quotations from Xi. On the times, Tie argues that writers must grasp the historical position of the new era and combine an eagle's overview with the rootedness of a tree in everyday life. Citing Zhou Libo's Great Changes in a Mountain Village and Liu Qing's fourteen years in a village, Tie calls for "historical initiative": writers should join the people's historical practice rather than merely observe it. On the people, Tie reads Xi's remark that the people are not an abstract symbol as a theoretical innovation, describing a dialectical movement from the concrete to the whole and back. On innovation, Tie presents the "guochao" works as creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture. Tie concludes that the new era needs and can produce literary masters. Tie sketches a second, spiritual "central axis" of Beijing, formed by generations of writers and artists, which binds people together emotionally. The closing hope is that the lamp of the Chinese spirit will shine on the new era's artistic peaks. Read the original if you want to see how a senior figure in China's official literary institutions applies Xi Jinping's cultural directives to creative work, or if you are interested in the rhetoric of the Chinese literary establishment in 2022.

The background and course of the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization 中华文明探源工程的“来龙去脉” Dai Sheng Published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) in 2022, this short explanatory piece follows the 39th collective study session of the Political Bureau (27 May 2022), which was devoted to deepening the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization. Dai Sheng asks what the project is, and what its aims, stages, value and significance are. The author's answer is that it is a long-running, multidisciplinary national undertaking whose first 20 years have produced substantial but only preliminary and stage-specific results. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the study session and then moves through three parts. The first explains how the project grew out of the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project (1996–2000). The second walks through the project's phases from the pre-study of 2001–2003 to the fifth phase of 2020–2024. The third sets out the results announced in 2018, the related "Archaeology China" programme launched in 2017, and the tasks ahead. Dai's account stresses how the project's scope widened. The chronology project, the author says, was meant to answer overseas scholars who denied the Xia dynasty because documented dates reach back only to 841 BCE. The origins project then extended its time range from 2500 BCE to 3500 BCE. Its geography grew from the Central Plains to the Yellow and Yangtze valleys, the West Liao River basin and the border regions. Its content grew from archaeological periodization and settlement patterns to environment, subsistence, resources and spiritual life. The author lists three achievements. These are the dating of the early emergence of civilization (signs around 5800 years ago, entry into the civilizational stage from 5300 years ago, a mature Central Plains form around 3800 years ago); a picture of diverse regional paths within a pattern of pluralistic unity; and a Chinese standard for judging civilization that goes beyond the Western "three elements" of metallurgy, writing and cities. Dai concludes that the work ahead is heavy. The author lists future tasks: study more regions, push back to 8,000 or even 10,000 years ago, deepen theory, popularize the findings, and build a discipline, academic and discourse system with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. The piece repeats Xi's call for coordinated planning and joint work between archaeology, history, and the humanities and natural sciences. Read the original if you want a compact official-style chronology of the project's phases, leaders and announced findings, or if you want to see how Party media present the project's scholarly and political aims.

Mao Zedong's thought on investigation and research in his family letters of the early People's Republic 新中国成立初期毛泽东家书中的调查研究思想探究 Yang Xinbin Yang Xinbin asks how Mao Zedong's habit of social investigation and research (diaoyan) continued after 1949, when he could no longer carry out fieldwork as he had before. The article argues that, between the founding of the People's Republic and the socialist transformation, Mao used letters to and from relatives as a special information channel. In Yang's reading, these letters served a function close to investigation and research and carried forward his earlier methods. The article draws on 46 published letters from 1949 to 1953, sent to 32 recipients among his paternal, maternal and wife's kin. Most of these were peasants, small producers, local cadres and intellectuals in rural Hunan. It has three parts: the historical setting of the family-letter route, the major problems Mao raised in the letters, and the principles of investigation they reveal. Yang links three recurring concerns in the letters to national policy. Grain shortages in 1950 are traced to wartime requisitions and a fiscal system not yet unified, which Mao answered by lowering requisition rates and unifying finance. Complaints about local work in 1950 are tied to coercive cadre conduct and the Party's rapid growth, which prompted rectification campaigns. Grain shortages in 1952 are read as showing the fragility of smallholder farming after land reform, and so as supporting Mao's push towards agricultural cooperation. Yang then identifies four principles in the letters. These are the people's standing as the subject of practice, typical-case analysis ("dissecting a sparrow"), the investigation meeting, and winning the trust of those surveyed. Kinship, Yang argues, made candid reporting more likely. Yang concludes that Mao's attention to family letters continued his pre-1949 approach and was an attempt to keep up the Party's good traditions while in power. The article presents investigation and research as a Party heirloom and calls for it to be inherited in the new era, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you are interested in Mao's working methods, in Hunan rural conditions in the early 1950s, or in how Chinese scholars use private correspondence as evidence of policy thinking.

The effects of developing the rural collective economy in the period of agricultural collectivisation and their lessons 农业集体化时期发展农村集体经济的效用及其启示 Wu Shuli Wu Shuli asks how rural revitalisation can overcome the weakness of fragmented smallholder farming ("dispersal") while drawing on the strength of a new type of collective economy ("unification"). The article argues that this question cannot be understood without tracing the history of rural collective ownership. Wu contends that the collective economy of the collectivisation period (c. 1951–1983) achieved real economic and social results, and that its experience offers guidance for today's "three rural issues" (agriculture, rural areas, farmers). Wu begins by criticising existing scholarship for three tendencies: stigmatising collective economy as inefficient and uniform, separating the collective era from the household contract responsibility system, and concentrating on political campaigns rather than everyday economic development. The article then has three parts: why the Party promoted collective economy, what it concretely achieved, and what lessons follow for the present. The evidence includes statistics, Mao Zedong's statements, local cases such as Shandong's Yantai and Henan's Shibanyan supply and marketing cooperative, and the views of foreign scholars such as Theda Skocpol. In Wu's account, collectivisation was needed for socialist industrialisation, for raising agricultural productivity, and for keeping a socialist direction in the countryside. Wu credits collective organisation with pooling land and labour, expanding mechanisation and irrigation, supporting commune and brigade enterprises that later fed township and village enterprises, running supply and marketing cooperatives, and providing schooling, cooperative medical care and the "five guarantees". Wu also credits it with reshaping farmers' political participation, values and family life. Wu concedes problems, including the price scissors between industry and agriculture, weak property and distribution rules, and tensions between administrative orders and farmers' voluntarism, but denies that these amount to the failure of the collective system. For the present, Wu proposes developing collective economy in forms suited to local conditions, on a voluntary basis and without "rushing" or mass campaigns, so that smallholders are linked to modern agriculture rather than eliminated. Wu also calls for collective channels and supply and marketing reform to reduce smallholders' exposure to merchant capital. Finally, Wu argues for Party branch leadership so that capital serves farmers and common prosperity is not undermined, citing Tangyue in Guizhou and Yantai as examples. Read the original if you want a favourable reassessment of the collective era, with historical detail and policy implications for rural revitalisation, from a Chinese academic perspective.

Practical explorations in China's forestry development, 1949–1966 1949—1966年我国林业建设的实践探索 Ren Ling Ren Ling asks how the Communist Party built up forestry in the first seventeen years of the People's Republic, starting from a country that, according to the author, had forest cover of only 8.6% in 1949. The article argues that this period laid the foundations of forestry work and that, by 1966, China had begun to find its own path of forestry development. It holds that this experience still offers lessons for forestry work and for building an ecological civilization today. The article runs from 1949 to the national forestry work conference of February 1966, which it treats as a historical turning point. It is organised in three parts: the leadership and the actors of forestry construction; the policy of protecting, planting and tending forests while harvesting and using them rationally; and the regulations, forest ownership rights and tree-planting funds that supported this work. Ren draws mainly on Party and State Council directives, ministerial regulations, and remarks by Mao Zedong, Chen Yun, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and others. Ren's first main point is that Party committees at each level were made responsible for forestry. Mass mobilisation under the mass line, state forest farms and specialised training institutions supplied the planters, the labour force and the expertise. Second, the founding guideline of 1950 was "universal forest protection, key-area afforestation, rational felling and use". It was adjusted over time by timber-saving measures, comprehensive use of wood and scientific research, and after the Great Leap Forward, which Ren says caused predatory logging. Third, institutional arrangements settled ownership and funding. These included the principle "whoever plants owns" (1961), a distinction between state, collective and individual forests, and a forest-nurturing fund drawn from timber sales costs. Ren says these steps tried to link ownership, management and income so as to protect peasants' enthusiasm for forestry. Ren concludes that by 1966 China had over 200 million mu of young plantations, more than 3,500 state forest farms and an annual planting capacity of about 40 million mu, according to the article's figures. The author credits the Party's leadership, the mass line and analysis of specific problems for these results, and holds that these lessons still bear on forestry work and ecological civilization today. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of early People's Republic forestry policy, ownership rules and funding mechanisms as presented in Party-history scholarship.

Enriching and developing the Marxist theory of productive forces: scientific guidance for accelerating the building of an innovation-oriented country 丰富和发展马克思主义生产力理论 为加快建设创新型国家提供科学指引 Liu Yapin This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in 2022, asks how Xi Jinping's statements on innovation-driven development relate to the Marxist theory of productive forces. Liu Yapin argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) these statements have enriched and developed that theory and give scientific guidance for accelerating the building of an innovation-oriented country. The piece sets out four propositions of Xi's, each paired with a claimed theoretical contribution. They are: innovation as the "primary driving force" of development; scientific and technological innovation as the strategic support for raising productive forces; the "three-stage leap" of scientific and technological achievements; and innovation as an important driver of world development. Liu's reasoning follows a repeated pattern. Each proposition is anchored in a Marxist premise: productive forces are the fundamental driving force of social development, science is part of productive forces, and science becomes a real, direct productive force only when applied in production. Xi's formulations are then presented as extending these premises. The author reads the "primary driving force" formulation as building on the earlier thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force. The "three-stage leap", from scientific research through experimental development to popularisation and application, is described as a path for turning technology into real productive forces. Liu concludes that Xi's expositions deepen the Party's understanding of how productive forces relate to scientific and technological innovation, and offer a global perspective for countries facing shared risks and challenges. The author credits the innovation-driven development strategy, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, with raising China's productive forces and comprehensive national strength. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style example of how Xi's innovation discourse is tied to the Marxist theory of productive forces.

Guiding the correct handling of the relationship between production and distribution: the contemporary significance of Marx's labour theory of value 指导正确处理生产与分配关系马克思劳动价值论的时代意义 Huang Shao'an Huang Shao'an, writing in the People's Daily in 2022, asks what Marx's labour theory of value offers for handling the relationship between production and distribution today. The author argues that, although the theory arose from analysis of private-ownership commodity economies, its account of general laws of commodity production and exchange still guides the building of a socialist market economy in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The short commentary first summarises the theory's main distinctions and then draws three practical implications. These are that labour creates wealth and value, that productive labour strengthens the country, and that income distribution should reflect labour's contribution. Huang identifies four distinctions in Marx's theory: concrete and abstract labour; necessary and surplus labour; social and private labour; and productive and non-productive labour. From these the author derives policy points. Because labour creates value, diligence and hard work should be promoted at the stage of promoting common prosperity, and labour's share in primary distribution should rise. Because productive labour creates material wealth, the real economy should be strengthened, avoiding what the author calls the 'shift from the real to the virtual' seen in some countries, and factor markets reformed so that factors are rewarded by their market-assessed contribution. Huang adds that productive labour now includes producing knowledge, technology, information and data, so the creative and complex labour of scientists, technicians and managers should be rewarded in line with its contribution. The author concludes that Marx's theory remains relevant to economic development and to distribution policy under common prosperity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese economist links Marx's labour theory of value to current policy on distribution, the real economy and technical labour.

The critical, revolutionary and practical logics of Marx and Engels's thought on spatial justice 马克思恩格斯空间正义思想的批判逻辑、革命逻辑与实践逻辑 Yuan Tangwei Zhang Zhiquan Western spatial theorists such as Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja, the authors report, treat classical Marxism as a 'spaceless' and closed system with four defects: an epistemological gap, an outdated critique, a useless theory of revolution and a hopeless vision of the future. Yuan and Zhang answer that Marx and Engels did hold a thought on spatial justice, and that Marxism is a 'double helix' of time and space, not a one-dimensional theory of time. They call on scholars to 'return to Marx and Engels' against the tendency to belittle or discard Marxism. The article first establishes that Marx and Engels's thought on space was present, drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Engels's writings on English cities. It then organises the argument in three logics: critique (how spatial injustice arises), revolution (how it is overcome) and practice (how it is realised). The last section turns to socialism with Chinese characteristics and ends with a brief afterword. On critique, the authors argue that Marx and Engels traced capitalism's spatial divisions to capital itself at three levels. These are class segregation within cities, the rural–urban rupture, and a global 'centre–periphery' structure.
