On revolution, they argue that Marx and Engels required a three-part programme: a revolution in productive forces, an ethical revolution and violent revolution. They hold that dialogue with capital and the reformist 'right to the city' leave the capitalist mode of production intact. They credit the Communist Party of China with adapting this to China through 'encircling the cities from the countryside'. On realisation, they say spatial justice means productive, distributive and ethical justice. They argue that China's land system, the rural revitalisation and targeted poverty-alleviation strategies, 'people's cities', ecological civilization and shared human values have put these into practice. In their view this refutes Harvey's claim that the communist prospect is spatially vague. The authors conclude that Xi Jinping's ideas, including 'lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets', the new development philosophy and 'joint contribution, joint governance and shared benefits' in social governance, uphold and extend Marx and Engels's thought on spatial justice. They present these ideas as a guide for building socialist equal space, regulating the production of urban space and realising spatial human rights. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja, or an example of how Chinese urban and rural policy is framed as spatial justice.

Advancing as one the efforts to make officials dare not, be unable to and not want to be corrupt 一体推进不敢腐不能腐不想腐 Song Wei This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in September 2022, takes up the Party's anti-corruption approach of making officials dare not, be unable to and not want to be corrupt. Song Wei argues that advancing these three aims as one is an important experience of the new era. In the author's account it has become the basic anti-corruption policy and a key strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The piece begins from Xi Jinping's recent speech to a seminar for provincial and ministerial-level leading cadres, which reviewed the previous five years. Song then explains the logic of the three aims, describes how enforcement and institution-building have been carried out, and closes by linking the campaign to the Party's long-term position. Song contends that corruption results from long-accumulated factors, personal, environmental and institutional, so no single measure can cure it. Not daring to be corrupt is the precondition and rests on punishment and deterrence. Being unable is the key and rests on institutional constraint. Not wanting to is the foundation and rests on education. The three are an organic whole, not three stages, and must work together. The author describes a policy of "no forbidden zones, full coverage, zero tolerance" and the pursuit of "tigers", "flies" and "foxes", alongside oversight reform and ideological education. Song also presents learning from cases, reforming and governing on the basis of cases as a working method that reduces existing corruption and curbs new cases. Song concludes that the anti-corruption struggle is a protracted battle of the Party's self-reform. The author holds that the Party must win it to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall and keep the people's trust. Song calls for greater ability to advance the three aims together. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of the rationale behind the Party's anti-corruption method.

Marx's view of capital and its contemporary significance 马克思的资本观及其现实意义 Yao Manlin Yao Manlin asks what Marx's analysis of capital, developed in the era of free-competition capitalism, offers for understanding and using capital in China today. The article argues that Marx's view of capital rests on three claims: capital is a production relation, it has both a barbaric and a civilising face, and the capitalist is the personification of capital as an economic category. Yao holds that each claim yields practical guidance for how capital should be regulated and guided under socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article has four sections. The first treats capital as a socio-historical phenomenon and sets Marx against bourgeois economists. The second examines the two faces of capital. The third examines the relation between capital and the capitalist, and the fourth sums up the theoretical contribution and present relevance of Marx's view. Each of the first three sections ends with implications for contemporary China, drawing on texts such as Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts, Wage Labour and Capital and The Communist Manifesto. Yao reads Marx as showing that money becomes capital only where the objective conditions of labour are separated from labour itself and labour-power becomes a commodity. Capital is therefore a relation of unpaid appropriation of surplus value, not a mere thing. On the second claim, Yao says capital's barbarism lies in primitive accumulation, in alienation driven by the pursuit of profit, and in the inherent limits of capitalist production. Its civilising role lies in advancing productive forces, dissolving feudal bonds and preparing the conditions for socialism. Yao insists that barbarism dominates and that the civilising side must not be stretched into a defence of exploitation. On the third claim, Yao says Marx held that capital implies the capitalist, but did not blame individuals for the system. From this Yao draws the conclusion that entrepreneurs in China are not capitalists. From these arguments Yao draws policy lessons. These include systemic thinking, with the market playing the decisive role in allocating resources and the government playing its role better. They also include bottom-line thinking against the disorderly expansion of capital, and rule-of-law thinking that sets "traffic lights" for capital. Yao adds that labour creates value, that wealth should be understood as use value, and that entrepreneurship should be promoted. Yao concludes that Marx's view of capital also offers a method that joins philosophy, political economy and socialism, a critical spirit that bears on Frankfurt School and ecological critiques, and resources for handling capital in an era of globalisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar derives current policy on regulating capital from Marx's texts.

Understanding "Marxism works" through the essence of the epoch 从时代精华角度读懂“马克思主义行” Jia Yingjian This short commentary in Guangming Daily takes up Marx's dictum that every true philosophy is the spiritual quintessence of its time. Jia Yingjian argues that the line explains why Marxist philosophy keeps pace with the demands of the epoch. The author presents Marxism as an innovative, open body of theory and an intellectual forerunner of social progress. The piece begins from Xi Jinping's reaffirmation of the saying at a Politburo study session of the 18th Central Committee. It then sets out four claims about how Marxist philosophy relates to its era, and closes with the task of building a modern socialist country. Jia argues that Marxist philosophy is a scientific theory grounded in its epoch and develops historically as social being and social life change. It advances through answering the questions of the age, and the author credits the Party leadership since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with answering the questions of what kind of socialism with Chinese characteristics to uphold and how. Marxist philosophy also marks the height of the spirit of the age, and the author says the Party has combined it with the creative transformation of traditional Chinese culture. Finally, it drives change in the epoch and shows the power of "changing the world". Jia concludes that applying contemporary Chinese Marxist theory in practice will let the Party meet the "great test" of building a modern socialist country. The author calls for stronger ability to grasp and steer the times. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary links Marx's view of philosophy and the epoch to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

Historical materialism and the historical summing-up of the Communist Party of China's century of struggle 唯物史观与中国共产党百年奋斗的历史总结 Li Weiwu Li Weiwu asks how the Party's 2021 Resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's centennial struggle, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, uses historical materialism to sum up the Party's history. Writing in 2022, the author argues that the Resolution is a model of researching and writing Party history on a historical-materialist basis, and that it works as a "mirror of history" showing where the Party has come from and where it is heading, and why this course is historically reasonable. The article rests on the long Chinese tradition of drawing lessons from history and on Mao Zedong's Yan'an-era call to study the Party's own history. It organises the Resolution's approach under five headings: its guiding principle (a correct view of Party history), its method (seeking truth from facts), its logic (examining the process and giving an overall assessment), its focal point (establishing the new era), and the lines of thought that follow for Party-history writing. Li draws on Feng Youlan's distinction between history as it happened and history as written, on Cai Hesen's early Party-history writings, and on Mao's and Xi Jinping's statements. Li's central claim is that correct Party history requires combining historical objectivity with the discovery of historical regularity. Merely listing facts, the author says, blurs the distinction between essence and surface, mainstream and tributary, and invites historical nihilism. The Resolution's division of the century into four periods and its account of three leaps in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context are presented as expressions of this method, as are its five-fold historical significance and ten lessons. Li also argues that the weight given to the new era under Xi Jinping rests on an objective change in the principal contradiction in society and in the Party's tasks. In this account, the Two Establishes follow from the historical reading. Li concludes that studying Party history from a historical-materialist standpoint means holding together three linked elements: historical objectivity, historical regularity and historical initiative, the last being the conscious activity of people acting within objective laws. Li treats the Resolution as having unified these elements, and as therefore giving the Party's "yesterday, today and tomorrow" a coherent reading. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how the official Party-history narrative is justified methodologically, or of how the 2021 Resolution is read within Chinese Marxist philosophy.

Accurately grasping the logic and path of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party in the new era 准确把握新时代全面从严治党逻辑路径 Ni Bangwen This commentary, published in Economic Daily in September 2022, asks how the Party's strategic policy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party should be understood in the new era. Ni Bangwen takes as a starting point the 2021 Sixth Plenum resolution on the Party's century of struggle. The author argues that the policy has a clear logic, with a starting point, a destination and a point of leverage, all tied to the Party's founding mission of seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation. The piece is built in three sections. The first, "everything for the people, everything relying on the people", deals with the Party's class basis and with democracy. The second concerns ensuring that the Party remains the strong leadership core, and the third concerns persisting in self-reform. Ni draws on Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and on the Marxist idea that a proletarian party has no interests separate from those of the proletariat as a whole. Ni's central move is to link Party discipline to popular legitimacy. The Party, in this account, has no special interests of its own, so it can examine its own faults honestly. Whole-process people's democracy, with its rights to information, participation, expression and supervision, is said to let the people supervise power and to keep it in a "cage" of institutions. The author then ties the Party's leadership to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to the risks the Party faces, listing four tests (holding power, reform and opening up, the market economy, the external environment) and four dangers (slackness, insufficient capacity, detachment from the masses, corruption). Self-reform is presented as three paired efforts: ideological education alongside rule-based governance, a healthy political culture and ecology, and campaigns against misconduct together with anti-corruption work. Ni concludes that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party must cover every area and stage and be sustained, so that the Party does not change in character. Specific proposals include continued centralised study campaigns, making the Party constitution the basic reference, upholding democratic centralism and the Two Upholds, strictly enforcing the eight-point regulations, and following a "zero tolerance" approach to corruption. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party-building and anti-corruption policy were justified in the run-up to the 20th Party Congress.

Did Marx really believe the circulation process creates value? Upholding the monism of "productive labour creates value" and its implications for the new era 马克思真的认为流通过程能创造价值吗？ Wang Xianpeng Does circulation, including transport and commerce, create value? Wang Xianpeng takes up a dispute that has run in Chinese scholarship since the 1960s and was revived by the growth of the tertiary sector. Through a close reading of Marx's texts, the article argues that Marx never held that circulation creates value. In Wang's account, Marx held a monist position: only productive labour creates value. The article has four parts. It first shows that productive labour creating value is the foundation of Marx's critique of political economy. It then examines the passages in Volume 2 of Capital that are most often cited to support value creation in circulation. Next it sets out four judgements on how to read Marx correctly. It ends with the significance of the monist position for contemporary China. Wang's first move is to read Marx's Economic Manuscripts of 1861–63 and the Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy as limiting the "labour" that creates value to labour that is directly exchanged with capital in capitalist production. In this reading, services and "total labour" fall outside that concept. The second move is a re-reading of the Capital passages on transport, storage and the "total circuit". Wang stresses Marx's wording: "adding" value rather than creating it; "for the individual capitalist" circulation costs may "act as value-creating", which concerns price mark-ups; and what transport sells is a "useful effect", not a commodity. Wang adds a logical test: if circulation created value, the same commodity transported short, long or not at all would have different values, and the "created" value would have nowhere to go. Wang also treats transport profit as a transfer of surplus value from industrial capital. Wang concludes that circulation labour is unproductive but still important, since it enables the realization of value and use-value. The author holds that abandoning the monism would split theory from practice, damage the theoretical legitimacy of a socialist state and open the door to claims that Marxism is outdated. Wang calls for upholding fundamental principles while supplementing them for new conditions, as an aid to strengthening the real economy, curbing the disorderly expansion of capital and advancing common prosperity. Read the original if you want a text-based case against value creation in circulation, or want to see how this debate is tied to current Chinese economic policy.

New trends in the development of left-wing parties amid Europe's political transformation 欧洲政治转型背景下左翼政党发展新动向 Wu Yunxi Postwar European party politics rested on a relatively stable contest between left and right mainstream parties. Wu Yunxi argues that since the 2010s, a series of crises has fragmented party systems and blurred the boundaries between old and new, mainstream and non-mainstream parties. The article's thesis is that Europe's left has entered a new phase of adjustment, marked by sharply divergent electoral results, flexible governing alliances and serious difficulties in office. The article treats the left as three families: social democratic parties, green parties and radical left parties, each with its own group in the European Parliament. It then proceeds in three steps: electoral performance across Western, Northern, Southern and Central-Eastern Europe, the forms of governing cooperation, and the challenges the left faces once in government. It draws on many national cases, including Germany, the Nordic states, Portugal, Spain, France, Britain, Greece and Finland, and on recent election figures. Wu's central claim is that social democracy is split between recovering parties (Germany, the Nordic countries, Portugal) and parties in steep decline (France, the Netherlands, Greece, much of Central and Eastern Europe). Greens have gained from climate politics, and new radical left parties such as Syriza and Podemos surged and then fell back, while old communist parties remain weak. Fragmentation, rightward drift and populism mean that single-party majorities are rare. Social democrats now depend on minority governments, multi-party coalitions and cross-camp deals, as in Portugal, Spain, Finland and Germany's three-party coalition. Wu identifies three challenges in office: policy differences and rivalry with partners, instability when partners withdraw, and limited resources and room for error amid economic weakness, polarisation and the pandemic. Wu concludes that social democracy suffers a deeper crisis of representation, policy effectiveness and social base than the centre-right, and that in some countries short-term weakness has become long-term decline. Greens and radical left parties, in this reading, have not yet shown they can replace it, and Syriza's brief tenure exposed the practical limits of new parties' programmes. The Portuguese Socialist Party is singled out as a useful model, having united the left, balanced growth, public spending, employment and deficit reduction, and won repeated re-election. Read the original if you want a dense, data-rich survey of European left parties' elections, coalitions and governing problems as of 2022.

Grasping the milestone significance of the great transformations of the past decade in the new era 深刻把握新时代十年伟大变革的里程碑意义 Zhong Xiaowu Published in Guangming Daily on 25 August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary by Zhong Xiaowu explains Xi Jinping's statement that the great transformations of the past ten years in the new era are of milestone significance. Xi made the statement in a speech to a study session for provincial and ministerial leaders. Zhong argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core has produced historic achievements and historic changes. In this account, China's development now stands at a new historical starting point. The article is organised around the areas in which Zhong sees these changes. It moves from the Party itself to the economy and the first centenary goal, then to reform, the road of socialism with Chinese characteristics and institutional development. It then turns to theory, Chinese modernization and global initiatives, and finally to the Chinese nation, ethnic unity and traditional culture. Zhong places the decade within the history of the Party, the People's Republic, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation. On the Party, Zhong argues that its leadership has been comprehensively strengthened. The author cites the Two Establishes, the Two Upholds, the campaign against corruption and the Party's self-reform as the means by which the Party found a path out of the historical cycle of rise and decline. On the economy, Zhong cites GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000, a rise in China's share of the world economy from 11.3% to over 18%, and the lifting of nearly 100 million people out of poverty. Zhong states that a moderately prosperous society has been built in all respects. Zhong also credits the decade with the creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, described as Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. It is also credited with a Chinese modernization that, in the author's words, breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and shifts the contest between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour. The article adds a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. It concludes that the nation is closer than ever to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which it calls irreversible. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary summarised the achievements of the Xi era on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

Accurately grasping the profound meaning of the "Two Integrations" 准确把握“两个结合”的深刻内涵 Xie Hui This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 24 August 2022, takes up how to understand the Two Integrations: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xie argues that the formula deepens understanding of the laws governing adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Grasping its historical necessity, theoretical logic and practical innovation, the author says, is essential for understanding how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era took shape. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's remarks at a seminar for provincial and ministerial-level leading officials ahead of the 20th Party Congress. The text is organised in three numbered sections: historical necessity, theoretical logic and practical innovation. The first traces the Party's theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, to Xi Jinping's thought. The second turns to the reception of Marxism in China after the Opium War and the October Revolution. The third addresses the practical orientation of the Two Integrations and what they require today. Xie's central claim is that Marxism succeeded in China because the Party rooted it in Chinese soil and because it can connect with fine traditional culture. The author cites ideas such as great harmony under heaven and the people as the foundation of the state, which are said to resonate with human emancipation, common prosperity and the free and all-round development of each person. Integration with tradition is described not as repeating particular cultural content but as drawing out its spirit through creative transformation and innovative development. In the article's account, the Party's revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture share a root with traditional culture, and this underpins the path of Chinese modernization. Theory, Xie says, becomes a material force once the masses grasp it, and the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) are attributed to the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought. Xie concludes that the Two Integrations must keep developing in step with practice. Contemporary China's social change and practical innovation are said to give them strong momentum and wide scope. The author calls for deep excavation of the ideas and moral essence of traditional culture, reinterpreted with the spirit of the times, so that Chinese civilisation regains its brilliance and Marxism in twenty-first-century China opens new horizons. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the Two Integrations just before the 20th Party Congress.

The strategic significance of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation 铸牢中华民族共同体意识的战略意义 Wang Yanzhong Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Wang Yanzhong asks why forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation (zhulao Zhonghua minzu gongtongti yishi) should be the main thread of the Party's ethnic work. The author presents it as a major original thesis put forward by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, in response to new conditions in ethnic affairs. Wang's answer is that its strategic importance can be understood on five levels: political, theoretical, practical, contemporary and cultural. The commentary is built as a sequence of five headed sections, each with two sub-points. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks during an inspection tour of Xinjiang, on the Central United Front Work Conference, on the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work, and on the Party's regulations on united front work. It is a short, programmatic piece that interprets official positions rather than introducing new empirical material. On the political level, Wang argues that the formulation embodies the Party's overall leadership of ethnic work, now placed within the "large united front work pattern", and keeps that work on course by subordinating ethnic consciousness to the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community. On the theoretical level, the author calls it the latest result of adapting Marxist ethnic theory to Chinese conditions and a basis for correct views of the nation and of history, one that requires education and countering hostile forces. In practical terms, Wang says it is a guide for ethnic work and a basic principle for handling major relationships, leading to the dialectical unity of commonality and difference. In terms of the times and culture, the author links it to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, to Chinese and overseas Chinese unity, and to the tradition of "great unity", which Wang says seeks common ground while accepting differences. Wang concludes that the concept is an inherent requirement of high-quality development in ethnic work and of building a modern socialist country. It is also, in the author's account, the ideological precondition for strengthening the "five identifications", especially identification with Chinese culture, without setting identification with one's own ethnic group against identification with the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Party scholars justify this central concept of current ethnic policy and which documents and formulations they rely on.

Seeking the code to the success of a century-old Party 探寻百年大党为什么能够成功的密码 Sang Donghua Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Sang Donghua asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to endure and succeed over a hundred years. Taking as his starting point the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Sang answers that the Party's ideals, original aspiration, fundamental purpose, theoretical character and political courage for self-reform have stayed constant through every change of circumstance. The article is a short commentary organised into four numbered sections, each describing the Party through a single identity: a mission-driven party, a party of the people, a party armed with scientific theory, and a team of revolutionaries. Each section runs through the revolutionary, socialist-construction, reform-era and post-2012 periods, drawing on quotations from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, on Party documents and on episodes from Party history. Sang argues that the Party has held to socialism and communism as its goal since its founding in 1921, citing a figure of more than 370 martyrs on record from 1921 to 1949. Its strength, in Sang's account, comes from adhering to a people's standpoint, and Sang points to the Long March story of the shared quilt and to the poverty-alleviation campaign, in which 98.99 million rural poor are said to have been lifted out of poverty under current standards. Sang also credits the Party's ability to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The last strand is self-reform: Sang holds that the Party's greatness lies not in avoiding mistakes but in confronting its own problems, through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and anti-corruption work. Sang concludes that the Party's century of history is one of striving for lofty social ideals, of unity with the people, of continuous theoretical innovation, and of using great self-reform to lead great social revolution. These four features are presented as the explanation of why the Party has remained the firm leadership core. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary summarises the sources of the Party's success for a general readership in the year of the 20th Party Congress.

The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of governing the Party through institutions 中国共产党制度治党的探索历程 Chi Buyun Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Chi Buyun asks how the Chinese Communist Party has come to rely on institutions to govern itself, and how that reliance has developed over a century. Chi defines governing the Party through institutions as the making and enforcement of intra-Party regulations, forming a system that regulates relations inside the Party and between the Party, the state and society. The author argues that this approach is an important support for keeping the Party advanced and for keeping Party building and the Party's cause moving in step. The short article follows four historical periods. It starts with the New Democratic Revolution, when the concept of intra-Party regulations was first put forward. It then covers socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and finally the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Chi draws on Party constitutions, regulations, and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping. Chi's account is of cumulative development. Before 1949, Party constitutions and regulations, such as those adopted in 1938 and the 1945 Seventh Congress constitution, established democratic centralism and rules for leadership bodies. After 1949, the Eighth Congress (1956) made specific arrangements for collective leadership. Chi concedes, however, that no broad consensus or lasting mechanism took shape across the Party. After 1978, Deng Xiaoping stressed that institutional questions are fundamental and long-term, and by the turn of the century institution-building was formally part of the overall layout of Party building. Since 2012, the author reports, there are over 3,600 Party regulations in force (as of July 2021), covering all levels and categories. Chi also lists the "seven focuses" guiding their improvement. Chi concludes that ideological and organisational Party building must be combined with institutional governance, with political discipline as the priority. Chi calls institutional governance the Party's "unique code" and claims that it offers a useful reference for party governance and political civilisation worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed chronology of how Party-regulation building is presented in Chinese Party-building discourse as of 2022.

Excellent Chinese etiquette culture should be integrated into the cultivation of core values 中华优秀礼仪文化应融入核心价值观培育进程 Han Yunzhong Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, Han Yunzhong asks how traditional Chinese etiquette culture can help root the core socialist values in everyday life. The author argues that etiquette and values are inherently consistent and mutually dependent, so that passing on the best of etiquette culture should be built into the cultivation of the core socialist values. The short commentary first defines traditional etiquette culture and shows that it already carries values such as harmony, civility, good faith and friendliness. It then explains the distinctive role etiquette plays in nurturing values, and ends with four practical routes for linking etiquette to the core socialist values. Han argues that etiquette has long shaped and transmitted values: coming-of-age, marriage, funeral, village-drinking and court rites each convey particular virtues, internalised as belief and externalised as conduct. Because rites cover every stage of life, they make abstract values visible and tangible and win emotional assent. Citing Xi Jinping on values as a form of virtue, Han holds that etiquette is the outward form of morality, so it promotes moral behaviour. Han calls for a Marxist-guided, creative transformation of etiquette that discards outdated elaborate ritual. The four routes are education, environmental influence through ceremonies and festivals, family traditions and instructions, and institutional norms such as citizens' pacts, village rules and codes of conduct. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the core socialist values are linked to traditional ritual culture in Chinese public discourse.

"People make their own history" “人们自己创造自己的历史” Ye Zexiong Zhao Ting Ye Zexiong and Zhao Ting, in a commentary first published in Guangming Daily in August 2022, ask what Marx and Engels meant by history and who makes it. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that the people are the creators of history, they argue that the formulation in The Holy Family, that history is nothing but the activity of human beings pursuing their own aims, offers a worldview and a method for grasping the direction of historical development. The piece has three sections. The first sets the masses as creators of history against idealist history. The second treats history as practical activity with purposes and an orientation. The third turns to the Chinese Communist Party's mass-line view of history, from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. The authors contend that idealist history, which credits emperors, generals and heroes, errs epistemologically by taking ideas and motives as causes, and errs in class terms by serving exploiting classes. Historical materialism instead starts from "real individuals" and the resultant of many wills (Engels's "parallelogram of forces"), and holds that the masses create material and spiritual wealth and decide social change. Ye and Zhao add that history is practice, and that its purposes are set by people from their own needs and the possibilities reality offers, not by "reason" or the "absolute spirit". They conclude that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has pursued a people-centred approach to development and has relied on the people to eliminate absolute poverty, build a moderately prosperous society and fight Covid-19. Reaching the second centenary goal of a modern socialist country, the authors say, requires fuller use of the masses' initiative and creativity. Read the original if you want a short, official-style statement of how the mass-line view of history is derived from Marx and Engels and applied in Party discourse.

Grasping the power of thought and drawing on the strength of truth On studying volume four of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China 感悟思想伟力 汲取真理力量 Wang Rui This commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 25 August 2022, is a study guide to the fourth volume of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China. Wang Rui presents the volume as an authoritative account of how the Party led the people in responding to changed circumstances and opening a new situation. The author argues that studying it closely helps Party members, cadres and the public to understand why the Party has succeeded so far and how it can keep succeeding, and so to understand the Chinese path, Chinese governance and the reasoning behind them. The piece is organised around five things readers are urged to grasp. They are the essence of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times; the Party's character of confronting risks and waging struggle; the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind; the political resolve to lead a great social revolution through a great self-reform; and the strengthening of historical confidence and a sense of responsibility. Wang draws throughout on the volume, on Xi's statements and on the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's historical achievements and experience. On theory, Wang follows the resolution in describing Xi's thought as twenty-first-century Marxism that has achieved a new leap, and says the volume sets out the "Ten Clarifications" and explains Chinese modernization. On struggle, the author describes a world of great change, the pandemic and mounting risks, and holds that national rejuvenation will not come easily, so cadres must sharpen their ability to struggle. On self-reform, Wang presents it as the Party's second answer to the question of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall, after Mao Zedong's 1945 answer of supervision by the people, and links it to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Wang also says the community with a shared future for mankind rejects zero-sum thinking and answers talk of a "China threat". The article ends by calling on cadres to treat the Party's centenary experience as a source of historical confidence, and to see the establishment of Xi's core position and the guiding status of his thought as the most important political outcome of the new era. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the official press framed the study of this volume in 2022.

The German Ideology in the development of Marx's thought 马克思思想发展中的《德意志意识形态》 Niu Ziniu Niu Ziniu asks what place The German Ideology should occupy in Marx's intellectual development. The commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, argues that the manuscript, now widely seen as a birthplace of the materialist conception of history, represents only a rudimentary form of that theory. In Niu's account, it comes before two decisive turning points and should be assessed with that in mind. Niu locates the manuscript between the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach on one side, and later works on the other. The first public statement of the materialist conception of history was The Poverty of Philosophy (1847), and its classic formulation is the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. The author marks two nodes: the 'historical principle' (every principle has its century) and the completion of the critique of political economy in the Grundrisse and the 1859 work. The text proceeds in three steps: what The German Ideology established, what it left unfinished, and how later work corrected it. Niu credits the manuscript with establishing the basic content of the materialist conception of history. It brings Marx's critique of German idealism and of Feuerbach's old materialism into a social-historical frame, moving from 'real individuals' and their life-process rather than from abstract categories. It also links this to a revolutionary political stance. Niu then argues that the manuscript does not apply the historicity of categories to itself. Its general concept of 'production' and its use of 'capital' for feudal society treat categories of capitalist society as timeless, and Niu says this shows a residue of Hegelian derivation from abstractions. Marx's own self-criticism in the Grundrisse is cited as evidence. There Marx holds that thought must move from the abstract to the concrete, and that materialism differs from idealism because it treats every abstraction as the product of a given historical concrete totality. Niu concludes that Marx did not first complete the materialist conception of history and then apply it to political economy. Rather, he built and refined it through the critique of political economy. The Hegelian residue is, in Niu's view, an immaturity and not a distinctive value of the manuscript. By 1859 its content had largely been sublated into the later work, which Niu offers as one reason Marx abandoned publishing it and left it to 'the gnawing criticism of the mice'. Niu grants its philological value but calls for a cautious, realistic assessment of its place. Read the original if you want a short, critical account of why The German Ideology should be read as an early stage in Marx's development and not as his mature statement of historical materialism.

Practical materialism from the perspective of the reconciliation of body and mind 从肉体与精神和解的视角看实践唯物主义 Wang Xiaosheng Since reform and opening up, Chinese Marxist philosophy has given weight to the foundational status of practice and has often understood itself as "practical materialism". Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, Wang Xiaosheng notes that scholars still disagree on how to read this, chiefly over whether practice or matter comes first. Wang argues that neither side can settle the dispute, because both assume that body and mind are separate, and that this assumption itself needs to be examined. The article's answer is that Marxism seeks a reconciliation of body and mind, and that practical materialism is best understood on that basis. The article is a short philosophical commentary in three parts. It begins with Engels's account of the basic question of philosophy and its roots in early humanity's belief that thinking is the activity of a soul. It then turns to Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment and to Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology. Finally it applies the reading to Marx's critique of the Young Hegelians, to the notion of "reality", and to the theory–practice relation. Wang argues that the opposition of body and mind is a basic fact of human survival, not merely a mistaken idea. Drawing on the Odysseus and Sirens episode in Dialectic of Enlightenment, Wang holds that humans must restrain their bodily nature to survive, and that this opposition underlies civilisation and the modern subject–object split. Fixing the opposition as the only mode of existence is also mistaken, in Wang's view, because it yields an instrumental reason that drives the body to self-harm. Body and mind are neither naturally unified nor wholly opposed; Wang reads Marx's account of communism as resolving the conflict between humans and nature, including their own nature, as pointing to a dialectical unity-in-opposition, or reconciliation. On this basis Wang treats dialectical and practical materialism as essentially the same: material priority is granted within the opposition, but thought is carried into practice, and Marx's "practical subject" is the reconciled living person. Wang concludes that Marx's critique of the Young Hegelians, his idea of "reality" as distinct from Hegel's, and his words as bound to reality all depend on this reconciliation. Wang warns that purely spiritual "love" can turn cold and even justify killing. In Wang's view, practical materialism overturns the body–mind and subject–object framework, marking a major change in the history of philosophy and offering guidance for present-day social practice. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese argument that links the debate over practice versus matter to the Frankfurt School and the early Marx.

The polyphonic character of Marx's early intellectual development 马克思早期思想发展的复调性特征 Li Yaxi Li Yaxi questions the standard account that Marx turned to Bruno Bauer's philosophy of self-consciousness in 1837 and wrote his doctoral dissertation on that basis. The article notes that Bauer only built his self-consciousness system after reaching Bonn in 1840, which leaves a gap in the history of ideas. Drawing on Marx's early notebooks in MEGA2, Li argues that Marx's early thought and dissertation are "polyphonic", combining heterogeneous and conflicting intellectual sources. The piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2022, is short. It begins with Marx's letter of November 1837 and his law studies in Berlin, then covers the dispute between the historical school and the rationalist school of jurisprudence, and Marx's teachers Savigny and Eduard Gans. It then turns to Marx's contact with the Doctors' Club and Bauer, and to the Epicurus Notebooks, the Berlin Notebooks and the Bonn Notebooks. Li argues that in 1837 Marx was still mainly absorbed in law, and that his move to philosophy extended the jurisprudential debate between Savigny and Gans. Bauer, then still a Hegelian of the right, had not yet developed his own system. In the Epicurus Notebooks Marx criticised a subjective spirit detached from substance and wanted to ask how philosophy relates to the world. Bauer rejected this in letters of 1841, and Marx probably compromised because he hoped for Bauer's help with the teaching-qualification exam. In the Bonn Notebooks Marx treated art through "social connection", which Li traces to the objective rationalism of Gans. Li concludes that the background of the time, independent research and practical needs left Marx's writing with incompatible sources, which form the polyphonic character of his texts and thought. Li also finds in Gans the roots of the rationalist view of the state Marx held at the Rheinische Zeitung. Read the original if you study the young Marx, the Bauer–Marx relationship or the MEGA2 notebooks and want a concise argument against a straight line from Bauer to the dissertation.

The theoretical responsibility of historical materialism 历史唯物主义的理论担当 Chen Lixin This short commentary, published in a Chinese newspaper in 2022, asks why Marx and Engels's The German Ideology deserves repeated reading today. Chen Lixin argues that the work gave the first relatively systematic statement of historical materialism's basic principles. In Chen's account, the doctrine shows a distinctive "theoretical responsibility" (lilun dandang) in how it faces both thought and the real world. The piece opens by noting that major world events send people back to Marxism, and cites Derrida's remark that failing to read and discuss Marx would be an error of the age. It then moves through three headings: raising philosophical ontology through the historical principle, entering the real life-process, and revealing the dialectical movement of modern society. Chen traces the lineage from Vico through Kant and Hegel to Marx. Chen's central claim is that Marx brought history into the ontology of philosophy. Earlier philosophy started from consciousness or self-consciousness and proved being through the deduction of categories. Marx, by contrast, started from real individuals and their sensuous activity, explained ideas from practice and ended the philosophy of conceptual deduction. Chen adds that historical materialism holds that the production and reproduction of real life is decisive in history. Because human activity is social by nature, the author says, individuals develop only in community, and the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse drives history. Chen holds that Capital, by showing the relation of capital and labour as the axis of modern society, extends this insight. Chen concludes that the historical principle, the demand of reality and the movement of society together display the unmatched theoretical responsibility of historical materialism. Chen argues that the doctrine helps people grasp the nature and likely course of the logic of capital today. It can also answer a modern "spiritual hunger" amid material abundance. Re-reading The German Ideology with this awareness is, for Chen, indispensable. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of why the classic text is still treated as central to Marxist philosophy.

The Bonn Notebooks and research on the young Marx's philosophical thought 《波恩笔记》与青年马克思的哲学思想研究 Liu Bingjing Liu Bingjing asks what pushed Marx away from Young Hegelian idealism in 1842–1843. The usual account stresses Feuerbach and the material-interest questions of the Rheinische Zeitung period. Drawing on the Bonn Notebooks as published in MEGA2, Liu argues that an earlier theoretical factor was already at work before the Rheinische Zeitung and prepared Marx's first intellectual turn. The short newspaper article describes the Bonn Notebooks as the remains of a failed plan to write a critique of religion with Bruno Bauer. Marx abandoned the plan in early 1842 and, from April to May in Bonn, excerpted works on the history of religion and art. These included Charles de Brosses, Karl August Böttiger, Benjamin Constant and Christoph Meiners. Liu concentrates on the Constant excerpts from On the Religion of the Ancients. Liu identifies two critical threads in Constant that Marx noted. The first is synchronic: religion arises from human society's real need to communicate with the invisible, yet priests monopolise that mediation and turn human-made religious power into domination. The second is diachronic: religious forms harden over time and obstruct religious feeling, so a church claiming to be eternal can be exposed as falsely so. Liu contends that this offered Marx a critique starting from human reality, as opposed to Bauer's self-consciousness, which treats religion as alienated self-consciousness to be overcome by the awakening of a few. Liu concludes that the Constant excerpts probably moved Marx towards Feuerbach's materialism. Marx's letter on his disagreement with Feuerbach about religion's essence and some materialist statements in his 1842 articles are offered as support. Together with the material-interest question of the Rheinische Zeitung period, the Bonn Notebooks are said to have driven Marx's turn to materialism. Read the original if you want a brief account of how the MEGA2 Bonn Notebooks bear on the debate over Marx's break with Bauer.

Mao Zedong's idea of people's constitution-making in the 1954 Constitution and its implications “五四宪法”中毛泽东人民立宪思想及其启示 Zhang Xiaoshuai Marking the 40th anniversary of the current 1982 Constitution, Zhang Xiaoshuai asks what the 1954 Constitution (the "Five-Four Constitution") reveals about Mao Zedong's idea of people's constitution-making (renmin lixian). The author argues that existing scholarship relies too heavily on hindsight or Western constitutional theory, and that the 1954 text should be read within Mao's own thought and the historical evolution of China's constitutional system. The article is a research article published in 2022. Zhang does not examine the Constitution's detailed provisions. Instead the article considers three aspects of how Mao's thought shaped it: its foundations (the creation of "democratic facts" and of "the people" as the constituent subject), its purposes (the state system, the system of people's congresses and the general line for the transition period), and its drafting methods. A final section draws four implications for implementing the current Constitution in full. On foundations, Zhang reports Mao's view that a constitution recognises democratic facts already won through revolution, so that earlier documents such as the Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China failed for lack of them. On purposes, the 1954 Constitution established people's democratic dictatorship and wrote the general line for the transition period into its preamble. Zhang contends that the Constitution lost force after socialist transformation was completed in 1956 not because it was instrumental, since all Chinese constitutions set development goals, but because it set only a transitional goal rather than a long-term one. The drafters, in this reading, also neglected constitutional amendment. On methods, Zhang cites Mao's combination of leadership and mass opinion (the author cites over 150 million participants in the draft's discussion), reliance on national conditions, critical borrowing from foreign constitutions, and a balance of principle and flexibility. Zhang draws four lessons for implementing the current Constitution: stress its legal character, including constitutional interpretation and review; protect human rights, understood through China's conditions and with subsistence and development rights as primary; improve whole-process people's democracy; and combine national conditions, traditional legal culture and critical borrowing from abroad while upholding Party leadership and rejecting Western "constitutionalism". Read the original if you want a Chinese constitutional-law reading of Mao's approach to the 1954 Constitution and the way it is linked to current official discourse on implementing the Constitution.

Always upholding the value pursuit of putting the people first 始终坚持人民至上的价值追求 Wan Guangxia Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Wan Guangxia comments on Xi Jinping's speech at a seminar for provincial and ministerial leaders held ahead of the 20th Party Congress. Wan reads the speech's call to serve the people wholeheartedly as a restatement of the historical lesson of "putting the people first", and as an expression of the value pursuit of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that the Party must keep to this principle on the new journey. The short piece is organised under three headings: placing the people's interests in the highest position, respecting the people's principal position, and promoting all-round human development and common prosperity for all. On the first, Wan holds that the people's stance is the Party's basic political stance, that the Party has no special interests of its own, and that the people are the foundation of its governing position. Wan cites the 19th Party Congress's adoption of "putting the people at the center" as a basic principle. On the second, Wan invokes historical materialism, Marx and Engels, and Mao Zedong to present the masses as the decisive force in history, and calls for using the mass line, respecting people's initiative and learning from them. On the third, Wan links human development to the aim of common prosperity. Wan concludes that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism and a feature of Chinese modernization. Wan describes it as prosperity of all, material and cultural, and neither the wealth of a few nor egalitarian levelling. Wan calls for high-quality development, social fairness and justice, and the balanced handling of competing interests. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's "people first" principle was presented to a general readership just before the 20th Party Congress.

The people's standpoint is the fundamental standpoint for promoting the spirit of historical initiative in the new era 人民立场是新时代弘扬历史主动精神的根本立场 Li Yuyan This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 24 August 2022, asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to hold the "historical initiative" through more than a century of changing tasks and crises. Li Yuyan argues that the root answer is the Party's consistent adherence to the people's standpoint, and that promoting the spirit of historical initiative in the new era requires keeping to it. The article defines the spirit of historical initiative as a state of mind: grasping historical laws under Marxist guidance, following the main trend of history, acting proactively and innovating. It is organised in three parts, treating the people's standpoint as, in turn, the logical premise for understanding historical laws, the greatest source of confidence for shouldering historical responsibility, and the solid foundation for recognising the people's status as the subject of history. In the first part, Li reads modern Chinese history as showing that earlier patriots failed to change the nation's fate because they did not stand with the people and so could not grasp historical laws. Marxism-Leninism, in Li's account, moved Chinese people from passivity to initiative because it takes the people's standpoint. In the second, Li surveys the Party's stages from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, presenting each as responsibility borne for the people. In the third, citing Engels and Xi Jinping, Li contends that only this standpoint sees the masses as creators of history, and illustrates it with poverty alleviation and epidemic control. Li concludes that promoting historical initiative means keeping close ties with the people, applying a people-centred philosophy of development, developing whole-process people's democracy, pursuing common prosperity, and relying on the people. Read the original if you want a short, representative example of how Party theorists in 2022 linked the spirit of historical initiative to the people's standpoint.

Leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform 以党的自我革命引领社会革命 Li Xiaodong Writing in Guangming Daily on 22 August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Li Xiaodong argues that the Communist Party of China can carry out a great social revolution only because it is also capable of great self-revolution. The commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at a seminar for provincial and ministerial leading cadres, to use the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. Li presents this as the key to consolidating the Party's long-term governing position and keeping the people's support. The piece is organised in three numbered sections. The first presents the principle as an inherent requirement of a Marxist party's historical mission. The second reads it as the accumulated experience of revolution, construction and reform, from the Gutian, Zunyi and Yan'an episodes to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the post-2012 period. The third treats it as the key to meeting the changes in the world, the times and history. Li defines social revolution, on Marxist premises, as grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, covering both the overthrow of the old political superstructure and the building of a new society. Self-revolution means continual self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. Citing Engels and Lenin on the value of internal struggle and of openly admitting mistakes, Li holds that the two processes are organically unified and reinforce each other. Li cites the fall of dynasties and of long-established parties abroad as evidence that failing to confront internal problems is fatal. For the new era, Li points to the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, the anti-corruption campaign and the cases it brought down, and Party education campaigns as a set of measures that, in the article's account, helped the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Li concludes that the Party's work is unprecedented in breadth, depth, sharpness, difficulty and complexity, and so calls for greater urgency, initiative and foresight in self-revolution. Li stresses that the "four dangers" and "four tests" remain severe, that problems of impurity in thought, politics, organisation and style are unresolved, and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is never finished. The article ends with confidence that a Party able to break an old world and build a new one will keep winning victories. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official line on self-reform was framed for a general readership on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The natural yardsticks and spatial dimensions of common prosperity 共同富裕的自然尺度与空间维度 Chen Huixiong Writing in a newspaper commentary of July 2022, Chen Huixiong asks how common prosperity can be given a concrete measure and an internal structure. Drawing on Marx's definition of wealth as a thing that satisfies human needs, Chen defines prosperity as the degree to which wealth adequately meets needs. Common prosperity is then a shared but differentiated sufficiency across people's different levels of need. The article proposes two "natural yardsticks" and three "spatial dimensions" for realising it. The piece is organised in two parts. The first sets out the two yardsticks: meeting people's reasonable needs as the goal, and the carrying capacity of natural resources as the limiting boundary. The second applies a systems perspective to divide common prosperity into three levels: harmony between humanity and nature, prosperity among people, and prosperity of body and mind. A short conclusion ties the two parts together. On the first yardstick, Chen distinguishes needs ("needs") from wants or desires ("wants"). Citing the economic happiness equation (happiness = utility/desire), Chen argues that no growth in productive forces can satisfy ever-rising desires for money, so common prosperity must be measured by reasonable needs. On the second, Chen calls for abandoning growth that ignores ecological capacity and for using the dual carbon goals and high-quality development to advance common prosperity. Of the three dimensions, Chen treats harmony between humanity and nature as the premise, holding that without it there can be no prosperity among people. Prosperity among people is to come from individuals' "productive effort", fair distribution and a mix of government-led design with market competition. Chen adds that psychological poverty now needs more attention than physical poverty. Chen links this three-level structure to the traditional Chinese idea of the unity of heaven and humanity. Chen concludes that common prosperity is an essential feature of socialism and that the two yardsticks and three dimensions are all indispensable. Only by taking people's growing need for a better life as the goal and natural carrying capacity as the limit can a more sustainable common prosperity be achieved. Chen presents this as the way to sustainable development of people, economy, society and ecology together. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how ecological limits and spiritual well-being are being built into the concept of common prosperity.

On accelerating the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics 关于加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学 Xi Ge Shu Yating This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks during his inspection of Renmin University of China. Xi Ge and Shu Yating argue that these remarks raise basic questions about the standard, substance and path of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, and that they call for systematic study and elaboration. The article is organised around three paired relationships. The first is between "Chinese characteristics" and "world-class" status, which the authors treat as the question of standards. The second is between building Chinese-characteristic philosophy and social sciences and building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, which they treat as the question of substance. The third is between philosophical and social science work and the training of talent, which they treat as the question of path. On standards, the authors invoke historical materialism: universal laws of civilizational progress are realised through particular national paths. They argue that a universal standard detached from particulars is a "pseudo-universal", so world-class university standards must be internalised and creatively transformed to fit China's conditions. On substance, they contend that answering the questions of the times and upholding the Two Integrations are the guiding requirements. Citing Xi, they hold that the field's main task is to build an autonomous knowledge system. In their view, whether the field has Chinese characteristics depends less on the "outward forms" of disciplinary, academic and discourse systems than on the "substantive core" of an original, autonomous body of knowledge. On path, the authors call on scholars to be "great teachers" (da xiansheng), combining teaching and research and uniting the roles of "teacher of classics" and "teacher of conduct". They conclude that a new path to a Chinese-characteristic, world-class university lies in unifying the building of Chinese-characteristic philosophy and social sciences with the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. They present this unity as an expression of the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-aligned account of how Chinese academics interpret Xi Jinping's 2022 remarks on academic autonomy and university building.

Deepening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to keep it vigorous 深化全面从严治党 永葆旺盛生命活力 Wang Yonghua Yang Shixue Published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, this short commentary asks why the Communist Party of China must keep deepening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Wang and Yang argue that governing the country requires first governing the Party, and that strict governance affects the fate of the Party, the state and the nation. They conclude that it is the necessary road for the Party to stay vigorous and to pass what the text calls the "new examination". The article is organised in three sections: a historical summary, the theoretical support, and practical requirements. The first traces the principle of strict Party governance from the Party's founding through the democratic revolution, the early People's Republic and the period of reform and opening up, to the new era. The second sets the policy within the "Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy" and Marxist Party-building theory, and the third lists concrete tasks. In the authors' account, strict governance has been a constant of Party history. It is credited with winning popular support, strengthening Party unity and discipline, and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), with ending lax and soft Party governance and securing an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle. Theoretically, Wang and Yang hold that the nature of a proletarian party decides what kind of party must be built. They hold that its fundamental purpose, serving the people wholeheartedly, requires strict discipline, since slack discipline and unpunished corruption would cost popular support. They also say the Party still faces the "four tests" and "four dangers", and that political building must come first. For practice, the authors propose four tasks: strengthening ideals and convictions education, improving conduct by tackling formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, enforcing political discipline and rules, and building a rule-based system of Party regulations. They call for Party members to uphold the Two Upholds, for zero tolerance in anti-corruption work, and for discipline that binds everyone without exception. They also call for integrating rule-based Party governance with law-based national governance. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 presented the historical logic, theoretical basis and practical agenda of Party discipline.

Accurately grasping the theoretical character and practical logic of "people-centredness" 准确把握“以人民为中心”的理论特质和实践逻辑 Gao Fengni Writing in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in July 2022, Gao Fengni asks what the "people-centred" development philosophy advanced by Xi Jinping consists of, and how it works in practice. The author argues that it draws on three sources: the historical-materialist view of the masses as makers of history, the "people as the root" (minben) tradition of Chinese culture, and the Chinese Communists' own view of the people. In Gao's account, Xi creatively developed these into the principle of upholding the people's principal position. The piece is a short commentary in three parts. It first traces the idea's historical lineage from Mao Zedong's 1945 call to serve the people wholeheartedly, through Deng Xiaoping, to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), citing the 2021 Resolution on the Party's century of struggle. It then sets out the idea's theoretical character, and finally its practical logic. On theory, Gao names three features. The first is the Marxist view of the masses as the creators of history, which the author says has been carried forward through the Party's purpose of serving the people and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The second is traditional minben thought, from the Shang and Zhou notion of protecting the people to the image of the ruler as a boat and the people as water. Gao treats this as compatible with historical materialism and as a cultural gene that Xi's formulation lifts to a higher level. The third is the value of people's free and all-round development, in which Gao reads the Party's concern with raising living standards and, since 2012, with people's sense of fulfilment and common prosperity. On practice, Gao argues that putting the people first means ranking the people's interests above all else, mobilising their initiative to raise labour efficiency, and using the people's own judgement as the measure of the Party's work. Pursuing common prosperity is presented as the route to realising those interests. Gao concludes that, with the principal social contradiction having changed in the new era, work must shift from meeting material and cultural needs to meeting the people's needs for a better life. The author calls for attention to livelihood issues, economic growth, better governance and stronger cultural soft power. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Chinese commentators trace the lineage of Xi Jinping's \"people-centred\" formula and relate it to Marxism and Chinese tradition.

The contemporary significance of Marx's labour theory of value 马克思劳动价值论的时代意义 Huang Shao'an This short commentary, published in People's Daily in August 2022, asks what Marx's labour theory of value still offers China today. Huang argues that, although Marx built the theory on an analysis of private-ownership commodity economies, its account of general laws of commodity production, exchange and market development guides the building and improvement of the socialist market economy. The piece first summarises the theory's content, then draws out its implications for production and distribution in what it calls the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It ends with the changing scope of productive labour in the modern economy. Huang identifies the dual character of labour as Marx's main advance over bourgeois classical economics. Labour is divided into concrete and abstract, necessary and surplus, private and social (private labour becoming social only through exchange), and productive and unproductive. From this Huang derives three values: labour creates wealth, productive labour strengthens the country, and income distribution should reflect labour's contribution. Policy follows: raise labour's share in primary distribution, strengthen the real economy and avoid economic 'hollowing out', and deepen market-based allocation of production factors so that rewards follow contribution. Huang adds that productive labour now includes producing knowledge, technology, information and data. Creative and complex labour by scientists, technicians and managers therefore deserves pay matching its contribution, which would also raise China's position in global industrial and value chains. The article presents the theory as a guide to common prosperity and to balancing production and distribution. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese economist links Marx's value theory to current policy on distribution and the real economy.

The pendulum effect in Latin American political development and the features of the new left-wing wave 拉美政治发展的钟摆效应与新一轮左翼浪潮的特点 Li Han Yuan Dongzhen Latin American politics, the authors argue, swings like a pendulum, with left- and right-wing parties competing and alternating in office. After the 'pink tide' of the early 2000s and a short rightward turn after 2014, left-wing parties returned to power in several countries, producing a second left-wing wave this century. The article contends that this wave is both a product of the pendulum effect and a reflection of the region's present economic, political and social conditions. The article first traces the left's fortunes from the late nineteenth century through the Cuban Revolution, Cold War repression, democratisation and the end of the Cold War. It then recounts the first pink tide (from Hugo Chávez's election in 1998), the rightward retreat from 2009 to 2019, and the left's recent victories in Mexico, Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Honduras and Nicaragua. The remaining sections set out the left's general traits, seven features of the new wave, its causes and its prospects. The authors say the left shares a base among the middle and lower strata, anti-elitism, support for state intervention and an anti-US orientation, though the boundary with the right is blurred and shifts over time. Compared with the first wave, the new one arises in a weaker economy, with Latin American output down 6.8% in 2020. Its governments are more pragmatic in their priorities and more moderate in their line, and they take a softer stance towards the United States. They also lack a regional leader, rest on weaker legislative support (the article cites Peru's Pedro Castillo and Chile's Gabriel Boric) and find continuous rule harder. The authors attribute the wave mainly to the pendulum effect after the right failed to reverse economic decline, to the appeal of the left's equality agenda amid rising poverty and unemployment, and to anti-establishment sentiment. In their reading, many voters were punishing incumbents rather than endorsing left-wing ideology. The authors conclude that the new wave shows the left's vitality, since poverty and inequality remain severe and keep its message attractive. Multiparty competition, entrenched elites, voter weariness of long incumbency and weak institutions, however, make long continuous left-wing rule unlikely. They expect the left cycle to be shorter than the first and the pendulum to swing faster. Read the original if you want a detailed, data-rich Chinese academic account of Latin America's second left-wing wave and its limits.

Mao Zedong's methodological characteristics in advancing the "Two Integrations" 毛泽东在推进“两个结合”中的方法论特质 Peng Bingbing How did Mao Zedong's thought emerge from the integration of Marxism with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture? Peng Bingbing argues that this integration, which the article calls the Two Integrations, did not happen spontaneously. It required the conscious subjectivity and methodological awareness of Marxist theorists. The article identifies three methodological traits in Mao's practice and presents them as essential for grasping the core of Mao Zedong Thought and for taking the Two Integrations further. Published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2022, the article is organised in four parts. Three main sections each take up one trait, quoting a phrase of Mao's as a heading: problem awareness and theory-building, the scientific system and its national form, and the people as subject together with mass-oriented discourse. A short conclusion links them to the unity of worldview and methodology. Peng draws on Mao's investigations, his texts from the 1920s to the 1940s, and classical statements by Marx and Engels. First, theory starts from real problems found through investigation. Peng traces Mao's founding of a Russian studies society (1920), his Hunan peasant report (1927), his rural surveys and his 1930 dictum that without investigation there is no right to speak. Mao's later "seeking truth from facts" line is read as a synthesis of Marxist principle and Chinese tradition, centred on the overall question "where is China headed?". Second, Marxism must take a national form with "Chinese style and Chinese manner". Peng points to Mao's 1938 call to make Marxism concrete in China, his recasting of traditional concepts such as knowing and doing, and his dialectics of contradiction. Third, the people are the subject of history. Peng links this to Mao's mass line and to his use of vivid popular idiom, noting a count of over 2,000 set expressions in the first four volumes of the Selected Works. Peng concludes that the worldview and methodology of Marxism must be unified in practice, which happens only when theory is made concrete. Because Marxist philosophy is a practical philosophy oriented to the activity of the people, the author holds that adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions must continually address problems that concern the masses. Its results must take national forms and a popular style. On this basis the article calls the sinicization, contemporisation and popularisation of Marxism internally unified. Read the original if you study Mao Zedong Thought, Marxism's adaptation to Chinese conditions, or how Chinese scholars derive method from Mao's practice.

The historical contributions and limitations of Chen Duxiu's atheist thought 陈独秀无神论思想的历史功绩与局限性 Cao Jialiang Li Hong Chen Duxiu, co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party and a pioneer of Marxist atheism in China, wrote on superstition and religion a century ago. Cao and Li ask how his atheist thought should be assessed today, at a time when the Party has passed its centenary. They argue that he made major contributions to spreading atheism in China, but that his thinking had clear limits: it was not thoroughly Marxist and remained entangled with religion. The article is published in the journal Science and Atheism (2022, no. 4). It has two main parts, followed by a short conclusion. The first part sets out Chen's merits under three headings: his critique of feudal ghost-and-spirit culture, his exposure of the worship of deities, and his dialectical reflections on basic questions about religion. The second part examines three limitations. The authors draw on Chen's essays, his polemics with Kang Youwei and Yi Yixuan, and his later writings on the Red Army. On the positive side, Cao and Li report that Chen denied that ghosts are objective matter, treated them as human inventions, and blamed fatalism and karmic belief for national weakness. He opposed idol-making and the revival of Confucianism as a state religion. He held that religion would not soon disappear, that it has both good and bad social effects, that freedom of belief includes freedom to criticise religion, and that mission schools served foreign domination. On the negative side, the authors argue that Chen rested his case on evolutionism, never clearly affirmed the primacy of matter, and drifted towards agnosticism. They also say he praised Buddhism, favoured a "better religion" to replace worse ones, and could not separate religious philosophy from theology. In their view, he lacked sympathy for peasants caught up in superstition, dismissing them as "vagrant proletarians" and bandits, unlike Mao Zedong and Li Dazhao, and so gave up leadership of anti-theistic work. They link this to his later "right-capitulationist" line.
