The authors conclude that Chen's insights helped spread Marxist atheism and open the way for its adaptation in China, so his contribution cannot be erased, while his errors and their negative effects cannot be ignored. They urge that he be judged within the historical conditions of his time, not by today's understanding alone. Read the original if you want a Party-journal assessment of Chen Duxiu's views on religion, with extensive quotation from his early essays.

Mao Zedong's thought on adult mass education in the revolutionary base areas during the New Democratic Revolution 论新民主主义革命时期毛泽东在根据地的成人民众教育思想 Ren Lin Du Junhua The article asks how Mao Zedong's thinking on educating the adult rural population took shape in the Communist-led base areas, and what it achieved. Ren and Du argue that adult education, built on literacy campaigns, was essential for mobilising peasants for revolutionary war. In their account it also left lasting experience for adult education in the People's Republic and in the present. The authors begin with the background: after 1927 the Party moved its centre of gravity to the countryside, where the base areas were poor, remote and overwhelmingly illiterate. They cite Xu Teli and Li Weihan on illiteracy of 95 to 99 per cent in the north-west. They then set out the content of Mao's ideas in two periods, the Soviet areas of the land revolution era and the Shaan-Gan-Ning base area during the War of Resistance against Japan. Next they review practice and results, and close with lessons for today. The central argument is that Mao tied education directly to the needs of war. In the Soviet areas the task was to eradicate illiteracy, raise class consciousness and give men and women equal educational rights. During the anti-Japanese war the stated aim became education that served a protracted war. The authors describe three channels of practice: literacy groups, night schools and winter schools; Lenin rooms, libraries and people's education centres, including the blackboard newspaper; and revolutionary folk songs and yangge and Qinqiang performances. They cite statistics, such as the figure that women made up 69 per cent of Xingguo night-school students, to claim lower illiteracy, better hygiene awareness and stronger collective and patriotic consciousness. In their reading, peasants thereby became a reserve force for the army and the war effort. The authors conclude that this experience opened a path of educational development suited to China's conditions, and that night schools, literacy groups and winter schools later became standard methods of adult education after 1949. For the present they propose linking adult education to production and daily life, encouraging technical training to ease skills shortages, and adding practical courses to compulsory and higher education. They also call for adult education guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and spread through websites, apps, film and television. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of base-area literacy and mass-education methods, and of how Chinese scholars link them to current adult-education policy.

A deep understanding of the new stage of development 深刻理解新发展阶段 Qu Qingshan Writing in Qiushi in 2022, Qu Qingshan sets out how the new stage of development (xin fazhan jieduan) should be understood. The article presents entering this stage as a major strategic judgement by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core. Qu argues that the stage is the period of comprehensively building a modern socialist country and marching towards the second centenary goal, and that studying Xi's statements on it has great practical and historical significance. The article is organised as a sequence of six topics, each introduced by a question and answered mainly through extended quotations from Xi Jinping. They are the stage's historical position, its material foundation, its goals, its relation to the primary stage of socialism, its relation to the new era, and its relation to Chinese modernization. A last section treats the link between the new stage, the new development philosophy and the new development pattern. Qu's first move is historical. He traces the quest for modernization from the Opium War, through Sun Yat-sen's plans and the founding of the Party in 1921, to the 1954 and 1964 modernization goals, reform and opening up, and the leap from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong" after 2012. The material basis, he says, is the completion of a moderately prosperous society and the poverty-alleviation campaign, for which he cites 832 counties lifted out of poverty and a GDP above 100 trillion yuan. His second move concerns periodisation: the new stage lies within the primary stage of socialism, which he describes as dynamic and not static, so that quantitative accumulation moves towards qualitative change. The new era and the new stage differ in length but share the same tasks and goals. Qu concludes that the new stage carries two phased goals: basic socialist modernization by 2035 and a modern socialist country by the middle of the century. This modernization must have Chinese characteristics, which he lists as huge population scale, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement, harmony with nature and peaceful development. He holds that the new stage supplies the historical position, the new development philosophy the guiding principle and the new development pattern the path for economic modernization. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the official 2022 account of the new stage of development, built on Xi Jinping's formulations, ahead of the 20th Party Congress.

Strengthening Marxist atheist propaganda in a targeted way 有针对性加强马克思主义无神论宣传 Zhu Xiaoming Writing in Science and Atheism (2022, no. 4), Zhu Xiaoming takes up the call of the 2021 National Conference on Religious Work to "strengthen Marxist atheist propaganda in a targeted way". Zhu argues that this requires first grasping the conference's spirit fully and accurately, then clearing away intellectual obstacles, and then making atheist education more precisely aimed in content and audience. The piece is a commentary linked to the work of the China Atheism Society. The article opens with the Party's theory of religious work for the new era, summarised in the "nine musts", and reports two advances by the China Atheism Society in 2022. These are a Marxist atheism teaching unit with three lectures in training courses for religious-affairs cadres, and support for a northwestern university's course for undergraduate and graduate students. It then proceeds in three parts: observing religious questions politically, three ideological obstacles to atheist education, and ways to make the propaganda more targeted. In the first part Zhu stresses that religious work is political and policy-driven, not merely administrative. Zhu distinguishes two "essences": religion's essence is illusory, while religious work is in essence mass work, so neither claim may cancel the other. Zhu also contends that the "freedom of religious belief" of the bourgeoisie differs fundamentally from the Party's policy, since the workers' party seeks to free belief from religion. In the second part Zhu rebuts three attitudes: that atheism needs no separate promotion because Marxism already covers it, that propaganda is useless, and that criticising theology is too risky. Zhu cites Lenin and the Indian controversy of 2022 over remarks about the Prophet. Zhu proposes limiting the critique of theology to the ideological sphere, aiming it at core ideas such as the immortality of the soul rather than at believers, and using education, not administrative measures. Atheist propaganda should not be conducted in religious venues or among believers. Zhu also calls for opposing the bundling of religion with ethnicity, for an alliance of social and natural scientists to answer questions at the edge of science, and for four target areas: cadre education, schools, public outreach and scholarship. Priorities are atheism courses in Party schools, universities and, in suitable form, primary and secondary schools. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese atheist-society scholar translates the 2021 religious-work conference into concrete educational and propaganda tasks.

Revering China's fine traditional culture 敬仰中华优秀传统文化 Cai Wencheng This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in July 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's call during an inspection in Sichuan to revere China's fine traditional culture and strengthen cultural confidence. Cai Wencheng argues that national strength rests on cultural flourishing and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires the development and prosperity of Chinese culture. The piece moves through four steps, each anchored in quotations from Xi Jinping. It treats culture as a force for national survival, describes the content of fine traditional culture, considers its role amid global upheaval, and links it to the Party's path of Chinese modernization. Cai contends that China's civilisation, which the author calls the only one in the world to have continued without interruption, sustained the nation through hardship. Fine traditional culture, in this account, carries the nation's "roots and soul" and helps people form correct views of history, nation, state and culture. Cai says that in an era of what the article calls changes unseen in a century and a pandemic, the Party must hold to Marxism, a Chinese cultural standpoint and openness to foreign cultures. The author adds that the Party succeeded because it combined Marxism with China's specific realities and with its fine traditional culture. Cai concludes that the Chinese Communist Party has taken root in Chinese culture and that contemporary social change offers scope for the creative transformation and innovative development of tradition. The author calls for giving this heritage new value through the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary presents cultural confidence and the Two Integrations in 2022.

The Communist Party of China's sublimation of fine traditional Chinese culture 中国共产党对中华优秀传统文化的升华 Liu Kaimei Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2022, Liu Kaimei asks how the Communist Party of China has related to fine traditional Chinese culture. The short commentary argues that the Party has not merely inherited this culture but raised it to a higher level. Liu presents this as the result of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional culture, and as a historical responsibility of the Party. The article is organised around five paired themes, each setting a traditional idea against a Party outlook. They are "the people as the root of the state" and the Party's view of the people; "change from ancient to modern" and its view of reform; the complementarity of virtue and law and its view of governing the country; "unity of heaven and humanity" and its view of development; and "great harmony under heaven" and its view of humankind. For each, Liu first traces the idea through classical sources, from the Book of Documents and Mencius to Sima Qian, Liu Zongyuan, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. Liu's core move is to claim a line of continuity from each classical idea to a current Party position, with the Party carrying the idea further. The tradition of people-centred governance is said to be realised in the Party's purpose of serving the people and in common prosperity. The tradition of change is linked to reform and innovation, the building of a socialist market economy and a community with a shared future for mankind. The Confucian pairing of virtue and law is linked to combining rule of law with rule by virtue, with socialist core values running through the whole process. Harmony between humans and nature is linked to the new development philosophy and the saying that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets. The ancient pursuit of an ideal society is linked to the Party's leadership from revolution through construction to reform. Liu says the traditional idea supplies the cultural foundation and the Party's outlook gives it fresh vitality. Liu concludes that over a century of revolution, construction and reform, the Party has absorbed the essence of traditional thought, brought out its moral core and raised its value for the present age. Liu calls this a great service to the Chinese nation at the level of its cultural roots. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2022 framed the Marxism–tradition relationship through five classical ideas.

Continuously deepening research on the Chinese national community 不断深化中华民族共同体研究 Zhang Jingze This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 13 July 2022, asks how universities for ethnic minorities should contribute to forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation. Taking Xi Jinping's description of this task as the "key link" of the Party's ethnic work in the new era, Zhang argues that such universities must keep deepening research on the Chinese national community and use it to educate students and teachers. The piece is organised under three headings, each opening with a statement by Xi Jinping: raising political standing and treating the forging of a strong sense of community as the main thread; building historical confidence to support the creation of model areas for ethnic unity and progress; and working quietly and steadily to help build a regular mechanism for publicity and education. Zhang contends that a strong sense of community is the foundation of national unity and ethnic solidarity, and that research should supply scholarly support for unity and stability and help guard against risks in the ethnic sphere. Drawing on the idea of a pluralistic and unified Chinese nation, the author describes Chinese history as one of many peoples jointly building the country. Zhang cites the Central University for Nationalities as an example of research that has informed policy. Research should move towards greater commonality while balancing commonality with difference. Zhang calls for research that traces the origins of Chinese civilization, presents the nation as a community with a shared destiny, and draws lessons from a century of Party ethnic work. It should help teachers and students grasp the relations between commonality and difference, and between national and ethnic consciousness. Zhang presents this as a contribution to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official ethnic-policy language is applied to the mission of ethnic universities.

Pushing forward the historic cause of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 把实现中华民族伟大复兴的历史伟业推向前进 Chinese Society of the History of the Communist Party of China This commentary was published in the People's Daily on 26 July 2022 under the name of the Chinese Society of the History of the Communist Party of China. It starts from Xi Jinping's statement that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires a strong force to lead the people, and that this force is the Communist Party. Its thesis is that history and present reality show there would be no New China and no national rejuvenation without the Party. The piece has four parts. It first explains why the Party took on the historic mission of national rejuvenation. It then reads the Party's century of history as one continuous struggle for that goal, divided into four periods. It next sets out the "new road to the examination" now facing the Party, and ends with a short statement of confidence in the Party leadership. The core argument has two steps. First, the author describes the decline of China after the Opium War of 1840 and argues that earlier movements, from the Taiping to the 1911 Revolution, failed because they lacked the correct path and leadership. In this account the Party emerged in 1921 from the combination of Marxism-Leninism and the workers' movement. The author presents it as armed with Marxism and as the vanguard of the working class, the Chinese people and the nation, so that its leading role was "the choice of history and of the people". Second, the author lists what the Party achieved in the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The author attributes the prospects of rejuvenation to the Party's leadership, its grasp of historical trends, its adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and its Party's self-reform. Looking ahead, the author warns that rejuvenation will not be easy, citing "changes unseen in a century", a harsher international environment and demanding domestic tasks. The author calls for applying the "ten upholds" of the 2021 historical resolution, keeping to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics (rejecting both a closed, rigid road and one of abandoning socialism), advancing Chinese modernization, and carrying forward the great founding spirit. It also calls for the broadest united front at home and abroad. Read the original if you want a compact example of the official Party-history narrative of national rejuvenation as it was presented in mid-2022.

Overseas scholarship on the relationship between Mao Zedong Thought and Marxism-Leninism Debates and four forms of misreading 海外视阈下毛泽东思想与马克思列宁主义的关系问题研究 Sun Shuai How have scholars outside China understood the relationship between Mao Zedong Thought and Marxism-Leninism, and what does that understanding imply for judging China's socialist road? Sun Shuai surveys the overseas debates and argues that much of this work misreads Mao Zedong Thought, whether through academic limitations, dogmatic textual reading or Cold War political motives. Sun holds that Mao Zedong Thought inherits and develops Marxism-Leninism. The first part traces the debate chronologically. It covers Edgar Snow, John King Fairbank, Benjamin Schwartz and Stuart Schram, the early-1960s exchange in The China Quarterly between Karl Wittfogel, Schwartz and Schram on the originality of 'Maoism', and the 1970s dispute in Modern China involving Richard Pfeffer, Maurice Meisner and others. It ends with Nick Knight's work from the late twentieth century. The second part sorts the misreadings into four types: utopian, populist, nativist and the 'vassal' reading. A conclusion assesses their academic and political significance. Sun credits some contributions: Pfeffer's call to read Mao against revolutionary practice, and Knight's reading of Mao as a modernist who upheld working-class leadership and developed Marxism through New Democracy. Sun then criticises Meisner for presenting Mao as a voluntarist utopian and as a populist who neglected the industrial proletariat. Against this Sun cites Mao's own writings on class analysis and on the shift of the Party's work to the cities in 1949. The nativist reading, exemplified by Terrill's biography, is said to reduce Mao to nationalism and tradition. The 'vassal' reading, associated with Cold War conservatives, Alexander Pantsov and the 1964 charge that On Contradiction copied Stalin, is described as politically motivated and as rebutted by Knight's textual findings. Sun concludes that overseas research has some value and has helped spread Mao Zedong Thought abroad. It is limited, however, by incomplete texts, Western political-science frameworks and ideological bias, and should therefore be read critically, with its new perspectives drawn on and its errors rebutted. Sun adds that clarifying these debates would help China's discourse and its voice abroad. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-side guide to the Western Mao studies controversies and to how Chinese scholars evaluate them.

Practical materialism from the perspective of the reconciliation of body and mind 肉体与精神和解的视角看实践唯物主义 Wang Xiaosheng Since reform and opening up, Chinese research on Marxist philosophy has given the foundational status of practice new weight and has come to read Marxism as "practical materialism". Wang Xiaosheng observes that scholars remain deeply divided over how to understand it, above all over whether practice or matter is primary. In this newspaper essay, Wang argues that the dispute cannot be settled because both sides assume the separation of body and mind, a premise that itself needs reflection. Wang's thesis is that Marxism seeks a reconciliation of body and mind, and that practical materialism and dialectical materialism are essentially the same when read from this angle. The essay has four parts. It first treats the opposition of body and mind as a basic fact of human existence, drawing on Engels's account of the fundamental question of philosophy and on Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment. It then turns to Marx's pursuit of reconciliation, citing the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology. A final part applies this reading to Marx's critique of the Young Hegelians, to the meaning of "reality" in Marx and Hegel, and to the unity of theory and practice. Wang holds that Engels traced the question of thought and being to the "ignorant notions of the age of savagery", yet the separation it names is real: Wang reads the Odysseus and the Sirens episode as showing that survival requires people to bind their own bodies and to control nature. Taken as an absolute, however, this opposition produces an instrumental reason that drives the body to self-harm, and Wang notes that only humans commit suicide. Simple unity of body and mind would be barbarism, so Wang argues that the two stand in a dialectical unity of opposites, which Wang calls reconciliation. Materialism then accepts the priority of matter within the opposition without being confined to it, and reconciliation is possible only in practice, where the "living human being" is the practical subject. On this basis Wang reads the Young Hegelians as thinkers who stayed in words, while Marx's concepts aim to be realised in life. Wang concludes that practical materialism overturns the philosophical framework that divides body from mind and subject from object. In Wang's view it is both a major transformation in the history of philosophy and a guide to contemporary social practice. Wang adds that purely spiritual "love" can turn cold and has been used to justify killing. Read the original if you want a compact example of a Chinese philosophical reading that tries to settle the "practice first or matter first" debate through the body–mind relation.

Reflecting on virtual reality through Baudrillard's philosophy of technology 于鲍德里亚技术哲学反思虚拟现实 Zhang Yungui Zhang asks what Jean Baudrillard's late philosophy of technology can offer for thinking about virtual reality. The article argues that his concept of the "perfect crime", set out in The Perfect Crime (1995), serves as a prophetic warning. In this crime, a technologically produced "perfect world" kills reality without leaving a trace. The short commentary first defines virtual reality in a broad sense as a digital world that interpenetrates the physical one. It then outlines three stages of development: digitising reality ("reality + virtual"), virtual–real symbiosis ("reality × virtual") and full fusion ("reality = virtual") through technologies such as brain–computer interfaces. Zhang acknowledges potential benefits, including expanded creativity and, ideally, features resembling a "free association of individuals". Zhang reads Baudrillard's simulacra and "hyperreality" as a forerunner of the virtual reality concept. At the third stage the author sees a "hyper-hyperreality" in which digital certainty replaces the real, and the real turns from being into nothingness. The same three stages are also read as the killing of illusion, which ends once virtual and real can no longer be told apart. In Zhang's account, people then become nodes in a network, living time becomes labour time, and the result is precise control of individuals, a "pure governance of consciousness". Zhang calls Baudrillard's thought pessimistically technologically determinist but still valuable as a warning. The author notes that many people already spend more time online than offline and take what they see there as the real world. Whether virtual reality brings a "perfect world" or a "perfect crime" is said to depend on balancing instrumental and value rationality and using technology with "good knowledge" and "good regulation". Read the original if you want a brief Chinese philosophical reading of virtual reality and the metaverse through Baudrillard.

The people are the Party's greatest source of confidence in governing and rejuvenating the country 人民是党执政兴国的最大底气 Yang Limin This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in July 2022, takes up the formula that "the people are the Party's greatest source of confidence in governing and rejuvenating the country". Yang draws it from the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which lists "putting the people first" among ten historical experiences. The author's thesis is that the Party's roots, lifeblood and strength lie in the people. The piece has three parts. The first treats the people's standpoint as the fundamental political position of the Communist Party of China. The second reviews the Party's history as one of close ties with the masses. The third turns to the people as the creators of history and to the tasks of the new journey ahead. Yang argues that the people's standpoint distinguishes a Marxist party from other parties, citing the Communist Manifesto on the proletarian movement as one of the great majority in the interest of the great majority. In this account the Party, unlike earlier political forces, has no particular interest of its own and was founded to seek the happiness of the people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Yang names its greatest political advantage as close ties with the masses and its greatest danger after taking power as separation from them. The author cites the mass line, whole-process people's democracy and the achievement of a moderately prosperous society across a population of over 1.4 billion as evidence, and invokes Xi Jinping on the people as the driving force of history. Yang concludes that the Party must keep its flesh-and-blood ties with the people, uphold the people's principal position and respect their initiative. On this basis the Party is to lead them towards the second centenary goal of a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary presents the people-centred rationale for the Party's long-term rule.

Promoting the better conversion of institutional advantages into governance effectiveness 推动制度优势更好转化为治理效能 Shuang Chuanxue Writing in the People's Daily in July 2022, Shuang Chuanxue takes up a judgement Xi Jinping made during the 2022 "two sessions": that China enjoys "five strategic favourable conditions", one of which is the distinctive advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics. The commentary argues that these advantages have been repeatedly proven in practice, and that the task on the new journey is to convert them better into effective national governance. The article has three parts. It first sets out the advantages of the system, which the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) summarised under 13 headings, and which Shuang groups as advantages of value, organisation and operation. It then explains how the institutional system and governance mechanisms should be integrated, and finally lists three requirements for upholding and improving the national system and the system of governance. Xi Jinping's statements are quoted at almost every step. Shuang's core argument is that institutions and governance are dialectically unified. The national system is the basis of governance, while the governance system and governance capacity are where institutional strength is concentrated and realised. A system is superior, the author holds, not only because its design is sound but because it operates effectively and brings tangible benefits. The article cites the response to Covid-19 and the campaign against poverty as proof. In the author's account, these showed the capacity to "concentrate resources on major undertakings" and to coordinate the country "as one chess game", and the author contrasts "China's governance" with "Western disorder". Shuang proposes three requirements: upholding the Party's overall leadership, described as the system's greatest advantage; keeping the people's principal position, which includes finding institutional flaws behind problems the public raises repeatedly; and adhering to fundamental principles while innovating, so that institutions are refined in the course of solving real problems. The author links this to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the second centenary goal. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the link between institutional advantages and governance capacity.

The rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered an irreversible historical process 中华民族伟大复兴进入不可逆转的历史进程 Ma Jiantang Writing in the People's Daily in July 2022, Ma Jiantang assesses the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012). He argues that, under the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, a moderately prosperous society has been fully built and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered an irreversible historical process. The short commentary is organised as five "over the decade" claims. These cover Marxism in China, the maturing of the socialist system, economic and social breakthroughs, the building of a community with a shared future for mankind, and Chinese modernization. Ma first presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the product of combining Marxism with China's realities and its fine traditional culture. He calls it a new leap in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. He then reports results: comprehensive deepening of reform, GDP above 110 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$12,000, victory in the poverty-alleviation campaign and high-quality development. Ma also states that China's contribution to world economic growth has stayed around 30 per cent for several years. On the international side, he credits the Belt and Road Initiative and the global development and security initiatives with addressing deficits in governance, trust, development and peace. Ma concludes that Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilization. In his account it is a modernization of huge population size, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony with nature and peaceful development. He contrasts it with a Western path he describes as capital-centred, polarising and expansionist, and says it offers developing countries a new route and a Chinese approach. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official People's Daily summary of the Party's achievements over the decade from 2012 to 2022.

Promoting steady results in common prosperity 推动共同富裕不断取得成效 Han Keqing This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 27 July 2022, asks how common prosperity can be advanced step by step. Han Keqing argues that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism and a key feature of Chinese modernization. In Han's account it means prosperity for all the people, neither wealth for a few nor egalitarian "eating from the same big pot". The article sets out the staged targets attributed to Xi Jinping: solid progress by the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan, more marked substantive progress and equalised basic public services by 2035, and basic realisation by the middle of the century. It then moves through development, livelihood protection, spiritual life and distribution policy. Han's central reasoning is that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and is the largest developing country. It must therefore first "make the cake bigger" through economic development, then divide it well through institutional arrangements that handle growth and distribution. Han also stresses that common prosperity covers both material and spiritual life and is closely tied to the all-round development of the person. Livelihood measures focus on education, healthcare, elderly care and housing, together with human capital and upward mobility. Cultural measures include core socialist values, patriotic and collectivist education, and public cultural services. Han concludes that common prosperity for over 1.4 billion people is a dynamic process that cannot be achieved at one stroke. Han calls for coordinated primary, secondary and tertiary distribution, stronger tax, social security and transfer-payment adjustment, a larger middle-income group, the abolition of illegal income, and an olive-shaped distribution structure. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line summary of how common prosperity was framed in mid-2022.

The threefold meaning of the essence of Marx and Engels's "science of history" and its contemporary significance 马克思恩格斯“历史科学”实质的三重蕴涵及其现实意义 Hu Haibo Hu Haibo takes up the concept of the "science of history" (历史科学), which Marx and Engels used from The German Ideology to Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy. Chinese scholars read it in conflicting ways: as the "one science" uniting natural science and the science of man, as historical materialism, or as a "genuine positive science" (the last disputed by those who treat historical materialism as philosophy). Hu argues that the concept means a science of human practical activity and its real development, and that this essence has three connected layers. The article has three parts. The first re-reads the concept across the whole corpus rather than through Marx's early texts alone, giving weight to Engels's later definitions in Anti-Dühring, the Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy review, Dialectics of Nature and the Marx graveside speech. The second sets out the three layers and the logic by which they unfold. The third draws lessons for building China's "independent knowledge system", a topic that became prominent after Xi Jinping's visit to Renmin University of China on 25 April 2022. Hu's central move is to show that Engels defined "science of history" as every science that is not natural science, covering human living conditions, social relations, legal and state forms and the ideological superstructure. Since Marx knew and approved this work, Hu holds that neither the "one science" reading nor the pure "historical materialism" reading is adequate. The three layers, set against German ideology, are: first, the basic principles and method of historical materialism (real individuals, life determining consciousness, the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production as a "natural historical process"); second, the "genuine knowledge" gained by applying that method to economics, politics, law, anthropology and other fields, with Capital as the main example; and third, the aim of human emancipation, so that scientific socialism is the proletariat's "science of history". Hu describes the three as mutually conditioning and forming a logical whole, with historical materialism as the foundation. Hu concludes that building China's independent knowledge system continues the Marx–Engels construction of the "science of history" in the new era. He proposes three requirements: adhering to the historical-materialist worldview and method; answering the major theoretical and practical questions facing the Party and country across all disciplines; and holding to a people-centred stance as the value orientation. Read the original if you want a text-based account of how Engels's later writings shape the interpretation of "science of history" and how that reading is tied to current Chinese debates on knowledge-system construction.

Examining and reflecting on Sohn-Rethel's genetic account of the origins of "historical materialism" from a Marxist perspective 马克思主义视域下索恩-雷特尔“历史唯物主义”发生学起源的审视与反思 Tan Yong Alfred Sohn-Rethel claimed to have discovered the "guiding principle of historical materialism". Theodor Adorno summed up his work in the formula "historical materialism is the recollection of origins". Tan Yong asks how this linking of historical materialism to the genetic question of "origin" should be understood, and what its rationality and limits are. The article's answer is that the approach has some kinship with Marx but is one-sided and differs fundamentally from his historical materialism. The article rests mainly on Sohn-Rethel's Intellectual and Manual Labour: A Critique of Epistemology. It first examines his account of the origin of rational knowledge, then his account of the origin of reification. It then turns to Marx's analysis of the origin of the money form in Capital, to test whether the "recollection of origins" has a Marxian basis. Tan also notes Habermas's own attempt to reconstruct historical materialism. Tan reconstructs Sohn-Rethel's argument in two steps. He distinguishes "real abstraction", which arises from people's exchange practice and not from thought, from abstraction in thinking. He then makes money, with its socially synthesising function, the bridge by which real abstraction passes into abstract thought and the theoretical subject. On reification, Sohn-Rethel finds three layers: identity, thing-form and "being-there" (Dasein). He holds that exploitation is its historical origin and that commodity exchange developed out of exploitation. Tan judges this reversal of the relation between commodity production and exploitation to be an error that departs from Marx. Tan then shows that Marx's account of the four value forms, from the simple form to the money form, is itself a tracing of origins. On that basis Tan finds a limited connection with Sohn-Rethel. Tan concludes that Sohn-Rethel's effort offers some reference value for understanding historical materialism. Tan argues, however, that it concentrates on micro-level foundations and stresses only the "recollection of origins". It thereby neglects the broad vision and rich content of historical materialism, and so differs in substance from Marx's own version. Tan urges readers to keep this clearly in mind. Read the original if you study Sohn-Rethel, real abstraction or Adorno's formula, or want a Chinese Marxist assessment of how far they square with Marx's Capital.

Firmly establishing a correct view of Party history 牢固树立正确党史观 Wang Guang Writing in 2022, as the Party marked its first centenary, Wang Guang argues that the study of Party history depends on the right view of history. In the author's account, a correct view of Party history, grounded in historical materialism, determines the attitude and method of historical research and whether lessons can be drawn from it. The commentary rests heavily on Xi Jinping's statements and on the communiqué of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). The piece is a short essay built around three claims about why a correct view of Party history is needed. It is needed for understanding the Party's hundred years of struggle, for uncovering historical laws that guide the Party and state, and for resisting historical nihilism. Wang closes with a note on the present task, at the junction of the "two centenary goals". On the first point, Wang sketches modern Chinese history as a passage from national humiliation under feudal rule and foreign aggression, through failed earlier attempts at salvation, to success under the Party's leadership. The author attributes that success to combining Marxism with Chinese realities and traditional culture and to treating the people as creators of history. On the second, Wang treats recognition of historical laws as the dividing line between historical materialism and idealism, and calls the Party's history one of exploring and applying such laws. Wang presents Xi Jinping's ideas as a new advance in understanding the laws of Communist Party governance, socialist construction and human social development. On the third, Wang lists forms of historical nihilism: exaggerating errors, linking Party history to current problems, and trivialising it with rumour and unofficial accounts. The author cites Xi's explanation of the Soviet collapse as the cost of totally negating Soviet and Soviet Party history. Wang reports that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the correct view has brought clarification of Party history and curbed nihilism, especially online. The author adds that more research and more popular forms of communication are still needed so that the official account becomes a consensus across the Party and society. Wang calls on readers to take Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as guidance and to draw spiritual strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation from history. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 framed the official view of Party history and the campaign against historical nihilism.

Cultivating the Communist's "philosophy of the mind" 修炼共产党人的“心学” Zhong Jun Zhong Jun's commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call to "cultivate the Communist's 'xinxue'" (literally 'learning of the mind', a term borrowed from Ming-dynasty Neo-Confucian thought). It reads the phrase as a demand that Party members, especially leading cadres, firm up their ideals and convictions and strengthen Party spirit. Zhong's thesis is that this inner cultivation rests on three lifelong tasks: steadfast ideals and convictions, remembering the original aspiration and founding mission, and the spirit of self-reform. Written in 2022, the piece is organised around these three tasks and draws heavily on Xi's speeches, notably his remarks at the opening of the Central Party School's training courses for young and middle-aged cadres in autumn 2021 and spring 2022. It also cites Lenin on a serious party's open admission of errors, Xi's 2020 visit to Hunan and the 'half a quilt' story, and the lessons Xi draws from the collapse of the Soviet Union. On ideals, Zhong argues that belief works as a 'master switch'. In the author's account, the loss of conviction explains why the Soviet party fell without resistance, while Chinese Communists' conviction rests on a rational understanding of Marxism and historical laws, not on emotion. Zhong calls for reading Marxist classics closely and for theoretical grounding. On the original aspiration, the author says that the Party's purity does not persist naturally and that members need regular ideological check-ups. Zhong also stresses that a correct view of performance means judging achievements by the people's real experience. On self-reform, Zhong holds that it distinguishes the Party from other parties. Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has achieved results since the 18th Party Congress (2012), but Zhong still points to cadres who are complacent, evade criticism or breach discipline and the central eight-point regulations. Zhong concludes that the 'thief in the heart' is harder to defeat than external enemies, so cadres must guard their inner selves, resist greed and keep to Party discipline from small matters upward. The piece offers a compact guide to how Party theorists present moral and ideological self-cultivation as part of Party building. Read the original if you want to see how a provincial academy head restates Xi Jinping's language on belief, discipline and cadre self-discipline in a Party-building journal.

Upholding and strengthening the Party's centralised and unified leadership over economic work 坚持和加强党对经济工作的集中统一领导 Ding Xiaoqin Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2022, Ding Xiaoqin takes up why and how the Communist Party of China should uphold and strengthen its centralised and unified leadership over economic work. Ding presents this as an important component of Xi Jinping's economic thought and as a necessary consequence of the Party's overall leadership. The central claim is that the authority of the Party Central Committee is the highest principle of Party leadership and the key guarantee that economic work stays on the right course. The article has four parts. It first places economic leadership within the principle of the Party's overall leadership, drawing on the 2021 Resolution on the Party's century of struggle and on Xi Jinping's statements. It then discusses the role of the Central Committee, followed by the institutions through which leadership is exercised at the central, local and state-owned enterprise levels. The last part sets out what is needed to raise the Party's capacity to lead economic work. Ding argues that the Central Committee sets direction, formulates strategy and policy, and bears overall responsibility for economic work. The article traces how the annual Central Economic Work Conferences from 2018 to 2021 increasingly named centralised and unified leadership as a core lesson, and in 2021 as the first priority. In Ding's account, this authority allows the concentration of resources on major undertakings and strengthens the reaction of the superstructure on the economic base. Institutionally, Ding points to the 2018 conversion of the leading small groups on finance and on deepening reform into commissions, the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission's quarterly reviews, local Party committees' collective decisions, and Party committees in state-owned enterprises that discuss major matters before boards and managers decide. Ding proposes three ways to raise the Party's capacity. Leaders should acquire professional expertise through study of Marxist political economy, fieldwork, use of think tanks and better selection and training of cadres. They should also govern the economy by law, and apply the method of seeking progress while maintaining stability, with stability focused on growth, employment, prices and financial risk, and progress on structural adjustment and reform. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how Party leadership over the economy is justified and institutionalised in the Xi Jinping era.

On ideological security in the new era 论新时代意识形态安全 Tang Aijun Writing in Studies on Marxism in 2022, Tang Aijun asks how China should conceive and safeguard ideological security amid what official discourse calls profound changes unseen in a century and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that the task requires a new concept, a "holistic view of ideological security" derived from the holistic view of national security, and that ideological struggle today is above all a competition for identification, or "winning hearts and minds". The article has four parts. It first defines ideological security and sets out the holistic view, tracing earlier Party strategic thinking from Mao Zedong to Hu Jintao. It then assesses the situation since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the main risks. A third part analyses the means of ideological contest, and a fourth proposes an ideological security system at the international and domestic levels. Tang defines ideological security as a state in which the mainstream ideology is relatively free of danger and external or internal threat, together with the capacity to sustain that state. Because ideology is both political and cultural, the author places it in the categories of both political security and cultural security. The holistic view is said to be comprehensive (a "big security" covering culture, values and online opinion), systematic and sustainable. Tang identifies four challenges: diverse social trends (the "6+1", including constitutional democracy, universal values and historical nihilism), market profit-seeking, infiltration and containment by hostile Western forces, and new media and technology. Tang says these contests are fought through three ideological functions: value orientation, social control and integration, and political legitimacy. Tang calls for a more actively combative international system: strategic confidence, stronger international communication, institutional discourse power, exposing the double standards behind "universal values", and confronting issues the West attacks. Domestically, the author proposes a system built on "hearts and minds", with an early-warning view that popular support equals security, and "six identifications": political, ideological, value, historical, practical and emotional. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how a Party School scholar frames ideological security as a competition for identification and what institutional measures follow.

Upholding the Party's leadership over ideological work in the new era: basis, value and paths of realisation 新时代坚持党对意识形态工作的领导权：基本依据、价值意蕴和实现路径 Xiao Guangwen Li Xiaotong Xiao Guangwen and Li Xiaotong take up the call in the historical resolution of the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) to "firmly grasp the leadership over ideological work" and build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power. They argue that upholding the Party's leadership over ideological work in the new era rests on historical, theoretical and practical grounds. In their account it serves the Party's ruling base, mainstream values, political security and spiritual unity, and it can be realised through four concrete paths. The article has three parts. The first sets out the basis for the leadership: the Party's century of ideological work, from the 1921 First Congress through Yan'an, the post-1949 period, the Cultural Revolution, reform and opening up, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012); the Marxist theory of ideology; and the demands of the "two overall situations". The second discusses its value in four respects. The third proposes ways to put it into practice. On theory, the authors draw on Marx and Engels on the ruling ideas of an age, Lenin's doctrine of "inculcation" and "scientific ideology", and Gramsci's concept of ideological hegemony. They read these as showing that a proletarian party must hold ideological leadership to prevent the dissolution of mainstream ideology and to defend its political legitimacy. On value, they hold that such leadership unites Party spirit and the people's character, fosters the core socialist values, and counters what they call erroneous trends of thought promoted from the West, including neoliberalism, "universal values" and historical nihilism. They also say it strengthens discursive power, which they break down into the rights to pose questions, to judge, to interpret and to criticise. For realisation, the authors propose four paths. The first is to be guided by Xi Jinping's statements on ideological leadership, including building Chinese philosophy and social sciences and governing online ideology. The second is to enforce the primary responsibility of Party committees under the 2015 and 2016 responsibility-system measures. The third is to raise the ideological capacity and fighting spirit of Party members and cadres. The fourth is to improve institutions, namely the fundamental system of Marxism's guiding role, Party management of ideology, and supervision, assessment and accountability. They conclude that only a sound institutional system and stronger execution can secure comprehensive Party leadership in this field. Read the original if you want a representative account of how Party-affiliated scholars justify and operationalise ideological leadership in the Xi Jinping era.

The main features of the interaction between Chinese modernization and world modernization 论中国现代化与世界现代化互动的主要特征 Wu Zhongmin Wu Zhongmin asks what the main features are of the interaction between China's modernization and the modernization of the world. Wu argues that, unlike many smaller states, China has built a benign, two-way relationship with world modernization, marked by economic interdependence, strong autonomy and a positive influence on the basic pattern of international relations. The article treats this as a necessary part of the study of Chinese modernization. The article is organised around three dimensions: whether the two processes are economically symbiotic, whether China's modernization has autonomous capacity, and whether it shapes the international order. A closing section sets out the mutual benefits and three tasks ahead. Wu draws on trade and GDP figures, comparisons with Japan, the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States, and quotations from foreign politicians and scholars. First, Wu argues that since reform and opening up China's trade and economic weight have grown so fast that the two processes are now interdependent and cannot be decoupled. In Wu's account, China's entry into the existing market-based world economic system, rather than building a rival one as the Soviet Union tried, explains its success. Wu also says deep integration limits how far US pressure can go and helps China avoid the "Thucydides trap". Second, Wu holds that integration must be paired with autonomy, which the article defines as national self-awareness, endogenous drive and defensive capacity. Japan is offered as a cautionary case of weak autonomy and prolonged stagnation. Third, Wu argues that a rising power changes the division of labour, technology flows and ideas in international relations. Wu contends that China, guided by the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and by support for the United Nations, exerts this influence peacefully and equally, in contrast to the unilateralism and quasi-colonial conduct the article attributes to Britain and the United States. Wu concludes that the interaction is a mutually beneficial win-win and that China will keep advancing and contribute more to the world. Wu names three tasks: upgrading the economy through a sound market system, a complete industrial chain and technological leadership; resolving domestic social contradictions by promoting social justice; and improving mutual understanding between China and other countries, partly to counter what Wu calls the demonization of China. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how Chinese official discourse frames China's relationship with the global economic and political order.

The threefold implication of the essence of Marx and Engels's "science of history" and its contemporary significance 马克思恩格斯“历史科学”实质的三重蕴涵及其现实意义 Hu Haibo Marx and Engels used the term "science of history" repeatedly, from The German Ideology to Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, yet Chinese scholars disagree about what it means. Some read it as the single unified science of nature and man found in the 1844 Manuscripts; most read it as historical materialism, and within that camp argue over whether historical materialism is a philosophy of history or a "genuine positive science". Hu argues that the concept's essence has three interlocking implications: the basic principles and method of historical materialism, the "genuine knowledge" obtained by applying them to social life, and the value aim of human emancipation. The article has three parts. The first re-reads the concept across the whole body of Marx's and Engels's texts, giving weight to Engels's later writings. The second sets out the three implications and the logic by which they unfold. The third draws lessons for building a Chinese independent knowledge system, a topic that became prominent after Xi Jinping's visit to Renmin University of China on 25 April 2022. Hu's first move is textual. Earlier readings concentrated on Marx and the early works and neglected Engels, who defined the history sciences as "all sciences that are not natural sciences" and, in Anti-Dühring, as the third class of science covering human living conditions, social relations and the ideological superstructure. Since Engels describes the two men's work as a joint effort, Hu holds that neither the "one science" reading nor the pure historical-materialism reading is adequate. In Hu's account, the term narrows from nature-plus-human history to "human history", the science of real people's practical activity, set against ideology. The second move is to show how the three implications are ordered. Historical materialism supplies the foundation. Its application yields genuine knowledge in political economy (Capital), politics, law and anthropology. Proletarian emancipation gives both the value aim and the practical test, so that science and value are united. Hu concludes that the construction of a Chinese independent knowledge system is the logical development of the "science of history" in China today. The author draws three implications. The system must rest on the worldview and method of historical materialism. It must answer major theoretical and practical problems facing the Party and the country, which calls for a comprehensive, cross-disciplinary system. Its value orientation must be a people-centred stance. Read the original if you want a text-based argument about the meaning of "science of history" in Marx and Engels, or an example of how the concept is linked to current Chinese debates on self-reliant knowledge production.

Building the national ideological security system in the new era 新时代国家意识形态安全体系建构研究 Wang Yonggui Writing in 2022, Wang Yonggui asks how China should build a systematic national ideological security system in the new era. Wang treats ideological security as a cornerstone of overall national security and argues that it needs institutionalised safeguards and systemic support. The article's answer is a framework of four sub-systems, supported by deliberate capacity-building. The article follows a path from strategic assessment to strategic layout to strategic capability. It first sets out the theoretical and contemporary grounds for the system, citing Xi Jinping's remarks and the National Security Strategy (2021–2025). It then describes the system's elements: supporting factors, driving forces and a layered structure. The longest section examines the four sub-systems in turn, and a final section turns to capabilities. Wang's central claim is that the system rests on four sub-systems, each with four subordinate parts. The leadership and organisation system has the commanding position and covers leadership, organisation, personnel and responsibility. The risk prevention and control system is the core and covers monitoring, early warning, feedback and assessment. The legal safeguard system is the leading one and works through legislation, enforcement, adjudication, compliance and legal education. The resource system is the foundation and covers personnel, social forces and material and financial support. Wang adds that legislation must balance freedom of thought and speech against national security. The system must then be turned into capacity in four areas: political ability, thinking ability (strategic, bottom-line and historical thinking), coordination and innovation. Wang concludes that ideological security work has become heavier in the new journey. Strong leadership, risk prevention, legal safeguards and resources are needed, together with improved capabilities, so that Marxist ideology can act as a stabilising anchor for socialism with Chinese characteristics amid great changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars conceptualise the institutional design of ideological security, including its monitoring, early-warning and legal mechanisms.

The contemporary value and transmission of the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists 中国共产党人精神谱系的时代价值与传承路径 Xu Lianlin Peng Shijie This commentary in Guangming Daily (September 2022) asks why the spiritual genealogy of Chinese Communists matters now and how it should be passed on. Xu and Peng argue that this genealogy, rooted in the great founding spirit of the Party, is a lasting resource for the new journey towards the second centenary goal. They hold that it supports socialism with Chinese characteristics, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and the Party's original aspiration and mission. The article first traces how the genealogy took shape over a century. It lists clusters of spirits from each period: the Jinggangshan, Long March and Yan'an spirits in the revolutionary years; the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" and Lei Feng spirits in socialist construction; and the special economic zone and flood-fighting spirits in reform and opening up. For the new era it names poverty alleviation, anti-epidemic, lunar exploration and Beidou spirits. It then sets out four contemporary values and four ways of transmitting the genealogy. On value, the authors present the genealogy as a spiritual support for opening new prospects, an ideological weapon for Party building, and a source of strength for the Party's mission. They add that it combines Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture and carries wider appeal. On transmission, they call for more rigorous scholarly research and interpretation, including rebutting views that distort Party history. They also call for effective publicity using new media, coordinated protection and use of "red resources" such as sites and museums, and mass cultural activities that link the genealogy to core socialist values. Xu and Peng conclude that the genealogy should be built into the Party's "blood and genes" and supply spiritual momentum for building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-school scholars frame the official "spiritual genealogy" and its practical dissemination.

The contest over discursive power between the Guomindang and the Communist Party in the New Democratic Revolution period A reading from the field of philosophy and social sciences 新民主主义革命时期国共两党的话语权博弈 Wang Dong Wang Dong asks how the Guomindang (Kuomintang) and the Communist Party contended for discursive power in philosophy and the social sciences between the 1920s and 1940s. The article argues that, besides its military campaigns, the Guomindang waged a reactionary 'cultural encirclement' to build a discourse guided by the Three People's Principles. In Wang's account, the Party met it with effective counter-measures that weakened that campaign, raised the influence of Marxist philosophy and social science, and strengthened popular identification with the revolution. Wang says existing scholarship on discursive power is mostly present-oriented and has not examined this period systematically. Drawing on archival and published historical sources, the article looks at three arenas: the publication and distribution of books and periodicals, academic controversy (using the debate on the nature of Chinese society as the case), and attitudes towards traditional culture. It closes by linking the history to present-day ideological work. On publishing, Wang documents Guomindang censorship laws and standards, the persecution of writers, raids on bookshops and postal inspection. The Party answered with disguised titles, nominal bookshops, use of legal periodicals and publishers, and a cultural united front calling for academic freedom. In the debate on Chinese society, Wang argues that Tao Xisheng's 'New Life' group and the Reorganization faction denied that China was semi-colonial and semi-feudal in order to undercut the Party's revolutionary discourse. Communist writers such as Pan Dongzhou, Wu Liangping and Jian Bozan countered with economic analysis, which the article says confirmed the scientific character of Marxism. On tradition, Wang describes the Guomindang drawing on Confucian ethics, the New Life Movement and Chiang Kai-shek's 'philosophy of vigorous action' to bolster authoritarian rule. The Party, in Wang's reading, criticised this revivalism through the New Enlightenment movement while practising sublation of tradition, which also advanced the adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions. Wang concludes that Marxist philosophy and social science rose from an emerging academic discourse to the mainstream, contributing to the revolution's victory. Today, Wang notes, historical nihilism, neoliberalism and democratic socialism challenge socialist ideology. The article calls on the Party to carry forward its revolutionary-era traditions and consolidate Marxism's discursive power in these fields in the new era, in support of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a source-rich, Party-historiographical account of Guomindang censorship and Communist counter-strategies in the Republican-era publishing and intellectual world.

The Communists' strategic vision for national rejuvenation in the New Democratic Revolution period 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党人实现民族复兴的战略设想 Liu Xiaomin Li Yongchun Liu Xiaomin and Li Yongchun ask how the Communist Party of China conceived of national rejuvenation during the New Democratic Revolution (roughly 1921–1949), the first stage of its century of struggle. Drawing on Party documents and leaders' writings, they argue that the Party developed a coherent strategy for rejuvenating the Chinese nation. In their account it rested on three "new" elements: a new politics, a new economy and a new culture. The article is organised in three parts, each following the same pattern: why the field matters for national rejuvenation, then how the Party explored it. It runs chronologically from the Party's early programmes and the 1922 statement on the political situation through the Great Revolution, the Soviet period, the War of Resistance against Japan and the late 1940s. Sources include Mao Zedong, Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying, Cai Hesen and Qu Qiubai. On politics, the authors say the Party treated national independence as the precondition of rejuvenation and democracy as both its goal and its means. Its formulas moved from workers' and peasants' democratic dictatorship to the New Democratic republic and finally to the people's democratic dictatorship, which they present as the political foundation for rejuvenation. On the economy, they argue that the Party saw prosperity and strength as the basis of independence, rejected capitalism for China, and planned a New Democratic economy led by the state sector before a gradual transition to socialism. It pursued tariff autonomy, land revolution and industrialisation. On culture, they report that the Party, responding to the 1930s debates over "wholesale Westernisation" and the Nationalist government's rejuvenation discourse, advanced a new culture that was national, scientific and mass-oriented. It stressed national self-respect and confidence, national spirit, and critical handling of foreign and ancient cultures. The authors conclude that this three-part vision grasped China's principal contradiction, answered the people's urgent needs and became the inevitable choice for independence and rejuvenation. They describe it as pioneering within the Party's hundred-year course and as a source of spiritual strength for socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era and for the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a source-heavy, documentary survey of how Party texts from 1921 to 1949 linked independence, democracy, economic development and cultural renewal to the idea of national rejuvenation.

Early explorations in building a rural social security system in New China, 1949–1957 新中国构建农村社会保障体系的初步探索（1949—1957） Zhou Xiao Zhou Xiao asks how the Party and the state began to build social security for the Chinese countryside between 1949 and 1957, and how informal, temporary relief turned into a more institutionalised system. Writing in the context of efforts to narrow the urban–rural gap and advance common prosperity, the author argues that early rural security should not be judged by modern or Western standards. It should be read as a broad set of measures covering peasants' birth, old age, illness and death, and the author holds that these measures offer historical experience for building a unified urban–rural system. The article has three main sections. The first covers state relief, divided into disaster relief and social relief, and begins with land reform as the basis of peasants' self-reliance. The second examines the collective economy through three institutions: the accumulation and welfare funds of cooperatives, rural cooperative medical care, and the "five guarantees" support system. The third treats rural medical and health work, including the patriotic health campaign, the building of health institutions, disease control, midwifery and drug supply. Evidence comes from policy documents, leaders' speeches, and local cases such as Zhejiang, Anhui, Hebei, Liaoning and the Wuhan suburbs. Zhou's central claim is that, because rural productive forces were weak and state finances limited, the state could not copy the labour insurance system it built for urban workers. Instead it relied on self-help through production, collective strength and mutual aid, with state relief as a supplement. After 1954 the relief policy was restated as "relying on the collective, mutual aid among the masses, production for self-rescue, supplemented by necessary state relief". Collectives then took on more functions through public funds, cooperative medical schemes and the five guarantees of food, clothing, fuel, education and burial. The author presents health campaigns, such as smallpox vaccination and the fight against schistosomiasis, as improving rural living conditions. Zhou concludes that the period brought real gains: land-based self-security, systematic disaster relief, a collective role in peasant welfare and much better rural health, which the author calls unprecedented in the history of agrarian society. The system also had limits: narrow coverage, unsystematic provision, a single funding channel, and an egalitarianism that dampened incentives. Zhou also notes that urban social security was tied to household registration and that the rural–urban dual structure took shape early. The author adds that the Great Leap Forward after 1958 damaged medical work. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of how the early People's Republic built rural relief, the five guarantees and cooperative medicine.

Two statistical reasons why economic growth before and after reform and opening up is underestimated by GDP 关于改革开放前后经济增长被低估的两类GDP统计原因 Wu Wen Yu Hongjun Wu Wen and Yu Hongjun ask whether China's official GDP series measures real economic growth accurately, particularly when growth before and after reform and opening up is compared. They argue that problems arising in the use of the GDP indicator, rather than in the indicator itself, lead to underestimation of true growth in both periods, and that the distortion is larger for the pre-reform period. In their words, real GDP is therefore not truly 'real'. The article is divided into two parts, each addressing one statistical problem. The first concerns the method of deriving real GDP from nominal GDP, illustrated with numerical examples and the National Bureau of Statistics' two GDP indices (base year 1978 = 100, and previous year = 100). The second concerns the 'monetary' character of GDP, drawing on a theory of macro-level optimal monetary deepening that the authors construct, and applies it to China's shift from a low-monetised planned economy to a monetised market economy. On the first problem, the authors compare an absolute base-year method with a relative (previous-year) one. With ongoing technological progress and industrial upgrading the two diverge sharply, yet the official Chinese series almost coincide. Wu and Yu infer that statisticians group new products into existing categories ('same-scope classification'), which treats the high prices of innovative goods as pure inflation and so understates real output. On the second problem, they argue that GDP captures only the monetised part of gross domestic product. In early monetary deepening, GDP growth exceeds real growth in rate but falls short in scale. Before 1978, they contend, administered prices below value, rationing coupons and little commodification made GDP understate real growth in both absolute and relative terms. The authors conclude that the GDP growth gap between the two periods cannot stand for the real gap, and that fair comparison would require decomposing growth into monetised and non-monetised components, using data not yet published. They add that, because pre-reform industrialisation was a leap 'from zero to one', its growth is underestimated more severely. They also welcome the central leadership's recent downplaying of GDP as a way of returning it to a purely statistical role. Read the original if you are interested in the statistical methods and monetary-deepening arguments behind claims about how China's pre-reform and post-reform growth should be compared.

Unite: an account of Mao Zedong's early idea of the "great union of the popular masses" 联合起来——毛泽东早期“民众的大联合”思想述论 Wang Shuyin Ouyang Shuo Around 1919, in the wake of the May Fourth Movement, the young Mao Zedong turned to the question of social transformation. In essays such as the inaugural declaration of the Xiang River Review and "The Great Union of the Popular Masses", he set out the idea of a great union of the masses. Wang and Ouyang argue that the idea follows a clear logic: why the masses must unite, how union is possible, how it is to be carried out, and what it will finally look like. They present it as an important marker in Mao's shift from democrat to Marxist. The article has four sections. It begins with union as the fundamental method for remaking state and society. It then covers the conditions that make union possible, the route from small unions to a great union, and Mao's prediction that China would achieve it first. The authors draw on Mao's 1915 and 1917 letters, his 1919 writings and his later 1920 reassessment, and they compare his class concepts with Lenin's definition of class. The authors argue that Mao saw union as the root remedy, whereas education, industry and constitutional reform were only branches. In their reading, he held that the powerful, nobles and capitalists monopolise knowledge, money and armed force, but that the common people, who outnumber them, are gradually learning these three methods. Mao's division into classes of the wise and foolish, rich and poor, strong and weak is judged still simple and abstract by Lenin's standard, yet it shows an early grasp of the economic roots of class. His call to build the great union on occupational "small unions" held together by common interests is said to contain the germ of the united front. The authors also note that his shift from relying on exceptional heroes to saying "we" shows an emerging mass view of history. They add that he still favoured a "bloodless" revolution of appeals, a position the failure of the Hunan self-government movement later overturned. Wang and Ouyang conclude that Mao rested his confidence in the idea on the masses' awakened consciousness, motive and capacity for union. They say the 1919 prediction was borne out in the course of the Chinese revolution. They concede that the idea was immature, with a shallow understanding of class and no concrete plan for moving from small to great unions, but they maintain that it was distinctive among contemporary proposals. Read the original if you study the formation of Mao Zedong's thought before 1921 or the early roots of the united front and of Mao's class analysis, as seen through official Chinese scholarship.

Building the industrial system and the national economic system, 1949–1978 1949年至1978年工业体系和国民经济体系建设研究 Jiang Changqing Jiang Changqing examines how the People's Republic of China, between 1949 and 1978, built what official texts call an independent and relatively complete industrial system and national economic system. The article starts from the humiliations of China since the Opium War and argues that, by 1978, this construction had been preliminarily achieved. It frames the period through four questions: why the systems were built, how, how long leaders expected it to take, and how progress was measured. The article is organised in four sections, drawing mainly on speeches, reports and annotations by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, along with Party congress and National People's Congress documents. It follows the stated targets from the early 1950s through the Great Leap Forward, the economic readjustment of the early 1960s and the 1975 Fourth National People's Congress. It closes with the physical indicators leaders used, such as coal, steel, grain and cotton output. On the reasons, Jiang identifies four: overcoming backwardness, building a strong socialist modern country, strengthening the socialist camp internationally, and fitting China's conditions as a large country with a big population and rich resources. On the path, Jiang lists a catch-up strategy of prioritising heavy industry, building scientific strength and a technical workforce, learning from the Soviet Union and other countries, and exploring a distinctively Chinese road to socialism. Jiang traces how time estimates shifted: twenty years from 1953 in Mao's 1951 draft, 1967 at the Eighth Party Congress (1956), over-optimistic targets around 1960, and later a two-step plan of fifteen years plus further modernization. Zhou Enlai's 1963 remark that an independent national economic system is a more complete aim than industry alone is highlighted. The article notes that state statistics followed the MPS (material product system) accounting method. Jiang concludes that the 1949–1978 effort was the most successful industrialisation China had undertaken since the Opium War. In this reading it changed China's socioeconomic base and the global balance of forces, and laid the industrial foundation for reform and opening up. The article cites the 1981 Party resolution on historical questions in support. Jiang acknowledges that early targets, especially around 1960, were unrealistic given an insufficient grasp of economic difficulties. Read the original if you want a documentary account of how Party leaders justified, planned and timed China's industrial system, with many dated quotations and target figures.

Marx's theory of "capital in general" and "many capitals" and the study of capital in China 马克思“资本一般”和“许多资本”理论与中国资本问题研究 Gu Hailiang Gu Hailiang asks how Marx's theory of capital can guide the study of regulating and guiding the healthy development of capital under China's socialist market economy. Writing in 2022, he argues that Marx never discussed capital in socialist countries, but that his categories \"capital in general\" and \"many capitals\" supply the basic ideas and method. Gu presents these as the root of the current Party formulation about understanding \"the characteristics and law of behaviour of capital\".
