The article first traces how the two categories emerged in the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse): from the \"five-part plan\" through the six-part and three-part structures of the capital theory to a two-part structure, and then to the six-book plan and a four-part structure for the book on capital. It then shows how Marx used the categories in Capital, volumes 1 to 3. The final section applies them to the Party's current discussion of capital, drawing on Xi Jinping's remarks of December 2021 and April 2022 and on the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Gu reads \"capital in general\" as capital's common determinations: the total form from which individual capitals abstract. \"Many capitals\" is its unfolding in competition among capitals, with accumulation, concentration, credit and joint-stock capital as its forms. He links this to Hegel's Logic, where the \"many\" arises from the \"one\" through repulsion. He holds that in Capital the categories no longer structure the work but act as a method: volumes 1 and 2 treat industrial capital in general, while volume 3 moves towards concrete forms such as commercial, bank and agricultural capital. Gu maps the pair onto Xi's two-sided framing. Capital's \"characteristics\" correspond to capital in general, and its \"behaviour\" to many capitals. He argues that the five coexisting forms of capital in China (state, collective, private, foreign and mixed) are \"many capitals\" under a dominant public sector, whose \"universal light\" alters the colour and weight of private capital without removing its profit-seeking nature. He draws on Marx's remarks on competition and personification to support \"orderly\" governance of capital, \"traffic lights\" and guiding private entrepreneurs away from capital personified, and he adds that Marx's unfinished treatment of the world market opens a research agenda. Read the original if you want a textual account of how the Grundrisse and Capital are being used to ground current Chinese policy on capital.")

Strengthening education for Party members and cadres on the essential nature of money 加强对党员干部金钱本质教育 Xu Baojian This short commentary, first published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) in 2022, asks how to make Party members and cadres genuinely unwilling to be corrupt. Xu Baojian argues that, besides ideals-and-convictions education and education in discipline and the legal system, education about the essential nature of money is an overlooked but necessary addition. The piece begins from the framework of making officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt, in which Xu treats unwillingness as fundamental. It then cites recent prosecutions of senior officials accused of taking bribes of hundreds of millions of yuan, and the case of Lai Xiaomin, who kept more than 200 million yuan in cash in a flat. Xu's central claim is that money is by origin a tool of exchange whose value lies in use and circulation, so hoarded cash is merely a number or a pile of waste paper. Officials who amass it, in Xu's reading, end up as custodians of property that must finally be returned to the people or the state. People load money with symbolic meanings and overlook its essence, which Xu links to Marx's critique of money fetishism and the alienation of people by things. The author compares excessive greed to Jia Rui and the mirror in Dream of the Red Chamber. Xu concludes that education should dispel illusions about money and teach that it is for sharing, not monopolising. Linking this to the Communist goal of common prosperity, Xu calls on cadres to be masters of money rather than its slaves and to use it for the people's benefit. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party press commentary frames anti-corruption education in moral and Marxist terms.

The fundamental guidelines for the Party's youth work A study of Xi Jinping's "On the Party's Youth Work" 党的青年工作的根本遵循 Liu Changjun This study essay, first published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) and posted in September 2022, reads Xi Jinping's collection On the Party's Youth Work as the basic guide for youth work in the new era. Liu argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Central Committee with Xi at its core has raised the Party's understanding of how youth work operates. In Liu's account, the book says what youth work is, why it matters and how to do it. The article has three parts. The first sets out why youth work bears on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the continuity of the Party's cause and the international outlook of Chinese youth. The second turns to the book's answers to the major questions of the new era, the path to follow and the theme of the youth movement. The third looks at the importance of youth work and what it requires of the Communist Youth League. Liu relies throughout on quotations from Xi's speeches and talks. Liu's central claim is that youth work is a strategic task and not a sectoral one. The article presents Xi's formulations: youth work is "extremely important" and "bears on the future and destiny of the Party and the country", and the Party must represent, win over and rely on young people. Liu reports the guiding questions as what kind of young people to cultivate, how to cultivate them, and what kind of Youth League to build and how. The answer is the path of mass organizations with Chinese characteristics, under unified Party leadership. The Youth League's fundamental task is to train socialist builders and successors, its political responsibility is to consolidate and expand the Party's support among young people, and its main line of work is to focus on the Party's central tasks and serve the overall interest. Liu also lists the demands for strict self-governance of the League and for staying close to young people. The League is to avoid becoming bureaucratic, administrative, aristocratic or entertainment-oriented, and its cadres are to be "friends of the young, not officials". Liu concludes that the book offers a rich body of ideas and working methods on the theoretical and practical questions of youth work. The author calls for careful study and thorough implementation, so that young people can be united, organized and mobilized for the second centenary goal and the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-school view of how Xi's youth-work ideas are organized and presented for study within the Communist Youth League system.

Forging a long-ruling Marxist party through full and rigorous self-governance and self-reform 在全面从严治党与自我革命中锻造长期执政的马克思主义政党 Liu Honglin Liu Honglin takes up a question that the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) placed among the core propositions of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era: what kind of long-ruling Marxist party should be built, and how. Liu argues that the question can only be understood through the practical, theoretical and institutional innovations in Party governance since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and through Xi Jinping's related speeches. The article's thesis is that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the effective route to the Party's self-reform, which Liu presents as the way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Liu organises the argument around six key terms: the Party's overall leadership, long-term rule, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, supervision and restraint of power, self-reform, and escaping the historical cycle. These are handled in three sections. The first defines the long-ruling Marxist party and its relation to Party leadership. The second examines Xi's judgement that self-reform is the "second answer" to the historical cycle. The third links self-reform to full and rigorous self-governance. Liu draws on comparisons with the Soviet Communist Party, Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party and other long-serving parties. In the first section Liu distinguishes the Chinese Communist Party from Western parties by six features: guiding ideology, nature, purpose, founding mission, essence of rule and standards of work. Liu holds that upholding overall leadership is the basic political precondition for long-term rule, and that this does not mean the planned-economy practice of the Party managing everything. In the second section, Liu reads Mao Zedong's 1945 Yan'an answer (supervision of government by the people) and Xi's answer (self-reform) as continuity and development. The "blade" moves from the government to the ruling Party itself, and the target widens from power corruption to power corruption plus political corruption. Liu treats political corruption as systemic and especially dangerous to a ruling party. Liu concludes that the two are mutually reinforcing: self-reform advances through full and rigorous self-governance, and the political awareness behind self-reform sustains it. Liu credits the decade since 2012 with turning Party governance from lax to strict and with an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle. Liu calls for continued strictness, strengthened Party-building, the Two Upholds, a cadre corps willing to reform itself and a more complete system of intra-Party regulations. Read the original if you want a representative account of how Party scholars link long-term rule, self-reform and Party discipline within Xi-era theory.

Full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the only path to lasting vitality and a successful "new road to the exam" 全面从严治党是党永葆生机活力、走好新的赶考之路的必由之路 Guo Guangyin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2022, Guo Guangyin takes up a remark by Xi Jinping to the Inner Mongolia delegation at the National People's Congress session: that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is the only way for the Party to keep its vitality and to pass the "new exam". Guo argues that this is a considered statement of how a long-ruling Marxist party must be built, and that it should run through every area of Party building. The article has three parts. The first sets out what full and rigorous self-governance means (comprehensive in scope, strict in practice, effective in governance) and goes through the areas of Party building one by one. The second claims that this self-governance is the route to the Party's lasting vitality. The third claims it is the route to meeting the demands of the "new road to the exam" of the new era. In the first part, Guo gives political building priority as the "foundation and soul" of the rest, tied to the Two Upholds. Ideological building comes next, then organisational building, work style (including the central Eight-point Regulation), discipline and rule-based Party governance through internal Party regulations. In the second part Guo lists the means: firm ideals and convictions, holding to the original aspiration and mission, and the courage for self-reform. Guo calls self-reform the mark that sets the Party apart from other parties and the way it escapes the "historical cycle of rise and fall". The Party must also grasp the laws of governing, which Guo says means better governing capacity and a more scientific level of Party building, backed by ideology and by institutions. Guo concludes that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the campaign has reversed lax and soft Party governance, secured an overwhelming victory against corruption and strengthened the Party's capacity for self-purification and self-improvement. The Party still faces long-term "four tests" and severe "four dangers". It should therefore keep a strict tone and treat Party building as the decisive "great new project" alongside the great struggle, the great cause and the great dream. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale for Party discipline and Party building in the new era, as presented in a Red Flag Manuscripts commentary.

Upholding and strengthening the Party's centralised and unified leadership over economic work 坚持和加强党对经济工作的集中统一领导 Ding Xiaoqin Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), Ding Xiaoqin takes up how the Communist Party of China should lead economic work. Ding presents upholding and strengthening the Party's centralised and unified leadership over economic work as an important component of Xi Jinping's economic thought and as a necessary consequence of the Party's overall leadership. The central claim is that the authority of the Party Central Committee is the key guarantee of this leadership, and that it requires both better institutions and stronger leadership capacity. The article is organised in four parts. It first places economic leadership within the Party's overall leadership, citing the 2021 historical resolution (adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee) and Xi Jinping's statements. It then explains why the Central Committee's role is decisive, followed by a survey of institutional mechanisms at the central, local and state-owned enterprise levels. The last part sets out three requirements for improving the Party's capacity to lead economic work. Ding's core argument draws on the Central Economic Work Conferences of 2018 to 2021, which the author says increasingly named centralised and unified Party leadership as a lesson of successful economic work, and finally placed it first. In this reading, the Central Committee sets direction, strategy and policy, which unifies thought and action and allows the nation to concentrate resources on major undertakings. On institutions, Ding points to the replacement of the central leading small groups by commissions, including the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, to quarterly economic analysis and to annual work conferences. Ding also describes local Party committees collectively deciding development plans, and state-owned enterprise Party committees discussing major matters before boards and managers decide. On capacity, Ding calls for three things. Cadres should acquire professional competence, through studying Marxist political economy, doing fieldwork, drawing on think tanks and improving selection and training. Economic leadership should be conducted according to law and in line with objective economic, social and natural laws. The method of seeking progress while maintaining stability should be applied, with "stability" meaning steady growth, employment, prices and financial security, and "progress" meaning structural adjustment and deeper reform and opening up. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official rationale and institutional channels for Party leadership over the economy in the period after the 19th Party Congress.

Strengthening Party building to lead the high-quality development of state-owned enterprises 加强党的建设引领国有企业高质量发展 Deng Weihua Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2022, Deng Weihua, a senior Party and corporate official at a state-owned construction firm, takes up how Party building can guide the development of state-owned enterprises (SOEs). The author's thesis is that Party leadership is the "root and soul" of SOEs, and that high-quality Party building is the fundamental guarantee of their high-quality development. SOEs, in this account, must keep Party leadership unwavering and fuse Party work with production and management. The article opens by citing the Central Committee's trial regulations on strengthening Party leadership in corporate governance and on Party grassroots organisations in SOEs, together with Xi Jinping's remarks on SOE Party building. It then proceeds through five headings: Party building as direction-setting, as part of management, as a means of rallying people, as a source of work style, and as a source of vitality. Deng draws on examples from corporate practice and on the Covid-19 response. Deng's central claim is that the Party's political advantage must be converted into development advantage and governance effectiveness. This is to be done through overall strategy, organisational structure, grassroots leadership arrangements and cadre training. Party organisations are to be embedded in governance through the management system, decision-making (major matters going first to the Party committee for prior review before the board's standing committee), work deployment and performance appraisal that links business results and Party-building targets. Deng also stresses the "people-centred" aim of SOEs: employment, income, benefit-sharing and care for employees. The article further urges SOEs to preserve their "red gene" and to distil a replicable "wartime Party building" model. It argues that Party members' conduct in the Covid-19 response showed the political advantages of the system. Deng concludes that, amid what the article calls changes unseen in a century and global competition, the Party must strengthen its governing capacity in the economic sphere. Its leadership should be built into every link of corporate governance, and Party work should adapt to a younger workforce born in the 1990s and 2000s. The stated goal is to raise the Party's organisational strength, cohesion and combat effectiveness. Read the original if you want an insider's view, from a practising SOE leader, of how Party committees are being built into corporate governance, appraisal and employee work in China's state sector.

The distinctive political character and powerful political strengths of the Communist Party of China 中国共产党鲜明的政治品格和强大的政治优势 Feng Pengzhi Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2022, no. 16), Feng Pengzhi takes up Xi Jinping's July 2022 statement, made at a seminar for provincial and ministerial leading cadres ahead of the 20th Party Congress. Xi said that being guided by Marxist scientific theory is the Party's distinctive political character and powerful political strength. Feng argues that this explains why the Party succeeds and why socialism with Chinese characteristics works: in the end, "Marxism works". The article has three parts. The first treats Marxism as the soul and banner of the Party. The second presents the continuous adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions as the Party's key historical experience. The third sets out how to grasp and apply Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, including its worldview and methodology. Feng relies heavily on Xi's statements and on the 2021 Party resolution on history. Feng's central claim is that Marxism has proved effective in China because the Party has kept "adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times" and has not treated it as dogma. Feng traces three historic leaps: Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Xi Jinping Thought. Each is tied to an era of Party work, from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Feng attributes the Party's strength to several habits: drawing on Chinese practice and traditional culture, keeping pace with the times, and absorbing the achievements of other civilizations. Feng then turns to practice. The Party must rely on the people, benefit the people and stay rooted among them, with whole-process people's democracy, common prosperity, and opposition to corruption, formalism and bureaucratism. Cadres should also master the materialist-dialectical principles in Xi Jinping Thought, such as the unity of the material world, contradiction, and the people as makers of history. They should apply its methods too: systemic thinking, strategic, historical, dialectical and bottom-line thinking, and a spirit of struggle. Feng presents these as the way to keep opening up new realms of Marxism in China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists in 2022 tied the Party's "Marxism works" formula to the three leaps and to study of Xi Jinping Thought.

A survey of Christian gathering points among urban migrant workers The case of Z migrant-worker church in Beijing 城市农民工基督徒聚会点调查 Cui Qi Zheng Hong'e As Christianity in China shifts, in the authors' account, from the countryside to the cities, the number of migrant-worker Christians is growing. Cui and Zheng take up a gap in earlier studies: most are about a decade old and focus on gathering points nurtured by rural church teams, not on those that migrants organise themselves. Using recent fieldwork on one self-organised Beijing congregation, the article argues that such churches give migrants belonging but remain fragile and weakly institutionalised. It closes with policy recommendations on religious work. The article rests on participant observation and interviews, with the researcher attending as a seeker (a prospective believer). It describes Z church, founded in the 1990s by migrants from Anhui in an urban village on Beijing's outskirts and affiliated since 2003 with a Three-Self church, which the authors call a "quasi-Three-Self" church. It then sets out the congregation's membership types, weekly and annual activities, and its relations with other churches and the neighbourhood committee. A third section discusses management and policy. The authors identify four features of Z church. It has a "mobile" meeting place, having moved nearly ten times within the community because of rent, demolition and neighbours' complaints. It relies on part-time pastors because a full-time clergy is unaffordable. Its members' spiritual needs are polarised: older members accept it as a temporary refuge, while a few younger members and seekers find it informal and want reform. Its membership is skewed towards older women with little schooling. In the authors' reading, the church is dual in character: it builds a "family of faith" and a sense of belonging, but its closed tendency and lack of outside contact deepen the social separation of migrant Christians. Cui and Zheng conclude that migrant churches will persist and propose three responses. They call for stronger legal management of religious affairs, with unregistered gatherings screened and, where they qualify, brought under legitimate religious bodies. They call for legal education so that migrant Christians understand the Party's policy of religious freedom and are less drawn to underground groups. They also urge better public services for migrants, since the authors see exclusion in the city as one reason for turning to the church. Read the original if you want detailed ethnographic material on a migrant church in Beijing, or an example of how Chinese scholars link research on religion to official policy.

Resources in Chinese cultural thought for the sinicization of religion 宗教中国化的中华文化思想资源探析 Qi Fujuan Qi Fujuan asks how traditional Chinese culture can supply ideas for the Party's policy of keeping religion on a "sinicizing" path (zongjiao zhongguohua). The article argues that Chinese culture has historically absorbed foreign religions and moderated their exclusivism. In the author's view, the same resources should now be used to "infuse" religion, above all Islam in southern Xinjiang, so that religion serves the mainstream ideology. The article begins with Xi Jinping's statements on the sinicization of religion at the 2015 United Front work conference, the 2016 national religious work conference and the 2020 Xinjiang work symposium. Part two lists five strands of cultural thought: harmony without uniformity and inclusiveness; moderation and non-extremism; the primacy of state over religion together with patriotic support for the state; the "distancing from spirits" tradition; and reciprocity and tolerance as moral ideas. Part three draws four practical conclusions for present-day religious work. Qi reads Chinese history as showing that Buddhism, Islam, Christianity and other religions survived by adapting to Confucian and wider Chinese thought. Examples include Ming–Qing Muslim scholars who explained Islamic doctrine through Confucian concepts, and Buddhist texts on filial piety. The author argues that Chinese rulers kept religion subordinate to political authority, citing Tang and Qing emperors, and that Confucian culture is oriented to this world rather than to spirits. From this, Qi concludes that religions must keep adapting, and that doctrines should be reinterpreted to fit socialist core values and fine traditional culture. Qi also points to the shared cultural heritage of Xinjiang's ethnic minorities, such as the Uyghur work Blessed Knowledge (Fule zhihui), as material for this work. Qi sets out four tasks: uphold Marxism's guiding position in ideology; follow the historical logic of sinicization by using cultural resources to shape religious teaching, including tolerance, respect for other faiths and a shared citizen identity; promote shared Chinese culture to forge a strong sense of community of the Chinese nation; and encourage religious circles to advance sinicization themselves, steadily and without haste. The author expresses confidence that, under Party leadership, religions can develop a system of religious thought suited to the new era. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of scientific atheism draws on historical and cultural arguments to justify current religious policy, especially in Xinjiang.

The theoretical positioning of Engels's critique of religion 恩格斯宗教批判思想的理论定位 Wang Beite Chen Tianjia How should Engels's critique of religion be placed within the history of Marxism? Wang and Chen take up three disputed questions: when the critique began, whether it can be divided into stages, and what function Engels assigned to atheism. They argue that it began in 1839 and forms one continuous whole grounded in historical materialism, and that atheism is, for Engels, a long-term practical and dialectical link on the way to communism. The article opens by surveying existing scholarship, which either folds Engels into a general Marxist atheism or studies him separately, with little treatment of his views as a system. It outlines two debates: whether the late Engels softened towards early Christianity, a reading traced to Kautsky, and four competing periodisations that separate his early piety from historical materialism. The authors then answer in three sections, on the starting point, the coherence of the thought, and the function of atheism. First, the authors date the beginning to the anonymous 1839 "Letters from the Wuppertal", when Engels was still a believer. They read it as an exposure of the social harm done by Pietism and of the exploitation of workers, and as already containing the goals of material and spiritual liberation and the working class as agent. Second, they reject fine periodisation. In their account Engels was always a firm critic, his critique developed in step with historical materialism, and it stayed tied to the workers' movement, from the Communist Manifesto and the polemic against Dühring to the study of early Christianity. The late, milder remarks on Christianity are read as tactics drawn from the movement's needs, not as a defence of religion. Third, they read Engels's remark that atheism is "a religion" as meaning only that atheism and theism are both worldviews and that atheism depends on its opponent. Marxism differs fundamentally from religion, they say, and atheism lasts as long as theism does. It should proceed by building a secular state, not by banning religion, and its dialectical basis helps resist idealism, pseudo-science and new theism. The authors conclude that Engels's critique should be treated as an organic whole running from 1839 to the 1894 essay on early Christianity, with an internal demand to move from criticising religion to transcending it. Atheism is presented as the bridge between pre-communist society and communism, ending its mission when alienation of ideas disappears. The authors say this retains guiding value today, including for ideological work in the primary stage of socialism, where they call for both active promotion of atheism and a pragmatic strategy of uniting more people. Read the original if you study Engels's writings on religion, the debates over periodising his thought, or how Chinese scholars present Marxist atheism.

A historical examination of the Sinicization of Islam in Xinjiang 新疆伊斯兰教中国化的历史考察 Yu Shangping Yu Shangping asks how Islam in Xinjiang has historically moved towards "Sinicization" (zhongguohua), a process the author treats as the main historical pattern of foreign religions in China. The article argues that after Islam arrived in Xinjiang around the 9th–10th centuries, it survived and spread mainly by adapting to local society, absorbing and merging with earlier beliefs and customs, and so took root as a religion with Chinese features. The article, published in Science and Atheism in 2022, surveys the historical record in four dimensions: politics, culture, customs and ideas. It draws on local regimes such as the Karakhanid dynasty, the Eastern Chagatai Khanate and the Yarkand Khanate, on the Qing administration, and on texts such as Wisdom of Royal Glory and the Compendium of the Turkic Dialects. It also uses accounts by travellers and Russian officers, and it closes with four conclusions and a policy note. Yu's central claims run through the four dimensions. Politically, the author holds that Xinjiang's regimes were marked by separation of religion and state, with religion subordinate to political authority, a pattern Yu says the Qing reinforced by imposing its legal code and curbing clerical interference. Culturally and in customs, Yu points to retained pre-Islamic terms, Sufi-influenced music such as the Twelve Muqam, flat-roofed vernacular mosques, shrine pilgrimage with Zoroastrian, shamanic and Buddhist traces, the Nowruz festival, and relaxed veiling. In terms of ideas, Yu cites the Karakhanid rulers' "Tabghach" identity, resistance to Yaqub Beg's invasion, and wartime anti-Japanese fundraising as signs of a developing national consciousness. Yu draws four lessons: Sinicization has had different standards in different periods; coexistence has been the mainstream of Xinjiang's religious relations; adapting to society is a general law of religious survival, which the author ties to Engels and Marxist views of religion; and gradual Sinicization is Xinjiang Islam's historical tradition. The author adds that its Sinicization remains shallow and slow, and that it has regressed when confronted by religious extremism and "Arabization". Citing Xi Jinping's statement at the Third Central Xinjiang Work Forum, Yu calls for guidance by core socialist values and permeation by Chinese culture. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of religion presents the history of Islam in Xinjiang to support current official policy on Sinicization.

Building a "four-part institutional system" to advance the Sinicization of religion in China 构建“四项制度体系”助推我国宗教中国化 Zhao Yan Li Jianfeng Zhao Yan and Li Jianfeng take up the question of how to put into practice the policy of keeping to the Sinicization of religion in China (zongjiao zhongguohua), which Xi Jinping has stressed repeatedly since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors argue that this direction needs institutional guarantees, because well-developed rules are the precondition for it to proceed. Their answer is a system of four sets of institutions: ideological guidance, building the ranks of clergy, management of religious affairs according to law, and accountability. The article opens by tracing Xi's statements from the 2015 United Front Work Conference to the National Conference on Religious Work of December 2021, and by stating that religion will persist for a long time and must be understood through a Marxist view of religion. Four main sections follow. Each lists concrete mechanisms: education and liaison systems for religious figures, a clergy training and appointment system, a regulatory system covering venues, schools, property, internet and publications, and a system of supervision and punishment. The authors' central move is to treat religious work as mass work that must above all "guide" religious circles ideologically. They propose regular political and policy education, themed campaigns, joint meetings of religious bodies and paired friendships with officials. For clergy they propose compulsory study at approved religious schools, state-funded academic degrees, annual rotating training and a database used to weed out and promote individuals. They also propose that religious teaching be reinterpreted in line with socialist core values. The authors then call for Party committees to lead, with government, society and religious bodies cooperating. They propose pre-approval and reporting rewards for activities, screening of candidates for clergy, a rule that at least 30 per cent of school hours go to political and legal content, and curbs on online preaching and foreign infiltration. Inspection teams and Party-discipline accountability would back all of this. The authors conclude that Sinicization is the only route to healthy religious development. They hold that it is a systemic project that must be supported by these four linked institutional systems if it is to take effect on the ground. The article is written as a policy proposal, not an analysis of how religious communities themselves respond. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the institutional measures that Chinese scholars propose for implementing religious Sinicization policy.

From integrating resources to the "Two Integrations" Reflections from Chinese linguistics 从资源融通到“两个结合” Zhang Bojiang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Zhang Bojiang takes up the sixth anniversary of Xi Jinping's 2016 symposium on philosophy and social sciences. The short commentary argues that the call to integrate Marxist, traditional Chinese and foreign intellectual resources is logically continuous with the Two Integrations, and that the former is the practical route to the latter. Zhang begins with Xi's instruction to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, and with the 14th Five-Year Plan for the field. The piece then turns to Chinese linguistics as a case, tracing its history from the pre-twentieth-century philological traditions to its establishment as an independent modern discipline. Zhang says that before the twentieth century, Chinese language scholarship was subordinate to literature and classical studies. Western influence and the New Culture Movement then brought it into a modern academic framework. In Zhang's account, development has been uneven: some traditional fields lack the habit of extracting distinctive concepts in a modern way, while imported fields lack experience in consciously applying Marxist standpoint and method. Integration of the three resources, Zhang says, is not yet a shared habit among scholars, although Party history study education has helped build it in Zhang's institute. Only with such an attitude, Zhang argues, can Marxist guidance take root and lead to the Two Integrations. Zhang concludes that the Two Integrations, which address theory's relation to reality and to culture, are the distinctive mark of the plan for the coming five years. Zhang pledges to strengthen them in building Chinese linguistics, with breakthroughs in basic theory, concepts, methods, disciplinary history and technical platforms. Read the original if you want a brief insider example of how a CASS researcher links the 2016 resource-integration directive to the Two Integrations in one discipline.

Forging ahead on a new journey of flourishing Chinese historiography in the new era 奋进新时代中国史学繁荣发展新征程 Li Guoqiang Marking six years since Xi Jinping's speech of 17 May 2016 on philosophy and social sciences, this commentary, published in 2022, takes stock of Chinese historiography. Li argues that historians, guided by the speech, have gained unprecedented vitality. In Li's account, building the "three systems" of historiography with Chinese characteristics is the central task of the new era, and the founding of the Chinese Academy of History has moved the field into high-quality development. The article first reviews achievements and then sets out three priorities. The achievements include the launch in June 2020 of the (New) General History of China project, listed in the 14th Five-Year Plan, and a special programme of major historical research that has set up 9 topics and 139 projects. Li also notes progress in traditional and emerging subfields and in interdisciplinary work using big data and artificial intelligence. Li contends that historians are linking research to the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They use a "grand view of history" to examine the historical roots of Chinese modernization, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. The three priorities are: firmly following Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; making full use of the Academy's role in coordinating national historical research; and carrying forward the tradition of applying scholarship to practical statecraft. Li concludes that these steps should produce works of intellectual depth, train historians versed in Chinese and Western learning, and contribute to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation ahead of the 20th Party Congress (2022). Read the original if you want an official-institutional view of how China's leading history body presents its achievements and agenda in 2022.

Applying the Marxist conception of justice to advance social fairness and justice 运用马克思主义正义观推进社会公平正义 Li Nan Li Nan asks how Marx's conception of justice can be revived and applied to the tasks of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article argues that returning to Marx's view of justice answers rival theories, especially liberal ones, helps defend mainstream values, and offers a way to resolve deep-seated social contradictions and conflicts of interest. In Li's view it should be tied to the modernization of state governance, so that the fruits of development reach all people more fairly. Published in People's Forum in 2022, the article has three parts. The first sets out four theoretical features of Marx's view of justice. The second explains the significance of applying it today, under four headings: historical position, value orientation, content system and spatial pattern. The third proposes four practical paths: building consensus on fairness, narrowing gaps in distribution, strengthening the rule of law, and improving public services. On Marx, Li argues that justice belongs to the superstructure and is a historical category, with no eternal justice. Its core is the question of social relations of production, and its ultimate aim is the free and all-round development of the human being. For the present, Li reads Xi Jinping's statement that fairness and justice are an inherent requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the Party's updated position. Justice is said to include both 'getting what one deserves' and 'getting what one needs', with the second protecting vulnerable groups through redistribution. Li presents the 'three fairnesses' (fairness of rights, opportunity and rules) as linking starting point, process and outcome. The article also ties the new development philosophy, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind to justice at home and abroad. Li's practical proposals include promoting the socialist core value of 'justice' through education and Party media. In distribution, Li calls for distribution according to labour as the main form, fiscal transfers, and charitable 'third distribution'. Li also stresses rigorous law-making and enforcement and fairer education, employment and public services. Achieving justice is described as long-term and complex, to be pursued on the basis of high-quality development. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese journals link Marx's theory of justice to Xi-era policy on common prosperity, law and livelihood.

Marx's thought on labour and its contemporary value 马克思的劳动思想及当代价值 Liu Huihui Writing in 2022, Liu Huihui asks what Marx's thought on labour can still offer at a time when modern science and technology have changed the forms and content of labour. The article argues that tracing how Marx's view of labour developed, from his school essay to Capital, yields practical guidance for China's present tasks, including the labour-capital relationship, distribution and common prosperity. The article follows Marx's intellectual path in stages. It begins with his early views (the essay on choosing a profession, the doctoral dissertation on Democritus and Epicurus, and his work at the Rheinische Zeitung), then turns to alienated labour in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 against the background of Hegel, Feuerbach and Moses Hess. It next covers the materialist conception of history in The German Ideology, and finally the labour theory of value in The Poverty of Philosophy, Wage Labour and Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital. Liu's central claim is that labour runs through Marx's whole development. Contact with material interests at the Rheinische Zeitung pushed him from idealism to materialism. In the 1844 Manuscripts he described four forms of alienation: from the product, from the act of labour, from species-being and from other people. The German Ideology then made labour and production the basis of history, and the dual character of labour (concrete and abstract) became, in Liu's account, the pivot for understanding political economy and for exposing capitalist exploitation. Liu draws four lessons for today. These are to respect labour and talent and keep workers as the main body of development; to uphold distribution according to work and tackle uneven distribution in pursuit of common prosperity; to advance a community with a shared future for mankind, presented as a contemporary expression of Marx's theory of labour emancipation; and to combine Marxist principles with the Chinese Dream. Liu stresses that labour's full emancipation belongs to communism. Read the original if you want a concise, textbook-style survey of the stages of Marx's labour thought and an example of how such scholarship is tied to current Chinese policy language.

The transformation of philosophy and the true task of human philosophy 哲学之变与人类哲学的真正任务 Zhang Nengwei Zhang Nengwei asks whether philosophy is, as Aristotle and Hegel held, a body of theoretical knowledge about the essence and laws of the world. The article, first published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in July 2022, answers no. It argues that modern science has ended philosophy's classical role as knowledge of essences. Philosophy survives in a changed form, and its true task is practical philosophy, which reflects on the meaning of human existence and action. The article is built in three steps, mostly through the work of Hans-Georg Gadamer, with Habermas, Rorty, Kant and Thomas Kuhn's notion of a paradigm in supporting roles. The first step describes how a scientised age and positivist philosophy of science have eroded philosophy's claim to a unified view of the world. The second step follows philosophy's turn towards art and the humanities. The third step proposes replacing the "theoretical paradigm" with a "practical paradigm", drawing on Aristotle's distinction between theoretical, practical and productive knowledge. Zhang's central move is to separate the end of metaphysics as a theory of knowledge from the end of philosophy itself. Following Gadamer, the author holds that philosophy still pursues an overall understanding of experience, but this "whole" exceeds what science can know. Philosophy therefore resembles art and the humanities: it offers no fixed or absolute answers and is an enterprise of understanding. Zhang then argues that practical philosophy should take the place of "first philosophy". Practice is not the application of scientific theory. Theoretical knowledge and technical capacity should be subordinated to human practice, not the reverse, and this is how the growing self-alienation of modern life can be countered. Zhang concludes that practical philosophy is the true task of philosophy. It is needed by a scientised present and by a future in which people ask how they ought to exist. The article closes on the claim that philosophy will not end so long as questioning does not end. It does not discuss Marxism explicitly and rests mainly on the hermeneutic tradition. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language account of Gadamerian arguments for practical philosophy and their use in rethinking philosophy's task.

Abstraction becomes domination: Marx and Lefebvre 抽象成为统治：马克思与列斐伏尔 Yan Jinggao This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in 2022, asks how Henri Lefebvre extends Marx's critique of the modern paradox that individuals are now ruled by abstractions. Yan argues that Lefebvre takes up Marx's formula of abstraction (capital) becoming dominant and concludes that abstract space has become dominant. Neither thinker, in Yan's reading, falls into despair, since both trust the emancipatory force of historical dialectics. The piece has three parts: abstract capital as ruler, abstract space as ruler, and the path to breaking abstract domination. It draws mainly on Marx's remarks on money, capital and the bourgeois state, and on Lefebvre's account of the production of space. For Marx, Yan says, the development of the market makes exchange value an alien power, money its embodiment, and money fetishism a reified social relation in which workers and capitalists alike serve capital's self-expansion. Economic globalisation extends this rule, and capitalist fetishism becomes the ideology of global capital. Lefebvre, Yan explains, moves from the production of things in space to the production of space itself: abstract space becomes the "subject" of social relations and daily life. It is an objective abstraction, understood through the dialectic from the abstract to the concrete. Its closest concrete form is state monopoly capitalism, and urbanisation, nationalisation and globalisation make up a spatial trinity. Yan concludes that this domination contains its own negation. Capital, for Marx, meets its limit in itself, and abstract space must generate spaces of difference that exist in negative form. The proletariat, in Marx's view, carries the task of liberating humanity, and Lefebvre locates possible spatial liberation in city margins, slums and prohibited spaces of resistance. Read the original if you want a brief overview of how Lefebvre's spatial theory is presented as a continuation of Marx's critique of capital.

Advancing Marxist research in depth and on solid foundations 深入扎实推进马克思主义研究 Xin Xiangyang Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Xin Xiangyang argues that studying Xi Jinping's 17 May speech on Marxism and his remarks at Renmin University of China should drive further research on twenty-first-century Marxism and contemporary Chinese Marxism. The piece is a short commentary tied to the 14th Five-Year Plan for philosophy and social sciences. The article has three parts. It first discusses why Marxism keeps its vitality, then sets out the original contributions it attributes to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and finally reports on the work of the Academy of Marxism at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Xin contends that Marxism stays vital when upholding it is combined with developing it, which the author links to the Two Integrations. Marxist guidance, in this account, is what distinguishes contemporary Chinese philosophy and social sciences. Xin says Xi Jinping Thought spans Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. Its philosophical contributions include the theory of the principal contradiction in the new era; its economic ones include the new development philosophy and common prosperity theory; its contributions to scientific socialism include theories of the Party's long-term governance and the Party's self-reform. Xin reports that the Academy of Marxism has published chronologies of Marx's and Engels's thought and is issuing an eight-volume history of Marxism's development. It has also launched book series on Xi Jinping Thought and completed over 300 policy reports. The author calls for taking this research to a higher level. Read the original if you want a brief official-institutional view of how the Academy of Marxism framed its research agenda in 2022.

Accelerating the building of the "three systems" of economics with Chinese characteristics 加快推进中国特色经济学“三大体系”建设 Huang Qunhui Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Huang Qunhui asks how economists should carry out Xi Jinping's 2016 call to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, applied here to economics. Huang's answer is that the work must be led by Marxism and, concretely, by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. This Thought is to guide the building of the discipline system, the academic system and the discourse system of Chinese economics. The short commentary first states the guiding principle. It presents the Party Central Committee's economic thinking since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a further theoretical leap in combining Marxist political economy with China's concrete realities. It then sets out three tasks for the 14th Five-Year Plan period, one for each system. Each task is illustrated with projects of the Institute of Economics at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. For the discipline system, Huang stresses foundational work: textbooks, handbooks and yearbooks. Examples are the Handbook of Chinese Economics, the Yearbook of Chinese Economics and the textbook Contemporary Chinese Economics. For the academic system, Huang calls for research on major theoretical and practical questions, such as high-quality development, the new development philosophy, common prosperity and the nature and behaviour of capital. The Institute's annual China Economic Report is cited as a collective effort on these themes. For the discourse system, Huang proposes turning political discourse into scholarly concepts, making academic discourse accessible to the public, and taking Chinese discourse abroad, so that distinctive concepts with world influence emerge. Huang concludes that studying and explaining Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is both a basic need of building a modern socialist country and a necessary condition for Marxism to lead economics. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line statement of how Chinese economists are told to organise textbooks, research programmes and public discourse around Xi's economic thought.

The theoretical power of a system comes from practical requirements of building that system 体系的理论力量来自服务于体系建设的实践要求 Mo Jihong Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Mo Jihong takes up the task, set by Xi Jinping in his May 2016 speech on philosophy and social sciences, of building a philosophy and social science with Chinese characteristics. Mo argues that legal scholarship should construct a theoretical system of socialist jurisprudence with Chinese characteristics by integrating its discipline system, academic system and discourse system. Two tasks are described as key. The short commentary is organised around those two tasks. The first concerns teaching: the discipline, curriculum and instruction systems of legal studies. The second concerns linking the "three systems" to the practical requirements of building a socialist system of rule of law with Chinese characteristics. On the first task, Mo notes that the revised national teaching quality standard for law (2021) changed the "10+X" core curriculum into "1+10+X", making the Introduction to Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law the foundational "1". Mo holds that this one course cannot by itself carry the Thought's spirit into the other legal disciplines, so its theoretical system must be unified with the discipline and curriculum systems. Mo describes the response of the CASS law school, which formed a teaching group of senior researchers. On the second task, Mo traces the path from the 15th Party Congress's goal of a legal system to the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2014) and its overall goal of a socialist system of rule of law with Chinese characteristics. Mo argues that scholarship must be problem-oriented and organised around the seven legal branches, so that it keeps lasting academic vitality. Mo concludes that legal scholars should keep to the Chinese path of rule of law and resist what the article calls blind worship of Western constitutionalism and rule-of-law theory. They should also tell China's rule-of-law story in terms the world can understand and hold discourse power. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a CASS legal scholar ties the "three systems" agenda to law teaching and legal-system building.

Implementing the speech's spirit, staying problem-oriented, and promoting the integrated development of basic and applied research 落实讲话精神 坚持问题导向 推动基础研究和应用研究融合发展 Sun Zhuangzhi Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Sun Zhuangzhi takes up how international studies in China should respond to Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences and to the national 14th Five-Year Plan for the development of philosophy and social sciences. Sun's answer is that research must stay problem-oriented, because theoretical innovation, in Xi's words, begins from problems. Doing so, Sun argues, would join basic theoretical research with applied, policy-oriented research. The short commentary sets out four tasks. These are strengthening the guiding role of theoretical innovation, the supporting role of disciplinary expertise, the policy-advisory role of think tanks, and the building of international communication capacity. It draws examples from the work of institutes in the international studies division of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS). It closes with a brief assessment of strengths and shortcomings. Sun contends that international studies should be guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, especially his thought on diplomacy, and should answer questions such as "what is happening to the world" and "where is humanity heading". Area studies, in Sun's view, need interdisciplinary methods from a Marxist standpoint and should avoid fragmented, low-level repetition. Think-tank output should be judged by whether it solves real problems and serves central decision-making, not by description alone. Sun cites the China–Russia strategic cooperation think tank and joint opinion polls with partner countries as cases of effective practice. Sun concludes that CASS has balanced its disciplines and improved its management, but still lacks enough high-quality outputs, wider international cooperation and sufficient talent. Sun calls for closing these gaps so that CASS can show "national team" standards. Read the original if you want a brief insider view of how a CASS institute links the Party's research guidelines to think-tank and international-communication work.

The deepening of Marx's view of the internal contradictions of capitalism From the Economic Manuscripts of 1857–1858 to the Economic Manuscripts of 1861–1863 马克思资本主义内在矛盾观的深化 Huang Lu Huang Lu asks how Marx's understanding of the internal contradictions of capitalism changed between two of his economic manuscripts. The article argues that in the 1857–1858 manuscripts Marx was still held within a framework of exchange between capital and labour, which limited his grasp of those contradictions. In the 1861–1863 manuscripts, Huang contends, he moved to the capitalist mode of production itself and reached the view that capital is its own real barrier, producing a fuller, systematic account. The article has three parts. It first traces the move from monetary relations to capital's process of valorisation, then the shift from the direct production process to the production process of large-scale machine industry, and finally the move from the collapse of the capitalist system of exchange value to a deepened account of crisis. Huang also links the study to the Chinese context, saying that as socialism with Chinese characteristics enters a new era and the socialist market economy is refined, the basic logic of capital must be understood more deeply. Huang argues that the 1857–1858 manuscripts locate the contradiction in the ratio of necessary to surplus labour: capital needs necessary labour and at the same time seeks to reduce it. Machinery, in the 'fragment on machines', pushes this ratio to its limit and is presented as undermining exchange value and the basis of capital. This still treats production as the realisation of unequal exchange. In the 1861–1863 manuscripts, Huang says, Marx analyses machinery as constant capital within production, covering the factory's simplified labour, intensified labour, the pull between absolute and relative surplus value, and the antinomy in the labour relation, which leads to the legal limiting of the working day and to class struggle. Science and general social productive forces are absorbed by capital, so machines replacing labour do not lead directly to collapse. Huang concludes that Marx came to see the contradictions of capitalism as arising in capital's production and reproduction as both a thing and a social relation. On this reading they reflect the logic of capital and the capitalist system, not merely unjust distribution or wasted productive forces, and this prepares Marx's treatment of crisis in Capital. Tracing the shift is said to show how Marx's critique of political economy extended and deepened. Read the original if you study the genesis of Capital, the 'fragment on machines' or Marx's theory of capitalist crisis, and want to see how a Chinese scholar reads the change between the two manuscripts.

The basic orientations and institutional failures of economic governance in capitalist states 资本主义国家经济治理的基本取向及制度性失灵 Wang Shengsheng Western economists remain divided over how far the state should govern the economy. After the 2008 financial crisis, neoliberals restated the case for a minimal state, while most left-wing scholars demanded stronger action on equality. Wang Shengsheng argues that the dispute can be resolved only by starting from the dialectical unity of economic base and superstructure. On this basis the article analyses the nature of the capitalist state and its "elastic structure", identifies the basic orientations of its economic governance, and explains why that governance fails at the level of institutions. The article first criticises Western theories of the "modern state" as public and autonomous, citing Skocpol, Mann, Evans and others, and sets against them Marx, Engels, Miliband and Poulantzas. It then derives a four-layered elastic structure of the capitalist state from four determinations of capitalist relations of production, and draws from each a basic orientation of governance. A fourth part sets out the institutional failures corresponding to each orientation, and a short closing section draws lessons for China. Wang's central claim is that the public and autonomous features of the capitalist state do not contradict its class character but are the concrete form in which bourgeois rule operates. Because capitalist economy and politics are relatively separated, the state can absorb part of the proletariat's economic claims while preserving the relations of production. The four layers are institutional (private property and freedom of contract), organisational (elections and party competition), operational (supporting accumulation and technical progress) and discursive (bourgeois ideology). The corresponding orientations are partial "de-commodification" of labour-power, balancing different fractions of capital under industrial capital, macroeconomic balance through demand management, and presenting governance as value-free economics. Each fails because the root cause of disruption, the antagonism between capital and labour, cannot be removed without negating capitalism itself. Wang cites the post-war shift from Keynesianism to neoliberalism, the rise of financial monopoly capital (with US profit-share figures), overproduction, and the dependence of mainstream economics on bourgeois ideology. Wang concludes that capitalist economic governance marks historical progress over earlier social forms but has insurmountable limits. The author argues that China should draw on its reasonable elements, coordinating the rule of law, political, educational and Party-building work, while going beyond its limits by consolidating socialist relations of production, putting the people at the centre, and relying on the Party's overall leadership. Read the original if you want a Marxist state-theory critique of Western debates on economic governance, with extensive engagement with Poulantzas, Polanyi, Arrighi and the autonomy-of-the-state literature.

The essence of climate capitalism and its transcendence 气候资本主义的实质和超越 Zhang Yunfei Zhang Yunfei asks how late capitalism has responded to the climate crisis and how that response can be overcome. Zhang argues that global warming is the climatic expression of capitalism's general crisis. To protect the realisation of surplus value, late capitalism has turned into "climate capitalism" through carbon markets and carbon technologies, and into "climate imperialism" through war, threats and manipulation of the global carbon agenda. The two are described as inner and outer faces of one phenomenon. The article was published in Marxist Studies in 2022. The article has four parts. It first traces the historical emergence of climate capitalism from "fossil capitalism", covering the energy base of capitalism, the climate crisis, international pressure and the climate policies of Western states. It then examines climate capitalism as an expression of neoliberal environmentalism, looking at carbon pricing, carbon finance, geoengineering and failures of social governance. The third part treats climate imperialism, and the fourth sets out how climate capitalism is to be transcended. Zhang's central claim is that warming stems from fossil capitalism and ultimately from the logic of capital, not from industrial civilisation as such. Carbon trading privatises the atmosphere as a public resource and opens new accumulation opportunities. Geoengineering is presented as technological optimism that preserves fossil capitalism. The article cites the 1984–85 British miners' strike and the Trump administration's withdrawal from the Paris Agreement to show climate policy being tied to class struggle. Climate imperialism, in Zhang's account, appears in oil wars, wavering US diplomacy, refusal of historical responsibility and a "climate encirclement" of China, which the article says bears less historical and current responsibility than the West. Zhang concludes that only a revolutionary change of social form can end the crisis. The path runs from the capitalist high-carbon society through a socialist low-carbon society to a communist "zero-carbon society" based on solar energy and public ownership, with climate struggle folded into class struggle. The article presents China's carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals, together with its ecological civilisation policy, as a bridge between reality and ideal, and as evidence that socialism offers hope for a low-carbon society. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of climate politics that links Western eco-Marxist literature to China's official climate strategy.

Embracing the world: the historical evolution of the Communist Party of China's international outlook 胸怀天下：中国共产党国际观的历史沿革 Zhang Shunyue Taking up the Sixth Plenum's 2021 Resolution on the Party's century of struggle, which names "embracing the world" as a historical lesson, Zhang asks how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has understood its relationship to the outside world. The article argues that the Party's international outlook is distinct from its theory of international relations or diplomacy. It covers the Party's views on world history, on other parties, on Chinese and world revolution, and on civilizations. Zhang holds that this outlook grew out of Marxist internationalism, Chinese traditional culture and changing conditions, and that it should be read within the history of the world socialist movement. The article traces four periods. These are the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For each, Zhang identifies the central problem the Party faced and the answers it gave. Zhang closes by drawing four lessons from the century as a whole. In the first period, Zhang argues, the young Party, then a section of the Communist International, absorbed Lenin's theory of world revolution. It copied Soviet urban-insurrection strategy and went through detours until Mao Zedong's Sinification of Marxism. Zhang points to the thesis that the Chinese revolution is part of the world revolution, to the strategy of encircling the cities from the countryside, and to the principle of independence and self-reliance. In the second period, the Party first took the Soviet Union as its teacher, then urged critical learning and a "second integration". After the Sino-Soviet split it developed the "intermediate zone" and "three worlds" ideas. In the reform era, Zhang says, "peace and development" became the theme of the age, and self-reliance was combined with opening up. This led to the idea of a harmonious world. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Zhang describes an outlook framed by the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and "changes unseen in a century", and expressed in a community with a shared future for mankind and Chinese modernization. Zhang concludes that the Party has "embraced the world" by following four principles. It upholds Marxist internationalism while taking its own road. It analyses situations realistically and sides with human progress. It maintains independence and self-reliance while learning from abroad. It pursues peace and mutual benefit while being ready to struggle against hegemonism and imperialism. The article presents these as the basis of the Party's current global role and of its claim to lead a revival of world socialism. Read the original if you want a periodised, officially framed account of how Party theorists link China's revolution, construction and reform to its view of world order.

Deeply understanding the "Two Establishes" and consciously achieving the "Two Upholds" 深刻理解“两个确立” 自觉做到“两个维护” Chen Li Writing in Qiushi (2022, no. 2), Chen Li takes up the Party's 2021 historical resolution, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which declared that establishing Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and the whole Party, and establishing the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, are of decisive significance. This is a theoretical commentary on the Party's line. It argues that the Two Establishes rest on theoretical, historical and practical grounds, and that understanding them should strengthen the Party's consciousness in carrying out the Two Upholds. The article has four parts. Three sections set out the theoretical, historical and practical bases of the Two Establishes. A final section describes how Party members and cadres should achieve the Two Upholds. Chen draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, on Party history from the First Congress through the Zunyi Meeting, Yan'an and Deng Xiaoping, and on developments since the 18th Party Congress (2012). On theory, Chen holds that upholding the authority of the Party centre and centralised, unified leadership is a principle of the Marxist doctrine of party-building. The article cites Engels on the Paris Commune and on authority, and Lenin on political leaders and revolutionary theory. It attributes the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party partly to its abandonment of centralised leadership. On history, Chen argues that the Party suffered repeated setbacks before the Zunyi Meeting because it lacked a mature leadership core. After Zunyi, a core around Mao Zedong formed, a point Chen reinforces with Mao's and Deng's remarks on the leadership core. On practice, Chen says the Party centre with Xi as its core has since 2012 strengthened Party leadership, handled major risks and achieved historic changes. Xi's core status and his Thought were then written into the Party constitution and the state constitution. Chen concludes that the Two Establishes reflect the will of the Party, army and people and provide a stronger political guarantee for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chen calls for turning support for them into the Two Upholds through five steps: firm belief in and faithful practice of Xi Jinping Thought, stronger Party political building, concrete action rather than slogans, loyalty to the Party, and better political capacity. Read the original if you want an authoritative statement of how the Party's theorists justify the Two Establishes and what they require of cadres.

The Communist Party of China and the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 中国共产党与中华民族伟大复兴 Ren Lixuan Writing in the People's Daily on 29 June 2022, Ren Lixuan argues that only the Communist Party of China could take on the historic mission of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and that this rejuvenation is the single theme running through the Party's century of struggle. The piece is an authoritative-style commentary that builds on Xi Jinping's statement that without the Party there would be no new China and no national rejuvenation, and on the 2021 Party resolution on its history. The article has three parts. The first explains why the Party was the only force able to carry the mission, citing four factors: scientific theory, its founding aspiration, reliance on the people, and self-reform. The second says that all the Party's struggles, sacrifices and creations since 1921 have served rejuvenation. The third looks ahead and sets out how to advance the cause by taking in hand the "four greats": great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream. In Ren's account, earlier political forces failed to save the nation because they lacked a lasting mass movement and did not recognise the strength of the people. The Party, by contrast, adapted Marxism to China, culminating in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and it pursues no special interests of its own. It also escaped the "historical cycle" of rise and fall through self-reform, which Ren presents as the second answer after Mao Zedong's answer of supervision by the people. The article cites more than 3.7 million identifiable martyrs between 1921 and 1949 as evidence of sacrifice, and it points to the building of a moderately prosperous society, Chinese modernization and institutional innovation as evidence of creation. Ren concludes that the country is closer than ever to rejuvenation but must expect harder struggle, including against a long-term external containment campaign that the author attributes to the United States. The author calls for implementing the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, continuing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and pursuing high-quality development and common prosperity along socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece also presents rejuvenation as contributing to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party narrative of rejuvenation in the run-up to the 20th Party Congress (2022).

Opening up a historic undertaking by upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership 在坚持和加强党的全面领导中开创历史伟业 Liu Tongfang Published in Guangming Daily on 1 July 2022, the centenary of the Party's founding, this commentary asks why the Communist Party of China's overall leadership must be upheld and how it should be strengthened. Liu Tongfang takes as the starting point the Resolution on the major achievements and historical experience of the Party's century of struggle, adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021). Liu argues that leadership by the Party is the first lesson of the century and that it must be maintained steadfastly and without wavering. The piece has three parts. The first grounds the principle in scientific socialism and the classical texts. The second sets out how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era places Party leadership first among its core contents. The third gives practical measures for the Party's leading role in the new era, and a short closing passage restates the main points. Liu's central claim is that leadership by a proletarian party is a basic principle of scientific socialism. The author gives four reasons: it realises the people's interests, it fulfils the proletariat's historical mission, it is needed for victory in struggle, and it is the precondition for moving socialism from theory to practice. Liu draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin for support. Liu then presents three formulations from Xi Jinping as an original contribution to scientific socialism in the twenty-first century. In them, Party leadership is the most essential feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the greatest strength of its system, and the supreme political leadership force. Liu says the Party's leading position is confirmed by history, set by the nature of the state and written into the constitution. Liu also contrasts China's peaceful development and stable economy with what the author describes as continuing local wars and weak growth in the West. For practice, Liu calls for three things. The first is to uphold the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership, with the Two Upholds as the basic political requirement. The second is to build an institutional system that carries Party leadership into state organs, the rule of law and grass-roots organisations, and to improve democratic centralism. The third is to pursue the Party's self-reform so as to keep it advanced and pure, including through anti-corruption work and better governing capacity. Liu concludes that Party leadership is the anchor for the new journey towards a modern socialist country and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official line on Party leadership as presented in a major Party newspaper at the 2022 centenary.

Summing up historical experience: the scientific method behind the Communist Party of China's major achievements 总结历史经验：中国共产党取得重大成就的科学方法 Han Zhenfeng Mi Ting Han Zhenfeng and Mi Ting ask how the Communist Party of China (CPC) has used the summing-up of historical experience as a working method, and why it counts as a decisive factor in the Party's achievements. They define the method as a scientific application of Marxist methodology, an expression of dialectical-materialist epistemology in practice. It turns knowledge gained in practice into rational conclusions and theory that then guide new practice. Drawing on the Party's third historical resolution (2021), the authors present it as a tradition of more than a century. The article proceeds chronologically through four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. For each period it identifies characteristic practices, from the 1927 August 7 Meeting and the Zunyi Meeting to Mao Zedong's rural investigations, the 1945 and 1981 historical resolutions, and Xi Jinping's call for a 'grand historical view' and the 2021 Party history study campaign. A final section draws out the method's basic dimensions and lessons. The authors identify three constant principles: integrating Marxist fundamentals with China's concrete conditions, using dialectical thinking to weigh positive and negative experience, and combining continuity with development. They argue that the Party sums up experience in several ways: through investigation and the mass line, through domestic and foreign experience, and through routine summing-up at congresses and anniversaries. They also stress raising experience into new theory. Their main analytical move is to distinguish fundamental, basic and specific experience. Fundamental experience, such as upholding the Party's overall leadership, Marxism and the socialist path, governs the other two; specific cases such as the 'Fengqiao experience' or 'Jinjiang experience' supplement and refine it. The authors conclude that summing-up must keep to the people's standpoint and respond to the demands of the times, guided by a problem-oriented approach. They call for the Party to draw lessons from mistakes while opposing exaggeration of errors or negation of Party history. They also urge it to treat foreign experience as reference, not as a model to copy, with its own experience primary. They add that experience should be promptly turned into theory and used on new problems, since summing-up serves present needs and is not an end in itself. Read the original if you want a systematic, Party-official account of how the CPC describes its own method of historical self-assessment, from Mao to Xi.

The great changes of the new era's ten years show the strong resilience and vitality of China's economy 新时代十年的伟大变革彰显中国经济强大韧性和活力 Ye Qi Huang Maoxing Published in Guangming Daily on 31 August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary takes Xi Jinping's speech to a seminar of provincial and ministerial leaders as its starting point. Ye and Huang argue that the decade since the 18th Party Congress (2012) brought historic changes that show the strength, resilience and vitality of China's economy. They present these changes as the basis for Chinese modernization and for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article has three parts. The first reviews economic achievements across six areas: economic strength, scientific and technological innovation, coordinated regional development, green development, opening up, and people's livelihoods. The second describes what the authors call a new outlook in the economy, covering resilience, strategic resolve, released vitality and China's contribution to the world economy. The third sets out the sources of this performance and the direction ahead. The authors rely on figures to make the case. They cite GDP of 114 trillion yuan in 2021, a global share rising from 11.4% to above 18%, per capita GDP of 12,500 US dollars, and R&D spending 2.7 times the 2012 level. They also cite a fall in the urban–rural income ratio from 2.88 to 2.50 and the poverty alleviation of 98.99 million rural people. They attribute resilience to a complete industrial system, a supply chain with strong supporting capacity, a flexible macroeconomic policy toolkit and a very large domestic market.
