They name Xi Jinping Thought on the economy, the Party's overall leadership of economic work, the people-centred approach, the new development philosophy, problem-oriented reform and integration into the world economy as the guiding factors. Leadership, in their account, supplies the capacity to concentrate resources on major undertakings and is the core advantage against risks. Ye and Huang conclude that the decade's changes give the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation a stronger institutional, material and spiritual footing and set a course for high-quality development. They contend that China followed an independent path rather than the old Western road to modernization. They also hold that China has acted as a builder of world peace and a contributor to global development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official-aligned scholars summarised the economic record of 2012–2022 on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The political-philosophical meaning of Marx's "illusory community" 马克思“虚幻的共同体”的政治哲学意涵 Wang Tian Wang Tian takes up a long-standing reading of Marx and Engels's phrase "illusory community" (illusory communality) in The German Ideology. On that reading, the state is simply the counterpart of the "real community" and is therefore a purely negative notion. The article argues that this equation of the state with the "illusory community" is too simple. It holds that the state does take a community form with real public functions, and that the charge of illusoriness has a specific target and a specific value standard. The article, published in Theory Journal in 2022, has three sections and a short conclusion. The first examines the state's community form (rule by a class, law, bureaucracy, ideological packaging) and its public functions. The second reconstructs the polemical context of the phrase, namely Marx and Engels's critique of Max Stirner in the "Saint Max" chapter. The third explains the phrase as an evaluation tied to individual freedom, drawing on the Grundrisse, Capital and other texts. Wang makes three main moves. First, the state arises from the division of labour and the clash between particular and common interests. It therefore takes a community form that mediates class conflict, keeps public order, builds public institutions and works, and takes part in world-market competition. The article describes this as the premise of the state's illusoriness. Second, Wang contends that the formulation was aimed first at Stirner's petty-bourgeois, idealist treatment of the "universal" as an abstraction opposed to the individual ego. It was not a general definition of the modern state. For the modern state Wang points to the "bourgeois manipulation" account, in which civil society determines the state and the bourgeoisie uses taxation and credit to make its interests universal. Third, "illusory" carries a value judgement. The state is separated from the individuals in it, who take part only as class members. The freedom it proclaims differs by class and rests on the contingency of living conditions and on the "limits of things", so it restricts individual freedom. Wang concludes that equating the state with the "illusory community" fits neither Marx and Engels's theory nor actual state relations. The bourgeois state, in Wang's account, does not stand apart from civil society. It pushes the opposition between bourgeoisie and proletariat deeper into the defence of private property. Wang says this is a dimension to remember when re-examining Marx's theory of the state and when considering how that theory bears on present-day state governance. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of the state, the Marx–Stirner dispute in The German Ideology, or Chinese scholarly debates on Marxist political philosophy.

On the Marxist shaping of "Chinese governance" by the Communist Party of China 论中国共产党关于“中国之治”的马克思主义塑造 He Changyu Wang Guiquan Scholars have read "Chinese governance" (zhongguo zhi zhi) through traditional culture, through comparison with the West, and through the Fourth Plenum document of 2019. He Changyu and Wang Guiquan argue that this literature lacks a Marxist account of the concept's scientific content. Their thesis is that "Chinese governance" is the result of the Communist Party of China applying Marxism to Chinese conditions, and that it has four linked dimensions: historic achievement, "Chinese wisdom", "Chinese institutions" and "Chinese capacity". The article first traces the term from the Song writer Su Shi through Lu Xun, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. In the authors' account, these earlier models failed to deliver order and prosperity. It then devotes one section to each dimension and ties each to a principle of historical materialism. It closes with practical measures for turning institutional strengths into governance effectiveness. The authors map the four dimensions onto Marxist categories. "Chinese wisdom" is social consciousness actively reflecting social being, and they place Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in this line. "Chinese institutions" are a superstructure resting on a particular economic base. The authors set out the fundamental, basic and important institutions of socialism with Chinese characteristics as three tiers, comparing them to a worldview, a methodology and concrete methods. "Chinese capacity" rests on Marx's view of practice. Here they argue that an institution is judged by the governance results it produces, citing GDP growth from 1952 to 2019 and long-term social stability as the "two miracles". To keep institutional advantages and convert them into effectiveness, the authors propose three measures. The first is to uphold and improve Party leadership. The second is to give full play to the people's role through people's congresses, multiparty cooperation and grassroots self-governance. The third is to improve government decision-making and implementation, with accountability for failures. They conclude that the Party's century of history is one in which "Chinese wisdom" guides, "Chinese institutions" are established and "Chinese capacity" is applied. Read the original if you want to see how Party theorists fit the official concept of governance into the base–superstructure and practice framework of historical materialism.

A century of relations between Chinese youth and the Communist Party of China: review and reflections 中国青年与中国共产党关系百年发展的回顾与思考 Peng Qinghong Tian Shan Writing in 2022, after the Party's centenary, Peng Qinghong and Tian Shan ask how young people and the Communist Party of China (CPC) have related over more than a hundred years, and how that relationship should be handled in future. They argue that the two are "interconnected and mutually thriving" (xiangtong gongrong): the Party's growth has depended on youth, and young people's development has depended on Party guidance. The authors treat this as a main reason for past success and a condition of future success. The article has three parts. The first traces the role of youth across five periods: founding of the Party, national liberation, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The second analyses the internal factors behind the relationship. The third proposes how to develop it going forward. The authors support their account with quotations from Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, and with Party membership statistics from 2022. In the authors' analysis, the relationship rests on three things. The first is affinity: young people's pursuit of truth, novelty, change and practicality is said to match the Party's righteousness, revolutionary character, creativity and practical orientation. The Party's "people-oriented" character and its collective organisation are said to supply young people with a foundation for growth and with socialisation. The second is shared prosperity: the Party offers a broad stage for young people, who give it vitality in return. The third is the Communist Youth League, which the authors describe as the bridge and link that gathers young people around the Party and addresses their practical problems. As evidence of structural closeness, they cite the 2022 Party statistical bulletin: 24.159 million members aged 35 or under, 25 per cent of the 96.712 million total, and 80.8 per cent of those recruited in 2021. For the future the authors propose a strategy of "four lines advancing together". The ideological line calls for strengthening ideals and convictions and for combating historical nihilism, money worship, hedonism and extreme individualism. The organisational line calls for extending Party and League organisation to young people in new occupations and for innovating forms of activity. The development line calls for supporting young people's growth, innovation and entrepreneurship. The problem-solving line calls for easing difficulties in employment, housing and education and for protecting young people's rights. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist-institute scholarly article presents the Party–youth relationship historically and sets out the youth-work agenda of the new era.

Grasping the milestone significance of the great changes of the new era's first decade 深刻把握新时代十年伟大变革的里程碑意义 Zhong Xiaowu This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2022 shortly before the 20th Party Congress, explains why Xi Jinping described the great changes of the past ten years as having "milestone significance". Zhong Xiaowu takes up Xi's statement that the decade is a milestone in the history of the Party, of the People's Republic, of reform and opening up, of socialist development and of the Chinese nation. The author argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core has achieved historic accomplishments and brought about historic change. The article is organised as a sequence of areas in which the author finds the decade decisive. It covers Party building, economic strength and the first centenary goal, reform and opening up, theory and international influence, and finally national rejuvenation and cultural foundations. Each section lists achievements in the official register, with figures such as GDP passing 100 trillion yuan and nearly 100 million people lifted out of poverty. On the Party, Zhong claims that the Two Establishes have become a broad consensus, that political awareness of the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds has risen, and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has cleaned up long-standing problems. The author presents the Party's self-reform as a successful path for escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall. On development, Zhong cites a rise in China's share of the world economy from 11.3% to over 18%, a move from 34th to 12th in the Global Innovation Index, the building of a moderately prosperous society, and more than 2,000 reform plans. Zhong then treats Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as "Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century". The article holds that Chinese modernization offers developing countries a new path, breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization, and has shifted the contest between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour. Zhong concludes that the Chinese nation has entered its best period of development since modern times, and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has become an irreversible historical process. The author links this to a stronger sense of the Chinese nation as a community, to the creative transformation of traditional culture, and to the proposal of a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official 2022 narrative of the "new era" decade was framed for a general readership before the 20th Party Congress.

The Communist Party of China's practice and experience in opposing historical nihilism 中国共产党反对历史虚无主义的实践与经验 Yang Jun Writing in mid-2022, Yang Jun asks how the Communist Party of China has responded to historical nihilism and how that struggle should continue as the phenomenon changes form. Yang treats historical nihilism as a political current fundamentally opposed to Marxism, not as the value-neutral 'academic discussion' it claims to be. The article argues that the Party's approach combines affirmative 'building' with 'refuting', that nihilism has taken a 'soft', harder-to-detect form, and that opposing it requires long-term persistence. The article has four parts. It first reviews the Party's measures since 2021, then describes five features of present-day historical nihilism. It next examines how nihilism interacts with other social currents, and finally gives three reasons why criticism must be sustained and what tasks follow. Yang's examples include the Party history study campaign, online rumour-refutation lists, legal punishment of insults to heroes and martyrs, and online controversies of 2021. On the Party's response, Yang points to the campaign launched in February 2021 and the 'four histories' publicity drive, backed by films and television series. On the 'refuting' side, Yang cites rumour-refutation lists and prosecutions under the Law on the Protection of Heroes and Martyrs. Yang says these measures raised public awareness of the concept and shrank nihilism's room for spread. Nihilism, in Yang's account, now focuses on Party history and the history of the People's Republic and reform era, and uses concealed rhetoric, recycled old online content, online disputes and 'fan circle' culture. It also draws on consumerism, pan-entertainment and online populism, which Yang says clothe a political aim in an 'invisibility cloak'. Yang concludes that the struggle must be long-term, for three reasons: Marxism has always developed through contending with hostile currents; nihilism threatens ideological security on the road to the second centenary goal; and global changes are sharpening the contest between socialism and capitalism. Yang calls for better analysis of nihilism's theory and trends, clear criteria separating scholarship from political agitation, and work on institutions, rule of law, education, internet governance and communication. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-affiliated scholar describes the current forms of historical nihilism and the state's strategy against it.

Bringing the Party's political advantage of overall leadership into play on the new journey 新征程上发挥党的全面领导的政治优势 Wu Jiaqing This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in August 2022, asks how the Party's overall leadership can be used as a political advantage on the new journey of building a modern socialist country. Wu Jiaqing, drawing on volume four of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, argues that the Party now faces conditions and tasks of rare complexity and difficulty. In Wu's view, making full use of this advantage will be the key to success on what the text calls a new "examination road". The piece is organised under two headings. The first concerns the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership. The second concerns the Party's capacity to set direction, take the overall view, formulate policy and promote reform. On the first, Wu argues that the Central Committee's authority is the basic support in times of difficulty. Wu credits the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) to the leadership of the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, and cites the Two Establishes as confirming this. Wu calls on Party members to practise the Two Upholds and to strengthen the institutional safeguards, citing intra-Party regulations, reporting requirements and a tightly linked organisational system. On the second, Wu treats each of the four capacities as a matter of ability and resolve for leading cadres: correct political direction, a focus on the "matters of national importance", policy grounded in investigation and a people-centred approach, and deepening reform. Wu concludes that leading cadres at every level must raise these capacities so that modernization stays on course. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars presented the Party's overall leadership as a source of strength shortly before the 20th Party Congress.

Seeking the code of why a century-old Party has succeeded 探寻百年大党为什么能够成功的密码 Sang Donghua Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Sang Donghua asks why the Communist Party of China has stayed vigorous, remained at the forefront of its era and continued to serve as the core of leadership after a hundred years. Drawing on the Resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Sang answers that five things have never changed: the Party's lofty ideals, its founding mission, its fundamental purpose of serving the people, its commitment to developing Marxism, and its political courage for self-reform. The commentary is organised into four sections, each describing the Party as a particular kind of political force: a mission-driven party, a party of the people, a party armed with scientific theory, and a party of revolutionaries. Each section runs through the revolutionary, socialist construction, reform and opening up, and post-18th Party Congress (2012) periods. It draws on speeches by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, early Party documents and episodes from the Long March and the Yan'an years. Sang argues first that the Party has held to socialism and communism since 1921, and cites the more than 3.7 million named revolutionary martyrs of 1921–1949 as proof of its commitment. Second, Sang holds that the Party's strength comes from its bond with the people, from the 1945 inclusion of serving the people in the Party constitution to the poverty-alleviation campaign, which the article says lifted 98.99 million rural poor out of poverty. Third, adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, is presented as the Party's ongoing theoretical innovation. Fourth, Sang stresses self-reform: the Party's greatness lies not in avoiding errors but in confronting its own problems, now through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Sang concludes that the Party's century of history is one of striving for lofty social ideals, of sharing the people's fate, of continually adapting Marxism, and of leading a great social revolution through a great self-revolution. The piece is a concise statement of the official account of Party success. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated historians present the sources of the Party's longevity, with the standard quotations and episodes used in that account.

Leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform 以党的自我革命引领社会革命 Li Xiaodong Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Li Xiaodong argues that the Communist Party of China has been able to lead what the article calls a great social revolution because it has repeatedly carried out a great revolution on itself. The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's recent remarks to provincial and ministerial leaders, which call for the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. Li presents this as essential to the Party's long-term rule. The commentary is organised in three numbered sections. The first treats self-reform as an inherent requirement of a Marxist party's historical mission. The second reads it as a lesson drawn from the Party's revolution, construction and reform. The third presents it as the key to coping with changes in the world, the era and history. Li defines social revolution as resting on the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, covering both the violent overthrow of old political structures and the building of new society. Self-reform, in this account, means continual self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. Li cites Engels and Lenin on internal struggle and on a party's attitude to its own mistakes. Li argues that the two revolutions form an organic unity, in which the height reached by self-reform determines the depth of social revolution. The historical record is traced through the Gutian, Zunyi and Yan'an rectification meetings, the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), and the anti-corruption campaign and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since 2012. Li contrasts this with dynasties and large parties elsewhere that, the article says, failed to resolve their own serious problems and fell into the pattern of rising quickly and collapsing quickly. Li concludes that the Party faces lasting "four dangers" and "four tests" and that impurities in ideology, politics, organisation and work style remain unresolved. Self-reform therefore has no end point, and the Party must strengthen its urgency, initiative and foresight to ensure it does not degenerate. Li ties this to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and to building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building discourse in 2022 justified full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as the precondition of the Party's leadership of social change.

The historical coordinates and world significance of Chinese modernization from the perspective of historical materialism 唯物史观视野下中国式现代化的历史坐标与世界意义 Huang Jianjun Huang Jianjun asks where Chinese modernization sits within the overall course of human modernization, and what significance it has for the world. Writing in 2022, Huang argues that, read through historical materialism, Chinese modernization is a non-capitalist path that goes beyond the logic of capital and puts people's value at its centre. In this reading it has far-reaching world-historical significance. The article has three parts. The first reconstructs how Marx and Engels understood the origin of modernization, and the problems of Western modernization. The second sets out the historical coordinates of Chinese modernization: its historical starting point, a vertical axis (the Communist Party's independent exploration) and a horizontal axis (comparison with the West). The third turns to the world significance of the Chinese path. It cites Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping throughout. Huang first argues that for Marx modernization is driven by changes in the mode of production, especially machine industry and the expansion of capital. Western modernization therefore brings a chain of problems: the expansionary logic of capital, polarisation between rich and poor, and the alienation of human beings. Against this, Huang presents Chinese modernization as the practical application of Marx's idea of bypassing the 'Caudine Forks' of capitalism. Its vertical coordinate is the Party-led path from passive to active exploration, ending in modernization that is socialist and has Chinese characteristics. Its horizontal coordinate is a 'parallel' (bingliánshì) model, centred on the people, which Huang contrasts with the West's capital-centred 'serial' model. Huang concludes that Chinese modernization points towards a future form of civilization beyond industrial civilization. It offers developing countries a way to avoid 'dependency', 'convergence' or 'decoupling' models, and it widens the field of practice for scientific socialism. The article cites an economy of more than 100 trillion yuan, and long-term social stability, as evidence that theories of socialism's failure and of the 'end of history' have been refuted. Huang calls for continued theoretical and practical exploration. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Chinese scholars use classical Marxist texts to place Chinese modernization within world history.

The "small organisation" problem in the early Chinese Communist Party 中共创建初期的“小组织”问题研究 Yang Yang Between the First and Third Congresses (1921–1923), the young Chinese Communist Party faced what later Party reports called the "small organisation problem" (xiao zuzhi wenti): a group of activists around Zhang Guotao that threatened central leadership and unity. Yang Yang argues that earlier accounts reduced the episode to Zhang's ambition against Chen Duxiu and drew mainly on memoirs. Drawing on Chinese and foreign archives, Yang contends that the group was internally diverse and was driven by a shared wish to tighten Party discipline. Yang also argues that resolving it strengthened the Party's organisational system. The article has four parts. It first traces how the term changed from a generic label for small groups into a specific name for factional activity after the Second Congress (1922). It then reconstructs the group's membership, its two sources of recruits (the China Labour Union Secretariat and returnees from Russia and France) and its effect on the central leadership. Next it covers the 1922 West Lake meeting, where the Comintern representative Maring (Henk Sneevliet) intervened. It ends with the group's dissolution at the Third Congress and the institutional changes that followed. Yang makes three main moves. First, the group is measured against Lenin's criteria for factionalism, a separate platform and separate group discipline. Yang finds neither: the members demanded stricter discipline and regular meetings, and criticised Chen Duxiu and the intellectual founders, such as Chen Wangdao and Li Hanjun, as lax. They are therefore described as an "organisation within the organisation" rather than a true faction. Second, Yang shows how the group marginalised Chen and the founding cadres while Zhang's rivalry for Party power, and his abrasive style, fuelled conflict in Wuhan and the Youth League. Third, Maring first sought to cultivate Zhang but backed Chen as the only capable leader. The group collapsed when Zhang lost Comintern support, was discredited after the 1923 Beijing–Hankou railway strike, and failed to be re-elected to the Central Committee at the Third Congress. Yang concludes that the episode left lasting distrust in the Party. It was also later used as a negative example, and the 1945 Party constitution banned small-organisation activity. The Third Congress produced the Party's first organisational regulation, which defined the chairman's powers, added a secretary's countersignature and fixed meeting schedules. Yang sees this as meeting the group's own demands, and says the case gave experience for applying democratic centralism. Read the original if you study early CPC organisational history, the Comintern's role in China, or the origins of Party discipline, and want an archive-based reassessment of Zhang Guotao's group.

Upholding historical thinking to advance the great cause 坚持历史思维 推进伟大事业 Dong Zhenhua This commentary, published in Economic Daily in August 2022, asks how historical thinking can guide the Party's management of economic and social development. Dong argues that it rests on historical materialism, has been an important tool for generations of Chinese communists, and is a methodological component of Xi Jinping's economic thought. The piece is organised under three headings: identifying the historical position and fixing basic strategy; drawing on historical experience for strategic planning; and following historical laws to advance historic undertakings. It draws on Deng Xiaoping's remarks on the primary stage of socialism, the 19th Party Congress (2017) judgement on a new era, and the Party's practice of periodic historical summing-up. Dong contends that historical development is both continuous and staged, so each period must first establish its historical premises and position. China, in the author's account, remains in the primary stage of socialism and is the world's largest developing country, while the new era shapes the response to changes in the principal contradiction. Dong holds that the new development philosophy grew out of lessons from China and abroad. The author also treats development as a qualitative change that follows economic, social and natural laws, with innovation, coordination and green development as examples. Dong concludes that, having taken the new historical position, the Party should apply historical materialism and a sense of historical initiative, learn from experience, grasp historical laws and seize opportunities. The aim is to raise the public's sense of gain, happiness and security and to create new historic achievements. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party School scholars present historical thinking as a method for economic policy.

Grasping the contemporary significance and essential features of common prosperity 把握共同富裕的时代意蕴和本质特征 Jia Liping Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Jia Liping asks how common prosperity should be understood as the country begins a new journey towards building a modern socialist country in all respects. Jia argues that common prosperity has its roots in Marxism, expresses the Chinese Communist Party's fundamental values, is an essential requirement of socialism, and is an important feature of Chinese modernization. The short commentary is organised under four headings, one for each of these claims. It draws on Marx and Engels, on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, and on Xi Jinping, and it cites the 2021 Party history resolution and the 19th Party Congress (2017) goals for 2035 and the middle of the century. Jia holds that Marx and Engels pictured a community of free individuals in which each person's free development is the condition for everyone's, so common prosperity is the basic aim of Marxism. In the Party's own history, Jia traces the same aim through Mao's "common" wealth and strength, Deng's statement that common prosperity is socialism's greatest advantage, and Xi's commitment to people-centred development. Jia also reads common prosperity as an institutional requirement tied to the basic socialist economic system and its distribution arrangements, and as a marker of Chinese modernization. Jia concludes that the Party must coordinate the Five-sphere Integrated Plan and the Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy, and must pursue high-quality development, so as to meet its goals for common prosperity and all-round human development. Jia presents these goals as having major significance for the history of the Party, of socialism and of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party theorists in 2022 linked common prosperity to Marxist classics and to the Party's own tradition.

The development path, defining categories and innovative value of the CPC's thought on building a moderately prosperous society 中国共产党小康社会建设思想的发展进路、标识范畴及拓新价值 Huang Rongsheng Following Xi Jinping's 2021 announcement that a moderately prosperous society (xiaokang) had been fully built, Huang Rongsheng asks how the Communist Party of China's thinking on building such a society developed, what its core categories are, and what it adds to theory and practice. The article argues that this thought answers the questions of how xiaokang is built and completed, and that it is a distinctive part of Chinese modernization that will continue to matter in the second centenary goal. The article has three parts. The first traces the development path through traditional Chinese culture, the Party's century of struggle, and the people's rising living standards. The second sets out five defining categories. The third assesses the innovative value of the thought for the Chinese nation, the modernization project, global poverty governance and Marxist theory. In Huang's account, the idea runs from the Book of Songs and the Confucian Book of Rites, through the late-Qing reformer Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen, to Deng Xiaoping's adoption of xiaokang in 1979 to explain a Chinese-style modernization. The five categories are a people-centred philosophy; social civilizational progress and all-round human development as the essence; poverty alleviation as the focus; Chinese modernization as the direction; and the Party's overall leadership as the key. Huang presents these as applications of historical materialism and of Marx's idea of free and all-round human development. The innovative value is said to lie in delivering the first centenary goal, laying material, institutional and popular foundations for a modernized socialist country, offering a Chinese sample for global poverty reduction, opening the path to common prosperity and a community with a shared future for mankind, and enriching contemporary Chinese Marxism. Huang also draws a favourable comparison between China and the West. Huang concludes that xiaokang thought fuses traditional culture, the Party's struggle and popular aspiration, and that it is a scientifically tested understanding with an original place in the Party's theoretical innovation. The author treats full xiaokang as a starting point rather than an endpoint, and calls for inheriting the thought in building a modernized socialist country and pursuing common prosperity. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theory account of how xiaokang is framed historically and conceptually, including its link to poverty alleviation and common prosperity.

A historical inquiry into the logical presuppositions of Western modernity Revisiting the origins of the early Marx's critique of political economy 西方现代性逻辑预设的历史追问 Zhang Xiong Fu Dongmei Taking up Arthur Herman's claim that the Scottish Enlightenment 'invented' the modern world, Zhang and Fu ask how the logic of Western modernity took shape and why it gave rise to the young Marx's critique of political economy. They argue that this critique opened within the dialectical movement of that logic and its history. The Scottish Enlightenment, Rousseau and Hegel are presented as decisive influences, and the relation between civil society and the state as the axis of Western modernity. The article moves through four stages. It first reconstructs three logical presuppositions set out by Scottish thinkers (Hutcheson, Hume, Ferguson, Smith). It then turns to British classical political economy as the system that elaborated these presuppositions, to Rousseau's and Sismondi's doubts about them, and to Hegel's reflection on modernity. It closes with the young Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and its Introduction, and a short conclusion. The authors identify the presuppositions as follows: civil society as the economic community of the future; state governance as the modern art of political philosophy; and sympathy or compassion as a psychological balancer of the opposition between rich and poor. In their account, classical economics made these concrete through four principles (everyone a merchant, economic freedom, market allocation, the state as 'night-watchman') and a dynamics of individual capital driven by desire for profit. Rousseau and Sismondi saw this logic as antinomic: civilization as alienation, and production for production's sake. Hegel recast the antinomy as a split between civil society and state, but resolved it idealistically in the movement of spirit. Marx reversed this, arguing that civil society determines the state and that property relations are its essence. The authors read this as the seed of historical materialism and of the critique of alienated labour. They add that the Introduction's distinction between political and human emancipation fixed his proletarian standpoint. Zhang and Fu conclude that Marx rejected both Hegel's idealism and the Scottish construction of modernity, which he saw as resting on human nature and private property and as favouring the form of freedom over its substance. He sought a new form of human civilization, an association of free individuals. They hold that the critique of political economy is a fundamental critique of modernity, and that the early works shaped the direction of Marx's later system. Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual-historical account, from Hutcheson to Hegel, of how Chinese scholars trace Marx's early turn to political economy.

What kind of road is the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics? An analysis based on four assertions by Xi Jinping 中国特色社会主义道路是一条什么样的道路 Xu Di Xu Hengbing Xu Di and Xu Hengbing ask what kind of road socialism with Chinese characteristics is. They take their answer from four assertions Xi Jinping made in his keynote speech at the World Economic Forum on 17 January 2017. In that speech Xi called it a road established from China's national conditions, one that puts the people's interests first, one of reform and innovation, and one that seeks common development through opening up. The authors argue that these four assertions show the road's content, distinctive features and practical requirements. The article is a research essay in five parts: one section for each assertion, followed by a short conclusion. Each section combines extended quotation from Xi with a historical account of the Party's work in the revolutionary, socialist construction and reform-era periods, and of the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also refers to the 2021 third historical resolution, Mao Zedong's 1939 writings and Deng Xiaoping's remarks on opening up. On national conditions, the authors say the road answers China's historic tasks, rests on the realities of the primary stage of socialism, and is rooted in Chinese cultural traditions. They present it as the product of the Two Integrations, which join Marxism with China's concrete realities and its fine traditional culture. On the people, they stress the people's principal position, the Party's priority on their fundamental interests, and the idea that the people are the final judge of the Party's work. They cite the "dynamic zero" anti-epidemic policy as an example. On reform, they distinguish theoretical, practical, institutional and cultural innovation. On opening up, they argue that China's development occurred under open conditions, that Chinese modernization offers a model for developing countries, and that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and Xi's global initiatives contribute to global governance. The authors conclude that the road is the "only correct" one and that the four assertions help to strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. They say that, by avoiding both a closed, rigid old path and an "evil path" of changing the Party's banner, China can build a modern socialist country and realise the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Party-school scholarship organises the official account of the socialist road around Xi Jinping's formulations.

Using digital technology to help comprehensively advance rural revitalization 以数字技术助力乡村全面振兴 Chen Fulong Writing in the People's Daily in August 2022, Chen Fulong asks how digital technology can serve the comprehensive advancement of rural revitalization after the victory in poverty alleviation. Chen argues that digital technology should be deeply integrated with agricultural development, rural governance and farmers' daily life, providing a scientific and technological guarantee for agricultural and rural modernization. This short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's statements on the shift in the focus of work on agriculture, rural areas and farmers, and on the 14th Five-Year Plan's call to speed up building digital villages. It then proceeds through three headings: modern agriculture, rural governance and farmers' quality of life. On agriculture, Chen holds that applying digital tools across ploughing, sowing, management and harvest changes business models as well as productivity. Examples include BeiDou positioning, artificial intelligence, QR-code traceability from field to table, and online sales of farm produce. On governance, Chen argues that digital tools suit grid-based management and allow more actors to take part in orderly co-construction, co-governance and sharing, for instance through village affairs posted on WeChat accounts and voting in WeChat groups. On living standards, Chen presents online services such as "at most one visit" and "no-face-to-face approval" as ways to widen the reach and accessibility of rural public services. Chen concludes that digital technology should drive agricultural modernization while respecting the laws of agricultural production, and should support governance led by Party organizations. Chen also calls for better rural information infrastructure, such as fibre-optic and mobile networks, so that farmers feel the convenience and gain a stronger sense of benefit and security. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned statement of how digital villages are framed in the policy discourse on rural revitalization.

Seizing the historical initiative to better uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era 掌握历史主动，在新时代更好坚持和发展中国特色社会主义 Hou Yanshe Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Hou Yanshe asks why the Party and the country must 'seize the historical initiative' (lishi zhudong) in the new era, and what supports it. Hou defines the term as the spirit and practical character of a party or state that respects historical laws and the people's主体 position while grasping major trends and opportunities. The article, based on Volume IV of Xi Jinping: The Governance of China, argues that this initiative is a requirement of historical materialism and a distinctive strength the Communist Party formed over its hundred-year struggle. The piece is organised into five numbered sections. The first sets out why the initiative matters, citing new domestic tasks and what it calls the unprecedented changes of the world in a century. The remaining four name its supports: theory, the path, the leadership and the people. Each section is built around quotations from Xi Jinping and ends with a 'must-take road' (bi you zhi lu) formula. Hou's central claim is that the initiative rests on four pillars. First, the Party must arm itself with the latest achievements in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, above all Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, combining strategic judgement with dialectical method. Second, socialism with Chinese characteristics is described as the only route to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and Chinese modernization is presented as going beyond both capitalist and traditional socialist modernization and as a new form of human civilisation. Third, Party leadership is called the most essential feature of the system and the fundamental guarantee, sustained by full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform, which Hou presents as the way to escape the historical cycle of rise and fall. Fourth, Hou treats the people as the creators of history and the source of the Party's strength, so unity and struggle under Party leadership are needed to carry the cause forward. Hou also calls for mobilising overseas Chinese and like-minded people worldwide to help build a community with a shared future for mankind. The article concludes that the Party's theory, path, leadership and popular support together let it keep the strategic initiative amid risks and challenges. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 presented 'historical initiative' as a framework tying together Xi Jinping Thought, Party leadership and the people's role.

The forward trajectory of Lenin's view of socialist society after the October Revolution 十月革命后列宁社会主义社会观的前进轨迹 Yu Min Yu Min asks how Lenin's view of what socialist society is developed after the October Revolution, once the Bolsheviks had taken power and were exploring paths of socialist construction. The article argues that this view moved along two traceable lines. One kept the communist society described by Marx and Engels as its direction of travel. The other explained what socialism is by reference to the practice and wishes of the masses. The article is organised in three parts. The first follows the first line through four Lenin texts: the Declaration of the Rights of the Working and Exploited People (1918), the draft Programme of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) (1919), The Tasks of the Youth Leagues (1920) and the 1922 article marking the tenth anniversary of Pravda. The second part gathers Lenin's remarks from 1918 and 1922 that identify socialism with specific popular practices. The third assesses the historical role and present-day value of the two lines. In Yu's reading, Lenin's definition of communism as common ownership of land and factories and common labour, his call on the young to build communist society, and his confidence in world revolution all show continuity with Marx and Engels. For the second line, Yu cites Lenin's statements that accounting and control, the wish of everyone to improve their lives, the fair distribution of grain, and whatever the masses judge "better than the old system" are socialism. Yu notes that Marx and Engels' basic theory contains no such formulations. Lenin made them, Yu argues, because he judged these practices to be what the people were actually doing and wanted. The two lines form an organic unity: the great goal stays fixed while tasks change with each period. Yu credits this unity with three historical effects. It gave the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) political steadiness during the New Economic Policy. It spread communist spirit, as in the "communist subbotniks". It affirmed the masses' own experience and so raised their enthusiasm. For the present, Yu argues that Lenin's view helps Chinese Communists, especially cadres, keep to the Party's founding mission and take a people-centred approach to development, and cites Xi Jinping's 2017 remarks on not forgetting the road travelled. Read the original if you want a close reading of how Lenin's post-1917 texts are used to link a communist goal with popular practice, and how that reading is applied to current Party-building themes in China.

New explorations in the French Communist Party's alliance strategy since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe 苏东剧变以来法国共产党的联合策略新探索 Tian Zhengxuan Tian Zhengxuan asks how the French Communist Party (PCF) has reshaped its strategy of alliances since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and why that strategy has yielded no breakthrough. The article argues that the PCF has widened and diversified its alliances at home and abroad, but that party disunity and weak appeal to the masses have limited their results. The article is built in four parts. It first traces the PCF's alliance positions under four national secretaries: Robert Hue, Marie-George Buffet, Pierre Laurent and Fabien Roussel. These run from the "citizen intervention" approach and the "plural left government" of 1997, through a "people's movement at the centre" approach, to the Left Front and the later call for a broad "people's and political alliance". It then identifies four features of the post-1991 period and two obstacles. It closes with lessons. Tian's four features are these. Partners are more varied, since the Socialist Party is no longer the automatic ally and the Greens and the Left Party have joined the field. The central place of mass alliances is reaffirmed. Cooperation in Europe and internationally has grown, notably through the Party of the European Left. The PCF now stresses the equality and autonomy of partners and no longer insists on leadership. The two obstacles are the weak cohesion and stability of party alliances, and insufficient pull on the masses. On the first, Tian cites the break-up of the Left Front, repeated shifts of partner and factional splits. On the second, the author cites falling parliamentary, presidential and European election results and a weakening link with the CGT trade union. The author attributes this to a shrinking industrial working class, a rising middle stratum, public distrust of party politics, and a policy agenda so broad that it blurs the party's distinct identity. Tian concludes that alliance will remain an important PCF strategy and that its effectiveness depends on the party's own development. The author calls for keeping a clear strategic position and for innovating theory with the stance and method of scientific socialism. Tian also calls for guarding against practices that turn alliance actions into part of capitalist rule, for strengthening unity within the party, and for combining parliamentary cooperation with extra-parliamentary mass struggle. Read the original if you want a detailed, period-by-period Chinese academic account of the PCF's alliance policy, with electoral data, since 1991.

Persistently advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party 持之以恒推进全面从严治党 Sang Xuecheng Shi Wei Xu Jiang Writing in the People's Daily in August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Sang Xuecheng, Shi Wei and Xu Jiang take up a speech by Xi Jinping to provincial and ministerial leaders. In it Xi said that building a modern socialist country depends above all on the Party. The authors' thesis is that this requires persistent full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the continued advance of the "new great project" of Party building in the new era. They say the task rests on five pairings that must be handled together. The piece is a theoretical commentary built around those five pairings, each introduced with a statement by Xi. They are: Party leadership and rigorous self-governance; ideological and institutional Party building; popular supervision and the Party's self-reform; comprehensive advance and a focus on key points; and treating symptoms and root causes. The authors draw on the experience accumulated since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They present the pairings as a method that the Party's central leadership summed up from the Party's history. The first argument is that the two halves of each pairing reinforce one another. The more the Party stresses its overall leadership, the more it must govern itself rigorously, because the quality of Party governance determines whether its leading role can be exercised. The authors describe ideological education and institutional rules as the soft and the hard side of Party building. In their view, ideals and convictions give rules their force, and rules give ideological work its backing. Second, the authors present popular supervision, together with whole-process people's democracy, and the Party's self-reform as two answers to the question of how to escape the historical cycle of rise and decline. Third, they present rigorous governance as covering all areas, all Party bodies and the whole process, while giving priority to leading cadres as the "critical minority". They also call for tackling corruption at once through deterrence and for the longer term through institutions and a clean political culture, so that officials "dare not, cannot and do not want to" be corrupt. The authors conclude that self-governance of the Party is "always on the road" and must never slacken. They hold that only persistence will keep the Party a strong leadership core in upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The text is mainly an authoritative restatement of Xi's thinking on Party building, with little new evidence. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of the Party's own rationale for its anti-corruption and Party-discipline policy on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

The Chinese Communist Party's century-long view of Marxism, as seen through the three historical resolutions 从三个历史决议看中国共产党的百年马克思主义观 Ouyang Qi Ouyang Qi asks what view of Marxism the Chinese Communist Party has built up over a century, and argues that the three historical resolutions (1945, 1981 and 2021) are the best place to read it. Writing in 2022, Ouyang holds that although each resolution was drafted in a different era, together they answer three questions: what Marxism is, how to treat it, and how to evaluate it. The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic content of the Party's view of Marxism under three headings: ontology (the nature of Marxism), practice (how to study and apply it) and value (its contemporary worth). The second discusses the significance of this view for the nation, for socialism and for human civilization. The third draws out the experience behind the view's formation, using examples from each resolution. On ontology, Ouyang reads the resolutions as presenting Marxism as a rigorous guide to action and a scientific truth that keeps pace with the times, in contrast to dogmatism and empiricism. On practice, they call for systematic study of the classics, for research and innovation, and for the leading role of Party leaders in theoretical creation. On value, Marxism appears as guiding ideology, scientific belief and a conception of civilization. The author argues that this view guided the choice of banner and path, helped revive socialism in the twenty-first century, and supported a community with a shared future for mankind. Its formation rests on three things: combining Marxism with China's concrete conditions, joining a sense of the times with a world outlook, and uniting Party leadership with putting the people first. Ouyang concludes that the Party's view of Marxism runs like a golden thread through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and explains why "Marxism works". The author presents it as an innovation in Marxist theory and also in the theory and practice of human civilization. Read the original if you want a close reading of the three resolutions as statements on Marxism itself, and a view of how Party theorists present the continuity between them.

New explorations in building domestic united fronts by communist parties in capitalist countries 资本主义国家共产党国内统一战线建设新探索 Shi Xiaohu Shi Xiaohu asks how communist parties in capitalist countries have approached building domestic united fronts in non-revolutionary periods since the start of the twenty-first century. The article argues that, faced with a complicated political environment, many of these parties have turned to more open and inclusive alliance-building. In Shi's view, these efforts are valuable for the parties' survival and for world socialism, though they cannot by themselves transform the parties' overall situation. The article first describes the difficult setting: social discontent after the 2008 financial crisis and the pandemic, a weakening traditional working-class base, the transformation of mainstream left and right parties into catch-all parties, the rise of populist parties, and coalition politics that often excludes communists. It then surveys how parties in countries such as Italy, Belgium, Greece, Australia, France, Brazil, Britain, Japan and Nepal conceive the united front. Next it reviews practical cases, and it closes with an assessment and outlook. Shi identifies four features of the new thinking: broader political composition and varied names (left front, left alliance, popular front); wider social representation that reaches the middle class; a more flexible stance on leadership, with fewer references to the vanguard role, though some theorists insist on retaining it; and more exchange between parties. In practice Shi finds four patterns: relying on structural alliances (the South African Communist Party in the tripartite alliance, the Uruguayan party in the Broad Front); looser electoral alliances (India, France, Chile); extra-parliamentary support for governments (Portugal, the Czech Republic); and temporary patriotic fronts against foreign aggression (Iraq, Armenia). The author argues these have advanced ideas, a culture of political cooperation, electoral gains and the conversion of party policies into government policy. Shi concludes that the united front is both strategy and tactic, but that most parties neither overrate it nor neglect their own party-building. Citing the Communist Party USA, the article notes that broad coalitions are fragile. It calls on these parties to combine principle with flexibility, to serve short-term goals while looking to the long term, and to win support among lower- and middle-income groups. The author expects gradual quantitative progress that might, for a few parties, lead to qualitative change. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of how communist parties outside China are approaching coalition politics, with many country examples.

Upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership and the centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee 坚持加强党的全面领导和党中央集中统一领导 Liu Jingbei Writing in the People's Daily on 3 August 2022, in the run-up to the 20th Party Congress, Liu Jingbei argues that upholding and strengthening the Party's overall leadership and the centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee has been a fundamental political guarantee of the achievements of the past decade. The commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech at a seminar for provincial and ministerial-level leading cadres, which described the previous five years and the changes of the new era. Liu's thesis is that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has produced original ideas, institutional arrangements and practical results that have unified the Party in thought, politics and action. The piece is organised in three parts: a set of original new concepts, thoughts and strategies; a series of important institutional arrangements; and a series of major practical results. The practical results are divided into strengthening leadership over the Party's own building and strengthening the Party's leadership over the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. The article ends with a short call for the Party to rally around the Central Committee. On ideas, Liu summarises Xi's statements: the Party's leadership is the defining feature and greatest strength of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Party leads everything "in east, west, south, north and centre", and it must be "comprehensive, systematic and holistic". Liu holds that these formulations raised understanding of Party leadership to a new level. On institutions, Liu stresses the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, then lists mechanisms: the Political Bureau Standing Committee hears annual work reports from the legislature, State Council and judicial bodies, Political Bureau members submit annual written reports, and systems of task allocation, supervision, review and accountability ensure that central decisions are carried out. On results, Liu cites full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point regulation, anti-corruption work described as having achieved an overwhelming victory, and Party leadership across the economy, politics, culture, society, ecological civilisation, diplomacy and defence. Liu concludes that the Central Committee's authority and unified leadership have been firmly secured, the Party's leadership system has been steadily improved, and its methods of leadership have become more scientific. Liu calls on Party members to understand the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, strengthen the "four consciousnesses" and practise the Two Upholds. Read the original if you want a compact example of how an official Party-school commentary of 2022 summarises the case for Party centralisation before the 20th Party Congress.

Keeping the Party forever young and vital through self-reform 在自我革命中永葆党的青春与活力 Yang Yang Writing in Guangming Daily on the eve of the 20th Party Congress (2022), Yang Yang asks why the Communist Party of China has stayed vital after more than a century, and answers that persistent self-reform (自我革命) is the reason. The commentary takes its cue from the 2021 historical resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which lists adherence to self-reform among the Party's valuable historical experiences. Yang also draws on Xi Jinping's recent address to provincial and ministerial leaders. Yang calls self-reform the Party's distinguishing mark, the "code" of its youthfulness and a guarantee of its leading role. The piece is organised under three headings. The first treats self-reform as what separates the Party from every other party, and traces its theoretical lineage from Marx, Engels and Lenin through Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to Xi Jinping. The second presents self-reform as the source of the Party's vitality, with an account of the campaigns since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third reviews the Party's history as a series of self-corrections and links self-reform to national rejuvenation. Yang defines self-reform as a conscious process of self-sublation by the Party as subject: upholding truth, correcting errors, renewing itself and turning the blade inward. In Yang's account, an advanced Marxist party is not born but is forged through this process. Yang argues that a party able to lead a great social revolution must keep its own advanced character and purity, which means removing whatever corrodes its body. Yang credits the post-2012 measures with solving long-standing problems: theoretical education, work-style rectification, stricter discipline, tighter cadre selection and the anti-corruption drive of "tigers, flies and foxes". The article says these produced an overwhelming victory against corruption, a healthier political ecology within the Party and closer Party–people ties. It also lists earlier milestones, from the 1927 August 7 Meeting and the Zunyi Meeting to the Yan'an rectification and the "Three Stresses" campaign. Yang concludes that the Party faces more numerous and complex risks as it enters a critical period for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, so it must never relax. Yang holds that without a Party armed with the spirit of self-reform, national rejuvenation would remain a fantasy. The author calls on readers to rally around the Central Committee with Xi at its core, apply Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and continue the new great project of Party building. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary on the eve of the 20th Party Congress framed self-reform and its lineage from the Marxist classics.

Advancing under the Party's banner towards the centenary goal of the army's founding 在党的旗帜下向着建军一百年奋斗目标前进 Zhao Zhouxian Marking the 95th anniversary of the founding of the People's Liberation Army on 1 August 2022, this commentary in the People's Daily argues that a strong country requires a strong military and that the army, under the Party's leadership, is now advancing along the path of building a strong military with Chinese characteristics. Zhao Zhouxian, a researcher at the National Defence University, presents the army's history and current agenda as guided by Xi Jinping's thought on strengthening the military and aimed at the centenary goal of 2027. The piece has three parts. The first reviews the army's record in the revolutionary period, the early decades of the People's Republic and the era of reform and opening up. The second sets out what the author calls the historic achievements and transformations in building the military since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third turns to the tasks that Zhao says must be carried out between now and 2027. On the historical record, Zhao credits the army with winning the revolutionary wars, building up defence science and industry (including the \"two bombs and one satellite\" programme), and providing security for reform and development. For the new era, the author identifies three levers. The first is ideological guidance, including the absolute leadership of the Party, the chairman responsibility system of the Central Military Commission and a political clean-up in which Guo Boxiong, Xu Caihou, Fang Fenghui and Zhang Yang are named. The second is top-level design: the broadest defence and military reform since 1949, a 300,000 cut in personnel, a new command structure, and the integrated development of mechanisation, informatisation and intelligentisation. The third is strategic guidance that focuses on combat readiness, legal governance of the military and the handling of external challenges, which the author says include deterring \"Taiwan independence\" separatism. For the period to 2027, Zhao calls for upholding the Party's absolute leadership, equipping the whole army with the Party's innovative theory, and carrying out the tasks in the 14th Five-Year Plan for military building. Zhao also calls for continuing the reforms, self-reliance in science and technology, and civil–military integration, with wider national defence education and the tradition of army–people unity. The author presents these as the means to build a world-class military and to support national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want an example of the official People's Daily framing of the PLA's history and its 2027 centenary goal on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.

A century of Chinese Communist Party grassroots Party building: practice and lessons 中国共产党基层党建的百年实践与启示 Jia Gangtao Gao Hongbo Published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, this short commentary asks what a century of Party-building at the grassroots offers for the present. Jia Gangtao and Gao Hongbo argue that attention to the grassroots is a "glorious tradition" of the Chinese Communist Party. In their account, it has been a key source of the Party's organisational strength and of its ability to carry central decisions through to the "last mile". The article has two main parts. The first traces the tradition across periods: the New Democratic Revolution, the early People's Republic, the era of reform and opening up under Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, and the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second sets out four requirements for grassroots work in the new era, drawing on Xi Jinping's remarks. In the authors' historical survey, each generation of leaders is credited with a Party-building task and a body of theory. They list Mao Zedong's "great undertaking" of building a Bolshevized mass Party, the Eighth Party Congress's theory of the ruling party, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development. They say these steadily made grassroots organisation more institutionalised and standardised. Since 2012, they say, campaigns such as the mass line education drive, the "Three Stricts and Three Honests" and the "Two Studies, One Action" campaign have improved Party conduct and revived the role of grassroots organisations. For the present, the authors call for four things: arming members with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, with the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds; full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; stronger organisational capacity; and institution-building. On organisation, they cite innovations such as branches "on the industrial chain" and "at the front line of epidemic control", plus internet-plus Party building. On institutions, they cite regulations for rural, state-owned enterprise, university and government-organ branches. The authors conclude that grassroots organisations are the "nerve endings" and the "foundation" of the Party's governance. They hold that the Party must neither relax this work nor stop innovating in it, if it is to consolidate its ruling base and support the building of a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed periodisation of Party grassroots work and the policy priorities it draws from that history.

The essence of the times of Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit 中华文化和中国精神的时代精华 Pang Lisheng This newspaper commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, takes up a formulation from the Party's 2021 historical resolution. The resolution describes Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the "essence of the times of Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit". Pang explains what this says about the relationship between the Thought, Chinese culture and the Chinese spirit, and argues that it gives the Thought an important place in the history of the Chinese nation and civilization. The article has three parts. The first treats the Thought as opening a new chapter for Chinese culture. The second treats it as the distillation of the Chinese spirit. The third presents it as pointing the direction of civilizational development for the world. On culture, Pang argues that Xi links cultural inheritance with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Pang cites Xi's stress on cultural confidence within the Four-sphere Confidence, on "Chinese cultural genes", and on the creative transformation of traditional culture through the Two Integrations. On the spirit, Pang defines it as the unity of national spirit, centred on patriotism, and the spirit of the times, centred on reform and innovation. Pang adds that Xi ties it to the Chinese Dream, to core socialist values and to the spiritual lineage that runs from the founding spirit of the Party onward. Pang concludes that, amid what is described as great changes unseen in a century, the world's problems have become problems of civilization. Concepts such as the people-centred approach to development, the new development philosophy, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind are said to offer original Chinese solutions. In Pang's view, Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization provide a framework with wide reference value. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary links Xi Jinping Thought to culture, national spirit and global civilization.

A concentrated presentation of one hundred years of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context The main content and distinctive features of the Chronicle of a Century of the Sinicization of Marxism (1921–2021) 马克思主义中国化一百年的集中展现 Third Research Department, Institute of Party History and Literature of the CPC Central Committee This piece, written by the research department of the institute that compiled the volume, introduces the newly published Chronicle of a Century of the Sinicization of Marxism (1921–2021), a chronological record of the Communist Party's efforts to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context. The authors argue that the book gives a full account of the process, its major theoretical results and its historical lessons. They present it as an aid to understanding the Two Establishes and to studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The chronicle opens with the founding of the Party in July 1921, with a brief look back at the spread of Marxism in China before that date. It closes with the sixth plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) and its resolution on the Party's century of struggle. It has 1,271 entries and about 410,000 characters. It draws on major documents and the collected works of the main leaders, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, and gives some space to older revolutionaries such as Zhou Enlai and Chen Yun. The article is organised around the book's features: its coverage of the historical course, its record of theoretical innovation, its emphasis on Xi Jinping Thought, and the lessons it draws. The authors describe three ways in which the book records innovation. It highlights pioneering ideas, such as Mao's 1957 speech on contradictions among the people and the first appearances of concepts like "xiaokang" and the Chinese Dream. It traces how ideas developed, for example the path from Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remark on the market economy to the decision of the 18th Central Committee's Third Plenum (2013) that the market should play a decisive role in allocating resources. It also shows the dialectical and historical materialist method, for instance in its treatment of Mao's On Practice and On Contradiction. The authors say the book gives most weight to Xi Jinping Thought, covering the new development philosophy and more than forty passages on a community with a shared future for mankind, and that it reflects Xi's recent assessments of Party history. The authors conclude that the chronicle shows, through what they call irrefutable facts, that Marxism works in China, which they say explains why the Party succeeded and why socialism with Chinese characteristics is good. They draw three lessons. China must uphold Marxism's guiding role, continue the Two Integrations and strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. It must also keep opening new horizons for Marxism as the times require. Read the original if you want an official account of how the Party presents its own theoretical history, and of the periodisation and framing used in this reference work.

The meaning of Lenin's thought on socialist state governance and its contemporary implications 列宁社会主义国家治理思想的内涵要义与当代启示 Zhang Kai Wang Hongsheng Zhang Kai and Wang Hongsheng ask what Lenin's exploration of governing the first socialist state can offer China as it works to modernise its system and capacity of state governance. Writing in 2022, with the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) having made this modernisation the overall goal of deepening reform, they argue that Lenin's thought is an important theoretical source for that task. They identify three pillars in it: the dictatorship of the proletariat as the fundamental precondition, proletarian culture as the spiritual consciousness, and participation by all the people as the value orientation. The article opens with a review of Chinese scholarship, which the authors sort into general accounts of Lenin's governance thought, studies of its essence and principles, and studies of its actors and measures. They say this literature has not examined governance through the proletarian dictatorship, communist culture or forms of popular participation, and has rarely linked Lenin to China's recent experience. Three sections then take Lenin's ideas in turn, and a final section draws four lessons for China. In the authors' reading, Lenin held that the state remains necessary after the revolution and should be a 'practical' and 'inexpensive' government. It would be led by the vanguard party through political, organisational and ideological leadership, and bound by socialist legality, including supervision through bodies such as the Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate. Because Russia's backwardness in culture and literacy obstructed governance, he stressed communist morality, political education of cadres and officials, and basic schooling for the masses. He combined direct democracy with party-led indirect democracy, and gave citizens rights of supervision and recall. The authors conclude that China should uphold the Party's overall leadership, citing the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party as a warning. They also call for whole-process people's democracy with a people-centred stance, for rule of law that turns institutional strengths into governance effectiveness, and for Party leadership of ideological work against Western ideological infiltration and historical nihilism. They add that Lenin's wartime communism and the New Economic Policy offer further lessons. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link Lenin's state-building thought to current Party-state governance doctrine.

A contemporary interpretation of Marx's thought on world history 马克思世界历史思想的当代阐释 Yu Han Yu Han takes up a weakness in research on Marx's thought on world history: its core content is often identified imprecisely, so that the idea is understood too broadly and loses its distinctive function. The article argues that the core is Marx's identification of the characteristic of his epoch, "history transformed into world history". It holds that this is a revolutionary weapon of theory rooted in historical materialism, and that its interpretation should also be tied to the Communist Party of China's century of practice. The article has three parts. The first traces Marx's intellectual sources, chiefly Hegel's philosophy of history. The second examines the epoch characteristic as set out in The German Ideology, Capital and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The third discusses the idea's contemporary value, ending with the Party's practice and the present international situation. Yu's argument turns on two moves. First, Marx inherited Hegel's strong sense of history but sublated it. Marx replaced the self-movement of "impersonal reason" with the practical activity of real human beings, and rejected any general philosophy of history that supplies one abstract formula for all epochs. He also criticised the Eurocentrism of Hegel and Herder as bourgeois ideology. Second, Yu reads the epoch characteristic through large-scale industry and the world market. Capitalism opened the world-historical age and dominated it, but in Marx's view it lacks full world-historical significance, which only communism, aimed at the free and all-round development of the human being, can attain. Yu adds that there is no world-history thought independent of historical materialism. Yu concludes that Marx's thought on world history completes the aims of his whole doctrine, since it reveals the temporary character of capitalist rule and points to the "changing of the world". For the present, Yu credits the Party's century of practice and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with grasping the pulse of the age, and says this practice opens a new world-historical period. Yu also says Marxist philosophy must keep widening its horizons to meet "changes unseen in a century", anti-globalisation sentiment and protectionism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how Marx's world-history thought relates to Hegel, historical materialism and the Party's current self-understanding.

Overseas scholarship on the Marxist theory of ownership and its assessment 海外学界关于马克思主义所有制理论的研究及其评价 Bao Weijie This literature review surveys how scholars outside China have treated the Marxist theory of ownership and China's ownership reforms. Bao notes that domestic Chinese research on the subject is extensive, whereas overseas work has been little introduced in China. The article argues that overseas research is thin, ideologically conditioned and strongest at the meso and micro levels, and it uses the comparison to propose directions for Chinese research. Drawing on searches of JSTOR, Web of Science and CNKI, on Chinese translation journals, and on Monthly Review, Historical Materialism and Radical Political Economy, Bao sorts the literature into three blocks. The first covers reflection on classical ownership theory and practice, including the analytical Marxism of G. A. Cohen and John Roemer, Coase-style property-rights theory, and debates on Soviet state ownership and post-Soviet privatisation, where David Kotz is cited as a critic.
