The second covers China's reforms: the household contract responsibility system, private enterprise and state-owned enterprise reform. The third covers future trends, citing Stiglitz, Samir Amin and comparisons of Chinese and American public enterprises. Bao credits overseas work with widening the methodological basis for comparing ownership forms and with offering a micro-level path that complements China's macro-level focus on the nature, structure and function of ownership. Two weaknesses are stressed. First, Western mainstream economics has since the marginal revolution taken capitalist private ownership as a given, so Marx's ownership theory has been marginalised; Bao reads Piketty's focus on distribution without ownership in this light. Second, overseas assessments of Chinese reform remain trapped in a Cold War binary of public versus private. In the article's account, they overlook the historical role of state-owned enterprises as the material and political foundation of the state in a late-developing country. Bao proposes three directions for Chinese research. One is to study contemporary capitalist ownership, including why private ownership has not met the fate Marx foresaw, and to demonstrate the strengths of socialist ownership by comparison. Another is to strengthen research on deepening state-owned enterprise reform in the new era, resisting privatisation and arguing how competitive state firms can become stronger, better and larger. The last is to study the effect of the digital economy and data ownership on traditional ownership relations, drawing on Christian Fuchs and Nick Dyer-Witheford. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly map of overseas ownership research and of how Chinese scholars assess and respond to it.

Early explorations in building a rural social security system in New China, 1949–1957 新中国构建农村社会保障体系的初步探索（1949—1957） Zhou Xiao How did the Party and state begin to provide social security for China's peasants after 1949, when the country was poor and the countryside vast? Zhou Xiao argues that early New China, lacking the means to copy the urban system, assembled a broad package of measures covering peasants' birth, old age, sickness and death. The author holds that this marked a shift from informal, temporary relief towards a modern social security system, and offers it as historical reference for building a unified urban–rural system and advancing common prosperity. The article covers 1949–1957 in three parts. The first treats state relief, divided into disaster relief and poor relief, after land reform gave peasants a basis for self-reliance. The second examines collective economy as the main support of rural security after agricultural cooperativization began in 1953. The third turns to rural health and disease prevention, and a closing section compares rural and urban arrangements. Zhou draws on policy documents, leaders' speeches and local cases from provinces such as Zhejiang, Hebei, Hubei and Liaoning. Zhou's central claim is that the relief approach was set out in the guideline revised in 1954: relying on the collective, mutual aid among the masses and production for self-rescue, with necessary state relief as a supplement. Under it, cooperatives created provident and welfare funds, experimented with cooperative medical care, and from 1956 established the "five guarantees" system for childless and infirm elderly people. In health, the author credits the "patriotic hygiene campaign", county and district health institutions, and campaigns against smallpox, plague and schistosomiasis with rapidly easing the shortage of doctors and medicine. Zhou also notes limits: egalitarianism under the guise of distribution according to work dampened incentives, provident-fund deductions sometimes cut members' incomes, the Great Leap Forward damaged rural health work, and Zhou Enlai acknowledged a marked urban–rural imbalance in medical resources. Zhou concludes that urban and rural areas ran two different models: urban security was tied to household registration and labour insurance, while the countryside relied on self-rescue, collectives, mutual aid and emergency state aid. The rural system was narrow in coverage, unsystematic, and funded through a single channel. Even so, the author sees collective security and improved rural health as unprecedented changes in China's agrarian history. Read the original if you want a detailed, documented account of how early PRC policy approached rural welfare, cooperative medicine and the five guarantees, from a Chinese official-academic perspective.

The "Two Establishes" in the perspective of democratic centralism 论民主集中制视阈中的“两个确立” Li Haiqing Li Haiqing takes up the formula, set out in the Sixth Plenum resolution of 2021, that the Party established Xi Jinping as the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party and established the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that the Two Establishes cannot be understood only through the circumstances and achievements of the new era. In Li's view they must be read through democratic centralism, the Party's fundamental organisational principle, and reading them otherwise invites misinterpretation. The article has three parts. It first explains democratic centralism as a principle governing relations inside the Party. It then asks how each of the Two Establishes rests on a democratic basis. Finally it describes the organisational advantages of correct centralisation in Party governance, state governance and global governance, and closes with a short conclusion. Li holds that democratic centralism combines centralisation on a democratic basis with democracy under centralised guidance, and that centralisation is the pivot, comparable to the brain. Because power and responsibility are concentrated level by level, the leadership core is the highest bearer of centralisation, and its theoretical output becomes the Party's guiding thought. Li describes the top level as in effect a "committee plus core" system. The first Establish is said to rest on step-by-step intra-Party election and testing, and the second on the way the thought gathers views from below and then refines them in the centralising stage, where the core's ability is decisive. Li says the Two Establishes show the system's strength in several fields. In Party governance, Li cites full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the Party's self-reform and the 2021 document on supervising top leaders. In state governance, Li points to the "Two Centenary Goals" and systematic reform. In global governance, Li points to Chinese modernization and a community with a shared future for mankind. Li concludes that the Two Establishes are the necessary result of centralisation on a democratic basis, resting on modern democratic politics and communist democratic values. Li also argues that a strong core and a guiding thought that is both orthodox and innovative produce institutional advantages. Further improvement of democratic centralism and effective implementation of the Two Establishes are said to help the Party meet opportunities and challenges on the new journey. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party School scholar justifies the Two Establishes in organisational and institutional terms rather than through historical achievements alone.

Rethinking the explanatory models of anti-corruption theory in contemporary China Corruption and anti-corruption as the production and use of domination and anti-domination power 当代中国廉政理论解释模式的再思考 Peng Bin Zhu Yajiao Peng Bin and Zhu Yajiao take up a gap in Chinese research on clean government. Existing studies explain corruption through institutions, rights, morality or class, and all treat abuse of power as its cause. The authors argue that this treats power as nothing but domination. In their view corruption is the conversion of official authority into "power as domination" for private gain, while anti-corruption is the Party and government producing, activating and using "power as anti-domination". They propose this as a new, power-centred account. The article has three parts. The first summarises four existing explanatory models: "institutional anti-corruption", "rights anti-corruption", "moral anti-corruption" and "class anti-corruption", each with representative Chinese scholars. The second sets out the authors' own perspective, including the case of Lai Xiaomin, former chairman of China Huarong Asset Management, as shown in the documentary series State Supervision. It also covers the anti-corruption system built since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third re-reads each of the four models through anti-domination power. The central move is to reject the equation of power with domination, which the authors link to Weber and to Lord Acton's dictum on power and corruption. Because actors can mobilise economic, social, cultural and symbolic resources against domination, the authors hold that power can also take an anti-dominating form. They describe an anti-domination power system inside the political system (the eight-point rules, the Supervision Law, the National Supervisory Commission, intra-Party supervision) and outside it (petitions, reporting, media exposure, litigation, inspection tours). The second move reinterprets the four models. Institutions supply channels for anti-domination power. Rights depend on state power to be realised. Moral settings shape tendencies toward domination. Class structure conditions whether such power can arise, and the authors tie common prosperity to this last point. The authors conclude that the power-centred approach does not oppose the four models but absorbs and complements them. In their account it implies a logic led by Party leadership, secured by institutions and law, supported by citizens' rights and morality, and focused on improving social structure. They claim it can correct misunderstandings of the link between power and corruption and yield a more comprehensive explanatory model. They add that building such a system is a long-term task that is "always on the road". Read the original if you study Chinese anti-corruption and discipline-inspection scholarship and want to see how one theoretical framework tries to integrate its main schools.

Several issues deserving attention in current research on world socialism 当前世界社会主义研究中值得关注的几个问题 Chai Shangjin Chai Shangjin asks how research on world socialism should define its object, read the current balance of forces and respond to new contradictions and challenges in the international communist movement. Writing in 2022, the author argues that the field needs clearer concepts and a more integrated approach. The article holds that world socialism should be studied as a whole, that communist parties remain its main force, and that the shifting relationship between socialism and capitalism favours socialism. The article has four parts. The first separates "world socialism" from scientific socialism and from the "international communist movement". The second asks who the main force of world socialism is today. The third places the socialism–capitalism relationship in the "great changes unseen in a century". The fourth turns to a community with a shared future for mankind and the prospects for world socialism. Chai first treats world socialism as an umbrella concept covering many left-wing currents and forces. Only strands guided by Marxism and committed to the socialist road count as scientific socialism, while democratic socialism and national socialism do not. The author reviews three views on whether the international communist movement still exists, and favours the term "world socialism movement". Chai lists new features of the movement: the unity of national and international character, a grounding in reality, and diverse exploration. The author also criticises "fragmentary" scholarship. Chai then argues that communist parties remain the main force because of their ideological and organisational strengths. The author names five ruling parties, the parties of developed countries, and those in the developing world, and points to cooperation with new social movements and the international meetings of communist and workers' parties. On the two systems, Chai describes an "East rising, West declining" trend. Chai presents the pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict as exposing weaknesses in Western institutions, and treats socialism's institutional advantages as shown by comparison. Chai describes Sino-US rivalry as the main variable in the two systems' relationship. Chai concludes that building a community with a shared future for mankind is consistent with Marx and Engels's "true community" and with the eventual replacement of capitalism by socialism. In the author's view, armed revolution is no longer the only road in an era of peace and development. Opposing Western hegemony and capitalist exploitation is presented as compatible with that project, and Chinese modernization is said to help revive world socialism. Read the original if you want an official-affiliated Chinese scholar's account of how the field of world socialism is defined, who its main force is, and how Chinese Party thinking links it to the two-systems rivalry.

Upholding the Communist Party of China's commitment to taking the whole world in view 坚持胸怀天下的中国共产党 Mu Zhaoyong This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, examines one of the historical experiences listed in the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021): "upholding a worldwide vision" (胸怀天下). Mu argues that the resolution's formulation of this experience is an original contribution. In Mu's reading, it is at once a sense of mission, a mode of strategic thinking and a political and spiritual quality. It helps explain why the Party's century of struggle has influenced the course of world history. The article has three parts. The first traces the sources of the commitment to Marxism and to traditional Chinese culture. The second surveys the Party's history from its founding to the present, in four stages: the revolutionary period, the early People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the years since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third sets out what the commitment requires on the "new journey". Mu's core argument is that the Party's worldwide vision follows from the Two Integrations, that is, from combining Marxism's basic principles with excellent traditional culture. Marxism supplies the aim of human liberation, while ideas such as "all under heaven as one family" and "harmony in diversity" supply cultural roots. Mu then reads the Party's record as handling China's development and the world's progress together. Examples include the Second Congress's 1922 resolution on the world situation, the anti-fascist war, the Korean War, reform and opening up, and recent Chinese modernization, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. In Mu's account these have given the world Chinese wisdom, solutions and strength. Mu concludes with three requirements for the future. The Party must study Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and keep a firm grasp of historical laws. It must take its own path, with independence and self-reliance, while learning from other countries. It must pursue peaceful development and major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics, building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Party historians present the Party's international outlook within its century-long narrative.

Overseas perceptions of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind 海外人士关于人类命运共同体理念的认知图景 Zhang Xiuping Zhang Guangzhe This literature-style survey, published in 2022, asks how scholars, politicians and commentators outside China understand Xi Jinping's concept of a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors want to know what overseas observers focus on, what main views have formed and what characterises them. They conclude that overseas views, while wide-ranging and often favourable, remain shallow in height, depth and breadth, and that China should respond actively. The review is organised around four themes: the grounds on which the concept was put forward (theoretical and practical), its basic meaning, its value and significance, and its practical paths. It cites many named figures from Europe, North America, Russia, Asia, Africa and Latin America, including academics, think-tank reports, Party leaders and former officials. It also devotes a section to views the authors regard as misunderstandings. On origins, the authors report that overseas commentators trace the concept to traditional Chinese 'all under heaven' thinking, to Marx's internationalism, to earlier Chinese Party leaders' diplomatic thought and to international law. Practical grounds are seen either as China's need for a favourable environment and greater influence, or as a response to deepening interdependence, global problems and an outdated hegemonic order. Meanings are read as a vision of the future, a wisdom for global governance, a new model of international relations, or a foreign policy. Overseas figures see the concept as going beyond Western zero-sum thinking. They propose paths through the Belt and Road Initiative, through particular fields (politics, security, economy, culture, ecology) and through regional or sectoral communities such as health or cyberspace. The authors attribute critical readings, for example that the concept implies Chinese domination or a deliberately vague definition, to a long-standing Western habit of binary, zero-sum thinking. The authors identify three weaknesses: overseas observers often view the concept through 'tinted glasses', treat it insufficiently in depth, and neglect its relation to capitalism and socialism. Little attention goes to cultural, ecological and micro-level aspects, or to who bears which responsibilities. They propose targeted rebuttal of mistaken views, a stronger cultural construction of the concept as a new civilisational outlook beyond capitalist alienation, and its translation into practice. Read the original if you want a catalogue of named overseas commentators and their positions on the concept, as framed by Chinese scholars.

The path of Chinese modernization and a new form of human civilization 中国式现代化道路与人类文明新形态 Hu Boxiang Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2022, Hu Boxiang takes up the Sixth Plenum (2021) resolution on the Party's century of struggle. It states that the Party has led the people along the path of Chinese modernization, created a new form of human civilization and widened the routes to modernization open to developing countries. Hu argues that this path is a modernization road without precedent and offers developing countries a new option. The article is organised in four numbered sections, each naming one "outstanding feature" of the path and of the civilization it produces. These are leadership by the Communist Party and socialism, independence and self-reliance, comprehensive and coordinated development, and peaceful development. Each section sets the feature against a Western theory or model that Hu says Chinese modernization surpasses. Hu contends that the Western view of modernization as Westernization is overcome by a path that the Party explored independently over a century. In this account China needed the Party's leadership to compress an industrialization that took developed countries centuries into a few decades, and it keeps a socialist orientation. That orientation rests on a public-ownership-based system of mixed ownership, distribution mainly according to work, and common prosperity as the goal. Hu rejects the notion that late developers must depend on imported Western civilization, citing Deng Xiaoping on not copying other countries' experience, while stressing that self-reliance does not mean closing the country. Against "pure economic growth" theory, Hu presents a modernization that coordinates material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization and treats human modernization as its essence, pursued through common prosperity and a people-centred rather than capital-centred logic. Against "a strong country inevitably seeks hegemony", the clash of civilizations and zero-sum thinking, Hu describes a path of peaceful development, mutual benefit and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Hu says Western modernization was bound up with expansion, colonialism and plunder. Hu concludes that the path and the new form of civilization come from the Party's grasp of national conditions, from Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions, and from the practice of reform and opening up. Hu presents peaceful development as a considered conclusion, not a diplomatic expedient, and claims it offers "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" to global problems. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement in Guangming Daily of how Chinese modernization is contrasted with Western modernization theory.

The Chinese Communist Party's understanding and practice of the eight-hour working day in the New Democratic Revolution period 新民主主义革命时期中国共产党对八小时工作制的认识与实践 Zhang Longping How did the Chinese Communist Party handle the eight-hour working day, a demand of the international labour movement, under Chinese revolutionary conditions? Zhang Longping argues that the Party never applied the principle mechanically. Over several decades it combined firm principle with flexibility and arrived at an eight-to-ten-hour flexible system, which Zhang reads as a concrete case of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The article follows four periods. It begins with the Party's founding and the First Revolutionary Civil War, when the eight-hour day entered Party programmes and labour congresses. It then covers the Soviet areas of the Agrarian Revolution period, the full War of Resistance against Japan, and the War of Liberation. Zhang draws on labour laws, Party directives, congress resolutions and statements by Mao Zedong, Chen Yun, Zhang Wentian, Liu Shaoqi and others. The account ends with the 1949 Common Program. Zhang's central claim is that each adjustment answered a practical constraint without abandoning the principle. Early petitions to the Beiyang government gave way, after the failures of the early 1920s, to the view that economic struggle must become political struggle. In the Soviet areas, laws first fixed the eight-hour day rigidly. Zhang Wentian and Chen Yun criticised this as detached from reality, and the 1933 revision added exceptions for overtime and for employers of auxiliary labour. During the War of Resistance, central directives from 1940 treated stressing the eight-hour day as an excessive demand. Mao Zedong then allowed a ten-hour day, which the March 1942 Outline of Labour Policy described as a stopgap given backward, dispersed industry and wartime needs. In 1947–48 the centre criticised excessive labour conditions in newly liberated cities, including the draft Harbin labour law, as a repeat of the 'Left' errors of 1931–34. Zhang concludes that Mao Zedong's 1945 formula of an eight-to-ten-hour day was adopted by the All-China Federation of Trade Unions in 1949 and confirmed by the Common Program, and that it continued into the early People's Republic. In Zhang's view this shows a Party that proceeds from the overall, long-term and fundamental interests of the people and links theory with practice. Read the original if you want a source-based account of Chinese labour-time policy and its Party-history justification from 1920 to 1949.

The basic connotation of the international discourse power of China's new-type party system and paths to enhance it 中国新型政党制度国际话语权的基本内涵与提升路径 Zang Xiuling Zang Xiuling takes up the question of how China's new-type party system can gain an international voice that matches its institutional performance. The author argues that the system has begun to break the discourse hegemony of "Western centrism" in party politics, but that its international discourse power remains weak. Zang contends that it can be raised by building on theory, culture, practice and a global mission, and through concrete changes in how the system is communicated abroad. The article opens with a short review of existing research, which Zang groups into party theory, party-system discourse and party diplomacy. It then defines international discourse power and analyses it in four dimensions: supply, competitiveness, attractiveness and influence. After that it sets out the opportunities and challenges, the principles for improvement, and four practical paths. Zang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Zhou Enlai and Xi Jinping. Zang reads international discourse power as having a dual nature, a right to speak and a power to affect others, and as resting on national strength. In the author's account, Western party systems are caught in a "institutional bottleneck" of vetoing party politics, procedural democracy and social division. The new-type party system is credited with unifying leadership and cooperation, supplying an institutional carrier for whole-process people's democracy and keeping policy continuous. The main obstacles named are Western labels such as "authoritarian" and "flower vase", an official-dominated and stiff propaganda style, and academic discourse that lags behind political discourse and leans on Western concepts. Zang therefore ties each dimension of discourse power to a foundation: the Sinicization of Marxism, traditional Chinese culture, the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a community with a shared future for mankind. Zang proposes that the Communist Party lead with strategy and trained personnel, that the democratic parties and non-party figures speak actively, and that ordinary people and scholars take part. The author also calls for less lecturing, more languages and media, stronger online presence, and a shift from rule-follower to rule-maker in international discourse. Party diplomacy and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference are to widen channels, with the aim of an international united front of parties friendly to China. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar frames discourse strategy for the party system, and how the argument ties culture, theory and diplomacy together.

Grasping the essential requirement and key features of common prosperity 深刻把握共同富裕的本质要求和重要特征 Zhang Guanzi Published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper on 30 June 2022, this commentary takes its cue from Xi Jinping's Qiushi article "Solidly promote common prosperity". Era characteristics of the Party's leadership in building a modern economic system 党领导建设现代化经济体系的时代特征 Fu Chunyu Zhao Xinpeng This short commentary, published in January 2022, asks how the Communist Party of China has led the building of a modern economic system and what distinguishes that leadership in the current era. The theoretical commitment of historical materialism 历史唯物主义的理论担当 Chen Lixin Why should The German Ideology still be read repeatedly today? On the second and third themes, Chen holds that Marx fastened on "real individuals" in their social relations, which exposes ideological illusion and locates the ultimate causes of social change in the economy. The article has three parts. The first sets out Marx's critique of old philosophy, which in Marx's words either distorts human history or leaves it aside altogether. Juan reads old materialism as leaving human history aside: after Bacon's lively sensuous matter, it turned mechanical and mathematical and became indifferent to human beings. Idealism touched human history but treated it abstractly, as the evolution of spirit. Both, in Juan's account, fail to see that sensuous practical activity is the foundation of the existing world. Historical materialism starts from real individuals and their activity. Production covers the production of life, one's own and others', and so contains both natural and social relations. For Juan this rules out an economic-determinist reading and makes the theory a set of principles and methods, not a formula to be applied everywhere. Its aim is human emancipation, through the common appropriation of social productive forces by associated individuals. Juan concludes that the nature Marx speaks of is not an absolutely objective nature outside humanity. It is a humanised nature that takes shape through practice, so that natural science will include the science of man and the reverse. Historical materialism is therefore both a science of man and a science of nature, united as the single science of history. These are narratives that, in the author's account, stigmatise the Party and China to build a false "consensus" and to display Western ideological dominance. The article argues that the Party has answered such traps for a century through a series of innovative international positions, and that today China should move from reactive denial to actively building its own discourse system. The article opens with a theoretical section on discourse, discourse power and discourse hegemony, drawing on Marx and Engels's account of ideology, Foucault and Joseph Nye. It then traces four historical "traps": the "communist red menace" and "collapse of China" theories from the Party's founding to the early People's Republic; the "end of history" thesis after the Soviet collapse; the comprehensive "China threat" theories of the 1990s and 2000s; and the "Thucydides Trap" and similar "trap" theories after the 2008 financial crisis. The 2021 "Xinjiang cotton incident" serves as the author's contemporary example of how a hegemonic narrative is manufactured. Zhang sets out the Party's responses in three stages. Version 1.0 is the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence (1955) and Mao Zedong's "three worlds" theory. Version 2.0 is the opening-up strategy of mutual benefit and win-win results and the path of peaceful development. Version 3.0 is the call for a community with a shared future for mankind, which the author presents as a historic move beyond Western "jungle law" and zero-sum thinking. Citing Engels's remark that economically backward countries can still "play first fiddle" in philosophy, Zhang argues that China's record shows that a rising economy need not produce hegemonic ambition. For the present, Zhang proposes three directions for renewing China's discourse system. The first is to replace passive rebuttal with proactive, positive self-expression and new concepts that connect China with other countries. The second is to build professional, academic discourse and describe China accurately and in its own terms, using stories such as targeted poverty alleviation and epidemic control. The third is to engage with a multipolar world, criticise Western-centrism and foster dialogue among civilizations. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese military-affiliated scholar periodises the Party's international discourse strategy and frames Western narratives about China as deliberate "traps".

Grasping the logic of strengthening Party spirit cultivation 把握加强党性修养的逻辑 Cao Jiangqiu Why should Party members and cadres keep working on their Party spirit (dangxing)? In this commentary, published in Guangming Daily on 19 July 2022, Cao Jiangqiu argues that strengthening dangxing xiuyang, the cultivation of Party spirit, is a lifelong obligation for Communists. The author grounds this in three "logics": theoretical, historical and practical. The piece opens with a statement by Xi Jinping that leading cadres must exercise self-discipline and check their conduct against the Party Constitution. It then takes the three logics in turn. The first draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi to define what a Marxist party is. The second surveys Party history from the Second Congress to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The third looks at the international, domestic and Party situation of the early 2020s. Cao's theoretical claim is that advancedness and purity are the essential attributes of a Marxist party, and that Party spirit and the people's character are unified: upholding one means upholding the other. The historical section lists milestones as evidence that attention to Party spirit explains the Party's endurance. These include the 1941 decision on strengthening Party spirit, the 1942 Yan'an rectification movement, and the intra-Party regulations issued since 2012. On practice, the author cites the Party's size (96.712 million members at the end of 2021) and says many young members lack experience of intra-Party political life. Cao adds that Party spirit does not rise automatically with seniority or rank, and that problems of impure thinking, politics, organization and work style persist. Cao concludes that the more complex the domestic and international environment, the more Party spirit must be cultivated. Members are urged to treat Party education as a discipline of the heart, to understand the decisive significance of the Two Establishes, and to carry out the Two Upholds. The author presents this as the way to advance the Party's self-reform and keep the Party from degenerating. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-school scholars present Party-building doctrine, with its standard historical milestones, in mid-2022.

The Communist Party of China is the most reliable backbone for achieving great undertakings 中国共产党是成就伟业最可靠的主心骨 Yan Xu Wang Yixin This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, takes its title from a statement by Xi Jinping: that the Communist Party of China is the most reliable backbone (zhuxingu) for achieving great undertakings. Yan and Wang read this as both a summary of past practice and a basic requirement for the future. They argue that, on the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects, the Party's centralised and unified leadership must be upheld and carried through every sphere of Party and state work. The piece has three sections. The first presents the Party as the author of a historic achievement for the Chinese nation and for the world. The second explains why Party leadership is the 'sea-stabilising needle' of the cause. The third turns to the present and asks how to win new victories in socialist modernization under that leadership. The authors support their points with Xi's statements, one quotation from Marx on the proletariat organising as a party, and remarks by the American writers Ted Fishman and Kenneth Lieberthal. The central argument is that Party leadership determines the nature, direction and destiny of socialism with Chinese characteristics, as well as its outlook and its capacity to meet major risks. The authors say the Party led the Chinese people through four great achievements, from the new-democratic revolution to the new era. In their account it also produced Chinese modernization, which they say broke the 'myth' that modernization means Westernization, and it revitalised world socialism after the Soviet and East European collapse. They cite China's GDP of 114 trillion yuan in 2021, about 18% of the world total, and the country's lead in contributing to global growth since 2006. They hold that the Party's leadership has been decisive in crises ranging from foreign aggression and natural disasters to the Covid-19 pandemic and pressure from the United States and the West. They also contend that some developing countries stall in modernization for lack of a strong party. Yan and Wang conclude that the Party's comprehensive leadership of modernization must be strengthened and made to cover every area. They call on leading cadres at all levels to raise their political capacity, strategic vision and professional competence, so as to meet a more complex 'great changes unseen in a century' than earlier modernizers faced. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary in 2022 tied Party leadership to modernization, global influence and crisis management.

Grasping the value implications and practical significance of putting the people at the centre 深刻把握以人民为中心的价值意蕴和现实意义 Zheng E This newspaper commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2022, starts from a line in the Party's 2021 historical resolution. The line says the Party has sought happiness for the Chinese people, rejuvenation for the Chinese nation, progress for humanity and "great harmony" for the world. Zheng argues that this formulation expresses the Marxist people's standpoint and the principle of putting the people at the centre. The author says it should be studied through its value implications and practical significance. The article takes the four aims in turn: the people, the nation, humanity and the world. For each it names a corresponding goal and cites Xi Jinping's statements and Party history. It then discusses how the four relate to one another and ends with China's international role. Zheng links the aims to concrete programmes. Seeking happiness for the people means pursuing common prosperity. Seeking rejuvenation for the nation means building a modern socialist country, with Chinese modernization traced from the Seventh Party Congress (1945) through Deng Xiaoping's three-step strategy to the present. Seeking progress for humanity means building a community with a shared future for mankind, and seeking great harmony means the Global Development Initiative and shared values of humanity. The author stresses that the four are an organic unity, so that serving humanity and the world also serves the people and the nation. Zheng presents this as drawing on Chinese tradition and on Marx and Engels's "association of free individuals". Zheng concludes that China will take on more international responsibilities as its strength grows. The author says Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilization and offers developing countries a fresh option. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party commentary ties domestic goals to its global vision in 2022.

The sources of strength behind the Communist Party of China's centenary of achievement 中国共产党铸就百年辉煌的力量源泉 Zhao Xiaohu Mao Junji Writing in Guangming Daily in June 2022, Zhao Xiaohu and Mao Junji ask what explains the Communist Party of China's achievements over its hundred-year history. They argue that four forces, acting together, kept the Party at the forefront of its era: the power of belief, of theoretical innovation, of bold practice and of self-reform. This is a short commentary with one section for each force, followed by a brief forward-looking passage. It draws on Xi Jinping's speech at the centenary of the Party's founding, the 2021 Party resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience, and statements by Mao Zedong. On belief, the authors hold that the Party's ideals rest on Marxism, on the patriotic traditions of Chinese culture and on the aim of national independence and liberation; they link these to the spirit of the Party's founding. On theoretical innovation, they point to historical, political and theoretical self-awareness, a practical, reality-based style of thought, and the unity of innovation with theoretical education within the Party. On practice, they describe an unprecedented firmness, spirit of sacrifice and thoroughness, running from revolution through construction to reform and opening up. On self-reform, they follow the resolution in calling it what distinguishes the Party from others, rooted in its having no interests of its own. They add that Mao's answer, supervision by the people, and Xi Jinping's answer, self-reform, now combine internal and external discipline. The authors conclude that, as the Party begins its journey toward the second centenary goal amid great changes unseen in a century, preserving these four forces will let it succeed in governing, building and strengthening itself under long-term rule. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned account of how Party writers explain the sources of its historical success.

Injecting new impetus into the innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture 为中华优秀传统文化创新发展注入新动力 Wang Zhenzhong This short commentary, published in the People's Daily on 6 June 2022, asks how excellent traditional Chinese culture can be given fresh momentum. Wang Zhenzhong builds on Xi Jinping's remarks at the 39th collective study session of the Political Bureau, where Xi called traditional culture the "root and soul" of the Chinese nation. Wang argues that its creative transformation and innovative development should proceed by upholding fundamental principles while innovating, and by fusing tradition with scientific culture. The piece has three parts. It first lists the values Wang finds in traditional culture, from harmony between humans and nature to ethics, self-improvement, people-based governance, national unity and peaceful international relations. It then treats transformation and development as a systematic project that needs top-level design and workable methods. It ends with a call to remain guided by Marxism. Wang's central claim is that traditional culture is open, inclusive and developing rather than fixed. In Wang's account, it evolves with its society and grows by absorbing and exchanging with other cultures. Wang names integration with scientific culture as an important route, citing the 14th Five-Year Plan's emphasis on science and technology. Concretely, Wang proposes carrying forward the tradition's esteem for innovation, bringing scientific spirit (seeking truth from facts, respect for laws of nature) and modes of thinking (dialectical, empirical, deductive) into its renewal. The two are described as mutually reinforcing, since scientific culture can in turn draw wisdom from tradition. Wang concludes that, under Marxist guidance and Xi's directives, traditional culture will show greater vitality. It will offer insight for understanding and changing the world, for state and social governance and for moral development, and will help build Chinese spirit, Chinese values and Chinese strength. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed tradition, science and Party guidance together.

The Communist Party of China and the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation 中国共产党与中华民族伟大复兴 Ren Lixuan Writing in the People's Daily on 29 June 2022, Ren Lixuan asks why the Communist Party of China (CPC) alone could take on the task of national rejuvenation, and what that task has meant across the Party's history. Ren answers by citing Xi Jinping's statement that without the Party there would be no new China and no rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article argues that the Party has fundamentally reversed the fate of the Chinese people since the modern era and is moving irreversibly towards rejuvenation along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The commentary has three parts. The first sets out four reasons why only the CPC can carry the historic mission: scientific theory, an unchanging founding mission, reliance on the people, and self-reform. The second presents rejuvenation as the single theme of all the Party's struggles, sacrifices and creations over a century. The third looks ahead and tells the Party to take charge of the "four greats": great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream. It closes by linking the Chinese Dream to a community with a shared future for mankind. Ren holds that earlier political forces and ideologies failed because they lacked scientific theory and did not understand the strength of the people. By contrast, Ren credits the Party's adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, culminating in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Ren also credits its refusal to pursue any special interest. Ren answers the question of how the Party escapes the historical cycle of rise and fall with self-reform, presented as a second answer after Mao Zedong's appeal to supervision by the people. Ren also points to Party leadership, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and the Two Establishes as guarantees. Sacrifice is illustrated by the figure of more than 3.7 million named martyrs between 1921 and 1949. Ren concludes that China is closer than ever to rejuvenation, but must expect harder struggles, including the pressures of trade friction with the United States and the pandemic, which Ren says will last until the second centenary goal. The article calls for the Two Upholds, the Four-sphere Confidence, high-quality development and common prosperity, and presents rejuvenation as a boost to human progress. Read the original if you want an authoritative example of how the Party's leadership framed its historical mission and its tasks in mid-2022.

The distinctive regional features of the anti-Japanese war behind enemy lines in South China 华南敌后抗战呈现鲜明地域特色 Guo Lu This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2022, asks what set the anti-Japanese war behind enemy lines in South China apart from that in North and Central China. Guo Lu argues that the region's rivers, coast, overseas-Chinese ties and border position gave it clearly regional characteristics. The article first notes that after Japan occupied Guangzhou in October 1938, soldiers and civilians led by the Communist Party built several bases, including Dongjiang, Qiongya and Wuguishan, known together as the South China anti-Japanese base areas. It treats these as one of the three main fronts behind enemy lines. It then examines three features in turn: maritime guerrilla warfare, mobilisation of overseas Chinese and Hong Kong and Macao compatriots, and support for Allied operations. On the first, Guo says South China forces used mountain and plain guerrilla tactics common elsewhere, and also developed maritime guerrilla warfare, citing Mao Zedong's 1938 remarks on rivers and coasts. Examples include the Dongjiang Column's sea units near Daya Bay and Dapeng Bay, which attacked Japanese transport with wooden sailing boats and home-made explosives, and the 'Sea Eagle' unit at the Pearl River estuary. On the second, the author lists returnees joining guerrilla units, more than thirty home-service groups and donations of money and supplies. On the third, Guo reports the rescue of 89 foreign friends from Hong Kong, the rescue of nearly 40 American and British airmen in 1944–45, and a joint intelligence station with US forces. Guo concludes that South China's forces achieved good results in all three areas and strongly supported the worldwide anti-fascist war. Read the original if you want a brief, example-based overview of how geography shaped the Communist-led resistance in Guangdong and its links to Hong Kong and the Allies.

The threefold identity of Chinese modernization 中国式现代化的三重身份特质 Chen Fulong Chen Fulong asks what shapes the path of Chinese modernization and why it differs from Western modernization. The article, a short commentary first published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2022, answers that three identities together form its basic character: socialist country, developing country and emerging country. Chen argues that these identities determine the model and path of Chinese modernization, which is therefore planned within both "China in the world" and "China's world". The commentary is organised in three sections, one for each identity, with a short closing summary. It draws on Marx's remarks on the world market and the modern history of capital, on passages from Xi Jinping and the report to the 19th Party Congress (2017), and on examples from Latin America, West Asia and North Africa. It also looks at the two world wars as episodes of shifting power among rising and established states. On the first identity, Chen contends that modernization began in the West on a capitalist basis, but that this historical priority gives capitalism no moral priority and no exclusive claim to the means of realising modernization. Chinese modernization, in this reading, goes beyond capital-centred logic, puts the people first, joins efficiency with fairness and aims at common prosperity. On the second, the author cites the "two unchanged" judgments (China remains in the primary stage of socialism and is the largest developing country) and argues that "modernization equals Westernization" is a prejudice. Countries that copied Western models, such as Argentina, Brazil, Peru and Chile, are said to have met similar internal contradictions. Developed countries modernised in "serial" fashion, while developing ones must compress industrialisation, informatisation, urbanisation and agricultural modernization into a "parallel" process. On the third, Chen argues that China has risen through interaction and cooperation, not through expansion or colonialism. As part of a collective rise of emerging and developing countries, it is said to push toward a more multipolar and equitable order. Chen concludes that the three identities show Chinese modernization to be a distinctive socialist "Chinese version" that dissolves the "modernization equals Westernization" narrative. The author presents it as offering Chinese wisdom and a Chinese approach to problems facing humanity, and as helping to build a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese official scholarship frames the international and developmental identity of Chinese modernization in 2022.

Recent advances in German MEGA research 近年来德国学界MEGA研究的新进展 Kaan Kangal Kaan Kangal (Kangal Kaan in the Chinese rendering) surveys German-language scholarship on the Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe (MEGA) over roughly the past five to six years; the piece first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in January 2022. The author notes that the 200th anniversaries of Marx (2018) and Engels (2020) produced a surge of publications in Germany. Many of these draw on MEGA2 materials but concern Marx's and Engels's theory in general rather than the edition itself. Kangal's review therefore focuses on debates that deal directly with MEGA. The survey identifies the main venues of these debates: the Marx-Engels-Jahrbuch, the Marx-Engels-Forschung. Neue Folge and, occasionally, the Zeitschrift für marxistische Erneuerung. It also lists five books bearing directly on MEGA research, among them works by Matthias Bohlender, Hagen Kleemann, Ulrich Pagel and Rolf Hecker. Kangal sorts the debates into four areas: The German Ideology, Marx's political philosophy and conception of critique, the history of MEGA1, and Marx's economic theory of the 1850s and 1860s. On The German Ideology, Kangal reports that after the MEGA2 volume appeared in 2017, Gerald Hubmann argued that no single work of that name exists. In his account, the manuscripts belonged to a planned journal, and the main target of Marx and Engels was Max Stirner rather than Feuerbach. Pagel and Bohlender develop this line, while Terrell Carver's English edition is criticised by Michael Quante as politically narrow. Lucas Rudolph holds that the text aimed to criticise German philosophy and "true socialism" rather than to construct historical materialism. A second debate concerns Marx's idea of critique as "critique in hand-to-hand combat" and his relation to utopian socialists. The third covers the Marx-Engels-Forschung volume on Boris Nikolaevsky, who helped Ryazanov's MEGA1 project and later the Amsterdam archive. The fourth turns on MEGA2 Section IV notebooks: Soichiro Sumida on the Asiatic form in the London Notebooks, Norman Jakob on Marx's publishing plans, and Kenji Mori and Hecker on the Crisis Notebooks of the 1857 crisis, which Hecker sees as an empirical test of Marx's crisis theory. Kangal does not offer a single conclusion; the article is a descriptive map of current German MEGA scholarship and its disputes. It shows how new editions and notebooks are reopening questions about Marx's texts, politics and economics. Read the original if you want a guide to the German authors, journals and books driving MEGA debates, particularly on The German Ideology and the Crisis Notebooks.

Abstraction becomes domination: Marx and Lefebvre 抽象成为统治：马克思与列斐伏尔 Yan Jinggao This short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2022, asks how Henri Lefebvre extends Marx's account of modern domination by abstraction. Yan argues that Lefebvre takes up Marx's claim that abstraction (capital) becomes dominant and concludes that abstract space has become dominant in contemporary capitalism. Despite the 'anonymous power' involved, both thinkers are presented as revolutionary optimists who trust the emancipatory force of historical dialectics. The piece has three parts: abstract capital as ruler, abstract space as ruler, and the path to breaking abstract domination. It draws on Marx's remarks on the second great social form, money, capital and the world market, and on Lefebvre's writings on the production of space, the state and everyday life. In Yan's reading, Marx shows that exchange value and money become alien powers, so that workers and capitalists alike serve the self-expansion of capital, and that globalisation spreads this rule worldwide. Lefebvre, in Yan's account, shifts the focus from the production of things in space to the production of space itself in abstract space, which codes social relations and admits nothing without exchange value. Its closest concrete form is state monopoly capitalism, and urbanisation, nationalisation and globalisation make up a 'spatial trinity'. Yan concludes that abstract domination carries its own negation. For Marx capital 'repels itself' and meets its limit in its own nature, and for Lefebvre abstract space must produce differential space that contests homogenisation. Yan notes that Marx locates the force of liberation in the proletariat, while Lefebvre locates it in urban margins, slums and forbidden spaces of resistance. Read the original if you want a brief comparison of Marx's critique of capital with Lefebvre's theory of space.

Reflecting on virtual reality through Baudrillard's philosophy of technology 基于鲍德里亚技术哲学反思虚拟现实 Zhang Yungui This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2022, asks what Jean Baudrillard's later philosophy of technology can contribute to thinking about virtual reality. Zhang argues that his concept of the "perfect crime" offers theoretical resources for judging whether virtual reality will bring a "perfect world" or carry out a crime against reality itself. The article first defines virtual reality in the broad sense as a digital world, parallel to and interpenetrating the physical one, in which people live with digital identities. It then sets out Zhang's three-stage model of its development and turns to Baudrillard's works Simulacra and Simulation, The Perfect Crime and others, before returning to present-day online life. Zhang's three stages run from digitising reality ("reality + virtual"), through symbiosis ("reality × virtual"), to fusion ("reality = virtual") via brain-computer interfaces. Reading Baudrillard, Zhang treats the third stage as a "hyper-hyperreal" condition in which digital certainty replaces the real and illusion disappears, because virtual and original intelligence can no longer be told apart. On this reading the human being becomes a node in a network, existence becomes labour time, and the result is control through "pure governance of consciousness". Zhang sees this as the true perfect crime for a humanity seeking emancipation, while acknowledging that virtual reality might in an ideal case stimulate creativity and resemble the "association of free individuals". Zhang calls Baudrillard's thought pessimistically technological-determinist but still valuable as a warning about the defects of a highly technologised society. Zhang notes that many people already spend more time online than offline and take what they see there as the real world. Whether virtual reality yields a perfect world or a perfect crime, Zhang concludes, depends on balancing instrumental and value rationality and using technology with "good knowledge" and "good regulation". Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist-oriented application of Baudrillard to debates on virtual reality and the metaverse.

Focus and breakthrough in Marx's doctoral research A reconstruction based on the MEGA2 edition of the Berlin Notebooks 马克思在博士论文研究中的聚焦与突破 Zhang Yixiu Zhang Yixiu asks how Marx's reading notes from his Berlin years supported the writing of his doctoral dissertation, The Difference between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature. The author argues that MEGA2 gives valuable documents but arranges and names them poorly, splitting Marx's Berlin notes into three parts. Zhang proposes treating all of them as one body, the "Berlin Notebooks", and re-periodising them by date and content. The article is a short newspaper piece that follows the notes in chronological order, from the winter semester of 1838 to the doctorate granted by Jena in 1841. It covers the Epicurus excerpts of 1839, the later notes and additions on atomism, the lost materials on Democritus and Aristotle, the drafting of the dissertation, and a final group of excerpts from early 1841. Zhang identifies two moments of focus and breakthrough. In the first group of notes Marx concentrated on Epicurus and engaged his critics, such as Plutarch. He built on Hegel's History of Philosophy but broke with it by valuing Epicurus's natural philosophy and his theory of celestial phenomena as expressions of self-consciousness. From mid-1839 Marx turned to atomism and compared Epicurus with Democritus. Zhang argues that Marx read the atom's swerve as freedom against determinism, in contrast to Hegel, who took it as an emphasis on contingency. According to Zhang, this idea is the core of the dissertation, where the "objectification of self-consciousness" expresses the pursuit of individual freedom. Zhang concludes that Marx's Berlin notes should be reconstructed as a whole, which would show more clearly how they supported his dissertation. The author also suggests that the last excerpts, from Leibniz, Hume, Spinoza and Rosenkranz, differ physically from the earlier notes and bear little relation to the dissertation. They were more likely preparation for a later teaching qualification examination. Read the original if you work on the early Marx, Marx's relation to Hegel, or the editorial arrangement of MEGA2.

The early intellectual context of the young Marx 青年马克思的早期思想构境 Zhang Yibing Zhang Yibing asks where the young Marx's early idealism and revolutionary-democratic stance came from, a question he says Chinese scholarship has neglected. Studies have concentrated on the materialist turn and on texts such as the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and The German Ideology. Zhang argues that the answer lies in Marx's early reading notes, and that the dominant influence was Bruno Bauer's subjective idealism rather than Hegel's objective idealism. This short newspaper commentary, published in 2022, proceeds through three questions. It asks first about Marx's initial relation to Hegelian philosophy and the Young Hegelians, then about how the philosophy of his doctoral dissertation took shape, and finally about the change in his thinking between the doctorate and the Rheinische Zeitung period. It draws on the Berlin Notebooks and the Bonn Notebooks. Zhang holds that Marx came to Hegel largely through the Young Hegelians, above all Bauer, whose concept of self-consciousness recast Hegel's system as subjective idealism and expressed bourgeois individual subjectivity. In the dissertation on Epicurus, Marx used self-consciousness to reinterpret an atomism that had appeared historically in a materialist guise. Zhang calls this Marx's first near-miss with materialism. In the Bonn Notebooks, Zhang sees the subjective idealism loosening. Marx grew dissatisfied with Bauer's detached theological critique, broke off their planned joint work, and first used the concept of fetishism in excerpts from de Brosses. His attention shifted from Hegelian spirit to real history. Zhang suggests that the fetishism excerpts may be an important source for Marx's later critique of fetishism, up to Capital. Zhang adds that materialist threads in the Bonn Notebooks may already have formed a tacit framework, although the materialist turn was not yet complete. Zhang notes that MEGA2 now publishes these notebooks and letters in full, and hopes for more research. Read the original if you want a brief guide to the early notebooks and to Bauer's influence on Marx before 1843.

The content and intellectual value of the Berlin Notebooks 《柏林笔记》的内容及其思想价值 Li Qiankun Li Qiankun asks how the young Marx's Berlin Notebooks (1839–1841) should be read and what they are worth. Li argues that they should be treated neither as a finished philosophical statement nor as mere preparatory material. In Li's view they are an indispensable link for understanding the early course of Marx's thought. The piece first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2022. Li follows MEGA2 in using the title for the eight notebooks of Excerpts from Classical Philosophers. The earlier seven notebooks on Epicurean philosophy and the two groups of Epicurus fragments can count as Berlin Notebooks in a wider sense, but they are already translated and well studied. Li therefore surveys the excerpts section by section: Aristotle's On the Soul, Leibniz, Hume's Treatise, Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise, and Rosenkranz's history of Kantian philosophy. Li describes two prior positions. One, represented by the MEGA2 editors and by Alexandre Matheron's French counterpart Lübbert-type studies such as Rubel's Marx Encounters Spinoza (1977), stresses Marx's distinctive philosophical exploration. The other, represented by Michael Heinrich's 2018 biography, reads the excerpts as preparation for a Bonn habilitation, supported by Bruno Bauer's letter of 1840. Li accepts a dialectical view of both. Marx at Berlin still worked within the older philosophical vocabulary, so over-reading is a postmodern textual reading detached from the author. Li nonetheless finds vivid traces of the period in the notebooks. These include Marx's remarks on Aristotle, his Hegelian vocabulary of consciousness, and his choice to excerpt the later chapters of Spinoza on freedom of thought and democracy first. Li reads these as signs of a preference for Hegel's philosophy of self-consciousness and a democratic political leaning. Read the original if you want a short guide to the contents of the notebooks and to the dispute over their significance.

Lessons of the Chinese modernization path for African development 中国式现代化道路对非洲发展的启示 Li Xinfeng Writing in 2022, Li Xinfeng asks what the Chinese modernization path means for Africa, where poverty reduction and development have not fundamentally improved. Li argues that Western modernization theory has constrained African development. Li holds that Chinese modernization shows that there is no single model, and that African states should choose paths suited to their own conditions rather than copy either West or East. The article has three parts. The first criticises Western modernization theory and reviews African critiques of it, including Samir Amin's dependency theory and Walter Rodney's How Europe Underdeveloped Africa. The second surveys Africa's poverty, its internal and external causes, and its failed attempts at development: African socialism, the structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s, the post-Cold War turn to multiparty democracy, and the African Union's Agenda 2063. The third draws five lessons from China. Li cites Afrobarometer survey data and African officials' remarks during a visit to Yan'an as evidence of African interest. Li contends that Western modernization theory is a product of Cold War mobilisation. In Li's account, it casts non-Western states as backward, and the West's own modernization rested on colonial plunder. Li treats Africa's poverty as stemming from colonial history, unequal economic relations and aid conditionality, as well as from single-commodity economies, conflict and weak governance. Against this, Li presents Chinese modernization, with its five features, as more open than the Western model and as ending the equation of modernization with Westernization. The five lessons are to choose a path from national conditions, to adopt a people-centred approach, to pursue a win-win of growth and environmental protection, to take Pan-Africanism as a guiding spirit, and to manage reform, development and stability while pursuing peace. Li compares common prosperity with the Southern African idea of ubuntu. Li concludes that the age of remaking the world in the West's image is over and that Africa should give modernization its own content. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Africa specialist presents Chinese modernization as a reference for African development and draws on African voices to do so.

A major work on the theory of the Party's self-reform On "Self-Revolution: The Second Answer to Escaping the Historical Cycle" 研究阐释党的自我革命理论的一部力作 Shen Chuanbao This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, of Self-Revolution: The Second Answer to Escaping the Historical Cycle, written by Zhen Zhanmin and others and published by People's Publishing House. Reviewer Shen Chuanbao presents the book as a first-rate study of Xi Jinping's statements on the Party's self-reform. In Shen's view it explores how self-reform relates to escaping the "historical cycle" of rise and decline. The book treats the theory of self-reform in eight parts: its scientific meaning, theoretical basis, successful practice, historical experience, main challenges, ethical consciousness, systemic framework and strategic guidelines. Shen organises the review around four qualities the book is said to have: it is systematic, scholarly, practical and innovative. On the first two points, Shen argues that earlier scholarship mostly analysed individual assertions, whereas this book builds a fairly complete analytical framework. It also starts from concepts and compares existing definitions. It then defines self-reform in four dimensions: spirit, practice, theory and politics. Its theoretical grounds are drawn from philosophy, political science and cultural studies. On practice, Shen notes the book's chapter on the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It covers Party building and the anti-corruption struggle, and the role of intra-Party regulations. It holds that theoretical, action-based and institutional consciousness must work together, which in Shen's account yields the second answer to the historical cycle. Shen credits the book with a fresh topic, new formulations such as six \"unities\" of experience, and up-to-date data from the 2022 plenary session of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. It also proposes a four-dimension system of goal, motivation, conduct and evaluation, and stresses ethical self-awareness. Shen's assessment is wholly favourable. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-affiliated reading of how this book frames self-reform theory in the 2022 discussion.

The Party's overall leadership profoundly shapes the political advantages of whole-process people's democracy 党的全面领导深刻塑造全过程人民民主政治优势 Chai Baoyong Li Tian This newspaper commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, asks why Chinese democracy can be described as covering the "whole process". Chai and Li argue that the Party's overall leadership is the deep driving force behind the political advantages of whole-process people's democracy. They say it supplies the fundamental political guarantee and the direction for building a broader and more effective operating system of democracy. The article is organised in five sections. Four of them examine how Party leadership works: it keeps the people's will present in every link of the process, turns institutional strengths into governance effectiveness, provides the political foundation for implementation, and strengthens the supervision and restraint of power. The last section places the model in the wider context of human political civilisation. Throughout, the authors contrast the Chinese practice with Western capitalist democracy, which they describe as limited to voting. In the authors' account, Western democracy replaces broad participation with episodic voting, and its checks and balances produce money politics, elite politics and a "veto politics" of reflexive opposition. Whole-process people's democracy instead builds the Party's people-centred stance into a full chain of democratic election, consultation, decision-making, management and oversight. The authors say this chain is supported by the Party's leadership system and the mass line. They draw on Engels's essay "On Authority" to argue that modern society requires political authority, and that the Party's leadership combines democracy with authority. In their view, this lowers the costs of democratic procedures, helps manage social disagreement and brings the separate mechanisms together. They add that the Party shapes the oversight system, so that Party supervision drives supervision in other fields. Chai and Li conclude that Party leadership gives whole-process people's democracy a supreme moral basis, scientific theoretical guidance, a deep mass base and a tight organisational structure. They present it as a new form of democratic civilisation distinct from the West, one that offers "Chinese wisdom" and a "Chinese approach" to political civilisation and strengthens China's international democratic discourse power. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2022 tied the Party's leadership to the claimed superiority of Chinese democracy over Western models.

The reasoning of empirical research on rural religion A response to "Rethinking the 'Western religion fever in rural China': myth or fact" 农村宗教实证研究的理路分析 Liu Yanwu Yang Hua Liu Yanwu and Yang Hua reply to a 2020 Kaifang shidai article by Wu Yue, Zhang Chunni and Lu Yunfeng (the "Lu article"). That article used China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) survey data to argue that a "Western religion fever" in the countryside is "a myth rather than a fact". It was a critique of the 2014 Xiyuan Foundation report on the spread of Western religion in rural China. Liu and Yang contend that the Lu article does not refute the report and that its own figures, read carefully, support it. They also argue that rural religion needs a different research approach. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's speeches on religious work (2015, 2016, 2021). It then takes up the Lu article's three claims in turn: whether a Western religion fever exists in the countryside, whether the countryside is more favourable than cities to Western religion, and whether typical regions can stand for the whole country. Liu and Yang check the CFPS 2016 raw data and questionnaire items and cite official figures. They close with methodological reflections and a statement on religious policy. The first move is definitional and logical. In the authors' account, the Lu article counts only registered Protestants and Catholics, drops the roughly 12 million "hidden Christians" and leaves out underground churches and heterodox groups. Liu and Yang say this removes about 45 percent of Western-religion adherents, and that the small overlapping part cannot refute the larger whole. Second, they recompute the rural–urban comparison by household registration. They find rural adherents slightly more numerous in proportion, and well over half a million more in absolute numbers. They also report that rural worshippers appear more active, not less. Third, they say the CFPS sample cannot capture clustered religious groups. They cite provincial counts, such as zero Christians in Sichuan and zero Catholics in Chongqing and Beijing, that conflict with official and church figures. On this basis they argue that the Lu article attacks partial evidence with partial evidence. Liu and Yang conclude that exact counts of believers matter less than trends, and that questionnaires cannot reliably classify folk religious practice. They call for solid fieldwork and first-hand qualitative data, with surveys only as a supplement. They add that the Xiyuan report used data from 2009 or earlier, and that conditions have since changed positively. They end by restating that religious freedom must be compatible with socialist society. They also hold that the rapid rural spread of Western religion could carry social risks. Read the original if you want a detailed example of a Chinese dispute over survey methods in religion research, and of how that dispute is tied to official religious policy.

An "industrial pathology" examination of the capitalist public health crisis 资本主义公共卫生危机的“工业病理学”考察 Li Ling Why do capitalist societies, which have had public health systems since nineteenth-century Britain, still fall into disarray when a pandemic such as COVID-19 strikes? Writing in 2022, Li Ling answers by returning to Marx's use of "industrial pathology" in Capital. The article argues that Marx took an existing medical genre, drawn from physicians' investigations of work-related illness, and recast it through historical materialism. In Li's account, this allows the root of recurrent public health crises to be traced to the capitalist mode of production rather than to administrative failings. The article draws mainly on Capital, especially the Public Health Reports edited by Dr John Simon, and on Engels, Marx's letters and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. It is organised in four parts: misplaced values, internal contradictions, functional failure of the health system, and a final section on remedies. Each diagnostic part moves from nineteenth-century Britain to the pandemic response in the United States and other Western countries. Li cites New York Times figures from May 2020 on deaths in US elderly-care facilities and higher mortality among ethnic minorities, as well as reports of an early US task-force recommendation rejected over fears for financial markets. Li's central argument is that capital's self-valorisation takes precedence over human life and health, so that workers, and above all the unemployed, become expendable. Economising on constant capital such as ventilation and housing, and maintaining an industrial reserve army that carries disease, are said to spread epidemics. Li also contends that, in Marx's analysis, doctors are subordinate to the bourgeoisie, medical care is merely the "repair of labour-power", and health spending is an "unproductive cost" to be cut precisely when it is most needed. Hence, Li argues, the health system tends to paralyse itself in a crisis. As remedies, Li draws on Marx three lessons: change the system of ownership of the means of production, since reform by technocrats and doctors cannot cure a crisis rooted in the mode of production; have doctors serve ordinary people, as the doctors of the poor-law dispensaries did; and respect medical science, as in Marx's proposal that factory inspectors be doctors. Li links these to the Chinese anti-epidemic spirit of putting life first. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar applies Marx's Capital to the COVID-19 response and to criticism of Western health systems.

Integrating Party history study and education into daily life and making it routine 把党史学习教育融入日常、抓在经常 Yuwen Li This short commentary in Guangming Daily (July 2022) takes up Xi Jinping's January 2022 instruction that a single campaign is not enough to make the whole Party study and use Party history well. Yuwen argues that Party history education must be made routine and long-term, and that this is important for consolidating the Party's leadership and strengthening Party building in the new era. The article first explains the purpose of studying Party history, then sets out the institutional mechanisms needed to make the study permanent, and ends with the wider attitudes required. Yuwen holds that studying history is meant to clarify principles, strengthen confidence and raise political awareness, so that Party members do not forget the Party's founding mission. The article puts study and implementation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era first. It lists five mechanisms: the study system of Party committee theory study groups; cadre education and training, with Party history as a compulsory and regular course in Party schools; ideological and political courses in schools; education using red resources; and the practice of 'doing practical things for the people'. Yuwen concludes that institutional rules are the key to removing obstacles to regular study. The author also calls for a lasting, lifelong and whole-course concept of learning, so that results show in Party members' and cadres' practical work toward building a modern socialist country. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line account of how Party history education is meant to be institutionalised after the 2021 campaign.

Keeping the clarity and purity proper to young cadres 永葆年轻干部应有的清澈和纯粹 Xu Huixia This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in July 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's call at the centenary of the Communist Youth League for young cadres to show "clarity and purity" (qingche and chuncui). Xu Huixia argues that these qualities are a long-standing Chinese and communist ideal, and that they now have a concrete content and a practical route of cultivation for young cadres. The article has two parts. The first traces the meaning of the two words through classical Chinese texts and through remarks by Marx, Lenin and Mao Zedong on the purity of the Party and of communists. It then sets out what Xi Jinping has required of young cadres since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second part proposes four ways of cultivating these qualities under the heading of the "new journey". Xu identifies five elements of clarity and purity: firm ideals and convictions as their soul; loyalty to the Party as their foundation; a work style of taking responsibility and striving; integrity and self-discipline as their bottom line; and the original aspiration of serving the people as their essence. For cultivation, Xu calls for study of the Party's theory and the "four histories" to replenish the "spiritual calcium". Xu also calls for loyalty grounded in the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, for pioneering and courage to take on responsibility, and for caution in the use of power. Finally, Xu stresses the mass line and fieldwork at the grassroots. Xu concludes that only by keeping clarity and purity can young cadres contribute to the second centenary goal and to a better China. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party-building discourse in 2022 frames the qualities expected of young cadres.
